The case of Vejdeland and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 1813/07) concerned four Swedish nationals—Tor Fredrik Vejdeland, Mattias Harlin, Björn Täng and Niklas Lundström—who alleged that their 2006 conviction by the Swedish Supreme Court for agitation against a national or ethnic group violated Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 7 (no punishment without law) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In December 2004 the applicants, together with three others, entered an upper secondary school and left approximately 100 leaflets in or on pupils’ lockers. The leaflets, produced by the organisation National Youth, were headed “Homosexual Propaganda” and contained statements describing homosexuality as a “deviant sexual proclivity” with a “morally destructive effect on the substance of society.” They urged pupils to tell teachers that HIV and AIDS had appeared early among homosexuals because of a promiscuous lifestyle and that homosexual lobby organisations were trying to play down paedophilia, asking whether that “sexual deviation” should be legalised.

The applicants were charged under Chapter 16, Article 8 of the Penal Code, which criminalises statements expressing contempt for a group on grounds including sexual orientation (an offence carrying up to two years’ imprisonment). They denied that the leaflets expressed contempt for homosexuals as a group and maintained that their purpose had been to start a debate about alleged lack of objectivity in Swedish school education.

On 11 July 2005 the Bollnäs District Court convicted them, finding the statements went beyond objective discussion and that the applicants had intended to express contempt. It imposed two months’ imprisonment on the first two applicants, a suspended sentence plus fine on the third, and probation plus community service on the fourth.

The Court of Appeal for Southern Norrland acquitted them on 14 December 2005, holding that a conviction would violate Article 10. The Prosecutor-General appealed.

On 6 July 2006 the Supreme Court (by a 3–2 majority) convicted the applicants. It held that, although the leaflets aimed to initiate debate on a matter of public interest, they had been distributed in a relatively sheltered school environment to a captive audience of young people who could not choose whether to receive them. The statements were offensive and disparaging to homosexuals as a group, violated the duty under Article 10 to avoid unwarrantably offensive language, and did not contribute to public debate capable of fostering mutual understanding. The majority distinguished an earlier Supreme Court case (NJA 2005 p. 805) in which a pastor’s sermon-based remarks had been protected. The minority considered conviction disproportionate. The first three applicants received suspended sentences plus fines (SEK 1 800–19 000); the fourth received probation.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 4 January 2007, complaining that the Supreme Court judgment interfered with their freedom of expression and that they had been punished without a sufficiently clear legal basis. The Court joined the admissibility and merits examination. Third-party comments were received from the International Centre for the Legal Protection of Human Rights and the International Commission of Jurists.

The case of Vejdeland and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 1813/07) involved four Swedish applicants who alleged that their conviction for distributing anti-homosexual leaflets violated Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights. They also claimed a violation of Article 7 (no punishment without law).

In December 2004, the applicants entered an upper secondary school and left approximately 100 leaflets in or on pupils' lockers. The leaflets, originating from the group National Youth and headed "Homosexual Propaganda," stated that society had shifted from rejecting homosexuality and other "sexual deviances" to embracing this "deviant sexual proclivity." They asserted that teachers knew homosexuality had a "morally destructive effect on the substance of society" yet presented it as normal. The text linked HIV/AIDS to homosexuals' "promiscuous lifestyle" as a main reason for the disease's spread and claimed homosexual lobby groups sought to "play down" paedophilia, asking whether this "sexual deviation" should be legalised.

The applicants were charged under Chapter 16, Article 8 of the Penal Code with agitation against a national or ethnic group. This provision, amended effective 1 January 2003 to cover sexual orientation, criminalises statements expressing contempt for groups based on race, origin, religion or sexual orientation. Preparatory works described homosexuals as an exposed group often targeted by extremist propaganda, including from national socialist organisations.

The applicants denied that the leaflets expressed contempt and stated their intent was to start a debate on alleged lack of objectivity in school education about homosexuality.

On 11 July 2005 the District Court convicted them, holding that the statements exceeded objective discussion and showed intent to express contempt. Sentences included two months' imprisonment for two applicants, a suspended sentence plus fine for one, and probation plus community service for the fourth.

The Court of Appeal acquitted them on 14 December 2005, citing a 2005 Supreme Court ruling (NJA 2005 p. 805) that had acquitted a pastor of similar charges over sermon remarks, on the basis that conviction would breach Article 10.

The Supreme Court convicted the applicants on 6 July 2006 by a 3-2 majority. It held that a conviction was compatible with Article 10 after a comprehensive assessment. Key factors included the school setting (a relatively sheltered environment without free access for outsiders), the fact that pupils received the leaflets involuntarily, and the offensive, disparaging nature of the statements towards homosexuals as a group. Although the claimed purpose was to debate educational objectivity, the wording constituted an unwarranted assault on others' rights and did not contribute to public debate or mutual understanding. The aims could have been achieved without such statements. This distinguished the case from the pastor's sermon delivered to a congregation. The interference was therefore necessary in a democratic society and proportionate to protecting homosexuals.

The minority considered conviction disproportionate under Article 10. Final sentences were suspended terms plus fines (SEK 1,800–19,000) for three applicants and probation for the fourth.

These facts—the leaflets' content and distribution method at a school, the applicants' claimed debate purpose versus the courts' findings of contempt, the Penal Code provision and its 2003 amendment, and the Supreme Court's contextual analysis of necessity and proportionality—formed the core of the alleged Article 10 and 7 violations.

The case of Vejdeland and Others v. Sweden originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by four Swedish nationals who alleged that their conviction by the Swedish Supreme Court violated their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention, as well as Article 7. In December 2004, the applicants and three others entered an upper secondary school and left approximately 100 leaflets in or on pupils' lockers. The leaflets, produced by the organisation National Youth, were titled “Homosexual Propaganda” and stated that society had shifted from rejecting homosexuality and other “sexual deviances” to embracing this “deviant sexual proclivity.” They asserted that teachers knew homosexuality had a “morally destructive effect on the substance of society” yet presented it as normal. The text urged readers to tell teachers that HIV and AIDS had appeared early among homosexuals due to their “promiscuous lifestyle,” which was a main reason for the “modern-day plague,” and that homosexual lobby organisations were trying to play down paedophilia, asking whether this “sexual deviation” should be legalised. The school principal intervened and required them to leave.

The applicants were charged with agitation against a national or ethnic group under Chapter 16, Article 8 of the Penal Code. This provision criminalises statements expressing contempt for a group with allusion to, inter alia, sexual orientation, an offence added in 2003. The applicants denied that the leaflets expressed contempt for homosexuals as a group and stated that their intent had been solely to initiate debate on the lack of objectivity in Swedish school education.

On 11 July 2005 the District Court of Bollnäs convicted them, finding that the statements went beyond objective discussion and that the applicants had intended to express contempt. It imposed two months’ imprisonment on the first two applicants, a suspended sentence plus fine on the third, and probation plus community service on the fourth. The Court of Appeal for Southern Norrland acquitted them on 14 December 2005, holding that a conviction would violate Article 10, relying on a 2005 Supreme Court decision that had interpreted the “contempt” requirement restrictively to comply with the Convention.

The Prosecutor-General appealed. On 6 July 2006 the Supreme Court (by a 3–2 majority) convicted the applicants. It held that an overall assessment was required. The leaflets had been distributed in a school, a relatively sheltered environment to which the applicants had no free access. Pupils received the material without any choice whether to accept it. Although the stated purpose was to start a debate of public interest on educational objectivity, the statements were offensive and disparaging to homosexuals as a group, constituting an unwarranted assault on their rights and contributing nothing to mutual understanding. The same purpose could have been achieved without such language. The majority distinguished the case from the 2005 pastor’s sermon, which had occurred before a congregation and been based on biblical quotations. The two dissenting judges considered conviction disproportionate and contrary to Article 10. The first three applicants received suspended sentences combined with fines; the fourth received probation.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the Supreme Court judgment interfered with their freedom of expression in a manner not necessary in a democratic society and that they had been punished without a sufficiently clear legal basis.
001-108431:
**CASE OF CRISTESCU v. ROMANIA (Application no. 13589/07), ECtHR (Third Section), 10 January 2012**

The applicant, Ioan Cristescu, a Romanian national living in Bucharest, alleged that Romanian authorities failed to enforce a final judicial decision granting him contact rights with his younger son, Th.N. (born 1996). He and I.R. had two sons: C.I. (born 1992) and Th.N. After I.R. initiated divorce and custody proceedings in 2001, the Bucharest First District Court of First Instance awarded custody of both children to the mother in October 2001, with specified visiting rights for the applicant (alternate weekends and holiday periods). Environment studies found both homes suitable. The applicant appealed, seeking custody of C.I. due to their close relationship.

In May 2002, the Bucharest County Court awarded C.I. to the applicant based on the child's preference, upholding the mother's custody of Th.N. The Bucharest Court of Appeal confirmed this in October 2002, emphasizing the children's best interests in maintaining sibling contact. I.R. refused to allow the applicant to collect Th.N., citing the child's reluctance. In April 2003, the County Court specified that the applicant could take Th.N. from I.R.'s home per the existing schedule.

Enforcement proceedings began in May 2002. Bailiff attempts repeatedly failed: I.R. was absent, premises were inaccessible despite signs of occupancy, or the child refused. I.R. claimed Th.N. opposed contact and agreed to public meetings, but cooperation lapsed. She objected to enforcement reports, citing psychological reports of the child's anxiety, nightmares, and enuresis linked to visits and alleged parental conflict; these objections were dismissed as going to the merits. I.R. frequently changed addresses without notice, complicating location. In 2004, after two weekends with the applicant, I.R. alleged Th.N. returned ill (benzodiazepine then nicotine intoxication) and sought to halt enforcement while filing a criminal complaint against the applicant. Courts rejected this, finding no proven fault by the father.

The applicant filed multiple criminal complaints against I.R. for non-compliance with the 2002 judgment. Prosecutors closed cases, citing Th.N.'s unwillingness rather than maternal obstruction (one administrative fine was imposed). I.R.'s criminal complaint against the applicant for endangering the child was also closed for lack of evidence of negligence. Parallel civil proceedings by I.R. sought to reduce the applicant's contact with Th.N. (citing "negative influence" and trauma) and later, in 2006, to obtain custody of C.I. after the boy moved to her home. Social reports and in-camera hearings of the children (then aged 10 and 14) highlighted strained relations, with both boys expressing fear or reluctance toward the applicant and preference for the mother's household. In April 2007, a first-instance court granted I.R. custody of C.I. with contact for the applicant, dismissing his counterclaim for Th.N.'s custody, noting disputes over enforcement were not sufficient grounds for change.

The applicant also sought school information about Th.N. (denied based on the visiting schedule) and a daily fine for non-enforcement; in 2006 a court imposed a modest fine on I.R., attributing the children's distress partly to her influence. Efforts spanned years with limited practical success in contact with Th.N. The case concerned alleged violations of Article 8 (family life) due to ineffective enforcement of contact rights amid parental conflict and the child's expressed reluctance.

The case of Cristescu v. Romania (Application no. 13589/07) concerns Romanian national Ioan Cristescu’s complaint that authorities failed to enforce a 2002 court judgment granting him contact rights with his younger son, Th.N. (born 1996). This formed the core alleged violation of his right to family life.

Cristescu and I.R. divorced following proceedings initiated in 2001. They had two sons: C.I. (born 1992) and Th.N. A first-instance court placed both children with the mother and granted the applicant weekend and holiday visitation. On appeal in 2002, the Bucharest County Court (upheld by the Court of Appeal) awarded custody of C.I. to the applicant based on the child’s preference and close relationship, while Th.N. remained with the mother. Contact with Th.N. was specified as the first and third weekends of each month plus holiday periods. A 2003 judgment confirmed the applicant could collect Th.N. from the mother’s home.

Enforcement began in May 2002. Repeated bailiff attempts through 2006 largely failed: the mother and child were frequently absent, addresses changed without notice (including a 2005 sale of the known residence), or Th.N. refused to go, citing fear. Temporary agreements for public meetings or shared holidays collapsed. Psychologist reports commissioned by the mother (from 2001–2003) described Th.N.’s anxiety, nightmares, bed-wetting and fear of kidnapping, attributing these to the applicant’s unscheduled visits, alleged insults toward the mother, and enforcement involving bailiffs. The mother claimed Th.N. simply did not want contact.

In 2004 the mother alleged that after two weekends with the applicant, Th.N. returned ill; tests showed benzodiazepine then nicotine. She filed a criminal complaint and sought to halt enforcement. Prosecutors and courts found no imputable fault or negligence by the applicant; the source of the substances could not be established, and her objection was dismissed. The applicant’s multiple criminal complaints against the mother for non-compliance were mostly closed, with prosecutors citing Th.N.’s unwillingness rather than the mother’s obstruction, though one imposed a small administrative fine.

The mother repeatedly sought to restrict the applicant’s contact (to a few hours monthly) and later to obtain custody of C.I. Courts largely rejected changes to Th.N.’s arrangements, finding no sufficient change in circumstances, though one dissenting judge highlighted the child’s trauma. In late 2006 C.I. (then 14) left the applicant’s home for the mother’s; a 2007 judgment granted her residence of C.I. (citing the child’s preference and reported neglect) while confirming similar contact rights for the applicant with both sons. The applicant’s counterclaim for Th.N.’s custody was rejected.

A 2006 civil action by the applicant resulted in a token daily fine (approximately EUR 0.75) against the mother for non-compliance. The applicant also complained unsuccessfully of school officials denying him information or access to Th.N. Numerous proceedings and complaints over years produced little effective contact. The Court examined whether Romanian authorities took adequate, timely measures to facilitate the applicant’s relationship with Th.N. despite the child’s apparent reluctance and parental conflict.

The case of Cristescu v. Romania (Application no. 13589/07) concerns a Romanian national, Ioan Cristescu, who alleged that domestic authorities failed to enforce a final judicial decision granting him contact rights with his younger son, Th.N.

Cristescu was married to I.R.; they had two sons, C.I. (born 1992) and Th.N. (born 1996). After I.R. initiated divorce and custody proceedings in 2001, the Bucharest First District Court of First Instance ruled on 9 October 2001 that both children should reside with their mother. Cristescu was granted contact every first and third weekend of the month (Friday 6 p.m. to Sunday 6 p.m.), plus two weeks in summer and one week in winter holidays. Environmental studies confirmed both homes were suitable. On appeal, the Bucharest County Court on 21 May 2002 awarded custody of C.I. to Cristescu, citing the child's preference and close relationship, while confirming Th.N.'s placement with I.R. The Bucharest Court of Appeal upheld this on 25 October 2002, stressing the children's best interests in maintaining sibling contact. A further 21 April 2003 judgment specified that Cristescu could collect Th.N. from I.R.'s home per the schedule.

Enforcement of contact with Th.N. proved problematic. Cristescu initiated proceedings on 24 May 2002. Bailiff attempts from June 2002 onward frequently failed: I.R. was absent, refused entry (despite signs of occupancy), claimed Th.N. refused contact, or was on vacation. The family changed addresses without notice, requiring repeated inquiries to authorities. I.R. attributed refusals to Th.N.'s unwillingness, alleging trauma from sibling separation and Cristescu's influence (e.g., insulting her in the child's presence). Psychologist reports from E.I.V. (2003) described Th.N.'s anxiety, nightmares, enuresis, and fear of "kidnapping," linked to visits involving bailiffs. Limited meetings occurred, including a 2003 agreement for public-place encounters and alternate summer stays, but these were not fully implemented.

I.R. lodged objections to enforcement, citing Th.N.'s alleged refusal and, in 2004, health incidents after two June weekends with Cristescu (urine tests showing benzodiazepine then nicotine). She filed a criminal complaint accusing Cristescu of endangering Th.N. Courts dismissed her objections (e.g., 14 July 2003; 20 September 2005; 12 April 2006), holding they concerned the merits rather than enforcement and that no fault was proven against Cristescu. The forensic report on the intoxications could not determine sources. Cristescu's multiple criminal complaints against I.R. for non-compliance (2003–2005) were mostly closed by prosecutors, who attributed obstruction to Th.N.'s trauma and reluctance rather than I.R.'s fault (one 2003 decision imposed a small administrative fine on I.R.). I.R.'s complaint against Cristescu was not pursued (decision 15 February 2006).

I.R. sought to modify contact in 2002–2003 proceedings, proposing reduced access (one Saturday monthly) due to Th.N.'s fear and "negative influence." Social worker reports noted both parents' affection but strained relations; C.I. was heard expressing preference for sibling-only visits. Courts rejected changes (9 October 2003; 25 March 2004), finding no substantial alteration in circumstances, though a dissenting judge cited trauma evidence. An appeal on points of law was struck out in 2009.

In 2006, I.R. sought custody of C.I. after he moved in with her (citing neglect at Cristescu's home with his new partner). Hearings of both children (now 10 and 14) revealed Th.N.'s fear of Cristescu, preference for his stepfather, and recollections of parental conflict; C.I. described feeling a burden and wanted limited paternal contact. A 5 April 2007 judgment granted I.R. custody of C.I. with similar contact for Cristescu, dismissing his counterclaim for Th.N.'s custody as enforcement issues did not justify change. Separately, on 28 September 2006, a court imposed a modest daily fine (ROL 20, ~EUR 0.75) on I.R. for non-compliance, noting both parents' conflict harmed the children but I.R. bore partial responsibility for Th.N.'s impressions.

Cristescu also reported unsuccessful attempts to obtain school information about Th.N., with complaints to authorities yielding no details. These facts highlight prolonged non-enforcement of contact despite bailiff action, court orders, and fines, amid parental conflict, child's expressed reluctance, address changes, and limited coercive measures by authorities.
001-109541:
The applicant, a sole-practice GP since 1978 with premises he owned and a list of around 1,400 (mostly Bangladeshi) patients, entered a 2004 NHS contract with Waltham Forest PCT. This required him to provide primary medical services (personally or via employees) in return for quarterly capitation payments based on list size, plus discretionary notional rent for NHS use of his premises. Inclusion on the PCT’s medical performers list was a statutory precondition to performing NHS services; suspension treated him as not included and barred personal performance (though the contract itself continued).

A 20 January 2005 monitoring visit prompted an immediate 21 January letter alleging he posed a “serious risk” to patients and imposing suspension pending investigation (citing Performers List Regulations 2004, r.13(1)(a)). Defects later particularised included inadequate records/registers, clinical knowledge gaps, sterilisation failures, and out-of-hours arrangements. The applicant offered voluntary absence; this was refused. A 31 January hearing proceeded in his absence (he had flu) and continued the suspension. After solicitors alleged unlawfulness, the PCT conceded procedural irregularities, treated the decisions as nullities, and held a 16 March hearing that imposed a six-month suspension. A further 3 August hearing (the prior suspension never having been revoked) imposed two months. Locums were arranged, but not at the applicant’s premises (deemed unsatisfactory), so NHS patients were diverted; notional rent ceased because the premises were no longer used for NHS work. During suspension he received 90% of contractual profits (10% deducted for expenses he no longer incurred). Patient numbers later fell from 1,380 (January 2005) to 1,013 (May 2006).

The High Court (March 2006) held every suspension unlawful: no prior notice or opportunity to respond (r.13(11)), unfairness in proceeding despite the voluntary-absence offer, failure to specify duration (r.13(2)), introduction of unparticularised allegations, and exceedance of the six-month aggregate limit. It treated list inclusion as an A1P1 “possession” akin to a licence with intrinsic economic value (enabling practice and affecting remuneration via list size). Because the interference was unlawful it was unjustified; damages might follow if recoverable loss were shown (though 90% payments complicated this).

The Court of Appeal (March 2007) allowed the PCT’s appeal on A1P1 only (unlawfulness was unchallenged). Statutory prohibition on sale of NHS-practice goodwill meant the patient list had no marketable value and thus was not a possession; mere future income (or a “legitimate expectation” of it) is unprotected. List inclusion was a regulatory qualification, not itself an asset or licence of economic value. Even if it were a possession there was no interference: the contract remained on foot, 90% remuneration continued, locums preserved the practice, and any list-size drop was simply a future-income effect. Notional-rent cessation likewise did not engage A1P1. The House of Lords refused leave after citing the Court of Appeal’s conclusion with approval in Countryside Alliance.

The applicant never resumed practice, attributing stress-related illness to the unlawful suspensions; GMC proceedings ended when he resigned on health grounds. He claimed the suspensions therefore violated A1P1 by interfering with his possessions (list inclusion, practice goodwill, contract and premises).

The case of Malik v. the United Kingdom (App. no. 23780/08) concerned the applicant's claim that successive suspensions from an NHS medical performers list violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). Mr Zafar Iqbal Malik, a British GP born in 1943, had practised as a sole practitioner from owned premises in London since 1978, with a list of around 1,400 patients (many from the local Bangladeshi community). In March 2004 he contracted with Waltham Forest Primary Care Trust (PCT) under the National Health Service (General Medical Services Contracts) Regulations 2004. The contract required him to ensure NHS services (personally or via employed doctors) and entitled him to quarterly payments based on registered patients plus discretionary notional rent for NHS use of his premises.

A PCT monitoring visit on 20 January 2005 identified multiple defects (inadequate records and disease registers; gaps in clinical knowledge on bipolar disorder, emergency contraception and smoking cessation; poor maternity services, sterilisation and vaccine storage; and deficient out-of-hours/opening arrangements). On 21 January the PCT suspended him under Regulation 13(1)(a) of the National Health Service (Performers Lists) Regulations 2004 “to protect patients” pending investigation, without prior notice or hearing. Locum cover was arranged but not at his premises because of their condition. A hearing on 31 January 2005 proceeded in his absence (he had flu and offered voluntary abstention, which was refused); the suspension continued. After the applicant’s solicitors alleged unlawfulness, the PCT treated the first two decisions as nullities and held a fresh hearing on 16 March 2005, imposing a six-month suspension. Further process irregularities occurred (new allegations without notice; failure to produce a promised witness). A later hearing on 3 August 2005 imposed a two-month suspension even though an existing suspension had not been revoked and the six-month aggregate limit had been exceeded.

During suspension the applicant received 90% of his contractual profits (the 10% deduction reflecting saved expenses) pursuant to Regulation 13(17) and a Secretary of State determination; notional rent ceased because the premises were unused for NHS purposes. His patient list fell from 1,380 (January 2005) to 1,013 (May 2006). He never resumed practice, citing stress-related ill-health that he attributed to the suspensions; he later resigned from the GMC register on health grounds.

In judicial-review proceedings the High Court (March 2006) held every suspension unlawful for breaches of Regulation 13 (lack of notice, unfair hearings, failure to specify duration, and exceeding time limits) and found that inclusion on the performers list was a “possession” (akin to a licence with present economic value via patient numbers). Because the interference was unlawful it was unjustified under A1P1. The Court of Appeal (March 2007) reversed the A1P1 finding: future income is not a possession; statutory prohibition on sale of NHS goodwill (Regulation 3 of the 2004 Sales of Goodwill Regulations) meant the practice had no marketable asset; list inclusion was merely a regulatory condition, not a possessory right. Even assuming a possession, there was no interference, because the contract remained in force, 90% payments continued, locums preserved the list, and any patient decline was mere future-income loss. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal, endorsing that analysis.

These facts formed the core of the alleged A1P1 violation: an unlawful, prolonged exclusion from NHS practice that the applicant claimed diminished the economic value of his list inclusion, patient base and premises.

The applicant, a British GP born in 1943, had practised as a sole practitioner from owned premises since 1978, serving around 1,400 patients (many from the local Bangladeshi community). In March 2004 he contracted with Waltham Forest Primary Care Trust (PCT) under the National Health Service (General Medical Services Contracts) Regulations 2004. The contract required him to provide NHS primary medical services (personally or via employed doctors) in return for quarterly payments calculated by patient numbers, plus discretionary notional rent for the use of his premises.

A PCT monitoring visit on 20 January 2005 led to his immediate suspension the next day under regulation 13(1)(a) of the National Health Service (Performers Lists) Regulations 2004, on the ground that he posed a “serious risk” to patients. Defects cited included inadequate records and disease registers, gaps in clinical knowledge, poor maternity and out-of-hours arrangements, and hygiene/equipment failures. The applicant’s insurers offered a voluntary four-week absence; this was refused. A locum was arranged, but not at his premises because of their condition.

A hearing proceeded in his absence (he had submitted a flu certificate) on 31 January 2005 and the suspension was continued. After his solicitors alleged unlawfulness, the PCT admitted procedural irregularities and treated the earlier decisions as nullities. A fresh hearing on 16 March 2005 imposed a six-month suspension. The applicant commenced judicial-review proceedings. Meanwhile the PCT paid him 90 % of his normal net contractual income (the 10 % deduction reflecting saved practice expenses) but stopped notional rent because the premises were no longer used for NHS purposes.

A further hearing on 3 August 2005 (the previous suspension never having been revoked) imposed a two-month suspension. In March 2006 the High Court (Collins J) declared all four purported suspensions unlawful for want of notice, fairness and compliance with the six-month maximum and other regulatory requirements. The judge held that inclusion on the performers list was a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (akin to a licence with intrinsic economic value that enabled practice and affected remuneration). Because the suspensions were unlawful the interference was unjustified; damages might be available if recoverable loss were proved.

The PCT and Secretary of State appealed only the Article 1 finding. The Court of Appeal (Auld, Rix and Moses LJJ) held there was no possession. Statute had prohibited sale of NHS practice goodwill since 1948, so the patient list had no marketable value. Inclusion on the performers list was a regulatory condition, not an asset; the underlying GMS contract remained in force and 90 % payments continued while a PCT-funded locum served the patients. Future income and non-marketable reputation were not protected. Even if a possession existed, there was no evidence of material economic interference. Leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused (after Countryside Alliance had approved the Court of Appeal’s approach).

The applicant never resumed practice; he attributed subsequent stress-related ill-health to the unlawful suspensions. His patient list fell from 1,380 to 1,013. GMC fitness-to-practise proceedings were begun but he later resigned on health grounds. The application to the European Court alleged that the series of unlawful suspensions violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Gąsior v. Poland (Application no. 34472/07) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 July 2007 by Wanda Gąsior, a Polish national born in 1931 and resident in Kraków. Represented by counsel from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, she alleged that her conviction for defamation violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The Court communicated the case to the Polish Government on 12 January 2010 and decided to examine admissibility and merits together.

The applicant’s son-in-law, J.D., owned a construction company that in 2002 built a villa for Z.W., a prominent politician, former prosecutor and parliamentary deputy. On 4 April 2003 the applicant wrote to the editor of a television programme, stating that Z.W. had owed the company 240,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) for six months after occupying the villa on 15 November 2002 and had paid nothing. She criticised members of the Law and Justice party for ignoring the matter, described Z.W. as greedy, mendacious and dishonest, and accused him of tricking her son-in-law. In a second letter of 2 June 2004 to the president of the Polish Television board she asserted that Z.W. had deceived and ruined three Polish companies and intimidated their owners and employees.

Journalists informed Z.W. of the letters. On 8 July 2004 he lodged a private indictment charging the applicant with defamation under Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 31 August 2006 the Kraków District Court convicted her, conditionally discontinued the proceedings, ordered her to pay Z.W. PLN 1,000, to publish a written apology and to reimburse PLN 300 in costs. The court found that expressions such as “liar”, “greedy and mendacious person” and “dishonest” were capable of undermining the public trust required for Z.W.’s political career. Although a civil dispute existed over the villa, expert evidence indicated that some of Z.W.’s complaints about construction quality were well-founded and that the building was not faultless. The court held that the applicant’s statements were untrue private opinions lacking objective justification, that she knew of the ongoing civil proceedings and therefore could not have been mistaken as to the facts, and that there was no evidence three companies had been ruined. It characterised the letters as an unjustified personal attack circulating untrue allegations about a private financial matter rather than Z.W.’s political activities.

On appeal, the Kraków Regional Court on 24 January 2007 upheld the conviction in substance but limited the sanctions to publication of an apology and reimbursement of costs. It agreed that the allegations were untrue, that the applicant knew this, and that she had not acted in the public interest but had expressed a personal, unsubstantiated negative opinion.

Parallel civil proceedings commenced by J.D. on 21 April 2004 sought PLN 40,492 from Z.W. and his wife. A summary order of 22 June 2004 directed payment, but the case was later transferred to ordinary procedure. On 10 June 2008 the Kraków Regional Court dismissed the claim, finding the works defective and noting that Z.W. had spent approximately PLN 100,000 on repairs, an amount that could be set off against any claim. The Kraków Court of Appeal confirmed this judgment on 28 November 2008.

Domestic law relevant to the alleged violation included Article 212 of the Criminal Code (defamation punishable by fine, restriction of liberty or imprisonment) and Article 213 (truth as a defence, with additional public-interest requirements and restrictions on allegations concerning private life). The Constitutional Court had upheld the compatibility of these provisions with the Constitution on 30 October 2006, observing that protection of dignity and reputation may in some circumstances outweigh freedom of expression and that criminal sanctions are not inherently disproportionate.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the criminal conviction and associated orders unjustifiably interfered with her freedom of expression.

The case of Gąsior v. Poland (no. 34472/07) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s complaint that her conviction for defamation violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, Wanda Gąsior (born 1931), is the mother-in-law of J.D., owner of a construction firm that in 2002 built a villa for Z.W., a prominent politician, former prosecutor and parliamentary deputy.

On 4 April 2003 the applicant wrote to the editor of a television programme stating that Z.W. had owed the firm 240 000 PLN for six months after moving into the villa and had paid nothing. She accused deputies of ignoring the matter because of Z.W.’s status and described him as “greedy and mendacious”, a person who had “tricked” her son-in-law through unexpected dishonesty from a public figure. In a second letter of 2 June 2004 to the president of Polish Television she asserted that Z.W. had “deceived and ruined three Polish companies” and intimidated their owners.

Z.W. learned of the letters and on 8 July 2004 lodged a private indictment for defamation under Article 212 of the Criminal Code, claiming the applicant had falsely alleged non-payment and imputed dishonesty and fraud. On 31 August 2006 the Kraków District Court convicted her. Proceedings were conditionally discontinued; she was ordered to pay Z.W. 1 000 PLN, publish an apology and reimburse 300 PLN costs. The court held that expressions such as “liar”, “greedy and mendacious” and “dishonest” could destroy the public confidence Z.W. needed for his political career. It noted an unresolved civil dispute over the villa (which it declined to decide) and expert evidence that the construction was faulty, contradicting the applicant’s portrayal of a flawless building. The statements were found to be untrue personal opinions lacking objective foundation; the applicant knew of the civil proceedings and no evidence supported the claim that three companies had been ruined. The letters constituted an unjustified personal attack on private matters rather than political activity.

On 24 January 2007 the Kraków Regional Court partly upheld the conviction, restricting the penalty to an apology and costs. It confirmed that the allegations were untrue, that the applicant knew this, and that she had not acted in the public interest but had voiced an unsubstantiated personal opinion.

In parallel civil proceedings J.D. claimed 40 492 PLN. After an initial summary order in his favour the case proceeded ordinarily. On 10 June 2008 the Kraków Regional Court dismissed the claim, finding the works defective; Z.W. had spent approximately 100 000 PLN on repairs, which could be offset. The Court of Appeal confirmed this on 28 November 2008.

Article 212 of the Criminal Code penalises imputations that lower a person in public esteem or undermine confidence needed for office; higher penalties apply if committed via mass media. Article 213 provides a defence of truth, or of a true statement made in the justifiable public interest (with restrictions where private or family life is concerned). In 2006 the Constitutional Court upheld these provisions as compatible with the Constitution, holding that criminal-law protection of dignity and privacy may, in appropriate cases, prevail over freedom of expression.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claim that punishing her letters criticising a public official in a commercial dispute unjustifiably restricted her freedom of expression.

The case of Gąsior v. Poland (no. 34472/07) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. Wanda Gąsior, a Polish national born in 1931 and living in Kraków, claimed that her criminal conviction for defamation arising from two letters she wrote about a politician infringed that right.

In 2002 the applicant’s son-in-law, J.D., whose construction company built a villa for Z.W. (a prominent politician, former prosecutor and parliamentary deputy), alleged that Z.W. had failed to pay approximately PLN 240,000. On 4 April 2003 the applicant wrote to the editor of a television programme stating that Z.W. had lived in the villa for six months without paying “a cent,” that deputies of his party ignored complaints because they believed his “lies and fibs,” and that he was a “greedy and mendacious person” who had “tricked” the company out of a large sum. On 2 June 2004 she wrote to the President of Polish Television claiming that Z.W. had “deceived and ruined three Polish companies” and intimidated their owners and employees.

Journalists informed Z.W. of the letters. On 8 July 2004 he lodged a private indictment for defamation under Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code, asserting that the letters falsely accused him of non-payment and imputed dishonesty, deceit and fraud. On 31 August 2006 the Kraków District Court convicted the applicant. The proceedings were conditionally discontinued; she was ordered to pay PLN 1,000 to Z.W., publish a written apology and reimburse PLN 300 in costs. The court held that expressions such as “liar,” “greedy and mendacious” and “dishonest” were capable of destroying the public trust necessary for Z.W.’s political career. Expert evidence obtained in both the criminal and parallel civil proceedings showed construction defects, so the villa was not the faultless work claimed by the applicant. The statements were therefore untrue private opinions lacking objective justification. The applicant, being aware of the ongoing civil dispute, could not have been mistaken. No evidence supported the claim that three companies had been ruined. The letters constituted an unjustified personal attack on Z.W.’s private financial affairs rather than comments on his political activity and therefore enjoyed reduced protection.

On 24 January 2007 the Kraków Regional Court partly upheld the conviction, requiring only publication of an apology and reimbursement of costs. It confirmed that the allegations were untrue, that the applicant knew they were untrue, and that she had not acted in the public interest but had merely expressed a personal negative opinion.

In the related civil action J.D. sought PLN 40,492 from Z.W. After an initial summary order in J.D.’s favour the case proceeded on the ordinary track. On 10 June 2008 the Regional Court dismissed the claim, finding the works defective and noting that Z.W. had spent about PLN 100,000 on repairs, which could be set off against any debt. The Court of Appeal confirmed the dismissal on 28 November 2008.

Domestic law (Article 212 of the Criminal Code) criminalises statements that lower a person in public esteem or undermine confidence required for office; Article 213 provides limited defences of truth and public interest (with stricter limits when private life is involved). In 2006 the Constitutional Court upheld the compatibility of Article 212 with constitutional free-speech guarantees, holding that criminal protection of reputation can be necessary and that civil remedies alone are insufficient.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 10 violation: a private individual’s critical letters about a public figure’s unpaid debt, the subsequent defamation conviction based on findings of untruth and lack of public interest, and the interplay with a civil construction dispute that ultimately went against the applicant’s family.

The case of Volodarskiy v. Russia (Application no. 45202/04) concerns a Russian national who alleged ill-treatment by police during his arrest and detention on 14-15 October 2003, an ineffective subsequent investigation, and a denial of a fair trial due to the refusal to summon key witnesses.

On the evening of 14 October 2003, the applicant attempted to steal Ms G.'s handbag. Ms G. and her acquaintance Mr Sh. located him at a nearby bus stop. Police officers M. and S. arrived to find the applicant already bleeding from the head with a torn jacket; they handcuffed him after he tried to flee. He was taken to Cheremushinskoye police station, given ambulance first aid at a hospital, returned to the station, questioned, and released the next day.

The applicant's account differed sharply. He claimed Ms G. pushed him and Mr Sh. struck him on the head with a handgun handle, causing bleeding; two security guards then joined in beating him before police arrived. At the station, he alleged being handcuffed to a cell bar, forced to sit on the floor, struck on the legs with a truncheon when he tried to stand, and mocked by officers who made him sing a children's song.

Medical examinations on 16 and 18 October 2003 documented multiple bruises on his head, neck and torso, an abrasion and infected wound on his head, and numbness in his right-hand fingers. Both records noted his claim of being beaten by Cheremushinskoye officers.

An inspection record of Ms G.'s handbag (listing a phone and cash) was signed by attesting witnesses P. and K. The next day it found the applicant had committed the offence but, citing his mental health, relieved him of liability and ordered psychiatric hospitalisation. The decision relied on G. and Sh.'s testimony, the inspection records, and the applicant's mother's statement that strangers had beaten him before handing him to police. The Moscow City Court upheld this on 11 August 2004.

001-108665:
The case of Krivošejs v. Latvia concerns allegations by Viktors Krivošejs (born 1974, a Latvian non-citizen) that he received inadequate medical care in prison and was not released despite his condition, raising issues under Article 3 ECHR regarding potential inhuman or degrading treatment.

The applicant had childhood diagnoses of conduct disorder from early CNS damage (1987 and 1991) but did not pursue recommended treatment. Arrested in December 1997, he was convicted in 1999 of aggravated murder and robbery (15 years) and in 2002 of aggravated theft, with sentences combined then reduced to 15 years.

Multiple forensic psychiatric examinations occurred. Early ones (2000–2001) identified antisocial/borderline personality disorders but no mental illness and affirmed full capacity. In March 2002, a CT scan discovered a 4x5x7 cm primary arachnoid cyst in the left temporal/frontal lobes. Experts diagnosed organic personality disorder, mild cognitive disorder, and temporary psychotic episodes, recommending prison hospital observation, treatment (including dehydration), and follow-up scans. One expert likened it to mental illness requiring seizure reduction to avoid dementia. A later 2002 scan showed the cyst grown to 10x10x5 cm (“huge”), but specialists advised only monitoring and avoiding head impacts, with no surgery needed; full capacity was confirmed.

The applicant was held mainly in Riga prisons (later Jelgava). After a December 1998 fight causing concussion, he received 10 days of hospital care. He later reported headaches, memory issues, and other symptoms (sometimes viewed as fabricated). He had multiple prison hospital admissions (2003–2007) involving specialist exams (neurologist, neurosurgeon, psychiatrist, etc.), CT scans, EEG tests, and medications. Further scans (2007–2008) showed stable cyst size. He was classified Category 3 disabled in 2008.

MADEKKI reviews (2003–2006) initially noted deterioration and recommended treatment/neurosurgeon input (partially followed), but later found care adequate, with biannual checks and no further interventions required.

Repeated release applications under laws allowing it for new severe/incurable illnesses (preventing sentence service) were denied. Prosecutors and panels (including a 2006 multi-specialist review) deemed the condition congenital, health satisfactory without sufficient deterioration, and forensic exams unnecessary.

These facts—cyst discovery/growth, mixed expert views on treatment urgency, provided care vs. complaints, and consistent refusals of release—underpin the alleged failures in medical assistance and continued detention.

The case of Krivošejs v. Latvia (no. 45517/04) was brought by Viktors Krivošejs, a Latvian non-citizen born in 1974 then serving a prison sentence. He alleged inadequate medical care in detention and failure to release him despite his health, contrary to the Convention.

Krivošejs had been diagnosed in 1987 and 1991 with conduct disorder linked to early central-nervous-system damage, but he never pursued recommended inpatient assessment. Arrested in December 1997, he was convicted in 1999 of aggravated murder and robbery and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment; the conviction was upheld after a first forensic psychiatric examination. Separate theft proceedings produced three further inpatient examinations. In 2002 the Jelgava Court convicted him of aggravated theft, imposing three years that was combined with the earlier term (later reduced on appeal to a total of 15 years). The court found him fully mentally capable, though it noted his health when fixing the sentence.

In December 1998, while in Riga Central Prison, Krivošejs was assaulted and suffered a concussion. He was hospitalised for ten days; no fractures or lasting neurological damage were recorded. Subsequent complaints of headache, memory loss, insomnia and auditory hallucinations were initially regarded by prison psychiatrists as fabricated. Outpatient and inpatient forensic examinations in 1998–2001 diagnosed antisocial and borderline personality disorders but no mental illness and confirmed full capacity. A March–May 2002 examination, however, revealed a 4 \times 5 \times 7 cm primary arachnoid cyst spanning the left temporal and frontal lobes. Experts diagnosed an organic personality disorder, mild cognitive impairment and episodic mild psychotic states, declared him temporarily unfit for trial and recommended observation, dehydration therapy and a follow-up CT scan. A later 2002 scan showed the cyst had doubled to 10 \times 10 \times 5 cm; neurosurgeons nevertheless advised only monitoring, stating that surgery was unnecessary and that the cyst could remain asymptomatic absent further trauma. One expert later testified that untreated seizures risked progressive brain-cell damage and dementia.

From 2003 onward Krivošejs spent multiple periods in the prison hospital, where he was seen by neurologists, neurosurgeons, psychiatrists and other specialists and underwent further CT scans (the cyst remaining stable). In 2008 he was classified as Category 3 disabled. The State Medical Care Quality Inspectorate (MADEKKI) investigated four times at his request. The first review (2003) found deterioration and recommended dehydration and a neurosurgical consultation; those steps were taken. Subsequent reviews confirmed regular specialist examinations, deemed further imaging or surgery unnecessary and ultimately found no shortcomings in care.

Krivošejs repeatedly sought release under provisions allowing a court to free a prisoner who develops a mental illness impairing insight or a severe incurable disease rendering continued detention impossible. Prosecutors and prison medical boards consistently refused to commission the required forensic examination, concluding that his condition was congenital, had not deteriorated to the statutory threshold, and that his health remained satisfactory. A 2006 multidisciplinary panel examination reached the same result.

These facts form the core of the allegations of inadequate treatment and unjustified continued detention.

The case of Krivošejs v. Latvia (no. 45517/04) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns allegations by applicant Viktors Krivošejs (born 1974, a Latvian non-citizen) of inadequate prison medical care and failure to release him despite his health. He was serving a lengthy sentence (initially combined to 15 years 10 months, later reduced to 15 years) after 1999 conviction for aggravated murder and robbery, plus a later theft conviction.

Krivošejs had a documented history of conduct disorder from early CNS damage, diagnosed at age 13 and reconfirmed at 17, though he did not follow up on recommended care. Arrested in 1997, he was held primarily in Riga’s Matīsa and Central Prisons (later merged), with periodic transfers to the prison hospital for somatic and psychiatric care. In December 1998 he suffered a head blow in a prison fight, causing concussion and brief unconsciousness; he was hospitalized for 10 days with headaches and dizziness but no detected neurological damage or fractures.

Subsequent complaints included headaches, insomnia, memory impairment, anxiety, and hearing voices. Multiple forensic psychiatric examinations followed. Outpatient reviews (1998, 2000) noted antisocial personality disorder but full mental capacity. Inpatient exams in 2000 and 2001 similarly found personality disorders without mental illness or significant memory issues interfering with capacity or trial participation. A 2002 inpatient exam (third) revealed via CT scan a primary arachnoid cyst (4x5x7 cm) across the left temporal and frontal lobes. Experts diagnosed organic personality disorder, mild cognitive disorder, and intermittent mild psychotic episodes, deeming him temporarily unfit for hearings and recommending prison hospital observation, dehydration, and a follow-up CT to assess neurosurgery. A fourth 2002 exam showed the cyst had grown to 10x10x5 cm (“huge”); neurologists and neurosurgeons advised monitoring only, with no immediate treatment or surgery, though he should avoid head impacts. Expert trial testimony varied: some warned untreated seizures risked dementia and urged specialist supervision; others stated a person could live long-term with such a cyst absent trauma.

Prison medical records show repeated hospital admissions (e.g., 2003–2006 periods totaling months) with examinations by neurologists, neurosurgeons, psychiatrists, ophthalmologists and others; multiple CT scans (cyst size later stable); and some medication (e.g., diazepam). In 2007 he received further consultations and short hospitalization. He was classified Category 3 disabled in 2008.

The MADEKKI inspectorate reviewed care four times at his request. A 2003 review found deterioration requiring treatment (including dehydration) and a neurosurgeon consult, which was implemented via CT and review. A 2004 review noted missing in-person neurosurgeon input but no surgery need, recommending a later scan. Later reviews (2005–2006) found regular specialist checks, no health damage, and no shortcomings.

Release applications from 2004–2006 were repeatedly refused. Prosecutors and prison medical panels declined forensic exams, citing the congenital (not newly acquired) nature of his condition and lack of a mental illness or other severe incurable disease rendering him unable to serve his sentence (per Criminal Law s. 59, Criminal Procedure provisions, and Sentence Enforcement Code s. 116). A 2006 multi-specialist panel examination confirmed no release grounds. These facts formed the basis of his claims of inadequate treatment and unlawful continued detention.
001-109076:
The case of Antwi and Others v. Norway (Application no. 26940/10) concerns a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that the first applicant’s expulsion from Norway, with a five-year re-entry ban, would violate the applicants’ right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention. The first applicant, Henry Antwi, is a Ghanaian national born in 1975. The second applicant, his wife Vivian Awere Osei, is a Norwegian citizen of Ghanaian origin born in 1979. The third applicant is their daughter, Nadia Ryan Pinto, a Norwegian national born in September 2001.

The first applicant arrived in Germany in 1998 and obtained a forged Portuguese passport and birth certificate under the false identity of Jose Joao Olas Pinto, born in 1969. He met the second applicant (who had moved to Norway in 1997 at age 17 to join her father and siblings) while she travelled in Germany. She invited him to Norway, where they began cohabiting in Oslo. In 2000 she acquired Norwegian citizenship. Using the forged documents, the first applicant applied on 23 December 1999 for an EEA work and residence permit, which the Norwegian authorities granted from April 2000 to April 2005. Their daughter was born in 2001. In 2003 his application for Norwegian citizenship was refused for insufficient residence. The couple married in Ghana on 11 February 2005; the second applicant then learned his true identity when he obtained a Ghanaian passport. He nevertheless used the false identity again when seeking renewal of his permit in spring 2005.

On 15 July 2005 he was arrested in the Netherlands travelling on the forged passport and thereafter disclosed his true identity to the Norwegian authorities. On 3 May 2006 the Directorate of Immigration ordered his expulsion under section 29(1)(a) of the Immigration Act 1988 for serious and repeated violations consisting of false information about identity, date of birth and nationality, supported by a forged passport. A five-year re-entry ban was imposed and the decision was entered in the Schengen Information System. Family-reunification and work-permit applications were rejected. The Directorate considered expulsion proportionate. The Immigration Appeals Board upheld the decision on 4 September 2007, stressing the gravity of the offences, the absence of any legitimate expectation of continued residence (given the false identity used throughout), and the limited weight of family ties formed under those circumstances. It found no incompatibility with Article 8 or the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, noting that the second applicant shared the first applicant’s country of origin and that the young child could accompany her parents.

The Oslo City Court quashed the decision on 28 March 2008, holding that while the conditions for expulsion were met, the measure was disproportionate vis-à-vis the eight-year-old daughter, an ordinary Norwegian girl who would lose close daily contact with her father. The Borgarting High Court, by a 2–1 majority, restored the expulsion order on 19 January 2010. It characterised the four instances of false identity information as serious, undermining immigration control that relies on trust. The first applicant had no legitimate expectation of remaining; the second applicant’s interests (Norwegian citizenship, family in Norway, employment) did not render expulsion disproportionate. The child’s best interests, while fundamental, were not decisive: she had no special care needs, her mother could provide satisfactory care, and the shared Ghanaian origin of the parents facilitated either visits or relocation. A five-year ban was consistent with practice and not an extraordinary burden. The minority favoured a two-year ban, emphasising the child’s developmental stage, her father’s primary role in schooling and activities, and the social and educational disruption of a longer separation or move to Ghana. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave to appeal on 28 April 2010.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ Article 8 complaint that implementation of the expulsion would unjustifiably interfere with their family life.

The case of Antwi and Others v. Norway (Application no. 26940/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The applicants are Henry Antwi (first applicant, Ghanaian national born 1975), his wife Vivian Awere Osei (second applicant, Norwegian citizen born in Ghana in 1979), and their daughter Nadia Ryan Pinto (third applicant, Norwegian national born September 2001). They claimed that Norwegian authorities’ decision to expel the first applicant and ban his re-entry for five years would, if implemented, breach their family life rights.

The first applicant arrived in Germany in 1998 and obtained a forged Portuguese passport and birth certificate under the false identity of Jose Joao Olas Pinto (born 1 March 1969). The second applicant arrived in Norway in 1997 at age 17 to reunite with her father and siblings. The couple met in Germany; she invited him to Norway, where they began cohabiting in Oslo. She obtained Norwegian citizenship in 2000. On 23 December 1999, using the forged documents, the first applicant applied for and received a five-year EEA work-and-residence permit (13 April 2000–13 April 2005). Their daughter was born on 23 September 2001. In 2003 he applied unsuccessfully for Norwegian citizenship due to insufficient residence. The couple married in Ghana on 11 February 2005, at which point the second applicant learned his true identity (he obtained a Ghanaian passport). He again used the false identity when seeking permit renewal in spring 2005.

On 15 July 2005, Dutch authorities arrested him en route to Canada after discovering the forged passport. He then disclosed his true identity to Norwegian authorities and later returned to Norway. On 12 October 2005 the Directorate of Immigration warned of possible expulsion. On 3 May 2006 it ordered his expulsion under section 29(1)(a) of the 1988 Immigration Act for serious/repeated violations (false identity, nationality and forged passport). The measure was not deemed disproportionate; a five-year re-entry ban was imposed and entered in the Schengen Information System. His work-permit and family-reunification applications were rejected. He was to leave by 24 July 2006. The Immigration Appeals Board upheld the decision on 4 September 2007, stressing repeated aggravated breaches, failure to depart, general-prevention interests, lack of legitimate expectation of residence (family ties formed under false identity), and the wife’s Ghanaian origin (facilitating accompaniment). The young child was said to have closest attachment to her parents. The Board found no incompatibility with Article 8 or the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

The first applicant challenged the decision in court (expulsion stayed). On 28 March 2008 the Oslo City Court quashed the Board’s decision as invalid. While expulsion conditions were met and general deterrence was weighty, the measure was disproportionate vis-à-vis the (then six-year-old) daughter, an ordinary Norwegian girl who would likely lose close contact with her father, risking developmental harm even with visits; relocation to Ghana was uncertain.

The State appealed. After a stay pending a parallel case, the Borgarting High Court (19 January 2010, 2–1) upheld the expulsion. The violations were serious (false information on four occasions, forged passport enabling an unwarranted EEA permit). The first applicant had grown up in Ghana with family there and no legitimate stay expectation. The second applicant (Norwegian citizen with family and work in Norway) had begun the relationship believing his residence lawful, but her interests alone did not render expulsion disproportionate. The eight-and-a-half-year-old daughter’s best interests were decisive: she was a Norwegian national, established in school, sports and her local environment, speaking mainly Norwegian. Her father provided close follow-up on school and hobbies. She had a recurrent skin rash (allegedly heat-aggravated, though documentation was weak). Expulsion would split the family or require relocation to Ghana—neither in her best interests—but ordinary strain was insufficient. Citing Supreme Court precedent, a child’s interests are not decisive absent special care needs if a remaining parent can provide satisfactory care. The mother (same origin, prior visits to Ghana with the child) could do so, enabling contact or settlement there. The five-year ban was not an “extraordinary burden.” The dissenting judge favoured a two-year ban as less severe given the father’s caregiving role, the child’s developmental years, unrealistic Ghana settlement, educational/social disruption, and the second applicant’s expectations.

On 28 April 2010 the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave to appeal. Throughout, the first applicant had legal representation. Interim measures under Rule 39 prevented deportation pending the Strasbourg proceedings.

**Case summary (approx. 500 words)**

The case concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life) arising from Norwegian authorities’ decision to expel Ghanaian national Henry Antwi (first applicant, born 1975) from Norway and ban his re-entry for five years. His wife, Vivian Awere Osei (second applicant, Norwegian citizen of Ghanaian origin, born 1979), and their daughter Nadia Ryan Pinto (third applicant, Norwegian national born September 2001) joined the application, arguing that implementation would disrupt their family life.

Antwi arrived in Germany in 1998 and obtained a forged Portuguese passport and birth certificate under the false identity “Jose Joao Olas Pinto” (claimed born 1969). He met the second applicant (who had arrived in Norway in 1997 aged 17 to reunite with her father and siblings) while she travelled in Germany. She invited him to Norway; they began cohabiting in Oslo. In December 1999 he applied for an EEA work-and-residence permit using the forged documents. Norwegian authorities granted a five-year permit (April 2000–April 2005). The couple’s daughter was born in 2001. Antwi applied unsuccessfully for Norwegian citizenship in 2003 (insufficient residence). They married in Ghana in February 2005; the second applicant learned his true identity around this time when he obtained a Ghanaian passport. He again used the false identity when seeking permit renewal in spring 2005.

In July 2005 Dutch authorities arrested him en route to Canada after discovering the forgery. He then disclosed his true identity (Henry Antwi, Ghanaian, born 9 May 1975) to Norwegian authorities and later returned to Norway.

On 3 May 2006 the Directorate of Immigration ordered expulsion under section 29(1)(a) of the Immigration Act 1988 for serious/repeated violations (false identity, nationality and date of birth supported by a forged passport). It found the measure proportionate and imposed a five-year re-entry ban (to be entered in the Schengen Information System). Family-reunification and work-permit applications were refused on the same ground. The Immigration Appeals Board upheld the decision in September 2007, stressing general-prevention interests, the lack of any legitimate expectation of continued residence (family life having been established under false pretences), the first applicant’s adult arrival and remaining ties to Ghana, the second applicant’s Ghanaian origin and knowledge of the true identity by 2005, and the child’s young age and ability to follow her parents. It considered the five-year ban compatible with Article 8 and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

The Oslo City Court quashed the decision in March 2008, holding expulsion disproportionate vis-à-vis the then six-year-old daughter, who would lose close paternal contact. The Borgarting High Court (2–1) reversed this in January 2010. It characterised the identity fraud (committed on four occasions) as serious, undermining immigration-control systems that rely on trust. Expulsion was not disproportionate for the first applicant (no legitimate expectation; family in Ghana). The second applicant had strong Norwegian ties but originated from Ghana and spoke the language. The decisive factor was the now 8½-year-old daughter (Norwegian, school-attending, sports-active, Norwegian-speaking, attached to both parents). The High Court majority held she had no special care needs, her mother could provide satisfactory care, shared parental origin facilitated contact or relocation to Ghana, and a five-year ban was not an “extraordinary burden.” A minority favoured a two-year ban, citing the father’s primary caregiving role, the child’s developmental stage, unrealistic relocation prospects, and the second applicant’s reasonable expectations. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave in April 2010.

The applicants complained that the expulsion and five-year ban, if executed, would breach Article 8 for all three family members. Interim measures under Rule 39 prevented deportation pending the Court’s examination. The core factual issues relevant to the alleged violation were the gravity and repetition of the immigration fraud, the circumstances in which family life was established, the duration and quality of ties to Norway versus Ghana, the child’s best interests and attachments, and the proportionality of a time-limited ban versus family disruption.

The case of Gas and Dubois v. France (application no. 25951/07) was brought by two French women, Valérie Gas (born 1961) and Nathalie Dubois (born 1965), who have cohabited in Clamart since 1989. Dubois gave birth in France on 21 September 2000 to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium by anonymous donor insemination. A. has no legally established father and has lived her entire life in the applicants’ shared home. Dubois formally recognised the child on 9 October 2000. The couple registered a civil partnership on 15 April 2002.

On 3 March 2006 Gas applied to the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance for a simple-adoption order in respect of A., with Dubois’s notarised consent. The public prosecutor opposed the application by reference to Article 365 of the Civil Code. On 4 July 2006 the tribunal found that the statutory conditions for adoption were satisfied and that the couple jointly provided the child with care and affection, but refused the order. Simple adoption of a minor transfers all parental responsibility to the adoptive parent and thereby extinguishes the birth mother’s rights, an outcome contrary both to the applicants’ intentions and to the child’s interests. The exception allowing shared parental responsibility applies only where the adopter is the spouse of the child’s parent.

The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld the refusal on 21 December 2006. It likewise accepted that the legal conditions were met and that Gas was actively involved in the child’s welfare, but held that the legal consequences of adoption would not serve the child’s interests: the applicants could not share parental responsibility (the statutory exception being confined to married spouses) and Dubois would therefore lose all rights in relation to her daughter. A subsequent delegation of parental responsibility would be insufficient to remove the resulting risks. The applicants lodged but did not pursue an appeal on points of law to the Court of Cassation; their right of appeal was declared forfeit on 20 September 2007.

The applicants complained under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 that French law discriminated against them on the ground of sexual orientation. Heterosexual married couples could obtain second-parent adoption while retaining joint parental responsibility; same-sex couples, who were excluded from marriage and whose civil partnership conferred no equivalent rights, had no comparable legal mechanism. They argued that this denied them a stable legal framework reflecting the social reality of their family life.

Under French law, simple adoption of a minor vests exclusive parental responsibility in the adopter unless the adopter is married to the child’s parent, in which case responsibility is shared (Article 365 Civil Code). Marriage is reserved to opposite-sex couples. Civil partnership creates no kinship ties and has no effect on adoptive parentage or parental responsibility. The Court of Cassation has consistently applied Article 365 to refuse simple-adoption applications by same-sex civil partners, holding that the resulting loss of the biological parent’s rights is incompatible with the child’s interests and that sharing of responsibility is available only to spouses. Delegation of parental responsibility remains possible but is temporary, does not create a legal parent-child relationship, and has been interpreted restrictively. Assisted-reproduction rules likewise limit access to opposite-sex couples. The Constitutional Council has upheld the legislature’s choice to confine the relevant adoption exception to married couples.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violation: the absence of any legal route by which a same-sex couple could establish a second parent-child relationship without depriving the birth parent of parental responsibility.

**Case of Gas and Dubois v. France (ECtHR, Application no. 25951/07)**

Valérie Gas and Nathalie Dubois, French nationals cohabiting since 1989, entered a civil partnership (PACS) in 2002. Dubois gave birth in France on 21 September 2000 to daughter A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. A. has no established legal father under Belgian law. She has lived her entire life in the applicants’ shared home in Clamart; Dubois formally recognised her on 9 October 2000, and her birth was registered locally.

On 3 March 2006, Gas applied to the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance for a simple-adoption order in respect of A., with Dubois’s notarised consent. The public prosecutor objected under Article 365 of the Civil Code. On 4 July 2006 the court found the statutory conditions for adoption satisfied and acknowledged the applicants’ active, joint involvement in the child’s upbringing and affection. It nevertheless refused the order because simple adoption would transfer all parental responsibility exclusively to the adoptive parent (Gas), thereby stripping the birth mother (Dubois) of her rights. Only spouses share parental responsibility after such an adoption; the applicants, as an unmarried same-sex couple, could not marry under French law (Article 144 of the Civil Code).

Gas appealed; Dubois intervened. The Versailles Court of Appeal, on 21 December 2006, upheld the refusal. It confirmed the applicants’ fulfilment of adoption conditions and Gas’s role in the child’s welfare but held that the legal consequences—exclusive transfer of parental responsibility without the sharing mechanism available to married couples—would not serve A.’s interests. Subsequent delegation of parental responsibility (Articles 376 et seq. of the Civil Code) was deemed insufficient to mitigate the risks of the mother’s loss of rights. The applicants did not pursue their appeal on points of law to the Court of Cassation; their right to do so was declared forfeit in September 2007.

French law distinguishes full adoption (which severs original ties) from simple adoption (which adds a legal parent-child relationship without extinguishing the original one). For a minor, simple adoption vests exclusive parental responsibility in the adopter unless the adopter is married to the child’s parent, in which case responsibility is shared (Article 365). Civil partnerships confer certain rights but create no kinship, inheritance, or adoptive ties and have no effect on parental responsibility. Assisted reproduction is available only to opposite-sex couples for therapeutic reasons. Court of Cassation rulings (notably 20 February 2007) consistently held that simple adoption by a civil partner of a child’s sole legal parent would unlawfully deprive that parent of responsibility; sharing is reserved to spouses. The Constitutional Council (6 October 2010) later confirmed that Article 365, as interpreted, does not violate constitutional equality or family-life guarantees and that the legislature may restrict simple adoption to married couples.

The applicants complained under Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 8 that they had suffered discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Unlike heterosexual married couples, they had no legal means of second-parent adoption that would create a formal parent-child link while allowing them to share parental responsibility, thereby recognising the child’s social and family reality. They argued this treatment interfered with respect for their private and family life.
