The case of Sitaropoulos and Giakoumopoulos v. Greece (Application no. 42202/07) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 September 2007 by three Greek nationals residing in Strasbourg, where they worked as officials of the Council of Europe. The second applicant’s complaint was later struck out, leaving Mr Nikolaos Sitaropoulos (born 1967) and Mr Christos Giakoumopoulos (born 1958) as the remaining applicants. They alleged that the Greek authorities’ refusal to allow them to vote from their place of residence in the parliamentary elections of 16 September 2007 constituted a disproportionate interference with their right to free elections under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

The relevant facts began with Presidential Decree no. 154/2007 of 18 August 2007, which dissolved the Greek Parliament and called a general election for 16 September 2007. On 10 September 2007 the applicants, who were permanently resident in France, sent a faxed letter to the Greek ambassador in France requesting to exercise their voting rights there. On 12 September 2007 the ambassador replied, relying on instructions from the Ministry of the Interior, that although the Greek State wished to enable citizens abroad to vote from their place of residence, no statutory rules existed for this purpose. Such rules could not be introduced by simple administrative decision; special measures would be required to set up polling stations in embassies and consulates. Consequently, the request could not be granted. The election proceeded on 16 September 2007. The applicants did not travel to Greece and therefore did not vote.

Greek electoral law in force at the time (Presidential Decree no. 96/2007) granted the right to vote to every Greek national aged 18 or over, subject only to limited exceptions such as legal incapacity or certain criminal convictions. However, Article 6 confined the actual exercise of that right to persons registered on the electoral roll of a municipality or local-authority area within a Greek constituency. Voting was mandatory. Article 51 § 4 of the 1975 Constitution (as amended in 2001) provided that the conditions governing the exercise of the vote by persons living outside the country “may be specified by statute” adopted by a two-thirds majority of Parliament, and that postal or other appropriate means could be used provided results were announced simultaneously with those inside Greece. No such statute had been enacted by September 2007.

A subsequent bill intended to implement out-of-country voting was introduced in February 2009. Parliamentary reports characterised the measure as fulfilling a constitutional “social right” under Article 108 (which obliges the State to maintain expatriates’ ties with the homeland) and as implementing Article 51 § 4. The Scientific Council of Parliament, however, concluded that the Constitution conferred only an option, not a duty, on the legislature. The bill was rejected on 7 April 2009 for lack of the required two-thirds majority; opposition deputies cited, inter alia, the potential impact of the large expatriate population on the composition of Parliament.

Thus the applicants, although fully entitled under Greek law to vote, were unable to do so from their long-term residence abroad because no legislative machinery existed to enable them to cast a ballot outside Greece. This factual and legal situation formed the core of the alleged violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

001-109581:
On 1 May 2001, police contained a large crowd at Oxford Circus in central London using a cordon (known as “kettling”) during anti-globalisation protests. The four applicants were held inside for up to seven hours and alleged this amounted to a deprivation of liberty contrary to Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.

Ms Austin, a protester, arrived around 2 p.m. She asked to leave at 3.45 p.m. to collect her infant daughter from a crèche but was refused and remained until about 9.30 p.m. Mr Black, intending only to visit a bookshop, was directed away from approaching demonstrators but was forced into the Circus by advancing riot police around 2.30 p.m. He was told there was an exit for non-protesters; none existed. He left at 9.20 p.m. Ms Lowenthal and Mr O’Shea, both local workers on lunch break and unconnected to the protest, were blocked by police lines and held until 9.35 p.m. and 8 p.m. respectively. Repeated requests to leave were refused.

Intelligence and recent history shaped the police response. Similar protests in London (1999–2000) and abroad had produced serious disorder, injuries and damage. Organisers of the 2001 “May Day Monopoly” events had not cooperated, had publicised 24 possible targets and a 4 p.m. rally at Oxford Circus, and had encouraged masks and violence. Special Branch estimated 500–1,000 hard-core activists intent on confrontation. Nearly 6,000 officers were deployed, the largest such operation then recorded.

By 2 p.m. more than 1,500 people (some masked) were already at Oxford Circus, earlier and in greater numbers than expected. A full cordon was imposed within 20–25 minutes under common-law powers to prevent a breach of the peace. Space inside permitted movement but no food, water, toilets or shelter were available; conditions worsened in cold rain. No public announcement was made until 4 p.m. for fear the cordon would be rushed.

Controlled collective release was repeatedly planned and then suspended because of missile-throwing, pushing, break-out attempts and violence both inside and outside the cordon, plus other disorderly crowds nearby. Individual releases totalled around 400 (mostly before 4 p.m.), including some identified as bystanders or vulnerable persons. Collective dispersal finally began in small groups after 8 p.m. and was largely complete by 9.45 p.m. Over 100 arrests followed. Peak numbers were estimated at 2,000 inside and 1,000 outside.

The High Court, after a three-week trial with extensive witness, documentary and video evidence, found the police had reasonable grounds to fear serious injury, death or property damage. An absolute cordon at 2 p.m. was the only practicable option and was proportionate. Earlier release was impossible given ongoing violence, non-cooperation (about 40 per cent of those inside actively hostile) and stretched resources. Distinguishing peaceful individuals from potential troublemakers was impracticable. The containment was a close confinement whose effects grew severe, but it was kept under constant review.

The applicants sued for false imprisonment and breach of Article 5. The High Court accepted necessity as a defence to false imprisonment and held there had been a deprivation of liberty, but that it was justified under Article 5 § 1(c). The Court of Appeal and House of Lords disagreed on Article 5, holding that the measure was not a deprivation of liberty at all. They characterised it as a necessary, non-arbitrary crowd-control operation analogous to holding football supporters or motorists after an accident, whose purpose (public safety) and circumstances (violence beyond police control) placed it outside Article 5. The unusually long duration did not alter that characterisation.

A pragmatic balance was required between individual liberty and public safety (tied to Article 2 positive obligations). Proportionate, good-faith measures of crowd control in the public interest—here, to prevent serious disorder, with continuous review and no punitive intent—did not constitute deprivation of liberty, even if unusually prolonged by external factors. 001-110164:
**Case of Boulois v. Luxembourg (Application no. 37575/04), ECHR Grand Chamber judgment of 3 April 2012**

The applicant, Thomas Boulois (French national, born 1972), was remanded in Luxembourg in December 1998 and convicted in October 2001 by the Court of Appeal to 15 years’ imprisonment (three years suspended) for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape and false imprisonment accompanied by torture. He was detained in Schrassig Prison when he lodged his application.

While serving his sentence, Boulois made repeated requests for prison leave (temporary absence, typically one day, counting toward the sentence). The first, in October 2003, sought leave for administrative tasks (renewing documents, collecting papers, banking/tax matters, meeting contacts, workshop measurements). Supporting psychologist certificates noted his therapy and desire to understand his offences and avoid reoffending. The Prison Board (Attorney-General or representative, a judge and a prosecutor) refused on 5 November 2003, citing deportation risk (pending Ministry of Justice application), absconding risk due to failure to reflect on the crime, and the need to begin paying civil damages.

A January 2004 repeat request (same programme, with lawyer arguing it would aid rehabilitation, reintegration and quicker damages payments) was refused in March 2004 as the prior decision remained valid.

Boulois sought judicial review of both refusals in the Administrative Court (May 2004). That court, of its own motion, declined jurisdiction in December 2004, holding that prison leave alters the “scope” of a sentence imposed by ordinary courts and is thus a judicial (not administrative) measure relating to sentence execution, unlike purely internal prison administration decisions. The Higher Administrative Court upheld this in April 2005, classifying it as a decision on the manner of sentence execution (not length). It rejected claims of denial of justice or Article 6 inapplicability, noting administrative courts could not rule on merits.

Further requests (August 2004 onward) were refused: ability to study in prison plus insufficient compensation efforts (September 2004); unestablished visiting rights for children (December 2004); lack of reasons (March 2005); absconding risk (July 2005); and failure to pay compensation or abide by conditions (May 2006). Later letters seeking repayment plans and explanations went largely unanswered.

Leave was eventually granted from October 2008 (initially one day with his girlfriend, then multiple two-day periods). In 2009 he transferred to Givenich semi-open prison, received further leave for work-seeking and formalities, signed a vocational contract, and obtained conditional release in September 2009. Sentence suspension followed in July 2010.

Domestic law (1986 Law) defines prison leave as a privilege for family reasons, rehabilitation/professional reintegration or trial toward conditional release, available to first offenders after one-third of the sentence, considering personality, progress and reoffending risk. Decisions for sentences over two years rest with the Prison Board (majority vote, chaired by the judge). Implementing rules require written requests, minimum intervals, and limited reapplications after refusal. No specific judicial appeal against Board decisions is provided. Luxembourg’s Ombudsman later recommended a post-sentencing judge with adversarial proceedings and appeals.

Council of Europe recommendations (R(82)16, Rec(2003)23, Rec(2006)2) urge granting leave on social/reintegration grounds (considering offence, behaviour, family situation), informing of refusal reasons, providing review, and treating leave as integral to sentence plans and gradual release, including for closed-prison long-term inmates.

The applicant alleged that the refusals, combined with administrative courts’ lack of jurisdiction and absence of other review, deprived him of a fair hearing and access to a court under Article 6 § 1. (A Chamber had found a violation by 4–3 votes before Grand Chamber referral.)

The case of Boulois v. Luxembourg (Application no. 37575/04) originated from an application by French national Thomas Boulois (born 1972), who was detained in Schrassig Prison. Remanded in custody on 15 December 1998, he was convicted on 22 October 2001 by the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape and false imprisonment accompanied by torture, receiving a 15-year sentence (three years suspended). While imprisoned, Boulois made repeated requests for prison leave (temporary absence of up to 24 hours, counting towards sentence length) under Luxembourg’s 1986 Law on execution of custodial sentences. This privilege, available after one-third of the sentence for first offenders, aims to facilitate family contact, rehabilitation, professional reintegration or trial of conditional release. Decisions rest with a Prison Board (Attorney-General’s representative, a judge and a prosecutor), exercising broad discretion based on the prisoner’s personality, progress and reoffending risk.

Boulois’s first request (October 2003) sought one day’s leave for administrative tasks: obtaining photos, renewing his driving licence and consular card, visiting police, a bank, tax office, lawyer, town hall and others, plus collecting documents and meeting contacts. He noted unpaid civil damages due to debts. Supporting psychologist certificates highlighted his therapy and efforts to understand his offences. On 5 November 2003 the Board refused, citing deportation risk (pending application), absconding risk from insufficient reflection on the crime, and the need to start compensating the victim. A January 2004 reiteration, endorsed by his lawyer as aiding reintegration and quicker compensation payments, was refused on 17 March 2004 as the prior decision remained valid.

On 25 May 2004 Boulois applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review of these refusals. At a 6 December 2004 hearing the court raised jurisdiction of its own motion. On 23 December 2004 it declined, distinguishing administrative prison-treatment measures from decisions altering a sentence’s “scope” (manner of execution), which it deemed judicial. The Higher Administrative Court upheld this on 14 April 2005, confirming the decisions as judicial (altering execution terms, not length), finding no denial of justice and holding Article 6 inapplicable to a body lacking merits jurisdiction.

Further requests followed. An August 2004 application to attend external accounting/computing classes was refused (21 September 2004) as courses were available in prison and compensation efforts remained insufficient. An October 2004 request for a St Nicholas weekend with his children (whose visiting rights were disputed post-divorce) was refused (14 December 2004) because rights were not established. A February 2005 request (reintegration, document renewal, debt solutions) was refused (23 March 2005) for lack of reasons. Subsequent requests were denied for absconding risk (July 2005) or inadequate compensation efforts and non-compliance with conditions (May 2006). Boulois’s later letters seeking repayment-plan assistance and condition explanations received no substantive reply.

From late 2008 leave was granted (initially one day with his girlfriend, later two-day periods). In March 2009 he transferred to Givenich semi-open prison, received ten days’ leave for work-seeking and formalities, signed a vocational contract, obtained conditional-release approval (September 2009) and had his sentence suspended on 15 July 2010.

The applicant alleged that the refusals deprived him of a fair hearing and court access under Article 6 § 1. Luxembourg law treats leave as a non-automatic privilege; Council of Europe recommendations urge leave on social grounds with review of refusals, while the Ombudsman advocated a post-sentencing judge with adversarial, appealable decisions. The Chamber found a violation; the Grand Chamber examined whether such discretionary decisions engaged civil rights attracting Article 6 safeguards.

**Case of Boulois v. Luxembourg (Application no. 37575/04), ECtHR Grand Chamber, 3 April 2012**

Thomas Boulois, a French national born in 1972, was remanded in custody on 15 December 1998. On 22 October 2001 the Luxembourg Court of Appeal’s Criminal Division sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment (three years suspended) for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape and false imprisonment accompanied by torture, committed on 10 December 1998. He was held at Schrassig Prison. After his divorce (finalised 19 October 2000) he litigated visiting rights concerning his three minor children.

While serving his sentence he made repeated requests for prison leave (temporary absence of part of a day or 24 hours, counting towards the sentence). Under the Law of 26 July 1986 such leave is a privilege that may be granted (after one-third of sentence for first offenders) for family reasons, preparation for rehabilitation/reintegration, or on a trial basis towards conditional release. Decisions for sentences over two years are taken by the Prison Board (Attorney-General or representative, a judge and a public prosecutor) after considering personality, progress and risk of reoffending; the Board enjoys wide discretion and leave is never automatic.

His first request (October 2003) sought one day’s escorted leave for administrative tasks (passport photos, driving-licence renewal, consular card, tax office, bank, lawyer, etc.). Supporting psychologists’ certificates noted ongoing therapy aimed at understanding the offences and avoiding reoffending. On 5 November 2003 the Prison Board refused, citing risk of deportation (an application to the Ministry of Justice was pending), risk of absconding, failure to reflect on the crime, and the need to begin paying civil-party damages. A second identical request (January 2004, supported by his lawyer as aiding rehabilitation and enabling damage payments) was refused on 17 March 2004 on the same grounds.

On 25 May 2004 Boulois applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review of both refusals. At a 6 December 2004 hearing the court raised jurisdiction of its own motion. On 23 December 2004 it declined jurisdiction, distinguishing ordinary prison-administration measures from decisions altering the nature or “scope” (manner of execution) of a sentence imposed by ordinary courts; the latter were judicial, not administrative. The Higher Administrative Court upheld this on 14 April 2005, classifying prison-leave decisions as judicial alterations of sentence-execution terms. It rejected arguments that no other remedy existed, that the decisions did not alter sentence scope, and that declining jurisdiction denied justice contrary to Article 6 § 1. It held Article 6 inapplicable to a body without power to rule on the merits.

Further requests followed. A third (August 2004, to attend accounting/computing classes) was refused (21 September 2004) because courses were available in prison and no substantial compensation payments had been made. A fourth (October 2004, to spend a day with his children) was refused (14 December 2004) because visiting rights were not clearly established. Later requests were refused for failure to give reasons, risk of non-return, lack of effort (especially on compensation) and refusal to abide by conditions. Between May and October 2006 he wrote repeatedly seeking a repayment plan and clarification of reintegration conditions; the Attorney-General’s representative declined to comment.

Leave was eventually granted: one day on 31 October 2008 (to be spent with his girlfriend) and five two-day periods thereafter. On 20 March 2009 he was transferred to Givenich semi-open prison and given ten days’ leave for job-seeking and administrative tasks, later placed under a semi-custodial regime. He obtained a vocational contract as a cook, started a sole-trader business, and was granted conditional release (25 September 2009). Sentence-suspension requests were refused until 15 July 2010, when the remaining sentence was suspended and he left prison.

Boulois alleged that the refusals of prison leave, coupled with the administrative courts’ lack of jurisdiction and the absence of any other judicial remedy, deprived him of a fair hearing and access to a court (Article 6). The Chamber (14 December 2010) found a violation by four votes to three; the Grand Chamber accepted the Government’s referral.
001-109788:
The applicant, an Austrian national born in 1953, had a lengthy criminal history in Austria (1968–1988) involving robbery, theft, assault and a 1981 rape conviction that led to more than ten years’ detention, including in an institution for mentally disturbed offenders. In June 1991 the Munich I Regional Court convicted him of three counts of sexual abuse of children (one involving attempted rape) committed in 1989–90, imposed a sentence of five years and six months’ imprisonment and ordered preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The court found he possessed a propensity to commit serious sexual offences causing physical or mental harm. An expulsion order of September 1991, which became final the following month, required his removal from Germany upon release and barred re-entry.

He served the full prison term until 20 March 1996 and was then placed in preventive detention in a separate wing of Straubing Prison. In July 1997 the Regensburg Regional Court confirmed that detention remained necessary. A psychiatric expert diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder and recommended social therapy followed by sex-offender treatment; the applicant had declined prison-based therapy out of fear of harassment. Transfer to a psychiatric hospital was refused. Subsequent attempts to place him in social-therapeutic institutions elsewhere failed: institutions cited the enforceable expulsion order (which made completion of a multi-year programme impossible) and, in one case, his age (then 45) as rendering him unsuitable for a facility geared to younger offenders. In January 2000 the same court again continued detention, noting that therapy had been denied solely because of his nationality and impending expulsion, and suggested examination of a transfer to Austria.

Repeated applications under Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure to discontinue execution of the measure in view of expulsion were rejected by prosecutors and courts on the ground that he remained dangerous to the public; he had also declined to request a transfer to Austria. In the proceedings that formed the subject of the Strasbourg application, the Regensburg Regional Court (May 2003) and Nuremberg Court of Appeal (July 2003) ordered further detention after hearing a new expert who found the personality disorder unchanged and a continuing risk of violent sexual reoffending. The expert proposed a discussion group or social therapy; the applicant refused the former because it would publicise his offences inside the prison. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint in March 2004.

Later reviews (2005–2007) likewise maintained detention. After ten years had elapsed the courts declined to terminate the measure under the post-1998 version of Article 67d § 3, again citing persistent risk and the applicant’s refusal of newly available prison therapies. Transfer requests to Austria were refused because Austrian law would have required his release after ten years. In January 2008 prosecutors finally dispensed with further execution upon expulsion; the applicant was released and removed to Austria on 16 April 2008. Austrian courts then revoked an earlier suspension and re-detained him.

The applicant alleged that the refusal of therapy—attributable solely to the expulsion order and his age—rendered his continued preventive detention arbitrary and therefore contrary to Article 5 § 1.

The case of Ostermünchner v. Germany (Application no. 36035/04) was brought by an Austrian national born in 1953, who alleged that his continued preventive detention in Germany, without access to therapy due to an impending expulsion order and his age, violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty). He also raised issues of retrospective application of law (abolition of a 10-year maximum duration for a first period of preventive detention after his conviction) and discrimination on grounds of nationality.

Between 1968 and 1988, Austrian courts convicted the applicant of multiple offences including robbery, theft, assault and rape (the latter in 1981, for which he received seven years’ imprisonment plus placement in an institution for mentally disturbed offenders). He spent over ten years detained. On 14 June 1991 the Munich I Regional Court convicted him of three counts of sexual abuse of children (committed in 1989–1990, including attempted rape and sexual assault), imposed a sentence of five years and six months’ imprisonment and ordered preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. Court-appointed experts described him as having an egocentric anti-social personality lacking empathy and a propensity to commit serious offences causing physical or mental harm. On 19 September 1991 the City of Munich issued a final expulsion order (effective on release from prison) prohibiting re-entry to Germany.

The applicant served his full prison term until 20 March 1996 and was then placed in preventive detention in a separate wing of Straubing Prison. On 15 July 1997 the Regensburg Regional Court ordered execution of the preventive detention (Article 67c § 1 Criminal Code). A psychiatric expert diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder and noted the applicant’s refusal of sexual-offender therapy in prison due to fear of harassment; the expert recommended social therapy first. The court refused transfer to a psychiatric hospital, finding social therapy more suitable for reintegration.

Subsequent attempts to obtain social therapy failed. Institutions in Baden-Württemberg (August 1997), Erlangen (November 1998) and Munich (December 1998) refused admission because of the enforceable expulsion order (which made completion of a multi-year programme impossible) or because the applicant (then aged 45) did not fit a programme for younger offenders. Administrative rules excluded prisoners subject to expulsion from transfer to socio-therapeutic institutions. On 13 January 2000 the Regensburg Regional Court continued detention, finding a continuing risk of sexual offences; it noted the applicant’s justified refusal of group therapy in Straubing and his unsuccessful efforts to obtain social therapy, and suggested examining a transfer to Austria.

Repeated requests under Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure to discontinue execution in view of expulsion were refused (1993–2003) on public-interest grounds, as the applicant remained dangerous; he had not requested transfer to Austria.

In the proceedings at issue, on 2 May 2003 the Regensburg Regional Court (after hearing a further expert) again continued detention under Article 67d § 2, finding the personality unchanged and a risk of further violent sexual offences. The expert recommended attempting therapy (discussion group or social-therapeutic institution) despite limited prospects. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 4 July 2003, endorsing the findings and noting the applicant’s refusal of a discussion group; it considered detention proportionate. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the constitutional complaint on 25 March 2004, holding the retrospective-punishment claim inadmissible (the applicant not yet affected by the 1998 amendments) and the remainder ill-founded.

Later reviews (2005–2006) confirmed continued detention after ten years, noting the applicant’s refusal of therapies that had become available in Straubing. Transfer-to-Austria requests were refused because he would have been released after ten years there. In January 2008 the prosecution finally dispensed with further execution under Article 456a; the applicant was released on 16 April 2008 and expelled. Austrian authorities then revoked the 1981 suspension of his earlier institutional placement, and he has been detained in Vienna since August 2008.

The applicant, Austrian national Franz Ostermünchner (born 1953), lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights alleging that his continued preventive detention in Germany, without access to therapy due to an impending expulsion order and his age, violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.

Between 1968 and 1988, Austrian courts convicted him of multiple offences including robbery, theft, assault and rape, resulting in over ten years' detention, partly in an institution for mentally disturbed offenders. On 14 June 1991, the Munich I Regional Court convicted him of three counts of sexual abuse of children (including attempted rape and sexual assault) committed in 1989–1990. It sentenced him to five years and six months' imprisonment and ordered preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code, finding that he had a propensity to commit serious offences causing physical or mental harm, based on expert evidence of an egocentric anti-social personality lacking empathy.

On 19 September 1991, the City of Munich issued a final expulsion order (effective on release) prohibiting his re-entry to Germany. He served his prison sentence until 20 March 1996 and was then placed in preventive detention at Straubing Prison.

In 1997, the Regensburg Regional Court ordered execution of the preventive detention, relying on expert reports diagnosing a dissocial personality disorder. The expert recommended social therapy followed by sex-offender treatment, but the applicant had refused in-prison therapy due to fear of harassment. Transfer to a psychiatric hospital was refused. Subsequent attempts to access social-therapeutic institutions in other prisons failed: one rejected him because the expulsion order prevented completion of a five-year programme; another cited administrative rules excluding those subject to expulsion; a third deemed its programme unsuitable due to his age (then 45).

In January 2000, the same court continued detention, noting the ongoing risk of sexual offences and that therapy had been refused solely due to his age and status as a foreigner facing expulsion. It suggested examining transfer to Austria. Repeated requests under Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure to discontinue execution in view of expulsion were rejected by prosecutors (confirmed on appeal) on grounds of public interest and ongoing dangerousness; the applicant declined to request transfer to Austria.

The impugned 2003 proceedings concerned a further review. On 2 May 2003, the Regensburg Regional Court, after hearing the applicant and expert H., ordered continued detention under Article 67d § 2 of the Criminal Code. The expert found the personality unchanged and a persistent risk of violent sexual offences, recommending therapy (including a discussion group or placement in other prisons) despite limited prospects, as the applicant expressed willingness. The applicant refused the in-prison group. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 4 July 2003, endorsing the risk assessment and finding detention proportionate given the applicant's refusal of available treatment.

The applicant's 2003 constitutional complaint alleged disproportionate detention without therapy (due to expulsion), retrospective application of the 1998 abolition of the ten-year maximum (Article 67d § 3), and nationality-based discrimination. On 25 March 2004, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider it, finding the retrospective complaint inadmissible (as the applicant was not yet affected) and the remainder ill-founded.

Subsequent reviews (2005–2006) again continued detention, noting no therapy received (partly due to the applicant's later refusals of newly available options) and ongoing risk even after ten years. Transfer requests to Austria were refused because he would have been released there after ten years. In 2008, prosecutors dispensed with further execution upon expulsion. He was released and expelled to Austria on 16 April 2008, after which Austrian authorities detained him pursuant to the earlier 1981 order. 

These facts centre on the German authorities' repeated decisions to maintain preventive detention while systematically denying the applicant access to recommended therapeutic measures solely on grounds of the enforceable expulsion order and his age, despite expert consensus on the need for such treatment to address his dangerousness.
001-110156:
The case of Chmura v. Poland originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Polish national Mariusz Chmura, who alleged that his criminal trial had been unfair in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant, born in 1973, was suspected of participating in an organised criminal gang. The key events centred on the abduction, beating and robbery of NA, a Bulgarian national allegedly involved in procuring prostitution, who claimed that several men (including the applicant) had demanded protection money related to foreign prostitutes.

In April 1999, NA identified the applicant from a photograph, in an identity parade and during a confrontation, reiterating that the applicant and accomplices had attacked him. Subsequent attempts to locate NA failed initially, as he was not at his indicated addresses and an arrest warrant existed against him in another case. The applicant was arrested in February 2002 on charges of kidnapping and robbing NA in November 1998 as part of a gang led by LC. Charges referenced testimony from NA and another victim.

On 19 March 2002, after NA was located and arrested, the prosecutor requested that a court hear him under Article 316 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing the risk that NA (a foreign national without a stable Polish address) might not be available at trial. The request was granted, and the hearing was set for 11 April 2002, with notification to the accused and counsel. The applicant's counsel claimed he learned of it by chance (though the Government disputed this) and appeared. Counsel sought an adjournment to consult the investigation file, particularly NA's prior statements, arguing that lack of access prevented effective questioning and defence. The prosecutor opposed, citing witness protection needs and stating that the file would become accessible the next day. The court refused the adjournment, holding it lacked competence to grant file access without prosecutorial permission. The applicant, counsel and some co-accused left the courtroom in protest. NA then testified, identifying the applicant as an attacker and answering questions from the prosecutor and two accused. The hearing was video-recorded.

A bill of indictment followed in April 2002, charging the applicant with gang participation, abduction, deprivation of liberty and robbery of NA. At the 2002–2003 trial (12 hearings), repeated unsuccessful efforts were made to summon NA, including via police and the Bulgarian embassy. The court therefore played the video of NA's April 2002 testimony. On 4 June 2003, the Kielce Regional Court convicted the applicant (and others) largely on NA's evidence, imposing a four-year prison sentence and fine. It noted the special hearing procedure was justified by the risk of unavailability, that counsel had waived the chance to question NA by leaving, and that questions could have been put even without the full file.

On appeal, counsel argued a breach of defence rights under Article 6, as denial of pre-hearing file access (despite the investigation being essentially complete) prevented identification of inconsistencies in NA's statements (e.g., regarding dates and the applicant's role) and rendered the defence illusory. The prosecutor's actions were said to have deliberately hindered rights, and NA had been allowed to leave Poland. The Kraków Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in February 2004, finding NA's testimony decisive but holding that file access at the investigation stage was at the prosecutor's discretion (important for confidentiality and safety, given other gang members at large). Counsel had not requested access in advance and, by leaving, had waived participation rights; questions could still have been asked based on the applicant's information or NA's live testimony. Inconsistencies were examined and rejected. The Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded in December 2004.

These facts concern the alleged unfairness arising from restricted defence participation in examining the sole key witness whose evidence proved decisive to conviction.

The case of Chmura v. Poland (Application no. 18475/05) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the unfairness of criminal proceedings against the applicant, Mariusz Chmura, a Polish national born in 1973. The applicant was suspected of involvement in an organised criminal gang. In 1999, NA, a Bulgarian national allegedly involved in procuring prostitution, filed a criminal complaint of abduction and robbery. On 19 April 1999 NA testified to the prosecutor that several men had abducted, severely beaten and robbed him while demanding protection money linked to the income of foreign prostitutes under his supervision. NA identified the applicant from a photograph. On 23 April 1999 NA identified the applicant at an identity parade and, during a confrontation the same day, reiterated his accusations; the applicant denied involvement, stating he had merely seen NA near a bar frequented by prostitutes.

Authorities later lost contact with NA. A summons sent to his Bulgarian address was returned, indicating he resided in Poland, but he could not be located. The investigation was adjourned pending legal assistance from Bulgarian authorities regarding another witness. On 12 February 2002 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of kidnapping and robbing NA in November 1998 as part of a gang led by LC. He was charged and detained. The statement of charges relied particularly on testimonies from another victim (PK) and NA.

Police efforts to trace NA continued; he had changed residence and an arrest warrant existed against him in another case. On 18 March 2002 NA was arrested and questioned. The applicant’s counsel submitted his power of attorney that day (transmitted to the prosecutor the next day). On 19 March 2002 the prosecutor requested the Kielce Regional Court, pursuant to Article 316 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, to hear NA on 11 April 2002 because of the risk he might not appear at trial. NA, a foreign national without a known permanent address in Poland, had only recently been located. The court granted the request and directed notification of the applicant, co-accused and counsel.

The applicant’s counsel maintained he was not formally notified but learned of the hearing by chance and attended. At the 11 April 2002 hearing (video-recorded), counsel sought an adjournment to consult the investigation file, at least regarding NA’s prior statements. The prosecutor opposed this, citing the need to protect the witness and stating the file would become accessible from the following day. The court refused the adjournment, holding it lacked competence over file access without prosecutorial permission. Counsel protested that proceeding without file access would prevent effective defence; the applicant, counsel and some co-accused then left the courtroom. NA described the alleged events, recognised the applicant as one of the perpetrators, and answered questions from the prosecutor and two co-accused.

A bill of indictment was filed on 26 April 2002 charging the applicant with participation in a criminal gang and the abduction, deprivation of liberty and robbery of NA. The trial, comprising twelve hearings from July 2002 to May 2003, included unsuccessful police and embassy efforts to locate NA. On 13 May 2003 the court played the 11 April video recording. On 4 June 2003 the Kielce Regional Court convicted the applicant (and others) largely on NA’s testimony identifying him, imposing a four-year prison sentence and a fine. It noted the special hearing under Article 316 § 3 CCP, the unsuccessful attempts to secure NA’s presence, and that the applicant and counsel had forfeited the chance to question NA by leaving.

On appeal the applicant’s counsel argued, invoking Article 6, that denial of prior file access (particularly NA’s earlier statements) prevented comparison of testimonies and identification of inconsistencies, rendering the defence illusory. The Kraków Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 26 February 2004, finding the applicant and counsel had been duly summoned, that file access during investigation required prosecutorial permission to protect confidentiality and witness safety (some gang members remaining at large), and that they could have requested access earlier or posed questions based on the client’s information or NA’s live testimony. By leaving they waived their right to participate. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded on 8 December 2004.

Relevant domestic provisions included Article 316 § 3 CCP (allowing a court hearing of a witness at risk of unavailability at trial) and Article 156 § 5 CCP (restricting investigation-file access to cases of prosecutorial permission). These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that restrictions on confronting and examining the decisive witness, combined with withheld file access, violated the fairness of the trial.

The case of Chmura v. Poland originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 April 2005 by Polish national Mariusz Chmura, born in 1973. He alleged that his criminal trial was unfair, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention.

The applicant was suspected of participating in an organised criminal gang. In 1999, NA, a Bulgarian national allegedly involved in procuring prostitution, complained of abduction, severe beating and robbery by men demanding protection money from foreign prostitutes. On 19 April 1999, NA identified the applicant from a photograph as one of his attackers. On 23 April 1999, NA identified him in an identity parade; during a confrontation the same day, NA reiterated the accusations while the applicant denied involvement, stating he knew NA only from seeing him near a bar frequented by prostitutes.

NA subsequently could not be located (a summons to his Bulgarian address indicated residence in Poland), and the investigation was adjourned. On 12 February 2002, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of kidnapping and robbing NA in November 1998 as part of a gang led by LC. He was charged and detained on remand. The written grounds for the charges, served on 20 February 2002, relied particularly on the testimonies of another victim (PK) and NA.

Police efforts to trace NA continued; an arrest warrant existed against him in a separate case. He was located and arrested on 18 March 2002. The applicant’s counsel submitted a power of attorney on 18 March. The prosecutor heard NA on 19 March 2002 (NA undertook to appear in court on 11 April) and requested the Kielce Regional Court to hear him pursuant to Article 316 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing the risk he might be unavailable at trial due to his foreign nationality and previously unknown whereabouts in Poland. The court granted the request on 20 March and decided to notify the accused and counsel.

On 2 April 2002, counsel was informed that the investigation file could be consulted from 12 April (final date 22 April). The applicant claimed counsel learned of the 11 April hearing only by chance (the Government maintained he was duly notified). At the video-recorded hearing on 11 April 2002, counsel requested an adjournment because he had not been able to consult the file, particularly NA’s prior statements, arguing this prevented effective defence. The prosecutor opposed, citing the need to protect the witness, and stated the file would be accessible from the next day. The court refused, holding it was not competent to decide file access without the prosecutor’s permission, and proceeded. The applicant, counsel and some co-accused left in protest. NA described the events, recognised the applicant as one of the perpetrators, and answered questions from the prosecutor and two accused.

The bill of indictment was filed on 26 April 2002, charging the applicant with participation in a criminal gang and with abducting, depriving of liberty and robbing NA. The trial (July 2002–May 2003, 12 hearings) included unsuccessful attempts to summon NA (police assistance and Bulgarian embassy). On 13 May 2003 the court decided to play the 11 April video. On 4 June 2003 the Kielce Regional Court convicted the applicant (and others) of the charges, sentencing him to four years’ imprisonment and a fine. The judgment relied to a decisive extent on NA’s testimony identifying the applicant. The court noted the pre-trial hearing under Article 316 § 3 due to unavailability risk, unsuccessful later summons, and that the applicant and counsel had freely forfeited the chance to question NA (even without the file they could have asked questions based on the testimony given).

Counsel appealed on 23 October 2003, complaining of a breach of defence rights (Article 6) because lack of prior file access (especially previous statements) prevented highlighting inconsistencies in NA’s accounts; the prosecutor had allegedly hindered the defence; and the authorities had allowed NA to leave Poland. The Kraków Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 26 February 2004. It held NA’s testimony was key evidence; the applicant and counsel had been summoned and appeared; file access during investigation required prosecutorial permission to protect confidentiality and the investigation’s outcome; participation in the hearing did not require access; adjournment would have caused significant delay; refusal was reasonable given safety concerns (gang members still at large); counsel should have requested access earlier (and could have appealed a refusal); and by leaving they waived the right to put questions. Alleged inconsistencies were rejected as ill-founded. A cassation appeal raising similar points was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 8 December 2004 as manifestly ill-founded.

Relevant domestic provisions included Article 316 § 3 CCP (court may hear a witness if there is a danger the witness cannot be heard at trial) and Article 156 § 5 CCP (file access during preparatory proceedings only with permission of the person conducting them).
001-109807:
The case of Granos Organicos Nacionales S.A. v. Germany (Application no. 19508/07) concerns a Peruvian corporation based in Lima that exported organic bananas to Europe. In 2001/2002 it concluded a commission contract with two German companies, providing that disputes would be brought before Hamburg courts (with an additional Hamburg arbitration clause). On 31 December 2005 the applicant, claiming insolvency of itself and its shareholder, applied to the Hamburg Regional Court for legal aid to sue the German companies for breach of contract, as it could not pay the required advance court fees.

On 4 January 2006 the Regional Court refused legal aid under section 116(2) of the German Code of Civil Procedure. That provision restricts legal aid for legal persons to those founded or based in an EU or EEA Member State (and only if neither the entity nor those financially interested can pay the costs and if non-litigation would run counter to the general interest). The court held the list of eligible entities exhaustive and declined to extend it to extra-European companies, stating Germany was under no duty to grant legal aid to all legal persons worldwide.

The applicant’s objection was rejected on 17 January 2006. On 23 January 2006 the Hanseatic Court of Appeal confirmed the refusal. It accepted that the restriction interfered with access to court but found the interference justified by reciprocity: automatic equality of treatment would remove any incentive for third States to afford comparable protection to German legal persons. Even if the applicant were treated as a domestic entity, the court (citing a 1973 Federal Constitutional Court decision) considered that a legal person must pursue its objects by its own means; non-litigation therefore did not run counter to the general interest.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint on 25 October 2006 (decision served 2 November 2006). The company applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 2 May 2007, alleging that the refusal of legal aid was discriminatory and violated its right of access to a court. The application was declared admissible on 12 October 2010.

German law further requires non-EU/EEA plaintiffs to give security for costs (section 110 CCP) and makes service of a claim contingent on payment of court fees unless legal aid is granted or certain hardship exceptions apply (Court Fees Act). Peruvian law grants legal aid only to natural persons. Germany is a party to the 1954 Hague Convention on Civil Procedure, which provides for reciprocal legal aid among contracting States, but Peru is not a party. Comparative material from 32 Convention States shows three models: many exclude legal aid for all legal persons; some restrict it to non-commercial entities; a minority (including Germany) allow it for commercial companies under limited conditions.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: a commercially active non-EU/EEA company, contractually bound to litigate in Germany and unable to pay fees, was denied legal aid solely because of its Peruvian nationality, while EU/EEA legal persons in comparable circumstances would have been eligible.

The case of Granos Organicos Nacionales S.A. v. Germany (Application no. 19508/07) originated in an application lodged on 2 May 2007 by a Peruvian corporation based in Lima. The applicant alleged that Germany’s refusal to grant it legal aid for civil proceedings was discriminatory and violated its right of access to a court under the Convention.

The company exported organic bananas to Europe. In 2001/2002 it concluded a commission contract with two German companies providing that disputes would be heard by Hamburg courts (with an additional Hamburg arbitration clause). On 31 December 2005 it applied to the Hamburg Regional Court for legal aid to sue the German companies for breach of contract, stating that it and its shareholder were insolvent and could not pay the required advance court fees.

On 4 January 2006 the Regional Court refused legal aid. It held that section 116(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure entitles only legal persons founded or based in an EU or EEA member State to such aid. On 17 January 2006 the same court rejected the company’s objection, ruling that the statute exhaustively defined eligible legal persons and that courts could not extend it to extra-European companies; Germany was under no obligation to furnish legal aid to legal persons worldwide.

On 23 January 2006 the Hanseatic Court of Appeal confirmed the refusals. It found the restriction on access to court justified by reciprocity: constitutional equality would eliminate any incentive for foreign States to afford comparable treatment to German legal persons. Even if the applicant were treated as a domestic entity, non-litigation would not run counter to the general interest. The court relied on a 1973 Federal Constitutional Court decision holding that a legal person retains its existence only if it can pursue its objects by its own means.

On 25 October 2006 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit the company’s constitutional complaint; the decision was served on 2 November 2006.

German law (Code of Civil Procedure ss. 114 and 116) grants legal aid to impecunious parties whose claims have prospects of success and are not frivolous, but for legal persons this is confined to those established in the EU/EEA, provided the costs cannot be met by the entity or those financially interested and non-litigation would be contrary to the general interest. Non-EU/EEA plaintiffs must generally provide security for costs (s. 110). The Court Fees Act requires advance payment of fees before an action is served, subject to exceptions for legal-aid recipients or cases of hardship or urgency.

Peruvian law confines legal aid to natural persons who would otherwise be unable to support themselves or their dependents. The Hague Convention on Civil Procedure (to which Germany but not Peru is a party) provides reciprocal legal aid among contracting States’ nationals.

A 2008 comparative survey of 32 Convention States revealed three approaches: most exclude legal aid for legal persons altogether; some restrict it to non-commercial entities; and a third group (including Germany) permits it for commercial companies under specified conditions.

The Court declared the application admissible on 12 October 2010; both parties thereafter filed observations on the merits.

The applicant, Granos Organicos Nacionales S.A., a Peruvian corporation based in Lima, exported organic bananas to Europe. In 2001/2002 it concluded a commission contract with two German companies providing that disputes would be heard by Hamburg courts (with an additional Hamburg arbitration clause). Claiming insolvency of itself and its shareholder, the company applied on 31 December 2005 for legal aid to sue the German companies for breach of contract before the Hamburg Regional Court, as it could not pay the advance court fees required to have the action served.

On 4 January 2006 the Regional Court refused legal aid. Section 116(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure confined such aid for legal persons to entities founded or based in an EU or EEA Member State. The applicant’s objection was dismissed on 17 January 2006: the provision was exhaustive and courts could not extend it to extra-European companies; Germany had no duty to finance litigation by all legal persons worldwide.

The Hanseatic Court of Appeal confirmed the refusal on 23 January 2006. Any interference with access to court was justified by reciprocity: treating foreign companies identically would remove any incentive for other States to grant equivalent protection to German entities. Even if the applicant were treated as a domestic legal person, non-litigation would not run counter to the general interest. A 1973 Federal Constitutional Court ruling established that a legal entity retains its existence under the legal order only if it can pursue its objects by its own means. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint on 25 October 2006 (served 2 November 2006).

German law further requires non-EU/EEA plaintiffs to furnish security for costs (s. 110). Legal aid is available to natural persons unable to pay if the claim has prospects and is not wanton (s. 114). For legal persons the same conditions apply only to EU/EEA entities, plus a public-interest test (s. 116). The Court Fees Act bars service of a claim until fees are paid, subject to limited hardship exceptions.

Peruvian law grants legal aid solely to natural persons at risk of destitution. Germany is a party to the 1954 Hague Convention on Civil Procedure, which provides reciprocal legal aid among contracting States, but Peru is not a party.

A 2008 comparative survey of 32 Convention States revealed three models: most exclude legal persons entirely; some restrict aid to non-profit entities; a minority (including Germany) allow commercial companies legal aid under specific conditions.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations of Articles 6 and 14: the nationality-based exclusion from legal aid prevented the insolvent applicant from having its claim served, thereby denying effective access to a court and discriminating against a non-European commercial company. The application was lodged on 2 May 2007 and declared admissible on 12 October 2010.

The case of Francesco Sessa v. Italy (ECtHR Application no. 28790/08, judgment of 3 April 2012) concerns an Italian Jewish lawyer’s allegation that Italian judicial authorities violated his freedom to manifest his religion. Sessa, born in 1955 and resident in Naples, represented one of two complainants in criminal proceedings against several banks. On 7 June 2005 he appeared before the Forlì investigating judge for a hearing on a request for the immediate production of evidence (incidente probatorio). The assigned judge being unavailable, the replacement invited the parties to select one of two already-identified dates—13 or 18 October 2005.

Sessa immediately objected that both dates fell on major Jewish holidays (Yom Kippur and Sukkot respectively) and that his religious obligations as a member of the Naples Jewish community prevented him from attending. He invoked sections 4 and 5 of Law no. 101 of 8 March 1989, which regulate relations between the Italian State and the Union of Italian Jewish Communities, grant Jews the right to observe the Sabbath (subject only to essential-service requirements) and treat the listed holidays equivalently. The replacement judge nevertheless fixed the hearing for 13 October. Sessa then lodged a formal adjournment application with the original investigating judge, who on 20 June simply placed it on the file without ruling.

On 11 July Sessa filed a criminal complaint against both judges for breach of section 2 of the same Law (which protects the free practice and manifestation of Judaism) and notified the Supreme Council of the Judiciary. At the 13 October hearing Sessa was recorded as absent “for personal reasons.” The judge invited submissions on the adjournment request: the prosecutor and defence counsel opposed it on the ground that it rested on no statutory basis, while counsel for the second complainant supported it. In an order issued the same day the judge refused the adjournment. He noted that Article 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires only the prosecutor and defence counsel to attend such hearings; the presence of complainants’ counsel is optional and the Code imposes no duty to adjourn for their legitimate unavailability. Given the large number of participants and the court’s heavy caseload (which would have postponed the matter until 2006), the request of a party lacking any legitimate entitlement to an adjournment had to be rejected in the interest of expedition.

The Supreme Council later declared itself incompetent because the complaint concerned the exercise of judicial functions. Sessa’s criminal complaint against the judges was ultimately discontinued by an Ancona investigating judge in February 2008 after a procedural detour through the Court of Cassation; the judge found no indication that either magistrate had intended to interfere with Sessa’s right to practise his faith or to offend his dignity on religious grounds.

These facts form the core of the alleged Convention violation: the authorities’ refusal to accommodate two recognised Jewish holy days, despite an express statutory framework treating them as equivalent to the Sabbath, and the subsequent dismissal of all domestic remedies. The case therefore turns on whether that refusal constituted an unjustified interference with the applicant’s freedom to manifest his religion.

The case of Francesco Sessa v. Italy (Application no. 28790/08) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of the applicant’s freedom to manifest his religion under Article 9 of the Convention. Francesco Sessa, an Italian national born in 1955 and resident in Naples, is a practising Jew and a lawyer. On 7 June 2005 he appeared before the Forlì investigating judge in his capacity as counsel for one of two complainants in criminal proceedings against several banks. The hearing concerned a request for the immediate production of evidence (incidente probatorio). The assigned judge being unavailable, a replacement invited the parties to select one of two possible dates already identified for the adjourned hearing: 13 or 18 October 2005.

Sessa immediately objected that both dates coincided with major Jewish religious holidays—Yom Kippur and Sukkot respectively—and that his religious obligations as a member of the Naples Jewish community would prevent his attendance. He expressly invoked sections 4 and 5 of Law no. 101 of 8 March 1989, which govern relations between the Italian State and the Union of Italian Jewish Communities and equate those holidays with the Sabbath, entitling Jewish persons who so request to observe them. The replacement judge nevertheless fixed the hearing for 13 October 2005 (Yom Kippur).

The same day Sessa filed a formal application to adjourn. On 20 June 2005 the investigating judge simply placed the application on the case file without ruling on it. On 11 July 2005 Sessa lodged a criminal complaint against both judges, alleging a breach of section 2 of Law no. 101 (which recognises the right freely to practise and manifest the Jewish religion) and notified the Supreme Council of the Judiciary.

At the 13 October hearing Sessa was absent “for personal reasons.” The prosecutor and defence counsel opposed any adjournment, arguing that no statutory ground existed; counsel for the other complainant supported the request. In an order issued that day the investigating judge rejected the application. He noted that Article 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires only the prosecutor and defence counsel to attend an incidente-probatorio hearing; the presence of counsel for the injured party is optional. The Code imposes no duty to adjourn merely because such optional counsel has a legitimate impediment. Given the large number of participants and the court’s heavy workload, which would have pushed the hearing into 2006, the judge held that the request—made by a person without a recognised right to demand adjournment—had to be refused in the interest of a reasonable time.

The Supreme Council of the Judiciary later declared itself incompetent because the matter concerned the exercise of judicial functions. Parallel criminal proceedings arising from Sessa’s complaint were ultimately discontinued. After a registry error that initially ignored his objection to a request for no further action, the Court of Cassation remitted the case. On 15 February 2008 the Ancona investigating judge discontinued the proceedings, finding no evidence that the Forlì judges had intended to impair Sessa’s right to practise his faith or to offend his dignity on religious grounds.

These facts formed the core of the alleged interference: a public authority scheduled and then refused to adjourn a hearing on a recognised Jewish holy day despite a timely, documented request, thereby forcing the applicant to choose between religious observance and professional participation (albeit optional) in proceedings in which he represented a complainant. Domestic law expressly protected such observance, yet the judicial authorities treated the request as lacking any legal foundation and subordinated it to considerations of court efficiency.

The European Court of Human Rights examined Francesco Sessa v. Italy (application no. 28790/08), brought by an Italian Jewish lawyer born in 1955 and living in Naples. He alleged a violation of his right to manifest his religion under the Convention, arising from a domestic court's refusal to adjourn a hearing that coincided with Jewish religious holidays.

On 7 June 2005 the applicant appeared before the Forlì investigating judge in an “incidente probatorio” (immediate production of evidence) as counsel for one of two complainants in criminal proceedings against several banks. The assigned judge being unavailable, a replacement offered two adjournment dates already selected by the original judge: 13 or 18 October 2005. The applicant objected that both dates fell on major Jewish holidays—Yom Kippur and Sukkot—and that his religious obligations as a member of the Naples Jewish community prevented his attendance. He invoked sections 4 and 5 of Law no. 101 of 8 March 1989, which govern relations between the Italian State and Jewish communities and require that those holidays be treated equivalently to the Sabbath, with corresponding workplace accommodations.

The replacement judge nevertheless fixed the hearing for 13 October 2005. That same day the applicant formally applied for an adjournment. On 20 June the investigating judge simply added the application to the case file without ruling. On 11 July the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against both judges, alleging a breach of section 2 of Law 101/1989 (which protects free practice and manifestation of the Jewish faith and penalizes religious intolerance). He also notified the Supreme Council of the Judiciary.

At the 13 October hearing the investigating judge recorded the applicant’s absence for “personal reasons” and invited the parties’ views. The public prosecutor and defence counsel opposed adjournment, arguing that the request did not rest on any statutory ground. Counsel for the co-complainant supported it. In an order issued the same day the judge rejected the application. He noted that Article 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the presence only of the prosecutor and defence counsel; the injured party’s counsel may attend but is not obligatory. The Code imposes no duty to adjourn merely because such optional counsel has a legitimate impediment. Given the large number of participants (defendants, complainants, experts) and the court’s heavy caseload, granting the request would have postponed the hearing until 2006, contrary to the duty to decide cases within a reasonable time.

The Supreme Council later declared itself incompetent because the matter concerned judicial activity. Parallel criminal proceedings initiated by the applicant were discontinued twice—first in 2006 after an apparent registry error overlooked his objection, then again in 2008 after Cassation remittal—on the ground that nothing indicated an intent to interfere with the applicant’s religious practice or to offend his dignity.

Law 101/1989 expressly recognises the right to observe Jewish holidays without prejudice to essential public services and treats manifestations of religious prejudice as punishable offences. These provisions formed the core of the applicant’s claim that the courts’ refusal to accommodate his religious calendar constituted an unjustified interference with his freedom to manifest his faith.
