The case of Shchebetov v. Russia (Application no. 21731/02) concerns a Russian national, Anatoliy Dmitriyevich Shchebetov (born 1972), who lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 April 2002. He alleged that he contracted tuberculosis (TB) and HIV while in custody, received inadequate medical care, lacked an effective domestic remedy for his health-related complaints, and suffered delays and interference with his correspondence to the Court.

Shchebetov was arrested in 1997, convicted of theft and robbery in 1998 (sentenced to 12 years), and later convicted of aggravated robbery in 2005 (sentenced to 9 years). He entered detention facility IZ-14/1 in Yakutsk on 1 October 1997. An initial medical examination (including blood tests and chest X-ray) showed him to be healthy, with no HIV, syphilis, or lung issues; he was housed with other healthy inmates. A follow-up X-ray on 30 April 1998 revealed focal TB in the right lung. Treatment was prescribed, but he was not transferred to the Sakha Republic prison hospital until 15 July 1998 (after his conviction became final). He received intensive anti-TB therapy there until 28 October 1998 and was subsequently readmitted on six occasions between 1999 and 2004 for antibacterial chemotherapy and monitoring. Medical records indicated clinical improvement, with no mycobacterium detected in 1999–2000 tests and a shift to prophylactic care by late 2001. Doctors noted the applicant’s sometimes negative or aggressive attitude toward treatment, though he received regular check-ups, psychological support for complaints such as sleep issues, and medicines. In 2001 he sued the Ministry of Justice and the facility for infection (claiming placement with an active TB patient). The Yakutsk Town Court dismissed the claim on 12 October 2001, finding no proven fault or infection in detention (possibly predating 1997 given his prior incarcerations); this was upheld on appeal in February 2002.

Regarding HIV, the applicant claimed that in late December 2001 a drunk medical assistant (P.) reused a syringe after drawing blood from an HIV-positive inmate (G.). The Government disputed this, stating that on 14 December 2001 a nurse used disposable equipment for tests on the applicant and others (negative for HIV), that P. was on leave, and that G.’s sample was taken separately later. Unclear results from 2002 tests led to an HIV diagnosis in November 2002. Thereafter he received clinical assessments, psychological support, enriched diet, vitamins, and hospital evaluations, though he refused a transfer in September 2005. Complaints prompted inquiries: prosecutors twice refused to open a criminal case (finding no shared syringe use or involvement by P.), with courts ordering further probes but ultimately dismissing the matter in December 2003 (upheld February 2004) after reviewing records, logs, and staff statements (G. refused to testify).

On correspondence, the applicant alleged delays, misrouting (e.g., a 28 November 2002 letter sent erroneously to domestic bodies, with attachments allegedly seized), and non-dispatch of letters to the Court. The Government produced logs showing 20 letters sent to the Court (2002–2004) plus hundreds of others, all in sealed envelopes except one delayed by addressing error (quickly resent after notification). Later complaints about seized documents were unsubstantiated by prosecutors in 2006. The Court received over 25 letters from him (with enclosures) in the relevant period.

These facts formed the basis for alleged violations under the Convention relating to health, medical care, remedies, and correspondence.

The case of Shchebetov v. Russia (no. 21731/02) concerns allegations by a Russian national (born 1972) that he contracted tuberculosis and HIV while in detention, received inadequate medical care, had no effective domestic remedy for his health complaints, and suffered delays or interference with his correspondence to the European Court of Human Rights.

The applicant was arrested in 1997, convicted of theft and robbery in February 1998, and sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment (conditionally released in 2004 after serving two-thirds). He was re-arrested shortly thereafter, convicted of aggravated robbery in April 2005, and sentenced to nine years.

On tuberculosis: He entered temporary detention facility IZ-14/1 in Yakutsk on 1 October 1997. An initial medical examination (including chest X-ray and blood tests) showed no tuberculosis or HIV, and he was housed with healthy inmates. A follow-up X-ray on 30 April 1998 revealed focal tuberculosis of the right lung. Treatment was prescribed, but hospital admission was delayed until 29 July 1998 (after his conviction became final). He received an intensive anti-tuberculosis course until 28 October 1998 and was readmitted for further treatment on six later occasions between 1999 and 2004. Medical records indicate regular examinations, chemotherapy, and prophylactic measures; microbiological tests from 1999–2000 showed no mycobacterium tuberculosis, and his condition later stabilised at a consolidation stage requiring only check-ups. Records also note the applicant’s occasionally negative or aggressive attitude toward treatment, though doctors explained its necessity. In 2001 he brought a civil claim against the Ministry of Justice and the facility, alleging infection from a cellmate with active tuberculosis. Domestic courts dismissed the claim in 2001–2002, finding no proof of infection in detention (or of fault) and considering it possible that he had contracted the disease earlier, given his prior incarceration history.

On HIV: The applicant alleged that in late December 2001 a drunken medical assistant used the same syringe on him after drawing blood from an HIV-positive inmate. The Government countered that a nurse took his blood (and that of other newcomers) on 14 December 2001 using disposable equipment, with negative results; the HIV-positive inmate’s sample was taken later by a different nurse, and the named assistant had been on sick leave. Subsequent tests in 2002 were initially inconclusive; HIV was diagnosed in November 2002. Thereafter he received clinical monitoring, psychological support, vitamins, hepatoprotective medicine, and an enriched diet, with assessments of readiness for antiretroviral treatment (which he later refused in 2005 without explanation). Inquiries into the alleged infection produced multiple prosecutorial refusals to open a criminal case (2003), some of which were quashed by courts ordering further steps such as record reviews and confrontations. Courts ultimately upheld the refusals, finding no evidence that the applicant’s and the HIV-positive inmate’s samples had been taken together or by the named assistant.

On correspondence: The applicant claimed delays, non-dispatch, or seizure of attachments in letters to the Court (citing examples from 2002–2003). The Government produced logs showing more than 20 letters sent in sealed envelopes (plus hundreds to Russian authorities); one delay was attributed to a mistaken routing that was promptly corrected, with the applicant informed. The Court itself received over 25 letters from him (many with voluminous enclosures) between 2002 and communication of the case.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment, lack of medical care, ineffective remedies, and interference with Court correspondence.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1972, was arrested in 1997, convicted of theft and robbery in 1998 (12-year sentence), conditionally released in 2004, then reconvicted of aggravated robbery in 2005 (9-year sentence). He alleged contraction of tuberculosis (TB) and HIV in detention due to authorities’ failures, inadequate medical care, lack of effective remedies, and interference with his correspondence to the ECtHR (Articles 3, 13 and 34).

On TB: The applicant entered IZ-14/1 detention facility on 1 October 1997. An initial medical exam (including HIV/syphilis tests and chest X-ray) was normal; he was housed with healthy inmates (TB patients held separately). A 30 April 1998 X-ray revealed focal TB of the right lung. Treatment was prescribed on 15 May 1998, but he was not admitted to the colony hospital until 29 July 1998 (after his conviction became final). He received intensive anti-TB therapy until 28 October 1998, then prophylactic/anti-relapse courses during six further hospitalisations (1999–2004). By 2000–2001 tests showed no mycobacterium, with the disease at resolution/consolidation stages requiring only check-ups and prophylaxis. Records indicated generally successful treatment, though he sometimes resisted care; other complaints (e.g., sleep issues) were addressed. In 2001 he sued the Ministry of Justice and facility for infection (claiming exposure to an infected cellmate). The Yakutsk Town Court dismissed the claim (12 October 2001), finding no proof of authorities’ fault or in-detention contraction (possible pre-existing given his prior incarcerations); this was upheld on appeal (4 February 2002).

On HIV: The applicant claimed that in late December 2001 a drunk medical assistant (P.) reused a syringe from an HIV-positive inmate (G.) to take his blood. The Government disputed this: on 13 December 2001 he and others were admitted for TB prophylaxis; nurse Z. drew samples on 14 December using disposables (negative for HIV); G. arrived 26 December and was tested by nurse S.; P. was on sick leave 12–18 December. Unclear/contradictory tests in March–September 2002 led to an HIV diagnosis in November 2002. He received counselling, monitoring (no immediate ARVs), enriched diet, vitamins and hospital evaluations, though he later refused a transfer. He complained of infection. A January 2003 prosecutor’s refusal to open a criminal case (finding P. uninvolved) was challenged; courts ordered further inquiry (April/July 2003), but after G. refused to testify, the Town Court dismissed the complaint (15 December 2003, upheld February 2004), concluding samples were taken separately by different nurses with no evidence of P.’s involvement or reused syringes.

On correspondence: The applicant alleged delays, non-dispatch or seizure of attachments (e.g., a 28 November 2002 letter sent erroneously then missing documents; a 13 November 2003 delay). Government logs showed ~20 letters to the Court (plus hundreds to officials) dispatched promptly in sealed envelopes, save one misdirected letter (to the Supreme Court) resent within days after notification. The Court received over 25 letters with enclosures. A 2005–2006 complaint about seized attachments yielded no proof of loss or responsible officials; a prosecutor refused criminal proceedings.

These facts formed the core of claims of inhumane treatment via infection/inadequate care, ineffective investigation/remedies, and hindrance of Court access.
001-110188:
The case of Van der Heijden v. the Netherlands (Application no. 42857/05) originated in a complaint by Ms Gina Gerdina van der Heijden, a Dutch national born in 1969 and resident in ’s-Hertogenbosch. She alleged that attempts to compel her testimony in criminal proceedings against her long-term unmarried partner, Mr A., violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life), both alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination).

On the night of 9–10 May 2004 a man was shot dead in a café in ’s-Hertogenbosch. The suspected perpetrator was Mr A., the applicant’s companion of 18 years; the couple had two children whom he had recognised. They had never married and had not entered a registered partnership. Mr A. had prior convictions, including one for attempted manslaughter with a firearm, and was on weekend prison leave at the time of the shooting. The applicant was believed to have been with him.

Summoned as a witness on 25 May 2004, she appeared before the investigating judge but refused to testify. She claimed the testimonial privilege (verschoningsrecht) afforded by Article 217(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to spouses and registered partners (and former spouses/partners). The investigating judge declined to order her detention for non-compliance, holding that her personal liberty interests outweighed those of the investigation. The public prosecutor appealed.

On 2 June 2004 the ’s-Hertogenbosch Regional Court, sitting in chambers, quashed that decision and ordered her detention. It held that the 1998 amendment extending privilege to registered partners had deliberately excluded other cohabitees, however stable or marriage-like. Extending the privilege judicially would exceed the courts’ function; Articles 8 and 14 did not require otherwise. Given the gravity of the offence, the public interest in discovering the truth outweighed her personal interests. She was taken into custody that afternoon.

On 3 June an investigating judge confirmed the detention. The following day the Regional Court, after hearing her (she persisted in her refusal), ordered her held for twelve days, renewable. On 15 June it refused a further extension and ordered her immediate release, noting that continued detention interfered with her Article 8 rights and that her personal interests now prevailed. The Court of Appeal upheld the 4 June decision on 24 June. The Supreme Court, on 31 May 2005, declared her cassation appeal inadmissible for lack of remaining interest (she having been released) but nevertheless examined the merits. It confirmed that Article 217(3) applied only to formal spouses and registered partners. Any difference in treatment of long-term cohabitees pursued the legitimate aim of legal certainty: the privilege was an exceptional derogation from the general duty to testify, deliberately and clearly delimited by the legislature so as to protect only those family relationships whose legal status was unambiguous.

Dutch law treats registered partnership as essentially equivalent to marriage for most civil-law purposes. The legislative history of Article 217 shows that the privilege exists to shield close family bonds from the moral conflict of having to choose between truth-telling and loyalty (or perjury). A 1985 survey and later committee reports had considered whether to include informal life partners, but the 1998 reform did not do so. Comparative material indicated that while most Council of Europe States exempt spouses and many also exempt registered partners, only a minority unconditionally exempt informal cohabitees.

These facts framed the alleged violations: the detention and attempted compulsion to testify against a de-facto spouse of 18 years, and the statutory distinction between formally recognised and informal family relationships.

The case of Van der Heijden v. the Netherlands (Application no. 42857/05) was brought by Ms Gina Gerdina van der Heijden, a Dutch national born in 1969 and living in ’s-Hertogenbosch. She alleged that compelling her to testify in criminal proceedings against her long-term unmarried partner violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life), taken alone and with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination).

On the night of 9–10 May 2004 a man was shot dead in a café. The suspected gunman was the applicant’s partner, Mr A., with whom she was believed to have been present. Mr A. had prior convictions for similar offences, including attempted manslaughter with a firearm.

On 25 May 2004 the applicant was summoned as a witness. She appeared before the investigating judge but refused to give evidence, claiming the testimonial privilege in Article 217 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Although they were neither married nor in a registered partnership, she and Mr A. had cohabited for 18 years and had two children recognised by him. She argued that this stable family relationship entitled her to the same exemption granted to spouses and registered partners.

The investigating judge refused to recognise the privilege but declined to order her detention, holding that her liberty outweighed the prosecution’s interest. The public prosecutor appealed. On 2 June 2004 the Regional Court, sitting in chambers, quashed that decision and ordered her detention for failure to comply with a judicial order. It held that the legislature, when extending the privilege to registered partners in 1998, had deliberately excluded other cohabitees. Extending it further would exceed the judicial function. Given the gravity of the homicide, the public interest in establishing the truth prevailed over the applicant’s personal interests. She was taken into detention that afternoon.

She was heard again on 3 June and persisted in her refusal. On 4 June the Regional Court ordered her continued detention for 12 days (extendable), again finding that investigative needs outweighed her interests. She appealed. On 15 June, considering a request to extend the detention, the same court ordered her immediate release. It now concluded that her personal interest—including the interference with her Article 8 rights caused by the detention itself—outweighed the interest in obtaining her evidence.

The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 24 June 2004 and upheld the 4 June decision. The Supreme Court, on 31 May 2005, declared her further appeal inadmissible for lack of interest (she had already been released) but observed that the statutory privilege was confined to spouses and registered partners in order to protect family life under Article 8. Any difference in treatment of long-term cohabitees was objectively justified by the need for a clear and workable exception to the general duty to testify, thereby serving legal certainty.

Under Dutch law a witness is obliged to answer questions on oath; refusal is a criminal offence. Article 217 excuses certain blood and marital relatives, spouses, former spouses and (since 1998) registered partners and former registered partners. The privilege exists to protect socially valued family relationships and to spare witnesses a moral conflict between truth-telling and loyalty. Registered partnership is created by formal registration and produces legal effects analogous to marriage (with limited exceptions concerning parentage). The legislature had surveyed distinctions between married and unmarried couples and had chosen not to extend the privilege to informal cohabitation.

The applicant was detained from 2 to 15 June 2004. She contended that the attempt to force her testimony against her de-facto spouse, and the consequent detention, unjustifiably interfered with her family life and discriminated against unmarried couples in a comparable situation to married or registered partners.

The case originated in an application lodged on 30 November 2005 by Ms Gina Gerdina van der Heijden, a Netherlands national born in 1969 and resident in ’s-Hertogenbosch, against the Kingdom of the Netherlands. She alleged violations of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life), taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The complaint arose from efforts to compel her testimony as a witness in criminal proceedings against her long-term unmarried companion, Mr A., with whom she shared a stable family relationship.

On the night of 9–10 May 2004, a man was shot and killed in a café in ’s-Hertogenbosch. The perpetrator was believed to be Mr A., who had prior convictions in 1998 and 2003 for similar offences, including attempted manslaughter with a firearm; the shooting occurred during weekend leave from his 2003 sentence. The applicant had been in Mr A.’s company at the relevant time. They had cohabited for 18 years and had two children, both recognised by Mr A., but they were neither married nor in a registered partnership.

Summoned as a witness on 25 May 2004, the applicant appeared before the investigating judge but refused to testify. She claimed entitlement to the testimonial privilege under Article 217 (opening sentence and sub-paragraph 3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which exempts spouses (or former spouses) and registered partners (or former registered partners) of a suspect from the duty to give evidence. The investigating judge declined to order her detention for non-compliance, but the public prosecutor successfully appealed.

On 2 June 2004 the ’s-Hertogenbosch Regional Court, sitting in chambers, quashed that decision and ordered the applicant’s detention. It held that the wording and legislative history of Article 217, as amended with effect from 1 January 1998, unambiguously confined the privilege to spouses and registered partners. The courts could not extend it to other long-term cohabitees; any such extension was a matter for the legislature. The seriousness of the offence meant that the public interest in discovering the truth outweighed the applicant’s personal interests. She was taken into detention that afternoon.

The Regional Court confirmed the detention for 12 days on 4 June 2004 after the applicant persisted in her refusal. She appealed. On 15 June 2004, however, the same court refused an extension and ordered her immediate release, finding that her personal interest (including the interference with Article 8 rights) now outweighed the investigative interest. The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 24 June 2004, upholding the 4 June ruling.

The Supreme Court declared her subsequent appeal on points of law inadmissible for lack of interest (she having already been released) but nevertheless examined the merits. It confirmed that Article 217 did not apply. Addressing Articles 8 and 14, it accepted that the privilege protected “family life” but held that the distinction between spouses/registered partners and other cohabitees was objectively and reasonably justified: the privilege was an exception to the general duty to testify, and the legislature had delimited it clearly in the interests of legal certainty.

The applicant had thus been detained for 13 days (2–15 June 2004) solely because of her refusal to testify against her long-term partner. The domestic courts consistently treated the absence of marriage or registered partnership as decisive, notwithstanding the acknowledged existence of family life.
001-110261:
The case of Silickienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 20496/02) concerned complaints by Jurgita Silickienė under Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) that criminal proceedings resulting in the confiscation of her property were unfair, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the deprivation of her property was unlawful. (Her late husband’s related application was declared inadmissible.)

The applicant’s husband, M.S., a senior tax police officer, was arrested in August 2000 and charged with fraud, forgery, and later with leading a criminal organisation that systematically smuggled large quantities of alcohol and cigarettes between 1999 and 2000. In 2000 investigators froze assets belonging to M.S., his mother and the applicant. The mother successfully appealed the seizure of some of her property; the applicant did not appeal the freeze on hers.

M.S. committed suicide in prison in April 2003. At the request of the applicant and M.S.’s mother the Kaunas Regional Court continued the proceedings against the criminal organisation (appointing a lawyer to represent the deceased) in order to examine possible rehabilitation. In January 2004 the court found ample evidence that M.S. had organised and led the group, which had completed 22 smuggling operations causing millions of litas in damage. Proceedings against him were discontinued solely because of his death; three co-accused were convicted. Applying Article 72 of the Criminal Code, the court confiscated property acquired from the crimes, including the applicant’s Vilnius apartment (purchased in 1999 with a sham loan from a co-accused’s mother) and her shares in a telecommunications company (obtained via an offshore vehicle used to conceal proceeds). Other family assets lacking proven illicit origin were released. The court devoted eight pages to explaining each confiscation decision.

On appeal the family lawyer argued that proceedings should have ended with M.S.’s death and that the applicant’s assets had a legitimate source. The Court of Appeal (October 2004) upheld the confiscations. It stressed that the applicant, although not charged in those proceedings, had been fully aware of the organisation’s activities: she was informed of loadings, unloadings and sales and herself received proceeds. Article 72 required confiscation of criminally obtained property transferred to third parties who knew or ought to have known of its origin, independently of any charge or conviction against those third parties. The property derived from the joint activities of all co-accused (including those convicted), not solely M.S. The Supreme Court (May 2005) confirmed that confiscation is a mandatory penal measure applicable even without a conviction or charge, provided the statutory conditions are met; the lower courts had thoroughly established the illicit origin and the third parties’ knowledge.

In separate proceedings in June 2005 the applicant was convicted of misappropriating property and forging documents after she admitted organising transfers to the same offshore companies in order to hide proceeds and shield her detained husband. She received a four-year sentence (later amnestied).

Lithuanian law at the time (Criminal Code Article 72 and the Code of Criminal Procedure) expressly permitted confiscation of proceeds held by third parties who knew or should have known of their criminal origin, irrespective of the third parties’ own criminal liability and even after the offender’s death. Comparative material showed that several Council of Europe states likewise allow non-conviction-based confiscation against knowing third parties, especially family members. Lithuania had also ratified the 1990 Council of Europe Convention on Laundering, Search, Seizure and Confiscation of the Proceeds from Crime.

The case of Silickienė v. Lithuania originated in an application by Jurgita Silickienė (and initially her husband) alleging violations of Article 6 (fair trial) in the criminal proceedings that led to confiscation of her property and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) on the ground that the deprivation was unlawful.

The applicant’s husband, M.S., a senior tax-police officer, was arrested in August 2000 on fraud charges that later expanded to include leading a criminal organisation that systematically smuggled large quantities of alcohol and cigarettes between 1999 and 2000. Investigators immediately froze assets belonging to M.S., his mother and the applicant. The applicant did not challenge the freeze on her own property.

M.S. committed suicide in remand prison in April 2003. Although the applicant and M.S.’s mother asked that the proceedings be discontinued, the Kaunas Regional Court continued them in order to establish the facts concerning the criminal organisation and appointed a lawyer to represent the deceased. In its January 2004 judgment the court found overwhelming evidence that M.S. had organised and directed the group, which had successfully carried out 22 smuggling operations, but it terminated the case against him because of his death. Three co-accused were convicted.

Pursuant to Article 72 of the Criminal Code the court confiscated assets it held to be proceeds of the crimes. These included the applicant’s Vilnius apartment, purchased in August 1999 with a sham loan of LTL 80 000 from the mother of one of the co-accused, and her shares in a telecommunications company (value LTL 29 997) acquired through an offshore vehicle used to conceal the organisation’s profits. The court released other items belonging to the applicant for which no illicit origin had been shown.

On appeal the applicant’s lawyer argued that the proceedings should have ended with M.S.’s death and that the confiscated assets had legitimate sources. The Court of Appeal rejected both contentions. It stressed that the applicant had been fully aware of the smuggling operations, had been kept informed of the movement and sale of the goods and had herself received proceeds. Consequently she knew that the property registered in her name originated from crime. Article 72 required confiscation of such proceeds from third parties who knew or ought to have known of their illicit origin, irrespective of whether those third parties had been charged or convicted and irrespective of the discontinuation of proceedings against the principal offender. The appellate court reviewed the trial court’s eight-page analysis of the provenance of each item and found it well-founded.

The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on points of law, confirming that confiscation under Article 72 is a mandatory penal measure that may be imposed even when no one has been convicted or even charged, provided the statutory conditions are met.

In separate but related proceedings concluded in June 2005 the applicant was convicted of misappropriation and document falsification committed in order to channel funds through offshore companies and thereby shield her husband; she received a four-year sentence (later remitted by amnesty).

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that she had been denied a fair hearing in the confiscation proceedings and that the taking of her property had been unlawful.

The case of Silickienė v. Lithuania originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Lithuanian nationals Mindaugas Silickis (who died by suicide in 2003) and his wife Jurgita Silickienė. The Court considered only her complaints under Article 6 of the Convention (fair trial) regarding the fairness of criminal proceedings that led to confiscation of her property, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) regarding the alleged unlawfulness of that deprivation.

In August 2000, Silickis, a senior tax police officer, was arrested and later charged with fraud, forgery, smuggling large quantities of alcohol, and forming and leading a criminal association that smuggled alcohol and cigarettes on 22 occasions between 1999 and 2000. In 2000, investigators froze assets belonging to Silickis, his mother, and the applicant. His mother successfully appealed the seizure of some items (an apartment, garage, and land), but a café and telecom shares were retained as proceeds of crime. The applicant did not appeal the freeze of her own property.

They later sought discontinuance, which the court refused, as evidence examination had begun. In its January 2004 judgment, the court found overwhelming evidence that Silickis had organized the criminal group but discontinued proceedings against him due to his death. Three co-accused were convicted and imprisoned. The court confiscated property acquired through the crimes under Article 72 of the Criminal Code, including the applicant’s Vilnius apartment (purchased in 1999 via a sham loan of 80,000 litai from a co-accused’s mother) and her telecom shares (worth about 8,700 euros, obtained via an offshore company used to conceal proceeds). Some of the applicant’s other assets were released for lack of illicit origin. The judgment devoted eight pages to justifying each confiscation.

The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in October 2004, describing the group as an exceptionally dangerous, systematic conspiracy that caused massive harm. It found the applicant “well aware” of the smuggling: she was informed of loadings, unloadings, and sales, and herself received proceeds. Confiscation applied independently of conviction or charging of third parties who knew or ought to have known of the illicit origin, and the property stemmed from the joint activities of all co-accused (including those convicted). The court re-examined the evidence and rejected claims of lawful provenance. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal in May 2005, confirming that confiscation of crime proceeds (a penal measure) was mandatory even without a conviction or charge, provided third parties knew or should have known of the illicit funding.

In separate 2005 proceedings, the applicant was convicted of misappropriation and document falsification for organizing transfers to the group’s offshore companies to hide money and help her detained husband evade liability; she confessed and received a four-year sentence (later pardoned under amnesty). Her mother-in-law received a shorter sentence for similar acts.

These facts formed the basis for the applicant’s claims that she lacked a fair opportunity to contest the confiscation (as a non-party whose assets were seized post-death) and that the measure was unlawful.

**Case of Balogun v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 60286/09), ECHR Fourth Section, judgment of 10 April 2012 (final 24 September 2012).**

The applicant, a Nigerian national born in 1986, alleged that his deportation from the United Kingdom to Nigeria would violate Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. He claimed to have arrived in the UK at age three, though official records first noted his presence in 1994 at age eight. In 1994, a family court inquired about his immigration status amid an aunt's residence order application. In 2003, the aunt sought indefinite leave to remain, listing him as a dependant. A further application by Southwark Social Services noted that the aunt had evicted him in January 2002, after which he entered foster care; he alleged long-term beatings by the aunt and her boyfriend. He received indefinite leave to remain outside the rules on 1 December 2003 and lived independently in council housing after turning 18.

In February 2007, at age 20, he was convicted of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply (pleading guilty on the basis of coercion following a 2005 shooting) and sentenced to three years' imprisonment. He had prior convictions for possession of Class A and B drugs (February 2004), handling stolen goods (April 2004), and possession of Class C drugs (June 2005). On 18 October 2007, the Secretary of State notified him of the intention to deport him as conducive to the public good under the Immigration Act 1971. Officials found no evidence of presence before age eight, limited lawful stay (four years), contact with his mother in Nigeria, and independence since majority; they rejected claims of UK family life.

His appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on 13 March 2008. The Tribunal rejected a claimed long-term relationship (inconsistent evidence, never previously mentioned) and close ties to a second aunt (who had not housed him and was unaware of his conviction) or half-brother. It found no protected family life. Private-life ties (long residence, education, some work) were insufficient to prevent interference, as he could re-establish life in Nigeria (possible family contact there). Applying *Üner v. the Netherlands*, deportation was proportionate given the public interest in removing a persistent offender. A deportation order was signed on 14 October 2008. Further human-rights representations were refused as not constituting a fresh claim (Immigration Rules, para. 353); judicial review was denied on 30 October 2009, with the High Court confirming no family life and a proportionate private-life interference. He did not renew the application.

Detained on 10 November 2009 with removal set for 19 November, he applied to the Court on 13 November, submitting a 14 September 2009 psychiatric report. It recorded a suicide attempt on 13 August 2009 (after the Secretary of State's refusal), inpatient treatment until 7 September, ongoing despair, and moderate depression. The Court indicated Rule 39 interim measures on 18 November 2009 (initially for two weeks, later prolonged), seeking Government comments on suicide risk. The Government, previously unaware of the attempt, confirmed constant supervision in detention, trained staff, and planned medical escorts if needed during removal, plus available Nigerian mental-health facilities; they invited lifting of the measure. The applicant reported a minor paracetamol overdose on 29 December 2009 (assessed as few tablets); he was released on 13 January 2010 with no further claimed attempts.

Domestic law included deportation powers (Immigration Act 1971, s. 3(5)(a)), appeal rights (Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002), and the Human Rights Act 1998. Relevant case-law (*J. v. Secretary of State*) set a high Article 3 threshold for suicide risk in expulsion cases: minimum severity, causal link to removal, particularly high bar for illness not caused by receiving-state authorities, assessment of whether fears are objectively well-founded, and availability of safeguards in the UK, transit, and receiving state. Risks are examined in three stages (UK, transit, receiving country), with a higher threshold abroad.

These facts underpin the Article 3 claim (suicide/mental-health risk upon/after removal, including during transit and in Nigeria) and Article 8 claim (interference with long-established private life, disputed family ties, and proportionality against criminality and public-order interests). The Court joined admissibility and merits.

A deportation order was signed on 14 October 2008. 001-110384:
The case of Tomić and Others v. Montenegro (applications nos. 18650/09 et al.) involves twelve Montenegrin nationals, former employees of the Aluminium Plant in Podgorica, who alleged that Montenegrin courts applied inconsistent practices by rejecting their claims while upholding identical ones from colleagues. This raised issues of legal certainty and equal treatment under the Convention.

The applicants (and a legal predecessor) were certified totally unfit for work due to disabilities partly stemming from work-related illnesses. Between 10 and 16 November 2005 they were made redundant and received severance payments. The Pension Fund later recognized their disability pensions, effective from the certification dates. They then sued their former employer for damages representing the difference between those pensions and the salaries they would have earned if not made redundant. Claims ranged from EUR 581 to EUR 9,273.64; the applicants characterized them as labour-related and thus exempt from court fees. Some succeeded at first instance in the Podgorica Court of First Instance, but all lost before the High Court (decisions of 7 November 2008–9 October 2009). Several then lodged appeals on points of law with the Supreme Court, which (between 18 February and 3 December 2009) upheld the High Court. Both higher courts reasoned that employment had ended through redundancy, not pension recognition; once unemployed the applicants had no salary, so no damage had occurred.

By contrast, in six contemporaneous judgments (Supreme Court, December 2006; High Court, up to February 2009) the same courts allowed identical claims by colleagues. Those decisions held that compensation was due according to the degree to which work-related illness had caused disability, and that redundancy and severance were legally irrelevant. The judgments became final and enforceable.

All applicants filed constitutional appeals. The Constitutional Court rejected one (the ninth applicant) for non-exhaustion (no Supreme Court appeal) and dismissed the rest (December 2009–March 2011) on the ground that the impugned rulings did not depart from established case-law.

A broader survey of 89 similar cases (2007–2010) showed later consistency against claimants: the High Court allowed only four of 88 appeals, and the Supreme Court rejected all 84 meritorious appeals on points of law (regardless of claim value). One earlier successful claimant had never been made redundant.

The applicants thus complained of simultaneous contradictory outcomes in factually and legally indistinguishable labour-damage cases, violating the principle of legal certainty. Domestic law (Constitution Arts. 17/19, 32, 124; Courts Act s. 5, 27; Civil Procedure Act provisions on labour disputes and appeals) required equal protection and consistent application of law, yet produced divergent results until the later uniform rejection of such claims. The case therefore centres on whether this judicial inconsistency itself constituted a Convention violation.

**Case Summary: Tomić and Others v. Montenegro (ECtHR, 2012)**

This ECtHR case (applications nos. 18650/09 et al.) concerned twelve Montenegrin nationals (some successors to a deceased claimant) who alleged inconsistent domestic court practice violating their Convention rights, specifically that identical labour-related damages claims by colleagues succeeded while theirs failed. The applicants, all former employees of the Aluminium Plant in Podgorica, were certified totally unfit for work (disability partly due to occupational illness). They were made redundant in November 2005 with severance pay. The Pension Fund later granted disability pensions effective from the certification dates.

The applicants sued their former employer for the difference between the pensions received and salaries they would have earned if not made redundant (claims ranging €581–€9,273). They classified these as labour claims exempt from court fees. First-instance outcomes in Podgorica varied, but the High Court uniformly dismissed all claims (judgments 7 Nov 2008–9 Oct 2009). Several applicants’ appeals on points of law to the Supreme Court were rejected (Feb–Dec 2009). The courts reasoned that termination occurred via redundancy, not pension recognition; as the applicants were already unemployed when pensions were granted, they had no salary and thus suffered no compensable damage.

In contrast, six contemporaneous judgments (Supreme Court Dec 2006 to High Court Feb 2009) awarded identical claims by colleagues. Those courts held that damages were justified by the disability itself, with the employer liable in proportion to the occupational illness’s contribution; redundancy and severance were irrelevant to the disability-based claim. These became final and enforceable. The applicants highlighted this divergence in their submissions.

All applicants filed constitutional appeals. The Constitutional Court rejected one (ninth applicant) for non-exhaustion (no Supreme Court appeal) and dismissed the rest (Dec 2009–Mar 2011), finding no departure from established case-law.

Broader practice confirmed inconsistency then alignment against claimants: of 89 similar colleague cases (2007–2010), one first-instance win became final unappealed; the High Court allowed four of 88 appeals (two becoming final); the Supreme Court examined 84 meritoriously (regardless of value, despite a €5,000/€10,000 threshold, with labour exceptions) and rejected all, including two High Court successes. One non-redundant colleague who retired after certification succeeded throughout.

Domestic law (1992/2007 Constitutions) guaranteed equal protection of rights and fair trial; the Supreme Court was tasked with consistent law application (Courts Act s. 27; Const. Art. 124). Civil Procedure Act provisions on appeals, finality, and labour-dispute exceptions applied, with 2006 amendments raising thresholds but lacking transitional rules. Court Fees Act exempted labour claims.

The alleged violation centred on this divergent treatment of factually and legally identical claims (redundancy vs. disability causation, relevance of severance), undermining legal certainty and equality before the courts, contrary to constitutional and Convention principles (esp. Art. 6 fair trial). The ECtHR examined these facts for potential breach via inconsistent jurisprudence. (Word count: 512)

**Case of Tomić and Others v. Montenegro (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 17 April 2012)**

Applications were communicated on 7 October 2010, with admissibility and merits considered together.

Between 10 and 16 November 2005 they were made redundant and received severance. The Pension Fund later recognised their disability pensions effective from the certification dates.

They then sued their former employer for damages equal to the difference between their pensions and the salaries they would have received absent redundancy (claims ranging from €581 to €9,273.64). They characterised the claims as labour-related and thus exempt from court fees. Those who filed appeals on points of law (revizija) saw the Supreme Court uphold the High Court (18 February–3 December 2009). All applicants lodged constitutional appeals. The Constitutional Court rejected one (ninth applicant) for failure to exhaust remedies (no revizija) and dismissed the rest (24 December 2009–10 March 2011) on the ground that the impugned judgments did not depart from established case-law.

Relevant domestic law included constitutional guarantees of equal protection of rights (1992 Art. 17; 2007 Arts. 19, 32) and the Supreme Court’s duty to ensure consistent application of law (2007 Art. 124 § 2; Courts Act s. 27). The Civil Procedure Act (as amended 2006) regulated appeals on points of law in labour disputes and pecuniary claims, with no transitional provisions for pending cases. Labour-rights proceedings were exempt from court fees.

The alleged violations centred on this conflicting judicial treatment of factually and legally identical labour-damage claims, raising issues of legal certainty, equality before the courts, and fair trial.
001-110272:
The applicant, Raymond Woolley, alleged breaches of Articles 5 § 1 and 6 § 1 ECHR arising from an alleged violation of the specialty rule after his extradition from Switzerland. He argued that enforcement of a default prison term for non-payment of a confiscation order rendered his detention unlawful.

Woolley was convicted in December 2002 at Birmingham Crown Court of conspiracy to cheat the public revenue (and related money-laundering offences) and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment. After serving 41 months he escaped from an open prison in February 2005 and fled to Switzerland, leaving 66 months of the sentence outstanding. An arrest warrant was issued for the escape.

On 3 March 2005 the Crown Court made a confiscation order of £9.5 million, payable by April 2006, with a consecutive four-year default term of imprisonment if unpaid. Woolley was represented but not present. Subsequent appeals against the order failed.

In February 2008 the United Kingdom requested extradition under the 1957 European Convention on Extradition both as a convicted person (to serve the remainder of the nine-year sentence) and as an accused person (for escape). The request expressly referred to the confiscation order and stated that any default term formed part of the overall penalty.

When the Swiss authorities asked whether extradition was also sought for non-payment of the confiscation sum, the United Kingdom replied in August 2008 that there was no such charge: extradition was sought only for the original offences and the escape, the confiscation order being merely part of the sentence already imposed. Activation of the default term was simply one method of enforcing that sentence.

Switzerland granted extradition solely for the original conspiracy and money-laundering offences (which satisfied dual criminality). It refused extradition for the escape (not an offence under Swiss law) and recorded that extradition had not been requested for non-payment of the confiscation order. Swiss courts at every level confirmed that the United Kingdom had thereby waived any claim to enforce the default term.

Woolley was surrendered in March 2009 and completed the original sentence. In April 2009 the UK prosecutor applied to activate the four-year default term. Switzerland immediately protested that this would breach specialty. After judicial-review proceedings the High Court held in January 2010 that the default term was an integral component of the original sentence, not a separate offence. Enforcement therefore neither violated section 151 of the Extradition Act 2003 nor Article 14 of the Convention. The Swiss “reservation” resulted from a misunderstanding of the United Kingdom’s consistently expressed position; there had been no abuse of process or deliberate misleading of the requested State.

The Magistrates’ Court accordingly activated the default term. After early-release provisions extinguished the original sentence in April 2010, Woolley remained in custody solely on the default term. Switzerland continues to regard this as a specialty violation and has asked either for a formal extension of the extradition request or for Woolley’s release.

When the Swiss authorities asked whether extradition was also sought for non-payment of the confiscation order, the United Kingdom replied that no such charge existed or was proposed; the confiscation order and its default term were integral components of the sentence already imposed for the extradition offences.

It refused surrender for escape (not a crime under Swiss law) and recorded that extradition had not been requested for non-payment. Woolley’s appeals in the Swiss courts were dismissed. He was surrendered in March 2009 and returned to prison.

In April 2009 United Kingdom prosecutors applied to activate the four-year default term. Switzerland immediately protested that this would violate specialty. After judicial-review proceedings the English High Court held in January 2010 that the default term formed part of the original sentence for the extradition offences, so neither section 151 of the Extradition Act 2003 nor Article 14 ECE was breached. The magistrates then ordered the default term to be served. After early release from the nine-year sentence, Woolley remained in custody solely under the default term. Switzerland continued to insist that extradition had never been granted for non-payment and that enforcement therefore breached specialty, requesting either a formal extension of the extradition request or Woolley’s release.

These facts constitute the core of the alleged violations: the applicant contends that the United Kingdom obtained his surrender on a limited basis and then detained him for a matter expressly excluded by the requested State, rendering his continued imprisonment arbitrary and the related proceedings unfair.
001-110675:
The case of Gennadiy Medvedev v. Russia (application no. 34184/03) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right under Article 6 of the Convention to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing during appeal proceedings.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1960, was arrested on 9 March 2001 on suspicion of murder and remanded in custody. On 15 July 2002 the Kemerovo Regional Court convicted him of murder, abduction, disturbance of the peace and illegal possession of firearms, imposing an 18-year prison sentence. Both the applicant and his lawyer lodged appeals.

The Supreme Court of the Russian Federation rejected the applicant’s request for appointment of a State-funded lawyer for the appeal, holding that the applicable rules of criminal procedure did not provide for a public defender at that stage. On 24 April 2003 the Supreme Court held the appeal hearing in the applicant’s absence and without any legal representation for him. The prosecutor attended and made submissions. The court acquitted the applicant of disturbance of the peace, upheld the remaining convictions and reduced the sentence to 17 years and 6 months.

In November 2007 the Deputy Prosecutor General sought supervisory review of the 24 April 2003 judgment, citing the failure to appoint counsel. On 28 December 2007 the Supreme Court remitted the matter. Counsel P. was appointed to represent the applicant in the supervisory-review proceedings. On 12 March 2008 the Presidium of the Supreme Court quashed the 2003 appeal judgment, expressly acknowledging a violation of the applicant’s right to legal assistance, and remitted the case for a fresh appeal. The applicant did not participate in that hearing; counsel P. did.

The applicant again requested a public defender and leave to attend the new appeal hearing. The Supreme Court appointed counsel K., who examined the case file on several dates in September 2008, and granted the applicant permission to participate by video-link from a remand prison in Kemerovo (approximately 3,742 km from Moscow). At the hearing on 1 October 2008 the applicant appeared via video-link and counsel K. attended in person. The court acquitted the applicant of disturbance of the peace and illegal possession of firearms, upheld the remaining convictions and reduced the sentence to 16 years. It also ordered the applicant to reimburse counsel K.’s fee of 5,967.50 Russian roubles.

According to the applicant, the video-link was of poor quality, with sound interruptions that rendered parts of the hearing unintelligible. He claimed the court interrupted him, refused to admit certain documents, prevented him from fully presenting his grounds of appeal, and denied him a final statement. He further asserted that counsel K. offered no meaningful defence, merely proposing that two charges be dropped on technical grounds, and that neither counsel, the prosecutor nor the court had properly studied the file.

These facts form the core of the alleged impairment of the applicant’s rights of defence on appeal, first through the complete absence of representation in 2003 and subsequently through the conditions of the 2008 rehearing conducted by video-link.

The case of Gennadiy Medvedev v. Russia (application no. 34184/03) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by a Russian national born in 1960, who at the relevant time was serving a lengthy prison sentence. The case of Gennadiy Medvedev v.
