001-110805:
The applicants in *Albu and Others v. Romania* (applications nos. 34796/09 and 63 others) were 64 Romanian civil servants employed by the Caraş Severin District Employment Agency. On 5 May 2008 they petitioned their employer to recognise two wage supplements—a grade allowance and a salary-step allowance—each quantified at 25% of basic salary under section 31(1)(c) and (d) of Law no. 188/1999 (the Public Servants’ Statute). They sought payment retroactively from April 2004 (despite statutory suspensions of the provisions until 31 December 2006) and prospectively, plus annotation in their employment records. The employer rejected the petition as unfounded on 19 May 2008.

The applicants challenged this before the Caraş Severin County Court, arguing that the suspensions did not extinguish the rights, that they violated the Constitution, and that the rights constituted a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 10 September 2008 the County Court dismissed the claim. While acknowledging that the Labour Code obliged payment of statutory allowances and that the Statute listed the two supplements as salary components, it held that no subsequent legislation or executive act had quantified them. Determining the amounts itself would violate the separation of powers by encroaching on the executive.

On appeal to the Timişoara Court of Appeal the applicants reiterated these points, invoked the principle that laws must produce effects, cited Article 38 of the Labour Code (acquired rights cannot be limited), and alleged discrimination contrary to Article 14. They pointed to consistent national case-law granting identical claims to other civil servants, including a colleague (S.S.M.) from the same agency whose similar claim had been upheld by the same first-instance court and, on 2 October 2008, by the same Court of Appeal. On 21 January 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It found no legal basis for a 25% figure, held that additional legislation or government instructions were required, and stated that courts lacked jurisdiction to create such norms. Precedents were not a source of law. There was neither a “possession” nor a “legitimate expectation” because case-law was not well-established. The Labour Code was inapplicable to civil servants appointed by administrative acts that omitted the allowances.

The Statute (originally section 29, later section 31) had been amended in 2003–2004 to include the supplements, but their application was suspended until the end of 2006; they were abolished entirely from 1 January 2010. Applicants produced judgments from the same Timişoara panel (23 January 2008) and the Suceava Court of Appeal (5 June 2008) that had granted analogous claims, reasoning that the absence of a quantified amount could not render the statutory provisions ineffective. The Government cited several other courts of appeal that had rejected similar claims on grounds later endorsed by the High Court of Cassation and Justice.

On 21 September 2009 that High Court, ruling on an appeal in the interests of the law, confirmed nationwide divergence and held that, without a legal determination of amount, the judiciary could not grant the allowances; they were merely “virtual rights” and not possessions. The ruling bound all courts prospectively and ended the divergence. International material cited in the judgment (Venice Commission, UN Special Rapporteur, CCJE) underscored that conflicting highest-court decisions undermine legal certainty, predictability and the rule of law.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights of a breach of Articles 6 and 14 arising from this prolonged, inconsistent case-law that had denied them the supplements while others in identical situations had received them.

The ECtHR case Albu and Others v. Romania (apps. 34796/09 et al., judgment 10 May 2012) involved 64 Romanian civil servants employed by the Caraş Severin District Employment Agency. They alleged violations of Article 6 (fair trial) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the Convention arising from prolonged divergence in domestic case-law on their entitlement to two salary supplements.

On 5 May 2008 the applicants petitioned their employer to recognise and pay (retroactively from April 2004 and prospectively) a grade supplement and a salary-step supplement, each quantified at 25 % of basic salary, pursuant to section 31(1)(c) and (d) of Law no. 188/1999 (the Public Servants’ Statute). They also sought annotation of the entitlements in their employment records. The employer rejected the request as unfounded.

The applicants then sued in the Caraş Severin County Court. They argued that the statutory suspension of the allowances until 31 December 2006 did not extinguish the rights, which therefore became payable from 1 January 2007, and that the suspension itself was unconstitutional. On 10 September 2008 the County Court acknowledged that the Labour Code and the Statute entitled civil servants to the supplements in principle, but dismissed the claim. It held that neither the original 2003 amendment nor subsequent salary legislation specified any amount or calculation method; determination of quantum was reserved to the executive. For a court to fix the figures itself would violate the separation of powers.

The applicants appealed to the Timişoara Court of Appeal, adding that acquired labour rights could not be limited, that unused legal provisions are inconceivable, that the rights constituted a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and that the lower court’s interpretation rendered the Statute ineffective. They further invoked Article 14, pointing to consistent case-law in which other civil servants (including a colleague from the same agency, whose claim had been granted by the identical first-instance court and then upheld by the same Court of Appeal) had obtained the supplements.

On 21 January 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It found no statutory basis for a 25 % figure and held that further legislation or governmental instructions were required. Courts lacked jurisdiction to supply missing norms or to treat precedents as binding sources of law. The applicants had not established a “possession” or even a “legitimate expectation,” given the unsettled case-law. The Labour Code was inapplicable to civil servants, whose administrative appointments made no mention of the allowances.

The Statute had introduced the two supplements (initially without quantum) from 2004; their application was repeatedly suspended until the end of 2006 and they were abolished entirely in 2010. Before unification, some Courts of Appeal (including Timişoara and Suceava) had granted identical claims, while others (Alba Iulia, Galaţi, Bacău, etc.) had rejected them on grounds later endorsed by the High Court. On 21 September 2009 the High Court of Cassation and Justice, ruling on an appeal in the interests of the law, held that in the absence of a legally determined amount the judiciary could not award the supplements; they were merely “virtual rights.” The ruling bound all courts prospectively and ended the divergence.

These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 6 complaint (lack of legal certainty and foreseeability caused by persistent conflicting interpretations) and the Article 14 complaint (unequal treatment vis-à-vis similarly situated civil servants who had obtained the allowances). International instruments cited in the judgment (Venice Commission report on the rule of law, UN Special Rapporteur observations, CCJE Opinion No. 11) underscored the necessity of coherent case-law to safeguard legal certainty.

The case of Albu and Others v. Romania (applications nos. 34796/09 and 63 others) was brought by 64 Romanian civil servants employed by the Caraş Severin District Employment Agency. They alleged violations of Articles 6 (fair trial) and 14 (non-discrimination) of the Convention arising from prolonged inconsistency in domestic case-law on their entitlement to two salary supplements.

In May 2008 the applicants petitioned their employer for a grade allowance and a salary-step allowance, each at 25 % of basic salary, pursuant to section 31(1)(c) and (d) of Law no. 188/1999 (the Public Servants’ Statute). They sought retroactive payment from April 2004, future payment until termination of employment, and notation in their records. The employer rejected the petition as ill-founded.

The applicants challenged this before the Caraş Severin County Court. They argued that, although Government Emergency Ordinance no. 92/2004 and subsequent instruments had suspended the relevant provisions until 31 December 2006, the suspension did not extinguish the rights; payment was therefore due from 1 January 2007 (or even from 2004, as the suspension itself breached the Constitution). On 10 September 2008 the County Court dismissed the claim. While acknowledging that the Labour Code required payment of all statutory allowances, it held that neither Law no. 188/1999 nor subsequent legislation specified the amounts of the supplements. Courts therefore lacked jurisdiction to quantify them, as doing so would encroach on the executive’s power and violate the separation of powers.

The applicants appealed to the Timişoara Court of Appeal, repeating their arguments and adding that acquired rights could not be limited (Labour Code, Art. 38), that a statute must produce effects, and that their claims constituted a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They also invoked Article 14, pointing to consistent case-law granting identical claims to other civil servants, including a colleague (S.S.M.) employed by the same agency whose claim had been upheld by the same County Court and, ultimately, by the Timişoara Court of Appeal itself.

On 21 January 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It found no statutory basis for a 25 % figure; additional legislation was required. Courts could not create norms or refuse to apply existing ones merely because they considered them discriminatory. Romanian law did not treat judicial precedents as a source of law. The applicants had not established a possession or legitimate expectation, given the unsettled case-law. Moreover, the Labour Code did not apply to civil servants appointed by individual administrative acts that made no mention of the allowances.

Law no. 188/1999 had introduced the supplements with effect from 2004, but their application was repeatedly suspended until the end of 2006; they were abolished altogether by Law no. 330/2009 with effect from 1 January 2010. No implementing measure ever quantified them.

Domestic practice was sharply divided. Several courts of appeal (including Timişoara in other cases and Suceava) granted analogous claims, holding that the absence of a specified amount could not render the statutory provisions ineffective. Other courts of appeal (Alba Iulia, Galaţi, Bacău, Constanţa, Cluj, Ploieşti, Bucharest) dismissed them for lack of quantification. On 21 September 2009—after the applicants’ proceedings had ended—the High Court of Cassation and Justice, on an appeal in the interests of the law, unified the interpretation: without a legal determination of amount the supplements were merely “virtual rights” that courts could not award. The ruling bound all courts thereafter, ending the divergence.

These facts—statutory rights whose quantification was left unspecified, prolonged conflicting judgments even within the same courts, and the applicants’ unsuccessful attempt to rely on a successful parallel claim by a co-worker—formed the basis of the alleged breaches of legal certainty under Article 6 and of equal treatment under Article 14.
001-110314:
The case of Stübing v. Germany (Application no. 43547/08) concerns Patrick Stübing’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that his criminal convictions for incest violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life).

Stübing was born in 1976. At age three he was placed in a children’s home and later adopted at age seven by foster parents, after which he had no contact with his biological family. His sister S.K. was born in 1984. After their mother’s death in 2000, Stübing re-established contact with his family of origin. From January 2001 the adult siblings engaged in a consensual sexual relationship, lived together for several years and had four children (born 2001, 2003, 2004 and 2005). Stübing underwent a vasectomy after the fourth birth. Three children were placed in foster care; the youngest remained with the mother.

Stübing was convicted under Section 173 § 2(2) of the German Criminal Code (punishing sexual intercourse between consanguine siblings). On 23 April 2002 the Borna District Court imposed a suspended one-year sentence for 16 counts. On 6 April 2004 he received 10 months’ imprisonment for a further count. On 10 November 2005 the Leipzig District Court convicted him of two more counts and, aggregating prior sentences, imposed a total of one year and four months’ imprisonment. Mitigating factors included childhood physical abuse by his father, a confession, media attention and an assault in detention; aggravating factors were reoffending and unprotected intercourse despite known pregnancy risks. S.K., charged with the same offence, was found only partially criminally liable owing to a serious personality disorder, extreme dependency on Stübing (especially after their mother’s death) and mild learning disabilities; she received no sentence.

The Dresden Court of Appeal dismissed Stübing’s appeal. His 2007 constitutional complaint (alleging violation of sexual self-determination, discrimination and disproportionality, plus interference with the parent-child relationship of children born of the union) was rejected 7-1 by the Federal Constitutional Court on 26 February 2008. The majority held that the narrowly drawn prohibition did not encroach on the core of private life. It pursued legitimate aims: protection of marriage and the family (incest produces overlapping roles that undermine family structure and children’s ability to form secure attachments); protection of sexual self-determination within interdependent family relationships; and eugenic considerations (elevated risk of genetic defects, supported by medical literature). The provision also performed a general-preventive, norm-reinforcing function consistent with a widespread societal and international conviction against incest. It was suitable, necessary (youth-welfare measures lack equivalent deterrent and signalling effects) and proportionate (courts may refrain from punishment where guilt is slight). A dissent argued the provision pursued no legitimate aim beyond morality, was both over- and under-inclusive (it ignored other sexual acts, same-sex siblings and non-blood relatives yet applied after siblings had left the family home), and that less intrusive family-court or welfare measures would suffice.

Stübing began serving his sentence on 4 June 2008 and was released on probation on 3 June 2009. Comparative material showed that roughly half of Council of Europe states criminalise adult sibling incest while half do not; even where decriminalised, siblings generally may not marry.

These facts—late-discovered biological siblinghood, a fully consensual adult relationship producing children, repeated prosecutions and imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court’s family-protection and eugenic justifications—form the core of the alleged Article 8 interference.

The case of Stübing v. Germany (no. 43547/08) was brought by Patrick Stübing, a German national born in 1976, who alleged that his criminal convictions for incest with his biological sister violated his right to respect for private and family life.

Separated from his family of origin at age three and adopted at seven, the applicant had no contact with them until 2000. His sister S.K. was born in 1984. After their mother's death, the siblings developed a close relationship and, from January 2001, engaged in consensual sexual intercourse while living together. They had four children (born 2001–2005). The applicant later underwent a vasectomy. The three older children were placed in foster care; the youngest remained with S.K.

German courts repeatedly convicted the applicant under Section 173 § 2(2) of the Criminal Code, which punishes sexual intercourse between consanguine siblings (with an exemption for those under 18). In April 2002 the Borna District Court imposed a suspended one-year sentence for 16 counts. A further conviction in April 2004 yielded 10 months’ imprisonment. In November 2005 the Leipzig District Court added convictions for two more counts and imposed a combined sentence of one year and four months, citing aggravating factors (reoffending and unprotected intercourse despite pregnancy risks) alongside mitigating ones (childhood abuse, confession, media exposure and prior prison assaults). S.K. faced the same charges but received no sentence: an expert report established her timid, dependent personality, exacerbated by family circumstances and mild learning disabilities, rendering her only partially responsible.

Appeals failed. The applicant’s 2007 constitutional complaint argued that the incest provision violated sexual self-determination, discriminated against him and disproportionately interfered with family relationships involving children born of incest. On 26 February 2008 the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint by 7–1. It held that the narrowly tailored ban did not touch the core of private life, because sibling intercourse could harm family structures, social roles and any resulting children. Legitimate aims included protection of marriage and the family (supported by empirical studies of role confusion and damage to family function), sexual self-determination within interdependent family settings, and eugenic considerations (elevated genetic-risk evidence). The provision also performed a signalling and general-preventive function consistent with widespread societal and international views. It was suitable, necessary (youth-welfare measures lacked equivalent deterrent effect) and proportionate, given courts’ discretion to refrain from punishment in cases of slight guilt.

A dissenting judge contended that the provision pursued no legitimate aim (eugenics being improper for criminal law, self-determination already covered by other offences, and family protection inconsistently applied, since only heterosexual intercourse between blood siblings was banned). It was both under- and over-inclusive, other family-law tools were available, and the measure was excessive.

The applicant served his sentence from June 2008 until his release on probation in June 2009. Comparative material showed that roughly half of surveyed Council of Europe states still criminalise consensual adult sibling incest, with no general movement toward repeal.

These facts—the late-discovered sibling relationship, repeated consensual adult intercourse producing children, successive convictions despite personality and welfare considerations, and the Constitutional Court’s multi-pronged justification—form the core of the alleged Article 8 interference.

The case of Stübing v. Germany (ECHR Application no. 43547/08) arose from Patrick Stübing’s allegation that his convictions for incest violated his right to respect for private and family life. Stübing, born in 1976, was placed in a children’s home at age three, later fostered, and adopted at age seven, after which he had no contact with his biological family. His sister S.K. was born in 1984. He first learned of her existence and re-established contact in 2000 after their mother’s death. From January 2001 they engaged in consensual sexual intercourse, lived together for several years, and had four children (born 2001, 2003, 2004 and 2005). Stübing later underwent a vasectomy. The three older children were placed in foster care; the youngest remained with the mother.

In April 2002 the Borna District Court convicted Stübing of 16 counts of incest under Section 173 § 2(2) of the Criminal Code and imposed a one-year suspended sentence. A further conviction in April 2004 produced a ten-month term. In November 2005 the Leipzig District Court convicted him of two additional counts and imposed a cumulative sentence of one year and four months (taking account of prior convictions). Mitigating factors included childhood physical abuse by his father, a confession, adverse media coverage and an assault while in detention; aggravating factors were reoffending and unprotected intercourse despite known pregnancy risks. S.K. was charged with the same offence but received no sentence: an expert report established a timid, withdrawn and dependent personality, extreme reliance on Stübing after their mother’s death, and mild learning disabilities, rendering her only partially responsible.

The Dresden Court of Appeal dismissed Stübing’s appeal in January 2007. He then lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that the incest provision violated sexual self-determination, discriminated against him, was disproportionate and interfered with parent–child relationships arising from incestuous unions. In February 2008 the Federal Constitutional Court rejected the complaint by seven votes to one. It held that the provision restricted sexual self-determination of biological siblings but did not touch the core of private life, given effects on family, society and any children. Legitimate aims included protection of marriage and the family (overlapping roles damage family structures and children’s ability to form trusting relationships), protection of sexual self-determination within close family settings, and eugenic concerns about genetic defects. The measure was suitable, necessary (youth-welfare interventions lack the same general-preventive and norm-reinforcing effect) and proportionate, since courts could refrain from punishment where guilt was slight. A dissenting judge contended that the provision pursued no legitimate aim (eugenics being an improper criminal-law objective and the text failing to protect self-determination or the family consistently, as it omitted other sexual acts, same-sex intercourse and non-blood relatives), was unsuitable and excessive, and merely enforced moral standards rather than protecting rights; less restrictive family-court or welfare measures were available.

Stübing began serving his sentence in June 2008 and was released on probation in June 2009. The facts underlying the alleged Article 8 violation are therefore the criminalisation of a consensual adult sibling relationship (formed after the siblings had been raised separately), the resulting convictions and sentences, the impact on their cohabitation and on the four children, and the domestic courts’ confirmation that the impugned provision pursued family-protection, self-determination and public-health objectives while remaining proportionate.
001-110866:
The ÖDP, a Turkish political party based in Ankara, was authorised by the Higher Electoral Commission (28 November 1998) to contest the 18 April 1999 parliamentary and municipal elections. Eligibility required parties to maintain branches in at least half of Turkey’s provinces for six months beforehand and to have held a party conference. On 23 September 1998 the ÖDP applied to the Ministry of Finance for the public funding that Article 68 of the Constitution requires the State to provide “sufficient and equitable[ly]” to political parties, with detailed principles to be set by ordinary legislation.

The Ministry refused the request on 23 November 1998, applying additional section 1 of Law no. 2820. That provision allocates a fixed share of the State budget (2/5 000ths, tripled in a parliamentary-election year and doubled in a municipal-election year) exclusively to parties already represented in Parliament (in proportion to their last election result) or to extra-parliamentary parties that obtained at least 7 % of the national vote in the preceding general election. Parties holding at least three seats are also eligible even if they did not contest the last poll. The ÖDP satisfied none of these criteria.

On 29 December 1998 the party sought judicial review in the Ankara Administrative Court. It argued that the 7 % threshold and the exclusion of parties lacking parliamentary representation contradicted the Constitution’s command of equitable funding, undermined the State’s duty to foster democratic pluralism, and discriminated against smaller parties that cannot campaign effectively without resources. The court dismissed the action on 29 September 1999 solely on the ground that the statutory criteria were unmet; it declined to examine the constitutional challenge. An appeal on points of law repeating the same arguments was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 25 April 2002 (notified 10 July 2002).

The ÖDP obtained 0.8 % of the vote in 1999, 0.34 % in 2002 and 0.15 % in 2007, and never received State funding. By contrast, several extra-parliamentary parties that cleared the 7 % bar did receive subsidies before each of those elections. In 2008 the Constitutional Court, by majority, upheld the 7 % threshold against a later unconstitutionality plea, reasoning that only parties with substantial electoral support meaningfully contribute to the formation of public opinion; a dissenting minority considered the threshold (almost three million votes) excessively high and the “contribution” criterion subjective.

The ÖDP therefore claimed that the refusal of funding, based solely on a high statutory threshold that systematically favoured already-established or large parties, constituted discrimination contrary to the Convention, impairing its ability to participate on equal terms in the democratic process.

The case of Özgürlük ve Dayanışma Partisi (ÖDP) v. Turkey (Application no. 7819/03) originated in an application by the Turkish political party ÖDP, based in Ankara, alleging discrimination arising from the refusal of its request for state financial assistance to political parties as provided under the Constitution. The ÖDP had been authorised to contest the parliamentary and municipal elections of 18 April 1999, appearing on the Higher Electoral Commission’s list of 18 qualifying parties published on 28 November 1998. Eligibility for those elections required parties to have maintained branches in at least half of Turkey’s provinces for six months beforehand and to have convened a party conference.

On 23 September 1998 the ÖDP applied to the Ministry of Finance for the funding envisaged by the final paragraph of Article 68 of the Constitution, which obliges the State to grant political parties “sufficient and equitable funding” according to principles laid down by law. The Ministry rejected the request on 23 November 1998 on the ground that only parties satisfying the criteria of Law no. 2820 on political parties were entitled to public money.

The ÖDP challenged the refusal before the Ankara Administrative Court on 29 December 1998. It argued that the statutory criteria unconstitutionally excluded parties not represented in Parliament, thereby violating the Constitution’s guarantee of equitable funding, the principles of a democratic State, the duty to promote democratic rights, the principle of non-discrimination, and relevant international instruments. The party emphasised the practical impossibility of conducting political activities and election campaigns without adequate resources.

In a judgment of 29 September 1999 the Administrative Court dismissed the action solely because the ÖDP failed to meet the conditions of Law no. 2820; it did not examine the plea of unconstitutionality. The ÖDP’s appeal on points of law, repeating the same arguments, was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 25 April 2002 (served 10 July 2002), which found the first-instance decision consistent with law and procedure.

Additional section 1 of Law no. 2820 allocates an overall sum equivalent to 2/5000ths of the state budget to parties represented in Parliament in proportion to their share of the vote in the preceding parliamentary elections. Non-parliamentary parties may also receive funding if they obtained at least 7 per cent of the valid votes in that election, and any party with at least three members of Parliament is eligible even if it did not contest the last election. The amount is tripled in parliamentary election years and doubled in municipal election years.

The ÖDP obtained 0.8 per cent of the valid votes in 1999, 0.34 per cent in 2002 and 0.15 per cent in 2007, and never received state funding. Ahead of the 1999 election six of 21 contesting parties (one of them extra-parliamentary) received assistance; comparable figures applied in 2002 and 2007.

In a later (2008) decision the Constitutional Court, by majority, rejected a similar challenge to the 7 per cent threshold, holding that parties lacking sufficient electoral support do not contribute equally to the expression of popular opinion and that the criterion of contribution to democratic life is objective, equitable and proportionate. A minority considered the threshold (almost three million votes in 2007) excessively high, unfairly advantageous to larger parties, and subjective, thereby breaching the rule of law.

OSCE/ODIHR and Venice Commission guidelines on political-party regulation (2010) underscore that public funding should promote equal opportunity, pluralism and the ability of all parties—including new and extra-parliamentary ones—to compete. Thresholds for eligibility ought not to be unreasonably high, allocation formulae should be objective and unbiased, and funding should not be monopolised by the largest parties. These facts formed the basis of the ÖDP’s claim that the denial of funding constituted unlawful discrimination contrary to the Constitution’s equitable-funding requirement and relevant Convention rights.

The case Özgürlük ve Dayanışma Partisi (ÖDP) v. Turkey (Application no. 7819/03) concerns a Turkish political party’s complaint of discrimination arising from the refusal of State financial assistance available under the Constitution. The ÖDP, based in Ankara, was included by decree of 28 November 1998 on the list of 18 parties authorised by the Higher Electoral Commission to contest the 18 April 1999 parliamentary and municipal elections. Eligibility for those elections required parties to have maintained branches in at least half of Turkey’s provinces for six months and to have held a party conference.

On 23 September 1998 the ÖDP applied to the Ministry of Finance for the public funding provided for in the final paragraph of Article 68 of the Constitution, which states that the State shall grant political parties “sufficient and equitable funding” and that the law shall define the applicable principles. The Ministry rejected the request on 23 November 1998, holding that only parties meeting the criteria of Law no. 2820 on political parties were eligible. Under additional section 1 of that Law, State assistance (amounting to 2/5000ths of the national budget) is given to parties represented in Parliament in proportion to votes obtained in the preceding parliamentary elections. Parties not represented in Parliament may receive funding if they obtained at least 7 % of the votes in those elections; parties with at least three members of Parliament are also eligible even if they did not contest the last election. Funding is tripled in a parliamentary-election year and doubled in a municipal-election year.

On 29 December 1998 the ÖDP brought proceedings in the Ankara Administrative Court seeking annulment of the refusal. It argued that the statutory criteria unconstitutionally excluded non-parliamentary parties, thereby violating the Constitution’s mandate of equitable funding, the principles of a democratic State, the State’s duty to promote democratic rights, and the prohibition of discrimination, as well as international human-rights instruments. The difficulty of conducting political activities and campaigning without financial resources was emphasised. In a judgment of 29 September 1999 the Administrative Court dismissed the action solely on the ground that the ÖDP failed to satisfy Law no. 2820; it did not address the plea of unconstitutionality. An appeal on points of law reiterating the same arguments was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 25 April 2002 (served 10 July 2002).

The ÖDP obtained only 0.8 % of the valid votes in the 1999 elections, 0.34 % in 2002 and 0.15 % in 2007, and never received State funding. Ahead of the 1999, 2002 and 2007 elections, funding was granted only to parties that either held seats or had exceeded the 7 % threshold (six parties out of 21 in 1999, six out of 15 in 2002, five out of 15 in 2007). In 2008 the Constitutional Court, by majority, later upheld the 7 % threshold against a similar unconstitutionality challenge, reasoning that parties lacking sufficient electoral support contribute less to the expression of popular opinion; a minority considered the threshold excessively high and the criterion subjective.

The ÖDP’s application to the European Court of Human Rights, lodged on 1 October 2002, alleged that the refusal of funding discriminated against it despite its qualification to contest elections. Relevant international standards (OSCE/ODIHR–Venice Commission Guidelines on political-party regulation) stress that public funding should promote equal opportunity and pluralism, should not be confined to parliamentary parties, and should employ reasonably low thresholds so that new or small parties can compete.

The applicants—Sladjan Nacic (b. 1969), his wife Jelena Nacic (b. 1971), and their sons Alexander (b. 1991) and Milan (b. 1994)—are of Roma descent from Kosovo Polje. After the 1999 conflict, Sladjan refused conscription and hid; the family suffered threats and beatings by Serbian forces, was driven from their home by Albanian militia, lost their documents, and lived in isolation in Suvi Do until fleeing to Sweden in 2006, where they sought asylum and residence permits.

The family was not deemed refugees or otherwise in need of protection. Their claimed Roma ethnicity was doubted because they lived among Serbs, spoke no Romani, and had no prior persecution on that basis. Medical issues were insufficient: Sladjan's hypertension was common and treatable; Jelena's psychological problems (supported by incomplete records) were not life-threatening; Alexander's depression lacked a clear diagnosis, with care available in Kosovo/Serbia.

On appeal, the family entered a children's home after authorities found the parents unable to cope. Further certificates indicated suicide risks for the parents if expelled, PTSD symptoms in Jelena (including a prior attempt), and Alexander's severe depression with a June 2008 overdose attempt, isolation, and apathy. The Migration Court rejected the appeal in December 2008, noting Alexander was nearly 18, psychiatric care existed (at least for those who could pay), and his development would not be irreparably harmed. Two lay judges dissented, citing his health and family unity.

The Migration Court of Appeal, in November 2009, granted Alexander a permanent residence permit. Certificates showed his severe, persistent mental illness originating in Kosovo events, requiring a safe, stable environment for treatment. Care existed but was inadequate given his history. The parents and Milan were refused; two dissents argued for the whole family (one viewing Alexander as an adult whose case should be assessed separately; the other stressing family circumstances as a whole).

A February 2010 request citing worsened health and new certificates was rejected: no new impediments existed, and Alexander's majority ended family-tie claims.

Interim measures under Rule 39 halted deportation. Later certificates (2009–2011) diagnosed grave depression, complex PTSD, and eating/sleep disorders in the parents (with suicidal ideation); Alexander's improvement after his permit was threatened by family separation; and Milan (spared earlier trauma due to age) faced severe trauma from family breakup. Country reports noted ongoing Roma discrimination in Kosovo (employment, services, movement, returns) and Serbia (health-insurance access requiring documentation often lacking for returnees), plus Kosovo's severely under-resourced mental-health system (few specialists, limited PTSD treatment, high population needs).

The case of Nacic and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 16567/10) concerns a Roma family from Kosovo who sought asylum in Sweden in 2006 and alleged that the deportation of three family members to Kosovo or Serbia would violate Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.

The applicants are Sladjan Nacic (born 1969), his wife Jelena Nacic (born 1971), and their sons Alexander (born 1991) and Milan (born 1994). They lived in Kosovo Polje. After the 1999 war outbreak, Sladjan hid from armed forces after refusing to fight. The family faced threats and beatings by Serbian military, then expulsion by Albanian militia. They fled to Suvi Do, losing identity papers, and hid isolated at a friend’s home until traveling to Sweden. They claimed harassment as Roma but no prior persecution due to isolation.

The Migration Board rejected their 2008 asylum and residence applications. Identity was not fully proven but Kosovo/Serbia origin was plausible. Neither country’s general situation warranted asylum, nor were they refugees or otherwise in need of protection. On ethnicity, the Board noted the first applicant’s Serbian mother, lack of Romani language or Roma contacts, life in Serb areas socializing only with Serbs, and no prior ethnicity-based persecution, concluding no return risk as Roma. Personal circumstances, including medical issues, were insufficient: Sladjan’s hypertension was common and treatable; Jelena’s psychological problems (supported by a non-compliant certificate and records) were not life-threatening; Alexander’s depression (certificate lacking diagnosis) had treatment available in both countries, with no improvement in Sweden.

On appeal, the family submitted further medical evidence after moving to a children’s home in 2008 due to parental inability to care for the children. Certificates indicated suicide risk for Sladjan and Jelena (who had attempted suicide and showed PTSD signs). Alexander’s certificate detailed severe depression, isolation, a 2008 suicide attempt by overdose, and poor condition (refusing food, bedridden), with high reattempt risk on expulsion. The Migration Court upheld the rejection in December 2008, noting Alexander nearing 18, available (paid) psychiatric care, and insufficient grounds for any applicant. Dissenters would have granted based on Alexander’s health and family unity.

The Migration Court of Appeal in November 2009 granted Alexander a permanent residence permit due to severe mental illness unlikely to improve without a safe, stable environment (issues originating in Kosovo/Serbia), despite available care there. It rejected the others. Dissenters split: one viewed Alexander (now 18) separately as an adult with available care; another saw severe illness across the family requiring unity.

A 2010 reapplication citing worsened conditions (new certificates) was rejected: no new circumstances, and Alexander’s majority ended family-tie claims. Further certificates (2009–2011) diagnosed grave depression, PTSD, and suicidal tendencies in Sladjan, Jelena, and Alexander; family disruption would fatally risk Jelena, worsen Alexander’s rehabilitation (needing family support), and traumatize young Milan. Reports highlighted Kosovo Roma discrimination, violence, and inadequate mental health care (limited professionals, PTSD untreated for 7–10% of population); Serbia posed access barriers for undocumented Roma.

These facts underpin claims of Article 3 risks (ill-treatment via ethnicity, health deterioration without care/access, suicide) and Article 8 (family separation from Alexander). Interim measures halted deportation pending the Court’s review.

**CASE OF FERNÁNDEZ MARTÍNEZ v. SPAIN (Application no. 56030/07), ECtHR Third Section, 15 May 2012 (referred to Grand Chamber)**

The applicant, José Antonio Fernández Martínez (born 1937), is a Spanish national living in Cieza. Ordained a Catholic priest in 1961, he applied in 1984 for Vatican dispensation from celibacy and married in a civil ceremony in 1985; he and his wife have five children.

From October 1991 he taught Catholic religion and ethics at a state secondary school in Murcia under a renewable one-year contract. Under the 1979 Spain-Holy See Agreement, the local Bishop had to confirm each renewal and the Ministry of Education was bound by that decision.

In November 1996 a regional newspaper published an article on the “Movement for Optional Celibacy.” It named the applicant (a former seminary rector and movement member), showed a photograph of him with his wife and children at a gathering, and quoted participants (including him) calling for optional celibacy, a more democratic Church, and disagreement with Catholic teaching on abortion, divorce, sexuality and contraception. Publicity reportedly deterred many members from attending.

On 15 September 1997 the Vatican granted the dispensation. The document barred the recipient from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the Bishop decided otherwise “according to his own criteria and provided that there [was] no scandal.” On 29 September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry it would not approve renewal for 1997/98. A later Diocese memorandum stated that publicity of the applicant’s personal situation created a “risk of scandal,” breaching the duty to teach discreetly and protecting the sensitivities of pupils’ parents.

The applicant’s administrative challenge failed. Murcia Employment Tribunal No. 3 (28 September 2000) found discrimination on grounds of marital status and movement membership, held the press appearance caused the non-renewal, declared the dismissal void and ordered reinstatement.

The Murcia High Court of Justice (26 February 2001) reversed. It characterised the relationship as one of trust on the “borderline” between ecclesiastical and employment law. The Bishop had lawfully exercised his prerogative once the applicant publicised his situation; there was no violation of constitutional rights to equality, private life or expression. The restrictions were legitimate and proportionate to avoid scandal. The contract was temporary and had simply expired.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, invoking constitutional Articles 14 (non-discrimination), 18 (private and family life) and 20 (expression). The Court (4 June 2007, two judges dissenting) dismissed it. It treated the case under Articles 16 (thought, religion and worship) and 20. The applicant’s situation had been known for years; non-renewal followed only after he publicised it. Religion teachers occupy a special status selected on religious criteria. The State’s duty of neutrality prevented it from reviewing the Bishop’s notion of “scandal.” The interference was justified by the Church’s collective religious freedom and parents’ right to choose their children’s religious education. Reasons were exclusively religious.

The applicant then asked the Constitutional Court to annul its judgment because two judges had known affinities with the Catholic Church (one belonged to the International Secretariat of Catholic Lawyers). The request was rejected as inadmissible; the only possible step was a request for clarification.

Before the ECtHR the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of lack of impartiality of those two Constitutional Court judges. Under Article 8 taken with Article 14 he alleged the non-renewal was an unjustified interference with private life. He further claimed that the public manifestation of his views on priestly celibacy caused the non-renewal, violating Articles 9 and 10.

The case of Epners-Gefners v. Latvia (no. 37862/02) was brought by Aivars Epners-Gefners, a Latvian national born in 1964, who alleged inadequate dental care and denial of long-term family visits during detention. He was arrested on 1 October 1999 for aggravated robbery, convicted on 11 April 2002 by the Kurzeme Regional Court and sentenced to six years and one month’s imprisonment. Appeals were dismissed on 5 June and 20 September 2002. He was released early on 23 August 2004.

His wife gave birth to their son on 18 May 2000. During pre-trial detention he received only two short-term visits from her (16 November 2000 and 20 November 2001) plus four from his aunt. Long-term visits (six from his wife, each lasting about 16 hours) were allowed only after 5 October 2002, once he began serving his sentence.

Remand-prison rules then in force (Minister of the Interior instruction of 1994, replaced in May 2001 by a Minister of Justice transitional instruction) permitted detainees one short-term visit of up to one hour per month, and only with written permission from the investigating authority or court. No provision existed for long-term visits during pre-trial detention. Later Constitutional Court rulings confirmed that the instructions were unpublished internal acts and that a subsequent one-hour monthly limit on short-term visits was disproportionate, but they also held that states were under no duty to allow long-term visits for remand prisoners.

Dental complaints began on 29 June 2000; the prison doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and advised a dentist. On 16 August 2000 further pain relief (Analgin) was given. Examination on 18 August 2000 revealed caries, two missing teeth, remnants of 21 damaged teeth and only eight healthy teeth; the applicant refused treatment. Headache complaints in 2001 were linked by a psychiatrist to dental cavities. On 25 October 2001 periodontal disease was diagnosed and four teeth extracted. A November 2001 complaint seeking prosthetics was answered by the Prisons Administration on 11 December 2001: extractions had been free, eight teeth remained (attributed to pre-detention neglect), and prosthetics were available only at the prisoner’s expense because no budgetary funds existed. Identical replies followed further complaints.

Cabinet Regulation no. 358 (1999) guaranteed detainees and convicts free emergency dental care and basic health services within budgetary limits, but excluded planned or prosthetic treatment. These facts underpinned the applicant’s claims of insufficient medical care and interference with family life.

Later Constitutional Court judgments confirmed that there was no obligation to provide long-term visits to remand prisoners, though a subsequent blanket one-hour monthly limit on short visits was found disproportionate (and later amended).

Similar complaints and prescriptions (Analgin) followed on 16 August 2000. On 18 August 2000 a dentist diagnosed caries in one tooth and recorded two missing teeth plus the remains of 21 damaged teeth (only eight healthy teeth remaining); the applicant refused the recommended treatment. Further pain complaints occurred in August 2001. A psychiatrist in September 2001 linked headaches to dental problems. On 25 October 2001 a dentist diagnosed periodontal disease (loose teeth) and extracted four teeth. On 26 November 2001 the applicant complained to the General Inspectorate about inadequate care and the need for prosthetics; the complaint was referred to the Prisons Administration. On 11 December 2001 (and again on 12 February 2002 after further correspondence) the Administration replied that extractions had been provided free of charge, that eight teeth remained, that poor pre-detention care was presumed, and that dental prosthetics were available only at the prisoner’s own expense because no budgetary funds were allocated for them.

Cabinet Regulation no. 358 (1999) required free emergency dental care and a minimum standard of health care for convicted and detained persons, but did not cover planned prosthetics. The applicant, Ardi Shuvalov, was a judge at Estonia’s Harju County Court. From 2003 he presided over a criminal case against businessman D. involving tax evasion, money laundering and other charges. In January 2006 D. told the security police that his business partner N. (who owed D. a large sum) had offered to arrange a favourable judgment through Shuvalov—his former university roommate—if D. waived repayment of the debt and paid bribes of EEK 200,000 as a “Christmas gesture” plus EEK 900,000 for acquittal.

A criminal investigation into accepting and arranging a bribe was opened. Covert surveillance and recordings of N. and later of Shuvalov were authorised, as was a simulated bribe-giving operation by D. On 6 April 2006 D. handed N. EEK 400,000; N. was arrested. Interviewed as a suspect, N. claimed he had merely relayed Shuvalov’s demand for EEK 900,000. That same day a further simulation was authorised: N., wearing a recording device, met Shuvalov and handed over EEK 200,000. Shuvalov was arrested, later released, and surrendered the cash.

On 9 April 2006 the Public Prosecutor’s Office issued a press release headed “A judge suspected of accepting a bribe.” It described the arrest during a simulation, the suspicion that the judge had demanded a large bribe through an intermediary for a more favourable judgment, and the acceptance of part of the sum. Prosecutor V., who led the case, subsequently made repeated statements to television and newspapers. These included remarks that the suspicion originated from the person from whom the bribe was demanded, that the simulation had been successful, that the proceedings had not been provoked by police, that Shuvalov himself had demanded the money, and that he had been “very careful.” After Shuvalov’s identity became public, V. named him and gave further details.

On 5 October 2006 a bill of indictment charged Shuvalov with the aggravated offence of demanding a large bribe (over EEK 300,000). A 6 October press release announced that the case had reached court and recited the prosecution’s version as established facts: Shuvalov had demanded a large bribe through an intermediary, promised favourable decisions and acquittal, and accepted EEK 200,000; he had thereby “committed” the offence. Further media comments by V. repeated the amounts, the instalment arrangement and the claim that the initiative had come from the judge.

At trial Shuvalov twice sought V.’s removal, arguing she had conducted a hostile public campaign that portrayed him as guilty. The courts refused, citing legitimate public interest in a case involving a judge and finding that the statements had not treated him as convicted. The prosecution later dropped the “demanding” element and sought conviction only for an attempted offence. In January 2008 Shuvalov was convicted of attempting to accept a bribe of EEK 200,000 and sentenced to three-and-a-half years’ imprisonment; appeals failed.

In parallel, Shuvalov brought an administrative claim for non-pecuniary damage, alleging that the prosecutor’s statements had violated his presumption of innocence and private life by presenting the prosecution case as proven fact. Domestic courts dismissed the claim, holding that the information had been released lawfully to meet high public interest, that wording such as “suspected” had been used, and that later statements merely summarised the indictment. The Supreme Court declined to hear further appeals.

These events formed the basis of Shuvalov’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that his presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention had been infringed by the public statements of the prosecuting authorities.

The case of Shuvalov v. Estonia (applications nos. 39820/08 and 14942/09) concerns an Estonian judge, Ardi Shuvalov, who alleged that public statements by the prosecutor during bribery proceedings against him infringed his presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention.

In January 2006, D. told the security police that his partner N. D. passed 200,000 EEK to N. in February 2006 and a further 400,000 EEK on 6 April; N. was immediately arrested. Under police instructions, N. then met Shuvalov the same day and handed over 200,000 EEK. Shuvalov was arrested as a suspect, surrendered the money the next day and was released.

On television she stated that suspicion arose when the person from whom the bribe was demanded contacted the police and that the simulation had succeeded. Newspapers quoted her as saying the case was not fabricated or provoked, proceedings had begun in January on “very specific information,” the applicant himself had demanded the money, he had been “very careful,” and the main evidence had already been gathered.

The Prosecutor’s Office replied that it was obliged to inform the public of a matter of high interest, had used the language of suspicion, and had based later statements on the indictment. Domestic courts rejected the claim. They held that a judge’s alleged bribery generated legitimate public interest justifying limited, objective information to counter rumours; the statements consistently referred to suspicion or charges, expressed no opinion on guilt, and did not exceed what was necessary.

The ECHR case of Shuvalov v. Estonia (apps. 39820/08 and 14942/09) concerns Estonian judge Ardi Shuvalov’s claim that prosecutors’ public statements during his bribery investigation and trial violated his presumption of innocence (Art. 6 § 2).

Police opened a bribery investigation, authorizing surveillance of N. and later Shuvalov, plus simulated offenses.

The judge’s identity soon became public. Prosecutor V. was quoted on TV and in newspapers stating that suspicion arose from the alleged victim’s report, the simulation succeeded, the investigation began in January on specific information, and it was not fabricated or provoked. Later comments asserted Shuvalov himself demanded the money and was “very careful.”

It presented alleged facts as established (proposal via N., installment payments, acceptance of EEK 200,000) and stated he breached rule-of-law principles by using his official position, damaging the reputation of Estonian law-enforcement. A 6 October press release titled “The judge’s criminal case has arrived at the court” repeated that he demanded a large bribe, promised favorable decisions and acquittal, accepted EEK 200,000, and committed the offence under the Penal Code.

During the trial V. was quoted detailing the charges, amounts, and names. Shuvalov’s requests to recuse V. for a “hostile campaign” presenting him as guilty were denied; courts found the articles did not treat him as convicted and that public interest in a judge’s case was justified.

The office replied that it had a duty to inform the public of a high-interest case involving a judge, used the word “suspected,” limited details, and later based statements on the indictment. Administrative courts dismissed the claim, holding that elevated public interest justified the communications, the information was objective and necessary to prevent rumors, no opinion on guilt was expressed, and there was no excessive interference. Higher courts upheld this.

These official statements and releases—made before a final conviction and using language presenting the prosecution’s version as fact—are the core facts underlying the alleged violation of the presumption of innocence.

The applicant, an Uzbek national born in 1974, left Uzbekistan for Russia in September 2009 in search of work and arrived in Kazan on 8 September. On 24 December 2009 Uzbek authorities charged him with attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, membership of the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan and dissemination of subversive materials; an arrest warrant was issued and he was placed on an international wanted list.

Russian police arrested him on 30 March 2010 at a migration office where he was applying for a temporary residence permit, relying on the wanted-list entry and the Minsk Convention. Uzbek authorities immediately confirmed that he remained wanted. A prosecutor applied for detention pending extradition. On 1 April 2010 the Vakhitovskiy District Court of Kazan upheld the arrest and authorised detention until 8 May 2010, citing the applicant’s foreign nationality, lack of a permanent address, the foreign warrant, the fact that he had fled justice, and the consequent risk of flight or further offending (Articles 97, 99, 108 and 466 of the Code of Criminal Procedure).

On 15 April 2010 the applicant sought asylum. Uzbekistan formally requested extradition on 4 May. The District Court extended detention to 8 July (7 May order) and then, without waiting for that period to expire, issued a fresh order on 25 May extending it to 30 September. The applicant regarded an appeal against the 7 May order as impracticable.

On 4 August the Russian Prosecutor General authorised extradition. Notified on 23 August, the applicant sought judicial review, arguing that pending asylum proceedings suspended enforcement and that he faced a real risk of torture if returned. Asylum was refused on 26 August and he appealed that decision. On 20 September the Tatarstan Supreme Court dismissed the extradition challenge, treating the ill-treatment allegations as mere assumptions and noting that asylum had been sought only after criminal proceedings had begun in Uzbekistan. The Russian Supreme Court later quashed that judgment and remitted the case.

Meanwhile, on 30 September the District Court extended detention to 30 November, informing the applicant of his right to participate in any appeal. His lawyer appealed on 4 October, contesting the risk of flight, citing the still-pending refugee application and alleging a breach of the seven-day rule for extension requests; no request for personal attendance was made. On 8 October the Tatarstan Supreme Court, after hearing only the prosecutor, upheld the extension. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer was present, although the Government asserted they had been notified of the hearing.

Detention was further extended to 30 January 2011. On re-examination, the Tatarstan Supreme Court on 10 December 2010 annulled the extradition order, relying on international reports, the Court’s own case-law and the systematic use of torture against persons accused of religious or extremist offences in Uzbekistan. The applicant was released the same day. On 3 February 2011 the Russian Supreme Court upheld the annulment, additionally noting a mismatch between the Uzbek charges and corresponding Russian offences, the fact that extradition had been authorised before a final asylum decision, and the absence of any diplomatic assurances.

These facts concern alleged violations of Article 3 (risk of ill-treatment upon return) and Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 (lawfulness of extradition detention and adequacy of its judicial review, including the applicant’s absence from the 8 October appeal hearing). Domestic law (CCrP Article 376, as interpreted by the Constitutional Court) required notification of appeal hearings and provision of legal assistance if requested, and applied equally to detention appeals.

**Case of Scoppola v. Italy (No. 3) (Application no. 126/05), ECHR Grand Chamber judgment of 22 May 2012**

Franco Scoppola, an Italian national born in 1940 and later held in compulsory residence at a hospital in Parma, alleged that his automatic, permanent disenfranchisement after conviction violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections). The application was lodged on 16 December 2004.

On 2 September 1999, following a violent family dispute, Scoppola killed his wife and injured one of his sons. He was arrested the next day. After investigation, he faced charges of murder, attempted murder, family ill-treatment, and unauthorized firearm possession. He elected the summary procedure. On 24 November 2000, the Rome preliminary hearings judge convicted him on all counts. Life imprisonment was indicated, but the summary procedure produced a 30-year sentence plus a lifetime ban from public office under Article 29 of the Criminal Code. The judge described the attack: Scoppola first tried to strangle his wife with the cable of the telephone she had used to call police; when she and the children fled down the stairs, he fired multiple shots at her at close range and at a son who had returned to help her. Aggravating factors included the crime against his own family, triggered by a trifling incident (children allegedly breaking his mobile phone). The judge rejected a clean record as mitigation, citing the applicant’s lack of remorse, denial of some acts, and blame of his family for “rebelling” against his authority. Witnesses described a 20-year history of insults, physical violence, and threats (including with weapons) against his wife and children.

The Public Prosecutor and applicant appealed. On 10 January 2002 the Rome Assize Court of Appeal imposed life imprisonment, confirming the aggravating and mitigating assessments. The Court of Cassation dismissed a further appeal on 20 January 2003. The life sentence automatically triggered a lifetime ban from public office (Article 28–29 Criminal Code), which under section 2 of Presidential Decree no. 223/1967 produced permanent loss of the right to vote. The ban was not mentioned in the sentencing judgments.

On 2 April 2003 the electoral committee removed Scoppola from the electoral roll. He complained on 30 June 2004, citing *Hirst v. United Kingdom (no. 2)* and arguing incompatibility with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. After rejection he appealed to the Rome Court of Appeal, contending that the automatic consequence of the life sentence and ban left no judicial assessment of proportionality or competing interests. On 29 November 2004 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, distinguishing *Hirst* on the ground that Italian law applied the measure only to particularly heavy sentences (including life), not to every custodial term. Scoppola’s cassation appeal—arguing the ban was an automatic ancillary penalty unrelated to the specific offence and imposed without court discretion—was dismissed on 17 January 2006. The Court of Cassation noted that Italian law limited disenfranchisement to sentences of at least three years (five-year ban) or five years/life (lifetime ban).

In a separate application (*Scoppola v. Italy (no. 2)*), the Grand Chamber found violations of Articles 6 and 7 concerning the life sentence and directed replacement by a term not exceeding 30 years. On 28 April 2010 the Court of Cassation therefore set the sentence at 30 years. A 30-year term still automatically entailed a lifetime ban from public office and thus permanent disenfranchisement.

Under Italian law a ban from public office is an ancillary penalty that forfeits voting rights. It applies automatically to any imprisonment of three years or more (temporary) or five years or more/life (permanent), and independently to certain listed offences (e.g., embezzlement, extortion, perjury, abuse of office). Rehabilitation (Articles 178–179 Criminal Code) can terminate ancillary penalties after three years of genuine good conduct following completion of the main sentence; early-release provisions also exist. The Chamber of the Second Section found a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 on 18 January 2011. Italy requested referral; the Grand Chamber accepted the case on 20 June 2011. The United Kingdom intervened.

The Court of Cassation rejected the further appeal (17 January 2006), noting that under Article 29 only sentences of at least three years trigger disenfranchisement (five years temporary for 3–<5 years; lifetime for 5+ years or life). 001-111373:
The case of Segame SA v. France (ECtHR, Application no. 4837/06, judgment of 7 June 2012) concerned a French limited company operating an art gallery in Paris. Following judicial reorganisation and compulsory liquidation ordered by the Paris Commercial Court in 1993 (terminated in 2004 after debts were cleared), the tax authorities audited the company's accounts for 1991–1993. They issued supplementary assessments for the fixed-rate tax on sales of precious metals, jewellery, works of art, collectors’ items and antiques (Articles 302 bis A–E, later 150 V bis–sexies of the General Tax Code). This 7% tax applied to sales exceeding a threshold (with reductions in a narrow band) and extended to intra-Community sales. The company was also charged late-payment interest plus a fine equal to 100% of the unpaid tax (Article 1788 ter/1770 octies GTC). A January 1995 demand sought FRF 15,927,514 (EUR 2,428,133), half of which was the fine.

The company (via its administrator) complained to the Director of Revenue in December 1997, seeking relief. It argued the tax was equivalent to VAT (contrary to Council Directives 77/388/EEC and 94/5/EC) or to a capital-gains tax amounting to an export restriction or internal taxation prohibited by Articles 34 and 95 of the Treaty of Rome. It further contended that the fines, akin to criminal convictions under the Convention, required imposition by a court. The Director rejected the complaint in June 1998, stating the tax was neither VAT nor a barrier to free movement (as it applied equally to domestic and Community sales) and citing Bendenoun v. France to confirm administrative penalties were compatible with Article 6 § 1 if subject to judicial supervision.

In July 1998 the company sued in the Paris Administrative Court for exemption from the tax and penalties on the same grounds. The court dismissed the action in November 2004. On the Article 6 § 1 complaint it held that tax courts possessed full review of the facts and their legal classification by the authorities. They could therefore uphold the statutory penalty or cancel it entirely if the infringement was not established, but they could not modulate the amount to the circumstances of the case. Article 6 § 1 did not require such a power of adjustment.

An appeal followed to the Paris Administrative Court of Appeal. In the interim, Ordinance No. 2005-1512 of 7 December 2005 reduced the fine from 100% to 25%. The authorities consequently reduced the fine by EUR 910,550 and the tax itself by EUR 28,735 (calculation error). The Court of Appeal, in November 2006, noted the reductions, slightly lowered one artwork valuation, and otherwise upheld the first-instance judgment. It rejected the Community-law arguments and, on Article 6, reiterated that full jurisdiction existed through review of facts and classification; a single statutory rate need not be adjustable downward.

The Conseil d’État dismissed the subsequent cassation appeal in June 2008. On the fine it observed that the 2005 ordinance had already made the rate proportionate, and that the tax court, after full review of facts and classification, either applied the statutory rate or cancelled the penalty. This constituted the “full jurisdiction” required by Article 6 § 1; the Convention did not oblige a court to apply a rate lower than that fixed by law.

Parallel proceedings challenged the ministerial interpretation of the tax base (selling price including commission, as set out in administrative documents of 1989 and 1993) as an ultra-vires exercise of legislative power reserved to Parliament, and the collection regulations as both ultra vires and insufficiently clear (invoking Article 7 of the Convention). The Conseil d’État rejected both sets of appeals in 2006, holding that the statute implicitly required inclusion of all purchaser costs and that the regulations merely implemented collection procedures without overstepping authority. Article 7 could not be invoked to quash the refusal to revoke the regulations.

French administrative courts in tax matters normally enjoy full jurisdiction to cancel assessments and penalties or to substitute their own figures within statutory limits; where multiple rates exist they may select the appropriate one according to the taxpayer’s conduct. The Conseil d’État consistently held that even a single-rate penalty satisfied Article 6 provided the court could review the facts and legal classification and then apply or refuse the penalty. (The Court of Cassation, by contrast, required an independent assessment of proportionality of both the principle and the quantum of certain other tax fines.) The Constitutional Council later confirmed the constitutionality of comparable graduated surcharges, emphasising that judicial review of classification already ensured individualisation.

These facts formed the core of the company’s complaint that it had been denied access to a court possessing full jurisdiction over a tax penalty of a criminal character.

**Case Summary: Segame SA v. France (ECtHR, Application no. 4837/06, Judgment of 7 June 2012, final 7 September 2012)**

Segame SA, a French limited company operating an art gallery in Paris, was placed in judicial reorganisation and then compulsory liquidation by the Paris Commercial Court in 1993; the liquidation ended in 2004. Between October 1993 and April 1994 the French tax authorities audited its accounts for 1991–1993 and issued supplementary assessments for the fixed-rate tax on precious metals, jewellery, works of art, collectors’ items and antiques (Articles 302 bis A–E, later 150 V bis–sexies of the General Tax Code). The tax applied to sales (including in other EC Member States) above a threshold, at 7 % of value, borne by the seller but paid by an intermediary or the buyer. The company was also charged late-payment interest and a statutory fine equal to 100 % of the unpaid tax (Article 1788 ter / later 1770 octies). A January 1995 demand totalled FRF 15.9 million (approx. EUR 2.43 million), of which the fine accounted for half.

The company (via its administrator) complained to the Director of Revenue in December 1997, arguing that the tax resembled VAT (contrary to EC Directives 77/388 and 94/5) or a capital-gains tax equivalent to a prohibited export restriction or internal tax (Articles 34 and 95 of the Treaty of Rome), and that the fine was a criminal penalty that should have been imposed by a court. The complaint was rejected in June 1998.

In July 1998 the company sued in the Paris Administrative Court for exemption from the tax and penalties on the same grounds. The court dismissed the action in November 2004. On the Article 6 § 1 point it held that tax courts had full review of facts and legal classification and could either apply the statutory penalty or cancel it entirely if the infringement was not established, but could not modulate the amount; Article 6 § 1 did not require such modulation when the law prescribed a single rate.

The company appealed to the Paris Administrative Court of Appeal. In December 2005 an ordinance reduced the statutory fine from 100 % to 25 %. The authorities later granted partial reductions for a calculation error and the lowered rate. In November 2006 the Court of Appeal noted the reductions, made a minor adjustment to the valuation of one work, and otherwise upheld the lower court. It rejected the Community-law challenges and, on Article 6 § 1, reiterated that full jurisdiction existed without the power to apply a rate below the single statutory figure.

The company appealed on points of law to the Conseil d’État, repeating the Community-law and Article 6 arguments and stressing the court’s inability to scale the fine to the seriousness of the conduct. The Conseil d’État dismissed the appeal in June 2008. It observed that the 2005 ordinance had already reduced the rate to 25 % and that the tax court, after full review of facts and classification, could only uphold or cancel the statutory surcharge; Article 6 § 1 did not require the court to apply a lower rate when the legislation fixed a single rate.

Separately, in 2005 the company challenged before the Conseil d’État ministerial interpretations of the tax base (selling price including commission) as ultra vires and lacking parliamentary authority. After the 2005 Budget Amendment Act incorporated the rules into statute, the Conseil d’État rejected the challenges in February 2006, holding that the law implicitly required inclusion of all purchaser costs. Parallel challenges to collection regulations (as exceeding the 1976 enabling law and violating Article 7 legality of offences and penalties) were rejected in May 2006; the Conseil d’État found the regulations merely implemented the statute and that Article 7 could not be invoked to quash the refusal to revoke them.

The proceedings therefore centred on whether the administrative tax courts possessed “full jurisdiction” under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in respect of a fixed-rate fiscal penalty of a criminal character, given their inability to reduce the statutory percentage to reflect individual circumstances, together with subsidiary questions of compatibility with EC law and the principle of legality.

**Case Summary: Segame SA v. France (ECHR, App. No. 4837/06, 7 June 2012)**

Segame SA, a French limited company operating an art gallery in Paris, entered judicial reorganization in September 1993 and compulsory liquidation in November 1993 (proceedings terminated in December 2004 after debts were cleared). From October 1993 to April 1994, tax authorities audited its accounts for 1991–1993 and issued supplementary assessments for a fixed-rate tax on sales of jewellery, works of art, collectors’ items and antiques (General Tax Code Arts. 302 bis A–E, later 150 V bis–sexies). The tax applied to sales above a threshold (including those in other EEC states), was borne by the seller (or intermediary), and could be opted out of in favour of capital-gains rules with proof of acquisition. Additional late-payment interest and a fine equal to 100% of unpaid tax (Art. 1788 ter, later 1770 octies) were imposed, producing a total demand of FRF 15,927,514 (EUR 2,428,133), half of which was the fine.

In December 1997 the company’s administrator sought relief from the Director of Revenue, arguing the tax equated to VAT (contrary to Council Directives 77/388/EEC and 94/5/EC) or a prohibited capital-gains/export measure (Arts. 34 and 95 of the Treaty of Rome), and that the fines, being criminal in nature under the Convention, required imposition by a court. The request was rejected in June 1998; the Director held the tax was neither VAT nor a barrier to free movement and cited *Bendenoun v. France* (1994) as confirming that administrative penalties are compatible with Article 6 § 1 provided they are subject to judicial supervision.

In July 1998 the company brought proceedings in the Paris Administrative Court seeking exemption from the tax and penalties on the same grounds. The court dismissed the claim in November 2004. It held that tax courts possess full review of the facts and of the authorities’ legal classification; they may therefore uphold the statutory penalty or cancel it entirely if the breach is not established, but they cannot modulate a single-rate fine to the circumstances of the case. Article 6 § 1 therefore did not require a power of adjustment.

An appeal was lodged with the Paris Administrative Court of Appeal. Meanwhile, Ordinance No. 2005-1512 of 7 December 2005 reduced the fine rate from 100% to 25%; the authorities subsequently reduced the fine by EUR 910,550 and the underlying tax by EUR 28,735 for a calculation error. In November 2006 the Court of Appeal noted the reductions, made a minor adjustment to the valuation of one work, and otherwise upheld the first-instance judgment. It rejected the EU-law arguments and confirmed that full jurisdiction under Article 6 § 1 existed even though the court could not reduce a single statutory rate.

The company appealed on points of law to the Conseil d’État, repeating the Community-law objections and the Article 6 § 1 complaint that the court lacked power to scale the fine to the seriousness of the conduct. In June 2008 the Conseil d’État dismissed the appeal. After noting the legislative reduction to 25%, it held that a tax court, having fully reviewed the facts and classification, may only apply or cancel the statutory rate; Article 6 § 1 does not require a power to impose a lower rate when the legislature has prescribed a single rate.

In parallel proceedings the company challenged, before the Conseil d’État, the Minister’s interpretation (in administrative documents) that the tax base was the selling price including commission, and the Prime Minister’s implicit refusal to revoke collection regulations issued under the 1976 enabling law. It argued that only Parliament could determine the tax base and that the collection rules were insufficiently clear, contrary to Article 7 of the Convention. Both challenges were rejected in 2006: the Conseil held that the legislation implicitly required inclusion of all purchaser costs, so the Minister had not created new rules; the regulations merely implemented collection procedures and did not overstep authority. The Article 7 argument was held inapplicable.

The central alleged violation was therefore the lack of access to a court possessing “full jurisdiction” under Article 6 § 1, specifically the inability of the administrative courts to modulate a fixed-rate tax penalty once the facts and legal classification had been reviewed. Subsidiary issues concerned compatibility of the tax itself with Community law and the alleged unclarity of the collection regime under Article 7.
