The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered its judgment in Szerdahelyi v. Hungary (Application no. 30385/07) on 17 January 2012 (final 17 April 2012). The case originated in an application lodged on 4 June 2007 by Dr Szabolcs Szerdahelyi, a Hungarian national born in 1943 and resident in Budapest. He was represented by counsel. After his death on 13 July 2009, his son and sole heir, Szabolcs Szerdahelyi, continued the proceedings.

The applicant complained of interference with his right to peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the Convention. On 24 November 2006 he notified the Budapest Police Department, as required by the Assembly Act 1989, of his intention to hold a demonstration on 9 December 2006 on Kossuth Square in front of the Hungarian Parliament. On 26 November 2006 the police refused to process the notification. They stated that on 23 October 2006 they had themselves declared the square a “security operational zone” of indefinite duration because of violent events in Budapest in September 2006. The area therefore fell outside their jurisdiction to permit or prohibit assemblies.

The Budapest Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s request for judicial review on 6 December 2006, holding that the police had taken no decision on the merits that could be reviewed. Subsequent complaints to senior police authorities were rejected. On 19 December 2006 the applicant brought an action challenging both the original designation of the security zone and later police decisions. On 12 February 2007 the National Police Department ordered the Budapest police to replace the indefinite measure with one of limited duration. The Regional Court nevertheless dismissed the applicant’s action on 5 March 2007, ruling that the proceedings concerned only the police’s finding of lack of competence and did not permit review of the underlying security-zone decision.

Further litigation followed. On 18 March 2008 the Regional Court quashed two police decisions and remitted the matter; the Supreme Court later quashed that ruling and remitted the case again. Proceedings were interrupted by the applicant’s death and resumed only after his son joined them as successor in 2011. The Government maintained that the pending litigation concerned the original security-zone designation itself.

A parallel set of proceedings initiated by another individual, Mr K., directly challenged the legality of the security-zone measure. After repeated administrative rejections, the Regional Court in 2010 quashed the relevant decisions for failing to demonstrate the necessity and proportionality of maintaining the zone after November 2006 and for not considering a less restrictive alternative (fencing only the immediate vicinity of Parliament). In April 2011 the Budapest police commander partly upheld Mr K.’s complaint, acknowledging that the proportionality of the measure had been successfully contested.

The core facts therefore centre on the police’s use of an open-ended “security operational zone” to place Kossuth Square outside the ordinary legal regime governing assemblies, thereby preventing the applicant from holding his notified demonstration and generating protracted, inconclusive domestic litigation that never produced a merits review of the restriction itself.

The European Court of Human Rights case Szerdahelyi v. Hungary (Application no. 30385/07) concerned an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of peaceful assembly. Dr Szabolcs Szerdahelyi, a Hungarian national born in 1943 and residing in Budapest, notified the Budapest Police Department on 24 November 2006 of his intention to organise a demonstration on 9 December 2006 on Kossuth Square in front of Parliament, as required under Hungary’s Assembly Act 1989. On 26 November 2006 the police refused to process the notification. They explained that on 23 October 2006 they had themselves declared the square a “security operational zone” of indefinite duration because of the violent unrest that had occurred in Budapest in September 2006. As a result, the area fell outside their jurisdiction to prohibit or authorise demonstrations. The Budapest Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s request for judicial review on 6 December 2006, holding that no decision on the merits had ever been taken by the administrative authorities and that therefore no review was possible.

The applicant lodged further complaints. On 11 December 2006 the Deputy Head of the National Police Department rejected his challenge. He then brought an action before the Budapest Regional Court attacking both the original 23 October 2006 designation and the later police decisions. Subsequent internal reviews produced mixed results: on 12 February 2007 the Deputy Head of the National Police instructed the Budapest Police to replace the indefinite measure with one of limited duration, but on 5 March 2007 the Regional Court again dismissed the applicant’s action, emphasising that the proceedings concerned only the police’s finding of non-competence and did not amount to a review of the original security-zone declaration. Later court rulings quashed certain decisions and remitted the matter, yet the litigation remained unresolved when the applicant died on 13 July 2009. His son and sole heir continued both the domestic proceedings and the Strasbourg application.

Parallel litigation initiated by another individual, Mr K., directly challenged the lawfulness of the security-zone designation itself. After several rounds of administrative and judicial review, the Budapest Regional Court on 11 November 2010 quashed the police decisions, noting that they contained no concrete elements demonstrating the necessity or proportionality of maintaining the zone after 22 November 2006 and that they had failed to consider a less restrictive alternative such as fencing off only the immediate vicinity of Parliament. In resumed proceedings the Budapest Police Commander partly accepted Mr K.’s complaint on 4 April 2011, acknowledging that, in the absence of contrary evidence, the proportionality of the measure had been successfully contested.

The applicant’s complaint therefore centred on the fact that an indefinitely maintained security zone, never subjected to a proper merits review in his own case, had rendered it impossible for the authorities even to consider his notification of an intended peaceful assembly. The resulting legal vacuum, combined with the later judicial findings that the zone lacked adequate justification, formed the core of the alleged interference with the right to peaceful assembly.

The case of Szerdahelyi v. Hungary (Application no. 30385/07) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Hungarian national Dr Szabolcs Szerdahelyi, who alleged that the authorities frustrated his right to peaceful assembly. The applicant notified the Budapest Police Department on 24 November 2006 of his intention to organise a demonstration on 9 December 2006 on Kossuth Square in front of Parliament, as required by the 1989 Assembly Act.

On 26 November 2006 the police refused to process the notification. They stated that on 23 October 2006 they had declared the area an indefinite “security operational zone” (biztonsági műveleti terület) because of violent events in Budapest in September 2006. This placed the square outside their jurisdiction to permit or prohibit demonstrations. On 6 December 2006 the Budapest Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s request for judicial review, holding that no decision on the merits had been taken by the administrative authorities and therefore no review was possible.

The applicant pursued further remedies. On 11 December 2006 the Deputy Head of the National Police Department dismissed his complaint. He then filed an action on 19 December 2006 challenging both the original 23 October declaration and the later decision. On 11 January 2007 the Head of Budapest Police rejected a renewed complaint; this was partly reversed on 12 February 2007, when the Deputy Head of the National Police instructed that the indefinite measure be replaced by one of definite duration. The Regional Court nevertheless dismissed the applicant’s ensuing action on 5 March 2007, stating that the proceedings concerned only the police’s finding of non-competence and did not review the original security-zone declaration.

Litigation continued. On 18 March 2008 the Regional Court quashed certain decisions and remitted the case; the Supreme Court later quashed that ruling and remitted it again. The applicant died on 13 July 2009; his son and heir joined the still-pending domestic proceedings.

A parallel challenge brought by Mr K. against the same security-zone declaration produced further relevant facts. After successive administrative rejections, the Budapest Regional Court on 11 November 2010 quashed the police decisions. It found they contained no concrete elements establishing the necessity or proportionality of maintaining the zone after 22 November 2006 and had failed to consider whether merely fencing off Parliament’s immediate vicinity would have been sufficient. On 4 April 2011 the Budapest Police Commander partly upheld Mr K.’s complaint, acknowledging that the proportionality of the measure had been successfully challenged.

These events meant the applicant’s planned demonstration never took place. The police’s refusal to process his notification, combined with the courts’ initial inability to review the underlying indefinite security-zone declaration, formed the core of the alleged interference with freedom of assembly. The applicant’s case before the Strasbourg Court was communicated in 2011; his son continued the application after his death.

The case of Vulakh and Others v. Russia (no. 33468/03) arose from an application by four relatives of the late Vitaliy Eduardovich Vulakh—his parents and two children—alleging violations of the presumption of innocence (in respect of Vitaliy) and of their own property rights.

Vitaliy was suspected of leading a criminal syndicate responsible for multiple murders, robberies and acts of property destruction. On 25 March 2002 three alleged members (S., N. and K.) were arrested. Upon learning of the arrests, Vitaliy shot his fiancée and then took his own life. Criminal proceedings against him were discontinued on 20 June 2002 solely because of his death.

On 3 October 2002 the Krasnodar Regional Court convicted S., N. and K. of serious offences and imposed lengthy prison sentences. The judgment expressly identified Vitaliy as the gang’s leader, stated that he had funded the group, purchased vehicles and paid members to commit crimes, and recorded that he had ordered the murder of a business competitor. Civil claims lodged by several victims were deferred to separate proceedings. Vitaliy’s father sought to appeal the criminal judgment, complaining that neither he nor defence counsel had been notified of the discontinuation or given an opportunity to study the file or plead innocence. He was told he had no standing because he was not a party. The Supreme Court of the Russian Federation later upheld the convictions.

On 5 March 2003 a notary issued the four applicants a certificate of succession in respect of Vitaliy’s house. Shortly afterwards the victims and a private company sued the applicants and the Kurganinskiy dairy factory (of which Vitaliy had been a minority shareholder) for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. On 4 September 2003 the Kurganinskiy District Court found against them. Relying on the criminal judgment, it held that Vitaliy had organised an armed gang and directed the commission of the crimes; that he, S., N. and K. were jointly liable; and that the applicants, as heirs who had accepted the inheritance, were liable for his debts under Article 1175 of the Civil Code. The court treated Vitaliy’s share in the dairy factory (valued at more than 18 million roubles) as part of the estate and awarded substantial portions of it to the claimants, ordering immediate enforcement.

The applicants appealed, arguing that Vitaliy had never been convicted by a court and therefore remained presumed innocent, that there was consequently no legal basis for joint liability of the heirs, and that a company could not be held liable for the personal debts of a shareholder. On 18 September 2003 the Krasnodar Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the final criminal conviction had established Vitaliy’s responsibility for the damage even though proceedings against him had been discontinued.

Domestic law required discontinuation of proceedings against a deceased person unless continuation was necessary for rehabilitation. Civil-law rules made heirs jointly liable for a testator’s debts in proportion to their shares, while a criminal judgment bound a civil court only as to whether the acts in question had been committed by the person concerned. A later Moscow City Court decision had criticised the practice of naming untried individuals as accomplices in a conviction.

These events formed the factual core of the applicants’ complaints that the courts had treated Vitaliy as guilty without a trial, thereby also stripping the heirs of inherited assets.

The case of Vulakh and Others v. Russia (application no. 33468/03) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by four Russian nationals—the parents and two children of the late Vitaliy Eduardovich Vulakh—who alleged a violation of the presumption of innocence in respect of their deceased relative and a violation of their own property rights.

A criminal investigation was opened into multiple murders, robberies and acts of property destruction attributed to an organised criminal syndicate of which Vitaliy Vulakh was suspected of being the leader. On 25 March 2002 three alleged members (S., N. and K.) were arrested. Upon learning of the arrests, Vitaliy Vulakh shot his fiancée dead and then committed suicide. On 20 June 2002 the criminal prosecution against him was discontinued solely on account of his death, pursuant to the then-applicable RSFSR Code of Criminal Procedure.

On 3 October 2002 the Krasnodar Regional Court convicted S., N. and K. of serious offences and sentenced them to lengthy terms of imprisonment. In its judgment the court expressly stated that Vitaliy Vulakh “had been the leader of the gang”, had funded its activities, had paid members to commit crimes and had instructed them to murder a business competitor. The first applicant (Vitaliy’s father) sought to appeal this judgment to the Supreme Court, complaining that neither he nor counsel had been notified of the discontinuation decision or permitted to study the file or argue innocence; a regional-court judge rejected the appeal on the ground that the father was not a party to the proceedings. The Supreme Court later upheld the convictions (2 April 2003).

Meanwhile the four applicants obtained a notarial certificate of succession in respect of Vitaliy’s house. Victims of the crimes (including G., F., B. and V., as well as a private company) then brought civil claims against the applicants and against the Kurganinskiy dairy factory, in which Vitaliy had been a minority shareholder, seeking compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. On 4 September 2003 the Kurganinskiy District Court found against the applicants. Relying directly on the statements contained in the 3 October 2002 criminal judgment (and the subsequent Supreme Court decision), it held that Vitaliy Vulakh had organised an armed gang that had committed murders and attempted murders. Invoking joint-and-several liability under the Civil Code and the rule that heirs who accept an inheritance become liable for the decedent’s debts in proportion to their shares, the court treated the applicants as having accepted Vitaliy’s 37.49 per cent interest in the dairy factory (valued at more than 18 million roubles). It therefore awarded substantial portions of that shareholding to the civil claimants and ordered immediate enforcement.

The applicants appealed, arguing that Vitaliy had never been found guilty by a court, that the presumption of innocence therefore applied, and that there was no legal basis for imposing liability on his heirs or on the company itself. On 18 September 2003 the Krasnodar Regional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the criminal convictions of the co-defendants had “established” Vitaliy Vulakh’s responsibility for the damage. Under the Code of Civil Procedure the findings of a final criminal judgment are binding in subsequent civil proceedings only as to whether the relevant acts occurred and whether they were committed by the person concerned; the domestic courts nevertheless treated the untried decedent as a co-perpetrator whose civil liability could be enforced against his estate.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints that the judicial statements imputing criminal responsibility to Vitaliy Vulakh after his death, and the subsequent attachment of inherited assets (including the company share), violated the presumption of innocence and the applicants’ property rights.

The case of Vulakh and Others v. Russia (Application no. 33468/03) was brought by four Russian nationals—the parents and two children of the late Vitaliy Eduardovich Vulakh—against the Russian Federation. The applicants alleged a violation of the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2 of the Convention) in respect of their deceased relative and a violation of their own property rights (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

A criminal investigation was opened into murders, robberies and property destruction committed by an alleged syndicate of which Vitaliy Vulakh was suspected of being the leader. On 25 March 2002 three co-suspects (S., N. and K.) were arrested. Upon learning of the arrests, Vitaliy Vulakh killed his fiancée and committed suicide. His criminal prosecution was discontinued on 20 June 2002 solely on account of his death.

On 3 October 2002 the Krasnodar Regional Court convicted the three co-suspects of serious offences and sentenced them to long prison terms. The judgment expressly described Vitaliy Vulakh as the gang’s leader who had financed the group, paid its members and ordered the murder of a business competitor. Victims (G., F., B. and V.) lodged civil claims against the convicted men; the court directed that those claims be examined separately. The first applicant attempted to appeal the criminal judgment to the Supreme Court, arguing that neither he nor his son’s counsel had been notified of the discontinuation or permitted to study the file or plead innocence. A Regional Court judge informed him that he lacked standing because he was not a party. On 2 April 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed the convicted men’s appeals and upheld the 3 October judgment.

A notary subsequently issued the four applicants a certificate of succession to Vitaliy Vulakh’s house. The same victims, together with a private company, then brought a civil action against the applicants and the Kurganinskiy dairy factory (of which Vitaliy Vulakh had been a minority shareholder) seeking pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. On 4 September 2003 the Kurganinskiy District Court found against the defendants. Relying on the 2002 criminal judgment (and its 2003 affirmation), the court treated Vitaliy Vulakh as the organiser of the armed gang that had committed the crimes, held him jointly liable with the convicted men, and concluded that his heirs were liable for his debts under Article 1175 of the Civil Code. Because the heirs had accepted the inheritance they were also deemed to have accepted his 37.49 % share in the dairy factory (valued at RUB 18 705 260). The court awarded percentages of that share to the plaintiffs and ordered immediate enforcement.

The applicants appealed, arguing that Vitaliy Vulakh had never been found guilty by a court, that he must be presumed innocent, that joint liability therefore could not attach to his heirs, and that the factory could not be held liable for its shareholders’ personal debts. On 18 September 2003 the Krasnodar Regional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the criminal conviction of the three co-defendants had established Vitaliy Vulakh’s responsibility for the damage.

Domestic law provided that criminal proceedings against a deceased person must be discontinued unless continued for rehabilitation (RSFSR Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 5 § 8). Civil-procedure rules made findings in a final criminal judgment binding only as regards whether particular acts had been committed by the person actually tried (Code of Civil Procedure, Article 61 § 4). Relevant case-law of the Moscow City Court Presidium had already criticised the naming of untried individuals as accomplices.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints that the civil courts had treated their deceased relative as guilty without a trial and had thereby deprived them of inherited property.
001-111180:
The applicant, an Uzbek national born in 1971, participated in Hizb-ut-Tahrir (HT) activities in Uzbekistan during the 1990s before moving to Russia in May 2000, leaving his wife and two children behind. He was arrested in Russia in June 2001 on drug charges, convicted, and released in August 2004. He then settled in Saratov, formed a relationship with a Belarusian national (then residing unlawfully), and had two children with her (born 2006 and 2008).

In March 2006, Uzbek authorities charged him in absentia with attempting to overthrow the constitutional order (UCC Art. 159-3) and later added charges of forming a criminal group, producing/disseminating materials threatening national security, and involvement in banned extremist organisations (UCC Arts. 242-1, 244(1)-3, 244(2)-1), all linked to his alleged role as an HT founder, manager, and financial supporter. He was placed on national and international wanted lists.

Arrested in Saratov on 26 February 2010 as a person wanted by Uzbekistan, he was held in remand. Uzbekistan formally requested extradition on 8 March 2010, offering assurances that he would not be re-extradited without Russian consent, would be prosecuted only for the requested offences, and could leave after any sentence. Russian authorities (FMS, FSB, MFA) found no bars to extradition; the FSB described him as a confirmed HT functionary. The Deputy Prosecutor General issued an extradition order on 9 August 2010, mapping the charges to equivalent Russian offences (RCC Arts. 210, 278) whose limitation periods had not expired and noting that classification differences were immaterial.

The applicant sought judicial review, citing a real risk of torture and ill-treatment because of his HT links and citing international reports of widespread torture in Uzbekistan. The Saratov Regional Court initially upheld the order (16 September 2010), relying on Uzbek assurances of compliance with procedural norms and the FMS’s refusal of refugee status. The Supreme Court quashed this on 17 November 2010 and remitted. On 28 December 2010 the Regional Court annulled the extradition order, citing errors in the comparative analysis of offences and the fact that refugee-status review remained pending, rendering the order premature under the Refugees Act. The applicant was released in court; the Supreme Court confirmed the annulment on 4 March 2011 and extradition proceedings ended.

He was detained solely with a view to extradition from 26 February to 28 December 2010. A district court authorised initial detention (to 6 April 2010) under CCrP Arts. 108 and 466, citing the gravity of the equivalent Russian charges, his lack of registered residence, and flight risk. Extensions followed: to 25 August (1 April), to 25 November (23 August, justified by pending extradition review and “particular complexity”), to 17 December (Supreme Court, 17 November), and to 25 February 2011 (22 November). Appeals against the orders were dismissed; requests for house arrest were refused. He was released only after the extradition order itself was quashed.

On 17/24 March 2010 the applicant applied for refugee status, invoking a well-founded fear of persecution and torture on account of his HT membership and supporting the claim with international reports. The regional FMS refused (1 July 2010), finding he had left for economic reasons, that the charges were ordinary (not political) offences, and that the application was delayed. The central FMS upheld the refusal (14 September 2010), stressing HT’s designation as a terrorist organisation in Russia and the applicant’s late claim after learning of Uzbek prosecutions of HT members. Judicial review by the Basmanny District Court (24 December 2010) and Moscow City Court (18 May 2011) confirmed the refusals, noting that he had never distanced himself from HT, had first raised fears only after arrest, and was fleeing prosecution rather than persecution; Uzbek constitutional guarantees were also cited. Temporary asylum was refused in March 2011.

On 5 July 2011 UNHCR independently recognised the applicant as a mandate refugee, concluding that he had a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of religion and imputed political opinion and that return would expose him to torture or other ill-treatment.

These facts underpin the complaints of a real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment upon return (despite diplomatic assurances and the eventual annulment of the extradition order) and of unlawful/unjustified Article 5 detention pending extradition.

The case of Khodzhamberdiyev v. Russia (Application no. 64809/10) concerns an Uzbek national, born in 1971, who had lived in Russia since 2000. In the 1990s he participated in Hizb-ut-Tahrir (HT), later banned in both Uzbekistan and Russia. After moving to Russia he was convicted there on drug charges and released in 2004; he subsequently formed a family in Saratov.

In 2006 Uzbek authorities charged him in absentia with attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, organising a criminal group and participating in a banned extremist organisation, all linked to his earlier HT activity. He was placed on national and international wanted lists. On 26 February 2010 he was arrested in Saratov. Uzbekistan formally requested extradition on 8 March 2010, furnishing diplomatic assurances that he would be treated in accordance with Uzbek procedure, would not face additional charges and would be free to leave after serving any sentence.

Russian prosecutors conducted an extradition check. On 9 August 2010 the Deputy Prosecutor General authorised extradition, finding the acts also constituted offences under the Russian Criminal Code, that limitation periods had not expired and that the applicant, an undocumented Uzbek national, enjoyed no statutory protection against removal. The applicant immediately sought judicial review, invoking a real risk of torture and ill-treatment in Uzbekistan because of his HT connections and citing international reports of systematic abuse of such suspects. The Saratov Regional Court initially upheld the order, relying on the Uzbek assurances and the contemporaneous refusal of refugee status. The Supreme Court quashed that decision on 17 November 2010. On 28 December 2010 the Regional Court annulled the extradition order on two grounds: inconsistencies in the comparative legal characterisation of the offences and the fact that refugee-status review proceedings remained pending, rendering the order premature under the Refugees Act. The applicant was released in court. The Supreme Court confirmed the annulment on 4 March 2011, rendering extradition legally impossible.

Throughout this period the applicant was held in remand prison no. 64/1 solely for the purpose of extradition. Detention was first authorised by the Kirovskiy District Court on 26 February 2010 until 6 April under Articles 108 and 466 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It was extended on 1 April to 25 August, on 23 August to 25 November, and thereafter by both the Supreme Court and the District Court until February 2011. The courts repeatedly cited the seriousness of the charges, the applicant’s lack of registered residence, and the “complexity” created by his judicial challenges. He was released on 28 December 2010 when the extradition order itself was quashed.

In parallel the applicant applied for refugee status in March 2010, expressly citing fear of torture linked to HT membership. The Federal Migration Service refused the claim, finding that he had left Uzbekistan for economic reasons, that the charges were ordinary criminal offences rather than political persecution, and that he had delayed applying until after his arrest. Domestic courts upheld the refusal, emphasising that he had never distanced himself from HT and had not sought protection when he first learned of the Uzbek investigation. In July 2011 UNHCR independently recognised him as a mandate refugee on grounds of well-founded fear of religious and imputed political persecution and of torture.

These facts form the basis of the complaints of a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 if returned to Uzbekistan, of arbitrary and excessively prolonged detention contrary to Article 5, and of the absence of an effective domestic remedy capable of examining those risks.

The applicant, an Uzbek national born in 1971, lived in Uzbekistan in the 1990s and participated in Hizb-ut-Tahrir (HT), a pan-Islamic group later banned as terrorist in Russia. He relocated to Russia in May 2000 for work, leaving a wife and two children in Andizhan. Arrested in Russia in June 2001 on drug charges, he was convicted and imprisoned until August 2004. He then settled in Saratov, formed a relationship with a Belarusian national (herself irregularly present), and fathered two children born in 2006 and 2008.

In March 2006 the Uzbek authorities charged him in absentia with attempting to overthrow the constitutional order (UCC Art. 159-3). Further charges followed in 2007 for organising a criminal group, producing and circulating materials threatening national security, and leading or participating in banned extremist organisations (UCC Arts. 242-1, 244(1)-3 and 244(2)-1), all linked to his HT role as a founding manager and financier who had created sub-groups and disseminated literature. An international arrest warrant was issued.

Russian police arrested him in Saratov on 26 February 2010. Uzbekistan formally requested extradition on 8 March 2010, supplying diplomatic assurances that he would be treated in accordance with domestic procedure, would not be re-extradited, and could leave after serving any sentence. The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office conducted an “extradition check.” The FMS, FSB and Foreign Ministry reported that the applicant held only Uzbek nationality, had never sought Russian citizenship or asylum, and was regarded by the FSB as an HT functionary; they identified no bar to surrender. On 9 August 2010 the Deputy Prosecutor General authorised extradition on the corresponding Russian offences (RCC Arts. 210 and 278), noting that dual-criminality differences did not preclude surrender and that limitation periods had not expired.

The applicant immediately challenged the order, invoking a real risk of torture because of his HT affiliation and citing extensive international reports on systematic ill-treatment of such suspects in Uzbekistan. The Saratov Regional Court initially upheld the order on 16 September 2010, relying on the Uzbek assurances and the contemporaneous refusal of refugee status. The Supreme Court quashed that judgment on 17 November 2010 and remitted the case. On 28 December 2010 the Regional Court annulled the extradition order on two grounds: material errors in the comparative legal characterisation of the offences, and the fact that judicial review of the refugee-status refusal remained pending, rendering extradition premature under the Refugees Act. The applicant was released in court. The Supreme Court confirmed the annulment on 4 March 2011; extradition proceedings were abandoned.

Throughout, the applicant remained in detention from 26 February to 28 December 2010. Successive court orders (26 February, 1 April, 23 August, 17 November and 22 November 2010) authorised and extended custody under CCrP Arts. 108–109 and 466, citing the gravity of the charges, the applicant’s lack of registered residence, alleged flight risk, and the “particular complexity” created by his appeals and asylum claim. Most appeals against the extensions failed.

Parallel refugee proceedings began on 17/24 March 2010. The applicant cited fear of persecution and torture on account of his former HT membership. The regional FMS refused status on 1 July 2010, finding that he had left Uzbekistan years earlier for economic reasons, that the charges were ordinary criminal rather than political, and that the late application indicated an attempt to evade prosecution. The central FMS and subsequent judicial review (Basmannyy District Court 24 December 2010; Moscow City Court 18 May 2011) upheld the refusal, emphasising that he had never distanced himself from HT and that UNHCR Handbook criteria distinguished genuine refugees from fugitives from justice. Temporary asylum was likewise denied in March 2011. In July 2011, however, UNHCR independently recognised the applicant as a mandate refugee, concluding that he faced a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of religion and imputed political opinion and a real risk of torture if returned.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of a real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment upon return, of detention contrary to Article 5 (lawfulness, time-limits and review), and of the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

The case of Mitrokhin v. Russia (no. 35648/04) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns complaints by Aleksandr Grigoryevich Mitrokhin (born 1973), a Russian national serving a prison sentence. 001-108670:
The case of Kronfeldner v. Germany (Application no. 21906/09) concerns a complaint by German national Franz Xaver Kronfeldner (born 1958) that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention beyond the 10-year maximum applicable at the time of his 1989 offence violated Article 5 of the Convention. Since age 16, the applicant had multiple convictions and spent only about four years outside prison. On 20 November 1990, the Regensburg Regional Court convicted him of rape (committed in July 1989, four months after a prior release) and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment plus preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. A psychiatric expert found no mental illness diminishing responsibility (though alcohol had done so at the time) and noted prior convictions including attempted rape (1973), sexual assaults (1978), and rape/coercion (1984). The court found a propensity for serious sexual offences making him a public danger.

After serving his full prison term, the applicant entered preventive detention on 13 November 1997. Its continuation was ordered in 1999 and 2002. In 2004 the Regensburg Regional Court directed execution in a detoxification facility (transfer March 2004); in October 2005 it directed transfer to a psychiatric hospital (December 2005) after an expert diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder with high reoffending risk treatable only there. Prolongation in hospital occurred in 2007. By 11 May 2008 he had served 10 years in preventive detention (interrupted by another sentence).

On 12 June 2008 the Regensburg Regional Court, after hearing the applicant, counsel and expert K., refused to terminate detention after 10 years or suspend it on probation. It found a high likelihood of further serious violent sexual offences (especially rapes) causing considerable harm, based on the applicant’s unchanged dangerousness, prior convictions and expert K.’s diagnosis of a serious dissocial personality disorder (no pathological sexual deviation, psychiatric illness or treatable mental disorder). The court quashed the hospital placement (as therapy had failed and the applicant had no psychiatric illness) and ordered return to prison (effected 19 June 2008). The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 22 July 2008, endorsing the findings and citing the Federal Constitutional Court’s 5 February 2004 ruling that retroactive extension beyond 10 years was constitutional. The Federal Constitutional Court declined the applicant’s 21 August 2008 constitutional complaint (alleging liberty and fair-trial violations, including inadequate expert report and withheld therapy information) without reasons on 3 November 2008.

Detention occurred in a separate prison wing with privileges (e.g., extra recreation, shorter lock-up, more visits and purchases, larger cells) versus ordinary prisoners. The applicant refused offered therapies, citing lack of motivation and questioning therapists’ expertise; no relaxations were granted.

Subsequent proceedings (after the Court’s M. v. Germany judgment) led the Nuremberg Court of Appeal, on 28 November 2011, to terminate the detention immediately as disproportionate under the Federal Constitutional Court’s 4 May 2011 criteria (no showing of high likelihood of the most serious violent/sexual offences due to specific personal circumstances). Provisional detention in a psychiatric hospital was then ordered under the 2011 Therapy Detention Act.

Relevant domestic law originally limited first-period preventive detention to 10 years (Article 67d § 1, pre-1998). The 1998 Combating of Sexual Offences Act abolished this maximum and applied the change retroactively (Article 67d § 3), initially upheld by the Federal Constitutional Court in 2004 but later held incompatible with legitimate expectations and liberty rights (2011 judgment). Transfers between measures (e.g., to hospital) were possible if they better promoted reintegration (Article 67a). The 2011 Therapy Detention Act allowed civil-court placement of those no longer detainable in preventive detention if they had a mental disorder creating high risk of serious harm.

**Case of Kronfeldner v. Germany (Application no. 21906/09), ECHR Fifth Section, Judgment of 19 January 2012 (final 19 April 2012).**

The applicant, a German national born in 1958, alleged that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention (a measure of correction and prevention under German criminal law) beyond the 10-year maximum applicable at the time of his offence violated Article 5 of the Convention (right to liberty). He had a lengthy criminal record from age 16, including attempted rape (1973), sexual assaults (1978), and rape/coercion (1984), spending most of his adult life in custody. On 20 November 1990 the Regensburg Regional Court convicted him of rape (committed shortly after prior release) and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment plus preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. A psychiatric expert found no mental illness diminishing criminal responsibility (though alcohol played a role), but a propensity for serious sexual offences making him a public danger. After serving his full sentence, preventive detention began on 13 November 1997 in Straubing Prison (with later transfers).

At the time of the 1989/1990 offence and conviction, Article 67d of the Criminal Code limited the first period of preventive detention to a maximum of 10 years, after which release was required. The Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act of 26 January 1998 (effective 31 January 1998) abolished this maximum and applied retroactively (via the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code). The applicant reached the 10-year mark on 11 May 2008. On 12 June 2008 the Regensburg Regional Court (after hearing the applicant, counsel, and expert K.) refused to terminate or suspend the detention on probation. Relying on expert K.’s report (reviewing hospital files and diagnosing a serious dissocial personality disorder reflected in prior sexual offences, but no pathological sexual deviation, psychiatric illness, or mental disorder diminishing responsibility or requiring therapy), the court found a high likelihood of further serious violent sexual offences (especially rapes) causing considerable harm if released. It quashed an earlier transfer to a psychiatric hospital (under Article 67a), finding therapy unsuccessful and reintegration not better served there, and ordered return to prison. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal upheld this on 22 July 2008, endorsing the risk assessment and citing a 2004 Federal Constitutional Court ruling upholding retroactive extension as constitutional. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s 2008 constitutional complaint (alleging liberty violations, inadequate expert reports, and fair-trial issues) without reasons.

Preventive detention was executed in a separate prison wing with some privileges (e.g., extra recreation, shorter lock-up, more visits, larger cells) compared to regular prisoners. The applicant received family visits/calls, worked later in a factory, but refused available therapies (group/individual social therapy for sex offenders) due to lack of motivation and distrust of therapists; no sentence relaxations were granted.

Subsequent developments (post-M. v. Germany) included a 2010 continuation order, referral amid evolving case law, and, after the Federal Constitutional Court’s 4 May 2011 judgment declaring relevant provisions incompatible with the Basic Law (for failing to distinguish preventive detention from punishment and protect legitimate expectations), the Nuremberg Court of Appeal terminated the detention on 28 November 2011 as disproportionate (no shown high likelihood of the most serious offences). Provisional detention under the new Therapy Detention Act (for mentally disordered violent offenders no longer holdable in preventive detention) was then ordered, with transfer to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital. The applicant was never previously placed under the Bavarian Mentally Ill Persons’ Placement Act.

These facts centre on the retroactive removal of the 10-year limit, continued detention after 2008 based on unchanged dangerousness assessments (personality disorder without qualifying mental illness), unsuccessful transfers/therapy, and prison-like conditions, all while the original legal framework at the time of the offence had imposed a firm temporal cap. The case was examined in light of the related M. v. Germany judgment finding similar retroactive extensions incompatible with Articles 5 and 7.

The case of Kronfeldner v. Germany (application no. 21906/09) concerns a German national, Franz Xaver Kronfeldner (born 1958), who alleged that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention beyond the ten-year maximum applicable at the time of his offence violated Article 5 of the Convention. After serving the full prison term he entered preventive detention on 13 November 1997; its continuation was ordered in 1999 and 2002. In March 2004 he was transferred to a detoxification facility and, in December 2005, to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital after an expert diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder and a high risk of reoffending. By 11 May 2008 he had completed ten years of preventive detention (the former statutory maximum under Article 67d § 1 as in force before 31 January 1998). On 12 June 2008 the Regensburg Regional Court, after hearing the applicant and a new expert, refused to terminate or suspend the measure. The expert diagnosed a serious dissocial personality disorder but no pathological sexual deviation, psychiatric illness or mental disorder diminishing responsibility or requiring hospital treatment. The court found a very high likelihood of further violent sexual offences and ordered his return to prison (implemented on 19 June 2008). The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 22 July 2008, relying on the Federal Constitutional Court’s 5 February 2004 ruling that the 1998 amendment (abolishing the ten-year limit and applying it retroactively via the Introductory Act) was constitutional. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to examine his complaint on 3 November 2008.

Preventive detention was served in a separate prison wing offering modest privileges (extra recreation, shorter lock-up, larger cells, etc.). The applicant refused available social therapies, citing lack of motivation and distrust of therapists, and received no sentence relaxations. Subsequent reviews in 2010 again continued detention. Following the Court’s judgment in M. v. Germany and the Federal Constitutional Court’s 4 May 2011 ruling (declaring the relevant provisions incompatible with the Basic Law), the Nuremberg Court of Appeal terminated the preventive detention on 28 November 2011 because the stricter “high likelihood of the most serious violent or sexual offences” plus a mental disorder (as defined by reference to Article 5 § 1 (e)) had not been shown. Provisional placement under the new Therapy Detention Act was then ordered and he was transferred to a psychiatric hospital.

These facts centre on the retroactive application of the 1998 legislation that converted a time-limited measure into an indefinite one after the applicant had already begun serving it, the domestic courts’ reliance on a personality disorder falling short of unsoundness of mind, and the absence of sufficient therapeutic differentiation from ordinary imprisonment.

The case of Proshkin v. Russia (Application no. 28869/03) concerns a Russian national, Sergey Anatolyevich Proshkin (born 1963), who alleged unlawful detention in 2003, the authorities’ failure to examine his appeals against a detention order, and their failure to ensure his personal presence at key hearings in criminal proceedings against him.

The proceedings originated from a 1996 traffic accident involving the applicant’s family and a Mr P., after which criminal charges against P. were dropped under an amnesty. The applicant then allegedly harassed P. and his mother with threats and demands for compensation. In 1999, criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant for aggravated defamation, insult, and later death threats and extortion. He was detained briefly, convicted in 2000 of defamation and extortion (seven-year sentence), but the conviction was quashed on appeal, with a retrial ordered only on the extortion charge; he was released. Psychiatric examinations followed, including one in late 2002 at a Moscow centre diagnosing schizophrenia based on personality traits, obsessive complaints, and alleged danger to society. A further examination was ordered in January 2003.

On 27 January 2003 the Industrialniy District Court, with the applicant present, issued two identically worded decisions (one handwritten, one typed) citing the seriousness of the charges and the schizophrenia diagnosis as posing a societal danger. One authorised placement in a psychiatric hospital; the other authorised detention in Perm’s ordinary detention facility no. IZ-59/1. The applicant was immediately taken into custody at the courthouse and held in the ordinary facility. He promptly appealed (statements received by the Perm Regional Court on 29 January, 31 January and 2 February 2003), arguing there was no evidence of danger justifying detention. The appeals received no examination or reply.

Trial hearings proceeded on 17–18 February 2003 without the applicant, despite his being in custody; his lawyer and mother attended. The court issued no formal ruling on his absence but concluded his presence was unnecessary. On 18 February it found he had committed aggravated extortion while mentally incapacitated, relieved him of criminal responsibility, and ordered compulsory intensive psychiatric treatment in a specialised hospital. A confirmatory psychiatric report was issued two days later. The applicant’s request to attend the 15 April 2003 appeal hearing was ignored; only his lawyer and mother appeared. The Regional Court upheld the decision, holding that domestic law did not require his presence given his representation.

Meanwhile the applicant remained in the ordinary detention facility (in a cell for mentally ill inmates) until 24 July 2003 because of delays obtaining transit visas for transfer to a Kaliningrad hospital. After that hospital refused him for lack of identity documents he stayed until 18 August 2003, when he was sent to a Kazan psychiatric hospital. He was released on 4 June 2004. Separately, on 6 May 2003 he was declared legally incapacitated (a decision he did not appeal).

These facts underpin the complaints of unlawful 2003 detention (including its form and prolongation in an ordinary facility rather than a hospital), the complete failure to process appeals against the 27 January order, and the exclusion of the applicant from both trial and appeal hearings despite his requests and the gravity of the potential outcome.

001-109070:
The case Arras and Others v. Italy (no. 17972/07) was brought by four Italian pensioners (former Banco di Napoli employees who retired before 31 December 1990) alleging a breach of Article 6 of the Convention through legislative interference in pending civil proceedings concerning their pension rights.

Prior to privatisation, Banco di Napoli employees enjoyed an exclusive welfare regime featuring a favourable equalisation mechanism (perequazione aziendale). Annual pension increases were calculated by reference to salary rises of serving staff of equivalent grade, rather than the less generous cost-of-living adjustment (perequazione legale) applicable under the general compulsory insurance scheme.

The 1990 Amato reform privatised public banks and replaced exclusive regimes with integrated schemes under the Istituto Nazionale della Previdenza Sociale (INPS). Subsequent 1992 legislation (Laws nos. 421/92 and 503/92) was interpreted by the bank as extinguishing perequazione aziendale even for already-retired staff. Pensioners contended that the 1992 laws expressly preserved more favourable treatment for those who had retired by 31 December 1990.

From the mid-1990s a series of civil actions produced a consistent line of authority, culminating in the Court of Cassation sitting as a full court (Sezioni Unite, judgment no. 9024/01 of 2001). The courts held that perequazione aziendale remained applicable to pre-1991 retirees, at least for the period 1 January 1994 to 26 July 1996.

The applicants themselves commenced proceedings in 1996. In February 2001 the Naples Labour Tribunal found in their favour and ordered payment of arrears. In April 2004 the Naples Court of Appeal confirmed the entitlement, albeit limited to the 1994–1996 window.

While the bank’s further appeal was pending, Parliament enacted Law no. 243/04. Section 1(55) purported to give an “authentic interpretation” of the 1992 texts, declaring that perequazione aziendale had been abolished for all Banco di Napoli pensioners irrespective of retirement date, with retroactive effect from 1992. The stated purpose was to secure homogeneous treatment and to extinguish outstanding litigation.

In October 2006 the Court of Cassation applied the new provision, reversed the lower courts and dismissed the applicants’ claims. It rejected arguments of unconstitutionality, holding that the legislator was entitled to clarify one of the possible meanings of the original text.

In 2008 the Constitutional Court (judgment no. 362) upheld the 2004 law in analogous cases, describing it as a legitimate interpretative measure based on a possible reading of the 1992 statutes and aimed at equal treatment.

The facts central to the Article 6 complaint are therefore the enactment, while the applicants’ cassation appeal was still pending, of a retroactive interpretative statute that overturned a settled line of case-law (including a Sezioni Unite ruling) which had hitherto guaranteed them the more favourable pension adjustment.

The case Arras and Others v. Italy (App. no. 17972/07) involved four Italian pensioners (Antonio Arras, Celestina Dede, Alessandro Dessi and Bachisio Zizi), former employees of Banco di Napoli who retired before 31 December 1990. Two later died and their heirs continued the application. They alleged a violation of Article 6 ECHR (fair trial) arising from retrospective legislative interference in their pending civil claims.

Banco di Napoli (originally a public entity later privatised) operated a special pension regime featuring perequazione aziendale: annual pension increases calculated by reference to salary rises of serving staff in equivalent grades. This was more generous than the general perequazione legale (cost-of-living adjustment) under the INPS compulsory insurance scheme. The 1990 Amato reform and subsequent 1992 legislation (Laws 421/92 and 503/92) suppressed exclusive bank pension regimes and brought employees into the INPS system, but the applicants maintained that those laws expressly preserved more favourable treatment for persons already retired by 31 December 1990.

From 1993 the bank nevertheless sought to apply only perequazione legale even to pre-1991 retirees. Numerous pensioners, including the applicants (who sued in 1996), brought civil actions claiming continued entitlement to the original mechanism and payment of arrears. Domestic courts, culminating in the Court of Cassation (Sezioni Unite) judgment no. 9024/01 of 3 July 2001, uniformly upheld the pensioners. The 1992 reforms were held to apply only to staff still in service; pre-1991 retirees retained perequazione aziendale for the period 1 January 1994–26 July 1996 (after which a special “Salvabanco” suspension applied). The applicants obtained first-instance judgment in their favour on 26 February 2001 (Naples Tribunal, Labour Section) and confirmation on appeal on 24 April 2004 (limited to the 1994–1996 window), with orders for arrears, inflation adjustment and interest.

While those proceedings remained pending, Parliament enacted Law 243/04, s. 1(55). The provision gave an “authentic interpretation” of the 1992 texts, declaring that perequazione aziendale was abolished for all Banco di Napoli pensioners irrespective of retirement date and applying the change retrospectively from 1992. Its stated purpose was to extinguish litigation and ensure homogeneous treatment of all pensioners under the new integrative regimes. (A 1997 finance law had already ended all azienda-style adjustments from 1 January 1998.)

The bank appealed to the Court of Cassation. In judgment no. 22701/06 of 19 September 2006 the Cassation reversed the lower courts, applying the 2004 interpretative statute (which had not existed when the Court of Appeal ruled). It rejected an unconstitutionality plea, holding that the legislature may clarify an original text by selecting one of its possible meanings. In 2008 the Constitutional Court (judgment no. 362) likewise upheld Law 243/04 as a legitimate interpretative measure that merely confirmed a meaning already present in the 1992 wording and in some earlier case-law; any incidental effects on pending cases were not sufficient to render it unconstitutional.

The applicants contended that the retroactive statute, introduced while their claims were still live, constituted legislative interference that determined the outcome of pending litigation and thereby deprived them of a fair hearing by an independent tribunal.

**CASE OF ARRAS AND OTHERS v. ITALY (Application no. 17972/07), ECHR, 14 February 2012 (final 14 May 2012)**

The four applicants (two of whom later died, with heirs continuing the case) were Italian pensioners who had retired before 31 December 1990 as former employees of Banco di Napoli. Prior to privatisation, that bank (originally a public entity) operated a special welfare regime under which pensioners received annual increases calculated on the basis of salary rises for serving employees of equivalent grade (*perequazione aziendale*). This was more favourable than the standard cost-of-living adjustment (*perequazione legale*) under the general compulsory insurance scheme administered by INPS.

The 1990 Amato reform privatised public banks such as Banco di Napoli and replaced their exclusive pension arrangements with integrated ones, registering employees with INPS. Further 1992 pension legislation (Laws nos. 421/92 and 503/92) was interpreted by the bank as suppressing *perequazione aziendale* even for those already retired, substituting the less generous legal adjustment. The applicants (and many similarly situated pensioners) contended that the 1992 laws, read with the 1990 reform, preserved more favourable treatment for pre-1991 retirees; only serving employees were affected, and they had been offered compensatory benefits via collective bargaining.

From the mid-1990s, pensioners brought civil claims seeking restoration of *perequazione aziendale* and payment of arrears. A consistent line of case-law developed in their favour. In 1994 a first-instance court upheld the claims. The Court of Cassation (including its Sezioni Unite in 2001) confirmed that the 1992 reforms did not abrogate *perequazione aziendale* for those who had already retired by 31 December 1990. Entitlement was recognised for the period 1 January 1994 to 26 July 1996 (after a general suspension of adjustments ended and before a bank-specific suspension began). Subsequent legislation in 1997 definitively ended *perequazione aziendale* from 1 January 1998 for most public-bank pensioners, but the Banco di Napoli’s employees had already been suspended earlier.

The applicants themselves commenced proceedings in 1996. In February 2001 the Naples Labour Tribunal found in their favour and ordered payment of arrears plus interest from January 1994. In April 2004 the Naples Court of Appeal confirmed the right, limited to the 1994–1996 window. Banco di Napoli appealed to the Court of Cassation.

In the meantime, section 1(55) of Law no. 243/04 (enacted 2004) provided an authentic interpretation of the 1992 provisions. It stated that the less favourable *perequazione legale* applied to *all* pensioners (regardless of retirement date) from 1994, with a view to extinguishing litigation, achieving homogeneous treatment under the integrated regimes, and placing the cost on the general insurance scheme. The law was given retroactive effect.

In October 2006 the Court of Cassation allowed the bank’s appeal, applied Law no. 243/04, reversed the lower courts and dismissed the applicants’ claims (costs to be shared). It rejected a constitutional challenge, noting that the legislature could adopt an interpretative statute selecting one possible meaning of the original text. In 2008 the Constitutional Court, seised in analogous cases, upheld the 2004 law as a legitimate interpretative measure that merely confirmed one possible reading of the 1992 texts, pursued the reasonable aim of equal treatment, and did not unconstitutionally interfere with pending proceedings or the role of the courts.

The applicants complained that the 2004 legislation constituted an impermissible legislative intervention in pending judicial proceedings, thereby violating their right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention by retrospectively altering the legal rules applicable to their established claims.

The case of Romet v. the Netherlands (Application no. 7094/06) originated from a complaint by Steven Benito Romet, a Dutch national born in 1968 and residing in Maastricht, alleging a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. He claimed that unknown persons had been able to misuse his driving licence after he reported it stolen, resulting in extensive fraudulent vehicle registrations in his name and severe repercussions for his private life.

On 3 November 1995 the applicant reported to police that his driving licence had been stolen in September of that year. A replacement licence was issued only on 14 March 1997 after he applied shortly beforehand. In the intervening period the Government Road Transport Agency registered 1,737 motor vehicles in the applicant’s name in the official vehicle registration system, without his consent. These registrations were effected upon presentation of the stolen licence.

As a direct result the applicant received large numbers of motor-vehicle tax assessments. He was repeatedly prosecuted under the Motor Liability Insurance Act and fined by the public prosecutor under the Traffic Regulations Administrative Enforcement Act for offences committed with the vehicles. After being ordered by courts to pay the fines he was detained (gijzeling) for non-payment. He ultimately paid fines imposed for offences he had not committed. On several occasions the Motor Traffic Guarantee Fund held him liable for damage caused by uninsured vehicles registered in his name. His welfare benefits were stopped because the sheer number of vehicles made his financial means appear adequate.

The applicant alleged that on 1 July 1996 he asked the Agency to annul all but one of the registrations and that he made unsuccessful complaints to the public prosecutor in 1996; the Government stated that no official records of these steps existed. In February 2004 he appealed to the Amsterdam Court of Appeal against the Public Prosecution Service’s refusal to prosecute those responsible for the malicious registrations. In its 22 June 2005 decision the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on the ground that too much time had elapsed for a viable investigation, although it favoured a one-off administrative remission of all related sanctions. No such remission occurred. The Tax and Customs Administration also initially blocked the applicant’s eligibility for statutory debt rescheduling.

On 16 January 2004 the applicant formally requested the Agency to cancel the registrations with retroactive effect. On 3 April 2004 the Agency cancelled the 240 registrations still standing in his name, but only as of that date, stating that retroactive cancellation would undermine the reliability of the registration system. His objection was dismissed on 2 September 2004 because retroactivity would create legal uncertainty and encroach on the competences of other authorities (prosecution and tax). The Rotterdam Regional Court upheld that decision, noting that the applicant had waited more than seven years after his 1996 complaints before initiating proceedings. On 7 December 2005 the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State confirmed that the Agency’s policy of refusing retroactive effect was reasonable in order to preserve the purity of the register and legal certainty. It also rejected arguments based on Directive 95/46/EC and other Convention provisions.

The facts thus centre on the ease with which a reported-stolen driving licence could be used to effect thousands of unauthorised registrations and on the authorities’ subsequent inability or refusal to restore the applicant’s situation retroactively, leaving him exposed to prolonged financial, legal and personal consequences.

The case of Romet v. the Netherlands (Application no. 7094/06) concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the abuse of the applicant’s stolen driving licence. The case of Karrer v. Romania (Application no. 16965/10) was brought by two Austrian nationals, Alexander Hannes Karrer (the first applicant, born 1982) and his daughter Alexandra Bianca Karrer (the second applicant, born 2006). They alleged a violation of their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from Romanian courts’ handling of international child abduction proceedings. The first applicant further complained of a lack of fair hearing under Article 6 § 1.

The first applicant married Romanian national K.T. in Salzburg, Austria, in April 2004. Their daughter was born in February 2006; the couple held joint custody under Austrian law and resided in Salzburg. They separated in February 2008. K.T. petitioned for divorce and obtained an interim injunction excluding the first applicant from the family home on grounds of alleged violence (later acquitted in related criminal proceedings). She also sought sole custody. In late September 2008, while Austrian custody proceedings remained pending, K.T. departed for Romania with the child without informing the first applicant.

In November 2008 the Salzburg District Civil Court awarded the first applicant temporary sole custody, relying on expert evidence that he was better suited as custodian. K.T. did not appeal. Divorce proceedings later continued in Romania.

On 30 September 2008 the first applicant requested the child’s return under Article 3 of the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, arguing the removal breached joint custody rights. The Austrian Central Authority transmitted the request to Romania’s Ministry of Justice on 7 October 2008. Romanian police confirmed the child’s presence with her mother and maternal grandparents. A social-services report recorded the mother’s account of events in Austria, the grandparents’ willingness to support the child, and the child’s apparent good material and emotional conditions and attachment to her mother.

The Ministry instituted return proceedings before the Bucharest County Court on 5 December 2008. On 28 January 2009 (communicated only on 28 May 2009) that court ordered the child’s return, finding the removal wrongful and no Article 13 exception applicable.

K.T. appealed, submitting witness statements from her parents (given in concurrent Romanian divorce/custody proceedings) and a welfare report from Timişoara City Hall that described her family circumstances and recommended she receive custody. On 8 July 2009 (written judgment 17 September 2009) the Bucharest Court of Appeal reversed the order. It held that return would expose the child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm under Hague Convention Article 13(1)(b). The court relied on the earlier Austrian interim injunction as evidence of the first applicant’s violence toward K.T., inferred similar risk to the child despite the absence of direct evidence, and treated the mother’s departure as confirmation of that risk. It disregarded the November 2008 Austrian custody order because the mother and child had already left Austria.

Throughout, the Romanian Ministry kept the Austrian authorities informed of hearing dates and procedural steps but had no direct contact with the first applicant. The applicants contended that these proceedings, including delays exceeding Hague Convention and EU Regulation 2201/2003 time-limits and the appellate court’s approach to evidence and the child’s best interests, failed to secure prompt restoration of family life.

**Case of Karrer v. Romania (Application no. 16965/10), ECtHR (Third Section), judgment of 21 February 2012 (final 21 May 2012)**

The applicants, Austrian nationals Alexander Hannes Karrer (born 1982) and his daughter Alexandra Bianca Karrer (born 2006), alleged that Romanian authorities infringed their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The father further claimed a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to an unfair hearing in determining his civil rights.

The father married Romanian national K.T. in Salzburg, Austria, in 2004. Their daughter was born in 2006; they shared joint custody under Austrian law and lived in Salzburg. The couple separated on 1 February 2008. K.T. petitioned for divorce on 25 February 2008; the father filed a counter-petition. On 29 January 2008, K.T. sought an interim injunction against the father citing violent behaviour, which the Salzburg District Civil Court granted on 8 February 2008 for three months, requiring his removal from the family home. Criminal proceedings for inflicting bodily harm were also opened against him.

K.T. applied for temporary sole custody during the divorce. At the end of September 2008, while those proceedings were pending, she took the child to Romania without informing the father, despite their joint custody. On 25 July 2008, the Salzburg District Criminal Court acquitted the father of bodily harm; the prosecutor reserved the possibility of charging K.T. with perjury. On 25 November 2008, the Salzburg District Civil Court awarded the father temporary sole custody until the divorce was finalised, relying on an expert opinion that he was better suited. K.T. did not appeal. Divorce proceedings later continued in Romanian courts.

On 30 September 2008 the father requested the child’s return to Austria under Article 3 of the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The Austrian authorities transmitted the request to Romania’s Central Authority (the Ministry of Justice). Romanian police confirmed the child lived with her mother and maternal grandparents. A social services report noted the child’s attachment to her mother and grandparents, adequate living conditions, and no signs of abuse or neglect.

On 5 December 2008 the Romanian Ministry initiated proceedings on the father’s behalf before the Bucharest County Court. On 28 January 2009 that court ordered the child’s return, finding the removal wrongful under Hague Convention Article 3 and that no Article 13 exceptions applied. K.T. appealed, submitting witness statements from her parents (given in Romanian divorce/custody proceedings) and a welfare report from Timişoara City Hall recommending she receive custody. On 8 July 2009 the Bucharest Court of Appeal reversed the order. It held that return would expose the child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm under Hague Convention Article 13 § 1(b). The court relied on the 8 February 2008 Austrian injunction as evidence of the father’s violence toward K.T., found he had breached the restraining order (prompting K.T.’s departure), and inferred a risk to the child from that violence even without direct evidence of harm to her. It disregarded the 25 November 2008 Austrian custody award because the mother and child had already left Austria.

Throughout, the Romanian Ministry informed the Austrian authorities of procedural steps but had no direct contact with the father. The applicants contended that these events—particularly the Romanian courts’ handling of the Hague return request, the reliance on the later-discredited violence allegations, the inference of risk to the child, the disregard of Austrian custody findings, and the lack of the father’s effective participation—breached Article 8 (family life) and, for the father, Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing). Relevant instruments included the Hague Convention (especially Articles 3, 11–13 on wrongful removal, expedition, and exceptions) and EU Regulation 2201/2003 (requiring expedition, hearing the requesting parent, and considering protective arrangements).

The case of Shumkova v. Russia concerns the death of the applicant's son, Vladimir Shumkov, while serving a prison sentence, and the ensuing official investigation. Shumkov, arrested in December 1993, was convicted in March 1995 of murder and perjury and sentenced to nine years and six months' imprisonment. He was held in successive correctional facilities in the Irkutsk region (ITK-19, IK-6, IK-15 and finally IK-20), with transfers prompted by conflicts with other inmates.

From 1995 onward he received repeated in-patient psychiatric and somatic treatment in prison hospitals. An initial diagnosis of epilepsy was later revised to psychopathic personality disorder of mixed (explosive-hysteroid) type. Medical records document irritability, aggressiveness, affective instability, demonstrative self-mutilation, simulation of fits and somatic complaints (duodenal ulcer, hypertension). He was discharged from hospital in June 2001 after further psychiatric treatment and returned to IK-20, where he incurred multiple disciplinary sanctions.

On 17 June 2001 he was confined to a disciplinary cell. On 1 August he slashed his left wrist. After first aid he refused to re-enter the cell, insulted and threatened officers and seized one officer's uniform; rubber truncheons and physical force were then used to return him to the cell. Bruises were later noted. The same day he was again placed in a disciplinary cell for the self-mutilation.

In the early hours of 4 August 2001 Shumkov knocked on his cell door claiming high blood pressure. Officers found he had slashed large vessels in both antecubital fossae and forearms with a fragment of a disposable razor blade (an item then permitted under internal regulations). He refused first aid from warders and insisted on seeing a doctor. The on-call prison doctor was summoned from home, arrived approximately 20–25 minutes later, dressed the wounds, administered stimulants and attempted resuscitation. Shumkov was transported to the medical unit but was pronounced dead from massive blood loss at around 02.40–02.45.

A post-mortem confirmed the cause of death. Initial decisions declining to open a criminal investigation were repeatedly quashed. An investigation was instituted in June 2002 but was discontinued several times, finally on 28 May 2003. Prosecutors concluded that officers had used force lawfully, that cell searches had revealed no prohibited objects, that the medical response had been timely, that Shumkov had been able to control his actions and that no offence (incitement to suicide, abuse of office or neglect) had been committed. A 2003 forensic psychiatric report diagnosed mixed psychopathy with self-harm tendencies but no temporary mental disorder or loss of insight at the material time.

The applicant unsuccessfully challenged the discontinuation before prosecutors and courts; the last domestic decision upholding it was given in September 2005. These circumstances raise issues concerning the State's positive obligation to protect the life of a mentally vulnerable prisoner with a history of self-harm and the effectiveness of the subsequent investigation.

The case of Shumkova v. Russia (Application no. 9296/06) concerns the death of the applicant’s son, Vladimir Shumkov, while serving a prison sentence, and the subsequent investigation. Medical records and later expert opinions indicated frequent hospitalisations between 1995 and 2001, during which he displayed unbalanced behaviour, mood swings, simulation of fits and a tendency toward self-mutilation; authorities maintained that he had been provided with adequate psychiatric and general medical care and that he retained the capacity to understand and control his actions.

On 17 June 2001 Shumkov was placed in a disciplinary cell for a breach of discipline. On 1 August 2001 he slashed his left wrist. After first aid he refused to return to the cell, prompting officers to use physical force and rubber truncheons; an internal inquiry later found the force lawful and proportionate. He was then returned to the disciplinary cell, where internal rules at the time permitted him to keep a disposable safety-razor blade.

In the early hours of 4 August 2001 Shumkov knocked on his cell door claiming high blood-pressure and requesting pills. Officers discovered he had slashed the veins in both elbows. He refused assistance from the warders and insisted on seeing the prison doctor. The doctor, who lived nearby and was on stand-by duty, arrived approximately 20–30 minutes later, dressed the wounds and administered injections, but Shumkov died of massive blood loss shortly after being taken to the medical unit (recorded time of death around 02.40–02.45). A post-mortem confirmed death from injuries to large blood vessels; bruises consistent with the earlier use of force were also noted.

Domestic inquiries initially declined to open a criminal case. After several quashings and additional steps (including a forensic psychiatric-psychological report concluding that Shumkov suffered from a personality disorder conducive to impulsive self-harm but was not psychotic and that no extreme circumstances had prompted suicide), proceedings were finally discontinued in May 2003. Prosecutors found no evidence of incitement to suicide, abuse of power, neglect of duty or failure to render aid: the razor fragment was permitted under the then-applicable regulations, cell searches had revealed no other prohibited items, supervision through the inspection hatch had been maintained, and the doctor’s response time was consistent with night-time stand-by arrangements. The applicant’s subsequent complaints to higher prosecutors and the courts were unsuccessful; the last domestic decision upholding the discontinuation became final in 2006.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the authorities failed to protect her son’s life (through inadequate monitoring of a known vulnerable prisoner, delayed medical response and the permitted presence of a cutting implement) and that the investigation into the death was ineffective.

The case originated in an application lodged by Mariya Nikolayevna Shumkova against Russia concerning the death of her son, Vladimir Shumkov, in custody. Shumkov was arrested in December 1993 on suspicion of murder, convicted in March 1995, and sentenced to nine years and six months' imprisonment. Officers found he had slashed veins in both elbows with a piece of disposable razor blade (permitted under then-applicable internal regulations). He refused first aid from staff, insisting on the prison doctor. Doctor G. was summoned from home and arrived at approximately 2:40 a.m., dressed the wounds, administered stimulants, and attempted resuscitation. Shumkov was transported to the medical unit but was pronounced dead from massive blood loss (around 2:40–2:45 a.m.). A post-mortem confirmed the cause as injuries to large vessels in the antecubital fossae and forearms.

The latter found chronic psychopathy with traits of impulsivity, demonstrative self-harm, and aggression, but concluded Shumkov retained the capacity to understand and control his actions; no extreme environmental stressors precipitating suicide were identified. On 28 May 2003 the prosecutor discontinued proceedings, finding no corpus delicti of incitement to suicide, abuse of office, or neglect of duty by staff. The decision cited lawful use of force on 1 August, permitted possession of the razor fragment, timely (if unsuccessful) medical response, and compliance with supervision rules. Subsequent complaints by the applicant were rejected by the Prosecutor General's Office and, after remittal for a procedural defect, by the Ust-Kuta District Court (5 April 2005) and Irkutsk Regional Court (6 September 2005). Additional prison certificates confirmed that detention conditions complied with regulations and that all medical care had been provided within the penal system.

These facts form the basis of complaints relating to the State's positive obligations to protect life in custody (including suicide-risk assessment, cell-search procedures, and prompt medical intervention) and to conduct an effective official investigation into a death occurring under State control.
