The European Court of Human Rights case of Melnītis v. Latvia (Application no. 30779/05, judgment of 28 February 2012) concerned allegations by Latvian national Aigars Melnītis (born 1969) that conditions during his pre-trial detention in Valmiera Prison from 19 May to 14 October 2005 amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

Melnītis was held in cell no. 26 of the remand wing. On 14 October 2005 the Valmiera District Court convicted him of resistance to a public official, imposing a suspended three-year sentence, and ordered his release. No appeal followed.

He alleged the cell was poorly lit and ventilated. Toilets were unseparated from the living area, producing a lingering foul smell that forced detainees to eat nearby. The cell was overcrowded, providing less than the domestic minimum of 2.5 m² per adult male detainee.

The Government contested these claims. Cell no. 26 measured 23.6 m² and held no more than eight men (including the applicant), yielding roughly 2.95 m² each. It had both natural and artificial lighting plus a ventilation system; the toilet area was screened off.

Melnītis further claimed he received almost no personal hygiene items, only a quarter-bar of laundry soap. He was denied toilet soap, a toothbrush, toothpaste and toilet paper, contrary to Cabinet Regulation no. 339 (2002). That regulation required a healthy adult male detainee to receive 200 g of laundry soap, 50 g of toothpaste and a 30 m roll of toilet paper each month, plus one toothbrush every six months (no toilet soap was mandated). The Government did not dispute the non-provision. Prison authorities repeatedly cited a lack of funds. In October 2005 Melnītis finally received 200 g of laundry soap, one toothbrush, 50 g of toothpaste and one 30 m roll of toilet paper.

He complained to the prosecutor’s office, prison administration and National Human Rights Office. The Prisons Administration and Valmiera Prison confirmed the funding shortfall, stating they could supply only 200 g of laundry soap per month. The National Human Rights Office replied in general terms that Latvian penal institutions failed to meet many legal standards and that it had already warned the Government in March 2005 about insufficient allocations for hygiene products.

Cabinet Regulation no. 211 (2003), in force at the time, set remand-wing standards but contained no toilet-partitioning requirement (later introduced). The European Prison Rules (2006) emphasise dignity, health, hygiene, adequate space, lighting, ventilation and the provision of toiletries.

001-109913:
The ECHR case Inderbiyeva v. Russia (no. 56765/08) was brought by Deshi Inderbiyeva, who alleged that Russian servicemen killed her sisters Shema (b. 1963) and Shamani (b. 1966) Inderbiyeva in Grozny in January 2000, in violation of Articles 2, 3, 6 and 13 of the Convention.

In late 1999 the applicant fled to a refugee camp in Ingushetia amid hostilities, while her sisters and mother Yakhita remained in their Staropromyslovskiy District apartment to safeguard property. Russian forces regained control of the area in early January 2000. The sisters and mother hid in a basement; on 1 January the sisters moved to another basement at 285 Derzhavina Street because of fire, leaving their ill mother behind and visiting her with food.

On 8 or 12 February 2000 the applicant found her mother in shock, repeating “Russian soldiers, smoke, fire.” She then discovered her sisters’ burnt corpses in the basement at 154B Pugacheva Street, identifying them by belongings, hair, residual features and dental crowns. She collected the remains in pillowcases. An elderly ethnic-Russian neighbour, Ms M.Z., recounted seeing three servicemen on 10 January 2000: a senior soldier pulled the mother out for an “identity check,” after which the others threw an explosive into the basement, causing an explosion, smoke and partial destruction of the pavilion. The soldiers laughed as the mother fainted.

The applicant buried the remains in Valerik cemetery on 10 February after a confrontation at the military commander’s office, where servicemen tried to detain her upon hearing her accusation. Her mother suffered a severe psychological breakdown and became mentally ill. Supporting materials included witness statements, a February 2000 Human Rights Watch report on civilian killings in the district, and references to prior ECHR judgments on identical Staropromyslovskiy events.

The Government did not contest the account but attributed the deaths to unidentified perpetrators, stating that an investigation remained open.

The deaths were first examined in criminal case no. 12038, opened 3 May 2000 after a Novaya Gazeta article on mass murders by the 205th brigade. A dedicated case (no. 50080) was opened on 2 July 2003 under Article 105 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The applicant was neither promptly informed nor granted victim status until October 2003. Steps included questioning relatives and neighbours (most of whom had heard that Russian troops using a flamethrower had killed the sisters during a “sweeping-up” operation in an area under complete federal control), two crime-scene examinations that yielded nothing, exhumation, and forensic analysis rendered inconclusive by burns and decomposition. Repeated requests sought identification of units (including 3737 and the 205th brigade) and the elderly couple who had spoken to the applicant.

The investigation was suspended at least six times for failure to identify perpetrators; supervising prosecutors repeatedly quashed the suspensions as unsubstantiated and premature, ordering further inquiries that were largely unimplemented. The applicant’s complaints of ineffectiveness and requests for file access produced only partial disclosure. Domestic courts rejected one complaint because the investigation had just resumed. The Government submitted an incomplete 171-page file to the Court and maintained that no State-agent involvement was proven, yet the proceedings were still pending years later.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the killings themselves and the prolonged, inadequate investigation (Article 2), the suffering inflicted (Article 3), related procedural shortcomings (Article 6) and the absence of an effective remedy (Article 13).

The ECtHR case Inderbiyeva v. Russia (no. 56765/08) arose from an application by Deshi Inderbiyeva, a Russian national born in 1968 and living in Grozny. She alleged that Russian servicemen killed her sisters Shema (b. 1963) and Shamani (b. 1966) in Grozny in January 2000, in violation of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (fair trial) and 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention.

Due to hostilities, the applicant fled to an Ingushetia refugee camp in 1999, while her sisters and mother Yakhita remained in their Staropromyslovskiy District flat to guard family property. Russian forces regained control of the district in early January 2000. In December 1999 the family moved to a basement; on 1 January 2000 the sisters hid in another basement (at Derzhavina Street) while their ill mother stayed behind. They visited her regularly.

On 8 or 12 February 2000 the applicant found her mother in shock in a basement, muttering about “Russian soldiers, smoke, fire.” She then discovered her sisters’ burnt corpses in a courtyard basement, identifying them by belongings, hair, facial features and dental crowns. An elderly Russian witness, Ms M.Z., reported seeing three servicemen on 10 January 2000 pull the mother from the basement for an “identity check,” after which one threw an object inside, causing an explosion that destroyed the pavilion. The soldiers laughed as the mother fainted. The applicant collected the remains, faced hostility (including gunfire) when seeking burial permission at a military commander’s office, and buried them in Valerik cemetery on 10 February 2000. Her mother suffered a severe psychological breakdown and became mentally ill.

A criminal investigation began on 3 May 2000 (case no. 12038/12583) after a Novaya Gazeta article on mass civilian killings by the 205th brigade. A separate case (no. 50080) was opened on 2 July 2003 for the sisters’ murder. The applicant was granted victim status only on 5 October 2003. Investigators examined the crime scene (collecting nothing), ordered forensic exams of exhumed remains (impossible due to burns and decomposition), and repeatedly requested information on military units (including unit 3737 and brigade 205) stationed in the area in January–February 2000. The applicant’s complaints of ineffectiveness (including a 2008 court challenge) were rejected on grounds that proceedings had resumed. The case of Inderbiyeva v. Russia (Application no. 56765/08) concerns the alleged killing of the applicant’s two sisters by Russian military servicemen in Grozny, Chechnya, during the Second Chechen War, and the subsequent failure of the authorities to investigate effectively. The applicant, Deshi Inderbiyeva (born 1968), claimed violations of Articles 2, 3, 6 and 13 of the Convention.

In late 1999, amid intense hostilities, the applicant fled to a refugee camp in Ingushetia. Her sisters Shema (born 1963) and Shamani (born 1966), together with their mother Yakhita, remained in their apartment at 154B Pugacheva Street in Grozny’s Staropromyslovskiy District to protect family property. Most other residents had already left. Russian forces retook control of the district in early January 2000. In December 1999 the sisters and their mother had moved into a basement under a pavilion in the courtyard. On 1 January 2000, owing to fire, the sisters hid in another basement at 285/287 Derzhavina Street; their mother, who was ill, stayed behind. The sisters continued to visit her.

On or about 8–12 February 2000 the applicant returned to Grozny. She found her mother in a basement, in a state of shock and repeatedly uttering “Russian soldiers, smoke, fire.” The next day she discovered the charred remains of her sisters in the Pugacheva Street basement. She identified them by personal belongings, hair, remaining facial features and dental work. An elderly Russian neighbour, M.Z., later told her that on 10 January 2000 three servicemen had approached the basement, pulled Yakhita out, and then thrown an explosive device inside. A powerful blast partially destroyed the pavilion; smoke poured from the basement. The soldiers laughed as Yakhita fainted. The applicant collected the remains and buried them on 10 February 2000 in Valerik cemetery. Yakhita subsequently suffered a severe psychological breakdown and became mentally ill.

The deaths were first investigated as part of criminal case no. 12038, opened on 3 May 2000 after a newspaper report of mass civilian killings by the 205th brigade. A separate investigation (case no. 50080) into the sisters’ murders was opened only on 2 July 2003. The applicant was granted victim status on 5 October 2003. Forensic examination of the remains proved impossible because of the advanced state of burning and decomposition. The investigation was suspended six times for failure to identify perpetrators; each suspension was later quashed by supervising prosecutors as premature and unsubstantiated. Ordered steps—identification of the military unit (variously described as the 205th brigade or unit 3737) that had operated in the district in January 2000, location of the elderly couple who had witnessed the explosion, and resolution of discrepancies in witness statements—were never adequately carried out. The applicant received only limited access to the file and was not kept informed of progress. The Government maintained that unidentified persons had killed the sisters and that the investigation remained ongoing.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that her sisters had been killed by State agents (Article 2), that the investigation had been ineffective (Article 2 procedural limb), that she and her mother had suffered inhuman treatment (Article 3), and that she had been denied an effective remedy (Articles 6 and 13).
001-110212:
The case of Popa and Tănăsescu v. Romania (Application no. 19946/04) concerned two Romanian nationals, Ioan Ştefan Popa and Aurelian Ştefan Tănăsescu, who alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that they had been subjected to an unfair trial resulting in an unfair conviction, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention.

The applicants were involved in the so-called “Car Boot Affair” of January 2000. Their friend R.V. was kidnapped and ill-treated for nearly five weeks by individuals paid by businessman B.M., who sought to recover money allegedly stolen from the boot of his car. On 11 January 2000, R.V. was lured to B.M.’s company headquarters under the pretence of clarifying the theft. There he admitted the theft under threat and was thereafter held captive in various locations until his escape on 14 February 2000.

The applicants’ role was disputed. Prosecutors portrayed them as B.M.’s paid accomplices who helped kidnap and guard R.V. The victim and several witnesses, however, described the applicants as R.V.’s friends who attended the initial meeting to protect him. They stated that the applicants untied R.V., tried to calm the situation and protect him from further harm, and later attempted to locate and free him after he was moved, but were outnumbered and threatened by B.M.’s armed men. Fearing reprisals (including arson and shootings targeting other friends), the applicants did not contact police and later hid in Moldova. They surrendered in May 2001 after publicly announcing their intention in order to obtain protection.

In May 2000 the applicants and ten others were indicted for conspiracy to commit a crime and unlawful deprivation of liberty. Arrest warrants were issued, but the applicants remained at large until they surrendered. At first instance, the Bucharest County Court acquitted them on 15 February 2002. It relied on the victim’s testimony that the applicants had not threatened, beaten or detained him but had instead protected him, together with consistent witness statements. The remaining defendants were convicted and received sentences of around seven years.

The prosecutor appealed. On 5 July 2002 the Bucharest Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal, holding that mere presence at B.M.’s headquarters was insufficient to establish guilt without incriminating evidence. The prosecutor then lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that even if not perpetrators the applicants should be convicted as accomplices.

On 18 September 2003 the High Court of Cassation and Justice heard only oral submissions on the admissibility of the appeals; no further evidence was taken. The applicants were permitted to speak solely at the very end and simply endorsed their lawyers’ arguments. Pronouncement was adjourned. On 13 October 2003 the High Court quashed the acquittals, retained the case for fresh examination without scheduling a new hearing or taking additional evidence, and convicted both applicants of the original charges, imposing seven-year prison sentences. It re-interpreted the same facts, concluding that the applicants had lured R.V. to the meeting and belonged to B.M.’s group, even though they had been present only on the first evening. The sentence was identical to that given to co-defendants who had held and ill-treated the victim for the entire five-week period.

At the material time Romanian criminal procedure did not require the appellate court to hear an accused who had been acquitted at first instance. Subsequent legislative amendments made such a hearing mandatory. The applicants contended that the High Court’s reversal, without hearing them on the merits or receiving new evidence, rendered the proceedings unfair.

The ECtHR case Popa and Tănăsescu v. Romania (no. 19946/04, 10 April 2012) concerned two Romanian nationals who alleged an unfair criminal trial (Article 6 ECHR) resulting in their conviction and seven-year sentences.

The background was the 2000 “Car Boot Affair.” The applicants’ friend R.V. was kidnapped and ill-treated for nearly five weeks by men paid by businessman B.M. over alleged stolen money. Prosecutors charged the applicants (with ten others) with conspiracy and unlawful deprivation of liberty, asserting they had been paid by B.M. to kidnap and guard R.V. R.V. and several witnesses, however, described the applicants as friends who attended an initial meeting only to protect him; they had not threatened, hit or detained him and had tried to ease his situation. The applicants themselves stated they had been present solely on the first evening, had informed other friends of R.V.’s detention, had attempted (unsuccessfully) to locate and free him, and had later fled to Moldova after threats and related violence, without contacting police.

After surrendering in May 2001 they were initially detained, then released under an obligation not to leave the city. On 15 February 2002 the Bucharest County Court acquitted them, relying on R.V.’s consistent statements that they had protected rather than harmed him, corroborated by witnesses. The remaining defendants were convicted. The prosecutor appealed, arguing the applicants belonged to B.M.’s group and had lured R.V. to the meeting. On 5 July 2002 the Bucharest Court of Appeal upheld the acquittals, holding that mere presence at the company headquarters, without incriminatory evidence, did not establish guilt.

The prosecutor then lodged an appeal on points of law to the High Court of Cassation and Justice, seeking conviction at least as accomplices. At the 18 September 2003 hearing only oral submissions on the admissibility of the appeals were heard; no new evidence was taken. The applicants were permitted to speak only at the very end (“last word of the accused”) and simply endorsed their lawyers. Pronouncement was adjourned. On 13 October 2003 the High Court allowed the appeal in part, quashed the two lower-court acquittals without setting a date for a fresh hearing or taking further evidence, and itself convicted the applicants, sentencing each to seven years—the same term imposed on co-defendants who had held R.V. captive for the entire five weeks and subjected him to constant ill-treatment. The High Court accepted the first-instance findings of fact as suitable for review but re-interpreted them, concluding that the applicants had lured R.V. to the site and were members of B.M.’s group, even though they had been present only on the first night.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure then in force, an appeal court was not required to hear an accused who had been acquitted at first instance. (A 2006 amendment later made such a hearing mandatory.) The applicants’ complaint of unfairness centred on this reversal of two acquittals by a court of last instance that recharacterised the facts and imposed heavy sentences without ever hearing them on the merits or allowing them to contest the new legal characterisation.

**Case Summary: Popa and Tănăsescu v. Romania (Application no. 19946/04, ECHR, 10 April 2012)**

The applicants, Romanian nationals Ioan Ştefan Popa (born 1971) and Aurelian Ştefan Tănăsescu (born 1974), alleged a violation of their right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed an unfair conviction arising from proceedings in the so-called “Car Boot Affair.” The first applicant began serving a seven-year sentence in 2007 (later suspended on probation in 2012); the second remained detained.

In January 2000, their friend R.V. was kidnapped and ill-treated for nearly five weeks by individuals paid by businessman B.M. to recover money allegedly stolen from B.M.’s car boot. R.V. was lured to B.M.’s company headquarters on 11 January 2000 after a call from D.C., admitted the theft under threat, and was held in various Bucharest locations before being moved to B.M.’s villa in Breaza. He escaped on 14 February 2000; B.M. then fled Romania.

The applicants’ involvement was disputed. Prosecutors alleged they were paid by B.M. to kidnap and guard R.V. However, R.V., D.C., P.C., and others stated the applicants were R.V.’s friends who attended the meeting to protect him and inform mutual acquaintances. R.V.’s lawyer later sought their acquittal, noting they had eased his situation. The applicants claimed they were present only on the first night, informed friends that R.V. would not be released until the money was returned, attempted (unsuccessfully) to locate and free him after he was taken away, and were forced to withdraw due to threats. They hid in Moldova after further intimidation (including arson and a bullet-riddled car) rather than contacting police, despite knowing they were wanted as witnesses.

A 25 May 2000 indictment charged the applicants and ten others with conspiracy (Article 323 of the Criminal Code) and unlawful deprivation of liberty (Article 189). Arrest warrants issued but they remained in hiding. They surrendered on 27 May 2001 after announcing it publicly for protection. On 18 July 2001 the Bucharest County Court replaced detention with an obligation not to leave the city.

On 15 February 2002 the Bucharest County Court acquitted the applicants. It relied on R.V.’s testimony that they neither threatened, hit, nor imprisoned him but protected him (“maybe if they had not been there he would be dead”) and consistent statements from witnesses B.F., D.C., and M.C. Other defendants were convicted and mostly sentenced to seven years.

The prosecutor appealed, arguing the applicants belonged to B.M.’s group and had invited R.V. to the kidnapping site. On 5 July 2002 the Bucharest Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal, holding that mere presence at the headquarters, without incriminating evidence, was insufficient.

The prosecutor then appealed on points of law, seeking conviction at least as accomplices. At the 18 September 2003 High Court of Cassation and Justice hearing, lawyers made oral submissions only on admissibility of the appeals; no new evidence was taken. The applicants spoke solely at the very end (“ultimul cuvânt”) and simply endorsed their lawyers’ statements. Pronouncement was adjourned.

On 13 October 2003 the High Court allowed the prosecutor’s appeal in part, quashed the acquittals, retained the file, and—without a new hearing or further evidence—convicted both applicants as charged and sentenced each to seven years’ imprisonment. It accepted the lower courts’ factual findings as suitable for review but re-interpreted them: the applicants had “lured” (ademenirea) R.V. to the headquarters and belonged to B.M.’s group. Although their role was limited to the first evening/night, they received the same seven-year term as co-defendants who held R.V. captive for five weeks and inflicted ongoing ill-treatment.

Relevant Romanian Code of Criminal Procedure provisions (as then in force) governed appeals on points of law (see Constantinescu v. Romania and Dănilă v. Romania). A 2006 amendment later required an appellate court quashing an acquittal to hear the accused and take statements.

These facts underpin the alleged unfairness: conviction after two acquittals by a last-instance court that recharacterised evidence, imposed equivalent punishment for a far lesser role, and afforded no meaningful opportunity to be heard or present new material.

001-109241:
The ECHR case Pashayev v. Azerbaijan (no. 36084/06) involves an Azerbaijani national born in 1957, serving a life sentence in Gobustan Prison. He alleged harsh detention conditions, inadequate medical care, unfair civil proceedings held in his absence, and denial of access to court/appeal regarding his 1991 criminal conviction.

The applicant belonged to an organized crime group that carried out robberies and murders across Soviet republics from 1987–1989. On 12 November 1991 the Supreme Court of Azerbaijan, acting as first-instance court, convicted him of organized crime and premeditated murder, imposing a death sentence plus property confiscation. The judgment was final with no appeal available under then-applicable rules. A de facto moratorium on executions operated from 1993. A 10 February 1998 law abolished the death penalty and automatically commuted such sentences to life imprisonment. The applicant spent about 7.5 years in Bayil Prison’s death-row wing before transfer to Gobustan Prison in March 1998.

A 2000 Transitional Law, enacted with a new Code of Criminal Procedure, permitted appeals against pre-2000 final judgments. In January 2005 the applicant lodged an appeal (plus a request to restore a missed time-limit) with the Court of Appeal, noting the original lack of appeal rights. A clerk advised him to apply to the Supreme Court. He did so; a deputy president replied that the complaint concerned only the legislative commutation (which the applicant claimed should have been to 15 years’ imprisonment rather than life) and therefore fell outside judicial jurisdiction, the original conviction being final. Later 2005 filings to both courts produced similar clerk letters directing him to first-instance courts for sentence-execution matters and ignoring the request to review the 1991 conviction itself. Separate 2005–2006 proceedings challenging the commutation as retroactive and seeking to set aside foreign-code sentences were rejected at all levels, confirming the life term.

On detention conditions the applicant described a 9–10 m² cell shared with one other inmate, containing two beds, a cupboard, a fixed table and chairs, and a separated toilet. Floors and ceiling were stone/concrete; heating was inadequate, producing extreme seasonal temperatures. The barred window lacked glass (covered only by polyethylene film in winter), causing stale, unventilated air. Food was poor, unvaried and lacking meat/vitamins; outdoor exercise lasted only 30 minutes daily. The Government countered that cells measured at least 12 m², met national/international standards, had openable windows admitting light and air, plus electric lighting, a ventilator and radio. From 2008 prisoners could watch television (4 hours weekdays, 6 hours weekends); a library existed; food and sanitation were acceptable; exercise lasted one hour.

Regarding medical care, the applicant said he had been healthy before arrest. A 1991 pre-trial X-ray showed a lung shadow, but treatment was refused. In Bayil he shared cells with two tuberculosis sufferers who later died; he began coughing blood and self-medicated with bought antibiotics (1992–1998) because TB patients were not transferred to specialized facilities and mortality was high. After transfer he received only a superficial 1998 examination (diagnosed with bronchitis) and was first seen by a TB specialist in November 1999. Brief 2004 admission to the Specialized Medical Establishment for Prisoners with Tuberculosis (SME) found pulmonary TB but deemed DOTS unnecessary. A 2005 SME stay provided DOTS (February–March), which he refused because of inadequate conditions; residual symptoms persisted from the 1998–2004 gap in care. The Government disputed infection in Bayil (the co-inmate’s TB was non-contagious) and asserted regular examinations from arrival in 1998, treatment of bronchitis, no TB reactivation, ICRC-observed 2004–2006 tests that were negative, DOTS that the applicant himself discontinued, and overall care meeting WHO standards (citing Green Light Committee reports). Residual symptoms were limited.

In February 2007 the applicant brought a civil claim against Bayil authorities for health damage from TB contracted through poor conditions and cell-sharing with infected inmates. He submitted inmate statements, requested that former prisoners be heard, and asked to attend hearings personally. The Sabail District Court dismissed the claim on 29 May 2007 (applicant represented but absent; judgment silent on the attendance request), finding no proof of deliberate placement or ill-treatment. The Baku Court of Appeal (30 November 2007) and Supreme Court (20 June 2008) upheld the dismissal after hearings likewise held in his absence (lawyer present) and remaining silent on the repeated personal-attendance requests. Domestic law permitted parties to appear in person or by representative but was silent on transferring prisoners for civil hearings.

The case of Pashayev v. Azerbaijan (no. 36084/06) involves Chingiz Pashayev (born 1957), an Azerbaijani national serving a life sentence in Gobustan Prison. He alleged harsh detention conditions, inadequate medical care (particularly regarding tuberculosis), unfair civil proceedings held in his absence, and denial of access to court plus the right of appeal against his 1991 conviction.

Pashayev belonged to an organized criminal group responsible for robberies and murders across Soviet republics from 1987 to 1989. On 12 November 1991 the Supreme Court of Azerbaijan, sitting as first-instance court, convicted him of organized crime and premeditated murder, imposing the death penalty plus property confiscation. The judgment was final with no appeal possible at the time. A de facto moratorium on executions existed from 1993. The death penalty was abolished in 1998; by Law of 10 February 1998 all such sentences, including the applicant’s, were automatically commuted to life imprisonment.

A 2000 Transitional Law accompanying the new Code of Criminal Procedure permitted appeals against pre-2000 final judgments. On 24 January 2005 Pashayev lodged an appeal with the Court of Appeal (plus a request to restore any missed time-limit), stressing that no appeal right had existed in 1991. A clerk advised him to apply to the Supreme Court. A Supreme Court deputy president replied that the matter (which the applicant framed as unlawful commutation to life rather than 15 years) lay outside judicial jurisdiction because the conviction was final and commutation was legislative. Later 2005 filings produced similar administrative letters directing him to first-instance courts for sentence-execution issues, without examining the 1991 conviction.

Separately, in August 2005 Pashayev sued in Garadagh District Court, arguing that commutation was retroactively detrimental and that sentences under other Soviet codes should be lifted. The district court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court (March 2006) all upheld the life sentence.

After conviction Pashayev spent about 7.5 years on death row in Bayil Prison’s 5th wing, then from March 1998 in Gobustan. He described a 9–10 m² cell shared with another inmate, inadequate heating, a window without glass (covered by plastic film in winter), stale unventilated air, poor monotonous food lacking meat and vitamins, and only 30 minutes’ daily outdoor exercise. The Government stated cells measured at least 12 m², windows opened, ventilation and lighting existed, television and library access were later granted, food and sanitation were adequate, and exercise lasted one hour.

Pashayev claimed he was healthy before arrest. In 1991 pre-trial detention an X-ray showed a lung shadow but treatment was refused. In Bayil he shared cells with two inmates who later died of tuberculosis; he began coughing blood and self-medicated with purchased antibiotics (1992–1998). Tuberculosis patients were generally untreated in cells, with high mortality. After transfer to Gobustan, examinations were incomplete; bronchitis was diagnosed in 1998 and tuberculosis in 1999. In November 2004 he spent seven days at the Specialised Medical Establishment (SME) for pulmonary tuberculosis but was not placed on WHO DOTS treatment. In 2005 he received DOTS but refused it because of conditions; he later claimed residual symptoms from years of inadequate care.

The Government disputed contraction in prison, noting a non-contagious cellmate. Examinations from arrival in 1998 recorded a prior history of tuberculosis without worsening. Bronchitis was treated successfully. Regular checks through 2004 showed no reactivation. SME examinations (some in ICRC presence) in 2004–2006 found focal tuberculosis without need for in-patient care or later negative results. DOTS began in February 2005 but stopped at the applicant’s refusal. Subsequent treatment was described as adequate and WHO-compliant, with only limited residual symptoms.

On 23 February 2007 Pashayev filed a civil claim against Bayil Prison authorities seeking compensation for contracting tuberculosis through poor conditions and placement with infected inmates. He requested personal attendance and witness hearings. Sabail District Court dismissed the claim on 29 May 2007, finding no proof of deliberate placement or ill-treatment; he was absent though represented, and the judgment ignored his attendance request. The Baku Court of Appeal (30 November 2007) and Supreme Court (20 June 2008) similarly dismissed appeals, always in his absence (lawyer present) and silent on the attendance request. Domestic civil procedure allows parties to appear in person or by representative, but prison rules are silent on transferring convicted persons for civil hearings.

These facts form the core of the alleged Convention violations concerning detention conditions, medical care, procedural fairness and access to appellate review.

The case of Panaitescu v. Romania (Application no. 30909/06) was brought by Romanian national Ştefan Panaitescu (born 1944), who died on 3 December 2006; his son continued the application as heir. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from the Romanian authorities’ failure to provide him with medically necessary cancer treatment despite his statutory entitlement and final court orders.

Under Law no. 189/2000, persons persecuted on ethnic grounds between 1940 and 1945 were entitled to priority free medical assistance and medicines, both as inpatients and outpatients. In 2002 the applicant successfully challenged a denial of these benefits; a 3 June 2002 Oradea Appeal Court decision (final 28 January 2003) confirmed his status. A commission decision of 2 April 2003 expressly recognised his right to such care from 1 April 2001.

In April 2005 the applicant was diagnosed with stage-III kidney cancer that had affected a lung; he underwent surgery at Oradea State Hospital on 4 May 2005. He claimed the hospital provided only supportive care (vitamins and saline) rather than specific oncological treatment. He therefore sought care at the Cluj-Napoca Oncological Institute. From July 2005 he self-funded Avastin and Roferon, achieving partial remission confirmed by his treating oncologist in letters of 16 September 2005 and 12 January 2006. Unable to continue paying, he submitted repeated requests (including a 27 September 2005 bailiff notification) to the Bihor Health Insurance Service (CAS), the Public Health Office and the National Health Insurance Service (CNAS), warning that refusal would endanger his life and amount to murder.

On 10 November 2005 he sued CNAS and CAS. By judgment of 12 December 2005 the Oradea Appeal Court ordered the defendants to supply Avastin and Roferon (and any other prescribed drugs) free of charge and with priority for the medically indicated period, and to reimburse costs already incurred. The court rejected the argument that Avastin was absent from the 2005 reimbursement list (Government Decision no. 235/2005, as amended), holding that lists could and should be updated promptly when a new drug had proven efficacy and no equivalent existed; delay would harm patients. The High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld this on 19 April 2006, noting Avastin had been nationally approved since June 2005.

The judgment was never enforced. On 23 May 2006 the applicant demanded urgent compliance, citing deterioration and invoking Article 2. CAS contested enforcement on 6 June 2006, claiming it lacked authority to purchase or compel pharmacies to dispense the drugs and that reimbursement amounts were unspecified; it also sought suspension. The applicant informed the Court that treatment ceased, substitutes caused side-effects, the disease progressed, and he entered a German experimental trial (Nexavar) in May 2006. The enforcement challenge was dismissed only on 22 March 2010 (after his death), the authorities arguing the claims were time-barred or rendered moot.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: despite a clear statutory right, a final 2003 recognition of status, and binding 2005–2006 court orders, the authorities’ administrative refusal, delays and procedural resistance deprived the applicant of potentially life-prolonging medication, causing physical decline and mental anguish until his death.

The case of Ali Güneş v. Turkey (App. no. 9829/07) before the European Court of Human Rights arose from events on 28 June 2004 during the NATO summit in Istanbul. The applicant, a 36-year-old high-school teacher, union executive and public-sector union member, joined fellow teachers at one of 13 officially designated demonstration sites (the square outside Mecidiyeköy Underground Station) to read a press statement.

The parties’ accounts diverge sharply. The applicant maintained that the group was unarmed and peaceful. Police nonetheless seized him and others by the arms, sprayed them with tear gas and beat them. He was held at a police station for eleven hours before a prosecutor ordered his release. The Government asserted that, after the statement had been read, officers twice ordered the group to disperse. The demonstrators refused, staged a sit-in and then attacked officers with stones and banner sticks, damaging nearby cars and injuring police. Tear gas was used only thereafter; the applicant was among eleven people arrested.

Contemporary documents and photographs paint a more precise picture. A police report recorded that the demonstrators, having been warned they could not march to Taksim Square, attacked officers with sticks and sat down; the Rapid Response Force then dispersed them and made arrests. A photograph published the same day in the newspaper Sabah shows the applicant held between two officers, one of whom is spraying gas directly into his nose and mouth at very close range.

Medical evidence obtained that day is consistent with both chemical and physical force. At 11.30 a.m. a doctor at Haseki Hospital noted bilateral ocular redness and referred the applicant to an ophthalmologist, who confirmed hyperaemia in both eyes. A later examination (report 3015) recorded two large bruises (8 cm and 5 \times 8 cm) below the shoulders together with reddened eyes. Ten co-arrestees likewise displayed injuries. A further medical form completed at 6.45 p.m. was left almost entirely blank.

In his statement to the prosecutor the applicant denied any offence, insisted he had been exercising democratic rights and specifically mentioned the use of pepper spray; a lawyer was present. On 7 September 2004 he lodged a formal complaint alleging truncheon blows, punches, kicks and close-range tear-gas spraying, identifying the officers from press photographs.

Unknown to him, a prosecutor had already, on 30 June 2004, decided not to prosecute the nine named officers, holding that they had acted within their statutory powers. The decision listed the applicant among sixteen “complainants” and stated that it would be notified, yet it was never served. Only after the applicant inquired in 2007 did he receive a copy (November 2007). His subsequent objection, which highlighted the ignored medical reports and photographs, was dismissed by the Beyoğlu Assize Court on 8 February 2008 as procedurally correct.

These facts—direct facial spraying of tear gas causing documented ocular injury, bruises consistent with beating, eleven-hour detention, and a prosecutorial decision taken within two days that was neither communicated nor based on the available medical and photographic evidence—form the core of the alleged Article 3 violation.

The case of Kaperzyński v. Poland (Application no. 43206/07) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, Przemysław Kaperzyński (born 1964, resident of Olsztyn), was editor-in-chief of the local weekly newspaper Iławski Tydzień.

On 17 October 2005 the newspaper published an article co-authored by the applicant, entitled “Municipality in danger; authorities fail to see problem.” It described serious deficiencies in the Iława municipality’s sewage system, warning of public-health risks, the need for costly investment, a shortage of funds, and the authorities’ slow and incompetent response. The piece accused officials of placing budgetary savings above residents’ safety, noted unsatisfactory water quality, and criticised the mayor for failing to resolve the problems despite two terms in office.

The same day the mayor sent a letter to the newspaper. Its opening paragraph was ironic, questioning the applicant’s motives, implying self-interest, and doubting whether the paper even had readers. Invoking sections 31 and 32 of the 1984 Press Act, the mayor formally requested publication of a rectification. He asserted that sewage development was a municipal priority, listed completed projects from the preceding five years and planned works for 2007–2013, and referred to water-quality monitoring and modernisation efforts.

The applicant neither replied nor published the letter (or any excerpt). The municipality subsequently lodged a private indictment charging him with the offence of failing to publish a rectification or reply under section 46 § 1 of the Press Act.

In written pleadings the applicant argued that the letter did not constitute a “rectification” within the meaning of section 31: it was not confined to facts, lacked objectivity, and contained personal attacks on his integrity and that of his journalists, rendering it more akin to a “reply” expressing value judgments. It also exceeded twice the length of the original article, contrary to section 33. He further maintained that the letter itself infringed personal rights, entitling him under the same provision to refuse publication as incompatible with principles of social coexistence.

On 13 December 2006 the Elbląg District Court convicted the applicant. It imposed a four-month restriction of liberty consisting of 20 hours of community service per month, suspended for two years; a two-year ban on practising journalism; and an order that the judgment be displayed at the Iława Municipal Office. The court found that the applicant had a statutory duty to publish the letter, that he had offered no legitimate grounds for refusal, and that he had not even informed the mayor of his reasons. Because the original article concerned a matter of significant public importance, the failure to publish the municipality’s response had prevented a fair public debate and undermined democratic confidence in the local executive.

The applicant’s appeal, which essentially reiterated his earlier arguments, was dismissed by the Elbląg Regional Court on 29 March 2007.

The 1984 Press Act obliged editors to publish, free of charge, factually based rectifications of inaccurate statements or replies to statements that might infringe personal rights. Refusal (or publication contrary to statutory conditions) was a criminal offence punishable by a fine or restriction of liberty. Subsequent Constitutional Court judgments (2004 and 2010) later found aspects of these provisions unconstitutionally imprecise, but they remained in force at the material time.

These events—the publication of criticism on a genuine matter of public interest, the mixed and polemical character of the requested “rectification,” the applicant’s refusal, and the ensuing criminal conviction that included a professional ban—constitute the core facts underlying the alleged breach of Article 10.

The case of *Kaperzyński v. Poland* (Application no. 43206/07), decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) on 3 April 2012 (final on 3 July 2012), originated in an application lodged on 28 September 2007 by Polish national Przemysław Kaperzyński. He alleged a violation of his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

At the relevant time, the applicant served as editor-in-chief of the local weekly newspaper *Iławski Tydzień*. On 17 October 2005, the paper published an article he co-authored, titled “Municipality in danger; authorities fail to see problem.” The piece described in detail the sewage system in the Iława municipality, asserting that it posed significant public-health risks requiring extensive investment amid a shortage of funds. It accused municipal authorities of handling the issues slowly and incompetently, prioritizing cost savings over prevention of health dangers, and failing to address unsatisfactory water quality. The article specifically criticised the mayor, who had served two terms, for not resolving these problems.

That same day the mayor wrote to the newspaper. The letter opened in ironic terms, questioning the applicant’s intentions, implying personal motives, criticising the article’s tone, and doubting whether the newspaper even had readers. It then formally requested publication of a rectification under sections 31 § 1 and 32 of the Press Act 1984. The letter listed sewage-network projects completed over the preceding five years, three projects planned for 2007–2013, and stated that water quality was monitored by the competent services, with further modernisation work under way.

The applicant neither replied nor published the letter (or any excerpts) as a rectification or reply. The municipality of Iława subsequently lodged a private bill of indictment charging him with the offence of failing to publish a rectification or reply, contrary to section 46 § 1 of the Press Act.

In written pleadings dated 4 December 2005 the applicant argued that the letter could not be regarded as a rectification: it was not factually based or objective, its opening contained personal criticism and innuendos about his character, motives and the newspaper’s journalists, and it more closely resembled a “reply” expressing value judgments. Even if viewed as a rectification, it exceeded twice the length of the original article, breaching section 33 requirements. He further contended that the letter infringed his personal rights and those of other journalists, entitling him under section 33 to refuse publication as incompatible with the principles of social coexistence.

On 13 December 2006 the Elbląg District Court convicted the applicant. It imposed a four-month restriction of liberty (20 hours of community service per month), suspended for two years, deprived him of the right to practise journalism for two years, and ordered the judgment displayed at the Iława Municipal Office. The court held that the applicant had a clear statutory duty to publish the letter, that he had previously published rectifications, and that no objective grounds justified refusal; he had not even notified the mayor of his reasons. The failure, the court found, had seriously harmed the municipality by preventing fair public debate and undermining public confidence in a democratically elected executive, especially given the article’s discussion of a matter of significant local importance.

The applicant appealed, reiterating his earlier arguments. On 29 March 2007 the Elbląg Regional Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction.

Relevant domestic law comprised the Press Act 1984. Section 31 required editors-in-chief to publish, free of charge, a factually based rectification of untrue or inaccurate statements or a factually based reply to statements that might infringe personal rights. Section 32 prohibited unauthorised alteration that would weaken the text’s significance. Section 33 permitted refusal if the submission failed to meet statutory requirements, with a duty to notify the claimant of the reasons. Section 46 § 1 made refusal (or non-compliant publication) a criminal offence punishable by a fine or restriction of liberty. Subsequent Constitutional Court judgments (2004 and 2010) criticised the lack of precision in these criminal provisions, finding them incompatible with the principle of *nullum crimen sine lege*, though they remained applicable for a transitional period.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the criminal conviction, professional ban and associated measures constituted an unjustified interference with his freedom of expression.

The mayor, despite two terms in office, was said to have failed to address the issues properly.

That same day the mayor wrote to the newspaper. The letter opened with ironic remarks questioning the applicant’s motives, suggesting self-interest, criticising the article’s tone, and doubting whether the paper had readers. It then formally requested publication of a rectification under sections 31 § 1 and 32 of the 1984 Press Act. The mayor listed sewage and sanitary projects completed over the previous five years, three further projects planned for 2007–2013, and asserted that water quality was monitored by the competent services.

The applicant neither replied nor published the letter. The municipality later lodged a private bill of indictment charging him with the offence of failing to publish a requested rectification or reply (Press Act s. 46 § 1).

In written pleadings of 4 December 2005 the applicant argued that the letter could not be treated as a “rectification.” It was not factually based or objective, contained personal criticisms and innuendos about his character, motives and the professionalism of the paper’s journalists, and exceeded twice the length of the original article. It more closely resembled a “reply” expressing value judgments. Even if it were a rectification, s. 33 of the Press Act obliged him to refuse publication because its form and content were incompatible with the principles of social coexistence and infringed personal rights.

On 13 December 2006 the Elbląg District Court convicted him. It imposed a four-month restriction of liberty consisting of 20 hours’ community service per month, suspended for two years; deprived him of the right to practise journalism for two years; and ordered the judgment displayed at the municipal office. The court found the facts essentially undisputed: the applicant had neither published the letter nor explained his refusal, despite a clear statutory duty of which he was aware. No legitimate grounds existed for non-compliance. The article had addressed a matter of significant local importance; by preventing publication of the municipality’s response the applicant had obstructed fair public debate and undermined democratic confidence in the elected authorities.

The applicant’s appeal, which reiterated his earlier arguments, was dismissed by the Elbląg Regional Court on 29 March 2007.

These events constitute the factual core of the alleged Article 10 violation: a criminal conviction, including a professional ban, imposed for refusing to publish a letter that the applicant considered neither a proper rectification nor a reply that he was legally required to print.
001-110253:
The case of İlbeyi Kemaloğlu and Meriye Kemaloğlu v. Turkey (no. 19986/06) arose from the death of the applicants’ seven-year-old son Atalay on 22–23 January 2004 and the subsequent administrative and criminal proceedings. The applicants alleged, inter alia, a violation of the right to life (Article 2) through the authorities’ failure to protect their child and of the right of access to court through the denial of legal aid that extinguished their compensation claim.

Istanbul was struck by a heavy snowstorm on 22 January 2004. The Ministry of Education ordered schools to close a day early. Atalay travelled to primary school on a free municipal shuttle. After school reports were distributed, classes ended in the early afternoon. Because the municipality had not been notified, the shuttle never arrived. Atalay set out on foot for the 4 km journey home. When he failed to return, his parents alerted the police; his frozen body was found the next day beside a riverbed.

School inspectors concluded that the deputy headmaster had been at fault for not informing the municipal shuttle service and issued a disciplinary warning. On 6 August 2004 the applicants brought two actions before the Istanbul Administrative Court against the Ministry of Education and two municipalities, claiming substantial pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for negligence. They applied for legal aid, producing muhtar certificates of indigence, District Governor attestations that they owned no immovable property, and evidence of tax debts. On 8 June 2005 the court rejected legal aid without reasons. The applicants were then required to pay court fees of approximately EUR 3 000 and EUR 2 600 within one month. Unable to do so, the court discontinued the proceedings on 29 December 2005.

In parallel the applicants lodged a criminal complaint against the headmaster, deputy headmaster and class teacher. The Ümraniye District Governor initially refused authorisation to prosecute, relying on a report that found no fault. The Istanbul Regional Administrative Court quashed that decision, holding that sufficient evidence existed. An indictment for misconduct in office followed; the applicants joined as civil parties. On 28 June 2006 the Ümraniye Criminal Court acquitted the accused, reasoning that the death was not the result of wilful neglect, that it was unreasonable to expect staff to supervise 2 400 pupils after dismissal, and that the child’s death in the storm could not have been foreseen. The court declined jurisdiction over any “service-related fault.” The Court of Cassation later quashed the judgment on a purely formal ground (missing clerk’s signature) and remitted the case. On 13 May 2011 the same court again acquitted the officials on identical reasoning. An appeal remained pending.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the State’s positive obligation under Article 2 to take reasonable steps to safeguard a young child’s life (timely notification of early closure, organisation of transport, and foreseeable weather risks) and the effective denial of access to a court for compensation because legal aid was refused despite documented poverty, while the criminal process produced only repeated acquittals that left the applicants without an effective domestic remedy.

The case of İlbeyi Kemaloğlu and Meriye Kemaloğlu v. Turkey (Application no. 19986/06) arose from the death of the applicants’ seven-year-old son Atalay on 22 January 2004 amid a severe snowstorm in Istanbul. Acting on Ministry of Education instructions, schools closed a day early for winter break. Atalay travelled to his primary school on a free municipal shuttle. After bulletins were distributed, classes ended in the early afternoon, well before the usual time. Because the municipality had not been notified of the early dismissal, the shuttle never arrived. Atalay set out on foot for his home four kilometres away. When he failed to return that evening the applicants alerted the police, but his frozen body was discovered the following day near a riverbed.

A subsequent inquiry by the Istanbul Education Directorate’s primary-school inspectors established that the deputy headmaster had failed to inform the municipal shuttle service of the premature closure; he received only a disciplinary warning. The applicants then brought two administrative actions against the Ministry of Education and the relevant municipalities, seeking substantial pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages on the ground that official negligence had caused their son’s death. They applied for legal aid, producing certificates from the local headman attesting to their indigence, confirmation that they owned no immovable property, and evidence of outstanding tax debts. The Istanbul Administrative Court rejected the legal-aid request without giving reasons. The applicants were then required to pay court fees of approximately EUR 3 000 and EUR 2 600 (well in excess of the prevailing monthly minimum wage of about EUR 245). Unable to do so, they saw the proceedings discontinued in December 2005.

In parallel the applicants lodged a criminal complaint against the school headmaster, deputy headmaster and Atalay’s class teacher. The district governor initially refused authorisation to prosecute, relying on a report that found no fault. The applicants successfully challenged that decision before the Istanbul Regional Administrative Court, which held that sufficient evidence existed to proceed. An indictment for misconduct in office was filed and the applicants joined as civil parties, reserving their compensation claims. At trial the class teacher stated that she had told pupils the previous day that their parents should collect them when bulletins were issued. A psychologist testified that a seven-year-old could not reasonably be expected to devise effective solutions in an unforeseen emergency or to appreciate the mortal danger of walking home alone in a blizzard. Nevertheless the Ümraniye Criminal Court acquitted all three defendants in 2006, reasoning that the death was not the product of deliberate neglect, that school staff could not be expected to supervise the departure of 2 400 pupils, and that they could not have foreseen the fatal outcome. The court also declined jurisdiction over any service-related fault. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on a purely procedural ground (a missing clerk’s signature) and remitted the case. A second acquittal on identical reasoning followed in 2011; the subsequent appeal remained pending.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: a failure by the authorities to take the elementary precaution of notifying transport providers of an early closure, thereby exposing a young child to lethal weather; an administrative investigation that resulted only in a minor disciplinary measure; the refusal of legal aid that effectively barred the parents from pursuing civil remedies; and criminal proceedings that twice ended in acquittal without a thorough examination of official responsibility.

The applicants, İlbeyi and Meriye Kemaloğlu, are the parents of seven-year-old Atalay Kemaloğlu, who died in January 2004. On 22 January 2004 a heavy snowstorm struck Istanbul. Following instructions from the Ministry of Education, schools closed a day early for the winter break. Atalay travelled to his primary school on a free municipal shuttle. After school bulletins were distributed, classes were dismissed in the early afternoon without notification to the municipality. The shuttle therefore did not arrive. Atalay, who had not enrolled for a paid school bus, attempted to walk the 4 km home. When he failed to return, his parents contacted the police, but he could not be located. His frozen body was found the next day near a river bed.

An internal investigation by Primary School Inspectors concluded that the deputy headmaster had been at fault for failing to inform the municipal shuttle service of the early closure. A disciplinary warning was issued.

The applicants instituted two sets of proceedings. In August 2004 they lodged administrative actions against the Ministry of Education and the relevant municipalities, seeking substantial pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for alleged negligence. They applied for legal aid, submitting certificates from the local headman confirming their indigency, from the District Governor confirming they owned no immovable property, and records of tax debts. In June 2005 the Istanbul Administrative Court rejected the legal-aid request without reasons. The applicants were then required to pay court fees of approximately EUR 3,000 and EUR 2,600 respectively (against a monthly minimum wage of about EUR 245). When they failed to do so, the court discontinued the proceedings in December 2005.

Separately, in February 2004 the applicants filed a criminal complaint against the school headmaster, deputy headmaster and class teacher. The public prosecutor sought authorisation to prosecute under the Law on the Prosecution of Civil Servants. The District Governor refused authorisation on the basis of a report finding no fault. The applicants successfully objected; the Istanbul Regional Administrative Court held that sufficient evidence existed. An indictment was filed in October 2004 charging the officials with misconduct in office. The applicants joined as civil parties.

At trial the class teacher stated she had told pupils the previous day that parents should attend for bulletin distribution. A psychologist’s expert opinion noted that a seven-year-old could not reasonably be expected to find effective solutions or foresee dangers when walking home alone in a severe storm. In June 2006 the Ümraniye Criminal Court acquitted all three accused, holding that the death was not the result of deliberate action, that it was unreasonable to expect school authorities to monitor 2,400 pupils after dismissal, that misconduct required wilful neglect, and that the officials could not reasonably have foreseen that Atalay would freeze to death. The court added that it lacked jurisdiction to examine service-related fault. The Court of Cassation later quashed the judgment on a procedural ground (missing clerk’s signature) and remitted the case. In May 2011 the same court again acquitted the accused on identical reasoning. The applicants’ appeal remained pending.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints concerning the authorities’ alleged failure to protect their son’s life and to provide an effective investigation, as well as their inability to obtain a determination of their compensation claim owing to the denial of legal aid.
001-110452:
The case of Kalucza v. Hungary (Application no. 57693/10) concerns a Hungarian national, Matild Kalucza (born 1969), who alleged that the authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligations under Articles 2, 3 and 8 of the Convention. She claimed this left her forced to cohabit in a jointly owned Budapest apartment with her former partner Gy.B., who subjected her to repeated physical and psychological abuse.

In July 2000 the applicant and her then-husband purchased an undivided shared-property flat (two-thirds registered to her). After their divorce she was to buy out his share. In April 2005 she entered an unregistered cohabitation with Gy.B., who paid the former husband’s share and later acquired title to that portion via a January 2006 sale. Gy.B. renovated the premises into two separate units. The applicant briefly lived with him elsewhere before returning to the apartment in March 2006; Gy.B. retained keys, slept there regularly and, from late 2006, resided there after registering the address as his official residence. Their relationship ended around January 2007, yet Gy.B. remained against her wishes. In April 2007 he sold his share to a third party but later challenged the sale; those proceedings remained pending.

From October 2005 onward the relationship deteriorated into frequent mutual verbal and physical violence. More than a dozen medical reports documented the applicant’s injuries, including contusions to the head, face, chest, neck and limbs (healing times of 8–10 days), a violently broken little finger (6–8 weeks healing) in June 2007, and a 2010 brain concussion with loss of consciousness that required two days’ hospitalisation. She lodged numerous criminal complaints against Gy.B. for rape, assault and harassment. Outcomes included his 2008 acquittal on rape charges (her allegations found not credible), mutual convictions for assault in 2009 (Gy.B. released on one-year parole, the applicant on three-year parole) and 2011 (both fined; each found to have initiated one incident and the other to have acted in self-defence), several acquittals of Gy.B. for lack of evidence, discontinued harassment investigations, and two still-pending assault cases against him. The applicant herself was convicted of disorderly conduct, grievous bodily harm and assault on several occasions; other investigations against her were discontinued.

She twice applied for restraining orders under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Both were dismissed (2010 decisions, upheld on appeal) because the courts found mutual animosity, both parties’ involvement in violence, and the statutory conditions unmet (no sufficient risk of recidivism attributable solely to Gy.B. or of his influencing proceedings). Parallel civil proceedings to determine ownership and to order Gy.B. to vacate the flat were repeatedly suspended pending resolution of related property disputes. When the applicant changed locks, police compelled her to grant Gy.B. access because of his registered residence. A notary later ordered him to provide her keys after he changed them, but subsequent requests to delete his registration and evict him were rejected as the notary lacked competence and he was actually living there. Criminal trespass proceedings were initiated against the applicant herself after she again changed the locks in 2010.

Domestic law provided limited protection: a 2009 statute on restraining orders for domestic violence did not apply to unregistered former partners, and registration of residence conferred no property rights. The applicant thus remained unable to exclude Gy.B. from the shared home despite repeated requests for assistance.

The applicant, Ms Matild Kalucza (born 1969), lodged her ECHR application against Hungary in September 2010. She alleged that the authorities had failed in their positive obligations under Articles 2, 3 and 8 (later examined under Articles 8 and 13) by not protecting her from repeated physical and psychological abuse by her former partner, Gy.B., with whom she was compelled to cohabit owing to unresolved property issues.

In 2000 the applicant and her then-husband purchased a Budapest flat (two-thirds registered in her name). After their divorce she was to acquire his share. In 2005 she began an unregistered relationship with Gy.B., who paid for the husband’s share and became its owner in January 2006. He renovated the property into two units. The applicant lived with him intermittently; he obtained keys, stayed regularly and had his residence registered at the flat in November 2006. Their relationship ended around January 2007, but Gy.B. remained against her wishes. In April 2007 he sold his share to a third party yet later challenged the sale; those proceedings remain pending.

From 2005 onward the applicant sustained numerous injuries (contusions to head, face, chest, neck and limbs; a broken finger; concussion with loss of consciousness) documented in more than a dozen medical reports, typically with 8–12 days’ healing time. Specific incidents included:
- October 2005: injuries; the court later found she had initiated the assault and Gy.B. had acted in self-defence, convicting her of disorderly conduct.
- December 2006: rape complaint; Gy.B. was acquitted in 2008 because her account was deemed not credible.
- June 2007: broken finger; both were convicted (Gy.B. of assault, the applicant of grievous bodily harm). Police had intervened but left; the assault resumed.
- April 2008 onward: further assault complaints and a first request for a restraining order. After delays (transport strike, postponements) the request was refused in January 2010 (upheld on appeal) because both parties were at fault and statutory conditions were unmet. Proceedings remain pending.
- December 2009–January 2010: additional injuries and complaints; one investigation was discontinued as injuries were not “serious”; another (including a failed psychiatric examination of Gy.B.) remains pending.
- April 2010: concussion requiring two days’ hospitalisation plus a further assault. Mutual complaints were joined. A second restraining-order request was refused (June 2010, upheld July 2010) on grounds of mutual involvement and lack of risk to the proceedings. In July 2011 both were convicted of assault and fined; each had initiated one of the two incidents.

Overall, Gy.B. was acquitted four times, convicted twice (parole and a fine) and faced two pending assault cases. The applicant was convicted several times; some of her complaints were discontinued or she declined to prosecute. Harassment investigations were dropped for insufficient evidence.

Efforts to remove Gy.B. from the flat were equally unsuccessful. His 2005 civil claim for renovation costs and her 2006 ownership action were both suspended pending related litigation. A 2006 trespass complaint was discontinued because he was then registered as owner. After he changed the locks (2007) a notary ordered him to provide keys; when the applicant later changed the locks, police forced her to admit him as a registered resident. A 2008 request to the notary to cancel his registered address and evict him was dismissed (2011) as the notary lacked competence and he was actually living there. Her April 2008 civil eviction action remains pending after suspension. In 2010 she again changed the locks and was herself charged with trespass.

Hungarian law permitted short-term restraining orders under the Code of Criminal Procedure and a 2009 domestic-violence statute, but the latter did not cover unregistered former partners. Residence registration conferred no property rights; civil possession-protection and interim measures existed but were not effectively applied.

The case of Kalucza v. Hungary (ECtHR, Application no. 57693/10, judgment 24 April 2012) concerns a Hungarian applicant's complaint that domestic authorities failed in their positive obligations under Articles 2, 3 and 8 of the Convention (communicated under Articles 8 and 13). The applicant moved between his house and the flat; she returned in March 2006. Gy.B. retained keys, slept there regularly, then moved in. His residence was registered at her address in November 2006. Their relationship ended around January 2007, but Gy.B. continued occupying the apartment against her wishes. In April 2007 he sold his share to a third party then challenged the sale (proceedings still pending).

From 2005 onward the relationship involved regular mutual verbal and physical assaults. Medical reports documented the applicant's injuries (contusions to head, face, chest, neck, arms, etc., typically healing in 8–12 days), including a 2005 report of finger/arm/ankle injuries, a 2007 report of a violently broken finger (healing 6–8 weeks), and a 2010 report of brain concussion with loss of consciousness (hospitalized two days). Outcomes were mixed: Gy.B. was acquitted four times (including of rape in 2008, for lack of credible evidence) and convicted twice of assault (parole or fine). The applicant was convicted of disorderly conduct, grievous bodily harm and assault. Some proceedings were discontinued (insufficient evidence or her failure to pursue); two assault cases against him and trespass against her remained pending. Both were dismissed (2010): courts found mutual fault, no well-founded risk justifying restraint only against Gy.B., and conditions unmet. Regulatory-offence trespass proceedings against him were discontinued because he was registered as owner. After he changed locks (2007), a notary ordered him to give her keys. When she changed locks, police forced access (his registered address). A 2008 request to delete his residence registration and order him out was dismissed (wrong authority; actual occupation prevented deletion). 2008 eviction proceedings remain pending (suspended). Her 2010 lock change prompted trespass charges against her.

Residence registration created no property rights; civil-law possession protection and interim measures existed but were not effectively used. The facts highlight repeated official inaction, delays, mutual-blame findings, and inability to separate the parties despite documented violence.
001-110449:
The case of Yordanova and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 25446/06) concerns 23 Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin who, with their families (including children), occupied informal homes in the Batalova Vodenitsa neighbourhood of Sofia. Some applicants or their ancestors had settled there in the late 1960s–1970s after state expropriation of the land for housing projects that left certain plots vacant (originally earmarked as unused green space). Others arrived in the 1990s. They constructed unauthorised single-storey dwellings without sewage, plumbing or official recognition; water came from public fountains. The settlement housed 200–300 people. The homes failed basic construction and safety standards and could not be legalised without major reconstruction. Applicants never applied for regularisation, citing poverty and social isolation.

Until 2005 the authorities took no eviction steps, despite the land becoming municipal property in 1996. Adverse possession of state/municipal land was impossible before 1996 and was later suspended by legislation (extended to 2014), preventing title acquisition. Neighbour complaints from the 1990s onward alleged sanitation problems, livestock, crime and aesthetic blight; non-Roma residents demonstrated for eviction and formed pressure groups. Media and politicians frequently called for clearance of “Roma ghettos.” In 2000 former owners whose land rights had been restored complained; the municipal council offered land swaps but produced no overall plan. A 2003 local plan envisaged development; adjacent plots were transferred to a private investor in 2005–2006.

On 8 September 2005 the district mayor ordered approximately 180 residents (including the applicants) to vacate within seven days under section 65 of the Municipal Property Act as unlawful occupiers, warning of police removal. After non-compliance a 17 September 2005 order set forcible eviction for 27 September and contemplated demolition. Applicants obtained a stay. A 28 September 2005 agreement promised alternative housing for registered residents in exchange for hygiene improvements, but the municipality never implemented it. Sofia City Court (January 2006) and the Supreme Administrative Court (June 2006) upheld the order solely because the applicants lacked a legal title; the houses therefore belonged to the municipality under the Property Act. The courts treated long-term occupation with official acquiescence, proportionality and Convention arguments as irrelevant.

A June 2006 eviction attempt was halted by European Parliament pressure. The district mayor publicly stated that the occupants, occupying land unlawfully, could not register as persons in housing need and would receive no priority over the waiting list; she disavowed the 2005 agreement as pre-electoral. Anti-Roma remarks by officials (e.g., comparing Roma settlement to a refuse tip) were reported. Later negotiations produced no viable relocation plan amid opposition from other neighbourhoods. In June 2008 the authorities issued a fresh notice to leave by 10 July, relying on the 2005 order. The European Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39, requiring information on housing for vulnerable persons. Limited social-home rooms were offered (unsuitable for families and rejected by applicants unwilling to leave their community). The mayor then suspended enforcement “pending resolution of housing problems” without quashing the order. Subsequent municipal and national Roma-housing programmes (including a 2005–2015 national plan and 2007 Sofia implementation plan) identified chronic over-crowding and discrimination but yielded no concrete alternative housing by late 2010.

The applicants alleged that the removal decision, taken after decades of tolerance, without proportionality assessment, consultation, or provision of alternative accommodation, and in a context of anti-Roma hostility, violated Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alone and together with Articles 13 and 14.

After 1996 the land became municipal property; acquisitive prescription was inapplicable to State/municipal land until then and was later suspended by Parliament. On 12 January 2006 the Sofia City Court upheld the order; the Supreme Administrative Court confirmed this on 12 June 2006. The courts held that lack of legal title sufficed, that the houses belonged to the municipality under the Property Act, and that Convention and discrimination arguments were unfounded. Long-term occupation with official acquiescence and proportionality were treated as irrelevant under then-applicable law (proportionality entered the Administrative Procedure Code only in July 2006).

A June 2006 eviction attempt was halted by political pressure. Officials publicly stated that the residents could not be prioritised for municipal housing because they occupied land unlawfully and were not on waiting lists; the 2005 agreement was dismissed as pre-electoral. In June 2008 a fresh notice required departure by 10 July. The Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39, seeking information on housing for vulnerable persons. The municipality offered a few rooms in social homes (unsuitable for families or community life). Enforcement was then suspended “pending resolution of housing problems,” but the order remained in force. National and municipal Roma-housing programmes (2005–2015) and later discussions produced no concrete alternative accommodation; other neighbourhoods opposed relocation. Four applicants temporarily registered elsewhere but regarded Batalova Vodenitsa as their only home.

The applicants, 23 Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin, alleged that Bulgarian authorities’ decision to evict them from long-occupied homes in Sofia’s Batalova Vodenitsa neighbourhood violated Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (alone and with Articles 13 and 14). The area housed 200–300 people in substandard conditions lacking sewage, plumbing or official recognition; residents used public fountains. Buildings failed construction and safety standards and could not be legalised without major reconstruction. Applicants never applied for regularisation, citing poverty and isolation. Domestic law precluded them from acquiring title: prescription against State/municipal land was unavailable until 1996 and then repeatedly suspended. Authorities tolerated the settlement for decades without action.

From the 1990s, tensions rose with non-Roma neighbours over sanitation, animals, alleged crime and aesthetics. Demonstrations, media coverage and political statements demanded clearance of “Roma ghettos.” In 2005 the district mayor ordered approximately 180 residents, including the applicants, to vacate municipal land within seven days under the Municipal Property Act, warning of police enforcement. After non-compliance a forcible-removal order followed, listing names and announcing planned demolition. Applicants obtained a stay pending appeal. An agreement promising alternative housing for registered residents was never implemented. Domestic courts (Sofia City Court and Supreme Administrative Court) upheld the order solely because occupants lacked legal title; houses therefore belonged to the municipality. Courts dismissed Convention, discrimination and proportionality arguments as irrelevant under then-applicable law (proportionality entered the Administrative Procedure Code only in 2006). Long-term occupation with official acquiescence was ignored.
