Officials publicly stated that residents were ineligible for municipal housing (they occupied land unlawfully and were not on waiting lists) and that lack of alternatives was irrelevant. Racist remarks by local politicians were reported. In 2008 authorities again served notice of eviction. The European Court indicated interim measures requiring arrangements for children, elderly and other vulnerable persons. Limited social-home places were offered, but not for intact families; applicants refused separation from their community. The mayor then suspended enforcement “pending resolution of housing problems,” without quashing the order. These facts underpin the complaints: decades of tolerated occupation created a de-facto home whose sudden removal, without genuine alternatives or proportionality review, threatened family life, privacy and potentially degrading homelessness (Arts 8 and 3); the structures, though illegal, represented possessions (Art. 1 Protocol 1); domestic courts afforded no effective examination of Convention rights (Art. 13); and the measure, set against anti-Roma rhetoric and unequal treatment of similarly situated communities, raised ethnic-discrimination issues (Art. 14). International bodies (Council of Europe Social Rights Committee, UN CESCR, EU FRA) had already criticised Bulgaria’s handling of Roma settlements and evictions.
001-110806:
The case of Bezrukovy v. Russia (no. 34616/02) involves two Russian nationals, Lyudmila Vitalyevna Bezrukova (born 1950) and her daughter Irina Sergeyevna Bezrukova (born 1976), both resident in Voronezh. They alleged that a final and enforceable domestic judgment in their favour was not enforced in a timely manner and that an extension of the time-limit for appealing that judgment permitted its subsequent quashing, in breach of their Convention rights (principally Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

In July–August 1998 the applicants deposited funds with the Voronezh branch of SBS-Agro Bank. During the 1998 financial crisis they sought repayment of capital plus interest; the bank refused. On 4 August 1999 the Zheleznodorozhniy District Court of Voronezh awarded them USD 24 490 and USD 32 931 respectively. Enforcement began in August 2000 but was discontinued on 10 July 2001 after the bank became insolvent; the judgment remained unenforced.

A moratorium on creditors’ claims against the bank was imposed by the Central Bank of Russia and later extended. Management of the bank was transferred to ARKO, a State corporation established to restructure credit institutions. On 9 November 2001 the applicants sued the Central Bank and ARKO, asserting that ARKO had assumed the bank’s liabilities. On 5 December 2001 the District Court held ARKO liable and awarded the same sums. The Voronezh Regional Court set that judgment aside on 12 March 2002.

After remittal, the District Court on 20 December 2004 again found for the applicants (and a co-plaintiff, Mr Kravchenko), ordering ARKO to pay the original amounts. The judgment was appealable within ten days. ARKO appealed and the Central Bank joined the proceedings. ARKO was liquidated on 25 February 2005. On 19 July 2005 the Regional Court discontinued the appeal because of the liquidation; the 20 December 2004 judgment therefore became final and enforceable. A writ of execution was issued on 2 August 2005.

On 6 December 2005 the Central Bank lodged an out-of-time appeal and requested an extension of the ten-day limit, arguing it had been deprived of the opportunity to have the judgment reviewed. On 2 March 2006 the Regional Court granted the extension, noting that the Central Bank had joined ARKO’s earlier appeal, which had not been examined on the merits. On 9 March 2006 the same court (hearing the same Central Bank representative who had appeared in July 2005) quashed the 20 December 2004 judgment, held that its earlier discontinuation decision had been legally incorrect, and terminated the proceedings on account of ARKO’s liquidation.

In a related case the Court later found a violation in respect of Mr Kravchenko arising from the quashing of a final judgment by supervisory review. Relying on that judgment, the applicants sought reopening of the 9 March 2006 decision under Articles 392–394 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the Presidium of the Voronezh Regional Court dismissed the application on 15 June 2011.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Bezrukovy v. Russia (application no. 34616/02) concerned two Russian applicants, Lyudmila Vitalyevna Bezrukova and her daughter Irina Sergeyevna Bezrukova, who alleged that a final domestic judgment in their favour had not been enforced promptly and that an extended time-limit for appeal had permitted its subsequent quashing.

In July and August 1998 the applicants deposited funds with the Voronezh branch of SBS-Agro Bank. During the ensuing financial crisis and currency devaluation they sought repayment of capital plus interest, which the bank refused. On 4 August 1999 the Zheleznodorozhniy District Court of Voronezh awarded them USD 24,490 and USD 32,931 respectively. Enforcement proceedings commenced in August 2000 but were discontinued in July 2001 after the bank became insolvent; the 1999 judgment therefore remained unenforced.

The Central Bank of Russia imposed a moratorium on creditors’ claims against SBS-Agro and transferred management of the bank to the state-established Agency on Restructuring of Lending Agencies (ARKO). The applicants then sued both the Central Bank and ARKO, arguing that ARKO exercised effective control over the bank. After an initial 2001 District Court judgment in their favour was set aside on appeal, the District Court on 20 December 2004 again found for the applicants on similar reasoning and ordered ARKO to pay the same sums (together with an award to a co-plaintiff, Mr Kravchenko). The judgment stated that it was appealable within ten days.

ARKO lodged an appeal, which the Central Bank joined. ARKO was dissolved on 25 February 2005. On 19 July 2005 the Voronezh Regional Court, noting ARKO’s liquidation, discontinued the appellate proceedings; the 20 December 2004 judgment thereby became final and enforceable. A writ of execution was issued on 2 August 2005.

On 6 December 2005 the Central Bank filed an out-of-time appeal against the December 2004 judgment and sought an extension of the ten-day time-limit, claiming it had been deprived of the opportunity to have the judgment reviewed. On 2 March 2006 the Regional Court granted the extension, observing that the Central Bank had joined ARKO’s earlier appeal, which had been dismissed without examination on the merits. On 9 March 2006 the same court, sitting with the same Central Bank representative who had appeared in July 2005, quashed the December 2004 judgment and discontinued the proceedings. It held that its earlier decision of 19 July 2005 had incorrectly applied the relevant procedural rules, given that both ARKO and the Central Bank were co-defendants and ARKO had been liquidated.

The applicants’ subsequent attempt to have the March 2006 decision reviewed on the basis of the Court’s 2009 judgment in the related case of Kravchenko v. Russia (which had found a violation arising from the quashing of a similar award by way of supervisory review) was dismissed by the Presidium of the Voronezh Regional Court in June 2011.

Under the Russian Code of Civil Procedure a court may restore an expired time-limit if a valid excuse is shown, and an appellate court must discontinue proceedings upon liquidation of a legal-entity party. A final judgment may also be reopened if the European Court has found a Convention violation in respect of the same proceedings.

The applicants complained that the final and enforceable judgment of 20 December 2004 had not been executed in a timely manner and that the unjustified restoration of the appeal time-limit had allowed its subsequent quashing, thereby frustrating their right to a court and to peaceful enjoyment of their possessions.

From 16 November 1999 the Agency for the Restructuring of Lending Agencies (ARKO), a State corporation established under federal law, temporarily assumed management of the bank.

On 9 November 2001 the applicants sued the Central Bank and ARKO for damages, arguing that ARKO exercised effective control over the bank. On 5 December 2001 the District Court held ARKO liable for the bank’s obligations and awarded the same USD sums. The Voronezh Regional Court set that judgment aside on 12 March 2002. After remittal, on 20 December 2004 the District Court again found for the applicants on similar reasoning, awarding the same amounts payable by ARKO (and a further sum to co-plaintiff Mr Kravchenko). On 19 July 2005 the Regional Court discontinued the appeal because ARKO had been liquidated; the 20 December 2004 judgment thereby became final and enforceable. A writ of execution was issued on 2 August 2005.

On 6 December 2005 the Central Bank lodged an out-of-time appeal and sought an extension of the time-limit, claiming it had been deprived of the opportunity to have the 2004 judgment reviewed. On 2 March 2006 the Regional Court granted the extension, noting that the Central Bank had earlier joined ARKO’s appeal (which had been dismissed without examination on the merits). On 9 March 2006 the same court, sitting with the same Central Bank representative who had appeared on 19 July 2005, set aside the 20 December 2004 judgment and discontinued the proceedings, holding that its earlier decision had misapplied the law.

The applicants, Fikret Murtić and Raska Ćerimović, were employees of Agrokomerc, a company in Velika Kladuša. In 1991, as part of its conversion to a joint-stock company, internal shares were issued to workers, with one-third of salaries allocated as instalment payments. 1993 board resolutions raised the internal share capital to 80.9 percent of the total (the rest State-owned). The process halted in August 1994 when the State assumed control amid the war. The applicants could no longer exercise shareholder rights, though the company continued listing the internal shares on balance sheets until mid-1999. Their employment was suspended in August 1995 and never restored.

In June 2000 they complained to the Human Rights Chamber. A March 2001 Revsar audit declared the internal-share measures unlawful, concluding the company was wholly State-owned. A July 2001 Federation decree placed it under State control.

On 8 March 2002 the Chamber (joining related cases) held that the applicants had acquired protected possessions consisting of their paid-up internal shares (via salary deductions, deposits and 1992 profit allocations). Cancellation of those shares by the Revsar audit and the Federation’s exclusive management control violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants had also been denied an effective opportunity to participate in determining ownership, violating Article 6. The Chamber ordered the Federation to appoint internationally recognised auditors to establish the full ownership structure in accordance with international standards, to value and formally register the applicants’ shares, and to issue them individual certificates. Interim measures regulated company management pending a shareholders’ meeting.

A November 2003 Deloitte audit found 90.33 percent State-owned and 9.67 percent private (only 3.34 percent assigned to named individuals). The applicants’ holdings were not valued, so they could not attend the March 2004 general meeting. In May 2004 the Human Rights Commission lifted the interim measures after receiving the audit and meeting minutes. Ownership changes were registered by the Bihać Cantonal Court in May 2005. A February 2006 meeting authorised distribution of the remaining unassigned private capital.

Individual certificates were finally issued on 29 October 2007: Murtić received 451 shares (market value BAM 4 510) and Ćerimović 1 086 shares (BAM 10 000). They were thereafter able to attend shareholders’ meetings. In January 2009 the Constitutional Court confirmed that the 2002 decision had been fully implemented.

The applicants’ 6 October 2005 application to the European Court complained of the prolonged non-enforcement of the Chamber’s decision. Domestic law (Criminal Code 2003, Article 239) makes refusal or obstruction of a Human Rights Chamber decision a criminal offence punishable by six months to five years’ imprisonment.

The case of Murtić and Ćerimović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by two Bosnian citizens, Fikret Murtić and Raska Ćerimović, both former employees of Agrokomerc, an agricultural company in Velika Kladuša. They alleged a violation arising from the prolonged non-enforcement of a Human Rights Chamber decision of 8 March 2002 that had recognised their property rights as shareholders.

In 1991 the company’s workers’ council decided to issue internal shares to employees as part of its conversion from a socially owned enterprise into a joint-stock company. One-third of employees’ salaries was deducted toward the purchase of these shares. Further board resolutions in 1993 increased the internal share capital to 80.9 per cent of the company’s total capital, the remainder remaining State-owned. The applicants thereby acquired paid-up internal shares through salary allocations, permanent deposits and profit distributions. After the outbreak of armed conflict the State assumed control of the company in 1994. Although the company’s accounts continued to record the internal shares until mid-1999, the applicants were unable to exercise any shareholder rights. Their employment was suspended in August 1995 and they were placed on a waiting list from which they were never recalled.

In June 2000 the applicants lodged complaints with the Human Rights Chamber. A 2001 audit by Revsar concluded that the internal shares had never been validly created and that the company was wholly State-owned. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina then placed Agrokomerc on its list of State-controlled enterprises. On 8 March 2002 the Chamber (joining the applicants’ cases with others) held that the applicants possessed “possessions” protected by Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Revsar audit and the Federation’s exclusive control had deprived them of those possessions and of their rights to participate in management and profits, without a legal basis. The Chamber further found a violation of Article 6 because the applicants had been afforded no effective judicial opportunity to contest the audit or the resulting ownership structure.

The Chamber ordered the Federation to engage internationally recognised auditors to determine the complete ownership structure in accordance with international standards, to establish and register the value of the applicants’ shares, and to issue individual certificates. Interim measures were imposed pending the new audit and the first shareholders’ meeting.

Implementation proved protracted. A 2003 Deloitte & Touche audit found only 9.67 per cent of capital privately held, of which merely 3.34 per cent had been assigned to identifiable individuals; the applicants’ holdings were not quantified, so they could not attend the March 2004 shareholders’ meeting. The Human Rights Commission lifted the interim measures in May 2004 after receiving the audit and meeting minutes. Ownership changes were registered by a cantonal court in 2005. Only in October 2007 were the applicants issued certificates (451 shares worth BAM 4 510 for the first applicant and 1 086 shares worth BAM 10 000 for the second) and formally registered, enabling them to attend subsequent meetings. In January 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the 2002 decision fully executed.

The applicants’ 2005 application to the Strasbourg Court therefore concerned the four-and-a-half-year delay in giving effect to the Chamber’s binding orders. Domestic law classified non-enforcement of Human Rights Chamber decisions as a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment. These facts formed the core of the alleged continuing violation of the applicants’ Convention rights.

The applicants, Fikret Murtić and Raska Ćerimović, were employees of Agrokomerc, a company in Velika Kladuša that began converting from social to joint-stock ownership in 1991. Its workers’ council decided to issue internal shares, with one-third of salaries deducted as instalment payments. Management resolutions in 1993 increased the internal share capital to 80.9 per cent of the total (the rest remaining state-owned). After the State assumed control of the company during the 1992–95 war, the applicants were unable to exercise any shareholder rights, although the company continued to record the internal capital on its balance sheets until mid-1999. Their employment was suspended in August 1995 and they were never rehired.

In June 2000 they lodged applications with the Human Rights Chamber. A March 2001 audit concluded that the 1991–94 measures had been unlawful, so no internal shares had ever been validly created and the company was wholly state-owned. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina then listed Agrokomerc as a state-controlled enterprise.

On 8 March 2002 the Chamber (joining the applicants’ cases with others) found that they had acquired possessions in the form of their paid-up internal shares. Cancellation of those shares by the 2001 audit, together with the Federation’s exclusive control of management, violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants had also been denied any real opportunity to participate in determining the company’s ownership structure, in breach of Article 6. The Chamber ordered the Federation to commission an internationally recognised audit of the complete ownership structure, to establish and formally register the value of the applicants’ shares, and to issue individual share certificates. Interim measures were imposed to regulate management pending the new audit and a general meeting of shareholders.

A November 2003 Deloitte & Touche audit found 90.33 per cent of the capital still state-owned and only 9.67 per cent privately held (of which just 3.34 per cent had been assigned to identified shareholders). The applicants’ individual holdings were not valued, so they could not attend the March 2004 general meeting. The Human Rights Commission (the Chamber’s successor) lifted the interim measures in May 2004 after receiving the audit report and minutes of that meeting. Ownership changes were registered by a cantonal court in May 2005. In February 2006 a shareholders’ meeting authorised distribution of the remaining unassigned private capital. Only on 29 October 2007 were the applicants issued share certificates (451 shares worth BAM 4 510 for Murtić and 1 086 shares worth BAM 10 000 for Ćerimović) and entered in the official register, after which they were permitted to attend meetings. In January 2009 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared the Chamber’s 2002 decision fully executed.

The applicants’ 2005 application to the European Court complained of the prolonged failure to enforce the Chamber’s binding decision. Under domestic criminal law, non-enforcement of such a decision constituted an offence punishable by imprisonment.
001-112086:
The case of K.M.C. v. Hungary (Application no. 19554/11) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 10 July 2012. The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1973, was a civil servant employed by an administrative inspectorate. On 27 September 2010 her employer dismissed her under section 8(1) of Act no. LVIII of 2010 on the Legal Status of Government Officials. That provision, in force from 6 July 2010 until 31 May 2011, permitted dismissal of government officials on two months’ notice without any statement of reasons.

The applicant did not bring court proceedings. She considered that the complete absence of reasons made any challenge futile. The statutory time-limit expired on 26 October 2010. On 18 February 2011 the Constitutional Court annulled section 8(1) as unconstitutional with effect from 31 May 2011. A later Constitutional Court decision of 6 May 2011 addressed the non-application of unconstitutional norms in pending litigation.

The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the lack of reasons rendered her dismissal incapable of effective judicial review.

Domestic constitutional provisions guaranteed equality before the law, a fair trial before an independent court (Article 57) and the right of Hungarian citizens to hold public office according to suitability and qualifications (Article 70(6)). The Labour Code generally required employers to give clear reasons for dismissal and to prove their genuineness and adequacy, subject to limited exceptions. Additional statutory bars existed during illness, pregnancy, maternity leave and similar periods. The Equal Treatment Act prohibited discrimination on a wide range of grounds and, once a claimant substantiated disadvantage linked to a protected characteristic, shifted the burden of proof to the employer. Improper exercise of rights (including harassment or suppression of opinion) was also prohibited.

The Constitutional Court held that public-service relationships are public-law in character because officials exercise state powers. The legislature therefore could not confer on the employer an unrestricted power of dismissal. Such a power violated the constitutional right to hold public office and endangered the political neutrality, impartiality and lawfulness of the administration, because officials could no longer be expected to voice professional views at the risk of losing their posts. It also disproportionately restricted the right to judicial protection under Article 57 (and thereby Article 6 of the Convention). Without statutory grounds or an obligation to give reasons, the range of justiciable claims (nullity, equal-treatment violations, misuse of rights) became extremely narrow and the employee bore the burden of proving unlawfulness. The resulting vulnerability of officials was held contrary to human dignity.

The Constitutional Court referred to the Strasbourg Court’s case-law extending Article 6 to civil-servant disputes and requiring genuine examination of claims on the merits. International instruments cited included Article 30 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and Article 24 of the revised European Social Charter, both of which protect workers against dismissal without valid reasons related to capacity, conduct or operational requirements and guarantee a right of appeal to an impartial body.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that Hungarian law had denied her an effective judicial remedy against an unreasoned dismissal.

The case of K.M.C. v. Hungary (Application no. 19554/11) concerned a complaint under Article 6 of the Convention that the applicant’s dismissal from public service could not be effectively challenged in court owing to the absence of any reasons given by her employer.

The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1973 and residing in Pécel, was employed as a civil servant in an administrative inspectorate. On 27 September 2010 her employer terminated her service by applying Section 8(1) of Act no. LVIII of 2010 on the Legal Status of Government Officials. That provision, in force from 6 July 2010 until 31 May 2011, permitted the dismissal of a government official with two months’ notice and without any obligation to state specific reasons. The applicant did not bring court proceedings to contest the dismissal. She considered that, in the absence of any stated grounds, she had no realistic prospect of success. The statutory time-limit for initiating such proceedings expired on 26 October 2010.

On 18 February 2011 the Hungarian Constitutional Court, in decision no. 8/2011. (II.18.) AB, declared Section 8(1) unconstitutional and annulled it with effect from 31 May 2011. The Court held that the legislature’s failure to prescribe statutory grounds for dismissal and to impose a duty to give reasons disproportionately restricted government officials’ right to hold public office (Article 70(6) of the Constitution then in force) and their right to judicial protection (Article 57(1), corresponding to Article 6 of the Convention). It emphasised that public-service relationships are public-law in nature; officials exercise State powers and must remain politically neutral and impartial. Unfettered power of dismissal without reasons or judicially reviewable criteria would expose them to political pressure, undermine the lawfulness of administrative decisions, and reduce them to mere “means” for accomplishing State tasks, contrary to human dignity. While the Constitutional Court recognised the legislature’s wide margin in regulating public-service relations and the general trend in Europe towards loosening the rigidity of closed career systems, it stressed that the employer’s right of dismissal could not be left entirely unrestricted. The duty to give reasons was not a mere privilege (as it might be in private-sector employment) but a constitutional guarantee inherent in the public-service relationship. Without it, the range of claims that could be examined on the merits—nullity, prohibition of dismissal, violation of equal-treatment rules or abuse of rights—was severely curtailed, rendering judicial review ineffective.

A subsequent Constitutional Court decision of 6 May 2011 (no. 35/2011. (V.6.) AB) clarified that unconstitutional provisions should not be applied in pending court cases and that judges were obliged to refer such provisions for constitutional review.

Domestic legislation also contained provisions on equal treatment (Act no. CXXV of 2003), which reversed the burden of proof once a claimant substantiated a protected characteristic and disadvantage, and on improper exercise of rights (Labour Code). The Labour Code itself generally required employers to give reasons for dismissal, except in limited cases such as retirement. International instruments cited included Article 30 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (protection against unjustified dismissal) and Article 24 of the revised European Social Charter (right not to be dismissed without valid reasons connected with capacity, conduct or operational requirements, together with a right of appeal to an impartial body).

The applicant’s complaint therefore centred on the practical impossibility of obtaining an effective judicial determination of the lawfulness of her dismissal, given the statutory regime that required no reasons and placed the burden of proving unlawfulness on the dismissed official.

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered its judgment in K.M.C. v. Hungary (Application no. 19554/11) on 10 July 2012. The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1973 and residing in Pécel, was a civil servant employed by an administrative inspectorate. On 27 September 2010, applying Section 8(1) of Act no. LVIII of 2010 on the Legal Status of Government Officials (in force from 6 July 2010), her employer dismissed her with two months’ notice but without stating any reasons.

The applicant did not bring court proceedings to challenge the dismissal. She considered that the complete absence of reasons left her with no realistic prospect of success. The statutory time-limit expired on 26 October 2010.

On 18 February 2011 the Constitutional Court annulled Section 8(1) as unconstitutional with effect from 31 May 2011. In decision 8/2011 (II.18.) AB it held that public-service relationships are public-law relations, not private contracts. The duty to give reasons is therefore a constitutional guarantee flowing from the nature of the relationship, not a mere privilege. Unrestricted power to dismiss without statutory grounds or reasons violates Article 70(6) of the Constitution (the right to hold public office) and Article 57(1) (right to a fair trial by an independent court). It also undermines the political neutrality, impartiality and lawfulness of the public administration, treats officials as mere instruments of the State, and is contrary to human dignity. The Constitutional Court observed that, without reasons, the only remaining avenues of challenge (equal-treatment claims under Act CXXV of 2003 or misuse-of-rights claims under the Labour Code) were extremely limited; the employee bore the burden of proving unlawfulness. A further decision of 6 May 2011 (35/2011 (V.6.) AB) clarified that judges must not apply unconstitutional laws in pending cases and may refer such issues to the Constitutional Court.

Domestic law otherwise required reasons for ordinary dismissals (Labour Code s. 89) and shifted the burden of proof in discrimination cases. Reopening of final judgments was possible only if a constitutional complaint produced a retroactive exclusion of the impugned provision (Code of Civil Procedure s. 262/A). International instruments (EU Charter Art. 30; revised European Social Charter Art. 24) likewise protect against unjustified dismissal and guarantee an appeal to an impartial body.

The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the lack of reasons rendered any judicial challenge illusory, thereby denying her effective access to a court. The Government were given an opportunity to comment; the Court examined admissibility and merits together. The facts therefore centre on a dismissal effected under a provision later struck down precisely because it precluded meaningful judicial scrutiny of the employer’s decision.
001-111682:
The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1961, was acquitted in 1996 by the Munich I Regional Court of multiple counts of assault (including dangerous assault), sexual assault and procuring. The court found he had committed serious violent and sexual acts between 1991 and 1995, primarily against his wife (whom he threatened with weapons, beat, attempted to strangle and forced into prostitution and other degrading acts, inflicting fractures and other injuries) as well as against another woman and a relative (including sexual assaults involving fettering, urination and insertion of objects). Experts diagnosed a brain disorder, borderline personality disorder with emotional instability and paranoid jealousy; he had also been intoxicated during some acts. Due to his pathological mental disorder, criminal responsibility could not be excluded. The court ordered his placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code, as he posed a danger of further serious offences.

He remained in various psychiatric hospitals from 1996 until 2007, with annual reviews confirming detention. After renouncing German nationality, an expulsion order to Romania was issued in 2005 and became final. In February 2007, the Paderborn Regional Court terminated the psychiatric placement under Article 67d § 6 of the Criminal Code. A psychiatric expert found a personality disorder with paranoid and dissocial elements that neither excluded nor diminished criminal responsibility; his ongoing dangerousness (particularly to women, including his ex-wife) stemmed from his attitude rather than a pathological disorder. He was transferred to prison and placed in provisional detention pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention.

On 30 July 2008, the Munich I Regional Court ordered retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b § 3 of the Criminal Code (introduced in 2004 to address cases where psychiatric placement ended but public danger persisted). It held that the original placement had been based on qualifying serious offences listed in Article 66 § 3 and that a comprehensive assessment of the applicant, his offences and his development in hospital showed a very high likelihood of further serious violent or sexual offences causing considerable harm if released. Two experts diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder (one adding sexual sadism), with one describing a combined disorder including psychopathic, paranoid and unstable elements and the other labelling him a psychopath. His violent, degrading and partly sadistic attitude toward women had not changed. The court deemed detention proportionate, including to protect potential victims abroad.

The applicant appealed, arguing that Article 66b § 3 and the order violated his right to liberty under the Basic Law and Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal on 13 May 2009. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint on 4 November 2009 without reasons.

In prison, multidisciplinary staff offered therapies and courses, but the applicant initially declined transfer to a social-therapeutic institution (claiming prior treatment) and later applications were refused; he did not pursue other programmes. He worked, had limited family contact and received no relaxations of detention due to the expulsion order. Later reviews of the detention (2010–2011) produced conflicting decisions on continuation, with one court terminating it in 2011 (finding no high risk of the most serious offences and applying stricter post-2011 Federal Constitutional Court criteria) only for the appeal court to reverse this. Parallel attempts at detention under other mental-health or therapy-detention statutes were also pursued.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the retrospective preventive-detention order lacked a sufficient legal basis under Article 5 § 1 and was not justified as detention “after conviction” or of a person of unsound mind.

The case of S. v. Germany (Application no. 3300/10) concerns a Romanian national born in 1961 who alleged that an order for his retrospective preventive detention violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty).

In February 1996, the Munich I Regional Court acquitted S. of multiple offences committed between 1991 and 1995—including repeated dangerous assaults, sexual assault, and procuring—on grounds of lack of criminal responsibility. The acts involved extreme violence against his wife (threats with weapons, beatings causing fractures and other injuries, forced prostitution, and public humiliation) as well as sexual assaults on others. Three medical experts diagnosed a brain disorder, borderline personality disorder with emotional instability and paranoiac jealousy, and partial intoxication. Finding him liable to commit further serious offences and thus a public danger, the court ordered his indefinite placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. S. remained in various hospitals from 1996, with annual judicial confirmations of the measure; he escaped once in 2002.

In 2004 S. renounced German nationality, prompting a final 2005 expulsion order to Romania. On 9 February 2007 the Paderborn Regional Court terminated the psychiatric placement under Article 67d § 6 of the Criminal Code. After examining S., an expert found a personality disorder with paranoiac and dissocial features that neither excluded nor diminished criminal responsibility. His ongoing danger to women (especially his ex-wife) arose from a chosen attitude rather than pathology. S. was transferred to prison and placed in provisional detention pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention.

On 30 July 2008 the Munich I Regional Court, applying Article 66b § 3 of the Criminal Code (inserted in 2004), ordered retrospective preventive detention. The original placement had been based on listed serious offences (including dangerous assault). A comprehensive assessment of S., his crimes, and his hospital progress—supported by two experts diagnosing a dissocial/psychopathic personality disorder (with possible sexual sadism) that did not affect responsibility—showed a very high likelihood he would commit similar serious violent or sexual offences causing substantial harm if released. The court deemed the measure proportionate, noting that it protected potential victims even in Romania.

S. appealed, arguing that Article 66b § 3 and the resulting order violated his liberty rights under the Basic Law and Article 5 of the Convention because the detention was retrospective and unforeseeable. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal in May 2009. In November 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint without giving reasons.

Later reviews (2009–2011) largely upheld continued detention. One regional court briefly terminated it in 2011 after a new expert report and the Federal Constitutional Court’s May 2011 ruling on preventive-detention provisions, but the court of appeal reversed this, finding a sufficient risk of serious offences. Parallel attempts to detain S. under Bavarian mental-health legislation or the 2011 Therapy Detention Act were initiated but remained unresolved at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.

These facts centre on the 2008 retrospective order, imposed years after the original 1996 psychiatric measure and after that measure had been terminated because S. no longer met the legal criteria for hospital placement, thereby raising questions about the lawfulness and justification of the detention under Article 5 § 1.

**CASE OF S. v. GERMANY (Application no. 3300/10, ECtHR Fifth Section, Judgment 28 June 2012)**

The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1961 and detained in Straubing Prison, alleged that a 2008 order for his retrospective preventive detention violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty).

On 23 February 1996 the Munich I Regional Court acquitted him of multiple counts of assault (including dangerous assault), sexual assault and procuring, finding a lack of criminal responsibility. Between 1991 and 1995 he had violently threatened, beaten and attempted to strangle his wife (using a gun, knife and teargas), inflicting fractures, lacerations and other injuries; forced her into prostitution; and committed degrading sexual assaults on her female friend and a relative. Three experts diagnosed a brain disorder, borderline personality disorder with emotional instability and paranoid jealousy (partly combined with alcohol use). The court ordered indefinite placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code because he remained liable to commit further serious offences and posed a public danger. He was held in successive psychiatric hospitals from 1996 (with one escape in 2002). Detention was reviewed and confirmed annually. In 2005 an expulsion order to Romania became final after he renounced German nationality.

On 9 February 2007 the Paderborn Regional Court terminated the psychiatric placement under Article 67d § 6 of the Criminal Code. An expert found a personality disorder with paranoid and dissocial features that neither excluded nor diminished criminal responsibility; his ongoing dangerousness to women (especially his ex-wife) stemmed from attitude rather than pathology. He was transferred to prison and placed in provisional detention pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention.

On 30 July 2008 the Munich I Regional Court ordered retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b § 3 of the Criminal Code (inserted in 2004). It held that the statutory conditions were met: the original psychiatric order had been based on listed serious offences (dangerous assault etc.), and a comprehensive assessment of the applicant, his crimes and his development in hospital showed it was very likely he would again commit similar serious violent or sexual offences against related women, causing considerable harm. Two experts diagnosed a dissocial/psychopathic personality disorder (one adding sexual sadism) without diminished responsibility. The court found a persistent violent, degrading and partly sadistic attitude toward women and held the measure proportionate, including for potential victims in Romania.

The Federal Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on points of law on 13 May 2009. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint (alleging a breach of the right to liberty) on 4 November 2009.

In prison, multidisciplinary staff offered therapy, social-therapeutic placement, anti-aggression courses and addiction counselling, but the applicant did not pursue most options (claiming prior treatment and that he was primarily a violent rather than sexual offender). He worked, had limited family contact and received no relaxations because of the expulsion order.

Subsequent reviews (2009–2011) produced mixed results. Some courts initially terminated detention after a 2011 Federal Constitutional Court judgment on retrospective measures, citing insufficient risk of the most serious offences or lack of a qualifying mental disorder under later legislation (the Therapy Detention Act). Appellate courts reversed, finding the risk of serious violent or sexual offences sufficient for continued detention under Article 66b § 3. Parallel requests for placement under Bavarian mental-health legislation and the Therapy Detention Act were also pursued, with mixed provisional outcomes.

These facts centre on the shift from psychiatric hospitalisation (after acquittal for lack of responsibility) to retrospective preventive detention years later, after the original mental-health grounds had lapsed, raising the Article 5 compatibility of the 2004 statutory basis and the 2008 order.
001-111631:
The case originated in an application by Armenian national Kamo Piruzyan (born 1978) against Armenia, alleging violations arising from his detention and trial on robbery charges.

On 18 October 2006, following an alleged armed assault that evening, the applicant was taken to a police station (an arrest he claimed was unrecorded and from which he was later released). Criminal proceedings were instituted the next day under Article 175 § 2(2) and (4) of the Criminal Code after a complaint by victim G.H., who lived in the same building and alleged that the masked applicant had attacked him with a metal rod and stolen a briefcase of jewellery. The applicant was formally arrested that evening and charged on 22 October 2006 (the charge sheet noting that the victim had pursued him, forcing him to drop the briefcase).

That same day the investigator applied to the Lori Regional Court for two months’ detention, citing previous convictions, the serious nature of the offence and a risk of absconding. The court granted the application, finding sufficient grounds that the applicant might abscond or obstruct the investigation given the offence’s nature and dangerousness. On 8 December the investigator sought a further two-month extension, arguing that additional biological examinations were needed, that the applicant (who had not admitted guilt) would abscond or reoffend because of his record and the seriousness of the crime, and submitting limited case materials. At the 12 December hearing the applicant (present with counsel) objected, denied any reasonable suspicion, sought bail and noted the lack of concrete evidence; the investigator conceded none was available beyond the need for a blood-sample comparison. After requesting the full case file the judge deliberated and extended detention by one month (to 19 January 2007) solely because the examination remained incomplete, refusing bail under Article 143 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the offence was classified as serious.

The applicant appealed, complaining of the absence of reasonable suspicion, generic reasoning, lack of evidence of flight or obstruction risk, and a non-adversarial procedure that denied him access to or comment on the full file. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 25 January 2007, holding that the materials established reasonable suspicion of involvement, that detention was justified by the offence’s dangerousness and the risks of absconding or obstruction, and that the first-instance decision was reasoned. A further one-month extension to 19 February 2007 was granted on 12 January on identical grounds (incomplete examinations); the applicant again objected and sought bail. His 27 January appeal was left unexamined by the Court of Appeal on 19 February because the investigation had concluded that day, the indictment had been approved and the case transmitted to the Regional Court.

Thereafter the authorised detention period expired. On 5 March the applicant applied to the Regional Court (and the detention-facility chief) claiming unlawfulness since 19 February and seeking release; both requests were refused by reference to Article 138 of the Code, which suspends the pre-trial time-limit once a case is sent to court. On 12 March the Regional Court set the case down for trial, leaving detention unchanged.

Throughout the ensuing nine-month trial (21 public hearings, some lasting up to seven hours and attracting family, friends, townspeople and students) the applicant was confined in a 4.5 m² metal cage in the courtroom. On 21 March he asked to be released from the cage; the request was adjourned. On 30 March he challenged the presiding judge, arguing that the cage constituted inhuman and degrading treatment and breached equality of arms and the presumption of innocence. The challenge was dismissed; a further request (according to the applicant) was refused on security grounds. He remained caged for the entire trial. On 8 August he again sought revocation of detention or bail, citing the elapsed time, completed witness examinations and absence of obstruction risk; the court refused because the trial was unfinished and no sufficient grounds existed. Charges were later dropped for insufficient evidence; proceedings were terminated on 5 December 2007 and the applicant released.

Domestic law classified the robbery as a serious offence (punishable by six to ten years), limited bail to minor or medium offences, and provided that pre-trial detention time-limits are suspended upon transmission of the case to court. Accused persons and counsel obtained full case-file access only after the investigation ended.

The case originated in an application by Armenian national Kamo Piruzyan (born 1978) alleging multiple Convention violations arising from his arrest, detention and trial on robbery charges.

On 18 October 2006 an armed robbery occurred in Alaverdi. The victim, a neighbour, reported that a masked man hit him with a metal rod and stole a briefcase of jewellery. The applicant was taken to the police station that morning but released without a record. Formal proceedings under Article 175 § 2 of the Criminal Code (robbery with violence/weapon, a “serious” offence carrying 6–10 years) were opened the next day. He was arrested at 8 p.m. on 19 October and charged on 22 October. The investigator immediately sought two months’ detention, citing prior convictions, the seriousness of the offence and a risk of absconding. The Lori Regional Court granted the request, finding sufficient grounds that the applicant might flee or obstruct the investigation.

On 8 December the investigator applied for a further two-month extension, arguing that examinations (including a biological test) remained unfinished, the applicant denied guilt, and he risked absconding or reoffending. At the 12 December hearing the applicant and his lawyer were present. He contested any reasonable suspicion, noted the absence of concrete evidence of flight risk, and requested bail. The investigator conceded that no supporting evidence had yet been produced and that a blood-sample comparison was still needed. The judge then obtained the entire case file from the investigator and retired to deliberate. The court extended detention by one month (until 19 January 2007) solely because of the pending examination and refused bail under Article 143 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which limited bail to offences of minor or medium seriousness.

The applicant appealed on 27 December, repeating the lack of reasonable suspicion, the court’s failure to examine the issue, the absence of evidence of any detention grounds, and the non-adversarial nature of the hearing (the judge having received unseen materials). On 25 January 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld the extension, stating that “certain evidence” established involvement and therefore a reasonable suspicion, and that the offence’s dangerousness justified continued detention and refusal of bail.

A further one-month extension (to 19 February) was granted on 12 January on identical grounds. The applicant again appealed. On 8 February the charges were amended to add recidivism and attempted murder. The investigation ended on 16 February and the file was disclosed. Detention authorised by the 12 January order expired on 19 February, the same day the indictment was approved and the case transmitted to the Regional Court. The Court of Appeal therefore left the 27 January appeal unexamined.

On 5 March the applicant applied for release, arguing that detention had been unlawful since 19 February. The Regional Court rejected the application on 12 March (the same day it listed the case for trial and ordered that detention “remain unchanged”), relying on the transmission of the file.

Throughout the ensuing nine-month trial (21 public hearings attended by family, friends, local residents and students) the applicant was confined in a 4.5 m² metal cage in the courtroom. On 21 March he asked to be released from it; the request was adjourned. On 30 March he challenged the judge, asserting that the cage constituted degrading treatment and violated equality of arms and the presumption of innocence. The challenge was dismissed. A further request was allegedly refused on security grounds. An 8 August application to revoke detention or grant bail was rejected because the trial was unfinished.

On 5 December 2007 the prosecutor dropped all charges for insufficient evidence. The Regional Court terminated the proceedings and the applicant was released the same day.

These facts form the basis of the complaints concerning degrading treatment in the cage, the lawfulness of detention after 19 February, the adequacy of reasons given for continued detention, the automatic exclusion of bail, the fairness of the 12 December hearing, the courts’ treatment of the reasonable-suspicion argument, and the Court of Appeal’s refusal to examine the January appeal.

The case of Piruzyan v. Armenia (Application no. 33376/07) concerns an Armenian national, Kamo Piruzyan (born 1978), who alleged multiple violations of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his arrest, pre-trial detention, court hearings and conditions of confinement. On 18 October 2006 an armed robbery occurred in Alaverdi: the victim, G.H., claimed that a masked man struck him with a metal rod and seized a briefcase of jewellery. Criminal proceedings were opened the next day under Article 175 § 2 of the Criminal Code (aggravated robbery, a “serious” offence punishable by six to ten years’ imprisonment). The applicant was formally arrested that evening and charged on 22 October.

The Lori Regional Court authorised two months’ detention on 22 October, citing the applicant’s prior convictions, the gravity of the offence and a risk of absconding. On 12 December 2006 the investigator sought a further two-month extension, arguing that outstanding biological tests (including blood-group comparison) were needed, that the applicant had not confessed, and that he might abscond or re-offend. At the hearing the applicant sat beside his lawyer and requested release on bail, asserting that no reasonable suspicion existed and that no concrete evidence of flight risk had been produced. The investigator conceded he had no such evidence and handed the entire case file to the judge, who then retired to deliberate. The court extended detention by one month (to 19 January 2007) solely because the biological examination was incomplete and refused bail because the offence was “serious.” The applicant appealed, complaining that the hearing had not been adversarial (he had been denied access to the file) and that the court had failed to address the absence of reasonable suspicion.

The Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 25 January 2007, stating that “certain evidence” substantiated involvement and that the nature of the offence justified continued detention and the refusal of bail. A further one-month extension was granted on 12 January 2007 on identical grounds. The applicant’s appeal of 27 January 2007 was left unexamined on 16 February because the investigation had been completed and the case transmitted to the Regional Court. Detention authorised until 19 February therefore expired without a new court order. The applicant’s applications of 5 March seeking release as unlawful were rejected by both the detention facility and the Regional Court, which on 12 March simply ordered that “detention remain unchanged” when it listed the case for trial.

Throughout the subsequent nine-month trial (21 public hearings) the applicant was confined in a 4.5 m² metal cage. He twice asked to be released from it; the court first adjourned the request and later refused, citing security. A challenge to the judge on the ground that the cage violated the presumption of innocence and equality of arms was dismissed. Hearings were attended by the applicant’s family, friends, local residents and students. On 8 August 2007 a further bail application was refused because the trial was unfinished and the offence remained classified as serious. Charges were ultimately dropped for insufficient evidence; the Regional Court terminated the proceedings on 5 December 2007 and the applicant was released.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints that his cage confinement constituted degrading treatment, that detention after 19 February 2007 lacked a legal basis, that successive detention orders were unreasoned, that bail was automatically unavailable because of the offence’s gravity, that the 12 December hearing breached equality of arms, that reasonable-suspicion arguments were ignored, and that the Court of Appeal unlawfully declined to examine his 27 January appeal.
001-112099:
The case of Trampevski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 4570/07) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s fair-trial rights under Article 6 of the Convention. Tome Trampevski, a taxi driver from Bitola born in 1958, claimed he had been unable to confront two key witnesses whose pre-trial statements formed the basis of his conviction for migrant smuggling.

On 1 November 2005, Albanian nationals E.J. and R.M. were stopped by Macedonian border police near the Greek frontier at Velushina crossroads. They told officers they had been driven from Bitola bus station by a taxi driver who knew they lacked travel documents and charged them approximately EUR 100 each to be taken to a point from which they could illegally enter Greece. The following day, 2 November 2005, an investigating judge of the Bitola Court of First Instance heard the two men in the presence of the public prosecutor only. Both waived an interpreter and spoke Macedonian. They described hailing a white taxi at the bus station, informing the driver of their intention to reach Greece without papers, agreeing a fare of EUR 100–160 each, receiving instructions to flee or lie if stopped by police, and being dropped near a water canal that they could not cross. They identified the applicant from photographs and, later the same day, in a live identification parade. At 19:30 that evening the pair were deported to Albania.

The investigating judge opened a formal investigation. The applicant, assisted by counsel, denied the allegations. He stated that he had driven the two men only as far as Bukovo village, a few kilometres from Bitola, for a fare of 120–150 Macedonian denars (approximately EUR 2–2.50) and had not suspected they were undocumented foreigners. He produced two eyewitnesses—kiosk staff S.S. and M.T.—who corroborated his version of a short, inexpensive trip to Bukovo. Police officers T.S. and B.G., who had arrested the migrants, confirmed the location of the arrest and the men’s account of the fare.

On 11 November 2005 the public prosecutor indicted the applicant for migrant smuggling. At the trial hearing of 23 March 2006 the applicant repeated his denial. S.S. and M.T. again supported him. The court then scheduled a final hearing for 13 April 2006. In the absence of the deported migrants, the court simply read their 2 November statements into the record without seeking the applicant’s or his lawyer’s consent. Counsel immediately objected that the defence had never been able to confront the witnesses on the drop-off point or the amount paid, and noted inconsistencies in their accounts of the fare. The trial court nevertheless convicted the applicant the same day and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. It relied principally on the migrants’ written statements to find that he had knowingly transported undocumented Albanians to a smuggling route near the Greek border for EUR 100 each. The court dismissed the defence witnesses as unreliable and treated the precise drop-off location as irrelevant.

The applicant appealed, arguing that he had been denied the opportunity to cross-examine the only witnesses who could establish his knowledge of the men’s status and the terms of the journey. The Bitola Court of Appeal, sitting in public session on 17 October 2006, upheld the conviction after a detailed review of the migrants’ statements, which it described as clear and consistent. It did not address the confrontation complaint. A further appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court, again raising the inability to examine the witnesses, was dismissed on 20 December 2006. The Supreme Court held that it could not re-examine facts or the specific procedural ground invoked by the applicant.

The core factual issue is therefore that the conviction rested almost entirely on the untested, uncross-examined statements of two witnesses who had been removed from the jurisdiction hours after they identified the applicant and who never appeared at trial.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Trampevski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 4570/07) concerned a Macedonian taxi driver, Tome Trampevski (born 1958), who alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. Specifically, he claimed he could not confront or cross-examine two key witnesses—Albanian migrants E.J. and R.M.—whose pre-trial statements formed the basis of his conviction for smuggling migrants.

On 1 or 2 November 2005, the migrants, attempting illegal entry into Greece, were apprehended by border police near Velushina after being dropped off by a taxi. That day, an investigating judge heard them (without the applicant or his counsel present) in the presence of only the public prosecutor. Both waived an interpreter and testified in Macedonian. They described arriving at Bitola bus station, approaching a taxi driver (whom they later identified as the applicant via photographs and a parade), and agreeing to pay him EUR 100–160 each after disclosing they lacked travel documents. The driver allegedly hid his vehicle, directed them toward a water canal to cross into Greece, advised them to flee or deny knowing him if police appeared, and mentioned his prior Greek prison sentence for similar offenses. They claimed he knew their intent and destination. Police officers T.S. and B.G. later confirmed apprehending the pair near the border; one carried an Albanian ID, and they mentioned a taxi ride costing EUR 100–150 each.

The applicant, heard the same day with counsel, denied the charges. He stated he drove an orange van, met the pair (who spoke Macedonian) at the bus station around 6:45 p.m., and agreed to take them to nearby Bukovo village for MKD 120–150 (about EUR 2–2.50) each after bargaining. He returned immediately, asked no questions about documents (suspecting nothing due to their language skills and local Albanian population), and rejected claims of euro payments or discussing his past sentence. Eyewitnesses S.S. (a kiosk saleswoman) and M.T. corroborated that the migrants requested a ride to Bukovo and obtained change there, with no suspicion of foreign status. The migrants were deported to Albania that evening, precluding any later confrontation.

On 11 November 2005, the prosecutor indicted the applicant for migrant smuggling, requesting the trial court read the migrants' statements and identification records, plus hear the police officers. At the 23 March 2006 hearing, the applicant reiterated his account, contesting the euro payments, drop-off point, and any conversation. S.S. and M.T. testified consistently with him. At the final 13 April 2006 hearing, without seeking applicant or counsel consent, the court read the migrants' unchallenged pre-trial statements. The defense lawyer analyzed inconsistencies (e.g., payment amounts, drop-off) and complained of no opportunity to confront the pair on key issues like location and price.

The trial court convicted the applicant that day, imposing one year's imprisonment. It relied primarily on the migrants' statements to find he knowingly transported undocumented Albanians from Bitola station to Velushina (a known smuggling spot) for EUR 100 each, aware of their illegal intent, and mentioned his Greek sentence. It dismissed S.S. and M.T. as unreliable and treated the drop-off discrepancy as minor, given police testimony.

The applicant appealed, arguing (under Criminal Proceedings Act s. 355) that the conviction rested on unconfronted statements establishing knowledge of migrant status, the Velushina drop-off, and euro payments, despite inconsistencies and his inability to question them during investigation. He noted their Macedonian fluency made suspicion unreasonable. The Bitola Court of Appeal (17 October 2006) upheld the judgment after reviewing the statements as "clear and consistent," deeming drop-off and language irrelevant (as the pair allegedly disclosed illegal intent), but ignored the confrontation complaint. The Supreme Court (20 December 2006) dismissed a further appeal on points of law, finding no basis to reassess facts or address s. 355(11) defense-rights violations, and again omitting comment on the lack of cross-examination.

These facts centered on the unavailability of the migrants (due to swift deportation) and the domestic courts' use of their untested statements as decisive evidence, without granting the defense any opportunity for confrontation despite repeated complaints.

The case of Trampevski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 4570/07) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the inability to confront and examine key prosecution witnesses whose pre-trial statements formed the basis of his conviction for smuggling migrants.

Tome Trampevski, a taxi driver born in 1958 and living in Bitola, was charged after events on 1 November 2005. Two Albanian nationals, E.J. and R.M., were apprehended by border police near the Velushina crossroads while attempting to enter Greece illegally. They carried no travel documents and claimed they had been driven from Bitola bus station by a taxi driver.

On 2 November 2005, an investigating judge heard the migrants in the presence of the public prosecutor only. Both waived an interpreter and spoke Macedonian. They stated they had approached a taxi driver at the bus station, informed him they wished to reach Greece without documents, and agreed to pay EUR 160 each (later described inconsistently as reduced to EUR 100 each). The driver, whom they later identified photographically and in an identification parade as the applicant, took them to a location near a water canal, instructed them on how to cross into Greece, and allegedly mentioned having served a prison sentence in Greece for similar conduct. He advised them to deny knowing him or his knowledge of their destination if stopped. The migrants were deported to Albania the same evening.

The applicant was heard the same day, assisted by counsel. He stated he drove an orange Mitsubishi van and had accepted a fare of MKD 120–150 (approximately EUR 2–2.50) to take two men speaking Macedonian to the nearby village of Bukovo. He denied any knowledge they were foreign nationals or intending illegal entry, denied requesting euros, and denied mentioning a prison sentence. He requested examination of two eyewitnesses present at the bus station, S.S. (a kiosk saleswoman) and M.T.

Police officers who arrested the migrants confirmed the pair had spoken of a taxi driver and payments of EUR 100–150 each. On 11 November 2005 the public prosecutor indicted the applicant for smuggling, alleging he transported the migrants to the Velushina area for EUR 100 each, and requested that the migrants’ statements be read at trial.

At the trial hearings in March and April 2006 the applicant maintained his account. S.S. and M.T. corroborated that the men had requested a short trip to Bukovo for a modest local-currency fare and that nothing suggested they were undocumented foreigners. The trial court then read out the migrants’ pre-trial statements without seeking the agreement of the applicant or his lawyer and without any opportunity for confrontation. The defence complained that the applicant had been unable to test the migrants on the drop-off location, the agreed price (noting inconsistencies in their accounts), and related details.

On 13 April 2006 the trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. It accepted the migrants’ statements as establishing that he knew they were undocumented Albanians intending illegal entry, that he had driven them toward the border, that they had paid EUR 100 each, and that he had referred to his Greek prison sentence. It treated the precise drop-off point as established by the location of the arrest (a known smuggling route) and dismissed the defence witnesses as unreliable.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the conviction rested on untested statements and that he had been denied confrontation on critical points such as payment and destination. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 17 October 2006, finding the migrants’ accounts clear and consistent and regarding the exact drop-off location as irrelevant; it did not address the confrontation complaint. The Supreme Court likewise rejected an appeal on points of law on 20 December 2006, declining to re-examine the facts or the defence-rights issue.

The migrants’ statements constituted the decisive evidence of the applicant’s knowledge and intent. Their immediate deportation prevented any subsequent examination, and the domestic courts neither secured the witnesses nor provided compensating safeguards.
001-112278:
The case of Jama v. Slovenia originated in Application no. 48163/08 lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 September 2008 by Vinko Jama, a Slovenian national born in 1914. Jama died later that year; his daughter Marija Preželj pursued the application. The proceedings concern the alleged excessive length of domestic court proceedings to determine compensation following expropriation of Jama’s house, raising issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a hearing within a reasonable time) and, relatedly, the effectiveness of domestic remedies under Article 13.

On 1 September 1970 a decision expropriating Jama’s house in favour of the Municipality of Ljubljana became final. In 1971 the municipality instituted non-contentious proceedings before the first-instance court to fix the compensation payable. Jama was a party. By 1988 the first-instance court had delivered four successive rulings, each of the first three having been quashed and remitted by the Ljubljana Higher Court. The fourth first-instance judgment of 15 July 1988 was itself quashed on 2 March 1989 because the facts had been insufficiently established; a further re-examination was ordered.

In 1989 the compensation proceedings were suspended pending the outcome of separate proceedings in which Jama challenged the validity of the expropriation itself. Thereafter hearings were repeatedly cancelled at Jama’s request because related denationalisation proceedings concerning the same house and land remained pending. A hearing listed for 5 April 2004 was informed that those denationalisation proceedings (UE 351-307/93) were still ongoing. The case was then transferred to a new judge who assumed it only in December 2005. Hearings took place in March, April and June 2006; at the last of these Jama stated that his related compensation claim arising from denationalisation was still pending before the Administrative Court.

Jama had already applied to the Strasbourg Court on 7 June 2006 complaining of the length of the compensation proceedings. That application was declared inadmissible on 11 December 2007 for failure to exhaust the remedies introduced by the 2006 Act on the Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay (supervisory appeal, motion for a deadline and, after final resolution, a claim for just satisfaction limited to EUR 5,000).

Meanwhile, on 14 November 2007 the first-instance court noted that the denationalisation compensation proceedings had reached the Supreme Court. Those proceedings ended on 25 February 2008 with an award of state certificates for the land and rejection of the claim for the house. The compensation proceedings for the house could therefore resume. On 21 February 2008 Jama lodged a supervisory appeal; a hearing was listed for 10 April 2008 at which an expert in construction was appointed. On 19 September 2008 the court formulated the questions for the expert. Jama lodged a further supervisory appeal on 29 July 2008 and a motion for a deadline on 1 September 2008. He died on 19 October 2008 aged 94.

The expert, delayed by hospitalisation and heart surgery, produced a report only on 25 March 2010. At a hearing on 13 January 2011 a new expert was appointed and the court requested identification of Jama’s successors. An inheritance decision of 7 May 2010 named Preželj as executor and sole manager of the estate, authorised to continue all pending proceedings; three other next-of-kin received statutory shares. Preželj’s representative lodged a further supervisory appeal on 6 June 2011, complaining that the 2008 motion for a deadline remained unanswered. Only on 9 September 2011 did the President of the Higher Court acknowledge receipt of that motion (transmitted three days earlier) and instruct the first-instance judge to treat the case as a priority and to submit three-monthly progress reports.

Thus, more than forty years after the 1971 institution of proceedings, and despite the availability of the 2006 Act remedies from 1 January 2007, the first-instance court had still not determined the compensation due for an expropriation that became final in 1970. The successive remittals, lengthy suspensions linked to parallel denationalisation litigation, judicial transfers, delayed expert evidence and slow processing of acceleration requests constitute the core factual matrix of the alleged violations.

**Case Summary: Jama v. Slovenia (Application no. 48163/08), ECtHR, 19 July 2012**

The case concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time) due to the excessive duration of domestic non-contentious proceedings to determine compensation for the applicant’s expropriated house. Vinko Jama (born 1914, died October 2008 at age 94) lodged the application on 18 September 2008. After his death his daughter, Marija Preželj (named in the inheritance decision as sole manager of the estate, executor and successor authorised to continue the relevant proceedings), pursued the application.

On 1 September 1970 a decision expropriating Jama’s house in favour of the Municipality of Ljubljana became final. In 1971 the municipality commenced non-contentious court proceedings to fix compensation; Jama was a party. By 1988 the first-instance court had issued four decisions, three of which had been remitted by the second-instance court. The last first-instance judgment (15 July 1988) was quashed by the Ljubljana Higher Court on 2 March 1989 for insufficient factual findings, with an order for re-examination.

In 1989 the compensation proceedings were suspended pending a challenge by Jama to the validity of the expropriation. Multiple hearings were later cancelled at Jama’s request because related proceedings remained pending. On 5 April 2004 his daughter (then representing him) informed the court that denationalisation proceedings (no. UE 351-307/93) concerning the house and land were still ongoing. A September 2004 hearing was cancelled because the case was transferred to another judge, who took it over only in December 2005. Hearings occurred on 30 March and 20 April 2006; on 8 June 2006 Jama stated that a related compensation claim arising from denationalisation of the same property was still pending before the Administrative Court.

Jama had already applied to the ECtHR in June 2006 complaining of delay; that application was declared inadmissible in December 2007 for non-exhaustion of the newly available remedies under the 2006 Act on the Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay. At a hearing on 14 November 2007 the Ljubljana Local Court noted that denationalisation compensation proceedings were then before the Supreme Court. Those proceedings ended on 25 February 2008: Jama received state certificates for the nationalised land, but his request for denationalisation of the house itself was rejected.

Jama lodged a supervisory appeal on 21 February 2008. A hearing was scheduled and, on 10 April 2008, the court recorded that the denationalisation case had concluded, allowing the compensation proceedings to resume; it appointed a construction expert. Questions for the expert were set on 19 September 2008. Further supervisory appeals and a motion for a deadline followed in July–September 2008. Jama died on 19 October 2008.

The expert (hospitalised and having undergone heart surgery) filed his report only on 25 March 2010. At a hearing on 13 January 2011 the court decided to appoint a new expert and requested details of Jama’s successors; these were supplied on 24 February 2011. The applicant’s representative lodged another supervisory appeal on 6 June 2011 complaining of continued delay and the unanswered 2008 motion for a deadline. The 2006 Act (in force from 1 January 2007) provides two acceleratory remedies (supervisory appeal and motion for a deadline) while proceedings are pending and, after final resolution, a claim for just satisfaction (capped at EUR 5 000 for non-pecuniary damage). At the time of the ECtHR’s examination the compensation proceedings, begun in 1971, remained unresolved. The Court later found a violation of Article 6 § 1 on account of the overall length (more than 40 years) and awarded just satisfaction.

001-112706:
The applicants, 30 Serbian nationals who served as Yugoslav Army reservists from March to June 1999 during the NATO intervention, were entitled to per diems under April 1999 army orders based on amended travel-expense rules. After demobilisation the State refused payment. Reservists protested, sometimes clashing with police. On 11 January 2008 the Government concluded an agreement solely with reservists resident in seven “underdeveloped” municipalities (Kuršumlija, Lebane, Bojnik, Žitorađa, Doljevac, Prokuplje and Blace). Those reservists received instalment payments through their municipalities in exchange for withdrawing all pending and future claims; a mixed local commission would set distribution criteria. The applicants, lacking registered residence in those municipalities, were excluded.

On 26 March 2009 they sued the State for the unpaid per diems, alleging discrimination. The Niš Court of First Instance dismissed the action on 8 July 2010, accepting a legal basis but holding the claim time-barred under the three-year limitation of Article 376 § 1 of the Obligations Act (running from demobilisation). The Niš Appeals Court upheld the judgment on 16 November 2010, adding that the five-year absolute period of Article 376 § 2 had also expired. The applicants then lodged a constitutional appeal (still pending when the Chamber sat), complaining that other Serbian appellate courts had applied the ordinary ten-year limitation of Article 371 on identical facts and that the 2008 agreement itself constituted residence-based discrimination.

Between 2002 and early 2009 first-instance and appellate courts across Serbia had produced conflicting results, some applying the three-/five-year periods and others the ten-year period. Supreme Court legal opinions of 2003 and 2004 favoured the shorter periods for “damages” claims against the State. From 2010 onward most appellate courts aligned with those opinions, although a few later judgments rejected similar claims as purely administrative and thus outside civil-court competence. A default judgment obtained by one reservist in Leskovac never became final.

A Government working group set up in August 2008 to examine remaining reservists’ demands ultimately rejected them, citing lack of funds, unharmonised requests and the assertion that many per diems had already been paid. On 26 July 2011 the Commissioner for the Protection of Equality found that the 2008 payments were per diems, not social assistance, because recipients had been required to waive legal claims and had never been asked to prove indigence. Differential treatment based solely on registered residence therefore lacked objective and reasonable justification; the Commissioner recommended that the Government extend the same payments to all reservists.

The Constitutional Court had, in several comparable cases, either dismissed appeals as unsubstantiated or found no discrimination because the impugned judgments had not been based on personal status; in one later decision it ordered a retrial solely for inconsistent case-law. The Chamber was thus confronted with two linked complaints: (i) that the applicants had been treated differently from equally situated reservists solely on account of residence, and (ii) that the domestic courts’ contradictory application of limitation periods had deprived them of a fair hearing and legal certainty.

They served from March to June 1999 and were entitled to per diems under April 1999 orders issued by the Army Chief of Staff pursuant to military bylaws on travel and other expenses.

After demobilization the Government refused payment. Reservists staged protests, some of which turned confrontational. On 11 January 2008 the Government concluded an agreement solely with reservists residing in seven designated “underdeveloped” municipalities (Kuršumlija, Lebane, Bojnik, Žitorađa, Doljevac, Prokuplje and Blace). Those individuals received payments in six instalments through their municipalities in exchange for waiving all outstanding 1999-related claims. Selection of the municipalities was justified by their economic status, implying the recipients’ indigence; individual means-testing was not required. The applicants, who lived elsewhere, were excluded.
