On 8 July 2010 that court accepted the legal basis of the claims but dismissed them as time-barred under the three-year limitation period running from demobilization (Art. 376 § 1 of the Obligations Act). The Niš Appeals Court upheld the dismissal on 16 November 2010, adding that the five-year absolute period had also expired. On 21 January 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional appeal, arguing that other appellate courts had applied the general ten-year limitation period (Art. 371) and had granted identical claims, and that the 2008 agreement itself constituted discriminatory exclusion. The Constitutional Court proceedings remained pending.

Supreme Court legal opinions of 2003 and 2004 indicated that the shorter periods governed such compensation claims. From 2010 most appellate courts followed those opinions. The applicants, 30 Serbian nationals represented by counsel, were army reservists drafted into the Yugoslav Army during the 1999 NATO intervention. They served from March to June 1999 and were entitled to daily allowances (per diems) under April 1999 army decisions and orders issued by the Chief of Staff, themselves based on amended army travel-and-expenses rules. After demobilisation the State refused to pay. Reservists organised protests, some of which turned confrontational. On 11 January 2008 the Government concluded an agreement solely with reservists resident in seven designated “underdeveloped” municipalities (Kuršumlija, Lebane, Bojnik, Žitorađa, Doljevac, Prokuplje and Blace). Those reservists received the sums in six monthly instalments channelled through their municipalities, in exchange for waiving all outstanding 1999-service claims still pending in the civil courts. The municipalities were selected on the stated ground of the reservists’ presumed indigence; no individual means test was required. All other reservists, including the applicants, were excluded.

On 26 March 2009 the applicants brought a civil action against the State seeking the unpaid per diems and alleging discrimination. The Niš first-instance court (8 July 2010) accepted that a valid legal basis existed but dismissed the claim as time-barred under the three-year prescription period of Article 376 § 1 of the Obligations Act, running from demobilisation. The Niš Appeals Court (16 November 2010) upheld the judgment, adding that the five-year absolute limit in Article 376 § 2 had also expired. The applicants then lodged a constitutional appeal (21 January 2011) complaining both of the exclusionary 2008 agreement and of inconsistent appellate case-law: other Serbian courts (district, high and appeals courts) had applied the ordinary ten-year prescription of Article 371 and had therefore awarded identical claims. Those constitutional proceedings remained pending when the European Court examined the applications.

Domestic jurisprudence on the same facts was divided. Between 2002 and early 2009 first-instance and appellate courts across Serbia had reached opposite results, some applying the short three-/five-year periods and others the ten-year period. Supreme Court legal opinions of 26 May 2003 and 6 April 2004 (published in the Court’s Bulletin) treated the claims as compensation for State malfeasance and therefore subject to Article 376. From 2010 onwards most appellate courts followed those opinions. A minority of claims were dismissed as purely administrative and thus outside civil-court jurisdiction. One default judgment in a reservist’s favour (Leskovac, July 2010) never became final. Earlier constitutional appeals by similarly situated reservists were rejected, the Constitutional Court either ignoring the 2008 agreement or holding that any jurisprudential inconsistency did not constitute discrimination because it was not based on a “personal characteristic.”

The Government later established a working group for the excluded reservists but ultimately rejected their demands, citing lack of funds, incomplete documentation, doubtful representative standing and the assertion that many per diems had already been paid. On 26 July 2011 the Commissioner for the Protection of Equality found that the 2008 agreement discriminated on the basis of registered residence. She characterised the payments as per diems (not social assistance), noting that recipients had been required to abandon legal claims and had never had to prove poverty. She recommended that the Government extend equivalent payments to all reservists; the Government did not implement the recommendation.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints of discriminatory treatment in the enjoyment of a pecuniary claim and of a violation of legal certainty arising from persistently contradictory domestic case-law.
001-113299:
The case of Najafli v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 2594/07) was brought by journalist Ramiz Huseyn oglu Najafli, editor-in-chief of the newspaper Boz Qurd, against Azerbaijan before the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been beaten by police during the dispersal of an unauthorised opposition demonstration in Baku on 9 October 2005 and that the authorities had failed to investigate the incident effectively.

On that date the applicant, wearing a journalist’s badge but not a distinctive blue vest, attended the demonstration with five colleagues to report on events. During the police dispersal the journalists were beaten and sustained injuries. The applicant stated that he identified himself as a journalist and asked officers to stop, but he was struck on the head with truncheons by a group of officers, lost consciousness and was hospitalised the same day. A medical certificate of 26 October 2005 diagnosed closed cranio-cerebral trauma, concussion and soft-tissue damage to the crown of the head. A further certificate of 10 July 2006 from Baku City Polyclinic no. 19 confirmed the diagnosis and noted that his condition required long-term treatment.

The six journalists lodged a joint criminal complaint. On 9 November 2005 the Sabail District Police Department opened proceedings under Article 132 of the Criminal Code (beating). The case was later re-qualified under Article 163 (obstruction of journalists’ lawful professional activity) and transferred to the Sabail District Prosecutor’s Office. On 12 January 2006 the applicant told the investigator that he had been beaten while observing the demonstration and submitted a photograph of A.V., head of the Riot Police Regiment; two other journalists corroborated his account. The Government claimed that a forensic examination was ordered on 28 January 2006 but that the applicant failed to attend; the applicant maintained he was never informed. The investigator asked the police to identify the officers involved; the police replied on 25 February 2006 that they had been unable to do so. A.V. was questioned on 1 March 2006 and denied any unlawful conduct.

On 9 March 2006 the investigator suspended the investigation on the ground that the perpetrators remained unidentified, relying on A.V.’s denial. The applicant was not notified until May 2006, when he was also refused a copy of the suspension decision. He complained to the Sabail District Court, arguing that the officers (including those under A.V.’s command) were identifiable and seeking quashing of the decision. On 26 May 2006 the court dismissed the complaint as lawful, without addressing A.V.’s role or hearing witnesses. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 13 June 2006.

Separately, on 9 November 2006 the applicant brought a civil claim against the Ministry of Internal Affairs for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, invoking Articles 3, 10 and 11 of the Convention. The Sabail District Court refused to admit the action for lack of a forensic report establishing the cause of injury, absence of any finding of individual police responsibility, and failure to name specific defendants rather than the Ministry. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the refusal in January and June 2007 respectively.

The facts thus centre on the alleged police beating of an identified journalist during a demonstration and the subsequent investigative and judicial responses that left the perpetrators unidentified and provided no effective remedy.

The case of Najafli v. Najafli informed the officers of his professional status and asked them to stop; they nevertheless struck him on the head, causing him to lose consciousness. He was taken to hospital the same day. A medical certificate issued on 26 October 2005 diagnosed closed cranio-cerebral trauma, concussion and soft-tissue damage to the crown of the head. A further certificate of 10 July 2006 confirmed the diagnosis and the need for long-term treatment.

The six journalists lodged a joint criminal complaint. On 9 November 2005 the Sabail District Police Department opened proceedings under Article 132 of the Criminal Code (beating). The case was re-qualified on 22 December 2005 under Article 163 (obstruction of journalists’ lawful professional activity) and transferred to the Sabail District Prosecutor’s Office. On 12 January 2006 the applicant described being beaten by a group of unidentified officers while observing the demonstration; he identified A.V., commander of the Baku Riot Police Regiment, from a photograph taken at the scene and noted that A.V. was in charge of the unit. Two other journalists corroborated his account. A.V. was later questioned and denied any unlawful conduct.

The investigator requested the police to identify the officers involved; the police replied on 25 February 2006 that they had been unable to do so. The Government claimed a forensic examination had been ordered on 28 January 2006 but that the applicant failed to appear; the applicant stated he had never been informed of the order. On 9 March 2006 the investigation was suspended on the ground that the perpetrators remained unidentified and that A.V. had denied wrongdoing. The applicant was not notified until he inquired in May 2006 and never received a copy of the suspension decision.

He challenged the suspension before the Sabail District Court, arguing that the authorities already knew the officers’ identities (particularly A.V.’s role) and that the failure to supply the decision prevented a proper appeal. On 26 May 2006 the court dismissed the complaint, holding that the decision had been lawful and had been sent to him; it did not address A.V.’s involvement or hear any witnesses. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 13 June 2006.

In parallel civil proceedings lodged on 9 November 2006 against the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Najafli sought damages under Articles 3, 10 and 11 of the Convention. The first-instance court refused to admit the claim for lack of a forensic report establishing causation, absence of any document identifying a responsible officer, and failure to name individual defendants rather than the Ministry. Subsequent appeals were rejected, culminating in a Supreme Court decision of 14 June 2007.

Azerbaijani law (Constitution Article 46 and the 1999 Police Act) prohibits torture and ill-treatment, requires that any use of physical force or special equipment (including truncheons) be strictly necessary and proportionate, mandates written reports and prosecutorial notification within 24 hours, and obliges the police to conduct an inquiry into every such incident. These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of both substantive ill-treatment by state agents and a structurally deficient investigation that never identified the officers responsible or produced an effective remedy.

The case of Najafli v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 2594/07) was brought by Azerbaijani journalist Ramiz Huseyn oglu Najafli, born in 1967 and living in Baku, who served as editor-in-chief of the newspaper Boz Qurd. He alleged that police officers beat him during the dispersal of an unauthorized opposition demonstration in Baku on 9 October 2005 and that domestic authorities failed to investigate the incident effectively.

Najafli attended the demonstration with five other journalists to report on events. He wore a journalist badge on his chest but not the special blue vest used to identify media personnel. During the police operation to disperse the crowd, Najafli and his colleagues were beaten and suffered various injuries. He informed the officers that he was a journalist and asked them to stop, but was struck on the head and lost consciousness.

Najafli was taken to hospital that day. A medical certificate dated 26 October 2005 diagnosed closed cranio-cerebral trauma, concussion, and soft-tissue damage to the crown of the head. A further certificate issued on 10 July 2006 by Baku City Polyclinic no. 19 confirmed the same diagnosis and indicated that his condition required long-term treatment.

The six journalists lodged a joint criminal complaint. On 9 November 2005 the Sabail District Police Department instituted proceedings under Article 132 of the Criminal Code (beating). The case was re-qualified on 22 December 2005 under Article 163 (obstruction of the lawful professional activity of journalists) and transferred to the Sabail District Prosecutor’s Office.

Najafli was questioned on 12 January 2006. He stated that a group of police officers had beaten him with truncheons while he was observing the demonstration in his capacity as a journalist. He did not know the officers who struck him but identified those in charge of the unit and submitted a photograph of A.V., head of the Riot Police Regiment of the Baku Police Office. Two other journalists present, E.M. and N.A., corroborated his account. The Government claimed that a forensic examination was ordered on 28 January 2006 but that Najafli failed to appear; he maintained that he was never informed of the order.

The investigator requested the police on 2 February 2006 to identify the officers involved. On 25 February 2006 the police replied that they had been unable to do so but would continue efforts. A.V. was heard on 1 March 2006 and denied any involvement or unlawful actions by himself or officers under his command. On 9 March 2006 the investigator suspended the proceedings pending identification of the perpetrators, relying on the failure to identify the officers and on A.V.’s statements.

Najafli received no information until May 2006. After inquiring on 9 May, he learned of the suspension but was not given a copy of the decision. He complained to the Sabail District Court on 12 May 2006, arguing that the lack of a copy prevented a proper challenge, that the officers had been under A.V.’s command, and that the photograph had been submitted. The court dismissed the complaint on 26 May 2006, holding that the suspension was lawful and had been sent to him; the decision was silent on A.V. and no witnesses were heard. The Court of Appeal upheld the ruling on 13 June 2006.

On 9 November 2006 Najafli brought a civil action against the Ministry of Internal Affairs seeking compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, relying on Articles 3, 10 and 11 of the Convention. The Sabail District Court refused to admit the claim on 20 November 2006 for failure to produce a forensic report on the cause of the injuries, absence of any document establishing an officer’s responsibility, and failure to name specific individuals as defendants. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the refusal in January and June 2007 respectively.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations concerning the beating itself and the effectiveness of the subsequent investigation. Domestic law, including Article 46 of the Constitution and the Law on Police, prohibits ill-treatment and requires inquiries into police use of force.
001-112444:
The case of Toziczka v. Poland (Application no. 29995/08) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to an impartial tribunal under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant, Bożenna Toziczka, a Polish national born in 1943 and resident in Opole, complained that the Supreme Court that dismissed her cassation appeal was not impartial because one of its members had already expressed a definitive view on the central legal issue while sitting in a lower court.

In 2003 the “Zgoda” Housing Cooperative sued the applicant in the Opole Regional Court, seeking a court order compelling her to sell several plots of land that the cooperative had long occupied de facto. The cooperative had constructed roads and parking areas on the land as part of an adjacent housing estate. On 16 June 2003 the Regional Court dismissed the claim. It interpreted section 35 of the Housing Co-operatives Act as authorizing compulsory sale only where a cooperative had erected residential buildings, not mere infrastructure.

The cooperative appealed. On 26 November 2003 the Wrocław Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case, holding that section 35 also covered other infrastructure such as roads and parking. Judge D.Z. sat on that bench (as rapporteur). After remittal the Regional Court granted the claim and ordered the applicant to sell approximately 2,000 square metres.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the courts had misapplied section 35 by departing from its clear wording and adopting an unduly broad, functional interpretation. She also invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, claiming an unlawful and excessive interference with her property rights. On 14 March 2007 the Wrocław Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, expressly endorsing its 2003 legal interpretation.

The applicant then lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court, repeating the same arguments on statutory interpretation and property rights. On 18 January 2008 a three-judge panel of the Supreme Court, sitting in camera, dismissed the cassation. It accepted that the case turned entirely on the proper construction of section 35 and agreed with the Court of Appeal. Judge D.Z., who had in the meantime been promoted to the Supreme Court, sat on that panel.

A second, unrelated set of proceedings (compensation for an electricity company’s long-term use of the applicant’s land) ended with the Supreme Court’s refusal, on 14 December 2007, to entertain a cassation appeal; that dispute did not form the basis of the impartiality complaint.

The applicant’s core allegation was that Judge D.Z.’s successive participation in the 2003 Court of Appeal decision (which established the contested interpretation) and in the 2008 Supreme Court decision (which upheld the same interpretation) meant that the cassation court could not be regarded as impartial. Domestic law (Articles 398³ and 401 of the Code of Civil Procedure) allows cassation only on specified grounds of law and permits reopening for an improperly composed court, but the applicant considered those remedies inadequate in the circumstances. The Court communicated the application solely on the impartiality issue.

The case of Toziczka v. Poland originated in an application lodged on 2 June 2008 by Polish national Ms Bożenna Toziczka (born 1943, resident in Opole) under Article 34 of the Convention. She alleged, in particular, that her civil proceedings had not been determined by an impartial tribunal.

The principal proceedings concerned a claim by the “Zgoda” Housing Cooperative in Brzeg for a court order compelling the applicant to sell it several plots of land that it had occupied de facto for a lengthy period. On 16 June 2003 the Opole Regional Court dismissed the claim. It interpreted section 35 of the Housing Co-operatives Act as permitting compulsory sale only where a co-operative had erected buildings (houses) on third-party land. Here the co-operative had merely constructed roads and parking areas.

The co-operative appealed. On 26 November 2003 the Wrocław Court of Appeal (Judge D.Z. sitting as rapporteur) allowed the appeal, quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. It held that section 35 also covered land on which infrastructure other than houses had been built.

On remittal the Opole Regional Court granted the claim and ordered the applicant to sell 2,000 m² of land. It found that the co-operative had constructed a nearby housing estate that extended, via roads and parking, onto the applicant’s property, thereby engaging section 35.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the court had misapplied substantive law. Section 35, she submitted, permitted compulsory sale solely in respect of land on which houses had been built; exceptions must be construed narrowly. The order also violated her rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 14 March 2007 the Wrocław Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, expressly endorsing the legal view it had expressed in 2003.

The applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. She reiterated that the courts had unlawfully preferred a functional interpretation of section 35 (extending it by analogy to roads and parking so as to further the co-operative’s acquisition of third-party land) over its clear literal wording, and that the resulting order disproportionately interfered with her property rights.

The Supreme Court examined the cassation in camera on 18 January 2008. Judge D.Z., meanwhile promoted to that court, sat on the bench. The court treated the appeal as turning on the correct interpretation of section 35, agreed with the Court of Appeal’s view, and dismissed the cassation.

A second, separate set of proceedings concerned compensation for an electricity company’s long-term use of the applicant’s land (a pipeline). On 1 February 2007 the Opole Regional Court awarded her PLN 388,000. The Wrocław Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and dismissed the claim on 25 April 2007. The Supreme Court refused to examine her subsequent cassation appeal (decision of 14 December 2007).

Relevant domestic provisions included Article 398³ of the Code of Civil Procedure (cassation grounds: erroneous interpretation or application of substantive law, or procedural defects capable of affecting the outcome) and Article 401 (reopening for invalidity arising from improper court composition or a judge disqualified by law).

The central facts relevant to the impartiality complaint are therefore Judge D.Z.’s successive participation, first as rapporteur in the 2003 appellate judgment that established the contested interpretation of section 35, and later as a Supreme Court justice in the 2008 cassation that reviewed and upheld precisely that interpretation.

The case of Toziczka v. Poland (Application no. 29995/08) originated from an application lodged on 2 June 2008 with the European Court of Human Rights by Bożenna Toziczka, a Polish national born in 1943 and residing in Opole. Represented by lawyer A. Sieradzki, she complained primarily that her civil proceedings had not been determined by an impartial tribunal, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention.

The key proceedings concerned a claim by the “Zgoda” Housing Cooperative in Brzeg against the applicant. The cooperative sought a court order compelling her to sell several plots of land that it had long occupied de facto. On 16 June 2003 the Opole Regional Court dismissed the claim. It interpreted section 35 of the Housing Co-operatives Act as permitting compulsory sale only where a cooperative had erected residential buildings on third-party land. In this instance the cooperative had constructed only roads and parking areas.

The cooperative appealed. On 26 November 2003 the Wrocław Court of Appeal, with Judge D.Z. sitting as judge rapporteur, allowed the appeal, quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. The appellate court held that the Regional Court had misapplied section 35: compulsory sale could also be ordered in respect of land on which a cooperative had built infrastructure other than houses.

After remittal the Opole Regional Court granted the cooperative’s claim and ordered the applicant to sell approximately 2,000 square metres of land. It found that the cooperative had constructed a housing estate nearby and had built parking areas and roads partly on the applicant’s property; section 35 therefore authorised the compulsory transfer.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the courts had erred in their interpretation of substantive law. She maintained that section 35 applied exclusively to land on which houses had been built and that any broader, functional reading violated the principle that exceptions must be construed narrowly. She also invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, asserting that the forced sale constituted an unlawful and excessive interference with her property rights.

On 14 March 2007 the Wrocław Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, expressly endorsing the legal view it had already expressed in its 2003 remittal judgment.

The applicant then lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court, reiterating that the lower courts had unlawfully departed from the clear wording of section 35 by employing a functional interpretation that extended the provision to roads and parking facilities. She again relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The cassation appeal was examined in camera on 18 January 2008. Judge D.Z., who had in the meantime been promoted to the Supreme Court, sat on the bench. The Supreme Court identified the interpretation of section 35 as the decisive issue, agreed with the Wrocław Court of Appeal’s construction, and dismissed the cassation appeal.

A second, separate set of proceedings concerned compensation for an electricity company’s long-term use of the applicant’s land for a pipeline. Those proceedings ended with the Supreme Court’s refusal, on 14 December 2007, to entertain a cassation appeal, but they do not form the core of the impartiality complaint.

The applicant’s principal allegation therefore centred on the participation of the same judge, D.Z., first in the 2003 appellate decision that remitted the case and later in the 2008 Supreme Court ruling that finally disposed of it. She contended that this sequential involvement compromised the objective impartiality of the tribunal that determined her property rights.
001-113390:
The case of Popenda v. Poland (Application no. 39502/08) concerns a Polish national, Krzysztof Popenda (born 1958), who lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 August 2008 alleging violations arising from two sets of criminal proceedings against him. These involved prolonged pre-trial detention, delays in investigation and trial, restricted access to case files, and limitations on family visits, among other issues.

In the first set of proceedings, Popenda was arrested on 26 September 2004 and remanded in custody on 28 September 2004 by the Łódź District Court. He was charged with offering a bribe to Member of Parliament A.P., alongside well-known businessman and lobbyist M.D., whose case attracted significant media and political attention. Detention was justified by a reasonable suspicion of the offence, the need to secure the proceedings, the risk of a severe sentence, and potential influence on witnesses. Appeals were dismissed, and detention was repeatedly extended by the District Court (December 2004, March and June 2005) and the Łódź Court of Appeal (September and December 2005; February, May, June, September, and December 2006). Courts cited the case's extraordinary complexity involving high-ranking officials, ongoing investigation delays, and the insufficiency of alternative measures. On 6 December 2006, bail of 300,000 PLN was set; Popenda paid it on 5 January 2007 and was released. A bill of indictment was filed on 20 January 2007 against Popenda, M.D., and A.P. The first hearing, scheduled for 27 September 2007, was cancelled. On 25 June 2012, the Pabianice District Court convicted Popenda of two years and ten months' imprisonment plus a fine (judgment not final; appeal pending).

The second set began around 20 July 2004, with charges later including money laundering (added 8 March 2005, severed 14 November 2005), tax offences, and forgery (added 2007–2008). Popenda was arrested on 14 January 2008 and detained on 15 January 2008 by the Katowice District Court due to reasonable suspicion and risk of a severe sentence, though the court found no risk of interference given the lengthy prior proceedings and his prior liberty without incident. Bail of 100,000 PLN was set but stayed pending the prosecutor's appeal. Detention was extended on 5 March 2008. On 11 April 2008, the Warsaw Regional Court refused further extension, imposing police supervision and a travel ban while criticizing the prosecutor for withholding investigative plans (citing ECHR Article 5 § 4). Popenda was released on 15 April 2008, but the Warsaw Court of Appeal reversed this on 27 May 2008, reinstating detention from 28 May 2008. Further extension to 31 May 2009 was granted on 25 February 2009 with 300,000 PLN bail; he was released on 8 April 2009 after payment. Some charges were discontinued (24 May 2011, no offence); bills of indictment followed in 2011–2012 for tax fraud-related matters. The main investigation (no. Ap V Ds. 6/09/s) remained pending and was stayed on 22 December 2011.

On 22 December 2009, the Warsaw Court of Appeal upheld Popenda's complaint under the 2004 Act on unreasonable delay, finding a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time in the investigation (started 20 July 2004, still pending). It awarded 10,000 PLN compensation, noting unrelated charges joined (mostly against M.D.), repeated supplements causing protraction, delays in evidence examination (e.g., witnesses heard years later, expert opinions delayed), inactivity in international legal assistance requests (often irrelevant to Popenda), and reduced hearings of the applicant after 2005. The court instructed termination by 30 March 2010, which did not occur.

Access to the case file was granted on several occasions in the first proceedings (2005–2008) but refused for parts in September 2006. In the second, temporary refusals occurred on 6 December 2006, 31 August 2007, and 29 January 2008 (appeals dismissed); later access was allowed, though a reasoned detention motion was initially withheld.

During detention, family visit requests (wife and children) were often denied, including a 4 July 2008 refusal without reasons. Popenda also alleged medical issues, including recommended surgery unavailable in detention and cell placement with a murder suspect awaiting medical transfer.

These facts underpin complaints relating to excessive detention length, procedural delays, defence rights, and private/family life. The Court communicated the case on 13 October 2008.

The case of Popenda v. Poland concerns Polish national Krzysztof Popenda (born 1958) and his lengthy pre-trial detentions plus related proceedings.

In the first criminal proceedings, Popenda was arrested on 26 September 2004 and remanded in custody two days later by the Łódź District Court on suspicion of bribing MP A.P. together with businessman-lobbyist M.D. Detention was justified by the need to secure the proceedings, the likelihood of a severe sentence and the risk of influencing witnesses. Extensions were granted repeatedly through 2006 by district and appellate courts, citing case complexity involving high-ranking officials and the inadequacy of lesser measures. All appeals and release applications failed. On 6 December 2006 the court set bail of PLN 300 000; this was paid on 5 January 2007 and Popenda was released. An indictment followed on 20 January 2007. The first hearing scheduled for September 2007 was cancelled. He was convicted on 25 June 2012 and sentenced to two years and ten months’ imprisonment plus a fine (judgment not yet final).

A second investigation, opened on 20 July 2004, added charges of money-laundering (March 2005, later severed), tax offences and forgery (January 2008). Popenda was re-arrested on 14 January 2008. The Katowice District Court detained him the next day, citing a reasonable suspicion and the risk of a severe sentence, but found no tampering risk given the already lengthy proceedings and set PLN 100 000 bail. The prosecutor’s appeal stayed enforcement; detention was extended on 5 March 2008. On 11 April 2008 the Warsaw Regional Court refused a further extension, imposed police supervision and a travel ban, and criticised the prosecutor for withholding planned investigative steps (a possible Article 5 § 4 breach). Popenda was released on 15 April but, after a successful prosecutorial appeal, re-detained from 28 May 2008. On 25 February 2009 detention was extended until 31 May with PLN 300 000 bail, which was paid; he was released on 8 April 2009. Some tax charges were discontinued in May 2011; others led to indictments in 2011–2012. The remaining investigation was stayed in December 2011 and remains pending.

On 22 December 2009 the Warsaw Court of Appeal, applying the 2004 Act, found that the investigation (running since July 2004) had exceeded a reasonable time and awarded PLN 10 000. It criticised the joinder of unrelated charges (mainly against M.D.), delays in witness hearings and expert examinations, prosecutorial inactivity, and irrelevant international-assistance requests. The prosecutor was ordered to finish by 30 March 2010 but failed to do so.

Access to the case file was granted on several occasions in both sets of proceedings but refused on 6 December 2006, 31 August 2007 and 29 January 2008 (the last also denying a reasoned copy of the detention motion). Appeals against the refusals were dismissed. Family-visit requests, including one by Popenda’s wife and sons on 4 July 2008, were rejected without reasons. Medical recommendations for surgery could not be implemented in detention, and he was housed with a detainee charged with murder.

These facts underpin alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 (excessive detention and inadequate review), Article 6 § 1 (unreasonable length of proceedings) and Article 8 (family-contact restrictions).

The case of Popenda v. Poland (no. 39502/08) originated in an application lodged on 5 August 2008 by Polish national Krzysztof Popenda (born 1958, resident in Częstochowa) against Poland. He was represented by counsel; the Government were represented by their Agent.

The facts centre on two overlapping sets of criminal proceedings involving charges of bribery, money-laundering, forgery and tax offences, together with the applicant’s associated periods of pre-trial detention, restrictions on access to the case file, and family-visit refusals.

In the first set of proceedings the applicant was arrested on 26 September 2004. On 28 September 2004 the Łódź District Court ordered his detention on remand on the ground of a reasonable suspicion that he had offered a bribe to a Member of Parliament, together with co-accused M.D. (a prominent businessman whose case attracted extensive media and political attention). The court cited the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation, the likelihood of a severe sentence and the risk that the applicant would influence witnesses. Subsequent extensions by the District Court (December 2004–June 2005) and the Łódź Court of Appeal (September 2005–December 2006) relied on the same grounds plus the “extraordinary complexity” of corruption charges involving high-ranking officials. The applicant’s appeals and applications for release were unsuccessful. On 6 December 2006 the Court of Appeal authorised release on bail of PLN 300 000 (approx. EUR 76 000). The applicant paid the sum and was released on 5 January 2007. A bill of indictment was lodged on 20 January 2007. The first hearing, scheduled for 27 September 2007, was cancelled. On 25 June 2012 the Pabianice District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to two years and ten months’ imprisonment plus a fine; the judgment was not yet final.

A second investigation, begun around 20 July 2004, led to additional charges of money-laundering (March 2005, later severed), further supplements in 2007 and a forgery charge in January 2008. The applicant was re-arrested on 14 January 2008. The next day the Katowice District Court ordered detention on the grounds of reasonable suspicion and the risk of a severe sentence, but found no risk of interference with the proceedings (the applicant having been at liberty without incident) and therefore set bail of PLN 100 000. Enforcement was stayed pending the prosecutor’s appeal. After further extensions the Warsaw Regional Court on 11 April 2008 refused a further extension, imposed police supervision and a travel ban, and criticised the prosecutor for withholding planned investigative steps, citing Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. The applicant was released on 15 April 2008. The Warsaw Court of Appeal allowed the prosecutor’s appeal on 27 May 2008 and re-imposed detention; the applicant returned to custody on 28 May 2008. On 25 February 2009 the Katowice Court of Appeal extended detention until 31 May 2009 but authorised release on bail of PLN 300 000, taking into account the volume of evidence already gathered, the length of detention already served and the availability of alternative measures. The applicant paid the bail and was released on 8 April 2009. Part of the investigation was discontinued in May 2011 (no offence established); bills of indictment on tax-fraud charges were lodged in 2011 and 2012; the remaining investigation was stayed in December 2011.

In December 2009 the Warsaw Court of Appeal, applying the 2004 Act on complaints about unreasonable delay, found a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time in the investigation that had begun in July 2004 and was still pending. It awarded PLN 10 000 (approx. EUR 2 300) compensation. The court criticised the joinder of numerous unrelated charges (mostly concerning co-accused M.D.), repeated supplementation of charges that prolonged the main investigation, delays in examining evidence and hearing witnesses, and periods of inactivity (including unanswered international letters of request that had no bearing on the applicant). It instructed the prosecutor to conclude the investigation by 30 March 2010; that deadline was not met.

At the pre-trial stage the prosecutor refused the applicant access to parts of the case file on several occasions (September 2006; 6 December 2006; 31 August 2007; 29 January 2008, the last also withholding the reasoned motion for detention). Appeals against the refusals were dismissed. Access was later granted. Family-visit requests were repeatedly lodged; one (4 July 2008) was refused without reasons. While detained the applicant was not given recommended surgery and was housed with a co-detainee charged with murder.

These facts underpin the complaints concerning the length and successive extensions of pre-trial detention, access to the file in the context of detention reviews, the overall length of the investigations, and restrictions on family contact.
001-113331:
The case of Ferenčíková v. Slovakia (Application no. 39912/09) concerns two Slovak nationals, Natália Ferenčíková (born 1976) and her daughter Jessica Júlia Ferenčíková (born 1997). The first applicant married a United States national, A., in the United States in May 1996 but returned to Slovakia in November 1996, remaining there thereafter. The marriage was dissolved by Slovak courts, with the second applicant placed in the first applicant’s care and custody. The application focuses on maintenance claims for the second applicant against A.

Three sets of proceedings addressed maintenance. In the first, a Bratislava Regional Court judgment that became final on 16 February 2004 dismissed the claim for the pre-divorce period. The court noted that the first applicant had not provided a usable address for A. in the United States, making it impossible to involve him; any order would be unenforceable there. The Regional Court specified that a fresh claim could be lodged if an address were later obtained.

A second judgment, final on 1 October 2004 and issued in the divorce proceedings, ordered A. to make monthly maintenance payments for the post-divorce period. A. was identified at the same address previously used and participated via a written submission and a court-appointed representative.

The third proceedings, initiated in February 2004 after the first dismissal, form the core of the application. The first applicant submitted a new address for A. The Bratislava IV District Court sought information from the Centre for the International Legal Protection of Children and Youth and requested assistance from United States authorities under the 1970 Hague Evidence Convention to question A. Reminders were sent, but responses were delayed or unhelpful. On 19 June 2008 the District Court split its ruling: it declared the claim for the period before 16 February 2004 (specifically from 5 February 2001) inadmissible as res judicata on the basis of the first judgment, while granting maintenance for the short subsequent period up to the second judgment.

The first applicant appealed, arguing that the first judgment had not decided the merits and had expressly left open a new application once an address was available. On 21 January 2009 the Regional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that A. still could not be made available for the proceedings, so the matter remained res judicata. A United States report responding to the 2005 evidence request arrived only in December 2009, after the proceedings had ended.

The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint on 9 April 2009, invoking Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (access to court and fair trial) and Article 5 of Protocol No. 7. They contended that they had supplied a confirmed address used successfully in other proceedings and that maintenance had previously been enforced through official channels. On 14 May 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible for failure to exhaust ordinary remedies. It held that, although Article 238 § 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure generally excludes appeals on points of law in Family Code matters, an appeal under Article 237(f) (serious procedural irregularity preventing a party from acting) remained available. The applicants then asked the Prosecutor General to lodge an extraordinary appeal; he replied that no such remedy existed in Family Code cases under Article 243f § 2(a).

Domestic practice on the availability of points-of-law appeals in family matters was inconsistent. Some Constitutional Court decisions required such an appeal even in Family Code cases, while a later 2009 judgment found that admitting one violated Article 6 § 1 because Article 238 § 4 excluded it. The Supreme Court had similarly mixed rulings.

These facts underpin the alleged violation of the right of access to court under Article 6 § 1, arising from the declaration of inadmissibility of the 2001–2004 maintenance claim despite the first judgment’s invitation to reapply and the applicants’ subsequent provision of an address. The Court also examined of its own motion whether the applicants had an effective remedy under Article 13, given the conflicting statutory provisions and case-law on further appeals.

**Case Summary: Ferenčíková v. Slovakia (Application no. 39912/09)**

The applicants, Natália Ferenčíková (born 1976) and her daughter Jessica Júlia Ferenčíková (born 1997), both Slovak nationals living in Bratislava, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 July 2009. They alleged that Slovak courts had violated their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention by declaring inadmissible a maintenance claim covering 5 February 2001 to 16 February 2004. The Court also examined of its own motion whether they had been denied an effective remedy under Article 13.

The first applicant married A., a United States national, in the United States in 1996. She returned to Slovakia later that year and remained there. Slovak courts later dissolved the marriage and awarded her custody of the second applicant. Maintenance for the child was addressed in three sets of proceedings, all in Slovakia.

In the first set, a judgment that became final on 16 February 2004 dismissed the first applicant’s maintenance claim. The Bratislava Regional Court held that she had failed to provide a usable address for A. in the United States, making it impossible to involve him; any order would be unenforceable there. The court explicitly stated that she could file a fresh claim if she later obtained an address.

In the second set, a ruling that became final on 1 October 2004 (attached to the divorce judgment) ordered A. to make monthly maintenance payments for the post-divorce period. A. was identified at the same address used previously and participated through a written submission and a court-appointed representative.

The third set of proceedings, which gave rise to the application, began in February 2004 when the first applicant filed a new claim using a different address for A. The Bratislava IV District Court made extensive efforts to locate him: it inquired of the Centre for the International Legal Protection of Children and Youth (which reported it had no relevant information and lacked investigative powers under the 1956 Convention on the Recovery Abroad of Maintenance); it sent a request to United States authorities under the 1970 Hague Evidence Convention (with reminders in 2007 and 2008); and it made further inquiries of the Centre in 2008. No usable information was obtained during the proceedings.

On 19 June 2008 the District Court split the claim. For the period before 16 February 2004 it declared the action inadmissible as res judicata, holding that the 2004 judgment had already decided the matter. For the subsequent period up to the second judgment it awarded the same monthly amount as previously ordered. The first applicant appealed only the inadmissibility ruling, arguing that the first judgment had not decided the merits and had expressly permitted a new claim once an address was available. On 21 January 2009 the Regional Court dismissed the appeal, finding that A. still could not be made available for the proceedings and that the matter therefore remained res judicata.

A report from the United States authorities on the questioning of A. arrived only on 14 December 2009, after the domestic proceedings had ended.

The applicants then filed a constitutional complaint under Article 127 of the Slovak Constitution, relying on Article 6 § 1 and Article 5 of Protocol No. 7. They asserted that they had identified a valid address (confirmed by A. himself in the divorce proceedings) and that earlier maintenance orders had been enforced through the Centre and its United States counterpart. On 14 May 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible for failure to exhaust ordinary remedies. It held that, although appeals on points of law are generally unavailable in Family Code matters (Article 238 § 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure), an appeal under Article 237(f) (denial of the right to act before the court) remained possible for serious procedural irregularities.

The applicants next asked the Prosecutor General to lodge an extraordinary appeal on points of law. On 20 July 2009 the Prosecutor General replied that no such remedy existed in Family Code cases (Article 243f § 2(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure).

The case of Ferenčíková v. Slovakia (Application no. 39912/09) concerns two Slovak applicants—a mother (born 1976) and her daughter (born 1997)—who alleged a violation of their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in connection with a child-maintenance claim. The Court also examined of its own motion whether they had been denied an effective remedy under Article 13.

The mother married A., a United States national, in the United States in 1996. She returned to Slovakia later that year and remained there. The marriage was later dissolved by Slovak courts and the child was placed in the mother’s custody. Three sets of maintenance proceedings followed, all in Slovak courts.

In the first set the Bratislava Regional Court, by a judgment that became final on 16 February 2004, dismissed the claim for maintenance covering the period before the divorce. It did so solely because the mother had not supplied a usable address for A. in the United States, rendering any order unenforceable there. The court expressly stated that the mother could file a fresh application once an address was obtained. (The first-instance court had merely “refrained from ruling”; the Regional Court recast this as a dismissal.)

A second judgment, final on 1 October 2004 and attached to the divorce decree, ordered monthly payments for the post-divorce period. A. participated to a limited extent.

In February 2004 the mother re-filed, this time indicating a new address, and sought maintenance for the earlier period (5 February 2001–16 February 2004). The District Court made repeated but unsuccessful attempts to locate A. through the Centre for the International Legal Protection of Children and Youth and through letters of request to United States authorities under the 1970 Hague Evidence Convention. On 19 June 2008 it declared the claim for the pre-16 February 2004 period inadmissible on grounds of res judicata. For the short subsequent interval it awarded the same monthly sum already ordered in the second judgment.

The mother appealed, relying on the first judgment’s explicit invitation to re-apply once an address was known and arguing that the matter had never been decided on the merits. The Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 21 January 2009, holding that A. still could not be made available and that the issue therefore remained res judicata. A United States report on A. arrived only after the proceedings had ended.

The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint alleging a breach of Article 6 § 1 (and of equality of spouses under Article 5 of Protocol No. 7). On 14 May 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible for failure to exhaust ordinary remedies. Although Article 238 § 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure generally excludes an appeal on points of law (dovolanie) in Family-Code matters, the court held that such an appeal remains available under Article 237(f) when a party has been prevented from acting before the court. It relied on academic commentary and one of its own earlier inadmissibility decisions.

The applicants then asked the Prosecutor General to lodge an extraordinary appeal on points of law. He refused, citing Article 243f § 2(a), which excludes that remedy in Family-Code cases.

Domestic practice on the availability of further appeals was inconsistent. Some Constitutional Court decisions required an Article 237(f) appeal even in family matters; a later 2009 Constitutional Court judgment held that admitting such an appeal violated Article 6 because it was barred by Article 238 § 4. The Supreme Court’s own case-law on the point was likewise non-uniform.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that they had been denied access to a court for a determination of the maintenance claim on its merits and that no effective domestic remedy existed.

The case of Jehovas Zeugen in Österreich v. Austria (Application no. 27540/05) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) on 25 September 2012. The applicant was a registered religious community in Austria under the 1998 Religious Communities Act (later granted religious society status in 2009). It alleged discrimination contrary to Article 9 of the Convention (freedom of religion) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) because, unlike legally recognised religious societies, it was subject to restrictions under the Employment of Aliens Act and inheritance/gift tax rules.

In 2002 the community sought to employ a Filipino couple, both ministers in the Religious Order of Jehovah’s Witnesses, to serve its Tagalog-speaking members. To obtain residence or settlement permits the couple needed either a work permit or confirmation that their pastoral work fell outside the Employment of Aliens Act. The community applied to the Vienna Labour Market Service for a declaratory ruling that the exemption in section 1(2) of the Act (covering pastoral work performed for a church or religious society recognised by law) applied to registered communities, or alternatively that the work did not constitute “employment.” Both the Labour Market Service and its appeal panel refused. They held that the statutory exemption was limited to recognised societies and that the proposed pastoral activity displayed the hallmarks of employment (hierarchical structure, instructions from superiors and economic dependence).

The community complained to the Constitutional Court, invoking Article 9 alone and together with Article 14. On 10 October 2003 the Court dismissed the complaint. It accepted that pastoral work and the associated employment contracts fell within Article 9, and that labour-market rules could interfere with that right, but found the interference justified. Recognition as a religious society conferred a special legal status enabling participation in the shaping of public life; the distinction drawn by the Act was therefore constitutional. The Administrative Court later rejected a further complaint on the same grounds.

Separately, in October 1999 the community received a donation. In May 2001 the Vienna Tax Office assessed inheritance and gift tax at 14 per cent, holding that the exemption in section 15(1)(14) of the 1955 Inheritance and Gift Tax Act applied only to legally recognised churches and religious societies. An appeal to the Independent Finance Panel was dismissed in January 2005. The Panel confirmed that a registered community could not claim the privilege reserved for recognised societies and that none of the other statutory exemptions applied. A subsequent Constitutional Court complaint was declined for lack of prospects of success (September 2005); the Administrative Court dismissed the remitted complaint in April 2006, adding that the community was not a “charitable institution” because its activities, according to its own constitutional documents, were directed essentially at its members rather than the general public.

Domestic law thus drew a clear line: only recognised religious societies enjoyed automatic exemption from work-permit requirements for foreign ministers and from gift tax on donations. The Constitutional Court consistently treated the distinction as compatible with the Federal Constitution on the ground that recognition carried public-law consequences that a mere registered community did not possess. These facts formed the basis of the community’s claim that it had been treated less favourably than recognised religious societies in the exercise of its religious and property rights.

The case of Jehovas Zeugen in Österreich v. Austria (no. 27540/05) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by an Austrian registered religious community (under the 1998 Religious Communities Act), which later obtained statutory religious-society status in May 2009. The community alleged discrimination, contrary to Article 9 of the Convention (alone and with Article 14) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because Austrian law subjected it to employment-of-aliens and inheritance/gift-tax rules from which legally recognised religious societies were exempt.

In 2002 the community sought to employ a Filipino couple, both ordained ministers of the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ Religious Order, to serve its Tagalog-speaking members. Residence or settlement permits required either a work permit or proof that the work fell outside the Employment of Aliens Act. The community therefore applied to the Vienna Labour Market Service for a declaration that the couple’s pastoral activities were exempt under section 1(2) of that Act. It argued that, after the 1998 Act, the exemption extended to all religious communities, or alternatively that the work did not constitute “employment.” Both the Service and its appeal panel refused, holding that the exemption applied solely to ministers of recognised churches and societies; they also classified the work as employment because it involved a hierarchical structure, instructions and economic dependence.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the subsequent complaint in October 2003. It accepted that pastoral work (including the conclusion of employment contracts) fell within Article 9 and that labour-market restrictions interfered with that right, but found the interference justified under Article 9 § 2. The statutory distinction was constitutional: recognition conferred a status enabling participation in public life and was available to any group meeting the prescribed conditions. The Administrative Court later rejected a further complaint on the same grounds.

Separately, in October 1999 the community received a donation. In May 2001 the Vienna Tax Office assessed 14 % inheritance and gift tax, denying the exemption in section 15(1)(14) of the 1955 Inheritance and Gift Tax Act, which applied only to recognised churches and societies. An appeal to the Independent Finance Panel failed in January 2005; the Panel relied on the Constitutional Court’s earlier reasoning that the distinction was constitutional and found no other exemption applicable. The Constitutional Court declined to examine a further complaint for lack of prospects of success, referring to its prior case-law. After remittal, the Administrative Court dismissed the case in April 2006, holding that the community was neither a recognised religious society nor a charitable institution (its activities being directed essentially at its own members rather than the general public).

The relevant statutory provisions confirmed the differential treatment: section 1(2) of the Employment of Aliens Act exempted only pastoral work performed for recognised churches or societies, while section 15(1)(14) of the 1955 tax statute likewise reserved its privilege to those same recognised bodies (or to purely charitable entities serving the public at large). These facts formed the core of the alleged violations.

The case of Jehovas Zeugen in Österreich v. Austria (Application no. 27540/05) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by the Jehovah’s Witnesses, then a registered religious community under Austria’s Religious Communities Act 1998 (later granted religious society status in 2009). The applicant alleged discrimination contrary to Article 9 of the Convention (freedom of religion) taken alone and with Article 14, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), because it was subjected to restrictions on employing foreign ministers and to inheritance/gift tax from which legally recognised religious societies were exempt.

In 2002 the community sought to employ a Filipino couple who were full-time ministers of the Jehovah’s Witnesses order, intending them to perform pastoral work among Tagalog-speaking members in Austria. Residence or settlement permits required either a work permit or confirmation that the Employment of Aliens Act did not apply. It argued that, after the 1998 Act, the statutory exemption for “pastoral work \ldots as part of a church or religious society recognised by law” had to be read as covering all registered religious communities, or alternatively that the work did not constitute employment. The Labour Market Service and its appeal panel rejected the request, holding that the exemption was confined to recognised societies and that the work displayed the hallmarks of employment (hierarchical structure, instructions and economic dependence). The Constitutional Court dismissed a subsequent complaint in October 2003. It accepted that pastoral employment contracts fell within Article 9 and that labour-market rules interfered with that right, but found the interference justified. Recognition conferred a distinct legal status enabling participation in the shaping of public life; because that status was available to any community meeting the statutory criteria, the distinction was constitutional. The Administrative Court later confirmed the same reasoning.

Separately, in 1999 the community received a donation. In 2001 the Vienna Tax Office assessed inheritance and gift tax at 14 per cent, refusing the exemption in section 15(1)(14) of the 1955 Inheritance and Gift Tax Act that applied to “domestic churches or religious societies recognised by law” (or to exclusively charitable bodies serving the general public). Appeals were unsuccessful. The Independent Finance Panel, relying on the Constitutional Court’s 2003 ruling, held that a registered community was not a recognised society and that the community’s activities, directed essentially at its own members, did not serve the general public. The Constitutional Court declined to entertain a further complaint for lack of prospects of success, and the Administrative Court dismissed the case on the same grounds in 2006.

Thus the domestic authorities consistently treated the community’s lack of recognised-society status as a lawful ground for withholding both the employment exemption and the tax privilege, notwithstanding the community’s religious character and the interference this created with its ability to organise pastoral work and to receive donations.

The case of Efe v. Austria (Application no. 9134/06) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mehmet Efe, a dual Austrian-Turkish national born in Turkey in 1955 and resident in Vienna since moving there in 1989, where he has lived and worked continuously. The applicant alleged discrimination arising from the Austrian authorities’ refusal to grant him family allowance and related tax credits for maintenance payments in respect of his two children, who resided permanently in Turkey.

On 17 June 2002 the applicant claimed family allowance, backdated to 1 June 1997, for his daughter (born 1978, who by 2002 had completed her studies and begun work as a teacher) and his son (born 1980, a student since 2000). He had previously received a reduced family allowance until 1996 pursuant to a bilateral social-security agreement between Austria and Turkey. The Vienna Tax Office dismissed the claim on 17 February 2003 on the ground that the children were not resident in Austria, a core statutory condition of entitlement.

The applicant appealed, invoking European Court of Justice case-law and arguing that the decision contravened EU legislation, though he made no request for a preliminary ruling. On 24 May 2004 the Independent Financial Panel dismissed the appeal, noting that Austria had terminated the 1985 Social Security Agreement with Turkey with effect from 30 September 1996 and that the children remained resident in Turkey; the applicant had never taken steps to relocate his family to Austria.

A parallel set of proceedings concerned tax credits for maintenance payments for 1999–2001. On 22 March 2004 the Independent Financial Panel rejected that claim, holding that Austrian law generally precluded such credits for children over the age of majority who were not in receipt of family allowance.

The applicant lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, including the failure to refer the matter to the ECJ. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with both complaints, finding them without prospect of success, refused legal aid, and remitted the cases to the Administrative Court. On 10 August 2005 the Administrative Court (having joined the two sets of proceedings) dismissed the complaints. It held that the legislation in force since 1 January 2001, which excluded family allowance for children over majority living abroad, was lawful; that a constitutional provision barred tax credits for maintenance where no family allowance was payable; that the rules applied equally to Austrian nationals and foreigners and therefore involved no discrimination; and that there was no legal basis for an ECJ referral. No oral hearing was required.

Relevant domestic law included section 2 of the Family Burden Equalisation Act 1967, which conditions family allowance on the claimant’s residence in Austria and on the child belonging to the household or being maintained by the claimant, together with section 5(4), amended in 1996 to exclude entitlement for children permanently resident abroad (the former reciprocity exception having disappeared with termination of the bilateral agreement). Section 34(5) of the Income Tax Act, a constitutional provision, similarly excludes tax credits for maintenance of adult children not entitled to family allowance. The 1985 Austria–Turkey Social Security Agreement had expressly permitted family allowance for children resident in the other State, but Austria denounced it in 1996.

The applicant contended that these refusals constituted discrimination contrary to the Convention, given his long-term residence and work in Austria and his prior receipt of benefits under the terminated treaty. The Turkish Government exercised its right to intervene as a third party.

The ECHR case of Efe v. Austria (App. no. 9134/06, judgment 8 January 2013) concerned alleged discrimination arising from the refusal of family allowances and related tax credits. The applicant, Mehmet Efe (born 1955 in Turkey; dual Austrian-Turkish national), had lived and worked in Vienna since 1989. His two children remained permanently resident in Turkey: a daughter born in 1978 (who had completed studies and begun teaching by 2002) and a son born in 1980 (a student from 2000). Until 1996 he had received reduced family allowance under a 1985 Austria-Turkey Social Security Agreement, which Austria terminated with effect from 30 September 1996.

On 17 June 2002 Efe claimed family allowance retroactive to 1 June 1997. The Vienna Tax Office rejected the claim on 17 February 2003 because the children were not resident in Austria, a core statutory condition. He appealed on 8 April 2003, citing ECJ case-law and arguing incompatibility with EU law, but did not request a preliminary ruling. The Independent Financial Panel dismissed the appeal on 24 May 2004, relying on the agreement’s termination and the children’s foreign residence; it noted that Efe had never sought to relocate his family.

In parallel proceedings the Panel, on 22 March 2004, refused tax credits for maintenance payments in 1999–2001. Austrian law generally precluded such credits once children reached majority and no family allowance was payable.

Efe lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court (Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14 ECHR plus Article 1 of Protocol No. 1), alleging, inter alia, failure to refer questions to the ECJ. The Court declined to hear the cases (no reasonable prospect of success), refused legal aid, and remitted them to the Administrative Court. That court, joining both sets of proceedings, dismissed the complaints on 10 August 2005. It held that legislation in force from 1 January 2001 lawfully barred family allowances for adult children living abroad, that a constitutional provision correspondingly excluded tax credits, that the rules applied equally to Austrian and foreign nationals (hence no discrimination), and that there was no basis for an ECJ reference or an oral hearing.

Domestic law (Family Burden Equalisation Act 1967, as amended 1996) granted family allowance only to persons whose centre of main interests lay in Austria, for minor children or those under 26 in training who belonged to the claimant’s household or for whom the claimant paid the majority of maintenance. The 1996 amendment removed any entitlement for children with permanent residence abroad (eliminating a prior treaty-reciprocity exception). A constitutional provision of the Income Tax Act likewise excluded tax credits for maintenance of adult children not receiving family allowance. The terminated 1985 bilateral agreement had previously allowed payment for children resident in the other State. The European Social Charter (Art. 12) requires equal treatment in social security; the European Committee of Social Rights regarded a child-residence requirement as compatible provided bilateral agreements were concluded where necessary, and found Austria in conformity.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s claim that the residence-based exclusion of benefits for his children in Turkey constituted discrimination in the enjoyment of family life and property rights.

The case of Efe v. Austria (App. no. 9134/06) arose from an application by Mehmet Efe, a dual Austrian-Turkish national born in Turkey in 1955. He moved to Austria in 1989, residing and working in Vienna thereafter. He alleged discrimination (primarily under Articles 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, with an additional Article 6 complaint) because Austrian authorities refused him family allowance and related tax credits for maintenance payments in respect of his two children, who lived permanently in Turkey.

On 17 June 2002 the applicant claimed family allowance retroactively from 1 June 1997. His daughter (born 1978) had by then completed her studies and begun work as a teacher; his son (born 1980) had been a student since 2000. Until 1996 he had received a reduced allowance under the 1985 Austria-Turkey Social Security Agreement (Article 26(1) of which entitled persons employed in one State to family allowance even for children residing in the other). Austria terminated that agreement with effect from 30 September 1996.

The Vienna Tax Office rejected the claim on 17 February 2003 because the children were not resident in Austria, a core condition of entitlement. The Independent Financial Panel (IFP) dismissed the appeal on 24 May 2004, citing the termination of the bilateral agreement, the children’s non-residence, and the absence of any steps by the applicant to relocate his family.

In separate proceedings the IFP, on 22 March 2004, also refused tax credits for maintenance payments covering 1999–2001. Austrian law (Income Tax Act, section 34(5), a constitutional provision) precludes such credits (or treatment as an extraordinary burden) for children over the age of majority who are not in receipt of family allowance.

The applicant lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court, alleging Convention violations (including failure to refer questions to the ECJ) and seeking legal aid. The Court refused legal aid, declined to examine the complaints on the ground that they lacked prospects of success, and remitted both sets of proceedings to the Administrative Court. It observed that the IFP was not a court obliged to make a preliminary reference, that Turkey was not an EU Member State, and that the relevant provisions did not breach the Constitution or EU law.

The Administrative Court joined the cases and, on 10 August 2005, dismissed both complaints. It held that the legislation in force since 1 January 2001 lawfully withheld family allowance for children over majority living abroad; that the tax-credit restriction followed automatically from the constitutional provision; and that the rules applied equally to Austrian nationals and foreigners, so there was no discrimination. No referral to the ECJ was required and no oral hearing was necessary.

Domestic law underpinning the refusals included section 2 of the Family Burden Equalisation Act 1967 (entitlement generally limited to persons whose centre of interests is in Austria and to children belonging to their household) and the 1996 amendment to section 5(4) of that Act, which removed the former exception for children residing abroad under reciprocal treaties. The European Social Charter (Article 12 § 4) was also cited in the materials, the European Committee of Social Rights having found Austria’s situation in conformity while noting the desirability of bilateral agreements with certain States, including Turkey.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged discriminatory denial of family-related benefits after the 1996 termination of the bilateral agreement.
