The case of Qama v. Albania and Italy (Application no. 4604/09) concerned an Albanian national, Flamur Qama (born 1960), who alleged that Albanian and Italian authorities failed to secure his right of contact with his son (born 25 August 1994), in breach of Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention. The son, then a minor, had been taken to Italy in 1999 by the applicant’s wife (who suffered from a serious illness) for medical treatment; the applicant later joined them irregularly. In August or September 2002, following family disagreements, the applicant was expelled from Italy for lack of a residence permit. His wife and son remained; the wife died on 7 October 2002.

On 17 October 2002 the sister-in-law Z. sought custody in the Ancona Youth Court. A December 2002 social-health report recorded the child’s fear of returning to the father because of alleged ill-treatment of the mother and the father’s abandonment at a critical time. On 4 June 2003 the Italian court granted Z. custody under social-service supervision, appointed the Mayor of Senigallia temporary guardian, suspended parental rights (on the ground that the parents had allowed the child to leave Albania without addressing subsequent difficulties), prohibited the child’s removal from Italy, and commissioned the International Social Service to investigate the applicant’s circumstances. No contact or visiting rights were provided for the applicant. Subsequent reports indicated that the child had been regularised, was well-settled, and (in 2007 statements) refused telephone contact, citing past ill-treatment and years of separation.

The applicant repeatedly sought to re-establish contact. In January–February 2007 he wrote to the Italian court (without a power of attorney) claiming abduction, requesting enforcement of an Albanian contact order, and asking that the child be allowed to travel to Albania. In November 2007 he invoked the Hague Child Abduction Convention before the Italian Ministry of Justice. In Albania he pursued both criminal and civil remedies. Criminal complaints under Article 127 of the Criminal Code for wrongful retention produced mixed results: one case was discontinued in 2003; Z. was later convicted and fined (2004, upheld on appeal; a further conviction in 2009), though a 2008 action was rejected on ne bis in idem and on the basis of the 2003 Italian decision. Civilly, the Durrës District Court on 30 June 2006 (in Z.’s absence, notified by public notice) ordered contact at least twice yearly during school holidays; an execution writ issued, but later Albanian courts noted that they could not compel travel or visas and that no international instrument then bound Italy to recognise or enforce the Albanian judgment. A 2009 Albanian order reiterated the contact right but left enforcement to the applicant’s own means.

Between 2003 and 2009 the applicant petitioned numerous Albanian authorities (Interior, Justice, Foreign Affairs, Ombudsman, Prime Minister, President). Responses indicated that Albania lacked a legal basis or international agreement for compelling Italian recognition of its civil judgments, that the Italian custody decision placed the matter beyond Albanian jurisdiction, and that consular inquiries had been made. Italy’s 2005 notification of the 2003 decision informed the applicant of a possible appeal, which he did not pursue. The child remained in Italy under Z.’s care; no effective contact was established. Albania had become party to the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention (2007) and the 1996 Hague Jurisdiction Convention (2007), and to the 2003 Contact Convention (2005); Italy was party only to the 1980 Convention and had signed but not ratified the others. These facts formed the basis of the alleged failures to protect family life and to enforce judicial decisions concerning contact.

The case of Qama v. Albania and Italy (Application no. 4604/09), decided by the ECHR on 8 January 2013, concerned an Albanian applicant’s allegations of violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention. These arose from the failure of Albanian and Italian authorities to enforce his right of contact with his son (born 1994), who resided in Italy.

In September 1999 the applicant’s seriously ill wife entered Italy irregularly with their son for medical treatment; the applicant later joined them. In August/September 2002, after disagreements with his in-laws, the applicant was expelled for lack of a residence permit. His wife and son remained; she died on 7 October 2002.

On 17 October 2002 the sister-in-law Z. sought custody in the Ancona Youth Court. A December 2002 social-health report stated that the child feared returning to the father because of alleged ill-treatment of the deceased mother and that the father had abandoned them when needed most. On 4 June 2003 the court awarded Z. custody under Senigallia social-services supervision, appointed the mayor temporary guardian, suspended parental rights (because the parents had allowed the child to leave Albania without addressing ensuing difficulties), and banned the child’s removal from Italy. No visiting or contact rights were granted. The International Social Service was tasked with investigating the applicant’s situation; he refused to speak to them, simply demanding the child’s return. Neighbours reported that he had remarried, that his wife was expecting, and that he was unemployed and living on her income.

By March 2004 the child’s Italian status had been regularised and his situation appeared balanced. In April 2005 the Italian Ministry of Justice informed the applicant of the 2003 decision and of the possibility of appealing through a lawyer. The child later told the court (January and December 2007) that he had had no contact for years and did not wish to speak to the applicant because of past alleged ill-treatment.

The applicant wrote to the Italian court in January and February 2007, claiming abduction, seeking contact and enforcement of a later Albanian order, and asking that the child travel to Albania. He did not seek permanent return. In November 2007 he invoked the Hague Conventions before the Italian Ministry of Justice.

In Albania the applicant brought successive criminal complaints under Article 127 of the Criminal Code for wrongful retention. Some resulted in fines against Z. (later subject to amnesty); others were discontinued or rejected, one explicitly relying on the 2003 Italian decision. On 30 June 2006, in civil proceedings conducted in Z.’s absence, the Durrës District Court ordered contact twice yearly during school holidays, noting the applicant’s new family, income and housing and the child’s good care in Italy. An execution writ issued, but enforcement proved impossible. Further Albanian decisions (2008–2009) confirmed contact rights but acknowledged the court’s inability to obtain an Italian visa or compel compliance.

From 2003 to 2009 the applicant repeatedly petitioned Albanian ministries, the Ombudsman and other institutions. They cited lack of jurisdiction, the Italian custody order, and the absence of treaties permitting recognition of Albanian civil judgments in Italy.

The Hague Child Abduction Convention (in force for Italy since 1995, Albania since 2007) and related instruments on jurisdiction and contact were potentially relevant, yet Italy had not ratified the 1996 Hague Jurisdiction Convention or the Council of Europe Contact Convention. Albanian and Italian domestic law provided for parental-responsibility measures, but Italian youth-court orders were non-final, revocable and not subject to ordinary appeal.

These facts—conflicting national proceedings, the child’s expressed opposition, the applicant’s expulsion and subsequent inability to travel, and the authorities’ limited practical cooperation—underpinned the alleged failures to protect family life and to provide effective access to justice for enforcement of contact rights.

001-116064:
The case of Mitić v. Serbia originated in an application by Najdan Mitić, father of Jovica Mitić (JM), a 28-year-old inmate who hanged himself on 8 October 2007 while serving a cumulative one-year-and-nine-month sentence at Leskovac District Prison. Relying on Article 2 of the Convention, the applicant alleged that the authorities failed to protect his son’s life in solitary confinement and that the subsequent investigation into the death was neither adequate nor effective.

JM was arrested on 14 August 2007 for larceny and detained. A prison medical file recorded recent traffic accidents injuring his sixth cervical vertebra and sleeping difficulties; he was prescribed diazepam and flormidal. On 21 August the police notified the prison of earlier final sentences (for larceny, forgery and enabling substance abuse) and of outstanding arrest warrants, requesting his transfer from detention to a high-security unit as a recidivist and fugitive. Placement occurred on 27 August. Standard examinations by the prison doctor and psychologist described JM as introverted, dishonest and dissimulative; he denied any family history of mental illness and mentioned prior sedative use.

Further medical visits followed. On 21 September bruises were observed on JM’s left shoulder, shoulder blades and right upper arm; he appeared nervous, refused to explain their origin or lodge a complaint, and received increased diazepam plus ibuprofen. He later complained of a dermatological condition, insomnia and minor anxiety, refused to see the psychologist, and had his diazepam dosage raised again.

On 3 October JM attempted to escape with three other inmates. Disciplinary proceedings resulted in 15 days’ solitary confinement for each. A pre-placement medical examination found him fit to continue existing therapy. In isolation he received daily doctor visits and medication administered by staff; he voiced no health complaints. The cell contained a heating pipe and CCTV that covered only the door and part of the toilet, transmitting live images (without recording) to the head of prison guards. Visits were prohibited under prison rules; the applicant was turned away on 7 October but left a package that was delivered the same day.

On the morning of 8 October JM received breakfast, was seen by the doctor at approximately 8.15 a.m. and was given medication between 8.45 and 9.00 a.m.; staff recalled him as calm and responsive. At around noon a guard and a correctional officer found him hanging from the heating pipe by a bed-sheet ligature; he was pronounced dead at 12.05 p.m.

An investigating judge immediately conducted an on-site examination, secured the cell, took photographs and reconstructed events from staff statements. Police interviewed the discovering officers, the doctor, medical staff and other personnel; all stated that JM had shown no suicidal tendencies. An autopsy performed that evening concluded death by asphyxia from hanging between 9.00 and 10.00 a.m., noted an old bruise, traces of alcohol and no poison. The applicant’s request for a second autopsy was deferred pending receipt of the first report; the body was released the same day.

The following day an inmate who had been isolated with JM reported that JM had spoken of staging a suicide attempt in order to obtain transfer to a special prison hospital. The applicant lodged a criminal complaint alleging murder and abuse of authority, asserting that solitary confinement had been arbitrarily imposed and had caused the suicide. The prosecutor obtained prison reports and re-interviewed staff, then declined to prosecute on 19 December 2007. Acting as subsidiary prosecutor, the applicant filed an indictment. After reviewing the file the investigating judge found insufficient grounds; a District Court chamber discontinued the investigation on 23 January 2008, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court on 12 March 2008.

Domestic law required a medical examination before placement in solitary confinement and daily medical checks thereafter. Relevant CPT standards stress the need for special observation of identified suicide risks and the removal of readily available ligature points.

The case of Mitić v. Serbia (Application no. 31963/08) was brought by Najdan Mitić against Serbia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He alleged a violation of Article 2, claiming that prison authorities failed to protect the life of his 28-year-old son, Jovica Mitić (JM), who hanged himself on 8 October 2007 while in solitary confinement at Leskovac District Prison, and that the subsequent investigation into the death was neither adequate nor effective.

JM was arrested on 14 August 2007 on suspicion of larceny and placed in pre-trial detention. A prison medical examination the next day recorded recent traffic accidents causing injury to his sixth cervical vertebra, along with denials of other illnesses. He later reported sleep difficulties and received prescriptions for diazepam and flormidal. On 21 August, authorities learned of outstanding sentences totalling one year and nine months for prior offences, including larceny, forgery and enabling substance abuse. As a recidivist and former fugitive, JM was transferred to a high-security unit on 27 August. A standard psychological assessment described him as introverted, dishonest and dissimulative. Subsequent medical visits addressed muscle pain, unexplained bruises (which he refused to explain), a dermato-venereal condition, insomnia and minor anxiety. He declined further psychological consultation. Daily diazepam was increased.

On 3 October 2007 JM attempted to escape with three other inmates. Disciplinary proceedings resulted in 15 days’ solitary confinement for each. A pre-placement medical examination found him fit to serve the sanction while continuing existing medication. Prison rules required daily medical visits, which occurred; JM voiced no health complaints. His cell contained CCTV covering the door and part of the toilet but produced no recordings, only a live feed to the guards’ office. Visits were prohibited during solitary confinement; the applicant was therefore turned away on 7 October, though a package was delivered.

On 8 October JM received breakfast, a doctor’s visit at approximately 8.15 a.m. and medication between 8.45 and 9.00 a.m. Staff described him as calm. Around noon a guard and correctional officer found him hanging from a heating pipe by a bed-sheet ligature; he was pronounced dead at 12.05 p.m. An investigating judge immediately conducted an on-site examination, securing the cell, taking photographs and recording staff statements. An autopsy performed that evening established death by asphyxia from hanging between 9.00 and 10.00 a.m.; toxicology showed no poison and only traces of alcohol. An old bruise was noted, consistent with earlier observations.

The following day another inmate reported that JM had spoken of staging a suicide attempt in order to obtain transfer to a special prison hospital. The applicant lodged a criminal complaint alleging murder and abuse of authority, asserting that solitary confinement had been arbitrarily imposed and had caused psychological harm. Police re-interviewed staff, all of whom denied any indication of suicidal intent. The public prosecutor declined to prosecute. Acting as subsidiary prosecutor, the applicant filed an indictment against the prison, its doctor and several officers. After reviewing files, an investigating judge found insufficient grounds; a three-judge chamber discontinued proceedings, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court of Serbia on 12 March 2008.

Domestic law required medical examination before and daily during solitary confinement and classified escape attempts as serious disciplinary offences warranting such placement. CPT standards emphasised suicide-proof cells, removal of ligature points and special observation for identified risks. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 2 complaints concerning both the authorities’ alleged failure to prevent a foreseeable suicide and the claimed deficiencies in the investigation.

The case of Mitić v. Serbia (Application no. 31963/08) concerns an application lodged on 20 June 2008 by Serbian national Najdan Mitić under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Serbian authorities violated Article 2 by failing to protect the life of his son, Jovica Mitić (JM), who hanged himself on 8 October 2007 at age 28 while in solitary confinement at Leskovac District Prison, and by conducting an inadequate investigation into the death.

JM was arrested on 14 August 2007 on suspicion of larceny and detained. A medical examination that day recorded recent cervical vertebra injuries from traffic accidents and sleeping difficulties, for which he received diazepam and flormidal. On 21 August, authorities learned of prior unserved sentences totalling one year and nine months (for larceny, forgery and related offences); as a recidivist and fugitive, JM was transferred on 27 August to the high-security unit. A psychologist described him as introverted, dishonest and dissimulative. He later presented bruises of unknown origin, appeared nervous and received increased sedatives. He missed one check-up and refused further psychological consultation.

On 3 October 2007 JM attempted to escape with three others. Disciplinary proceedings on 5 October resulted in 15 days’ solitary confinement for each. A pre-placement medical examination found him fit to continue existing medication. Daily doctor visits occurred in solitary, with no health complaints recorded. The cell had live CCTV covering only the door and part of the toilet (no recordings). Visits were prohibited under prison rules. The applicant was denied a visit on 7 October but left a package that was delivered.

On 8 October, JM received breakfast, was seen by the doctor at 08:15 and given medication between 08:45 and 09:00; staff described him as calm. He was found hanging from a heating pipe by a bed-sheet ligature around noon and pronounced dead at 12:05. An investigating judge conducted an on-site inspection that afternoon, photographing the cell and body; staff statements were collected. The applicant filed a criminal complaint alleging murder and abuse of authority, claiming arbitrary solitary placement (asserting only JM was so punished) caused psychological harm leading to suicide. Acting as subsidiary prosecutor, the applicant indicted the prison, doctor and officers, adding that the fitness assessment for solitary was erroneous. After reviewing files, the investigating judge found insufficient grounds; a District Court chamber discontinued proceedings on 23 January 2008, upheld by the Supreme Court on 12 March 2008.

Domestic law required medical examination before and daily during solitary confinement, and authorised the victim to take over prosecution if the public prosecutor declined. CPT standards emphasised suicide-proof conditions, special observation for at-risk prisoners and adequate solitary-cell furnishings without ligature points.

These facts form the core of the alleged substantive failure to identify and mitigate suicide risk in solitary (despite prior injuries, medication, bruises, escape attempt and psychologist’s notes) and the procedural claim that the investigation omitted a second autopsy, full forensic scrutiny of bruises/timing discrepancies and effective inquiry into staff responsibility.

The case of *Martirosyan v. Armenia* (no. 23341/06) involves Armenian national Vahagn Martirosyan (born 1969), former Lori Regional Branch Manager of Credit Service Bank. He alleged that his pre-trial detention was lengthy and unjustified and that his conviction rested on an unforeseeable application of criminal law.

Proceedings opened on 19 March 2002 into embezzlement of entrusted funds by former bank management through abuse of official capacity. A search warrant issued on 8 April 2002. The applicant was questioned as a witness from 22 April 2002 onward (eight times in total). An expert examination of records was ordered in November 2002.

He was arrested on 1 April 2003 and charged the next day under the former Criminal Code with embezzlement by abuse of office and official falsification (ten co-accused, including A.D.). The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court immediately ordered two months’ detention, citing the acts’ nature and danger plus all grounds in CCP Article 135 § 1 (flight risk, interference, further crime, evasion of liability). An appeal was dismissed on 2 May 2003. Extensions followed on 23 May (two months) and 23 July (one month, to 1 September 2003) for further investigation; neither was appealed.

A new Criminal Code entered force on 1 August 2003; charges were adapted on 11–12 August. The applicant accessed the 34-volume file from 26 August to 10 November 2003. On 11 November he complained of detention without court order since 1 September; the prosecutor rejected this. The indictment was approved on 14 November and the case sent to the same District Court, which admitted it on 17 November and, on 1 December, listed it for trial while maintaining detention.

The trial comprised 57 hearings (eight December 2003–13 September 2005; ten adjourned). On 15 December 2004 the applicant moved for release; examination was deferred. At the 27 December hearing, amid disorder after an emotional outburst, the judge treated the motion as withdrawn and left it unexamined—an account the applicant disputed, supported by a co-accused’s and his mother’s statements.

On 14 November 2005 the District Court convicted him of abetting embezzlement (new CC Article 179 § 2(3) with Article 38) and sentenced him to two years six months’ imprisonment; the Article 325 § 1 falsification count was discontinued under the statute of limitations. He was released, having already served the term.

The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 10 April 2006, holding that any legally capable person aged 16 or over (including a private employee) could be a perpetrator under Article 325 § 1. The Court of Cassation dismissed a further appeal on 1 June 2006, ruling that “official documents” include those issued by commercial banks (such as credit agreements) because they possess legal significance.

These facts frame the detention lasting from 1 April 2003 until 14 November 2005 (with a possible gap after 1 September 2003 and only perfunctory later reviews) and the novel interpretation that private-bank records fall within Article 325.

The applicant, an Armenian national born in 1969, served as Lori Regional Branch Manager of Credit Service Bank. On 19 March 2002 criminal proceedings were opened into embezzlement of funds entrusted to the Bank by a third company, allegedly committed through abuse of official capacity by former management. The applicant was questioned as a witness on multiple occasions in 2002–2003. He was arrested on 1 April 2003 and formally charged the next day under the former Criminal Code with large-scale embezzlement through abuse of office and official falsification (preparation and use of false accounting documents). Ten co-accused were charged alongside him.

On 2 April 2003 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan authorised two months’ pre-trial detention, citing the gravity of the offences and all five grounds listed in Article 135 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (risk of absconding, interference with the investigation, commission of further offences, evasion of liability and obstruction of sentence enforcement). The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 2 May 2003. Detention was extended by two months on 23 May 2003 and by a further month on 23 July 2003 (until 1 September 2003), both times on the ground that additional investigative steps were required; the applicant did not appeal either extension.

A new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 August 2003. Charges were reformulated under Articles 179 § 3 and 325 § 2. The investigation closed on 26 August 2003; the applicant finished studying the 34-volume file on 10 November 2003. On 11 November he complained to the prosecutor that he had been held without a court order since 1 September and sought release. The prosecutor rejected the complaint. The indictment was approved on 14 November and transmitted to the District Court, which admitted the case on 17 November and, on 1 December, listed it for trial while confirming that there were no grounds to vary or revoke detention.

The trial ran from 8 December 2003 to 13 September 2005 (57 hearings, ten of them adjourned). On 15 December 2004 the applicant applied for release; examination was deferred. At the next hearing he stated that the motion need not be considered; the court left it unexamined. (The applicant later claimed the statement was an emotional outburst following the judge’s failure to rule on the motion together with other applications, but the court treated it as a withdrawal.)

On 14 November 2005 the District Court convicted the applicant of abetting large-scale embezzlement (Article 179 § 2 read with Article 38) and of falsifying and using credit agreements (Article 325 § 1). He received two years and six months’ imprisonment on the embezzlement count; proceedings on the document-falsification count were discontinued under the statute of limitations. Having already served the sentence, he was released immediately.

The Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 10 April 2006, holding that any legally competent person over 16, including a private-sector employee, could be a perpetrator under Article 325 § 1. The Court of Cassation rejected a further appeal on 1 June 2006, ruling that “official documents” include instruments issued by commercial banks that possess legal significance (such as credit agreements). The applicant argued that this interpretation was unforeseeable because private-bank papers fell outside the scope of official-document offences both under the former Code and under a proper reading of the new Code.

These facts form the basis of the complaints that pre-trial detention lasting more than two and a half years was neither justified nor regularly reviewed, and that the conviction under Article 325 § 1 rested on an unforeseeable extension of criminal law.

The case of Martirosyan v. Armenia (no. 23341/06) was brought by Vahagn Martirosyan, an Armenian national born in 1969 and former Lori Regional Branch Manager of Credit Service Bank. He alleged that his pre-trial detention had been excessively lengthy and unjustified, and that his conviction had resulted from an unforeseeable application of criminal law.

Proceedings began on 19 March 2002 into alleged embezzlement of entrusted funds by former bank management. The applicant was questioned as a witness on multiple occasions. He was arrested on 1 April 2003 and charged the next day under the former Criminal Code with embezzlement by abuse of official capacity (Article 90 § 4, including in conjunction with Article 17) and official falsification (Article 187). The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan immediately authorised two months’ pre-trial detention, citing the nature and dangerousness of the alleged acts together with all grounds listed in Article 135 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (risk of absconding, interference with the investigation, further offences, evasion of liability, and obstruction of judgment). An appeal against this order was dismissed on 2 May 2003.

Detention was extended on 23 May 2003 for a further two months and again on 23 July 2003 until 1 September 2003, each time solely on the ground that additional investigative steps were required. No appeals were lodged against these extensions. A new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 August 2003; the charges were re-characterised on 11 August under Articles 179 § 3(1) (including with Article 38) and 325 § 2. The investigation was declared complete on 26 August 2003 and the applicant was given access to a 34-volume case file, which he finished reviewing on 10 November. On 11 November he complained that he had been held without a court order since 1 September; the prosecutor rejected the complaint.

The indictment was approved on 14 November 2003 and the case assigned to Judge A. On 1 December the judge listed the trial for 8 December and declined to alter the detention. Between December 2003 and September 2005 the District Court held 57 hearings (ten of them adjourned). On 15 December 2004 the applicant applied for release; examination was postponed to 27 December. Amid a courtroom dispute the applicant stated that the judge should not examine the motion if it caused his family further distress; the judge treated the statement as a withdrawal and left the application unexamined.

On 14 November 2005 the District Court convicted the applicant of abetting embezzlement (new Criminal Code Article 179 § 2(3) in conjunction with Article 38) and of document falsification (Article 325 § 1, proceedings on which were discontinued under the statute of limitations). He received two years and six months’ imprisonment and was released immediately, having already served the term. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 10 April 2006. The Court of Cassation dismissed a further appeal on 1 June 2006, holding that credit and other financial documents issued by commercial banks constitute “official documents” because they possess legal significance.

The applicant remained in detention from 1 April 2003 until 14 November 2005. After the initial periods of judicial authorisation, further detention (particularly during the lengthy trial, for which Armenian law set no maximum) received only cursory or no review. On the conviction issue, the applicant argued that Article 325 could not apply to private-bank documents, which fell outside the notion of official documents; the domestic courts applied a broad interpretation that he contended was unforeseeable.
001-116333:
The case of Bubnov v. Russia (Application no. 76317/11) concerns a Russian national, Vasiliy Viktorovich Bubnov (born 1982), who alleged violations of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to ineffective medical care while detained and the authorities’ refusal to release him despite his deteriorating health, which he claimed caused extreme physical and mental suffering. The European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined the application, granting it priority, and delivered its judgment on 5 February 2013 (final on 5 May 2013).

Bubnov was arrested on 18 May 2006 on suspicion of murder. On 28 November 2006, the Kaliningrad Leningradskiy District Court convicted him of murder and attempted murder, sentencing him to 13 years’ imprisonment in a strict-regime correctional facility. He was transferred to a colony in the Kaliningrad Region after the judgment became final.

Prior to his arrest, in December 2005, Bubnov tested positive for HIV and hepatitis C at a drug clinic due to his opiate addiction. On 23 March 2006, the AIDS Centre diagnosed him with clinical stage 3 HIV infection, chronic viral hepatitis C with minimal activity, and drug addiction. He received monitoring there until April 2006.

Upon admission to detention facility no. 1 on 20 May 2006, tests confirmed the diagnoses. Subsequent transfers and tests showed progression of the HIV infection. In April 2007, antiretroviral therapy (ART) was recommended, but Bubnov requested a postponement. After transfer to correctional colony no. 13, he expressed willingness to start ART, but it was not initiated despite further progression, including a CD4 cell count drop below 498 cells/mm³ by mid-2007 and later to approximately 290 cells/mm³ by March 2008. ART (Combivir and Stocrin) finally began on 18 April 2008. Immunological tests in July 2008 showed a further drop below 240 cells/mm³, with no regimen change. By November 2008, he had clinical stage 4 HIV (B2), biliary dyskinesia, and progressing hepatitis, though ART continued.

In May 2009, a new ART regimen (Epivir, Zerit, and Kaletra) was recommended and started after slight deterioration. Transfers followed: to colony no. 9 in March 2010 (where he was declared category 3 disabled in April 2010) and to a regional prison hospital in June 2010 for examination, with a diagnosis including progressing HIV despite ART, secondary illnesses, chronic hepatitis with acute episodes, bronchitis, polyneuropathy, and addiction. Released in a satisfactory condition, tests in August 2010 showed a CD4 rise above 342 cells/mm³ but high viral load. Further transfer to prison hospital in colony no. 8 occurred in October 2010 due to stage 4 progression; the regimen was expanded, and he was returned to the colony after stabilization. From April 2011, he remained in the hospital, receiving adjusted ART, regular specialist examinations (including from the AIDS Centre), and monitoring. His condition was deemed stable by April 2012, though he was reclassified as category 2 disabled in March 2012. Secondary issues (e.g., dermatological problems, infections, psychological complaints) were generally addressed promptly.

On 24 June 2011, a prison hospital medical panel recommended Bubnov’s release under paragraph 39 of the List of Illnesses Warranting Relief from a Sentence (Government Decree of 6 February 2004), citing progressing stage 4 HIV despite ART, secondary illnesses affecting the central nervous system (encephalopathy and polyneuropathy), chronic hepatitis C and B with acute episodes, and accompanying conditions like bronchitis and lesions. The colony governor applied to the Kaliningrad Tsentralniy District Court, which Bubnov supported, alleging inadequate care including for HIV.

On 8 August 2011, the District Court dismissed the application. It noted that release for illness is discretionary, considering not only the listed illness but also its impact on serving the sentence, the crime’s seriousness (particularly grave, with less than half the term served), Bubnov’s poor prison behavior (34 unexpired penalties, declared a persistent offender in 2009, prone to provocation), inadequate and aggressive conduct, lack of demonstrated improvement, and risk of reoffending. The court emphasized available prison hospital care (with specialists) versus potential civilian hospital limitations and his mother’s offer to fund medicines. The Kaliningrad Regional Court upheld this on 4 October 2011.

Separate proceedings in 2011 awarded Bubnov minor compensation (RUB 2,000 and RUB 3,000) for poor conditions during brief earlier detentions in 2002 and 2007, but these were unrelated to the primary allegations.

The facts highlight delays in initiating ART despite declining immunity and the court’s balancing of health recommendations against behavioral and public safety factors in refusing release.

**Case of Bubnov v. Russia (Application no. 76317/11), ECtHR, 5 February 2013 (final 5 May 2013)**

Vasiliy Viktorovich Bubnov, a Russian national born in 1982, was arrested on 18 May 2006 on suspicion of murder. On 28 November 2006, the Kaliningrad Leningradskiy District Court convicted him of murder and attempted murder, sentencing him to 13 years’ imprisonment in a strict-regime correctional colony. He was transferred there after the judgment became final.

Bubnov had been diagnosed in late 2005–early 2006 (prior to detention) with clinical stage 3 HIV infection, chronic hepatitis C (minimal activity), and opiate addiction, following testing at a drug clinic and the AIDS Centre. Upon admission to detention facility no. 1 on 20 May 2006, tests confirmed these diagnoses. He was later transferred to other facilities, including colony no. 13.

Medical records show that antiretroviral therapy (ART) was first recommended in April 2007 after immunological testing indicated HIV progression, but it was postponed at Bubnov’s request pending a meeting with his mother. Upon arrival at colony no. 13, he requested ART, which was recorded but not immediately started. Further tests in July–August 2007 confirmed progression (CD4 count below 498 cells/mm³) and elevated liver enzymes. He experienced symptoms including throat pain, coughing, dizziness, fatigue, and fever, diagnosed as acute respiratory disease, with later issues including localized lymphadenopathy.

ART (initially Combivir and Stocrin) commenced on 18 April 2008 after a March 2008 test showed a CD4 drop to approximately 290 cells/mm³. Therapy continued with adjustments: a new regimen (Epivir, Zerit, Kaletra) was recommended by the AIDS Centre and started around August 2009 after further deterioration. Subsequent monitoring (including CD4 counts, viral load, and clinical tests) occurred at intervals, with treatments for secondary conditions such as dermatological problems, biliary dyskinesia, chronic bronchitis, polyneuropathy, and hepatitis exacerbations. He received inpatient care in prison hospitals (e.g., June 2010, October–November 2010, and from April 2011 onward in colony no. 8 hospital), including specialist consultations (infectious diseases, neurology, psychiatry) and regimen adjustments. A medical panel declared him category 3 disabled in April 2010 and category 2 in March 2012. Records indicate ongoing ART, regular examinations (at least every three days in hospital), and responses to complaints and side effects, with his condition described as stabilized at times despite progression to clinical stage 4 HIV and a high viral load in some tests (e.g., August 2010).

On 24 June 2011, a prison hospital medical panel recommended release under paragraph 39 of the 2004 List of Illnesses Warranting Relief from a Sentence, citing progressing stage 4 HIV despite ART, secondary illnesses affecting the central nervous system (encephalopathy, polyneuropathy), acute hepatitis C and B episodes, and accompanying conditions. The colony governor applied to the Kaliningrad Tsentralniy District Court for release, which Bubnov supported, alleging inadequate HIV care.

On 8 August 2011, the District Court refused, noting that release for illness is discretionary. It considered the particularly serious offence, less than half the sentence served, Bubnov’s negative prison characterization (34 unexpired penalties, declared a persistent offender in 2009 with provocative behaviour), inadequate/aggressive conduct requiring psychiatric assessment, and the availability of prison medical facilities (including infectious diseases and neurology specialists) capable of providing necessary free treatment. It found he might pose a danger if released and that external hospital admission was not guaranteed. The Kaliningrad Regional Court upheld this on 4 October 2011.

Separate 2011 proceedings awarded Bubnov modest compensation (RUB 2,000 and 3,000) for earlier poor detention conditions (2002 and 2007), unrelated to the main health claims.

The alleged violations centre on ineffective medical care for HIV and related conditions in detention (including delayed ART initiation and management of progression) and the refusal of release despite a medical recommendation and advanced illness, purportedly causing extreme suffering. Domestic law and WHO guidelines on ART initiation (based on CD4 counts and clinical staging) were referenced as relevant.

The case of Bubnov v. Russia (Application no. 76317/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Russian national, Vasiliy Viktorovich Bubnov (born 1982), who alleged that Russian authorities failed to provide effective medical care during his detention and refused to release him despite his deteriorating health, thereby subjecting him to severe physical and mental suffering (primarily under Article 3 of the Convention).

Bubnov was arrested on 18 May 2006 on suspicion of murder. On 28 November 2006, the Kaliningrad Leningradskiy District Court convicted him of murder and attempted murder, imposing a 13-year sentence in a strict-regime correctional colony. He had already been diagnosed with HIV and hepatitis C prior to detention. In December 2005, while undergoing testing as a drug addict, he tested positive for both viruses. A March 2006 diagnosis at an AIDS Centre confirmed clinical stage 3 HIV infection, chronic viral hepatitis C with minimal activity, and opiate addiction. Upon admission to detention facility no. 1 on 20 May 2006, blood tests confirmed these diagnoses.

HIV progressed in detention. In April 2007, antiretroviral therapy (ART) was advised after immunological tests, but Bubnov postponed it and was transferred after being deemed fit. Upon arrival at colony no. 13, he requested ART, but it was not started. Tests in July–August 2007 showed a CD4 count below 498 cells/mm³ and elevated liver enzymes. By March 2008, the CD4 count had fallen to approximately 290 cells/mm³. ART (Combivir and Stocrin) finally began on 18 April 2008, with strict adherence required. Subsequent tests in July 2008 showed a further drop below 240 cells/mm³; the regimen was unchanged. In November 2008, he was diagnosed with clinical stage 4 HIV (B2), progressing chronic hepatitis, and biliary dyskinesia, with a severe CD4 decline. The same ART continued. In August 2009, following AIDS Centre recommendations, the regimen changed to Epivir, Zerit and Kaletra.

Transfers followed: to colony no. 9 in March 2010 (diagnosed with progressing HIV, chronic hepatitis, possible polyarthritis, and heroin addiction; ART continued with added medication and frequent monitoring); a regional prison hospital stay in June 2010 for in-depth examination (diagnoses included secondary illnesses, chronic bronchitis, polyneuropathy, and joint pain); and hospitalisation from October 2010 onward in colony no. 8 (further HIV progression to stage 4, regimen expansion with additional antivirals, hepatoprotectors and other drugs). He was declared category 3 disabled in April 2010 and category 2 in March 2012. Throughout 2010–2012, records show regular specialist examinations (infectious diseases, neurology, psychiatry, etc.), immunological monitoring, responses to secondary issues (dermatological problems, lymphadenopathy, side-effects), and adjustments to therapy. CD4 counts fluctuated (e.g., rising above 342 cells/mm³ in August 2010 with high viral load; later slight drops but reduced viral load). By April 2012, his condition was described as stable after overcoming intermittent negative changes, with ongoing hospital care and AIDS Centre input.

On 24 June 2011, a prison hospital medical panel (report no. 39-11) recommended release under paragraph 39 of the Government’s 2004 List of Illnesses Warranting Relief from a Sentence, citing progressing stage 4 HIV despite ART, secondary illnesses (encephalopathy, polyneuropathy), chronic hepatitis C/B with acute episodes, and accompanying conditions (bronchitis, dermatitis, fungal lesions). The colony governor applied for release; Bubnov supported it, alleging inadequate HIV care. On 8 August 2011, the Kaliningrad Tsentralniy District Court refused, noting that release is discretionary. It weighed the particularly serious offence, less than half the sentence served, 34 unexpired disciplinary penalties (including “persistent offender” status since 2009 and provocative behaviour), aggressive/uncontrolled conduct, and risk of reoffending. The court emphasised available prison hospital resources (including specialists) equivalent to civilian infectious diseases care, plus family support for medicines. The Kaliningrad Regional Court upheld this on 4 October 2011.

Separate 2011 proceedings yielded modest compensation (RUB 2,000 and RUB 3,000) for earlier poor detention conditions (2002 and 2007), unrelated to the core health complaints.

These facts centre on delayed ART initiation amid falling CD4 counts, ongoing HIV progression with complications, provided (if delayed/adjustable) treatment in prison facilities, and judicial refusal of medically recommended release based on criminality, conduct and institutional care capacity.
001-116836:
The case of Gani v. Spain (Application no. 61800/08) originated in a 2008 application by Albanian national Leci Gani to the European Court of Human Rights. He alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention, claiming he was denied a proper opportunity during investigation and trial to challenge or question N., his former partner (and mother of their son) and the sole direct witness against him for all but one of the offences of which he was convicted.

Gani was arrested on 3 June 2004 at Barcelona airport after N. reported him to police. An investigating judge opened a probe into alleged bodily harm, abduction and rape. Gani, represented by an officially appointed lawyer (whom he later confirmed as counsel), was questioned twice. On 22 July 2004 N. testified before the judge, confirming and elaborating on her police statement; Gani’s counsel was summoned but failed to attend without excuse. Gani later replaced his lawyer.

The trial opened on 19 April 2006 before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial. N. attended after a psychological assessment confirmed her fitness to testify. She began answering the prosecutor but broke down with medically confirmed post-traumatic stress symptoms that prevented further testimony. The hearing had already been adjourned once for the same reason; the court had ordered psychological support, relaxation techniques, breaks and attempts to fragment her account, all to no avail. The court described her condition as extreme psychological annihilation and, invoking victim-protection principles, declared live examination impracticable. It therefore ordered that N.’s pre-trial statements be read out. Gani gave his own account.

On 5 May 2006 the court convicted Gani as principal offender of serious threats, violent breaking-and-entering, minor injuries to N. and to J. (a friend of N.), kidnapping of both N. and J. (with family-tie aggravation for N.), an offence against N.’s moral integrity, rape of N. (again with family-tie aggravation) and forgery of official documents. Sentences included 15 years for rape and 8 years for N.’s kidnapping, plus other terms, house arrest, fines and €30,525 damages. The court relied principally on N.’s pre-trial statements (whose credibility it found enhanced by Gani’s implausible testimony and partial admissions of non-criminal details), corroborated by J.’s live evidence, medical reports consistent with the injuries and with PTSD, a defence witness’s contradictions, and the court’s own observation of N.’s incapacity.

Gani’s cassation appeal was partly allowed by the Supreme Court on 21 February 2007: some penalties were reduced, threats were reclassified, and the moral-integrity count was absorbed into the rape conviction. The remainder of the judgment was upheld. The Supreme Court held that the defence right to examine witnesses had not been breached: the trial court had exhausted every reasonable effort to obtain live testimony; Spanish law permits reading of pre-trial statements when a witness’s appearance is impossible for reasons beyond the parties’ control (here a tested psychological impediment); counsel had been duly summoned to N.’s investigative interview; and the trial court had applied the required caution when relying on a sole-victim statement by identifying corroborative evidence and finding no material inconsistencies or improper motive. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible.

The facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation therefore centre on the combination of counsel’s unexplained absence from N.’s only pre-trial examination, N.’s subsequent inability (despite extensive court measures) to give live evidence at trial, the consequent use of her untested statements as the principal evidence of conviction, and the domestic courts’ conclusion that those circumstances did not render the trial unfair.

The case of Gani v. Spain originated in an application lodged by Albanian national Leci Gani on 10 December 2008, alleging a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. He claimed he had been denied a proper opportunity, at both the investigative stage and trial, to challenge and question N., his former partner and the sole witness against him on all charges except forgery of official documents.

Gani was arrested on 3 June 2004 at Barcelona airport following reports by N., the mother of his child. Investigating judge no. 5 of Gavà opened a pre-trial investigation into allegations of serious bodily harm, abduction and rape. Gani was questioned by the judge on 5 June and 6 July 2004 in the presence of his officially appointed lawyer, whom he confirmed as his private counsel. On 22 July 2004 N. testified before the investigating judge and confirmed her police statement with additional details. Gani’s counsel failed to attend without justification; the statement was recorded and added to the file. Gani later dismissed that lawyer and appointed new counsel. No negligence proceedings were brought against the first lawyer.

The trial took place before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial on 19 April 2006. N. attended after a psychological assessment confirming her fitness to testify. She began answering the public prosecutor’s questions but her evidence was interrupted by medically confirmed post-traumatic stress symptoms that prevented her from continuing. The hearing had already been adjourned once for the same reason; psychological support, relaxation techniques, fragmentation of her account and recesses had all been provided, yet she remained unable to complete her testimony. The court therefore ordered that her pre-trial statements to the police and investigating judge be read out. Gani gave his own account of events.

On 5 May 2006 the Audiencia Provincial convicted Gani of making very serious threats, breaking and entering, minor injuries to N. and J., kidnapping of both (with family-ties aggravation for N.), a crime against N.’s moral integrity, rape (again with family-ties aggravation) and forgery. Sentences totalled more than 30 years’ imprisonment plus fines and damages. The court relied principally on N.’s pre-trial statements, whose credibility it found enhanced by the implausibility of Gani’s testimony. Corroborative evidence included J.’s in-court statement, contradictions in a defence hearsay witness, medical reports confirming N.’s injuries were consistent with the alleged assaults, a forensic opinion linking later injuries to the events, an expert diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder, and the court’s own observation of N.’s psychological collapse when she attempted to recount the facts.

Gani appealed on points of law. The Supreme Court, in a judgment of 21 February 2007, partially quashed the decision: it reduced the kidnapping penalty, reclassified the threats, and acquitted Gani of the moral-integrity offence (absorbed into rape). It otherwise upheld the convictions, holding that N.’s pre-trial statements had been properly admitted. The trial court had exhausted every possibility of obtaining live testimony; Spanish law permitted reading of investigation records when a witness was physically or psychologically unable to testify; and Gani’s counsel had been duly summoned to the investigative examination but had not attended. The Supreme Court also found that the trial court had applied the requisite caution when relying on a sole victim’s evidence, given the existence of independent corroboration and the absence of material inconsistencies or improper motives.

Gani’s subsequent amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 for lack of constitutional content. He remained imprisoned in Spain at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.

The case of Gani v. Spain originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Albanian national Leci Gani, who alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. He complained that he had not been given a proper and adequate opportunity, either at the investigative stage or at trial, to challenge and question N., his former partner and the sole witness against him in respect of all offences of which he was convicted except forgery of official documents.

Gani was questioned by the judge on 5 June 2004 in the presence of that lawyer, whom he then formally appointed as his private counsel; he was questioned again on 6 July 2004 with counsel present.

On 22 July 2004 N. gave evidence before the investigating judge. Gani’s counsel was duly summoned but failed to attend without justification. N. confirmed her earlier police statement, adding further details; the statement was recorded and placed on the case file. Gani later dismissed that lawyer and appointed a new one.

The trial took place before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial on 19 April 2006. N. attended after a psychological assessment confirmed her fitness to testify. She began answering the prosecutor’s questions but was overcome by severe post-traumatic stress symptoms that prevented her from continuing. The hearing had already been adjourned once for the same reason; psychological assistance had been provided before and during the resumed hearing, yet proved ineffective. The court described an extreme reaction of psychological annihilation that rendered further examination impossible, despite every available measure (breaks, relaxation techniques, fragmentation of testimony, support from victim services). It therefore ordered that N.’s statements from the investigation stage be read out in lieu of live testimony. Gani gave his own account of events.

The court held that use of the pre-trial statements did not infringe the defence, because they were introduced only after live cross-examination had become impracticable and remained open to challenge.

Gani appealed on points of law. On 21 February 2007 the Supreme Court partially quashed the judgment, reducing certain penalties and acquitting him of the moral-integrity offence (absorbed into the rape), but otherwise upheld the convictions. The trial court had exhausted all reasonable efforts to obtain live testimony, including medical examination and support; Spanish law permitted the reading of investigation-stage statements when a witness’s evidence could not be produced because of a tested physical or psychological impediment. Counsel had been summoned to N.’s investigative interview but had not attended. The Supreme Court emphasised that special caution is required when a victim is the sole direct witness, yet it was satisfied that the trial court had relied on sufficient corroboration and that N.’s account contained no material inconsistencies.

An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 for lack of constitutional content.

The case of Krisztián Barnabás Tóth v. Hungary (application no. 48494/06) was lodged on 24 November 2006 by a Hungarian national born in 1974 and living in Budapest. He complained under Article 8 of the Convention that he had been unable to establish his biological paternity of a child.

From January 2004 the applicant cohabited with Ms H.K. in a common-law marriage. Her pregnancy was confirmed on 5 April 2004, but cohabitation ended on 1 September 2004. On 26 November 2004 Mr P. made a declaration of paternity of the unborn child, with the mother’s consent. The girl was born on 4 January 2005. On 13 January 2005 Mr P.’s wife adopted her; the Gyomaendrőd Custody Board endorsed the adoption with the mother’s consent.

On learning of these events the applicant, on 20 January 2005, asked the Pest County Administrative Office to appoint an ad hoc guardian so that he could bring an action to establish his paternity. The request was transferred to the Gyomaendrőd Custody Board, which refused. It held that the child’s family situation was already settled and that it was not in her interest to have paternity litigated. An administrative appeal failed.

The applicant challenged the refusals in court. On 15 September 2005 the Békés County Regional Court heard him on his personal circumstances and plans for raising the child, then dismissed the action. It confirmed that challenging the presumption of paternity was not in the child’s interest. The applicant had had an opportunity after conception to make his own declaration with the mother’s consent, but that window had closed. Mr P. had acknowledged paternity and the child had been adopted by Mrs P., so her legal status was settled. Evidence from a home visit and interviews showed she was being raised in a loving family; it was not in her interest to be removed from that environment merely for medical tests. A successful challenge would leave the father’s status vacant, yet the applicant’s declaration would not take full effect without the mother’s consent, so the child would lose her settled family status. Granting the request would have been a grave breach of the law, potentially depriving the child of her family and of the atmosphere needed for her physical, mental and moral development.

On 17 May 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s petition for review. It accepted that the child’s interest in knowing her biological father was significant, but held that her overall welfare was paramount. She was being brought up in a loving family with adequate means; a lawsuit at that stage was not in her best interest. The child herself could bring such an action once she reached the age of 14.

These successive refusals by administrative authorities and courts form the factual basis of the applicant’s Article 8 complaint that he was prevented from establishing biological paternity.

The case of Krisztián Barnabás Tóth v. Hungary (Application no. 48494/06) concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1974 and living in Budapest, alleged that Hungarian authorities prevented him from establishing his biological paternity of a child born to his former partner, thereby violating his right to respect for private and family life.

The applicant cohabited with Ms H.K. in a common-law marriage from January 2004. On 5 April 2004, her pregnancy was confirmed. Their cohabitation ended on 1 September 2004. On 26 November 2004, a Mr P. made a legally effective declaration of paternity regarding the unborn child, to which the mother consented. The girl was born on 4 January 2005. Shortly thereafter, on 13 January 2005, Mr P.’s wife adopted the child. The Gyomaendrőd Custody Board endorsed the adoption, and the mother consented.

Upon discovering these developments, the applicant, on 20 January 2005, applied to the Pest County Administrative Office for appointment of an ad hoc guardian for the infant. This would have enabled him to bring a court action to establish his own paternity. The matter was transferred to the Gyomaendrőd Custody Board, which refused the request. It reasoned that the child’s family situation was already settled and that litigation over paternity would not serve her interests. The applicant’s administrative appeal was unsuccessful.

He then challenged the refusals in court. On 15 September 2005 the Békés County Regional Court held a hearing, at which the applicant described his personal circumstances and plans for raising the child. The court dismissed the action that same day. It confirmed that proceedings to challenge the existing presumption of paternity were not in the child’s interest. The court noted that the applicant had had an opportunity after conception to make his own declaration of paternity with the mother’s consent, but had not done so. In the meantime Mr P. had acknowledged paternity and the child had been adopted by Mrs P. The child’s legal status was therefore settled. Evidence gathered by the custody authorities, including a home visit and interviews, showed that she was being raised in a loving family atmosphere. It was not in her interest to be removed from that environment merely to allow medical tests of biological paternity. The court added that a successful challenge would leave the legal “status of father” vacant; the applicant’s subsequent declaration would still lack the mother’s consent and therefore would not take full effect. The child would consequently lose her settled family status. Granting the applicant’s request would have constituted a grave breach of law, as it risked depriving the child of her existing family relationships, which were necessary for her harmonious physical, mental and moral development.

On 17 May 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s petition for review. It endorsed the authorities’ view that questioning paternity was not in the child’s interest. While acknowledging the potential value to the child of knowing her biological father, the Supreme Court stressed that the child’s interest remained paramount. She was being brought up in a loving family with appropriate means. A lawsuit challenging paternity was not, at that time, in her best interest. The court observed that the child herself could later bring such an action once she reached the age of fourteen.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint: successive administrative and judicial decisions had blocked any possibility of establishing biological paternity, on the ground that the child’s welfare in her adoptive family outweighed the putative father’s interest in legal recognition of the biological link.

**CASE OF ZARZYCKI v. POLAND (Application no. 15351/03, ECtHR, 12 March 2013)**

The applicant, Adam Zarzycki (born 1976), a Polish national, lost both forearms in a 1996 accident and held a first-degree disability certificate requiring assistance from another person. He alleged that his detention from June 2002 onward in Szczytno and Olsztyn Remand Centres violated Article 3 of the Convention due to conditions unadapted to his disability and special needs.

On 19 June 2002, the Szczytno District Court remanded him in custody on suspicion of offences against a minor and coercing perjury. Courts cited strong evidence, the risk of a severe penalty, and the need to secure proceedings (he had attempted to influence witnesses). His disability and a March 2002 medical certificate stating he could not live independently were considered, but detention was upheld. He had previously been detained for four months in Szczytno without reported issues. Prosecutors and courts repeatedly rejected requests to lift or replace detention, noting no risk to life or health and that prison authorities could transfer him to a hospital if needed. Witness testimony on his independence was mixed. He was convicted on 31 October 2002 and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment; the conviction was largely upheld on appeal in February 2003. Detention continued during the appeal.

He was held in Szczytno (19 June 2002–5 March 2003 and 28 March–7 July 2003) and briefly in Olsztyn (5–28 March 2003), then granted six months’ leave (later extended to July 2004) for external orthopaedic care. After failing to return, he was re-arrested in July 2004 and detained alternately in the two centres until parole on 21 October 2006.

Without prostheses (first period), he was placed in standard multi-occupancy cells. He claimed he could not independently perform daily tasks such as serving meals, making his bed, cutting toenails, washing, shaving, dressing, or post-toilet hygiene, forcing dependence on inmates. The Government maintained he was largely self-sufficient (eating, dressing, making his bed, reading) with only occasional inmate help for minor tasks, was excused from cell-cleaning, received privileges (longer visits, extra parcels, more showers), saw a psychologist 11 times, and received unsupervised leaves as rewards. A prison doctor found no medical reason for transfer or release, describing his needs as non-medical. A remand-centre memorandum and governor’s letter confirmed he managed most routines independently.

Authorities assisted with prostheses: a prior 2001 approval had lapsed due to funding shortages; a new application led to approval of basic mechanical prostheses (cost ~PLN 3,600 / EUR 860, fully reimbursable). He was transferred to Olsztyn for fittings but rejected them, insisting on more expensive bio-mechanical prostheses (~PLN 50,000 / EUR 12,000, only PLN 3,600 reimbursable). He declined to pay the difference, so no transfer to Poznań occurred. A psychiatrist diagnosed depression linked to prosthesis fears (noting prior suicide attempts as a minor) but made no detention recommendations. Courts found detention posed no danger to life or health, only minor difficulties. He received ~12 specialist consultations.

After obtaining basic mechanical prostheses and physiotherapy while at liberty (around March 2004), he still required help for precise tasks (washing, small clothing items, shaving, bathroom use). A rehabilitation centre confirmed the prostheses allowed only simple tasks. Prison requests for transfer for further therapy were refused due to pending proceedings; he declined in-house physiotherapy. Some doctors certified inadequate prison care. A June 2005 expert report (cardiology/orthopaedics) found him well-adapted, in good health (despite hypertension), and fit for detention, though needing staff assistance for daily routines. Olsztyn had no adapted cells for disabled prisoners. He received ~60 specialist consultations. Numerous complaints were dismissed; a prosecutor’s inquiry concluded authorities had made extensive efforts regarding prostheses.

Domestic law provided a “therapeutic regime” for disabled prisoners needing specialised care or rehabilitation, with possible adaptations to medical, hygiene, and sanitary needs, and exceptions to standard rules justified by health (including physical disability). No further specific regulation existed for disabled detainees.

The case of Ostendorf v. Germany (Application no. 15598/08) originated from a complaint by Henrik Ostendorf, a German national born in 1968 and resident in Bremen, who alleged that his preventive detention on 10 April 2004 violated Article 5 of the Convention. Ostendorf was a regular supporter of Werder Bremen football club and had been registered since 3 September 1996 in Bremen police and nationwide databases as a person prepared to use violence at sports events, with eight incidents listed against him between 1996 and 2003.

On 10 April 2004, Ostendorf travelled by train from Bremen to Frankfurt am Main with 30–40 other fans to attend the Eintracht Frankfurt versus Werder Bremen match. Bremen police had alerted Frankfurt counterparts that the group included “category C hooligans” prepared to use violence; Ostendorf was identified as a “gang leader.” Upon arrival, police verified identities, searched the group and seized a mouth guard and quartz-sand-filled gloves (typical hooligan weapons) from members other than the applicant. The group, placed under surveillance, went to a pub. When they left, Ostendorf was missing and was located in a locked cubicle in the ladies’ toilet. He was arrested at approximately 2.30 p.m., taken to a police station near the stadium and had his mobile phone seized. He was released at 6.30 p.m., one hour after the match ended; the phone was returned on 15 April 2004.

Ostendorf complained to Frankfurt Police Headquarters that the detention and seizure were unlawful. The police president dismissed the complaint on 17 August 2004 as both inadmissible (the measures having become moot) and unfounded. Relying on section 32(1) no. 2 of the Hessian Public Security and Order Act, the president held that detention had been indispensable to prevent the imminent commission of a criminal or regulatory offence of considerable public importance (assault or breach of the peace). Police information indicated that an arranged hooligan confrontation was likely; Ostendorf had tried to evade surveillance, was known as a gang leader, had spoken to a Frankfurt hooligan and had hidden in the toilet. The phone seizure under section 40 no. 4 of the same Act was likewise necessary to stop him arranging the clash.

Ostendorf then sued the Land of Hesse in the Frankfurt Administrative Court, denying any plan to arrange violence and claiming he had used the ladies’ toilet because the men’s was unusable. After a hearing on 14 June 2005 at which a police officer testified that the group had been drinking heavily, that weapons had been found, that Ostendorf had been identified as leader and that his phone had displayed a Frankfurt number when it rang, the court dismissed the action. It found the four-hour detention lawful under the Hessian Act: the police reasonably concluded it was necessary to avert imminent offences of assault and public-order breach, given Ostendorf’s known status, his evasion of surveillance and the established practice of pre-arranged hooligan fights. The phone seizure was similarly justified.

The Hessian Administrative Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 1 February 2006, confirming that detention required a very high likelihood of an imminent serious offence and that the facts met that threshold. It noted that Frankfurt police had not relied on (and were not responsible for) the Bremen database entries. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider Ostendorf’s constitutional complaint on 26 February 2008 without giving reasons.

The relevant Hessian provisions authorise police custody if indispensable to prevent an imminent criminal or regulatory offence of considerable public importance, with release required as soon as the grounds cease (or after 24 hours at latest). No prior judicial order is needed for short detentions. These facts formed the core of Ostendorf’s Article 5 complaint that his liberty had been restricted without sufficient justification.

**CASE OF OSTENDORF v. GERMANY (Application no. 15598/08)**

The applicant, Henrik Ostendorf (born 1968, resident in Bremen), a regular Werder Bremen football supporter, challenged his four-hour preventive detention on 10 April 2004 as a violation of Article 5 of the Convention (right to liberty). He had been registered since 1996 in Bremen police and nationwide databases as a person prepared to use violence at sports events (a “category C hooligan”), with eight listed incidents between 1996 and 2003; he was also identified by Bremen police as a “gang leader.”

On 10 April 2004, Ostendorf travelled by train from Bremen to Frankfurt am Main with 30–40 other fans for the Eintracht Frankfurt–Werder Bremen match. Bremen police had alerted Frankfurt police that the group consisted of persons prepared to use violence. Upon arrival at Frankfurt station, police checked identities, classified most as hooligans, and identified Ostendorf as the group’s “gang leader.” A search of the group (not including Ostendorf) yielded a mouth guard and quartz-sand-filled gloves—items typically used in hooligan clashes involving assault or breach of the peace (Landfriedensbruch). The group, placed under police surveillance, proceeded to a pub. Ostendorf then left the group and was found locked in a cubicle in the ladies’ bathroom. He was arrested at approximately 2.30 p.m., taken to a police station near the stadium, and had his mobile phone seized. He was released at 6.30 p.m., one hour after the match ended; the phone was returned five days later.

Ostendorf complained that the detention and seizure were unlawful. The president of the Frankfurt police rejected the complaint as inadmissible (the measures had become moot) and, in any event, unfounded. Detention was authorised under section 32(1) no. 2 of the Hessian Public Security and Order Act as indispensable to prevent the imminent commission of a criminal or regulatory offence of considerable public importance. Police expected an arranged altercation between Bremen and Frankfurt hooligans that would involve offences such as bodily assault and breach of the peace. Ostendorf was viewed as having evaded surveillance to organise such a clash (he was a known gang leader, had spoken to a Frankfurt hooligan in the pub, and had hidden in the bathroom). Separating him was necessary; release after the match, once both groups had dispersed, was sufficient. The phone seizure (section 40 no. 4 of the same Act) was likewise necessary to prevent him from arranging a clash.

Ostendorf then brought an action in the Frankfurt Administrative Court, denying he was a gang leader or had planned any offence and claiming he had used the ladies’ bathroom only because the men’s facilities were unusable. (who confirmed heavy alcohol consumption by the group, the typical use of the seized items, the warning that anyone leaving the group would be arrested, Ostendorf’s leadership role, the presence of a Frankfurt man in the bathroom, Ostendorf’s lack of explanation, and an incoming call on Ostendorf’s phone displaying a male name plus “Ftm.”), the court dismissed the action on 14 June 2005. The Hessian Act authorises police custody only when indispensable to prevent an imminent criminal or regulatory offence of considerable public importance (or to enforce a banning order), subject to prompt judicial review (unless the measure would expire first), release as soon as grounds cease, a 24-hour maximum without a judge, and an overall six-day judicial maximum. Objects may be seized if there are concrete reasons they will be used to commit an offence. Relevant Criminal Code provisions include breach of the peace (Art. 125), bodily injury (Arts. 223–224) and participation in a brawl (Art. 231).

The case of Ostendorf v. Germany (Application no. 15598/08) originated from a complaint by Henrik Ostendorf, a German national and regular Werder Bremen football supporter born in 1968, alleging that his four-hour preventive detention on 10 April 2004 violated Article 5 of the Convention (right to liberty). Ostendorf had been registered since 1996 in Bremen and nationwide police databases as a person prepared to use violence at sports events, with eight listed incidents between 1996 and 2003 involving him in football-related contexts.

On 10 April 2004, Ostendorf travelled by train from Bremen to Frankfurt am Main with 30–40 other fans for the Eintracht Frankfurt–Werder Bremen match. Bremen police had notified Frankfurt counterparts that the group included “category C” hooligans likely to use violence. Upon arrival at Frankfurt station, police checked identities, classified most of the group as violent hooligans and identified Ostendorf as their “gang leader.” A search of the group (not including Ostendorf) yielded a mouth-protection device and quartz-sand-filled gloves, items typically used in hooligan clashes involving assault or breach of the peace.

Placed under surveillance, the group entered a pub. When they departed, Ostendorf was absent. Police located him at about 2.30 p.m. locked in a cubicle in the ladies’ toilet; he offered no plausible explanation. He was arrested, taken to a nearby police station and had his mobile phone seized. He was released at 6.30 p.m., one hour after the match ended (the phone was returned five days later).

Ostendorf’s subsequent complaint to Frankfurt police was rejected. The police president held the detention lawful under section 32(1) no. 2 of the Hessian Public Security and Order Act as indispensable to prevent an imminent criminal or regulatory offence of considerable public importance. Given Ostendorf’s reputation, his observed contact with a Frankfurt hooligan, his evasion of surveillance and the known practice of pre-arranged hooligan confrontations, police reasonably feared he intended to organise a clash involving assault and public-order offences. Detention separated him from the group; release followed once opposing fans had dispersed. Phone seizure (under section 40 no. 4 of the same Act) was likewise justified to stop coordination of the fight.

Ostendorf then sued the Land of Hesse in the Frankfurt Administrative Court, denying any leadership role or violent intent and claiming he had used the ladies’ toilet only because the men’s was unusable. After hearing Ostendorf and a participating officer (who confirmed heavy drinking on the train, the seized items, a prior warning that anyone leaving the group would be arrested, Ostendorf’s leadership status and an incoming call displaying a Frankfurt number), the court dismissed the action. It found detention necessary and proportionate to avert imminent assaults and breaches of the peace.

The Hessian Administrative Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal, confirming that concordant facts made an altercation highly likely and that milder measures (continued escort of the group or mere separation) would have been insufficient, since such clashes typically occur away from stadiums. Data transferred from Bremen police could be relied upon; its original lawfulness was not at issue in proceedings against Hesse. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider Ostendorf’s constitutional complaint.

Hessian law authorises custody only when indispensable to prevent an imminent offence of public importance, subject to strict time-limits (normally 24 hours, or six days if a court so orders). Criminal provisions cover rioting, bodily injury and participation in brawls. These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 5 breach: purely preventive detention without charge or judicial authorisation at the time of arrest.

The case of Luković v. Serbia (Application no. 43808/07) originated from a complaint by Velibor Luković, a Serbian national and Customs Department Anti-Smuggling Team employee born in 1973, that his pre-trial detention was unlawful and excessively long.

On 1 December 2006 an investigating judge of the Belgrade District Court extended his detention (along with that of 18 co-accused) under Article 142 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The stated grounds were: risk of absconding (professional contacts including international ones and illicit profits that could facilitate flight); risk of obstructing justice by influencing witnesses (as superior to other customs officers to be heard); risk of reoffending (multiple offences in a short period); and the seriousness of the charges (offences punishable by over ten years’ imprisonment, committed in a manner that exploited his anti-smuggling role).

He was suspended from work effective from the arrest date. Detention was extended on the same grounds on 27 December 2006 and 23 February 2007.

On 28 May 2007 the prosecutor issued a 247-page indictment against Luković and 27 others, charging him with organising a criminal group and eight counts of large-scale corruption. The District Court extended detention that day, noting 81 witnesses still to be examined given the case’s complexity. Luković was not served the indictment until 13 June 2007, missing the 24-hour limit of Article 270 § 1. He applied for release, arguing that this delayed “issuance” breached the six-month maximum pre-trial detention period of Article 144. The District Court rejected the application (no appeal possible). The Supreme Court later held that an indictment is issued upon delivery to the court, not service on the accused, consistent with established jurisprudence.

Luković repeatedly challenged the grounds, arguing that witnesses were unspecified so influence risk could not be assessed; that he had not held the team-leader post at the relevant time; that suspension eliminated reoffending risk; and that the severity/aggravating-circumstances ground lacked legal basis.
