From 4 December 2009 it rested solely on absconding risk, the courts holding that reoffending risk had ceased given elapsed time since the alleged activity, suspension, lack of prior record, time already spent in detention and disbandment of the group.

After December 2009 four applications offering a mortgage over family property were refused for insufficient value and lack of supporting financial evidence. On 9 July 2010 the High Court accepted bail of EUR 388,416.50; the Court of Appeal quashed the decision pending clarification of whether assets under financial investigation were included. Bail was re-accepted and upheld, and Luković was released on 27 August 2010 after approximately three years and nine months in detention.

The case of Luković v. Serbia (Application no. 43808/07) concerns a Serbian customs officer, Velibor Luković (born 1973), who alleged that his pre-trial detention was both unlawful and excessively lengthy, in violation of Article 5 of the Convention.

Luković, a team leader in the Customs Department’s Anti-Smuggling Team, was arrested on 28 November 2006 on suspicion of organising a criminal group and large-scale corruption. An investigating judge of the Belgrade District Court immediately extended his detention (along with that of 18 co-accused). The stated grounds were: (i) a risk of absconding, given his professional contacts (including international ones that could facilitate border crossing) and illicit profits; (ii) a risk of influencing witnesses, as he was the superior of other customs officers who would be called to testify; (iii) a risk of reoffending, based on multiple offences committed in a short period; and (iv) the gravity of the charges (punishable by more than ten years’ imprisonment) and the aggravating circumstance that he had used his anti-smuggling post to enable the very crimes he was supposed to prevent.

He was suspended from duty with effect from the date of arrest. Detention was confirmed and extended on 27 December 2006 and 23 February 2007 on identical grounds.

On 28 May 2007 the prosecutor filed a 247-page indictment against Luković and 27 others, charging him with organising a criminal group and eight counts of large-scale corruption. The District Court extended detention the same day, reiterating the original grounds and noting that 81 witnesses remained to be examined. Luković was served with the indictment only on 13 June 2007. He applied for release, arguing that the statutory 24-hour service deadline (Article 270 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) had been missed, so the six-month maximum pre-trial detention period (Article 144) had expired. The application was rejected; the Supreme Court later held that an indictment is “issued” when delivered to the court, not when served on the accused.

Detention was thereafter reviewed every two months. Luković repeatedly challenged the orders, arguing that the courts had failed to identify which witnesses he could still influence, that he had not in fact been team leader at the relevant time, that his suspension eliminated any risk of reoffending, and that the gravity/aggravating-circumstances ground was legally insufficient.

On 19 November 2007 the Supreme Court dropped the gravity ground, holding that the facts relied upon (his official position and the scale of profit) were already constituent elements of the charged offences and therefore could not constitute additional “particularly aggravating circumstances.” Subsequent orders specified two remaining co-accused who were at large and one named witness as persons Luković might influence.

From 13 April 2009 detention rested only on risks of absconding and reoffending; from 4 December 2009 it rested solely on the risk of absconding, the courts having found that the passage of time, his suspension, lack of prior convictions, the length of detention already served and the disbanding of the alleged group had extinguished any realistic fear of reoffending.

Bail applications were initially declared inadmissible (bail being available only for absconding risk). After December 2009 they were refused on the ground that the offered security (a family property mortgage) was insufficiently valued. Bail of EUR 388,416.50 was finally accepted in August 2010 and Luković was released on 27 August 2010 after nearly three years and nine months in custody.

The domestic courts’ successive reasoning, the timing of the indictment, the evolving (and eventually narrowing) grounds of detention, and the handling of bail therefore form the core factual matrix against which the alleged unlawfulness and excessive length of detention must be assessed.

The ECHR case Novaya Gazeta and Borodyanskiy v. Russia (no. 14087/08) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) arising from civil libel proceedings in Russia. The first applicant was the editorial house of Novaya Gazeta, a national daily newspaper with a 500,000 circulation. The second applicant, journalist G. Borodyanskiy, contributed regional reporting.

On 27 November 2006 the newspaper (print and online) published Borodyanskiy’s article “Personalities received loans.” It described alleged fraudulent schemes used to obtain unpaid Sberbank loans of up to EUR 147 million. The piece named individuals involved and focused on Mr R.M., a Kazakh politician and businessman with substantial agricultural interests in Omsk Region, including control of the Kirovskiy Grain Elevator (the region’s largest flour producer) and other enterprises. Key passages stated that R.M.’s success would have been “inconceivable” without the “benevolence” of Omsk Governor Mr P., who had held senior office in Kazakhstan for over 20 years, creating “fraternal bonds.” The article also described how the grain elevator’s CEO issued forged certificates of non-existent grain, each costing 50–70 thousand roubles, enabling loans of half a billion roubles. A brief note on a related criminal inquiry closed the piece.

On 11 December 2006 Governor P. sued both applicants in the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of Omsk for libel. He sought a finding that the statements about him were defamatory, a rectification, and RUB 500,000 in non-pecuniary damages.

The District Court heard the case on 15 January 2007 in the applicants’ absence after refusing a further adjournment. It held that the statements had been widely disseminated, were discrediting, and were unproven. “Benevolence” was interpreted as implying the Governor’s approval of R.M.’s business control, which, taken with the surrounding allegations of fraud, created a negative image of P. as abusing office to confer privileges. The court ordered rectification in both print and online editions and jointly awarded RUB 60,000 (approx. EUR 1,623) in damages plus RUB 100 in fees.

The Omsk Regional Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 25 July 2007. It rejected the argument that the passages were unverifiable value judgments and confirmed they tarnished P.’s reputation by alleging improper approval of R.M.’s control. One fragment (the forged-certificate scheme) was held non-defamatory because it did not mention P. Rectification of the remaining passages and payment of RUB 60,100 were confirmed. The applicants complied.

Russian law (Civil Code Article 152 and a 2005 Supreme Court Plenum decree) required proof of truth for damaging statements of fact but distinguished them from non-actionable opinions. The applicants contended that the domestic courts’ characterisation of journalistic comment on a public official and possible high-level financial irregularities as unproven facts, together with the modest but still punitive award and forced rectification, constituted an unjustified interference with press freedom on a matter of public interest.

The case of C.B. v. Austria (Application no. 30465/06) concerned criminal proceedings in Austria against the applicant, an Austrian national born in 1966. In 2005, the Krems an der Donau Regional Court tried him for attempted and completed sexual abuse of minors and juveniles, plus offences under the Drug Offences Act. The court appointed a neurological-psychiatric expert to assess, inter alia, whether the applicant met the criteria under Article 21 § 2 of the Criminal Code for placement in an institution for mentally ill offenders. The applicant did not object to the expert or the remit.

The court-appointed expert’s report of 4 March 2005, based on an examination of the applicant, the case file and an MMPI-2 test, concluded that the applicant was fully criminally responsible but suffered from a disorder of sexual preference (paedophilia) and a narcissistic personality disorder. It found a very high risk of reoffending with severe consequences, noting that the age of victims had decreased. The report was served on defence counsel.

On 8 June 2005 counsel submitted comments together with a private psychiatric-neurological expert opinion dated 12 May 2005. The private expert agreed on homosexual paedophilia and a sexual-preference disorder but found no narcissistic disorder. He assessed the risk of non-violent reoffending as low to moderate and criticised the court expert’s methods, factual statements and interpretations as insufficiently explained. Counsel asked that the private report be read to the court-appointed expert at the hearing and that a further court expert be appointed if the two opinions diverged.

The court-appointed expert filed a written supplement on 22 June 2005 addressing each criticism. At the oral hearing of 30 June 2005 the court expert summarised and expanded his opinion and was questioned at length by counsel. The court, however, disallowed questions that referred to the private report or probed the expert’s qualifications. Counsel applied for the private report to be admitted, for the private expert to be heard as a witness (on an assessment performed after the applicant’s five-week solitary detention), for a second court expert, and for three lay witnesses (B.S., J.H. and A.U.) to testify that the applicant had no difficulty forming relationships, possessed empathy and lacked a pathological need to control others, and that the facts relied on by the court expert were inaccurate or incomplete.

The public prosecutor opposed all requests. The Regional Court refused them, holding that: (1) the private expert could not testify as a witness on psychiatric assessment or legal issues reserved to the court and its appointed expert; (2) a second expert was unnecessary because the first expert’s findings were complete, conclusive and certain (Articles 118, 125 and 126 of the Code of Criminal Procedure); (3) the private report could not be read out without the prosecutor’s consent (Article 252); and (4) the three lay witnesses were not shown to possess relevant knowledge and could not draw medical conclusions.

The same day the court, sitting as a Schöffengericht, convicted the applicant, imposed a two-year sentence and ordered institutional placement under Article 21 § 2. It found he had sexually abused a minor born in 1992 on at least ten occasions (2003–2004) and two juveniles born in 1988 on approximately 26 occasions by offering money, and had supplied hashish five times. The judgment relied entirely on the court-appointed expert, whom it described as experienced, consistent and logical; it dismissed the private report and proposed witnesses as legally irrelevant.

A plea of nullity was rejected by the Supreme Court on 22 December 2005; the appeal was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal on 30 March 2006. Both courts held that the refusals were correct under domestic law, that the defence had had ample opportunity to question the court expert (including on points raised by the private report), and that no fairness violation under Article 6 ECHR had occurred. Austrian law at the time treated privately commissioned opinions as having no evidentiary value; they served only to assist the defence in formulating questions. A second court expert was required only if the first report was incomplete or inconclusive. Witnesses were confined to personal perceptions of facts, not opinions or medical assessments.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the refusals violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) by denying him a fair opportunity to challenge the expert evidence that led to his conviction and preventive detention.

It agreed on homosexual paedophilia and a disorder of sexual preference but rejected the narcissistic diagnosis and assessed only a low-to-moderate risk of non-violent reoffending. Counsel asked that the private opinion be read to the court expert at the hearing and that a second expert be appointed if they disagreed. The court expert replied in writing on 22 June 2005.

At the 30 June 2005 hearing the court expert presented and supplemented his views. Counsel questioned him at length but was barred from referring to the private opinion or probing the expert’s qualifications. Requests to admit the private opinion, to hear the private expert (Dr W.B.) as a witness on the Article 21 § 2 criteria and on his later examination of the applicant, and to call three further witnesses (B.S., J.H. and A.U.) to speak to the applicant’s capacity for relationships, empathy, lack of pathological control needs and alleged inaccuracies in the court expert’s factual basis were all refused.

The court held that a private expert could not give valid evidence as either expert or witness; assessments were reserved to court-appointed experts. No second expert was required because the appointed expert had answered all questions conclusively and with certainty. The private report could not be read out in the absence of the prosecutor’s consent and of any statutory ground. The three proposed witnesses were unsuitable: they could not themselves make psychiatric assessments, the request failed to specify the facts they would address, and witnesses may not draw conclusions.

The same day the court convicted the applicant, imposed two years’ imprisonment and ordered institutional placement. It relied entirely on the court expert’s “comprehensible, logical and consistent” opinion, finding no grounds under Articles 125–126 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for further expertise or for treating the private material as evidence.

The Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s plea of nullity on 22 December 2005, holding that the refusals caused no prejudice: the court expert had been conclusive, private-expert testimony was inadmissible, the defence had been able to explore the private opinion’s criticisms during lengthy questioning, and the witness request was too vague. The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the remaining appeal on 30 March 2006, confirming that the court expert’s prognosis was convincing and that no legal basis existed for a further expert.

These evidentiary refusals constitute the facts underlying the alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d).
001-118477:
The case of Tarantino and Others v. Italy (Applications nos. 25851/09, 29284/09 and 64090/09) involves eight Italian nationals who alleged a violation of their right to education under Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. They claimed that Law no. 127/1997, introducing a numerus clausus (limited access) to university faculties, pursued illegitimate aims and imposed a disproportionate restriction.

Ms Claudia Tarantino failed the entrance examination for the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Palermo in 2007 (when 2,000 candidates competed for 210 places), as well as in 2008 and 2009. In December 2007, she and others complained to the President of the Republic that Law no. 264/1999’s two binding criteria for setting quotas—universities’ capacity and resources, plus society’s need for the profession—were incompatible with EU law (including the Treaty, Directive 2005/36/EC on professional qualifications, and the Charter of Fundamental Rights), the principle of equality, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. She also challenged the extension of limits to private universities and the adequacy of the entrance examinations, seeking provisional admission. The Supreme Administrative Court rejected her request for an interim measure. In April 2009 the President dismissed the complaints, holding the restrictions reasonable in light of universities’ human and material resources and noting a 10-20% increase in medical-faculty admissions for 2008-09 to meet societal demand. The professional examination after graduation was characterised as a standard State exam, and the entrance test’s content was deemed adequate.

The remaining seven applicants, who had worked for years as dental technicians or hygienists, failed the 2009 (and other) entrance examinations for the Faculty of Dentistry. Mr Carmelo Marcuzzo had passed the exam in 1999/2000 but lost student status in 2009 after eight consecutive years of inactivity caused by serious family problems, pursuant to university rules implementing Royal Decree no. 1592/1933. These applicants did not pursue domestic remedies, considering them futile: the Supreme Administrative Court had consistently held limited university access compatible with the Constitution and EU law, and had ruled that subjective reasons such as family difficulties could not interrupt the eight-year continuity requirement.

Law no. 127/1997 first introduced the numerus clausus for both public and private universities, leaving the Ministry of Universities to set limits without specified criteria. The Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 1998, finding ministerial discretion constrained by EU directives aimed at adequate educational standards and calling on Parliament to legislate. Law no. 264/1999 then required the Ministry to fix quotas for medicine, dentistry and related faculties according to the two criteria of capacity/resources and societal professional need. In 2009 the Antitrust Authority criticised the system for relying on occupational-demand data (especially public-sector demand) supplied by health-ministry and professional-body representatives, arguing that this artificially restricted competition, raised fees and ignored private demand.

Admission depended on an 80-question multiple-choice test covering high-school subjects (general culture, biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics) designed to assess aptitude. Domestic courts repeatedly confirmed that the numerus clausus complied with the Constitution and EU law. They treated university capacity as the primary criterion necessary to guarantee proper scientific training, with societal need merely secondary and applicable only if resources were abundant. EU directives on medical training and recognition of qualifications set minimum standards but left implementation, including any access limits, to the Member States.

These facts underpin the applicants’ claim that the statutory restrictions unlawfully interfered with their access to higher education.

**CASE OF TARANTINO AND OTHERS v. ITALY (Apps. nos. 25851/09, 29284/09 and 64090/09), ECtHR (Second Section), 2 April 2013 (final 9 September 2013)**

Eight Italian nationals (Ms Claudia Tarantino and seven others, including dental technicians/hygienists) alleged a violation of their right to education under Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. They challenged Italy’s *numerus clausus* (limited university access) under Law no. 127/1997 (as implemented by Law no. 264/1999), claiming its aims were illegitimate and the restrictions disproportionate. The Ministry of Universities set annual quotas for faculties including Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Architecture and Nursing, based on two binding criteria: (1) universities’ capacity and resources, and (2) society’s need for the profession (*fabbisogno di professionalità*). Admission required passing a standardised multiple-choice entrance exam (80 questions on general culture, biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics, drawn from the high-school syllabus).

Ms Tarantino failed the Palermo Medicine entrance exam in 2007 (2,000 candidates for 210 places), 2008 and 2009. In December 2007 she and others petitioned the President of the Republic, arguing the quotas (especially the societal-need criterion) and identical limits on private universities violated EU law (including Treaty provisions on equality, Directive 2005/36/EC on professional qualifications, and the EU Charter), as well as Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. She also contested exam adequacy and sought interim admission. The Supreme Administrative Court (*Consiglio di Stato*) refused interim relief in July 2008. By presidential decree of 28 April 2009 (based on the Court’s November 2008 advisory opinion), her complaints were rejected: restrictions were reasonable given universities’ human and material resources, selected only meritorious students, and were compatible with EU standards. Admissions had risen 10–20% in 2008–09 to meet demand for doctors; the post-degree professional exam was a standard State test.

The other seven applicants (experienced dental technicians or hygienists) failed the Dentistry entrance exam in 2009 (and other years). Mr Marcuzzo had passed in 1999/2000 but lost student status in July 2009 after eight consecutive years without sitting exams, owing to serious family problems (under Royal Decree no. 1592/1933, Art. 149, and university rules; the time-limit was treated as a non-interruptible lapse of the right). They did not exhaust domestic remedies, viewing them as futile: consistent Supreme Administrative Court case-law (e.g., judgments of 2008) held *numerus clausus* compatible with the Constitution and EU law, and family circumstances did not excuse the eight-year rule.

The 1998 Constitutional Court (judgment no. 383) had upheld Law no. 127/1997, finding ministerial discretion constrained by EU directives ensuring educational standards; Parliament later enacted the two-criteria system. Domestic courts repeatedly confirmed compatibility (e.g., *Consiglio di Stato* nos. 1931/2008, 5418/2008). Capacity/resources was the primary criterion, ensuring scientific training meeting EU minimum standards (directives left methods to States and did not prohibit *numeri clausi*); societal need was secondary and applied only to avoid market saturation. The Antitrust Authority (2009 recommendation) criticised the system: assessments focused solely on public (National Health Service) demand, ignored private demand, involved interested professional bodies, artificially limited dentists, raised fees and restricted competition, contrary to the Constitutional Court’s emphasis on educational quality.

The Court joined the applications and examined admissibility and merits together. The facts centre on repeated exam failures despite (in some cases) relevant professional experience, the statutory quotas and exam process, unsuccessful or unpursued domestic challenges, and the applicants’ core claim that the restrictions pursued illegitimate aims and were disproportionate, impairing access to higher education.

The case of Tarantino and Others v. Italy (applications nos. 25851/09, 29284/09 and 64090/09) concerns eight Italian nationals who alleged that Italy’s numerus clausus (restricted-access) regime for university admission violated their right to education under Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. They contended that the aims of Law no. 127/1997 (as implemented by Law no. 264/1999) were illegitimate and the restrictions disproportionate.

Ms Claudia Tarantino sat the entrance examination for the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Palermo in 2007 (2 000 candidates for 210 places) and failed; she failed again in 2008 and 2009. In December 2007 she and others petitioned the President of the Republic, arguing that the two binding ministerial criteria used to fix admission numbers—university capacity/resources and society’s professional needs—were incompatible with EU Treaty provisions on free movement and non-discrimination, Directive 2005/36/EC on professional qualifications, the EU Charter, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. She also challenged the application of the same limits to private universities and the adequacy of the examination, and sought provisional enrolment. The Consiglio di Stato refused interim relief. By decree of 28 April 2009 the President, relying on an advisory opinion of 12 November 2008, rejected the petition: the restrictions were reasonable in the light of human and material resources, selected the most meritorious students, and were compatible with EU law; admissions had in any event been increased by 10–20 % to meet growing demand for doctors. The examination itself was held to be adequate.

The remaining seven applicants, all practising dental technicians or hygienists, failed the Dentistry Faculty entrance examination in 2009 (and in other years). One of them, Mr Marcuzzo, had been admitted in 1999/2000 but lost student status in July 2009 after failing to sit examinations for eight consecutive years because of family difficulties, pursuant to a 1933 royal-decree rule that the Consiglio di Stato treats as a non-interruptible forfeiture period. These applicants did not exhaust domestic remedies, considering them futile in view of consistent Consiglio di Stato case-law upholding both the constitutionality of the numerus clausus and the strict application of the eight-year rule.

Law no. 127/1997 first introduced limited access to public and private universities, leaving the Ministry of Universities to set the numbers without statutory criteria. The Constitutional Court (judgment no. 383/1998) upheld the provision, holding that ministerial discretion was bounded by the legal framework and by EU directives requiring adequate educational standards. Parliament then enacted Law no. 264/1999, requiring the Ministry to fix quotas for Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Architecture and Nursing on the two criteria already mentioned. In 2009 the Antitrust Authority criticised the Dentistry quota as based solely on public-sector demand, thereby artificially restricting supply, inflating fees and involving professional bodies with a vested interest. Domestic courts have repeatedly confirmed that the primary criterion is university capacity (necessary for scientifically adequate, theory-plus-practice training) and that society’s needs are merely secondary; EU law does not prohibit numeri clausi and leaves States free to choose the means of ensuring minimum training standards.

Admission is by an 80-question multiple-choice test drawn from the high-school syllabus (general culture, biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics). The applicants maintained that these arrangements pursued illegitimate aims and were disproportionate, particularly given their professional experience or repeated attempts.

001-119969:
The case originated in an application against Russia by OOO ‘Vesti’ (a limited liability company serving as publisher and editorial board of the Gubernskie Vesti, Kirov newspaper) and its editor-in-chief Sergey Ukhov. On 16 August 2002 the newspaper published Ukhov’s article (under a pen-name) criticising a press conference held by Mr P., the Chief Federal Inspector for the Kirov Region, together with the city’s mayor. The article mocked the cultural project “Kirov, cultural capital of the Volga region” and quoted unnamed businessmen who had been “pestered” with sponsorship requests. They refused, some because they wanted no part in P.’s “political games” and others because they feared their money “might be wasted on the lovers of the collector of funds rather than spent on cultural events.”

P. sued the editorial board and the anonymous author for defamation under Article 152 of the Civil Code. He claimed the final sentence identified him as the collector, implied he was capable of embezzlement and alleged he had lovers, thereby damaging his honour, dignity and professional reputation. He sought a retraction in wording he himself drafted (apology, promise to discipline the author, undertaking to obey media law) plus non-pecuniary damages.

On 13 September 2002 the Leninskiy District Court, sitting as a single judge (Judge S.), refused an adjournment requested because Ukhov (the only person who knew the author’s identity and the article’s background) was on leave. It held that the article as a whole, and other local papers’ interpretation of it, showed the impugned sentence referred to P. The defendants had produced no proof of truth. The court ordered the editorial board (later “rectified” of its own motion, without hearing the parties, to the company OOO ‘Vesti’) to pay 20 000 roubles plus costs and to publish P.’s retraction immediately. Enforcement began at once; the retraction appeared on 20 September.

The claim against the author was then resumed. Ukhov, now identified, objected to Judge S. on the ground that the judge had already formed a view in the first judgment; lay assessors rejected the objection. On 3 October the same court found that the article “read as a whole” and third-party newspaper reports established that the statements concerned P., were untrue and damaging, and that Ukhov had failed to prove their truth. He was ordered to pay 2 500 roubles.

Both applicants appealed, arguing that the sentence did not name or concern P., that it merely reported businessmen’s reservations, that the hearing had been unfairly rushed, and that Judge S.’s participation in the second case predetermined the outcome. The Kirov Regional Court joined the appeals. On 24 December 2002 it quashed the original rectification order because it had been issued in the parties’ absence, but upheld a later identical order as a mere clerical correction. It confirmed that the District Court had correctly analysed title, structure and content and had rightly placed the burden of proving truth on the defendants. It held that severance of the claims and the presence of counsel had not violated procedural rights. It nevertheless deleted from the retraction the apology and disciplinary promise (neither of which had a basis in Russian law) and reduced the company’s award to 10 000 roubles. An amended retraction was published in January 2003. The company was later declared insolvent.

The applicants complained that the defamation judgments violated their freedom of expression (Article 10) by treating journalistic reporting of third-party concerns about a public official as unproven facts, and that the proceedings themselves were unfair (Article 6) because of the refusal of an adjournment, the same judge’s participation, the ex-parte substitution of defendant and the predetermined outcome.

The ECtHR case OOO ‘Vesti’ and Ukhov v. Russia (no. 21724/03) concerned a Kirov newspaper publisher (first applicant, a State-founded LLC whose main activity was issuing Gubernskie Vesti) and its editor-in-chief Sergey Ukhov (second applicant, also the article’s author under a pen-name). They alleged violations of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression) arising from domestic defamation findings against a critical 16 August 2002 article, and of Article 6 (fair trial) due to procedural defects in those proceedings.

The article, headlined “The Chief Federal Inspector has brought the media to its knees. But not the businessmen,” covered a press conference by Mr P. (Chief Federal Inspector for Kirov Region) and the Kirov mayor on media coverage of the “Kirov, cultural capital of the Volga region for 2002” project. It criticised the events’ cultural value, ironised about Mr P.’s role, quoted him complaining of insufficient funds and local businesses’ reluctance to sponsor (allegedly for lack of the Governor’s endorsement), and reported businessmen’s views that they had been “pestered” with sponsorship “offers.” The final sentence stated that some businessmen feared their money “might be wasted on the lovers of the collector of funds rather than spent on cultural events.”

On 30 August 2002 Mr P. sued the newspaper’s editorial board and author Semyon Volkov for defamation under Article 152 of the Civil Code. He claimed the last paragraph falsely portrayed him as collector and distributor of project funds capable of embezzlement and as having lovers, thereby damaging his honour, dignity and professional reputation. He sought a retraction (including an apology, a promise to discipline the author and an undertaking to obey media law) plus non-pecuniary damages.

The Leninskiy District Court first heard the claim against the editorial board on 13 September 2002 before Judge S., refusing an adjournment sought because Ukhov (the only person who knew the author’s identity and the relevant facts) was on leave. Counsel argued the statements did not identify Mr P. as collector (the Town Administration collected the funds). The court nevertheless held that the article as a whole, and especially its last sentence, referred to Mr P., contained unproven false information implying waste of funds on lovers, and awarded 20 000 RUB damages plus costs; it ordered immediate publication of Mr P.’s drafted retraction. Enforcement began at once. An interim decision of 19 September (issued without the parties) later “rectified” the defendant’s name from the unregistered editorial board of Gubernskie Vesti to the first applicant LLC. The newspaper published the retraction on 20 September.

Once Ukhov identified himself as author, separate proceedings against him were heard on 2–3 October 2002 by Judge S. sitting with two lay assessors. An objection to Judge S.’s impartiality (on the ground that he had already decided the identical issues against the publisher) was rejected. The court again found that the article as a whole and other local newspapers’ interpretations showed the last sentence targeted Mr P., that the statements accused him of spending public money on lovers, and that Ukhov had failed to prove their truth; it awarded 2 500 RUB damages.

On appeal the Kirov Regional Court joined the cases, quashed the 19 September rectification for having been made in the parties’ absence but upheld a subsequent identical rectification, and confirmed the first-instance judgments on the merits. It held that the District Court had correctly analysed title, structure and content and had properly placed the burden of proving truth on the defendants. It nevertheless found the required apology, disciplinary promise and law-abiding undertaking had no legal basis, reduced the first applicant’s damages to 10 000 RUB, and ordered an amended retraction (published 14 January 2003). The first applicant was later declared insolvent and dissolved.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints that the statements were not of and concerning Mr P., constituted value judgments or reported third-party opinions rather than verifiable facts, concerned a public figure and a matter of public interest (funding of a cultural project), and that the proceedings were unfair because of the un-adjourned hearing, the same judge’s successive determinations, the ex-parte “rectification” that in substance substituted a defendant, the unlawful immediate-enforcement and apology orders, and the overall failure to examine whether the impugned sentence was actually directed at Mr P.

The case originated in an application by the limited-liability company OOO ‘Vesti’ (the first applicant, publisher of the Gubernskie Vesti newspaper) and its editor-in-chief Sergey Ukhov (the second applicant) against Russia. They alleged a violation of their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention arising from defamation proceedings, as well as unfairness in those proceedings under Article 6.

The first applicant, founded in 1997 by the Kirov Regional Government’s State Property Department, published the Gubernskie Vesti, Kirov newspaper, of which Ukhov was also editor-in-chief. On 16 August 2002 the newspaper carried an article written by Ukhov under the pen-name Semyon Volkov, headed “The Chief Federal Inspector has brought the media to its knees. But not the businessmen.” The piece criticised a regional cultural project and a press conference given by Mr P., the Chief Federal Inspector for the Kirov Region. It quoted businessmen as saying that Mr P.’s office had “pestered” them with sponsorship “offers.” The final sentence recorded their concern that money “might be wasted on the lovers of the collector of funds rather than spent on cultural events.”

On 30 August 2002 Mr P. sued the newspaper’s editorial board and the unidentified author for defamation. He claimed the last paragraph falsely portrayed him as the collector of funds who might embezzle them on lovers, thereby damaging his honour, dignity and professional reputation. He demanded a retraction in wording he himself supplied (including an apology and a promise of disciplinary action) plus compensation.

The Leninskiy District Court of Kirov first heard the claim against the board on 13 September 2002, refusing an adjournment sought because Ukhov (the only person who knew the author’s identity) was on leave. The court found the statements referred to Mr P., were untrue and unproven, and ordered the board to pay 20,000 roubles and to publish the retraction immediately. It later rectified the defendant’s name from the unregistered editorial board to the first applicant company. Enforcement followed at once; the retraction appeared on 20 September 2002.

Proceedings against Ukhov (now identified as the author) were heard by the same judge sitting with two lay assessors. An objection of bias was rejected. On 3 October 2002 the court again held that the article as a whole, and similar reporting in other newspapers, showed that the impugned sentence concerned Mr P., accused him of spending public money on lovers, and had not been proved true. Ukhov was ordered to pay 2,500 roubles.

Both judgments were appealed. The Kirov Regional Court joined the cases, quashed the original rectification order for procedural irregularity but upheld a later identical order, and confirmed the substance of both defamation judgments. It found that the district court had correctly linked the statements to Mr P. and that the applicants had failed to prove their truth. It nevertheless deleted the apology and other extra-legal elements from the retraction, reduced the company’s award to 10,000 roubles, and held that the order for immediate enforcement had been unlawful. An amended retraction was published on 14 January 2003. The first applicant was later dissolved in insolvency proceedings.

The domestic courts treated the statements as factual assertions of criminal and immoral conduct rather than value judgments or reports of others’ opinions, placed the burden of proof on the defendants, and proceeded despite objections concerning the identity of the proper defendant, the refusal of an adjournment, and the same judge’s prior determination of the identical issues. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints of an unjustified interference with freedom of expression and of procedural unfairness.
001-119678:
The case of Radu v. Germany (Application no. 20084/07) concerns a German national, Fredy Radu (born 1962), who alleged that his continued detention in a psychiatric hospital violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty). This followed domestic findings that he did not suffer from any condition diminishing or excluding criminal responsibility, as required to justify such placement.

In 1983, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court convicted Radu of two counts of murder (stabbing his girlfriend’s parents 25 times) and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment, finding full criminal responsibility. He was released in 1987. In 1995, the Gießen Regional Court convicted him of homicide (stabbing his former partner eight times after she began a new relationship) and sentenced him to eight-and-a-half years’ imprisonment plus placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. Experts found diminished responsibility (Article 21) due to a profound consciousness disorder and a serious personality disorder with violent outbursts; the court held that he was likely to kill again in similar relational crises.

Radu served four years in prison before transfer to Haina Psychiatric Hospital in 1998. The hospital’s medical director later concluded that Radu had never had a persisting pathological mental disorder (merely an “accentuated personality” within normal range, not a WHO-defined personality disorder) but remained highly likely to reoffend in a relationship crisis due to lack of therapeutic motivation. He was returned to prison in 2000 to complete his sentence. In 2002, the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal upheld refusal to suspend the remainder of the sentence or terminate the psychiatric placement. An expert found no serious mental abnormality (Article 20) and no medical justification for hospital detention. The court held that the original order rested on an erroneous legal qualification of correctly established facts, which execution courts could not correct without violating the constitutional principle of finality of judgments.

Since October 2003, after fully serving his prison term, Radu has been detained in psychiatric hospitals (initially Hanau, later Riedstadt). In 2006 review proceedings under Article 67e of the Criminal Code, the Gießen Regional Court refused to suspend the placement or grant probation. Experts (including B.) confirmed no pathological or serious mental abnormality, only a non-pathological personality disorder with emotional instability and uncontrolled violence; however, he remained disposed to similar offences if released. Retrospective preventive detention (Article 66b) was legally unavailable (no new evidence of particular dangerousness; the 1983 conviction was too old). The court distinguished this legal-qualification error from a factual error (which would permit termination under Article 67d § 6, as the person never had a qualifying condition and need not undergo treatment independent of guilt). Correcting the legal error would breach finality; continued detention was necessary and proportionate given the risk of a fourth killing.

The Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal dismissed Radu’s appeal, confirming that Article 67d § 6 (codifying prior case-law) applied only to factual errors or subsequent recovery, not legal misclassification of correctly diagnosed facts. The applicant remained dangerous, having killed three people, and had not learned to control his conduct. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear his complaint (19 October 2006), finding the lower courts’ application of ordinary law non-arbitrary. Even considering the right to liberty, constitutional law did not require applying Article 67d § 6 to legal errors; finality (legal certainty) competed with material justice, a balance for the legislature.

Subsequent annual reviews (2007–2012) consistently continued detention on identical grounds: no qualifying disorder existed, yet personality traits created a high risk of capital offences in conflicts, and Radu lacked motivation for therapy (though hospitals remained obliged to offer it). Retrospective preventive detention remained unavailable. Radu thus remains confined solely on the basis of the unappealable 1995 legal qualification, despite unanimous expert consensus that the statutory conditions for psychiatric placement were never met.

The case of Radu v. Germany (Application no. 20084/07) concerns a German national born in 1962 who alleged that his continued detention in a psychiatric hospital after serving his prison sentence violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, as experts had established that he never suffered from a pathological mental disorder diminishing his criminal responsibility.

In 1983 the applicant was convicted of two murders (stabbing his girlfriend’s parents) and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment on a finding of full criminal responsibility; he was released in 1987. In 1995 the Gießen Regional Court convicted him of homicide for stabbing his former partner eight times and sentenced him to eight years and six months’ imprisonment plus placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. The court, relying on experts, found diminished responsibility under Article 21 due to a “profound consciousness disorder” arising from a serious personality disorder with violent outbursts, and a risk of further killings in similar relationship conflicts. The sentence was mitigated accordingly.

After serving four years in prison the applicant was transferred to a psychiatric hospital in 1998. Subsequent reviews by hospital staff and independent experts (including in 2001) concluded that he had never suffered from a persisting pathological mental disorder as defined by the WHO or required by Article 20 of the Criminal Code. He was an “accentuated personality” with a non-pathological disposition to uncontrolled violence in crises and lacked motivation for therapy, making reoffending likely. He was therefore returned to prison in 2000 to finish his sentence.

From October 2003, after completing his prison term, he has remained in psychiatric hospitals. In 2002 the Frankfurt Court of Appeal refused to terminate the placement, holding that the sentencing court’s error was one of legal qualification of correctly established facts and could not be corrected by execution courts without violating the finality of judgments.

In the 2006 review proceedings at issue, the Gießen Regional Court (after consulting expert B., who confirmed the absence of any pathological disorder or “serious mental abnormality” but a continuing risk of similar offences) declined to suspend the order. It held that Article 67d § 6 of the Criminal Code (requiring termination when the conditions for placement no longer persist) applied only to factual errors by the sentencing court, not legal ones; retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b was unavailable. Continued detention was necessary and proportionate given the risk of a fourth killing. The Frankfurt Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 16 June 2006, reiterating that the error was purely legal and thus not remediable under Article 67d § 6 (which merely codified prior case-law limited to factual mistakes). The Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain the constitutional complaint on 19 October 2006, finding the courts’ approach non-arbitrary and stressing that the legislature, not the courts, must balance legal certainty (finality) against material justice.

Later annual reviews (2007–2012) uniformly continued the detention. Experts consistently found no qualifying mental abnormality, only a high risk of capital offences in conflicts and insufficient motivation for therapy (which hospitals remained obliged to offer). These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that his detention lacked a lawful basis, as the statutory conditions for psychiatric confinement had never been met.

The applicant, Fredy Radu (born 1962), a German national, alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention due to his continued detention in a psychiatric hospital after fully serving a prison sentence. Domestic courts had determined that he did not suffer from a mental condition diminishing his criminal responsibility, yet they refused to terminate the placement ordered in 1995.

In 1983, Radu was convicted of two counts of murder (committed at age 19) and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment, which he served with full criminal responsibility; he was released in 1987. In 1995, the Gießen Regional Court convicted him of homicide for stabbing his former partner to death in 1994 and sentenced him to eight years and six months’ imprisonment plus placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. The court found diminished criminal responsibility under Article 21 due to a profound consciousness disorder and a serious personality disorder marked by violent outbursts. Experts concluded he was likely to reoffend lethally in similar relationship conflicts. The sentence was mitigated accordingly, and the judgment became final.

Radu served four years in prison before transfer to Haina Psychiatric Hospital in 1998. Subsequent reviews found the placement erroneous: he lacked a persisting pathological mental disorder (being merely an “accentuated personality” without a WHO-defined personality disorder) and showed insufficient motivation for therapy. He was retransferred to prison in 2000 to complete his sentence. In 2002, the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal upheld non-termination of the hospital order, accepting an expert’s view that Radu had never had a serious mental abnormality under Article 20. The court treated the 1995 finding as an uncorrectable legal misqualification of correctly established facts, protected by the finality of judgments. After completing his prison term in October 2003, Radu remained detained in psychiatric hospitals (initially Hanau, later others including Riedstadt).

In the 2006 review proceedings under Article 67e, the Gießen Regional Court declined to suspend the order or grant probation. Hospital staff and expert B. confirmed no pathological disorder existed (only emotional instability and impulsive violence, insufficient for Article 20), but a high risk of further killings persisted due to unlearned conflict-management skills. Retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b was unavailable (no new evidence of particular dangerousness; the 1983 conviction was too old). The court held that Article 67d § 6 (allowing termination if conditions for placement no longer persist) applied only to factual errors or subsequent changes, not legal misqualifications; correcting the latter would breach res judicata. Continued detention was deemed necessary and proportionate given the risk of a fourth killing.

The Court of Appeal dismissed Radu’s appeal in June 2006, reiterating that the 1995 error was purely legal (the sentencing court had failed to require a persisting condition) and thus uncorrectable in execution proceedings. Article 67d § 6 merely codified prior case-law excluding legal errors. The applicant’s unchanged dangerousness (three prior killings, no behavioural change) rendered detention proportionate. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit his complaint in October 2006, finding the lower courts’ approach non-arbitrary and consistent with the constitutional balance between legal certainty and justice.

Subsequent annual reviews (2007–2012) consistently reached the same conclusions: experts uniformly found no qualifying mental disorder, only personality traits creating a high reoffending risk in crises, plus the applicant’s lack of therapy motivation. Courts stressed hospitals’ duty to offer treatment and the applicant’s need to engage, while rejecting termination. Retrospective preventive detention remained unavailable. Radu has remained detained solely under the 1995 psychiatric-hospital order.
001-120966:
The applicant, an Austrian national born in 1941, was employed as a photographer at the US embassy in Vienna from 1978 under an indefinite contract from 1981. After accidents in 1983 and 1987, she was classified as disabled under Austrian law. The embassy dismissed her in September 1987, but Austrian labour courts later voided the dismissal for lack of the required authority approval, rejecting the US claim of state immunity on the ground that employment contracts constitute acta iure gestionis. The Supreme Court upheld this in 1990. The applicant thus retained a valid employment contract, though the embassy refused to utilise her services.

During her employment the applicant self-registered for Austrian social security under a statutory exception for extraterritorial employers and paid both the employee’s and employer’s contributions. The United States reimbursed the employer’s share (initially 53 per cent, later 55 per cent of the total) pursuant to embassy administrative notices until 1987 or 1988. After the dismissal was declared void she obtained a labour-court judgment awarding salary arrears for September 1988–June 1995; the United States paid approximately EUR 269,000 in 1996, corresponding to gross salary (from which employee contributions remained payable). The embassy’s lawyer simultaneously declared that the payment implied no acceptance of Austrian jurisdiction and that any further claims would be met with diplomatic immunities. Subsequent salary claims for later periods failed because the United States refused service of process, a refusal treated by Austrian courts as an immune sovereign act (later found by the European Court to violate Article 6).

In 1999 the competent ministry issued a declaratory decision confirming that the applicant remained an employee for social-security purposes by virtue of the still-valid contract. The Vienna Health Insurance Board then demanded payment of both employee’s and employer’s contributions for the 1988–1995 period already remunerated. After objections and a transfer of jurisdiction, the Regional Governor in June 2000 ordered her to pay ATS 1 088 677 (EUR 79 117). She paid the employee’s share (EUR 36 528) but appealed, arguing that embassy notices constituted an agreement to bear the employer’s share and that the special rule of section 53(3)(a) of the General Social Security Act was inapplicable or unconstitutional.

The Federal Ministry initially allowed the appeal in 2001, holding the embassy obliged to pay the employer’s contributions. The Health Insurance Board challenged that decision. In March 2005 the Administrative Court quashed the Ministry’s ruling, applying section 53(3)(a): where an extraterritorial employer fails to pay contributions the employee must bear the entire amount. The Ministry thereupon issued a fresh decision in June 2005 repeating the order for EUR 79 177. The Constitutional Court declined to entertain the applicant’s complaint, citing among other things Article 29 of the 1972 European Convention on State Immunity (which excludes social-security proceedings) and the practical impossibility of enforcing payment against an extraterritorial employer.

Parallel attempts by the applicant to recover the employer’s share from the United States were equally unsuccessful: service of summons was refused and treated as immune. She terminated the employment upon reaching pensionable age in 2002 and applied for an old-age pension.

The relevant Austrian provision, section 53(3)(a) of the General Social Security Act, was introduced in 1962 precisely to cover the rare cases of non-paying extraterritorial employers who cannot be compelled to comply with domestic law; it therefore shifts the whole contribution burden (normally shared and collected from the employer) onto the employee. The applicant contended that this imposition of the employer’s share constituted an unjustified and disproportionate interference with her possessions.

The applicant, Roswitha Wallishauser, an Austrian national born in 1941 and living in Vienna, worked as a photographer at the US Embassy in Vienna from March 1978 under a contract of indefinite duration from 1981. After a 1983 accident, she qualified for protection under the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act. The embassy dismissed her in September 1987 following a work-related accident that March. Austrian courts later voided the dismissal, as it required prior authority approval under the Act; the US immunity objection (acta iure imperii vs. acta iure gestionis) was not maintained, so the employment contract remained valid. The embassy, however, refused her services.

During employment, the applicant self-registered for social security under section 35(4)(a) of the General Social Security Act (due to the employer's extraterritorial status) and paid both employee and employer contributions to the Vienna Health Insurance Board until August 1988. The US reimbursed the employer's share (initially 53%, then 55% of totals per embassy notices) until March 1987 or August 1988.

She obtained salary arrears for 1 September 1988 to 30 June 1995 via a 1995 Vienna Labour and Social Court judgment (upheld despite US immunity claims). The US paid ATS 3.7 million (approx. EUR 269,000), covering gross salary including her employee's social security contributions (which she remitted to the Board). The US lawyer's letter stated this implied no acceptance of the judgments and that the contract was terminated.

A 1999 Federal Ministry decision confirmed her continued employee status (section 4 of the Act) due to the valid contract, thus requiring social security affiliation.

The Health Insurance Board then ordered her to pay both employer and employee contributions for 1988–1995 (ATS 1,088,676.76 / EUR 79,117.22), citing section 53(3)(a): the employee pays the full amount if an extraterritorial employer (like the US) does not contribute. She paid the employee's share (ATS 502,631.67 / EUR 36,527.70) but appealed.

The Federal Ministry initially allowed the appeal in 2001, holding the embassy obliged to pay the employer's share based on its 1982 reimbursement undertaking. The Administrative Court quashed this in 2005 (joining complaints), ruling section 53(3)(a) applied regardless of any reimbursement promise, as the US had extraterritorial status and paid nothing. The 1962 provision addressed rare cases of unenforceable contributions from such employers, making the employee the debtor for the full amount (exception to the usual sharing under sections 51(3) and 58(2), where the employer is debtor and deducts the employee's share).

The Ministry then ordered full payment (EUR 79,177.22). The applicant's Constitutional Court complaint (alleging property rights violation via disproportionate burden, discrimination vs. other employees, and unconstitutionality, as public international law treated employment as acta iure gestionis without justification for differential treatment) was refused in 2005 for lack of prospects. The Court cited the 1972 European Convention on State Immunity (Article 29 excluding social security proceedings) and practical extraterritoriality effects.

Parallel proceedings to recover the employer's share from the US stalled: the US refused to serve summons (deemed acta iure imperii), preventing default judgments (Supreme Court 2001). These were stayed pending the Administrative Court ruling and later noted as unservable.

The applicant alleged this full-contribution imposition (for salary already received) disproportionately burdened her possessions, violating peaceful enjoyment thereof, especially as recovery from the US was blocked by immunity. She reached pensionable age in 2002 and applied for an old-age pension.

The case of Balakin v. Russia (Application no. 21788/06) concerned a Russian national, Sergey Vyacheslavovich Balakin, who alleged a violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, he claimed that domestic courts, by declining to examine his complaint about local authorities’ failure to provide his family with additional social housing, had deprived him of his right of access to a court.

The applicant, a municipal school employee in Orel, lived with his wife (a librarian) and their two children in a privately owned two-room apartment measuring 27.9 square metres. Their daughter suffered from severe diabetes and was classified as handicapped. In 1988 the family was placed on the municipal “general” waiting list for improved social housing on account of sub-standard living conditions. From 1997 the applicant repeatedly petitioned the Orel authorities for better accommodation, citing his daughter’s illness. In 1999 the family was transferred to the “first-priority” waiting list reserved for households with disabled children.

In July 2004 the applicant met senior regional and municipal officials, who allegedly promised a three-room flat in the town centre. The following month the Housing Authority instead offered an old three-room apartment in a remote suburb; the applicant rejected it because of poor transport links and distance from medical facilities, pharmacies and relatives. On 5 December 2005 he lodged a claim with the Sovetskiy District Court of Orel, complaining of prolonged official inaction. He asked the court to order the municipality to allocate a three-room apartment (with privatisation rights) in exchange for the family’s existing dwelling and to award non-pecuniary damages. The statement of claim invoked Soviet and Russian decrees that placed families with diabetic children on first-priority lists, the 1993 Constitution, the UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child and the Convention itself. It emphasised that the family had waited nine years, that living conditions were harming the daughter’s health, and that earlier official promises had not been honoured.

The District Court required the applicant to reformulate his pleadings. He then sought recognition of his right to additional housing and an order compelling the authorities to provide a three-room apartment in a specified central district. At a preliminary hearing on 9 February 2006 the applicant confirmed that he was seeking housing “out of turn” on the basis of the lengthy delay, his child’s deteriorating health and repeated official assurances. The court discontinued the proceedings for lack of jurisdiction. Relying on a 1987 USSR Supreme Court ruling and the Russian Code of Civil Procedure, it held that ordinary courts could entertain housing claims only where a person was entitled to “extraordinary” (immediate) allocation or where a statutory time-limit had been breached. The applicant was merely on a first-priority list; neither the 1996 Government Decree nor the Law on Social Protection of Disabled Persons prescribed any time-limit for first-priority allocations. Such matters therefore fell exclusively within the competence of administrative bodies.

On 15 March 2006 the Orel Regional Court upheld the decision, reiterating that the courts lacked competence over ordinary or first-priority social-housing allocations and that the applicant did not fall into the “extraordinary” category. Subsequent supervisory-review applications were unsuccessful. In January 2007 the authorities invited the applicant to apply for a cash grant instead of housing in kind; he did not do so. The family remained without new accommodation.

Domestic law (the 1983 Soviet Housing Code, the 2004 Russian Housing Code, Decree No. 330 of 1983 and Government Decree No. 901 of 1996) created waiting lists but imposed no deadlines for first-priority housing. Only persons entitled to extraordinary allocation (for example, those whose dwellings were unfit or who suffered from certain severe chronic illnesses, a list that excluded diabetes) could compel immediate provision through the courts. The Code of Civil Procedure and Supreme Court guidance confirmed that allocation of ordinary or first-priority social housing was an administrative, not a judicial, function.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the courts’ refusal to hear the merits of his claim constituted a denial of access to court under Article 6.

**Case of Balakin v. Russia (Application no. 21788/06), ECtHR First Section Judgment of 4 July 2013 (final 9 December 2013)**

The applicant, Sergey Vyacheslavovich Balakin, a Russian national working at a municipal school in Orel (his wife a librarian), alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention. He claimed that domestic courts’ refusal to examine his complaint about the local authorities’ failure to provide additional social housing deprived him of his right of access to a court.

The family owned a two-room apartment of 27.9 square metres shared with their two children. Their daughter suffered from severe (type 1) diabetes, a condition listed in USSR Ministry of Health Decree No. 330 (1983) as entitling families to “first-priority” status for improved housing. In 1988 the family was placed on Orel’s general waiting list for those in need of better housing. From 1997 the applicant made repeated requests citing his daughter’s illness. In 1999 they were placed on the local “first-priority” list. In July 2004 officials reportedly promised a new three-room flat in the town centre, but the family was later offered an old three-room flat in a distant suburb; the applicant declined it because of poor transport links, distance from medical facilities, a pharmacy and relatives, and the effect of cramped conditions on his daughter’s health. He had waited nine years without allocation.

On 5 December 2005 the applicant sued the local authorities in the Sovetskiy District Court of Orel. He sought an order requiring them to provide a three-room apartment (with privatisation rights) in exchange for his existing flat, plus compensation for non-pecuniary damage caused by prolonged inaction. He relied on Decree No. 330, Government Decree No. 901 (1996) placing families with disabled children on separate first-priority lists, the Constitution, the UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child and the Convention. The court invited him to reformulate the claim. He then asked the court to recognise his right to additional housing and to compel the authorities to provide a three-room apartment in a specified area.

At a preliminary hearing on 9 February 2006 the applicant confirmed he sought housing “out of turn” after more than nine years of inaction, deteriorating health of his child and unfulfilled promises; he acknowledged there was no statutory time-limit for families with disabled children. The District Court discontinued the proceedings for lack of jurisdiction under Article 134 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It cited a 1987 USSR Supreme Court Plenary Ruling (as amended) holding that courts could hear disputes about “extraordinary” (immediate) housing allocation or cases where a statutory time-limit had been missed, but not ordinary claims by persons on waiting lists for improved living conditions. The applicant was on the general and first-priority lists (and first on his employer’s list) but not entitled to extraordinary provision. The 1996 Decree created first-priority lists without time-limits; the Law on Social Protection of Disabled Persons likewise set none. The Orel Regional Court upheld the decision on 15 March 2006, confirming courts lacked competence over social-housing allocation except for extraordinary claims. Supervisory-review complaints failed; the applicant again confirmed his list status.

In January 2007 the authorities invited him to apply for a financial housing grant; he did not. No new housing had been provided by the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.

Domestic law (old 1983 Housing Code, 1996 Decree and 2004 Housing Code) established waiting lists that conferred only an order of priority when housing became available, not a right to allocation within a fixed period. “Extraordinary” entitlement (immediate allocation) applied only to specified severe chronic illnesses (diabetes was not included after 2006) or other narrow categories. Courts could review administrative inaction under the Constitution and Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but the housing-specific rulings confined their role in allocation disputes to extraordinary cases.

These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 6 violation: the courts’ blanket refusal to examine the merits of a claim concerning prolonged failure to honour first-priority status and official promises, despite the existence of a civil right to housing under domestic law and constitutional guarantees of judicial protection against official inaction.

The case of Balakin v. Russia (Application no. 21788/06) originated in a complaint by Sergey Vyacheslavovich Balakin, a Russian national employed at a municipal school in Orel, whose wife worked as a librarian. The couple owned a two-room apartment of 27.9 square metres, which they shared with their two children. Their daughter suffered from severe diabetes and was handicapped.

In 1988, the family was placed on Orel’s general waiting list for residents with sub-standard housing entitled to more spacious social housing. From 1997, Balakin submitted numerous requests to local authorities seeking improved accommodation on account of his daughter’s illness. In 1999, the family was transferred to the first-priority list for persons needing better living conditions due to the disability. In July 2004, after meetings with the regional governor and the head of the municipal Housing Authority, the family was offered an old three-room flat in a suburb; Balakin declined it owing to its remoteness from medical facilities, poor transport links and distance from relatives.

On 5 December 2005, Balakin lodged a claim with the Sovetskiy District Court of Orel alleging inaction by the local authorities in failing to provide better social housing. Invoking a 1983 USSR Ministry of Health decree listing diabetes as conferring a first-priority right to additional space and a 1996 Government decree requiring families with disabled children already on the general list to be placed on a separate first-priority list, he asked the court to order the allocation of a three-room apartment (with privatisation rights) in exchange for the existing two-room flat, plus compensation for non-pecuniary damage caused by nine years of delay and the adverse effect on his daughter’s health. After the court invited him to reformulate the claim, he sought recognition of his right to additional housing and an order requiring the authorities to provide a three-room apartment in a specified area of town.

At a preliminary hearing on 9 February 2006, the District Court discontinued the proceedings for lack of jurisdiction. Relying on Article 134 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a 1987 USSR Supreme Court Plenary Ruling (as amended), it held that courts could examine only certain housing disputes, including those of persons entitled to “extraordinary” (immediate) provision of housing where a statutory time-limit had been missed. The applicant, however, was merely on the general and first-priority waiting lists; neither the 1996 decree nor the Law on Social Protection of Disabled Persons prescribed any time-limit for allocation to families with disabled children. Consequently the claim fell outside the court’s competence and within that of other State bodies.

The Orel Regional Court upheld the decision on 15 March 2006, confirming that courts lacked jurisdiction over ordinary social-housing allocations and that the applicant’s entitlement was only first-priority, not extraordinary. Supervisory-review applications were unsuccessful. In January 2007 the authorities invited Balakin to apply for a financial housing grant, which he did not do. No new housing had been provided by the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention, namely that the domestic courts’ refusal to examine the substance of the housing complaint deprived the applicant of his right of access to a court.
001-120062:
The applicant, Rafał Kostecki (born 1974), was arrested in Poland on 29 October 2003 on suspicion of drug trafficking within an organised criminal group and remanded in custody. He fled a psychiatric hospital on 1 August 2004 during observation. Recaptured in Belgium on 23 September 2005 pursuant to a European arrest warrant, he was extradited to Poland on 30 November 2005 and re-detained. A bill of indictment dated 15 December 2005 charged him with trafficking a significant quantity of drugs, leading an organised armed group, attempted armed robbery, arms trafficking and escape. Detention was repeatedly extended. Trial began on 13 February 2006 before the Białystok District Court.

Witness Ł.K. could not be located; police inquiries established he resided in England at an unknown address with no known return date. On 10 July 2006 the court, over the applicant’s objection, ordered his investigation statements (and those of M.K.) read out under Article 391 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the witnesses were abroad and unavailable. The applicant admitted selling Ł.K. only small quantities of drugs, described the statements as untrue and requested an opportunity to question him. He later supplied an Irish address and, with eventual prosecutorial support, sought examination via international judicial assistance; the court refused on 15 September 2006 because the statements had already been read. A further request that a probation officer (who supervised Ł.K.) locate him was likewise dismissed as immaterial. Statements of K.M., who was not at his registered address, were also read out; the applicant again contested their veracity. Live testimony from D.B. and Ł.B. (who identified the applicant as their sole supplier of dozens of transactions) was received and the applicant was permitted to question them. A request to call thirteen additional witnesses on drug quantities and alternative suppliers was rejected as irrelevant.

On 12 December 2006 the District Court convicted the applicant of trafficking significant quantities of drugs (relying principally on the concordant, detailed testimonies of Ł.K., D.B., Ł.B. and K.M.), trespass (reclassified from armed robbery), arms trafficking and escape, imposing a cumulative five-year sentence; it acquitted him of leading an organised group. It treated the unread statements as credible despite the witnesses’ absence and deemed the applicant’s late, limited admissions self-serving. The Białystok Regional Court (24 September 2007) quashed the escape conviction (absent from the European arrest warrant), increased the drug-trafficking term to five years six months and the cumulative sentence to six years six months, and otherwise upheld the judgment, finding that reasonable efforts had been made to secure Ł.K., that Article 391 had been properly applied and that the additional witnesses were unnecessary. The Supreme Court (24 June 2008) quashed the trespass conviction on the same warrant ground and dismissed the remainder of the cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded, noting that the witness and procedural complaints had already been considered.

Separately, detention-centre records confirmed that the applicant’s correspondence with his lawyer had been opened on 20 March and 4 September 2006. The application to the European Court was lodged on 22 December 2008.

The ECHR case of Kostecki v. Poland (Appl. no. 14932/09) concerns Rafał Kostecki (b. 1974), a Polish national, and his criminal trial for serious offences. Arrested on 29 October 2003 on suspicion of drug trafficking in an organised group, he was remanded in custody. He escaped a psychiatric hospital on 1 August 2004 during observation. Recaptured in Belgium on 23 September 2005 via European Arrest Warrant, he was extradited to Poland on 30 November 2005 and re-detained. The 15 December 2005 indictment charged trafficking in significant drug quantities, leading an organised armed group, attempted armed robbery, arms trafficking and escape. Detention was repeatedly extended (to June 2007).

Trial opened on 13 February 2006 in the Białystok District Court. Central to the alleged fair-trial issues was witness evidence. Ł.K. could not be summoned (resident in England, address and return unknown). Over objection, the court on 10 July 2006 read his and M.K.’s investigation statements under Article 391 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (witness abroad, return date unknown). Kostecki admitted only small sales to Ł.K., disputed the amounts, and later supplied an Irish address, requesting examination via international judicial assistance. The court refused on 15 September 2006 (statements already read). D.B. and Ł.B. testified in court that Kostecki was their sole supplier in dozens of transactions; he later admitted limited sales to them. On 16 November 2006 K.M.’s statements were likewise read (unlocatable at his residence). A request to locate Ł.K. via his probation officer was refused. A bid to call 13 further witnesses (to contest quantities and exclusivity of supply) was dismissed as irrelevant.

On 12 December 2006 Kostecki was convicted of trafficking significant drug quantities (relying mainly on the “concordant, detailed and complementary” accounts of Ł.K., D.B., Ł.B. and K.M.), reclassified trespass, arms trafficking and escape, and sentenced to five years. He was acquitted of leading the group. The court held the reading of statements lawful and the applicant’s late partial admissions self-serving.

On appeal the Regional Court (24 September 2007) quashed the escape conviction (charge omitted from the EAW) but raised the trafficking sentence to 5½ years and the cumulative term to 6½ years, citing the applicant’s leading role, large quantities, priors and flight. It found no procedural breach: efforts had been made to hear key witnesses, reading was permitted, and the 13 witnesses were irrelevant. Cassation to the Supreme Court (24 June 2008) succeeded only on the trespass count (likewise absent from the EAW); complaints about Ł.K.’s unread statements, unused location methods and the 13 witnesses were rejected as already examined or directed at the first-instance judgment.

Separately, detention-centre records confirmed that two letters from Kostecki’s lawyer were opened on 20 March and 4 September 2006.

These facts underpin the alleged Convention violations: Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) (inability to examine key absent witnesses whose unread statements underpinned the “significant quantity” finding that the applicant only partially admitted, despite unused alternatives such as international assistance) and Article 8 (monitoring of lawyer–client correspondence).
