The case of Kostecki v. Poland (Application no. 14932/09) originated from an application lodged on 22 December 2008 by Polish national Rafał Kostecki (born 1974), represented by lawyer H. Łapiński. It concerned alleged violations of the Convention arising from his criminal trial for serious drug-related and other offences, as well as interference with his legal correspondence while detained.

The applicant was arrested on 29 October 2003 on suspicion of drug trafficking within an organised criminal group and remanded in custody. On 1 August 2004, during psychiatric observation, he fled hospital. He was arrested in Belgium on 23 September 2005 under a European Arrest Warrant, unsuccessfully contested extradition, and was returned to Poland and re-detained on 30 November 2005. A bill of indictment was filed on 15 December 2005 with the Białystok District Court charging him with: (I) trafficking significant quantities of drugs; (II) leading an organised armed criminal group; (III) attempted armed robbery; (IV) arms trafficking; and (V) escaping from hospital.

The trial opened on 13 February 2006. Key witness Ł.K. could not be summoned: police inquiries established he lived in England at an unknown address with no known return date. On 10 July 2006, over the applicant’s objection, the court ordered the reading-out of Ł.K.’s and M.K.’s investigation statements under Article 391 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (allowing this where a witness is abroad or unsummonable). The applicant denied the accuracy of Ł.K.’s statements, admitted only small-quantity sales to him, and requested his address be established so he could put questions. At a later hearing he supplied an Irish address and sought examination via international judicial assistance; the prosecutor initially supported this, but the court dismissed the request on 15 September 2006 because the statements had already been read. Similar reading-out occurred for K.M.’s statements after he could not be located at his residence. The applicant’s request to hear 13 additional witnesses (to show others supplied drugs and to contest quantities) was refused as irrelevant.

Witnesses D.B. and Ł.B. testified in person that the applicant had been their exclusive supplier over dozens of transactions. On 12 December 2006 the District Court convicted the applicant of trafficking significant quantities of drugs (relying principally on the mutually corroborative, detailed testimonies of Ł.K., D.B., Ł.B. and K.M., which it found credible despite two witnesses not appearing), trespass (reclassified from robbery), arms trafficking and escape, imposing a five-year sentence. He was acquitted of leading the group. The court dismissed the applicant’s partial admissions as tactical and unreliable.

The applicant appealed, arguing excessive reliance on unread statements (violating the principle of directness and defence rights), failure to hear the 13 witnesses, and that escape was not listed in the EAW. On 24 September 2007 the Regional Court quashed the escape conviction and discontinued that part of the proceedings (EAW limitation), but increased the drug-trafficking sentence to 5 years 6 months (citing the applicant’s leading role, large quantities, prior convictions and flight) for a cumulative 6 years 6 months. It upheld the evidence assessment, finding sufficient efforts to hear witnesses and no breach of Article 391 or defence rights; quantities had been assessed conservatively.

The applicant’s cassation appeal to the Supreme Court repeated the witness complaints (including that Ł.K. was under probation supervision, so could have been located or examined abroad) and challenged the trespass conviction (also absent from the EAW). On 24 June 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the trespass conviction and discontinued that part, but dismissed the remainder as manifestly ill-founded, holding that witness issues had already been properly rejected on appeal and could not be re-litigated against the first-instance judgment.

Separately, detention-centre authorities confirmed that the applicant’s correspondence with his lawyer had been interfered with on 20 March and 4 September 2006.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: principally Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) (fair trial and right to examine witnesses), given the trial courts’ heavy reliance on unread statements of key incriminating witnesses (especially Ł.K.) without adequate efforts to secure their attendance or alternative examination, and the refusal of other evidence; and Article 8 (respect for correspondence) arising from the documented interference with lawyer communications. Domestic law (Article 391 CCP) permitted the readings, but the applicant contended the courts had not exhausted available means and had thereby undermined confrontation rights essential to a fair trial. The drug-trafficking conviction turned on the contested “significant quantity” findings drawn from those statements.
001-122365:
The case of Węgrzynowski and Smolczewski v. Poland originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by two Polish lawyers from Katowice. They alleged that Polish courts had failed to protect their rights to private life and reputation (under Article 8 of the Convention) after a defamatory newspaper article remained publicly accessible online.

On 8 May 2002 the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the applicants’ civil claim under Articles 23 and 24 of the Civil Code. Journalists working for the daily Rzeczpospolita had published an article accusing the applicants of enriching themselves through shady political deals while acting as liquidators of bankrupt state-owned companies, thereby obtaining unjustified benefits at public expense. The court found that the journalists had not contacted the applicants, had relied largely on gossip and hearsay, and had failed to take even minimum steps to verify the allegations, which lacked any plausible factual basis. The article therefore unlawfully damaged the applicants’ good name. The court ordered the journalists and editor-in-chief jointly to pay PLN 30,000 to a charity and to publish an apology. The Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the defendants’ appeal on 24 April 2003, and the newspaper complied with the orders.

In July 2004 the applicants brought a fresh action after discovering that the identical article remained freely available on the newspaper’s website and ranked prominently in Google searches. They argued that this constituted a continuing publication that rendered the earlier judgments ineffective, exposed them to a large new readership, and again infringed their personal rights. They sought an order requiring the newspaper to remove the article, to publish a further apology, and to pay PLN 11,000 in non-pecuniary damages.

The defendants pleaded res judicata, noting that the article now appeared only in the website archive, that printed copies existed in libraries nationwide, and that the applicants had been aware of the online version during the first proceedings yet had not then sought any internet-specific remedy.

On 28 September 2005 the Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the new claim. It accepted that the later discovery of an additional publication source (the website) created a fresh cause of action, so the matter was not strictly res judicata. Nevertheless, it held that removing the article would amount to unconstitutional censorship, rewriting history and a breach of archiving principles. The applicants had already received an apology and compensation; had they requested a footnote, a hyperlink to the 2002–2003 judgments, or a website apology, the court would have considered it. Instead they should have sought reopening of the first proceedings.

The Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 20 July 2006. It emphasised that the online version had existed since December 2000—well before the first judgments—and that the applicants’ failure to request specific internet measures at that time barred them from basing a new claim on facts already then known or discoverable. Each subsequent reading of an archived article did not constitute a fresh publication. Subsequent cassation proceedings were unsuccessful: the first applicant’s appeal was rejected for non-payment of the required court fee, and the Supreme Court refused to entertain the remaining cassation.

The applicants maintained before the Strasbourg Court that the domestic courts’ refusal to order removal of the article or any other effective online remedy left their reputations unprotected against a continuing, easily accessible defamation.

The case of Węgrzynowski and Smolczewski v. Poland originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by two Polish lawyers, Szymon Węgrzynowski and Tadeusz Smolczewski. They alleged a violation of their rights to respect for private life and reputation under Article 8 of the Convention, arising from the continued online availability of a newspaper article previously found to be defamatory.

On 8 May 2002, the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the applicants’ claim under Articles 23 and 24 of the Polish Civil Code. Journalists B.K. and A.M. of the daily newspaper Rzeczpospolita had published an article accusing the applicants of enriching themselves through involvement in shady political business deals and of abusing their roles as liquidators of bankrupt State-owned companies at public expense. The court held that the journalists had failed to contact the applicants or take even minimal steps to verify the allegations, which rested largely on gossip and hearsay and lacked a plausible factual basis. While acknowledging journalists’ freedom of expression and duty to inform the public, the court found the article smeared the applicants’ reputation. It ordered the journalists and editor-in-chief jointly to pay PLN 30,000 to charity and to publish an apology. The Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the newspaper’s appeal on 24 April 2003, and the newspaper complied with the judgment.

In July 2004 the applicants brought a fresh action under the same Civil Code provisions after discovering that the article remained freely accessible on the newspaper’s website and ranked prominently in Google searches. They argued that this created a continuing infringement, rendering the earlier judicial protection ineffective. They sought an order for the article’s removal, a written apology for the online publication, and PLN 11,000 in non-pecuniary damages.

The newspaper contended that the matter was res judicata, that the article formed part of a historical archive that could not be erased, and that the applicants had been aware of the online version during the first proceedings but had not sought specific relief in respect of it.

On 28 September 2005 the Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the claim. It accepted that discovery of a new publication source (the website) could in principle found a fresh action and that the issues were not res judicata. Nevertheless, it held that removing the article would amount to censorship, rewriting history and a breach of archiving principles. The applicants had already received an apology and compensation; a further printed apology would serve no purpose. The court observed that it might have considered a request for a footnote or hyperlink referring to the 2002–2003 judgments, but no such request had been made. It added that any newly discovered facts should have been raised by an application to reopen the original proceedings rather than by a new action.

The applicants appealed, arguing that each online reading constituted a fresh publication and that an internet “archive” differed fundamentally from a traditional paper archive. On 20 July 2006 the Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It stressed that the article had been placed online in December 2000 and that the applicants’ failure to seek specific remedies for the internet version in the first set of proceedings precluded them from relying on facts that already existed at that time.

Procedural complications followed. The Warsaw Court of Appeal rejected the first applicant’s cassation appeal for non-payment of the full court fee. The Supreme Court, on 7 February 2007, refused to entertain the second applicant’s cassation appeal.

The applicants maintained before the Strasbourg Court that the Polish courts’ refusal to order removal of the article or any other effective online remedy left their reputation unprotected and rendered the original judgments illusory.

**Case Summary: Węgrzynowski and Smolczewski v. Poland (ECtHR, Application no. 33846/07)**

Two Polish lawyers, Szymon Węgrzynowski and Tadeusz Smolczewski, alleged that Polish courts failed to protect their reputation and private life after a defamatory newspaper article remained freely available online.

In December 2000, journalists at the national daily *Rzeczpospolita* published an article claiming the applicants had amassed a fortune by exploiting their roles as liquidators of bankrupt state-owned companies. The piece alleged they assisted politicians in shady deals that harmed the public purse. In May 2002 the Warsaw Regional Court found the article defamatory. The journalists had not contacted the applicants, had not taken even minimal steps to verify the claims, and had relied largely on gossip and hearsay. Although journalists enjoy freedom of expression and a duty to inform the public, the court held that the allegations lacked a plausible factual basis and had smeared the applicants’ good name. It ordered the journalists and the editor-in-chief jointly to pay PLN 30,000 to charity and to publish an apology. The Warsaw Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in April 2003; the newspaper complied.

In July 2004 the applicants sued again. They had discovered that the identical article remained on the newspaper’s website and ranked prominently in Google searches. Anyone searching their names could easily read it. They argued that this constituted a continuing publication that rendered the earlier judicial protection illusory. They sought an order that the article be removed, a written apology for the online dissemination, and PLN 11,000 in non-pecuniary damages.

The newspaper contended that the matter was *res judicata*. The applicants had already obtained a remedy; the article now sat in the website’s archive, so readers would understand it was historical; printed copies existed in libraries nationwide and could not be erased from history. The defendants also noted that the applicants had mentioned the website version in the first proceedings but had not then sought any specific online remedy.

In September 2005 the Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the new claim. It accepted that the internet publication constituted a new source and therefore a new cause of action, so *res judicata* did not apply. Nevertheless, it refused to order removal, describing such a step as purposeless, equivalent to censorship and the rewriting of history, and contrary to archiving principles. The applicants had already received a public apology and compensation. The court observed that, had they asked for a footnote or hyperlink to the 2002–2003 judgments or for an online apology, the request would have received serious consideration.

The applicants appealed, arguing that each online viewing amounted to a fresh publication, that an internet “archive” is not comparable to a traditional paper archive, and that Article 24 of the Civil Code obliged the court to consider other suitable remedial measures. In July 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It stressed that the article had been online since 2000—well before the first judgment. Because the applicants had not specifically claimed against the internet version in the original proceedings, they could not now rely on facts that already existed at that time.

Subsequent cassation proceedings encountered procedural obstacles. The court fee paid covered only one appellant; the first applicant’s appeal was therefore rejected. The Supreme Court later refused to entertain the remaining cassation appeal.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ complaint that domestic courts left their reputation exposed to a continuing, easily accessible online publication despite earlier findings of defamation, thereby failing to secure effective protection of their private life and reputation.
001-122892:
The case of Lay Lay Company Limited v. Malta originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights alleging that the applicant company had been denied access to a court, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, to contest the authorities’ refusal of its building-permit application and that this had also violated its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In July 1984 the applicant company and a co-owner purchased approximately 4 500 m² of land in Ghaxaq, described in the deed as a “field” but claimed by the company to constitute a building site under the Building Development Areas Act 1983. An application to erect garages with overlying dwellings was submitted in August 1984 in the co-owner’s name. After the company became sole owner in September 1985, the Planning Area Permits Board (PAPB) approved the plans on 10 July 1986 subject to payment of road-contribution costs. The company nevertheless commenced construction. A contribution bill issued in May 1987 to the original applicant remained unpaid; a minute of 30 June 1987 recorded that no permit had been issued and that works were proceeding without one. A warning letter followed in July 1987. Criminal proceedings for illegal construction were later instituted but ultimately suspended without judgment.

Subsequent legislation (the Building Permits (Temporary Provisions) Act 1988 and the Development Planning Act 1992) replaced the PAPB with the Planning Authority (later MEPA). A fresh bill was issued in August 1992 and paid by the company on 14 December 1992; clearance was granted. Under transitional rules the company’s architect lodged a “Notice for Consideration” in January 1993. The file was thereafter transferred internally, misplaced, and no permit issued. In October 1996 a Development Control Unit manager wrote that the permit could not be granted because the original 1986 bill had “fallen through” after six years. Meetings between 1996 and 1999 produced no decision.

In June 1999 the company filed a judicial protest seeking issuance of the permit and damages. MEPA immediately issued a stop notice. An appeal against that notice was dismissed by the Development Appeals Board in August 2003 on the ground that the 1986 recommendation did not constitute a permit and that payment of the contribution did not automatically confer one. A further appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected in 2004 as not raising points of law. The authorities treated the 1996 letter as a final refusal against which the thirty-day appeal period had expired.

Constitutional proceedings instituted in September 2004 alleged that the failure to issue a formal decision, the stop notice and the informal rejection had denied the company access to court and interfered with its possessions. Both the Civil Court (First Hall) in 2009 and the Constitutional Court in 2011 rejected the claims. They held that the company possessed only the land itself, not a permit; that it had built without authorisation and had failed to seek regularisation; that the 1996 letter was appealable (or alternatively reviewable by judicial review); and that the company had remained passive. The permit requirement, the refusal and the enforcement measures were found to be lawful, in the public interest (rational planning, environmental protection and the rule of law) and proportionate. The land later fell outside the development zone under the 2006 South Malta Local Plan. The contribution of approximately EUR 7 970 was never refunded.

These circumstances form the factual basis of the alleged denial of access to a court to challenge the permit refusal and the consequent interference with the company’s property rights.

The applicant company, Lay Lay Company Limited, purchased approximately 4,500 square metres of land in Ghaxaq, Malta, in 1984. The land was described as a “field” but the company regarded it as a developable building site under the Building Development Areas Act 1983, given its road frontage and proximity to a built-up area. An application to construct garages with overlying dwellings was submitted later that year in the name of a co-owner. In July 1986 the Planning Area Permits Board (PAPB) approved the application subject to payment of road-contribution costs. The company commenced construction without first paying the contribution or receiving a formal permit.

Contribution bills were issued to the original applicant but remained unpaid for years. Criminal proceedings for illegal construction were instituted in 1988 and later suspended without judgment. Meanwhile, legislative changes occurred: the 1988 Act introduced temporary schemes, and the 1992 Development Planning Act established the Planning Authority (later MEPA) and new procedures. A fresh bill was issued in August 1992 and paid by the company in December 1992; clearance was granted. Under transitional regulations the company notified the new authority in January 1993 that it wished the original application to be considered. The file was subsequently misplaced and no permit issued.

In October 1996 a Development Control Unit manager wrote that the permit could not be granted because payment six years after the original bill meant the bill had “fallen through.” The company treated the letter as unofficial and did not appeal within the 30-day statutory period. After further unsuccessful correspondence it lodged a judicial protest in June 1999 seeking issuance of the permit and damages. The same day MEPA issued a stop notice. The company’s appeal against the notice was dismissed by the Development Appeals Board in 2003 and the Court of Appeal in 2004 on the ground that no permit had ever been issued; the 1996 letter was regarded as a final refusal.

In 2004 the company instituted constitutional proceedings claiming that the absence of a proper, appealable decision on its permit application had denied it access to court under Article 6 § 1 and that the refusal and stop notice had violated its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Civil Court (2009) and Constitutional Court (2011) rejected both claims. They held that the 1996 letter constituted a refusal against which an appeal or judicial-review action could have been brought, that the company therefore had access to court but failed to use it, and that it possessed no legitimate expectation of a permit because construction had begun without one and payment had been delayed. The requirement of a permit and the subsequent stop notice were lawful, pursued the public interest in orderly planning, and were proportionate. The contribution paid was never refunded. By 2006 a local plan placed the land outside the development zone.

These facts form the basis of the company’s complaints to the European Court of Human Rights that it was denied an effective judicial determination of the refusal of its long-standing permit application and that its peaceful enjoyment of possessions was thereby unlawfully interfered with.

The case of Lay Lay Company Limited v. Malta (Application no. 30633/11) concerns alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the ECHR (right of access to a court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applicant company, registered in Malta in 1979, purchased approximately 4,500 sq. m of land in Ghaxaq in July 1984 (initially jointly with a third party, C.). The land was described as a “field” but claimed by the applicant as a building site under the Building Development Areas Act 1983 due to its road frontage and proximity to a built-up area.

In August 1984, an application was submitted in C.’s name to the Planning Area Permits Board (PAPB) for permission to construct garages with overlying dwellings. The applicant became sole owner in September 1985. On 10 July 1986, the PAPB approved the application subject to payment of road contribution costs, but no formal permit was issued. The applicant began development works. Contribution bills and reminders were sent to C. (not the applicant) from 1987 onward; none were paid. A 1987 file note recorded that no permit had issued due to non-payment and that works were underway. Criminal proceedings for illegal construction were initiated in 1988 but later suspended without judgment.

Legislative changes followed: the 1988 Building Permits (Temporary Provisions) Act and the 1992 Development Planning Act, which established the Planning Authority (later MEPA) and its Development Control Commission. A fresh contribution bill was issued in August 1992 (again to C.), which the applicant paid on 14 December 1992. Clearance was granted, but no permit issued. In January 1993 the applicant’s architect submitted a transitional notice to the new authority (still naming C. as owner). The file was delayed, transferred repeatedly, and later misplaced. In 1996 the applicant’s new architect requested issuance of the permit and notified the authority of the change in ownership. On 7 October 1996 a MEPA manager (G.C.) wrote that the permit could not issue because the 1986 bill had “fallen through” after six years and payment had been refused.

The applicant held meetings with MEPA between 1996 and 1999 but received no definitive decision. After a February 1999 letter went unanswered, the applicant lodged a judicial protest on 15 June 1999 seeking issuance of the permit and damages. The same day MEPA issued a stop notice. The applicant appealed the notice to the Development Appeals Board, which in August 2003 held that no permit had ever been granted; PAPB approval and payment of the contribution did not constitute a permit. The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal in June 2004 as not raising points of law. During those proceedings it emerged that MEPA regarded the 1996 letter as a final refusal whose 30-day appeal period had expired.

In September 2004 the applicant instituted constitutional proceedings, claiming that the failure to issue a permit, the stop notice, and the informal manner of refusal (denying an opportunity to contest it) violated Article 6 (access to court and length of proceedings) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Civil Court (First Hall) in 2009 and the Constitutional Court in 2011 rejected the claims. They held that the applicant possessed only the land, not a permit or legitimate expectation of one; payment of the contribution did not compel issuance, especially after delay and unauthorised works. The 1996 letter constituted a refusal that could have been appealed to the Planning Appeals Board or subjected to judicial review; the applicant’s inaction meant it had not been denied access to court. The requirement of a permit, the refusal, and the stop notice were lawful, in the public interest, and proportionate.

In 2006 the South Malta Local Plan placed the land outside the development zone. The contribution payment of approximately EUR 7,970 was never refunded.
001-122373:
The ECHR case of Remuszko v. Poland (no. 1562/10, judgment of 16 July 2013) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention arising from newspapers’ refusals to publish a paid advertisement for the applicant’s book.

Stanisław Remuszko, a Polish journalist born in 1948 and resident in Warsaw, published a book in 1999 (second edition 2003) entitled “Gazeta Wyborcza. Beginnings and Beyond.” The work presented an unfavourable account of the 1989 founding of Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily that emerged from the Round Table talks. No press reviews of the book appeared. Remuszko then submitted an identical paid advertisement to seven daily and weekly newspapers. The proposed text read: “It does not make for pleasant reading for [the editor-in-chief] of Gazeta Wyborcza, friends. The truth about Gazeta Wyborcza. Previously unseen documents and new witnesses. Stanisław Remuszko, a former journalist [at the newspaper], today working freelance, has written the first ever book in Poland, Europe and the world about Gazeta Wyborcza and its background. Do you have the faintest idea where the wealth of Gazeta Wyborcza comes from? Information available at www.remuszko.pl.”

All seven titles (Nasz Dziennik, Wprost, Metropol, Newsweek, Polityka, Rzeczpospolita and Gazeta Polska) refused publication. Gazeta Polska initially signed a contract but later withdrew and refunded the fee.

On 12 June 2003 Remuszko lodged seven identical civil claims in the Warsaw Regional Court seeking orders that the newspapers publish the advertisement. He relied on section 36 of the 1984 Press Act (which permits paid advertisements provided they do not breach the law or principles of social coexistence and allows refusal only if the advertisement’s content or form is incompatible with the newspaper’s editorial profile) and on constitutional freedom of expression (Article 54). He argued that the text itself contained nothing unlawful or injurious to third-party personal rights.

The Regional Court dismissed the claims against five newspapers. The Court of Appeal subsequently ordered Wprost and Metropol to publish (those judgments became final). The appeal against Newsweek was rejected on formal grounds, the appeal against Polityka was dismissed, and the Gazeta Polska proceedings were settled without publication.

The application before the ECHR focused on the proceedings against Rzeczpospolita. On 30 March 2004 the Regional Court dismissed the claim, holding that publication could be understood as an endorsement of the book’s content and thus as a breach of third parties’ personal rights, obliging the editors to refuse. The Court of Appeal (4 November 2004) remitted the case, criticising the absence of reasons and emphasising that only the advertisement’s own wording—not the book’s content—could be examined under the Press Act; it also stated that advertisements fell outside freedom of expression.

On remittal the Regional Court (30 January 2007) again dismissed the claim. It found the advertisement incompatible with Rzeczpospolita’s editorial profile, liable to be read as an endorsement of views the paper rejected, and potentially damaging because the two titles were market competitors. Publishers enjoyed commercial freedom and were not obliged to accept every paid advertisement. The Court of Appeal (7 February 2008) upheld this reasoning. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 26 March 2009, confirming that the press market is governed by commercial freedom, that section 36(4) validly permits refusal on profile grounds, and that any limitation of commercial speech must satisfy the principle of proportionality (citing Appleby v. the United Kingdom).

These facts formed the basis of Remuszko’s complaint that the domestic courts’ endorsement of the refusals unjustifiably interfered with his right to impart information under Article 10.

The case of Remuszko v. Poland (Application no. 1562/10) originated from a complaint lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Polish journalist Stanisław Remuszko on 22 December 2009. He alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention arising from the refusal of the newspaper Rzeczpospolita to publish a paid advertisement for his book, a refusal upheld by the Polish courts.

In 1999 the applicant published Gazeta Wyborcza. Beginnings and Beyond, a critical account of the founding of Gazeta Wyborcza (a leading national daily established after the 1989 Round Table talks). A second edition appeared in 2003. After no reviews were published, the applicant submitted an identical paid advertisement to seven newspapers, including Rzeczpospolita. The advertisement stated: “It does not make for pleasant reading for [the editor-in-chief] of Gazeta Wyborcza, friends. The truth about Gazeta Wyborcza. Previously unseen documents and new witnesses. Stanisław Remuszko, a former journalist [at the newspaper], today working freelance, has written the first ever book in Poland, Europe and the world about Gazeta Wyborcza and its background. Do you have the faintest idea where the wealth of Gazeta Wyborcza comes from? Information available at www.remuszko.pl.” All seven titles refused publication.

The applicant brought civil claims under section 36 of the 1984 Press Act, arguing that the advertisement complied with the law, did not infringe third-party rights and was compatible with the newspapers’ editorial policies. The present application concerns only the proceedings against Rzeczpospolita.

On 30 March 2004 the Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the claim, holding that publication could be viewed as endorsement of the book’s content and thus a breach of third parties’ personal rights, creating a risk of civil liability that the editors were obliged to avoid. The Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 4 November 2004 and remitted the case, criticising the first-instance court’s failure to give adequate reasons and its incorrect reliance on the book’s content rather than the advertisement itself. It also observed that advertising fell outside the scope of freedom of expression.

On remittal the Regional Court again dismissed the claim on 30 January 2007. It found the advertisement incompatible with Rzeczpospolita’s editorial profile, capable of being read as an endorsement of views the paper did not share, and liable to suggest that one competitor was seeking to denigrate another. Publishers were under no duty to disseminate opinions they rejected. The Court of Appeal upheld this reasoning on 7 February 2008.

The applicant’s cassation appeal, expressly invoking Article 10 and the Polish Constitution, was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 26 March 2009. The Court held that the press market was governed by commercial freedom; a publisher without a monopoly was not obliged to accept every advertisement. Section 36(4) of the Press Act validly authorised refusal where an advertisement was incompatible with a newspaper’s profile. It referred to the Court’s judgment in Appleby and Others v. the United Kingdom and accepted that commercial speech attracted Article 10 protection, but maintained that horizontal relations permitted proportionate limitations.

Section 36 of the Press Act permits paid advertisements provided they do not breach the law or principles of social co-existence, are clearly distinguishable from editorial content, and are compatible with the paper’s editorial profile. The Supreme Court had already expressed similar views on the provision in other proceedings brought by the same applicant. Article 54 of the Constitution guarantees freedom of expression, subject to the limitations set out in Article 31.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the courts’ endorsement of the newspaper’s refusal constituted an unjustified interference with his right to impart information.

The European Court of Human Rights examined Stanisław Remuszko’s application alleging a violation of Article 10 of the Convention arising from Polish newspapers’ refusals to publish a paid advertisement for his book and the domestic courts’ subsequent confirmation of those refusals.

Remuszko, a journalist born in 1948 and living in Warsaw, published “Gazeta Wyborcza. Beginnings and Beyond” in 1999 (second edition 2003). The work portrayed the 1989 founding of Gazeta Wyborcza—one of Poland’s leading dailies, established after the Round Table talks—in a strongly unfavourable light. No press reviews appeared. Remuszko then submitted an identical paid advertisement to seven national dailies and weeklies. The text read: “It does not make for pleasant reading for [the editor-in-chief] of Gazeta Wyborcza, friends. The truth about Gazeta Wyborcza. Previously unseen documents and new witnesses. Stanisław Remuszko, a former journalist [at the newspaper], today working freelance, has written the first ever book in Poland, Europe and the world about Gazeta Wyborcza and its background. Do you have the faintest idea where the wealth of Gazeta Wyborcza comes from? Information available at www.remuszko.pl.”

Every title, including Rzeczpospolita (the defendant in the present proceedings), refused publication. Gazeta Polska initially contracted to run the advertisement but later withdrew and refunded the fee. Remuszko brought seven identical civil actions in the Warsaw Regional Court, invoking section 36 of the 1984 Press Act. He argued that the advertisement neither breached the law nor third-party personal rights and was not contrary to any editorial policy except, possibly, an unstated duty to protect Gazeta Wyborcza’s interests. He also relied on Article 54 of the Constitution (freedom of expression) and section 1 of the Press Act.

The Regional Court dismissed the claim against Rzeczpospolita on 30 March 2004. It held that publication could be perceived as endorsement of the book’s content, thereby exposing the newspaper to civil liability for infringement of third-party rights; editors were therefore entitled—and even obliged—to refuse. The Court of Appeal remitted the case on 4 November 2004, criticising the first-instance court’s failure to give reasons and its reliance on the book rather than the advertisement itself. On re-examination the Regional Court again dismissed the claim (30 January 2007), finding the advertisement incompatible with Rzeczpospolita’s editorial profile, capable of being read as an attack on a commercial rival, and therefore outside the statutory duty to publish. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 7 February 2008.

Remuszko’s cassation appeal, expressly invoking Article 10 of the Convention, was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 26 March 2009. The Court emphasised the commercial freedom of the press market and the absence of any monopoly that would compel a publisher to accept every paid advertisement. It cited Appleby v. the United Kingdom and held that section 36(4) validly authorised refusal where an advertisement conflicted with a newspaper’s character. Parallel Supreme Court rulings in Remuszko’s other actions reached the same conclusion.

Section 36 of the Press Act permits paid advertisements provided they do not breach the law or “principles of social co-existence,” are visually distinguishable from editorial content, and are compatible with the paper’s profile. Articles 54 and 31 of the Constitution guarantee freedom of expression subject to proportionate statutory limitations. The domestic courts consistently treated the refusal as a legitimate exercise of contractual and editorial autonomy rather than an unjustified restriction on the applicant’s speech.
001-122429:
The applicant, a Liechtenstein national born in 1925, owned two plots in Triesenberg that a February 2000 municipal land-development plan (adopted by referendum) classified as non-buildable. She objected that the plan breached equality and property rights and sought reclassification as building land. The municipality dismissed the objection in November 2000 (decision issued January 2001), citing incomplete water infrastructure, the plan’s status as the first for the area, environmental and landscape protection, and the plots’ location outside year-round habitation. The Government rejected her complaint in April 2004, holding the plan lawful, finding no vested claim even if the plots had been buildable under 1983 provisional rules, and deeming a personal hearing or site inspection unnecessary because the facts were clear from the file.

The applicant then complained to the Administrative Court, requesting a public oral hearing, production of planning documents, witness evidence of alleged referendum manipulation, reclassification or compensation for de facto expropriation, and a declaration that the referendum was void. The court obtained additional documents and photographs but, without a hearing, dismissed the complaint on 30 June 2004. It found no breach of legitimate expectations (any prior official statements could not override the plan as submitted to referendum) and no proof of manipulation, rendering further evidence or a hearing unnecessary.

Before the Constitutional Court the applicant alleged, inter alia, an Article 6 violation because the Administrative Court had refused an adversarial public oral hearing despite her request and despite having held hearings in comparable cases; evidence had been taken solely in writing. She also raised property and procedural complaints and sought an oral hearing. The Administrative Court explained that the plots’ situation was notorious and documented by photographs, that the applicant had commented in writing, and that public hearings were not normally held in land-development matters. The Constitutional Court held one public hearing in May 2006; after a change in composition it declined a further hearing.

In its November 2008 judgment (served April 2009) the Constitutional Court declared the request to void the referendum inadmissible for failure to exhaust a separate remedy and rejected the remaining complaints as unfounded. It found, however, that the length of its own proceedings had violated the right to a hearing within a reasonable time and ordered Liechtenstein to pay the applicant’s costs. On the hearing issue it held that Liechtenstein’s 1982 reservation (modified 1991) to Article 6 § 1 validly limited the publicity requirement to the principles of listed statutes, including the 1922 National Administrative Justice Act. Under section 100 of that Act the Administrative Court enjoyed discretion to decide on the file; because all factual and legal questions (including good-faith and manipulation issues) could be resolved from the written submissions and documents and were not complex, the discretion had been exercised compatibly with the unreserved right to a fair trial. Other complaints were either unexhausted or, in any event, unfounded: the plan merely regulated use rather than expropriating the land, and the applicant had had access to a court of full jurisdiction.

Hearings before the Administrative Court are not public as a matter of practice. The reservation lists the 1922 Act among the laws whose principles continue to govern publicity.

The case concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the Liechtenstein Administrative Court’s refusal to hold a public oral hearing or take evidence adversarially. The applicant, a Liechtenstein national born in 1925 and residing in Triesenberg, owned two plots of land. In February 2000 a municipal referendum adopted a land-development plan that placed those plots in a non-building zone. She objected, arguing that the plan was unlawful, breached equality and property rights, and that her land should be designated building land.

The municipality dismissed the objection in November 2000, citing incomplete water installations, environmental and landscape-protection reasons, and the plots’ location outside the year-round inhabited area. The Government rejected her 2001 complaint in April 2004, endorsing those reasons and stating that a personal hearing or site inspection was unnecessary because the relevant facts emerged clearly from her written submissions and the planning documents.

In May 2004 the applicant appealed to the Administrative Court. She requested a public oral hearing, the production of planning documents, the examination of witnesses whose evidence would allegedly show that the referendum had been manipulated, designation of her plots as building land or compensation for de-facto expropriation, and a declaration that the referendum was void. The municipality and Government filed written observations and additional documents and photographs. On 30 June 2004 the Administrative Court, without holding a hearing, dismissed the complaint. It held that nothing indicated a breach of legitimate expectations, that even if municipal officials had earlier raised hopes of future building-land status the adopted plan itself made the opposite designation clear, and that neither witness evidence nor an oral hearing was therefore required. It also found no proof of referendum manipulation.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint. She argued that the Administrative Court’s exclusive reliance on written procedure, despite her express request and contrary to its practice in comparable cases, violated Article 6 because no prior authority had held an oral hearing and the court had declined to examine her witnesses. She also raised complaints about the plan’s adoption procedure and an alleged interference with property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Constitutional Court held a public hearing in May 2006 (its composition later changed without a further hearing). In its November 2008 judgment it declared the request to annul the referendum inadmissible for failure to exhaust remedies and rejected the remaining complaints as ill-founded, while finding, of its own motion, a violation of the reasonable-time requirement in its own proceedings.

On the oral-hearing issue the Constitutional Court noted Liechtenstein’s reservation to Article 6 § 1, which limits the publicity requirement to the principles then embodied in specified statutes, including the 1922 National Administrative Justice Act. That reservation, it held, remained valid, so the Convention’s public-hearing obligation did not apply. The right to a fair trial (not covered by the reservation) did apply. Under the Administrative Justice Act the Administrative Court enjoyed discretion to decide whether an oral hearing was necessary, provided the discretion was exercised consistently with fundamental rights. The Constitutional Court concluded that the Administrative Court had been able to determine all factual and legal questions from the written observations and the file (including photographs showing the well-known location of the plots) and that the legal issues of good faith, protection of legitimate expectations and alleged manipulation were not complex. Consequently the refusal of a hearing did not breach the right to a fair trial.

The case concerns Karolina Schädler-Eberle, a Liechtenstein national born in 1925 and residing in Triesenberg. In February 2000 a municipal referendum adopted the first land-development plan for the area, placing two of her plots in a non-building zone for environmental and landscape-protection reasons (they lacked full water installations and lay outside the permanently inhabited settlement).  

She lodged a written objection with the municipality, alleging a breach of equality and property rights and seeking reclassification as building land. The municipality dismissed the objection in November 2000 (notified January 2001). A further written complaint to the Government was rejected in April 2004; the Government held that even if the plots had been building land under earlier provisional rules, no legitimate expectation of reclassification existed, and that an oral hearing or site inspection was unnecessary because the facts were clear from the file.  

In May 2004 the applicant complained to the Administrative Court. She requested a public oral hearing, the examination of witnesses (to prove alleged manipulation of the referendum), production of documents, reclassification of the plots or compensation for de-facto expropriation, and annulment of the referendum. The court obtained additional documents and photographs, invited written comments, but on 30 June 2004 dismissed the complaint without a hearing. It found no breach of legitimate expectations: any informal hopes raised by officials could not override the plan actually submitted to referendum. Witness evidence was therefore unnecessary and there was no proof of manipulation.  

A constitutional complaint followed in August 2004. The applicant alleged that the Administrative Court’s refusal to take evidence adversarially in a public oral hearing—despite her express request, the absence of any prior oral stage, and the court’s practice in comparable cases—violated Article 6. She also invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Constitutional Court itself held a public hearing in May 2006 (though its composition later changed without a further hearing). In its November 2008 judgment (served April 2009) it declared the request to annul the referendum inadmissible for failure to exhaust a separate remedy. On the hearing complaint it noted Liechtenstein’s reservation to Article 6 § 1, which validly limited the publicity requirement in proceedings under the 1922 National Administrative Justice Act. The right to a fair trial (not covered by the reservation) nevertheless required the court to exercise its statutory discretion consistently with fundamental rights. Because all factual and legal issues could be resolved from the written file, the situation of the plots was notorious and documented by photographs, and the legal questions (good faith, protection of legitimate interests, alleged manipulation) were not complex, the refusal of an oral hearing did not breach Article 6. Other complaints were rejected for non-exhaustion or as unfounded: the plan merely regulated use of property and the Administrative Court had full jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court did, however, find of its own motion that the length of its own proceedings had violated the reasonable-time guarantee and awarded costs.  

These facts—the successive written-only stages, the applicant’s repeated requests for an adversarial public hearing and witness examination, the Administrative Court’s discretionary refusal on the ground that the outcome would be unaffected, and the Constitutional Court’s subsequent review of that discretion in light of the reservation and Strasbourg case-law—form the core of the alleged Article 6 violation submitted to the European Court.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1974 and living in St Petersburg, suffered from an organic brain lesion causing manic syndrome and had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. His wife, who had the same diagnosis, gave birth to their son D. on 10 April 2002. The couple later separated; the wife died in 2012. Shortly after D.’s birth, owing to the parents’ inability to provide care (particularly the mother’s deteriorating condition), the child was placed with his maternal grandparents. The applicant continued to visit regularly, spend time with D., take him to events and provide gifts.

In August 2006 the local custody authority appointed the maternal grandmother, T.K., as guardian, noting that the mother was hospitalised and that the applicant neither lived with nor financially supported the child. T.K. then sued to restrict the mother’s parental rights and terminate the applicant’s. The applicant counterclaimed for revocation of the guardianship and transfer of D. to his care. Living-condition inspections confirmed that T.K.’s two-bedroom flat was suitable, while the parents occupied one room in a shared flat. The applicant later withdrew his request to take D. into his own home, accepting that the child should remain with the grandparents, but sought unrestricted contact (visits, overnight stays, holidays) after prior notice to T.K.

Medical evidence was uniformly favourable to the applicant. His treating psychiatrist stated that, although he experienced periodic mood swings, he displayed no psychotic symptoms, aggression or personality deterioration and that his condition neither impaired his capacity to raise a child nor endangered D. A subsequent clinic examination reached the same conclusion. The custody authority nevertheless recommended restriction of both parents’ rights “in D.’s best interests.”

On 29 August 2007 the Nevskiy District Court restricted the parental rights of both parents under Article 73 of the Family Code. It found that T.K. had discharged all parental duties since D.’s birth, that the mother had completely neglected them because of illness, and that the applicant, despite not having wholly abandoned the child, had neglected his duties owing to his chronic disorder and difficult circumstances. The court held that living with the applicant would be dangerous for D. independently of the applicant’s will. It rejected the argument that no actual danger had been proved, citing both the psychiatric diagnosis and the applicant’s alleged avoidance of upbringing. Contact of the types requested by the applicant was authorised, but only “with the consent of guardian T.K.” The court noted that the restriction could later be lifted if the underlying reasons ceased.

The applicant appealed, arguing that no danger to D. had been established and that making contact dependent on T.K.’s consent—given their evident conflict—rendered the right illusory; he asked that consent be required only from the custody authority. On 25 October 2007 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment, relying on the first-instance findings, the custody authority’s opinion and Article 75 of the Family Code, which permits contact with a parent whose rights have been restricted only with the guardian’s or authority’s consent.

Subsequent official reports (2011) confirmed that D. was thriving under T.K.’s care, that the applicant exercised contact twice monthly without obstruction, and that the boy regarded the relationship as positive, although the applicant remained relatively passive and had not sought to lift the restriction.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaint that the restriction of his parental rights, based essentially on his mental-health diagnosis despite contrary medical evidence, and the conditioning of all contact on the opposing guardian’s consent, violated his rights under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention.

The case of Dmitriy Ryabov v. Russia (no. 33774/08) concerns the restriction of the applicant’s parental rights over his son D., alleged to violate Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1974, has an organic brain lesion causing manic syndrome and paranoid schizophrenia. His wife, also diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, gave birth to D. on 10 April 2002. The couple later separated (the wife died in 2012). Shortly after D.’s birth, the parents placed him with the maternal grandparents because of the mother’s worsening health. The applicant maintained regular contact, visiting D., taking him on outings and providing gifts.

In August 2006 the local authority appointed the maternal grandmother, Ms T.K., as D.’s guardian despite the parents’ written objections. The decision recorded the mother’s hospitalisation and the father’s failure to live with, raise or financially support the child. Home inspections confirmed the grandparents’ two-bedroom flat provided good conditions, while the parents occupied a single 16 m² room in a shared flat; both were employed.

T.K. sued to restrict the mother’s parental rights and terminate the applicant’s. The applicant counterclaimed for revocation of the guardianship and transfer of D. to him. T.K. later limited her claim to restriction of the applicant’s rights. The mother consented in writing to T.K. remaining guardian, citing her own health and the applicant’s alleged drinking and absences. Two 2007 medical reports stated that the applicant displayed no aggression, psychotic symptoms or socially dangerous tendencies and that his condition neither impaired his parental capacity nor endangered the child.

The custody authority nevertheless advised that restriction of both parents’ rights was in D.’s best interests. The applicant then withdrew his request for custody, accepting that D. should remain with the grandparents, but maintained his request to revoke the guardianship and asked the court to grant him extensive, specified contact rights.

On 29 August 2007 the District Court restricted both parents’ rights under Article 73 of the Family Code. It found that D. had lived with T.K. since birth, that the mother had wholly neglected her duties because of illness, and that the applicant, although not wholly uninvolved, had neglected his duties for a prolonged period. The court held that the applicant’s chronic mental disorder rendered cohabitation independently dangerous to the child and therefore justified restriction. It refused to revoke the guardianship but granted all requested contacts, subject to T.K.’s consent, noting that the restriction could later be lifted if the grounds ceased.

The applicant appealed, arguing that no danger had been proved and that making contact dependent on T.K.’s consent (given their conflict) rendered the rights illusory; he asked that consent be required only from the custody authority. On 25 October 2007 the City Court dismissed the appeal, relying on D.’s long residence with the grandparents, the parents’ health problems and non-involvement, the authority’s opinion and Article 75 of the Family Code, which permits contact with a restricted parent only with the guardian’s or authority’s consent.

Later evidence (2011) showed D. thriving at school under T.K.’s care. The applicant had exercised contact twice a month without hindrance, maintaining a good relationship, though he remained relatively passive regarding studies and illness. He never applied to lift the restriction.

Domestic law (Family Code Arts. 73–76) allows restriction, even without parental fault, where remaining with a parent is dangerous because of a psychiatric disorder or similar circumstances. Restricted parents lose the right to personal upbringing but retain support duties; contact requires the guardian’s or authority’s consent; the restriction may be lifted if the grounds disappear.

The case of Dmitriy Ryabov v. Russia (Application no. 33774/08) concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights by a Russian national born in 1974, who lives in St Petersburg and suffers from an organic brain lesion causing manic syndrome as well as paranoid schizophrenia. He and his wife, Ms O.R. (who also had paranoid schizophrenia and later died in 2012), had a son, D., born on 10 April 2002. Shortly after the birth, D. was placed in the care of his maternal grandparents because the parents could not look after him owing to the mother’s deteriorating mental health. The applicant nonetheless maintained regular contact, visiting the child, taking him to events and providing gifts.

On 30 August 2006 the local custody authority appointed the maternal grandmother, Ms T.K., as D.’s guardian at her request, noting that the mother was hospitalised and that the applicant was not living with or supporting the child. Ms T.K. then brought proceedings to restrict the mother’s parental rights and terminate the applicant’s. The applicant counterclaimed for revocation of the guardianship and transfer of the child to him. Living-condition inspections showed that D. had a well-furnished home with his grandparents, while the parents occupied a single room in a shared flat.

In May 2007 Ms T.K. amended her claim to seek only restriction (rather than termination) of the applicant’s rights. The mother submitted a statement agreeing that Ms T.K. should remain guardian, citing her own health and the applicant’s health and lifestyle (including drinking and absences). Two psychiatric reports stated that the applicant displayed no psychotic symptoms, aggression or socially dangerous tendencies and that his condition neither impaired his ability to raise his son nor posed any danger to the child’s life or health. Nevertheless, the custody authority opined that restriction of both parents’ rights would be in D.’s best interests.

The applicant later withdrew his request for transfer of the child (accepting that D. should stay with the grandparents) but still sought revocation of the guardianship and a detailed contact schedule (visits at the grandparents’ home, collection from school, overnight stays twice a month, and holiday travel). On 29 August 2007 the Nevskiy District Court restricted both parents’ rights under Article 73 of the Family Code. It found that the mother had completely neglected her duties because of illness and that the applicant, although he had not entirely abandoned the child, had neglected his responsibilities for a prolonged period owing to his mental impairment and difficult circumstances. The court considered that the nature of the applicant’s disorder could make it dangerous for D. to live with him (circumstances independent of the applicant) and also cited the applicant’s conduct in avoiding upbringing. It rejected revocation of the guardianship but granted all requested forms of contact, subject to the guardian’s consent. The court noted that the restriction could later be lifted under Article 76 if the grounds ceased to exist.

On appeal the applicant argued that danger to the child had not been proven and that making contact dependent on Ms T.K.’s consent (given their conflict) rendered the right illusory; he asked that consent instead be required from the custody authority. The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment on 25 October 2007, relying on the first-instance findings, the parents’ mental-health problems, the fact that D. had always lived with his grandmother, and Article 75 of the Family Code (which permits contact only with the consent of the guardian or the custody authority).

Subsequent official statements in 2011 confirmed that D. was thriving at school, that the applicant exercised contact twice a month without hindrance (museums, theatres, shopping, pocket money and occasional telephone calls), and that the applicant had never sought to lift the restriction. Interviews indicated that the applicant was regarded as relatively passive and did not assist with homework or visit during illness.

The applicant alleged that the restriction of his parental rights, based largely on his mental-health diagnosis despite contrary medical evidence and despite the later practical exercise of contact, was incompatible with his right to respect for family life (Article 8) and was discriminatory (Article 14).
001-126027:
The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Somali national K.A.B. (born 1960), who entered Sweden in April 2009 and claimed asylum days later. He alleged that enforcing a deportation order to Somalia would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention (right to life and prohibition of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment). The Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39 to prevent his removal pending its decision.

The applicant stated he was born in Mogadishu, belonged to the Sheikal clan, and had lived there most of his life (apart from childhood years in Baydhabo). He trained as a teacher and worked as an administrator for the American Friends Service Community (a humanitarian organisation) from 1992 until its 2005 closure due to insecurity. He then taught from home. In 2007 he received threatening calls from people claiming to represent the Islamic courts, accusing him of spreading Christianity; he insisted he was Muslim and had ceased the work, but the threats continued. After a lull amid fighting, al-Shabaab issued similar threats in early 2009. On 2 March 2009 armed members visited his home looking for him; he fled immediately. His wife and children later also left Mogadishu. He claimed he faced serious assault by al-Shabaab on return, with no effective clan protection available.

Swedish authorities rejected the claim. The Migration Board (September 2009) accepted his Somali origin and clan affiliation as generally credible but found he had not substantiated residence in Mogadishu in the years immediately before departure. Family members’ earlier statements to Swedish authorities (a brother in 2002 and a nephew’s wife in 2008) placed him elsewhere, including Ethiopia. His account of the threats was deemed vague and lacking detail, especially given the unproven recent presence in Mogadishu. The employment certificate and expired identity card carried little weight. The Board therefore found no well-founded fear of persecution.

The Migration Court (February 2010), after an oral hearing, similarly held that the applicant had not proved his identity or recent Mogadishu residence. His explanations for the contradictory family statements and for trips to Ethiopia lacked credibility. Details of his work for the humanitarian organisation were insufficient, and it was unexplained why Islamist groups would target him years after he had stopped that work. The court examined the claim on the basis of return to Somalia as a whole and found no real personal risk established. Leave to appeal was refused by the Migration Court of Appeal in July 2010. Subsequent requests to re-examine on the ground of impediments to enforcement were also refused.

Country information before the Court showed that al-Shabaab had withdrawn from Mogadishu by mid-2012. Conventional front-line fighting had ceased, infrastructure had improved modestly, and some returns (mainly of resourceful diaspora members) were occurring. Nevertheless, the city remained fragile: al-Shabaab still conducted targeted assassinations, grenade and IED attacks (several per week), and hit-and-run operations, mainly against government affiliates, journalists, NGO workers and other visible figures, though civilians were also caught in the violence or crime. Criminality, unpaid security forces, and weak policing created additional risks, especially for internally displaced persons lacking clan networks. Authorities no longer regarded the general situation in Mogadishu as amounting to armed conflict exposing every inhabitant to a real risk of ill-treatment, but they noted political instability, high criminality and unpredictable incidents. Internal relocation to Somaliland was generally unavailable to persons originating from south-central Somalia who lacked clan ties there.

These personal credibility findings and the evolving security picture formed the core factual matrix against which the Court assessed whether return would expose the applicant to a real risk of treatment contrary to Articles 2 or 3.

The case of K.A.B. v. Sweden (Application no. 886/11) concerns a Somali national born in 1960 who entered Sweden in April 2009 and claimed asylum. He alleged that his forcible return to Somalia would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to a real risk of death or ill-treatment.

The applicant stated that he was born and had lived almost his entire life in Mogadishu, belonging to the Sheikal clan. He worked as an administrator for the American Friends Service Community, a humanitarian organisation, from 1992 until its closure in 2005 amid deteriorating security. He then taught from home. In 2007 he received telephone threats from individuals claiming to represent the Islamic courts, accusing him of spreading Christianity; he replied that he had ceased working for the organisation and was a Muslim, but the threats continued. After a lull, similar threats resumed in early 2009 from al-Shabaab. On 2 March 2009 al-Shabaab members visited his home looking for him. He fled immediately. His wife and children later left Mogadishu. He claimed that upon return he would face serious assault by al-Shabaab and that his clan could no longer protect him.

Swedish authorities rejected the claim. The Migration Board accepted that he originated from Somalia but found his account of recent residence in Mogadishu unconvincing, citing contradictory statements by relatives (one brother reported no siblings in Mogadishu; a relative’s wife said they had been neighbours in Addis Ababa). The alleged threats were deemed vague. The Migration Court, after an oral hearing, similarly held that he had not substantiated identity or residence in Mogadishu between 2006 and 2009, nor the nature of his earlier work or why threats began years after he left the organisation. It examined the case on the basis of return to Somalia as a whole and found no real personal risk. Leave to appeal was refused, as were later applications alleging new impediments to deportation.

Relevant country information at the time of the Court’s examination showed a complex and evolving security situation. Earlier UNHCR guidelines (2010) described widespread disregard of international humanitarian law in southern and central Somalia, with civilians routinely caught in indiscriminate bombardment, bombings and targeted attacks; no internal flight alternative existed and clan protection had been undermined. By 2012–2013, however, reports from Lifos, Danish/Norwegian fact-finding missions and others indicated that al-Shabaab had withdrawn from Mogadishu, ending front-line fighting. AMISOM and government forces controlled the city. Improvements included greater freedom of movement, reconstruction and some returns (mainly by resourceful diaspora members). Nevertheless, al-Shabaab remained present and conducted frequent grenade attacks, IEDs, suicide bombings and targeted killings of government affiliates, journalists and others. Criminality, unpaid soldiers, illegal checkpoints and a security vacuum persisted. Civilians risked being in the “wrong place at the wrong time.” IDPs remained highly vulnerable. Somaliland and Puntland were relatively safer but generally accepted only persons with local clan ties or prior residence; internal relocation there was therefore limited for those from the south.

The Court applied Rule 39 to stay deportation pending its decision. The core issue was whether, given both the applicant’s personal profile and the general conditions in Mogadishu (or Somalia more broadly), implementation of the expulsion order would expose him to a real risk of treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3.

**CASE OF K.A.B. v. SWEDEN (Application no. 886/11)**

The applicant, a Somali national born in 1960, entered Sweden on 18 April 2009 and claimed asylum on 24 April 2009. He stated he was born and had lived almost his entire life in Mogadishu (except a few childhood years in Baydhabo), belonging to the Sheikal clan. Trained as a teacher, he worked from 1992–2005 as an administrator for the American Friends Service Community, a humanitarian organisation that closed due to insecurity. Thereafter he taught from home. In 2007 he received threats by telephone from people claiming to represent the Islamic courts, accusing him of spreading Christianity; he replied that he had stopped working for the organisation and was Muslim, but this made no difference. Calls ceased temporarily during fighting with Ethiopian forces but resumed in early 2009 from al-Shabaab with similar accusations. On 2 March 2009 al-Shabaab members visited his home looking for him (he was absent). He immediately fled; his wife and children later also left Mogadishu. He claimed that on return he faced serious assault by al-Shabaab with no effective clan protection.

Swedish authorities rejected the claim. The Migration Board (18 September 2009) accepted his Somali origin and clan but found he had not credibly shown recent residence in Mogadishu (contradicted by a brother’s 2002 statement and a relative’s 2008 application mentioning him in Addis Ababa). Threats were vague and unparticularised, and he had not proved presence in Mogadishu when they allegedly occurred. Documents (expired ID and employment certificate) were given little weight. The application was assessed on return to Somalia generally. The Migration Court (25 February 2010, after oral hearing) agreed: identity unproved, recent Mogadishu residence unsubstantiated, work details vague, and no explanation why threats arose years after the organisation closed or how the groups learned of his work. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal (7 July 2010). Later claims of new impediments to deportation were also rejected.

The applicant alleged that enforcement of the deportation order would violate Articles 2 and 3 ECHR. Interim measures under Rule 39 prevented removal pending the Court’s examination. The Court later sought updated observations on Mogadishu’s security situation.

Country information before the Court described a deteriorating then evolving situation. UNHCR 2010 Guidelines recorded widespread IHL violations, indiscriminate attacks, and high civilian casualties in Mogadishu, concluding that anyone returned to south/central Somalia faced a real risk of serious harm with no internal flight alternative; clan protection had been undermined. Later reports (Swedish Lifos 2012; Danish/Norwegian fact-finding 2013) noted al-Shabaab’s withdrawal from territorial control of Mogadishu by mid-2012, the end of front-line fighting, some infrastructure improvements, returning diaspora (often temporary, elite or business-oriented), and reduced conventional conflict. However, al-Shabaab remained capable of asymmetric attacks (grenades, IEDs, targeted killings) affecting civilians as well as officials; criminality, weak policing, clan militias, and “wrong place, wrong time” risks persisted. Ordinary civilians, IDPs, NGO-associated persons, and returnees without strong networks or resources remained vulnerable. Somaliland was relatively safer but generally accepted only those originating from or closely affiliated with the territory; it was not regarded as a viable alternative for most southern/central Somalis.

These facts framed the core issue: whether the applicant’s personal circumstances and the general conditions in Mogadishu (or Somalia more broadly) created a real risk of treatment contrary to Articles 2 and/or 3 if the deportation order were implemented.
001-126451:
**Case of Sardón Alvira v. Spain (Application no. 46090/10), ECtHR (Third Section), 24 September 2013 (final 24 December 2013)**

The applicant, Anibal Sardón Alvira, a Spanish national, complained of a violation of his right to a fair trial. In 2001, Spain’s National Securities Market Commission (CNMV) assumed control of investment firm GESCARTERA amid concerns over its finances and client funds. This led to a criminal investigation by Audiencia Nacional investigating judge no. 3 into executives and associates for continuous fraud, misappropriation, and false commercial statements. The applicant, an agent for GESCARTERA’s commercial office Asesoría y Gestión de Patrimonios, S.A. (AGP), was among those investigated.

Fourteen people, including the applicant, were charged. Prosecutors sought compensation under Article 116 of the Criminal Code (civil liability of those found guilty of an offence causing damage). Relatives and others were summoned under Article 122 (liability of those who gratuitously benefited from crime proceeds, unaware of their criminal origin, limited to the gain received). On 25 March 2008, the Audiencia Nacional convicted the applicant of continuous misappropriation and false statements. It held he was not a mere AGP agent but its de facto administrator, who had premeditatedly cooperated in stripping assets from GESCARTERA clients, prepared false documents to attract/retain investors, and, as an investor himself, owed the firm €88,671.78 (net withdrawals exceeding deposits). He received a seven-year prison term plus fines for misappropriation and two years plus fines for false statements. Jointly with co-convicts, he was ordered under Article 116 to pay €87,995,626.91 (estimated losses plus interest from CNMV intervention). Other parties, including relatives, were ordered under Article 122 to repay their net gains, based on Supreme Court case-law requiring gratuitous enrichment from crime, lack of knowledge of its origin, and restoration limited to actual participation (a civil obligation rooted in unjust enrichment, not the crime itself).

The applicant and others appealed on points of law. He sought acquittal, argued his GESCARTERA investments/gains were lawful, and challenged the net-amount calculation. After a hearing attended by his counsel (28–29 September 2009), the Supreme Court on 13 October 2009 acquitted him. It found insufficient evidence that he managed funds or prepared false documents, thus quashing facts implying active criminal participation and upholding the presumption of innocence. However, it left intact the first-instance finding that he was an investor owing €88,671.78 and imposed Article 122 liability for that sum. It applied the same reasoning used for co-appellant M.A.V.: although M.A.V. (and the applicant) had been charged under Article 116, their defence that gains were lawful investments also addressed potential Article 122 liability, so no violation of the right of defence occurred.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court on 5 January 2010, alleging a fair-trial breach. He argued the Supreme Court had unexpectedly recharacterised him as an unwitting economic beneficiary (Article 122) rather than a principal offender (Article 116), without prior accusation, notice, or opportunity to challenge this new capacity or adapt his defence strategy. The legal requirements and available defences differed substantially. On 11 February 2010 the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible for failure to demonstrate particular constitutional significance.

The applicant further alleged insufficient reasoning by both the Supreme and Constitutional Courts and discriminatory treatment, as other GESCARTERA investors were treated as victims rather than beneficiaries of the misappropriation.
