The case of Sardón Alvira v. Spain (no. 46090/10) involved a Spanish applicant alleging unfair proceedings, insufficient reasoning, misapplication of civil liability rules, and discrimination. He claimed the Supreme Court imposed civil liability on him as an economic beneficiary of crime proceeds—a capacity he could not challenge—after acquitting him of related criminal charges, without prior accusation or hearing on that basis. Other investors were treated as victims rather than beneficiaries.

In 2001, Spain’s CNMV intervened in the investment firm GESCARTERA due to opaque finances and fund destinations. Criminal probes followed at the Audiencia Nacional for continuous fraud, misappropriation, and false commercial statements. The applicant, an agent for related firm AGP, was charged with misappropriation and false statements. Prosecutors sought joint civil compensation from the accused under Criminal Code Article 116. Relatives and others were summoned under Article 122 as potential gratuitous beneficiaries of crime proceeds.

In its 2008 judgment, the Audiencia Nacional convicted the applicant as AGP’s de facto administrator. It found he had premeditatedly cooperated in systematic asset-stripping of GESCARTERA, misappropriating client funds and issuing false documents to attract/retain investors. As an investor himself, he owed the firm €88,671.78 (net withdrawals exceeding deposits). He received prison terms (seven years plus two years) and fines, plus joint and several civil liability under Article 116 for €87,995,626.91 in estimated losses (plus interest). Applying Supreme Court case-law on Article 122 (requiring gratuitous benefit from crime, the beneficiary’s unawareness of its criminal origin, and restitution limited to actual gain under civil rules), the court ordered others—including relatives—to repay their net gains.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, seeking full acquittal and arguing his gains were lawful investments while challenging the net-withdrawal calculation. After a hearing attended by his counsel, the Supreme Court on 13 October 2009 acquitted him. It held that the trial court had violated the presumption of innocence: there was insufficient evidence he managed funds or prepared false documents. It quashed findings of his active criminal role. However, it left intact his investor status and the €88,671.78 figure, ordering repayment under Article 122. It reasoned by analogy to co-appellant M.A.V. (similarly charged under Article 116 but held under Article 122): M.A.V.’s defence of lawful investment gains had addressed both the criminal accusation and potential Article 122 liability. The same applied to the applicant.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, arguing the Supreme Court had unexpectedly recharacterised the facts, imposing beneficiary liability he could not contest. No party had accused him under Article 122, and there had been no hearing on it. The legal elements for perpetrator liability (Article 116) differed from those for an unaware gratuitous beneficiary (Article 122), so his defence strategy would have differed. The Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible in February 2010 for failure to demonstrate special constitutional significance.

These facts centre on the alleged lack of notice, opportunity to be heard, and specific defence against the recharacterised civil claim, as well as the treatment of other investors as victims. Relevant provisions include Constitution Article 24 (rights to judicial protection, information on charges, and a fair trial) and Criminal Code Articles 116 and 122.

The case of Sardón Alvira v. Spain (Application no. 46090/10) concerns alleged violations of the applicant’s fair-trial rights under Article 6 of the Convention, arising from the manner in which Spanish courts imposed civil liability on him after acquitting him of criminal charges.

The applicant, a Spanish national, was linked to GESCARTERA, a registered investment agency. In June 2001 the Spanish stock-exchange regulator (CNMV) took control of the agency after discovering irregularities in its finances and the destination of client funds. Criminal proceedings followed before the Audiencia Nacional against executives and associated persons, including the applicant (in his role as de-facto administrator of one of GESCARTERA’s commercial offices). He was charged with continuous misappropriation and the continuous making of false commercial statements. Prosecutors also sought civil compensation under Article 116 of the Criminal Code (joint and several liability of those found guilty of an offence that caused damage).

In March 2008 the Audiencia Nacional convicted the applicant, finding that he had premeditatedly misappropriated client funds in concert with GESCARTERA’s principal shareholders and had supplied false documents to attract and retain investors. It sentenced him to imprisonment and fines and held him jointly liable, together with co-defendants, for approximately €88 million in estimated losses (plus interest). Separately, the court recorded that the applicant, as an investor, had withdrawn €88,671.78 more than he had deposited; that sum was treated as an amount he owed the company. Other persons (including some of the applicant’s relatives) who had received gratuitous benefits from the scheme were ordered to make restitution under Article 122 of the Criminal Code, which imposes a purely civil obligation on anyone who has innocently increased his wealth by the proceeds of a crime.

The applicant appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court, seeking acquittal and arguing that any personal gain had been the product of ordinary, lawful investment rather than crime. He also contested the calculation of his deposits and withdrawals. After a hearing attended by his counsel, the Supreme Court, in October 2009, quashed the conviction. It held that there was insufficient evidence that the applicant had managed GESCARTERA’s funds or prepared false documents, and that the first-instance court had therefore violated the presumption of innocence. The criminal findings of fact against him were set aside. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court left untouched the finding that he had been an investor who owed €88,671.78 and, applying Article 122, ordered him to repay that sum as a gratuitous beneficiary of the proceeds of crime. It justified the re-characterisation by reference to a co-appellant whose similar “lawful-investment” defence was deemed to have covered both the criminal charge and the possible Article-122 liability.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, complaining that the Supreme Court had suddenly recast the case, finding him liable in a capacity (innocent beneficiary) that had never been charged and that he had been given no opportunity to contest. He argued that the legal requirements and defence strategy for Article 122 liability differed materially from those applicable to a convicted principal under Article 116, so that he had been deprived of a fair hearing. In February 2010 the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible for lack of special constitutional significance.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that he had been denied a fair hearing because the Supreme Court imposed civil liability under a new legal characterisation that he could not challenge, that the domestic courts had misapplied the civil-liability provisions, that they had failed to give adequate reasons, and that he had been treated differently from other investors who were recognised as victims rather than beneficiaries.

The case of Brzuszczyński v. Poland (Application no. 23789/09) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention due to an unfair trial. The applicant, Piotr Brzuszczyński (born 1959), was convicted of aiding and abetting murder, illegal firearm possession, and aiding extortion, and sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment. The murder of E.U. occurred on 19 May 2001, committed by R.N., who was arrested with the applicant on 6 June 2001 while carrying a loaded gun. R.N. was questioned four times: twice on 7 June 2001, then on 8 June and 25 July 2001. In his initial statements, R.N. confessed to the murder, stating that the applicant had provided him with a Walther pistol (handed over in a plastic bag near a warehouse in Kobyłka in mid-May 2001) knowing it would be used to obtain money, possibly by killing the victim, and that they planned to split proceeds. R.N. confirmed this in subsequent early statements and later identified the burial site. On 25 July, he altered his account slightly (mentioning an unnamed third person and claiming he had been kidnapped), then broke off. R.N. died by suicide on 31 August 2001.

A bill of indictment was filed on 23 May 2002 charging the applicant with aiding the murder by supplying the gun, illegal possession, and (with P.D.) attempted extortion of a ransom from the victim's family. The applicant denied all involvement. In the first trial, the Warsaw Regional Court convicted him on 27 May 2003 of aiding armed robbery (reclassified), possession, and aiding extortion, imposing 8 years, relying primarily on R.N.'s statements as credible (noting his detailed self-incrimination and lack of motive to lie). The applicant appealed, arguing selective reliance on R.N.'s testimony, ignored inconsistencies, and contradictory witness evidence (e.g., that R.N. possessed a gun earlier, never told the truth, or used drugs). The prosecutor sought a murder conviction. On 9 December 2003, the Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the judgment for incomplete evidence assessment and insufficient scrutiny of the deceased witness's statements, remitting the case with instructions to examine the gun's origin, fingerprints, and permits.

After 19 hearings, the Regional Court reconvicted the applicant on 27 November 2007 of aiding murder, possession, and aiding extortion (15 years; P.D. received 4 years for related offences). The 135-page judgment relied on R.N.'s early spontaneous statements (deemed credible as self-incriminating, detailed, and made without pressure), corroborated by ~40 witnesses, phone records (frequent calls around the murder and extortion dates), site inspection, autopsy, firearms expert opinion, and other documents. It established the applicant's financial motive, ongoing contact/help to the hiding R.N., provision of the gun with awareness of possible lethal use, and role in proposing/supervising the ransom (supported by voice analysis implicating P.D.). Later R.N. changes and certain witnesses (suggesting earlier gun possession by R.N.) were deemed unreliable, biased, or inconsistent. The applicant refused to testify.

On appeal (20 March 2008), the applicant reiterated errors in facts and evidence assessment, particularly over-reliance on selected R.N. statements contradicted by witnesses. The Court of Appeal dismissed it on 30 July 2008, affirming the trial court's thorough, rigorous analysis of the "incriminating evidence" from the deceased co-suspect (applying Supreme Court criteria: complex/self-incriminating nature, spontaneous timing, no motive to fabricate given good relations, corroboration, and free expression). Cassation was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 10 December 2008 as manifestly ill-founded. Domestic law (Article 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) permitted reading the deceased's prior statements. The core facts relevant to the unfairness claim thus centred on the unavailability of R.N. for confrontation, the decisive weight given to his statements despite later inconsistencies, and the extent of corroboration and judicial scrutiny.

The case of Brzuszczyński v. Poland (Application no. 23789/09) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention arising from the applicant’s conviction for aiding and abetting murder (and related offences). The conviction rested substantially on the untested pre-trial statements of a co-suspect, R.N., who died by suicide before trial and thus could not be examined or cross-examined in court.

R.N. murdered E.U. on 19 May 2001. Both men were arrested on 6 June 2001; R.N. was found in possession of a loaded gun. Questioned four times (twice on 7 June, then on 8 June and 25 July 2001), R.N. immediately confessed, stating that the applicant had supplied him with the Walther pistol (in a plastic bag, near a warehouse in Kobyłka) knowing it would be used to obtain money from a prospective car buyer, that they planned to share the proceeds, and that the applicant later proposed extorting a ransom from the victim’s family after no cash was found. R.N. identified the burial site and described the killing in detail. In his final interview he introduced inconsistent new claims (an unnamed third person present, his own alleged kidnapping) before breaking off. He hanged himself on 31 August 2001.

The applicant, who denied all involvement and later refused to testify, was indicted for aiding murder by providing the gun, illegal firearm possession, and attempted extortion (together with P.D.). After an initial conviction for the lesser offence of aiding armed robbery (eight years), the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment for incomplete and inconsistent assessment of evidence, stressing that R.N.’s unread statements required especially rigorous scrutiny. On remittal the Regional Court, after 19 hearings, convicted the applicant of the original murder-aiding charge plus the other counts and imposed 15 years’ imprisonment. Its 135-page judgment treated R.N.’s early, spontaneous statements as credible “incriminating evidence” (pomówienie). It found no motive for R.N. to fabricate the applicant’s role (they had been close friends and business partners; the applicant had helped R.N. hide from creditors by supplying clothes and toiletries). The statements were corroborated by telephone-traffic data showing intense contact immediately after the murder and during the ransom demand, by the applicant’s financial difficulties and prior interest in firearms, by the absence of the applicant’s fingerprints on the bagged gun, and by other forensic and witness evidence confirming the killing itself. Testimonies suggesting R.N. already possessed a gun earlier were dismissed as unreliable or biased.

The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, applying Supreme Court criteria for evaluating such statements (complex rather than simple incrimination, spontaneity, absence of motive to lie, consistency with other evidence, and freedom of expression). It confirmed that later inconsistencies in R.N.’s account had been properly discarded as illogical. A cassation appeal arguing that the conviction rested solely on the deceased co-suspect’s words was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded. Domestic law (Article 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) expressly permits the reading of a deceased witness’s prior statements.

These facts form the core of the Article 6 complaint: the decisive use of hearsay from a person the defence could never confront.

The case of Brzuszczyński v. Poland concerns the applicant’s complaint of an unfair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. Piotr Brzuszczyński (born 1959) was convicted of aiding and abetting the murder of E.U. (committed by R.N. on 19 May 2001), illegal firearm possession, and aiding extortion of a ransom from the victim’s family; he received a 15-year sentence.

R.N. and the applicant were arrested on 6 June 2001 (R.N. carrying the murder weapon). R.N. was questioned four times. On 7 June he confessed, stating the applicant had given him the gun in mid-May 2001 near a Kobyłka warehouse so they could obtain money (possibly by killing) and split the proceeds. He confirmed this on 8 June and 25 July, though on the last date he added an unnamed accomplice and his own alleged kidnapping before breaking off. R.N. hanged himself in prison on 31 August 2001. The applicant denied any involvement or knowledge of the gun.

The Warsaw Regional Court first convicted him in May 2003 of aiding armed robbery (reclassified), illegal possession and aiding extortion (8 years), treating R.N.’s statements as credible despite his death. The applicant appealed, arguing selective use of those statements and disregard of witnesses who said R.N. already possessed a gun, never told the truth and used drugs. The Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in December 2003 for incomplete and inconsistent evidence assessment, remitting with instructions for a particularly rigorous review of the untested statements and further inquiries into the gun’s origin.

After 19 hearings the Regional Court reconvicted him in November 2007 of the original charges (15 years). It relied on R.N.’s statements, the two accused’s prior accounts (they refused to testify), some 40 witnesses and documents. It found the men were close friends in financial distress; the applicant had helped R.N. hide from creditors (clothes, supplies, frequent calls) and had a prior interest in firearms. R.N.’s statements were deemed spontaneous, detailed, largely self-incriminating and unmotivated by animus; they were corroborated by the burial site, autopsy, ballistics, event witnesses and phone records showing call spikes around the murder and ransom demand. Testimonies suggesting R.N. already had a gun were inconsistent, changed and biased. The applicant’s explanations were contradictory.

The applicant again appealed, claiming over-reliance on selected parts of R.N.’s testimony contradicted by other witnesses. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in July 2008, finding the first-instance court had applied the required strict criteria for “incriminating evidence” from a deceased co-suspect (complex nature, spontaneity, lack of motive to lie, corroboration, free expression). Inconsistencies were addressed and other evidence analysed. The Supreme Court dismissed cassation in December 2008 as manifestly ill-founded.

Article 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows previous statements of a deceased witness to be read. These facts centre on the decisive use of R.N.’s untested statements as the principal basis for conviction.

**Case Summary: Print Zeitungsverlag GmbH v. Austria (Application no. 26547/07), ECHR (First Section), Judgment of 10 October 2013 (final 10 January 2014)**

The applicant, Print Zeitungsverlag GmbH, an Austrian limited liability company based in Innsbruck, publishes the free weekly newspaper *Bezirksblatt, Lokalausgabe Hall/Rum*, which circulated 17,440 copies in a Tyrol region. In January 2006, an anonymous letter styled as a “survey” was mailed to around 300 recipients, including members of the supervisory board of the Hall and Wattens tourism association. It targeted two brothers, C.M. and J.M. (referred to as “M&M”). C.M., a practising lawyer, chaired the tourism association and was seeking re-election. J.M., also a lawyer, served as Hall City Council member responsible for public finance and chaired the supervisory board of the municipal utility Stadtwerke Hall. The letter posed rhetorical questions implying dishonesty, lack of qualifications, and untrustworthiness in professional, private, and family matters, urging readers not to support them in their positions.

A journalist for the applicant’s newspaper learned of the letter, contacted both men, and received their comments that it formed part of a political smear campaign. C.M. later telephoned to object to any publication and threatened legal action. On 18 January 2006 the newspaper published an article headed “Anonymous campaign against M&M,” which recounted the letter’s circulation, reproduced the men’s denials and characterisation of the accusations as personal insults, included their photographs, and reprinted the full text of the anonymous letter.

C.M. and J.M. sued the publisher under section 6 of the Media Act for defamation, seeking damages and an order to publish the judgment. The applicant argued that it had merely reported a third-party statement from which it had distanced itself and that the matter was of public interest. On 24 March 2006 the Innsbruck Regional Court found for the claimants, ordering publication of the judgment and payment of EUR 2,000 to each. It accepted that the article itself commented objectively and did not endorse the letter, and that the claimants, as holders of public offices, were already in the public eye. However, it held that the reproduced letter itself constituted defamation by accusing them of contemptible characteristics and conduct that lowered their public esteem. The men had suffered professional repercussions as lawyers. Although section 6(2)(4) of the Media Act permits truthful quotation of a third-party statement (even if the author is unknown) where there is an overriding public interest, the court balanced that interest against the claimants’ reputational rights. Local public interest existed in knowing of a campaign against the tourism-association chairman and a local politician, but did not justify reprinting the letter; the newspaper could have reported the campaign without disseminating the defamatory content to a far larger audience.

The applicant appealed, invoking the “law on quotations” under section 6(2)(4) and stressing that the tourism association was a public-law body and that both men were local public figures. On 10 August 2006 the Innsbruck Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that the quotation defence was unavailable because the original author remained anonymous (the defence applies, it said, only when the speaker’s identity is known so that the victim can sue that person directly). In any event, there was no overriding public interest in publishing the letter itself. The judgment was served on 3 January 2007.

The applicant company lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 May 2007, complaining that the domestic courts’ decisions violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The Court communicated the case on 2 December 2009 and joined the questions of admissibility and merits.

The case of Print Zeitungsverlag GmbH v. Austria (Application no. 26547/07) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). The applicant, an Austrian limited liability company, publishes the weekly free newspaper Bezirksblatt (Lokalausgabe Hall/Rum), which circulated 17,440 copies of the relevant edition in a Tyrol region.

In January 2006, approximately 300 copies of an anonymous letter styled as a “survey” about C.M. and J.M. (referred to as “M&M”) were circulated, including to members of the supervisory board of the Hall and Wattens tourism association. C.M., a practising lawyer and then-chairman of the association, was standing for re-election to that post. His brother J.M., also a lawyer, served as a City Council member responsible for public finance and as chairman of the supervisory board of the local utility Stadtwerke Hall. The letter posed rhetorical questions implying that the brothers lacked honesty, qualifications, and integrity in both professional and private spheres (e.g., whether one would buy a car from them, stake money on their promises, or allow them to execute a will) and urged recipients to vote them out of their positions.

A journalist for the applicant’s newspaper learned of the letter and contacted C.M. and J.M., who characterised it as a politically motivated campaign and personal insult. C.M. subsequently telephoned to object to any publication and threatened legal action. Nonetheless, the 18 January 2006 edition carried an article entitled “Anonymous campaign against M&M,” which recounted the letter’s circulation, reproduced the brothers’ comments, included their photographs, and printed the full text of the anonymous letter.

C.M. and J.M. sued the applicant under section 6 of the Media Act, which imposes strict liability on publishers for defamation (defined by reference to Article 111 of the Criminal Code as attributing contemptible characteristics or dishonourable conduct capable of lowering public esteem). They sought damages and publication of any judgment. The applicant contended that the article merely quoted a third-party statement from which it had distanced itself and that the matter was one of public interest.

On 24 March 2006 the Innsbruck Regional Court found the newspaper liable. It accepted that the accompanying text was objective and did not endorse the letter, but held that the reproduced letter itself constituted defamation by accusing the claimants of dishonesty and other disreputable traits. The claimants had suffered professional repercussions as lawyers. Although section 6(2)(4) of the Media Act permits quotation of a third-party statement if it is truthful and there is an overriding public interest, the court concluded that public interest in reporting a campaign against local office-holders did not extend to reproducing the letter itself; the newspaper could have informed readers of the campaign without disseminating the defamatory content to a far larger audience.

The applicant appealed, invoking the “law on quotations” and stressing the public-law character of the tourism association and the claimants’ status as local political figures. On 10 August 2006 the Innsbruck Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that the quotation defence was unavailable because the original author remained anonymous (so that the persons concerned could not pursue the source directly) and, in any event, that there was no overriding public interest justifying publication of the letter. The applicant was ordered to pay each claimant EUR 2,000 and to publish the judgment. The decision became final after service on 3 January 2007.

The applicant thereafter complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the domestic rulings constituted an unjustified interference with its right to impart information on a matter of local public concern.

**Case of Print Zeitungsverlag GmbH v. Austria (Application no. 26547/07), ECtHR (First Section), 10 October 2013 (final 10 January 2014)**

The applicant, Print Zeitungsverlag GmbH, an Austrian limited liability company based in Innsbruck, publishes the free weekly newspaper Bezirksblatt (Lokalausgabe Hall/Rum), which circulated 17,440 copies of the relevant edition. It alleged a violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression) arising from domestic defamation proceedings.

In January 2006, an anonymous letter styled as a survey was circulated in approximately 300 copies, many to members of the supervisory board of the tourism association for Hall and Wattens in Tyrol. It targeted two brothers, C.M. and J.M. (referred to as “M&M”). C.M. was a practising lawyer, chairman of the tourism association (and a candidate in ongoing elections for that post), while J.M. was a practising lawyer, a long-time local politician in Hall, City Council member responsible for public finance, and chairman of the supervisory board of the municipal utility Stadtwerke Hall. The letter posed rhetorical questions implying the brothers were dishonest, unqualified, unreliable in professional and personal matters (e.g., “Would you buy a car from this man?” “Is this man honest with his own family?”), and urged voters not to support them.

A journalist from the applicant company learned of the letter, contacted C.M. and J.M. (who described it as a political smear), and was warned by C.M. against publication. On 18 January 2006 the newspaper published an article headed “Anonymous campaign against M&M,” reporting the letter’s existence and the brothers’ comments that it sought to harm their political activities and constituted a personal insult. The article included their photographs and reproduced the full text of the anonymous letter.

C.M. and J.M. sued the publisher under section 6 of the Media Act (strict liability of the publisher for defamation, insult, etc., with a damages claim). The applicant argued it had merely quoted a third-party statement, had distanced itself from the content, and that publication served the public interest.

On 24 March 2006 the Innsbruck Regional Court found for the claimants, ordering the applicant to publish the judgment and pay EUR 2,000 compensation to each brother. It held that the article itself was objective and did not endorse the letter, but that the reproduced letter itself met the definition of defamation under Article 111 of the Criminal Code by attributing contemptible characteristics (dishonesty, lack of qualifications) affecting both professional and private life. The brothers had suffered professional repercussions as lawyers. Although the claimants were public figures often in local media, section 6(2)(4) of the Media Act (the “law on quotations”) permitted truthful quotation of a third-party statement only where there was an overriding public interest. The court accepted a public interest in knowing of a campaign against the tourism association chairman and a local politician, but found this did not justify reprinting the full defamatory letter; the newspaper could have reported the campaign without it and had thereby disseminated the allegations far more widely.

The applicant appealed, invoking the quotations defence and stressing the public-law nature of the tourism association and the claimants’ status as public figures. On 10 August 2006 the Innsbruck Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held the quotations provision inapplicable because the original author was anonymous (so the victims could not pursue the source directly). In any event there was no overriding public interest in publishing the letter itself. The judgment was served on 3 January 2007. The application to the ECtHR followed on 30 May 2007.

The case of Haxhia v. Albania (ECtHR, 8 October 2013) concerns Albanian national Ismet Haxhia (b. 1954), former head of traffic police at Bajram Curri commissariat. He alleged violations of Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Convention arising from his arrest, detention, trial and conviction in connection with the 12 September 1998 assassination in Tirana of opposition MP Azem Hajdari and one bodyguard (a second bodyguard was wounded). Albania was then experiencing residual anarchy after the 1997 pyramid-scheme collapse.

Haxhia was arrested on 22 January 2001 pursuant to a prosecutor’s warrant of 13 January and charged with two counts of murder (Criminal Code Arts 78 and 79(c)) and one of attempted murder. He was questioned the next day, informed of the charges and allowed counsel of his choice. On 24 January the Tirana District Court validated the arrest and ordered pre-trial detention of undefined duration, citing “reasonable suspicion” that he had acted as an accomplice. On appeal the Supreme Court held that the District Court had failed to justify a risk of flight, rendering the initial detention unlawful, yet upheld remand because of the gravity of the offence and danger to public order.

The indictment of 13 March 2001 listed Haxhia and four co-accused as organisers or participants. The investigation file (1 409 pages) was disclosed on 16 March. At trial Haxhia repeatedly complained of inadequate time to study the file, late or incomplete disclosure (especially driver A.L.’s 8 May 2001 statement), and the trial court’s refusal of expert examinations (handwriting, visibility from a well-lit café veranda into a dark street). Witness M. (already serving a sentence in Italy) testified by video-link; Haxhia and another accused walked out, claiming no legal basis. Witness Ç. (a prisoner) had given a pre-trial “secured” statement on 11 March 2001 that implicated Haxhia; although summoned later, his evidence was criticised as contradictory and the court refused a visibility test. Several alibi witnesses placed Haxhia at dinner in a nearby restaurant at the moment of the shooting; surviving bodyguard Z.N. never identified him.

On 29 April 2002 the District Court convicted Haxhia of aiding and abetting premeditated murder committed for revenge (new Art. 78 § 2, in force only from 24 January 2001) and sentenced him to 20 years’ imprisonment. It reclassified the charge from politically motivated murder (Art. 79(c)) after finding the motive was blood-feud revenge linked to F.H.’s brother. The court relied on circumstantial evidence: Haxhia’s car having travelled in convoy with the later perpetrators from Bajram Curri on 10–11 September, his presence near the crime scene, continued contact with F.H., and attendance at N.C.’s funeral 40 days later. It rejected Ç. and M. as unreliable vis-à-vis other accused but accepted A.L., co-accused J.M. and K.G. Haxhia was acquitted of the remaining charges.

The Court of Appeal (9 July 2002) and Supreme Court (14 February 2003) upheld the conviction, holding that disclosure had been adequate, the video-link lawful under the CCP and Mutual Assistance Convention, and reclassification permitted. An impartiality challenge to the trial bench (29 October 2001) was dismissed in Haxhia’s absence; the Supreme Court later treated the ensuing appeal as improperly lodged. The Constitutional Court (9 July 2003) declared the complaint inadmissible without reasons.

Haxhia’s core complaints were that detention lacked reasonable suspicion and prompt information (Art. 5); that the trial was unfair because of delayed disclosure, inability to test key witnesses, unlawful video-link evidence, unreasoned rejection of defence motions, lack of judicial impartiality, and inadequate reasoning based on circumstantial evidence (Art. 6); and that the reclassification applied a heavier post-offence provision (Art. 7).

**CASE OF HAXHIA v. ALBANIA (Application no. 29861/03, ECtHR, 8 October 2013)**

Ismet Haxhia, an Albanian traffic police chief in Bajram Curri born in 1954, applied to the ECtHR alleging violations of Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Convention arising from his arrest, detention, trial and conviction in connection with the 12 September 1998 assassination of opposition MP Azem Hajdari and his bodyguards in Tirana. Hajdari and one bodyguard were killed; another was wounded. The murder, amid Albania’s post-1997 instability, sparked political violence.

Haxhia was arrested on 22 January 2001 on warrants issued 13 January 2001. He was charged with two murders (Articles 79(c) and 78 CC) and attempted murder (Article 78 CC). On 24 January 2001 the Tirana District Court validated the arrest and ordered undefined pre-trial detention, citing reasonable suspicion of complicity. Haxhia appealed. On 9 February 2001 the Supreme Court found the initial detention unlawful for lack of justification of flight risk but upheld remand due to the crime’s circumstances, public-order danger and suspicion of complicity. Haxhia later complained he was not promptly informed of the reasons for detention and that no reasonable suspicion existed.

The prosecutor filed the indictment on 13 March 2001. Haxhia received a 1,409-page investigation file of 324 documents on 16 March 2001. He repeatedly sought more time to study it and objected to non-disclosure of certain materials, including witness A.L.’s 8 May 2001 statement (disclosed later). The trial court granted limited extra time but rejected many requests for expert examinations (e.g., visibility tests regarding witness Ç., handwriting analysis, car inspections) without reasons. A.L. testified that he saw Haxhia’s Fiat Tipo in a convoy travelling from Bajram Curri to Tirana on 10-11 September 1998 and parked at a hotel; Haxhia denied joining the group or being at the hotel. Co-accused J.M. gave similar evidence. Eye-witnesses P.G. and surviving bodyguard Z.N. did not place Haxhia at the scene. Witness Ç. (whose testimony was “secured” pre-trial on 11 March 2001) later testified he saw Haxhia and his car near the scene immediately before and after the shooting, despite darkness, rain and distance (later contradicted by the café owner). Italian prisoner M. testified by video-link (admitted over Haxhia’s objection of no legal basis and boycott of the hearing); M. did not implicate Haxhia. Haxhia and alibi witnesses (E.B., A.P., H.A.) said he was dining in a nearby restaurant at the time of the shooting. Haxhia also challenged the District Court’s impartiality; the Court of Appeal dismissed the request in his absence.

On 29 April 2002 the District Court convicted Haxhia of aiding and abetting premeditated murder on revenge grounds (reclassified from political-motive murder under Article 79(c) to Article 78 § 2 CC, which had been amended on 24 January 2001 after the 1998 crime). It relied on circumstantial evidence: escorting the perpetrators, presence of his car, contacts with a suspect’s family and a funeral visit. He was acquitted of the other charges and sentenced to 20 years. The Court of Appeal (9 July 2002) and Supreme Court (14 February 2003) upheld the conviction, rejecting complaints about disclosure, time to prepare, video-link evidence, rejected motions, impartiality, reasoning and reclassification (the latter held lawful under Article 375 CCP as amended). The Supreme Court also declined to examine Haxhia’s earlier impartiality appeal on formal grounds. The Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible without reasons on 9 July 2003.

Haxhia alleged Article 5 violations (unlawful detention lacking reasonable suspicion and prompt information), Article 6 violations (insufficient time and facilities to prepare a defence, non-disclosure, unlawful evidence, rejection of evidence requests, lack of impartiality and inadequate reasoning) and Article 7 issues arising from the post-offence reclassification of charges.

The applicant, Ismet Haxhia (born 1954), headed traffic police in Bajram Curri. On 12 September 1998, amid post-1997 anarchy, MP Azem Hajdari and a bodyguard were assassinated near Democratic Party headquarters in Tirana; another bodyguard was wounded. Hajdari’s killing sparked riots. No autopsies occurred; forensics and early witness statements (including a surviving bodyguard who later recanted identifications) did not implicate the applicant. He voluntarily stated in 1999 that he dined nearby and inquired after shots, fearing for his brother.

On 13 January 2001 arrest warrants issued for five officers, including the applicant, for the murders and attempted murder. He was arrested 22 January and charged under then-applicable Criminal Code Articles 79(c) and 78. The District Court validated detention on 24 January, citing reasonable suspicion of complicity. The Supreme Court on 9 February found the initial detention unlawful for lack of flight-risk reasons but upheld remand due to the offence’s gravity, public-order risk and accomplice suspicion.

The indictment of 13 March 2001 (with 1,409 pages) reached the applicant on 16 March. He obtained extra time to 13 April but later objected to undisclosed cassettes, extra witness statements and late production of driver A.L.’s 8 May 2001 statement (placing the applicant’s Fiat Tipo in a convoy to Tirana and at a hotel, but not at the crime scene). Expert requests (vehicle inspection, handwriting, visibility tests from a lit café into a dark street) were rejected without reasons. Co-accused J.M. testified they merely crossed paths. M. (in Italian prison) testified by video-link; the applicant boycotted, alleging no legal basis. Eye-witness Ç.’s testimony, secured on 11 March 2001 amid haste, later placed the applicant arguing with Hajdari then arriving post-shooting; a café owner contradicted the closing time and distance. Alibi witnesses placed the applicant dining nearby; the surviving bodyguard did not mention him.

On 29 April 2002 the District Court convicted the applicant as an aider/abettor of premeditated revenge murder (reclassified from political-motive Article 79(c) to Article 78 § 2, enacted 24 January 2001), sentencing him to 20 years; it acquitted him of the other counts. It relied on circumstantial acts (escorting the group, car proximity, later funeral attendance and prior acquaintance) and testimonies of A.L., K.G. and J.M., dismissing other witnesses as unreliable. An impartiality challenge of 29 October 2001 was dismissed the same day in the applicant’s absence; a further appeal was never examined.

The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 9 July 2002 after admitting some extra documents. The Supreme Court on 14 February 2003 confirmed, finding adequate defence time, lawful video-link evidence, opportunity to question A.L. at trial, and permissible reclassification. The Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible on 9 July 2003 without reasons. These events formed the basis of complaints under Articles 5, 6 and 7 concerning detention lawfulness and information, equality of arms, disclosure, witness examination, reasoning, impartiality, appellate review and retrospective reclassification.
001-126551:
The case of Zrilić v. Croatia (Application no. 46726/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns complaints by Croatian national Slavica Zrilić that national courts’ order for judicial sale (rather than physical partition) of a family house she co-owned with her former husband violated her right to respect for her home under Article 8 of the Convention and her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 1992 the applicant and G.Z. built a two-storey house of 176.42 m² on a 455 m² plot in Vinkovci. They occupied the finished ground-floor living areas (rooms, bathroom, hallway, dining room and kitchen); the upper floor remained unfinished. After their May 2005 divorce both continued to reside in the house.

The applicant brought civil proceedings to determine her ownership share in the house, land and a jointly owned car. An expert valued the property at EUR 55,158.48 and attributed investments 66:34 in G.Z.’s favour. A final May 2009 judgment of the Županja Municipal Court accordingly awarded the applicant one-third ownership and G.Z. two-thirds (and equal car shares). The shares were registered in the land registry.

In August 2009 G.Z. applied to the Vinkovci Municipal Court for partition, offering to buy out the applicant’s share or, alternatively, a judicial sale. The applicant initially accepted the established proportions but later sought partition in kind, arguing that the parties had already lived separately in different parts of the house for years (a de facto partition) and citing pending separate proceedings in which she claimed reimbursement of her construction contributions.

An expert (S.Ž.) appointed at a hearing the applicant’s representative missed for unverified health reasons reported in January 2010 that the property was worth EUR 55,674 and that physical partition was impossible: the house was a single unit with one entrance giving access to all rooms, held a building permit only for the ground floor and lacked a use permit. Creating two independent flats would require major extra construction, a new building permit and further administrative proceedings. After hearing the expert (who confirmed his findings) the court rejected the applicant’s request for a second expert.

On 22 April 2010 the court ordered sale of the house and land, holding that in-kind partition would substantially impair the property’s value, that the parties’ de facto living arrangements did not themselves create registerable separate units proportionate to their shares, and that the pending contribution claim did not warrant a stay because ownership shares were already finally settled. The Vukovar County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in February 2011, endorsing the expert report and the sale order. Enforcement proceedings followed. The applicant’s March 2011 constitutional complaint (invoking fair-trial, home, private-life and property rights) was declared manifestly ill-founded in May 2011.

In September 2012 the house and land were sold to G.Z.; the applicant received HRK 135,333.34 as her share and was ordered to vacate. These events form the core of the alleged violations: the courts’ insistence on sale, rather than physical division reflecting the applicant’s long-term occupation of part of the house as her home, resulting in loss of both her dwelling and her co-ownership interest.

**Case of Zrilić v. Croatia (Application no. 46726/11), ECtHR, 3 October 2013 (final 20 January 2014)**

The applicant, Slavica Zrilić (born 1958, resident in Vinkovci, Croatia), alleged violations of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for her home) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). These arose from Croatian courts’ order for judicial sale (rather than partition in kind) of a house she co-owned with her former husband, G.Z., resulting in her eviction from her long-term residence.

In 1992, the couple built a 176.42 m² two-level house on a 455 m² plot. They occupied the finished ground floor (two rooms, bathroom, hallway, dining room and kitchen); the upper level remained unfinished. They divorced in May 2005 but continued living in the house.

The applicant brought proceedings in the Županja Municipal Court to determine ownership shares. An expert valued the property at EUR 55,158.48 and assessed investment proportions at 66:34 in G.Z.’s favour. On 8 May 2009 the court, unopposed by G.Z., declared the applicant owner of one-third and G.Z. of two-thirds. Shares were registered; a related car-division order was also made.

On 28 August 2009 G.Z. applied to the Vinkovci Municipal Court for partition, offering to buy out the applicant’s share or, alternatively, judicial sale. The applicant did not oppose partition itself but, on 14 October 2009, sought division in kind. She argued they had already lived in separate parts for years (a de-facto partition) and cited pending civil proceedings in which she claimed reimbursement of her construction contributions.

G.Z. replied that they still shared most living space and that in-kind partition was technically impossible given the share ratio. After the applicant’s representative missed a hearing (health reasons, no evidence submitted), the court commissioned expert S.Ž. The applicant later complained she had not been heard on the expert’s selection.

S.Ž.’s January 2010 report valued the property at EUR 55,674 and found in-kind partition impossible: the house was a single unit with one entrance giving access to all rooms; it lacked a use permit (building permit covered only the ground floor). Creating two independent flats would require a new building permit, administrative proceedings and substantial construction work. At a March 2010 hearing the expert reiterated these findings; creating separate units would not be feasible without major extra investment. The applicant requested a second expert.

On 22 April 2010 the Vinkovci Municipal Court ordered judicial sale. It rejected a stay pending the contribution-reimbursement action (shares already finally determined) and a new expert (the report was objective). Separate occupancy did not itself constitute legally partitionable, registerable units proportional to the parties’ shares. The Vukovar County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 17 February 2011, accepting the expert evidence and finding no procedural unfairness.

Enforcement proceedings for sale began on 22 March 2011. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 10 October 2011. Her April 2011 constitutional complaint (invoking fair trial, equality, private/family life, home and ownership rights, and requesting a stay) was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 12 May 2011. On 18 September 2012 the house and plot were sold by court order to G.Z.; the applicant received HRK 135,333.34 as her share and was ordered to vacate.

These facts centre on the applicant’s continuous post-divorce residence in the family house (her home) and her registered one-third ownership. Domestic courts, relying on expert evidence that physical division into independent, registerable units was impractical without significant extra works and permits, preferred civil termination by sale over the applicant’s preferred in-kind solution, despite her claims of existing de-facto separation and a related pending claim. The resulting forced sale and eviction order formed the core of the alleged interferences with her home and possessions.

The case of Zrilić v. Croatia (Application no. 46726/11) was brought by Slavica Zrilić, a Croatian national born in 1958 and resident in Vinkovci, against Croatia. She alleged that national court orders for the partition and judicial sale of a house she jointly owned with her former husband G.Z. violated her right to respect for her home (Article 8 of the Convention) and her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

In 1992 the applicant and G.Z. built a two-level family house of 176.42 m² on a 455 m² plot in Vinkovci. They occupied the ground floor (two rooms, bathroom, hallway, dining room and kitchen); the upper floor remained unfinished. After their divorce in May 2005 they continued to live in the house. The applicant then sued in the Županja Municipal Court to have her ownership share determined. An expert valued the property at EUR 55,158.48 and attributed investments 66:34 in G.Z.’s favour. By a final judgment of 8 May 2009 the court declared the applicant owner of one-third and G.Z. of two-thirds; the shares were registered in the land registry.

On 28 August 2009 G.Z. applied to the Vinkovci Municipal Court for partition, proposing to buy out the applicant’s share or, alternatively, a judicial sale. The applicant initially accepted the established shares but later sought partition in kind, arguing that they had already lived separately for years (a de-facto partition) and that pending civil proceedings for reimbursement of her construction contributions should first be resolved. G.Z. replied that they still shared the same living areas except bedrooms and that physical division was technically impossible given the shares.

After a hearing from which the applicant’s lawyer was absent (her adjournment request on unsubstantiated health grounds having been refused), the court commissioned an expert report from S.Ž. The report of 4 January 2010 valued the property at EUR 55,674 and concluded that partition in kind was impossible: the house was a single unit with one entrance leading to all rooms, possessed a building permit only for the ground floor, and lacked a use permit. Creating two independent flats would require a new building permit, fresh administrative proceedings and substantial construction. At a later hearing the expert reiterated that a “flat” under Croatian law needed a cohesive group of rooms forming a self-contained unit with a separate entrance—criteria the house did not meet without major extra investment. The applicant’s request for a second expert was refused.

On 22 April 2010 the Municipal Court, relying on the report, ordered a judicial sale. It held that current separate occupation did not constitute legal partition into registerable units proportional to the shares, and that the pending reimbursement action was irrelevant because the shares had already been finally determined. The Vukovar County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 17 February 2011, endorsing the expert’s findings and the first-instance reasoning. Enforcement proceedings followed; on 18 September 2012 the house was sold to G.Z., the applicant received HRK 135,333.34 as her share, and she was ordered to vacate.

A constitutional complaint alleging breaches of fair-trial, equality, private-life and property rights (and seeking a stay of enforcement) was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 12 May 2011. Croatian property law (Property Act, ss. 47, 50, 53, 67) prefers partition in kind when possible without substantial detriment to value; otherwise it requires sale and division of proceeds. A “flat” is defined (Lease of Flats Act, s. 2) as a self-contained group of rooms with a separate entrance.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged interferences with the applicant’s long-term home and her one-third ownership interest.
001-127610:
The case of Pauliukienė and Pauliukas v. Lithuania (ECtHR, Application no. 18310/06) concerned a complaint by the second applicant, Vytautas Pauliukas (a public official elected as Kaunas city centre elder in 2003), that a newspaper article had defamed him, violating his Article 8 right to respect for his reputation. His wife, the first applicant, was also involved as co-owner of the relevant property.

The couple had long-running disputes with neighbours over a plot of land and house at 40 Raseinių Street/13 Telšių Street in Kaunas, purchased by the first applicant in 1995–1996. Authorities issued multiple administrative-law penalty notices against the first applicant (some later quashed on procedural grounds) for unauthorised reconstruction of a warehouse/house, continuing works without permits, occupying State land, and related violations. The second applicant had separately been found liable for demolishing a neighbour’s fence. Neighbours (including Č.P.) formally complained in 2003 that the applicants had ignored the law for years, lied, used connections, occupied others’ and State land, and that the second applicant had abused his official position for personal gain. Official replies confirmed some violations.

On 11 November 2003 the daily Respublika published an article headed “The elder was occupying the neighbours’ land.” It stated that the second applicant (explicitly identified as the newly elected elder) was illegally building on the plot after occupying neighbours’ and State land, ignoring official prohibitions on reconstructing a derelict house, and that the couple had enlarged their plot at others’ expense in 1995. It further noted that housing authorities had ordered them to submit a reconstruction project or demolish the building (which they ignored, instead building a new house inside the old one without permission) and that the second applicant had previously worked as deputy director of Inkaras, an EBSW-group company then under criminal investigation for insolvency. The article relied on neighbours’ complaints and official documents.

The second applicant requested a correction, arguing the statements were false and damaging to his reputation as elder; the newspaper refused. He sued for rectification and non-pecuniary damages. The first-instance court dismissed the claim, finding the journalist had spoken to neighbours, reviewed official documents (which the press could trust without further verification), and that the couple’s property was jointly owned, so both could be linked to the violations. Language was not insulting, and the Inkaras reference was essentially accurate.

The appellate court partly allowed the claim and ordered a rectification. It held that the Real Estate Registry showed the first applicant as sole registered owner, so linking the second applicant to the illegal acts was inaccurate; the Inkaras job description was also misleading. This damaged his authority as a public figure and breached the journalist’s duty of accuracy.

The Supreme Court reversed, upholding the first-instance dismissal. It emphasised that the article concerned a genuine neighbour dispute over illegal construction and land occupation. Official documents provided a sufficient factual basis. Even though the property was registered in the first applicant’s name, it was joint marital property; a public figure such as the second applicant had a duty to prevent his co-owner from violating others’ rights. The journalist had acted in good faith. The appellate court had therefore erred in finding a deliberate breach of journalistic standards.

The second applicant alleged that the domestic courts’ failure to protect him from the article’s imputations of illegal conduct and improper associations violated Article 8. (The ECtHR later examined the balancing of his reputation against freedom of expression.)
