The case of Pauliukienė and Pauliukas v. Lithuania (Application no. 18310/06) originated from an application lodged on 2 May 2006 by Lithuanian nationals Zita Pauliukienė (born 1954) and her husband Vytautas Pauliukas (born 1953), both resident in Kaunas. The second applicant alleged that a newspaper article defamed him, violating his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicants were involved in long-running disputes with neighbours over a plot of land and house at 40 Raseinių Street and 13 Telšių Street in Kaunas. In December 1995 the first applicant purchased a share of the land, which was registered in her name. Multiple administrative proceedings followed. In 2003 the Kaunas territorial planning authorities issued penalty notices against the first applicant for unauthorised construction works inside a warehouse and unlawful reconstruction of a house, imposing fines of LTL 1,000. These were later quashed on procedural grounds (absence of the first applicant or timing of the offence). Further notices concerned arbitrary occupation of State land (also discontinued after courts found boundaries had been established only after construction) and an unlawful wall on State land. Separately, the second applicant was found administratively liable and ordered to pay damages for demolishing a neighbour’s fence in 2002.

Neighbours (including Č.P.) submitted written complaints in 2003 accusing the applicants of ignoring laws, occupying others’ and State land, and the second applicant of exploiting his position as Kaunas city-centre elder (elected that year) for personal gain. Copies of complaints and official replies were later provided to a journalist.

On 11 November 2003 the daily Respublika published an article stating that the second applicant, as newly elected elder, was illegally building, occupying neighbours’ and State land, ignoring reconstruction bans, and continuing works despite official orders. It also noted his former role at Inkaras (part of the EBSW group then under criminal investigation for insolvency). The second applicant requested a correction, which was refused. He then brought a civil defamation claim seeking rectification and non-pecuniary damages.

The Vilnius City Second District Court dismissed the claim on 3 December 2004. It held that the journalist had spoken to neighbours, examined official documents confirming administrative liabilities for both applicants, and contacted the second applicant. Official replies from authorities constituted reliable sources, so the newspaper had acted in good faith and was not required to verify further. The plot was presumed joint marital property, justifying mention of both applicants. References to Inkaras were not shown to be insulting, and the article contained no manifestly offensive language.

The Vilnius Regional Court partially allowed the appeal on 13 April 2005, ordering rectification. It found the published statements inaccurate because the property was registered solely in the first applicant’s name and the second applicant had worked at a subsidiary (Inkaro padai), not Inkaras itself. Linking the second applicant (a public figure) to the alleged violations and EBSW damaged his authority and breached the journalist’s duty of fairness and impartiality.

On 2 November 2005 the Supreme Court quashed the appellate ruling and reinstated the first-instance decision. It emphasised that the land and house constituted joint marital property under the Code of Marriage and Family, giving both spouses equal management rights and imposing on the second applicant (as public official) a duty to prevent his co-owner’s unlawful actions. Official documents referring to violations by both applicants provided a sufficient factual basis. The journalist had not acted in bad faith or breached journalistic ethics under the Law on the Provision of Information to the Public. The neighbours had acted in good faith to protect their rights and ensure a public figure’s compliance with the law.

Domestic law (Civil Code Articles 2.23–2.24 and the Law on the Provision of Information to the Public) protected honour and dignity while permitting publication of information about public figures where there was a lawful public interest, provided the media acted in good faith and presented information fairly. The Supreme Court found these conditions met.

The case of Pauliukienė and Pauliukas v. Lithuania (no. 18310/06) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life, encompassing reputation) arising from a newspaper article that the second applicant claimed defamed him.

The applicants, a married couple living in Kaunas, were embroiled in protracted disputes with neighbours over a plot of land and house at 40 Raseinių Street/13 Telšių Street. The first applicant had purchased a share of the land in 1995, registered solely in her name. From 2003 onward, territorial planning authorities repeatedly issued administrative penalty notices against her for unauthorised reconstruction of a warehouse/house, occupation of State land, and related breaches. Several notices were later quashed on purely procedural grounds (absence of the applicant, expiry of the six-month limitation period). Parallel proceedings confirmed that the second applicant had unlawfully demolished a neighbour’s fence. Neighbours (including Č.P.) lodged formal complaints with municipal and State bodies, asserting that the applicants had enlarged their plot at others’ expense, built without permits and ignored stop-work orders; official replies largely substantiated these allegations.

On 11 November 2003 the daily Respublika published an article describing the conflicts. It identified the second applicant as the newly elected elder of Kaunas city centre and stated that he (and his wife) were illegally constructing on the plot, occupying neighbours’ and State land, disregarding institutional prohibitions and continuing works inside an old building without authorisation. The piece also noted his former post at the Inkaras factory, part of the EBSW group then under criminal investigation for insolvency.

The second applicant requested a correction; when the newspaper refused, he sued for rectification and non-pecuniary damages. He argued that the property was registered only in his wife’s name, that the article therefore falsely attributed illegal acts to him, and that the Inkaras reference was misleading and damaging to his public reputation.

The Vilnius City Second District Court dismissed the claim (3 December 2004). It held that the journalist had acted in good faith: she interviewed neighbours, examined official documents and contacted the applicant. Official replies from authorities constituted reliable sources exempt from further verification. The land, acquired during marriage, was presumed joint property; the Inkaras statement was sufficiently accurate.

The Vilnius Regional Court allowed the claim in part (13 April 2005) and ordered a rectification. It found the statements factually incorrect because title was registered solely in the first applicant’s name and the employment detail was imprecise.

The Supreme Court reversed (2 November 2005) and reinstated the first-instance judgment. It reasoned that marital property remained jointly owned and managed regardless of registration. As a public official, the second applicant bore a duty to prevent his co-owner from violating the law. Official documents therefore provided a sufficient factual basis; the journalist had not acted in bad faith or breached the statutory duty of accuracy and impartiality.

The applicants lodged their application with the Court on 2 May 2006, complaining that the article and the domestic courts’ refusal to grant redress had unlawfully interfered with the second applicant’s reputation.
001-128035:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) case of Galina Kostova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 36181/05) originated from a 27 September 2005 application by Bulgarian lawyer Galina Georgieva Kostova, born in 1970 and a Sofia Bar Association member. She alleged that the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) refused to review the proportionality of the Minister of Justice’s decision to remove her from the official list of persons qualified to serve as liquidators of insolvent companies.

In December 2001 the Minister included Kostova on the list under the Commerce Act 1991. In December 2003 the Sliven Regional Court appointed her liquidator of State-owned company T., which had entered winding-up proceedings. The company’s management objected to her work and repeatedly but unsuccessfully sought her replacement. On 31 March 2004 they complained to the Minister. The Deputy Minister opened proceedings under section 655(3) of the 1991 Act, invited written representations, and received several further complaints. Kostova submitted explanations and documents in May and June 2004, arguing that any delay in compiling lists of creditors’ claims was not her fault: the relevant case file had been sent to another town.

An inspector concluded that Kostova had nevertheless failed to identify the creditors within the statutory time-limit. On 2 August 2004 the Minister struck her off the list, citing that failure: the deadline expired on 8 May 2004, yet the lists reached the insolvency court only on 18 June 2004. The decision was published in the State Gazette on 20 August 2004.

Kostova sought judicial review. She reiterated that circumstances beyond her control had caused the delay, that procedural rules had been ignored, and that removal—the harshest available sanction—was disproportionate because the delay had caused no harm to the company or its creditors. Section 655(3) was reserved for serious or repeated breaches, and lighter measures existed under section 663.

A three-member SAC panel heard the case on 7 October 2004 and, in a judgment of 18 October 2004, dismissed the challenge. It examined the facts in detail, found that Kostova had culpably missed the deadline, and held the Minister’s decision lawful. On proportionality the court stated that the conditions of section 655(3) were met, that the choice of the heaviest sanction was a matter of administrative expediency within the Minister’s competence, and that the court lacked power to assess whether the sanction matched the gravity of the breach. The statutory provision did not require a “serious” breach; timely preparation of creditor lists was a pivotal stage of insolvency proceedings.

Kostova appealed on points of law, contesting both the finding of fault and the refusal to review proportionality. She argued that courts must quash decisions inconsistent with the object and purpose of the law, that section 655(3) existed to protect participants in insolvency proceedings from liquidators who actually endangered their interests, and that a single missed non-decisive deadline did not justify permanent disqualification from all future appointments.

A five-member SAC panel heard the appeal on 28 January 2005 and, in a final judgment of 28 March 2005, upheld the lower decision. It accepted that Kostova had been prevented from meeting the original 8 May deadline but held she could still have complied by 14 June; submission on 18 June therefore remained a breach. On proportionality the panel ruled that the Minister retained the right to select any lawful measure and that the severity of the sanction relative to the breach was unreviewable, a principle equally applied in labour-disciplinary cases. Procedural fairness had been observed because Kostova had been notified and allowed to make representations.

These facts form the core of the alleged Convention violation: the SAC’s consistent refusal to examine whether striking Kostova off the list was a proportionate response to a single missed deadline, despite her arguments that the measure was excessively harsh and inconsistent with the protective purpose of the statute. The courts confined themselves to verifying the existence of a formal breach and treated the choice and gravity of the sanction as non-justiciable discretion.

The applicant, a Bulgarian lawyer and member of the Sofia Bar, was added in December 2001 to the official list of persons qualified to act as liquidators of insolvent companies, maintained by the Minister of Justice under the Commerce Act 1991. In December 2003 the Sliven Regional Court appointed her liquidator of the state-owned company T. after opening winding-up proceedings. The company’s management repeatedly but unsuccessfully sought her replacement and, on 31 March 2004, complained to the Minister about her performance.

The Deputy Minister opened proceedings under section 655(3) of the 1991 Act, which empowers the Minister to strike a person off the list upon establishment of breaches connected with liquidator activity. The applicant submitted written representations and documents on several occasions (May–July 2004) after receiving successive invitations to respond to further complaints, including an allegation that she had missed the statutory deadline for drawing up lists of creditors’ claims. An inspector concluded that the missed deadline constituted a breach justifying removal; the Minister therefore struck the applicant off the list on 2 August 2004, noting that the time-limit had expired on 8 May while the lists were filed only on 18 June. The decision was published in the State Gazette.

The applicant sought judicial review, arguing that any delay was not her fault (the file had been sent elsewhere), that procedural rules had been ignored, and that the sanction was disproportionate. She stressed that the delay caused no harm to the company or its creditors and that section 655(3) reserved the heaviest possible penalty—permanent disqualification from acting as liquidator for any company—for serious or repeated breaches. Lighter measures existed under section 663.

A three-member panel of the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) dismissed the challenge on 18 October 2004. After examining the facts in detail it found that the applicant had, through her own fault, failed to meet the deadline. It held that the statutory conditions for striking-off were therefore satisfied and that the Minister had lawfully exercised his power. The choice of the “heaviest sanction” was a matter of expediency lying within the Minister’s competence; the court was not entitled to assess whether the penalty matched the seriousness of the breach. The panel added that the law imposed no “seriousness” requirement and that timely submission of claim lists was a key stage of insolvency proceedings.

The applicant appealed, reiterating that she had not been at fault and that the SAC was obliged to review whether the decision was consistent with the object and purpose of the law (protection of participants in insolvency proceedings). A five-member SAC panel upheld the judgment on 28 March 2005. It accepted that the applicant had been prevented from meeting the original 8 May deadline but found she could still have complied by 14 June; filing on 18 June therefore remained a breach. It confirmed that the Minister alone decided which lawful measure to apply and that the proportionality of the sanction was not reviewable, a position said to be settled both in administrative and in labour-law disciplinary cases. Procedural fairness was found to have been observed.

Under the applicable domestic law (Constitution Article 120 and the Administrative Procedure Act 1979 / Supreme Administrative Court Act 1997) courts were required to verify that administrative decisions were consistent with the object and purpose of the enabling statute, yet SAC case-law consistently treated the Minister’s choice whether and how severely to sanction a liquidator as unreviewable discretion once a breach had been established. The later Code of Administrative Procedure 2006 introduced an express proportionality principle, but it post-dated the impugned decisions.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaint that the SAC refused to examine the proportionality of her permanent removal from the liquidators’ list.

The case originated in an application by Bulgarian lawyer Galina Kostova, born in 1970 and living in Sofia, against Bulgaria. She complained that the Supreme Administrative Court refused to examine the proportionality of the Minister of Justice’s decision to strike her off the list of persons qualified to act as liquidators of insolvent companies.

In December 2001 the Minister included her on that list. In December 2003 the Sliven Regional Court appointed her liquidator of State-owned company T. The company’s management disapproved of her work and unsuccessfully sought her replacement by the insolvency court. On 31 March 2004 they complained to the Minister. Proceedings under section 655(3) of the Commerce Act 1991 were opened. The applicant submitted written representations and documents on several occasions (11 May, 16 June and 12 July 2004) in response to successive complaints, including an allegation that she had missed the statutory deadline for drawing up lists of creditors’ claims. She maintained that any delay was not her fault because the relevant case file had been sent to another town.

On 28 July 2004 a Ministry inspector concluded that she had failed to ascertain the creditors within the time-limit and proposed her removal from the list. On 2 August 2004 the Minister struck her off, citing her failure to submit the lists by 8 May 2004 (they were presented only on 18 June 2004). The decision was published in the State Gazette on 20 August 2004.

The applicant sought judicial review. She repeated that she had been prevented from acting in time, alleged procedural irregularities, and argued that removal from the list was disproportionate: the delay had caused no harm to the company or its creditors, the sanction was the harshest available and was intended for serious or repeated breaches, and lighter measures existed under the Act.

A three-member panel of the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the challenge on 18 October 2004. After a detailed examination of her conduct it found that she had, through her own fault, missed the deadline. The statutory conditions for striking her off were therefore met. The choice of the heaviest sanction was a matter of expediency within the Minister’s competence; the court had no power to assess whether its severity matched the seriousness of the breach. Arguments that the delay was not serious were rejected because the statute contained no “seriousness” requirement and the lists of claims formed a key stage of insolvency proceedings subject to strict time-limits. Procedural complaints were also dismissed.

On appeal the applicant again contested the finding of fault and the refusal to review proportionality. She submitted that courts must quash administrative decisions inconsistent with the object and purpose of the law (here, protecting participants in insolvency proceedings) and that total disqualification was excessive for a single, harmless delay.

A five-member panel upheld the first-instance judgment on 28 March 2005. It accepted that the applicant had been delayed until 8 May but held that she could still have complied by 14 June; submission on 18 June therefore remained late. The Minister was entitled to select any measure provided by law. The question whether the sanction’s severity corresponded to the breach was not reviewable, either in administrative judicial review or in disciplinary proceedings. The Minister had given her notice and an opportunity to be heard.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violation: the domestic courts’ categorical refusal to examine the proportionality of the striking-off decision, treating the Minister’s choice of sanction as unreviewable discretion.
001-126793:
The case of Mulosmani v. Albania arose from the 12 September 1998 assassination of opposition MP Azem Hajdari and one of his bodyguards (with a second bodyguard seriously wounded) outside Democratic Party headquarters in Tirana. The applicant, then head of public order at the Bajram Curri police commissariat, was immediately publicly named as the killer by Democratic Party chairman Sali Berisha; a party press statement reportedly confirmed this identification. The applicant denied involvement in a recorded telephone conversation with the Interior Minister (the tape later vanished). Turmoil, including the storming of government buildings, followed.

A criminal investigation collected forensic and ballistics evidence (no autopsies were performed) and statements from witnesses, some of whom later changed accounts to implicate the applicant. Key later statements came from a surviving bodyguard (Z.N., obtained via mutual legal assistance in Belgium), a prisoner (M., who first implicated others then the applicant), and a convicted observer (Ç.). The prosecutor did not initially question the applicant or Berisha. Charges under Articles 79(c), 78 and related Criminal Code provisions (intentional murder of an official and premeditated murder) were filed in December 1999; an arrest warrant issued and the applicant was declared a fugitive. He was arrested in May 2001 and questioned by the prosecutor without a lawyer present (though informed of his right to counsel). He later elected self-representation at a remand hearing.

The indictment (March 2001) listed the applicant and co-accused as organisers/participants. Trial began in April 2001 (initially in absentia with a court-appointed lawyer who promptly withdrew). The applicant first appeared in May 2001 and obtained counsel of choice. Multiple witnesses testified, including: the applicant’s former superior (applicant absent from a post-assassination meeting); M. (via video-link from Italy under CCP Article 151(3) and the Mutual Assistance Convention, over some co-accused objections); a bar owner and childhood friend of the victim (hearsay of applicant’s presence and prior threats); police driver A.L. (whose pre-trial statement was disclosed late, prompting an adjournment for cross-examination; he described a convoy to Tirana, the applicant in a Mercedes with a police siren, and post-shooting transport of a wounded co-accused); the applicant himself (admitted travelling to Tirana at a co-accused’s request, parking near the scene, and dragging the wounded man to hospital after others fired, but denied shooting or prior knowledge of a murder plan); an eyewitness (P.G., who identified the applicant in military clothing firing from the passenger seat); and Ç. (secured in advance under CCP Articles 316–322; claimed to see the applicant fire despite darkness and a closed café 60–200 m away). Berisha was repeatedly summoned but never appeared; a Constitutional Court reference on compelling an MP went unanswered.

The District Court (29 April 2002) convicted the applicant as organiser and executor of premeditated murder for revenge (reclassifying from official-position murder under Article 79(c) to Article 78 § 2, a provision in force only from January 2001). It relied on A.L., P.G. and others, rejected Ç. and M. as unreliable for co-accused, found no political motive, and imposed life imprisonment. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court (2002–2003) upheld the conviction, finding no violation of defence rights (late disclosure remedied by questioning; video evidence lawful; time to prepare adequate; reclassification permitted by CCP Article 375). The Constitutional Court dismissed a fair-trial complaint without reasons.

These facts underpin the applicant’s Article 6 complaints (fair-trial guarantees including confrontation, equality of arms, time to prepare, and reasoned assessment of contradictory/hearsay evidence obtained amid public accusations and political tension) and Article 7 complaint (reclassification under a post-offence statutory provision).

The case of Mulosmani v. Albania (Application no. 29864/03) concerned an Albanian police officer, Jaho Mulosmani (born 1977), convicted of involvement in the 12 September 1998 assassination of opposition Democratic Party (DP) MP Azem Hajdari and one bodyguard outside DP headquarters in Tirana. A second bodyguard was wounded. Mulosmani, then head of public order at the Bajram Curri police commissariat, alleged violations of Articles 6 (fair trial) and 7 (no punishment without law) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He is serving a life sentence.

Immediately after the shooting, DP chairman Sali Berisha publicly named Mulosmani as the perpetrator, a claim echoed in a DP press statement. This sparked political violence, including the storming of government buildings. No autopsies were performed. Early investigation included ballistics on weapons found at the scene and statements from five witnesses, one of whom claimed a clear view of the killer. The surviving bodyguard, Z.N., initially described an unknown shooter from a police-siren vehicle but later (in 2000, while in Belgium) implicated Mulosmani. Other witnesses, including prisoner M. (questioned in Italy) and recidivist Ç., eventually named Mulosmani and co-accused, though their accounts were inconsistent on details such as vehicles, clothing, and positions. The prosecutor did not question Mulosmani or Berisha at this stage.

Mulosmani was charged in December 1999 under Criminal Code provisions including Articles 78, 79(c), and 25 (premeditated murder, murder of an official, and collaboration). The District Court ordered his arrest, citing Berisha’s statements. Declared a fugitive in January 2001, he was arrested in May 2001 and questioned without a lawyer present (though informed of his right to one). He denied involvement, claiming he was dining nearby.

The trial began in April 2001. Mulosmani appeared in May and obtained counsel. Key testimonies included: K.G. (police chief) stating Mulosmani was reported ill at home; M. (via video link from Italy, admitted under CCP Article 151 § 3 and the Mutual Assistance Convention) describing Mulosmani procuring a car and being present near the scene; A.L. (police driver) placing Mulosmani at the scene in a siren-equipped Mercedes after a trip from Bajram Curri, armed and helping a wounded man; P.G. identifying Mulosmani (in military uniform) as a shooter after an argument; and Ç. claiming to have seen Mulosmani fire an automatic weapon from 60 meters in the dark (contradicted by the café owner, who said the venue closed early and was farther away). Z.N.’s later written statement was equivocal. Mulosmani testified that he drove F.H. and N.C. to the scene at F.H.’s request for a discussion with Hajdari, remained unarmed in the car, and only helped the wounded N.C. He requested Berisha’s testimony regarding an alleged deal with F.H.; despite multiple summonses, Berisha (an MP) did not appear, and a Constitutional Court referral on compulsory appearance went unresolved.

On 29 April 2002 the District Court convicted Mulosmani as organizer and executor. It rejected some witness accounts as unreliable but relied on others (A.L., P.G., etc.) and ballistics linking a 9 mm pistol (attributed to Mulosmani by A.L.) to the scene. Finding the motive was revenge (F.H. blaming Hajdari for his brother’s death) rather than Hajdari’s official position, it reclassified the charges under the post-2001 Article 78 § 2 (premeditated murder for revenge, punishable by 25 years to life) instead of Article 79(c). Life imprisonment was imposed.

The Court of Appeal (July 2002) and Supreme Court (February 2003) upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court rejected complaints about investigation disclosure, video-link evidence, A.L.’s statement, forensic testimony, time to prepare, and the reclassification (citing CCP Article 375, later amended). It noted the applicant’s participation, cross-examination opportunities, and that assessment of evidence was for lower courts. The Constitutional Court (July 2003) dismissed a further complaint as disclosing no fair-trial breach.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 6 issues (e.g., evidence admissibility, witness non-appearance, defense preparation, and reclassification) and Article 7 issues (application/reclassification of criminal provisions post-dating the 1998 events).

The case of Mulosmani v. Albania (Application no. 29864/03) before the European Court of Human Rights arose from the conviction of Jaho Mulosmani, then head of public order at the Bajram Curri police commissariat, for the 12 September 1998 assassination of Democratic Party MP Azem Hajdari and one bodyguard (with the attempted murder of a second bodyguard, Z.N.). Hajdari was shot outside DP headquarters in Tirana as he left the building. Democratic Party chairman Sali Berisha immediately publicly named Mulosmani as the perpetrator on television and in a party press statement, triggering widespread unrest.

Mulosmani denied involvement in a telephone interview with the Interior Minister the following day (a recording of which later vanished). An arrest order was issued but not executed amid the ensuing turmoil. Initial investigation included ballistics on weapons found at the scene (no autopsies were performed) and statements from five witnesses, one of whom claimed a clear view of the shooter and another who described two men exiting a green Mercedes with police markings. Z.N. initially described an unknown assailant from a car with a police siren and did not name Mulosmani. In 2000, prisoner M. (then in Italy) implicated Mulosmani and two other Bajram Curri officers after initially giving confused statements; he later admitted providing a vehicle. Recidivist Ç. also implicated Mulosmani. Z.N., questioned in Belgium, later suggested Mulosmani as the shooter (contradicting his earlier account).

On 14 December 1999 the prosecutor charged Mulosmani under Articles 79(c), 78 and related provisions of the Criminal Code, citing Berisha’s accusation as a key factor; the District Court ordered his arrest on the same basis. Declared a fugitive in January 2001, Mulosmani was arrested in May 2001 and questioned without a lawyer present (though informed of his right to counsel). He claimed an alibi of dining nearby and later admitted presence at the scene but denied shooting, asserting that co-accused F.H. (motivated by revenge over his brother’s killing) had fired.

The indictment of 13 March 2001 charged Mulosmani and co-accused with the assassination and related offences. Trial began in April 2001. Key witnesses included police colleague K.G. (who said Mulosmani was reported ill at home that evening); M. (via video-link from Italy, describing helping Mulosmani obtain a black Mercedes and later hearing shots); bar owner G.B. (reporting rumours and a prior threat by Mulosmani); driver A.L. (detailing a convoy to Tirana organised by Mulosmani, parking near the scene, and later transporting the wounded N.C.); eye-witness P.G. (identifying Mulosmani in military uniform as a shooter); and Ç. (claiming to have seen Mulosmani fire despite darkness and rain; the café owner later said the premises closed at 7 p.m.). Z.N.’s written statement suggested Mulosmani “could have been” the shooter. Berisha ignored multiple summonses; the court referred the question of compelling an MP’s attendance to the Constitutional Court (unresolved). Mulosmani testified, admitting driving F.H. and N.C. to the scene but denying any organisational role or firing a weapon.

On 29 April 2002 the District Court convicted Mulosmani as organiser and executor, relying particularly on A.L., P.G., G.B. and S.L. It reclassified the charges from murder of an MP on account of his position (Article 79(c)) to premeditated murder committed for revenge (Article 78 § 2, as amended in January 2001 after the offence), finding the motive to be F.H.’s vendetta rather than Hajdari’s parliamentary status. Mulosmani received life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing insufficient evidence (contradictory and speculative witness accounts, no proof he possessed or used a 9 mm pistol, no autopsy), lack of proven premeditation or motive, unlawful reclassification (a prerogative of the prosecutor), denial of adequate time to prepare further statements, unlawful admission of M.’s video evidence, failure to summon key witnesses, and media/political influence. The Court of Appeal (July 2002), Supreme Court (February 2003) and Constitutional Court (July 2003, declaring the complaint inadmissible) all upheld the conviction, finding no fair-trial breach, lawful reclassification under Article 375 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and proper handling of evidence and defence rights.

Mulosmani alleged violations of Article 6 (fair trial, including equality of arms, examination of witnesses, time and facilities for defence, and reasoned judgments) and Article 7 (retrospective application of the 2001 amendment via reclassification of the 1998 offence).

**CASE OF BOGDEL v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 41248/06)**

The applicants, Piotras Bogdel and his daughter Snežana Bogdel, Lithuanian nationals living in Trakai, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that domestic courts breached legal certainty by their interpretation of the statutory limitation period applicable to a public authority’s claim to annul their land title. They further alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from the annulment of their ownership of a plot of land.

In March 1992 the Trakai City Council leased a 22 m² State-owned plot at 41 Karaimų Street (at the entrance to Trakai castle) to Galina Bogdel (Piotras’s wife and Snežana’s mother) for five years to construct a kiosk. The kiosk was completed by February 1993. A December 1993 territorial plan for Trakai old town, based on cultural-heritage expertise, stipulated that the plot was not to be divided or privatised. In July 1994 the plot was enlarged to 134 m² and re-leased for five years. On 18 January 1995 the Trakai District Executive Council approved its sale to Galina for LTL 2,874; the purchase agreement was signed on 10 February 1995 and registered, making her the owner. After her death later that year the applicants inherited the land and kiosk, which they converted into a café.

In July 1998 the applicants sought to enlarge the plot further for hygiene reasons connected with public catering. Public consultation in 1999 provoked local opposition: residents complained of a noisy café in the historically sensitive Trakai Historical National Park immediately in front of the castle. A private complaint to the Seimas prompted the State Audit Office (SAO) to investigate. Its 3 July 2000 decision found that the 1994 lease and 1995 sale had breached the Law on Protected Territories, the 1992 Trakai Historical National Park regulations and the 1993 territorial plan, all of which prohibited privatisation of land in the protected urban-heritage site. The SAO invited the Head of Vilnius County Administration (HVCA) to act.

The HVCA sued in April 2001 to annul the lease, sale decision and purchase agreement. The applicants argued the claim was time-barred. On 11 July 2005 the Trakai District Court held that the three-year limitation period under the 1964 Civil Code (Article 84, starting when the claimant knew or ought to have known of the violation—Article 86) began only on 3 July 2000, the date of the SAO report. Counties had assumed State-land competence in 1995 but had no duty to review earlier municipal contracts. The court found the transactions unlawful, declared them void and ordered unilateral restitution of the land to the State (no refund). The Vilnius Regional Court (8 November 2005) upheld the limitation ruling but ordered double restitution, refunding the LTL 2,874 purchase price. The Supreme Court (10 May 2006) confirmed both courts’ reasoning: the limitation period ran from the authorities’ actual knowledge of the breach, not from the 1995 sale, because the new county administration was not obliged to audit past municipal acts. It reiterated that 1992–1993 legislation and the 1993 plan had already rendered the plot inalienable.

After the Supreme Court judgment the applicants retained ownership of the café building and obtained 87-year leases of the land from the HVCA.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centre on the 1995 acquisition of land already designated non-privatisable, the six-year delay before the HVCA acted, the courts’ choice of the 2000 SAO report as the starting point of limitation, the subsequent annulment of title and the modest monetary restitution.

The case of Bogdel v. Lithuania (no. 41248/06) involves Lithuanian applicants Piotras Bogdel and his daughter Snežana, who alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (legal certainty in applying statutory limitation) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property rights) after Lithuanian courts annulled their title to a plot of land.

In March 1992 the Trakai City Council leased Galina Bogdel (Piotras’s wife and Snežana’s mother) a 22 m² State-owned plot at 41 Karaimų Street, at the entrance to Trakai Castle, for five years to build a kiosk. On 18 January 1995 the District Council approved the sale of that plot to Galina for LTL 2 874; the purchase agreement was signed on 10 February 1995 and registered, conferring ownership.

Galina died later that year. The applicants inherited the land and kiosk and, with municipal permission, converted the kiosk into a café. In 1998 they sought to double the plot’s size to meet hygiene standards for the expanding tourist trade; the municipality tasked them with preparing a new territorial plan. Publication of the draft in 1999 provoked local protests. Residents complained that a “noisy café” now stood in a historically sensitive location inside Trakai Historical National Park, immediately in front of the castle. A private citizen wrote to Parliament alleging that the plot, which could never have been privatised, had been obtained illegally.

The State Audit Office (SAO) investigated. Its 3 July 2000 decision found that the 1994 lease and 1995 sale had breached the Law on Protected Territories, the park regulations and the 1993 territorial plan. A municipal audit reached the same conclusion. The Head of the Vilnius County Administration (HVCA) was instructed to take remedial action.

In 2001 the HVCA sued to annul the lease, the sale decision and the purchase agreement. The applicants pleaded that the three-year limitation period under the 1964 Civil Code had expired. The Trakai District Court (11 July 2005) held that time began to run only on 3 July 2000, when the SAO report first made the HVCA aware of the breach. Newly created county administrations had no duty to review earlier municipal contracts. On the merits the court declared the transactions void for violation of heritage-protection and planning laws, ordered restitution of the land to the State and awarded no compensation. The Vilnius Regional Court (8 November 2005) confirmed the limitation ruling but directed repayment of the original LTL 2 874. The Supreme Court (10 May 2006) dismissed the applicants’ further appeal, reiterating that limitation started when the HVCA acquired knowledge of the unlawfulness and that the plot had been inalienable since 1992–93.

After the final judgment the applicants retained ownership of the café building and were granted 87-year leases of the same land. These facts form the basis of their complaints that the courts’ calculation of limitation (starting in 2000 rather than 1995) destroyed legitimate expectations of title stability, and that the annulment of an inherited, registered and improved property without adequate compensation violated their property rights.

The applicants, Piotras and Snežana Bogdel, inherited a 134 m² plot at 41 Karaimų Street in Trakai (at the entrance to Trakai Castle, within the Trakai Historical National Park) after Galina Bogdel (Piotras’s wife and Snežana’s mother) died in 1995. The plot originated as State land. In March 1992 the Trakai City Council leased 22 m² of it to Galina for five years to build a kiosk; by February 1993 the kiosk existed. Nonetheless, in July 1994 the District Executive Council enlarged the lease to 134 m² and, in January–February 1995, sold the plot to Galina for LTL 2 874. The sale was registered and she became owner. The applicants later converted the kiosk into a café.

In 1998 they sought to enlarge the plot further; the municipality authorised them to coordinate a new plan. Public controversy followed in 1999: neighbours objected to a “noisy café” in a historically sensitive location, a public hearing was held, and a private complainant wrote to the Seimas alleging unlawful privatisation of protected land. The complaint reached the State Audit Office (SAO). In July 2000 the SAO found that the 1994–1995 lease and sale violated the Law on Protected Territories, the park’s regulations, the 1993 territorial plan and cultural-heritage rules; a municipal audit reached the same conclusion. The SAO instructed the Head of Vilnius County Administration (HVCA) to act.

In 2001 the HVCA sued to annul the lease, sale decision and sale contract. The applicants argued the claim was time-barred. The 1964 Civil Code prescribed a three-year limitation period running from the date the claimant knew or ought to have known of the violation. The Vilnius Regional Court (November 2005) upheld the finding on limitation and merits but ordered restitution of the original LTL 2 874. The Supreme Court (May 2006) confirmed both points, stressing that starting the clock in 1995 would have been unreasonable and that the plot had been inalienable since the park’s creation in 1992 and the 1993 legislation and plan.

After the final judgment the applicants retained title to the café building and obtained an 87-year lease of the same plot. They complained to the Court that the domestic courts’ interpretation of the limitation period violated legal certainty (Article 6 § 1) and that the annulment of their title violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Arsovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (no. 30206/06) was brought by Macedonian nationals Stojko Arsovski, Stefan Arsovski (continued by his widow and daughters after his 2007 death), and Verka Arsovska, also originally on behalf of the late Milan Arsovski. They alleged that the State deprived them of the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicants’ predecessor held title since 1952 to plot no. 1339, a pasture. A 1968 gift transferred it first to Stojko Arsovski and then to all the applicants. In 1973 the State was erroneously registered as owner. In 1977 the Kratovo City Council authorised company S. to use the land for intensive agriculture, but the company never did so. In April 1996 the applicants (and Milan Arsovski) sued the State for recognition of title to several plots including no. 1339. That same year the Ministry authorised the company to conduct geological research. On 19 March 2002 the Kratovo Court of First Instance recognised the applicants’ title; the Skopje Court of Appeal confirmed the judgment on 26 June 2002, noting that the applicants had always had actual possession.

Immediately thereafter, on 26 July 2002, company S. applied for expropriation of the plot so that it could extract mineral water. It relied on an 8 May 2000 concession contract granting it a renewable 30-year right to exploit geothermal mineral water in return for payments to the State. On 9 December 2002 the Kratovo Office of the Ministry of Finance ordered full expropriation under sections 2 § 1 (6) and 3 § 1 (3) of the Expropriation Act, to enable construction of a pit. The applicants appealed, arguing that mineral-water extraction was not mentioned in any relevant plan and that the Act permitted only partial expropriation (an easement, lease or temporary restriction) or a maximum three-year lease for research into and exploitation of mineral resources (sections 4 and 6), not outright loss of title.

The Government Appeal Commission dismissed the appeal on 2 June 2003, holding that the expropriation served the public interest and that the company would pay compensation. The Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on 16 November 2005 (served January 2006), reiterating that the measure pursued the public interest of constructing objects for research into and exploitation of natural resources, that the company had supplied the required documents, and that compensation had been fixed in separate proceedings.

In those non-contentious proceedings the first-instance court, relying on an expert report, awarded the applicants jointly the equivalent of EUR 880—the plot’s market value based on location, size, quality, construction potential and access—while ordering them to pay the company EUR 475 in costs. The Court of Appeal confirmed the award on 15 September 2005.

In 2009 the Constitutional Court, in proceedings brought by two individuals including applicant Verka Arsovska, declared section 3 § 1 (3) of the Expropriation Act unconstitutional (ex nunc). It held that the State’s margin of appreciation in defining public interest does not permit expropriation for the commercial benefit of private persons without first exhausting less restrictive measures such as a long-term lease or concession. Allowing confiscation “always and on every occasion \ldots for the benefit of economically powerful recipients” would subordinate owners’ constitutional rights to private commercial interests.

Subsequent land-register extracts recorded the company as owner in 2008 and the State as owner with the company as beneficiary in 2010. These facts underlie the complaint that the full expropriation was neither lawful nor proportionate.

The applicants (Macedonian nationals, one of whom died during the proceedings, with heirs continuing) held title since 1952 to plot no. 1339, a pasture later gifted among them. The State was erroneously recorded as owner in 1973. In 1977 the Kratovo City Council authorised a company to use the plot for intensive agriculture, but no such activity occurred. In 1996 the applicants sued the State for recognition of title to several plots including this one. Courts of first instance and appeal in 2002 confirmed their title, noting they had always been in actual possession.

Meanwhile, in 1996 the Ministry authorised the company to conduct geological research. In 2000 the State granted the company a 30-year renewable concession to exploit geothermal mineral water from the plot, in return for fixed annual payments plus a share of profits. Immediately after the 2002 title judgment, the company requested expropriation so that it could extract the water. On 9 December 2002 the Ministry of Finance ordered full expropriation under sections 2 § 1 (6) and 3 § 1 (3) of the Expropriation Act, citing the public interest in constructing objects for research into and exploitation of natural resources.

The applicants appealed, arguing that mineral-water extraction was not specifically provided for in any applicable plan, that the Act envisaged only partial expropriation (an easement or temporary restriction) or a three-year lease under sections 4 and 6 for mineral-resource activities, and that full expropriation therefore violated legal certainty and the Constitution. The Government Appeal Commission dismissed the appeal in June 2003, holding that the required documents had been submitted, that a 1996 City Council decision contemplated exploitation, that the measure served the public interest, and that the company would pay compensation. The Supreme Court rejected a further appeal in November 2005, reiterating that expropriation was in the public interest for research and exploitation of natural resources and that compensation had been fixed in separate proceedings.

In those non-contentious proceedings the first-instance court, relying on an expert valuation of location, size, land quality, construction potential and access, awarded the applicants jointly the equivalent of EUR 880 (the plot’s market value). They were ordered to pay the company EUR 475 in costs. The award was confirmed on appeal in 2005. Subsequent land-register extracts recorded first the company and later the State as owner, with the company as beneficiary.

In 2009 the Constitutional Court, in proceedings brought by two individuals including one applicant, declared section 3 § 1 (3) of the Expropriation Act unconstitutional. It held that merely listing categories of works as being in the public interest was insufficient, that construction for private commercial purposes could not automatically be treated as public interest, and that less restrictive measures (long-term lease or concession) had to be exhausted first; otherwise the commercial interests of economically powerful private parties would prevail over owners’ constitutional rights.

The applicants alleged that the full expropriation deprived them of the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions contrary to the Constitution, the Expropriation Act and the Convention. Relevant domestic law confirmed that mineral resources belong to the State regardless of surface title, that concessions govern their exploitation, and that the Act itself contemplated leases of limited duration for such activities.

The case of Arsovski and Others v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (no. 30206/06) was brought by three Macedonian nationals (Stojko Arsovski, the late Stefan Arsovski whose heirs continued the claim, and Verka Arsovska), also on behalf of the late Milan Arsovski. They alleged that the State unlawfully deprived them of the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions.

The applicants’ predecessor had held title to pasture plot no. 1339 since 1952. A 1968 gift transferred possession first to Stojko Arsovski and then to all of them. In 1973 the State was wrongly registered as owner. In 1977 the Kratovo City Council authorised company S. to use the land for intensive agriculture, but the company never did so. In 1996 the applicants (and Milan) sued the State for recognition of title to several plots including no. 1339. That same year the Ministry authorised the company to conduct geological research. On 19 March 2002 the Kratovo Court of First Instance recognised the applicants’ title; the Skopje Court of Appeal confirmed the judgment on 26 June 2002, noting that the applicants had always been in actual possession.

On 26 July 2002 the company applied for expropriation so that it could extract mineral water. It produced a May 2000 concession contract under which the State had granted it a renewable 30-year right to exploit geothermal mineral water in return for fixed and profit-based payments. On 9 December 2002 the Kratovo office of the Ministry of Finance ordered full expropriation under sections 2(1)(6) and 3(1)(3) of the Expropriation Act so that the company could construct an extraction pit.

The applicants appealed, arguing that mineral-water extraction was not provided for in any relevant plan and that the Act permitted only partial expropriation or a three-year lease (ss. 4 and 6), not the complete loss of title. The Government Appeal Commission dismissed the appeal on 2 June 2003, holding that the expropriation served the public interest, the company had filed the necessary documents, a 1996 municipal decision existed, and the company would pay compensation. The Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on 16 November 2005, repeating that the measure was in the public interest for the construction of facilities for research into and exploitation of natural resources and that compensation had been fixed separately. The public prosecutor later declined to seek a legality review.

In parallel non-contentious proceedings the first-instance court, relying on an expert valuation that took account of location, size, soil quality, building potential and access, awarded the applicants jointly the equivalent of EUR 880 (they were also ordered to pay the company EUR 475 in costs). The award was confirmed on appeal in September 2005.

In February 2009 the Constitutional Court, on an application brought by Verka Arsovska and another person, declared section 3(1)(3) of the Expropriation Act unconstitutional. It held that the State’s margin of appreciation in defining public interest could not be exercised in a manifestly unreasonable way; merely listing types of construction as being in the public interest was insufficient, especially when the beneficiary was a private person. Expropriation could be used only after less restrictive measures such as a long-term lease or concession had been exhausted; otherwise private commercial interests would prevail over both the public interest and the constitutional right to property.

The relevant constitutional provisions (Arts. 8(1)(6) and 30) protect property and permit deprivation only in the public interest and as provided by law. The Expropriation Act treated the construction of facilities for the research and exploitation of natural resources as being in the public interest and allowed expropriation for the benefit of private legal or natural persons. Section 6 expressly contemplated a maximum three-year lease for such activities. The Mineral Resources Act classified mineral water as a State-owned resource irrespective of surface title and required a concession for its exploitation.

These facts—rapid full expropriation of land whose title had only just been judicially confirmed, the availability of statutory alternatives (lease or concession) that would have preserved ownership, the modest compensation awarded, and the subsequent constitutional invalidation of the enabling provision—form the core of the applicants’ complaint that the interference with their possessions was neither lawful nor proportionate.
001-115853:
The case of Baltiņš v. Latvia originated in an application (no. 25282/07) lodged on 12 June 2007 by Latvian national G. Baltiņš (born 1970), who alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention. He claimed that unlawful operational investigative measures had resulted in an undercover police agent inciting him to acquire and sell narcotic substances, for which he was later convicted, thereby denying him a fair trial.

The applicant had been convicted in July 2003 of unauthorised acquisition and storage of 0.5108 grams of methamphetamine for personal use (he pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence). He also had four prior theft convictions. Since 2002 the Anti-Drugs Office (ONAP) held information of his involvement in drug trafficking. In February 2004 new unofficial information prompted a preliminary inquiry (including Supreme Court-authorised phone tapping). This confirmed his involvement, leading to the opening of operational case no. 7019304 on 27 October 2004, which involved surveillance, further telephone interception and other measures.

On 2, 11 and 30 November 2004 a specially authorised prosecutor approved investigative tests under section 15(3) of the Law on Operational Activities (LOA). These authorised an undercover agent (I.) to make “test” purchases of amphetamine from the applicant in order to record his behaviour in a situation that might result in criminal activity. The operations proceeded as follows. On 3 November 2004 I. telephoned the applicant, arranged a meeting and handed over LVL 500 in marked notes; later that day the applicant delivered approximately 100 grams of amphetamine (conversations were recorded). On 8 November they met again; the applicant stated he had 300 grams available that day and described drug trafficking as his “only bread.” On 25 November I. requested the same quantity and type of drugs; the applicant accepted another LVL 500 and later delivered a further 100 grams. On 1 December I. proposed purchasing 400 grams for LVL 2,000. The applicant accepted half-payment, later complained that the notes were marked, and thereafter became uncontactable.

Criminal proceedings were instituted on 1 December 2004 for aggravated unauthorised acquisition and possession of narcotic substances with intent to sell. The applicant was arrested on 6 December. A search of his home yielded a scale bearing traces of psychotropic substances, money and a SIM card. At first-instance trial the Rīga Regional Court convicted him on 21 October 2005 and imposed a ten-year sentence. It relied on police reports of the tests of 3 and 25 November and 1–6 December, recorded conversations, forensic reports confirming the seized drugs and traces on the scale and the applicant’s hands, and physical evidence (including the scale and storage devices). Agent I. did not attend; his pre-trial statements were read out. A surveillance officer testified that the applicant had evaded tracking and met suspicious persons; a currency-exchange worker confirmed he had presented the marked notes for verification.

On appeal the applicant initially requested I.’s attendance but later withdrew the request. The Rīga Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 15 September 2006, treating the incitement plea as a mere defence tactic. In cassation the Senate of the Supreme Court likewise rejected the plea. It noted that the former Code of Criminal Procedure had not regulated special investigative activities, that the prosecutor had duly authorised the tests, that there was no evidence the officer had incited the applicant or overcome any resistance, and that the police had possessed sufficient prior information to suspect him of drug-related offences. The LOA itself prohibits incitement and confines investigative tests to recording behaviour in situations liable to result in crime, without forcing the suspect to act.

The case of Baltiņš v. Latvia (Application no. 25282/07) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial). The applicant, a Latvian national born in 1970, claimed that undercover police operations unlawfully incited him to commit the offence of acquiring and selling narcotic substances, for which he was later convicted.

The applicant had a criminal record, including four prior theft convictions and a July 2003 conviction for unauthorised acquisition and storage of 0.5108 grams of methamphetamine for personal use, resulting in a suspended sentence. Latvian police asserted that since 2002 the Anti-Drugs Office had information suggesting his involvement in drug trafficking. In February 2004, following new unofficial information, they opened an operational verification case (No. 7004204), involving inquiries and Supreme Court-authorised phone tapping. This led to an operational case (No. 7019304) in October 2004, incorporating surveillance and further interceptions.

On 2, 11 and 30 November 2004, a specially authorised prosecutor approved “investigative tests” under section 15(3) of the Law on Operational Activities. These permitted an undercover agent (I.) to attempt test purchases of amphetamine from the applicant, aiming to record his behaviour in a situation potentially conducive to crime while leaving him free to refuse.

The operations unfolded as follows. On 3 November 2004, I. contacted the applicant, who initially declined a meeting but later arranged one. I. handed over 500 Latvian lati (approximately €700) in marked notes; the applicant subsequently delivered around 100 grams of amphetamine at a petrol station. Conversations were recorded. On 8 November, they met in a supermarket to build trust. The applicant inquired about the prior deal, stated that drug trafficking was his “only bread,” and offered 300 grams for sale that day or the next (portions of this exchange were inaudible on recordings). On 25 November, I. requested a similar quantity; after receiving another 500 lati, the applicant delivered approximately 100 grams by concealing it under a restaurant chair cover. On 1 December, I. proposed purchasing 400 grams for 2,000 lati, paying half in advance. The applicant later complained that the notes were marked and thereafter became uncontactable.

Criminal proceedings commenced on 1 December 2004 for aggravated unauthorised acquisition and possession of narcotics with intent to sell. The applicant was arrested on 6 December and refused to make statements. A search of his home yielded a weighing scale bearing traces of amphetamine and cocaine, cash and a SIM card. He was charged and committed for trial. At the Rīga Regional Court hearing on 21 October 2005, I. did not appear and his pre-trial statements were read out. The court convicted the applicant and imposed a ten-year sentence, relying on officers’ reports of the tests, recorded conversations, forensic analyses of seized items and substances, and related documentary evidence.

On appeal, the applicant initially sought I.’s attendance but withdrew the request. The Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 15 September 2006, characterising the incitement claim as a mere defence tactic. In cassation proceedings, the Senate of the Supreme Court rejected the plea on 2007, holding that the operations complied with the Law on Operational Activities, that police possessed sufficient prior information to suspect the applicant, and that there was no evidence I. had overcome any reluctance or applied pressure. The applicant remained free to decline participation.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that the undercover measures constituted prohibited incitement, rendering the subsequent trial unfair through reliance on evidence obtained thereby.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Baltiņš v. Latvia (Application no. 25282/07) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant, a Latvian national born in 1970, claimed he had been denied a fair trial after undercover police operations incited him to commit the drug offences of which he was later convicted.

The applicant had a prior criminal record, including four theft convictions and a July 2003 suspended sentence for unauthorised acquisition and storage of 0.5108 grams of methamphetamine for personal use. Latvian Anti-Drugs Office records indicated that unofficial information of his involvement in narcotics trafficking had existed since 2002. Fresh unofficial information in February 2004 prompted a preliminary inquiry, operational records, authorised telephone tapping and, on 27 October 2004, a formal operational case. The stated aim of subsequent undercover measures was to place the applicant in a situation in which he could either supply narcotics or refuse to do so.

On 2, 11 and 30 November 2004 a specially authorised prosecutor approved “investigative tests” under section 15(3) of the Law on Operational Activities. An undercover officer, I., then contacted the applicant. On 3 November I. initiated a telephone call, arranged a meeting and handed over 500 lati in marked notes; later that day the applicant supplied approximately 100 grams of amphetamine. On 8 November I. met the applicant again “to gain his trust” and inquired about larger quantities; the applicant offered 300 grams and remarked that trafficking was his “only bread.” On 25 November I. again requested the same quantity, paid another 500 lati and received a further 100 grams. On 1 December I. offered 2 000 lati for 400 grams, paid half in advance and obtained a small discount; the applicant later complained that the notes were marked and thereafter ceased contact.

Criminal proceedings for aggravated unauthorised acquisition and possession with intent to sell were opened on 1 December 2004. The applicant was arrested on 6 December; a search of his home yielded a scale bearing traces of amphetamine and cocaine, cash and a SIM card. He declined to make statements. Officer I. did not appear at the Rīga Regional Court trial; his pre-trial statements and audio recordings of the conversations were read into evidence, together with surveillance reports, forensic analyses and the testimony of a currency-exchange clerk who had examined the marked notes. On 21 October 2005 the court convicted the applicant and imposed a ten-year sentence. The incitement plea was rejected on appeal (15 September 2006) as a mere defence tactic and again by the Senate of the Supreme Court, which held that the police had possessed sufficient prior suspicion, that the operations merely recorded the applicant’s existing criminal intent, and that no pressure or inducement capable of overcoming reluctance had been applied. The authorising decisions themselves remained classified and were never disclosed to the defence or placed in the case file.

These facts formed the core of the Article 6 complaint: that the police, lacking adequate independent verification of pre-existing criminal activity, had themselves instigated the offences through repeated solicitations and the creation of opportunities that would not otherwise have arisen.
001-115874:
The case of Mitrofan v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 50054/07) concerns a Moldovan national, Valeriu Mitrofan (born 1963), who alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his criminal conviction and subsequent detention. At the relevant time, Mitrofan served as head of a private high school (V.) and acting head of a state-funded industrial college. In 2004, he faced investigation for alleged fraud and abuse of power, specifically for accepting tuition payments from two students at V. without recording them in the school accounts.

Mitrofan was briefly detained in September 2004 but released after the Chișinău Court of Appeal found no flight risk. On 20 November 2006, the Grigoriopol District Court convicted him of fraud and sentenced him to three years' imprisonment (acquitting him of remaining charges for lack of evidence). He was immediately placed in Chișinău Prison no. 13. On 8 February 2007, the Chișinău Court of Appeal reclassified the offence as negligent performance of duties under Article 329(1) of the Criminal Code—based on his admission of students after the Ministry of Education had suspended V.'s licence in December 2003—and reduced the sentence to eight months.

Mitrofan appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice, arguing that two essential elements of the offence were absent. First, as head of a private institution, he was not a “public official” (persoană cu funcţii de răspundere) as defined in Article 123 of the Criminal Code. Second, the alleged damage (MDL 3,020) fell well below the “large-scale” threshold of MDL 10,000 set by Articles 64 and 126. He further contended that his court challenge to the 2003 licence-suspension order had automatically suspended its effect. On 28 June 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed these arguments as “unsubstantiated and contradicted by the material evidence,” citing only the enrolment contract, payment receipts and the licence-suspension order themselves. It did not engage with the legal definitions of “public official” or “large-scale damage.” Taking account of mitigating factors (no prior convictions, good social standing), the court replaced imprisonment with a fine and ordered Mitrofan’s immediate release after approximately seven months’ detention; time already served extinguished the fine.

The second limb of the application concerned the conditions of that detention. Prison no. 13 occupied a 165-year-old building. Mitrofan was held in a 26 m² cell with 11–14 other inmates (well below the statutory 4 m² per person required by the Enforcement Code). The cell lacked proper ventilation (air entered only through holes in a window net), was unheated in winter and overheated in summer, had damp walls and ceiling, and contained an unseparated toilet. For the first five months he received no bedding and slept on a bare mattress infested with insects; bedding, once supplied, was changed infrequently and never coincided with the weekly shower, perpetuating infestation. Lighting was inadequate for reading, food portions (especially protein) fell short of government norms, and the cell was never cleaned. Mitrofan submitted 44 written complaints requesting reduced occupancy, extra exercise, ventilation, a non-smoking cell, proper food, insect control and materials for cell repairs. The authorities sent only five replies, none of which substantively addressed the complaints. A window opposite the cell was eventually opened; a request to use a reading room was refused because none existed. A prison doctor later noted a tuberculosis-exposure risk.

Domestic reports (Ombudsman 2010, parliamentary and ministerial evaluations of the 2004–2008 National Human Rights Action Plan) and the CPT’s 2007 visit confirmed systemic overcrowding (average 2 m² per prisoner), inadequate sanitation, ventilation and nutrition throughout the Moldovan prison estate, including Prison no. 13, attributing the problems to chronic underfunding despite legislative and policy reforms.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s claims that his detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment and that the Supreme Court failed to examine the principal legal arguments of his defence.

His sentence was reduced to eight months.

Mitrofan appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice, arguing that two essential elements of Article 329(1) were absent: he was not a “public official” (as defined in Article 123) because V. was private, and the alleged damage (MDL 3,020) fell below the “large-scale” threshold of MDL 10,000 (Articles 64 and 126). It substituted a fine for imprisonment (waived because of time already served) and ordered his release after approximately seven months in custody.

**CASE OF MITROFAN v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA (Application no. 50054/07), ECtHR (Third Section), Judgment of 15 January 2013 (final 15 April 2013)**

The applicant, Valeriu Mitrofan (born 1963), a Moldovan national and head of private high school V. (also acting head of a state-funded college), faced a 2004 criminal investigation for fraud and abuse of power. He was accused of accepting undisclosed tuition payments (MDL 3,020 total) from two students at V. After brief arrest and release in September 2004 (Court of Appeal finding no flight or interference risk given his family ties and fixed address), the Grigoriopol District Court on 20 November 2006 convicted him of fraud, imposing a three-year prison sentence (acquitting him of other charges for lack of evidence). He was immediately detained in Chișinău Prison no. 13.

On 8 February 2007 the Chișinău Court of Appeal reclassified the offence under Article 329(1) of the Criminal Code (negligent performance of duties by a public official causing large-scale damage). It found he had improperly admitted the students after a 25 December 2003 Ministry of Education order suspended V.’s licence (requiring transfer of pupils) and reduced the sentence to eight months. In his appeal on points of law the applicant argued two core elements of Article 329(1) were absent: (i) as head of a private institution he was not a “public official” (defined in Article 123 as a person exercising public-authority, administrative or economic functions in a state or local body); and (ii) the damage (MDL 3,020) fell well below the “large-scale” threshold of 500 conventional units (MDL 10,000) under Articles 64 and 126. He further contended that his pending court challenge to the 2003 order had suspended its effect.

On 28 June 2007 the Supreme Court of Justice rejected these arguments as “unsubstantiated and contradicted by the material evidence” (citing enrolment contracts, receipts and the 2003 order) without addressing the statutory definitions or the “public official”/damage-threshold issues. It noted mitigating circumstances (no prior convictions, good social standing) and replaced imprisonment with a fine, from which he was dispensed after already serving approximately seven months; he was released that day.

Throughout detention the applicant described inhuman conditions in a 165-year-old prison: a 26 m² cell holding 11–14 detainees (far below the statutory 4 m² minimum under the Enforcement Code), no ventilation (air only through netted window holes), extreme seasonal temperatures, damp walls/ceiling, unseparated toilet, no bedding for the first five months (thereafter rarely changed and infested with parasites), weak lighting, weekly showers misaligned with bedding changes, and inadequate food (portions below government standards, especially meat, fish, eggs and dairy). He submitted 44 complaints seeking reduced occupancy, extra exercise, ventilation, a non-smoking cell (citing passive smoking as worse than his sentence), insect control, repairs and proper food. Authorities issued only five generic replies (mostly that transfer depended on final conviction) and made two minor adjustments (corridor window opened; confirmation of no library reading room). He also protested placement in a closed rather than semi-open regime and, on 2 July 2007, was medically assessed as at risk of tuberculosis.

Domestic reports (Ombudsman 2010, Ministry of Justice and parliamentary reviews of the 2004–2008 National Human Rights Action Plan) and the CPT’s 2007 visit confirmed systemic overcrowding (average 2 m² per detainee), dilapidated infrastructure, poor sanitation, ventilation, lighting and nutrition across Moldovan prisons, including Prison no. 13, despite reform plans and falling inmate numbers. These facts underpinned the applicant’s complaints of inhuman detention (Article 3) and failure of the courts to examine his principal defence arguments (Article 6).
