The applicant, Samuel Betteridge (born 1954), was convicted of rape in 2005 and sentenced to an IPP (imprisonment for public protection) with a tariff of 3.5 years (less 98 days on remand). His tariff expired on 18 December 2008. IPPs, introduced in 2005 for dangerous offenders, are indeterminate sentences requiring Parole Board review after tariff expiry to determine if continued detention is necessary for public protection; the Secretary of State must then release if directed.

A few months before expiry, the Secretary of State referred the case to the Parole Board (under s.239(2) Criminal Justice Act 2003) for possible recategorisation to open conditions. On 15 September 2008, the Board (including psychologist and psychiatrist members) declined to recommend this. It cited remaining treatment needs, underestimated risk (including sadistic elements of the offences), insufficient attention in prior assessments, and the applicant's only superficial understanding of his offending and risk-management strategies. Balancing sentence progression against public safety, it found insufficient evidence that his risk of sexual/violent reoffending could be safely managed outside closed conditions.

On 13 October 2008 (two months before expiry), the Secretary of State referred the case for post-tariff review under s.28 Crime (Sentences) Act 1997. No hearing occurred by tariff expiry. On 20 February 2009 the Board agreed to an oral hearing, but resource constraints (a backlog of cases) meant the earliest slot was May 2009; even then, no panel could be provided. It was rescheduled for September 2009. The applicant sought judicial review of the delay.

In those proceedings, the Parole Board conceded a breach of Article 5 § 4 (right to speedy judicial review of detention lawfulness) due to the May-to-September delay. The Secretary of State disagreed, arguing the September 2008 pre-tariff opinion showed no realistic prospect of release. On 23 June 2009 the High Court found a breach: the delay stemmed from Parole Board manpower shortages (panels for lifers/IPPs requiring a judicial chair), rendering the review unspeedy. Article 5 § 4 requires a speedy hearing even if the outcome is inevitable detention. However, no damages were payable, as a timely hearing would not have ordered release (the 2008 opinion made this clear; at best, open conditions might have been considered later). No declaration or mandatory order (to prioritise the applicant over others) was granted; the judgment itself recorded the breach, and queue-jumping was inappropriate amid a systemic backlog. The judge noted IPP numbers had overwhelmed the system (contrary to resource-neutral intentions), that remedial steps were underway (though delayed), and that future claims should generally be discouraged absent special circumstances.

The September 2009 hearing did not occur. A review finally took place on 13 January 2010, recommending (and obtaining) transfer to open conditions. Counsel advised that an appeal against the High Court decision would fail, as the Court of Appeal would not prioritise one case amid systemic resource shortages.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 5 § 4 violation (delayed post-tariff review due to Parole Board capacity issues following the IPP influx) and the claim of no effective domestic remedy (refusal of declaration or mandatory relief despite conceded breach).

The case Betteridge v. the United Kingdom (App. No. 1497/10, ECtHR 29 January 2013) concerned alleged violations of Article 5 § 4 ECHR (right to speedy review of detention lawfulness) and lack of effective domestic remedy. The applicant, Samuel Betteridge (born 1954), was convicted of rape in 2005 and received an IPP sentence (indeterminate, for public protection) with a 3.5-year tariff (less 98 days on remand), reduced on appeal from life imprisonment. Tariff expiry was 18 December 2008, after which continued detention required Parole Board direction that public protection no longer necessitated confinement.

In September 2008, shortly before expiry, the Parole Board reviewed a pre-tariff referral for possible transfer to open conditions. It made no recommendation, citing remaining treatment needs, underestimated risk (including sadistic elements of the offence), the applicant’s only superficial understanding of his offending and risk-management strategies, and insufficient evidence that sexual/violent risk had reduced enough for safe management outside closed conditions. On 13 October 2008 the Secretary of State referred the case for post-tariff review. No hearing occurred by tariff expiry.

An oral hearing was later agreed (20 February 2009), with the earliest slot in May 2009 due to a large backlog. No panel could be provided, so it was rescheduled for September 2009. The applicant brought judicial review against the Parole Board over the delay. The Board conceded an Article 5 § 4 breach arising from inability to hold the May hearing and the further postponement. The Secretary of State disputed this, relying on the September 2008 opinion as showing no realistic prospect of release at tariff expiry.

The High Court (23 June 2009) found a breach. The referral dossier had arrived only two months (not the usual six) before expiry, placing the case later in the queue. Delay stemmed from Parole Board manpower shortages, particularly the need for a judicially headed panel in lifer/IPP release cases. Article 5 § 4 independently requires a speedy hearing to determine lawfulness of detention, even if the outcome is inevitably continued detention. “Speedy” is fact-sensitive; here the cause was systemic resource lack. The court recorded the breach but granted neither damages (a timely hearing would not have produced release; the best realistic outcome was possible later open-conditions transfer) nor a declaration or mandatory order (the latter would allow queue-jumping at other prisoners’ expense). It noted that remedial steps (extra manpower, more flexible prioritisation of stronger-release-prospect cases) were underway, though they would take time, and discouraged future claims absent “very special circumstances.”

The September 2009 hearing did not occur. A review on 13 January 2010 recommended transfer to open conditions, which the Secretary of State accepted.

Relevant domestic context included the 2003 Act’s introduction of IPPs, which rapidly created a large cohort of indeterminate prisoners that overwhelmed existing Parole Board resources (later addressed by 2008 amendments). Earlier authority (Noorkoiv) had held that even three-month post-tariff delays breached Article 5 § 4 and that resource constraints did not excuse the State. James indicated that Article 5 § 4 requires a functioning system of reasonably intervalled assessments; total breakdown rendering detention arbitrary would trigger a damages remedy. Later High Court decisions (Alcock, Hoole) followed the same approach of recording delay breaches but refusing declarations or prioritisation without special circumstances.

These facts—late referral, resource-driven backlog delaying the first post-tariff hearing until well after expiry, the conceded/established Article 5 § 4 breach, and the limited domestic relief granted—underpinned the Strasbourg application.

**Case Summary: Betteridge v. United Kingdom (App. no. 1497/10, ECtHR, 29 January 2013)**

Samuel Betteridge, a British national born in 1954, was convicted of rape in 2005. His original life sentence with a five-year tariff was reduced on appeal to an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection (IPP) under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, with a tariff of three-and-a-half years (less 98 days on remand). IPPs required detention until the Parole Board was satisfied the prisoner no longer posed a significant risk of serious harm; the Secretary of State had to refer cases routinely, and the Board directed release only if confinement was no longer needed for public protection.

A few months before tariff expiry, the Secretary of State referred the case to the Parole Board for possible transfer to open conditions. On 15 September 2008 the Board (including a psychologist and psychiatrist) declined to recommend this. It noted remaining treatment needs, an apparent underestimate of risk (including sadistic elements of the offences), and the applicant’s only superficial understanding of his offending and risk-management strategies. Balancing progression against public safety, it found insufficient evidence that risk of sexual or violent offending had reduced to a level manageable outside closed conditions.

On 13 October 2008 the Secretary of State referred the case again in anticipation of tariff expiry under the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997. The tariff expired on 18 December 2008 with no hearing held. On 20 February 2009 the Board agreed to an oral hearing; backlog meant the earliest slot was May 2009. No panel could be provided then, so the hearing was rescheduled for September 2009.

Betteridge brought judicial review against the Parole Board over the delay. The Board conceded a breach of Article 5 § 4 (right to speedy judicial review of detention lawfulness). The Secretary of State disagreed, citing the September 2008 opinion as showing no realistic prospect of release. On 23 June 2009 the High Court found a breach: the delay stemmed from insufficient Parole Board manpower (especially judicial chairs required for lifer/IPP release decisions), not a fact-sensitive “speedy” period. The 2008 opinion did not itself determine post-tariff lawfulness, but it made release inconceivable even with a prompt hearing; the best realistic outcome would have been a later recommendation for open conditions. No damages were therefore payable. The court declined a formal declaration (the judgment itself recorded the breach) and any mandatory order (which would let one prisoner jump the queue at others’ expense). It noted systemic backlog from the 2005 introduction of IPPs, which had overwhelmed resources despite later 2008 amendments making IPPs discretionary; steps were being taken to recruit staff and introduce flexibility for priority cases, but improvement would take time. Future claims against the Board were discouraged absent “very special circumstances.” Counsel advised against appeal, as the Court of Appeal would not prioritise one case amid systemic shortages.

The September 2009 hearing did not occur. A review on 13 January 2010 recommended transfer to open conditions, which the Secretary of State accepted.

Betteridge alleged a violation of Article 5 § 4 from the non-speedy review after tariff expiry and no effective remedy (Article 13) because domestic courts refused a declaration or mandatory relief. Domestic authorities (R (Noorkoiv), James, Alcock, Hoole) had already recognised that even shorter delays could breach Article 5 § 4, that resource constraints did not excuse the State, and that declarations or priority orders were often inappropriate without exceptional features or a realistic prospect of earlier release. The case illustrated post-2005 IPP backlogs that left many prisoners without timely Board reviews of continued detention.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Pashov and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 20875/07, judgment of 5 February 2013) concerned three Bulgarian nationals from Sofia who alleged, in particular, that civil tort proceedings they brought were excessively lengthy and that a final judgment in their favour went unenforced for years.

On the night of 10-11 January 1997 a political rally outside Parliament in Sofia turned violent. Around 3 a.m. the applicants, who lived nearby, stepped outside and encountered a group of armed police officers. They retreated into their apartment building and locked the door, but officers forced entry and beat them with batons on the top floor. The applicants sustained head wounds (two requiring stitches), bruises and a broken finger. Forensic medical examinations later confirmed that the injuries were consistent with being struck by hard objects at the time and in the manner alleged.

A criminal investigation into police conduct during the rally was opened in January 1997. It involved interviews with hundreds of participants and officers plus collection of documentary and video evidence. In November 1999 a prosecutor discontinued the proceedings, finding that individual perpetrators could not be identified and that officers had acted in self-defence; the applicants’ specific incident was not addressed. The decision was upheld in July 2000.

Meanwhile, on 13 November 1997 the applicants filed a tort claim against the Ministry of the Interior under the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act, seeking non-pecuniary damages. The Sofia District Court held at least twelve hearings between February 1998 and March 2000, several adjourned for improper service. In May 2000 it found against the Sofia Directorate of Internal Affairs. The Sofia City Court remitted the case in October 2001 for legal error. After further hearings and the addition of defendants, the City Court remitted again in December 2003, holding that the State itself was not the proper defendant. On 22 July 2004 the District Court, relying on medical expert reports and three witness statements, held that the officers had used unjustified force against unresisting civilians. It awarded each applicant 1,000 BGN (approximately €510) plus interest and costs against the Sofia Directorate. The judgment became final on 15 October 2004.

The applicants obtained a writ of execution in November 2004 and submitted it, together with repeated payment requests in 2006, to the Directorate. Under the Code of Civil Procedure then in force, enforcement proceedings could not be instituted against a State body. By December 2010 the award remained unpaid.

The civil action thus lasted from November 1997 until October 2004 (nearly seven years, including two remittals and adjournments), after which the final judgment went unenforced for more than six years. These facts formed the core of the complaints of excessive length and ineffective enforcement.

The ECHR case of Pashov and Others v. Bulgaria (App. no. 20875/07, judgment 5 February 2013) concerned three Bulgarian nationals who alleged that civil proceedings they brought were excessively lengthy and that a final judgment in their favour was not enforced for a prolonged period.

On the night of 10–11 January 1997 a political rally outside the Bulgarian Parliament in Sofia turned violent. Around 3 a.m. the applicants (two of whom lived nearby) went outside after hearing reports of unrest. They encountered armed police running towards them, fled back into their apartment building and locked the door. Officers forced entry, chased the applicants to the top floor and beat them with batons for several minutes before leaving.

The applicants delayed seeking medical help until morning because they were too frightened to go out. All three had head wounds and bruises; two required stitches and the third had a broken finger. Forensic examination on 22 January 1997 confirmed the injuries were consistent with being beaten by hard objects at the time and in the manner alleged. The first and second applicants promptly lodged a criminal complaint.

A criminal investigation into police conduct during the rally was opened. It involved interviews with hundreds of officers and participants plus documentary and video evidence. In November 1999 prosecutors discontinued the proceedings, finding that although police had used batons, individual perpetrators could not be identified and the force used appeared to have been in self-defence. The applicants’ names appeared on a list of 85 injured persons, but the decision did not address the specific circumstances of their beating. An appeal was rejected in July 2000; thereafter the applicants received no further information.

Meanwhile, on 13 November 1997 the applicants began a civil claim for non-pecuniary damages against the Ministry of the Interior under the State Responsibility for Damage Act. Between 1998 and 2000 the Sofia District Court held at least twelve hearings, several adjourned for defective service. The applicants later sought to add further defendants. A May 2000 first-instance judgment in their favour was set aside on appeal in October 2001 and remitted. Further procedural complications followed, including the court’s own-motion joinder of the State. After another remittal in December 2003, a July 2004 judgment found that police had used unjustified force, identified the Sofia Directorate of Internal Affairs as the proper defendant and awarded each applicant BGN 1 000 (approximately EUR 510) plus interest and costs. That judgment became final on 15 October 2004.

Enforcement proved impossible for years. The applicants obtained a writ of execution on 3 November 2004 and repeatedly demanded payment from the Directorate (November 2004, January, April and October 2006). Under then-applicable rules, enforcement proceedings could not be instituted against a State body. As of December 2010 the judgment remained unpaid.

The Court examined these facts in the light of Article 6 § 1 (reasonable-time requirement) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The civil proceedings lasted almost seven years from lodging to final judgment, marked by repeated remittals caused by errors in identifying the correct defendant and adjournments attributable to the authorities. Non-enforcement then continued for more than six years after the judgment became final, leaving the applicants without the compensation awarded for police ill-treatment.

In March 1999 the applicants sought to join additional defendants, including the Sofia Directorate of Internal Affairs. Under the Code of Civil Procedure then in force (and remaining unchanged after 2008), no enforcement proceedings could be instituted against a State body. 001-116031:
The European Court of Human Rights case of Şükran Aydın and Others v. Turkey (applications 49197/06, 23196/07, 50242/08, 60912/08 and 14871/09) arose from five applications by Turkish nationals convicted for using Kurdish during election campaigns, contrary to domestic electoral law. The applicants (born 1952–1973) lived in Diyarbakır, Şanlıurfa, Kars, Ankara and Siirt. They included sitting mayors and candidates for parties such as DEHAP and SHP, or independents.

Şükran Aydın, then mayor of Bismil and a 2002 parliamentary candidate, addressed a rally in Kurdish on 26 October 2002. She explained that the audience was predominantly Kurdish-speaking, including many elderly people and women who did not understand Turkish. The Lice Criminal Court convicted her in January 2005 under section 58 of Law no. 298, imposing six months’ imprisonment plus a heavy fine. The sentence was reduced, commuted to a fine and then suspended in view of her character and lack of prior record. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction (with a minor adjustment to the fine) in May 2006.

Ayşe Gökkan, a DEHAP parliamentary candidate in Şanlıurfa, used Kurdish on 27 October 2002 to address Kurdish women who spoke no Turkish. The Viranşehir court convicted her in December 2005 on identical statutory grounds; the prison term was commuted to a fine and suspended. The Court of Cassation declined to consider her appeal because it was not written in Turkish and otherwise upheld the judgment.

Ayhan Erkmen, mayor of Dağpınar, spoke Kurdish at a July 2007 rally supporting an independent candidate. He argued that many listeners would otherwise not understand him. The Digor court convicted him in March 2008, reduced the six-month term slightly and suspended pronouncement of judgment for five years. An objection was dismissed.

Orhan Miroğlu, an independent candidate in Mersin, used some Kurdish greetings at a June 2007 rally. Convicted by the Mersin court in April 2008, he likewise received a suspended pronouncement of a six-month sentence. His objection failed.

Mesut Beştaş campaigned in Kurdish during the March 2004 municipal elections in Siirt. After successive first-instance convictions (some quashed by the Court of Cassation) and conversion of the prison term into a fine, the Siirt court in October 2008 suspended pronouncement of judgment for five years. An objection was rejected.

At the material time, section 58 of Law no. 298 absolutely prohibited the use of any language other than Turkish in election campaigning “on radio or television or by other means.” Section 151 prescribed imprisonment of six months to one year plus a fine. (The provision was amended in 2010 to require only that candidates “primarily use Turkish.”) All convictions rested on video transcripts confirming the use of Kurdish. The applicants maintained that they had spoken Kurdish solely to communicate effectively with constituents who did not understand Turkish and that such speech was not criminal.

These facts constitute the alleged interferences with freedom of expression (Article 10 of the Convention) in the context of political campaigning and minority-language use. International instruments cited in the case (ICCPR Art. 27, the UN Minorities Declaration, the UNESCO Cultural Diversity Declaration, the Framework Convention for National Minorities and related recommendations) affirm the right of persons belonging to linguistic minorities to use their language freely in public life and election campaigns. Comparative material from 22 Council of Europe States showed that none imposed criminal sanctions for the use of minority languages at public election meetings.

**Case of Şükran Aydın and Others v. Turkey (ECtHR, 2013)**

This ECtHR judgment (applications 49197/06 et al.) arose from five Turkish nationals prosecuted for using Kurdish during election campaigns, contrary to then-applicable domestic law. The applicants—Şükran Aydın (b. 1957, Diyarbakır), Ayşe Gökkan (b. 1965, Şanlıurfa), Ayhan Erkmen (b. 1973, Kars), Orhan Miroğlu (b. 1952, Ankara), and Mesut Beştaş (b. 1966, Diyarbakır)—were represented by counsel and complained of convictions interfering with their political expression.

Aydın, then mayor of Bismil and a DEHAP parliamentary candidate for the 3 November 2002 elections, addressed a crowd partly in Kurdish on 26 October 2002. She explained this was necessary for elderly people and women who did not understand Turkish. Proceedings began in January 2003. In January 2005 the Lice Criminal Court of First Instance, relying on a video transcript, convicted her under section 58 of Law no. 298 (forbidding any language other than Turkish in election campaigning by any means) and section 151(2) (six months’ imprisonment plus a heavy fine). The sentence was reduced, commuted to a fine, and payment suspended due to her clean record and the court’s belief she would not reoffend. The Court of Cassation adjusted the fine and upheld the conviction in May 2006.

Gökkan, a DEHAP candidate in Şanlıurfa for the same elections, spoke in Kurdish on 27 October 2002 to a crowd of Kurdish women who did not understand Turkish. Convicted in December 2005 on similar evidence and legal grounds, her prison term was commuted to a fine that was then suspended. The Court of Cassation in November 2006 refused to examine her appeal because it was not in Turkish, adjusted the fine, and upheld the judgment.

Erkmen, mayor of Dağpınar, gave a Kurdish speech on 18 July 2007 at a rally for an independent Kars parliamentary candidate so that non-Turkish speakers in the crowd could understand him. In March 2008 the Digor Magistrates’ Court convicted him and imposed six months’ imprisonment (reduced to five), but suspended pronouncement of the judgment for five years under the Code of Criminal Procedure. An objection was dismissed in May 2008.

Miroğlu, an independent Mersin parliamentary candidate, was found to have spoken partly in Kurdish at a 27 June 2007 rally (he claimed he had only greeted Kurdish speakers). Convicted in April 2008, he received a six-month sentence whose pronouncement was likewise suspended for five years. An objection failed in July 2008.

Beştaş, an SHP municipal candidate in Siirt, campaigned in Kurdish on 20 March 2004 ahead of the 28 March 2004 elections. After multiple first-instance convictions (six months plus a fine, later commuted), quashings by the Court of Cassation, and a re-trial, the Siirt court in October 2008 suspended pronouncement for five years. An objection was dismissed in December 2008.

At the relevant time section 58 of Law no. 298 absolutely prohibited non-Turkish languages or scripts in campaigning; section 151 prescribed imprisonment of six months to one year plus a fine. The provision was amended in 2010 to require that parties and candidates “primarily use Turkish.” International materials cited included ICCPR Article 27, the 1992 UN Minorities Declaration, the UNESCO Cultural Diversity Declaration, Framework Convention Articles 9, 10 and 15, and Council of Europe/UN recommendations that minority languages should not be banned in election campaigns. Comparative material from 22 Council of Europe states showed no other country imposed criminal sanctions for using a minority language at public election meetings.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints of unjustified interference with political speech (primarily Article 10 ECHR), given the blanket ban, criminal penalties (even if later mitigated or suspended), and the context of addressing Kurdish-speaking voters.

The case of Şükran Aydın and Others v. Turkey originated in five applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Turkish nationals Şükran Aydın, Ayşe Gökkan, Ayhan Erkmen, Orhan Miroğlu and Mesut Beştaş. All concerned criminal convictions for using Kurdish rather than Turkish while campaigning in elections, contrary to section 58 of Law no. 298 (which at the relevant time forbade any language or script other than Turkish in election campaigning by any means). Section 151(2) prescribed a prison term of six months to one year plus a fine. The applicants argued that the prohibition and resulting sanctions interfered with their rights, particularly freedom of expression, given that they had addressed Kurdish-speaking audiences (often including women and the elderly) who would not otherwise have understood them.

Aydın, then mayor of Bismil and a DEHAP parliamentary candidate, addressed a crowd partly in Kurdish on 26 October 2002. The Lice Criminal Court convicted her in January 2005 after reviewing a video transcript, imposing a six-month sentence and fine that was reduced, commuted and ultimately suspended. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction (with a modified fine) in May 2006.

Gökkan, a DEHAP candidate in Şanlıurfa, spoke Kurdish to an audience of Kurdish women on 27 October 2002. The Viranşehir court convicted her in December 2005 on similar video evidence, again commuting and suspending the sentence. The Court of Cassation declined to consider her appeal because it was not written in Turkish and upheld the judgment in November 2006.

Erkmen, mayor of Dağpınar, delivered a Kurdish speech at a July 2007 rally supporting an independent parliamentary candidate. The Digor court convicted him in March 2008, reduced the sentence and suspended pronouncement of judgment for five years under Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. An objection was dismissed in May 2008.

Miroğlu, an independent candidate in Mersin, used some Kurdish (which he described as greetings) at a June 2007 rally. The Mersin court convicted him in April 2008 and likewise suspended pronouncement for five years; an objection failed in July 2008.

Beştaş, an SHP municipal candidate in Siirt, campaigned in Kurdish on 20 March 2004. After a protracted process involving two quashings by the Court of Cassation, the Siirt court ultimately suspended pronouncement of judgment for five years in October 2008; an objection was dismissed in December 2008.

In 2010 the impugned provision was amended to require only that Turkish be used “primarily.” International instruments cited in the case (ICCPR Article 27, the UN Minorities Declaration, the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities, and related recommendations) affirm the right of persons belonging to linguistic minorities to use their language in public, including during election campaigns, and to participate effectively in public life. Comparative material available to the Court indicated that none of 22 other Council of Europe states imposed criminal sanctions for the use of minority languages by candidates at public election meetings.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: a blanket criminal ban on a minority language in political speech that the applicants maintained was necessary to communicate with their constituencies, resulting in convictions (even if sentences were later mitigated or their pronouncement suspended).

The case of Claes v. Belgium (Application no. 43418/09) concerns Belgian national André Claes (born 1952), who alleged that his prolonged detention in prison psychiatric wings unsuitable for his mental disability violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the Convention.

Claes was first detained on 4 April 1978 after the Louvain Criminal Court found him not criminally responsible for raping his underage sisters between 1973 and 1977. He was released on 24 April 1978 subject to psychiatric hospital treatment. On 20 August 1982, he was re-detained for sexually assaulting a child and placed under observation at Merksplas Prison. The Mental Health Board ordered transfer to the Bierbeek clinic on 7 March 1983, but he returned to Merksplas in October 1984 due to aggression and another assault. After trial release to the Dr Guislain institute in December 1985 and later authorization to live alone with daily treatment, he was arrested again on 12 June 1987 for indecent assault on a girl and held at Turnhout Prison until September 1989, when he was released on condition of hospital admission.

Incidents involving girls and staff, plus reports describing him as manipulative and dangerous, led to his return to Merksplas in 1994. Intelligence tests in 1998 classified him as mentally disabled (IQ 72). Attempts to place him in non-prison institutions failed. Between 1999 and 2009 he received sporadic consultations (typically monthly or fewer) from rotating prison psychiatrists. Reports from 2002–2008 documented unsuccessful searches for a structured residential facility to reduce reoffending risk; he was on a waiting list but none would accept him due to his behavioural problems and offence history. Staff noted worsening suffering, frustration, rigidity, and little progress or insight. The Board repeatedly extended detention pending placement in the Flemish disability integration system, citing public safety (especially of children) and insufficient rehabilitation prospects.

A July 2008 visit to Merksplas found Claes spending days in communal areas with social workers for those with mental deficiencies, sharing a 24-person dormitory at night, and facing unsatisfactory sanitation. In December 2007 and February 2008 he sought injunctions to force placement in a suitable institution, arguing prison care was inadequate. These were dismissed: urgent-applications judges lacked jurisdiction, as placement was the exclusive remit of the Mental Health Boards. Appeals, including to the Higher Board and Court of Cassation, failed. In March 2009 the Board rejected release, acknowledging treatment shortfalls but denying any Article 3 or 5 violation (no intent to harm; detention lawful under Article 5 § 1(e) to protect society) and stating it could not compel institutions to accept him. The Antwerp Court of Appeal confirmed this in April 2009.

A new “De Haven” secure unit opened at Merksplas in June 2009 (capacity 60 for those with mental disabilities), but Claes disputed being moved there from the older F-block. He was trial-released on 10 September 2009 to the Martine van Camp Centre but returned to Louvain Prison’s psychiatric wing in June 2011 after aggressive behaviour threatened safety. An appeal on points of law remained pending.

Belgium’s psychiatric detention system comprises high-security forensic centres, medium/low-security hospitals, and prison wings originally meant only for temporary observation. By 2010 over 1,000 patients (about 10% of the prison population) were held in the latter, including hundreds at Merksplas, owing to capacity shortages. These facts—decades of prison confinement despite recognised disability, rotating/minimal treatment, failed placement efforts, poor living conditions, and ineffective domestic remedies—underpin the alleged violations.

The case of Claes v. Belgium (Application no. 43418/09) concerns a Belgian national, André Claes (born 1952), who alleged that his prolonged detention in prison psychiatric wings, rather than a suitable institution for persons with mental disabilities, violated Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 (lawful detention of persons of unsound mind and right to speedy review) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Claes was first detained in 1978 after the Louvain Criminal Court found him not criminally responsible for the repeated rape of his underage sisters between 1973 and 1977. He was diagnosed with severe mental disabilities and released on condition of psychiatric treatment. In 1982 he was re-detained for sexually assaulting a child and placed under observation in Merksplas Prison. Subsequent transfers to private clinics (Bierbeek in 1983, Dr Guislain in 1985) failed due to his aggressive behaviour and further sexual assaults, leading to returns to prison psychiatric wings. After more incidents in 1987 and 1994 involving young girls and female staff, he was returned to Merksplas. Intelligence testing in 1998 recorded an IQ of 72, classifying him as mentally disabled. Multiple attempts from 1998 onward to place him in non-prison psychiatric institutions failed; psychologists described him as manipulative, immature and potentially dangerous, requiring structured care to reduce reoffending risk, but no facility would accept him. He remained on waiting lists (e.g., Borgenstein care home) while receiving only sporadic prison psychiatric consultations (typically one per month, with rotating doctors).

From 2005 the Mental Health Board extended his detention at Merksplas pending placement in the Flemish social-integration system for persons with disabilities. In 2007–2008 Claes sought injunctions from the Turnhout Court of First Instance and later the Antwerp Court of Appeal, arguing that prison conditions (overcrowded 24-person dormitories, poor sanitation, inadequate specialised care) were unsuitable and seeking an order that the State find him a place, subject to penalty. Both courts declined jurisdiction, holding that placement decisions belonged exclusively to the Mental Health Boards under the Social Protection Act. Prison reports noted his growing frustration, resignation and suffering; a 2008 visit report confirmed communal daytime activities with social workers but unsatisfactory night-time conditions. The Boards repeatedly confirmed detention, citing insufficient rehabilitation prospects and danger to society (especially children), while acknowledging they lacked power to compel institutions to accept him or to order specific treatment. They stressed that release was impossible given the risk he posed.

In June 2009 Claes was moved to the new “De Haven” secure unit at Merksplas (opened for mentally disabled patients). In September 2009 he was granted trial release to the Martine van Camp Centre, a facility for persons with mental disabilities. After aggressive incidents that endangered staff and residents, he was re-arrested in June 2011 and placed in the psychiatric wing of Louvain Prison, where he remains. At the time of the Court’s examination, an appeal on points of law concerning the 2009 Court of Appeal ruling was still pending.

Belgian law provides three categories of placement: high-security “social protection” forensic-psychiatry centres (few in number, none originally in Flanders until “De Haven”); medium- or low-security traditional psychiatric hospitals; and prison psychiatric wings originally intended only for short-term observation. By 2010 those wings held 1,094 patients (about 10 % of the prison population), far exceeding capacity; Merksplas alone housed 625. Two new high-security centres planned for Flanders were not expected before 2015. These facts formed the core of Claes’s claim that his detention, lasting decades in facilities unequipped for his disability and treatment needs, was unlawful and degrading.

The case of Claes v. Belgium (Application no. 43418/09) involves André Claes, a Belgian national born in 1952 with severe mental disabilities (IQ of 72, classified as mentally disabled), who alleged that his long-term detention in prison psychiatric wings unsuitable for his condition violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the Convention. He was first interned on 4 April 1978 after a Louvain Criminal Court judgment of 2 February 1978 found him not criminally responsible for repeatedly raping his under-age sisters between 1973 and 1977. Released shortly after on condition of psychiatric hospital treatment (following a 1977 diagnosis of severe mental disabilities), he was re-detained in August 1982 for sexually assaulting a child and placed under observation in Merksplas Prison.

Subsequent Mental Health Board decisions repeatedly sought transfers to specialised private psychiatric clinics or institutes (e.g., Bierbeek in 1983, Dr Guislain in 1985), but these failed due to his aggressive behaviour and further sexual assaults, leading to returns to prison psychiatric wings (Merksplas, Turnhout). A 1987 trial release to live alone with daily treatment ended after another indecent assault on a young girl. In 1994, following incidents involving young girls and staff plus psychologist reports describing him as manipulative, potentially dangerous and unfit for society, the Board ordered his return to Merksplas, citing the 1978 judgment. Multiple non-prison institutions approached from 1998 onward refused him.

Prison mental welfare reports from 2002–2008 documented unsuccessful searches for residential care (e.g., waiting lists for homes like Borgenstein), his dull-witted immature personality, growing frustration and resignation from delays, and the need for structured intensive treatment to reduce reoffending risk. He received infrequent consultations (roughly monthly, often with rotating psychiatrists). A 2008 Ghent Mental Health Board visit to Merksplas F-block noted he spent days in communal areas with social workers from a disability association, shared a 24-person dormitory at night, and faced unsatisfactory sanitation.

In 2005 the Board extended detention until placement in the Flemish disability integration system. Claes applied in 2007–2008 for court injunctions (Turnhout Court of First Instance, Antwerp Court of Appeal) to compel transfer to a suitable institution, citing inadequate prison care, unsuitability for the mentally disabled, and Convention violations. These were dismissed: judges lacked jurisdiction as placement was the exclusive remit of Mental Health Boards (under the Social Protection Act). Appeals to the Higher Mental Health Board and Court of Cassation failed; the Board acknowledged treatment was often insufficient and conditions suboptimal but stressed it could not force institutions to accept him, prioritised public safety (especially protecting children from sexual abuse), and found no Article 3 violation or unlawful detention under Article 5 § 1(e). A 2009 psychologist report confirmed priority funding status for disability care, but placement remained elusive. He was briefly transferred to the Martine van Camp Centre in September 2009 but returned to Louvain Prison's psychiatric wing in June 2011 after aggressive behaviour endangered residents and staff.

Prison psychiatric wings (originally for short-term observation) housed over 1,000 such detainees nationally by 2010 amid capacity shortages; specialised forensic centres were limited and delayed (new Flemish facilities planned for 2015). These facts highlight prolonged unsuitable detention without adequate therapeutic environment or effective judicial remedy to secure transfer.

The case of Gurenko v. Russia (Application no. 41828/10) concerns allegations by Mr Georgiy Grigoryevich Gurenko, a Russian national born in 1941, of inadequate medical care while detained. Convicted on 29 September 2006 by the Kursk Leninskiy District Court of beating his partner to death and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment (upheld on appeal on 14 December 2006), he was held from January 2006 first in facility IZ-46/1 in Kursk and then, from 26 December 2006, in a correctional colony in the Kursk Region until his early release in April 2012.

Gurenko had a severe pre-existing cardiac history. In November 2001 he suffered a large transmural myocardial infarction requiring lengthy cardiology-clinic treatment. By October 2002 he had been diagnosed with coronary artery disease, postinfarction cardiosclerosis, cardiac aneurysm, severe chronic arterial hypertension and latent urolithiasis, and classified as permanently disabled (category 2). A further myocardial infarction occurred in March 2005.

Immediately after arrest on 2 January 2006 an ambulance attended him for severe chest pain; emergency doctors recorded stage-3 arterial hypertension and coronary artery disease, gave urgent treatment and authorised continued detention. Persistent complaints of pressing chest pain and dyspnoea followed. Ten days later the facility’s medical-unit head confirmed severe essential hypertension (stage 2–3) with high risk of further cardiovascular events and prescribed four medicines (nitroglycerine, aspirin, isosorbide dinitrate and lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide). Subsequent examinations merely copied this regimen. In March 2006, after complaints of unrelieved angina, syncope, tachycardia and extreme hypertension, he spent two months in the Kursk Regional prison hospital, where his condition was assessed as moderately severe. Diagnoses included recurrent myocardial infarction, extensive left-ventricular scarring, postinfarction cardiosclerosis, chronic left-ventricular aneurysm, stage-3 hypertension and premature ventricular complexes. He received eleven ECGs and blood/urine tests but was never seen by a cardiologist; attending staff were general physicians, a dermatologist, an ophthalmologist and a dentist. On discharge his condition was called satisfactory, yet a third infarction in 2006 was noted and only symptomatic treatment prescribed.

Further episodes included a suspected infarction during a July 2006 court hearing, after which hospitalisation was recommended if he deteriorated. A subsequent August 2006 hospital stay involved blood/urine tests and a chest X-ray but no ECG and no cardiologist. After transfer to the colony he was placed on a close-supervision list. Periodic examinations (sometimes by a tuberculosis or drug-addiction specialist acting as duty doctor) and short medical-unit admissions continued; ECG traces often could not be interpreted and ultrasound was unavailable for want of specialists. Medicines were sometimes supplied by his son. Repeated hypertensive crises and anginal attacks from 2007 to 2011 were treated symptomatically with nitrates, antihypertensives, magnesium or papaverine injections; hospital stays (April–May 2008, April 2009, June 2010) again featured limited diagnostics and no cardiologist even when attending physicians themselves recommended ECG monitoring, cardiac ultrasound, Doppler studies and specialist consultations.

Gurenko repeatedly complained to prison authorities, the Ministry of Health, prosecutors and the courts that facilities lacked cardiologists, equipment and resuscitation capacity. Responses were perfunctory; one official letter stated that additional specialist care (including a cardiologist) could be obtained only at the inmate’s own expense. An action for damages lodged in January 2009 was returned without examination. On 29 March 2012 the District Court ordered his release after prison-hospital doctors confirmed that his advanced heart disease precluded continued detention and that necessary treatment could not be provided. Upon release he was admitted to a civilian cardiology department and later diagnosed with cancer.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s claim that the medical assistance furnished throughout his detention was inadequate given the gravity and progression of his cardiac condition.

The case of Gurenko v. Russia (Application no. 41828/10) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Russian national Georgiy Grigoryevich Gurenko (born 1941). He alleged inadequate medical care during detention, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment). The Court granted the application priority and examined admissibility and merits together.

Gurenko was convicted on 29 September 2006 by the Kursk Leninskiy District Court of beating his female partner to death while intoxicated, receiving an eight-year prison sentence upheld on appeal. He had a serious pre-existing cardiac history: a large transmural myocardial infarction in November 2001 requiring lengthy cardiology treatment, followed by diagnoses in 2002 of coronary artery disease, postinfarction cardiosclerosis, cardiac aneurysm, severe chronic arterial hypertension and latent urolithiasis, rendering him permanently disabled (category 2). He suffered a second infarction in March 2005.

Arrested in January 2006, Gurenko immediately required an ambulance for severe chest pain. Emergency doctors confirmed stage-3 hypertension and coronary disease but authorised detention in facility IZ-46/1 in Kursk. He repeatedly complained of pressing chest pain and shortness of breath. Ten days after admission a prison doctor confirmed severe essential hypertension (stage 2–3) with high risk of further complications and prescribed four medications (nitroglycerine, aspirin, isosorbide dinitrate and lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide). Subsequent examinations merely repeated this regimen without specialist input.

In March 2006, after complaints of unrelievable angina, loss of consciousness and extremely high blood pressure, he was transferred to the Kursk Regional prison hospital for two months. Doctors recorded a third infarction (2006), extensive scarring, chronic aneurysm and other conditions, performing 11 ECGs and blood/urine tests, but no cardiologist examined him. He was attended only by general physicians and other non-specialists. Released in “satisfactory” condition, he continued to suffer fatigue and chest pain on exertion.

Further crises followed: a suspected fourth infarction during a July 2006 court hearing led to emergency treatment and another hospital stay (August 2006) without ECGs or cardiology review. Transferred to correctional colony no. 2 in December 2006, he was placed under “close supervision” but received only general-physician or non-specialist consultations, occasional medication adjustments and short medical-unit stays. A February 2007 medical panel confirmed his disabilities. Ultrasound and ECG interpretation were impossible due to lack of specialists. Medicines were sometimes supplied by his son.

Between 2007 and 2011 he endured repeated hypertensive emergencies, angina attacks and hospital admissions (April–May 2008, April 2009, June 2010). Recommended specialist investigations (cardiologist, neurologist, cardiac surgeon, heart ultrasound, Doppler scans) were almost never performed; only isolated ECGs occurred. Treatment remained symptomatic—nitrates, antihypertensives, painkiller injections—administered by tuberculosis specialists, psychiatrists or medical assistants. He was frequently released despite ongoing complaints of stabbing pain, dizziness and panic attacks.

Gurenko lodged complaints with prison authorities, prosecutors, the Ministry of Health and a district court (January 2009, returned unexamined). A July 2009 official reply stated that a prisoner could obtain extra specialist care (including a cardiologist) only at his own expense. In March 2012 the same district court ordered his early release after prison doctors confirmed that his condition precluded continued detention and that necessary treatment was unavailable. Upon release he was immediately hospitalised in a civilian cardiology unit and later diagnosed with cancer.

These facts establish a pattern of untreated progression of life-threatening heart disease, absence of specialist care and diagnostic tools, and official indifference despite repeated requests, forming the core of the alleged Article 3 violation.

The case of Gurenko v. Russia (no. 41828/10) concerns the applicant’s allegation of inadequate medical care in detention, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. Georgiy Grigoryevich Gurenko, born in 1941, was convicted on 29 September 2006 of beating his partner to death and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment (final on 14 December 2006). Arrested in January 2006, he was held in pre-trial facility IZ-46/1 in Kursk before transfer to a correctional colony on 26 December 2006. He was released in April 2012 on health grounds.

Gurenko had a grave pre-existing cardiac history. In 2001 he suffered a large transmural myocardial infarction and was later diagnosed with coronary artery disease, post-infarction cardiosclerosis, left-ventricular aneurysm, stage-3 arterial hypertension and urolithiasis; he was classified category-2 disabled. A second infarction occurred in March 2005.

On the day after arrest an ambulance treated him for severe chest pain and confirmed his diagnoses, yet authorised continued detention. Persistent complaints of crushing chest pain and dyspnoea produced only the copying of earlier prescriptions (nitroglycerine, aspirin, isosorbide dinitrate, lisinopril). In March 2006 he was admitted to the Kursk Regional prison hospital for two months with a diagnosis that now included a third infarction, extensive scarring and chronic aneurysm. He received eleven ECGs and laboratory tests but was never examined by a cardiologist—only general physicians, a dermatologist, ophthalmologist and dentist. Discharged as “improved,” he continued to suffer angina.

A suspected fourth infarction during a July 2006 court hearing led to another hospitalisation (August 2006) again without ECG or cardiologist. After transfer to colony IK-2 he was placed on “close supervision.” Subsequent admissions (April 2007, April–May 2008, April 2009, September 2009–January 2010, June 2010) followed the same pattern: symptomatic treatment with nitrates and antihypertensives, occasional ECGs that could not even be interpreted for lack of a specialist, no ultrasound or Doppler studies, and never a consultation with a cardiologist. Medicines were frequently supplied by the applicant’s son. Examinations were performed by tuberculosis specialists, psychiatrists or general duty doctors. In June 2010 hospital doctors themselves recommended daily ECGs, echocardiography, vascular imaging and cardiological/surgical review; only two ECGs were performed and he was discharged still complaining of rest angina, panic attacks and nocturnal sweats.

Hypertensive crises and heart attacks recurred monthly through 2011, each time treated with injections and a return to the cell. Official complaints, including a 2009 civil action, were either ignored or met with the reply that he could pay for a private cardiologist. On 29 March 2012 the District Court ordered his release, accepting the prison hospital’s own admission that his condition was incompatible with continued detention and that necessary care could not be provided. Immediately after release he was admitted to a civilian cardiology ward and later diagnosed with cancer.

The facts demonstrate years of exclusively symptomatic management of a high-risk, multi-infarct patient without specialist assessment, essential diagnostic investigations or equipment, despite repeated life-threatening episodes and the authorities’ own recognition that adequate treatment was unavailable in the prison system.

The case of Eduard Popa v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 17008/07) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by a Moldovan national born in 1981. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the Convention, stemming from his alleged ill-treatment by police officers and the subsequent ineffective investigation, which left him with life-altering injuries including amputations.

At the time, the applicant was serving a sentence in an open prison in Goian, working outside during the day. On 18 November 2005, his request for home leave was denied, but he stayed overnight at his parents’ home in Ialoveni. The next morning, around 9 a.m., he visited a pharmacy for back-pain medication. Around 10 a.m., a red car stopped; a police officer allegedly punched him in the face, pushed him inside, and he lost consciousness. The Government did not confirm this but accepted it as possible. Simultaneously, around 9:30 a.m., two officers searched the parents’ home. After phone calls, they left abruptly; the mother followed, begging them not to beat her son. A neighbour overheard them say they had found the “criminals.”

On 20 November, two men found the applicant near a pond 1.5 km from Ialoveni. He was unresponsive, with facial injuries consistent with assault, wet and dirty clothes, and later exhibited odd behaviour including eating mud. They warmed him but, believing him to be a drug user, sent him away without calling an ambulance (a claim disputed by the family). He was found again the next day nearby; an ambulance took him to hospital in critical condition. He told his parents he had been beaten by police and abandoned by the lake. Due to frostbite from low temperatures, both feet and eight fingers were amputated on 8 December 2005. Medical records confirmed no alcohol or drugs in his system.

The applicant’s mother promptly complained to prosecutors, alleging police ill-treatment and stating he could identify the officers. One officer later expressed surprise that the applicant was alive. Initial questioning was limited; prosecutors asked no questions during key interviews. Criminal proceedings opened on 20 January 2006 but focused on robbery (theft of a watch and coat) rather than police involvement. A forensic report confirmed bruises, scratches, and the amputations but was based solely on documents.

Despite repeated requests for an identity parade of Ialoveni officers, none occurred. The investigation was dismissed multiple times (September 2007, July 2009, March 2011) for vague statements and lack of cooperation, even after the applicant identified one officer in March 2009. Higher prosecutors repeatedly quashed these decisions, citing superficial inquiries, failure to question all involved, lack of confrontations, and delays; the case was even transferred to the military prosecutor. A later forensic report suggested injuries could result from a fall. As of the Court’s consideration, the investigation remained pending after more than five years, with no identification of perpetrators or resolution of the police-assault allegations.

These facts highlight the core issues: the applicant’s detention-like encounter with police, the beating and abandonment causing severe, potentially life-threatening harm (frostbite leading to amputations), and the authorities’ persistent failure to conduct a prompt, thorough, and independent investigation into possible official involvement.

The case of Eduard Popa v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 17008/07) concerns alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from claimed police ill-treatment of the applicant and a subsequent ineffective investigation. The applicant, a Moldovan national born in 1981, was serving a prison sentence in an open detention facility in Goian at the relevant time. He worked outside the facility during the day but was required to return at night. On 18 November 2005 his application for home leave was refused, yet he spent the night at his parents’ home in Ialoveni.

On 19 November 2005 the applicant went to a pharmacy for back-pain medication. According to his account, at around 10 a.m. a red car stopped, a police officer punched him in the face, pushed him into the vehicle and he lost consciousness. The Government did not confirm the details but accepted that such an incident was possible. Around the same time two police officers arrived at the applicant’s parents’ house, searched it and inquired about his whereabouts. After receiving telephone calls they left abruptly. A neighbour later heard the officers state that they had found the criminals they were seeking. The applicant’s mother followed them and pleaded with them not to beat her son.

On 20 November the applicant was discovered lying near a pond approximately 1.5 km from Ialoveni. He was unable to speak or walk, displayed facial injuries consistent with assault, and his clothes were wet and dirty. After being warmed he exhibited strange behaviour, including eating mud, which led those who found him to believe he was under the influence of drugs. They gave him a coat and boots and sent him away rather than calling an ambulance. The following day the same people found him again nearby, called an ambulance and he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Medical records confirmed he had not been under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

The applicant later told his parents that police officers had beaten him and left him by the lake. He suffered severe frostbite; on 8 December 2005 both feet and eight fingers were amputated. His mother lodged a complaint with the prosecutor’s office alleging police ill-treatment and stated that the applicant was prepared to identify the officers. She later encountered one of the officers who had visited her home; he appeared surprised that her son was still alive.

A criminal investigation was opened on 20 January 2006 but initially focused on a suspected robbery of the applicant’s watch and coat rather than on the police-assault allegation. The applicant’s statements describing the red-car incident were recorded, yet no identity parade of Ialoveni police officers was arranged despite repeated requests. Forensic reports confirmed bruises, scratches and the amputations; a later report noted that the facial injuries could have resulted from a fall. The Prosecutor General’s Office initially stated there was no reason to believe police were involved.

The complaint was dismissed several times on grounds that the applicant’s statements were vague and that he had not cooperated. Higher prosecutors repeatedly quashed these decisions, citing a superficial investigation, failure to question all relevant persons, absence of confrontations and identity procedures, and delays. The case was transferred between prosecutors’ offices but, as of the Court’s judgment, remained pending more than five years after the events. These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Articles 2 and 3 concerning both the alleged life-threatening ill-treatment and the lack of an effective official investigation.

The case of Eduard Popa v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 17008/07) concerns complaints under Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arising from the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment by police officers on 19 November 2005 and the subsequent ineffective investigation into those events. The applicant, a Moldovan national born in 1981, was at the time serving a sentence in an open prison facility in Goian, from which he was permitted to work outside during the day. On 18 November 2005 his request for home leave was refused, yet he failed to return that evening and instead spent the night at his parents’ house in nearby Ialoveni.

The following morning, around 9 a.m., the applicant went to a pharmacy to obtain medication for back pain. At approximately 10 a.m., while walking home, a red car stopped beside him. According to his later account, a police officer emerged, punched him in the face and forced him into the vehicle, after which he lost consciousness. The Government did not confirm this version but accepted it as one possible scenario. Meanwhile, at about 9.30 a.m., two police officers arrived at the applicant’s parents’ home, searched the premises and enquired about his whereabouts. One officer received telephone calls, after which the pair left abruptly. The applicant’s mother followed them, begging them not to beat her son; a neighbour who knew the officers was told they were looking for criminals and had found them.

On 20 November 2005, around 11 a.m., two men discovered the applicant lying near a pond 1.5 km from Ialoveni. He was unable to speak or walk, displayed facial injuries consistent with a violent assault, and was wet and dirty. After being taken to a nearby lodge, warmed and given dry clothing, he exhibited odd behaviour (including eating mud) that led those present to believe he was under the influence of drugs. He was given a coat and boots and set off on foot towards Ialoveni; his mother later disputed that he had left of his own accord, claiming he had been turned out because he was thought to be an addict. The next day the same men found him again, only 30 metres from the lodge, and called an ambulance. He was admitted to hospital in Chișinău in a critical condition. Medical records confirmed that he had not been under the influence of alcohol or drugs. He told his visiting parents that police officers had beaten him and left him by the lake. Severe frostbite necessitated the amputation, on 8 December 2005, of both feet and eight fingers.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the psychiatric detentions and the children’s removal lacked lawful procedure, adequate safeguards and effective judicial control.

The ECHR case Asen Kostov v. Bulgaria (no. 48445/06) concerns a Bulgarian national's claims that detention exceeding a one-year prison term set on 10 May 2004 was unlawful and that he lacked an enforceable right to compensation.

Kostov (born 1961) had multiple convictions for crimes from 1991–1998 (cases including 70/1995, 343/1998, 805/2001, 751/2002, 660/2002, 868/2003 and 1732/2002). On 13 October 2003 a plea bargain in case 868/2003 imposed one year's imprisonment for robbery; he began serving it on 28 October 2003. On 19 December 2003 the Plovdiv District Court set an overall two-year term incorporating four other convictions. On appeal, the Plovdiv Regional Court on 10 May 2004 quashed that decision and imposed a one-year overall term solely for cases 343/1998 and 868/2003. It deducted six months already served in case 343/1998 plus time served in case 868/2003, but did not state an expiry date. For the remaining cases it held that a separate overall sentence (potentially beneficial to Kostov) fell to another court.

Kostov sought suspension of the sentence under the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure. The regional prosecutor refused on 14 May 2004, citing the still-pending overall sentence for other convictions. Kostov was released on 1 June 2004 once the 10 May 2004 decision became final (unappealed). In 2005 new overall-sentence proceedings began because case 1732/2002 had been omitted. On 13 December 2005 the District Court imposed a one-year-three-month overall term for cases 343/1998, 1732/2002 and 868/2003; this was upheld on 21 April 2006. It is unclear whether an overall sentence was ever set for the remaining cases.

On 1 October 2004 Kostov sued the Plovdiv District Court and prosecutor's office under the 1988 State and Municipalities' Responsibility for Damage Act, alleging he had served one year, two months and ten days rather than the one-year term. On 13 May 2005 the Pazardzhik Regional Court accepted that, after deductions for prior service and prison work, two months and ten days had been served in excess, but dismissed the claim: pending overall-sentence proceedings would credit the excess time. Kostov was ordered to pay BGN 480 in fees. The Plovdiv Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 12 December 2008, holding the detention lawful because case 1732/2002 should have been included in the 10 May 2004 decision (a defect later cured) and overall-sentence proceedings were incomplete in May 2004; it added BGN 240 in fees. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave on the merits on 5 February 2010 but, applying 2008 amendments to the 1988 Act, later reduced the fees to a flat BGN 15.

Bulgarian law (Criminal Code Art. 25) requires an overall prison term for multiple pre-first-conviction offences, with prior time served deducted. The 1974 Code provided that sentences are enforced only once final, via prosecutorial order to prison authorities, and allowed interruption of imprisonment on compelling grounds. The 1988 Act (as amended) governed state liability and court fees.

Kostov alleged the excess detention after the 10 May 2004 decision was unlawful and that he had no effective compensation remedy.

The case of Krylov v. Russia (no. 36697/03) involves a Russian national born in 1981 who alleged that criminal proceedings against him were unfair. On 6 January 2002 he was arrested on charges of aggravated murder, robbery, theft, use of forged documents and failure to report a crime (along with co-defendant Mr I.). After the investigation ended on 5 September 2002 the applicant, assisted by counsel Ms K., reviewed the four-volume case file (1,214 pages) in limited sessions between 10 September and 8 October 2002, totalling roughly 22.5 hours. He claimed the investigator pressured him to finish quickly by promising extra visits from his mother and copies of the materials (neither of which materialised). On 8 October both signed a statement confirming they had studied the entire file and had no further requests.

The jury trial began on 15 November 2002 in the Ivanovo Regional Court. The applicant was represented by privately retained counsel Mr S., who never sought to examine the file. On 25 December the jury convicted the applicant of aggravated murder, robbery, theft and failure to report a crime; on 9 January 2003 he received a 23-year sentence. He lodged an appeal on 14 January, Mr S. filed submissions on 20 January, and the applicant submitted further grounds (including a request to attend) on 7 April. A local newspaper published an article about the offences on 18 February.

The appeal was listed for 25 June 2003 before the Supreme Court. The applicant was moved to a Moscow remand centre and appeared by video link; Mr S., although notified, did not attend. The applicant asserted that he asked for an adjournment and for counsel to be appointed, but the court refused, saying there was no legal basis. He also claimed to have faxed additional submissions that day (complaining of insufficient time to study the file) and to have read them aloud; the video connection was poor and repeatedly broke. The Government denied any record of such requests or submissions. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal the same day, holding that it could not re-examine the jury’s factual findings and that the investigation and trial had been procedurally regular.

Domestic law (Articles 51 and 52 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) made counsel mandatory for offences carrying more than 15 years’ imprisonment and for jury trials, and the Constitutional Court later confirmed that this obligation extended to appeal proceedings. These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of inadequate time and facilities to prepare his defence and of the absence of effective legal assistance, particularly at the appeal stage.

The same day the Supreme Court upheld the conviction, holding that it lacked competence under Article 379 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to review the jury’s factual findings and that the investigation and trial had complied with procedural law.

Domestic law (Articles 51 and 52 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) made legal representation mandatory for charges carrying more than 15 years’ imprisonment and for jury trials; a later Constitutional Court ruling confirmed that this obligation extended to appeal proceedings. Article 376 required 14 days’ notice of the hearing date and allowed video-link participation. These facts formed the basis of Krylov’s complaints concerning inadequate time and facilities to prepare his defence and the absence of effective legal assistance, particularly on appeal.

The case of Krylov v. Russia (application no. 36697/03) concerns a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that criminal proceedings in Russia violated the applicant’s right to a fair trial. Dmitriy Yevgenyevich Krylov, born in 1981, was arrested on 6 January 2002 and charged with multiple counts of aggravated murder, robbery, theft, use of forged documents and failure to report a crime. A co-defendant, Mr I., faced the same charges.

The pre-trial investigation ended on 5 September 2002. The case file consisted of four volumes totalling 1,214 pages. Krylov and his then-counsel, Ms K., examined it over a series of short sessions in September and October 2002: four days of 2.5 hours each, two days of 2 hours each, one day of 2.5 hours, one day of 3.5 hours and one further day of 2.5 hours. Krylov later claimed that the investigator had pressured him to accelerate his review by promising extra visits from his mother and copies of the materials; the copies were never supplied. On 8 October 2002 both Krylov and Ms K. signed a statement confirming that they had studied the entire file and had no further requests.

The trial opened on 15 November 2002 before a jury in the Ivanovo Regional Court. Krylov was then represented by a new lawyer, Mr S., whom his mother had retained. According to Krylov, Mr S. never sought permission to study the case file. On 25 December 2002 the jury convicted both defendants of aggravated murder, robbery, theft and failure to report a crime. On 9 January 2003 the Regional Court sentenced Krylov to 23 years’ imprisonment.

Krylov lodged an appeal on 14 January 2003; Mr S. filed submissions on 20 January; Krylov submitted further grounds on 7 April together with a request to attend the hearing. The appeal was listed for 25 June 2003 before the Supreme Court of Russia. Krylov was transferred to a Moscow remand centre and appeared by video link. Mr S. did not attend. Krylov asserted that he asked the court to adjourn the hearing and to appoint replacement counsel, but was told there was no legal basis for the request. He also claimed that a warder had faxed additional written submissions (repeating, among other points, that he had been given insufficient time to study the file) and that he read those submissions aloud. The video connection was of poor quality and was interrupted several times. The Government disputed that any request for counsel or additional submissions had been made or recorded.

The same day the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It held that, because the verdict had been returned by a jury, it lacked competence to re-examine the facts and confined itself to the legal issues, concluding that the investigation and trial had complied with the prescribed procedure.

Domestic law in force at the time made legal representation mandatory for anyone facing a possible sentence of more than 15 years or a jury trial. The Constitutional Court later confirmed that this obligation extended to appeal proceedings and that courts were required to appoint counsel if the accused so requested or if the statutory conditions were met. A waiver of counsel had to be initiated by the accused in writing. Appellate courts reviewed the lawfulness, validity and fairness of first-instance judgments, but after a jury trial the grounds of appeal were limited to procedural breaches, misapplication of the criminal law or an unjust sentence. Prisoners who asked to take part in the appeal hearing were entitled to appear in person or by video link, the choice being for the court.

These facts form the core of Krylov’s complaint that the criminal process was unfair, particularly as regards the time and facilities afforded to prepare his defence, the effectiveness of legal assistance at trial and on appeal, and the conditions of his participation in the appeal hearing.
