**Summary of Iurcu v. the Republic of Moldova (ECtHR, Application no. 33759/10, 9 April 2013)**

The case arose from the aftermath of Moldova’s 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections, in which the ruling Communist Party was declared the narrow winner. On 6–7 April 2009, protests against alleged electoral fraud grew from a few hundred to several thousand people in Chișinău. Initially peaceful, the demonstration on 7 April turned violent after poorly planned police interventions; approximately 250 protesters occupied and looted the lower floors of the Presidential Palace and Parliament, setting fires. From around 1 a.m. on 8 April, police and special forces launched a large-scale operation using excessive force. Arrests continued for days, including of people uninvolved in violence; video and media reports showed beatings of youths by uniformed and plain-clothes officers even after the protests had ended.

The applicant, Vitalie Iurcu (born 1994, then aged 15), alleged he was walking home from a birthday party along a main boulevard around 10.20 p.m. on 7 April 2009 when a group in military uniforms ordered him to the ground and beat him with kicks and batons to his body and head. He was released but stopped again shortly afterward by persons in black clothing and balaclavas, who beat him again (including a kick near his right eye) and forced him into a vehicle with other youths. At the police station he was held in the basement with others, forced to kneel with hands on his head for about three hours, and punched in the back by an officer. Around 2.30 a.m. on 8 April he was briefly questioned about the demonstrations, then transferred to a temporary detention centre for minors, where he and others slept on the floor of a crowded room. A doctor later documented bruises on his back and around his right eye. He was released to his mother on 8 April. Subsequent examination at a torture-victim rehabilitation centre recorded cranial trauma and psychological symptoms typical of torture victims. National television later portrayed the detained youths, including the applicant, as responsible for the building damage.

The Government accepted the facts of arrest and detention but not the ill-treatment claims, relying on the domestic version of events.

On 19 June 2009 the applicant filed a criminal complaint of ill-treatment with the Prosecutor General’s Office. On 15 October 2009 the prosecutor dismissed it without opening a formal investigation, concluding that the applicant had been taken in as a vagrant minor rather than a protester, that an officer present denied any ill-treatment, and that the injuries were insufficient to match the claimed beating. The Buiucani District Court quashed this decision on 3 December 2009, holding that the injuries remained unexplained and the preliminary inquiry incomplete. A criminal investigation was then opened on 18 December 2009; the applicant was granted victim status on 5 February 2010. One police officer was questioned on 9 February 2010; no further investigative steps are recorded in the case materials.

The applicant complained of ill-treatment by police contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, of an ineffective investigation into that complaint, and of a lack of effective domestic remedies (Article 13). The Court examined these together with the admissibility and merits.

**Summary of Iurcu v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 33759/10)**

This ECHR case (Third Section judgment of 9 April 2013) involves a Moldovan national, Vitalie Iurcu (born 1994, aged 15 at the time), who alleged police ill-treatment during post-election unrest in Chișinău on 7-8 April 2009, an ineffective investigation into those claims, and lack of effective remedies. The facts relevant to the alleged Article 3 (prohibition of torture/inhuman or degrading treatment, both substantive and procedural limbs) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) violations are as follows.

On 5 April 2009, general elections were held in Moldova. Preliminary results showed a narrow win for the ruling Communist Party, prompting discontent over alleged fraud. Protests began on 6 April and resumed on 7 April with 5,000-6,000 participants. Though initially peaceful, they turned violent after poorly planned police and fire-truck interventions. Protesters occupied lower floors of the Presidential Palace and Parliament, looting and setting fires. Around 1 a.m. on 8 April, police and special forces launched a large-scale operation using excessive force, arresting all remaining in the square regardless of involvement. Arrests and reported beatings by uniformed and plain-clothes officers continued for days.

According to the applicant, on the evening of 7 April 2009 he was walking home along a main boulevard after a birthday party (unrelated to the protests). Around 10:20 p.m., persons in military uniforms ordered him to lie on the ground with hands on his head. He complied but was kicked and beaten with batons on his body and head; he screamed that he was only 15. Released, he ran but was stopped hundreds of metres later by persons in black clothing and balaclavas, beaten again (including a kick near his right eye), forced into a truck with other youths, and taken to a police station.

At the station, he and others were held in the basement, forced to kneel with hands on heads for about three hours. An officer punched him in the back and told him to straighten up. Around 2:30 a.m. on 8 April he was briefly questioned (about 10 minutes) regarding involvement in the demonstrations. Around 3 a.m. he was transferred to a centre for temporary detention of minors and placed in a small overcrowded room with two beds, sleeping on the floor. The next day a doctor treated him for facial injury; a later report noted bruises on his back and around his right eye. His mother collected him around 4 p.m. on 8 April after being notified around 1 p.m. National television later depicted him and the group as responsible for the disorders.

After release the applicant suffered kidney-area pain and headaches. On 29 April 2009 he obtained a report from the “Memoria” Rehabilitation Centre for Torture Victims documenting cranial trauma and psychological problems typical of torture victims.

The Government accepted the arrest and detention facts but not the ill-treatment allegations, relying on the domestic version.

On 19 June 2009 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint with the Prosecutor General’s Office. On 15 October 2009 prosecutors dismissed it without opening an investigation, concluding he had been taken as a vagrant minor rather than for protest involvement; a police officer denied ill-treatment; and he would have had more bruises if beaten as claimed. The Buiucani District Court quashed this on 3 December 2009, noting the prosecutors had not explained the documented injuries and that the preliminary inquiry was incomplete.

A criminal investigation was formally opened on 18 December 2009; the applicant received victim status on 5 February 2010. On 9 February 2010 one police officer from the station was questioned. No further investigative steps appear to have been taken by the time of the Strasbourg application.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims of police ill-treatment of a minor (including during detention) and of a delayed, superficial investigation that failed to identify perpetrators or properly address the medical evidence of injuries.

**Case Summary: Iurcu v. the Republic of Moldova (App. No. 33759/10, ECtHR, 9 April 2013)**

The applicant, Vitalie Iurcu (born 1994), a 15-year-old Moldovan national, alleged violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his arrest and ill-treatment by police during post-election unrest in Chișinău, followed by an ineffective investigation.

On 5 April 2009, parliamentary elections in Moldova produced a narrow victory for the ruling Communist Party, sparking allegations of fraud. Protests began on 6 April with several thousand mostly young people gathering in central Chișinău. On 7 April, a demonstration of 5–6,000 people turned violent after poorly planned police interventions; protesters occupied and looted lower floors of the Presidential Palace and Parliament, setting fires. From around 1 a.m. on 8 April, police and special forces conducted mass arrests using excessive force against all present in the square, continuing for days regardless of individual involvement in violence. Media footage showed beatings of youths by uniformed and plain-clothes officers after the protests had ended.

The applicant stated that on the evening of 7 April 2009 he was walking home from a birthday party along a main boulevard. Around 10:20 p.m., persons in military uniforms ordered him to lie down with hands on his head; he complied and received multiple kicks and baton blows to his body and head. He screamed that he was only 15 and was briefly released. After running a few hundred metres he was stopped by persons in black clothes and balaclavas, beaten again (including a kick to the right eye), forced into a pick-up truck with other youths, and taken to a police station. There he and others were held in the basement, forced to kneel with hands on heads for about three hours; a police officer punched him in the back. Around 2:30 a.m. on 8 April he was questioned briefly about the demonstrations. At 3 a.m. he was transferred to a juvenile detention centre, where he slept on the floor of an overcrowded room with only two beds. A doctor later recorded bruises on his back and around the right eye. His mother collected him at 4 p.m. after being notified around 1 p.m. National television on 9 April portrayed the detained youths, including the applicant, as responsible for the violence and destruction.

After release the applicant suffered kidney pain and headaches. On 29 April 2009 he attended the “Memoria” Rehabilitation Centre for Torture Victims, which diagnosed cranial trauma and psychological symptoms typical of torture victims.

On 19 June 2009 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint with the Prosecutor General’s Office. On 15 October 2009 prosecutors dismissed it without opening a formal investigation, classifying him as a vagrant minor rather than a protester, relying on a police officer’s denial of ill-treatment, and stating that more bruises would have been expected. The Buiucani District Court quashed this decision on 3 December 2009, finding the preliminary inquiry incomplete and noting the failure to explain the injuries. A criminal investigation was opened on 18 December 2009; the applicant received victim status on 5 February 2010. The only investigative step recorded was the questioning of one police officer on 9 February 2010. No further measures appear to have been taken.

The Government accepted the facts of arrest and detention but rejected the ill-treatment allegations, adopting the domestic prosecutors’ version. The applicant complained of both the ill-treatment itself and the lack of an effective investigation, as well as the absence of effective domestic remedies.

001-118276:
The case of Zorica Jovanović v. Serbia (Application no. 21794/08) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by a Serbian national born in 1953. She alleged a continuing violation arising from the Serbian authorities’ failure to provide any information about the fate of her infant son, who was reported to have died in a state hospital in 1983, or to offer any other form of redress.

On 28 October 1983 the applicant gave birth to a healthy boy at the state-run Ćuprija Medical Centre. She had regular contact with the child until the evening of 30 October, when he was taken to a nursery room as part of standard procedure; no medical problems had been noted. The following morning a doctor informed her that the baby had died. She attempted to reach the nursery but was physically restrained by staff, one of whom tried to administer a sedative. She left the hospital in shock. Relatives were told that an autopsy would be performed in Belgrade, so the body could not be released—an unusual departure from normal hospital practice. The body was never given to the family, no autopsy report was ever produced, and they were never told when or where the child was supposedly buried.

From 2001 onwards Serbian media reported numerous similar “missing baby” cases. In 2002 the applicant requested her son’s records. The hospital replied that he had died of an unknown cause at 07:15 on 31 October 1983 and that its archives had later been destroyed by flooding. Municipal records confirmed the birth but contained no death registration. In January 2003 the child’s father lodged a criminal complaint alleging abduction by hospital staff. The public prosecutor dismissed it in October 2003 as unsubstantiated, citing evidence of death but offering no indication that any investigation had occurred. Subsequent municipal and hospital correspondence simply restated the earlier positions. Death was never formally registered.

The applicant later received psychiatric treatment for depression linked to the events. Hundreds of other parents whose newborns had allegedly died in hospitals during the 1970s–1990s petitioned parliament. A 2006 parliamentary investigating-committee report found serious legislative and procedural shortcomings that justified parental doubts, noted that criminal limitation periods now barred prosecution, and called for legislative change and coordinated state action. A 2010 Ombudsman report concluded that there had been no coherent procedures for hospital deaths of newborns, that autopsy reports were often incomplete or unreliable, that unlawful removal of infants could not be excluded, and that the state’s response between 2006 and 2010 had been inadequate. A parliamentary working group later reported that constitutional non-retroactivity rules prevented any extension of limitation periods and that existing criminal and health-care provisions were sufficient.

Domestic law at the relevant time made unlawful abduction of a minor punishable, but prosecution became time-barred after twenty years. Civil claims for non-pecuniary damage arising from interference with family life were subject to short limitation periods, although case-law held that time did not begin to run until the impugned situation had ended. Later health-care legislation introduced detailed rules on notification, access to the body, autopsy and police involvement when a newborn dies in hospital.

The core facts relevant to the alleged continuing violation are therefore the unexplained disappearance of a healthy infant from a state hospital, the persistent absence of a body, autopsy or death registration, the summary rejection of a criminal complaint without apparent investigation, and the state’s failure, despite parliamentary and Ombudsman findings, to furnish the applicant with any reliable information or effective remedy.

**CASE OF ZORICA JOVANOVIĆ v. SERBIA (Application no. 21794/08), ECtHR judgment of 26 March 2013 (final 9 September 2013)**

The applicant, Zorica Jovanović (born 1953), a Serbian national, complained of the Serbian authorities’ continuing failure to provide information on the real fate of her son, who allegedly died in a State-run hospital in 1983, or any other redress. This was treated as a potential violation of her right to respect for family life.

On 28 October 1983, she gave birth to a healthy boy at the Ćuprija Medical Centre (ĆMC). She had regular contact with him until 30 October, when doctors said both would be discharged the next day. That evening, he was taken to the newborns’ room with no reported medical issues. At 6:30 a.m. on 31 October, a doctor informed her that the baby had died. She ran toward the room but was physically restrained by orderlies; a nurse tried (unsuccessfully) to sedate her. In shock, she left the hospital. Relatives were told an autopsy would occur in Belgrade (a departure from normal ĆMC practice), so the body could not be released. The body was never given to the family, no autopsy report was provided, and they received no information on any burial.

From 2001–2002, Serbian media reported numerous similar “missing babies” cases from the 1970s–1990s. On 24 October 2002, the applicant requested ĆMC records. On 12 November 2002, ĆMC stated the child died at 7:15 a.m. on 31 October 1983 from an unknown cause, but archives had flooded and documents were destroyed. The Municipality of Ćuprija confirmed the birth was registered but the death was not (reaffirmed in 2004 and 2007). On 10 January 2003, her husband filed a criminal complaint against ĆMC staff for abduction. On 15 October 2003, the public prosecutor rejected it as unsubstantiated, citing evidence of death, with no indication of any investigation. In 2004, ĆMC supplied internal records. In 2007, the municipality provided the birth certificate. The applicant received ongoing treatment for depression-related symptoms from 1999/2001.

Hundreds of similarly affected parents petitioned Parliament in 2005. A 14 July 2006 parliamentary investigating committee report found serious legislative and procedural shortcomings at the time, which justified parental doubts about what happened to the children. Criminal redress was barred by limitation periods (20 years under the 1976 Yugoslav Criminal Code for abduction under the 1977 Serbian Criminal Code). It called for coordinated government action and legislative changes. A 2010 Ombudsman report, after investigation, noted the absence of coherent hospital procedures for newborn deaths, a medical view that parents should be spared burial, incomplete/inconclusive autopsies of dubious reliability, and the possibility of unlawful removal of babies. Government responses from 2006–2010 were inadequate; parents were entitled to the truth via a *lex specialis*. A 2010 parliamentary working group concluded existing laws (including the 2005 Criminal Code on abduction/trafficking and the Health Care Act’s procedures for determining time/cause of death, informing families, autopsies, and police notification) were sufficient, with constitutional bars (Article 34) preventing retroactive criminal extensions.

Domestic civil law (Obligations Act) allowed claims for non-pecuniary damage from breaches of personal rights, including family life (per Supreme Court), but with short limitation periods (3–5 years, extendable only if linked to a criminal offence). New 2003 burial procedures required parental or institutional declarations. The ĆMC’s 1983 actions, lack of body/autopsy/death registration, uninvestigated complaint, destroyed records, and unaddressed systemic issues left the applicant without answers or redress for decades.

From 2001 (and especially 2002) Serbian media extensively reported numerous similar cases of newborn babies who had “gone missing” after alleged hospital deaths in the 1970s–1990s. In October 2002 the applicant requested all relevant documentation from the ĆMC. It replied that the child had died on 31 October 1983 at 7.15 a.m. of unknown cause, adding that its archives had been flooded and many documents destroyed. The Municipality of Ćuprija confirmed that the birth had been registered but the death had not (a fact later reaffirmed). The Ombudsman’s July 2010 report, after extensive investigation, found no coherent procedures for newborn deaths in hospital, a prevailing medical view that parents should be “spared” burial of newborns (possibly leading to deliberate deprivation of that opportunity), incomplete/in conclusive autopsies of dubious veracity, and that unlawful removal of babies could not be ruled out. Government responses between 2006 and 2010 had been inadequate; parents remained entitled to know the truth, which required a *lex specialis*. A December 2010 parliamentary working-group report, however, concluded that existing (already-amended) legislation needed no further change except as to medical data, that the Constitution barred extending limitation periods or introducing new/harsher offences for past crimes, and that current criminal and health-care laws already addressed child abduction/trafficking and newborn-death procedures.

Domestic law at the time made criminal prosecution for unlawful detention/abduction of a minor time-barred after 20 years. Civil claims for non-pecuniary damage arising from breach of “personal rights” (including respect for family life) were possible, with some Supreme Court case-law indicating that limitation periods do not begin until the complained-of situation has ended. Subsequent health-care legislation now requires prompt family notification, access to the body, autopsies, storage of biological samples, and police/municipal notification.

These facts underpin the alleged continuing violation consisting of the authorities’ failure to provide information about the child’s fate or any other redress.
001-118335:
The case of Abdi v. the United Kingdom (no. 27770/08) concerns Somali national Mustafa Abdi (born 1975). He arrived in the UK on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. The claim was refused, but he received exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 23 July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment.

On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to make a deportation order and authorised detention pending it. The applicant appealed and submitted a fresh asylum claim; appeal rights were exhausted on 4 December 2003. Automatic release from the criminal sentence occurred on 3 September 2003, but he remained in immigration detention. A deportation order was issued on 5 April 2004 (served 19 April).

The applicant claimed Isaaq-clan origins in Somaliland (though born in Mogadishu). Authorities first pursued return there, which required bio-data he did not supply, then switched to Somalia. In August 2004 the last carrier accepting enforced returns withdrew, leaving only voluntary returns (requiring a signed disclaimer). The applicant refused in November 2004. Bail was refused in December 2004 and October 2005 (the latter hearing receiving inaccurate information that enforced removals were imminent). Further representations in March 2005 were not accepted as a fresh claim. An airline agreement in July 2006 restored enforced removals (first flight November 2006).

Judicial review of the detention was granted in September 2006. The Administrative Court (7 December 2006) held detention lawful to August 2004 (pending appeals/formalities plus re-offending/absconding risks) but unlawful from 3 December 2004 to 30 June 2006 (excessive length, impossibility of removal, and misleading statements). Detention after 30 June 2006 was lawful once removal prospects revived. The Court of Appeal (30 July 2007) reversed this, finding the entire period lawful: the applicant could have returned voluntarily, and his high re-offending risk (given the nature of his offences) outweighed other factors. Leave to the House of Lords was refused.

A parallel challenge to the deportation order itself produced mixed results. After an Immigration Judge allowed an appeal, the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal (reconsideration and rehearing) dismissed it. The Court of Appeal (23 April 2010) found an Article 3 risk on return to Mogadishu; the Supreme Court reversed this (24 November 2010). Removal directions were then set for 8 December 2010, but the ECtHR issued a Rule 39 indication on 7 December 2010 preventing expulsion.

The applicant was released on bail shortly after 13 April 2007 (the end of the period at issue here) but re-detained in April 2008 after breaching conditions. Monthly detention reviews occurred on 22 dates between November 2003 and March 2007. From April 2006 an unpublished “secret” policy imposed a near-blanket presumption of detention for foreign national prisoners, contrary to the published policy of a presumption of release. The UK Supreme Court later held this policy unlawful in Lumba (2011), though only nominal damages followed because detention would have been authorised under the published policy.

These facts go to the alleged Article 5 violation concerning the lawfulness and duration of immigration detention pending deportation (Hardial Singh principles: purpose limited to deportation, reasonable period, continuing prospect of removal, and due diligence).

The applicant, a Somali national born in 1975, arrived in the United Kingdom in May 1995 and claimed asylum. His claim was refused, but he received exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. In July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. In May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to deport him and authorised his detention pending a deportation order. His appeal and fresh asylum claim failed, with appeal rights exhausted in December 2003. Probation assessments found him unsuitable for parole, noting fourteen prison disciplinary charges (six involving fighting) and a high risk of sexual reoffending plus a medium risk of general reoffending.

His sentence expired automatically on 3 September 2003, after which he remained in immigration detention. A deportation order was issued in April 2004. The authorities first sought removal to Somaliland (based on his claimed clan origins) but, after he declined to provide the necessary bio-data, switched to Somalia. From August 2004 no airline would accept enforced returns; only voluntary returns were possible, and the applicant refused to sign a disclaimer in November 2004. Enforced removals resumed only in late 2006 after a new airline agreement. Bail applications were refused in December 2004 and October 2005 (the latter after the immigration judge was wrongly told that enforced removals were imminent). Further asylum representations in 2005 were rejected.

Judicial review of the detention was granted in September 2006. The Administrative Court (December 2006) held detention lawful until August 2004 (owing to pending appeals, absence of a deportation order, and risks of reoffending/absconding) and after June 2006 (once removal prospects revived), but unlawful between December 2004 and June 2006 because of its length, the impossibility of removal, and misleading internal statements. The Court of Appeal (July 2007) reversed the finding of unlawfulness, ruling that the applicant’s refusal of voluntary return and high reoffending risk justified continued detention; permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused. The applicant was released on bail in April 2007 (ending the period under challenge) but later re-detained after breaching conditions. Monthly detention reviews occurred throughout, though not always at precise monthly intervals.

From April 2006 a secret, unpublished Home Office policy created a near-blanket presumption in favour of detaining foreign national prisoners, contrary to the published policy of a presumption in favour of release. Domestic law (Immigration Act 1971 and Hardial Singh principles) permits detention pending deportation only for a reasonable period, with due diligence, and only while a realistic prospect of removal exists. Subsequent Supreme Court rulings (Lumba and Kambadzi) confirmed that application of the unpublished policy, or failure to conduct required reviews, rendered detention unlawful (though damages might be merely nominal if the detainee would have been held anyway).

These facts underpin the applicant’s claim that his detention of approximately three years and seven months pending deportation was arbitrary and unlawful, particularly during periods when removal was practically impossible.

The applicant, Mustafa Abdi (a Somali national born in 1975), arrived in the United Kingdom on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. Although the claim was refused, he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 23 July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to deport him and authorised his detention pending a deportation order. Appeals against deportation and a fresh asylum claim were exhausted on 4 December 2003. Although the applicant became eligible for automatic release on 3 September 2003, he remained in immigration detention under the 2002 authority. A deportation order (including continued detention) was issued on 5 April 2004 and served on 19 April 2004.

Removal proved difficult. The applicant claimed membership of the Isaaq tribe from Somaliland (though born in Mogadishu) but declined to provide the bio-data required by Somaliland authorities, prompting the Government to pursue return to Somalia instead. In August 2004 the last carrier willing to accept enforced returns to Somalia withdrew, rendering involuntary removal impossible until an agreement with African Express Airlines in July 2006 enabled the first such removal in November 2006. In November 2004 the applicant refused a formal request to sign a voluntary-return disclaimer. Bail applications were refused in December 2004 and October 2005 (the latter after an immigration judge was wrongly told that enforced removals would soon resume). Further asylum representations in March 2005 were not treated as a fresh claim.

The applicant obtained permission for judicial review of his detention in September 2006. Removal directions set for 29 November 2006 were cancelled pending that challenge. In a 7 December 2006 judgment the Administrative Court, applying the Hardial Singh principles, held detention lawful from September 2003 to August 2004 (owing to pending appeals, the absence of a deportation order until April 2004, and risks of re-offending and absconding) and after 30 June 2006 (when removal again became feasible). It found the period 3 December 2004–30 June 2006 unlawful because of its length, the impossibility of removal, and misleading official statements. Both parties appealed. On 30 July 2007 the Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal and dismissed the applicant’s, ruling the entire detention lawful: the applicant could have returned voluntarily, the risk of re-offending (especially given the sexual nature of his offences) was high, and his objections to Somalia were irrelevant once removal had been held compatible with the Refugee Convention and Article 3. Permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 13 December 2007.

A parallel challenge to the deportation order itself produced mixed results. An immigration judge allowed an appeal in 2007, but the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal later dismissed it; the Court of Appeal found an Article 3 risk in Mogadishu in April 2010, only for the Supreme Court to reverse that finding in November 2010. Fresh removal directions were then issued, but the European Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39 on 7 December 2010. The present application concerns only the first period of detention, which ended shortly after the applicant’s release on bail on 13 April 2007 (he was later re-detained after breaching conditions). Monthly detention reviews occurred throughout most of the period.

From April 2006 an unpublished Home Office policy created a near-blanket presumption in favour of detaining foreign national prisoners, contrary to the contemporaneous published policy of a presumption of release. The policy was not disclosed until mid-2008. Subsequent Supreme Court decisions (Lumba and Mighty; Kambadzi) later held that such an unpublished policy, and failures to conduct the reviews required by published policy, rendered detention unlawful, albeit often attracting only nominal damages where detention would have occurred in any event.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of unlawful detention contrary to Article 5 of the Convention, arising from the overall duration, periods of no realistic prospect of removal, the unpublished policy, and related procedural shortcomings.
001-118729:
The case of Yevgeniy Ivanov v. Russia (Application no. 27100/03) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant's complaint that he was denied an adequate opportunity to question key prosecution eyewitnesses at his criminal trial, in alleged breach of Article 6 of the Convention (fair trial rights, including the right to examine witnesses).

Yevgeniy Ivanov, a Russian national born in 1979, was charged on 20 September 2002 with manslaughter under Article 111 § 4 of the Criminal Code. The charge arose from a fight on 28 August 2002 in which Mr S. suffered fatal injuries. It relied particularly on pre-trial statements given to investigators by eyewitnesses Mr M., Mr O. and Mr I. M. and O. described how they and S. had fought with three strangers after S. kicked a passing red VAZ car; the driver struck S. in the face, after which others joined the assault and the three lost consciousness. S. was found injured the next day and later died. In later interviews M. and O. stated that S. had fallen immediately after the driver's blows and that they had not seen further hits. I. recounted seeing the car stop, an argument and fight outside a bar, after which he left.

The trial opened on 21 January 2003 before the Kalininskiy District Court of Cheboksary. Ivanov pleaded not guilty. He admitted hitting one of three men twice in the chest during an incident he insisted occurred on 30 August 2002 (a date he sought to prove by calling a tax inspector, whose evidence the court deemed irrelevant). He claimed the men had left uninjured. Other witnesses testified at trial about seeing Ivanov in a bar on 28 August, observing bruises on M., last seeing S. that morning, discovering S. unconscious nearby, and overhearing talk of hitting a man who had kicked a car. Medical evidence showed S. died of a craniocerebral injury after at least nine blows; a police report confirmed he was found on 29 August.

M., O. and I. never appeared. The court repeatedly ordered bailiffs to secure their attendance. Attempts on 22 January 2003 established that O. had moved and that a summons for I. could only be left with his daughter. After adjournment to 3 February, bailiffs learned O.'s mother did not know his address, left a summons for M. at a university campus, and were told I. was at a country house. Further failed efforts followed: on 7 February I. was reported on an indefinite business trip and O. still absent from his former address; similar results occurred on 10–12 February. On 11 February the prosecutor requested that the witnesses' pre-trial statements be read out. Ivanov and his counsel did not object, and the transcripts were read. The next day Ivanov insisted the witnesses must be produced and objected to closing the trial without their examination. The court nevertheless terminated proceedings, citing unsuccessful efforts to locate them.

On 13 February 2003 the District Court convicted Ivanov of manslaughter and sentenced him to eleven years and six months' imprisonment. It held that guilt was established by the pre-trial statements of M., O. and I. (who had witnessed the incident and contradicted Ivanov's account that he had struck only the chest and that S. had left uninjured), together with other trial testimony and the medical and police reports.

Ivanov appealed, arguing that the court had failed to secure the witnesses' attendance, that he had been misled into not objecting to the reading of their statements (believing it would not substitute for live examination), and that he had consistently demanded they be questioned. On 26 February the District Court ruled that the witnesses could not be traced despite bailiffs' efforts, making the reading of statements permissible under Article 281 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 27 March 2003 the Supreme Court of the Chuvashiya Republic dismissed the appeal without addressing the witness issue.

Domestic law required witnesses to be examined directly (Article 278 CCP). Pre-trial statements could be read, with the parties' consent, if a witness failed to appear (Article 281). Courts could order forced attendance (Article 113). These facts formed the core of the complaint that the conviction rested to a decisive extent on untested hearsay evidence.

The case of Yevgeniy Ivanov v. Russia (Application no. 27100/03) concerns a complaint by a Russian national, born in 1979 and living in Cheboksary, that his criminal trial for manslaughter violated his right to a fair hearing. Represented by lawyer N. Mulyakov, Ivanov lodged the application with the European Court of Human Rights on 25 June 2003. The Russian Government was represented by V. Milinchuk. The Court communicated the application on 15 March 2007 and examined admissibility and merits together.

On 20 September 2002 Ivanov was charged under Article 111 § 4 of the Criminal Code with manslaughter arising from a fight on 28 August 2002. The charge relied principally on pre-trial interviews of three eyewitnesses: Mr M., Mr O. and Mr I. According to M. and O., they and their friend Mr S. had argued with three men who emerged from a red VAZ car after S. kicked it. The driver struck S. twice in the face; seven or eight others then joined in. All three victims lost consciousness. S. was found unconscious in the street the next morning and died in hospital from his injuries. In later interviews M. and O. adjusted their accounts, stating that S. fell immediately after the first blows and that they did not see others strike him. I. told investigators he had seen the car stop, two men enter a nearby bar, and the driver begin fighting with three people outside; he left at once.

Trial opened on 21 January 2003 before the Kalininskiy District Court of Cheboksary. Ivanov pleaded not guilty. He admitted striking one of three strangers twice in the chest on 30 August 2002 (not 28 August) and then retreating into a bar; he claimed the men left uninjured. He asked the court to hear tax inspector Ms Sh. to confirm he had taken his mother to pay taxes that day, but the request was refused as irrelevant. Other witnesses testified about seeing Ivanov in the bar on 28 August, seeing bruises on M., hearing O. describe a beating, last seeing S. on the morning of 28 August, finding S. injured, and overhearing men near a red VAZ boast of hitting someone who had kicked their car. A medical expert report recorded that S. died of a craniocerebral injury after at least nine blows and displayed numerous bruises. A police report confirmed S. was found on 29 August.

M., O. and I. never appeared. The court repeatedly ordered bailiffs to secure their attendance (21 January, 22 January, 3 February, 7 February, 11 February). Bailiffs’ reports showed O. had left the address on file (confirmed by new occupants and his mother, who did not know his current address or employer); I. was at work, then at a country house, then on an extended business trip (his daughter received summonses); M. was said to live on a university campus but was never found there. On 11 February the prosecutor asked that the pre-trial transcripts be read out. Ivanov and his counsel did not object; the transcripts were read. The next day Ivanov insisted the witnesses still be produced and objected to closing the trial. The court nevertheless terminated proceedings, holding that all reasonable efforts had failed.

On 13 February 2003 the District Court convicted Ivanov of manslaughter and sentenced him to eleven years and six months’ imprisonment. It found his guilt established by the unread statements of M., O. and I., the other trial testimony, and the medical and police reports. It rejected his claim that he had struck S. only in the chest and that S. had left uninjured, relying expressly on M.’s and O.’s accounts. Ivanov appealed, arguing he had been misled into consenting to the reading of the transcripts, that he had never been warned the reading would replace live examination, and that he had consistently demanded the witnesses’ presence. On 26 February the District Court held that Article 281 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permitted the reading because the witnesses could not be traced despite bailiffs’ efforts. On 27 March 2003 the Supreme Court of the Chuvashiya Republic dismissed the appeal without addressing the witness issue.

Domestic law required witnesses to be examined directly (Article 278 CCP) but allowed pre-trial statements to be read with the parties’ consent if a witness failed to appear (Article 281). Failure to obey a summons could be met by forcible production (Article 113). The applicant’s complaint therefore centred on whether these provisions, as applied, afforded him an adequate opportunity to examine the three key prosecution witnesses whose statements formed the core of the conviction.

The case of Yevgeniy Ivanov v. Russia (Application no. 27100/03) originated from a complaint by a Russian national born in 1979 that he had been denied an adequate opportunity to question key prosecution witnesses at trial, contrary to fair-trial guarantees.

On 20 September 2002 the applicant was charged with manslaughter (Criminal Code Art. 111 § 4) following the death of Mr S. The charge rested principally on pre-trial interviews with three eyewitnesses—Mr M., Mr O. and Mr I. M. and O. described a fight on 28 August 2002 after S., who was drunk, kicked a passing red VAZ car. The driver struck S. in the face; others then joined the assault and the three victims lost consciousness. S. was found the next morning and died in hospital from his injuries. In later interviews M. and O. added that S. had fallen immediately after the driver’s blows and that they had not seen anyone else strike him. I. stated that he had watched the argument and fight from a nearby bar before leaving.

Trial opened on 21 January 2003 before the Kalininskiy District Court of Cheboksary. The applicant pleaded not guilty, insisting the incident had occurred on 30 August (when he had taken his mother to the tax office) and that he had only punched one stranger twice in the chest before retreating to a bar. A request to call the tax inspector was refused as irrelevant. Other witnesses placed the applicant in the bar on the evening of 28 August, confirmed that M. had bruises that night and that S. had last been seen alive that morning, and described finding S. unconscious near the bar at the end of August. A medical expert report recorded death from a craniocerebral injury caused by at least nine blows; a police report confirmed S. had been discovered on 29 August.

M., O. and I. never appeared. The court repeatedly ordered bailiffs to produce them, adjourning the hearing on 21 January, 22 January, 3 February, 7 February, 11 February and 12 February. Bailiffs’ reports documented unsuccessful visits: O. had permanently left the address on file (confirmed four times by new occupants and by his mother, who did not know his whereabouts); I. was successively at work, at a country house or on an extended business trip (summonses left with his daughter); M. lived on a university campus (summons left with a guard) and his mother stated he did not reside with her.

On 11 February the prosecutor asked for the pre-trial transcripts to be read out. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer objected, and the statements were admitted. The next day the applicant insisted that the three witnesses still be produced and objected to closing the trial without their examination. The court nevertheless ended the proceedings, holding that all reasonable efforts to locate them had failed.

On 13 February the applicant was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to eleven years and six months’ imprisonment. The court treated the unread pre-trial statements of M., O. and I. as decisive, finding that they refuted the applicant’s account that he had struck only the chest and that S. had left uninjured. Other trial testimony and the expert reports were cited as corroboration.

In his appeal the applicant argued that he had been misled into consenting to the reading of the transcripts (the judge never warning that this would replace live examination) and that he had consistently demanded the witnesses’ attendance. On 26 February the District Court ruled that Art. 281 of the Code of Criminal Procedure authorised the reading because the witnesses could not be traced despite bailiffs’ efforts. The Supreme Court of the Chuvashiya Republic dismissed the appeal on 27 March 2003 without addressing the witness issue.

001-118738:
The case of Zahirović v. Croatia (no. 58590/11) arose from criminal proceedings against Zajko Zahirović, a stateless person born in 1975 and living in Zagreb. An investigation opened on 22 October 2003 concerning events of 5 July 2003, when he allegedly fired two shots at a wall in his partner’s flat while two others were present, endangering their lives, and of 6 July 2003, when after a verbal dispute he allegedly fired multiple shots in a nightclub, attempting to murder three persons (K.G., A.P. and M.V.). He remained at large until appearing before an investigating judge on 28 April 2004, when he was questioned and remanded in custody. He was indicted on 24 June 2004 on both counts.

Judge Z.K. initially presided over the trial panel at Zagreb County Court. On 2 September 2004 a three-judge panel including Judge M.G. extended detention on grounds of risk of reoffending under Article 102 § 1(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The decision highlighted the applicant’s alleged “brutality, determination, high degree of criminal resolve and obvious propensity towards such criminal behaviour.” On 28 April 2006 another panel including M.G. ordered his release after the statutory maximum detention period expired. In September 2008, after Z.K. was appointed to the Supreme Court, the case was reassigned to M.G. as president of the trial panel.

On 27 November 2009 the panel presided by M.G. convicted the applicant of attempted murder of the three persons (the prosecution having withdrawn the endangerment charge) and sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment. Both parties appealed to the Supreme Court: the prosecutor sought a more severe sentence; the applicant raised multiple complaints, including that M.G. lacked impartiality because he had already expressed views on the applicant’s character while extending detention.

The Supreme Court forwarded the file and appeals to the State Attorney’s Office of the Republic of Croatia under Article 373 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 16 March 2010 that office submitted a written opinion supporting the prosecutor’s appeal (arguing the first-instance sentence was unduly lenient given aggravating factors such as grave injuries to K.G., lack of remorse and the applicant’s flight) and rejecting the defence appeal (including on impartiality, asserting that a judge’s impartiality is presumed and that no objective circumstances existed to doubt M.G.). This opinion was never communicated to the defence.

A public hearing was scheduled for 20 April 2010. The applicant’s lawyer was invited, but the applicant (then in detention) was expressly not summoned, despite his request to attend with counsel. At the hearing the lawyer reiterated the appeal arguments; the Deputy State Attorney endorsed the uncommunicated 16 March opinion. The Supreme Court then deliberated in private, dismissed the applicant’s appeal, upheld the conviction and increased the sentence to eight years. It held that M.G.’s prior detention ruling did not require his exclusion, as no additional circumstances raising doubts about impartiality had been shown, and that the applicant’s presence at the hearing was not useful.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging violations of fair-trial rights, inter alia through M.G.’s lack of impartiality, non-communication of the State Attorney’s submissions (equality of arms) and his exclusion from the Supreme Court hearing (particularly as the sentence was increased without examining him). The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as ill-founded on 23 March 2011, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning. The decision was served on 4 April 2011; the application to the European Court followed on 6 September 2011.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 6 violations concerning judicial impartiality (objective doubts arising from M.G.’s earlier characterisation of the applicant’s criminal propensity), equality of arms (undisclosed prosecutorial opinion influencing the Supreme Court) and the applicant’s absence from the appeal hearing at which his sentence was increased.

The case of Zahirović v. Croatia (Application no. 58590/11) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 September 2011 by Zajko Zahirović, a stateless person born in 1975 and residing in Zagreb. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial), specifically concerning the impartiality of the trial court, equality of arms, and his absence from the appeal hearing.

On 22 October 2003, an investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court opened an investigation into suspicions that the applicant had endangered life and limb by firing shots in his partner’s flat on 5 July 2003 and attempted to murder three persons by shooting at them in a nightclub on 6 July 2003. Detention was ordered, but the applicant remained at large until he appeared on 28 April 2004, was questioned, and remanded in custody. He was indicted on 24 June 2004.

Judge Z.K. initially presided over the trial panel. On 2 September 2004, a three-judge panel of the Zagreb County Court, including Judge M.G., extended the applicant’s detention under Article 102 § 1(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (risk of reoffending). The decision highlighted the applicant’s alleged brutality, determination, and propensity for criminal behaviour based on the charges. On 28 April 2006, another panel including Judge M.G. ordered the applicant’s release after the maximum statutory detention period expired.

On 16 September 2008, the case was reassigned to Judge M.G. as president of the trial panel after Judge Z.K. was appointed to the Supreme Court. On 27 November 2009, the trial panel, presided over by Judge M.G., convicted the applicant of attempted murder of three persons (dismissing the endangerment charge after its withdrawal by the prosecution) and sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment.

The Zagreb County State Attorney’s Office appealed on 2 February 2010 seeking a harsher sentence. The applicant appealed on 16 February 2010, raising substantive and procedural flaws, including that Judge M.G. lacked impartiality because his prior involvement in the detention decision showed he had already formed an opinion on the charges.

The Supreme Court forwarded the case file and appeals to the State Attorney’s Office of the Republic of Croatia. On 16 March 2010, that office submitted a detailed opinion supporting the prosecutor’s appeal for a more severe sentence and dismissing the defence appeal (including on impartiality, arguing no objective circumstances raised doubts and that impartiality is presumed). This opinion was not communicated to the defence.

On 22 March 2010, the Supreme Court scheduled a public hearing for 20 April 2010, inviting the applicant’s lawyer but expressly excluding the applicant (then in pre-trial detention pending final judgment). At the hearing, attended by the lawyer and the Deputy State Attorney, the lawyer reiterated the appeal arguments, while the Deputy endorsed the 16 March opinion. The applicant was not present or heard.

The same day, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction but increased the sentence to eight years. It rejected the impartiality complaint, stating that prior involvement in a detention ruling did not require exclusion absent specific circumstances raising doubts. It found it unnecessary to have the applicant brought from detention. The sentence increase cited underestimation of aggravating factors (grave injuries to one victim, lack of remorse, flight abroad) and argued against applying more lenient penalty rules.

On 31 May 2010, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging unfair trial due to Judge M.G.’s lack of impartiality, non-communication of the State Attorney’s submissions, and failure to examine him before increasing the sentence. The Constitutional Court dismissed it as ill-founded on 23 March 2011 (served 4 April 2011), endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 6 violations regarding judicial impartiality, equality of arms (non-disclosure of the opinion), and the right to be present/heard at the appeal stage where the sentence was increased.

The case of Zahirović v. Croatia (Application no. 58590/11) originated from criminal proceedings against a stateless applicant born in 1975. An investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court opened an investigation on 22 October 2003 into events of 5–6 July 2003: the applicant had allegedly endangered others by firing two shots at a wall in his partner’s flat (despite the presence of others) and had attempted to murder three persons by shooting at them in a nightclub after a dispute. The applicant was questioned and remanded in custody on 28 April 2004. He was indicted on 24 June 2004.

Judge Z.K. initially presided over the trial panel. On 2 September 2004 a three-judge panel that included Judge M.G. extended the applicant’s detention on the ground of risk of reoffending. The decision described the alleged facts in detail and characterised the applicant as displaying “brutality, determination, high degree of criminal resolve and obvious propensity towards such criminal behaviour.” A later panel that also included Judge M.G. ordered the applicant’s release on 28 April 2006 after the statutory maximum period of detention had expired.

In September 2008 the case was reassigned to Judge M.G. after Judge Z.K. was appointed to the Supreme Court. On 27 November 2009 a trial panel presided over by Judge M.G. convicted the applicant of attempted murder of three persons, withdrew the endangerment charge, and imposed a six-year sentence.

The Zagreb County State Attorney’s Office appealed, seeking a heavier sentence. The applicant also appealed, arguing (among other points) that Judge M.G. lacked impartiality because he had already formed an opinion on the charges when extending detention. The Supreme Court forwarded the file and both appeals to the State Attorney’s Office of the Republic of Croatia. That office submitted a detailed opinion dated 16 March 2010 that supported a heavier sentence, rejected the impartiality complaint (asserting that impartiality is presumed and that no objective circumstances raised doubt), and addressed the remaining grounds of appeal. The opinion was never communicated to the defence.

The Supreme Court scheduled a public hearing for 20 April 2010. Although the applicant (then in detention) and his lawyer had requested that both attend, the court expressly excluded the applicant while inviting only the lawyer. At the hearing the lawyer reiterated the appeal; the Deputy State Attorney endorsed the undisclosed 16 March opinion. The Supreme Court immediately upheld the conviction and increased the sentence to eight years. It held that prior participation in a detention decision did not of itself require exclusion of Judge M.G. and that the applicant had failed to substantiate any other circumstances capable of casting doubt on impartiality. The court also analysed sentencing factors, treating certain circumstances as additional aggravating elements.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint, which raised the same issues of judicial impartiality, non-communication of the State Attorney’s submissions, and his exclusion from the hearing at which the sentence was increased, was dismissed as ill-founded on 23 March 2011.

These facts form the core of the complaints concerning lack of impartiality of the trial court, inequality of arms, and the applicant’s absence from the Supreme Court hearing.
001-118578:
The case of A.B. v. Hungary (application no. 33292/09) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 16 April 2013 (final 16 July 2013). The Hungarian applicant, a security guard born in 1975, alleged that his pre-trial detention was of unjustified length in violation of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention. He further complained under Article 5 § 4 that equality of arms was not respected in proceedings challenging his detention, as he lacked access to relevant investigation materials.

Criminal proceedings began on 17 January 2007 against the applicant and alleged accomplices for aggravated extortion, endorsement of and profiteering from prostitution, and other offences. Upon learning police were seeking him, the applicant voluntarily presented himself at a police station. On 18 January 2007 the prosecution sought his pre-trial detention, citing risks of absconding, reoffending, and collusion. The Pest Central District Court ordered detention on 19 January 2007 solely on collusion grounds. It rejected absconding risk in light of the applicant’s settled family life, legal income, and lack of prior convictions (deeming the prospect of a severe sentence insufficient), and found the offence’s continuous nature did not necessarily imply a reoffending risk.

On 1 February 2007 the Budapest Regional Court upheld detention on all three grounds, noting the applicant’s lack of legal income, unknown personal circumstances, and an accomplice’s flight. Detention was thereafter repeatedly prolonged at statutory intervals, primarily citing collusion and witness intimidation. Courts referred to investigation-file material indicating that the applicant and an associate had tried to influence witnesses and that police had seized from a defendant a summons issued to a witness who later withdrew testimony.

On 4 May 2007 the defence unsuccessfully sought substitution of a less severe measure, arguing that any collusion risk had dissipated at that stage. On 7 May the applicant’s lawyer complained of no access to prosecution evidence supporting the intimidation risk. Similar unsuccessful motions followed on 31 May and 13 September 2007, stressing that no evidence known to the defence substantiated collusion. A 12 September 2007 prolongation order added a reoffending risk; on appeal this was dropped but absconding risk retained, the court citing the organised nature of the alleged crimes and the accused’s attitude toward witnesses even after the investigation ended.

A bill of indictment was filed on 17 October 2007. Detention was prolonged on 19 October 2007 for absconding and collusion. The applicant appealed, highlighting his settled background (negating absconding) and the absence of any communicated material indicating a genuine collusion risk. The appeal was dismissed on 28 November 2007, though the collusion ground was dropped. At the first hearing on 18 December 2007 one co-accused was released on bail, but the applicant’s request was refused because the proposed sum would not guarantee his appearance given the severe potential sentence. A further bail request was denied on 19 February 2008 on absconding grounds linked to charge seriousness; subsequent appeals and requests for less coercive measures failed, courts repeatedly invoking the risk of flight due to possible severe punishment. The applicant was released on 10 December 2008 subject to a residence restriction.

Hungarian Code of Criminal Procedure provisions (sections 211(3) and 186) required the prosecution to present evidence supporting detention motions and permitted the defence to examine it (and obtain copies of inspectable documents) unless investigation interests would be harmed, with restrictions on victim/witness personal data.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: detention spanning nearly two years, with shifting and sometimes internally inconsistent justifications that the applicant contended were inadequately substantiated or no longer relevant, and repeated unsuccessful attempts to obtain the underlying investigative material said to justify continued detention.

The case of A.B. v. Hungary (Application no. 33292/09) involves a Hungarian national born in 1975, employed as a security guard in Budapest. On 17 January 2007, criminal proceedings began against him and alleged accomplices for aggravated extortion, endorsement of and profiteering from prostitution, and related offenses. The applicant voluntarily surrendered to police upon learning they sought him.

On 18 January 2007, prosecutors sought pre-trial detention citing risks of absconding, crime repetition, and collusion. The Pest Central District Court ordered detention on 19 January 2007, retaining only the collusion risk. It rejected absconding, given the applicant’s settled family life, legal income, and lack of prior convictions, and found the offense’s continuous nature did not inherently imply repetition risk.

On 1 February 2007, the Budapest Regional Court upheld detention on all three grounds, citing the applicant’s lack of legal income, unknown personal circumstances, and an absconded accomplice. Detention was repeatedly extended at statutory intervals, primarily for collusion and witness intimidation. Courts referenced investigation file materials showing the applicant and an associate had attempted to influence witnesses, plus a seized summons linked to a witness who later withdrew testimony.

The defense unsuccessfully sought less stringent measures on 4 May 2007, arguing collusion risk had become irrelevant. On 7 May, 31 May, and 13 September 2007, the applicant’s lawyer complained of no access to prosecution evidence supporting witness-intimidation claims, with the risk unsubstantiated by any material known to the defense.

A 12 September 2007 extension invoked repetition and absconding risks. On appeal, repetition was dropped but absconding retained, based on the organized nature of the alleged crime and defendants’ attitudes toward witnesses, even after the investigation ended.

A bill of indictment issued on 17 October 2007. Detention was extended on 19 October 2007 for absconding and collusion. The applicant appealed, stressing his settled background and absence of disclosed evidence of collusion. The appeal was rejected on 28 November 2007, though collusion risk was no longer cited.

At the first hearing on 18 December 2007, an accomplice received bail, but the applicant was refused because the proposed sum would not secure his attendance given the severe potential sentence. A further bail request was denied on 19 February 2008, again citing absconding risk from the charges’ seriousness. Subsequent appeals and requests for milder measures failed, with courts repeatedly invoking the risk of flight due to a potentially harsh penalty.

The applicant was released on 10 December 2008 subject to a residence restriction, after nearly 23 months in detention.

Under Hungarian law (Act XIX of 1998, Code of Criminal Procedure, Sections 211(3) and 186), the prosecution must present evidence supporting detention motions, and parties may inspect it subject to investigation-interest limits. Suspects and counsel may inspect expert opinions freely but other documents only if this does not harm the investigation; copies of witness/victim statements omit personal data, and certain internal communications are withheld.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 that detention lacked sufficient, evolving justification over its duration, and under Article 5 § 4 that equality of arms was breached by restricted access to the materials used to justify continued detention.

The case of A.B. v. Hungary (application no. 33292/09) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 16 April 2013. The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1975 and living in Budapest, lodged the application on 8 June 2009, requesting anonymity. He was represented by counsel. He alleged that his pre-trial detention violated Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention due to its unjustified length, and Article 5 § 4 because the principle of equality of arms was breached when he challenged the detention, as he lacked access to relevant investigation materials.

Criminal proceedings were instituted on 17 January 2007 against the applicant (then a security guard) and alleged accomplices for aggravated extortion, endorsement of and profiteering from prostitution, and related offences. Upon learning the police were seeking him, the applicant voluntarily presented himself at the police station. The prosecution moved for pre-trial detention on 18 January 2007, citing risks of absconding, crime repetition, and collusion.

On 19 January 2007, the Pest Central District Court ordered detention solely on collusion grounds. It rejected absconding risk because of the applicant’s settled family life, legal income, and lack of prior convictions, holding that a potential severe sanction alone was insufficient. It also found that the continuous nature of the alleged offence did not necessarily imply a risk of repetition.

On 1 February 2007, the Budapest Regional Court upheld detention, restoring all three grounds. It noted the applicant’s lack of legal income, unknown personal circumstances, and an absconded accomplice.

Thereafter, detention was prolonged at statutory intervals, mainly citing collusion and witness intimidation. Courts referred to investigation-file elements indicating that the applicant and an associate had attempted to influence witnesses, and that police had seized from a defendant a summons sent to a witness who later withdrew testimony.

The defence repeatedly sought substitution of detention by a less stringent measure, arguing that any collusion risk had become irrelevant at an advanced stage. On 7 May 2007 the applicant’s lawyer specifically complained that no supporting evidence of witness intimidation had been made accessible. Similar unsuccessful motions and complaints were filed on 31 May and 13 September 2007.

A 12 September 2007 prolongation order reintroduced the risk of crime repetition (later discarded on appeal) together with absconding. Even after the investigation ended, courts retained detention because of the organised character of the alleged offences and the accused persons’ attitude toward witnesses.

A bill of indictment was filed on 17 October 2007. Detention was then prolonged for absconding and collusion; an appeal was rejected and the collusion ground dropped. At the first hearing on 18 December 2007 an accomplice was released on bail, but the applicant’s corresponding request was refused because the proposed bail would not adequately secure his appearance given the severity of the potential sentence. Further applications for bail or alternative measures (including one decided on 19 February 2008) were likewise rejected, the courts repeatedly invoking absconding risk solely on the basis of the seriousness of the charges.

The applicant was finally released on 10 December 2008 subject to a prohibition on leaving his domicile. The pre-trial detention thus lasted from 19 January 2007 until 10 December 2008.

Relevant domestic provisions (Act XIX of 1998 on the Code of Criminal Procedure) require the prosecution, at detention hearings, to present the evidence supporting its motion, and grant those present an opportunity to examine that evidence (Section 211). However, access to investigation documents is restricted: the suspect and counsel may inspect expert opinions and certain other materials only insofar as this does not injure investigation interests, and copies of documents containing victim or witness data are withheld (Section 186).

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: nearly two years of detention justified by shifting grounds that frequently reduced to the abstract severity of possible punishment, despite the applicant’s voluntary surrender, family ties and lack of criminal record, coupled with persistent non-disclosure of the concrete evidence said to underpin collusion or intimidation risks.
001-118645:
The case of Baksza v. Hungary originated in an application lodged on 2 December 2008 by István Baksza, a Hungarian national born in 1974 and residing in Gödöllő. He complained under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that the length of his pre-trial detention was excessive and unjustified, and under Article 5 § 4 that equality of arms was not respected in detention reviews because he and his lawyer lacked detailed access to the investigation materials supporting the risks cited against him.

Baksza, who was married and the father of a minor child, was arrested on 18 January 2006 after police found suspicious spare car parts, documents and tools in his vehicle. He was interrogated that day on suspicion of attempted aggravated larceny of a van. On 20 January 2006 the prosecution sought pre-trial detention, arguing on the basis of the seized items that there was reasonable suspicion he and an accomplice, together with unknown others, were involved in car theft. The Dunakeszi District Court ordered detention the same day, citing (but not substantiating) risks of absconding, collusion and repetition of crime; the accomplice was also detained.

Baksza appealed, challenging the suspicion and stressing his clean record, legal income and family responsibilities as making flight or reoffending unlikely. The Pest County Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 27 January 2006 without addressing those arguments in detail. Detention was prolonged on 13 February 2006 with reference to eight counts of larceny. Baksza pointed out that evidence for one theft did not connect him to the vehicle and that he had not been formally suspected of the remaining seven. The Regional Court rejected the appeal on 28 February 2006, stating it could not assess the evidence at that stage.

Thereafter detention was extended at statutory intervals with essentially identical reasoning, despite persistent discrepancies in the number of charges. A request for release on 24 April 2006 citing deteriorating family circumstances was refused. On 10 July 2006 the prosecution sought prolongation on four counts; the District Court granted it and added a further count. An expert was appointed on 29 August 2006 to determine whether the seized items linked Baksza to any thefts. Further extensions occurred in October and November 2006. Additional charges were brought on 21 December 2006. On 15 January 2007 the Regional Court again prolonged detention; Baksza complained that the expert opinion had never been disclosed to him.

A bill of indictment was filed on 16 May 2007 charging 17 counts of car theft or attempted theft plus one count of document forgery. Detention continued on grounds of absconding and reoffending risk. The first trial hearing took place on 21 November 2007; the court maintained detention solely because a potentially severe sentence created a flight risk and gave no reason for any reoffending risk. Subsequent requests for release or a milder measure failed. Apart from the July 2006 motion, none of the prosecution’s prolongation applications specified the evidence said to underpin the alleged risks. Baksza’s lawyer repeatedly protested the lack of access (notably on 17 July and 20 November 2006); the omission was never remedied and the courts did not dispute the defence’s claim of non-access. Of 24 detention decisions only one distinguished the two co-detainees. Less restrictive measures were considered on three dates in 2006 but never applied.

Baksza was released on 2 June 2008 subject to a prohibition on leaving his domicile. He was convicted at first instance on 24 May 2011; the appeal remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment. Hungarian law (Code of Criminal Procedure ss. 131–132, 186 and 211) sets time-limits and review intervals for pre-trial detention and restricts defence inspection of investigation documents where this would injure the interests of the investigation.

The case of Baksza v. Hungary originated in an application lodged on 2 December 2008 by István Baksza, a Hungarian national born in 1974 and residing in Gödöllő. He alleged violations of Article 5 § 3 (unjustified length of pre-trial detention) and Article 5 § 4 (breach of equality of arms in detention reviews) of the Convention.

On 18 January 2006, police arrested the applicant after finding suspicious spare car parts, documents and tools in his vehicle. He was interrogated on suspicion of attempted aggravated larceny of a van. On 20 January 2006 the prosecution sought pre-trial detention, relying on the seized items as indicating that the applicant and an accomplice (with unknown helpers) were engaged in car theft. That day the Dunakeszi District Court ordered detention, citing risks of absconding, collusion and reoffending but without substantiating them. An accomplice was likewise detained.

The applicant appealed, contesting the suspicion and stressing his unblemished record, legal income, marriage and support of family members including a minor child as rendering the risks implausible. On 27 January 2006 the Pest County Regional Court dismissed the appeal without addressing these arguments in detail. Detention was prolonged on 13 February 2006 by reference to eight counts of larceny. The applicant observed that evidence for one count did not link him to the vehicle and that he had not even been formally suspected of the remaining seven. The Regional Court rejected his appeal on 28 February 2006, stating that it could not yet assess the evidence.

Further prolongations occurred at statutory intervals, repeating essentially the same reasoning despite fluctuating numbers of charges. The applicant’s requests for release, citing worsening conditions for his dependants, were refused. On 10 July 2006 the prosecution invoked four counts; the District Court added a fifth. An expert was appointed on 29 August 2006 to determine whether the seized items connected the applicant to any thefts, yet the opinion was never disclosed to him. Additional counts were added in December 2006. A bill of indictment of 16 May 2007 charged 17 counts of (attempted) car theft plus document forgery. Detention was maintained on grounds of absconding and reoffending risk.

The first trial hearing took place on 21 November 2007; the court cited only the prospect of a severe sentence as justifying continued detention for absconding and gave no reason for any reoffending risk. Subsequent requests for release or a less restrictive measure failed. Apart from the 10 July 2006 motion, none of the prosecution’s applications specified the evidence said to support the risks. The applicant’s lawyer repeatedly sought access to that material (notably on 17 July and 20 November 2006) but was refused; the courts neither granted access nor rebutted the complaint. Of 24 detention decisions, only one distinguished between the two co-detainees. Alternatives to detention were considered on three dates in 2006 but never applied.

The applicant was released on 2 June 2008 (after more than two years and four months) subject to a residence restriction. He was convicted at first instance on 24 May 2011; the appeal remains pending. These facts form the basis of the complaints that the detention was unduly prolonged by stereotyped reasoning that ignored personal circumstances and alternatives, and that the defence was denied effective access to the evidence underpinning the alleged risks.

He was interrogated that day on suspicion of attempted aggravated larceny involving a van. On 20 January 2006, the prosecution sought pre-trial detention, asserting reasonable suspicion that Baksza and an accomplice, with unknown helpers, were involved in car theft, based primarily on the seized items. Baksza appealed, contesting the suspicion and arguing that his stable background made the risks improbable. The Pest County Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 27 January 2006 without addressing his arguments in detail.

Baksza appealed, noting that evidence for one count failed to link him to the vehicle and that he had not been formally implicated in the other seven. The Regional Court rejected this on 28 February 2006, stating it could not assess evidence at that stage. A 24 April 2006 release request, citing deteriorated family living conditions, was denied. On 14 July, the District Court upheld this after a hearing and added another theft suspicion; subsequent appeals and requests failed. A 15 January 2007 extension used the same grounds; Baksza noted that the expert opinion had never been disclosed to him.

A bill of indictment was filed on 16 May 2007 charging 17 counts of car theft or attempted theft plus document forgery. Detention continued due to risks of absconding and repetition. The first trial hearing was held on 21 November 2007, with detention upheld solely because a potentially severe sentence created an absconding risk (no explanation was given for repetition risk). Later release or alternative-measure requests failed. Of the prosecution’s motions, only the 10 July 2006 filing specifically referenced underlying evidence. Baksza’s lawyer repeatedly complained (notably on 17 July and 20 November 2006) of denied access to the materials supporting the alleged risks; courts neither remedied this nor refuted the claims. Of 24 detention decisions, only one provided separate reasoning for each co-detainee. Less stringent measures were considered on three dates in 2006 but never applied.
