The European Court of Human Rights case of Udeh v. Switzerland (Application no. 12020/09) arose from a 3 March 2009 application by Nigerian national Kinsley Chike Udeh (born 1972), his then-Swiss wife Michèle Udeh (born 1984), and their twin daughters (born 2003, dual Swiss-Nigerian nationals). They alleged that Swiss authorities’ refusal to renew the first applicant’s residence permit, and a subsequent entry ban, violated their Article 8 right to respect for family life.

The first applicant, using a false identity and claiming a later birth year, received a suspended four-month sentence in Austria in August 2001 for possessing a small quantity of cocaine. He entered Switzerland in November 2001; his asylum claim was rejected as inadmissible. He departed and re-entered in September 2003. On 1 November 2003 he married a Swiss national who had just given birth to their twins and obtained a residence permit on that basis.

In August 2006 he was arrested in Germany and, on 24 November 2006, sentenced to 42 months’ imprisonment for attempting to import 257 grams of pure cocaine (55 doses) by body-packing. Because he had been outside Switzerland for more than six months, the Basle-Rural Migration Office declared his permit void on 23 August 2007 and refused a new one, citing the conviction and the family’s dependence on social assistance.

Cantonal appeals failed. On 8 January 2009 the Federal Court dismissed the final appeal. It stressed the gravity of the German offence (more than 18 grams of pure cocaine, a “serious case” under Swiss narcotics law carrying a minimum one-year sentence) and the applicant’s two drug convictions. The family had received some CHF 165 000 in benefits. The applicant had lived with his family only since late 2003, had no stable employment (partly linked to tuberculosis), spoke German poorly, mixed mainly with co-nationals and was therefore poorly integrated. Re-offending could not be excluded given his poor employment prospects. Although a genuine family life existed and the Swiss wife and children could not be required to follow him to Nigeria, the applicant retained family ties there that would ease reintegration.

He was ordered to leave by 31 March 2009. A request for interim measures was refused. He was detained pending removal, disappeared, was recaptured and released in January 2011. On 25 January 2011 an entry ban until 26 January 2020 was imposed (suspensible for humanitarian reasons). He remained in Switzerland, later divorced, retained limited access to the twins (one afternoon every two weeks) and fathered a third child in 2012 with another Swiss national, with whom he cohabited and planned to marry.

Under the former Residence and Settlement of Aliens Act a Swiss spouse was entitled to a permit unless expulsion grounds existed (serious conviction or significant, continuous welfare dependence) and expulsion was appropriate in all the circumstances. The later Foreign Nationals Act authorised entry bans after removal orders, public-order threats or welfare costs, normally for five years but extendable, and suspendible on humanitarian grounds.

These facts frame the Article 8 complaint: the interference with family life (including two Swiss children and, later, a third Swiss child) versus Switzerland’s interests in immigration control, public order and the prevention of serious drug crime.

The case of Udeh v. Switzerland (Application no. 12020/09) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 March 2009 by Nigerian national Kinsley Chike Udeh (born 1972), his then-wife Michèle Udeh (a Swiss national born 1984), and their twin daughters Naira Johanna Udeh and Uzoma Elisa Udeh (born 2003, holding dual Swiss-Nigerian nationality). The applicants alleged that Swiss authorities’ refusal to grant or renew the first applicant’s residence permit, followed by an entry ban, violated their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The first applicant, using a false identity and claiming to have been born in 1983, received a suspended four-month sentence from an Austrian court in August 2001 for possessing a small quantity of cocaine. He entered Switzerland in November 2001; his asylum claim (also under a false identity) was declared inadmissible, after which he left and re-entered on 2 September 2003. On 1 November 2003 he married the second applicant, who had recently given birth to the twins; the marriage entitled him to a residence permit.

In August 2006 he was arrested in Germany for attempting to import 257 grams of pure cocaine (55 doses) by body-packing and sentenced to 42 months’ imprisonment. Because he had been outside Switzerland for more than six months while serving that sentence, the Canton of Basle-Rural Migration Office declared his permit void on 23 August 2007 and refused to reissue it, citing the conviction and the family’s dependence on social welfare. Appeals were rejected by the cantonal government and the Basle-Rural Cantonal Court. After early release in May 2008, the Federal Court dismissed a final appeal on 8 January 2009. It treated the German offence as serious (qualifying as a “serious case” under Swiss narcotics law), noted two drug convictions, observed that the family had received approximately CHF 165 000 in benefits, recorded the first applicant’s limited stay in Switzerland since October 2003, lack of stable employment (partly linked to tuberculosis), poor German and limited social integration, and found a risk of reoffending. Although it acknowledged a genuine and close family life that would be severely affected, and accepted that the Swiss wife and children could not be expected to relocate to Nigeria, it held that the first applicant retained family ties there and could reintegrate relatively easily.

He was ordered to leave by 31 March 2009. A Rule 39 request for interim measures was refused. He was detained pending removal in September 2009, disappeared, was re-arrested in September 2010 and held until January 2011. On 25 January 2011 the Federal Office of Migration imposed an entry ban until 26 January 2020 (suspensible on humanitarian grounds). The couple later separated and divorced in September 2012; custody of the twins was awarded to the mother, with the first applicant granted access one afternoon at least every two weeks. By late 2012 he was living with another Swiss national, with whom he had a third child born in August 2012, and intended to marry her. He remained in Switzerland and claimed to maintain contact with the twins.

These facts—the first applicant’s criminal record, welfare dependency, incomplete integration, the genuine family unit (later fractured by divorce yet involving access rights and a new Swiss family), and the lengthy entry ban—formed the core of the Article 8 claim. Relevant domestic law at the time (former Residence and Settlement of Aliens Act, ss. 7, 10 and 11, and later Federal Act on Foreign Nationals, s. 67) permitted expulsion or an entry ban after serious criminal convictions or significant welfare reliance, subject to an overall assessment of the circumstances.

**Case summary (approx. 500 words)**

In *Udeh v. Switzerland* (App. no. 12020/09), the applicants—Nigerian national Kinsley Chike Udeh (born 1972), his then Swiss wife Michèle Udeh (born 1984), and their twin daughters (born 2003, dual Swiss-Nigerian nationality)—alleged that Swiss authorities’ refusal to grant the first applicant leave to remain after his drug convictions violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life). The couple later divorced; the first applicant remained in Switzerland and had a further child with another Swiss national.

The first applicant entered Switzerland in November 2001 under a false identity (claiming birth in 1983). His asylum claim was rejected as inadmissible. He left and re-entered in September 2003. On 1 November 2003 he married the Swiss national who had just given birth to their twins and obtained a residence permit on that basis.

He already had a 2001 Austrian conviction (under the false identity) for possessing a small quantity of cocaine, resulting in a suspended four-month sentence. In August 2006 he was arrested in Germany for attempting to import 257 grams of pure cocaine (55 doses) by body-packing and was sentenced to 42 months’ imprisonment.

In August 2007 the cantonal migration office treated his permit as lapsed because he had been outside Switzerland for more than six months while imprisoned in Germany. It refused to re-issue a permit, citing the conviction and the family’s reliance on social-welfare benefits. Appeals failed. The Federal Court (January 2009) held that the German offence was a “serious case” under Swiss narcotics law (more than 18 grams of pure cocaine, punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment). The family’s receipt of some CHF 165,000 in benefits was noted, as was the first applicant’s limited integration: he had lived with the family in Switzerland only since late 2003, had no real professional activity (possibly linked to tuberculosis), spoke German poorly and socialised mainly with Nigerian migrants. Re-offending could not be ruled out given his bleak job prospects. The Court accepted that a genuine, close family life existed and that expulsion would affect the family badly, especially as they could not be required to follow him to Nigeria. It nevertheless found that he retained an intact family network in Nigeria and could reintegrate there.

He was ordered to leave by 31 March 2009. An application for interim measures under Rule 39 was refused. He was detained pending removal (September 2009), disappeared, was recaptured (September 2010) and detained again until January 2011. An entry ban was imposed until January 2020 (suspensible for good cause). He remained in Switzerland, separated from his wife and later divorced (September 2012). Custody of the twins was awarded to the mother; he received limited access (at least one afternoon every two weeks) and claimed to maintain contact. In August 2012 he had a third child with another Swiss woman and wished to marry her.

These facts—established family life in Switzerland, the children’s best interests and Swiss nationality, the seriousness of the drug offences, limited integration, welfare dependence, risk of re-offending, and the subsequent family developments—were central to the Article 8 complaint concerning the refusal of leave to remain, the expulsion order and the entry ban.

**CASE OF M.S. v. CROATIA (Application no. 36337/10), ECtHR (First Section), 25 April 2013 (final 25 July 2013)**

The applicant, a Croatian national living in a flat in L. above a restaurant operated by M.M. (leased from the municipality), made 137 police calls between 2002 and 2007 regarding noise, smells, and disturbances from the premises. Neighbours and other residents submitted petitions and complaints about nightly noise, rubbish odours, and related issues; some minor-offence convictions followed against M.M. and employee M.Č. for public-order breaches involving excessive noise during works. Occupants (including the applicant) unsuccessfully sought termination of the lease.

On 10 May 2003 the applicant alleged M.Č. kicked and struck her repeatedly around 1 a.m., causing documented injuries (swollen right ankle and hand, contusions/haematomas to hand, shin, hip, and neck pain) confirmed by contemporaneous and follow-up medical reports. She and her sister initiated a private prosecution in the O. Municipal Court for bodily injury and verbal assault. Parallel proceedings against them for insult were joined. After hearings (including forensic-medical evidence supporting her account of the injuries), a 2005 first-instance judgment convicted M.Č. of inflicting injury (and the applicant/sister of insult), imposing warnings. All appealed. In 2007 the R. County Court quashed the judgment because some hearings had been conducted by a judge’s assistant rather than a judge. Fresh proceedings ensued. In April 2009 the trial judge learned that the O. Social Welfare Centre had instituted non-contentious proceedings to divest the applicant and her sister of legal capacity and had appointed special guardians. The judge requested extension of guardianship to the criminal case. The guardians declined to consent to continuation. The Municipal Court terminated the prosecution on 28 April 2009 for lack of an authorised prosecutor’s request. The County Court later held the appeal obsolete because the offence had become time-barred. A constitutional complaint by the sister was declared inadmissible.

Separately, in 2006 M.M. brought a private prosecution against the applicant and her sister for defamation, alleging they had shouted from their balcony (as a visiting dignitary entered the restaurant) that he engaged in illegal weapons trafficking. They denied knowing the visitor’s identity and said the remark was private. The applicant filed detailed submissions alleging record discrepancies. A psychiatric report was commissioned; psychiatrist K.R. prepared it solely from case-file documents (the applicant refused examination) and diagnosed persistent psychotic disorder, concluding both women were unaccountable at the material time. Proceedings were terminated in April 2010 on that basis.

In April–June 2008 the same psychiatrist and the trial judge notified the Social Welfare Centre of the diagnosis. The psychiatrist warned of possible aggression arising from paranoid ideas directed at M.M. and others. The Centre requested the Municipal Court to open capacity-divestment proceedings (under the Family Act, which permits total or partial deprivation where mental illness prevents a person from protecting their own interests or endangers others). A Centre employee was appointed guardian ad litem after unsuccessful attempts to contact the applicant. A psychiatric/psychological assessment was ordered in January 2009; those proceedings remained pending. The applicant’s 2006 civil claim against M.M. for repossession of a woodshed and compensation was stayed in 2010 because of the capacity proceedings (appeal pending).

Independent medical evidence contradicted the court psychiatrist’s conclusions: a 1999 psychological report found the applicant mentally healthy with normal cognitive function; 2009 reports (psychologist and psychiatrist) recorded above-average intelligence, no psychotic symptoms or prior psychiatric treatment, euthymic affect, and no hallucinations, though they noted defensiveness, authority conflict, insomnia linked to neighbour disputes, and past physical attacks. In July 2010 she reported further injuries from an alleged assault.

Domestic law required private prosecution for simple bodily injury and provided that social-welfare centres initiate capacity proceedings, appoint guardians, and obtain expert medical opinion. Relevant international standards (UN CRPD Art. 12; Council of Europe Recommendation R(99)4) emphasise equal legal capacity, maximum reservation of capacity, proportionality, the right to be heard, and safeguards against abuse.

These facts centre on delays and termination of the applicant’s private prosecution (rendering it time-barred), the initiation and conduct of capacity proceedings based on an unexamined psychiatric report, the stay of her civil claim, and conflicting medical evidence concerning her mental state.

The case of Eremia v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 3564/11) was brought by Lilia Eremia and her daughters Doina and Mariana against Moldova. They alleged that authorities failed to meet positive obligations under Articles 3, 14 and 17 ECHR to protect them from domestic violence by Lilia’s husband A. (a police officer) and to punish him.

A. frequently assaulted Lilia (often in the daughters’ presence) after the second daughter’s birth and verbally abused the family. Lilia petitioned for divorce on 2 July 2010 after an assault. On 30 August 2010 she reported being punched in the head; A. was fined 200 MDL. He received a formal warning on 30 September. Further assaults followed in November, including one in which A. nearly suffocated Lilia. A 23 November forensic examination found no injuries.

On 29 November the applicants applied for a protection order, granted on 9 December. It required A. to stay 500 m from the home for 90 days and barred contact or violence. Police oversaw it with visits and cautions, and A. temporarily moved out. He nevertheless breached it by harassing Lilia on 16 December and entering the home on 19 December (assaulting her, destroying property and abusing a daughter). The Government claimed the applicants had permitted his return; they denied this. Lilia reported the breaches.

On 10 January 2011 police pressured Lilia to withdraw her criminal complaint, citing harm to the daughters’ prospects if A. lost his job. At a 11 January meeting (with A. present) she said she wanted a divorce but no trouble for him. The prosecutor initially declined to investigate. A. then returned, assaulted Lilia (simulating strangling) and threatened her; medical evidence confirmed injuries.

A criminal investigation began on 17 January 2011. Social workers advised reconciliation, remarking that Lilia was “neither the first nor the last” beaten wife. Despite requests, A. was not promptly fined for further breaches. On 1 April a prosecutor noted A.’s admission of physical and psychological abuse of three family members, medical reports and prior sanctions, but treated the offence as “less serious.” Citing A.’s lack of drug/alcohol issues, three minors to support, good reputation and absence of danger to society, the investigation was suspended for one year under a plea bargain (to be reopened only if A. reoffended). The applicants’ appeal was rejected on the ground that suspension afforded better protection.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal later partly revoked the protection order, removing the 500 m zone and explicit bans on harassment/violence. Social services never enforced the original order owing to a clerical error. Divorce proceedings also faced delays.

These facts illustrate alleged failures: delayed or inadequate responses to reports, ineffective enforcement of protection measures, victim-pressuring, stereotypical official attitudes, and suspension of proceedings despite evidence of ongoing abuse, including of children.

The case of Eremia v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 3564/11) concerns three applicants—Lilia Eremia (born 1973) and her daughters Doina (born 1995) and Mariana (born 1997)—who alleged that Moldovan authorities failed to protect them from domestic violence by A., Lilia’s husband and a police officer at Călăraşi station, in violation of Articles 3, 14 and 17 of the Convention.

Following the birth of their second daughter, A. frequently returned home drunk and assaulted Lilia, often in the children’s presence. On 1 July 2010 he assaulted her and verbally abused the daughters; she petitioned for divorce the next day. Violence intensified. On 30 August 2010 she reported being punched in the head; A. was fined 200 MDL (approximately EUR 12) on 18 September and formally warned by the Ministry of Internal Affairs on 30 September. Further assaults occurred on 5, 11 and 12 November 2010; on the last occasion A. nearly suffocated her. A forensic examination on 23 November found no injuries. The applicants applied for a protection order on 29 November. On 9 December the Călăraşi District Court issued a 90-day order requiring A. to stay 500 metres from the home, refrain from contact or violence, and leave the family residence. The order was served on 12 December.

Police visited A. six times between 12 December 2010 and 17 January 2011 to warn him. Despite this, A. harassed Lilia in the street and a shop on 16 December, then entered the home on 19 December (the parties disputed whether permission had been given), assaulting her, destroying property and abusing Mariana. These incidents were reported on 23 December. On 10 January 2011 police pressured Lilia to withdraw her complaint, citing the harm a criminal record would cause the children’s future. At a meeting the next day (with A. present) she stated she wanted a divorce but did not wish to cause trouble. The prosecutor declined to open an investigation on 12 January. A. returned on 13 January, assaulted and threatened Lilia (simulating strangling) and warned he would kill her and her aunt if she persisted. A medical expert on 14 January documented four haematomas on her neck and one on her clavicle.

A criminal investigation finally opened on 17 January 2011. Social workers advised Lilia on 19 January to reconcile, remarking that she was “neither the first nor the last woman to be beaten up by her husband.” A. continued to breach the protection order. On 1 April 2011 the prosecutor accepted A.’s plea bargain, noting he had admitted physical and psychological abuse of three family members. Citing the “less serious” nature of the offence, A.’s lack of prior convictions, his three dependent minors, good standing at work and in the community, and the absence of danger to society, the prosecutor suspended the investigation for one year (to be reopened only if A. reoffended). The applicants’ appeal was rejected on 18 April on the ground that suspension afforded better protection. Meanwhile, on 14 April the Chișinău Court of Appeal partially revoked the protection order, removing the 500-metre exclusion zone and explicit bans on harassment and violence because the law did not expressly provide for them. Social services later admitted a clerical error had prevented enforcement of the original order.

These facts illustrate repeated, documented violence (including in the children’s presence), non-enforcement of a protection order, delays in investigation, pressure on the victim to withdraw complaints, social-service comments reflecting tolerance of domestic abuse, and the ultimate suspension of criminal proceedings against a police officer, all of which underpinned the applicants’ claims of a failure to fulfil positive obligations to prevent and punish ill-treatment and to provide equal protection.

The case of Eremia v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 3564/11) was brought by Lilia Eremia and her two daughters, Doina and Mariana, against Moldova. The first applicant was married to A., a police officer at the Călăraşi station. Following the birth of their second daughter, A. frequently returned home drunk and physically assaulted the first applicant, sometimes in the presence of the children. On 2 July 2010, after an assault the previous day and verbal abuse of the teenage daughters, the first applicant petitioned for divorce. Violence then intensified, with regular assaults and insults directed at both the first applicant and the daughters.

On 30 August 2010 the first applicant reported being punched in the head; A. was fined 200 Moldovan lei (approximately EUR 12.40) by an administrative court. On 30 September 2010 the Ministry of Internal Affairs formally warned him to cease his violent behaviour. Further assaults occurred on 5, 11 and 12 November 2010, the last involving attempted suffocation that left the first applicant voiceless for a day and a half. A forensic examination on 23 November 2010 found no injuries.

On 29 November 2010 the applicants sought a protection order from the Călăraşi District Court. On 9 December 2010 the court granted a 90-day order requiring A. to stay 500 metres from the family home, prohibiting contact and any violence. The order was served on 12 December 2010. Police opened an enforcement file and visited A. six times between 12 December 2010 and 17 January 2011, issuing cautions. Nevertheless, on 16 December 2010 A. followed, insulted and tried to apprehend the first applicant in the street and in a shop. On 19 December 2010 he entered the home (the parties disputed whether permission had been given), assaulted the first applicant, destroyed property and verbally abused the third applicant. These incidents were reported on 23 December 2010.

On 10 January 2011 police allegedly pressured the first applicant to withdraw her criminal complaint, warning that a conviction would harm the daughters’ future because A. would lose his job. The next day, in A.’s presence, she told a prosecutor she wanted a divorce but did not wish to cause her husband trouble. On 12 January the prosecutor declined to open a criminal investigation. On 13 January A. returned, simulated strangling the first applicant and threatened to kill her and her aunt unless she withdrew the complaint. A medical examination the following day documented four haematomas on her neck and one on her clavicle.

Social services later admitted a clerical error had prevented enforcement of the protection order. On 14 April 2011 the Chișinău Court of Appeal partly revoked the order, removing the 500-metre exclusion zone and the explicit bans on harassment and physical violence on the ground that they were not expressly required by law. A criminal investigation was opened on 17 January 2011. On 1 April 2011 a prosecutor, citing A.’s admission of physical and psychological abuse, medical reports, witness statements and prior sanctions, nevertheless suspended the proceedings for one year under a plea bargain. The prosecutor classified the offence as “less serious,” noted that A. supported three minors, was respected at work and in the community, and did not pose a danger to society. An appeal against the suspension was rejected on the basis that it afforded better protection to the applicants. Social workers had earlier advised the first applicant to reconcile, remarking that she was “neither the first nor the last woman to be beaten up by her husband.”

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the authorities had failed to protect them from domestic violence and to punish the perpetrator.

The case concerns the protracted examination of a 1990 Norwegian patent application (no. 19905214) filed by Arne Kristiansen for a propulsion method applicable to aircraft and sea vessels. NIPO issued a March 1991 preliminary view that the application was not patentable for want of a concrete technical solution or demonstrated effect, and it demanded independent practical tests. Kristiansen contested the necessity and cost of tests, offering instead to demonstrate prototypes.

Correspondence on confidentiality (including a 1993 military-security check that proved negative) occupied 1992–1994. NIPO restated the test requirement in February 1995; Kristiansen replied with theoretical arguments and a 1965 research report, asserting that tests were superfluous. After he complained of delay in November 1996, NIPO apologised and promised priority, yet continued to insist on tests through 1997 (when two academic statements were submitted) and set a November 1999 deadline in May 1999. Non-compliance led NIPO to shelve the application; the decision was confirmed in February 2000.

A March 2001 petition to the Parliamentary Ombudsman prompted NIPO to resume the file in August 2001 and impose a February 2002 deadline. Kristiansen’s September 2001 reply added nothing new, and NIPO refused the application on 2 October 2001 for lack of probable technical effect. An appeal was lodged with NIPO’s Board of Appeals in November 2001, but the Board first met only in September 2004. It suggested a reformulation limited to sea vessels. After a February 2005 hearing and the transfer of a 50 % interest to Tyvik AS, the Board held in November 2005 that the invention possessed technical effect yet, because the applicants refused to amend the claims, remitted the case without deciding remaining patentability criteria.

NIPO promptly found the subject-matter lacking novelty. Further Ombudsman complaints about alleged bias were deferred pending final disposal. After unsuccessful 2006 exchanges in which NIPO proposed claim amendments that the applicants rejected, NIPO formally refused the application on 20 June 2007. A second appeal produced a November 2007 Board indication that a patent might be granted only for a narrowly defined class of sea vessels; the applicants were warned that failure to adopt the suggested wording would result in confirmation of the refusal. They responded in January 2008 by altering the claims. On 22 September 2008 the Board upheld the refusal, noting the applicants’ unwillingness to exclude aviation (although, unlike NIPO, it accepted industrial applicability). No further challenge was brought before the Norwegian courts.

The entire administrative process thus lasted from November 1990 until September 2008—almost eighteen years—against the background of a patent term that would in any event have expired in November 2010. Prolonged periods of inactivity (notably 1997–1999, 2001–2004 and 2005–2007) and repeated, ultimately unsuccessful, invitations to recast the claims constitute the principal facts relied upon in support of the alleged violation of the reasonable-time requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The case of Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on account of the excessive length of proceedings concerning a patent application. On 30 November 1990 the first applicant filed patent application no. 19905214 with the Norwegian Industrial Property Office (NIPO) for a propulsion method applicable to aircraft and sea vessels. In March 1991 NIPO issued a preliminary opinion that the application, as formulated, was not patentable and required independent tests to demonstrate a concrete technical effect. The applicant disputed the necessity and cost of such tests, offering instead to demonstrate prototypes.

Subsequent correspondence addressed confidentiality issues, including a negative military assessment on national-security grounds completed by mid-1993. NIPO reiterated its test requirement in 1995; the applicant responded with theoretical arguments and a 1965 report, insisting tests were superfluous. After a 1996 complaint about delays, NIPO’s Director-General apologised and promised priority, yet maintained the test demand through 1997–1999. A November 1999 deadline was not met with the requested evidence, leading NIPO to shelve the application. Although the filing was later accepted as timely, the decision was confirmed in February 2000 for failure to satisfy substantive requirements.

Following a March 2001 petition to the Parliamentary Ombudsman, NIPO annulled the shelving in August 2001 and set a new deadline. The applicant supplied no new material, and NIPO refused the application on 2 October 2001 for lack of probable technical effect. An appeal was lodged with NIPO’s Board of Appeals on 27 November 2001. After prolonged file circulation, the Board first met on 13 September 2004. It suggested reformulating the claims to cover only sea vessels. Ownership of 50 per cent of the application was transferred to the second applicant in February 2005. On 14 November 2005 the Board accepted that a technical effect existed but, because the applicants declined to amend the claims, remitted the case to NIPO.

NIPO then found the invention lacked novelty. After further exchanges and another Ombudsman complaint (which merely assumed future diligence), NIPO formally refused the application on 20 June 2007. A second appeal followed. In November 2007 the Board indicated that a limited sea-vessel patent might be granted if aviation claims were excluded, warning that otherwise the refusal would be confirmed. The applicants made only partial adjustments. On 22 September 2008 the Board upheld the refusal, concluding that the application as presented lacked novelty for aviation and that the applicants had refused to limit it to a potentially patentable maritime field.

The administrative proceedings thus lasted almost eighteen years. Any patent granted would have expired on 30 November 2010. The applicants later obtained patents in other jurisdictions, but the Government maintained these were based on distinct later filings. No domestic judicial challenge was brought against the final Board decision. The protracted timeline, punctuated by multi-year periods of inactivity especially before the Board of Appeals, constitutes the core of the alleged violation of the right to a determination within a reasonable time.

The case concerns a lengthy patent application process in Norway, lodged on 30 November 1990 by the first applicant (Arne Kristiansen) with the Norwegian Industrial Property Office (NIPO) for a propulsion method applicable to aircraft and sea vessels (application no. 19905214). NIPO, a government body under the Ministry of Trade and Industry, issued a preliminary opinion on 21 March 1991 that the application was not patentable in its submitted form, as it failed to demonstrate a concrete technical solution or any effect. Invoking the Patents Act regulations, NIPO required independent testing at a research institute. The applicant disputed this, citing high costs, and noted that prototypes could be tested with NIPO present.

From 1992 to 1994, exchanges addressed confidentiality and national security (the military confirmed no secrecy was needed). The applicant provided further details in May 1994, but NIPO reiterated the test demand in February 1995. The applicant responded in May 1995 with theoretical arguments and a 1965 research report, claiming tests were unnecessary. After a delay complaint in November 1996 (prompting an apology and priority promise from NIPO's Director General), NIPO maintained the test requirement in December 1996. Further protests followed, including academic statements in 1997 questioning NIPO's competence.

In May 1999, NIPO set a 5 November 1999 deadline. The applicant's late October 1999 response (received 11 November) reiterated complaints without new substance. NIPO then discontinued examination under Patents Act section 15(2) for non-compliance, upholding this in February 2000 despite the response arriving in time, citing unmet substantive requirements. A March 2001 petition to the Parliamentary Ombudsman led NIPO to resume proceedings in August 2001 (annulling discontinuation and setting a February 2002 deadline). The applicant's September 2001 reply added nothing new, and NIPO refused the application on 2 October 2001 for failure to show probable technical effect. The Ombudsman closed the matter in January 2002.

An appeal to NIPO's Board of Appeals was filed on 27 November 2001. After file circulation, the Board first met in September 2004 and suggested reformulating claims for possible patentability limited to sea vessels. Meetings and correspondence ensued through 2005; 50% ownership transferred to the second applicant (Tyvik AS) in February 2005. On 14 November 2005, the Board found technical effect existed but referred the case back to NIPO, as the applicants refused to amend claims. NIPO then held in November 2005 that the invention lacked novelty.

A March 2006 Ombudsman complaint alleged examiner prejudice; the Ombudsman deferred pending completion, assuming due diligence. Further 2006 exchanges saw NIPO propose claim changes (rejected by applicants). NIPO formally refused the application on 20 June 2007 for lack of novelty. A second Board appeal followed in August 2007. In November 2007, the Board indicated potential success only for limited sea-vessel claims (mirroring 2004 suggestions) and warned of confirmation of refusal otherwise, or possible division of the application (with aircraft claims likely rejected). After the applicants' January 2008 observations and amendments, the Board confirmed refusal on 22 September 2008 (on differing grounds: industrial applicability existed, but no aviation novelty, and applicants declined to exclude aircraft claims). No court challenge was brought. Any granted patent would have expired by 30 November 2010.

The applicants later obtained related patents abroad (US, Russia, China, Singapore, and via EPO), though the Government noted these did not claim priority from the 1990 application and involved additional features. The core facts highlight an 18-year administrative process marked by repeated NIPO demands for evidence/tests, applicant resistance, appeals, remittals, and delays (including multi-year Board circulation), without final grant.
001-119972:
The case of Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 31848/07) concerns an Azerbaijani farmer, Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov (born 1935), who alleged a violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to the Supreme Court’s examination of his criminal case. The proceedings arose from a land ownership dispute with the Sadan Municipality (in the former Davachi district). The applicant was charged under Article 188 of the Criminal Code with violating a lawful owner’s rights through unauthorised occupation, alteration or cultivation of land.

On 29 December 2004 the Davachi District Court convicted the applicant and imposed a fine of 100 conventional financial units (approximately EUR 84). It found that he had unlawfully occupied and cultivated 0.8 hectares belonging to the Municipality, relying on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography (SCLC). The applicant appealed, contending that the plot formed part of a larger 50-hectare parcel used by his family farming business. On 18 March 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction.

The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the lower courts had misassessed the facts. On 9 August 2005 a three-judge Supreme Court panel, which included Judge N.H., quashed the Court of Appeal’s judgment and remitted the case for fresh examination. The Supreme Court held that the conviction rested on insufficient evidence.

Following the remittal, the Court of Appeal sought additional information. The Municipality confirmed that official records showed the plot belonged to it. The SCLC carried out an on-site inspection and likewise reported that the land formed part of the Municipality’s estate. On 12 July 2006 the Court of Appeal delivered a new judgment upholding the original conviction, concluding that the applicant had cultivated municipal land and that the relevant law had been correctly applied.

The applicant appealed once more. On 10 October 2006 another three-judge Supreme Court panel, again including Judge N.H., dismissed the appeal. It found that the Court of Appeal had examined all relevant evidence and had committed no breaches of substantive or procedural law.

The applicant’s complaint focused on the participation of the same judge in both Supreme Court examinations of the identical criminal case. Domestic law expressly prohibited this. Article 109 of the Code of Criminal Procedure required a judge to recuse himself (or to be disqualified) if he had already participated as a judge in the same criminal case at first instance, on appeal or before the Supreme Court. The Plenum of the Supreme Court, in its decision of 24 November 2005, confirmed that such recusal was a legal duty even in the absence of an objection by the parties, and that a judge who had previously sat in cassation could not take part in any re-examination of the same matter.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 6 violation: the repeated involvement of Judge N.H. was said to have deprived the applicant of an impartial tribunal, contrary both to the Convention and to clear domestic rules designed to safeguard judicial impartiality. The application was lodged on 9 April 2007 and communicated to the Government on 10 November 2010. The Court examined admissibility and merits together.

The case of Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 31848/07) was brought by Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov, an Azerbaijani national born in 1935 and residing in Siyazan, who works as a farmer. Represented by lawyer A. Nağıyev, he lodged the application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 April 2007, alleging that the Supreme Court’s examination of criminal proceedings against him failed to comply with the fair-trial guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. The Azerbaijani Government was represented by its Agent, Ç. Asgarov. The Court communicated the case on 10 November 2010 and decided to examine admissibility and merits jointly.

The proceedings arose from a land-ownership dispute between the applicant and the Sadan Municipality (in the former Davachi district). Criminal charges were brought against Zeynalov under Article 188 of the Criminal Code, which prohibits violation of a lawful owner’s rights to land by unauthorised occupation, alteration or cultivation. On 29 December 2004 the Davachi District Court convicted him of unlawfully occupying and cultivating 0.8 hectares of municipal land. It imposed a fine of 100 conventional financial units (approximately 84 euros at the time) and based its findings on witness statements and data supplied by the State Committee of Land and Cartography (SCLC).

The applicant appealed, maintaining that the plot formed part of a 50-hectare parcel belonging to his family farm. On 18 March 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. He then lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the lower courts had misassessed the facts. On 9 August 2005 a three-judge Supreme Court panel that included Judge N.H. quashed the appellate judgment for insufficient evidence and remitted the case for fresh examination.

In the remitted proceedings the Court of Appeal requested additional information from the Municipality and the SCLC. The Municipality produced official records confirming its ownership; the SCLC conducted an on-site inspection and likewise reported that the land formed part of the municipal estate. On 12 July 2006 the Court of Appeal again upheld the original conviction, holding that the applicant had cultivated municipal land and that the relevant law had been correctly applied.

The applicant appealed once more. On 10 October 2006 another three-judge Supreme Court panel, again including Judge N.H., examined the appeal. It found that the Court of Appeal had considered all available evidence and had committed no substantive or procedural errors, and therefore dismissed the appeal, thereby rendering the conviction final.

The core facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation concern the repeated participation of Judge N.H. in two successive cassation reviews of the identical criminal case. Domestic law, specifically Article 109.1.6 of the 2000 Code of Criminal Procedure, expressly precludes a judge from sitting in a case if he or she has previously examined the same matter at first instance, on appeal or before the Supreme Court. Article 109.2 requires the judge to recuse himself or herself whenever any such ground exists. The Plenum of the Supreme Court, in its 24 November 2005 decision (no. 3), confirmed that this recusal duty is automatic and obligatory even in the absence of an objection by the parties; a judge who has already heard a criminal case at any level cannot take part in its re-examination.

These statutory and interpretative rules form the factual backdrop against which the applicant contended that the Supreme Court’s second examination lacked the impartiality required by Article 6. The same judge who had earlier found the evidence insufficient later sat on the panel that endorsed the conviction after the gathering of further material. The application therefore focused on whether this dual involvement compromised the objective impartiality of the cassation court.

001-119703:
The case of Gross v. Switzerland (no. 67810/10) concerns Swiss national Alda Gross (born 1931), who for years wished to end her life due to progressive frailty and declining physical/mental faculties, without any terminal illness. After a failed 2005 suicide attempt and six months of psychiatric inpatient treatment that did not change her resolve, she sought a painless death via lethal sodium pentobarbital to avoid further failed attempts. She contacted the assisted-suicide organisation EXIT, which indicated difficulty finding a doctor willing to prescribe the substance.

Psychiatrist Dr T. examined her twice in August 2008 and confirmed her full capacity for judgment, a persistent, well-considered wish unconnected to psychiatric illness, and no medical objection to a prescription. He declined to issue it himself to avoid mixing expert and treating roles. Three further doctors also refused: one cited professional-conduct rules because Gross was not ill; another found the wish understandable but would not proceed without a guarantee against professional or legal repercussions, which counsel could not provide.

Gross then applied to the Canton of Zurich Health Board (December 2008) for 15 g of the substance without a prescription, arguing she could not reasonably continue searching for a willing physician. The Board rejected the request (April 2009), holding that neither Article 8 ECHR nor the Swiss Constitution obliged the State to supply a chosen means of suicide. The Administrative Court of Zurich dismissed her appeal (October 2009). It recalled that assisting suicide is criminal under Criminal Code Article 115 only if done for selfish motives, so a physician may lawfully supply pentobarbital to a terminally ill patient. The prescription requirement nevertheless served public-health and safety interests, prevented abuse and hasty decisions, and ensured medical justification and free will. Dr T.’s report was insufficient because it had not assessed whether Gross suffered from a treatable condition or was near death; further medical examination was therefore required.

The Federal Supreme Court rejected her further appeal (April 2010). Relying on Pretty v. United Kingdom and its own Haas jurisprudence, it held that Article 8 created no positive obligation to furnish a dangerous substance for a painless, reliable death. The prescription rule pursued legitimate aims of protecting individuals from rash decisions and safeguarding public health. Gross did not meet the Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences (SAMS) end-of-life guidelines (patients whose clinical course indicated death within days or weeks). Although an earlier ruling had allowed, with “utmost restraint,” a prescription for persons with incurable, severe psychological illness, this did not compel doctors or the State to supply the drug. A thorough examination plus long-term specialist supervision remained indispensable and could not be waived.

Gross complained under Articles 2, 3 and 8 that the refusals rendered her right to decide the manner and moment of her death theoretical and ineffective, imposing a positive duty on the State to furnish the necessary means. Domestic law (Drugs Act, Therapeutic Products Act) classified pentobarbital as a prescription-only substance issuable only after personal examination and in accordance with medical science. SAMS guidelines confined physician-assisted suicide to the terminal phase. These facts—persistent wish of a competent but non-terminally ill person, repeated professional refusals, and the authorities’ insistence on an unobtainable prescription—formed the core of the alleged Article 8 violation.

The case of Gross v. Switzerland (Application no. 67810/10) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Swiss national Alda Gross (born 1931) on 10 November 2010. She alleged that Swiss authorities had breached her right under Article 8 of the Convention (and, in substance, Articles 2 and 3) to decide how and when to end her life. The Second Section of the Court delivered its Chamber judgment on 14 May 2013 (later referred to the Grand Chamber).

For many years Gross had expressed a persistent wish to die. She was not suffering from any terminal or serious physical or psychiatric illness. Instead, she cited advancing age, growing physical frailty, declining mental faculties (memory, concentration and attention), reduced mobility, a shrinking circle of friends and activities, eczema, back pain, and an overall monotonous and diminishing quality of life that she found increasingly unbearable. A 2005 suicide attempt led to six months of inpatient psychiatric treatment, which did not change her resolve. Fearing another failed attempt, she decided to obtain a lethal dose of sodium pentobarbital through an assisted-suicide organisation (EXIT). The organisation warned that locating a willing physician would be difficult.

In August 2008 a psychiatrist, Dr T., examined her twice and issued an expert opinion confirming that she possessed full capacity to form her own judgement. Her wish was reasoned, well-considered and of several years’ duration; it was not the product of psychiatric illness. From a psychiatric standpoint he saw no objection to a prescription, yet he declined to issue one himself in order to avoid mixing the roles of expert and treating doctor.

Gross then approached three further physicians. All refused. One cited the code of professional conduct, emphasising that Gross suffered from no illness; another was prepared to consider the request only if counsel could guarantee immunity from professional or judicial consequences—an assurance that could not be given.

On 16 December 2008 Gross applied to the Health Board of the Canton of Zurich for 15 grams of sodium pentobarbital, arguing that further searches for a prescribing doctor were unreasonable. The Board rejected the request on 29 April 2009, holding that neither Article 8 nor the Swiss Constitution obliged the State to supply a person wishing to die with the means of her choice.

The Administrative Court of the Canton of Zurich dismissed her appeal on 22 October 2009. It recalled that assisting suicide is not a criminal offence under Article 115 of the Swiss Criminal Code unless committed for selfish motives. A medical prescription for sodium pentobarbital nevertheless remained mandatory: it served public-health and safety interests, prevented abuse and hasty decisions, and guaranteed that the act was medically justified and based on free will. Dr T.’s opinion had addressed only capacity and persistence, not the existence of an illness that would place death in the near future or the possibility that the wish itself was a treatable condition. Further medical examination was therefore required; the prescription requirement could not be waived.

The Federal Supreme Court rejected Gross’s further appeal on 12 April 2010. Relying on its own earlier case-law and on Pretty v. the United Kingdom, it found no positive obligation on the State to furnish a dangerous substance so that an individual could die painlessly. The prescription requirement pursued legitimate aims of protecting the individual from precipitate action and safeguarding public health. Ethical questions surrounding assisted suicide were primarily for the democratically elected legislature (a reform process was then under way). Gross did not meet the Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences (SAMS) guidelines on end-of-life care, which apply only to patients whose death is expected within days or weeks. Although an exception might exist, with “utmost restraint,” for persons suffering from a serious, incurable psychological disorder, that exception did not apply and did not compel either the medical profession or the State to supply the drug. Thorough examination and long-term specialist supervision could not be circumvented.

Sodium pentobarbital is classified as a controlled drug under Swiss narcotics and therapeutic-products legislation and may be obtained only on medical prescription issued after personal examination and in accordance with recognised medical practice. The SAMS guidelines, while not formally binding, define the professional standard: assistance in suicide is not part of a doctor’s ordinary task and is contemplated only in the final phase of life after alternatives have been explored, capacity confirmed and the last act performed by the patient.

These facts formed the basis of Gross’s claim that the combination of the prescription requirement, the refusal of physicians and the authorities’ insistence on further medical examination rendered her Convention right to decide the manner and timing of her death theoretical and illusory.

The case of Gross v. Switzerland (Application no. 67810/10) originated in a 2010 application by Alda Gross, a Swiss national born in 1931 and resident in Greifensee. She alleged a breach of her Article 8 right to decide how and when to end her life (also invoking Articles 2 and 3). The applicant had long expressed a wish to die owing to progressive frailty, declining physical and mental faculties (impaired memory, concentration, mobility and social circle), eczema, back pain and reduced quality of life. She had no serious or terminal illness.

After a failed 2005 suicide attempt she received six months’ inpatient psychiatric care, which did not alter her wish. Fearing another unsuccessful attempt, she sought a lethal dose of sodium pentobarbital via the assisted-suicide organisation EXIT, which warned that finding a willing doctor would be difficult.

In October 2008 psychiatrist Dr T., after examining her, confirmed she possessed full capacity to form her own judgement. Her wish was reasoned, persistent for years and unconnected to psychiatric illness; from a medical/psychiatric standpoint he had no objection to a prescription, but declined to issue one himself so as not to mix expert and treating roles. Three further doctors refused: one on professional-ethics grounds because the applicant was not ill; another would consider the request only if guaranteed immunity from disciplinary proceedings, which could not be given.

On 16 December 2008 the applicant asked the Zurich Cantonal Health Board to supply 15 g of sodium pentobarbital (or to authorise a pharmacy to do so). The Board rejected the request on 29 April 2009, holding that neither Article 8 nor the Swiss Constitution obliged the State to furnish the means of suicide of an individual’s choice.

The Zurich Administrative Court dismissed her appeal on 22 October 2009. Assisting suicide is not criminal under Article 115 of the Criminal Code unless done for selfish motives. A medical prescription is nonetheless required to ensure a thorough examination of competence, persistence of the wish and medical justification; it serves public health, safety, crime prevention and the avoidance of abuse. Dr T. had assessed only capacity and the considered nature of the wish, not whether an illness indicated that death was near or whether the wish itself was a treatable condition. A mere persistent wish to die was insufficient. Further medical assessment was therefore necessary and no exemption from the prescription requirement could be granted.

The Federal Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on 12 April 2010. Relying on Pretty v. the United Kingdom and its own earlier case-law, it held that Article 8 imposed no positive obligation to guarantee access to a dangerous substance so that an individual could die painlessly. The prescription requirement pursued the legitimate aims of preventing hasty decisions and abuse and of protecting public health and safety. Ethical questions surrounding medically assisted suicide were primarily for the democratically elected legislature (a reform process was then under way). The applicant did not meet the Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences end-of-life guidelines, which apply only to patients expected to die within days or weeks. Even the limited exception previously recognised for incurable, persistent psychological illness had to be applied with “utmost restraint” and created no duty on doctors or the State to supply the drug. Thorough examination and long-term specialist supervision could not be circumvented by a request for an exemption.

Sodium pentobarbital is classified as a controlled substance under the Drugs Act and a category-B medicinal product under the Therapeutic Products Act; it may be prescribed only by a doctor who has personally examined the patient and only if the prescription is medically acceptable. The applicant maintained that the domestic decisions rendered her right to choose the manner and moment of her death purely theoretical.

The case of Davitidze v. Russia (Application no. 8810/05) concerned a Georgian national, Levan Aleksandrovich Davitidze (born 1960), who alleged violations of Articles 3 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his arrest on 20 August 2003, subsequent detention, and criminal trial in Moscow.

On that date, police at Obruchevskiy station authorised a “test purchase” of drugs based on a statement by Mr S., who reported that a Georgian man named Levan (around 40 years old) supplied heroin. After a body search confirming S. had no drugs, officers gave him photocopied money (USD 100 and RUB 3,000). According to the Government, Davitidze handed S. a 6.9 g parcel of heroin (one of two parcels totalling 13.4 g that Davitidze had acquired); both parcels and the money were seized at the station, and Davitidze was arrested in flagrante delicto.

Davitidze’s account differed sharply. He claimed he was undergoing outpatient psychiatric treatment for cyclothymic disorder and had gone to meet Mr T. (a former addict he had helped) to deliver two anti-anxiety pills; the money was repayment of a debt. T. introduced him to S., who sought drugs, but Davitidze refused. Police then stopped him, requested his passport, and attempted to handcuff him. He resisted only by pressing one arm to his body against painful twisting. Officers applied a “suffocating” technique twice, beat him, and struck him with a gun, causing concussion, a closed jaw fracture, and multiple bruises. At the station (entered via a back door without formal recording), officers punched and kicked him, demanded a confession and “surrender” of drugs (which he denied possessing), and withheld medical aid and family contact until he complied. He briefly called his wife.

Davitidze was held in temporary detention from 20/21–24 August 2003. Remand centre no. 77/2 refused admission due to visible injuries; he was taken to hospitals, where a jaw fracture was confirmed. He received treatment in the medical unit of remand centre no. 77/1 (24 August–8 September 2003) before transfer to no. 77/2. He alleged inadequate care, unrecorded complaints about his health and the force used, and no prompt inquiry.

On 21 August 2003, investigator A. interviewed him in the presence of lawyer To. (later disbarred for failing to act on Davitidze’s psychiatric condition and injury). Davitidze made self-incriminating statements (later invalidated for lack of proper warnings). He was charged with unlawful procurement, possession and supply of heroin. At trial before the Gagarinskiy District Court (November 2003–April 2004), he recanted, claiming the drugs were planted and the operation was entrapment. Witnesses included Ma. (who saw officers twist Davitidze’s arms and use “wrestling techniques”), T. (who described arranging the meeting after S. offered money and denied Davitidze supplied drugs), and Ko. (who called S. a police informant). Police officers K., Su. and M. testified that Davitidze actively resisted, requiring combat techniques; they denied visible injuries or difficulty speaking. The court admitted most evidence, including S.’s pre-trial statements (S. died in October 2003), despite handwriting doubts and the physical items’ absence. On 30 April 2004 Davitidze was convicted and sentenced to eight years; this was upheld on appeal (17 August 2004). Supervisory review in 2009 recharacterised the offence as attempted supply, reducing the sentence to seven years and six months.

Meanwhile, inquiries into alleged police brutality (opened after complaints by Davitidze and his wife) produced repeated refusals to prosecute the officers for abuse of power or related offences. Officers claimed Davitidze resisted and that they used proportionate force; a prosecutor cited trial testimony. Decisions were repeatedly annulled by higher prosecutors and courts for insufficient thoroughness (failure to interview key persons, obtain full medical files or X-rays, or commission timely forensics). Forensic reports confirmed a jaw fracture, haematoma and bruises inflicted by blunt objects but could not date them precisely due to incomplete records. Final refusals in 2007–2008 were upheld, with courts concluding injuries resulted from lawful resistance during arrest. Davitidze also alleged no effective investigation into his complaints and inadequate post-arrest medical care.

The case of Davitidze v. Russia (Application no. 8810/05) concerns allegations by Georgian national Levan Davitidze of violations of Articles 3 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his arrest on 20 August 2003 and subsequent criminal proceedings.

Police conducted a “test purchase” after informant S. reported that a Georgian man named Levan supplied heroin. S. was searched (finding no drugs), given photocopied money, and met the applicant, who handed over 6.9 g of heroin. Officers then arrested the applicant; they seized the remaining 6.5 g parcel and the marked money from him at the station.

The applicant, then receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment for cyclothymic disorder, maintained that T. had requested two anti-anxiety pills. After delivering them and receiving money as debt repayment, he met S., refused any involvement in drugs, and recommended hospital treatment. Two officers stopped him, demanded his passport, and attempted to handcuff him. He offered only slight resistance to one arm being twisted, which he described as a natural reaction to pain. Officers then applied a “suffocating” technique twice, beat him, and struck him with a gun, causing concussion, a closed jaw fracture and multiple bruises. At the station (entered via a back door with no formal record) he was punched, kicked and threatened until he agreed to confess and “surrender” drugs he did not possess.

The next day he made self-incriminating statements in the presence of counsel (later disbarred for failing to seek a forensic examination or file motions). Those statements were subsequently excluded because he had not been properly cautioned. He later retracted them, alleging the drugs had been planted. S. died in October 2003. The applicant was charged with unlawful procurement, possession and supply of heroin.

At trial before the Gagarinskiy District Court the applicant repeated his version of events and complained of excessive force. Witnesses included the driver who had seen officers twisting his arms and using wrestling techniques, T. (whose accounts were inconsistent), and the arresting officers, who claimed the applicant had actively resisted, requiring combat techniques that caused both men to fall. The officers denied seeing injuries or hearing complaints. The court admitted most of the test-purchase evidence, including S.’s pre-trial statements, and convicted the applicant on 30 April 2004, sentencing him to eight years’ imprisonment. The conviction was upheld on appeal; a 2009 supervisory review reclassified the offence as attempted supply and reduced the sentence to seven-and-a-half years.

Immediately after arrest the applicant was held in a temporary detention centre. Remand centre no. 77/2 refused him admission because of visible injuries. He was taken to two hospitals, where a jaw fracture was confirmed, then treated in a prison medical unit from 24 August to 8 September 2003 before transfer to another remand facility. No prompt inquiry into the origin of the injuries was conducted at any of these institutions.

From March 2004 onward the applicant’s wife lodged complaints of fabricated evidence and ill-treatment. A series of prosecutorial inquiries followed. Officers stated that force had been necessary because of resistance and that the applicant had appeared uninjured. Multiple refusals to open a criminal case (under abuse-of-power and related provisions) were issued and repeatedly annulled for incompleteness. Forensic reports established a haematoma, bruises consistent with blows from a solid object, and a jaw fracture, but could not determine the precise date of the injuries or whether they had been inflicted during the arrest. Judicial review of the final refusals was unsuccessful.

The applicant also alleged that the test purchase amounted to entrapment and that the trial was unfair because of contradictory evidence, the unavailability of S., and the admission of improperly obtained statements.

The case of Davitidze v. Russia (Application no. 8810/05) involves a Georgian national, Levan Davitidze (born 1960), who alleged violations of Articles 3 and 6 of the ECHR. These concerned excessive force and ill-treatment during his arrest on 20 August 2003, the lack of an effective investigation into those events, inadequate medical care thereafter, and an unfair trial tainted by police entrapment in a drug offence.

According to the authorities, informant S. reported that a Georgian man named “Levan” supplied heroin. Police authorised a “test purchase.” After a body search confirming S. carried no drugs, he was given photocopied marked money (USD 100 and RUB 3,000). S. obtained 6.9 g of heroin from the applicant, who was immediately arrested; a further 6.5 g parcel and the marked notes were seized from him at the station.

The applicant’s account differed sharply. He said he had gone to repay a debt to T. by delivering two anti-anxiety pills (he was then an outpatient for cyclothymic disorder). T. introduced S., who requested drugs; the applicant refused. Officers then approached, asked for his passport and began handcuffing him. He pressed one arm to his body in reaction to pain. Officers applied “suffocating” holds, beat him and struck him in the face with a gun, causing concussion, a closed jaw fracture and multiple bruises. At the station he was further assaulted and pressured to confess and “surrender” drugs he did not have.

From 20–24 August he was held in temporary detention. On 24 August a remand prison refused him because of visible injuries. He was taken to two hospitals, where the jaw fracture was confirmed, then held in a prison medical unit until 8 September before transfer to ordinary remand.

He was charged with unlawful procurement, possession and supply of heroin. After an initial confession (later invalidated because he had not been properly cautioned), he recanted and alleged the drugs had been planted. At the Gagarinskiy District Court trial, officers testified that combat techniques and handcuffing were required because he resisted and tried to flee. Witnesses called by the defence (including T. and the driver Ma.) partly corroborated his version of the meeting and the arrest. S. had died in October 2003; his statements were nonetheless admitted. On 30 April 2004 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to eight years. The conviction was upheld on appeal; a 2009 supervisory review reclassified the offence as attempted supply and reduced the sentence to seven years six months.

Complaints of ill-treatment prompted a series of prosecutorial inquiries between 2004 and 2008. Officers consistently claimed only necessary force had been used. Successive refusals to open a criminal case were repeatedly quashed by higher prosecutors or courts for incompleteness (failure to interview key persons, obtain X-rays or commission proper forensic reports). Later forensic examinations confirmed a haematoma, bruises consistent with blows from a blunt object, and the jaw fracture, but could not establish precise timing or causation because of missing original medical records. Final refusals to prosecute were ultimately upheld by the courts in 2008.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the nature and extent of the force used, the protracted and repeatedly deficient inquiries, delays and gaps in medical recording and treatment, and the circumstances of the test purchase (including the role of T. and S.) that the applicant characterised as entrapment.

The case of Prizzia v. Hungary (ECtHR Application no. 20255/12) concerns a US national, Gary Prizzia, who alleged that Hungarian authorities failed to enforce court-ordered visiting rights with his son T.M.P. (born 2000), in violation of Article 8 of the Convention, and that related proceedings lasted unreasonably long, contrary to Article 6 § 1.

Prizzia married Hungarian national J.B.; the family lived in Virginia. After a 2003 visit to Hungary, J.B. remained there with the child and sought divorce. Prizzia invoked the Hague Convention on child abduction. Hungary’s Supreme Court held the retention unlawful but declined a return order (14 September 2004). Interim access measures applied pending divorce. After the 2005 divorce, the child was placed with the mother. A final Supreme Court judgment of 27 March 2007 granted Prizzia four consecutive days’ access monthly plus one summer month (including travel to the USA), with the mother obliged to provide travel documents. The court stressed the child’s interest in maintaining paternal and linguistic ties and found no risk the father would fail to return him.

Enforcement repeatedly failed. In August 2007 the mother claimed the child was ill, then absconded. The Guardianship Authority warned of a fine; Prizzia’s enforcement attempt failed. On 1 July 2008 the mother again refused, citing an alleged US warrant. A 100,000 HUF fine was imposed and handover ordered for 1 August 2008; she still refused US travel. Later she was ordered to pay the fine plus Prizzia’s travel costs (circa 396,000 HUF), upheld in 2010. A July 2008 bailiff order required delivery of the child’s passport within three days. The mother instead gave it to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which returned it to her rather than Prizzia. Prizzia’s criminal complaint against a ministry employee was discontinued in 2010 (no offence). A further 200,000 HUF fine plus cost reimbursement was imposed in September 2009 for the 2008 default; judicial review was rejected in June 2010. Monthly access otherwise occurred, but June and November 2009 visits were missed.

Parallel 2007 actions (Prizzia seeking custody change and passport deposit; the mother seeking to bar US travel) were joined and both rejected in December 2008, though summer visits were shifted to July (upheld January 2010). The 2009 summer visit (rescheduled to August) did not occur; the mother demanded discontinuation of alleged US criminal proceedings against her and absconded despite police accompaniment. A 300,000 HUF penalty followed (confirmed 2011). A 2011 summer-visit enforcement claim was dismissed in 2012 after the mother claimed she had been available.

In a new custody action, an interim measure confined the 2010 summer visit to Hungary. A May 2011 judgment dismissed the custody claim and restricted all holiday access to Hungary until the child turned 16, citing the child’s fears of non-return, alienation from the father, and parental conflict; specific bi-monthly Hungarian visit days were fixed. This was upheld in November 2011 (no flexibility granted). A Supreme Court review petition remained pending.

Domestic rules (Government Decree 149/1997) empower guardianship authorities to enforce contact orders within 30 days, impose warnings, costs, fines, mediation or child-protection measures, and, for persistent alienation, seek placement change or file criminal complaints. Despite repeated fines and orders, US-travel access was never realised and monthly contact was intermittently frustrated, while related litigation continued for years.

The case of Prizzia v. Hungary (Application no. 20255/12) concerns a US national, Gary Prizzia, who alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for family life) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant claimed that Hungarian authorities failed to enforce judicial decisions granting him access rights to his minor son, T.M.P. (born 3 February 2000), and that related proceedings were excessively lengthy.

Prizzia married Hungarian national J.B. and the family resided in Virginia, USA. In 2003, after a visit to Hungary, J.B. retained the child there without the applicant's consent and initiated divorce proceedings. The applicant sought the child's return under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. On 14 September 2004, the Hungarian Supreme Court held the retention unlawful but refused a return order. Interim measures regulated visiting rights pending divorce.

On 19 March 2005, following the divorce, the Budapest Central District Court awarded custody to the mother. After appeals, the Supreme Court on 27 March 2007 finally granted the applicant access of four consecutive days per month plus one month of summer vacation (including travel to the USA), with the mother obliged to provide travel documents. The court emphasised the child's best interests in maintaining ties with his father and found no risk of non-return.

Enforcement difficulties arose immediately. In August 2007 the mother failed to make the child available, claiming illness, then left Budapest with him. The Budapest XII District Guardianship Authority established non-compliance, warned of a fine, but the applicant's enforcement request failed. In July 2008 the mother again refused (citing an alleged US warrant). The XIII District Guardianship Authority imposed a HUF 100,000 fine and ordered handover; later proceedings added a further fine and reimbursement of the applicant's travel costs (upheld April 2010). A bailiff ordered surrender of the child's passport, but the mother delivered it to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which returned it to her rather than the applicant. A related criminal complaint was discontinued in 2010.

Further non-compliances occurred in August 2008 (another HUF 200,000 fine plus costs, upheld June 2010), July/August 2009 (police accompaniment unsuccessful as mother and child had left; HUF 300,000 penalty imposed, confirmed July 2011), and at least June and November 2009 (monthly access missed). The applicant's 2011 action over a missed summer visit was dismissed in August 2012 on the mother's assertion of availability. Some domestic contacts otherwise occurred.

Parallel civil proceedings (joined 2007) seeking custody change and passport deposit, or restriction of US travel, were rejected in December 2008 (upheld January 2010), though summer visits were rescheduled. A 2010 interim measure confined 2010 summer access to Hungary. In a May 2011 judgment (upheld November 2011), the Pest Central District Court dismissed a further custody claim and limited remaining access (until the child's 16th birthday) to Hungary only, citing the child's reluctance and parental conflict; review remained pending before the Supreme Court.

These repeated frustrations, despite fines, warnings, cost orders and police involvement, formed the core of the Article 8 complaint. Multiple overlapping enforcement, custody-modification and related proceedings spanning years underpinned the Article 6 length complaint. The Court examined the authorities' positive obligations to take all necessary, adequate and effective measures to enforce contact.

**Case Summary: Prizzia v. Hungary (App. No. 20255/12)**

The applicant, Gary Prizzia (a U.S. national born in 1962, living in Virginia), alleged that Hungarian authorities failed to enforce court-ordered visiting rights with his son T.M.P. (born 3 February 2000), in breach of Article 8 of the Convention, and that related proceedings lasted unreasonably long under Article 6 § 1.

Prizzia married Hungarian national J.B.; the family lived in Virginia. In 2003, after a Hungary visit, J.B. stayed with the child and began divorce proceedings. Prizzia sought the child’s return under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. On 14 September 2004 the Hungarian Supreme Court found the mother’s retention illegal but refused a return order. Interim measures governed visiting rights during the divorce.

After the divorce, the Budapest Central District Court on 19 March 2005 placed the child with the mother. On 27 March 2007 the Supreme Court finally granted Prizzia four consecutive days of access every month plus one month of summer vacation (including travel to the USA), requiring the mother to provide travel documents. It held this served the child’s best interests in maintaining paternal ties and linguistic environment, finding no evidence the father would fail to return the child.

From August 2007 the mother repeatedly obstructed access, especially USA travel. She claimed the child was ill, absconded, or refused cooperation citing fears of non-return, alleged U.S. warrants, or demands that U.S. proceedings against her cease. The Budapest XII (later XIII) District Guardianship Authority recorded non-compliance (e.g., August 2007, July–August 2008, 2009 summers). It warned her, imposed successive fines (HUF 100,000 / ~EUR 360 in 2008; HUF 200,000 / ~EUR 720 in 2009; HUF 300,000 / ~EUR 1,000 later), and ordered cost reimbursement (e.g., HUF 396,375 / ~EUR 1,300 for travel). Courts upheld these. A 2008 bailiff order for the child’s passport was ignored; the mother gave it to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which returned it to her rather than Prizzia. A criminal complaint against a ministry employee was discontinued in 2010 for lack of offence.

Police accompaniment failed when the mother left with the child. Some monthly contacts occurred, but others (June/November 2009) did not. A 2011 enforcement claim was dismissed on the mother’s assertion she had been available. Prizzia’s 2007 action for custody change and passport deposit, joined with the mother’s request to bar USA travel, was rejected in 2008 (upheld 2010), though summer timing was adjusted.

An interim 2010 measure confined that year’s summer access to Hungary. On 19 May 2011 the Pest Central District Court dismissed Prizzia’s further custody claim, restricted remaining summer (and other holiday) access to Hungary until the child’s 16th birthday, and scheduled specific Hungarian visits, citing the child’s reluctance, lack of family identification with the father, and parental conflict. The Budapest Regional Court upheld this on 29 November 2011; a Supreme Court review petition remained pending.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged failures to secure effective enforcement of access rights and of excessive delay in the various civil, administrative and enforcement proceedings.
