The case of Sereny v. Romania (no. 13071/06) concerns complaints by Romanian national Ştefan Sereny under Articles 3 and 6 ECHR. He alleged inadequate medical care in detention (Ploieşti Prison and Dej Prison Hospital), excessive length of proceedings on his 22 October 2007 request for temporary suspension of his prison sentence due to serious illness, and excessive length of criminal proceedings begun against him on 2 June 1998.

Sereny (born 1953) owned a company that bought a campsite in 1993. In 1997 the company obtained a first-instance judgment acknowledging title to 42,000 m² of land, which it then mortgaged for large bank loans. The judgment was overturned on appeal in 1998–1999. Criminal proceedings were opened against Sereny on 2 June 1998 for fraud, accessory to forgery and using a non-final court order to mortgage public land. The case was joined to proceedings against the first-instance judge.

The criminal case proceeded through multiple courts with numerous adjournments (for legal representation, witness summonses, evidence, unconstitutionality pleas later dismissed, absences and co-accused’s illness). The Bacău Court of Appeal convicted Sereny on 2 November 2004 to 3 years 6 months’ imprisonment plus repayment of loans. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 2 November 2005, finalising the conviction after more than seven years.

Sereny suffered a serious heart condition, undergoing emergency surgery in 2002. He was detained in Ploieşti Prison from 11 November 2006 to 8 January 2007. There he received multiple medical consultations, a cardiological examination, prescribed medication, a special diet and advice on lifestyle. He occasionally refused parts of the treatment, stating he already possessed the drugs. He was later hospitalised in Dej Prison Hospital (January–February 2007, December 2007–February 2008 and April–May 2008), where he again received the recommended treatment and a low-sodium diet.

In late 2005 and early 2006 the Bacău Court of Appeal twice postponed execution of the sentence for three months each on forensic-medical evidence that revascularisation surgery could not be performed in a prison hospital. A third request was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 16 October 2006: alternative non-surgical treatment was available in prison hospitals, Sereny had already had two postponements in which to undergo surgery, and he had not proved intervening infections had prevented the operation.

On 22 October 2007 Sereny applied to the Cluj Court of Appeal for suspension of the remaining sentence on medical grounds. The court ordered a fresh expert report from the Mina Minovici Forensic Institute rather than relying on earlier reports. The report, completed in January 2008, confirmed the worsening heart condition requiring civilian-hospital surgery (or, if consent were withheld, prison-hospital medical treatment). Further adjournments followed while the court sought clarification whether surgery was an emergency. The Higher Forensic Commission later stated that surgery was recommended (with a mortality risk exceeding 50 %) but was not urgent, having been advised since 2005, and that consent was legally required. On 4 June 2008 the Cluj Court of Appeal granted a three-month suspension; the judgment became final on 9 June 2008 and Sereny was released the same day.

Subsequent proceedings to extend the suspension (because surgery had been scheduled for 23 September 2008) were delayed by questions of territorial competence. Fearing recall to prison, Sereny left Romania for Austria in September 2008 and sought asylum.

The ECtHR case of Sereny v. Romania (no. 13071/06) involved a Romanian applicant, Ştefan Sereny (born 1953), who alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman/degrading treatment via inadequate medical care in detention, especially at Ploieşti Prison and Dej Prison Hospital) and Article 6 (excessive length of criminal proceedings begun 2 June 1998, plus the 22 October 2007 request to suspend his sentence on medical grounds).

The background was a 1993 campsite purchase by the applicant’s company, followed by 1997 civil proceedings that initially recognised property rights over 42,000 m² of land. The applicant mortgaged it for loans despite a pending appeal. The recognition was overturned in 1998–1999. This prompted 1998 criminal charges against him (joined to those against the original judge) for fraud, accessory to forgery and using forged documents by relying on a non-final order to mortgage public land and failing to repay loans. After an initial 1998 discontinuation, proceedings reopened. The applicant was indicted in December 2000. The Constanţa Court of Appeal adjourned repeatedly (2001) for legal representation, absences, witness summoning, evidence and co-accused illness. It remitted the case for further investigation in July 2001. Cassation appeals followed, with further adjournments (2001–2003) for representation, illness, an unconstitutionality objection (dismissed November 2002) and deliberations. The case transferred to the Bacău Court of Appeal (April 2003), which adjourned (2003–2004) for representation, absences, medical issues, summoning errors, witnesses, evidence, another unconstitutionality objection (dismissed May 2004) and deliberations. Conviction (3 years 6 months’ imprisonment plus repayment orders) came on 2 November 2004. Cassation adjourned (2005) for summoning errors, representation and illness before dismissing the appeal on 2 November 2005, upholding the evidence assessment and land status findings. Total duration exceeded 7.5 years.

The applicant had a serious heart condition, with 2002–2003 hospitalisations (including April 2002 emergency surgery) and ongoing monitoring. After two 2005–2006 postponements of sentence execution (based on forensic reports that revascularisation surgery could not occur in a prison hospital, plus a dental delay), a third request was dismissed on 16 October 2006: alternative treatment was available in prison hospitals, prior postponements had been granted, and infection claims lacked evidence.

Detention began 11 November 2006–8 January 2007 at Ploieşti Prison. He received a cardiological exam (15 November), treatment, a special diet, and nine medical-office visits (diagnoses and medication); he refused some treatment as he already had medication. He was hospitalised at Dej Prison Hospital (January–February 2007, December 2007–February 2008, April–May 2008), receiving recommended treatment and a low-sodium diet each time.

On 22 October 2007 he sought suspension on medical grounds. The Cluj Court of Appeal ordered a new forensic report (14 November 2007), adjourning pending it. The 11 January 2008 report confirmed worsening condition needing civilian-hospital surgery (or prison alternatives if no consent). Further delays ensued from requests for amendments on urgency/postponability (February–May 2008), with adjournments and a Higher Forensic Commission reply (9 May: surgery recommended, high-risk/not emergency given 2005 advice and unused prior postponements, consent mandatory). On 4 June 2008 the court granted 3 months’ suspension (life-threatening condition requiring civilian surgery); it became final 9 June 2008 and he was released. (Later extension efforts were overtaken by his flight to Austria.)

These facts framed the alleged inadequate care (despite documented treatments, diets and hospitalisations) and delays (numerous adjournments in the criminal case; forensic-report bottlenecks in the 2007 request).

The case of Sereny v. Romania (Application no. 13071/06) concerns a Romanian national born in 1953 who alleged violations of Articles 3 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Article 3 claim related to inadequate medical care during detention in Ploieşti Prison and Dej Prison Hospital. The Article 6 claims related to the length of criminal proceedings opened against him on 2 June 1998 and the length of proceedings on his 22 October 2007 request for temporary suspension of his prison sentence due to a serious medical condition.

The underlying events began with a 1993 purchase of a Black Sea campsite by the applicant’s company. In 1997 the company obtained a first-instance judgment acknowledging property rights over 42,000 sq. m of land, which it used (while an appeal was pending) to mortgage the land as security for bank loans totalling approximately 114,895 USD. The appeal succeeded in June 1998, and the company’s action was finally dismissed in November 1999. The applicant was later held personally liable for the company’s debts, and the company was declared bankrupt.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant for fraud, accessory to forgery and use of forged documents (joined to related proceedings against the first-instance judge) were opened on 2 June 1998. After an initial discontinuance was quashed, he was indicted in December 2000. Multiple adjournments followed at both first-instance and appellate levels for reasons including the need to obtain legal representation, witness summoning, examination of evidence, the co-accused’s illness, unconstitutionality objections (dismissed in 2002 and 2004), and court transfers. The Bacău Court of Appeal convicted him in November 2004 and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment plus repayment of the loans with interest. His appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 2 November 2005.

The applicant suffered from a serious heart condition. He underwent emergency surgery in April 2002 and received subsequent monitoring and treatment in a civilian hospital. After his 2005 conviction he obtained two three-month postponements of sentence execution (December 2005 and April 2006) on the basis of forensic reports recommending revascularisation surgery that could not be performed in prison. A third postponement request was dismissed in October 2006 because alternative treatment was available in prison hospitals and he had already had opportunities for surgery.

There he received cardiological examination, medication, a special diet and nine further medical-office visits (during some of which he declined part of the offered treatment). The report confirmed a worsening heart condition requiring high-risk surgery in a civilian hospital (with a mortality rate exceeding 50 per cent) but noted that non-surgical treatment was available in prison and that the applicant had previously failed to undergo the recommended operation. On 4 June 2008 the court granted a three-month suspension; the judgment became final on 9 June 2008 and the applicant was released the same day. Subsequent attempts to extend the suspension encountered competence disputes between courts. Fearing recall to prison before scheduled surgery, the applicant left Romania for Austria in September 2008.

The case of Martin v. Estonia (Application no. 35985/09) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arising from interference with his defence rights during a murder investigation and prosecution.

Keijo Martin, born in 1988, was 17 when 16-year-old J. was killed in a forest near Pärnu-Jaagupi on 21 May 2006. Martin was interviewed as a witness on 29 May. He turned 18 on 1 July 2006. Lawyer Paul Järve, already representing other suspects A. and K., was engaged by Martin’s parents on 25 July 2006 as his counsel. Martin, who had initially received appointed legal-aid counsel R. after his 19 July arrest, agreed to Järve’s representation and consistently denied involvement in the killing during multiple meetings.

On 7 August 2006 Martin produced two handwritten notes terminating Järve’s services and requesting R. instead, citing his adult status and, in one version, shame and a wish that neither Järve nor his parents be told of “the act I have committed.” The investigator immediately appointed R. That evening Martin was interrogated in R.’s presence, confessed in detail, and participated in a video-recorded crime-scene reconstruction. He later produced two written “confessions,” one denying and one admitting guilt. Järve was denied access to Martin to verify that the waiver was voluntary; the investigator first claimed a written instruction already existed and then offered to have one written immediately. Järve complained that the change of counsel had been coerced, citing Martin’s earlier reports of threats by investigators (including being taken handcuffed to the crime scene to force a confession). Prosecutors dismissed the complaints, finding the waiver valid and noting a potential conflict because Järve also represented A. and K. The Bar Association likewise found no ethical breach by R.

Martin subsequently obtained new counsel G. and recanted. A letter he wrote to his father from detention, confessing to the killing, was seized. Psychiatric experts diagnosed an adjustment disorder but found him competent. Other suspects, including A. and K., were later dropped from the case.

At trial Martin, again represented by Järve, claimed his pre-trial statements had been obtained under police pressure and threats of transfer to a violent cell; he also alleged a cellmate had forced the letter to his father. The County Court convicted him of murder committed in a cruel and torturous manner and of theft, relying inter alia on the reconstruction video, the 10 August video-recorded confession, the letter, phone records showing Martin made the last call to J., and items found at locations Martin had indicated. He received a ten-year sentence.

The Court of Appeal excluded all pre-trial statements (including videos) as procedurally tainted, noting that counsel’s presence was mandatory throughout because the offence had been committed while Martin was a minor and that he had been questioned twice without counsel. It nevertheless upheld the conviction for murder in a torturous manner on the remaining evidence, finding Martin’s trial testimony implausible. The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal.

These circumstances—the disputed waiver of chosen counsel, denial of access for verification, possible coercion, absence of counsel at certain interrogations, and subsequent use (or attempted use) of the resulting statements—formed the core of the complaint that Martin’s defence rights had been violated, rendering the trial unfair.

The case of Martin v. Estonia (Application no. 35985/09) concerned an Estonian national, Keijo Martin (born 1988), who alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to infringements of his defence rights during a murder investigation and trial. The European Court of Human Rights communicated the application in 2010 and delivered judgment on 30 May 2013.

On 21 May 2006, 16-year-old J. was killed near Pärnu-Jaagupi. The applicant, then 17, was interviewed as a witness on 29 May. He turned 18 on 1 July 2006. Arrested on 19 July 2006 on suspicion of murder, he requested legal aid and was interrogated with appointed counsel R., denying the charges. On 25 July, his parents signed an agreement with lawyer Paul Järve to represent him. Järve met the applicant multiple times; the applicant continued to deny involvement and complained of feeling unwell.

On 7 August 2006, the applicant signed two handwritten requests terminating Järve’s services (chosen by his parents) and requesting R. instead, citing his adulthood. One request asked that Järve and his parents not be informed of his “act,” as he felt ashamed. That evening, with R. present, the applicant confessed in detail and participated in a video-recorded crime-scene reconstruction. He later wrote “sincere confessions,” one denying and one admitting the killing. Järve was not promptly informed and was denied a meeting to confirm the waiver’s voluntariness. He complained that the waiver was coerced, alleging investigator threats (including being handcuffed and taken to the crime scene to confess). Prosecutors dismissed the complaints, noting the applicant’s written requests, his confirmation of trust in R., and a potential conflict of interest (Järve also represented other suspects). Internal police inquiries found no criminal offences. The Bar Association found no ethical breach by R.

The applicant later recanted, claiming pressure (threats of transfer to a violent cell, a cellmate’s demands). He was interrogated without counsel on some occasions. Psychiatric experts found him capable of understanding and controlling his actions, with no mental disorder impairing the relevant proceedings.

At trial in Pärnu County Court (with Järve as counsel), the applicant denied guilt, claiming pre-trial statements resulted from police pressure and a cellmate’s influence (including a seized letter to his father confessing). The court convicted him of murder in a cruel and torturous manner plus theft, sentencing him to 10 years. It relied on the reconstruction (video shown), forensic evidence, phone records (applicant’s last call to J.), recovered items matching the applicant’s indications, the letter, and witness statements.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal (2008) acquitted him of cruel murder and theft but upheld conviction for torturous murder. Citing procedure and Supreme Court case-law, it excluded all pre-trial statements (as court-hearing statements are decisive, and contradictions required disregard of earlier ones; a video of an interview had been improperly shown). Nonetheless, it found the conviction safe based on remaining evidence: crime-scene facts, expert opinions, inspection reports, witnesses, the letter (deemed voluntary), and the implausibility of the applicant’s trial account. It acknowledged mandatory counsel participation (as the offence occurred when the applicant was a minor) and two uncounselled interrogations, but held that exclusion of pre-trial statements meant any defence-rights breach had no effect. The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal.

These facts centred on the disputed voluntariness of the counsel waiver, access restrictions, potential coercion, uncounselled questioning, and the domestic courts’ handling of resulting evidence and procedural complaints.

The case of Martin v. Estonia originated in an application by Estonian national Keijo Martin (born 1988) alleging a violation of his Article 6 defence rights in unfair murder proceedings.

On 21 May 2006, 16-year-old J. was killed near Pärnu-Jaagupi. The applicant, then 17, was interviewed as a witness on 29 May. He turned 18 on 1 July. Arrested on 19 July 2006 as a murder suspect, he requested legal aid and was interrogated with appointed counsel R., denying the charges. His parents hired lawyer Mr Järve on 25 July; Järve met him repeatedly. On 7 August the applicant signed two handwritten requests terminating Järve (chosen by his parents) in favour of R., citing his adult status and a wish that Järve and his parents not be informed of the offence due to shame. That evening he was interrogated with R., confessed in detail, and the next day took part in a video-recorded crime-scene reconstruction (R. present). He produced two “sincere confessions” with inconsistent accounts.

Järve learned of the change only on 8 August, was refused a meeting to verify the waiver’s voluntariness, and complained that it was involuntary (alleging investigator threats to handcuff the applicant and force a confession). Prosecutors rejected the complaints, citing the written requests, the applicant’s oral confirmation that he trusted R., and a possible conflict of interest (Järve also represented other suspects). The Bar Association found no ethical breach by R. A county court later held that the legal-services contract remained valid until proper notice to the parents and Järve; the waivers were then served. The applicant was later questioned twice without counsel (mandatory under Estonian law because he had been a minor at the time of the offence). He recanted, claiming police pressure (threats of transfer to a violent cell) and coercion by a cell-mate who induced a confessing letter to his father (later seized). Psychiatric experts found him mentally capable of understanding and controlling his actions and of participating in the proceedings, though they could not scientifically assess the voluntariness or truthfulness of his statements from video recordings.

In the Pärnu County Court (represented by Järve) the applicant denied the charges, repeating the pressure allegations. On 17 June 2008 he was convicted of murder in a cruel and torturous manner and of theft, relying inter alia on the crime-scene inspection, forensic reports, phone records showing he made the last call to J., the reconstruction and 10 August confession videos, the seized letter, and witness statements. He was sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal (28 October 2008) excluded all pre-trial statements as improperly relied upon (court statements being decisive) and noted the uncounselled questioning, but held that any defence-rights breach had no effect once those statements were disregarded. It acquitted the applicant of some charges yet upheld the murder conviction on remaining evidence, finding his trial account incoherent and the letter genuine. The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the abrupt, unverified change of counsel, subsequent interrogations and reconstructions, and use of the resulting material had violated his defence rights and rendered the trial unfair.
001-120961:
**CASE OF BANEL v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 14326/11)**

On 6 June 2005, 13-year-old E.B. was playing with other children on the balcony of a derelict ancillary building containing cellars, adjacent to his mother's apartment in Vilnius's Naujamiestis district. The balcony collapsed, killing E.B. instantly from spinal injuries and crushed organs; two other children suffered minor injuries. Police immediately opened a pre-trial investigation into the accident, surveying the scene and confirming the cause of death via forensic examination. The applicant was granted victim status.

The building's poor condition was known to municipal authorities. Vilnius city municipality discussed its future shortly after the incident, and an expert inspection in July 2005 recommended fencing it off pending demolition, which a municipal enterprise completed in December 2005 after approval. The applicant filed a civil claim within the criminal proceedings for substantial non-pecuniary damages, arguing that municipal bodies had failed to supervise the dangerous structure.

Investigators charged two municipal employees with negligent failure to perform official duties under Article 229 of the Criminal Code: one for not inspecting buildings or reporting their condition despite assigned responsibilities, and another for failing to notify authorities of the danger posed by empty municipal buildings. However, prosecutors repeatedly discontinued the investigation (in 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010), citing contradictory evidence on ownership and maintenance duties amid administrative reforms in 2004–2005 that redistributed responsibilities. They concluded no specific individual could be identified as criminally liable, as duties were unclear or unassigned during the relevant period, and a short time (three months) had elapsed between the municipality learning of the building's state in February 2005 and the collapse. Prosecutors repeatedly advised pursuing separate civil claims against the municipality or its enterprise under Civil Code Article 6.266 (strict liability of building owners/managers for collapse or defects).

The applicant appealed multiple discontinuations, arguing that both the municipality and its enterprise had long known of the building's dangerous state yet failed to repair or demolish it, and that investigations consisted mainly of inter-institutional correspondence without identifying responsible parties. A district court in January 2009 quashed one discontinuation as insufficiently thorough, ordering specific steps such as reviewing 1970s archived documents to establish ownership and why no timely maintenance decision was made. Subsequent investigations still failed to pinpoint liability. In 2010, a court refused to reopen proceedings because the five-year limitation period for the offense had expired (investigation opened in 2005), without addressing investigation flaws. A regional court upheld this as final.

Domestic law imposed municipal duties to supervise building use and manage owned property (Law on Local Self-Government; Law on Construction Article 42, allowing authorities to demand safety measures or evacuate if structures threatened life). The Constitution protects the right to life. Civil provisions allowed claims for non-pecuniary damage from death or health impairment, and municipal liability for unlawful acts or building defects regardless of individual fault.

The applicant alleged that Lithuania failed to protect her son's life by not maintaining the known-dangerous building and that the investigation into his death was ineffective, failing to identify those responsible despite multiple reopenings and court directives. The facts highlight prolonged investigative delays, inability to resolve ownership/responsibility amid bureaucratic changes, time-barring of charges, and the State's prior knowledge of the hazard without preventive action. The case of Banel v. Lithuania (Application no. 14326/11) arose from an application by Ms Venata Banel, a Lithuanian national living in Vilnius, alleging that the State failed to protect her son's right to life and that the investigation into his death was ineffective.

On 6 June 2005, the applicant's 13-year-old son E.B. was playing with other children on the balcony of a dilapidated ancillary building containing cellars, located near her apartment in Vilnius's Naujamiestis district. The balcony collapsed, with a portion falling onto E.B. and causing his immediate death from a broken spine and crushed internal organs. Two other children suffered minor injuries. Police opened a pre-trial investigation that same day, surveyed the scene, and a forensic expert confirmed the cause of death the following day. The applicant was granted victim status on 4 July 2005.

The building's poor condition was known to authorities. Municipal discussions followed the accident, an expert recommended fencing it off pending demolition, and it was demolished in December 2005 by a municipal enterprise. In September 2006, within the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim for 3,000,000 LTL in non-pecuniary damages against the Vilnius city municipality, asserting that its failure to supervise the buildings caused her son's death and her resulting suffering.

An employee of the municipal enterprise Naujamiesčio būstas, A.J., was charged in January 2007 with negligent failure to perform official duties (Criminal Code Article 229) for not inspecting the buildings as assigned in 2004. Later, in December 2009, a Naujamiestis district specialist, K.G., was similarly charged for failing to report the danger after being tasked in January 2005 with monitoring empty municipal buildings.

The investigation was discontinued on multiple occasions (October 2007, July 2008, July 2009, and May 2010). Prosecutors cited contradictory evidence on ownership and responsibility between the municipality and Naujamiesčio būstas, as well as 2004-2005 administrative reforms that redistributed duties and left no one specifically assigned to manage derelict buildings. Although the municipality knew of the building's condition (at least by February 2005), the short timeframe before the accident and lack of proof of specific duty breaches meant no individual could be held criminally liable. Corporate entities could not be prosecuted under the relevant provision. Charges against A.J. and K.G. were dropped each time.

The applicant repeatedly appealed, arguing that authorities had long known the building was dangerously derelict yet failed to act until after the collapse, and that the investigation was passive, delayed, and limited to inter-institutional correspondence. A district court in January 2009 found the probe insufficiently thorough, noting that ownership had not been established, and ordered specific further steps (including retrieval of 1970s archival records) to identify those who failed to decide on the building's maintenance. The applicant also complained to the Attorney General about stalling. Despite several reopenings, the investigation was not completed. In August 2010 a court refused to reopen it, as the five-year statute of limitations for the offence (running from June 2005) had expired; this was upheld in September 2010.

Prosecutors consistently suggested that the applicant pursue separate civil proceedings against the owner or manager under Civil Code Article 6.266 (strict liability for damage from collapsing structures). However, the criminal investigation, which the applicant used to seek identification of those responsible, ended after more than five years without any person being held to account.

These facts concern the State's alleged failure to take preventive measures regarding a known hazardous structure under municipal supervision and the subsequent delays, incompleteness, and ultimate time-bar that prevented an effective inquiry into the death.

The case of Banel v. Lithuania (Application no. 14326/11) concerns the death of the applicant’s 13-year-old son, E.B., on 6 June 2005 in Vilnius. E.B. was playing with other children on the balcony of a derelict ancillary building containing cellars when the structure collapsed. Part of the balcony fell on him, causing fatal injuries (broken spine and crushed internal organs). Two other children sustained minor injuries.
