The building, located in the Naujamiestis district, was known to be in poor condition. An expert inspection shortly after the accident recommended fencing it off pending demolition, which occurred in December 2005 following municipal approval. The applicant later lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings for 3 million LTL in non-pecuniary damages, alleging that Vilnius city municipality and related bodies had failed to supervise and maintain the building.

Investigation focused on potential criminal liability under Article 229 of the Criminal Code (failure to perform official duties). Charges were brought against A.J., an employee of the municipal enterprise Naujamiesčio būstas, for not inspecting buildings or reporting their condition as assigned in 2004. Later, K.G., a Naujamiestis district specialist tasked in January 2005 with monitoring empty municipal buildings, was also charged for failing to warn of the danger.

Prosecutors discontinued the investigation on multiple occasions (November 2007, July 2008, July 2009, and May 2010). They cited contradictory evidence on ownership and maintenance responsibility between the municipality and Naujamiesčio būstas, noting administrative reforms in 2004–2005 that redistributed duties and left no one specifically assigned to derelict buildings. Documents showed the municipality was aware of the building’s poor state by February 2005 (about three months before the accident), but prosecutors found insufficient evidence of stalling or failure to perform clearly prescribed duties. They repeatedly advised the applicant to pursue a separate civil claim under Article 6.266 of the Civil Code (strict liability of building owners/managers for collapse or defects).

The applicant appealed each discontinuation, arguing that both the municipality and Naujamiesčio būstas had long known the building was dangerous (avarinės būklės) yet took no action to repair or demolish it, and that the investigation consisted of unproductive correspondence between institutions unwilling to accept responsibility. A district court in January 2009 quashed one discontinuation, finding the investigation insufficiently thorough (ownership still unidentified) and ordering specific further steps, including retrieval of 1970s archival documents. A higher prosecutor later reopened proceedings, instructing identification of any person or unit responsible for ownerless buildings and consideration of liability of municipal managers if duties were unassigned.

Despite these orders, the investigation was again discontinued in May 2010. On 9 August 2010 a district court refused to reopen it because the five-year statute of limitations for the offence had expired (investigation opened 7 June 2005). The Vilnius Regional Court upheld this on 15 September 2010, without addressing the applicant’s complaints about investigative shortcomings.

The applicant alleged that Lithuania had failed to protect her son’s life and that the investigation into his death had been ineffective. Relevant domestic provisions included constitutional protection of life, municipal duties under the Law on Local Self-Government and Law on Construction to supervise building use and act against threats to life, and civil-code rules on owner/manager liability and state/municipal liability for unlawful inaction.
001-120188:
The case of Lavida and Others v. Greece (application no. 7973/10) was brought by 23 Greek nationals of Roma origin (15 children of compulsory school age in 2009–2010 and their 8 parents) against Greece. Represented by the Greek Helsinki Monitor, they alleged a violation of Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of discrimination) taken together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education). The complaint centred on the authorities’ placement and continued schooling of the children in an ethnically segregated primary school.

Sofades, in Thessaly, had a Roma population of around 3,000 (nearly half the town), concentrated in an old subdivision and a newer “model” settlement known as Nea Zoé (84 families). Four public primary schools operated in municipal buildings. The 4th Primary School, established by presidential decree in 1986 and housed in a 1996 building with 12 classrooms, a gym and a computer lab, stood in the old Roma subdivision and was mapped (by an August 2008 decision of the Karditsa primary-education office) as the catchment school for both Roma areas. In the 2009–2010 year it had 511 pupils on the roll (the applicants disputed actual attendance, claiming only about 200 regularly attended for lack of space). After a 2011 merger three schools remained: the 1st (89 pupils), the 2nd (193) and the 4th (550 enrolled, of whom the applicants said 250 attended). The 4th school’s pupil body was exclusively or overwhelmingly Roma; non-Roma children living nearby attended the other schools.

The 15 child applicants (one kindergartener, the rest in years 1–6) lived in Nea Zoé and were enrolled at the 4th school, 2.5 km away, rather than the nearer 1st school (2.4 km). Only one family later obtained a transfer. The Government stated that no other parents had requested a transfer; the applicants asserted that the 1st-school director had refused enrolment in September 2009, saying the authorities required the children to remain at the 4th school. Roma pupils from Nea Zoé were bused to the 4th school even though the distance was comparable.

In May–July 2009 the Greek Helsinki Monitor wrote to the Ministry of Education’s special secretary for intercultural education and to the Minister, describing “clear ethnic segregation” that violated both domestic law and the Convention as interpreted in Sampanis v. Greece. The letters noted that non-Roma children living closer to the 4th school were sent to the 1st school and that teaching quality at the Roma-only school was poor. No reply was received. A further letter in November 2009 and a complaint to the Ombudsman likewise went unanswered.

A September 2009 report by the Thessaly Regional Directorate of Education recorded 511 sporadically attending Roma pupils at the 4th school and the resulting district boundaries. It recommended new school construction and redistricting so that Roma children would not be educated in exclusively Roma establishments, but the municipal council opposed closing the 4th school. The Directorate considered immediate integration into the other Sofades schools impracticable because of numbers and inadequate infrastructure. Isolated attempts to enrol individual Roma children in non-Roma schools provoked “vehement reactions” from non-Roma parents and municipal authorities.

In December 2011 the Ministry proposed transferring first-graders from the 4th school to five other schools and ceasing new enrolments there from 2012–2013. After public outcry a January 2012 meeting (Minister, special secretary, mayor, parents’ associations) decided instead to retain the 4th school with extra resources, to build another school for Roma children, and to allow only a limited number of “fit” pupils into mixed preparatory classes subject to a 20 % cap. EU Commissioner Viviane Reding publicly stated that these steps were insufficient to end racial segregation.

Domestic provisions required enrolment according to residence (Presidential Decree 201/1998) and prohibited racial discrimination in education (Law 3304/2005 and Ministry circulars of 2008 and 2010 that set a 50 % ceiling on “intercultural” pupils per class and declared segregation contrary to the Constitution and the Convention). International instruments cited by the Court (Committee of Ministers Recommendation CM/Rec(2009)4, ECRI’s 2009 report on Greece, CERD General Recommendation 27 and the UNESCO Convention against Discrimination in Education) likewise condemned the de-facto segregation of Roma pupils and required desegregation measures.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ claim that the State had maintained, and failed to dismantle, a system of ethnically segregated schooling that denied them equal access to education.

**CASE OF LAVIDA AND OTHERS v. GREECE (ECtHR, Application no. 7973/10, judgment 30 May 2013, final 30 August 2013)**

This European Court of Human Rights (First Section) case was brought by 23 Greek nationals (15 children of compulsory school age in 2009–2010 and eight parents) from the Roma community in Sofades, Thessaly. Represented by the Greek Helsinki Monitor (GHM), they alleged a violation of Article 14 of the Convention (prohibition of discrimination) taken with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education) due to ethnic segregation in primary schooling.

Sofades had a large Roma population (around 3,000 people, nearly half the town). Many lived in the old Roma subdivision or the newer “Nea Zoé” area. Four public primary schools operated (later merged to three). The 4th Primary School, established by 1986 presidential decree and housed in a 1996 building with 12 classrooms plus facilities, stood in the old Roma subdivision and was assigned (via 2008 school-mapping decision) to serve both Roma areas. Government figures listed 511 pupils enrolled there in 2009–2010 (127 completing primary education); applicants claimed roughly 200 enrolled annually with many not attending due to overcrowding, and that children from Nea Zoé (closer to the 1st school) were bused 2.5 km to the 4th school instead of the nearer 1st school. Non-Roma children living near the 4th school attended other schools. After the 2011 merger the 4th school still had 550 pupils (applicants said only about 250 attended regularly), far more than the other schools.

The 15 child applicants (except one kindergartener) were enrolled in various grades at the 4th school. Two finished primary education that year; one later transferred at parental request to the 2nd school. The Government stated that no other parents requested transfers from the 4th school or the Karditsa education office, and the Ministry of Education’s intercultural-education secretary confirmed receiving none. In May 2009 a GHM delegation visited and wrote (May–July 2009) to the intercultural-education secretary and Education Minister, describing the 4th school as a de facto “school for Gypsy students” that only Roma children attended while nearby non-Roma children went elsewhere, constituting ethnic segregation contrary to Greek law and the Convention (citing *Sampanis v. Greece*). They urged integration into nearer mixed schools plus support programmes. The letters went unanswered. Parents later alleged they asked the 1st-school director in September 2009 to enrol their children and were refused on the ground that authorities required continued attendance at the 4th school. A September 2009 regional-education report acknowledged sporadic attendance at the 4th school (511 pupils), noted the 2008 mapping that kept Roma children in an exclusively Roma school, recorded municipal opposition to closing those schools, and described vehement parental protests when isolated Roma pupils were briefly allowed into other schools. The report viewed mixing as currently impracticable because of numbers and infrastructure and favoured new schools inside the Roma area plus later redistricting.

Further GHM letters in late 2009 also went unanswered. Education officials later proposed ending exclusive Roma schooling by building a new school and redrawing maps. In December 2011 ministry services suggested transferring first-graders from the 4th school to other local schools with extra teachers and ceasing new enrolments at the 4th school from 2012–2013. After press reports and parental outcry, a January 2012 meeting instead decided to keep the 4th school operating (with added amenities), build a new Roma school, place a few “fit” beginners in preparatory classes physically located at an exclusively Roma kindergarten, and from 2012–2013 limit Roma pupils in mixed schools to 20 percent. An EU commissioner later called these steps insufficient to end racial segregation.

Domestic rules required enrolment of all children of compulsory age and transfers when a new school opened in a child’s district. Ministry circulars (2008, 2010) limited intercultural pupils to 50 percent per class, declared Roma integration into ordinary classes official policy, and stated that exclusion or segregation violated the Constitution, anti-discrimination law, the Convention and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. International instruments cited (Council of Europe recommendation, ECRI report, CERD, UNESCO Convention) likewise condemned racial or ethnic segregation in education and called for effective desegregation measures.

The facts therefore centre on the long-standing assignment of Roma children to a school attended almost exclusively by Roma pupils, official knowledge of the resulting segregation, unsuccessful attempts at mixed-school enrolment, and subsequent official proposals that were scaled back amid local opposition.

The case of Lavida and Others v. Greece (Application no. 7973/10) concerns 23 Greek Roma nationals (15 schoolchildren of compulsory-education age and their 8 parents) from Sofades, Thessaly. They alleged a violation of Article 14 ECHR (prohibition of discrimination) read with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), claiming racial segregation in primary schooling.

Sofades has a large Roma population (around 3,000 people, nearly half the town) concentrated in an old settlement and the newer “Nea Zoé” subdivision. Four municipal primary schools operated at the relevant time. The 4th Primary School, built in 1996 inside the old Roma settlement (and close to Nea Zoé), had 12 classrooms plus ancillary facilities. For 2009–2010 it officially enrolled 511 pupils, virtually all of them Roma; attendance was sporadic. School-district maps assigned both Roma areas to this school. Non-Roma children living nearer the 4th school were instead sent to the 1st school. Roma children from Nea Zoé were bused 2.5 km to the 4th school even though the mixed 1st school was only 2.4 km away. After a 2011 merger the 4th school still had 550 enrolled pupils (only about 250 regular attendees), remaining almost exclusively Roma.

The child applicants (except two who finished primary school that year) were all registered at the 4th school. Their parents say they asked the 1st-school head teacher in September 2009 to enrol them and were refused on the ground that the authorities wanted them to stay at the 4th school. Only one family later obtained a transfer. The Greek Helsinki Monitor (GHM) visited the settlement and school in May 2009 and wrote repeatedly to the Ministry of Education and the Ombudsman, describing a “clear ethnic segregation” contrary to Greek law and the Court’s earlier ruling in Sampanis v. Greece. No replies were received.

A September 2009 report by the regional education directorate itself noted that the 4th school was a Roma-only institution, recommended new mixed schools and redistricting, and recorded “vehement reactions” from non-Roma parents whenever individual Roma children were placed in other schools. The municipal council nevertheless opposed closing the Roma-area schools. In late 2011 the Ministry proposed transferring first-graders and phasing out new enrolments at the 4th school; local protests forced a retreat. The January 2012 compromise kept the 4th school open, promised a new Roma-only building, allowed only nine selected children into mixed preparatory classes, and capped future Roma enrolment at 20 % in other schools. EU Commissioner Reding publicly stated that these steps were insufficient to end racial segregation.

Greek law (Presidential Decree 201/1998) ties enrolment to residence zones; Ministry circulars expressly prohibit Roma concentrations above 50 % per class and any ethnic segregation. International instruments cited by the Court (CoE Recommendation CM/Rec(2009)4, ECRI’s 2009 report on Greece, CERD General Recommendation 27 and the UNESCO Convention against Discrimination in Education) likewise condemn separate schooling of Roma children and require their integration into mainstream classes. The facts therefore disclose a persistent, officially tolerated pattern of ethnic isolation of Roma pupils, maintained by local resistance despite repeated acknowledgements that such isolation contravenes both domestic and international standards.
001-121564:
The applicant, Oleg Ivanovich Abashev, a Russian national born in 1967, was charged with false denunciation and had given an undertaking to appear. On 3 April 2006 he was due at a preliminary hearing before the Aleksandrovskiy District Court. At 9.30 a.m. he telephoned the court registry to say that he and his counsel would be delayed by concurrent civil proceedings. The court, sitting as a single judge, nevertheless opened the hearing at 2 p.m. in his absence. The prosecutor applied for the applicant to be remanded in custody on the ground that he had failed to appear. The court granted the application, holding that the applicant had not supplied a valid explanation or supporting evidence and that there was therefore reason to believe he had fled from justice. It ordered a change of preventive measure from an undertaking to appear to pre-trial detention, while noting that the offence was minor, the applicant had no prior record, was married with a young child and was in poor health. The applicant was taken into custody at 4 p.m. the same day and immediately began a hunger strike. His counsel appealed, alleging judicial bias and lack of justification.

On 18 May 2006 the Tomsk Regional Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the first-instance judge had reasonably concluded that the applicant had absconded. In the interim, on 14 April 2006 the District Court substituted bail of 50 000 roubles for detention. Being unable to pay at once, the applicant remained in custody until 21 April, when counsel posted the sum and he was released. On 29 May 2006 the Regional Court quashed the bail decision, observing that the applicant had a known address, had merely been delayed, and that the original detention order had been made in the absence of both the applicant and his lawyer, in breach of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The bail money was later returned. On 13 December 2006 the Presidium of the Regional Court, acting by way of supervisory review, quashed both the original detention order and the appeal judgment of 18 May. It held that a delayed appearance did not amount to flight from justice and that the lower courts had failed to apply the relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure correctly.

On 10 January 2007 the applicant was convicted as charged and given a suspended sentence of eighteen months, later upheld on appeal. Relying on the Presidium’s decision, he brought a civil claim against the regional treasury and the Ministry of Finance for compensation for the period of detention from 3 to 21 April 2006. On 23 May 2008 the Kirovskiy District Court dismissed the claim, holding that Chapter 18 of the Code of Criminal Procedure confined the right to rehabilitation (and thus to compensation) to persons who had been acquitted or otherwise cleared of charges. Because the applicant had been convicted, no such right arose. The Regional Court upheld that judgment on 29 July 2008. It added that Article 1070 § 2 of the Civil Code required proof of a judge’s criminal guilt before compensation could be awarded for damage caused in the administration of justice, and that no such conviction existed. The Presidium had characterised the detention as unjustified rather than unlawful, so Article 1100 of the Civil Code (which provides for compensation irrespective of fault in cases of unlawful detention) was inapplicable.

The applicant complained that these decisions had denied him an enforceable right to compensation for a period of detention later found to have been imposed in breach of domestic procedure.

The case of Abashev v. Russia (application no. 9096/09) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Russian national's complaint that he had been denied an enforceable right to compensation for a period of pre-trial detention later found to have been imposed in breach of domestic procedure.

The applicant, Oleg Ivanovich Abashev (born 1967), faced a charge of false denunciation and had given an undertaking to appear. On 3 April 2006 he telephoned the Aleksandrovskiy District Court to report that he and his counsel would be delayed by concurrent civil proceedings. The court, sitting as a single judge, nevertheless opened the hearing in their absence at 2 p.m. The prosecutor sought a remand in custody on the ground of non-appearance. The court granted the request, concluding that the applicant had fled justice, and ordered his detention. He was taken into custody the same afternoon and began a hunger strike.

Counsel immediately appealed, alleging judicial bias and lack of justification. On 18 May 2006 the Tomsk Regional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the first-instance judge had reasonably inferred an attempt to abscond. In the interim, on 14 April 2006 the District Court offered release on bail of 50 000 roubles. Unable to pay at once, the applicant remained detained until 21 April, when counsel posted the sum.

On 29 May 2006 the Regional Court quashed the bail decision. It found that the applicant had a known address, had merely been delayed, and had not evaded justice; the original detention order had moreover been issued in the absence of both the defendant and his lawyer, contrary to the Code of Criminal Procedure. The bail money was later returned. On 13 December 2006 the Presidium of the Regional Court, exercising supervisory review, quashed both the 3 April detention order and the 18 May appeal judgment. It held that a late arrival, of which the court had been informed, could not constitute flight and that the lower courts had failed to apply the relevant statutory criteria for imposing custody.

The applicant was subsequently convicted of the underlying offence on 10 January 2007 and received a suspended sentence, upheld on appeal.

Relying on the Presidium’s decision, he brought a civil action against the regional treasury and the Ministry of Finance seeking compensation for the 18 days of detention (3–21 April 2006). On 23 May 2008 the Kirovskiy District Court dismissed the claim. It reasoned that Article 1070 of the Civil Code and Chapter 18 of the Code of Criminal Procedure confined the right to compensation for unlawful preventive measures to persons who had been rehabilitated (i.e., acquitted or otherwise cleared). Because the applicant had been convicted, no such right existed. On 29 July 2008 the Regional Court affirmed, adding that Article 1070 § 2 required a final criminal conviction of the judge who issued the detention order—an element that was absent—and that the Presidium had characterised the measure merely as “unjustified” rather than “unlawful.” Article 1100 of the Civil Code (which provides for compensation irrespective of fault in cases of unlawful custody) was held inapplicable.

Domestic law distinguished between full, no-fault compensation under Article 1070 § 1 and the rehabilitation provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (available only to those cleared of charges) and the stricter fault requirement of Article 1070 § 2 for damage caused “in the framework of the administration of justice.” The applicant’s claim therefore failed on the combined grounds that he had not been rehabilitated and that no judicial criminal liability had been established.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s allegation that Russian law afforded him no effective, enforceable right to compensation for the period of detention that the highest regional court had itself found to have been imposed in violation of procedural guarantees.

The case of Abashev v. Russia (Application no. 9096/09) originated in a complaint by Russian national Oleg Ivanovich Abashev, born in 1967 and residing in Nizhnevartovsk, lodged on 28 January 2009. He alleged a denial of an enforceable right to compensation for a period of detention, raising issues under Article 5 § 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Abashev stood accused of false denunciation and had given an undertaking to appear. On 3 April 2006, he was due at a preliminary hearing before the Aleksandrovskiy District Court of the Tomsk Region. At 9:30 a.m., he telephoned the court registry to explain that he and his counsel were occupied that morning with concurrent civil proceedings and would attend later. At 2 p.m., the court (Judge K., sitting alone) proceeded in his absence. The prosecutor requested remand in custody on the ground of non-appearance. The court granted the request, holding that Abashev had failed to explain his absence or produce evidence of valid reasons, had not asked for the hearing to proceed without him, and therefore appeared to have fled justice. Despite noting the minor nature of the charge, his lack of criminal record, family circumstances, unemployment, and health issues, the court replaced the undertaking to appear with a custodial measure.

Abashev was taken into custody at 4 p.m. that day at the Aleksandrovskiy district police station and began a hunger strike. His counsel appealed, alleging judicial bias and lack of justification. On 18 May 2006 the Tomsk Regional Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the first-instance judge had reasonably concluded that Abashev had absconded. Meanwhile, on 14 April 2006 the District Court offered release on bail of 50,000 roubles (approximately €1,500). Unable to pay immediately, Abashev remained in detention until 21 April 2006, when counsel posted the sum.

On 29 May 2006 the Regional Court quashed the bail decision. It observed that Abashev had notified the court of the delay, had a known address, had not fled or breached the earlier measure, and that detention had been ordered in the absence of both him and his lawyer, contrary to the Code of Criminal Procedure. The bail itself was later refunded. On 13 December 2006 the Presidium of the Tomsk Regional Court, by way of supervisory review, quashed both the original detention order and the 18 May 2006 appeal judgment. It held that the courts had failed to apply Articles 97, 99 and 110 of the Code of Criminal Procedure properly: the hearing record showed only that Abashev and counsel would be delayed, which could not constitute flight from justice warranting custody.

Abashev was convicted on 10 January 2007 and given a suspended sentence of one and a half years with two years’ probation; the conviction was upheld on 20 August 2007.

Relying on the Presidium’s decision, Abashev brought civil proceedings against the Tomsk Regional Treasury and the Ministry of Finance, seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damage arising from the detention of 3–21 April 2006. On 23 May 2008 the Kirovskiy District Court of Tomsk dismissed the claim. It held that Article 1070 of the Civil Code and Chapter 18 of the Code of Criminal Procedure confined the right to compensation for unlawful custody to persons who had been fully rehabilitated (acquitted or otherwise cleared). Because Abashev had been convicted, no such right existed. On 29 July 2008 the Tomsk Regional Court upheld the dismissal. It added that damage caused in the administration of justice was compensable under Article 1070 § 2 only if the judge’s personal guilt had been established by a final criminal conviction, which had not occurred. The Presidium had characterised the detention as unjustified rather than unlawful, and Article 1100 of the Civil Code (which allows compensation irrespective of fault for unlawful custody) was inapplicable because Article 1070 § 2 specifically governed judicial acts.

The relevant domestic provisions thus distinguished between compensation available to rehabilitated persons (Article 1070 § 1 and Articles 133–139 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) and the stricter requirement of a criminal conviction of the judge for damage arising from judicial decisions (Article 1070 § 2). These rules formed the core of the alleged denial of an enforceable compensation right for the period of detention later found to have been improperly imposed.
001-139903:
**CASE OF A.A. v. SWITZERLAND (Application no. 58802/12), ECtHR (Second Section), 7 January 2014 (final 7 April 2014)**

The applicant, a Sudanese national claiming birth in 1985 in Zalingei near Kutum, North Darfur, alleged that his expulsion to Sudan would violate Article 3 ECHR (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) due to risks from his Darfuri origins and political activities. He further claimed a violation of Article 13 combined with Article 3, arguing Swiss authorities provided no effective remedy concerning the determination of his origins.

He entered Switzerland on 23 August 2004 and sought asylum the same day, stating he belonged to the Fur ethnic group paternally and Bergo maternally. He claimed he fled on 25 July 2004 after Janjaweed militia killed his father, mistreated him, burned his village, killed inhabitants, and stole cattle. He travelled via Port Sudan by boat, arriving in France then Geneva. Lacking identity papers, the Federal Office for Refugees (FOR) conducted a 13 September 2004 “Lingua analysis” of his cultural knowledge and Arabic dialect, plus a hearing. On 25 October 2004, the FOR rejected asylum, finding he originated from Sudan but was most probably socialised in Central or East Sudan (not Darfur) based on dialect. His statements on the region, flight itinerary, relatives, neighbouring towns, refugee camps, street conditions, climate, and Janjaweed knowledge were deemed contradictory, incomplete, or incorrect, rendering his Darfur origin and expulsion claims implausible. Return was considered safe under Article 3.

The applicant appealed to the Swiss Appeal Board for Asylum. He stated he never had identity papers and that documents were burned in the attack; he knew his birth date from his parents. On 15 February 2005 the Board upheld the decision, noting the FOR had breached his right to be heard on the Lingua results but that this was remedied by comments submitted to the Board.

After assumed departure, he was arrested in January 2009 for illegal stay. On 7 January and 2 February 2009 he lodged a second asylum request with the Federal Office for Migration (FOM), citing new political activism: membership in the Sudan Liberation Movement-Unity (SLM-Unity) in Switzerland from 2006, appointment as its human rights officer, participation in public activities, membership in the Darfur Peace and Development Centre, a local TV interview, and press releases mentioning his name. He argued Sudanese authorities would identify him, leading to arrest at the airport and Article 3 treatment, especially given his claimed Darfur origin, foreign asylum claim, and years abroad. He submitted a 26 July 1987 Sudanese birth register extract listing birth in Kutum, North Darfur, and a petition from 20 Darfuris in Switzerland confirming his origin.

The FOM dismissed the request on 15 May 2009, but the Federal Administrative Court (FAC) quashed this on 28 May 2009, requiring a merits assessment and hearing. After a hearing, the applicant provided SLM-Unity membership documents, photos of demonstrations, and UN Human Rights Council entry passes. On 8 June 2012 the FOM rejected asylum, finding activities began after departure and the 2005 rejection (subjective post-flight grounds under Asylum Act Art. 54). He lacked in-depth knowledge of SLM-Unity structure or his officer duties; the TV interview was vague and not nationally/internationally broadcast. Sudanese authorities monitored only high-profile opposition, not low-level actors like him. Combined with failed identity documents, contradictory ethnicity statements, and Lingua analysis showing non-Darfur origin (even if from Darfur, internal relocation to Khartoum was possible given family ties and work experience), return posed no Article 3 risk.

On appeal, the applicant argued the FOM ignored the birth certificate versus Lingua discrepancies (he learned Arabic pronunciation at madrasa, not home; activism proved Darfur experience). He detailed high-level involvement, including meeting the Sudanese president’s brother at the UN in Geneva, CNN appearance, and newspaper photo. On 6 August 2012 the FAC dismissed the appeal. Flight itinerary lacked credibility (impossible to reach Calais without documents amid border controls). The birth certificate had no evidentiary value (possible forgery via bribes; even authentic, it showed birthplace but not socialisation). Lingua analysis clearly indicated Central Sudan origin. Political profile was insufficient to attract Sudanese attention or create persecution risk. Expulsion would not breach Article 3.

On 27 August 2012 the applicant’s lawyers sought the Lingua transcript. The FOM allowed listening at its offices but withheld the full transcript as confidential, disclosing only that the expert (Central Sudan origin, 30 years’ residence, linguistics degree, FOM employee since 2003) tested knowledge of government, agriculture, geography/transport, traditions, and daily life (all answered correctly); he failed Bargu counting (1-10) and a common Darfur plant, with dialect resembling Central/East Sudan. Conclusion: Sudan origin, not Darfur.

Domestic law (Asylum Act Arts. 3, 7, 29, 54) required credible proof of refugee status (serious harm from race, religion, nationality, social group, or political opinion) on the balance of probabilities; post-flight grounds generally insufficient. Country reports (US State Department 2011, UK FCO 2012-2013, UN OHCHR 2008, Amnesty/HRW 2013) documented Sudanese abuses including extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention of opposition/civil society/journalists (especially Darfuris linked to rebels or returning from abroad), monitoring of exiles, and conflict in Darfur. UK tribunal and Swiss FAC case-law indicated risks for non-Arab Darfuris or those with public SLM involvement.

These facts formed the basis for the applicant’s claims of Article 3 risk on return (origin plus activism) and ineffective remedy on origin determination.

The case of A.A. v. Switzerland (Application no. 58802/12) concerns a Sudanese national’s challenge to his expulsion under Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment) and a related complaint under Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) taken with Article 3. The applicant, who requested anonymity, claimed to have been born in 1985 in Zalingei near Kutum in North Darfur. He asserted membership of the Fur ethnic group paternally and the Bergo group maternally. He stated that he fled in July 2004 after Janjaweed militias killed his father, burned his village, stole cattle and mistreated him. He travelled via Port Sudan and Calais to Switzerland, entering on 23 August 2004 and immediately claiming asylum.

Unable to produce identity documents, he underwent a Lingua analysis assessing cultural knowledge and Arabic dialect. The Federal Office for Refugees (FOR) concluded that while he originated from Sudan, his dialect indicated socialisation in Central or East Sudan rather than Darfur. His accounts of geography, itinerary, relatives and the Janjaweed were found contradictory or incomplete. Asylum was refused on 25 October 2004; an appeal was dismissed on 15 February 2005 after the Appeal Board remedied a procedural failure to allow comment on the Lingua results.

The applicant was later assumed to have left Switzerland but was arrested in January 2009 for illegal stay. He lodged a second asylum claim, asserting that he had become an active member and human-rights officer of the Sudan Liberation Movement-Unity (SLM-Unity) in Switzerland since 2006, as well as a member of the Darfur Peace and Development Centre. He cited a local television interview, press coverage, photographs of demonstrations, UN Human Rights Council passes, an SLM-Unity membership card and confirmation letter. He also submitted a 1987 Sudanese birth-register extract recording birth in Kutum, North Darfur, and a petition signed by twenty Darfuris in Switzerland. He argued that these activities, combined with his Darfuri origin, asylum claim and long absence, would expose him to arrest, interrogation and ill-treatment on return.

The Federal Office for Migration (FOM) initially rejected the claim but the Federal Administrative Court (FAC) quashed that decision, requiring a hearing on the merits. After hearing the applicant, the FOM again refused asylum on 8 June 2012. It characterised his political involvement as low-level “subjective post-flight grounds” created after the first refusal, noting insufficient knowledge of SLM-Unity structures and vague descriptions of his television appearance. Sudanese authorities, it held, monitored only high-profile opposition figures and lacked resources to track persons such as the applicant. The Lingua analysis remained decisive: he did not originate from Darfur. Even if he did, internal relocation to Khartoum was feasible given family ties and work experience.

The FAC dismissed the subsequent appeal on 6 August 2012. It found the flight itinerary implausible given border controls and the absence of any travel documents. The birth certificate was of no evidential value (possibly obtained by bribery) and, even if authentic, showed only place of birth, not subsequent socialisation. The Lingua analysis, conducted by an expert from Central Sudan, demonstrated Central Sudanese origin: the applicant could not count in Bargu, lacked knowledge of a common Darfur plant, and spoke a Central/East Sudanese dialect. His political profile was insufficiently prominent to attract Sudanese attention. Expulsion therefore posed no Article 3 risk.

Country reports cited in the proceedings documented ongoing conflict in Darfur, extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention of opposition members, journalists and returnees (especially those with rebel-group contacts or who had travelled abroad), and particular vulnerability of Darfuris in Khartoum. Swiss and UK case-law indicated that high-profile sur-place activities or non-Arab Darfuri ethnicity could generate real risk, though Swiss practice by 2013 required additional distinguishing features beyond ethnicity alone.

The applicant further complained that Swiss authorities had failed to investigate his origins adequately and had denied him an effective remedy on that point, including incomplete access to the Lingua transcript. Interim measures under Rule 39 were granted pending the Court’s examination.

The case of A.A. v. Switzerland (Application no. 58802/12) involved a Sudanese national who claimed birth in 1985 in Zalingei, North Darfur, to Fur (paternal) and Bergo (maternal) ethnic groups. He alleged fleeing on 25 July 2004 after Janjaweed militia killed his father, mistreated him, burned his village, killed inhabitants, and stole cattle. He traveled via Port Sudan by boat to Calais, then France and Switzerland, entering on 23 August 2004 and applying for asylum the same day without identity documents.

The Federal Office for Refugees (FOR) conducted a 13 September 2004 Lingua analysis of his cultural knowledge and Arab dialect, concluding he originated from Sudan but was most likely socialized in Central or East Sudan, not Darfur. His statements on origins, flight itinerary, relatives' whereabouts, neighboring towns, refugee camps, street conditions, climate, and Janjaweed knowledge were deemed contradictory, incomplete, or inaccurate. Asylum was denied on 25 October 2004, finding no Article 3 risk on return. The Appeal Board dismissed his appeal on 15 February 2005 (remedying a prior hearing right breach on the Lingua results). He later claimed never having identity papers, with documents burned in the assault; he knew his birthdate only from parents.

Assumed to have left Switzerland after January 2008, he was arrested on 2 January 2009 for illegal residence. On 7 January and 2 February 2009, he lodged a second asylum request, citing political activism since 2006 as SLM-Unity human rights officer in Switzerland, participation in public activities, DFEZ membership, a local TV interview, and press releases naming him. He argued Sudanese authorities would identify him, risking airport arrest and Article 3 treatment due to claimed Darfur origins, asylum application, and time abroad. He submitted a 26 July 1987 Sudanese birth register extract listing Kutum, North Darfur birth, and a petition from 20 Swiss-based Darfuris confirming origins.

The Federal Office for Migration (FOM) dismissed on 15 May 2009, but the Federal Administrative Court (FAC) quashed this on 28 May 2009, requiring merits consideration of political activities and an oral hearing. After submissions including SLM-Unity membership pass, president's confirmation, demonstration photos, and 2009-2010 UN Human Rights Council passes, FOM rejected on 8 June 2012. It found activities post-flight (joining after 2005 denial), lacking in-depth SLM-Unity knowledge or precise human rights officer duties, thus creating subjective post-flight grounds. The TV interview was vaguely described and not nationally/internationally broadcast; Sudanese monitoring targeted high-profile figures, not low-level ones like the applicant. Lingua analysis (not Darfur origin) allowed return even if assuming Darfur origins, via relocation to Khartoum, with family ties and professional experience aiding this.

On appeal, the applicant argued FOM ignored the birth certificate versus Lingua discrepancies (claiming madrasa-learned pronunciation, not parental; political involvement motivated by Darfur suffering). He cited high-profile activities (UN meetings, argument with Sudanese president's brother, CNN/newspaper appearances). FAC dismissed on 6 August 2012, finding flight itinerary incredible (impossible without documents amid border controls). The birth certificate lacked evidential value (potentially forged via bribes, or proving only birth, not socialization). Lingua analysis reliably showed Central Sudan origins. Political profile was insufficient to attract Sudanese attention or create persecution risk, so expulsion posed no Article 3 breach.

On 27 August 2012, the applicant sought the Lingua transcript. FOM allowed listening but disclosed limited details due to confidentiality: expert (Central Sudan origin, 30 years there, linguistics degree, FOM work since 2003) interviewed on government, agriculture, geography/transport, traditions, daily life (all answered correctly); Bargu language test failed (could not count 1-10); dialect resembled Central/East Sudan; lacked knowledge of a common Darfur plant. Conclusion: Sudanese but not Darfuri origin.

The applicant alleged expulsion would violate Article 3 (ill-treatment risk from origins/politics) and Article 13 combined with Article 3 (no effective remedy on origins, due to authorities' failures). Country reports noted Sudanese abuses including torture of opposition/Darfuris suspected of rebel links, especially returnees from abroad.
001-121906:
The case of R.M.S. v. Spain concerns a Spanish applicant of mixed Guinean-Spanish origin who alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention after authorities permanently separated her from her daughter G. (born 3 October 2001) without sufficient justification and deprived her of all contact.

At the time of G.’s birth the applicant lived on her grandmother’s olive farm within a mutually supporting extended family that included her great-uncle (a lawyer), her two older sons and, periodically, other relatives. The two sons were formally under provincial guardianship but lived with the family under the great-uncle’s foster care; the applicant combined seasonal agricultural work in Andalusia with grape-picking in France.

On 23 August 2005 the applicant, her partner and the nearly four-year-old G. approached municipal social services in Motril seeking work, food and housing. A social worker, citing the applicant’s agitated state, summoned police; G. was immediately removed and placed in a Granada children’s home while the applicant was hospitalised. Two days later the provincial child-protection office issued a provisional declaration of abandonment, citing the applicant’s extreme poverty, G.’s dirty appearance, summer clothing, dry scarred skin and food anxiety. Guardianship was assumed and residential placement ordered. Subsequent medical notes described G.’s overall condition as acceptable and attributed her skin problems to atopic dermatitis.

The applicant repeatedly requested G.’s return and contact. She was told visits would not be allowed until she underwent psychiatric treatment. Three supervised meetings occurred in September 2005; the last took place on 27 September. A social-worker report then described the applicant as violent and aggressive, recommended suspension of all contact and relocation of G. to an undisclosed home. On 5 October 2005 the office confirmed the abandonment declaration, moved G. without notice or consent, prohibited visits and withheld her whereabouts. The applicant made more than twenty further requests for information or contact between November 2005 and early 2006; all were refused.

On 1 February 2006 the office formally declared G. abandoned, citing “poor prospects” of reunification, the mother’s undiagnosed “manic” state and alleged lack of interest in the child’s welfare, and initiated pre-adoption foster care. The applicant opposed the measures and reported the matter to the Ombudsman. A couple was selected as foster parents in April 2006; temporary pre-adoption placement was ordered in February 2007.

Domestic courts consistently upheld the authorities. In May 2007 a first-instance judge rejected the applicant’s challenge to the abandonment declaration, relying on the 2005 file and noting the child’s lack of attachment and the applicant’s “violent” conduct during visits. The prohibition on contact was confirmed. Appeals were dismissed in 2008. In 2009 another first-instance judge approved pre-adoption foster care, declining to hear the great-uncle as a witness or consider family placement, on the ground that G. (now eight) had had no contact with her mother for years. Although the public prosecutor supported the applicant, the judgment was upheld on appeal in 2010; a psychological report submitted by the applicant was dismissed as self-serving. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible in 2011. Follow-up reports recorded that G. had integrated well with the foster family since February 2007. Adoption proceedings were opened in 2011 but had not been concluded by early 2013; the applicant had not seen or received news of her daughter since September 2005.

These facts form the core of the alleged unjustified and irreversible interference with family life and possible discriminatory treatment linked to the applicant’s socio-economic circumstances and origin.

The applicant, a Spanish national of mixed Guinean-Spanish origin born in 1979, lived with her extended family (including her grandmother, a lawyer great-uncle, and two older sons) on a family olive farm in Jaén province. She worked seasonally as an agricultural labourer in Andalusia and France. Her two older sons were formally under provincial guardianship but remained in the extended family's care. Her daughter G. was born on 3 October 2001.

On 23 August 2005 the applicant, her partner and G. (then aged three years and ten months) approached municipal social services in Motril seeking work, food and housing. Owing to the applicant's agitated state, social workers summoned the police; G. was immediately removed and placed in a Granada children's home, while the applicant was hospitalised. Two days later the Granada provincial child-protection office issued a provisional declaration that G. was legally abandoned, citing the family's extreme poverty, the child's poor hygiene, unsuitable summer clothing, dry and scarred skin, and food anxiety. The office assumed guardianship and informed the applicant she could seek legal aid to challenge the decision. Contact was refused unless the applicant first obtained psychiatric treatment.

A children's-home report of 29 August 2005 described G.'s overall condition as acceptable, noting only dry skin and minor scratches later attributed to atopic dermatitis. Without the applicant's knowledge or consent, G. was transferred on 14 September 2005 to another home. The applicant had three supervised, police-escorted visits (the last on 27 September 2005) during which G. reportedly mentioned being taken to a house with a swimming pool. A social-work report of 4 October 2005 portrayed the applicant as violent, aggressive and disrespectful, accused her of encouraging G. to cry and of threatening publicity, and recommended suspending all contact and concealing G.'s location. On 5 October 2005 the office confirmed the abandonment declaration, moved G. again, and barred all communication and information.

The applicant repeatedly petitioned for G.'s return, a transfer closer to home, and visiting rights, approaching the office at least seventeen times between November 2005 and January 2006. On 1 February 2006 the office issued a final abandonment declaration, citing poor prospects of family reunification, the applicant's "moderately manic" state and alleged lack of interest in G.'s welfare, and initiated pre-adoption foster-care proceedings. It also asserted, without supporting evidence, that the great-uncle was unsuitable. The applicant opposed the measures, reported the matter to the Ombudsman and, once legally aided, challenged both the abandonment finding and the contact ban.

Domestic courts upheld the authorities. In May 2007 a first-instance judge confirmed wholesale physical and psychological neglect at the time of removal, noted the older sons' existing foster placement, and refused contact because of G.'s lack of attachment and the applicant's disruptive behaviour. The Granada Audiencia Provincial affirmed the ruling in June 2008, observing that any later change of circumstances could be examined in separate proceedings. Parallel proceedings concerning pre-adoption foster care produced the same outcome: in September 2009 another first-instance judge approved placement with a couple selected in 2006, rejected the great-uncle as a carer, and held that G. (now almost eight and without contact for years) needed stability. The Audiencia Provincial confirmed this in June 2010, finding the applicant's psychological report unconvincing and no proof that the original risk had disappeared. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible in October 2011 for lack of constitutional significance. Follow-up reports indicated G. was fully integrated with the foster family, who had been living with her since February 2007. Adoption proceedings began in 2011 but had not concluded by early 2013.

The applicant alleged that the removal, the total and permanent severance of contact, the concealment of G.'s whereabouts and the progression toward adoption, all based on poverty, unproven mental-health concerns and her protestations, violated her right to respect for family life (Article 8) and amounted to discrimination (Article 14).

The case of R.M.S. v. Spain concerns a Spanish national of mixed Guinean-Spanish origin who alleged that Spanish authorities violated her rights under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights by removing her daughter G. (born October 2001) from her care in 2005 and thereafter denying all contact without sufficient justification.

At the time of G.’s birth the applicant lived in an extended family unit on her grandmother’s olive farm in Andalusia, together with her two older sons, her grandmother and a great-uncle (a lawyer). The older sons were formally under public guardianship and placed with the great-uncle, but in practice remained within the household. The applicant combined seasonal agricultural work in Spain and France with family life.

On 23 August 2005 the applicant, her partner and G. (then aged nearly four) attended municipal social services in Motril seeking work, food and housing. Because of the applicant’s agitated state a social worker called the police; G. was immediately removed and placed in a children’s home while the applicant was hospitalised. Two days later the Granada provincial child-protection office issued a provisional declaration of abandonment, citing the applicant’s extreme poverty, G.’s alleged lack of hygiene, inappropriate clothing, dry scarred skin and anxiety about food. The office assumed guardianship and informed the applicant she could apply for legal aid to challenge the decision.

The applicant repeatedly requested G.’s return and a transfer to a closer home. She was told contact would not be allowed until she began psychiatric treatment. After three supervised visits in September 2005 (during which officials described her as violent and disruptive), all contact was suspended, G. was moved to another institution without the applicant’s knowledge or consent, and her whereabouts were concealed. The applicant made at least 17 further approaches between November 2005 and January 2006 seeking information and access; none was granted.

In February 2006 the office formally declared G. abandoned, citing poor prospects of family reunification, the mother’s “moderately manic” state and alleged lack of interest in the child’s welfare, and initiated pre-adoption foster-care proceedings. The applicant opposed the measure, reported the matter to the Ombudsman and continued to demand contact. Domestic courts successively upheld the abandonment declaration (2007–2008) and the pre-adoption placement (2009–2010), relying on the original 2005 findings of neglect, the applicant’s purported mental instability and the fact that G. (by then aged eight) had had no contact with her mother for years. Alternative placement with the great-uncle was rejected. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible in 2011. By 2013 G. was fully integrated with her pre-adoptive foster family, although formal adoption had not yet been completed.

The applicant maintained throughout that the initial removal was based solely on her poverty and ethnic origin, that no serious neglect or mental illness had been established by independent evidence, and that the complete and permanent severance of all family ties was disproportionate.

The ECHR case Ojala and Etukeno Oy v. Finland (no. 69939/10) arose from an alleged Article 10 violation of freedom of expression. Finnish publisher Kari Markus Ojala and his company Etukeno Oy co-authored and published an autobiographical book with the former girlfriend of Finland’s Prime Minister (in office 2003–2010). Released on 19 February 2007, the book recounted nine months of their relationship from the girlfriend’s viewpoint as a single mother, including their dating life and intimate interactions. The Prime Minister had previously divorced and publicly discussed aspects of his family, habits, and this relationship via a 2005 autobiography, interviews, a blog, and home photographs, though he tightly controlled his image.

On 5 October 2007 the public prosecutor charged Ojala (and the girlfriend) under Penal Code Chapter 24, section 8 for disseminating information violating personal privacy that could cause damage, suffering, or contempt. Forfeiture of the company’s proceeds was also sought under Chapter 10, section 2. The Prime Minister endorsed the charges and joined a compensation claim. The book was withdrawn from sale on 15 February 2008. The girlfriend later lodged a separate ECHR application.

On 5 March 2008 the Helsinki District Court (by majority) dismissed the charges and the forfeiture request. It held that while the book revealed private details, the Prime Minister had already disclosed much of his personal life; new information merely completed that picture and was undisputed as true. The girlfriend was entitled to recount her own experiences, describing the Prime Minister compassionately. Although the material had no direct bearing on his official functions, it related to his character (ministers must be “known to be honest and competent”) and illustrated social contrasts. Criminal liability, as a last resort, was disproportionate; Ojala also lacked intent after obtaining legal advice.

The prosecutor and Prime Minister appealed. On 10 February 2009 the Helsinki Appeal Court convicted Ojala of disseminating privacy-violating information, imposing 60 day-fines (840 euros), 1,000 euros non-pecuniary damages plus 9,344 euros costs to the Prime Minister, and forfeiture of 4,260 euros in proceeds (the company recovered 4,000 euros in costs). Intimate dating details and the children’s feelings unnecessarily invaded the core of the Prime Minister’s private life, which he had not waived despite prior disclosures. Consent was required for another’s intimate information; the book served no public-interest purpose concerning his political role or qualities.

Leave to appeal was granted. On 16 June 2010, after an oral hearing, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction but quashed the forfeiture against Ojala and reduced costs (6,000 euros for lower courts plus 4,500 euros for itself; the company received 2,000 euros). Drawing on ECHR case-law, it gave a narrower reading of protected private life. Details of how the couple met, the relationship’s rapid development, lifestyle disparities, data-protection issues, and protection of high officials were relevant to public debate on the Prime Minister’s honesty and judgment. Information about the children (the girlfriend’s interpretations of their attitudes) was not damaging. However, seven specific passages on the couple’s sex life—its commencement, brief passionate moments, mutual massages, and sexual intercourse—had never been disclosed, lay at the core of private life, and were liable to cause suffering and contempt. Restriction of expression was therefore necessary to protect privacy. Ojala’s prior legal advice did not negate intent.

These facts—the publication of previously undisclosed intimate sexual details, the successive court assessments balancing expression against privacy, and the final conviction with modest penalties—formed the basis of the Article 10 complaint.

The applicants—publisher Kari Markus Ojala and his company Etukeno Oy—collaborated with the former girlfriend of Finland’s then-Prime Minister to produce an autobiographical book about their nine-month relationship. Published on 19 February 2007, the book recounted their dating life and intimate interactions from the girlfriend’s perspective as a single mother; the Prime Minister (in office 2003–2010) had previously divorced. It included previously undisclosed details of their sex life, passionate moments, massages, and intercourse, alongside other personal information.

On 5 October 2007 the public prosecutor charged Ojala (and the girlfriend, in a related case) under Chapter 24, section 8 of the Penal Code with disseminating information violating the Prime Minister’s private life, seeking forfeiture of the company’s proceeds. The Prime Minister joined the charges and claimed compensation. The book was withdrawn from sale on 15 February 2008.

The Helsinki District Court acquitted Ojala on 5 March 2008, finding no criminal offence. Although the book revealed private details, the Prime Minister had already publicised much of his family life, habits, and the relationship (via a 2005 autobiography, interviews, a blog, and home photographs). New facts merely completed that picture; their truth was undisputed. The girlfriend was entitled to describe her own life, including a compassionate portrait of the Prime Minister. Even without direct bearing on his official duties, the material was relevant to assessing his personal honesty and competence (constitutionally required of ministers) and illustrated a clash between a wealthy politician’s world and everyday financial struggles. Criminal sanctions were a last resort, and Ojala’s prior legal advice negated intent.

The prosecutor and Prime Minister appealed. On 10 February 2009 the Helsinki Appeal Court convicted Ojala of disseminating information violating personal privacy, imposing 60 day-fines (€840), €1,000 non-pecuniary damages plus costs to the Prime Minister, and forfeiture of €4,260 proceeds. It held that passages on intimate dating and the children’s feelings unnecessarily invaded the core of private life, which the Prime Minister had not previously disclosed or waived. A girlfriend’s right to recount her own life still required consent for another’s intimate details. The book’s aim was private-life gossip with no bearing on official functions or personal qualities such as honesty.

Ojala and the company appealed. After granting leave and holding an oral hearing, the Supreme Court on 16 June 2010 upheld the conviction (quashing forfeiture against Ojala and reducing costs). Drawing on ECHR case-law, it narrowed the protected private sphere. Information on how the couple met, the relationship’s rapid development, lifestyle disparities, data-protection issues, and protection of high officials had public-interest value for assessing the Prime Minister’s honesty and judgment. Descriptions of the children’s attitudes were not damaging. However, seven specific passages—on the start of their sex life, brief passionate encounters, mutual massages, and sexual intercourse—fell within the core of private life, had never been disclosed, and were capable of causing suffering and contempt. Their unauthorised publication therefore required restriction of the applicants’ freedom of expression to protect the Prime Minister’s privacy.

Finnish law (Constitution Articles 10 and 12; Penal Code Chapter 24, section 8) balances privacy against expression, with an exception for public figures when disclosure is necessary to evaluate their official activities. The applicants alleged that the conviction and sanctions violated Article 10 of the Convention.

The case of Ojala and Etukeno Oy v. Finland (Application no. 69939/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression). Finnish publisher Kari Markus Ojala and his company Etukeno Oy, together with the former girlfriend of Finland’s then-Prime Minister, published an autobiographical book on 19 February 2007. The work covered a nine-month period of their relationship from the girlfriend’s viewpoint as a single mother, including details of their dating life and intimate interactions. The Prime Minister (in office 2003–2010) had previously divorced and had himself publicised aspects of his family life, habits and the relationship via a 2005 autobiography, interviews, a blog and home photographs, though he was known for tightly controlling his public image.

On 5 October 2007 the public prosecutor charged Ojala and the girlfriend under Chapter 24, section 8 of the Penal Code with disseminating information violating the Prime Minister’s private life (an offence punishable by fine or up to two years’ imprisonment). The prosecutor also sought forfeiture of the company’s proceeds. The Prime Minister joined the charges and claimed compensation. The book was withdrawn from sale on 15 February 2008.

The Helsinki District Court (5 March 2008) acquitted Ojala, finding that the Prime Minister had already disclosed much of the material, that new details merely completed the existing picture, that the girlfriend was entitled to recount her own life, and that the information retained some relevance to assessing the Prime Minister’s personal qualities (honesty and competence being constitutionally required of ministers). Criminal liability was a last resort; Ojala had obtained prior legal advice and therefore lacked intent.

On appeal the Helsinki Appeal Court (10 February 2009) convicted Ojala, imposing 60 day-fines (EUR 840), EUR 1 000 non-pecuniary damages plus costs, and forfeiture of EUR 4 260 proceeds. It held that passages concerning intimate dating and the children’s feelings unnecessarily invaded the core of private life, which the Prime Minister had neither previously disclosed nor waived. The book pursued no public-interest purpose linked to his political functions.

The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and, after an oral hearing, delivered judgment on 16 June 2010. It upheld the conviction but quashed forfeiture against Ojala and reduced costs. Drawing extensively on ECHR case-law, it confined the criminal interference to seven specific passages describing the commencement of their sex life, brief passionate encounters, mutual massages and sexual intercourse. These details had never been made public, fell within the core of private life, and were capable of causing suffering or contempt; their unauthorised publication therefore justified a restriction of expression. Other information (how the couple met, the speed of the relationship, disparities in living standards, lifestyle, data-protection issues) possessed public-interest value for assessing the Prime Minister’s honesty and judgment and did not attract liability.

Finnish law (Constitution Arts 10 and 12; Penal Code Ch. 24 s. 8) balances private-life protection against freedom of expression, creating an exception for public figures when the information may affect evaluation of their official activities and is necessary for a matter of societal importance. The applicants contended that the conviction nevertheless violated Article 10.

The case of Lillo-Stenberg and Sæther v. Norway (ECHR, Application no. 13258/09) concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) arising from a Norwegian Supreme Court ruling that permitted publication of photographs and details of the applicants’ wedding.

The applicants, a well-known musician and actress, married on 20 August 2005 in a private outdoor ceremony on a small islet in Tjøme, in the Oslo fjord. The event was not open to the press. Shortly afterwards, the celebrity magazine Se og Hør published a two-page article illustrated by six photographs. These included images of the bride arriving by rowing boat with her father and bridesmaids, the couple surrounded by guests on the islet, and the pair returning to the mainland across stepping stones (the bride barefoot, her dress held above her knees). Additional pictures showed wedding guests (including a couple with a baby) and older photographs of the applicants and their young son. The accompanying text described the ceremony as “touching,” noted guests’ emotional reactions, named some attendees, and mentioned a subsequent garden party. The magazine had contacted the applicants’ manager shortly before publication; they declined to comment and refused consent, but the issue was already in print. The photographs had been taken without the couple’s knowledge from a headland some 250 metres away, using a 300–400 mm zoom lens.

The applicants sued the magazine, its editor, journalist and photographer, claiming a violation of privacy under section 390 of the Penal Code (which prohibits public disclosure of personal or domestic relations) and Article 8 of the Convention. They sought compensation. Oslo District Court (22 November 2006) found for them, awarding each NOK 50,000 plus smaller sums from the individuals involved. The Borgarting High Court upheld this on 13 February 2008.

The Supreme Court, by a 3–2 majority (2 September 2008), reversed the lower courts. The majority held that, although the material concerned private and family life, publication was not unlawful. A wedding has a public dimension as a legal affirmation of cohabitation. The photographs did not depict the actual ceremony, the location was publicly accessible under Norway’s Outdoor Recreation Act and highly visible, the arrangements were unusual and attention-grabbing, and there was no element of harassment or breach of confidence. The article contained no criticism or reputation-damaging content. The majority balanced Article 8 against Article 10 (freedom of expression), concluding that the entertainment-oriented piece did not constitute an unlawful intrusion. The minority viewed the wedding as a clearly private event whose personal details (arrangements, guests, emotional atmosphere) lacked sufficient public-interest justification; they analogised the distant zoom photography to a hidden camera.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Supreme Court’s decision itself breached Article 8. The Court communicated the application in 2010 but awaited the Grand Chamber judgments in Von Hannover (no. 2) and Axel Springer AG before proceeding.

The ECHR case of Lillo-Stenberg and Sæther v. Norway (no. 13258/09) concerned an alleged breach of the applicants’ Article 8 right to respect for private life arising from a 2 September 2008 Norwegian Supreme Court judgment (3-2) that rejected their privacy claim against a magazine.

The applicants, a well-known Norwegian musician and actress, held a private outdoor wedding ceremony on 20 August 2005 on an islet in Tjøme (Oslo fjord). The weekly magazine Se og Hør later published a two-page article with six photographs taken without invitation or the couple’s knowledge, from ~250 metres away using a 300-400 mm zoom lens. Images showed the bride (with father and bridesmaids) arriving by rowing boat, being escorted to the groom amid guests, and the couple returning barefoot across stepping stones (dress lifted); a guest couple with baby; and older photos of the applicants plus their young son. Text described the “touching” ceremony, guests’ tears, a choir singing “To live is to love,” named guests, and a garden party at a guest house, noting the applicants (via manager) declined comment.

The applicants sued in Oslo District Court under Penal Code s. 390 (public disclosure of personal/domestic relations) and Article 8. On 22 November 2006 the court found a privacy violation and awarded NOK 50,000 each from the magazine plus smaller sums from the editor, journalist and photographer. Borgarting High Court upheld this on 13 February 2008.

The Supreme Court majority (Justice U. et al.) held the publication lawful. Information on family relations and the wedding was private, and no consent existed (the couple learned of it only after printing began). Yet a wedding also has a public legal dimension; a neutral, non-critical report from a reliable source does not violate privacy. The couple were public figures but not political ones, so the article’s purely entertainment value carried little Article 10 weight. The location was publicly accessible under the Outdoor Recreation Act and visible; the unusual, attention-drawing ceremony (open boat, choir) occurred in a popular holiday area. Photos depicted only arrival/departure, not the core ceremony itself, and were not taken from a closed space where privacy was reasonably expected. Use of a child’s previously published photo raised no separate issue. A parallel copyright claim (Copyright Act s. 45c) failed for the same balancing reasons. No costs were awarded given the novel public-interest questions.

The minority (Justice T. et al.) found a s. 390 violation. The event was private: the couple had arranged it to restrict attendance (landowner permission obtained; linked to a private hotel garden), even though the islet was publicly accessible. Published details of the personalised ceremony, guests (including named families with children) and families constituted “personal matters.” Pure entertainment lacked the minimum public interest needed to override privacy, especially for so significant an occasion. Celebrities retain equivalent privacy rights. The concealed zoom photography resembled a hidden camera and confirmed awareness of the event’s private character.

The ECHR application (lodged 5 March 2009) was communicated on 26 May 2010 after the Court awaited Grand Chamber rulings in von Hannover (no. 2) and Axel Springer. The facts centre on whether secretly photographing and publishing details of a celebrity couple’s outdoor wedding, held on publicly accessible land yet intended as private, unlawfully interfered with Article 8.

The case of Lillo-Stenberg and Sæther v. Norway (Application no. 13258/09) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) on 16 January 2014. The applicants, Norwegian nationals Lars Lillo-Stenberg (a musician born in 1962) and Andrine Sæther (an actress born in 1964), both well-known public figures living in Oslo, alleged that a 2 September 2008 Norwegian Supreme Court judgment violated their Article 8 right to respect for private life.

On 20 August 2005, the applicants held a private outdoor wedding ceremony on an islet in Tjøme municipality in the Oslo fjord, about 100 km south of Oslo. The weekly magazine Se og Hør subsequently published a two-page article accompanied by six photographs. These included images of the bride, her father and bridesmaids arriving by small rowing boat; the bride being escorted to the groom amid guests; the couple returning to the mainland across stepping stones (with the bride barefoot and her dress lifted above her knees); a guest couple with their baby; and two older photographs (one of the applicants framed in a heart, and one of the second applicant with their young son at a musical festival a month earlier). The text described the ceremony as touching, noting guests’ tears during a male choir’s performance of “To live is to love,” a subsequent garden party at a named guesthouse, and the applicants’ manager’s statement that they did not wish to comment.

The magazine had not been invited. Photographs were taken without the applicants’ knowledge from approximately 250 metres away using a 300–400 mm zoom lens. The journalist contacted the first applicant’s manager shortly before publication and was told the couple would not comment; later that day, after being informed they withheld consent, the magazine stated the issue was already at press.

The applicants sued in Oslo District Court, invoking Penal Code section 390 (public disclosure of personal or domestic relations) and Article 8. On 22 November 2006 the District Court found for them, awarding NOK 50,000 each in compensation plus smaller sums from the editor, journalist and photographer. Borgarting High Court upheld this on 13 February 2008.

The Supreme Court, by a 3–2 majority, reversed on 2 September 2008. The majority, led by Justice U., held that while the article as a whole concerned private family matters and was published without consent, it did not unlawfully violate privacy. A wedding has a public dimension as a legal and social affirmation. The text and photos were not unfavourable, contained no criticism, omitted the actual ceremony, and were taken in a publicly accessible location under the Outdoor Recreation Act that was visible and likely to attract attention due to the unusual, spectacular arrangements (open-boat arrival, choir). The photographs did not constitute harassment or a breach of confidence. Although the applicants were well-known cultural figures rather than political ones, and the piece had purely entertainment value rather than contributing to public debate, the overall circumstances (public setting, lack of intrusion into the core ceremony) meant no violation occurred. The same conclusion applied under copyright provisions on image use, interpreted consistently with Articles 8 and 10 ECHR. No costs were awarded given the public-interest legal questions.

The minority, led by Justice T., found a privacy violation. The wedding, including its personal touches and linked hotel reception, was a private event despite public access rights; consent from the landowner had been obtained. Publication of ceremonial details, guest names (including children) and family relations concerned a personal matter. Using a zoom lens from concealment resembled a hidden camera and indicated awareness that presence would have disrupted the event. The piece served only entertainment with no public-interest contribution sufficient to override privacy, especially given the emotional significance of a wedding. Well-known persons retain such protection. The minority would have upheld the compensation awards.

The applicants claimed the Supreme Court judgment itself breached Article 8 by failing to protect their private life against the unconsented publication. The Court communicated the application on 26 May 2010, awaiting related Grand Chamber cases on privacy and press freedom.
