The case of Ruusunen v. Finland (Application no. 73579/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). Finnish national Susan Ruusunen, a former girlfriend of then-Prime Minister Matti Vanhanen (in office 2003–2010), published an autobiographical book on 19 February 2007 describing their nine-month relationship. As a single mother, she detailed their dating life, including intimate interactions. The Prime Minister had previously divorced and publicly shared aspects of his family life, habits, and the relationship via an autobiography, interviews, a blog, and home photographs, though he tightly controlled his public image.

On 5 October 2007, the public prosecutor charged Ruusunen (along with her publisher and its representative) under Chapter 24, section 8 of the Penal Code with unlawfully disseminating information about the Prime Minister’s private life that was conducive to causing damage, suffering, or contempt. The prosecutor also sought forfeiture of the book’s proceeds (approximately €4,270). The Prime Minister did not bring private charges or claims. The book was withdrawn from sale on 15 February 2008.

The Helsinki District Court dismissed the charges on 5 March 2008. It held that much of the information had already been disclosed by the Prime Minister himself, with new details merely completing the public picture. The facts were undisputed as true. Ruusunen had a right to recount her own life, and the book portrayed the Prime Minister compassionately. Although the material lacked direct relevance to his official duties, it concerned his personal qualities (honesty and competence, as required of ministers by the Constitution) and illustrated social contrasts. Given the Prime Minister’s prior disclosures, criminal liability was disproportionate; Ruusunen, not a professional writer, lacked the requisite intent.

The prosecutor and Prime Minister appealed. On 10 February 2009, the Helsinki Appeal Court convicted Ruusunen of dissemination of information violating personal privacy, imposing 20 day-fines totaling €300 and ordering forfeiture. It found that previously undisclosed passages about intimate dating and the children’s feelings and behaviour unnecessarily invaded the core of the Prime Minister’s private life. His earlier disclosures did not waive remaining privacy rights, nor did he consent. The book’s focus on private matters had no bearing on his political functions or personal qualities relevant to office. Ruusunen’s actions were intentional.

Ruusunen appealed to the Supreme Court, which granted leave and, after an oral hearing, on 16 June 2010 upheld the conviction but quashed the forfeiture. Referring extensively to ECHR case-law, it narrowed the protected private sphere: only seven specific passages concerning the start of their sex life, brief passionate moments, mutual massages, and sexual intercourse constituted unauthorised disclosure of core private-life details capable of causing suffering or contempt. Other elements—how and when they met, the relationship’s rapid development, lifestyle differences, data-protection issues, and the children’s attitudes—were relevant to public debate on the Prime Minister’s honesty, judgment, and the protection of high officials. The Prime Minister had not waived protection for the sexual details, and consent to use his photograph on the cover did not extend to them. Restriction of Ruusunen’s expression was therefore necessary to protect his private life.

Domestic law invoked includes Article 10 of the Finnish Constitution (guaranteeing private life) and Article 12 (freedom of expression), as well as the cited Penal Code provisions. The European Court of Human Rights communicated the application on 2 July 2012 and joined admissibility and merits. The alleged violation centres on whether the conviction, limited to intimate sexual revelations in an autobiography about a public figure who had already publicised much of his private life, constituted a proportionate interference with freedom of expression.

The case of Ruusunen v. Finland (Application no. 73579/10) concerns Finnish national Susan Ruusunen, a former girlfriend of Finland’s Prime Minister (in office 2003–2010). On 5 October 2007 the public prosecutor charged the applicant (along with the publisher and its representative) under Chapter 24, section 8 of the Penal Code with unlawfully disseminating information, an insinuation or an image of another person’s private life that was conducive to causing damage, suffering or contempt. The new material merely completed that picture; all facts were undisputed. The applicant was entitled to narrate her own life and had done so compassionately. It held that passages concerning intimate dating and the children’s feelings and behaviour invaded the core of the Prime Minister’s private life—details he had never disclosed. Prior publicity did not constitute a waiver of all privacy rights, nor did consent to a cover photograph. The book’s aim was purely private and irrelevant to the evaluation of the Prime Minister’s official functions or personal fitness for office. The applicant’s acts were intentional.

Information about how and when the relationship began, differences in living standards, lifestyle, data-protection issues and the security of high officials possessed public-interest value and could legitimately inform debate on the Prime Minister’s honesty and judgment. The case of Ruusunen v. Finland (Application no. 73579/10) before the European Court of Human Rights originated in a complaint by Susan Ruusunen, a Finnish national born in 1970 and living in Helsinki. She alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) after her conviction for publishing an autobiographical book that disclosed details of her relationship with Finland’s then-Prime Minister.

The applicant, a single mother, dated the recently divorced Prime Minister for nine months. Her book, published on 19 February 2007, described their daily life together and included references to intimate interactions. The Prime Minister served from June 2003 until June 2010. On 5 October 2007 the public prosecutor charged the applicant (and the publisher) under Chapter 24, section 8 of the Penal Code with disseminating information that violated personal privacy. Forfeiture of the proceeds of the offence was also sought. The Prime Minister brought no private prosecution or compensation claim. The book was withdrawn from sale in February 2008.

On 5 March 2008 the Helsinki District Court dismissed the charges. It accepted that the book revealed substantial private information but observed that the Prime Minister had already publicised aspects of his family life, habits and the relationship itself through an autobiography, interviews, a blog and photographs of his home. Previously unpublished details merely completed that existing picture; their truth was never disputed. The court held that the applicant was entitled to recount her own life, that her portrayal was compassionate, and that the material had some relevance to the Prime Minister’s personal qualities (honesty and competence being constitutional requirements for ministers). It also noted the societal contrast between a wealthy political leader and a financially struggling single mother. Criminal sanctions were regarded as a last resort and disproportionate once information had entered the public domain; moreover the applicant, not a professional writer, lacked the requisite intent.

The prosecutor and the Prime Minister appealed. On 10 February 2009 the Helsinki Court of Appeal convicted the applicant, imposing 20 day-fines (300 euros) and ordering forfeiture of 4 270 euros. It found that passages concerning intimate dating, sexual relations and the feelings and behaviour of the Prime Minister’s children invaded the core of his private life—matters he had never previously disclosed. Prior publicity of other aspects of his life did not constitute a waiver of remaining privacy rights, nor did consent to the use of his photograph on the book cover. The court considered the book’s purpose to be purely private and irrelevant to the Prime Minister’s official functions or to any assessment of his public character.

The applicant obtained leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, arguing that a precedent was needed on freedom of expression in autobiographies. After an oral hearing the Supreme Court, on 16 June 2010, upheld the conviction but quashed the forfeiture order. Drawing extensively on Strasbourg case-law, it adopted a narrower view of protected private life than the Court of Appeal. Information about how and when the couple met, the speed of the relationship, lifestyle differences, data-protection issues and the protection of high office-holders contributed to legitimate public debate about the Prime Minister’s honesty and judgment. Descriptions of the children’s attitudes were merely the applicant’s interpretation and not damaging. However, seven specific passages describing the onset of their sexual relationship, brief passionate encounters, mutual massages and sexual intercourse had never been made public. These details belonged to the core of private life; their unauthorised publication was capable of causing suffering and contempt. Restriction of the applicant’s expression was therefore necessary to protect the Prime Minister’s privacy.

The relevant domestic provisions were Article 10 of the Finnish Constitution (protection of private life) and Article 12 (freedom of expression), together with Chapter 24, section 8 of the Penal Code, which criminalises unauthorised dissemination of private information apt to cause damage, suffering or contempt, subject to an exception for information about public figures that is necessary for the evaluation of their official activities and for the discussion of matters of societal importance.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that her criminal conviction for publishing the intimate passages violated Article 10.

The case of Pentikäinen v. Finland (Application no. 11882/10) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Finnish journalist and photographer Markus Veikko Pentikäinen. He alleged a violation of his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention, arising from his arrest and subsequent conviction for disobeying police orders while covering a demonstration in his professional capacity.

On 9 September 2006, Pentikäinen was assigned by the weekly magazine Suomen Kuvalehti to photograph a large protest in Helsinki against the Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM). Finnish authorities had been warned that the “Smash ASEM” event would likely be hostile rather than a conventional political demonstration, and they were unable to contact its organisers. A designated media area was established so that journalists could observe and photograph safely.

The protest began at 6 p.m. Violence quickly erupted: bottles, stones and paint-filled jars were thrown at police, and some demonstrators physically assaulted officers. Police repeatedly announced over loudspeakers that a stationary, peaceful gathering was permitted but that a march would not be allowed. When the crowd attempted to breach police lines, officers declared the demonstration over and ordered everyone to disperse. Hundreds left voluntarily. Police then sealed off the area, initially restricting exits before establishing controlled routes where identities were checked and belongings searched.

A core group of approximately 20 people, including Pentikäinen and a former member of parliament, remained. Police instructed them to leave or face arrest. Pentikäinen later claimed he believed the order applied only to demonstrators, that he displayed his press badge, and that an officer acknowledged it. After consulting a colleague by telephone, he chose to stay to document the unfolding events. He was arrested shortly afterwards along with the remaining individuals. In total, 121 people were detained in connection with the protest. Pentikäinen was held for 17.5 hours, from 9.26 p.m. on 9 September until 3.05 p.m. the following day.

On 23 May 2007 he was charged under Chapter 16, section 4(1) of the Penal Code with disobeying a police order issued for the maintenance of public order. On 17 December 2007 the Helsinki District Court found him guilty but, exercising its discretion under Chapter 6, section 12 of the Penal Code, imposed no penalty. The court accepted that he had heard the dispersal orders yet remained, that he had not identified himself as a journalist to the arresting officer (who learned of his profession only later), and that two other photographers in the same area had left without incident. It held that the orders were clear, applied to everyone, and pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder. The interference with Pentikäinen’s journalistic activity was therefore prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society to end a violent situation. The court regarded the offence as excusable because the applicant faced conflicting professional and legal duties.

Pentikäinen appealed, arguing that his arrest and conviction were unnecessary in a democratic society and that he had neither participated in the demonstration nor caused disorder. On 30 April 2009 the Helsinki Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal without additional reasoning. On 1 September 2009 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicant maintained that the police action and the finding of guilt had prevented him from performing his journalistic function of informing the public about an event of significant public interest. The Chamber of the Court (Fourth Section) examined the application under Article 10, noting the importance of press freedom while also recognising the authorities’ duty to restore public order after the protest had turned into a riot. (The Chamber judgment of 4 February 2014 was later referred to the Grand Chamber.)

**Case Summary: Pentikäinen v. Finland (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 4 February 2014; Application no. 11882/10)**

Markus Veikko Pentikäinen, a Finnish photographer and journalist for the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*, alleged a violation of his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. He claimed the police arrested him and that domestic courts later found him guilty of disobeying police orders while he was attempting to carry out his professional duties covering a demonstration.

On 9 September 2006, Pentikäinen’s employer sent him to photograph the large “Smash ASEM” protest in Helsinki against the Asia-Europe Meeting. Finnish security services had warned police that the event would be hostile and lack a clear political message; organizers could not be contacted. Authorities reserved a separate area for media to observe and photograph safely. The demonstration began at 6 p.m. Violence quickly erupted: participants threw bottles, stones and paint-filled jars at police and bystanders, and some assaulted officers. Police announced repeatedly over loudspeakers that a static peaceful protest was permitted but marching was not. When the crowd attempted to break police lines, officers declared the event over, ordered the crowd to disperse, and repeated the announcements. Hundreds left voluntarily.

Police then treated the event as a riot, sealed the area, and later opened exit routes where leavers showed identification and submitted to searches. A core group of about 20 people, including Pentikäinen and a former member of parliament, remained. They were ordered to leave or face arrest. Pentikäinen later stated he believed the order applied only to demonstrators, that he displayed his press badge, that an officer accepted it, and that he chose to stay after consulting a colleague in order to document the unfolding events. Shortly thereafter police arrested the remaining group, including him. In total, 121 people were arrested. Pentikäinen was detained for 17.5 hours (from 9.26 p.m. on 9 September until 3.05 p.m. on 10 September).

On 23 May 2007 he was charged under Chapter 16, section 4(1) of the Penal Code with contumacy toward the police for failing to obey an order issued to maintain public order. On 17 December 2007 the Helsinki District Court found him guilty but imposed no penalty. The court established that he had heard the clear orders applying to everyone yet remained; witness evidence showed he had not identified himself as a journalist to the arresting officer (who learned of his status only later from the magazine). Two other photographers had left the sealed area without incident shortly before his arrest. Balancing Article 10 against public-order needs, the court held the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder, and was necessary in a democratic society to end violence. Punishment was waived under Chapter 6, section 12 of the Penal Code because the journalist faced conflicting professional and legal demands, rendering the offence excusable.

Pentikäinen appealed, arguing that as a non-participating journalist his arrest and conviction violated the Finnish Constitution and Article 10 and that the District Court had failed to explain why the measures were necessary. The Helsinki Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 30 April 2009 without additional reasoning. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 1 September 2009.

The relevant domestic provisions include the Penal Code’s offence of disobeying a police order issued to maintain public order or security (punishable by fine or up to three months’ imprisonment) and the court’s power to waive punishment for minor or excusable acts. The Criminal Records Act requires certain convictions to be recorded, though no penalty was imposed here.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 10 complaint: that arrest, detention and a finding of guilt, even without punishment, interfered with a journalist’s ability to report on a matter of public interest (a large, violent demonstration) and that the interference was neither necessary nor proportionate. Two other photographers in the sealed area had left without incident. The applicant appealed, arguing that the conviction and arrest violated the Finnish Constitution and Article 10 because he had not participated in the disorder and the District Court had failed to demonstrate necessity. **CASE OF VELLA v. MALTA (Application no. 69122/10, ECtHR, 11 February 2014)**

Maltese national Francis Vella (born 1939) alleged that civil Court of Appeal judgments and their declarations violated his Article 6 § 2 right to be presumed innocent after criminal acquittals on most charges.

In criminal proceedings, Vella was charged with thefts (burglaries 1976–1983) and/or receiving stolen goods. On 26 October 1992 the Court of Magistrates found him guilty of receiving stolen goods (acquitting him of the thefts themselves, as he had “nothing to do with” them) and imposed five years’ imprisonment. It noted his detailed (later denied) police admissions of buying items known to be stolen due to his antique fascination; victims’ identifications; and possession of melting tools plus silver bullion. On 30 October 2001 the Criminal Court of Appeal affirmed the theft acquittals (no evidence) but reversed most receiving convictions. It held he was a collector/dealer who purchased without checking origins and was aware some items were stolen (some hidden), but police negligence in losing documents/receipts meant he should not suffer prejudice. Receiving was proved only for antiquarian items from three venues (A., B., C.; two burglaries). Sentence reduced to two years, suspended.

While criminal proceedings were pending, alleged owners of items seized from Vella (claimed theft victims) brought civil claims for return or damages. Appeals followed the 2001 criminal judgment.

In *Maurice Meli Bugeja et v. Francis Vella* (items from 1983 burglary at venue P.; all charges later acquitted), the Civil Court (26 January 2001) found claimants owners (except five items claimed by others) but declined premature return. It cited a police officer’s evidence that Vella admitted some seized items “had not been purchased honestly,” inferred improper acquisition, noted Vella’s inability to evidence origins or trade details versus identifications, and preferred claimants’ version given multiple identifications. The Court of Appeal (16 April 2004) upheld this, observing Vella’s vague origin accounts (deceased individuals, lost receipts), hesitation-free purchases of “dubious or suspicious, if not illicit” items, the officer’s testimony of admissions (including dishonest sofa purchase and incomplete receipts), and insufficient proof of Vella’s ownership.

In *Ian Ellis et v. Francis Vella* (items from 1983 burglary at venue BC; charges acquitted), the Civil Court (29 January 2001) found for claimants (premature return). It preferred their corroborated identifications/photos over Vella’s purchase claims (including a 1983 receipt), citing the officer’s evidence of admissions that items “had not been purchased honestly.” The Court of Appeal (16 April 2004) upheld, noting Vella’s unreliable explanations, the officer’s testimony of buying items of “dubious origins,” inconsistent/untruthful testimony, inability to produce seized receipts or living witnesses, versus claimants’ pre-theft photos.

In *Baroness Maria Testaferrata Bonici et v. Francis Vella* (items from venue B., including alleged melted silver; theft acquitted but receiving conviction stood), the Civil Court (22 June 2001) found claimants owners, ordered return, and held Vella liable for damages in bad faith (MTL 64,870 / ~EUR 151,100). It admitted criminal-investigation statements (Vella rarely acquired lawfully; sellers told him items were stolen; “I go blind” for antiques), found him the “very image of a receiver of stolen goods,” and inferred melted-down stolen silver from home-made bullion and tools (no credible explanation). The Court of Appeal (9 November 2004) upheld (no return of missing items), confirming admissibility of unsigned statements witnessed by the officer, proper evidence assessment, and Vella’s responsibility for melting damage.

Vella’s 2008 constitutional proceedings claimed the civil judgments (plus one pending) violated the presumption of innocence. The Civil Court (constitutional jurisdiction, 29 September 2009) rejected this: civil cases sought ownership/return/compensation, not criminal guilt; different burdens applied; he was no longer accused; conclusions properly assessed evidence without violating innocence. The Constitutional Court (25 May 2010) upheld, stressing separate criminal (State punishment, higher proof, accused-favouring rules) and civil (individual restitution, balance of probabilities) proceedings. Acquittal did not confer ownership; civil findings concerned only title, requiring return regardless of acquisition manner.

Domestic law treats criminal and civil actions independently (different proof standards); a party’s declaration against interest is admissible evidence.

The case of Vella v. Malta (Application no. 69122/10) concerns Francis Vella’s complaint that Maltese Court of Appeal civil judgments (and declarations therein) violated his Article 6 § 2 right to be presumed innocent after his partial criminal acquittal.

Vella faced charges of theft (burglaries 1976–1983) and receiving stolen goods. On 26 October 1992 the Court of Magistrates convicted him of receiving stolen goods (acquitting him of thefts) and imposed five years’ imprisonment. It cited victims’ identifications of items in his possession, his police admissions of knowingly buying stolen antiques due to his fascination with them, his possession of metal-melting tools and silver bullion, and the organised nature of the thefts.

Vella appealed, complaining that police had lost documents proving the items’ origins. On 30 October 2001 the Criminal Court of Appeal affirmed his innocence of theft (no evidence existed) and reversed most receiving convictions. It described him as an antiques collector who bought items without checking origins, attributed missing proof to police negligence, and declined to infer guilt from the tools (normal for coin collecting). It convicted him only of receiving items stolen from three venues (A, B and C) in two burglaries, reducing the sentence to a two-year suspended term.

Alleged owners then brought civil actions for return of the seized items or damages. These were decided after the criminal appeal.

In Maurice Meli Bugeja et v. Vella (items from venue P, of which Vella had been acquitted), the Civil Court (26 January 2001) declared the claimants owners. It relied on a police officer’s testimony that Vella had admitted some items “had not been purchased honestly,” Vella’s inability to prove origins, and multiple identifications by third parties. The Court of Appeal (16 April 2004) upheld the decision, noting Vella’s vague accounts, the same admissions, and evidence of purchases of dubious origin.

In Ian Ellis et v. Vella (items from venue BC, likewise acquitted), the Civil Court (29 January 2001) favoured the claimants on the basis of photographs, witnesses and the officer’s testimony of admissions of dishonest purchases. The Court of Appeal (16 April 2004) confirmed this, finding Vella’s testimony inconsistent and uncorroborated (no receipts; named sellers deceased) while the claimants produced pre-theft photographs.

In Baroness Maria Testaferrata Bonici et v. Vella (items from venue B, of which Vella had been convicted of receiving), the Civil Court (22 June 2001) found the claimants owners, ordered return of remaining items and awarded damages (MTL 64,870) for bad-faith possession and melting of silver objects. It admitted Vella’s unsigned investigation statements (Article 632(1) of the Code of Organisation and Civil Procedure) and concluded he “rarely acquired items lawfully,” knew their stolen origins and was “the very image of a receiver of stolen goods.” The Court of Appeal (9 November 2004) upheld the findings (except return of items no longer in Vella’s possession), confirming the statements’ admissibility and Vella’s liability for melting damage.

Vella instituted constitutional proceedings on 22 January 2008, alleging the civil judgments (and one still pending) violated the presumption of innocence. The Civil Court in its constitutional jurisdiction (29 September 2009) rejected the claim: the civil actions sought only restitution or compensation, not a criminal finding; they applied the civil standard of proof (balance of probabilities) rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt; and they determined ownership without convicting him of any crime. The Constitutional Court (25 May 2010) dismissed his appeal, stressing the independence of criminal and civil proceedings and that an acquittal does not confer ownership of items found in a defendant’s possession.

Maltese law treats criminal and civil actions as independent, with distinct burdens of proof; Article 632(1) admits a party’s declarations against interest as evidence.

These facts centre on the civil courts’ use of criminal-investigation statements and language implying criminal-like conclusions despite the acquittals.

**CASE OF VELLA v. MALTA (Application no. 69122/10), ECtHR (Fourth Section), Judgment of 11 February 2014 (final 7 July 2014)**

The applicant, Francis Vella (born 1939), a Maltese antique collector and dealer, alleged that civil Court of Appeal judgments violated his Article 6 § 2 right to be presumed innocent. He had faced criminal charges of theft (burglaries 1976–1983) and/or receiving stolen goods.

In 1992, the Court of Magistrates convicted him of receiving stolen goods (acquitting him of theft) and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It relied on his detailed police statements admitting purchases of items he knew were stolen due to his interest in antiques, victim identifications of seized items, and possession of metal-melting tools and silver bullion.

On appeal, the Criminal Court of Appeal (30 October 2001) affirmed his innocence on all theft charges (no evidence) and reversed convictions for most receiving-stolen-goods charges. It noted police loss of the applicant’s documents/receipts, that tools were consistent with coin collecting, and that he should not be prejudiced by inability to prove origins. It convicted him only of receiving antiquarian items from three specific venues (A, B, and C; two burglaries) and reduced the sentence to a two-year suspended term. He thus stood acquitted of theft and of receiving goods from other venues.

Meanwhile, alleged owners of seized items brought civil actions seeking return of property or damages. These proceeded independently (different burdens of proof: balance of probabilities versus beyond reasonable doubt) and were decided after the criminal acquittals on most charges.

In *Maurice Meli Bugeja et v. Vella* (items from a 1983 burglary at venue P, charges of which he was acquitted), the Civil Court (2001) and Court of Appeal (16 April 2004) found the claimants were owners. They cited police testimony that the applicant admitted items “had not been purchased honestly,” his vague explanations, inability to produce receipts (seized by police), and practice of buying items of “dubious or suspicious, if not illicit, origins.” They rejected his ownership claim despite his collector status.

In *Ian Ellis et v. Vella* (items from venue BC, also acquitted charges), similar 2001/2004 judgments favored the claimants. The Court of Appeal noted inconsistent testimony, lack of receipts, police evidence of purchases with “dubious origins,” and claimants’ photographs/witnesses. It found the applicant’s explanations unreliable.

In *Baroness Maria Testaferrata Bonici et v. Vella* (items from venue B, including alleged melted silver; he had been convicted of receiving some), the Civil Court (2001) and Court of Appeal (9 November 2004) held the claimants were owners, found the applicant possessed items in bad faith, and awarded damages (~EUR 151,100) for melted items. It described him as the “very image of a receiver of stolen goods (*ricettatur*),” relied on unsigned investigation statements (admissible under domestic law), and inferred melting to hide identity despite no proof he stole the goods.

The applicant’s 2008 constitutional challenge (that the civil judgments repeated criminal findings and used incriminating language despite acquittals) was rejected in 2009–2010. Domestic courts held the proceedings distinct: civil actions concerned ownership/restitution (not criminal guilt), with a lower burden of proof, and did not find him guilty of crime.

The ECtHR application focused on whether the civil courts’ language and reasoning (imputing knowledge of illicit origins, bad faith, and receiver-like conduct even for acquitted items) undermined the criminal acquittals and presumption of innocence.
001-140020:
The applicant, an Iranian national born in 1962, applied for asylum in Sweden on 16 November 2009. He claimed that expulsion to Iran would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention due to a real risk of persecution, death or ill-treatment arising from his political activities against the Iranian regime and his conversion from Islam to Christianity.

He stated that he had worked with university-linked opponents of the regime, primarily creating and publishing web pages. He was arrested in April 2007, released after 24 hours and hospitalised. Before the June 2009 presidential elections he supported the Green Movement (backing Mousavi) by disseminating its message online. He was arrested the day before the elections and detained overnight at a polling station. After the elections he took part in demonstrations and was arrested again in September 2009, imprisoned for 20 days, then brought before the Revolutionary Court in October 2009. He was released on condition that he cooperate by spying on friends, providing his business premises as a guarantee and undertaking not to demonstrate. Upon release he discovered that the premises had been searched, politically sensitive material removed and his passport taken. Summoned to appear at Evin prison on 2 November 2009, he fled Iran with a smuggler’s help. He converted to Christianity after arriving in Sweden.

The Migration Board rejected the claim on 29 April 2010. It accepted that the applicant had rendered his identity and nationality probable but found his political activities too limited to attract genuine official interest. It noted inconsistencies (varying accounts of arrests; inability to name the park of his release) and observed that he had continued his web work after the 2007 questioning even though the authorities allegedly knew of it. On conversion, the Board recorded that he had initially declined to rely on it as an asylum ground (calling it a private matter) and had produced no baptism certificate; it therefore found no plausible risk.

On appeal the applicant submitted a baptism certificate and a summons. He explained that he had initially withheld the conversion so as not to trivialise his faith, added that a computer containing critical material had been seized, and stated that his family had not been targeted. The Migration Court dismissed the appeal on 9 March 2011. It accepted that earlier inconsistencies had been clarified but held the political account vague and lacking in detail. The summons, even if authentic, was a mere citation without stated reason and could not by itself establish a protection need. The absence of further summonses or family targeting indicated that the authorities had no special interest in him; he had exaggerated the significance of his activities.

Leave to appeal was refused on 8 June 2011. In September 2011 the applicant sought a stay and re-examination, arguing that apostasy is punishable by death. Both the Migration Board (13 September 2011) and the Migration Court (6 October 2011) rejected the request: the conversion had already been known and could not constitute a “new circumstance.” Leave to appeal was again refused.

The applicant lodged his application with the Court on 12 July 2011 and requested an interim measure. He emphasised both his pre- and post-election political activism and, more particularly, his conversion (which he now dated a couple of years earlier). He produced a pastor’s certificate confirming that he had been met in summer 2010, had converted, had been a congregation member since February 2011, and that services were broadcast online. On 25 October 2011 the Court applied Rule 39, indicating that the applicant should not be expelled pending the proceedings.

Swedish law (Aliens Act, Chapters 4, 5 and 12) grants residence permits to refugees or persons otherwise in need of protection and prohibits expulsion where there are reasonable grounds to believe the person faces capital punishment, torture or inhuman treatment. New circumstances may justify a stay or re-examination only if they could not have been invoked earlier.

The case of F.G. v. Sweden (Application no. 43611/11) involves an Iranian national born in 1962 who applied for asylum in Sweden on 16 November 2009, alleging that expulsion to Iran would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention due to risks of death, persecution or ill-treatment arising from his political opposition activities and subsequent conversion from Islam to Christianity.

F.G. claimed he had collaborated with university-linked regime opponents in Iran by creating and publishing critical web pages. He was arrested in April 2007, detained for 24 hours and hospitalised for high blood pressure. Ahead of the 12 June 2009 presidential elections he supported the Green Movement and candidate Mousavi by disseminating messages online. He and associates were arrested the day before the poll and held overnight at a polling station. After the elections he joined demonstrations and was re-arrested in September 2009, spending 20 days in prison. In October 2009 the Revolutionary Court released him on condition that he spy on friends and refrain from further protests, using his business premises as security. Upon release he discovered the premises had been searched, politically sensitive material noticed and his passport and documents seized. A summons required him to appear at Evin prison on 2 November 2009; he fled Iran with a smuggler’s help. After arriving in Sweden he converted to Christianity. He produced the summons and, later, a baptism certificate dated 13 April 2011 confirming membership of a congregation whose services were broadcast on the internet.

The Migration Board rejected the claim on 29 April 2010. While accepting his Iranian nationality as probable, it found his political activities too limited to generate a real risk: he had continued web-page work even after the 2007 arrest, his account of arrests contained inconsistencies (including inability to name the park of release), and mere participation in demonstrations or Green Movement affiliation was insufficient. Conversion was not invoked as an asylum ground initially and lacked contemporaneous documentary proof, rendering any religious-risk claim implausible.

On appeal F.G. submitted the baptism certificate, explained that he had initially treated faith as a private matter to avoid trivialising it, and added that a computer containing critical e-mails and caricatures had been seized. The Migration Court dismissed the appeal on 9 March 2011, accepting the narrative in outline but finding the activities vague, lacking detail and exaggerated; the summons alone (even if genuine) did not prove official interest, especially as no further summons had been issued and his family had not been targeted. Conversion had already been disclosed and therefore could not constitute a new circumstance.

Subsequent requests for reconsideration on the ground that apostasy is punishable by death were rejected by the Board and courts (September–November 2011) because the conversion had been known throughout the earlier proceedings and F.G. had chosen not to rely on it.

F.G. lodged his application with the Court on 12 July 2011 and obtained a Rule 39 indication staying expulsion. Swedish aliens legislation (Chapters 4, 5 and 12 of the Aliens Act) grants residence to refugees fearing persecution on political or religious grounds or to persons at risk of capital punishment, torture or inhuman treatment, and permits re-examination only where genuinely new circumstances arise that could not previously have been invoked. The Chamber judgment of 16 January 2014 (later referred to the Grand Chamber) thus turned on whether the Swedish authorities’ assessment of the political and religious risks was Convention-compliant.

The applicant, an Iranian national born in 1962, sought asylum in Sweden on 16 November 2009. He claimed to have collaborated with university-linked opponents of the Iranian regime by creating and publishing critical web pages. He was arrested in April 2007, held for 24 hours and later hospitalised. Ahead of the June 2009 presidential elections he supported the Green Movement and Mousavi via the internet; he was detained overnight at a polling station the day before the vote. After the elections he joined demonstrations, was arrested again in September 2009 and imprisoned for 20 days. In October 2009 the Revolutionary Court released him on condition that he spy on associates and refrain from further protests; he pledged his business premises as security. Those premises were subsequently searched, politically sensitive material and his passport were seized, and he received a summons to appear at Evin prison on 2 November 2009. He fled Iran with a smuggler’s assistance. After arriving in Sweden he converted from Islam to Christianity.

The Migration Board rejected his claim on 29 April 2010. It accepted his Iranian nationality as probable but found his political activities limited and his account inconsistent (he had altered the number of arrests and could not identify the park where he was released). It doubted that the authorities had any special interest in him, noting that he had continued his web-page work after 2007. His conversion was not regarded as a plausible risk factor: he had initially declined to invoke it, calling it a private matter, and had produced no baptism certificate.

On appeal the applicant supplied a baptism certificate, explained that he had not wished to trivialise his faith, and added that a computer containing regime-critical material had been confiscated. The Migration Court dismissed the appeal on 9 March 2011. It accepted that earlier inconsistencies had been clarified but held that the summons, even if genuine, was insufficient on its own. His political activities remained vague, he had not been re-summoned after November 2009 and his family had not been targeted. The court concluded he had exaggerated both his activities and the authorities’ interest in him. Conversion was not advanced as a ground of asylum, though the applicant asserted it would create difficulties on return.

Leave to appeal was refused on 8 June 2011. In September 2011 the applicant sought a stay and reconsideration, arguing that apostasy is a capital offence in Iran. Both the Migration Board and the Migration Court rejected the request, holding that conversion was not a “new circumstance” because it had already been known (though not relied upon) in the earlier proceedings. Further leave was refused in November 2011.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 12 July 2011, invoking Articles 2 and 3. He stressed both his pre-election political work and, more prominently, his conversion, which he said had occurred before any Swedish decision. He produced a pastor’s certificate dated 13 April 2011 confirming that he had been met in summer 2010, had converted, had been a church member since February 2011, and that services were broadcast on the internet. The Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39, preventing expulsion pending the proceedings.

Swedish law (Aliens Act, as amended 2010) entitles refugees and persons otherwise in need of protection to residence permits and prohibits expulsion where there are reasonable grounds to fear the death penalty, torture or persecution. New circumstances that create lasting impediments to enforcement may justify a stay or re-examination, but the domestic authorities found no such circumstances here.
001-140402:
The case concerns the extraordinary quashing of a final administrative restitution order in favour of the applicant, Mr Aleksandar Vikentijevik, which he alleged violated his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

In 1945 the applicant’s grandfather (V.D.M.) and three others (A.J., T.K. and L.L.), as members of the executive board of company T., were convicted of wartime collaboration. A 1946 confiscation order transferred the company’s entire property to the State, comprising buildings totalling 3,496 m², 60,549 m² of land and specified movables. The four men were described as “convicted shareholders” in actual possession of the company.

After company restructuring in 1995, a 1996 contract transferred certain buildings (1,240 m², excluding workers’ apartments) and preference shares worth DEM 2,158,831 to the State. In December 1999 a first-instance court quashed the 1945 confiscation insofar as it concerned V.D.M.; the judgment became final in January 2000. In July 2000 the same court declared the applicant heir to V.D.M.’s restitution rights over the confiscated property.

On 14 August 2000 the applicant filed a restitution claim. An on-site inspection on 12 September 2000 recorded that only some original buildings remained and that much larger structures (34,617 m²) now stood on the land. On 15 September 2000 the Restitution Commission granted the claim in full: it restored the 1996-contract buildings plus workers’ apartments (694 m²) and the entire 60,549 m² of land, transferred the preference shares as compensation for movables, and awarded additional State shares (circa EUR 51,400) for other objects. The file had been sent to the Solicitor General, who declined to comment, stating he was under no statutory duty to do so. No appeal was lodged and the order became final on 13 October 2000. Title to the shares and immovable property was thereafter registered in the applicant’s name (62,755 m²).

Enforcement difficulties subsequently arose. In November 2003 an expert commission found the land could not be physically restored because it now served existing buildings. After further requests for enforcement, a Coordinating Commission in 2004 noted “irregularities” but the Government Appeal Commission declined supervisory review.

On 1 December 2004 the Solicitor General applied under section 267 § 1 (3) and (5) of the 1986 Administrative Proceedings Act to have the 2000 order declared null and void. He argued that the applicant had received the entire company property although it had been jointly owned by four persons, that the restored buildings did not correspond to those confiscated, that the land had been extensively developed, and that the shares exceeded V.D.M.’s putative share. On 26 April 2006 the Commission granted the application, quashed the order and remitted the case. It held that the applicant was entitled only to a notional one-quarter share, that the land was developed construction land incapable of restitution under the Restitution Act, and that the entire share package had been wrongly awarded to him alone, rendering the order legally unenforceable.

The applicant challenged the quashing before the Supreme Court, arguing that the order had already been executed, that the Solicitor General had failed to use the ordinary appeal, that mere factual errors could not justify the extraordinary remedy, and that the five-year delay violated legal certainty. On 16 March 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the claim, confirming that the original order violated imperative provisions of the Restitution Act (sections 13, 21, 28, 33 and 36) and was therefore legally impossible to enforce. The public prosecutor declined to seek a legality review.

Resumed restitution proceedings were later suspended pending a civil determination of V.D.M.’s exact share in the company; those civil proceedings remain pending. The applicant maintained that the belated annulment of a final, executed administrative decision awarding him specific property and shares deprived him of a legitimate expectation and violated the principle of legal certainty.

The case of Vikentijevik v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 50179/07) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s property rights arising from the extraordinary quashing of a final restitution order issued in his favour.

In 1945 the applicant’s late grandfather, V.D.M., and three other individuals were convicted of wartime offences and the immovable and movable property of company T. was confiscated by court order in 1946. The confiscated assets included buildings totalling 3,496 sq. m and 60,549 sq. m of land. In 1996, as part of company restructuring, certain buildings and preference shares were transferred to the State. In 1999–2000 the confiscation was overturned with respect to V.D.M. and the applicant was declared his heir entitled to claim restitution of the company’s property.

On 14 August 2000 the applicant lodged a restitution claim. Following an on-site inspection, the Restitution Commission of the Ministry of Finance issued an order on 15 September 2000 restoring to him the buildings listed in the 1996 contract, residential apartments and adjacent structures, the entire 60,549 sq. m of land, the preference shares as compensation for movable property, and additional State-owned shares. The order was served on the Solicitor General, who submitted no comments and lodged no appeal. It became final on 13 October 2000 and was subsequently rectified in a minor respect. Title to the shares and buildings was transferred to the applicant, he was registered as owner of 62,755 sq. m of land, and he was entered in the company’s shareholder records.

Enforcement difficulties later arose because the land supported existing buildings. In 2003 an inspection confirmed that the original confiscated structures no longer existed and that far larger modern buildings (approximately 34,617 sq. m) had been constructed. In December 2004 the Solicitor General applied under section 267 of the Administrative Proceedings Act for the restitution order and the rectifying decision to be declared null and void. He argued that the applicant had received the entire company property although it had been jointly owned by four persons, that the restored buildings did not correspond to those confiscated, that the land had been extensively developed, and that the shares awarded exceeded the applicant’s putative share.

On 26 April 2006 the Government Appeal Commission granted the request, quashed both decisions and remitted the case. It held that the applicant, as heir of only one of four former owners, was entitled at most to a one-quarter share; that the confiscated buildings no longer existed and had been replaced by far larger constructions; that the developed land could not be restored under the Restitution Act; and that the entire package of preference shares had been wrongly transferred to him alone. The Commission characterised the Solicitor General’s earlier failure to appeal as a “manifest omission.”

The applicant challenged the quashing before the Supreme Court, arguing that the original order had already been enforced, that the extraordinary remedy had been misused to correct alleged factual errors after more than five years, and that legal certainty had been violated. On 16 March 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the restitution order was legally unenforceable because it contravened several imperative provisions of the Restitution Act (concerning identification of entitled persons, valuation of improved property, restoration of developed land, and allocation of reserved shares). The public prosecutor declined to seek further review.

In the resumed restitution proceedings an expert inspection in 2008 found that part of the land was now designated for new residential construction. In December 2010 the Restitution Commission suspended the case and directed the applicant to bring civil proceedings to determine V.D.M.’s precise share in the company, noting that other claimants had also asserted inheritance rights over the same property. Those civil proceedings remain pending.

The applicant complained that the belated extraordinary annulment of a final and partially executed restitution order arbitrarily deprived him of property in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Vikentijevik v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 50179/07) concerns the applicant’s complaint that the extraordinary quashing of a final restitution order in his favour violated his property rights.

In 1945 the applicant’s grandfather, V.D.M., together with three other individuals, was convicted of wartime offences and the property of company T. (of which they were treated as convicted shareholders) was confiscated. The 1946 confiscation order covered buildings totalling 3,496 m² and 60,549 m² of land, together with movable assets. In December 1999 the 1945 conviction was overturned in so far as it related to confiscation; that judgment became final in January 2000. In July 2000 the applicant was declared the heir entitled to claim restitution of his grandfather’s property.

In August 2000 the applicant lodged a restitution claim. After an on-site inspection, the Restitution Commission of the Ministry of Finance, by decision of 15 September 2000, restored to him specified buildings (including those transferred to the State under a 1996 privatisation contract), residential apartments and adjacent structures (694 m²), the entire 60,549 m² of land, preference shares previously reserved for the State as compensation for movables, and additional State-owned shares as compensation for remaining objects. The Solicitor General was notified of the claim but declined to comment; no appeal was lodged and the order became final on 13 October 2000. Title to the buildings, land and shares was subsequently transferred and registered in the applicant’s name.

In 2004, following complaints by residents of the apartments, the Solicitor General sought to have the 2000 order and a subsequent rectifying decision declared null and void under section 267 of the Administrative Proceedings Act. He argued that the applicant had been awarded the entire company property although it had been jointly owned, that the restored buildings differed in size and character from those confiscated (the site now contained modern structures of some 34,000 m²), that the land was developed construction land that could not be returned, and that the applicant had received the whole package of preference shares rather than a proportionate share.

On 26 April 2006 the Government Appeal Commission granted the request, quashed both decisions and remitted the matter. It held that the applicant, as heir of only one of four former owners, was entitled at most to a notional one-quarter share; that the original buildings no longer existed; that the developed land could not be restored under the Restitution Act; and that the order was therefore legally unenforceable.

The applicant challenged the quashing before the Supreme Court, arguing that the order had already been executed, that the Solicitor General had failed to use the ordinary appeal, that alleged factual errors were not a proper ground for the extraordinary remedy, and that the five-year delay violated legal certainty. On 16 March 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the claim, confirming that the original order had violated mandatory provisions of the Restitution Act (wrongful award of the entire property, restoration of developed land, and transfer of the full share package) and was therefore legally incapable of enforcement.

Resumed restitution proceedings were later suspended so that the applicant could bring a civil action to establish his grandfather’s precise share in the company; those proceedings remain pending. The quashing of the final and partially executed restitution order forms the basis of the applicant’s complaint of a violation of his proprietary rights.
001-141369:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (the Mormon Church), a UK-registered religious organisation with around 180,000 members in the UK and Ireland, brought this application to the European Court of Human Rights. It alleged that the UK’s refusal to grant full exemption from business rates to its Preston temple violated Article 9 of the Convention (freedom of thought, conscience and religion), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), both taken alone and with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy).

The Church maintains local chapels (wards) open to all, plus two UK temples (London and Preston) regarded as the holiest places on earth. Only “worthy” members holding a current “recommend”—issued after a private interview confirming moral conduct, tithing, loyalty and other standards—may enter. The Preston temple hosts services for an average of 950 worshippers weekly. Under the Local Government Finance Act 1988, buildings used wholly or mainly for charitable purposes receive 80% rates relief, while places of “public religious worship” (and associated halls) are fully exempt. The valuation officer treated the temple as charitable (so 20% rates remained payable) but denied the full exemption because it was closed to the general public. The on-site stake centre (chapel) received the exemption; other buildings did not. In 1999/2000 the Church paid £117,360 in rates for the Preston site.

The Church applied in 2001 to have the temple removed from the rating list. The Lancashire Valuation Tribunal granted the exemption in 2004, but the Lands Tribunal reversed that decision in 2005. The Court of Appeal dismissed the further appeal in 2006. Convention arguments were first raised (with permission) before the House of Lords, which unanimously dismissed the appeal in 2008, relying on its 1964 Henning precedent. That case held that “public religious worship” requires premises open to the general public, reflecting a long-standing legislative policy of exempting only those religious activities that confer a public benefit.

Four Law Lords held that the 20% rates liability did not even fall within the ambit of Article 9: Mormons remained free to worship, the rule applied equally to all closed religious buildings, and any financial disadvantage was too remote from the right to manifest religion. Even if it constituted indirect discrimination, it was justified by the State’s wide margin of appreciation in defining public-benefit tax exemptions; public access itself constituted such a benefit. Lord Hope added that the case more readily engaged Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but the second paragraph of that provision preserved the State’s power to levy taxes, and Parliament’s choice of exemption criteria lay within its discretion. Lord Scott, concurring, considered the measure did fall within Article 9’s ambit and involved discrimination between open and closed places of worship. He nevertheless found it justified: while religion can benefit individuals and society, it can also be divisive; secrecy fosters suspicion, whereas openness dispels prejudice. A general policy favouring publicly accessible worship therefore pursued a legitimate aim and remained within the State’s margin.

The Church had not raised Convention points before the lower tribunals. The application to Strasbourg followed, with the Court adjourning proceedings pending its judgment in Eweida. The core dispute thus centres on whether requiring public access as a condition of full rates exemption, applied to a closed Mormon temple, unlawfully interfered with religious manifestation or property rights or constituted unjustified discrimination.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (applicant), a UK-registered religious organisation with ~180,000 members in the UK/Ireland (part of 12 million worldwide), alleged that denial of full business-rates exemption for its Preston temple violated Article 9 ECHR (manifestation of religion), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property), both alone and with Article 14 (discrimination), plus Article 13 (effective remedy). Temples are the Church’s holiest sites, used for sacred “ordinances.” Access is restricted to members holding a current “recommend,” issued after private interview confirming worthiness (moral conduct, full tithing of ~10% income, lifestyle, loyalty, no apostate ties). This is a core tenet: only the worthy may enter.

Under the Local Government Finance Act 1988, occupied premises are liable for non-domestic rates. Charitable use attracts 80% relief; “places of public religious worship” (plus associated halls) are wholly exempt. The Preston temple received only the 80% charitable relief (thus 20% liability). The on-site stake centre/chapel (open congregational services, ~950 weekly attendees) was fully exempt as public worship; ancillary buildings paid full rates. For 1999/2000 the Church paid £117,360 across the site.

In 2001 the Church sought full exemption for the temple. The Valuation Tribunal granted it (2004), but the Lands Tribunal reversed (2005). The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal (2006). The House of Lords unanimously dismissed the further appeal (Gallagher [2008] UKHL 56), following its 1964 Henning precedent on an earlier Mormon temple. “Public religious worship” requires the premises to be open to the general public, not merely members. This traces to the 1833 Act extending the historic Anglican open-door exemption to other denominations’ similar public worship; closed-door worship does not confer the intended public benefit.

Convention arguments (raised only at the Lords with permission) were rejected by a 4-1 majority. The 20% liability did not fall within Article 9’s ambit: it neither prevented manifestation of Mormon faith nor targeted Mormons; it merely withheld a tax advantage because the religion’s restricted access failed the public-benefit test applied equally to all faiths. Even assuming indirect discrimination, it was justified. Parliament enjoys a wide margin in defining sufficient public benefit for tax exemption; requiring public access to worship services was a legitimate choice. Lord Hope added that Article 1 Protocol 1 was engaged but the tax-reservation clause preserved the State’s power, and the exemption’s scope lay within its discretion.

Lord Scott (concurring in result) found the measure within Article 9’s ambit for Article 14 purposes, as taxing a place of worship could in principle engage religious freedom, creating a difference in treatment (open vs closed worship) requiring justification. He held it justified: states may view religion as beneficial yet potentially divisive in diverse societies; openness dispels suspicion and prejudice, while secrecy fosters them. Withholding relief from closed-door worship was therefore a permissible general policy.

The application (lodged 2009) was communicated in 2011 and adjourned pending Eweida. These facts go to whether the tax treatment constituted an interference with religious manifestation or property, whether it was discriminatory on religious grounds, and whether any difference was justified by the public-access requirement.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (the applicant), a UK-registered religious organisation with some 180,000 members in the UK and Ireland, challenged the denial of full business-rates exemption for its Preston temple. The temple is regarded as one of the holiest sites, accessible solely to “worthy” members holding a current recommend issued after a private interview confirming moral conduct, tithing, family duties and loyalty. Congregational services there attract about 950 worshippers weekly. Adjacent public chapels and a stake centre on the same site were treated as places of public religious worship.

Under the Local Government Finance Act 1988 a valuation officer compiles a non-domestic rating list. Charitable use attracts 80 % relief; a place of “public religious worship” is wholly exempt. The temple received only the 80 % charitable relief and remained liable for 20 % rates (together with other non-exempt buildings the site paid £117,360 in 1999/2000). In 2001 the Church applied to have the temple removed from the list. The Lancashire Valuation Tribunal granted exemption in 2004, but the Lands Tribunal reversed that decision in 2005. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in 2006. Convention arguments were first advanced, with leave, before the House of Lords, which in 2008 unanimously dismissed the further appeal (Gallagher v Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints).

The Lords relied on the 1964 Henning precedent: “public religious worship” requires openness to the general public, an interpretation rooted in the historic exemption of Anglican churches with open doors and later extended to comparable denominations. Closed worship was held not to confer the public spiritual benefit that justified fiscal privilege. Four Law Lords found the 20 % liability outside the ambit of Article 9, because it neither prevented Mormons from practising their faith nor targeted them specifically; it merely withheld a tax advantage from those whose beliefs precluded public access. Any indirect discrimination was justified by Parliament’s wide margin in defining public benefit. Lord Hope added that Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 expressly preserves the State’s power to levy taxes. Lord Scott, concurring in the result, considered the measure within Article 9’s ambit (taxation of a place of worship) and therefore requiring Article 14 justification, but held the “open-doors” policy justified: it promotes social cohesion and dispels suspicion that secrecy in religion can foster.

The applicant alleged that the differential treatment violated Article 9 (alone and with Article 14) by interfering with manifestation of a religion whose ordinances demand exclusivity, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (alone and with Article 14) by imposing an unjustified fiscal burden. It further claimed that domestic courts afforded no effective remedy (Article 13). The facts therefore centre on the statutory requirement of public access, the temple’s restricted entry as an article of Mormon faith, the resulting 20 % rates liability, and the House of Lords’ conclusions that the measure neither fell within the relevant Convention rights nor lacked objective and reasonable justification.

The case of Karaman v. Germany (Application no. 17103/10) concerns a Turkish national, Zekeriya Karaman (born 1952, resident in Istanbul), who founded the Turkish television station Kanal 7 and served as director of its operating company. Kanal 7 programming, including content from a related German station, featured appeals by the non-profit associations Deniz Feneri Yardimlasma Dernegi (Turkey) and Deniz Feneri Dernegi e.V. (Germany). These associations, linked to Karaman and associates through shared personnel and companies (including Euro 7 Fernseh- und Marketing GmbH, of which Karaman was a shareholder and sometimes managing director or authorised signatory), solicited donations via television for purported charitable aid projects, emphasising exclusive use for social purposes.

In 2006, Frankfurt am Main prosecutors opened investigations into Karaman and several co-suspects, including G. (a fellow shareholder and former chairman of the German association), on suspicion of aggravated fraud. The allegation was that the majority of donated funds had been diverted to commercial activities and personal benefit rather than charity. In March 2008, proceedings against Karaman were formally separated from those against the co-suspects. Parallel fraud investigations began in Turkey later that year.

On 17 September 2008, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court’s Extended Economic Crimes Chamber convicted co-suspects G. and T. of aggravated fraud as members of a joint criminal enterprise led from Turkey, and E. of aiding and abetting. Sentences ranged from suspended terms to over five years’ imprisonment. The 32-page written judgment (delivered by early November 2008) repeatedly named Karaman in full, describing him as a separately prosecuted leader who coordinated the scheme, issued instructions to G., received over €4.5 million in diverted funds, and held a “pre-eminent role” as director of the Turkish company. It stated that G. acted “in coordination with and upon the instructions of” Karaman; that unofficial accounts were kept on Karaman’s orders; that Karaman decided on the use of funds; and that G. was merely an “executing organ” below Karaman and other “persons behind the scenes in Turkey.” The court rejected G.’s claim of sole responsibility, relying in part on co-accused testimony placing Karaman at the hierarchy’s apex. These findings were based on plea-bargain confessions and other trial evidence.

Media reports immediately quoted the presiding judge and prosecutors describing Karaman as the “main perpetrator and leader of the whole organisation,” with “strings pulled at the level of Kanal 7” and “main persons in charge located in Turkey.” The judgment was published on the court’s website on 25 November 2008 (names anonymised), accompanied by a disclaimer that it bound only the convicted persons and that references to others (including the separately prosecuted) were non-binding, with the presumption of innocence remaining intact. The judgment itself contained no such caveat. It became final on 13 November 2008.

Karaman lodged a constitutional complaint in December 2008, arguing that the judgment’s references to his role violated the presumption of innocence (a component of the fair-trial right under German constitutional law, interpreted in light of the Convention). The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as inadmissible on 3 September 2009. It held that the presumption of innocence does not shield a person from all factual mentions in third-party proceedings; such statements have no binding effect on later proceedings against the applicant and do not constitute a finding of guilt or a penalty against him. Complex cases inevitably involve overlapping facts, and authorities remain free to assess suspicion.

Charges were subsequently brought against Karaman in Germany (August 2009) and Turkey (2012). The German main hearing opened in 2013; both sets of proceedings remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg application. A 2009 request for Turkish legal assistance to examine Karaman went unanswered in the record.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation of Article 6 § 2: judicial statements in a co-suspects’ judgment that portrayed Karaman as a principal offender before any determination of his own guilt.

The applicant, Zekeriya Karaman, a Turkish national and founder of the Turkish television station Kanal 7 (with related German broadcasting companies in which he held roles as shareholder, managing director or authorised signatory), was linked to the German non-profit association Deniz Feneri. From 1998/1999, the association used a dedicated TV slot to solicit donations, publicly representing that funds would be used exclusively for charitable and social projects.

In March 2008 the proceedings against the applicant were severed from those against the co-suspects. Parallel investigations later began in Turkey.

On 17 September 2008 the Frankfurt Regional Court’s Extended Economic Crimes Chamber convicted G. and T. of aggravated fraud as members of a joint criminal enterprise directed from Turkey, and convicted E. of aiding and abetting. Sentences ranged from a suspended term to over five years’ imprisonment. The written judgment (approximately 32 pages) repeatedly named the applicant in full as one of the “separately prosecuted” persons “behind the scenes.” It found that G. had not acted autonomously but had coordinated with and taken instructions from the applicant (who held a “pre-eminent role” as director of Kanal 7’s operating company). The court recorded that the applicant and others had decided on the use of funds, that unofficial accounts had been kept at their instruction, that monthly coordination of those accounts had occurred with the applicant, and that €4.5 million in cash had been handed to him. It rejected G.’s claim of sole responsibility, preferring the trial confessions of T. and E. that G. operated within a hierarchy whose leaders (including the applicant) were in Turkey. These findings were used both to establish the facts and to mitigate G.’s sentence on the basis that he was merely an “executing organ.”

Media reports of the oral delivery quoted the presiding judge as stating that “strings were pulled” from Kanal 7, specifically naming the applicant. An anonymised internet version of the judgment later carried an introductory disclaimer that findings concerning separately prosecuted persons were not binding on them and that those persons still enjoyed the presumption of innocence; the body of the judgment itself contained no such caveat.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that the references amounted to a public finding of his guilt without trial, violating the presumption of innocence (an aspect of the fair-trial guarantee and the rule of law). In September 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. It held that a third-party judgment does not determine an absent person’s guilt, has no binding effect in subsequent proceedings, and cannot be treated as a penalty; any factual impact is an inevitable consequence of complex, multi-accused cases and does not itself breach the presumption.

Charges were subsequently brought against the applicant in both Germany (2009) and Turkey (2012); the German trial remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.
