The applicant, a Polish national born in 1974, was in a relationship with R (unmarried) when she gave birth to son D on 27 October 1995. They married four days later. On 2 November 1995 the applicant formally acknowledged paternity of D before the registry office, with R’s consent as required by Article 77 of the Family and Custody Code. The couple divorced in January 2000; custody of D was awarded to R and the applicant was ordered to pay maintenance. No paternity issues were raised. R subsequently remarried and had another child.

In January 2007 the applicant, having developed doubts, arranged a private DNA test which excluded him as D’s biological father. By then the one-year time-limit under Article 80 § 1 of the Code for a man personally to seek annulment of his own recognition on grounds of a defective declaration of will had long expired. He therefore asked the district prosecutor to bring proceedings in his name (permitted at any time under Article 86 while the child is alive). The prosecutor interviewed the parties. The applicant stated he had never believed himself to be the father, had been told the child was conceived at a party, had known R had other partners, and had acknowledged paternity only because he saw no alternative; contact with D was sporadic. R countered that the applicant had always known he might not be the father, had recognised the child voluntarily, and that D (who suffered from ADHD and was certified disabled) regarded the applicant as his father; annulment would be traumatic. R’s husband confirmed he had no intention of adopting D.

On 22 March 2007 the prosecutor issued a claim for annulment, citing the DNA result, R’s other relationships at the relevant time, the new family unit and the limited contact. A guardian ad litem appointed for D opposed the claim as contrary to the child’s interests. After hearing the parties the Nowa Sól District Court dismissed the action on 20 June 2007. It found that the couple had cohabited but both had other partners of which each was aware; R had told the applicant he was the father and his mother had pressed for marriage. Although the DNA evidence was accepted, the court held that the applicant had knowingly recognised a child who might not be his; there was therefore no defect of will (deception or otherwise) that would have invalidated the recognition even had the time-limit still run. The prosecutor was not bound by that time-limit, but the court had to weigh the child’s welfare and the rule of law. Recognition of paternity, it observed, is intended to protect the child’s interest and family stability even if it creates a legal fiction; there is no obligation to verify biological truth. Annulment would be contrary to D’s interests: he still regarded the applicant as his father, the stepfather would not adopt him, and revelation of non-paternity after twelve years, especially given D’s ADHD and the impossibility of identifying the true father, would be traumatic. The applicant had made a conscious choice and must bear its consequences. The legislature treats recognition as a definitive act, challengeable only for defects of will or exceptional circumstances incompatible with public order or social co-existence; none existed.

The applicant appealed, arguing that DNA evidence and the principle of biological truth should prevail. The Zielona Góra Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 29 November 2007. It first noted (relying on a 1975 Supreme Court resolution) that a legally recognised father has no standing to appeal the dismissal of a prosecutor’s claim, the right to contest non-biological paternity belonging to the child upon majority (Article 81). Even assuming standing, the first-instance reasoning was sound: the child’s welfare justified departure from biological truth, the applicant had treated D as his own during the marriage, and Polish law accords no absolute priority to genetic reality. The Supreme Court refused to entertain a cassation appeal in October 2008.

(The Code was later amended, effective June 2009, to allow a man six months from learning he is not the biological father to challenge recognition, reflecting a greater emphasis on biological reality; that change post-dated the events.)

The applicant’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights concerned the unfavourable outcome of these proceedings, which left him legally bound as D’s father despite conclusive DNA evidence and his lack of any personal right of action after the statutory time-limit.

The case of A.L. v. Poland (Application no. 28609/08) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns a Polish national's unsuccessful efforts to annul his legal recognition of paternity over a child shown by DNA evidence not to be his biological son. The applicant (born 1974) had a relationship with R, who gave birth to son D on 27 October 1995. The pair married on 31 October 1995, and on 2 November 1995 the applicant formally acknowledged paternity before the registry office, with R's consent as required by Article 77 of the Family and Custody Code. They divorced in January 2000; custody went to the mother and the applicant was ordered to pay maintenance. No paternity issue was raised. R later remarried D.S. and had another son.

The applicant subsequently doubted his paternity and obtained a private DNA test on 4 January 2007 that excluded him as D's father. Because the one-year time-limit under then-applicable Article 80 § 1 of the Family and Custody Code had long expired, he could not himself institute denial-of-paternity proceedings. He therefore asked the district prosecutor to bring a claim in the child's interest (Article 86 permitted the prosecutor to challenge recognition at any time while the child lived).

The prosecutor interviewed the parties. The applicant stated he had never believed he was the father, had no recollection of intercourse with R at the relevant time, knew she had other partners, and had acknowledged paternity only because he felt he had no choice; contact with D remained sporadic. R maintained that the applicant had always known he might not be the father and had acknowledged voluntarily; she warned that annulment would traumatise D, who had ADHD, regarded the applicant as his father and had emotional ties with him. D.S. indicated he had no intention of adopting D.

On 22 March 2007 the prosecutor sued for annulment, citing the DNA result, R's other sexual contacts, the new family unit and the limited contact. A guardian ad litem opposed the claim as contrary to D's interests. After hearing the parties, the Nowa Sól District Court dismissed the action on 20 June 2007. It found that the couple had been aware of each other's other partners, that the applicant had known at the time of recognition that he might not be the father, and that no defect of will (Articles 82, 84, 86 or 87 of the Civil Code) therefore existed. Even though the prosecutor was not bound by the statutory time-limit, annulment was not required by the child's interest or the rule of law. D still viewed the applicant as his father; D.S. would not adopt him; disclosure after many years would be traumatic given D's ADHD and the impossibility of identifying the biological father. Recognition of paternity was treated by the legislature as a definitive act that could create a legal fiction in the interests of the child's welfare and family stability; the applicant, having acted with full knowledge, must bear the consequences.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the DNA evidence and the principle of biological truth had been disregarded. The prosecutor now contended that the child's interest no longer favoured the claim and questioned the applicant's standing. On 29 November 2007 the Zielona Góra Regional Court dismissed the appeal. Relying on a 1975 Supreme Court resolution, it held that a legally recognised father had no standing to appeal dismissal of a prosecutor's claim; the Code reserved the right to challenge recognition on biological grounds to the child himself once he reached majority (Article 81). Even assuming standing, the first-instance court had correctly given priority to the child's welfare and the stability of the existing legal relationship over biological truth. A cassation appeal was refused by the Supreme Court on 17 October 2008.

(The Family and Custody Code was later amended, with effect from June 2009, to allow a man to challenge recognition within six months of learning he was not the biological father.)

These facts form the core of the applicant's complaint that the domestic courts' refusal to give effect to the DNA evidence and to annul the recognition violated his Convention rights.

The case of A.L. v. Poland (application no. 28609/08) arose from the applicant’s unsuccessful domestic efforts to annul his legal recognition of paternity of a child later shown by DNA evidence not to be his biological son. On 2 November 1995 the applicant formally acknowledged paternity of D before the registry office, with R’s required consent under the Family and Custody Code. They later divorced on 12 January 2000; the court awarded custody of D to R and ordered the applicant to pay monthly child maintenance (initially PLN 300, later PLN 400). No paternity questions were raised in those proceedings. R subsequently remarried and had another son.

The applicant later developed doubts about his paternity. On 4 January 2007 he took D to a private laboratory for a DNA test, which excluded him as the biological father. Because more than one year had passed since the 1995 acknowledgment, Article 80 § 1 of the Family and Custody Code barred him from personally seeking annulment on grounds of a defective declaration of will. He therefore asked the Nowa Sól District Prosecutor to bring the action instead (permitted at any time under Article 86 while the child lived).

The prosecutor filed the claim on 22 March 2007 against the applicant, R and D, relying on the DNA results, R’s admission of other sexual partners around the time of conception, the applicant’s limited contact with D, and statements that R’s new husband treated D as part of the family. A guardian ad litem for D opposed the claim as contrary to the child’s interests. After hearing the parties, the District Court dismissed the action on 20 June 2007. It found that the applicant and R had both had other partners and that the applicant had been fully aware he might not be D’s father when he acknowledged paternity; there had been no deception or other defect of will. Even though the prosecutor was not bound by the one-year limit, the court held that neither the child’s interests nor the rule of law required annulment. D (then a primary-school pupil with ADHD and certified educational needs) still regarded the applicant as his father; the stepfather had no intention of adopting him; revealing the truth after many years would be traumatic, especially as the biological father remained unidentified; and a man who had consciously assumed paternity should bear the consequences for the child’s stability. The court emphasised that Polish law treats recognition of paternity as a definitive act that may create a legal fiction of parentage in the service of family stability.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the DNA evidence had been disregarded and that biological truth plus the child’s and public interest required ending the legal fiction. The Zielona Góra Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 29 November 2007. It first held, citing Supreme Court precedent, that a recognised father lacked standing to appeal a judgment refusing the prosecutor’s claim. Even assuming standing, the first-instance reasoning was sound: the child’s well-being justified departure from biological truth, and the applicant’s own divorce-file statements showed he had treated D as his son. The Supreme Court refused to entertain a cassation appeal on 17 October 2008.

(The Family and Custody Code was later amended in 2009 to allow a recognised father six months from the date he learns he is not the biological parent to challenge recognition, reflecting a greater emphasis on biological reality.) These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights about the unfavourable outcome of the annulment proceedings.
001-141384:
The applicant, a Russian national born in 1966, alleged violations of Articles 3, 6 and 8 of the Convention arising from his arrest on 1 June 2005, subsequent ill-treatment, detention conditions, the investigation thereof, a house search and the fairness of his criminal trial for drug trafficking.

On 1 June 2005 police arranged a test purchase after suspecting the applicant of opium trafficking. An undercover officer arranged to buy two doses; the applicant sold two sachets to undercover agents around 11.30 a.m. Officers G. and K. then arrested him near his flat in the presence of his partner E. and her sister B., taking him to the local police station. He declined counsel. He alleged that over the next eight hours G. and K. beat him (including with a water-filled plastic bottle to the lower back) to extract a confession of trafficking, injuring his kidneys; he did not confess. His hands were later examined for drug traces in the presence of witnesses and money was taken from his pocket. At 9.12 p.m. he was transferred to a temporary detention facility, where a paramedic recorded back pain and a knee scratch the applicant attributed to the arrest. Officers then searched his flat at 11.27 p.m. (in his absence, despite his request to attend) and found opium; he did not challenge the search. In detention he repeatedly complained of lower-back pain (1–10 June), receiving painkillers; a paramedic diagnosed soft-tissue bruising. An August hospital examination (X-ray and tests) found no anomalies.

On 9 June 2005 the applicant requested criminal proceedings against the officers for ill-treatment. Prosecutors refused on 18 July 2005 (unfounded). A higher prosecutor quashed this as perfunctory on 17 August, ordering further steps (questioning G. and B., a medical examination). A further refusal on 20 August was similarly quashed on 16 September (paramedics to be questioned). After interviewing K., the applicant, B., E. and paramedic Zyu., prosecutors refused again on 21 September 2005, finding no evidence of force or pressure (witnesses to the arrest saw none; no visible injuries beyond the scratch; later tests negative). The applicant’s court appeal was dismissed on 10 February 2006 but quashed by the regional court on 25 April 2006 for incompleteness (failure to question emergency doctors, ignore contradictions, omit pre-existing kidney issues or the cause of pain). Additional interviews (including E., who reported the applicant’s prior prison beating causing kidney/rib pain treated only with pharmacy painkillers, never doctors; paramedics noting no hematomas; surgeon Tr. finding no anomalies) led to a final refusal on 24 April 2007 (allegations an attempt to evade liability; no abuse of power). The applicant did not appeal this. In 2011 E. recanted, claiming her statements were false due to a housing dispute.

In his trial the applicant denied trafficking, alleging police fabrication. He claimed he could not cross-examine two prosecution witnesses and that the court failed to secure a defence witness. On 18 October 2005 he was convicted and sentenced to four years six months. His appeal (which omitted the witness complaints) was dismissed on 31 January 2006. Supervisory review on 21 September 2006 re-characterised the offence as an attempt and reduced the sentence to four years three months.

At trial the applicant denied the charges (claiming fabrication) and said he could not cross-examine two witnesses or have a defence witness called. He was convicted of trafficking on 18 October 2005 (4 years 6 months). His appeal (omitting the witness complaints) was dismissed (31 January 2006). The applicant claimed that over the ensuing eight hours, officers G. and K. beat him repeatedly (including with a water-filled plastic bottle on the lower back) to extract a confession of trafficking, causing kidney damage and other injuries. He was then taken to officer M.’s office, where his hands were examined for drug traces in the presence of attesting witnesses and money was removed from his pocket for inspection.

At 9:12 p.m., he was transferred to a temporary detention facility. A paramedic noted his complaint of back pain and a knee scratch he attributed to the arrest, with no other visible injuries recorded. He repeatedly complained of lower-back pain in the following days; a paramedic diagnosed soft-tissue bruising, and he received painkiller injections. On 15 August 2005, hospital examination (X-ray and tests) revealed no anomalies, though an ultrasound of the kidneys was not completed.

A search of his flat at 11:27 p.m. on 1 June uncovered opium. He brought no domestic challenge to its lawfulness.

On 9 June 2005 the applicant requested that the prosecutor institute criminal proceedings over the alleged ill-treatment. Multiple refusals followed (18 July, 20 August, 21 September 2005, and 24 April 2007), several of which were quashed by higher prosecutors or courts for being perfunctory. Investigators questioned the officers, E., B., detention paramedics, a hospital surgeon, and others. E. initially stated that the applicant had pre-existing kidney, rib, and liver pain from a prior prison beating and had self-medicated without seeking formal care. In a 2011 statement obtained for the Strasbourg proceedings, she recanted, claiming she had lied out of fear of eviction and resentment over paying household costs. The 24 April 2007 decision (which the applicant did not appeal) concluded there was no evidence of offences by the officers and that the allegations were an attempt to evade liability. Courts reviewing earlier refusals noted failures to interview all relevant medical staff, unresolved contradictions in witness accounts, and the investigators’ failure to determine the cause of the applicant’s pain or any pre-existing conditions.

In the criminal proceedings, the applicant denied trafficking and claimed the case had been fabricated. On 18 October 2005 the Volgodonsk Town Court convicted him and imposed a sentence of four years and six months’ imprisonment. He appealed, reiterating the fabrication claim but not raising alleged inability to cross-examine two prosecution witnesses or to secure attendance of a defence witness. The conviction was upheld on 31 January 2006; on 21 September 2006 a higher court recharacterised the offence as an attempt and reduced the sentence to four years and three months.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints of physical ill-treatment, deficient investigation, detention conditions, trial unfairness, and an unlawful search.
001-141644:
The case of Avotiņš v. Latvia (Application no. 17502/07) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair hearing). The applicant, a Latvian national, complained that Latvian courts breached this right by recognising and enforcing a default judgment issued against him by a Cypriot court, despite his not having been properly summoned or afforded an opportunity to defend himself in the original proceedings.

In May 1999 the applicant signed a notarial deed acknowledging a debt of USD 100,000 to F.H. Ltd., a Cypriot company, which he undertook to repay with interest by 30 June 1999. The deed contained choice-of-law and jurisdiction clauses conferring non-exclusive jurisdiction on the Cypriot courts. In 2003 F.H. Ltd. sued the applicant in the Limassol District Court for non-payment. Because the applicant resided in Latvia, the company obtained an order for service of the summons at an address in G. Street, Riga (the address at which the 1999 documents had been signed). The applicant maintained that this was neither his home nor his place of business and that service there was objectively impossible. An affidavit later indicated that the summons had been sent by recorded delivery on 16 November 2003 and received on 18 November 2003 (a Latvian public holiday). The applicant denied ever receiving it.

On 24 May 2004 the Limassol District Court, sitting in the applicant’s absence, entered a default judgment ordering him to pay the principal sum plus interest at 10 % per annum from 30 June 1999, together with costs. The judgment recorded that the applicant had been duly informed of the hearing but contained no statement of finality or available remedies.

In February 2005 F.H. Ltd. applied to the Riga City Latgale District Court for recognition and enforcement of the Cypriot judgment under Council Regulation (EC) No 44/2001 (the Brussels I Regulation) and sought a protective charge over the applicant’s real property in Garkalne. After procedural corrections concerning the applicant’s address, the District Court, sitting without the parties, granted the application on 27 February 2006.

The applicant first learned of both the Cypriot judgment and the Latvian enforcement order on 16 June 2006. He did not challenge the Cypriot judgment in Cyprus. He did, however, lodge an ancillary appeal against the Latvian order; the District Court extended the time-limit after finding that he had not been notified of the 27 February 2006 decision and no longer lived at his declared address. Before the Riga Regional Court he argued that recognition violated Article 34(2) of the Brussels I Regulation (and the corresponding provision of Latvian law) because the originating document had not been served in sufficient time and in such a manner as to enable him to arrange his defence. He further contended that the judgment had not been shown to be enforceable in Cyprus, the required certificate (Annex V to the Regulation) having been omitted and the judgment itself containing no indication of finality.

On 2 October 2006 the Regional Court allowed the appeal and refused recognition. F.H. Ltd. then appealed to the Senate of the Supreme Court. At the hearing on 31 January 2007 the company produced, for the first time, an Annex V certificate dated 18 January 2007 stating that service had occurred on 27 November 2003. The Senate quashed the Regional Court’s decision, holding that the Cypriot judgment was final (no appeal having been lodged) and that the applicant’s complaints of defective notification were therefore irrelevant. It ordered recognition, enforcement and inscription of the charge. The applicant immediately paid the sum due (approximately EUR 129 000) and the charge was later lifted.

The applicant maintained that the Latvian courts had thereby given effect to a judgment obtained in violation of his defence rights, contrary to Article 6 § 1.

**CASE OF AVOTIŅŠ v. LATVIA (Application no. 17502/07)**

This ECtHR Chamber judgment (25 February 2014; later referred to the Grand Chamber) arose from a Latvian national’s complaint that Latvian courts, by recognising and enforcing a Cypriot default judgment, violated his Article 6 § 1 right to a fair hearing. The application against Cyprus itself was declared inadmissible for missing the six-month time-limit.

In May 1999 the applicant signed a notarial deed acknowledging a USD 100,000 loan from Cypriot company F.H. Ltd., repayable by 30 June 1999. The deed was governed by Cypriot law and conferred non-exclusive jurisdiction on Cypriot courts. In 2003 F.H. Ltd. sued in the Limassol District Court for non-payment. Because the applicant lived in Latvia, the company obtained an ex parte order for service at a Riga address (G. Street) that the applicant later said was merely the place where the deed had been signed and was neither his home nor his business premises. An affidavit recorded that a recorded-delivery summons was sent on 16 November 2003 and received on 18 November 2003 (a Latvian public holiday). The applicant denied receipt. He did not appear. On 24 May 2004 the Limassol court, sitting in his absence, gave judgment for the principal, 10 % interest and costs, stating that he had been “duly informed.” The judgment contained no statement of finality or available remedies.

In February 2005 F.H. Ltd. applied to the Riga City Latgale District Court for recognition and enforcement under the Brussels I Regulation (No 44/2001) and Latvian Civil Procedure Law, simultaneously seeking a charge over the applicant’s Garkalne property. It now listed a different Riga address (Č. Street). After procedural adjournments the District Court, sitting without the parties on 27 February 2006, granted recognition, enforcement and the charge. The applicant first learned of both the Cypriot judgment and the Latvian order on 16 June 2006. He did not challenge the Cypriot judgment in Cyprus but lodged an ancillary appeal in Latvia; the time-limit was extended because he had not been served with the order.

He argued two grounds under Article 34(2) of the Regulation (mirrored in Latvian law): (1) he had not been served with the originating process in sufficient time and in such a manner as to enable him to arrange his defence—the claimant’s lawyers knew his actual business and registered addresses yet used an address at which he could not be reached; and (2) the judgment had not been shown to be enforceable in Cyprus (no Annex V certificate had been produced, the judgment itself was silent on finality, and no proof of enforceability existed). On 2 October 2006 the Riga Regional Court allowed the appeal and refused recognition.

F.H. Ltd. appealed to the Senate of the Supreme Court. At the 31 January 2007 hearing it produced, for the first time, an 18 January 2007 Annex V certificate stating that service had occurred on 27 November 2003 (the field identifying the person against whom the judgment was enforceable was left blank). The Senate quashed the Regional Court, holding that the Cypriot judgment was final (no appeal had been lodged) and that the applicant’s complaints about service were therefore “of no importance.” Article 36 of the Regulation forbade review of the merits. Recognition, enforcement and the property charge were ordered. The applicant immediately paid approximately LVL 90,245 (EUR 129,000) under the writ of execution; the charge was later lifted.

The core facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation are therefore: (a) disputed service of the Cypriot originating process at an address the applicant said was unusable; (b) the Latvian first-instance court’s ex parte recognition; (c) the Senate’s refusal to examine whether service had in fact enabled a defence, on the sole ground that the applicant had not appealed in Cyprus; and (d) the late production and uncritical acceptance of the incomplete Annex V certificate. These elements formed the basis of the claim that Latvian courts had failed to afford the applicant a fair opportunity to contest enforcement of a foreign default judgment.

The case of Avotiņš v. Latvia originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Latvian national Pēteris Avotiņš. He alleged that Latvian courts, by recognising and enforcing a Cypriot default judgment against him, violated his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. (His parallel complaint against Cyprus was declared inadmissible for exceeding the six-month time-limit.)

In May 1999 Avotiņš signed a notarial deed acknowledging a USD 100,000 debt to the Cypriot company F.H. Ltd., payable with interest by 30 June 1999. The deed was governed by Cypriot law and conferred non-exclusive jurisdiction on the Cypriot courts. In 2003 F.H. Ltd. sued in the Limassol District Court for non-payment. Because Avotiņš was not resident in Cyprus the claimant obtained an order for service at a G. Street address in Riga that Avotiņš later described as merely the place where the 1999 documents had been signed, not his home or business address. A recorded-delivery summons was sent on 16 November 2003; postal records indicated receipt on 18 November (a Latvian public holiday). Avotiņš denied ever receiving it.

He did not appear. On 24 May 2004 the Limassol court entered a default judgment ordering him to pay the principal, 10 % annual interest from 30 June 1999, and costs. The judgment stated that he had been duly notified but contained no mention of its finality or of available remedies.

In February 2005 F.H. Ltd. applied to the Riga City Latgale District Court for recognition and enforcement of the Cypriot judgment under the Brussels I Regulation and for a protective charge on Avotiņš’s Garkalne property. After procedural delays, the District Court granted the application on 27 February 2006 without the parties present. Avotiņš learned of both the Cypriot judgment and the Latvian order only by chance on 16 June 2006. He was granted an extension of time to appeal, the District Court accepting that he had not been notified of the order and that he no longer resided at the declared Č. Street address.

On appeal Avotiņš argued two grounds under Article 34(2) and Article 38(1) of the Regulation (mirrored in Latvian law). First, he had not been served with the originating process in sufficient time and in such a manner as to enable him to arrange his defence; the claimant’s lawyers knew his actual business and registered addresses yet deliberately used an inaccessible one. Second, the claimant had produced neither the required Annex V certificate nor proof that the judgment was enforceable in Cyprus.

The Riga Regional Court accepted these arguments on 2 October 2006 and refused recognition. F.H. Ltd. then appealed to the Senate of the Supreme Court. At the 31 January 2007 hearing it produced, for the first time, an 18 January 2007 certificate stating that the originating document had been served on 27 November 2003. The Senate reversed the Regional Court, holding that the Cypriot judgment had become final because Avotiņš had never appealed it in Cyprus; his complaints about service were therefore “of no importance.” Article 36 of the Regulation prohibited any review of the merits. Recognition and a charge on the Garkalne property were ordered. Avotiņš immediately paid the full sum (approximately EUR 129 000) and later obtained the lifting of the charge.

These facts formed the basis of Avotiņš’s Article 6 complaint: that the Latvian courts had mechanically enforced a default judgment without satisfying themselves that his defence rights had been respected, contrary to both the Convention and the safeguards contained in the Brussels I Regulation.
001-142636:
The European Court of Human Rights case of Oran v. Turkey (applications nos. 28881/07 and 37920/07) arose from complaints by Baskın Oran, a Turkish national born in 1945 and living in Ankara. A professor of political science at Ankara University, Oran stood as an independent candidate (unaffiliated with any political party) in Istanbul’s second electoral district during the early parliamentary elections of 22 July 2007.

These elections followed a political crisis over Parliament’s failure to elect a successor to President Ahmet Necdet Sezer. Fourteen parties participated amid 84% turnout. Parties employed strategies to evade the 10% national threshold: the DSP ran under the CHP banner, while the pro-Kurdish DTP fielded candidates as independents under the “A thousand hopes” slogan (supported by smaller left-wing groups). Over 60 independents ran; 27 were elected, including more than 20 “thousand hopes” candidates who later joined the DTP (enabling it to form a parliamentary group). The AKP secured an absolute majority.

Oran alleged violations of Articles 10 (freedom of expression) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention, read with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), plus Article 13 (effective remedy).

The first application concerned voting by Turkish nationals resident abroad for over six months. Under Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298 (as amended), they could vote only for political parties—not independents—at customs-post polling stations. A 27 May 2007 Higher Electoral Council decree set voting from 25 June to 22 July 2007 exclusively for parties. On 3 July 2007 Oran sought annulment, invoking constitutional Articles 67 and 90 § 6 plus Protocol No. 1 Article 3. The Council rejected this on 4 July 2007, holding that only legislative amendment could alter the provision.

The second application addressed campaign media access. Section 52(1) of Law no. 298 allowed participating parties limited election broadcasts on national radio and television (TRT), overseen by the Higher Electoral Council (with sanctions for breaches). Broadcasts ran 15–21 July 2007. Independents such as Oran were barred from national or private-channel electioneering. Oran emphasised the unusually high number of independents, attributing this to the 10% threshold and widespread dissatisfaction with established parties (whether in government or opposition).

These facts underpin claims of discriminatory treatment of independents relative to parties, impairing equal electoral participation, campaign opportunities, and the free expression of the people’s opinion in choosing the legislature, without effective domestic redress.

The case of Oran v. Turkey (applications nos. 28881/07 and 37920/07) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) in a judgment of 15 April 2014 (final on 8 September 2014). The applicant, Baskin Oran, a Turkish national born in 1945 and living in Ankara, was a professor of political science at Ankara University. He stood as an independent candidate (not affiliated with any political party) in the second electoral district of Istanbul during Turkey’s parliamentary elections of 22 July 2007.

These elections were called early amid a political crisis over the failure to elect a successor to President Ahmet Necdet Sezer. They featured a high turnout of 84 percent and were shaped by Turkey’s 10 percent national electoral threshold. Fourteen parties participated. To circumvent the threshold, some groups (including the pro-Kurdish DTP) fielded candidates as independents under slogans such as “A thousand hopes.” More than sixty independents stood nationwide; twenty-seven were elected (including over twenty “thousand hopes” candidates who later joined the DTP, enabling it to form a parliamentary group). The ruling AKP obtained 46.58 percent of the vote and 341 seats; the CHP and MHP also surpassed the threshold.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 10 (freedom of expression) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention, read in conjunction with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), as well as a violation of Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The complaints arose from two sets of restrictions that, in his view, systematically disadvantaged independent candidates relative to those of political parties.

The first application concerned out-of-country voting. Under Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298 (as amended), Turkish electors who had resided abroad for more than six months could vote at polling stations established at customs posts, but only for political parties—not for independent candidates such as the applicant. A Higher Electoral Council decree of 27 May 2007 confirmed the dates (25 June–22 July 2007) and the restriction to party lists. On 3 July 2007 the applicant applied to the Council for annulment of the decree, invoking Articles 67 and 90 § 6 of the Turkish Constitution and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The Council dismissed the request the following day, holding that the statutory provision could be altered only by fresh legislation.

The second application concerned election broadcasts. Section 52(1) of Law no. 298 permitted political parties to transmit campaign broadcasts on the national broadcaster TRT (subject to airtime limits and other restrictions) during the week preceding the poll (15–21 July 2007). The Higher Electoral Council supervised compliance and could impose sanctions. The law contained no equivalent provision for independent candidates. The applicant maintained that this exclusion extended to private channels as well, thereby denying him any access to radio or television electioneering. He stressed that the 2007 elections were marked by an unusually large number of independents, a phenomenon he attributed both to the 10 percent threshold and to widespread public dissatisfaction with established parties.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s claims that the legal framework treated independents unequally, impairing their ability to campaign effectively and to receive votes from a significant segment of the electorate (those voting at customs posts). The Higher Electoral Council’s decisions were presented as leaving him without an effective domestic remedy. The Court communicated the applications to the Turkish Government on 14 March 2011.

The case of Oran v. Turkey (applications nos. 28881/07 and 37920/07) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 15 April 2014. The applicant, Baskin Oran, a Turkish national born in 1945 and resident in Ankara, was a professor of political science. He stood as an independent candidate (not affiliated with any political party) in the second electoral district of Istanbul during Turkey’s parliamentary elections held on 22 July 2007.

These elections were called early amid a political crisis over the failure to elect a new president before the incumbent’s term expired. Fourteen parties participated, with an 84% turnout. To circumvent the national 10% electoral threshold, some parties fielded candidates as independents or under other banners. This produced an unusually high number of independent candidates (over 60 in around 40 constituencies), of whom 27 were elected, including more than 20 “thousand hopes” candidates who later joined the DTP parliamentary group.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 10 and 14 of the Convention (taken together with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1) and of Article 13. The facts relevant to these claims fall into two parts.

In the first application, Turkish law (Article 94 II a of Law no. 298, as amended) permitted voters at polling stations established at customs posts (for Turkish nationals resident abroad for more than six months) to cast ballots only for political parties, not for independent candidates. A Higher Electoral Council decree of 27 May 2007 confirmed the relevant dates and restated this restriction. On 3 July 2007 the applicant applied to the Council for annulment of the decree, invoking Articles 67 and 90 § 6 of the Turkish Constitution and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The Council dismissed the request the following day, holding that the statutory provision could be altered only by fresh legislation.

In the second application, section 52(1) of Law no. 298 granted participating political parties the right to election broadcasts on the national public broadcaster TRT (subject to airtime and other limits), with the Higher Electoral Council supervising compliance and imposing sanctions. Broadcasts were permitted only during the week of 15–21 July 2007. Independent candidates such as the applicant were excluded from these broadcasts, both on TRT and, according to the applicant, on private channels as well. He attributed the large number of independents in 2007 to the 10% threshold and widespread voter dissatisfaction with established parties.

These restrictions—on the ability of overseas voters to support independents and on independents’ access to broadcast media—formed the factual core of the applicant’s complaints concerning the right to free elections, freedom of expression, non-discrimination and the availability of an effective remedy.
001-142406:
The case of Krasicki v. Poland (Application no. 17254/11) concerns a Polish father's complaint that the authorities failed to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his two sons, A. and J. (born 1999 and 2000 out of wedlock). The applicant never cohabited with the mother, J.J. In 2004, after the mother withdrew an application to strip him of parental authority, a Warsaw-Mokotów District Court confirmed both parents' authority, placed the children with the mother, assigned a court guardian to supervise the applicant, and granted him unspecified contact rights.

Difficulties arose immediately. In 2005 the applicant sought specified contact away from the mother's home. A December 2005 expert report from the Regional Family Consultation Centre found the children had close emotional ties with both parents, praised the applicant as a competent father who paid support, and criticised the mother's hostility and wish to exclude him. The experts recommended frequent contact. The applicant last saw the boys in October 2005 and thereafter avoided visits because of the mother's verbal aggression.

A February 2006 court order granted the applicant unsupervised contact on the first, second and fourth Saturdays of each month (10 a.m.–7 p.m.) plus one week in summer. The mother ignored the order. The applicant repeatedly complained to police and the court. Successive guardian reports (2006–2009) documented her obstruction, including refusal to open her door. In November 2006 she allegedly told the children their father was dead and sent him a funeral wreath. The court imposed successive fines (PLN 1 000 in April 2007, PLN 1 000 in September 2007 and PLN 1 200 in May 2008) with 30-day compliance deadlines, convertible to detention. The mother paid none.

In April 2008 the applicant, accompanied by a guardian and police, was refused entry; officers declined to intervene. In December 2008 the court converted unpaid fines into 32 days' detention. The applicant declined to take the children if the mother were imprisoned, citing inadequate housing. Further deadlines and a December 2009 detention order followed; the grandmother temporarily housed the children. In 2010 the grandmother paid the fines (PLN 3 200). Attempts by the bailiff to arrest the mother failed; police again refused to assist and medical certificates delayed enforcement.

Meanwhile the court, acting of its own motion in November 2007, limited the mother's parental authority in March 2008 and appointed a supervisory guardian, citing detriment to the children. The mother's 2009 counter-application to strip the applicant of authority was dismissed in December 2009; the court found her hostility, not the children's interests, motivated her obstruction.

In October 2010 the applicant sought forcible removal of the children. The court authorised guardian-assisted visits. Between January and March 2011 six attempts produced only one 30-minute meeting with the older boy; the children expressed hostility and refused further contact. The applicant then waived further coercive enforcement, arguing it would deepen alienation, and requested a fresh psychological assessment.

Guardians continued to report the mother's total seclusion and the children's irregular school attendance, neglect and aggression. In March–April 2012 the court opened further proceedings, heard evidence and ordered emergency placement. The mother ignored the order; four collection attempts (even with police) failed. In November 2012 she applied to revoke the placement, briefly admitted police, and was assessed as unfit. Expert examinations were ordered; those proceedings remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

The applicant contended that, despite repeated court orders, fines, detention threats and guardian involvement spanning more than six years, the Polish authorities never secured even minimal contact, thereby violating his right to family life.

The case of Krasicki v. Poland (Application no. 17254/11) concerns a Polish father’s complaint that domestic authorities failed to take effective measures to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his two sons, born in 1999 and 2000 to a former partner with whom he never cohabited. Both parents retained parental authority, with the children residing with their mother; a court-appointed guardian was assigned to supervise the father’s exercise of his rights. In February 2006, following an expert psychological assessment confirming the children’s emotional ties to both parents, the father’s competence, and the mother’s hostile desire to exclude him, a Warsaw district court specified contact on three Saturdays per month (without the mother present) plus one week of summer holidays. The mother was ordered to comply.

The mother systematically obstructed contact from the outset. She refused to open her door to the father, guardians, or police; told the children their father was dead and sent him a funeral wreath in their names; and consistently failed to facilitate visits. Guardians’ reports from 2006 onward documented her non-cooperation, verbal aggression, and isolation of the children, though they noted no overt neglect of the boys’ basic needs or schooling at that stage. The father repeatedly applied for enforcement. The court imposed successive fines (PLN 1,000–1,200) in 2007–2008, convertible to detention if unpaid, and in December 2008 ordered 32 days’ detention. A 2009 order threatened enforcement of that detention; the children were to be placed with their grandmother during any incarceration. The mother promised compliance but did not deliver. Attempts by the bailiff to arrest her in 2010 failed when no one answered the door and police declined to intervene; medical certificates delayed matters until the grandmother paid the accumulated fines.

Parallel proceedings produced limited results. In March 2008 the court, acting ex officio, restricted the mother’s parental authority and appointed a supervisor, citing her detrimental attitude. It dismissed her 2009 counter-application to strip the father of all rights, finding her motivated solely by personal hostility rather than the children’s welfare. In late 2010 the father sought forcible removal of the children. The court authorised guardian-assisted visits. Six such attempts in early 2011 yielded only one 30-minute meeting with the older son; thereafter the boys (now aged 11–12) refused contact, echoing their mother’s narrative that the father had never cared for them. The father then waived further coercive assistance, arguing it would deepen their hostility, and requested a fresh psychological assessment.

By 2011–2012 guardians and school officials reported the children were irregularly attending school, becoming neglected, disturbed and aggressive; the mother lived in total seclusion and evaded all contact. In April 2012 the court ordered emergency care placement. The mother ignored the order; repeated attempts by the guardian (with police) to collect the children failed. She later applied to revoke the order, cooperated briefly, and submitted her own psychologist’s report denying neglect. An official expert assessment was ordered; those proceedings remained pending.

Over more than five years the authorities employed fines, detention orders, guardians, police accompaniment and care-removal proceedings, yet never secured regular contact. The father’s last uncontested visit occurred in late 2005; by 2011 the children openly rejected him. The applicant contended these measures were neither timely nor sufficiently robust to overcome the mother’s persistent defiance.

**Case Summary: Krasicki v. Poland (Application no. 17254/11)**

The applicant, Artur Krasicki (born 1970), alleged that Polish authorities failed to take effective steps to enforce his court-ordered right to contact with his two sons, A. and J. (born January 1999 and December 2000), whom he had recognised as his own from a non-cohabiting relationship with their mother, J.J.

In January 2004, J.J. applied to divest the applicant of parental authority, citing his alleged failures, but withdrew the claim. The Warsaw-Mokotów District Court discontinued those proceedings, maintained joint parental authority, placed the children with the mother, assigned a court-appointed guardian to supervise the applicant, and granted him unspecified contact rights. In May 2005 the applicant sought specific arrangements away from the mother’s home due to access difficulties. A December 2005 expert report from the Regional Family Consultation Centre found strong emotional bonds between the children and both parents, described the father as competent and committed (including payment of support), criticised the mother’s hostile and exclusionary attitude, and recommended frequent father-child contact. The applicant last saw the boys in October 2005 and thereafter avoided visits because of the mother’s aggression.

On 8 February 2006 the court specified unsupervised contact on the first, second and fourth Saturdays of each month (10 a.m.–7 p.m.) plus one week of summer holidays; the mother’s appeal was dismissed. She consistently refused compliance. The applicant repeatedly complained to police and the court. Successive guardian reports (2006–2009) documented her obstruction, refusal to open her door, and verbal hostility; teachers confirmed no neglect of the children at school but noted the mother’s attitude. In November 2006 she allegedly told the boys their father was dead and sent him a funeral wreath.

The court imposed fines of PLN 1,000–1,200 on the mother in April and September 2007 and May 2008, each with a 30-day compliance deadline (unpaid fines convertible to detention). She did not pay. In April 2008 the applicant, guardian and police were refused entry; police declined to intervene. A December 2008 order converted unpaid fines into 32 days’ detention and directed the bailiff to enforce it. A July 2009 guardian report recorded no contact since 2005 and the applicant’s view that the children believed him dead; he declined to take the boys if the mother were detained because of inadequate housing. Further court orders (September and December 2009) set deadlines on pain of detention; the mother made insincere promises of compliance. Attempts by the applicant, grandmother and police in November 2009 failed. The grandmother later paid the accumulated fines (PLN 3,200) in October 2010, after medical certificates delayed the mother’s detention and a July 2010 arrest attempt found no one at home.

In November 2007 the court, acting *ex officio* on guardian reports, limited the mother’s parental authority (March 2008) and assigned a supervising guardian, finding her conduct detrimental. Her August 2009 application to strip the applicant of authority and contact was dismissed in December 2009; the court praised his persistent efforts, condemned her arbitrary hostility as contrary to the children’s interests, and warned of the risk that the boys would internalise her attitude.

In October 2010 the applicant sought forcible removal of the children. The court authorised guardian assistance for scheduled visits (December 2010). Six assisted attempts (January–March 2011) produced only one brief meeting with the older son; the children thereafter refused contact. Citing their hostility and best interests, the applicant waived further coercive assistance in March 2011 and requested a new psychological assessment.

Guardian reports from 2010–2012 showed the mother remaining secluded, refusing all access, and the children becoming irregular school attendees who displayed neglect, disturbance and aggression. In March–April 2012 the court, acting *ex officio*, joined proceedings and ordered the children placed in emergency care. The mother failed to deliver them; four subsequent attempts by the guardian (with police and school officials) in August–November 2012 were unsuccessful. She then applied to revoke the care order (November 2012), claiming readiness to cooperate; enforcement was stayed. A January 2013 home assessment found her unable to discharge her duties and distrustful of officials; further expert examinations were ordered. Those proceedings remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

Throughout, Polish courts repeatedly issued orders, imposed (and later converted) fines, threatened detention, limited parental authority, authorised guardians and police assistance, and even ordered emergency care, yet none of these measures secured meaningful or regular contact. The applicant’s last substantial contact occurred in 2005; by 2011 the children’s induced hostility led him to abandon coercive enforcement. The facts demonstrate a pattern of maternal obstruction met by incremental but ultimately ineffective state responses over more than seven years.
001-141929:
The case of Palanci v. Switzerland (Application no. 2607/08) concerns a Turkish national, Erol Palanci (born 1971), who alleged that his expulsion from Switzerland violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). Palanci first entered Switzerland in 1989, sought asylum, and worked in the gastronomic sector until his claim was rejected in 1993, prompting his departure to Germany. There, on 10 February 1994, he married a Turkish national holding a Swiss residence permit. He re-entered Switzerland on 15 July 1994 and obtained a residence permit. The couple had three daughters born in Switzerland (1995, 1997 and 2000); the wife's daughter from a prior marriage (born 1985) also lived with them.

Palanci's record included a 1995 charge for working without a permit and a 1997 warning for forging his wife's signature on an official document. The couple separated in August 1999; the children remained with the wife, and Palanci was ordered to pay maintenance. On 1 December 1999 he received a three-month suspended sentence for multiple assaults on his wife, some involving a dangerous object. Further warnings followed in December 1999 and September 2001 owing to growing debts and the family's reliance on social welfare. By May 2002 debts stood at approximately CHF 177,850 and unpaid maintenance at CHF 46,150. His permit was extended for six months in August 2002 with a warning to improve his finances. In March 2003 he was sentenced to 60 days' imprisonment for wilful non-payment of maintenance. A final warning in December 2003 required proof of financial stability and maintenance payments by June 2004.

The wife filed for divorce in March 2001 (later withdrawn) and again in March 2004, also lodging a criminal complaint for aggression (withdrawn in August 2004). The case of Đekić and Others v. Serbia (no. 32277/07) was brought by three Serbian nationals—Dragan Đekić, Zoran Đekić and Dragan Končar—who alleged police ill-treatment after a minor traffic accident and an ineffective investigation into those claims. They relied on Articles 3, 6 and 13 of the Convention.

On 18 September 2004 at about 2.30 a.m. the applicants were involved in a minor road accident in Prokuplje. Police arrived shortly afterwards. The applicants stated that they were immediately handcuffed and taken to Prokuplje Police Station, where they were beaten. Official reports prepared by three duty officers recorded that the applicants were drunk and violent on the officers’ arrival, tried to flee and attacked an officer attempting to stop them. They were therefore arrested. At the station they continued to behave violently; the officers struck them a few times with truncheons in order to subdue them and then handcuffed them. While resisting, Zoran Đekić and Dragan Končar struck their heads against office furniture.

After spending the night in custody the applicants were taken to hospital. Medical reports recorded a bruise on Dragan Đekić’s right shoulder; bruises on Zoran Đekić’s head, right arm and right shoulder; and bruises on Dragan Končar’s head, chest, abdomen, back and right shoulder.

That same morning the police lodged a criminal complaint against the applicants for obstructing an officer in the discharge of his duty. At approximately 8.30 a.m. they were brought before an investigating judge and complained that they had been beaten; the judge took no action. They were released around 1 p.m.

Between 21 and 27 September the Inspector General’s Service (the Ministry’s internal-control body) conducted an internal inquiry. It interviewed the applicants, 18 police officers and 19 civilians (eyewitnesses to the arrest and the doctor who examined the applicants). All except the applicants stated that they had been drunk and violent. The Service concluded on 27 September that the police had acted lawfully; the report was not disclosed to the applicants.

On 18 November 2004 the public prosecutor charged the applicants; they were later convicted and received suspended sentences.

On 8 December 2004 the applicants themselves lodged a criminal complaint against three officers for ill-treatment. The case of Safaii v. Austria (no. 44689/09) involved Afghan national Hanif Safaii, who alleged that Austria’s transfer of him to Greece under the Dublin Regulation exposed him to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant and his wife arrived in Austria in August 2008 and claimed asylum on 19 August. They had reached Greece via Iran. There they first stayed in a camp, then with traffickers for three months, and later in public parks. The applicant stated that he had queued to seek asylum but was beaten by police and driven away; without money or support they slept rough. After four failed attempts, traffickers brought the couple to Austria. In Austria he cited Taliban persecution, including the kidnapping of two brothers years earlier.

On 14 October 2008 the Federal Asylum Office rejected the claim as inadmissible, holding Greece responsible under the Dublin II Regulation and the 2005 Asylum Act, and ordered expulsion. It found no real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment, citing UNHCR (April 2008) and Swedish Migration Board reports. While acknowledging criticism of Greek reception, access and procedure, it deemed the applicant’s account of his Greek experiences not credible. Only Norway had briefly halted transfers; other states continued them. UNHCR had welcomed Greek reforms and a joint working group; EU directives bound Greece; the Swedish fact-finding mission of April 2008 had concluded there were no humanitarian reasons to stop returns. Persons never previously registered in Greece would have full access to asylum procedures. The sovereignty clause was therefore unnecessary.

The applicant appealed, stressing Greek systemic deficiencies, risk of chain refoulement to Afghanistan and destitution. On 11 November 2008 the Asylum Court dismissed the complaint. Frequent use of the sovereignty clause would undermine the effectiveness of EU law. Dublin rests on the presumption that all Member States are safe, so counter-arguments require special substantiation. The Swedish report showed that all 26 monitored cases had obtained access to procedure; Greek authorities had confirmed the applicant would have access. Reception support was acceptable and work was permitted; refoulement risk was absent. Hence there was no real Article 3 risk.

The Constitutional Court declined to examine the case on 30 January 2009. The wife was transferred on 25 November 2008 and the applicant on 8 April 2009. Thereafter his lawyer lost all contact and could supply no current address.

Contemporaneous international material (CPT reports 2006–2008, Pro Asyl 2007, Amnesty International 2008, UNHCR studies 2007–2008) documented overcrowded and unsanitary detention, homelessness, police violence, virtually automatic rejection of claims without individual assessment, and obstacles to fair procedure. UNHCR’s April 2008 position paper, while noting reform efforts, advised states to refrain from Dublin transfers to Greece and to apply the sovereignty clause. Norway suspended transfers for several months. A May 2008 Swedish report acknowledged housing shortages but found adult reception generally tolerable and refoulement risk low. These materials formed the backdrop against which the Austrian authorities assessed the applicant’s transfer.

The case of Rumor v. Italy (Application no. 72964/10) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 27 May 2014. The applicant, an Italian national born in 1968, alleged that Italian authorities failed to protect and support her after she suffered domestic violence at the hands of her former partner, J.C.N., a Kenyan national, thereby causing her ongoing anguish and fear in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. She further claimed, under Article 14 read with Article 3, that she had been discriminated against on the basis of her gender.

The couple’s relationship began in 2003 and produced two children, born in 2006 and 2008. It deteriorated rapidly. On 16 November 2008, during an argument about the applicant’s involvement with a mutual friend, J.C.N. repeatedly struck her and threatened her with a knife and scissors. He locked her inside their flat and took the keys. One of the children, awakened by the noise, witnessed part of the assault. Neighbours summoned the carabinieri. The applicant was hospitalised in a state of shock and diagnosed with concussion, head injuries and multiple bruises.

J.C.N. was arrested and charged with attempted murder, kidnapping, aggravated assault and threats. He elected the abbreviated procedure. On 2 April 2009 the first-instance court convicted him and imposed a sentence of four years and eight months’ imprisonment. The applicant did not constitute herself as a civil party. On appeal the sentence was reduced to three years and four months; the Court of Cassation dismissed a further appeal in October 2010.

While serving his sentence J.C.N. applied twice for house arrest. The first request, seeking placement in a facility only 2 km from the applicant’s home, was refused in November 2009 because of the proximity, his psychological state and the risk of contact. A second request, for a centre 15 km away that already housed other prisoners under house arrest and was regularly monitored by the carabinieri, was granted on 18 June 2010. In September 2010 he was authorised to work outside the centre during the grape harvest. He completed his sentence on 2 August 2011 and chose to remain at the same facility.

In parallel juvenile-court proceedings the applicant obtained sole custody in May 2009. In February 2010, after hearing both parents, the court stripped J.C.N. of parental rights and prohibited all contact with the children, noting that he could later apply for restoration once he had served his sentence and acquired adequate parenting skills. In January 2012 he sought restoration of those rights and suspension of his maintenance obligation; the outcome of that application is not known.

After the assault the applicant lived in constant fear of further violence against herself and her children. Both she and her older son received psychological therapy. She obtained material, psychological and legal assistance from a victims’ association. Nevertheless she visited J.C.N. five times while he was in prison (November 2008–June 2010). After his release the two exchanged e-mails.

The Venice Court of Appeal refused on 3 November 2009, citing the proximity, J.C.N.'s psychological condition and the risk of contact. A second application in June 2010 sought house arrest at a centre 15 km away. After a carabinieri inspection confirming the facility's suitability and regular surveillance, the court granted the request on 18 June 2010. The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1960, is the father of three children. His eldest daughter (born 1986, from a prior relationship) lived with him. He married in 1995 and had two further children (born 1996 and 1999). The couple separated in 2002. The Civil Court of East Vaud awarded custody of the younger children to the mother, citing their young age, while granting the applicant extensive contact rights: Thursdays after school until Friday mornings, alternate weeks from Thursday to Monday, and half the school holidays (around seven weeks yearly). The applicant estimated this amounted to 42% of the children’s time. His eldest daughter continued residing with him.

In January 2005 the applicant petitioned for divorce; a joint petition followed in January 2006, with both parents seeking sole parental authority and custody. The Civil Court commissioned two psychiatric expert reports (July 2006 and March 2008). Both found the children trapped in loyalty conflicts and wishing to split time equally. The parents remained deeply antagonistic, unable to agree on child-related matters, and each had difficulty recognising the other’s parenting skills. Although both were competent parents, the mother opposed shared authority, alleging the applicant had pressured her and used improper tactics to obtain custody of his eldest daughter, whom he had allegedly turned against her mother. The experts noted the applicant’s sense of being reduced to a “paying father,” his lingering resentment from the divorce, and his criticism of the mother’s abilities. They concluded that shared authority was not in the children’s best interests and recommended awarding sole authority to the mother while preserving the applicant’s extensive contact rights, thereby ensuring continuity. The youngest child also expressed a preference to remain close to the mother, and the children were well integrated in her household and school.

The applicant withdrew his claim for sole authority and custody in May 2008. On 15 December 2009 the Civil Court granted the divorce, awarded parental authority and custody to the mother, and confirmed the applicant’s existing contact rights. Witnesses testified that he fully exercised those rights and engaged actively with the children, but that the parental relationship remained highly conflictual, with greater animosity emanating from him.

The applicant appealed, invoking the European Court’s judgment in Zaunegger v. Germany and arguing that a father who had demonstrated his parenting capacity since 2002 could not be deprived of authority. The Cantonal Appeal Court dismissed the appeal on 9 February 2010, holding that Article 133 § 1 of the Swiss Civil Code required parental authority to be awarded to one parent only, unless both parents jointly requested shared authority (Article 133 § 3) and the arrangement served the child’s best interests. Shared authority could not be imposed against the mother’s opposition. The court emphasised that the child’s welfare was paramount and that, where both parents were capable, the parent showing greater willingness to cooperate should prevail; the experts had identified the mother as that parent.

The Federal Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on 11 August 2011. It distinguished Zaunegger (which concerned unmarried parents under German law that privileged mothers) on the grounds that the present case involved a divorced couple, Swiss law treated both parents equally, and either could seek sole authority. There was no sex-based privilege or maternal veto; the sole criterion was the children’s best interests.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (right to family life) and Article 14 (discrimination on grounds of sex) arising from the automatic award of sole authority to the mother in the absence of a joint request and from the alleged inability of a divorced father to obtain shared authority against the mother’s wishes. The case of Buchs v. Switzerland (Application no. 9929/12) concerns a Swiss father's complaints to the European Court of Human Rights that Swiss divorce courts violated his right to family life under Article 8 of the Convention and discriminated against him on grounds of sex under Article 14 by awarding sole parental authority over his two younger children to their mother.

The applicant, born in 1960 and living in the Canton of Vaud, is the father of three children. His eldest daughter (born 1986, from a prior relationship) resides with him. He married his ex-wife in 1995; they had two children (born 1996 and 1999). The couple separated in 2002. The Civil Court of the District of East Vaud granted the mother custody, citing the children's young ages, while awarding the applicant extensive contact rights. These included overnight stays every Thursday after school until Friday morning, every other weekend from Thursday to Monday morning, and half of school holidays (approximately seven weeks yearly). The applicant estimated this amounted to 42% of the children's time. The eldest daughter continued living with him.

The Civil Court commissioned two expert reports from child psychiatrists (July 2006 and March 2008). Both experts found the parents in ongoing high conflict, with the children experiencing loyalty conflicts and wishing to split time equally. Both parents were assessed as having good parenting skills and providing adequate environments. However, the experts noted the applicant's difficulties distinguishing his feelings about the divorce from those about the children, his criticism of the mother's abilities, his sense of being a mere “paying father,” and his earlier inappropriate methods of obtaining custody of his eldest daughter. The mother opposed shared authority, fearing the applicant would use it to distance the children from her, though she supported extensive contact. The youngest child wished to remain close to the mother; the children were well-integrated at her home and school. Both experts recommended awarding parental authority to the mother (for continuity and her greater willingness to cooperate) while maintaining the applicant's extensive contact rights. Shared authority was deemed contrary to the children's best interests given the lack of parental cooperation.

After the second report, the applicant withdrew his request for sole authority and custody. Witnesses confirmed he fully exercised his contact rights and engaged in many activities with the children, but that parental relations remained conflictual, with greater animosity from the applicant. On 15 December 2009 the Civil Court granted the divorce, awarded the mother sole parental authority and custody, and confirmed the applicant's extensive contact rights.

The applicant appealed to the Cantonal Appeal Court, arguing (with reference to Zaunegger v. Germany) that parental authority could not be withdrawn from a father who had demonstrated parenting abilities since 2002, criticizing the mother's conduct, and noting he could no longer afford a lawyer. The Appeal Court dismissed the appeal on 9 February 2010. Under Article 133 of the Swiss Civil Code then in force, parental authority after divorce was awarded to only one parent unless both made a joint request (which the mother refused). The child's best interests were paramount; both parents had good skills, but the mother had shown greater willingness to cooperate.

The Federal Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 11 August 2011. It distinguished Zaunegger (which concerned unmarried parents and a maternal veto under German law). Swiss law treated married/divorced parents equally without sex-based privilege or maternal veto; decisions turned solely on the child's best interests. The applicant had been able to apply for sole authority on the same terms as the mother.

(The Swiss Civil Code was later amended, effective 1 July 2014, to make shared parental authority the default after divorce without requiring a joint request, with limited retrospective application possible.)

These facts framed the applicant's claims that the legal framework and its application automatically privileged the mother, preventing him from seeking shared authority despite his proven involvement, thereby interfering with his family life and discriminating against him as a father.

**Case of Buchs v. Switzerland (Application no. 9929/12), ECtHR (Second Section), Judgment of 27 May 2014 (final 27 August 2014)**

The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1960 and residing in Cully (Canton of Vaud), is the father of three children. His eldest daughter (born 1986, from a prior relationship) lived with him. He married in 1995 and had two further children (born 1996 and 1999). The couple separated in 2002. On 16 May 2002 the Civil Court of the District of East Vaud awarded custody of the two younger children to the mother, citing their young age, while granting the applicant extensive contact rights. These comprised overnight stays every Thursday after school until Friday morning, every other week from Thursday after school until Monday morning, and half of school holidays (around seven weeks annually), amounting to approximately 42% of the time.

The applicant filed for divorce in January 2005. After a joint petition in January 2006, both parents sought sole parental authority and custody. The Civil Court commissioned two expert reports from child and adolescent psychiatry specialists (July 2006 and March 2008). Both reports documented ongoing parental conflict, loyalty conflicts for the children (who wished to divide time equally), and the mother's opposition to shared parental authority. She alleged the applicant used pressure and inappropriate tactics (including those previously employed regarding his eldest daughter) that risked distancing the children from her, though she supported his extensive contact. The applicant felt reduced to a “paying father.” Experts found both parents competent but concluded shared authority was not in the children's best interests due to the lack of cooperation and the applicant's residual hostility and difficulty separating personal feelings from parenting. They recommended sole parental authority and custody to the mother for continuity, with the applicant retaining extensive contact rights. The children were well integrated socially and at school with the mother; the younger child wished to remain close to her.

In May 2008 the applicant withdrew his claim for sole authority and custody. On 15 December 2009 the Civil Court granted the divorce, awarded sole parental authority and custody to the mother, and maintained the applicant's existing contact rights. Witnesses confirmed the applicant fully exercised those rights and engaged actively with the children, but the parental relationship remained conflictual, with greater animosity from the applicant.

The applicant lodged a partial appeal, arguing the award of sole authority to the mother violated his rights in light of *Zaunegger v. Germany* (2009) and that he had demonstrated his parenting abilities. The Vaud Appeal Court dismissed the appeal on 9 February 2010, holding that Article 133 § 1 of the Swiss Civil Code required parental authority after divorce to be awarded to one parent only. Shared authority under Article 133 § 3 required a joint parental request and could not be imposed on an opposing parent. The child's best interests (Article 133 § 2) were paramount; where both parents were competent, the more cooperative parent (here the mother, per the experts) should receive authority.

The Federal Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 11 August 2011. It distinguished *Zaunegger* (which concerned unmarried parents under German law privileging the mother) on the grounds that Swiss law treated divorced parents equally: either could seek sole authority, there was no sex-based privilege or maternal veto, and the decision rested solely on the child's best interests. The applicant had not been treated differently from the mother.

Subsequent legislative amendments (adopted 21 June 2013, in force 1 July 2014) made shared parental authority the default after divorce without requiring a joint request, while still permitting sole authority if in the child's best interests. Transitional rules allowed applications in certain prior cases.

The applicant alleged that the domestic decisions infringed his right to respect for family life (Article 8 ECHR) by denying shared parental authority despite his proven involvement and that they discriminated against him as a father on grounds of sex (Article 14 taken with Article 8), in circumstances comparable to *Zaunegger*. The facts centre on the statutory requirement of a joint request for shared authority, the mother's opposition, expert assessments of ongoing conflict and the children's best interests, the applicant's extensive de facto involvement, and the domestic courts' emphasis on equal treatment of parents and the child's welfare rather than any automatic preference based on sex.
