The case of P.K. v. Poland (Application no. 43123/10) concerns a Polish father’s complaint that the authorities failed to take effective measures to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his son, allegedly violating Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

P.K. married in 1999; his son P. was born in 2001. In December 2001 he petitioned for divorce, initially seeking that the child reside with the mother and challenging paternity (a claim later dismissed after DNA confirmation that he was the father). He subsequently sought custody himself. On 28 October 2003 the Lublin Regional Court dissolved the marriage, attributing fault to both parties, awarding joint parental authority, fixing the child’s residence with the mother, and granting the applicant contact every third Sunday from 10 a.m. to noon at the mother’s home in her presence. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in May 2004.

The mother persistently refused to comply. In September 2006 the applicant commenced enforcement proceedings. Courts repeatedly set compliance deadlines and imposed escalating fines on the mother (PLN 600, then 700, 800 and 1,300). A court guardian was appointed in July 2008 to accompany visits and later authorised to remove the child if necessary. Despite these orders, numerous scheduled visits failed because the mother did not answer the door, even when police attended. The applicant himself missed some appointments. Parallel applications by the mother sought to restrict or terminate the applicant’s parental rights, citing his earlier disinterest (he had not seen the child between 2001 and 2006 and had defaulted on maintenance). The applicant in turn sought a change of residence and later the mother’s deprivation of parental authority.

In November 2010 the District Court limited the mother’s parental authority, assigned a supervisory guardian and ordered her to attend family therapy. It recorded the applicant’s prior lack of involvement. A 2012 expert report from the Regional Family Consultation Centre found strong emotional bonds between mother and child, none between father and son, and the child’s unwillingness to have contact; it criticised the applicant’s focus on formal rights over the child’s needs. Brief encounters occurred in 2012, during one of which the child told the applicant he was not wanted.

From 2011 the courts imposed punitive damages on the mother (ultimately PLN 7,000) for repeated non-compliance. Criminal complaints alleging unlawful restriction of the child’s liberty were consistently discontinued: prosecutors found no offence, and a court held that a parent exercising parental authority could not be a perpetrator even if acting against the other parent’s wishes.

The facts therefore describe a protracted sequence of judicial measures—fines, guardians, removal orders, damages and therapy directives—that failed over many years to secure regular contact, against a background of mutual parental hostility, the child’s alienation from the father, and unsuccessful criminal avenues.

**Case Summary: P.K. v. Poland (ECHR, Application no. 43123/10, Judgment 10 June 2014)**

The applicant, a Polish national born in 1978, married in 1999; his son P. was born in 2001. In December 2001 he petitioned for divorce, initially claiming he was not the biological father (a claim later disproved by DNA tests) and requesting that the child reside with the mother. He later sought custody himself and (according to the Government) placement of the child in public care. On 28 October 2003 the Lublin Regional Court dissolved the marriage, finding both parents at fault. Joint parental authority was retained, but P.’s residence was fixed with the mother. The applicant was granted contact every third Sunday from 10 a.m. to noon at the mother’s home and in her presence. The court criticised the applicant’s conduct and expressed doubt about his genuine interest in contact. His appeal was dismissed in May 2004.

Thereafter the mother persistently refused to comply. In September 2006 the applicant began enforcement proceedings. He could not recall when he had last seen his son; the mother claimed he had shown no interest until she sought higher maintenance. In June 2007 the District Court set a one-month compliance deadline, backed by a PLN 600 fine. Further fines (PLN 700, 800, 1 300) and successive deadlines followed in 2007–2008. In July 2008 a court guardian was appointed to accompany every visit. The mother applied to restrict the applicant’s parental rights and ban contact; the applicant applied for a change of residence. Both applications were largely unsuccessful; the court found the child’s living conditions with the mother satisfactory.

From 2009 the court authorised the guardian to remove the child if necessary. Repeated attempts (August 2009, January, April–June 2010, December 2010, April–May 2011) failed because no one answered the door, even when police attended. Enforcement orders automatically expired after three months, requiring fresh applications. The applicant sometimes failed to attend scheduled visits. He and the guardian repeatedly notified prosecutors of the mother’s obstruction. Investigations were discontinued on the ground that her conduct did not constitute a criminal offence of unlawful restriction of a minor’s liberty; a 2011 indictment was likewise dismissed because a custodial parent could not be the perpetrator of that offence.

In November 2010 the District Court dismissed the mother’s application to deprive the applicant of parental authority, limited her own authority by appointing a supervisory guardian, and ordered family therapy. A 2012 expert report from the Regional Family Consultation Centre found strong emotional bonds between mother and child, none between father and child, and a lack of willingness on the child’s part to have contact. The experts criticised the applicant for focusing on his legal rights rather than the child’s needs and for seeking to deprive the mother of authority. After legislative changes in August 2011 the court imposed punitive damages (initially PLN 1 000 per breach, later increased on appeal to PLN 7 000 for seven instances of non-compliance or obstruction in 2012). Occasional brief contacts occurred in 2012, during one of which the child told the applicant he was not wanted.

Throughout, the authorities imposed fines, appointed guardians, authorised removal of the child, and later awarded damages, yet contact remained sporadic or non-existent for years because of the mother’s non-cooperation, the automatic expiry of enforcement orders, the inapplicability of criminal sanctions, and the applicant’s own intermittent non-attendance. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the State had failed to take effective measures to secure his right to contact, thereby violating Article 8 of the Convention.

The case of Dončev and Burgov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 30265/09) concerns two Macedonian police officers, Dragan Dončev (born 1971) and Stojan Burgov (born 1970), both from Strumica, who alleged a violation of their defence rights under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Their complaint focused on the use of evidence from an unidentified undercover agent, treated as a protected witness, in proceedings that led to their conviction for accepting a bribe.

On 3 March 2005, the public prosecutor authorised special investigative measures under the Criminal Proceedings Act, including secret surveillance, audio-visual recording, a simulated bribe offer, and undercover agents. These targeted suspected bribery by traffic police and ran from 15 March to 13 May 2005. On 28 April 2005, the applicants stopped a speeding vehicle near Strumica, driven by K.N. (an undercover agent). They recorded a warning in official notes but neither issued a formal report nor brought charges. The Ministry of the Interior later alleged they had accepted 500 Macedonian denars (MKD) from K.N. to forgo those steps. A criminal complaint followed on 8 June 2005, noting partial admissions by the applicants.

An investigating judge opened proceedings on 12 July 2005; the applicants remained silent. The 19 September 2005 indictment charged them with accepting the bribe and sought admission of photographs plus audio-visual recordings of the 28 April encounter. On 28 November 2005 the trial court admitted this evidence and, on 30 November, convicted the applicants, imposing six-month suspended prison sentences. It relied on the audio recording to find that K.N. had exceeded the speed limit, offered money, and that the applicants had accepted it in lieu of a fine (MKD 4,000–12,000) or 30 days’ imprisonment plus a driving ban.

The applicants appealed, arguing the recording showed only an offer, not acceptance; no pre-marked notes were recovered; they had been entitled to issue a warning; the transcript was incomplete; and they had neither examined nor confronted K.N. On 28 June 2006 the Štip Court of Appeal quashed the conviction for inadequate fact-finding and insufficient reasons, directing re-examination of the evidence, questioning of K.N., and possible confrontation.

At the 15 May 2007 retrial hearing the applicants denied receiving money and challenged the recording’s integrity. Their lawyer requested examination of K.N. and information on whether the money had been marked. The Ministry later confirmed the notes were unmarked (as audio-visual measures had been used) and that the undercover agent could testify as a protected witness. On 7 December 2007 the trial court examined K.N. as a protected witness under statutory provisions designed to safeguard identity. Because no secure room existed, the applicants, their lawyers and the public were excluded by prior agreement (to which they did not object at the time). K.N. described deliberately speeding, being stopped, witnessing another alleged bribe, offering 500 MKD after the applicants indicated they would not punish him, and handing over the money. After K.N. left, the applicants were given a transcript and invited to submit written questions via the court; they instead sought recusal of the judges, claiming unlawful exclusion and denial of confrontation. Recusal requests were rejected.

Subsequent hearings (April–May 2008) saw the applicants receive the transcript, decline to question K.N. in writing, and object to the record as contradictory. On 16 May 2008 they were reconvicted and given six-month suspended sentences. The court found the protected-witness statement consistent with the audio recording and declined confrontation because of the witness’s protected status. The applicants appealed, reiterating insufficient evidence of acceptance, unmarked notes, lawful use of a warning, challenges to the recording, and the fact that they already knew K.N., rendering protected-witness status unreasonable. They stressed that the statement had been taken in their absence and that they had been denied questions or confrontation.

On 18 November 2008 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the special measures and protected-witness examination lawful. It noted the applicants’ agreement to the in-absentia hearing and their subsequent opportunity to pose written questions. The convictions became final after the judgment was served in December 2008. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court on 3 June 2009, complaining specifically that reliance on the anonymous undercover agent’s evidence had breached their Article 6 rights to a fair trial and to examine witnesses against them.

The applicants, two Macedonian traffic police officers, were convicted of accepting a 500 MKD bribe from a speeding motorist in April 2005 in exchange for issuing only an oral warning rather than a formal report and charges. The motorist was in fact an undercover police officer acting pursuant to a March 2005 public-prosecutor order authorizing special investigative measures (secret surveillance, audio-visual recording, simulated bribe and undercover agents) against traffic police suspected of corruption.

The applicants remained silent during the investigation. At first-instance trial they were convicted on the basis of four photographs and an audio recording of the stop, which the court treated as proving both the speeding offence and the acceptance of money. On appeal the Štip Court of Appeal quashed the conviction, holding that neither the photographs nor the audio established that money had actually changed hands and that the driver had never been examined. It remitted the case with instructions to re-hear the existing evidence, to question the driver and, if necessary, to confront him with the accused.

On remittal the trial court requested the Ministry of the Interior to identify the driver and to state whether the notes had been marked. The Ministry replied that the notes were unmarked (the audio-visual measures rendered marking unnecessary) and that the undercover agent could be heard only as a protected witness under the Criminal Procedure Act. At a hearing on 7 December 2007 the court therefore examined the witness (pseudonym K.N.) in a separate room in the presence of only the judge and prosecutor; the applicants and their lawyers were excluded after an “advance agreement.” The witness described deliberately speeding, witnessing another bribe, offering 500 MKD himself and receiving the reply “there is no price-list, it’s up to you.” After the statement the applicants were given a transcript and invited to submit written questions through the court. They immediately protested, demanded the judges’ recusal and asserted that no genuine examination had occurred.

Subsequent hearings were adjourned because the witness could not be produced. On 9 May 2008 defence counsel formally declined to examine the protected witness and challenged the 7 December record as contradictory. The court nevertheless read the statement into evidence, admitted the prosecutor’s order, the photographs and the audio-visual recording, and again convicted the applicants. It relied on the consistency between the protected-witness account and the audio transcript and explained that confrontation had been withheld because the witness’s identity was classified.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the conviction rested decisively on the untested statement of a person they had already met, that they had been denied any opportunity to question or confront him, that the notes were unmarked and that the audio did not prove acceptance of money. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the special measures had been lawfully ordered, that the examination in the applicants’ absence had been by agreement and that they had been given the chance to put written questions. It found the witness’s detailed narrative corroborated by the audio recording.

The applicants complained to the European Court that these arrangements violated their Article 6 defence rights: they had been convicted on the decisive evidence of an anonymous undercover agent whom they had never been able to confront or cross-examine.

The case of Dončev and Burgov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 30265/09) concerns two traffic police officers, Dragan Dončev and Stojan Burgov, who alleged a violation of their Article 6 defence rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. The complaint centred on their conviction for bribery, which relied on evidence from an anonymous undercover agent whose identity was never disclosed and whom they were not permitted to confront or cross-examine directly.

In March 2005 the public prosecutor authorised special investigative measures—including secret surveillance, audio-visual recording, a simulated bribe offer and the deployment of undercover agents—after the Ministry of the Interior suspected traffic police of accepting bribes. The order remained valid until mid-May. On 28 April 2005 the applicants stopped a vehicle driven by an undercover officer known only as “K.N.” for exceeding the speed limit by more than 30 km/h. They recorded a verbal warning but neither drew up an official report nor instituted misdemeanour proceedings.

In June 2005 the Ministry filed a criminal complaint alleging that the applicants had accepted 500 Macedonian denars from K.N. in exchange for forgoing formal action. An investigating judge opened an inquiry; the applicants remained silent. The September 2005 indictment requested admission of four photographs and an audio-visual recording of the encounter. The first-instance court convicted the applicants in November 2005 on the basis of the recording, imposing a six-month suspended sentence. The applicants appealed, arguing that the recording showed only an offer of money, not acceptance; that no pre-marked notes had been recovered; that a warning was a lawful alternative; and that the court had neither heard nor confronted them with the driver.

The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction in June 2006, holding that the photographs and audio material did not prove acceptance and that the driver had not been examined. It instructed the trial court to re-hear the evidence, question the driver and, if necessary, arrange a confrontation. At the retrial the applicants again denied receiving money. The court requested the Ministry to identify K.N. so that he could be examined and confronted. The Ministry replied that the notes had not been marked (because other special measures were already in place) and that the undercover officer could be heard only as a protected witness whose identity remained classified.

On 7 December 2007 the trial court examined K.N. in the applicants’ absence, citing the absence of a special room and an alleged prior agreement. The witness gave a detailed account of offering and handing over 500 denars, which one applicant allegedly accepted. After the examination the applicants were given a transcript and told they could submit written questions through the court. They immediately challenged the procedure, asserting that they had already met the driver and that no genuine statement had been taken. Their recusal requests were rejected. At subsequent hearings the driver failed to appear. The applicants’ lawyer formally declined to examine the protected witness and objected to the record as contradictory. In closing submissions the defence argued that the term “protected witness” was inapplicable because the applicants already knew the driver, that they had been denied confrontation, and that neither the audio material nor unmarked notes proved acceptance.

In May 2008 the trial court again convicted the applicants, finding the protected-witness statement consistent with the audio recording and holding that confrontation was unnecessary once identity protection had been invoked. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in November 2008, confirming that the special measures had been lawfully ordered, that the witness had been examined by agreement in the applicants’ absence, and that they had subsequently been given the opportunity to put written questions. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 June 2009, complaining that their conviction rested to a decisive extent on the untested testimony of an anonymous undercover agent whose identity had never been disclosed.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Australian national Lee Sydney Harrison McKee against Hungary (no. 22840/07). The applicant, born in 1948 and residing in Australia, alleged that Hungarian courts imposed excessive court fees in his civil action for compensation, thereby violating his Convention rights.

In 2003 the applicant, represented by Hungarian counsel, sued a public prosecutor attached to the Budapest Regional Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Office itself, and the Office of the Attorney General. He claimed that a letter the prosecutor sent to the Pest Central District Court during criminal proceedings against him contained false statements that infringed his personality rights, specifically his honour, dignity and reputation. Because of the subject-matter, section 64 of the 1990 Stamp Duties Act exempted him from advancing court fees.

The applicant later amended his claim to seek HUF 390 million (approximately EUR 1.314 million) in non-pecuniary damages. This figure reflected his personal valuation of his reputation rather than amounts typically awarded in comparable Hungarian cases; he nevertheless maintained the claim throughout.

On 22 September 2005 the Budapest Regional Court discontinued the action against the Regional Prosecutor’s Office for lack of standing. It found that the prosecutor’s statements had violated the applicant’s right to reputation and ordered her to apologise, but it dismissed the damages claim as excessive and unsupported by proof of actual harm. Applying section 39 of the Stamp Duties Act (6 % of the claim, subject to a HUF 15 000 minimum and HUF 900 000 maximum), the court ordered the applicant to pay HUF 879 000 (approximately EUR 2 900). It explained that fees must be calculated on the dismissed portion of the claim and noted that the sum sought far exceeded awards normally granted in similar actions.

Both sides appealed. On 3 October 2006 the Budapest Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the first-instance costs ruling. It additionally ordered the applicant to pay HUF 900 000 (approximately EUR 3 000) in appellate fees, again calculated as a percentage of the unsuccessful claim.

The respondents then sought review. On 4 July 2007 the Supreme Court quashed the lower courts’ judgments and dismissed the entire action. It held that the prosecutor’s statements, made in the exercise of her official functions within the criminal proceedings, could not constitute an unlawful interference with personality rights. The Supreme Court ordered the applicant to pay aggregate court fees of HUF 1 836 000 (approximately EUR 6 000) for all three instances—less than the theoretical maximum of HUF 4.3 million (approximately EUR 14 200) that would have applied under sections 42, 46 and 50 of the Stamp Duties Act (6 %, 8 % and 10 % respectively, with statutory ceilings).

The relevant Hungarian rules (Code of Civil Procedure ss. 75, 77, 81, 84 and 85/A; Stamp Duties Act ss. 39, 42, 46 and 50) provide that court fees are generally a percentage of the value of the claim or of the unsuccessful part thereof, subject to statutory minima and maxima. In actions involving judicially quantified damages, a court may still require the unsuccessful party to bear costs in proportion to the amount claimed if that amount is not regarded as manifestly excessive. Natural persons of limited means may obtain exemption or reduction, but the applicant did not rely on such provisions once the proceedings had begun. The case of Harrison McKee v. Hungary (application no. 22840/07) concerns an Australian national’s complaint that Hungarian courts imposed excessive court fees on him after he brought unsuccessful civil proceedings against public prosecutors and related offices for alleged violations of his personality rights. Because of the subject-matter of the action he was initially exempt from having to advance court fees under the then-applicable stamp-duty legislation.

The applicant later amended his claim to seek non-pecuniary damages of HUF 390 million (approximately EUR 1.314 million). It found that the prosecutor’s statements had violated the applicant’s right to reputation and ordered her to apologise, but it dismissed the claim for compensation as excessive and unsupported by proof of actual damage. Applying the statutory rule that stamp duty in civil cases was 6 per cent of the value of the claim (subject to a floor of HUF 15 000 and a ceiling of HUF 900 000), the court ordered the applicant to pay HUF 879 000 (approximately EUR 2 900). The relevant domestic provisions (Code of Civil Procedure and Stamp Duties Act) provided that court costs generally followed the event, with fees assessed as a percentage of the value of the claim or of the part remaining in dispute (6 per cent at first instance, 8 per cent on appeal, 10 per cent on review), subject to statutory minima and maxima. The case of Marčan v. Croatia (no. 40820/12) concerned an application by Goran Marčan, a Croatian lawyer born in 1967 and living in Rijeka. He alleged that summary minor-offence proceedings against him were unfair, in violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) and (d) of the Convention (right to a fair trial, including to defend oneself and examine witnesses).

On 7 July 2010 the applicant was stopped near Vrgorac by a police officer who alleged he had dangerously overtaken another vehicle and was driving with inappropriate tyres. The officer prepared a report. On 6 October 2010 the applicant received a penalty notice dated 12 July 2010 from the Dubrovnik-Neretvanska Police Department. It imposed a fine of HRK 1,500 for offences under sections 12 and 236 of the Road Traffic Safety Act. The notice stated that the facts had been established by the officer’s personal observations and report.

The applicant lodged a request for judicial review on 7 October 2010, denying the offences and asking to be heard. Summary proceedings opened before the Vrgorac Minor Offences Court. He was summoned for questioning on 23 February and 30 March 2011 but did not appear, citing professional commitments, and asked instead to be questioned by the Rijeka Minor Offences Court (where he lived). On 3 May 2011 the case file was forwarded to Rijeka, giving him access to it.

On 17 October 2011 a Rijeka judge questioned him. He maintained that he had not overtaken any car when stopped, claimed his tyres were factory-standard, and promised supporting documents (but later failed to submit them). He offered no other evidence. The file was returned to Vrgorac on 28 October 2011.

On 21 November 2011 the Vrgorac court convicted him, issuing a caution, a reduced fine of HRK 500 and HRK 100 in costs. It relied solely on the 7 July 2010 police report, finding that the applicant’s defence had not cast doubt on it. No hearing was held and the police officer was not examined.

The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court on 2 March 2012 that he had never seen the report, had been given no opportunity to challenge its accusations, and that the court had based its verdict solely on the untested report without allowing cross-examination. On 2 May 2012 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, holding that no constitutional rights had been violated and that the lower court had not acted arbitrarily. The decision was served on 18 May 2012. Enforcement of the fine remains pending.

Relevant domestic law included constitutional fair-trial guarantees and the Minor Offences Act, which provided for summary procedure (no main hearing) in cases involving modest fines. After an objection to a mandatory penalty notice, the court could decide on the basis of the case file and any questioning, without applying ordinary hearing rules. The conviction thus rested entirely on the unchallenged police report.

The case of Čačko v. Slovakia (Application no. 49905/08) concerns a Slovak national, Róbert Čačko (born 1970), who alleged that his irreducible life sentence violated Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. He is serving the sentence in Leopoldov prison.

On 7 September 2005, Čačko was taken to a police station and questioned about the death of his stepfather, whom he was accused of stabbing fourteen times. He was formally arrested early on 8 September 2005 and remanded in custody. During the investigation, he repeatedly admitted the stabbing in his lawyer’s presence but later claimed he had not intended to kill and sought reclassification as causing bodily harm. He was indicted on 5 December 2005.

On 13 July 2007 the Košice Regional Court convicted him of murder. Relying on witness statements, expert medical and forensic opinions, and other evidence, it found he had deliberately stabbed the heavily intoxicated victim with intent to kill, acting in a particularly contemptible manner while intoxicated and exhibiting an abnormally antisocial personality. An expert reported that Čačko was pathologically aggressive, lacked self-control, had virtually no prospects of re-socialisation and posed an extremely high risk of re-offending. He had five prior convictions, including rape and murder (the latter committed only months after conditional release from a similar sentence). The court therefore imposed life imprisonment without parole under the 1961 Criminal Code (Articles 219 § 2, 29 §§ 1 and 3, 30 § 1(c), 43 § 1 and 35 § 3). It also quashed an unrelated six-month sentence.

Čačko appealed, arguing that his admissions had been made under shock, fatigue and alleged police pressure, that there was no direct evidence, that relevant facts had not been established and that certain witnesses and reconstructions had been omitted. On 27 February 2008 the Supreme Court quashed only the sentencing part, re-imposed life imprisonment and expressly excluded parole under the correct provision (Article 30 § 1(d)). It otherwise upheld the conviction, noting that Čačko’s detailed admissions (known only to the perpetrator) and corroborating physical evidence (including a blood-stained T-shirt) were reliable. The statutory conditions for an irreducible life sentence were met.

An appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Supreme Court’s cassation chamber on 2 March 2009. It found no errors of law; the pre-trial interrogations had been lawful and the three-strike rule and discretionary exclusion of parole had been correctly applied.

On 7 May 2009 Čačko lodged a constitutional complaint alleging, inter alia, breaches of Articles 3 and 13 (as well as other Convention rights) in connection with his conviction and sentence. He asked the Constitutional Court to quash the ordinary-court decisions and requested legal aid. On 21 September 2009 a Constitutional Court judge set the complaint aside under section 23(a) of the 1993 Constitutional Court Act because it failed to specify an enforceable outcome within the Court’s powers.

Domestic law at the time of sentencing (1961 Criminal Code) permitted an exceptional life sentence for murder in particularly dangerous circumstances with no prospect of reform by a 15–25-year term (Article 29 § 3) and, under the three-strike rule (Article 43 § 1), required life imprisonment for a third serious violent offence. Article 30 § 1(d) allowed exclusion of parole for such offenders, and Article 62 § 3 barred conditional release. The 2005 Criminal Code (in force from 1 January 2006) initially maintained the bar on parole for three-strike whole-life prisoners (Article 67 § 3), but an amendment effective 1 January 2010 limited the bar to those given whole-life sentences more than once. Transitional provisions and Supreme Court practice allow the 2005 Code’s more favourable parole rules to apply to earlier sentences. Presidential pardon (Constitution Article 102 and Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 472–475) remains available, including conditionally, on the Minister of Justice’s recommendation.

Čačko later filed a fresh (inadmissible) appeal on points of law in 2013, which remained pending. He also complained of media coverage implying his guilt and of being ordered to reimburse detention costs.

The Constitutional Court set the complaint aside on 21 September 2009 because it failed to specify an enforceable outcome within the court's powers.

Domestic law at the time of sentencing (1961 Criminal Code) permitted life imprisonment without parole for repeat serious offenders when there was no prospect of reform by a determinate term. The 2005 Criminal Code, applicable after 1 January 2006, initially maintained the same exclusion for whole-life sentences under the three-strike rule; an amendment effective 1 January 2010 limited the exclusion to persons who had received whole-life sentences more than once, allowing others to seek parole after 25 years. Transitional provisions apply the newer rules to sentences imposed under the old Code. The Constitution also empowers the President (with countersignature of the Prime Minister or a minister) to grant individual pardons or commute sentences, a process prepared by the Ministry of Justice and subject to possible conditions.

The applicant remains in Leopoldov Prison serving the life term. Periods of earlier detention were credited against the sentence, though he was required to reimburse detention costs. Newspaper articles at the time portrayed him as a brutal offender, which he attributed to leaks from prosecutors. In November 2013 he filed a further (still-pending) appeal on points of law.

These facts form the basis of the applicant's claim that the life sentence was de facto and de jure irreducible, constituting inhuman and degrading treatment contrary to Article 3, and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.
001-146383:
The case of P.F. v. Poland (Application no. 2210/12) concerns a Polish father's complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that domestic authorities failed to take effective measures to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his twin daughters, born in April 2004. The applicant and the girls' mother, A.W., began a relationship in 2003 and separated in February 2005. Contact thereafter became irregular.

On 2 November 2007 the applicant applied to the Warsaw Mokotów District Court for contact arrangements and an interim order. Simultaneously A.W. alleged that he had sexually abused the children. The prosecutor opened a criminal investigation in February 2008; the family court stayed the contact proceedings. An interim order of 21 January 2008 nevertheless granted the applicant visits every other Sunday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The criminal investigation was discontinued on 31 October 2008 for lack of evidence; a court-appointed expert found no psychological signs of abuse, though a private expert commissioned by A.W. reached the opposite conclusion. A.W.'s appeal against discontinuance failed.

Contact proceedings resumed in January 2009. Successive interim orders followed: 10 June 2009 (every Saturday 9 a.m.–6 p.m. at the mother's home); 24 February 2010 (every Saturday 10 a.m.–2 p.m. at home, plus expert assessments); and 9 March 2011 (every other Saturday and Sunday 10 a.m.–4 p.m. away from the mother's home). Experts from the Regional Family Consultation Centre reported that the mother had drawn the children into the parental conflict, that the girls themselves sought contact with their father, and that joint therapy was needed. The mother repeatedly cancelled or refused visits, citing the children's alleged unavailability or her own safety concerns; from September 2011 until February/March 2012 she blocked all contact. A final first-instance decision of 16 December 2011 mixed supervised home visits with the mother present and visits at the father's home with a court-appointed guardian. That decision was later quashed on procedural grounds (incorrect joinder of custody-limitation proceedings). A fresh decision of 3 December 2012 allowed unsupervised contact every other weekend 10 a.m.–4 p.m. outside the mother's home, plus limited holiday time, but prohibited overnight stays.

Throughout, the applicant sought enforcement of the successive orders by applying for fines against A.W. under the Code of Civil Procedure. A May 2010 order threatened a 500-zloty fine if she failed to comply within 30 days, yet subsequent enforcement applications were discontinued once a later interim order superseded the one being enforced. A further fine was imposed only in January 2013. Regular Saturday visits at the mother's home eventually resumed in early 2012, but by then several years of disrupted or non-existent contact had already elapsed. The applicant maintained that the authorities' delays, repeated modifications of orders, and ineffective enforcement left his right to family life unprotected.

The case of P.F. v. Poland (no. 2210/12) involves a Polish applicant's claim under Article 8 that authorities failed to enforce his contact rights with his twin daughters effectively.

The applicant and A.W. started a relationship in May 2003; twins A. and J. were born 13 April 2004. They separated in February 2005. On 2 November 2007, the applicant sought contact arrangements and an interim order from the Warsaw Mokotów District Court. A.W. alleged sexual abuse of the children, prompting a prosecutor's notification, a social enquiry, and a criminal investigation from 19 February 2008. An interim order of 21 January 2008 allowed visits every other Sunday, 10 a.m.–2 p.m. Custody proceedings were stayed on 28 March 2008 pending the criminal case; the court separately initiated limitation of the applicant's custody rights on 15 June 2008.

Criminal proceedings ended on 31 October 2008 for insufficient evidence. A court expert found no psychological signs of abuse, contrary to A.W.'s private expert; her appeal failed. Contact proceedings resumed on 20 January 2009. An interim order of 10 June 2009 permitted Saturday visits, 9 a.m.–6 p.m., at the children's home (appeals dismissed November 2009). The applicant reported non-compliance. A.W. sought reduced visits. On 24 February 2010 the order became Saturdays, 10 a.m.–2 p.m., at home, with expert assessments ordered. A September 2010 Regional Family Consultation Centre report stated the mother had involved the children in the conflict; they wanted contact with their father (including at his home) and recommended therapy. Experts confirmed no abuse symptoms.

A 9 March 2011 interim order allowed every-other-weekend visits, 10 a.m.–4 p.m., outside the home to preserve the emotional bond. A.W. refused compliance (appeal dismissed July 2011) and cancelled or blocked visits, refusing all contact from 10 September 2011. Her modification request was dismissed. A 16 December 2011 decision mixed home visits (with mother) and applicant-home visits (with guardian); the applicant appealed. Weekly Saturday contact at A.W.'s home resumed from March 2012. On 29 May 2012 the Regional Court quashed the decision as the joined proceedings used an incorrect court composition and were void.

At a 30 November 2012 hearing, the applicant described irregular post-2005 contact, A.W.'s absences, and total refusal from September 2011 to February 2012. A.W. cited abuse concerns (despite experts) and planned a move to Gdańsk. A 3 December 2012 order granted every-other-weekend visits, 10 a.m.–4 p.m., outside the home without A.W., plus holiday time, but no overnights. Both appealed.

The applicant repeatedly sought fines for non-compliance under the Code of Civil Procedure. A 17 May 2010 order required A.W. to obey the February 2010 interim terms within 30 days or pay 500 PLN, noting some earlier visits occurred under a prior order due to legal advice and that the applicant had shortened some. Proceedings were discontinued in March 2011 after a new order (appeal dismissed August 2011). A November 2012 motion produced a fine on 4 January 2013.

These events—prolonged delays, frequent order changes, dismissed abuse claims, persistent maternal obstruction, and limited enforcement—underpin the alleged failure to protect the applicant's family-life rights.

The case of P.F. v. Poland (Application no. 2210/12) concerns a Polish father's complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that domestic authorities failed to take effective measures to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his twin daughters.

P.F. (born 1963) began a relationship with A.W. in May 2003. Their daughters, A. and J., were born on 13 April 2004. The couple separated in February 2005. On 2 November 2007, P.F. applied to the Warsaw Mokotów District Court for contact arrangements and an interim order. Simultaneously, A.W. reported alleged sexual abuse of the girls to the prosecutor, prompting a social enquiry and a criminal investigation launched on 19 February 2008.

An interim order of 21 January 2008 permitted P.F. visits every other Sunday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Custody proceedings were stayed on 28 March 2008 pending the criminal case, and the court later initiated proceedings of its own motion to limit P.F.'s parental rights. The criminal investigation was discontinued on 31 October 2008 for insufficient evidence; a court expert found no psychological signs of abuse in the children (though A.W. produced a conflicting private opinion). The discontinuation was upheld on appeal. Contact proceedings resumed on 20 January 2009.

Subsequent interim orders progressively adjusted contact: 10 June 2009 (every Saturday, 9 a.m.–6 p.m. at the mother's home); 24 February 2010 (every Saturday, 10 a.m.–2 p.m. at home, with expert assessments ordered); and 9 March 2011 (every other Saturday and Sunday, 10 a.m.–4 p.m. outside the home). Expert reports from the Regional Family Consultation Centre (RODK) in 2010–2011 indicated that the mother had drawn the children into the parental conflict, that the girls desired contact with their father (including at his home), and that family therapy was advisable. A court expert similarly found no typical signs of sexual abuse. A.W. repeatedly failed to comply, cancelling visits or refusing access (including a complete refusal from September 2011 until early 2012). She also sought modifications, citing concerns for the children's welfare and later announcing plans to relocate to Gdańsk.

A first-instance decision of 16 December 2011 allowed contact every other weekend (partly at each parent's home, with a guardian present at the father's) but was quashed on 29 May 2012 by the Regional Court on procedural grounds (improper joinder of proceedings and incorrect court composition). A fresh decision of 3 December 2012 granted contact every other weekend outside the mother's home (without her presence), plus specified holiday periods, but barred overnight stays. Both parties appealed. From March 2012 onward, limited weekly contact resumed at A.W.'s home.

P.F. repeatedly sought enforcement of the interim orders through applications for fines under the Code of Civil Procedure. One motion (November 2009) led to a 17 May 2010 order requiring A.W. to comply within 30 days or face a 500 PLN fine; the court noted some cancellations attributable to P.F. himself and an initial misunderstanding of the order's finality. Later enforcement proceedings were discontinued in March 2011 after a new interim order superseded the previous one (appeal dismissed August 2011). A further fine was imposed on A.W. on 4 January 2013. Relevant domestic provisions (Family and Custody Code Article 106 and CCP Articles 730, 1050–1051, later supplemented by a specific 2011 chapter on contact enforcement) permitted modification of arrangements in the child's interest and coercive fines for non-compliance, but P.F. alleged these mechanisms proved ineffective over several years of obstruction.

The Court granted the applicant anonymity. The facts highlight prolonged delays, repeated modifications, expert findings of maternal interference, and limited coercive success in securing regular, meaningful contact.
001-145572:
The case of Ashlarba v. Georgia (Application no. 45554/08) originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Georgian national Izet Ashlarba, who alleged a violation of Article 7 of the Convention. He claimed that Article 223(1) § 1 of the Georgian Criminal Code, under which he was convicted of membership in the “thieves’ underworld,” lacked the precision and foreseeability needed for him to regulate his conduct.

The applicant, born in 1956 and resident in the Ajarian Autonomous Republic, became involved after a February 2006 investigation into Mr. A.K., suspected of being a “thief in law” who ran criminal syndicates and resolved private disputes through illicit means. Witnesses, including prison officers and associates, confirmed A.K. had received the title via a 1999 “baptism” ritual and thereafter managed the underworld according to its special rules. Phone taps revealed A.K., then a fugitive, regularly instructed others, including the applicant. The probe expanded accordingly, and the applicant was arrested on 31 July 2006 alongside another suspect. Questioned that day, he admitted a 30-year acquaintance with A.K. and knowledge of his title, describing a “thief in law” as “a righteous man.”

On 27 March 2007 the Batumi City Court convicted the applicant under Article 223(1) § 1 and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. It found he had publicly supported the underworld through his lifestyle, actively pursued its goals by securing profits, terrorizing and coercing ordinary people, disseminating its rules, and assisting A.K. The conviction rested on three episodes corroborated by witnesses and taps.

First, A.K. asked the applicant to resolve an apartment dispute between A.K.’s mother-in-law and another person. Between 24 June and July 2006 the applicant became involved, invoking A.K.’s criminal authority. He unsuccessfully argued he had merely sought a friendly settlement for an acquaintance and had not known such conduct was criminal, noting the parties were already in civil court.

Second, on 24 July 2006 A.K. asked him to locate two young men who had refused to pay a taxi fare and to persuade them, using his own and A.K.’s authority, to settle the debt. The applicant implicitly acknowledged the request but claimed he had taken no action and therefore could not be liable.

Third, on 8 July 2006, while visiting an imprisoned acquaintance regarded as a future “thief in law,” the applicant discussed finances of the underworld’s common fund (the “kitty” or obshyak) and remarked that the Interior Minister’s possible removal would strengthen the authority of thieves in law. He argued this was merely an expression of opinion.

Appeals reiterating these arguments were dismissed by the Kutaisi Court of Appeal on 10 July 2007 and by the Supreme Court on 29 February 2008.

Article 223(1), inserted by a 20 December 2005 amendment, punishes membership in the thieves’ underworld with five to eight years’ imprisonment. An accompanying Law on Organised Crime and Racketeering defines the underworld as any group acting under special self-adopted rules whose aim is profit through intimidation, threats, coercion, a code of silence, dispute settlement via a thief-in-law’s authority, youth recruitment, or the commission or encouragement of offences. A member is anyone who recognises those rules and actively furthers the group’s goals. Settlement of disputes using such authority is defined as resolution of a private quarrel accompanied by threat, coercion or other illicit conduct. The official explanatory memorandum stated that existing organised-crime provisions were insufficient to address these syndicates.

Socio-legal studies submitted by the Government describe the post-Soviet “thieves’ underworld” as a hierarchical structure with initiation rituals, a strict code, and elite “thieves in law” who rarely commit crimes themselves but exercise reputation-based authority, administer the kitty, settle disputes, recruit youth and coordinate lower-level criminals. Georgian thieves in law historically formed one of the most influential ethnic groups within this network.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s contention that the newly enacted provision was too vague for him reasonably to foresee that his ordinary social interactions and expressions of opinion would constitute a criminal offence.

The case originated from an application by Izet Ashlarba, a Georgian national born in 1956, alleging a violation of Article 7 of the Convention. He claimed that Article 223(1) § 1 of the Georgian Criminal Code, under which he was convicted of membership in the “thieves’ underworld,” lacked sufficient precision and foreseeability to allow him to regulate his conduct.

A criminal investigation began on 15 February 2006 into Mr A.K., suspected of being a “thief in law” who directed criminal syndicates and resolved private disputes through illicit means. Witnesses, including prison officers and A.K.’s associates, confirmed that A.K. had received the title via a “baptism” ritual in 1999 and thereafter managed the underworld according to its special rules. Telephone taps revealed A.K.’s regular instructions to the applicant. The probe was expanded accordingly.

On 31 July 2006 the applicant was arrested under Article 223(1) § 1. He admitted knowing A.K. for thirty years and being aware of his status as a “thief in law,” whom he described as “a righteous man.” The investigation was closed on 29 September 2006 and the case sent to trial.

On 27 March 2007 the Batumi City Court convicted the applicant of membership in the thieves’ underworld and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. The court found that he had publicly supported the underworld through his lifestyle, obtained profits for its members, terrorised ordinary people, disseminated its rules, and assisted A.K. in running it. Guilt rested on three episodes corroborated by witness statements and further telephone intercepts.

First, A.K. asked the applicant to settle a dispute over an apartment involving A.K.’s mother-in-law. Between 24 June and July 2006 the applicant unofficially adjudicated the matter by invoking A.K.’s criminal authority. The applicant contended he had merely sought an amicable resolution for a close acquaintance and had not realised such conduct was criminal.

Second, on 24 July 2006 A.K. asked the applicant to locate two young men who had refused to pay a taxi fare and to compel payment by using his own and A.K.’s authority. The applicant maintained he had taken no practical steps.

Third, on 8 July 2006, while visiting an imprisoned associate regarded as a future “thief in law,” the applicant discussed the underworld’s common fund (obshyak) and remarked that the Interior Minister’s possible removal would strengthen the authority of “thieves in law.” He argued he had merely expressed a personal opinion.

The Kutaisi Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 10 July 2007. The Supreme Court rejected his cassation complaint as inadmissible on 29 February 2008.

Article 223(1), inserted by a 20 December 2005 amendment, punishes membership of the thieves’ underworld with five to eight years’ imprisonment and being a “thief in law” with seven to ten years. An accompanying Law on Organised Crime and Racketeering defined the key terms: the “thieves’ underworld” as any group acting under special rules to obtain profit through intimidation, threats, coercion, the “rule of silence,” settlement of disputes by a thief in law’s authority, induction of youth into crime, or the commission or encouragement of offences; a “member” as anyone who recognises those rules and actively further their goals; and “settlement of disputes using the authority of a thief in law” as unofficial resolution of a private dispute accompanied by illicit pressure.

The provision formed part of a legislative response to post-Soviet organised crime. The thieves’ underworld, originating in Imperial Russia and evolving through the Soviet period, is a hierarchical network with initiation rituals, a strict code of conduct, and “thieves in law” as its elite leaders. These figures rarely commit crimes themselves but exercise control through reputation, communications networks, management of the common fund, recruitment, and unofficial dispute resolution. Georgian “thieves in law” historically constituted one of the most influential ethnic groups within this structure. The 2005 laws were intended to close a previous legislative gap that had allowed such figures to operate with relative impunity.

The case of Ashlarba v. Georgia (Application no. 45554/08) originated in an application lodged on 22 April 2008 by Georgian national Izet Ashlarba (born 1956), who lived in the Ajarian Autonomous Republic. He alleged a violation of Article 7 of the Convention, claiming that Article 223(1) § 1 of the Georgian Criminal Code—under which he was convicted of membership in the “thieves’ underworld”—lacked the precision and foreseeability required for him to regulate his conduct.

The proceedings began with a 15 February 2006 investigation by the Ministry of the Interior into Mr A.K., suspected of being a “thief in law” who ran criminal syndicates and settled private disputes through criminal means. Witnesses, including prison officers, family members and associates, confirmed that A.K. had obtained the title via a 1999 “baptism” ritual and thereafter managed the “thieves’ underworld”—a hierarchical network of criminal groups operating under a special code of conduct. A 5 March 2006 search warrant noted A.K.’s residence in Ukraine or Russia and his telephone contacts with regional criminal figures. Judicially authorised tapping revealed that the applicant regularly received instructions from A.K. on dispute settlement, leading to expansion of the probe.

The applicant and another individual, Mr Y.A., were arrested on 31 July 2006. When questioned, the applicant acknowledged a 30-year acquaintance with A.K. and awareness of his “thief in law” status, describing such a figure as “a righteous man.” The investigation concluded on 29 September 2006 and was referred for trial.

On 27 March 2007 the Batumi City Court convicted the applicant of membership in the thieves’ underworld (Article 223(1) § 1), imposing a seven-year sentence (Y.A. received five years; A.K. was convicted as a “thief in law” under § 2 and received ten years). The court described the applicant’s conduct in general terms as publicly supporting the underworld through his lifestyle, actively pursuing its goals of profit for members and others, terrorising and coercing ordinary people, disseminating its rules, and assisting A.K. in its management. Guilt rested on three specific episodes corroborated by witness testimony and telephone intercepts.

First, between late June and July 2006 the applicant, at A.K.’s request, intervened in an apartment dispute involving A.K.’s mother-in-law, employing A.K.’s criminal authority. The applicant maintained he had merely sought an amicable settlement as a friend of the woman and had not realised such action was criminal. Second, on 24 July 2006 A.K. asked him to locate two young men who had refused to pay a taxi fare and to pressure them, using both his own standing and A.K.’s authority, to settle the debt. The applicant conceded the request but insisted he had taken no practical steps. Third, on 8 July 2006, while visiting an imprisoned acquaintance regarded as a future “thief in law,” the applicant discussed financial matters relating to the underworld’s common fund (the “kitty” or obshyak) and remarked that the possible removal of the Interior Minister would strengthen the authority of thieves in law. He argued this was merely an expression of personal opinion.

The Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 10 July 2007; the Supreme Court declared the cassation appeal inadmissible on 29 February 2008.

Article 223(1), inserted by a 20 December 2005 amendment, punishes membership in the thieves’ underworld by five to eight years’ imprisonment. An accompanying Law on Organised Crime and Racketeering defined the underworld as any group acting under special rules to obtain profit through intimidation, threat, coercion, the rule of silence, dispute settlement by thief-in-law authority, recruitment of youth, or the commission or encouragement of offences. A member is any person who recognises those rules and actively furthers the group’s aims. “Settlement of disputes using the authority of a thief in law” means illicit resolution of private disputes accompanied by threat or coercion. A thief in law is a member who directly runs or coordinates the underworld.

Socio-legal studies described the thieves’ underworld as the backbone of post-Soviet organised crime, featuring initiation rituals, a strict code, hierarchy and control over both criminals and parts of society. Thieves in law constitute its elite, exercising reputation-based authority (physical presence being unnecessary), administering the common fund, recruiting, and settling disputes. Georgian thieves in law historically ranked among the most influential ethnic groups within this elite.

These facts—centred on the applicant’s long-standing association with a recognised thief in law, his receipt of instructions, and his involvement in unofficial dispute resolution and underworld discussions shortly after the new provision’s enactment—formed the basis of the alleged lack of foreseeability under Article 7.
001-145789:
**CASE OF A.A. AND OTHERS v. SWEDEN (Application no. 34098/11)**

The applicants, four Somali nationals (a father born in 1964 and his three children born in 1990, 1994 and 1997), entered Sweden on 1 June 2009 and applied for asylum the next day. They alleged that deporting them to Somaliland would violate Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). The Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 preventing their removal pending proceedings.

The first applicant stated the family belonged to the Sheikal clan and had lived in Hosingo village in southern Somalia since 1999. He claimed Al-Shabaab seized the village after Ethiopian forces withdrew in mid-2008. He described participating in a protest or negotiation that ended in disagreement; the village’s spiritual leader was killed (accounts varied on whether this occurred immediately or six days later), and he was placed on a hit list. Armed men later searched his home for him. He asserted the family could not relocate elsewhere in Somalia because their clan had no other presence and Al-Shabaab operated nationwide. Passport stamps from Djibouti (2000 and 2005) and Somaliland locations (Lowyacado, Borama, Berbera up to 2005) were explained as travel via Djibouti to Saudi Arabia; he maintained the family had remained in Hosingo.

The second applicant (then 19) initially said her mother and husband remained in Hosingo but later stated her husband had fled (location unknown) while six siblings, uncles and cousins stayed. She reported Al-Shabaab burning their house in 2006 (leaving her with upper-body burn scars) and a village leader’s killing in 2008 that forced her father and husband to flee. She feared rape by Al-Shabaab on return.

The Migration Board rejected the claims on 11 September 2009. It noted Somalis often lacked verifiable identity documents, making narratives decisive. The first applicant gave detailed information about Hosingo but displayed northern Somali pronunciation; his passport contained Somaliland airport stamps (2000–2005) with none from the south; and his accounts of the 2008 events were contradictory and vague regarding conditions in south/central Somalia. Language analysis of the second applicant indicated Somaliland origin, and she provided insufficient verifiable details about the village or clan. The Board concluded it was more likely the family’s most recent home had been in northern Somalia (Somaliland) rather than Hosingo.

The Migration Court upheld the decision on 2 June 2010 after an oral hearing (written witness statements were admitted but two witnesses were not heard). It accepted the first applicant originated from Hosingo but found language analyses and explanations did not support a last domicile in southern Somalia or refugee/protection status. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 3 September 2010, making the deportation order enforceable.

Later requests to re-examine based on alleged enforcement impediments (October 2010, early 2011, January and March 2012) were rejected by the Board and, where appealed, the Migration Court, as no new circumstances justifying reconsideration were shown.

Swedish law (2005 Aliens Act) grants residence to refugees or those facing death, corporal punishment, torture or inhuman treatment, or in particularly distressing circumstances. Enforcement is barred where there are reasonable grounds to believe such risks exist. Re-examination is possible only on new circumstances indicating lasting impediments that could not previously have been invoked.

Country information available to the Court (UNHCR 2014 guidelines, UK Home Office reports, fact-finding missions) described ongoing conflict, displacement and Al-Shabaab control in southern/central Somalia, with limited internal protection options. Somaliland was relatively more stable with some social/economic progress, though it faced security incidents, clan tensions, rape (including gang rape and cases involving minors), weak judicial independence and restrictions on movement for those from the south. UNHCR viewed internal relocation to Somaliland/Puntland as generally unavailable for southern/central Somalis except in individual cases depending on clan ties and origin. Women and girls faced heightened risks of FGM and sexual/gender-based violence.

These facts formed the core of the dispute over whether return to Somaliland (the authorities’ assessed origin) would expose the applicants to Article 3 risks, given the credibility findings on their claimed southern origins and Al-Shabaab threats.

The case of A.A. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 34098/11) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by four Somali nationals—a father born in 1964 and his three children born in 1990, 1994 and 1997. They entered Sweden on 1 June 2009 and applied for asylum the next day, alleging that their forced return to Somaliland would expose them to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicants claimed membership of the Sheikal clan and residence since 1999 in the southern Somali village of Hosingo. The first applicant, a university graduate, stated that Al-Shabaab seized the village in mid-2008 after Ethiopian forces withdrew. Village elders, including him, attempted negotiations that failed; the spiritual leader was subsequently killed (accounts varied as to whether this occurred immediately or six days later). Armed men later sought the first applicant at his home, placing him on a kill list after he had protested the takeover. The family maintained they could not relocate internally because their clan had no other base and Al-Shabaab operated nationwide. The second applicant added that Al-Shabaab had burned the family home in 2006, leaving her with upper-body scars, and that she feared rape on return. She initially said her mother and husband remained in Hosingo but later stated her husband had fled.

Swedish authorities rejected these accounts as incredible. Language analysis of the first and second applicants indicated northern Somali (Somaliland) origins. The first applicant’s passport bore entry stamps from Somaliland airports (Lowyacado, Borama, Berbera) between 2000 and 2005 and from Djibouti, with no corresponding stamps from southern Somalia; he offered inconsistent explanations for travel to Saudi Arabia. He also gave contradictory versions of the 2008 events and vague descriptions of conditions in south-central Somalia. The second applicant could supply no verifiable details about the village or clan. The Migration Board therefore concluded on 11 September 2009 that the family’s most recent residence had been in northern Somalia, not Hosingo, and refused asylum.

The Migration Court upheld the decision on 2 June 2010 after an oral hearing (written but not oral witness testimony was admitted). It accepted that the first applicant originated from Hosingo but found the language evidence and inconsistencies fatal to the claim of recent southern residence or a well-founded fear of persecution. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 3 September 2010, rendering the deportation orders enforceable. Subsequent requests to the Migration Board and Migration Court citing new circumstances or impediments to enforcement were rejected in 2010–2012.

Under the 2005 Aliens Act, protection is available to refugees or persons facing a real risk of death, torture or inhuman treatment; deportation is barred where such a risk exists. The authorities considered the applicants fell outside these categories. Country information available to the Court (UNHCR 2014 Guidelines and later UK and Nordic reports) described south-central Somalia as remaining highly insecure under Al-Shabaab influence, with listed risk profiles including perceived opponents, women and children. Somaliland was comparatively stable, yet reports noted judicial interference, incidents of rape (including of minors) and limited protection for certain groups. Internal relocation from south-central Somalia to Somaliland was generally regarded as unavailable.

The Court indicated under Rule 39 that the applicants should not be removed pending its examination. The core factual dispute thus centred on the applicants’ true place of origin and the consequent risk, if any, of Article 3 ill-treatment upon return to Somaliland.

The case of A.A. and Others v. Sweden (no. 34098/11) concerns four Somali nationals—the father A.A. (born 1964) and his three children (born 1990, 1994 and 1997)—who entered Sweden on 1 June 2009 and claimed asylum the next day. They alleged that enforcement of their deportation to Somaliland would violate Article 3 of the Convention. Interim measures under Rule 39 were applied on 12 July 2011 to prevent removal pending the Court’s examination.

The applicants claimed to belong to the Sheikal clan and to have lived in the southern Somali village of Hosingo since 1999. They asserted that Al-Shabaab seized the village in mid-2008 after Ethiopian forces withdrew. The father described participating in a protest or in failed negotiations by village elders with Al-Shabaab, after which the village spiritual leader was killed (accounts varied as to whether this occurred immediately or six days later). Armed men subsequently sought him at home, placing him on a kill list. The family maintained that their clan had no presence elsewhere and that Al-Shabaab operated throughout Somalia, precluding internal relocation. The second applicant (then 19) initially said her mother and husband remained in Hosingo but later stated her husband had fled; she still had siblings, uncles and cousins there. She described Al-Shabaab burning the family home in 2006 (leaving her with upper-body burn scars) and expressed fear of rape on return. The father, who held a Saudi university degree, initially denied travel since 1999 but, when confronted with Djibouti stamps from 2000 and 2005, recalled visits via Djibouti to Saudi Arabia (one to see a niece). His passport also bore stamps from Somaliland airports (Lowyacado, Borama, Berbera) up to 2005; he insisted the family had never left Hosingo.

A language analysis conducted by a Mogadishu-born analyst found the father’s pronunciation typical of northern Somalia. The second applicant’s speech likewise indicated a Somaliland origin, and she supplied only vague, unverifiable details about the village and clan. The Migration Board rejected the claims on 11 September 2009, concluding it was not credible that the family had resided in southern Somalia until departure; their most recent home was far more likely in northern Somalia (Somaliland). The Board noted the absence of southern entry/exit stamps, the father’s contradictory accounts of the 2008 events and his targeting, and his vagueness about conditions in south-central Somalia.

An oral hearing was held before the Migration Court, which declined to hear two proposed witnesses but admitted their written statements. On 2 June 2010 the Court accepted that the father might originate from Hosingo but, like the Board, found that the language evidence and inconsistent explanations did not establish recent southern domicile or a need for protection. Leave to appeal was refused on 3 September 2010, rendering the deportation orders enforceable. Subsequent applications citing new circumstances or impediments to enforcement (autumn 2010, early 2011, January–March 2012) were rejected by the Board and, where appealed, by the Migration Court, as no qualifying new facts had been presented.

Country information contemporaneous with the proceedings underscored intense fighting, displacement and Al-Shabaab control in southern and central Somalia, with UNHCR listing multiple risk profiles (including women, children and perceived opponents) and advising against forced returns. Somaliland was comparatively more stable, with economic progress, though it experienced political tensions, isolated clashes, high rates of (often unreported) rape—including gang rape of minors and women from host communities as well as IDPs—and FGM. Judicial interference and weak protection for relocators from the south were also documented. UNHCR generally considered internal relocation from south-central Somalia to Somaliland unavailable except for those originating there or belonging to majority clans.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ Article 3 complaint: that return to Somaliland, the destination implied by the Swedish authorities’ credibility findings, would expose them to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment.
