The ECHR case Jüssi Osawe v. Estonia (App. no. 63206/10) involved Estonian national Veronika Jüssi Osawe, who alleged a lack of access to court (Article 6 ECHR) in seeking to establish her daughter's paternity.

The applicant married Nigerian national O. in Copenhagen on 29 June 2005. They separated from 1 November 2005. In 2006 she began Danish divorce proceedings. On 2 November 2007 the Copenhagen City Court granted separation (not divorce), as O. (believed in Nigeria) failed to appear after public-notice summons. The marriage remained legally intact.

In September 2008 the applicant moved to Estonia and gave birth on 4 October 2008 to daughter A., whom she said was fathered by D. Municipal officials nevertheless registered O. as father under marital presumption, despite her objections.

On 28 September 2009 she sued in Harju County Court to have the birth-register entry declared incorrect. She supplied O.'s last Copenhagen address (from the population register) but stated he no longer lived there and her actual address was unknown; she requested public-notice service.

On 15 December 2009 the court declined to proceed. It noted under-payment of the state fee (EEK 1,000 instead of 5,000) and, more critically, that filiation cases require personal appearance and personal summons of the parties (Code of Civil Procedure). Public service was inappropriate given the likely need for evidence-taking abroad under EU Regulation 1206/2001. The court held the applicant's efforts to locate O. insufficient, given her status as his wife and pending Danish proceedings, and gave her 30 days to pay the balance and ascertain his residence (e.g., via acquaintances, relatives or colleagues).

She asked the court to declare the relevant procedural provisions unconstitutional and sought extra time to query Danish police. On 12 February 2010 the court rejected the constitutional challenge but granted the extension. She never reported any inquiries. On 16 April 2010 the court therefore refused to entertain the claim; she did not appeal.

Meanwhile, on 18 March 2010 she filed a second claim seeking to establish filiation from D. (a British national in the UK), supplying addresses and requesting a DNA test via British authorities. On 20 April 2010 the same court refused, relying on 1996 Supreme Court case-law: filiation from another man cannot be established until the existing register entry has first been declared incorrect; simultaneous examination is forbidden. Appeals to the Tallinn Court of Appeal (17 June 2010) and Supreme Court (leave refused 8 September 2010) failed.

Estonian Family Law Act § 39 presumed the mother's husband to be the father of a child born or conceived in wedlock and required his entry in the birth register. § 42 allowed court establishment of paternity only if the parents were unmarried and paternity unascertained. § 44 permitted a court to declare a register entry incorrect (one-year limitation from knowledge of the error). The Code of Civil Procedure mandated personal appearance and personal summons in filiation matters, with public service available only in limited circumstances (and potentially refused if it would impede foreign recognition/enforcement). Supreme Court precedent barred concurrent claims.

These sequential-procedure, personal-appearance and unknown-address requirements effectively blocked any judicial determination of the child's paternity.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Jüssi Osawe v. Estonia (Application no. 63206/10) arose from the applicant’s complaint of being denied access to court to challenge her child’s registered paternity and establish the true father’s identity.

The applicant, an Estonian national, married O. (a Nigerian national) in Copenhagen on 29 June 2005. The couple separated from 1 November 2005. She initiated Danish divorce proceedings; on 2 November 2007 the Copenhagen City Court granted a legal separation (not a full divorce) after O., believed to be in Nigeria, failed to appear despite public summons. The marriage remained undissolved.

In September 2008 the applicant moved to Estonia and gave birth to daughter A. on 4 October 2008, whom she stated was fathered by D. Municipal officials nevertheless registered O. as the father solely because of the existing marriage, over the applicant’s objections.

On 28 September 2009 she lodged a claim in Harju County Court to have the birth-register entry declared incorrect. She supplied O.’s last registered Danish address but stated that he no longer lived there and that she did not know his current whereabouts; she requested service by public notice.

On 15 December 2009 the County Court declined to proceed. It noted that only EEK 1,000 of the required EEK 5,000 state fee had been paid and that, in filiation proceedings, both parties must appear in person and be summoned personally. Because O. was a Nigerian national probably residing in Denmark, any evidence-taking would require cooperation under EU Regulation 1206/2001, which in turn demanded knowledge of his address. The court held that locating him was the applicant’s duty and that her efforts had been insufficient; as his wife with pending Danish proceedings she was better placed to inquire through acquaintances, relatives or colleagues. A 30-day deadline was set both to pay the outstanding fee and to supply the address.

The applicant then asked the court to declare the relevant Code of Civil Procedure provisions unconstitutional and sought an extension, announcing an intended inquiry with the Danish police. On 12 February 2010 the court rejected the constitutionality request but granted the extension. The applicant never informed the court of any inquiries or results.

On 16 April 2010 the County Court refused to entertain the action for failure to remedy the deficiencies. No appeal was filed.

Meanwhile, on 18 March 2010 the applicant filed a second claim seeking a court declaration of filiation from D. (a British national living in the United Kingdom) and a DNA test to be arranged through British authorities, supplying D.’s and his parents’ addresses.

On 20 April 2010 the County Court refused to examine this claim, relying on Supreme Court case-law of 12 September 1996 that filiation from a man other than the registered father cannot be established until the existing register entry has first been declared incorrect and removed; the two claims could not be heard simultaneously.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 17 June 2010; the Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal on 8 September 2010.

Estonian Family Law Act s. 39 created an irrebuttable presumption that a child born or conceived during marriage descends from the husband, who must be entered in the birth register. An incorrect entry could be challenged within one year (s. 44), but only after that entry was removed could filiation from another man be established (s. 42). The Code of Civil Procedure required personal appearance in filiation cases (Art. 346) and permitted public service only in limited circumstances (Art. 317), which the first-instance court declined to use.

The Government later cited appellate decisions in which unknown (including foreign) addresses had not barred proceedings and one first-instance judgment that had established filiation after public-notice service. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the combined procedural obstacles—fee, personal-appearance rule, sequential-claim requirement and inability to locate the registered father—effectively denied her access to court to determine her child’s paternity.

The applicant, Veronika Jüssi Osawe (Estonian, born 1979), married Nigerian national O. in Copenhagen on 29 June 2005. They separated from 1 November 2005. Danish proceedings she initiated in 2006 led to a 2 November 2007 Copenhagen City Court decision granting legal separation (not divorce); O. was presumed in Nigeria, summoned by public notice but did not appear. The marriage remained undissolved.

In September 2008 the applicant moved to Estonia and gave birth to daughter A. on 4 October 2008, whom she asserted was fathered by D. Municipal officials registered O. as father because of the existing marriage, despite her objections.

On 28 September 2009 she claimed in Harju County Court that the birth-register entry was incorrect. She supplied O.’s last known Copenhagen address but stated he no longer lived there and her actual location was unknown, requesting service by public notice.

On 15 December 2009 the court declined to proceed. It noted underpayment of the State fee (EEK 1 000 instead of 5 000) and required her, within 30 days, both to pay the balance and to ascertain O.’s current residence. Filiation proceedings demand personal appearance and personal service; without an address the court could not continue. Because O. was a Nigerian national likely living in Denmark, evidence might have to be taken under EU Regulation 1206/2001, necessitating knowledge of his whereabouts. The court held that locating him was the plaintiff’s duty and that her efforts (as his wife, with pending Danish proceedings) had been inadequate.

On 30 December 2009 the applicant asked the court to declare the relevant Code of Civil Procedure provisions unconstitutional, announced an intention to seek information from the Danish police, and requested extra time. On 12 February 2010 the court rejected the constitutional challenge but granted the extension. She never informed the court of any inquiries or results.

On 16 April 2010 the court therefore refused to entertain the claim for unrectified deficiencies. No appeal was lodged.

Meanwhile, on 18 March 2010 she filed a fresh claim seeking to establish A.’s filiation from D. (a British national living in the United Kingdom), supplying his and his parents’ addresses and requesting a DNA test via British authorities.

On 20 April 2010 the County Court refused to examine the claim, relying on Supreme Court case-law of 12 September 1996 that filiation from a third man cannot be established until an existing birth-register entry has first been declared incorrect; the two claims cannot be heard together.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 17 June 2010; the Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal on 8 September 2010.

Under the Family Law Act then in force, a child born or conceived during marriage is presumed to descend from the mother’s husband, who is entered as father. A court may later declare the entry incorrect, after which filiation from another man may be established; simultaneous examination is forbidden. The Code of Civil Procedure requires personal appearance and personal service in filiation matters (though public service is in principle available if an address cannot be found) and permits a court to decide even in a party’s absence if the facts are sufficiently clear. The applicant’s two successive actions therefore never reached a hearing on the merits.

The case of Y v. Latvia (Application no. 61183/08) before the European Court of Human Rights arose from events on 1 November 2007 in the courtyard of the applicant’s apartment building in Liepāja. Two municipal police officers, J.M. and J.L., approached her in connection with an alleged administrative offence of washing a car in a public area. According to the applicant, after she declined to speak with them at their vehicle and suggested they come to her apartment instead, the officers grabbed her arms, twisted them behind her back, and attempted to force her into their car while shouting about teaching her a lesson for resisting. Neighbours intervened, after which the officers released her. The applicant immediately experienced chest pain, elevated blood pressure, pain in her back, neck and head, and numbness in her hands. She summoned an ambulance, received an injection, and the next day obtained a sick-leave certificate until 12 November 2007 together with prescriptions for painkillers and sedatives. A subsequent forensic examination recorded two haematomas on each upper arm, consistent with her account and classified as minor injuries not expected to produce health effects lasting more than six days.

On 2 November 2007 the applicant requested the Liepāja City Public Prosecutor to open a criminal investigation; proceedings were instituted the same day and transferred to the State police. She simultaneously complained to the head of the municipal police, seeking investigation of the officers’ conduct and compensation for mental, material and psychological harm. An internal police inquiry later imposed disciplinary sanctions on the officers solely for failing to document the administrative offence properly; it did not address the use of force.

On 21 January 2008 a police inspector terminated the criminal investigation. The decision recited the officers’ version (that the applicant had walked away after being invited to their car, prompting them to take her by the arms), the applicant’s account, statements of three eyewitnesses who described her resistance, the forensic report, and the internal disciplinary outcome. The inspector found that the applicant had committed an administrative offence by disobeying a lawful order, thereby justifying the use of restraint techniques. However, the officers had breached section 13 of the Law on Police, which at the time prohibited special restraint techniques against women except in narrowly defined exceptional circumstances. Despite this breach, the inspector held that the officers had not exceeded their official authority under section 317 of the Criminal Law because no “substantial harm” had been caused. Infliction of minor injuries under section 130 was an offence subject only to private prosecution by the victim. Proceedings were therefore discontinued for lack of corpus delicti. The applicant was notified of her right to appeal within ten days or to institute a private prosecution.

She did not appeal the termination. On 29–30 April 2008 she lodged a private-prosecution complaint with the Liepāja Court under sections 130 and 156 of the Criminal Law, claiming injuries and both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. A single judge rejected the complaint on 7 May 2008, holding that the six-month limitation period (running from 1 November 2007) had expired and that the complaint failed to specify the applicable paragraph of section 130 or to substantiate the section 156 claim. The Kurzeme Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 2 June 2008 as final. It observed that even if the complaint had been received on 30 April, the necessary procedural steps could not have been completed by the last possible day (1 May), criticised the applicant’s almost three-month delay after the January decision, and reiterated the possibility of a civil claim for compensation (which the applicant did not pursue).

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the use of physical force against a woman in circumstances prohibited by domestic law, resulting in documented injuries, and the subsequent inability to obtain either criminal accountability or compensation through the available domestic procedures.

The applicant, a Latvian woman born in 1959, alleged that municipal police officers subjected her to inhuman and degrading treatment on 1 November 2007 and that she had no effective means of obtaining compensation. While in the courtyard of her apartment building, two officers (J.M. and J.L.) approached her after she had been washing a car. They ordered her to approach their vehicle so they could record an administrative violation. When she declined and began walking away, they seized her arms, twisted them behind her back, and attempted to force her into the car. Neighbours intervened and the officers released her. Immediately afterwards she experienced chest pain, elevated blood pressure, pain in her back, neck and head, and numbness in her hands. An ambulance was called; she received an injection and was later issued a sick-leave certificate and prescribed painkillers and sedatives. A forensic examination confirmed two haematomas on each upper arm, classified as minor injuries not expected to impair health for more than six days.

On 2 November 2007 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint with the public prosecutor, who opened an investigation that same day and transferred the file to the State police. She also complained to the municipal police. On 21 January 2008 an inspector terminated the criminal proceedings. The decision accepted that the officers had used “special restraint techniques” after the applicant disobeyed a lawful order and had thereby inflicted the documented injuries. It further accepted that the use of such techniques against a woman violated section 13 of the Law on Police, which prohibits them except in exceptional circumstances (armed resistance or danger to life or health). Nevertheless the inspector found no corpus delicti of exceeding official authority under section 317 of the Criminal Law, because the applicant’s own resistance and the absence of “substantial harm” to State authority or individual rights negated the offence. Infliction of minor bodily injury under section 130 is a privately prosecuted offence; the inspector therefore left any further action to the applicant and merely suggested that the municipal police consider disciplinary sanctions. The officers were in fact disciplined only for failing to document the original administrative violation.

The termination decision, notified on 24 January 2008, informed the applicant that she could appeal to the prosecutor within ten days or initiate a private prosecution herself. She did not appeal. On 29–30 April 2008 she filed a private-prosecution complaint seeking damages. A first-instance judge rejected it on 7 May as time-barred: the six-month limitation period under the Criminal Procedure Law expired on 1 May 2008, and the court considered it impossible to complete the necessary procedural steps in the remaining hours. An appeal to the regional court was dismissed on 2 June 2008. The appellate judge added that the applicant had waited almost three months after learning of the police decision and that she remained free to bring a civil claim for compensation.

Domestic law at the time authorised police use of force to stop “intentionally wrongful disobedience” but expressly forbade special restraint techniques against women except in narrowly defined emergencies. Article 92 of the Constitution guaranteed compensation for unjustified rights violations, and the Civil Law provided a general delictual action for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The applicant never pursued a civil claim.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 violation (the physical force used against a woman in circumstances that domestic law itself treated as prohibited) and the alleged lack of an effective remedy or compensation (the termination of the public investigation, the rigid six-month private-prosecution deadline, and the practical unavailability of timely redress).

The applicant, a Latvian national born in 1959, alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention arising from an incident on 1 November 2007. While in the courtyard of her apartment building, she was approached by two municipal police officers (J.M. and J.L.) responding to a report of a car being washed in a public space (an administrative infraction). After a brief exchange, the officers twisted her arms behind her back and attempted to force her toward their vehicle. Neighbours intervened, and she was released. She immediately experienced chest pain, elevated blood pressure, and numbness in her hands, requiring an ambulance and subsequent medical treatment, including sick leave and painkillers. She reported lingering health effects more than a year later. A forensic examination confirmed two haematomas on each upper arm, classified as minor injuries consistent with her account but not expected to cause health issues beyond six days.

On 2 November 2007, the applicant complained to the Liepāja City Public Prosecutor, requesting a criminal investigation and forensic examination. Proceedings were opened and referred to the State police. She also complained to the municipal police chief, alleging mental anguish and harm. Witnesses confirmed that she had ignored the officers’ requests, prompting them to attempt detention; she resisted, after which her arms were twisted until she complied and was released. The officers stated they used restraint only after she refused to approach their vehicle for documentation of the infraction and then released her once she ceased resisting. An internal municipal police inquiry (16 November 2007) disciplined the officers solely for failing to properly record the administrative violation, without addressing the use of force.

On 21 January 2008, a police inspector terminated the criminal investigation. The decision found that the applicant had committed an administrative offence by disobeying a lawful order, justifying the officers’ use of “special restraint techniques.” However, this violated section 13 of the Law on Police, which generally prohibits such techniques against women except in cases of danger to life/health or armed resistance. The resulting minor injuries fell under section 130 of the Criminal Law (intentional infliction of minor bodily harm), a privately prosecutable offence. The officers had not exceeded official authority under section 317, as there was no “substantial harm” given the applicant’s resistance. Proceedings were thus ended for lack of corpus delicti, with any further discipline left to the municipal police. The applicant was notified of her right to appeal the termination within 10 days and of the private-prosecution option for section 130.

She did not appeal the termination. Instead, on 30 April 2008 she applied to the Liepāja Court to initiate a private prosecution under sections 130 and 156 of the Criminal Law, seeking damages. A single judge rejected the application on 7 May 2008, citing expiry of the six-month limitation period (calculated from the incident date) and deficiencies in specifying the relevant paragraph of section 130. Her appeal was dismissed on 2 June 2008 by the Kurzeme Regional Court, which noted that even her 30 April filing made timely initiation of proceedings on 1 May 2008 practically impossible, that she had delayed nearly three months after the January decision, and that a civil claim for compensation remained available. The decision was final.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims of inhuman and degrading treatment through excessive force, as well as the absence of an effective avenue for compensation.

**Case of Dillon v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 32621/11), ECtHR (Fourth Section), judgment of 4 November 2014 (final 4 February 2015).**

The applicant, John Dillon (born 1955, British national, detained at HMP Whatton), alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. He claimed his post-tariff detention was unlawful because the authorities failed to provide resources enabling him to show the Parole Board that his risk had reduced, rendering reviews a meaningless exercise. Other complaints were declared inadmissible; the Article 5 § 1 complaint was communicated.

On 25 April 2007 Dillon received an indeterminate sentence for public protection (IPP) for sexual assault of a 15-year-old girl, committed while on licence from a prior sentence for indecent assault of girls under 16 and while undertaking the community Sex Offender Treatment Programme (SOTP). A four-year tariff was fixed, expiring 26 April 2011.

He was first held at HMP Armley, where SOTP completion was recommended in 2007. Transferred to HMP Rye Hill in June 2008, he completed an Enhanced Thinking Skills course (2008), the core SOTP (8 March 2009) and an Alcohol Awareness course. An August 2009 Structured Assessment of Risk and Need (SARN) report identified outstanding risk-reduction work and recommended the extended SOTP (74 interactive sessions plus individual work, lasting around six months) and possibly a Better Lives Booster (BLB).

A 7 September 2009 Parole Board review found substantial remaining work needed and directed that he stay in closed conditions. Transferred to HMP Acklington in September 2009 (where he believed the extended SOTP was available), a 24 August 2010 memo confirmed suitability but required transfer as the course was not offered there. He completed the Thinking Skills Programme on 27 August 2010.

A January 2011 pre-tariff paper Parole Board review refused release. The 24 February 2011 decision credited completed work but required the extended SOTP (and possibly BLB) to address remaining risk factors; significant work in closed conditions was needed. The Secretary of State agreed on 6 April 2011, identifying outstanding factors (sexual offending, grievance, distorted thinking, alcohol misuse, anger). She expected the interventions (or equivalent) before the next review but could not guarantee places due to resource limits. A 21-month review period was set (transfer, course, post-course reviews, skill consolidation, BLB assessment, alcohol work), scheduled to start March 2012 and conclude November 2012 with a September oral hearing.

After tariff expiry Dillon’s solicitors wrote to HMP Acklington about delays and contemplated judicial review. He transferred to HMP Whatton on 22 September 2011. On 10 October 2011 he requested assessment timing and was told it would occur as soon as possible. Officials (28 October 2011) cited a necessary settling-in period; assessments were prioritised by tariff expiry, risk and readiness. Four extended programmes were planned for 2012; if suitable he would be considered. A SARN would follow within 26 weeks of completion. On 12 November 2011 Dillon expressed concern about prioritisation given the forthcoming review; the reply (18 November 2011) noted limited resources and a large number of post-tariff IPP and life-sentence prisoners.

Solicitors wrote to the Governor on 6 January 2012 threatening judicial review and seeking an undertaking for an April 2012 course. Reassessed on 19 January and 6 February 2012, Dillon was found insufficiently motivated (the second meeting ended because of abusive, disrespectful language and an aggressive tone). Although tariff expiry would have given priority for April 2012, he was not ready; individual work with his offender supervisor was recommended, with reassessment in June/July 2012.

A 13 June 2012 Parole Board paper review refused release or transfer to open conditions. It noted the index offence (committed on extended licence after prior sexual offences), breach of trust, risk factors, completed core SOTP and Thinking Skills, but outstanding extended SOTP, possible BLB and Healthy Sexual Functioning programmes, plus a CALM programme for violence and emotion management. High risk of harm to children remained; considerable accredited work was still required, so an oral hearing had no merit.

Reassessed suitable in July 2012, he was considered for an October 2012 course, completed the extended SOTP in March 2013 and received a SARN report in March 2014 identifying any further needs.

The facts highlight repeated delays, transfers, resource constraints, prioritisation issues and one unsuccessful motivation assessment after tariff expiry, against a background of Parole Board insistence on further accredited work before any progress. Relevant domestic law and practice on IPP sentences and rehabilitation resources appear in James, Wells and Lee v. the United Kingdom.

The case of Dillon v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 32621/11) was brought by British national John Dillon (born 1955) under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He argued that the authorities had failed to provide the resources (specifically, offending-behaviour programmes) needed for him to demonstrate reduced risk to the Parole Board, rendering reviews a meaningless exercise. The complaint was communicated to the UK Government on 23 September 2013; other complaints were declared inadmissible.

On 25 April 2007 Dillon received an IPP with a four-year tariff after conviction for sexual assault of a 15-year-old girl. The offence occurred while he was on licence from a prior sentence for indecent assault of underage girls and while undertaking the Sex Offender Treatment Programme (SOTP) in the community. He was initially held at HMP Armley, where SOTP completion was recommended in 2007.

In June 2008 he transferred to HMP Rye Hill and completed an Enhanced Thinking Skills course (2008), the core SOTP (8 March 2009) and an Alcohol Awareness course. An August 2009 Structured Assessment of Risk and Need (SARN) report identified outstanding risk factors and recommended the extended SOTP (74 interactive sessions lasting around six months) plus possible Better Lives Booster (BLB) work. A September 2009 Parole Board review concluded that substantial risk-reduction work remained, so Dillon should stay in closed conditions.

He transferred to HMP Acklington in September 2009, believing the extended SOTP was available there. A 24 August 2010 memo confirmed suitability but stated the course was not offered at Acklington, requiring another transfer. Dillon completed a Thinking Skills Programme there on 27 August 2010. A January 2011 paper Parole Board review (pre-tariff expiry) refused release, citing the need for the extended SOTP (and possibly BLB). The Secretary of State agreed in April 2011, listing outstanding risks (sexual offending, grievance, distorted thinking, alcohol misuse, anger) and noting that resource limits prevented any guarantee of course placement. A 21-month review cycle was set, expecting course completion by the next hearing (scheduled for 2012). Dillon’s tariff expired on 26 April 2011.

After solicitors raised delay concerns, Dillon transferred to HMP Whatton on 22 September 2011. Assessment was deferred to allow “settling in.” He was told four extended SOTP programmes would run in 2012, with priority based on tariff expiry, risk and readiness, but resources were limited amid many post-tariff IPP and life prisoners. In February 2012 a reassessment found him insufficiently motivated (due to abusive, aggressive behaviour during interview); individual work was recommended instead, delaying group treatment. A June 2012 paper Parole Board review again refused release or open conditions, noting the still-outstanding extended SOTP, CALM programme and possible further courses, and declining an oral hearing because core risks remained unaddressed.

Dillon was reassessed as suitable in July 2012 and completed the extended SOTP in March 2013. A follow-up SARN report appeared only in March 2014. Throughout, official correspondence repeatedly cited resource constraints and high demand as reasons for delays in assessment, transfer and placement.

These facts formed the basis of Dillon’s claim that post-tariff detention lacked the necessary rehabilitative opportunities, rendering it arbitrary and the Parole Board process ineffective. The Court referred to its earlier judgment in James, Wells and Lee v. the United Kingdom for the relevant domestic IPP framework.

001-140021:
The case originated in an application to the ECHR by Turkish national Zübeyir Perihan (born 1966, residing in Istanbul) and Mezopotamya Basın Yayın A.Ş. (Mesopotamia Publishing), a joint-stock company incorporated in Turkey in 1991 and dissolved in 2001. Perihan was appointed the company's Director General on 24 December 2001. The company maintained branch offices in Şanlıurfa, Diyarbakır and Izmir. The facts centre on police searches, confiscations of publications, related criminal proceedings (mostly unsuccessful for the authorities), and the company's subsequent judicial dissolution, which formed the basis of complaints concerning the fairness of those proceedings and related interferences with the company's operations as a publisher.

On 26 October 1997 the Şanlıurfa branch was inaugurated and immediately searched by police from the Security Directorate. Newspapers, magazines, books, cassettes and documents alleged to be illegal were confiscated. The next day the Deputy Governor of Şanlıurfa asked the Ministry of Industry and Trade to seek the company's dissolution. Criminal proceedings were opened against the branch manager and the then Director General for storing banned books; these were discontinued on 6 June 2000 as time-barred.

In December 1997 the Diyarbakır office was searched on multiple dates. Books, publications and a calendar produced by the company were seized. The Governor closed the office (the judgment records the date as 14 January 1997, almost certainly a clerical error for 1998) and later requested dissolution proceedings, asserting that the company had disseminated propaganda in favour of the PKK. Criminal charges against board members relating to the calendar were instituted in the Istanbul State Security Court but suspended in September 1999 pursuant to a law on media-related offences.

On 26 December 1997 the Izmir office was searched; allegedly illegal publications and a satellite decoder were seized. The Governor requested dissolution on the ground of PKK propaganda. The branch manager was acquitted by the Izmir Magistrate's Court in May 1998.

Following the governors' complaints, the Ministry of Industry and Trade commenced dissolution proceedings on 24 February 1998 in the Istanbul Beyoğlu Commercial Court under Article 274 § 2 of the Commercial Code (acts contrary to law, public order or the company's articles). The writ and related documents were served on 12 March 1998 and collected by a Mr M.B., who signed as an authorised representative. Additional evidence (incident and seizure reports) was later added to the file. The company did not appear at the first hearing on 3 April 1998 or at subsequent hearings. The court obtained further material from the relevant public prosecutors, stayed the case pending the criminal proceedings, and on 19 October 2001 ordered the company's dissolution. It held the company responsible for the Şanlıurfa and Diyarbakır incidents, which it found had breached public order, and appointed a liquidator. Notification of the judgment was again recorded in the commercial registry.

On appeal the company argued that service on M.B. (not a board member) had been invalid, that it had not been notified of later evidence, and that the dissolution rested on incidents that had produced no convictions. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on 17 October 2002 after a hearing and rejected a request for rectification in January 2003. Domestic notification rules required service on an authorised representative (or, if none was present, on an officer or employee at the premises). These facts—disputed service, the company's non-participation, reliance on unconvicted incidents involving publications, and the resulting dissolution of a media company—were the core circumstances underlying the alleged Convention violations.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Perihan and Mezopotamya Basın Yayın A.Ş. v. Turkey (Application no. 21377/03) concerns the 2001 court-ordered dissolution of a Turkish publishing company, Mezopotamya Basın Yayın A.Ş. (Mesopotamia Publishing), and related proceedings. The first applicant, Zübeyir Perihan (born 1966, residing in Istanbul), was appointed the company's Director General on 24 December 2001. The company, incorporated in 1991, was dissolved that year. The applicants were represented by lawyer M. İriz; the Turkish Government by its Agent. The application was lodged on 23 May 2003 and communicated to the Government on 23 November 2006.

Key background facts involve searches of the company's branch offices. On 26 October 1997, police searched the newly inaugurated Şanlıurfa office, confiscating newspapers, magazines, books, cassettes and documents alleged to be illegal. The Şanlıurfa Deputy Governor requested dissolution proceedings. Criminal charges were brought against the branch manager (Murat Gökdağ) and then-Director General (Nuray Şen) for storing banned books; these were discontinued on 6 June 2000 as time-barred.

In December 1997, the Diyarbakır office was searched multiple times, with books, publications and a company calendar seized. The office was closed by gubernatorial order on 14 January 1998. The Diyarbakır Governor sought dissolution. Criminal proceedings were later instituted against board members in the Istanbul State Security Court for alleged PKK propaganda via the calendar; these were suspended on 17 September 1999 under a media-offences amnesty law.

On 26 December 1997, the Izmir office was searched; publications alleged to be illegal and a satellite decoder were seized. The Izmir Governor requested dissolution for alleged PKK propaganda. The branch manager (Hatice Çoban) was acquitted on 14 May 1998.

On 24 February 1998, following gubernatorial complaints, the Ministry of Industry and Trade initiated dissolution proceedings in the Istanbul Beyoğlu Commercial Court under Article 274 § 2 of the Commercial Code (acts against public order). The court registered the case on 27 February 1998, scheduled a 3 April 1998 hearing, and ordered notification of the Ministry's submissions and evidence per the Code of Civil Procedure (warning that non-appearance would not prevent a merits decision). On 12 March 1998, documents were served at the Trade Commercial Registry and received by M.B., who signed as authorised representative.

The Ministry submitted further evidence (incident/seizure reports), admitted on 17 March 1998. At the 3 April 1998 hearing, the company was absent (notification deemed duly served). Evidence was read; the court sought additional documents from prosecutors. Proceedings were stayed on 28 July 1999 pending related criminal cases.

On 19 October 2001, the court dissolved the company, noting its failure to attend or submit observations despite notification. It held the company responsible for Şanlıurfa and Diyarbakır incidents that breached public order. A liquidator was appointed. The decision was served via the registry.

The company appealed on 28 March 2002, arguing improper notification (M.B. was not a board member), non-notification of later-admitted evidence, and that dissolution rested on unconvicted incidents. After a 15 October 2002 hearing, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on 17 October 2002. A rectification request repeating substantive grounds was dismissed on 24 January 2003.

Domestic law required notification to authorised representatives (or, if unavailable, a present officer/employee). The Commercial Code permitted dissolution for proven unlawful or public-order-violating acts.

These facts centre on alleged procedural defects in the dissolution (notification, participation, evidence access, and reliance on unadjudicated incidents) and the underlying seizures tied to publications.

**CASE OF PERİHAN AND MEZOPOTAMYA BASIN YAYIN A.Ş. v. TURKEY (Application no. 21377/03), ECtHR Second Section, Judgment of 21 January 2014 (final 2 June 2014)**

The applicants were Zübeyir Perihan (born 1966, Istanbul resident, appointed Director General of the second applicant on 24 December 2001) and Mezopotamya Basın Yayın A.Ş. (“Mesopotamia Publishing”), a Turkish joint-stock company incorporated in 1991 and later dissolved. They complained of the company’s court-ordered dissolution.

In late 1997, police searched the company’s branch offices. On 26 October 1997, Şanlıurfa officers confiscated newspapers, magazines, books, cassettes and documents alleged to be illegal. The Şanlıurfa Deputy Governor then asked the Ministry of Industry and Trade to seek dissolution. Criminal proceedings against the branch manager and then-Director General for storing banned books were discontinued as time-barred on 6 June 2000.

The Diyarbakır office was searched on multiple dates in December 1997; books, publications and a company calendar were seized. The Governor closed the office on 14 January 1998 (note: the judgment text states 14 January 1997) and requested dissolution proceedings, citing PKK propaganda. Criminal proceedings against board members for the calendar were later suspended under a media-offences amnesty law.

On 26 December 1997 the Izmir office was searched; alleged illegal publications and a satellite decoder were seized. The Governor sought dissolution for PKK propaganda. The branch manager was acquitted on 14 May 1998.

On 24 February 1998 the Ministry instituted commercial-court proceedings in Istanbul Beyoğlu Commercial Court to dissolve the company under Article 274 § 2 of the Commercial Code for acts contrary to law, public order and its articles of association. The court notified the company of the hearing and the plaintiff’s submissions. On 12 March 1998 the documents were collected from the Trade Commercial Registry by one M.B., who signed as an authorised representative. Additional seizure reports were added to the file on 17 March 1998. The company did not appear at the 3 April 1998 hearing or subsequent hearings. The court stayed the case pending related criminal proceedings, then on 19 October 2001 dissolved the company, finding it responsible for the Şanlıurfa and Diyarbakır incidents that had breached public order, and appointed a liquidator. The decision was served via the registry.

The company appealed, arguing that notification had been defective because M.B. was not a board member at the time, that it had not been notified of later-admitted evidence, and that dissolution had been ordered on the basis of two incidents for which the company itself had never been convicted. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on 17 October 2002 after hearing the parties and examining the file; a request for rectification repeating the same grounds was rejected on 24 January 2003.

Domestic notification rules required service on an authorised representative of a legal entity (or, if none was present, on an officer or employee at the office). The Commercial Code permitted the Ministry to seek dissolution of a company proven responsible for unlawful or public-order-violating acts.

These facts centre on the searches, confiscations, unsuccessful or time-barred criminal cases against individuals, the uncontested civil dissolution proceedings, the disputed service of process, the company’s non-participation, and the appellate courts’ rejection of both procedural (notification) and substantive (lack of company conviction) objections. The case therefore raises issues of whether the applicants were afforded a fair opportunity to defend the company against dissolution.

The case of Pozaić v. Croatia (Application no. 5901/13) was brought by Vladimir Pozaić, a Croatian national born in 1977, who alleged that conditions of his detention in Bjelovar Prison violated Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) due to overcrowding, unsanitary cells, and inadequate medical care, and that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The applicant had been convicted of drug-related offences and robbery, receiving successive prison sentences that were later combined. He began serving time in Bjelovar Prison on 22 March 2010 and was transferred to Zagreb Prison on 5 January 2011 after roughly ten months.

During that period he occupied four cells. According to the applicant, three cells each measured 17.13 m² (including sanitary facilities) and were shared with between four and seven other inmates, while a fourth cell of 6.24 m² was shared with one other person. He described open toilets, dirt, insufficient lockers, poor ventilation, and a lack of adequate medical attention that caused him additional distress.

The Government disputed these figures, stating that the applicant enjoyed an average of 3.46 m² of personal space. Official measurements placed him in a 21.75 m² cell with four to seven others for 141 days, a 9.72 m² cell with one other inmate for 22 days, a 19.7 m² cell for 125 days, and a 22.36 m² cell for two days. They asserted that toilets were fully or partially partitioned with independent ventilation, that cells had running water, windows admitting daylight and air, central heating, and had been refurbished in 2007–2010. Inmates were permitted three hours of free movement daily and had access to a gym, outdoor sports courts, table tennis, chess, library books, television and films.

On medical care, records showed the applicant reported no serious health problems on arrival or at a June 2010 examination. He later saw a psychiatrist for sleep difficulties but twice refused treatment. He received eight dental consultations and six prison-doctor examinations.

The applicant pursued domestic remedies. He complained to the Government Office for Human Rights, requested a friendly settlement from the State Attorney (refused), and petitioned the sentence-execution judge of Bjelovar County Court. After inspecting the prison, the judge dismissed the complaint, finding no overcrowding, clean sanitary facilities, adequate medical care and sufficient outdoor activity. A three-judge panel upheld that decision. The Prison Administration acknowledged general overcrowding but claimed it was offset by activities and maintenance. A constitutional complaint alleging violations of equality, humane treatment and fair-trial rights was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 5 June 2012.

Croatian law required at least 4 m² per prisoner and provided complaint routes to prison authorities and judges. The CPT’s 2012 visit had already identified systemic overcrowding and recommended a minimum of 4 m² living space excluding sanitary facilities.

These contested facts concerning personal space, hygiene, medical treatment and the availability of effective remedies constitute the core of the alleged Convention violations.

**Case Summary: Pozaić v. Croatia (ECHR Application no. 5901/13, Judgment 4 December 2014)**

The applicant, Vladimir Pozaić (born 1977), a Croatian national, alleged violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his detention conditions in Bjelovar Prison and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. He was serving a consolidated prison sentence of two years and eight months (stemming from convictions for drug abuse and robbery) and was held in Bjelovar Prison from 22 March 2010 until his transfer to Zagreb Prison on 5 January 2011.

The applicant claimed severe overcrowding and inadequate facilities. He was housed in four cells. Three cells measured 17.13 m² (including sanitary facilities) and were shared with seven others (cell 5, 22 March–4 August 2010), four others (cell 4, 4–10 August 2010), and five others (cell 1, 3 September 2010–5 January 2011). A fourth cell (no. 11) measured 6.24 m² and was shared with one other person (10 August–3 September 2010). He alleged open (unpartitioned) sanitary facilities, dirtiness, insufficient lockers, and inadequate medical care that caused additional distress.

The Government contested these details, stating the applicant had an average of 3.46 m² of personal space. Specifics included 141 days in cell 5/I (21.75 m², shared with 4–7 others); 22 days in cell 11/1 (9.72 m², shared with one other); 125 days in cell 1/O (19.7 m²); and two days in cell 4/O (22.36 m²). Inmate numbers for the last two cells were not specified. The Government asserted that toilets in most cells were fully separated with independent ventilation (a partial wall in cell 11/1), all cells had drinking water, windows for light and air, central heating, and regular maintenance/refurbishment (documented in 2007, 2009, and 2010). The applicant had three hours of daily free movement outside his cell (4–7 p.m.), plus access to a gym, basketball court, other sports, library books, television, and films.

On medical care, the Government provided records showing the applicant reported no serious issues upon arrival and in a June 2010 examination. He received six prison-doctor examinations, eight dental treatments, and one psychiatric consultation (for sleep problems, which he declined to treat). The applicant had requested a psychiatrist on 29 September 2010 but refused treatment.

The applicant pursued multiple complaints. On 14 September 2010 he wrote to the Government’s Office for Human Rights (forwarded to the Prison Administration) and invited the Bjelovar Municipal State Attorney’s Office to a friendly settlement (declined on 10 December 2010 after finding no violation). On 21 September 2010 he complained to a Bjelovar County Court sentence-execution judge, who dismissed the complaint on 11 October 2010 after visiting the prison and reviewing records; she found no overcrowding, adequate sanitary facilities, sufficient medical care, and adequate recreational opportunities. A three-judge panel dismissed his appeal on 21 October 2010. The Prison Administration replied on 5 November 2010, acknowledging general overcrowding but arguing it was offset by out-of-cell time and activities; it listed slightly different cell measurements and confirmed the medical examinations. The applicant later filed a constitutional complaint (alleging inadequate space, medical care, and discrimination), which the Constitutional Court declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 5 June 2012.

Domestic law (Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act, s. 74) required a minimum of 4 m² and 10 m³ per prisoner. The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) 2012 visit report highlighted Croatian prison overcrowding and recommended at least 4 m² living space per prisoner in multi-occupancy cells (excluding sanitary facilities), plus improved activities and medical-record standards.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 violation (overcrowding below statutory/CPT minima, combined with claimed hygiene and medical shortcomings) and Article 13 violation (ineffectiveness of the sentence-execution judge, administrative, and constitutional complaint procedures, all of which rejected the claims). The applicant was represented by counsel; the Government was represented by its Agent.

The case of Pozaić v. Croatia (no. 5901/13) concerns complaints by Croatian national Vladimir Pozaić (born 1977) of inadequate detention conditions in Bjelovar Prison from 22 March 2010 to 5 January 2011, in alleged violation of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. Pozaić had been sentenced to a consolidated term of two years and eight months’ imprisonment for drug offences and robbery.

He was housed in four cells. On his account, three cells of 17.13 m² (including sanitary facilities) were shared with four to seven others, yielding well under 4 m² personal space, while a 6.24 m² cell was shared with one other inmate. The cells were dirty, had open sanitary facilities, insufficient lockers and poor ventilation; medical care was also inadequate, causing further distress.

The Government stated that Pozaić had on average 3.46 m² of personal space. He spent 141 days in a 21.75 m² cell with four to seven others, 22 days in a 9.72 m² cell with one other, 125 days in a 19.7 m² cell and two days in a 22.36 m² cell (occupancy of the last two cells unspecified). Sanitary facilities were fully partitioned in three cells and separated by a 168 cm wall in the fourth, all with independent ventilation. Cells had drinking water, windows admitting daylight and air, and central heating; they had been refurbished in 2007, 2009 and 2010. Pozaić enjoyed three hours of daily out-of-cell movement plus access to a gym, basketball and other sports facilities, a library, television and films.

Medical records showed that Pozaić had initially reported no serious health problems. He received six prison-doctor examinations, eight dental treatments and one psychiatric consultation for sleep difficulties (treatment refused).

Pozaić complained on 14 September 2010 to the Government’s Office for Human Rights (forwarded to the Prison Administration) and invited the municipal State Attorney to settle; the latter declined on 10 December 2010, finding no violation. A sentence-execution judge of the Bjelovar County Court dismissed his complaint on 11 October 2010 after visiting the prison, concluding that cells were not overcrowded, sanitary facilities were clean, medical care had been provided and outdoor activities were adequate. A three-judge panel upheld that decision on 21 October 2010. The Prison Administration’s 5 November 2010 reply acknowledged general overcrowding but maintained that free movement, sports and regular maintenance compensated for it and that medical attention had been sufficient.

Pozaić later sought review by the County Court and, on 22 November 2011, lodged a constitutional complaint alleging inadequate space, medical care and discrimination. The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 5 June 2012.

Croatian law requires at least 4 m² and 10 m³ per prisoner, prohibits ill-treatment and guarantees humane treatment, and provides administrative and judicial complaint procedures (including protection by sentence-execution judges). The CPT’s 2012 visit report recorded widespread overcrowding in Croatian prisons and recommended a minimum of 4 m² living space (excluding sanitary facilities), together with improved activity programmes and medical-record standards.

These facts underpin the Court’s examination of whether the conditions reached the Article 3 threshold and whether an effective domestic remedy existed.

The case of Maravić Markeš v. Croatia originated in Application no. 70923/11 lodged on 20 April 2011 by a Croatian national, Ms Dragica Karla Maravić Markeš (born 1949, resident in Zagreb). She alleged a breach of the principle of equality of arms in administrative proceedings concerning her claim for severance pay following termination of her employment.

The applicant had been employed since 1985 as an inspector for Zagreb Municipal Council. On 25 June 1991 its Executive Board removed her from her post. She was made available for redeployment and temporarily assigned to the Council’s Secretariat for Planning, Public Utilities, Transport and Infrastructure until 30 September 1991. On that date the Secretariat concluded that no permanent post could be found and terminated her employment upon expiry of her notice period on 31 March 1992. No severance pay was paid at the time. Termination occurred under section 383 of the Public Administration Act (then in force), which addressed redundancy arising from restructuring of units or posts and contained no entitlement to severance pay. Section 383(a), which later provided for severance pay where a civil servant was made available for redeployment to meet the needs of the service, entered into force only on 8 October 1991—after the notice decision had already been issued.

On 29 July 2006 the applicant requested severance pay from the successor Municipal Office, relying on section 383(a). On 10 October 2006 the Office declared the request inadmissible as time-barred, holding that the three-year limitation period under section 138 of the Labour Act had begun to run on 1 April 1992. Her appeal was dismissed on 9 November 2006; the appellate body confirmed that the claim was statute-barred both under the five-year period of the Obligations Act applicable at the date of termination and under the later Labour Act.

On 23 December 2006 the applicant brought an administrative action before the Administrative Court. The court transmitted the case file to the Municipal Office for comment. On 15 February 2007 the Office submitted written observations that, for the first time, contested entitlement on the merits: even had the request been timely, the applicant would not have been entitled to severance pay because her employment had been terminated under section 383 rather than section 383(a). These observations were never forwarded to the applicant.

Between September 2007 and December 2008 the applicant repeatedly asked the Administrative Court to expedite the proceedings and to hold an oral hearing. She also sought the recusal of the assigned judge and the Court’s President, citing unexplained delay; both requests were refused. On 6 May 2009 the Administrative Court dismissed the action. It held that termination had occurred under section 383, not 383(a), so no statutory basis for severance pay existed, and that the request was in any event time-barred. The court thereby adopted the new merits argument that had first appeared in the uncommunicated observations.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint on 10 July 2009 alleging, inter alia, a lack of adversarial procedure. On 30 March 2011 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, finding that she had merely repeated her earlier submissions and had not demonstrated any arbitrary interpretation of statute or violation of constitutional rights.

(The applicant also pursued a separate complaint about the length of the administrative proceedings, which the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rejected; those proceedings are not central to the equality-of-arms allegation.)

The facts relevant to the alleged violation therefore centre on the Administrative Court’s failure to communicate the Municipal Office’s 15 February 2007 observations—observations that introduced a previously unraised ground of decision—and the Court’s subsequent reliance on that ground without giving the applicant any opportunity to reply, either in writing or at an oral hearing.
