**Case of Placì v. Italy (Application no. 48754/11)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 21 January 2014 (final 21 April 2014) in this application by Italian national Luigi Placì (born 1975), represented by counsel. He alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention arising from the lack of a proper pre-conscription fitness assessment and from the compulsory military service itself, including intensive training and punishments inflicted on him, which he claimed amounted to prohibited treatment. He also alleged a violation of Article 6 on account of unfairness in the ensuing domestic proceedings for damages.

In 1993, at age 18, the applicant was called up for compulsory military service. A combined psychological evaluation and physical examination on 3 December 1993 found him fit. The detailed report (disclosed to him only in 2010 during later proceedings) recorded slowness in understanding and executing tasks, a tendency to give up, and scores of 4 out of 10 in language/cultural skills, motivation, mental performance and behaviour. A further medical examination on 14 June 1994 again declared him fit, with no illness detected. He was assigned to Battalion no. 123 in Chieti and subjected to intensive physical and mental training, including firearms instruction.

On 9 July 1994 he was transferred to the provincial command in Aquila, remaining until 30 December 1994 (with a temporary posting to its logistical battalion from September to November). During this period he received eight punishments amounting to 24 days of confinement, including solitary confinement, for infractions such as negligent care of his camp-bed area, failure to report to a supervisor, and informal behaviour towards a superior. He was hospitalised at least four times for unrelated medical issues. On 30 December 1994 he was moved to Lecce, where a commander observed nervous tics and twitches, difficulty socialising and learning, and absent-minded behaviour, prompting a specialised fitness assessment.

On 24 January 1995 he was hospitalised and diagnosed with an anxiety disorder and a fragile mental state. An NHS report of 6 February 1995 noted a youth history of affection-relational problems and learning difficulties; he was physically weak, insecure, isolated, dysfunctional, and had a slight intellectual deficit (IQ 67) with impaired logic, memory and orientation. Military life provoked anxiety and fear of colleagues. He remained on medical leave until April 1995, when a further assessment diagnosed dysphoria and borderline personality disorder; he was discharged as unfit on 8 April 1995.

Subsequent examinations showed some improvement after discharge (cessation of tics and dysphoria) but persistent insecurity, isolation and intellectual deficit. The applicant’s doctor identified at least a causal link to military service. In 1996 he sought damages from the Defence Ministry. Military medical commissions in 1999–2000 diagnosed chronic obsessive-compulsive disorder as a pre-existing condition unrelated to service (no significant events or duties having influenced it) and deemed the claim out of time. The Ministry rejected the request in July 2000. The applicant repeatedly sought, and only partially obtained, military health, disciplinary and administrative records.

He instituted proceedings before the Lecce Regional Administrative Tribunal in July 2000, seeking recognition of a causal link (or, alternatively, liability for recruiting an unfit person) and damages. After delays, including a court-appointed expert’s failure to report, the TAR in 2007 found the condition pre-existing and the 1994 fitness examination inaccurate but did not award damages. On appeal the Consiglio di Stato in 2010 ordered a further assessment by the Defence Ministry’s Medical Board (composed mainly of military doctors plus an external neurologist). The Board confirmed a pre-existing condition (chronic OCD, intellectual disability, personality changes) neither caused nor aggravated by ordinary service. The applicant’s expert argued that service (isolation, lack of support, repeated punishments) had triggered or worsened latent vulnerabilities. The Consiglio di Stato in 2011 rejected the appeal, adopting the Board’s findings that the infirmity predated service and had not been detectable in 1994, while declining to review the report’s merits.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 3 claim (inadequate screening exposing a vulnerable conscript to training and disciplinary measures) and the Article 6 claim (delays, incomplete disclosure, and questions over the impartiality of the military-composed Medical Board).

The case of Placì v. Italy (ECtHR, Application no. 48754/11) concerns an Italian conscript's complaints under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 6 (right to a fair hearing) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Luigi Placì, born in 1975, was called up for compulsory military service in 1993 at age 18. A combined psychological and physical examination on 3 December 1993 found him fit, though an undisclosed report (released only in 2010) noted slowness in understanding and executing tasks, a tendency to give up, and low scores (4/10) in language/cultural skills, motivation, mental performance and behaviour. A further examination on 14 June 1994 again declared him fit, with no illness identified. He was assigned to Battalion 123 in Chieti for intensive physical and mental training, including firearms use.

On 9 July 1994 he was transferred to the Aquila provincial command (remaining until 30 December 1994, with a temporary logistical posting). There he received eight punishments totalling 24 days' confinement (including solitary confinement) for minor infractions such as poor camp-bed care, failure to report and informal behaviour towards superiors. He was hospitalised at least four times for non-mental-health reasons. After transfer to Lecce, a commander observed nervous tics, social and learning difficulties and absent-minded behaviour, prompting a specialist assessment.

On 24 January 1995 Placì was hospitalised and diagnosed with anxiety disorder and a fragile mental state. A 6 February 1995 NHS report detailed pre-existing affection-relational problems, learning difficulties, physical weakness, insecurity, isolation, dysfunctionality, inability to take responsibility, impaired cognition (logic and memory deficits) and an IQ of 67. He was deemed incapable of positive relationships and lived military life in anxiety and fear (perceiving even jokes as aggression). Prolonged service was predicted to worsen his condition. After medical leave he was diagnosed on 8 April 1995 with dysphoria and borderline personality disorder and discharged as unfit.

Post-discharge examinations (October 1995) showed some improvement once service ended, but persisting insecurity, isolation, instability and intellectual deficit. Placì's doctor identified a causal link to military service (or at least aggravation). In January 1996 he claimed damages from the Defence Ministry. Military medical commissions (1999–2000) diagnosed chronic OCD as pre-existing and unrelated to service, rejecting the claim as untimely. A 1999 NHS certificate noted treatment since 1977 for a fragile mind, low IQ and OCD, with post-service violent outbursts. Repeated requests for service documents went unanswered for years.

In July 2000 Placì sued in the Lecce Regional Administrative Tribunal (TAR) seeking recognition of a causal link or, alternatively, liability for recruiting an unfit person, plus damages. Access to documents remained incomplete (the Aquila unit having been disbanded). A court expert appointed in 2002 never reported; the TAR refused replacement in 2007 (citing the applicant's inaction) and dismissed the claim, accepting the commissions' view of a pre-existing condition while noting the 1994 fitness examination had been inaccurate.

On appeal the Supreme Administrative Court (CS) ordered a 2010 examination by the Defence Ministry's Medical Board (predominantly military members plus one police doctor and an external neurologist). The Board confirmed pre-existing chronic OCD, slight intellectual disability and personality changes, finding no causation or aggravation by ordinary service. Placì's expert argued the opposite: a previously healthy conscript developed dysphoria (later chronic OCD) due to isolation, inability to relate, lack of support and repeated punishments, which triggered or at least contributed to the illness even if predisposition existed. The CS (February 2011) rejected the appeal, endorsing the Board's findings (noting the 1994 problems may not have been detectable without stimuli), dismissing impartiality and disclosure complaints, and holding that it could not reassess the report's merits. The applicant alleged Article 3 violations arising from conscription despite unfitness and from the training and punishments inflicted, plus Article 6 violations from delayed, incomplete and non-independent proceedings.

The case of Placì v. Italy (Application no. 48754/11) concerns an Italian applicant, Luigi Placì (born 1975), who alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 6 (right to a fair hearing) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his compulsory military service and subsequent domestic proceedings.

In 1993, at age 18, the applicant was conscripted. A combined psychological and physical examination on 3 December 1993 found him fit for service, though an undisclosed detailed report (released only in 2010) noted slowness in understanding and executing tasks, a tendency to give up, and scores of 4/10 in language/cultural skills, motivation, mental performance and behaviour. A further examination on 14 June 1994 again declared him fit, with no illness identified. He was assigned to intensive physical and mental training, including firearms use.

Transferred in July 1994, he faced eight punishments over five months, totalling 24 days of confinement (including solitary) for minor infractions such as poor camp-bed maintenance, failure to report or informal behaviour towards superiors. He was hospitalised at least four times. A commander later observed nervous tics, socialisation and learning difficulties and absent-mindedness, prompting a specialist assessment.

Hospitalised in January 1995, he was diagnosed with anxiety disorder and a fragile mental state. A February 1995 NHS report detailed pre-existing affection-relational problems, learning difficulties, physical weakness, insecurity, isolation, dysfunction, inability to assume responsibility, impaired cognition (IQ 67, logic and memory deficits) and fear of fellow soldiers. Prolonged service was expected to worsen his anxiety. After medical leave he was discharged in April 1995 as unfit, diagnosed with dysphoria and borderline personality disorder.

Post-discharge examinations showed some improvement (cessation of defensive attitudes, dysphoria and tics) but persistent insecurity, isolation and intellectual deficit. His doctor identified a causal link to military service. In 1996 he sought damages from the Defence Ministry. Military medical commissions in 1999–2000 diagnosed pre-existing obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), unrelated to service events or duties, and deemed the claim time-barred. The Ministry rejected the request. Repeated applications for service records, health files, disciplinary details and commission minutes went largely unanswered or produced only partial, delayed disclosures.

In 2000 the applicant sued before the Lecce Regional Administrative Tribunal (TAR) for recognition of a causal link or, alternatively, liability for recruiting an unfit person, plus damages. After years of delay (an appointed expert failed to report), the TAR in 2007 dismissed the claim, accepting the commissions’ finding of a pre-existing condition while noting the 1994 fitness examination had been inaccurate.

On appeal the Supreme Administrative Court (CS) in 2010 ordered a further assessment by the Defence Ministry’s Medical Board (composed largely of military doctors). The Board confirmed pre-existing chronic OCD, slight intellectual disability and personality changes, concluding the condition was neither caused nor aggravated by ordinary service. The applicant’s expert countered that military stresses, isolation, lack of support and repeated punishments had triggered or precipitated the disorders in a predisposed individual. The CS in 2011 rejected the appeal, adopting the Board’s findings as neither contradictory nor illogical and declining to review their merits. It held any undisclosed documents were irrelevant to the service period and that health problems might not have manifested without particular stimuli.

These facts underpin the Article 3 complaint of inadequate pre-conscription assessment exposing a vulnerable recruit to intensive training and punishments amounting to prohibited treatment, and the Article 6 complaint of unfair proceedings marked by delayed or withheld evidence, an expert aligned with the defendant Ministry, and courts’ failure to address liability despite acknowledged examination shortcomings.
001-140238:
The case of Buhaniuc v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 56074/10) concerns allegations of ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation arising from events in Chișinău in April 2009. Following disputed parliamentary elections on 5 April, large-scale protests erupted. On the evening of 7 April the applicant, then aged 19, was arrested amid the unrest and the next day sentenced to ten days’ administrative detention.

The applicant claimed that a plain-clothes officer punched him in the eye at the moment of arrest. He was then taken first to Buiucani police station and later to the General Police Directorate, where he was beaten by groups of five to twelve officers, some in uniform and some in civilian clothes. He described being forced to run a “death corridor” of lined-up officers who kicked and struck detainees as they passed, being subjected to the “telephone” (simultaneous blows to both ears), being punched and struck with rubber truncheons on the head while handcuffed behind his back, and being forced to hold his arms raised for prolonged periods while being hit. He lost consciousness several times. Psychological pressure included threats of long-term imprisonment, rape and death, as well as interrogation by multiple officers and coercion to sign blank documents.

Detention conditions were also alleged to constitute ill-treatment. The applicant was held with eight others in a 4 m × 4 m damp cell without daylight, any means of telling the time or date, or contact with the outside world, relatives, a lawyer or a doctor. No water was supplied for the first 24 hours; thereafter dirty water was distributed in shared, unhygienic bottles. No food was provided. Overcrowding and humidity prevented sleep for three days. There was no toilet inside the cell and access to one outside was irregular and accompanied by humiliation. He later developed hepatitis of unknown origin.

Medical evidence included a haematoma on the left eye recorded by a doctor on 11 April 2009. A detailed examination on 29 April 2009 at the “Memoria” Rehabilitation Centre for Torture Victims (an EU-funded NGO) produced a report dated 15 December 2009 documenting sequelae of head injury (intracranial hypertension syndrome), post-traumatic stress disorder and a post-traumatic ear condition.

On 15 April 2009 the applicant lodged a complaint of ill-treatment with the military prosecutor. Officers involved in the arrest denied using force. On 29 May 2009 the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation for lack of evidence of a crime. The applicant learned of the decision only in January 2010; the Prosecutor General’s Office upheld it on 18 February 2010. On 19 April 2010 an investigating judge quashed both decisions, noting that they rested solely on the accused officers’ statements and that one prosecutor had conceded force might have been used during arrest while the officers themselves denied any force. A formal investigation was then opened. The applicant was recognised as a victim, gave a statement and participated in a photographic identification parade (without recognising anyone). On 25 May 2010 the investigation was suspended because no suspect had been identified.

After the European Court of Human Rights communicated the application in December 2011, the Prosecutor General’s Office in February 2012 instructed the Chișinău Military Prosecutor to reopen the case, listing twelve specific investigative steps (hearings of co-arrestees and cell-mates, examination of medical records including the Memoria report, cross-examination of the applicant and arresting officers, etc.). In March 2012 the doctor who had examined the applicant at Buiucani station was heard and two officers were formally declared suspects. No further progress was reported to the Court.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning both the alleged ill-treatment itself and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation.

The ECtHR case of Buhaniuc v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 56074/10) concerns a Moldovan applicant’s claims of police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation after his arrest during post-election unrest.

General elections occurred on 5 April 2009. Large protests against alleged fraud followed on 6–7 April, prompting hundreds of arrests. Applicant Sergiu Buhaniuc (born 1990) was arrested on the evening of 7 April and the next day received a 10-day administrative detention sentence.

He alleged that a plain-clothes officer punched him in the eye during arrest. At Buiucani police station and the General Police Directorate he was beaten by groups of 5–12 uniformed and plain-clothes officers and forced through a “death corridor” in which lined-up officers kicked and struck passing detainees. Specific acts included simultaneous blows to both ears (“the telephone”), fists and rubber sticks to the head while his hands were cuffed behind his back, and being forced to keep his arms raised for long periods while being hit. He lost consciousness several times.

He was confined with eight others in a 4 \times 4 m damp cell lacking daylight or any means of telling time, and was denied contact with family, a lawyer or a doctor. No water was supplied for the first 24 hours; thereafter only dirty water in shared unhygienic bottles was provided (he later developed hepatitis of unknown origin). No food was given and congestion prevented sleep for three days. Toilet access was irregular and humiliating. He was threatened with lengthy imprisonment, rape and death, interrogated by several persons at once and forced to sign blank papers.

A doctor on 11 April recorded a left-eye haematoma. Examination at the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre for Torture Victims (29 April; report issued December) documented sequelae of head trauma, including intracranial hypertension, post-traumatic stress disorder and a post-traumatic ear condition.

The applicant complained to the military prosecutor on 15 April. Arresting officers denied using force. On 29 May the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation for lack of evidence of a crime. The applicant received the decision only in January 2010 and appealed; the Prosecutor General confirmed the refusal on 18 February 2010.

A court challenge succeeded on 19 April 2010: the investigating judge annulled both decisions, criticising exclusive reliance on the accused officers’ statements and noting inconsistencies about whether force had been used at all, and ordered a supplementary investigation.

A formal probe began around May 2010. The applicant was granted victim status on 19 May, gave a detailed account and viewed a photo parade but recognised no one. The investigation was suspended on 25 May because no suspect had been identified.

After the Court communicated the application (December 2011), the Prosecutor General in February 2012 recommended reopening and listed twelve specific steps (hearings of co-arrestees and the examining doctor, collection of all medical records including Memoria’s, examination of the underlying case file, and confrontations). In March 2012 the doctor confirmed he had recorded all injuries without pressure being applied, and two officers were named suspects and interviewed. No further developments were reported.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 3 violations (ill-treatment and lack of an effective investigation).

The case of Buhaniuc v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 56074/10) concerns allegations of police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation following the applicant’s arrest amid post-election protests. Sergiu Buhaniuc, a Moldovan national born in 1990 and living in Chișinău, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 September 2010. He claimed he had been subjected to physical and psychological ill-treatment during and after his arrest on 7 April 2009, and that the authorities failed to investigate his complaints effectively.

General elections occurred in Moldova on 5 April 2009. Large protests against alleged electoral fraud took place on 6 and 7 April, resulting in hundreds of arrests. The applicant was arrested on the evening of 7 April 2009 and sentenced the next day to ten days’ administrative detention. He alleged that a plain-clothes officer punched him in the eye during the arrest. He was then beaten at the Buiucani police station and the General Police Directorate (GPD) by groups of five to twelve officers, some in uniform and others in civilian clothes. Officers formed a “death corridor” through which detainees were forced to pass while being kicked and struck. The applicant was subjected to “the telephone” (simultaneous blows to both ears), punched and hit on the head with fists and rubber truncheons while handcuffed behind his back, and forced to hold his hands up for prolonged periods while being struck. He lost consciousness several times.

Detention conditions were also alleged to constitute ill-treatment. He was held with eight others in a 4 x 4 metre damp cell without daylight or any means of telling time, and without access to relatives, a lawyer or a doctor. No water was provided for the first 24 hours; thereafter only dirty water in unhygienic shared bottles was available. He later developed hepatitis of unknown origin. No food was given and he could not sleep for three days. There was no toilet in the cell and access to one outside was irregular and accompanied by humiliation. Psychologically, he was threatened with lengthy imprisonment, rape and death, interrogated by several persons at once and forced to sign blank papers.

On 11 April 2009 a doctor recorded a haematoma on the applicant’s left eye. He complained to the military prosecutor on 15 April 2009. On 29 April 2009 he was examined at the “Memoria” Rehabilitation Centre for Torture Victims, which later issued a report documenting consequences of head injury (including intracranial hypertension and post-traumatic stress disorder) and a post-traumatic ear condition.

The prosecutor interviewed the arresting officers, who denied using force, and on 29 May 2009 decided not to open a criminal investigation for lack of evidence. The applicant received the decision only in January 2010 and complained to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which upheld it on 18 February 2010. He challenged both decisions in court. On 19 April 2010 the Buiucani District Court quashed them, noting that they relied solely on the accused officers’ statements and contained internal contradictions about whether force had been used during arrest. A formal investigation was opened. The applicant was recognised as a victim on 19 May 2010 and took part in a photo identification parade without recognising anyone. The investigation was suspended on 25 May 2010 because no suspect had been identified.

After the Court communicated the application on 12 December 2011, the Prosecutor General’s Office on 8 February 2012 recommended reopening the case and listed twelve specific investigative steps, including hearing co-detainees, the examining doctor, obtaining medical records and conducting confrontations. The station doctor was heard on 22 March 2012 and confirmed noting the applicant’s injuries. On 26 March 2012 two officers were declared suspects and interviewed. No further developments were reported to the Court.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning both the alleged ill-treatment itself and the adequacy of the subsequent investigation.
001-140259:
The case concerns the disappearance of Zhamalayl Yanayev (b. 1961) after his detention on 28 December 2004 at Beslan airport, North Ossetia. The first applicant (Ms Z., his sister, living in Austria) and second applicant (Yakha Khatuyeva, his wife, living in Grozny) alleged that state agents abducted him.

Yanayev was in the departure lounge after checking in for a Moscow flight. Two armed men in camouflage uniforms, presenting themselves as RUBOP colonels of the Ministry of the Interior, entered the office of FSB Lt-Col V.T. (head of airport security). Without producing any arrest documents, they had Yanayev summoned. They took him to a personal-inspection room, then left via a service exit and drove away in two UAZ-469 vehicles and a Niva (one registration noted as 33-03 65-86 OA 12 RUS). Unnamed witnesses later supplied names and ranks of possible servicemen from Chechnya. The family has had no news of him since.

Relatives learned of the incident when he failed to arrive in Moscow and immediately contacted airport staff, prosecutors and other agencies. On 2 January 2005 the airport police chief confirmed to the second applicant that unidentified “power-structure” officers had entered the security zone in the same vehicles, collected Yanayev and driven off.

On 10 February 2005 the Vladikavkaz transport prosecutor’s office opened criminal case no. 2553005 for kidnapping (Art. 126 CC); the second applicant was granted victim status the next day. The investigation was later reclassified to include murder because of Yanayev’s prolonged absence and was transferred to military prosecutors. Despite numerous complaints to the General Prosecutor’s Office, the Ministry of the Interior, the Presidential Council and others, no progress was made in identifying the perpetrators or locating Yanayev. CCTV footage of the vehicles proved illegible. The last recorded decision to reopen the file dates from June 2009; the investigation remained pending without result.

A parallel inquiry examined V.T.’s conduct. He stated that the men had produced apparently genuine RUBOP identity papers and that he had escorted them in accordance with airport-access regulations, without demanding detention documents. Criminal proceedings for abuse of power were opened against him in September 2005, discontinued in January and April 2006 for lack of the constituent elements of a crime, and the discontinuances were upheld by the garrison military court. Subsequent appeals and complaints by the second applicant were unsuccessful.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints of an unacknowledged detention and disappearance implicating state agents, together with an ineffective official investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights case of *Z. and Khatuyeva v. Russia* (applications nos. 39436/06 and 40169/07) concerns the alleged abduction and subsequent disappearance of Zhamalayl Yanayev (born 1961) on 28 December 2004. The first applicant (Ms Z., his sister, residing in Austria) and second applicant (Mrs Yakha Khatuyeva, his wife, residing in Grozny) claimed that State agents detained him at Beslan airport in North Ossetia, after which he vanished without trace. Neither applicant witnessed the events; their account derives from family inquiries and official investigation materials.

Yanayev, then living in Vladikavkaz, had checked in for a Moscow flight and passed security into the departure zone. Around 3 p.m., two armed men in camouflage uniforms approached Lieutenant-Colonel V.T. (FSB, head of airport security). They displayed RUBOP (Ministry of Interior organised-crime unit) credentials identifying them as colonels but produced no arrest warrant. Accompanied by V.T., they had a police officer summon Yanayev to a personal-inspection room. The men then escorted him out a service exit to three waiting vehicles (two UAZ-469s and a Niva) that had entered the secure perimeter. Family members later obtained (from unnamed eyewitnesses, including security staff) names, ranks and one vehicle registration (33-03 65-86 OA 12 RUS) linking the group to Ministry of Interior units based in Chechnya and to military personnel. Yanayev has not been seen or heard from since.

The family immediately contacted airport authorities, prosecutors and other agencies. On 2 January 2005 the airport police chief confirmed to the second applicant that unidentified “power-structure” officers had taken Yanayev after requesting his flight be delayed. Criminal investigation no. 2553005 was opened on 10 February 2005 by the Vladikavkaz transport prosecutor’s office under Article 126 § 1 of the Criminal Code (kidnapping); the second applicant was granted victim status the next day. The case was later reclassified to include murder given the prolonged disappearance. Despite repeated family complaints to prosecutors, the Interior Ministry, the FSB and human-rights bodies, the investigation (transferred at various times to military prosecutors) identified neither perpetrators nor Yanayev’s fate. CCTV footage proved unusable; listed vehicles were never traced. The last recorded reopening occurred on 8 June 2009; the file remained pending without progress.

Parallel proceedings examined V.T.’s role. He stated that the men had shown authentic RUBOP identity papers, that airport regulations permitted such access, and that he had not demanded an arrest warrant. After an initial refusal to prosecute, a case for abuse of power (Article 286) was opened then twice discontinued (January and April 2006) on the ground that V.T. had acted within his duties. Military courts rejected the second applicant’s challenges to those decisions. No further investigative steps established the identities of the men who removed Yanayev or any official records of his detention.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints of a State-orchestrated disappearance and an ineffective investigation.

The case of *Z. and Khatuyeva v. Russia* (ECtHR, 2014) involves applications by Ms Z (sister of Zhamalayl Yanayev, born 1961) and Mrs Yakha Khatuyeva (his wife) alleging that Russian State agents detained and disappeared Yanayev on 28 December 2004 at Beslan airport in North Ossetia. Neither applicant witnessed the events; accounts derive from family inquiries and official files.

Yanayev, living in Vladikavkaz, had checked in for a Moscow flight and passed security by about 3 p.m., waiting in the departure zone. Two armed men in camouflage uniforms approached Lieutenant-Colonel V.T. (FSB, head of airport security). They presented RUBOP (Ministry of Interior anti-organised crime) identity documents as colonels, requested Yanayev be summoned, but produced no arrest warrant or legal basis. V.T. accompanied them; a police officer called Yanayev to an inspection room. The men then escorted him from the building via a service exit into three waiting vehicles (two UAZ-469s and a Niva) that had entered the security perimeter. Eyewitnesses, including airport guards, later provided the family with names, ranks, and a vehicle plate (33-03 65-86 OA 12 RUS) linking the men to Ministry of Interior or military personnel based in Chechnya (Khankala). Yanayev has not been seen or heard from since.

The family realised the abduction when Yanayev missed his flight. On 2 January 2005, the second applicant spoke to airport police, who confirmed that unidentified “power structure” officers had requested a flight delay, entered with V.T., and taken Yanayev away in the described vehicles. Relatives immediately contacted airport authorities, prosecutors, the Interior Ministry, military prosecutors, administrative bodies, the media, and human-rights organisations (including the Red Cross), supplying details of the incident but receiving no information on Yanayev’s whereabouts.

On 18 January 2005 the second applicant petitioned the Vladikavkaz transport prosecutor. Criminal case no. 2553005 was opened on 10 February 2005 for kidnapping (Criminal Code Art. 126); she was granted victim status. Given Yanayev’s prolonged absence the events were later also classified as murder. The investigation was transferred around May 2005 to the Northern Caucasus military prosecutor. Despite establishing that unidentified persons posing as FSB/RUBOP officers, with V.T.’s assistance, had detained Yanayev, investigators identified neither the perpetrators nor Yanayev’s fate. Requests for case-file access were refused while the inquiry remained pending. The latest reopening occurred on 8 June 2009; the Government reported no subsequent progress.

Separate proceedings examined V.T. for abuse of power (Art. 286). Questioned in June 2005, he stated the men showed genuine-looking RUBOP IDs, he followed airport access rules allowing FSB/MVD officers into the security zone on presentation of service documents, he did not demand an arrest warrant, and he later learned they came from Khankala. After an initial decision not to prosecute, proceedings were opened then repeatedly discontinued (most recently 20 April 2006) for lack of criminal elements, the investigators concluding V.T. had acted in accordance with regulations and his duties. The second applicant’s complaints were dismissed by military courts (June 2006, upheld on review). No one has been held accountable and Yanayev remains missing.

These facts underpin the applicants’ claims of an unacknowledged detention by State agents followed by an ineffective investigation into a possible enforced disappearance.
001-140232:
The case of Węgrzyn v. Poland (Application no. 29423/05) originated from an application lodged on 5 August 2005 by Jan Węgrzyn, a Polish national born in 1955 and residing in Widełka. He alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property) arising from the ex officio reopening of social-security proceedings that quashed a final decision awarding him an early-retirement pension.

The applicant, who had two children and had previously been employed while paying social-security contributions, applied on 13 February 2002 to the Rzeszów Social Security Board for an “EWK” pension. This benefit, governed by a 1989 Ordinance, was available to persons raising children whose serious health conditions required constant parental care. He submitted a medical certificate dated 21 December 2001 stating that his daughter (born 1991) suffered from neurogenic bladder dysfunction and needed constant care.

On 18 February 2002 the Board granted the pension. After the applicant’s employment contract ended on 28 February 2002, monthly payments of 943.88 PLN net (approximately EUR 232) began on 1 March 2002. He received a pensioner’s identity card marked “valid indefinitely” and continued to draw the benefit without interruption.

The Board later consulted its chief medical officer, who concluded from the existing documents that the child had never required permanent parental care. On 8 October 2002 the Board simultaneously issued two decisions: one immediately discontinuing payment and the other revoking the original award and refusing the pension on the ground that the statutory condition of necessary permanent care had not been met.

The applicant appealed, relying on the original medical certificate and invoking the principle of vested rights. The Rzeszów Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 20 November 2003. The Court of Appeal confirmed the dismissal on 16 April 2004, holding that the applicant had never satisfied the permanent-care requirement. A cassation appeal prepared by a professional lawyer was rejected by the Supreme Court on 17 September 2004 because it failed to specify admissible grounds.

The applicant was not required to repay benefits already received. He had not worked while receiving the pension. After revocation he resumed employment on 28 October 2002, initially on successive three-month contracts paying PLN 1 000 (less than 50 % of the then-average wage of approximately PLN 2 133). Later earnings rose to between 82 % and 104 % of the national average. Before the pension his income had consistently exceeded the average (102–140 %). His son later obtained employment as well.

These facts—initial grant of a seemingly final pension on the basis of submitted medical evidence, subsequent unilateral revocation without repayment obligation, unsuccessful domestic challenges, and the applicant’s subsequent modest earnings—form the core of the alleged interference with a possession under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The domestic legal framework and practice were those described in the Court’s earlier judgment in Moskal v. Poland.

The case of Węgrzyn v. Poland (Application no. 29423/05) was decided by a Committee of the European Court of Human Rights on 28 January 2014. The applicant, a Polish national born in 1955, alleged that the ex officio reopening of social-security proceedings that quashed a final decision granting him an early-retirement pension violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, who had two children and had previously been employed while paying social-security contributions, applied on 13 February 2002 to the Rzeszów Social Security Board for an “EWK” early-retirement pension available to persons raising children whose serious health conditions required constant parental care. He submitted a 21 December 2001 medical certificate stating that his daughter (born 1991) suffered from neurogenic bladder dysfunction and needed her parent’s constant care. On 18 February 2002 the Board granted the pension. Payment was initially suspended because the applicant was still working; his employment ended on 28 February 2002 and monthly payments of PLN 943.88 net (approximately EUR 232) began on 1 March 2002. He received a pensioner’s identity card marked “valid indefinitely” and continued to receive the pension without interruption until its later revocation.

On an unspecified date the Board consulted its chief medical officer, who concluded from the existing documents that the child had never required permanent parental care. On 8 October 2002 the Board issued two simultaneous decisions: one immediately discontinuing payments and the other revoking the original grant and refusing the pension under the 1989 Ordinance. The applicant appealed, arguing that the medical certificate confirmed the need for constant care and that revocation violated the principle of vested rights.

On 20 November 2003 the Rzeszów Regional Court dismissed the appeal. On 16 April 2004 the Rzeszów Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, holding that the applicant had not satisfied the statutory requirement of necessary permanent care. A professionally prepared cassation appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court on 17 September 2004 because it failed to specify grounds justifying examination.

The applicant was not ordered to repay any benefits already received. He had not worked while receiving the pension. After revocation he resumed employment on 28 October 2002, initially on short-term contracts at PLN 1,000 per month (less than half the then-average national wage of approximately PLN 2,130). Government figures later showed his annual income fluctuating around or slightly below the national average, compared with 102–140 per cent of average earnings in the years immediately before the pension. His son began working in 2007.

The relevant domestic social-security provisions and practice are those set out in Moskal v. Poland (no. 10373/05). The case therefore centres on whether the retrospective administrative reopening and judicial confirmation of the revocation of a formally final pension award constituted an unjustified interference with a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Węgrzyn v. Poland (no. 29423/05) was brought by a Polish national, Jan Węgrzyn (born 1955), who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He claimed that the authorities’ ex officio reopening of social-security proceedings, which quashed a final decision awarding him an early-retirement “EWK” pension, unlawfully interfered with his possessions.

On 13 February 2002 the applicant applied to the Rzeszów Social Security Board for an EWK pension, a benefit payable to persons raising children whose serious health conditions required constant parental care. He submitted a specialist medical certificate of 21 December 2001 stating that his daughter (born 1991) suffered from neurogenic bladder dysfunction and needed such care. On 18 February 2002 the Board granted the pension. Payment was briefly suspended because the applicant was still employed; after his contract ended on 28 February 2002, monthly net payments of 943.88 PLN (approximately EUR 232) began on 1 March 2002. He received a pensioner’s card marked “valid indefinitely” and received the benefit without interruption.

The Board later asked the Main Social Security Board’s doctor to review the file. The doctor concluded, on the basis of the medical documents, that the child had never required permanent care. On 8 October 2002 the Board issued two simultaneous decisions: one immediately stopping payment and the other revoking the original award and refusing the pension under the 1989 Ordinance.

The applicant appealed, relying on the original medical certificate and the principle of vested rights. The Rzeszów Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 20 November 2003. The Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 16 April 2004, finding that the statutory requirement of necessary permanent care had not been met. A professionally drafted cassation appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court on 17 September 2004 because the lawyer had failed to specify grounds that would justify examination of the appeal.

The applicant was not ordered to repay any sums already received. He had not worked while drawing the pension. He resumed employment on 28 October 2002, initially on short-term contracts paying PLN 1 000 (less than half the national average wage). Subsequent earnings fluctuated around or slightly below the national average. Before the pension award his income had generally exceeded the average. His son later obtained work, but the applicant remained the principal earner.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference: a formally final pension award, based on documents the applicant had submitted in good faith, was unilaterally reopened and withdrawn after payments had begun, without any finding of fraud or misrepresentation by the applicant and without any obligation to reimburse past benefits. The domestic courts confirmed the revocation solely on a fresh medical assessment that the child had never needed constant care, thereby extinguishing a right the applicant had treated as vested.
001-140260:
The applicant, a Russian national born in 1977, was arrested on 31 March 2003 on suspicion of murder and detained at the Shchelkovo IVS. He alleged that police officers, acting under the command of officer N., repeatedly took him to special cells for questioning in an effort to extract a confession or obtain his signature on blank sheets of paper. When he refused, they handcuffed him to a chair and beat him on the back and sides until he signed a confession.

On 21 April 2003 the applicant was transferred to SIZO-50/8. Medical staff there refused admission after documenting a contusion of the spine and a contusion of the left chest with suspected rib fractures; they required further specialist examination. He was returned to the IVS and taken the same day to Shchelkovo town hospital, where a physician, neuropathologist and radiologist confirmed the spinal and chest contusions and excluded fractures. He was finally admitted to the SIZO on 25 April 2003. Certificates issued by the SIZO in 2011 recorded no complaints by him during his subsequent detention there and noted that the initial refusal of admission had not been entered in the prison register because he had not actually been received.

On 16 August 2007 the applicant lodged a formal complaint of police ill-treatment, expressly relying on the 21 April 2003 medical report. Over the following three years the investigating authorities issued seven successive refusals to open a criminal case. Each refusal asserted that no injuries had been recorded at the IVS, that hospital records showed only influenza and an unrelated tendon rupture, and that the applicant’s allegations were unfounded. The 21 April 2003 report was either ignored or later dismissed as unverifiable because it did not appear in the applicant’s personal file and the hospital archive contained no corresponding X-ray. Officers N. and the investigators who had handled the original murder case denied any use of force. Supervising prosecutors repeatedly quashed the refusals as incomplete, ordering interviews, retrieval of SIZO and hospital documents, and other steps that were never fully carried out. Domestic courts, acting under Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, dismissed the applicant’s challenges, often on the ground that the latest refusal had already been set aside. One appellate decision in 2011 identified specific defects (failure to examine the medical report, reliance on non-existent witness statements, and an unaddressed recusal application) but the subsequent re-examination again rejected the complaint.

Meanwhile the applicant had been convicted of murder on 28 August 2003 and the conviction had been upheld on appeal. A later recantation by a prosecution witness did not lead to any reopening of that case.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning both the alleged ill-treatment itself and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation.

**Case of Velikanov v. Russia (Application no. 4124/08)**

The applicant, Vadim Vladimirovich Velikanov (born 1977), a Russian national later serving a prison sentence, alleged ill-treatment by police and an ineffective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention. He was arrested on 31 March 2003 on suspicion of murder and detained in the Shchelkovo IVS (temporary detention facility). He claimed officers under police officer N. took him to special cells, sought a confession or his signature on blank papers, handcuffed him to a chair when he refused, and beat him on the back and sides until he signed a confession.

On 21 April 2003 he was transferred to remand prison SIZO-50/8. Authorities refused admission after a medical examination documented injuries including a spinal contusion and left-chest contusion with suspected rib fracture, requiring further expert examination. He was returned to the IVS, then taken to Shchelkovo town hospital for examination (including X-ray). Physicians and a neuropathologist confirmed the contusions in the SIZO report (barely legible). A radiologist’s 23 April 2003 note similarly confirmed spinal contusion without fracture. He was admitted to SIZO-50/8 on 25 April 2003. Later SIZO certificates (2011) stated he made no complaints while held there (April 2003–January 2004) and that the 21 April refusal of admission was for additional medical confirmation, with no register entry as he was not admitted.

On 16 August 2007 the applicant complained of police beatings, citing the 21 April 2003 report. Investigators issued successive refusals to open a criminal case (24 August 2007, 29 September 2007, 11 February 2008, 5 March 2008, 4 July 2008, 16 April 2009, and 4 October 2010). Early decisions claimed no IVS records of medical requests or injuries during pre-trial detention, cited a hospital certificate diagnosing influenza and spontaneous tendon rupture (unrelated to the alleged injuries), noted no forensic examination in his criminal case, and ignored the 21 April report. Documents from the IVS were said to have been lost by a former head. Later decisions added that SIZO-50/8 and the hospital had no records of the 21 April examination or X-ray (image no. 1478), that interviewed officers (including N.) and investigators denied using or witnessing force, that the applicant first complained four years later, and that his claims aimed to mislead authorities and accuse officials. One decision noted he named only N. (who allegedly brought civilians who used force) and did not identify other officers.

Supervising prosecutors repeatedly quashed the refusals as incomplete or premature, ordering identification/interview of officers and investigators, retrieval of SIZO medical documents and the applicant’s file, and other steps. The applicant lodged Article 125 complaints with Shchelkovo Town Court challenging several refusals. Courts often dismissed them because the decisions had already been quashed and further inquiry ordered; he did not always appeal. A December 2010 dismissal (which noted but did not examine the 21 April report and referenced missing explanations) was quashed on appeal in March 2011 for failure to consider a recusal, the medical report, and absent evidence. A May 2011 re-dismissal stated the report’s authenticity could not be verified (no file record of the examination) and that the applicant had not alleged ill-treatment during his original investigation or trial. It is unclear if he appealed further. A 2010 re-submission was dismissed as already investigated and unsubstantiated.

The applicant was convicted of murder on 28 August 2003 and sentenced to 11 years; the conviction was upheld on 12 February 2004. A later witness recantation led to unsuccessful attempts (2006–2009) to prosecute that witness. Domestic law (Article 125 CCP and related jurisprudence) allowed judicial review of investigative decisions but generally not after the main case reached trial, except in limited circumstances involving possible criminality compromising fairness.

These facts centre on the documented injuries shortly after alleged police questioning, the four-year delay in formal complaint, and the protracted, repeatedly quashed inquiries that consistently failed to engage the key medical report or locate corroborating records.

The applicant, Vadim Velikanov, a Russian national born in 1977, alleged that he had been subjected to ill-treatment by police officers after his arrest on suspicion of murder and that the ensuing investigation had been ineffective, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

On 31 March 2003 Velikanov was arrested and placed in the temporary detention facility of the Shchelkovo Office of the Interior (Shchelkovo IVS). He claimed that officers under the command of officer N. repeatedly took him to special cells, demanded that he confess or sign blank sheets of paper, and, when he refused, handcuffed him to a chair and beat him on the back and sides until he signed a confession.

On 21 April 2003 he was transferred to remand prison SIZO-50/8. Medical staff there refused to admit him after documenting a spinal contusion and a chest contusion with suspected rib fractures; they required further expert examination. He was taken to Shchelkovo town hospital the same day for an X-ray and clinical assessment. The attending physicians and radiologist confirmed the spinal and chest contusions but found no fracture. Velikanov was finally admitted to SIZO-50/8 on 25 April 2003. Subsequent prison certificates recorded that he made no complaints while held there and that the initial refusal of admission had been solely for additional medical checks.

Velikanov first formally complained of the beatings on 16 August 2007, citing the 21 April 2003 medical report. The Shchelkovo prosecutor’s office issued seven successive refusals to open a criminal investigation (24 August 2007, 29 September 2007, 11 February 2008, 5 March 2008, 4 July 2008, 16 April 2009 and 4 October 2010). Each decision asserted that no injuries had been recorded at the IVS, that relevant registers had been lost, that hospital records showed only influenza and a spontaneous tendon rupture, and that officers and investigators denied any violence. None of the decisions examined the 21 April 2003 report. Supervising prosecutors repeatedly quashed the refusals as incomplete or premature and ordered further steps (identification and questioning of officers, retrieval of SIZO medical records, etc.). Those steps were never adequately performed.

Velikanov challenged several of the refusals in the Shchelkovo Town Court under Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court either returned the complaints for formal defects, dismissed them because the impugned decisions had already been quashed, or, on one occasion, held the inquiry complete without addressing the medical report. The Moscow Regional Court later quashed one such dismissal for failure to examine the report and for relying on statements that were not in the file; on remittal the Town Court again dismissed the complaint, stating that the report’s authenticity could not be verified.

Velikanov was convicted of murder on 28 August 2003 and sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment; the conviction was upheld on appeal in February 2004. He did not raise the ill-treatment allegations during the criminal trial. Later unsuccessful attempts to prosecute a recanting witness did not form part of the Article 3 complaint.

The Court found that the documented injuries, occurring while Velikanov was entirely under police control, gave rise to a presumption of ill-treatment that the State had failed to rebut. The investigation, marked by repeated refusals that ignored key medical evidence, lost documents, untraced witnesses and a four-year delay before any inquiry began, fell well short of the requirement of effectiveness. Both the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3 were therefore violated.
001-140753:
The case of Franek v. Slovakia (Application no. 14090/10) originated from an application lodged on 18 February 2010 by Ján Franek, a Slovak enforcement officer born in 1964. He alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention, specifically his right to a fair hearing by a tribunal, arising from civil proceedings and their review by the Constitutional Court.

In enforcement proceedings, Franek seized movable property belonging to a debtor company. Bankruptcy proceedings were then initiated against the debtor, prompting the administrator to demand transfer of the property in line with legal requirements. Franek stored certain items at the premises of one creditor, whose representatives initially retained the property to secure the outstanding debt before later revoking that stance.

On 21 October 2003 the Liptovský Mikuláš District Court, acting on the administrator’s application, ordered Franek to transfer the property within 15 days and to pay costs of EUR 1,130. The Žilina Regional Court quashed that judgment on 14 April 2005, holding that the first-instance court had failed to examine properly whether Franek had standing as defendant given that a third party was retaining the items.

A fresh hearing was listed for 21 March 2006. On 14 March Franek requested an adjournment on grounds of incapacity for work. The District Court proceeded in his absence after noting the absence of supporting documentary evidence and, on 21 March 2006, again ordered transfer of the property (which it held was at Franek’s disposal under sections 14 and 18 of the Bankruptcy Act 1991) together with costs of EUR 1,964. It rejected the argument that the storing creditor’s retention right excused Franek.

Franek appealed, enclosing a medical certificate dated 17 February 2006 that confirmed his inability to work from 16 February to 2 May 2006 following an accident; he explained that he had been bedridden and therefore unable to produce the certificate earlier. The Regional Court nevertheless upheld the judgment on 6 September 2007; the decision became final on 10 December 2007.

Franek then lodged an appeal on points of law. Invoking Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, he complained that the first-instance court had refused his excuse and thereby prevented him from participating. He further argued that neither he nor the administrator had standing, that the lower courts had applied the law incorrectly and arbitrarily, and that the order was unenforceable because the property was not in his possession.

The Supreme Court rejected the appeal as inadmissible on 7 April 2009. It observed that, although a written request for adjournment had been sent, no documentary proof of illness had been submitted to the District Court in time; the court was therefore entitled to proceed. Lack of standing (as opposed to lack of legal capacity) was not a permissible ground under Article 237(b). Consequently the Supreme Court did not examine the alleged errors of fact or law.

On 12 June 2009 Franek filed a constitutional complaint alleging breaches of Article 6 by all three levels of ordinary court: factual and legal errors, arbitrariness, absence of standing, and the decision to proceed in his absence despite a broken leg that had prevented timely production of a medical certificate.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint on 17 September 2009. It held that the challenge to the first-instance and appellate judgments was out of time (the two-month statutory limit having expired after 10 December 2007) and that the Supreme Court’s declaration of inadmissibility did not restart the clock. After a detailed review it found the Supreme Court’s reasoning neither arbitrary nor otherwise contrary to the right to a fair hearing.

These facts centre on whether Franek was afforded a genuine opportunity to be heard, whether the courts correctly determined standing and applied the Bankruptcy Act, and whether the Constitutional Court’s application of time-limits and the subsidiarity principle itself respected Article 6.

The case of Franek v. Slovakia (application no. 14090/10) was brought by Slovak enforcement officer Ján Franek, who alleged a violation of his Article 6 ECHR right to a fair hearing by a tribunal in civil proceedings concerning seized property and in the Constitutional Court’s subsequent review.

In the course of enforcement proceedings Franek seized movable property belonging to a company. Bankruptcy proceedings were then opened against the debtor. The bankruptcy administrator demanded that Franek transfer the assets in accordance with the Bankruptcy Act 1991. Franek had stored some of the items at the premises of one of the creditors; that creditor initially asserted a right of retention but later revoked it.

On 21 October 2003 the Liptovský Mikuláš District Court, on the administrator’s application, ordered Franek to hand over the property within 15 days and to pay the administrator’s costs. The Žilina Regional Court quashed that judgment on 14 April 2005, holding that the first-instance court had failed to examine whether Franek had standing as defendant given that a third party was retaining the property.

A fresh hearing was fixed for 21 March 2006. On 14 March Franek requested an adjournment on grounds of incapacity for work, but he submitted no supporting medical evidence at that time. The District Court proceeded in his absence, again ordered the transfer of the property (relying on sections 14 and 18 of the Bankruptcy Act) and awarded further costs. It found that the property remained at Franek’s disposal and that the storing creditor owed no duty to the bankruptcy estate.

Franek appealed, explaining that he had been bedridden from 16 February to 2 May 2006 following an accident and enclosing a medical certificate dated 17 February 2006. On 6 September 2007 the Regional Court upheld the District Court’s judgment; the decision became final on 10 December 2007.

Franek then lodged an appeal on points of law. He invoked Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, arguing that the first-instance court had unlawfully prevented him from participating by rejecting his excuse and proceeding in his absence. He also contended that neither he nor the administrator had standing, that the lower courts had applied the law incorrectly and arbitrarily, and that the order was unenforceable because the property was not in his possession. The Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible on 7 April 2009. It held that Franek’s failure to produce contemporaneous documentary evidence entitled the District Court to continue in his absence and that lack of standing (as opposed to lack of legal capacity) was not a ground for an appeal on points of law under Article 237(b).

On 12 June 2009 Franek filed a constitutional complaint alleging breaches of Article 6 on three principal grounds: (i) errors of fact and law and arbitrary reasoning by the ordinary courts; (ii) his lack of standing as defendant; and (iii) the District Court’s decision to proceed despite his medically certified inability to attend. The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint on 17 September 2009. It found the complaints directed at the District and Regional Courts time-barred (the two-month statutory period having begun to run from the date those judgments became final). Because the Supreme Court had declared the appeal on points of law inadmissible, that remedy did not interrupt the time-limit. The Constitutional Court examined the Supreme Court’s reasoning in detail and concluded that it was neither arbitrary nor otherwise incompatible with the right to a fair hearing.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 6 violations: denial of an opportunity to be heard, questions of standing and the enforceability of the transfer order, alleged arbitrariness in the application of bankruptcy law, and the Constitutional Court’s approach to time-limits and the principle of subsidiarity.

The case of Franek v. Slovakia (no. 14090/10) arose from civil proceedings in which the applicant, a Slovak enforcement officer, alleged a breach of his Article 6 right to a fair hearing, including before the Constitutional Court.

The applicant had seized movable property of a debtor company. After bankruptcy proceedings commenced, the administrator demanded transfer of the assets. The applicant stored some items with a creditor, which initially retained them to secure its claim but later revoked that stance. On 21 October 2003 the Liptovský Mikuláš District Court ordered the applicant to hand over the property within 15 days and pay costs of EUR 1,130. The Žilina Regional Court quashed that judgment on 14 April 2005, finding that the first-instance court had failed to examine whether the applicant had standing as defendant, given third-party retention of the goods.

A new hearing was set for 21 March 2006. On 14 March the applicant sought an adjournment for incapacity to work. The District Court proceeded in his absence, holding that he had supplied no documentary proof of illness, that the property remained at his disposal under sections 14 and 18 of the Bankruptcy Act 1991, and that the storing creditor owed no duty to the estate. It again ordered transfer and costs of EUR 1,964. The applicant appealed, enclosing a 17 February 2006 medical certificate confirming bedridden status until 2 May 2006 after an accident. The Regional Court upheld the judgment on 6 September 2007 (final on 10 December 2007).

In an appeal on points of law the applicant invoked Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, arguing that the first-instance court had wrongly ignored his timely excuse and thereby denied him access to court. He further contended that neither he nor the administrator had standing: the goods were not in his possession (rendering any order unenforceable) and the administrator could not realise assets subject to a creditor’s retention right; once that right was abandoned the action should have been discontinued. He also alleged arbitrary fact-finding and misapplication of law.

The Supreme Court rejected the appeal as inadmissible on 7 April 2009. It accepted that a written request for adjournment had been filed but noted the absence of contemporaneous medical evidence, so the District Court had been entitled to continue. Article 237(f) was therefore not engaged. Lack of standing did not fall within Article 237(b), which concerns only legal capacity. Consequently the Court could not review alleged errors of fact or law.

On 12 June 2009 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 6, repeating the complaints of arbitrary decisions, lack of standing and proceeding in his absence (he had been immobilised by a broken leg and unable to produce the certificate in time). The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint on 17 September 2009. The challenge to the first-instance and appellate judgments was out of time (two-month limit from 10 December 2007). Because the Supreme Court had declared the appeal on points of law inadmissible, that decision did not interrupt the time-limit. After examining the Supreme Court’s reasoning the Constitutional Court found it neither arbitrary nor otherwise contrary to Article 6.

These facts—the decision to proceed in the applicant’s absence, the standing and enforceability arguments, the Supreme Court’s restrictive reading of the cassation grounds, and the Constitutional Court’s time-bar and subsidiarity analysis—form the core of the alleged fair-hearing violations.
001-140769:
The case of Cēsnieks v. Latvia (Application no. 9278/06) originated from a complaint by Latvian national Valters Cēsnieks, lodged on 26 January 2006. He alleged that police officers ill-treated him on 21 March 2002 in violation of Article 3 of the Convention to extract a confession to the murder of Ģ.Č., that there was no effective investigation into this (Article 13), and that the resulting evidence was used to convict him in breach of his fair-trial rights under Article 6 § 1. On 6 March 2012 the Court struck out the Article 3 and 13 complaints after accepting a Government unilateral declaration that acknowledged the ill-treatment in custody and the lack of an effective investigation. The present judgment examines only the remaining Article 6 § 1 complaint.

On 21 March 2002 police telephoned the applicant and asked him to attend a station. He alleged that, before any charges were laid, officers accused him of the murder and used physical force (including beating that broke his nose) to obtain a confession; he was held at the station until the early hours of 23 March before transfer to a short-term detention facility. An investigation into possible police misconduct opened on 23 May 2002 but was later terminated by a prosecutor who relied on a subsequent Supreme Court finding that dismissed the ill-treatment allegation.

The impugned statements were as follows. On 21 March, questioned as a witness (5.20–6.40 p.m.), the applicant described providing company documents and facilitating bank withdrawals via acquaintance Z.K. for Ģ.Č.; he said he learned of the murder only from the officers that day. On 22 March he wrote a handwritten confession stating that he had borrowed LVL 4,500 he could not repay, had travelled to Moscow with O.O. in late January 2002, had informed O.O. of an impending LVL 17,000 transfer to Ģ.Č., and that O.O. had said he would murder Ģ.Č. Later that day, questioned as a suspect (11 a.m.–12.30 p.m. and again 11.30 p.m.–12.50 a.m.), he confirmed the confession, added that O.O. had threatened him over the debt and decided to kill Ģ.Č., and then admitted that he himself had requested the killing in order to keep the LVL 17,000 (needed to pay for car parts). He described phone calls from Moscow and a bus using his telephone to arrange the murder with an acquaintance of O.O. (later identified as V.Z.). Both suspect interviews recorded that he wished to speak without a lawyer.

At first instance the Riga Regional Court (11 October 2004) convicted two co-accused of the aggravated murder of Ģ.Č. on 2 February 2002 but acquitted the applicant and O.O. It accepted the applicant’s recantation, noting that he had been held for many hours after his witness interview without explanation, that medical evidence confirmed injuries sustained in custody, and that Article 3 had therefore been violated. The court found the 22 March statements contradictory, rejected an expert report that the confession showed no signs of distress (the report lacked a proper study section), and held that no other evidence (financial dealings or telephone records of a call from the applicant’s phone to V.Z.) proved that he had organised or incited the murder.

On appeal the Criminal Cases Chamber of the Supreme Court (26 April 2005) reversed the acquittal, convicted the applicant of aggravated murder and sentenced him to eleven years’ imprisonment. It held that the Regional Court had wrongly accepted the recantation: there was no impartial evidence of ill-treatment, the criminal case against the officers had been terminated (and the defence had not challenged that termination), the expert report was valid and showed free-style handwriting, and a comparison with a later complaint confirmed the confession was genuine. The court therefore admitted and relied on the 22 March statements.

The Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the subsequent cassation appeal (26 August 2005) without a hearing, ruling that the defence merely sought a re-evaluation of facts (outside cassation competence) and that the Convention arguments were formal and unsupported by the case file.

At the material time the Criminal Procedure Code contained no explicit rule rendering evidence obtained by ill-treatment inadmissible (unlike the later 2005 Criminal Procedure Law). Constitutional provisions prohibited torture and guaranteed a fair trial; proceedings may be reopened if an international court finds a violation of a binding international norm.

The case of Cēsnieks v. Latvia (Application no. 9278/06) concerned a Latvian national, Valters Cēsnieks, who alleged that police subjected him to ill-treatment in violation of Article 3 of the Convention after he appeared at a State Police station on 21 March 2002, that there was no effective investigation into that ill-treatment contrary to Article 13, and that evidence obtained thereby was used at his trial in breach of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1. On 6 March 2012 the Court struck the Article 3 and 13 complaints out of its list following a unilateral declaration in which the Government acknowledged that the applicant had been ill-treated in police custody and that there had been no effective investigation. The remaining Article 6 complaint is the subject of the present judgment.

On 21 March 2002 the police telephoned the applicant and asked him to attend their station. Before any formal charges were laid he was accused of murdering Ģ.Č. Police officers used physical force to obtain a confession, as a result of which he made a written statement. He was transferred to a short-term detention facility only on 23 March. An investigation into alleged police misconduct was opened on 23 May 2002 but later terminated.

The applicant was first questioned as a witness on 21 March from 5.20 p.m. to 6.40 p.m. He described documents he had given Ģ.Č. concerning his late father’s company, money withdrawals arranged through an acquaintance Z.K., a trip to Moscow at the end of January 2002, and learning of the murder only from the police that day. On 22 March he produced a handwritten confession stating that he had borrowed LVL 4,500 which he could not repay, had travelled to Moscow with acquaintance O.O., had told O.O. about forthcoming transfers of LVL 17,000 intended for Ģ.Č., and that O.O. had said he would murder Ģ.Č. In subsequent interviews as a suspect the same day the applicant confirmed the confession, added that he had concealed the purpose of the Moscow trip, that O.O. had demanded repayment and decided to kill Ģ.Č., and later that he himself had sought the killing in order to obtain the money because of financial difficulties. He stated that he wished to give these statements without a lawyer.

The applicant and three co-accused were tried before the Riga Regional Court on charges related to Ģ.Č.’s murder. On 11 October 2004 that court convicted two co-accused but acquitted the applicant and O.O. It accepted the applicant’s recantation at trial, noting that he had been detained at the police station for many hours after being questioned as a witness, that expert reports confirmed he had suffered bodily injuries while in custody, and that his 22 March statements were contradictory. It therefore ruled those statements unusable and found no other evidence that the applicant had organised, assisted or incited the murder.

On appeal the Criminal Cases Chamber of the Supreme Court, on 26 April 2005, overturned the acquittal and convicted the applicant of aggravated murder, sentencing him to eleven years’ imprisonment. It held that the first-instance court had wrongly treated the pre-trial statements as untruthful, that there was no impartial evidence of ill-treatment, that the criminal case against the police officers had been terminated, and that an expert report confirming the confession was written in the applicant’s free style was reliable. It admitted and relied upon the 22 March statement. The Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed an appeal on points of law on 26 August 2005 without a hearing, stating that the appeal sought an impermissible re-evaluation of evidence and that the Convention complaint was purely formal.

At the material time the Criminal Procedure Code contained no provision rendering evidence obtained through ill-treatment automatically inadmissible (unlike the later 2005 Criminal Procedure Law). The applicant remained in detention serving his sentence.

The case of Cēsnieks v. Latvia (Application no. 9278/06) concerned a Latvian national, Valters Cēsnieks (born 1975), who alleged violations of Articles 3, 13 and 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. On 21 March 2002 police summoned him to a station, where officers accused him of murdering Ģ.Č. before any charges were laid and applied physical force to extract a confession. He produced a written confession under this duress. He was held at the station until 23 March before transfer to a short-term detention facility. Medical evidence later confirmed he had suffered bodily injuries while in custody.

His pre-trial statements comprised a 21 March witness interview (describing document and money dealings involving Ģ.Č. and Z.K.), a 22 March handwritten confession (detailing a debt to O.O., a Moscow trip, and O.O.’s stated intent to murder Ģ.Č.), and two subsequent suspect interviews the same day (in which he first confirmed the confession and later admitted having solicited the killing to obtain LVL 17 000). He waived a lawyer for these interviews.

The Riga Regional Court acquitted him on 11 October 2004. It found that his recantation at trial was credible: he had been detained for hours after his witness interview, witnesses could not explain the delay, expert reports documented injuries, and the statements of 22 March were internally contradictory. The court held that Article 3 had been breached and excluded the statements. It found no other evidence that he had organised or incited the murder (phone records were deemed inconclusive).

On appeal the Supreme Court reversed the acquittal on 26 April 2005, convicting him of aggravated murder and imposing an 11-year sentence. It ruled there was no impartial evidence of ill-treatment, noted that the separate police-misconduct investigation had been terminated, accepted an expert handwriting report, and admitted the 22 March statements as the principal evidence of guilt. A cassation appeal arguing that the conviction rested on evidence obtained in violation of Articles 3 and 6 was dismissed on 26 August 2005 as raising only factual issues outside the Senate’s competence.

In 2012 the Court struck the Article 3 and 13 complaints out of its list after a Government unilateral declaration that acknowledged both the ill-treatment and the absence of an effective investigation. The remaining complaint—whether the use at trial of statements obtained through that ill-treatment rendered the proceedings unfair under Article 6 § 1—was examined in the present judgment. (The 2005 Criminal Procedure Law, adopted after the events, later rendered evidence obtained by ill-treatment formally inadmissible.)
