001-140781:
The case of Gábor Nagy v. Hungary (ECtHR Application no. 33529/11, judgment of 11 February 2014) concerns a Hungarian national born in 1990 who alleged violations arising from his pre-trial detention. He was apprehended on 4 December 2010 together with an alleged accomplice. On 6 December 2010 the Pest Central District Court ordered his detention on remand on charges of multiple thefts (breaking into three cars and attempting a fourth, all on a single day, with an aggregate value of approximately €400). Detention was based on a risk of repetition of crime under section 129(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court cited the applicant’s lack of employment or other income and the alleged serial character of the acts. The applicant was present but his public defender was not. On 14 December 2010 the Budapest Regional Court dismissed his appeal, repeating the same grounds and adding that no less restrictive measure was available.

On 20 December 2010 the applicant applied for release. He argued that the courts had failed to identify any concrete facts supporting a risk of reoffending, produced documents showing he was about to start work and that his mother would cover his living expenses in the interim, and emphasised his clean criminal record. On 12 January 2011 the District Court rejected the application without hearing him and without addressing his new arguments, relying instead on stereotyped references to the “serial nature” of the offences and his financial situation. The Regional Court dismissed the ensuing appeal on 22 February 2011 without a hearing; the entire set of proceedings was conducted in writing.

Meanwhile the prosecution sought prolongation of detention without notifying defence counsel. On 28 December 2010 the District Court extended detention until 6 March 2011 without hearing the applicant, again citing unemployment and the serial character of the alleged offences. The Regional Court upheld this order on 19 January 2011 in the applicant’s absence. A further prolongation request was examined on 3 March 2011; although the defence had been notified, the court did not wait for its observations and maintained detention on the same grounds previously invoked.

The applicant was ultimately released on 13 April 2011 after a successful appeal. The Regional Court observed that his financial situation was now secured, that mere unemployment did not establish a risk of reoffending (especially in the absence of a prior record), and that several thefts committed on a single day did not constitute serial crime. The relevant domestic provisions (sections 129–136, 210–215 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) required courts to give reasoned decisions, to consider personal circumstances, to examine motions on their merits, and, in certain circumstances, to hold sessions at which the defence could comment on evidence.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints that the detention lacked justification (Article 5 § 1), lasted an unreasonable time (Articles 5 § 1 and 6 §§ 1, 3(b)–(c)), and that equality of arms was denied in the review proceedings (Article 5 § 4), given the absence of hearings, the failure to notify or await defence submissions, and the courts’ repeated use of formulaic reasoning that ignored contrary evidence.

**Case of Gábor Nagy v. Hungary (Application no. 33529/11), ECtHR (Second Section), Judgment of 11 February 2014 (final 11 May 2014)**

The applicant, Gábor Nagy (born 1990, Budapest resident), lodged an application on 27 May 2011 complaining that his pre-trial detention was unjustified and excessively long (Articles 5 § 1 and 6 §§ 1, 3(b) and (c) of the Convention) and that equality of arms was not respected in challenges to his detention (Article 5 § 4). He was represented by counsel; the Hungarian Government was represented by its agent.

On 4 December 2010, police apprehended the applicant and an alleged accomplice. On 6 December 2010, the Pest Central District Court ordered his pre-trial detention on charges of multiple thefts (breaking into three cars and attempting a fourth, all on one day, total value around €400) due to a feared risk of reoffending under section 129(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The court cited the applicant’s lack of job or income and the “serial nature” of the acts. The applicant attended without his public defender. On 14 December 2010, the Budapest Regional Court dismissed his appeal, repeating the unemployment finding and stating no less-restrictive measure was suitable.

On 20 December 2010, the applicant applied for release, arguing that courts had not specified facts supporting a risk of repetition. He provided documents showing imminent employment, his mother’s willingness to cover living expenses until salary arrival, and his lack of criminal record. On 12 January 2011, the District Court refused release without hearing him or addressing his arguments, using stereotyped language about serial crime and financial circumstances. On 22 February 2011, the Regional Court dismissed his appeal without a hearing. These proceedings occurred entirely in writing.

Meanwhile, prosecutors sought prolongation without notifying the applicant’s lawyer. On 28 December 2010, detention was extended until 6 March 2011 without hearing the applicant, repeating that unemployment and lack of income meant he would reoffend in serial crime. A co-accused’s release application was also dismissed. On 19 January 2011, the Regional Court rejected the applicant’s appeal against prolongation without his attendance, citing unemployment and serial nature.

A further prolongation request was processed on 3 March 2011. Although the defence was notified, the District Court did not await observations and maintained detention on prior grounds. The applicant successfully appealed and was released on 13 April 2011. The Regional Court observed that his financial situation was now secured, unemployment alone did not establish a reoffending risk (especially with no prior record), and multiple larcenies in one day did not constitute serial crime.

Domestic law (Act XIX of 1998) permits pre-trial detention for imprisonment-punishable offences if there is reasonable cause to believe the defendant would reoffend (section 129(2)(d)), with alternatives like home detention available (section 130(2)). Detention before indictment is initially limited to one month, extendable under strict conditions (section 131). Courts must examine release motions on the merits with reasoned decisions (section 133), minimise detention duration with extraordinary procedures (section 136), and hold sessions for initial orders or extensions based on new circumstances (section 210). Prosecutors present evidence at sessions, with opportunities for examination (section 211). Decisions require reasoned rulings (section 214) and are appealable, though immediately executable (section 215).

These facts highlight alleged shortcomings: stereotyped justifications ignoring new evidence of employment prospects, family support, and clean record; repeated written proceedings without hearings or defence notification; failure to await observations; and initial absence of counsel. Detention lasted from 6 December 2010 to 13 April 2011. The case centred on whether these elements rendered the detention unjustified, overly prolonged, and procedurally unfair under the Convention, particularly regarding equality of arms in detention reviews.

The case of Gábor Nagy v. Hungary (Application no. 33529/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned complaints by a Hungarian national born in 1990 regarding his pre-trial detention. The applicant alleged that this detention was unjustified and unreasonably prolonged, invoking Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty) as well as Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b)-(c) (fair trial rights, including adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence and legal assistance). He further complained under Article 5 § 4 that equality of arms had not been respected in proceedings challenging his detention.

The applicant and an alleged accomplice were arrested on 4 December 2010. On 6 December 2010 the Pest Central District Court ordered his pre-trial detention on charges of multiple thefts involving breaking into three cars and attempting a fourth, all on the same day and valued at approximately 400 euros. Detention was based on a perceived risk of reoffending under section 129(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, with the court citing the applicant’s lack of employment or income and the serial nature of the alleged acts. The applicant attended this hearing without his public defender.

On 14 December 2010 the Budapest Regional Court dismissed his appeal, reiterating his unemployment and adding that no less restrictive measure was suitable. On 20 December 2010 the applicant applied for release, arguing that the courts had not specified facts supporting a risk of repetition. He submitted documents showing imminent employment and his mother’s willingness to cover living expenses, and noted his lack of a criminal record.

The Pest Central District Court refused this application on 12 January 2011 without hearing the applicant or addressing his arguments, repeating in stereotyped terms that the serial nature of the alleged crimes and his financial circumstances created a risk of reoffending. The Regional Court dismissed his appeal on 22 February 2011 without a hearing; all related proceedings were conducted in writing.

Meanwhile, the prosecution sought prolongation of detention without informing the applicant’s lawyer. On 28 December 2010 detention was extended until 6 March 2011 without hearing the applicant, again relying on unemployment and the serial character of the alleged offences. The Regional Court dismissed the related appeal on 19 January 2011 in the applicant’s absence, citing the same grounds.

A further prolongation request was processed on 3 March 2011. Although the defence was notified, the District Court did not await its observations and maintained detention on previously stated grounds. The applicant’s subsequent appeal succeeded, leading to his release on 13 April 2011. The Regional Court observed that his financial situation was now secured, that unemployment alone (especially without a prior record) did not establish a risk of reoffending, and that several larcenies committed in a single day did not constitute serial crime.

These facts highlight issues of stereotyped reasoning, failure to consider new evidence of the applicant’s circumstances, absence of hearings in several instances, lack of notification to counsel of the prosecution’s motions, and decisions taken without awaiting defence submissions, all occurring over a detention period of just over four months.
001-140775:
The case of Maširević v. Serbia (Application no. 30671/08) originated from an application lodged on 13 May 2008 by Milan Maširević, a Serbian national born in 1940 and a practising lawyer living in Sombor. He alleged, in particular, that he had been unlawfully denied access to the Supreme Court of Serbia, in violation of his Convention rights (notably the right of access to a court under Article 6).

The underlying civil proceedings began on 8 July 1998, when the applicant sued a private insurance company in the Municipal Court in Novi Sad for unpaid legal fees under a 1995 fee agreement. On 17 September 1998 the court issued a payment order, which the respondent challenged. In September 2001 the respondent lodged a counter-claim seeking to have the 1995 contract declared null and void. The two sets of proceedings were joined in September 2002. On 24 November 2003 the Municipal Court quashed the payment order, rejected the applicant’s claim, declared part of the contract void and left the remainder in force.

The applicant appealed. On 24 February 2005 the District Court in Novi Sad upheld the first-instance judgment. In April 2005 the applicant himself filed an appeal on points of law (revizija) with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court returned the file in November 2006 because the District Court had not fully adjudicated the appeal; a supplementary District Court judgment of 25 April 2007 rejected the remaining points.

On 24 October 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the revizija as inadmissible. It held that Article 84 of the Civil Procedure Act 2004 (in force from 23 February 2005) required that such an appeal be lodged by a practising attorney and that parties—even if they were themselves attorneys—had lost the capacity to file it in person. The decision was served on 14 January 2008.

The applicant then turned to the Constitutional Court (11 February 2008). After being asked to specify his complaint and submitting an amended appeal, the Constitutional Court dismissed the application as incomplete on 25 March 2009.

The alleged violation centres on the Supreme Court’s refusal to examine the merits of the revizija. The 1977 Civil Procedure Act (in force when the original claim was filed) had permitted parties to lodge such appeals themselves. The 2004 Act introduced a mandatory-representation rule, but its transitional provision (Article 491 § 4) stipulated that the old rules continued to apply to appeals on points of law in proceedings begun before 23 February 2005. Later Constitutional Court case-law (2010) confirmed that the Supreme Court had misapplied the 2004 Act to pre-2005 cases and that even under the 2004 Act a registered lawyer could file his own revizija. The 2011 Act later expressly restored the right of lawyer-parties to represent themselves.

These facts—particularly the timing of the original claim, the applicant’s status as a practising lawyer, the Supreme Court’s reliance on the new representation rule, and the subsequent domestic jurisprudence holding that rule inapplicable—constitute the core of the alleged denial of access to the highest court.

The case of Maširević v. Serbia (Application no. 30671/08) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right of access to a court under Article 6 of the Convention. Milan Maširević, a Serbian national born in 1940 and a practising lawyer residing in Sombor, claimed that the Supreme Court of Serbia unlawfully prevented him from pursuing an appeal on points of law in his own civil proceedings.

On 8 July 1998 the applicant instituted civil proceedings in the Municipal Court in Novi Sad against a private insurance company. He sought payment of professional fees pursuant to a 1995 legal-fee agreement. On 17 September 1998 the court issued a payment order; the respondent objected. In September 2001 the respondent lodged a counter-claim seeking a declaration that the 1995 contract was null and void. The two actions were joined in September 2002. On 24 November 2003 the Municipal Court quashed the payment order, dismissed the applicant’s claim, declared part of the contract void and left the remainder in force. The applicant appealed. On 24 February 2005 the District Court in Novi Sad upheld the first-instance judgment.

In April 2005 the applicant personally filed an appeal on points of law (revizija) with the Supreme Court. After the file was returned because part of the appeal had not been examined, the District Court issued a supplementary judgment on 25 April 2007 rejecting the remaining grounds. On 24 October 2007 the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible. It relied on Article 84 of the Civil Procedure Act 2004 (which entered into force on 23 February 2005) and held that an appeal on points of law could be lodged only by an attorney-at-law, not by a party in person—even if that party was himself a practising lawyer. The decision was served on the applicant on 14 January 2008.

The applicant then turned to the Constitutional Court. He lodged a constitutional appeal on 11 February 2008, supplied additional particulars on 6 June 2008 after a request for clarification, and saw the appeal dismissed as incomplete on 25 March 2009.

The procedural history is governed by two successive codes. Under the Civil Procedure Act 1977 (applicable when the action was commenced) any party could file an appeal on points of law personally. The 2004 Act introduced a mandatory-counsel rule for such appeals and, in Article 401 § 2(2), provided that an appeal lodged by a person who was not a practising lawyer would be inadmissible. A transitional provision (Article 491 § 4) nevertheless stipulated that appeals on points of law in proceedings instituted before 23 February 2005 remained subject to the earlier legislation. Subsequent Constitutional Court rulings (2010) confirmed that the Supreme Court had misapplied the 2004 Act to pre-2005 cases and that a registered attorney could validly lodge an appeal on his or her own behalf. The later Civil Procedure Act 2011 expressly restored that possibility.

The applicant’s complaint therefore centres on the Supreme Court’s refusal, on the basis of an erroneous interpretation of the 2004 Act and in disregard of the transitional rule, to examine the merits of an appeal that he, as a qualified lawyer and a party to proceedings begun under the 1977 Act, was entitled to bring. The Constitutional Court’s subsequent dismissal of his appeal as incomplete left that denial unremedied. These facts form the core of the alleged violation of the right of access to the highest domestic court.

The case of Maširević v. Serbia (Application no. 30671/08) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 May 2008 by Milan Maširević, a Serbian national and practising lawyer born in 1940 and residing in Sombor. Represented by counsel, the applicant complained that he had been unlawfully denied access to the Supreme Court of Serbia, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing, encompassing the right of access to a court). The Court joined the admissibility and merits examination.

The underlying domestic dispute began on 8 July 1998 when the applicant filed a civil claim in the Municipal Court in Novi Sad against a private insurance company. He sought payment of professional fees pursuant to a legal-fee agreement concluded in 1995. On 17 September 1998 the Municipal Court issued a payment order. The respondent objected. During a hearing on 27 September 2001 the respondent lodged a counter-claim seeking a declaration that the 1995 contract was null and void. The two sets of proceedings were joined on 16 September 2002. By judgment of 24 November 2003 the Municipal Court quashed its earlier payment order, rejected the applicant’s claim, declared part of the contract void and left the remainder in force. The applicant appealed. On 24 February 2005 the District Court in Novi Sad dismissed the appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment.

In April 2005 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law (revizija) with the Supreme Court. On 30 November 2006 the Supreme Court returned the file because the District Court had failed to determine one part of the appeal. The District Court issued a supplementary judgment on 25 April 2007 rejecting the remaining limb of the appeal. On 24 October 2007 the Supreme Court declared the applicant’s revizija inadmissible. It relied on Article 84 of the Civil Procedure Act 2004 (which had entered into force on 23 February 2005) and held that only a practising attorney, not a party acting in person, could lodge such an appeal; even a party who was himself a lawyer had lost the capacity to file the remedy personally. The decision was served on 14 January 2008.

The applicant filed a constitutional appeal on 11 February 2008. After the Constitutional Court requested clarification, he submitted an amended appeal on 6 June 2008. On 25 March 2009 the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal as incomplete.

The 1977 Civil Procedure Act, in force when the original proceedings were instituted, expressly permitted a party to lodge a revizija without professional representation. The 2004 Act introduced a mandatory-counsel rule for such appeals (Articles 84 § 2 and 401 § 2(2)). However, its transitional provision (Article 491 § 4) stipulated that the pre-2005 rules continued to govern revizija in cases commenced before the new Act’s entry into force. Subsequent Constitutional Court jurisprudence (decisions of 27 January 2010, 13 May 2010 and 16 December 2010) confirmed both that the 2004 Act was inapplicable to pre-2005 proceedings and that, even under the 2004 Act, a registered lawyer acting in person could validly lodge a revizija. Those later rulings were not available to the applicant when his own constitutional complaint was rejected.

The facts therefore centre on the Supreme Court’s application of the 2004 mandatory-counsel requirement to a 1998 case, its rejection of an appeal filed by a lawyer-applicant in person, and the Constitutional Court’s subsequent failure to examine the complaint on the merits. These events formed the basis of the alleged violation of the right of access to the highest domestic court.
001-141200:
**CASE OF LUČIĆ v. CROATIA (Application no. 5699/11), ECtHR (First Section), 27 February 2014 (final 27 May 2014)**

The applicant, Mirko Lučić (born 1970), a Croatian national living in Zagreb, alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention (fair trial and right to examine witnesses) because he was convicted of rape without ever examining the complainant, J.N., whose pre-trial statement was decisive.

On 3 May 1999 J.N. reported to Zagreb police that the previous night the applicant, who had offered her a lift home from bar A. where she worked, had instead driven into nearby woods and raped her in his car before dropping her at nightclub “S.”. He was arrested that evening and identified by J.N. Medical examination that night found no injuries on J.N.’s body or genitals; the applicant had abrasions on his right arm, elbow and knee, which he later attributed to consensual intercourse.

Questioned by an investigating judge on 4 May 1999, the applicant admitted sexual intercourse but insisted it was consensual. He was released. J.N.’s lawyer later claimed the applicant had contacted and threatened her, and that she had sought psychiatric help. An investigation for rape was opened on 6 July 1999; detention was refused.

On 9 July 1999 J.N. (accompanied by her lawyer) gave a detailed oral statement to the investigating judge repeating the rape allegation. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer was informed or present. Other investigation evidence included statements from colleague S.S. (who had asked the applicant to give J.N. a lift and later heard conflicting accounts), musician K.N. (who took J.N. home from “S.” and observed nothing unusual), and J.M. (to whom J.N. reported the rape the next morning while distressed). Forensic reports noted biological traces of J.N. on the applicant’s underwear; medical experts found J.N. had no objective injuries and that the applicant’s abrasions could have resulted from scratches, a fall or friction.

The applicant was indicted in February 2001. At the first trial J.N. never appeared despite summonses, police attempts to locate her, and her lawyer’s request for postponement because she was living abroad (later confirmed as Spain). The trial court admitted the written record of her 9 July 1999 statement over defence objection and convicted the applicant on 10 April 2006, sentencing him to one year. The Supreme Court quashed the judgment in December 2007, holding that the trial court had not taken all reasonable steps to secure J.N.’s presence even though her evidence was decisive.

On retrial the court again sought J.N. through Spanish authorities (obtaining an address and telephone number) and issued summonses; she did not appear and gave no reason. The defence again objected that it had never been able to question her (including at the 1999 hearing) and that her whereabouts could have been pursued more vigorously. The court admitted her written statement, heard K.N. again, and on 21 January 2009 again convicted the applicant of rape, relying on J.N.’s account as corroborated by S.S., J.M. and medical/forensic evidence. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in May 2009, stating that J.N. had been lawfully questioned during the investigation, had thereafter lived abroad, and that the trial court had no means of compelling her attendance, so reading the record was permitted under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint in July 2010.

The alleged violation centred on the use, as decisive evidence, of J.N.’s untested pre-trial statement given in the absence of the defence, combined with the domestic courts’ subsequent inability or failure to secure her attendance at trial despite her status as a Croatian citizen whose location became known.

The case of Lučić v. Croatia (Application no. 5699/11) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Mirko Lučić, a Croatian national, complained that he had not received a fair trial because he was denied the opportunity to examine the key witness against him, J.N., the alleged victim of rape.

On 3 May 1999, J.N. reported to Zagreb police that the applicant had raped her the previous night. She stated that he had offered her a lift home from the bar where she worked, driven into nearby woods, and raped her in his car before dropping her at a nightclub. The applicant was arrested that evening and identified by J.N. A medical examination of J.N. found no injuries to her body or genitals, while the applicant had abrasions on his arm, elbow and knee. Questioned by an investigating judge on 4 May 1999, the applicant admitted sexual intercourse but claimed it was consensual, attributing his injuries to friction. He was released.

J.N.’s lawyer later alleged that the applicant had contacted and threatened her in an effort to have the complaint withdrawn and that she had sought psychiatric help. Requests to detain the applicant were refused. On 9 July 1999, J.N. gave a detailed oral statement to the investigating judge repeating her rape allegation. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer was informed of or present at this hearing.

The investigation included testimony from other witnesses. S.S., a colleague, confirmed asking the applicant to drive J.N. home and later hearing J.N.’s rape claim, though she knew of no prior similar conduct by the applicant. K.N., a musician at the nightclub, said J.N. appeared normal when she arrived and made no mention of rape. J.M. described J.N. as distressed the next morning when reporting the incident. Forensic evidence confirmed biological traces from J.N. on the applicant’s underwear; medical experts found J.N. had no objective injuries and the applicant’s abrasions were consistent with scratches or friction.

The applicant was indicted for rape in February 2001. During the first trial, J.N. repeatedly failed to appear despite summonses. Information indicated she had lived in Spain for years. After unsuccessful efforts including police inquiries and international legal assistance (including a failed attempt via the Netherlands), the Zagreb County Court on 10 April 2006 admitted the written record of her 1999 investigative statement over the defence’s objection that she must be examined given the gravity of the charge. The court convicted the applicant and imposed a one-year sentence, finding her account corroborated by other evidence.

The Supreme Court quashed the conviction in December 2007, holding that not all reasonable steps had been taken to secure J.N.’s attendance even though her evidence was decisive. In the retrial the court obtained J.N.’s Spanish address from her parents and through the Spanish authorities and summoned her twice. She failed to appear. On 21 January 2009 the court again admitted her investigative statement (the defence objecting that it had never had the chance to question her) and convicted the applicant once more, relying principally on her account as supported by S.S., J.M. and medical evidence.

The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in May 2009, reasoning that J.N. had been lawfully questioned during the investigation, that she now lived abroad and could not be compelled to attend, and that reading her statement was therefore permitted under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Constitutional Court dismissed a further complaint in July 2010.

The applicant maintained throughout that the inability to examine the decisive witness whose statement was given in his absence rendered the proceedings unfair.

**Summary of Lučić v. Croatia (Application no. 5699/11)**

The case arose from a rape allegation against Croatian national Mirko Lučić. On 3 May 1999, J.N. reported to Zagreb police that the previous night Lučić had offered her a lift home from bar A., where she worked, but instead drove into woods and raped her in his car before dropping her at nightclub S. Lučić was arrested the same evening and identified by J.N. Medical examination of J.N. found no injuries to her body or genitals. Lučić had abrasions on his right upper arm, elbow and knee, which he attributed to friction during what he claimed was consensual intercourse. He was questioned by an investigating judge on 4 May 1999, admitted the intercourse but denied rape, and was released.

J.N.’s lawyer later alleged Lučić had contacted and threatened her to withdraw the complaint and that she had sought psychiatric help. An investigation for rape was opened on 6 July 1999. On 9 July 1999 J.N. gave oral evidence to the investigating judge, repeating her rape account. Neither Lučić nor his lawyer was notified of or present at this hearing, although Croatian law (Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 198) permitted their attendance if requested or if the witness’s later non-appearance was probable. Other investigation evidence included statements from colleague S.S. (who had asked Lučić to give J.N. a lift and later heard conflicting accounts from both), musician K.N. (who saw J.N. appear normal later that night with no mention of rape), and J.M. (who saw J.N. distressed the next morning reporting rape). Medical and forensic reports were mixed and inconclusive on injuries or traces.

Lučić was indicted in February 2001. At trial J.N. repeatedly failed to appear despite proper summonses. She was living abroad (initially reported as Spain, later possibly the Netherlands). The Zagreb County Court made multiple efforts: police inquiries with her family, orders to locate and bring her, adjournments at her request, and requests for international legal assistance. Addresses and a telephone number were eventually obtained, and she was summoned at least twice after her Spanish address was confirmed, but she did not attend and gave no reasons.

In April 2006 the court admitted the written record of J.N.’s 1999 investigation statement over defence objections that she must be examined in person given the gravity of the charge. Lučić was convicted and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. The Supreme Court quashed the judgment in December 2007, holding that the trial court had not taken all reasonable steps to secure the decisive witness’s presence.

On retrial similar efforts were renewed, including further international requests and summonses to the confirmed Spanish address. J.N. again failed to appear. In January 2009 the court again admitted her 1999 statement (defence having been denied the chance to question her at that earlier stage) and convicted Lučić on the same sentence, finding her account corroborated by S.S., J.M. and medical evidence. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in May 2009, reasoning that J.N. had been lawfully questioned during investigation (with no contemporaneous defence request to attend and no then-indication she would later be unavailable), that she subsequently lived abroad and appeared unwilling to attend, and that the trial court therefore could not compel her presence and was entitled to read her statement under Art. 331 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Constitutional Court dismissed Lučić’s complaint in July 2010, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning.

The application to the European Court of Human Rights alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention on the ground that Lučić had been denied a fair trial because he never had an opportunity to examine the key prosecution witness against him.
001-140912:
The case of Novruz Ismayilov v. Azerbaijan concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging violations of Article 5 of the Convention arising from the applicant’s pre-trial detention. The applicant, born in 1961, founded the private Borçalı Bank and Borçalı Association and chaired the bank’s supervisory board. Criminal proceedings for tax evasion under Article 213 of the Criminal Code were instituted on 19 April 2004 in connection with the Association’s activities. The applicant initially cooperated as a witness, appearing for questioning on 16 July 2004 and confrontations on 20 July, 18 August and 26 August 2004. He missed two July requests, which he attributed to illness. In early September the investigator could not locate him and ordered his compulsory attendance. On 28 September 2004 the applicant appeared and was charged with fraud, embezzlement and official forgery (Articles 178, 179 and 313). That same day the prosecutor sought remand in custody, citing the seriousness of the offences and risks of absconding or obstruction. The Khatai District Court ordered three months’ detention, relying on the charges and the prosecutor’s request and stating that the applicant had committed a serious crime and might abscond, influence participants, hide or falsify evidence, or fail to appear. The applicant appealed, arguing that he had cooperated, that all relevant documents had already been seized so he could not hide or falsify them, and that the court had ignored his family status, health and other personal circumstances. On 5 October 2004 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in a brief formulaic ruling that the order was “lawful and justified.”

On 16 December 2004 the investigator requested an extension because further investigative steps remained. The Deputy Prosecutor General asked the court to prolong detention until 28 February 2005, listing the need to obtain audit records, question additional witnesses, conduct confrontations and analyses, seek reimbursement of damage, prefer extra charges and identify co-offenders. On 23 December 2004 the Khatai District Court granted a two-month extension, reproducing the prosecutor’s list almost verbatim and concluding that the investigation could not be completed by 28 December. The hearing took place in the applicant’s absence; the official record claimed that his lawyer F.A. had attended and voiced no objection. F.A. immediately protested that he had never been notified, had not attended and that the record was false. Telephone transcripts of conversations with a court clerk, the investigator and the judge himself confirmed his non-attendance; the judge acknowledged a “mistake” but refused to correct the record. On 28 December the same judge rejected F.A.’s rectification request. The applicant appealed, repeating that neither he nor his lawyer had been present and that the extension lacked any individualised justification. On 6 January 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the extension, again reciting the list of remaining investigative acts, adding that release would be “inappropriate” and that the first-instance court had correctly considered the seriousness of the offences and the risk of influence or obstruction. It did not address the complaints of absence or record falsification. That hearing also occurred without the applicant, although his lawyers were present.

Further extensions followed (including one to 28 April 2005 after additional charges on 15 April 2005), but the Government failed to produce the relevant decisions despite the Court’s request. On 31 January 2006 the Assize Court convicted the applicant of fraud, embezzlement and tax evasion and sentenced him to nine years’ imprisonment. The facts therefore centre on stereotypical, non-individualised detention orders, hearings conducted in the applicant’s absence, failure to notify counsel, an allegedly falsified record, and appellate courts’ refusal to examine those specific procedural and substantive complaints.

The applicant, Novruz Ismayilov (born 1961), a founder and supervisory board chairman of Borçalı Bank and the associated Borçalı Association, alleged violations of Article 5 ECHR arising from his pre-trial detention. Criminal proceedings for tax evasion began on 19 April 2004. He cooperated initially as a witness, attending questioning and confrontations in July and August 2004 (with two non-attendances attributed to illness). After the investigator could not locate him in early September, compulsory attendance was ordered. On 28 September 2004 he appeared and was charged with fraud, embezzlement and official forgery, based on a financial audit and witness statements. The prosecutor immediately sought remand in custody, citing the seriousness of the offences and risks of absconding or obstruction.

At the same-day hearing the applicant and his lawyer argued that he had never absconded or obstructed the investigation and that any missed attendances were health-related. The Khatai District Court nevertheless ordered three months’ detention, reciting the charges and the prosecutor’s request and listing generic risks (absconding, influencing witnesses, hiding or falsifying evidence, failing to appear). On appeal the applicant reiterated the absence of concrete evidence of those risks, his prior cooperation, his family and health circumstances, and the fact that all relevant documents had already been seized. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 5 October 2004 in a single sentence stating that the order was “lawful and justified,” without addressing the specific submissions.

On 16 December 2004 the investigator sought an extension because further investigative steps (obtaining audit records, questioning additional witnesses, confrontations, possible expert examinations, and possible further charges) remained outstanding. The Deputy Prosecutor General forwarded the request the same day, asking for an extension until 28 February 2005. On 23 December 2004 the Khatai District Court granted the request in a decision that essentially copied the prosecutor’s wording and cited the same unfinished investigative actions. The hearing took place in the applicant’s absence; the official record stated that his lawyer F.A. had been present and had raised no objection. F.A. immediately protested that he had never been notified of the hearing, had not attended, and that the record was false. Phone transcripts with the court clerk, investigator and judge confirmed his absence; the judge privately admitted a “mistake” but refused to correct the record. A formal rectification request was rejected the same day on the ground that the lawyer had in fact been present.

The applicant appealed, complaining of his and his lawyer’s absence, the lack of any fresh or specific justification for continued detention, and the court’s failure to address his arguments. The Court of Appeal, sitting on 6 January 2005 in the applicant’s absence (though his lawyers were present), upheld the extension. It repeated the list of unfinished investigative steps, added that release would be “inappropriate” at that stage, and invoked the seriousness of the charges and the generic risks of influencing participants or obstructing proceedings. It did not examine the complaints about absence from the 23 December hearing or the alleged falsification of the record.

Domestic law (CCrP Articles 51 and 155, and two Plenum of the Supreme Court decisions) required that remand be an exceptional measure, that each statutory ground be verified against concrete case material (including personal circumstances), that the accused be present unless exceptional circumstances existed, and that extensions be justified by reasons distinct from those originally used. None of these requirements was met in the decisions under challenge. Subsequent extensions (including one to 28 April 2005) were not produced despite the Court’s request. The applicant was convicted on 31 January 2006 and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment.

The applicant, Novruz Ismayilov (born 1961), an Azerbaijani national and founder/chairman of Borçalı Bank and the associated Borçalı Association, faced criminal proceedings initiated on 19 April 2004 by the Ministry of Taxes under Article 213 of the Criminal Code for tax evasion linked to the Association's activities. He initially cooperated as a witness, appearing for questioning on 16 July 2004, a confrontation on 20 July 2004, and further sessions on 18 and 26 August 2004. He missed some July summonses, citing health issues, and his whereabouts were temporarily unknown in early September, prompting a 14 September 2004 compulsory participation order. On 28 September 2004, he appeared and was charged with fraud (Article 178), embezzlement (Article 179), and official forgery (Article 313), based on a financial audit and witness statements from business associates.

That same day, the prosecutor sought pre-trial detention (remand in custody), citing the seriousness of the offences and risks of absconding or obstructing the investigation. At the Khatai District Court hearing, the applicant and his lawyer argued he had never absconded or obstructed, attributing missed appearances to illness. The court ordered three months' detention, reasoning that he had committed a serious crime with risks of absconding, influencing participants, obstructing by hiding or falsifying evidence, failing to attend without reason, or otherwise evading responsibility. The applicant appealed, claiming insufficient evidence of any offence, lack of justification for detention, his prior cooperation, unconsidered personal circumstances (family, health), and impossibility of tampering with already-seized documents. On 5 October 2004, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, stating only that the order was lawful and justified, without addressing specifics.

On 16 December 2004, the investigator sought an extension for further investigative steps, including obtaining audit records, questioning witnesses, conducting confrontations and analyses, pursuing restitution, adding charges, and identifying other suspects. The Deputy Prosecutor General requested extension until 28 February 2005. On 23 December 2004, the Khatai District Court granted it, largely copying the prosecutor's wording about needed actions and the detention expiry, without independent assessment of detention necessity. The hearing occurred in the applicant's absence (with the investigator present). The record claimed his lawyer F.A. attended and raised no objections. F.A. later objected in writing that he had not been notified, did not attend, and that the record was falsified; phone transcripts with court staff, the investigator, and the judge confirmed his absence, though the judge admitted an error unofficially but refused formal correction. The court rejected the rectification request, insisting the lawyer had participated.

The applicant appealed the extension, citing his and his lawyer's absence, lack of notification, absence of justification, and failure to substantiate the decision; he also sought a special ruling on the alleged falsification. On 6 January 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld the extension, repeating the list of pending actions, stating release was inappropriate, and noting the seriousness of the charges plus risks of influencing others or obstructing via evidence tampering. It ignored complaints about absences and record falsification. That hearing also excluded the applicant (though his lawyers attended). Further charges were added on 15 April 2005, with detention extended until 28 April 2005 (no supporting decisions provided despite request). The applicant was convicted on 31 January 2006 of fraud, embezzlement, and tax evasion and sentenced to nine years' imprisonment.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 5 violations: detention orders (initial and extensions) relied on stereotypical, unparticularized grounds without assessing specific risks or alternatives, despite cooperation evidence and seized documents; hearings proceeded without the applicant (and, for the 23 December 2004 hearing, without notifying or including his lawyer); and courts failed to address his arguments or the record discrepancy. Domestic law (CCrP Article 51.7 on hearing records; detention provisions) and Supreme Court Plenum decisions (2006 and 2009) required exceptional use of detention, individualized reasoning, accused presence except in rare cases, and distinct justification for extensions versus initial orders.
001-141383:
The case of Allahverdiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 49192/08) concerns an Azerbaijani student, Amil Allahverdiyev (born 1985), who alleged breaches of his right to liberty under Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, he claimed that domestic judicial decisions ordering and extending his pre-trial detention lacked reasonable grounds, and that he was held without any court order from 19 to 29 July 2008.

On 15 March 2008, the applicant and his adult girlfriend, A.M., travelled with three others from Baku to Ganja intending to marry. A.M.’s father reported her “kidnapping” to police. Proceedings were instituted the next day under Article 144.2.3 of the Criminal Code (kidnapping by a group). A.M. contacted her family, who retrieved her; the applicant returned to Baku on 17 March. After police visits to his home, he voluntarily presented himself at a station on 19 March and was detained for 48 hours as a suspect.

On 21 March he was formally charged. The prosecutor sought remand in custody, citing the offence’s gravity and risks of absconding or obstruction. The Narimanov District Court granted a three-month detention order, referring only to “sufficient evidence,” the crime’s gravity and character, and possible absconding or obstruction. The applicant appealed, arguing that his lack of criminal record, permanent residence, youth, status as an internally displaced person, family and financial difficulties, and the impact on his university studies had been ignored and that a non-custodial measure sufficed. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3 April, relying on the offence’s gravity, public dangerousness and the fact that it carried more than two years’ imprisonment.

On 11 June the investigator sought a one-month extension to complete inquiries. On 14 June the District Court extended detention until 19 July, again citing the applicant’s “personality,” the offence’s gravity, character, circumstances and dangerousness, plus the need for further investigative acts. The applicant’s appeal, proposing alternatives such as police supervision, an undertaking not to abscond or house arrest and repeating his personal circumstances, was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 20 June on essentially identical grounds, adding a risk of influencing witnesses.

The indictment was filed with the Assize Court on 11 July. The applicant’s authorised detention expired on 19 July. He immediately requested release from the Ministry of Justice and, on 22 July, complained to the Prosecutor General that he remained detained without a court order. At a preliminary hearing on 29 July the Assize Court refused to vary the measure and declared the intervening detention lawful solely because the indictment had already been lodged. Subsequent attempts to appeal that decision or to obtain release through a civil action against the prison authorities failed on procedural or formal grounds.

The applicant was later convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. Throughout, the courts used stereotyped language, failed to examine concrete risks or the applicant’s individual situation, and provided no reasoned justification for continued custody after the authorised period had expired.

The case of Allahverdiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 49192/08) concerns an Azerbaijani student, Amil Allahverdiyev (born 1985), who alleged breaches of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He claimed detention from 19 to 29 July 2008 without a court order and that judicial decisions imposing and extending his pre-trial detention lacked reasonable grounds.

On 15 March 2008, the applicant and his adult girlfriend, A.M., travelled from Baku to Ganja with three others intending to marry. A.M.’s father reported her kidnapping to police that day. Criminal proceedings were instituted on 16 March under Article 144.2.3 of the Criminal Code (kidnapping by a group). A.M. contacted her family the same day to explain she had left voluntarily with her boyfriend; her parents retrieved her from Ganja.

The applicant returned to Baku on 17 March. After police visits to his home, he presented himself at a police station on 19 March and was arrested. An investigator ordered 48-hour detention as a suspect. On 21 March he was charged with kidnapping. The prosecutor sought remand in custody, citing the gravity of the offence and risks of absconding or obstructing the investigation. That day the Narimanov District Court granted the request and ordered three months’ detention. It referred to “sufficient evidence,” the gravity and character of the crime, and possibilities of absconding or obstruction, without addressing the applicant’s personal circumstances or alternatives.

The applicant appealed, arguing lack of justification and failure to consider that he had no criminal record, a permanent residence, youth, internally displaced person status, family and financial difficulties, and that detention would interrupt his university studies and risk expulsion. On 3 April 2008 the Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, relying on the offence’s gravity, public dangerousness, circumstances of commission, and the fact that it carried a potential sentence exceeding two years’ imprisonment.

On 11 June the investigator requested a one-month extension to complete the investigation. On 14 June the Narimanov District Court extended detention until 19 July 2008, citing the applicant’s personality, the offence’s gravity, character, circumstances, public dangerousness, and the need for further investigative actions. The applicant again appealed, proposing less restrictive measures (police supervision, an undertaking not to abscond, or house arrest) and repeating his personal circumstances (internally displaced person, voluntary surrender, student status, no record, permanent residence). On 20 June the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the extension, reiterating the offence’s seriousness, risks of absconding, influencing witnesses or obstructing the investigation, and the need for further actions.

The indictment was filed with the Assize Court on 11 July 2008. The applicant wrote to the Ministry of Justice on 16 July requesting release on 19 July when authorised detention expired, and complained to the Prosecutor General on 22 July that he remained detained. At a 29 July preliminary hearing he argued the detention since 19 July was unlawful and sought a change of measure. The Assize Court rejected the request, held that the measure remained unchanged, and declared the post-19 July detention lawful because the indictment had been filed on 11 July. It refused to entertain an appeal, stating that preliminary-hearing decisions were not appealable.

On 30 July the applicant sued the prison department seeking release because the authorised period had expired. The Azizbayov District Court dismissed the claim on 11 August, noting that the Assize Court had already upheld the detention’s lawfulness; the Baku Court of Appeal confirmed this on 11 September. The applicant was convicted of group kidnapping on 19 March 2009 and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment.

The courts’ reasoning throughout consisted of formulaic references to the offence’s gravity and abstract risks, without specific evidence of those risks or meaningful consideration of the applicant’s circumstances or non-custodial alternatives. After 19 July he remained in custody for ten days without a fresh judicial authorisation of continued detention.

The case of Starokadomskiy v. Russia (No. 2) (Application no. 27455/06) concerns a Russian national, Nikolay Anatolyevich Starokadomskiy (born 1971), who alleged violations of Articles 5 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, he claimed that his detention from 2 October to 10 November 2004 was unlawful; that his criminal trial was conducted in camera without valid justification; and that the overall proceedings were excessively lengthy.

Starokadomskiy was arrested on 31 January 1998 on suspicion of murder and charged with aggravated murder on 6 February 1998. He and co-defendants faced additional charges of violent crimes, including conspiracy to commit murder; the cases were joined and investigated by Moscow prosecutors, concluding in December 1998. He reviewed the file in June–July 1999 and requested a jury trial.

The indictment was approved on 19 July 1999 and sent to Moscow City Court. On 5 August 1999, noting the absence of juries there despite most defendants’ requests, the court referred the matter to the Supreme Court, which assigned it to Moscow Regional Court (where juries existed). A Regional Court judge then queried the Constitutional Court on jurisdictional compatibility, suspending proceedings on 17 February 2000 and extending detention due to the seriousness of the charges. The Constitutional Court ruled on 13 April 2000 that the venue change violated the Constitution. The case returned to the Supreme Court, which on 6 September 2000 confirmed City Court competence.

Trial scheduling began on 29 September 2000 for 13 October 2000 (professional judge plus two lay judges) but was adjourned due to the presiding judge’s other commitments. Hearings from 2001 to early 2003 were repeatedly postponed—primarily because of absences by the prosecutor, interpreter, or defence lawyers, and the judge’s involvement in other cases (May/October 2001; May/September/October 2002). The applicant’s 24 December 2001 request for more time to study the file went unanswered. Merits consideration started around March 2003, but hearings on 4 March and 29 April 2003 were adjourned due to lawyers’ absences. On 12 March 2003 the judge removed the applicant from the courtroom for contempt until the end of pleadings; he missed subsequent March hearings. A 9 April 2003 request for a witness list also went unanswered. Hearings on 26 January and 2 February 2004 were adjourned. From February 2004, hearings occurred inside remand centre no. 77/1 (where the applicant was held). The judge declined to explain or provide the venue-change order.

On 1 July 2004 the trial bench extended detention until 1 October 2004. The trial closed on 12 August 2004 and deliberations began. The remand-centre governor repeatedly notified the City Court in October 2004 that the detention order had expired on 1 October and a new one was urgently needed. On 18 October the court replied that the deliberating bench could not issue detention decisions. On 27 October 2004 the applicant was convicted of conspiracy to murder and other offences and sentenced to 10.5 years’ imprisonment, with time served since 31 January 1998 credited. Delivery of the judgment concluded on 10 November 2004; the operative part ordered continued detention pending finality. An appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 15 November 2005 (sentence reduced to 10 years).

The applicant challenged the post-1 October 2004 detention via Article 125 CCrP complaints against the remand-centre governor and supervising prosecutor (dismissed in 2005) and civil proceedings (also dismissed). Domestic law permitted another judge of the same court to extend detention during deliberations and required the governor to release a detainee if no extension arrived by expiry. Public hearings were the rule, with in-camera exceptions limited to state secrets, minors, private-life details or safety. These facts underpin the alleged unlawful detention (no valid order after 1 October until 10 November), closed trial (hearings inside the remand centre) and overall delay (arrest in 1998 to final conviction in 2005).

On 15 November 2005, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to 10 years.

These were dismissed at first instance and on appeal, with authorities finding no basis to prosecute the governor.

Article 241 required public hearings, with limited exceptions (state secrets, minors, private-life details, or participant safety).

These facts centre on the alleged unlawful detention (expired order during deliberations, no timely extension despite notifications, and continued custody until 10 November 2004), potential in-camera aspects (hearings in the remand centre without disclosed justification), and overall length (arrest in 1998 to final appeal in 2005, with repeated adjournments, venue disputes, and procedural interruptions).

Russia (No. 2) (Application no. 27455/06) concerns a Russian national arrested on 31 January 1998 on suspicion of murder and charged on 6 February 1998 with aggravated murder, later joined with other violent offences involving co-defendants. The Constitutional Court ruled on 13 April 2000 that the venue change violated the Constitution. The case returned to the Supreme Court, which on 6 September 2000 confirmed City Court competence.

The court replied on 18 October that it could issue no decisions while deliberating. Judgment delivery concluded on 10 November 2004; the operative part maintained detention pending finality. A related complaint against the supervising prosecutor failed. Civil proceedings against the remand centre were rejected in 2005. The case of Gál v. Hungary originated in an application by György Gál, a Hungarian national born in 1954 and a former Budapest Municipal Council member and economic committee chairman. Arrested on 25 November 2008 on charges of aggravated fraud, corruption, forgery and related offences (with proceedings also against associates), he alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1(c) and 4 (unjustified and unreviewed pre-trial detention), Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (unfair trial and excessive length), Article 8 (family contact restrictions) and Article 13 (ineffective remedy).

On 27 November 2008 the Pest Central District Court ordered detention on remand under Criminal Procedure Code s. 129(2)(b), (c) and (d), citing absconding risk (serious charges, foreign contacts), collusion risk and outstanding investigation. House arrest was refused. The Budapest Regional Court upheld this on 8 December 2008, adding reoffending risk because the alleged acts occurred over a long period through companies he and associates operated, despite his employment and income. From 25–27 November 2008 the prosecutor restricted family contacts (supervised correspondence and visits only; telephone solely with counsel).

Detention was extended at statutory intervals (e.g., 22 December 2008, 24 March, 26 May, 26 August and 26 November 2009; January, March, May, July and November 2010). Courts repeatedly invoked the same grounds: absconding (foreign property/contacts, “underworld” backing, severe sentence, “another reason”), collusion (unspecified information that he and an associate planned to destroy evidence) and reoffending (organised crime, luxurious lifestyle, continued municipal allowance). Applicant arguments—settled family life with five minor children, voluntary return from abroad during the investigation, cessation of his municipal mandate (eliminating reoffending opportunity), and completion of evidence-gathering—were routinely dismissed. Less severe measures were seldom assessed. After indictment on 9 November 2010 (121 pages, 25 defendants, ~10 000-page file), the court dropped collusion risk but maintained detention solely on absconding grounds, again without considering alternatives.

Procedural defects affected reviews. Oral appeals against the 26 May and 21 July 2010 extensions were decided (28 June and 28 July) before written elaborations arrived and before the written first-instance decisions were served. Motions for further evidence (e.g., appointment of a specific valuer) were rejected as superfluous or because the expert might have been involved in the transactions.

Family-contact restrictions lasted until 4 December 2009, after which general prison rules applied (60-minute visits, three 10-minute weekly calls, daily correspondence). Earlier requests for unsupervised or telephone contact with his wife were initially refused.

On 25 January 2011 the court granted release on HUF 100 million bail (~EUR 332 000), which the applicant could not pay. House arrest ordered on 13 May 2011 (citing family responsibilities) was reversed on prosecution appeal on 16 June 2011; the appellate court simply reaffirmed earlier reasons without analysing changed circumstances. Further release requests were refused. Detention ended on 16 December 2011 (over three years). The applicant was convicted on 24 February 2012 and sentenced to eight years six months; further appeal remained pending.

These facts underpin the claims of stereotyped, insufficiently individualised detention justifications, delayed or incomplete reviews, disregarded defence motions, protracted proceedings, and unjustified interference with family life.

Hungary (Application no. 62631/11) concerns a Hungarian national, György Gál (born 1954), a Budapest municipal councillor and economic committee chairman arrested on 25 November 2008 on charges of aggravated fraud, corruption, document forgery and related offences. 001-141629:
The case of Kiisa v. Estonia (ECtHR, applications nos. 16587/10 and 34304/11) arose from protracted Estonian civil proceedings over child alimony between former spouses Karin Kiisa (first applicant) and Aare Kiisa (second applicant). Married from 1989 to 2006, they had a child K. born in September 2002, with the second applicant listed as father in civil records. The first applicant initiated divorce and property proceedings in October 2003.

On 25 October 2004 she sued in Harju County Court for alimony (case 2-04-1467). Preliminary hearings occurred in January and April 2005 amid evidence exchanges. On 27 April 2005 the second applicant filed a separate filiation action (case 2-3307/109) contesting paternity and the civil-status record. He sought suspension of the alimony case; the first applicant did not oppose it. On 14 October 2005 the County Court suspended alimony proceedings pending the filiation judgment.

In the filiation case, the County Court ordered DNA testing of the child and second applicant on 12 May 2005 and required the first applicant to present the child. She appealed unsuccessfully; the Supreme Court refused leave on 31 January 2007. She never produced the child. The filiation action was ultimately dismissed only on 10 May 2012.

Alimony proceedings resumed on 20 June 2007 after the first applicant invoked Supreme Court practice that a paternity challenge does not extinguish the subsistence obligation. A hearing set for August 2007 was postponed at the second applicant’s request. He later proposed a compromise (time-limit extended) and sought further delays or non-resumption; the first applicant supplemented her claim. The court requested bank and tax records and compelled document production. A hearing took place on 30 November 2007.

On 11 January 2008 the County Court awarded partial alimony of EEK 3 000 (approx. EUR 192) per month. Both parties appealed. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the award on 9 May 2008. The Supreme Court quashed that judgment on 19 November 2008 and remitted the case. On 21 May 2009 the Court of Appeal quashed the County Court judgment and remitted it to first instance; the Supreme Court refused the first applicant leave to appeal that remittal on 7 September 2009.

In January 2010 the first applicant amended her claim, filed voluminous new evidence and sought interim measures. A February 2010 hearing (representatives only) led the court to order personal attendance next time. On 17 February 2010 interim alimony of EEK 2 175 (EUR 139) monthly was granted. A April 2010 hearing was postponed for the second applicant’s representative’s illness. Further supplements, evidence and exchanges followed. After a June 2010 hearing the County Court, on 5 July 2010, ordered EEK 5 000 (EUR 320) monthly. The Court of Appeal reduced it to EEK 3 550 (EUR 227) on 6 October 2010. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 26 January 2011, ending the proceedings after more than six years and three months from inception.

The timeline featured multiple adjournments, party-driven delays, evidence-gathering from third parties, two remittals after appellate reversals, and the lengthy (ultimately unsuccessful) filiation suspension. These facts formed the core of the alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (reasonable-time guarantee in civil proceedings) and, given contemporaneous domestic developments on length-of-proceedings remedies, possibly Article 13. Estonian law (Constitution Arts. 14, 15, 25; State Liability Act; Supreme Court rulings such as Osmjorkin) provided a constitutional right to an effective remedy including reasonable duration, with compensation claims directed to administrative courts, though practice at the time of the applications remained evolving mainly in the criminal context.

The county court resumed the case, but further postponements, compromise talks, evidence requests (including from banks and tax authorities), and adjournments followed. A November 2007 hearing produced a January 2008 judgment awarding EEK 3,000 monthly alimony. In May 2009 the Court of Appeal again quashed and remitted to first instance (Supreme Court refusal of leave September 2009).

The county court awarded EEK 5,000 monthly in July 2010; the Court of Appeal reduced it to EEK 3,550 in October 2010. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 26 January 2011, ending the proceedings after more than six years.

Administrative-court compensation claims face a three-year limit. Supreme Court rulings (2008 Constitutional Review Chamber; 2011 plenary Osmjorkin judgment) confirmed that non-pecuniary damage from excessive length may be claimed in administrative courts under the State Liability Act or directly under the Constitution; later administrative-court awards implemented this.

The facts centre on the protracted alimony litigation (multiple remittals, suspensions linked to an unresolved paternity dispute, repeated adjournments and evidence-gathering), raising issues of reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the availability of an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.
