In April 2005 the second applicant began parallel filiation proceedings to contest paternity and the civil-status record. He successfully applied to suspend the alimony case; suspension was granted on 14 October 2005 pending the filiation outcome. In the filiation case the court ordered DNA testing, but the first applicant refused to produce the child. Her appeals were exhausted by January 2007 when the Supreme Court refused leave. (The filiation action was eventually dismissed in May 2012.)

Relying on intervening Supreme Court practice that a paternity challenge did not suspend the duty of support, the first applicant obtained resumption of the alimony proceedings on 20 June 2007. Hearings were postponed, a compromise proposal was made, further evidence (including from banks and the tax authority) was gathered, and the first applicant enlarged her claim. On 11 January 2008 the County Court awarded monthly alimony of EEK 3 000 (approximately EUR 192). Both parties appealed. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the award on 9 May 2008, but the Supreme Court quashed that judgment on 19 November 2008 and remitted the case. On 21 May 2009 the Court of Appeal itself remitted the matter to the first-instance court; the first applicant’s further appeal was refused by the Supreme Court on 7 September 2009.

The first applicant then filed voluminous additional evidence and sought interim measures. A hearing occurred in February 2010; an interim order of EEK 2 175 per month was made. After further exchanges and a hearing in June, the County Court, on 5 July 2010, increased the award to EEK 5 000. The Court of Appeal reduced it to EEK 3 550 on 6 October 2010. Both parties sought cassation; the Supreme Court refused leave on 26 January 2011, thereby terminating the proceedings.

The alimony action therefore lasted more than six years and three months across three levels of jurisdiction, involving a 20-month suspension, two remittals that restarted examination, multiple postponements, and repeated evidentiary submissions. The applicants complained of the overall duration. Domestic law at the time offered no statutory compensation for non-pecuniary damage caused by delay in civil proceedings; later Supreme Court jurisprudence (Osmjorkin, 2011) recognised a constitutional right to an effective remedy and directed claimants to administrative courts under the State Liability Act, but that avenue was not yet established when the applications were lodged.

The facts thus centre on the protracted civil litigation, successive remittals, the interplay with unfinished filiation proceedings, and the absence of a contemporaneous compensatory remedy for delay.
001-142075:
The case of Artemov v. Russia (ECtHR, Application no. 14945/03) involves a former police officer arrested on 30 August 2002 on suspicion of organised-group kidnapping and extortion, based on an eyewitness statement. He was remanded in custody the next day by the Kuzminskiy District Court without any time-limit, citing the offence’s gravity and risks of witness interference, further crime or absconding. Formal charges followed on 6 September 2002 (later expanded then refined to exclude abuse of power).

Detention was extended repeatedly: to 30 November 2002, 30 December 2002, 28 February 2003, 20 May 2003, 30 August 2003, 20 November 2003, 20 February 2004, 1 March 2004, and thereafter until the applicant finished studying the voluminous case file. Extensions rested almost exclusively on the seriousness of the charges (punishable by up to 15 years), incomplete investigative steps (alibi checks, locating co-accused, identification parades, reconstructions) and presumed risks of flight or obstruction. Positive character evidence, family ties and stable residence were acknowledged but dismissed. Several orders lacked specific expiry dates. Pre-trial detention lasted 1 year, 7 months and 8 days until the case reached court on 7 April 2004; detention continued through trial until conviction on 11 October 2004 (total 2 years, 1 month and 12 days). The applicant and/or his lawyer were frequently neither notified of nor present at appeal hearings reviewing these orders (e.g., 19 March 2003, 8 January 2004, 20 April 2004, 27 April 2004). Some appeals took months.

The trial began publicly, but on 1 June 2004 the District Court, without questioning the alleged victim or examining supporting material, granted the prosecutor’s request for in-camera hearings after claims that the applicant had threatened him. All subsequent sessions (including witness examination) were closed. The applicant alleged that records distorted or abridged testimony. On 11 October 2004 he and co-accused were convicted of armed kidnapping and robbery on the basis of more than ten eyewitnesses, co-accused statements, identification records and medical evidence; he received eight years. Sentence was announced publicly. The Moscow City Court upheld the conviction and closed-trial ruling on 11 July 2005, citing participant safety under Article 241 CCrP.

Conditions complaints concerned 30 August–16 September 2002 solitary confinement in the Vikhino facility (infrequent meals every 1–3 days, wooden sleeping boards without mattress, no sanitary facilities) and later remand prison IZ-77/1. Approximately 40 transports (31 August 2002–11 October 2004) involved 5 a.m. cell extraction, overcrowded holding cells and windowless, unventilated vans mixing healthy detainees with those having tuberculosis or lice; journeys lasted 2–5 hours amid traffic. Court holding cells designed for two people regularly held three or four, sometimes all day.

These facts underpin alleged breaches of Article 3 (detention/transport conditions), Article 5 (unjustified, unlimited or excessively long detention and deficient judicial review) and Article 6 (lack of publicity and unfair trial).

The case of *Artemov v. Russia* (Application no. 14945/03) involved a Russian national and former police officer, Artem Aleksandrovich Artemov (born 1977), who alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his arrest, prolonged pre-trial and remand detention, conditions of confinement and transport, closed trial hearings, delayed charges, and unfair proceedings.

On 30 August 2002, Artemov was arrested on suspicion of armed kidnapping and extortion as part of an organised group, based on an eyewitness statement. The next day, the Moscow Kuzminskiy District Court remanded him in custody without a time limit, citing the seriousness of the offence and risks of witness intimidation, continued criminality, or absconding. Formal charges followed on 6 September 2002 (later updated to include robbery, with abuse of power dropped).

Detention was extended repeatedly by the District Court and Moscow City Court: to 30 November 2002, 30 December 2002, 28 February 2003, 20 May 2003, 30 August 2003, 20 November 2003, 20 February 2004, 1 March 2004, and then indefinitely until the applicant finished reviewing the case file. Extensions typically invoked the gravity of charges (offences carrying up to 15 years' imprisonment), incomplete investigations (alibi checks, locating co-accused, identification parades), and presumed flight or interference risks. The applicant's lack of prior convictions, family ties, stable Moscow residence, and positive references were often noted but dismissed. Several appeal hearings (e.g., 19 March 2003, 8 January 2004, 20 April 2004, 27 April 2004) proceeded without notifying or securing the presence of Artemov or his counsel. Pre-trial detention lasted 1 year, 7 months and 8 days until the case reached court on 7 April 2004; remand continued until conviction on 11 October 2004 (total detention: 2 years, 1 month and 12 days). Additional complaints concerned the absence of time limits in April 2004 and alleged unlawfulness of detention from 7–11 October 2004.

On 14 May 2004 the District Court ordered open hearings, but on 1 June 2004 it granted the prosecutor's request for *in camera* proceedings after unexamined claims that victim Mr R. had received threats. Subsequent hearings, including witness examinations, were closed. On 11 October 2004 Artemov was convicted of armed kidnapping and robbery and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment, based on eyewitness, co-accused and documentary evidence. The Moscow City Court upheld the conviction and closed-hearing decision on 11 July 2005, citing participant safety.

Conditions complaints covered 30 August–16 September 2002 in Moscow's Vikhino facility (solitary confinement, food every 1–3 days, wooden sleeping boards without mattresses, no sanitation) and later remand prison IZ-77/1. Transportation on approximately 40 occasions (31 August 2002–11 October 2004) involved overcrowded holding cells and windowless, unventilated vans mixing healthy and ill prisoners (tuberculosis, lice), with 2–5 hour journeys. Court holding cells, designed for two, held three or four occupants for entire days.

These facts underpin alleged breaches of Article 3 (conditions amounting to inhuman treatment), Article 5 (unjustified, excessive or unreasoned detention and inadequate review) and Article 6 (non-public trial and procedural fairness). The application was communicated in 2008; the judgment became final on 3 July 2014.

The case of Artemov v. Russia (no. 14945/03) involves a Russian national (born 1977, former police officer living in Moscow) who alleged violations arising from his arrest, detention, trial and conditions of confinement.

On 30 August 2002 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of kidnapping and extortion committed as part of a group, based on an eyewitness statement. The next day the Kuzminskiy District Court remanded him in custody without a time-limit, citing the seriousness of the offence and risks of pressuring witnesses, interfering with justice, reoffending or absconding. Official charges of armed kidnapping and accessory to extortion by an organised group (aggravated by prior association) followed on 6 September 2002. Further charges of abuse of power and robbery were added in January 2003 (the former later dropped). There were four co-accused.

Detention was extended repeatedly: 24 October 2002 (to 30 November), 26 November (to 30 December), 24 December (to 28 February 2003), 18 February 2003 (to 20 May), 14 May 2003, 4 August 2003 (to 30 August), 15 August 2003 (to 20 November), 17 November 2003 (to 20 February 2004), 17 February 2004 (to 1 March) and 26 February 2004 (until the accused finished studying the case file). Courts relied on the gravity of the charges (punishable by 15 years or more than two years’ imprisonment), unfinished investigative steps (checking alibis, locating co-accused, identification parades, reconstructions) and risks of flight or obstruction. Positive personal circumstances (no record, family, residence, employment references) were noted but deemed insufficient to change the measure.

The applicant or his lawyer were frequently absent from (and unnotified of) appeal hearings on these orders before the Moscow City Court and Supreme Court. Pre-trial detention lasted 1 year, 7 months and 8 days until the case reached the District Court on 7 April 2004. Detention continued during trial (extended without specific reasons) until conviction, adding 6 months and 4 days (total 2 years, 1 month and 12 days). A complaint of unlawful detention from 7–11 October 2004 was also raised, as was the absence of time-limits in April 2004.

On 14 May 2004 open hearings were ordered. On 1 June the prosecutor alleged threats against victim Mr R.; the court granted an in-camera request without questioning Mr R. or examining supporting statements. Subsequent hearings (including witness testimony) were closed. On 11 October 2004 the applicant was convicted of armed premeditated kidnapping with violence threats and robbery, and sentenced to eight years on the basis of more than ten eyewitnesses, co-accused statements, identification records, medical documents and other evidence. The sentence was announced publicly. The City Court upheld the conviction and closed hearings on 11 July 2005, citing participant safety under Article 241 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant also complained of late service of charges, unfair proceedings, misrepresentation of evidence and excessive length of appeal reviews of detention orders.

From 30 August to 16 September 2002 he was held in solitary confinement at the Vikhino temporary facility, receiving food only every 1–3 days, sleeping on wooden boards without a mattress and lacking sanitary facilities; he was later moved to IZ-77/1. On approximately 40 transport occasions (31 August 2002–11 October 2004) he was taken from his cell at 5 a.m., held in overcrowded reception cells, then placed in windowless, unventilated prison vans so crowded that half the inmates (including those with tuberculosis or lice) had nowhere to sit. Journeys lasted 2–5 hours amid traffic. Court cells designed for two people held three or four all day.
001-141763:
**Summary of Dilipak and Karakaya v. Turkey (ECHR, 2014 extracts)**

Two Turkish journalists, Abdurrahman Dilipak (b. 1949) and Hasan Karakaya (b. 1953), both then working for the Akit newspaper in Istanbul, alleged violations of Article 6 (access to court) and Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the ECHR arising from a civil defamation judgment against them.

On 25–26 June 2000, shortly after the funeral of Admiral Güven Erkaya (former navy commander and National Security Council member associated with the 28 February 1997 “post-modern coup”), the applicants published critical articles. Karakaya’s piece, under the headline “We will not waive our rights,” faulted the admiral’s role in that process and stated the author would not attend the funeral or waive claims against him. Dilipak’s article used phrases such as “may your land be abundant” (normally reserved for non-Muslims) and argued that injunctions against speaking ill of the dead did not apply, analogizing to historical tyrants while noting Erkaya’s place in public consciousness.

On 29 September 2000 the deceased’s family brought a civil damages action in the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance against the applicants and the newspaper company, also lodging a criminal complaint. Summonses sent to the newspaper’s registered office could not be served; the muhtar confirmed the applicants were not there. Police inquiries yielded a business address in Aksaray for Karakaya (where service was effected on an “authorised employee”) and an address in Mecidiyeköy for Dilipak (where he was unknown). Service on Dilipak therefore proceeded by newspaper publication.

On 21 January 2003 the court, sitting in the defendants’ absence, ordered them jointly to pay TRY 30 000 (approx. EUR 17 000) plus interest from June 2000 for non-pecuniary damage. It held that the articles exceeded the bounds of permissible criticism by launching personal attacks on a “valorous army commander who served the nation.” Specific passages were cited as implying that Erkaya’s cancer and death were deserved retribution and as employing language reserved for historical villains.

The judgment was never validly served on the applicants. For Karakaya it was treated as served at his last-known address under s. 35 of the Notification Act because he had not notified a change of address; for Dilipak it was published on 14 April 2003 and became final on 29 May 2003. Enforcement began on 9 June 2003; payment orders were posted to the applicants’ actual home addresses (Acıbadem for Dilipak, Beylikdüzü for Karakaya), which they received.

They immediately sought leave to appeal, arguing they had only just learned of the judgment. The first-instance court rejected the appeals as out of time. The Court of Cassation dismissed further appeals in December 2003 and February 2005. Dilipak contended that service by publication was unlawful because the court had made only perfunctory police inquiries instead of checking civil-status, press, social-security, land-registry and other official records (all of which listed his long-term Acıbadem address). He noted that the claimants themselves had known his address from related criminal proceedings and had supplied it promptly for enforcement. Karakaya argued that service at a business address on a non-employee was invalid. Both invoked Court of Cassation case-law requiring exhaustive official inquiries before publication or deemed service. A 2007 appeal in the interests of the law by the Public Prosecutor was also dismissed.

In 2012 the applicants applied to reopen the proceedings on the basis of subsequent criminal investigations into the 1997 events (which, they said, undermined the court’s laudatory characterisation of Erkaya) and the pending Strasbourg applications. Enforcement was suspended pending payment of a large surety; the outcome of the reopening request is not recorded in the extract.

These facts form the core of the complaints: that defective notification deprived the applicants of any opportunity to defend the action, and that the resulting damages award punished legitimate journalistic comment on a public official’s official conduct.

The case of Dilipak and Karakaya v. Turkey originated in applications lodged in 2005 by two Turkish journalists, Abdurrahman Dilipak (born 1949) and Hasan Karakaya (born 1953), both then working for the Akit newspaper in Istanbul. They alleged violations of their right of access to a court (Article 6) and freedom of expression (Article 10) arising from civil defamation proceedings.

On 25 June 2000, following the funeral of Admiral Güven Erkaya (former navy commander and National Security Council member), Karakaya published an article headlined “We will not waive our rights.” It criticised Erkaya’s role in the 28 February 1997 NSC meeting (described by some as a “post-modern coup”). The next day Dilipak published a similar piece. Both articles used strong language: Dilipak invoked historical tyrants and the phrase “may your land be abundant” (typically reserved for non-Muslims); Karakaya suggested the admiral’s cancer and death were retribution for suffering inflicted on the people and stated he would not attend the funeral or waive his rights.

On 29 September 2000 the Erkaya family brought a civil damages action in the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance against the applicants and the newspaper company, also lodging a criminal complaint. They gave only the newspaper’s registered office as the defendants’ address. Service attempts failed there. Police inquiries yielded two Istanbul addresses: a business address in Aksaray for Karakaya and another in Mecidiyeköy for Dilipak. Karakaya’s summons was left with an “authorised employee” (N.G.). Dilipak was unknown at the given address, so service was effected by newspaper publication. Neither applicant appeared.

On 21 January 2003 the court, sitting in the defendants’ absence, awarded the family TRY 30,000 (then about EUR 17,000) jointly plus interest from 25 June 2000 for non-pecuniary damage. It held that the articles exceeded the limits of permissible criticism by constituting personal attacks on a “valorous army commander who served the nation.” The judgment was never served on Karakaya at a current address (he had not notified any change, so service was deemed effected under section 35 of the Notification Act at the last-known address). Dilipak’s judgment was served by publication on 14 April 2003 and became final on 29 May 2003.

Payment orders were issued on 9 June 2003 and sent to the applicants’ actual home addresses (which the family evidently knew). Only then did the applicants learn of the judgment. Their requests for leave to appeal were rejected on 17 June 2003 because the decision had become final. The Court of Cassation dismissed their subsequent appeals on points of law (24 December 2003) and requests for rectification (14 February 2005), finding the first-instance judgment procedurally and substantively lawful. Dilipak argued that the court had failed to make the wide-ranging enquiries required by law and Cassation case-law (e.g., to journalists’ associations, civil-status registries, the press directorate or social-security records) before resorting to publication; he had lived at the same Acıbadem address for more than 20 years and the police even assigned him a bodyguard. Karakaya contended that service at a business address had not complied with statutory conditions.

In 2007 the Ministry of Justice invited the Cassation prosecutor to lodge an appeal in the interests of the law; it was dismissed. In 2012 the applicants sought reopening on the basis of new coup-related prosecutions of 1997 NSC members and the pending Strasbourg applications; enforcement was stayed pending payment of a large surety. The Notification Act (Law no. 7201) governed service: documents could be left with a permanent employee at a workplace only if the addressee was absent; unknown-address procedures required enquiries of relevant public bodies and police investigation before publication.

These facts underpin the applicants’ claims that they were deprived of any genuine opportunity to defend themselves and that the domestic courts’ characterisation of their articles as unlawful personal attacks unjustifiably restricted political speech.

The case of Dilipak and Karakaya v. Turkey (Applications nos. 7942/05 and 24838/05) originated from two applications lodged by Turkish journalists Abdurrahman Dilipak and Hasan Karakaya against Turkey. Both worked for the Akit newspaper and alleged violations of their right of access to a court (Article 6) and freedom of expression (Article 10) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 25 June 2000, coinciding with the funeral of Admiral Güven Erkaya (former navy commander and National Security Council member), Karakaya published an article headlined “We will not waive our rights.” It criticised Erkaya’s role in the 28 February 1997 National Security Council meeting (termed a “post-modern coup d’état” by some). The piece suggested the admiral’s cancer-related death was deserved retribution for suffering he inflicted, stating he made people weep, invented lies about Koranic schools, and that the author felt no sadness and would not attend the funeral. On 26 June 2000, Dilipak published a similar article insinuating Erkaya would face justice for wrongdoing. It used the phrase “may your land be abundant” (typically for non-Muslims) and referenced figures like Hitler, Mussolini, Stalin, Nimrod, and Pharaoh, while noting Erkaya held a particular place in public consciousness.

On 29 September 2000, Erkaya’s family initiated a civil damages action in the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance against the applicants and the newspaper’s owner, also filing a criminal complaint. They listed the newspaper’s registered office as the defendants’ address. Service failed there, as confirmed by the neighbourhood leader (muhtar). Police inquiries yielded addresses: Küçüklanga Caddesi no. 103 (Aksaray) for Karakaya and Mecidiye Caddesi no. 7/50 (Mecidiyeköy) for Dilipak. Karakaya’s summons was handed to N.G., described as an “authorised employee.” Dilipak was unknown at his listed address, so service occurred via press publication.

On 21 January 2003, in the applicants’ absence (they never appeared), the court awarded the family 30,000 TRY (about 17,000 EUR) plus interest from 25 June 2000 for non-pecuniary damage. It held that Dilipak implied Erkaya would pay for misdeeds and that the “do not speak ill of the dead” rule did not apply, exceeding criticism limits via personal attack. For Karakaya, it found implications that the death (especially from cancer) was fitting, plus statements of no sadness or funeral attendance. The court described Erkaya as a “valorous army commander who served the nation” and noted inquiries into the defendants’ finances.

The judgment was not properly served: Karakaya had moved from Küçüklanga Caddesi without notifying the court, so it was deemed served under Notification Act section 35. Dilipak’s was published on 14 April 2003, becoming final on 29 May 2003. Enforcement proceedings began on 9 June 2003, with payment orders sent to the applicants’ actual home addresses (Acıbadem for Dilipak, Beylikdüzü for Karakaya), which they received.

The applicants sought to appeal, learning of the judgment via the orders, but the court rejected this on 17 June 2003 as the ruling was final. The Court of Cassation dismissed their points-of-law appeals on 24 December 2003, finding the judgment procedurally and statutorily compliant. Rectification requests were rejected on 14 February 2005. Dilipak argued insufficient address inquiries (contrary to Court of Cassation case-law requiring checks with municipal, civil status, land registry, and professional bodies, not just police). He provided evidence of his long-term Acıbadem residence, known to journalists’ associations, press directorate, social security, and others, plus that the family knew his address from related criminal proceedings. Karakaya contested service at a non-employee’s business address without noting his absence. A 2007 appeal in the law’s interests by the Public Prosecutor (citing notification rule breaches) was also dismissed.

In 2012, the applicants sought reopening based on new coup-related prosecutions of 1997 Council members (undermining the “valorous commander” characterisation) and the pending ECHR applications. Enforcement was suspended pending a large surety.

These facts highlight alleged Article 6 issues from defective notification (failing Notification Act sections 17, 28, and 35, plus case-law on exhaustive inquiries), resulting in an in absentia judgment without defence opportunities, and Article 10 issues from the damages award penalising journalistic criticism of a public official’s actions.
001-142073:
The case of Enache v. Romania (Application no. 10662/06) originated from a 7 March 2006 application by Marian Enache, a Romanian national born in 1977, then serving a life sentence for murder in Giurgiu Prison. He alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions (Article 3) and hindrance of his right of individual petition to the Court (Article 34). He had been held mainly in Craiova Prison from 2 December 1997 to 26 June 2008 (with brief transfers), then Poarta Albă Prison, and Giurgiu Prison from 2 September 2010.

In Craiova, classified as a dangerous prisoner, Enache described solitary confinement in a cell cluttered with unused bunk beds, leaving insufficient space. He claimed total isolation, prohibition on sharing the cell or meeting other inmates, and virtually no out-of-cell activities except limited educational programmes in 2002–2003. Water was scarce, with hot water available only once weekly for one hour in crowded showers; heating ran just two hours morning and evening, causing winter cold; food was inadequate in quantity and quality, leading to hunger; lighting was poor due to a narrow window and evening-only artificial light; and he was systematically handcuffed whenever leaving his cell, even for religious services. These conditions allegedly caused chronic depressive psychopathy (with a suicide attempt) plus chronic gastritis and duodenitis from 2004.

The Government stated the 9.03 m² cell contained three rows of fixed bunk beds (1.90 m × 0.80 m each), a table and two chairs. Enache sometimes shared it and once planned an escape with a cellmate. He attended some educational activities. Cold drinking water was constant; hot water became available daily for at least one hour from mid-2001 (previously weekly baths). Winter heating averaged eight hours daily. Food met European and domestic standards. A 1.50 m × 0.75 m window provided daylight, with electricity until 22:00. Handcuffing followed regulations for dangerous prisoners and was removed during programmes or visits.

In Giurgiu, Enache described detention alone in a 7 m × 1.50 m cell whose small barred and netted window overlooked a rubbish dump producing unbearable odours. He received only three hours of daily outdoor exercise and no other activities. Knocking on the door for attention resulted in discipline by masked special intervention units.

The Government reported five similar 10.24 m² cells each with two beds (1.93 m × 0.83 m) and a bedside table. The dump lay about 100 m away and was collected monthly; occasional smells were remedied. They supplied only general prison activity regulations.

Concerning petition rights, the Court sent letters to Craiova Prison on 23 January 2007 and 14 May 2009; the second was returned “recipient unknown.” After confirming Enache’s location, further letters of 21 September and 30 November 2010 reached him only on 1 October and 10 December 2010. Enache alleged systematic refusal to forward his correspondence, threats that continued complaints would see him “leave prison only in a coffin,” a transfer intended to force abandonment of the application, and coercion (by the section director and three masked guards) to sign a 4 February 2011 statement withdrawing interest because of the transfer. The letters arrived late and opened.

The Government produced incoming-mail registers, escort-planning sheets and internal rules showing staff collected mail (signing postal receipts) and detainees confirmed receipt. Correspondence was opened only to check for forbidden items and never read; Court letters were never opened. Delays resulted from transfers. They submitted Enache’s 4 February 2011 statement that he no longer wished to pursue the case.

CPT reports after 1999 and 2006 visits to Craiova documented severe overcrowding, inadequate heating and hygiene, poor food, nighttime water cuts, total isolation and inactivity for lifers (automatically classed dangerous), systematic unjustified handcuffing, and the intimidating use of masked intervention units, concluding that conditions could amount to inhuman and degrading treatment.

These facts underpin the alleged violations.

The case of Enache v. Romania (Application no. 10662/06) was brought by Marian Enache, a Romanian national born in 1977 and serving a life sentence for murder, who alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions under Article 3 of the Convention as well as interference by State agents with his right of individual petition to the Court under Article 34.

Enache was held in Craiova Prison from December 1997 until June 2008 (with brief transfers), then Poarta Albă Prison, and finally Giurgiu Prison from September 2010. Classified as a dangerous prisoner due to his sentence, he was kept in solitary confinement. He described his Craiova cell as overcrowded with unnecessary fixed bunk beds occupying space in a 9.03 m² room, leaving him isolated with no cellmate contact or out-of-cell activities except limited educational sessions in 2002–2003. He reported chronic shortages of drinking water and hot water (available only one hour weekly in collective showers until mid-2001, later one hour daily), inadequate heating (two hours morning and evening, causing winter cold), insufficient poor-quality food leading to hunger, and poor lighting from a narrow window with artificial light only in the evenings. He was systematically handcuffed whenever leaving his cell, including for religious services. These conditions allegedly caused chronic depressive psychopathy, a suicide attempt, and chronic gastritis/duodenitis from 2004. The Government countered that the cell sometimes housed others (including one escape-planning cellmate), cold water was constant, heating averaged eight hours daily in winter, food met standards, the window (1.50 m × 0.75 m) provided adequate daylight plus evening electricity until 10 p.m., and handcuffing followed regulations for high-risk inmates (removed during programmes and visits). CPT reports from 1999 and 2006 visits to Craiova corroborated severe overcrowding, hygiene and heating failures, poor food, nighttime water cuts, total isolation of life-sentence prisoners, unjustified handcuffing, and the intimidating use of masked special intervention units.

In Giurgiu, Enache claimed detention alone in a 7 m × 1.50 m cell with a barred, netted window overlooking a rubbish dump that produced unbearable odours; he received only three hours of daily outdoor exercise with no other activities and was disciplined (often by masked units) for tapping on his door to summon guards. The Government stated cells measured 10.24 m² with two beds, the dump was 100 m away and collected monthly (with remedial steps for smells), and activities followed internal rules.

Regarding petition rights, Court letters of January 2007 and May 2009 were sent to Craiova (the second returned undelivered). After confirmation of Enache’s transfer, 2010 letters to Poarta Albă reached him only after further delays and transfers to Giurgiu. Signatures on postal receipts differed from his application form. The Government produced registers showing later receipt (1 October and 10 December 2010) and a 4 February 2011 statement in which Enache purported to withdraw his application because earlier complaints no longer interested him. Enache later alleged that prison staff in all three facilities systematically blocked or delayed his correspondence, threatened that continued complaints would result in his leaving prison “in a coffin,” transferred him specifically to induce withdrawal, and coerced the statement under the presence of three masked guards; the letters arrived late and already opened. The Government maintained that all incoming mail was briefly checked for prohibited items but that Court correspondence was never read and was delivered unopened and on time.

These facts formed the basis of the Court’s examination of whether the cumulative detention conditions reached the Article 3 threshold and whether the authorities’ handling of correspondence and the contested statement constituted hindrance of the Article 34 right of petition.

001-142430:
The applicant, Gayratbek Saliyev, a Kyrgyz national of Uzbek ethnicity born in 1988, fled southern Kyrgyzstan for Russia in July 2010 amid inter-ethnic violence between Kyrgyz and Uzbek groups that erupted in June 2010 in areas including Osh and the Jalal-Abad Region (where he lived in Suzak village). He claimed he had not participated in any violence and left to escape ethnically motivated attacks; his relatives remained in Kyrgyzstan. In Russia he was convicted of robbery in September 2011, served a prison term and was released in January 2012. He had not previously sought refugee status or asylum.

In August 2010 the Osh Region Prosecutor’s Office charged him in absentia with serious violent offences (later amended to include illegal firearms use, murder, robbery, property destruction and ethnically aggravated rioting) committed during the June 2010 unrest. A Kyrgyz court ordered his pre-trial detention and he was placed on an international wanted list. Russian police arrested him on 25 March 2012 while travelling by train. The transport prosecutor’s office ordered his remand in custody pending an extradition request (received on 18 April 2012). Detention was repeatedly extended by Moscow courts (to September 2012, December 2012, March 2013 and September 2013), with some appeal delays of several weeks.

On 28 April 2012 Saliyev applied for refugee status, arguing that the charges were ethnically motivated fabrications and that he faced a real risk of ill-treatment if returned, citing Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International reports. The Moscow migration authority refused the application on 21 August 2012, finding that he feared lawful prosecution rather than persecution on ethnic or other Convention grounds and that he had not proved such persecution. The Federal Migration Service upheld the refusal; judicial review by the Basmannyy District Court and Moscow City Court confirmed it. A later temporary-asylum application was also initially refused (later quashed for re-examination).

Kyrgyzstan provided diplomatic assurances that Saliyev would receive legal assistance, would not be tortured or ill-treated, that the request concerned ordinary crimes without ethnic or political persecution, and that Russian diplomats could visit him in detention. On 27 February 2013 the Russian Deputy Prosecutor General granted extradition without addressing the ill-treatment risk. Saliyev appealed, relying on international reports of ethnic Uzbeks’ particular vulnerability after the 2010 violence. On 16 April 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the order, refusing to consider most of the reports (describing them as general and unproven), noting that the refugee refusal had already dismissed persecution claims, and accepting the assurances as sufficient. The Supreme Court of Russia dismissed a further appeal on 19 June 2013, endorsing that reasoning and finding no political or discriminatory motivation.

On 17 June 2013 the European Court of Human Rights indicated under Rule 39 that Saliyev should not be extradited pending its examination. He was released from custody on 4 September 2013 under a personal guarantee. Relevant UN, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch materials documented widespread torture and ill-treatment in Kyrgyzstan (especially of ethnic Uzbeks linked to the 2010 events), impunity, coerced confessions, biased prosecutions targeting Uzbeks, courtroom violence against defence lawyers, and failures to investigate or review such cases despite legislative prohibitions.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: that extradition would expose Saliyev to a real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3, that he lacked effective domestic remedies (Article 13) to challenge that risk, and that detention pending extradition lacked effective judicial review (Article 5).

The applicant, Gayratbek Saliyev, a Kyrgyz national of ethnic Uzbek origin born in 1988, left southern Kyrgyzstan in 2010 amid inter-ethnic clashes between Kyrgyz and Uzbek groups in Osh and Jalal-Abad (including his village of Suzak). These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints that extradition would violate Article 3 (real risk of ill-treatment given his ethnicity and the documented pattern of abuse), that he lacked an effective domestic remedy for that claim (Article 13) and that judicial review of his lengthy pre-extradition detention was ineffective (Article 5).

The case of Gayratbek Saliyev v. Russia (Application no. 39093/13) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a Kyrgyz national of Uzbek ethnicity. He alleged that extradition to Kyrgyzstan would expose him to a real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, that he lacked effective domestic remedies in this regard (Article 13), and that there had been no effective judicial review of his detention pending extradition.

The applicant was born in 1988 and originated from the village of Suzak in Kyrgyzstan’s Jalal-Abad Region. In June 2010, inter-ethnic violence erupted between Kyrgyz and Uzbek communities in southern Kyrgyzstan, including his home area. He claimed he took no part in the violence and fled to Russia in July 2010 to escape ethnically motivated attacks. His family remained in Kyrgyzstan. In Russia he was convicted of robbery, served a sentence and was released in January 2012. He made no asylum claim at that stage.

On 24 August 2010 the Osh Region Prosecutor’s Office charged him in absentia with serious violent offences—including murder, robbery, illegal use of firearms and participation in rioting aggravated by ethnic hatred—allegedly committed during the June 2010 events. A Kyrgyz court ordered his remand in custody and he was placed on an international wanted list.

Russian police arrested him on 25 March 2012. He was detained pending receipt of an extradition request under the Minsk Convention. The request arrived on 18 April 2012. Detention was repeatedly extended by the Meshchanskiy District Court (and upheld on appeal) for periods of several months while the extradition check proceeded.

He relied on reports by Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. The Moscow migration authority refused the application on 21 August 2012, finding that he was fleeing lawful criminal prosecution rather than persecution and that he had produced no evidence of ethnic targeting. The Federal Migration Service and the domestic courts upheld the refusal.

Kyrgyzstan furnished diplomatic assurances that the applicant would receive legal assistance, would not be subjected to torture or inhuman treatment, that the request concerned ordinary criminal offences and was not politically or ethnically motivated, and that Russian diplomats would be allowed to visit him in detention. On 27 February 2013 the Russian Deputy Prosecutor General granted extradition. The applicant appealed, citing extensive international material showing that ethnic Uzbeks charged in connection with the 2010 violence were systematically subjected to torture, coerced confessions, biased investigations and unfair trials, and that impunity for such abuses was widespread. The Moscow City Court (16 April 2013) and the Supreme Court (19 June 2013) dismissed the appeals. They relied on the earlier refugee-status refusal, treated the Kyrgyz assurances as sufficient to eliminate any risk, and regarded general country reports as unproven and inapplicable to the individual case.

On 17 June 2013 the Court indicated under Rule 39 that the applicant should not be extradited pending further notice. He was released from custody in September 2013 after his lawyer gave a personal guarantee of appearance.

The relevant international material (UN Committee against Torture, Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch reports from 2012–2014) documented a persistent pattern of torture in Kyrgyz detention facilities, especially against ethnic Uzbeks linked to the 2010 events, the almost total absence of effective investigations or prosecutions of perpetrators, heavy reliance on coerced confessions, and courtroom violence and harassment of defence lawyers. These facts formed the core of the applicant’s claims concerning the risk of ill-treatment, the adequacy of the remedies available to him and the lawfulness of the successive detention orders.

The applicant, a stateless Palestinian from Gaza born in 1988, suffered paraplegia from a 2007 Israeli missile strike that he claimed targeted him personally (following earlier attacks and the loss of many relatives). A humanitarian group brought him to Turkey in March 2008 with other injured Palestinians for medical care. He received short-term residence permits, then married his Turkish physiotherapist in April 2009 and obtained a long-term permit valid to May 2010.

On 12 August 2009 police collected him from home under the pretext of an interview. At headquarters he was told his permit had been cancelled and he would be deported, without reasons, destination or timing. He was detained at the Kumkapı Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre. A same-day police record (never served on him) recorded a 27 July 2009 deportation order based on National Intelligence Agency material alleging telephone contacts with Israeli numbers about arms procurement, recruitment and operational security, deemed a national-security threat under the Passport Act and Residence and Travel of Foreigners Act. Documents supporting the order were never disclosed to him.

As a paraplegic he could not use the centre’s squat toilets and had to be taken to a nearby hotel (sometimes accompanied by his wife); he slept on a table and his medical treatment was interrupted. His wife alerted an NGO and UNHCR.

On 14 August 2009 he sued the Ministry of the Interior in the Ankara Administrative Court to annul the order and stay its execution, arguing it was unlawful (given his marriage and valid permit), unnotified, unsupported by evidence, would expose him to torture or death by Israeli forces, destroy family unity, halt vital treatment and constitute degrading detention lacking disability accommodations. The court immediately stayed execution and requested the underlying documents. He was released on 18 August 2009.

The Ministry later cited the intelligence report (still undisclosed). On 16 September 2009 the court lifted the stay. His appeal, repeating the risks and adding his UNHCR refugee application plus the detention conditions, was dismissed without reasons by the Regional Administrative Court on 14 October 2009. On 22 December 2009 he was given 15 days to leave or face forced removal.

He applied to UNHCR (interviewed October 2009) and claimed asylum in Turkey on 24 December 2009, citing persecution, ongoing treatment needs and the risk of Israeli torture. His lawyer noted that the order had never been served and that a 2005 National Action Plan required suspension of deportation during pending judicial review.

On 4 January 2010 the ECHR indicated under Rule 39 that he should not be deported to Israel or Gaza pending the UNHCR decision. Temporary residence was then granted. In April 2010 the administrative court quashed the deportation order because the interim measure rendered it unfeasible; the Supreme Administrative Court upheld this in 2010–2012. He received further temporary permits as an asylum-seeker, later withdrew both his asylum claim (2011) and UNHCR application (2013) to avoid possible resettlement away from his wife, and in March 2013 obtained a one-year renewable residence permit based on genuine family life.

These facts concern the lawfulness and conditions of detention, the risk of ill-treatment upon removal, interference with family life and the availability of effective remedies.

The applicant, İslam H.M. Asalya, a stateless Palestinian born in 1988, lived in the Gaza Strip until March 2008. He alleged losing around 25 relatives to Israeli attacks and personally surviving three missile strikes between 2000 and 2007. The most recent, in 2007, followed an anonymous call confirming his identity and left him paraplegic. On 25 March 2008 a Turkish humanitarian organisation evacuated him and 49 other injured Palestinians to Turkey for medical care. The Interior Ministry issued short-term residence permits in June 2008. After marrying his Turkish physiotherapist on 30 April 2009 he received a long-term temporary residence permit valid until 17 May 2010.

On 12 August 2009 police collected him from home on the pretext of an interview. At headquarters he was told his permit had been cancelled and he would be deported; no reasons, destination or timetable were given. He was taken to the Kumkapı Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre. A police record of the same day stated that a 27 July 2009 ministerial deportation order, issued at the National Intelligence Agency’s request, cited intelligence of possible involvement in international terrorism. Neither the order nor the record was served on him.

His wife alerted a human-rights organisation, which contacted UNHCR and reported the centre’s unsuitability for a paraplegic: he slept on a table, could not use squat toilets (requiring police escorts to a nearby hotel), and his treatment had been halted. On 14 August 2009 he sued in the Ankara Administrative Court to quash the order and stay its execution, arguing that it was unnotified, unsupported by evidence, unlawful given his marriage and valid permit, and would expose him to targeted killing or torture by Israeli forces, interrupt vital treatment and destroy family life. He also challenged the detention’s lawfulness and its degrading conditions.

The court immediately stayed execution pending further examination and requested the underlying documents. The applicant was released on 18 August 2009. On 9 September the Ministry disclosed that the order rested on a 16 July 2009 intelligence report alleging telephone contacts with Israeli numbers concerning arms procurement, recruitment and operational secrecy; supporting documents were withheld from him. On 16 September the court lifted the stay; an appeal was rejected without reasons on 14 October.

Meanwhile the applicant applied to UNHCR (25 September) and later claimed asylum in Turkey (24 December), citing persecution, ongoing treatment, marriage and the risk of Israeli targeting or torture. On 22 December authorities ordered him to leave within 15 days. On 4 January 2010 the European Court indicated under Rule 39 that he should not be deported to Israel or Gaza pending UNHCR’s decision. Turkey then issued renewable temporary residence permits. In April 2010 the Ankara Administrative Court quashed the deportation order because of the interim measure; the Supreme Administrative Court upheld this in 2010–2012. The applicant later withdrew both his Turkish asylum claim (2011) and UNHCR application (2013) to remain with his wife. In March 2013 he received a one-year renewable residence permit based on established family life.

These facts concern alleged violations arising from unnotified detention and deportation proceedings based on undisclosed intelligence, the centre’s failure to provide reasonable accommodation for his disability (contrary to CRPD standards), interruption of medical care, and the real risk of death or ill-treatment if returned to Gaza, together with interference with family life and the absence of an effective domestic remedy capable of suspending expulsion.

The case of Asalya v. Turkey (Application no. 43875/09) concerned a stateless Palestinian applicant, İslam H.M. Asalya (born 1988), who held a Palestinian Authority passport and lived in Istanbul. He originated from the Gaza Strip, where he claimed to have lost around 25 relatives to Israeli attacks and to have been personally targeted in a 2007 missile strike following an anonymous call confirming his identity. The attack left him paraplegic and severely injured. In March 2008, a Turkish humanitarian organisation (İHH) transported him and 49 other injured Palestinians to Turkey for medical treatment. The Ministry of the Interior granted the group short-term residence permits in June 2008. In April 2009, the applicant married his Turkish physiotherapist, obtaining a long-term residence permit valid until May 2010.

On 12 August 2009, police officers took the applicant from his home to Istanbul Police Headquarters under the pretence of an interview, after which he was verbally informed that his residence permit had been cancelled and that he would be deported. He was detained at the Kumkapı Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre without service of the 27 July 2009 deportation order (issued at the request of the National Intelligence Agency based on a 16 July 2009 report alleging contacts with Israeli telephone numbers concerning arms procurement, recruitment, and operational confidentiality, deemed a national security threat under the Passport Act and Residence and Travel of Foreigners Act). No reasons, destination, or timeline were provided. Detention conditions were unsuitable for his disability: he slept on a table, could not use squat toilets (requiring police escorts to a nearby hotel, sometimes with his wife), and his medical treatment was interrupted.

The applicant’s wife contacted Mazlumder, which alerted the UNHCR. On 14 August 2009, he challenged the deportation before the Ankara Administrative Court, seeking annulment and a stay of execution. He argued the order was unlawful given his marriage, valid permit, lack of notification or opportunity to respond, absence of concrete evidence of a security threat, risks to life and physical integrity (targeted killings or torture by Israeli forces), family unity, and health (irreversible harm from treatment interruption). He also alleged unlawful detention and degrading conditions lacking disability accommodations (no accessible toilets or lifts). The court immediately requested the order and supporting documents and granted a stay due to potential irreversible harm. The applicant was released on 18 August 2009.

The Ministry later submitted the intelligence report and undisclosed annexes. On 16 September 2009, the court lifted the stay. The applicant’s appeal, reiterating lack of evidence, health and family risks, pending UNHCR application, and detention conditions, was rejected without reasons by the Ankara Regional Administrative Court on 14 October 2009. He applied to the UNHCR on 25 September 2009 and claimed asylum in Turkey on 24 December 2009, citing Gaza persecution, ongoing treatment, marriage, and Israeli targeting. Authorities demanded he leave within 15 days or face forcible deportation. His lawyer highlighted non-service of the order, pending merits proceedings, and Turkey’s National Action Plan requiring suspension of deportation during challenges.

On 4 January 2010, the ECHR indicated under Rule 39 that the applicant not be deported to Israel or Gaza pending UNHCR proceedings. He received renewable temporary residence permits. The Ankara Administrative Court quashed the deportation on 22 April 2010 as unfeasible due to the interim measure (upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court). The applicant later withdrew his asylum and UNHCR claims to remain with his wife and was granted a one-year renewable residence permit in 2013 based on established family life.

These facts underpin alleged violations relating to detention conditions (particularly for a disabled person), the lawfulness and notification of detention and deportation, risks upon return to Israel/Gaza (targeted killings, torture, treatment interruption), interference with family life, and lack of effective domestic remedies or disclosure of evidence. Relevant standards include the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (reasonable accommodation in detention) and reports on Israeli practices of targeted killings and ill-treatment of Palestinian detainees.

The case of Duško Ivanovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 10718/05) concerns alleged violations of the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Ivanovski, a Macedonian national born in 1971, claimed that domestic courts convicted him of drug trafficking on the basis of unlawfully obtained evidence and denied him the opportunity to examine defence witnesses or obtain independent expert evidence.

On 4 February 2003 police apprehended Ivanovski in Skopje and conducted a personal search without a court warrant or witnesses, confiscating 13 keys and a mobile phone. An investigating judge then issued warrants to search two apartments and related premises belonging to the applicant’s father, based on suspicion of drug trafficking. During the searches, conducted in the presence of the father and two neighbour-witnesses, seven packages were discovered in cellar no. 10 of the building. The cellar belonged to a third party and was opened with a key seized from Ivanovski. Ivanovski, who had been waiting in a police car, was later brought to the scene, photographed beside the packages, and signed a confiscation certificate. He later claimed police had forced him to touch the packages, both at the scene and at the police station, in order to obtain his fingerprints, and that he had been physically ill-treated.

Expert examinations by the Ministry of the Interior’s Criminal Investigations Bureau established that the padlock on cellar no. 10 could be opened with any key (including those taken from Ivanovski), that five packages contained 2.296 kg of heroin and two others contained cutting agents, and that a fingerprint on one package matched Ivanovski’s right middle finger. The Bureau’s reports were prepared without a prior judicial order for expert examination and without the defence present.

Ivanovski was indicted for possessing and offering the heroin for sale. At trial he denied any connection to the drugs, stating that the cellar was not his and that he had been compelled to touch the packages. His father testified that police had pushed Ivanovski against the packages so that he touched them, that the cellar belonged to another apartment, and that a pair of keys (one held by the father) fitted the padlock. Defence counsel argued that the cellar search lacked a specific warrant, that the personal search was unlawful, that the fingerprint had been obtained without an expert present and was unreliable, that the Bureau’s experts (employed by the prosecuting Ministry) were biased, and that the quantity of heroin was inconsistent with the small package sizes. Counsel requested examination of the neighbour-witnesses, the police officers who secured the fingerprint, and the Bureau experts, as well as alternative independent expert examinations of the fingerprint and the substances.

The Skopje Court of First Instance convicted Ivanovski on 20 March 2003 and sentenced him to two-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. It found the searches lawful (the personal search being permitted by statute on reasonable suspicion), accepted the Bureau’s reports as scientifically valid, and dismissed the father’s account as biased. It regarded the fingerprint as sufficient to link Ivanovski to the drugs irrespective of ownership of the cellar.

Ivanovski’s appeals to the Court of Appeal and an extraordinary-review application to the Supreme Court reiterated the complaints of unlawfully obtained evidence, lack of impartiality of the Bureau experts, and the refusal to hear additional witnesses or commission alternative expertise. Both higher courts upheld the conviction, holding that the searches complied with the Criminal Proceedings Act, that the Bureau was competent to perform expert examinations, that the signed search records rendered examination of the neighbours unnecessary, and that the evidence as a whole established guilt. A request for protection of legality was refused by the public prosecutor.

These facts form the core of the alleged fair-trial violations: reliance on evidence obtained through searches whose lawfulness was contested, admission of expert reports from a body attached to the investigating Ministry, and the courts’ refusal to allow the defence to confront key witnesses or obtain independent scientific evidence.

The case of Duško Ivanovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 10718/05) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s complaint of an unfair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. A Macedonian national born in 1971 and living in Skopje, he alleged that domestic courts convicted him of drug trafficking on the basis of unlawfully obtained evidence and that he was denied the chance to examine defence witnesses or obtain alternative expert evidence.

On 4 February 2003 police detained the applicant in Skopje and performed a personal search without a warrant or witnesses, seizing 13 keys and a mobile phone under statutory exceptions for reasonable suspicion of concealing evidence. An investigating judge then issued warrants for two apartments belonging to the applicant’s father, citing suspicion of drug trafficking. Searches of the apartments and associated cellars, conducted in the presence of the father and two neighbour witnesses, uncovered seven packages in cellar no. 10, opened with one of the seized keys. The applicant, brought to the scene afterwards, signed a confiscation certificate. The Criminal Investigations Bureau of the Ministry of the Interior later reported that five packages contained 2.296 kg of heroin (the remainder being mixing agents), that the padlock could be opened by any key including those taken from the applicant, and that a fingerprint on one package matched the applicant’s right middle finger.

A criminal complaint followed. The applicant, examined with counsel present, remained silent but confirmed his signatures on the records. He was indicted for possessing and offering the heroin for sale. At the 19 March 2003 trial he denied any link to the drugs, asserting that the cellar belonged to a third party. He claimed police forced him to handle the packages for photographs, ill-treated him, and obtained his fingerprints under duress. His father testified that the drugs were found in a third-party cellar opened with matching keys and that officers pushed the applicant against the packages, causing accidental contact. Counsel argued that no warrant authorised the personal search or the search of cellar no. 10, that the fingerprint had been secured without an expert present, that the Bureau’s reports were biased because the Ministry had initiated the prosecution, and that the courts should hear the officers, experts and neighbours and commission independent analyses.

On 20 March 2003 the trial court convicted the applicant and imposed a two-and-a-half-year sentence. It treated the search records as lawful, relied on the signed certificate, the keys and the expert reports, dismissed the father’s account as biased, and saw no need for further witnesses or experts. The applicant appealed, repeating the complaints of unlawful searches, unreliable and partisan expertise, and the refusal to examine additional persons. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 20 May 2004, holding that the searches complied with the Criminal Proceedings Act, that the Bureau was statutorily authorised to perform the examinations, and that the neighbours’ signatures rendered their testimony unnecessary. The Supreme Court rejected an extraordinary-review application on 2 November 2004, confirming that the evidence was admissible and the facts correctly established.

These circumstances form the core of the alleged Article 6 violation: the legality of the warrantless searches, the circumstances in which the fingerprint was obtained, the impartiality of Ministry experts, and the courts’ consistent refusal to hear defence witnesses or order independent expert evidence.

The applicant, a Macedonian national born in 1971, was arrested by police in Skopje on 4 February 2003 on suspicion of drug trafficking. He was subjected to a personal search without a court warrant or witnesses (permitted under the Criminal Proceedings Act in cases of reasonable suspicion of concealing evidence). Thirteen keys and a mobile phone were seized. Later that day, an investigating judge issued warrants to search two apartments and associated premises owned by the applicant’s father. The searches of the apartments and cellars occurred in the presence of the father and two neighbour-witnesses. Seven packages of unknown substance were discovered in cellar no. 10 (belonging to a third-party apartment), which had been opened using a key taken from the applicant. The applicant, brought to the scene afterwards, signed a confiscation certificate for the packages without objection. Search records were signed by all present, including a note that the packages were found in the third-party cellar.

On 5 February 2003, the Ministry of the Interior’s Criminal Investigations Bureau issued expert reports: the cellar padlock was damaged and openable with any key (including those seized); five packages contained 2.296 kg of heroin and two others contained 0.991 kg of common cutting agents; and a fingerprint on one package matched the applicant’s right middle finger via automated comparison. A criminal complaint followed, and the applicant (who remained silent when examined by an investigating judge) was detained pending trial.

The public prosecutor indicted the applicant for possessing and offering for sale the heroin found in the cellar. At the 19 March 2003 trial hearing, the applicant denied any connection to the drugs or cellar (claiming it belonged to an unknown third party). He alleged that police had forced him to handle the packages (first in the cellar, then at the station) to photograph him and obtain his fingerprint, including by physical ill-treatment; he had signed documents under pressure and had not requested medical help or reported the abuse out of fear. His father testified that police had opened the third-party cellar with seized keys (one of which matched a key the father also possessed), found the packages in a ventilation shaft, and pushed the applicant against them so that he touched them accidentally; the officer had not worn gloves initially. The defence argued that no warrant authorised the cellar search, there were no eyewitnesses linking the applicant to the drugs (hidden in a third-party space openable by any key), the fingerprint had been obtained improperly without an on-site expert, the expert reports were unclear, imprecise, and biased (as the Bureau formed part of the prosecuting Ministry), the package dimensions were inconsistent with the reported quantities, and the examinations had occurred in the defence’s absence. The defence requested examination of the father (already heard), the attending neighbours, the police officers who secured the fingerprint, and the Bureau experts, plus alternative independent expert examinations of the fingerprint and substances.

On 20 March 2003 the trial court convicted the applicant (who had a prior suspended sentence) of drug trafficking and imposed a 2½-year prison term. It found that he had stored the heroin for sale, relying on the (lawfully obtained) search records, the signed confiscation certificate, the keys, and the Bureau reports confirming the heroin and matching fingerprint. The father’s testimony was dismissed as biased; the court saw no reason for police to have used force and held that the fingerprint rendered the third-party ownership of the cellar irrelevant. Requests for further witnesses or alternative experts were implicitly rejected.

The applicant appealed, reiterating that the cellar search lacked a warrant, the fingerprint and substance examinations were unlawful/unreliable/biased, and the trial court had failed to hear the neighbours (regarding alleged forcing of the fingerprint), police officers, or experts, or to order alternative examinations. On 20 May 2004 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal (and a prosecutor’s appeal on sentence leniency). It held that the searches complied with the Act (personal search without warrant permitted on suspicion; home search conducted pursuant to warrant in the presence of witnesses and the occupier), that the Ministry was authorised to request Bureau examinations, that the reports were scientifically valid, and that examination of the neighbours was unnecessary as they had signed the records without objection. The fingerprint, keys, and signed certificate established guilt.

The applicant’s July 2004 extraordinary-review application to the Supreme Court repeated the complaints of no direct evidence, unlawful cellar search, need to hear police/experts/neighbours, and biased/unreliable Bureau reports (requesting alternatives). On 2 November 2004 the Supreme Court dismissed it, affirming that the searches and examinations were lawful under the Act, the evidence was properly assessed, and no procedural violation affecting the outcome had occurred. A subsequent request for a legality review was refused by the public prosecutor.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the conviction rested on unlawfully obtained evidence (warrantless personal search and cellar search) and that he had been denied the opportunity to examine defence witnesses and obtain alternative expert evidence, in violation of his right to a fair trial.

The applicant, Marija Božić (born 1940), was insured as an agricultural entrepreneur with the Croatian Pension Fund from 1 January 1980 until 30 November 1992 while residing in Klokočevik. In November 1992 she relocated to Lipovača (in the self-proclaimed Serbian Independent Region of Krajina) and ceased contributions.

In April 1998 the Fund accepted her payment of contributions for November 1992–December 1994 and issued a certificate confirming registration of the qualifying period from 1980 to 1994. In November 2000 it accepted a further payment covering January 1995–May 2000 and issued another certificate.

On 22 November 2000, having reached the then-applicable retirement age of 60, she applied for an old-age pension (requiring 15 years of contributions). In April 2002 the Fund, acting of its own motion, ruled that she had lost insured status on 30 November 1992 upon winding up her agricultural activities. It therefore counted only 12 years and 11 months of qualifying service and refused the pension. She did not appeal the refusal itself but challenged the status decision, arguing that she had paid the contributions at the Fund’s invitation.

The Central Office dismissed her appeal without addressing the payments. The Administrative Court upheld the decision in September 2006, holding that departure from the territory where she had exercised her activity automatically terminated her status; any activity on occupied territory would have required validation under the Validation Act, which she had not sought. The Constitutional Court dismissed her complaint in April 2009, finding no interference with property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In January 2012 she lodged fresh administrative requests seeking recognition of the entire 1980–2000 period, formal validation of the 1992–1994 interval, and a pension from November 2000. After initial refusals, the Central Office in December 2012 accepted her appeals, recognised the full period as agricultural-entrepreneur service on the strength of the earlier payments, and treated the validation issue as already resolved. On 21 March 2013 the competent office awarded an old-age pension only from 1 August 2011, applying the six-month retroactivity rule of the Pension Insurance Act to the 2012 application date.

The application to the Court, lodged in August 2009, complained that the successive refusals had deprived her of a pension to which the accepted contributions entitled her.

The case of Marija Božić v. Croatia (application no. 50636/09) concerns the applicant’s complaint that Croatian authorities deprived her of a pension to which she claimed entitlement on the basis of contributions she had paid, in alleged violation of her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, born in 1940, was insured with the Croatian Pension Fund as an agricultural entrepreneur from 1 January 1980 until 30 November 1992 while living in Klokočevik. In November 1992 she moved to Lipovača in the self-proclaimed “Serbian Independent Region of Krajina” and ceased making contributions. In April 1998 she paid HRK 4,978 covering the period 30 November 1992 to 31 December 1994 and received a certificate confirming registration of a pension-qualifying period from 1980 to 1994. In November 2000 she paid a further HRK 11,663 covering 1 January 1995 to 31 May 2000 and obtained a second certificate. Having reached pensionable age, she applied for an old-age pension on 22 November 2000.

On 12 April 2002 the Slavonski Brod Office of the Pension Fund decided of its own motion that her insured status had ended on 30 November 1992 when she wound up her agricultural activity. Ten days later the same office refused her pension claim, holding that her qualifying period was only twelve years and eleven months (January 1980–November 1992) and therefore insufficient. The applicant appealed solely against the status decision, arguing that she had paid the requested contributions. The Central Office dismissed the appeal on 13 May 2002 without addressing the payments. The Administrative Court upheld that decision on 28 September 2006, stating that her departure from the territory where she had been insured meant she had lost status and that any continued activity on occupied territory required validation under the Validation Act; the payments were therefore irrelevant. The Constitutional Court rejected her subsequent complaint on 8 April 2009, finding no interference with property rights.

In January 2012 the applicant lodged a fresh request with the Vukovar Office seeking recognition of the full period 1980–2000, formal validation of 1992–1994 and payment of pension from November 2000. That office refused both requests in March 2012. On 12 December 2012 the Central Office annulled the refusal and recognised the entire period 1 January 1980 to 31 May 2000 as a qualifying period on the strength of the 1998 and 2000 payments. On 21 March 2013 the Vukovar Office granted an old-age pension effective only from 1 August 2011, applying section 32(3) of the Pension Insurance Act and treating the 2012 request as the relevant application date. The applicant thus received no pension between meeting the age and contribution conditions in 2000 and August 2011, and the authorities had initially treated the contributions she had been invited to pay as legally ineffective.

These facts form the core of the alleged deprivation of a pension asset in which the applicant claimed a legitimate expectation.

The applicant, Marija Božić (born 1940), was insured with the Croatian Pension Fund as an agricultural entrepreneur from 1 January 1980 to 30 November 1992 while living in Klokočevik. In November 1992 she moved to Lipovača (then part of the self-proclaimed “Serbian Independent Region of Krajina”) and stopped contributing.

On 6 April 1998 the Slavonski Brod Office accepted her payment of HRK 4,978 covering contributions from 30 November 1992 to 31 December 1994 and issued a certificate confirming registration of the pension-qualifying period from 1 January 1980 to 31 December 1994. On 21 November 2000 it accepted a further payment of HRK 11,663 for 1 January 1995–31 May 2000 and issued a second certificate.

Having reached pensionable age, she applied for an old-age pension on 22 November 2000. On 12 April 2002 the same office, acting of its own motion, declared that she had lost insured status on 30 November 1992 when she wound up her agricultural activities. Ten days later it refused her pension claim, counting only the 12 years and 11 months from January 1980 to November 1992 (insufficient under the then-applicable 15-year requirement). She did not appeal the refusal but challenged the status decision, arguing that she had paid the contributions requested by the Fund itself.

The Central Office dismissed her appeal on 13 May 2002 without addressing the payments. The Administrative Court rejected her subsequent action on 28 September 2006, holding that she had left the territory that formed the basis of her insurance, that any activity on occupied territory would have required validation under the Validation Act, and that the later payments were irrelevant. The Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional complaint on 8 April 2009, finding no interference with the right of property or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the termination of insured status could not violate those rights. That decision was served on 22 April 2009 and formed the basis of her application to the Court, in which she alleged deprivation of her pension.

In January 2012 she lodged fresh administrative proceedings. After initial refusals, the Central Office on 12 December 2012 recognised the entire period 1 January 1980–31 May 2000 as pension-qualifying time on the strength of the earlier payments. On 21 March 2013 the Vukovar Office granted her a pension with effect from 1 August 2011, applying the six-month retroactivity rule in section 32(3) of the Pension Insurance Act to her 2012 request. These later decisions occurred after the application had been lodged.

The case thus centres on the authorities’ initial refusal to treat the post-1992 contributions (which they themselves had calculated and accepted) as creating a pension entitlement, their insistence that she had lost insured status merely by changing residence, and the consequent delay of more than a decade before any pension was awarded.
