**CASE OF ZENKOV v. RUSSIA (Application no. 37858/08), ECtHR (First Section), Judgment of 30 April 2014 (final 30 July 2014)**

The applicant, Andrey Anatolyevich Zenkov (born 1983), a Russian national from Blagoveshchensk, complained under the European Convention on Human Rights that the conditions of his pre-trial detention were incompatible with Convention standards (primarily Article 3), that a period of that detention was unlawful (Article 5), and that his subsequent claim for damages was unsuccessful (related to Articles 5 and/or 13).

On 11 March 2006, Zenkov was arrested on suspicion of fraud. The Blagoveshchensk Town Court authorized his detention the next day, citing charges of moderately serious offences (up to five years’ imprisonment) committed in a group, and risks that he might abscond, fail to appear, obstruct proceedings, pressure witnesses, or destroy evidence. Detention was extended multiple times during investigation and trial. Charges were later reclassified as several counts of theft and robbery. Trial opened on 21 November 2006 against him and seven co-defendants.

On 29 June 2007, the Town Court extended detention of Zenkov and four co-defendants until 21 October 2007, noting charges of grievous and moderately serious property offences and rejecting a less strict measure. On 16 November 2007, it extended detention until 21 January 2008 using identical reasoning. Zenkov appealed, arguing he had been held without a court order from 21 October to 16 November 2007. On 17 December 2007, the Town Court convicted him and imposed a 10-year sentence.

On 21 February 2008, the Amur Regional Court quashed the 16 November 2007 order, acknowledging the review occurred more than three weeks late in breach of criminal procedure rules. It declined to examine the merits or order release because of the intervening conviction. On 31 July 2008, the Regional Court upheld the conviction in substance, reduced the sentence to eight years, quashed one theft count, and remitted it. That count was discontinued on 13 October 2008. Supervisory review on 8 June 2009 further reduced the sentence to seven years and six months. Zenkov was released on parole on 5 February 2010.

Zenkov claimed RUB 150,000 in damages for unlawful detention from 21 October to 17 December 2007. On 29 September 2008, the Town Court dismissed the claim, holding that the period had been offset against his sentence and thus was not unlawful, and that the non-pecuniary claim was unsubstantiated. This was upheld on appeal on 19 November 2008. After supervisory review was granted, the Regional Court Presidium on 19 April 2010 quashed those decisions, recognized the detention as unlawful under the Convention and Russian Civil Code, and awarded RUB 15,000, taking into account the length of the period, its offset against the sentence, and the absence of proven health deterioration.

Zenkov was held in remand prison IZ-28/1 in Blagoveshchensk from 11 March 2006 to 11 March 2008, 19 February–19 March 2009, and 28 May–20 August 2009 (plus short periods in disciplinary cells). Government data showed frequent overcrowding: e.g., a 12 m² cell with 2–4 inmates; a 49.2 m² cell with 22 beds holding 17–31 inmates (well below the statutory 4 m² per person at times); and smaller cells similarly populated. The Government stated he always had an individual bed and bedding, three meals daily, working ventilation, temperatures of 18–24°C, screened toilets at adequate distances, regular cleaning, daily outdoor exercise, and 20–23 hours’ daily cell confinement, with lighting and heating meeting standards.

Zenkov accepted the measurements but claimed he lacked an individual bed, cells were dirty and infested with insects and mice, and inmates with tuberculosis were sometimes held there. A prosecutor’s inspection (following his complaint) on 31 October 2008 confirmed numerous statutory violations: insufficient furnishings (tables, benches, cabinets, sinks), absent or inadequate ventilation and toilet screens, missing radios and wooden floors in many cells, incomplete disinfection, insect infestation (bed bugs, cockroaches), mould, flaking plaster, cracks, humidity, stuffy air, and non-compliant temperatures. Some cells required complete refurbishment.

These facts formed the core of the alleged violations concerning detention conditions, a specific unlawful detention interval, and the adequacy of the later compensation award.

**Case Summary: Taranenko v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 19554/05, Judgment 15 May 2014)**

Yevgeniya Taranenko, a Russian national born in 1981, alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 10 and 11 of the Convention arising from her arrest, pre-trial detention and conviction after events on 14 December 2004 at the President’s Administration building in Moscow.

Media reports and the prosecution case described a group of about 40 National Bolsheviks Party members entering the reception area without authorisation, pushing past guards, occupying an office, locking and barricading the door with a safe, waving “Putin, resign!” placards, throwing leaflets listing alleged constitutional failures by the President and calling for his resignation, and remaining for roughly one hour until police forced entry. The prosecution alleged they damaged furniture, walls and ceiling. The applicant, who denied Party membership, stated she was a sociology master’s student researching radical movements; she claimed she attended only to observe, take notes and photographs, and did not occupy the office or participate in any disorder. Defendants at trial described a planned peaceful protest to deliver a petition; they said guards pushed them into the office, prompting them to lock the door out of fear, after which they chanted slogans and distributed leaflets. They denied causing damage (attributing it to police) or resisting arrest.

The applicant was arrested on 14 December 2004. On 16 December the Khamovnicheskiy District Court ordered her detention, citing suspicion of an especially serious offence and risks of absconding, reoffending or interfering with witnesses. On 22 December she was charged with attempted violent overthrow of the State (Criminal Code Art. 278) and intentional destruction of property (Arts. 167 § 2 and 214). Release requests citing her clean record, Moscow residence and employment as a teacher were refused. Charges were later amended to participation in mass disorder (Art. 212 § 2). Detention was extended by courts on 7 February, 8 April and 30 June 2005 (and subsequent applications rejected) on grounds of the gravity of the charges and continued risks of flight or obstruction, without individualised assessment of her circumstances. The investigation ended on 7 June 2005; she remained in custody through the trial.

On 8 December 2005 the Tverskoy District Court convicted her and co-defendants of mass disorder, finding unauthorised entry, pushing a guard, barricading the office, conducting an unauthorised political meeting that disrupted Administration functions, and damaging property. The court held the action was not peaceful. Taking into account compensation paid for damage (approx. EUR 2,200) and her positive character references, it imposed a three-year sentence suspended for three years’ probation; she was released immediately. The Moscow City Court dismissed her appeal (in which she invoked Article 10) on 29 March 2006.

From 16 December 2004 to 8 December 2005 she was held at remand centre IZ-77/6. She claimed her cell (housing up to 40 inmates) was overcrowded and that she received inadequate treatment for psoriasis, chronic pyelonephritis, bronchitis and allergies. The Government produced records showing cells of 123–132 m² housing 27–32 inmates (or a smaller cell with two inmates for one week), individual bunks, partitioned toilets, ventilation, lighting, daily exercise, weekly showers, regular disinfection, and medical examinations with prescribed treatment.

These facts formed the basis of her complaints of inhuman detention conditions, excessive length of pre-trial detention (approximately one year), and interference with freedom of expression and assembly through prosecution and conviction for a protest against the President’s policies.

The case of Taranenko v. Russia (Application no. 19554/05), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 15 May 2014, concerned allegations by applicant Yevgeniya Vladimirovna Taranenko (a Russian national born in 1981 and living in Moscow) of inhuman detention conditions, excessively long pre-trial detention, and violations of her rights to freedom of expression and assembly arising from her prosecution and conviction for a protest against presidential policies.

On 14 December 2004, around 40 National Bolsheviks Party members occupied the reception area of the President’s Administration building in Moscow. They locked themselves in a ground-floor office, waved “Putin, resign!” placards through the window, distributed leaflets listing ten alleged constitutional failures by the President and calling for his resignation, and chanted slogans. They remained for about 90 minutes until police forced entry; they offered no resistance. The applicant, a sociology master’s student researching radical political movements (not a party member), claimed she attended solely as an observer to take notes and photographs and did not participate in the occupation. Prosecutors alleged unauthorised entry by pushing guards, occupation of the office, blocking the door with a heavy safe, waving placards, throwing leaflets, chanting, destroying furniture/equipment, and damaging walls and ceiling.

The applicant was arrested on 14 December 2004. On 16 December the Khamovnicheskiy District Court ordered her detention on grounds of suspicion of an especially serious offence and risks of absconding, reoffending or interfering with the investigation. She was charged on 22 December with attempted violent overthrow of the State and intentional destruction of property. Her request for release (citing a clean record, Moscow residence and employment as a teacher) was refused. Charges were later amended to participation in mass disorder (Criminal Code Article 212 § 2). Detention was extended on 7 February 2005 until 14 April 2005 and on 8 April 2005 until 14 July 2005, citing charge gravity and flight/interference risks. After the investigation ended on 7 June 2005, 39 defendants including the applicant were committed for trial. At a 30 June 2005 preliminary hearing the Tverskoy District Court refused release, finding sufficient reasons to believe the defendants would flee or interfere despite considering their youth, health, family situations and stable lives. Further release applications in July and August 2005 were rejected on similar grounds (the 30 June order remaining valid for six months).

From 16 December 2004 to 8 December 2005 the applicant was held in Moscow facility IZ-77/6. She alleged overcrowding (a cell holding 40 inmates) and inadequate medical care for psoriasis, chronic pyelonephritis, bronchitis and allergies. The Government submitted that cells were larger and less crowded (e.g., 123.4 m² housing 27–30 inmates), with individual bunks/bedding, partitioned toilets, ventilation, adequate lighting, monthly disinfection, three daily meals, daily walks and weekly showers; medical records showed regular specialist examinations and treatment.

At trial the defendants described a planned peaceful protest to deliver a petition and speak to journalists; they claimed guards pushed them inside, they locked the door out of fear, and police (not they) damaged furniture. Witnesses described the group rushing past security, occupying the office, locking the door and chanting, with some resistance to police. On 8 December 2005 the Tverskoy District Court convicted them of mass disorder, finding unauthorised aggressive entry (bypassing checks, pushing a guard), occupation, door-blocking, an unauthorised meeting that disrupted administration functions, and property damage. The applicant’s claimed academic purpose was irrelevant because she had participated. Accounting for compensation of damage (approximately €2,200) and positive character references, she received a three-year suspended sentence with three years’ probation and was released. Her appeal (claiming the conviction breached Article 10 for peaceful assembly and political expression) was dismissed on 29 March 2006.

The case of Paulet v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 6219/08), decided by the ECtHR on 13 May 2014, concerned an Ivorian national, Didier Pierre Paulet (born 1984, living in Leeds). He alleged that a confiscation order violated his rights, principally under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

Paulet entered the UK illegally on 26 January 2001 and resided in Bedford. Using a false French passport, he obtained three jobs between April 2003 and February 2007 (recruitment agency, cash-and-carry, and forklift driving). Employers later stated they would not have hired him if aware of his immigration status. He earned a gross salary of £73,293.17, paid all taxes and national insurance, and accumulated savings of £21,649.60 (later assessed at £21,949.60).

In January 2007 he applied for a provisional driving licence using the same false passport. This led to his arrest. On 4 June 2007 he pleaded guilty at Luton Crown Court to three counts of dishonestly obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception, possessing a false identity document with intent, driving while disqualified, and driving without insurance. On 29 June 2007 he received concurrent 15-month prison sentences for the first four offences plus a consecutive two-month term for driving while disqualified, together with a deportation recommendation.

The prosecution also sought a confiscation order under section 6 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. The trial judge accepted that the applicant had genuinely performed the work and paid all taxes, calculating his “benefit” (after tax/NI) at £50,000. Because only £21,949.60 remained available, a confiscation order for that exact sum was imposed, with 12 months’ imprisonment in default. The order stripped him of all savings accumulated over nearly four years of employment.

Paulet appealed, first arguing that the earnings were not a “benefit” from criminal conduct and later that the prosecutor’s decision to seek confiscation was an abuse of process because it produced a disproportionate and oppressive result incompatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. After an adjournment pending DPP guidance, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 28 July 2009. Relying on R v Carter [2006] EWCA Crim 416, it held that the false representation was a continuing and operative cause of the employment and therefore of the wages. A wider public interest existed in preventing illegal working. The court emphasised that it had no discretion to refuse a confiscation order that complied with the statute merely because the result appeared harsh; abuse of process was confined to true oppression and could not be used to rewrite the legislative scheme.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused. Enforcement proceedings followed. Separate asylum and deportation challenges failed on procedural grounds.

Domestic law (POCA 2002, ss. 6–9 and 76) treats as “benefit” any property or pecuniary advantage obtained as a result of or in connection with particular criminal conduct. Subsequent Supreme Court authority (R v Waya [2012] UKSC 51) later required courts to refuse confiscation orders that would be disproportionate under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but that development post-dated the decisions in Paulet’s case. The core factual issue before the Strasbourg Court was therefore whether the total confiscation of legitimately earned (and taxed) savings, obtained solely through the deception that secured the jobs, constituted a disproportionate interference with the applicant’s possessions.

The case of Paulet v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 6219/08) arose from a confiscation order imposed on an Ivorian national, Didier Pierre Paulet, following his conviction for immigration-related deception offences. Paulet entered the UK illegally in January 2001. Using a false French passport, he obtained three successive jobs between April 2003 and February 2007, earning a gross salary of £73,293.17. He paid all due taxes and national insurance; his remaining savings stood at £21,649.60. His employers later confirmed they would not have hired him had they known his true immigration status.

In January 2007 the same false passport was used to apply for a provisional driving licence, leading to his arrest. He pleaded guilty to three counts of dishonestly obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception, possessing a false identity document with intent, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance. He received concurrent 15-month prison terms for the first four offences plus a consecutive two-month term for driving while disqualified, together with a recommendation for deportation.

The prosecution then sought a confiscation order under section 6 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. The trial judge accepted that the wages had been genuinely earned and that tax and national insurance had been paid. After those deductions the “benefit” was assessed at £50,000. Because Paulet’s remaining realisable assets totalled only £21,949.60, a confiscation order was made in that exact sum, with 12 months’ imprisonment in default. The order therefore stripped him of all savings accumulated over four years of work.

Paulet appealed, arguing that the order was disproportionate and violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). He contended that the earnings were not “benefit” obtained “as a result of or in connection with” the offences and that seeking confiscation of the entire savings amounted to an abuse of process. After the Court of Appeal granted leave, counsel accepted (in light of R v Carter) that the wages constituted relevant benefit, but maintained that the resulting figure was oppressive because it far exceeded the gravity of the deception and pursued none of the legitimate aims of the confiscation regime.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in July 2009. It held that a court has no residual discretion to refuse a confiscation order once the statutory conditions are met; any complaint of oppression must be confined to true abuse of process, which was absent. The false representation had been a continuing operative cause of the employment and therefore of the wages. A wider public interest existed in preventing illegal working. The court distinguished hypothetical situations in which the deception had become remote or the employment would have continued even after the truth was known.

Paulet also claimed asylum on the basis of ethnic persecution in Côte d’Ivoire; the claim was refused, a deportation order was made, and subsequent judicial-review and appeal applications were rejected as out of time.

The alleged Convention violation therefore centred on whether the confiscation of legitimately earned (but deceptively obtained) wages constituted a disproportionate interference with property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Domestic authorities treated the order as a straightforward application of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and existing case-law, while Paulet argued that the measure went beyond what was necessary to deprive him of the proceeds of crime and thereby failed the proportionality test.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Paulet v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 6219/08) arose from an application by Ivorian national Didier Pierre Paulet, who challenged a confiscation order imposed after his conviction for immigration-related deception offences. The core alleged violation concerned the order’s compatibility with the Convention, in particular Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), on the grounds that it was disproportionate, oppressive and an abuse of process.

The money was accepted as having been “truly earned” through actual labour.

The deception came to light when he submitted the same false passport with a driving-licence application. On 4 June 2007 he pleaded guilty to three counts of obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception, possession of a false identity document with intent, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance. He received a 17-month custodial sentence and a recommendation for deportation.

The prosecution then sought a confiscation order under section 6 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. The Crown Court treated the entire post-tax earnings (£50,000) as “benefit” obtained through the continuing deception that enabled him to work. Because his realisable assets were only £21,949.60, an order in that sum was made, with 12 months’ imprisonment in default. The order stripped him of every pound he had saved.

Paulet appealed, first arguing that the wages were not “benefit” within the statutory meaning and later that the decision to seek confiscation was an abuse of process. He contended that Parliament intended the 2002 Act to be applied compatibly with the Convention; a confiscation figure far exceeding any identifiable criminal gain was therefore disproportionate and oppressive. After the Court of Appeal adjourned the case pending DPP guidance, it dismissed the appeal on 28 July 2009. Following its earlier decision in R v Carter, the court held that the false representation remained an operative cause of the employment throughout. A wider public interest existed in preventing illegal work. Once the statutory conditions were met, the court had no residual discretion to refuse an order merely because the outcome appeared harsh. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

Parallel asylum and deportation proceedings (claim based on ethnic risk in Côte d’Ivoire) failed on credibility and timing grounds and are not central to the property complaint.

The facts therefore centre on whether the complete confiscation of savings generated by genuine labour, obtained only because of an immigration deception, constituted a disproportionate interference with property rights under the Convention.
001-144109:
The case of László Magyar v. Hungary originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a Hungarian national born in 1966, who remains detained at Szeged Prison. He alleged that his irreducible whole-life sentence and prison conditions violated Article 3 of the Convention, while the length of his criminal trial and the impartiality of the convicting court breached Article 6 § 1.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant and nine accomplices commenced in 2002. The investigation, generating a 25-box case file, established that the group had carried out a series of burglaries targeting isolated elderly people in various villages. Victims were tied up, beaten or threatened until they revealed the location of valuables, then left bound and alone; some died shortly afterwards. The applicant was repeatedly interrogated as a suspect.

A 48-page bill of indictment dated 26 June 2003 charged ten defendants. The applicant faced three counts of homicide, 19 of robbery, 19 of infringement of personal liberty, four of assault causing grievous bodily harm, seven of trespass and three of theft or attempted theft. Seventy-two witnesses and two forensic experts were proposed.

The Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok County Regional Court held 34 hearings from 4 February 2004. On 12 May 2005 it convicted the applicant, in a 135-page judgment, of murder, robbery and other offences and, as a multiple recidivist, imposed life imprisonment without eligibility for parole (tényleges életfogytiglan).

The Debrecen Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 25 January 2006 after a preparatory meeting and hearing, remitting the case. An amended indictment was filed on 31 August 2006. Twenty-seven further hearings took place between 25 October 2006 and 19 November 2008. Extensive expert evidence (forensic medical and graphological) was obtained concerning a co-defendant’s claimed alibi involving knee surgery performed under a false name; the issue was irrelevant to the applicant.

On 19 November 2008 the Regional Court again convicted the applicant in a 161-page judgment covering 33 incidents and reimposed the irreducible life sentence. The applicant observed that the trial judge had previously been a trainee of the judge who had sat in the first set of proceedings.

On appeal the Debrecen Court of Appeal held four hearings in 2009. Its 16 December 2009 judgment re-characterised certain offences but confirmed the whole-life term. A co-defendant who had shown remorse and assisted the court received a sentence permitting parole. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 28 September 2010.

The applicant’s cell at Szeged Prison measures five by two metres, is occupied by a second inmate, and has a toilet adjacent to the bed and table.

Under the Criminal Code then in force, a court imposing life imprisonment could either fix a minimum term before parole eligibility (at least 20 or 30 years) or exclude parole altogether. Presidential pardon, requiring ministerial countersignature, remained theoretically available, but no clemency had ever been granted to a prisoner serving a whole-life term since the exclusion of parole became possible in 1999.

These facts underpin the complaints of an irreducible life sentence lacking any realistic prospect of release, allegedly degrading detention conditions, proceedings lasting approximately eight years from investigation to final confirmation, and a perceived lack of judicial impartiality arising from the professional relationship between the two Regional Court judges.

The case of László Magyar v. Hungary (Application no. 73593/10) concerns a Hungarian national born in 1966, detained at Szeged Prison, who alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman or degrading treatment) due to his irreducible whole-life sentence and poor prison conditions, as well as Article 6 § 1 (fair trial) due to excessive length of proceedings and lack of impartiality in the convicting court.

The 48-page indictment of 26 June 2003 charged the applicant with three homicides, 19 robberies, 19 infringements of personal liberty, four grievous bodily harm assaults, seven trespasses, and three thefts or attempts.

The first trial at the Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok County Regional Court comprised 34 hearings from 4 February 2004. On 12 May 2005, in a 135-page judgment, the court convicted the applicant (a multiple recidivist) of murder, robbery and related offences, imposing life imprisonment without parole eligibility (“tényleges életfogytiglan”).

Presidential pardon existed, requiring a government member’s countersignature, with requests routed via the trial court and justice minister. However, no whole-life prisoner had received clemency since non-parole life terms were introduced in 1999.

These facts framed the Article 3 claims of an irreducible sentence lacking realistic release prospects and of degrading detention, plus Article 6 claims of an eight-year process (investigation to final judgment) and judicial bias from the second-instance judge’s prior professional link.

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined László Magyar v. Hungary (application no. 73593/10), lodged on 9 December 2010 by a Hungarian national born in 1966 and detained at Szeged Prison. The applicant, represented with legal aid, alleged violations of Article 3 (life sentence without parole eligibility and degrading detention conditions) and Article 6 § 1 (excessive trial length and lack of impartiality of the convicting Regional Court). The applicant faced three homicide counts, 19 robberies, 19 personal-liberty infringements, four grievous-bodily-harm assaults, seven trespasses and three thefts/attempts.

The Debrecen Court of Appeal, after a preparatory meeting and hearing, quashed the judgment on 25 January 2006 and remitted the case.

001-144107:
The case of Binişan v. Romania (Application no. 39438/05) originated in an application lodged on 24 October 2005 by Romanian national Dan-Liviu Binişan (born 1974). He alleged that staff negligence at the State-owned National Railway Company (CFR) put his life at risk, causing a severe accident, and that authorities failed to investigate effectively or punish those responsible, in violation of the State's positive obligations under the Convention (primarily Article 2).

On 20 September 2002, a private exporter (company E) used five CFR wagons at Lugoj station for export operations, including customs inspection, under a contract with CFR's Lugoj Merchandise Subsidiary and another firm. Around 1 p.m., the applicant, a designated customs inspector, arrived with company E's manager and associate S.V. After payment of transport taxes and stamping of the CIM consignment note, CFR employee M.M. accompanied them to the wagons, reportedly on electrified track no. 7 (instead of the designated non-electrified industrial track no. 20). While applying seals atop a wagon at 1.19 p.m., the applicant was electrocuted. He suffered burns over 70% of his body, required 138 days of care (including two months in a coma in Hungary, multiple skin grafts, and treatment for breathing difficulties), and was later classified as permanently disabled. Official reports confirmed his life had been at risk.

A special commission (from labour inspectorate, customs, and CFR) investigated from 24 September, reporting on 16 October that the accident stemmed from improper inspection organisation, non-compliance with a 24 June 2002 framework agreement, and health/safety lapses. It blamed company E's manager (for poor organisation), the applicant (for rule breaches), his superior (for inadequate training), and company E. Customs authorities objected, noting M.M. had assured the applicant of safety, that he had received training on 3 June 2002, and that CFR violated Order no. 26/2000 (prohibiting work on wagon roofs on electrified tracks).

The commission fined company E and its manager, but Lugoj District Court cancelled both in September 2003, attributing liability to CFR for leaving wagons on high-voltage tracks without warning, failing to shunt them as required, and breaching transit rules obliging it to ensure safe inspections. Courts noted M.M. had assured safety and that the manager could not have known of electrification.

Criminal proceedings against company E's manager, requested by the labour inspectorate, ended with prosecutors declining to investigate (24 April 2003, upheld 31 July), citing the applicant's sole fault (ignoring a warning sign and agreement). The applicant complained of unresolved contradictions (e.g., M.M.'s presence, absent from some colleague statements; a warning sign appearing only in later photos). Further reviews, including by Lugoj District Court (21 January 2005), upheld this, finding no CFR employee liability despite noting inspections should have occurred at track no. 20.

Separately, the applicant complained that CFR's manager forged a backdated "Declarație" (signed post-accident but dated 16 September) to shift liability by requiring inspections only at track no. 20. After initial refusals, the manager was indicted and convicted (25 January 2006, upheld on appeal) of abuse of office, forgery, and using forged documents to protect CFR.

The applicant sought review of the 21 January 2005 decision citing this conviction and new witnesses, but it was dismissed as inadmissible/unfounded. In civil proceedings (18 October 2005) against CFR and M.M. for damages, Lugoj District Court (20 June 2006) rejected res judicata, found shared fault (CFR/M.M. negligent in duties like shunting and documentation), and awarded half the claimed sums. Higher courts (2008–2009) reversed this, applying res judicata from the criminal findings of the applicant's sole responsibility.

These facts highlight alleged State failures in preventing electrocution risks via CFR staff and in conducting a thorough, impartial probe that addressed contradictions, the forged document's role, and CFR's organisational duties.

The case of Binişan v. Romania (Application no. 39438/05) originated from an application lodged on 24 October 2005 by Romanian national Dan-Liviu Binişan, born in 1974 and residing in Lugoj. The applicant alleged that negligence by staff of the State-owned National Railway Company (CFR) had put his life at risk, resulting in a severe electrocution accident, and that State authorities had failed to investigate the incident effectively or punish those responsible. These complaints engaged the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 2 of the Convention (right to life).

On 20 September 2002 a private exporter (company E) used five wagons supplied by the National Railway Company’s Lugoj subsidiary under a contract for customs inspection prior to export. At approximately 1 p.m. the applicant, designated as customs inspector, accompanied company E’s manager and employee S.V. to the station. An employee of the railway company, M.M., reportedly escorted them to the wagons. While the applicant was on top of a wagon applying seals at 1.19 p.m., he was electrocuted. He required 138 days of medical care, suffered burns over 70 percent of his body, spent nearly two months in a coma in Hungary, underwent multiple skin grafts, and was later classified as permanently disabled.

A special commission of labour, customs and railway experts investigated from 24 September 2002 and reported on 16 October 2002 that the accident resulted from improper organisation of the inspection. It identified concurrent causes, including failure to receive the wagons in accordance with a 24 June 2002 framework agreement (requiring use of non-electrified industrial track no. 20) and non-observance of health-and-safety rules. The commission attributed responsibility to company E’s manager, the applicant, his superior and company E. Customs authorities objected, noting that M.M. had assured the applicant there was no danger and that the applicant had received training; they argued the railway company had breached Order no. 26 of 11 January 2000, which prohibits work on wagon roofs on electrified tracks.

Administrative fines imposed on company E and its manager were later quashed by the Lugoj District Court. The court held the railway company grossly negligent for leaving the wagons on high-voltage tracks without moving them to the unelectrified industrial line or informing those involved, thereby failing its obligation under transit rules to ensure safe inspection conditions.

Criminal proceedings against company E’s manager were discontinued by prosecutors in April 2003 on the ground of the applicant’s sole fault. The applicant’s complaints were rejected; prosecutors and courts found he had ignored a warning sign and the framework agreement. Courts refused to hear further witnesses or reconstruct the scene, dismissed evidence that the warning sign was added after the accident, and concluded M.M. had not accompanied the party. A request to reopen the decision after the railway manager was convicted in 2006 of back-dating a “Declarație” document (signed after the accident to shift inspections to track 20) was declared inadmissible.

The applicant’s 2005 civil action against the railway company and M.M. succeeded in part at first instance (shared liability and half damages awarded), but was dismissed on appeal in 2008–2009 on res judicata grounds stemming from the earlier criminal finding of the applicant’s exclusive fault.

Relevant domestic rules (Order no. 26) mandated communication of safety regulations and prohibited roof-level work on electrified tracks; railway companies acting as principals under CIM/T1 transit procedures were required to ensure safe inspection conditions. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that State agents had failed to protect his life and that the subsequent investigation had been ineffective.

The case of Binişan v. Romania (application no. 39438/05) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 October 2005 by Dan-Liviu Binişan, a Romanian national born in 1974 and resident in Lugoj. The applicant alleged that staff negligence at the state-owned National Railway Company had put his life at risk, causing a severe accident, and that the authorities had failed to investigate it effectively or punish those responsible.

On 20 September 2002 a private exporter (company E) arranged, under contract with the Lugoj subsidiary of the National Railway Company and another firm, to use railway wagons for customs inspection prior to export. The applicant, a customs inspector, attended the station that afternoon with company E’s manager and an associate (S.V.). After documentation was stamped at the cash desk, an employee of the railway company (M.M.) allegedly accompanied them to the wagons. At 1.19 p.m., while standing on top of a wagon to apply seals, the applicant was electrocuted. He suffered burns over 70 per cent of his body, required 138 days of medical care (including two months in a coma in Hungary and multiple skin grafts), experienced severe respiratory problems and was later classified as permanently disabled.

A police on-site report was prepared the same day. A special commission comprising experts from the labour inspectorate, regional customs department and the railway company itself investigated from 24 September and reported on 16 October 2002. It identified multiple concurrent causes, including failure to transfer the wagons to a non-electrified industrial track as required by a framework agreement, non-observance of health-and-safety rules (Order no. 26 of 11 January 2000, which prohibits work on the upper parts of wagons on live tracks), and inadequate training. The commission attributed responsibility to company E’s manager, the applicant himself, his superior and the company. The customs department objected, stressing that M.M. had assured the applicant there was no danger, that he had received training and that the railway company had breached the safety order.

Administrative fines imposed on company E and its manager were later cancelled by the Lugoj District Court. The court held the railway company solely liable for leaving the wagons on electrified tracks without warning those involved, thereby failing in its statutory duty to ensure safe conditions for customs inspection. A criminal investigation requested against company E’s manager was closed by prosecutors in April 2003 on the ground that the accident was the applicant’s own fault; his complaints seeking further inquiries (including witness confrontations, reconstruction and examination of contradictory statements about M.M.’s presence and a warning sign allegedly added after the event) were rejected. The Lugoj District Court ultimately upheld the decision not to prosecute, finding no railway-employee responsibility and blaming the applicant for ignoring a warning sign and the framework agreement.

Separately, the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against the railway-company manager for forging and back-dating a document (“Declarație”) after the accident in order to shift liability. The manager was convicted in January 2006 of abuse of office, forgery and use of forged documents; the conviction became final. An application for judicial review of the earlier non-prosecution decision, relying on this conviction as new evidence, was dismissed.

In civil proceedings begun in October 2005 the applicant sought damages from the railway company and M.M. The first-instance court found shared responsibility and awarded partial compensation, but the appellate courts reversed the judgment on res-judicata grounds, holding that the criminal court’s factual findings bound the civil courts. The applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed in January 2009.

These events form the factual basis of the applicant’s complaints that a state-owned entity had negligently exposed him to a life-threatening risk and that the subsequent investigations had been incomplete, contradictory and ineffective.
001-144351:
The applicant, a Turkmen-Russian national and former deputy chair of Turkmenistan’s Central Bank (1992–1998), moved to Bulgaria in 2001 amid political opposition activities. He obtained permanent residence, co-founded a human-rights organisation, and was granted humanitarian status in 2004 after family members faced persecution in Turkmenistan.

In October 2002 Turkmen authorities charged him with embezzling USD 40 million via SWIFT transfers between July and September 2002—a period when he no longer worked at the bank and already resided in Bulgaria—and requested extradition. After brief police and prosecutorial detention he was released on bail. On 22 May 2003 the Varna Regional Court refused extradition under the 1975 Bulgaria–USSR Legal Aid Treaty, holding that he could not have committed the offence, that the request was politically motivated, and that extradition would risk a breach of Article 3 of the Convention. The decision became final.

Bulgarian prosecutors then charged him with money-laundering based on the identical alleged facts; those proceedings were terminated in 2004 because no crime had been committed.

In February 2006 Interpol issued a red notice repeating the same 2002 charges and arrest warrant. On 19 February 2007 the applicant was arrested in Bulgaria. A prosecutor ordered provisional detention under Article 65 of the 1975 Treaty (and the 2005 Extradition Act) citing a risk of flight. The Varna Regional Court extended detention for 40 days, treating the Interpol warrant and the seriousness of the charge as sufficient and stating it was not bound by the 2003 refusal. Appeals were dismissed on similar grounds, the courts declining to examine whether the charges were identical or whether extradition was even possible.

An official extradition request received on 9 March 2007 contained no new evidence. Detention was further extended for the duration of the proceedings; courts again treated it as mandatory and ignored the earlier refusal. On 12 April 2007 the Varna Regional Court refused extradition a second time, finding the request identical, the 2003 judgment binding, the alleged conduct not a crime under Bulgarian law, and extradition barred by the applicant’s humanitarian status and Article 3 risks. The Court of Appeal upheld the refusal. The applicant was released the same day after 52 days in custody.

The applicant complained that this second period of detention was unlawful and arbitrary: it rested on an already-rejected identical request, followed a domestic finding that no crime had occurred, and was ordered without any assessment—required by the Treaty—of whether extradition could lawfully proceed.

**Case Summary: Khadzhiev v. Bulgaria (ECHR, Application no. 44330/07, Judgment 3 June 2014)**

The applicant, Annadurdy Karlievich Khadzhiev (Turkmen/Russian national), served as deputy chair of Turkmenistan’s Central Bank from 1992–1998. After criticizing the Turkmen regime as a member of the “Watan” movement, he moved to Bulgaria in October 2001 with his family, obtained permanent residency, and co-founded the Turkmen Helsinki Foundation. He received humanitarian status in March 2004 (later upgraded to refugee status in 2007) due to political persecution risks, including the 2006 murder of his sister in a Turkmen prison.

In October 2002, Turkmen authorities charged him with embezzling USD 40 million (via SWIFT transfers, July–September 2002) plus document forgery, issuing an arrest warrant. They requested extradition under the 1975 Bulgaria-USSR Legal Aid Treaty (applicable to Turkmenistan). Bulgarian authorities detained him briefly in December 2002 (police custody then 72-hour prosecutor’s order, extended 30 days then lifted on bail). In May 2003, the Varna Regional Court refused extradition: the applicant was already in Bulgaria (not employed at the bank) during the alleged period, making the acts impossible; charges were politically motivated; and extradition risked Article 3 ECHR violations. This became final.

Related Bulgarian money-laundering charges (same facts, transfers to Dubai) were discontinued in 2004 (prosecutor: insufficient evidence of predicate crime) and terminated by the court (no crime committed, politically motivated accusations, relying on the extradition refusal).

In February 2006, Interpol issued a red notice on the identical 2002 charges/warrant. On 19 February 2007, Bulgarian police detained the applicant for 24 hours; a prosecutor then ordered provisional detention under the 1975 Treaty (citing exigency, flight risk, and the 2002 warrant), referencing the 2005 Extradition Act. He was detained that day. On 22 February, the Varna Regional Court extended it 40 days (seriousness of charges, 2002 warrant, flight/reoffending risk; court not bound by 2003 refusal; no evidence of political persecution). Appeals were dismissed (27 February: Interpol notice sufficed; 21 March: no new facts justifying release). After the official extradition request (identical charges, no new evidence) arrived 9 March, the court on 30 March extended detention for the proceedings’ duration (same risk factors). The Court of Appeal upheld this on 3 April, treating detention as mandatory and rejecting identity arguments.

No authority examined extradition’s possibility, as required by Article 65 of the 1975 Treaty (immediate arrest except where extradition cannot occur). The applicant was released 12 April 2007 after the Varna Regional Court refused extradition (alleged conduct not a crime under Bulgarian law per prior findings/Article 61(г) Treaty; Article 3 risks given humanitarian status and unchanged Turkmen conditions; 2005 Act obstacles). The Court of Appeal upheld this 3 May, noting the identical request and binding 2003 judgment, precluding re-examination.

The applicant alleged the second detention (19 February–12 April 2007) was unlawful and arbitrary under Article 5 ECHR, given the identical prior request, terminated domestic proceedings finding no crime, humanitarian/refugee status, and failure to assess extradition feasibility. (He also described poor detention conditions but the communicated complaint focused on lawfulness/arbitrariness.) Separate 1988 Act damages claims for the first detention failed, with courts citing Treaty obligations.

The case of Khadzhiev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 44330/07) concerns a complaint by Annadurdy Karlievich Khadzhiev, a dual Turkmen-Russian national, that his second period of detention in Bulgaria pending extradition to Turkmenistan was unlawful and arbitrary.

The applicant served as deputy chair of Turkmenistan’s Central Bank from 1992 to 1998. In 2000 he joined the opposition movement “Watan.” He moved to Bulgaria in October 2001, obtained permanent residency, established a construction business, and co-founded the Turkmen Helsinki Foundation. Family members remaining in Turkmenistan faced persecution; his sister was tortured and murdered in prison in 2006. Bulgaria granted him humanitarian status in March 2004 and refugee status in September 2007.

Turkmen authorities charged him in October 2002 (supplemented February 2003) with aggravated embezzlement of USD 40 million allegedly transferred via SWIFT between 25 July and 3 September 2002 while acting as a bank official, plus document forgery. An arrest warrant was issued. Because he already lived in Bulgaria, Turkmenistan requested extradition under the 1975 Bulgaria-USSR Legal Aid Treaty.

He was detained briefly in December 2002 (police order later quashed, then 72-hour prosecutor’s detention under the Treaty, extended 30 days but lifted on bail). On 22 May 2003 the Varna Regional Court refused extradition with final effect. It found that during the alleged period the applicant no longer worked at the bank, could not have used SWIFT, and that the request was politically motivated, aimed at persecution for his beliefs, and would risk an Article 3 violation.

Related Bulgarian money-laundering charges based on the identical facts were terminated in 2004 because no crime had been committed.

In February 2006 Interpol issued a red notice repeating the 2002 charges and warrant. On 19 February 2007 Bulgarian police detained the applicant for 24 hours; a prosecutor then ordered provisional detention under the 1975 Treaty citing exigency, flight risk and the 2002 warrant. The Varna Regional Court (22 February 2007) and Court of Appeal (27 February 2007) confirmed 40-day detention, treating the Interpol notice and charge seriousness as sufficient and holding they were not bound by the 2003 refusal. After the identical extradition request arrived on 9 March 2007, detention was extended for the proceedings (30 March and 3 April 2007). Neither prosecutors nor courts examined whether extradition remained possible, as required by Article 65 of the Treaty. The Varna Regional Court refused extradition on 12 April 2007 (upheld 3 May 2007), citing the 2003 judgment as binding, identity of the requests, absence of a dual-criminality offence, the applicant’s humanitarian status and continuing Article 3 risk. He was released the same day after roughly seven weeks in detention.

The applicant maintained that this second detention, based on an unchanged and previously rejected politically motivated request, lacked any lawful basis or genuine extradition purpose and was therefore arbitrary.
001-144115:
The case of McDonald v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 4241/12) originated from an application lodged on 5 January 2012 by Elaine McDonald, a British national born in 1943 and resident in London. It concerned her complaints of a failure by the local authority (Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea) to meet her assessed night-time care needs, amounting to an unlawful interference with her right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention, as well as related claims under domestic disability discrimination law. These arose from the substitution of incontinence pads for personal night-time assistance, which she regarded as an affront to her dignity.

McDonald suffered an incapacitating stroke in 1999, leaving her with severely limited mobility. Further falls in 2006 (including a multi-place hip fracture) and thereafter required additional hospitalisation. She has a small neurogenic bladder, typically needing to urinate two to three times nightly, but cannot safely access a toilet or commode unaided.

In March 2007 she applied to the Independent Living Fund for full day-and-night support. Pending a decision, the local authority provided a care package including 70 hours of weekly night-time care. The Fund application later failed when she turned 65 in 2008. Early assessments (April 2007 care plan; January 2008 FACE Overview) identified a substantial need for night-time toileting assistance. Subsequent assessments (February and October 2008) similarly recorded a substantial need for help to use a commode at night, the latter later characterised as a temporary concession.

On 17 October 2008 the authority decided to reduce weekly care funding from £703 to £450, on the basis that incontinence pads would suffice in place of a night carer. This was confirmed by letter of 21 November 2008, citing the need to meet eligible needs under Fair Access to Care Services criteria while having regard to public resources. McDonald, who refused pads as undignified, sought judicial review on 22 December 2008, alleging unreasonable failure to meet assessed needs and an Article 8 interference causing her to “lose all sense of dignity” and suffer distress. A holding compromise thereafter provided night care five nights weekly (November–December 2008) then four nights (until September 2011), with her partner assisting otherwise; all night care ended in September 2011.

The High Court refused permission in March 2009, treating the assessed need as safety (meetable by pads or a carer) and Article 8 claims as parasitic. Later Care Plan Reviews (November 2009 and April 2010) maintained that pads or absorbent sheets were a practical, safe solution offering privacy and independence, while noting McDonald’s refusal and her view of them as an affront; extra-care sheltered housing was offered but declined. The Court of Appeal (October 2010) held that, until the 2009 review, the assessed need had been commode assistance, so a statutory duty had been breached (mitigated by the partner’s help and later reassessment), but found no Article 8 violation (the error arising from resource-balancing, not disrespect) and no Disability Discrimination Act 1995 breach. The Supreme Court (majority) agreed that needs had been validly reassessed from November 2009, that there was thereafter no Article 8 interference (or any interference was justified under Article 8(2) by economic well-being, the interests of other service-users, safety, privacy, independence and cost savings of some £22,270 yearly), and that consultations had respected dignity and autonomy (including choices as to hours, direct payments and housing). Lady Hale dissented, viewing the needs as irrationally confused.

Domestic law (National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990, s. 47; Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970, s. 2) required needs assessment and, where eligible, provision of practical home assistance, with resources relevant both to assessment and to the manner of meeting needs (R v Gloucestershire CC ex p Barry). FACS Guidance required broadly similar outcomes and periodic reviews. International instruments (UNCRPD Arts. 3, 17, 19; EU Charter Art. 1) emphasise dignity, autonomy, physical integrity and community living with support.

These facts centre on the tension between McDonald’s assessed need for assisted night-time toileting, her dignity-based objection to pads, the authority’s resource-driven alternative, and the resulting Article 8 claim.

The case of McDonald v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 4241/12) concerned alleged violations of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private life) arising from a local authority's decision to reduce night-time care for a disabled woman, substituting incontinence pads for personal assistance with toileting. The applicant, Elaine McDonald, a British national born in 1943 and resident in London, suffered an incapacitating stroke in 1999 that left her with severely limited mobility. In 2006 she experienced multiple falls, including one that fractured her hip in several places, leading to further hospitalisations. She has a small neurogenic bladder requiring urination two to three times nightly but cannot safely reach a toilet or commode unaided due to her mobility impairments.

In March 2007, following her third fall, she applied to the Independent Living Fund for comprehensive day-and-night support. While that application (ultimately unsuccessful after she turned 65) was pending, the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea provided a care package including 70 hours of weekly night-time care. Contemporary assessments (April 2007 care plan; January and February 2008 FACE overviews; October 2008 needs assessment) recorded a “substantial need” for assistance with night-time toileting or commode use. The applicant explicitly rejected incontinence pads, viewing them as an affront to her dignity.

On 17 October 2008 the authority decided to reduce weekly care funding from £703 to £450, intending to meet her needs via pads rather than a night carer. The decision, notified on 21 November 2008, cited the need to respect public resources and the authority’s Fair Access to Care Services criteria. The applicant sought judicial review, arguing the reduction failed to meet her assessed eligible needs and would cause indignity amounting to an Article 8 interference. A “holding compromise” continued limited night care (five then four nights weekly) until September 2011, when all night-time care ceased; her partner assisted on other nights.

Domestic courts reached mixed conclusions. The High Court (March 2009) refused permission, recategorising her need as safety from falls (meetable by pads or a carer) and treating Article 8 as parasitic. Subsequent 2009–2010 care-plan reviews reaffirmed pads as a practical, safety-enhancing solution offering privacy and independence, while noting the applicant’s refusal and exploring (and rejecting) extra-care housing. The Court of Appeal (October 2010) held that, between November 2008 and November 2009, the assessed need remained commode assistance, so the authority breached its statutory duty under the National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990 and Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970; the breach was, however, mitigated and later superseded by lawful reassessment. No Article 8 violation or Disability Discrimination Act 1995 breach was found, the error stemming from resource-balancing rather than disrespect for dignity. The Supreme Court (majority) agreed that needs were validly reassessed from November 2009, that any Article 8 interference thereafter was justified under Article 8(2) by economic well-being, other service-users’ interests, injury prevention, privacy, independence and cost savings, and that extensive consultation respected the applicant’s autonomy. Lady Hale dissented, finding it irrational to treat the distinct needs of toileting assistance and continence protection as interchangeable.

These facts framed the Strasbourg complaint that the reduction, particularly the initial period of unlawfulness and the subsequent imposition of pads, unjustifiably interfered with the applicant’s physical and psychological integrity, dignity and independent living.

The ECtHR case *McDonald v. the United Kingdom* (no. 4241/12) concerned an alleged Article 8 violation arising from a local authority's decision to reduce the applicant's night-time care.

Ms Elaine McDonald (born 1943) suffered a 1999 stroke causing severe mobility limits. 2006 falls produced hip fractures. A neurogenic bladder required 2–3 nightly urinations, but she could not safely reach a toilet or commode unaided.

Kensington and Chelsea initially supplied 70 hours of weekly night care. 2007–2008 assessments recorded a “substantial need” for night-time toileting help.

In October 2008 funding fell from £703 to £450 weekly, substituting incontinence pads for a carer on grounds of excess provision and scarce public resources. The applicant was notified in November 2008 and sought judicial review, arguing the change failed to meet her assessed needs and breached Article 8 by inflicting indignity (pads would cause her to “lose all sense of dignity”).

The High Court refused permission, holding her true need was safety (meetable economically by pads) and that the statute allowed flexibility; Article 8 claims were parasitic.

2009–2010 reviews reaffirmed pads as practical for safety, privacy and independence; she refused them and extra-care housing.

The Court of Appeal found a statutory breach from November 2008 to November 2009 because the assessed need (commode assistance) was unmet (though mitigated by her partner). After the 2009 reassessment there was no ongoing breach. Article 8 was not violated: the error reflected resource-balancing, not disrespect. The Disability Discrimination Act was likewise satisfied.

The Supreme Court majority confirmed the 2009 reassessment and found no subsequent Article 8 interference. Extensive consultation had respected dignity, autonomy, safety and other users. Any interference would have been justified under Article 8(2) as necessary for economic well-being and proportionate (greater safety, privacy, independence and cost savings). Lady Hale dissented, calling it irrational to treat a need for toilet assistance as equivalent to incontinence management.

Domestic law (NHS and Community Care Act 1990 s. 47 and Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970) requires a needs assessment that may take resources into account; eligible needs (per FACS bands) must then be met. International instruments (UNCRPD Arts. 3, 17, 19; EU Charter Art. 1) emphasise dignity, autonomy and community living.

The facts therefore pit the applicant’s claim to dignity in intimate personal care against the authority’s duty to allocate limited funds across all service users.

The case of Velyo Velev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 16032/07) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 March 2007 by Bulgarian national Velyo Nikolaev Velev (born 1977). He alleged a breach of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 due to denial of education access while detained in Stara Zagora Prison, and a breach of Article 6 § 2 because he was treated as a “recidivist” before any final conviction in pending proceedings.

Velev was convicted of fraud in 2003 and served a prison sentence in Stara Zagora Prison from 11 February 2003 to 9 August 2004. Arrested on 1 October 2004 for unlawful firearms possession, he was held on remand in the same prison from 29 November 2004 until 20 April 2007 (initially with prisoners classified as recidivists). Having not completed secondary education, he sought enrolment in the prison school.

In August 2005 he requested enrolment for the 2005/06 school year from the prison governor, receiving no reply before term began on 15 September. Further requests followed on 29 September to the governor, Ministry of Education and Prosecutor’s Office. The Prosecutor replied on 6 October that the administration had considered his study request in light of his prior sentence and that denial of access was unconfirmed. The Ministry of Education stated on 24 October that persons deprived of liberty could continue education in prison, without distinguishing remand prisoners.

Velev submitted further requests in October 2005. On 7 December the Head of the Execution of Punishments Directorate rejected enrolment, noting that Velev was unconvicted and, once convicted, would be transferred to a recidivists’ prison. Including recidivists in programmes at a non-recidivist prison would violate separation rules for inmate categories.

Velev appealed on 21 December 2005, arguing that without a second imprisonment sentence he could not be treated as a recidivist. He invoked Article 53 of the Bulgarian Constitution, Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Rule 77), the Execution of Punishments Act 1969 (which he claimed imposed equivalent education duties for remand and sentenced prisoners), the National Education Act 1991 and the UN Convention against Discrimination in Education. At the hearing he noted that others in similar positions had been allowed to study and that no legal basis for refusal had been shown. The governor acknowledged a discontinued prior practice of access, citing concerns over recidivists’ influence, and confirmed Velev was treated as a recidivist under the 1969 Act (section 158), precluding school attendance to avoid mixing with non-recidivists.

On 24 March 2006 the Stara Zagora Regional Court allowed the appeal and ordered enrolment. It held that Velev was not a recidivist, as the 1969 Act required two or more imprisonment sentences (or a dangerous recidivism conviction) after actual service of a term; pending proceedings meant the separation rule did not apply.

The governor appealed, arguing that Velev was housed with remand prisoners who would become recidivists if convicted, that Stara Zagora Prison was for non-recidivists, and that recidivist (including remand) accommodation there was exceptional.

Before the appeal hearing, Velev requested 2006/07 enrolment on 9 August 2006 (unanswered) and again on 21 September to the Directorate. On 26 September 2006 the Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling. Although the prosecutor supported the first-instance decision as correctly interpreting the law, the Court held that the right to education (mandatory or voluntary) applied solely to those deprived of liberty after final conviction, not remand detainees. Whether Velev was wrongly treated as a recidivist was therefore irrelevant. The Directorate confirmed non-enrolment on 6 November 2006, citing this judgment.

Velev was later convicted of the firearms offence, transferred to Pazardjik Prison on 20 April 2007 (which had no school) and released on 27 July 2008. He submitted no education requests there. Documents indicated at least one classified recidivist had successfully participated in the Stara Zagora programme.

Domestic law at the time (Execution of Punishments Act 1969 and implementing rules) made education mandatory for convicted prisoners under 16 and available on request for older convicted prisoners serving at least one year; section 128 applied convicted-prisoner provisions to remand detainees absent specific rules. Recidivists (defined as those with two or more served imprisonment sentences for intentional offences, or dangerous recidivism) were to be held separately, with corresponding rules for certain remand prisoners. Council of Europe instruments, including the 1987 and 2006 European Prison Rules and Recommendation R(89)12, stressed education access for all prisoners (including untried persons presumed innocent) and encouraged participation without undue restrictions.

The case of Velyo Velev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 16032/07) was brought by a Bulgarian national born in 1977 who alleged two Convention violations arising from his pre-trial detention. First, he claimed a breach of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 because prison authorities refused him access to the school inside Stara Zagora Prison, thereby denying him the opportunity to complete his secondary education. Second, he alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) because he was classified and treated as a “recidivist” before any final conviction on the charge for which he was remanded.

In 2003 Velev was convicted of fraud and served a sentence in Stara Zagora Prison until August 2004. On 1 October 2004 he was arrested on suspicion of unlawful possession of firearms and held on remand in the same prison from 29 November 2004 until 20 April 2007. During this period he asserted that he was housed with sentenced “recidivist” prisoners.

Having never finished secondary school, Velev submitted repeated written requests, beginning in August 2005, to the prison governor, the Ministry of Education and the Prosecutor’s Office seeking enrolment for the 2005/06 academic year. The prosecutor’s office replied that the administration had taken the request into account; the Ministry of Education stated that persons “deprived of their liberty” were entitled to education but did not address remand prisoners specifically. On 7 December 2005 the Directorate for the Execution of Punishments formally refused enrolment, stating that Velev had not yet been convicted, that once convicted he would be transferred to a recidivist prison, and that allowing a person treated as a recidivist to attend classes with non-recidivists would breach the statutory requirement of category separation.

Velev appealed. At first instance the Stara Zagora Regional Court (24 March 2006) upheld his claim, holding that he could not be regarded as a recidivist under section 158 of the 1969 Execution of Punishments Act because he had not received a second final sentence of imprisonment; the separation rule was therefore inapplicable and the governor was ordered to enrol him. The governor appealed, arguing that Velev was correctly placed among remand prisoners who, if convicted, would become recidivists and that Stara Zagora Prison was designated for non-recidivists.

Meanwhile Velev renewed his request for the 2006/07 school year. On 26 September 2006 the Supreme Administrative Court reversed the lower court. It held that domestic legislation conferred a right to education only on persons serving a final sentence of imprisonment of at least one year; remand prisoners had no such right. The question whether Velev had been wrongly labelled a recidivist was therefore irrelevant. The Directorate then confirmed that he would not be enrolled.

Velev was subsequently convicted of the firearms offence, transferred on 20 April 2007 to Pazardjik Prison (which had no school) and released on 27 July 2008. He produced evidence that at least one prisoner classified as a recidivist had been permitted to study at Stara Zagora Prison, and he maintained that other remand prisoners in his situation had previously been allowed to attend classes.

The relevant domestic framework (the 1969 Execution of Punishments Act and its implementing regulations) made education mandatory only for prisoners under 16 and available, on request, for older convicted prisoners serving at least one year. A general clause provided that, unless otherwise stipulated, the rules applicable to convicted prisoners also applied to those on remand. Recidivists were defined as persons sentenced twice or more to imprisonment (or convicted of “dangerous recidivism”) and were required to serve their sentences separately; remand prisoners with a prior unsuspended sentence were likewise to be kept apart from other remand prisoners.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints that he was both denied education while presumed innocent and prematurely treated as a recidivist.

The case of Velyo Velev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 16032/07) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 March 2007 by a Bulgarian national born in 1977. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education) due to his exclusion from the prison school while detained on remand, and a breach of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) because he was treated as a “recidivist” before any second final conviction.

In 2003 the applicant was convicted of fraud and served a prison sentence in Stara Zagora Prison until August 2004. On 1 October 2004 he was arrested on suspicion of unlawful possession of firearms and held on remand in the same prison from 29 November 2004 until 20 April 2007. He claimed he was housed with recidivist prisoners. Having never completed secondary education, he applied in August 2005 to enrol in the prison school for the 2005/06 academic year. Receiving no timely reply, he repeated the request to the prison governor, the Ministry of Education and the Prosecutor’s Office. The Prosecutor’s Office stated that the administration had considered his situation in light of his prior sentence and that his claim of refusal was unconfirmed. The Ministry of Education confirmed that persons deprived of liberty were entitled to continue their education but made no specific reference to remand prisoners.

Further requests in October 2005 were rejected on 7 December 2005 by the Head of the Execution of Punishments Directorate. The refusal stated that the applicant had not yet been convicted, would upon conviction be transferred to a recidivist prison, and that allowing him (as a prospective recidivist) to join educational programmes with non-recidivists would violate the statutory requirement to keep different categories of inmate separate. The applicant appealed, arguing that without a second conviction he could not be classified as a recidivist under the Execution of Punishments Act 1969, that domestic law (including section 128 of that Act) extended educational rights to remand prisoners, and that the refusal lacked a legitimate aim and contravened constitutional and international provisions on education.

On 24 March 2006 the Stara Zagora Regional Court upheld the appeal and ordered his enrolment. It held that he did not meet the statutory definition of a recidivist (section 158 of the 1969 Act) because the current proceedings remained pending; the separation rule was therefore inapplicable. The prison governor appealed, maintaining that the applicant was housed with remand prisoners who, if convicted, would be treated as recidivists and that Stara Zagora Prison was designated for non-recidivists. Before the appeal was decided, the applicant again sought enrolment for the 2006/07 school year.

On 26 September 2006 the Supreme Administrative Court delivered a final ruling dismissing the applicant’s claim. It interpreted the 1969 Act (as amended in 2002) as conferring a right of access to education solely on persons serving a final sentence of imprisonment of one year or more, not on remand prisoners. The question of recidivist status was therefore irrelevant. Relying on that judgment, the authorities refused enrolment for 2006/07. After conviction for the firearms offence the applicant was transferred on 20 April 2007 to Pazardjik Prison (which he stated had no school) and was released on 27 July 2008. He produced documents showing that at least one prisoner classified as a recidivist had previously been allowed to study at Stara Zagora Prison.

Domestic law at the time provided that, absent specific contrary rules, provisions applicable to convicted prisoners also applied to remand prisoners. Recidivists (those previously sentenced to imprisonment for intentional offences and who had served that sentence) were required to be held separately. European Prison Rules and related recommendations encouraged access to education for all prisoners, including untried detainees, while permitting joint organised activities.
