The case of Veits v. Estonia (application no. 12951/11) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Estonian national Anneli Veits (born 1990). She alleged that a domestic confiscation order violated her ownership rights and that she had not been involved in the proceedings deciding the confiscation of her property.

In 1995 the applicant’s grandmother N privatised an apartment at 9 Mahtra Street, Tallinn, and in 1996 gifted it to the then-minor applicant (represented by her mother V). On 21 April 2003 Zh authorised N (via notarised power of attorney) to sell his apartment at 33 Punane Street. On 20 May 2003 N sold it to V; in return N acquired for Zh a far cheaper rural apartment (worth about one-twentieth as much). Zh, who suffered from paranoid schizophrenia, later died on 3 January 2004 of ethylene glycol poisoning. On 7 August 2003 V obtained social-security approval to sell the applicant’s Mahtra apartment, stating she had bought the Punane apartment on loan and wished to repay it from the sale proceeds then gift the new apartment to her daughter. The Mahtra apartment was sold and, on 28 October 2003, V gifted the Punane apartment to the applicant (again acting as her legal representative).

Criminal investigations were opened into multiple apartment sales by vulnerable persons (including Zh), some of whom died soon afterwards. An attachment of the Punane apartment was ordered in November 2003 but later quashed and the related proceedings discontinued in 2005. In spring 2007 investigations were reopened and joined; N was remanded in custody. On 14 June 2007 the Harju County Court attached the Punane apartment (and another) at the prosecutor’s request, finding it had been acquired fraudulently from Zh, immediately registered in V’s name, then transferred to the applicant (then a minor) to avoid confiscation. Copies of the attachment order were sent to V and the applicant; V signed for receipt. The applicant (interviewed as a witness on 31 July 2007) stated she had been a young child in 2003, did not recall details, knew the apartment was in her name but had never lived there, and that her mother paid for it.

N and V (with two others) were committed for trial in October 2007. N was charged inter alia with Zh’s murder and multiple frauds; V with frauds and aiding attempted murder. The applicant turned 18 on 27 April 2008. At trial N and V claimed the Punane apartment had always been intended for the applicant and that funds originated from legitimate sources (including sale of the Mahtra apartment with social-security approval). On 12 January 2010 the County Court convicted N (15 years) and V (8 years). It found Zh had not understood the 2003 transaction, received no payment, and that the accused’s explanations of the purchase funds were implausible. Relying on Penal Code Article 83 § 3(2), it confiscated the Punane apartment from the applicant as property obtained through crime against Zh. The applicant, aged 13 in 2003, could not have been a bona-fide acquirer because her mother V had concluded the transaction on her behalf, shortly after the purchase, to prevent confiscation.

V and N appealed, arguing the apartment belonged to the applicant and had been acquired via the legitimate sale of her Mahtra apartment. On 14 June 2010 the Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals, holding the apartment was the object of the offenders’ fraud, acquired by the then-minor applicant on account of their actions, and thus confiscable under Articles 83 § 3(2) and 83-1 § 2. The Supreme Court declined to examine further appeals on 18 August 2010, rendering the judgments final.

Relevant domestic law (Penal Code Articles 83, 83-1 and 85) permitted exceptional confiscation of third-party property acquired as a gift from the offender or at a price far below market value, or where the third party knew transfer was intended to avoid confiscation; third-party rights otherwise survived confiscation except in specified cases. The Code of Criminal Procedure allowed involvement of third parties whose rights might be affected and attachment of their property to secure confiscation. Later Supreme Court case-law (2011–2013) emphasised that a person whose property was to be confiscated had to be involved as a third party, that attachment required a demonstrated link to the specific offence, and that an uninvolved alleged owner retained title (with civil or administrative remedies available). Estonian civil law further held that a minor’s knowledge of circumstances was assessed through her representative and that gratuitous transfers to close relatives did not confer bona-fide status.

The case of Veits v. Estonia (Application no. 12951/11) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 February 2011 by Estonian national Anneli Veits (born 1990). She alleged a violation of her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention due to the confiscation of her apartment, and a related breach of fair-trial rights because she was not a party to the criminal proceedings in which that confiscation was ordered.

In 1995 the applicant’s grandmother N. privatised an apartment at 9 Mahtra Street, Tallinn, and in 1996 transferred it to the then-minor applicant, who was represented by her mother V. In April 2003 Zh. granted N. a notarised power of attorney to sell his apartment at 33 Punane Street. On 20 May 2003 N., acting for Zh., sold that apartment to V. and acquired for Zh. a far cheaper rural property. V. then obtained municipal social-security approval to sell the applicant’s Mahtra apartment (the applicant being 13 years old) in order to repay a loan used to buy the Punane apartment; she subsequently gifted the Punane apartment to the applicant on 28 October 2003, again acting as the child’s legal representative.

Criminal investigations were opened into a series of similar apartment transactions involving vulnerable vendors, some of whom (including Zh., who died of ethylene glycol poisoning on 3 January 2004) died shortly afterwards. After an initial attachment of the Punane apartment was lifted and proceedings discontinued, a fresh investigation began in 2007. On 14 June 2007 the Harju County Court attached the Punane apartment (then registered in the applicant’s name) together with another property, finding that it had been acquired fraudulently from Zh. and registered in the applicant’s name solely to avoid confiscation. Copies of the attachment order were sent to V. and the applicant “for information.” The applicant, interviewed as a witness on 31 July 2007, stated that she had no recollection of the 2003 transactions, had never lived in the Punane apartment, and that her mother paid for it.

N. and V. were committed for trial on charges including murder, attempted murder and multiple counts of fraud. At trial N. claimed the Punane apartment had always been intended for the applicant; V. asserted that it had been purchased with the proceeds of the approved sale of the Mahtra apartment. On 12 January 2010 the County Court convicted both women (N. to 15 years, V. to 8 years). Relying on a psychiatric report that Zh. (suffering from paranoid schizophrenia) had not understood the power-of-attorney transaction and had received no payment, the court ordered confiscation of the Punane apartment under Articles 83 § 3(2) and 83-1 § 2 of the Penal Code as property obtained through crime. It held that the 13-year-old applicant could not have been a bona-fide acquirer because the gift had been effected by her mother shortly after the fraudulent purchase in order to defeat confiscation.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals on 14 June 2010, confirming that the apartment had been the object of the fraud and had been acquired by a minor incapable of understanding the transaction. The Supreme Court declined to examine further appeals on 18 August 2010, rendering the confiscation final. Throughout, the applicant was never formally joined as a third party under Article 40-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, nor given an opportunity to contest the confiscation in her own right.

The ECHR case Veits v. Estonia (App. no. 12951/11) arose from an application by Anneli Veits (born 1990), alleging that Estonian courts’ confiscation of her Tallinn apartment at 33 Punane Street violated her property rights and that she had not been involved in the proceedings deciding that confiscation.

In 1995 Veits’ grandmother N. privatised an apartment at 9 Mahtra Street and gifted it to the then-minor Veits in 1996 (Veits represented by her mother V.). In 2003 N., acting under a notarised power of attorney from Zh., sold Zh.’s Punane Street apartment to V. V. then obtained social-services approval to sell Veits’ Mahtra Street apartment, using the proceeds to repay a loan taken to acquire the Punane apartment, which she then gifted to Veits (again acting as Veits’ representative). Zh., who suffered from paranoid schizophrenia, received little or no consideration and died shortly afterwards of ethylene glycol poisoning.

Investigations into a pattern of similar transactions with vulnerable persons (some of whom also died) led to charges against N. and V. for fraud (and, in N.’s case, murder of Zh.). In June 2007 the Harju County Court attached the Punane apartment (among others) to secure possible confiscation, finding it had been obtained fraudulently from Zh. and registered in Veits’ name to avoid confiscation. Copies of the attachment order were sent to V. and Veits. Veits, then a minor, was later interviewed as a witness and said she recalled little of the 2003 transactions.

N. and V. were convicted in January 2010. The County Court held that Zh. had not understood the 2003 sale, received no payment, and that the subsequent gift to Veits (then 13) was not a bona fide acquisition because it had been effected by V. to prevent confiscation. Relying on Penal Code Articles 83 § 3(2) and 83-1 § 2, the court confiscated the apartment as the object/proceeds of crime belonging to a third party acquired as a gift or at an undervalue from the offenders. Appeals by N. and V. (Veits not a party) were dismissed; the Supreme Court declined to hear further appeals.

Veits (who turned 18 in 2008) complained that the apartment had been acquired with proceeds of her own prior property (sold with official approval) and that she had never been joined as a third party despite her ownership interest being at stake. Domestic law permitted exceptional confiscation from third parties who received crime-derived assets as gifts or knowing they were transferred to evade confiscation, but also provided for involvement of third parties whose rights might be affected (Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 40-1). Subsequent Supreme Court case-law emphasised that a person not an accused could be the object of a confiscation order only if joined as a third party, otherwise ownership did not pass to the State.

The facts thus centre on a third-party minor’s acquisition of property later found to be crime proceeds, the absence of her procedural participation, and the domestic courts’ conclusion that she could not be a bona fide owner.
001-144619:
The case of Albergas and Arlauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 17978/05) concerns two Lithuanian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed they were deprived of their property by a domestic court decision without receiving adequate compensation.

In 1994, the Vilnius City municipality assigned a 0.08-hectare plot of land to the first applicant, Eduardas Albergas (born 1949), for construction of an individual house. As a family member of a deportee, he was entitled to acquire the land under then-applicable law. On 5 September 1995, he purchased the plot from the State for 422 Lithuanian litai (approximately EUR 122) plus 423 single-use investment vouchers and registered title in his name. In April 1997, he sold the plot to the second applicant, Jurijus Arlauskas (born 1955), for LTL 6,000 (approximately EUR 1,740). The second applicant registered the land in his own name.

The second applicant later sued a neighbouring landowner, R.A., claiming she had unlawfully fenced off his plot and thereby interfered with his peaceful enjoyment of the property. R.A. counterclaimed against both applicants, seeking annulment of the 1995 and 1997 contracts and of the original municipal assignment. She asserted that the plot formed part of her late father’s land, which had been nationalised by Soviet authorities. R.A. had applied for restoration of her rights in 1991; in 1999 those rights were restored in natura, but only to part of the original holding.

Lower courts upheld the applicants’ position and dismissed the counterclaim. They noted that, under the 1991 Law on Restitution I then in force, R.A. was entitled to no more than 0.2 hectares in natura and that the municipality had taken this limit into account when assigning the plot in 1994–1995. Subsequent legislative changes (Law on Restitution II of 1997, allowing up to 1 hectare) did not automatically invalidate earlier decisions.

On 27 November 2002 the Supreme Court reversed those rulings. Applying a principle of priority for former owners developed in earlier case-law, it held that the authorities had been prohibited from selling land to third parties while restitution claims remained pending. The Court characterised both applicants as having acted in “bad faith,” although it offered no specific substantiation regarding the first applicant and merely assumed the second applicant must have known of third-party claims. The 1994 assignment and both sale contracts were annulled; the land reverted to the State. The first applicant was ordered to repay the second applicant LTL 6,000, while the State was to refund him only the LTL 422 cash portion of the original purchase price (the vouchers having become worthless).

The applicants then sought redress. In 2004 they asked the National Land Service to allocate a replacement plot of equivalent size and value; the request was refused. Administrative courts (Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, 1 October 2004; Supreme Administrative Court, 19 January 2005) confirmed the refusal, observing that the statutory provisions under which the first applicant had originally obtained land were no longer in force and that the second applicant had never been eligible. The first applicant complied with the Supreme Court’s order and repaid LTL 6,000 in August 2005. A subsequent civil claim against the Vilnius municipality for damages was dismissed by the Vilnius City First District Court on 29 September 2005 on the ground that the applicants had purchased in bad faith; no appeal was lodged.

The applicants maintained that they had acquired the land in good faith, that the Supreme Court’s decision deprived them of their property, and that the sums awarded (or not awarded) failed to constitute adequate compensation, particularly given the unreturned investment vouchers and the refusal of any substitute plot. These facts form the core of their complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Albergas and Arlauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 17978/05) concerns two Lithuanian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed they were deprived of their property by a domestic court decision without receiving adequate compensation.

In 1994 the Vilnius City municipality assigned a plot of land measuring 0.08 hectares to the first applicant, Eduardas Albergas (born 1949), for the construction of an individual house. Similar plots were assigned to other private persons at the time. Due to his status as a family member of a deportee and in accordance with then-applicable domestic law, the first applicant was entitled to acquire the land. On 5 September 1995 he signed a contract with the Vilnius Region Administration and purchased the plot from the State, paying 422 Lithuanian litai (approximately 122 euros) plus 423 single-use investment vouchers. He subsequently registered the plot in his name.

On 10 April 1997 the first applicant sold the plot to the second applicant, Jurijus Arlauskas (born 1955), for 6,000 litai (approximately 1,740 euros). The second applicant registered the land in his own name.

The second applicant later brought a civil claim against a neighbouring private person, R.A., alleging that she had unlawfully fenced off the plot and thereby interfered with his peaceful enjoyment of the property. R.A. lodged a counterclaim seeking annulment of the 1995 and 1997 sale contracts (as well as the underlying 1994 assignment decision) and restoration in natura of her ownership rights. She asserted that the plot formed part of land belonging to her father that had been nationalised by the Soviet authorities. R.A. had applied for restoration of her rights in 1991; those rights were partially restored in natura in 1999, but only in respect of part of her father’s original holding.

Lower courts at two instances granted the second applicant’s claim and dismissed the counterclaim. They observed that, under the Law on Restitution I then in force, R.A. had been entitled to restitution in natura of no more than 0.2 hectares. The local authorities had taken this limit into account when assigning the plot to the first applicant. The fact that a later statute (Law on Restitution II, in force from July 1997) increased the possible restoration area to one hectare did not automatically invalidate the earlier administrative decisions.

On 27 November 2002 the Supreme Court overturned those rulings. Applying a principle of priority for former owners’ rights (developed in earlier case-law), it held that the authorities had not been entitled to sell plots to third parties before outstanding restitution claims had been resolved. The Supreme Court further found that both applicants had acted in “bad faith” when acquiring the land, although it provided no substantiation of that finding in respect of the first applicant and merely assumed that the second applicant had known of third-party claims. The 1994 assignment decision and both sale contracts were annulled; the plot was returned to the State. The first applicant was ordered to repay the second applicant the 6,000 litai he had received, while the State was ordered to repay the first applicant only the 422 litai cash component of the original purchase price. The investment vouchers were not restored, as they had by then lost all pecuniary value.

In 2004 both applicants requested the National Land Service to assign them a new plot of equivalent size and value. The request was refused. They then applied to the administrative courts, arguing that they had acquired the land in good faith and that the sums awarded by the Supreme Court did not adequately compensate their loss (particularly given the unpaid vouchers). They sought a replacement plot. The case of Albergas and Arlauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 17978/05) concerns two Lithuanian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed that a domestic court decision had deprived them of their property without adequate compensation.

In 1994 the Vilnius City municipality assigned a 0.08-hectare plot to the first applicant, Eduardas Albergas, for construction of a house. As a deportee’s family member he was entitled to acquire it under then-applicable law. On 5 September 1995 he purchased the plot from the State for LTL 422 plus 423 single-use investment vouchers and registered title. On 10 April 1997 he sold it to the second applicant, Jurijus Arlauskas, for LTL 6,000; the latter also registered title.

The second applicant later sued a neighbour, R.A., who had fenced the land. R.A. counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the 1995 and 1997 contracts and restoration in natura of her late father’s nationalised land. She had applied for restitution in 1991 and received partial restoration in 1999. Lower courts granted the second applicant’s claim and rejected the counterclaim, holding that under the 1991 Law on Restitution I R.A. could recover no more than 0.2 hectares and that the 1994–95 administrative decisions therefore remained valid even after a 1997 law raised the limit to one hectare.

On 27 November 2002 the Supreme Court reversed. Applying a principle of priority for former owners, it held that the authorities had been barred from selling the plot while restitution claims were pending. It found both applicants had acted in “bad faith” (though it gave no reasons regarding the first applicant and merely assumed knowledge on the part of the second). The contracts and the 1994 assignment were annulled, title reverted to the State, the first applicant was ordered to repay LTL 6,000 to the second applicant, and the State was ordered to repay only LTL 422 to the first applicant (the vouchers having become worthless).

The applicants then sought a replacement plot of equivalent size and value from the National Land Service; the request was refused. Administrative courts dismissed their subsequent claims in October 2004 and January 2005, noting that the legal basis for the original assignment no longer existed and that the second applicant was ineligible. The first applicant paid the LTL 6,000 in August 2005. A civil claim for damages against the municipality was dismissed in September 2005 on the same “bad-faith” ground; no appeal was lodged.

Domestic law (Constitution Articles 23 and 30, the two Restitution Laws, Civil Code Article 6.271 and Constitutional Court jurisprudence) required just compensation for expropriation, recognised a restricted form of restitution that balanced former owners’ rights against those of good-faith purchasers and legitimate expectations, and imposed State liability for unlawful official acts. Supreme Court case-law treated land subject to unresolved restitution claims as “disputed” and therefore inalienable. The applicants maintained that they had acquired the plot in good faith and that the sums awarded (especially the non-reimbursement of the vouchers) were inadequate.

The case originated in an application by Slovenian national Zdravko Mihelj, born in 1965 and resident in Ljubljana, alleging a violation of his defence rights under the Convention due to a trial conducted in his absence after modification of the indictment.

Following a request by M.K. on 25 March 1999 (amended 9 July 1999), the applicant was summoned on 30 July 1999 to appear as accused before the Ljubljana District Court investigating judge on a charge of aggravated fraud under section 217 § 2 of the Criminal Code. He was heard on 6 September 1999, denied the charge, submitted supporting documents claiming the accusations were fabricated, but declined to answer questions from M.K.’s counsel. An investigation order was issued on 17 September 1999. Two witnesses confirming M.K.’s account were examined in the applicant’s absence; although notification was ordered, court records showed no proof of service of a summons.

The investigation closed on 10 November 1999. The Ljubljana District State Prosecutor’s Office took over and, on 4 February 2000, filed an indictment for attempted aggravated fraud (Article 217 §§ 1 and 2 in conjunction with Article 22). It alleged that the applicant had deceived M.K., exploiting her age and naivety, into signing a fictitious loan agreement for DEM 50,000 (SIT 4,691,500) secured by a mortgage on her share of the family house (despite knowing she owed him nothing), obtaining her authority to execute it, registering the mortgage (thereby prejudicing her property), and receiving SIT 225,000 from her in instalments.

The applicant objected that the accusations were fabricated and that a mortgage could not be registered without M.K.’s cooperation. The objection was rejected on 7 July 2000; the pre-trial panel reclassified the offence as attempted fraud under Article 217 § 1 with Article 22 (as the value did not meet the significant-damage threshold) and transferred the case to the Ljubljana Local Court for summary proceedings. The applicant’s appeal against the transfer was dismissed.

The applicant failed to collect the first two summonses for a hearing scheduled for 22 January 2002; it was postponed to 29 March 2002. Summonses were served on 4 February 2002 (by courier at home and work) and 6 February 2002 (by post at both addresses). On 28 March 2002 he wrote objecting to four identical, unexplained summonses mentioning only the legal classification; the letter arrived on 29 March.

On 29 March 2002 the Local Court held the hearing in the applicant’s absence, finding he had been duly summoned, had given no justification, had already been questioned in the investigation, and that his presence was unnecessary to establish the facts. M.K. and the two witnesses (whose accounts matched their earlier statements) were examined. In closing, the prosecutor modified the indictment, reclassifying the offence as completed fraud (not attempted) and adding that the applicant had lied about land-registry expenses, for which M.K. had paid him SIT 225,000. The court convicted him on the modified indictment and imposed a seven-month prison sentence, leaving M.K.’s pecuniary claim for civil proceedings.

The applicant appealed to the Ljubljana Higher Court, arguing that his investigation statement was insufficient (no indictment yet existed to dispute), that in-absentia rules applied only after indictment, that the witnesses lacked credibility, that documents showed M.K. was evading contractual obligations, and that the sentence was excessive. On 18 September 2002 the Higher Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the applicant had a right (but not an obligation) to attend, had been heard earlier, had received the indictment, had been duly summoned (and thus could have made a statement and examined witnesses), and that the facts were already fully established; a hearing need be discontinued only for a substantial change in the description of the offence, which had not occurred.

He further appealed on points of law, reiterating that trial in absentia was improper because he had been questioned only before indictment and that he had been denied the chance to cross-examine witnesses. On 13 November 2003 the Supreme Court upheld the conviction, finding the investigated and charged offences identical, no new facts at the hearing, the statutory conditions for trial in absentia satisfied (right to attend but waivable; due summons and warning given), and the earlier lack of notification of witness examinations remedied by their re-examination at the hearing he could have attended.

A constitutional complaint was declared admissible on 29 May 2006. On 9 November 2006 the Constitutional Court found no violation of constitutional rights: the applicant had been heard during the investigation; the request for investigation and the later indictment concerned the same acts and offence (misleading M.K. into a fictitious agreement for illicit gain) despite wording differences; although the indictment was modified at the hearing (reclassification from attempted to completed fraud plus added expense details), the charge remained the same in substance as to the applicant’s conduct and circumstances; he had been duly summoned without valid excuse and had not requested an adjournment; and the witness issue had been remedied as the Supreme Court held. He had not even claimed the investigated offence differed from that tried, but had merely noted that a prosecutor could in theory file a different indictment after investigation.

He had been warned that the hearing might proceed without him and had given no valid reason for his absence.

001-152647:
**Case of Bohlen v. Germany (Application no. 53495/09), ECHR Fifth Section judgment of 19 February 2015 (final 19 May 2015)**

Dieter Bohlen, a German musician and producer born in 1954, published the book *Backstage* (Hinter den Kulissen) in autumn 2003. Certain passages were redacted following urgent court proceedings against him.

On 27 October 2003, British American Tobacco (Germany) GmbH published a full-page advertisement for Lucky Strike cigarettes in *Der Spiegel* (circulation 1.42 million) and *Bild* (4.67 million). The ad showed two cigarette packets, a lit cigarette, and a black marker pen, with the large heading: “Look, dear Dieter, how easy it is to write super books.” Words including “dear,” “easy,” and “super” were blacked out but still readable. The slogan “Lucky Strike. Nothing else.” appeared at the bottom. This formed part of a long-running campaign (1989–2004) of over 500 humorous ads alluding to current events and individuals.

Bohlen viewed the ad as an unauthorized use of his forename that exploited his publicity around the censored book. The company undertook not to republish it with the heading but refused his demand of €70,000 for a “notional licence” (compensation as if a licence had been granted).

Bohlen sued in the Hamburg Regional Court for €100,000. On 3 September 2004 the court found that “Dieter” clearly referred to him, given the campaign’s style of commenting on topical events and the unique publicity around his redacted book. Balancing rights, it held that personality rights (the right to control commercial use of one’s name) prevailed over the company’s freedom of expression under Article 5 of the Basic Law. The ad pursued primarily commercial aims (boosting cigarette sales) with only superficial contribution to public debate and no genuine link to the product. Drawing on comparable cases involving celebrities, it awarded €100,000, considering the ad’s wide reach (over 6 million readers) but noting it used neither his image nor surname.

The Hamburg Court of Appeal (29 November 2005) upheld the finding of unlawful interference, emphasising commercial use of the name, but reduced the award to €35,000 under unjust-enrichment principles. It noted the ad’s humorous, non-debasing character, single publication, and Bohlen’s own seeking of publicity. Leave to appeal on points of law was refused.

The Federal Court of Justice granted leave and, on 5 June 2008, quashed the decision. It held there was no unlawful interference with the pecuniary aspects of personality or name rights. Those pecuniary interests enjoy only ordinary civil-law protection, whereas freedom of expression (including commercial advertising that shapes public opinion, even via entertainment or satire) is constitutionally protected. The ad humorously referenced a matter of public debate (the book’s publication and redactions) shortly after the event, without exploiting Bohlen’s image, implying endorsement of the cigarettes, or containing degrading content. Because Bohlen had sought the limelight, his interest in preventing unconsented mention carried less weight. No notional licence was due. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear Bohlen’s appeal (7 April 2009).

Bohlen applied to the ECHR, alleging that the refusal of a notional licence violated Article 8 (right to respect for private life) by failing to protect his personality rights against commercial exploitation of his name.

The advertisement constituted satirical comment on a matter of public debate (the circumstances of Bohlen’s book publication) without exploiting his image, implying endorsement of the product, or containing degrading content. Because Bohlen had himself courted publicity, his interest in preventing unauthorised mention of his name was of lesser weight. No notional licence was therefore due.

**Case of Bohlen v. Germany (ECtHR, Application no. 53495/09, 19 February 2015)**

Dieter Bohlen, a German musician, artistic producer, and public figure born in 1954, published his book *Backstage* (*Hinter den Kulissen*) in autumn 2003. Certain passages were redacted following urgent judicial proceedings. Shortly thereafter, on 27 October 2003, British American Tobacco (Germany) GmbH launched a full-page advertisement as part of its long-running Lucky Strike campaign (1989–2004). The ad depicted two cigarette packets, a lit cigarette, and a marker pen, with the headline: “Look, dear Dieter, how easy it is to write super books.” Words such as “dear,” “easy,” and “super” were blacked out but remained legible, accompanied by the slogan “Lucky Strike. Nothing else.” It appeared in *Der Spiegel* (circulation 1.42 million) and *Bild* (4.67 million). The campaign frequently used humorous slogans alluding to current events and involved persons.

Bohlen viewed the ad as an unauthorized commercial exploitation of his forename and the public controversy surrounding his book. The company undertook not to republish it but refused his demand for €70,000 as a “notional licence” (fiktive Lizenz) compensating for the use of his name/personality. He sued in the Hamburg Regional Court for €100,000.

The Regional Court (3 September 2004) found a clear reference to Bohlen, given the campaign’s practice of commenting on topical events and the unique publicity around his censored book. It balanced his personality rights (protecting against unauthorized commercial use of one’s name) against the company’s freedom of expression under Article 5 § 1 of the Basic Law, which extends to commercial speech contributing to public opinion. The court held that personality rights prevailed because the ad was primarily commercial (promoting cigarette sales) and entertaining rather than genuinely contributing to debate; it lacked a direct link between Bohlen or the ad’s content and the product. Compensation of €100,000 was awarded based on his fame, the ad’s wide reach, and comparable cases (e.g., involving Boris Becker), though noting the absence of his photograph or surname.

The Hamburg Court of Appeal (29 November 2005) upheld the finding of unlawful interference with personality rights, emphasizing the commercial purpose, but reduced the award to €35,000. It considered the ad’s humorous, non-degrading nature, its single publication, use of only part of the name, and Bohlen’s own seeking of publicity. Leave to appeal on points of law was initially refused.

The Federal Court of Justice (5 June 2008) quashed this. It accepted an interference with the pecuniary aspects of personality rights and the right to one’s name but held it was not unlawful. These pecuniary elements enjoy only ordinary civil-law protection, whereas freedom of expression (including advertising that comments on matters of general interest, even humorously or entertainingly) is constitutionally protected. The ad satirically alluded to a publicly known event shortly after it occurred, without exploiting Bohlen’s “brand image” or implying his endorsement of the product. Bohlen’s interest in preventing unauthorized mention thus yielded to the company’s expression rights. No notional licence was due.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear Bohlen’s constitutional complaint (7 April 2009). He applied to the ECtHR, alleging that the refusal of compensation for the unauthorized use of his forename in the advertisement violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention, as it failed to adequately protect his personality rights against commercial exploitation.

The case of Mileusnić and Mileusnić-Espenheim v. Croatia (no. 66953/09) concerns Croatian nationals of Serbian origin, Petar Mileusnić (born 1936, died 2013) and his son Goran Mileusnić-Espenheim (born 1967). On returning in July 1992 he found his house occupied by refugees and his possessions gone.

In March 1992 the military prosecutor dropped charges against I.G. and Z.P. for insufficient ballistic evidence. 001-150778:
The case of Hutchinson v. the United Kingdom (Appl. no. 57592/08) was brought by Arthur Hutchinson, a British national born in 1941 and detained at HM Prison Durham. He alleged that his whole-life prison sentence violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment) because it was irreducible, offering no realistic prospect of release.

In October 1983 Hutchinson broke into a family home, stabbed a man, his wife and their adult son to death, and repeatedly raped their 18-year-old daughter after dragging her past her father’s body. He pleaded not guilty, denying the killings and claiming the sex was consensual. On 14 September 1984 he was convicted at Sheffield Crown Court of aggravated burglary, rape and three murders. The trial judge imposed life imprisonment and initially recommended an 18-year tariff. In 1988 the same judge described the case as “genuinely a life case” for retribution and deterrence; the Lord Chief Justice recommended a whole-life term, stating that the applicant should never be released. The Secretary of State imposed a whole-life order on 16 December 1994.

After the Criminal Justice Act 2003 came into force, Hutchinson applied to the High Court for a review of his tariff. On 16 May 2008 Tugendhat J confirmed the whole-life order: the starting point was a whole-life term because of the exceptional seriousness of the offences, and there were multiple aggravating factors (including sadistic and sexual conduct described in the surviving victim’s impact statement) with no mitigation. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 6 October 2008.

Under s. 30 of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997 the Secretary of State may release a life prisoner on licence if “exceptional circumstances” justify release on compassionate grounds. Chapter 12 of the Lifer Manual (PSO 4700) lists restrictive criteria: terminal illness with death imminent (typically within three months), or being bedridden/incapacitated; minimal risk of re-offending; imprisonment reducing life expectancy; adequate external care arrangements; and significant benefit to the prisoner or family. The Human Rights Act 1998 requires the Secretary of State to act compatibly with Article 3 and legislation to be interpreted accordingly.

The Grand Chamber in Vinter and Others v. the United Kingdom (2013) had found a violation of Article 3. Although s. 30 could in principle provide a review mechanism, the law was insufficiently clear: the Lifer Manual’s exhaustive, highly restrictive conditions had not been revised, and it was uncertain whether the Secretary of State would apply those conditions or a broader Article 3 test. Compassionate release of the terminally ill was not a genuine “prospect of release.”

In R v Newell; R v McLoughlin (2014) a specially constituted Court of Appeal responded. It held that domestic law was clear. The Secretary of State’s s. 30 power cannot be fettered by the Manual; he must consider all exceptional circumstances. “Compassionate grounds” must be read compatibly with Article 3 and given a wide meaning developed case-by-case. Decisions must be reasoned and are subject to judicial review. Thus a whole-life prisoner has a realistic hope of release if later exceptional circumstances render continued detention no longer justified.

The key facts relevant to the Article 3 complaint are therefore the extreme gravity of the original offences (justifying a whole-life term at the outset), the successive confirmations of that term, the statutory release power and its restrictive policy guidance, the lack of clarity identified in Vinter, and the subsequent Court of Appeal clarification that an Article 3-compliant review exists.

The case of Hutchinson v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 57592/08) was brought by Arthur Hutchinson, a British national born in 1941 and detained at HM Prison Durham. He alleged that his whole life sentence violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment), as it was irreducible and thus incompatible with human dignity.

In October 1983 Hutchinson broke into a family home, stabbed to death a man, his wife and their adult son, and repeatedly raped their 18-year-old daughter after dragging her past her father's corpse. Arrested weeks later, he pleaded not guilty at Sheffield Crown Court, denying the murders and claiming the sexual activity was consensual. On 14 September 1984 he was convicted of aggravated burglary, rape and three counts of murder.

The trial judge imposed life imprisonment and recommended an 18-year minimum tariff. In January 1988 the same judge confirmed it was “genuinely a life case” for retribution and deterrence. The Lord Chief Justice recommended a whole-life term, stating he did not think the applicant should ever be released (quite apart from risk). On 16 December 1994 the Secretary of State imposed a whole-life tariff.

After the Criminal Justice Act 2003 came into force, Hutchinson applied to the High Court for a review of his minimum term. On 16 May 2008 Tugendhat J upheld the whole-life order: the offences’ seriousness alone made that the starting point, and there were multiple serious aggravating factors, including the surviving victim’s impact statement describing sadistic as well as sexual conduct. There were no mitigating factors. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 6 October 2008.

Domestic law on possible release is contained in section 30 of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997, which permits the Secretary of State to release a life prisoner on licence at any time if exceptional circumstances justify release on compassionate grounds. Chapter 12 of the Lifer Manual (Prison Service Order 4700) lists highly restrictive criteria: terminal illness with death likely within about three months, or being bedridden or similarly incapacitated; minimal risk of re-offending; imprisonment reducing life expectancy; adequate external care arrangements; and significant benefit to the prisoner or family. The Secretary of State, as a public authority, must act compatibly with the Convention (Human Rights Act 1998, s. 6) and interpret legislation accordingly (s. 3).

The complaint arose against the background of Vinter and Others v. the United Kingdom (Grand Chamber, 2013), which found whole-life orders incompatible with Article 3 because of a lack of clarity about any review mechanism, rendering the sentences apparently irreducible. The Grand Chamber noted that the Lifer Manual’s exhaustive, restrictive conditions (especially compassionate release only for the terminally ill or incapacitated) did not provide a genuine prospect of release, and it was uncertain whether the Secretary of State would apply the broader Article 3-compatible approach set out in earlier Court of Appeal case-law (Bieber, Oakes).

In response, a specially constituted Court of Appeal (R v Newell; R v McLoughlin [2014] EWCA Crim 188) held that English law was in fact clear and compatible. Section 30 requires the Secretary of State to consider all exceptional circumstances that may render continued detention no longer justifiable; the Lifer Manual cannot fetter that discretion; “compassionate grounds” must be given a wide, Convention-compliant meaning developed case-by-case; and any refusal is subject to reasoned decision and judicial review. Thus a whole-life prisoner has a real possibility of release if exceptional circumstances arise that make the original just punishment no longer tenable.

These facts—the extreme gravity of the offences, the successive confirmations of the whole-life order, the statutory power of release, the restrictive published policy, and the subsequent judicial clarification of its true legal scope—are the core elements relevant to whether the sentence was irreducible and therefore violated Article 3.
001-152679:
The case of Ernst August von Hannover v. Germany (App. no. 53649/09) arose from the applicant's claim that German courts' refusal of a notional licence fee for unauthorised commercial use of his forenames in a cigarette advertisement violated his Article 8 right to respect for private life.

The applicant (born 1954, resident in Monaco) became publicly known through his relationship with Princess Caroline of Monaco and two well-publicised incidents of violence: striking a cameraman with an umbrella outside his property in 1998, and a 2000 assault conviction after a fight with a discotheque manager on Lamu Island.

On 27 March 2000, British American Tobacco (Germany) GmbH ran a 10-day campaign of full-page magazine advertisements and 6,364 billboards across 18 cities (potential reach 2.97 million people, plus media coverage). Each showed a crumpled Lucky Strike packet with the slogan “Was it Ernst? Or August?” and “Lucky Strike. Nothing else.” The applicant demanded cessation. The advertising agency agreed; the company refused. Hamburg Regional Court granted an interim injunction on 31 March 2000 (confirmed 14 April). The company stopped the campaign but refused to reimburse the applicant's notice costs. He then claimed €250,000 in damages (unanswered) before suing for a €100,000 notional licence, at least €500 non-pecuniary compensation for personality-rights infringement, and costs.

On 21 January 2005 the Regional Court awarded €60,000 for the notional licence plus costs, but no non-pecuniary damages. It held that the distinctive name combination, the applicant's fame and the clear allusion to his fights made the advertisement an unauthorised use of his name. Personality rights generally outweighed commercial expression; a notional licence prevented unjust enrichment (fee assessed by fame, media used and limited use of forenames only). Non-pecuniary harm was not serious enough because the ad merely mocked a public event.

The Hamburg Court of Appeal (15 May 2007) largely upheld the decision. Even forenames were identifiable; the purely commercial, mocking ad contributed nothing of substance to public debate and therefore yielded to personality rights. A notional licence was due as the unauthorised use of name for commercial gain (akin to image use) irrespective of whether consent would have been given. The amount was justified by the campaign's scale and the applicant's profile.

The Federal Court of Justice (5 June 2008, I ZR 96/07) quashed the award. It accepted an interference with the name but held it lawful under Article 5 of the Basic Law. Only the non-pecuniary aspects of personality rights enjoy constitutional rank; the pecuniary aspects (including a notional licence) are merely civil-law protections and cannot automatically prevail over freedom of expression. The satirical, derisive allusion to already-public incidents formed part of a debate of general interest; it neither exploited the applicant's advertising value nor suggested endorsement of the product. Hence there was no unlawful interference and no entitlement to a licence fee or costs.

On 6 April 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the applicant's constitutional complaint without giving reasons. The applicant complained to the European Court that this outcome violated Article 8.

The case of Ernst August von Hannover v. Germany (Application no. 53649/09) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private life). The applicant, a German national born in 1954 and resident in Monaco, complained that German courts' refusal to award him a notional licence fee for the unauthorised use of his forenames in a commercial advertisement infringed his personality rights.

In 1998, the applicant was involved in a public altercation outside his property, striking a cameraman with an umbrella. In January 2000, he was involved in another scuffle with a nightclub manager in Kenya, leading to an assault conviction. These incidents received press coverage, partly due to the applicant's relationship with Princess Caroline of Monaco, which had raised his public profile.

On 27 March 2000, British American Tobacco (Germany) GmbH launched a 10-day advertising campaign featuring full-page magazine ads and 6,364 posters across 18 cities. The ads displayed a crumpled Lucky Strike cigarette packet alongside the slogan “Was it Ernst? Or August?” and “Lucky Strike. Nothing else.” The campaign reached an estimated 2.97 million people and alluded satirically to the applicant's known propensity for physical confrontations. The applicant demanded discontinuation; the advertising agency agreed, but the company refused. An interim injunction was granted by the Hamburg Regional Court on 31 March 2000 (confirmed 14 April 2000), after which the company halted the ads but declined to cover the applicant's notice costs.

In 2001, the applicant sought €250,000 in damages. In December 2003, he sued the company and agency in the Hamburg Regional Court for a €100,000 notional licence (compensation for unauthorised commercial use of his name, based on a hypothetical reasonable fee), at least €500 non-pecuniary damages for personality rights infringement, and notice costs. On 21 January 2005, the Regional Court awarded €60,000 for the notional licence plus costs, but dismissed non-pecuniary compensation. It held that the distinctive combination of forenames, combined with the applicant's fame and the crumpled packet's allusion to his fights, constituted unauthorised use of his name. Personality rights generally prevailed over commercial advertising's contribution to public debate, though the applicant's own public actions reduced the interference's severity. No “unavoidable need” existed for extra non-pecuniary damages given the ads' merely derisive nature.

The Hamburg Court of Appeal largely upheld this on 15 May 2007 (varying only notice costs). It found interference with both the applicant's name rights and the pecuniary aspect of personality rights, as the ads commercially exploited his identity for sales without consent, contributing little to public opinion beyond entertainment of celebrity gossip. The notional licence was justified regardless of whether the applicant would have consented, based on the campaign's scale, the company's size, and the applicant's prominence.

The Federal Court of Justice quashed this on 5 June 2008. It accepted interference and the theoretical availability of a notional licence under unjust enrichment principles but held there was no unlawfulness. Freedom of expression under Article 5 of the Basic Law protected even satirical advertising contributing to public debate, including entertainment-oriented coverage of the applicant's incidents (already of public interest due to his status). Pecuniary components of personality and name rights, protected only by ordinary civil law, did not automatically prevail over constitutionally guaranteed expression. The ads merely alluded cleverly to known events without exploiting the applicant's “brand image,” implying endorsement, or containing seriously degrading content. Thus, no violation of pecuniary or non-pecuniary rights occurred, precluding any licence fee or costs.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the applicant's complaint on 6 April 2009 without reasons. The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 5 October 2009, arguing the Federal Court of Justice's approach failed to protect his Article 8 rights against commercial appropriation of his identity. British American Tobacco intervened in the Strasbourg proceedings.

**Case of Ernst August von Hannover v. Germany (ECHR, App. no. 53649/09, 19 Feb. 2015)**

Ernst August von Hannover (born 1954, resident in Monaco) alleged that German courts’ refusal to award him a “notional licence” (fiktive Lizenz) for the unauthorised commercial use of his forenames in an advertisement violated his Article 8 right to respect for private life.

In 1998 the applicant struck a cameraman with an umbrella outside his property. In January 2000 he was convicted of assault after a scuffle with a discotheque manager on Lamu Island, Kenya. Both incidents received press coverage, amplified by his relationship with Princess Caroline of Monaco.

On 27 March 2000 British American Tobacco (Germany) GmbH launched a ten-day campaign. Advertisements (full-page magazine placements and 6,364 posters at bus stops and busy locations across 18 towns, with a potential reach of 2.97 million people, plus media reports) showed a crumpled Lucky Strike packet with the headline “Was it Ernst? Or August?” and the tagline “Lucky Strike. Nothing else.” The crumpled packet alluded to the applicant’s fights.

The applicant demanded the campaign cease. The advertising agency agreed in writing, but the company refused. On 31 March 2000 the Hamburg Regional Court granted an interim injunction (confirmed 14 April 2000). The company discontinued the ads but refused to reimburse service costs. In March 2001 the applicant sought €250,000 damages; the company did not reply.

In December 2003 he sued for €100,000 as a notional licence, at least €500 non-pecuniary compensation for infringement of personality rights, and costs. On 21 January 2005 the Regional Court awarded €60,000 for the notional licence plus costs, rejecting non-pecuniary damages. It held that the relatively uncommon combination of forenames, the applicant’s fame, and the clear allusion to his public scuffles constituted unauthorised use of his name. Advertising enjoyed some freedom-of-expression protection if it shaped public opinion, but here the commercial, humorous nature of the ads meant personality rights (protected equally with expression under the Basic Law) prevailed. A notional licence prevented unjust enrichment; the amount reflected the applicant’s profile, media used, and limited use of forenames only. Non-pecuniary compensation was unnecessary given the public nature of the original incidents, the merely derisive tone, and the licence award.

On 15 May 2007 the Hamburg Court of Appeal largely upheld the judgment (varying only the costs order). It confirmed interference with the right to one’s name (well-known through press reports and the princely connection) and the pecuniary aspect of personality rights. The ads generated commercial advantage with negligible contribution to public debate; the incidents were not political or societal events of genuine interest but were exploited for entertainment. Unauthorised commercial use of a name required payment of a reasonable fee irrespective of whether consent would have been given. The fee was justified by the company’s size, the campaign’s scale and success, the applicant’s prominence, and public attention generated.

On 5 June 2008 the Federal Court of Justice quashed the decision. It accepted that a notional licence could in principle compensate unjust enrichment from unauthorised name use but held there was no unlawful interference. Only the non-pecuniary components of personality rights enjoy constitutional protection; pecuniary components are protected solely by ordinary civil law and therefore yield to the constitutional right of freedom of expression (Article 5 § 1 Basic Law). That right covers advertising that contributes to public opinion, including entertainment-oriented content. The satirical, derisive ads merely alluded (in a clever, indirect way) to already-publicised events of public interest arising from the applicant’s royal connection. They neither exploited his image/advertising value, suggested endorsement of the product, nor contained seriously degrading content. Consequently personality rights (pecuniary or non-pecuniary) were not violated, so neither a notional licence nor costs reimbursement was due.

On 6 April 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint, giving no reasons.

The applicant complained that this outcome failed to protect him against commercial appropriation of his identity, violating Article 8. (British American Tobacco was granted leave to intervene.)

The case of Momčilović v. Croatia (Application no. 11239/11) concerns three Croatian applicants—Barica Momčilović (born 1938), Nikola Momčilović (born 1938) and Darko Momčilović (born 1963)—who alleged a violation of their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Their claim for compensation against the State, arising from the unlawful killing of a close relative by a serving soldier, was declared inadmissible by the domestic courts on procedural grounds.

On 1 April 1993 the first and second applicants’ daughter (the third applicant’s sister) was killed in a bar by Z.R., then a soldier in the Croatian army. Z.R. was convicted of murder by the Karlovac Military Court and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment; on appeal the Supreme Court increased the sentence to nine years, rendering the conviction final on 17 February 1994.

On 15 January 1998 the applicants submitted a request to the State Attorney’s Office seeking an out-of-court settlement of their damages claim, as required by the then-applicable Military Service Act. After the request was refused they instituted civil proceedings on 5 March 1998 in the Zagreb Municipal Court against both the State and Z.R. They later withdrew the claim against Z.R. but maintained the action against the State. Because their representative failed to appear at several hearings, the Zagreb Municipal Court, applying section 216(4) of the Civil Procedure Act, deemed the action withdrawn on 14 March 2003. That decision became final. A subsequent attempt in 2005 to have the statement of finality quashed and to file a belated appeal was unsuccessful.

On 9 May 2005 the applicants lodged a fresh civil action in the now-competent Karlovac Municipal Court, again seeking damages from the State and Z.R. The State Attorney’s Office objected that the applicants had not submitted a new request for settlement before bringing the 2005 action, as required by section 186(a) of the Civil Procedure Act (introduced by 2003 amendments that entered into force on 1 December 2003). That provision obliges any person intending to sue the Republic of Croatia first to request a settlement from the competent State Attorney’s Office; only if the request is refused or remains undecided after three months may an action be filed. The court must declare any action lodged without compliance inadmissible.

On 17 March 2010 the Karlovac Municipal Court declared the claim against the State inadmissible for failure to seek a prior settlement. The Karlovac County Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 29 July 2010, holding that the duty under section 186(a) is a procedural prerequisite that must be fulfilled at the moment each action is lodged. The earlier 1998 request and the 2003 deemed withdrawal did not exempt the applicants from repeating the step. Section 193 of the Civil Procedure Act treats a withdrawn action as never having been submitted, so a new action must satisfy all current admissibility requirements. The Supreme Court, on 3 April 2013, endorsed this reasoning and rejected the applicants’ argument that the requirement unreasonably restricted access to court. It noted that a settlement request interrupts the limitation period and that an action may still be brought if the request is refused or unanswered, so the rule neither extinguishes the claim nor prevents a merits decision. The Constitutional Court declared the applicants’ constitutional complaint inadmissible on 23 March 2011, finding that the lower-court decisions did not determine civil rights or obligations.

The applicants contended that they had already complied with the settlement obligation in 1998 for an identical claim, that the State Attorney’s Office had already refused it and had contested the claim on the merits in the first proceedings, and that requiring a second request after a deemed withdrawal served no legitimate purpose and impaired their access to court. The domestic courts maintained that each new action, being treated as never previously submitted, independently triggered the statutory prerequisite.

The case of Momčilović v. Croatia (Application no. 11239/11) concerns three Croatian applicants—Barica Momčilović, Nikola Momčilović and Darko Momčilović—who alleged that domestic court decisions impaired their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Their claim arose from the 1 April 1993 killing of their daughter and sister by Z.R., a serving Croatian army soldier, in a bar. Z.R. was convicted of murder by the Karlovac Military Court and, after an appeal, received a final nine-year sentence from the Supreme Court on 17 February 1994.

In January 1998 the applicants first requested an out-of-court settlement of their damages claim from the State Attorney’s Office, as then required by the Military Service Act. After refusal they issued civil proceedings on 5 March 1998 in the Zagreb Municipal Court against both the State and Z.R. They later withdrew the claim against Z.R. The action against the State was deemed withdrawn on 14 March 2003 under section 216 § 4 of the Civil Procedure Act because their representative had failed to attend several hearings. That decision became final; subsequent attempts to revive it were unsuccessful.

On 9 May 2005 the applicants re-filed an identical claim in the now-competent Karlovac Municipal Court. By then, 2003 amendments to the Civil Procedure Act had introduced section 186(a), which made a fresh request for settlement with the State Attorney a mandatory precondition for any civil action against the Republic of Croatia. If the request is refused or unanswered within three months, an action may be lodged; otherwise the court must declare it inadmissible. The State Attorney objected that no such request had preceded the 2005 action.

On 17 March 2010 the Karlovac Municipal Court declared the claim against the State inadmissible. The Karlovac County Court upheld that ruling on 29 July 2010, holding that the settlement duty is a procedural requirement that must be satisfied at the moment each action is filed. The 1998 request and the later withdrawal of those proceedings (treated under section 193 as if the action had never been submitted) did not exempt the applicants from repeating the step. Section 186(a) applied only to actions lodged after 1 December 2003, so the 2005 claim was a new proceeding. The Supreme Court dismissed an appeal on points of law on 3 April 2013, adding that the requirement did not impair access to court because a timely request interrupts limitation periods and, if refused, still permits a meritorious action. A constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 23 March 2011 on the ground that the lower-court decisions did not determine civil rights.

The applicants maintained that insisting on a second, identical settlement request after the State had already rejected the claim and actively opposed it in court was an unreasonable formalistic barrier that denied them a hearing on the merits of their compensation claim. The case therefore turns on whether the domestic courts’ strict application of the post-2003 procedural precondition to a re-filed action, after an earlier attempt had been made and the first proceedings deemed withdrawn, unlawfully restricted access to court.

The applicants (Croatian nationals Barica, Nikola and Darko Momčilović) complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that Croatian courts had unreasonably restricted their right of access to a court by declaring inadmissible their civil claim for damages against the State arising from the 1993 killing of their close relative (the first and second applicants’ daughter and the third applicant’s sister) by a serving Croatian soldier, Z.R. Z.R. was convicted of murder by a military court (sentence increased on appeal to nine years’ imprisonment).

In January 1998 the applicants first requested an out-of-court settlement from the State Attorney’s Office, as then required by the Military Service Act. After refusal they lodged a civil action in March 1998 in the Zagreb Municipal Court against both the State and Z.R. They later withdrew the claim against Z.R. In March 2003, after their representative twice failed to appear at hearings, that court treated the remaining claim against the State as withdrawn pursuant to section 216(4) of the Civil Procedure Act. The decision became final.

In May 2005 the applicants re-lodged an identical claim in the now-competent Karlovac Municipal Court. The State Attorney objected that they had not first submitted a fresh settlement request. By then, 2003 amendments to the Civil Procedure Act (section 186(a), in force from 1 December 2003) had made such a request a mandatory precondition for any civil action against the State: the request interrupts prescription; if refused or unanswered within three months the claimant may sue; and any action filed without compliance is to be declared inadmissible. The first-instance court therefore declared the 2005 action against the State inadmissible. The County Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal, holding that the duty applied at the moment the new action was lodged, that the earlier (withdrawn) 1998 proceedings did not exempt them, and that section 186(a) did not apply to claims filed before December 2003. The Supreme Court later endorsed this reasoning, adding that the requirement did not impair access to court because a claimant who complies loses no substantive rights and can still obtain a merits decision once the three-month period expires or the request is refused. The Constitutional Court declared a related complaint inadmissible on the ground that the decisions did not determine civil rights.

The applicants argued that a second settlement request was pointless: they had already complied in 1998, the State Attorney had both refused settlement and contested the claim in court, and treating a withdrawn action as never having existed (section 193(3)) while simultaneously insisting on a new pre-action request created an unjustified formal obstacle. Relevant provisions of the Obligations Act (interruption and revival of limitation periods) and the unchanged Military Service Act were also in play, as were Council of Europe recommendations encouraging pre-litigation settlement.

The case of Muršić v. Croatia (Application no. 7334/13) concerns a Croatian national’s complaints under Articles 3 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding inadequate prison conditions and lack of an effective domestic remedy. The applicant, Kristijan Muršić (born 1987), was convicted of robbery and theft and received a combined sentence of two years and eleven months’ imprisonment. He was transferred to Bjelovar Prison on 16 October 2009 and remained there until 16 March 2011.

The applicant alleged that he spent eleven months sharing an 18 m² cell (including sanitary facilities) with seven other inmates. He claimed the cell was dirty, poorly maintained, and inadequately furnished, with insufficient lockers and chairs. He further complained of a complete lack of prison work opportunities and insufficient access to recreational or educational activities.

The Government provided a detailed occupancy table covering four cells. Personal space averaged 3.59 m² and frequently fell below 4 m² (the domestic statutory minimum under section 74 of the Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act). Periods of 2.80–2.86 m² occurred on multiple dates, while other intervals reached 3.19–3.81 m² or occasionally exceeded 4 m². The Government stated that each cell had a fully separated, ventilated toilet, drinking water, natural light and air, central heating, and regular maintenance (with documented renovations in 2007, 2009 and 2010). Hygiene facilities and nutrition met professional standards and were subject to official monitoring. The applicant had three hours of free movement daily (16:00–19:00), plus access to a gym, basketball and badminton courts, ping-pong, chess, library books, television and films.

The applicant lodged multiple domestic complaints. In March–May 2010 he requested a transfer to Varaždin Prison for family reasons and alleged inadequate food, ignored meeting requests and lack of work. The Ministry of Justice Prison Administration rejected these claims in July 2010, noting seven meetings with the governor, twenty-five meetings with other officials, expert-supervised diet and insufficient work posts. In August 2010 he applied to a sentence-execution judge, citing the transfer request, absence of work and overcrowding in an 18 m² cell. After obtaining a prison report and hearing the applicant, the judge dismissed the complaint in October 2010, finding conditions, hygiene and sanitation adequate and work unavailable to all inmates. A three-judge panel of the Bjelovar County Court upheld this decision, observing that temporary non-compliance with the 4 m² standard did not automatically violate prisoners’ rights.

The applicant then complained to the Constitutional Court (invoking equality and fair-trial provisions) and the Ombudsman. The Ombudsman confirmed in April 2011 that personal space fell short of the statutory 4 m² requirement but noted 2010 renovations, compliance with hygiene/health standards and the same work shortage affecting 92 other inmates. On 5 June 2012 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, finding no violation of constitutional rights or arbitrary application of law.

Relevant domestic law (Articles 23 and 25 of the Constitution) prohibits ill-treatment and requires humane treatment of detainees. The Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act guarantees 4 m² and 10 m³ per prisoner and provides complaint and judicial-protection mechanisms (sections 15 and 17). The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture’s 2012 visit report highlighted Croatian prison overcrowding and recommended at least 4 m² of living space (excluding sanitary facilities) plus improved work and activity programmes.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 violation (conditions falling below Convention standards, particularly personal space and purposeful activity) and the Article 13 complaint (ineffectiveness of the available remedies, culminating in the Constitutional Court’s summary dismissal). The Chamber judgment of 12 March 2015 was later referred to the Grand Chamber.

The case of Muršić v. Croatia (Application no. 7334/13) originated in a 2012 application by Croatian national Kristijan Muršić (born 1987) alleging violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention due to inadequate conditions of detention at Bjelovar Prison (particularly insufficient personal space and lack of work opportunities) and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

Muršić was convicted of robbery (two-year sentence, final in 2009) and theft (one-year sentence, final in 2010). These were combined into a single term of two years and eleven months. He was transferred to Bjelovar Prison on 16 October 2009 and held there until 16 March 2011, when he was moved to Varaždin Prison.

The applicant claimed he spent eleven months sharing an 18 m² cell (including sanitary facilities) with seven other inmates. He described the cell as poorly maintained, dirty, and inadequately furnished (insufficient lockers and chairs). He also alleged no prison work opportunities and insufficient access to recreational or educational activities.

The Government submitted detailed records showing the applicant was detained in four different cells, with personal space averaging 3.59 m². Occupancy fluctuated, with multiple periods of eight inmates in cells of 22.36–22.88 m², yielding as little as 2.80–2.86 m² per person, and numerous other periods below 4 m² (and some below 3 m²). Cells had fully separate, ventilated toilets; access to drinking water; windows providing natural light and air; and central heating in winter. Facilities were maintained, with documented reconstructions in 2007, 2009, and 2010. Hygiene and sanitary provisions were supplied, and nutrition (expert-assessed and state-monitored) was adequate.

The applicant had three hours of free movement outside his cell daily (4–7 p.m.), plus access to a gym, basketball court, badminton, ping-pong, chess, library books from the local service, television, and films.

Muršić made repeated complaints seeking transfer closer to his family and raising conditions issues. A March 2010 transfer request and April 2010 general complaint to the Ministry of Justice Prisons Administration (alleging ignored requests, lack of meetings, and poor food) were rejected in July 2010 as unfounded; officials noted sufficient family contact, insufficient work posts prison-wide, multiple meetings with staff, and supervised diet. In August 2010 he complained to a sentence-execution judge of the Bjelovar County Court about the transfer denial, unanswered work request, and detention of eight inmates in an 18 m² cell that was poorly equipped and maintained. After obtaining a prison report and hearing the applicant, the judge dismissed the complaint in October 2010, finding conditions and hygiene adequate and work unavailable to all inmates. A subsequent appeal to a three-judge panel was dismissed; the panel acknowledged the statutory 4 m² standard but held there was no automatic rights violation from temporary shortfalls.

Further submissions to the county court detailed specific cells and occupancies (including six or eight inmates in cells of about 17 m²). A November 2010 constitutional complaint (invoking equality and fair-trial provisions) alleging lack of space and work was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded in June 2012. A contemporaneous Ombudsman complaint yielded a 2011 reply noting that accommodation fell short of the statutory 4 m² standard but that the relevant cell had been renovated in 2010, met hygiene/health standards, and that work posts were insufficient for 93 inmates including the applicant.

Relevant domestic law included constitutional prohibitions on ill-treatment and requirements of humane, dignified treatment of prisoners, plus the Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act requiring clean, dry, spacious premises with a minimum of 4 m² and 10 m³ per prisoner, a qualified right to work, and complaint/judicial-protection procedures (to governors, the Prisons Administration, or sentence-execution judges, with appeals). The CPT’s 2012 visit report highlighted overcrowding across Croatian prisons and recommended at least 4 m² of living space per prisoner in multi-occupancy cells (excluding sanitary facilities) plus improved work and activity programmes.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 issues of overcrowding and inadequate conditions, and the Article 13 claim that domestic mechanisms failed to provide effective redress despite clear statutory space standards.

The case of Muršić v. Croatia (no. 7334/13) was brought by Croatian national Kristijan Muršić (born 1987) under Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. He alleged inhuman/degrading detention conditions in Bjelovar Prison—chiefly insufficient personal space, no work opportunities and inadequate activities—plus the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

Following convictions for robbery and theft, Muršić received a combined sentence of two years and eleven months. He was held in Bjelovar Prison from 16 October 2009 until 16 March 2011.

The applicant claimed he spent eleven months with seven other inmates in an 18 m² cell (including sanitary facilities) that was dirty, poorly maintained and insufficiently furnished. He was given no prison work and insufficient recreational or educational opportunities.

The Government supplied occupancy data showing the applicant occupied four cells whose personal space averaged 3.59 m² and fluctuated between 2.80 m² and 7.39 m². Periods of eight inmates in 22.88 m² cells produced 2.86 m² per person for several weeks; similar shortfalls occurred in other cells. Each cell had a fully partitioned, ventilated toilet, drinking water, windows for light and air, and central heating. Facilities had been renovated in 2007, 2009 and 2010; hygiene, sanitation and nutritionally supervised meals met official standards. The applicant enjoyed three hours of free movement outside the cell daily plus access to a gym, outdoor sports courts, indoor games, a library, television and films.

Muršić repeatedly sought transfer to Varaždin Prison for family reasons and complained about conditions. A March 2010 transfer request and April 2010 complaint to the Ministry of Justice (ignored meetings, food, transfer) were rejected in July 2010: family contact was adequate, work posts were limited, he had had numerous official meetings, and the diet was expert-supervised. In August 2010 he applied to a sentence-execution judge, highlighting overcrowding (cell 8, claimed 18 m² with eight inmates), lack of work and the transfer request. After a prison report and personal hearing the judge dismissed the complaint in October 2010, finding conditions and hygiene adequate and work unavailable to all inmates. A three-judge panel upheld that decision, observing that the statutory 4 m² standard need not be observed at every moment. Subsequent complaints to the County Court, the Ombudsman (who acknowledged the space shortfall but noted 2010 renovations, hygiene compliance and the general unavailability of work) and the Constitutional Court (declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded in June 2012) failed.

Relevant domestic law comprised Constitution Articles 23 and 25 (prohibition of ill-treatment and duty of humane treatment) and the Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act (ss. 15 and 17: administrative and judicial complaints; s. 74: minimum 4 m² and 10 m³ per prisoner; s. 80: entitlement to work according to capacity and available posts). The CPT’s 2012 visit recorded systemic overcrowding in Croatian prisons and recommended a minimum of 4 m² (excluding sanitary annexes) together with expanded work and activities.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 violation (whether the space, hygiene, activities and duration reached the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment) and the Article 13 claim (whether the complaint, judicial-protection and constitutional procedures constituted an effective remedy).
