**CASE OF DIMECH v. MALTA (Application no. 34373/13), ECtHR (Fifth Section), 2 April 2015 (final 2 July 2015)**

Martin Dimech, a Maltese national born in 1960, alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) due to the absence of legal assistance during pre-trial police questioning. Maltese law introduced a right to legal assistance at the pre-trial stage by Act III of 2002, but this only entered into force in 2010 via Legal Notice 35 of 2010. Prior to that date, suspects had no right to a lawyer during police questioning or investigative magistrate inquiries, though they were cautioned about the right to remain silent and the possible use of any statements as evidence. No adverse inferences could then be drawn from silence. Statements could later be confirmed on oath before the Court of Magistrates with a lawyer present.

On 30 April 2009 a magistrate authorised a search of residence F. The search on 1 May 2009 uncovered five bags of heroin (925.26 g at 35% purity), €755 in cash, weighing scales and cut plastic bags. Dimech was arrested on 2 May 2009, cautioned and questioned without a lawyer on suspicion of drug trafficking. He gave a signed statement admitting possession of approximately 800 g of heroin, which he said he had accepted as security for a debt and hidden in his fridge, while asserting that his partner knew nothing of it. He denied ownership of the drugs and any personal use or sale. He confirmed the statement was voluntary, given without threats or inducements, and that he did not wish to alter it.

A magisterial inquiry (in genere) took place on 13 May 2009. Dimech was arraigned on 20 May 2009; both the inquiry record and his police statement were adduced as evidence. Further evidence was gathered during committal proceedings. A bill of indictment issued on 8 July 2010. Dimech asked the Criminal Court to refer the legal-assistance complaint to the constitutional courts; the request was granted.

The Civil Court (First Hall), acting in its constitutional jurisdiction, examined the merits while the criminal case remained pending. On 10 January 2012 it found a breach of the fair-trial right because Dimech had been unassisted when he made his statement. It held that the caution and the statement’s voluntary character did not cure the defect, since it was impossible to know what he would have said with legal advice. The court directed the Criminal Court to take the breach into account when assessing the evidence.

Both parties appealed. On 26 April 2013 the Constitutional Court reversed the finding. It treated the right to counsel as a safeguard against abusive questioning, not a mere formality whose absence automatically invalidated a trial. Relying on its reading of Salduz v. Turkey, it required additional elements of vulnerability or prejudice. Dimech had admitted he was not pressured; the statement was therefore neither illicit nor abusive. He was an adult of mature years with no special vulnerability, and he had not demonstrated that the lack of a lawyer created an objective risk of an unfair trial. Consequently no Convention violation had occurred and no remedy was needed.

Dimech’s jury trial, scheduled for 23 October 2013, was stayed after he lodged further constitutional proceedings and the Strasbourg application. The Strasbourg Court later granted the case priority under Rule 41.

The relevant domestic provision (Article 355AT of the Criminal Code, in force from February 2010) now entitles an arrested person to consult a lawyer privately for up to one hour before questioning and requires the police to inform the suspect of that right. Constitutional redress is available under Article 4 of the European Convention Act. Early 2011 Constitutional Court judgments (Privitera, Pullicino, Lombardi) had applied Salduz strictly and found violations where unassisted statements formed the sole or principal evidence, even without proven coercion. Subsequent decisions, including the one in Dimech’s case, adopted a more restrictive approach requiring proof of vulnerability, pressure or concrete prejudice.

The case of Dimech v. Malta (Application no. 34373/13) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). The Maltese applicant, Martin Dimech (born 1960), claimed he was denied a fair trial due to the lack of legal assistance during pre-trial police questioning.

At the material time, Maltese law (prior to Legal Notice 35 of 2010 bringing into force 2002 amendments) did not entitle suspects to a lawyer during investigations or questioning by police or an inquiring magistrate. Suspects were merely cautioned of their right to remain silent (with no adverse inferences permitted from silence at that stage). Statements could later be confirmed on oath before a court with legal assistance available then.

On 30 April 2009 a search warrant was issued. On 1 May 2009 a search of residence F uncovered 925.26 grams of heroin (35% purity), €755 in cash, scales, and cut plastic bags. The applicant was arrested on 2 May 2009, cautioned, and questioned without a lawyer on suspicion of drug trafficking. He gave a signed statement admitting certain facts while denying others: he explained that he held approximately 800 grams of heroin found at his home as a guarantee for a debt owed to him, knowing the drugs would serve as that guarantee when he lent the money; he had hidden the drugs in his fridge; and his partner was unaware and uninvolved. He denied that the drugs belonged to him and denied ever using or selling drugs. He confirmed the statement was made voluntarily, without threats or promises, and that he did not wish to alter it.

A magisterial inquiry (in genere) occurred on 13 May 2009. The applicant was arraigned on 20 May 2009, at which point the inquiry report (procès verbal) and his statement were produced as evidence. Additional witness and documentary evidence was later collected during committal proceedings. A bill of indictment issued on 8 July 2010.

During the criminal case the applicant sought a referral to the constitutional courts regarding the absence of legal assistance. The Civil Court (First Hall), sitting in its constitutional jurisdiction, examined the merits on 10 January 2012 despite the ongoing criminal trial. It found a violation of the right to a fair trial because the applicant had made his statement to police without a lawyer. The court held that the statement’s voluntary nature and the caution given did not remedy the deficiency, as it was impossible to know how the applicant would have acted with legal advice. It directed the Criminal Court to take the breach into account when assessing all evidence.

Both sides appealed. On 26 April 2013 the Constitutional Court reversed the finding. It held that the right to legal assistance is not a mere formality whose absence automatically vitiates proceedings. A breach occurs only if a statement is taken abusively (without legitimacy guarantees) or if the suspect is particularly vulnerable; the mere making of a mixed admission/denial statement without a lawyer does not suffice. The applicant had admitted he was not pressured, so there was nothing illicit in the taking of the statement. He lacked the vulnerability present in cases such as Salduz v. Turkey. No prejudice sufficient to endanger a fair trial had been shown. Consequently no violation existed and no remedy was required.

The applicant’s jury trial (scheduled for 23 October 2013) was suspended on 23 September 2013 pending the Strasbourg proceedings and a separate Article 7 constitutional claim.

Subsequent Maltese law (Article 355AT of the Criminal Code) entitled arrested persons to a private one-hour consultation with a lawyer (in person or by telephone) as soon as practicable and required police to inform them of this right before questioning. Early 2011 Constitutional Court decisions had applied Salduz more strictly and found violations in analogous cases (even without full admissions). Later domestic jurisprudence required additional elements such as vulnerability, pressure or lack of caution before finding a breach.

The case of Dimech v. Malta (Application no. 34373/13) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial) due to the absence of legal assistance during the applicant’s pre-trial police questioning. Martin Dimech, a Maltese national born in 1960, was arrested on 2 May 2009 on suspicion of drug trafficking after a search of his residence the previous day uncovered 925.26 grams of heroin (35% purity), cash, weighing scales and packaging materials.

At the relevant time, Maltese law (prior to Legal Notice 35 of 2010) provided no right to a lawyer during police investigation or questioning. Suspects were merely cautioned that they could remain silent and that statements could be used as evidence; no adverse inferences could be drawn from silence. After the caution, Dimech—unassisted—gave a signed statement admitting he had knowingly accepted and hidden approximately 800 grams of heroin as security for a debt, while denying ownership, use or sale of drugs and insisting his partner was unaware. He confirmed the statement was voluntary and truthful.

A magisterial inquiry followed. On 20 May 2009 Dimech was arraigned; his statement and the inquiry procès-verbal were produced as evidence, together with later witness and documentary material. A bill of indictment issued on 8 July 2010. Dimech applied to the Criminal Court to refer the legal-assistance issue to the constitutional courts.

The Civil Court (First Hall), sitting in its constitutional jurisdiction, found a violation of Article 6 on 10 January 2012. It held that the caution and the statement’s apparent voluntariness could not compensate for the lack of counsel, because it was impossible to know how Dimech would have acted had a lawyer been present. It directed the Criminal Court to take the breach into account when assessing the evidence.

The Constitutional Court reversed that judgment on 26 April 2013. Interpreting Salduz v. Turkey restrictively, it ruled that the mere absence of a lawyer does not automatically breach Article 6. A violation arises only when a statement is obtained abusively or the suspect is shown to have been particularly vulnerable, thereby compromising the overall fairness of the trial. Dimech had admitted he was not pressured; he displayed no special vulnerability (age, immaturity or similar factors); and no objective prejudice had been demonstrated. Consequently no remedy was required.

Dimech’s jury trial, scheduled for October 2013, was stayed pending further constitutional proceedings and the Strasbourg application lodged on 22 May 2013. The European Court of Human Rights later examined whether the systemic denial of legal assistance at the investigative stage, and the use of the resulting statement, rendered the criminal proceedings unfair.

The case of Sarközi and Mahran v. Austria concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to private and family life) arising from an eight-year exclusion order against the first applicant and her 2012 expulsion to Slovakia.

Jana Sarközi (first applicant), a Slovak national born in 1966, entered Austria in 1990 and obtained permanent residence in 1997. She married an Austrian citizen; their son Mohamed Mahran (second applicant), an Austrian national born in Vienna in 2002, resulted from the marriage. The couple later divorced but retained joint custody. The first applicant has further family in Austria (a daughter from a prior marriage plus the daughter's husband and child, her brother, and her parents). The second applicant lives in Vienna with his father and has additional relatives there (grandparents, uncle, half-sister and her family).

The first applicant has seven convictions (1993–2008): bodily harm (1993, fine); attempted aggravated fraud (1994, five months suspended); property damage (1995, fine); property damage, bodily harm and assault on a police officer (2002, three months suspended); fraud (2003, two months suspended, jointly with her ex-husband); aggravated fraud (2006, six months); and partly attempted/completed aggravated fraud on a commercial basis (2008, three years' imprisonment). She served the last sentence from September 2007 to December 2010, during which the second applicant lived with his father.

After a 1994 warning, an unlimited exclusion order was issued in September 2008 under the Aliens Police Act, citing her as a threat to public order/security (especially repeated fraud as a source of income) that outweighed her long residence and family ties. Her appeal was dismissed in April 2009: the panel stressed her persistent offending from soon after arrival, disregard for property and physical integrity, the fact that family ties had not deterred her, Slovakia's proximity (one hour by train, facilitating visits), her capacity to reintegrate there, and the possibility of later review. Higher courts rejected further complaints. After a legal amendment capping such orders for EEA citizens at ten years, the duration was reduced in 2011 to eight years (to September 2016). Later applications to lift it failed. She was expelled on 4 December 2012; the second applicant remained with his father (joint custody continuing).

Evidence of impact included a 2012 Youth and Family Office statement that the imprisonment separation had already traumatized the child and that another would re-traumatize him and impair his development. Psychological reports diagnosed the second applicant with PTSD, emotional disorder and separation anxiety (including suicidal ideation after learning of the expulsion). The first applicant was diagnosed with depression, anxiety, claustrophobia and pre-suicidal syndrome.

These facts underpin the claim that the measures disproportionately interfered with family life, particularly the child's best interests, given the first applicant's long-term residence and integration.

The case of Sarközi and Mahran v. Austria (Application no. 27945/10) concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention arising from an eight-year exclusion order imposed on the first applicant (a Slovak national) and her subsequent expulsion from Austria, which the applicants claimed interfered disproportionately with their right to respect for private and family life.

The first applicant, Jana Sarközi (born 1966), entered Austria in 1990 on a visa, obtained temporary residence permits, and was granted a permanent residence permit in 1997. She married an Austrian citizen; their son, the second applicant Mohamed Mahran (born 2002 in Vienna and an Austrian national), was the product of that marriage. The couple later divorced but retained joint custody. The first applicant’s other close relatives in Austria included a daughter from a prior marriage (together with that daughter’s husband and child), her brother, and her parents. The second applicant resided in Vienna with his father; his additional Austrian-based relatives comprised his grandparents, an uncle, a half-sister and her family.

The first applicant accumulated seven criminal convictions between 1993 and 2008. These comprised offences of deliberately causing bodily harm (1993, fine), attempted aggravated fraud (1994, five months’ imprisonment suspended), causing damage to property (1995, fine), causing damage to property, bodily harm and assault on a police officer (2002, three months’ imprisonment suspended), fraud (2003, two months’ imprisonment suspended, jointly with her former husband), aggravated fraud (2006, six months’ imprisonment), and partly attempted, partly completed aggravated fraud committed on a commercial basis (2008, three years’ imprisonment). She served the final sentence from September 2007 until December 2010; during that period the second applicant lived with his father. The Aliens Police had formally warned her in 1994 that a further conviction could trigger an exclusion order.

Following the 2008 conviction the Vienna Federal Police Authority issued an unlimited exclusion order under the Aliens Police Act, holding that her continued presence endangered public order and safety and that the public interest in preventing crime and protecting Austria’s economic well-being outweighed her private- and family-life interests. On appeal the Vienna Independent Administrative Panel confirmed the order in April 2009. It emphasised the long-term, income-generating nature of her property offences, her earlier violent convictions, and the absence of any indication that the risk she posed had diminished. Although it recognised her 17-plus years of residence, integration and family ties (especially to her then seven-year-old son), it found the interference proportionate, noting the short travel distance to Slovakia and her ability to reintegrate there. Subsequent complaints to the Constitutional Court and Administrative Court were rejected. After a change in the law limiting exclusion orders against EEA nationals to a maximum of ten years, the duration was reduced to eight years (expiring 29 September 2016). Further applications to lift the order were unsuccessful.

Medical evidence later submitted included a 2012 statement by the Vienna Youth and Family Office that the first applicant’s imprisonment had already traumatised the second applicant and that a further separation would re-traumatise him and jeopardise his psychosocial development. Psychological and neurological reports diagnosed the child with post-traumatic stress disorder, emotional disorder and separation anxiety (including suicidal ideation) and the first applicant with depression, anxiety, claustrophobia and a pre-suicidal syndrome. The first applicant was expelled to Slovakia on 4 December 2012; the second applicant has since lived with his father in Vienna, the parents retaining joint custody.

These facts formed the core of the applicants’ complaint that the exclusion order and expulsion constituted a disproportionate interference with their Article 8 rights, particularly given the child’s Austrian nationality, the family’s long-established ties in Austria, and the documented risk of serious psychological harm from renewed separation.

**Summary of Sarközi and Mahran v. Austria (ECHR, Application no. 27945/10, Judgment 2 April 2015)**

The applicants—Jana Sarközi (first applicant, Slovak national born 1966) and her son Mohamed Mahran (second applicant, Austrian national born 2002)—alleged that an eight-year exclusion order against the first applicant and her 2012 expulsion from Austria to Slovakia violated their right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first applicant entered Austria in 1990 on a visa, obtained successive temporary residence permits, and was granted a permanent residence permit in 1997. She married an Austrian citizen; their son (the second applicant) was born in Vienna in 2002. The couple later divorced but retained joint custody. Additional family members of both applicants resided in Austria, including the first applicant’s daughter from a prior marriage (and that daughter’s family), brother, and parents, as well as the second applicant’s grandparents, uncle, and half-sister. The first applicant was well integrated in Austria after nearly two decades of lawful residence.

The first applicant had a substantial criminal record comprising seven convictions between 1993 and 2008. These included causing bodily harm (1993, fine), attempted aggravated fraud (1994, five months’ imprisonment suspended), property damage (1995, fine), bodily harm, property damage and assault on a police officer (2002, three months’ imprisonment suspended), fraud (2003, two months’ imprisonment suspended, jointly with her former husband), aggravated fraud (2006, six months’ imprisonment), and partly attempted/partly completed aggravated fraud on a commercial basis (2008, three years’ imprisonment). She served the final sentence from September 2007 to December 2010; during this period the second applicant lived with his father.

In 1994 the Aliens Police had already warned her that a further conviction could lead to an exclusion order. Following the 2008 conviction, the Vienna Federal Police Authority issued an unlimited exclusion order in September 2008 under the Aliens Police Act. The authorities cited her persistent criminality—particularly property offences used as a source of income and earlier violent offences—as creating a serious, ongoing threat to public order and safety. They acknowledged interference with her private and family life (children and parents in Austria) but held that the public interest in protecting Austria’s economic well-being and preventing crime outweighed her interests. The Independent Administrative Panel dismissed her appeal in April 2009, emphasising the duration and nature of her offending, her personality profile, and the fact that she was still serving her sentence (so the risk had not diminished). It noted her integration and family ties, including to her then seven-year-old son, but found the order proportionate: the short distance between Vienna and Bratislava would allow frequent family visits, she spoke Slovak and could reintegrate in her country of origin, and family presence in Austria had not previously deterred her. An unlimited duration was justified because it was impossible to predict when the risk would cease; she could later apply for lifting if circumstances changed. The Constitutional Court and Administrative Court rejected further challenges.

In 2010 the first applicant applied to have the order lifted. In 2011 the Independent Administrative Panel reduced its duration to eight years (expiring September 2016) after a change in the law limiting exclusion orders against EEA citizens. Subsequent attempts to lift the order failed. She was expelled to Slovakia on 4 December 2012; the second applicant thereafter lived with his father in Vienna, with both parents retaining joint custody.

Medical and social-welfare evidence highlighted the impact of separation. A 2012 Youth and Family Office statement described the earlier imprisonment-related separation as already traumatising for the second applicant and warned that further separation would re-traumatise him and jeopardise his psychosocial development. Psychological and neurological reports diagnosed the second applicant with post-traumatic stress disorder, emotional disorder and separation anxiety, noting suicidal thoughts after learning of the planned expulsion. The first applicant was diagnosed with depression, anxiety, claustrophobia and a pre-suicidal syndrome.

These facts formed the core of the Article 8 complaint: a long-term integrated resident and mother of a young Austrian child was excluded and expelled on public-order grounds arising from repeated (mainly property) offences, despite close family ties and documented mental-health consequences of separation. The domestic authorities had balanced the competing interests but concluded that the measure remained necessary and proportionate.

The case of O’Donnell v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 16667/10) concerned an Irish national, Matthew O’Donnell (born 1980, IQ of 62 placing him in the bottom 1% of the population, with spoken-English comprehension equivalent to a six-year-old), who alleged that his murder trial in Northern Ireland violated Article 6 § 1 ECHR. Specifically, the trial judge permitted the jury to draw an adverse inference from O’Donnell’s failure to testify and failed to direct the jury that they must first find a case to answer on the prosecution evidence.

On 13 October 2004, the body of Mr Williamson was discovered on the banks of the Blackwater River in County Tyrone. He had been extensively beaten and suffered knife wounds, including severance of the carotid artery. The previous day, O’Donnell had spent time drinking in public with the deceased and Samuel Houston. Witnesses described both Houston and O’Donnell as threatening and aggressive toward various individuals, including the deceased. One witness reported that when Houston produced a knife and threatened to kill the deceased, O’Donnell encouraged him to “just kill him.” The pair also challenged the deceased to a fight after being refused entry to a public house. The three men were last seen alive around 1:30 a.m. heading toward a park by the river.

A search of O’Donnell’s flat uncovered two sets of clothing heavily stained with the deceased’s blood (including beige-and-navy tracksuit bottoms bearing O’Donnell’s name tag) and a plastic bag containing a knife with matching blood. Medical evidence indicated the knife could have inflicted the wounds. Houston admitted manslaughter and received a 10-year sentence. O’Donnell was arrested in the Republic of Ireland, where videotaped interviews took place, then extradited to Northern Ireland in April 2007.

At trial, the prosecution sought to rely on those interviews, but the judge excluded them after a voir dire because procedures for interviewing a mentally handicapped suspect had not been followed. At the close of the prosecution case, the judge rejected a defence submission of no case to answer. The defence then applied under Article 4(1)(b) of the Criminal Evidence (Northern Ireland) Order 1988 for a ruling that O’Donnell’s mental condition made it undesirable for him to give evidence, which would have precluded any adverse inference from silence. In a second voir dire, psychologist Dr Davies was barred from referring to the excluded interview tapes but testified that O’Donnell’s low IQ would make him highly suggestible, impair his understanding of questions, and hinder coherent responses. Psychiatrist Dr Kennedy’s report, however, indicated that with simply phrased material and adequate consultation, O’Donnell should be capable of following proceedings and contributing.

The judge refused the application, stating he could control questioning to avoid unfairness, and indicated he would give an adverse-inference direction if O’Donnell did not testify. O’Donnell elected not to give evidence; Dr Davies was permitted to testify to the jury about his vulnerabilities. The prosecution invited an adverse inference. In summing up, the judge reminded the jury of the right to silence and the prosecution’s burden, explained that inferences could be drawn if they considered it proper, highlighted Dr Davies’s evidence of limited intellect and difficulties, but noted the absence of any claim of unfitness to stand trial, inability to instruct lawyers, or memory loss (citing O’Donnell’s reply on charge: “I didn’t go near him”). He emphasised that the court would have ensured simplified, non-leading questions and that silence could not alone prove guilt, though it might provide additional support if unexplained.

O’Donnell was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment with a 12-year minimum term. Appeals on three grounds—exclusion of tape-related evidence from Dr Davies, the ruling that testifying was not undesirable, and the lack of a “case to answer” direction—were refused by a single judge and dismissed by the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal held that the omitted tape evidence was immaterial, that the trial judge had reasonably preferred Dr Kennedy’s evidence, and that the strong prosecution case (bloody clothing, knife, and circumstantial evidence of joint enterprise) made a specific “case to answer” direction unnecessary under then-prevailing Northern Ireland practice (unlike the mandatory approach in England and Wales). It nonetheless recommended aligning Northern Ireland specimen directions with the latter.

The European Court of Human Rights examined whether these rulings rendered the trial unfair.

**CASE OF O’DONNELL v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (Application no. 16667/10), ECtHR (Fourth Section), Judgment of 7 April 2015 (final 7 July 2015)**

Irish national Matthew O’Donnell (born 1980, IQ 62 in the bottom 1% of the population, spoken English comprehension equivalent to a six-year-old) was convicted in Northern Ireland of the murder of Mr Williamson, whose body was found on 13 October 2004 by the Blackwater River. The previous day the applicant, the deceased and Samuel Houston had been drinking; witnesses described threats and aggression, including Houston producing a knife and the applicant allegedly encouraging him to “just kill him.” The three were last seen around 1:30 a.m. heading to a riverside park. The deceased had been beaten and suffered knife wounds, including a severed carotid artery.

Police found two sets of blood-stained clothing (including items with the applicant’s name tag) matching the deceased’s blood at the applicant’s flat, plus a knife in a bag with matching blood. Houston admitted manslaughter and received 10 years. The applicant, arrested in Ireland and interviewed on videotape, was extradited. At trial the interviews were excluded after a voir dire, as proper procedures for a mentally handicapped suspect had not been followed.

The trial judge rejected a no-case-to-answer submission. The defence then sought a ruling under Article 4(1)(b) of the Criminal Evidence (Northern Ireland) Order 1988 that the applicant’s mental condition made it undesirable for him to give evidence, which would have precluded an adverse inference from silence. In a second voir dire, clinical psychologist Dr Davies testified to the applicant’s high suggestibility, difficulty understanding questions, and likely incoherent responses. Consultant psychiatrist Dr Kennedy opined that, with simplified phrasing and consultation, he could follow proceedings and contribute. The judge refused the application, stating he could control questioning to avoid unfairness, and indicated he would give an adverse-inference direction if the applicant did not testify.

The applicant did not give evidence. Dr Davies testified to the jury about his vulnerabilities. The prosecution invited an adverse inference. The judge directed the jury on the right to silence, that they might draw proper inferences from failure to testify, and that they should consider Dr Davies’s evidence of limited intellect and comprehension difficulties. He also noted no suggestion of unfitness to stand trial or inability to instruct lawyers, the applicant’s reply on charge (“I didn’t go near him”), that the court would have ensured simplified, non-leading questions, and that silence alone could not prove guilt but could provide additional support if there was no adequate explanation (such as having no answer that would withstand cross-examination). The applicant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment with a 12-year minimum term.

He appealed on three grounds: exclusion of Dr Davies’s evidence from the interview tapes; error in rejecting the “undesirable to testify” ruling; and failure to direct the jury that they must find a case to answer before drawing an adverse inference. The Court of Appeal (Northern Ireland) dismissed the appeal. It held that the tapes, while potentially admissible on expression/suggestibility, were not material (suggestibility was undisputed). The judge had properly balanced competing expert evidence and preferred Dr Kennedy’s view; the conclusion was not unreasonable. On the third ground, unlike in England and Wales (where R v Cowan requires a “case to answer” direction before inferences), Northern Ireland practice left it to the trial judge according to the strength of the evidence. Here the prosecution case was substantial, so no such direction was required and the trial was not unfair. The court nonetheless recommended aligning the specimen direction with Cowan.

The applicant alleged that permitting an adverse inference from his silence (given his intellectual disability) and omitting a “case to answer” direction violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). These facts formed the core of the complaints communicated to the Government.

**Case of O'Donnell v. the United Kingdom (ECtHR, App. No. 16667/10, 7 April 2015)**

The applicant, Matthew O'Donnell (Irish national, born 1980, IQ of 62 equivalent to a six-year-old's spoken English comprehension), was convicted in Northern Ireland of murdering Mr Williamson (found beaten and knifed on 13 October 2004) and sentenced to life with a 12-year minimum. He alleged an Article 6 § 1 fair-trial violation because the trial judge permitted the jury to draw an adverse inference from his silence and failed to direct them to consider whether there was a case to answer.

Key facts of the offence: The applicant, the deceased, and Samuel Houston (who later admitted manslaughter) spent 12 October 2004 drinking. Witnesses described threats and aggression by Houston and the applicant toward others, including the deceased; one said Houston produced a knife and threatened to kill the deceased, with the applicant urging “just kill him.” They were last seen around 1:30 a.m. heading to a riverside park. Two bloodstained clothing sets (one with the applicant’s name tag) matching the deceased’s blood, plus a knife in a bag with matching blood, were found at the applicant’s premises. The two clothing sets supported the prosecution theory of two killers.

The applicant was arrested in Ireland, interviewed on videotape (later excluded at a voir dire because procedures for a mentally handicapped suspect were not followed), and extradited. At trial, after the prosecution case, the judge rejected a “no case to answer” submission. The defence then applied under Article 4(1)(b) of the Criminal Evidence (Northern Ireland) Order 1988 for a ruling that the applicant’s mental condition made it “undesirable” for him to give evidence, which would have barred any adverse-inference direction.

A second voir dire featured psychologist Dr Davies (who expressed doubts the applicant could give a coherent account even with simplified questions, citing high suggestibility and limited comprehension) and psychiatrist Dr Kennedy (who considered him capable of following proceedings and contributing if material was simply phrased and consultation allowed). The judge refused to let Davies rely on the excluded interview tapes. Preferring Kennedy’s evidence, the judge ruled the applicant could testify fairly (the court would control questioning) and indicated an adverse-inference direction would follow if he remained silent. The applicant did not testify; Davies gave evidence to the jury on his vulnerabilities.

The prosecution invited an adverse inference. The judge directed the jury that silence was the applicant’s right, the prosecution still had to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and they could draw proper inferences from silence. He summarised Davies’ evidence on IQ, suggestibility, and difficulties, but noted the applicant was fit to stand trial, could instruct lawyers, had replied “I didn’t go near him” when charged (implying possible knowledge), and that difficulty giving evidence (even for children) does not automatically excuse silence. The court would have ensured simple, non-leading questions. If Davies’ evidence provided no adequate explanation, they could treat silence as supporting the prosecution (but not as the sole or main basis for conviction) and consider what questions the applicant would have faced. The applicant was convicted.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal (NI) refused leave. It held exclusion of the tapes was immaterial (suggestibility was undisputed). The “undesirable” ruling was balanced and reasonable given competing expert evidence. Unlike England and Wales (where R v Cowan requires a “case to answer” direction before any inference), Northern Ireland left this to the judge’s discretion based on case strength; here the evidence was substantial, so the omission did not render the trial unfair (though the court recommended aligning the specimen direction with Cowan). Questions of public importance were not certified.

Relevant law (Art. 4 of the 1988 Order) permits inferences from silence unless the accused’s mental/physical condition makes giving evidence undesirable; it does not compel testimony. English authorities (Cowan) emphasise that juries must find a case to answer before inferring, an inference cannot prove guilt alone, and silence must be attributable only to having no answer. Northern Ireland practice at the time differed on the case-to-answer direction.

**Case summary: Muradeli v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 72780/12)**

The applicant, a Georgian national born in 1969, alleged that Russia’s 2011 administrative removal order violated his Article 8 right to respect for private and family life. He had long-term ties to Russia through marriage and a child.

He first arrived in Penza around 1992–1993. In 1994 he married L., a Russian national; their son G. was born in 1995. The family later bought a flat financed by a loan repayable until 2027. After a period in Georgia (1996–1999), he returned and lived with his family in Penza. He obtained a residence permit in 2002 (valid until 2004, later renewed to 2009). He was required to apply for renewal six months before expiry and to submit annual stay notifications.

He incurred repeated immigration breaches. In 2006 he was found guilty under Article 18.8 of the Code of Administrative Offences for failing to renew his permit after it expired. His 2009 renewal application (submitted two weeks before expiry) was refused because it was late (despite a notification he claimed not to have received after a move) and because of two prior offences. He had also failed to notify an address change and to submit annual notifications. After expiry he remained in Russia without a permit from August 2009 until March 2011. In March 2011 he was fined for staying illegally; he obtained a short transit visa and left. His wife’s subsequent invitations were refused until September 2013 because of his three immigration offences (plus traffic offences).

In October 2011 he re-entered via Belarus (no visa required for Georgians) and was told he could stay two or three weeks. On 24 October 2011, during an identity check, he had no authorisation to stay. The Oktyabrskiy District Court of Penza convicted him under Article 18.8, fined him 3,000 roubles, ordered administrative removal and detention pending removal. The court noted his family and financial situation, personality, 2011 offence, lengthy unregistered stay after 2009, and the existing re-entry ban until 2013; it found no circumstances preventing removal. He was deported on 8 November 2011.

On appeal he argued the order disrupted family life: his 16-year-old son needed him and his wife faced sole childcare plus the housing loan. The Penza Regional Court (April 2012) and the Supreme Court (supervisory review, November 2012) upheld the order as lawful and proportionate. They confirmed the lower court had considered his family/financial circumstances, prior offences, unregistered stay and the invitation ban, and noted his own statement that he had entered for business and intended to leave.

Relevant domestic law (Foreigners Act, Code of Administrative Offences, Entry and Leave Procedures Act) required departure on permit expiry, allowed refusal of permits after two or more residency offences in a year, imposed a five-year re-entry ban after removal, and provided that removal decisions must be taken by a judge with a right of appeal. Russian Supreme Court case-law required courts to weigh Article 8 considerations and to ensure removal was necessary to balance public and private interests.

The case thus centres on whether the removal, despite acknowledged family ties built over nearly two decades, was a proportionate interference given the applicant’s pattern of immigration violations, illegal stay and prior sanctions.

The case of Lhermitte v. Belgium (Application no. 34238/09) originated from an application lodged on 5 June 2009 by Belgian national Geneviève Lhermitte, born in 1966 and detained in Forest Prison. She alleged a violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically her right to a fair trial, due to the absence of reasons in the jury’s verdict and the Assize Court’s judgment imposing a life sentence.

On 28 February 2007, Lhermitte contacted emergency services to report that she had killed her five children and attempted suicide. Upon arrival, authorities discovered her injured and the bodies of the children, each with a slit throat. An order of 17 June 2008 by the Indictments Division of the Brussels Court of Appeal committed her for trial on charges of knowingly and intentionally killing the five children with premeditation in Nivelles.

The indictment of 16 October 2008 detailed that, upon admission to intensive care, a doctor observed depressive and self-destructive thoughts amid psychotropic, anti-anxiety, and antidepressant medication. In her initial police interview, Lhermitte attributed her actions to despair over her family’s financial dependence on Dr S., who lived with them. The investigating judge commissioned psychological reports. Two psychologists, reporting on 30 October and 8 November 2007, found that Lhermitte exhibited inner fragility requiring rigid defences to maintain a facade of perfection. She had developed maternal omnipotence and a lack of psychological distance from her children; by killing them—objects of over-investment—she was in effect killing herself as a person and mother.

A psychiatric panel of three experts, in a report dated 30 October 2007, concluded that Lhermitte was in a severe state of anxiety and depression that encouraged her acts and profoundly impaired (but did not destroy) her judgment. She was not suffering from a mental disorder or severe disturbance rendering her incapable of controlling her actions at the time or subsequently.

The trial occurred before the Assize Court of Walloon Brabant from 8 to 19 December 2008. During proceedings, Lhermitte’s psychiatrist, Dr V., produced two previously undisclosed letters she had sent him days before the killings. The court president ordered an additional psychiatric report. On 14 December 2008 the same three psychiatrists unanimously found that the 13 February 2007 letter indicated melancholic major depression warranting hospital admission. Lhermitte had entered a transient dissociative state of depersonalisation, leaving only operational thought and no reflective consciousness, rendering her incapable of controlling her actions at the time. She currently required long-term treatment for a severe mental disturbance.

The jury was asked five questions by the president: (1) whether Lhermitte was guilty of knowingly and intentionally killing the five children; (2) whether the homicides were premeditated (if yes to 1); (3) whether she had committed the act classified as a serious crime of intentional killing (if no to 1); (4) whether that act was premeditated (if yes to 3); and (5) whether she currently suffered from a mental disorder or severe disturbance making her incapable of controlling her actions (if yes to 1 or 3). The jury answered “yes” to questions 1 and 2 and “no” to question 5.

In its judgment of 19 December 2008, the Assize Court (three professional judges plus the jury) endorsed the verdict and imposed life imprisonment. It reasoned that while Lhermitte’s family burdens, isolation, dependence, mental fragility, depression and character explained a desire for freedom, these factors—and even a suicidal wish or lack of help—could not sufficiently account for the extreme violence carried out in cold blood. Her genuine difficulties did not constitute mitigating circumstances given the offences’ gravity. Ancillary penalties included deprivation of titles, ranks and functions and permanent loss of certain civic rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Criminal Code, plus public display of the judgment under Article 18.

On 8 January 2009 Lhermitte appealed on points of law, raising the same complaints later submitted to the European Court. On 6 May 2009 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that the Assize Court had properly addressed a plurality of serious crimes rather than a single collective offence, that the parties had accepted the questions’ wording, that Article 6 did not require a court composed solely of professional judges, and that the statutory yes/no format of the verdict (Article 348 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) was compatible with the Convention. The Assize Court’s reference to Lhermitte’s cold-blooded determination explained why it rejected a finding of mental disturbance rendering her incapable of control. No statutory bar prevented the court from concluding that the facts precluded mitigation, and the judgment had not punished her for denying guilt but had simply found no mitigating circumstances. Ancillary penalties were mandatory and required no reasons; public display did not reach the severity threshold of Article 3; and the absence of appeal against the verdict (Article 350) was extraneous to the judgment itself.

The Chamber judgment in Lhermitte v. Belgium (no. 34238/09, 26 May 2015) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention arising from the absence of reasons for a jury’s guilty verdict and the Assize Court’s life sentence. The applicant, a Belgian national born in 1966, telephoned emergency services on 28 February 2007 to report that she had killed her five children and attempted suicide. Police and medical personnel found her injured and the children dead from slit throats.

An order of 17 June 2008 committed her for trial on a charge of knowingly and intentionally killing the five children with premeditation. Psychiatric and psychological assessments followed. Two psychologists reported inner fragility, rigid defences, maternal omnipotence and a lack of psychological distance from the children, such that killing them amounted to a form of self-destruction. A panel of three psychiatrists concluded on 30 October 2007 that she had been in a severe state of anxiety and depression that impaired but did not destroy her judgement and that she was not suffering from a mental disorder rendering her incapable of controlling her actions.

The trial took place before the Assize Court of Walloon Brabant from 8 to 19 December 2008. Mid-trial the applicant’s psychiatrist produced two letters she had written days before the killings. The President directed the same three psychiatrists to prepare a supplementary report. On 14 December 2008 they unanimously found that the letters evidenced melancholic major depression, a transient dissociative state of depersonalisation and a complete lack of reflective consciousness, so that at the material time she had been suffering from a severe mental disturbance that rendered her incapable of controlling her actions and that she currently required long-term treatment.

The President put five questions to the jury: (1) whether the applicant was guilty of the intentional killings; (2) if so, whether they were premeditated; (3)–(4) alternative formulations if the first answer was negative; and (5) whether she was then suffering from a mental disorder rendering her incapable of controlling her actions (the social-protection question). The jury answered the first two questions in the affirmative and the fifth in the negative.

On 19 December 2008 the Assize Court (three professional judges sitting with the jury) endorsed the verdict and imposed life imprisonment. The judgment contained reasoning solely for the sentence: the applicant’s family burdens, isolation, dependence, mental fragility and depression might explain a desire for personal freedom or even suicide, yet they could not account for the cold-blooded, extremely violent acts; those circumstances therefore furnished no mitigating factors given the heinous nature of the offences. Ancillary penalties (loss of civic rights and public display of the conviction) were imposed as mandatory consequences of a life sentence.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, repeating the complaints later submitted to Strasbourg. On 6 May 2009 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that the Assize Court had correctly treated the five killings as a plurality of crimes, that the yes/no form of the verdict was prescribed by statute, that Article 6 did not require professional judges or experts on the jury, that the applicant had shown no specific ground for fearing impartiality, and that the Assize Court judgment had adequately explained why the social-protection conditions were not met (by referring to the cold-blooded execution of the crimes) and why no mitigating circumstances existed.

The applicant’s central contention before the Court was that the unreasoned jury answers and the limited reasoning of the Assize Court judgment deprived her of a fair trial. (The Chamber judgment itself was later referred to the Grand Chamber.)

**Case Summary: Lhermitte v. Belgium (ECtHR, Application no. 34238/09)**

The applicant, Geneviève Lhermitte (born 1966), a Belgian national, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 June 2009 alleging a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). She complained specifically of the lack of reasons in the Assize Court jury’s guilty verdict and in the court’s judgment imposing a life sentence. The Chamber of the Second Section delivered its judgment on 26 May 2015 (later referred to the Grand Chamber).

On 28 February 2007 the applicant telephoned emergency services, stating that she had killed her five children and attempted suicide. Police and medical personnel found her injured at the family home in Nivelles together with the bodies of the five children, all of whom had had their throats cut. She was later committed for trial by the Indictments Division of the Brussels Court of Appeal for having “knowingly and intentionally killed” the children “with premeditation.”

The indictment recorded that, on admission to hospital, she displayed depressive and self-destructive thoughts against a background of psychotropic medication. In her first police interview she attributed her actions to despair arising from the family’s financial and emotional dependence on a doctor, Dr S., who lived with them and supported them. Two psychological reports described her as possessing rigid psychological defences, maternal omnipotence and an absence of distance between herself and her children; the killings were interpreted as a form of self-destruction. A panel of three psychiatrists initially concluded (30 October 2007) that she had been in a severe state of anxiety and depression that impaired but did not destroy her judgment and that she was not suffering from a mental disorder rendering her incapable of controlling her actions.

At the Assize Court trial (8–19 December 2008) previously undisclosed letters written by the applicant shortly before the killings were produced. The same psychiatrists then issued a supplementary report concluding that she had been suffering from melancholic major depression, a transient dissociative state of depersonalisation and a severe mental disturbance that made her incapable of controlling her actions at the material time; they also found that she currently required long-term treatment.

The jury was required to answer five questions. It answered “yes” to the principal questions of guilt and premeditation and “no” to the question whether she was presently suffering from a mental disorder making her incapable of controlling her actions. The Assize Court, composed of three professional judges and the jury, endorsed the verdict and sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment. The judgment contained reasons only for the sentence, stressing the “particularly heinous” nature of the acts and holding that neither her family responsibilities, isolation, mental fragility nor desire to escape a “dead-end situation” constituted mitigating circumstances. Ancillary penalties (loss of civic rights and public display of the judgment) were also imposed.

The applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 6 May 2009. The court held that the simple “yes/no” form of the jury’s answers was prescribed by law, that the Assize Court’s judgment adequately explained why the Social Protection Act (providing for internment of the mentally ill) did not apply, and that the sentence reasons were sufficient. It rejected arguments concerning jury impartiality, the absence of a further appeal against the verdict, and alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 6.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 6 violation: the jury’s unexplained “yes/no” answers on guilt, premeditation and criminal responsibility, coupled with the Assize Court’s limited reasoning confined to sentencing, were said to deprive the applicant of a sufficiently reasoned decision enabling her to understand why she had been convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment despite conflicting expert evidence on her mental state.

The case of Manole and “Romanian Farmers Direct” v. Romania (Application no. 46551/06) concerns an alleged violation of Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of association). The first applicant, Benieamin Manole (born 1956, residing in Priponesti, Galaţi county), is a Romanian farmer. On 15 January 2006, he and 48 others met in a constituent assembly and decided to form a trade union named “Agricultural trade union Romanian Farmers Direct,” electing Manole as President. The group (the second applicant) sought to register the union under Romanian law to obtain legal personality.

On 23 January 2006, Manole applied to the Tecuci District Court for registration, enclosing the union’s statutes and a notarized authority form from the assembly. The statutes identified the union’s purpose as defending the interests of members—farmers and those providing related services (including transport). Manole explained that the union aimed to help Romanian farmers shift from subsistence farming to market-oriented production as practiced in the European Union, thereby securing a decent living standard. It planned to establish local centers across Romania’s counties to offer legal information, accountancy advice, and judicial assistance, enabling farmers to act collectively for agricultural success.

On 27 January 2006, the Tecuci District Court (single judge) declared the request inadmissible. It held that only employees (persoanele încadrate în muncă) and civil servants could form trade unions. The applicant union appealed. On 21 March 2006, the Galaţi County Court quashed the decision, finding the request had been wrongly deemed inadmissible and that the district court should have examined the merits.

On remittal, the same district-court judge, on 12 April 2006, rejected the request as ill-founded. Citing Law No. 54/2003 on trade unions, the court ruled that farmers could not establish trade unions and could only join existing ones. The union appealed on points of law, arguing that the same judge had sat after the earlier invalidation and that the refusal infringed Article 40 of the Romanian Constitution (guaranteeing trade-union rights).

On 30 May 2006, the Galaţi County Court accepted the appeal insofar as it concerned the first-instance court’s composition. Assessing the merits, however, it again refused registration. It held that only employees with employment contracts and civil servants could form trade unions; farmers and other self-employed persons were excluded and could merely join pre-existing unions.

These successive refusals, grounded in the interpretation of national legislation that reserved the right to form trade unions to salaried employees and civil servants, constitute the facts underlying the alleged Article 11 violation. (The applicants were represented before the Court by counsel appointed via a November 2006 authority form signed by Manole in his dual personal and representative capacities.)

The case of Manole and “Romanian Farmers Direct” v. Romania concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 11 of the Convention (freedom of association). The first applicant, Benieamin Manole, a Romanian farmer born in 1956 and residing in Priponesti, Galaţi county, together with 48 other persons, sought to establish a trade union. On 15 January 2006, they met in a constituent assembly and decided to form the “Agricultural trade union Romanian Farmers Direct,” electing Manole as president. The union’s statutes defined its purpose as defending the interests of farmers and persons providing related services (including transport). It aimed to assist members in shifting from subsistence farming to market-oriented production typical of the European Union, thereby securing a decent living standard. The union planned to establish local centres (covering three or four adjacent municipalities) in all Romanian counties to furnish legal information, accountancy advice and judicial assistance, encouraging farmers to act collectively.

On 23 January 2006 Manole applied to the Tecuci District Court for registration of the union so that it could acquire legal personality. He submitted the statutes and a notarised authority form dated 27 January 2006. By judgment of 27 January 2006 the district court, sitting as a single judge (Judge N.M.), declared the application inadmissible on the ground that only employees (persoanele încadrate în muncă) and civil servants were entitled to form trade unions.

The union appealed. On 21 March 2006 the Galaţi County Court quashed the decision, holding that the district court had wrongly declared the action inadmissible and should have examined the merits. On 12 April 2006 the same district-court judge rejected the application as ill-founded, relying on Law No. 54/2003 on trade unions, which, the court held, barred farmers from establishing unions and permitted them only to join pre-existing ones.

The union lodged a further appeal, arguing that the same judge who had delivered the quashed judgment had sat again and that Article 40 of the Romanian Constitution (guaranteeing trade-union rights) had been infringed. On 30 May 2006 the county court accepted the appeal insofar as it concerned the composition of the first-instance court, but, examining the merits itself, dismissed the registration request. It confirmed that only persons holding contracts of employment and civil servants could found trade unions; farmers and other self-employed persons were excluded from that right and could merely join existing unions.

The applicants contended that this persistent refusal to register their union constituted an unjustified interference with their freedom of association. They were represented before the Court by Italian lawyer G. Perin pursuant to an authority form signed by Manole on 12 November 2006 in his personal capacity and as union president.

The facts therefore centre on the Romanian courts’ consistent interpretation of domestic trade-union legislation as prohibiting self-employed farmers from creating their own organisation, thereby denying the applicants legal personality and the ability to pursue their stated collective aims.

Relying on Law No. 54/2003 on trade unions, the court held that farmers could not establish their own unions but could only join existing ones.

A further appeal followed. The county court, on 30 May 2006, allowed the complaint that the same judge had sat after the earlier judgment had been quashed, but itself examined the merits and again refused registration. It confirmed that only persons holding contracts of employment and civil servants could found trade unions; farmers and other self-employed persons were limited to joining pre-existing unions.

They were represented by Italian lawyer G. Perin pursuant to an authority form dated 12 November 2006.

Relevant international instruments cited in the case (ILO Conventions Nos. 87, 11 and 141, together with associated recommendations and ILO supervisory comments) underscore that agricultural and self-employed workers should, in principle, enjoy the same rights of association as other workers, a standard Romania had undertaken to respect.

The case Banović v. Croatia (ECtHR application no. 44284/10) originated from an application by Croatian national Maja Banović, who alleged that domestic decisions dismissing her request for recognition as a family member of a Homeland War veteran deprived her of access to a court.

In February 1997 Banović’s father G.B. applied to the Rijeka Office for recognition as a disabled war veteran, claiming he had contracted tuberculosis and developed psychosis during 1995 military service. G.B. died on 19 December 1997; Banović continued the proceedings as heir. The Rijeka Office dismissed the claim in September 1998, finding the conditions unrelated to service. Multiple appeals and remittals followed. After the 2004 Veterans Act entered into force on 1 January 2005, unfinished proceedings were to be decided under its more favourable terms. In September 2006 the County Office terminated the case because G.B.’s death made certain facts unascertainable. The Ministry reversed this in April 2007, recognising G.B. as a fourth-category disabled veteran (80 % disability) on account of tuberculosis contracted while defending Croatia; the psychosis claim was rejected. The decision reached Banović in June 2007. Separately, the Supreme Court later found the length of these proceedings excessive and awarded her HRK 10 500.

On 2 July 2007 Banović applied to the County Office for family-member status and the associated disability benefit. The Office declared the application inadmissible as out of time. Section 124(2) of the Veterans Act required that, where a veteran had died of a war-related illness before the Act’s entry into force, claims had to be lodged within twelve months of 1 January 2005 (i.e., by 31 December 2005). The Ministry upheld the decision in December 2007.

Banović challenged the rulings before the Administrative Court, arguing they were overly formalistic: her father’s status—the indispensable legal basis for her own claim—had been established only in 2007 after a decade of litigation, so any earlier application would have been premature and doomed. The Administrative Court dismissed the action in June 2009, holding that the two sets of proceedings were legally distinct and that the statutory deadline was preclusive. Banović’s constitutional complaint repeating these arguments was declared manifestly ill-founded by the Constitutional Court in December 2009.

Domestic law (Veterans Act ss. 3, 5, 75 and 124) defined a “fallen veteran” as one who died of a war-related illness no later than 31 December 1997 and made family disability benefit dependent on that status. The Administrative Procedure Act (s. 144) permitted adjournment of proceedings pending resolution of a preliminary issue. The Government produced examples of such adjournments in other administrative contexts and one comparable veterans case in which the Administrative Court required the authorities to decide a family-benefit request irrespective of pending status proceedings.

These facts form the core of Banović’s complaint that the rigid application of a time-limit she could not meet until after the prerequisite status decision effectively barred her from court.

The case Banović v. Croatia (application no. 44284/10) concerns a complaint by Maja Banović, a Croatian national born in 1984, that the dismissal of her application for recognition as a family member of a Homeland War veteran (and the associated family disability benefit) violated her right of access to a court.

On 28 February 1997 the applicant’s father, G.B., applied to the competent administrative office for recognition as a disabled Homeland War veteran. He claimed that tuberculosis and psychosis had arisen from his military service (which included periods in 1991–1992 and 1995). G.B. died on 19 December 1997; the applicant continued the proceedings as his heir. After successive dismissals, appeals and remittals—including a 1999 finding that the claim had lapsed on death, a 2001 finding of inadmissibility for lack of formal discharge, and a 2006 remittal after the 2004 Veterans Act entered into force—the Ministry, on 21 April 2007, recognised G.B. as an 80-per-cent disabled veteran on account of tuberculosis contracted while defending Croatian sovereignty (psychosis was rejected). The decision was served on the applicant in June 2007.

On 2 July 2007 the applicant applied for recognition as the family member of a fallen veteran and for the corresponding family disability benefit. The first-instance body declared the application inadmissible as out of time. Section 124(2) of the 2004 Veterans Act (in force from 1 January 2005) required that, where a veteran had died of a service-related illness before the Act’s entry into force, any claim for family-member status and benefit had to be lodged within twelve months, i.e., by 31 December 2005. The Ministry and, on 17 June 2009, the Administrative Court upheld that ruling, stressing that the time-limit was preclusive and that the earlier proceedings concerning G.B.’s own status were legally distinct. The Constitutional Court, on 3 December 2009, declared the subsequent constitutional complaint manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant argued that the approach was excessively formalistic: she could not have lodged a well-founded claim until her father’s status had been finally established in 2007. She also relied on section 144 of the Administrative Procedure Act, which permitted an administrative body to adjourn proceedings pending resolution of a preliminary issue. Domestic practice included examples of such adjournments in other administrative contexts, and one comparable veterans case in which proceedings for a family benefit had been stayed pending determination of the deceased’s status (although the Administrative Court later emphasised that a decision on the benefit claim was still required).

Separately, the Supreme Court found in 2011 that the ten-year duration of the father’s-status proceedings had violated the reasonable-time guarantee and awarded the applicant HRK 10 500; she did not pursue a further appeal.
