The case of Banović v. Croatia (Application no. 44284/10) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Croatian national Maja Banović, born in 1984. She alleged that Croatian courts’ dismissal of her request for recognition as a family member of a Homeland War veteran (and associated family disability benefit) deprived her of access to a court, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention.

In February 1997 the applicant’s father, G.B., applied to the Rijeka Office of the Department for Croatian Homeland War Veterans for recognition as a disabled war veteran. He claimed he had contracted tuberculosis and developed psychosis during military service in 1991–1992 and 1995. G.B. died on 19 December 1997; the applicant continued the proceedings as his heir. After multiple dismissals, appeals, remittals and changes in applicable legislation, the Ministry of Family, Veterans’ Affairs and Intergenerational Solidarity, on 21 April 2007, recognised G.B. as a fourth-category disabled Homeland War veteran with 80 % bodily damage caused by tuberculosis contracted while defending Croatian sovereignty. The decision was served on the applicant in June 2007. (A later Supreme Court finding of excessive length in those proceedings awarded her modest compensation; she did not appeal further.)

On 2 July 2007 the applicant applied to the competent County Office for recognition as a family member of a fallen war veteran and for family disability benefit. The Office declared the application inadmissible as out of time. Section 124(2) of the Act on the Rights of Croatian Homeland War Veterans and their Family Members (in force from 1 January 2005) required that, where a veteran had died of a service-related illness before the Act entered into force, such applications be lodged within twelve months of that date—i.e., by 31 December 2005. The Ministry confirmed the decision on 20 December 2007, stressing that the statutory time-limit was preclusive and could not be extended.

The applicant brought an administrative action arguing that the authorities’ approach was overly formalistic. She could not have lodged a well-founded application before her father’s status had been definitively established in June 2007; an earlier request would have been premature. On 17 June 2009 the Administrative Court dismissed the action, holding that the father’s-status proceedings were legally distinct from the family-member claim and that the time-limit had therefore expired. The Constitutional Court, on 3 December 2009, declared her subsequent complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded.

Relevant domestic law included the 2004 Veterans Act (ss. 3, 5, 75 and 124), which defined a “fallen Homeland War veteran” as one who died of an illness directly caused by defence of Croatian sovereignty no later than 31 December 1997, and which granted family members disability benefit once that status was recognised. Section 144 of the Administrative Procedure Act permitted an authority to adjourn proceedings pending resolution of a preliminary issue falling within another body’s competence. The Government supplied examples of such adjournments in unrelated administrative contexts, but none involving the precise interplay between a veteran’s status determination and a subsequent family-benefit claim.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: the rigid application of a time-limit that expired before the applicant could obtain the very administrative decision on which her claim necessarily depended.
001-153481:
The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of two Croatian nationals, Marija Nježić and Ana Štimac, who alleged that Croatian authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the 1991 killings of their parents and grandmother, in violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention.

On 16 October 1991 Croatian Army personnel discovered the bodies of seven civilians in the village of Bukovac, including Mile and Ana Pocrnić and Marija Pocrnić. The bodies were taken to Gospić Medical Centre, where a pathologist confirmed they had been shot. An investigating judge was notified but declined an on-site inspection because of the risk of further attacks. On 28 December 1991 the Gospić police filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons for murder.

Limited inquiries followed. In September 1992 police interviewed I.P., who identified two Serbian paramilitary members (B.G. and Č.B.) as having boasted of killings in Bukovac, and brothers P.J. and I.J., who reported similar remarks made in a Knin prison. A report naming these men was sent to the military prosecutor. After Operation Storm in August 1995 most Serbian forces left Croatia. In 1996 the second applicant supplied a letter from relative D.P. (then in Canada) listing fourteen named perpetrators and several commanders of the Široka Kula group that had entered Bukovac and killed civilians.

A 2001 internal-security report reiterated these names and noted that the only surviving eyewitnesses, D.P. and his father J.P., lived in Canada. The Gospić County State Attorney requested an investigation and asked that the two men be heard. In 2004 police interviewed three former Serbian paramilitaries detained in Zagreb; they described operations in the area but could not identify the killers of the Pocrnić family. Efforts to locate D.P. and J.P. continued into 2006, when Canadian addresses were obtained. Canadian authorities invited them to testify on three occasions; they refused, stating they had already given written accounts.

Further activity occurred years later. In 2010 an investigating judge heard M.Ć., who had only hearsay information from a deceased source. In 2011 police re-interviewed earlier witnesses, learned that B.G. and Č.B. had been convicted in Belgrade of unrelated war crimes, and interviewed a Croatian soldier who had found the bodies. In 2012 a report by another former paramilitary, M.Š., stating that “they had killed seven people” on 16 October 1991 was received; two named suspects were confirmed dead and a third (D.V.) was in Serbian custody. A criminal complaint against B.G. and Č.B. was forwarded to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor, who later reported that the men denied involvement. Additional interviews in 2013 produced no new evidence. A police summary listed four deceased suspects, fourteen living in Serbia, three in the United States and two of unknown whereabouts. The Croatian authorities transmitted the list to Serbia and requested further questioning.

By the time the application was lodged in April 2013—more than twenty-one years after the killings—no indictment had been issued in Croatia and the investigation remained open, relying on sporadic interviews, foreign legal assistance and the 2006 Croatia–Serbia cooperation agreement on war-crimes prosecution. The applicants contended that these steps did not constitute an effective official response to the deaths of their relatives.

The case of Nježić and Štimac v. Croatia (Application no. 29823/13) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by two Croatian nationals whose parents and grandmother were among seven civilians killed by unidentified persons in the village of Bukovac on 16 October 1991, during the Croatian War of Independence. The applicants alleged a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention, claiming that Croatian authorities had failed to conduct an adequate investigation into the killings.

The victims’ bodies were discovered that day by Croatian Army members and transferred to the Gospić Medical Centre, where a pathologist’s autopsy confirmed they had been shot dead. An investigating judge of the Gospić County Court was notified but declined an on-site inspection owing to security risks from nearby Široka Kula. On 28 December 1991 the Gospić police filed a criminal complaint against unknown perpetrators with the Gospić County State Attorney’s Office.

In September 1992 police interviewed I.P., a nearby resident who identified two Serbian paramilitary members (B.G. and Č.B.) from photographs after they allegedly boasted of killings in Bukovac; brothers P.J. and I.J. provided similar hearsay linking the same men to civilian killings in the area. These leads were forwarded to a military prosecutor, but no further immediate action followed. Most Serbian paramilitary forces fled Croatia after Operation Storm in August 1995.

Little investigative progress occurred until 2001. That year a report from the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order transmitted letters from surviving relatives D.P. and J.P. (then living in Canada) that named numerous alleged perpetrators and commanders from Široka Kula. The Gospić County State Attorney’s Office requested an investigation and the hearing of D.P. and J.P. Subsequent police interviews of former Serbian paramilitaries (2004) yielded only general accounts of operations in the region, without specific information on the Bukovac killings. Efforts to locate the Canadian witnesses were delayed; when contacted via the Canadian authorities they declined further interviews, citing earlier written statements.

Additional steps were taken only from 2010 onward. Witnesses were re-interviewed, repeating earlier accounts; B.G. and Č.B. were noted to have been convicted in Belgrade in 2011 of unrelated war crimes. In 2012–2013 Croatian authorities transmitted a criminal complaint and suspect lists to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor pursuant to a 2006 cooperation agreement. Serbian interviews of B.G., Č.B. and another named individual produced denials of involvement. By March 2013 police reports identified a group of suspects, four of whom had died, fourteen of whom had relocated to Serbia (where extradition of nationals is barred), three of whom were in the United States, and two of whom could not be traced. One further suspect died later that year.

The investigation remained open at the time of the application in April 2013, more than twenty-one years after the killings, with no indictments issued in Croatia. The Court communicated only the procedural Article 2 complaint.

The case of Nježić and Štimac v. Croatia (Application no. 29823/13) was brought by two Croatian nationals, Marija Nježić and Ana Štimac, who alleged a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed that Croatian authorities had failed to conduct an adequate investigation into the 1991 killings of their close relatives.

On 16 October 1991, seven civilians were killed in the village of Bukovac. Croatian Army members discovered the bodies and transported them to the Gospić Medical Centre. Two victims were identified as the applicants’ parents, Mile and Ana Pocrnić, and a third as their grandmother, Marija Pocrnić. An investigating judge of the Gospić County Court was notified but declined an on-site inspection owing to the risk of further attacks by unidentified persons from nearby Široka Kula. A pathologist performed autopsies the same day and confirmed that the three relatives had been shot dead.

On 28 December 1991 the Gospić police filed a criminal complaint with the Gospić County State Attorney’s Office against unknown perpetrators for the murders. In September 1992 the police interviewed several witnesses. I.P. stated that three members of Serbian paramilitary forces had fired at him in December 1991 and that two men he later identified from photographs as B.G. and Č.B. had boasted of killing people in Bukovac. Brothers P.J. and I.J. reported meeting B.G. and Č.B. in a Knin prison, where B.G. allegedly admitted killing civilians near Lički Osik. The police forwarded a report identifying B.G. and Č.B. as possible suspects to the Karlovac Military Prosecutor. Most Serbian paramilitary members fled Croatia after Operation Storm in August 1995.

In March 1996 the second applicant supplied police with a letter from relative D.P. A 2001 report by the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order named numerous alleged perpetrators from Široka Kula paramilitary units, identified D.P. and his father J.P. (then living in Canada) as the only surviving witnesses, and enclosed their letters describing the 16 October 1991 attack. The Gospić County State Attorney’s Office requested an investigation and sought to hear D.P. and J.P. Subsequent interviews in 2004 with former paramilitary members S.Ɖ., D.S. and B.Č. yielded general information about operations in the Bukovac area but nothing specific to the killings.

Efforts to locate D.P. and J.P. were delayed; their Canadian address was obtained only in 2006. Canadian authorities invited them to testify on three occasions, but they refused, citing earlier written statements. Further police interviews between 2010 and 2013 with witnesses, including the second applicant, soldiers who found the bodies, and previously interviewed individuals, largely repeated earlier accounts or produced no new evidence. In 2011 it was noted that B.G. and Č.B. had been convicted in Belgrade of unrelated war crimes. A 2012 report listed numerous suspects, several of whom had died or moved to Serbia or the United States. Croatian authorities sent a criminal complaint against B.G. and Č.B. to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor and requested interviews with other suspects in Serbia. Those interviewed by Serbian authorities denied involvement. Additional requests for interviews of remaining suspects in Serbia were transmitted in 2013.

By the time the application was lodged in April 2013, more than twenty-one years after the killings, no perpetrators had been identified or prosecuted in Croatia despite the accumulation of names, witness statements and international cooperation requests. The investigation remained open, with several suspects deceased or residing abroad.

The case of J.K. and Others v. Sweden (no. 59166/12) concerns three Iraqi nationals (a married couple born in 1964 and 1965, and their son born in 2000) who alleged that deportation from Sweden to Iraq would violate Article 3 ECHR due to a real risk of treatment by al-Qaeda contrary to that provision.

The husband had operated a business exclusively serving American clients from an office at Baghdad’s Victoria Camp US base since the 1990s. Employees had been warned against such cooperation. On 26 October 2004 he survived an al-Qaeda assassination attempt and spent three months in hospital (where unknown men inquired after him). In 2005 al-Qaeda kidnapped his brother, citing the collaboration; the brother was released after bribes and fled. The family escaped to Jordan until December 2006. Upon return a bomb was placed by their house; the wife detected it and US forces arrested the perpetrator, who confessed he had been paid by al-Qaeda and named 16 persons assigned to watch the family. They then moved to Syria (the husband continuing business in Iraq), after which al-Qaeda destroyed their home and stocks.

They returned to Baghdad in January 2008. In October that year the husband and a daughter were shot at while driving; the daughter died in hospital. He ceased work and the family moved frequently within Baghdad. Stocks were attacked four or five times. No personal threats occurred after 2008 because of their mobility. The son stayed indoors most of the time. They did not seek state protection, believing the authorities infiltrated by al-Qaeda and fearing disclosure of their address. The husband had a lingering infected abdominal wound; the wife had cysts. Identity papers, the daughter’s death certificate and medical certificates were submitted.

After interviews the Migration Board rejected asylum on 22 November 2011. It accepted identity and credibility but noted that collaboration had ended in 2008, two years had passed without personal attacks (only stock threats), three daughters remained unharmed in Baghdad, they had not sought protection despite reduced infiltration, and their health was not sufficiently poor.

On appeal they produced a neighbour’s attestation that masked terrorists had sought the husband on 10 September 2011, a report that their house had been burned on 12 November 2011, a 2008 television debate video, and further medical evidence. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 23 April 2012, finding the attacks several years old, no remaining American business ties, Iraqi authorities willing and able to protect if any threat persisted, and health not exceptionally distressing. Leave to appeal was refused. A later re-examination request (citing political activity and videos) was also refused.

The Court noted post-2014 country information: ISIS offensives capturing Mosul and other cities, mass displacement, sectarian killings, executions by government-aligned militias, and UNHCR’s October 2014 call against forced returns given the fluid nationwide violence and unsuitability of internal relocation. Interim measures under Rule 39 prevented deportation pending the proceedings.

The case of J.K. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 59166/12) was decided by a Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 4 June 2015 (later referred to the Grand Chamber). Three Iraqi nationals—a married couple born in 1964 and 1965 and their son born in 2000—alleged that their deportation from Sweden to Iraq would violate Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) due to a real risk of persecution by al-Qaeda.

The applicants, originally from Baghdad, claimed the husband had operated a business exclusively serving American clients from an office at the U.S. “Victoria Camp” base since the 1990s. Employees had received warnings against such cooperation. On 26 October 2004 the husband was the target of an al-Qaeda assassination attempt, requiring three months’ hospitalisation during which unknown men inquired after him. In 2005 al-Qaeda kidnapped his brother, threatening to kill him because of the husband’s collaboration; the brother was released after bribes and immediately fled Iraq. The family then left for Jordan, remaining until December 2006.

Upon return a bomb was placed beside their house but was discovered by the wife; U.S. forces arrested the perpetrator, who confessed to being paid by al-Qaeda and named 16 persons assigned to watch the family. The applicants moved to Syria (the husband continuing his Iraqi business), after which al-Qaeda destroyed their home and business stocks. They returned to Baghdad in January 2008. In October 2008 the husband and a daughter were shot at while driving; the daughter later died in hospital. The husband ceased working and the family moved repeatedly within Baghdad. Business stocks were attacked four or five more times and guards threatened. The husband received no further personal threats after 2008. The son remained indoors most of the time and attended school only for examinations. The family never sought state protection, citing the authorities’ inability to safeguard them and fear that al-Qaeda had infiltrated official structures. The husband still suffered an open, infected abdominal wound from the 2004 shooting; the wife had cysts on her liver and uterus. Supporting documents included identity papers, the daughter’s death certificate and a medical certificate.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected the asylum claims on 22 November 2011, accepting the applicants’ identities and the credibility of their account but noting that the husband had ended American collaboration in 2008, had thereafter lived two years in Baghdad without personal attack (apart from stock raids), and that three daughters remaining in Baghdad were unharmed. The Board held that the applicants had not shown they could not obtain state protection (al-Qaeda infiltration having diminished) and that their health problems were insufficiently severe. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 23 April 2012, emphasising the lapse of time since the last personal attacks and finding that Iraqi authorities possessed both the will and capacity to protect the family; health issues did not amount to exceptionally distressing circumstances. Leave to appeal to the Migration Court of Appeal was refused on 9 August 2012. A subsequent request for re-examination, based on alleged political activity and additional videos, was rejected on 26 September 2012.

On 13 September 2012 the applicants lodged their application with the Court. Interim measures under Rule 39 were indicated, preventing deportation pending the proceedings. Relevant country information available at the time of the Chamber judgment included the 2014 ISIS offensive, large-scale displacement, sectarian violence, infiltration of security forces, and UNHCR’s position against forced returns to Iraq given the fluid security situation and humanitarian crisis.

The case of *J.K. and Others v. Sweden* (Application no. 59166/12) concerns three Iraqi nationals—a married couple born in 1964 and 1965 and their son born in 2000—who alleged that their deportation from Sweden to Iraq would violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) issued its Chamber judgment on 4 June 2015 after applying interim measures under Rule 39 to halt deportation pending proceedings. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber.

The applicants, whose religious affiliation is unknown, originated from Baghdad. The husband had operated a business exclusively serving American clients from an office at the U.S. military base Victoria Camp since the 1990s. Employees received warnings against cooperating with Americans. On 26 October 2004, al-Qaeda targeted the husband in a murder attempt, hospitalizing him for three months; unknown men later inquired about him at the hospital, prompting transfers between facilities. In 2005, al-Qaeda kidnapped his brother, citing the husband's collaboration, but released him after bribes; the brother fled Iraq immediately. The family then fled to Jordan until December 2006 before returning to Iraq.

Shortly after their return, al-Qaeda planted a bomb beside their house (detected by the wife); U.S. forces arrested the perpetrator, who confessed to being paid to kill the husband and named 16 individuals assigned to watch the family. The applicants relocated to Syria while the husband continued his Iraqi business; al-Qaeda subsequently destroyed their home and business stocks. They returned to Baghdad in January 2008. In October 2008, gunmen shot at the husband and their daughter while driving; the daughter died in hospital. The husband ceased work, and the family frequently relocated within Baghdad. Al-Qaeda attacked their business stocks four or five times, threatening guards, but the husband reported no personal threats after 2008 due to their mobility. Their son remained mostly indoors out of fear and attended school only for exams. The family never sought protection from Iraqi authorities, citing those authorities' inability to help and fears of address disclosure given al-Qaeda's alleged infiltration. The husband retained an open, infected wound from the 2004 shooting; the wife had liver and uterine cysts. They submitted identity documents, their daughter's death certificate, and medical records.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected their asylum applications on 22 November 2011 after multiple interviews (with counsel). It accepted their identities and found their account credible but noted the husband had ended U.S. collaboration in 2008 and lived two years in Baghdad without personal attacks (beyond stock threats). Three daughters remaining in Baghdad faced no harassment. The Board held that the applicants had not shown they could not obtain state protection, as al-Qaeda infiltration had diminished, and their health issues were insufficient for asylum.

On appeal, the applicants argued Iraqi authorities could not protect them. They had contacted police after 2006/2008 fires and their daughter's murder but later feared revealing their location. They submitted a neighbour's attestation of masked terrorists seeking the husband on 10 September 2011, a police report of their house being burned on 12 November 2011, a 2008 TV debate video (in which the husband participated), and updated medical certificates. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 23 April 2012, finding the al-Qaeda acts dated years earlier, the husband no longer collaborated with Americans, Iraqi authorities could provide protection if any threat persisted, and health issues were not exceptionally distressing. Leave to appeal to the Migration Court of Appeal was refused on 9 August 2012.

A subsequent re-examination request (claiming political activity and submitting further videos) was denied on 26 September 2012 without appeal. Swedish law (Aliens Act) grants residence to refugees or those facing a real risk of death, torture, or similar treatment, or in particularly distressing circumstances (including severe health issues). Enforcement is barred if such risks exist.

The applicants thus claimed a real risk of al-Qaeda persecution upon return, based on past targeted violence (including a family member's death), alleged ongoing interest (2011 incidents), and inadequate Iraqi state protection amid infiltration and later ISIS-related instability.
001-155359:
**Case of Selahattin Demirtaş v. Turkey (ECHR Application no. 15028/09, judgment 23 June 2015)**

The applicant, Selahattin Demirtaş (born 1973, resident in Diyarbakır), was a DTP (pro-Kurdish Party for a Democratic Society) member of the Turkish Parliament at the relevant time; the DTP was later dissolved by the Constitutional Court in 2009, and he became HDP co-chair. The case arose from an article published on 11 October 2007 in the Bolu Express newspaper (and online) titled “Turk, here is your enemy” by journalist I.E. The piece listed recent PKK attacks killing soldiers, village guards and others, criticised the state and army for failing to defeat “three to five thousand ‘looters’”, and identified DTP leaders—including the applicant by name, along with other MPs, executives, mayors and officials—as the “real murderers.” It accused them of using PKK colours, backing PKK bullets, calling terrorists “brothers and sisters,” and instigating murder. The author declared these individuals “the enemy of Turks” and potential targets of “civilian patriots” unless they denounced the PKK as a separatist terrorist organisation. It proposed “wiping out” a few “microbes,” suggested that for every security officer killed one named person should “share the same fate,” and referred to cutting out “organs which suffer from necrosis.”

On 2 November 2007 the applicant’s lawyer petitioned the Bolu public prosecutor to investigate I.E. for incitement to commit a crime (Criminal Code Art. 214), incitement to disobey the law (Art. 217) and defamation/insult (Art. 125), noting the offences were committed via the press. The petition highlighted two recent murders (of priest Andrea Santoro and journalist Hrant Dink) that followed similar online articles and argued the piece openly incited society to kill the named DTP figures, including the applicant, while insulting him as a “murderer.”

I.E. submitted a defence asserting lifelong support for the Republic and military, claiming any offence was committed under severe provocation because the applicant had not condemned the PKK and called its members “brothers and sisters.” He portrayed the article as solidarity with martyrs’ families, criticism of DTP ideology, and an attempt to inform society; he analogised it to the Chief Public Prosecutor’s indictment seeking DTP dissolution and insisted he targeted only terrorists. He questioned the applicant’s “Turkishness.”

On 7 December 2007 the Bolu public prosecutor declined to prosecute. He characterised the article as a reaction to internationally recognised PKK terrorism, public anger at killings of civilians and soldiers, and criticism of both the state and the DTP (for failing to condemn the PKK or stand with society). The prosecutor viewed the piece as protected media freedom of information, criticism and comment, even if it used strong or exaggerated language against a political party and its members. He cited a domestic judgment (referencing ECHR case-law such as *Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria*) holding that expressions with a factual basis are not extreme, and noted Turkey’s culture of tolerance had prevented ethnic conflict despite inflammatory publications.

The applicant’s lawyer objected on 30 July 2008, repeating that the article marked DTP members as targets for their political opinions and posed a societal threat; he argued the prosecutor had improperly considered the applicant’s political identity. On 21 August 2008 the Düzce Assize Court dismissed the objection as unfounded. In October 2008 the Minister of Justice publicly stated that the article’s content should not be protected as freedom of expression and that the Ministry would seek cassation. On 15 October 2008 the Ministry applied via the Court of Cassation public prosecutor. On 30 September 2009 the Court of Cassation rejected the application: the applicant’s original objection had been lodged out of time, so the Assize Court should not have examined the merits, yet the dismissal produced the correct result.

The application (lodged 13 February 2009) was communicated under Article 8 (private life/reputation). The Chamber later invited observations under Articles 2 (right to life) and 13 (effective remedy). The Government initially responded on Article 8 then withdrew those observations (accepted by the President). They later filed observations on Articles 2 and 13; the applicant made none. Domestic provisions cited include Criminal Code Articles 125 (defamation, including via media), 214 (incitement to offence, including arming groups to kill) and 217 (incitement to disobey laws if capable of breaching public order). These facts centre on the article’s alleged incitement and targeting of a politician, the authorities’ refusal to prosecute, and the ensuing procedural history relevant to claims of inadequate protection of life, reputation and access to an effective remedy.

The case concerns an application by Selahattin Demirtaş, a Turkish national and prominent pro-Kurdish politician (then a DTP parliamentarian, later HDP co-chair), lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 February 2009. It arose from a highly inflammatory newspaper article published on 11 October 2007 in the Bolu Express (print and online) titled “Turk, here is your enemy.” The piece listed recent PKK attacks that had killed Turkish soldiers and village guards, expressed public fury at the state’s inability to defeat the group, and identified DTP politicians—including the applicant by name—as the “real murderers.” It accused them of using PKK colours, calling terrorists “brothers and sisters,” and instigating killings. The author declared these individuals “the enemy” of the Turkish nation and stated that if they did not denounce the PKK they would become targets of “civilian patriots.” He advocated “wiping out” a few “microbes” and suggested that for every security officer killed, one of the named politicians should “share the same fate,” invoking society’s desire to “cut out those organs which suffer from necrosis.”

On 2 November 2007 the applicant’s lawyer complained to the Bolu public prosecutor, seeking prosecution of the author (I.E.) for incitement to commit an offence, incitement to disobey the law, and public insult (Criminal Code Articles 214, 217 and 125). The complaint stressed that the article openly called for the murder of the named politicians and noted that similar internet writings had preceded the killings of priest Andrea Santoro and journalist Hrant Dink. I.E. responded that the article merely criticised DTP ideology, expressed solidarity with martyrs’ families, and reacted to the applicant’s failure to condemn the PKK or to utter the phrase “How happy is he who says ‘I am a Turk.’”

On 7 December 2007 the prosecutor declined to prosecute, characterising the article as a legitimate, if exaggerated, expression of public anger at PKK terrorism and of criticism of a party perceived as insufficiently opposed to it. He placed the piece within media freedom to comment and criticise, citing domestic case-law and the Court’s judgment in Prager and Oberschlick. The applicant’s objection of 30 July 2008, which argued that the article marked DTP members as assassination targets and that the prosecutor had improperly taken political identity into account, was dismissed by the Düzce Assize Court on 21 August 2008. The decision was served on 18 September 2008.

In October 2008 the then Justice Minister publicly stated that the article should not have been protected by freedom of expression and that the Ministry would seek cassation. The Ministry applied on 15 October 2008, but on 30 September 2009 the Court of Cassation rejected the request on the ground that the original objection had been lodged out of time; although the Assize Court had wrongly examined the merits, the outcome (dismissal) was correct.

The application was communicated under Article 8 (private life/reputation) and later under Articles 2 and 13 (right to life and effective remedy). The key facts therefore centre on the publication of an article that explicitly designated a sitting parliamentarian as a legitimate target for lethal “civilian patriot” action, the domestic authorities’ refusal to treat it as incitement, and the subsequent procedural termination of review, raising questions about the State’s positive obligations to protect life against publicly issued death threats and to provide an effective investigative and remedial response.

The case of Selahattin Demirtaş v. Turkey (Application no. 15028/09) concerns a 2007 newspaper article that named the applicant—a serving Member of Parliament for the pro-Kurdish DTP party—as one of the “real murderers” responsible for PKK terrorism and called for him and other listed DTP figures to be targeted and killed by “civilian patriots.”

On 11 October 2007 the Bolu Express published an article entitled “Turk, here is your enemy.” After listing recent PKK attacks that had killed soldiers and village guards, the author, I.E., accused the State of failing to defeat “three to five thousand looters.” He then identified the “real murderers” as those who used PKK colours, called PKK members “brothers and sisters,” and thereby instigated the killings. He named the DTP president, 18 DTP MPs (explicitly including the applicant), members of the DTP executive, and all DTP mayors and local officials. The article declared that these persons would become the targets of “civilian patriots” unless they denounced the PKK as a terrorist organisation, suggested that “a few microbes should be wiped out,” and stated that “for every security officer who is killed, one of these people should share the same fate.” It concluded that it was time “to cut out those organs which suffer from necrosis.” The piece also appeared on the newspaper’s website.

On 2 November 2007 the applicant’s lawyer lodged a criminal complaint with the Bolu public prosecutor, alleging incitement to commit crime (Criminal Code Art. 214), incitement to disobey the law (Art. 217) and public defamation (Art. 125). The complaint emphasised that similar internet publications had preceded the murders of priest Andrea Santoro and journalist Hrant Dink, and that the article openly called for the listed individuals, including the applicant, to be killed.

I.E. submitted a defence claiming he had acted under severe provocation, was expressing solidarity with the families of “martyrs,” and was merely criticising the DTP’s ideology in terms similar to the Chief Public Prosecutor’s indictment seeking the party’s dissolution. He maintained that he had targeted only terrorists; if the applicant felt implicated, that confirmed he was a legitimate target.

On 7 December 2007 the Bolu public prosecutor decided not to prosecute. He characterised the article as a legitimate expression of public anger at PKK violence, a critique of the DTP’s failure to condemn terrorism, and an exercise of media freedom that used strong but permissible language. Citing a domestic judgment that itself referred to Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria, he held that a factual basis existed for the criticism and that no ethnic conflict had resulted.

The applicant’s lawyer objected, arguing that the article marked DTP members as targets solely because of their political identity and that the prosecutor had improperly taken that identity into account. On 21 August 2008 the Düzce Assize Court dismissed the objection. The Ministry of Justice later asked the Court of Cassation to quash the decision, considering the article unprotected speech. On 30 September 2009 the Court of Cassation refused, finding that the original objection had been lodged out of time and that the Assize Court’s dismissal, though based on an erroneous merits examination, had produced the correct formal result.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints that the Turkish authorities failed to take the death threats seriously, thereby exposing him to a real risk to his life (Article 2), failed to protect his reputation and private life from targeted hate speech (Article 8), and provided no effective remedy (Article 13).
001-154399:
The case of Magee and Others v. the United Kingdom (ECtHR, 12 May 2015) arose from three applications by Irish nationals Gabriel Magee, Colin Francis Duffy and Teresa Magee. All three were arrested without warrant on 14 March 2009 under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 on reasonable suspicion of being terrorists. The first and third applicants were suspected of involvement in the murder of a police officer on 9 March 2009; the second applicant was suspected of involvement in the murders of two soldiers at Massereene Barracks on 7 March 2009. Each was detained at Antrim police station and interviewed repeatedly.

Under Schedule 8 to the 2000 Act, initial detention without charge is limited to 48 hours, after which a judicial authority (a designated County Court or District Judge) may issue a warrant of further detention of up to seven days if satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing further detention is necessary to obtain or preserve relevant evidence or pending forensic analysis, and that the investigation is being conducted diligently and expeditiously. On 16 March 2009 the County Court granted five-day warrants of further detention in respect of all three applicants. Each was then interviewed a further twelve times.

On 21–22 March 2009 the Director of Public Prosecutions applied for seven-day extensions under paragraph 36 of Schedule 8, citing the need to await additional forensic results from a laboratory in Great Britain so that further questioning (and possible charging) could take place. Judge Philpott QC granted the extensions, authorising detention until 28 March. In written and oral rulings she expressly confined herself to the statutory necessity test and held that neither the 2000 Act nor Article 5 of the Convention conferred power on her to examine the lawfulness of the original arrests or to consider bail.

The applicants immediately sought judicial review. On 25 March 2009 the High Court of Northern Ireland quashed the extension warrants. It held that paragraphs 5 and 32 of Schedule 8 had to be read compatibly with Article 5 § 3, so that the reviewing judge was required to examine the basis of the arrest (albeit without a detailed merits analysis). The High Court nevertheless found that Judge Philpott had adequately addressed the need for continued detention and had given sufficient (if brief) reasons. The applicants were released without charge later that same day. The second applicant was immediately re-arrested, charged on 27 March 2009 with the two murders and related firearms offences, refused bail, and ultimately acquitted after a non-jury trial in January 2012. The first and third applicants were never charged in connection with the police officer’s murder.

A later High Court judgment (24 February 2011) rejected a freestanding compatibility challenge to Schedule 8. It held that the designated judge constituted a “judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power” for Article 5 § 3 purposes; that a power to order release must be implied; that the necessity test imported a requirement of proportionality; and that the statutory power to exclude the detainee and withhold sensitive information from him or her could be exercised in a manner compatible with an adversarial procedure and equality of arms. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

The applications to the Strasbourg Court therefore centred on whether the applicants’ detention after the initial 48-hour period, the limited scope of the judicial review actually conducted, the absence of an express bail power, the possibility of closed material, and the overall length of detention without charge were compatible with Article 5 §§ 1(c), 2 and 3 of the Convention.

The case of Magee and Others v. the United Kingdom (applications nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) arose from the arrests and detentions of three Irish nationals—Gabriel Magee (born 1972), Colin Francis Duffy (born 1967) and Teresa Magee (born 1978)—under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000. On 14 March 2009 the first and third applicants were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the 9 March murder of a police officer and detained at Antrim police station. They were interviewed multiple times over the following two days. On 16 March the Director of Public Prosecutions applied to the County Court under paragraph 29 of Schedule 8 for five-day warrants of further detention to permit additional questioning and forensic examination. After a hearing at which the first applicant gave evidence, the warrants were granted.

Each applicant was then interviewed twelve times. On 21 March the DPP sought seven-day extensions under paragraph 36, citing the need to await further forensic results. At hearings on 22 March a police superintendent testified and submissions were made. Judge Philpott granted both applications, extending detention until 28 March. She held that the 2000 Act conferred no power (express or implied) to review the lawfulness of the original arrests or to grant bail; her sole task was to decide whether continued detention was necessary for a diligent and expeditious investigation. Forensic evidence was central and the investigation met that standard.

The second applicant was arrested the same day on suspicion of involvement in the 7 March murders of two soldiers. A five-day extension was granted on 16 March. After twelve interviews and negative forensic results, a further seven-day extension was sought on 21 March to await tests from a laboratory in Great Britain. Judge Philpott granted it until 28 March.

The applicants sought judicial review of the 21–22 March decisions. They argued that the judge had wrongly declined to examine the lawfulness of their arrests, had failed to consider whether detention (as opposed to release) was required pending forensic results, had given inadequate reasons, and that Schedule 8 was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention. Permission was granted and the High Court of Northern Ireland heard the matter on 25 March. It ruled that paragraphs 5 and 32 of Schedule 8 must be read consistently with Article 5 § 3, so that judicial review of detention necessarily included examination of the arrest’s basis (albeit not a detailed merits review). Judge Philpott’s refusal to undertake that review vitiated her decisions, which were therefore quashed. The court accepted, however, that she had sufficiently considered the necessity of detention and had given adequate reasons.

The compatibility challenge was adjourned. In a February 2011 judgment the High Court held Schedule 8 compatible with Article 5. The “competent legal authority” need not be the trial court; a power to order release could be implied; the “reasonable grounds” test imported proportionality; closed-material provisions (paragraphs 33(3) and 34) could still permit an adversarial hearing; and Article 5 did not require a charge well before the 28-day maximum. Points of law of general public importance were certified, but the High Court and subsequently the Supreme Court (14 November 2011) refused permission to appeal.

The applicants were released without charge on 25 March 2009 (eleven days after arrest). The first and third were never charged in connection with the police officer’s murder. The second was immediately re-arrested, charged on 27 March with the soldiers’ murders and related offences, and remanded in custody. Bail was repeatedly refused. He was tried without a jury and acquitted on all counts on 20 January 2012.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints that the statutory scheme for extending pre-charge detention of terrorist suspects, the limited scope of judicial scrutiny, the absence of an express power of release or bail, and the possibility of closed hearings violated Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 3.

The case of Magee and Others v. the United Kingdom (applications nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) on 12 May 2015. It concerned three Irish nationals—Gabriel Magee (born 1972), Colin Francis Duffy (born 1967) and Teresa Magee (born 1978)—who alleged violations of Article 5 of the Convention arising from their arrests and pre-charge detention under the Terrorism Act 2000.

On 14 March 2009 the first and third applicants were arrested under section 41 of the 2000 Act on suspicion of involvement in the murder of a police officer five days earlier. They were taken to Antrim police station and interviewed over the following two days. The second applicant was arrested the same day on suspicion of involvement in the murder of two soldiers at Massereene Barracks on 7 March 2009. He was likewise detained at Antrim.

Under the statutory scheme, initial detention was limited to 48 hours, after which further detention required a warrant from a designated judicial authority (a County Court judge or District Judge). On 16 March 2009 the Director of Public Prosecutions applied successfully for five-day warrants of further detention in respect of all three applicants so that questioning and forensic examinations could continue. Each applicant was then interviewed twelve times.

On 21–22 March 2009 the DPP sought seven-day extensions under paragraph 36 of Schedule 8. A police superintendent gave evidence that further detention was necessary to await forensic results from a laboratory in Great Britain and to enable additional questioning. Judge Philpott granted the extensions, authorising detention until the early hours of 28 March. She expressly declined to examine the lawfulness of the original arrests, holding that her only statutory task was to decide whether continued detention was necessary for investigative purposes. She found that the investigation was being conducted diligently and that the outstanding forensic evidence was central.

The applicants immediately sought judicial review. On 25 March 2009 the High Court of Northern Ireland quashed the extension warrants. It held that, in order to comply with Article 5 § 3, the reviewing judge was required to examine the basis of the original arrest; otherwise a person could be held for up to 28 days without any judicial scrutiny of the arrest itself. The High Court accepted, however, that the review need not be a detailed merits examination and that the judge’s reasons, though brief, were adequate on the necessity question.

The applicants were released without charge later that day. The first and third applicants were never charged in connection with the police officer’s murder. The second applicant was immediately re-arrested, charged two days later with the soldiers’ murders and related offences, refused bail, tried without a jury and ultimately acquitted in January 2012.

In a later judgment of 24 February 2011 the High Court rejected the applicants’ remaining challenge that Schedule 8 itself was incompatible with Article 5. It held that a County Court judge constituted a “judge or other officer authorised by law” for Article 5 § 3 purposes, that a power to order release could be implied, that the “reasonable grounds” test incorporated proportionality, that the absence of an express bail power did not arise on the facts, and that the provisions permitting exclusion of the detainee and withholding of sensitive information could be operated in a manner consistent with an adversarial procedure. The Supreme Court refused permission to appeal.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints to the Strasbourg Court that their detention, the limited scope of the judicial reviews initially granted, the possibility of closed hearings and the length of detention without charge violated Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4.
001-153909:
**Case of Khan v. Germany (Application no. 38030/12), ECtHR Fifth Section, 23 April 2015 (referred to Grand Chamber)**

The applicant, Farida Kathoon Khan, a Pakistani national born in 1963, alleged that her planned expulsion from Germany to Pakistan would violate Articles 8 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. She had lived in Germany since 1991, initially as the spouse of a recognised refugee (her husband, whom she married in Pakistan in 1990 after converting to the Ahmadiyya faith). Her own asylum claim was refused, but she received a temporary residence permit in 1994 and a permanent one in 2001. Their son was born in 1995. The couple separated in 1998 (divorced 2004); the son initially lived with the applicant but later resided with the father after custody was transferred in 2005. The applicant worked as a cleaner until unemployment in 2004 linked to emerging psychological issues. She had limited German language skills, was not economically integrated, and maintained only restricted contact with her former husband and son.

On 31 May 2004, while in an acute psychotic state, the applicant killed a neighbour by strangling her and pushing her down stairs. She was detained, then committed to a psychiatric hospital after a self-harm attempt. In July 2005 the Gießen Regional Court found her to have committed manslaughter while mentally incapacitated (schizophrenia symptoms and diminished intelligence). She lacked insight into her condition, was deemed a continuing public danger, and was ordered to remain in hospital; a legal guardian was appointed.

In June 2009 the Waldeck-Frankenberg administrative authority ordered her expulsion under section 55(2) of the Residence Act, citing the offence, her mental state, and the resulting threat to public safety. Personal ties (long residence, permit status) were treated as secondary; she was not integrated, spoke little German (hindering therapy), had limited family contacts in Germany, remained familiar with Pakistani culture, and could access adequate psychiatric care there with family assistance and a small pension.

The applicant’s condition later improved. She received hospital privileges, worked full-time in the laundry, and showed better behaviour. In March 2011 the Kassel Administrative Court upheld the expulsion, emphasising the gravity of the offence, lack of insight, high reoffending risk, and poor integration. It held Article 8 inapplicable due to insignificant family ties. Basic psychiatric care existed in Pakistani cities such as Lahore; the applicant could fund treatment via her pension (~€250). Although relatives had refused to take her in, they might assist if paid small sums. As she held no prominent Ahmadiyya role, no specific religious risk was found. Leave to appeal was refused; a complaint that her improved health, her sister’s death, expected conditions in Pakistan, and regular visits by her son had been ignored was unsuccessful.

In November 2011 the Marburg Regional Court lifted the hospital order on medical advice, releasing her on five years’ probation with conditions to stay in contact with clinicians and take medication. The residual risk was deemed tolerable. A report noted remaining cognitive deficits and language-barrier problems in therapy, but she was compliant, worked, took medication, and displayed balanced behaviour. Her son visited regularly and wished greater involvement (limited by his studies). She was transferred to nearby sheltered accommodation providing structure. A constitutional complaint was not admitted (December 2011) and a parliamentary petition failed. No removal date had been set.

The case thus centred on whether expulsion, despite her long residence, mental-health improvements, family contacts, and possible difficulties obtaining care or support in Pakistan (including as an Ahmadiyya convert), disproportionately interfered with her private and family life or denied her a fair hearing in the expulsion proceedings. Domestic law provided for discretionary expulsion of foreigners whose stay endangered public safety, with special protection for long-term residents holding settlement permits (expulsion only on serious grounds).

The case of Khan v. Germany (Application no. 38030/12) was brought by a Pakistani national, Ms Farida Kathoon Khan (born 1963), who alleged that her planned expulsion to Pakistan would violate Articles 8 and 6 of the Convention. She has lived in Germany since 1991, initially arriving with her husband (granted refugee status); she obtained a temporary residence permit in 1994 as his spouse and a permanent permit in 2001. She converted to the Ahmadiyya faith upon marriage in Pakistan. Their son was born in 1995. The couple separated in 1998 (divorcing in 2004), after which the son lived with the applicant until 2005, when a family court transferred custody to the father.

In 2004 the applicant became unemployed amid emerging psychological problems. On 31 May 2004 she killed a neighbour by strangling and pushing her down stairs. After pre-trial detention and a suicide attempt she was committed to a psychiatric hospital. On 13 July 2005 the Gießen Regional Court found that she had committed manslaughter in a state of mental incapacity caused by acute psychosis; she exhibited schizophrenia symptoms and diminished intelligence, lacked insight into her condition, and posed a continuing public danger. Indefinite hospitalisation and appointment of a legal guardian were ordered.

On 4 June 2009 the Waldeck-Frankenberg administrative authority issued an expulsion order under section 55(2) of the Residence Act, citing the offence and her mental state as creating a danger to public safety that outweighed her long residence, status, lack of economic integration, limited German-language skills, sparse contacts with her former husband and son, and familiarity with Pakistani culture. Adequate psychiatric care was said to exist in Pakistan, where her family could assist.

The Kassel Administrative Court dismissed her challenge on 1 March 2011, stressing the gravity of the crime, her lack of insight (raising a high risk of reoffending) and her poor societal integration. It held Article 8 inapplicable because family ties were insignificant. Basic psychiatric care was available in cities such as Lahore and affordable with her small German pension; although relatives had refused to house her, they might assist in exchange for money. As a non-prominent Ahmadiyya member she faced no particular risk. Leave to appeal was refused. The applicant unsuccessfully invoked her right to be heard, arguing that improved health, her sister’s death in Pakistan, expected living conditions there and regular visits from her son had been ignored.

On 24 November 2011 the Marburg Regional Court, relying on a medical report, lifted the hospital order and released her on five years’ probation requiring continued medication and clinic contact. The report noted that, despite remaining cognitive deficits and language-barrier difficulties in therapy, she had become reachable, worked full-time in the hospital laundry, took her medication, displayed balanced behaviour and received regular visits from her son (who wished greater involvement). The residual risk was deemed tolerable. She was placed in nearby sheltered accommodation.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit her complaint. A subsequent parliamentary petition failed. No removal date has been set.

These facts—two decades of lawful residence, residual son–mother contact, a serious but mentally incapacitated offence, subsequent clinical improvement under structured care, language and integration deficits, and the contested availability of equivalent treatment plus family support in Pakistan—form the core of the alleged Article 8 interference with private (and limited family) life and the Article 6 complaint concerning the fairness of the expulsion proceedings.

The case of Khan v. Germany (Application no. 38030/12) was brought by Farida Kathoon Khan, a Pakistani national born in 1963, who alleged that her planned expulsion from Germany to Pakistan would violate Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and 6 (right to a fair hearing) of the European Convention on Human Rights. After pre-trial detention and a suicide attempt she was committed to a psychiatric hospital. On 13 July 2005 the Gießen Regional Court found that she had committed manslaughter while in a state of mental incapacity caused by acute psychosis; she displayed schizophrenic symptoms and diminished intelligence and lacked insight into her condition. The court therefore ordered her indefinite detention in a psychiatric hospital and appointed a legal guardian, considering her a continuing danger to the public.

On 4 June 2009 the Waldeck-Frankenthal administrative authority ordered her expulsion under section 55(2) of the Residence Act, citing the offence and her mental state as posing a threat to public safety that outweighed her long residence and status. The authority noted her lack of economic integration, poor German-language skills (which impeded therapy), limited contact with her former husband and son, familiarity with Pakistani culture, and the availability of adequate psychiatric care in Pakistan with possible family assistance.

Khan later obtained leave privileges, worked full-time in the hospital laundry and showed improved health. On 1 March 2011 the Kassel Administrative Court dismissed her challenge, holding that the seriousness of the offence, her lack of insight and the high risk of reoffending justified expulsion; she was insufficiently integrated and Article 8 was inapplicable because she had no significant family ties in Germany. The court accepted that basic psychiatric care existed in large Pakistani cities, that she would receive a modest German pension of approximately €250, and that relatives (who had refused to house her) might nevertheless assist if paid small sums. It found no particular risk arising from her Ahmadiyya affiliation. Leave to appeal was refused on 23 May 2011. Khan unsuccessfully invoked her right to be heard, complaining that the courts had ignored her improved health, her sister’s death in Pakistan, expected living conditions there, and regular visits from her son.

On 24 November 2011 the Marburg Regional Court lifted the hospital order on medical advice, releasing Khan on five-year probation with conditions of continued medication and clinic contact. The court accepted that treatment had reduced the risk of reoffending to a residual level that society must tolerate. A medical report described her as reachable despite cognitive deficits and language barriers, compliant with medication, behaviourally stable, and receiving regular visits from her son, who wished greater involvement (limited by his studies). Prognosis was positive. She was transferred to nearby sheltered accommodation. Her constitutional complaint was not admitted for review and a parliamentary petition failed. No removal date has been set.

These facts form the core of the Article 8 claim (length and quality of private life in Germany, residual family ties, integration, mental-health progress and conditions of return) and the Article 6 complaint (alleged failure to consider updated evidence of health, family circumstances and Pakistan conditions). Domestic law provided for discretionary expulsion even of long-term residents on serious public-safety grounds, subject to balancing of personal ties.

**Abdulla Ali v. the United Kingdom (ECHR, 2015) concerned an alleged Article 6 § 1 violation (fair trial by an impartial tribunal) arising from extensive prejudicial media publicity between the applicant’s first trial and retrial on terrorism charges.**

Abdulla Ahmed Ali, a British national born in 1980, was arrested in August 2006 with others in a major counter-terrorism operation. Prosecutors alleged he conspired to construct and detonate improvised explosive devices (IEDs) on transatlantic passenger aircraft using suicide bombers.

The first trial of eight defendants, including Ali, began in the Crown Court on 4 April 2008. Charges included conspiracy to murder (Count 1, specified as by mid-flight IED detonation) and conspiracy to endanger aircraft safety (Count 2). After the prosecution case, the indictment was amended to add Count 1A (conspiracy to murder without specifying means). On 8 September 2008, Ali was convicted on Count 1A; the jury hung on Count 1 (and on counts against several co-defendants). One defendant was fully acquitted.

The verdicts attracted massive press and broadcast coverage, including material never presented to the jury and criticism of the jury for failing to convict on Count 1. Illustrative inadmissible reports included: Ali’s alleged telephone contact with the ringleader of the failed 21 July 2005 London bombings; deeper links to 7/7 and 21/7 bombers (including concurrent Pakistan trips); connections to Rashid Rauf and Al-Qaeda leadership (including Abu Ubaydah Al Masri); interception of a text message urging action and communications suggesting a dummy run; and claims that US pressure on Pakistan prompted premature arrests that deprived investigators of further evidence. Sources were attributed to police, intelligence officials, counter-terrorism sources, and US/UK officials. Coverage appeared in virtually all national newspapers, on television/radio, and remained online. The judge later described it as an “avalanche of objectionable material” asserting the defendants’ guilt of the airline plot.

The Crown Prosecution Service announced a retrial on 10 September 2008 and reminded media of the need for responsible reporting to protect fair-trial rights. Defence lawyers wrote to the Attorney General seeking steps to prevent prejudicial reporting.

Ali applied to stay proceedings on Count 1, arguing that State-orchestrated briefings (intelligence, police, or government) had leaked non-evidential material to vilify the defendants and manipulate any retrial. On 18 December 2008, Mr Justice Henriques refused the stay. He rejected claims of secret Executive briefings or deliberate process abuse as fanciful, noting multiple alternative information sources (especially from the US) and standard pre-verdict briefing practices. He held that a fair trial remained possible: five months would elapse before the February 2009 retrial; juries could be trusted to follow tailored directions and decide solely on courtroom evidence; other terrorism trials had intervened; and defendants had already admitted related conspiracies (public nuisance via martyrdom videos and, for some, causing explosions), rendering alleged terrorist links less prejudicial if remembered. He cited domestic authorities on the “fade factor,” the focusing effect of trial evidence, and juries’ ability to disregard publicity.

The retrial of seven defendants (including Ali on Count 1) began in February 2009 but was aborted twice. A new jury was sworn on 2 March 2009. The judge questioned potential jurors about preconceptions of guilt, media employment, recent broadcasts discussing the plot, and internet research. He repeatedly instructed the selected jury not to conduct research, discuss the case outside the jury, or consider media reports, emphasising that only courtroom evidence counted and that prior reporting had been inaccurate. Similar warnings were given throughout the trial, including at the close of speeches and during summing-up.

On 7 September 2009, Ali was convicted on Count 1 (two co-defendants convicted, three acquitted, one hung). He received life imprisonment with a 40-year minimum term. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal (including the publicity ground) on 19 May 2011. It found the trial process capable of coping with the publicity; no evidence of juror internet research or disobedience of oath; and that a fair-minded observer would conclude a properly directed jury could try the case impartially after the elapsed time. It distinguished the case as involving post-conviction (rather than purely pre-trial) publicity but still held a fair trial possible.

Ali applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 15 May 2012, alleging that the publicity between trials denied him a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal. (The Court later examined whether domestic safeguards sufficed.)

On 8 September 2008, Ali was convicted on Count 1A, but the jury could not agree on Count 1. Similar hung verdicts occurred for most co-defendants; one was acquitted.

This encompassed Ali’s alleged telephone contacts with the 21 July 2005 London bombers, travel overlaps with 7 July 2005 bombers, links to Rashid Rauf and Al-Qaeda figures such as Abu Ubaydah Al Masri, intercepted texts and calls suggesting a dummy run, and claims that US pressure led to premature arrests in Pakistan that limited evidence-gathering. Defence lawyers wrote to the Attorney General seeking measures to protect the process. Applying domestic principles from cases such as Montgomery v HM Advocate, he held that a fair trial remained possible. Juries could be trusted to follow directions, the five-month interval would allow fading of memories, and other terrorist cases had since occupied the media. Ali’s admissions of related offences (public nuisance via martyrdom videos and, for some defendants, causing explosions) further reduced any residual prejudice. The retrial was fixed for February 2009.

The judge questioned potential jurors about preconceived views, family media connections, and recent broadcasts; none disqualified themselves on publicity grounds. He repeatedly directed the jury not to research the case, ignore media reports, and decide solely on courtroom evidence, repeating these instructions throughout the trial and summing-up. On 7 September 2009 Ali was convicted on Count 1 and sentenced to life imprisonment with a 40-year minimum term. Two co-defendants were also convicted on Count 1; others were acquitted or the jury hung.

Ali appealed, arguing the publicity rendered the retrial unfair. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 19 May 2011, endorsing Henriques J’s approach. It noted that no application had been made to postpone reporting of the first verdicts, that worldwide interest made suppression impractical, and that the trial process (including time elapsed and judicial directions) could counteract residual effects. Leave to appeal further was refused.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Abdulla Ali v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 30971/12) arose from an allegation under Article 6 § 1 that extensive adverse publicity after a first trial prevented a fair retrial by an impartial tribunal.

Abdulla Ahmed Ali, a British national born in 1980, was arrested in August 2006 during a major counter-terrorism operation. He was accused of conspiring to construct and detonate improvised explosive devices on transatlantic passenger aircraft in mid-flight using suicide bombers.

The first trial of eight defendants, including Ali, began on 4 April 2008 in the Crown Court on charges of conspiracy to murder by detonating devices on aircraft (Count 1) and conspiracy to endanger aircraft (Count 2). After the prosecution case closed, Count 1A was added, alleging conspiracy to murder without specifying the means. On 8 September 2008, Ali was convicted on Count 1A but the jury could not agree on Count 1. Results for co-defendants were mixed, with one acquitted of all charges.

The verdicts generated intense media coverage across newspapers, television, radio and the internet. Reports included inadmissible material never put to the jury, such as Ali’s alleged telephone contact with the ringleader of the failed 21 July 2005 London bombings, overlapping trips to Pakistan with those responsible for the 7 July 2005 attacks, connections to Rashid Rauf (who allegedly linked the plot to Al-Qaeda leadership), possible oversight by Abu Ubaydah Al Masri, intercepted texts and calls suggesting a dummy run, and claims that US pressure on Pakistan prompted premature arrests before more evidence could be gathered. Coverage also criticised the jury’s failure to convict on Count 1 and the trial judge’s management of proceedings.

The Crown Prosecution Service announced a retrial on 10 September 2008 and cautioned the media. Ali applied for a stay, arguing that the publicity—allegedly the product of orchestrated State briefings—had irretrievably prejudiced any future jury.

On 18 December 2008 Mr Justice Henriques refused the stay. He catalogued seven illustrative examples of non-evidential material published from sources including police, intelligence officials and government figures. He described an “avalanche” of reports asserting the defendants’ guilt of the aircraft plot, categorising the offending content as undisclosed terrorist links, blame on the United States for incomplete evidence, monitoring of communications, claims of lives saved, attacks on the jury’s competence and criticism of the judge. He rejected as fanciful the suggestion of deliberate secret briefings designed to taint a retrial, noting multiple independent sources of information. He held that a fair trial remained possible: juries could be trusted to follow directions, more than five months would elapse, intervening high-profile cases would fade public memory, and the defendants’ own admissions of related conspiracies diminished the impact of any remembered links.

A retrial began in February 2009 but was aborted twice. A new jury was sworn on 2 March 2009. The judge screened potential jurors for preconceived views arising from publicity, media connections, specific broadcasts and internet research. Once selected, the jury received repeated, detailed directions not to conduct research, discuss the case outside the jury room or consider media reports, and to decide solely on courtroom evidence. These warnings were reiterated throughout the trial.

On 7 September 2009 Ali was convicted on Count 1 and sentenced to life imprisonment with a 40-year minimum term. Two co-defendants were also convicted, three acquitted and one produced a hung jury. The Court of Appeal dismissed Ali’s appeal on 19 May 2011, endorsing the trial judge’s assessment that the trial process, the passage of time and jury directions were capable of ensuring impartiality.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the publicity had rendered the retrial unfair.

**CASE OF A.S. v. SWITZERLAND (Application no. 39350/13), ECtHR (Second Section), Judgment of 30 June 2015 (final 30 September 2015)**

The applicant, a Syrian national of Kurdish origin born in 1988, entered Switzerland from Italy on an unspecified date and applied for asylum on 18 February 2013. He alleged persecution, detention and torture in Syria. On 8 May 2013 the Federal Office of Migration (FOM) rejected his claim. Fingerprints registered in EURODAC showed prior entry to Greece (16 August 2012) and Italy (21 January 2013). Italy had accepted Switzerland’s 17 April 2013 take-back request under Article 10(1) of the Dublin Regulation. The FOM held that the applicant’s two sisters (resident in Switzerland since 2006 and January 2012) were not “family members” under Article 2(i) of the Regulation. It found no barrier to transfer arising from the applicant’s back problems, as Italy was obliged to provide medical care.

The applicant appealed to the Federal Administrative Court (FAC). He produced medical evidence of severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and back problems requiring twice-monthly psychotherapy, daily Sertraline, sleeping pills and painkillers. A 6 June 2013 report stated that without treatment his condition would deteriorate rapidly, creating high risks of substance abuse and suicide (higher still if returned to Syria). It described the sisters’ involvement as “an absolute necessity” for emotional stability. The sisters declared that the applicant spent virtually all his time with their families, could not be left alone and needed their support to recover. He also argued that Greece, not Italy, was the responsible Dublin State (citing M.S.S. v. Belgium and Greece) and that Article 15(2) of the Regulation required that he remain with his dependent relatives.

On 13 June 2013 the FAC dismissed the appeal. It confirmed Italy’s responsibility (Italy having been informed of the Greek entry) and noted that the applicant might have left the Dublin area after Greece. It found he was not so ill as to be dependent on his sisters, rendering Article 15(2) and Article 8 of the Convention inapplicable. There were no established structural deficiencies in Italy’s asylum reception or medical systems that would expose him to treatment contrary to Article 3. The Swiss authorities would inform Italy of his health needs upon transfer.

Before the Court the applicant alleged that removal to Italy would expose him to inhuman or degrading treatment (Article 3) because of his PTSD, back problems and lack of family support, and would interfere with his family and private life (Article 8). He further complained under Article 13 taken with Article 3 that the domestic authorities’ refusal of interim relief pending his appeal deprived him of an effective remedy.

He alleged that transfer to Italy would expose him to treatment contrary to Article 3 ECHR and interfere with his family and private life under Article 8. The FOM held that the applicant’s two sisters (legally resident in Switzerland since 2006 and January 2012) did not constitute “family members” under the Regulation. He was not so ill as to be dependent on his sisters, so neither Article 15 § 2 nor Article 8 applied. No structural deficiencies in Italy’s asylum reception system had been shown, and thus no Article 3 risk existed. Swiss authorities should inform Italy of his health problems upon transfer.

He had been allocated an individual asylum-seeker apartment but spent virtually all waking hours with his sisters’ families, remaining alone only at night. The sisters confirmed his intense emotional needs and their capacity and willingness to support his recovery.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: inadequate Italian reception and healthcare for a severely traumatised individual (Article 3), disruption of essential family support (Article 8), and the absence of suspensive interim relief (Article 13 + 3).
