The case of Kardišauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 62304/12) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged violations of Article 3 of the Convention. The Lithuanian applicant, Markas Kardišauskas (born 1979), claimed that prison authorities failed to protect him from a violent assault by fellow inmates and that the subsequent investigation into the attack was ineffective.

On 3 January 2003, the applicant began serving a sentence at Pravieniškės Prison following convictions for rape and theft (later supplemented by a 2013 Supreme Court ruling on murder and robbery charges, resulting in a combined 13-year term). On 25 May 2003, he was discovered beaten and unconscious after an attack by other prisoners. Prison authorities immediately opened a pre-trial investigation and inspected the scene, notifying the Kaišiadorys prosecutor. The applicant was rushed first to the Prison Department Hospital and then to Vilnius University Emergency Hospital for surgery. A forensic examination the next day confirmed head beatings and hematoma. A 28 August 2003 medical certificate established a severe skull fracture from two blows with blunt objects, rendering him unconscious and necessitating neurosurgery and prolonged rehabilitation. He was classified as Category II disabled in August 2003 (later downgraded), though by February 2008 he was deemed 90% able to work. After discharge on 28 August 2003, he received outpatient care and was transferred between facilities.

The applicant’s mother, informed a week later, complained of unsafe prison conditions and demanded punishment of those responsible. She was told an investigation (including a medical assessment of injury severity) was underway. The applicant, granted victim status on 10 July 2003, was questioned twice that summer but initially recalled nothing due to his condition. On 10 September 2003 he described being lured to Wing 5 living quarters, where a tall, well-built man (aged 40-45, previously convicted of murder, and known from outside prison) struck him with a knife. On 25 September he identified a photograph of E.J. as the attacker. Prison records later showed E.J. had been transferred to Lukiškės Remand Prison on 5 September 2002 and did not return until 29 May 2003, four days after the assault.

Investigators questioned 28 witnesses (prisoners and others), conducted medical exams, showed suspect photographs, and repeatedly requested operational measures from police (in 2003, 2004, 2005 and later) to identify perpetrators and the weapon. A November 2003 prison report and December 2003 internal investigation confirmed these steps but yielded no identifications. Police reported in March 2004 that no reliable leads existed. Further witness questioning in 2005 and a 2007 report on former inmates produced nothing. The prosecutor dismissed the mother’s 2007 complaint of ineffectiveness, noting that despite numerous actions the attackers remained unidentified; she was advised of appeal rights. A separate 2008 request to investigate prison officials’ alleged failure to protect the applicant was refused, as the main investigation was pending and any official liability or damages would be addressed once suspects were named (with prosecutors potentially filing a civil claim under Article 117 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the applicant could not). As of 2013–2014 the investigation remained open with no suspects identified and no procedural decisions taken.

In October 2010 the applicant, granted legal aid, sued the State in administrative courts for damages arising from the failure to protect his safety and the ineffective investigation. He attributed delay to his health, ongoing detention, lack of timely information about civil claims or legal aid, and prosecutors’ statements that a claim required identification of the attacker. The Kaunas Regional Administrative Court dismissed the health-damage claim in March 2011 as time-barred (three-year limit under Civil Code Article 1.125 from the May 2003 injury). After remittal, the same court in February 2012 again refused examination, noting health improvement by 2004, available family support and legal aid, and the applicant’s unfounded belief that identification was a prerequisite. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this on 7 June 2012, rejecting claims of prosecutorial misleading or health barriers and observing that the applicant had not used his rights under Article 28 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to appeal investigators’ or prosecutors’ actions. The investigation was still pending.

Domestic law (Civil Code Articles 6.271 and 6.283) imposes strict State liability for unlawful acts or omissions by public authorities causing health damage, while the Code of Criminal Procedure requires prompt, thorough investigation of crimes (Article 2), grants victims rights to request actions and appeal (Articles 28, 62–63), and assigns prosecutors supervisory powers (Articles 164, 170). Court practice confirms the limitation period starts on the date of injury.

The case of Kardišauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 62304/12) concerns a Lithuanian national’s complaints under Article 3 of the Convention that prison authorities failed to protect him from assault by other inmates and that the subsequent criminal investigation into the attack was ineffective.

The applicant began serving a sentence at Pravieniškės Prison on 3 January 2003 following convictions for rape and theft (later increased to 13 years after a separate murder-and-robbery conviction). On 25 May 2003 he was found beaten and unconscious. Prison authorities immediately opened a pre-trial investigation, inspected the scene, and transferred him first to the Prison Department Hospital and then to Vilnius University Emergency Hospital, where he underwent neurosurgery. A forensic examination the next day recorded beatings to the head and haematoma. A later medical certificate established a severe skull fracture caused by two blows with blunt objects; the applicant had been unconscious, required lengthy rehabilitation, and was classified Category II disabled (later reduced to Category III). By 2008 his working capacity had recovered to 90 percent. He was returned to prison for outpatient care in late August 2003.

The applicant’s mother, informed only a week later, demanded that those responsible be identified and punished. Investigators granted the applicant victim status on 10 July 2003 and questioned him twice; he initially stated he could not recall the attack because of his injuries. On 10 September 2003 he described being lured to another wing, seeing a tall, well-built man of 40–45 whom he recognised from outside prison, and being struck on the head with a knife. He later identified a photograph of E.J. as the attacker. Prison records showed, however, that E.J. had been transferred to Lukiškės Remand Prison on 5 September 2002 and did not return until 29 May 2003—four days after the incident. Prison authorities therefore concluded E.J. could not have been the assailant.

Over the following years investigators questioned 28 witnesses (including fellow inmates), ordered operational measures, circulated photographs, and repeatedly asked police forces in Kaunas and Plungė to identify suspects and locate the weapon. No reliable information emerged. The applicant’s mother repeatedly complained of inaction; prosecutors replied that all possible steps had been taken and that she could appeal to a court (which she did not do). In 2008 a prosecutor refused to open a separate inquiry into possible official negligence, stating that any such question would be examined within the existing investigation once perpetrators were identified. By 2010 still no suspect had been named. The investigation remained formally open in 2012–2014 “until new circumstances came to light.”

In October 2010 the applicant, granted legal aid, brought an administrative action against the State for damages arising from both the failure to protect him and the ineffective investigation. The prison administration noted that he had never reported feeling in danger. Domestic courts dismissed the claim as time-barred: the three-year limitation period for health-related damage ran from the date of injury, and the applicant had filed more than seven years later. They rejected arguments that his health, detention, or alleged prosecutorial advice that a civil claim could be lodged only after identification of the attacker excused the delay. The courts also observed that he had never exercised his statutory rights as a victim to challenge investigative decisions.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 violations: an unexplained violent assault causing life-threatening injury inside a State prison, followed by a decade-long investigation that produced no identifications despite numerous formal steps.

The applicant, a Lithuanian national born in 1979, began serving a prison sentence at Pravieniškės Prison on 3 January 2003 following a conviction for rape and theft. In later proceedings he was also convicted of murder and robbery committed as part of an organised group, receiving a combined sentence of 13 years.

On 25 May 2003 he was found beaten and unconscious after an attack by other inmates. A pre-trial investigation was opened the same day by prison authorities, who inspected the scene and notified the prosecutor. The applicant was hospitalised, first at the prison hospital and then at a university emergency hospital, where he underwent neurosurgery. Medical evidence established a severe skull fracture caused by two blows to the head with blunt objects; he remained unconscious for a period and required lengthy rehabilitation. He was classified as Category II disabled in August 2003 and Category III in March 2004; by 2008 his working capacity had recovered to 90 percent. He was discharged from hospital in late August 2003 and later moved between prisons and the prison hospital.

The applicant’s mother, who learned of the incident a week later, immediately complained that the prison was unsafe and demanded that those responsible be identified and punished. Investigators granted the applicant victim status in July 2003 and questioned him twice; he initially claimed no memory of the attack because of his injuries. In September 2003 he described being lured to another wing by an inmate, seeing a tall, well-built man aged 40–45 (previously convicted of murder) holding a knife, and being struck on the head. From photographs of 43 persons he identified a suspect, E.J. Prison records subsequently showed that E.J. had been transferred to another facility in September 2002 and did not return until 29 May 2003—four days after the attack.

Over the following years investigators questioned 28 witnesses (including fellow inmates), ordered operational police measures, conducted further medical examinations and showed additional photographs. Repeated written requests were sent to police and prosecutors in 2004–2005 asking that additional inmates be questioned, suspects identified and the weapon located. Police reported that no reliable information had been obtained. A 2007 prison report confirmed that former inmates questioned about the 2003 events had provided nothing useful. The prosecutor dismissed the mother’s complaints about the pace of the investigation, stating that despite numerous steps the perpetrators could not be identified; she was told she could appeal to a court. A request to open a separate investigation into alleged prison-staff negligence was also refused on the ground that any official failure would be examined within the existing inquiry and that a civil claim for damages would be considered once suspects were found. The investigation remained open without any suspect being named, and no procedural decision terminating or concluding it had been taken by 2014.

The first-instance court held the claim time-barred under the three-year limitation period applicable to health-damage actions, which ran from the date of injury. After remittal, the courts again rejected the claim, finding that the applicant’s health had sufficiently improved by 2004, that relatives and free legal aid had been available, and that he had not needed to wait for identification of the attacker. They also noted that he had never used his rights under the Code of Criminal Procedure to complain about investigative steps. The Supreme Administrative Court confirmed the dismissal on 7 June 2012, observing that the criminal investigation was still pending.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 3 of the Convention that the prison authorities had failed to ensure his safety and that the subsequent investigation had been ineffective.

On the evening of 25 September 2002, E. visited M.V. at his Braşov business headquarters demanding repayment of an alleged USD 50,000 loan. M.V. then telephoned the applicant, asking him to come by car to transport someone to Bacău. The applicant arrived to find E. badly beaten and pleading for mercy. The attackers bound E., placed him in the boot of his own car, drove away, murdered him, and staged a road accident as cover. The applicant then drove the attackers home.

On 5 October 2002 the applicant contacted S.S. (then on holiday) and reported the events. They met after S.S.’s return; on 23 October 2002 S.S. transmitted the information to the police via his superiors. No investigation occurred until a year later, when another participant confessed.

On 27 October 2003 the applicant was informed of the accusations and made a statement in the presence of counsel. On 18 January 2004 he and the others were committed for trial on charges of illegal deprivation of liberty and extremely aggravated murder. Throughout the proceedings the applicant maintained that he had infiltrated M.V.’s group as an SRI informant and that M.V. had coerced his participation by threats to him and his family.

The court relied on witness testimony, accused persons’ statements, expert reports and police documents. It found that the applicant’s arrival at M.V.’s headquarters, his accompaniment of the car carrying the victim, and his driving of the perpetrators home constituted assistance in the crimes. The court acknowledged the applicant’s information-sharing with S.S. but noted the SRI’s denial that this arose from any collaboration concerning the murder. The court held that the applicant could not claim informant status under the Prevention and Combat of Organised Crime Act (Law No. 39/2003), as no indications of those specific crimes existed and he had not been used to gather data on them. It rejected the coercion defence, observing that the applicant could have left or called the police (even claiming a blocked mobile-phone keypad was unconvincing).

The Braşov Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 26 January 2006. S.S. testified that his collaboration with the applicant was based on long-standing friendship, that M.V.’s group posed no national-security threat and was therefore of no SRI interest, and that he could not disclose meeting details or whether the applicant had been infiltrated because the information was classified. The court concluded that the applicant had assumed an informant role on his own initiative without official request or permission to participate in crimes.

On 24 October 2006 the High Court of Cassation and Justice increased the sentence to ten years; the decision was final.

The applicant sought revision of the final judgment, arguing that classified information prevented him from proving his SRI informant status (S.S. risked his job by disclosing it) and that police inaction on his report had denied him the more lenient treatment given to the later confessor. He requested declassification. On 25 July 2007 the County Court granted the request in principle, considering the information potentially relevant and previously unavailable.

S.S. again refused to confirm infiltration or the nature of the information, citing classification. On 12 September 2007 the SRI partially declassified S.S.’s report (describing the facts as related by the applicant) but stated that the applicant’s own written report had been destroyed after verification and transmission to the police; collaboration details remained classified under the Protection of Classified Information Act (Law No. 182/2002) because disclosure could severely affect national security.

On 20 November 2008 the County Court quashed the convictions in part and acquitted the applicant, finding that the SRI’s incomplete information and the cumbersome declassification procedure (left to the SRI’s discretion) had undermined defence rights under Article 6. Given the difficulty of obtaining conclusive proof, the court accorded increased weight to the available material and concluded that the applicant had participated solely as an informant, his fear, horror and despair at the scene removing criminal responsibility.

On appeal by the prosecutor, the Braşov Court of Appeal on 22 October 2009 quashed the acquittal and dismissed the revision request. It held that revision could not serve merely to introduce new evidence (already examined by the ordinary courts) and that the absence of a legal framework regulating intelligence informants created a risk of abuse; such status could not exonerate criminal acts. The High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 28 October 2010.

Relevant domestic law included the SRI Act (Law No. 14/1992), the National Security Act (Law No. 51/1991) (permitting agents to receive informant reports but not to initiate investigations), and the Organised Crime Act (providing limited immunity or sentence reduction for cooperating participants or informants, but only in exceptional circumstances where other identification methods were unavailable).

**Case Summary: Berland v. France (ECHR, Application no. 42875/10, judgment of 3 September 2015)**

Daniel Berland (born 1987), a French national, alleged a violation of Article 7 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (no punishment without law, including the prohibition on retrospective application of harsher criminal legislation). He claimed that French courts had applied a 2008 statute retrospectively to impose coercive measures for a 2007 offence that would not have been available under the law in force at the time.

On 12 September 2007, when aged 20, Berland went to the workplace of his former girlfriend C.G. after she had ended contact due to his threats and violence. He inflicted multiple stab wounds, killing C.G. by massive haemorrhage from injuries to the throat and thorax, and wounding two other persons. On 14 September 2007 he was placed under judicial investigation for premeditated murder and intentional wounding, remanded in custody, and simultaneously subjected by prefectural order to compulsory admission to the Sevrey specialised hospital centre (CHS). Two boards of expert psychiatrists concluded that, at the material time, he suffered from a mental disorder that had impaired his discernment and ability to control his actions within the meaning of Article 122-1 of the Criminal Code (which excludes criminal liability).

The Law of 25 February 2008 on preventive detention and declarations of criminal insanity introduced new procedural provisions (Articles 706-120 et seq. of the Code of Criminal Procedure). On 8 September 2008 the public prosecutor requested referral to the Investigation Division of the Dijon Court of Appeal for a ruling of lack of criminal liability under the new framework. The investigating judge, finding sufficient evidence that the offences had been committed and plausible grounds for applying Article 122-1, transmitted the file. After a public hearing (which Berland could not attend for medical reasons), his representative argued that the new procedure required the Investigation Division to make findings of fact amounting to a conviction and to impose indefinite compulsory treatment and other sanctions that had not existed at the time of the 2007 acts, thereby violating the principle of non-retrospectivity of harsher criminal law.

In its judgment of 18 February 2009 the Investigation Division held that there was sufficient evidence that Berland had “intentionally killed C.G.” but that he lacked criminal liability because of his mental disorder. It ordered his compulsory hospitalisation pursuant to new Article 706-135 on the ground that his disorder posed a risk to others and required long-term hospital care. It also imposed, under new Article 706-136, a twenty-year prohibition on contacting the complainants and on possessing or carrying a weapon. The civil claims were remitted to the ordinary criminal court. The Division rejected the non-retrospectivity objection, characterising the measures as preventive rather than penal: hospitalisation would be administered by medical and administrative authorities according to the patient’s evolving health, not as a court-imposed sentence of unlimited duration.

Berland appealed to the Court of Cassation, repeating that Article 7 and the principle of legality precluded immediate application of a procedure that attached court-ordered coercive measures to a declaration of insanity. The Advocate General observed that a finding of “intentional” commission was legally incompatible with insanity (which negated the mental element). On 14 April 2010 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that the 2008 measures were preventive, not penalties, and therefore fell outside Article 112-1 of the Criminal Code (which confines penalties to those applicable at the date of the offence). It confirmed that sufficient evidence existed that Berland had committed the offences of premeditated murder and wounding.

In February 2011 the Prefect of Saône-et-Loire refused Berland unescorted leave from hospital, citing the 2009 contact prohibition even though psychiatric assessments had tentatively supported such leave as part of rehabilitation. The ongoing operation of the twenty-year bans thus continued to constrain his treatment.

These facts formed the basis of Berland’s complaint that the 2008 legislation had been applied retrospectively to attach punitive consequences (indefinite hospitalisation and long-term prohibitions recorded in his criminal record) to acts committed before the statute’s entry into force.

The case of Berland v. France (Application no. 42875/10) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 7 § 1 of the Convention (no punishment without law), arising from the retrospective application of a 2008 French law imposing coercive measures after a finding of criminal irresponsibility due to mental disorder.

On 12 September 2007, 20-year-old Daniel Berland stabbed his former girlfriend C.G. to death at her workplace and wounded two others, following prior threats and violence. Charged with premeditated murder and intentional wounding, he was remanded in custody and immediately placed under compulsory psychiatric admission by prefectural order. Expert psychiatrists concluded that a mental disorder had abolished his discernment and self-control at the time of the acts, engaging Article 122-1 of the Criminal Code (which excludes criminal liability).

The proceedings then applied the Law of 25 February 2008 (on preventive detention and declarations of criminal insanity), enacted after the offences. This law created a new public procedure before the Investigation Division of the Court of Appeal to declare lack of criminal liability while simultaneously ordering long-term compulsory hospitalisation (Article 706-135 CCP) and other restrictions (Article 706-136), such as contact bans and weapons prohibitions, recorded in the criminal record. The investigating judge found sufficient evidence of the offences and referred the case. At the 2008 hearing (which the applicant could not attend for medical reasons), his lawyer objected that the new procedure required a finding that he had committed the acts and then imposed indefinite hospitalisation plus 20-year prohibitions—measures that constituted a conviction and sentence unavailable under the law in force in 2007.

On 18 February 2009 the Investigation Division held there was sufficient evidence that the applicant had “intentionally killed” C.G. (and wounded the others) but that he lacked criminal liability owing to his mental disorder. It ordered compulsory hospitalisation because the disorder posed a risk to others requiring long-term inpatient care, plus 20-year bans on contacting the complainants or possessing weapons. It classified these as preventive rather than penal measures, so the 2008 law applied immediately; the case was remitted solely for civil damages.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, arguing that Article 7 precluded immediate application of a procedure that attached “quasi-criminal sanctions” to a declaration of insanity. The public prosecutor noted an inconsistency in describing the acts as “intentional,” given that insanity precluded the mental element. On 14 April 2010 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, ruling that the non-retroactivity rule of Article 112-1 of the Criminal Code applied only to penalties, not to the preventive measures in Articles 706-135 and 706-136.

Subsequent events illustrated the measures’ lasting effect: in 2011 the prefect refused unescorted leave, despite favourable medical assessments, because the 2009 court-ordered prohibitions made it impossible to guarantee no contact with the victims. The applicant remained detained in the specialised hospital.

These facts centre on the 2008 law’s retrospective use to establish that the applicant had committed the 2007 acts and to impose hospitalisation and restrictions that he claims amounted to punishment not prescribed at the time.

The case of Peruzzi v. Italy (no. 39294/09) arose from an application by Italian lawyer Piero Antonio Peruzzi, who alleged that his conviction for defamation violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression).

In 2001 the applicant, then practising as a lawyer, sent a complaint to the National Legal Service Commission (CSM) about the conduct of Judge X of the Lucca District Court in inheritance-partition proceedings involving the applicant’s clients. He later circulated a letter (without naming X) to other judges of the same court. The letter described how, despite a pending appeal, an investigating judge had rejected repeated requests to suspend the auction of a flat and had ultimately sold it. The applicant praised judges who performed their duties with dedication, commitment and decorum, but criticised others for acting “in a partial manner, perhaps with a display of arrogance”, for showing “total indifference and lack of commitment”, for treating judicial autonomy as “absolute discretionary power \ldots bordering on or tantamount to arbitrariness”, and for making “wilful mistakes, by malicious intent, serious misconduct or negligence”. He argued that such conduct showed disrespect for lawyers’ work, deprived clients of certainty and eroded public confidence in the justice system.

Judge X lodged a criminal complaint for defamation. Because X sat in Lucca, the file was transferred to Genoa. X joined the proceedings as a civil party. The public prosecutor initially charged the applicant with both defamation and (later) proffering insults.

On 3 February 2005 the Genoa District Court convicted the applicant of both offences and sentenced him to four months’ imprisonment, reimbursement of X’s costs (EUR 2 000) and an advance of EUR 15 000 toward non-pecuniary damage. The court held that while criticism of a judge’s legal interpretation was permissible, the quoted passages overstepped the limits of legitimate criticism. They accused X of arrogance, indifference, a sense of impunity arising from power, and wilful error, thereby impugning his honour. Parallel letters that named X confirmed that he was the intended target. The defence of provocation was rejected because the circular letter, sent four months after the contested decisions, was not an immediate reaction.

The Genoa Court of Appeal, on 12 March 2007, quashed the insults conviction (no complaint had been filed on that charge) and replaced the prison sentence with a remitted fine of EUR 400. It nevertheless confirmed the defamation conviction and awarded X EUR 15 000 in damages plus further costs. The court found that fellow judges had readily identified X as the addressee, that X’s decisions were at most erroneous (and had been partly upheld by the Court of Cassation), and that circulating the letter inside a small court necessarily damaged X’s dignity and his image as an independent judge.

The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 12 November 2008, holding that the Court of Appeal’s reasoning was logical and complete.

These facts—the content and circulation of the letter, the identification of Judge X, the domestic courts’ characterisation of the remarks as exceeding fair criticism, and the resulting criminal conviction and damages award—constitute the core of the alleged interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression.

The case of Peruzzi v. Italy originated in an application by Italian lawyer Piero Antonio Peruzzi, who alleged that his 2005 conviction for defamation (later reduced on appeal) violated Article 10 of the Convention. In 2001, following decisions by Judge X of the Lucca District Court in inheritance partition proceedings involving Peruzzi’s clients, the applicant first complained to the Consiglio Superiore della Magistratura (CSM) and other bodies. He then circulated a letter to other Lucca civil-division judges. Although the circular did not name X, it recounted the case in detail: the court had ordered sale of a jointly owned flat occupied by a cohabitee and her daughter despite a pending cassation appeal, which the applicant said was forbidden by Article 791 of the Code of Civil Procedure. After two unsuccessful auctions the property was conveyed to a third party.

The letter mixed general praise for the judiciary with pointed criticism. Peruzzi wrote that judicial autonomy “cannot be turned into an absolute discretionary power because that would be bordering on or tantamount to arbitrariness”; that rights could be decided “in a partial manner, perhaps with a display of arrogance, or \ldots with total indifference and lack of commitment”; that a judge “cannot allow himself not to respect the work of others, including that of the lawyer”; and that judges “cannot and must not wilfully make mistakes, by malicious intent, serious misconduct or negligence.” He portrayed such conduct as damaging lawyers’ professional dignity and public confidence in justice.

X lodged a criminal complaint for defamation. Because X sat in Lucca the file was transferred to Genoa. X joined the proceedings as a civil party. The Genoa District Court convicted Peruzzi in February 2005 of defamation and insult, imposing four months’ imprisonment, an order to pay X’s costs (€2,000) and a provisional award of €15,000 damages. It held that the letter, read with the earlier named complaints to the CSM, unmistakably targeted X, accused him of arrogance, indifference, a sense of impunity and deliberate error, and thereby exceeded legitimate criticism of judicial work.

On appeal the Genoa Court of Appeal (March 2007) quashed the insult count for lack of a specific complaint, converted the remaining sentence to a remitted fine of €400, but confirmed the €15,000 damages and a further €2,000 costs. It found that other Lucca judges had readily identified X as the addressee and that the letter was not merely a general lament about the justice system. X’s rulings might have been erroneous but were not “unfair”; the National Bar Council had even regarded Peruzzi’s correspondence as an attempt to pressure the bench. Circulating such language inside a small court necessarily undermined X’s dignity and appearance of independence.

The Court of Cassation dismissed Peruzzi’s further appeal in November 2008, holding that the lower courts’ reasoning on the offensive character of the statements and the absence of provocation was logical and complete. These domestic findings—that the circular personally impugned a named judge’s integrity rather than offering admissible professional criticism—form the factual core of the Article 10 complaint later examined by the European Court.

The case R.H. v. Sweden (Application no. 4601/14) concerns a Somali national born in 1988 who alleged that her deportation from Sweden to Somalia would violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by exposing her to a real risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment.

The applicant first applied for asylum in Sweden on 27 December 2011, claiming arrival on 11 December 2011. A EURODAC search showed she had sought asylum in the Netherlands in December 2006 under a different identity. She later admitted arriving in Sweden in 2007 after time in the Netherlands and remaining illegally to avoid transfer to Italy, where she said she had no housing or means of support. She had relatives (cousins) in Sweden. Dutch authorities declined a Dublin transfer because she had previously applied in Italy under yet another name. Italian authorities did not respond in time, so the Swedish Migration Board ordered her transfer to Italy on 24 April 2012. The transfer became time-barred.

She reapplied for asylum on 30 November 2012. In a lengthy interview she described a forced marriage in November 2004, arranged by her family to an older man. She had been in a secret relationship with a schoolboy; days after the marriage they attempted to flee Mogadishu by truck but were discovered by her uncles, beaten and thrown off. She suffered hip injuries requiring months of hospitalisation. She remained at home until August 2005, when her father deemed her fit to join her husband. She then fled with her boyfriend via Ethiopia, Sudan and Libya. Their boat to Italy sank and he drowned. She later learned her father had died in 2010 and her mother in 2011. She feared that return would force her back to the husband or expose her to a death sentence (by stoning) for having fled the marriage and the country, threats she said would be carried out by her uncles. She claimed she lacked any male support network, would be at high risk of sexual assault as a single woman, could not rent accommodation or organise her life, and would become a social outcast. She also cited Somalia’s dire humanitarian conditions and the ongoing need for treatment of her hip injury. An x-ray showing hip prostheses was later produced.

The Migration Board rejected the claim on 8 March 2013 and ordered deportation to Somalia. It found she had not substantiated her identity (multiple aliases) but accepted she originated from Mogadishu. The four-year delay in seeking asylum after arriving in 2007 undermined any genuine fear of persecution. Material credibility problems existed: she first claimed to be unmarried and invoked only the general armed conflict, later introducing the 2004 forced marriage and changing details about her hip injury and living arrangements. The Board concluded she had not made plausible any past ill-treatment by relatives and therefore had not shown she lacked male protection (her brother and uncles still lived in Mogadishu). Country information from a 2012 fact-finding mission indicated the situation in Mogadishu was not so severe as to prevent return for a person with a male network. She had never lived in a refugee camp.

The Migration Court dismissed her appeal on 4 June 2013, endorsing the credibility findings and noting further inconsistency (marriage dated 2004 then 2010). The x-ray did not prove assault in Somalia. Leave to appeal was refused. A later request to re-open the case, alleging an uncle had joined al-Shabaab, killed her sister and forced her brother to join (raising a risk of stoning), was rejected on 7 September 2013 as presenting no new circumstances; the uncle-related threats had already been examined and her general lack of credibility meant a mere assertion was insufficient. She did not appeal that decision.

The European Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39 preventing deportation pending its examination. The alleged Article 3 risk therefore rested on the combination of her personal history of forced marriage, family violence and flight, the claimed absence of male protection, gender-specific dangers for a single woman in Mogadishu, possible targeting by al-Shabaab-linked relatives, and her medical condition, all set against the Swedish authorities’ findings that her account was not credible and that she retained family support in Mogadishu.

The case of R.H. v. Sweden (Application no. 4601/14) concerned a Somali woman born in 1988 who claimed that her deportation from Sweden to Somalia would violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). She arrived in Sweden around 2007 after unsuccessful asylum claims in Italy and the Netherlands (under different identities) and remained illegally until applying for asylum in December 2011. After an initial Dublin Regulation transfer order to Italy expired, she reapplied in November 2012.

In her asylum interview, the applicant described being forcibly married in November 2004 to an older man. She had a secret boyfriend; they were caught attempting to flee Mogadishu, beaten by her uncles, and she suffered hip injuries requiring months of hospitalisation. After living at home until August 2005, she fled with her boyfriend via Ethiopia, Sudan and Libya. Their boat sank and he died. Her parents later died. She claimed return would force her back to the husband or result in death (stoning) by uncles for fleeing the marriage and country. As a single woman without a male support network she risked sexual assault, social ostracism and inability to secure housing or organise her life. She also invoked Somalia’s dire humanitarian conditions and her ongoing need for hip treatment (evidenced later by an x-ray of prostheses). After rejection she added that an uncle had joined al-Shabaab, killed her sister and forced her brother to join, heightening the risk of being stoned.

Swedish authorities rejected her claims. The Migration Board (March 2013) found her identity unsubstantiated due to prior inconsistent identities abroad and noted her four-year delay in seeking protection after arriving in 2007. It identified major credibility problems: she initially claimed to be unmarried and invoked only general armed conflict, later introducing the forced marriage; accounts of her hip injury, pre-departure living arrangements and marriage timing also conflicted. The Board accepted she was from Mogadishu but held she had not shown past ill-treatment or lack of a male network (her brother and uncles remained there). Country information from a 2012 fact-finding mission indicated Mogadishu’s situation was not so severe as to prevent return, especially with family protection; she had not lived in a refugee camp and faced no such risk.

The Migration Court (June 2013) upheld the decision, endorsing the credibility findings and adding further inconsistencies (e.g., marriage date). It discounted the x-ray as proof of assault. Leave to appeal was refused. A later request to re-examine based on the uncle’s al-Shabaab involvement was rejected (September 2013) as not constituting new circumstances given her lack of credibility.

Domestic law (Aliens Act) provides protection for refugees or those at risk of death, torture or inhuman treatment, plus residence on particularly distressing grounds (including health). Enforcement is barred where such risks exist. Country information before the Court (Danish/Norwegian reports 2013–2014, Swedish Migration Board 2014, UK Upper Tribunal 2014, UNHCR 2014 and others) described improved security in Mogadishu after al-Shabaab’s 2011–2012 withdrawal, with no frontline fighting but persistent targeted attacks (IEDs, assassinations) mainly against officials, security forces and affiliates; ordinary civilians faced lower (though not zero) risk if they avoided high-profile sites. Civilian casualties had declined. For women, however, sexual and gender-based violence remained widespread and committed with impunity by state forces, militias and others. Single women or female heads of household without nuclear-family or clan (male-network) protection faced heightened vulnerability to rape, abuse and inability to access housing, livelihoods or customary-law representation. Clan support had weakened as a protection mechanism. Returnees without family, resources or diaspora remittances risked destitution or IDP-camp conditions. UNHCR identified women and girls as a potential risk profile.

The Court applied an interim measure preventing deportation pending its examination.

The applicant, a Somali woman born in 1988, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights alleging that her deportation from Sweden to Somalia would violate Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). She first applied for asylum in Sweden in December 2011, claiming arrival that month, but EURODAC records showed a prior 2006 application in the Netherlands under a different identity. She later admitted arriving via the Netherlands in 2007 and remaining illegally thereafter, fearing onward transfer to Italy. Under the Dublin Regulation, Italy was deemed responsible after failing to respond, but the transfer decision lapsed. She reapplied in November 2012.

In her January 2013 interview, she described a forced marriage in November 2004 to an older man arranged by her family in Mogadishu, despite a secret relationship with a schoolboy. Days later, she and her boyfriend attempted to flee but were intercepted by her uncles, beaten, and thrown from a truck, causing hip injuries requiring months of hospitalisation. She lived with her parents until August 2005, when her father deemed her fit to join her husband. She then fled with her boyfriend via Ethiopia, Sudan and Libya; he drowned when their boat to Italy sank. She later learned of her parents’ deaths in 2010–2011. She feared return to her husband or execution by uncles for fleeing the marriage and country. As a single woman lacking a male support network, she claimed she risked sexual assault, inability to secure housing or livelihood, social ostracism, and inadequate care for her hips amid Somalia’s humanitarian crisis.

The Migration Board rejected her claim on 8 March 2013, finding her identity unsubstantiated (multiple aliases used) but accepting Mogadishu origins. It questioned her delayed application after years of illegal stay and identified credibility problems: she initially claimed to be unmarried and cited only general conflict, later introducing the forced marriage, inconsistent accounts of her injury and pre-flight living arrangements, and varying marriage dates. The Board concluded she had not shown past ill-treatment or absence of male protection (brother and uncles remained in Mogadishu). Country information from a 2012 fact-finding mission indicated Mogadishu’s situation, including for women, was not sufficiently severe to preclude return given her network; she had not previously lived in a camp.

The Migration Court dismissed her appeal on 4 June 2013, endorsing the credibility findings and noting further inconsistencies. An X-ray of hip prostheses did not prove assault. Leave to appeal was refused. A subsequent request citing new claims—that an uncle had joined al-Shabaab, killed her sister and forced her brother to join, creating a stoning risk—was rejected as insufficiently new or credible; she did not appeal.

Swedish law (Aliens Act) grants protection to refugees or those facing death, torture or inhuman treatment, including from non-state actors if authorities cannot protect, plus residence on particularly distressing grounds (e.g., health). Enforcement is barred where such risks exist.

Extensive country material (Danish/Norwegian reports 2013–2014, Swedish Migration Board missions 2013–2014, UK Upper Tribunal 2014, UNHCR 2014, UN OCHA) described Mogadishu’s post-2011 improvement after al-Shabaab’s withdrawal: reduced frontline fighting, economic activity and returns, but persistent targeted attacks, IEDs, assassinations and criminality by various actors, including government forces. Civilian casualties declined but remained daily. Women faced widespread sexual and gender-based violence (rape, exploitation) by soldiers, militias and others, often with impunity; state protection was ineffective due to weak institutions, corruption and discriminatory customary law (Xeer). Single women or female heads of household without nuclear family or clan/male networks (fathers, husbands, uncles, brothers) were at heightened risk of violence, isolation and inability to access housing, livelihoods or legal representation. Clan support had weakened as a protective mechanism. Ordinary civilians (non-profiled) faced no general Article 3 risk from indiscriminate violence, but individual assessment was required for those lacking family/clan/economic support, who might face destitution below humanitarian standards. Diaspora returnees often had resources; those without faced precarious conditions.

These facts formed the basis for assessing whether substantial grounds existed for believing the applicant would face a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 upon return.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Krasnodębska-Kazikowska and Łuniewska v. Poland (application no. 26860/11) concerned two Polish applicants, legal successors of owners of land near Warsaw (Willa Janówka) that was expropriated by the State Treasury in 1971 without compensation under an administrative scheme. In 2005 the Local Self-Government Board of Appeal declared the 1971 decision to have been issued in flagrant breach of the law then in force and confirmed that the declaration created a right to compensation for the resulting damage.

The applicants lodged a civil claim for compensation in August 2006. In May 2009 the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the claim and awarded each applicant PLN 64,487, representing the value of the expropriated land. It found that all elements of State liability in tort were present and that, because the original decision pre-dated the 1 September 2004 amendments to the Civil Code, the new Article 417¹ (read with the general tort provisions) applied. Consequently the three-year limitation period began only when the 2005 corrective decision became final and had not expired.

The State Treasury appealed. In November 2009 the Warsaw Court of Appeal accepted the first-instance findings on damage and causation but reversed the legal characterisation of the limitation period. It held that, given the practical impossibility of suing the State under the communist regime, the ten-year period in former Article 442 of the Civil Code started to run on 4 June 1989 (the date of the first partially free elections). The applicants were therefore required to have obtained a declaration of unlawfulness before June 1999; their claim was time-barred.

The applicants’ cassation appeal argued that the Court of Appeal’s approach violated Article 77 of the 1997 Constitution (the right to compensation for unlawful acts of public authorities) and highlighted a significant legal issue arising from contradictory domestic case-law on the applicable limitation regime for pre-2004 decisions declared unlawful after that date. In October 2010 the Supreme Court, sitting as a single judge, refused to entertain the appeal on the ground that it raised no significant legal issue.

Meanwhile, two other legal successors of owners affected by the identical 1971 expropriation and the same 2005 corrective decision succeeded in their own compensation actions. In September 2010 the Warsaw Regional Court awarded one claimant PLN 110,187, applying the three-year period that ran from the 2005 decision. In July 2012 the same court awarded another claimant PLN 82,988, expressly relying on a March 2011 Supreme Court resolution (III CZP 112/10) that confirmed the applicability of former Article 160 of the Code of Administrative Procedure and the three-year period commencing with the corrective decision. The Regional Court noted that earlier conflicting interpretations had created serious difficulties in judicial practice.

The applicants therefore found themselves denied compensation solely because of divergent interpretations of the same transitional provisions, while identically situated co-owners obtained awards after the Supreme Court had clarified the law. The discrepancy formed the core of their complaint that they had been arbitrarily deprived of a property claim that the domestic legal system itself recognised as well-founded.

The applicants, legal successors of owners of land near Warsaw (including “Willa Janówka”), were affected by a 1971 administrative decision that expropriated the property to the State Treasury without compensation as part of a broader scheme. On 30 December 2005 the Local Self-Government Board of Appeal declared that the 1971 decision had been issued in flagrant breach of the law then in force and informed the parties that this “corrective” decision gave rise to a compensation claim for the resulting damage.

The applicants lodged their claim on 28 August 2006. On 15 May 2009 the Warsaw Regional Court awarded each of them PLN 64,487 (the value of the expropriated land). It found that the conditions of State liability in tort were satisfied once the 2005 decision had established the unlawfulness of the original act. Because the original decision pre-dated 1 September 2004 (when the Civil Code was amended), the court applied Article 417^{1} of the Civil Code; the three-year limitation period therefore began only when the 2005 decision became final and had not expired.

The State appealed. On 26 November 2009 the Warsaw Court of Appeal set aside the award. While it accepted the existence of pecuniary damage and the causal link, it held that the ten-year limitation period under the former Article 442 of the Civil Code had begun to run on 4 June 1989 (the date of the first partially free elections, after which it had become politically possible to challenge communist-era decisions). The applicants ought therefore to have obtained a declaration of unlawfulness before 4 June 1999; their claim was time-barred.

The applicants’ cassation appeal argued that the appellate judgment violated Article 77 of the 1997 Constitution (right to compensation for damage caused by public authorities) and that the case raised a significant legal issue because of well-known divergences in the case-law on the law and limitation periods applicable to pre-2004 decisions declared unlawful after that date. On 21 October 2010 the Supreme Court, sitting as a single judge, refused to examine the appeal, finding that no significant legal issue arose.

Parallel claims brought by other successors affected by the identical 1971 expropriation and the same 2005 corrective decision produced opposite results. A.C.’s claim, lodged on 30 August 2006, was allowed by the Warsaw Regional Court on 30 September 2010 (PLN 110,187); the court applied the three-year period running from the 2005 decision. R.W.’s claim, lodged on 5 September 2006, was allowed on 10 July 2012 (PLN 82,988) after the court relied on a subsequent Supreme Court resolution.

The relevant legal framework comprised Article 77 of the Constitution, the former Article 160 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (compensation for actual damage caused by an unlawful decision), and, after 1 September 2004, Articles 417 and 417^{1} of the Civil Code (which require a prior declaration of unlawfulness). These provisions generated persistent and acknowledged discrepancies among Polish courts—including within the Supreme Court itself—concerning which statute applied and, consequently, when the limitation period began and how long it lasted. In March 2011 (after the applicants’ case had become final) the full Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court resolved that former Article 160 governed and that the three-year period ran from the date of the corrective decision.

The applicants therefore alleged that the inconsistent domestic jurisprudence had arbitrarily deprived them of compensation that was granted to identically situated claimants.

The case of Krasnodębska-Kazikowska and Łuniewska v. Poland (Application no. 26860/11) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by two Polish nationals, Ms Maria Krasnodębska-Kazikowska and Ms Hanna Łuniewska, born in 1942 and 1943. As legal successors of former owners of the property known as Willa Janówka near Warsaw, they alleged that discrepancies in Polish judicial case-law had denied them compensation for damage caused by an unlawful expropriation.

In 1971, an administrative decision compelled the then-owners, including the applicants’ mother, to transfer the land to the State Treasury without compensation as part of a broader expropriation scheme. On 30 December 2005, the Local Self-Government Board of Appeal in Warsaw issued a corrective decision declaring the 1971 measure to have been issued in flagrant breach of the law then in force. The decision explicitly informed the parties, including the applicants and other successors, that it gave rise to a compensation claim for the damage inflicted by the original unlawful act.

The applicants lodged their civil claim for compensation on 28 August 2006. On 15 May 2009 the Warsaw Regional Court allowed the claim and awarded each applicant PLN 64,487, equivalent to the value of the expropriated land. The court found that the conditions of State liability in tort were satisfied and applied the post-1 September 2004 Civil Code provisions (in particular Article 417¹), under which the three-year prescription period began only when the 2005 corrective decision became final. That period had not expired.

The State Treasury appealed. On 26 November 2009 the Warsaw Court of Appeal reversed the award and dismissed the claim. While endorsing the first-instance findings on the existence of damage and the causal link, the appellate court held that the ten-year prescription period under the former Article 442 of the Civil Code had begun to run on 4 June 1989 (the date of the first partially free elections, after which claims against the communist-era State became realistically possible). The applicants had therefore been required to obtain a declaration of unlawfulness of the 1971 decision before 4 June 1999; having failed to do so, their claim was time-barred.

The applicants’ cassation appeal argued that the appellate judgment violated Article 77 of the 1997 Constitution (guaranteeing compensation for unlawful State acts) and highlighted a significant legal issue arising from divergent case-law on the temporal application of the 2004 amendments and the applicable prescription rules. On 21 October 2010 the Supreme Court, sitting as a single judge, refused to examine the appeal on the ground that it raised no significant legal issue.

Parallel proceedings brought by other successors of the same 1971 expropriation, also relying on the 2005 corrective decision, produced opposite outcomes. In a judgment of 30 September 2010 the Warsaw Regional Court awarded A.C. PLN 110,187, applying the three-year period running from the 2005 decision. On 10 July 2012 the same court awarded R.W. PLN 82,988, expressly following a 31 March 2011 resolution of the Supreme Court sitting as a full Civil Chamber. That resolution (III CZP 112/10) acknowledged serious discrepancies in judicial practice and held that the former Article 160 of the Code of Administrative Procedure applied, so that the three-year limitation period started only upon the issuance of the corrective decision.

The applicants therefore found themselves in an identical factual situation to co-owners who later obtained compensation, yet their claim was rejected solely because of one of the competing interpretations of the transitional provisions governing State liability for pre-2004 administrative decisions. The Supreme Court’s refusal to take their case at a time when the divergence was already well-documented left them without a remedy for the acknowledged unlawfulness of the 1971 expropriation.

The case of Lecomte v. Germany concerned the conditions of the applicant’s preventive detention in two police stations, which she alleged violated Article 3 of the Convention.

Cécile Lecomte, a French environmental activist known for climbing-based protests, was arrested on 6 November 2008 at 2.40 p.m. after she and three others from Robin Wood scaled a railway bridge arch, unfurled anti-nuclear banners, and refused to descend. Police mountain rescuers lowered them; only Lecomte was detained. A commuter train had been halted due to the risk. At 5.30 p.m. the Lüneburg District Court ordered her detention under section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act until the scheduled radioactive-waste (“castor”) transport reached Dannenberg (at latest 10 November). The court found an imminent risk that she would again climb to block the transport, thereby committing serious regulatory offences. She was taken home briefly to collect clothes and medication, then held in Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m.

Her cell there was small, containing only a mattress and chair, lit by a ventilation slot and electric light. She remained until approximately 1.40 p.m. on 7 November, when she was taken to the Regional Court. After the hearing she waited in police offices and was walked outdoors three times. The Regional Court dismissed her appeal that evening. En route to Braunschweig Police Station (deemed better equipped) she reported breathing difficulties; an ambulance and police doctor found her fit, and she arrived at 2.10 a.m. on 8 November.

In Braunschweig she occupied a cell with a bed, empty desk, chair, open cupboard and barred frosted-glass window. Photographs of shackled persons, including one “hog-tied,” hung in the corridor. On the first night the light stayed on because she climbed onto the 1.90 m cupboard and refused to descend; police left the light burning rather than forcibly removing her. She received writing materials, three visits from a friend, two from her doctor, and several telephone calls to her lawyer and partner. Outdoor time totalled 42 minutes on 8 November (loosely shackled to an officer because of escape risk and lack of a closed courtyard) and 13 minutes on 9 November (unshackled; she climbed a tree). She suffered from rheumatism requiring constant movement; her joints stiffened and her mental state deteriorated. On 9 November at 5.25 p.m. the District Court quashed the detention order, citing her health and the consequent absence of any remaining risk of climbing. She was released at 6.32 p.m.

Lecomte later sought a declaration that both the detention and its conditions had been unlawful. The District Court and Regional Court rejected the claim, holding that the cells met Police Custody Regulations (adequate lighting, ventilation, furnishings), that the constant light was required for her own safety, that the photographs were tasteless but not intimidatory, that outdoor exercise complied with staffing and infrastructure limits, and that health deterioration had not been independently proven before the release decision. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to examine the complaints.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 3 complaint concerning the material conditions, lighting, photographs, limited outdoor access, shackling and the applicant’s health in police custody lasting just over three days.

**Case of Lecomte v. Germany (Application no. 80442/12), ECtHR Fifth Section, 6 October 2015 (final 6 January 2016).**

French national Cécile Lecomte (born 1981), an anti-nuclear activist known for climbing protests, alleged that conditions of her short preventive police detention in two German stations violated Article 3 ECHR (inhuman or degrading treatment).

On 6 November 2008 around 11 a.m., she and three others from Robin Wood climbed a railway bridge arch, hung protest banners against scheduled radioactive “castor” waste transport (7–9 November) from France to Gorleben, and refused police orders to descend. Police mountain rescue lowered them; only she was arrested at 2:40 p.m. (banners and gear seized). A Federal Police doctor found her healthy. At 5:30 p.m. the Lüneburg District Court ordered preventive detention under Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act s.18(1) no. 2 (to prevent imminent serious regulatory offences of public importance) until the train arrived or at latest 10 November 00:00, citing her climbing history, prior law-breaking in protests, and risk of blocking the transport (a commuter train had already been halted). She was taken home briefly (5:45–6:45 p.m.) for clothes and medication.

Detention began at 7 p.m. in a small Lüneburg Police Station cell (mattress, chair; lighting via ventilation slot plus electric light). She stayed until ~1:40 p.m. on 7 November, then appeared before the Regional Court (which dismissed her appeal at 9:15 p.m.). Meanwhile she waited in the station office area and was taken for three walks by the river. Transfer to better-equipped Braunschweig Police Station followed; en route she reported breathing problems, an ambulance and police doctor confirmed fitness, and she arrived at 2:10 a.m. on 8 November. Her cell had a bed, empty desk, chair, open cupboard and barred frosted-glass window. Corridor photos showed shackled persons, including one hogtied (ankle- and hand-cuffs chained behind the back on a mattress).

Lights remained on her first Braunschweig night because she climbed a 1.90 m cupboard and refused orders to descend; police left them on for safety monitoring rather than forcing her down. Outdoor time: 8 November 2:20–3:02 p.m. (loosely shackled to a female officer, no closed courtyard, given her climbing skill and non-compliance risk); 9 November 12:22–12:35 p.m. (unshackled; she climbed a tree). She received writing materials, three friend visits, two doctor visits (C., who confirmed serious rheumatism requiring constant movement, joint stiffening from limited mobility, poor mental state, and likely inability to climb soon), and multiple calls to her lawyer and partner. Some 200 calls from sympathisers (some abusive) disrupted operations.

On 9 November at 5:25 p.m. the District Court quashed the order due to her deteriorating health (no remaining risk of climbing offences; detention no longer proportionate) and released her at 6:32 p.m. (total custody ~3 days). Later domestic review (District and Regional Courts 2009; Constitutional Court declined 2010/2012) upheld the detention order and conditions as lawful and compliant with Police Custody Regulations (cells adequately lit/ventilated/equipped; night rest right not breached—noise individual, lights for her protection; outdoor time as staffing/infrastructure allowed; visits not unlawfully restricted; photos tasteless but not intimidatory). CPT recommendations on police cells (size, natural light, 1-hour daily outdoor exercise after 24 hours) were treated as inapplicable.

These facts—short duration, basic cell furnishings, security-driven lighting/shackling/outdoor limits, health impact from rheumatism and restricted movement, and limited visits amid disruption—formed the core of the Article 3 complaint about preventive police custody.
