The European Court of Human Rights case of Uğur v. Turkey (Application no. 37308/05) concerned two brothers, Ferdi Uğur (born 1985) and Atilla Uğur (born 1987), who alleged violations of Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention arising from their treatment as minors following a 23 November 2002 shooting in Istanbul.

Around 2:30 a.m., the applicants’ neighbour B.S. was shot in the street and later died. The applicants, then aged 17 and 15, helped take him to hospital. Police arrived and took the applicants and several friends to Beyoğlu police station, ostensibly as witnesses. Police reports recorded their arrival at 5:30 a.m. after they had been “apprehended in connection with the incident.” They remained there for over 24 hours without being entered in custody ledgers, without notification of rights or family, without a lawyer, and without transfer to a specialised minors’ station as required by domestic regulations. Hand swabs were taken from the first applicant. On 24 November, officers from the minors’ station were summoned to Beyoğlu station and questioned the applicants (still without a lawyer). The resulting statements, recorded as having been taken at the minors’ station, had the applicants admitting they had tried to rob an off-duty officer, A.Ö., whose pistol discharged and killed B.S. during a scuffle. The applicants later maintained these statements were false, extracted under duress, and that they had never said the things attributed to them.

The applicants alleged they were stripped, doused with cold water, kicked, punched, grabbed by the throat and beaten with truncheons to force self-incrimination. They said they were released around 4–5 p.m. on 25 November after further blows and told never to return. Medical examinations on 26 November (Human Rights Foundation) and subsequently (including 12 December hospital reports and 31 December Forensic Medical Institute reports) documented injuries on both applicants, including bruises, scratches and cuts consistent with the alleged beatings; the first applicant was deemed unfit for three days and the second for five days. An investigation against the second applicant for attempted robbery was discontinued for lack of evidence; B.S. had in fact been killed by A.Ö.

On 29 November the applicants lodged a formal complaint. The prosecutor’s investigation was delayed by the then-chief of Beyoğlu station, K.Ş.S., who failed to produce officers for questioning. Twenty officers, including K.Ş.S., were eventually indicted for ill-treatment (later reclassified as torture). The applicants identified several officers. They later alleged that police pressure—including threats and the forced appointment of a new lawyer—led them to withdraw their complaints and recant in June 2004. They subsequently reappointed their original lawyer and maintained their claims. Other detained youths corroborated the beatings. Many defendant officers repeatedly failed to attend hearings. An unscheduled hearing on 15 December 2004 heard K.Ş.S. in the applicants’ absence.

On 29 December 2009 the Assize Court acquitted ten officers for lack of evidence of torture and discontinued proceedings against the remaining ten (including K.Ş.S.) after reclassifying the offence as ill-treatment, for which the limitation period had expired. It found the applicants had been “unnecessarily kept” and injured by “pushing and jostling.” The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment in 2011, holding that the applicants lacked standing because they had withdrawn their complaints. A parallel disciplinary inquiry imposed no sanctions on the officers.

The applicants argued that these events constituted unlawful detention (Article 5) and both substantive ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation (Article 3). Domestic regulations required custody records, immediate family notification, compulsory legal representation for minors, and questioning only by a prosecutor in a lawyer’s presence—none of which occurred.

The applicants, brothers Ferdi and Atilla Uğur (aged 17 and 15), were among a group who took their neighbour B.S. to hospital after he was shot in Istanbul around 2.30 a.m. on 23 November 2002; B.S. died on arrival. Police, already aware an off-duty officer A.Ö. had shot him nearby, took the group (including the applicants) from the hospital to Beyoğlu police station around 3 a.m. as purported witnesses. Police reports recorded arrival at 5.30 a.m. and described them as “apprehended” and “placed in custody” for transfer to a special minors’ station; hand swabs were taken. They remained overnight. On 24 November the station chief obtained telephone permission to question them as “statement makers.” Officers from the minors’ station then took statements at Beyoğlu station (falsely recorded as taken at the special station) without a lawyer, contrary to rules requiring legal representation, family notification and prosecutor involvement for minors. The statements described an attempted robbery of the drunken A.Ö. during which B.S. was shot; an investigation of the second applicant was later dropped for lack of evidence. No custody logs, rights notifications or release records exist; special-station records for the period are missing. The applicants were released around 4–5 p.m. on 25 November.

They alleged they were stripped, doused with cold water, kicked, punched and beaten with truncheons to extract the self-incriminating statements, then struck again on release without a medical examination. Medical reports of 26 November (Human Rights Foundation) recorded bruises and a scratch on the first applicant consistent with truncheon blows and a compatible account from the second (no visible marks). Hospital and forensic examinations in December confirmed injuries rendering the first applicant unfit for three days and the second (lip, arm and leg wounds) for five days.

On 29 November they complained to the prosecutor of ill-treatment and procedural violations. The investigation was delayed by non-cooperation from station chief K.Ş.S. Twenty officers (including K.Ş.S.) were indicted for ill-treatment, later reclassified as torture. The applicants identified several officers. Under alleged police pressure they withdrew the complaint on 8 June 2004, dismissed their lawyer, appointed another who opposed them, and claimed the injuries resulted from a street fight while intoxicated. They later recanted, reappointed original counsel and alleged threats. Other teenagers corroborated beatings aimed at forcing a confession that they (not A.Ö.) had killed B.S. Trial irregularities included an unscheduled hearing of K.Ş.S. in the applicants’ absence and repeated non-attendance by defendants. In 2009 the Assize Court acquitted ten officers and found the remaining ten (including K.Ş.S.) guilty only of ill-treatment (unnecessary detention and injuries from “pushing and jostling”) rather than torture, but discontinued the case as time-barred. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicants’ appeal because they had withdrawn their complaint. A parallel complaint of unlawful detention was dismissed on the ground that they had merely been questioned as witnesses.

The case of Uğur v. Turkey (Application no. 37308/05) involves brothers Ferdi Uğur (born 1985) and Atilla Uğur (born 1987), who were 17 and 15 years old in 2002. They alleged ill-treatment by police (Article 3) and unlawful deprivation of liberty (Article 5) after being taken to Beyoğlu police station following a shooting.

On 23 November 2002 at around 2:30 a.m., neighbour B.S. was shot in an Istanbul street and died after the applicants and friends took him to hospital. Police arrived at the hospital around 3 a.m. and took the applicants (and four other teenagers) to Beyoğlu police station, recording their arrival as 5:30 a.m. Official reports described them as “apprehended in connection with the incident” and “placed in the custody of the police.” Hand swabs were taken from the first applicant and others, indicating they were treated as suspects. An off-duty police officer, A.Ö., had in fact shot B.S.; A.Ö. was found injured nearby with his pistol.

The applicants, as minors, were not transferred promptly to a special station for minors. No custody ledgers recorded their identities, detention times, or medical examinations. They were not informed of their rights, allowed to contact a lawyer or family, or given food. They remained at the station for over 24 hours without prosecutor authorisation for any extension. On 24 November, after telephone permission from a prosecutor to question them as “statement makers,” two officers from the minors’ station took statements between 9:30 and 11:30 a.m. (recorded as taken at the minors’ station). The statements claimed the teenagers tried to rob the drunken A.Ö., leading to a scuffle in which B.S. was shot. The officers later testified they had refused to sign pre-prepared statements and that Beyoğlu officers ignored requests to release the minors as their detention was unlawful. No documents record the exact release time; the applicants stated they were beaten with truncheons and told to leave around 4–5 p.m. on 25 November, without a medical examination.

The applicants alleged they were stripped naked, doused with cold water, grabbed by the throat, kicked, punched and beaten with truncheons to force self-incriminating statements they could not verify as they were illiterate and unrepresented. On 26 November doctors at the Human Rights Foundation found the first applicant had a 4 cm scratch and multiple linear bruises (up to 14 cm) compatible with his account; the second applicant showed no external injuries but a compatible nervous state requiring further tests. Prosecutor-ordered examinations on 29 November and 12 December confirmed injuries rendering the first applicant unfit for three days and the second (cuts and grazes to lip, arms and legs) unfit for five days. An investigation against the second applicant for attempted robbery was discontinued for lack of evidence.

The applicants complained to the prosecutor on 29 November 2002. Police chief K.Ş.S. delayed the investigation by failing to produce officers. Twenty officers (including K.Ş.S.) were indicted for ill-treatment (later reclassified as possible torture). The applicants identified K.Ş.S. and others. Under alleged police pressure they withdrew complaints in June 2004 and changed lawyers, later reversing this. Trial irregularities included an unscheduled hearing of K.Ş.S. in their absence, widespread non-attendance by defendants, and delays. On 29 December 2009 ten officers were acquitted of torture; the remaining ten (including K.Ş.S.) were found to have committed ill-treatment by unnecessarily detaining the applicants and causing injuries through “pushing and jostling,” but proceedings were discontinued as time-barred. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicants’ appeal on the ground they had withdrawn their complaints. A disciplinary inquiry imposed no sanctions. Domestic regulations required custody records, lawyer appointment for minors regardless of wishes, family notification and prosecutor-led questioning of children.
001-157966:
The case of Jovanovic v. Sweden (Application no. 10592/12) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 December 2011 by Ljiljana Jovanovic, a Serbian national residing in Eskilstuna, Sweden. The applicant alleged that Swedish authorities’ refusal to terminate the compulsory public care of her son, X, violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.

X was born on 25 July 2008 to the applicant and her then-husband, B., both of Serbian origin. Shortly after birth, X was hospitalized with genital bruises. The following day he developed cramps and extensive brain bleeding. Medical staff suspected severe ill-treatment consistent with shaken-baby syndrome, resulting in lasting brain injuries and probable lifelong disabilities. On 25 August 2008 the local Social Council took X into immediate provisional public care under the 1990 Act with Special Provisions on the Care of Young Persons. The County Administrative Court confirmed the order; a full care order was granted on 28 October 2008 after an oral hearing. The court found that the injuries had occurred while X was in his parents’ care and that the parents had demonstrated a serious lack of protective capacity, regardless of which parent had inflicted the harm. The Administrative Court of Appeal and the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the order.

X was initially placed with his parents in an evaluation home, where staff noted the applicant’s practical caregiving skills but significant emotional shortcomings, including objectification of the child and denial of his injuries. In March 2009 X was moved to a Swedish foster family. A criminal investigation against both parents was discontinued for lack of proof as to the perpetrator.

In February 2010, after divorcing B. and obtaining interim sole custody, the applicant requested termination of public care, asserting she had never harmed X, had no reason to suspect risk, and was now capable of caring for him. An investigation by social services, incorporating expert medical evidence confirming shaken-baby syndrome, led the Social Council to refuse. On appeal the County Administrative Court, after hearing the parties and considering the applicant’s competing medical certificate, rejected the request on 31 August 2010. It held that the original circumstances had not been clarified, that the applicant’s life changes were insufficient, and that X needed stability with his foster parents.

The Administrative Court of Appeal obtained an independent expert opinion from the National Board of Health and Welfare, which corroborated the diagnosis of non-accidental trauma. At a hearing on 18 March 2011 the applicant revised her account, suggesting B. had likely shaken X while she was out of the room and had threatened her into silence. The court nevertheless upheld the care order on 12 April 2011, stressing the child’s best interests, the still-unresolved identity of the abuser, and a continuing clear risk of impairment to X’s health and development. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court was refused.

Parallel decisions restricted the applicant’s contact to as little as one hour per month because visits reportedly distressed X. Requests to transfer X to a Serbian foster family were refused as contrary to his best interests. Subsequent six-monthly reviews in 2012 and 2013 confirmed continuation of care; the applicant did not appeal those decisions. By late 2013 contact had been modestly increased and the applicant was working as a kindergarten teacher, yet public care remained in force.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 8 complaint: that the authorities’ persistent refusal to restore X to his mother’s care, despite her improved circumstances and eventual acknowledgment of the abuse, unjustifiably interfered with family life.

The case of Jovanovic v. Sweden originated in an application by Serbian national Ljiljana Jovanovic (born 1982), residing in Eskilstuna, Sweden. She alleged that Swedish authorities' refusal to end the compulsory public care of her son X violated her Article 8 right to family life.

The applicant married B., a Serbian man in Sweden, in August 2007 and moved there in January 2008. Their son X was born on 25 July 2008. After a brief postnatal hospital stay for a suspected infection, X was discharged in good health. On 20 August 2008, the parents took him to hospital with bruises on his genitals. The next day, X suffered cramps and extensive brain bleeding. A physician suspected severe ill-treatment, specifically shaken baby syndrome, involving tight gripping and violent shaking. X remained hospitalised with severe brain injuries expected to cause lifelong disabilities.

On 25 August 2008, the Social Council placed X in immediate provisional public care under the 1990 Act on Care of Young Persons, citing suspected child abuse. The County Administrative Court confirmed this on 2 September 2008. The Council then applied for a full care order. On 28 October 2008, after an oral hearing, the County Administrative Court granted it, holding that the injuries (genital bruises, brain bleeding, and a chest mark) occurred while X was in his parents' care. The parents had shown a serious lack of ability to protect him, regardless of who inflicted the harm. The Administrative Court of Appeal upheld this on 9 March 2009, and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 17 June 2009. A criminal investigation against the parents was discontinued in December 2008 for lack of proof.

X and his parents initially stayed in an evaluation home, where staff noted the applicant's good physical care but significant emotional interaction flaws, including objectification of X and denial of his injuries. B. was often absent. In March 2009, X was placed in a Swedish family home. The applicant later reported B. for threats.

In February 2010, the applicant sought to terminate the care, citing her divorce from B., interim sole custody, completed Swedish studies, and job plans. She denied any abuse or knowledge of risk. An investigation (completed 22 February 2010) referenced a specialist certificate confirming shaken baby syndrome, X's life-threatening injuries, and lifelong care needs. The Social Council rejected the request on 25 March 2010, stressing its duty to ensure X's safety given the unexplained harm.

The applicant appealed, contesting the medical findings (claiming hospital malpractice and submitting a conflicting certificate of anoxic injury), alleging procedural flaws, and arguing X's rights to language and religion were violated. The County Administrative Court rejected her appeal on 31 August 2010 after a hearing, finding her claims unsubstantiated speculation and the original circumstances unchanged by her divorce or custody status. It emphasised X's need for stability in the family home.

The Administrative Court of Appeal obtained a further expert opinion (January 2011) confirming the injuries resulted from severe violence matching shaken baby syndrome, not illness, accident, or birth trauma. At a March 2011 hearing, the applicant accepted the medical conclusions, suggested B. might be responsible (citing his temper and a specific incident), and described her now-stable life. On 12 April 2011, the court upheld the care order. While noting her improved situation, it prioritised X's best interests and extensive needs. The perpetrator remained unidentified, past family conditions had caused life-threatening harm, and a clear risk of impairment persisted. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave on 20 June 2011. Care continued after later reviews in 2012–2013.

Contact rights were restricted due to X's negative reactions, reduced from weekly to monthly or less, with unsuccessful appeals. A request to move X to a Serbian family home was denied as contrary to his interests. A 2012 filmed interaction later showed positive mother-child interplay, leading to modestly extended visits. The applicant works as a kindergarten teacher. These facts underpin the Article 8 complaint regarding ongoing care and limited family contact.

The applicant, a Serbian national residing in Sweden, married B. (also Serbian) and gave birth to their son X on 25 July 2008. Shortly after X’s discharge from hospital, the parents returned him with bruises on his genitals. The next day he suffered seizures and extensive brain bleeding. Hospital staff suspected severe physical abuse consistent with shaken-baby syndrome; X was left with lifelong mental and physical disabilities. On 25 August 2008 the local Social Council placed X in immediate compulsory public care under the 1990 Care of Young Persons Act. The County Administrative Court confirmed the order on 2 September 2008. In October 2008 the same court issued a full care order, finding that the injuries had occurred while X was in his parents’ care and that they had failed to protect him, demonstrating a serious lack of parental capacity. The Administrative Court of Appeal and Supreme Administrative Court upheld the decision. A criminal investigation against both parents was discontinued for lack of evidence identifying the perpetrator.

X and his parents were first placed together in an evaluation home. Staff reported that the applicant met X’s physical needs but displayed significant emotional deficits, objectified the child and refused to acknowledge his injuries or future disabilities. In March 2009 X was moved to a Swedish foster family. Contact with the parents, initially several times a week, was progressively restricted (to once a month or less) because visits visibly distressed X. The applicant later sought a Serbian foster placement and the right to speak Serbian and practise Orthodox Christianity with X; these requests were refused as contrary to the child’s best interests.

In February 2010, after divorcing B. and obtaining interim sole custody, the applicant applied for termination of care. She denied any abuse, claimed hospital malpractice, and pointed to her completed language studies and planned employment. The Social Council’s investigation, relying on specialist medical evidence, concluded that X still required protection regardless of which parent had caused the injuries. All three levels of administrative court rejected the application (final refusal of leave to appeal in June 2011). They held that the original circumstances remained unexplained, that the applicant’s improved personal situation and later admission that B. had probably shaken the child were insufficient, and that X’s extensive care needs and need for stability in the foster home outweighed the change in family circumstances. Subsequent six-monthly reviews by the Social Council (2012–2013) continued the care order; the applicant did not appeal those decisions. A 2012 filmed observation later showed positive emotional interaction between mother and child, prompting a modest increase in contact, but the care order itself remained in force.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the persistent refusal to end public care violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.
001-157760:
The case of Medžlis Islamske Zajednice Brčko and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 17224/11) originated in a January 2011 application by four Brčko District NGOs: the Brčko Branch of the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Bosniac Cultural Society “Preporod”, the Bosniac Charity Association “Merhamet”, and the Council of Bosniac Intellectuals. They alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) arising from domestic defamation judgments against them.

In May 2003 the applicants sent a letter to the International Supervisor for Brčko District, the President of the Assembly and the Governor. The letter criticised the composition of a selection panel for the director of the public radio station as contrary to the Statute’s requirement of proportional representation of the three constituent peoples (three Serbs, one Croat, one Bosniac). It opposed the candidacy of M.S., then entertainment editor, whom the Serb panel members had allegedly proposed. The applicants asserted that M.S. lacked the requisite professional and moral qualities, citing four pieces of information they had received: (1) in a published interview she had said Muslims were not people, possessed no culture and that destroying mosques could not therefore be regarded as destruction of cultural monuments; (2) on radio premises she had ostentatiously removed and torn up a calendar listing Ramadan religious services; (3) she had covered the coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina with that of Republika Srpska; and (4) as entertainment editor she had banned sevdalinka songs on the ground that they lacked cultural or musical value. They described these acts as disqualifying her for the post of director of a multi-ethnic radio station and warned that, absent action by the addressees, they would approach the media and other competent bodies.

The letter was shortly afterwards published in three daily newspapers. On 29 May 2003 M.S. brought a civil defamation action seeking BAM 50,000. She had learned of the letter soon after it was sent but did not know who had given it to the press. Following publication the Governor annulled the appointment procedure.

The Brčko District Court of First Instance dismissed the claim on 29 September 2004, holding that the applicants had sent the letter privately to the competent authorities rather than to the media and that they could not therefore be held liable for its subsequent publication.

The Appellate Court quashed that judgment on 16 May 2005 and, after hearing witnesses (including the two radio employees who had supplied the applicants with the information), delivered a fresh judgment on 11 July 2007. It found that the letter mixed value-judgments with statements of fact that were untrue and damaging to M.S.’s reputation. Liability under section 6(1) of the 2003 Defamation Act did not require the applicants themselves to have published the letter. The court ordered them, within 15 days, to inform the three original addressees of the retraction of the statements or, in default, to pay BAM 2,500 plus statutory interest, and to publish the judgment at their own expense.

The applicants paid BAM 2,825 in December 2007; enforcement proceedings were closed in March 2009.

They then complained to the Constitutional Court of a violation of Article 10. On 13 May 2010 that court held that the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation of others, and was necessary in a democratic society. Witness evidence had established that the factual allegations were false: there were inconsistencies between what the sources had actually said and what the letter reported; a further witness confirmed that M.S. had not given the alleged interview; and the applicants had produced no proof of the coat-of-arms incident. They had therefore failed in their duty to verify information before disseminating it and had exceeded the bounds of acceptable criticism of a candidate for public office. The award of non-pecuniary damages was proportionate to the mental anguish caused and did not go beyond the Appellate Court’s discretion. Consequently there had been no violation of Article II/3.h of the Constitution or of Article 10.

The Chamber communicated the Article 10 complaint and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicants—four Bosniak NGOs based in Brčko District (the local Islamic Community branch, the cultural society Preporod, the charity Merhamet, and the Council of Bosniak Intellectuals)—wrote a private letter in May 2003 to the International Supervisor, the District Assembly President, and the District Governor. The letter concerned the selection of a new director for the District’s public radio station. It objected that the selection panel (three Serbs, one Croat, one Bosniak) violated statutory ethnic-proportionality rules. It specifically opposed the candidacy of M.S., then the station’s entertainment editor, asserting she lacked the necessary professional and moral qualities.

The letter listed four concrete allegations said to have been received from unnamed sources: (1) M.S. had stated in a NIN interview that Muslims were not people, possessed no culture, and that the wartime destruction of Brčko mosques therefore did not constitute destruction of cultural monuments; (2) she had torn a Ramadan prayer-calendar from the wall on radio premises; (3) she had covered the Bosnia and Herzegovina coat of arms with that of Republika Srpska; and (4) she had banned sevdalinka songs from the airwaves on the ground that they lacked cultural or musical value. The applicants warned that if the authorities took no action they would publicise the matter in the media and before other domestic and international bodies.

The letter was leaked and appeared in three daily newspapers. M.S. then sued the four NGOs for defamation, seeking 50 000 convertible marks (BAM). She acknowledged learning of the letter shortly after it was sent but denied knowing who had given it to the press. Following publication the Governor annulled the entire selection procedure.

The Brčko Court of First Instance dismissed the claim in September 2004, holding that the letter had been a private communication to the competent authorities, not a publication, and that the NGOs had not themselves given it to the media. On appeal the Appellate Court quashed that judgment, held a fresh hearing (including testimony from the two radio employees who had supplied the information), and in July 2007 found the applicants liable. It characterised parts of the letter as value judgments but held that the four factual assertions were untrue, had damaged M.S.’s reputation, and had not been adequately verified. Under the District Defamation Act it was irrelevant that the NGOs had not themselves published the letter. The court ordered them either to send a retraction to the original addressees within 15 days or to pay BAM 2 500 in non-pecuniary damages (plus statutory interest) and to publish the judgment at their own expense.

The applicants paid BAM 2 825 in December 2007 to satisfy the judgment; enforcement proceedings were closed in 2009. They then complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, alleging a violation of freedom of expression. In May 2010 that court upheld the Appellate Court’s decision. It accepted that the interference was prescribed by the 2003 Defamation Act and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting reputation. It found the interference “necessary in a democratic society”: the factual statements had been shown to be false (witness testimony contradicted the calendar and sevdalinka allegations; a later check established that M.S. had not given the NIN interview; the coat-of-arms allegation remained unproved), the applicants had failed in their duty to verify, and the statements exceeded the bounds of acceptable criticism of a public official. The modest damages award was held to be proportionate.

The applicants then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that the domestic judgments violated Article 10 of the Convention. (The Chamber’s 2015 judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber.)

001-158155:
The case of Konstantin Stefanov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 35399/05) concerns a Bulgarian lawyer’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions was violated when he received no remuneration for court-appointed legal-aid work and was instead fined for refusing to act.

In early 2005 the Plovdiv District Court, trying two accused of aggravated theft (maximum sentence 15 years), concluded that the interests of justice required appointed counsel because the defendants wished to be represented but could not pay. The court asked the Plovdiv Bar to nominate two lawyers and stated that remuneration would be fixed in accordance with the 2004 Remuneration Ordinance. On 31 May 2005 the Bar nominated the applicant to represent one defendant, N.R. Its letter reminded him of his statutory duty to appear (section 44 of the Bar Act) and warned that the court was obliged to fix his fee at or above the Ordinance minimum; otherwise he must refuse the appointment or face disciplinary proceedings under section 132(6) of the Bar Act.

At the hearing on 10 June 2005 the District Court formally appointed the applicant and asked whether there was any obstacle to proceeding. The applicant replied that he would act only if the court immediately determined his remuneration at the Ordinance minimum of BGN 550 (approximately EUR 280), as required by section 44(2) of the Bar Act. The presiding judge refused to fix any figure at that stage, warning that a refusal to act would be punished by a fine. The applicant then declined the appointment and left the courtroom.

The court immediately imposed a fine of BGN 500 (approximately EUR 260) on the applicant under Article 269 § 7 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure. It held that asking for a fee before evidence had been heard displayed “manifest disrespect,” that the lawyers had caused an unjustified adjournment, and that the defendants had to be represented. After a one-hour break a substitute lawyer present in court was appointed, acquainted himself with the file, and the case ended the same afternoon by plea bargain. The substitute was awarded only BGN 30.

The applicant appealed the fine, arguing that the court had itself breached section 44(2) by failing to indicate the remuneration in the appointment order and by refusing to apply the Ordinance minimum. His refusal was therefore lawful and the fine unlawful. On 11 July 2005 the Plovdiv Regional Court dismissed the appeal in a final decision. It accepted that the Bar Act required the fee to be stated in the appointment order and not to fall below the Ordinance minimum (BGN 550 for a 15-year offence, reduced to BGN 150 if the case ended by plea bargain). It nevertheless held that the precise amount could be known only at the end of the proceedings, because the court could not foresee a plea bargain. The applicant’s insistence on an immediate determination was therefore contrary to the Bar Act, had caused an adjournment, and justified the maximum fine, which the court found proportionate.

Domestic law at the material time obliged a court-appointed lawyer to act (section 44(1) Bar Act) and permitted resignation only for objective impossibility. Courts were simultaneously required to fix remuneration in the appointment decision itself at or above the Ordinance rates. After 1 January 2006 a new Legal Aid Act removed both the obligation to state the fee at appointment and the applicability of the Remuneration Ordinance to legal-aid work.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference with the applicant’s possessions: he performed no work and received no fee, yet was fined the statutory maximum for declining an appointment that, in his view and on the face of the Bar Act, the court had itself rendered unlawful by refusing to determine the fee in advance.

The case of Konstantin Stefanov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 35399/05) arose from events in 2005 involving the applicant, a practising lawyer in Plovdiv. He alleged a breach of his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions (under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention) because he received no fee for work as court-appointed legal aid counsel and was unlawfully fined in the process.

In criminal proceedings before the Plovdiv District Court against two accused charged with aggravated theft (punishable by up to 15 years' imprisonment), the court determined that the interests of justice required appointment of defence counsel. The accused could not afford lawyers but wished to be represented. The court requested the Plovdiv Bar to nominate two lawyers, noting that remuneration would follow the National Bar Council's 2004 Remuneration Ordinance on minimum fees.

On 31 May 2005 the Bar nominated the applicant to represent one accused (N.R.). Its letter stressed that, under section 44 of the Bar Act, he was obliged to appear and act as counsel or face disciplinary action and possible civil liability. It further stated that the court's appointment decision must set remuneration at or above the Ordinance minimum (BGN 550, or about EUR 280); otherwise the applicant should refuse representation to avoid disciplinary sanctions for breaching the Bar Act.

At the 10 June 2005 hearing the District Court appointed the applicant and asked whether the hearing could proceed. He replied that he would act only if the court immediately complied with section 44(2) of the Bar Act by fixing his fee at or above the BGN 550 minimum. The presiding judge refused to determine the amount at that stage and warned of a fine if the applicant declined to serve. The applicant then refused and left the courtroom.

The court immediately fined him BGN 500 (about EUR 260) under Article 269 § 7 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure. It reasoned that appointed counsel should not raise the remuneration question before the close of evidence and pleadings; the precise sum could be calculated only then. By insisting on a minimum of BGN 550 at the outset, the applicant had shown “manifest disrespect,” breached the Code, and caused an adjournment despite a warning. A one-hour break was granted so that a replacement lawyer present in court could be appointed. That lawyer reviewed the file, accepted the appointment, and received a fee of only BGN 30. The case concluded that day by plea bargain.

The applicant appealed the fine, arguing that the District Court had itself violated section 44(2) of the Bar Act by failing to fix remuneration (at least the Ordinance minimum) in the appointment order. His refusal was therefore justified; he had neither caused an unjustified adjournment nor acted disrespectfully, so the fine was unlawful.

On 11 July 2005 the Plovdiv Regional Court dismissed the appeal in a final ruling. It accepted that section 44(2) required the appointment order to indicate a fee not lower than the Ordinance minimum. However, it held that the exact amount could be fixed only at the end of proceedings, because the Ordinance prescribed a reduced fee of BGN 150 if the case ended by plea bargain. The trial court could not predict the outcome, so the applicant's demand for an advance determination of BGN 550 contradicted the Bar Act. He had therefore caused an unjustified delay and the fine was both lawful and proportionate.

Domestic law at the time obliged courts to appoint counsel in specified circumstances (including where an accused of limited means wished representation and the interests of justice required it). Appointed counsel had a duty to act and could resign only for “objective reasons” making performance impossible. Lawyers could not charge below the Ordinance minima. For court-appointed work the appointment decision itself had to state the fee (not below the relevant minimum of BGN 550, or BGN 150 on a plea bargain). A 2006 Legal Aid Act later removed the requirement to fix the fee at the moment of appointment and introduced a post-proceedings reporting and payment system administered by a central bureau.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant's complaint that both the unpaid (and unperformed) work and the fine constituted an unlawful interference with his possessions.

The case of Konstantin Stefanov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 35399/05) concerns a Bulgarian lawyer’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was violated when a criminal court refused to fix his legal-aid fee at the statutory minimum upon appointing him and then fined him for declining to act.

In early 2005 the Plovdiv District Court was trying two defendants charged with aggravated theft (punishable by up to fifteen years’ imprisonment). Because the accused could not afford counsel and the interests of justice required representation, the court asked the Plovdiv Bar to nominate two lawyers. The Bar’s letter of 31 May 2005 nominated the applicant and expressly reminded him of section 44 of the Bar Act: he was obliged to appear, the court was obliged to fix his remuneration at no less than the BGN 550 minimum prescribed by the 2004 Remuneration Ordinance, and failure to obtain that minimum would expose him to disciplinary sanctions.

At the hearing on 10 June 2005 the court formally appointed the applicant but refused to determine the fee immediately, stating that the exact amount could be assessed only after all evidence had been heard and final pleadings delivered. The applicant insisted that the Bar Act required the fee to be fixed in the appointment order itself. When the court persisted and warned that refusal would attract a fine, the applicant declined to act and left the courtroom. The court immediately imposed a fine of BGN 500 (approximately EUR 260) under Article 269 § 7 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure, holding that the demand for an advance determination of fees showed “manifest disrespect” and had caused an unnecessary adjournment.

The prosecutor then requested a short break; another lawyer who happened to be present was appointed, familiarised himself with the file in minutes, and the case proceeded to a plea-bargain that same afternoon. The replacement counsel was awarded only BGN 30.

The applicant appealed the fine, arguing that the appointment had been unlawful because the court had failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of section 44(2) of the Bar Act to indicate a remuneration not lower than the Ordinance minimum. Consequently his refusal to act had been justified and the fine itself unlawful. On 11 July 2005 the Plovdiv Regional Court dismissed the appeal in a final ruling. It accepted that the Bar Act obliged the trial court to state a fee in the appointment order, but held that the precise amount could be known only at the close of proceedings because the Ordinance itself provided a reduced tariff (BGN 150) if the case ended in a plea bargain. Relevant domestic provisions confirm that, at the material time, court-appointed counsel could resign only for “objective reasons” rendering performance impossible, that lawyers were forbidden to charge below the Ordinance minima, and that the court was under a statutory duty to fix the fee at the moment of appointment. After 1 January 2006 a new Legal Aid Act removed the requirement that the fee be stated in the appointment order and transferred payment to a central bureau, but those reforms post-dated the events.

The applicant’s central contention is that the court’s refusal to set the statutory minimum fee at the outset deprived him of a legitimate expectation of remuneration and that the subsequent fine constituted an unlawful interference with his possessions.

The case of Fazia Ali v. the United Kingdom concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (the right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal) in the determination of the applicant’s entitlement to homelessness assistance.

The Council accepted that she was homeless, eligible for assistance, in priority need and not intentionally homeless. It therefore owed her the “main housing duty” under section 193 of the Housing Act 1996 to secure that suitable accommodation was available for her and her family.

An initial offer of accommodation in November 2006 was refused on grounds of location. After a successful review, a further offer of a property at 16 Bromford Lane was made in March 2007. The Council maintained that a written offer letter (warning that refusal without good cause would discharge its duty) had been posted on 14 March. The applicant denied receiving any such letter and said she had obtained the address only by telephoning the housing office. She viewed the property on 19 March and refused it because of the dirty communal areas and lack of a lift, which she considered a risk to her youngest child’s health.

On 21 March 2007 the Council notified her that its duty had been discharged by reason of the refusal. The applicant requested a statutory review, again asserting that no written offer had been received. A Council Homelessness Review Officer (an employee of the same authority that had made the original offer) conducted a telephone interview on 1 May. The officer recorded that the applicant had admitted receiving the letter but had refused the property for reasons of suitability. Both courts applied the House of Lords’ earlier decision in Runa Begum, concluding that the limited judicial-review jurisdiction of the County Court supplied sufficient review for Article 6 purposes. The Supreme Court additionally held that the discharge decision did not determine a “civil right” at all, because the statutory housing duty involved evaluative, discretionary judgments rather than a precisely defined individual entitlement.

The applicant contended that the Review Officer’s decision had turned on a simple, disputed primary fact (whether a letter had arrived) that required no specialist expertise. She argued that, following Tsfayo v. the United Kingdom, Article 6 therefore demanded a full appellate fact-finding jurisdiction, and that the restriction of all homelessness appeals to points of law was incompatible with the Convention. The domestic courts rejected any such distinction, emphasising the practical difficulties of separating “gateway” facts from evaluative assessments of suitability and the existence of procedural safeguards in the review regulations.

**CASE OF FAZIA ALI v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (Application no. 40378/10)**

The applicant, a British national born in 1980 and living in Birmingham, was a homeless parent of two young children in priority need under Part VII of the Housing Act 1996. Birmingham City Council, as the local housing authority, accepted in November 2006 that it owed her the “main housing duty” to secure accommodation after finding her homeless, eligible, in priority need and not intentionally homeless. It made an initial offer, which she refused on location grounds; a review succeeded and a further offer followed.

On 14 March 2007 the Council claimed it sent a written offer of a property at 16 Bromford Lane, warning that refusal without good cause would discharge its duty under section 193. The applicant denied receiving the letter and said she had telephoned to obtain the address and viewing details. She viewed the property on 19 March but refused it because of the condition of the communal areas. On 21 March the Council notified her that her refusal had discharged its duty. She requested a review, asserting she had never received a written offer.

A Council Homelessness Review Officer (not independent of the authority) interviewed her by telephone on 1 May 2007. The officer recorded that the applicant had admitted receiving the letter but refused the property due to the lack of a lift and dirty entrance, which she feared would affect her son’s health. The applicant later claimed she had thought the questions related to a subsequent Part VI offer. On 2 May the officer upheld the discharge decision, finding the letter had been sent and received and that the refusal was based on perceived unsuitability rather than non-receipt.

The applicant appealed to Birmingham County Court under section 204 of the 1996 Act, limited to points of law (a judicial-review jurisdiction). She argued the Council had taken irrelevant considerations into account, failed to make adequate inquiries, acted irrationally, fettered its discretion and breached natural justice. The judge accepted the review officer was not independent but declined to hear evidence on whether the letter had arrived, holding that this factual question was properly for the officer. The only ground pursued was non-receipt of the letter.

She appealed to the Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court. She contended that the review officer’s decision determined her civil rights under Article 6 § 1; that the officer was neither independent nor impartial; that the case turned on a simple disputed primary fact requiring no specialist knowledge; and that, following Tsfayo v. the United Kingdom, Article 6 required a full appeal on that fact (or, alternatively, that restricting all appeals to points of law was incompatible with Article 6).

Both appellate courts followed the House of Lords decision in Runa Begum v. London Borough of Tower Hamlets. They held that, even assuming Article 6 applied, the composite procedure (internal review plus limited County Court appeal) provided sufficient review. The findings of fact were merely staging posts toward broader evaluative judgments on suitability and local housing conditions, for which the officer possessed specialist knowledge. Statutory safeguards (a more senior, uninvolved reviewer, opportunity to make representations, and appeal on legal error) ensured fairness. Distinguishing Tsfayo (a housing-benefit scheme with different financial incentives and no equivalent evaluative judgments), the courts saw no need for a full fact-finding jurisdiction. The Supreme Court further doubted that the case engaged Article 6 at all, characterising the homelessness duty as a benefit in kind dependent on a series of discretionary administrative judgments rather than a precisely defined individual civil right.

The applicant’s challenge therefore centred on whether the absence of an independent tribunal with full jurisdiction over a disputed primary fact (receipt of the offer letter) violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The domestic courts rejected that argument, emphasising the specialised, discretionary nature of homelessness decision-making and the adequacy of the existing safeguards.

The case of Kuppinger v. Germany (Application no. 62198/11) concerns a German father’s complaint that domestic courts failed to implement his right of contact with his son born out of wedlock in December 2003. The mother refused all contact shortly after the birth. The applicant’s 2005 request for regulation of contact rights led to protracted proceedings before the Frankfurt/Main District Court. An earlier ECHR judgment of 21 April 2011 found those proceedings (lasting until March 2010) violated Article 6 § 1 (reasonable time) and Article 13 (effective remedy). An interim order of May 2007 had permitted limited supervised visits, of which only three occurred.

On 12 May 2010 the Frankfurt Court of Appeal issued an interim decision granting the applicant six three-hour visits between May and August 2010 (the first three supervised). It warned the mother of administrative fines up to EUR 25 000 for non-compliance and found no risk to the child’s welfare; the boy’s refusals were attributed to maternal influence rather than autonomous choice. Most visits failed or were truncated. The child left early, the mother cancelled dates for holidays without consent, or she induced refusals. The applicant repeatedly sought fines, citing urgency and ECHR case-law.

The District Court imposed a total fine of only EUR 300 in November 2010, treating the mother’s responsibility as limited because professional mediation had also failed, she had brought the child to some meetings, and a contact custodian had since been appointed. The court viewed the fine as primarily punitive rather than coercive. Complaints about the amount and the length of the fine proceedings were rejected by the Court of Appeal (February 2011) and the Federal Constitutional Court (August 2011). The fine was eventually paid.

On 1 September 2010 the Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s earlier one-year suspension of contact, granted fortnightly three-hour visits (initially supervised), and appointed a time-limited contact custodian. It again held that the child’s verbal refusals stemmed from loyalty to the mother and that contact posed no welfare risk. Implementation collapsed: the first custodian reported the applicant uncooperative; a replacement could not be found promptly despite extensive judicial efforts; the mother refused handover; and the applicant lodged multiple unsuccessful requests for further fines. The District Court later held that unsupervised contact could not proceed without prior successful supervision, a question now pending in new review proceedings it had instituted ex officio.

Those review proceedings, begun in February 2011, were marked by successive delays: judicial recusals, expert-bias challenges, the applicant’s unavailability and health-related absences, and cancelled hearings. In November 2013 the District Court suspended all personal contact until October 2015, finding that forced meetings against the now eleven-year-old child’s consistent wishes would endanger his psychological development. The Court of Appeal confirmed the suspension in September 2014, while permitting monthly letters. It observed that the earlier fine may have been insufficient and that a decade-long denial of contact resulted from parental (especially maternal) obstruction as well as shortcomings of the judiciary and youth-welfare services.

The applicant complained that the courts’ failure to enforce contact orders, the derisory fines, and the successive delays violated his Article 8 right to family life (and implicitly Articles 6 and 13). The facts relevant to those allegations centre on the repeated non-implementation of two 2010 contact orders, the courts’ reluctance to impose meaningful sanctions, and the multi-year protraction of enforcement and review proceedings that ultimately produced a further suspension of contact.

Germany (Application no. 62198/11) concerns a German father's complaint that domestic courts failed to implement his right of contact with his son, born out of wedlock in December 2003. Germany, no. 41599/09) finding violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 on account of their length.

In July–August 2010 the applicant applied for fines. On 12 November 2010 the District Court imposed a total fine of only EUR 300, holding the mother’s responsibility limited, the child’s resistance relevant, and coercive effect unnecessary once a contact custodian had been appointed. Appeals and a constitutional complaint were unsuccessful. The fine was paid in instalments by June 2011.

On 1 September 2010 the Court of Appeal, in the main proceedings, quashed an earlier suspension of contact, ordered fortnightly three-hour visits (supervised at first, then unsupervised up to eight hours) and appointed a contact custodian until 31 March 2011. The custodian reported the applicant uncooperative; the applicant sought the custodian’s removal. After the custodianship expired, the mother refused to hand over the child. The District Court rejected further fine applications in August 2011, reasoning that unsupervised contact could not begin without a prior supervised phase and that fresh review proceedings were pending. A complaint was dismissed.

Those review proceedings, instituted ex officio in February 2011, were marked by repeated postponements, recusal motions, expert-appointment disputes and the applicant’s non-attendance (citing health). On 12 November 2013 the District Court suspended all personal contact until 31 October 2015, finding that contact against the now eleven-year-old child’s consistently expressed will would endanger his welfare. The Court of Appeal confirmed the suspension on 17 September 2014, permitting only monthly letters, while observing that the earlier fine may have been insufficient and that the decade-long refusal of contact also reflected failures by the judiciary and youth services.

German law (Civil Code s. 1684) gives each parent a right and duty of contact and empowers courts to appoint time-limited contact custodians and to impose fines up to EUR 25,000. The Family Procedure Act (s. 155) requires priority treatment and a hearing within one month. Direct force against the child is prohibited. A 2011 Remedy Act later provided compensation for excessive length, but most of the impugned measures pre-dated it.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s claim that the authorities failed to take effective, timely steps to realise his contact rights.

The case of N.D. v. Slovenia concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging that criminal proceedings against the applicant’s uncle for the rape and continuous sexual assault of the applicant (then a child) were excessively lengthy and lacked the required diligence, in violation of the reasonable-time requirement under Article 6 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1986, was raped by her then-19-year-old uncle J.D. in 1992 while living with her family in her grandparents’ house. J.D. thereafter forced her to have sexual intercourse approximately twice a week until March 1994, when the family moved; thereafter he continued to touch her inappropriately and once attempted intercourse. On 24 November 2000, aged 14, the applicant reported the abuse to her school counsellor. The matter was promptly referred to social services and the police, who took statements from the applicant, J.D., family members and others. A criminal complaint for sexual assault of a person under 15 was filed with the Celje District Public Prosecutor on 7 December 2000. A request to open a judicial investigation followed on 29 December 2000; the investigating judge issued the relevant decision on 29 March 2001 after hearing J.D.

In May 2001 the investigation was expanded to include similar allegations concerning the applicant’s younger sister. The applicant (then receiving hospital treatment for psychological trauma) and her sister were questioned; she gave a detailed account. Two clinical psychologists were appointed; their reports, confirming post-traumatic stress disorder in the applicant, were submitted in November 2001 and April 2002. An indictment for sexual assault of a person under 14 (the applicable provision at the time of the offences) was issued on 28 May 2002. A legal representative was appointed for the still-minor applicant in September 2002.

Thereafter the case stagnated. In January 2003 a police statement by J.D. was excluded from the file. No further activity occurred until 22 January 2007, when the assigned judge withdrew after inadvertently reviewing the excluded material. The first trial hearing was not scheduled until 19 February 2008 (for 14 April 2008). Four further hearings took place between June 2008 and April 2009; two were adjourned for several months because of defence counsel’s sick leave. The applicant testified, reiterating her earlier account but declining to give a full fresh narrative because of the trauma of reliving the events. Expert evidence was updated. On 8 April 2009 the District Court convicted J.D. of continuous sexual assault of both girls and sentenced him to three years and four months’ imprisonment, expressly taking the lengthy delay into account as a mitigating factor. The applicant’s compensation claim was left to civil proceedings. The Higher Court dismissed J.D.’s appeal on 10 March 2010, rendering the conviction final.

The entire criminal process thus lasted more than nine years from the initial complaint, with a four-year period of complete inactivity. In February 2009 the applicant had lodged a supervisory appeal under the 2006 Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay Act. After unsuccessful settlement talks she brought a compensation claim under that Act. On 27 May 2011 the Celje Local Court found a violation of the reasonable-time guarantee, emphasising the especial need for expedition in cases of sexual assault of children and the additional distress caused by repeated testimony. It awarded the applicant EUR 4 000 (close to the statutory maximum). The Higher Court upheld the award in December 2011.

These facts form the core of the alleged Convention violation: the protracted, insufficiently diligent handling of a particularly sensitive prosecution involving a child victim of intra-familial sexual abuse.

The case of N.D. v. Slovenia (Application no. 16605/09), decided by the ECtHR on 15 January 2015, concerned a complaint by a Slovenian national (born 1986) that criminal proceedings over her childhood rape were unduly prolonged and lacked the required diligence.

Between 1992 and 1994, when the applicant was aged 6–8, her 19-year-old uncle J.D. raped her and thereafter forced sexual intercourse roughly twice weekly while they cohabited in her grandparents’ house. After the family moved in March 1994, abuse persisted during visits in the form of inappropriate touching and one further attempted intercourse.

The applicant first disclosed the abuse to a school counsellor on 24 November 2000 (aged 14). Police took her statement and interviewed family members, her doctor and the counsellor. A criminal complaint for sexual assault of a person under 15 was filed on 7 December 2000. A judicial investigation was requested on 29 December 2000 and opened on 29 March 2001 after J.D. was heard. On 16 May 2001 the investigating judge questioned the applicant (then hospitalised for psychological trauma), her similarly abused younger sister S., their mother and the counsellor; the applicant gave a detailed account. Two psychologists were appointed. The applicant’s report (November 2001) diagnosed PTSD consistent with sexual-abuse victims; J.D.’s report followed in April 2002.

J.D. was indicted on 28 May 2002 (the charge later adjusted to the 1977 Criminal Code provision applicable at the time, covering a victim under 14). A legal representative was appointed for the still-minor applicant in September 2002. Thereafter the case languished. In January 2003 an earlier police statement by J.D. was excluded. In January 2007 the assigned judge recused himself after reviewing excluded material. The first hearing was not listed until February 2008 and held on 14 April 2008 (public excluded for privacy); J.D. denied the charges and the applicant’s representative was discharged because she had reached majority.

Four further hearings took place between June 2008 and April 2009. The applicant’s testimony remained consistent with her earlier statements, though she later declined a full re-narration because of trauma. Family members invoked testimonial privilege. Additional expert evidence (including a psychiatric report confirming J.D.’s full criminal responsibility) was obtained; hearings were adjourned while defence counsel was ill. The applicant lodged a civil claim for non-pecuniary damage (raised to €53 000) and was granted free legal aid in October 2008. In February 2009 she filed a supervisory appeal under the 2006 Act; a hearing was promptly listed.

On 8 April 2009 the Celje District Court convicted J.D. of continuous sexual assault of the applicant (March 1992–1994) and of S., imposing 3 years 4 months’ imprisonment. The long interval since the offences was treated as a mitigating factor, offset by J.D.’s lack of remorse. The compensation claim was remitted to the civil courts. The Celje Higher Court dismissed J.D.’s appeal on 10 March 2010, rendering the conviction final.

The applicant then sued the State under the 2006 Act for non-pecuniary damage caused by the delay. The Celje Local Court (27 May 2011) found a breach of the reasonable-time guarantee, awarding €4 000 (the statutory maximum being €5 000). It stressed the overall duration of some 9 years 2 months, the complete inactivity between January 2003 and January 2007, and the especial need for promptness and sensitivity in child-sexual-abuse cases so as to minimise repeated traumatisation of the victim. The Higher Court largely upheld the award (2 December 2011).

These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation: proceedings that began in late 2000 and ended only in 2010, marked by protracted inactivity despite the vulnerability of the child victim and the statutory duty of special diligence.
