The ECHR case *Malika Yusupova and Others v. Russia* (applications 14705/09, 4386/10, 67305/10, 68860/10 and 70695/10) concerns the alleged 2001–2002 abductions in Chechnya of six men by Russian federal servicemen, followed by ineffective investigations. The applicants (close relatives) claimed their kin vanished after unlawful detention in areas under full Russian military control, with no subsequent news of them. They alleged violations arising from the disappearances themselves and the authorities’ failure to investigate.

On 23 March 2002 in Gudermes, Arbi Yusupov and his brother were stopped by ~10 armed men (some masked, of Slavic appearance speaking unaccented Russian) using an unregistered APC. Taken via a police-manned checkpoint to a basement, they were separately interrogated about illegal armed groups. The brother was released after several days (handcuffed, unfed) with a warning not to complain; Arbi was never seen again. Their Niva car was later impounded at the local military commander’s office.

On 30 October 2001 in Goyty (under curfew with federal checkpoints), ~10 masked armed men in camouflage, arriving in two APCs, a Ural lorry and UAZ cars, broke into Khasan Khadzhiyev’s house. After checking documents they took him away, radioing “Vostok” that the operation was complete. Relatives were later told he was held at the Urus-Martan military commander’s office but he was never released.

On 24 September 2001 during a special operation in Alkhazurovo, armed men in camouflage (using an APC, UAZ, Ural and Kamaz lorries) beat family members and abducted brothers Mayrbek and Aslambek Shavanov. The Urus-Martan military commander unofficially confirmed they were held at the FSB office on the commander’s premises.

On 5 November 2002 in Achkhoy-Martan, armed Slavic-looking men speaking Russian broke into Ibragim Dzhabrailov’s house, locked relatives in a room, and took him (in underwear) in an APC accompanied by a UAZ and Ural. The local military commander’s office acknowledged the detention and promised same-day release, which never occurred; he was later said to have been taken to Grozny.

On 5 September 2002 in Urus-Martan (under curfew), ~40 masked men in camouflage arriving in an APC and two Ural lorries entered Mayrbek Minayev’s flat, locked his father in the kitchen, checked documents, and took him (bag over head, beaten) after stating they were transferring him to the military commander’s office.

In each instance, applicants immediately complained to police, prosecutors and military authorities. Criminal cases were opened (between January and November 2002) but consisted largely of formal information requests and operational-search orders that received negative or no replies. Investigations were repeatedly suspended (often for years, sometimes without notice) and resumed, remaining pending without identifying perpetrators or producing results despite evidence of military vehicles, uniforms, Slavic appearance, radio codes, and unofficial acknowledgements of detention. The Government did not contest the applicants’ factual accounts but maintained there was insufficient proof of State-agent involvement.

These facts underpin the alleged Convention violations: the disappearances (implicating the right to life, prohibition of ill-treatment, and liberty/security) occurring under exclusive State control, and the protracted, fruitless inquiries demonstrating a lack of effective investigation or remedy.

The European Court of Human Rights considered five joined applications against Russia concerning the alleged abduction of six Chechen men by federal servicemen between 2001 and 2002, followed by ineffective investigations. All incidents occurred in areas under full Russian control; relatives have had no news of the missing men since. Applicants complained of unlawful detention by State agents (typically groups of 10–40 armed, often-masked men of Slavic appearance speaking unaccented Russian, using APCs, UAZ vehicles, Ural/Kamaz lorries and radios) and of investigations that consisted mainly of unanswered information requests, were repeatedly suspended/resumed without identifying perpetrators, and remained pending years later with no tangible results. The Government did not dispute the factual accounts but maintained there was no proof “beyond reasonable doubt” of State-agent involvement.

On 23 March 2002 in Gudermes, Arbi Yusupov (b. 1973) and his brother Ilman were stopped at a bridge by ~10 armed servicemen, some masked. They were forced into an unmarked APC, taken first to a nearby checkpoint manned by an Ivanovo Region police unit, then to a basement where they were held separately, interrogated about illegal armed groups, and denied food. Ilman was released after four–five days near Isti-Su and ordered not to complain; Arbi vanished. Criminal case 57041 was opened in June 2002. Military investigators later questioned Gudermes commander’s-office personnel who denied involvement (one claimed they had merely towed an empty car). The file was transferred between civilian and military prosecutors; proceedings were suspended for more than five years (2003–2008) despite ICRC inquiries. Victim status was granted only in 2008 after the mother’s request. Periodic resumptions produced no new leads; the investigation remains pending.

On 30 October 2001 in Goyty (under curfew), ~10 masked armed men in two APCs, a Ural lorry and two UAZs broke into the Khadzhiyev home at 4 a.m., handcuffed Khasan Khadzhiyev (b. 1969), checked documents and drove him toward Urus-Martan after radioing “Vostok.” Relatives later heard he was held at the Urus-Martan military commander’s office but he was never released. Case 25191 opened in January 2002; the crime scene was examined and witnesses (family and neighbours) questioned, all corroborating the account. Proceedings were suspended and resumed multiple times (2002–2011); applicants repeatedly complained of ineffectiveness and obtained limited file access only after court orders. No perpetrators were identified; the case is still pending.

On 24 September 2001 in Alkhazurovo, armed camouflage-clad men using an APC, UAZ, Ural and two Kamaz lorries (one from the local police station) beat family members and abducted brothers Mayrbek (b. 1976) and Aslambek Shavanov (b. 1977) at 4 a.m. The Urus-Martan military commander unofficially confirmed they were held at the FSB office on the commander’s premises. Case 25192 opened in January 2002. Witnesses refused statements out of fear; military units could not be identified. Proceedings were suspended for years (2002–2006, then intermittently); court-ordered resumptions in 2010–2011 yielded no results. The investigation remains pending.

On 5 November 2002 in Achkhoy-Martan, armed men (unmasked of Slavic appearance) locked relatives in a room, dragged Ibragim Dzhabrailov (b. 1976) outside in underwear and took him in an APC accompanied by a UAZ and Ural. The local military commander’s office acknowledged detention and promised same-day release, which never occurred. Case 63090 opened days later; a police report noted Ibragim’s alleged prior involvement with illegal groups. After a 2003 suspension, the case was resumed in 2008 and 2010 following complaints; questioning of relatives produced no new evidence. It remains pending.

On 5 September 2002 in Urus-Martan (under curfew), ~40 masked servicemen arrived in an APC and two Urals; 15 entered the Minayev flat, locked the father in the kitchen, threatened a brother, and dragged Mayrbek Minayev (b. 1972) (bag over head) to a vehicle after saying they were taking him to the commander’s office. Case 61138 opened in November 2002. The father was questioned; the wife obtained victim status. Proceedings were suspended for years (2003–2007, then 2010–2011); later questioning of neighbours and relatives corroborated the account but identified no perpetrators. The case remains pending.

In all five investigations the authorities failed to establish the identity or affiliation of the abductors despite the presence of military vehicles, checkpoints and commander’s offices, and despite repeated prosecutorial criticism of investigative shortcomings.

The case of Malika Yusupova and Others v. Russia concerns five applications by Russian nationals (close relatives of six disappeared men) alleging that between 2001 and 2002 their relatives were abducted by Russian State servicemen during special operations in Chechnya, in areas under full federal-force control, with no subsequent news of the missing persons. Official investigations were opened but proved ineffective: they were repeatedly suspended and resumed over years, consisted mainly of unanswered or negative information requests, and failed to identify any perpetrators. The Government did not contest the applicants’ factual accounts but maintained there was no proof beyond reasonable doubt of State-agent involvement.

In application no. 14705/09, Arbi Yusupov (born 1973) and his brother were stopped at 8 a.m. on 23 March 2002 in central Gudermes by about ten armed servicemen (some masked, of Slavic appearance). They were taken in an unmarked APC to a nearby checkpoint manned by Ivanovo-region police, then to a basement where they were held separately. The brother was interrogated about illegal armed groups, held for five days without food, and released on 27 March after being warned not to complain; Arbi vanished. Case no. 57041 was opened on 3 June 2002. Early inquiries confirmed that Gudermes military-commander’s-office intelligence officers had seized the pair; the file was transferred to military prosecutors, who later denied military involvement and returned it. The investigation remained pending after multiple suspensions, with no identifications.

In no. 4386/10, Khasan Khadzhiyev was taken at 4 a.m. on 30 October 2001 from his Goyty home by ten masked, armed men in camouflage who arrived in two APCs, a Ural truck and two UAZ vehicles and radioed “Vostok.” Relatives were told he was held at the Urus-Martan military commander’s office for a check but he was never released. Case no. 25191 (opened January 2002) involved repeated witness interviews confirming the account, yet produced no results despite numerous resumptions.

In no. 67305/10, Mayrbek and Aslambek Shavanov were abducted at 4 a.m. on 24 September 2001 during a special operation in Alkhazurovo by armed camouflaged men who beat family members and used an APC, UAZ, Ural and Kamaz trucks (some from the local police station). The Urus-Martan military commander unofficially admitted they were held at the FSB office on the commander’s premises. Case no. 25192 (opened January 2002) yielded only similar witness statements and remained pending after long suspensions.

In no. 68860/10, Ibragim Dzhabrailov was seized at 5–6 a.m. on 5 November 2002 from his Achkhoy-Martan home by armed camouflaged men (some of Slavic appearance) who locked relatives in a room, dragged him out in underwear and took him away in an APC accompanied by a UAZ and Ural. The local military commander’s office initially acknowledged detention and promised same-day release, later claiming Grozny servicemen had taken him. Case no. 63090 (opened November 2002) noted prior alleged membership in illegal groups but produced no identifications.

In no. 70695/10, Mayrbek Minayev was taken at 2–3 a.m. on 5 September 2002 from his Urus-Martan flat by some 40 masked camouflaged men from an APC and two Ural trucks who said they were taking him to the military commander’s office; relatives saw him beaten with a bag over his head. Case no. 61138 (opened November 2002) likewise remained pending without results.

In all five cases the investigations never established the servicemen’s identities or the victims’ fates.
001-150643:
The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1952, worked for years as a tractor and heavy-machine driver, developing nervous-system dysfunctions. In 1985 she was classified with third-degree disability (50–70 % loss of working capacity) and began receiving a disability pension. Seven subsequent re-examinations by the Territorial Expert Medical Commission (TEMC) between 1985 and 2000 confirmed the same classification and diagnoses (vegetative polyneuropathy of the upper extremities, coxarthrosis, cervical spondylosis and radiculopathy).

On 14 November 2000 the TEMC reduced her assessed loss of capacity to 40 % (below the pension threshold), listing only two of the earlier conditions. The National Expert Medical Commission (NEMC) went further on 14 February 2001, declaring her fully fit for work. She sought judicial review. A court-appointed expert found multiple chronic, occupational conditions that had permanently impaired her health and typically produced a significant reduction in working capacity. On 27 December 2002 the Sofia City Court quashed the NEMC decision as unlawful for failing to consider all relevant medical elements, remitted the case and directed the NEMC to fix the precise percentage of reduced capacity. The judgment became final on 11 February 2003.

The NEMC re-examined her on 9 October 2003 and assessed only 30 % loss, omitting vegetative polyneuropathy and treating some conditions as non-occupational. A second court-appointed expert confirmed the full set of chronic occupational diseases and irreversible locomotor damage. On 6 January 2005 the Sofia City Court again quashed the NEMC decision for ignoring relevant circumstances and the applicant’s actual health; the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment on 15 July 2005.

On 28 October 2005 the NEMC nevertheless assessed a 40 % loss (still insufficient for a pension), listing only vegetative polyneuropathy as occupational and stating that it “quashes and decides anew the question of percentage of disability” while confirming the remaining elements. The applicant did not challenge this last decision. Pension payments had already been stopped from 2 October 2000; no later restoration is recorded.

At the relevant time Bulgarian law contained no mechanism that could compel an administrative body to comply with a final court judgment other than a separate action for a modest pecuniary fine; implementation timing was left entirely to the administration. These repeated refusals by the NEMC to follow binding judicial instructions on the medical assessment, and the consequent continued denial of the pension, form the core facts underlying the alleged Convention violations.

The case of Yagnina v. Bulgaria (Application no. 18238/06) concerns a Bulgarian national, Denka Angelova Yagnina (born 1952), who lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 April 2006. She had worked as a tractor and heavy-machine driver until 1985, when occupational exposure caused nervous-system dysfunctions. She was then classified as having a “third-degree disability” (50–70 % loss of working capacity) and began receiving a disability pension.

Between 1985 and 2000 she underwent seven re-examinations by the Territorial Expert Medical Commission (TEMC). Each confirmed the third-degree classification and the diagnoses of vegetative polyneuropathy of the upper extremities, coxarthrosis, cervical spondylosis and radiculopathy.

On 14 November 2000 a further TEMC examination recorded only vegetative polyneuropathy and myotendinosis, omitting the earlier diagnoses, and assessed her loss of capacity at 40 %—below the pension threshold. She appealed to the National Expert Medical Commission (NEMC), which, on 14 February 2001, declared her fully fit for work under the diagnosis “spondylosis and related diseases.”

The Sofia City Court, after appointing an independent medical expert, quashed the NEMC decision on 27 December 2002 (final on 11 February 2003). The expert found chronic, progressive conditions (cervical spondylarthrosis, vegetative polyneuropathy, myotendinosis and coxarthrosis) that had permanently reduced her working capacity. The court remitted the case, instructing the NEMC to reassess the exact percentage on the basis of the actual medical picture.

The NEMC re-examined her on 9 October 2003, recorded a 30 % reduction, classified only some conditions as occupational and again excluded vegetative polyneuropathy. A second court-appointed expert confirmed all the earlier diagnoses as occupational, chronic and irreversible. On 6 January 2005 the Sofia City Court quashed the 2003 decision; the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment on 15 July 2005. The courts again directed the NEMC to apply the expert findings and to determine the percentage itself.

On 28 October 2005 the NEMC assessed a 40 % reduction (still insufficient for a pension), listing only vegetative polyneuropathy as occupational. The applicant did not seek judicial review of this last decision. Payment of her pension had already ceased on 2 October 2000; no subsequent information on restoration appears in the file.

At the relevant time Bulgarian law (Administrative Procedure Act 1979 and Supreme Administrative Court Act 1997) contained no time-limit for an administrative body to implement a final court judgment and provided only for a separate action seeking a pecuniary fine. Mandatory instructions issued by the courts therefore lacked an effective enforcement mechanism. (The 2006 Code of Administrative Procedure later introduced weekly fines and other coercive measures, but those provisions post-dated the events.)

The sequence of medical assessments, successive court quashings and the NEMC’s persistent low-percentage findings, together with the absence of an effective means of compelling compliance, form the core factual matrix of the alleged Convention violations.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Denka Angelova Yagnina, a Bulgarian national born in 1952 and residing in Voyvodinovo, lodged in April 2006. Yagnina had worked for years as a tractor and heavy-machinery driver until 1985, when occupational strain produced chronic nervous-system and locomotor disorders. That year she was classified with “third-degree disability” (50–70 % loss of working capacity) and awarded a disability pension. Seven subsequent re-examinations by the Territorial Expert Medical Commission (TEMC) between 1985 and 2000 confirmed the same classification and the same cluster of diagnoses: vegetative polyneuropathy of the upper extremities, coxarthrosis, cervical spondylosis and radiculopathy.

On 14 November 2000 a new TEMC examination omitted the earlier diagnoses except polyneuropathy and myotendinosis, assessing only 40 % loss of capacity—below the pension threshold. Yagnina appealed to the National Expert Medical Commission (NEMC), which on 14 February 2001 declared her fully fit, citing merely “spondylosis and related diseases.” She sought judicial review. The Sofia City Court, relying on an independent expert who documented the original conditions (now worsened) and their irreversible impact on working capacity, quashed the NEMC decision on 27 December 2002 as unlawful and remitted the file with instructions that the NEMC must reassess all relevant medical facts and determine the precise percentage of reduced capacity. The judgment became final on 11 February 2003.

The NEMC re-examined Yagnina on 9 October 2003, listing cervical spondylarthrosis and radiculopathy as occupational but excluding polyneuropathy, and fixing reduced capacity at 30 %. A second round of judicial review followed. A new court-appointed expert confirmed the full set of occupational diseases and their permanent degenerative effects. On 6 January 2005 the Sofia City Court again quashed the NEMC decision for failing to take all relevant circumstances into account; the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that ruling on 15 July 2005, reiterating that only the NEMC could set the exact percentage but that its assessment had to reflect the applicant’s actual health.

On 28 October 2005 the NEMC issued a third decision assessing 40 % reduced capacity (again insufficient for a pension). It listed only vegetative polyneuropathy as occupational and purported to “quash and decide anew” the percentage while “confirming the rest.” Yagnina did not seek further judicial review. Payment of her disability pension had already ceased on 2 October 2000; the file contains no indication that it was ever restored.

At the material time Bulgarian law (Administrative Procedure Act 1979 and Supreme Administrative Court Act 1997) contained no mechanism to compel an administrative body to implement a final court judgment within a fixed period; the only available remedy was a separate action for a modest pecuniary sanction. The 2006 Code of Administrative Procedure later introduced weekly fines and time-limited enforcement orders, but those provisions post-dated the events. Claims for damages under the State and Municipalities Liability for Damage Act required the prior setting-aside of the impugned administrative act.

These facts—repeated judicial annulments of NEMC assessments that systematically understated established occupational disabilities, followed by fresh assessments that still denied pension entitlement, and the absence of effective means to enforce the courts’ instructions—form the core of the alleged Convention violations concerning the right to a fair trial (enforcement of judgments) and the peaceful enjoyment of possessions (the discontinued pension).
001-150998:
The applicant, Ms Béláné Nagy (born 1959), a Hungarian national, was assessed in 2001 as having suffered a 67% loss of working capacity from 1 April 2001 and was granted a disability pension under Act LXXXI of 1997. Subsequent assessments in 2003, 2006 and 2007 confirmed this level. In December 2009, following a change in assessment methodology (without any material improvement in her health), her disability was re-rated at 40%. Her pension was therefore withdrawn with effect from 1 February 2010. She was also required to repay sums received after that date. The Nyíregyháza Labour Court dismissed her challenge on 1 April 2011 despite expert evidence that her condition had not improved since 2007.

A 2011 reassessment produced ratings of 45% (first instance) then 50% (appeal). The 50% rating would have entitled her to a disability pension had rehabilitation been deemed impossible, but the authorities instead directed a 36-month rehabilitation programme with a corresponding allowance. Act CXCI of 2011, which entered into force on 1 January 2012, replaced the former pension scheme with a new system of allowances for persons of reduced working capacity. Eligibility now required (i) a health rating of 60% or less and (ii) at least 1 095 days of social-security coverage in the five years preceding the claim, or alternatively uninterrupted career coverage or receipt of a disability pension on 31 December 2011. Rehabilitation or disability allowances were payable according to whether rehabilitation was recommended.

The applicant’s February 2012 claim was refused in June 2012 because she possessed only 947 qualifying days and had not been in receipt of pension on the relevant date; rehabilitation was not recommended. A fresh August 2012 claim, again based on a 50% rating with no rehabilitation envisaged, was likewise refused by the authorities (November 2012 and February 2013) and by the Nyíregyháza Administrative and Labour Court (20 June 2013). A 2014 legislative amendment (2 555 days in ten years or 3 650 days in fifteen years) did not assist her. She has since lived on social aid.

The applicant complained under Article 6 that the successive methodological and legislative changes, applied without regard to the unchanged state of her health, had deprived her of her sole means of livelihood. Similar complaints were later lodged with the Constitutional Court, which rejected them as inadmissible without requiring prior recourse to the Kúria.

The former law had treated disability pension as a mixed insurance/social-security benefit requiring a 67% (later 50–79%) loss of capacity plus the requisite service period. The 2011 Act introduced stricter insurance-period conditions while preserving a transitional exception only for those already in receipt of pension on 31 December 2011. ILO Convention No. 102 and WHO ICF guidelines, cited in the domestic material, emphasise continuity of invalidity benefit once the contingency of lasting incapacity is established.

The case of Béláné Nagy v. Hungary (application no. 53080/13) concerns a Hungarian national born in 1959 who alleged that successive legislative and administrative changes deprived her of her disability pension—her sole means of livelihood—despite no improvement in her health. She invoked Article 6 of the Convention.

In 2001 the applicant’s work-capacity loss was assessed at 67 percent and she was awarded a disability pension under Act LXXXI of 1997. The same rating was confirmed in 2003, 2006 and 2007. In December 2009, following a change in assessment methodology but without any medical improvement, her disability was re-rated at 40 percent. The pension was withdrawn with effect from 1 February 2010 and she was ordered to repay sums received thereafter. Her challenge before the Nyíregyháza Labour Court was dismissed in April 2011, even though an expert report confirmed that her condition had remained unchanged since 2007.

A further assessment in 2011 produced a 50-percent rating. Under the then-applicable rules this would have entitled her to a disability pension had rehabilitation been deemed infeasible; instead, a 36-month rehabilitation programme was prescribed and she received a temporary rehabilitation allowance.

On 1 January 2012 Act CXCI of 2011 entered into force. It replaced the former service-period requirement with a new eligibility condition: at least 1 095 days of social-security coverage in the five years preceding the claim. Persons who had been in receipt of a disability pension on 31 December 2011 were exempted. In February and August 2012 the applicant submitted fresh claims. Her disability was again assessed at 50 percent and rehabilitation was no longer envisaged, yet both claims were refused because she possessed only 947 covered days and had not been receiving a pension on the cut-off date. Administrative and judicial appeals, culminating in a June 2013 judgment of the Nyíregyháza Administrative and Labour Court, were unsuccessful. A 2014 legislative amendment that lengthened the look-back periods still left her ineligible. She thereafter survived on social assistance.

The old pension statute had required a 67-percent (later 50–79 percent without rehabilitation prospect) loss of capacity plus a prescribed insurance period. The 2011 Act instead demanded a health-status rating of 60 percent or less together with the 1 095-day rule (or one of the listed derogations). The Hungarian Constitutional Court characterised disability benefits as mixed social-security and social-assistance payments that did not confer “purchased” property rights, although legitimate-expectation safeguards still applied. International instruments cited in the file (ILO Convention No. 102 and the WHO ICF ethical guidelines) emphasise that established entitlements should not be withdrawn solely by methodological or legislative change.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaint that the authorities applied the new rules without equity, extinguishing a long-standing entitlement on which she had reasonably relied.

**Case of Béláné Nagy v. Hungary (App. no. 53080/13), ECtHR Second Section, 10 February 2015 (referred to Grand Chamber)**

The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1959 and living in Baktalórántháza, alleged that legislative changes, applied without equity, caused her to lose her sole source of livelihood—a disability allowance—despite no improvement in her health. She invoked Article 6 of the Convention.

In 2001 her work capacity loss was assessed at 67% from 1 April 2001, entitling her to a disability pension under Act no. LXXXI of 1997. This rating was confirmed in 2003, 2006 and 2007. Following a change in assessment methodology (with no material health improvement), her disability was re-rated at 40% from 1 December 2009. Pension entitlement was withdrawn from 1 February 2010. She challenged the decision; the Nyíregyháza Labour Court dismissed her claim on 1 April 2011 despite an expert opinion confirming her condition had not improved since 2007. She was required to repay sums received after 1 February 2010.

A 2011 re-assessment initially produced 45%, raised on appeal to 50% (re-assessment due March 2015). Under then-applicable rules this level would have restored pension entitlement if rehabilitation were impossible, but the authorities instead directed 36 months of rehabilitation, during which she would receive a rehabilitation allowance.

Act no. CXCI of 2011 entered into force on 1 January 2012, introducing stricter eligibility: a person whose health status was 60% or less had to have at least 1,095 days of social-security coverage in the five years before the claim, not be engaged in gainful activity, and not receive other regular cash benefits. Exceptions existed for those whose cover had never been interrupted by more than 30 days or who were already receiving a disability pension (or equivalent) on 31 December 2011. The applicant’s February 2012 claim (50% disability, no rehabilitation envisaged) was rejected because she lacked the required coverage period. A further August 2012 claim produced the same 50% rating and the same refusal: she had not been in receipt of pension on 31 December 2011 (it having ended in February 2010) and possessed only 947 of the requisite 1,095 days. Administrative authorities and the Nyíregyháza Administrative and Labour Court (20 June 2013) upheld the refusals.

A 2014 amendment relaxed the contribution test (2,555 days in ten years or 3,650 days in fifteen years), but the applicant still failed to qualify. She thereafter lived on social aid.

The Constitutional Court had considered similar challenges to the 2011 Act (decisions 40/2012, 3227/2013 etc.). It distinguished contributory “purchased-right” benefits (old-age or survivors’ pensions) that enjoy property-like protection from mixed social-security/social-assistance disability pensions, which are subject only to rule-of-law requirements of legitimate expectations and adequate transition time. Disability pensions were characterised as special, non-constitutional entitlements for those below retirement age whose reduced work capacity created a need for income replacement.

Relevant international material included ILO Convention No. 102 (minimum standards for invalidity benefit, including qualifying periods of contribution or employment) and the WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health ethical guideline that ICF data should not be used to deny established rights or restrict legitimate entitlements.

The core facts thus concern successive methodological re-assessments that reduced the applicant’s disability rating without health improvement, followed by a legislative overhaul whose new contribution conditions she could not meet precisely because her earlier pension had already been terminated. The result was total loss of disability-related income despite a 50% impairment that, under both old and new medical criteria, would otherwise have supported an allowance.

001-150312:
The European Court of Human Rights case of Nogin v. Russia (application no. 58530/08) concerned allegations by Russian national Vladimir Rufimovich Nogin (born 1981) that he received inadequate medical treatment during imprisonment, in violation of his rights. Nogin had suffered from insulin-dependent Type 1 diabetes since age four, with complications including diabetic angioretinopathy, polyneuropathy, nephropathy, arterial hypertension, chronic renal insufficiency, and progressing cataracts that severely impaired his vision.

Criminal proceedings for aggravated rape led to his pre-trial detention from 8 August to 9 November 2006 in SIZO no. 1, Syktyvkar. He was convicted on 8 December 2006 and sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment, returning to the same facility before transfer on 11 April 2007 to prison IK-31 in Mikun. He was released on 6 March 2009 upon sentence expiry.

Pre-detention examinations in April and November 2006 showed very low visual acuity (right eye 0.02, allowing finger-counting at 1 metre; left eye limited to hand movements near the face). A cataract operation was recommended. Upon post-conviction detention in December 2006, prison hospital B-18 confirmed advanced diabetes with immature/almost mature diabetic cataracts (visual acuity 0.02 right, 0.004 left). By late 2008 a medical commission found him able only to detect hand movements with the right eye and blind in the left, with nearly mature and mature cataracts. Post-release in March 2009, an ophthalmologist confirmed this and urged urgent surgery. May 2009 hospital admission led to a recommendation for specialised care due to the advanced stage. July 2009 Moscow clinic diagnosis included complicated immature cataract, proliferative retinopathy and retinal detachment (right eye: light perception only) plus neo-vascular glaucoma and advanced detachment (left eye: blind). Successful right-eye cataract surgery occurred on 14 July 2009, restoring hand-movement detection, but September 2009 assessment found complete right-eye retinal detachment, rendering further surgery futile.

During imprisonment Nogin was frequently hospitalised (SIZO hospital December 2006; B-18 on multiple occasions 2006–2008; IK-31 hospital 2007–2009). He received regular examinations by doctors, an endocrinologist and ophthalmologist, plus blood/urine tests, ultrasounds, ECGs and other diagnostics. Treatment included insulin, hypotensive drugs, microcirculation improvers, vitamins and nootropics. Special diabetic diets (nos. 7a/7b, sugar replaced by milk) were prescribed in 2006–2007, though Nogin claimed they were unavailable from April–July 2007 and from early 2008. Authorities stated diets were provided in hospital and insulin was supplied (with substitutions when specific types like Humalog or Lantus were temporarily unavailable). Nogin alleged receipt of expired insulin in July 2008 (denied by prison records showing valid expiry dates).

Ophthalmologists repeatedly recommended cataract surgery from September 2006 onward, noting it was feasible in civilian Ministry of Health facilities and that vision loss was not irreversible. Prison authorities sought admission to the specialised Gaaza prison hospital in St Petersburg from mid-2008; initial requests were refused for incomplete documentation, but approval came in December 2008 with a mid-January 2009 arrival deadline. Nogin refused transfer on 30 December 2008, citing lack of assistance (he was nearly blind), inability to travel unaccompanied, and only 69 days remaining on his sentence. Authorities deemed him fit to travel and the refusal unfounded. Further persuasion attempts in February 2009 failed; he again declined.

Nogin sought parole on medical grounds in 2008, emphasising deteriorating vision and untreated cataracts. Courts rejected both applications (April 2008 and January 2009, upheld on appeal), holding that his conditions were not on the governmental list of diseases precluding imprisonment and did not prevent sentence service. He also claimed eyesight had worsened to the point of needing a (normally prohibited) walking stick.

These facts centre on whether prison medical care—particularly delayed or unavailable specialised cataract surgery, inconsistent diet and insulin issues—adequately addressed his serious, progressive diabetic complications, leading to near-total blindness.

The case of Nogin v. Russia (no. 58530/08) concerns the applicant Vladimir Rufimovich Nogin’s allegation of inadequate medical treatment during imprisonment, stemming from his longstanding insulin-dependent Type 1 diabetes (diagnosed at age four) and related complications including diabetic angioretinopathy, nephropathy, polyneuropathy, hypertension, renal insufficiency and bilateral cataracts.

Nogin was detained pre-trial in SIZO no. 1, Syktyvkar (8 August–9 November 2006), then, after conviction for aggravated rape and a sentence of two years six months, from 8 December 2006 (again in SIZO no. 1) until transfer on 11 April 2007 to IK-31, Mikun. He was released on sentence expiry on 6 March 2009.

Vision had already deteriorated markedly before and during detention. An April 2006 examination recorded right-eye acuity of 0.02 (finger-counting at 1 m) and left-eye ability only to perceive hand movements near the face. By November 2006 right-eye acuity had fallen to 0.01. Upon prison-hospital admission in December 2006 he presented with an immature left cataract and almost-mature right cataract (acuities 0.004 and 0.02). By late 2008 he was blind in the left eye and could detect only hand movements with the right; both cataracts were now mature or nearly so. Post-release examinations in 2009 confirmed proliferative retinopathy, retinal detachments and terminal glaucoma, rendering further surgery futile after a limited right-eye cataract extraction.

While detained Nogin was repeatedly hospitalised in SIZO, B-18 and IK-31 facilities, where he received regular endocrinological and ophthalmological reviews, laboratory and imaging tests, insulin and symptomatic medication. Special diabetic diets (nos. 7a/7b, sugar substituted by milk) were prescribed, yet Nogin asserted they were withheld from April–July 2007 and from early 2008 onward. He further claimed receipt of expired insulin in July 2008; the prison produced supply records showing valid expiry dates and stated that only equivalent substitutes were used when the prescribed formulations were temporarily unavailable.

Ophthalmologists repeatedly recommended elective cataract extraction and lens implantation, feasible in civilian Ministry of Health hospitals. From mid-2008 the prison submitted successive transfer requests to the specialised Gaaza prison hospital in St Petersburg. After initial refusals for incomplete paperwork, admission was authorised in December 2008 (arrival by 15 January 2009). Nogin refused in writing, citing his inability to travel unassisted given near-total blindness and the fact that only 69 days of sentence remained. Prison doctors later attempted to obtain consent at his mother’s request, but he again declined. Two applications for medical parole were rejected on the grounds that his conditions neither featured on the statutory list of illnesses precluding imprisonment nor prevented service of the sentence.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: despite documented progression of sight-threatening complications and repeated specialist recommendations, timely specialised surgery was never arranged, while diet and insulin provision remained contested.

The case of Nogin v. Russia (no. 58530/08) concerns inadequate medical care during the applicant’s imprisonment. Vladimir Nogin, born in 1981, has had insulin-dependent Type 1 diabetes since age four, with complications including polyneuropathy, nephropathy, hypertension, renal insufficiency, retinopathy and diabetic cataracts that severely impaired his vision. Pre-conviction examinations in 2006 showed visual acuity of 0.02 in the right eye (counting fingers at 1 m) and only hand movements near the face in the left; he could still navigate familiar spaces.

Convicted of aggravated rape on 8 December 2006 and sentenced to two years six months, he was held in SIZO No. 1 Syktyvkar then transferred to IK-31 Mikun (April 2007–March 2009). He was repeatedly admitted to prison hospitals (SIZO, B-18 and IK-31) for monitoring. He received regular examinations by doctors, endocrinologists and ophthalmologists, blood/urine tests and other diagnostics, plus insulin, hypotensive drugs, circulation-improving medication, vitamins and nootropics. Special diabetic diets (sugar replaced by milk) were prescribed, though Nogin claimed they were not consistently supplied after April 2007. Prison records showed valid insulin stocks; Nogin’s claim of receiving expired insulin in July 2008 was denied.

The principal complaint was failure to treat his cataracts. From September 2006 onward, ophthalmologists repeatedly recommended elective surgery (cataract removal and intraocular-lens implantation) in Ministry of Health or specialised prison facilities, noting that poor vision caused by cataracts was not irreversible. The Federal Service for Execution of Sentences itself acknowledged the need. Nevertheless, no operation occurred. In 2008 IK-31 twice requested admission to Gaaza prison hospital, St Petersburg; after initial rejection for incomplete paperwork, admission was granted in December 2008 with a deadline of 15 January 2009. Nogin refused transfer on 30 December, citing his near-blindness, lack of medical escort and only 69 days remaining on his sentence. Authorities considered him fit to travel and the refusal groundless. Further persuasion in February 2009 failed.

Vision deteriorated sharply: by late 2008 he required a walking stick (normally prohibited), was blind in the left eye and could detect only hand movements with the right. Post-release examinations (March–July 2009) confirmed mature cataracts, proliferative retinopathy, retinal detachment and glaucoma. Cataract surgery on the right eye in a Moscow clinic restored light perception temporarily, but complete retinal detachment rendered further intervention futile.

Parole applications in 2008–2009 citing the need for surgery and progressive blindness were rejected; courts held that the conditions did not prevent service of sentence and were not on the official list of diseases warranting release.

Domestic Diabetes Algorithms require frequent ophthalmological review and specific treatments (laser photocoagulation being impossible once cataracts form). WHO guidance stresses consistent insulin, dietary management and regular eye care to prevent blindness. These facts form the basis of the alleged violation of the right to adequate medical treatment in detention.

The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1972, had lived since birth in a privately owned house (84.6 sq m, including 58.8 sq m habitable space) in Baku’s Khutor settlement, on a 257 sq m plot (93.4 sq m built upon, the rest courtyard). He acquired formal ownership of the house itself on 8 October 2005, though the land was never registered in his name. He resided there with his wife, two young children and elderly mother.

On 14 May 2004 the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) issued an order assigning several neighbourhoods, including the applicant’s, to a private developer (Kaspi Nur LLC) on lease for construction of cottage-type houses, as part of urban development. The applicant was never notified of this order. In December 2008 a subordinate body, the Narimanov District Executive Authority (NDEA), noted difficulties relocating residents of “old, hostel-type and squatter houses” in the area. On 24 April 2009 the NDEA authorised another private company (Azyevro LAU LLC) to build replacement housing elsewhere “in connection with the construction of an important State facility.”

From mid-2009 NDEA officials orally demanded that the applicant vacate his house in exchange for an occupancy voucher for a 123 sq m five-room flat in the new development. He refused, insisting on prior monetary compensation equal to market value of the house and land. Surrounding demolitions, power cuts and debris forced the family (except the mother) to leave in October 2009. On 8 December 2009 the NDEA evicted the mother and demolished the house together with remaining belongings.

The applicant sued the NDEA (later joined by the BCEA, Ministry of Finance and Azyevro) seeking an end to the interference, restoration of the property or, alternatively, substantial pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages plus daily compensation for lost opportunity. The first-instance court (4 November 2010) dismissed the claims. It accepted his ownership of the house but not the land, treated the 2004 BCEA order and the 2009 voucher as lawful “compensation in kind” under the repealed 1982 Housing Code (applicable to state/public housing stock), cited but did not apply Civil Code expropriation rules, and relied on an unofficial valuation claiming the offered flat was larger and more valuable. Subsequent appeals (Baku Court of Appeal, 18 March 2011; Supreme Court, 8 July 2011) largely upheld this reasoning, merely substituting two other flats (vouchers back-dated to the same day) as compensation. The courts never examined whether a proper expropriation order by the Cabinet of Ministers existed, whether the purpose fell within the exhaustive statutory grounds (roads, borders, defence), whether prior market-value compensation had been paid, or whether the 2009 Housing Code purchase procedure applied after 1 October 2009. They also ignored the applicant’s claim that, by virtue of house ownership and 1997 regulations, he was entitled to the land free of charge.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that he had been arbitrarily deprived of his home and property without lawful procedure or genuine compensation, in violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8, and that the domestic courts had failed to address the lawfulness of the interference or provide an effective remedy, contrary to Articles 6 and 13.

The applicant was never notified of this order. It treated the 2004 BCEA order as still valid, relied on the 1982 Housing Code (in force only until 1 October 2009) governing allocation of state/public housing, and characterised the September 2009 voucher as lawful “compensation in kind.” An unofficial valuation supplied by the NDEA was accepted as showing the new flat to be larger and more valuable. Claims for cash compensation and non-pecuniary damage were dismissed.

The Baku Court of Appeal (18 March 2011) largely upheld the judgment but substituted two smaller flats for the original five-room offer. These facts form the core of the complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (unlawful deprivation of possessions without prior compensation or court order), Article 8 (interference with home), and Articles 6 and 13 (failure of the civil courts to examine the lawfulness of the taking or provide an effective remedy).

The case of M.A. v. Slovenia (application no. 3400/07) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns a Slovenian applicant's complaint that criminal proceedings arising from her 1983 rape were excessively lengthy and lacked the required diligence.

On 3 November 1983 the applicant, then eight months pregnant, was returning from work when three men (A.M., T.D. and N.T.) dragged her into a car, drove her to a remote location and raped her in succession. She reported the attack immediately; the suspects were arrested that night, medically examined the victim and released on 24 November 1983. A criminal complaint was lodged on 5 November and an investigation formally opened three days later. Crime-scene reports were prepared and the accused and witnesses were interviewed. T.D. and N.T. admitted intercourse but denied force; A.M. denied any sexual contact. On 13 March 1984 all three were indicted for aggravated rape (minimum three-year sentence). The trial was held in camera to protect privacy.

The first hearing was listed only in August 1988—more than four years after indictment and well beyond the two-month statutory deadline—and was adjourned because A.M. and N.T. failed to appear. A February 1989 listing likewise failed because N.T. could not be served. N.T. (a Roma national of another Yugoslav republic) absconded; a detention order and national arrest warrant (1990) and later an international warrant (2004) proved fruitless. His case was severed in October 1995 and the charges dropped in 2008.

Proceedings against A.M. and T.D. began in November 1996. Between late 1995 and 2002 thirty-one further hearings were postponed, almost invariably because of the defendants’ or counsel’s absence. Attempts to compel T.D.’s attendance, including a rejected 2000 detention request, failed. T.D. died in July 2003; his case was severed the following January.

Evidence was finally taken in May and November 2004. On 3 November 2004 A.M. was convicted and given 2½ years (below the statutory minimum) expressly because of the enormous delay, which the court attributed mainly to the co-accused. The Higher Court quashed the verdict in November 2006 and remitted for further inquiry into whether the offence had been completed and into the victim’s credibility. After five more hearings A.M. was reconvicted in November 2007 with the same sentence, again citing the lapse of time. On appeal the Higher Court reduced the term to one year (July 2008), taking into account the delay, A.M.’s youth at the time, subsequent good character, health and family circumstances. The Supreme Court rejected a final appeal in September 2009.

The criminal process thus lasted more than 25 years from investigation to final decision, punctuated by systemic failures to secure the defendants’ presence and repeated remittals. A subsequent civil claim for damages was settled in 2011, but the applicant stated she had received nothing.

The case of M.A. v. Slovenia (application no. 3400/07) arose from an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging that criminal proceedings relating to the applicant’s rape had been unduly lengthy and not pursued with the required diligence.

The applicant, a Slovenian national born in 1962, was eight months pregnant when, on the evening of 3 November 1983, three men (A.M., T.D. and N.T.) attacked her as she returned from work in Maribor. They dragged her into a car, drove to a remote location and raped her in succession. She reported the attack immediately; the police arrested the three men that night. They were detained until 24 November 1983. The applicant was medically examined. A police criminal complaint for rape was filed on 5 November 1983 and an investigation opened three days later. During the investigation the crime scene was examined and the suspects and witnesses were heard. T.D. and N.T. admitted intercourse but denied force; A.M. denied any sexual contact.

On 13 March 1984 the three men were charged with aggravated rape (minimum sentence three years). Proceedings were conducted in camera. The first hearing, listed for August 1988, was adjourned because two defendants failed to appear. A further hearing in February 1989 was adjourned because N.T. could not be served. All three accused were of Roma origin and had been born outside Slovenia; N.T. lived in another part of the then Yugoslavia. A detention order against N.T. was issued in December 1989 on flight-risk grounds, but he could not be found. An arrest warrant followed in April 1990. Inquiries in 1995 located A.M. and T.D. but not N.T. After a hearing adjournment caused by A.M.’s counsel, charges against N.T. were severed in October 1995. He was never located; an international warrant issued in 2004 was later revoked and the charges against him were dropped in 2008.

The trial of A.M. and T.D. opened in November 1996 and continued at hearings in 1998–1999. Thirty-one further hearings scheduled between late 1995 and early 2002 were postponed, principally because of the absence of the defendants or their lawyers. From 2000 the court took steps to secure T.D.’s attendance after he left Slovenia; a proposal to detain him was rejected in favour of milder coercive measures. T.D. died in July 2003 and his case was severed. After hearings in May and November 2004 the District Court convicted A.M. of aggravated rape and sentenced him to two-and-a-half years’ imprisonment, citing the long delay (mainly attributable to the other two accused) as a mitigating factor.

The Higher Court quashed the conviction in November 2006 and remitted the case, directing the first-instance court to consider whether the offence had been completed or merely attempted and whether the applicant had previously known A.M. After further hearings in 2007 the District Court again convicted A.M. and imposed the same sentence, again referring to the extreme lapse of time. On appeal the Higher Court reduced the sentence to one year in July 2008, taking account of the delay, A.M.’s age at the time of the offence, his subsequent clean record, his health and the fact that he had a young child. A further appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court in September 2009.

In July 2009 the applicant brought a civil claim against A.M. for €50 000 in non-pecuniary damages. After a default judgment, an appeal and several adjournments the parties settled in May 2011 for €15 000 payable in instalments; the applicant stated that she had received nothing.

The criminal proceedings therefore lasted from the 1983 investigation until the 2009 Supreme Court decision—more than twenty-five years—with repeated adjournments caused by the difficulty of locating and securing the attendance of defendants who had little connection to Slovenia.

The case of Guseva v. Bulgaria (Application no. 6987/07) concerns Ms Lyubov Viktorovna Guseva, a Bulgarian national and Board member of the Animal Protection Society in Vidin, authorised to represent it. She alleged that the mayor of Vidin’s failure to enforce three final administrative court judgments ordering disclosure of public information breached her Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The information was sought to contribute to public debate on animal protection.

On 11 April 2002 the applicant requested details of an agreement between the municipality and “Cleanliness” EOOD for collecting stray animals. The mayor refused after the company withheld consent, citing the Access to Public Information Act 2000. The Vidin Regional Court allowed her claim on 27 June 2003, holding that the information did not affect third-party rights. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this on 25 May 2004, finding the information of high public interest and the refusal unreasoned, and ordered disclosure.

On 20 January 2003 she requested 2001–2002 statistics on animals held at the “Municipal Care” shelter (numbers placed, deaths, euthanasia and municipal costs). The mayor again refused after “Titan Sever” OOD withheld consent. The Vidin Regional Court on 27 June 2003 ordered provision (if necessary without disclosing third-party parts). The Supreme Administrative Court confirmed this on 25 May 2004, reiterating public interest.

On 17 June 2003 she requested information on a public procurement procedure to reduce stray dogs (number of tenderers, those passing pre-selection, their qualified staff, facilities, proofs of capacity and prices). The mayor refused on 1 July 2003, stating the information concerned candidates’ bids, was economic in nature and related only to preparatory administrative acts. The Vidin Regional Court allowed the claim on 10 December 2003 and ordered disclosure, including of the winning organisation and contract terms. The Supreme Administrative Court on 20 October 2004 partly upheld the judgment, quashing the order relating to the winner and contract conditions but requiring the remainder of the information.

On 10 June 2004 (first two judgments) and 10 December 2004 (third judgment) the applicant asked the mayor to comply. On 27 December 2004 he issued a decision repeating that he need not disclose the winning organisation and remaining silent on the rest of the ordered information. He did not respond to the earlier requests. By letter of 15 September 2010 the applicant informed the Court that none of the information had been provided.

The persistent non-enforcement of the three final judgments granting access to information of high public interest in municipal animal-control practices formed the core of the alleged violation.

After the company withheld consent, the mayor refused access on 4 June 2002 under the Access to Public Information Act 2000. On 20 January 2003 she sought 2001–2002 statistics from the “Municipal Care” shelter (numbers of animals housed, deaths, euthanasias and municipal costs). The mayor again refused (14 February 2003) after “Titan Sever” OOD withheld consent. Both courts (same dates as above) ordered release, noting that even if third-party data existed it could be redacted, and that the refusal was unreasoned.

On 17 June 2003 she requested information about a public-procurement tender to reduce stray dogs: number of bidders, those that passed pre-selection, their staffing, facilities, capacity proofs and prices. The mayor refused on 1 July 2003, arguing the data concerned only the bidders’ economic bids and had no independent significance. The Regional Court (10 December 2003) ordered disclosure; the Supreme Administrative Court (20 October 2004) largely upheld that order, requiring all information except the identity of the winning contractor and the contract terms.

The case of Colac v. Romania (Application no. 26504/06) concerns the applicant Doru Colac, a Romanian national born in 1969. On 20 February 2003, the Iaşi Prosecutor’s Office indicted him (and a co-accused) for procurement and unlawful deprivation of liberty, alleging that they had threatened and forced five underage girls (C.R.R., M.A., F.P.D., I.A.P. and G.S.S.) into prostitution. The indictment relied primarily on the girls’ pre-trial statements, minutes of confrontations, a search of the applicant’s home, telephone records, and statements by the applicant, co-accused and other witnesses.

Before the Iaşi District Court (2003–2004), the applicant’s lawyer repeatedly requested that all pre-trial witnesses be heard in person. The court issued warrants and adjourned proceedings 15 times. Bailiffs attempted enforcement 17 times, but numerous witnesses could not be located: several (including F.P.D., I.A.P. and M.M.K.) had left Romania; others had moved to unknown addresses, changed names or sold property without updating records. Population, passport and border authorities confirmed they had no current addresses. By interlocutory decisions the court declared it impossible to hear C.R., G.C.R., F.P.D., I.A.P., T.E.P., M.M.K. and I.I.C., and ordered that certain pre-trial statements be read out (though the file confirms this occurred only for I.I.C.). I.I.C. appeared once but left for medical reasons before being examined; he was never located thereafter. The court later refused a further adjournment to find him.

Five witnesses who could be produced (M.A., G.S.S., D.V.D., F.H.A. and J.L.A.) were examined. M.A. confirmed being forced into prostitution; G.S.S. recanted and alleged police pressure; others either confirmed earlier accounts or withdrew them. On 22 June 2004 the District Court acquitted the applicant of deprivation of liberty but convicted him of procurement and imposed nine years’ imprisonment. It treated the unheard pre-trial statements of the girls, C.R., G.C.R., I.I.C., T.E.P. and M.M.K. as decisive, holding that they were closer in time to the events and were corroborated by the search report, objects belonging to one victim, a letter, and telephone logs linking the applicant to clients. Recanting trial testimony was discarded as inconsistent.

On appeal the Iaşi County Court (17 October 2005) upheld the conviction (adjusting classification) and sentence, reiterating that the girls’ statements were corroborated by other pre-trial evidence (including I.I.C.’s account that the applicant sought girls to work abroad). The Iaşi Court of Appeal, after an extraordinary appeal and remittal, ultimately reduced the sentence to seven years (21 December 2010). It held that the lower courts had taken all reasonable steps to secure attendance, that Article 327 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure permitted reliance on unread pre-trial statements when witnesses were unavailable, and that the evidence as a whole established guilt. The applicant consistently argued that the decisive statements had never been tested by him in open court and that the girls should have been treated as victims rather than mere witnesses.

These facts formed the basis of the complaint that the conviction violated Article 6 because the applicant had been unable to examine the principal witnesses against him.

The case originated in an indictment of 20 February 2003 by the Iași Prosecutor’s Office charging the applicant, Doru Colac, and a co-accused with procurement and unlawful deprivation of liberty. Prosecutors alleged they had threatened and forced five underage girls (C.R.R., M.A., F.P.D., I.A.P. and G.S.S.) into prostitution.
