It based the conviction principally on the pre-trial statements of the five girls and of the absent witnesses (C.R., G.C.R., I.A.P., F.P.D., I.I.C., T.E.P., M.M.K.), treating those statements as more reliable because they were closer in time to the events and were corroborated by the search report, objects belonging to C.R.R., a letter found in the applicant’s home, and telephone lists linking the applicant to alleged clients. Recantations given in court were dismissed as inconsistent with the remainder of the file.

The applicant appealed, complaining that the girls had been summoned only as witnesses, not as victims, that their statements lacked independent support and that essential witnesses had never been heard. The Iași County Court (17 October 2005) reclassified the offence but upheld the conviction, holding that the girls’ accounts were corroborated by client statements and by I.I.C. and G.C. After an extraordinary appeal prompted by the applicant’s medical absence, the Iași Court of Appeal, sitting as last-instance court, reduced the sentence to seven years (final judgment of 21 December 2010). It found that the lower courts had taken all reasonable steps to secure attendance, that the witnesses’ departure from Romania constituted a valid reason for applying Article 327, and that the conviction rested on a combination of pre-trial and trial evidence.

Separately, G.S.S. was investigated for perjury after recanting; the proceedings were discontinued and she was fined because the courts had already disregarded her in-court statement.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 that he was unable to examine the witnesses whose statements constituted the principal basis of his conviction.

The case of Colac v. Romania concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). The applicant, Doru Colac, a Romanian national, claimed he had been unable to examine all witnesses whose pre-trial statements formed the main basis of his conviction for procurement.

On 20 February 2003 the Iaşi Prosecutor’s Office indicted the applicant and a co-accused for procurement and unlawful deprivation of liberty. It alleged they had threatened and forced five underage girls (C.R.R., M.A., F.P.D., I.A.P. and G.S.S.) into prostitution. The indictment relied on the girls’ statements, minutes of confrontations, a search report of the applicant’s home, telephone records, medical documents and the accused’s own statements.

Proceedings before the Iaşi District Court (March 2003–June 2004) were adjourned fifteen times to secure the attendance of pre-trial witnesses. Bailiffs attempted seventeen times to enforce warrants. Several witnesses could not be located: M.M.K., F.P.D. and I.A.P. had left Romania (the latter two for Italy and Austria respectively); others (T.E.P., C.R.R., C.R., G.C.R.) had moved to unknown addresses or sold property and left the country; I.I.C. was registered at an address but never found at home. The court repeatedly requested information from population-records offices, passport services and border guards, which confirmed the absences and provided no further addresses.

By interlocutory judgments the court declared it impossible to hear C.R., G.C.R., F.P.D., I.A.P., T.E.P., M.M.K. and I.I.C. and, invoking Article 327 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure, ordered that their pre-trial statements be read out. I.I.C. appeared once but left for surgery before being examined; he was never located thereafter. The applicant’s request to adjourn in order to find him was refused.

Five witnesses who could be traced (including two of the girls, M.A. and G.S.S.) testified at trial. M.A. confirmed her earlier account of being threatened and sold into prostitution. G.S.S. recanted, claiming police pressure. Other witnesses either confirmed or withdrew their pre-trial statements. The court preferred the earlier versions as closer in time to the events and better corroborated by the remaining evidence (telephone lists linking the applicant to clients, objects belonging to one girl found in his home, a letter referring to rumours of prostitution). On 22 June 2004 it acquitted the applicant of deprivation of liberty but convicted him of procurement and sentenced him to nine years’ imprisonment, relying heavily on the unread witnesses’ statements together with those of the girls.

On appeal the Iaşi County Court (17 October 2005) reclassified the offence but upheld the conviction and sentence, holding that the girls’ accounts were corroborated by other pre-trial testimony. The Iaşi Court of Appeal first reduced the sentence to eight years (21 February 2006). After an extraordinary appeal succeeded because the applicant had been medically unable to attend, the same court, on 21 December 2010, further reduced the sentence to seven years. It found that the lower courts had taken all reasonable steps to hear the missing witnesses, that their departure from Romania justified reading the statements, and that the conviction was supported by the totality of the evidence.

Throughout the appeals the applicant argued that key witnesses (including some of the girls, treated as witnesses rather than victims) had never been examined in open court, that summonses had been sent to incomplete addresses, and that the proceedings therefore lacked an adversarial character. The domestic courts rejected these complaints, emphasising the practical impossibility of locating the witnesses and the corroborative value of the remaining evidence.
001-152892:
The case of Kolakovic v. Malta (Application no. 76392/12) concerns a British national, Jovica Kolakovic, who alleged a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his continued pre-trial detention for approximately 16 months after bail had been formally granted, due to financial conditions he could not meet.

Kolakovic was arrested on 8 September 2009 after a search of a nearby hotel room uncovered approximately 15 kg of cannabis. The next day he was questioned, and on 10 September 2009 he and co-suspects were charged with possession of cannabis not for exclusive personal use and conspiracy to traffic drugs. He was remanded in custody by the Court of Magistrates sitting as a Court of Criminal Inquiry. Repeated bail applications were refused.

On 25 March 2010 he commenced constitutional proceedings complaining of a breach of Article 5 § 3 and seeking release under Article 5 § 4. The Civil Court (First Hall) dismissed the claims on 12 August 2010 after examining the facts and Strasbourg case-law, without prejudice to future remedies. While the appeal was pending, the investigating court granted bail on 18 January 2011 subject to a curfew, twice-daily police reporting, residence in a designated apartment, a cash deposit of EUR 50,000 and a personal guarantee of EUR 15,000. Because the sums were not paid, Kolakovic remained in custody.

On 14 February 2011 the Constitutional Court found a violation of Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 on account of the continued refusals after the first-instance judgment. It awarded EUR 1,000 but declined to order release or modify the conditions, noting that bail had already been granted.

Kolakovic then applied repeatedly to reduce the financial requirements. On 22 February 2011 the deposit was lowered to EUR 40,000 and the guarantee raised to EUR 60,000. On 4 May 2011 the deposit was reduced to EUR 15,000 and the guarantee to EUR 30,000 (with a surety option requiring proof of means). A further reduction request was refused on 22 July 2011; the court relied on documents showing the couple still owned a substantial mortgaged home in the United Kingdom and inferred that the sale of a family shoe business had generated significant funds. Kolakovic argued that the business had merely closed because of his detention and his wife’s illness, that the family lived on diminishing savings and benefits, and that the house could not realistically be sold.

On 12 August 2011 he brought a second set of constitutional proceedings, asserting that the guarantees were so high as to render bail illusory. The Civil Court rejected the claim on 16 January 2012, holding that Kolakovic had initially failed to supply adequate financial evidence. On appeal the Constitutional Court upheld that decision on 12 November 2012, observing that early evidence had been limited (a house valued at approximately GBP 700,000 subject to a large mortgage and a former business) but that later reductions had occurred once further information emerged.

Meanwhile the investigating court continued to adjust conditions. On 14 March 2012 the deposit was cut to EUR 7,000 (guarantee raised to EUR 60,000). On 23 April 2012 it was reduced to EUR 5,000 (guarantee EUR 70,000) with a lighter reporting obligation. Kolakovic deposited the sum and was released the same day.

The criminal inquiry itself proceeded slowly, with numerous hearings, adjournments, and delays caused by letters rogatory to the United Kingdom for telephone data that ultimately proved irretrievable. After release, further applications to vary conditions (including permission to travel to the United Kingdom) were largely refused for want of additional guarantees.

These facts formed the basis of the complaint that the financial terms of bail, persistently set beyond the applicant’s means despite successive reductions and constitutional findings, had deprived him of the practical benefit of the right to release pending trial guaranteed by Article 5 § 3.

**CASE OF KOLAKOVIC v. MALTA (Application no. 76392/12)**

The applicant, a British national born in 1956, was arrested in Malta on 8 September 2009. A search of a nearby hotel room uncovered approximately 15 kg of cannabis. On 10 September 2009 he and others were charged with possession of cannabis not for exclusive use and conspiracy to traffic drugs. He was remanded in custody by the Court of Magistrates sitting as a Court of Criminal Inquiry.

Multiple bail applications were refused. The applicant commenced constitutional proceedings alleging a breach of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and seeking release under Article 5 § 4. The Civil Court (First Hall) dismissed the claims on 12 August 2010. While the constitutional appeal was pending, on 18 January 2011 the applicant was granted bail subject to a curfew, twice-daily police reporting, residence in a rented apartment, a cash deposit of EUR 50,000 and a personal guarantee of EUR 15,000. Unable to pay the deposit, he remained detained.

On 14 February 2011 the Constitutional Court found a violation of Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 arising from the passage of time and repeated refusals after the first-instance judgment. It awarded EUR 1,000 but declined to order release or vary the bail terms.

The applicant repeatedly sought reductions of the financial conditions, citing his family's lack of means. His wife testified that the family (four dependent children) had limited resources: the applicant had been detained for nearly two years, the family shoe business had closed (not been sold) because she was too ill to run it, savings had been exhausted on living costs, school fees and the mortgage, and she was receiving state benefits. On 22 February 2011 the deposit was reduced to EUR 40,000 and the personal guarantee raised to EUR 60,000. On 4 May 2011 the deposit fell to EUR 15,000 and the personal guarantee to EUR 30,000 (with the option of a third-party surety upon proof of means). A further reduction request was refused on 22 July 2011; the court noted the couple still owned a substantial mortgaged home (indicating they were not an average family) and inferred a “substantial” inflow of money from the supposed sale of the business.

On 12 August 2011 the applicant lodged a second set of constitutional proceedings complaining that the high guarantees rendered bail illusory and violated Article 5 § 3. Additional evidence showed the bank had foreclosed on the family home, the family was living on benefits with no savings, household goods and a car had been sold, and the wife was sending money to the applicant while renting a flat in Malta as a bail address. On 16 January 2012 the Civil Court (First Hall) rejected the claim, holding that earlier evidence had been insufficient and that the applicant was responsible for the delay in providing clear financial information; it invited the investigating court to re-evaluate the conditions. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 12 November 2012, observing that initial evidence (ownership of a GBP 700,000 house subject to a large mortgage and a shoe business) had been scanty, but that guarantees had later been lowered once more information emerged and the grounds for detention had weakened with the passage of time.

Following the first-instance constitutional judgment, the deposit was reduced to EUR 7,000 (personal guarantee raised to EUR 60,000) on 14 March 2012 and then to EUR 5,000 (personal guarantee EUR 70,000) on 23 April 2012, with some relaxation of reporting conditions. The applicant paid the deposit and was released the same day—approximately fifteen months after bail had first been granted.

The criminal inquiry itself was marked by numerous adjournments, delays in obtaining telephone data via letters rogatory (some data ultimately lost), witness issues and a restart of proceedings under Article 432 of the Criminal Code. Domestic law (Criminal Code Articles 576–578) required the amount of security to take into account the accused’s circumstances, the nature of the offence and the possible penalty; release on mere recognizance was possible in certain cases.

The applicant’s core complaint, communicated by the Court, was that the sixteen-month period of detention after bail had been granted, caused by financial conditions he could not meet, violated Article 5 § 3. (The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.)

**CASE OF KOLAKOVIC v. MALTA (Application no. 76392/12)**

The applicant, Jovica Kolakovic (a British national born in 1956), was arrested in Malta on 8 September 2009. A search of a nearby hotel room uncovered approximately 15 kg of cannabis. On 10 September 2009 he and others were charged with possession of cannabis not exclusively for personal use and conspiracy to traffic drugs. He was remanded in custody by the Court of Magistrates (as a Court of Criminal Inquiry).

Multiple bail applications were refused. On 25 March 2010 he began constitutional redress proceedings alleging a breach of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and seeking release under Article 5 § 4. The Civil Court (First Hall) dismissed the claims on 12 August 2010 after examining the facts and relevant Strasbourg case-law, without prejudice to future remedies. He appealed.

While the appeal was pending, on 18 January 2011 the applicant was granted bail subject to a curfew, twice-daily police reporting, residence in a rented apartment, a EUR 50,000 cash deposit and a EUR 15,000 personal guarantee. He could not pay and remained detained. On 14 February 2011 the Constitutional Court found a violation of Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 because of the time that had elapsed since the first-instance judgment and the continued refusals of bail. It awarded EUR 1,000 but declined to order release or vary the conditions, noting that bail had already been granted formally.

He then made repeated applications to reduce the financial guarantees. On 22 February 2011 the deposit was lowered to EUR 40,000 and the personal guarantee raised to EUR 60,000. After further evidence from his wife that the family lacked funds, on 4 May 2011 the deposit was reduced to EUR 15,000 and the personal guarantee to EUR 30,000 (with proof of a surety’s means required). A July 2011 request citing four dependent children in the United Kingdom, his wife’s illness, the winding-up of the family shoe business, mortgage arrears and exhausted savings was rejected on 22 July 2011. The court noted that the couple still owned a substantial mortgaged home and inferred that the sale of the business had generated funds; it considered EUR 15,000 commensurate with the charges and the applicant’s lack of ties to Malta.

A clarification that the business had closed rather than been sold was unsuccessful. On 12 August 2011 the applicant instituted a second set of constitutional proceedings, arguing that the guarantees were so high that release was impossible in practice. His wife testified in September 2011 that the shop had closed, stock had been sold at a loss, the bank had repossessed the family home, the family was living on state benefits with no savings, and she was renting a flat in Malta as a bail address. On 16 January 2012 the Civil Court rejected the claim, holding that earlier evidence of means had been insufficient and that the applicant bore responsibility for the delay in providing fuller information; it invited the investigating court to reassess the conditions. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 12 November 2012, observing that initial evidence (including ownership of a GBP 700,000 house subject to a large mortgage) had been scanty, after which the guarantees had been progressively lowered.

On 14 March 2012 the deposit was reduced to EUR 7,000 (personal guarantee EUR 60,000). On 23 April 2012 it was further reduced to EUR 5,000 (personal guarantee EUR 70,000, with less onerous reporting). The applicant paid the deposit and was released the same day—approximately fifteen months after bail had first been granted. Later applications to vary conditions (including permission to travel to the United Kingdom) were largely refused because he could not provide additional financial guarantees.

(The criminal investigation continued with numerous hearings, adjournments and letters of request to the United Kingdom for telephone data, most of which proved unobtainable; those proceedings are not the subject of the communicated complaint.)

The communicated complaint under Article 5 § 3 concerned solely the period of continued detention after formal grant of bail, caused by guarantees that the applicant maintained were disproportionate to his means. Domestic law (Criminal Code Arts. 576–578) required the amount of security to take account of the accused’s condition, the nature of the offence and the possible penalty.
001-152625:
The case of M.C. v. Poland originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by a Polish national born in 1987. Arrested in January 2007 on robbery charges and later additionally charged with sexual abuse of a minor, he was remanded in custody and convicted in 2008 of all offences, receiving a seven-year prison sentence plus ancillary bans related to contact with minors. In August 2007 he was transferred to Warsaw-Mokotów Detention Centre for psychiatric observation and placed in a nine-person “observation cell” in the psychiatric wing, located opposite the nurses’ room and equipped with CCTV.

Between Friday 7 and Monday 10 September 2007 two fellow inmates (T.G. and P.O.) subjected him to physical and psychological abuse. They held him while attempting to rape him with a broomstick, tried to force a third (mentally disabled) inmate to insert his penis into the applicant’s mouth, poured cold water over him while he lay in bed, spat on him, scrubbed his head with a toilet brush, struck him, verbally abused him and threatened to kill him if he reported the events. The applicant twice requested private conversations with a doctor and a warden during routine checks; both requests were refused. On Monday morning another inmate reported the weekend events; the applicant was immediately examined (revealing bruises and haematomas on his legs lasting no more than seven days) and transferred to another cell.

A prison inquiry confirmed the abuse but characterised it as neither lengthy nor of significant severity and mostly psychological. It found no shortcomings by staff, noting that the applicant had not reported the incidents immediately and that swift action followed once he did. The two perpetrators received only minor disciplinary sanctions (short bans on shopping or receiving parcels). The applicant lodged a criminal complaint alleging ill-treatment of a person deprived of liberty. After an initial police inquiry was discontinued for insufficient evidence, a prosecutor confirmed the decision. The district court upheld the discontinuation, holding that the isolated acts over less than four days did not meet the statutory definition of “ill-treatment” (which required a series of repeated acts causing significant pain or suffering) and amounted at most to privately prosecutable minor offences of personal inviolability or light bodily injury. Subsequent private-prosecution proceedings against the inmates were ultimately discontinued on limitation grounds. After the case was communicated to the Government the public investigation was reopened, charges were laid, but it was again discontinued on ne bis in idem and lack-of-evidence grounds; an inquiry into alleged staff negligence was likewise closed.

In parallel civil proceedings the Warsaw Regional Court held the State Treasury liable for infringement of the applicant’s personal rights (dignity, health, inviolability). Despite the cell’s special observation status and CCTV, staff had ignored requests for private talks, failed to notice a wet bed and visible injuries, and thereby failed in their duty to ensure the applicant’s safety. The court awarded 3 000 PLN (approximately €750) in non-pecuniary damages; the sum was upheld on appeal. Separate civil actions against the two inmates produced a settlement of 1 250 PLN and a final judgment of 2 500 PLN.

The applicant also complained of later incidents of alleged assault, unsafe cell-mates, disciplinary measures, inadequate medical and psychological care, and poor material conditions in other Warsaw remand centres; domestic authorities consistently rejected those complaints as unfounded. The application to the Court focused on the September 2007 events, the authorities’ failure to prevent or promptly halt the abuse, and the alleged ineffectiveness of the subsequent investigations.

**Case Summary: M.C. v. Poland (ECtHR, Application no. 23692/09, Judgment 3 March 2015)**

The applicant, a Polish national born in 1987, was arrested on 5 January 2007 on robbery charges and remanded in custody. He was later additionally charged with sexual abuse of a minor and recording a pornographic image of a minor. On 14 August 2008, the Warsaw-Mokotów District Court convicted him as charged, imposing a seven-year prison sentence plus lengthy bans on activities involving minors. The conviction was upheld on appeal.

The core allegations concern events while the applicant was held in the psychiatric wing of Warsaw-Mokotów Remand Centre (24 August–24 October 2007) for examination. Between Friday 7 and Monday 10 September 2007, two fellow inmates (T.G. and P.O.) allegedly subjected him to physical and sexual abuse in a nine-person observation cell equipped with CCTV and located opposite the nurses’ room. They attempted to rape him with a broomstick, forced a third inmate (J.C., who had a mental disability) to expose himself and attempt oral contact, poured cold water over him in bed, spat on him, scrubbed his head with a toilet brush, verbally abused him, and issued death threats. The applicant claimed he unsuccessfully sought to alert staff privately during checks; a doctor and warden refused private conversations. On Monday 10 September, another inmate reported the events; the applicant was examined (revealing haematomas on his legs causing health impairment of no more than seven days) and promptly moved to another cell.

A prison inquiry ordered by the Governor on 12 September 2007 confirmed the abuse (holding the applicant, threats of sexual violence, hitting with a stick, spitting, water-pouring, and use of a toilet brush), attributing it to inmates learning of the applicant’s sex-offence charges (the applicant denied making sexual advances). It found no staff shortcomings, noting the applicant had not reported immediately and that action followed once he did. Perpetrators received minor disciplinary sanctions (shopping and parcel bans). The inquiry characterised the treatment as mostly psychological and not of significant degree.

The applicant filed a criminal complaint on 10 September 2007; the Governor also notified prosecutors. An investigation into ill-treatment of a detainee (Article 247 § 1 Criminal Code) and related offences was opened but discontinued in March 2008 for insufficient evidence, despite witness statements (including from inmate A.S. corroborating the abuse) and the internal findings. The applicant appealed, arguing disregard of the inquiry, injuries, and unused CCTV evidence. In October 2008, the District Court upheld discontinuation, holding the acts were neither lengthy/continuous nor sufficiently serious for Article 247 (requiring repeated acts causing significant pain/suffering) and amounted at most to privately prosecutable offences (light injury or inviolability breach). It noted disciplinary action and the possibility of a private indictment.

A later private prosecution by the applicant against T.G. and P.O. (for inviolability breach and light injury) was ultimately discontinued in 2010–2011 due to expiry of the limitation period (after earlier quashed decisions citing *ne bis in idem*). After the ECtHR application was communicated, public prosecutors resumed proceedings in 2011, charged the inmates, but discontinued in 2012 on *ne bis in idem* grounds (referencing the private-prosecution termination) and found no staff negligence (no immediate report, no CCTV recordings, isolated acts over fewer than four days, prompt transfer once notified). Courts upheld this in 2013.

In related civil proceedings, the Warsaw Regional Court (2010, upheld on appeal) found the State Treasury liable for infringement of the applicant’s personal rights (dignity, health, inviolability). Despite the observation cell’s CCTV and the applicant’s requests, wet bedding, and visible injuries, staff failed to intervene over three days. The court awarded 3,000 PLN (approximately €750) in non-pecuniary damages (deeming the claimed 80,000 PLN excessive). Separate civil claims against the inmates yielded a settlement (1,250 PLN from T.G.) and a 2,500 PLN award against P.O.

Other detention complaints (conditions, assaults, medical care, disciplinary measures) were raised but largely rejected by domestic authorities as unfounded or addressed (e.g., single-cell placement after reported risks). The case centres on the State’s alleged failure to protect the applicant from inter-prisoner violence (given his vulnerability as a sex-offence suspect in an observed cell) and the ineffectiveness of subsequent investigations. The case of M.C. v. Poland (Application no. 23692/09) originated from a complaint by Polish national M.C. (born 1987) to the European Court of Human Rights. He alleged that, while detained, fellow inmates ill-treated him without adequate intervention by prison authorities, and that no effective investigation followed, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment).

M.C. was arrested on 5 January 2007 on robbery suspicions and later charged with sexual abuse of a minor (plus related recording of a pornographic image). He was remanded in custody. On 24 August 2007 he was transferred to Warsaw-Mokotów Detention Centre for psychiatric examination and housed in its psychiatric wing (cell no. 6, an “observation cell” opposite the nurses’ room and equipped with CCTV) from 31 August to 12 October 2007.

Between Friday 7 and Monday 10 September 2007, inmates T.G. and P.O. abused him. They held him down and attempted to rape him with a broomstick; they used the mental disability of a third inmate (J.C.) to force J.C. to expose his penis near M.C.’s face and attempt oral sex; they poured cold water over him (including his bed), spat on him, struck him with a broom and mop (causing facial bruises, haematomas and abrasions), scrubbed his head with a toilet brush, tattooed a mark on his arm, verbally abused him, ordered him to clean and sit in a corner, and threatened to kill him if he reported the events. M.C. sought private conversations with a doctor and warden during checks, but both refused. On 10 September another inmate (A.S.) alerted a doctor; M.C. was examined (yellow-brown haematoma marks on his legs, impairing health for under seven days) and promptly moved to another cell.

An internal prison inquiry (ordered 12 September, reported 20 September) confirmed the physical and psychological ill-treatment and death threats. It attributed the motive to the inmates learning of M.C.’s sexual-offence charges (they also claimed, and he denied, that he had made sexual advances). The inquiry found no staff failings, noting M.C. had not reported immediately and that action followed once he did. T.G. received a three-month food-parcel ban and P.O. a one-month shopping ban. The Governor notified prosecutors of an offence.

M.C. filed a criminal complaint on 10 September 2007. After delays (including failure to notify him of the inquiry’s opening), an investigation into ill-treatment of a detainee (Criminal Code Article 247 § 1) and related offences was opened. Witness A.S. largely corroborated the abuse, including the broomstick attempt; T.G. and P.O. denied it, claiming mere teasing over M.C.’s hygiene, appearance and alleged advances; a guard reported seeing nothing on CCTV and receiving no complaints. On 28 March 2008 the police discontinued for insufficient evidence; this was confirmed by the prosecutor and, on 22 October 2008, by the District Court, which added that the brief, non-continuous acts causing only light injuries did not meet Article 247’s threshold of repeated significant pain or suffering (they might constitute privately prosecutable offences of inviolability or light injury).

M.C.’s private bill of indictment against T.G. and P.O. (Articles 217 § 1 and 157 § 2) faced repeated discontinuations (ne bis in idem or limitation) before a final 4 November 2010 ruling of time-bar, upheld on appeal. After the Strasbourg application was communicated, prosecutors reopened the public case in 2011, charged T.G. and P.O. under Article 247, but discontinued in 2012 on ne bis in idem (citing the private case) and found no staff offence (no CCTV recordings existed; M.C. reported only on day four; staff then acted swiftly). The District Court upheld this in 2013.

In parallel civil proceedings M.C. sued the State Treasury (and the two inmates) for infringement of personal rights. On 3 March 2010 the Regional Court found the State liable: despite CCTV, M.C.’s unheeded requests, a wet bed and visible injuries, staff failed to intervene over three days in a specially monitored cell, violating his dignity. It awarded PLN 3,000 (circa EUR 750), upheld on appeal as proportionate. M.C. settled with T.G. for PLN 1,250 and obtained a final PLN 2,500 award against P.O.

M.C. also raised other detention complaints (assaults, conditions, medical care, placement with smokers), which authorities investigated and largely rejected as unfounded or already addressed (e.g., isolation for safety). The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights intervened as a third party. (Word count: 512)
001-153925:
The case concerns the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Vadim Pisari by a Russian soldier at a mixed peacekeeping checkpoint on the Dniester River bridge in Moldova on 1 January 2012, and the subsequent investigations.

Vadim, from a Moldovan-controlled village on the left bank, had been drinking at a New Year’s party. Around 7 a.m. he and a passenger took a friend’s car toward a petrol station on the right bank. At the left checkpoint (commanded by Russian sergeant V.K., the only soldier with a loaded machine gun), the car struck a “stop” sign and barrier and did not halt. V.K. radioed the right checkpoint, but the car also evaded obstacles there. After refuelling, the pair returned. They passed the right checkpoint unhindered (its soldiers alerted the left post). At the left checkpoint V.K. ordered them to stop; the car accelerated past deployed hedgehogs (and, according to later Russian-account statements, spike strips). V.K. claimed he had to jump aside to avoid being hit—an assertion absent from the contemporaneous affidavits given to Moldovan police. He fired a warning shot into the air, then three shots at the tyres. One bullet struck Vadim in the back. He died hours later in a Chișinău hospital. Blood-alcohol readings indicated light to moderate intoxication; visibility was poor because of ice on the windscreen.

Moldovan police arrived promptly, took statements from mixed-force soldiers and examined the scene, car and body, but the Russian command refused to surrender the weapon. Moldova opened a criminal investigation, granted the parents victim status and issued an international arrest warrant. V.K. was immediately transferred to Russia. A joint commission (chaired by a Russian colonel and unsigned by its Moldovan member) blamed Vadim for a serious breach of checkpoint rules while noting inadequate non-lethal stopping equipment; it provisionally found V.K.’s use of force consistent with 2003 JCC instructions (verbal warning, warning shot, then shots at tyres only if lives were threatened). A separate Russian military report reached the same conclusions.

Russia opened its own manslaughter inquiry, questioned its own and Transdniestrian soldiers (whose later statements aligned with V.K.’s account of two hedgehogs plus spike strips and of personal danger), conducted a ballistic test, an investigative experiment and a psychiatric examination of V.K. On 17 May 2012 it discontinued the case for lack of an offence. The parents were never granted victim status, never received the termination decision and were told they lacked standing to challenge it. Moldova later closed its file because the suspect had absconded. Neither the family nor the Moldovan authorities ever obtained the Russian decision.

These facts raise issues under Article 2 concerning both the necessity and proportionality of lethal force at a peacekeeping post and the adequacy, independence and participatory nature of the ensuing investigations.

The case of Pisari v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 42139/12) concerns the fatal shooting of the applicants’ 18-year-old son, Vadim Pisari, by a Russian soldier at a joint peacekeeping checkpoint in Moldova’s Transdniestrian security zone on 1 January 2012. The applicants, Simion and Oxana Pisari, alleged violations of Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) arising from both the killing itself and the subsequent investigations, particularly their exclusion from the Russian proceedings.

Vadim Pisari lived in Pirita, a village on the left bank of the Dniester River under Moldovan control. After an all-night New Year’s party involving alcohol, he and a passenger took a friend’s car to refuel at a station across the river in Vadul lui Vodă. They needed to cross a bridge with peacekeeping checkpoints at each end, manned by mixed Russian, Moldovan and Transdniestrian soldiers. The left checkpoint, commanded by Russian sergeant V.K. (the only soldier armed with a loaded machine gun), featured concrete blocks and barriers requiring vehicles to slow down.

Around 7:10 a.m., Vadim’s car failed to stop at the left checkpoint, striking the “stop” sign and barrier. Visibility was poor due to ice on the windshield. V.K. ordered a halt, but the car continued and also evaded the right checkpoint. After refuelling, the pair returned around 7:30 a.m. They passed the right checkpoint unhindered (though it was alerted). At the left checkpoint, obstacles including “hedgehogs” and possibly spike strips had been deployed. V.K. ordered a stop; Vadim accelerated and avoided the barriers. V.K. later claimed the car headed toward him, forcing him to jump aside—a detail absent from his and other soldiers’ immediate affidavits to Moldovan police, though later given to Russian investigators.

V.K. fired a warning shot in the air, then three shots at the tyres. One bullet struck Vadim in the back. The car stopped after about 30 metres; Vadim collapsed and later died in hospital. Another soldier’s coat was reportedly pierced by a bullet. Vadim’s blood-alcohol level was later measured at 0.7–1.13%. Moldovan police quickly took statements from soldiers present but were refused the weapon by Russian commanders.

Moldova opened a criminal investigation, granting the applicants victim status and issuing an international arrest warrant for V.K., who was promptly transferred to Russia. Russia announced a parallel probe. A joint commission (chaired by a Russian colonel, unsigned by its Moldovan member) and a Russian military report blamed Vadim for breaching checkpoint rules and endangering lives, while citing inadequate vehicle-stopping equipment and poor local awareness of procedures. The case of Pisari v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 42139/12) concerns the killing of the applicants’ 18-year-old son, Vadim Pisari, by a Russian peacekeeping soldier at a security checkpoint in Moldova, and the subsequent investigations. The applicants, Moldovan nationals Simion and Oxana Pisari, alleged a breach of Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) both in its substantive aspect (the killing itself) and its procedural aspect (their exclusion from the Russian criminal proceedings).

Vadim Pisari lived in Pirita, a village on the left bank of the Dniester under Moldovan control. In the early hours of 1 January 2012, after a New Year’s party at which he had consumed alcohol, he and a passenger took a friend’s car for a joyride. Needing fuel, they drove toward a petrol station on the right bank, requiring them to cross a bridge with mixed peacekeeping checkpoints at each end. These were manned by Russian, Moldovan and Transdniestrian soldiers. The left checkpoint was commanded by Russian sergeant V.K., the only soldier armed with a loaded machine gun. Concrete blocks and metal barriers forced vehicles to slow down.

Around 7.10 a.m. Vadim failed to stop at the left checkpoint, hitting a “stop” sign and barrier. V.K. ordered him to halt, but he continued. The right checkpoint was alerted, yet the car did not stop there either (accounts differ on whether obstacles were deployed). After refuelling, the pair returned. They passed the right checkpoint unhindered; soldiers there immediately notified the left checkpoint.

At approximately 7.30 a.m. V.K. again ordered the car to stop. According to V.K., two “hedgehogs” and two spike strips had been placed (other soldiers mentioned only one hedgehog). Vadim accelerated and evaded the obstacles. V.K. later claimed the car came toward him, forcing him to jump aside, though this detail was absent from his immediate statement to Moldovan police and from contemporaneous affidavits of other witnesses. V.K. shouted a warning that he would shoot and fired once into the air. When the car continued, he fired three single shots at the tyres. One bullet struck Vadim in the back. The car stopped about 30 metres on; Vadim collapsed. Soldiers bandaged the wound and summoned an ambulance. He died hours later in a Chişinău hospital. Blood-alcohol readings were 0.7 % and 1.13 %. One of V.K.’s bullets nearly struck another soldier.

Moldovan police arrived promptly, took statements and sought the weapon, which Russian commanders refused to surrender. Moldova opened a criminal investigation. V.K. was immediately transferred to Russia. A joint commission headed by a Russian colonel (unsigned by its Moldovan member and thus lacking legal effect) blamed Vadim for a serious breach of checkpoint rules and for endangering lives, noted inadequate vehicle-stopping equipment, and provisionally found V.K.’s actions consistent with firearms rules. A separate Russian military report reached similar conclusions.

Moldova granted the applicants victim status, examined the scene, vehicle, body and bullet, questioned its own soldiers, and issued an international arrest warrant for V.K. Russia opened a parallel manslaughter inquiry, questioned its soldiers (who corroborated V.K.’s later account), conducted a reconstruction, ballistic tests and a psychiatric examination of V.K. On 17 May 2012 Russia discontinued the case, finding no offence, and refused extradition. The applicants were never recognised as parties, received no copy of the decision and were denied standing to appeal. Moldova later discontinued its own proceedings because the suspect had absconded. The applicants never obtained the Russian termination decision.

Peacekeeping operations in the security zone are governed by the 1992 Russia–Moldova agreement establishing the Joint Control Commission. 2003 instructions permitted firearms to stop a vehicle that ignored orders only if soldiers’ lives were threatened, and only after a verbal warning, a warning shot, and then shots aimed at the ground or tyres, with all necessary precautions for bystanders’ safety.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 2 violations: the circumstances and necessity of the lethal force used by V.K., and the applicants’ complete exclusion from an effective investigation capable of establishing accountability.

The case of Volkov and Adamskiy v. Russia (applications nos. 7614/09 and 30863/10) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by two Russian nationals who alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention. They claimed their convictions for copyright infringement (distributing counterfeit software) resulted from police entrapment via undercover “test purchase” operations under the 1995 Operational-Search Activities Act. Mr Volkov additionally alleged that he had been denied free legal assistance on appeal.

Both men advertised computer-repair services (Volkov online, Adamskiy in a newspaper). On 6 December 2007 an undercover officer, V, telephoned Volkov and asked him to install software including Photoshop and Windows XP. Volkov purchased counterfeit CDs and installed the programs for 3,300 roubles. A recorded conversation showed Volkov explaining that licensed software would cost far more (Photoshop 500 dollars) and that other firms charged higher prices because they feared “licensing inspections,” whereas he operated “semi-legally.” Volkov was charged under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. At the 3 July 2008 trial he testified that he had performed similar work for relatives, that V had not specifically requested unlicensed software, and that the police had incited the offence. V stated the operation followed prior intelligence of Volkov’s involvement in counterfeit distribution. The Golovinskiy District Court convicted him and imposed a suspended sentence of one year and three months’ imprisonment with one year’s probation.

Volkov, who had a privately retained lawyer only at the pre-trial stage and thereafter a legal-aid lawyer, lodged an appeal requesting to attend in person but not requesting counsel. The court notified his former lawyer, Ms D, who had no retainer for the appeal. At the 20 August 2008 hearing before the Moscow City Court Volkov appeared alone; Ms D did not attend. It is unclear whether he sought an adjournment or replacement counsel. The conviction was upheld.

On 10 December 2008 undercover officer M telephoned Adamskiy, who was in financial need, and requested several programs. Adamskiy downloaded “cracked” unlicensed copies from the internet and installed them the next day for 3,000 roubles. The recording captured him admitting he had not bought the software “to go bankrupt,” that it came from peers, and warning M about possible inspections and the need to “keep it quiet.” At the 28 September 2009 trial Adamskiy confirmed he had told M the software was counterfeit and did not claim M had asked for unlicensed copies; he pleaded guilty but alleged incitement. M said the operation verified existing intelligence. The Timiryazevskiy District Court imposed a suspended sentence of one year and six months with one year’s probation. The Moscow City Court dismissed his appeal on 16 November 2009.

Domestic law made copyright infringement punishable by fine, community service or up to two years’ imprisonment. Undercover operations and the use of their results as evidence were regulated by the Operational-Search Activities Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure. Appeal courts reviewed lawfulness, validity and fairness and could examine additional evidence. Constitutional Court and Supreme Court case-law confirmed this obligation applied equally to appeal proceedings. Article 413 permitted reopening of a case following a finding of a Convention violation by the Strasbourg Court.

001-153518:
**Case of Gallardo Sanchez v. Italy (ECHR, Application no. 11620/07, judgment of 24 March 2015)**

The applicant, Venezuelan national Manuel Rogelio Gallardo Sanchez (born 1965), was detained in Italy pending extradition to Greece on an arson accusation. He alleged that the length of this detention violated Article 5 § 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights; the Court examined the complaint under Article 5 § 1 (f), which permits detention of a person against whom action is being taken with a view to extradition.

On 19 April 2005, Rome police took the applicant into custody pursuant to an arrest warrant issued by the Athens Court of Appeal on 26 January 2005 under the 1957 European Convention on Extradition. On 22 April 2005 the L’Aquila Court of Appeal validated the arrest and ordered detention. The Ministry of Justice requested an extension on 26 April. At a 27 April hearing the applicant’s identity was confirmed and he refused consent to extradition.

On 9 June 2005 the Ministry informed the Court of Appeal that Greece had transmitted a formal extradition request and supporting documents on 25 May 2005. The public prosecutor sought approval of the request on 21 June. A hearing set for 15 December 2005 was postponed, at the applicant’s request, to 12 January 2006. On that date, without further investigation, the Court of Appeal authorised extradition (decision deposited 30 January 2006). It verified compliance with the Extradition Convention, the principles of ne bis in idem and double criminality, and the absence of discriminatory or political motives.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation on 3 March 2006, arguing that the request had arrived after the 40-day limit in Article 16 § 4 of the Extradition Convention (rendering detention unlawful) and that the Greek charges lacked serious indications of guilt. In a judgment of 11 May 2006 (deposited 18 September 2006) the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal in a one-page decision, holding that the request had arrived in time and that it lacked jurisdiction to assess the strength of the evidence of guilt.

Meanwhile the applicant made three unsuccessful applications for release to the Rome Court of Appeal between June and September 2005. In its last decision of 27 October 2005 the court reiterated the risk of flight (despite confiscation of the applicant’s passport) and Italy’s international obligations.

On 9 October 2006 the Minister of Justice signed the extradition order. The applicant was surrendered to Greece on 26 October 2006. Detention therefore lasted from 19 April 2005 until 26 October 2006—approximately 18½ months.

Italian law (Code of Criminal Procedure Arts. 714–718, 704–708) implements the Extradition Convention. Provisional arrest may last no more than 40 days pending receipt of the formal request; once confirmed, a custodial measure may not exceed 18 months (extendable by three months). The Court of Appeal examines legal conditions for extradition in private after hearing the parties; when the Convention applies it may not review the existence of serious indications of guilt. Release may be sought at any time, but the Court of Cassation has repeatedly held that it lacks jurisdiction to re-examine the risk of absconding once that risk has been found by the Court of Appeal. The Minister must decide on extradition within 45 days of the Cassation decision; failure to do so or a refusal requires release.

These facts—the duration of detention, the sequence of procedural steps, the unsuccessful release applications, and the applicable time-limits—formed the basis of the alleged violation of the right to liberty in the context of extradition proceedings.

The case of Gallardo Sanchez v. Italy (Application no. 11620/07) was brought by Venezuelan national Manuel Rogelio Gallardo Sanchez, born in 1965 and residing in Cape Town. He alleged that the duration of his detention in Italy pending extradition to Greece violated Article 5 of the Convention. Although initially framed under Article 5 § 3, the Court examined it under Article 5 § 1 (f), which authorises detention of a person against whom action is being taken with a view to extradition.

On 19 April 2005 the applicant was arrested in Rome pursuant to an Athens Court of Appeal warrant of 26 January 2005 issued under the 1957 European Convention on Extradition for an alleged arson offence. On 22 April 2005 the L’Aquila Court of Appeal validated the arrest and ordered detention. At a hearing on 27 April 2005 the applicant refused to consent to extradition.

The Greek authorities transmitted the formal extradition request and supporting documents on 25 May 2005; the Italian Ministry of Justice notified the Court of Appeal on 9 June 2005. The public prosecutor sought approval of extradition on 21 June 2005. A hearing listed for 15 December 2005 was adjourned to 12 January 2006 at the applicant’s request. On that date the Court of Appeal granted extradition, confirming compliance with the Extradition Convention, the ne bis in idem principle, dual criminality and the absence of political or discriminatory motives. The decision was filed on 30 January 2006.

On 3 March 2006 the applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, arguing that the request had arrived after the 40-day limit in Article 16 § 4 of the Extradition Convention (rendering detention unlawful) and that the Greek charges lacked serious indications of guilt; he sought release. In a judgment of 11 May 2006 (filed 18 September 2006) the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, holding that the request was timely and that it had no jurisdiction to review the existence of serious indications of guilt.

In the interim the applicant made three unsuccessful applications for release between June and September 2005. In its last decision of 27 October 2005 the Rome Court of Appeal, sitting in camera, maintained detention on the grounds of a continuing risk of absconding (even after confiscation of the applicant’s passport) and Italy’s duty to honour its international obligations.

The Minister of Justice signed the extradition decree on 9 October 2006 and the applicant was surrendered to Greece on 26 October 2006. Detention therefore lasted from 19 April 2005 until 26 October 2006—approximately 18 months and one week.

Italian law (Article 714 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) caps such detention at 18 months, extendable by a further three months. Provisional arrest under Articles 715–717 must be confirmed within 96 hours and the foreign request received within 40 days; thereafter the Court of Appeal examines the request in camera, verifying Convention compatibility and fundamental-rights safeguards but, where the Extradition Convention applies, without assessing the strength of the evidence of guilt. Release applications are decided by the Court of Appeal and may be challenged only on points of law; the Court of Cassation has consistently declined jurisdiction to re-examine the risk of flight.

These facts— the overall duration, the sequence of hearings and appeals, the unsuccessful release applications, the timing arguments under the Extradition Convention, and the domestic statutory limits—form the core of the complaint that the detention pending extradition was excessively long and therefore unlawful.

The case of Nagiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 16499/09) concerns an Azerbaijani national, Asif Nagiyev (born 1980), who alleged that his detention from 18 September 2008 to 10 March 2009 was unlawful. In November 2007 a bomb exploded in Moscow, leading Russian authorities to charge Nagiyev on 13 December 2007 with unlawful possession of explosives. On 21 December 2007 a Moscow court issued an arrest warrant and ordered his remand in custody; the warrant was forwarded to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) on 26 December 2007. Azerbaijani police contacted Nagiyev in January 2008. He appeared voluntarily, denied involvement, and was questioned again on 31 January 2008 in the presence of Russian officers, after which he was released without further action.

According to Nagiyev, he was summoned to the MIA’s Organised Crime Department (OCD) on 18 September 2008 in connection with his own complaint about property misappropriation. Upon arrival he was arrested without documentation, denied contact with family or a lawyer, and held in the OCD’s temporary detention facility. His family reported him missing on 21 September; the OCD confirmed his detention by telephone the next day. A brother visited on 24 September but received no explanation of the grounds. A privately retained lawyer was prevented from seeing him on 27 September and was not notified of that evening’s court hearing, at which a state-appointed lawyer appeared. The Narimanov District Court, relying on the Russian warrant and Azerbaijani extradition provisions (CCrP Art. 495.1), ordered two months’ remand.

The Government maintained that Nagiyev was arrested only at noon on 27 September 2008, as recorded in official documents, and taken to the detention facility at 4 p.m. after the court order. Detention was subsequently extended on 27 November 2008 (two months), 27 January 2009 (one month) and 27 February 2009 (one month). Each extension invoked CCrP Art. 159 (applicable to pending domestic criminal proceedings) and cited the time needed to obtain the case file from Russia after Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General requested its transfer, given that Nagiyev, as an Azerbaijani citizen, could not be extradited (Constitution Art. 53(II); Criminal Code Art. 13).

Nagiyev repeatedly appealed, arguing that: (i) his undocumented detention began on 18 September; (ii) no criminal proceedings existed in Azerbaijan; (iii) no official extradition or transfer request had been received from Russia (CCrP Arts. 495.3, 497.1 require release after 48 hours without such a request); and (iv) the courts failed to address these points. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals of 7 November 2008, 5 December 2008 and 2 February 2009 without examining the specific complaints. On 10 March 2009 it finally quashed the latest extension, noting that Nagiyev had already been held for 163 days, that no additional materials had arrived from Russia, that extradition of a citizen was constitutionally impossible, and that the first-instance court had erred. He was released that day.

Relevant domestic and international rules (CCrP Chapter LVII, 1993 Minsk Convention Arts. 60–62) permit provisional arrest pending an extradition request but require prompt release if the request and supporting documents are not received within 40–48 hours. No such request ever materialised, and no Azerbaijani investigation was opened during the entire period of detention.

The case of Nagiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 16499/09) concerns the alleged unlawful detention of Azerbaijani national Asif Nagiyev from 18 September 2008 to 10 March 2009.

In November 2007 a bomb exploded in Moscow, prompting Russian criminal proceedings. The applicant was charged on 13 December 2007 with unlawful possession of explosives. A Moscow court issued an arrest warrant on 21 December 2007, which was forwarded to Azerbaijani authorities on 26 December. In January 2008 the applicant voluntarily attended the Azerbaijani Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA), denied any involvement, and was questioned (including with Russian officers present) but released without further action.

On 30 June 2008 the applicant complained to the MIA’s Organised Crime Department (OCD) of property misappropriation by others. Dissatisfied with progress, he later complained to other authorities.

The applicant stated that on 18 September 2008 he was summoned to the OCD, arrested without documentation, and denied contact with family or a lawyer. His family reported him missing on 21 September. On 22 September they learned he was held at the OCD facility; his brother visited on 24 September but received no explanation of the reasons. A privately retained lawyer contracted on the morning of 27 September was refused access. That evening the applicant was brought before a Narimanov District Court judge (represented only by a state-appointed lawyer) who ordered two months’ remand.

The Government maintained that arrest occurred at noon on 27 September 2008, as recorded in an official protocol, with the applicant arriving at the facility later that day after the court order.

The 27 September detention order relied on the Russian warrant and Azerbaijani Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP) provisions permitting arrest pending an extradition decision. Yet Azerbaijan’s Constitution (Article 53) and Criminal Code (Article 13) absolutely prohibit extradition of its citizens. The applicant’s lawyer obtained the documents only on 8 October and appealed, arguing the arrest actually began on 18 September, that no Azerbaijani proceedings existed, that extradition was legally impossible, and that Russia had never submitted a formal request.

The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 7 November without addressing these points. Detention was then extended on 27 November 2008 (two months), 27 January 2009 (one month) and 27 February 2009 (one month). The courts cited CCrP Article 159 (extensions in pending domestic proceedings) and the time needed to obtain transfer of the Russian case file, even though no Azerbaijani investigation had been opened.

The applicant repeatedly appealed, stressing the absence of any official Russian request (CCrP Articles 495 and 497 require release within 48 hours if none arrives), the impossibility of extradition, the lack of pending Azerbaijani proceedings, and the courts’ failure to examine the undocumented 18–27 September detention. These appeals were rejected until 10 March 2009, when the Baku Court of Appeal ordered release. It noted that five months had elapsed without any materials from Russia, that extradition was barred, and that the applicable CIS conventions (Minsk Convention Articles 61–62) required release if a formal request did not arrive within 40 days.

The central facts are therefore the disputed commencement date of detention, the initial lack of documentation or legal access, the use of extradition provisions that could never apply to an Azerbaijani citizen, and the successive extensions of custody in the complete absence of instituted domestic proceedings or timely supporting documents from Russia.

In each appeal the applicant repeated that no Azerbaijani proceedings had been instituted, that the courts had ignored the undocumented detention of 18–27 September, that no extradition request had ever been received (triggering the 48-hour release rule in CCrP Article 497.1 and the 40-day rule in the relevant CIS convention), and that continued detention therefore lacked any legal basis.
