In Solomun v. Croatia (Application no. 679/11), Croatian police officer Ivica Solomun alleged that the quashing of a final civil judgment in his favour breached legal certainty under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Born in 1974 and resident in Sisak, the applicant joined the Sisak-Moslavina Police Department in 1993. From 1 January 1998 he was posted to Dvor Police Station. Dvor was classified as an area of special State support under the Special State Support Act, entitling public-sector employees to a 50 per cent salary bonus. Amendments effective 29 July 2000 limited eligibility to those who both held registered domicile and actually resided in such an area.

In May 2001 the applicant was reassigned to Sisak. On 29 September 2000 he sued the State for the bonus. The case reached the Hrvatska Kostajnica Municipal Court. The State Attorney’s Office challenged territorial jurisdiction and entitlement, pointing to travel expenses paid between Sisak and Dvor as evidence that the applicant in fact lived in Sisak (not a supported area), although Majur (also supported) had been mentioned. The applicant stated that his registered domicile and actual residence were in Majur, that incomplete post-war reconstruction of his house had led him to spend some time in Sisak, and that he had been authorised to use a police vehicle.

On 2 October 2003 the Municipal Court awarded the applicant HRK 67,214.69 plus statutory interest for the period 1 February 1998–1 May 2001, together with costs of HRK 7,978.80. It found his evidence of domicile and residence credible; the State had adduced no contrary proof and had itself asserted that he lived in Majur. Travel expenses were held irrelevant to the residence question.

The State appealed, repeating that the expenses demonstrated residence in Sisak. On 26 February 2004 the Sisak County Court dismissed the appeal and endorsed the first-instance findings, rendering the judgment final. Enforcement proceedings were opened on 19 April 2004 and the award was paid in full on 26 April 2004.

On 20 May 2004 the State Attorney’s Office lodged a request for the protection of legality with the Supreme Court, attacking only the portion of the award (HRK 19,238.59) covering 11 August 2000–5 May 2001. It argued that, after the 2000 amendments, the applicant no longer resided in a supported area, as shown by the travel expenses and the Sisak address given in his original claim. The applicant objected that the request contradicted a 13 June 2003 general position of the Supreme Court’s Civil Division that the amendments did not apply to rights already accrued.

On 14 April 2005 the Supreme Court granted the request, quashed the relevant part of the County Court judgment and remitted the case, holding that the amendments required both domicile and actual residence. On 7 December 2006 the County Court reversed the first-instance award for that period, ordered repayment of HRK 19,238.59 plus interest, and adjusted the costs order, finding that the applicant had not resided in a supported area.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint on 30 January 2007 challenging the use of the extraordinary remedy. On 29 April 2010 the Constitutional Court dismissed it as ill-founded, holding that the lower courts had applied the law correctly. The decision was served on 31 May 2010. The applicant subsequently repaid a total of HRK 28,700 from his salary.

Under the Civil Procedure Act then in force, the State Attorney could seek protection of legality within three months of a final decision on grounds of incorrect application of substantive law; the provision remained applicable because first-instance proceedings had ended before its repeal. Supreme Court case-law treated employment, domicile and residence as cumulative conditions.

The case of Solomun v. Croatia (Application no. 679/11) concerns Croatian national Ivica Solomun, a police officer born in 1974 and living in Sisak. He alleged that the quashing of a final civil judgment in his favour violated the principle of legal certainty under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Solomun began work with the Sisak-Moslavina Police Department in 1993 and was posted to Dvor Police Station from 1 January 1998. Dvor was designated an area of special State support under the relevant Act, entitling public-sector employees to a 50% salary bonus. Amendments effective 29 July 2000 restricted the bonus to those who both registered their domicile and actually resided in such an area. In May 2001 Solomun was reassigned to Sisak.

On 29 September 2000 he sued the State in the Kutina Municipal Court for the bonus covering February 1998 to May 2001. The case was transferred to the Hrvatska Kostajnica Municipal Court. The State contested territorial jurisdiction and entitlement, noting that Solomun received travel expenses between Sisak and Dvor and had given a Sisak address, suggesting he did not actually reside in a special-support area (Majur, where he claimed domicile). Solomun testified that he lived in Majur—partly in his war-damaged house and partly with his sister—and had used an official car.

On 2 October 2003 the first-instance court accepted his claim, awarding HRK 67,214.69 plus statutory interest and costs of HRK 7,978.80. It found his evidence of domicile and residence credible and uncontradicted by the State. The Sisak County Court dismissed the State’s appeal on 26 February 2004, rendering the judgment final. Enforcement proceedings led to full payment on 26 April 2004.

On 20 May 2004 the State Attorney’s Office filed a request for the protection of legality with the Supreme Court, challenging only the post-amendment portion of the award (HRK 19,238.59 for August 2000–May 2001). It argued that travel expenses and the Sisak address showed Solomun had not resided in a special-support area after the 2000 amendments, citing Supreme Court judgment Gzz-190/03. Solomun objected that the request was an improper remedy and contradicted the Supreme Court’s June 2003 general position that the amendments were not retrospective.

On 14 April 2005 the Supreme Court granted the request, quashed the relevant part of the second-instance judgment and remitted the case, holding that the amendments required both domicile and actual residence. On 7 December 2006 the Sisak County Court reversed the first-instance award for that period, ordered Solomun to repay HRK 19,238.59 plus interest, and adjusted costs, finding he had not resided in a qualifying area. His constitutional complaint, lodged on 30 January 2007, was dismissed as ill-founded on 29 April 2010 (served 31 May 2010). A 2013 Ministry of the Interior certificate confirmed he had repaid HRK 28,700 from his salary.

The Civil Procedure Act (as applicable) allowed the State Attorney to seek protection of legality against final decisions for substantial procedural flaws or incorrect application of substantive law, within three months of finality. Amendments effective 1 December 2003 repealed the remedy, but transitional provisions preserved it for cases whose first-instance proceedings had ended earlier. Supreme Court practice treated the 2000 amendments as requiring cumulative employment, domicile and residence criteria, yet also held they did not apply retrospectively to previously accrued rights.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: a final, enforced judgment was reopened via an extraordinary remedy after payment, resulting in an order to repay a portion of the awarded sum.

The case of Solomun v. Croatia originated in an application lodged on 26 November 2010 by Croatian national Ivica Solomun. He alleged that quashing a final civil judgment in his favour breached legal certainty under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, a police officer born in 1974, was assigned from 1 January 1998 to Dvor Police Station in a municipality receiving special State support. Under the Special State Support Act, public-sector employees there were entitled to a 50% salary bonus. Amendments effective 29 July 2000 limited the bonus to those with both registered domicile and actual residence in such an area. In May 2001 the applicant was reassigned to Sisak.

On 29 September 2000 he sued the State for the bonus covering February 1998 to May 2001. After transfer to the Hrvatska Kostajnica Municipal Court, the State contested jurisdiction and entitlement, citing the applicant’s travel expenses between Sisak and Dvor and arguing he resided in Sisak (outside a special-support area). The applicant maintained he resided in Majur (also a special-support area), using an authorised police car and staying there despite incomplete post-war house reconstruction, while occasionally being in Sisak.

On 2 October 2003 the Municipal Court awarded the applicant HRK 67,214.69 plus statutory interest for the claimed period and HRK 7,978.80 in costs. It accepted his residence evidence as credible, noting the State had neither adduced contrary proof nor properly challenged his account and had itself acknowledged Majur ties. Travel expenses were held irrelevant to domicile/residence. The Sisak County Court dismissed the State’s appeal on 26 February 2004, rendering the judgment final. It was fully enforced by payment on 26 April 2004.

On 20 May 2004 the State Attorney lodged a request for protection of legality with the Supreme Court against the portion of the award (HRK 19,238.59) for 11 August 2000–5 May 2001. It argued travel expenses and the applicant’s Sisak address showed he no longer resided in a special-support area after the 2000 amendments, citing Supreme Court case-law that employment, domicile and residence were cumulative requirements.

On 14 April 2005 the Supreme Court granted the request, quashed the relevant part of the County Court judgment and remitted the case for reassessment of whether the post-amendment criteria were met. On 7 December 2006 the County Court reversed the first-instance award for that period, ordered repayment of HRK 19,238.59 plus interest, and adjusted costs. It found the evidence showed the applicant had not actually resided in a special-support area.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint, challenging use of the legality-protection request, was dismissed on 29 April 2010 (served 31 May 2010) as the courts had applied the law correctly. He ultimately repaid HRK 28,700 from his salary.

The request remained available because first-instance proceedings had ended before 1 December 2003 amendments abolishing it. A 13 June 2003 Supreme Court Civil Division position had held that the 2000 amendments did not apply retroactively to rights already granted; the applicant argued the later rulings contradicted this.

These events—the finality and enforcement of the original judgment, followed by its partial quashing via an extraordinary State remedy and the resulting repayment—form the factual core of the alleged violations of legal certainty and property rights.
001-154148:
The applicants, seven Turkish nationals, are the mother and siblings of Mustafa Döleksoy, a lawyer born in 1952 who was found dead in his unfurnished summer house near Erdemli on 25 August 2007. Neighbours detected a strong odour around 10 a.m.; the caretaker and security guard saw the body through a gap under the locked door and summoned the gendarmerie. A local doctor accompanying officers examined the scene at 10.30 a.m. and attributed death to cerebral haemorrhage and circulatory failure from head trauma after a fall from a kitchen worktop, estimating it had occurred four to five days earlier. The Erdemli prosecutor arrived at 11.40 a.m., noted copious dried blood from the head, advanced decomposition (swollen, blackened corpse), two fractures and cuts on the occipital region, and a clump of hair clutched in the left hand. No firearm or stab wounds were visible. Hair samples (from the hand and the deceased’s head) were sealed; clothes were released as lacking evidential value; a wallet and phone were seized. Because the house was empty and hair was present in the hand, the prosecutor ordered a full autopsy at the Adana Forensic Medicine Institute despite the doctor’s view that the cause was already clear. Crime-scene officers recorded the same head lesions, found no struggle marks, and sketched the scene.

The 25 August 2007 autopsy (report dated 12 November 2007) contradicted the prosecutor: the skull was intact with no fractures; the “cuts” were likely decomposition artefacts. Toxicology (24 September) showed no poisons. Hair analysis (28 September) found the hand sample unresponsive to DNA testing, though stains on the wrapping paper matched the deceased’s own hair. Experts concluded there was no evidence of an external factor and could not determine the precise cause of death owing to decomposition, nor confirm whether the clutched hair belonged to the deceased.

The family repeatedly petitioned the prosecutor from December 2007 onward, citing suspicious circumstances: their son had recently filed for divorce after prolonged, acrimonious proceedings in which his wife refused to cooperate and allegedly threatened to “make him suffer”; she and relatives had previously approached his farmhouse (deterred by dogs later poisoned); a similar unexplained death had befallen the wife’s sister’s husband in 2001, whose autopsy report the deceased had given his parents as a precaution. They requested examination of his law office, mobile-phone records (alleging threatening calls), interviews with neighbours, and fingerprint searches. Further forensic work (report 20 October 2008) established the clutched hair was human, forcibly extracted, and macroscopically similar to the deceased’s, yet still yielded no DNA.

On 4 December 2008 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding no evidence of homicide or other external cause. The first applicant’s objection (deficient inquiries, unexamined phone records and witnesses, unexplained DNA failure) was rejected by the Tarsus Assize Court on 26 March 2009 as adequately reasoned. Subsequent petitions to the Ministry of Justice and a request for the hair samples for private DNA testing produced a further non-prosecution decision (13 October 2009) that released the file but refused the samples; that decision was likewise upheld. All domestic remedies were exhausted by March 2010.

When the European Court of Human Rights communicated the application, it sought clarification of the DNA impasse. The Forensic Medicine Institute’s 17 August 2012 report confirmed that autosomal, gonosomal and mitochondrial DNA could not be extracted from the clutched hair despite the methods employed. The applicants alleged that these investigative shortcomings—contradictory forensic findings, failure to pursue leads concerning marital conflict and possible threats, inadequate scene examination, and unexplained forensic gaps—rendered the inquiry into a potentially unnatural death ineffective, violating the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention.

The applicants (mother and six siblings of Mustafa Döleksoy, a lawyer born in 1952) complained under Article 2 of the Convention that the investigation into his death was ineffective. Döleksoy was found dead on 25 August 2007 in his locked, unfurnished summer house near Erdemli. Neighbours detected a strong smell around 10 a.m. The complex caretaker and security guard observed the body lying on its back through a gap under the door and summoned the gendarmerie.

Gendarmes and a local doctor arrived at 10.30 a.m. A locksmith opened the door. The doctor immediately reported that Döleksoy had died four to five days earlier from cerebral haemorrhage and circulatory failure caused by head trauma after falling from a kitchen worktop. The Erdemli prosecutor arrived at 11.40 a.m. and, assisted by the same doctor, recorded a large quantity of dried blood from the head, advanced decomposition (swollen body, blackened face), two fractures and two cuts in the occipital region, and no firearm or stab wounds. A clump of hair was found in the deceased’s left hand; it and comparison samples from his own scalp were separately sealed. Personal effects (wallet, money, credit cards, mobile phone) were seized, but clothing was returned to the family as having no evidential value. Because the house was empty and hair was clenched in the hand, the prosecutor ordered a full post-mortem at the Adana Forensic Medicine Institute.

Crime-scene officers noted the head lesions, recorded no signs of struggle, and prepared a sketch. The 12 November 2007 autopsy report contradicted the initial findings: the skull was intact with no fractures; the “cuts” were attributed to decomposition. Toxicology showed no poisons. The hair in the hand yielded no DNA profile, though stains on its wrapping paper matched Döleksoy’s own hair. Experts could not determine whether the clutched hair was his and, given the advanced decomposition, could not establish the precise cause of death. They found no medical evidence of an external factor.

From December 2007 the family repeatedly petitioned the prosecutor. They alleged suspicious circumstances, requested examination of Döleksoy’s law office and mobile-phone records, and asked that neighbours be interviewed. They reported that Döleksoy had received threatening calls, was locked in protracted divorce proceedings with his wife (who had allegedly threatened to “make him suffer”), and that the wife and her sister might have been involved; they produced a 2001 post-mortem report of a similar unexplained death of the sister’s husband that Döleksoy had given them for precisely this eventuality. They also queried why the clutched hair had not yielded DNA while his own hair had.

A further 20 October 2008 forensic report confirmed the hair was human, had been pulled from a scalp with force, and was microscopically similar to Döleksoy’s, but still produced no DNA. On 4 December 2008 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, concluding there was no evidence of homicide or any external cause. The family’s objections—citing unexamined witnesses, absence of fingerprint or other forensic searches, unanalysed telephone records, and unexplained DNA results—were rejected by the Tarsus Assize Court (26 March 2009) and the Ministry of Justice (13 May 2009). A later request for the hair samples themselves so that a university laboratory could attempt DNA testing was refused; a second non-prosecution decision followed and was likewise upheld.

After the application was communicated, the Court sought an explanation of the DNA failure. A 17 August 2012 report from the Forensic Medicine Institute reiterated that autosomal, gonosomal and mitochondrial DNA could not be obtained from the clutched hair. These facts form the core of the applicants’ claim that the investigation was neither thorough nor independent and failed to pursue obvious leads.

The case of Sultan Dölek and Others v. Turkey concerns the death of Mustafa Döleksoy (born 1952), a lawyer, whose body was discovered on 25 August 2007 in his locked, unfurnished summer house near Erdemli. Neighbours reported a strong odour; the complex caretaker and security guard observed him lying on the floor and summoned gendarmes and a doctor, who arrived around 10.30 a.m. A locksmith opened the door. The doctor estimated death four to five days earlier from cerebral haemorrhage and circulatory failure caused by head trauma after a fall from the kitchen worktop.

The Erdemli prosecutor examined the scene at 11.40 a.m., noting extensive dried blood from the head, advanced decomposition (swollen body, blackened face), two apparent occipital fractures with overlying cuts, and no firearm or stab wounds. A clump of hair was found in the deceased’s left hand and sealed separately from samples of his own hair. Personal effects (wallet, phone) were seized as evidence, but clothing was returned to the family as lacking evidentiary value. Despite the doctor’s view that a full autopsy was unnecessary, the prosecutor ordered one at the Adana Forensic Medicine Institute because the house was empty and hair was clenched in the hand. Crime-scene officers recorded no signs of struggle.

The November 2007 autopsy report contradicted the initial findings: the skull was intact, the “cuts” likely resulted from decomposition, toxicology was negative, and the hand-held hair yielded no DNA (though stains on its wrapping matched the deceased’s hair). Experts could not determine the exact cause of death owing to decomposition and found no medical evidence of an external factor.

The applicants (the deceased’s mother and six siblings) repeatedly petitioned the prosecutor, alleging suspicious circumstances. They highlighted a contentious divorce, threats from the wife, a similar unexplained death of the wife’s sister’s husband in 2001, and possible phone threats. They requested examination of the law office, mobile-phone records, interviews with neighbours and other witnesses, and further analysis of the hair. A 2008 forensic report confirmed the hair was human, forcibly pulled from a scalp, and microscopically similar to the deceased’s, but again produced no DNA.

On 4 December 2008 the prosecutor closed the investigation, finding no evidence of homicide or other external cause. The first applicant objected, citing unexamined leads, inadequate crime-scene processing, unexplained DNA failure, and failure to hear key witnesses. The Tarsus Assize Court rejected the objection in March 2009; the Ministry of Justice declined to intervene. A later request for the hair samples (to enable private DNA testing) was refused, prompting a further non-prosecution decision upheld on identical grounds. An additional 2012 forensic report, obtained after the application was communicated, reiterated that no autosomal, gonosomal or mitochondrial DNA could be extracted.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ complaint that the investigation into a potentially unnatural death was neither thorough nor effective, contrary to the procedural obligations of Article 2.
001-154149:
The case of Milić and Nikezić v. Montenegro (Applications nos. 54999/10 and 10609/11) concerns allegations by two Montenegrin nationals, Igor Milić (born 1974) and Dalibor Nikezić (born 1981), that they were tortured and ill-treated by prison guards at the Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) in Podgorica on 27 October 2009, while sharing a cell with five other detainees, and that there was no effective official investigation into the events. The first applicant was to be transferred to a disciplinary unit that day, prompting a cell search.

According to the applicants, several guards entered the cell, grabbed the first applicant, threw him onto the concrete corridor floor, handcuffed him, and beat him with batons and fists while swearing at him; two rows of guards then beat him as he was led away. The second applicant protested and was kicked and beaten with fists and batons by four guards inside the cell, then by eight more in the corridor, with the beating continuing after his return to the cell. The Government contended that the applicants resisted the guards’ lawful actions; specifically, the second applicant unprovokedly attacked and injured a guard, prompting necessary intervention.

The first applicant refused examination by the prison doctor that day, stating he was uninjured and had not been ill-treated. The second applicant was examined at the Deputy Ombudsman’s request; the resulting reports were barely legible and inconsistent. An external forensic doctor examined the second applicant on 4 November 2009, finding light injuries including an 8 x 15 cm haematoma on his left thigh (about 10 days old) and haematomas on both lower eyelids, noting also an undated prison report of bruises around his eyes and describing the IECS medical records as largely illegible. The first applicant refused external examination as his bruises were already fading. His mother observed facial bruises and haematomas on 5 November 2009 and reported them; she later lodged a criminal complaint describing fading bruises on his temple and leg plus difficulty sitting. The second applicant’s mother observed closed eyes and extensive bruises after a visit and also lodged a complaint.

The State prosecutor requested investigative actions, including the external examination, video recordings, identification of involved guards, and witness statements. Questioning from 4 November to 9 December 2009 produced mixed accounts: some detainees confirmed seeing both applicants beaten; some guards described resistance by the first applicant (cursing, kicking) and one admitted striking him once with a baton; others claimed the second applicant had grabbed a colleague’s collar, causing a fall, without further blows. A guard later noted a cut under the first applicant’s eye and a leg injury. The first applicant’s lawyer observed a bruise under one eye, a large calf bruise, and a frightened, “mentally broken” client.

On 12 February 2010 the prosecutor rejected complaints against two named guards, finding that limited baton use (three strikes on the first applicant, one on the second) was within their powers to overcome resistance, caused only light injuries, and did not violate human dignity or constitute an offence prosecutable ex officio. Other participating guards were identified. The applicants then lodged a private indictment against 16 guards for torture and severe injuries; this was reclassified as a complaint and ultimately rejected. Subsequent requests for investigation were dismissed by the Court of First Instance and High Court for lack of reasonable suspicion that force exceeded what was needed to overcome resistance. The Constitutional Court rejected a related appeal on procedural grounds.

The Deputy Ombudsman visited the applicants, recorded visible injuries on the second applicant and corroboration from other detainees, and issued an opinion on 29 March 2010 finding that the applicants had offered no resistance and that the force used was unjustified. Disciplinary proceedings followed against three guards, who were fined 20 % of one month’s salary for using excessive, disproportionate force (one baton strike each on the applicants, plus a kick). Four other staff members were transferred. In civil proceedings the applicants sought compensation under Article 3. After remittal, the first-instance court awarded each EUR 1,050 (later increased by the Supreme Court to EUR 1,500) for non-pecuniary damage, finding that the guards had exceeded their powers and degraded human dignity, but that the treatment did not amount to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment and that the applicants had contributed by offering resistance.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ Article 3 complaints regarding both the alleged ill-treatment itself and the alleged inadequacy of the subsequent criminal investigation.

The applicants, Igor Milić and Dalibor Nikezić, were detainees sharing a cell at Montenegro’s Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) on 27 October 2009. That day, Milić was to be moved to a disciplinary unit and the cell searched. Their accounts of what followed differed sharply from the Government’s.

Milić stated that several guards entered the cell, seized him, threw him onto the concrete corridor floor, handcuffed him and beat him with batons and fists while swearing at him. Two further rows of guards then struck him as he was led away. Nikezić said he protested; four guards kicked and beat him with fists and batons inside the cell, after which eight more guards continued the assault in the corridor and back in the cell. The Government maintained that both men resisted lawful orders, that Nikezić unprovokedly attacked and injured a guard, and that the force used was a necessary and proportionate response.

Milić refused examination by the prison doctor, telling him he had no injuries and had not been ill-treated. Nikezić was examined after the Deputy Ombudsman intervened; the resulting reports were barely legible. An external forensic doctor later confirmed Nikezić had a large haematoma on his left thigh and haematomas around both eyes (classified as light injuries). Milić refused the same examination, claiming his bruises were already fading. Both men’s mothers later observed extensive facial and bodily bruising and lodged criminal complaints.

The State prosecutor initiated investigative steps. Witnesses (fellow detainees, some guards, the prison doctor and Milić’s lawyer) gave conflicting evidence: detainees described seeing both men beaten; certain guards admitted limited baton use or claimed Nikezić had initiated violence. On 12 February 2010 the prosecutor rejected complaints against two named guards, holding that the force they used (three baton blows to Milić, one to Nikezić) remained within official powers to overcome resistance and did not constitute a criminal offence. The applicants were told they could pursue a subsidiary prosecution.

They filed an indictment against 16 guards. The first-instance court treated it as a mere criminal complaint; subsequent appeals and a fresh complaint were rejected. A request for investigation was dismissed in 2011 for lack of reasonable suspicion that the force exceeded what was necessary. The Constitutional Court rejected a related appeal on procedural grounds.

The Ombudsman, after visiting the applicants and interviewing cell-mates, concluded on 29 March 2010 that the men had offered no resistance and that the force used was unjustified. Disciplinary proceedings followed against three guards, who were fined 20 % of one month’s salary for excessive force. Civil proceedings later awarded the applicants €1,500 each for non-pecuniary damage; the domestic courts found the guards had exceeded their powers and degraded human dignity but expressly held that the conduct did not amount to torture or inhuman treatment.

The applicants also complained of later threats and of an ineffective investigation, noting family ties between senior prosecutors and the prison governor. These facts form the core of their Article 3 complaints (substantive ill-treatment and procedural failure to investigate).

The ECtHR case of Milić and Nikezić v. Montenegro (applications nos. 54999/10 and 10609/11) involved two Montenegrin detainees, Igor Milić (born 1974) and Dalibor Nikezić (born 1981), who alleged that prison guards at the Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) in Podgorica tortured and ill-treated them on 27 October 2009, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, and that the ensuing official investigation was ineffective.

The applicants shared a cell with five others. On the date in question the first applicant was due to be transferred to a disciplinary unit and the cell was to be searched. The applicants stated that several guards entered, seized the first applicant, threw him onto the concrete corridor floor, handcuffed him and beat him with fists and batons while swearing at him; two further rows of guards then beat him as he was led away. When the second applicant protested, four guards kicked and beat him with fists and batons inside the cell; eight more continued the beating in the corridor and it resumed after he was returned to the cell. The Government maintained that both men resisted lawful orders: the second applicant attacked a guard without provocation, injuring him, and force (including batons) was used only to overcome that resistance.

The first applicant refused examination by the prison doctor, telling him he was uninjured and had not been ill-treated. The second applicant was examined after the Deputy Ombudsman intervened; the doctor’s reports were later described as barely legible. An external forensic doctor examined the second applicant on 4 November 2009 and recorded light injuries (an 8 × 15 cm haematoma on the left thigh and haematomas under both eyes). The first applicant declined a later forensic examination, claiming his bruises were already fading. Both mothers subsequently observed extensive bruising and filed criminal complaints.

The State prosecutor requested an investigation. Witness statements were taken between November and December 2009. Two fellow detainees corroborated the first applicant’s beating; some guards admitted striking him once with a baton because he continued to resist; three detainees confirmed the second applicant was beaten by several guards. On 12 February 2010 the prosecutor rejected complaints against two named guards, finding that the limited force used was within their official powers and did not constitute a criminal offence. The applicants then sought to act as subsidiary prosecutors by lodging an indictment against 16 guards. The courts treated the indictment as a fresh criminal complaint, which the prosecutor again rejected in October 2010. A subsequent request for a formal investigation was dismissed in 2011 for lack of reasonable suspicion that the force used had been unlawful.

The Ombudsman, after visiting the applicants and interviewing witnesses, issued an opinion on 29 March 2010 concluding that the men had offered no resistance and that the force employed was unjustified. Disciplinary proceedings followed: three guards were fined 20 % of one month’s salary for using excessive force. In separate civil proceedings the applicants were ultimately awarded €1 500 each for non-pecuniary damage. Domestic courts accepted that the guards had exceeded their powers and degraded the applicants’ dignity, but held that the conduct did not amount to torture or inhuman treatment; they also found that the applicants’ own resistance had contributed to the harm.

No criminal prosecution of any guard ever took place. Subsequent complaints of threats and further ill-treatment were either rejected or remained pending. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ dual complaints under Article 3.
001-154163:
The case of Ilievska v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 20136/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s allegation of a violation of Article 3 of the Convention due to police brutality during her forced transfer to a psychiatric hospital.

Marina Ilievska, a Macedonian national born in 1976, underwent stomach cancer surgery in April 2009 followed by chemotherapy. On 29 October 2009, while feeling anxious and distressed, her husband sought help from Kriva Palanka hospital (110 km from Skopje). A general practitioner and a neuropsychiatrist (Dr C.T.) instructed her transfer to a Skopje psychiatric clinic with police assistance, without examining her in person.

Around 5 p.m., an ambulance arrived at her village home with officers M.N. and I.A. The applicant claimed the officers forcibly dragged her from the house (ignoring post-surgery pain), handcuffed her hands behind her back, laid her on a bed, and had I.A. sit on her legs. During the high-speed journey she alleged being hit, punched, threatened, and having her hair grabbed and handcuffs tightened. She arrived at Bardovci psychiatric hospital bleeding and bruised, remaining until 31 October.

The hospital’s discharge notice recorded her as malnourished and dehydrated, with several recent haematomas of varying sizes, plus a depressed, anxious, and paranoid state (focused on her cancer and husband). She was discharged untreated at her husband’s request. Subsequent examinations at Kriva Palanka hospital documented haematomas (2x6 cm on both forearms near the wrists; 1x2 cm on lower legs and hip), plus scratches and haematomas on the stomach, back, and legs. One doctor classified these as light bodily injury from hitting and punching. Photographs corroborated the injuries, which the applicant attributed to kicks, blows, and restraints.

Police notes from third parties offered alternative explanations. A doctor who treated her on 27 October described self-inflicted injuries from hitting a wall and bed during a breakdown. A neighbour claimed the applicant’s husband regularly beat her while drunk.

In January–February 2010 the applicant filed criminal charges against Dr C.T. (malpractice), an accompanying nurse, and officers M.N. and I.A. (ill-treatment and mild bodily injury). The public prosecutor obtained a Ministry of Interior internal report containing the officers’, nurse’s, and driver’s denials of force; they described the applicant as aggressive, screaming, using offensive language, and attempting self-harm by hitting her head, requiring them only to hold her hands. The prosecutor rejected the complaint as not warranting state prosecution.

Acting as subsidiary prosecutor, the applicant pursued private charges. At a single hearing the trial court heard the doctor, officers, applicant, and her husband. The officers denied using force, handcuffs, or a truncheon and said they acted professionally after being warned she might have a knife. The husband confirmed helping lift her by the legs but denied mentioning a knife. The court acquitted all defendants for lack of evidence, finding the doctor had acted properly on the husband’s request, the officers had used no force, and the injuries (though recent) were not proven to have occurred during the transfer. The Court of Appeal upheld this, confirming the police had acted lawfully.

The applicant insisted she had never suffered from a mental disorder. These facts formed the basis for her Article 3 complaint regarding both the alleged ill-treatment and the adequacy of the domestic investigation.

The applicant, Marina Ilievska (born 1976), underwent surgery for stomach cancer in April 2009 followed by chemotherapy. On 29 October 2009, while anxious and distressed, her husband sought help from Kriva Palanka hospital. General practitioner Dr M. and neuropsychiatrist Dr C.T. instructed her transfer to a Skopje psychiatric clinic with police assistance.

Around 5 p.m., an ambulance arrived at her home in Uzem village. Police officers M.N. and I.A. assisted in transporting her to Bardovci psychiatric hospital, where she remained until 31 October. The hospital discharge notice recorded her first admission with police aid, based on her husband’s account of post-cancer melancholia, lethargy and suicide threats. She presented malnourished and dehydrated, with several recent haematomas of varying sizes, appearing depressed, anxious and paranoid toward her husband. She was discharged untreated at his request.

The same day she was admitted to Kriva Palanka hospital. Certificates noted 2 x 6 cm haematomas around both wrist joints (consistent with handcuffing), plus smaller haematomas on the lower legs and right hip. Dr M. recorded additional scratches and haematomas on the legs, stomach and back, attributing them to trauma from hitting and punching and classifying them as light bodily injury. The applicant stated that officers had grabbed and dragged her (ignoring post-surgical pain), handcuffed her hands behind her back, that I.A. had sat on her legs, and that she had been hit, punched and threatened en route; hospital staff had also treated her violently. Photographs confirmed scratches on the back and stomach plus lower-leg haematomas.

Police inquiries produced conflicting accounts. Dr S.V. reported that on 27 October the applicant had self-injured by striking her head and body against a wall and bed, suggesting the visible injuries predated the transfer. Neighbour L.S. claimed the applicant’s husband regularly beat her while intoxicated. Officers denied using force, stating the applicant was aggressive, screamed, used offensive language and tried to harm herself by hitting her head against the ambulance window, requiring them to restrain her. The nurse and driver corroborated this. The applicant’s husband gave mixed statements: he had helped officers carry her (taking her legs to avoid injury) and that M.N. had handcuffed her, but later denied some details.

In January–February 2010 the applicant filed criminal charges of medical malpractice against Dr C.T. and of ill-treatment and mild bodily injury against the officers and nurse. The public prosecutor rejected the complaint after an internal-control report. Acting as subsidiary prosecutor, she pursued the case. At a single hearing on 6 October 2010 the trial court heard the parties and acquitted the accused for lack of evidence, finding Dr C.T. had acted properly and the officers had used no force. It accepted medical evidence of recent injuries but held they could not be linked to the transfer. The Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal on 15 December 2010; a further prosecutorial review was refused.

The applicant maintained she had never suffered from mental disorder and that her injuries resulted solely from police brutality during the transfer, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant, a Macedonian national born in 1976, alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention arising from police brutality during her transfer on 29 October 2009 from her home in the village of Uzem (near Kriva Palanka) to Bardovci psychiatric hospital in Skopje. She had undergone surgery for stomach cancer in April 2009 followed by chemotherapy. That afternoon, while anxious and distressed, her husband requested assistance from Kriva Palanka hospital (approximately 110 km from Skopje). A general practitioner (Dr M.) and a neuropsychiatry specialist (Dr C.T.) instructed that she be transferred to a Skopje psychiatric clinic with police assistance.

An ambulance arrived at around 5 p.m., accompanied by two officers (later identified as M.N. and I.A.). The applicant claimed the officers forcibly removed her by grabbing her arms and dragging her (while she was on her knees and crying out in pain from recent surgery), ignoring her protests. They placed her in the ambulance, forced her to lie down with her hands handcuffed behind her back, and one officer (I.A.) sat on her legs. En route, the officers allegedly hit and punched her (including on the legs and head with a truncheon), grabbed her hair, tightened the handcuffs, held her mouth closed, and threatened her. The ambulance first stopped at Kriva Palanka hospital (where a nurse allegedly received telephone instructions from Dr C.T. to administer a tranquilliser, which the applicant denied receiving). She was then taken to Bardovci hospital, where she remained until 31 October 2009.

Bardovci's 2 November 2009 discharge notice recorded her first admission there (with Kriva Palanka police assistance). Limited information from her husband indicated that, following her cancer diagnosis, she had become melancholic, lethargic, and suicidal. On admission she was malnourished and dehydrated, with several haematomas of different sizes, most probably of recent date. She was depressed, anxious, tearful, fixated on her cancer, burdened by depressive ideas, and paranoid toward her husband. She was discharged untreated at her husband's request.

The same day she was admitted to Kriva Palanka hospital. A medical certificate noted haematomas measuring 2 x 6 cm on both forearms around the wrists, three haematomas of 1 x 2 cm on both lower legs, and one of 1 x 2 cm on the right hip; the applicant attributed these to kicks and blows while handcuffed. Dr M. examined her and recorded additional injuries: haematomas and 4–5 scratches (1 x 2 cm or 2 x 2 cm) on the lower legs, haematomas and two scratches (3 x 1 cm) on the stomach, and five scratches (5 x 6 cm) on the back, plus small haematomas. These were assessed as light bodily injuries from trauma (hitting and punching). The applicant also claimed violent treatment by hospital staff on arrival. Photographs showed five scratches on her back, two scratches and a haematoma on her stomach, and haematomas on her lower legs.

Police later obtained statements suggesting alternative causes for the injuries. Dr S.V. (who had attended the applicant on 27 October after she reportedly hit her body and head against a wall and bed, leaving her face bloody) opined that the injuries shown in a subsequent television interview were likely self-inflicted then. A neighbour (L.S.) claimed the applicant's husband had beaten her on multiple nights and that the injuries were inflicted by him while intoxicated.

The applicant lodged criminal charges in January–February 2010 against Dr C.T. (for malpractice, alleging he ordered transfer without examining her), a nurse (V.S., who sat in the front of the ambulance), and officers M.N. and I.A. (for ill-treatment and mild bodily injury). She attached the medical records. The public prosecutor obtained a Ministry of Interior "special report" containing further statements: the husband confirmed the officers grabbed her arms and dragged her while he held her legs to avoid harm, after which they handcuffed her and I.A. sat on her legs; the applicant added that M.N. struck her with a baton before she entered the ambulance and that officers punched her and tightened the cuffs during the journey (driven at excessive speed). Officers, the nurse, and the driver denied using force, claiming the applicant was aggressive, used offensive language, screamed, and tried to harm herself (hitting her head against the window), requiring them to restrain her hands. They also claimed a warning that she had a knife. The prosecutor rejected the complaint as not subject to State prosecution. The applicant proceeded as a subsidiary prosecutor.

At a single hearing on 6 October 2010, the trial court heard Dr C.T., the officers, the applicant (unrepresented), and her husband. Officers denied force or handcuffs, stating they took her arms (husband took her legs) after she refused to enter the ambulance and held her down with their hands; a tranquilliser was administered. The husband largely corroborated the applicant's account of dragging and handcuffing. The court acquitted all accused for lack of evidence, finding Dr C.T. acted properly on the husband's request and officers acted professionally without using force or inflicting injury. It accepted that recent haematomas and scratches existed (as documented medically and photographically) but held they were not proven to have been inflicted during the transfer. The Court of Appeal upheld this on 15 December 2010. The applicant maintained she had never suffered from any mental disorder.

The case of S.L. and J.L. v. Croatia (Application no. 13712/11) concerns two Croatian sisters (born 1987 and 1992) who alleged a violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. In June 1997 their mother V.L., acting as their representative, agreed to purchase a rundown villa of 87 m² plus a 624 m² courtyard in a seaside area of P. The purchase was formalised that December for HRK 450 000; the sisters were registered as equal owners in November 1999.

In 2000 V.L. sought the Social Welfare Centre’s mandatory consent to sell the property. She and her husband Z.L. (father of the younger sister) told the Centre they had already spent substantial sums on renovation, lacked funds for further work, intended to live with relatives, and would deposit the proceeds in accounts for the children. In February 2001 Z.L. was arrested, later convicted of attempted murder and sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. His defence lawyer was M.I.

In October 2001 M.I. applied to the Centre for approval of a swap: the sisters would transfer the house to D.M. (M.I.’s mother-in-law) in exchange for D.M.’s 78 m² fourth-floor flat and garage. The draft stipulated that the properties were of equal value and waived any claim for lesio enormis. A supplement recorded that D.M. would reimburse the parents for renovation costs. At interview V.L. explained that Z.L.’s imprisonment had forced her to close the family business; she was unemployed, had borrowed money for household bills, and the children’s school performance had declined. She estimated the value difference at DEM 100 000 and promised to register the flat in the sisters’ names. The Centre authorised both the swap and a payment of DEM 5 000 to each sister, concluding that the transaction would not harm their interests because they would obtain suitable accommodation. The swap was executed on 16 December 2001 and registered; the declared value was HRK 400 000.

In November 2004 the sisters, now represented by Z.L., sued D.M. to have the contract declared null and void. They contended that the house (by then recorded as 225 m² plus courtyard) was worth approximately EUR 300 000, while the flat and garage were worth no more than EUR 70 000; that they had been only 14 and 9 years old; that no statutory ground for disposing of a minor’s property existed; and that the Centre had neither inspected the properties nor obtained an independent valuation. They also noted M.I.’s conflict of interest and V.L.’s later-documented drug-abuse problems. The Municipal Court refused all proposed evidence, holding that it could not review a final administrative authorisation. The County Court, Supreme Court and Constitutional Court upheld that approach, finding no failure to protect the children’s best interests.

Subsequent official reports confirmed that the Centre had been unaware of V.L.’s addiction (treatment began only in 2003) and of M.I.’s family link to D.M. The house remains registered in D.M.’s name. These facts form the core of the applicants’ complaint that the State, through the Centre’s perfunctory authorisation and the courts’ refusal to examine the transaction’s substance, failed to safeguard their property as minors.

The applicants, sisters S.L. (born 1987) and J.L. (born 1992), alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from an unfavourable real-estate swap of property they owned as minors. In 1997 their mother V.L. arranged the purchase of a dilapidated seaside villa (87 m² plus 624 m² courtyard) in P. for HRK 450 000; the girls were registered as equal owners in 1999. Under Croatian family law a parent may dispose of a child’s property only with Social Welfare Centre authorisation and only for the child’s maintenance, education or similarly urgent needs.

In April 2000 V.L. and the girls’ father Z.L. told the Centre they had already spent DEM 80 000 on renovation, lacked further funds and intended to sell the house and live with relatives, depositing the proceeds in the children’s accounts. In February 2001 Z.L. was arrested and later sentenced to six years’ imprisonment for attempted murder. His defence lawyer M.I. then applied to the Centre (October 2001) for approval of a swap with D.M.—M.I.’s mother-in-law—exchanging the villa for D.M.’s fourth-floor 78 m² flat and garage. The draft contract declared the properties of equal value (later set at HRK 400 000) and waived any claim of lesion beyond moiety; a supplement provided only DEM 5 000 to each child as “compensation for investments.”

V.L., now unemployed after the family business collapsed, told the Centre that the swap would also bring a further DEM 100 000 difference. On 13 November 2001 the Centre authorised both the swap and the modest cash supplement, finding that the children would receive “fully suitable living accommodation” and that their property rights would not be reduced. No site visit, independent valuation or inquiry into M.I.’s conflict of interest occurred. The notarial contract was signed on 16 December 2001 and title transferred. Subsequent land-register data showed the villa actually measured 225 m² plus a 476 m² courtyard.

In 2004 the applicants (then still minors, represented by Z.L.) sued D.M. to have the swap declared null and void. They argued that the villa, five minutes from the sea, was worth approximately EUR 300 000 while the flat and garage were worth at most EUR 70 000; that none of the statutory grounds for disposing of a child’s property existed; and that the Centre had failed to protect their interests. The Municipal Court refused all proposed evidence (including expert valuation and witness testimony) and dismissed the action on the sole ground that it could not review a final administrative authorisation. Appeals to the County Court, Supreme Court and Constitutional Court were rejected on the same formal basis.

Later official reports confirmed that the Centre had been unaware both of V.L.’s drug addiction (treatment began only in 2003) and of M.I.’s family relationship with the counter-party. The applicants therefore contended that the State, through the Centre’s uncritical authorisation and the courts’ subsequent refusal to examine the substance of the transaction, had failed to safeguard the property rights of two minors.

**Case of S.L. and J.L. v. Croatia (ECtHR, Application no. 13712/11, Judgment of 7 May 2015)**

The applicants, Croatian sisters S.L. (born 1987) and J.L. (born 1992), alleged a violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Represented by their mother V.L., they purchased a seaside villa (initially described as 87 m² with a 624 m² courtyard) in P. in 1997 for 450,000 HRK. They registered equal ownership shares in 1999. The property later proved larger (225 m² house plus 476 m² courtyard).

In 2000, V.L. sought Social Welfare Centre authorisation (required under Family Act s. 265 for disposing of a minor’s property, limited to the child’s maintenance, treatment, upbringing, education or other important needs). Parents stated they had invested ~80,000 DEM in renovations but lacked funds for more work, owned a retail business, and planned to sell and live with relatives while depositing proceeds in the children’s accounts. Children were doing well at school.

In February 2001 the second applicant’s father Z.L. was arrested, later convicted of attempted murder and unlawful firearms possession and sentenced to six years. His defence lawyer was M.I. In October 2001 M.I. (whose mother-in-law was D.M.) applied for Centre approval of a swap: the applicants’ house for D.M.’s 78.27 m² fourth-floor flat plus garage. Draft terms asserted equal values, waived claims of lesion, and provided for D.M. to reimburse documented renovation costs (later fixed at 5,000 DEM per applicant). V.L. told the Centre that Z.L.’s imprisonment had closed the family business, she was unemployed, bills required borrowing, and the children were struggling at school; she estimated a 100,000 DEM value difference. The Centre authorised the swap and the 5,000 DEM payments on 13 November 2001, concluding they served the children’s best interests because they would receive suitable accommodation. No site inspection or independent valuation occurred. The Centre was unaware of V.L.’s drug-abuse history (treatment began in 2003) or M.I.’s conflict of interest.

The swap was executed on 16 December 2001 before a notary. Parties declared the properties equally valued at ~400,000 HRK with no further claims. Ownership was registered. Each applicant paid 10,000 HRK transfer tax.

In 2004 the applicants (then still minors, represented by Z.L.) sued D.M. in the P. Municipal Court to have the swap declared null and void as unlawful and contrary to public morals. They contended the house (comprising two flats, five minutes from the sea) was worth ~€300,000 while the flat and garage were worth at most €70,000; they had been 14 and 9 years old; Family Act s. 265 conditions were unmet; and the Centre had failed to inspect or obtain an expert valuation. They sought witness evidence and an expert report.

The Municipal Court (2005) dismissed the claim without taking evidence, holding it could not review the Centre’s final administrative decision and that the contract was at most voidable (a claim not pleaded). The County Court (2007), Supreme Court (2007) and Constitutional Court (2010, declaring the complaint manifestly ill-founded) upheld this approach, finding the Centre had adequately protected the children’s interests.

The applicants argued that the State, through the Centre and the courts, had failed to safeguard the property of minors, permitting an unconscionable exchange that extinguished valuable real-estate rights without proper assessment of best interests or market values.

The case of Aleksandr Dmitriyev v. Russia (no. 12993/05) was brought by a Russian national (born 1980) alleging violations of the Convention arising from poor detention conditions and unreasonably prolonged pre-trial detention.

The applicant was arrested on 20 April 2003 on suspicion of inflicting injuries causing death. On 22 April 2003 the Kozelskiy District Court authorised continued detention, citing the gravity of the charges and a prior theft conviction, and finding a risk of obstruction or further offending; this was upheld on 7 May 2003. Detention was extended on 18 June 2003 on similar grounds (plus unemployment and a “serious case”). He was released on 22 July 2003 subject to an undertaking not to leave his residence.

On 19 May 2004 he was convicted and sentenced to 10½ years’ imprisonment and immediately remanded (prior detention credited). On 20 July 2004 the Regional Court quashed the conviction, ordered a retrial and directed that he remain in custody, citing neither legal basis nor time-limit. The case was remitted to the prosecutor on 8 October 2004, 9 December 2004 and 20 January 2005 for indictment defects; on each occasion the District Court ordered continued detention without legal grounds (or, in one instance, merely citing charge gravity). On 20 January 2005 detention was extended to 20 April 2005 solely because trial was pending.

After a (later-withdrawn) guilty plea, he was reconvicted on 7 April 2005. On 10 June 2005 that judgment was quashed for admission of uncounselled statements; a retrial was ordered and custody continued without reasons, extended to 1 August 2005. A July 2005 release application was refused on 25 July (gravity and prior conviction), with detention extended to 1 November 2005; the appeal, which stressed the applicant’s earlier compliant release, was dismissed on 2 September 2005. He was released on 26 October 2005 under an undertaking.

He was convicted again on 20 December 2005 (seven years) and remanded; the conviction became final on 21 February 2006. In November 2008 a court ordered compulsory psychiatric treatment.

The conditions complaint concerned a temporary stay in Kazan’s IZ-16/1 (15 August–24 September and 22–24 October 2008) while serving sentence, for psychiatric assessment. The applicant alleged overcrowding, absence of an individual bed (except two weeks) and shift-sleeping with two or three others, leaving insufficient rest. The Government stated he occupied four cells (12.4–20.98 m², three to five bunks) whose occupancy never exceeded capacity (registers showed two to five inmates), that he always had his own bunk and linen, and that temperature (+20 °C), ventilation, natural light and partitioned toilets were adequate. They produced governor certificates, later inmate statements and daily population extracts.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 (conditions) and Article 5 (length and reasoning of detention) violations.

The case of Aleksandr Dmitriyev v. Russia (Application no. 12993/05) concerns a Russian national born in 1980 who alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from unreasonably prolonged pre-trial detention and inadequate conditions of detention.

Dmitriyev was arrested on 20 April 2003 on suspicion of inflicting bodily injuries that caused death. On 22 April 2003 the Kozelskiy District Court authorised his continued detention, citing the gravity of the charges and his prior theft conviction, and finding a risk that he would obstruct proceedings or reoffend if released. The Kaluga Regional Court upheld this on 7 May 2003. Detention was extended on 18 June 2003 on similar grounds, including unemployment and the strength of the prosecution case; he did not appeal. He was released on 22 July 2003 under an undertaking not to leave his residence after investigative measures concluded.

Following his conviction on 19 May 2004 and sentence of ten years and six months (with the earlier detention credited), he was immediately re-detained. On 20 July 2004 the Regional Court quashed the conviction and ordered a retrial, directing that he remain in custody without citing any legal basis or setting a time-limit. On 8 October, 9 December 2004 and 20 January 2005 the District Court returned the case to the prosecutor owing to indictment deficiencies, each time ordering continued detention. The first and third of these decisions gave no reasons; the second referred only to charge gravity. An extension to 20 April 2005 mentioned solely that the trial was pending.

After a further conviction on 7 April 2005, the Regional Court on 10 June 2005 again quashed the judgment (because certain statements had been taken without counsel) and ordered a retrial, extending detention to 1 August 2005 without reasons. On 25 July 2005 the District Court refused release, citing charge gravity and the prior conviction, and prolonged detention to 1 November 2005; the Regional Court upheld this despite the applicant’s argument that he had previously complied with a residence undertaking. He was released on 26 October 2005 under a fresh undertaking. He was convicted a third time on 20 December 2005 and sentenced to seven years; the conviction became final on 21 February 2006.

A separate complaint concerned conditions in remand facility IZ-16/1 in Kazan. The applicant initially stated he was held there from 15 July to 24 September 2008 (later corrected to 15 August–24 October 2008) and that, except for two weeks, he had no individual bunk and slept in shifts with two or three others, resulting in insufficient rest. The Government stated he was transferred there only for a psychiatric assessment and occupied four cells (nos. 5, 6, 11 and 46) of 12.4–21 m² containing three to five bunks. Official registers, a governor’s certificate and later inmate statements showed occupancy never exceeded the number of bunks, that he always had his own bed and linen, and that cells had adequate temperature, ventilation, natural light and partitioned toilets. He was held in a psychiatric hospital between the two short periods of detention in IZ-16/1.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that successive detention orders after July 2004 lacked adequate reasoning and time-limits, rendering the overall period of pre-trial custody excessive, and that the Kazan facility was overcrowded and unsanitary.

The case of Aleksandr Dmitriyev v. Russia (Application no. 12993/05) originated from a complaint lodged on 18 February 2005 by a Russian national born in 1980. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been subjected to poor conditions of detention and that his pre-trial detention had been unreasonably lengthy.

The applicant was arrested on 20 April 2003 on suspicion of involvement in inflicting bodily injuries that led to death. On 22 April 2003 the Kozelskiy District Court authorised his continued detention, citing the gravity of the charges and his prior conviction for theft, and finding that he might otherwise obstruct the proceedings or reoffend. This decision was upheld on appeal. Detention was extended on 18 June 2003 on similar grounds (gravity of the charges, criminal record, unemployment and risk of reoffending or obstruction). The applicant was released on 22 July 2003 under an undertaking not to leave his place of residence after certain investigative steps had been completed.

On 19 May 2004 the district court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to ten years and six months’ imprisonment; he was taken into custody immediately. On 20 July 2004 the Kaluga Regional Court quashed the conviction and ordered a retrial, directing that the applicant remain in custody without citing any legal basis or time-limit. The case was repeatedly returned to the prosecutor on 8 October 2004, 9 December 2004 and 20 January 2005 because of deficiencies in the indictment. On each occasion the district court ordered that the applicant stay in custody, frequently without giving reasons or legal grounds (one decision referred only to the gravity of the charges). Detention was extended until 20 April 2005 solely because the trial was pending.

The applicant was convicted again on 7 April 2005. On 10 June 2005 the regional court quashed that judgment on the ground that certain testimonies had been taken without counsel, ordered a further retrial and, again without reasons, directed that the applicant remain in custody until 1 August 2005. A request for release was refused on 25 July 2005 by reference to the gravity of the charges and the prior conviction; detention was extended until 1 November 2005 and the refusal was upheld on appeal. The applicant was released on 26 October 2005 under a residence restriction. He was reconvicted on 20 December 2005 and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment; that judgment became final on 21 February 2006.

While serving his sentence the applicant was transferred to remand facility IZ-16/1 in Kazan for a psychiatric assessment, first from 15 August to 24 September 2008 and again from 22 to 24 October 2008. He alleged that, except for two weeks, he had had no individual sleeping place and had been forced to sleep in shifts with two or three other inmates, leaving him insufficient rest. The Government produced cell measurements (12.4–20.98 m² with three to five sleeping places), occupancy extracts, certificates and later inmate statements showing that the number of detainees never exceeded the number of beds, that the applicant always had his own sleeping place and bedding, and that the cells had ventilation, natural light, a temperature of around 20 °C and partitioned toilets.

001-154400:
The case concerns a 17 May 2012 peaceful march in Tbilisi organised by Identoba (an LGBT-rights NGO) and 14 individual participants to mark the International Day Against Homophobia. Organisers notified the City Hall and Interior Ministry eight days in advance of the route and expected turnout and, citing known hostility toward sexual minorities, expressly requested police protection. Authorities acknowledged the notice and confirmed that officers would be deployed.

Approximately 30 marchers assembled near Tbilisi Concert Hall carrying rainbow flags and banners such as “Love is love.” A police patrol was initially present. Counter-demonstrators from two Orthodox groups (numbering 100 or more) soon blocked the route, formed a human chain, and encircled the marchers. They subjected the group to homophobic insults (“fagots,” “sinners,” “perverts,” “sick”) and threats of burning or crushing. Police vehicles then withdrew. Officers who remained on the scene refused to intervene, stating it was not their duty.

The confrontation escalated: banners were seized and torn, and marchers in the front line were punched and kicked. The sixth applicant was knocked to the ground, beaten and kicked until a later-arriving officer pulled him away. Three other applicants were briefly detained by police (the Government later claimed this was for their own protection and to prevent a traffic offence). Medical examinations confirmed injuries: closed-head trauma and chest bruises (sixth applicant), a haematoma, grazes and a bruised knee (third applicant), and a wrist contusion (fourteenth applicant). Television footage broadcast the same evening clearly showed the victims and assailants.

On 18 May Identoba and the individual applicants lodged complaints with the Interior Ministry and Chief Prosecutor, describing the discriminatory violence and police inaction and invoking Article 53 of the Criminal Code (which treats bias based on sexual orientation as an aggravating circumstance). An investigation into light bodily harm to the fourteenth applicant was opened the next day; a similar inquiry into the sixth applicant’s beating began only on 24 October. Neither victim was granted formal victim status. Two counter-demonstrators received modest administrative fines (approximately €45 each) for a minor public-order breach; no criminal charges were brought and the homophobic motive was never examined. Police conduct was deemed lawful, so no inquiry into official inaction was opened. Both criminal files remained pending years later, with no identifications or prosecutions.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints under Articles 3, 10, 11 and 14 of the Convention: that the State failed to protect a peaceful assembly from foreseeable, hate-motivated violence and thereafter failed to conduct an effective investigation capable of identifying and punishing the perpetrators while treating the discriminatory motive as an aggravating factor.

The case of Identoba and Others v. Georgia (ECtHR, Application no. 73235/12) arose from events on 17 May 2012, when Identoba, a Georgian NGO promoting LGBT rights, organised a small peaceful march in Tbilisi to mark the International Day Against Homophobia. The first applicant (Identoba) and 14 individual Georgian applicants alleged that counter-demonstrators subjected them to homophobic violence and that the authorities failed to provide effective protection or investigation, in violation of Articles 3, 10, 11 and 14 of the Convention.

On 8 May 2012 Identoba notified Tbilisi City Hall and the Ministry of the Interior of the planned route (from the Tbilisi Concert Hall to Orbeliani Square) and the expected number of participants (around 30). It specifically requested police protection in light of known hostility toward sexual minorities. The City Hall acknowledged the notice and set out demonstrators’ legal rights and duties. On 15 May a senior Interior Ministry officer confirmed that police would be deployed to keep the event peaceful.

On the day, the LGBT marchers (including 13 of the individual applicants) gathered at about 1 p.m. carrying rainbow flags and banners with slogans such as “Love is love.” A police patrol was initially present. Members of two Orthodox religious groups arrived and began arguing that the event promoted “perversion” contrary to Georgian traditions. As the marchers reached Rustaveli Avenue they were encircled by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators who blocked their path, formed a human chain and subjected them to threats of physical assault together with slurs such as “sick,” “immoral,” “perverts,” “fagots” and “sinners.” The escorting police vehicles then withdrew. When the marchers telephoned for reinforcements and approached other officers present, those officers stated it was not their duty to intervene.

After 20–30 minutes the counter-demonstrators tore up banners and launched a physical attack, pushing and punching those in the front row. The sixth applicant was knocked down, beaten and kicked. Additional police cars eventually arrived; officers stopped the beating of the sixth applicant and stood between the two groups while the counter-demonstrators continued to shout that the marchers “should be burnt to death.” Several applicants were briefly placed in police cars and driven around the city (the third, sixth, seventh and tenth applicants); the Government later said this was both to protect them and to prevent an alleged traffic obstruction. Three applicants later received medical treatment for documented injuries (bruises, a closed-head trauma, a haematoma and a wrist contusion). The entire incident was filmed by journalists and broadcast nationally, making the participants recognisable.

The following day Identoba and the individual applicants lodged complaints with the Interior Ministry and the Chief Prosecutor, describing the discriminatory violence and the police’s failure to intervene. Only two criminal investigations were opened—both limited to “light bodily harm” inflicted by unidentified persons on the sixth and fourteenth applicants—and those files remained pending years later. The two applicants were never granted victim status. Two counter-demonstrators received modest administrative fines for a minor public-order breach. No investigation examined police conduct, nor was the recently enacted aggravating circumstance of homophobic motive (Criminal Code Article 53) applied. The authorities maintained that the police had merely called on both sides to remain peaceful.

These facts—the advance request for protection, the foreseeable hostility, the police withdrawal and delayed intervention, the homophobic insults and physical assaults, the brief detentions of several marchers, the documented injuries and the subsequent failure to investigate the bias motive—form the core of the applicants’ complaints under the Convention.

**Identoba and Others v. Georgia (ECtHR, Application no. 73235/12, Judgment of 12 May 2015)**

The case was brought by Identoba, a Georgian NGO established in 2010 to promote LGBT rights, and 14 individual Georgian applicants (mostly Identoba staff and LGBT activists). They alleged that violence by private counter-demonstrators, combined with inadequate police protection and ineffective subsequent investigations, during a peaceful 17 May 2012 demonstration in Tbilisi marking the International Day Against Homophobia, violated Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 10 (freedom of expression), 11 (freedom of assembly), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Identoba notified Tbilisi City Hall and the Ministry of the Interior on 8 May 2012 of the planned march from the Tbilisi Concert Hall grounds to Orbeliani Square, providing the route and expected numbers. Citing foreseeable hostility toward sexual minorities in Georgia, it specifically requested adequate police protection. The City Hall acknowledged the notice on 14 May. On 15 May a senior Interior Ministry officer confirmed that police would be deployed to ensure a peaceful event.

On 17 May around 1 p.m., approximately 30 LGBT marchers (including the 13 individual applicants besides Identoba itself) gathered holding banners such as “I am gay,” “Love is love,” rainbow flags and umbrellas. A police patrol was present as agreed. Members of two religious groups (the Orthodox Parents’ Union and Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali’s Brotherhood) arrived, along with journalists. After initial verbal confrontations about 200 metres from the start, the marchers reached Rustaveli Avenue, where more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators blocked their path, formed a human chain, encircled them, issued threats of physical assault, and hurled insults including “sick,” “immoral,” “perverts,” “fagots” and “sinners.” The escorting police patrol cars then withdrew. Marchers called for reinforcements; some officers present refused to intervene, stating it was not their duty.

After 20–30 minutes the counter-demonstrators tore banners and physically attacked the front row, knocking down, beating and kicking the sixth applicant (G. Demetrashvili). Additional police arrived, stopped the beating of that applicant and stood between the groups, but threats of burning the marchers to death or crushing them continued. Police then detained the third applicant (L. Berianidze) for about 20 minutes (later explained by the Government as protective distancing) and briefly drove the sixth, seventh and tenth applicants around the city (explained as preventing a traffic offence and providing protection). The third applicant later received medical treatment for a bruised knee, grazes, a haemorrhagic forearm and a haematoma; the sixth applicant for closed head trauma, cerebral contusions and chest bruises; and the fourteenth applicant (M. Tsutskiridze) two days later for a left-wrist contusion. The events were filmed and broadcast nationally, with faces clearly visible.

On 18 May Identoba board members filed complaints with the Interior Ministry and Chief Public Prosecutor about the violence. An investigation into light bodily harm to the fourteenth applicant by unidentified persons opened on 19 May; she was not granted victim status.
