The case of Mukhitdinov v. Russia (Application no. 20999/14) concerns an Uzbek national (also known as Sattarov after acquiring and later losing Russian citizenship) who alleged that his extradition from Russia to Uzbekistan would expose him to a real risk of torture or ill-treatment, in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He further complained that a period of his detention pending extradition was unlawful under Article 5 and that domestic courts ignored his arguments on this point. The European Court of Human Rights indicated interim measures under Rule 39, prohibiting his removal and requiring protective measures against irregular transfer; these were allegedly disregarded when he disappeared.

The applicant, born in 1967 in the Uzbek SSR, left Uzbekistan in 1992 for Saudi Arabia and settled in Russia in 1997. He obtained Russian nationality in 2001 (later cancelled in 2013 as fraudulently acquired) and was deemed to have forfeited Uzbek nationality due to prolonged absence. In 1998 Uzbekistan charged him with illegal border crossing. In December 2009 additional charges were added under Articles 159 and 242 of the Uzbek Criminal Code for alleged membership in the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan (a designated extremist/terrorist group), meetings with its members in Saudi Arabia, and dissemination of its ideas. An arrest warrant followed.

Russian authorities arrested him on 30 June 2013 in Tyumen. Detention was ordered and extended (initially to 30 July, then 30 December 2013). On 11 December 2013 the Prosecutor General authorised extradition solely on the extremist-organisation charge, citing Uzbek diplomatic assurances against torture or ill-treatment. Domestic courts (Tyumen Regional Court on 21 January 2014 and Supreme Court on 19 March 2014) upheld the order, dismissing the applicant’s claims of a real risk of torture or political persecution as unsubstantiated or unconvincing. They relied on the assurances, the absence of contrary information from Russian ministries, and the lack of a Russian procedural finding that the charges were politically motivated.

A further detention extension to 30 March 2014 was granted on 26 December 2013 but later quashed for lack of reasoning; a replacement order of 21 February 2014 was itself quashed on 11 March 2014. The Regional Court held that, under Article 109 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, detention for a medium-gravity offence could not exceed the initial six-month limit, and the applicant was released.

On 17 March 2014 the Court indicated that Russia must not extradite or otherwise remove the applicant to Uzbekistan (or any third country) and must implement an effective protective mechanism, especially after release, against unlawful transfer. Priority was granted to the application.

On 22 July 2014, seven uniformed Federal Migration Service officers took the applicant from his home. His lawyer was prevented from following them by traffic police. Officials later told his family he had been released after an identification check during a routine anti-illegal-migration operation. Prosecutors confirmed he was brought in, identified and released; they stated there was no subsequent arrest and no information on his whereabouts. A criminal investigation into his disappearance was opened on 25 August 2014. The Government maintained that State agents had neither detained him further nor transferred him across the border.

The alleged Article 3 risk rested on the nature of the charges (religious extremism), consistent NGO reports of systematic torture in Uzbekistan of persons accused of such offences, and a pattern of similar renditions from Russia. The detention complaint focused on the period after the statutory six-month limit. The disappearance, occurring despite the interim measure, raised additional issues of possible State involvement in an irregular transfer, non-cooperation with the Court, and frustration of the right of individual petition.

The case of Tychko v. Russia (no. 56097/07) was brought by Viktor Vladimirovich Tychko, a Russian national born in 1965 and resident in Volgograd. He alleged violations arising from the conditions of his detention, transport and holding at court, the excessive duration of criminal proceedings against him, and the absence of effective domestic remedies.

Criminal proceedings for large-scale fraud began on 15 August 2001. Tychko was arrested and remanded in custody on 28 September 2001. Charges followed on 2 October 2001 and 22 July 2002; the file reached the Tsentralniy District Court of Volgograd on 7 August 2002. The first hearing took place on 8 October 2002 under Judge A. Tychko was released on 26 November 2002. On 30 December 2002 the case was reassigned to Judge G. and, under the rule of immutability of the court’s composition, the trial began afresh. Between March–June 2003 and June 2004–January 2005 the court adjourned seven times (five because of absences of the accused, counsel or witnesses; two at Tychko’s request to study the file). In a separate case opened on 19 January 2003 for unlawful possession of firearms and narcotics, Tychko was again remanded on 20 January 2003 and convicted on 19 June 2003 to eight years’ imprisonment.

Judge G. took maternity leave in March 2005; the file passed to Judge S. on 26 April 2005 and the trial restarted. Two further adjournments occurred in 2005 for non-attendance. Judge S. resigned in December 2005; Judge M. received the case on 14 February 2006 and again restarted the trial. Three more adjournments followed in 2006. Judge M. resigned in July 2006; Judge Mar. took over and the trial restarted for a fourth time. Five additional adjournments took place between November 2006 and June 2008. On 6 August 2008 the District Court convicted Tychko of complicity in large-scale fraud and imposed three years and six months’ imprisonment; the sentences were aggregated to nine years. The Volgograd Regional Court upheld the judgment on 1 December 2009. The proceedings thus spanned more than eight years, with repeated restarts caused by successive judicial reassignments and numerous delays attributable to non-attendance.

Tychko spent lengthy periods (October 2001–November 2002, January–August 2003, September 2003–May 2005, July 2005–April 2008 and May–September 2008) in Volgograd remand prison IZ-34/1. He described severe overcrowding and insanitary conditions. The cell he occupied most recently measured approximately 30 m², contained 18 bunks and routinely held 20–30 inmates, so that prisoners slept in shifts. The toilet consisted of an unflushed hole in the floor, raised 0.4 m and screened by a 0.6 m partition that afforded no privacy; a tap above it served as the only wash-stand. A dining table seated ten inmates one metre from the toilet; the remainder ate on the concrete floor. Food was of poor quality and drinking-water tanks stood on the floor. The cell was lit continuously by two 100-watt bulbs, poorly ventilated and filled with the stench of tobacco, laundry and the toilet. It was infested with insects and rodents. Prisoners received a five-minute shower once a week; exercise yards were small and unequipped. Tychko contracted tuberculosis twice and suffered deteriorating eyesight. Domestic complaints produced no redress.

He was transported between the prison and the courthouse more than one hundred times in a windowless metal van comprising three compartments (two for twenty prisoners each, one for a single occupant). The vehicle lacked natural or artificial light, ventilation, seat-belts or other safety features and was stiflingly hot in summer and freezing in winter. At the courthouse he was held for seven or eight hours in cells of about 3 m² that contained five or six inmates, only one bench seating three persons, and mixed prisoners suffering from hepatitis, tuberculosis, HIV and other diseases.

These facts underpin the complaints concerning inhuman and degrading treatment, the right to a trial within a reasonable time, and the lack of an effective remedy.

The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1962, was deprived of liberty in Slovakia continuously from 25 June 2002 until his expulsion on 19 September 2013. This consisted mainly of successive and overlapping periods of pre-trial detention on various charges (some later severed into separate proceedings), a four-year sentence for attempting to legalise criminal proceeds (against which earlier detention was credited), and brief administrative detention pending expulsion.

On 13 July 2010 the applicant was released after serving the credited sentence. He was immediately detained administratively pending expulsion. The next day he was seized from the foreigners’ detention centre and brought before the Bratislava I District Court. After questioning and a private session the court remanded him that same day (16 July 2010) on a murder charge. Immediately after the oral pronouncement he announced an interlocutory appeal, stating that written reasons would follow service of the reasoned order. He filed reasons in Russian on 19 July (received 21 July). The written order (in Slovak) was served on 21 July and the file was sent the same day to the Regional Court. Further reasons were sent on 26 July (received 28 July). On 28 July the Regional Court dismissed the appeal as unfounded, observing that no reasons had been submitted. The Constitutional Court later declared a complaint inadmissible, holding that the submissions had not reached the Regional Court in time, that detention appeals must be decided within five working days, that the applicant had been heard at first instance and that his lawyer had taken no steps to protect his interests.

On 27 July 2011 the applicant was acquitted of the murder and released. He was re-arrested the same afternoon and served with a 2003 charge of conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist group (a charge that had formed part of the original 2002–2005 detention). On 29 July 2011 a pre-trial judge of the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him, citing flight risk (non-national status, unregistered residence, frequent foreign travel) and risk of further offending (other pending charges and a prior conviction). An interlocutory appeal raising unlawfulness of the arrest, lack of grounds, the already nine-year overall detention and a pattern of consecutive remands was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 8 August 2011. The Constitutional Court declared a subsequent complaint inadmissible, finding that the applicant had been informed of the charges, that the Supreme Court had examined lawfulness (if only implicitly), and that the length of this particular detention (then only a few weeks) was not yet unconstitutional.

The applicant was released on 22 February 2012 after the Supreme Court held that adding the earlier 2002–2005 detention on the same charges to the post-27 July 2011 period exceeded the statutory maximum and that the matter remained one single criminal case; it expressed concern that the repeated splitting of charges risked arbitrary prolongation of detention. Subsequent Constitutional Court judgments concerning later remands on still other charges similarly found violations of Article 5, emphasising that statutory time-limits could not be applied separately to each consecutively severed charge, otherwise detention could be prolonged indefinitely. The applicant was finally expelled on 19 September 2013 after a last period of administrative detention.

The case of Yegorov v. Slovakia (Application no. 27112/11) concerns a Ukrainian national, Volodymyr Yegorov (born 1962), who alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention. From 25 June 2002 until his expulsion to Ukraine on 19 September 2013, he was continuously deprived of liberty in Slovakia, primarily through successive and overlapping periods of pre-trial detention on various charges (including fraud, money-laundering, murder, and conceiving/setting up/supporting a criminal and terrorist group). Some charges were pursued in parallel or consecutively after being detached into separate proceedings.

The first set of relevant facts concerns the remand order of 16 July 2010 (on a murder charge). The applicant had been detained since 2002, including on the terrorist-group charge until that prosecution was detached in May 2005. Subsequent detention was later offset against a four-year sentence for attempted money-laundering, from which he was released on 13 July 2010. Immediately thereafter, he was placed in administrative detention pending expulsion. On 16 July 2010, police seized him from the Medveďov detention centre and brought him before the Bratislava I District Court. After a private session that day, the court remanded him pending trial on the murder charge (prosecution of which had begun in 2007 while he was already detained). He immediately announced an interlocutory appeal, stating he would provide reasons after receiving the written order. He submitted reasons in Russian on 19 July 2010 (received 21 July) and further reasons on 26 July (received 28 July). The written order was served on 21 July, and the file was transmitted to the Bratislava Regional Court the same day. On 28 July 2010, the Regional Court dismissed the appeal as unfounded, observing that no reasons had been submitted. The applicant’s subsequent constitutional complaint (alleging an unlawful bringing before the court, an arbitrary remand, and failure to consider his written reasons) was declared inadmissible by the Constitutional Court on 7 December 2010 as manifestly ill-founded. That court noted the need for swift determination of detention appeals (within five working days), that the submissions had not reached the Regional Court in time, that the applicant had been heard at first instance, and that his lawyer had taken no steps.

The second set of facts concerns the arrest of 27 July 2011 and remand of 29 July 2011. On 27 July 2011 the applicant was acquitted of the first murder charge and released, only to be immediately re-arrested the same afternoon and served with a 2003 charging document for the terrorist-group offence. On 29 July 2011 a pre-trial judge of the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him, citing risk of flight (as a non-national who had not lived at his registered address and had travelled abroad) and of reoffending (given other pending charges and a prior conviction). The applicant’s interlocutory appeal (contesting the lawfulness of the arrest for lack of information on its reasons, the detention grounds, the overall nine-year deprivation of liberty, and a pattern of consecutive remands) was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 8 August 2011. His constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 18 October 2011. The Constitutional Court held that the arrest report (signed by the applicant) had informed him of the charges, that the Supreme Court had considered the lawfulness arguments by implication, and that the length of detention since 27 July 2011 had not yet become unconstitutional (even though total detention exceeded nine years). The Supreme Court later ordered his release on 22 February 2012, observing that earlier detention on the same charges (2002–2005) had to be aggregated, that maximum statutory durations had been exceeded, and that the successive remands risked appearing arbitrary and self-serving.

These facts formed the core of the communicated complaints regarding the lawfulness and length of the relevant arrests/remands and the fairness/speed of the related review proceedings. Later domestic decisions (including several Constitutional Court judgments) recognised similar patterns of consecutive remands as violating Article 5 rights in related proceedings, though often without awarding just satisfaction.

The case of Yegorov v. Slovakia (application no. 27112/11) concerns a Ukrainian national born in 1962 who alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention arising from his arrest, remand in custody and related review proceedings in Slovakia. From 25 June 2002 until his expulsion on 19 September 2013 he was continuously deprived of liberty, almost entirely in pre-trial detention on a succession of charges pursued partly in parallel and partly consecutively.

The first contested period began immediately after his release on 13 July 2010 from a four-year sentence (already served in detention) for attempting to legalise the proceeds of crime. He was taken into administrative detention pending expulsion and a five-year re-entry ban. On 16 July 2010 police seized him from the Medveďov detention centre and brought him before the Bratislava I District Court. After questioning, a private session ordered his remand on a murder charge that had been pending since 2007. The applicant immediately announced an interlocutory appeal, stating that he would file reasons once he received the written decision. He submitted those reasons in Russian on 19 July (received 21 July) and further reasons on 26 July (received 28 July). The written decision was served on him in Slovak on 21 July and the file was transmitted the same day to the Regional Court. On 28 July that court dismissed the appeal as unfounded, recording that no reasons had been submitted. A subsequent constitutional complaint alleging an unlawful arrest, an arbitrary remand and failure to consider the written reasons was declared manifestly ill-founded: the Regional Court had been obliged to decide within five working days, the submissions had not reached it in time, the applicant had been heard at first instance and his lawyer had taken no steps to protect his rights.

The second contested period began on 27 July 2011, the day the applicant was acquitted of the murder charge and released. He was re-arrested the same afternoon and served with a 2003 charge of conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist organisation (a charge that had been severed from earlier joint proceedings in 2005). The following day the prosecution sought remand on that charge together with three other old charges. On 29 July a pre-trial judge of the Specialised Criminal Court ordered detention, citing flight risk (the applicant was a foreigner who had not lived at his registered address and had travelled frequently) and a risk of re-offending (other pending charges and a previous conviction). An interlocutory appeal complaining of an uninformed arrest, lack of grounds and a nine-year pattern of successive remands was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 8 August. A further constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible: the arrest report (signed by the applicant) showed he had been informed of the charges, the Supreme Court had examined lawfulness implicitly, and the length of detention since 27 July 2011 had not yet become unconstitutional.

The applicant was released on 22 February 2012 after the Supreme Court itself observed that the 2002–2005 detention on the same charges (two years and 329 days) plus the seven months since July 2011 already exceeded the statutory maximum, that the successive remands risked appearing arbitrary, and that the splitting of charges had left the legal basis of detention unclear. Subsequent Constitutional Court judgments concerning later remands on a second murder charge confirmed that the authorities’ practice of remanding the applicant immediately after each release, treating each charge as permitting a fresh maximum period, produced a recurring pattern incompatible with Article 5.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the lawfulness of the 16 July 2010 seizure and remand, the failure of the Regional Court to examine the applicant’s timely written reasons, the lawfulness and length of the 29 July 2011 detention (including its continuity with earlier periods on the same charges), and the overall pattern of consecutive remands that effectively prolonged detention far beyond statutory limits.
