The case of Bratanova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 44497/06) concerned a complaint by Ms Ilka Georgieva Bratanova, a Bulgarian national born in 1944 and resident in Las Vegas, that the mayor of Sofia’s Bankya district had unlawfully failed to comply with final court judgments requiring him to issue documents essential to her restitution claim.

The applicant’s mother had owned a 1,000-square-metre plot of agricultural land expropriated in 1952 and later incorporated into Bankya’s urban territory. As sole heir, the applicant applied in 1992 under the Agricultural Land Act for restoration of ownership. In September 1994 the Bankya land commission (later the Agriculture and Forestry Department) ruled that, because the land was now urban, restitution could proceed only after production of a plan of the plot and a certificate indicating whether any part had been built upon. The commission repeated this requirement in June 2000. The applicant then asked the Bankya district mayor to issue the documents. Over subsequent years the municipal authorities repeatedly demanded additional papers, which she supplied, yet neither the plan nor the certificate was produced.

On 27 February 2007 the applicant sought judicial review of the mayor’s tacit refusal. After an initial inadmissibility ruling was quashed by the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) on 19 May 2008—the SAC observing that the authorities had for years unlawfully withheld the documents while inundating the applicant with correspondence—the Sofia Administrative Court, on 9 January 2009, quashed the refusal. It held that the mayor enjoyed no discretion and ordered him to issue the documents within one month, noting that they were indispensable for resumption of the restitution procedure and that the refusal impaired the applicant’s restitution rights. The judgment became final.

The mayor nevertheless issued further instructions on 5 March 2009. When they were not followed, he formally refused on 24 February 2010. A second round of judicial-review proceedings followed. After another inadmissibility decision was set aside, the Sofia Administrative Court dismissed the claim on the merits in June 2011. On 8 May 2012 the SAC reversed that ruling, declared the refusal null and void, remitted the matter and again ordered the mayor to issue the documents, emphasising that he had already been bound by the 2009 judgment and that the documents remained prerequisites for the stayed restitution process.

Between October 2012 and January 2013 the Bankya administration merely sent three letters seeking land-register information from the Sofia municipality and took no further steps; the applicant’s lawyer eventually obtained the information herself at the end of 2013. On 18 August 2014 a Supreme Administrative Court judge imposed a BGN 1,000 fine on the mayor for non-compliance with the 2012 judgment; the fine was upheld on 30 October 2014.

Under the Regulations implementing the Agricultural Land Act, a plan and certificate issued by the local authorities are mandatory before any decision on restitution of former agricultural land now within urban territory; only unbuilt portions may be restored in kind, the remainder giving rise to compensation. Enforcement of administrative-court judgments is governed by the 2006 Code of Administrative Procedure, which provides for weekly pecuniary sanctions or court-imposed fines of BGN 200–2,000 for official non-compliance.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s allegation that the persistent failure of the Bankya mayor to execute two final judgments had violated her Convention rights.

The case of Bratanova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 44497/06) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 October 2006 by Ms Ilka Georgieva Bratanova, a Bulgarian national born in 1944 and residing in Las Vegas. She alleged that the mayor of Sofia’s Bankya district had unlawfully refused to comply with a final domestic court judgment issued in her favour.

The applicant’s mother had owned a 1,000-square-metre plot of agricultural land that was expropriated in 1952 and later incorporated into the urban territory of Bankya. As her mother’s sole heir, the applicant sought restitution of the property under the 1991 Agricultural Land Act. In a 7 September 1994 decision, the Bankya land commission ruled that the procedure could proceed only after submission of a plan of the plot and a certificate indicating whether any part had been built upon. These documents were required under the implementing regulations of the Act, which provided that only unbuilt portions of such land could be restored in kind (with compensation otherwise available). A 19 June 2000 letter from the commission reiterated the same requirements.

Thereafter the applicant repeatedly asked the Bankya district mayor to issue the plan and certificate. Over subsequent years the municipal authorities demanded numerous additional documents, all of which she supplied, yet they never produced the required plan or certificate. On 27 February 2007 she sought judicial review of the mayor’s tacit refusal. The Sofia Administrative Court initially rejected the application as inadmissible, but on 19 May 2008 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed that ruling and remitted the case, observing that the municipal bodies had for many years unlawfully withheld the documents while inundating the applicant with requests and explanations.

On 9 January 2009 the Sofia Administrative Court quashed the mayor’s refusal, held that he possessed no discretion in the matter, and ordered him to issue the documents within one month. It emphasised that the plan and certificate were indispensable for the Agriculture and Forestry Department to resume the restitution procedure and that the refusal therefore impaired the applicant’s restitution rights. The judgment became final. Nonetheless, on 5 March 2009 the mayor again demanded further documents. When these were not supplied he issued a fresh refusal on 24 February 2010.

A second application for judicial review followed. After the Sofia Administrative Court dismissed it as concerning enforcement of the 2009 judgment, the Supreme Administrative Court on 23 September 2010 held that the new refusal was independently reviewable. On 27 June 2011 the Sofia court rejected the application on the merits, but on 8 May 2012 the Supreme Administrative Court set that decision aside, declared the mayor’s refusal null and void, remitted the matter and again ordered issuance of the documents, stressing that the mayor had already been bound by the 2009 judgment.

Between October 2012 and January 2013 the Bankya administration sent three letters seeking information from the Sofia municipal land register but took no further steps; the applicant’s lawyer eventually obtained the data at the end of 2013. On 18 August 2014 a Supreme Administrative Court judge, acting under Article 304 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, fined the mayor 1,000 Bulgarian levs for non-compliance with the 2012 judgment. A three-member panel upheld the fine on 30 October 2014, noting the continued absence of the documents and the lack of any explanation from the mayor.

These facts centre on the prolonged failure of the Bankya mayor to execute two final administrative-court judgments that required him to issue documents essential to the applicant’s restitution claim, despite repeated judicial findings that he enjoyed no discretion and that his inaction unlawfully obstructed her property rights.

The case of Bratanova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 44497/06) concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights lodged on 7 October 2006 by Ilka Georgieva Bratanova, a Bulgarian national born in 1944 and residing in Las Vegas. She alleged that the mayor of Sofia’s Bankya district had unlawfully refused to comply with a final court judgment in her favour, thereby obstructing her efforts to restore property rights over land formerly owned by her late mother.

The land in question was a 1,000-square-metre agricultural plot expropriated in 1952 and later incorporated into Bankya’s urban territory. As her mother’s sole heir, the applicant applied in 1992—following enactment of the Agricultural Land Act—for restitution of the property. In September 1994 the Bankya land commission ruled that the procedure could proceed only after she submitted a plan of the plot and a certificate indicating whether any part had been built upon. These documents, required under the Regulations implementing the Act, had to be issued by the local authorities; only unbuilt portions were eligible for restitution in kind, with compensation available for the remainder.

The applicant repeatedly sought the documents from the Bankya district mayor. Over subsequent years the authorities demanded additional paperwork, which she supplied, yet never issued the plan or certificate. In February 2007 she applied for judicial review of the mayor’s tacit refusal. The Sofia Administrative Court initially declared the application inadmissible, but the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) in May 2008 remitted the case, observing that municipal bodies had for years unlawfully withheld the documents while inundating her with irrelevant requests.

On 9 January 2009 the Sofia Administrative Court quashed the refusal, held that the mayor enjoyed no discretion, and ordered him to issue the documents within one month. The judgment became final. Nevertheless, in March 2009 the mayor again demanded further documents and, in February 2010, formally refused to issue the plan and certificate. A fresh application for judicial review followed. After another inadmissibility ruling (later overturned by the SAC), the Sofia Administrative Court dismissed the claim in June 2011. On 8 May 2012 the SAC set that decision aside, declared the mayor’s refusal null and void, remitted the matter and again ordered issuance of the documents, stressing that the 2009 judgment already imposed that obligation.

Administrative inaction persisted. Between October 2012 and January 2013 the district administration sent three letters requesting land-register information but took no further steps; the applicant’s lawyer ultimately obtained the data herself at the end of 2013. In August 2014 a Supreme Administrative Court judge, acting under Article 304 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, fined the mayor BGN 1,000 for non-compliance with the 2012 judgment; the fine was upheld on appeal.

The facts demonstrate a prolonged pattern of administrative obstruction that prevented the applicant from completing the statutory restitution procedure. Two final court orders compelling issuance of the essential documents were ignored, despite available enforcement mechanisms (weekly pecuniary sanctions under Article 290 and fines under Article 304 of the Code of Administrative Procedure). The applicant’s property claim therefore remained stalled for more than two decades after her initial 1992 request.
001-155088:
The case of Becker v. Austria (Application no. 19844/08) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 11 June 2015. Austrian national Michael Becker alleged a violation of his rights under the Convention arising from the withdrawal of his driving licence. He specifically complained that he had been denied an oral hearing before the Administrative Court in those proceedings.

On 3 October 2000, police stopped Becker while he was driving and ordered a breathalyser test. He made nine attempts, of which only one produced a valid result; the test was then discontinued. The police treated this as a refusal to undergo the test and temporarily withdrew his licence. Two sets of proceedings followed.

On 15 December 2000 the Melk District Administrative Authority withdrew Becker’s licence for four months as a preventive road-safety measure. It relied on the statements of two officers and the print-outs showing nine attempts with only one valid reading. When Becker claimed the device was defective, one officer performed two successful tests using the same mouthpiece. The device had been independently verified as fully functional both before and after the incident. The authority therefore concluded that Becker had refused the test. It also ordered driver-improvement training and denied suspensive effect to any appeal.

Becker appealed, arguing that a technical expert should have examined the breathalyser. On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor dismissed the appeal. The print-outs and the officer’s successful tests demonstrated that the device had functioned correctly and that the officers, who were specially trained, had handled it properly. A request for an expert report that failed to specify any particular malfunction was an inadmissible fishing expedition. The Governor treated refusal of the test as equally serious as driving under the influence, because it prevented verification of actual intoxication, and therefore upheld the additional training measure.

On 8 February 2006 Becker lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and requested an oral hearing. He argued that the Regional Governor had lacked territorial competence (Becker resided in Vienna), that the officers’ statements were contradictory and that they should be questioned about the precise circumstances of the test, and that the refusal to commission a technical expert had been unlawful.

On 27 September 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the complaint. It held that the authorities’ assessment of the evidence was neither contradictory nor implausible and that Becker had advanced no substantial arguments against it. Pursuant to section 39(2) of the Administrative Court Act, the court refused a hearing on the ground that it was not likely to clarify the case. The decision was served on 25 October 2007.

In parallel penal proceedings a fine for refusal of the breathalyser test was imposed on 20 April 2001 but expired ipso iure because no decision was reached within the statutory 15-month period.

The relevant domestic provisions (Driving Licence Act ss. 3, 7, 24 and 25; Road Traffic Act s. 99) authorised withdrawal of a licence for lack of trustworthiness, treated refusal of a breathalyser test as a serious administrative offence equivalent to driving with a high blood-alcohol concentration, and permitted additional training measures. The Convention itself has constitutional rank in Austria.

These facts formed the basis of Becker’s complaint that the absence of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court violated his right to a fair trial.

The case of Becker v. Austria (no. 19844/08) originated in an application lodged on 22 April 2008 by Austrian national Michael Becker (born 1959, resident in Vienna) against Austria. Represented by counsel, he alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention, specifically that he was denied an oral hearing before the Administrative Court in proceedings to withdraw his driving licence.

On 3 October 2000 at 11:05 p.m., police stopped the applicant while he was driving on a public road and ordered a breathalyser test. After nine attempts (only one valid), the test was discontinued. His conduct was treated as a refusal, his licence was temporarily withdrawn, and two sets of proceedings were opened.

On 15 December 2000 the Melk District Administrative Authority withdrew the licence for four months as a preventive road-safety measure. It relied on statements of officers W. and R. plus the device print-outs showing nine attempts with only one valid result. The applicant had claimed the breathalyser was defective, but officer R. produced two valid results using the same mouthpiece. Subsequent technical tests (15 May and 9 November 2000) confirmed the device functioned properly. The authority therefore found a refusal. The appeal was given no suspensive effect and the applicant was ordered to complete driver-improvement training.

The applicant appealed, insisting a technical expert report on the device was required.

On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor dismissed the appeal. The print-out showed insufficient air on eight attempts; officer R.’s successful tests with the same mouthpiece indicated no malfunction or mishandling by trained officers. A request for an expert opinion lacking any concrete indication of defect constituted an inadmissible fishing expedition. Refusal of the test was as serious as drink-driving, justifying the additional training measure.

On 8 February 2006 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and expressly requested an oral hearing. He argued that the Regional Governor lacked territorial competence (the applicant lived in Vienna), that the officers’ statements were contradictory and they should be examined on the precise circumstances of the test, and that refusal of a technical expert opinion constituted a misapplication of the law.

On 27 September 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the complaint. It held that the authorities’ conclusion of refusal was supported by the evidence; the applicant had advanced no substantial arguments showing the assessment to be contradictory or implausible. Invoking section 39(2) of the Administrative Court Act, it refused a hearing on the ground that an oral hearing was unlikely to contribute to clarification of the case. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 25 October 2007.

(A parallel penal order imposing a fine for the same refusal, issued on 20 April 2001, later expired by operation of law after the 15-month time-limit for deciding the appeal was exceeded.)

The facts therefore centre on the licence-withdrawal proceedings, the repeated rejection of the applicant’s request for further evidence (including an expert report and oral questioning of officers), and the Administrative Court’s subsequent denial of an oral hearing under the applicable statutory provision.

The ECtHR case Becker v. Austria (no. 19844/08) arose from an Austrian national’s complaint that licence-withdrawal proceedings denied him an oral hearing before the Administrative Court, allegedly breaching Article 6 of the Convention.

On 3 October 2000 police stopped the applicant at 23:05 while he was driving and ordered a breathalyser test. After nine attempts only one reading was valid; the test was abandoned and his conduct treated as a refusal. His licence was provisionally seized and two parallel proceedings begun.

In the preventive (administrative) track the Melk District Administrative Authority, on 15 December 2000, withdrew the licence for four months. Austrian case-law treated four invalid blows out of five as refusal; the applicant had been given nine chances. Officer R. then produced two valid readings with the same mouthpiece. Subsequent laboratory checks (May and November 2000) confirmed the device was serviceable. An appeal was given no suspensive effect and driver-improvement training was imposed as a condition of restoration.

The applicant appealed, insisting a technical expert must examine the device. On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor dismissed the appeal. The print-out showed insufficient air on eight attempts, officer R.’s tests succeeded, and no concrete defect had been alleged; the request for an expert was therefore an inadmissible fishing expedition. Refusal of the test was held equivalent in gravity to drink-driving, justifying the extra training.

On 8 February 2006 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and expressly requested an oral hearing. He argued (i) territorial incompetence (he lived in Vienna), (ii) contradictory police statements that required the officers to be questioned, and (iii) unlawful refusal of the expert report.

On 27 September 2007 the Administrative Court rejected the complaint. The authorities’ evaluation of the evidence was neither contradictory nor implausible, and the applicant had advanced no substantial counter-arguments. Pursuant to s. 39(2) of the Administrative Court Act an oral hearing was refused because it would not assist clarification. The decision was served on 25 October 2007.

A separate penal order of 20 April 2001 imposing a fine for the same refusal lapsed automatically in 2005 after the Independent Administrative Panel found that the statutory 15-month decision deadline had been missed.

Domestic law (Driving Licence Act ss. 3, 7, 24–25 and Road Traffic Act s. 99) treated refusal of a breath test as a ground for withdrawal of a licence on grounds of untrustworthiness for road traffic, with a statutory minimum period of three months and power to add rehabilitative measures. The Convention itself enjoys constitutional rank in Austria.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 6 violation: a purely written determination of a licence-withdrawal measure that the applicant claimed required an oral hearing to test contested evidence and legal characterisation.
001-155187:
**CASE OF RAFAILOVIĆ AND STEVANOVIĆ v. SERBIA (Applications nos. 38629/07 and 23718/08), ECtHR (Third Section), 16 June 2015 (final 16 September 2015)**

The applicants, Serbian nationals Milan Rafailović (born 1958) and Svetlana Stevanović (born 1964), alleged that they could not obtain enforcement of final judicial decisions in their favour against local communities (mesne zajednice). Local communities are legal persons established by municipalities to deliver services of general local interest; they have limited legal personality based on founding statutes, act as indirect State budget beneficiaries, could levy self-imposed local taxes (SILT) in certain periods, and cannot undergo insolvency. Municipalities (their founders) were represented by solicitors general in the proceedings. Sole-proprietor businesses lack separate legal personality; owners succeed to claims and liabilities.

**First applicant (no. 38629/07).** As a sole proprietor running a transport business (1979–1995), he provided services in 1990–1991 to the Pocerski Metković local community (Šabac Municipality). After the business ceased, he succeeded to the unpaid claim. On 11 May 2001 the Valjevo Commercial Court ordered the community to pay RSD 24,400 plus interest and (jointly with other claimants) RSD 54,520 in costs. The judgment became final and enforceable. On 29 April 2003 he sought enforcement by bank transfer. On 6 October 2003 the court ordered enforcement (plus RSD 4,664 costs) and transmitted the order to the Central Bank. The debtor’s account had been frozen since 13 November 2003; he was registered as a second-class priority creditor. Inquiries in 2006–2007 confirmed this. The Government claimed the case was archived as terminated on 19 December 2003, but no decision was served or produced. After five years the case file was destroyed in 2010 without minutes or records. The judgment remains unenforced.

**Second applicant (no. 23718/08).** Her sole-proprietor installation business contracted with the Sokobanja local community to maintain a cable-satellite system. After non-payment she obtained a 9 October 2002 Zaječar Commercial Court order for direct enforcement of invoices, later suspended and referred to civil proceedings. On 17 April 2003 that court ordered payment of RSD 342,098.80 (principal), RSD 18,672 (enforcement costs), interest on various sums, and RSD 36,172 (civil costs). The High Commercial Court partly upheld this on 25 December 2003 and remitted costs; on 2 February/25 March 2004 the first-instance court awarded RSD 67,750 in civil costs. Enforcement by account transfer was ordered in May–June 2004 (plus further costs). In January 2005 the applicant reported that the municipality was routing funds through other accounts (including a SILT account), leaving the debtor’s account empty, and requested a change to auction of the cable-satellite system. The Niš Commercial Court joined the cases, repealed the transfer order, and transferred the matter to the Sokobanja Municipal Court. On 9/30 May 2005 that court ordered assessment and auction. On 13 March 2007 it suspended enforcement because an expert could not determine the exact ownership split of the system (financed by citizens) and public interest would be compromised by sale; it instructed the applicant to start new proceedings to identify the debtor’s assets. The decision was upheld on 12 June 2007; the Supreme Court dismissed a legality request on 29 November 2007. She did not start new proceedings. The decisions remain unenforced.

An Administrative Court president’s letter (2011) confirmed that local-community financial liabilities and any broader municipal/State responsibility were not regulated as administrative matters and that the underlying contracts fell within the communities’ competences. SILT-related disputes are generally treated as administrative, with municipalities sometimes treated as the relevant creditors.

These facts concern the persistent non-enforcement of final, enforceable judgments against public-law local communities whose accounts were frozen or empty, whose assets proved difficult to seize, and whose files were later destroyed, without effective alternative execution or State assumption of liability.

The case of Rafailović and Stevanović v. Serbia (applications nos. 38629/07 and 23718/08) concerns two Serbian nationals who alleged that they were unable to obtain enforcement of final judicial decisions in their favour against local communities, in violation of their Convention rights (typically Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1). The applicants, Mr Milan Rafailović (born 1958) and Ms Svetlana Stevanović (born 1964), lodged their applications in 2007 and 2008 respectively. Both had operated as sole proprietors whose businesses provided services to local communities (mesne zajednice) but were left unpaid.

For the first applicant, who ran a transport business from 1979 to 1995, services were provided in 1990–91 to the Pocerski Metković local community in Šabac, which had levied self-imposed local taxes (SILT). After his business ceased in 1995, he succeeded to its claims and, with two others, sued the community (represented by the Šabac Municipality’s Solicitor General). On 11 May 2001 the Valjevo Commercial Court ordered the community to pay him RSD 24,400 plus interest and jointly to pay RSD 54,520 in costs; the judgment became final and enforceable. On 29 April 2003 he sought enforcement by bank transfer. The court ordered it on 6 October 2003 (plus RSD 4,664 in enforcement costs) and transmitted the order to the Central Bank. The debtor’s account had been frozen since 13 November 2003, and he was registered as a second-class priority creditor. The case was archived as terminated on 19 December 2003 (though no such decision reached the applicant). The file was later destroyed without records. The 2001 judgment remains unenforced.

For the second applicant, whose installation business contracted with the Sokobanja local community for maintenance of its cable-satellite system, unpaid invoices led to an enforcement action. On 9 October 2002 the Zaječar Commercial Court ordered direct enforcement, but this was suspended on appeal and the matter referred to civil proceedings (the community again represented by the municipal Solicitor General). On 17 April 2003 the court ordered payment of RSD 342,098.80 principal, RSD 18,672 enforcement costs, various interest sums, and RSD 36,172 civil costs. After partial appeal success, the High Commercial Court remitted costs, which were fixed at RSD 67,750 in 2004. Enforcement by account transfer was ordered in May–June 2004 (plus further costs). In January 2005 the applicant reported that the municipality was routing funds through other accounts to evade payment and requested auction of the cable-satellite system. Jurisdiction was transferred to the Sokobanja Municipal Court, which in May 2005 ordered assessment and auction (later revised upward). On 13 March 2007, however, that court suspended enforcement, citing inability to determine the precise ownership split of the system (financed in part by citizens) and instructing the applicant to start new proceedings to identify the debtor’s assets. A panel upheld this; the Supreme Court dismissed a legality challenge. She did not launch new proceedings. The 2003–04 decisions remain unenforced.

Local communities are separate legal persons created by municipalities to deliver local services; they have limited legal capacity, are indirect budget beneficiaries, may levy SILT in some periods, and cannot enter insolvency. Municipalities (or the State) ultimately stand behind them, and their assets form part of public property. Neither community’s debts were discharged, and the applicants’ judgments remained unenforced years later, with enforcement frustrated by frozen accounts, insufficient funds, or judicial reluctance to seize community assets. The facts thus centre on the existence of final, enforceable awards against public-law entities that the State failed to satisfy.

The European Court of Human Rights examined two applications by Serbian nationals Milan Rafailović and Svetlana Stevanović alleging that Serbian authorities failed to enforce final court judgments in their favour against local communities, rendering the decisions ineffective.

Rafailović operated a sole-proprietor transport business from 1979 until 1995. In 1990–1991 he provided services to the Pocerski Metković local community, which levied self-imposed local taxes. After non-payment he and two others sued in 1994; upon the business’s dissolution he succeeded to the claim. The community was represented by the Šabac Municipality solicitor-general. On 11 May 2001 the Valjevo Commercial Court ordered the community to pay him RSD 24 400 plus interest and, jointly with the co-claimants, RSD 54 520 in costs. The judgment became final. Enforcement by bank transfer was sought on 29 April 2003 and ordered on 6 October 2003 (with additional costs of RSD 4 664). The Central Bank reported that the debtor’s account had been frozen since 13 November 2003 and that Rafailović ranked as a second-class creditor. The Government claimed the file was archived as terminated on 19 December 2003, yet no such decision reached the applicant. In 2010 the file was destroyed without record. The 2001 judgment remains unenforced.

Stevanović ran a sole-proprietor installation business that contracted with the Sokobanja local community to maintain a cable-satellite system. After non-payment she obtained a 9 October 2002 enforcement order based on invoices; it was later suspended and the dispute converted into ordinary civil proceedings. The community was represented by the Sokobanja Municipality solicitor-general. On 17 April 2003 the Zaječar Commercial Court awarded RSD 342 098.80 principal, interest, and costs; subsequent decisions of 2 February and 25 March 2004 fixed additional costs at RSD 67 750. Enforcement by account transfer was ordered in May–June 2004. Stevanović informed the court that the municipality channelled funds through other accounts, leaving the debtor’s account empty, and requested seizure and auction of the transmission system. After transfer of the case, the Sokobanja Municipal Court initially authorised auction but on 13 March 2007 suspended enforcement, citing an expert’s inability to determine ownership shares and the public interest in preserving a citizen-financed system. She was directed to bring new proceedings to establish ownership; she did not do so. The Supreme Court rejected a legality challenge. The 2003–2004 decisions remain unenforced.

Under Serbian law local communities are separate legal persons of limited capacity, created by municipalities to perform daily local-interest functions. They are indirect State-budget beneficiaries, may collect self-imposed taxes (until 2006), and cannot enter insolvency. Municipalities and the State have no clearly defined residual liability for their debts. Both applicants, as sole proprietors, personally succeeded to the claims. The protracted, fruitless enforcement proceedings against these public-law entities form the core of the alleged violations of the right to effective enforcement of final judgments.
001-155374:
The case of Kovárová v. Slovakia (Application no. 46564/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the rights of access to a court and to a fair hearing. The applicant, Eva Kovárová, a Slovak national born in 1947 and residing in Bratislava, complained that domestic courts discontinued her civil proceedings without examining the merits of her claim and that the Constitutional Court wrongly declared her subsequent complaint inadmissible.

On 9 May 2007, the applicant filed an action with the Bratislava V District Court seeking a declaration that a meeting of flat owners held on 24 April 2007 in her apartment building was unlawful and that the decisions adopted there were void. The defendant was a registered community of owners of residential and non-residential premises in the building, an entity with legal personality entered in the register of the local District Authority.

On 2 January 2008 a lawyer acting for the defendant informed the District Court that the entity had been struck off the register on 14 December 2007 and had thereby ceased to exist; responsibility for administering the building had been transferred to a specialised agency. The applicant learned of the deregistration only later and, on 24 January 2008, requested that a scheduled hearing be adjourned so that she could analyse the legal situation. The hearing was postponed.

On 3 March 2008 the District Court discontinued the proceedings. It held that the defendant no longer existed and had no legal successor: neither the individual flat owners nor the new management agency could be regarded as having succeeded to the defendant’s procedural position.

The applicant appealed on 20 March 2008. She argued, first, that the management agency was the legal successor and that the action should therefore continue against it. Alternatively, she submitted that the court should have stayed the proceedings pending the outcome of a separate action (lodged on 26 September 2007 by another owner) that challenged the 11 September 2007 decision of the flat owners to wind up the original defendant. If that winding-up decision were later declared void, the striking-off of the defendant would lose its legal basis and the original proceedings could resume.

On 30 May 2008 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the discontinuance. It simply noted that the defendant had lost capacity to be a party and that discontinuance was therefore mandatory, without addressing the applicant’s two arguments or providing any further reasoning.

The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, relying on Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure (which permits such an appeal when a court has prevented a party from pursuing a case). She complained of the Regional Court’s lack of reasoning and reiterated her successor and stay arguments. On 7 May 2009 the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible, holding that the alleged defects (including the failure to stay the proceedings) did not fall within Article 237(f). It therefore did not examine the merits.

On 17 August 2009 the applicant filed a constitutional complaint under Article 127 of the Constitution against all three ordinary courts, alleging that the discontinuance had unlawfully deprived her of access to a court and a fair hearing. On 16 December 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. It found the part directed at the Regional Court time-barred and held that the Supreme Court’s decision on admissibility was reasoned and not arbitrary. It observed that a successful outcome in the parallel winding-up challenge might theoretically allow the applicant to seek reopening, but stressed that even a judicial declaration of invalidity would not automatically resurrect the defendant; a fresh administrative decision of the District Authority would still be required.

The parallel challenge to the winding-up decision was dismissed at first instance and on appeal; a constitutional complaint against those judgments remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the Slovak courts had arbitrarily terminated her action without considering possible successors or staying the case, thereby denying her effective access to a court.

The case of Kovárová v. Slovakia (Application no. 46564/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (access to court and fair hearing). The applicant, Eva Kovárová, challenged the discontinuation of her civil action and the Constitutional Court’s rejection of her related complaint.

On 9 May 2007 the applicant sued a registered community of flat owners (the defendant) before the Bratislava V District Court, seeking a declaration that a 24 April 2007 owners’ meeting was unlawful and its decisions void. On 2 January 2008 the defendant’s lawyer informed the court that the entity had been struck from the register on 14 December 2007 after building administration transferred to a specialised agency. The applicant, learning of this, obtained an adjournment of the scheduled hearing.

On 3 March 2008 the District Court discontinued the action, holding that the defendant had ceased to exist without a legal successor (neither individual owners nor the new agency). The applicant appealed, arguing that the agency succeeded to the defendant or, alternatively, that the court should have stayed the action pending parallel proceedings (also before the same District Court) challenging a 11 September 2007 decision to wind up the defendant. If that winding-up were later declared void, the striking-off would lose its legal basis.

The Bratislava Regional Court upheld the discontinuation on 30 May 2008, stating that loss of legal personality left no alternative; it cited statutory provisions but offered no further reasoning. The applicant’s appeal on points of law (invoking Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure) was declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 7 May 2009. The Supreme Court held that alleged defects in reasoning, errors of fact or law, and the failure to stay proceedings did not fall within the cited provision (staying being discretionary). Merits were therefore not examined.

On 17 August 2009 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against all three ordinary courts, repeating that the discontinuation unlawfully prevented examination of her claim and violated Article 6 § 1. The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 16 December 2009. The part directed at the Regional Court was out of time. As to the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Court found the inadmissibility decision adequately reasoned and non-arbitrary; it observed that a successful challenge to the winding-up might later permit reopening, though even a judicial declaration of invalidity would not automatically restore the defendant’s existence (fresh incorporation by the District Authority would be required). The decision was served on 5 February 2010.

In the parallel winding-up challenge (filed 26 September 2007), the action was ultimately dismissed (District Court 4 April 2012; Regional Court 19 March 2014). A constitutional complaint lodged on 14 July 2014 remained pending.

These events form the factual core of the applicant’s complaint that she was denied access to a court capable of determining her civil claim on the merits.

The case of Kovárová v. Slovakia (App. no. 46564/10) was brought by Slovak national Eva Kovárová (born 1947, resident in Bratislava) against Slovakia under Article 34 of the ECHR. Represented by lawyer P. Arendacký, she alleged that domestic courts’ discontinuation of her civil claim and the Constitutional Court’s declaration of her related complaint as inadmissible violated her Article 6 § 1 rights of access to court and to a fair hearing. The application was lodged on 3 August 2010 and communicated on 2 April 2014. The Third Section Chamber (President Casadevall) delivered judgment on 23 June 2015 (final 23 September 2015).

On 9 May 2007 the applicant sued the community of owners of a Bratislava block of flats (a registered legal entity) in the Bratislava V District Court. She sought a declaration that a 24 April 2007 owners’ meeting was unlawful and its decisions void.

On 2 January 2008 the defendant’s lawyer informed the court that the entity had been struck from the District Authority register on 14 December 2007 (administration having transferred to a specialised agency) and had thus ceased to exist. The applicant, learning of this, obtained an adjournment of the 28 January 2008 hearing to consider her position.

On 3 March 2008 the District Court discontinued the action, holding that the defendant no longer existed and had no legal successor. Neither the individual owners nor the new agency could be treated as successors.

The applicant appealed on 20 March 2008. She argued (i) that the agency was the successor so the action should continue against it, and (ii) that, even if not, the court should have stayed rather than terminated the proceedings pending a parallel District Court action (brought 26 September 2007) challenging an 11 September 2007 owners’ decision to wind the defendant up. Success in that action would remove the legal basis for the striking-off.

On 30 May 2008 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld discontinuation, noting only that the defendant had been struck off and therefore lacked capacity; it supplied no reasons why there was “no alternative” to termination.

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law on 7 July 2008 under Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure (denial of the right to pursue a case). She criticised the Regional Court’s complete lack of reasoning (rendering the decision unreviewable) and reiterated her successor and stay arguments.

On 7 May 2009 the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible. The alleged defects (inadequate reasoning, errors of fact/law, failure to stay) fell outside Article 237(f); a stay was discretionary, not obligatory. Merits were therefore not examined.

On 17 August 2009 the applicant filed a constitutional complaint (Article 127 of the Constitution) against all three ordinary courts, repeating her arguments and claiming an unlawful denial of a merits determination in breach of Article 6 § 1.

On 16 December 2009 (served 5 February 2010) the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. The Regional-Court limb was out of time (two-month limit). The Supreme Court had given relevant, non-arbitrary reasons for inadmissibility and had not ruled out that the Regional Court might have erred. Even if the parallel winding-up challenge later succeeded, reopening might become possible, yet the defendant would not automatically revive; re-incorporation by the District Authority would still be required.

The parallel action itself was dismissed by the District Court (4 April 2012) and Regional Court (19 March 2014); a constitutional complaint against those rulings (filed 14 July 2014) remained pending.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaint that the courts’ handling of the defendant’s dissolution, the refusal to stay or continue the action, the absence of reasons, and the successive inadmissibility rulings collectively denied her access to a court and a fair hearing.
001-155102:
The case originated in an application by PSMA, spol. s r.o., a Slovak private limited company, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The complaint centred on the quashing of a final and binding judgment in its favour after the Prosecutor General (PG) lodged an extraordinary appeal on points of law, pursuant to a petition by the opposing party, Slovak Radio.

In 1995 the applicant company contracted with Slovak Radio, a public-service broadcaster, to act as exclusive agent for the sale of advertising airtime. The arrangement operated until 2004, when relations deteriorated. Slovak Radio billed the applicant for an alleged shortfall in 2003 profits and, upon non-payment, terminated the contract (effective 30 September 2005). The applicant later withdrew a challenge to the termination’s validity. Slovak Radio separately sued for the shortfall (outcome unknown).

On 1 June 2006 the applicant sued Slovak Radio for an indemnity of approximately EUR 693 000 (average annual commission over five years, including barter transactions) plus interest. The Bratislava I District Court granted the claim in full on 14 May 2007. Slovak Radio had submitted no observations and attended no hearings; the court therefore proceeded on the available evidence under the Code of Civil Procedure, finding the termination valid, the applicant eligible for indemnity, and barter transactions properly included.

Slovak Radio appealed, acknowledging the legal basis of the indemnity but disputing only the barter element (conceding roughly EUR 526 000) and the decision to proceed in its absence. On 28 November 2007 the Bratislava Regional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the principal had effectively conceded all but the barter claim (which it treated as distinct from a separate counter-claim in the shortfall proceedings) and that the first-instance court’s assessment of the defendant’s passivity was justified. The judgment became final and binding on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

Slovak Radio’s subsequent constitutional complaint (alleging arbitrariness and a failure to seek a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the EU) was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 for non-exhaustion of an ordinary appeal on points of law.

On 25 April 2008 Slovak Radio petitioned the PG to file an extraordinary appeal. The PG did so on 23 October 2008, arguing that the courts had wrongly treated the termination’s validity as undisputed (a legal question requiring independent examination) and had incorrectly included barter transactions contrary to the parties’ subsequent practice. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability on 8 December 2008.

The applicant submitted observations contending that the principal had failed to use available ordinary remedies (including a direct appeal on points of law), that an extraordinary appeal was statutorily excluded where an ordinary one existed, that the PG had exceeded the petition’s scope, and that the procedure itself undermined legal certainty and res judicata.

On 12 August 2009 the Supreme Court allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower-court judgments and remitted the case for fresh examination. It held that the courts had omitted to examine the validity of the underlying contract and, consequently, of the termination notice, rendering it impossible to determine the indemnity claim. The case has remained pending at first instance since.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint (20 November 2009) alleged that the extraordinary appeal was inadmissible, belated and beyond the petition’s scope; that it nullified a completed judicial process in breach of legal certainty; that the Supreme Court had ignored the applicant’s observations and denied file access; and that the decision was biased and unreasoned. On 25 November 2010 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint manifestly ill-founded, finding no constitutionally relevant arbitrariness and holding that file-access denial lacked significance given the nature of extraordinary-appeal proceedings.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation, namely the interference with a final judgment through an extraordinary mechanism initiated by the opposing party via the PG.

The applicant company PSMA, spol. s r.o. (established 1995) concluded a 1995 contract with Slovak Radio, a public-service broadcaster, to act as exclusive agent for selling advertising airtime. The contract, amended multiple times and valid until 31 December 2007, functioned well until 2004, when the principal grew dissatisfied with 2003 business volumes. It billed the applicant for the gap between estimated and actual profit. Non-payment prompted the principal to terminate the contract (notice expiring 30 September 2005). The applicant initially challenged the termination but later withdrew; the principal separately sued for the profit differential (outcome unknown).

On 5 December 2006 the applicant claimed an indemnity of approximately EUR 693,000 (average annual commission over five years, including barter transactions). It sued on 1 June 2006. The Bratislava I District Court held hearings in April–May 2007. Despite representation, the principal filed no observations and failed to appear (its excuses later disputed). On 14 May 2007 the court applied Article 101 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (allowing judgment on available material after unjustified non-cooperation) and granted the claim in full. It treated the termination as valid (unchallenged), found no disqualifying factors, and included barter transactions in the calculation.

The principal appealed, formally attacking the entire judgment but substantively conceding the legal basis for indemnity while disputing only the barter element (reducing the conceded sum to about EUR 526,000). It also alleged arbitrariness in proceeding in its absence. On 28 November 2007 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It noted the principal’s acknowledgment of the core claim, distinguished the barter indemnity from any offset in the parallel profit-differential action, and confirmed that the principal’s non-attendance had been unjustified. The judgment became final and binding on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

The principal’s subsequent constitutional complaint (alleging arbitrary refusal of a preliminary ruling to the Court of Justice of the EU) was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 for failure to exhaust an ordinary appeal on points of law.

On 25 April 2008 the principal petitioned the Prosecutor General to lodge an extraordinary appeal on points of law. The Prosecutor General did so on 23 October 2008, arguing that the courts had wrongly treated the termination’s validity as undisputed (a legal question requiring independent examination) and that barter transactions should be excluded by reference to the parties’ subsequent practice. Enforceability was suspended on 8 December 2008. The applicant objected that the principal had failed to use the ordinary cassation remedy (to avoid fees), that an extraordinary appeal was statutorily barred when an ordinary one was available, that the Prosecutor General had exceeded the petition’s scope, and that reopening a final judgment violated legal certainty.

On 12 August 2009 the Supreme Court allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower judgments, and remitted the case. It held that the courts had failed first to examine the contract’s validity and then the termination notice, rendering any assessment of the indemnity claim impossible. The remitted proceedings remain pending. The applicant’s constitutional complaint against the Supreme Court decision (alleging belatedness, excess of scope, violation of legal certainty, lack of reasoning, ignored observations, and denied file access) was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 25 November 2010.

The applicant alleged that the Prosecutor General’s successful extraordinary appeal, lodged at the losing party’s request after a final and binding judgment, violated Article 6 § 1 by undermining legal certainty and the principle of res judicata.

The applicant company PSMA, spol. s r.o., a Slovak private limited company, alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention arising from the quashing of a final judgment in its favour. In 1995 it concluded a contract with Slovak Radio, a public-service broadcaster, under which it acted as exclusive agent for the sale of advertising airtime. The contract, amended several times, was due to run until the end of 2007. Relations deteriorated in 2004 when the broadcaster billed the company for an alleged shortfall between estimated and actual profit. Non-payment led the broadcaster to terminate the contract with effect from 30 September 2005.

The company sued in 2006 for an indemnity of approximately EUR 693 000, calculated as its average annual commission over the preceding five years and including barter transactions. The Bratislava I District Court, sitting in the broadcaster’s absence, granted the claim in full on 14 May 2007. It treated the termination notice as valid because it had not been contested and found the company entitled to the indemnity, including the barter element. The Regional Court upheld the judgment on 28 November 2007, noting that the broadcaster had accepted the legal basis of the claim except as regards barter and that the company’s counter-claim in related proceedings concerned a different cause of action. The judgment became final on 9 January 2008 and enforceable three days later.

The broadcaster’s subsequent constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion of an ordinary appeal on points of law. It then petitioned the Prosecutor General, who on 23 October 2008 lodged an extraordinary appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. The Prosecutor General argued that the lower courts had failed independently to examine the validity of both the contract and the termination notice and had wrongly included barter transactions. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability and, on 12 August 2009, allowed the appeal, quashed both judgments and remitted the case for a fresh first-instance hearing. It held that the courts had omitted to scrutinise the contract’s validity and, consequently, the notice of termination, rendering it impossible to determine the claim’s foundation and scope.

The company complained to the Constitutional Court that the extraordinary appeal had been inadmissible, belated and ultra vires the petition, that it destroyed legal certainty, and that the Supreme Court had ignored its submissions and denied it access to the file. On 25 November 2010 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint manifestly ill-founded, finding no constitutionally relevant arbitrariness and holding that file-access denial lacked significance given the nature of the proceedings. The remitted action remains pending.

The company contended before the European Court that the Prosecutor General’s intervention and the Supreme Court’s decision violated the principles of legal certainty, res judicata and equality of arms, particularly because an ordinary appeal on points of law had been available to the broadcaster and the extraordinary appeal exceeded the petition’s scope.
001-155711:
The case of Serce v. Romania (Application no. 35049/08) was brought by Ali Serce, a Turkish national born in 1966, against Romania before the European Court of Human Rights. Detained in Giurgiu Prison at the time of the proceedings, Serce is married with four children residing in Turkey. On 28 June 2005, the Bucharest County Court convicted him of aggravated murder and sentenced him to 18 years’ imprisonment, with deportation to Turkey upon completion of his term. In his application lodged on 15 July 2008, Serce alleged that his detention conditions in Rahova Prison (until January 2009) and subsequently Giurgiu Prison amounted to inhuman treatment, and that the Romanian authorities’ refusal to transfer him to Turkey to serve his sentence violated his right to family life, as his impoverished family could not visit him.

Regarding detention conditions, Serce described severe hygiene deficiencies in both facilities, including insufficient cleaning and personal hygiene products supplied by the authorities, infestation by bed bugs that disrupted his sleep, and food unsuitable for his type II diabetes (diagnosed in 2008, along with a sleep disorder). He further claimed exclusion from educational, recreational, or work activities, preventing his reintegration, re-education, or any sentence reduction.

The Government contested these claims. In Rahova Prison, Serce occupied a 21 sq m cell with seven other inmates (2.62 sq m personal space), featuring eight beds, a 1.2 by 1.2 m window, and an en-suite bathroom (shower, sink, toilet). Cold water was constantly available, hot water twice weekly, and winter heating reached 18°C. Disinfection occurred two to three times yearly when infestations were noted. His diet substituted pork with beef to accommodate diabetes. Participation in activities was limited by his health. In Giurgiu Prison (from 17 January 2009), he shared a 21.47 sq m cell with five others (3.57 sq m personal space), equipped with six beds, furniture, a 1.5 by 1.8 m window, and a bathroom. Winter temperatures were 19°C, with hot water twice weekly. Monthly hygiene kits included two soaps, toothpaste, a toothbrush, shaving cream, a razor, and toilet paper; prisoners cleaned cells using provided products, with quarterly disinfection. His diabetes menu included 125 grams of meat daily. Activities were minimal: a 2011 folk concert, a 2012 religious discussion, and quizzes in 2013 and 2014.

Independent reports from the NGO APADOR-CH in 2009 corroborated overcrowding and inactivity in Rahova, plus hygiene issues in Giurgiu’s showers and food areas, with unused activity spaces. The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture had not inspected the relevant sections.

On the transfer issue, Serce applied in 2007 to the Romanian Ministry of Justice under the 1992 Romania-Turkey Convention on the Transfer of Convicted Persons, seeking proximity to his family. The Ministry initiated proceedings; on 5 June 2007, an Ankara court recognized the Romanian conviction and approved serving the remainder in Turkey. However, on 4 April 2008, the Bucharest Court of Appeal rejected the request, citing Turkey’s more lenient parole rules, which could result in earlier release and undermine the sentence’s punitive and educational aims. A renewed request was similarly denied on 15 December 2011. Romanian Law no. 302/2004 permitted optional refusal of transfers if they risked unduly short remaining sentences compared to domestic law. The Convention itself allowed refusals on sovereignty, public order, or enforcement grounds.

These facts formed the basis of Serce’s complaints under the European Convention on Human Rights, communicated to the Romanian Government in 2013 (with Turkey declining to intervene).

The case of Serce v. Romania (Application no. 35049/08) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 30 June 2015. The applicant, Ali Serce, a Turkish national born in 1966, was convicted on 28 June 2005 by the Bucharest County Court of aggravated murder and sentenced to 18 years’ imprisonment, with deportation to Turkey ordered at the end of his term. He has been detained first in Rahova Prison and, from 17 January 2009, in Giurgiu Prison. He is married with four children; his family lives in modest circumstances in a Turkish village and cannot travel to Romania.

The applicant alleged two main violations. First, his detention conditions amounted to inhuman treatment. He described severe hygiene deficiencies in both prisons, including insufficient cleaning and personal-hygiene products supplied by the authorities, infestation by bed bugs that prevented sleep, and a diet unsuited to the type-II diabetes and sleep disorder diagnosed in 2008. He further claimed he was excluded from educational or work programmes, frustrating any prospect of re-education or sentence reduction.

The Government contested these accounts. In Rahova, cells of 21 m² held eight prisoners (2.62 m² personal space), each equipped with a window, eight beds and a private bathroom. Cold water was constantly available and hot water twice weekly; winter heating reached 18 °C. Disinfection against insects occurred two or three times a year. The applicant’s diet replaced pork with beef. Participation in activities was limited by his health. In Giurgiu, a 21.47 m² cell housed six prisoners (3.57 m² personal space) with similar facilities and 19 °C heating. Monthly hygiene kits and quarterly disinfection were provided; prisoners cleaned their own cells. A diabetes-adapted menu included 125 g of meat daily. The applicant attended a concert in 2011, a religious discussion in 2012 and two history quizzes in 2013–2014.

Second, the applicant complained that repeated refusals to transfer him to Turkey under the 1992 Romania–Turkey Convention on the Transfer of Convicted Persons breached his right to family life. In 2007 the Romanian Ministry of Justice initiated transfer proceedings; the Ankara District Court recognised the Romanian conviction and authorised continued imprisonment in Turkey. The Bucharest Court of Appeal nevertheless rejected the request on 4 April 2008 (and a fresh request on 15 December 2011) because Turkish early-release rules were more lenient and would undermine the punitive and educational aims of the Romanian sentence. Domestic law (Law no. 302/2004) expressly permits optional refusal where transfer would result in release “after much too short a term” compared with Romanian law.

Relevant domestic standards include Law no. 275/2006 on prisoners’ rights and CPT/APADOR-CH reports noting overcrowding, poor hygiene and unused activity spaces in the two prisons. Isolated domestic decisions have ordered provision of cleaning products or awarded modest compensation for specific failures, but none directly resolved the applicant’s complaints.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 (inhuman conditions) and Article 8 (family-life) violations examined by the Court.

The case of Serce v. Romania (Application no. 35049/08) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 30 June 2015.
