001-155826:
The case of Mafalani v. Croatia (Application no. 32325/13) concerns allegations under Article 3 of the Convention of ill-treatment by police during the applicant’s arrest and custody, as well as the lack of an effective official investigation into those claims.

On 23 October 2008 a car bomb killed journalist I.P. and his associate N.F. in Zagreb. Intelligence implicated the applicant, Amir Mafalani (born 1982). On 29 October 2008 an antiterrorist unit (ATJ) of the Special Police Forces stormed his flat at around 6.05 p.m., where he was present with his sister and grandmother. According to the applicant, officers immediately threw him to the floor and punched him about the head and body. He was then blindfolded, taken to a remote riverside location, beaten again and subjected to water immersion to extract a confession, with further assaults continuing en route to the police station. Once there he was tightly restrained, beaten and threatened into silence about his injuries. The Government’s account differs: six ATJ officers ordered him to lie down; when he resisted they applied a “foot-sweep” technique, causing him to fall and strike a table with his head. Medical help was offered and refused. He was held in an ATJ van in the station car park from approximately 6.45–8.30 p.m. before being placed in an office with two inspectors (M.A. and M.M.). Handcuffs were removed shortly after arrival. Visible injuries to the head and nose were noted; emergency services were summoned only on superior orders.

An emergency-service record of 10.55 p.m. documented a 1.5 cm open wound above the left eye and nasal contusion/haematoma with possible fracture; the applicant again declined hospital treatment. He remained at the station until 8.30 p.m. on 30 October, undergoing questioning (in the presence of a lawyer and a prosecutor) and searches. Transfer documents to the Police Detention and Escort Unit gave conflicting descriptions of visible injuries. On 31 October, before an investigating judge, the applicant stated that he had fallen in his flat, sustaining a probable nasal fracture, and had refused treatment so as to leave the station quickly. The judge asked no further questions and took no action. Prison-hospital records of 3 November 2008 recorded head, nose and shoulder contusions, an undisplaced nasal fracture and haematoma; later notes mentioned testicular problems.

An ATJ officer’s contemporaneous report described resistance, use of the foot-sweep and a facial impact with a table. The Police Director promptly declared the force lawful under the Police Act and related by-laws. No independent inquiry followed. In 2011 the applicant sought medical and police records; the latter were refused as confidential. His November 2011 complaint to the State Attorney’s Organised Crime Office produced only a suggestion that he lodge a criminal complaint. He did so in February 2012. The County State Attorney’s Office rejected it in March 2014, relying solely on police reports and finding no reasonable suspicion of an offence. Parallel civil proceedings for damages, in which family members testified to seeing the applicant beaten, remain pending. The applicant was later convicted of aiding the 2008 murders and sentenced to sixteen years’ imprisonment.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the disputed circumstances of the arrest and subsequent custody, the documented injuries, and the absence of any prompt, independent and thorough investigation capable of establishing the truth or identifying those responsible.

The case of Mafalani v. Croatia (Application no. 32325/13) concerns allegations of police ill-treatment of Amir Mafalani (born 1982) during his 29 October 2008 arrest and subsequent custody, plus the lack of an effective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

Mafalani was a suspect in the 23 October 2008 car-bomb murders of journalist I.P. and associate N.F. Special antiterrorist police (ATJ) stormed his flat at around 6.05 p.m. He claimed officers immediately threw him to the floor and punched his head and body. The Government maintained that he resisted verbal orders to lie down; officers then used a “foot-sweep” technique, causing him to strike a table with his face. An official ATJ report of 30 October 2008 confirmed the use of force, the facial impact, and an offer of medical aid (refused). Mafalani further alleged that he was then blindfolded, taken to a riverside location, beaten, subjected to water immersion to extract a confession, and beaten again en route to the station. The Government stated he was held only in an ATJ van in the police-station car park from approximately 6.45/7.00 p.m. until 8.30 p.m.

At the station he was placed with inspectors M.A. and M.M. They later acknowledged seeing head and nose injuries, initial handcuffing (removed shortly afterwards), and an offer of medical help that he refused; emergency services were summoned only on superiors’ orders. The 10.55 p.m. medical note recorded a 1.5 cm open wound above the left eye, nasal contusion/haematoma with possible fracture; Mafalani again refused hospitalisation. He remained at the station until 8.30 p.m. on 30 October, participating in searches and being questioned (with a lawyer and prosecutor present). He alleged continued beating, tight restraint and threats; the Government denied this, stating he sat unrestrained on a chair with access to water and toilet. Transfer documents to the JZP detention unit recorded no injuries, yet the receiving officer noted visible facial injuries. Mafalani said jaw pain prevented him from eating the sandwich provided.

On 31 October he told an investigating judge that he had fallen in his flat, sustaining a probably dislocated nasal fracture, and had refused treatment only to leave the station quickly. The judge asked no further questions and took no action. Prison-hospital examination on 3 November diagnosed head, nose and shoulder contusions, an undisplaced nasal fracture, facial and shoulder haematomas, and displacement of an old metal hand implant. Some records referred to a fall, others to blows. Later notes mentioned testicular problems.

Internal police review on 30 October 2008 deemed the force lawful. In 2011 Mafalani obtained medical records but was refused police documents (classified). His November 2011 complaint to the specialised prosecutor elicited only advice to file a criminal complaint. He did so in February 2012 against unidentified officers. The complaint was rejected in March 2014 for lack of reasonable suspicion, relying on police reports and the existing file. Parallel civil proceedings for damages, begun in January 2012 and still pending, included family testimony of an immediate beating, a co-suspect’s account of seeing serious injuries, and police denials. CPT reports from 2007 and 2012 had already criticised Croatian police for excessive force, inadequate investigation of allegations and poor detention conditions.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 violations.

The case of Mafalani v. Croatia (Application no. 32325/13) concerns alleged violations of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the applicant’s claimed ill-treatment by Croatian police during his arrest and subsequent custody, as well as the alleged failure to conduct an effective official investigation into those claims.

The applicant, Amir Mafalani (born 1982), was arrested on 29 October 2008 in connection with a car-bomb attack the previous year that killed journalist I.P. and his associate N.F. An antiterrorist unit (ATJ) of the Special Police Forces executed an oral order from the Police Director to storm the applicant’s flat at approximately 6.05 p.m., where he was present with his sister and grandmother. According to the applicant, officers immediately threw him to the floor and punched him about the head and body. He was then blindfolded, taken to a remote riverside location, beaten again, and subjected to water immersion to extract a confession; the beating continued en route to the police station. The Government maintained that the applicant resisted verbal orders to lie down, prompting two officers to apply a “foot-sweep” technique; while falling he struck a table with his face. He was offered medical assistance at the scene but refused it. An official ATJ report dated 30 October 2008 corroborated the Government’s account of the use of force and the head injury.

The applicant was transferred to the parking area of the Zagreb Organised Crime police station and held in an ATJ minivan until approximately 8.30 p.m. He was then placed in a room under the control of inspectors M.A. and M.M. Both inspectors later recorded that they observed visible injuries to his head and nose, that an ATJ officer initially guarded him, and that handcuffs were removed shortly after arrival. Emergency medical services attended at 10.55 p.m. and documented a 1.5 cm open wound above the left eye together with nasal contusion and haematoma possibly involving fracture; the applicant again refused hospitalisation. He remained at the station until 8.30 p.m. the following day, during which time searches and questioning (in the presence of a lawyer and a prosecutor) took place. The applicant alleged continued tight restraint, further beatings and threats. The Government stated that he was kept in an ordinary office, was not handcuffed after arrival, had access to toilet and water, and made no requests for rest or food.

On 30 October he was transferred to the Police Detention and Escort Unit (JZP). The accompanying police report recorded no visible injuries, yet the receiving officer noted facial injuries. The applicant claimed he could not eat because of jaw pain. On 31 October he appeared before an investigating judge, remaining silent on the criminal charges but stating that he had fallen in his flat and sustained a nasal fracture; he had refused treatment in order to leave the station quickly. The judge asked no further questions and took no investigative steps. A subsequent examination at Zagreb Prison Hospital on 3 November diagnosed head, nasal and shoulder contusions, an undisplaced nasal fracture and an old metal-implant displacement in the hand. Some medical notes attributed the injuries to a fall, others to multiple blows. Later records mentioned testicular problems.

Internal police review on 30 October 2008 deemed the force used during arrest lawful. In 2011 the applicant obtained medical records and requested police documents, which were refused as confidential. He then lodged a criminal complaint in February 2012 alleging ill-treatment. The complaint was rejected in March 2014 for lack of reasonable suspicion, the authorities relying exclusively on police reports and existing medical and procedural records. Parallel civil proceedings for damages, commenced in January 2012, remain pending; the applicant’s grandmother and sister testified to an immediate physical attack, while police witnesses denied any abuse.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints of both substantive ill-treatment and a deficient investigation.
001-159789:
The case of Treskavica v. Croatia (Application no. 32036/13) was brought by three Croatian nationals of Serbian origin—Draginja Treskavica (widow) and her daughters Nataša and Valentina Treskavica—against Croatia. They alleged an ineffective investigation into the 1995 killing of their husband and father, J.T., during Operation Storm, claiming it failed to consider that he was targeted solely due to his ethnicity. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under the procedural limb of Article 2 (right to life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing), and Article 13 (effective remedy).

In 1991–1992, Serbian paramilitary forces seized about one-third of Croatian territory, establishing the self-proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, including Knin where the family lived. In early August 1995, Croatian forces launched Operation Storm (4–7 August) to recapture the area. Most Krajina Serbs (estimated 100,000–150,000) fled beforehand. During the operation, Croatian artillery shelled Knin. The applicants hid in their building’s basement. J.T. was later found dead near a petrol station after one attack and buried in Knin’s New Cemetery.

On 25 April 2001, during ICTY-supervised exhumations, Draginja approached police, identifying her husband as buried there. She described seeing his body on the pavement in civilian clothes after the shelling, assuming a shell killed him; Croatian soldiers then took her to a UNPROFOR camp. She had no further information on the body. Remains were exhumed in May–June 2001 and examined at Zagreb’s Institute for Forensic Medicine. A 20 June 2001 ICTY autopsy on the remains later confirmed as J.T.’s indicated a gunshot wound to the neck as the probable cause of death. Initial DNA comparison in November 2003 yielded no match.

In February 2007 the applicants lodged a damages claim with the State Attorney’s Office (later refused), prompting police to open an inquiry. Witnesses interviewed in late 2007–early 2008 (neighbours Lj.M., Z.M., and I.M.) confirmed seeing J.T.’s body on 5 August 1995 in civilian clothes with no visible injuries; they stated he was not in the RSK army or police and had last been seen alive that morning after hiding in the basement. Police noted they could not interview Draginja (then in England) and had not established J.T.’s military status.

In November 2009 J.T.’s brother supplied ante-mortem details to the Serbian Red Cross. Family DNA samples in February 2010 enabled identification of the remains as J.T.’s on 16 April 2010; Draginja confirmed this in June. The remains were reburied on 19 July 2010. A July–August 2010 police note recorded the death date and burial but added no further investigative steps. In 2014 the Ministry of War Veterans confirmed the identification to the Interior Ministry’s War Crimes Department.

Separately, on 14 June 2007 the applicants sued the State in Knin Municipal Court under the 2003 Liability Act (covering damage from terrorist acts or violence aimed at seriously disturbing public order). The court dismissed the claim on 17 December 2008, finding no evidence that J.T.’s death resulted from such acts. This was upheld by the Šibenik County Court (1 March 2010), the Supreme Court (21 February 2012), and the Constitutional Court (3 October 2012).

These facts highlight prolonged delays (initial police contact only in 2001, substantive inquiry only after 2007, identification only in 2010), the discrepancy between the assumed shelling death and forensic gunshot evidence, limited witness interviews, and failure to pursue possible ethnic motive or identify perpetrators—issues central to the alleged violations of the duty to investigate a wartime killing effectively and without discrimination.

The case Treskavica v. Croatia (Application no. 32036/13) was brought by three Croatian nationals of Serbian origin—Draginja Treskavica (the widow) and her daughters Nataša and Valentina—against Croatia. They complained that the investigation into the 1995 killing of their husband and father, J.T., during Operation Storm was ineffective and failed to consider that he was targeted solely because of his Serbian ethnicity. They invoked the procedural limbs of Articles 2 and 14 of the Convention, as well as Articles 6 § 1 and 13.

The relevant events occurred against the backdrop of the Croatian War of Independence. In 1991–1992 Serbian paramilitary forces seized roughly one-third of Croatian territory and proclaimed the “Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina.” In early August 1995 Croatian forces launched Operation Storm to recapture the area. Knin, the regional capital where the applicants lived, was subjected to intense artillery bombardment. The family sheltered in the basement of their building. After one of the attacks J.T. was found dead near a petrol station. The first applicant later stated that she saw his body lying on the pavement; she assumed he had been killed by a shell. Croatian soldiers then took her to a nearby UNPROFOR camp. J.T. was buried in Knin’s New Cemetery.

In April 2001, during official exhumations at that cemetery (conducted under the auspices of the ICTY and the Šibenik County State Attorney’s Office), the first applicant informed the police of her husband’s burial there. She was interviewed and gave a detailed description of the body and clothing. Remains were forensically examined in Zagreb, but J.T. was not identified at the time. A June 2001 autopsy report later linked to his remains recorded the probable cause of death as a gunshot wound to the neck, contradicting the initial assumption of death by shelling.

DNA extraction in 2003 produced no match. Only after the applicants filed a 2007 damages claim with the State Attorney’s Office did the Knin police open a formal inquiry. Witnesses interviewed in 2007–2008 (neighbours and others present in Knin on 5 August 1995) confirmed seeing J.T.’s body in civilian clothes with no visible injuries; they also stated that he had not been a member of the Krajina army or police and had not worn a uniform. Identification was finally achieved in April 2010 after family members supplied blood samples. The remains were released and reburied in July 2010.

The applicants’ civil action under the 2003 Liability Act (which imposes State liability for damage caused by terrorist or violent acts aimed at seriously disturbing public order, irrespective of whether the perpetrator is identified) was dismissed at every instance. The Knin Municipal Court, Šibenik County Court, Supreme Court and Constitutional Court all held that there was no evidence the death resulted from such an act.

These facts—delayed identification revealing a gunshot rather than shrapnel, limited and late witness interviews that did not pursue a possible ethnic motive, and the civil courts’ rejection of any terrorist or public-order element—formed the core of the applicants’ complaints of an ineffective investigation and lack of an effective remedy.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Draginja Treskavica and her two daughters, Croatian nationals of Serbian ethnicity residing in the United Kingdom, concerning the death of their husband and father, J.T., during Croatia’s 1995 Operation Storm. The applicants alleged that the investigation into J.T.’s killing had been ineffective and had ignored evidence that he had been targeted solely because of his Serbian origin, in violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 (right to life) taken alone and together with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). Related complaints under Articles 6 and 13 were also communicated.

J.T. lived with the applicants in Knin, then part of the self-proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina. On 5 August 1995 Croatian artillery shelled the town. The family hid in a basement; J.T. was later found dead on the pavement near a petrol station, dressed in civilian clothes. Croatian soldiers removed the first applicant to a UNPROFOR camp. She assumed a shell had killed him. His body was buried in Knin’s New Cemetery.

In April 2001, during ICTY-supervised exhumations, the first applicant identified the burial site and gave a statement to Knin police. An autopsy of the remains (later confirmed as J.T.’s) recorded a gunshot wound to the neck as the probable cause of death. DNA extracted in 2003 produced no match. Only after the applicants lodged a damages claim in February 2007 did the police open a formal inquiry. Witnesses interviewed in 2007–2008 confirmed that J.T. had never belonged to Krajina military or police forces, had last been seen alive that morning, and had been found dead in civilian clothing with no visible injuries. The first applicant, living in England, was not re-interviewed. DNA identification was completed in April 2010; the remains were reburied in July 2010. Police notes issued that August merely recorded the date of death and burial; no further investigative steps or perpetrator identification followed.

Parallel civil proceedings under the 2003 Liability Act (which imposes state liability for terrorist or politically motivated violence irrespective of whether perpetrators are identified) were dismissed at every instance. The Knin Municipal Court, Šibenik County Court, Supreme Court and Constitutional Court held that there was no evidence the death resulted from “terror or violence aimed at gravely disturbing public order.”

The factual record thus shows a fifteen-year delay between the killing and identification of remains, an autopsy inconsistent with the initial shelling theory, witness testimony that J.T. was an unarmed civilian, and an investigation that began in earnest only after civil proceedings were instituted and that never examined a possible ethnic motive. These elements formed the core of the applicants’ complaints that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective, independent inquiry capable of establishing the circumstances of the death and of addressing whether J.T. had been killed because he was Serbian.

The case of S.S. v. the Netherlands (Application no. 39575/06) concerns an Afghan national of Pashtun origin, born in 1964, who entered the Netherlands on 3 August 1998 and applied for asylum the next day. He claimed that expulsion to Afghanistan would expose him to a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In interviews, the applicant stated that after graduating from the Kabul military academy in 1982 he joined an administrative department of the KhAD/WAD security service (under the communist PDPA regime) as a second lieutenant, handling confidential documents. He became head of the department in 1988 and was promoted to lieutenant-colonel in 1990, remaining in post until the regime’s fall in 1992. His directorate negotiated paid cooperation agreements with mujahideen groups. He attended meetings assessing commanders’ performance and payment decisions, taking minutes. He believed certain mujahideen held him personally responsible for pay cuts and sought to eliminate him to conceal their past collaboration.

After Kabul fell in 1992, mujahideen searched for him at his office. He fled with his family to Mazar-e-Sharif, living quietly until 1997 when those groups arrived, searched his house, and forced him into hiding; the family then fled to Pakistan.

Dutch authorities rejected the asylum claim on 18 July 2000, applying Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention. Official reports (including one dated 29 February 2000 on Afghan security services 1978–1992) described KhAD/WAD as systematically using torture, arbitrary arrests, and executions, with a climate of terror. Higher-ranking officers, including those promoted after initial operational assignments, were presumed to have participated in or known of such acts. The applicant’s decade of service, high rank, promotions, and attendance at executive meetings established “serious reasons for considering” his personal and knowing participation in crimes against humanity. He had not distanced himself from the organisation. No humanitarian residence permit was granted; even if an Article 3 risk existed, it did not create a right to remain, as hosting such individuals would undermine the Netherlands’ international credibility.

Subsequent objections and hearings confirmed this analysis under the “personal and knowing participation” test. The applicant’s claims of a purely administrative desk job obtained via bribes, ignorance of abuses, and distinction from operational units were rejected as implausible and inconsistent, especially given his processing of classified information. Official reports were deemed reliable, drawing on UN, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch sources. The lower standard of proof for Article 1F (“serious reasons”) was applied.

A Regional Court judgment of 10 February 2005 upheld the Article 1F finding but remitted the case because the authorities had not adequately examined whether Article 3 lastingly barred expulsion. A fresh decision of 2 August 2005 rejected any real Article 3 risk: mere former PDPA/KhAD membership or differing political views did not suffice; the applicant was not publicly known; relatives (including his father and brother) remained in Afghanistan without incident; and fears of specific mujahideen commanders were unsubstantiated speculation, as he could not prove their current influence or whereabouts and had lived safely in Afghanistan until 1997.

The Regional Court sitting in Amsterdam dismissed a further appeal on 12 April 2006, holding that while some former KhAD officers might face risks from authorities or victims’ families (absent protection from influential groups), the applicant had not established such a personal risk. No further domestic appeal was possible.

The applicant lodged his application with the Court on 4 October 2006. Interim measures under Rule 39 were indicated on 20 November 2008 to prevent expulsion pending the proceedings; his identity was withheld from the public. The Government and applicant exchanged observations on the facts and the Article 3 claim. Later UNHCR and EASO materials on Afghanistan (2003–2015) were considered, noting risks for some former communist-era officials but not automatically for all KhAD/WAD members, depending on individual role, rank, and current circumstances. The case focused on whether expulsion would violate Article 3 given the applicant’s profile and the situation in Afghanistan.

The case of A.W.Q. and D.H. v. the Netherlands concerns two Afghan nationals (a married couple born in 1956 and 1966) and their children, who entered the Netherlands in December 1999 and applied for asylum. They feared persecution or treatment contrary to Article 3 of the ECHR (and later Article 2) if returned to Afghanistan, based on the first applicant’s career under the communist regime.

The first applicant joined the PDPA in 1978 and served as a conscript before pursuing a professional army career. After language training, he studied in the Soviet Union (1982–1986), graduating with a master’s degree. Assigned as a captain to the political affairs division of a border security unit (Division 5), he handled propaganda, literacy programmes, patriotic education, and the apprehension of roughly 300 deserters (of whom 15 were handed to military prosecutors after refusing to resume service). Promoted to senior captain, he later became deputy director of the Army Museum in Kabul (1990–1992), collecting weapons.

After the mujahideen takeover in 1992, he was briefly detained in the museum basement and pressured to help remove arms; he resigned in 1994. A death threat followed, their house was destroyed, and the family relocated to Kunduz. In 1998, after the Taliban seized Kunduz, relatives allegedly betrayed him; Taliban forces arrested him, detained and interrogated him (including ill-treatment and forced labour), and he feared execution. He escaped during transport to Kabul; the family fled Afghanistan in November 1999.

Dutch authorities accepted his career history but applied Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention, excluding him from protection. Official reports established that army political-affairs units consisted of loyal professionals who supplied the KhAD/WAD security service (notorious for torture, disappearances and executions) with information and helped remove disloyal soldiers. Applying the “personal and knowing participation” test, they concluded he knew or should have known of KhAD’s crimes and had facilitated them through his duties. For Article 3, they found no sufficiently specific, individualised risk: general fears of mujahideen or mere PDPA membership were insufficient according to country reports. Domestic courts upheld the refusals in 2005.

A fourth child was born in 2006. A subsequent regular-residence application failed. In 2008 the second applicant and younger children (and separately the eldest daughter) lodged fresh asylum claims based on westernisation; these were granted in 2010. The first applicant’s 2009 fresh claim (citing a deteriorated security situation, his ex-communist and atheist status, long absence and prominence) was rejected for lack of “nova,” a decision confirmed by the courts in 2011–2012.

The applicants complained to the ECtHR that expulsion would expose them to a real risk of treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3. Interim measures under Rule 39 prevented removal pending the proceedings. Relevant UNHCR materials noted possible risks for former communist officials or KhAD-linked personnel from authorities, victims’ families or insurgents, while stressing careful individual assessment of exclusion clauses and later omitting ordinary former armed-forces members from core risk profiles.

**Case Summary: S.D.M. and Others v. the Netherlands (Application no. 8161/07)**

The applicants, three Afghan nationals of Tajik origin (S.D.M., born 1969; his then-wife M.A., born 1975; and their child O.M., born 2002), resided in the Netherlands from 1996. They alleged that expulsion to Afghanistan would expose them to a real risk of death or treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, primarily due to the first applicant’s past employment with the communist-era security service KhAD/WAD.

The first applicant entered the Netherlands on 10 March 1996 and claimed asylum. He stated that he had performed compulsory military service from 1988, initially as a conscript in KhAD/WAD Department 5 in Herat (focused on national reconciliation and negotiations with mujahideen rather than combat). After one year of guard and administrative duties (e.g., propaganda, minutes, archiving), he became a professional soldier (Second Lieutenant, later claiming First Lieutenant) performing administrative tasks processing intelligence on mujahideen commanders. He left KhAD/WAD in April 1992 after the communist regime’s fall, then worked for mujahideen authorities in Herat until the Taliban captured the city in January 1996, prompting his flight via Turkmenistan.

His initial asylum claim was rejected in September 1996 for lack of personal risk (Tajik ethnicity alone insufficient; continued work under mujahideen without problems; Taliban likely unaware of his past). However, he received a one-year conditional residence permit due to Afghanistan’s poor conditions, later converted to an indefinite permit in 1999. An objection was rejected; he did not appeal.

In June 1998 he filed a second claim based on new facts: a possible child from a 1993 relationship; fuller details of KhAD work; and a Taliban Islamic Court judgment (October/November 1995, in absentia) convicting him and others of conspiracy against the Taliban, imposing a death sentence, and appending his photograph. He learned of this via his mother in Iran in November 1997 (she had also reported his brother’s capture and torture). He provided a detailed written account of his KhAD activities.

In February 2001 the second claim was rejected and Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention applied (serious reasons to believe he committed crimes against humanity). Official reports described KhAD/WAD as an elite, cruel organization systematically engaging in torture, murder, arbitrary executions and other violations. Given its recruitment of only loyal individuals, initial placement in investigative departments involving violations, and the first applicant’s operational-adjacent role (accompanying superiors on field missions, taking minutes of negotiations), authorities rejected his claims of purely administrative work and ignorance of abuses. Individual responsibility was found via the “knowing and personal participation” test: he knew or should have known of the crimes (common knowledge; his admission of ubiquitous fear of the regime) and bore responsibility by failing to prevent them. His indefinite permit was revoked for incomplete initial disclosure. Prosecution was requested but no outcome reported. The second applicant’s dependent permit (granted 2000) was also revoked; their child was born in 2002.

Objections were rejected in 2003. The Minister acknowledged a possible Article 3 risk but required departure. Appeals to the Regional Court of The Hague were joined. In May 2005 the court upheld the Article 1F finding but quashed the decisions for failure to assess whether Article 3 lastingly barred expulsion, remitting the case.

A fresh October 2005 decision maintained Article 1F and ineligibility for residence. On Article 3, a July 2005 official report noted risks for some former KhAD officials from current authorities, victims’ families or mujahideen (absent protection via contacts). Relevant factors included identification with communist ideology, rank and family ties. The first applicant had attracted no particular attention pre-Taliban and readily obtained work under mujahideen governor Ismail Khan (later Energy Minister). The general situation had improved since 2004, with Taliban activity concentrated outside Herat. The 1995 death sentence was unlikely to be known or enforced (poor records; Taliban judgments required verification against current law; the conviction concerned anti-Taliban conspiracy). He obtained an Afghan passport in 1999 via the Rabbani-era embassy in the UK (Jamiat-e-Islami, well-represented in the post-2001 government), indicating no negative attention. He had no mentioned family ties to the communist regime and had not been identified with communist ideology post-1992. Thus no real Article 3 risk was found.

The Regional Court rejected the appeal in August 2006. After the first and second applicants’ divorce, the latter and the child obtained asylum in 2009 as a single woman and child.

The applicants—an Afghan man of Tajik origin born in 1969 (the first applicant), his wife born in 1975 (the second applicant) and their child born in 2002 (the third applicant)—have resided in the Netherlands since 1996. The first applicant claimed asylum on arrival, stating that he had performed compulsory military service from 1988 and then served as a professional officer (rising to first lieutenant) in Department 5 of the KhAD/WAD security service in Herat until the communist regime fell in 1992. His duties, he said, were essentially administrative: processing reports on mujahideen commanders, taking minutes and producing propaganda in support of national-reconciliation talks. After the mujahideen took power he continued working for the local authorities without incident until the Taliban captured Herat in January 1996, at which point he fled.

His first asylum claim was refused in 1996 on the ground that he had not shown a personal risk, although he received a one-year humanitarian residence permit that later became indefinite. A second claim lodged in 1998 relied on new material, including a 1995 Taliban court judgment (in absentia) sentencing him to death for conspiracy, together with a photograph, and information that his brother had been detained and tortured. In 2001 the Dutch authorities applied Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention, finding serious reasons to believe he had been implicated in KhAD/WAD crimes against humanity. They relied on an official report describing the service’s systematic use of torture, extra-judicial killings and other abuses, and on the applicant’s own statements that he had accompanied senior officers on field missions. They concluded that he knew or ought to have known of the crimes and had personally participated in them. His residence permit (and the derived permit of his wife) was therefore revoked. The public prosecutor was asked to consider criminal proceedings, but no prosecution followed.

Subsequent domestic proceedings confirmed the Article 1F exclusion. On the question of Article 3 ECHR risk, the authorities accepted that some former KhAD officials remained vulnerable to reprisals from victims’ families or mujahideen factions unless they enjoyed protection. They nevertheless found no such risk in this case: the applicant had worked unmolested for the mujahideen governor of Herat after 1992; the Taliban judgment was unlikely to be known to, or executed by, the post-2001 authorities; he had obtained an Afghan passport in 1999 from an embassy still loyal to the previous (Jamiat-e-Islami) government, now well represented in Kabul; and he had not demonstrated any remaining identification with communist ideology. The Regional Court upheld these findings in 2006. After the couple divorced, the second and third applicants were granted asylum in 2009 on the basis of the risks facing a single woman and child in Afghanistan.

The applicants complained to the Court that expulsion of the first applicant (and, at the time of the application, of the whole family) would expose them to a real risk of death or of treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3.

The applicants, three Afghan nationals of Tajik origin, complained that their expulsion from the Netherlands to Afghanistan would expose them to a real risk of death or ill-treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. The first applicant (born 1969) entered the Netherlands and claimed asylum on 10 March 1996. He stated that he had performed compulsory military service from 1988, being assigned to Department 5 of the KhAD/WAD (the communist-era security service) in Herat. After basic training he performed guard and administrative duties, including propaganda and record-keeping related to the national reconciliation policy of negotiating with mujahideen groups. He later became a professional officer (Second Lieutenant, later claimed First Lieutenant) whose work involved processing intelligence on mujahideen commanders and accompanying superiors on field missions. He left the service in April 1992 after the fall of the Najibullah regime, returned after a mujahideen amnesty, and worked in local administration until the Taliban captured Herat in January 1996, whereupon he fled.

His initial asylum claim was rejected in September 1996 for lack of personal risk, though he received a one-year conditional residence permit on account of the general situation in Afghanistan; an objection was dismissed and he did not appeal. A second claim in June 1998 relied on new material, including a 1995 Taliban court judgment (sent by his mother in 1997) convicting him in absentia of conspiracy and sentencing him to death, together with a photograph, and reports that his brother had been tortured. The conditional permit was converted into an indefinite permit in 1999. In February 2001 the authorities rejected the second claim, applied Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention (serious reasons for considering him implicated in crimes against humanity), and revoked the residence permit because he had not disclosed the full extent of his KhAD service. They relied on a 2000 Ministry of Foreign Affairs report describing the KhAD/WAD as systematically responsible for torture, extrajudicial killings and other atrocities. The first applicant’s rank, posting to an operational directorate and field activities were held to establish both knowledge of those crimes and personal participation; mere administrative duties were rejected as implausible.

The second applicant (born 1975) had joined him and obtained a dependent permit in 2000; it was revoked in 2001. Their child (the third applicant, born 2002) was also affected. Objections were dismissed in 2003. The Regional Court of The Hague, in May 2005, upheld the Article 1F finding but quashed the decisions for failure to assess whether Article 3 lastingly prevented expulsion. A fresh decision of October 2005 maintained the exclusion and found no Article 3 risk. The authorities noted that the first applicant had worked without difficulty for mujahideen governor Ismail Khan after 1992, that the general situation had improved, that Taliban insurgents were not concentrated in Herat, that the 1995 judgment was unlikely to be known or executed by current authorities, and that he had obtained a passport in 1999 from an embassy still representing the former Rabbani government. No family links to the communist regime were alleged. The Regional Court dismissed a further appeal in August 2006; no further domestic remedy existed.

After the couple’s divorce the second and third applicants lodged a fresh claim in 2008, which was granted in 2009 on the ground that a single woman and child would face particular hardship in Afghanistan. The first applicant remained subject to the exclusion and the expulsion order. The Court was therefore required to examine whether, on the facts as they stood, his return would give rise to a real risk under Articles 2 and 3.
001-160315:
**CASE OF KIRAKOSYAN v. ARMENIA (No. 2) (Application no. 24723/05)**

The applicant, Lavrenti Kirakosyan, an Armenian national born in 1960 and living in Karakert, headed local offices of the opposition National Democratic Union party. In March–April 2004 he participated in opposition protest rallies criticizing irregularities in the 2003 presidential election. On 10 April 2004 he was arrested, charged administratively with disobeying police orders, and sentenced that day by the Armavir Regional Court to 10 days’ detention, which he served in Ejmiatsin.

On 20 April 2004, hours before his sentence expired, the same court granted an investigator’s motion (lodged that day) for a search of his home. The warrant cited an incident on 27 March 2004 in which two men allegedly used a weapon while inflicting violence on local officials. “Operative information” suggested they had given the weapon to the applicant, a member of the Union of Yezidis, who might have hidden it (or other relevant items) at his home. Criminal proceedings had already been opened over the incident. The warrant could be appealed within 15 days.

The official search record stated that seven Baghramyan police officers, with two neighbour attesting witnesses (G.G. and M.S.), searched the house from 5.10 p.m. to 6.55 p.m. The applicant was asked to surrender any illegal weapon; he denied possessing illegal objects. A plastic bag containing a cannabis-like herb was found in a hallway boiler. The applicant said he did not know what it was or who owned it and refused to sign the record.

The applicant and the witnesses alleged a different sequence. Police escorted him home from detention. He found his pregnant wife in a critical condition (apparently miscarrying) and his infant son crying; she fainted on seeing him. A doctor and female neighbours arrived. Officers then briefly showed him the warrant and began searching. The applicant claimed the two witnesses (one a disabled war veteran, the other 74 years old) were summoned only after the search had started. More than ten officers, using two trained dogs, searched the house, then the yard and outbuildings. The front door was left open with people, including officers, entering and leaving. After finding nothing outside, officers announced a second indoor search (to which G.G. objected). The bag was then “found.” The witnesses said their objections were not recorded and they were pressured into signing the record.

The applicant alleged he was returned to the police station, where the chief offered to drop the matter if he resigned from his party; he refused. He claimed he was held overnight, given a meal that made him violently ill (allegedly laced with drugs), and required an ambulance.

On 21 April 2004 proceedings were opened against him for illegal drug possession (Article 268 § 2 of the Criminal Code). He was formally arrested that evening, subjected to a forensic toxicological examination (urine sample taken; he alleged he received no copy of the decision), and questioned (denying the charges). A lawyer was engaged. The substance (approx. 59 g) was confirmed as cannabis. On 23 April he was charged and detained; a toxicology report later indicated cannabis traces in his urine.

The defence repeatedly challenged the search: motions and complaints to the prosecutor (23 and 27 April, 7 May, 9 June 2004) alleged the warrant lacked proper grounds, the search involved numerous procedural violations (warrant not properly presented/signed, witnesses not present from the start, objections unrecorded, possible planting of evidence, failure to question neighbours/doctor or hold confrontations), and the bag had been planted. A request for further forensic examination of the bag was refused. Police allegedly pressured the witnesses not to attend confrontations.

At trial the defence moved to exclude the search results as unlawfully obtained (Article 105 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). The Armavir Regional Court did not rule on the motion. On 22 June 2004 it convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 1½ years’ imprisonment, relying on police and witness testimony plus the urine analysis. The two attesting witnesses testified they had followed officers as best they could; G.G. helped retrieve the dusty bag and plate from the boiler; neither recalled being informed of their right to have objections recorded.

The Court of Appeal (10 August 2004) upheld the conviction, finding no significant procedural violations (relying on the same evidence except police testimony). No timely further appeal was lodged, so the judgment became final. The applicant was released on parole on 6 September 2004. A later appeal on points of law (15 November 2004) alleging the same violations was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 10 December 2004, which found no significant procedural flaws requiring remittal.

The alleged violations centred on an unlawful search (insufficient grounds based on unparticularised “operative information,” plus multiple execution irregularities under Articles 225–231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) whose results were admitted as evidence despite defence motions, contrary to Articles 105–106.

**CASE OF KIRAKOSYAN v. ARMENIA (No. 2) (Application no. 24723/05)**

The applicant, Lavrenti Kirakosyan (born 1960), an Armenian national and opposition activist heading local offices of the National Democratic Union since 1997, alleged an unlawful search of his home (as to both its legal grounds and manner of execution) whose results were used as evidence against him in subsequent criminal proceedings.

In March–April 2004, opposition parties organised protest rallies in Yerevan criticising alleged irregularities in the February–March 2003 presidential election. The applicant participated. On 10 April 2004 at 5.10 p.m. he was arrested and, that same day, sentenced by the Armavir Regional Court to 10 days’ administrative detention for disobeying police officers. He served the sentence in Ejmiatsin.

On 20 April 2004 the same court granted an investigator’s motion (apparently lodged the same day) for a search of the applicant’s home in Karakert village. The warrant recited that on 27 March 2004 two residents had used violence against local officials and that “operative information” indicated they had given a weapon to the applicant (a member of the Union of Yezidis) who might have hidden it, together with other relevant objects, in one of his homes. Criminal proceedings had been opened on that date. The warrant was appealable within 15 days.

The applicant stated that, several hours before his administrative sentence expired, he was taken to the Baghramyan Police Department and then escorted home by at least ten officers. The official search record states that seven officers conducted the search from 5.10 p.m. to 6.55 p.m. in the presence of two neighbouring attesting witnesses (G.G. and M.S.). The applicant was asked to surrender an illegal weapon; he denied possessing anything illegal. A plastic bag containing a cannabis-like herb (later confirmed as approximately 59 grams of cannabis) was found in a hallway boiler. The applicant refused to sign the record.

According to the applicant and the two witnesses (whose statements were appended to the application), he arrived to find his pregnant wife in a critical condition (apparently suffering a miscarriage) and their one-year-old son crying; she fainted and a doctor and female neighbours attended. The search warrant was briefly shown. The witnesses were invited only after the search had begun; G.G. was a seriously disabled war veteran and M.S. was 74. More than ten officers and two dogs searched the house, yard and outbuildings. The front door was left open, with people (including officers) coming and going. After finding nothing outside, officers re-searched the house over G.G.’s objection and then “discovered” the bag. The witnesses’ objections were not recorded and they were pressured to sign the record.

The applicant was returned to the police station, where he alleged he was offered a deal to abandon his political activities in exchange for no further action on the cannabis; he refused. He further alleged he was kept overnight, given a meal that made him ill (vomiting and loss of consciousness), and that the meal had been laced with a drug.

On 21 April 2004 criminal proceedings were opened against him for illegal drug possession (Article 268 § 2 of the Criminal Code). He was formally arrested that evening. A urine sample taken that day later showed traces of cannabis consumption. He denied the allegations. On 23 April he was charged and remanded in custody. His lawyer repeatedly complained to the prosecutor that the search lacked proper grounds, had been executed with numerous procedural violations (including possible planting of the bag), that the investigator had not investigated these claims (e.g., by questioning neighbours or the doctor present, or holding confrontations), and that the attesting witnesses had been pressured. Requests for further forensic examination of the bag and contents were refused.

The case reached the Armavir Regional Court, where the defence moved to exclude the search results as unlawfully obtained. The court never ruled on the motion. Both attesting witnesses testified: they had followed officers as best they could; G.G. helped retrieve a dusty bag and even dustier plate from the boiler; they did not recall being told of their right to record objections; the applicant refused to sign, saying the bag was not his. On 22 June 2004 the court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 18 months’ imprisonment, relying inter alia on the officers’ testimony, the witnesses’ accounts and the urine analysis.

On appeal the defence reiterated that the warrant was based on fabricated material, that the search violated procedure (warrant not properly presented or signed for, objections unrecorded) and that police officers’ testimony on their official duties should not have been relied upon. On 10 August 2004 the Criminal and Military Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding no significant procedural violations (relying on the same evidence except the officers’ testimony). No further appeal was lodged in time, so the judgment became final. The applicant was released on parole on 6 September 2004. A later cassation appeal raising the search irregularities was dismissed on 10 December 2004 on the ground that no significant violations requiring remittal had occurred.

The 2004 Annual Report of Armenia’s Human Rights Defender cited the case as an example of a court failing to address a motion to declare search-derived evidence inadmissible despite alleged procedural defects (insufficient witnesses and officers not remaining visible to them). Domestic law (Code of Criminal Procedure) required a judicial warrant for a home search based on sufficient grounds, presence of attesting witnesses and the occupant (or adult family member), presentation of the warrant against signature, recording of all actions and objections, and exclusion of evidence obtained in violation of investigative procedure.

In Kirakosyan v. Armenia (No. 2) (Application no. 24723/05), the applicant, a 1960-born opposition activist heading local offices of the National Democratic Union, alleged an unlawful home search (on grounds and execution) whose results were used against him criminally. Amid 2004 post-election protests he attended, he claimed authorities targeted supporters.

On 10 April 2004 he was arrested at 5:10 p.m. for disobeying police and given 10 days’ administrative detention in Ejmiatsin. On 20 April, hours before release, the Armavir Regional Court authorised a search of his Karakert home. The warrant cited a 27 March incident in which two men allegedly assaulted village officials while armed, then passed the weapon to the applicant for hiding; criminal proceedings existed and “sufficient grounds” existed to expect an illegal weapon, ammunition or other items there.

Escorted home by at least ten officers, the applicant found his pregnant wife in distress (apparent miscarriage) and infant son crying; she fainted and a doctor plus neighbours attended. The warrant was shown briefly. Officially, seven officers searched 5:10–6:55 p.m. with two neighbour witnesses (G.G., a disabled veteran; M.S., aged 74). After the applicant denied possessing illegal items, a bag containing ~59 g of cannabis was found in a hallway boiler; he refused to sign the record, saying he knew nothing of it.

He and the witnesses alleged the search started before they were invited, involved over ten officers plus dogs, left the door open (people entering/exiting), found nothing initially, then resumed inside over objection, discovering the bag. Objections went unrecorded and witnesses were pressured to sign. Returned to the station, he was allegedly offered impunity if he quit the party (he refused) and, after a meal, became violently ill, requiring an ambulance; he claimed the food was drugged.

On 21 April proceedings opened for illegal drug possession. He was arrested, a urine sample showed cannabis traces, and he was charged and detained on 23 April. His lawyer repeatedly complained the warrant lacked real grounds (fabricated “operative information”) and the search violated procedure (CCP Arts. 225, 227–228, 230: warrant presentation/signature, contemporaneous witnesses, record of objections, presence of family). He alleged planting, sought further forensics (refused), and asked that neighbours, the doctor and witnesses be examined or confronted; investigators ignored this. A motion to exclude the search fruits as inadmissible (Art. 105) received no ruling.

At trial the witnesses described retrieving a dusty bag (the plate dustier) and confirmed the applicant’s denial of ownership, but recalled little about objection rights. On 22 June 2004 the Regional Court convicted him (1.5 years) on the officers’ and witnesses’ testimony plus the urine result. Appeals reiterated the defects and argued police testimony could not rebut the irregularities; both the Court of Appeal (10 August) and Court of Cassation (10 December) found no significant violations. He was paroled on 6 September. Armenia’s Human Rights Defender later cited the case as an example of courts ignoring inadmissibility motions despite non-compliant searches.

The case of Neškoska v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (no. 60333/13) was brought by the mother of M.N., a 21-year-old killed on 6 June 2011. She alleged under Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention that the investigation into her son's death was ineffective and that she lacked an effective remedy.

The killing occurred around 12.20 a.m. at Skopje's central square amid post-election celebrations and a cultural event. I.S., an off-duty member of the Ministry of the Interior's Special Police Forces Unit attending privately, confronted M.N. after the latter tried to climb a podium to approach politicians. After a warning, M.N. fled. I.S. chased him, struck the back of his neck (causing him to fall and hit his head), then punched and kicked him repeatedly despite pleas to stop. M.N. died at 12.30 a.m. from brain haemorrhage due to severe injuries, as confirmed by a 6 June 2011 forensic report. Initial Ministry statements were conflicting.

The incident triggered 40 days of protests involving thousands, evolving into the "Stop Police Brutality" movement. Over 6,000 signed a petition demanding the truth, punishment of those responsible, and reforms to police accountability. The Ombudsman later described the events as resulting from irresponsible police conduct.

Proceedings against I.S. began promptly. On 8 June 2011 the public prosecutor sought an investigation. I.S. surrendered on 7 June after an identity parade. The Professional Standards Inspectorate reported that I.S. had been off duty after midnight, that two uniformed officers (Z.J. and P.K.) arrived post-incident, that I.S. and others (including civilian V.B.) moved the body to nearby greenery to aid ambulance access, and that I.S. then left. An indictment for murder followed on 3 October 2011. The trial court examined over 30 witnesses (including Z.J., P.K., V.B., and medical staff who noted no visible injuries initially), identity-parade records, expert evidence, and photographs. On 16 January 2012 I.S. was convicted of murder and sentenced to 14 years' imprisonment; the applicant (who had joined as injured party) was directed to seek civil damages separately. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 9 July 2012; the Supreme Court dismissed an extraordinary review request on 7 May 2013.

On 12 October 2011 the applicant filed a criminal complaint against Z.J., P.K., V.B. and an unidentified officer (later D.I.) alleging they assisted the perpetrator after the crime, failed to report it or identify I.S., allowed him to leave, moved the body to conceal evidence, and (via D.I.) falsely suggested a drug overdose, thereby deterring an immediate judicial on-site inspection. The public prosecutor rejected the complaint on 29 December 2011, finding no intent to obstruct: the officers arrived after the assault, believed M.N. was merely ill, acted to facilitate medical help, reported the incident, and did not conceal evidence. A higher prosecutor confirmed this on 12 March 2012. The applicant then acted as subsidiary prosecutor and lodged an indictment, but a trial-court panel rejected it on 10 May 2012 for lack of grounds; the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 10 September 2012.

In 2015 the applicant submitted leaked audio recordings of high-ranking officials discussing the perpetrator shortly after the incident. These facts underpin the claims of an ineffective investigation (particularly regarding possible official involvement, initial shortcomings, and failure to pursue others) and the absence of a remedy.

The applicant, Lenka Neškoska, is the mother of M.N., a 21-year-old killed on 6 June 2011 at around 12:20 a.m. in Skopje’s central square during post-election celebrations coinciding with a cultural event. I.S., a Special Police Forces member off duty and in civilian clothes, killed M.N. after the latter tried to climb a podium near high-ranking politicians. I.S. warned M.N., who fled; I.S. pursued, struck him on the back of the neck (causing him to fall and hit his head), then punched and kicked him despite pleas to stop. A post-mortem established death at 12:30 a.m. from brain haemorrhage due to severe injuries. Courts later confirmed I.S. attended privately, not on duty.

The Ministry’s Professional Standards Inspectorate (PSI) reported on 28 June that I.S. had left duty at midnight, gone to the square, argued with M.N., chased and beaten him, attempted resuscitation with water, then with others moved the body to nearby greenery to aid ambulance access before leaving. Uniformed officers Z.J. and P.K. (securing the event) arrived later; I.S. had earlier identified himself to them as Prime Minister’s security and asked them to watch M.N. They called emergency services after I.S. claimed M.N. had fallen ill, noticed no visible injuries, and stayed until the ambulance arrived. Civilian V.B. (an electricity-company employee) witnessed the beating, helped move the body, and remained until medics came; he too saw no injuries. Ambulance staff (L.K. and V.C.) confirmed no visible injuries. I.S. surrendered on 7 June; an identity parade followed. On 3 October 2011 I.S. was indicted for murder.

The Skopje Court of First Instance heard over 30 witnesses, examined identity-parade records, medical and other expert evidence, photographs and documents. On 16 January 2012 it convicted I.S. of murder and imposed 14 years’ imprisonment, directing the applicant (who had joined as injured party) to seek damages separately. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and sentence on 9 July 2012; the Supreme Court dismissed I.S.’s extraordinary review request on 7 May 2013.

Meanwhile, on 12 October 2011 the applicant filed a criminal complaint against Z.J., P.K., V.B. and unidentified officer D.I. (later identified), alleging they had assisted the offender after the crime and failed to report it (Criminal Code Arts. 364–365). She claimed the officers failed to identify or detain I.S. (who left), V.B. helped conceal the crime by moving the body, and D.I. wrongly told the prosecutor and investigating judge that death resulted from overdose, so neither attended the scene. On 29 December 2011 the prosecutor rejected the complaint: the officers arrived after the assault, believed M.N. merely ill, acted to save him, and reported the incident; V.B. likewise lacked intent to assist a known crime; D.I. reported “unknown death” possibly involving drugs. No obstruction occurred; the inspection unit attended. The higher prosecutor confirmed this on 12 March 2012.

The applicant then took over as subsidiary prosecutor and filed an indictment. On 10 May 2012 a trial-court panel, following the adjudicating-panel president’s recommendation, rejected it as unfounded. The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 10 September 2012 (served 20 March 2013).

The Ombudsman, writing to M.N.’s brother in September 2011, described the incident as resulting from irresponsible, unprofessional police conduct. In June 2015 the applicant submitted leaked audio (publicly released by the opposition in May 2015) of conversations among high-ranking officials shortly after the killing that allegedly concerned the perpetrator’s identity.

Domestic law (2005 Criminal Proceedings Act) obliged the public prosecutor to prosecute where sufficient evidence existed of an ex-officio offence. An injured party could assume the role of subsidiary prosecutor if the public prosecutor declined, enjoying similar rights except those reserved to the State.

The applicant, Lenka Neškoska, is the mother of M.N., a 21-year-old killed on 6 June 2011. Around 12.20 a.m. at Skopje’s central square during election celebrations coinciding with a cultural event, I.S.—a Special Police Forces member attending privately and off-duty—killed M.N. A post-mortem found numerous severe injuries, with death from brain haemorrhage at 12.30 a.m.

M.N.’s brother asked the Ministry’s Professional Standards Inspectorate to examine officers’ actions, alleging assistance to an offender and failure to report. The Inspectorate confirmed I.S. had left duty at 12.10 a.m., described the assault and subsequent (ineffective) revival attempts, noted two uniformed officers arriving later (after which I.S. left), and recorded an on-site inspection, autopsy, witness interviews, I.S.’s surrender, an identity parade, a murder complaint, and I.S.’s remand and dismissal.

The Ombudsman later criticised police unprofessionalism. On 3 October the prosecutor indicted I.S. for murder. The trial court heard over 30 witnesses plus extensive evidence. Uniformed officers Z.J. and P.K. said I.S. (claiming to be Prime Ministerial security) had asked them to watch M.N.; they later found I.S. and others attempting resuscitation and claiming illness, then moved the body for ambulance access. Eyewitness V.B. described the pursuit, blows, unconsciousness and movement of the body; ambulance staff saw no visible injuries. On 16 January 2012 I.S. was convicted of murder and sentenced to 14 years (applicant joined as victim’s representative and was directed to civil damages). Appeals failed, with the Supreme Court dismissing extraordinary review in May 2013.

Meanwhile the applicant complained against Z.J., P.K., V.B. and (later-identified) officer D.I., alleging they allowed I.S. to leave unidentified, moved the body to conceal the crime, and falsely suggested a drug overdose (preventing prosecutor/judge attendance). The prosecutor rejected this on 29 December 2011: the officers arrived post-assault, believed it was illness, acted to aid the ambulance, and reported the death; there was no intent to obstruct. The applicant then acted as subsidiary prosecutor, but a trial-court panel (May 2012) rejected the indictment, following the prosecutor; the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal (served March 2013).

In 2015 the applicant submitted leaked audio of officials discussing the perpetrator shortly after the killing.

The prosecutor could dismiss complaints lacking reasonable suspicion and notify the injured party accordingly.

These facts underpin the applicant’s Articles 2 and 13 complaints of an ineffective investigation into the death and lack of remedy.
001-160377:
The case of Partei Die Friesen v. Germany (Application no. 65480/10) concerns a complaint by the political party “Partei Die Friesen” (founded 2007 in Aurich) that the 5% electoral threshold applied in Lower Saxony parliamentary elections discriminated against it as the representative of the Frisian ethnic minority. The party confines its activities to Lower Saxony, home to an estimated 100,000 people of Frisian origin (out of a total population of approximately 7.9 million). East Frisians share linguistic and cultural ties with Frisian groups in the Netherlands and Schleswig-Holstein, though they have largely ceased using their language.

Lower Saxony’s electoral system allocates parliamentary seats (beyond those won by constituency majorities) by the D’Hondt method of proportional representation. Section 33(3) of the Lower Saxony Electoral Law and Article 8(3) of the Land Constitution restrict seats to parties obtaining at least 5% of valid votes. In 2007 the applicant party unsuccessfully requested an exemption from this threshold for the forthcoming elections. In the 27 January 2008 elections it received 10,069 votes (approximately 0.3%), a figure insufficient for a seat even without the threshold.

The party lodged an objection to the election result, arguing that the Frisians constitute a national minority under the Council of Europe Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities and that the threshold factually excluded it from parliament while other small parties remained theoretically able to meet it. The case of Partei Die Friesen v. Germany (no. 65480/10) was brought by a political party founded in 2007 in Aurich, Lower Saxony. Article 15 of the Framework Convention, which requires states to create conditions for effective minority participation in public affairs, leaves Contracting Parties a wide margin of appreciation as to the means employed. The Court therefore found it unnecessary to decide whether Frisians constitute a national minority or whether the applicant party represents them.

Supporting instruments include Germany’s ratification declaration, an Advisory Committee commentary noting that threshold exemptions can facilitate minority representation, and a Venice Commission report recommending that electoral thresholds should not impair minorities’ chances of obtaining seats.

**The applicants, Spaska Mitrova (mother, first applicant, Macedonian/Bulgarian national born 1983) and her daughter Suzana Savik (second applicant, born 2007), alleged that the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia violated their Article 8 right to respect for family life.** The first applicant married V. Savik in 2006; their daughter was born in February 2007. The Gevgelija Court of First Instance dissolved the marriage on 10 May 2007 and awarded the mother custody.

The Gevgelija Social Welfare Centre issued successive contact orders for the father. An initial May 2007 order allowed two-hour weekly visits at the mother’s home. The mother’s refusals in June 2007 led to her first conviction under Article 198 of the Criminal Code (unlawful prevention of contact or enforcement of a custody order), resulting in a six-month suspended prison sentence. Further refusals produced a second conviction in December 2007 (eight-month sentence suspended for two years), with an order to permit contact or face enforcement of the sentence. The Centre then moved meetings to its premises (five hours weekly from November 2007) and later extended them (full days from April 2008), citing the child’s need for an emotional bond with the father and the mother’s obstruction. A May 2008 enforcement order required the mother to produce the child on 2 June 2008, warning of criminal liability and possible temporary custody transfer to the father; an appeal would not suspend enforcement.

Non-compliance with the April/May 2008 orders prompted a third prosecution. On 10 July 2008 Judge I.S. (who had sat in the prior cases) convicted the mother of the 2 June 2008 failure and sentenced her to three months’ immediate imprisonment. The court treated the earlier convictions as aggravating, found no mitigating factors, and held that suspended sentences had failed to deter her. Appeals to the Skopje Court of Appeal (December 2008) and Supreme Court (May 2009) failed. Execution was postponed because of the child’s illness; the mother served the sentence from 30 July to 8 October 2009.

On the day she began the sentence, the Centre granted the father temporary custody (Family Act s. 87(6)) because of the mother’s ongoing obstruction and incarceration; no contact rights were specified for her. After release the mother sought contact. The Centre later arranged meetings (February 2010: Fridays 10 a.m.–3 p.m.; March 2010: every second weekend). She first saw the child on 19 February 2010.

Meanwhile the father applied in August 2008 to vary the 2007 custody order. After an initial grant to him was remitted, the first-instance court in October 2010 retained custody with the mother, finding both parents capable, the mother’s past non-cooperation attributable to distrust rather than incapacity, and current parental communication sufficient. The Court of Appeal upheld this in February 2011. On 1 March 2012 the Supreme Court reversed on an appeal on points of law, awarding custody to the father. It held that the mother’s persistent non-compliance (three convictions and Centre findings) had deprived the child of the father’s care, that the child’s age was not decisive, and that the father’s cooperative conduct better served the child’s development and right to both parents.

A July 2012 Centre order, based on parental agreement, provided that the child would live with the mother Monday–Friday and with the father on specified weekends and holidays; the parties confirmed compliance. Subsequent custody proceedings initiated by the mother remained pending.

These events—repeated criminal sanctions culminating in the mother’s imprisonment while the child was an infant, the unaccompanied transfer of custody during detention, delays in restoring the mother’s contact, and the Supreme Court’s 2012 custody reversal predicated on the enforcement history—formed the core of the alleged Article 8 interferences with family life.

**Summary of key facts in Mitrova and Savik v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (ECHR, 2016)**

The applicants, Spaska Mitrova (first applicant, a Macedonian and Bulgarian national born 1983) and her daughter Suzana Savik (second applicant, born February 2007), alleged a violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for family life) arising from contact arrangements, criminal sanctions against the mother for non-compliance, her imprisonment, and related custody changes. The first applicant married V. Savik in October 2006; their marriage was dissolved by the Gevgelija Court of First Instance on 10 May 2007, with custody awarded to the mother.

On 31 May 2007 the Gevgelija Social Welfare Centre ordered the father two hours of contact every Friday at the mother’s home. The mother’s refusals at scheduled meetings in June 2007 led to her conviction on 2 July 2007 under Article 198 of the Criminal Code (unlawfully preventing a child from being with an authorised person or hindering a custody order). She received a six-month prison sentence suspended for one year. Further refusals from July to October 2007 produced a second conviction on 17 December 2007 (eight months suspended for two years), plus an order to permit contact within 30 days or face revocation of the suspension. Both judgments (by Judge I.S.) dismissed her defences concerning lack of notice, the child’s health, the father’s alleged intoxication or disinterest, and harassment.

The Centre later increased contact (November 2007: five hours weekly at the Centre; April 2008: 09:00–16:00 every Monday), citing the need to build an emotional bond given the child’s age and breastfeeding status, and warning of criminal proceedings or temporary custody transfer. The mother failed to comply fully. An enforcement order of 28 May 2008 (appealed without suspensory effect) required production of the child on 2 June 2008. Non-attendance prompted new charges. On 10 July 2008 Judge I.S. convicted her again and imposed an unsuspended three-month prison term, relying on prior convictions as aggravating and finding no mitigating factors; appeals and an extraordinary review were dismissed. She served the sentence from 30 July to 8 October 2009 (execution briefly postponed due to the child’s illness).

On 30 July 2009 the Centre, of its own motion, granted the father temporary custody pending his August 2008 custody application, noting the mother’s recent non-compliance, the family’s hiding, the child’s health needs, and the incarceration; no contact rights were specified for the mother. After release she requested contact; arrangements were eventually set (first meeting February 2010; later every second weekend). The father obtained full custody from the Supreme Court on 1 March 2012 (reversing lower courts), which emphasised the mother’s three convictions, persistent obstruction of the child’s right to both parents, and the Centre’s expert view that the father’s custody better served the child’s development and dual-parental contact. The child’s age and biological link to the mother were held insufficient to outweigh these factors.

Later Centre orders (July 2012, based on parental agreement) allowed the mother weekday residence with the child plus holidays; the parties complied. Further custody litigation by the mother remained pending. The facts centre on successive criminal prosecutions and imprisonment of the custodial mother of a very young (initially breastfed) child for contact non-compliance, the resulting physical separation, unnotified or delayed contact arrangements during and after detention, and the subsequent transfer of custody justified primarily by that non-compliance and the Centre’s assessments.

The case of Mitrova and Savik v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 42534/09) concerns alleged violations of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The first applicant, Spaska Mitrova (Macedonian and Bulgarian national, born 1983), is the mother of the second applicant, Suzana Savik (born February 2007). The family lived in Gevgelija.

Mitrova married V. Savik in October 2006. Their marriage was dissolved by the Gevgelija Court of First Instance in May 2007, with custody of the infant daughter awarded to the mother. Shortly afterwards, on the father's application, the Gevgelija Social Welfare Centre ordered contact: two hours every Friday at the mother's home. The mother refused four meetings in June 2007. She was convicted under Article 198 of the Criminal Code of hindering a child's contact with a parent and received a six-month prison sentence, suspended for one year. The court cited the child's age and rejected her defences (lack of notice, the child's health, and the father's lack of interest). A second conviction followed in December 2007 for further refusals (July–October 2007), resulting in an eight-month sentence suspended for two years, with an order to permit contact within 30 days or face enforcement of the sentence. The same judge (I.S.) sat in both cases.

The Centre then increased contact to five hours weekly at its premises (November 2007) and later to a full day each Monday (April 2008), citing the need to build an emotional bond and protect the child's rights. The mother continued to miss meetings. An enforcement order of 28 May 2008 required her to produce the child on 2 June 2008, warning of criminal liability and possible transfer of custody. She did not comply. In July 2008 the public prosecutor charged her; after a hearing at which she remained silent, Judge I.S. sentenced her to three months' immediate imprisonment, noting her two prior convictions and the ineffectiveness of suspended sentences. Appeals and an extraordinary review were dismissed. Sentence execution was postponed once for the child's illness; she served from 30 July to 8 October 2009.

On the day imprisonment began, the Centre, acting of its own motion, granted the father temporary custody pending his August 2008 custody application, citing the mother's non-compliance and the child's concealment. No contact rights were specified for the mother. After release she encountered delays: she was not immediately served with the custody order, invitations to interviews were missed, and she refused some notifications. Contact was eventually arranged from February 2010 (initially Fridays, later alternate weekends).

In the custody proceedings the first-instance court initially awarded the father custody (March 2010) but this was set aside. After a remittal it dismissed the father's claim (October 2010), finding both parents fit and that the child's young age favoured remaining with the mother; an appeal was upheld. The Supreme Court, however, in March 2012 overturned the lower courts, awarding custody to the father. It relied on the mother's repeated non-compliance, her three convictions, and the Centre's expert view that her conduct had deprived the child of a relationship with both parents. The first applicant was ordered to pay modest maintenance. Subsequent Centre orders (with parental consent) allowed the mother weekday residence with the child and shared holidays. Later custody applications by the mother remained pending at the time of the facts.

The applicants complained that the criminal convictions, imprisonment, and resulting transfer of custody constituted a disproportionate interference with their family life.
