The case of Dallas v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 38395/12) concerns a Greek national, Theodora Dallas, who was convicted of common-law contempt of court for conducting internet research while serving as a juror. She alleged a violation of Article 7 of the Convention, claiming that her conviction related to conduct that did not constitute a criminal offence at the time it occurred, due to insufficient clarity and foreseeability in the applicable law.

Dallas was summoned for jury service at Luton Crown Court on 4 July 2011. Jurors received multiple warnings against internet research: a video presentation, verbal instructions from the jury officer, and notices in the waiting room stating that using the internet to research cases or defendants could constitute contempt of court, punishable by fine or imprisonment. After selection for a trial involving a defendant charged with grievous bodily harm with intent, Dallas took an oath to try the case according to the evidence. The trial judge then directed the jury not to discuss the case or conduct any independent research, including on the internet, Facebook or Twitter, emphasising that verdicts must be based solely on courtroom evidence. He referenced a recent juror who had faced severe consequences for similar conduct.

On 5 July 2011 the judge admitted evidence of the defendant’s previous conviction for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, without disclosing a related rape charge of which the defendant had been acquitted. The jury retired on 6 July. After court rose, another juror reported that Dallas had conducted internet research revealing the rape allegation and had shared this with the jury. The trial judge discharged the jury and aborted the trial.

Police interviewed Dallas under caution. She stated that, as a Greek speaker, she had searched “grievous bodily harm” and then “Luton” to understand the charge and its local frequency, inadvertently encountering a newspaper article about the defendant. She denied searching by name, claimed no recollection of the judge’s specific prohibition on internet research, and insisted she had no intention of disobeying instructions. She admitted disclosing the information to fellow jurors. Statements from other jurors confirmed that most had immediately recognised the material as extraneous and contrary to the directions they had received.

The Attorney General sought Dallas’s committal for contempt on the basis that her research and disclosure created a substantial risk of seriously prejudicing the administration of justice. In the Divisional Court, the parties initially debated whether the offence required specific intent to impede or prejudice justice (or merely foresight of that risk). After evidence and submissions, the court formulated the test as whether a juror had deliberately disobeyed a judicial direction, thereby creating a risk of prejudice. The court rejected Dallas’s account of accidentally stumbling upon the article as incredible. It found, to the criminal standard, that she knew of the unequivocal direction not to seek internet information, appreciated it as an order, and deliberately disobeyed it. By arming herself with extraneous information that could influence her verdict, and then disclosing it, she caused actual prejudice: the jury was discharged, a retrial ordered, the complainant forced to testify again, and public resources wasted. Dallas received a six-month custodial sentence (serving three months).

Dallas argued that this test reformulated the common law after the close of evidence, departing from authorities requiring specific intent to prejudice justice, and treating a mere “direction” as equivalent to an “order.” She contended this lacked foreseeability under Article 7 (and fairness under Article 6). The Supreme Court refused permission to appeal, holding that any distinction between “direction” and “order” was untenable in context and that deliberate disobedience of a specific judicial order not to use the internet constituted contempt at common law.

Domestic authorities (including Attorney-General v Fraill) confirmed that jurors’ internet research into defendants constituted contempt because it breached the oath and directions requiring verdicts based solely on courtroom evidence. Subsequent Law Commission analysis highlighted residual uncertainties about the precise scope of juror-research contempt, leading to a statutory offence in 2015. The ECtHR ultimately examined whether the common-law offence, as applied, satisfied Article 7’s requirements of accessibility, precision and foreseeability.

After the jury retired on 6 July, another juror reported that Dallas had researched the internet and discovered the rape allegation. The judge discharged the jury and aborted the trial. Statements from the remaining jurors confirmed that Dallas had told them of her research during deliberations.

An article referring to the defendant appeared in the results. She denied searching by name, claimed she did not recall any instruction forbidding research, and insisted she had had no intention of disobeying the judge.

The Attorney General applied to the Divisional Court for committal, alleging that Dallas’s internet research and subsequent disclosure to fellow jurors had created a substantial risk of seriously prejudicing the administration of justice. In written submissions the parties initially framed the common-law test as requiring an act or omission creating a real risk of prejudice, done with the specific intent to create that risk. During the hearing the court proposed, and both sides ultimately accepted, a reformulated test: that it is contempt for a juror deliberately to disobey the judge’s direction and thereby create a risk of prejudice to the due administration of justice.

The Divisional Court rejected Dallas’s account that she had “stumbled across” the information. It found, to the criminal standard, that she knew the judge had given an unequivocal order not to seek information about the case on the internet, appreciated that it was an order, and deliberately disobeyed it. The research itself, even before disclosure, had already prejudiced the administration of justice; the subsequent sharing of the information compounded the prejudice, necessitating a retrial. She was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment (of which she served three).

The Supreme Court refused permission, holding that the distinction between a “direction” and an “order” was untenable and that deliberate disobedience of a specific judicial instruction not to use the internet in connection with the case unquestionably constituted contempt at common law. Subsequent domestic cases (e.g., Attorney General v Davey and Beard) treated the four-element analysis used in Dallas as the ordinary approach to juror internet research. A Law Commission report later identified remaining uncertainties in the common-law framework, leading to the creation of a specific statutory offence in 2015.

001-160990:
The case of Prade v. Germany (Application no. 7215/10) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). The applicant, Hans-Otto Prade (born 1955), a German civil servant and lawyer for the Hamburg tax authorities, claimed that evidence coincidentally discovered during an unlawful house search had been improperly admitted against him in subsequent criminal proceedings.

In 1995 the applicant, then a board member of the “Red Aid” association, opened a bank account for it; the account details were publicly available. In 2003 police investigated an eBay sale of a counterfeit watch linked to an email address registered to that account (and used for other sales of computer programmes). Although a third party, Mr D., was initially implicated, he was cleared. On 21 September 2004 the Munich District Court issued a search warrant for the applicant’s Hamburg flat (and those of other authorised account users) on suspicion of copyright piracy. The warrant authorised seizure of computers and documents relating to the sales.

The search on 8 December 2004 yielded none of the targeted items. Police instead discovered, coincidentally, 463.732 grams of hashish (containing 39.09 grams of THC, sufficient for 2,606 consumption units) plus two defective scales. Piracy proceedings were discontinued, but the applicant was charged with possessing and trafficking a substantial quantity of drugs.

The applicant challenged the warrant. On 13 November 2005 the Federal Constitutional Court found a violation of Article 13 of the Basic Law (inviolability of the home), quashed the warrant and declared the search unlawful. It held that the weak indications of piracy did not justify so intrusive a measure; less restrictive investigative steps should first have been taken. The court left open whether an initial suspicion had even existed.

In the drug proceedings the Hamburg District Court convicted the applicant on 24 January 2006 solely on the basis of the hashish, imposing a ten-month suspended sentence. The Hamburg Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 5 September 2006 (finding insufficient inquiry into whether the drugs belonged to the applicant, who shared the flat) but ruled the evidence admissible. It applied Federal Constitutional Court case-law that unlawfully obtained evidence is not automatically excluded; a balancing exercise is required. The public interest in prosecuting a serious drug offence involving a substantial quantity outweighed the applicant’s interest in respect for his home, especially as the infringement had not been deliberate or arbitrary.

On remittal the District Court acquitted the applicant on 18 April 2007, holding the violation so severe that the evidence must be excluded. The Regional Court reversed this on 5 October 2007, convicting him of possession in less serious circumstances and imposing a six-month suspended sentence; it treated the Court of Appeal’s earlier admissibility ruling as binding (or, independently, reached the same conclusion after balancing). The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal on 16 September 2008, repeating that the public interest prevailed. A second constitutional complaint was rejected by the Federal Constitutional Court on 2 July 2009: the domestic courts’ balancing had been neither arbitrary nor unreasonable, and the fair-trial principle had been applied without injustice.

Disciplinary proceedings against the applicant as a civil servant were noted but discontinued without sanctions. German law contains no general exclusionary rule for unlawfully obtained evidence (save for confessions obtained by torture). Courts must weigh all evidence to establish guilt, exclusion remaining exceptional and reserved for serious, deliberate or arbitrary breaches affecting the core of private life. Admissibility is decided case-by-case.

Copyright-piracy proceedings were discontinued; new proceedings for possession and trafficking of a substantial quantity of drugs were opened against the applicant.

The applicant challenged the warrant. After unsuccessful complaints to the Munich District and Regional Courts, the Federal Constitutional Court, on 13 November 2005, declared the search unlawful. It held that the warrant violated Article 13 of the Basic Law (inviolability of the home) because the scant indications of copyright piracy were disproportionate to the severe intrusion; less invasive investigative steps should have been taken first. The warrant and lower-court decisions were quashed.

On 29 July 2005 the applicant was indicted in Hamburg for drug offences. On 24 January 2006 the Hamburg District Court convicted him of possession of a substantial quantity of drugs in less serious circumstances and imposed a ten-month suspended sentence, relying exclusively on the hashish found during the search. On appeal the Hamburg Court of Appeal (5 September 2006) quashed the conviction and remitted the case, holding that it had not been established whether the drugs belonged to the applicant rather than a flatmate. It nevertheless ruled the evidence admissible: although the search had seriously infringed the applicant’s rights, the public interest in prosecuting a serious drug offence involving a large quantity outweighed his interest in respect for his home. The violation had not been deliberate or arbitrary, and the quantity of drugs would itself have justified a search. A subsequent constitutional complaint was rejected as inadmissible.

In resumed proceedings the applicant stated that the room containing the drugs was used exclusively by him. On 18 April 2007 the District Court acquitted him, finding the initial suspicion too vague and the rights violation too severe to permit use of the evidence. On prosecution appeal the Hamburg Regional Court (5 October 2007) quashed the acquittal, convicted the applicant and imposed a six-month suspended sentence. It treated the Court of Appeal’s earlier admissibility ruling as binding and, in the alternative, reached the same balancing conclusion. The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal on 16 September 2008, repeating that the public interest prevailed. A second constitutional complaint was rejected on 2 July 2009; the Federal Constitutional Court held that the domestic courts’ balancing exercise was neither arbitrary nor unreasonable and that neither Article 13 of the Basic Law nor the fair-trial guarantee had been infringed.

The case of Prade v. Germany originated in an application by Hans-Otto Prade, a German civil servant and lawyer employed by the Hamburg tax authorities. In 1995, as a board member of the “Red Aid” association, he opened a bank account for the group (to which he and others had access); he left the board in 2000. In 2003, police investigated the sale of a fake watch on eBay. The seller’s email was linked to the Red Aid account, which other eBay users had also cited. A related eBay fee transaction had been protested and reversed. A named individual was questioned and cleared of involvement.

On 21 September 2004 the Munich District Court issued a search warrant for the applicant’s (shared) Hamburg flat on suspicion of copyright piracy through the sale of counterfeit goods. The warrant authorised seizure of computers and documents relating to those sales. The search on 8 December 2004 uncovered none of the sought items. Instead, police coincidentally discovered 463.732 grams of hashish (containing 39.09 grams of THC) and two defective scales—enough for 2,606 consumption units. Copyright proceedings were discontinued; drug-possession and trafficking charges were opened.

The applicant challenged the warrant. Lower courts rejected his complaints, but on 13 November 2005 the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) held the search unlawful and disproportionate under Article 13 of the Basic Law (inviolability of the home). Weak indications of suspicion did not justify the severe intrusion; less intrusive measures should have been exhausted first. The warrant and related decisions were quashed.

Drug proceedings followed. On 24 January 2006 the Hamburg District Court convicted the applicant of possessing a substantial quantity of drugs in less-serious circumstances and imposed a ten-month suspended sentence, relying exclusively on the hashish. The Hamburg Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 5 September 2006 and remitted the case because ownership of the drugs (found in a shared flat) had not been adequately examined. It nevertheless ruled the evidence admissible: after balancing interests, the public interest in prosecuting a serious offence involving a large quantity outweighed the applicant’s rights. There had been no deliberate or arbitrary violation, and the quantity found would theoretically have justified a search. German case-law (FCC and Federal Court of Justice) treats exclusion of unlawfully obtained evidence as exceptional, required only for grave, purposeful breaches or core privacy violations.

A further FCC complaint was rejected as inadmissible. On remittal the applicant stated that the room was exclusively his. The District Court acquitted him on 18 April 2007, holding the infringement (an entirely unjustified warrant based on vague suspicion) so severe that public-interest considerations could not prevail. On prosecution appeal the Regional Court convicted him on 5 October 2007 (six-month suspended sentence), treating the earlier admissibility ruling as binding or independently reaching the same balancing conclusion. The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal on 16 September 2008 after similar balancing. The FCC rejected a constitutional complaint on 2 July 2009, finding the domestic courts’ balancing neither arbitrary nor unreasonable and no violation of fair-trial rights.

Disciplinary proceedings against the applicant as a civil servant were adjourned pending the criminal case, then noted the offence but discontinued without further measures.

German law (Articles 102–108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) permits searches and the incidental seizure of objects indicating other offences (Article 108). There is no general rule excluding unlawfully obtained evidence except in cases of torture or comparable coercion. Courts must consider all available evidence; exclusion remains exceptional and is decided case-by-case.

The applicant alleged that admitting the coincidentally seized drugs—found during a search later declared unlawful and not even covered by the original warrant—rendered his trial unfair under Article 6 § 1, as the conviction rested solely on that evidence.

The case of Meier v. Switzerland (Application no. 10109/14) concerns a Swiss national born in 1946 who, following a 2003 conviction for multiple sexual offences against minors, was placed in preventive detention in 2010 after serving part of a custodial sentence. In December 2011, having reached retirement age, the applicant requested exemption from the statutory obligation to work while detained. Work had to be adapted to individual abilities and could take a therapeutic form. Because prison labour occurred inside a closed system rather than on the open market, ordinary pension-age rules were inapplicable. Voluntary occupation was deemed insufficient to achieve the statutory purposes.

Swiss law (Criminal Code Articles 74, 75, 81 and 90 and the Zürich implementing ordinance) requires all capable prisoners, including those under preventive measures, to perform assigned work matched to their skills and interests. Constitutional provisions protecting dignity and personal liberty were held not to preclude the obligation. A comparative survey of 28 Council of Europe States showed that 16 expressly exempt prisoners of retirement age; the remainder contain no formal prohibition but generally provide medical or individualised exemptions.

The case of Meier v. Switzerland (application no. 10109/14) was brought by Beat Meier, a Swiss national born in 1946 and detained in Regensdorf prison. Prison work is not comparable to employment on the open market, so ordinary pension-age rules do not apply; purely voluntary occupation would not achieve the same aims.

These circumstances constitute the factual matrix of the alleged violations.

The case of Klinkenbuß v. Germany (Application no. 53157/11) concerns a German national, Andreas Klinkenbuß (born 1964), who alleged that his prolonged confinement in a psychiatric hospital violated Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to liberty). The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined the complaint regarding continuation of his detention, communicating it to the German Government in 2014 while declaring other parts of the application inadmissible.

On 21 January 1983, the Münster Regional Court convicted him—then aged 17 at the time of the June 1982 offence—of attempted rape, sexual assault, dangerous assault, attempted murder and assault. Applying juvenile criminal law, it imposed a five-year prison sentence plus indefinite detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. The offence involved forcing a 14-year-old girl into a forest, attempting rape, assaulting her with a stick and attempting to strangle her. The court found diminished responsibility (Article 21) due to infantile brain damage causing a consciousness disorder and sadistic sexual tendencies, amounting to a “serious mental abnormality” (Articles 20–21). A comprehensive personality assessment concluded he posed a public danger of further serious unlawful acts.

Detention in a psychiatric hospital began on 29 January 1983 and has continued since. During 1990 leave, he attacked a 26-year-old cyclist with a knife and tried to force her into a forest; related proceedings were discontinued in light of the prior conviction. Periodic reviews under Articles 67d and 67e of the Criminal Code (requiring at least annual judicial scrutiny of whether detention should be suspended on probation or terminated if the person is no longer expected to reoffend or if continuation is disproportionate) followed. On 5 February 2010 the Paderborn Regional Court ordered continuation, citing the applicant’s refusal of therapeutic discussions and treatment stagnation, with hospital staff indicating that personality changes via sex therapy were no longer feasible.

The impugned 28 January 2011 decision of the same court again ordered continuation. External expert T.’s January 2010 report diagnosed Klinefelter syndrome causing an endocrine personality syndrome with retardation, dissocial and schizoid traits; sadistic paraphilia was unclear. Hormonal, social and psychotherapeutic treatment had yielded partial improvements, but the expert highlighted the applicant’s history of sadistic offences against children, the gravity of the 1983 offence and the 1990 incident. Risk of reoffending under stress from residual sadistic tendencies was difficult to quantify without further therapy. Hospital representatives confirmed the applicant’s limited engagement (occasional psychologist meetings but inability to reflect on offence motives) and the resulting uncertainty about current dangerousness. The court found insufficient probability that he would not reoffend if released, noting possible persistence of sadistic tendencies, absence of proper therapy and hospitalism. Continuation was deemed proportionate given the original offence’s seriousness, the 1990 relapse and expert/staff-confirmed risk.

His April 2011 constitutional complaint to the Federal Constitutional Court argued that 28-plus years of detention based on decades-old events, without ongoing therapy and amid uncertainty as to current dangerousness, was disproportionate and violated liberty and the rule of law. He was being prepared for renewed individual or group therapy but declined offers. He worked in the hospital factory and received occasional escorted family visits. A further continuation order issued on 18 January 2012 (upheld on appeal) cited incurable sadism and high risk of serious offences against life or sexual self-determination.

No maximum duration applies, unlike the ten-year prison maximum for juveniles. These facts formed the basis for assessing whether the continued detention remained lawful under Article 5 § 1.

The case of Klinkenbuß v. Germany (Application no. 53157/11) concerns a German national born in 1964 who has been detained in a psychiatric hospital in Lippstadt since 29 January 1983. Yearly reviews are mandatory; detention must be suspended or terminated if further offences are no longer expected or if continuation becomes disproportionate.

The case of Klinkenbuß v. Germany (Application no. 53157/11) concerns a German national born in 1964 who has been continuously detained in a psychiatric hospital in Lippstadt since 29 January 1983. He alleged that the prolongation of this confinement after more than 28 years violated his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.

The court found diminished criminal responsibility under Article 21 of the Criminal Code, attributing the acts to infantile brain damage that had produced a consciousness disorder and sadistic sexual tendencies amounting to a “serious mental abnormality.” A comprehensive assessment of his personality led the court to conclude that he remained dangerous to the public and therefore ordered his indefinite placement in a psychiatric hospital pursuant to Article 63 of the Criminal Code, in addition to a five-year prison sentence.

In December 1990, while on leave from the hospital, the applicant attacked a 26-year-old cyclist, threatened her with a knife and tried to force her into a forest; criminal proceedings were discontinued in view of the existing detention order. Periodic judicial reviews thereafter confirmed the need for continued hospitalisation. By 2010 the treating institution reported that the applicant had refused therapeutic discussions and that substantial personality change through sex therapy was no longer considered feasible.

On 28 January 2011 the Paderborn Regional Court, relying on an external psychiatric report of 28 January 2010 and statements from hospital staff, ordered continuation of detention under Articles 67d and 67e of the Criminal Code. The expert diagnosed Klinefelter syndrome that had produced an endocrine personality syndrome, retardation, and a dissocial/schizoid personality; it remained unclear whether sadistic paraphilia persisted. Sadistic tendencies could not be excluded; he was not undergoing therapy “in the proper sense” and displayed hospitalism. **Case of Rusu v. Romania (Application no. 25721/04), ECtHR, 8 March 2016 (final 8 June 2016)**

The applicant, Romanian journalist Sergiu-Cristian Rusu, alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). He claimed that domestic courts infringed this right by ordering him to pay non-pecuniary damages after he published a newspaper article.

On 26 August 2003, Rusu published an article in *Monitorul de Suceava* titled “An inhabitant of Verneşti is wanted by police across the country, having been accused of breaking into the headquarters of the local branch of the Social Democratic Party.” Accompanied by a photograph of S.A. (then a suspect), it stated that S.A., aged 35, was accused of stealing two television sets and approximately 17 million Romanian lei from the PSD local headquarters. As he had fled to avoid investigation for aggravated theft, a general (nationwide) search had been launched and his photograph distributed to judicial police across the country. The article described the Christmas Eve 2002 burglary: thieves vandalized offices, broke doors, and stole the items. Police identified S.A. as the main suspect; he had been missing from his residence. It explained procedures for escalating searches if a suspect fled.

S.A.’s father then wrote to the newspaper stating that his son had been in Italy (not Romania or Suceava County) at the time, that police had confirmed a mistake and cancelled the search, and requesting a retraction. The letter was published unedited on 29 August 2003.

On 15 September 2003, S.A. filed a criminal complaint against Rusu for defamation (then Article 206 of the Criminal Code). He asserted he had been in Italy, making participation impossible; the article contained serious allegations damaging his public image and causing suffering. He sought conviction and 100 million lei in non-pecuniary damages, noting that while his father’s letter was published, nothing further was done.

Rusu defended that the information and photograph came from the Suceava judicial service on 25 August 2003, giving him no reason to doubt it, and that the search order was valid at publication. He argued that publishing the father’s letter constituted a retraction.

Police later confirmed to the court that a general search had been issued on 31 December 2002 (Order no. 124000) because S.A. was suspected of theft and attempting to avoid investigation, but it was revoked on 3 September 2003 (Order no. S/150522) after clarification of his situation.

On 19 November 2003, the Suceava District Court acquitted Rusu of criminal defamation, finding no *mens rea* because he obtained the information from an official police source. However, it held him jointly liable with the newspaper to pay S.A. 10 million lei in civil damages. The court reasoned that defamation in the civil sense involved public communication of a distorted negative image causing suffering, reputational damage, social embarrassment, and injury to self-esteem. Publishing the article caused such damage. Although S.A.’s father notified the newspaper that the facts were false, no retraction of the original article was published.

On 23 January 2004, the Suceava County Court dismissed Rusu’s appeal and upheld the judgment. It confirmed the absence of criminal *mens rea* given the official source at the time of publication, but held that the civil obligation to pay compensation could not be set aside. After discovering the error, Rusu failed to publish a retraction to rectify it. The article caused non-pecuniary damage repairable only as ordered by the first-instance court.

Relevant domestic law included Criminal and Civil Code provisions on insult, defamation, and damages (as described in prior ECtHR cases such as *Cumpănă and Mazǎre v. Romania*), plus the Press Act (Law no. 3/1974, as amended), which allowed persons defamed by untrue press statements to request publication of a reply, retraction, or declaration within 30 days, with court enforcement possible if refused.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 10 interference: a civil sanction imposed on a journalist for reporting information obtained from official police sources concerning a criminal investigation into a burglary of a political party headquarters, despite acquittal of criminal defamation and publication of a related letter.

It stated that S.A. had fled to avoid investigation for aggravated theft, that a general (nationwide) search had been launched, and that his photograph had been circulated to police judicial services throughout Romania. A photograph of S.A. accompanied the piece.

Three days later the newspaper published an unedited letter from S.A.’s father. The letter asserted that S.A. had been in Italy at the relevant time, that the Suceava police had confirmed the search was a mistake and had already been called off, and that supporting documentation was available. The father requested a retraction.

He sought both a conviction and 100 million lei in non-pecuniary damages. Rusu’s defence was that both the information and the photograph had been supplied to him by the Suceava judicial police service on 25 August 2003, that a valid general-search order was in force at the moment of publication, and that the father’s letter constituted a published retraction.

A police letter of 17 October 2003 confirmed that a general-search order had indeed been issued on 31 December 2002 and had been revoked only on 3 September 2003 after S.A.’s situation had been clarified.

On 19 November 2003 the Suceava District Court acquitted Rusu of the criminal offence of defamation, finding that he had not acted with the requisite intent (mens rea) because he had relied on official police information. It therefore ordered Rusu, jointly with the newspaper, to pay 10 million lei in non-pecuniary damages. The court also noted that, although S.A.’s father had notified the newspaper of the error, no retraction of the original article had been published.

Rusu appealed. On 23 January 2004 the Suceava County Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the damages award. It reiterated that the absence of criminal intent did not extinguish civil liability once the error had been discovered, because Rusu had failed to publish a retraction that would have mitigated the non-pecuniary harm caused by the original report.

The applicant contended that these civil sanctions, imposed despite his good-faith reliance on official sources and the publication of the father’s letter, constituted an unjustified interference with his right to impart information of public interest. Relevant domestic provisions included the then-applicable criminal and civil rules on defamation and the Press Act’s right-of-reply and retraction procedures, which required publication of an answer within fifteen days of receipt.

(aged 35) had stolen two television sets and approximately 17 million lei from the PSD headquarters in Suceava on the night before Christmas Eve 2002. It stated that S.A. had fled to avoid investigation for aggravated theft, that a general (nationwide) search had been launched, and that his photograph had been circulated to police judicial services throughout Romania. The article described how the thieves had vandalised offices and how, after local investigations identified S.A. as the main suspect, he had been missing from his residence.

On 29 August 2003 the newspaper published, unedited, a letter from S.A.’s father. The letter asserted that S.A. had been in Italy (not Romania or Suceava county) at the relevant time, that Suceava County Police had promptly informed him of a mistake, that the general search had been called off, and that supporting documentation was publicly available. The father requested a retraction of the original article.

On 15 September 2003 S.A. lodged a criminal complaint for defamation (then Article 206 of the Criminal Code) with the Suceava District Court. He explained that he had been in Italy and therefore could not have committed the theft, noted that his father’s letter had been published but that nothing further had been done, and claimed that the article’s serious allegations had damaged his public image and caused personal suffering. He sought a criminal conviction and 100 million lei in non-pecuniary damages.

In defence the applicant stated that both the information about the search and S.A.’s photograph had been supplied to him on 25 August 2003 by the Suceava judicial service, that the search order had been valid at the time of publication, and that the father’s letter constituted a published retraction. A police statement of 17 October 2003 confirmed that a general search had been issued on 31 December 2002 by the General Inspectorate of the Romanian Police because S.A. was suspected of theft and attempting to avoid investigation; the measure was revoked on 3 September 2003 once S.A.’s situation had been clarified.

On 19 November 2003 the District Court acquitted the applicant of criminal defamation, finding no mens rea because he had obtained the information from official police sources. However, it held him jointly liable with the newspaper to pay 10 million lei in civil damages. The court reasoned that the article had communicated a distorted negative image causing reputational harm, social embarrassment and injury to self-esteem, and that, although notified of the falsity of the facts, the newspaper had not published a retraction of the original article.

The Suceava County Court, by final judgment of 23 January 2004, dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the civil award. It accepted the absence of criminal intent given the official source of the information at the date of publication, but held that the applicant’s failure to publish a retraction once the error became known meant that the non-pecuniary damage caused by the article could be repaired only by the compensation already ordered.

At the material time the Romanian Press Act (Law no. 3/1974, as amended) entitled any person considering himself or herself defamed by untrue press statements to request, within 30 days, publication of a reply, retraction or declaration. The press was obliged to publish a free, objective answer seeking to re-establish the truth within 15 days; unjustified refusal could be challenged in court, which could then order publication.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the civil damages award constituted an unjustified interference with his freedom of expression.

The case of Sousa Goucha v. Portugal (Application no. 70434/12) concerns a Portuguese television presenter’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that the dismissal of his domestic defamation proceedings amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention.

Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, born in 1954, is a well-known Portuguese television host with nearly forty years’ experience in the media. He publicly declared his homosexuality in 2008. On the night of 28 December 2009 a live comedy talk-show, “Five Minutes to Midnight”, was broadcast on the State channel RTP2. During a quiz the presenter asked guests “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?”, listing three women and the applicant as the four possible answers, with the applicant designated the “correct” one. The exchange was framed as humorous banter, including comments that one guest was a “fan” of the applicant and that choosing him might be “bad”.

The applicant filed a criminal complaint for defamation (Article 180 of the Criminal Code) and insult (Article 181) against RTP, the production company, the presenter and two programming directors, alleging that the inclusion of his name had damaged his reputation and dignity. The public prosecutor discontinued the case in March 2011, finding no intent to offend. The applicant then joined the proceedings as an assistant prosecutor and lodged a private accusation. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge of the Lisbon Criminal Investigation Court declined to send the individual defendants to trial, holding that there was insufficient evidence of the required subjective intent. The judge observed that the applicant, as a public figure, must expect comedians to caricature his “characteristics \ldots attributed to the female gender, such as his way of expressing himself, his colourful [feminine] clothes, and the fact that he has always lived in a world of women”. The judge added that the applicant had recently made his homosexuality public and that the defendants had never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. Corporate defendants were excluded from liability under Article 11 of the Criminal Code.

The applicant appealed, arguing that his name had been included precisely because of his sexual orientation. On 17 April 2012 the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It quoted the investigating judge’s remarks at length and added that, in the context of a comedy programme, the remark was “one of the many jokes” typical of the show. Even if in bad taste, the expression did not reach the threshold of an offence to honour as understood by “the majority of reasonable people”. The court reiterated that the defendants had not intended to criticise the applicant’s homosexuality.

These domestic rulings form the core of the alleged violation: the applicant contended that the courts’ repeated references to his homosexuality and stereotypically feminine traits, together with their conclusion that such a joke was socially acceptable, demonstrated discriminatory treatment based on sexual orientation. The Government maintained that the decisions turned solely on the absence of criminal intent and the humorous context, not on the applicant’s sexual orientation. Third-party comments from Alliance Defending Freedom emphasised the importance of protecting satirical speech. The Court’s subsequent examination of whether the national courts’ reasoning disclosed a difference of treatment on a prohibited ground, and whether that difference was objectively justified, rests on the facts set out above.

The case of Sousa Goucha v. Portugal (application no. 70434/12) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, a well-known Portuguese television presenter who had publicly come out as homosexual in 2008. The applicant alleged that the dismissal of his domestic criminal complaint for defamation and insult amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in violation of Article 14 of the Convention.

The relevant events occurred during a live late-night comedy talk show, “Five Minutes to Midnight,” broadcast on the state channel RTP2 on 28 December 2009. In a quiz segment the presenter asked guests to identify “the best Portuguese female TV host,” listing three women and the applicant as options, with the applicant’s name designated the “correct” answer. The ensuing banter treated the applicant as female (“she was the one telling me not to say it”), emphasised his popularity among the guests, and framed the choice as humorous. The applicant regarded the inclusion of his name on a list of female presenters as an attack on his honour and dignity that exploited his sexual orientation and perceived feminine traits.

In 2010 he lodged a criminal complaint against the public broadcaster, the production company, the presenter and two programming directors, alleging defamation (Article 180 of the Criminal Code) and insult (Article 181). The public prosecutor discontinued the case in March 2011, finding no intent to offend. The applicant then joined as an assistant prosecutor and filed a private indictment. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge of the Lisbon Criminal Investigation Court declined to send the natural persons to trial, holding that the subjective element of the offences was absent: the defendants had neither intended nor foreseen any attack on honour. The judge observed that the applicant, as a public figure, must expect comedians to caricature his well-known “female-gender” characteristics—his manner of speech, colourful clothing and long professional association with women’s programming. The court added that the applicant had recently disclosed his homosexuality and that the defendants had never intended to criticise that orientation. Liability of the two corporate defendants was excluded under Article 11 of the Criminal Code.

The Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 17 April 2012. It endorsed the first-instance reasoning, stressing the playful, irreverent context of a comedy programme. While the joke might be regarded as being in bad taste, it did not, in the view of a reasonable observer, cross the legal threshold for injury to honour. The appellate court repeated the lower court’s characterisation of the applicant’s public persona and sexual orientation as relevant background that rendered the remark non-offensive.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s Article 14 complaint: he argued that the domestic courts’ reliance on his homosexuality and stereotypically feminine attributes to justify the dismissal of his claim itself constituted discriminatory treatment. The Government maintained that the decisions turned solely on the absence of criminal intent and the humorous setting, not on sexual orientation. The case therefore turned on whether the Portuguese courts’ assessment of the joke and of the applicant’s reputation reflected an unjustified difference of treatment based on sexual orientation.

The European Court of Human Rights case Sousa Goucha v. Portugal (Application no. 70434/12, judgment of 22 March 2016) arose from a complaint by Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, a prominent Portuguese television presenter who had publicly declared his homosexuality in 2008. He alleged that the dismissal of his domestic criminal claims for defamation and insult amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention.

On 28 December 2009, the late-night talk show Five Minutes to Midnight, broadcast live on the state channel RTP2 and presented by F.C., featured a quiz. The key question, highlighted as the most important, asked: “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?” The multiple-choice options listed three well-known female presenters together with the applicant, who was identified as the “correct” answer. The ensuing banter treated the pairing as a joke. One guest hesitated, praised the female hosts as “gorgeous,” and ultimately selected a woman; the presenter then revealed the applicant’s name, prompting comments about the guest’s supposed fandom of Goucha and an implication that naming him would have been “bad.” The exchange portrayed the applicant’s inclusion as humorous, playing on perceived feminine traits.

In 2010 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against RTP, the production company, the presenter and the relevant directors, alleging that listing him among female hosts damaged his honour and reputation (Articles 180 and 181 of the Portuguese Criminal Code). The public prosecutor discontinued the case on 2 March 2011, finding no intent to offend. The applicant then intervened as an assistant prosecutor and filed a private indictment. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge of the Lisbon Criminal Investigation Court refused to send the case to trial. The judge held that the defendants had neither intended nor foreseen any attack on the applicant’s honour. As a public figure, the applicant was expected to tolerate comedic exaggeration of his publicly known characteristics—his manner of speech, colourful (feminine) clothing and long association with women’s programming. The judge added that the applicant had only recently come out and that the defendants had not sought to criticise his sexual orientation. Corporate defendants were excluded from liability under Article 11 of the Criminal Code.

The applicant appealed to the Lisbon Court of Appeal, insisting that his name had been included precisely because of his sexual orientation. On 17 April 2012 the appeal was dismissed. The court endorsed the investigating judge’s reasoning, stressing the playful, irreverent context of a comedy programme. It recalled that an insult is not whatever the complainant subjectively regards as offensive, but what reasonable people would consider an attack on honour. While the joke might be regarded as being in bad taste, it did not cross the statutory threshold. The court again noted the absence of any intention to disparage the applicant’s homosexuality and the need to balance reputation against freedom of expression in satirical television.

These facts—the stereotypical joke equating a gay male host with female presenters, the applicant’s claim that the remark was motivated by his sexual orientation, and the domestic courts’ consistent findings of no criminal intent, insufficient gravity and legitimate humorous context—formed the core of the alleged violation.

The case of Lukats v. Romania (Application no. 24199/07) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) on 5 April 2016 (final on 5 July 2016). The applicant, Maria Lia Lukats, a Romanian national born in 1936 and residing in Skokie, USA, lodged her application on 2 May 2007. She alleged that Romania’s domestic mechanism for compensating properties lost from former Romanian provinces (following pre- and World War II border changes) was ineffective.

On 31 August 1998, the applicant applied to the Bucharest County Commission under Law no. 9/1998 for compensation relating to assets owned by her ancestors and transferred to Bulgaria under the 1940 Treaty of Craiova. On 29 April 2004, the Commission granted her compensation of ROL 4,991,284,506 (approximately EUR 123,500 at the time). Between 2005 and 2008, she repeatedly applied to the National Authority for Property Restitution and the President of Romania for payment; she was informed each time that her file required ratification by the competent authority. On 20 February 2009, the National Authority ratified the award at RON 499,128.43 (approximately EUR 117,000), to be paid in two annual instalments per the applicable methodological rules (originally in force from 30 November 1998 and amended 26 October 2007). By the time of the Court’s judgment in 2016, the applicant had received neither the compensation nor any indication of a payment date.

Law no. 9/1998 (in force 14 March 1998, later amended) created a compensatory scheme for Romanian citizens whose immovable property was confiscated without compensation under the Treaty of Craiova. Claims had to be filed within initially 18 months (later extended). County Commissions (under prefectural authority) were to assess claims within six months; their decisions were then to be ratified (or rejected) by a Central Commission within 60 days, with further judicial challenge possible. Methodological rules provided for inflation adjustment of awards at the time of payment, initially limited to two consecutive years. Subsequent Government Decisions transferred ratification powers first to a department under the Prime Minister’s Chancellery and then (from 2005) to the National Authority. Later rules (2007) assigned payment responsibility to the National Authority. Parallel laws (nos. 290/2003 and 393/2006) established analogous mechanisms for properties lost in other former territories.

Subsequent measures underscored ongoing implementation problems. Emergency Government Ordinance no. 10/2013 provided for payment in ten equal annual instalments from 2014 (minimum RON 20,000 per instalment), citing budgetary constraints; the Constitutional Court struck it down in December 2013 as imposing an excessive, disproportionate burden and an unreasonable ten-year period. The ordinance was abrogated in March 2014. Emergency Government Ordinance no. 10/2014 then suspended (for six months) both the issuance of new decisions and voluntary payments of already-granted compensation. Law no. 164/2014 (in force 18 December 2014) aimed to accelerate resolution: it limited remedies to pecuniary compensation, transferred remaining Central Commission powers to the National Authority, set new ratification and payment deadlines (generally five years of equal annual instalments from 2015, with inflation adjustment via the consumer price index), imposed time limits on County Commissions based on caseload, and provided for court applications if deadlines were missed. Efficiency measures included a temporary staffing increase at the National Authority.

The applicant’s claim thus remained unpaid nearly 18 years after filing, despite a 2004 award and 2009 ratification, amid repeated legislative changes, administrative transfers of competence, and payment suspensions or extensions. These facts formed the basis of her complaint that the compensation mechanism was ineffective.

**CASE OF LUKATS v. ROMANIA (Application no. 24199/07), ECtHR Fourth Section, judgment of 5 April 2016 (final 5 July 2016)**

The applicant, Maria Lia Lukats (born 1936, resident in the USA), a Romanian national, alleged that Romania’s domestic compensation mechanism for properties lost in former Romanian territories was ineffective. She claimed under Article 34 of the Convention that this violated her rights, specifically in relation to delayed and unpaid compensation for ancestral assets transferred to Bulgaria under the 1940 Treaty of Craiova.

On 31 August 1998, she lodged a claim with the Bucharest County Commission (under Law no. 9/1998) for compensation relating to properties owned by her ancestors and transferred to the Bulgarian State following the treaty, which mandated resettlement and placed compensation responsibility on Romania for abandoned rural possessions. The County Commission, required by law to decide within six months, issued a decision only on 29 April 2004 (nearly six years later), awarding her ROL 4,991,284,506 (approximately EUR 123,500).

Between 2005 and 2008, she repeatedly applied to the National Authority for Property Restitution and the President of Romania seeking payment. She was informed each time that her file required ratification by the implementing authority. On 20 February 2009, the National Authority ratified the award, confirming entitlement to RON 499,128.43 (approximately EUR 117,000), payable in two annual instalments per the 1998 methodological rules (amended 2007). These rules provided for inflation adjustment based on salary or consumer price indices. As of the 2016 judgment, the applicant had received neither the compensation nor any indication of a payment date.

Law no. 9/1998 (in force from 14 March 1998, later amended) created an administrative process for such claims, involving County Commissions and a Central Commission (later replaced by departments and then the National Authority). Claimants had initially 18 months to file (deadlines later extended). Decisions could be challenged administratively and then in court. Similar mechanisms applied under Laws nos. 290/2003 and 393/2006 for other lost territories (Bessarabia, Northern Bukovina, Hertza, and former Yugoslav areas). Compensation was to come from the State budget, unlike nationalized property schemes.

Subsequent legislation highlighted systemic issues. Emergency Government Ordinance no. 10/2013 proposed 10-year instalments from 2014 (minimum RON 20,000 per instalment) due to budget difficulties but was struck down by the Constitutional Court in December 2013 as imposing an excessive, disproportionate burden with an unreasonable deadline. It was abrogated in March 2014. EGO no. 10/2014 then suspended decisions and payments for six months. Law no. 164/2014 (in force December 2014) aimed to accelerate processing: it limited remedies to pecuniary compensation, transferred ratification powers fully to the National Authority (with 18-month deadlines), set 5-year equal annual instalments from 2015 (or later for new ratifications), required inflation adjustments, and allowed court applications for missed deadlines. County Commissions faced staggered decision deadlines based on caseload (9–36 months from January 2015). Efficiency measures included extra staffing.

These facts illustrate prolonged delays: over five years from claim to initial decision (versus a six-month statutory limit), another five years to ratification, and then non-payment for years thereafter despite a confirmed award. Multiple authority changes, instalment stretching attempts (later invalidated), suspensions, and budget-related justifications compounded the ineffectiveness. The compensation constituted a “possession” or legitimate expectation under the Convention, yet the applicant remained without payment or a reliable timeline more than 17 years after lodging her claim. The case was communicated to the Government in 2010.

001-161738:
The case concerns John Edward Seton’s 2008 conviction at the Central Criminal Court for the murder of Jon Bartlett, shot dead at around 7.40 pm on 31 March 2006. Witnesses described the gunman as wearing a baseball cap and fleeing in a silver Vauxhall Vectra, later found burned nearby. Seton, then in his early twenties, fled to the Netherlands and was extradited to stand trial. His co-defendant was acquitted of assisting an offender.

Seton’s defence, formalised in a 1 April 2008 statement, was that the killer was Mr Pearman, a man in his fifties already serving a life sentence for murder and with prior convictions for serious drugs and firearms offences. Seton claimed involvement in a drugs deal with Pearman and Bartlett. On the morning of the murder Pearman and Bartlett asked him to obtain a car to collect a shipment; he bought the Vectra that afternoon in the presence of Pearman and co-defendant Osborne, but Pearman drove it away. Seton said he later met Pearman at 7.30 pm to hand over money while Pearman was still in the Vectra, after which Seton left with Osborne in a white van and went to his parents’ home. During the night he visited a petrol station and called a friend whose mother lived near the burning Vectra.

Police interviewed Pearman on 4 July 2008; he answered “no comment.” That evening and later he telephoned his son and wife (calls recorded, as he knew they would be as a Category A prisoner) and denied knowing Seton or any involvement in the murder.

At trial (starting 11 August 2008) the central issue was whether Seton or Pearman was the gunman. Pearman refused to make a statement or give evidence. The prosecution successfully applied under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 to admit the recorded calls as hearsay in the interests of justice. The trial judge, applying the statutory factors in section 114(2), found the recordings of strong probative value (Pearman appeared genuinely outraged at being implicated), important, and reliable (being taped), while noting Pearman’s refusal to testify, the self-serving nature of the denials, and the fact that he knew the calls were recorded. The judge considered there was no real prejudice to Seton.

Additional prosecution evidence included Seton’s and Bartlett’s involvement in substantial drug dealing; a debt list showing Seton owed Bartlett £24,000; Seton’s previous arrest while in possession of a firearm (which he denied); extensive telephone contact between Seton and Bartlett, including a final call at 7.22 pm; the Vectra seller’s evidence that Seton arranged collection around 6 pm; hire of a distinctive white van later seen near the scene; cell-site data placing Seton’s phone near the murder (switched off 7.28–7.50 pm) and later near the burning car; CCTV of Seton in the van wearing a baseball cap and calling an associate near the car’s location; eyewitness descriptions of a young man of average build wearing a baseball cap (matching Seton, not 54-year-old Pearman); a photograph of Pearman; and police evidence of no connection between Pearman and either Seton or Bartlett.

The judge directed the jury on the limitations of the hearsay (no opportunity to see or cross-examine Pearman, self-serving statements known to be recorded) and on Pearman’s bad character. The jury requested and heard the tapes again before convicting Seton by majority on 26 August 2008 (life imprisonment, 30-year minimum term).

The Court of Appeal granted leave but dismissed the appeal in March 2010. It held the judge had properly applied section 114(2); compelling Pearman would have been fruitless given his refusal and the privilege against self-incrimination. Even without the tapes, the circumstantial evidence was overwhelming and the conviction safe. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

The case of *Seton v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 55287/10) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant’s 2008 conviction for murder and the fairness of his trial, particularly the admission of hearsay evidence from a reluctant but available witness.

Jon Bartlett was shot dead around 7.40 p.m. on 31 March 2006. Witnesses described a gunman in a baseball cap who fled in a silver Vauxhall Vectra, later found burned nearby. The applicant, John Edward Seton, fled to the Netherlands and was extradited. His defence statement alleged that the killer was Mr Pearman, a category A prisoner already serving life for murder with prior convictions for serious drugs and firearms offences. Seton claimed involvement in a drugs deal with Pearman and Bartlett; he said he bought the Vectra that afternoon (in Pearman’s presence) for them to collect a shipment, later met Pearman (who was driving it) to hand over money, and then went to his parents’ home. He admitted visiting a petrol station overnight and calling a friend whose mother lived near the burning car.

Police interviewed Pearman, who made no comment. Two recorded prison telephone calls (which he knew were monitored) to his son and wife contained denials that he knew Seton or had any involvement in the killing.

At the Central Criminal Court trial (starting 11 August 2008), the sole issue for the jury was whether Seton or Pearman was the gunman. Pearman refused to make a statement or testify; this was confirmed by a prison officer. The prosecution applied under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 to admit the recordings in the interests of justice. The defence objected. The judge admitted them after considering the statutory factors in section 114(2): they had extremely strong probative value (appearing to show genuine outrage at a false implication); Pearman could not be called because of his refusal (police enquiries having found no link to the crime); the evidence was extremely important; the circumstances (self-serving statements, known recording) were matters of weight for the jury rather than exclusion; the tapes were reliable; the defence had already explored Pearman’s bad character; and there was no real prejudice. Other prosecution evidence included the parties’ drugs involvement and a £24,000 debt list showing Seton owing Bartlett; Seton’s prior arrest with a firearm; extensive telephone contact culminating in a last call at 7.22 p.m.; purchase of the Vectra by Seton and hire of a distinctive white van (seen near the scene) by his co-accused’s father; cell-site data placing Seton’s phone near the murder (switched off 7.28–7.50 p.m.) and the burning; unchallenged eyewitness descriptions of a young man in a baseball cap matching Seton (then 25) rather than Pearman (then 54); CCTV of Seton in the van, wearing a cap, calling an associate near the burning site; and a police superintendent’s evidence of exhaustive (negative) enquiries into Pearman. A photograph of Pearman was shown.

The judge directed the jury on the hearsay’s limitations (no opportunity to see or cross-examine the speaker; self-serving nature; known recording) and on Pearman’s bad character (relevant both to propensity and credibility of his denials). The jury asked to hear the tapes again and convicted Seton by majority. He received life imprisonment with a 30-year minimum term.

The Court of Appeal granted leave but dismissed the appeal. It held that the trial judge had correctly applied section 114(2); compelling Pearman would have been fruitless given his refusal and the privilege against self-incrimination. In any event the remaining circumstantial evidence was overwhelming (motive, late allegation, flight, absence of any Pearman link, eyewitness descriptions, vehicle and cell-site evidence). The Supreme Court refused certification.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint to the Strasbourg Court that the untested hearsay, from a witness who was available yet refused to testify, rendered his trial unfair.

**Case of Seton v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 55287/10), ECtHR (First Section), judgment of 31 March 2016 (final 12 September 2016).**

The applicant, a British national born in 1983, was convicted at the Central Criminal Court of the murder of Jon Bartlett, who was shot dead at about 7.40 pm on 31 March 2006. Witnesses described the gunman as wearing a baseball cap and driving off in a silver Vauxhall Vectra, which was later found burned nearby. The applicant fled to the Netherlands and was extradited to stand trial. A co-defendant was acquitted of assisting an offender.

The applicant’s defence, set out in a statement of 1 April 2008, was that Bartlett had been murdered by Pearman, a man with prior convictions for serious drug and firearms offences who was then serving a life sentence for another murder. The applicant claimed involvement in a drug deal with both men. On the morning of the murder he was asked to provide a car; he purchased the Vectra that afternoon in the presence of others, but Pearman drove it away. The applicant later met Pearman (then driving the Vectra) around 7.30 pm to hand over money and thereafter went to his parents’ home, later visiting a petrol station and making a call.

Police interviewed Pearman on 4 July 2008; he answered “no comment.” That evening and later he made recorded telephone calls from prison (as a Category A prisoner, he knew they were recorded) to his son and wife, denying any knowledge of the applicant or involvement in the murder. Pearman refused to make a statement or give evidence at trial; this was confirmed by a prison officer’s statement.

The trial began on 11 August 2008. The key issue for the jury was whether the applicant or Pearman was the killer. The prosecution sought to admit the recordings of Pearman’s calls under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (hearsay admissible if in the interests of justice). The defence objected. The trial judge admitted the recordings after considering the factors in section 114(2): they had extremely strong probative value (Pearman expressing genuine outrage at being implicated); Pearman refused to testify and police enquiries confirmed no involvement; the evidence was extremely important; any self-serving nature or knowledge of recording could be considered by the jury on weight; the tapes were reliable; the defence had already cross-examined on Pearman’s convictions; and there was no real prejudice.

Other prosecution evidence included: the applicant and victim’s known involvement in substantial drug dealing, with the applicant owing Bartlett £24,000; the applicant’s prior arrest while possessing a firearm (he admitted drug dealing but denied the firearm); mobile phone records showing contact on the day of the murder (last call 7.22 pm) and in the preceding days; evidence that the applicant arranged purchase of the Vectra that afternoon, collected with a distinctive hired white van; witnesses seeing a matching van near the shooting; cell-site evidence placing the applicant’s phone near the murder scene (switched off around the time of the shooting) and later near the burned car; multiple eyewitness descriptions of a young gunman (20s–30s, average build, baseball cap) matching the applicant but not the 54-year-old Pearman, whose photo was shown; CCTV of the applicant in the van wearing a cap and calling near the burned-car location; and police confirmation of no link between Pearman and the victim or applicant.

In summing up, the judge directed the jury on the limitations of the hearsay (no opportunity to see/hear/cross-examine Pearman; statements were self-serving and known to be recorded) and on Pearman’s bad character. The jury requested and reheard the tapes. On 26 August 2008 the applicant was convicted by majority and sentenced to life with a 30-year minimum term.

The Court of Appeal initially granted leave, noting arguable issues around not producing Pearman and the best-evidence principle. On 12 March 2010 it dismissed the appeal. It held the judge’s finding that Pearman would not testify was unimpeached, so compelling him would have been fruitless (he would invoke privilege against self-incrimination); the judge had properly addressed section 114(2) factors. Independently, the conviction was safe due to overwhelming circumstantial evidence even without the tapes (motive via drugs/debt; late allegation against Pearman; flight; no links found; phone/cell-site/car/van evidence; eyewitness descriptions fitting the applicant not Pearman; prior firearm connection). Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

These facts centre on the admission of untested hearsay from an unavailable (refusing) witness to rebut the defence, in the context of otherwise strong circumstantial evidence, raising issues under Article 6 of the Convention concerning the fairness of the trial and the right to examine witnesses.

The applicant, Valdas Bagdonavičius (born 1964), was arrested in March 2009 on suspicion of large-scale drug trafficking as part of an organised group and placed in pre-trial detention. He was held at Lukiškės Remand Prison from 30 March 2009 to 14 June 2010 in cells of approximately 8 m² housing 2–4 inmates. He was then transferred to Kaunas Remand Prison, where personal space sometimes fell below 3 m². The Prisons Department later admitted overcrowding at Lukiškės. In 2013 the applicant sought damages for those conditions, but the claim was dismissed as time-barred; the Supreme Administrative Court held he could have obtained legal aid earlier.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined four joined applications (nos. 5623/09, 12460/09, 33656/09 and 20758/10) brought by seven Russian nationals against the Russian Federation under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that final and enforceable domestic civil judgments delivered in their favour had been unlawfully quashed by way of the supervisory-review procedure that operated between 2008 and 2012.

All applicants had been successful claimants in first-instance proceedings. Those judgments were upheld on appeal and thereby became final and enforceable under Russian procedural law. At the defendants’ subsequent request, the presidia of the competent regional courts nevertheless quashed the judgments by supervisory review.

Two of the applications (Trapeznikov and Bychkov and Others) were brought by former participants in the Chernobyl clean-up operation. They had sued the competent authorities for an inflation adjustment to their social-security payments. The first-instance and appeal courts granted the claims. The regional-court presidia later set the judgments aside, holding that the lower courts had failed to apply the specific indexation method prescribed by the Government for that particular category of benefits.

The remaining two applications arose from property disputes. In Markova the applicant, asserting sole ownership of a flat after her late son had purportedly renounced his share, sought the eviction of her daughter-in-law and granddaughter. In Ryabchikov the applicant, who had inherited a house under his mother’s will, discovered that she had transferred two land plots to an agricultural company in 1994; he claimed the transfer had never been properly formalised and that the plots therefore formed part of the estate. Both claims succeeded at first instance and on appeal. The respective presidia subsequently quashed the judgments, finding that the lower courts had applied the relevant legislation retrospectively.

Under the Code of Civil Procedure then in force, a judgment became final and enforceable once the ordinary time-limit for appeal had expired or the appeal court had ruled. Until the 2012 reform such judgments remained open to supervisory review at three successive levels (regional-court presidia, the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court, and the Presidium of the Supreme Court). The 2008 amendments that governed the present cases reduced the time-limit for lodging a supervisory-review application to six months, abolished the regional-court presidents’ power to override a single judge’s refusal to admit an application, and required exhaustion of ordinary appellate remedies. The 2012 reform later converted the first two supervisory instances into cassation courts, leaving only the Supreme Court’s Presidium with residual supervisory jurisdiction.

The applicants maintained that the quashing of already-final and enforceable decisions violated the principle of legal certainty inherent in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court communicated the applications to the Russian Government on 27 March 2013. The judgment, adopted on 15 March 2016 and becoming final on 5 July 2016, examined whether the particular grounds invoked by the supervisory-review courts (misapplication of indexation rules or retrospective application of law) were compatible with the Convention requirement that final judgments be set aside only in exceptional circumstances and for compelling reasons of a substantial and compelling character.

**Summary of Trapeznikov and Others v. Russia (ECHR, 5 April 2016)**

This case joined four applications (nos. 5623/09, 12460/09, 33656/09 and 20758/10) by seven Russian nationals against Russia. The applicants complained that final, enforceable domestic civil judgments in their favour were quashed via Russia’s supervisory-review procedure (as it existed 2008–2012). This procedure, repeatedly amended but still permitting reopening of res judicata decisions, formed the core of the alleged Convention violations, principally of Article 6 § 1 (legal certainty and fair hearing) and, where pecuniary rights were at stake, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

All applicants had been successful claimants. In Trapeznikov and Bychkov and Others the applicants were former Chernobyl liquidators who sued state authorities for inflation-linked indexation of social benefits. First-instance courts granted the claims; appellate courts upheld the awards, rendering the judgments final and enforceable under Russian procedural law. In Markova the applicant sought eviction of her late son’s wife and granddaughter from a flat she occupied, asserting sole ownership after her son had renounced his share in her favour. Lower courts accepted her title and ordered eviction; the decision became final. In Ryabchikov the applicant inherited a house under his mother’s will. He later discovered two land plots she had transferred in 1994 to an agricultural cooperative of which she was a member. He sued to recover the plots, arguing the transfer had never been properly formalised and therefore formed part of the estate. The courts of first instance and appeal found for him; the judgment became enforceable.

At the defendants’ request the presidia of the competent regional courts then quashed all four final judgments by supervisory review. In the Chernobyl cases the presidia held that the lower courts had failed to apply the specific governmental formula prescribed for indexation of this category of benefits. In Markova and Ryabchikov they held that the favourable findings rested on an impermissible retrospective application of later legislation.

Under the Code of Civil Procedure then in force, a judgment became final once the ordinary appeal period expired or the appeal court ruled. Yet it remained subject to supervisory review at up to three successive levels (regional-court presidium, Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court, Presidium of the Supreme Court). A single judge first screened the application; a refusal could still be overridden by the court president (a power abolished at regional level in 2008). The 2003 Code had restricted standing to the parties and introduced a one-year time-limit; 2008 amendments shortened the limit to six months, required exhaustion of ordinary appeals and removed regional presidents’ discretionary override. Even after these changes the procedure still allowed a higher court, on a party’s or official’s initiative, to re-examine both facts and law and to annul a decision that had already acquired the force of res judicata. Only the 2012 reform converted the first two levels into cassation courts and confined true supervisory review to the Supreme Court’s Presidium.

These facts—final awards creating legitimate expectations, followed by their subsequent annulment on grounds that could have been raised earlier—constituted the alleged interference with legal certainty and, where money or property was involved, with the applicants’ possessions. The Court examined whether the 2008–2012 version of supervisory review still failed to satisfy the Convention’s requirements of finality and foreseeability.

**Case of Trapeznikov and Others v. Russia (ECHR, Third Section, 5 April 2016, final 5 July 2016)**

This judgment concerns four applications (nos. 5623/09, 12460/09, 33656/09 and 20758/10) lodged by seven Russian nationals against the Russian Federation under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that final and enforceable domestic judgments in their favour were unlawfully quashed via the supervisory-review procedure then in force (2008–2012). The Court communicated the cases to the Government on 27 March 2013.

All applicants were successful claimants in civil proceedings. First-instance courts ruled in their favour; those judgments were upheld on appeal and thereby became final and enforceable under Russian law. Defendants subsequently applied for supervisory review, and the presidia of the relevant regional courts quashed the judgments.

Two applications (Trapeznikov and Bychkov and Others) were brought by former Chernobyl clean-up participants who had sued the authorities for inflation-linked adjustments to social benefits. The regional-court presidia held that the lower courts had failed to apply the specific Government-prescribed method of calculating indexation for that category of benefit.

In Markova the applicant sought eviction of her late son’s widow and granddaughter from a flat she occupied, asserting sole ownership because her son had previously renounced his share in her favour. In Ryabchikov the applicant inherited a house under his late mother’s will and later discovered two land plots she had transferred in 1994 to an agricultural company of which she was a member. He claimed the transfer had not been properly formalised and that the plots therefore formed part of the estate. In both of these cases the presidia concluded that the lower courts’ findings favourable to the applicants rested on the retrospective application of later legislation.

Russian procedural law treated a judgment as final and enforceable once the ordinary appeal time-limit expired or an appellate court had ruled. Until 2012 such judgments remained open to supervisory review at three successive levels (regional-court presidia, Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court, and Presidium of the Supreme Court). A single judge first screened each application; a refusal could formerly be overridden by the court president’s unfettered discretion (abolished at regional level in 2008). The 2003 Code of Civil Procedure had already restricted the right to initiate review to the parties and introduced a one-year time-limit; 2008 amendments shortened that limit to six months, required prior exhaustion of ordinary appeals, and removed the regional presidents’ discretionary override. A further 2012 reform converted the first two levels into cassation courts and confined true supervisory review to the Supreme Court’s Presidium.

The applicants’ complaints therefore centred on the compatibility of this multi-tiered, post-finality review mechanism—and the particular quashing decisions—with the principle of legal certainty inherent in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court had previously examined earlier versions of the same procedure and found them capable of undermining the finality of judicial decisions. The present cases raised the same issue under the 2008–2012 regime, specifically whether the grounds invoked by the regional presidia (misapplication of an indexation formula or retrospective application of law) justified reopening otherwise binding judgments.
