**Case Summary: Vasileva v. Bulgaria (Application no. 23796/10)**

The applicant, Maria Ivanova Vasileva (born 1948), a Bulgarian national from Plovdiv, alleged that Bulgarian law lacked an effective system to ensure impartiality of medical experts in medical malpractice proceedings. This, she claimed, prevented her from obtaining compensation for injuries from 2003 surgery and rendered those proceedings unfair (under the Convention).

In January 2000, she underwent a left mastectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma. From early 2002, she experienced left-chest pain. Multiple bone scintigraphies (February, May, August 2002; January 2003) indicated pathological uptake in the sixth left rib. Contrasting CT scans (May 2002, February 2003) suggested a suspected metastasis in the eighth/ninth left ribs. A February 2003 radiography also pointed to a lesion in the sixth rib. On 26 February 2003, a panel of five doctors approved surgical removal of the suspected metastasis.

The applicant, concerned that the exact location remained unconfirmed, questioned the surgeon, Dr K.M. He stated that existing imaging sufficed and he could identify the site intraoperatively. A doctor who had performed her 2000 mastectomy advised that the small suspected metastasis could not be localized visually and required precise preoperative identification. Despite her repeated requests for further tests, Dr K.M. reassured her. She signed an informed-consent form and underwent surgery on 13 March 2003. Dr K.M. removed fragments of the fourth and fifth left ribs (not the sixth, eighth, or ninth). The operation report incorrectly stated that the eighth and ninth ribs had been removed; Dr K.M. later told her the same and that he had inspected her lungs. Histology (ready 25 March 2003) showed no cancerous tissue in the removed fragments.

Upon reviewing her discharge report (24 March 2003), the applicant discovered the discrepancy. Follow-up scintigraphy and CT (September 2003) confirmed removal of parts of the fourth and fifth ribs, a fractured sixth rib, and continued increased uptake in the sixth rib. Dr K.M. denied error. She underwent years of radiotherapy and hormonal therapy.

She complained to the Ministry of Health (late 2003). An inquiry concluded that inconclusive imaging had led the team to make a wide thoracic opening (fourth to ninth ribs) and remove parts of the fourth and fifth based on macroscopic changes; the report’s reference to the eighth/ninth ribs was a clerical error. The hospital’s ethics commission found no misconduct.

On 27 January 2004 she sued Dr K.M. and the state-owned hospital for damages, alleging: (a) unauthorized removal of healthy fourth/fifth ribs; (b) unnecessary lung inspection; (c) fracture of the sixth rib; and (d) failure to remove the suspected metastasis.

Before the Plovdiv Regional Court, experts were appointed (oncologist nominated by applicant, thoracic surgeon by Dr K.M., radiologist by the court; later a replacement thoracic surgeon after one was disqualified as a hospital employee). Reports (October 2004 and later) generally found no medical error: imaging was inconclusive; visual/tactile intraoperative findings justified rib removal (histology could not be obtained intraoperatively); lung palpation was standard; rib fractures were common; and no categorical proof of a remaining sixth-rib metastasis existed. The court dismissed the claim on 11 January 2006, relying on these opinions and noting that consent had not specified a particular rib.

The Plovdiv Court of Appeal appointed further experts, including a dissenting thoracic surgical oncologist (Dr V.T.) who opined the operation was unnecessary and carelessly performed. The majority reports aligned with prior experts. The court disregarded Dr V.T.’s view as contrary to other evidence and upheld the dismissal (2006).

The Supreme Court of Cassation quashed and remitted (29 July 2008), holding that the appeal court had failed to take an active role in formulating expert questions, fully clarify necessity of surgery/fracture/rib removal, or adequately explain rejection of Dr V.T.’s opinion. On remittal, new Sofia-based experts reiterated that surgery was imperative, the sixth-rib fracture predated the operation (due to prior treatment), rib removal was not erroneous given inconclusive imaging and intraoperative suspicion, and no proven metastasis remained. The Court of Appeal again upheld dismissal (11 May 2009), preferring the majority expert views.

The Supreme Court of Cassation refused a second cassation appeal (10 November 2009) as raising only factual issues with no conflicting case-law.

Domestic law required courts to appoint experts for specialized issues, allowed party nominations and replacement if contested, and mandated detailed, reasoned reports. Experts could be disqualified for familial ties, personal interest, or (per case-law) employment by a party. Courts were not bound by expert conclusions but had to analyze them with other evidence and explain any rejection. Informed-consent rules required explanation of diagnosis, treatment, risks, and alternatives.

These facts highlight the applicant’s core complaints: successive expert panels (some party-nominated or later replaced) largely exonerated the surgeon despite imaging inconsistencies and the dissenting view; limited disqualification grounds and judicial deference to majority medical opinions; and inability to obtain damages after multi-year proceedings.

In Vasileva v. Bulgaria, the applicant alleged that Bulgarian law lacked effective safeguards for the impartiality of medical experts in malpractice cases. This, she claimed, blocked compensation for harm from a 2003 surgery and made her civil proceedings unfair.

The applicant had a 2000 mastectomy for breast cancer. Scans in 2002–2003 conflicted on the site of a possible rib metastasis (sixth versus eighth/ninth left ribs). A medical panel approved surgery. Despite her doubts about localization, surgeon Dr K.M. operated on 13 March 2003 and removed fragments of the fourth and fifth ribs (healthy, per later histology). The report wrongly listed the eighth and ninth ribs. Later imaging showed a sixth-rib fracture and uptake there. She alleged unauthorized removal of healthy ribs, needless lung inspection, an intraoperative fracture, and failure to excise the metastasis.

Ministry and hospital inquiries found no misconduct (report error was clerical; removal followed observed changes). She sued Dr K.M. and the state hospital in 2004.

The Plovdiv Regional Court ordered expert reports (oncologist, thoracic surgeons, radiologist). One hospital-employed surgeon was disqualified for conflict. Experts generally found the operation necessary given inconclusive imaging; intraoperative visual/tactile findings justified the rib removals (intra-op histology impossible); lung palpation was standard; fractures were common or pre-existing; and remaining metastasis was unproven. The court dismissed the claim (2006), citing the non-specific consent form and expert consensus.

The Court of Appeal heard further experts. A dissenter (Dr V.T.) called the surgery unnecessary and careless; the majority agreed with prior reports. The court disregarded the dissent as contrary to the evidence and upheld dismissal.

The Supreme Court of Cassation quashed and remitted (2008), faulting inadequate fact-finding, passive questioning of experts, and insufficient reasons for ignoring Dr V.T. It required a fresh report with party input on questions.

On remittal, new experts again found surgery imperative, the fracture pre-existing (from prior treatment), the rib removals non-erroneous given imaging limits and intra-op findings, and no proven leftover metastasis. The Court of Appeal upheld dismissal (2009), preferring the consensus as reflecting practical surgical necessity. Cassation was refused (2009) as raising only factual issues.

Bulgarian law permits damages claims against doctors or their employers (not no-fault public-authority liability). Courts must appoint experts for specialized issues (parties may nominate; multiples possible if complex). Courts are not bound by opinions but must analyze them with other evidence and give reasons for preferring or rejecting any (including why one view over another). Disqualification originally covered close relatives or personal interest (an employee could not report against his employer); the 2007 Code aligned grounds with judicial recusal. Experts are warned of criminal liability for false/biased opinions and must pledge impartiality. Reports must be detailed.

These facts underscore the applicant’s impartiality complaint: an expert with a hospital tie required recusal; courts repeatedly deferred to a pro-defense expert majority (despite one dissent and remittal for better reasoning); and domestic rules left courts wide latitude to weigh conflicting medical views without stronger structural guarantees of expert independence.

**Case Summary: Vasileva v. Bulgaria (Application no. 23796/10), ECtHR (Fifth Section), 17 March 2016 (final 12 September 2016)**

The applicant, Maria Ivanova Vasileva (born 1948, resident in Plovdiv), alleged that Bulgarian law lacked an effective system to ensure the impartiality of medical experts in medical malpractice proceedings. A February 2003 panel of five doctors decided on surgical removal. The applicant expressed concern to the operating surgeon, Dr K.M., that the location was unconfirmed and requested further tests. He stated the existing images sufficed and that he could identify the site intraoperatively. Another doctor (who had performed the 2000 mastectomy) advised that the lesion was too small for visual localization and required precise pre-operative mapping. The applicant raised this with Dr K.M., who again reassured her.

She signed an informed consent form (which did not specify the exact rib) and underwent surgery on 13 March 2003. Dr K.M. removed fragments of the fourth and fifth left ribs (healthy, with no pre-operative lesions detected). The operation report erroneously recorded removal of the eighth and ninth ribs; Dr K.M. told the applicant the next day that he had removed those ribs and inspected her lungs. Histology (25 March 2003) found no cancerous tissue. Upon discharge (24 March 2003), the applicant discovered the discrepancy. Confronting Dr K.M., he denied error but ordered further imaging (September 2003), which showed increased uptake in the sixth rib (and fourth/fifth) plus a sixth-rib fracture and confirmed partial removal of the fourth and fifth ribs. He again denied mistake. She later received radiotherapy and hormonal therapy.

In late 2003 she complained to the Ministry of Health. An inquiry concluded that, given inconclusive imaging, the team made a wide thoracic opening (fourth to ninth ribs), removed fourth/fifth fragments due to observed macroscopic changes (none seen on the sixth), and that the report error was clerical. The hospital ethical commission found no misconduct by Dr K.M.

On 27 January 2004 the applicant sued Dr K.M. and the state-owned hospital for damages, alleging unauthorized removal of healthy fourth/fifth rib fragments, unnecessary lung inspection, fracture of the sixth rib, and failure to remove the suspected metastasis.

Before the Plovdiv Regional Court, experts were appointed (oncologist, thoracic surgeons, radiologist), with one thoracic surgeon later disqualified as a hospital employee. Reports generally found no breach of good practice: imaging was inconclusive; intraoperative visual/tactile findings justified removal of the fourth/fifth fragments (histology could not be obtained intraoperatively); lung palpation was standard; rib fractures were common/inevitable risks; regeneration occurred; presence of a sixth-rib metastasis was not categorically proven. The court dismissed the claim (11 January 2006), relying on most experts (excluding the disqualified one), holding that consent was given, no error occurred, and damage/causation were unproven.

On appeal, the Plovdiv Court of Appeal obtained further reports. A minority report by Dr V.T. (whom the defence alleged was biased due to prior acquaintance with the applicant) found the operation unnecessary and careless. The majority disagreed. The court disregarded Dr V.T.’s view as contrary to other evidence and upheld the dismissal (2006).

The Supreme Court of Cassation quashed and remitted (29 July 2008), criticizing inadequate fact-finding, insufficient explanation for disregarding Dr V.T., and failure to involve parties in formulating expert questions. On remittal, new experts reached similar conclusions (operation necessary; no error in removal based on intraoperative findings; fracture pre-existed due to treatment-related fragility; no proven untreated metastasis). The Court of Appeal again upheld (11 May 2009), explaining its preference for the majority views given the practical clinical context. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused a second cassation appeal (10 November 2009) as concerning facts rather than divergent law.

Domestic law allowed damages claims against practitioners or employers (not no-fault state liability for hospitals). Expert rules (1952 Code of Civil Procedure, later 2007 Code) permitted appointment (including by parties/court), disqualification for close relationships or personal interest (expanded to match judicial recusal grounds; employees barred from cases against employers), warnings against bias, and required courts to reason their preference among conflicting opinions rather than being bound by them. Informed consent rules existed but were distinguished from malpractice claims.

The proceedings highlighted repeated reliance on (mostly concordant) expert opinions, limited disqualifications, and courts’ choices among conflicting views, which the applicant linked to systemic impartiality defects in the medical-expert regime for malpractice cases.

The case originated in an application lodged on 20 June 2008 by Lithuanian national Vaidas Dungveckis (born 1978), alleging that he had been punished twice for the same offence.

On 6 February 2004 the Financial Crime Investigation Service notified the applicant of a criminal investigation into fraud committed in an organised group (Criminal Code Arts. 25 § 3 and 182 § 2). It was suspected that, from October 2001 to May 2002, he and accomplices had used specially acquired companies to buy large quantities of fish without paying VAT, forged payment documents purporting to show VAT had been paid, and then sold the fish at a VAT-inclusive price, thereby appropriating 261,854.65 LTL (approximately EUR 75,838) that should have been paid to the State. The same day he was subjected to a preventive measure prohibiting him from leaving home or the country without investigators’ approval.

An indictment of 6 May 2004 charged him with several counts of fraud and document forgery committed in an organised group (Arts. 25 § 3, 182 § 2 and 300 § 2). He admitted guilt and cooperated. On 3 February 2005 the Kaunas Regional Court convicted him on all charges and imposed a fine of LTL 18,750 (EUR 5,430).

On 3 February 2006 the Court of Appeal acquitted him of fraud but upheld the forgery conviction, imposing a two-year prison sentence suspended for two years together with an injunction forbidding him from leaving home for more than seven consecutive days without the supervising institution’s consent. He began complying immediately, reporting every two months from March 2006.

On 5 December 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the fraud acquittal and remitted that part of the case while upholding the remainder of the appellate judgment. On 4 July 2007 the Court of Appeal, after re-examination, convicted him of fraud. Taking into account aggravating factors (the well-organised nature of the offence, his leading role and the high value of the property appropriated) and mitigating factors (admission of guilt, family and employment, and prior compliance with the injunction), it imposed a sentence of two years and three months’ imprisonment—close to the statutory minimum. Because fraud is classified as a serious crime, the sentence could not be suspended. The court combined it with the earlier forgery sentence into a single consolidated sentence of two years and three months’ imprisonment.

The applicant’s cassation appeal sought restoration of the original fine. On 31 July 2007 the Supreme Court stayed execution of the July 2007 judgment pending the appeal; the applicant continued to observe the injunction. On 8 January 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, confirmed that a serious-crime conviction precluded suspension, but applied a 2002 amnesty law reducing the sentence by one-fifth, leaving a final consolidated term of one year and nine months.

The applicant then applied to be released from the consolidated sentence, arguing that he had virtually completed the two-year suspended term for the (longer) forgery sentence and that serving the shorter consolidated term would constitute double punishment. On 28 January 2008 the Kaunas Regional Court rejected the request, noting that one of the two crimes was serious and therefore unsuspendable. On 28 February 2008 the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, holding that completion of a suspended term required a district-court decision (which had not been issued), that an injunction imposed during suspension did not amount to serving the sentence, and that his compliance had already been taken into account when the consolidated sentence was fixed.

Subsequent attempts to obtain a court declaration that the suspended term had expired, or to compel the prison department to request such a declaration, were refused: only the supervising institution could apply, the later judgment had annulled the suspension, and administrative courts lacked competence over sentencing matters. The applicant began serving the consolidated sentence on 16 April 2008 and was released on probation on 26 January 2009 after serving one-third.

Domestic law (Constitution Art. 31 and Criminal Code Art. 2 § 6) prohibits punishment twice for the same criminal act. Constitutional Court jurisprudence permits concurrent sanctions of different types or for distinct offences, and sentencing rules (Criminal Code Art. 63) allow a consolidated sentence covering the most severe penalty when offences of markedly different gravity are committed. Suspension (Art. 75) is available only for minor or less-serious crimes. Supreme Court practice treats self-forged documents used in fraud as concurrent offences of forgery and fraud.

The case of Dungveckis v. Lithuania concerns an alleged violation of the ne bis in idem principle (prohibition of double punishment for the same offence). The applicant, Vaidas Dungveckis, a Lithuanian national born in 1978, was investigated from 6 February 2004 for fraud committed in an organised group. From October 2001 to May 2002, he and accomplices allegedly bought large quantities of fish without paying VAT, forged payment documents purporting that VAT had been paid, and resold the fish at prices including VAT, thereby appropriating approximately EUR 75,838 that should have gone to the State budget. On the same day he was placed under a restriction order prohibiting him from leaving home or the country without approval.

An indictment of 6 May 2004 charged him with fraud and document forgery in an organised group. He admitted guilt and cooperated. On 3 February 2005 the Kaunas Regional Court convicted him on all counts and imposed a fine of approximately EUR 5,430. On 3 February 2006 the Court of Appeal acquitted him of fraud but upheld the forgery conviction, imposing a two-year prison sentence suspended for two years with an injunction not to leave home for more than seven consecutive days without approval from the supervising authority. The applicant began complying with this injunction (reporting every two months from March 2006).

On 5 December 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the fraud acquittal and remitted that part for re-examination while upholding the rest of the judgment. On 4 July 2007 the Court of Appeal convicted him of fraud. Taking into account aggravating factors (the organised nature of the offence, his leading role and the high value involved) and mitigating factors (admission of guilt, family and employment, and compliance with the existing injunction), it imposed two years and three months’ imprisonment—near the statutory minimum. It then combined this with the earlier forgery sentence into a single consolidated sentence of two years and three months, which could not be suspended because fraud is classified as a serious crime.

The Supreme Court delayed execution pending cassation. The applicant continued to observe the injunction. On 8 January 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, applied an amnesty reducing the term by one-fifth, and confirmed a final consolidated sentence of one year and nine months’ imprisonment.

In January 2008 the applicant sought release, arguing that he had nearly completed the two-year suspended term (longer than the consolidated sentence) by complying with the injunction and that serving prison would constitute double punishment. The Kaunas Regional Court and Court of Appeal rejected this: he had been convicted of two distinct crimes (one serious), the injunction did not constitute service of the sentence, and the term of suspension had not been formally declared completed. Subsequent requests to confirm completion of the suspension were refused on procedural grounds (only the supervising institution could apply) and because the 2007 judgment had superseded the earlier suspension. Administrative courts likewise declined jurisdiction.

The applicant began serving the prison sentence on 16 April 2008 and was released on probation on 26 January 2009 after serving one-third.

Domestic law treats fraud and self-forged documents used to commit it as concurrent offences. The Constitution and Criminal Code prohibit double punishment for the same act, but the Constitutional Court has held that this does not preclude different forms of liability or multiple sanctions of the same type for a single violation, nor does it bar combining sentences for concurrent crimes. Suspension of sentence with injunctions is available only for less serious offences and is not equivalent to actual service of the sentence.

The case of Merčep v. Croatia (Application no. 12301/12) concerns the applicant Tomislav Merčep’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that domestic courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for his prolonged pre-trial detention on war-crimes charges.

Merčep, a Croatian national born in 1952, was arrested on 10 December 2010 after the Zagreb police lodged a criminal complaint alleging that, as commander of a reserve police unit in 1991, he had ordered or condoned arbitrary arrests, torture, robbery and killings of civilians during the armed conflict. The investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court immediately ordered 48-hour remand on grounds of risk of witness interference and the gravity of the offences. The same day Merčep, who had suffered a stroke in 2007, was placed in a prison hospital. An investigation was opened on 13 December 2010; thirty-one witnesses were heard, international legal assistance was sought, and extensive forensic material (DNA, autopsy and exhumation reports) was gathered.

On 9 June 2011 the State Attorney indicted Merčep on twenty-two counts of war crimes against civilians, including the murder of a twelve-year-old girl. Detention was thereafter maintained solely under Article 102 § 1(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (particularly grave circumstances of an offence carrying a sentence of at least twelve years). Successive extensions by three-judge panels of the Zagreb County Court, the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court repeatedly invoked the scale of the alleged atrocities (more than twenty civilian victims subjected to electric-shock torture, mutilation and execution), the public-order need to prevent “great disturbance” and to preserve confidence in the judiciary, and the fact that many witnesses had yet to be examined. Collusion risk was cited only until the indictment; thereafter gravity alone was deemed sufficient. Merčep’s health arguments were consistently rejected on the basis that adequate medical care was available in detention.

Hearings were adjourned twice because of deterioration in Merčep’s condition. On 18 April 2012 the Constitutional Court, while upholding detention, instructed the lower courts to examine his health more thoroughly. After two remittals by the Supreme Court for inadequate reasoning on medical care, the Zagreb County Court on 5 July 2012 revoked detention, holding that the quality of treatment in custody risked violating Article 3 and that the time already spent in detention, the age of the alleged events and the probable length of the trial outweighed the remaining public-interest justification.

Throughout the nineteen-month period of detention the domestic courts therefore relied first on a combination of collusion risk and gravity, then exclusively on the particularly grave nature of the charges, while repeatedly finding that Merčep’s chronic illness did not preclude continued custody. The trial itself remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings. These facts form the core of the alleged violation of the requirement that pre-trial detention be justified by relevant and sufficient reasons that are reviewed with increasing scrutiny as time passes.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Merčep v. The investigation involved 31 witnesses, international legal assistance, DNA analyses, exhumations and unit documents. The indictment detailed his command responsibility and acceptance of subordinates’ crimes. His objection to the indictment was dismissed in September 2011; a medical expert later confirmed he could stand trial with proper arrangements. Hearings were adjourned in 2012 due to his deteriorating health. Proceedings remained pending at the time of the Court’s judgment.

Initial 48-hour remand, followed by successive extensions, was based on Article 102 § 1(2) and (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (risk of collusion and particularly grave circumstances). After indictment, detention continued solely under Article 102 § 1(4). Health concerns were dismissed because adequate care was available in prison hospitals and a rehabilitation facility.

The Constitutional Court eventually directed fuller health assessments. After remittals by the Supreme Court, the County Court released him on 5 July 2012, holding that inadequate medical treatment in detention raised an Article 3 issue that outweighed even the grave public-interest grounds for continued custody.

Domestic law (Article 102 § 1(4) CCP and Constitutional Court practice) permitted such detention for the most serious offences when particularly grave circumstances existed, to protect public order and judicial reputation. International materials cited included Council of Europe Recommendation Rec(2006)13 and ICTY/ICTR/ICC case-law on the exceptional nature and reasonableness of pre-trial detention in grave-crime cases.

The applicant complained that the domestic courts had failed throughout to give relevant and sufficient reasons, to consider less restrictive measures, or to reassess proportionality as time passed, thereby violating Article 5 § 3.

The case of Kashlev v. Estonia concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to a fair trial. Janek Kashlev, of undetermined citizenship and born in 1987, was charged with causing serious health damage. The charges alleged that at 4.30 a.m. on 22 April 2006, he and I.J. repeatedly struck L. on the head outside a nightclub; L. fell and was kicked, suffering life-threatening head injuries and permanent damage. Proceedings against I.J. were discontinued after his death in a car accident.

The Harju County Court heard the applicant and nine witnesses and examined forensic evidence on L.’s injuries, a telephone activity report, photographic identification reports, CCTV footage, and I.J.’s pre-trial statements. It found the witness accounts incoherent and contradictory as to the number of people present, the attackers’ actions, and events after L. fell. It accepted I.J.’s account that he had struck L. twice, after which L. fell and the applicant arrived, and gave credit to S.G. (a friend of the applicant) who described a fight solely between L. and I.J. The court rejected the statements and identifications of K.A., K.S. and K.M. because they were inconsistent with their in-court testimony and lacked credibility (for example, K.M. claimed to recognise the applicant’s eyes but not his jacket). Concluding that only indirect evidence existed, the court held that guilt had not been established beyond doubt and acquitted the applicant on 30 April 2007.

The prosecutor appealed, challenging the assessment of the evidence but not requesting re-examination of witnesses, and asked the Tallinn Court of Appeal to quash the acquittal and convict. The applicant was notified and elected in writing not to attend. At the 4 September 2007 hearing his counsel confirmed this, the prosecutor did not object, and the first-instance records were disclosed without objection. Arguments were heard; no witnesses were summoned or examined.

The Court of Appeal, relying on the case file, reassessed the same evidence and found guilt established. It held that the statements were complementary rather than contradictory, as witnesses had focused on different details. It accepted the previously rejected statements and identifications, reasoning that witnesses need not recall every detail (for instance, eyes and eyebrows rather than clothing), that courtroom stress could explain failed recognition, that differing perceptions were normal, and that there were no radical inconsistencies. It rejected S.G.’s account as inconsistent with independent witnesses and noted the friendship among the applicant, S.G. and I.J. It found I.J. not credible in assuming sole responsibility and highlighted inconsistencies in the applicant’s own statements, together with overheard remarks matching his appearance that implied knowledge of the quarrel’s origin. Because the pair had acted jointly, it was irrelevant who delivered the blow that felled L. (though one witness attributed the last blow to the applicant). The court found indirect intent to cause serious injury and convicted the applicant, imposing a five-year sentence of which two months were to be served immediately and the rest suspended, taking account of his youth and lack of prior convictions.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the Court of Appeal had not directly examined the evidence, that witness demeanour (for example K.M.’s hesitation) was crucial yet unrecorded, and that the reassessment was selective and arbitrary. On 14 November 2007 the Supreme Court declined to examine the appeal.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure an appellate court may base its decision on evidence examined at first instance and merely disclosed on appeal. Settled Supreme Court case-law requires particularly thorough reasoning, including identification of the first-instance court’s errors, whenever an appellate court reaches the opposite conclusion on the same body of evidence.

The court accepted I.J.’s statement that he alone had struck L. twice before the applicant arrived, and it saw no reason to discount the testimony of the applicant’s friend S.G., who described a fight solely between L. and I.J. It rejected as unreliable the statements and identifications of K.A., K.S. and K.M. because they diverged from their later courtroom testimony (for example, K.M. claimed to recognise the applicant by his eye colour yet could not describe his jacket). Concluding that only indirect evidence existed, the court acquitted the applicant on 30 April 2007, holding that guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The prosecutor appealed, challenging solely the assessment of the existing evidence and requesting a conviction; he did not ask for witnesses to be reheard. The applicant and his counsel were notified. The applicant informed the Tallinn Court of Appeal in writing that he did not wish to attend and consented to the case being heard in his absence. At the 4 September 2007 hearing his counsel confirmed this, the prosecutor raised no objection, the first-instance records were read out without protest, and no request was made to summon any witness. No witnesses were examined.

It held that the witnesses had merely focused on different details rather than contradicted one another. It restored the statements and identifications of K.A., K.S. and K.M., explaining that a witness need not recall every detail, that courtroom stress could explain a failure to recognise the applicant, and that minor verbal discrepancies did not undermine reliability. It discounted S.G. as biased (he, the applicant and I.J. were friends) and found I.J. incredible for assuming sole responsibility. The applicant’s own accounts were inconsistent, and a remark overheard from a person matching his description (“Why then did he come to start a quarrel?”) showed he had been present from the outset. Acting jointly rendered it legally irrelevant which blow felled L.; the court nevertheless noted K.S.’s evidence that the applicant delivered the last blow. After analysing the mental element it found indirect intent and convicted the applicant, imposing a five-year sentence of which two months were to be served immediately (the remainder suspended) in view of his youth and clean record.

The applicant’s further appeal to the Supreme Court complained that the Court of Appeal had never directly observed the witnesses (whose demeanour, especially K.M.’s hesitation, was not recorded), had assessed the evidence selectively and had failed to give the benefit of the doubt. On 14 November 2007 the Supreme Court declined to admit the appeal.

Estonian law (Articles 15, 335 and 340 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) permits an appellate court to rely on first-instance evidence once it has been disclosed and to substitute a conviction for an acquittal. Subsequent Supreme Court case-law nevertheless requires particularly thorough reasoning, including identification of the first-instance court’s specific errors, whenever an appellate court reaches the opposite conclusion on the same body of evidence.

The case of Sulejmani v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 74681/11) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention about the confiscation of the applicant’s vehicle following criminal proceedings against a third party.

The applicant, Osman Sulejmani, a Macedonian national born in 1958 and residing in Tetovo, purchased a concrete-mixing and transport lorry from Sh.A. on 12 April 2006 for the equivalent of EUR 5,000. He later lent the vehicle to his company. On 6 October 2008 the Ministry of the Interior temporarily seized the vehicle and its registration certificate to examine the chassis, issuing a record of temporarily seized objects.

On 1 February 2010 the Struga Court of First Instance acquitted Sh.A. of forging a document relating to the vehicle’s chassis number, finding that it had not been established that Sh.A. had altered the chassis. An indictment against another person, I.S., was also rejected. The applicant, who had sought compensation in those proceedings, was directed to pursue any claim by separate civil action. The judgment became final on 21 July 2010.

On 16 November 2010 the applicant applied for return of the vehicle. At a hearing on 3 December 2010 he stated that he had paid EUR 25,000 and could not have known of any chassis-number forgery. On 6 December 2010 the first-instance court, applying Article 100-a(3) of the Criminal Code, held that there were no grounds for confiscation because the applicant had neither known nor could have known that the vehicle had been used to commit a crime, and ordered return of the registration certificate.

The public prosecutor appealed. On 24 January 2011 the Bitola Court of Appeal quashed the decision, relying on Article 100-a(2) of the Criminal Code. It found that the chassis had been forged, that the vehicle could not be declared roadworthy in the interest of public safety, and that the first-instance court should assess whether continued use would constitute the offence of using a forged public document.

On 22 February 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s request and ordered confiscation of both the vehicle and the registration certificate. It held that the forged chassis number meant the vehicle could be used to commit an offence and that confiscation was required for reasons of road safety and general safety, even though no proceedings had been brought against the applicant himself. The court cited section 532(1) of the Criminal Proceedings Act, which permits confiscation of objects that must be confiscated under the Criminal Code even when criminal proceedings do not end in a conviction.

The applicant appealed, arguing misapplication of Article 100-a(2) and (3) and stressing that he had not known of the forgery. On 19 May 2011 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It accepted that the applicant had not known the chassis was forged and had registered the vehicle, obtained a licence and paid a substantial sum, but held that Article 100-a(2) required confiscation of objects used or intended for an offence, irrespective of ownership by a third party, whenever general safety, public health or ethics so required. Continued use of a vehicle with forged identification numbers would endanger road users and therefore general safety; the conditions of Article 100-a(3) protecting bona-fide third-party owners were not therefore satisfied.

The decision was served on the applicant on 2 June 2011. Relevant domestic provisions include Article 100-a of the Criminal Code (confiscation of instrumentalities even from third parties when public-safety interests so require, subject to a knowledge proviso in paragraph 3), Article 380 (use of a false document), and section 532 of the Criminal Proceedings Act (confiscation possible without a conviction). The Obligations Act also imposes seller liability for legal defects. Domestic case-law confirmed both seller responsibility for such defects and the practice of confiscating vehicles with altered chassis numbers even in the absence of a conviction.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s claim that the confiscation of his lawfully acquired vehicle, of which he was a bona-fide owner, interfered with his right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The case of Sulejmani v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 74681/11) concerns Osman Sulejmani’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the confiscation of his vehicle, following criminal proceedings against a third party, unlawfully interfered with his property rights.

On 6 October 2008 the Ministry of the Interior temporarily seized the vehicle and its registration certificate to inspect the chassis, issuing a formal record of seizure.

On 1 February 2010 the Struga Court of First Instance acquitted him, holding that alteration of the chassis had not been proved, and rejected an indictment against another person. The applicant, who had sought compensation in those proceedings, was directed to pursue a civil claim. The judgment became final on 21 July 2010.

On 6 December 2010 the first-instance court, applying Article 100-a(3) of the Criminal Code, refused confiscation because the applicant neither knew nor ought to have known that the vehicle had been used in a crime, and ordered return of the certificate.

The public prosecutor appealed. On 24 January 2011 the Bitola Court of Appeal quashed the decision, noting that the forged chassis rendered the vehicle unroadworthy and that public safety required its confiscation. It remitted the matter for consideration of whether continued use would itself constitute the offence of using a forged document (Article 380).

It held that the forged identification numbers created a risk of further offences and endangered road safety, so confiscation was required even though the applicant himself faced no charges. Section 532 of the Criminal Proceedings Act allows such confiscation even without a conviction. Parallel civil provisions (Obligations Act, ss. 496–498) make a seller liable for legal defects and entitle a buyer to termination and damages. Domestic practice consistently confiscated vehicles with altered chassis numbers irrespective of the owner’s innocence or the outcome of related prosecutions.

These facts establish that a bona-fide purchaser lost title to his vehicle solely because of a prior, unproven alteration of its chassis, the courts relying exclusively on an abstract public-safety rationale after the original accused had been acquitted.

The case of Sulejmani v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 74681/11) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the confiscation of the applicant’s vehicle. Osman Sulejmani, a Macedonian national born in 1958 and residing in Tetovo, purchased a concrete-mixing and transport lorry from Sh.A. on 12 April 2006 for the equivalent of EUR 5,000. He later lent the vehicle to his company. On 6 October 2008 the Ministry of the Interior temporarily seized the vehicle and its registration certificate in order to examine the chassis; a record of temporarily seized objects was issued.

On 1 February 2010 the Struga Court of First Instance acquitted Sh.A. of forging a document relating to the vehicle’s chassis number and rejected an indictment against another individual. The court found that it had not been established that Sh.A. had altered the chassis. Pursuant to section 102(3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act it instructed the applicant, who had claimed compensation in those proceedings, to pursue any claim in separate civil proceedings. The judgment became final on 21 July 2010.

On 16 November 2010 the applicant applied for the return of the vehicle. He was heard on 3 December 2010 and stated that he had paid EUR 25,000 and could not have known the chassis number had been forged. On 6 December 2010 the first-instance court, applying Article 100-a(3) of the Criminal Code, held that there were no grounds for confiscation because the applicant had neither known nor could have known that the vehicle had been used to commit a crime; it ordered the return of the registration certificate.

The public prosecutor appealed. On 24 January 2011 the Bitola Court of Appeal quashed the decision. It found that the chassis had been forged, that the vehicle could not be declared roadworthy for reasons of public safety, and that the first-instance court should assess whether continued use would itself constitute the offence of using a forged document. On 22 February 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s application and ordered confiscation of the vehicle and certificate under Article 100-a(2) and (3) of the Criminal Code and section 532(1) of the Criminal Proceedings Act. It held that the forged chassis number meant the vehicle could be used to commit an offence and that confiscation was required for road-safety and general-safety reasons, even though no criminal proceedings had been brought against the applicant and he was not an offender.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the courts had misapplied Article 100-a and that he had been unaware of any forgery. On 19 May 2011 the appellate court dismissed the appeal. It accepted that the applicant had not known of the forged chassis, had registered the vehicle, obtained a licence and paid a substantial sum, but held that Article 100-a(2) required confiscation of objects used or intended for use in a crime, irrespective of ownership by a third party, whenever general safety, public health or ethics so demanded. Continued use of a vehicle with forged identification numbers would endanger road users and therefore general safety; the conditions of Article 100-a(3) were therefore not met.

The relevant domestic provisions included Article 100-a of the Criminal Code (confiscation of objects used in crime even from third-party owners if general safety so required, or if the third party knew or ought to have known of the intended use) and section 532(1) of the Criminal Proceedings Act (permitting confiscation even in the absence of a conviction). The applicant maintained that the confiscation of a vehicle belonging to a bona-fide purchaser who had no knowledge of the forgery, following the acquittal of the seller, constituted an unjustified interference with his property rights.
001-162219:
The case of Buchleither v. Germany (App. no. 20106/13) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for family life) arising from the indefinite suspension of all contact between the applicant (a German national born in 1965) and his daughter H. (born 29 June 2003). The unmarried parents separated shortly after H.’s birth. The mother holds sole parental authority and H. lives with her. Parental conflict over contact began in late 2003.

The applicant first applied to the Neustadt/Weinstraße Family Court for contact in April 2004. Supervised contact was agreed in 2004 but faltered due to the parents’ conduct, prompting youth-office and child-protection associations to withdraw. The applicant repeatedly sought coercive fines against the mother and appointment of facilitators. After further disputes, the Family Court in December 2008 suspended contact until 31 December 2009 (a constitutional complaint failed).

In January 2010 the applicant sought resumption. After hearing H., the Family Court ordered fortnightly contact with directions and sanctions, but none occurred. In September 2010, again after hearing H., it suspended contact pending the main proceedings and refused coercive measures.

In the main proceedings the Family Court (April 2011) heard the parents, H. and her guardian ad litem. Relying on psychiatrist Dr B. (written and oral evidence), it granted two hours’ contact every fortnight and appointed a guardian with instructions for preparation and organisation. The mother appealed. The applicant also sought regular information on H.’s development.

The Court of Appeal obtained further evidence from Dr B., who now considered suspension the less damaging option in H.’s best interests: contact itself was not harmful, but the parental conflict made it presently impossible. The mother refused mediation (which the applicant accepted). The guardian favoured at least letter/present contact to avoid long-term harm.

On 19 October 2012 the Zweibrücken Court of Appeal indefinitely suspended all contact under Civil Code Arts. 1684 § 4 and 1696. It noted four years without contact had made the father a stranger to H. (then aged 9). H. firmly stated she did not wish to see him and had only limited negative memories; she appeared age-appropriately developed, understood the issues and would resist being forced. Her guardian reported she cried and left the room when her father was mentioned. The court found her attitude shaped by loyalty to the mother (who spoke negatively of the applicant), creating a loyalty conflict; H. rejected her father to preserve her mother’s love and end the dispute. She was mature enough to decide consciously. Expert evidence showed forced contact amid unresolved parental communication problems (requiring at least mediation) would cause more harm than exclusion. The parents’ history made successful mediation unforeseeable. The court left open later resumption if the parents improved communication or H., with greater maturity, herself sought contact.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the applicant’s complaint (February 2013, no reasons). Subsequent administrative notes on the file indicated no further action.

Domestic law (Civil Code Art. 1684) entitles a child to contact with both parents but permits restriction or exclusion (including long-term/permanent) only if otherwise the child’s best interests would be endangered; Art. 1696 requires cancellation if the risk ceases. Family-procedure rules mandate ex-officio fact-finding and periodic review of long-term child-protection measures.

These facts—the decade-long high-conflict history, H.’s expressed wishes and loyalty dilemma, the expert’s assessment that unprepared contact would harm more than suspension, and the courts’ finding that parental communication could not be improved—underpin the applicant’s claim that the indefinite bar violated Article 8.

The case of Buchleither v. Germany (Application no. 20106/13) concerns the applicant Lucian Buchleither (born 1965), a German national, who alleged that the indefinite suspension of all contact with his daughter H. (born 29 June 2003) violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life. The unmarried parents separated shortly after H.'s birth. H. lives with her mother, who holds sole parental authority.

Disputes over contact began in late 2003. In April 2004 the applicant sought contact rights in the Neustadt/Weinstraße Family Court. Supervised contact occurred until October 2004 under a June 2004 agreement, followed by a further court-approved supervised-contact agreement in December 2004. Subsequent requests to replace the supervising Youth Office (2005), impose coercive fines on the mother, and appoint an access facilitator (2006) yielded mixed results, with contact occurring irregularly amid ongoing parental conflict.

In May 2007 the applicant sought extended contact and a coercive fine; the mother requested a two-year suspension. After expert evidence, the Family Court in December 2008 suspended contact until 31 December 2009. The applicant's constitutional complaint failed.

In January 2010, after the suspension expired, the applicant sought renewed contact. The Family Court granted fortnightly contact in April 2010 (with compliance directions and sanctions) after hearing H., but no contact occurred. In September 2010, after a further hearing of H., the court suspended contact pending the main proceedings and refused a coercive fine.

In the main proceedings the Family Court, on 15 April 2011, heard the parents, H. and her custodian ad litem. Relying on psychiatrist Dr B.'s written and oral evidence, it ordered two hours' fortnightly contact and appointed a guardian with instructions on preparing H. The mother appealed. The Court of Appeal obtained further evidence from Dr B., who now considered indefinite suspension the less damaging option given the parents' unresolved conflict (the applicant having agreed to mediation, which the mother refused). The guardian recommended minimum contact via letters and presents to avoid long-term harm.

On 19 October 2012, after hearing the parents, guardian, H. and Dr B., the Zweibrücken Court of Appeal indefinitely suspended all contact pursuant to Articles 1684 § 4 and 1696 of the Civil Code. It noted that the 2006 court-approved agreement remained formally valid but held that contact would endanger H.'s welfare. H. had had no contact with her father for four years and regarded him as a stranger. When heard, H. (who had developed age-appropriately) firmly stated she did not wish to see him, citing limited bad memories, and indicated she would resist being forced. The guardian had been unable to overcome her aversion; she cried and left the room when her father was mentioned.

The Court of Appeal attributed H.'s attitude to loyalty towards her mother, who spoke negatively of the applicant, creating a loyalty conflict that H. resolved by rejecting her father to preserve her mother's affection. H. was deemed mature enough to understand the consequences. While loss of parental contact generally harms a child's development, forced contact amid ongoing parental dispute could also cause serious harm. Dr B. had originally found contact itself non-damaging but required improved parental communication (via professional help such as mediation) as a prerequisite; this had been ignored by the Family Court. The parents had taken no such steps. Given their courtroom and extra-judicial conduct, the Court of Appeal ruled out successful mediation in the foreseeable future, making exclusion of contact the only option. It noted that the mother needed to overcome her aversion and the applicant needed patience and restraint; H. might later, with greater maturity, initiate contact herself. The decision did not preclude future possibilities.

The Federal Constitutional Court refused to entertain the applicant's complaint on 6 February 2013 without reasons. After the ECHR communicated the application, the family-court file was reviewed in July 2014 and marked “nothing to be done.”

The case of Buchleither v. Germany (ECHR Application no. 20106/13) concerns the applicant’s claim that an indefinite court-ordered suspension of all contact with his daughter violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life.

The applicant (born 1965) and the unmarried mother of his daughter H. (born 29 June 2003) separated shortly after the birth. The child lives with the mother, who has sole parental authority. Contact disputes began in late 2003. From 2004 the applicant repeatedly sought access through the Neustadt/Weinstraße Family Court. Supervised-contact agreements were reached in 2004 and 2006, but implementation repeatedly failed because of parental hostility; youth-welfare bodies and child-protection associations successively withdrew. In 2007 the applicant applied to extend contact and impose coercive measures; the mother sought a two-year ban. After expert evidence, the Family Court suspended all contact until 31 December 2009 (upheld on constitutional complaint).

When that period expired the applicant applied to resume access. In April 2010, after hearing the child, the Family Court ordered fortnightly meetings with detailed directions and sanctions, but none occurred. In September 2010, again after hearing the child, the court suspended contact pending the main proceedings.

In those proceedings the Family Court (April 2011), relying on psychiatrist Dr B., granted two hours’ contact every fortnight and appointed a guardian to prepare the child. The mother appealed. Dr B. then advised the Zweibrücken Court of Appeal that, given the unrelenting parental conflict, suspension was currently the less damaging option for the child; contact itself was not harmful, but the parents’ communication breakdown made it impossible. The child’s guardian recommended at least written contact. On 19 October 2012, after hearing the parents, the child (then aged nine), the guardian and Dr B., the Court of Appeal indefinitely suspended all contact under Civil Code Arts. 1684 § 4 and 1696. It found that four years without contact had made the father a stranger; the child clearly and firmly refused to see him, displayed distress at any mention of him, and possessed sufficient maturity to understand the consequences. Her attitude was shaped by loyalty to the mother, who persistently denigrated the father, creating an acute conflict of loyalties. Forced contact amid continuing parental warfare would itself endanger the child’s welfare. Mediation was unrealistic given the parents’ history; the mother refused it and the father could not unilaterally arrange access. The court noted that the child might later initiate contact herself as she matured, but saw no present means of protecting her welfare other than total exclusion.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain the applicant’s complaint (February 2013). After the Strasbourg application was communicated, the family-court file was returned and a judge recorded “nothing to be done.”

These facts—the protracted high-conflict history, the child’s expressed wishes and psychological dilemma, the expert’s assessment that current contact would cause greater harm than suspension, and the indefinite character of the ban—form the core of the alleged Article 8 violation.
001-163665:
The applicant, Tassos Philippou, a Cypriot national born in 1949, worked in Cyprus's Department of Lands and Surveys from December 1971. Promoted to assistant officer in 1996, he was authorised in 1998 to sign payment orders. In May 2002 an irregularity in a compulsory acquisition case led to an investigation revealing that compensation cheques had been issued but never reached the named payees.

Criminal proceedings followed against the applicant (and an accomplice), involving 223 charges. On 18 January 2005, after a plea bargain, the Nicosia Assize Court convicted him on 24 charges (including obtaining approximately €390,000 by false pretences, forging documents, abuse of office and concealment). He received concurrent sentences of two to five years' imprisonment. As part of the bargain he repaid CYP 150,000 (approximately €255,000), and a confiscation order was made. The court took account of eight further pending similar cases. His appeal against sentence was later withdrawn.

Following the conviction the Public Service Commission (PSC) opened disciplinary proceedings, the Attorney-General having advised that the offences involved dishonesty or moral turpitude. After hearing mitigation (the applicant's financial hardship, partial repayment, existing criminal sentence, long service and the lighter penalty given to his accomplice), the PSC dismissed him on 13 June 2005. It characterised the case as among the most serious it had encountered: a well-organised fraud that undermined the Department's prestige and the public service's credibility. The applicant was described as the mastermind who had exploited his position. Under section 79(7) of the Public Service Law 1990, dismissal automatically entailed forfeiture of all retirement benefits (lump sum and monthly pension) after 33 years' service. Withheld salary during suspension was not restored. The same provision entitled his wife to a widow's pension of €15,600 per year, calculated as if he had died on the date of dismissal.

The applicant sought judicial review, arguing that the automatic forfeiture of pension rights (a “possession”) violated Article 23 of the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and was disproportionate. He later added that reliance on his marital status for mitigation amounted to discrimination contrary to Article 28 of the Constitution, Article 14 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The Supreme Court (first instance) held the pension a possession but found the interference justified by the gravity of the offences. It noted the statutory proviso for a family pension reduced hardship, though it criticised the automatic nature of forfeiture and suggested legislative reform to allow discretion. On appeal the Supreme Court confirmed that the right to pension constituted a possession arising on appointment. It held that the PSC had exercised discretion by choosing dismissal rather than compulsory retirement (which would have preserved benefits). The measure pursued the legitimate aim of protecting public administration and was not disproportionate, given the seriousness of the conduct. Unlike Apostolakis v. Greece, the applicant retained social-insurance pension rights (which he later received from age 63, reducing his wife's pension). Comments about marital status were hypothetical and disclosed no discrimination.

The applicant has received a social-security pension since August 2012.
