The applicant, Tassos Philippou, a Cypriot national born in 1949, began public service in the Department of Lands and Surveys in 1971. He was promoted to assistant officer in 1996 and authorised in 1998 to sign payment orders. In 2002 irregularities emerged in compulsory land-acquisition compensation: cheques were issued but never reached named payees. Criminal proceedings followed against the applicant (and an accomplice) on 223 charges.

On 18 January 2005 the Nicosia Assize Court sentenced him, on a guilty plea to 24 charges after a plea bargain, to concurrent terms of two to five years’ imprisonment. Offences included obtaining approximately CYP 225,644 (EUR 390,000) by false pretences, issuing false documents, forging cheques, abuse of office and concealment. He agreed to repay CYP 150,000 (EUR 255,000), and a confiscation order was made. The court also took eight further pending similar cases into account. The applicant later withdrew his appeal against sentence.

After the Attorney-General advised that the offences involved dishonesty or moral turpitude, the Public Service Commission (PSC) opened disciplinary proceedings. On 13 June 2005, having heard mitigation (financial hardship after suspension, partial repayment, length of service, and the lighter penalty given to the accomplice), the PSC dismissed the applicant. It described the case as one of the most serious it had encountered: a well-organised fraud that undermined the Department’s prestige and the public service’s credibility. The applicant had been the mastermind, exploiting his trusted position with “unprecedented effrontery.” Dismissal under section 79(7) of the Public Service Law 1990 automatically forfeited all retirement benefits (lump sum and pension) after 33 years’ service. His wife received a widow’s pension (EUR 15,600 per year) as if he had died on the date of dismissal. Withheld salary during suspension was not returned.

The applicant sought judicial review, arguing that the automatic forfeiture of pension rights (a “possession”) violated Article 23 of the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, being disproportionate. On 7 May 2007 the Supreme Court (first instance) dismissed the recourse. It accepted that pension rights were possessions but held the interference justified by the offences’ gravity, which damaged administrative trustworthiness. Non-forfeiture would have rewarded him. Although automatic loss created hardship, the widow’s pension mitigated it; the court noted that a different outcome might have followed had there been no spouse. It recommended legislative amendment to allow discretionary (rather than automatic) forfeiture, modelled on English law.

Both sides appealed. On 18 May 2010 the Supreme Court (appellate) dismissed the appeals. It confirmed pension rights as possessions created by appointment. The PSC had exercised discretion in choosing dismissal (one of ten possible penalties) rather than compulsory retirement, which would have preserved benefits; the choice served the public interest of deterring serious misconduct and protecting administration. Forfeiture was a consequence of dismissal, not a separate punishment, and was not disproportionate given the offences’ scale. Unlike Apostolakis v. Greece, the applicant retained social-insurance rights (later paid from age 63, reducing the widow’s pension by EUR 855 monthly). Comments on marital status were hypothetical and did not establish discrimination under Article 28 of the Constitution.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the forfeiture breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and that the first-instance court’s reliance on his marital status (widow’s pension) constituted discrimination contrary to Article 14 taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The case of Philippou v. Cyprus (Application no. 71148/10) concerned a Cypriot public servant’s complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) regarding the automatic forfeiture of his retirement benefits upon disciplinary dismissal, as well as alleged discrimination on the basis of marital status under Article 14 of the Convention read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The applicant, born in 1949, joined the Department of Lands and Surveys in 1971 and was later authorised to sign payment orders. In 2002 an investigation revealed that numerous cheques issued as compensation in compulsory land-acquisition cases had never reached the named payees. He faced 223 criminal charges. Following a plea bargain he was convicted in January 2005 on 24 counts, including obtaining approximately CYP 225,643 (EUR 390,000) by false pretences, forgery, abuse of office and concealment. He received concurrent sentences of two to five years’ imprisonment; the Assize Court also took into account eight further pending cases. As part of the plea he repaid CYP 150,000 (EUR 255,000), secured by a confiscation order. He later withdrew his sentence appeal.

After the Attorney-General advised that the offences involved dishonesty or moral turpitude, the Public Service Commission (PSC) opened disciplinary proceedings. On 13 June 2005, having heard mitigation (financial hardship, partial restitution, length of service and a socio-economic report), the PSC dismissed the applicant. It characterised the case as one of the most serious it had encountered: a well-organised fraud that undermined public confidence in the Lands Department and the civil service as a whole. The applicant was identified as the mastermind. Dismissal under section 79(7) of the Public Service Law 1990 automatically entailed forfeiture of all retirement benefits (a lump sum and monthly pension) after 33 years’ service. A statutory proviso, however, directed that a widow’s pension calculated on actual years of service be paid to his wife (EUR 15,600 per year). His withheld salary during suspension was not restored.

The applicant sought judicial review of both the dismissal and the forfeiture. The Supreme Court (first instance) held that the pension rights constituted a possession under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It nevertheless found the interference justified by the gravity of the offences and the need to protect administrative integrity. Although it noted the automatic nature of the forfeiture and the applicant’s partial restitution, it regarded the payment to his wife as sufficiently mitigating family hardship. It suggested that the legislature consider introducing discretionary forfeiture. Both parties appealed. In May 2010 the Supreme Court (appellate) confirmed that pension rights were possessions but held the deprivation proportionate: the PSC had exercised discretion in selecting dismissal rather than compulsory retirement (which would have preserved benefits), the measure served the public interest in deterring serious misconduct, and the applicant remained entitled to a social-insurance pension. The Court distinguished Apostolakis v. Greece, in which the applicant had lost all means of subsistence. Comments about marital status were treated as hypothetical and did not establish discrimination.

From August 2012 the applicant himself received a social-insurance pension, which correspondingly reduced his wife’s pension. The domestic courts therefore found no violation of the property or non-discrimination provisions.
001-163347:
The case of Vukušić v. Croatia (Application no. 69735/11) concerns Croatian national Filip Vukušić (born 1946), who alleged that domestic courts violated his property rights by annulling his title to a flat in Sisak that he occupied. The European Court of Human Rights communicated the application on the property complaint (implicitly under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention).

In 1965 the socially owned Sisak Ironworks granted a specially protected tenancy of the flat to employee S.K. and his family. Amid 1991–1992 conflict, Serbian paramilitaries controlled nearby territory and Croatian forces carried out targeted killings of Serb civilians in the Sisak area. S.K. and his wife Z.K. (both of Serb origin) therefore fled to relatives in Rijeka, leaving furniture and appliances behind. The Ironworks was later restructured into state-controlled entities, including Sisak Ironworks Flat (which managed the company’s former flats) and Sisak Ironworks Fortis.

The 1991 Specially Protected Tenancies (Sale to Occupier) Act entitled holders of such tenancies of socially owned flats to purchase them on favourable terms (normally one flat only). The applicant, displaced from his house in occupied Petrinja, moved to Sisak, obtained employment with Fortis, and in 1992 moved into the flat. He claimed his employer allocated it; the Government noted he produced no allocation document. S.K. allegedly consented by telephone to temporary occupation by the displaced family.

In July 1992 the Flat company sued to terminate S.K. and Z.K.’s tenancy on abandonment grounds. The applicant testified that he did not know S.K.’s whereabouts. A guardian ad litem was appointed. The Sisak Municipal Court terminated the tenancy in October 1992; the County Court upheld the judgment, which became final. In December 1993 S.K. and Z.K. applied to reopen those proceedings. The application was granted on 12 April 1994 (with the applicant intervening for the company). On the same day the Holding and Fortis sold the flat to the applicant under the Sale to Occupier Act; the State Attorney approved the contract. In 1996–1997 the reopened proceedings ended with dismissal of the termination claim, restoring the tenancy to S.K. and Z.K.

After Croatian forces retook Petrinja the applicant obtained reconstruction assistance (HRK 29,900) for his house there and confirmed his family’s return in January 1998. He maintained registered residence in Petrinja from February 1993 to December 1999, yet continued occupying the Sisak flat.

In 2003 S.K. and Z.K. sued the parties to the 1994 sale, seeking its annulment. After S.K.’s death the Municipal Court dismissed the claim, holding the sale lawful because the applicant then held a specially protected tenancy. The County Court reversed in November 2007: Z.K.’s tenancy had been restored, so the sale breached mandatory provisions of the Sale to Occupier Act. The applicant had known both the circumstances of the original tenants’ departure and their reopening request; the contract was therefore contrary to morals and constitutional principles and void under section 103(1) of the Obligations Act. The Supreme Court upheld this in January 2010. The applicant’s March 2008 constitutional complaint (invoking inviolability of ownership, equality and fair-trial guarantees) was declared inadmissible in June 2011 on the ground that it raised no constitutional issues. He remains in the flat.

These facts centre on whether the applicant acquired a legitimate expectation or protected possession through the 1994 purchase (concluded after he knew of the original tenants’ challenge) and whether the later annulment, based on restoration of the prior tenancy and his knowledge, was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim and was proportionate.

The case of Vukušić v. Croatia (Application no. 69735/11) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s property rights arising from the annulment of his title to a flat in Sisak. Filip Vukušić, a Croatian national born in 1946, complained that domestic courts had unlawfully deprived him of ownership of the flat he had occupied since 1992.

In 1965 the socially-owned Sisak Ironworks granted a specially protected tenancy of the flat to its employee S.K. and his family. During the 1991–1992 conflict, Serbian paramilitary forces controlled parts of Croatia and proclaimed the “Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina.” Sisak, near the border, saw targeted killings of Serbian civilians. S.K. and his wife Z.K., both of Serbian origin, fled to Rijeka, leaving their belongings in the flat.

The applicant and his family, themselves displaced after Serbian forces occupied Petrinja in September 1991, moved to Sisak. The applicant obtained work with Sisak Ironworks Fortis, a successor entity of the original company. In 1992 he and his family entered the flat. He later claimed his employer had allocated it to him, though no such document was produced in domestic proceedings. S.K. had agreed by telephone that the displaced family could occupy the premises temporarily.

In July 1992 the company managing the flat sued S.K. and Z.K. for termination of their tenancy on grounds of abandonment. The applicant testified that he did not know their whereabouts. A guardian ad litem was appointed and, in October 1992, the Sisak Municipal Court terminated the tenancy; the decision became final in March 1993. S.K. and Z.K. successfully applied in December 1993 to reopen the proceedings. On the same day the reopening was granted (12 April 1994), the company sold the flat to the applicant under the 1991 Sale to Occupier Act, which permitted holders of specially protected tenancies to purchase socially-owned flats on favourable terms. The State Attorney approved the contract.

The reopened proceedings ended in 1996–1997 with final judgments restoring S.K. and Z.K.’s tenancy. Meanwhile the applicant obtained state reconstruction aid for his damaged house in Petrinja and registered residence there from 1993 to 1999, confirming his return in January 1998.

In 2003 S.K. and Z.K. sued the parties to the 1994 sale, seeking its annulment. After S.K.’s death the Sisak Municipal Court dismissed the claim, holding that the applicant had himself held a specially protected tenancy at the time of purchase. The Sisak County Court reversed that judgment in November 2007. It found that Z.K.’s tenancy had been restored, so the sale breached mandatory provisions of the Sale to Occupier Act. The court also held that the applicant had known both the circumstances of the original tenants’ departure and their application to reopen the termination proceedings; the contract was therefore contrary to morals and constitutional principles and null and void under the Obligations Act. The Supreme Court upheld the decision in January 2010.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint invoking, inter alia, the inviolability of ownership. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible in June 2011, finding no constitutional issue. The applicant continues to occupy the flat.

These facts—wartime displacement, temporary occupation with the original tenant’s consent, contemporaneous sale during reopened proceedings, subsequent restoration of the original tenancy, and the courts’ finding that the applicant knew of the competing claim—form the core of the alleged interference with his property rights.

The case of Vukušić v. Croatia (Application no. 69735/11) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to property under the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the judicial annulment of his ownership title to a flat in Sisak that he occupied.

In 1965 the socially owned Sisak Ironworks granted a specially protected tenancy over the flat to its employee S.K. and his family. During the 1991–1992 conflict, Serbian paramilitary forces controlled nearby territory. Targeted killings of Serbian civilians occurred in the Sisak area, prompting S.K. and his wife Z.K. (both of Serbian origin) to flee to relatives in Rijeka, leaving their furniture and household goods behind. The company was later restructured into Sisak Ironworks Holding (initially state-owned), which managed the flats through a subsidiary.

Croatia’s 1991 Sale to Occupier Act allowed holders of specially protected tenancies of socially owned flats to purchase them on favourable terms. The applicant, a Croatian national born in 1946, had lived with his family in a house in Petrinja until Serbian forces occupied that town in September 1991. Displaced, they relocated to Sisak, where the applicant obtained work with a related company. In 1992 they moved into S.K. and Z.K.’s flat. The applicant claimed his employer allocated it to him; the Government noted he produced no allocation document. S.K. had, however, agreed by telephone that the family could occupy the premises temporarily as displaced persons.

In July 1992 the managing company sued to terminate S.K. and Z.K.’s tenancy for abandonment. The applicant testified as a witness that he did not know S.K.’s whereabouts. A guardian ad litem was appointed. The Sisak Municipal Court terminated the tenancy in October 1992; the decision became final in 1993. In December 1993 S.K. and Z.K. applied to reopen those proceedings; the application was granted on 12 April 1994. That same day the company sold the flat to the applicant under the Sale to Occupier Act; the State Attorney approved the contract. The applicant joined the reopened proceedings as an intervener. In 1996–1997 the courts ultimately dismissed the termination claim and restored Z.K.’s tenancy.

After Croatian authorities recaptured Petrinja in 1995, the applicant obtained reconstruction grants for his damaged house there and confirmed his family’s return in January 1998 (with registered residence in Petrinja from 1993 to 1999).

In 2003 S.K. and Z.K. sued to annul the 1994 sale. The Municipal Court rejected the claim, finding the applicant had held a valid tenancy at the time of purchase. The Sisak County Court reversed this in November 2007, holding that Z.K.’s tenancy had been restored, that the sale therefore breached mandatory provisions of the Sale to Occupier Act, and that the applicant had known both of the original tenants’ circumstances of departure and of their reopening application. The contract was consequently contrary to morals and constitutional principles and void under the Obligations Act. The Supreme Court upheld the judgment in January 2010. The applicant’s 2008 constitutional complaint, invoking inviolability of ownership, was declared inadmissible in 2011 for raising no constitutional issue.

The applicant remains in occupation of the flat. These facts form the core of the claimed interference with his property rights.
001-163451:
The case of R.B.A.B. and Others v. the Netherlands (Application no. 7211/06) concerns five Sudanese nationals—a married couple (Mrs R.B.A.B. and Mr H.S.) and their three children (daughters X, born 1991, and Y, born 1993; son Z, born 1996)—who arrived in the Netherlands in April 2001 and sought asylum. They claimed to have fled Dilling in South Kordofan after Mr H.S. drew official attention through opposition activities. Dutch authorities rejected their initial 2001 applications as lacking credibility, citing contradictions, inability to describe their tribes or local topography, and Mr H.S.’s ignorance of the opposition movement. Appeals failed on procedural grounds. A 2003 repeat application on the same grounds was dismissed for want of new facts; no appeal followed.

In June 2005 the family lodged a third application, now asserting that expulsion would expose the still-uncircumcised daughters to female genital mutilation (FGM) under tribal and social pressure, contrary to Article 3. The parents opposed FGM but said they could not protect the girls. The Minister rejected the claim, doubting its sincerity (it had never been raised before) and noting that official policy, drawn from a 2004 Ministry of Foreign Affairs report, distinguished urban, highly educated women (university or higher-vocational level) who could refuse FGM without stigma from rural, poorly educated women who had little choice. Because the applicants had never substantiated their identities, origins or educational level, they had not shown they fell outside the latter group. Mr H.S. was also deemed a public-order risk after settling a shoplifting charge.

The Regional Court of The Hague (sitting in Zwolle) quashed the refusals. Nationality was no longer disputed, the daughters remained uncircumcised, and earlier credibility findings about the parents’ political claim were irrelevant to the children’s protection. The policy required only a real risk of FGM, state inability or unwillingness to protect, and absence of internal relocation. The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State reversed, holding that section 31 of the Aliens Act 2000 placed the burden on the applicants. Prior res judicata findings of implausibility entitled the Minister to conclude that the conditions of the FGM policy had not been met.

Subsequent developments included X’s grant of a residence permit (she withdrew her application) and unsuccessful later requests by Y and Z. Official Dutch reports (2010, 2015) confirmed FGM’s 89–90 % prevalence in northern Sudan, the absence of effective criminalisation or prosecution, and the decisive role of parental and community attitudes. Educated urban families could generally refuse the practice without difficulty; rural or less-educated families could not. Relocation to avoid FGM was unknown in practice and no shelters existed. International sources (WHO, UNICEF, UNHCR, UK Home Office, US State Department) likewise described FGM as widespread, typically performed on girls aged 4–11, and as a form of torture or inhuman treatment, while noting limited state action and continuing social pressure even after some urban decline.

The applicants maintained that return would place the remaining daughter at real risk of FGM in breach of Article 3. The Government relied on the applicants’ failure to prove identity, origin or educational status and on the policy distinction between those able and those unable to resist the practice.

The case of R.B.A.B. and Others v. the Netherlands (Application no. 7211/06) concerns a Sudanese family of five—parents Mrs R.B.A.B. and Mr H.S., daughters X (born 1991) and Y (born 1993), and son Z (born 1996)—who entered the Netherlands in 2001 and sought asylum. They claimed a real risk that the daughters would face female genital mutilation (FGM) if expelled to Sudan, in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Initial asylum claims in 2001 cited Mr H.S.’s opposition activities with movement M. in Dilling, South Kordofan. Interviews revealed contradictions, inability to describe tribes, local topography, or the movement’s details. The Deputy Minister rejected the claims in January 2002 as lacking credibility. Appeals failed on procedural grounds.

A 2003 repeat claim, supported by documents, was rejected as not based on new facts; it was not appealed. In June 2005 a third claim invoked FGM risk for the uncircumcised daughters (then aged 14 and 11) due to tribal/social pressure. Parents opposed FGM but said they could not protect the girls. A Sudanese Embassy document confirmed nationality.

The Minister intended to refuse, doubting sincerity (the claim was raised late) and citing 2004 policy based on a Foreign Affairs report: educated urban women (university/higher vocational level) could refuse FGM without stigma, while rural/uneducated women had little choice. Applicants had not proven identities, origins, or that they fell outside the educated group able to resist. Mr H.S. also posed a public-order risk after a shoplifting settlement. Applicants argued the mother had only primary education and offered an IQ test; this was refused as the burden lay on them.

The Minister rejected the claims. A Regional Court provisional-measures judge quashed the decisions in 2005, noting undisputed Sudanese nationality and the daughters’ uncircumcised status. Policy required a real FGM risk, lack of state protection, and no internal relocation; FGM was widespread, laws unenforced, and choice cultural. Prior incredibility was irrelevant to protecting the daughters. The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State reversed this in August 2005: applicants must prove eligibility. Prior findings of incredibility (now res judicata) meant they had not shown they met policy conditions or lacked protection/relocation options.

After the application, X had two children and obtained a residence permit in 2015, withdrawing her complaint. Y’s later application was refused in 2015: parents opposed FGM so would not force it, and identity/origin remained unproven. Z’s 2013 claim under a long-term-resident-children regulation (and family extensions) failed because the family had evaded monitoring for over three months. Discretionary admission was also refused.

Dutch reports (2010, 2015) and international sources confirmed FGM’s prevalence (~89–90% in northern Sudan, practiced by most groups, typically ages 4–11 or later at marriage). No effective national ban existed; prosecutions were rare. It was a parental/cultural decision with community pressure, especially rural/less-educated families; urban/educated families increasingly refused without problems. Relocation to avoid FGM was not practised; no shelters existed. Some decline occurred among younger girls amid campaigns, but protection remained inadequate. FGM constituted ill-treatment under international standards.

These facts framed the Article 3 claim: whether expulsion created a real, personal risk of FGM for the daughters given their background, family opposition, and Sudanese conditions.

The applicants, a Sudanese married couple (Mrs R.B.A.B. and Mr H.S.) and their three children (daughters X and Y, born 1991 and 1993, and son Z, born 1996), entered the Netherlands in April 2001 and sought asylum. They claimed to have fled Dilling in South Kordofan after the father attracted official attention through opposition activities. Dutch authorities rejected the claims in 2002 as lacking credibility, citing contradictions, inability to describe claimed tribal affiliations, local topography or the opposition movement, and an implausible overall account. Appeals failed on procedural grounds. A 2003 repeat application on the same grounds was likewise rejected for lack of new facts; no appeal followed.

In June 2005 the family lodged a third asylum request, now alleging a real risk that X and Y would face female genital mutilation (FGM) upon return owing to tribal and social pressure. The parents stated they opposed the practice but could not protect their daughters. They produced an embassy document confirming Sudanese nationality. The Minister rejected the claim, doubting its sincerity (it had not been raised earlier) and relying on official guidance that educated urban women could refuse FGM without stigma while rural, poorly educated women could not. Because identity, origin and educational level remained unproven, the family had not shown they fell outside the group able to resist the practice. The father was also deemed a public-order risk after a shoplifting settlement.

A Regional Court provisional-measures judge quashed the refusals, noting that Sudanese nationality and the daughters’ uncircumcised status were undisputed. Policy required assessment of (i) a real FGM risk, (ii) inability or unwillingness of Sudanese authorities to protect, and (iii) absence of an internal-relocation alternative. Official reports described FGM as widespread, barely prosecuted despite a general health-act prohibition, and determined by family and community attitudes. Educated city dwellers generally faced no problems if they refused; rural women of low education had little choice. The judge held that earlier credibility findings about the parents’ first claim were irrelevant to the daughters’ protection needs and remitted the case.

The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State reversed that ruling. Under the Aliens Act the applicants bore the burden of making their case. Prior, now-final findings that their identity, origin and asylum account lacked credibility entitled the Minister reasonably to conclude they had not shown they met the FGM-protection criteria, that state protection was unavailable, or that internal relocation was impossible.

Later developments included X’s grant of a Dutch residence permit in 2015 (she withdrew her application). Y, now adult, had a 2012 residence request refused; the Minister considered parental opposition made forced circumcision unlikely and again noted the absence of identity or origin documents. Z’s 2013 application under a transitional scheme for long-resident children was rejected because the family had evaded immigration monitoring for more than three months. Discretionary admission was also refused.

Country material consistently records FGM prevalence of approximately 88–90 % among northern Sudanese women, typically performed on girls aged 4–11 (occasionally later, including at marriage). There is no specific criminal prohibition and virtually no prosecutions. Parental decision, shaped by education, urban/rural residence and community pressure, is decisive; families do not relocate to avoid the practice and no shelters exist. Educated urban families can generally refuse without social penalty; less-educated rural families cannot. Some state-level bans and awareness campaigns exist, but national criminalisation has repeatedly failed and enforcement remains negligible.

**CASE OF PETSCHULIES v. GERMANY (Application no. 6281/13), ECtHR (Fifth Section), Judgment of 2 June 2016 (final 2 September 2016)**

The applicant, Dirk Petschulies (born 1952), a German national, complained under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that his preventive detention, retrospectively extended beyond the former 10-year statutory maximum and executed in a supervised residential facility affiliated with a psychiatric hospital, was unlawful.

He had a history of convictions for burglary, assault and related offences. In 1977 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted him of offences committed while drunk, imposed a one-year sentence and ordered psychiatric-hospital detention under Article 63 of the Criminal Code, finding diminished responsibility due to infantile brain damage combined with intoxication. He was detained in psychiatric hospitals until 1980. In 1981 the Göttingen Regional Court quashed that judgment, convicted him of intentional offences while drunk, imposed a longer sentence and found (after expert evidence and re-examination) that he had never suffered a pathological mental disorder, was not a psychopath or alcoholic, and had acted with full responsibility.

On 11 December 1984 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted him of multiple counts of dangerous assault, assault, coercion and attempted coercion committed 1982–1984 against mostly male victims (including schoolchildren and strangers), often involving punching, kicking to the head or setting a dog on them, and in two cases a knife attack on sleeping homeless persons. It imposed six years’ imprisonment plus preventive detention under Article 66 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Experts found he had acted with (almost entirely) full responsibility; alcohol was not causative; he had no pathological mental disorder under Article 21 but a non-pathological personality marked by lack of empathy, a self-image as dominant, and a propensity to commit serious violent offences causing significant injury.

After serving his sentence he entered preventive detention in May 1990 (primarily Salinenmoor Prison). By August 2000 he had completed ten years; the Lüneburg Regional Court nonetheless ordered continuation. A 2001 conviction for assaulting his daughter while on leave added a short prison term. In 2003 he was transferred to a detoxification department and in 2005 to a psychiatric department of Moringen Hospital (the court finding rehabilitation better served there under Article 67a). Further extensions followed. From March 2011 he was authorised to reside provisionally in a supervised residential facility (Friedland Castle, later Gestorf Castle), with regular hospital-staff visits, limited escorted outings, work therapy and no specific treatment for his diagnosed condition or alcohol abuse; the aim was independent coping with daily life. After a conflict he briefly returned to hospital before another supervised placement. He was released on 15 September 2014 pursuant to a July 2014 court decision.

In the proceedings at issue, on 19 July 2011 the Göttingen Regional Court again ordered continued preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under the amended Article 67d § 3. Applying the Federal Constitutional Court’s 4 May 2011 transitional criteria (high likelihood of the most serious violent/sexual offences plus a “mental disorder” under the 2011 Therapy Detention Act, interpreted consistently with Article 5 § 1(e)), it endorsed an expert report (based on files after the applicant refused examination) diagnosing a dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements (ICD-10), confirmed by treating doctors. This, plus alcohol abuse (not addiction), created a high risk of life-threatening attacks (kicking heads, dog attacks) on unprovoked random victims due to lack of empathy and impulse control; the risk was especially high when drunk. Detention remained proportionate given the danger and absence of sufficiently monitored alternative accommodation. Rehabilitation was still better served in a psychiatric setting. The Braunschweig Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal; the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the constitutional complaint.

The applicant argued the stricter criteria were unmet: the offences were 27 years old, he had not drunk since, conditions were relaxed, experts/courts had not shown the disorder caused the original offences or that he was alcoholic, and there was no convincing present risk of serious violence. Originally Article 67d limited an initial period of preventive detention to ten years (release required thereafter); the 1998 amendment abolished the cap with immediate effect, allowing continuation if serious-offence risk persisted. The 2011 Constitutional Court judgment declared retrospective extensions incompatible with the Basic Law (protection of legitimate expectations and liberty) unless Article 5 § 1(e) conditions were satisfied (unsound mind, appropriate institution, high risk of gravest offences) and ordered release by end-2011 if unmet. “Mental disorder” under the Therapy Detention Act (and thus Article 5 § 1(e)) covered personality/conduct disorders including dissocial personality disorder, even if they did not diminish criminal responsibility.

The case of Petschulies v. Germany (Application no. 6281/13) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that his preventive detention, retrospectively extended beyond the former statutory maximum of ten years and executed in a supervised residential facility affiliated to a psychiatric hospital, was unlawful.

The applicant, born in 1952, had a history of convictions including burglary and assault. In 1977 he was convicted of offences committed while drunk and ordered detained in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code on the basis of diminished responsibility due to alleged infantile brain damage; this was later quashed in 1981 after experts found no pathological mental disorder. In 1984 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted him of multiple counts of dangerous assault, assault and coercion (committed 1982–1984) against mostly male victims, including schoolchildren and strangers. Offences involved punching, kicking fallen victims, setting a dog on them (causing bites to the neck, face and stomach) and attacking sleeping homeless people with a knife; victims had not provoked the attacks. He was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment plus preventive detention under Article 66 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Experts found he had acted with full (or, in two cases, possibly diminished) responsibility, suffered from no pathological mental disorder, but had an abnormal personality marked by lack of empathy and a propensity to commit serious violent offences.

After serving his prison term, the applicant entered preventive detention in May 1990. By August 2000 he had completed ten years (the former statutory maximum under Article 67d § 1 of the Criminal Code). Detention was continued. In 2001 he received a further short sentence for assaulting his daughter while on leave. From 2003 he was transferred first to a detoxification facility and then (2005) to the psychiatric department of Moringen Hospital under Article 67a, the courts considering that his rehabilitation could be better promoted there. From March 2011 he resided provisionally in a supervised residential facility (initially Friedland Castle, later Gestorf Castle) affiliated to the hospital, with regular staff visits, limited escorted outings, work therapy and no specific treatment for his diagnosed conditions.

On 19 July 2011 the Göttingen Regional Court, applying the Federal Constitutional Court’s 4 May 2011 transitional criteria, ordered continued preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under the amended Article 67d § 3. An expert (who examined only the files after the applicant refused an interview) diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements (ICD-10), confirmed by treating doctors and said to have caused the original offences. There remained a high risk of the most serious violent offences (e.g., kicking heads or setting a dog on victims) if released, especially when the applicant abused alcohol (he was not addicted). Detention remained proportionate given the risk and the absence of suitable less-restrictive accommodation. The Braunschweig Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal; the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the subsequent constitutional complaint.

(The applicant was released in September 2014 pursuant to a later court decision.) The 1998 legislative amendment had abolished the ten-year maximum with retrospective effect. Following M. v. Germany, the Federal Constitutional Court held such extensions compatible with the Basic Law (and Article 5 § 1 (e)) only if the detainee suffered from a “mental disorder” within the meaning of the 2011 Therapy Detention Act (explicitly encompassing personality disorders) and posed a high risk of the most serious violent or sexual offences, and if detention occurred in an appropriate institution.

The case of *Petschulies v. Germany* (Application no. 6281/13) concerns a German national born in 1952 who alleged that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention beyond the former statutory 10-year maximum, implemented in a supervised residential facility affiliated with a psychiatric hospital, violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.

The applicant had a history of convictions for violent offences. In 1977 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted him of offences committed while drunk, imposing one year’s imprisonment plus detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code after finding diminished responsibility due to alleged infantile brain damage. He was detained until 1980. In 1981 that judgment was quashed; the Göttingen Regional Court found no pathological mental disorder, only an abnormal personality, and substituted a sentence of one year and eight months without psychiatric detention.

In 1984 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted him of seven counts of dangerous assault, four counts of assault and related offences committed 1982–1984 against mostly male victims (including schoolchildren and strangers), involving punches, kicks to the head and incitement of a dog to bite. He received six years’ imprisonment plus an order for preventive detention under Article 66 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Experts concluded he had acted with full criminal responsibility (save possibly two offences linked to alcohol), suffered no pathological mental disorder, but possessed a non-pathological lack of empathy and a propensity to commit serious violent offences.

After serving his prison term he entered preventive detention on 7 May 1990. By August 2000 he had completed ten years; the Lüneburg Regional Court nevertheless ordered continuation. Further short sentences followed. In 2003 he was transferred to a detoxification unit and, in 2005, to a psychiatric hospital under Article 63, the courts considering this better for rehabilitation. From March 2011 he was permitted provisional residence in supervised facilities (Friedland Castle, later Gestorf Castle) attached to Moringen Hospital, with limited escorted outings, work therapy and regular staff visits but no ongoing specific treatment for his diagnosed condition.

On 19 July 2011 the Göttingen Regional Court, applying the Federal Constitutional Court’s 4 May 2011 transitional criteria, again prolonged detention under Article 67d § 3. Relying on a 2010–2011 psychiatric report (prepared without examination, as the applicant refused), it found a dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements (ICD-10) constituting a “mental disorder” under the 2011 Therapy Detention Act and causative of the original offences. It identified a high risk of the most serious violent crimes (e.g., kicking victims’ heads or setting a dog on them) if released, especially when intoxicated, and held continued detention proportionate and better served in a psychiatric setting. The Braunschweig Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 19 September 2011. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain a constitutional complaint on 18 July 2012 without reasons.

The applicant was released on 15 September 2014 pursuant to a later court order. He argued that the original offences were decades old, that he had long abstained from alcohol, that no causal mental disorder had been established at the time of conviction, and that the risk assessment was unconvincing given the relaxed conditions of detention.

Relevant domestic law included the 1998 amendment abolishing the 10-year cap with retrospective effect, provisions allowing transfer between preventive-detention and psychiatric facilities, and the Therapy Detention Act (enacted after *M. v. Germany*). The Federal Constitutional Court’s 2011 leading judgment declared the retrospective-extension regime incompatible with the Basic Law unless, during the transitional period, a detainee suffered a mental disorder (interpreted consistently with Article 5 § 1 (e)) and presented a high likelihood of the most serious violent or sexual offences, and was held in an appropriate institution. Subsequent decisions confirmed that personality disorders fell within that notion.
001-163817:
The case of Lähteenmäki v. Estonia (Application no. 53172/10) concerns an Estonian national who alleged breaches of her right to the presumption of innocence and to a fair civil trial under the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 31 January 2006 the applicant submitted a traffic accident report to her insurer regarding an incident on 26 January 2006. She later provided explanations claiming she had been present, completed the report at the scene, and been collected by her friend P. The insurer suspected fraud and notified the police. Criminal proceedings opened on 6 April 2006. The applicant was charged with insurance fraud (submitting false information about an insured event, the persons involved, and the circumstances) and with inciting P. to give false testimony. A 16 May 2008 bill of indictment stated that mobile-phone positioning, call records and P.’s statement established that the applicant had not been at the scene. No pecuniary damage had occurred because the insurer had refused payment.

At a hearing on 2–3 December 2008 the prosecutor requested discontinuance of the proceedings against the applicant and P. under Article 202(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecutor cited the second-degree nature of the offences, the applicant’s lesser guilt (she had acted at the instigation of co-accused), her lack of prior convictions and her situation as a single mother of a small child. The applicant and her counsel expressly accepted this reasoning and consented to the requested obligations (payment of procedural costs and 80 hours of community service). By ruling of 3 December 2008 the Tartu County Court discontinued the proceedings, reciting the charges in detail and finding that the statutory conditions (second-degree offence, negligible guilt, no damage, no public interest) were met. The ruling noted the applicant’s consent.

On the same day the same court, in settlement proceedings, convicted the co-accused K., T. and V. of insurance fraud. The judgment stated that the applicant (referred to by initials) had not been present, that she had drafted and signed false documents, and that she, together with the others, had created the illusion of an insured event in order to obtain payment.

The applicant later claimed compensation from the insurer, which was refused on the ground that the criminal judgment had established that the accident had been staged. She then brought a civil action. The insurer relied on both the 3 December 2008 judgment and the discontinuance ruling. On 23 December 2009 the Tartu County Court dismissed the claim, holding that the criminal judgment had established that the accident had been staged and that the applicant had not been present; the discontinuance ruling likewise showed she had submitted false information. The court interpreted Article 202 as presupposing that guilt existed (albeit negligible) and that the accused had begun to remedy the offence.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the civil court had treated her as guilty despite the absence of a criminal conviction, thereby violating the presumption of innocence. On 3 May 2010 the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal. It held that discontinuance under Article 202 does not prove that the act was not committed; on the contrary, the provision presupposes that the offence occurred, that guilt was merely negligible, and that the accused had consented to obligations. The court found that the 3 December 2008 ruling had established the applicant’s participation in creating the illusion of an insured event. The applicant’s mere denial, without contrary evidence, was insufficient. The Supreme Court declined to examine a further appeal.

Domestic law and case-law confirm that Article 202 discontinuance requires the existence of the elements of an offence, unlawfulness and guilt, and therefore possesses an inculpatory effect, although it is not equivalent to a conviction and rests on a less rigorous evidentiary basis. Court decisions from other proceedings constitute documentary evidence in civil cases and may be used to prove facts, subject to possible contestation.

The case originated in an application by Estonian national Signe Kristiina Lähteenmäki against Estonia, alleging a breach of her right to the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2 of the Convention) and a lack of a fair civil trial (Article 6 § 1).

On 31 January 2006 the applicant reported a traffic accident of 26 January 2006 to her insurer and later provided explanations claiming she had been present, completed the report on site, and been collected by her friend P. The insurer suspected fraud and notified police. Criminal proceedings opened on 6 April 2006. The applicant was charged with insurance fraud (submitting false information about an insured event jointly with co-accused P., K., T. and V.) and inciting P. to give false testimony. A May 2008 indictment stated that phone records and other evidence showed she had not been at the scene; the co-accused had created a false impression of an accident to obtain an insurance payout. No actual payout had occurred.

At a 2–3 December 2008 hearing the prosecutor requested discontinuance of proceedings against the applicant and P. under Article 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP). The offence was of the second degree, the applicant’s involvement had been at others’ instigation (demonstrating lesser guilt), she had no prior convictions, and she was raising a young child alone. The applicant and her counsel explicitly accepted this reasoning and consented to payment of procedural costs plus 80 hours of community service. By a 3 December 2008 ruling the Tartu County Court discontinued the proceedings, imposing those obligations (resumable if unfulfilled). The ruling reproduced the charges in detail, noted that all legal conditions were met (second-degree offence, negligible guilt, no proprietary damage, no public interest in continuation) and recorded the parties’ consent. The same day, in related settlement proceedings, the court convicted K., T. and V. of insurance fraud, stating that the applicant had not been present, that she and others had drafted and submitted false documents, and that they had jointly created the illusion of an insured event.

The applicant later claimed insurance compensation. The insurer refused, citing the criminal judgment that the accident had been staged. After completing her obligations, she sued the insurer in June 2009, submitting the discontinuance ruling among other evidence. The insurer relied on the conviction judgment. On 23 December 2009 the County Court dismissed the claim, holding that the criminal judgment and ruling established that the accident had been staged, that the applicant had submitted false information, and that she had been charged with creating the illusion of an insured event. It interpreted Article 202 CCrP as confirming that guilt existed (albeit negligible). The applicant appealed, arguing that the civil court had treated her as guilty despite the absence of a conviction. On 3 May 2010 the Court of Appeal upheld the decision, stating that discontinuance under Article 202 presupposed that the act had been committed and that the applicant had participated in staging the accident; she had adduced no contrary evidence. The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal.

Domestic law (Article 202 CCrP) permits discontinuance of second-degree cases involving negligible guilt, remedy of damage or payment of costs, and no public interest, with the accused’s consent; obligations of a penal nature may be imposed. Supreme Court case-law confirms that such discontinuance presupposes establishment of the elements of an offence, unlawfulness and guilt, producing an inculpatory effect, though it is not equivalent to a conviction and rests on a lesser evidentiary basis. Civil courts may treat other courts’ decisions as documentary evidence.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: the civil courts’ reliance on the discontinuance ruling (and related conviction of co-accused) to treat the applicant as having committed insurance fraud, thereby denying her claim, despite the lack of a criminal conviction.

The case of Lähteenmäki v. Estonia (Application no. 53172/10) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 September 2010 by Estonian national Signe Kristiina Lähteenmäki. She alleged a breach of her right to the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, as well as a lack of a fair civil trial under Article 6 § 1, arising from how Estonian courts treated her in subsequent civil proceedings.

On 31 January 2006, the applicant reported a traffic accident involving her car (allegedly occurring on 26 January 2006) to her insurance company, providing further explanations on 3 March 2006 in which she claimed not to know the other parties and that a friend (P.) had collected her from the scene. The insurer suspected fraud and alerted police, leading to criminal proceedings opened on 6 April 2006. The applicant was charged with insurance fraud (intentionally causing or creating the illusion of an insured event) and inciting P. to give false testimony, alongside co-accused P., K., T. and V.

A bill of indictment dated 16 May 2008 asserted that mobile-phone positioning, call records and P.’s statement proved the applicant had not been at the scene. It alleged that she and the others had submitted false information about the accident, persons involved and circumstances, though no payout had been made. At a hearing on 2–3 December 2008, the prosecutor requested discontinuance of the proceedings against the applicant and P. under Article 202(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP). The prosecutor cited the second-degree nature of the offences, the applicant’s lesser involvement at the instigation of others, her lack of prior convictions, and her status as a single mother of a small child. The applicant and her counsel explicitly accepted this reasoning and consented to the imposition of obligations (payment of procedural costs of EEK 1,178 and 80 hours of community service).

By ruling of 3 December 2008, Tartu County Court discontinued the proceedings on the basis of Article 202(1) and (2) CCrP. The ruling reproduced the charges in detail, recorded the prosecutor’s reasons (negligible guilt, no proprietary damage, no public interest) and the parties’ consent, and imposed the requested obligations (failure to perform which would allow resumption of proceedings). On the same day, in related settlement proceedings, the same court convicted K., T. and V. of insurance fraud. That judgment (using initials for the applicant) stated that she had not been present at the alleged accident, had drafted false documents with K., and had signed and submitted them with T. and V., thereby jointly creating the illusion of an insured event.

The applicant later claimed EEK 190,282.71 in insurance compensation. The insurer refused, relying on the 3 December 2008 judgment that the accident had been staged. After completing the imposed obligations, she brought a civil action on 2 June 2009, submitting the discontinuance ruling among other documents. The insurer adduced the conviction judgment. Tartu County Court dismissed the claim on 23 December 2009, holding that the criminal judgment had established the accident was staged and that the ruling had confirmed the applicant’s absence from the scene and her submission of false information. It treated the discontinuance under Article 202 as confirming that her guilt existed (albeit negligible) and that no genuine insured event had occurred.

On appeal, the applicant complained that the civil court had treated her as guilty despite the absence of any conviction. Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3 May 2010, stating that discontinuance under Article 202 presupposes that the charged act was committed (guilt being merely negligible) and that the ruling itself established her participation in staging the accident. She had adduced no contrary evidence. The Supreme Court declined to examine her further appeal on 22 June 2010.

Domestic law (Article 202 CCrP) permits discontinuance for second-degree offences of negligible guilt with the accused’s consent and the imposition of obligations; Supreme Court case-law treats such a ruling as having an inculpatory effect because it presupposes the elements of an offence, unlawfulness and guilt, though it is not equivalent to a conviction and is generally not appealable. Civil courts may treat other courts’ decisions as documentary evidence (Article 272(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure), but facts established in criminal proceedings may in principle be contested. These elements formed the core of the applicant’s complaints that the civil courts had violated the presumption of innocence by treating the discontinuance ruling as establishing her guilt and had thereby rendered the civil trial unfair.
001-162704:
The applicants, Stanislava Poletan and Alija Azirovik, were convicted in North Macedonia of unauthorized group trafficking of narcotics under Article 215(2) of the Criminal Code and sentenced to 14 years and six months’ imprisonment. On 7 January 2007, customs officials at the Blace border crossing discovered 434.555 kg of cocaine hidden in rectangular packs submerged in hermetically sealed cans of acrylic paint. The cargo, loaded onto a truck driven by Azirovik in Bar, Montenegro, was destined for Greece. Poletan had arranged the shipment, contacting Azirovik on 29 December 2006, paying him €1,100, and providing documentation plus contact details for Montenegrin forwarding agents.

Expert reports by the Criminal Investigations Bureau (part of the Ministry of the Interior) initially identified the substance as pure cocaine, with quantities variously reported as 438.170 kg, 486.705 kg, and later a net weight of 436.879 kg ± 2.324 kg via statistical sampling. An investigation opened on 8 January 2007. Both applicants, represented by counsel, denied knowledge of the drugs during questioning. Poletan was extradited from Serbia. Her lawyer requested case-file access multiple times during the investigation (granted per notes, with later inspections confirmed); she was heard after being informed of the charges.

The indictment charged trafficking of 486.705 kg. At trial, the court heard the applicants, who reiterated their denials. It commissioned a fresh Bureau report (no. 1399/07) on quality/quantity, analyzing 27 randomly selected packages per UNDCP/ENFSI guidelines after preliminary tests on all 432. Experts testified that all packages underwent initial screening, with full analysis of a square-root sample; the Bureau was the sole accredited national lab. Applicants objected to the experts’ lack of independence (as a prosecuting body), sampling methods (not examining every package fully), quantity discrepancies, and paint-type inconsistencies. They requested an independent alternative examination (national or foreign), which the court refused, citing statutory permission for State-body experts in complex cases and compliance with international recommendations. An on-site inspection of 27 sample packages occurred in the applicants’ presence.

Montenegrin witnesses N.V. and L.S. (forwarding agents contacted by Poletan) were examined via letters rogatory by a Podgorica court, answering 14 trial-court questions under oath. Their statements (describing contacts but denying knowledge of contents or the applicants personally) were read at trial after they could not attend; applicants raised no contemporaneous objection. Phone records showed intense communication between the applicants (and with the witnesses). The Greek recipient company did not exist. The trial court convicted both as a group, inferring knowledge and intent from circumstances: the implausible economics of shipping low-value paint from Venezuela, non-existent buyer, extensive contacts, and Azirovik’s transport of the concealed drugs. Azirovik’s unawareness claim was rejected as unsupported.

Appeals and Supreme Court extraordinary reviews were dismissed. The Court of Appeal found no file-access violation (Poletan was questioned after opportunities to consult counsel/evidence), upheld expert evidence (court-ordered, unchallenged in substance, with testimony under warning), deemed witness statements lawfully obtained (no objection or request to attend), and confirmed intent from the evidence. The Supreme Court agreed the “for sale” purpose (absent from the operative part) was implicit from the quantity and actions, which could not be for personal use.

Applicants alleged Article 6 violations (fair trial: file access, expert independence/equality of arms, witness confrontation, and judgment reasoning, especially on intent) and Article 7 issues (offense qualification).

The case of Poletan and Azirovik v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (applications nos. 26711/07, 32786/10 and 34278/10) concerns two Macedonian nationals convicted of drug trafficking. On 7 January 2007, Macedonian customs at the Blace border crossing discovered 434.555 kg of cocaine concealed in 432 rectangular packs submerged in hermetically sealed cans of acrylic paint. The cargo had been loaded onto a truck driven by the second applicant (Azirovik) in Bar, Montenegro, and was destined for Greece.

An investigation was opened the next day against both applicants for trafficking approximately 438 kg of cocaine. The second applicant, heard immediately, admitted agreeing with the first applicant (Poletan) on 29 December 2006 to transport paint for €1,100 but denied any knowledge of drugs. He described searches of the truck in Kosovo and overnight parking at Blace before the discovery. The first applicant, arrested in Serbia and extradited, was heard in May 2007 after claiming she needed to review the evidence. She confirmed hiring the second applicant and providing contacts for Montenegrin agents N.V. and L.S., but denied awareness of the cocaine or any related discussions. Her lawyer's requests to inspect the case file during the investigation were noted as granted, though she later alleged they were unanswered until after indictment.

The public prosecutor indicted them in June 2007 for trafficking 486.705 kg. At trial before the Skopje Court of First Instance, the applicants reiterated their denials. The court commissioned expert reports from the Ministry of the Interior’s Criminal Investigations Bureau on the substance’s nature, quality and quantity. Initial reports (7 and 11 January 2007) identified pure cocaine. A further court-ordered report (9 November 2007) analysed 27 randomly selected packages per UNDCP and ENFSI sampling guidelines, confirming cocaine with a total net weight of 436.879 kg ± 2.324 kg. Experts testified at hearings in October and November 2007, explaining colour tests on all packages and full analysis of samples. The applicants objected that the Bureau, as part of the prosecuting Ministry, lacked independence (citing Stoimenov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia) and requested an alternative examination by an independent national or foreign body, plus analysis of every package. The court refused, noting that domestic law permitted state-body experts in complex cases and that the latest report followed a judicial order. An on-site inspection of sampled packages revealed colour variations, which the defence argued indicated inconsistent purity.

The court also admitted statements from Montenegrin witnesses N.V. and L.S., examined via letters rogatory by a Podgorica judge after the applicants raised no objection at the 14 September 2007 hearing. The witnesses described telephone contacts with a “Sandra” or “Sandrina” linked to the first applicant’s company and with a driver named Alija, but denied knowledge of the cargo’s contents. Their transcripts were read out on 17 October 2007.

On 30 November 2007 the trial court convicted both applicants under Article 215(2) of the Criminal Code of unauthorised transportation of 434.555 kg of cocaine as a group, imposing 14 years and six months’ imprisonment each. It relied on their admissions of arranging and executing the transport, intensive telephone traffic (over 150 calls between them plus contacts with the Montenegrin agents), the non-existence of the designated Greek recipient company, and the economic implausibility of shipping cheap paint from Venezuela. Knowledge of the drugs was inferred from these circumstances and the second applicant’s actions, despite his denials.

The Skopje Court of Appeal (18 April 2008) and Supreme Court (20 October 2009) dismissed appeals. They held that the first applicant had been informed of the charges, given statements after consultation opportunities, and that her lawyer inspected the file before objecting to the indictment. Expert evidence was accepted as court-commissioned, consistent across reports, and challengeable at trial. Witness statements were lawfully obtained given the lack of contemporaneous objection. The second applicant’s lack of knowledge was rejected as contrary to the evidence. The omitted phrase “for the purpose of selling” in the operative part was deemed implied by the quantity and conduct, which could not relate to personal use.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints under Article 6 (fair-trial rights, including access to the file, confrontation of witnesses, and independent expertise) and Article 7 (precision of the criminal charge).

The case involves two Macedonian nationals, Stanislava Poletan and Alija Azirovik, convicted of large-scale cocaine trafficking. On 7 January 2007, customs officials at the Blace border crossing (with Kosovo) discovered 434.555 kg of cocaine concealed in hermetically sealed cans of acrylic paint aboard a truck driven by Azirovik. The cargo had been loaded in Bar, Montenegro, and was destined for Greece. Poletan had arranged the shipment, hiring Azirovik for €1,100, providing documentation from her company, and furnishing contacts for Montenegrin forwarding agents N.V. and L.S.

An investigation opened on 8 January 2007. Azirovik, heard immediately, admitted transporting the paint but denied knowledge of the drugs. Poletan, extradited from Serbia and heard later, similarly denied awareness, claiming she was settling a debt via paint imported from Venezuela through an unknown Greek contact. Phone records showed intense communication between the applicants (over 150 calls) and with the Montenegrin agents. Expert reports by the Ministry of Interior’s Criminal Investigations Bureau (using UN/ENFSI sampling protocols on randomly selected packages) confirmed the substance as pure cocaine, though initial reports listed varying quantities (438 kg, then 486 kg) before a court-commissioned report settled on a net weight of 436.879 kg ± 2.324 kg.

At trial, the applicants challenged the experts’ independence, noting the Bureau’s affiliation with the prosecuting Ministry of Interior, and requested an alternative examination by an independent body (national or foreign). They also argued that all packages should have been fully analysed and highlighted inconsistencies (e.g., paint type descriptions). The trial court refused, citing statutory permission for state-body experts in complex cases and compliance with sampling standards. It also admitted transcripts of statements by N.V. and L.S., obtained via letters rogatory after they were unable to attend; the applicants had not objected at the time the request was made or when the statements were read out.

On 30 November 2007 the Skopje Court of First Instance convicted both of unauthorised transportation of narcotics as a group under Criminal Code Article 215(2), sentencing each to 14 years and six months’ imprisonment. The court inferred knowledge and intent from the applicants’ actions, the implausible economics of shipping inexpensive paint from Venezuela, the non-existent Greek recipient company, the volume of drugs (far exceeding personal use), and their communications. It held that the drugs were transported for sale, even though this purpose was not expressly stated in the operative part of the judgment.

The Court of Appeal (18 April 2008) and Supreme Court (20 October 2009) upheld the conviction. They found that Poletan had been granted file access after questioning (as required by domestic law) and had inspected the file before objecting to the indictment; that the experts’ reports were consistent on the presence of cocaine and had been adequately tested at trial; that the Montenegrin witnesses’ evidence was lawfully obtained; and that intent could be deduced from the circumstances. The applicants alleged that these proceedings violated Article 6 (fair-trial rights concerning access to the file, expert independence/equality of arms, and confrontation of witnesses) and Article 7 (insufficient establishment of the mental element and purpose of sale).

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered its judgment in Soares v. Portugal (Application no. 79972/12) on 21 June 2016 (final 21 September 2016). The Portuguese applicant, António Alberto Mota Soares (born 1957), a chief corporal in the National Republican Guard (GNR) stationed at the Góis territorial post, alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention. He claimed his criminal conviction for reporting suspected misuse of public funds interfered with his freedom of expression.

On 7 November 2009 the applicant emailed the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration under the subject “Suspected misuse of money.” He reported rumours heard from colleagues at the Arganil territorial post that Commander M.C. had misused funds. In December 2008 the Coimbra GNR Territorial Group had allocated money to posts for a Christmas dinner. Only Commander M.C. and one corporal attended the Arganil dinner; the full sum was paid to the restaurant in exchange for a receipt. The applicant stated it appeared the commander subsequently dined there with his family, with meal costs deducted from unspent funds. He requested an investigation and secrecy, citing fear of reprisals as a fellow serviceman.

The Inspectorate forwarded the email to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor. The prosecutor opened a criminal investigation but discontinued it on 28 February 2010 after the Judicial Police found no evidence of an offence. The Inspectorate’s own inquiry ended on 21 June 2010. The GNR launched an internal inquiry on 4 December 2009; Commander M.C. was heard on 23 December 2009 and thereby learned of the email. The inquiry became disciplinary proceedings against him on 9 February 2010 because of apparent lack of transparency in cafeteria management, but these were discontinued on 30 July 2010 for insufficient evidence (taking into account the prosecutor’s earlier decision).

On 22 April 2010 Commander M.C. filed a criminal complaint accusing the applicant of defamation through injurious statements. The public prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated defamation on 7 July 2011, asserting the email deliberately attacked the commander’s honesty, honour and professional reputation. M.C. also claimed €5,000 in damages. On 17 January 2012 the Lousã Criminal Court convicted the applicant, imposing 80 day-fines (€720) and ordering him to pay €1,000 damages. The court found no proof that the rumoured misuse existed; it concluded the applicant knew the allegation was untrue, intended to undermine the commander’s honour, and could easily have verified the facts with the restaurant owner. Whistle-blowing, the court held, is a duty only when based on personally observed facts within the reporter’s competence and must not be used to cast unsupported suspicion. The applicant appealed, denying any intent to attack honour. On 19 September 2012 the Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding no grounds to alter the first-instance factual findings or legal conclusions.

Separately, the GNR instituted disciplinary proceedings against the applicant on 3 August 2011. A 20 February 2013 report found he had breached the duty of loyalty by failing to inform hierarchical superiors and by bypassing the chain of command. The report noted that all prior investigations had been discontinued and that the applicant had already been convicted of defamation. On 27 March 2013 he received a six-day suspension (enforcement suspended for twelve months). He did not appeal this sanction.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 10 complaint concerning the criminal conviction for reporting alleged public-fund misuse.

The case of Soares v. Portugal (Application no. 79972/12) concerns a Portuguese National Republican Guard (GNR) chief corporal’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for aggravated defamation, following an email report of suspected misuse of public funds, unlawfully interfered with his freedom of expression.

In November 2009 the applicant, then serving at the Góis territorial post, emailed the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration. Citing rumours circulating among colleagues at the Arganil post, he reported that leftover funds allocated by the Coimbra GNR Territorial Group for a December 2008 Christmas dinner had been used by Commander M.C. to pay for subsequent family meals at the same restaurant. Only the commander and one corporal had attended the dinner; the full allocation was paid to the restaurant against a receipt. The applicant requested an investigation and confidentiality, citing fear of reprisals.

The Inspectorate forwarded the email to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor. The prosecutor opened a criminal investigation that was discontinued in February 2010 after the Judicial Police found no evidence of an offence. The Inspectorate’s own inquiry was closed in June 2010. An internal GNR inquiry, begun in December 2009, heard Commander M.C. and was converted into disciplinary proceedings against him because of apparent lack of transparency in the post’s cafeteria accounts. Those proceedings were discontinued in July 2010 for insufficient evidence, taking into account the prosecutor’s earlier decision.

In April 2010 Commander M.C. lodged a criminal complaint of defamation. In July 2011 the prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated defamation, asserting that the email had deliberately impugned the commander’s honesty, honour and professional reputation. The commander also claimed €5,000 in damages.

On 17 January 2012 the Lousã Criminal Court convicted the applicant. It found that the existence of the rumoured leftover-credit arrangement had not been proved and that the applicant, knowing the allegation to be a mere rumour, had acted with the specific intent of undermining the commander’s honour. The court held that whistle-blowing is a duty only when confined to facts actually observed and that the applicant had accused the commander of a dishonourable act without any supporting evidence and without taking the elementary step of checking with the restaurant owner. The applicant was sentenced to 80 day-fines (€720) and ordered to pay €1,000 damages. The Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and reasoning on 19 September 2012.

Parallel disciplinary proceedings were opened against the applicant in August 2011. A February 2013 report concluded that he had breached his statutory duty of loyalty by failing to report the alleged irregularities through the chain of command. Taking into account the discontinued investigations and the criminal conviction, the GNR imposed a six-day suspension (itself suspended for twelve months) in March 2013.

Portuguese criminal law (Article 180 of the Criminal Code) penalises statements that slur another’s honour or reputation, even when framed as suspicion; the penalty is increased when the victim is a public official (Article 184). Military statutes and disciplinary regulations further require GNR members to report irregularities exclusively through hierarchical channels and forbid statements that damage the force’s cohesion or reputation.

These facts—the content and circumstances of the email, the successive investigations that found no misconduct, the domestic courts’ findings of malicious intent and lack of verification, and the resulting criminal and disciplinary sanctions—constitute the core of the alleged Article 10 violation.

The case of Soares v. Portugal (Application no. 79972/12) concerns a complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights by António Alberto Mota Soares, a Portuguese national and chief corporal in the National Republican Guard (GNR) stationed at the Góis territorial post. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for defamation, arising from an internal report of suspected misuse of public funds, violated his right to freedom of expression.

On 7 November 2009, the applicant emailed the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration to report rumours he had heard from colleagues at the Arganil territorial post. The email alleged that Commander M.C. had misused leftover funds from a December 2008 Christmas dinner allocation (distributed by the Coimbra Territorial Group). Only the commander and one corporal had attended the dinner; the full allocated sum was paid to the restaurant, after which the commander supposedly deducted subsequent family meals from the unused balance. The applicant requested secrecy during any investigation, citing colleagues’ fear of reprisals and his own military status.

The email was forwarded to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor opened a criminal investigation but discontinued it on 28 February 2010 after the Judiciary Police found no evidence of an offence. A parallel Inspectorate inquiry was closed on 21 June 2010. The GNR’s own internal inquiry, launched on 4 December 2009, heard Commander M.C. on 23 December 2009 (thereby revealing the email’s contents) and was converted on 9 February 2010 into disciplinary proceedings against him because of apparent lack of transparency in the post’s cafeteria accounts. Those proceedings were discontinued on 30 July 2010 for insufficient evidence, taking into account the prosecutor’s earlier decision.

On 22 April 2010 Commander M.C. filed a criminal complaint accusing the applicant of defamation. Charges of aggravated defamation were brought on 7 July 2011 on the ground that the email had intentionally attacked the commander’s honesty, honour and professional reputation. Commander M.C. also claimed €5,000 in damages. On 17 January 2012 the Lousã Criminal Court convicted the applicant, imposing 80 day-fines totalling €720 and ordering him to pay €1,000 in damages. The court found that the alleged rumour had never been proved, that the applicant knew the accusation was untrue and could easily have checked it with the restaurant owner, and that he had therefore acted with the specific intent of undermining the commander’s honour. The court emphasised that whistle-blowing must rest on personally observed facts within the reporter’s competence and cannot serve as a vehicle for unsupported suspicions.

The Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 19 September 2012, confirming both the factual findings and the legal characterisation. Separately, the GNR instituted disciplinary proceedings against the applicant on 3 August 2011. A report of 20 February 2013 concluded that he had breached his duty of loyalty by failing to report the matter through the proper hierarchical channels rather than directly to an external inspectorate. The report noted the earlier discontinued investigations and the criminal conviction; a prior fine imposed by Commander M.C. on the applicant was treated as irrelevant. On 27 March 2013 the applicant received a six-day suspension (enforcement itself suspended for twelve months). He did not appeal the disciplinary measure.

Under Portuguese law, defamation (Criminal Code Article 180) is aggravated when the victim is a public official (Article 184). Good faith is excluded if the speaker fails to verify the information. Military statutes and disciplinary regulations further require GNR members to respect hierarchical channels and to refrain from statements that damage the force’s cohesion or reputation.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s Article 10 complaint: that a criminal conviction (and associated disciplinary sanction) for an internal report of possible public-fund misuse, later found unsubstantiated, constituted an unjustified interference with freedom of expression.
