The ECtHR case of Manerov v. Russia (App. No. 49848/10) concerned complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention about the applicant’s inability to obtain a prompt judicial review of the lawfulness of his pre-trial detention. Aleksandr Manerov, a former military commander born in 1963, was arrested on 28 May 2008 on suspicion of fraud but released two days later on an undertaking not to leave his residence. On 1 July 2009 the Vladivostok Garrison Military Court convicted him of fraud committed in abuse of office and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment; he was taken into custody immediately. On 29 January 2010 the Pacific Fleet Military Court quashed the conviction and ordered a retrial, but left the detention measure in force until 1 April 2010 because of the gravity of the charges and the risks of absconding and witness intimidation.

On 15 February 2010 the Garrison Court dismissed the applicant’s application for release, repeating the same grounds. The decision stated that it could be appealed to the Fleet Court within three days; the applicant lodged such an appeal. On 26 March 2010, however, the Fleet Court discontinued the appeal proceedings. It relied on Article 355 § 5(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which precludes a separate appeal against intermediate trial decisions (including refusals of release) until the final judgment on the merits. The court considered that the refusal did not impair the applicant’s access to court or the reasonable-time requirement and did not delay the trial. This approach sat uneasily with earlier Constitutional Court rulings (nos. 44-O of 2004 and 4-P of 2005) that detention-related decisions must be open to immediate appellate review because they produce irreparable effects on personal liberty.

In the meantime, on 22 March 2010 the Garrison Court extended detention until 1 July 2010. It again cited the seriousness of the charges, a medical report confirming the applicant’s fitness to stand trial, and his earlier removal from the courtroom for disruptive conduct, which the court treated as evidence that, if released, he might influence witnesses or abscond. A copy of the extension order was served on the applicant only on 25 March, after the three-day appeal period had expired. He filed an appeal on 27 March; the time-limit was restored on 8 April. The file reached the Fleet Court on 21 April, which listed a video-link hearing for 23 April. The applicant, notified only on the day of the hearing and suffering from a hearing impairment that made video participation ineffective, successfully requested an adjournment and physical presence. The hearing was reset for 30 April.

On 29 April the Garrison Court convicted the applicant of nine counts of fraud and imposed the same four-year sentence. The following day the Fleet Court dismissed the appeal against the 22 March extension order. The applicant later withdrew his appeal against the conviction itself. These events formed the basis of his complaints that he had been denied an effective, speedy review of the lawfulness of his continued detention.

The case of Manerov v. Russia (application no. 49848/10) concerns complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the applicant’s pre-trial detention during criminal proceedings for fraud. The applicant, a former military unit commander born in 1963 and residing in Vladivostok, was arrested on 28 May 2008 on suspicion of fraud but released two days later subject to an undertaking not to leave his place of residence. On 1 July 2009 the Military Court of the Vladivostok Garrison convicted him of fraud committed in abuse of position and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment; he was taken into custody immediately. On 29 January 2010 the Military Court of the Pacific Fleet quashed the conviction on appeal and remitted the case for retrial, while maintaining the applicant’s detention until 1 April 2010. The Fleet Court cited the seriousness of the charges and a risk of absconding or threatening witnesses, the latter supported by a witness statement.

On 15 February 2010 the Garrison Court dismissed the applicant’s application for release, again relying on the gravity of the charges and the risks of flight and witness interference. The decision expressly stated that it could be appealed to the Fleet Court within three days. The applicant lodged such an appeal. Nevertheless, on 26 March 2010 the Fleet Court discontinued the appeal proceedings. Invoking Article 355 § 5 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it held that a refusal of release was an intermediate procedural decision that could not be challenged separately before the final judgment on the merits, because it did not impair access to court, delay the trial, or otherwise affect the applicant’s rights in a manner requiring immediate review.

In parallel, on 22 March 2010 the Garrison Court extended the applicant’s detention until 1 July 2010. The court again referred to the seriousness of the charges, a medical report confirming the applicant’s fitness to stand trial, and his earlier removal from the courtroom for disruptive behaviour, which it considered indicative of a continuing risk that he would influence witnesses or abscond. A copy of this order was served on the applicant only on 25 March 2010, after the statutory three-day appeal period had expired. He nevertheless filed an appeal on 27 March 2010. On 8 April 2010 the Garrison Court restored the time-limit. The appeal file reached the Fleet Court on 21 April 2010; a video-link hearing was scheduled for 23 April 2010 and notice was sent to the remand prison. The applicant learned of the hearing only on the day itself and requested an adjournment on grounds of late notification and a hearing impairment that, he claimed, prevented him from following proceedings by video link; he also sought to appear in person. The Fleet Court granted the adjournment and listed the matter for 30 April 2010.

On 29 April 2010 the Garrison Court convicted the applicant of nine counts of fraud and again imposed a four-year sentence. The following day the Fleet Court dismissed the appeal against the 22 March extension order. Subsequent appeal proceedings against the conviction were discontinued after the applicant withdrew them.

These facts form the basis of the two Article 5 § 4 complaints: first, that the outright discontinuation of the appeal against the 15 February refusal of release deprived the applicant of any judicial review of the lawfulness of his detention; and second, that the examination of the appeal against the 22 March extension order was not conducted “speedily,” given the delayed service of the order, the late restoration of the time-limit, the belated notification of the hearing, and the further postponement. Domestic provisions (Articles 108 and 355 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) and Constitutional Court rulings of 2004 and 2005, which require prompt review of detention decisions even when they arise during trial, were invoked as relevant background.

The case of Manerov v. Russia (Application no. 49848/10) originated in a complaint lodged on 25 July 2010 by Aleksandr Vyacheslavovich Manerov, a Russian national and former military unit commander born in 1963 and living in Vladivostok. He alleged violations of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention concerning the lawfulness and speed of judicial review of his pre-trial detention. The Court communicated these complaints on 27 August 2013 while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicant was arrested on 28 May 2008 on suspicion of fraud but released two days later after giving an undertaking not to leave his place of residence. On 1 July 2009 the Military Court of the Vladivostok Garrison convicted him of fraud committed in abuse of position and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment with dishonourable discharge. He was arrested in the courtroom and placed in a remand prison.

On 29 January 2010 the Military Court of the Pacific Fleet quashed the conviction on appeal and ordered a retrial. It nevertheless maintained the applicant’s detention until 1 April 2010, citing the seriousness of the charges and the risk of absconding or threatening witnesses (supported by a witness statement). On 15 February 2010 the Garrison Court rejected the applicant’s application for release, repeating the same grounds. The decision expressly stated that it could be appealed within three days to the Fleet Court. The applicant lodged such an appeal.

On 26 March 2010 the Fleet Court discontinued the appeal proceedings. Invoking Article 355 § 5 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it held that a refusal of release during trial was not amenable to a separate appeal before the final judgment, as it did not impair the applicant’s right of access to a court or the right to a hearing within a reasonable time and did not delay the proceedings.

In the meantime, on 22 March 2010 the Garrison Court extended the applicant’s detention until 1 July 2010. It again relied on the seriousness of the charges, a medical report confirming that the applicant’s health permitted his participation in the trial, and his earlier removal from the courtroom for unacceptable behaviour, which the court treated as evidence that he might influence witnesses or abscond if released.

A copy of the extension order was served on the applicant only on 25 March 2010, after the three-day time-limit for appeal had expired. He nevertheless filed an appeal on 27 March 2010. The Garrison Court restored the time-limit on 8 April 2010. The appeal file reached the Fleet Court on 21 April 2010; a hearing by video-link was immediately scheduled for 23 April 2010 and notice was sent to the remand prison.

The applicant was informed of the hearing only on 23 April. He requested an adjournment because of the late notification and asked to be brought physically to court, explaining that a hearing impairment prevented him from following the proceedings effectively by video-link. The Fleet Court granted both requests and adjourned the hearing to 30 April 2010.

On 29 April 2010 the Garrison Court convicted the applicant of nine counts of fraud in abuse of office and again sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. The following day the Fleet Court examined the appeal against the 22 March extension order and upheld it. The applicant later withdrew his appeal against the conviction itself, and those proceedings were discontinued on 2 December 2010.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 5 § 4 violations are therefore: (i) the Fleet Court’s discontinuation, on purely procedural grounds, of the appeal against the 15 February 2010 refusal of release, despite the first-instance court’s indication that an appeal was available and despite Constitutional Court jurisprudence suggesting that detention-related decisions require prompt separate review; and (ii) the interval between the 22 March 2010 extension order and its appellate examination on 30 April 2010 (more than five weeks), during which the time-limit was restored only after expiry, notification of the hearing was late, the applicant’s hearing disability was raised, and the review ultimately took place one day after a fresh conviction had already been pronounced. These circumstances formed the basis of the complaints that the lawfulness of the applicant’s continued detention was not decided speedily by a court.
001-160318:
**Case summary (key facts on alleged violations):** Hilal Mammadov (born 1959), an Azerbaijani mathematician, journalist, and activist (editor of the Talishi Sedo newspaper and involved in minority rights and detainee rehabilitation), alleged police ill-treatment during arrest, an ineffective investigation, unlawful pre-trial detention without reasonable suspicion or justification, and hindrance of his right of petition to the ECHR.

On 21 June 2012, the applicant claimed that six or seven unidentified plain-clothes officers assaulted him near a Baku metro station, striking him below the knees, kicking his ribcage, planting drugs in his pocket, handcuffing him, and beating him in a car while insulting his ethnicity and threatening him over a YouTube video. He was not informed of the arrest reasons until taken to the Narcotics Department, where a search (without a lawyer) found 5 grams of heroin-like substance. A later unwarranted search of his flat (same attesting witnesses, no lawyer) found more drugs, which he denied owning. He alleged being held handcuffed without food or water on 21-22 June. The Government denied any ill-treatment.

He was charged on 22 June under Criminal Code Art. 234.4.3 (large-quantity drug offences). A court ordered three months’ detention, citing charge gravity, a potential sentence over five years, and absconding risk; appeals failed. Additional charges of high treason and incitement to hatred were added on 3 July 2012. House-arrest requests were refused due to alleged absconding/obstruction risks; detention was extended. He was convicted on all counts on 27 September 2013 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment (upheld on appeal). The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention later found the detention arbitrary (linked to expression rights and fair-trial issues).

The applicant complained of ill-treatment during 21 June questioning. A 22 June forensic exam found abrasions on his left calf and right thigh, possibly inflicted that day by a blunt object (he received no copy). Police (including one named officer) denied force in identical statements; guards reported no complaints; his clothes were undamaged. An additional forensic exam attributed injuries to contact with a vehicle’s protruding parts during arrest and found no traces matching claimed beatings to the head, neck or chest. On 27 August 2012 the Deputy Prosecutor General refused to open a criminal case, relying on the forensics and police/guard statements. The applicant learned of this (and received forensic copies) only after a court complaint about delay; subsequent judicial challenges were dismissed without hearing requested experts or officers.

Later, the applicant’s ECHR representative (Mr Bagirov) had his advocacy suspended in December 2014 during disciplinary proceedings. Prison authorities then denied him meetings with the applicant (even for pending ECHR cases), citing the suspension.

These facts underpin the alleged Art. 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation), Art. 5 (detention lawfulness/justification) and Art. 34 (petition hindrance) complaints.

**Hilal Mammadov v. Azerbaijan** (ECHR, 2016) concerns an Azerbaijani activist (born 1959), physicist, mathematician, editor-in-chief of the Talishi Sedo newspaper, chairman of the Talish Cultural Centre, and head of the Committee for Rehabilitation of Detainees. He alleged ill-treatment by police during arrest (Article 3), an ineffective investigation thereof, unlawful pre-trial detention lacking reasonable suspicion or justification (Article 5), and hindrance of his right of petition (Article 34).

On 21 June 2012, near Neftchilar metro station, six or seven plain-clothes officers allegedly assaulted him without identification, restrained and beat him (kicks below the knees and to the ribcage), planted drugs in his pocket, handcuffed him, and continued beating him in a car while insulting his ethnicity and threatening him over a YouTube video. He was unaware of the arrest until taken to the Narcotics Department. A search there (1:45–2 p.m., no lawyer) found 5g of heroin-like substance. A warrantless search of his flat (6:10–7:55 p.m., same witnesses, no lawyer) found more narcotics, which he denied owning. He claimed he was held in handcuffs without food or water on 21–22 June.

Charged on 22 June under Criminal Code Article 234.4.3 (large-quantity narcotics), he was ordered detained for three months by the Nizami District Court (upheld on appeal) due to charge gravity, possible >5-year sentence, and absconding risk. On 3 July he faced additional charges of high treason (Article 274) and incitement to hatred (Article 283.2.2). House-arrest requests were denied (absconding/obstruction risks cited); detention was extended. On 27 September 2013 the Baku Assize Court convicted him on all counts, sentencing him to five years (upheld on appeal).

He complained of ill-treatment during 21 June questioning. A 22 June forensic exam found abrasions on his left calf and right thigh (possible 21 June blunt-object injuries, not health-harming). Police denied force; detention-centre guards reported no complaint. An additional exam concluded injuries arose from contact with vehicle protrusions during arrest, with no supporting injuries to head/neck/chest. On 27 August 2012 the Deputy Prosecutor General refused to open proceedings, citing unproven allegations. Courts dismissed his complaints of investigative failure and later challenges to the refusal, finding a thorough inquiry.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (2013) deemed his detention arbitrary (categories II and III), tied to his expression and minority-rights work, with grave fair-trial flaws, and recommended release plus compensation.

After his lawyer K. Bagirov’s Bar Association suspension/disbarment proceedings (December 2014, for courtroom remarks), prison authorities refused him access to the applicant for the ECHR case, despite requests citing Strasbourg representation.

The case concerns Azerbaijani national Hilal Mammadov (b. 1959), a mathematician/physicist who became a Talysh minority activist, editor-in-chief of the bilingual newspaper Talishi Sedo, chairman of the Talish Cultural Centre, and head of the Committee for Rehabilitation of Detainees.

On 21 June 2012 around noon, near Neftchilar metro station in Baku, six or seven plain-clothes officers (who did not display identification) assaulted Mammadov. They restrained his arms, struck him below the knees, kicked his right ribcage, planted a narcotic-like substance in his trouser pocket, handcuffed him, and dragged him into a vehicle, where they continued beating him, insulted his ethnic origin, and threatened him over a YouTube video he had uploaded. He was not informed of any reasons for arrest and only realised he was in police custody upon arrival at the Narcotics Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (NDMIA). A search there (1.45–2 p.m., no lawyer present) found 5 grams of a heroin-like substance. A later search of his flat (6.10–7.55 p.m., again without a lawyer or court order, using the same attesting witnesses) found further narcotics, which Mammadov stated were planted. He was held handcuffed without food or water on 21–22 June.

On 22 June he was charged under Criminal Code Article 234.4.3 (large-scale illegal narcotics offences). The Nizami District Court ordered three months’ pre-trial detention, citing the gravity of the charge and risk of absconding; this was upheld on appeal. On 3 July further charges of high treason (Art. 274) and incitement to ethnic/racial/religious hatred (Art. 283.2.2) were added. Applications for house arrest were refused on similar grounds (absconding/obstruction risk). Detention was extended; he was convicted on all counts on 27 September 2013 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment (upheld through the Supreme Court).

Mammadov immediately alleged ill-treatment. A 22 June forensic examination recorded abrasions on his left calf and right thigh consistent with infliction on 21 June by a hard blunt object. An inquiry followed. Four arresting officers (identical statements) and three detention-centre guards denied force or complaints. Clothes were undamaged. A second forensic examination (23 August) attributed the injuries to contact with angular vehicle parts during arrest and found no traces of the claimed beating to head/neck/chest. On 27 August the Deputy Prosecutor General refused to open a criminal case, relying on the police statements and second forensic report. Domestic courts dismissed Mammadov’s complaints, holding the inquiry adequate.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (Opinion 59/2013) later found the detention arbitrary (categories II and III), as the treason/hatred charges related to legitimate exercise of freedom of expression and there were serious fair-trial violations; it recommended immediate release and compensation.

After Mammadov’s ECHR application was lodged, his representative (Bar member K. Bagirov) had his advocacy activity suspended (December 2014) pending disbarment proceedings arising from remarks in an unrelated case. Prison authorities thereafter refused Bagirov meetings with Mammadov concerning the Strasbourg proceedings, citing the suspension.

These facts underpin the complaints of police ill-treatment and ineffective investigation (Art. 3), absence of reasonable suspicion and inadequate justification of pre-trial detention (Art. 5), and interference with the right of individual petition (Art. 34).
001-164197:
The case of Józef Woś v. Poland (ECtHR Application no. 6058/10) arose from events on 26 January 2009, when the applicant (born 1966) and his wife were driving a borrowed car. After the wife overtook a police vehicle (claiming an accidental horn use), officers stopped them for a non-functioning rear light and unlit registration plate. A prolonged inspection followed, lasting around two hours, involving document checks, a trip to an unmanned police station, and identification of further faults (undersized fire extinguisher). Officers planned a 200 PLN fine for the wife. The applicant, viewing the officers as possibly seeking a bribe amid his wife's distress, told her not to sign anything for “those beggars.” Officers deemed this an insult and announced his arrest.

Accounts diverged. The applicant described a routine check turning aggressive, with him defending his anxious wife. Domestic courts later found (in proceedings against the officers) that he pushed an officer and fled; in proceedings against him, that he resisted apprehension, prompting Officer J.B. to force him to the ground and kneel on him. The applicant allegedly kicked J.B.’s leg (which he later claimed may have been involuntary). Officer D.B. then used pepper spray. The applicant was handcuffed, taken to the station, and—after his wife noted heart issues—examined at Nowy Targ Hospital (bruising on the right hand; chemical burn to the right eye). He spent the night in custody and was re-examined in Myślenice the next day (confirming the injuries plus reddish conjunctivitis from pepper spray). An undated urgent note sought ophthalmological review for spray burns. He alleged he was released via a back door without jacket or money, forcing him to find a taxi while his waiting wife was uninformed.

On 28 January 2009 the applicant complained to the Nowy Targ District Court about the arrest, alleging forceful grounding, excessive spray use, and injuries. On 4 February 2009 the court dismissed it as lawful (suspicion of influencing a witness; possible expedited proceedings for insulting officers under Criminal Code Article 226 § 1), relying solely on police notes without hearing witnesses or addressing force allegations.

Police indicted the applicant for insulting officers and kicking one. On 28 May 2009 the District Court found him guilty but conditionally discontinued proceedings (ordering a 200 PLN charity payment). He appealed, denying intent and claiming victimization while restrained. On 8 September 2009 the Nowy Sącz Regional Court quashed the judgment and discontinued the case due to insignificant public harm.

Separately, the applicant reported the officers for abuse of power. An investigation opened on 25 February 2009; both sides were questioned. On 16 April 2009 the prosecutor discontinued it, holding force lawful under the 1990 Police Act (applicant disobeyed, acted nervously, and fled). The applicant appealed, citing unjustified arrest, excessive force (grounding face-down, officers sitting on him, spray), injuries requiring a month’s sick leave, and release issues. On 12 August 2009 the District Court upheld discontinuation, rejecting his version as incredible, noting prior arrest-complaint review, and finding non-notification of his wife reprehensible but not criminal.

Relevant law authorized arrests on reasonable suspicion of an offence plus risks (e.g., influencing evidence or expedited proceedings) and limited force to what was necessary and proportionate for compliance. These facts underpin the alleged violations: disproportionate force causing documented injuries during a minor traffic matter, and investigations that uncritically accepted police accounts while ignoring the applicant’s evidence and medical records.

The case of Józef Woś v. Poland originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging that Polish police used excessive force during the applicant’s arrest on 26 January 2009 and that subsequent domestic investigations into those events were inadequate.

That evening the applicant and his wife were travelling in a borrowed car when they encountered a police vehicle attempting to stop another car on a narrow road. The applicant’s wife overtook the police car (claiming she honked accidentally). Officers then stopped their vehicle after noticing an unlit rear registration plate and a non-functioning left rear light. An inspection of documents followed; the car’s registration papers were considered partly illegible. After unsuccessful attempts to contact the local police station, the group drove to the Jabłonka station, which was unstaffed, so the check continued on the street. Officers identified an undersized fire extinguisher and proposed a 200-zloty fine for the wife.

The applicant then remarked that his wife should “not sign anything for those beggars.” Officers took offence and announced they would arrest him for insulting them. The applicant later claimed the two-hour inspection had become tense, that his wife was crying, and that the officers’ repeated comments that the faults “will cost a lot” suggested they were soliciting a bribe. Domestic courts later recorded two versions of the ensuing physical confrontation. In proceedings against the officers it was found that the applicant pushed an officer and attempted to flee. In proceedings against the applicant, officers testified that he resisted arrest, stepped back, was forced to the ground by officer J.B. who knelt on him, continued resisting and kicked J.B. several times in the leg, after which officer D.B. deployed pepper spray. The applicant was then handcuffed.

He was taken to the station, where an ambulance was called after his wife mentioned heart problems. Hospital notes from Nowy Targ recorded bruising on the right hand and a chemical burn to the right eye. Further examination the next day at Myślenice hospital confirmed the same injuries plus reddish conjunctivitis; an urgent ophthalmology referral cited pepper-spray burns. The applicant was held overnight and released the following day via a rear exit, without jacket or money and without his waiting wife being informed.

On 28 January 2009 the applicant complained to the Nowy Targ District Court about the lawfulness of the arrest and the force used. The court dismissed the complaint solely on the police note and arrest records, without hearing witnesses or addressing the force allegations, finding the arrest lawful because of a suspicion that the applicant might influence a witness and because expedited proceedings were possible.

The police charged the applicant with insulting officers and violating an officer’s bodily integrity by kicking. He maintained any leg movements were involuntary while he was pinned down. The District Court found him guilty but conditionally discontinued the case; the Regional Court later quashed the conviction entirely, holding that any harm caused was socially insignificant.

Separately, the applicant reported the officers for abuse of power. After questioning the parties, the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, concluding that force had been justified because the applicant had disobeyed orders, acted nervously and tried to flee. The District Court upheld that decision, treating the applicant’s account as incredible, noting that the arrest itself had already been reviewed, and dismissing the failure to notify the wife as merely reprehensible rather than criminal. The court did not examine the documented injuries or the necessity and proportionality of the knee restraint and pepper spray.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints communicated to the Government concerning both the alleged ill-treatment and the effectiveness of the domestic investigation.

The case of Józef Woś v. Poland (Application no. 6058/10) originated in a 26 January 2010 application to the European Court of Human Rights. The Polish applicant alleged that police used excessive force during his 26 January 2009 arrest and that domestic authorities failed to investigate this properly.

That evening, the applicant and his wife were driving a borrowed car when they overtook a police vehicle attempting to stop another car on a narrow road. The wife sounded the horn, which she claimed was accidental. Police noticed the car lacked a functioning left rear light and an illuminated registration plate, so they stopped it for inspection. They found the registration document partly illegible (though the applicant read it aloud) and the fire extinguisher undersized. After about 30 minutes by the roadside, all parties drove to the Jabłonka police station (which was empty) and continued the check outside. Officers proposed a 200 PLN fine for the wife. Frustrated after what he described as a two-hour “routine” stop during which officers repeatedly said “this will cost a lot” (which he interpreted as seeking a bribe), the applicant told his wife not to sign anything for “those beggars.” Officers took offence and announced they would arrest him for insulting them. His wife became upset and cried at the prospect of being taken in for questioning.

Police versions, later accepted by some domestic courts, held that the applicant then pushed an officer, resisted, and tried to flee. Officer J.B. forced him to the ground and pressed a knee into him; the applicant kicked J.B. several times in the leg (the applicant later claimed these were involuntary movements while pinned). Officer D.B. then used pepper spray. Once subdued, the applicant was handcuffed and taken to the station. Informed of his heart problems, officers summoned an ambulance. He was examined at Nowy Targ Hospital (bruising on the right hand; chemical burn to the right eye) and later at Myślenice Hospital (same findings plus reddish conjunctivitis). He was held overnight in police custody and released the next day via a back door without his jacket or money; his waiting wife was not informed.

On 28 January 2009 the applicant complained to the Nowy Targ District Court about the arrest, citing forceful takedown, use of an entire pepper-spray container, injuries, and the circumstances of release. On 4 February 2009 the court dismissed the complaint without hearing witnesses, relying solely on police notes. It found the arrest lawful under Article 244 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (reasonable suspicion of an offence under Article 226 § 1 of the Criminal Code—insulting officers—and grounds for expedited proceedings) and did not address the force used.

Separately, police indicted the applicant for insulting officers and violating an officer’s personal inviolability by kicking. On 28 May 2009 the District Court found him guilty but conditionally discontinued proceedings, ordering a charitable payment. On appeal, the Nowy Sącz Regional Court on 8 September 2009 quashed the judgment and discontinued the case entirely, holding the acts caused only insignificant social harm.

The applicant also reported the officers for abuse of power. The District Prosecutor opened an investigation, questioned the parties, then discontinued it on 16 April 2009, finding the force lawful under the 1990 Police Act and implementing ordinance because the applicant disobeyed orders, behaved nervously and tried to run. The District Court upheld this on 12 August 2009, deeming the applicant’s account not credible, noting the arrest complaint had already been dismissed, and briefly acknowledging (but not treating as an offence) the failure to notify his wife of his release. It did not examine the injuries.

These facts—prolonged stop escalating over a verbal insult, physical takedown plus pepper spray producing documented injuries, and investigations that accepted the police account without independently assessing proportionality or medical evidence—formed the core of the communicated complaints concerning the use of force and the quality of the domestic inquiry.
001-159803:
The case of Salamov v. Russia (Application no. 5063/05) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applicant, Aslambek Salamov, a Russian national born in 1960 and residing in Grozny, Chechnya, claimed that Russian military forces unlawfully seized and damaged his truck during counter-terrorist operations, without providing compensation.

In early October 1999, the Russian Government initiated a counter-terrorist operation in Chechnya. On 14 December 1999, during an identity check at the applicant’s family home in Shali, military servicemen seized his KAMAZ-53212 truck (1991 model, khaki, with specified engine, chassis, and cab numbers). The vehicle was in working order and in use. No authorizing document was presented.

The applicant’s father, Abu-Sultan Salamov, repeatedly complained to military, civilian, police, and prosecutorial authorities between December 1999 and February 2000, seeking the truck’s return. A letter from Major-General V., head of the “East” zone group of internal troops, confirmed that the truck was at military unit no. 3702, unused, sealed, and parked among seized vehicles. Ownership checks were underway against lists of vehicles taken in 1994–1995 and 1999–2000 operations; it would be returned if not military property.

The truck was returned on 24 April 2000. A certificate from Colonel K. confirmed the seizure on 14 December 1999 and return, noting that registration documents and number plates had been lost at the military unit. On 27 April 2000, a Shali town council commission, in the presence of the applicant’s father, documented 69 missing parts and assessed damage at 147,650 RUB. A 2003 forensic examination found the engine number erased but the cab number intact.

In August 2003, the Oktyabrskiy District Court of Grozny recognized the applicant as the truck’s owner. It relied on his testimony, two witnesses, and remaining documents, noting that military officers had lost the registration papers and that state archives had been destroyed in the conflict. The judgment became final in September 2003.

The applicant then pursued compensation. He lodged detailed complaints with Chechen administrative and law-enforcement bodies, including the military prosecutor, alleging use of the truck by a unit in Avtury and describing the damage. In May 2004 he sued military unit no. 3702 in the Prikubanskiy District Court of Krasnodar for unlawful seizure, missing parts, repair costs, military use of the vehicle, and non-pecuniary damage, invoking Civil Code Articles 151 and 1064.

On 22 July 2004 the court dismissed the claim. It found no record of the seizure in the unit’s log book for 14–16 December 1999 and heard two servicemen deny any alien truck at the base. It doubted the 2000 letter from Major-General V. (which lacked sources) and noted that ownership had been unclear at the time. The April 2000 evaluation was rejected as lacking expertise. Applying Articles 1069 and 1070, the court held that the unit was not the proper defendant; any liability for unlawful official acts lay with the relevant treasury. The Krasnodar Regional Court upheld the decision on 14 September 2004.

After the case was communicated, the Government submitted 2009 materials from a military prosecutor’s check. Unit no. 3702 stated it had conducted no operations in Shali on 14 December 1999 (operations in nearby Gudermes were classified) and held no relevant records or complaints. The regional command centre confirmed the unit was not involved in Avtury that day, had no information about the truck, and noted that Major-General V. had not served there. Servicemen’s affidavits recalled no such seized KAMAZ. An internal investigation concluded it could not be established that the truck had been kept at the unit.

These facts underpin the alleged unlawful interference with the applicant’s property rights through seizure, loss of documents, erasure of markings, missing parts, and denial of compensation.

The case of Salamov v. Russia (no. 5063/05) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Aslambek Salamov, born in 1960 and resident in Grozny, claimed that Russian military personnel unlawfully seized his KAMAZ-53212 truck (1991 model, khaki, specific engine/chassis/cab numbers) from his family home at 90 Shkolnaya Street, Shali, Chechnya, on 14 December 1999. This occurred during an identity check amid the Russian counter-terrorist operation launched in Chechnya in October 1999. No authorising document was produced. The truck was in working order and in use at the time.

The applicant’s father repeatedly complained to military, civilian, police and prosecutorial bodies between December 1999 and February 2000 seeking its return. A letter from Major-General V. (head of the “East” zone group of internal troops) confirmed the vehicle was at the base of military unit no. 3702, unused, sealed and parked among seized cars. Enquiries were being made to check if it had been stolen in earlier operations; it would be returned if not belonging to the forces. The truck was handed back on 24 April 2000. A certificate issued that day by Colonel K. recorded the seizure and return, noting that registration documents and number plates had been lost while in military custody. A Shali town council commission (in the presence of the applicant’s father) inspected the vehicle on 27 April 2000 and listed 69 missing parts, estimating damage at 147,650 roubles. A 2003 forensic examination found the engine number erased, though the cab number remained intact.

In 2003 the applicant obtained a final judgment from the Oktyabrskiy District Court of Grozny recognising his ownership. The court relied on witness statements and remaining documents, noting that military officers had lost the papers and that state archives had been destroyed in the conflict.

The applicant then sought compensation from the military authorities. After being directed to civil proceedings, he sued unit no. 3702 in the Prikubanskiy District Court of Krasnodar in May 2004 for the unlawful seizure, missing parts, repairs, unauthorised use and non-pecuniary damage, relying on Civil Code Articles 151 and 1064. On 22 July 2004 that court dismissed the claim. It found no mention of the truck in the unit’s December 1999 log-book, heard two servicemen deny any alien vehicle had been present, and doubted the reliability of Major-General V.’s letter (which cited no sources and was written when ownership was still unclear). The 2000 evaluation report was rejected as lacking specialist expertise. The court held that unit no. 3702 was the wrong defendant: under Civil Code Articles 1069 and 1070, liability for unlawful acts of state bodies or officials lies with the relevant treasury. The Krasnodar Regional Court upheld the decision on 14 September 2004.

After the case was communicated, the Government produced 2009 military-prosecutor materials. These stated that unit no. 3702 had not operated in Shali or Avtury on 14 December 1999, that archives contained no relevant records or complaints, that four former servicemen recalled no such truck, and that an internal investigation could not confirm the vehicle had ever been held at the unit. Major-General V. had not served in the relevant command.

These events constitute the factual core of the alleged interference with property: an unauthorised seizure lasting more than four months, physical deterioration and loss of documents, followed by the domestic courts’ refusal to award compensation on both evidentiary and procedural grounds.

The case of Salamov v. Russia (Application no. 5063/05) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Mr Aslambek Salamov, a Russian national born in 1960 and resident in Grozny, Chechnya, claimed that Russian military personnel unlawfully seized his KAMAZ-53212 truck (1991 model, khaki, with specified engine, chassis and cab numbers) from his family home at 90 Shkolnaya Street, Shali, on 14 December 1999 during an identity check amid the Russian counter-terrorist operation launched in Chechnya in October 1999. A letter dated around February 2000 from Major-General V., head of the “East” zone group of internal troops, confirmed to the Shali district prosecutor that the truck was held (unused and sealed) at the base of military unit no. 3702 pending ownership checks against lists of vehicles seized or lost in 1994-1995 and 1999-2000 operations. An internal investigation concluded that it could not be established that the truck had been held at the unit.

The applicant maintained that the seizure, prolonged retention, damage, loss of documents and subsequent inability to obtain compensation amounted to an unjustified interference with his property rights. The Government disputed the involvement of the identified unit and the reliability of contemporaneous documents.
001-160089:
The applicant, Varya Safaryan (born 1934), an Armenian national residing in Yerevan, owned an 815 m² plot of land in the city centre together with two houses and a garage. She shared the household with her four children. Prior to 1993 she had constructed, without planning permission, a pavilion of approximately 230 m² on the plot, which she used for commercial purposes. The pavilion was recorded on her 30 November 1998 ownership certificate merely as a “half-ruined construction.”

On 1 August 2002 the Armenian Government adopted Decree No. 1151-N, designating extensive expropriation zones (totalling 345 000 m²) within Yerevan’s Kentron District for State construction projects. The applicant’s plot fell inside one such zone.

In May 2004 she asked a notary to formalise a donation of the entire property to her four children. The notary refused, citing the expropriation decree. After the first-instance court dismissed her challenge, the Civil Court of Appeal on 28 July 2004 ordered the notary to complete the transaction. It held that Article 163 of the Civil Code entitled the owner to dispose of her property and that Decree 1151-N imposed no restriction on donations. The judgment became final.

Separately, the applicant applied to the State Real Estate Registry (SRER) seeking (i) partition of the plot into four lots to be registered in her children’s names and (ii) registration of her title to the pavilion. The SRER refused both requests on 23 February 2004, invoking Article 221 of the Civil Code and Government Decree No. 1748-N. In subsequent litigation the domestic courts consistently upheld the refusals. The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court (20 May 2004), the Civil Court of Appeal (29 April 2005) and the Court of Cassation (17 June 2005) reasoned that partition of land already earmarked for expropriation would contravene Decrees 1151-N and 2020-N, and that paragraph 3 of Decree 1748-N expressly excluded unauthorised structures located inside expropriation zones from the regularisation procedure. The courts also noted that the applicant remained the sole registered owner and that the pavilion, being an unauthorised construction, could not be regularised.

The applicant argued throughout that the refusals ignored the Court of Appeal’s earlier final judgment of 28 July 2004, unlawfully restricted her rights of disposal under Article 163 of the Civil Code, and, by denying registration of the pavilion, would deprive her of compensation when the land was ultimately expropriated. She therefore complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the authorities’ successive refusals violated her right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) and her right to respect for her home (Article 8 of the Convention).

Relevant domestic provisions confirmed that an owner normally retains full powers of possession, use and disposal until an expropriation agreement or court order is reached (Civil Code, Arts. 163 and 221), but that unauthorised buildings attract no ownership rights unless regularised under a special 2003 Law whose implementing decree (1748-N) expressly excluded constructions situated in designated expropriation zones.

The applicant, Varya Safaryan (born 1934), an Armenian national residing in Yerevan, owned an 815 sq. m plot of land in the city centre, together with two houses and a garage on it. She shared the household with her four children. Prior to 1993 she had constructed, without planning permission, a pavilion of approximately 230 sq. m on the plot, which she used for commercial purposes. The structure appeared in her November 1998 ownership certificate merely as a “half-ruined construction”.

On 1 August 2002 the Armenian Government adopted Decree no. 1151-N, designating large expropriation zones (totalling 345 000 sq. m) in Yerevan’s Kentron District for State construction needs. The applicant’s land fell inside one of those zones.

In May 2004 the applicant asked a notary to formalise the donation of her entire property to her four children. The notary refused, citing the expropriation decree. She successfully challenged the refusal: on 28 July 2004 the Civil Court of Appeal held that the decree imposed no restriction on the contemplated transaction and that the refusal violated Article 163 of the Civil Code (which guarantees an owner’s right to dispose of property). That judgment became final.

Separately, the applicant applied to the State Real Estate Registry (SRER) for two things: (i) division of the plot into four parts and transfer of title to her children, and (ii) registration of her ownership of the pavilion. On 23 February 2004 the SRER rejected both requests. It relied on the expropriation decrees and on Article 221 of the Civil Code, and also invoked Government Decree no. 1748-N, whose paragraph 3 expressly excluded unauthorised constructions located inside expropriation zones from the regularisation procedure.

The applicant brought judicial proceedings. The first-instance court dismissed her claims on 20 May 2004, holding that she remained the sole owner and that division was therefore unnecessary, and that the pavilion regularisation procedure did not apply inside an expropriation zone. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 29 April 2005. The Court of Cassation rejected her further appeal on 17 June 2005, repeating that the property’s location inside an expropriation zone and the unauthorised character of the pavilion justified the refusals.

The applicant contended that these successive refusals violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) by preventing her from disposing of her land as she wished and from obtaining legal title to the pavilion, thereby exposing her to the risk of receiving no compensation when the land was eventually expropriated. She further argued that the same measures interfered with her family life, contrary to Article 8 of the Convention, because they blocked the planned transfer of the family home to her children.

Domestic law relevant to the dispute included Civil Code Article 163 (owner’s right of free disposal), Article 188 (no automatic ownership of unauthorised structures), and Article 221 (continued right of disposal pending formal expropriation). The 2003 Law on unauthorised buildings and Decree no. 1748-N set out a regularisation procedure, but expressly excluded structures situated in designated expropriation zones.
