The case of Safaryan v. Armenia (Application no. 576/06) was lodged on 10 December 2005 by Varya Safaryan, an Armenian national born in 1934 and living in Yerevan. She alleged that the authorities' refusals to divide her property and transfer ownership to her four children, and to register her title to a pavilion on her land, violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life/home) of the Convention.

The applicant owned an 815 sq. m plot in central Yerevan, plus two houses and a garage, which she shared with her children. Before 1993 she had built an unauthorised pavilion of about 230 sq. m for commercial use; her 1998 ownership certificate listed it as a "half-ruined construction."

On 1 August 2002 the Government adopted Decree no. 1151-N, designating expropriation zones (totalling 345,000 sq. m) in Yerevan's Kentron District for state needs. The applicant's plot fell within one such zone.

On 7 May 2004 she asked a notary to formalise a donation of the property to her children. The notary refused, citing the expropriation decree. She challenged the refusal. The District Court dismissed her claim on 14 June 2004, but the Civil Court of Appeal allowed it on 28 July 2004. It held that the refusal violated Article 163 of the Civil Code (owners' rights to possess, use and dispose of property as they see fit, provided they do not contravene the law or others' rights) and that the decree imposed no relevant restrictions. The judgment became final.

Separately, the applicant applied to the State Real Estate Registry (SRER) to divide the property into four parts for transfer to her children and to register title to the pavilion. The SRER refused on 23 February 2004, citing Article 221 of the Civil Code and Decree no. 1748-N. She sued. The District Court dismissed the claim on 20 May 2004, finding division unnecessary because she was the sole owner and holding that the pavilion, as an unauthorised structure in an expropriation zone, was excluded from regularisation under paragraph 3 of Decree no. 1748-N. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld this on 29 April 2005, adding that division would also contravene Decrees nos. 1151-N and 2020-N. The Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal on points of law on 17 June 2005.

In her cassation submissions the applicant argued that the appellate court had ignored the earlier final judgment permitting the donation, that location in an expropriation zone could not restrict her Article 163 rights, and that refusal to register the pavilion (an immovable asset) would deprive her of compensation upon expropriation.

Relevant domestic provisions included Civil Code Article 188 (unauthorised structures generally confer no ownership rights unless a court grants them, and such grants may be refused if the structure harms others' rights or safety); Article 221 (owners of land earmarked for state needs retain possession, use and disposal rights until agreement or court order); a 2003 law and implementing decrees on regularising unauthorised buildings (applicable only to structures registered before certain dates and explicitly excluding those in expropriation zones); and Decree no. 1151-N itself, which required notification, valuation and eventual taking of the designated properties.

These events constitute the core facts of the alleged interferences: the authorities' reliance on the expropriation designation and the unauthorised status of the pavilion to block both the inter vivos transfer of the land and houses and the formal recognition of title to the pavilion.
001-160422:
The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered its judgment in Nazyrova and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 21126/09, 63620/09, 64811/09, 32965/10 and 64270/11) on 9 February 2016. The five applications, lodged by Russian nationals who lived in the Chechen Republic, alleged that their relatives had been abducted by State servicemen between 2000 and 2003 and that the authorities had failed to investigate the disappearances effectively. The events occurred in areas under the full control of Russian federal forces. The applicants had received no news of the missing men since their alleged arrests. Official investigations were opened after the abductions were reported, but they were repeatedly suspended and resumed, remaining pending for years without identifying perpetrators or yielding results. They consisted mainly of formal information requests that produced negative or no responses. The Government did not contest the applicants’ accounts of the circumstances but maintained that there was no proof beyond reasonable doubt of State-agent involvement.

In application no. 21126/09, Ms Maret Nazyrova alleged that her brother Badrudi Nazyrov (born 1973) was abducted on 20 April 2000 from her house in Gekhi. Around 30–40 armed Perm Region OMON servicemen, some in balaclavas, cordoned off the area, broke into the house, beat Nazyrov and a friend, covered their heads and took them in UAZ minivans to the Urus-Martan military commander’s office. Witnesses included the applicant and residents; two unmasked Kuznetsov brothers apparently commanded the unit. A food package was accepted the next day, but detention was later denied. Nazyrov has not been seen since. His father reported the abduction on 4 May 2000. Criminal case no. 24074 was opened on 25 November 2000 (after an initial refusal). The investigation was dormant from 2000 to 2007, then suspended and resumed several times (applicant granted victim status in 2007). It remains pending.

In application no. 63620/09, Ms Satsita Babuyeva alleged that her husband Muma Babuyev (born 1958), a driver at the Khankala military base, disappeared on 30 August 2002 after entering the base to collect salary arrears. He never emerged; an admissions-office employee confirmed an entrance pass was issued. Babuyeva waited fruitlessly for days. She reported the disappearance on 22 September 2002. Case no. 52112 was opened the same day under the kidnapping provision. She was granted victim status on 16 October 2002. Military prosecutors’ inquiries found no servicemen involvement. The investigation was suspended (unnotified) in November 2002, later resumed at her request, and remains pending. Babuyev was declared missing in 2004.

In application no. 64811/09, Mr Adam Kagermanov and Ms Zura Yakhayeva alleged that their relative Ruslan Kagermanov (born 1963) was abducted around 4 a.m. on 4 February 2002 from his dwelling in Gekhi (under curfew) by armed servicemen who arrived in a Ural lorry, broke down the door and drove toward Urus-Martan. Neighbours heard the vehicle; tyre tracks and military-boot footprints were found. Later that morning 50–60 servicemen in APCs and Ural lorries searched the premises and destroyed Kagermanov’s oil refinery during a sweeping operation. He has not been seen since. His mother reported the abduction the same day. Case no. 61023 was opened on 18 February 2002. Witnesses (applicants, relatives, neighbours) were questioned in 2002 and again in 2009; the crime scene was examined in 2009 with no evidence collected. The investigation was dormant for years, then suspended and resumed; it remains pending.

In application no. 32965/10, Ms Khedi Tchapanova alleged that her husband Eduard Zaynadinov (born 1974), a former member of illegal armed groups, was abducted between 3 and 4 a.m. on 30 July 2002 from their Shali flat by armed servicemen in balaclavas who arrived in APCs, placed a plastic bag over his head and took him away. Servicemen later searched the house, finding documents and firearms. He had been briefly detained weeks earlier. Zaynadinov has not been seen since; Tchapanova later moved to France. His father reported the abduction. Case no. 59229 was opened on 16 September 2002. Neighbours and relatives were questioned. The investigation was suspended (unnotified) in November 2002, later resumed with further questioning and a crime-scene examination yielding nothing; it remains pending. Zaynadinov was declared missing in 2007 and dead in 2008.

In application no. 64270/11, Ms Ayna Alkhotova alleged that her husband Ayndi Diniyev (born 1971) was abducted at about 1 a.m. on 16 August 2003 from their Grozny flat (under curfew) by 10–15 armed servicemen in camouflage and balaclavas who arrived in three UAZ vehicles and an APC, searched the flat, dragged him out and drove through a checkpoint toward the city centre. He has not been seen since. Alkhotova reported the abduction on 18 August 2003. Case no. 50094 was opened on 29 August 2003. Witnesses were questioned and the crime scene examined (no evidence collected). The investigation was suspended and resumed multiple times (applicant granted victim status); a prosecutor criticised investigators in 2011 for failing to take basic steps. It remains pending. Diniyev was declared missing in 2004.

The Court referenced its earlier summary of relevant domestic law and reports on Chechen disappearances.

The ECtHR case of Nazyrova and Others v. Russia (applications 21126/09, 63620/09, 64811/09, 32965/10 and 64270/11) concerns five Russian nationals whose close relatives disappeared after alleged abductions by State servicemen in Chechnya between 2000 and 2003. The applicants claimed the relatives were unlawfully detained during special operations in areas under full control of Russian federal forces, with no subsequent news of them. Official investigations were opened but repeatedly suspended and resumed over years, consisting mainly of unproductive information requests and yielding no identification of perpetrators or tangible results. The Government did not dispute the applicants’ accounts of events but denied proof beyond reasonable doubt of State-agent involvement.

In Nazyrova, on 20 April 2000 around 30–40 armed Perm-region OMON servicemen (some masked) arrived in Gekhi, cordoned the area, searched the applicant’s house, beat her brother Badrudi Nazyrov (b. 1973) and a friend, hooded them and took them in minivans to the Urus-Martan military commander’s office. The unit was locally stationed; two unmasked Kuznetsov brothers (unit leaders) were identifiable. A food package was initially accepted for Nazyrov but detention was later denied. The applicant and locals witnessed the events. Reported in May 2000, a criminal case (no. 24074) opened only in November 2000 after an initial refusal, noting an unconfirmed special operation. The probe was dormant until 2007, then suspended/resumed multiple times (including after a 2008 court complaint), remaining pending without results.

In Babuyeva, on 30 August 2002 Muma Babuyev (b. 1958), a driver at the Khankala military base, entered the base with a pass to collect salary arrears while his wife waited at the checkpoint. He never emerged. An admissions-office employee confirmed a pass issued that day (and one unused for the next). Reported in September 2002, case no. 52112 opened for kidnapping. Victim status granted; military-prosecutor inquiries found no servicemen involvement. Suspended in 2002 (unnotified), with later unsuccessful information requests; resumed in 2011 and still pending. A 2004 court declared him missing.

In Kagermanov and Yakhayeva, on 4 February 2002 (under curfew) armed servicemen in a Ural lorry broke into Ruslan Kagermanov’s (b. 1963) Gekhi dwelling around 3–4 a.m. and took him toward Urus-Martan. Tyre tracks and military-boot prints were found. Later that morning 50–60 servicemen in APCs and lorries searched the family compound and destroyed his oil refinery (part of a sweeping operation). Reported immediately, case no. 61023 opened in February 2002. Witness statements consistent; suspended April 2002 (unnotified). Largely dormant until 2009 questioning of relatives/neighbours and a crime-scene exam (no evidence). A 2009 court noted seven years of inaction and granted file access. Suspended again; still pending.

In Tchapanova, Eduard Zaynadinov (b. 1974, former illegal-armed-group member) was taken from his Shali flat around 3–4 a.m. on 30 July 2002 by balaclava-clad armed servicemen in APCs, bag over his head. Servicemen later searched, finding documents/firearms. Neighbours heard commotion and saw APCs. Reported August 2002, case no. 59229 opened September 2002. Suspended November 2002 (unnotified). Applicant fled Chechnya in 2004 (to France 2007). Declared missing (2007) then dead (2008). Resumed 2011 with further questioning/scene exam (no new information); suspended 2012, still pending.

In Alkhotova, around 1 a.m. on 16 August 2003 (under curfew) 10–15 camouflaged/balaclava-clad armed servicemen in three UAZ vehicles and an APC broke into Ayndi Diniyev’s (b. 1971) Grozny flat, searched it, and drove him through a checkpoint. Reported immediately, scene examined (no evidence), case no. 50094 opened August 2003. Consistent witness statements; victim status granted. Suspended October 2003 (unnotified). Declared missing 2004. Resumed/suspended multiple times (2005, 2011–2012) with prosecutor criticism of inaction and repeated questioning; still pending.

These facts underpin allegations of State-orchestrated disappearances and systemic investigative failures in Chechnya. (Word count: 512)

**CASE OF NAZYROVA AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA (Applications nos. 21126/09 etc., ECtHR, 9 February 2016)**

This judgment addresses five applications by Russian nationals whose close relatives disappeared after alleged abductions by State servicemen in Chechnya between 2000 and 2003. The applicants claimed their relatives were unlawfully detained during special operations in areas fully controlled by Russian federal forces, with no subsequent news of them. They reported the incidents, prompting official investigations that were repeatedly suspended and resumed over years without identifying perpetrators or producing results. Investigations largely involved unproductive information requests. The Government did not contest the applicants' accounts of events but denied evidence proving State agent involvement beyond reasonable doubt.

In *Nazyrova v. Russia*, Ms Maret Nazyrova alleged that on 20 April 2000, her brother Badrudi Nazyrov (born 1973) was at her home in Gekhi when 30–40 armed Perm OMON servicemen (some in balaclavas) arrived in vehicles, cordoned the area, searched the house, beat Nazyrov and a friend, and took them in UAZ minivans to the Urus-Martan military commander's office. Neighbours witnessed this. The unit was stationed nearby; two identifiable (unmasked) commanders from the Kuznetsov family were allegedly involved. A food package was accepted the next day, but detention was later denied. Criminal case no. 24074 opened in November 2000 after initial refusals (noting an unconfirmed special operation). The probe was largely inactive until 2007, with further suspensions; it remains pending. Nazyrova received victim status in 2007; court complaints about delays were rejected as the case had resumed.

In *Babuyeva v. Russia*, Ms Satsita Babuyeva claimed her husband Muma Babuyev (born 1958), a driver for a military-linked department, entered the Khankala federal military base on 30 August 2002 to collect salary arrears and never emerged. An admissions office confirmed issuing him a pass (and preparing one for the next day unused). Case no. 52112 opened in September 2002 (kidnapping). Inquiries by military prosecutors found no servicemen involvement. The investigation suspended in November 2002 (applicant uninformed), with later resumptions; it remains pending. He was declared missing in 2004. Information requests yielded little.

In *Kagermanov and Yakhayeva v. Russia*, Mr Adam Kagermanov and Ms Zura Yakhayeva alleged that on 4 February 2002 (during curfew in Gekhi), armed servicemen in a Ural lorry abducted their relative Ruslan Kagermanov (born 1963) from his home after breaking down the door. Neighbours heard them drive toward Urus-Martan; APCs were seen nearby. Morning evidence included lorry tracks and military boot prints. Later, 50–60 servicemen in APCs/lorries searched the family compound and destroyed Kagermanov's oil refinery. Case no. 61023 opened February 2002. It lay dormant for years; 2009 questioning of relatives/neighbours and a crime-scene exam added nothing. A court noted seven years of inactivity and granted file access. The case remains pending.

In *Tchapanova v. Russia*, Ms Khedi Tchapanova claimed her husband Eduard Zaynadinov (born 1974; prior illegal armed group member) was taken from their Shali flat around 3–4 a.m. on 30 July 2002 by armed balaclava-clad servicemen in APCs, who bagged his head. Neighbours heard cries and saw APCs leave. Servicemen later searched, finding group member lists, IDs, and hidden firearms. Case no. 59229 opened September 2002 after a father's report. It suspended in November 2002 (family uninformed); later police searches found nothing. He was declared missing (2007) then dead (2008). 2011–2012 questioning and a crime-scene exam added nothing; the case remains pending after a 2011 resumption.

In *Alkhotova v. Russia*, Ms Ayna Alkhotova alleged that around 1 a.m. on 16 August 2003 (Grozny curfew), 10–15 armed camouflaged/balaclava-clad servicemen in three UAZ vehicles and an APC broke into her flat at 186 Pugacheva Street, searched it, and took her husband Ayndi Diniyev (born 1971) through checkpoint 24. Case no. 50094 opened August 2003. Crime-scene exams yielded no evidence; questioning of relatives was consistent but unidentifying. Multiple suspensions/resumptions occurred (e.g., 2003, 2005, 2011, 2012); prosecutors criticised basic-step failures. He was declared missing in 2004. The case remains pending.

These facts concern alleged State-perpetrated enforced disappearances and systemic investigative failures in Chechnya, typically implicating Convention Articles 2 (life), 3 (ill-treatment of relatives), 5 (liberty), and 13 (remedy). The judgment became final on 6 June 2016.
001-160009:
The case of Bilbija and Blažević v. Croatia concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights by two Croatian sisters alleging that domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into their mother's death, which they attributed to medical negligence. This was claimed to violate Articles 2, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

The applicants' mother was admitted to the public Jordanovac Clinical Hospital Centre on 13 February 2001 with respiratory problems and died the following day. An autopsy by Zagreb University Medical Faculty pathologists identified the cause as respiratory insufficiency leading to cardiac complications. The family was informed of the results and the treatment provided, but they sought fuller medical records and details of the circumstances.

The first applicant pursued the matter. In July 2001 she complained to Ministry of Health inspectors about the lack of records and the death, but no action followed. In October 2002 she complained to the Croatian Medical Chamber (CMC). After correspondence, the CMC's Professional Supervisory Commission found no malpractice in May 2003. The first applicant objected, stressing the absence of concrete documents on the cause of death. The CMC Executive Board dismissed the objection in October 2003, informing her she could bring an administrative action.

She did so in November 2003, arguing the CMC had not properly assessed the death. After delays due to court backlog (prompting complaints to the Ministry of Justice and even the President's Office), the Administrative Court declared the action inadmissible in October 2007, holding that the CMC decision was not an administrative act affecting her rights or obligations. A constitutional complaint lodged in January 2008 was dismissed by the Constitutional Court in December 2013 as ill-founded; supplementary complaints on length and other issues were declared inadmissible for being out of time or for non-exhaustion of remedies.

Separately, in February 2004 the first applicant filed a criminal complaint with the Zagreb Municipal State Attorney's Office, alleging that hospital staff had administered a drug to which her mother was allergic, triggering a fatal reaction. After prolonged inactivity (including a lost file that had to be reconstructed), the police interviewed the relevant doctors, who denied any such administration or malpractice. An expert report in January 2008 found no negligence. The State Attorney rejected the complaint for lack of reasonable suspicion, allowing the applicant to take over as subsidiary prosecutor.

She instituted proceedings and submitted an indictment. Further expert reports in 2010 (by two doctors) confirmed no irregularities, no use of the allergenic drug, and no allergic reaction. After procedural steps requiring her to seek a formal investigation, an investigating judge questioned the doctor (who again denied wrongdoing). A three-judge panel of the Zagreb County Court dismissed the request for investigation in February 2012 for lack of evidence of malpractice. The Supreme Court upheld this in November 2012. A constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible in February 2013 on the ground that the decisions did not concern the applicant's rights or a criminal charge against her. A subsequent request to reopen the proceedings was rejected.

Throughout both sets of proceedings there were significant delays; the Supreme Court awarded modest compensation for excessive length in the criminal case. The applicants also lodged unsuccessful complaints against the medical experts and approached numerous other authorities. All official inquiries consistently found no medical negligence, yet the family maintained that the procedures had failed to elucidate the circumstances of the death or provide an effective remedy.

The case of Bilbija and Blažević v. Croatia (Application no. 62870/13) was brought by two Croatian sisters whose mother died on 13 February 2001 at the public Jordanovac Clinical Hospital Centre after admission for respiratory problems. An autopsy the following day attributed death to respiratory insufficiency leading to cardiac complications. The applicants were informed of this and of the treatment provided, but they alleged medical negligence, including administration of a drug to which their mother was allergic, and they complained of an ineffective domestic response to establish the circumstances of the death, contrary to Articles 2, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

The first applicant pursued remedies. In July 2001 she met Ministry of Health inspectors about the family’s inability to obtain medical records and the circumstances of death, but no action followed. In October 2002 she complained to the Croatian Medical Chamber (CMC). After she specified the hospital, its director and the intensive-care head (doctor B.S.), the CMC’s Professional Supervisory Commission found no malpractice in May 2003. The first applicant objected, citing the absence of concrete documents on the cause of death and inadequate reasoning. The CMC Executive Board dismissed the objection in October 2003, informing her she could seek judicial review. An administrative action in the Administrative Court was declared inadmissible in October 2007 on the ground that the CMC decision did not determine any of her rights or obligations. A constitutional complaint lodged in January 2008 was dismissed as ill-founded in December 2013; additional complaints about delay were rejected for non-exhaustion of remedies.

Separately, in February 2004 the first applicant filed a criminal complaint with the Zagreb Municipal State Attorney’s Office alleging negligence by unknown hospital staff. Progress was slow. She made repeated inquiries; the Ministry of Justice requested reports. In December 2007 the file was found to have been lost and was reconstructed. Police interviewed the mother’s general practitioner and doctor B.S. (who denied giving the allergic drug). An expert report of January 2008 found no malpractice. The State Attorney rejected the complaint later that month for lack of reasonable suspicion, advising that the first applicant could proceed as a subsidiary prosecutor.

She did so, filing an indictment against doctor B.S. Further delays ensued. Additional expert reports (March 2010) confirmed no irregularity and that the disputed drug had not been used. The first applicant challenged the reports as incomplete. In April 2011 the Municipal Criminal Court returned the indictment, requiring her to seek an investigation. An investigating judge questioned B.S. and disagreed with opening an investigation; a County Court panel dismissed the request in February 2012 for lack of evidence. The Supreme Court upheld this in November 2012. A subsequent constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible in February 2013 on the ground that the decisions did not concern the applicant’s rights or a criminal charge against her. A request to reopen proceedings was rejected in 2014. A later complaint against the experts for false evidence was also rejected.

Throughout both sets of proceedings the applicants encountered protracted delays (including a lost criminal file), successive findings of no negligence, limited access to records at the outset, and judicial decisions treating the complaints as not engaging their personal rights. The first applicant repeatedly urged authorities and complained to higher bodies, including the President’s Office and Parliament, without obtaining an effective elucidation of the death. The Supreme Court later awarded modest compensation for the length of the criminal proceedings, but the core complaints about the adequacy of the investigation remained unresolved at the domestic level.

The applicants, two Croatian sisters, alleged that domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into their mother's death from possible medical negligence, in violation of Articles 2, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

Their mother died on 13 February 2001 at a public hospital after admission for respiratory problems. An autopsy the next day attributed death to respiratory insufficiency causing cardiac complications. The applicants were informed of the results and treatment but claimed they never received complete records or a satisfactory explanation. They alleged specifically that staff administered a drug to which she was allergic, triggering a fatal reaction.

The first applicant pursued remedies. In July 2001 she complained to health inspectors about missing records and the circumstances of death, but they took no action. In October 2002 she complained to the Croatian Medical Chamber (CMC). After delays and requests for specification, she named the hospital, its director and the intensive-care head. The Ministry of Health obtained a hospital report. In May 2003 the CMC's supervisory commission found no malpractice. Her objection was dismissed by the CMC executive board in October 2003. She brought an administrative action in November 2003. After repeated urgings amid backlog, the Administrative Court declared it inadmissible in October 2007 on the ground that the CMC decision was not an administrative act affecting her rights or obligations. A January 2008 constitutional complaint was dismissed as ill-founded in December 2013 (additional length complaints were rejected as out of time or for non-exhaustion).

Separately, she lodged a criminal complaint in February 2004 alleging negligence by unknown hospital staff. After inquiries, a lost file that had to be reconstructed, and a police investigation (including interviews denying the allergic-drug claim), an expert report found no malpractice. The State Attorney rejected the complaint in January 2008 for lack of reasonable suspicion. She took over as subsidiary prosecutor and filed charges against the intensive-care doctor. Further delays ensued. A 2010 expert report again found no irregularity and excluded use of the allergenic drug or death from allergy. After she challenged it, a court panel in 2011 returned the indictment, requiring her to seek a formal investigation. An investigating judge questioned the doctor (who denied malpractice); a county-court panel then dismissed the investigation request in February 2012 for lack of evidence. The Supreme Court upheld this in November 2012. A February 2013 constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible because the decisions concerned neither her rights/obligations nor a criminal charge against her. A reopening request was rejected in 2013–14. A later complaint that the experts gave false evidence was also rejected.

Throughout both tracks the first applicant repeatedly urged authorities, complained of inactivity to the Ministry of Justice, presidential and prime-ministerial offices and a parliamentarian, and received acknowledgements of delay (including a 2012 Supreme Court finding of unreasonable length with a small award). Domestic law (Criminal Code Arts. 240 and 249) criminalises negligent medical treatment causing deterioration, serious injury or death. Victims may act as subsidiary prosecutors if public authorities decline to prosecute. Constitutional-court practice generally treated such decisions as not engaging the complainant's rights, though later cases showed some evolution.

These facts—the unexplained death, conflicting or incomplete information, multiple rejected complaints, lost files, successive expert reports finding no fault, and serial dismissals on procedural or evidential grounds—form the core of the applicants' claim that no effective official inquiry ever elucidated the circumstances or afforded them an effective remedy.
001-160620:
The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined eleven applications against Russia from detained Russian nationals (Yevdokimov, Rezanov, Morozov, Makhov, Resin, Anikanov, Lebetskiy, Gromovoy, Gordeyev, Vinokhodov and Martirosyan). All were serving sentences in penal facilities when they became parties to civil proceedings. Three (Yevdokimov, Rezanov, Morozov) sued private persons for defamation. Seven others claimed compensation for allegedly inhuman detention conditions. Martirosyan sought damages for the allegedly unlawful institution of criminal proceedings against him.

None of the applicants was permitted to attend the hearings of their claims. Domestic courts refused personal appearance on the ground that Russian law contained no provision allowing convicted prisoners to be brought to court for civil cases. They cited Article 77.1 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences (which authorises transfer only for participation as a witness, victim or suspect in a criminal investigation) together with the Code of Civil Procedure. In several instances the courts simply ignored the applicants’ requests to be present.

The applicants raised the issue of their absence on appeal (some filing separate motions for leave to appear). Appellate courts either dismissed the arguments or held that non-attendance was lawful and did not breach fairness. All claims were rejected at two levels of jurisdiction.

The Code of Civil Procedure allows parties to appear in person or by representative, to use letters of request, and (after later amendment) video-conferencing. It requires oral, direct examination of evidence. The Legal Aid Act, however, limits State-funded representation to a narrow list of disputes that did not cover the applicants’ claims. Article 77.1 of the Execution Code remains silent on civil proceedings. Russia’s Constitutional Court, while declaring similar complaints inadmissible, has repeatedly stated that a detained party must still be able to present his case (via representative, video-link, hearing at the prison, or letters of request) and that courts must give reasoned decisions on whether personal presence is required by the interests of justice. The Supreme Court later instructed lower courts that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention confers on prisoners a right to participate in their civil hearings.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints that they were denied an effective opportunity to take part in the determination of their civil rights, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention.

The case originated in eleven applications by Russian nationals detained in penal colonies, who complained that they were denied the chance to appear in person at hearings in their own civil cases, in alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing).

Three applicants (Yevdokimov, Rezanov and Morozov) brought defamation actions against private individuals. Seven others (Makhov, Resin, Anikanov, Lebetskiy, Gromovoy, Gordeyev and Vinokhodov) claimed compensation for allegedly inhuman conditions of detention. Martirosyan sought damages on the ground that criminal proceedings against him had been instituted unlawfully. All claims were examined while the applicants remained in custody.

Domestic courts refused every request for personal attendance. They relied principally on Article 77.1 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences, which authorises the transfer of a convicted person to a remand facility only for participation in criminal investigations as a witness, victim or suspect, and contains no provision for civil proceedings. In several cases the courts simply ignored the issue of presence. First-instance hearings therefore took place in the applicants’ absence. Appeals raising the same point were dismissed on the ground that the absences complied with domestic law and did not undermine fairness. All claims were rejected at both levels of jurisdiction.

The Code of Civil Procedure permits parties to appear in person or through a representative and, since 2013, to participate by video-conference from a penitentiary facility if the necessary equipment exists (Article 155.1). It also allows a court to issue a letter of request to another court to take evidence locally. Proceedings must be oral and the court must take direct cognisance of the evidence. A hearing may nevertheless proceed in a party’s absence if that party has been duly notified and has not shown a valid reason for non-attendance. Legal aid for court representation is available only in a narrow range of disputes that did not cover the applicants’ claims.

The Constitutional Court had previously held that the absence of an express transfer provision does not, of itself, restrict access to court, but that a detainee must still be able to present his case—through a representative, by video-link, by a hearing held at the prison, or by a letter of request. The trial court is required to weigh all relevant circumstances, including the nature of the rights at stake and the need for oral evidence, and to give a reasoned decision on the mode of participation. In 2013 the Supreme Court similarly instructed ordinary courts that, under Article 6 of the Convention, an imprisoned person has the right to take part in the hearing of his civil case.

None of these alternative means of participation was employed. The applicants therefore alleged that they had been deprived of a fair opportunity to present their cases in person.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered its judgment in Yevdokimov and Others v. Russia on 16 February 2016 (final 16 May 2016). The case joined eleven applications lodged by Russian nationals detained in penal facilities who alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention arising from their inability to appear in person at hearings in civil proceedings to which they were parties.

At the relevant times all applicants were serving sentences in Russian correctional colonies. While detained, three (Yevdokimov, Rezanov and Morozov) brought defamation claims against private individuals. Seven others (Makhov, Resin, Anikanov, Lebetskiy, Gromovoy, Gordeyev and Vinokhodov) sought compensation for allegedly inhuman conditions of detention. Martirosyan claimed compensation on the ground that criminal proceedings against him had been instituted unlawfully.

None of the applicants was permitted to attend the first-instance hearings at which their claims were examined. Domestic courts systematically refused requests for their personal appearance, citing the absence of any statutory provision authorising the transfer of convicted prisoners for civil proceedings. They relied in particular on Article 77.1 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences, which permits transfer only for participation as a witness, victim or suspect in criminal investigations, and on corresponding provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. In some cases the courts did not even address the applicants’ presence.

The applicants appealed, expressly raising their exclusion from the hearings (some also filing separate applications for leave to appear). Appellate courts either dismissed the arguments or held that the absences complied with domestic legislation and did not breach fairness. All claims were ultimately rejected at two instances of jurisdiction.

Domestic law offered limited alternatives. The Code of Civil Procedure permitted representation, letters of request, and (after later amendments) video-conferencing, but contained no general mechanism for bringing detainees to court. Legal aid was available only in narrowly defined categories of disputes, none of which matched the applicants’ claims. The Constitutional Court, while declaring similar complaints inadmissible, had repeatedly stated that the legislative silence did not itself restrict access to court; detainees must still be able to make submissions through a representative, video-link, or by holding the hearing at the place of detention or issuing a letter of request. Courts were required to give reasoned decisions taking account of the nature of the rights at stake and the need for oral evidence. In 2013 the Supreme Court Plenary similarly instructed lower courts that Article 6 required an imprisoned person to be able to participate in the hearing of his civil case.

These facts formed the core of the alleged violation: the systematic denial, without individualised assessment, of any effective opportunity for the detained applicants to present their cases in person, despite the civil character of the disputes and the absence of any countervailing security or organisational justification appearing in the domestic decisions.
001-161004:
The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Andrey Borisovich Lavrov, a Russian national born in 1967, who alleged inadequate medical care during detention after his 2013 arrest and convictions for fraud, robbery and theft. While serving an earlier sentence in 2012, he had been diagnosed with lymphoma, received two chemotherapy courses in a prison hospital, and obtained early release on health grounds that December. He continued chemotherapy as a civilian but was re-arrested in September 2013 and, after conviction, transferred in March 2014 to a prison tuberculosis hospital.

On 13 March 2014 a prison medical panel diagnosed progressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma at acute stage III B, involving multiple lymph-node groups, and confirmed the condition appeared on the official list of serious illnesses that preclude continued imprisonment. Lavrov applied for early release. The Metallurgicheskiy District Court rejected the application on 26 May 2014, accepting that the illness was listed and describing his state as “stable but serious,” yet holding that necessary drugs were available and that post-release care arrangements were unclear. A prison-hospital certificate subsequently stated that the required chemotherapy drugs were in fact unavailable. A further panel examination on 1 July 2014 recorded progression to stage IV B; another release request was refused on 12 September 2014. Although a hospital doctor testified that chemotherapy and radiotherapy were medically necessary but impossible in the facility for lack of equipment, the court cited a supposed tendency to reoffend and asserted that care remained adequate.

In October 2014 Lavrov sought a Rule 39 interim measure, relying on the hospital’s own confirmation that chemotherapy drugs were absent. On 16 October the Court indicated that independent experts (including an oncologist unaffiliated with the prison system) must immediately examine him to determine (1) whether existing treatment was adequate, (2) whether his health was compatible with continued detention, and (3) whether specialised hospitalisation or release was required. The Government’s 7 November reply contained no independent examination. Instead it supplied internal records showing only basic analgesics, anti-inflammatories and psychotropic drugs, together with assertions that Lavrov had refused chemotherapy (though he had declined to sign a refusal form). Prison officials described his condition as life-threatening, with severe pain, asthenia, haemoptysis and enlarging nodes, yet claimed the hospital possessed an oncologist and the necessary medicines. The Government itself answered the Court’s three questions, stating that treatment would resume once blood-test results permitted and consent was given, that the illness was incurable, and that a further prison-panel review was scheduled.

On 28 November 2014 the Chelyabinsk Regional Court quashed the September refusal, holding that the lower court’s finding of adequate care contradicted the doctor’s testimony and that family care had been offered. Lavrov was released shortly afterwards. The facts centre on the progressive, listed malignancy, the documented unavailability of indicated oncological treatment, repeated domestic refusals of release despite medical eligibility, and the authorities’ failure to arrange the independent examination required by the interim measure.

The case of Andrey Lavrov v. Russia (Application no. 66252/14) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Russian national born in 1967 who alleged a lack of adequate medical care during detention, in circumstances raising issues under Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) as well as potential non-compliance with an interim measure under Rule 39 that could engage Article 34.

While serving a prior prison sentence in 2012, the applicant was diagnosed with lymphoma and received two courses of chemotherapy in a prison hospital. A court authorised his early release on health grounds in December 2012. Thereafter he was monitored by a civilian oncologist and continued chemotherapy, though he did not complete all examinations or treatment. He was re-arrested on 10 September 2013 and later convicted of fraud, robbery and theft. He was held first in a detention facility and, from 3 March 2014, in a prison tuberculosis hospital.

A medical panel of prison doctors examined him on 13 March 2014 and diagnosed progressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma at acute stage III B, with lesions of cervical, axillary and abdominal lymph nodes. The panel found him eligible for early release because the illness appeared on the official list of serious diseases incompatible with continued detention. His application for release was refused by a district court on 26 May 2014. Although the court accepted that the disease was on the list and described the applicant’s condition as “stable but serious,” it held that the necessary drugs were available in the prison hospital, that he was receiving appropriate procedures, and that it was unclear who would care for him if released. The applicant did not appeal.

A later certificate from the prison hospital confirmed that chemotherapy drugs were in fact unavailable. On 1 July 2014 a further panel examination recorded progression to stage IV B. A second release application was lodged, supported by a written undertaking from the applicant’s sister to care for him. At a hearing on 12 September 2014 a prison doctor testified that the applicant required chemotherapy and radiation therapy that could not be provided in detention because the necessary equipment was lacking. The district court nevertheless dismissed the application, citing a risk of reoffending and asserting that care was adequate. The applicant appealed.

In October 2014 the applicant sought an interim measure under Rule 39, arguing that he was being denied essential treatment for a rapidly progressing, life-threatening illness. On 16 October 2014 the Court indicated that the applicant should be examined immediately by medical experts independent of the prison system to determine (1) whether his current treatment was adequate, (2) whether his health was compatible with detention, and (3) whether he required transfer to a specialised hospital or release. The Government were also instructed to transfer him if the experts so recommended.

The Government’s response of 7 November 2014 consisted of prison-hospital documents rather than an independent expert examination. These showed that the applicant had received only basic analgesics, anti-inflammatories and similar drugs; they asserted (without a written record from the applicant) that he had refused chemotherapy. The documents confirmed that his condition was life-threatening, that he was in severe pain, coughing blood and experiencing growing lymph nodes and increasing weakness. The Government themselves answered the Court’s three questions, claiming that treatment was adequate, that specialists and drugs were available, and that the illness was incurable, while noting that domestic courts had already refused release.

On 28 November 2014 the regional court quashed the September refusal, holding that the lower court’s findings on the adequacy of treatment contradicted the evidence, including the doctor’s testimony, and that it had ignored the sister’s undertaking. The applicant was released shortly thereafter.

These facts formed the core of the alleged violations: the claimed failure to provide chemotherapy and specialist care for advanced lymphoma while the applicant remained in detention, and the Government’s failure to comply with the terms of the Rule 39 indication.

**Case of Andrey Lavrov v. Russia (Application no. 66252/14), ECHR (Third Section), judgment of 1 March 2016 (final 1 June 2016).**

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1967, alleged inadequate medical assistance in detention (primarily under Article 3 of the Convention) and, relatedly, issues arising from the Government’s response to an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court (potentially engaging Article 34).

In 2012, while serving a prison sentence, he was diagnosed with lymphoma and received two courses of chemotherapy in a prison hospital. A court granted early release on health grounds in December 2012. He continued monitoring and chemotherapy in a civilian facility. An in-depth examination in May 2013 at the Chelyabinsk regional hospital confirmed lymphoproliferative disorder affecting multiple lymph nodes, but he did not complete further examinations or treatment. He was arrested on 10 September 2013 and later convicted of fraud, robbery and theft. He was placed in detention facility no. 3 and transferred on 3 March 2014 to the prison tuberculosis hospital.

On 13 March 2014 a prison medical panel diagnosed progressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma (acute stage III B) with lesions of cervical, axillary and abdominal lymph nodes. The panel found him eligible for early release, as the condition appeared on the official List of serious illnesses precluding detention in correctional institutions (Government Decree no. 54 of 6 February 2004). He applied for release on 10 April 2014. On 26 May 2014 the Metallurgicheskiy District Court dismissed the application. It accepted that the illness was on the List and described his condition as “stable [but] serious,” but held that necessary drugs were available, that he was receiving required procedures, and that it was unclear who would care for him if released. He did not appeal. His sister later provided a written undertaking (30 June 2014) to care for him.

A prison hospital certificate confirmed that chemotherapy drugs were unavailable. On 1 July 2014 the same panel re-examined him, now diagnosing progressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma (acute stage IV B) with abdominal lymph-node lesions, and again found him eligible for release. He reapplied at the end of July 2014, citing disease progression to its final stage and family care. At a 12 September 2014 hearing, a prison doctor (B.) testified that chemotherapy and radiation therapy were required but unavailable due to lack of equipment. The District Court again dismissed the application, citing a tendency to reoffend and concluding that adequate care was being provided. The applicant appealed.

In October 2014 the applicant sought a Rule 39 interim measure for immediate release, arguing that he was receiving no necessary treatment for a life-threatening, rapidly progressing illness (supported by the certificate on missing chemotherapy drugs). On 16 October 2014 the Court indicated that the applicant should be examined immediately by independent medical experts (including an oncologist) from outside the prison system to determine: (1) adequacy of current treatment; (2) compatibility of his health with detention in a colony or prison hospital; and (3) whether specialised hospital placement or release was required. Transfer to a specialised hospital was to occur if indicated.

The Government replied on 7 November 2014 without an independent examination. They submitted the applicant’s detention medical history (showing only basic analgesics, anti-inflammatories, antihistamines, sleeping pills, antidepressants, antiemetics and neuroleptics), certificates claiming he had refused chemotherapy (no written refusal obtained) when offered in March and June 2014, notes of four oncologist examinations, and descriptions of his deteriorating condition (severe pain, increasing asthenia, coughing blood, growing lymph nodes). They asserted that the hospital employed an oncologist and possessed necessary medicines; that treatment was adequate (subject to consent and blood-test results); that his condition was compatible with detention; and that the illness was incurable and on the List, though domestic courts had refused release. A further internal panel examination was scheduled for November 2014.

On 28 November 2014 the Chelyabinsk Regional Court quashed the 12 September 2014 decision and ordered release. It held that the District Court’s finding of adequate treatment contradicted the established facts (including B.’s testimony) and that the court had failed to address the sister’s care undertaking. The applicant was released shortly thereafter.

These facts centre on the progression of untreated or inadequately treated advanced lymphoma in detention, repeated domestic medical findings of eligibility for release that courts initially disregarded, the provision of only palliative rather than oncological treatment, and the authorities’ substitution of internal assessments for the independent expert examination required by the interim measure.
001-160619:
The case of A.K. v. Liechtenstein (No. 2) involves a German national's application to the ECHR alleging breaches of Article 6 § 1 (impartial tribunal and reasonable time) and Article 13 (effective remedy) arising from protracted civil litigation in Liechtenstein over corporate share ownership.

Since 2004 the applicant and F.H. have disputed title to 75 % of the bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. On 10 June 2005 F.H. sued the applicant in the Regional Court for delivery of the shares and a declaration that the applicant had never owned them. The applicant immediately challenged jurisdiction. Interlocutory proceedings on that issue, including a failed appeal and a constitutional complaint, occupied almost two years and ended only on 27 March 2007 when the Constitutional Court dismissed the challenge. Hearings on the merits then took place on 31 May, 28 June and 6 September 2007. Although the applicant requested judgment in April 2009, the Regional Court did not deliver its 66-page decision until 28 December 2009—an unexplained interval of two years and three months. The court found for F.H., holding that the applicant’s mother had never validly acquired the shares and that the applicant therefore lacked good-faith title. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 27 May 2010 and the Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law on 13 January 2011.

On 18 February 2011 the applicant lodged an 80-page constitutional complaint. He invoked Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, stressing that the nearly seven-year proceedings (to which he claimed not to have contributed) concerned his livelihood and that Liechtenstein law provided no mechanism, such as an application to accelerate, to enforce the reasonable-time guarantee.

On 20 April 2012 the President of the Constitutional Court notified the applicant that he and four other judges (Bu., Sn., S. and W.) would sit on 15 May. Eight days later the applicant challenged the entire bench for bias. He alleged that all five judges had previously rendered arbitrary decisions against him, that the court was subject to executive influence and discriminated against foreigners, and that individual members were compromised by personal friendship with the court’s Vice-President (F.H.’s brother), by government consultancy work, by academic writings on judicial tenure, by membership of a state-owned company’s board, and by professional links to lawyers involved in related litigation.

On 15 May 2012 the same five judges dismissed the recusal applications. They stated that each challenged judge had withdrawn from the deliberation on his own recusal, leaving the remaining four to decide. They held that prior rulings against the applicant, five-year renewable terms of office, collegial relations with the Vice-President, and the other personal or professional connections did not give rise to objectively justified doubts as to impartiality.

The same day the Constitutional Court delivered its judgment on the merits. It accepted that the two-year-three-month inactivity at first instance violated the reasonable-time requirement of Article 6 § 1 and of the Liechtenstein Constitution, even though the overall duration of seven years was not itself excessive given the applicant’s interlocutory manoeuvres and the complexity of the evidence. Finding a legislative gap as to the consequences of such a violation, the court filled it by awarding limited costs relief: reimbursement of the CHF 170 complaint fee, exemption from the CHF 1 700 judgment fee, and payment of the opponent’s lawyers’ fees of CHF 2 694.40. All remaining complaints—property rights, judicial independence and alleged discrimination—were dismissed.

These events form the factual core of the three complaints declared admissible: the procedure by which the challenged judges themselves disposed of the recusal applications; the overall length of the civil action from June 2005 until service of the Constitutional Court’s judgment on 27 June 2012; and the alleged absence of any effective domestic remedy capable of either preventing or adequately redressing delay.

**CASE OF A.K. v. LIECHTENSTEIN (No. 2) (Application no. 10722/13)**

The applicant, A.K. (a German national living in Switzerland), alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 ECHR (impartial tribunal and reasonable-time requirement) and Article 13 ECHR (effective remedy for delay) arising from lengthy Liechtenstein civil proceedings over ownership of bearer shares and from the Constitutional Court’s handling of his related bias complaints.

Since 2004, A.K. and F.H. had disputed ownership of 75% of the bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies (EMK and EMK Engineering). In June 2005 F.H. sued A.K. in the Regional Court seeking handover of the shares and a declaration that A.K. had never owned them. A.K. challenged jurisdiction; this was rejected in July 2005, with the appeal dismissed in February 2006. A.K.’s subsequent constitutional complaint (with suspensory effect) was dismissed in March 2007 after nearly two years of interlocutory proceedings.

The Regional Court then held hearings in May–September 2007 but did not deliver judgment until 28 December 2009 (over two years and three months later), despite A.K.’s April 2009 request. It found for F.H., holding that A.K. had not acquired good-faith title. The Court of Appeal dismissed A.K.’s appeal in May 2010; the Supreme Court rejected his further appeal in January 2011. Total duration from the 2005 action to the Supreme Court decision was nearly six years.

On 18 February 2011 A.K. lodged an 80-page constitutional complaint alleging (inter alia) excessive length, lack of an effective acceleration remedy, and other Convention breaches. The Constitutional Court President granted suspensory effect. In April 2012 the President (Judge B.) named a five-judge bench (himself plus Judges Bu., Sn., S. and W.) to decide the case in camera on 15 May 2012. A.K. immediately challenged all five for bias. He cited their prior rulings against him, alleged executive influence and anti-foreigner discrimination, and specific ties: Judge B.’s delay in assigning the case and close friendship with Vice-President H. (F.H.’s brother); Judge Bu.’s government work and collaboration with H.; Judge Sn.’s academic views on judicial tenure; Judge S.’s role on a state-owned company’s board; and Judge W.’s law-firm links to A.K.’s inheritance opponent, to the companies, and to H.’s former firm.

On 15 May 2012 the same five judges dismissed the bias challenges. Each judge recused himself only from the decision concerning himself, leaving the other four to rule. They held that prior adverse decisions, five-year renewable terms, professional/government work, and friendships or collaboration with H. did not create objectively justified doubts as to impartiality, and that A.K. had not shown executive influence.

The same day the Court partly allowed the constitutional complaint. It found a breach of the reasonable-time guarantee under Article 6 § 1 and the Liechtenstein Constitution solely because of the Regional Court’s 27-month inactivity after the last hearing; other periods (including A.K.’s own interlocutory challenges) were justifiable given the case’s complexity. Liechtenstein law contained no explicit remedy for delay, so the Court filled the gap by ordering the State to reimburse A.K.’s lodging fee (CHF 170) and to bear remaining court costs (including the CHF 1,700 judgment fee) as compensation; it also ordered the State to pay F.H.’s Constitutional Court lawyers’ fees (CHF 2,694.40). All other complaints (including property-rights and independence arguments) were rejected; H. had not sat on any relevant bench.

A.K. argued these mechanisms, and the recusal procedure, were inadequate. The ECtHR application focused on whether the Constitutional Court’s composition and self-judging of bias complaints satisfied objective impartiality, whether the overall length (including Constitutional Court delay) was reasonable, and whether an effective length-of-proceedings remedy existed.

The case of A.K. v. Liechtenstein (No. 2) (Application no. 10722/13) was brought by a German national residing in Switzerland against Liechtenstein. The applicant alleged that the Constitutional Court judges were partial, particularly due to the procedure used to examine his bias complaints, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 10 June 2005 F.H. sued in the Regional Court for delivery of the shares and a declaration that the applicant had never owned them. The applicant challenged jurisdiction. The Regional Court rejected the challenge on 15 July 2005; the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 1 February 2006. A constitutional complaint produced a stay of proceedings until the Constitutional Court dismissed it on 27 March 2007.

The Regional Court then heard the parties, counsel and twelve witnesses on 31 May, 28 June and 6 September 2007 and examined extensive documentary evidence. After the applicant requested judgment on 22 April 2009, the court delivered a 66-page decision on 28 December 2009 upholding F.H.’s claims. It found the applicant’s mother had never acquired title and that the applicant lacked good faith.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 27 May 2010, rejecting late evidence as an attempt to delay. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 13 January 2011.

On 18 February 2011 the applicant lodged an 80-page constitutional complaint alleging, among other things, excessive length (then nearly six years) of proceedings that affected his livelihood, and the absence of any remedy to accelerate them. The President granted suspensory effect. On 20 April 2012 the applicant was notified that President B. and Judges Bu., Sn., S. and W. would decide the case in camera on 15 May 2012.

On 8 May 2012 the applicant challenged all five judges for bias. He cited their prior rulings against him, alleged executive influence, and specific ties: President B. was a close friend of Vice-President H. (F.H.’s brother); Judge Bu. produced government expert reports and worked regularly with H.; Judge Sn. was a university professor who had written on judicial tenure; Judge S. sat on a state-owned company’s board; and Judge W. practised with lawyers previously involved against the applicant or with H.

On 15 May 2012 the same five-judge bench dismissed the bias challenges. Each challenged judge abstained from the vote on his own impartiality, which was decided by the remaining four. The court held that prior adverse rulings, five-year terms, professional associations with H., and the other alleged connections did not create objectively justified doubts as to impartiality.

The same day the Constitutional Court partially allowed the complaint. It found a violation of the reasonable-time guarantee because of a two-year-three-month period of inactivity after the last first-instance hearing, notwithstanding the case’s complexity and the almost two years consumed by the applicant’s own interlocutory jurisdictional proceedings. Liechtenstein law contained no express consequences for such a breach; the court therefore filled the gap by ordering the State to reimburse the applicant’s CHF 170 lodging fee, to bear the CHF 1,700 judgment fee, and to pay F.H.’s lawyer’s fees of CHF 2,694.40. All remaining complaints, including those concerning property rights and judicial independence, were rejected.

Domestic law provided for supervisory complaints about delay (Court Organisation Act) and official-liability actions, while the Constitutional Court Act regulated recusal and composition. The court’s own case-law treated a finding of delay plus cost-shifting as sufficient redress. The judgment became final on 18 May 2016.

The case of Aleksandr Andreyev v. Russia (Application no. 2281/06) concerns a 17-year-old Russian national who alleged, under the European Convention on Human Rights, that he was unlawfully deprived of liberty and ill-treated while in police custody on 15 February 2005, and that no effective investigation followed.

Andreyev received a summons to appear at 11 a.m. at the Sovetskiy district police department in Orsk. He arrived with his father and a friend. Investigator K. was absent; officer M. took Andreyev to an office. After the father completed an investigative measure, he could not locate his son. Police told the father and friend to leave. They waited until about 7 p.m. before being informed Andreyev had left. Subsequent inquiries indicated he had gone to police station no. 2 with officer Sh. and remained until 8 p.m. Station logs recorded Andreyev leaving the first station at 3:20 p.m.

Andreyev stated that Sh. took him to an experts’ room for photographing and fingerprinting, then via a back exit to station no. 2. There, department head P. and officer E. questioned him about shop thefts. After he denied involvement, E. shackled his hands behind his back, forced him to sit with legs crossed, tied his legs with a rope, looped it around his neck, and pulled it taut over a chair, causing severe back pain. Officer K. later demanded a confession. Fearing further abuse, Andreyev ran and struck his head against a glass bookcase door, sustaining cuts above his left eyebrow and on his scalp. E. then bound his hands and legs, passed a metal bar under the bindings, and hung him between a table and chair for about eight minutes. After being untied, Andreyev began writing a confession under pressure. Lawyer S. arrived and offered representation, which Andreyev declined. An ambulance (called after the glass incident) provided first aid. Two other (allegedly intoxicated) officers then struck him on the ears and punched his head. He was hung again until officer B. untied him and insisted he finish the confession. Andreyev complied and was released; he walked home, arriving around 9:40 p.m.

He was hospitalised at 11:05 p.m. with headache, nausea, vomiting and dizziness. Records noted an abrasion over the left eyebrow, scalp bruises and concussion; he remained an in-patient until 4 March. Police records showed E. documenting Andreyev’s “conveyance” at 7 p.m. “for examination,” a search in the presence of witnesses, and notification of rights as an administrative “violator.”

The hospital alerted police the same evening. The Sovetskiy district prosecutor’s office received complaints from Andreyev’s father on 21 February and 4 March. Investigator B. conducted a preliminary inquiry, collecting statements. Officers and witnesses claimed Andreyev had been at the first station only until 3:20 p.m. for an identity parade, was later brought to station no. 2 on theft suspicion, and had self-inflicted the head injuries by striking the bookcase. Lawyer S. confirmed seeing blood but said Andreyev attributed it to the bookcase. Ambulance staff noted facial cuts but no other visible injuries or obvious concussion. Hospital roommates later recounted Andreyev describing being hung and beaten. A forensic expert found the injuries (concussion, eyebrow wound, scalp bruises) caused by hard blunt objects shortly before hospitalisation, constituting light health damage; concussion could have resulted from either the bookcase or punches.

On 17 March 2005 investigator B. refused to open a criminal case, citing no elements of abuse of power, unlawful detention or coercion. A deputy prosecutor quashed the decision as incomplete. After further statements, B. again refused on 24 March, concluding the injuries were self-inflicted and the allegations unfounded. Andreyev’s father challenged the refusal under Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Sovetskiy District Court dismissed the appeal on 20 May 2005, finding the inquiry thorough and impartial. The Orenburg Regional Court upheld this on 16 June 2005, noting Andreyev had not been arrested as a criminal suspect.

These facts formed the basis of the claims of arbitrary detention, police ill-treatment and inadequate investigation.
