001-160863:
The case of Elena Apostol and Others v. Romania (applications nos. 24093/14 and 16 others) concerns 17 Romanian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 2 of the Convention due to the lack of an effective investigation into the deaths of their relatives during the violent suppression of anti-government protests in December 1989.

The events unfolded after President Nicolae Ceaușescu ordered military operations against demonstrators starting on 17 December 1989 in Timișoara, then spreading to Bucharest, Reșița, Brașov and other cities. Official documents later recorded more than 1,200 deaths, over 5,000 injuries, and thousands of unlawful detentions and instances of ill-treatment. Thousands of servicemen, supported by tanks and armed vehicles, deployed substantial quantities of ammunition against civilians between 17 and 30 December.

Most applicants lost relatives who were shot in Bucharest; one applicant’s husband was killed in Reșița and another’s son in Brașov. Military prosecutors opened investigations in 1990 into the use of lethal force and related offences. The principal file (originally 97/P/1990, later 11/P/2014) remained the main vehicle for examining violence against civilian demonstrators both before and after Ceaușescu’s overthrow.

The investigation was repeatedly interrupted. In October 2010 the military prosecutor’s office decided not to prosecute, holding that parts of the case were statute-barred and the remainder ill-founded; civilian aspects were severed and transferred. That decision was set aside in April 2011 because the inquiry was incomplete and not all victims or perpetrators had been identified. Jurisdiction then oscillated between military and civilian prosecutors. After classified documents were released in 2010 the case was re-registered in 2012. The new Code of Criminal Procedure, which entered into force in February 2014, returned the file to military prosecutors on the ground that they must investigate offences committed by military personnel. On 14 October 2015 the prosecuting authorities discontinued the proceedings. No information was provided on whether that decision was appealed.

Domestic law treats military judges and prosecutors as part of the ordinary judiciary, granting them formal independence and stability of tenure. Nevertheless, their appointment, ranking and promotion require the assent of the Ministry of Defence, and they retain military status. These features raised persistent doubts about institutional and hierarchical independence when investigating members of the armed forces. The Committee of Ministers, supervising earlier related judgments, invited Romania to assess the implications of those doubts and to ensure fuller cooperation from bodies holding relevant information.

The combination of extreme delay (more than 25 years), repeated discontinuances, jurisdictional transfers, and questions over the independence of the investigating authorities formed the core factual matrix of the alleged procedural violation of the right to life.

**Case Summary: Elena Apostol and Others v. Romania (Applications nos. 24093/14 et al., ECHR Fourth Section, Judgment of 23 February 2016)**

This case comprises 17 applications by Romanian nationals whose relatives were killed during the violent suppression of anti-government demonstrations in December 1989. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to life), specifically the State's procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation into those deaths. (Other complaints were declared inadmissible.)

The events began on 17 December 1989 after protests against Nicolae Ceaușescu's regime. On presidential orders, military operations were launched in Timișoara and subsequently in Bucharest, Reșița, Brașov and other cities. Over 1,200 people were killed, more than 5,000 injured, and thousands unlawfully detained and ill-treated. Thousands of servicemen, using tanks, armed vehicles and large quantities of ammunition, were deployed against civilian demonstrators between 17 and 30 December 1989. The applicants' relatives were shot dead during this period, primarily in Bucharest; one relative died in Reșița and another in Brașov.

Military prosecutors opened investigations in 1990 in several cities into the use of force and unlawful detentions. The principal file (originally 97/P/1990, later 11/P/2014) addressed violence against civilians both before and after Ceaușescu's overthrow. The investigation remained pending for more than 25 years, with repeated jurisdictional transfers between military and civilian prosecutors, incomplete inquiries, and incomplete identification of victims and perpetrators. Key developments after 2009 included a 18 October 2010 decision by the military prosecutor's office at the High Court of Cassation and Justice not to prosecute military personnel (partly on statute-of-limitations grounds and partly as ill-founded). This was set aside on 15 April 2011 because the investigation was unfinished. Jurisdiction then shifted to civilian prosecutors, the case was re-registered in 2012 after declassification of documents, and it returned to military prosecutors after the 2014 Code of Criminal Procedure took effect. On 14 October 2015 the proceedings were discontinued; no information on any appeal was provided.

The applicants contended that this protracted process failed to meet Convention standards of promptness, thoroughness, independence and effectiveness. Structural concerns included the status of military prosecutors, who investigate military personnel yet are appointed with Ministry of Defence involvement and operate within a military framework, raising questions of hierarchical independence (as previously noted by the Court and the Committee of Ministers in related cases such as Association “21 December 1989” and Others v. Romania). The investigation's length, multiple discontinuations or transfers, and failure to produce a conclusive outcome regarding the deaths formed the core of the alleged violation. The facts thus centre on the 1989 killings of the applicants' relatives by State forces and the subsequent decades-long, inconclusive domestic inquiry.

The case of Elena Apostol and Others v. Romania (applications nos. 24093/14 and 16 others) was brought by 17 Romanian nationals whose relatives were killed during the violent suppression of anti-government demonstrations in December 1989. The applicants complained under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) of the lack of an effective official investigation into those deaths.

The background events, which occurred mainly between 17 and 30 December 1989, involved military operations ordered by President Nicolae Ceaușescu against civilian protesters in Timișoara, Bucharest, Reșița, Brașov and other cities. Official records later indicated more than 1,200 deaths, over 5,000 injuries and thousands of unlawful detentions and instances of ill-treatment. Thousands of troops, tanks and armed vehicles were deployed and large quantities of ammunition were used against demonstrators. The applicants’ relatives were among those shot dead, principally in Bucharest (with two exceptions, in Reșița and Brașov).

Military prosecutors opened investigations in 1990 in several cities into the use of lethal force and related abuses. The principal file (originally 97/P/1990, later 11/P/2014) concerned violence against civilians both before and after Ceaușescu’s overthrow. Despite the passage of more than two decades, the inquiry remained incomplete. On 18 October 2010 the military prosecutor’s office decided not to prosecute members of the armed forces, holding parts of the complaints statute-barred and others unfounded, while transferring the civilian aspects of the case. That decision was set aside on 15 April 2011 because the investigation had not identified all victims and perpetrators. Jurisdiction then passed to the civilian prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice. After previously classified material was released in 2010 the file was re-registered in March 2012. The entry into force of a new Code of Criminal Procedure in 2014 returned the case to military prosecutors. On 14 October 2015 the proceedings were discontinued; no information was provided about any appeal.

Domestic legislation applicable to military prosecutors (Laws nos. 303/2004 and 304/2004 and the 2014 joint regulation on appointments) placed their appointment, transfer and promotion under the joint authority of the High Council of the Judiciary and the Ministry of Defence, requiring the latter’s assent after medical, physical and psychological assessments. The new Code of Criminal Procedure also reserved investigation of offences committed by military personnel exclusively to military prosecutors. These arrangements raised structural questions about institutional and hierarchical independence when the persons under investigation belonged to the armed forces.

The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, supervising execution of an earlier related judgment, had already invited Romania to assess the implications of those independence concerns and to ensure full cooperation by bodies holding relevant information.

Taken together, the facts show an investigation that lasted more than 25 years, was repeatedly transferred between military and civilian authorities, failed to identify all those responsible, and was ultimately terminated without any person being held accountable. The combination of excessive delay, incomplete inquiries and doubts about the independence of the investigating authorities formed the core of the alleged violation of the procedural limb of Article 2.
001-160621:
The case originated in an application against Russia by Magomed Dalakov, uncle of Apti Dalakov (born 1986). The applicant alleged that State agents killed his nephew during a special operation on 2 September 2007 in Karabulak, Ingushetia, and that the authorities failed to investigate the death effectively, in violation of Article 2 of the Convention.

The circumstances of the killing were disputed. According to the applicant, Apti Dalakov and his friend I.D. left a computer club around 5 p.m. Armed men (some in camouflage and balaclavas, others in civilian clothes) emerged from two unmarked Gazel minivans with tinted windows, pointed weapons at them without identifying themselves, and opened fire. Apti ran; he was struck by a car in Dzhabagiyeva Street, limped into a nursery-school courtyard, and was shot several times—including after he had fallen face-down—by pursuers. One of the men then placed an object (later identified as a grenade with its pin pulled) under the body. Local police and OMON officers arrived to find a crowd insisting Apti had been unarmed and had offered no resistance. The pursuers, later identified as FSB officers, refused to identify themselves; a scuffle ensued, they were briefly detained, and they were released without their identities being logged after senior officials intervened. Apti’s body was returned for burial that night. These accounts were supported by statements from local residents who witnessed parts of the chase, shooting, and aftermath.

The Government, relying on the investigation file, stated that FSB officers attempting to detain Apti and I.D. as suspected members of an illegal armed group identified themselves and ordered the pair to the ground. I.D. complied; Apti fled. After warnings, including a shot in the air, Apti stopped, produced a grenade and prepared to pull the pin. An FSB officer then shot him to neutralize the threat to life. I.D. was detained briefly and later left for Kazakhstan.

A criminal case was opened the same day against Apti for assaulting a law-enforcement official and unlawful possession of arms. The crime-scene examination recovered 40 cartridge cases and a grenade under the body (none in Apti’s hands). An internal police inquiry noted that the FSB operation had not been coordinated with local police, that the FSB officers had refused to identify themselves and had behaved aggressively, and that residents claimed the grenade had been planted. Forensic examination found Apti had died from gunshot wounds, including two in the back and one in the back of the head. Several local witnesses and OMON officers described an unarmed, non-resistant victim and FSB refusal to identify themselves. FSB officers, questioned weeks later and granted victim status, maintained they had identified themselves, that Apti had fled and produced a grenade, and that the grenade was found in his hand.

The investigation against Apti was terminated three times on account of his death, with decisions repeatedly overruled as incomplete: I.D. and the shooter had not been questioned, legal grounds for the use of lethal force had not been examined, and the planting allegation had not been probed. The firearms-use material was transferred to military investigators, who refused to open a case against the shooter on the basis of his statement that he had fired only after Apti produced the grenade. The applicant repeatedly complained that no investigation into the killing itself had been opened, that civilian eyewitnesses had not been interviewed, and that he had not been granted victim status. His Article 125 CCrP complaint to the district court was rejected; he disputed whether a proper hearing had occurred and whether he had been notified. No criminal proceedings against the FSB officers were ever instituted.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that the use of lethal force had been unjustified and that the subsequent investigation had been neither independent nor effective.

The case of Dalakov v. Russia originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 May 2009 by Magomed Dalakov, a Russian national born in 1933 and living in Karabulak, Ingushetia. He is the uncle of Apti Dalakov (born 1986), whose parents and brother had died in a 1998 car accident. The applicant alleged that State agents killed his nephew during a special operation on 2 September 2007 and that the authorities failed to investigate the death effectively, raising issues under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life).

The circumstances of Apti Dalakov’s death are disputed. According to the applicant, at about 5 p.m. on 2 September 2007 Apti and his friend I.D. left a computer club and were walking along Oskanova Street when two unmarked Gazel minivans with tinted windows stopped. Armed men (some in camouflage and balaclavas, others in plain clothes) emerged, pointed weapons at the pair without identifying themselves, and opened fire. Apti fled and was pursued. In Dzhabagiyeva Street he was struck by a car, fell, rose and limped into a nursery-school courtyard. A man from the car shot him with a pistol; other armed men then fired several more rounds while he lay face-down. One placed an object (later identified as a grenade with its pin pulled) under the body. Local police and OMON officers arrived to find a crowd of residents insisting that Apti had been unarmed and had offered no resistance. The armed men (Ingushetia FSB officers) refused to identify themselves; a scuffle ensued and they were arrested, though later released without their names being logged. I.D. was briefly detained and then released. Apti’s body was examined and returned to relatives that night. The account is supported by statements from nearby residents.

The Government, relying on the investigation file, stated that FSB officers had identified Apti and I.D. as members of an illegal armed group. They alighted from their vehicle, identified themselves as FSB and ordered the pair to the ground. I.D. complied; Apti ran. During the chase an officer warned that he would fire. Apti stopped, produced a grenade and prepared to pull the pin. The officer, perceiving an imminent threat, shot to kill. I.D. was arrested, questioned and later left for Kazakhstan.

A criminal case (no. 27520028) was opened the same day against Apti for assault on a law-enforcement officer and unlawful possession of arms. Forty cartridge cases and a grenade (found under the body, nothing in Apti’s hands) were recovered. An internal inquiry noted that local police had not been informed of the operation, that residents claimed the grenade had been planted, and that a confrontation had occurred because the FSB officers refused to identify themselves. Forensic examination established that Apti died from gunshot wounds (two to the back, one to the back of the lower leg and one to the back of the head). Several local witnesses and police officers described an unarmed young man being pursued and shot; FSB officers later gave consistent accounts of a warning, a grenade and necessary lethal force. They were granted victim status.

The investigation against Apti was repeatedly terminated on the ground of his death (2 November 2007, 3 January 2008, 6 February 2008) and equally repeatedly reopened because key witnesses (including I.D. and the shooter) had not been questioned, the legal basis for the use of firearms had not been examined and the planting allegation had not been investigated. Material concerning the shooting was sent to a military investigator, who on 30 January 2008 refused to open a case, finding no corpus delicti. No criminal proceedings were ever instituted against the FSB officers.

The applicant lodged multiple complaints seeking an investigation into the killing and victim status. On 14 August 2008 he applied to the Karabulak District Court under Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, complaining of inaction. The court rejected the complaint on 23 September 2008 as unsubstantiated. The applicant disputed whether a proper hearing had occurred and whether he had been notified of the decision. No further investigative steps were taken.

These facts form the core of the alleged substantive violation (unjustified lethal force by State agents against an unarmed man) and the alleged procedural violation (a series of incomplete, repeatedly terminated inquiries that never examined the use of force or the planting claim, together with the domestic court’s failure to compel an effective investigation).

The case of Dalakov v. Russia concerns the killing of the applicant’s nephew, Apti Dalakov (born 1986), on 2 September 2007 in Karabulak, Ingushetia, and the subsequent failure to investigate it. Apti’s parents and brother had died in a 1998 car accident; the applicant, his uncle, lived in the same town.

The parties dispute the circumstances. According to the applicant, Apti and his friend I.D. left a computer club around 5 p.m. Unidentified armed men (some in camouflage and balaclavas, others in civilian clothes) emerged from two unmarked, tinted Gazel minivans, pointed weapons at them without identifying themselves, and opened fire. Apti fled. He was struck by a car on Dzhabagiyeva Street, limped into a nursery-school courtyard, and was shot several times on the ground by the pursuers (later identified as Ingushetia FSB officers). One officer then placed an object (a pin-pulled grenade) under the body. Local police and OMON arrived; residents told them Apti had been unarmed and offered no resistance. The FSB officers refused to identify themselves, leading to a scuffle in which police arrested them and I.D. (later released). The grenade was deactivated and Apti’s body returned after a post-mortem showing gunshot wounds to the back, leg and head.

The Government’s account, drawn from the investigation file, is that FSB officers conducting a special operation to detain suspected members of an illegal armed group identified themselves, ordered the pair to the ground, and fired only after Apti fled, ignored warnings, and prepared to use a grenade, posing an imminent threat.

A criminal case (no. 27520028) was opened the same day against Apti for assaulting a law-enforcement officer and unlawful possession of arms. The crime-scene examination recovered 40 cartridge cases and the grenade under the body (none in Apti’s hands). An internal Interior Ministry inquiry found the FSB had not coordinated with local police; the latter initially mistook the FSB for terrorists, disarmed them amid an angry crowd claiming the grenade had been planted, and released them without logging identities after the FSB and Interior ministers intervened.

Witness statements from nearby residents and arriving police/OMON officers largely described a crowd alleging an unarmed man had been shot and a grenade planted; FSB officers refused identification and threatened police. Forensic examination showed the grenade’s fuse was incomplete but the device itself viable. FSB officers (granted victim status) later claimed they had identified themselves, Apti had fled and produced a grenade, and they had then fired. I.D. was not questioned (he left for Kazakhstan).

The investigation against Apti was terminated three times (November 2007, January 2008, February 2008) on grounds of his death, each time relying on FSB statements and finding sufficient evidence of his guilt. These decisions were repeatedly quashed as premature: I.D. and the shooting officer had not been questioned, the legal basis for lethal force had not been examined, and the planted-grenade allegation had been ignored. Materials on the use of force were transferred to military investigators, who in January 2008 refused to open a case against the FSB shooter for lack of corpus delicti. No investigation into the killing itself was ever opened.

The applicant repeatedly complained to prosecutors and investigators from September 2007 onward, requesting a case into the killing, witness interviews (including police/OMON who arrested the FSB team), and victim status; he received no adequate response. In August 2008 he applied to the Karabulak District Court under Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, alleging investigative inaction. After hearings marked by disputed attendance and notification, the court rejected the complaint in September 2008, holding that the FSB’s actions had been lawful and no further witnesses existed. The applicant alleged the decision was backdated and never properly served. No further effective domestic investigation occurred.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) concerning both the alleged unjustified use of lethal force by State agents and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation.
001-161048:
The case of Y.Y. v. Russia (Application no. 40378/06) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to respect for her private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Russian national born in 1966 and resident in St Petersburg, claimed that public health authorities obtained, examined and disclosed her confidential medical information and that of her newborn twins without her consent.

In April 2003 the applicant gave birth prematurely to twins at a St Petersburg maternity hospital. One twin, a girl, died nine hours after birth. The surviving twin, a boy, was transferred to a children’s hospital resuscitation unit twenty hours after birth. The applicant believed prompt transfer of the girl would have saved her life.

The applicant’s mother, Mrs D., sent three telegrams to the President of the Russian Federation in May, June and August 2003. She complained of fatal delays caused by waiting lists for neonatal resuscitation, described the twins’ cases, and demanded official action. The Presidential Administration forwarded the telegrams to the Ministry of Healthcare. The Ministry instructed the St Petersburg Committee for Healthcare to investigate.

The Committee convened a two-member expert panel (the city’s chief neonatologist and a paediatrics professor). Without notifying or obtaining consent from the applicant, the panel obtained the full medical records of the applicant and both twins from the maternity and children’s hospitals. The resulting report, dated September 2003, concentrated on the deceased infant. It recorded that the girl had been born at 31 weeks’ gestation as the product of the applicant’s eighth pregnancy and first delivery, noted possible prenatal viral infection, and diagnosed severe respiratory distress syndrome with atelectasis. A post-mortem finding of interstitial emphysema was identified as the immediate cause of death. The experts concluded that the treatment given had been appropriate given an 80 per cent mortality risk and that earlier transfer would not have guaranteed survival. The surviving twin’s milder respiratory problems were mentioned only briefly.

On 5 September 2003 the Committee sent the report to the Ministry. On 12 September it informed Mrs D. of the conclusions and, in a separate letter to the Ministry, added that a hospital commission had attributed the premature delivery to the applicant’s obstetric history (seven prior abortions) and urogenital mycoplasmosis. The applicant herself received a similar summary letter only on 3 December 2003. After further litigation she obtained the full report and covering letter on 30 November 2004.

On 25 February 2005 the applicant sued the Committee in the Kuybyshevskiy District Court. She argued that the collection, examination and onward transmission of her and her children’s medical data without consent violated Article 61 of the Basic Principles of Public Health Law, which treats such information as confidential and lists exhaustive exceptions (none of which, she said, applied). She also relied on constitutional guarantees of privacy and family confidentiality.

The District Court dismissed the claim on 14 December 2005. It held that the Ministry had lawfully requested information, that the Committee had a corresponding duty to respond, that the records had been reviewed only by doctors bound by professional secrecy, and that only the experts’ report (not the raw records) had been forwarded. The court further considered the action time-barred because the applicant had learned of the examination in December 2003. The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment on 14 March 2006, endorsing the lower court’s reasoning in full.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that the unauthorised handling of highly sensitive medical data constituted an unjustified interference with her private life.

The case of Y.Y. v. Russia (Application no. 40378/06) concerned an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention, arising from the unauthorised collection, examination and disclosure of her confidential medical data (and that of her newborn twins) by public health authorities.

In April 2003 the applicant, a Russian national born in 1966 and resident in St Petersburg, gave birth prematurely (at 31 weeks) to twins at a local maternity hospital. The daughter died nine hours later; the son was transferred to a children’s hospital resuscitation unit after 20 hours and survived. The applicant believed prompt transfer might have saved her daughter.

The applicant’s mother, Mrs D., sent three telegrams to the Russian President (25 May, 15 June and 1 August 2003) alleging that delays and “waiting lists” for neonatal resuscitation had caused the infant’s death and constituted criminal negligence. The President’s Administration forwarded the complaints to the Ministry of Healthcare, which instructed the St Petersburg City Administration’s Committee for Healthcare to investigate.

The Committee convened a two-member expert panel (its chief neonatologist and a paediatrics professor). Without the applicant’s knowledge or consent, the panel obtained and reviewed the full medical records of the applicant and both twins from the two hospitals. Its report concentrated on the deceased infant: it recorded the applicant’s obstetric history (eighth pregnancy, first delivery, seven prior abortions, urogenital mycoplasmosis), diagnosed severe respiratory-distress syndrome with air-leak complications, and concluded that the treatment given had been appropriate given an 80 % mortality risk; earlier transfer would not have guaranteed survival. Limited observations were made about the surviving twin.

On 5 September 2003 the Committee transmitted the full report to the Ministry. On 12 September it sent Mrs D. a summary of the conclusions and separately informed the Ministry that the applicant’s abortions and infection had caused the premature birth. On 3 December 2003 the Committee sent the applicant a similar letter revealing that the children’s records had been examined. After separate litigation she obtained the report itself only on 30 November 2004.

On 25 February 2005 the applicant sued the Committee in the Kuybyshevskiy District Court, seeking a declaration that the collection, examination and onward transmission of the medical data (including highly sensitive details of her reproductive history) without her consent violated Article 61 of the 1993 Basic Principles of Public Health Law. That provision treated all information about a patient’s request for treatment, diagnosis or health status as confidential medical data that could not be disclosed except in an exhaustive list of statutory situations (none of which, she argued, applied). She also invoked the constitutional guarantees of privacy and data-protection (Articles 23 and 24). She stressed that she had never requested any review of the quality of care or the cause of death and that the information had been circulated to an unknown number of officials in two public bodies.

The District Court dismissed the claim on 14 December 2005. It held that the Ministry was entitled to request, and the Committee obliged to supply, the information needed to answer the presidential complaints; the records had been seen only by doctors bound by professional secrecy; and only the report, not the raw records, had been sent onwards. The court additionally found the action time-barred, calculating the three-month limitation period from 3 December 2003. The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment in full on 14 March 2006.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that public authorities had systematically interfered with her medical confidentiality in a manner not “in accordance with the law” and not necessary in a democratic society.

The case of Y.Y. v. Russia (Application no. 40378/06) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to respect for private life under the European Convention on Human Rights, arising from the unauthorised collection, examination and disclosure of her confidential medical data (and that of her newborn twins) by Russian public health authorities.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1966 and resident in St Petersburg, gave birth prematurely to twins in April 2003 at a local maternity hospital. The first twin died nine hours after birth; the second, transferred after twenty hours to a children’s hospital intensive-care unit, survived. The applicant believed the deceased infant would have lived had transfer occurred sooner. Her mother, Mrs D., sent three telegrams (25 May, 15 June and 1 August 2003) to the President of the Russian Federation complaining of fatal delays caused by waiting lists for neonatal resuscitation and demanding official action.

The President’s Administration forwarded the telegrams to the Ministry of Healthcare, which instructed the St Petersburg Committee for Healthcare to investigate. The Committee assembled a panel (the city’s chief neonatologist and a paediatrics professor) that obtained and reviewed the full medical records of the applicant and both twins from the two hospitals. The resulting expert report of September 2003 focused on the deceased infant, recording her premature birth at 31 weeks of an eighth pregnancy (first delivery), possible prenatal viral infection, respiratory-distress syndrome, atelectasis and post-mortem interstitial emphysema. It concluded that treatment had been entirely appropriate given an 80 % mortality risk and that earlier transfer would not have guaranteed survival. The surviving twin’s milder distress was noted without criticism of care.

On 5 September 2003 the Committee transmitted the report to the Ministry. On 12 September it summarised the findings to Mrs D. and, in a separate letter to the Ministry, added that a hospital commission had attributed the premature delivery to the applicant’s obstetric history—specifically seven prior artificial abortions and urogenital mycoplasmosis. The applicant received a comparable letter on 3 December 2003. After further proceedings she obtained copies of the report and the 5 September letter on 30 November 2004.

On 25 February 2005 she sued the Committee, seeking a declaration that its actions were unlawful. She argued that the records had been collected and examined, and the report containing her intimate medical data forwarded to the Ministry, without her consent, contrary to Article 61 of the Basic Principles of Public Health Law (then in force). That provision classified all information about requests for treatment, diagnoses and examination results as confidential medical data whose disclosure was prohibited except in exhaustively listed circumstances (none of which, she contended, applied). She further claimed the information had been seen by numerous officials at both the Committee and the Ministry.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court dismissed the claim on 14 December 2005. It held that the Ministry had lawfully requested information and the Committee had a corresponding duty to supply it; the records had been reviewed only by doctors bound by professional secrecy; and only the report, not the raw records, had been transmitted. The court also found the action time-barred, the applicant having known of the records’ use since December 2003. The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment in full on 14 March 2006.

Domestic law invoked included Articles 23 and 24 of the Russian Constitution (inviolability of private life and prohibition on collecting or disseminating private information without consent) and the Constitutional Court’s confirmation that Article 61 established a closed list of exceptions. Regulations governing both the Ministry and the Committee authorised them to examine citizens’ complaints and to obtain necessary documents, while a 1996 order on quality-control reviews made examination of medical records compulsory in cases of neonatal death.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference: state authorities accessed and circulated highly sensitive personal medical information in response to a third-party complaint, without the data subject’s knowledge or consent and outside the statutory exceptions.
001-161373:
The case of Ciorap v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 5) (Application no. 7232/07) originated in a 2006 application by Tudor Ciorap, a Moldovan national born in 1965 then serving an 11-year sentence in Chișinău Prison no. 13. He alleged ill-treatment in detention contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, an ineffective investigation of that complaint, and lack of an effective remedy. The Court communicated those complaints in 2013.

Ciorap, who had a personality disorder and Category 2 disability, occupied cell no. 20 (reserved for mentally ill detainees) with five others, three of them also disabled. Around 3 p.m. on 28 October 2006, several men—some masked, armed with rubber truncheons and metal shields, from the Pantera special forces—entered to search for prohibited items. They ordered the occupants out. The applicant claimed they shouted insults, hit and pushed the detainees. The Government denied any force or improper conduct. Detainees stood facing the wall in the corridor for about 30 minutes while the search took place; one officer filmed it.

Ordered back inside, Ciorap saw possessions (including relatives’ food, medication and documents) scattered in disorder. He refused to re-enter until a prosecutor or prison official documented the search. He alleged he was then hit, thrown to the floor, kicked in the stomach and had the cell door slammed on his foot, causing intense pain; a masked man smashed his reading glasses. The Government maintained that no force was used and the cell remained orderly.

Around 7 p.m. Ciorap was taken by ambulance to hospital. A doctor diagnosed contusion of the soft tissues of the right ankle and a suspected fracture; the foot was plastered. A 28 November 2006 examination confirmed a broken bone and a haematoma consistent with violence causing health problems lasting over 21 days. Later forensic reports (December 2006, May 2007) supported an injury to the right foot according to the applicant; the Government cited a 31 October 2007 report finding no conclusive evidence of a fracture. Full copies of the later reports were not submitted.

On 31 October 2006 Ciorap and four cellmates complained to the Prosecutor General, military prosecutor and other authorities. A Chișinău Military Prosecutor declined to open a criminal investigation on 6 December 2006, but a Chișinău Prosecutor started one on 8 December. Between late November and early December 2007 several Pantera members who participated in the 28 October action were charged with exceeding their powers by using excessive force.

On 15 February 2008 the investigation was discontinued. The prosecutor found that Ciorap had disobeyed lawful orders, acted provocatively and refused to return to the cell, so force was required; self-infliction of injury could not be excluded. Detainee witnesses (S.B., A.G., V.Z., B.I.) corroborated insults, truncheon blows, disorder and the slamming of the door on Ciorap’s foot; they described the video as selective, short (about 6 minutes versus a 30-minute incident) and non-chronological. One detainee returning from exercise saw the mess and heard complaints of being hit. Prison staff witnesses mostly denied seeing violence or disorder, though some acknowledged hearing conflict, seeing scattered items, the applicant’s post-search complaints of sharp foot pain, swelling, limping and the hospital transfer. The 6-minute-36-second video showed voluntary exit, an initially orderly cell, Ciorap’s refusal to re-enter, him sitting on the ground demanding a prosecutor, the door closing, interior banging and Ciorap shouting about self-harm and missing documents. The prosecutor concluded the footage proved no violence and suggested possible self-infliction.

The deputy Prosecutor General quashed the decision on 10 March 2008 and ordered a more thorough investigation. It was discontinued again on 17 April 2008 for essentially the same reasons. An investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court upheld that decision on 12 August 2008, holding that the complaint concerned evaluation of evidence, which lay outside his competence. Ciorap’s extraordinary appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court of Justice on 1 October 2009, which found the district court’s decision lawful.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of the prohibition of ill-treatment and the duty to investigate it effectively.

The case of Ciorap v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 5) (Application no. 7232/07) originated from an application lodged on 15 November 2006 by Moldovan national Tudor Ciorap, born in 1965. The applicant, serving an 11-year prison sentence in Prison no. 13 in Chișinău, alleged ill-treatment during detention on 28 October 2006 and an ineffective subsequent investigation, in violation of his rights (primarily under Article 3 of the Convention, concerning prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, including the duty to investigate).

On that date, the applicant—who had a Category 2 disability and a diagnosis including personality disorder—was held with five other detainees (three with disabilities) in cell no. 20, reserved for those with mental health issues. Around 3 p.m., several men, some wearing dark masks and armed with rubber truncheons and metal shields (from the “Pantera” special forces battalion), entered to search for prohibited items. They ordered the detainees out. The applicant claimed the masked men shouted insults, hit, and pushed them. The Government disputed any use of force or improper conduct. The detainees stood facing the wall in the corridor for about 30 minutes during the search, which was partially video-recorded by a prison officer.

Upon being ordered back into the cell, the applicant saw their possessions—including food from relatives, medication, and documents—scattered in disorder. He refused to re-enter until a prosecutor or prison representative documented the search and mess. He alleged he was then hit, thrown to the floor, kicked in the stomach, and that the cell door was slammed shut on his foot, causing severe pain; his glasses were also smashed. The Government maintained no force was used and the cell remained in order. Around 7 p.m., the applicant, complaining of a swollen foot, was taken by ambulance to a Chișinău hospital. A doctor diagnosed contusion of the soft tissues of the right ankle with a suspected bone fracture; the foot was plastered.

On 31 October 2006, the applicant and four fellow detainees complained of ill-treatment to the Prosecutor General’s Office, military prosecutors, and other authorities. Subsequent medical examinations (28 November 2006, December 2006, and May 2007) confirmed a broken bone, a haematoma consistent with violence, and long-lasting health issues (over 21 days). A later 2007 forensic exam, per the Government, found no conclusive evidence of a fracture (full reports were not submitted by the parties).

A prosecutor initially declined to investigate on 6 December 2006, but another started a criminal probe on 8 December 2006. Between November and December 2007, several Pantera members were charged with exceeding powers by using excessive force. On 15 February 2008, a prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding the applicant had disobeyed lawful orders, acted provocatively, and required force to re-enter the cell; self-inflicted injury to accuse authorities could not be ruled out. The decision noted consistent detainee statements confirming insults, hitting with truncheons, disorder, and the door crushing the applicant’s foot (with threats). One detainee who returned from exercise described scattered items and complaints of beatings. Prison staff testimonies were mixed: some denied violence or disorder, while medical and supervisory staff reported seeing/hearing conflict, disorder, the applicant’s swollen/painful foot, limping, and immediate post-search complaints (he had not complained earlier that day). Coordinators claimed no force was needed or reported.

A 6-minute-36-second video showed detainees leaving voluntarily, masked men present, the applicant refusing to re-enter without a report, sitting on the ground, and the door closing amid sounds of hitting from inside and the applicant’s shouts about self-harm and missing documents. The prosecutor found it did not prove violence and suggested possible self-infliction from the door-striking sounds.

The investigation was reopened on 10 March 2008 but discontinued again on 17 April 2008 for similar reasons. On 12 August 2008, an investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court upheld this, ruling the complaint concerned evidence evaluation in criminal proceedings (beyond the judge’s competence for fundamental rights violations). The applicant’s extraordinary appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court of Justice on 1 October 2009, affirming the lower court’s lawful analysis of the evidence.

These facts highlight the alleged physical ill-treatment (injuries, force, disorder) during the search of a vulnerable detainee and the investigation’s handling, including witness discrepancies, incomplete video, possible self-harm findings, and judicial deference on evidence, which the applicant claimed rendered it ineffective and without adequate remedy.

**CASE OF CIORAP v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA (No. 5)** (Application no. 7232/07, ECtHR, 15 March 2016)

This ECtHR case concerns allegations of ill-treatment of a prisoner (Art. 3 ECHR) during a cell search and an ineffective investigation into those claims, plus lack of an effective remedy (Art. 13). Tudor Ciorap (born 1965), serving an 11-year sentence in Prison no. 13 in Chișinău, was held on 28 October 2006 in cell no. 20 (reserved for detainees with mental problems). He had a Category 2 disability and a personality disorder diagnosis; two of five co-detainees also had Category 2 disabilities.

Around 3 p.m., several men (some wearing dark masks and armed with rubber truncheons and metal shields) entered to search for prohibited items and ordered the detainees out. The applicant claimed the masked men shouted, insulted, hit and pushed the detainees. The Government denied any force or improper behaviour. Detainees stood facing the wall in the corridor for about 30 minutes while an officer filmed the search. They were then ordered back.

The applicant alleged that, seeing possessions (including food from relatives, medication and documents) scattered in disorder, he refused to re-enter until a prosecutor or prison administrator documented the search and mess. He was then hit, thrown to the floor, kicked in the stomach, and had the cell door slammed on his foot (causing great pain); his glasses were smashed. The Government maintained no force was used and the cell was left in order.

The applicant complained of a swollen foot and was taken by ambulance to hospital around 7 p.m. A doctor diagnosed contusion of the soft tissues of the right ankle with suspected bone fracture; the foot was plastered. Later examinations (28 November 2006 onwards) confirmed a broken bone, haematoma consistent with violence, and lasting health effects (over 21 days). The Government cited a later (31 October 2007) forensic report finding no conclusive fracture evidence; full copies of later reports were not submitted.

On 31 October 2006 the applicant (and four co-detainees) complained of ill-treatment to the Prosecutor General, military prosecutor and others. A Chișinău military prosecutor declined to open a criminal investigation on 6 December 2006, but a Chișinău prosecutor opened one on 8 December 2006. Members of the “Pantera” special forces battalion who participated were charged (late 2007) with exceeding powers by using excessive force.

The investigation was discontinued on 15 February 2008. The prosecutor found the applicant had disobeyed lawful orders, acted provocatively, refused to return to the cell and had to be forced back; self-inflicted injury could not be ruled out. Detainee witnesses (S.B., A.G., V.Z., B.I. and the applicant) described insults, hits with truncheons, disorder, the door crushing the applicant’s foot, and threats; they said the video was selective, incomplete (~6 minutes vs. ~30-minute event) and out of chronological order. One detainee returning from exercise confirmed disorder and complaints of being hit. Prison staff/medical witnesses were mixed: some saw no violence or disorder; others noted disorder, the applicant’s post-search complaints of pain, swelling, limping, and his account of being beaten; the medical unit head heard conflict but saw no violence (while admitting force might have been used). Coordinators reported no force used except that the uncooperative applicant was eventually persuaded back without it. A 6-minute-36-second video showed detainees leaving voluntarily, masked men, an initially orderly cell, the applicant’s refusal and request for a prosecutor, him sitting on the ground, the door closing with internal hitting, and the applicant shouting about suicide/self-harm and missing documents. The prosecutor viewed the video as not proving violence and as permitting an inference of self-inflicted injury.

The deputy Prosecutor General quashed the discontinuation on 10 March 2008 and ordered a more thorough investigation. It was discontinued again on 17 April 2008 on essentially the same grounds. An investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court upheld this on 12 August 2008 (final at that level), holding that the complaint concerned evaluation of evidence (beyond the judge’s competence). The Supreme Court of Justice rejected an extraordinary appeal on 1 October 2009, finding the lower court’s decision lawful after reviewing the file.

These facts formed the basis of the communicated complaints of ill-treatment, inadequate investigation and lack of effective remedy.

The case of Butrin v. Russia (Application no. 16179/14) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 22 March 2016 (final 22 June 2016). The applicant, Sergey Georgiyevich Butrin (born 1949), a Russian national serving a 19-year sentence for aggravated murder, robbery and firearms possession (imposed in 2006 after arrest that year), complained under the Convention that conditions in correctional colony IK-17/1 (Kochubeyevskoe, Stavropol Region, where he arrived in February 2010) were unsuitable for a totally blind detainee and that no effective domestic remedy existed.

Upon arrival, doctors recorded the applicant’s first-degree disability: total blindness from mature cataracts in both eyes (developed in detention), rendering him unable to move independently. He also suffered coronary disease, hypertension, gallstones and chronic pancreatitis, requiring enhanced medical attention. He was placed in unit no. 10 (a 149.6 m² dormitory for 46 special-needs inmates with various disabilities/illnesses, plus dining, toilet, shower and office space). Official figures indicated 2.82 m² living space per person after accounting for bunks and furniture. Premises were unadapted for visual impairment (no tactile markings, lighting adjustments or other aids). An unpaid fellow inmate with cardiac issues was assigned to assist with mobility, showers and meals; the applicant performed no work and remained in the unit. After that inmate’s release in September 2014, the applicant (who refused other inmate help) was left unaided.

The applicant regularly stumbled, slipped and fell due to disorientation, causing anguish, despair and a 2011 diagnosis of emotionally unstable personality disorder. Medical commissions (February 2011 and November 2012) confirmed disability and recommended a walking stick, white cane, audiobook player, vocal thermometer and tonometer; these were never supplied. Officials recorded (but the applicant did not confirm in writing) alleged refusals of the items.

In February 2013 the applicant sought a medical examination for early release on health grounds. An April 2013 commission found his blindness listed in Government Decree no. 54 (2004) as potentially warranting release. The Kochubeevskoe District Court dismissed the application (April 2013), citing crime gravity, remaining sentence length and Supreme Court Ruling no. 21 (2011) that listing alone did not mandate release. The Stavropol Regional Court upheld this; the Supreme Court rejected a cassation appeal as out of time (July 2014).

Russian law (Code of Execution of Sentences and Internal Regulations) grants disabled inmates (categories 1-2) improved accommodation, extra food/parcels, free clothing/toiletries, enriched diet and roll-call exemptions, but contains no specific rules for visually impaired or blind detainees. International standards (UN CRPD Arts. 1, 14-15, 20; CPT reports; Council of Europe recommendations) require reasonable accommodation, mobility aids, non-discrimination and prevention of ill-treatment for disabled prisoners, including structural adaptations and trained assistance to avoid dependence or harm.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: unadapted facilities, overcrowding, lack of prescribed aids, inadequate/unpaid assistance leading to falls and psychological harm, and ineffective remedies (including denial of release despite medical findings). The Court had granted priority and communicated the detention-conditions and remedy complaints.

The case of Butrin v. Russia (Application no. 16179/14) concerns a Russian national, Sergey Georgiyevich Butrin (born 1949), who alleged that his detention conditions in a correctional colony were incompatible with his total blindness and that he lacked an effective remedy. He was arrested in March 2006 on charges of aggravated murder, robbery and firearms possession, convicted in July 2006 by the Stavropol Regional Court, and sentenced to 19 years’ imprisonment.

In February 2010 he was transferred to correctional colony IK-17/1 in Kochubeyevskoe, Stavropol Region. Upon arrival a prison doctor recorded first-degree disability due to total blindness from mature cataracts in both eyes, a condition that had developed in detention and left him unable to move independently. He also suffered from coronary disease, hypertension, gallstones and chronic pancreatitis and was placed on a list of inmates requiring enhanced medical supervision.

He was housed in unit no. 10, a special-needs dormitory for 46 disabled or seriously ill detainees. The dormitory measured 149.6 m², of which a substantial portion was occupied by bunk beds, tables and chairs, yielding 2.82 m² of living space per person. The premises contained no adaptations for the visually impaired. Another inmate with cardiac problems was assigned (without remuneration) to help him move around the dormitory, shower and eat; the applicant himself performed no work and remained in the unit all day.

He frequently stumbled over objects, slipped and fell, experiences that produced anguish and despair. In 2011 he was diagnosed with an emotionally unstable personality disorder. A medical commission in 2011 and 2012 confirmed his disability and recommended a walking stick, white cane, audiobook player, talking thermometer and talking tonometer. These items were never supplied; prison records merely note that officials asked him whether he wanted them and that he allegedly refused without making a written statement. After his assigned helper was released in September 2014 the authorities claimed he declined assistance from other inmates, leaving him unaided.

In February 2013 he sought a medical examination with a view to early release. A commission concluded that total blindness appeared on the statutory list of illnesses that could justify release. The Kochubeevskoe District Court nevertheless refused the application in April 2013, citing the gravity of the original offences and the length of sentence still to be served; the decision was upheld on appeal and a subsequent cassation appeal was rejected as out of time.

Russian law grants disabled prisoners improved accommodation, extra food parcels and exemption from roll-calls, but contains no specific rules for visually impaired inmates. The applicant therefore argued that the combination of unadapted premises, absence of mobility aids, dependence on unpaid fellow prisoners and subsequent isolation constituted inhuman and degrading treatment, and that no effective domestic remedy existed to challenge those conditions.

Russia ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2012, which requires reasonable accommodation and personal mobility aids for disabled detainees. Council of Europe instruments similarly emphasise structural adaptations and staff sensitivity toward handicapped prisoners.

The ECtHR case Savca v. Moldova (no. 17963/08, judgment 15 March 2016) concerns a high-ranking police officer, Corneliu Savca (b. 1970), who alleged unlawful pre-trial detention without reasonable suspicion or sufficient grounds, plus inhuman and degrading conditions.

Savca was arrested on 26 March 2008 after a large heroin seizure in Chișinău, suspected of involvement in a smuggling ring targeting the EU. He was charged under Criminal Code Article 217/1 (large-scale narcotics circulation, 7–20 years). The investigation ended on 5 September 2008 and the file went to trial. On 21 October 2009 he was convicted of different offences (negligence, abuse of power, aiding and abetting) and sentenced to 5 years 9 months. The Chișinău Court of Appeal quashed the conviction on 21 June 2010 and released him; the case remains pending.

He spent the entire period in remand. Monthly detention orders recited the same formula: a serious offence carrying more than two years’ imprisonment plus risks of flight or interference with the investigation. Every habeas corpus application was dismissed.

He was held in solitary confinement at the CFECC facility until 17 November 2008, then in Prison no. 13 until release. He described the latter as dirty and overcrowded (2.5 m² per inmate), with poor food, constant smoking, vermin, no bed linen, and co-detention with violent convicts who threatened him because he was a police officer.

His health deteriorated (gastritis, duodenitis, pancreatitis, hepatitis, hypertension). Doctors recommended hospitalisation. He spent 7 October–17 November 2008 in a Ministry of Justice prison hospital but refused treatment, seeking instead a military hospital accredited by the Ministry of Healthcare; the request was refused.

Domestic law originally limited remand under Constitution Article 25 to 30 days, extendable to 6 (or exceptionally 12) months. A 1999 Constitutional Court decision confined the cap to the investigation stage, leaving trial-stage detention unrestricted. A 2001 amendment set a 12-month overall court-controlled maximum. CCP Article 186 imposes 6- or 12-month limits (depending on maximum sentence) for both investigation and trial phases, after which three-month extensions are possible only in exceptional circumstances.

Contemporary reports confirm systemic failings. The 2008 UN Special Rapporteur found Prison no. 13 holding 931 inmates against a 600 capacity, with poor hygiene, limited healthcare and inadequate food. Ombudsman reports for 2009–2010 recorded failure to issue soap, nationwide overcrowding well below the 4 m² statutory minimum, budget-driven shortfalls in meat and fish, and dilapidated cells that were dark, damp, unventilated and smoke-filled.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 5 violations (unlawful detention lacking reasonable suspicion and relevant/sufficient grounds, including possible exceedance of statutory time-limits) and Article 3 complaints (overcrowding, hygiene, diet, inter-prisoner violence and inadequate medical care).

The case of Savca v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 17963/08) was brought by Corneliu Savca, a Moldovan national born in 1970 and resident in Chișinău, who at the relevant time held a senior position as a police officer. He lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 April 2008, alleging that his detention on remand had been unlawful, lacked any reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence, and was not supported by relevant and sufficient grounds. He further complained that the conditions of that detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

On 26 March 2008 Savca was arrested following the seizure of a large quantity of heroin in Chișinău. He was suspected of belonging to an organised group that smuggled heroin through Moldova destined for the European Union and was charged under Article 217/1 of the Criminal Code with circulating large quantities of narcotics, an offence carrying a sentence of between seven and twenty years’ imprisonment. The investigation was completed on 5 September 2008 and the file was sent to a trial court. On 21 October 2009 the first-instance court convicted him of entirely different offences—negligence, abuse of power and aiding and abetting—and imposed a sentence of five years and nine months. That judgment was quashed by the Chișinău Court of Appeal on 21 June 2010, after which Savca was released. The criminal proceedings remained pending at the time the European Court delivered its judgment.

Throughout the period from his arrest until the 2009 conviction Savca was held in pre-trial detention. Warrants were issued monthly and invariably recited the same two justifications: the seriousness of the charge (an offence punishable by more than two years’ imprisonment) and a risk that he might abscond or interfere with the investigation. Every habeas-corpus application he lodged was rejected. After the investigation phase ended, the detention continued into the trial phase, raising issues under both the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure, which impose statutory ceilings of six or twelve months (depending on the maximum penalty) that may be exceeded only in exceptional circumstances and by reasoned judicial decision.

Savca was first held in solitary confinement at the detention facility of the Centre for Combating Economic Crime and Corruption until 17 November 2008, then transferred to Prison no. 13, where he remained until his release in June 2010. He described the cells in Prison no. 13 as dirty, vermin-infested and severely overcrowded, affording each inmate only 2.5 square metres of space. Food was of very poor quality, inmates smoked constantly, and no bed linen was supplied. Because of his former police rank he was housed with prisoners convicted of violent crimes who threatened him with physical harm. Independent reports contemporaneous with his detention corroborated these conditions. The United Nations Special Rapporteur on torture, after visiting Moldova in July 2008, recorded that Prison no. 13 was holding 931 inmates against an official capacity of 600 and noted widespread problems of overcrowding, inadequate hygiene, insufficient food and restricted medical care. The Moldovan Ombudsman (Human Rights Centre) similarly documented, in its 2009 and 2010 reports, systematic overcrowding well below the statutory four square metres per person, chronic shortages of soap and bedding, poor ventilation, dampness and insufficient nutrition, attributing the situation to dilapidated Soviet-era infrastructure and budgetary shortfalls.

During detention Savca’s health deteriorated; a medical panel diagnosed gastritis, duodenitis, pancreatitis, hepatitis and hypertension and recommended in-patient treatment. He was admitted to a Ministry of Justice prison hospital from 7 October to 17 November 2008 but refused the treatment offered, requesting instead transfer to a military hospital accredited by the Ministry of Healthcare. That request was denied for reasons never communicated to the European Court.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaints concerning the lawfulness and justification of his prolonged remand and the compatibility of the prison conditions with the prohibition of inhuman and degrading treatment.

The case of Savca v. the Republic of Moldova (application no. 17963/08) was decided by a Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights on 15 March 2016 (final on 15 June 2016). The applicant, Corneliu Savca (born 1970), a high-ranking Moldovan police officer living in Chișinău, alleged violations arising from his pre-trial detention, specifically that it was unlawful, lacked reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence, and was not based on relevant and sufficient grounds, and that the conditions of his detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

On 26 March 2008 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership in a criminal gang involved in smuggling large quantities of heroin through Moldova toward the European Union. The arrest followed the seizure of a substantial quantity of heroin in Chișinău. He was charged under Article 217/1 of the Criminal Code with circulating large quantities of narcotics, an offence carrying a sentence of seven to twenty years’ imprisonment. The investigation concluded on 5 September 2008 and the case was sent for trial. On 21 October 2009 a first-instance court convicted him not of the original charge but of unrelated offences of negligence, abuse of power and aiding and abetting an offence, imposing a sentence of five years and nine months. The Chișinău Court of Appeal quashed that judgment on 21 June 2010 and ordered his release; the criminal proceedings remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

Throughout the period from arrest until the 2009 conviction the applicant was held on remand. Detention warrants were issued monthly on identical grounds: that he was accused of a serious offence punishable by more than two years’ imprisonment and that there was a risk he would abscond or obstruct the investigation. All of his habeas-corpus applications were rejected.

He was first held in solitary confinement at the Centre for Combating Economic Crime and Corruption until 17 November 2008, then transferred to Prison no. 13 in Chișinău, where he remained until his release in June 2010. He described the conditions in Prison no. 13 as overcrowded (approximately 2.5 m² of personal space), filthy, infested with vermin and lacking bed linen. Food was of very poor quality, inmates smoked continuously, and he was housed with convicted violent offenders who threatened him because of his police status. His health deteriorated; a medical panel diagnosed gastritis, duodenitis, pancreatitis, hepatitis and hypertension and recommended in-patient treatment. He spent 7 October–17 November 2008 in a Ministry of Justice prison hospital but refused treatment there, requesting transfer to a military hospital accredited by the Ministry of Health; the request was denied for undisclosed reasons.

Relevant domestic law included Article 25 of the Constitution (as amended in 2001), which limited remand detention to a maximum of twelve months, and Articles 186(3), (8) and (9) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which imposed six- or twelve-month ceilings (depending on the maximum penalty) for both the investigation and trial phases, with possible three-month extensions thereafter only in exceptional circumstances. A 1999 Constitutional Court ruling had interpreted an earlier version of Article 25 as applying solely to the investigation stage.

Independent reports contemporaneous with the applicant’s detention corroborated systemic problems. A 2008 UN Special Rapporteur report and 2009–2010 reports of the Moldovan Human Rights Centre (Ombudsman) documented severe overcrowding in Prison no. 13 (official capacity 600, actual occupancy exceeding 900), inadequate hygiene, insufficient nutrition, poor ventilation and lighting, and limited medical care—conditions falling short of both national standards and international norms.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaints under Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention concerning the lawfulness, justification and physical conditions of his prolonged remand detention.
001-161380:
**Summary of M.G.C. v. Romania (ECtHR, Application no. 61495/11)**

The applicant, a Romanian girl born in 1997, alleged that Romanian authorities failed in their positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the ECHR to protect her from inhuman/degrading treatment and respect her private life after sexual abuse at age 11. In 2008, while living in a village and playing at a neighbouring family's house (the B. family, with ten children), she encountered J.V., a 52-year-old unemployed relative living in their vacant stable. She later told police that J.V. had forcibly dragged her from play in August and December 2008, taken her to an empty room or barn, and raped her while holding her down and covering her mouth. Between August 2008 and February 2009, four of the B. brothers and their friend G.I. also raped her under similar circumstances, with threats of violence (including a knife once). She became pregnant and, with parental consent, had a termination. On 10 March 2009, after missing her period, she disclosed the abuse to her mother, citing shame and J.V.'s threats of beatings if she told anyone.

Her parents filed a complaint that day. Police questioned the suspects. The brothers admitted sexual acts but claimed she initiated or consented, often describing her as scantily dressed and "provocative"; J.V. said she came to him first and had prior experience with the boys. G.I. was under 14 and not liable. A forensic exam found no traces of violence. A July 2009 psychiatric report diagnosed post-traumatic stress, noting her shame, vivid memories, fear for her and her family's safety, difficulties foreseeing consequences, and insufficient discernment due to age.

The prosecutor indicted only J.V. for sexual intercourse with a minor (repeated acts), fining the brothers administratively for the same offence. He concluded the evidence (perpetrators' and sisters' statements) did not prove lack of consent, citing her attire and visits to the house. Her challenges failed. The Deva District Court convicted J.V. of the lesser offence (3 years' imprisonment, ~EUR 2,000 non-pecuniary damages). It relied on no physical injuries, perpetrators' claims she initiated acts and continued playing afterward, and her clothing, concluding force or incapacity was unlikely.

On appeal, the Hunedoara County Court reclassified it as rape (4 years, same damages), citing Article 197 of the Criminal Code (intercourse by constraint or exploiting inability to express will) and an absolute presumption of incapacity under age 14 (Article 99 and related civil law). It noted the minimum consent age of 15. The Alba Iulia Court of Appeal, however, restored the original conviction. It distinguished rape (requiring constraint or lack of will) from consensual intercourse with a minor under 15, holding the incapacity presumption applied only to child perpetrators, not victims. It credited J.V., the brothers, and sisters' statements that she initiated acts, plus her delayed reporting, while ignoring the psychiatric report.

Domestic practice was inconsistent: some courts found valid consent in similar-aged victims based on non-reporting, lack of screaming, or clothing; others treated young age as precluding consent, sometimes using expert reports. The applicant argued the authorities failed to treat the acts as rape given her age, threats, force, and incapacity, instead accepting perpetrators' accounts and overlooking expert evidence of trauma and limited discernment. This formed the basis of her claims that the investigation and judicial response were inadequate to protect her rights. (Word count: 512)

The case of M.G.C. v. Romania (Application no. 61495/11) concerns an 11-year-old girl (born 1997) who alleged that Romanian authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights to protect her from sexual abuse amounting to inhuman and degrading treatment and to safeguard her private life. The events occurred in a small village in 2008–2009, where the applicant regularly played at the home of a neighbouring family (the B. family) with ten children. The family also housed J.V., an unemployed 52-year-old relative living in a vacant cattle stable.

According to the applicant’s later statements to police, J.V. twice dragged her by force into an empty room or barn (in August and December 2008), held her down, covered her mouth to prevent screaming, and raped her. Between August 2008 and February 2009 she was similarly forced into sex by four of the B. family’s sons (F.B., A.B., G.B. and P.B.) and their friend G.I. (who was under 14 and thus not criminally liable). She became pregnant and, after telling her mother on 10 March 2009 that she had been too ashamed and frightened (owing to J.V.’s threats of beatings) to speak earlier, underwent a surgical termination.

A criminal complaint was lodged the same day. The suspects were questioned immediately. They admitted sexual acts but claimed the applicant had initiated them, often while “scantily dressed,” and that she had previously had sex with others among them. A forensic examination found no traces of violence. A July 2009 psychiatric report diagnosed post-traumatic stress, noted her vivid, shame-filled recollection of the events and her fear for her safety, and concluded that, owing to her age, she had insufficient discernment and difficulty foreseeing the consequences of her actions.

The prosecutor indicted only J.V. for the lesser offence of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 198 of the Criminal Code), imposing administrative fines on the four brothers. The prosecutor found it unproven that the applicant had not consented. The applicant’s challenge to this decision was rejected. In April 2010 the Deva District Court convicted J.V. of the lesser offence, sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment and awarded modest compensation. It relied on the absence of physical injuries, the perpetrators’ and sisters’ statements that the applicant had always taken the initiative, and her continued visits to the house, concluding that these facts showed she had not been forced and possessed capacity to consent.

On appeal the Hunedoara County Court reclassified the offence as rape (Article 197), citing an absolute legal presumption that persons under 14 lack capacity to consent, and increased the sentence to four years (below the statutory minimum, citing mitigating circumstances). The Alba Iulia Court of Appeal reversed this in March 2011, restoring the original conviction. It held that the presumption of incapacity applied only to child perpetrators, not victims, and that the applicant’s alleged initiation of the acts, failure to tell her parents sooner, and the sisters’ evidence demonstrated valid consent. The psychiatric report was neither mentioned nor discussed.

Romanian law at the time distinguished rape (non-consensual intercourse or intercourse taking advantage of inability to express will, with an aggravated penalty if the victim was under 15) from the separate offence of intercourse with a minor under 15 (regardless of consent). Domestic case-law submitted by the parties revealed inconsistent approaches: some courts treated very young victims as incapable of valid consent; others inferred consent from a child’s silence, lack of visible resistance, continued contact with the perpetrator, or “provocative” clothing, even in the absence of forensic or psychological assessment. NGO reports contemporaneously documented systemic shortcomings in the treatment of child victims of sexual violence, including re-victimisation, lack of specialised questioning, and insufficient regard for children’s vulnerability.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that the investigation and judicial process had failed to treat her as a child incapable of giving meaningful consent, had given decisive weight to the accused’s narrative, and had thereby denied her effective protection.

The case of M.G.C. v. Romania (Application no. 61495/11) concerns an 11-year-old girl (born 1997) from a small village who alleged repeated sexual abuse. In 2008 she regularly played at the home of a neighbouring family with ten children. A 52-year-old unemployed relative, J.V., lived in their unused stable. According to the applicant’s later police statement, J.V. twice dragged her into an empty room or barn, held her down, covered her mouth and raped her (August and December 2008). Between August 2008 and February 2009 four of the neighbours’ sons and their friend G.I. likewise forced her to have sex, claiming J.V. had instructed them. She was threatened with beatings (and once with a knife) if she told anyone.

In March 2009 her mother noticed a missed period; the applicant then disclosed the abuse, citing shame and fear. She was pregnant and, with parental consent, underwent a termination. A complaint was lodged the same day. The five adult suspects were questioned immediately. J.V. and the brothers claimed the applicant had initiated every encounter, dressed provocatively and previously had sex with others. A forensic examination found no traces of violence. A July 2009 psychiatric report diagnosed post-traumatic stress, noted her vivid but shame-filled recollection, her fear for her family’s safety, and her age-related lack of discernment.

The prosecutor indicted only J.V. for the lesser offence of sexual intercourse with a minor, imposing administrative fines on the brothers (G.I. was under 14 and not liable). The prosecutor accepted the perpetrators’ accounts of the applicant’s “provocative” dress and concluded consent had not been disproved. The applicant’s complaint against this decision was rejected.

In April 2010 the Deva District Court convicted J.V. of sexual intercourse with a minor (three years’ imprisonment plus modest compensation). It relied on the absence of physical injuries, the perpetrators’ and the two sisters’ statements that the applicant initiated the acts and continued visiting afterwards, and her “scantily dressed” appearance. It dismissed any lack of capacity.

On appeal the Hunedoara County Court reclassified the offence as rape, applying an absolute presumption that a child under 14 cannot give valid consent, and increased the sentence to four years. The Alba Iulia Court of Appeal reversed this in March 2011, restoring the original conviction. It treated the statutory presumption of incapacity as applying only to child offenders, not victims, and again credited the perpetrators’ and sisters’ testimony that the applicant had consented. The psychiatric report was ignored.

Romanian law distinguished rape (constraint or taking advantage of incapacity to express will; 3–10 years, or 10–25 if the victim is under 15) from sexual intercourse with a minor under 15 (3–10 years). Domestic case-law was inconsistent: some courts treated young age itself as precluding valid consent; others inferred consent from delayed disclosure, continued contact or “provocative” clothing. International instruments (UNCRC, Lanzarote Convention, Istanbul Convention) emphasise that children cannot freely consent, that investigations must be child-sensitive and that evidence of a child’s sexual history is generally irrelevant.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claim that the authorities failed in their positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8: they did not treat an 11-year-old’s alleged repeated abuse as rape, relied on the accused’s narrative and stereotyped notions of “provocation,” disregarded expert evidence of trauma and incapacity, and thereby failed to afford effective protection or a child-appropriate investigation.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered its judgment in Didov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 27791/09) on 17 March 2016 (final 17 June 2016). The applicant, Stoyan Dimitrov Didov, a Bulgarian national born in 1972 and living in Burgas, alleged that his police detention of approximately six and a half hours on 11 July 2007 violated his right to liberty.

Around 6 a.m. that day, police officers visited the applicant’s home with a summons requiring him to report to the Pomorie police station “as a witness” in an investigation. The applicant stated he was absent and learned of the visit by telephone from his wife; the summons recorded that he had refused to accept it.
