The case of Zherebin v. Russia (Application no. 51445/09) concerns the pre-trial detention of Russian national Pavel Mikhaylovich Zherebin, born in 1983 and resident in Tula. He was arrested on 9 March 2009 on suspicion of participating in a December 2008 organised-group offence involving a flagrant breach of public peace and order, punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

On 10 March 2009 the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow remanded him in custody. It cited the seriousness of the charge, the offence’s public-order nature, the applicant’s lack of residence in Moscow or at his registered address (he claimed to be staying with a friend in the Moscow Region), his two-year leave from university studies, unemployment, unknown means of subsistence, prior administrative offences, and the use of improvised weapons by an organised group at night. The court concluded he might abscond or interfere with justice (including by pressuring witnesses). The applicant appealed, arguing that the court had failed to justify detention or consider less restrictive measures, that no evidence showed any attempt to interfere or abscond, and that he lived with his pregnant wife at a known address. The Moscow City Court upheld the order on 30 March 2009.

On 27 April 2009 the District Court extended detention until 15 June 2009, repeating that the offence was serious and committed with unidentified co-perpetrators, that the applicant lacked a registered Moscow-region address and was unemployed, and that neither he nor his lawyer had disproved the risk of absconding or interference. Personal-guarantee statements were rejected as not submitted to the investigator, not presented in person, or of doubtful authenticity. This extension was upheld on 18 May 2009.

On 29 May 2009, after the investigation had ended and the trial had been scheduled, the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court continued detention pending trial, again invoking the seriousness of the charges, the applicant’s lack of registered address, unemployment, and unchanged circumstances. Completion of the investigation was held irrelevant. On 24 June 2009 the applicant sought release after his wife gave birth, relying on sureties; the court dismissed the request on identical grounds, stating that the birth changed nothing. The City Court confirmed the 29 May decision on 22 July 2009.

The applicant was convicted on 28 October 2009 and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment; the conviction was upheld on 22 December 2009. Throughout, domestic courts applied stereotyped reasoning focused on the gravity of the charge and generic personal circumstances, without examining concrete evidence of flight or interference risk, without adequately considering the applicant’s family situation or completed investigation, and without seriously evaluating alternatives such as sureties or house arrest.

Russian criminal-procedure law (CCrP Arts. 97–99, 108) requires “sufficient grounds” for believing an accused will abscond, reoffend or interfere, plus consideration of character, family status and other circumstances; detention is a last resort for offences punishable by more than three years. Supreme Court rulings (2006, 2013) have repeatedly criticised courts for formalistic recitation of statutory grounds without specific facts and for failing to treat detention as exceptional. Council-of-Europe materials similarly stress that remand must be strictly necessary, individually justified and used only when alternatives cannot address identified risks.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint of unjustified and excessively prolonged pre-trial detention.

It concluded he posed a risk of absconding or interfering with justice, including by pressuring witnesses.

The District Court repeated the seriousness of the offence (committed in concert, with some co-perpetrators still unidentified), the applicant's lack of a registered Moscow address or employment, and asserted that neither he nor his lawyer had disproved the risk of absconding or interference. The court maintained custody, referencing the same factors (seriousness, character, lack of registered address or employment) and holding that completion of the investigation changed nothing. A further request for release on 24 June 2009—now citing the 16 June birth of his child and surety statements—was dismissed on identical grounds, with the court stating that the child's birth had "no effect." The case of Zherebin v. Russia (application no. 51445/09) concerns the applicant’s pre-trial detention in Moscow courts between March and October 2009. Pavel Mikhaylovich Zherebin, a Russian national born in 1983, was arrested on 9 March 2009 on suspicion of having committed a flagrant breach of public peace and order as part of an organised group in December 2008. The following day the Taganskiy District Court remanded him in custody, citing the seriousness of the charge (punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment), the fact that the offence was directed against public order, the applicant’s lack of a registered address in Moscow, his temporary residence with a friend, his unemployment and unknown source of income, his prior administrative offences, and the use of improvised weapons by an organised group at night. The court concluded that, if released, he might abscond or interfere with the investigation, including by putting pressure on witnesses.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the court had given no specific reasons, had failed to consider less restrictive measures, and had ignored the absence of any evidence that he had attempted to abscond or influence witnesses. He also pointed out that he lived with his pregnant wife at an address known to the authorities. On 30 March 2009 the Moscow City Court upheld the detention order.

On 27 April 2009 the District Court extended detention until 15 June, repeating that the applicant was charged with a serious offence committed in concert (some co-perpetrators still unidentified), that he had no registered address in the Moscow Region, and that he was unemployed. It held that neither the applicant nor his lawyer had produced evidence negating the statutory risks of absconding or interference, and it dismissed statements of guarantee as improperly submitted. The City Court confirmed the extension on 18 May.

When the case was committed for trial on 29 May 2009 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court again refused release, relying on the same factors (seriousness of the charges, lack of a Moscow address, unemployment) and stating that completion of the investigation did not alter the original grounds. A further application for release after the birth of the applicant’s child on 16 June 2009 was rejected on 24 June on identical grounds; the court expressly held that the birth “has no effect to the contrary.” The City Court dismissed the appeal on 22 July. The applicant was convicted on 28 October 2009 and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment; the conviction was upheld in December.

Throughout the proceedings the domestic courts invoked Articles 97–99 and 108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which require “sufficient grounds” to believe that an accused will abscond, reoffend or obstruct justice and oblige the court to consider the accused’s personal circumstances and the possibility of less restrictive measures. The case of Dimitar Yanakiev v. Bulgaria (No. 2) (Application no. 50346/07) concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic court judgment awarding the applicant compensation for nationalised property. The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1936 and residing in Sofia, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 November 2007. He complained solely of the Sofia regional governor’s failure to implement a final judgment in his favour (the remainder of the application having been declared inadmissible).

The background lies in Bulgaria’s 1997 Compensation for Owners of Nationalised Real Property Act, which provided for compensation (typically via “housing compensation bonds”) where physical restitution of property taken under earlier punitive or redistributive laws was impossible. On 27 November 1997 the applicant applied to the Sofia regional governor for compensation in respect of an apartment that had belonged to his ancestor and had been nationalised in 1949. Receiving no reply, he challenged the governor’s tacit refusal. On 18 June 1999 the Sofia City Court quashed the refusal and held that compensation in bonds was due. The applicant appealed the form of compensation. On 9 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the lower court’s ruling and remitted the case for determination of the precise amount.

After the file was erroneously archived, the Sofia City Court (administrative bench) delivered its decision on 19 July 2005. It fixed the total compensation at BGN 23 604, held the governor liable for costs, and awarded the applicant his inheritance share in bonds. The court recorded that a 1994 heirs’ certificate showed the applicant and his brother as the sole heirs, who inherited in equal parts under the Inheritance Act. The decision became enforceable on 6 September 2005.

The applicant formally requested enforcement on 26 June and 8 August 2006. In February 2007 the deputy governor demanded a certified copy of the judgment, a fresh heirs’ certificate and a notary-certified declaration of the applicant’s inheritance share, citing Ordinance No. 9 of 1998. The applicant supplied the certified copy and pointed out that the heirs’ certificate had already been lodged in 1997 and that the 2005 judgment itself established the two heirs and their equal shares; he also queried the legal basis for the declaration. The governor insisted the declaration remained obligatory.

Meanwhile the applicant obtained a writ of execution (16 March 2007) and initiated forced-enforcement proceedings. The bailiff issued invitations to the governor for voluntary compliance, warning of weekly fines. The governor replied that proceedings could not be completed without the missing declaration and that an original writ was required for costs. The applicant argued that the 1998 Ordinance applied only when the administration itself calculated compensation, not when a court had already done so. The governor unsuccessfully challenged the bailiff’s invitations; both the Sofia City Administrative Court (2 July 2007) and the Supreme Administrative Court (21 December 2007) held the invitations were not reviewable acts of forced enforcement.

In March 2009 the applicant again requested enforcement. The bailiff renewed the demand, now threatening weekly fines of BGN 1 200 and possible prosecution. The governor reiterated the need for the declaration and, on 29 April 2009, himself imposed a weekly fine of BGN 1 000 on the applicant. That fine was quashed by the Sofia City Administrative Court on 8 January 2010 on the ground that the governor, being the debtor rather than an enforcement authority, lacked competence to fine the creditor.

As of 19 August 2013 the 19 July 2005 judgment remained wholly unenforced. The applicant’s complaint before the Strasbourg Court therefore centres on the authorities’ persistent refusal to implement a binding judicial award of compensation, despite multiple formal requests, a writ of execution and bailiff proceedings, and despite the fact that the 2005 judgment itself had already determined both the amount due and the applicant’s entitlement as one of two equal heirs.

**CASE OF DIMITAR YANAKIEV v. BULGARIA (No. 2) (Application no. 50346/07)**

This ECHR case concerns the prolonged failure of Bulgarian authorities to enforce a final domestic court judgment awarding the applicant compensation for nationalized property, which formed the core of his complaint (communicated as a non-enforcement issue under Article 6 of the Convention).

The applicant, Dimitar Pavlov Yanakiev (born 1936, resident in Sofia), sought compensation under the 1997 Compensation for Owners of Nationalised Real Property Act for an apartment nationalized in 1949 that had belonged to his ancestor. On 27 November 1997 he applied to the Sofia regional governor. Receiving no reply, he challenged the tacit refusal. The Sofia City Court quashed the refusal on 18 June 1999 and held that restitution was impossible, so compensation should take the form of housing compensation bonds. The applicant appealed the form of compensation. On 9 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the lower court and remitted the case for determination of the amount.

The Sofia City Court archived the file; it was restored to the roll only after the applicant’s complaint on 5 July 2002. On 19 July 2005 the court (administrative bench) quantified total compensation at BGN 23,604 and held the governor liable for costs. It awarded the applicant his legal share (one-half, as one of two heirs of the original owner, per the 1949 Inheritance Act) in housing compensation bonds. The decision became enforceable on 6 September 2005.

The applicant sent the judgment to the governor on 26 June and 8 August 2006 requesting enforcement. On 14 February 2007 the deputy governor demanded a certified copy, an heir certificate, and a notary-certified declaration. The applicant supplied the certified copy on 19 February 2007, noted that the 1997 request already included an heir certificate, and explained that the court itself had identified the two heirs and that the law automatically gave him a one-half share. The governor continued to insist on the declaration under Ordinance No. 9 of 1998 (which the applicant argued did not apply once a court had already fixed the amount and shares).

In parallel the applicant obtained a writ of execution (16 March 2007) and initiated forced-enforcement proceedings. The bailiff issued invitations to the governor on 3 April and 27 April 2007, warning of weekly fines for non-compliance. The governor replied that proceedings remained incomplete because of the missing declaration and that an original writ was needed for costs. He then challenged the bailiff’s invitations; both the Sofia City Administrative Court (2 July 2007) and the Supreme Administrative Court (21 December 2007) declared the challenge inadmissible because the invitations were not themselves acts of forced enforcement.

In March 2009 the applicant again asked the bailiff to act. The bailiff wrote on 31 March 2009 reiterating the possibility of weekly fines of BGN 1,200 and prosecution. The governor responded that the declaration was still missing and, on 29 April 2009, imposed a weekly fine of BGN 1,000 on the applicant. The Sofia City Administrative Court quashed that fine on 8 January 2010, holding that the governor was the debtor, not an enforcement body, and that the applicant was the creditor.

As of 19 August 2013 the 19 July 2005 judgment remained wholly unenforced. Under the 1997 Act and the 2002 Transactions with Compensation Instruments Act the governor was obliged, within seven days of receiving a final judgment, to transmit the necessary data to the Privatisation Agency so that compensatory instruments could be registered. The 2006 Code of Administrative Procedure empowered bailiffs to impose weekly fines (BGN 50–1,200) on officials who failed to perform non-substitutable acts required by final judgments, and provided for judicial review of bailiffs’ inaction. Domestic case-law showed both successful and unsuccessful attempts to obtain damages under the State and Municipality Responsibility for Damage Act for similar delays.

The facts thus establish an eight-year (and counting) period of non-enforcement after a final, enforceable court decision that had already determined both the amount and the applicant’s precise share, despite repeated requests, a writ of execution, and bailiff interventions.

The case of Dimitar Yanakiev v. Bulgaria (No. 2) (Application no. 50346/07) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 31 March 2016. The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1936 and living in Sofia, complained under the Convention that the regional governor of the Sofia region had failed to implement a final domestic judgment in his favour awarding compensation for nationalised property.

The 1997 Compensation for Owners of Nationalised Real Property Act provided for compensation, typically via “housing compensation bonds,” where physical restitution of property taken under earlier punitive or redistributive laws was impossible. On 27 November 1997 the applicant applied to the Sofia regional governor for compensation in respect of an apartment belonging to his ancestor and nationalised in 1949. Receiving no reply, he challenged the tacit refusal. On 18 June 1999 the Sofia City Court quashed the refusal and held that compensation in bonds was appropriate. The applicant appealed the form of compensation. On 9 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the lower court’s ruling on entitlement but remitted the case for determination of the amount.

The file was then archived and only restored to the roll after the applicant’s complaint. On 19 July 2005 the Sofia City Court (administrative bench) quantified the total compensation at BGN 23,604 and held that the applicant, as one of two heirs (himself and his brother), was entitled to half that sum in housing compensation bonds. The decision became enforceable on 6 September 2005.

The applicant forwarded the judgment to the governor on 26 June and 8 August 2006 and requested enforcement. The deputy governor replied on 14 February 2007 demanding a certified copy of the judgment, a fresh heir’s certificate and a notarised declaration. The applicant supplied the certified copy, recalled that the heir’s certificate had already been lodged in 1997, and pointed out that the court itself had already identified the two heirs and their equal shares under the 1949 Inheritance Act. The deputy governor insisted the declaration was required by a 1998 ordinance that in fact applied only to administrative (not judicial) determinations of compensation.

On 16 March 2007 the applicant obtained a writ of execution and instructed a bailiff. The bailiff issued successive invitations to the governor (3 and 27 April 2007, 31 March 2009) warning of weekly fines of up to BGN 1,200 and possible prosecution. The governor responded that enforcement was blocked solely by the missing declaration and even attempted, in April 2009, to impose weekly fines of BGN 1,000 on the applicant himself; those fines were quashed by the Sofia City Administrative Court on 8 January 2010 because the governor was the debtor, not an enforcement organ. The governor’s earlier attempt to obtain judicial review of the bailiff’s invitations was likewise dismissed as inadmissible by both the Sofia City Administrative Court (2 July 2007) and the Supreme Administrative Court (21 December 2007).

Domestic law (Articles 271, 290 and 294 of the 2006 Code of Administrative Procedure) authorised bailiffs to impose recurring fines on officials who failed to perform non-substitutable acts ordered by final administrative judgments, and allowed applicants to challenge a bailiff’s inaction. Separate provisions of the Transactions with Compensation Instruments Act 2002 required the governor, within seven days of receiving a final judgment, to transmit the necessary data to the Privatisation Agency so that the bonds could be registered. None of these mechanisms produced compliance. By letter of 19 August 2013 the applicant’s lawyer informed the Court that the 19 July 2005 judgment remained wholly unenforced.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Dzhabarov and Others v. Bulgaria (applications nos. 6095/11, 74091/11 and 75583/11) involved three Bulgarian nationals—Mr Deyan Georgiev Dzhabarov, Mr Stanislav Dimitrov Petkov (whose mother pursued the claim after his 2014 death), and Ms Vaska Kirilova Nikolova—who alleged unlawful police detention and the unjustified dismissal of their subsequent claims for non-pecuniary damages.

On 20 December 2007, around 3 a.m., Dzhabarov, Petkov and a friend were stopped by police in Stara Zagora while travelling by car. They were arrested at approximately 3.10 a.m. and taken to a local police station. Detention orders under section 63(1)(1) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs Act 2006 (MIAA) were issued much later: at noon for Dzhabarov (citing burglary/theft provisions of the Criminal Code) and at 1.30 p.m. for Petkov (citing robbery). Neither order stated factual grounds. They were released at noon on 21 December 2007 after roughly 33 hours in custody.

Both men obtained judicial review. The Stara Zagora Administrative Court quashed the orders in 2008, finding no reasonable suspicion at the time of arrest (evidenced by later-drawn police reports, discrepancies, and, in Petkov’s case, witness accounts of a robbery occurring after the arrest), delayed issuance of the orders contrary to the MIAA’s purpose, and lack of contemporaneous evidence. The Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) upheld these rulings.

Dzhabarov and Petkov then claimed damages (including BGN 2,000 each in non-pecuniary compensation for psychological trauma) under section 1(1) of the State and Municipalities Liability for Damage Act 1988. The Burgas Administrative Court dismissed the claims, holding that they had not proved non-pecuniary harm (such as stress or discomfort) because they provided no medical expert evidence; witness testimony about events and conditions was insufficient. The SAC confirmed that claimants bore the full burden of proving all tort elements, including damage, and that only medical expertise—not witnesses—could establish mental suffering from unlawful detention. Pecuniary claims for unreimbursed judicial-review costs were also rejected.

Separately, on 9 September 2006 around 11 a.m., Nikolova (head of an audit unit at the National Revenue Agency) entered the Sandanski office with an acquaintance, Mr B.T., triggering an alarm. Police found them accessing personal data in the Agency’s database and escorted them to the station at 11.15 a.m. Unidentified National Security Agency officers interviewed Nikolova without identifying themselves or explaining her detention. She was briefly returned to the office for a police record, then released at about 3.40 p.m. after roughly 4.5 hours; no written detention order was issued as required by section 65(1) MIAA.

Criminal proceedings against her for divulging confidential information were discontinued in 2007 for lack of prejudice. Complaints to prosecutors about the police action were rejected. Nikolova claimed BGN 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages for stress, humiliation and health aggravation from the unlawful (orderless) detention. The Blagoevgrad Administrative Court dismissed the claim, finding she had not proved damage: officers’ consistent testimony showed no physical or psychological abuse, her assertions were general and contradicted, and the short detention (under 24 hours) was lawful under section 64 MIAA to elucidate a possible offence. The SAC fully agreed, without addressing Convention arguments that unlawful detention inherently causes non-pecuniary harm.

These facts centre on police actions lacking reasonable suspicion or required written orders, followed by domestic courts’ refusal to presume damage from the deprivation of liberty itself.

The case of Dzhabarov and Others v. Bulgaria concerns three applications by Bulgarian nationals alleging unlawful police detention and the unjustified dismissal of their related claims for non-pecuniary damages.

Mr Dzhabarov (born 1975) and Mr Petkov (born 1981, who died in 2014; his mother pursued the claim) were travelling by car in Stara Zagora when stopped by police at around 3 a.m. on 20 December 2007. They were arrested and taken to a police station at 3:10 a.m. Detention orders were issued much later that day (noon for Dzhabarov; 1:30 p.m. for Petkov), citing section 63(1)(1) of the 2006 Ministry of Internal Affairs Act (MIAA) in connection with suspected burglary/theft or robbery under the Criminal Code. The orders contained no factual grounds. Both men were released at noon on 21 December 2007 after roughly 33 hours in custody.

They sought judicial review. The Stara Zagora Administrative Court quashed both orders. For Dzhabarov, it found no specified offence, no contemporaneous evidence of reasonable suspicion (later police reports being post-arrest and discrepant), and a nine-hour delay in issuing the order contrary to the law's purpose. The Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) upheld this in December 2008. For Petkov, the court similarly found no reasonable suspicion at the time of arrest (witness statements referred to a robbery occurring after his detention) and a mismatch between the actual arrest time and the order. The police appeal was dismissed as out of time.

Each then claimed damages under section 1(1) of the 1988 State and Municipalities Liability for Damage Act against the regional police directorate, seeking BGN 2,000 in non-pecuniary damages for psychological trauma plus unreimbursed judicial review costs. The Burgas Administrative Court dismissed both claims, holding that the applicants had not proved non-pecuniary damage (e.g., stress or discomfort) via medical expert reports; witness evidence of events or conditions was insufficient. Costs from judicial review could not be recovered this way. The SAC upheld these rulings in 2010 and 2011, confirming that claimants bore the full burden of proving all tort elements, including damage, which required expert medical evidence rather than witnesses.

Ms Nikolova (born 1962), a tax audit official, entered her Sandanski office around 11 a.m. on Saturday 9 September 2006 with an acquaintance, B.T., to check personal data for court papers. An alarm sounded; police arrived, found them accessing a database, and escorted them to the station at 11:15 a.m. Unidentified National Security Agency officers interviewed her without explanation. She was released around 3:40 p.m. after about 4.5 hours, having briefly returned to the office for a police record. Criminal proceedings for divulging confidential information were discontinued in 2007 for lack of proven prejudice. Prosecutorial complaints about the detention were refused.

In 2010 she claimed BGN 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages under the 1988 Act against the police and National Security Agency, citing the absence of a written order (required by MIAA section 65(1)) and resulting stress, humiliation and health effects. The Blagoevgrad Administrative Court dismissed the claim, accepting the detention occurred but finding no proven non-pecuniary damage or officer abuse; it was a lawful short detention under MIAA section 64 to investigate a possible offence. The SAC fully agreed in 2011, without addressing Convention arguments.

Under the MIAA, police may detain for suspected offences (among other grounds) for up to 24 hours, requiring a written order specifying grounds. The 1988 Act allows claims for damage from unlawful official acts, but the SAC's case-law has been inconsistent on whether mere unlawful detention automatically causes non-pecuniary harm or requires specific (often expert) proof.

The case of Dzhabarov and Others v. Bulgaria concerned three Bulgarian applicants who alleged unlawful police detention and the subsequent dismissal of their claims for non-pecuniary damages without adequate justification.

Mr Dzhabarov (born 1975) and Mr Petkov (born 1981, died 2014; his mother continued the application) were travelling in a car in Stara Zagora on 20 December 2007. At approximately 3 a.m. they were stopped by police, arrested, and taken to a police station at 3.10 a.m. Detention orders were issued much later: at noon for Dzhabarov (under s. 63(1)(1) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs Act 2006, citing burglary/theft using a vehicle) and at 1.30 p.m. for Petkov (citing robbery). Neither order stated factual grounds. They were released at noon on 21 December 2007.

Both sought judicial review. The Stara Zagora Administrative Court quashed the orders in 2008. For Dzhabarov, it found no specified offence, no contemporaneous evidence of reasonable suspicion (later police reports were post-arrest and discrepant), and the order issued over nine hours after de facto arrest, contrary to the law’s purpose. For Petkov, witness statements concerned a robbery at 4.50 a.m., after his 3.10 a.m. arrest, so no reasonable suspicion existed at the time; the order also misstated the detention start time. The Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) upheld these rulings (or declared the appeal inadmissible in Petkov’s case). Partial costs were awarded, but further costs claims were not fully addressed.

Each then claimed damages under s. 1(1) of the 1988 State and Municipalities Liability for Damage Act against the police directorate, seeking BGN 2,000 (EUR 1,023) non-pecuniary damages for psychological trauma plus remaining judicial-review costs. Burgas Administrative Court dismissed the claims (2009–2010), holding they failed to prove non-pecuniary damage (stress, negative emotions) via medical expert evidence; witness statements described events or conditions but not mental suffering. Costs from review proceedings could not be recovered this way. The SAC upheld this in 2010–2011, confirming claimants bear the full burden of proving all tort elements, including damage, which required expert medical evidence rather than witnesses.

Ms Nikolova (born 1962), a National Revenue Agency audit head, went to the Sandanski office on Saturday 9 September 2006 to practise ethics tests. She met acquaintance B.T., who asked her to check identities for court papers. They entered, triggering an alarm. Police arrived, found them accessing a computer database, and escorted them to the station around 11.15 a.m. Unidentified National Security Agency officers interviewed her without explanation. She was briefly returned to the office then released around 3.40 p.m. No written detention order was issued.

Criminal proceedings against her for divulging confidential data were discontinued in 2007 for lack of prejudice. Prosecutorial complaints about the detention were refused. In 2010 she claimed BGN 10,000 (EUR 5,113) non-pecuniary damages under the 1988 Act, alleging unlawful detention without a written order (required by s. 65(1) MIAA) and resulting stress/humiliation. Blagoevgrad Administrative Court dismissed the claim: detention occurred (confirmed by register and officers) but she failed to prove non-pecuniary damage or abuse; officers’ consistent evidence showed no ill-treatment, and detention under s. 64 MIAA (max. 24 hours) was to clarify a possible offence. The SAC fully agreed in 2011, without addressing Convention arguments.

Relevant domestic law permitted police detention for up to 24 hours on indications of an offence, requiring a prompt written order stating grounds. Damages claims were available after (or with) review of unlawfulness, but SAC case-law was inconsistent on whether mere unlawful detention presumed non-pecuniary harm or required specific (even expert) proof.
001-161735:
The case of Karen Poghosyan v. Armenia (no. 62356/09) concerns the 2009 quashing of a final 2001 judgment recognizing the applicant’s property rights, alleged to violate legal certainty (Article 6) and peaceful enjoyment of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

In 1991 the applicant, without permission, built a 500 sq m structure (shop/storage plus unfinished construction) on an unused 1,000 sq m plot in a Yerevan suburb. He occupied and used the property openly for more than ten years.

In 2001 he brought non-contentious proceedings in the Shengavit District Court seeking ownership of the building by acquisitive prescription (Civil Code Art. 187) and a right of use over the land. On 8 June 2001 the court granted both claims, finding no registered owners and good-faith, open, continuous possession exceeding ten years. No appeal was lodged within the 15-day limit, so the judgment became final.

A State Real Estate Registry certificate of 9 April 2002 confirmed building ownership and a 99-year lease of the land (Land Code Art. 118 § 4). On 20 May 2003 the applicant paid the cadastral value (AMD 1,465,500). Land ownership was registered on 22 May 2003. He thereafter paid property taxes on both assets. A 2008 topographic survey commissioned by the Yerevan Mayor’s Office identified him as owner.

A third party’s 16 June 2008 auction purchase of overlapping land prompted inquiries. On 24 February 2009 the Registry informed the Mayor’s Office of the 2001 judgment (letter received 18 March 2009).

On 7 May 2009 the Deputy Prosecutor General appealed the 2001 judgment, arguing that the land had always belonged to the State (Civil Code Art. 168) and was therefore not ownerless, rendering acquisitive prescription inapplicable; the District Court had also failed to join the Registry and Mayor’s Office as parties. Restoration of the appeal time-limit was sought because the Mayor’s Office had been unaware of the judgment until 2009. The Mayor’s Office lodged a similar appeal on 18 May 2009.

The applicant replied that the authorities must have known earlier: he had paid the cadastral value (constituting a direct sale under Land Code Art. 61), continued to pay taxes, and registration itself notified all entities (Law on State Registration of Rights, Art. 6).

On 12 June 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal restored the time-limit (CCP Art. 207 § 5, allowing non-parties three months from actual or constructive knowledge, subject to a 20-year outer limit) and admitted both appeals. On 18 July 2009 it quashed the 2001 judgment, holding that the building was an unauthorised construction on State land (Civil Code Arts. 168 and 188) so that only the State could acquire title. The Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s further appeal inadmissible on 9 September 2009.

Subsequent State proceedings annulled the applicant’s registered titles.

These facts—eight years of reliance on a final judgment, official registrations, substantial payment and tax collection, followed by a late appeal by previously uninvolved State bodies—form the core of the alleged breaches of legal certainty and property rights.

The case of Karen Poghosyan v. Armenia (Application no. 62356/09) concerns the 2009 quashing of a final 2001 judgment that had recognised the applicant’s property rights, which he alleged violated legal certainty (res judicata) and his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

In 1991 the applicant, without permission, built a 500 sq m structure (shop/storage plus unfinished construction) on an unused 1,000 sq m plot in a Yerevan suburb. He used the property openly for ten years. In 2001 he brought non-contentious proceedings in the Shengavit District Court seeking ownership of the building by acquisitive prescription (Civil Code Art. 187) and a right of use over the land.

On 8 June 2001 the District Court granted the claim, finding that the building had no registered owner and that the applicant had possessed it in good faith, openly and continuously for more than ten years. No appeal was filed within the 15-day statutory period and the judgment became final. On 9 April 2002 the State Real Estate Registry issued an ownership certificate for the building and recorded a 99-year lease of the land (Land Code Art. 118 § 4). On 20 May 2003 the applicant paid the cadastral value (AMD 1,465,500) and, pursuant to Art. 118 § 7, obtained registered ownership of the plot itself on 22 May 2003. He thereafter paid property taxes on both assets.

In July 2008 a municipal topographic survey still listed the applicant as owner. In November 2008 a third party who had purchased an adjoining plot at auction discovered an overlap and wrote to the Yerevan Mayor’s Office. Correspondence ensued with the Real Estate Registry. On 24 February 2009 the Registry informed the Mayor’s Office (letter received 18 March 2009) that the applicant’s rights derived from the 2001 judgment.

On 7 May 2009 the Deputy Prosecutor General, invoking the State’s pecuniary interest (CCP Art. 37), appealed the 2001 judgment out of time. He argued that the land had always been State property, so acquisitive-prescription rules were inapplicable (wrong articles of the Civil Code had been used) and that the Mayor’s Office and Registry should have been joined as parties. The Mayor’s Office filed a parallel appeal on 18 May 2009, claiming it first learned of the judgment from the 24 February letter. Both requested restoration of the time-limit under the post-2008 version of CCP Art. 207 § 5 (three months from actual or constructive knowledge for non-parties).

The applicant replied that the Mayor’s Office had itself alienated the land to him in 2003, received payment, levied taxes thereafter, and was deemed notified of the registered rights by the Law on State Registration of Rights. The authorities therefore could not plausibly claim ignorance until 2009.

On 12 June 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal restored the time-limit, finding the motions “substantiated.” On 18 July 2009 it quashed the 2001 judgment and dismissed the original claim, holding that the structure was an unauthorised construction on State land (Civil Code Arts. 168 and 188) of which only the State could become owner. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law as inadmissible on 9 September 2009. Subsequent proceedings initiated by the authorities then annulled the applicant’s registered titles.

The eight-year delay, the restoration of an expired time-limit despite evidence of earlier official knowledge, and the subsequent loss of both building and land constitute the core factual matrix of the alleged violations of legal certainty and property rights.

**Case of Karen Poghosyan v. Armenia (App. no. 62356/09, ECtHR, 31 March 2016)**

The applicant, an Armenian national born in 1969 and living in Yerevan, complained that the 2009 quashing of a final 8 June 2001 District Court judgment violated the principle of legal certainty (Article 6) and his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1). The Court communicated those complaints; the rest of the application was inadmissible.

In 1991 the applicant built, without permission, a 500 sq. m. structure (shop/storage plus unfinished construction) on a 1,000 sq. m. unused suburban plot in Yerevan that he had cleaned at his own expense. He used the property openly for more than ten years.

In 2001 he brought special (non-contentious) proceedings in the Shengavit District Court seeking recognition of ownership of the building by acquisitive prescription under Civil Code Article 187 and a right of use of the land. On 8 June 2001 the court granted the claims, finding no registered owners and that the applicant had possessed and used the property openly, in good faith and continuously for over ten years. No appeal was lodged within the 15-day time-limit, so the judgment became final.

On 9 April 2002 the State Real Estate Registry issued a certificate confirming the applicant’s ownership of the building and, pursuant to Land Code Article 118 § 4, a 99-year lease of the land. On 20 May 2003 he paid the cadastral value (AMD 1,465,500) under Article 118 § 7 and acquired full ownership of the plot; this was registered on 22 May 2003. He thereafter paid property tax regularly. A July 2008 topographic survey conducted for the Yerevan Mayor’s Office recorded him as owner.

In November 2008 a third party who had bought an overlapping plot at auction in June 2008 informed the Mayor’s Office of the conflict. After correspondence, the Registry wrote to the Mayor’s Office on 24 February 2009 (received 18 March 2009) enclosing the 2001 judgment and confirming that the applicant’s rights had been registered on its basis.

On 7 May 2009 the Deputy Prosecutor General appealed the 2001 judgment, arguing that the land was State (public) property under Civil Code Article 168, not ownerless, so acquisitive-prescription rules (Articles 178 and 187) did not apply; the building was an unauthorised construction under Article 188, of which only the State could become owner. Procedurally, the District Court had wrongly used special proceedings and had failed to join the Registry and the Mayor’s Office (the authority managing Yerevan public land). Restoration of the expired appeal time-limit was sought on the ground that the Mayor’s Office had been unaware of the judgment until 2009 and the Prosecutor’s Office had learned of it only from the Mayor’s February letter. The Mayor’s Office lodged a similar appeal on 18 May 2009, claiming it first learned of the judgment from the 24 February Registry letter.

The applicant replied that the Mayor’s Office had known of his title through the 2003 direct sale (Land Code Article 61), subsequent tax collection, and the constructive-notice effect of registration under the Law on State Registration of Rights in Respect of Property (Article 6).

On 12 June 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal admitted the late appeals under Code of Civil Procedure Article 207 § 5, accepting that the appellants had only recently become aware of the judgment. On 18 July 2009 it quashed the 2001 judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim, holding that the first-instance court had misapplied the law: the land was State property and the building unauthorised, so only the State could acquire ownership. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law as inadmissible on 9 September 2009. Subsequent proceedings brought by the authorities resulted in annulment of the applicant’s registrations.

These facts—the eight-year finality of the 2001 judgment, the applicant’s subsequent payments, registrations and tax compliance, the authorities’ late appeals based on claimed unawareness, and the quashing that extinguished his title—form the core of the alleged breaches of legal certainty and property rights.

The case of Paić v. Croatia originated in an application (no. 47082/12) lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 July 2012 by Zoran Paić, a Croatian national born in 1974 and residing in Šibenik. Represented by lawyer A. Giljanović, Paić alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention, specifically that he had been denied a fair trial because he had no opportunity to question the sole prosecution witness in criminal proceedings against him.

The relevant events began on 12 July 2005 in Betina, Croatia. E.R., a tourist from the Czech Republic, later claimed that after her children threw water-filled balloons at Paić, he approached the house where her family was staying. Through a window she allegedly saw him steal her mobile telephone from a table on the terrace. She and her stepdaughter followed him home and demanded the phone’s return, which he denied taking. On 26 August 2005 the Šibenik Municipal State Attorney’s Office opened an investigation into the suspected theft.

On 20 September 2005 an investigating judge heard Paić, who denied the accusation. He confirmed the balloon incident, stated that he had knocked on the house door without response, and then returned home, where two women later asked for the phone (which he again denied taking). In response to a Croatian request for international legal assistance, the Chomutovo County Court in the Czech Republic heard E.R. on 9 June 2006. She repeated her account of witnessing the theft through the window and confronting Paić.

Paić was indicted on 9 November 2006 before the Šibenik Municipal Court. During the trial he testified on 18 May 2010, reiterating his earlier denial and attributing the incident to a dispute over the children’s behaviour. His former wife, called as a witness, essentially corroborated his version. At a hearing on 27 October 2010 the court decided, over Paić’s objection, to admit the written record of E.R.’s 2006 statement without examining her in person.

On 28 October 2010 the Municipal Court convicted Paić of theft under Article 216 of the Criminal Code and imposed a four-month suspended prison sentence. Guilt was based solely on E.R.’s untested statement. The court invoked Article 331 § 1(12) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing the four-year delay since her testimony, the unlikelihood of new relevant facts, the approaching July 2011 limitation period, and the fact that she was a foreign national whose appearance would unnecessarily prolong proceedings. It found her account “credible and truthful” and saw no motive for her to accuse Paić falsely.

Paić appealed on 28 January 2011, arguing that E.R. had never been summoned and that he had been unable to question her; he also noted that the telephone had never been found in his possession. On 3 March 2011 the Šibenik County Court dismissed the appeal, endorsing the first-instance reasoning and observing that no search of Paić’s home had even been conducted. On 13 May 2011 Paić lodged a constitutional complaint asserting a fair-trial violation. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 8 December 2011 (served 12 January 2012).

Domestic law included Article 29 of the Constitution (fair trial and the right to question prosecution witnesses) and Code of Criminal Procedure provisions allowing written witness records to be read only in limited circumstances (death, untraceability, etc.). The Supreme Court had previously held that conviction based on an untested witness statement obtained without defence participation violated Article 6 § 3(d). The conviction thus rested exclusively on hearsay from a witness whom Paić never confronted, despite his consistent denial and the absence of any other incriminating evidence.

The case of Paić v. Croatia (no. 47082/12) originated in an application by Croatian national Zoran Paić, born 1974 and resident in Šibenik, alleging a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. Specifically, he complained that he had been denied any opportunity to question the sole prosecution witness whose evidence formed the exclusive basis for his conviction of theft.

E.R., a tourist from the Czech Republic, alleged that after her children threw water-filled balloons at the applicant, he approached the holiday house where she was staying; she claimed to have seen him, through a window, take her mobile telephone from a table on the terrace. She and her stepdaughter then followed him to his home and demanded the phone’s return, which he denied having taken.

The applicant consistently denied the theft. Questioned by an investigating judge of the Šibenik County Court on 20 September 2005, he stated that he had merely knocked at the door after the balloon incident, received no answer, and left. Later two young women had come to his house asking for the telephone; he told them he had not taken it. His former wife later gave evidence at trial that corroborated this account in substance.

An investigation was opened by the Šibenik Municipal State Attorney’s Office on 26 August 2005. In response to a request for international legal assistance, E.R. was heard on 9 June 2006 by the Chomutovo County Court in the Czech Republic; her statement repeated the account summarised above. The applicant was indicted on 9 November 2006.

At trial before the Šibenik Municipal Court the applicant again gave evidence on 18 May 2010, maintaining his innocence. On 27 October 2010 the court decided, over the applicant’s objection, to admit the written record of E.R.’s 2006 statement without examining her in person. It cited the lapse of more than four years, the unlikelihood of obtaining new relevant information, the approaching expiry of the limitation period in July 2011, and the delay that would be caused by summoning a foreign witness.

The following day the court convicted the applicant of theft (Criminal Code, Article 216) and imposed a four-month prison sentence suspended for one year. Guilt was based solely on E.R.’s statement, which the court found “credible and truthful” because she had no reason “to blame the accused without basis.”

On appeal the applicant argued that E.R. had never been summoned and that he had therefore been unable to question her; he also noted that the telephone had never been found in his possession and that his home had not even been searched. The Šibenik County Court dismissed the appeal on 3 March 2011, holding that the first-instance court’s reasons for reading the statement were sound, that defence rights had not been violated, and that the conviction stood even without recovery of the phone.

A constitutional complaint lodged on 13 May 2011, reiterating the inability to examine the only prosecution witness, was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded by the Constitutional Court on 8 December 2011. The application to the European Court of Human Rights followed on 9 July 2012.

These facts centre on the admission of untested hearsay from the sole accusing witness, the court’s justifications based on delay and limitation, and the domestic courts’ rejection of the applicant’s complaints that he had been deprived of the opportunity to challenge that decisive evidence.

The case of Paić v. Croatia (Application no. 47082/12) concerns Zoran Paić, a Croatian national born in 1974 and resident in Šibenik. He alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the inability to question the sole prosecution witness against him.

On 12 July 2005 in Betina, Croatia, Czech tourist E.R. reported that her mobile telephone had been stolen. Her children had thrown water-filled balloons at Paić, who then approached the house where she was staying. Through a window, she claimed to have seen him take the phone from a table on the terrace. She and her stepdaughter followed him home and demanded its return, but he denied taking it.

Croatian authorities opened an investigation on 26 August 2005. On 20 September 2005, an investigating judge heard Paić, who denied the theft. He stated that after the balloon incident he knocked at the house but received no answer and left. Later, two women asked for the phone, which he again denied taking. Via international legal assistance, E.R. gave a statement on 9 June 2006 before a Czech court, repeating her account of seeing Paić steal the phone.

Paić was indicted on 9 November 2006. At trial in the Šibenik Municipal Court, he testified on 18 May 2010, reiterating his denial and attributing the dispute to the children's behaviour. His former wife gave evidence supporting his version. On 27 October 2010 the court admitted E.R.'s 2006 statement as evidence without calling her, despite Paić's objection. The next day it convicted him of theft and imposed a four-month prison sentence suspended for one year. Guilt rested solely on E.R.'s unchallenged statement, which the court deemed credible; it noted no motive for her to accuse him falsely. The court justified reading the statement because it was more than four years old (so her memory would have been fresher then), the prosecution would become time-barred in July 2011, and summoning a foreign witness would unnecessarily prolong proceedings.

Paić appealed, arguing he had never been able to question E.R. and that the phone had never been found in his possession. On 3 March 2011 the Šibenik County Court dismissed the appeal. It endorsed the first-instance reasons and observed that the police had never searched Paić's home (a procedural error) but that this did not undermine the finding of guilt.

On 13 May 2011 Paić lodged a constitutional complaint claiming a denial of the opportunity to examine the decisive witness. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 8 December 2011; the decision was served on 12 January 2012. Paić then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 9 July 2012.

The conviction therefore depended entirely on a pre-trial statement given abroad by a witness who was never summoned or examined at trial, despite the applicant's persistent objections and the availability of domestic rules permitting the reading of such statements only in limited circumstances (death, untraceability, or similar obstacles). No search of the applicant's home had occurred, and no other corroborating evidence was adduced. These facts formed the core of the alleged breach of the right to examine witnesses under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d).
001-162761:
The case of Babajanov v. Turkey (Application no. 49867/08) concerns an Uzbek national who fled persecution and was forcibly removed from Turkey to Iran in 2008 while his asylum claim remained pending. Born in 1975, the applicant left Uzbekistan in 1999 after police pressure linked to his Islamic practices; he feared imprisonment and torture, and his name appeared on a 2003 Uzbek Interior Ministry “wanted” list for attempting to overthrow the constitutional order. He travelled through Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan before reaching Iran in 2005, where UNHCR recognised him as a refugee. In 2007, facing Iranian deportation threats, he entered Turkey illegally via Van on 18 November, applied to UNHCR in Ankara, obtained an asylum-seeker certificate in Van, registered with local police and received a temporary residence permit valid until 24 September 2008, subject to thrice-weekly reporting.

On 12 September 2008, while reporting at Van police headquarters, the applicant and 28 other Uzbek (and Afghan) asylum seekers were detained, their documents, money and phones confiscated, and they were driven to an unmarked mountainous border point and forced to walk into Iran. He alleged beatings and threats (including of rape against women and girls). In Iran the group was immediately seized by smugglers who demanded a US$5,000 ransom; after payment they walked back across the border to Yüksekova and re-entered Turkey illegally. On 11 October 2008 police attempted a second round-up of the same group; the applicant escaped only because officers lacked his correct address. He has since lived in hiding, unable to approach Turkish authorities or instruct a lawyer (lacking identity papers for a power of attorney) for fear of further expulsion. UNHCR has continued to examine his claim but he has received no decision from the Turkish authorities.

The Government maintained that the applicant had told officials he already held UNHCR refugee status in Iran, that he had left Van without permission, and that he was lawfully returned to a “safe third country” after an assessment under the 1951 Refugee Convention, the ECHR, the UN Convention against Torture and domestic law. They denied any deprivation of liberty or confiscation of documents.

Independent reports corroborated the events. Council of Europe Human Rights Commissioner Thomas Hammarberg, the US State Department, Amnesty International and UNHCR all recorded the September (and subsequent October) collective expulsion of UNHCR-recognised Uzbek refugees, including ill-treatment at the border and the risk of onward refoulement to Uzbekistan. NGOs and a Turkish parliamentarian publicly condemned the action as lacking legal basis and possibly politically motivated. Turkish official replies merely confirmed that Iran was treated as a safe third country.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints of a real risk of torture or inhuman treatment (direct or chain refoulement), unlawful detention and expulsion without procedural safeguards, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

The case of Babajanov v. Turkey (Application no. 49867/08) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an Uzbek national, Mohammad Kuranbay Babajanov (born 1975), who alleged violations arising from his treatment by Turkish authorities, including a forced deportation to Iran in 2008 and related risks of further removal. The applicant had fled Uzbekistan in 1999 after police suspected him of anti-constitutional activities linked to his Islamic beliefs and practices. He feared persecution, imprisonment, and torture, similar to that suffered by fellow Muslims. Supporting this, a 2003 list compiled by the Moscow-based Human Rights Centre “Memorial” from Uzbek Interior Ministry documents named him as charged under Article 159 § 4 of the Uzbekistan Criminal Code for attempting to violently overthrow the constitutional order.

From Tajikistan he travelled via Afghanistan and Pakistan, arriving in Iran in 2005. There he applied to UNHCR in Zahedan for refugee status and lived without major incident for two years. In 2007, facing deportation threats from Iranian authorities (reportedly over living-condition disputes), he and other Uzbek asylum seekers fled to Turkey, entering illegally via Van on 18 November 2007. He applied to UNHCR in Ankara, was referred to its Van office, received an asylum-seeker certificate, registered with Van police, and obtained a temporary residence permit valid until 24 September 2008, with a requirement to report three times weekly.

On 12 September 2008 the applicant attended the police station for his routine signature. He and some 28 other asylum seekers (mainly Uzbeks) were detained; their documents, money and telephones were confiscated. That evening they were driven to the border and forcibly deported to Iran. The applicant alleged ill-treatment and threats by police during the operation. Once in Iran the group was seized by people-smugglers who demanded a US$5,000 ransom; after payment they were released near Yüksekova and re-entered Turkey illegally. On 11 October 2008 police collected several of the same Uzbeks from their homes and deported them again; the applicant escaped because officers lacked his correct address.

The applicant has since lived in hiding in Turkey, unable to approach authorities for fear of further deportation. His UNHCR refugee claim remained pending (with interviews in 2013–2014). He could not obtain identity documents or appoint a lawyer. NGOs (including Amnesty International), UNHCR and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights documented the 12 September collective expulsion as unlawful, noting the deportees held valid residence permits, alleged beatings and rape threats, and the risk of onward refoulement to Uzbekistan. A second deportation of the group occurred in October 2008. UNHCR had requested Turkey to regularise their status.

The Turkish Government stated that the applicant had informed authorities he already held UNHCR refugee status in Iran. After leaving Van without permission in February 2008 and returning in August, his claim was assessed under refugee-convention and human-rights instruments and he was removed to Iran as a “safe third country.” Officials denied any deprivation of liberty or confiscation of documents. A police-military record confirmed the 12 September removal of 29 Uzbek and Afghan nationals.

These facts formed the core of complaints concerning collective expulsion, absence of procedural safeguards, alleged ill-treatment during removal, and ongoing risk of refoulement to Iran or Uzbekistan, where the applicant claimed a real risk of torture or persecution. The Court later examined victim status regarding threatened future deportation and requested further observations after Turkey’s 2014 Foreigners and International Protection Act.

The applicant, an Uzbek national born in 1975, fled Uzbekistan in 1999 amid police pressure over his Islamic practices, fearing persecution, imprisonment and torture. A 2003 list compiled by the NGO Memorial from Uzbek interior ministry sources named him as charged under Article 159 § 4 of the Uzbek Criminal Code (attempted violent overthrow of the constitutional order). He transited Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan before reaching Iran in 2005, where UNHCR recognised him as a refugee; he lived in Zahedan for two years. In 2007, facing deportation threats linked to disputes over living conditions, he and other Uzbek asylum-seekers left Iran.

He entered Turkey illegally via Van on 18 November 2007, applied to UNHCR in Ankara, was referred to Van, received an asylum-seeker certificate, registered with police and obtained a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008, with a weekly reporting obligation. On 12 September 2008, while reporting for signature, he and 28 other Uzbek and Afghan nationals were detained, their documents, money and phones confiscated, and driven to the Iranian border that evening. They were forcibly expelled on foot; the applicant alleged beatings and rape threats. After crossing, the group was seized by smugglers who demanded USD 5 000; ransom was paid via contacts in Turkey and they walked back, re-entering illegally.

On 11 October 2008 police again collected several of the same group from their homes and deported them to Iran; the applicant escaped because police lacked his address. NGOs (including Amnesty International), UNHCR, the Van Bar Association and a parliamentarian publicly condemned the operations as unlawful collective expulsions of persons holding valid permits, motivated by political rapprochement with Uzbekistan. Parliamentary and gubernatorial replies asserted that Iran was a “safe third country” and the removals complied with law.

UNHCR later confirmed the September 2008 deportation as illegal and asked Turkey to regularise the group pending refugee-status determination. The applicant has lived in hiding since 2008, interviewed by UNHCR in 2013–2014 but never informed of any Turkish asylum decision. He dares not approach the authorities for fear of further removal and cannot issue a power of attorney for lack of identity documents.

The Government maintained that the applicant had informed them of prior UNHCR status in Iran, left Van without permission, and was lawfully returned to that “safe third country”; they denied detention or confiscation of documents. A 2009 Council of Europe Commissioner report, a US State Department report and Amnesty statements corroborated the round-ups, ill-treatment and refoulement risk, noting that UNHCR-recognised refugees and registered asylum-seekers had been returned to Iran, from where they feared onward expulsion to Uzbekistan.

These facts underpin complaints of unlawful collective expulsion, risk of ill-treatment in Uzbekistan (or via Iran), ill-treatment and arbitrary detention during removal, and absence of an effective remedy or legal status in Turkey.
