**CASE OF TOPALLAJ v. ALBANIA (Application no. 32913/03), ECtHR (First Section), Judgment of 21 April 2016 (final 21 July 2016)**

The applicant, Marketin Topallaj (born 1951, later a US citizen living in the USA), alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair trial) and Article 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). He acted as a third party or contracting party in lengthy Albanian property restitution and related civil proceedings.

In 1995–1996, the Tirana District Court recognised inherited property rights of certain landowners over 24 hectares of land and a petrol station’s installations and fuel tanks. The applicant concluded agreements (January–February 1996) with one landowner (acting for the heirs) to finance privatisation and exercise a right of first refusal, with plans for a joint company. On 23 May 1996 he signed a notarised sales contract purchasing nearly all the tanks and installations for USD 100,000 (allegedly paid); he obtained a Mortgage Office property certificate registering title. Separate loan agreements (USD 200,000) were also signed.

A Commission on Property Restitution initially refused restitution (land outside city boundaries). On 24 April 1996 the District Court quashed this, allocated 56,500 sq m to the landowners, and ordered restoration of the installations (value under 20% of the land) at no cost. Title was registered. The station was later expropriated. Multiple State challenges to the landowners’ rights (1996–1998) failed or were discontinued; the applicant participated as a third party. A 1998 Ministry challenge was dismissed by the Supreme Court (1999). Supervisory reviews were accepted (2000), leading to remittals. After three further sets of proceedings involving remittals, the landowners’ rights were ultimately upheld (final Constitutional Court decision 20 September 2009). In 2007 an agency recognised rights over the full 24 hectares and ordered compensation for the unallocated portion (subject of a separate application).

In October 2002 the landowners sued to declare the 1996 agreements and contract absolutely null and void (fictitious, no legal effect). Proceedings were discontinued (2005) for non-attendance. A fresh claim (April 2005, signed only by their lawyer) succeeded. The District Court (18 April 2006) found the transactions fictitious under Civil Code Article 92(ç): they were concluded while the State still administered the property (no transfer to landowners yet), installations had been restored free, no joint company formed, and no loans actually advanced. It ordered erasure of the applicant’s 1996 registration.

The applicant appealed, alleging bias (recusal requests, disciplinary issues involving a judge, bench composition), time-bar, defective representation (power of attorney limited/outdated, claim unsigned by landowners), non-admission of evidence and counterclaims, failure to summon his spouse as co-owner, and excess of the claim. The Court of Appeal (25 May 2007, three judges including two from the Military Court of Appeal after recusals) upheld the finding of fictitiousness, rejected a limitation period for absolute nullity, and dismissed his arguments; one judge dissented, citing lack of landowner signatures, real party intent (evidenced by later powers of attorney), time-bar, and unreasoned rejection of evidence. The Supreme Court stayed execution then declared the appeal inadmissible (25 January 2010, no valid grounds). The Constitutional Court rejected an extensive appeal (22 November 2010), finding no impartiality issue (prior involvement in unrelated cases) and holding that remaining complaints concerned facts/outcome within lower-court jurisdiction.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: protracted, remitted proceedings with recusal, composition, evidence-admission, representation, reasoning, and access-to-court issues (Articles 6 § 1 and 13), plus interference with registered property rights via annulment of contracts (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1). Domestic law distinguished absolute nullity (no limitation period, no legal effects from inception) from relative invalidity.

The case of Topallaj v. Albania (Application no. 32913/03) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 August 2003 by Marketin Topallaj, an Albanian national (later a U.S. citizen) born in 1951. He alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court delivered its judgment on 21 April 2016.

In late 1995 and early 1996 the Tirana District Court recognised inherited property rights of certain landowners over a 24-hectare plot and the installations and fuel tanks of a petrol station situated on it. The applicant, acting through his company, entered into two agreements (January and February 1996) and a notarised sales contract (23 May 1996) with one landowner acting for all heirs. Under the agreements the applicant would finance privatisation of the installations in return for ownership; the sales contract transferred almost all of those installations to him for USD 100,000 (which the contract stated had been paid). The Mortgage Office issued him a property certificate the same day. Separate loan agreements for USD 200,000 were also signed.

On 24 April 1996 the District Court, quashing a Commission decision, allocated the landowners 56,500 sq m of the land and ordered restoration of the installations (valued at less than 20 per cent of the land) free of charge. That judgment became final. The landowners later obtained recognition of rights over the remaining land and an order for compensation, but the applicant’s own title derived from the 1996 contracts.

Between 1996 and 2009 the landowners’ title was repeatedly challenged by State bodies, giving rise to multiple remittals, supervisory-review applications and rehearings before the District Court, Court of Appeal, Supreme Court and Constitutional Court. The applicant participated as a third party. The courts ultimately upheld the landowners’ rights.

In parallel, the landowners themselves sought annulment of the 1996 agreements and sales contract as fictitious and absolutely null. A first action (2002) was discontinued for non-attendance. A second action (2005) proceeded despite the applicant’s challenges to the composition of the bench, requests to stay the case pending a criminal forgery complaint, counter-claims about lack of proper authorisation of the landowners’ lawyer, time-bar and fictitious nature of the loans, and numerous requests for evidence. On 18 April 2006 the District Court declared the instruments null, holding that the property had still been State-administered when the contracts were signed, no joint company had been formed and no money had changed hands. It ordered erasure of the applicant’s register entry.

The Court of Appeal (25 May 2007), sitting with three military judges appointed after all its own judges recused themselves, upheld the decision. One judge dissented, finding the transactions genuine, the claim time-barred and the applicant’s evidence improperly rejected. The Supreme Court declared the applicant’s 72-ground appeal inadmissible (25 January 2010) for lack of valid grounds. The Constitutional Court dismissed an 83-page appeal (22 November 2010), holding that complaints about impartiality, reasoning, assessment of evidence and length of proceedings either lacked foundation or concerned matters of fact outside its jurisdiction.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of unfair and excessively lengthy proceedings (including issues of tribunal established by law, impartiality, admission of evidence and lack of reasons), absence of an effective remedy, and unlawful interference with his registered property rights.

The applicant, Marketin Topallaj (later a US citizen who renounced Albanian nationality), alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair trial), Article 13 (effective remedy) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property) arising from Albanian proceedings over inherited land and petrol-station installations.

In 1995–96 the Tirana District Court recognised landowners’ inherited rights over 24 ha of land and the installations/fuel tanks thereon. On that basis the applicant’s company concluded two 1996 agreements with one landowner (acting for all heirs) to finance privatisation in exchange for ownership of the installations, followed by a notarised sales contract of 23 May 1996 transferring almost all installations to the applicant for USD 100 000 (registered that day). Two contemporaneous loan agreements for USD 200 000 were also signed. The landowners then obtained a final 24 April 1996 District Court judgment allocating them 56 500 m² and restoring the installations free of charge (their value being under 20 % of the land). A mortgage certificate confirmed their title; the site was later expropriated.

State bodies repeatedly challenged the landowners’ title (1996–99). After unsuccessful first-instance and Supreme Court proceedings, two 1999–2000 applications for supervisory review were accepted by the Supreme Court’s Joint Benches, remitting the cases. After further remittals (2003, 2005) the landowners ultimately prevailed in 2009. The applicant participated throughout as a third party. A 2007 administrative decision later recognised a larger 24 ha claim, with unpaid compensation forming a separate application.

In 2002 the landowners sued to have the 1996 contracts declared absolutely null (fictitious under Civil Code Art. 92(ç)). Those proceedings were discontinued for non-appearance. A fresh 2005 action (signed only by their lawyer) succeeded: on 18 April 2006 the District Court held the contracts fictitious because the installations were still State-administered, no joint company had been formed and the loans were simulated; it ordered erasure of the applicant’s registration. The applicant’s recusal requests, counter-claims (including time-bar and defective power of attorney) and 24 evidence motions were rejected.

The Court of Appeal (reconstituted with three Military Court of Appeal judges after the regular bench recused itself) upheld the judgment on 25 May 2007, finding no statutory limitation for absolute nullity. A dissenting judge considered the claim unsigned, time-barred, lacking standing and unsupported by the evidence of the parties’ subsequent conduct. The Supreme Court declared the applicant’s 72-ground appeal inadmissible (25 January 2010) for lack of valid grounds. The Constitutional Court rejected an 83-page appeal (22 November 2010) as concerning factual assessment and showing no impartiality defect.

The applicant complained of excessive length (multiple remittals spanning 1996–2011), a tribunal not established by law, rejected recusals and evidence, unreasoned decisions, and the consequent loss of his registered title without effective domestic redress.
001-162419:
The case of Cerf v. Turkey (Application no. 12938/07) arose from the 3 October 1994 killing of the applicant’s husband, Sefer Cerf, a HADEP district leader in Yüreğir, Adana, and the investigation that followed. The applicant alleged that the killing was carried out by or with the collusion of state agents (in violation of the substantive limb of Article 2 of the Convention) and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation (procedural limb of Article 2).

Sefer Cerf and his family had faced years of harassment, intimidation and threats from plainclothes police officers linked to his political activities. On 1 October 1994 a gunman fired at their 11-year-old son outside the family home, narrowly missing him. Two days later Sefer Cerf left home at around 8 a.m. and joined fellow HADEP board member R.Ç. on the terrace of a town-centre café. Eyewitnesses heard six gunshots and saw two men with pistols flee. Sefer Cerf died at the scene; R.Ç. died while being taken to hospital; a third man was wounded in the foot by a ricochet. No police or anti-terrorism vehicles were present in an area they normally patrolled, the authorities arrived only after a considerable delay, and telephone lines had been cut, preventing an ambulance from being called.

Police later collected six spent cartridges and two deformed bullets. Witnesses, including Sait Macir (who helped the victims), were questioned more about political connections than the shooting; Macir’s café was closed and he was later killed in a similar attack. Ahmet Dizman, who had tried to take R.Ç. to hospital, was detained, beaten (his jaw broken) and threatened. Harassment of the applicant’s family continued, including surveillance, threatening notes thrown into their garden, and the detention and questioning of their daughter.

A standing search order was issued on 20 October 1994, but no suspects were identified until Hizbullah operations in 2000. M.D. was arrested on 19 January 2000, confessed to the killing, and gave a detailed account; he was taken to the scene. Further arrests followed (H.T., A.A., A.Y., K.G. and others). The file was transferred to Diyarbakır. When the applicant sought documents in 2005 the prosecutor supplied only a limited selection, citing confidentiality and stating that the papers would be used against Turkey. Later requests produced similarly restricted information.

Criminal proceedings against several Hizbullah members ensued. A.A. was convicted (sentence reduced on appeal because he had been a minor) and served periods of detention. M.D. and K.G. received life sentences in 2009 (upheld 2011) for this and numerous other killings, but were released in January 2011 after exceeding the statutory detention limit and fled to Syria; arrest warrants were later issued. M.A.O. received a life sentence and remains in prison; A.Y. was sentenced to 12 years and 6 months. The suspects subsequently retracted their confessions, alleging they had been extracted under torture.

The Government maintained that no prior complaints of police harassment had been lodged, that the investigation began immediately (scene examination, forensics, witness statements, post-mortem), and that the later Hizbullah prosecutions demonstrated effectiveness. The applicant contended that the circumstances of the shooting, the pattern of prior and subsequent police harassment, the long initial inactivity, the restricted access given to the family, the reliance on later-retracted confessions and the eventual release of two of the principal convicts all pointed to state involvement or collusion and an ineffective investigation.

The case of Cerf v. Turkey (Application no. 12938/07) arose from an application lodged on 15 March 2007 by Yaşar Cerf, a Turkish national born in 1946 and living in Adana. She alleged under Article 2 of the Convention that her husband, Sefer Cerf, had been killed by state authorities or persons acting with their aid, and that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the killing.

Sefer Cerf was the district leader and administrative board member of HADEP (People’s Democracy Party, later dissolved) in Yüreğir, Adana. In the years before 1994, he and his family faced harassment, intimidation, and threats from plainclothes police officers linked to his political activities. On 1 October 1994, a shot was fired at the applicant’s 11-year-old son outside their home, narrowly missing him.

On 3 October 1994, around 8 a.m., Sefer Cerf left home for a café in the town centre. Eyewitnesses reported that he sat on the terrace with HADEP colleague R.Ç. Six gunshots were heard; two men with pistols then fled. Sefer Cerf died at the scene. R.Ç. was fatally wounded and died en route to hospital, while a bystander, S.S., was injured in the foot by a ricochet. Unusually, no police or anti-terrorism vehicles were present, despite regular patrols. Authorities were slow to arrive, and telephone lines had been cut, preventing calls for an ambulance.

Police collected six spent bullet cases and two deformed bullets, took witness statements (including from HADEP board member Sait Macir, who saw the assailants flee), and prepared a scene sketch. The prosecutor concluded an incident-scene investigation that day and conducted a post-mortem, recovering a bullet from the body for forensic analysis. Clothes and other evidence were also seized. On 20 October 1994, the Adana prosecutor issued a standing search order for the perpetrators, requiring periodic updates until the limitation period expired.

Subsequent events included further alleged harassment: Macir was later killed at the same café (30 December 1994); Ahmet Dizman (who tried to take R.Ç. to hospital) was detained, beaten (resulting in a broken jaw), and threatened; and the applicant’s family faced ongoing surveillance, notes threatening her daughter, and her daughter’s detention and questioning about the killing. The applicant claimed no police complaints of prior harassment had been lodged by her or her husband.

Investigation stagnated until 2000, when operations against Hizbullah (an illegal group linked to assassinations of pro-Kurdish figures) led to arrests. On 19 January 2000, M.D. was arrested and confessed to participating in the killings of Sefer Cerf and R.Ç., providing details and implicating others. He was taken to the scene for a “scene report.” H.T., A.Y., A.A., K.G., and others were subsequently arrested. A.A. described K.G.’s leadership role. The file was transferred to Diyarbakır State Security Court (later Assize Court after abolition of security courts). Suspects later retracted confessions, claiming they were extracted under torture.

Criminal proceedings followed. M.D. and K.G. were convicted in a 1,153-page 30 December 2009 judgment (joining cases involving 181 killings) of attempting to undermine the constitutional order and sentenced to life imprisonment (upheld 26 January 2011). They were released on 3 January 2011 after exceeding the 10-year custody limit, fled to Syria, and had arrest warrants issued. A.A. was convicted of Hizbullah membership and attacks (including the killing), initially sentenced to 14 years (quashed due to his age under 18 at the time), then to 5 years 6 months 20 days in 2013; he served periods in detention. M.A.O. received life imprisonment in 2008 (upheld 2009) and remains in prison. A.Y. was sentenced to 12 years 6 months in 2012 (upheld 2013).

The applicant encountered obstacles accessing files: in 2005, the Adana prosecutor provided limited copies citing confidentiality (the investigation covered multiple 1994–1995 killings) and stated documents would be used against Turkey. Further requests in 2006–2007 and 2012 yielded partial information, including the 2009 judgment, but no details on all suspects’ whereabouts.

The Government maintained that no harassment complaints were filed, the scene was promptly processed with evidence secured and witnesses interviewed, and prosecutions resulted from 2000 operations. The facts highlighted delays from 1994 to 2000, limited victim involvement, retractions, and incomplete accountability (e.g., releases and flight), relevant to claims of possible state collusion and investigative shortcomings.

These facts raise issues of possible state involvement or collusion (HADEP context, scene irregularities, police harassment of witnesses/family) and of investigative effectiveness (delayed suspect identification, confession retractions, limited victim access, incomplete sentences).
001-162862:
The case of Răchită v. Romania (Application no. 15987/09) concerned a Romanian national, Doru Răchită (born 1949), who lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 17 March 2009 alleging violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement). He died on 2 May 2009; his son Răzvan Răchită (born 1975) pursued the application.

On 31 October 2002 the Bucharest Commission for the Enforcement of Law no. 18/1991 acknowledged the applicant’s property rights over 350 m² of previously nationalised land on V. Street in Bucharest and granted him possession. An unidentified owner of land opposite the applicant’s plot later erected a fence that encroached onto the public street, significantly reducing its width. The applicant, who intended to build on his land, found that vehicular access was no longer possible; only pedestrian access remained.

In 2007 he applied to the Department of Discipline in Constructions (SDC) attached to the Mayor of Bucharest District No. 5 seeking removal of the encroaching portion of the fence. By letter of 17 September 2007 the SDC dismissed the request, stating that a building permit had been issued to C.M. On 23 November 2007 the applicant wrote to the Mayor of Bucharest and the Bucharest General and Local Councils, informing them that the SDC had misidentified the owner: C.M. occupied an adjoining plot, not the opposite one, and asking them to verify the situation and restore access.

On 22 April 2008 the applicant brought administrative-court proceedings against the Mayor and the two Councils. He sought an order requiring the Mayor to notify the fence’s owner to remove it or, failing compliance, to remove it without consent; alternatively, he asked the Councils to commence expropriation proceedings to widen the road. He stressed that the authorities had never answered his November 2007 requests and had confused his complaint with an unrelated one against C.M.

On 17 June 2008 the Bucharest County Court dismissed the action. It held that the applicant had never identified the neighbour or supplied an address, so the authorities could not be regarded as having refused to act. The Mayor could not issue an order against an unnamed person, and the street served several owners. The court rejected as unnecessary the applicant’s requests for witness evidence, an on-site inspection and an expert report that would have shown the obstruction. It nevertheless rejected the authorities’ arguments that the action was inadmissible or that they lacked standing, because the street formed part of the public domain they administered.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the rejected evidence would have established the owner’s identity, that he had already told officials the fence belonged to the opposite (unidentified) neighbour, and that it was the authorities’ duty, not his, to identify the occupant of empty property lacking a visible postal number. On 15 August 2008 he wrote again to the Public Domain Administration clarifying that the complaint did not concern C.M. On 19 September 2008 that office replied that it had contacted the tax and land-register authorities to identify the owner; the file contains no information on the outcome.

By final judgment of 3 November 2008 the Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It noted that no new evidence had been adduced and that the authorities had filed no observations. Relying on the SDC letter, it treated C.M. as the relevant owner and held that the authorities had not unjustifiably refused to act, being incompetent to issue orders over private property. The applicant had failed to inform the administrative authorities of their alleged identification error. Whether eviction proceedings were appropriate was a matter solely for those authorities.

An urban-planning certificate issued on 22 January 2009 confirmed that construction could be authorised on the land. After inheriting the plot, the applicant’s son sold it on 30 October 2015, reserving all rights arising from the Strasbourg application. He later claimed additional loss (extra tax of EUR 414 and a reduced sale price of EUR 20 725) caused by the absence of road access and utilities.

The alleged violations therefore centred on the domestic courts’ refusal to examine evidence that would have clarified the fence-owner’s identity, their acceptance of an acknowledged administrative error as fatal to the applicant’s claim, and the resulting obstruction of access that prevented the applicant from using, building on or selling his restored property.

He died on 2 May 2009, after which his son Răzvan Răchită pursued the application. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement).

Street in Bucharest and issued him a property title with possession. Subsequently, an unidentified owner of the plot opposite constructed a fence that encroached onto the public street. The error arose from confusion with a similar complaint against C.M. by another resident. On 23 November 2007, the applicant wrote to the Mayor of Bucharest and the Bucharest General and Local Councils, highlighting the SDC’s misidentification (confirmed by a land expert) and requesting removal of the fence to restore access. These authorities provided no substantive response.

On 22 April 2008, the applicant sued the Mayor, General Council, and District No. 5 Local Council in the Bucharest County Court. He sought an order requiring the Mayor to notify the fence owner to remove it (or for authorities to remove it without consent) or, alternatively, for the councils to initiate expropriation proceedings to widen the road. (who had a permit) and replied generally about area development. The court refused the applicant’s requests for testimonial evidence, an onsite investigation, and an expert report as unnecessary. It rejected claims of inadmissibility or lack of standing by the authorities, noting the street was public domain.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the rejected evidence would have identified the owner, that he had informed authorities it was not C.M., that the opposite property was empty with no visible postal number (making identification his duty rather than theirs, per relevant rules), and that the fence blocked vehicular access needed to use or develop the land.

On 15 August 2008, the applicant notified the Public Domain Administration that the complaint concerned the unidentified opposite neighbour, not C.M. On 19 September 2008, that office stated it had contacted the tax and land register to identify the owner, but no outcome appears in the file.

On 3 November 2008, the Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as ill-founded. It relied on the SDC’s 17 September 2007 letter identifying C.M. as the owner and held that authorities had not unjustifiably refused to act, as they lacked competence over private property. It stated that the applicant had failed to inform authorities of the identification error so they could clarify it. The court added that only administrative authorities could assess eviction or similar measures.

The applicant contended that the domestic courts failed to examine the evidence properly, particularly by incorrectly finding he had not notified authorities of the misidentification, denying him a fair hearing. He further alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision obstructed access to his property, breaching his rights to property and freedom of movement by preventing him from using, building on, or selling the land.

In January 2009, an urban planning certificate confirmed that construction could be authorised on the land. The son later sold the land in 2015 (reserving rights from the application) at a reduced price due to lack of access and utilities, incurring extra tax and claiming additional losses.
001-163437:
The case of *Pilav v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 41939/07) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 9 June 2016. It concerned an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the European Convention on Human Rights (general prohibition of discrimination). The applicant, Ilijaz Pilav (born 1964), a Bosniac citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Srebrenica in the Republika Srpska (one of the two Entities established by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement), complained that he was legally barred both from standing as a candidate for the tripartite Presidency and from voting for a Bosniac candidate from his Entity.

Pilav, a politically active member of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina and a former member of the Republika Srpska National Assembly, declared affiliation with the Bosniacs, one of the three “constituent peoples” (alongside Croats and Serbs) recognised by the Constitution. In 2006 he submitted his candidacy for the Presidency elections. On 24 July 2006 the Central Election Commission rejected it, citing Article V of the Constitution and Article 8.1 of the 2001 Election Act: the Presidency member elected from the Republika Srpska must be a Serb, while the Bosniac and Croat members are elected from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. His request for reconsideration was refused on 1 August 2006 and his appeal to the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina was dismissed on 10 August 2006 as contrary to the Constitution and Election Act.

A subsequent constitutional appeal invoking Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 was rejected by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 29 September 2006 (decision AP 2678/06). The majority held that the ethnic-territorial restriction, though limiting, pursued a legitimate aim of preserving the post-war peace, dialogue and the position of the constituent peoples under the Dayton settlement; it was therefore objectively justified and proportionate in the prevailing circumstances. A concurring opinion emphasised that the Constitutional Court could not render an express constitutional provision (Article V) ineffective. A dissent argued that the combination of ethnic and territorial criteria produced unjustified discrimination inconsistent with the equality of constituent peoples throughout the State and with Protocol No. 12.

Pilav renewed his candidacy in 2010; it was again rejected on the same grounds.

The relevant constitutional and statutory framework distinguishes “constituent peoples” from “Others.” Article V of the Constitution provides that the Presidency comprises one Bosniac and one Croat directly elected from the Federation and one Serb directly elected from the Republika Srpska. Voters in each Entity vote only for the member(s) allocated to that Entity. Consequently a Bosniac resident in the Republika Srpska can neither stand for the Presidency from that Entity nor vote for a Bosniac candidate; he may vote only for the Serb member. Analogous restrictions apply to Croats in the Republika Srpska and Serbs in the Federation. These rules were the direct legal basis for the successive rejections of Pilav’s candidacies and formed the core of his discrimination complaint.

The case of Pilav v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 41939/07) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of any right set forth by law. The applicant, Ilijaz Pilav, a Bosniac citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1964, resides in Srebrenica in the Republika Srpska (RS), one of the country's two Entities. He is a member of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina and has held elected positions, including in the RS National Assembly. As a self-declared Bosniac (one of the three “constituent peoples” under the Constitution), he sought to stand for election to the tripartite Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In 2006, Pilav submitted his candidacy for the Presidency elections. On 24 July 2006, the Central Election Commission (CEC) rejected it, citing Article V of the Constitution and Article 8.1 of the Election Act 2001. These provisions require that the Presidency member elected from the RS territory must be a Serb; Bosniacs and Croats may only stand from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while Serbs may only stand from the RS. Voters in each Entity elect one member, so RS voters (including Bosniacs like the applicant) cannot vote for a Bosniac or Croat candidate. The CEC rejected Pilav’s request for reconsideration on 1 August 2006. The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina dismissed his appeal on 10 August 2006, finding the candidacy contrary to the Constitution and Election Act.

Pilav and his party then lodged a constitutional appeal invoking Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. On 29 September 2006, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina (decision AP 2678/06) found no violation. The majority held that the restrictions, though limiting candidacy of Bosniacs and Croats from the RS (and Serbs from the Federation), served a legitimate aim of ensuring representation of the three constituent peoples as agreed in the Dayton Peace Accords, thereby preserving peace and dialogue. They were deemed proportionate given Bosnia and Herzegovina’s post-conflict situation. A concurring opinion emphasised that the Constitutional Court must uphold the Constitution’s express terms, even if they conflict with international standards. A dissenting opinion argued that the ethnic-territorial combination produced unjustified discrimination, inconsistent with the equality of constituent peoples across the entire territory and with Protocol No. 12 and Article 25 of the ICCPR; it called for removing the territorial criterion.

Pilav submitted another candidacy in 2010, which the CEC rejected on 29 July 2010 on identical grounds.

The Constitution distinguishes “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats, Serbs) from “Others.” Only the former may run for the Presidency, which consists of one Bosniac and one Croat elected from the Federation and one Serb from the RS. The Election Act implements this by restricting both candidacy and voting along ethnic and territorial lines. Bosnia and Herzegovina’s post-accession commitments to the Council of Europe included reviewing electoral legislation with Venice Commission assistance. Venice Commission opinions (2005 and 2006) criticised the system as mixing territorial and ethnic criteria in a manner incompatible with Protocol No. 12, excluding members of constituent peoples living in the “wrong” Entity from standing or electing candidates of their affiliation, and recommended reforms to ensure multi-ethnic representation without such discrimination.

These facts form the basis of the alleged discrimination in access to the Presidency on grounds of ethnicity and residence.

**Case of Pilav v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 41939/07), ECtHR (Fifth Section), judgment of 9 June 2016 (final 9 September 2016).**

The applicant, Ilijaz Pilav (born 1964), a Bosniac citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Srebrenica (Republika Srpska), was politically active as a member of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina and held elected posts, including in the Republika Srpska National Assembly. He alleged that domestic law made it impossible for him, as a Bosniac living in the Republika Srpska, to stand as a candidate for the tripartite Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina or to vote for a candidate from his own constituent people. He invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination). The Court communicated only this complaint; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

In 2006 the applicant submitted his candidacy for the Presidency. The Central Election Commission rejected it on 24 July 2006 (and again on reconsideration) because, under Article V of the Constitution and Article 8.1 of the Election Act 2001, the Presidency member elected from the Republika Srpska must be a Serb. The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina dismissed his appeal. On 29 September 2006 the Constitutional Court (decision AP 2678/06) found no violation of Protocol No. 12. The majority held that the restrictions, while limiting Bosniacs and Croats from the Republika Srpska (and Serbs from the Federation) from standing, pursued a legitimate aim of preserving the Dayton Agreement’s ethnic balance and peace; they were proportionate given the country’s post-conflict situation. A concurring opinion stressed that the Constitutional Court could not render an express constitutional provision ineffective. A dissent argued that the combination of ethnic and territorial criteria produced unjustified discrimination inconsistent with the equality of constituent peoples and the State’s multi-ethnic character. The applicant’s 2010 candidacy was likewise rejected.

The Constitution distinguishes “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats, Serbs) from “Others.” Article V provides that the Presidency consists of one Bosniac and one Croat elected from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and one Serb elected from the Republika Srpska. Voters in each Entity vote only for the seat allocated to that Entity. Consequently, only a Serb may be elected from the Republika Srpska, and Republika Srpska voters (including Bosniacs) may vote only for the Serb member. Analogous bars apply to Serbs in the Federation. These rules implement the Dayton Peace Agreement’s power-sharing architecture.

The Venice Commission had repeatedly criticised the arrangement as mixing territorial and ethnic criteria in a manner that excludes members of constituent peoples living in the “wrong” Entity, raising serious compatibility issues with Protocol No. 12. The case thus concerns whether the applicant’s ineligibility, and the related limitation on his voting rights, constituted discrimination in the enjoyment of a right set forth by law.

001-163357:
The case originated in an application by Slobodan Mitrov, a Macedonian national born in 1974 and living in Strumica, against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. He alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention concerning the impartiality of the trial court and equality of arms in criminal proceedings arising from a traffic accident.

On 26 November 2006, the applicant, driving a car, was involved in an accident that killed the 18-year-old daughter of Judge M.A. Judge M.A. served as president of the criminal section of the Strumica Court of First Instance (the trial court). At the relevant time, that section comprised only four judges: M.A., C.K., T.D. and G.M. Judge C.K. had worked at the court as a clerk from 2002 and specifically with Judge M.A. from 2004 until her appointment as a judge in February 2005. Additional judges included investigating judge B.B., Judge V.D. (handling minor offences) and Judge S.D. (on sick leave).

Investigating Judge B.B. opened proceedings against the applicant on 19 January 2007 after examining him in his lawyer’s presence. Between 25 January and 7 February 2007, B.B. heard five eyewitnesses, two experts and the victims’ representative; the applicant’s representative attended only two eyewitness statements. On 8 February 2007, B.B. commissioned an expert report from the Forensic Bureau on the accident’s causes, the applicant’s speed, avoidability and related issues. The Bureau issued its first report on 14 March 2007, relying in part on the earlier witness statements.

The public prosecutor charged the applicant on 20 April 2007 with severe crimes against traffic safety. A three-judge panel presided by T.D. dismissed the applicant’s objection to the indictment on 15 May 2007. In June 2007 the applicant obtained a second, alternative expert report from a private agency.

On 12 July 2007 the applicant applied to the trial-court president for the exclusion of C.K., T.D., G.M. and S.D., citing the death of a criminal-section colleague’s daughter and alleging an unfair, partial investigation by B.B. He also hoped the case would be transferred to another first-instance court. C.K. and T.D. submitted written statements that the death would not influence them. The president dismissed the exclusion applications concerning C.K. and T.D. (finding the statutory conditions unmet) and rejected those concerning G.M. and S.D. as inadmissible because they were not sitting on the case. A further application to exclude T.D., based on his prior role in dismissing the indictment objection, was granted the next day.

The trial proceeded before a panel initially including C.K. (presiding) and later V.D., together with three lay judges. The second expert report was admitted, but the applicant requested examination of the experts who prepared both reports because their findings appeared contradictory. The court instead commissioned a third report from three different Bureau experts, issued on 31 January 2008; one of those experts was later examined. In closing submissions on 5 March 2008 the applicant’s lawyer argued that the court was deciding a case involving a colleague’s daughter’s death and that practice in similar cases required withdrawal to avoid doubts about impartiality.

That same day the trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. It found he had driven at excessive speed while under the influence of alcohol, rejected his claims that the victim had ignored a stop sign or been unbelted, and relied on the third expert report and oral evidence while giving no weight to the second report. It also upheld a compensation claim by Judge M.A., her husband and her other daughter against the applicant’s insurer.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the case should have been transferred to another court, that C.K. had worked for years as clerk to the victim’s mother, that there were grounds for exclusion, that the second report had been ignored without reasoning, and that the third report merely repeated the first and contradicted the second on speed. He requested remittal to a different panel or court. On 24 September 2008 the appellate court dismissed the appeal, increased the sentence to six years, and held the impartiality complaints groundless because of the judges’ statements and the president’s decision. It further stated that the second report had not been court-ordered, that the experts had not been sworn, and that the trial court was not obliged to accept all proposed evidence.

The applicant then sought extraordinary review by the Supreme Court, citing Articles 6 and 8 and complaining that C.K. (former clerk to the victim’s mother, who headed the criminal section) had sat on the case and that transfer to another court had been refused. On 13 January 2009 the Supreme Court dismissed the request, endorsing the lower courts’ findings without further reasoning on alleged bias. Subsequent requests for extraordinary mitigation of sentence were also dismissed.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the trial court lacked objective impartiality owing to the close professional and hierarchical links between the sitting judges and the victim’s mother, and that equality of arms had been breached by the limited participation of the defence during the investigation, the court’s treatment of conflicting expert evidence, and the refusal to transfer the case.

The case of Mitrov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 45959/09) concerns an applicant convicted of causing a fatal traffic accident who alleged violations of Article 6 ECHR due to the trial court's lack of impartiality and a breach of equality of arms.

On 26 November 2006 the applicant, driving a car, was involved in an accident that killed the 18-year-old daughter of Judge M.A. At the time the Strumica Court of First Instance's criminal section comprised only four judges (M.A., C.K., T.D. and G.M.). Judge M.A. was president of that section. Judge C.K. had worked as a clerk assisting M.A. from 2004 until her own appointment as a judge in February 2005.

An investigation was opened on 19 January 2007 by investigating Judge B.B. Between 25 January and 7 February 2007 B.B. heard five eyewitnesses, two experts and the victims' representative; the applicant's lawyer was present for only two of the eyewitness statements. On 8 February B.B. commissioned an expert report from the Forensic Bureau on the accident's causes, the applicant's speed, avoidability and related issues. The first report, issued on 14 March 2007, relied in part on the earlier witness statements.

The applicant was charged on 20 April 2007 with serious traffic offences endangering life and property. A three-judge panel (presided over by T.D.) dismissed his objection to the indictment on 15 May 2007. In June 2007 the applicant obtained a second expert report from a private agency.

On 12 July 2007 the applicant applied to the court's president for the exclusion of C.K., T.D. and other judges, citing the death of their colleague's daughter and the risk of bias, and asked that the case be transferred to another first-instance court. C.K. and T.D. provided written statements that the event would not influence them. The president dismissed the application against them, holding that section 36(2) of the Criminal Proceedings Act (doubts as to impartiality) was not met, and rejected the remainder as inadmissible because those judges were not assigned to the case. A further application succeeded in excluding T.D. on the ground that he had already ruled on the indictment.

The trial continued under C.K. (later joined by V.D.). The second report was admitted on 26 September 2007; the applicant requested examination of the experts who had prepared both reports because of contradictions. On 19 October the court commissioned a third report from different Bureau experts. That report was issued on 31 January 2008; one of its authors was examined on 4 March.

On 5 March 2008 the court convicted the applicant of driving at excessive speed while under the influence of alcohol, sentenced him to four years and six months' imprisonment, dismissed his arguments that the victim had ignored a stop sign and was not wearing a seatbelt, and gave no weight to the second report. It also upheld the compensation claim brought by Judge M.A., her husband and surviving daughter (acknowledged by the applicant's insurer).

On appeal the applicant again argued that the case should have been transferred because of C.K.'s prior working relationship with the victim's mother and the small size of the court, that the second report had been ignored without reasons, and that proposed evidence had been refused. On 24 September 2008 the appellate court dismissed the impartiality complaint by simply referring to the first-instance president's decision, increased the sentence to six years, and held that the second report (not court-commissioned and whose authors had not been sworn) could be disregarded at the trial court's discretion; the court was not obliged to accept every piece of proposed evidence. The Supreme Court later dismissed an extraordinary review request, endorsing the lower courts' reasoning without additional analysis of bias.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 6 violations: the objective appearance of bias arising from the presiding judge's recent professional subordination to the victim's mother (herself a senior colleague in the same tiny section), the refusal to recuse or transfer the case, and the unequal treatment of expert evidence and incomplete defence participation in the investigation.

The case of Mitrov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 45959/09) concerned alleged violations of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the impartiality of the trial court and the principle of equality of arms in criminal proceedings arising from a fatal traffic accident.

The applicant, Slobodan Mitrov, was involved as the driver in a traffic accident on 26 November 2006 in which the 18-year-old daughter of Judge M.A. was killed. At the relevant time, the Strumica Court of First Instance had a small criminal section comprising Judges M.A. (president of the section since 2004), C.K., T.D. and G.M. Judge C.K. had previously served as a court clerk from 2002 and worked directly with Judge M.A. from 2004 until her appointment as a judge in February 2005. Other judges included investigating Judge B.B., Judge V.D. (handling minor offences) and Judge S.D. (on sick leave).

An investigation was opened against the applicant by Judge B.B. on 19 January 2007. Witnesses and experts were heard between January and February 2007, though the applicant’s representative was present for only some statements. A first expert report on the accident’s circumstances was prepared by the Forensic Bureau on 14 March 2007, relying partly on those statements. The applicant was charged in April 2007 with severe crimes against the safety of people and property in traffic. A three-judge panel including Judge T.D. dismissed his objection to the indictment.

In June 2007 the applicant obtained a second expert report from a private agency. On 12 July 2007 he requested the exclusion of several judges (including C.K. and T.D.) on the grounds that the case involved the death of a colleague’s daughter in the same small criminal section, and he sought transfer of the case to another court. The court president dismissed the recusal applications concerning Judges C.K. and T.D. after they declared they would remain impartial, finding no statutory grounds under section 36(2) of the Criminal Proceedings Act. A subsequent recusal of Judge T.D. (who had sat on the indictment panel) was granted. The trial proceeded before a panel presided over by Judge C.K. (later joined by Judge V.D.).

The trial court commissioned a third expert report from different Bureau experts. It admitted the applicant’s second report but gave it no weight, examined only one expert from the third report, and declined to hear all experts to resolve contradictions (particularly regarding the applicant’s speed). On 5 March 2008 the court convicted the applicant, finding he had driven at excessive speed while under the influence of alcohol, and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. It rejected his arguments that the victim had ignored a stop sign and was not wearing a seatbelt, relying on the third report and oral evidence. It also upheld a compensation claim by Judge M.A., her husband and surviving daughter against the applicant’s insurer.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the case should have been transferred due to the victim’s mother’s position and Judge C.K.’s prior working relationship with her, that the second report had been improperly disregarded, and that proposed evidence had been refused. The appellate court dismissed the impartiality complaint by referring only to the first-instance recusal decision, increased the sentence to six years, and held that the trial court was not obliged to accept all evidence or the privately commissioned report (which had not been court-ordered or sworn). The Supreme Court later dismissed an extraordinary review request, endorsing the lower courts without further addressing the bias allegations.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the trial court’s composition created an appearance of bias (given the personal and professional links to the victim’s mother within a small specialised section) and that equality of arms was breached through unequal treatment of expert evidence and refusal of proposed examinations.
001-162203:
The case of Başbilen v. Turkey (Application no. 35872/08) was brought by the parents of Hüseyin Başbilen, an engineer at Aselsan (a defence contractor for the Turkish Armed Forces). On 4 August 2006 Hüseyin disappeared; his locked car was found the next evening near Aydıncık village cemetery containing his body. His head lay under the passenger-side glove compartment and his feet on the driver’s seat. Autopsy (body already decomposed) established a superficial 8 cm throat cut and a fatal 8–10 cm left-wrist cut causing exsanguination. A blood-stained box-cutter, a typed and signed “FAREWELL” suicide note (citing emotional pain, no family/work problems, and instructions for property), a briefcase and personal items were recovered. Crime-scene processing yielded photographs, sketches, fingerprints (many unusable; two unmatched to the deceased or databases), blood/hair samples (matching the deceased) and the note. A matching file existed on a USB drive in Hüseyin’s office drawer (printed by gendarmerie officer Ş.K.); the drive itself later vanished.

Hüseyin’s wife reported psychiatric treatment for depression and accepted suicide; his parents and sister rejected it, citing a psychiatrist’s view of no suicidal ideation. The Ankara prosecutor closed the first investigation (no. 2006/131472) on 28 November 2006 as suicide, relying on the note’s authenticity, matching traces, and autopsy. The applicants’ objection highlighted omitted statements (wife, psychiatrist, colleagues), unexamined computer/emails/phone content beyond a call list, undated note file, and uninventoried briefcase. The Sincan Assize Court obtained a Forensic Medicine Institute opinion (majority: both wounds possibly self-inflicted; minority: homicide, given body position, lack of suicidal state and injury pattern) and upheld the closure in December 2007.

In November 2010, after press reports of an alleged naval-intelligence ring stealing Aselsan technology and staging suicides of non-cooperators, Hüseyin’s twin brother triggered a fresh investigation (no. 2010/142387). Additional steps included seizure and laboratory examination of Hüseyin’s work computer, recovery of briefcase documents (initially handed to his wife then Aselsan), further fingerprint analysis (more unmatched prints), and interviews. Ş.K. (now retired) claimed he had given the USB to commander E.Ş., who denied receiving it; no creation-date analysis occurred. A crime-scene expert flagged anomalies (briefcase placed after blood dried; unexplained rear-seat stains; body movement after cutting). The treating psychiatrist confirmed severe depression without suicidality but allowed a possible trigger. Colleagues described Hüseyin as stable and his project as non-critical. Some of his contacts appeared in Ergenekon/espionage files. Village witnesses recalled rumours of three cars and a quarrel the previous day. Graphology reconfirmed the signature. Multiple later forensic reports remained divided (majority possible self-infliction; others homicide or undetermined). Financial and medical records were gathered; all Aselsan staff had office/computer access.

In 2014 a prosecutor ordered a gendarmerie task force to re-examine this death and four similar Aselsan-engineer fatalities, targeting remaining gaps: unexplained crime-scene features, mishandling of the briefcase, the missing USB (and any related disciplinary/criminal action), and unused petrol-station CCTV from the morning of disappearance. The investigation remained open at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaint of an ineffective investigation into a suspicious death: initial premature closure despite evidentiary gaps, lost physical evidence, unpursued leads (unmatched prints, rumours, possible organisational links), conflicting expert opinions, and multi-year delays.

The case of Başbilen v. Turkey (Application no. 35872/08) was brought by Vehbi and Keziban Başbilen, parents of Hüseyin Başbilen, an engineer at Aselsan (a Turkish defence contractor). They alleged a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention, claiming that Turkish authorities failed to take reasonable and adequate steps to investigate the circumstances of their son's death, citing shortcomings and excessive delays.

Hüseyin Başbilen was reported missing on 4 August 2006. His body was found the following evening in his locked car near a village cemetery. A crime-scene examination noted a 15-20 cm cut to the throat and a 10 cm cut to the left wrist, bloodstains, a bloodied box cutter, personal items, a briefcase, and a typed, signed suicide note titled "FAREWELL" stating emotional pain, no family or work problems, and instructions for his property. Fingerprints, blood, and hair samples were collected; photos and sketches were made. An autopsy on 6 August 2006 found advanced decomposition, a fatal wrist wound causing excessive bleeding, and a superficial throat cut.

The suicide note matched a file on a USB drive from his work computer (not the hard drive). Experts confirmed the signature as his. Most fingerprints were unusable; two of four analysable ones were his, two unmatched. Blood and hair belonged to him. His wife stated he suffered depression and believed it was suicide; his parents and sister denied this. On 7 September 2006 the applicants requested expanded inquiries (phone records, emails, computer files, creation date of the note, and a psychiatrist's view that he had no suicidal tendencies). The prosecutor closed the investigation on 28 November 2006 as suicide, citing the note, matching evidence, and autopsy.

The applicants objected, highlighting failures to interview the wife, psychiatrist, or colleagues; examine the computer/emails/phone data or briefcase (absent from inventory); or determine the note's creation date. They suspected murder linked to his Aselsan work. On 12 April 2007 the Sincan Assize Court sought a Forensic Medicine Institute opinion. A 28 September 2007 majority report held both cuts possibly self-inflicted; a minority, citing his mental state, body position, and injuries, concluded it was not suicide. The court dismissed the objection on 13 December 2007, relying on the majority view.

A second investigation opened in November 2010 after the twin brother cited media reports of a criminal organisation stealing Aselsan technology, killing non-collaborators, and staging suicides. The father reiterated murder suspicions (including anonymous calls blaming foreign intelligence). Authorities searched his computer (files later analysed), but the USB drive had vanished; gendarmerie officers gave inconsistent accounts (one claimed confiscation and handover; another denied receipt). Further fingerprint analysis identified three unmatched prints. A relative noted little blood, an adjusted seat (inconsistent with the deceased's height), and unauthorised persons at the scene. The treating psychiatrist confirmed serious depression but no suicidal tendencies (though a trigger was possible). Colleagues described him as intelligent and sociable, with no critical project impact from his death. Some names from his files (including his) appeared in unrelated espionage/Ergenekon files. A crime-scene reconstruction suggested he inflicted the cuts while seated, then crawled; the briefcase appeared placed after blood dried, and some stains were unexplained. Graphology reconfirmed the signature. Financial, medical, and access records were gathered; colleagues and villagers (who mentioned seeing multiple cars and a quarrel the prior day) were interviewed. Air Force inquiries found no relevant software request.

A 2012 Forensic Medicine Institute majority again found self-inflicted injuries possible. A 2014 plenary (17-7-14 split) held self-infliction possible but many members deemed suicide undetermined or excluded. In July 2014 a new task force was ordered amid public interest and similar engineer deaths, targeting remaining gaps (briefcase handling without examination, missing USB, petrol-station CCTV from the morning of disappearance, and a reconstruction of 2011 doubts). The investigation remained ongoing as of the 2016 judgment.

These facts underscore the alleged investigative failings: initial rushed closure without key forensic/digital/witness steps; lost evidence; inconsistent official accounts; mixed expert opinions; and prolonged delays despite new leads.

The applicants, Vehbi and Keziban Başbilen, alleged that Turkish authorities failed to conduct an adequate and timely investigation into the 2006 death of their son Hüseyin, an Aselsan defence engineer, in violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 ECHR. They rejected the official suicide finding and suspected murder linked to his work.

Hüseyin vanished on 4 August 2006. His locked car was found the next evening near a village cemetery containing his body (head under the passenger glove box, feet on the driver’s seat), a bloody box-cutter, and a signed computer-typed “FAREWELL” suicide note stating he had no personal or work problems but wished to die from emotional pain. Autopsy (6 August) showed advanced decomposition, a fatal 8 cm left-wrist cut causing haemorrhage, and a superficial throat cut. The identical note existed on a USB drive in his office computer. His wife cited depression and psychiatric treatment as consistent with suicide; the applicants, his sister and later his psychiatrist denied any suicidal tendency.

Initial steps included crime-scene photography, sketches, fingerprinting (most unusable; two unidentified prints unmatched in databases), blood/hair analysis (his own), and signature verification. Phone records were obtained but not analysed. On 28 November 2006 the prosecutor closed the file as suicide, citing the note, signature, prints/blood/hair and autopsy. The applicants’ objection highlighted omitted statements (wife, psychiatrist, colleagues), no computer/email/phone or file-creation-date analysis, and the unexamined briefcase given to the widow. The Sincan Assize Court obtained a Forensic Medicine report (September 2007: majority possible self-infliction; minority, citing mental state, body position and injuries, homicide). The objection was dismissed in December 2007.

In November 2010 Hüseyin’s twin, citing press reports of an alleged naval-espionage ring that stole Aselsan technology and staged “suicides,” prompted a fresh investigation. Further measures included computer seizure, statements from the father (anonymous calls alleging foreign-intelligence murder over a project; briefcase missing), a relative (scant blood, odd seat position, unidentified men at the scene), the psychiatrist (serious depression but no suicide risk), and six colleagues (no known problems; project non-critical). A 2011 photographic reconstruction suggested the cuts occurred in the driver’s seat, after which the victim crawled passenger-side; the briefcase appeared placed post-mortem and some bloodstains unexplained. The USB had vanished; officer Ş.K. claimed he seized it and handed it to commander E.Ş., who denied receipt. No creation-date analysis occurred. Re-fingerprinting confirmed unidentified prints. Names on the computer appeared in Ergenekon/espionage files. Air-Force records showed no relevant software contract. The box-cutter yielded no prints. Graphology reconfirmed the signature. Financial and medical records were collected; Aselsan stated all staff could access the office and computers.

Forensic Medicine reports remained divided (2012 majority self-inflicted; 2014 plenary: 17 possible self-infliction, 7 homicide, 14 undetermined). In July 2014 a further prosecutor ordered a gendarmerie task force to re-examine this and four other Aselsan engineer deaths, specifically the unexplained photographic anomalies, the unexamined briefcase, the missing USB (and any disciplinary action), and unsecured petrol-station CCTV from 4 August. The investigation remained open at the time of the Court’s judgment.
001-163808:
The applicant, a Russian national born in 1955 and suffering from rectal cancer (with prior colorectal surgeries in 1994–1995) plus comorbidities including heart disease, was arrested on 1 November 2006 on suspicion of large-scale bank fraud. After initial release, a court ordered his remand detention on 3 November 2006 in Omsk prison IZ-55/1, citing risks of absconding, obstructing justice and influencing witnesses. Detention was repeatedly extended (to March, June, September, November and December 2007) by district and regional courts, which dismissed defence arguments that his deteriorating health rendered him unfit to pose such risks and that the investigation lacked urgency. The Supreme Court upheld one extension. The applicant was committed for trial in late 2007. Only after colorectal surgery in December 2007 did a court, on 8 February 2008, find that the original grounds had ceased and order his release on an undertaking not to leave his locality; the trial was stayed.

Upon admission the prison doctor recorded the applicant’s history. In December 2006 a large segment of sigmoid colon prolapsed, causing faecal incontinence. A surgeon prescribed adult nappies (never supplied by the authorities; a few were obtained from relatives) and twice-daily washing; a proctologist consultation was recommended but not arranged. Fellow inmates described acute nocturnal pain causing loss of consciousness, mobility limited to tiny steps, and complete absence of hygiene products. In January 2007 an independent colorectal specialist found serious anal-sphincter dysfunction and rectal strictures, stating that only a civilian hospital could perform the necessary endoscopy and surgery and that delay risked death. A prison surgeon nevertheless declared the condition “satisfactory.” A second independent doctor in February recorded progressive inflammation that could prove fatal without urgent specialised tests unavailable in the penitentiary system. The applicant was shuttled between the prison medical unit and the penitentiary hospital from March to October 2007, receiving only pain-killers and antispasmodics. Repeated examinations confirmed advancing inflammation, macerated perineal skin, and possible hepatic metastases (later disproved). By August independent doctors insisted on immediate colorectal surgery; the prison authorities maintained that none was required. Fellow prisoners described the applicant as emaciated, surrounded by a pungent faecal odour, forced to support a fist-sized prolapsed bowel while defecating standing up, and obliged to wash with cold water in full view of cell-mates.

On 23 November 2007 the European Court indicated under Rule 39 that colorectal surgery, a CT scan and a liver puncture be performed urgently. Diagnostic tests were carried out immediately and a colostomy was performed in a civilian hospital on 24 December 2007. The applicant was returned to prison and released three weeks later.

Detention conditions were disputed. The Government produced certificates showing the applicant had been held in cells of 10–41 m² with two to ten occupants and lavatory partitions of 1.1–1.6 m, plus hot water and weekly showers. The applicant and three former cell-mates asserted constant overcrowding (2.05–2.5 m² per person), showers at most once a week (often missed because walking caused agony), and the necessity of washing after each uncontrolled defecation while standing over an unscreened toilet in front of others, prompting insults and the need to “compensate” cell-mates with cigarettes and tea supplied by relatives. No special hygiene arrangements were ever made.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of inadequate medical care amounting to inhuman treatment, detention conditions incompatible with his health, and unjustified pre-trial detention lasting more than 15 months.

The case of G. v. Russia concerns a Russian national born in 1955 who suffered from rectal cancer (with prior colorectal surgeries in 1994–95 and second-degree disability certification). Arrested on 1 November 2006 on suspicion of large-scale bank fraud, he was initially released after questioning but detained from 3 November 2006 in Omsk remand prison IZ-55/1. Courts repeatedly extended his pre-trial detention (until 14 March, 14 June, 14 September, 1 November and 1 December 2007, then pending trial) citing risks of absconding or influencing witnesses, case complexity and the need to complete investigations or serve the indictment. Defence appeals stressing his fragile health, inability to receive specialist care (no proctologist available) and deteriorating condition were dismissed; courts held that health was not decisive, treatment was legally guaranteed, and the gravity of charges plus other risks warranted continued custody. On 8 February 2008, after surgery, a court found his condition now too serious for detention, ordered release on a written undertaking and stayed proceedings.

Upon admission, doctors noted his history plus coronary disease, hypertension and other ailments. In December 2006 his sigmoid colon prolapsed, causing faecal incontinence. A prison surgeon prescribed absorbent briefs (supplied only by relatives) and twice-daily washing; a proctologist consultation was advised but not arranged. Civilian colorectal specialists examined him in January–February 2007 at his lawyer’s request, diagnosing severe sphincter dysfunction, strictures and inflammation. They prescribed urgent inpatient examination and rectal surgery in a civilian hospital, warning that prison facilities lacked equipment and specialists and that delay risked complications or death. Prison doctors instead deemed his condition “satisfactory,” provided only painkillers and exempted him from drills. He was repeatedly transferred between the prison medical unit and Penitentiary Hospital no. 11, receiving symptomatic drugs while the prolapse enlarged, surrounding tissue became macerated and inflamed, and secondary heart problems worsened. Independent ultrasound in June 2007 suggested possible liver metastasis (later disproved). By August–October 2007 doctors recorded stage-2 colorectal cancer and again urged imminent surgery, which prison authorities postponed as “not urgent.” Fellow inmates described acute nocturnal pain, fainting, restricted mobility, a pungent smell, and the need to wash himself with cold water after uncontrolled defecation.

Detention conditions compounded these problems. The Government asserted non-overcrowded cells (10–41 m² for 2–10 persons) with partitions, running water and weekly showers. The applicant and three former cell-mates stated that cells were shared and overcrowded (approximately 2–2.5 m² per person), partitions were too low for privacy, showers were available only weekly (sometimes missed because walking caused pain), and after each incontinence episode he had to wash over the toilet in full view of others, using cold water and compensating cell-mates for the inconvenience. No special hygiene arrangements were made.

On 23 November 2007 the Court indicated interim measures requiring colorectal surgery, CT scan and liver puncture. Diagnostic tests showed no metastasis; a colostomy was performed in a civilian hospital on 24 December 2007. The applicant was released 17 days after discharge from hospital.

These facts underpin the complaints of inadequate medical care, detention conditions incompatible with his health, and insufficiently justified lengthy pre-trial detention.

**Case of G. v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 42526/07, judgment 21 June 2016)**

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1955 with a history of rectal cancer, two prior colorectal surgeries (1994–1995), and second-degree disability, was arrested on 1 November 2006 on suspicion of large-scale bank fraud by abuse of position. Released after questioning, he was ordered into pre-trial detention on 3 November 2006 by the Kuybishevskiy District Court of Omsk, which cited risks of absconding, hampering the investigation, and influencing witnesses. He was held in remand prison IZ-55/1 in Omsk. Detention was repeatedly extended (to March, June, September, November, and December 2007) by district and regional courts, which generally endorsed the original risks, noted the case’s complexity, and downplayed health arguments, stating that health was not decisive and that Russian law guaranteed medical care. Appeals were dismissed, often without fully addressing defence claims of deteriorating health and inadequate prison care. The applicant was committed for trial; a preliminary hearing in November 2007 again extended detention. He was released on 11 February 2008 against a written undertaking after the District Court found his health had become seriously incompatible with continued detention; proceedings were stayed.

Upon admission, a prison doctor noted his surgical history and comorbidities (coronary disease, angina, hypertension, obesity, gastritis, enterocolitis). In December 2006, prolapse of a large part of the sigmoid colon caused faecal incontinence. A surgeon prescribed adult absorbent briefs (not supplied by authorities; only a few came from relatives) and twice-daily washing, plus a proctologist consultation. Fellow inmates described acute pain (including loss of consciousness), limited mobility, and lack of hygiene products or toilet paper (supplied by relatives). Independent civilian doctors (Dr N. in January 2007; Dr Z. in February) found moderately serious to serious dysfunction, rectal strictures, inflammation of the prolapsed bowel, and risk of complications or death; they prescribed inpatient specialist examination, fibre endoscopy, CT imaging, and urgent colorectal surgery, noting that prison facilities lacked equipment and specialists. Prison doctors variously deemed the condition satisfactory or non-urgent.

The applicant was shuttled between the prison medical unit and Penitentiary Hospital no. 11 (March–October 2007), receiving only painkillers, antispasmodics, and limited endoscopy. Independent assessments recorded progressive inflammation, enlargement of the prolapse, macerated/oedematous skin, possible liver metastasis (ultrasound), and stage 2 colorectal cancer. Doctors repeatedly urged urgent surgery; delays risked irreparable harm or death. Inmate statements described a sallow, exhausted applicant with a pungent smell, fist-sized bleeding prolapse, inability to control defecation, and washing with cold water over a toilet while supporting the bowel. The authorities insisted there was no urgent need.

On 1 October 2007 the applicant applied to the ECHR and sought a Rule 39 interim measure. On 23 November 2007 the Court indicated urgent colorectal surgery in a specialist hospital, CT scan, and liver puncture. Tests (21–26 November) showed no metastasis. Surgery (colostomy) occurred on 24 December 2007 at Omsk Regional Hospital after further deterioration. He was discharged after a month, returned briefly to prison, and released shortly thereafter. The interim measure was lifted in October 2008 after compliance.

Detention conditions were disputed. The Government claimed non-overcrowded cells meeting standards, with partitions, water, and showers. The applicant and fellow inmates described shared, overcrowded cells (often 2–2.5 m² per person), weekly showers (sometimes inaccessible due to pain), low partitions offering no privacy for frequent washing after incontinence, exposure to cellmates, insults, and the need to compensate them with goods. These conditions, combined with untreated incontinence and pain, were alleged to be incompatible with his health.

The facts centre on prolonged pre-trial detention without sufficient justification in light of health, delayed and inadequate specialist care despite clear medical warnings of serious risk, and hygiene/privacy failures exacerbating a debilitating condition.
