The European Court of Human Rights examined the case of Rudolfer v. Slovakia (Application no. 38082/07), brought by Slovak national Tomáš Rudolfer against restrictions imposed by a national rent-control scheme on his property rights. He alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The property is a house in Bratislava-Ružinov built by the applicant’s parents in 1937. In the late 1950s the family was compelled to donate it to the State. Under restitution legislation it was returned on 31 July 1992 (three-quarters to the applicant’s mother and one-quarter to him). The applicant became sole owner on 30 September 1996.

At the time of restitution the house contained nine flats subject to the rent-control scheme: one measuring 30 m² and eight measuring 70 m² each. The scheme required the owner to accept the sitting tenants, to charge no more than the State-fixed maximum rent, to refrain from unilateral termination of the leases, and to sell the flats only to the tenants.

Two of the larger flats became vacant in 1996 and 2000 and thereby escaped the scheme. Two further 70 m² flats left the scheme in January 2008 and November 2012. Five flats remained subject to rent control at the time of the Court’s examination.

Between 1992 and 1999 the maximum monthly rent was the equivalent of €3–8. After successive increases the applicant could charge approximately €35 for the smaller flat and €65 for each larger flat in 2007. The applicant, relying on National Association of Real Estate Agencies data, asserted that 2007 market rents for comparable 70 m² flats reached €553 and for 30 m² flats €375. A government expert valued 2010 market rents at €330 and €160.50 respectively.

The Court noted that the legal framework and historical background of the Slovak rent-control regime had already been set out in Bittó and Others v. Slovakia. In that judgment the Court had found the scheme to violate Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because it imposed a disproportionate burden on landlords. Subsequent legislation (Law no. 260/2011) allowed landlords to terminate tenancies by 31 March 2012 (subject to a twelve-month notice period) and to raise rents by 20 % annually until 2015, while requiring municipalities to rehouse tenants in material hardship by the end of 2016; thereafter landlords could claim the difference between market and regulated rents. Law no. 150/2013 also offered preferential modernisation loans. These measures, however, did not retroactively compensate owners for the period before their adoption and only fully eliminated the restrictions from 2017. Implementation of the Bittó judgment, including the Court’s call for a specific compensatory remedy, remained pending.

The facts therefore centre on the long-term application of a statutory rent-control regime to restituted property, the resulting disparity between controlled and market rents, and the continuing restrictions on the owner’s ability to use, terminate or dispose of the flats.

The case of Rudolfer v. Slovakia (Application no. 38082/07) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 August 2007 by Tomáš Rudolfer, a Slovak national born in 1946 and residing in Bratislava. Represented by lawyer R. Procházka, the applicant complained that Slovakia’s rent-control scheme violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 4 January 2012, after which the parties submitted observations on the merits.

The property at issue is a house in Bratislava-Ružinov built by the applicant’s parents in 1937. In the second half of the 1950s they were compelled to donate it to the State. It was restored on 31 July 1992 under restitution legislation, with a three-quarters share going to the applicant’s mother and a one-quarter share to the applicant. He became sole owner on 30 September 1996.

At restitution the house contained nine flats subject to rent control: one of 30 sq m and eight of 70 sq m each. The scheme obliged the owner to accept the sitting tenants, capped rent at a State-fixed maximum, barred unilateral termination of leases, and restricted sales of the flats to the tenants only.

Two of the larger flats became vacant in 1996 and 2000, ending rent control for them. Two further 70 sq m flats left the regime in January 2008 and November 2012. Five flats remain subject to it.

Between 1992 and 1999 the maximum monthly rent was the equivalent of EUR 3–8. After successive increases, in 2007 the applicant could charge approximately EUR 35 for the smaller flat and EUR 65 for each larger one. The applicant, citing National Association of Real Estate Agencies data, asserted that 2007 market rents for comparable 70 sq m and 30 sq m flats were EUR 553 and EUR 375 respectively. The Government produced an expert valuation placing 2010 market rents at EUR 330 and EUR 160.50.

The domestic legal framework and historical background of the scheme are set out in Bittó and Others v. Slovakia. Law no. 260/2011, which entered into force on 15 September 2011, aimed to phase out restrictions. Landlords could give notice of termination by 31 March 2012 (effective after twelve months). Tenants facing material hardship could remain at regulated rent until a municipal tenancy was arranged. Landlords were permitted 20 % annual rent increases until 2015. Municipalities were required to house hardship tenants by 31 December 2016, failing which landlords could claim the difference between market and regulated rent. Law no. 150/2013, effective 1 January 2014, entitled owners of restituted properties to preferential modernisation loans.

In Bittó the Court held that the scheme violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, observing that it originated in a systemic legislative problem affecting numerous owners and that thirteen similar applications (involving some 170 persons) were pending. It noted that the 2011 measures would eliminate the scheme’s effects only from 2017 and did not address the prior situation, and called for a specific compensatory remedy. Implementation of that judgment remains pending.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claim that the long-standing restrictions on use, rent, termination and disposal of his restored property, together with the substantial disparity between controlled and market rents, constituted an unjustified interference with his possessions.

These facts establish the alleged interference: long-term, state-imposed occupation of restituted property at rents far below market levels, combined with inability to terminate tenancies or dispose freely of the flats.
001-164459:
The case of Lazu v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 46182/08) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s complaint that criminal proceedings against him were unfair, in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The applicant, Anatolie Lazu (born 1954, resident in Chișinău), was a bank armoured-vehicle driver. On 12 August 2005 at around 10.55 a.m. he drove around an illegally parked bus. As he completed the manoeuvre the bus began to move then stopped abruptly to avoid a collision. Passenger C. fell from her seat and suffered moderately severe injuries.

A criminal investigation opened on 1 September 2005. The prosecutor interviewed the applicant, C., bus driver D., a witness in the applicant’s vehicle and two bus passengers (S. and V.). On 7 October 2005 D. was charged with a traffic-rule violation causing injury. After a face-to-face interview on 10 October, in which the applicant stated he had completed the manoeuvre while the bus was stationary, signalled and sounded his horn, while D. claimed an unsignalled turn forced an emergency stop, proceedings against D. were discontinued for lack of evidence and he was treated as a witness. The applicant was charged on 21 October 2005.

The Botanica District Court heard the same witnesses and examined a site-investigation report and sketch map prepared hours later (12.20 p.m.) in D.’s presence only. On 27 March 2006 it acquitted the applicant. It found C.’s and the passengers’ accounts unreliable because they had not independently seen the events and appeared influenced by D.; D.’s evidence was unreliable given the earlier charge against him; the charge against the applicant rested on D.’s post-discontinuance statements without re-interviewing others; and the delayed report and map (drawn up without the applicant, omitting his objections and inconsistent with contemporaneous statements) were unreliable. The prosecution had failed to prove that the applicant’s actions caused the sudden stop. The prosecutor appealed.

On 23 May 2006 the Chișinău Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the acquittal, holding that the first-instance court had properly scrutinised the evidence. The prosecutor appealed on points of law. On 17 October 2006 the Supreme Court of Justice (parties present) quashed the appellate judgment and remitted the case for rehearing under first-instance rules, criticising the appeal court’s failure thoroughly to assess the statements of C., D. and the passengers.

After rehearing, the Court of Appeal again dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal on 28 December 2006, analysing the testimony, report and map and explaining their unreliability. The prosecutor again appealed. On 26 June 2007 the Supreme Court (parties present) again remitted the case for similar reasons.

At the 25 October 2007 hearing the applicant and his lawyer did not object to proceeding without recalling C. or the witnesses. The Court of Appeal then quashed the first-instance acquittal, convicted the applicant, imposed a 3,000 MDL fine (approximately EUR 194) and ordered 2,500 MDL damages (approximately EUR 162) to C. It merely listed the evidence, including the disputed statements, without additional reasoning.

The applicant appealed, highlighting unclarified discrepancies in the witness statements identified at first instance. On 13 February 2008 the Supreme Court examined the appeal in the parties’ absence and declared it inadmissible. The applicant was served on 24 May 2008 and lodged his Strasbourg application on 10 September 2008.

Domestic law required that a rehearing after cassation follow first-instance rules, with assessed evidence recorded in the hearing minutes. Proceedings could later be reopened if the Court found a continuing violation remediable only by review of the final judgment.

The case of Lazu v. the Republic of Moldova (application no. 46182/08) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention arising from unfairness in criminal proceedings that resulted in the applicant’s conviction for a traffic offence.

The applicant, a bank armoured-vehicle driver born in 1954, was involved in an incident at approximately 10.55 a.m. on 12 August 2005. While manoeuvring around an illegally parked bus, the bus began to move and then stopped abruptly, causing passenger C. to fall from her seat and sustain moderately severe injuries. A criminal investigation opened on 1 September 2005. The prosecutor interviewed the applicant, victim C., bus driver D., a witness travelling in the applicant’s vehicle, and two bus passengers (S. and V.). On 7 October 2005 D. was charged with violating traffic rules causing injury. In a face-to-face interview on 10 October 2005 the applicant stated that he had completed the manoeuvre while the bus remained stationary, signalled a right turn and sounded his horn; D. claimed the applicant had turned without warning, forcing an abrupt stop. The same day proceedings against D. were discontinued for lack of evidence and he was re-interviewed as a witness. On 21 October 2005 the applicant was charged instead.

At first instance the Botanica District Court heard the same witnesses and examined a site-investigation report and sketch map prepared at 12.20 p.m. on the day of the incident in D.’s presence alone. It found C.’s and the two passengers’ testimony unreliable, concluding they had not personally observed the events and had formed their views from D.’s accusations. D.’s evidence was likewise unreliable because he had previously faced the same charges. The court noted that the applicant had been charged solely on the basis of D.’s post-discontinuance statements without re-interviewing other witnesses, that the site documents had not been compiled immediately, that only D. had attended, that the applicant’s objections were unrecorded, and that the sketch did not match contemporaneous witness accounts. On 27 March 2006 the court acquitted the applicant, holding that the prosecution had failed to produce reliable evidence that his actions had caused the bus to stop suddenly.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal on 23 May 2006, endorsing the first-instance court’s scrutiny of the evidence. The Supreme Court of Justice, on 17 October 2006, quashed that decision and ordered a full rehearing under the first-instance rules, finding that the appeal court had not adequately assessed the statements of C., D. and the passengers. After rehearing, the Court of Appeal again acquitted on 28 December 2006, giving detailed reasons for rejecting the same evidence. The Supreme Court quashed this ruling on 26 June 2007 on similar grounds.

At a hearing on 25 October 2007 the applicant and his lawyer did not object to proceeding without recalling the victim or witnesses. The Court of Appeal then quashed the acquittal, convicted the applicant and imposed a fine of MDL 3,000 (approximately EUR 194) plus damages of MDL 2,500 (approximately EUR 162) to C. It simply listed the previously disputed statements without further reasoning. The applicant appealed, highlighting the unresolved discrepancies identified at first instance. On 13 February 2008 the Supreme Court, sitting in the parties’ absence, declared the appeal inadmissible. The applicant was served with that decision on 24 May 2008.

Domestic law required that a rehearing after cassation follow first-instance procedure and that assessed evidence be recorded in the hearing minutes. These successive quashings, the appeal court’s eventual conviction without hearing the key witnesses whose credibility had been repeatedly doubted, and the Supreme Court’s summary rejection form the core facts underlying the unfair-trial complaint.

The case of Lazu v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 46182/08) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial) arising from criminal proceedings against Anatolie Lazu, a Moldovan bank armoured-vehicle driver. The applicant complained that the proceedings leading to his conviction were unfair.

On 12 August 2005, at around 10.55 a.m., Lazu manoeuvred his vehicle around an illegally parked bus. The bus then moved and stopped abruptly to avoid a collision, causing passenger C. to fall from her seat and sustain moderately severe injuries. A criminal investigation began on 1 September 2005. The prosecutor interviewed Lazu, C., bus driver D., a witness from Lazu’s vehicle, and two bus passengers (S. and V.). On 7 October 2005, D. was charged with violating traffic rules. In a 10 October 2005 confrontation, Lazu claimed he had completed the manoeuvre while the bus remained stationary, signalled, and used the horn; D. claimed Lazu turned without warning, forcing an abrupt stop. Proceedings against D. were discontinued that day for lack of evidence, and he was treated as a witness. Lazu was charged on 21 October 2005.

The Botanica District Court heard the same witnesses, plus a site investigation report and sketch map prepared hours later (at 12.20 p.m. on 12 August) in D.’s presence only. On 27 March 2006, it acquitted Lazu. It found C., S., and V. unreliable, as they had not personally observed the events and appeared influenced by D.’s blame. D.’s testimony was unreliable given the prior charges against him. The court criticised the prosecution’s reliance on D.’s post-discontinuance statements without re-interviewing others, and noted flaws in the delayed site report and sketch (which omitted Lazu’s objections and mismatched early witness statements). The prosecution had failed to prove Lazu’s actions caused the sudden stop.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal on 23 May 2006, agreeing the first-instance court had properly scrutinised the evidence. The Supreme Court of Justice quashed this on 17 October 2006 (with parties present) and ordered a full rehearing under first-instance rules, finding the appellate court had not thoroughly assessed the statements of C., D., S., and V. After rehearing, the Court of Appeal again acquitted on 28 December 2006, analysing the testimony, report, and map with reasons for unreliability. The Supreme Court quashed this on 26 June 2007 (parties present) on similar grounds, ordering another rehearing.

At the 25 October 2007 rehearing, Lazu and his lawyer did not object to proceeding without recalling C. or request recalling other witnesses. The Court of Appeal convicted Lazu, imposing a 3,000 MDL fine (approx. EUR 194) and 2,500 MDL damages (approx. EUR 162) to C. It listed evidence including the previously disputed statements of C., D., S., and V., without further reasoning. Lazu appealed, highlighting unclarified discrepancies noted at first instance. On 13 February 2008 the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible in the parties’ absence. Lazu received the judgment on 24 May 2008 and applied to the European Court on 10 September 2008.

Domestic law (Articles 413(6), 419, and 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) required reheard cases to follow first-instance examination rules, with evidence listed in the hearing record. These facts formed the basis of the alleged unfairness, particularly the conviction based on untested, previously rejected evidence after repeated remittals.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered its judgment on 12 January 2017 (final on 12 April 2017) in Sarbyanova-Pashaliyska and Pashaliyska v. Bulgaria (Application no. 3524/14). The applicants, Bulgarian nationals Niya Ivanova Sarbyanova-Pashaliyska (born 1960) and her daughter Maria Ivanova Pashaliyska (born 1999), both of Sofia, complained under the Convention about the murder of their husband and father, Ivan Mirchev Pashaliysky. They alleged that the investigation into the killing was ineffective due to its excessive duration and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy for this.

Pashaliysky was killed on 2 June 2000 in a Sofia hotel office. He suffered fatal trauma to his brain, chest, torso and limbs from kicks, punches and blows with objects, causing irreversible damage to vital organs. A security guard, called to a reported brawl, glimpsed the victim lying helpless and bloody on the floor; S.V. opened the door holding a long oval object and claimed there was no problem. Earlier that day, S.V. had used the office telephone to threaten Pashaliysky’s business partner Ch.M. with death unless an undisclosed sum was paid immediately.

Police arrested S.V. that night after traces of the crime were found on his hands and clothes. He was charged with murder on 3 June 2000 and indicted on 5 June. The pre-trial investigation suffered repeated delays. On 20 April 2001 a prosecutor returned the case, noting missing DNA analysis of material under the victim’s nails, unquestioned key witnesses, unheld confrontations despite statement discrepancies, and lack of information on S.V.’s state at arrest. The file was returned three more times (17 July 2001, 18 July 2003 and 2 October 2003) with specific further instructions.

The case reached the Sofia City Court in November 2003. Both applicants were named private prosecutors; the daughter also joined as a civil party seeking non-pecuniary damages. First-instance proceedings ended on 11 June 2007 with a 15-year sentence for S.V. and an order to pay damages to the daughter. On appeal, S.V. argued the indictment lacked any description of the killing’s manner, a fundamental defect under Supreme Court of Cassation interpretative decision no. 2 of 2002. On 18 July 2008 the Sofia Court of Appeal quashed the conviction and returned the case to the pre-trial stage.

S.V. was re-indicted on 16 August 2008. Fresh first-instance proceedings began, with hearings postponed because defence counsel failed to appear. The court initially refused to name both applicants private prosecutors, a decision later quashed. Witnesses were reheard. Sixteen further hearings followed, during which the applicants repeatedly requested additional evidence. The trial restarted when the presiding judge became President of the Supreme Administrative Court; a new judge was appointed but no hearing occurred for about a year. The applicants complained to the Inspectorate of the Supreme Judicial Council, which on 21 February 2012 acknowledged that 11 years of proceedings exceeded a reasonable time but declined to sanction the judge. The new judge was later transferred, forcing another restart.

On 9 December 2013 the Sofia City Court convicted S.V. of murder, imposing 12 years’ imprisonment and awarding the daughter approximately EUR 50,000 in damages. On 22 December 2014 the Sofia Court of Appeal, after thorough review of witness statements, the crime-scene examination, searches, expert reports and autopsy, upheld the conviction but reduced damages to around EUR 8,000. The Supreme Court of Cassation dismissed S.V.’s cassation appeal on 2 November 2015, rendering the judgment final.

Bulgarian law required an indictment to specify the crime’s place, time and manner (1974 and 2006 Codes of Criminal Procedure). The same bench had to hear a trial from start to finish; any change necessitated a complete restart. Next of kin could participate as private prosecutors or civil parties, with rights of access to the file, to present evidence and to request investigative measures. Compensatory remedies for excessive length existed under the Judiciary Act 2007 (administrative, for concluded proceedings) and the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act 1988 (judicial, for pending or unsatisfactorily remedied concluded proceedings). The Court had previously held these remedies, taken together, to be effective for length complaints in civil, criminal and administrative cases.

The proceedings thus spanned more than 15 years from the 2000 killing until the 2015 final judgment, featuring multiple returns for investigation, two complete trial restarts caused by judicial changes, and acknowledged excessive duration.

The applicants, a mother and her daughter, alleged that the investigation into the 2000 murder of their husband and father, Ivan Pashaliysky, was ineffective due to its excessive duration and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy (under Articles 2 and 13 ECHR). Pashaliysky was beaten to death on 2 June 2000 in a Sofia office, suffering fatal trauma from kicks, punches, and blows with objects. A security guard glimpsed him injured on the floor as S.V. (holding a long object) claimed there was no issue. S.V. had earlier telephoned threats over money. Police arrested S.V. that night; traces of the crime were found on him. He was charged with murder on 3 June and indicted on 5 June 2000.

Pre-trial proceedings faced repeated returns by prosecutors for incomplete evidence. On 20 April 2001, a prosecutor ordered DNA analysis of material under the victim’s nails, questioning of key witnesses on their presence and movements, a confrontation over statement discrepancies, and details of S.V.’s arrest state. The case was returned three more times (July 2001, July 2003, October 2003) with specific further instructions. It reached Sofia City Court in November 2003. Both applicants joined as private prosecutors (with rights to access files, present evidence, and request measures); the daughter also joined as a civil party seeking damages.

The first trial ended on 11 June 2007 with S.V. sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment and ordered to pay damages. Appeals followed. S.V. argued the indictment omitted any description of how the killing occurred, a fundamental flaw (per a 2002 Supreme Court of Cassation interpretative decision) that should have returned the case earlier. On 18 July 2008 the Sofia Court of Appeal agreed, quashed the conviction, and returned the matter to the pre-trial stage so the defect could be cured, as it had prevented the defendant from exercising his rights.

A fresh indictment was issued on 16 August 2008 and new first-instance proceedings opened. Initial hearings were postponed due to the defence lawyer’s absence. In February 2009 the court initially refused to recognise both applicants as private prosecutors (while accepting the daughter as civil party); this was overturned on appeal in March 2009, requiring witnesses to be reheard. Sixteen further hearings occurred, during which the applicants made numerous requests for evidence and testimony. The presiding judge was then elected President of the Supreme Administrative Court, forcing the trial to restart. A replacement judge was appointed, yet no hearing was scheduled for about a year. The applicants complained to the Inspectorate of the Supreme Judicial Council, which in February 2012 acknowledged that the proceedings had already lasted 11 years (incompatible with a reasonable time) but declined to sanction the judge because her other cases were timely. The new judge was later transferred back to her original court, requiring yet another restart.

The Sofia City Court convicted S.V. of murder on 9 December 2013, imposing 12 years’ imprisonment and ordering payment of approximately EUR 50,000 in damages to the daughter. On appeal the Sofia Court of Appeal (22 December 2014) thoroughly reviewed witness statements, the crime-scene examination, search-and-seizure records, expert reports and the autopsy, then upheld the conviction while reducing damages to about EUR 8,000. The Supreme Court of Cassation confirmed the appellate judgment in full on 2 November 2015. The entire process thus lasted more than 15 years from the killing to final conviction.

Bulgarian law required an indictment to specify the place, time and manner of the offence; failure regarding an element of the corpus delicti justified return to an earlier stage. Trials had to be heard by the same bench throughout, otherwise restarting. Next-of-kin could participate as private prosecutors or civil parties with corresponding rights. Compensatory remedies for excessive length existed: an administrative procedure under the 2007 Judiciary Act (for concluded proceedings, capped at 10,000 levs) and a judicial claim under the 1988 State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act (available for pending cases or after unsuccessful administrative redress). The Court had previously regarded the two remedies, taken together, as effective for length complaints in civil, criminal and administrative proceedings.

The case of *Sarbyanova-Pashaliyska and Pashaliyska v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 3524/14) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 12 January 2017 (final on 12 April 2017). A security guard briefly saw him bloodied on the floor after S.V. opened the door, holding an oval object. S.V. had earlier telephoned a business associate of the victim, threatening murder unless money was paid. Police arrested S.V. that night after traces of the crime were found on him. He was charged with murder on 3 June 2000 and indicted on 5 June 2000.

The pre-trial investigation suffered repeated returns to investigators for deficiencies: on 20 April 2001 (no DNA analysis of material under the victim’s nails, unquestioned key witnesses, no confrontation of discrepant statements, no details of S.V.’s state at arrest); then on 17 July 2001, 18 July 2003 and 2 October 2003, with specific further instructions each time. The case reached the Sofia City Court in November 2003. Both applicants were named private prosecutors and the daughter a civil party claiming non-pecuniary damages.

The first-instance trial ended on 11 June 2007 with S.V. sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment and ordered to pay damages to the daughter. On appeal, the Sofia Court of Appeal on 18 July 2008 quashed the conviction, holding that the indictment lacked any description of the manner of killing (a fundamental defect under Supreme Court of Cassation interpretative decision no. 2 of 2002 and Articles 235/246 of the criminal procedure codes), preventing the defence from exercising its rights. The case returned to the pre-trial stage.

A fresh indictment was issued on 16 August 2008. New first-instance proceedings faced delays: two hearings postponed due to the defence lawyer’s absence; the applicants initially denied private-prosecutor status (later restored on appeal, requiring re-hearing of witnesses); sixteen further hearings with numerous evidence requests by the applicants; then two complete restarts of the trial after changes of presiding judge (one elected President of the Supreme Administrative Court; another transferred back to her original court). After the first restart, no hearing was scheduled for about a year. The applicants complained to the Inspectorate of the Supreme Judicial Council, which on 21 February 2012 acknowledged that the 11-year duration was incompatible with a reasonable time but declined to sanction the judge.

The Sofia City Court convicted S.V. of murder on 9 December 2013, sentencing him to 12 years and awarding the daughter approximately EUR 50,000 in damages. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 22 December 2014 after reviewing all evidence but reduced damages to around EUR 8,000. The Supreme Court of Cassation confirmed the judgment in full on 2 November 2015.

Bulgarian law required the same bench throughout a trial (restarting if a judge left) and allowed victims’ heirs to participate as private prosecutors or civil parties with rights to access files, present evidence and request measures. Compensatory remedies for excessive length existed (administrative under the 2007 Judiciary Act for concluded proceedings, judicial under the 1988 State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act for pending or inadequately remedied cases), but the applicants alleged these were ineffective for them as next of kin in a murder investigation.

001-164449:
The applicant, a Portuguese first-instance judge, faced three separate disciplinary proceedings before the High Council of the Judiciary (HCJ) in 2010–2012. These arose from alleged breaches of professional duties (propriety, loyalty and honesty) and resulted in sanctions that were later aggregated into a single 240-day unpaid suspension.

In the first set of proceedings the applicant was accused of calling a judicial inspector a “liar” in a telephone conversation and of accusing him of inertia. After the original inspector recused himself (having described himself as the applicant’s “sworn enemy”), a substitute inspector proposed a 15-day fine. The HCJ plenary (six judges and nine non-judicial members) imposed a 20-day fine. A dissenting opinion by four non-judicial members questioned the evidential basis and considered the remarks protected by freedom of expression. On appeal the Judicial Division of the Supreme Court of Justice (SCJ) confined itself to reviewing the reasonableness of the HCJ’s fact-finding, treated the applicant’s use of allegedly false testimony as an aggravating factor, and upheld the sanction.

The second set of proceedings concerned the same alleged false testimony. The inspector’s initial submissions did not propose a specific penalty; his later report recommended 60 days’ suspension. The HCJ (seven judges and five non-judicial members present) reclassified the conduct as a breach of honesty rather than loyalty and imposed 100 days’ suspension, relying inter alia on the applicant’s mobile-phone records. The SCJ Judicial Division again limited its review to lawfulness and reasonableness, held that the applicant had been adequately informed of the proposed penalty, accepted the reclassification as a mere change of legal characterisation of unchanged facts, and found the sanction proportionate.

The third set arose from an alleged private request by the applicant that the inspector refrain from disciplining the witness who had given evidence in the first proceedings. The inspector recommended dismissal. The HCJ (eight judges and six non-judicial members) imposed 180 days’ suspension for breaches of loyalty and propriety; one judge dissented in favour of dismissal. The applicant’s request for a public hearing at which she could call a witness and produce documents was refused by the SCJ Judicial Division on the ground that its jurisdiction did not extend to a fresh examination of the facts; the court also rejected the documents as exceeding the scope of the proceedings and declined to review the legal classification or the decision not to suspend the penalty.

In all three appeals the SCJ Judicial Division (composed of the most senior Vice-President and one judge from each division) characterised the proceedings as a special administrative action limited to verifying the lawfulness and internal coherence of the HCJ’s decisions. It therefore refused to re-hear evidence, to hold a public hearing, or to substitute its own assessment of proportionality except in cases of manifest error. The applicant complained that these limitations, together with the composition and functioning of the Judicial Division (whose president is also president of the HCJ), denied her access to a court with full jurisdiction, an independent and impartial tribunal, and a public hearing, and that the HCJ’s reclassification of the charges and its reliance on circumstances not set out in the inspectors’ original submissions further breached Article 6.

The case involves Portuguese judge Paula Cristina Ramos Nunes de Carvalho e Sá, who alleged unfair disciplinary proceedings violating Article 6 ECHR (fair trial). Three sets of proceedings by the High Council of the Judiciary (HCJ) led to appeals before the Supreme Court of Justice's Judicial Division.

In the first (no. 57728/13), started November 2010, the applicant was accused of calling inspector H.G. a "liar" by phone and accusing him of "inertia and lack of diligence" during her appraisal, breaching propriety. Inspector F.M.J. proposed 20 day-fines. She sought his recusal for bias and violating presumption of innocence (he had ties to H.G.); he recused after calling himself her "sworn enemy." Replacement inspector A.V.N. proposed 15 day-fines. A witness (called by her) denied the remarks. In January 2012, the HCJ plenary (15 members: 6 judges, 9 non-judges) imposed 20 unpaid day-fines, refusing suspension. Four non-judges dissented, finding insufficient evidence of the "liar" remark and that "inertia" comments fell under free expression. She appealed, seeking fact review and arguing disproportionality. In March 2013, the Judicial Division unanimously upheld, noting it verifies only reasonableness of facts (not a full review), rejected a CJEU referral, treated her witness as false testimony (aggravating the penalty), and held the remarks insulted H.G. beyond free expression. No suspension review was needed (not a custodial sentence).

The second (no. 55391/13) concerned alleged false testimony in the first case (asking a witness to lie). Inspector A.D.P.R. initially proposed no specific penalty, then 60-day suspension for loyalty breach in his final report. She pleaded nullity (penalty not in initial submissions); this was rejected. In October 2011, HCJ plenary (12 of 17 members: 7 judges including President, 5 non-judges) imposed 100-day suspension for honesty breach, based on her consented phone records. She appealed, citing no hearing on the (unspecified) penalty, HCJ's legal reclassification and altered circumstances of involvement, omitted reasons for not suspending the penalty, and disproportionality. In June 2013, the Judicial Division upheld, citing limited review powers (action to set aside, not full fact/law appeal, per Administrative Courts Code); the final report informed her of the penalty; HCJ could increase it as her defence addressed facts; reclassification was a different legal view of unchanged facts (rights safeguarded); no suspension assessment required (not criminal/custodial); penalty not disproportionate; and false testimony via a third party justified aggravation.

The third (no. 74041/13) alleged she privately asked inspector F.M.J. not to discipline the first-case witness. Inspector A.D.P.R. proposed dismissal for honesty breach. She admitted the conversation but denied the request. In April 2012, HCJ plenary (14 of 17: 8 judges including President, 6 non-judges) imposed 180-day suspension for loyalty/propriety breaches. One judge dissented, seeking dismissal/early retirement. She appealed, requesting a public hearing (to call a witness and submit documents), complaining of reclassification, no reasons for not suspending, and disproportionality. In May 2013, the Judicial Division refused the hearing (its role is not fact review, only checking evidence principles, coherence, and reasonableness; pleadings sufficed without oral argument; witness request breached confidentiality; documents exceeded scope). It held HCJ has broad discretion on offences (reviewable only for gross error); penalty review is limited to appropriateness/proportionality; and no suspension ruling was needed (not criminal).

In September 2014, HCJ combined penalties into a final 240-day suspension (12 of 17 members: 7 judges including President, 5 non-judges), which was enforced.

These facts centre on limited Supreme Court review (no full fact re-examination or public hearing), HCJ's mixed composition and penalty changes (reclassification without specified initial proposals or extra hearings), inspector recusals/overlaps, and use of evidence like phone records/witnesses, all relevant to claims of inadequate court access, impartiality/independence issues (HCJ-Supreme Court links, including shared presidency), and procedural unfairness.

The applicant, a Portuguese first-instance judge, faced three sets of disciplinary proceedings before the High Council of the Judiciary (HCJ) for alleged breaches of professional duties (propriety, honesty and loyalty). These led to Article 6 complaints of unfairness, specifically lack of access to a court with full jurisdiction, insufficient independence/impartiality of the reviewing Judicial Division of the Supreme Court of Justice (SCJ), absence of a public hearing, and (in two cases) prejudicial legal reclassification of the facts plus consideration of circumstances beyond the inspector’s original submissions.

In the first case (2010), the applicant was accused of calling a judicial inspector a “liar” and of “inertia and lack of diligence” during a telephone call. After the initial inspector recused himself following her challenge (he described himself as her “sworn enemy”), a replacement inspector proposed a 15-day fine. The HCJ plenary (15 members: 6 judges, 9 non-judges) imposed a 20-day fine (20 days’ unpaid salary) and refused to suspend it. A dissenting opinion questioned the evidential basis and viewed the remarks as protected expression. The applicant’s appeal to the SCJ Judicial Division sought a full factual review and argued disproportionality. The Division (unanimously) limited itself to checking whether the HCJ’s fact-finding was “reasonable and coherent”; it treated her use of allegedly false witness testimony as an aggravating factor, held that no suspension assessment was required (no custodial sentence being involved), and confirmed that the remarks fell outside freedom of expression.

The second case concerned alleged subornation of that same witness (false testimony) in the first proceedings. Phone records (obtained with the applicant’s consent) were used. The inspector’s submissions alleged a loyalty breach but proposed no penalty; his later report recommended 60 days’ suspension. The applicant unsuccessfully pleaded nullity for lack of prior notice of the penalty. The HCJ plenary (12 of 17 members: 7 judges including the President, 5 non-judges) reclassified the conduct as a honesty breach and imposed 100 days’ suspension. On appeal the SCJ Division again confined itself to a legality/reasonableness review, held that the final report had given adequate notice, accepted the HCJ’s power to increase the penalty and reclassify the same facts, and found the sanction proportionate (again treating recourse to a third party as aggravating).

The third case alleged that the applicant had privately asked an inspector not to discipline the witness. She admitted the conversation but denied the request. The inspector proposed dismissal; the HCJ (14 members: 8 judges including the President, 6 non-judges) imposed 180 days’ suspension for loyalty and propriety breaches (one dissent favoured dismissal). The applicant requested a public hearing, a witness and documents. The SCJ Division refused the hearing, stating that its statutory role was not a full merits review of facts but only verification of lawfulness, coherence and the absence of “manifest or gross error” in the HCJ’s broad discretionary assessment of disciplinary seriousness and penalty. It likewise declined to examine new evidence or to review the non-suspension of the penalty.

The three penalties were later aggregated by the HCJ into a single 240-day suspension, which was enforced. Under Portuguese law the HCJ (presided over by the SCJ President, with a mixed judicial/non-judicial membership) conducts confidential written proceedings; its decisions are challengeable only by a “special administrative action” before a specially constituted SCJ Judicial Division whose review is limited to legality, reasonableness and proportionality and does not permit a de novo examination of the evidence or a public oral hearing. The applicant contended that this structure denied her access to a court of full jurisdiction, that the SCJ Division lacked independence and impartiality (given institutional overlaps with the HCJ), that no public hearing had been held at either level, and that the reclassifications and extra-factual considerations violated her defence rights.
001-170059:
The applicant, a Czech national, alleged a violation of his defence rights under Article 6 of the Convention in domestic criminal proceedings for coercion of his former partner, C. Between late 2005 and June 2006, the applicant sent C. numerous emails containing threats of violence, abduction, trafficking, forced pornography, harm to her family, and other intimidation after she ended their relationship. C. reported the threats to UK police on 7 June 2006 and changed her contact details. An anonymous complaint of child sexual abuse involving C. (later attributed by her to knowledge only the applicant possessed) prompted Czech police questioning of several people, including the applicant, in July 2006. C.’s mother and a friend provided statements describing C.’s accounts of being tied up, threatened, and subjected to ongoing harassment.

On 8 August 2006, before any charges were brought against the applicant, police interviewed C. in the Czech Republic as an “urgent or non-repeatable measure” under Article 158a of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in the presence of a judge but without the applicant or counsel. The request cited C.’s UK residence and employment (making frequent travel difficult) and her fear for her safety. C. detailed the 29 December 2005 incident in the applicant’s flat (being tied to a bed, partially undressed, and threatened with heroin, a bag abduction, trafficking to Turkey, and pornographic recordings) plus later car threats and communications. She submitted emails, voicemails, and SMS messages. Further investigative steps included telephone and email records, searches of the applicant’s premises in April 2007, and interviews of additional witnesses (including C.’s mother and psychotherapist).

Criminal proceedings began in April 2007. The applicant was charged with unlawful restraint, coercion, defamation, and false accusation, then indicted in June 2008 solely for the more serious offence of coercion (without prior notification of the reclassification, contrary to domestic law). At the October 2008 trial, C. did not appear; the court read her 2006 statement over the applicant’s objection that her foreign residence did not justify the urgent-measure procedure or preclude later examination. A further summons via her mother went unanswered; C. wrote that she had lived and worked abroad for years, intended to remain there permanently, and found the proceedings stressful. The court made no further attempts to secure her attendance or use videoconference facilities available under EU mutual-assistance conventions.

In December 2009 the District Court convicted the applicant of coercion and imposed a suspended 2½-year sentence. It relied principally on C.’s unread statement, corroborated by her mother’s and friend’s accounts, emails, SMS messages, a letter C. had written, a psychotherapist’s testimony, and expert reports. The applicant appealed, arguing that C.’s untested statement was the sole direct evidence, that contradictions existed, and that she should be heard (including by video-link if necessary). The Municipal Court upheld the conviction in March 2010 (in the applicant’s absence after he requested a postponement), finding C.’s statement legally admissible under Article 211 § 2 of the Code because she was unreachable abroad, and sufficiently corroborated. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rejected further appeals, holding that the statement was not the sole evidence and that procedural irregularities (including the reclassification and searches) did not taint the verdict.

The applicant also complained of the failure to notify him of the reclassified charges and of the lawfulness of the searches, but the core alleged violation concerned the inability to confront or cross-examine the principal witness whose pre-trial statement formed the foundation of the conviction.

The case of Štulíř v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 36705/12) originated in a complaint by Czech national Emil Štulíř, lodged on 8 June 2012, alleging a violation of his defence rights under the Convention in criminal proceedings for coercion of his former partner, C.

Between 30 December 2005 and 8 June 2006, the applicant sent C. numerous emails containing explicit threats, including of physical restraint, abduction, trafficking to Turkey, production and distribution of pornographic material, harm to her family, and violence if she did not resume their relationship. C. reported threatening calls and emails to Surrey police in the United Kingdom on 7 June 2006 and, on advice, changed her telephone number and email address.

An anonymous complaint of 23 June 2006 alleging child sexual abuse involving C. prompted investigations. C.’s mother stated on 13 July 2006 that C. had confided in her about the applicant tying her up, threatening annihilation, and demanding sexual relations, and that C. feared for her family’s safety after an email referencing them. Friend D.B. reported a January 2006 letter from C. describing forcible coercion on 29 December 2005 and later threats to her life and family.

On 8 August 2006, while C. was visiting from the United Kingdom (where she worked as an au pair and felt unsafe in the Czech Republic), police interviewed her as a witness under Article 158a of the Code of Criminal Procedure as an “urgent or non-repeatable measure,” in a judge’s presence but before any charges against the applicant, who was therefore absent and unable to participate. C. detailed the 29 December 2005 incident (tied to a bed, partially undressed, threatened with heroin, trafficking, and pornography) and a 1 January 2006 car incident involving threats of abandonment or a fatal crash, plus ongoing emails, calls, and messages. She submitted emails, voice recordings, and SMS messages, and commented on the anonymous complaint as containing information only the applicant knew.

The applicant was charged on 20 April 2007 with unlawful restraint, coercion, defamation, and false accusation (following searches of his flat and premises). He was indicted on 16 June 2008 solely for the more serious offence of coercion, without prior notification of the reclassification as required by Article 176 § 2 of the Code.

At the trial commencing 14 October 2008, C. did not attend. The Prague 6 District Court read out her August 2006 statement. The applicant objected that her residence abroad did not justify the urgent-measure procedure or reading the statement under Article 211 § 2. Further summonses via her mother failed; C. wrote on 24 April 2009 that she had lived abroad for over four years, intended to remain permanently, and found the matter too stressful.

On 8 December 2009 the District Court convicted the applicant of coercion and imposed a two-and-a-half-year suspended sentence. It relied principally on C.’s testimony, corroborated by emails, a letter from C. to D.B., statements from C.’s mother and therapist (to whom C. had described being held against her will), a schoolfriend’s evidence, expert opinions, and other materials.

The applicant appealed, arguing that C.’s uncorroborated statement was decisive, requesting her examination to resolve contradictions, a psychiatric assessment of her reliability, and additional witnesses. He was absent from the 30 March 2010 Municipal Court hearing (citing personal reasons and requesting postponement) but represented by counsel, who did not renew the evidence requests. The court upheld the conviction, finding C.’s statement admissible as she was unreachable, corroborated by a consistent chain of indirect evidence (including the UK complaint and contemporaneous messages), and the reclassification harmless. The Supreme Court rejected an appeal on points of law on 30 November 2010. The Constitutional Court dismissed a constitutional complaint on 1 December 2011, confirming the evidence was sufficient and searches lawful.

A later claim for compensation due to delays was rejected as time-barred. Mutual legal assistance conventions permitted videoconference testimony, but this was not used.

The case of Štulíř v. the Czech Republic originated in an application by Czech national Emil Štulíř alleging a violation of his defence rights in domestic criminal proceedings for coercion of his former partner, C.

Between 30 December 2005 and 8 June 2006, the applicant sent C. multiple emails containing threats of violence, abduction, physical restraint, trafficking, production of pornographic material, and harm to her family unless she resumed their relationship. C., then working as an au pair in the United Kingdom, reported the threats to Surrey police on 7 June 2006 and, on police advice, changed her telephone number and email address. An anonymous criminal complaint of child sexual abuse involving C. was received by Czech prosecutors on 23 June 2006, prompting investigations in which the applicant and others were questioned.

On 8 August 2006, before any charges were brought against the applicant, police interviewed C. as a witness pursuant to Article 158a of the Code of Criminal Procedure (an “urgent or non-repeatable measure”) in the presence of a judge. The applicant was neither charged nor present. C. described in detail an incident on 29 December 2005 in the applicant’s Prague apartment in which he tied her to a bed, partially undressed her, and threatened to drug her with heroin, conceal her in a bag, and traffic her to Turkey unless she resumed their relationship. She also recounted further threats of a car accident, production and distribution of pornographic recordings, and later intimidation via telephone, SMS and email. C. submitted copies of the emails, voice recordings and SMS messages. She stated that she had returned to the Czech Republic solely for the interview because her UK employment and fear of the applicant made further travel impractical.

The applicant was charged in April 2007 (and later indicted in June 2008, with a more serious legal classification of which he claimed he had not been notified as required). A search of his premises was conducted. At the trial beginning on 14 October 2008, C. did not appear; her 2006 statement was therefore read out. The applicant objected that the conditions of Article 211 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been met. The District Court issued a further summons via C.’s mother. C. replied in writing that she had lived and worked abroad for more than four years, intended to remain there permanently, and found the proceedings too stressful to attend. No further attempt was made to secure her attendance, including by video-link under available mutual-assistance instruments.

On 8 December 2009 the District Court convicted the applicant of coercion and imposed a two-and-a-half-year suspended sentence. It relied principally on C.’s untested pre-trial testimony, which it found corroborated by her mother’s statements, a letter C. had written to a friend, matching emails, expert psychiatric and cyber-forensic reports, and other circumstantial evidence.

The applicant appealed, requesting that C. be examined to resolve alleged contradictions and that further evidence be taken. The Municipal Court heard the appeal on 30 March 2010 in the applicant’s absence (he had requested a postponement for personal reasons, which was refused; his counsel did not renew the request for additional evidence). The court upheld the conviction, holding that C.’s statement was not the sole evidence, that her long-term residence abroad justified both the original urgent interview and the subsequent reading of the statement, and that the procedural defect in the reclassification of charges was not decisive.

The Supreme Court rejected an appeal on points of law and the Constitutional Court dismissed a subsequent constitutional complaint, both endorsing the lower courts’ assessment that C.’s testimony had been adequately corroborated and that the procedures followed were lawful.
001-170057:
The case of Bátěk and Others v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 54146/09) concerned three Czech customs officers—Roman Bátěk (born 1969), Radek Blažej (born 1968) and Karel Elsner (born 1972)—who alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. They claimed that evidence from absent truck drivers and an anonymous undercover police agent, which they could not effectively challenge, proved decisive in their convictions for abuse of public office and accepting bribes.

From September 2003 to January 2004 the applicants worked at the Lanžhot Customs Office on the Slovak border. An undercover police agent infiltrated the office on 1 December 2003 pursuant to Article 158e of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) and remained until 6 February 2004. Her observations led to suspicions that officers routinely accepted small bribes (typically €5) from truck drivers in exchange for priority or trouble-free clearance.

In March–April 2004, before any charges were laid, twenty foreign truck drivers were interviewed in the presence of a judge as an urgent or non-repeatable investigative measure under Article 158a CCP. The applicants were neither present nor represented. Four statements later treated as significant described a general practice of paying bribes to avoid delays but contained only vague or no identifications of individual officers. One Romanian driver recalled paying on two or three occasions; another described a single corpulent officer with thinning hair; a third said he paid on every one of ten trips but could describe no one; a fourth confirmed corruption without naming anyone.

The applicants were charged on 22 April 2004 (together with fifteen co-accused) and indicted in February 2005. At trial on 14 December 2005 the Břeclav District Court heard the undercover agent as an anonymous witness under Articles 55 § 2 and 209 CCP. She testified by audio link from outside the courtroom, stating only that her written reports were reliable and offering no concrete instances of bribe-taking. Only the third applicant was present; the other two were represented by a substitute counsel. Cross-examination was limited to a single question from the third applicant. Defence arguments that the agent’s workstation gave her no view of other officers, that workplace cameras captured nothing, and that numbered stamps could have been used by others were noted but not accepted.

On 25 May 2006 the District Court convicted the applicants, imposing one-year suspended sentences and fines. It treated the agent’s contemporaneous reports as directly incriminating and corroborated them with customs documents bearing the applicants’ personal stamp and identification numbers, duty-rotation records, and computer logs that linked the applicants to the precise times the interviewed drivers were cleared. The drivers’ pre-trial statements were read out under Article 211 § 2(b) CCP because they were foreign nationals unlikely to return. The agent’s anonymity was justified by her possible future undercover work.

The Brno Regional Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 22 March 2007, holding that the drivers’ interviews constituted a non-repeatable act, that international letters of request had not been required, and that the agent’s anonymity and the limited questioning complied with the CCP. The Constitutional Court rejected a further complaint on 2 April 2009 as manifestly ill-founded, finding that the domestic courts had adequately explained the lawfulness of the evidence.

The applicants maintained throughout that the combination of unread, unchallengeable driver statements and an unseen, untested anonymous agent had deprived them of a fair opportunity to test the decisive evidence against them.

The case of Bátěk and Others v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 54146/09) concerns three Czech customs officers – Roman Bátěk, Radek Blažej and Karel Elsner – who alleged a violation of their right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, they claimed that their convictions for abuse of public authority and accepting bribes rested on decisive evidence from absent foreign truck drivers and an anonymous undercover police agent, whose testimonies they could not effectively challenge or confront.

The applicants worked at the Lanžhot Customs Office on the Slovak border from September 2003 to January 2004. An undercover police agent infiltrated their team from 1 December 2003 until 6 February 2004. Her observations led to suspicions that officers accepted small bribes (typically around 5 euros) from truck drivers in exchange for priority or trouble-free customs clearance.

In March and April 2004, before any charges were brought, twenty truck drivers of various nationalities were interviewed in the presence of a judge as an urgent or non-repeatable measure under Article 158a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicants, not yet charged, were absent from these interviews. Four testimonies were of particular significance: three from Romanian drivers and one from a Bulgarian driver. The drivers generally confirmed paying bribes to avoid delays or inconvenience but could not identify or describe specific officers, nor recall individual incidents in detail.

On 22 April 2004 the applicants (together with fifteen others) were charged; they were formally indicted in February 2005. At the trial before the Břeclav District Court on 14 December 2005, the undercover agent was heard as an anonymous witness pursuant to Articles 55 § 2 and 209 of the Code. She testified from outside the courtroom via audio link, confirming the reliability of her earlier written reports but providing no specific accounts of bribe-taking. Only the third applicant attended and put a question to her; the first two applicants were represented by substitute counsel.

The applicants argued that the agent could not have observed other officers from her workstation, that workplace cameras had recorded no relevant acts, and that personal rubber stamps might have been used by others.

On 25 May 2006 the District Court convicted the applicants, imposing one-year suspended prison sentences and fines. It treated the agent’s written reports as directly incriminating. It further relied on customs documents bearing the applicants’ personal stamp numbers and identifiers, service-rotation records, and a database matching the applicants to the times when the interviewed drivers had obtained clearance. These documents were compared with the drivers’ statements, which were read out at trial under Article 211 § 2(b) of the Code because the foreign drivers were considered unreachable at a later stage.

The applicants appealed, contending that the drivers could have been examined later through letters rogatory under the European Convention on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters and bilateral treaties with Romania and Bulgaria, possibly with immunity in return for testimony. They also challenged the necessity of the agent’s anonymity, arguing that Article 55 § 2 required a real risk of bodily harm or other serious interference with fundamental rights, not merely the preservation of her future undercover work; they further suggested that delays in her replies indicated she had consulted notes or another person.

The Brno Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 22 March 2007, holding that the interviews of transient foreign drivers were properly classified as non-repeatable and that the agent’s anonymity was justified by her potential future operations. The Constitutional Court rejected a subsequent complaint on 2 April 2009 as manifestly ill-founded, finding that the evidence had been obtained in accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure and that earlier arguments had been adequately addressed.

These circumstances formed the core of the applicants’ claim that they had been denied an effective opportunity to test the evidence that proved decisive to their convictions.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint of three Czech customs officers (Roman Bátěk, Radek Blažej and Karel Elsner) that their 2006 convictions for abuse of public office and accepting bribes from truck drivers violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. They argued that the decisive evidence consisted of statements from absent foreign truck drivers (whom they could never question) and an anonymous undercover police agent (whom they could neither see nor effectively challenge).

From September 2003 the applicants worked at the Lanžhot border customs post. In December 2003 an undercover female police officer was inserted into the team; she remained until early February 2004 and later reported that officers routinely demanded small cash payments for prompt or problem-free clearance. In March–April 2004, while the applicants were still uncharged, twenty foreign truck drivers were interviewed as an “urgent or non-repeatable” investigative measure under Article 158a of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in the presence of a judge but without the future defendants. Four of those statements (three Romanian, one Bulgarian) were later treated as particularly incriminating. The drivers described a general practice of paying €5 to avoid delays, but none identified any applicant by name and most could give only vague physical descriptions or none at all.

The applicants were charged in April 2004 and tried at Břeclav District Court. On 14 December 2005 the undercover agent testified as an anonymous witness under Articles 55 § 2 and 209 of the Code. She spoke from outside the courtroom via audio link, declined to describe any specific bribe she had personally observed, and merely affirmed that her written reports were reliable. Only the third applicant was present; he put one question. The other two applicants were represented by substitute counsel who asked nothing. The applicants objected that the agent’s work-station had no line of sight to the other officers, that workplace cameras had recorded nothing, and that numbered rubber stamps could have been used by anyone.

On 25 May 2006 the District Court convicted all three applicants (one-year suspended sentences plus fines). It treated the agent’s reports as “directly incriminating” and corroborated them with customs documents bearing the applicants’ personal stamp numbers and identification numbers, duty-roster records and the pre-trial driver statements (which were simply read out under Article 211 § 2(b)). The court held that the foreign drivers’ evidence was properly taken as a non-repeatable act because they had no ties to the Czech Republic and would be almost impossible to locate later, and that the agent’s anonymity was justified by her possible future undercover work.

The Brno Regional Court dismissed the appeals in March 2007, repeating that foreign-driver interviews were non-repeatable and that the agent’s identity had been lawfully concealed. The Constitutional Court rejected a further appeal in April 2009 as manifestly ill-founded, finding the domestic courts’ reasons adequate.

The applicants’ core complaint to the Strasbourg Court was therefore that they had never been given a proper opportunity to test the two categories of evidence that the national courts themselves described as decisive: the uncross-examined driver statements and the unseen, minimally questioned anonymous agent.
001-170389:
The case of Béres and Others v. Hungary (Applications nos. 59588/12, 59632/12 and 59865/12) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by eleven Hungarian nationals who alleged violations of Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applicants, political activists affiliated with the party “Politics Can Be Different,” claimed that the termination of criminal proceedings against them on the basis of an amnesty law infringed the presumption of innocence and damaged their reputations.

On 23 December 2011 the applicants took part in a demonstration outside the Hungarian Parliament. They blocked a car-park entrance adjacent to the building by chaining themselves to one another and to concrete columns. The Budapest police subsequently opened a criminal investigation against twenty-nine individuals, including all the applicants, on suspicion of violating personal liberty under Article 175(1) of the 1978 Criminal Code, an offence punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment.

Bulgaria (application no. 20440/11) was brought by Tsveta Dimitrova Dimova (born 1980) and her daughter Emma Lachezarova Peeva (born 2005) against Bulgaria under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They alleged that the Supreme Court of Cassation’s final refusal of 1 November 2010 to permit the child to travel abroad with her mother without the father’s consent violated both applicants’ rights to respect for private and family life under Article 8, and that no effective domestic remedy existed under Article 13.

The mother received parental rights and primary care of the child, who was to live with her; the father obtained contact rights (first and third weekends monthly, 30 days in summer, and one week in winter or spring), use of the family home, and an obligation to pay modest child support. No specific residence address was stipulated. In November 2009 a further agreement slightly extended weekend contact and required the father to collect and return the child at the mother’s home in Kazanlak; the mother had to notify any address change by registered mail.

On 18 March 2009 the mother applied to the Varna District Court under Article 72 of the 1985 Family Code for authorisation to take the child abroad without the father’s consent. She explained that she was in a committed relationship with a Bulgarian ship engineer living and working in the United Kingdom, that they planned to marry and that she wished to settle there with her daughter to provide better living conditions. She stated that she would remain in Bulgaria if permission were refused.

The District Court rejected the claim on 30 October 2009, holding that unrestricted travel was not in the child’s interests: the mother had shown neither a fixed residence nor a secure income abroad, and the child’s absence would impede the father’s contact rights.

The Varna Regional Court allowed the mother’s appeal on 22 February 2010. It found that her parental qualities—already accepted when she was awarded custody—remained unchanged by crossing a border and that she could provide an emotionally and financially stable environment. Given the parents’ strained relations, it granted permission for the child to travel with the mother alone until majority, noting that a change of residence might justify altering the contact regime but not deciding that issue.

The father appealed. The Supreme Court of Cassation suspended enforcement pending its decision and, on 1 November 2010, refused permission. It identified conflicting lower-court practice but followed its own established case-law that unrestricted travel with one parent could never serve a child’s best interests: it risked taking the child to war zones or disaster-prone areas and, in non-EU countries lacking judicial-assistance agreements, would prevent enforcement of the other parent’s contact rights. Permission could be granted only for specified destinations and limited periods when demonstrably in the child’s interest. In the present case the mother had offered no concrete guarantees of destination or of how contact would be exercised, had not applied to vary the contact regime in light of a possible move, and had produced only unsubstantiated assertions about an uncertain future marriage. Given the child’s young age, unlimited travel to unknown destinations until majority was not in her interest.

Domestic law (Article 72 of the 1985 Family Code and section 76(9) of the Identity Documents Act) required joint parental consent, or a court order, for a minor to leave Bulgaria; enforcement mechanisms existed for contact orders. After the Court’s later Penchevi judgment an interpretative procedure and draft legislative amendments were initiated.

In December 2011 the parents married in Bulgaria and the father thereafter regularly signed annual consent declarations. The applicants have lived in the United Kingdom since January 2012; the child maintains regular telephone and Skype contact with her father and spends summers with him.

Relying on criminological and psychiatric experts, it found persistent violent sexual fantasies and a high risk of further serious sexual offences, including murder. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on 9 March 2010. On 4 May 2011 the Federal Constitutional Court quashed those decisions, remitted the case and held that both the retrospective order and the earlier provisional detention violated the applicant’s right to liberty and the protection of legitimate expectations.

The applicant immediately sought release. On 6 May 2011 the Regional Court re-ordered provisional preventive detention, finding “weighty grounds” that retrospective detention would again be imposed under the Constitutional Court’s new, stricter standards. The applicant appealed on 29 June 2011 (with further submissions through late July). The Regional Court refused to amend its order on 4 July; the Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 16 August 2011 (after considering prior expert reports and the 2011 Constitutional Court judgment) and rejected a further complaint on 29 August. A constitutional complaint lodged on 7 September 2011 (also alleging delay) was communicated in October; an interim stay was refused on 25 October. The Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint, without reasons, on 22 May 2012 (notified 30 May).

On 2 January 2012 the Regional Court dismissed the challenge, holding that even if the remark had been made it merely applied the court’s own risk findings in a confidential setting and did not demonstrate present impartiality two years later after a fresh hearing.

A comprehensive assessment showed a high risk, arising from the applicant’s person and conduct, of the most serious violent and sexual offences. The case of Habran and Dalem v. Belgium (ECHR Applications nos. 43000/11 and 49380/11) involved two Belgian nationals convicted in connection with a 1998 attempted robbery of an armoured van near Waremme, during which two occupants were killed. A weapon recovered at the scene was ballistically linked to a prior 1996 mail-van attack. The applicants alleged that their convictions, based primarily on statements from “criminals turned informers,” rendered the proceedings unfair under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that the overall length of the proceedings was excessive.

An anonymous witness initially implicated L.C. (a convicted organised-crime offender and informer) and L.M. (later a co-defendant). L.C. claimed the second applicant had invited him to reconnoitre the area beforehand. The anonymous witness was later murdered. In 2002, R.C.—a detained career robber facing other charges—offered to cooperate in exchange for advantages. He named the applicants and others, was granted emergency witness protection, and testified under oath before the investigating judge. He admitted earlier involvement in planning an attack, identified the second applicant as an instigator, and relayed hearsay from another individual (M.A.) implicating the first applicant. R.C. was soon released on licence. The applicants were arrested, denied any role (asserting that L.C. and R.C. had fabricated evidence), and were later released for lack of sufficient evidence to continue detention.

In 2004 L.M. was murdered. D.S., another figure from organised-crime circles who scarcely knew R.C., then approached police fearing for his life and offered information on the murder and the Waremme attack in return for protection. He officially testified, naming the applicants on the basis of what L.M. had told him and stating that L.M. had purchased from the first applicant one of the weapons later found at the scene (previously used in the 1996 attack). D.S. received provisional protection (later lifted). L.M.’s widow, H.P., also testified under protection and named the second applicant. The applicants were re-arrested; they challenged the new evidence as coming from an untrustworthy source seeking impunity. The first applicant later conceded that his earlier alibi had been invented.

The investigation closed in late 2006. Twelve defendants, including the applicants, were committed for trial before the Liège Assize Court. At the 2008–2009 trial it emerged that R.C. had received a €50,000 bounty (paid in two instalments). Nine defendants, including the applicants, were convicted (first applicant 15 years; second applicant 30 years). The Court of Cassation quashed the convictions for lack of reasons and remitted the case to the Brussels-Capital Assize Court.

In the 2010 retrial the applicants formally challenged the lawfulness of the prosecution insofar as it rested on the statements of R.C. and the now-deceased D.S. The challenge was rejected. The jury convicted both applicants of the Waremme attack as leaders of a criminal organisation, relying on the “concurring” (albeit largely hearsay) statements of R.C., D.S. and H.P., said to be corroborated by objective elements such as the recovered Kalashnikov and ballistic links. Sentences of 15 and 25 years were imposed. The Court of Cassation dismissed the subsequent appeals, holding that a witness’s personal motives go only to credibility (a matter for the trial court), that an informer’s later sworn testimony subjects the evidence to adversarial debate, and that confidentiality surrounding protection measures and prior informer contacts does not of itself breach fairness when the defence can test the statements in open court. The Court of Cassation also rejected the claim that the overall duration of the proceedings (investigation commencing in 1998, final domestic judgment in 2011) was excessive.
