Belgium (applications nos. 43000/11 and 49380/11) concerns two Belgian nationals, Marcel Habran (born 1933) and Thierry Dalem (born 1958), who alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed their convictions for involvement in a violent armed robbery were unfair because they rested on statements from “criminals turned informers” who received protection and financial benefits, and that the overall length of the proceedings was excessive.

On 12 January 1998 an attempted robbery of a B.Z. armoured van near Waremme left two of the three occupants dead. Firearms recovered at the scene were later ballistically linked to a 1996 mail-van attack. An investigating judge opened a case of assault and robbery accompanied by murder. Early leads included an anonymous witness (later murdered) who named L.C., a convicted organised-crime figure acting as an informer, and L.M. (subsequently a co-defendant). L.C. himself implicated Dalem in reconnaissance for the Waremme attack.

In 2002 a detained career robber, R.C., offered to cooperate in exchange for advantages. After his arrest warrant in an unrelated case was quashed, police questioned him unofficially and then under oath. R.C. admitted helping prepare the Waremme attack in 1994, identified Dalem as an instigator, and relayed hearsay from another participant, M.A., that Habran had also been involved. The Witness Protection Board granted R.C. emergency protection; he was released on licence shortly afterwards. The applicants were arrested in late 2002, denied any role and offered (later admitted to be false) alibis; they were released in 2003 for insufficient evidence.

In 2004 L.M. was murdered. Another organised-crime figure, D.S., approached police fearing for his life and, in exchange for protection, gave statements based on information received from L.M. He named both applicants, described long-term planning by a different team, and said L.M. had bought one of the recovered weapons from Habran. D.S. received emergency protection (later lifted). L.M.’s widow, H.P., also questioned under protection, implicated Dalem. Confrontations were held; the witnesses maintained their accounts. The applicants were re-arrested in 2005.

The investigation closed in 2006. Twelve defendants, including the applicants, were committed for trial before the Liège Assize Court. At the 2008–2009 trial R.C. disclosed he had received a €50 000 bounty. Nine defendants were convicted: Habran received 15 years as leader of a criminal organisation (murder and firearm aggravations not found); Dalem received 30 years, with the murder aggravation established. The Court of Cassation quashed the verdicts for lack of reasons (following Taxquet) and remitted the case to the Brussels-Capital Assize Court.

At the 2010 retrial the applicants argued that the prosecution was unlawful because it relied on the statements of R.C. and the now-deceased D.S., both of whom had testified from self-interest after receiving protection and, in R.C.’s case, money. The Assize Court rejected the plea. The jury convicted both men of the Waremme attack as leaders of a criminal organisation, citing the “concurring” statements of R.C., D.S. and H.P., corroborated by the recovered Kalashnikov (recognised by D.S. as having been sold by Habran) and ballistic links to ammunition linked to Dalem. Sentences were 15 years (Habran) and 25 years (Dalem).

The Court of Cassation dismissed appeals in March 2011. It held that a trial court may assess the credibility of a witness motivated by personal advantage; that an informer’s later sworn testimony becomes subject to adversarial debate; that confidentiality of earlier informer contacts and of protection measures need not be disclosed; and that lack of judicial supervision of protection decisions did not render the trial unfair. It also found the length of proceedings (investigation from 1998, arrests 2002/2005, final domestic judgment 2011) not excessive.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints that the use of incentivised, protected “supergrass” testimony, combined with limited disclosure and an eight-to-thirteen-year overall duration, deprived them of a fair trial.

The case of Bubon v. Russia (Application no. 63898/09) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns a Russian lawyer and legal writer’s unsuccessful attempts to obtain official statistical data from regional authorities for academic and journalistic research, which he alleged violated his rights under Article 10 of the Convention.

The applicant, Konstantin Vladimirovich Bubon, regularly published articles on legal topics under contracts with Russian journals and databases. In May 2009, having been commissioned to write on prostitution and related law-enforcement measures in the Khabarovsk Region, he sent a registered letter to the head of the regional police department. He requested aggregated statistics covering 2000–2009 on: administrative liability under Article 6.11 of the Code of Administrative Offences (prostitution), broken down by sex, residence, nationality and year; criminal cases opened under Articles 241, 242, 242.1 and 127.1 of the Criminal Code (offences linked to sexual exploitation), similarly itemised; numbers of persons convicted under those articles, with demographic and other breakdowns; and types of sentences imposed. He expressly stated that he sought only general statistical information, not any personal data.

No reply arrived within the 30-day statutory period. On 26 June 2009 the applicant therefore brought proceedings in the Tsentralniy District Court of Khabarovsk, relying on the Information Act and Article 10. He argued that the implied refusal was unlawful because the requested material was neither confidential, a State secret nor internal operational information, but merely routine statistical data held by the police Information Centre.

On 18 July 2009 the Information Centre wrote that it compiled such detailed figures only on the written order of a deputy minister, a regional police chief or a prosecutor, and never at the request of a private individual; general statistics were forwarded to the Federal State Statistics Service, to which the applicant should apply. He promptly did so. The Khabarovsk Statistics Service replied on 23 July that the police had never supplied it with the specific data sought.

The District Court dismissed the claim on 4 August 2009. It held that the Information Centre was not authorised to answer private requests, that the Statistics Service was the designated disseminator of official figures (even though it lacked the data), that the applicant had not first consulted open sources such as libraries or the internet, and that, under section 8(2) of the Information Act, a citizen is entitled only to information that directly affects his or her own rights and freedoms. Because the statistics did not concern the applicant personally, the refusal was lawful.

On appeal the applicant stressed that the police alone possessed the information, that no alternative source existed, and that Russian law did not confine access to public statistical data to persons whose individual rights were affected. On 16 September 2009 the Khabarovsk Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment, repeating that the authorities were under no duty to supply material that did not touch the applicant’s rights or legitimate interests.

The applicant maintained that the successive refusals had prevented him from completing the commissioned research and thereby interfered with his right to receive and impart information.

It directed him to the regional office of the Federal Service of State Statistics. It held that the Information Centre lacked authority to process private requests, that official statistical dissemination was the task of the Statistics Service, that the applicant had not first consulted open sources, and that the information did not affect his personal rights or legitimate interests and therefore need not be disclosed under section 8(2) of the Information Act.

Public authorities must provide such information without requiring the requester to justify the request.

The facts therefore centre on a journalist-researcher’s unsuccessful attempt to obtain exclusively held official statistics of public interest, the authorities’ successive refusals on formal and statutory grounds, and the domestic courts’ confirmation that no right of access existed because the data did not concern the applicant personally.

The case of Mkhchyan v. Russia (Application no. 54700/12) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (protection of property). The applicant, Sergey Tatevosovich Mkhchyan (born 1933, resident in Moscow), complained that the demolition of his garage without compensation interfered with his possessions.

In March 1994, the Russian Ministry of Railways approved construction of a line of reinforced-concrete garages 5.5 metres from the Oktyabrskaya railway in Moscow, to function as a noise shield; 10% of the units were reserved for railway employees. A town-planning assignment issued in April 1994 by the Moscow architecture and planning directorate confirmed that the land belonged to the City of Moscow and reiterated the noise-shield purpose. Local authorities raised no objection to the garage-building cooperative “Kashenkin Lug” (GSK) proceeding. The applicant joined the GSK on 3 December 1994 and paid his share (USD 6,500). The one-storey capital garages were certified ready for use on 30 December 1996 and approved the following day. Garage no. 169 was allotted to the applicant, who received a local-administration certificate of possession dating from 3 December 1994; he never registered title in the real-estate register.

A 2000 lease between the Moscow Land Committee and the GSK (valid until August 2004) covered 324 garage boxes. A 2003 lease with the Federal State unitary enterprise “Oktyabrskaya Railway” (later succeeded by Russian Railways, RZD) allocated the plot for garage boxes, prohibited permanent structures without written approval, required removal of temporary structures at the lease’s end, and permitted unilateral termination if the land was needed for railway purposes (one month’s notice). The lease was extended and then tacitly renewed; the GSK paid rent until July 2007.

In 2008 the Federal Agency for State Property Management leased the same federal railway-right-of-way land to RZD. In July 2010 RZD terminated the GSK lease, citing railway needs, and demanded vacation by August 2010. The GSK refused and identified the applicant as owner of garage 169. After the applicant declined to vacate, RZD sued in September 2011 for removal.

On 21 November 2011 the Ostankinskiy District Court of Moscow ordered the applicant to remove the garage within ten days of the judgment becoming final (authorising RZD to demolish it otherwise). The court held that the plot (cadastral number 77:02:21017:032) lay within a federal railway right of way reserved exclusively for rail-transport facilities; a private garage was therefore an unauthorised construction under Article 222 of the Civil Code (built on land not allocated for that purpose and without federal permission). The applicant had acquired no property rights, the lease had ended, and RZD (as lawful user) was entitled under Article 305 of the Civil Code to restore unimpeded use of the land. The Moscow City Court upheld the judgment on 10 February 2012, adding that domestic law provided no compensation for demolition of an unauthorised construction. Enforcement followed; the applicant refused to comply and RZD demolished the garage in 2012. A fourth main track was later built on the site (opened 2013) and noise barriers installed (2014).

Poland (Application no. 28768/12) concerns a Polish father's complaint that domestic authorities failed to take effective steps to enforce his contact rights with his son J., born in December 2002. The applicant initially lived with J. and the mother, M.K., but moved out in 2003 following a family dispute. In 2005 he complained that M.K. was obstructing contact. A December 2005 court settlement granted him visits on two Saturdays and Sundays monthly (10 a.m.–6 p.m., arranged in advance) plus two weeks' summer holiday. Some 2006 visits were hindered or cancelled for illness, though most occurred.

M.K. sought to reduce access in June 2006, citing a planned move to Germany. The applicant counter-applied for expanded rights. After procedural delays, a March 2007 regional-court ruling noted that access was not being respected because M.K. had already taken J. to Germany in January 2007 without consent (the parties disputed whether an address was provided). The applicant obtained a Hague Convention return order from German courts in late 2007; mother and child returned to Poland in January 2008.

Parallel Polish custody proceedings (applicant seeking sole custody and residence with him; M.K. seeking the reverse) were stayed pending the Hague case. An April 2008 settlement established revised access (alternate weekends, holiday periods, telephone contact) and required notice of any residence change. Contact thereafter proceeded without major interruption; a September 2009 modification further increased the applicant's time (two full weekends monthly, three summer weeks, one winter week). Expert reports and court-ordered counselling/mediation followed amid ongoing parental conflict. In March 2011 the district court left J. with M.K., retained joint custody, and refused to curtail visits, finding the father-son bond had improved after 2008. On appeal the regional court (November 2011) limited the applicant's parental authority to major decisions on health, education and upbringing, citing the parents' inability to cooperate.

From February 2012 the applicant alleged that relations deteriorated because of M.K.'s influence; he sought enforcement of the 2009 arrangements, a guardian's presence, and later modification. M.K. applied to annul the settlement, claiming J. refused contact. Interim measures first restricted visits to brief public meetings with M.K. or grandparents present, then (after the applicant's successful appeal) allowed three-hour alternate-weekend meetings in a neutral place with a guardian initially required. J. (then 11) told a psychologist he no longer wished to see his father, describing inattentive visits. A November 2013 meeting at a restaurant was hostile. Subsequent expert reports (2014) attributed J.'s negative attitude to maternal influence and recommended counselling for both parents and psychological support for the child. The applicant ceased attending after November 2013, citing the boy's aggression. A February 2015 order lengthened meetings and again mandated counselling; proceedings remained pending.

Enforcement efforts included a 2007 complaint, a 2008 fine threat (unused because visits occurred), and 2012 applications for a guardian and penalty payments. In February 2013 the district court imposed PLN 200 per missed visit and PLN 50 per missed telephone call, noting M.K. had blocked contact for about a year; the order was upheld on appeal. The applicant never sought actual collection of those penalties. Domestic law (CCP Arts. 1050 and, after August 2011, 59815–59821) provided for court-imposed fines or penalty payments for non-compliance with access orders.

These facts illustrate prolonged parental conflict, intermittent obstruction by M.K., the child's progressive alienation, multiple court settlements and interim measures, expert interventions, and limited use of available coercive tools, forming the basis of the alleged failure to secure effective contact.

The case of Wdowiak v. Poland concerns the applicant Robert Wdowiak’s allegation that Polish authorities failed to take effective measures to enforce his access rights to his son J. (born December 2002), in breach of his right to family life.

The applicant lived with J. and the boy’s mother M.K. until 2003, when he moved out after a family disagreement. In 2005 he complained that M.K. was obstructing contact. A December 2005 court settlement granted him two Saturdays and two Sundays per month (10 a.m.–6 p.m.) plus two weeks in summer, with pick-up from M.K.’s home. Some 2006 visits were missed owing to illness or the mother’s actions.

In mid-2006 M.K. sought to reduce access and announced a planned move to Germany; the applicant sought expanded access. After M.K. withdrew her application, the district court discontinued proceedings, but the regional court reversed this in March 2007, noting that access was already being denied because M.K. had taken J. to Germany in January 2007 without the applicant’s consent. The applicant commenced Hague Convention proceedings. German courts in November and December 2007 ordered J.’s return to Poland (though not necessarily into the applicant’s care). Mother and child returned on 6 January 2008.

Both parents then applied for sole custody. Those proceedings were stayed during the Hague case. On 1 April 2008 a new settlement was approved: every-other-weekend visits (9.30 a.m.–6.30 p.m.), specified holiday periods, two weeks in July, and an obligation to notify any change of residence. Contact initially occurred as agreed and was further expanded by a September 2009 modification (Friday-to-Sunday weekends twice monthly, three weeks summer, one week winter, plus telephone contact). The court later ordered counselling (which M.K. abandoned) and expert reports.

In March 2011 the district court rejected both sole-custody applications, retained joint custody and found that the parent–child bond, weakened before 2008, had improved after the April 2008 settlement. The November 2011 regional court, however, limited the applicant’s parental authority to major decisions on health, education and upbringing because of the parents’ inability to co-operate.

From February 2012 the applicant asserted that M.K. was again obstructing contact and that J. had become hostile. In May 2012 he sought both modification of the 2009 arrangements (including supervised visits) and enforcement by way of fines under the newly introduced Articles 59815–59821 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On 19 February 2013 the district court ordered M.K. to pay the applicant PLN 200 for each missed visit and PLN 50 for each missed Wednesday telephone call, expressly finding that she had prevented contact for approximately one year. The regional court dismissed her appeal in June 2013. The applicant never applied to enforce those penalty orders.

Meanwhile the courts imposed successive interim measures restricting contact to short, supervised public meetings (initially at McDonald’s) in the presence of M.K. or her parents. J., then aged 11, told a psychologist he no longer wished to see his father. Expert reports in 2014 attributed the child’s hostility to the mother’s influence and recommended counselling. After a November 2013 meeting marked by aggression, the applicant ceased attending. In February 2015 the district court again lengthened contact periods and reiterated the counselling order; those proceedings remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg application.

Throughout, the authorities produced multiple expert opinions, ordered mediation and counselling, approved successive settlements, imposed (but did not themselves execute) financial penalties, and adjusted interim contact regimes. Contact nevertheless deteriorated sharply after 2011, culminating in a complete breakdown.

The case of Wdowiak v. Poland concerns a Polish father’s complaint that authorities failed to enforce his contact rights with his son, J. (born December 2002). The applicant lived with J. and the mother (M.K.) until moving out in 2003 after a family dispute. In 2005 he complained that M.K. was obstructing access. A December 2005 court-approved settlement granted him two Saturdays and two Sundays monthly (10 a.m.–6 p.m., pre-arranged) plus two summer weeks.

Most visits occurred in 2006, though some were blocked by M.K. or cancelled for illness. Both parents then sought to vary access. In January 2007 M.K. took J. to Germany without consent. Hague Convention proceedings followed: a German court (November 2007, upheld December 2007) found abduction and ordered return to Poland (where the parents held joint custody). Mother and child returned on 6 January 2008.

An April 2008 settlement restored contact (alternate weekends, holidays and two summer weeks). Visits occurred as agreed and were expanded in September 2009 (full weekends, longer holidays and telephone contact). Parallel custody proceedings produced expert reports and counselling/mediation orders. In March 2011 the District Court left J. with M.K. under joint custody, finding the parent–child bond had recovered after 2008. On appeal the Regional Court (November 2011) limited the applicant’s parental authority to major decisions because of parental conflict.

Relations deteriorated from early 2012. The applicant blamed M.K. and sought supervised contact plus enforcement of the 2009 settlement (May 2012). M.K. applied to terminate contact, citing J.’s refusal. Interim measures first restricted visits to short public meetings with M.K. or grandparents (February 2013), then (after the applicant’s appeal) to three-hour fortnightly meetings with a guardian initially (September 2013). J., aged 11, told a psychologist he no longer wished to see his father. A November 2013 meeting was hostile. Expert reports (2014) attributed J.’s rejection to maternal influence and recommended counselling. The applicant ceased visits after November 2013. In February 2015 the court ordered longer meetings and counselling (proceedings remained pending).

Enforcement attempts were limited. A 2007 complaint coincided with the abduction. A 2008 fine threat proved unnecessary because visits resumed. In May 2012 the applicant sought fines for non-compliance with the 2009 settlement (telephone access blocked; all meetings cancelled after November 2011). In February 2013 the District Court imposed penalties (PLN 200 per missed visit, PLN 50 per missed call), noting a year’s obstruction; the order was upheld on appeal. The applicant never sought to execute it.

These facts form the core of the alleged failure to take effective, timely steps to secure contact.
