The case of Ahmed v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 59727/13) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) on 2 March 2017 (final 3 July 2017). The applicant, Somali national Liban Mohamud Ahmed (born 1977, resident in London), challenged the lawfulness of his lengthy immigration detention pending deportation, alleging a violation of Article 5 of the Convention (right to liberty).

Ahmed left Somalia for the Netherlands in 1992 aged 15, claimed asylum there, married and had a son in 1994. His family moved to the UK in 1998. He arrived on 11 December 1999 and claimed asylum using a false name and history to avoid return to the Netherlands. The claim failed, but he received exceptional leave to remain until 2004.

He incurred ten criminal convictions from November 2001 to August 2005, plus a December 2007 conviction for a public order offence and failing to surrender (4.5 months' imprisonment). On 29 January 2008 the Secretary of State notified intention to deport him and refused indefinite leave. His appeal was dismissed on 30 June 2008 (rights exhausted 8 July 2008).

Detention under paragraph 2(2) of Schedule 3 to the Immigration Act 1971 began on 8 February 2008 (after he served half his sentence) pending a deportation order signed on 29 October 2008. Removal directions for 17 June 2009 were cancelled on 16 June 2009 after Ahmed lodged an ECHR application (no. 26023/09) that prompted a Rule 39 interim measure.

Monthly detention reviews cited the Rule 39 barrier to enforced removal but noted Ahmed could shorten detention by withdrawing the application and returning voluntarily under the Facilitated Return Scheme. Three bail applications were refused (9 November 2009, 21 April 2010, 14 July 2010) because immigration judges found a significant absconding risk; one explicitly linked recent detention length to ECHR delays. Ahmed had six prior absconding convictions.

Further representations in June 2010 were treated as an application to revoke the deportation order (refused 17 November 2010). Ahmed appealed; the refusal was withdrawn on 12 July 2011. He issued judicial review proceedings on 19 November 2010 claiming unlawful detention. Permission was granted on 17 June 2011 but bail was again refused. He was released on bail on 13 July 2011, two weeks after the ECHR's lead judgment in Sufi and Elmi v. the United Kingdom (28 June 2011) on returns to Mogadishu.

In the Administrative Court Ahmed argued detention breached the Hardial Singh principles (detention must be for deportation, of reasonable duration, and with a realistic prospect of removal within a reasonable time; authorities must act diligently) from 16 June 2009 (Rule 39), June 2010 (revocation application) or November 2010 (refusal). The court dismissed the claim on 14 November 2011. It treated absconding and reoffending risks as paramount (though not decisive), noted high reoffending risk despite later offences becoming less serious, and found alternatives such as tagging insufficient given his history. A realistic prospect of removal existed when the Rule 39 was granted (timing of Sufi and Elmi uncertain; success not inevitable) and later. Two weeks' detention after that judgment was lawful.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 20 October 2012. It reviewed the wider Somali-removal litigation (fact-insensitive Rule 39s; 116 adjourned applications; correspondence with the ECHR registry). A realistic prospect could exist without a specified date. Review-form references to voluntary return involved no public-law error and were not material. Article 5 § 1(f) added nothing. The Supreme Court refused leave on 26 March 2013.

These facts concern whether the approximately 41-month detention (February 2008–July 2011), prolonged by ECHR interim relief, domestic challenges and the unresolved Somalia situation, remained non-arbitrary given the documented risks of absconding and reoffending.

The applicant, a Somali national born in 1977, left Somalia for the Netherlands in 1992 at age 15 and later claimed asylum there, receiving temporary leave. He married and had a son in 1994. His family moved to the UK in 1998; he followed in December 1999, claiming asylum under a false identity and history to avoid return to the Netherlands. Though unsuccessful, he obtained exceptional leave to remain until 2004.

He accumulated ten criminal convictions between 2001 and 2005. In December 2007 he was convicted of a public-order offence and failing to surrender, receiving a 4.5-month sentence. In January 2008 the Secretary of State issued a deportation notice and refused indefinite leave. His appeal was dismissed in June 2008, with rights exhausted in July.

On 8 February 2008, after serving half his sentence, he was detained under the Immigration Act 1971 pending a deportation order (signed 29 October 2008) and subsequent removal. Removal directions set for 17 June 2009 were cancelled on 16 June after he lodged an ECHR application (no. 26023/09) and obtained a Rule 39 interim measure blocking removal to Somalia.

Monthly detention reviews cited his high absconding and reoffending risks and noted that he could shorten detention by withdrawing the ECHR application and returning voluntarily via the Facilitated Return Scheme. Bail applications were refused in November 2009, April 2010 and July 2010 because judges found a significant absconding risk; one decision attributed part of the lengthy detention to delays from his own ECHR application.

Further representations in June 2010 were treated as a revocation request, refused in November 2010 (later withdrawn by the Secretary of State in July 2011). He issued judicial-review proceedings in November 2010 alleging unlawful detention. Permission was granted in June 2011; a further bail application failed. He was released on bail on 13 July 2011, two weeks after the ECHR’s Sufi and Elmi judgment (28 June 2011) on Somalia returns.

In the judicial-review claim he argued that detention breached Hardial Singh principles (detention only for deportation, reasonable period, release if deportation not reasonably imminent, due diligence) from the date of the Rule 39 measure, the revocation application, or the November 2010 refusal. The Administrative Court dismissed the claim in November 2011. It found a substantial absconding risk (six prior convictions, family ties notwithstanding) and a high reoffending risk (offences including robbery). Alternatives such as tagging were inadequate. At the time of the Rule 39 indication there remained a realistic prospect of removal within a reasonable period, given uncertainty over the timing and outcome of Sufi and Elmi. The same conclusion applied to later dates; two weeks’ consideration after Sufi and Elmi was reasonable.

The Court of Appeal (October 2012) upheld this analysis after reviewing the extensive litigation on Somalia returns (including 116 adjourned ECHR cases and correspondence showing a fact-insensitive Rule 39 policy). A realistic prospect of removal existed even without a precise date. Review-form references to voluntary return were inelegant but not legally erroneous and were not material to the detention decisions. Article 5 § 1(f) added nothing; Mikolenko did not require a defined removal period. Elias LJ dissented solely on the two-week post-Sufi delay. The Supreme Court refused leave in March 2013.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 5 complaint that his detention from February 2008 to July 2011 (approximately 41 months, 25 of them after the Rule 39 measure) was arbitrary.

The case of Ahmed v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 59727/13) concerned a Somali national, Liban Mohamud Ahmed (born 1977), who alleged that his prolonged immigration detention in the United Kingdom pending deportation violated Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to liberty).

Ahmed left Somalia for the Netherlands in 1992 at age 15. After claiming asylum there, he married and had a son in 1994. His family moved to the UK in 1998; he followed in December 1999 and claimed asylum using a false name and history to avoid return to the Netherlands. Though unsuccessful, he received exceptional leave to remain until 2004.

Between 2001 and 2005, Ahmed accumulated ten criminal convictions. In December 2007 he was convicted of a public-order offence and failing to surrender, receiving a 4.5-month sentence. On 29 January 2008 the Secretary of State issued a deportation notice and refused indefinite leave to remain. Ahmed’s appeal was dismissed in June 2008 and his rights exhausted in July 2008.

He was detained on 8 February 2008 under paragraph 2 of Schedule 3 to the Immigration Act 1971, first pending a deportation order (signed 29 October 2008) and thereafter pending removal. Removal directions set for 17 June 2009 were cancelled after the European Court of Human Rights indicated a Rule 39 interim measure in a related application (no. 26023/09). Detention continued, reviewed monthly. Review forms repeatedly noted that Ahmed could shorten detention by withdrawing his Strasbourg application and returning voluntarily under the Facilitated Returns Scheme. Bail applications were refused in November 2009, April 2010 and July 2010 because of a high absconding risk (six prior absconding convictions).

Further representations in June 2010 were treated as a revocation application, refused in November 2010 (later withdrawn in July 2011). Ahmed sought judicial review of his detention in November 2010. Permission was granted in June 2011; bail was again refused. He was released on bail on 13 July 2011, two weeks after the Court’s judgment in Sufi and Elmi v. the United Kingdom (which addressed returns to Mogadishu).

The Administrative Court dismissed the judicial-review claim in November 2011, applying the Hardial Singh principles (detention must be for the purpose of deportation, of reasonable duration, and the authorities must act with due diligence). It found a substantial absconding risk and a high re-offending risk that could not be adequately mitigated by alternatives such as tagging. Despite the Rule 39 measure and uncertainty surrounding Sufi and Elmi, a realistic prospect of removal within a reasonable period existed at each relevant stage.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in October 2012, confirming that a realistic prospect of removal need not include a precise date, that the detention reviews contained no material public-law error regarding voluntary return, and that Article 5 § 1(f) added nothing of substance. One judge dissented solely on the two-week post-Sufi and Elmi delay. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in March 2013.

The key facts bearing on the alleged Article 5 violation were therefore the 41-month duration of detention, the intervening Rule 39 barrier, the applicant’s extensive criminal and absconding history, the monthly reviews, the rejected bail applications, and the domestic courts’ repeated conclusions that a realistic prospect of deportation persisted and that detention remained lawful under both domestic law and the Convention.
001-171776:
The case of R.L. and Others v. Denmark (Application no. 52629/11) concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR arising from Danish courts' refusal to reopen paternity proceedings for two children. The first applicant (M, born 1965 in Tanzania) married the second applicant (F, born 1951) in 2001 and moved to Denmark. Their son L was born in January 2004; F was registered as his legal father by operation of the Children Act due to the marriage. The couple legally separated in June 2005 but cohabited until June 2006. Their second son S was born in October 2006. Although F no longer lived with M and had had no sexual contact with her since 2004, he co-signed a declaration with her assuming joint responsibility for S, resulting in his registration as S's father.

Unknown to F, M had maintained a sexual relationship with E from 2003 to 2008. In October 2008, after that relationship ended, M informed F that E was S's biological father and probably also L's. In November 2008 the applicants requested that both paternity cases be reopened to establish E's fatherhood formally. The State Administration refused in April 2009. The applicants then brought the matter before the Copenhagen City Court, where E opposed reopening, as did the children (represented by counsel).

Testimony established that M and E had frequent unprotected sexual relations during the relevant fertile periods, including a planned pregnancy for S; E visited the children, took L swimming, gave modest gifts (including a birthday card signed “daddy”), and was known to them as “uncle E.” He never provided financial support and later denied any fatherly role. F had believed L to be his son, acknowledged S to treat the boys equally and to assist M (who was HIV-positive), and continued some contact even after learning of E. A subsequent DNA test (after the High Court decision) showed 0 % compatibility, confirming F was not the biological father of either child.

On 11 February 2010 the City Court reopened both cases. It found sexual relations in the fertile periods, that E had assumed a limited paternal role, that reopening would not unduly inconvenience the children, and that paternity was likely to be established. E appealed. On 26 November 2010 the High Court of Eastern Denmark (majority) refused reopening. It emphasised the delayed disclosure that F and M had had no sexual contact at the time of S’s conception, F’s continued treatment of the children as his own until late 2008, and the uncertainty that a new legal father would be identified. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in January 2011.

Under the Children Act then in force, paternity could be challenged freely within six months of birth. Thereafter, reopening within three years required new facts making a different outcome probable, assessed against elapsed time, knowledge of possible non-paternity, treatment of the child as one’s own, delay in seeking reopening, and the likelihood of establishing another man’s paternity. After three years, reopening was possible only for exceptional reasons, if highly appropriate, and without material nuisance to the child. These statutory criteria, applied by the High Court to deny reopening despite the DNA evidence and the parties’ wishes, formed the factual core of the Article 8 complaint that the applicants’ right to respect for their private and family life (including the children’s right to know their biological identity) had been disproportionately restricted.

The applicants in R.L. and Others v. Denmark were a Tanzanian-born mother (M, b. 1965), her Danish husband (F, b. 1951), and their two sons L (b. 2004) and S (b. 2006). M married F in 2001 and moved to Denmark. Under the marital presumption in the Children Act, F was registered as L’s legal father at birth. The couple legally separated in June 2005 but continued cohabiting until June 2006. S was born in October 2006. Although F and M had not had sexual relations since 2004, they jointly declared to the State Administration that they would assume responsibility for S; F was accordingly registered as S’s father.

Unknown to F, M had maintained a sexual relationship with another man, E, from 2003 until October 2008. The relationship included unprotected intercourse on several occasions. After it ended, M informed F that E was the biological father of S and probably also of L. In November 2008 the applicants applied to reopen both paternity cases so that E’s paternity could be formally established. The State Administration refused in April 2009.

The applicants appealed to the Copenhagen City Court. M testified that she and E had planned S’s conception around her ovulation cycle, that E had visited the children, given them gifts (including a birthday card to L signed “love daddy”), and that both boys regarded E as their father. F confirmed the absence of sexual contact after L’s birth, stated that he had treated both boys equally until learning the truth, and wished the biological father to assume financial and other responsibility. E admitted possible paternity, some contact, and that he had told his mother he might be the father, but denied any paternal role, stated he had never intended to have children, and refused a DNA test. The children, represented by counsel, opposed reopening.

In February 2010 the City Court reopened both cases. It found that both men had had sexual relations with M during the relevant fertile periods, that E had played a paternal role, and that reopening would not cause the children unnecessary inconvenience; paternity was expected to be established. The court regarded the circumstances as exceptional.

E appealed. In November 2010 the High Court of Eastern Denmark (majority) refused reopening. It noted that the applicants had not promptly disclosed the lack of sexual contact regarding S, that F had continued to treat the children as his own until late 2008, and that it remained uncertain whether paternity would be established. The stricter conditions applicable to L (born more than three years earlier) were likewise not met. A dissenting judge would have upheld the City Court.

A subsequent DNA test (submitted to the Appeals Permission Board) showed 0 % compatibility between F and both children, proving he was not the biological father. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in January 2011.

Under the Children Act then in force, paternity registrations become final six months after birth unless reopened. Thereafter reopening within three years requires new facts making a different outcome probable and an overall assessment of delay, knowledge, whether the registered father was allowed to treat the child as his own, and whether paternity can be expected to be established without material nuisance to the child. After three years, exceptional reasons and a high degree of appropriateness are required. The Act’s underlying policy is to secure a legal father and rapid stability for the child. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the refusal to reopen violated their Article 8 rights to private and family life, including the children’s right to know their biological identity.

The case of R.L. and Others v. Denmark (Application no. 52629/11) was brought by four Danish nationals: M (first applicant, born 1965 in Tanzania) and F (second applicant, born 1951), on behalf of themselves and M’s two children, L (born 2004) and S (born 2006). They alleged that Danish courts’ refusal to reopen paternity proceedings violated Article 8 of the Convention.

M married F in 2001 and moved to Denmark. L was born in January 2004 and F was registered as his legal father by marriage under the Children Act. The couple legally separated in June 2005 but cohabited until June 2006. S was born in October 2006. Although F no longer lived with M and had had no sexual contact with her since 2004, he co-signed a declaration (received January 2007) acknowledging joint responsibility for S and was registered as S’s father.

Unbeknownst to F, M maintained a relationship with E from 2003 to 2008. After it ended in October 2008, M informed F that E was the biological father of S and probably also of L. In November 2008 M and F applied to reopen both paternity cases so that E’s paternity could be formally established. The State Administration refused in April 2009.

The applicants appealed to the City Court. E opposed reopening; the children, represented by counsel, also objected. M testified that she met E in 2003, had unprotected sex, became pregnant with L, was diagnosed HIV-positive in late 2003, continued relations with E after separating from F, and planned S’s conception around her ovulation cycle. E visited the children (who called him “uncle”), knew of possible paternity, never provided financial support, and ended contact when M insisted he assume responsibility. F confirmed no sexual relations since L’s birth, treated both boys equally despite knowing S was not his, overheard E refer to them as “our children,” and believed the biological father should assume financial and identity-related responsibility. E described a purely sexual relationship, possible paternity, visits as an “uncle” rather than a father, and stated he would not voluntarily take a DNA test.

In February 2010 the City Court reopened both cases. It found E had sexual relations with M in the relevant fertile periods, new facts suggested a possible different outcome for S, E had assumed a paternal role with frequent contact, and reopening would not unduly inconvenience the children while paternity was expected to be established.

E appealed. Additional evidence included limited post-2008 contact, alleged gifts from E (including a birthday card signed “daddy”), and F’s partial withdrawal after learning the truth. In November 2010 the High Court (majority) refused reopening. It emphasised that the applicants had not earlier disclosed the lack of sexual contact regarding S, that F continued treating the children as his own until late 2008, and that it was uncertain whether paternity would be established. The stricter conditions of the Children Act (sections 24 and 25) were therefore not met. A minority judge would have upheld the City Court, noting F’s late discovery, his subsequent withdrawal, and the children’s identification of E as their father.

F later obtained DNA results showing 0 % compatibility with both children. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in January 2011.

These circumstances—the concealment of E’s possible paternity, the applicants’ subsequent joint request to establish biological truth, the children’s interest in knowing their origins, and the courts’ refusal to reopen despite DNA evidence—formed the factual core of the Article 8 complaint.
001-172134:
The case of A.-M.V. v. Finland (Application no. 53251/13) concerns a Finnish national born in 1990 who is intellectually disabled. He alleged violations of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement and right to choose one's residence). The applicant claimed these rights were breached by decisions preventing him from living with his former foster family in northern Finland and forcing him to remain in his southern hometown.

In February 2001, the applicant (then aged 11) and his two brothers were taken into public care and placed with a foster family in a village about 50 km from their hometown, after already living with them since August 2000. In June 2006, the foster family, the applicant and one brother moved north without authorization from child welfare authorities. After the applicant finished special-needs schooling in 2007, the foster parents planned (again without authorization) to send him to a vocational school 300 km away.

On 11 July 2007, authorities removed the applicant from the foster family and placed him in a disabled children's home in his southern hometown. They cited the foster parents' unauthorized decisions as evidence of unsatisfactory care. Appeals by the foster parents were dismissed by the Administrative Court in February 2008 and the Supreme Administrative Court in December 2008. The applicant was placed in the children's home on 31 July 2007; one brother joined him later that year.

The applicant turned 18 on 23 July 2008 and began local vocational studies. A mentor was initially appointed only for non-personal matters, leaving him free to decide personal issues. However, conflict arose between authorities and the former foster parents over his residence. In December 2008, authorities sought a mentor for personal matters as well. On 25 January 2009, the former foster parents took the applicant north at his request (he viewed them as his real family). Authorities, assisted by police, retrieved him the next day against his will and placed him in a special living unit for intellectually disabled adults in his hometown.

On 18 June 2009, the District Court appointed a mentor (a public legal-aid official) for the applicant's property, finances and personal matters he could not understand, citing medical evidence of diminished faculties, gullibility and child-like interests. In February 2011, after a psychologist's report, the mentor decided—against the applicant's wishes—that he should remain in his hometown. The mentor cited better educational/work opportunities, proximity to biological family, and the applicant's limited understanding of the consequences of moving to an isolated northern village where he knew only his elderly former foster parents. Holidays with the foster parents were permitted.

In April 2011, the applicant applied to the District Court to replace the mentor for decisions on residence and education with a person of his choosing. After hearing the applicant, mentor, former foster mother, brother and housing staff, the court refused on 22 June 2011. A November 2010 psychologist's report indicated decision-making skills equivalent to a 6- to 9-year-old; the applicant could not realistically assess consequences. Evidence showed he had no major complaints about his current life, enjoyed his apartment and work, and had developed well with a support network, job, hobbies and independent mobility. The court doubted the strength of his wish to move, attributing it to influence from the foster parents, and found a remote location would deprive him of these benefits. Daily long-distance travel to school was deemed unreasonable. As the applicant could not grasp the decision's significance, the mentor was required to act in his best interests rather than follow his wishes.

The Turku Court of Appeal upheld this (2-1) on 9 May 2012 after an oral hearing, endorsing the evidence assessment. The dissenter emphasized the applicant's long-standing bond with the foster mother as his only safe adult relationship and the lack of specific reasons for the 2007 removal. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 8 February 2013.

By 2015, the applicant lived in sheltered accommodation, worked five days a week in a disability shelter (described as well-liked and efficient), played floorball and had a girlfriend. He maintained telephone contact with his former foster mother (who later moved east) but had not recently discussed moving; he claimed this was because authorities would not allow it, and his sincere wish remained to live with or near her. These facts formed the basis of the alleged interferences with his family life and choice of residence.

The applicant, a Finnish man born in 1990 with an intellectual disability, was taken into public care in 2001 (aged 11) along with his two brothers and placed with a foster family in southern Finland. In June 2006 the foster family moved unauthorized to a remote northern village. After the applicant completed special-needs schooling in 2007, the child-welfare authorities removed him from the foster family (citing the unauthorized move and plans for distant vocational schooling) and placed him in a children’s home in his hometown; the decision was upheld by the Administrative Court and Supreme Administrative Court.

He turned 18 in July 2008 and began local vocational studies. A mentor was first appointed for financial matters. In June 2009 the District Court, relying on medical evidence of his limited development and gullibility, also appointed the same public official as mentor for personal affairs to the extent he could not grasp their significance. In January 2009 the former foster parents had taken him north at his request; police immediately retrieved him against his will.

In February 2011, after a psychologist’s report concluded that the applicant’s decision-making corresponded to that of a 6- to 9-year-old and that he could not assess the realism or consequences of his plans, the mentor decided—against his expressed wish—that it was in his best interests to remain in his hometown. There he had family, a support network, work, hobbies and educational opportunities unavailable in the isolated north; he would be allowed holiday visits.

In April 2011 the applicant asked the District Court to discharge the mentor in respect of residence and education and to appoint a person of his own choosing. After hearing him and several witnesses, the court refused. It found he did not comprehend the implications of a move to a remote location (including daily long-distance travel to school), that his will was likely influenced by the foster parents, and that his current situation was satisfactory and improving. Because he could not understand the significance of the decision, Finnish law required the mentor to act on an objective best-interests assessment rather than the applicant’s wishes. The Turku Court of Appeal upheld the ruling by 2–1 in May 2012 (the dissent emphasizing the unique long-term emotional bond with the foster mother and the resulting distrust of the mentor). The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in February 2013.

Thereafter the applicant lived in supported housing, worked five days a week in a sheltered workshop, and developed local friendships and a girlfriend. He nevertheless continued to regard the former foster family as his real family and maintained that his strongest wish was to live with or near his foster mother (who later moved east). He ceased expressing the wish only because the authorities would not permit it. These facts formed the basis of his complaints that the mentor’s override of his choice of residence and family life, confirmed by the domestic courts, violated Article 8 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The case of A.-M.V. v. Finland concerned an intellectually disabled Finnish man (born 1990) who alleged that decisions preventing him from living with or near his former foster family violated Article 8 ECHR (respect for private and family life) and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom to choose residence).

In 2001 the applicant (then aged 11) and his brothers were taken into public care and placed with a foster family 50 km from his southern hometown. In 2006 the foster family relocated north without child-welfare authorisation. After the applicant completed special-needs schooling in 2007, the authorities, citing unauthorised decisions by the foster parents (including plans to send him to a vocational school 300 km away), removed him and placed him in a children’s home in his hometown. Administrative courts upheld the removal.

Upon turning 18 in 2008 a mentor was appointed for financial matters only; the applicant retained capacity in personal affairs. Conflict over his residence prompted the authorities to seek a mentor for personal matters as well. In January 2009 the former foster parents took him north against official wishes; police returned him the next day to a specialised unit for intellectually disabled adults. In June 2009 a court appointed an official mentor for property, finances and personal matters the applicant could not understand, relying on medical evidence of diminished faculties, gullibility and child-like play. In February 2011, after a psychologist’s report, the mentor ruled (against the applicant’s wishes) that remaining in the hometown served his best interests: family members, better education/work opportunities and a support network existed there, whereas the remote northern village offered only elderly former foster parents. Holiday visits were permitted.

The applicant applied to the District Court to replace the mentor solely for residence and education decisions, arguing a lack of trust and invoking the constitutional right to choose residence. After hearing the applicant, mentor, former foster mother, brother and housing staff, the court refused. A 2010 psychological evaluation equated his decision-making to that of a 6- to 9-year-old; he could not grasp the consequences of relocation (isolation, loss of work/hobbies/network, daily 85 km school commute). Witnesses confirmed he enjoyed his current apartment, job and independence. The court found his expressed wish likely influenced by the foster parents given his gullibility; his development had improved in the south. Under the Guardianship Services Act the mentor was neither required nor permitted to follow wishes the applicant could not understand and had to decide on objective best interests. The Court of Appeal upheld the ruling 2–1; the dissent emphasised the unique long-term bond with the foster mother, the absence of reasons for the original 2007 removal, resulting distrust, and the equal competence of a replacement mentor enjoying the applicant’s confidence. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

By 2015 the applicant lived in sheltered two-room accommodation, worked five days a week in a sheltered workshop (where he was well-liked), played floorball and had a girlfriend. He maintained telephone contact with his former foster mother (who later moved east) but stated he no longer voiced his desire to move because authorities would not permit it; he insisted that wish remained his sincerest preference.

Finnish law (Constitution Art. 9; Guardianship Services Act ss. 8, 29, 42–43) permits a mentor for personal matters only when the adult cannot understand their significance, requires consultation of wishes where possible, and balances protection with dignity, necessity and proportionality. International materials (UNCRPD Art. 12; CoE Recommendation R(99)4) stress supported rather than substitute decision-making, respect for will and preferences, and the least-restrictive measures.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged interference with family life and freedom of residence.
001-172845:
The case originated from an application by Lithuanian national Adelė Valančienė against Lithuania, alleging that authorities unlawfully selected monetary compensation rather than returning land in natura or providing an equivalent plot to restore her inherited property rights, miscalculated the land's value, and caused unreasonable delays in the restitution process.

The applicant's father-in-law owned 9.24 hectares of land in the Telšiai region, nationalized in 1940. In 1991 his sons applied for restitution. In 1993 they agreed to divide it equally into 3.08-hectare portions, and the applicant's husband V.V. requested return of his share in natura.

From November 1999 the Plungė District Land Service informed V.V. that the original land was occupied by others and could not be returned in kind. Alternatives offered included monetary compensation, land in another cadastral area, or an equivalent-value plot. V.V. consistently refused, reiterating his 1991 in natura choice. Meetings and correspondence through 2005 showed him rejecting specific offered plots (e.g., 2.5 and 0.5 hectares) as non-equivalent and declining to select another form, despite warnings that authorities would decide otherwise.

V.V. died in November 2005; the applicant became his heir. She likewise insisted on in natura restitution or a genuinely equivalent plot, refused to sign a required land-transfer document without first viewing an equivalent plot and concluding a preliminary agreement (neither of which domestic law permitted), and rejected authorities' valuation procedures.

In November 2007 authorities, citing her failure to specify an alternative, opted for monetary compensation and gave her time to object. On 13 May 2008 they awarded 3,437 Lithuanian litai (later indexed to 5,499 litai, approximately EUR 1,593). The applicant challenged this in court, seeking annulment, damages, an explanation of inactivity between 1993 and 1999, and a higher sum.

On 29 September 2008 the Šiauliai Regional Administrative Court dismissed the claim, holding that V.V.'s original in natura request was valid but, once that became impossible, neither he nor the applicant had properly chosen another statutory form; authorities therefore lawfully selected compensation, and no damages were due. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed her appeal on 21 September 2009, noting a minor delay in notifying the statutory choice deadline (letter sent 27 March 2003 instead of by 1 March) was immaterial because V.V. had already stated he would never change his mind. The applicant's insistence on extra-legal conditions (preliminary agreement, prior viewing) was incompatible with the prescribed procedure, and she had failed to demonstrate that the compensation amount violated valuation rules.

Payment of the compensation itself was delayed until 14 November 2016 owing to missing inheritance documentation and the applicant's bank details (later attributed by the Government to human error). The applicant subsequently brought separate proceedings for interest.

These events underpin the complaints of an unlawful choice of compensation over in-kind or equivalent restitution, an allegedly incorrect valuation, and excessive overall duration of the process spanning from 1991 until 2008 (decision) and 2016 (payment). Domestic law prioritized in natura return where possible but allowed authorities to select compensation if the claimant failed to choose another available form by the statutory deadline.

The case originated in an application by Lithuanian national Adelė Valančienė (born 1940) alleging that Lithuanian authorities unlawfully selected monetary compensation rather than in-kind restitution for nationalized family land, miscalculated its value, and delayed the process unreasonably.

The land (9.24 hectares in Telšiai region) belonged to the applicant’s father-in-law and was nationalized in 1940. After independence, in 1991 the husband’s brother sought its return. In 1993 the three brothers agreed to divide it equally (3.08 hectares each); the applicant’s husband V.V. requested restitution in natura.

From 1999 the Plungė District Land Service repeatedly informed V.V. that the original land was occupied by others and could not be returned in kind. Alternatives offered included monetary compensation, land in another cadastral area, or an equivalent-value plot. V.V. consistently refused, insisting on the original plot. Meetings and correspondence in 2000–2005 confirmed this stance; authorities warned that failure to choose would allow them to decide the form. V.V. died in November 2005; the applicant inherited the claim.

She likewise refused any form other than in-natura return or a genuinely equivalent plot, declining to sign the required land-transfer document unless she first inspected and approved a specific plot (a sequence not permitted under domestic procedure). Authorities included the claim in a territorial plan but, in November 2007, concluded that her refusal to choose entitled them to select monetary compensation. A 13 May 2008 decision awarded LTL 3,437 (approx. EUR 995), indexed to LTL 5,499 (EUR 1,593). Payment was made in December 2008 but recorded in V.V.’s name; administrative errors (missing inheritance certificate and account details) delayed transfer to the applicant until November 2016.

In June 2008 the applicant sued to annul the 2008 decision, claiming she had always sought equivalent land and that the sum was too low. Both the Šiauliai Regional Administrative Court (September 2008) and the Supreme Administrative Court (September 2009) upheld the authorities: V.V. and the applicant had never clearly selected an available alternative, her additional conditions were legally impossible, and she had not substantiated any valuation error. The overall process ran from 1991 to 2008 (with a noted gap 1993–1999).

These facts underpin the complaints that monetary compensation was unlawfully imposed, the amount incorrectly calculated, and the restitution unreasonably protracted.

The case originated in an application by Lithuanian national Adelė Valančienė (born 1940) against Lithuania, lodged in December 2009. She alleged that authorities unlawfully selected monetary compensation rather than in-kind restitution of property rights, miscalculated the land's value, and caused unreasonably lengthy restitution proceedings.

The applicant's husband's father owned 9.24 hectares of land in the Telšiai region, nationalized in 1940. In 1991, one brother applied for its return to the three brothers. In 1993 they agreed to divide it equally (3.08 hectares each); the applicant's husband, V.V., requested return in natura.

In November 1999, at a meeting of the Plungė District Land Service, V.V. learned the land was occupied by others and could not be returned in kind. He was offered monetary compensation, restoration in another cadastral area, or an equivalent-value plot, but refused all. From 2000 onward, authorities repeatedly asked him to select another form. V.V. insisted on in-kind return, stating he had already chosen it in 1991. Meetings in 2002 offered specific plots (2.5 and 0.5 hectares); he delayed or refused. In July 2003, authorities warned that if he did not choose (monetary compensation, equivalent land/forest, or government bonds), they would decide. He did not attend a November 2003 meeting.

In 2005 V.V. inquired about damages for non-return in kind or equivalent land and rejected offered plots as unequal. He again refused other forms. After his death in November 2005, the applicant became his heir. Authorities asked her to request a transfer document and actively select a plot. She refused unless the original land or a truly equivalent plot was provided first, and declined to sign documents without a preliminary agreement (not provided for in law).

In 2006–2007, authorities explained valuation procedures and urged her to sign the transfer document so a plot could be allocated; she insisted on seeing an equivalent plot first. In November 2007, because she had not clearly chosen, they proposed monetary compensation and gave her time to object. She did not. On 13 May 2008 they decided to restore rights via compensation of LTL 3,437 (later indexed to LTL 5,499, or about EUR 1,593), naming V.V. as payee. The decision was sent on 28 May 2008; payments occurred in December 2008.

The applicant sued in June 2008 to annul the decision and claim damages, arguing she wanted in-kind or equivalent land, did not understand repeated demands to re-choose, questioned inactivity from 1993–1999, and called the amount too low. The Šiauliai Regional Administrative Court (September 2008) and Supreme Administrative Court (September 2009) dismissed her claims. They held V.V. had validly requested in-kind return in 1991, knew it was impossible, and never chose another form despite repeated invitations; the applicant similarly persisted without complying with legal procedures for equivalent-land transfer. Authorities thus lawfully selected compensation. Her valuation challenge lacked substantiation.

Compensation was not transferred to the applicant until November 2016, due to missing inheritance documents and her account details (later acknowledged as human error). In 2016 she sued for the unpaid sum plus interest.

Domestic law (1991 Law, 1997 Law on Restitution and implementing resolutions) prioritized in-kind return where possible but allowed compensation or equivalent property if not; citizens had until 1 April 2003 (or later invitations) to choose, failing which authorities decided. Transfer of equivalent land required a signed document. Courts and the Constitutional Court confirmed these principles and the need for fair compensation.
001-171529:
The case of Šimaitienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 55056/10) was brought by Birutė Šimaitienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1948 and residing in Kaunas. She alleged that the restitution of her late father's property rights—concerning buildings and land nationalized in 1940—was unreasonably delayed and that she received inadequate compensation, in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 1991 the applicant applied for restitution of the property. Authorities later informed her that the buildings had been privatized and sold in 1992 because she had supplied an incorrect address. In 1995–1996 they suggested monetary compensation but stated that her documents failed to prove her father's ownership, recommending that she seek a court declaration of that legal fact.

She lodged such a claim in April 1999. The Kaunas District Court left it unexamined on grounds of a legal dispute and advised her to proceed under contentious rules. Only on 28 May 2003 did the same court establish the ownership fact. The applicant then elected compensation in securities. On 14 July 2003 the Centre of Registers valued the buildings at LTL 36 000 (approximately EUR 10 426). On 9 October 2003 the authorities decided to restore rights by paying that sum (shared with her sister) in securities.

The applicant immediately challenged the valuation as too low. Procedural defects led the Kaunas District Court to treat her 2004 claim as not lodged; after an appeal the case was remitted. In 2005 the civil courts rejected her complaints about the timing of the assessment. The Supreme Court then transferred the matter to the administrative courts (December 2005). After further postponements and a modified claim, the Kaunas Regional Administrative Court appointed an expert in June 2006. The expert's April 2007 report put the July 2003 market value at LTL 56 850 and the then-current value at LTL 164 900. On 21 September 2007 the court annulled both the 2003 valuation and the corresponding portion of the restoration decision; the ruling became final on 5 October 2007.

The applicant next sought an urgent re-issue of the annulled decision and later claimed LTL 82 450 plus LTL 96 370 in damages. In May 2009 the Regional Administrative Court dismissed the claim, holding that a valuation produced no legal effects and that courts could not dictate compensation amounts to the authorities. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that decision in July 2010, noting that the 2003 decision had not yet been amended and that the valuation issue had already been settled. A request to reopen proceedings was refused in December 2010.

Meanwhile the authorities commissioned a fresh assessment (requested late 2007, delivered March 2008) that valued the buildings at LTL 57 000 (applicant's share LTL 28 500). This figure was formally adopted on 5 June 2009, amending the 2003 decision. In August 2010 the applicant requested securities; she received 11 875 units whose real value equalled LTL 28 500, transferred on 1 February 2011. Subsequent requests to revalue the property as of 2011 were rejected because the restitution procedure had been completed. An attempt to challenge the June 2009 decision failed when she did not remedy formal defects; the claim was left unexamined in October 2010 and she did not pursue it further.

These events, stretching from the 1991 application to the 2011 transfer of securities, involved repeated procedural setbacks, transfers between civil and administrative jurisdictions, expert delays, and successive official valuations that never reflected later market prices.

The applicant, Birutė Šimaitienė, alleged that Lithuania’s restitution of her late father’s nationalised property was unreasonably prolonged and that the compensation ultimately awarded was unfair. She first applied in 1991 for the return of buildings and land that her father had owned before the 1940 nationalisation. By 1992 the buildings had already been privatised; the authorities later attributed this to an incorrect address she had supplied. In 1996 they invited her to accept monetary compensation instead and indicated that her documents did not prove ownership, so she would have to obtain a court declaration of the relevant legal fact.

She instituted those proceedings in 1999. After an initial procedural setback the Kaunas District Court established the ownership fact in May 2003. She then opted for compensation in securities. The Centre of Registers valued the buildings at LTL 36 000 (approximately EUR 10 426) in July 2003; a restoration decision of October 2003 awarded that sum, to be shared with her sister.

She immediately challenged the valuation as both too low and premature. Civil-court proceedings were eventually transferred to the administrative courts. An expert appointed in 2006 assessed the 2003 market value at LTL 56 850 and the contemporaneous value at LTL 164 900. In September 2007 the Kaunas Regional Administrative Court therefore annulled both the 2003 valuation and the corresponding part of the restoration decision.

A fresh official valuation of LTL 57 000 (applicant’s share LTL 28 500) was obtained in March 2008 and formally adopted by an amending decision of June 2009. Securities with a real value matching that figure were transferred to her in February 2011. Parallel claims seeking an even higher award based on later market prices, plus damages, were dismissed by the administrative courts in 2009–2010 on the grounds that valuation itself produced no legal consequences, the original decision remained in force until amended, and the courts lacked jurisdiction to instruct the authorities on the amount of compensation. A subsequent attempt to have the 2009 amending decision quashed failed for uncorrected procedural defects. A 2012 request to recalculate the value as of 2011 was likewise rejected as the restitution process had already been completed.

Thus more than nineteen years elapsed between the original 1991 request and the 2011 transfer of securities, a period marked by repeated court proceedings, valuation disputes, jurisdictional transfers and delays in administrative action. The compensation finally paid reflected 2003/2008 figures rather than subsequent market values that the applicant regarded as the only fair measure.

The case of Šimaitienė v. Lithuania concerns the applicant’s request for restitution of her late father’s buildings and land, nationalized in 1940. In 1991 she applied for their return in natura. The buildings were nonetheless sold to third parties in 1992. In 1995 the authorities informed her that her original request had given an incorrect address and that the properties had already been privatized.

In 1996 the authorities invited her to accept monetary compensation and requested further proof of ownership. After she failed to supply the documents, she applied to the Kaunas District Court in April 1999 to have her father’s pre-nationalization ownership established as a legal fact. The court left the claim unexamined, citing a dispute over the applicable procedure, and directed her to start contentious proceedings. Only on 28 May 2003 did the same court finally establish the required legal fact.

In July 2003 the applicant chose compensation in State securities. The Centre of Registers valued the buildings at LTL 36 000 (approximately EUR 10 426). On 9 October 2003 the authorities issued a restoration decision awarding that sum in securities to the applicant and her sister. She immediately challenged the valuation as too low and as having been prepared several months before the restoration decision. After procedural defects, transfers between the civil and administrative courts, and repeated adjournments, an expert was appointed in June 2006. The expert reported a July 2003 market value of LTL 56 850 and a contemporaneous (2007) value of LTL 164 900. On 21 September 2007 the Kaunas Regional Administrative Court annulled both the original valuation and the corresponding part of the 2003 restoration decision; the ruling became final on 5 October 2007.

The applicant then sought an urgent replacement decision and later claimed LTL 82 450 plus substantial damages. The administrative courts dismissed these claims in 2009–2010, holding that the 2003 decision remained formally in force, that valuation questions had already been resolved, and that courts could not dictate the amount of compensation to the executive.

A fresh official valuation performed in March 2008 set the buildings at LTL 57 000 (the applicant’s half-share being LTL 28 500). This figure was approved by an amending decision of 5 June 2009. The applicant received the corresponding securities only on 1 February 2011. Subsequent requests to recalculate the award on the basis of 2011 market prices were refused on the ground that the restitution procedure had been completed. An attempt to have the 2009 amending decision quashed was rejected for formal deficiencies.

Thus the restitution process lasted from 1991 until 2011. The applicant’s core complaints were that this twenty-year delay was excessive and that the compensation ultimately awarded—based on 2003/2008 valuations—was not equivalent to the true market value of the property at the time it was finally paid.
001-172553:
The case of Klein and Others v. Germany (applications nos. 10138/11, 16687/11, 25359/11 and 28919/11) concerns five German nationals who alleged that the levying of church taxes or special church fees in mixed-religion marriages violated their freedom of religion under Article 9 of the Convention.

German churches with public-law status, notably the Catholic and Protestant Churches, are entitled under Article 140 of the Basic Law (incorporating Article 137 of the 1919 Weimar Constitution) to levy church tax on their members, typically at 8–9% of income tax and collected by state authorities. Membership can be terminated by declaration to the authorities to escape liability. In “glaubensverschiedene Ehen” (marriages where only one spouse belongs to a tax-levying church), tax is calculated solely on the church member’s income-tax share. Where that member has no taxable income, church tax cannot be imposed on the non-member’s income (Federal Constitutional Court, 14 December 1965). In several Länder (Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Thuringia), churches instead impose a “special church fee” (besonderes Kirchgeld)—approximately one-third of ordinary church tax—on the member. The fee is based on the member’s living expenses, themselves derived from the couple’s joint income, but only if the spouses elect joint tax assessment (which confers income-splitting and other advantages). The fee is formally levied solely on the church member, yet it may be offset against any tax reimbursement due to the non-member spouse.

The first applicant (Klein, Baden-Württemberg) left his church in 2005; his wife remained a Protestant. For 2008 they filed jointly. A special church fee of €2,220 was assessed against the wife (whose own income was below the taxable threshold) and offset against Klein’s €3,423 tax credit, leaving him €1,203. His objection was dismissed by reference to Federal Constitutional Court case-law.

The second applicant (Nussbaum, Bavaria), a Protestant with modest income (€10,144), was married to a non-member with high income (€162,522). Joint assessment for 2005 produced a special church fee of €1,500 calculated on their combined living expenses. Domestic courts, including the Federal Tax Court, upheld the levy; the Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain his 2010 complaint, holding the issue settled since 1965.

The third and fourth applicants (the Redekers, Thuringia) filed jointly in 2004–2006. The husband, a Protestant with the higher income, was charged ordinary church tax calculated as a percentage of the income tax attributable to him rather than his share of total household income. They argued that this indirectly incorporated the wife’s (non-member) earnings. Tax courts rejected the claim; the Federal Constitutional Court again declined review.

The fifth applicant (Gloeckner, Bavaria), a Protestant with no income, was married to a non-member. Joint assessments for 2004 and 2005 yielded special church fees of €1,860 and €3,600 based on joint living expenses. Objections and subsequent court challenges failed on the same settled case-law.

In each instance the applicants contended that the system either compelled a church member to rely on a non-member spouse’s resources (or to leave the church) or effectively taxed the non-member, thereby interfering with freedom of religion and discriminating against mixed marriages. Domestic authorities consistently applied the 1965 Federal Constitutional Court rulings that the special fee, being based on living expenses rather than the non-member’s income, was constitutionally permissible.

The case of Klein and Others v. Germany (applications nos. 10138/11, 16687/11, 25359/11 and 28919/11) was brought by five German nationals before the European Court of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the imposition of church taxes or special church fees in mixed-religion marriages violated their freedom of religion under Article 9 of the Convention.

German churches with public-law status, such as the Protestant and Catholic Churches, may levy taxes on their members (typically 8-9% of income tax), collected by state authorities. Membership can be ended by declaration to avoid liability. In marriages where only one spouse belongs to a taxing church (glaubensverschiedene Ehe) and the couple opts for joint income-tax assessment (which yields benefits such as income-splitting), the member’s liability is assessed on the portion of income tax attributable to him or her. Where the member has no taxable income of his or her own, certain Länder (including Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria and Thuringia) permit a “special church fee” calculated on the member’s living expenses, themselves derived from the couple’s joint income. The fee, legally treated as a tax, is levied solely on the church member but may be offset against any tax reimbursement due to the non-member spouse.

The first applicant (Klein) left his church in 2005; his wife remained a Protestant member. For 2008 they filed jointly. Because the wife’s income fell below the taxable threshold, a special church fee of €2,220 was assessed on her living expenses (joint income). The tax bill offset this sum against Klein’s €3,423 reimbursement, leaving him a net credit of €1,203. His objection was dismissed by reference to Federal Constitutional Court case-law.

The second applicant (Nussbaum), a Protestant with modest 2005 income (€10,144), was married to a non-member whose income was €162,522. A special church fee of €1,500 was levied on him on the basis of joint living expenses. Domestic courts and the Federal Constitutional Court rejected his challenge, citing the Court’s 1965 rulings.

The third and fourth applicants (the Redekers) are a couple in Thuringia. The husband, a Protestant with the higher income, was assessed church tax for 2004–2006 on the share of income tax attributable to him rather than on his proportional share of total household income. They contended that the wife’s (non-member) income had thereby been taken into account. Tax-court and Federal Constitutional Court proceedings failed.

The fifth applicant (Gloeckner), a Protestant with no income in 2004–2005, was married to a non-member. Special church fees of €1,860 and €3,600 were imposed on the basis of joint living expenses. She argued that she could remain in her church only if her husband agreed to finance the fee. Her complaints were likewise rejected by reference to settled constitutional case-law dating from 1965.

In all instances the applicants maintained that the use of a non-member’s income (or the offset of a member’s fee against a non-member’s tax credit) either compelled an unwilling spouse to contribute to a church or placed the church member in a position of financial dependence that interfered with the freedom to remain, or to leave, a religious community. The Federal Constitutional Court consistently declined to entertain the constitutional complaints, holding that the relevant questions had been settled in 1965 and that calculation of living expenses from joint income remained constitutionally valid.

The case of Klein and Others v. Germany (applications nos. 10138/11, 16687/11, 25359/11 and 28919/11) concerns five German nationals who alleged that the levying of church taxes or special church fees in mixed-faith marriages violated their freedom of religion under Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Under German law, certain religious societies with public-law status, including the Protestant and Catholic Churches, may levy church tax (typically 8-9% of income tax) solely on their members. Collection is usually handled by state authorities. Members may leave the church by declaration to avoid liability. In “glaubensverschiedene” marriages (only one spouse a church member), church tax is normally calculated solely by reference to the member spouse’s income-tax assessment. If that spouse has no taxable income under the Income Tax Code, no church tax is due. However, in several Länder (including Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria and Thuringia), churches may instead levy a “special church fee” (treated legally as a tax and amounting to roughly one-third of ordinary church tax). The fee is charged only when spouses elect joint income-tax assessment (which confers advantageous income-splitting and progression benefits). It is calculated on the member’s “living expenses,” using the couple’s joint income as a proxy. The fee is formally imposed only on the church member, yet it may be offset against any tax reimbursement due to the non-member spouse. Either spouse may object to the portion of the assessment that concerns them.

The first applicant (Klein) had left the church in 2005; his wife remained a Protestant member. For 2008 they opted for joint assessment. The resulting tax bill levied a special church fee of €2,220 on the wife (her own income being below the taxable threshold). This sum was offset against Klein’s tax reimbursement of €3,423, leaving him a net credit of €1,203. His objection was dismissed by reference to Federal Constitutional Court case-law.

The second applicant (Nussbaum), a Protestant with an annual income of €10,144, was married to a non-member whose income was €162,522. Joint assessment for 2005 produced a special church fee of €1,500 calculated on their combined income. Successive objections and actions before the tax courts and the Federal Constitutional Court were rejected as settled by a 1965 leading judgment.

The third and fourth applicants (the Redekers) were a Protestant husband with substantially higher income and a non-member wife. For 2004–2006 they chose joint assessment. Church tax was levied on the husband by reference to the portion of income tax attributable to him rather than to his share of total household income. Their objections and subsequent court actions, including a constitutional complaint, were unsuccessful.

The fifth applicant (Gloeckner), a Protestant with no income, was married to a non-member. Joint assessments for 2004 and 2005 produced special church fees of €1,860 and €3,600 respectively, again calculated on the couple’s joint income. Her objections and constitutional complaint were likewise dismissed.

The Federal Constitutional Court, joining the later complaints, held on 28 October 2010 that the issues had been resolved by its 1965 rulings: a non-member cannot be made liable for church tax, but a special church fee based on the member’s living expenses (proxied by joint income) is constitutionally permissible. Domestic tax courts consistently applied this jurisprudence.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ Article 9 complaints: that the system either compelled non-members to finance a church they had not joined or placed church members under pressure to leave if their spouses declined to subsidise the levy, thereby interfering with both positive and negative aspects of religious freedom.
001-171971:
The case of Fröbrich v. Germany originated in an application lodged on 10 April 2011 by a German national born in 1934, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention due to the absence of an oral hearing in domestic proceedings on the withdrawal of compensation and a special pension awarded for his imprisonment in the former GDR.

In 1958 a GDR court convicted the applicant of assault against state bodies and sentenced him to imprisonment, of which he served 14 months. After reunification, the Frankfurt (Oder) Regional Court rehabilitated him in 1994 under the Criminal Rehabilitation Act, finding the conviction incompatible with the rule of law. He applied for compensation, declaring on the form (which warned of ineligibility for those who had offended against humanity or the rule of law or worked for the Stasi) that he had never done so. He received DM 8,250 (about EUR 4,218) in 1995. After a legislative amendment he applied in 2007 for a monthly special pension of EUR 250, again confirming the same, and was granted it subject to verification of Stasi records.

In February 2008 the Federal Commissioner for Stasi Records informed the Regional Court President that the applicant had served as a secret informant for the Ministry of State Security from September 1953 to November 1954 while in the police, based on documents including a commitment declaration and 32 handwritten reports. In February 2009 the President withdrew both awards with retrospective effect and ordered reimbursement. The decisions had been unlawful from the outset because the applicant had obtained them by substantially incorrect information and his informant activities (at least five reports placing others at real risk of persecution) disqualified him under Section 16 § 2 of the Act.

The applicant sought judicial review and requested a personal hearing. He contended that the Stasi records were incomplete and inaccurate; that he had been only 19 and severely traumatised by wartime flight from Silesia, the Dresden bombing and subsequent homelessness; that his father had returned disabled from Soviet captivity; that he had been unaware of working for agencies other than the police; and that the commitment declaration might have been dictated while he was intoxicated, of which he had no memory and whose wording was not his own.

Sitting as a chamber of three judges, the Regional Court dismissed the request on 16 February 2010. It held that the nature, scope and duration of the informant work were sufficiently reprehensible to exclude compensation: the reports (including two additional ones) concerned contacts with West Germany and possible unauthorised departure, information of value capable of causing severe persecution. The applicant’s claim of unawareness was not credible given that he had already reported twice before signing the handwritten commitment. An oral hearing was unnecessary. Personality and recruitment circumstances would be relevant only if there were indications of insupportable pressure; none existed, the applicant had made no such claim, he had reported even before formal recruitment, and no causal link could be seen between his wartime experiences and his later cooperation.

The Brandenburg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 24 August 2010, endorsing those reasons. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain a constitutional complaint on 28 October 2010.

Under the Brandenburg Administrative Procedure Act an unlawful beneficial administrative act may be withdrawn retrospectively if obtained by substantially incorrect or incomplete information. Section 16 § 2 of the Criminal Rehabilitation Act excludes payments to persons who voluntarily collected and passed information to the Stasi in a targeted manner that condoned its use to others’ detriment (actual harm need not be proved; capability of endangering suffices). Insupportable pressure would prevent application of the exclusion. Section 11 § 3 of the Act provides that courts normally decide without an oral hearing unless they find one necessary to establish the facts.

The case of Fröbrich v. Germany (Application no. 23621/11) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that domestic courts denied him an oral hearing in proceedings withdrawing rehabilitation benefits awarded for his imprisonment under the former GDR regime.

The applicant, born in 1934, served in the GDR police from 1952 to 1954. In June 1958 a GDR court convicted him of “criminal assault against the local bodies of the State” after he attacked a parliamentarian of the ruling Socialist Unity Party; he was sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment and served 14 months.

After reunification, the Frankfurt (Oder) Regional Court in February 1994 annulled the conviction as incompatible with the rule of law and rehabilitated him under the Criminal Rehabilitation Act. He applied for compensation, declaring on the official form that he had never offended against the principles of humanity or the rule of law and had never worked for the Ministry of State Security (Stasi). In February 1995 he received a lump-sum payment of 8,250 DM (approximately EUR 4,218). After a legislative amendment he applied in August 2007 for a monthly special pension of EUR 250 for former prisoners, repeating the same declarations. The pension was granted in November 2007 subject to verification of Stasi records.

In February 2008 the Federal Commissioner for Stasi Records informed the authorities that the applicant had acted as a secret informant between September 1953 and November 1954. The information rested on documents including a handwritten commitment declaration and 32 reports attributed to him.

In February 2009 the President of the Regional Court withdrew both awards with retrospective effect and ordered reimbursement. The decisions had been unlawful from the outset because the applicant had obtained them by supplying substantially incorrect information and because his informant activities excluded entitlement under Section 16 § 2 of the Rehabilitation Act.

The applicant sought judicial review and expressly requested a personal hearing. He contended that the Stasi files were incomplete and inaccurate. At recruitment he had been only 19 and severely traumatised by wartime flight from Silesia, the Dresden bombing and subsequent homelessness; his father had returned from Soviet captivity disabled. While in the police he had not realised he was reporting to the Stasi; the commitment might have been dictated to him while intoxicated and he had no memory of it; the wording was not his own.

It held that the applicant’s informant work—reports on contacts with West Germany and possible unauthorised departure that were capable of triggering severe persecution—was of such nature, scope and duration as to constitute an offence against the principles of humanity and the rule of law, thereby excluding compensation. His claim of unawareness was not credible in light of the handwritten commitment given after he had already submitted two reports. An oral hearing was unnecessary: personal circumstances of recruitment would have been relevant only if there were indications of unbearable pressure, which the applicant had neither alleged nor substantiated; no connection existed between his wartime trauma and his cooperation with the Stasi.

The Brandenburg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in August 2010, endorsing the Regional Court’s reasoning. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint in October 2010.

Domestic law (Brandenburg Administrative Procedure Act, Section 48) permits withdrawal of a beneficial administrative act obtained by substantially incorrect information. Section 16 § 2 of the Rehabilitation Act excludes payments where a person voluntarily collected and transmitted information that could be used to suppress others’ human rights; courts need not weigh the claimant’s own suffering against harm caused, nor prove actual detriment. Section 11 § 3 of the Act provides that courts normally decide such cases without an oral hearing, unless they consider one necessary to establish the facts.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation arising from the refusal of the requested oral hearing.

**CASE OF KRASNIQI v. AUSTRIA (Application no. 41697/12), ECtHR (Fourth Section), 25 April 2017 (final 25 July 2017)**

The applicant, Agron Krasniqi (born 1974), a Kosovar national, alleged that his expulsion from Austria to Kosovo violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life). He entered Austria in January 1994 at age 19. After arrest for illegal work, a five-year residence ban was issued in November 1994. His January 1995 asylum claim was dismissed as unfounded; he voluntarily returned to Kosovo in September 1997.

He re-entered Austria on 1 July 1998 and lodged a fresh asylum claim with his wife and daughter. Asylum was refused, but they received subsidiary protection and temporary residence permits, extended until December 2009 (when the applicant did not renew). He has four children (born 1997, 1999, 2000 and 2006). His parents, three siblings and their families also lived in Austria (parents and older brother recognised as refugees); he shared a house with his parents, worked as a maintenance man and Albanian-German translator, and his wife also worked, giving the family regular income. His father owned land and three shops in Kosovo, then run by relatives.

The applicant accumulated nine criminal convictions in Austria. These included bodily harm (2003, 2006), aggravated burglary (2003, with prison time), participating in a brawl (2004), drugs offences and aggravated threat (2007, with prison time and revocation of earlier suspension), a further drugs offence (2010), attempted bodily harm and related offences (2010), and aggravated threat (2012, seven months’ imprisonment). He served multiple periods of detention and imprisonment.

In September 2007 the Dornbirn District Administrative Authority issued a ten-year ban on his return to Austria (confirmed November 2007), which had no effect while subsidiary protection remained valid. In March 2010 the Federal Asylum Office began proceedings to withdraw that status. At interview the applicant described his Austrian family and work situation, expressed a preference to stay so his children could continue school, and said he had a “bad feeling” about return but no fear of repression; his wife and children would probably join him if expelled. He noted the security situation and societal views in Kosovo.

On 17 May 2010 the Federal Asylum Office withdrew subsidiary protection (section 9(1) Asylum Act), finding no remaining risk of Article 2 or 3 violations given improved security in Kosovo, and declared expulsion admissible. On Article 8 it acknowledged his established private and family life but held that the public interest in preventing crime (especially the drug convictions) outweighed his interest in remaining. He retained ties to Kosovo (language, upbringing, physical capacity to work) and his father’s property; his wife could support the family and he could send maintenance.

The Asylum Court confirmed this on 27 June 2011, noting the convictions equated to substantial imprisonment (fines converting to nearly 24 months plus 22 months actual prison time). He had reoffended after the return ban. He could re-apply for residence after the ban expired in 2017. The applicant later mentioned one daughter born of an extra-marital relationship with an Austrian citizen (living with her mother); the Asylum Court considered that family life less established and held maintenance could continue from Kosovo. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint on 14 December 2011.

The case of Krasniqi v. Austria (no. 41697/12) concerns the applicant’s complaint that his expulsion from Austria to Kosovo violated Article 8 of the Convention by interfering with his established private and family life.

Agron Krasniqi, a Kosovar national born in 1974, first entered Austria in January 1994 aged 19. Arrested for illegal work, he received a five-year residence ban in November 1994. His asylum claim was dismissed as unfounded and he voluntarily returned to Kosovo in September 1997.

He re-entered Austria on 1 July 1998 with his wife and daughter and lodged a fresh asylum claim. Although the claim was rejected, the family was granted subsidiary protection and successive temporary residence permits. The last permit expired in December 2009 because the applicant did not apply for renewal.

Between 2003 and 2012 the applicant incurred nine criminal convictions in Austria. These comprised repeated offences of bodily harm, aggravated burglary, participation in a brawl, drugs-related offences, aggravated threats, attempted bodily harm, negligent injury and endangering physical integrity. Sentences included fines (some suspended) and prison terms totalling more than twenty months, with actual periods of detention in 2003, 2007, 2009–2010 and 2012. He reoffended both while serving sentences and after a ten-year return ban had been issued against him in September 2007 (the ban remaining ineffective so long as subsidiary protection lasted).

In March 2010 the Federal Asylum Office opened proceedings to withdraw subsidiary protection. At interview the applicant stated that he had four children (born 1997, 1999, 2000 and 2006), that his parents, three siblings and their families all lived in the same Austrian city (his parents and eldest brother being recognised refugees), that he worked as a maintenance man and Albanian–German translator, and that his wife was also employed. He expressed a “bad feeling” about returning to Kosovo, citing primitive societal attitudes, but did not claim a risk of persecution. His father still owned land and three shops there, then run by relatives. He said his wife and children would probably follow him if he were expelled, although he preferred to remain in Austria where the children attended school.

On 17 May 2010 the Federal Asylum Office withdrew subsidiary protection, finding that the security situation in Kosovo had improved and that return would no longer engage Articles 2 or 3. Balancing Article 8 interests, it accepted that the applicant had a well-established family and private life in Austria but held that the public interest in preventing further crime—especially the two drugs convictions—outweighed his personal interest. He retained linguistic, cultural and family-property ties to Kosovo and was capable of working; his wife could support the family and he could send remittances.

The Asylum Court confirmed the decision on 27 June 2011, converting the applicant’s fines into an equivalent of almost two years’ imprisonment and noting that he had continued to reoffend after the 2007 ban. He could reapply for a residence permit once the ban expired in 2017. After the applicant disclosed that one daughter was the product of an extra-marital relationship with an Austrian citizen and lived with her mother, the Asylum Court observed that this family life was less established and that financial maintenance could continue from Kosovo.

The Constitutional Court declined to examine the complaint in December 2011. After further detention the applicant was expelled to Kosovo on 5 January 2013; his family remained in Austria. The return ban remained in force until 16 November 2017.

These facts form the core of the Article 8 complaint: a lengthy period of residence, close family ties (wife, four children, parents and siblings) and a degree of social and economic integration set against a persistent pattern of serious criminality that the Austrian authorities considered to justify withdrawal of protection and expulsion as a proportionate measure for the prevention of crime.
