The case of Golubar v. Croatia (Application no. 21951/15) concerns Josip Golubar, a Croatian national born in 1955, who began serving a three-year prison sentence on 26 February 2014, initially at Zagreb Prison Hospital (ZPH). He alleged that detention facilities failed to provide appropriate medical care for his serious neurological conditions.

Shortly after incarceration, on 28 February 2014, Golubar requested suspension of his sentence due to health risks. He had suffered a stroke in early February 2014 requiring hospitalization, and had two brain arteriovenous malformations (one treated via gamma knife radiosurgery in 2013, with a high-risk three-year recovery period still ongoing). He also had basal ganglia posing hemorrhage risk, worsened by prison stress, plus epileptic fits that could prove life-threatening. A 6 March 2014 ZPH report confirmed these issues, noting a permanent high risk to himself and the institution, the need for two-to-three years of stabilization, and that suspension was medically justified.

A Zagreb County Court judge dismissed the request on 18 April 2014, relying solely on Dr. B. (internal medicine/cardiology expert), who found no acute illness, no worsening of chronic conditions, and that ZPH could treat him or arrange transfers if needed. Golubar appealed, citing ongoing deterioration, the ZPH recommendation, and Dr. B.'s lack of neurological expertise. A three-judge panel quashed the decision on 8 July 2014, ordering a neurologist's opinion.

The request was dismissed again on 21 August 2014 based on neurologist Dr. M., who reported no acute illness, improvement in his chronic condition, adequate ZPH care and staffing. Golubar appealed, contesting Dr. M.'s qualifications, noting she failed to address ZPH's actual capabilities, highlighting contradictions with the ZPH report, and arguing only a specialist institution could treat him properly.

On 29 September 2014, following ZPH advice that further hospitalization was unnecessary, he was transferred to Zagreb Prison. His appeal seeking transfer to a suitable medical facility was dismissed. On 19 November 2014, while being transported in a police van to Sisters of Mercy Hospital for tests, Golubar suffered an epileptic fit and lost consciousness; this was discovered only upon arrival, after which he spent 10 hours in hospital before returning to prison.

Golubar lodged a constitutional complaint against the suspension and transfer decisions, adding complaints about conditions: at ZPH, delayed access to toilets (requiring guards), no lift forcing stair-climbing to the second floor (a health risk), no neurology department or neurologist, and failure to provide recommended monthly check-ups. In Zagreb Prison, he was housed in a cell with seven others, lacking fresh air (worsening his condition), with an unprivate squat toilet emitting a foul smell; inmates ate in cells, and there was no lift. A second suspension request on 31 December 2014 reiterated health arguments and noted construction blocking daylight and fresh air since mid-October.

Hospital visits in January 2015 found high concentrations of certain drugs but no need for urgent measures. The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 27 January 2015. The second request was dismissed on 18 March 2015, citing prior opinions plus a neuropsychiatry expert (Dr. S.) confirming no acute issues and ZPH's capacity, along with reports that Golubar was not following treatment and was risking his health (with no comment on air/daylight complaints). His appeal was dismissed on 21 April 2015.

These facts center on conflicting medical assessments, inadequate specialist care, risky transport, and detention conditions aggravating health risks.

**Case of Golubar v. Croatia (App. no. 21951/15), ECtHR (Second Section), 2 May 2017**

Josip Golubar (born 1955), a Croatian national, began a three-year prison sentence on 26 February 2014 and was placed in Zagreb Prison Hospital (ZPH). Shortly before, he had been hospitalised (5–12 February 2014) after a stroke. He had two brain arteriovenous malformations; one had been treated by gamma-knife radiosurgery in February 2013, with a high-risk recovery period still underway. He also suffered epileptic fits. Medical documents noted basal ganglia in the ventricular system with haemorrhage risk, said to be increased by prison stress.

On 28 February 2014 he applied to the Zagreb County Court sentence-execution judge and the Prisons Administration for suspension of sentence on health grounds, arguing his conditions were life-threatening in combination with epilepsy. A ZPH report of 6 March 2014 confirmed his claims, stating he posed a permanent high risk to himself and the institution and that two to three years were needed for brain stabilisation; it considered the request medically justified.

On 18 April 2014 the judge dismissed the request, relying solely on an internist/cardiologist (Dr B.) who found no acute illness, no worsening of chronic conditions, and that ZPH could treat him (with transfer possible if needed). Golubar appealed, citing deteriorating health, the ZPH doctors’ own recommendation, and Dr B.’s lack of neurological expertise. On 8 July 2014 a three-judge panel quashed the decision and ordered a neurologist’s opinion.

On 21 August 2014 the same judge again dismissed the request, now relying mainly on neurologist Dr M., who found no acute illness, improvement in chronic conditions, good care at ZPH, and adequate staff. Golubar appealed, contesting Dr M.’s qualifications, her failure to address whether ZPH had proper staff/equipment, contradictions with the March 2014 ZPH report, and the need for specialist care. The appeal was dismissed on 31 October 2014.

Following a ZPH suggestion that hospitalisation was no longer needed, he was transferred to Zagreb Prison on 29 September 2014. His appeal seeking urgent transfer to a suitable diagnostic facility was dismissed on 14 October 2014.

On 19 November 2014, during transfer by police van to Sisters of Mercy Hospital for neurological tests, he suffered an epileptic fit and lost consciousness; this was discovered only on arrival. He spent ten hours at the hospital before return to prison.

Golubar lodged a constitutional complaint (plus later requests) covering inadequate medical care (no neurology department or neurologist at ZPH; monthly specialist check-ups recommended by prior treating hospitals not provided) and conditions: in ZPH, delayed access to toilets (he had to request guards, sometimes untimely), no lift so he climbed stairs to a second-floor cell (health risk), and later construction blocking daylight/fresh air. In Zagreb Prison he was held in a cell with seven others, with poor ventilation worsening his condition, an unprivate squat toilet emitting foul smells, eating in cells, and no lift.

A further suspension request of 31 December 2014 was dismissed on 18 March 2015, relying on prior opinions plus neuropsychiatrist Dr S. (no acute illness, no worsening, ZPH adequate) and ZPH reports that Golubar was non-compliant, not following treatment, and deliberately risking his health. No comment was made on daylight/air complaints. His appeal was dismissed on 21 April 2015. Hospital visits in January 2015 (Rebro) found no urgent need but high concentrations of tramadol, benzodiazepine and olanzapine.

The Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible on 27 January 2015 (not concerning civil rights/obligations or a criminal charge).

The communicated complaint concerned the alleged inability of detention facilities to provide appropriate medical care (likely Article 3 ECHR). Domestic law (Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act) allowed complaints, judicial protection, and sentence suspension for serious acute/worsening chronic illness if care could not be provided in prison.

**CASE OF GOLUBAR v. CROATIA (Application no. 21951/15, ECtHR, 2 May 2017)**

The applicant, Josip Golubar (born 1955), a Croatian national, began serving a three-year prison sentence on 26 February 2014 and was placed in Zagreb Prison Hospital (ZPH). He alleged that detention facilities could not provide appropriate medical care for his serious neurological conditions, in violation of the Convention (the complaint on medical care was communicated; other parts of the application were declared inadmissible).

On 28 February 2014, shortly after incarceration, the applicant requested suspension of his sentence from a Zagreb County Court judge and the Prisons Administration. He had been hospitalised in Dubrava Hospital from 5–12 February 2014 after a stroke. He had two brain arteriovenous malformations; one had been treated by gamma knife radiosurgery in February 2013, and the high-risk three-year recovery period had not ended. Medical documents showed basal ganglia in the ventricular system with haemorrhage risk, heightened by prison stress, plus epileptic fits that could prove life-threatening.

A ZPH report of 6 March 2014 confirmed these claims, stating the applicant posed a permanent high risk to himself and the institution, that two or three years were needed for brain stabilisation after surgery, and that suspension was medically justified.

On 18 April 2014 the judge dismissed the request, relying solely on an opinion by Dr B. (internal medicine and cardiology). Dr B. found no acute illness, no worsening of chronic conditions at ZPH, that sudden deterioration could be handled by transfer to an appropriate facility, and that ZPH could treat his problems.

The applicant appealed on 25 April 2014, arguing constant deterioration since incarceration, that ZPH doctors themselves had recommended suspension, and that Dr B. lacked neurological expertise. On 8 July 2014 a three-judge panel of Zagreb County Court quashed the decision and ordered a neurologist’s opinion.

On 21 August 2014 the same judge again dismissed the request, relying mainly on Dr M. (neurologist). She found no acute illness, improvement in chronic conditions, good medical care at ZPH, and appropriate staff for his needs. The applicant appealed on 27 August and 4 September 2014, contesting Dr M.’s qualifications and opinion (she had not addressed whether ZPH could properly treat him), contradictions with the ZPH report of 6 March 2014, and the need for a specialist institution.

Following ZPH’s suggestion that further hospitalisation was unnecessary, the Prisons Administration ordered transfer to Zagreb Prison on 29 September 2014. The applicant appealed on 2 October 2014, claiming ZPH lacked staff and equipment for proper diagnostic examinations, and seeking urgent transfer to a suitable facility. The appeal was dismissed on 14 October 2014. A three-judge panel dismissed his appeal against the 21 August decision on 31 October 2014.

On 19 November 2014 the applicant was taken to Sisters of Mercy Hospital for neurological tests. During transfer in a police van he suffered an epileptic fit and lost consciousness; this was discovered only on arrival when officers opened the van and found him on the floor. He spent ten hours at the hospital before return to Zagreb Prison.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the suspension and transfer decisions. He added that during eight months at ZPH he had lacked proper access to sanitary facilities (had to request guards, sometimes unanswered in time), that absence of a lift forced him to climb stairs to a second-floor cell (a health risk), that ZPH had no neurology department or neurologist, and that recommended monthly check-ups from prior treating hospitals had not occurred. He also complained of Zagreb Prison conditions: a cell with seven other inmates, lack of fresh air worsening his condition, a non-private squat toilet with foul smell, eating in the cell, and no lift preventing access to fresh air.

On 31 December 2014 he again requested suspension, reiterating prior arguments and adding that since 19 October 2014 he had lacked daylight and that lift construction blocked fresh air. He was taken to Rebro Hospital on 5, 9, 15 and 17 January 2015; a 15 January report found no need for urgent measures but high concentrations of tramadol, benzodiazepine and olanzapine.

The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 27 January 2015 (not concerning merits of civil rights/obligations or a criminal charge). On 18 March 2015 the judge dismissed the December request, relying on prior opinions plus Dr S. (neuropsychiatry), who confirmed no acute illness, no worsening, and ZPH’s adequate capacity. ZPH reports of 20 and 28 January 2015 stated the applicant was not following doctors’ orders and was deliberately risking his health. There was no comment on daylight or air access. His 27 March 2015 appeal (reiterating health arguments but omitting daylight/air complaints) was dismissed on 21 April 2015.

Relevant domestic law (Enforcement of Prison Sentences Act) provided for complaints, judicial protection against unlawful restrictions of rights, and suspension of sentence if a prisoner suffered serious acute illness or worsening chronic illness that could not be appropriately treated in the facility.

The case of Osipkovs and Others v. Latvia (application no. 39210/07) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, namely that Latvian authorities deprived the applicants of property without any compensation. The four individual applicants and two Latvian companies claimed ownership of plots derived from a 30-hectare forest in Jurmala that had been nationalised in 1940.

Following Latvia’s independence, 1991 property-reform legislation permitted former owners or their heirs to reclaim nationalised land. In 1999 the second applicant and two co-heirs of A.S. successfully obtained a Riga Regional Court judgment recognising their title to an equivalent-value plot (precise historic boundaries being unidentifiable). The judgment became final in June 1999. After enforcement difficulties, the Jurmala City Land Commission allocated four plots in December 2002; title was registered in January 2003 and the plots were immediately sold to the fifth applicant company (then owned and directed by the second applicant).

In October 2003 the President of the Civil Division of the Senate of the Supreme Court sought supervisory review of the 1999 judgment, citing fresh archival material showing that the forest had been undivided co-owned land and that A.S. had never been registered as sole owner after 1937. On 17 December 2003 the Senate quashed the judgment and remitted the case. Meanwhile the fifth applicant sold portions of the land to the third, fourth and sixth applicants and, via an intermediary, to the first applicant. Several of these contracts contained express warranties that the land was free of dispute.

In 2004 the Prosecutor General, acting for the Ministry of Finance, brought a reivindicatory action against all applicants, the original co-heirs and Jurmala City Council, seeking cancellation of the allocations, deletion of land-register entries and recognition of State (later municipal) title. The first-instance court dismissed the claim, but on 22 June 2006 the Civil Division of the Supreme Court allowed the appeal in part: the allocations were revoked, the register entries were ordered deleted and the land was returned to the municipality to complete land reform. The court held that the applicants could not be regarded as bona-fide acquirers because the contested transfers had occurred after the 1999 judgment had been quashed and, in some instances, while the prosecutor’s action was already pending (Civil Law, s. 1055). On 17 January 2007 the Senate dismissed the applicants’ cassation appeal, confirming both the lack of original title and the finding of bad faith. The register entries were thereafter deleted.

Latvia’s instrument of ratification contains a reservation excluding Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 from laws governing restoration of property nationalised during the Soviet period; the Government invoked that reservation. The applicants maintained that the supervisory-review procedure had retroactively extinguished rights acquired in reliance on a final judgment and that no compensation had been offered.

The applicant, a Turkish national born in Austria in 1990 to parents of Turkish origin, had his parents divorce in 1992, with sole custody awarded to his father. That year, his grandparents took him and his sister to Turkey (where he lived until 1998 and attended school for three years). His mother also returned to Turkey, started a new family, and lost contact. In 1998, at age 8, he and his sister returned to Austria to live with their father and he was granted a residence permit.

Beginning at age 14, the applicant committed violent offenses. On 30 December 2004, he and friends assaulted a man (jumping on him from behind, beating and kicking him, causing serious injuries) and stole money and cigarettes. He attempted shoplifting on 20 January 2005 and used a moped without consent on 29 August 2005. On 8 November 2005, he and friends stole an item from a man. Between 15 and 30 January 2006 (when he was 15), he and friends robbed nine elderly women of handbags using threats or force: he ripped bags away, grabbed one victim from behind (covering her mouth and dragging her down), hit another on the head and kneed her back, and beat others. Two victims were seriously injured.

On 13 March 2006, the Vienna Regional Criminal Court convicted him of aggravated robbery, attempted theft, and unauthorized use of a vehicle, imposing a one-year prison sentence (suspended for three years). Mitigating factors were his lack of prior record, confession, and willingness to compensate the victim; aggravating factors included multiple offenses. The court noted his notoriety for excessive violence, multiple school changes, lack of age-appropriate reflection, and strong aggressive tendencies used as a problem-solving strategy.

On 31 May 2006, the same court convicted him of aggravated robbery as a member of a criminal organization and theft, imposing 2.5 years’ imprisonment (with the prior probation extended to five years). His confession was mitigating, but repeated offending was aggravating. He had taken a leading role, targeting elderly women expected not to resist, and was a main perpetrator, leaving no room for a lighter sentence.

On 7 August 2006, the Vienna Federal Police Authority imposed a 10-year exclusion order under the Aliens Police Act, citing the offenses’ severity as justifying it to protect public order and security despite most of his family living in Austria. He appealed, arguing he had acted as a juvenile with the wrong friends; authorities had insufficiently weighed his interests given his father, paternal grandparents, siblings, and half-siblings in Austria; and his youth made independent life in Turkey impossible.

The Vienna Security Authority reduced the order to eight years on 16 March 2007. He was released from prison on 30 April 2007 after serving half his sentence due to good conduct. After a jurisdictional ruling, the Independent Administrative Panel (IAP) on 21 July 2008 (following a hearing) confirmed the order’s legality but limited it to five years. The IAP emphasized the robberies’ seriousness, showing severe disrespect for others’ well-being and property; victims were mostly frail elderly women; two were severely injured; he was a main perpetrator; and his violence/aggression had increased. His youth (still maturing at 14–15) was offset by the multiple, particularly brutal offenses.

The IAP assessed ongoing risk: his probation officer reported he had developed a sense of justice, cooperated well, apprenticed in prison, joined training programs post-release, and sought work, with no reoffending in over a year. However, the short post-release period did not prove he no longer endangered society.

On Article 8, the IAP noted stricter criteria for “second-generation migrants.” Unlike in Maslov, he had repeatedly committed serious violent crimes. Family and social integration in Austria meant an interference, but he was nearly of majority when the order issued, unemployed (no economic integration), spoke Turkish, last visited Turkey in 2001, and had a mother there (no current contact, but possible). The offenses’ seriousness and public interest outweighed his interest in remaining; five years sufficed given his age.

The Constitutional and Administrative Courts declined to hear his appeals. He was expelled to Turkey on 10 February 2010 (age 19) after not leaving voluntarily. The five-year order expired in July 2013.

Relevant Aliens Police Act provisions allowed exclusion if a stay endangered public order/security (supported by convictions to certain prison terms) or other Article 8 § 2 interests, with duration based on case circumstances (unlimited in some cases, otherwise up to 10 years). An exception barred exclusion for those grown up in Austria from early childhood with long legal residence, except for severe sentences (domestic courts interpreted “early childhood” as from age 3 or younger). Expulsion interfering with private/family life was admissible only if strictly necessary for Article 8 § 2 aims.

Protection for those who had grown up in Austria “from early childhood” applied only from age three or younger; the applicant, who returned at eight, did not qualify.

001-173463:
**Summary of Murtazaliyeva v. Russia (Application no. 36658/05, Chamber judgment of 9 May 2017)**

The applicant, an ethnic Chechen woman, arrived in Moscow in 2003 and befriended two recent Muslim converts, V. and Ku. Police placed her under court-authorised secret video and audio surveillance in a police-owned dormitory flat (where officer A. had arranged her housing) from 5 February to 4 March 2004, suspecting terrorist links. On 4 March 2004 she was stopped for an identity check, taken to a police station over expired registration, and searched by officer I. in the presence of attesting witnesses B. and K. Two foil-wrapped packages later identified as 196 grams of Plastit-4 explosive were found in her bag; hexogen traces were also detected on her bag lining and jacket. Police seized from the flat a handwritten note (critical of Russian policy in Chechnya, glorifying suicide bombers and jihad) and photographs of an escalator in Moscow’s Okhotnyi Ryad shopping centre. Tape transcripts recorded her discussing hatred of Russians, holy war, and Chechen insurgent camps while allegedly preparing V. and Ku. for terrorism. A. stated pre-trial that he had cultivated her trust on superiors’ orders. She was charged with preparing a terrorist explosion and inciting others to terrorism.

At trial she denied the charges, claiming the explosives were planted (her fingerprints taken before and after the search, only the latter recorded) and that she had not incited anyone. She requested the surveillance tapes be played; the court granted this. She and her lawyers later complained on appeal that only one of 16 tapes was shown, with “technical reasons” preventing them from highlighting transcript inaccuracies, though no contemporaneous objections were recorded. They also sought to call A. (whose pre-trial statement was read without defence objection) and attesting witnesses B. and K. The court refused A. because he was on a work mission (without further verification of his availability) and refused B. and K. because the applicant alleged planting occurred before they arrived, so they could not usefully testify. After four days the parties agreed to close the evidence and proceed to pleadings despite the absences.

The Moscow City Court convicted her on 17 January 2005 of preparing terrorism, incitement, and carrying explosives, sentencing her to nine years. It relied on V. and Ku.’s (partly contradictory) statements, police officers’ accounts, the forensic report, search record, photos, note, tape transcripts, and A.’s statement. It rejected the planting claim, citing official records that the search preceded fingerprinting and officers’ denials. The Supreme Court of Russia dismissed the appeal on 17 March 2005 (reducing the sentence to eight years six months), holding that the tape had been shown at the defence’s request with no contemporaneous complaints, that A.’s absence was justified and his statement read with consent, and that B. and K. were unnecessary given the planting timeline alleged plus the parties’ agreement to close the case.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that she could not effectively examine the surveillance videotapes used against her and could not question A. (a witness whose evidence she wished to test) or the two attesting witnesses, raising issues under Article 6 of the Convention concerning the fairness of the trial, equality of arms, and the right to examine witnesses.

**CASE OF MURTAZALIYEVA v. RUSSIA (Application no. 36658/05)**

Zara Khasanovna Murtazaliyeva, a Russian national of Chechen ethnicity born in 1983, alleged violations of her right to a fair trial (Article 6 ECHR). She claimed she could not effectively examine secret surveillance videotapes used as evidence and could not question police officer A. (who had testified for her at the pre-trial stage) or two attesting witnesses present at her personal search.

In September 2003, the applicant arrived in Moscow from Chechnya and began working at an insurance company. In October she met V. and Ku., two young Russian converts to Islam, at a mosque. After an identity check in December 2003 she was dismissed from work; she was later reinstated with help from A., an ethnic Chechen police officer in the organised crime division. A. also arranged a flat for her in a police-department dormitory, which she shared with V. and Ku. The Moscow City Court authorised secret audio- and videotaping in the flat from 5 February to 4 March 2004 because the applicant was suspected of links to a Chechen terrorist group. Transcripts later showed her discussing Islam, hatred of Russians, “holy war,” and Chechen insurgent camps.

On the evening of 4 March 2004 police stopped the applicant for an identity check (her appearance allegedly matched a wanted-person profile and her Moscow registration had expired). After she telephoned A., she was taken to the police station. There she was formally apprehended. Officer I. searched her bag in the presence of attesting witnesses B. and K. and found two foil-wrapped packages later identified as 196 grams of the industrial explosive Plastit-4 (based on hexogen). The inner lining of her bag and jacket pockets also tested positive for hexogen. Police did not swab her hands for residue or check the packages for her fingerprints. Fingerprints were taken (the official record placed this after the search). The same day she was arrested on terrorism charges. A search of the flat yielded a handwritten note she had written that criticised Russian policy in Chechnya, glorified suicide bombers and jihad, and contained harsh comments about Russians, plus photographs of an escalator in the Okhotnyi Ryad shopping centre.

The applicant was charged with preparing an explosion at that shopping centre and inciting V. and Ku. to commit a terrorist act. At her December 2004 trial before the Moscow City Court she pleaded not guilty, claiming the explosives had been planted, that her fingerprints had been taken both before and after the search (only the second occasion being recorded), and that she had been questioned without a lawyer and later beaten. She said she had copied the note from the internet and had taken the photographs randomly for recreation. V. and Ku. gave mixed testimony: V. described the applicant’s praise of terrorism, mention of a training camp near Baku, photographs of the escalator, and questions about whether they could carry out a suicide attack; some of V.’s trial statements contradicted her more incriminating pre-trial account. Ku. was less damning. Several police officers described a routine stop and search and denied prior knowledge of the explosives.

The defence asked for the surveillance tapes to be played; the court granted the request and one tape was shown. No contemporaneous complaint about quality or completeness appears in the record. The defence also asked to summon A.; the court refused because he was on a work mission and his pre-trial statement (describing how he had befriended the applicant on orders, found her housing, and advised her to accompany the police on 4 March) was read with the defence’s consent. The request to call attesting witnesses B. and K. was refused on the ground that the applicant herself said the planting had occurred before they arrived. After four days the parties agreed to close the evidence and proceed to pleadings without the missing witnesses.

On 17 January 2005 the court convicted the applicant of preparing a terrorist explosion, inciting terrorism and illegally carrying explosives, sentencing her to nine years. It rejected the planting claim, relying on police testimony and the official sequence of the search and fingerprinting, and found she had composed (not copied) the note. The Supreme Court of Russia, on 17 March 2005, reduced the sentence to eight years and six months. It held that the single tape had been shown at the defence’s request without objection, that A.’s absence was justified and his statement had been read by consent, and that B. and K. were unnecessary given the applicant’s own account of when the planting allegedly occurred; the defence had also agreed to close the evidence.

001-174119:
**Summary of Van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium (apps. 67496/10 and 52936/12)**

The applicant, Dutch national Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, complained to the ECHR of a violation of Article 6 § 1 (fair trial) and Article 6 § 3(d) (right to examine witnesses) because his defence rights were restricted by non-access to a confidential investigative file and because he could not question undercover agents whose evidence contributed to his conviction.

In May 2006 the Hasselt public prosecutor authorised a proactive investigation (under Article 28bis § 2 CIC) into suspected drug trafficking, participation in an international criminal organisation and money laundering. Special methods of infiltration and later observation were used; a separate confidential file was created pursuant to Articles 47septies and 47nonies CIC. The proactive phase lasted until 17 September 2008. Police reports of 17 and 18 September 2008 summarised the evidence obtained (including by infiltration and observation) and were placed in the ordinary criminal file. The prosecutor then requested a judicial investigation; additional measures (telephone tapping and mutual legal assistance) were employed. The Federal Prosecutor’s Office later assumed conduct of the case. Observation and infiltration ended on 14 June 2009 with the arrest of several suspects, including the applicant.

In December 2009 the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal was asked to review, under Article 235ter CIC, the conformity of the confidential file with the ordinary file and the absence of irregularities (and, at the parties’ request, also under Article 235bis CIC). The Division first heard the prosecutor in the parties’ absence and inspected the confidential file, then heard the defendants. An interim judgment of 20 May 2010 required the addition of certain materials relating to both the proactive and reactive phases. After those additions, a judgment of 24 June 2010 found the file complete and declared that the special methods (including during the proactive stage) had complied with the statutory conditions of reasonable suspicion, proportionality and subsidiarity and that no Convention violation had occurred. An appeal on points of law by the applicant (complaining of the absence from the ordinary file of the original 2006 authorisation and related documents) was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 21 September 2010 as raising questions of fact.

The applicant and co-defendants were committed for trial. On 16 March 2011 the Hasselt Court of First Instance convicted him of the charged offences and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment plus a fine; the lengthy judgment relied in part on evidence obtained by the special methods. The court refused a request for a confrontation with the undercover agents, citing the prior independent review by the Indictments Division, the existence of contemporaneous reports that had been compared with objective material (seized items, intercepted communications, SMS messages), the hearing of other witnesses, the agents’ safety and anonymity (photographs of them had been posted online; long-term infiltration had created personal contacts), the risk of reprisals, and the lack of specific questions that could not be addressed from the existing record. It also rejected a claim of incitement, noting that the agents’ involvement was limited to a later period and that other offences had been established independently of them.

The Antwerp Court of Appeal first confirmed the conviction in absentia and, after adversarial proceedings, again on 13 October 2011. It adopted the first-instance reasoning, added that the agents’ statements had only relative evidential value and that guilt was established by other evidence, and observed that the applicant’s non-appearance rendered the confrontation request somewhat academic. A further appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 20 March 2012. The Court held that the restriction on access to the confidential file was justified by the need to protect investigative techniques and the safety and anonymity of those employing them, was counterbalanced by the independent review of the Indictments Division (which verified correspondence between the ordinary and confidential files), and did not affect the outcome because the confidential file itself was not used as evidence. On the request to examine the agents, it recalled that Article 6 § 3(d) does not deprive the trial court of discretion to assess the necessity of a requested witness.

These national proceedings formed the factual basis for the applicant’s complaints that he had been denied a fair opportunity to challenge the special-methods evidence and to examine the undercover agents.

The case of van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium originated in two applications to the European Court of Human Rights by a Dutch national, Adrianus van Wesenbeeck. The investigation employed the special methods of infiltration (undercover agents) and, from 1 August 2006, observation. A separate confidential case file was opened. The proactive phase lasted until 17 September 2008, after which summary reports of the evidence gathered (including by infiltration and observation) were placed in the ordinary criminal file. A judicial investigation then began under an investigating judge; it included telephone tapping and mutual legal assistance. The special operations ended on 14 June 2009 with the applicant’s arrest.

The Federal Prosecutor later asked the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal to examine the confidential file under Article 235ter of the Code of Criminal Procedure to verify that it corresponded to the material in the ordinary file and that no irregularities had occurred; the parties also requested a review of lawfulness under Article 235bis. The Division inspected the confidential file in the prosecutor’s presence alone. In an interim decision of 20 May 2010 it held that both the proactive and reactive phases had to be scrutinised and that certain documents still needed to be added to the ordinary file. After those documents were supplied, a judgment of 24 June 2010 declared the file complete and found no nullity, irregularity or Convention violation. In particular it held that the proactive investigation (including the special methods) had complied with the statutory conditions of reasonable suspicion, proportionality and subsidiarity.

It refused a request for a confrontation with the undercover agents, citing the prior review by the Indictments Division, the existence of written reports that could be compared with objective evidence (searches, SMS messages, tapped conversations), the hearing of other witnesses, the agents’ safety (photographs had been posted online and personal relationships had developed during the lengthy infiltration, creating a real risk of reprisals) and the lack of specific questions beyond a point already covered in a report. It also found no incitement, noting that the agents’ involvement post-dated the start of the judicial investigation and that other offences had been committed independently of them.

The Court held that denial of access to the confidential file was justified by the need to protect investigative techniques and the agents’ anonymity and safety, and was counterbalanced by the independent review carried out by the Indictments Division; the confidential material itself had not been used as evidence. The case of Arnarson v. Iceland originated in an application by journalist Ólafur Arnarson against a domestic defamation ruling that he claimed unjustifiably restricted his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. Arnarson, a freelance writer for the online site Pressan, had published articles criticising the Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners (LIU) and its long-serving chief executive, A. The LIU represented fishing-vessel owners and defended their economic and legal interests. Arnarson alleged that a private website (B) regularly published anonymous blogs that lobbied for the LIU and attacked its critics.

On 21 July 2010 the newspaper DV reported rumours that the LIU was paying website B 1.5 million Icelandic krónur (ISK) per month. That same day Arnarson published an article on Pressan headed “LIU pays 20 million for offensive material,” citing the DV report. A promptly denied any such support; his statement appeared on Pressan two days later. On 24 July Arnarson responded, writing that A “had to do better” than a bare denial of direct payments and that the LIU, “directed by A,” remained “accountable for the offensive material” published anonymously on website B. He also asked whether the “respectable representatives” of LIU member companies would accept their organisation’s funds being channelled through intermediaries to “gossips such as the owners of website B.”

A third article, published on 26 July 2011, asserted that the LIU “supposedly supports website B with almost ISK 20 million annually through companies owned by [Mr Y],” the site’s owner. Arnarson added that he “knew” some board members were unaware of the payments because they were “well-disguised in the organisation’s financial statements.” He had been told it was “possible that no LIU board members know” of the expenditure and that “the CEO alone decided to use the organisation’s funds in this way,” although he noted he had not confirmed the last claim. A photograph of A accompanied the text.

In December 2011 A sued Arnarson in the Reykjanes District Court, seeking a declaration that four statements (labelled A–D) were null and void. On 29 November 2012 the court held only statement D defamatory. It ordered Arnarson to pay A ISK 300 000 (approximately EUR 2 500) in non-pecuniary damages plus interest and ISK 450 000 in costs, and declared the passage void.

The court reasoned that statement D applied directly to A, who as CEO was responsible for the LIU’s accounts. The claim that payments had been “well-disguised” implied A condoned accounting deception. The suggestion that A had acted alone and against the board’s will amounted to an insinuation of fraud by abuse of position (umboðssvik) and professional negligence. Because Arnarson could not prove the allegations, they were treated as untrue and therefore damaging to A’s honour and reputation under Article 241(1) of the Penal Code. The court acknowledged the constitutional and Convention guarantees of free expression and the public interest in the fisheries-management debate, but concluded that the unproven accusation against a named individual crossed the line into unprotected defamation.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 25 February 2013. Arnarson then lodged his application with the European Court, arguing that the domestic judgment constituted an interference with his journalistic speech that was not necessary in a democratic society.

The applicant had not proved the allegations. The court therefore declared the statement null and void, awarded A ISK 300 000 (approximately EUR 2 500) in non-pecuniary damages plus interest under the Tort Liability Act, and ordered the applicant to pay ISK 450 000 (approximately EUR 3 750) in costs.

In its reasoning the District Court recalled the constitutional and Convention guarantees of freedom of expression, noting that they may be restricted to protect the reputation of others when such restrictions are necessary in a democratic society. It observed that A, by virtue of his office, participated in public debate on fisheries policy—a matter of high public interest—while the applicant regularly criticised aspects of that policy. Nevertheless, the court concluded that readers would understand the impugned statement as an accusation of criminal misconduct that damaged A’s honour. **Case of Wrona v. Poland (Application no. 74568/11), ECtHR, 15 June 2017**

The applicant, Arkadiusz Wrona (born 1979), a Polish national living in Warsaw, alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 of the Convention. He claimed his detention on remand was unlawful, exceeded a reasonable time, and that he could not obtain compensation for it.

On 11 February 2004 he was charged with domestic violence. A bill of indictment followed on 27 February 2004 but was later returned for amendment. On 20 August 2004 the Warsaw District Court ordered a six-week psychiatric assessment in hospital; the applicant did not appeal. On 11 April 2005 police brought him to the Warsaw Psychiatric Hospital, but he refused to stay. Ordered to return on 18 April 2005 under threat of detention, he appeared but again refused, citing urgent matters.

On 7 June 2005 the District Court ordered his detention on remand under Articles 249 § 1 and 258 § 1(1)–(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP). It found a reasonable suspicion of the offences based on family testimonies and a risk that he would obstruct proceedings or abscond. This was supported by his irregular presence at home, repeated non-compliance with the assessment order, his parents’ reports of his poor mental condition and need for treatment, and a prior incident in which he had left a psychiatric hospital after one day in 2001. An appeal was dismissed on 20 September 2005, the Regional Court emphasising the still-pending assessment and irregular home stays.

Detention was extended on 28 September 2005 (to 4 January 2006), 27 December 2005 (to 4 February 2006) and 1 February 2006 (to 4 March 2006) on the same grounds; all appeals failed. On 18 October 2005 the court directed assessment in the hospital wing of the Warsaw Detention Centre, which took place from 21 November 2005 to 1 February 2006. An amended indictment charging domestic violence plus possession of 1.15 grams of marijuana was filed on 3 February 2006. Detention was again extended on 16 February 2006 (to 4 May 2006) because of the risk of obstruction or flight, given his earlier refusals.

At a hearing on 23 March 2006 the applicant’s father and sister refused to testify; he was released the same day. His mother later also refused. After further hearings the District Court on 12 March 2007 acquitted him of domestic violence and convicted him of the minor drug offence, imposing a five-month suspended sentence. The conviction was quashed on appeal (9 August 2007) and the proceedings discontinued (6 November 2007) on the ground that the act lacked significant social harm.

On 5 November 2008 the applicant sought compensation under Article 552 CCP for “undoubtedly unjustified” pre-trial detention, arguing that the principal justification had been a six-week assessment yet he had been held for nearly a year, the assessment having begun only five months after arrest, and that no genuine risk of obstruction existed. The Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the claim on 18 March 2010, citing a 1999 Supreme Court resolution. It held there had been no breach of Chapter 28 CCP; detention was justified by the applicant’s repeated refusals to comply with court orders, even though he was later acquitted. The Court of Appeal upheld this on 16 July 2010, adding that he had obstructed the proceedings by refusing assessment, that a risk of absconding existed, and that he was released once the family witnesses withdrew. The Supreme Court rejected his cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded on 31 May 2011.

Thus the applicant was detained from 7 June 2005 until 23 March 2006 (approximately nine and a half months). Domestic courts consistently treated the detention as lawful under the CCP because of reasonable suspicion, flight/obstruction risks and non-compliance with the psychiatric order, and therefore not “undoubtedly unjustified” for compensation purposes.

Relevant domestic law permits preventive detention only where evidence shows a significant probability of an offence and a risk of absconding or obstruction, and only if milder measures are insufficient. Compensation is available for “undoubtedly unjustified” detention, interpreted as a breach of procedural rules causing undue hardship in light of all circumstances, including the final outcome.

The case of Giesbert and Others v. France originated in three applications to the ECtHR by Franz-Olivier Giesbert (publication director of Le Point), journalist Hervé Gattegno, and the magazine’s operating company. They alleged a breach of Article 10 (freedom of expression) arising from sanctions for publishing extracts from a criminal file in two articles on the “Bettencourt affair” before those documents were read in open court.

Liliane Bettencourt, principal L’Oréal shareholder, had given her friend B. (a photographer and writer) gifts worth hundreds of millions of euros. In 2007 her daughter lodged a complaint of undue influence. A preliminary investigation followed, involving interviews and searches; B. was held in police custody. The public prosecutor discontinued the case in 2009, but the daughter pursued a private prosecution in the Nanterre Criminal Court. Hearings were deferred, including for a medical assessment of Mrs Bettencourt, which she refused. The affair received extensive press coverage.

On 10 December 2009 Le Point published a four-page article quoting investigation material: B.’s custody statements, employee and accountant testimony alleging his psychological hold and Mrs Bettencourt’s vulnerability, a neurologist’s report, and a prosecution summary concluding there were strong presumptions of undue influence. A second, eight-page article on 4 February 2010 (prominently advertised on the cover) reproduced lengthy exclusive extracts from staff statements describing B.’s pressure, her declining health, and his “web” around her. Both pieces integrated the quotes into analysis suggesting B. had exploited her.

Mrs Bettencourt brought urgent proceedings after the second article, invoking section 38 of the 1881 Press Law (prohibiting publication of criminal-file documents before they are read in court) and privacy rights. The Paris tribunal de grande instance held the statements were “procedural documents” (even from a discontinued investigation later joined to the private prosecution) and ordered a €3,000 advance. The Court of Appeal raised this to €10,000, finding the quotes portrayed her as weak and easily manipulated. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal in April 2011.

B. brought parallel urgent proceedings. The courts ordered a published notice, €3,000 compensation and costs, holding the extracts depicted him as unscrupulous and guilty before trial, thereby undermining his presumption of innocence. The Court of Cassation upheld this in July 2011.

B. then sued on the merits. First-instance judges dismissed the claim, ruling that applying section 38 strictly would prevent journalists from citing sources on matters of public interest. The Court of Appeal reversed, finding both articles (especially their timing just before hearings and their selection of incriminating quotes) breached B.’s fair-trial rights and presumption of innocence. It awarded €1 per article, costs and a notice. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal in May 2013.

The applicants argued the publications served the public interest in a high-profile case involving vast sums and prominent figures; quoting documents was necessary to demonstrate the seriousness of their reporting; and section 38 (a public-interest provision reserved to the prosecutor) should not apply to a private prosecution that did not impair judicial authority.

(Subsequent criminal proceedings, transferred to Bordeaux, resulted in B.’s 2015 conviction for undue influence, later varied on appeal.)

The Court referred to Council of Europe Recommendation Rec(2003)13 on media reporting of criminal proceedings.

The 10 December 2009 piece (“Investigation into a very dear friend”) quoted extensively from investigators’ interviews, B.’s custody statements, Mrs Bettencourt’s testimony and a neurologist’s report, presenting B. as having exploited her declining health and suggesting strong presumptions of the offence. The 4 February 2010 cover story (“Bettencourt affair: how to gain one billion (without any effort)”) reproduced lengthy extracts from household employees’ statements accusing B. of weaving a “web” around Mrs Bettencourt, applying pressure and taking advantage of her weakness.

Mrs Bettencourt and B. each instituted urgent proceedings, and B. later sued on the merits, claiming an unlawful nuisance, damage to reputation, and infringement of the presumption of innocence and defence rights.

Orders included monetary awards (advances of €3,000–€10,000, later €1 per article plus costs), publication of judicial notices, and website notices. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeals in 2011 and 2013, confirming that Article 10 did not preclude the interference.

The applicants contended that the sanctions prevented them from informing the public on a matter of general interest involving prominent figures and vast sums, and that section 38 was incompatible with Article 10. Subsequent criminal proceedings against B. (transferred to Bordeaux) ended in his 2015–2016 conviction for undue influence.

The case originated in an application lodged by Ms Vladislava Ramunė Lekavičienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1942 and resident in Vilnius, against Lithuania. She complained of the authorities’ refusal to readmit her to the Bar after a criminal conviction, alleging a violation of her Convention rights (communicated by the Court in 2010).

The applicant was admitted to the Bar on 27 September 1996, took the required oath of fidelity to the Constitution and laws, honest performance of duties, observance of moral norms and protection of professional secrets, and thereafter practised law from her registered office. At her own request, her name was removed from the list of practising advocates on 19 December 2003, a step she later acknowledged was taken because of a pending criminal investigation.

On 13 August 2004 she was convicted of forgery of documents and fraud (Articles 300 § 1 and 182 § 1 of the Criminal Code). The courts established that, while practising as an advocate, she had on more than thirty occasions submitted false written claims that she had provided legal services under the State-paid legal-aid scheme, forged the signatures of pre-trial investigation officers on those documents, and thereby obtained payment. The offences were classified as minor intentional crimes (maximum penalty of three years’ imprisonment). She was fined and paid the fine on 24 August 2004; the conviction expired three years later, on 24 August 2007.

On 12 September 2007 she applied to the Lithuanian Bar Association for readmission. The Association refused on 20 September 2007, holding that she lacked the “high moral character” required by Articles 7 § 4 and 8 § 4 of the Law on the Bar. Only a little over three years had elapsed since the conviction, the offences consisted of systematic misappropriation of public funds for non-existent services, and the ethical demands of advocacy made it reasonable to conclude that she had not yet regained an irreproachable reputation.

She challenged the decision before the Vilnius Regional Court. On 25 April 2008 that court, after hearing six character witnesses (most of whom knew her from her earlier work at the Ministry of Justice), partly annulled the Association’s decision and ordered reconsideration. It reasoned that the conviction had expired and therefore no longer constituted an automatic bar under Article 8(1) of the Law on the Bar.

The Association appealed. On 7 October 2008 the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and restored the refusal. It emphasised that advocates are subject to higher ethical standards because they participate in the administration of justice and must not discredit the profession, the oath or the ideal of justice (Code of Professional Ethics, points 1.2–1.3 and 2.2). Although the expired conviction removed the formal obstacle of Article 8(1), Article 8(4) still required compliance with the ethics code. The offences had been committed in the course of professional practice, had been repeated more than thirty times, and insufficient time had passed for objective rehabilitation to be established. The applicant had not produced clear and persuasive evidence that she had observed ethical and disciplinary rules in the intervening period.

The Supreme Court dismissed her further appeal on 23 February 2009, confirming that expiry of a conviction for a minor intentional crime is only one of several criteria. Article 8(4) independently required that a candidate satisfy the ethical standards applicable to advocates. Given the nature of the acts—systematic professional dishonesty—the lower court had been entitled to find that she had not proved restoration of high moral character.

Relevant domestic law (Law on the Bar, Articles 7–8 and 39; Code of Professional Ethics) and Supreme Court case-law consistently treat high moral character as an autonomous, ongoing requirement that goes beyond the mere absence of an unexpired criminal record and encompasses honesty, respect for the law and the dignity of the profession. The applicant did not argue before the domestic courts that the restrictions imposed on advocates were more severe than those applied to other legal professions.

These facts form the core of the complaint that the refusal to restore her right to practise law interfered with her private and professional life.

The case of Lekavičienė v. Lithuania concerns the applicant’s complaint that Lithuanian authorities refused to readmit her to the Bar after a criminal conviction, allegedly violating her Convention rights (likely involving professional life and reputation under Article 8).

The applicant, a Lithuanian national born in 1942 and living in Vilnius, was admitted to the Bar on 27 September 1996. She swore an oath of fidelity to the Republic, its Constitution and laws, honest performance of duties, observance of moral norms and citizens’ rights, and protection of professional secrets. She then registered a law office and began practising.

On 19 December 2003 she requested removal from the list of practising advocates because a criminal case was pending against her. On 13 August 2004 she was convicted of document forgery and fraud. While practising, she had on more than 30 occasions falsely claimed in writing that she had provided legal services under the State-paid legal-aid scheme, forged signatures of pre-trial investigation officers, submitted the documents and obtained payment. These were minor intentional crimes (maximum three years’ imprisonment). She was fined, paid the fine on 24 August 2004, and the conviction expired on 24 August 2007.

On 12 September 2007 she applied for readmission. The Bar Association refused on 20 September 2007, holding that she lacked the required “high moral character.” Only three years and 24 days had elapsed since conviction; given the nature of the offence (misappropriation of funds for non-existent services) and the demands of advocacy, she had not regained the character required by Articles 7 § 4 and 8 § 4 of the Law on the Bar.

She challenged the decision. On 25 April 2008 the Vilnius Regional Court, after hearing six character witnesses (most of whom knew her from pre-1996 Ministry of Justice work), partly annulled the refusal and ordered reconsideration. Because the conviction for a minor crime had expired, the Association had erred under Article 8(1).

The Association appealed, stressing that she failed the ethical criteria of Article 8(4) in light of the nature of her acts. The applicant submitted a favourable character reference from a subsequent employer but did not argue that the restrictions were harsher than those applied to other legal professions.

On 7 October 2008 the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal. Advocates must meet higher standards because they participate in the administration of justice; mere compliance with criminal law is insufficient. The Code of Professional Ethics requires observance of legal and moral duties toward clients, courts, the profession and society, and forbids conduct that discredits the advocate’s name, oath or the ideal of justice. Although the conviction had expired (so Article 8(1) did not apply), the offences had been committed in and for the purpose of professional practice and numbered more than 30. Expiry of the conviction did not automatically restore an irreproachable reputation. Insufficient time had passed. An applicant must produce clear, persuasive evidence of rehabilitation and adherence to ethical rules; the court must independently verify the nature of the breaches, the circumstances that produced them, subsequent conduct and whether those factors still obtain. Four years after the offences there was still no sufficient basis to find high moral character under Article 8(4).

The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 23 February 2009. No breach of law permanently bars readmission, yet expiry of a conviction is only one criterion. Article 8(4) additionally requires compliance with advocates’ ethical standards. Given the nature of the criminal acts, the Court of Appeal had correctly concluded that the applicant had not demonstrated regained high moral character.

Domestic law (Law on the Bar and the Code of Professional Ethics) and consistent case-law impose exacting ethical requirements on advocates that go beyond the absence of a criminal record. Analogous but differently timed “high moral character” rules apply to judges and prosecutors. These facts form the core of the alleged Convention violation.

The case of Dimcho Dimov v. Bulgaria (No. 2) concerns allegations by a Bulgarian prisoner that Varna Prison authorities failed to protect him from a known risk of inter-prisoner violence and then provided inadequate medical care for the resulting injury, in breach of Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1968, was serving an 18-year sentence for serious offences including aggravated murder. He had chronic medical conditions and a personality disorder marked by self-harm attempts. In early 2012 he shared a prisoner group with K.I., who was serving 6.5 years for racketeering, murder threats and hooliganism and who himself had a mixed personality disorder featuring dissocial, paranoid and emotionally unstable traits; K.I. had been admitted repeatedly to the prison psychiatric hospital.

On 15 February 2012 the applicant entered another cell to retrieve a mattress and argued with K.I. A guard removed him. The applicant later claimed K.I. then grabbed and struck him through bars, though no other inmate corroborated this and he sought no immediate medical examination. A social worker intervened, isolated the applicant after further shouting, and received complaints from five other inmates that the applicant systematically bullied them. The applicant himself requested separation from K.I. On 21 February the social worker recommended his permanent transfer to another group, citing risks to group relations, his emotional state and his security; he was already being held provisionally elsewhere.

That same day a guard nevertheless escorted the applicant back to his old corridor to collect belongings. The applicant swore at and threatened K.I., who punched him on the jaw. Eight inmates confirmed the sequence. The applicant suffered a fractured right condyloid process, but this went undetected at the time. K.I. received only a disciplinary warning three weeks later.

Immediately after the punch the applicant was seen by the prison feldsher (the sole doctor being on long-term sick leave). She recorded redness in the ear and pain in the jaw but no other injuries and, according to the applicant, refused an X-ray. He received analgesics, anti-inflammatories and antibiotics over the following days. On 7 March he complained of hearing loss and was referred to an external specialist, but the consultation occurred only on 26 April. The otolaryngologist noted pain, reduced hearing and eardrum redness and recommended a maxillofacial surgeon. After further delay for funding, a panoramic X-ray on 19 May revealed an improperly healed fracture and post-traumatic arthritis. Physiotherapy was advised. The applicant initially refused transfer to Sofia Prison Hospital but later accepted; he was admitted in mid-July, by which time the fracture had healed and could no longer be operated on. He received physiotherapy, psychiatric medication and later treatment for a related nasal deviation.

CPT reports of 2010 and 2012 documented endemic inter-prisoner violence at Varna Prison, attributed to severe overcrowding and critically low staffing that prevented effective supervision or dynamic security, together with chronic shortages of medical personnel that produced delayed access to doctors and specialists and over-reliance on feldshers.

A prosecutor initially declined to prosecute anyone, but after further appeal K.I. was convicted in 2015 of causing moderate bodily harm, sentenced to six years and ordered to pay BGN 2 000 in damages. The applicant’s civil claim against the prison authorities for inadequate care was withdrawn before judgment.

These facts underpin the two alleged failures of the State’s positive obligations under Article 3.

The applicant later claimed K.I. followed and struck him through bars, but a social worker’s report found no corroboration and noted no request for medical examination. Further shouting ensued; the social worker isolated the applicant after warning both men. The next day other inmates complained of bullying by the applicant, who in turn requested separation from K.I. On 21 February the social worker recommended transferring the applicant, citing risks to group relations, his emotional state and security; he was provisionally held elsewhere.

That same day a guard escorted the applicant back to collect belongings. According to the guard and eight inmates, the applicant swore at and threatened K.I., who punched him on the jaw, fracturing it (undetected at the time). A disciplinary warning was issued to K.I. only on 13 March. The applicant later obtained a criminal conviction against K.I. in 2015 for moderate bodily harm (six-year sentence plus BGN 2,000 damages), confirmed on appeal; prosecutors declined to proceed against staff, finding no omissions.

The case originated in an application by Lithuanian national Ramūnas Jankauskas against Lithuania, complaining of the authorities’ decision to remove him from the list of trainee advocates. Born in 1972, the applicant graduated in law in 1996 and worked as a police investigator in Šiauliai. On 3 October 2000 the Šiauliai Regional Court convicted him of abuse of office and bribery committed in 1995–1996: while an investigator he had solicited (and sometimes obtained) bribes to discontinue criminal proceedings, threatening victims (suspects or their relatives) that “the case would end badly” and in some instances sexually harassing them. He showed no remorse and sought to evade responsibility. He was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment under a strict regime, confiscation of all property and a five-year ban on working in law enforcement or the justice system. The conviction was upheld on appeal (29 June 2001) and by the Supreme Court (18 December 2001). After the new Criminal Code entered into force the sentence was reduced in 2003 to four years and seven months; he was released on 8 September 2003. On 17 June 2005 the same regional court expunged the conviction, noting that the offences were of medium severity, that he had served his sentence, committed no further administrative offences, was raising a child alone, received positive character references and had “drawn the right conclusions.”

From May 2004 the applicant worked as an in-house lawyer and loan administrator in private companies. On 12 January 2007 he applied to the Lithuanian Bar Association to be enrolled as a trainee advocate, requesting that advocate V.S.B. supervise him. He declared in writing that none of the statutory grounds barred his admission and submitted an application form listing his employment from 1991–1999 (police) and from 2004 (private sector), omitting any reference to the intervening period or the conviction. The Bar placed him on the trainee list on 25 January 2007.

On 13 June 2007 a private individual informed the Bar of the conviction. The Bar initiated disciplinary proceedings, holding that the applicant had withheld information material to an assessment of his reputation and thereby acted dishonestly and disrespectfully, breaching points 1.3, 12.1 and 13.2 of the Code of Professional Ethics for Advocates. The Disciplinary Committee confirmed the breach and referred the matter to the Advocates’ Court of Honour. A regional prosecutor wrote that the applicant’s work in Šiauliai created professional tensions with former colleagues, investigators, prosecutors and judges involved in his original case, though the Law on the Bar did not permit territorial restrictions.

At hearings in September–November 2007 the applicant attended, denied any duty to disclose the conviction and unsuccessfully sought the recusal of the Court of Honour’s president for alleged bias. On 23 November 2007 the Court of Honour (three advocates) found a disciplinary violation and struck him from the trainee list under Articles 13 § 1 and 54 § 2 of the Law on the Bar. It reasoned that, although the application form did not expressly require disclosure, Article 8(4) of the Law (high moral character) and the Ethics Code imposed a duty of honesty; the applicant, a law graduate formerly employed in the legal field, had deliberately concealed cynical crimes committed while in office, knowing that their nature would have barred admission. The profession of advocate demanded adherence to ethical standards that protected its prestige and society’s expectations of justice.

The applicant appealed to the Vilnius Regional Court, alleging procedural irregularities, lack of impartiality and an overly strict interpretation of “high moral character” compared with the rules applicable to bailiffs and civil servants. On 24 October 2008 that court dismissed the appeal, finding no bias or decisive procedural defects (postponements were not merits decisions; a change of composition was not material). Although the conviction had expired, the crimes’ nature, manner and context in law enforcement meant the applicant had not automatically regained high moral character; he had a moral (if not express statutory) duty to disclose the information comprehensively so that his reputation could be assessed. The Court of Appeal (7 April 2009) upheld the judgment, confirming that the Ethics Code applied to trainee candidates and that the proceedings complied with Article 6. The Supreme Court refused cassation on 13 May 2009 (and a second identical attempt on 10 July 2009), holding that the case followed settled case-law: advocates form part of the justice system and are subject to higher legal and ethical standards; ignorance of those standards cannot be pleaded.

The case of Trivkanović v. Croatia (Application no. 12986/13) was brought by Croatian national Stoja Trivkanović, who alleged that the Croatian authorities failed to meet their procedural obligations under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to life) in investigating the 1991 killing of her former husband N.T. and the disappearance of her two sons, Z.T. and B.T. Complaints under the procedural aspects of Articles 2 and 14 were communicated to the Government.

On 25 August 1991, during the Croatian War of Independence, members of the Sisak police “Wolves” unit abducted N.T., Z.T., and B.T. from Z.T.’s house. N.T.’s body was found the next day in the Sava River; an autopsy confirmed he had been shot. The sons vanished and were later declared dead as of that date. The applicant promptly informed the Ministry of the Interior and lodged a criminal complaint in 1993 (and again in 2006). Immediate police enquiries began under Sisak police commanders, later expanding into a broader investigation of killings of Serb civilians in the Sisak area.

Early witness interviews (pre-1997 Convention ratification and later) yielded no concrete perpetrator information. From 2002 onward, some former soldiers and relatives reported seeing the victims beaten at the ORA military base near Sisak. A 2004 police report listed the sons as missing. In 2005 the State Attorney’s Office directed county offices to identify perpetrators of 1991–1995 civilian killings. The case was classified as a war crime against civilians in 2006. Further interviews occurred in 2008–2009, alongside a 2008 State Attorney instruction stressing impartial investigation of war crimes regardless of ethnicity.

In June 2011 a criminal complaint was filed against three former Sisak police officials (Đ.B., who died shortly thereafter; V.M.; and D.B., a Wolves member) for war crimes, including the applicants’ relatives’ abduction and killing. An investigation followed, and in December 2011 an indictment charged V.M. and D.B. with command responsibility for a series of civilian killings (July 1991–June 1992). At trial, multiple witnesses, including the applicant, confirmed the abduction by Wolves members and transfer to ORA.

On 9 December 2013 the Osijek County Court convicted V.M. of war crimes against the civilian population. As commander of police forces and deputy head of Sisak police, he had allowed killings of Serbs and failed to prevent them. The judgment specifically described the 25 August 1991 abduction of N.T. and his sons, their beating at ORA, N.T.’s execution, and the unknown fate of the sons. V.M. received eight years’ imprisonment (increased to ten by the Supreme Court in 2014). D.B. was acquitted. These facts highlight the 20-year delay in charging officials, the initial police involvement in the events, and the eventual (but limited) accountability obtained.

The case of Trivkanović v. Croatia (Application no. 12986/13) concerns an application by Croatian national Stoja Trivkanović to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention (right to life). The applicant claimed that Croatian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the 1991 killing of her former husband, N.T., and the disappearance (later presumed death) of their two sons, Z.T. and B.T.

On 25 August 1991, during the Croatian War of Independence, members of the “Wolves” (Vukovi) unit of the Sisak police entered Z.T.’s home and abducted N.T., Z.T. and B.T. N.T.’s body was found the next day in the River Sava; an autopsy confirmed he had been shot. The sons vanished. The Sisak police filed a criminal complaint on 2 September 1991 and began enquiries under Đ.B. (head of Sisak police) and his deputy V.M. The applicant notified the Ministry of the Interior on 9 September 1991 and lodged a criminal complaint in June 1993. The Wolves commander, J.G., died in a 1992 accident.

Croatia ratified the Convention on 5 November 1997. Pre-ratification police interviews of the applicant and several witnesses yielded no concrete information on perpetrators. Broader enquiries into killings of Serb civilians in the Sisak area later incorporated this case. In 2002–2003, further interviews occurred. Witness Z.G. (a former Croatian soldier) stated he had seen all three victims at the ORA military base near Sisak, where the sons appeared beaten. Other former soldiers described wartime arrests and detentions at ORA but provided no specifics about these victims. Witness D.M. confirmed seeing the arrest by men in camouflage uniforms and hearing they were taken to ORA. The applicant testified that she had heard similar accounts from family and acquaintances.

A 2004 police report listed the sons as missing. In 2005 they were declared dead as of 25 August 1991. In October 2006 the Sisak County State Attorney’s Office classified the events as war crimes against the civilian population. The applicant filed another complaint in December 2006, alleging Croatian army involvement and naming B.B. as ORA commander. Additional interviews in 2007–2009 produced little new evidence; some witnesses remained fearful or uninformative.

The case formed part of wider police enquiries into Sisak police officials as suspects in 34 similar incidents. On 20 June 2011 a criminal complaint was lodged against Đ.B., V.M. and D.B. (a Wolves member) for war crimes, including these killings; all three were arrested. Đ.B. died on 13 July 2011. An investigation followed. In December 2011 an indictment was filed against V.M. and D.B. for command responsibility over the unit that committed multiple crimes against civilians between July 1991 and June 1992.

On 9 December 2013 the Osijek County Court convicted V.M. of war crimes against the civilian population. It found that, as commander of police forces in the Sisak-Banovina area and deputy head of Sisak police, he had allowed killings of Serb civilians and failed to prevent them. The judgment specifically recorded that Wolves members abducted the three victims to ORA, where they were beaten; N.T. was then taken away and shot, while the sons’ fate remained unknown. V.M. received an eight-year sentence; D.B. was acquitted. On 10 June 2014 the Supreme Court upheld the conviction and increased the sentence to ten years.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the investigation was ineffective, particularly given delays spanning two decades from the 1991 events until indictment and trial.

The case of Trivkanović v. Croatia concerns an application lodged in 2013 by Stoja Trivkanović, a Croatian national, alleging that Croatia failed to fulfil its procedural obligations under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) in investigating the 1991 killing of her former husband N.T. and the disappearance of their two sons, Z.T. and B.T. (The Court also communicated a related Article 14 complaint.) The applicant was born in 1950 and lived in Sisak; she had divorced N.T. in 1985.

On 25 August 1991, during the Croatian War of Independence, members of the “Wolves” (Vukovi) unit of the Sisak police forcibly entered Z.T.’s house and abducted N.T., Z.T. and B.T. N.T.’s body was found the next day in the River Sava; an autopsy confirmed he had been shot. The sons vanished and were never found. The Sisak police immediately opened a criminal complaint regarding N.T.’s killing; enquiries were led by Đ.B. (head of Sisak police) and his deputy V.M. The applicant notified the Ministry of the Interior on 9 September 1991. She lodged a criminal complaint with the State Attorney’s Office in June 1993. Broader police enquiries into killings of Serb civilians in the Sisak area later incorporated this case.

Croatia ratified the Convention in November 1997. Prior to that date the police had interviewed the applicant and several witnesses, none of whom identified perpetrators. In 2002 an investigating judge heard former soldier Z.G., who stated (after initially denying knowledge) that he had seen all three victims at the ORA military base near Sisak, where the sons appeared beaten. Subsequent police interviews of numerous former soldiers yielded no information on the victims’ fate, though some described arrests and detentions at ORA. Witness D.M. confirmed seeing the abduction by men in camouflage and hearing they were taken to ORA. The applicant herself testified in 2003 that she had not witnessed the arrest but had heard consistent accounts from family and others placing the victims at ORA.

In 2004 police listed the sons as missing. A 2005 State Attorney’s Office document directed county offices to identify perpetrators of 1991–1995 civilian killings. The sons were judicially declared dead as of 25 August 1991. In October 2006 the killing and disappearances were reclassified as war crimes against civilians. The applicant filed a further complaint in December 2006 naming Croatian army members and ORA commander B.B. Additional witness interviews in 2007–2009 (including D.F.T., Z.T.’s widow) produced no new identifications of direct perpetrators. A 2008 State Attorney’s instruction stressed impartial investigation of all war crimes regardless of ethnicity.

The enquiries formed part of a wider investigation into Sisak police officials as suspects in 34 civilian deaths. On 20 June 2011 police lodged a criminal complaint against Đ.B., V.M. and D.B. (a Wolves member) for war crimes, including the Trivkanović killings; the three were arrested that day. Đ.B. died in July 2011. An indictment against V.M. and D.B. was filed in December 2011, charging command responsibility for crimes (including these) committed by unnamed Wolves members between July 1991 and June 1992. Trial witnesses (including the applicant, D.M. and D.F.T.) confirmed the abduction by Wolves members and transfer to ORA.

On 9 December 2013 the Osijek County Court convicted V.M. of war crimes against civilians for failing, as commander of police forces in the Sisak–Banovina area and deputy head of Sisak police, to prevent killings of Serbs. The judgment recorded that Wolves members abducted the three victims, took them to ORA for beating and interrogation, shot N.T. that day (body recovered 26 August), and left the sons’ fate unknown. V.M. received eight years’ imprisonment (increased to ten by the Supreme Court in June 2014). D.B. was acquitted. Direct perpetrators of the abduction and killings were never identified or prosecuted. These facts underpin the applicant’s claim of an ineffective, delayed investigation into a 1991 killing and disappearance.
