The case of Zdjelar and Others v. Croatia (Application no. 80960/12) concerns nine Croatian nationals, children of Milan Zdjelar (killed on 8 August 1995). They alleged that Croatia failed to fulfil its procedural obligations under Articles 2 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the investigation into their father's death, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

During the 1991–1995 Croatian War of Independence, Serbian paramilitary forces controlled the Krajina region, including the village of Crni Potok where part of the Zdjelar family (of Serbian origin) resided. In August 1995, Croatian forces launched Operation Storm (4–7 August) to recapture the area; most Krajina inhabitants fled. Milan Zdjelar and his daughter Dragica remained. On 8 August 1995, around 12:50 p.m., while they sat outside their house, a military vehicle stopped nearby. Three camouflage-clad soldiers (identified by Dragica as from the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade) approached. Milan fled toward woods; Dragica followed and heard shots. She saw him shot in the chest and leg; he died shortly after. The soldiers departed. Dragica hid for two days, then reported the killing to Croatian Army personnel, who buried the body.

Authorities first learned of the death via a 11 October 2001 list of Operation Storm killings submitted to the State Attorney’s Office (SAO), noting Milan was shot in the head and leg by Tigers brigade members. Police photographed the grave and interviewed Dragica (who confirmed the date and location). The body was exhumed in 2002; a post-mortem on 20 September 2002 failed to establish the cause of death, noting only a broken collarbone.

In 2004, Dragica gave a detailed police statement identifying the perpetrators as Tigers soldiers and describing the shooting. Her mother provided no relevant information. Police reported the allegation to the Sisak County State Attorney. In 2005, following a SAO instruction to prioritize identifying perpetrators of 1991–1995 civilian killings, the applicants filed a criminal complaint classifying the death as a war crime against an unarmed civilian of Serbian ethnicity. The SAO requested an investigation, but police repeatedly reported no progress through 2008. Military Police provided no information in 2007.

A 2008 SAO instruction stressed impartiality in war-crimes probes regardless of ethnicity. In 2009, an investigating judge heard Dragica (who repeated her account). Neighbours confirmed Croatian soldiers’ presence but offered no perpetrator details. The Ministry of Defence stated that members of Croatian Army brigade 153 (under a commander named M.) had buried Milan and listed relevant personnel (one deceased). Interviews with Tigers brigade members and brigade 153 soldiers yielded denials of knowledge or involvement in civilian killings.

In 2012, former Tigers soldier Ž.L. filed a complaint mentioning a Crni Potok civilian killing days after Storm, allegedly tolerated by Third Battalion command. He described a logistics officer bringing a “četnik” civilian, who was taken away by officers P.Z. and J.M.; later, an elderly man was found shot in the back and head (with a gun nearby), and an old woman was also killed. Police interviewed Ž.L. and Dragica (who described two soldiers). Further statements were taken from Dragica and a neighbour in 2013–2014; Ž.L. later refused to testify, citing health issues and recanting his allegations as unfounded.

In 2015 the investigation (covering multiple Operation Storm victims) was reassigned to the Osijek County State Attorney’s Office. Further 2016–2017 inquiries sought locations of named individuals and interviewed additional soldiers and villagers; some witnesses had died, and interviewees denied seeing civilians or involvement in killings. No suspects were identified or prosecuted.

Separately, in 2004 the applicants sued the State for compensation under the 2003 Liability Act. Courts dismissed the claim as time-barred (finalised 2011); a 2012 constitutional complaint failed.

These facts highlight prolonged investigative delays, repeated lack of progress, inconsistent forensic findings, unfollowed leads (including Ž.L.’s account), and the civil claim’s dismissal, forming the basis of the alleged violations of the duty to conduct an effective, prompt, and impartial investigation into a potential unlawful killing, possibly motivated by ethnicity, without adequate domestic remedies.

The case of Zdjelar and Others v. Croatia (Application no. 80960/12) was brought by nine Croatian nationals, the children of Milan Zdjelar (killed on 8 August 1995). They alleged that Croatia had failed to meet its procedural obligations under Articles 2 (right to life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights in investigating their father’s death, and that they had no effective remedy under Article 13.

Milan Zdjelar, of Serbian ethnicity and a civilian, lived with part of his family in Crni Potok in the Krajina region, which Croatian forces recaptured in Operation Storm (4–7 August 1995). His daughter Dragica (the third applicant) remained with him. She stated that on 8 August 1995, around 12.50 p.m., three camouflage-clad soldiers from the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade approached their house. Her father ran into the woods; she followed and heard three shots. She saw him shot in the chest and leg; he died shortly afterwards. She hid for two days while his body lay in the grass. Soldiers later buried him.

The investigation began years later. In October 2001 a list of persons killed during or after Storm, including Zdjelar (noted as shot in the head and leg by Tigers brigade members), reached the authorities. Police photographed the grave and interviewed Dragica. In 2002 the body was exhumed; a post-mortem recorded only a broken collarbone and did not establish the cause of death, inconsistent with the shooting account.

In 2004 Dragica repeated her detailed statement. A police report followed, but little progress occurred. In September 2005 the applicants lodged a criminal complaint treating the killing as a war crime against a civilian. The State Attorney’s Office requested an investigation, yet police repeatedly reported “no progress” through 2007–2008 and later years. In 2008 authorities issued instructions stressing impartial investigation of all war crimes regardless of ethnicity. Dragica testified before an investigating judge in 2009. Neighbours and members of relevant army units (including Tigers and the brigade that buried Zdjelar) were interviewed in 2009–2010 and provided no information identifying perpetrators.

In 2012 a former Tigers soldier, Ž.L., mentioned in a separate complaint that civilians had been killed in Crni Potok shortly after Storm, describing soldiers taking away a man labelled a “četnik” and later finding an elderly man with gunshot wounds to the back and head (a logistics officer claiming to have shot him “to shorten his pain”). Police interviewed Ž.L. and Dragica again. Subsequent efforts to hear Ž.L. formally stalled; he later refused further statements, citing health issues, the passage of time, and prior official conclusions that his information did not establish a crime. The investigation was reassigned in 2015. Further interviews in 2016–2017 with former soldiers produced denials of any killings or even of the Tigers’ presence in the village. No suspects were identified.

Separately, the applicants’ 2004 civil claim for compensation against the State was dismissed in 2005 as time-barred under the applicable statute of limitations. The dismissal was upheld by appellate and supreme courts and by the Constitutional Court in 2012.

These facts—the multi-year delay before any meaningful inquiry, repeated inactivity despite specific witness identifications of army units, contradictory forensic findings, and failure to pursue or secure key witness evidence—underpin the alleged breaches of the duty to conduct a prompt, effective and independent investigation into a death potentially involving state agents, as well as the lack of any effective domestic remedy.

The applicants, nine children of Milan Zdjelar (a Croatian national of Serbian ethnicity who died on 8 August 1995), alleged that Croatia had failed to meet its procedural obligations under Articles 2 and 14 of the Convention regarding the investigation into their father’s killing, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

Milan Zdjelar and part of his family lived in Crni Potok, a village in the Krajina region that had been under the control of Serbian paramilitary forces since 1991–1992. In early August 1995 the Croatian Army launched Operation Storm to recapture the area. Most of the local Serb population fled. According to the account given by the third applicant (Dragica Zdjelar), she and her father remained at their isolated house. Around midday on 8 August a military transport vehicle carrying three soldiers in camouflage uniforms (later identified by her as members of the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade) stopped nearby. When her father ran toward the woods the soldiers fired; she saw him hit in the chest and leg. He died shortly afterwards. She hid for two days, then reported the killing to Croatian soldiers, who buried the body.

No official investigation began until October 2001, after a third-party list of Operation Storm victims (including Milan Zdjelar, noted as having been shot by the Tigers) was submitted to the State Attorney’s Office (SAO). Police photographed the grave and interviewed Dragica. In 2002 the body was exhumed; the autopsy recorded only a broken collarbone and did not establish the cause of death. Further interviews of Dragica and her mother in 2004 produced the detailed account summarised above. The applicants and their mother lodged a formal criminal complaint in September 2005 classifying the killing as a war crime against a civilian. The SAO referred the matter for investigation.

Thereafter the investigation proceeded in fits and starts. Between 2005 and 2011 the SAO repeatedly asked the police for progress reports and received the same answer: none. Limited steps included a 2007 enquiry to the Military Police (which yielded nothing), a 2009 judicial hearing of Dragica, interviews of two neighbours who confirmed only that Croatian soldiers had entered the village, and requests to the Ministry of Defence that produced a list of members of brigade 153 (the unit said to have buried the body). In 2010 five former Tigers soldiers and three members of brigade 153 were interviewed; all denied knowledge of any civilian killings. A 2008 SAO instruction had emphasised the need for impartial investigation of all war crimes regardless of the ethnicity of victims or perpetrators, yet no suspects were identified.

In late 2012 a former soldier, Ž.L., submitted a complaint mentioning a killing of a civilian (or civilians) in Crni Potok shortly after Operation Storm, allegedly tolerated by officers of the Tigers’ Third Battalion. When interviewed he described an elderly man found shot in the back and head; a logistics officer had then “finished him off.” Dragica was re-interviewed and gave descriptions of the two soldiers she had seen. Ž.L. was later summoned but cited health problems, stated that his earlier allegations were unfounded and that he had not actually witnessed any crime, and ultimately refused to give further evidence. In 2015 the file was transferred to the Osijek County State Attorney’s Office, which in 2016–2017 requested further information and interviews. Several potential witnesses had died; remaining former Tigers members denied having been in Crni Potok or having killed civilians. By the time of the Court’s judgment in July 2017 the investigation remained open and no perpetrator had been identified or prosecuted.

A parallel civil claim for compensation, lodged in 2004 under the 2003 Liability Act, was dismissed as time-barred by the municipal court (2005), the county court (2009) and the Supreme Court (2011); a constitutional complaint was rejected in 2012.

The applicants contended that the more than twenty-year delay, the inconclusive autopsy, the lack of progress despite repeated prosecutorial prompting, and the failure to follow up promising leads (including Ž.L.’s statement) demonstrated that the investigation had been ineffective and possibly tainted by ethnic bias.

The European Court of Human Rights case S.C. Service Benz Com S.R.L. v. Romania (Application no. 58045/11) concerns a Romanian fuel distribution company’s complaint over the confiscation of its two tankers. The applicant alleged that the vehicles were seized even though it had committed no offence and no fault on its part had been established, invoking Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

On 11 May 2010 the applicant contracted with company N. SARL to carry “automobile lubricants and other goods.” The contract placed responsibility on N. to complete transport documents accurately. That same day the tankers were loaded in Bulgaria in the presence of a tax official who sealed them. Romanian fraud-squad officers later stopped the vehicles. Laboratory tests showed the liquid did not match the specifications given in the documents.

By official report of 7 June 2010 the authorities fined N. (the owner of the goods) RON 100 000 (approximately EUR 23 000) under Article 220 § 1 (k) of the Code of Tax Procedure for transporting excise goods without proper documentation or with damaged seals. They also confiscated both the liquid and the applicant’s two tankers pursuant to Article 220 § 2 (a) and (b).

The applicant challenged only the confiscation of the tankers before the Slobozia Court of First Instance. It argued that it had merely transported a customer’s goods and therefore bore no responsibility for their legal conformity, and that the documents in its possession indicated that the cargo was not subject to excise duty. On 15 November 2010 the first-instance court allowed the challenge and annulled the confiscation. It held that the transporter could not verify the goods’ conformity, that a tax official had sealed the tankers after loading, and that confiscation was therefore unlawful.

The tax authorities appealed. On 28 February 2011 the Ialomiţa County Court allowed the appeal, quashed the lower judgment and dismissed the applicant’s challenge. The court reasoned that Article 220 § 2 (b) authorised confiscation of the means of transport used in the offence without requiring that the property belong to the administrative offender. Articles 24 and 25 of Government Ordinance No. 2/2001 expressly contemplated confiscation of property belonging to a third party. Because the applicant was not itself the offender, the court saw no need to examine fault on its part; confiscation was an ancillary penalty imposed by law and could be set aside only for breach of the relevant statutory provisions. The court added that the transporter had been negligent in failing to ensure the safety and lawfulness of the goods.

Domestic law treated the transport of improperly documented excise goods as an administrative offence punishable by fine and by confiscation of the tanks, recipients and vehicles used. The Romanian Constitutional Court had repeatedly upheld the constitutionality of these provisions, holding that an owner who entrusts a vehicle to another accepts the risk of its unlawful use, that the owner may seek contractual compensation from the offender, and that a contrary interpretation would allow offenders to evade confiscation simply by using hired vehicles.

Civil-law rules required proof of damage, an unlawful act, negligence and causation before contractual liability could arise. The Commercial Code placed responsibility for the content and lawfulness of transport documents on the forwarder, not the carrier.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the confiscation violated its right to a fair hearing and its right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions, because no offence or fault attributable to it had ever been lawfully established.

The case of S.C. Service Benz Com S.R.L. v. Romania (no. 58045/11) arose from the confiscation of two fuel tankers owned by the applicant, a Romanian company founded in 1993 and engaged in retail fuel distribution. On 11 May 2010 the applicant contracted with company “N.” SARL to transport “automobile lubricants and other goods,” the contract placing on “N.” the duty to complete transport documents accurately. The tankers were loaded that day in Bulgaria in the presence of a tax-office official who sealed them.

Before reaching their destination the tankers were stopped by the Romanian fraud squad. Laboratory tests showed that the liquid did not match the specifications recorded in the transport documents. By official report of 7 June 2010 the squad fined “N.” RON 100 000 (approximately EUR 23 000) under Article 220 § 1 (k) of the Code of Tax Procedure for transporting goods subject to excise duty without proper documentation, and confiscated both the liquid and the two tankers under Article 220 § 2 (a) and (b).

The applicant challenged only the confiscation of its vehicles, arguing that it had merely carried its customer’s goods, bore no responsibility for their legality, and that the documents in its possession did not indicate excise goods. On 15 November 2010 the Slobozia Court of First Instance upheld the challenge and annulled the confiscation. It held that the transporter could not verify the goods’ conformity, especially as a tax official had sealed the tankers, rendering the confiscation unlawful.

The tax authorities appealed. On 28 February 2011 the Ialomiţa County Court allowed the appeal, quashed the first-instance judgment and dismissed the applicant’s challenge. It reasoned that Article 220 § 2 (b) authorised confiscation of the means of transport without regard to ownership, and that Articles 24 and 25 of Government Ordinance No. 2/2001 expressly contemplated confiscation of property belonging to a third party. Because the applicant was not the administrative offender, no examination of its fault was required; confiscation was an ancillary penalty that could be set aside only for breach of the relevant legal provisions. The court added that the transporter had been negligent as regards the safety and lawfulness of the goods.

Relevant domestic law included Government Ordinance No. 2/2001, which treats confiscation of property used to commit an administrative offence as an ancillary penalty even when the owner is not the offender, and Article 220 of the Code of Tax Procedure, which specifically mandates confiscation of tanks used to transport undocumented excise goods. The Constitutional Court had repeatedly upheld the constitutionality of these provisions, holding that an owner who entrusts a vehicle accepts the risk of its misuse, can seek contractual compensation from the offender, and that a contrary interpretation would allow easy circumvention of the law. Civil-law rules on contractual liability require proof of damage, an unlawful act, negligence and causation; the Commercial Code and the later Civil Code allocate responsibility for transport documents between forwarder and carrier.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s complaint that the confiscation, effected without any offence or fault being established against it, violated Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of S.C. Service Benz Com S.R.L. v. Romania (Application no. 58045/11) involves a Romanian commercial company’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights over the confiscation of its two fuel tankers. The applicant, whose main business is retail fuel distribution, alleged that the confiscation took place even though it had committed no offence and no fault on its part had been lawfully established. It relied on Article 6 of the Convention (fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

On 11 May 2010 the applicant entered a contract with company N. for the carriage of automobile lubricants and other goods. The contract made N. responsible for completing transport documents accurately. That same day the applicant’s two tankers were loaded in Bulgaria in the presence of a tax-office representative, who then sealed them.

Before reaching their destination the tankers were stopped by the Romanian fraud squad. Laboratory analysis showed that the liquid did not match the specifications given in the transport documents.

By an official report of 7 June 2010 the authorities fined N. (the owner of the goods) RON 100 000 (approximately EUR 23 000) under Article 220 § 1 (k) of the Code of Tax Procedure for transporting goods subject to excise duty with incomplete or inaccurate documentation. They also confiscated the liquid and the applicant’s two tankers under Article 220 § 2 (a) and (b).

The applicant challenged the confiscation of the tankers before the Slobozia Court of First Instance. It argued that it was merely the carrier and bore no responsibility for the goods’ legal conformity, and that the documents in its possession showed it was not transporting excise goods.

On 15 November 2010 the first-instance court allowed the challenge and annulled the confiscation. It held that the transporter could not verify the goods’ conformity, particularly as the tankers had been sealed by tax authorities, rendering the confiscation unlawful.

The tax authorities appealed. On 28 February 2011 the Ialomiţa County Court allowed the appeal, quashed the lower judgment and dismissed the applicant’s challenge. It reasoned that Article 220 § 2 (b) authorised confiscation of the means of transport without requiring the property to belong to the administrative offender, and that Articles 24 and 25 of Government Ordinance No. 2/2001 expressly contemplated confiscation of third-party property. Because the applicant was not the offender, no examination of its fault was required; confiscation was an ancillary penalty that could be set aside only for breach of the relevant legal provisions. The court also found the transporter negligent in respect of the safety and lawfulness of the goods.

Relevant domestic law included Government Ordinance No. 2/2001, which treats confiscation as an ancillary administrative penalty for property used in an offence and requires identification of the owner if different from the offender. Article 220 of the Code of Tax Procedure specifically provides for confiscation of tanks and vehicles used in irregular transport of excise goods.

The Romanian Constitutional Court (decisions of 2006, 2011 and 2012) had upheld the constitutionality of these provisions, holding that an owner who entrusted property to another accepted the risk of its unlawful use, could seek contractual compensation, and that a contrary reading would allow easy circumvention of the law.

Civil and commercial rules in force at the time required fault, damage and causation for contractual liability; the forwarder was responsible for the accuracy and lawfulness of transport documents, while the transporter remained liable to third parties but could recoup from the forwarder.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: confiscation of an innocent third party’s vehicles without any finding of fault, raising issues of lawfulness, proportionality and procedural fairness.
001-170171:
The case of Boacă and Others v. Romania (Application no. 40374/11) originated from events on 27 August 2008 at the home of I.B., a Roma man whose heirs (the seven applicants) pursued the matter after his death in April 2010. The applicants, all of Roma origin, alleged police brutality, unlawful entry into their home, and discrimination.

Background facts established that on 15 August 2008, 16-year-old L.N. (from a non-Roma family) moved in with her boyfriend (the fifth applicant) at I.B.’s house. She and a neighbour promptly informed police that she was there voluntarily. On 21 August she repeated this to local officials, including the deputy mayor and police, and requested that her belongings be returned to her mother.

On 27 August, L.N.’s father reported her missing and claimed she might be held against her will or drugged. A police team, reinforced by five members of the Giurgiu Rapid Intervention Squad because of the Boacă family’s reputation for violence, arrived at the house. According to the applicants, officers demanded to know if a girl was being detained, punched I.B. when he asked for a warrant (stating their “warrant” was “a fist and a gun”), then broke a gate and windows, dragged L.N. out, fired rubber bullets (one striking the 15-year-old sixth applicant in the buttocks), deployed tear gas, and caused two young children to lose consciousness. No search warrant existed. Medical examination of the sixth applicant confirmed bruising but found no gunshot residue.

The Government, relying on domestic findings, described a lawful inquiry: officers were invited in, spoke with L.N. (who agreed to leave), and were then attacked by family members wielding bats and knives and throwing projectiles. Police used tear gas and fired warning shots solely in self-defence; they reported no injuries.

I.B. promptly lodged criminal complaints alleging excessive force, property damage and anti-Roma discrimination. Investigators interviewed only the eight participating officers, L.N. and her parents. The Boacă family were not heard; summonses were posted after alleged refusal. The prosecutor’s office (May 2009) and Giurgiu County Court (November 2009) concluded that force had been proportionate and defensive, that the sixth applicant’s injury was unrelated to firearms, and that no racial motive existed. The Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed the final appeal in December 2010.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints to the European Court of Human Rights concerning the use of force, the integrity of the home, the adequacy of the investigation, and possible discriminatory treatment on grounds of ethnic origin.

The ECHR case Boacă and Others v. Romania (no. 40374/11) was brought by seven Romanian nationals of Roma origin, heirs of I.B. (who died in April 2010). They pursued both his and their own claims arising from a 27 August 2008 police operation at I.B.’s home and the ensuing investigation.

On 15 August 2008, 16-year-old L.N. (from a non-Roma family) moved in with her boyfriend, I.B.’s son (fifth applicant). The next day she and a neighbour confirmed in writing to Clejani police that her stay was voluntary. On 21 August she repeated this at a meeting with the deputy mayor, social services and police officers, and asked that her jewellery and phone be given to her mother.

On 27 August a team comprising the Clejani police chief, Rapid Intervention Squad (R.I.S.) officers and two plain-clothes policemen arrived at the house. According to the applicants, an officer asked I.B. whether he was holding L.N. against her will. I.B. denied it, summoned L.N. (who again confirmed she was there freely) and asked for a search warrant. He was punched in the face and told the warrant was “a fist and a gun.” Masked R.I.S. officers then forced their way in, breaking a gate and five windows, dragged L.N. out, fired rubber bullets (one striking the 15-year-old sixth applicant in the buttocks), discharged shots into the air and threw tear-gas canisters. Two toddlers present lost consciousness. The sixth applicant was taken to hospital; the medical report recorded a superficial wound and bruising consistent with a hard object but not a firearm (no gunpowder residue). The family later established at the mayor’s office that no warrant had existed.

The Government, relying on domestic findings, stated that L.N.’s father had reported her missing and possibly drugged. Because the boyfriend had a violent record and the family was known to police, the local team was reinforced by five R.I.S. officers. They displayed badges, were invited inside and spoke to L.N., who eventually agreed to leave. The family then became violent (shouting, wielding bats and knives, throwing stones, bricks and glass at the police vehicle). After ignored warnings, officers used tear gas and fired vertical warning shots. Police statements asserted that no one was injured.

I.B. lodged criminal complaints in September and November 2008 alleging brutality, property damage and racial discrimination. He offered documents and named eyewitnesses. Investigators interviewed only the eight participating officers plus L.N. and her parents; the family was never heard (summonses were posted after alleged refusal). The report concluded that force had been used solely in self-defence, lasted only while violence continued, and had no racial motive; the sixth applicant’s injury was deemed irrelevant. On 7 May 2009 the prosecutor decided not to prosecute.

I.B. challenged the decision for failure to hear witnesses. The chief prosecutor upheld it. The Giurgiu County Court dismissed his complaint on 11 November 2009, finding the officers had acted within their authority to protect themselves and L.N. After I.B.’s death his heirs (except the seventh applicant, who did not actively participate) continued the appeal. On 14 December 2010 the Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed it, rendering the non-prosecution final.

These facts—forceful entry without a warrant, use of rubber bullets, tear gas and physical violence against a Roma family (including a minor), property destruction, and an investigation that relied exclusively on police accounts while ignoring the applicants’ evidence and discrimination claim—form the core of the alleged Convention violations.

The case of Boacă and Others v. Romania (Application no. 40374/11) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by seven Romanian nationals of Roma origin, acting as heirs of I.B. (who died in April 2010 while domestic proceedings were pending). The applicants pursued complaints both on I.B.’s behalf and their own, alleging that a police operation on 27 August 2008 involved unjustified force, property damage, and racial discrimination, compounded by an ineffective investigation.

The events began on 15 August 2008, when 16-year-old L.N. (from a non-Roma family) moved into the home of her boyfriend, the fifth applicant, at I.B.’s residence. The following day, L.N. voluntarily informed the Clejani police chief in writing of her wish to live there. A neighbour corroborated this. On 21 August, L.N. repeated her statement before local officials, including police, and requested that her belongings be returned to her mother.

According to the applicants, on 27 August around noon a team comprising the Clejani police chief, members of the Giurgiu Rapid Intervention Squad (R.I.S.), and two plain-clothes officers arrived at I.B.’s house. One officer asked whether a girl was being held against her will. I.B. explained L.N.’s voluntary presence (as previously declared) and asked for a search warrant; he was punched in the face and told the “warrant” was “a fist and a gun.” L.N. emerged and confirmed her free will. Masked R.I.S. officers then entered the yard. Police broke a gate and five windows, dragged L.N. away, fired rubber bullets (one striking the 15-year-old sixth applicant in the buttocks as he fled), discharged tear gas, and fired into the air. Two young children present lost consciousness. The sixth applicant was hospitalised with a superficial wound and bruising inconsistent with a gunshot (no gunpowder residue). Family members later learned at the mayor’s office that no warrant existed.

The Government, relying on domestic findings, stated that L.N.’s father had reported her disappearance, suspecting she was being held against her will (possibly drugged). Given the family’s reputation for violence and the boyfriend’s criminal record, local police were reinforced by five R.I.S. officers. Upon arrival, officers displayed badges and were invited inside. After speaking with L.N., who ultimately chose to leave with police, the family allegedly became violent: the seventh applicant shouted threats, and men armed themselves with bats and knives. Police issued warnings, used tear gas, and fired vertical warning shots after stones, bricks and glass were thrown at the vehicle containing L.N. Police reports claimed no injuries occurred and that force was used solely in self-defence.

I.B. lodged criminal complaints in September and November 2008 alleging police brutality, property damage and racial discrimination (citing prior incidents). He offered documents and eyewitnesses. The Giurgiu prosecutor interviewed only the eight participating officers, L.N. and her parents; no Boacă family members were heard (the prosecutor recorded that I.B. and the fifth applicant refused summonses, which they denied). A 7 May 2009 decision not to prosecute found the force defensive, proportionate and free of racial motive; the sixth applicant’s injury was deemed irrelevant. Hierarchical and judicial reviews (Giurgiu County Court, 11 November 2009; Bucharest Court of Appeal, 14 December 2010) upheld this, accepting that officers acted lawfully to protect themselves and L.N. I.B. died during the appeal; his recognised heirs continued the case.

These facts underpin the alleged violations, centred on the use of force during the unauthorised entry, injuries and damage, possible ethnic motivation, and the investigation’s failure to hear the victims or independent witnesses. (Word count: 512)

The case of Ioniță v. Romania (Application no. 81270/12) concerns a complaint by Romanian parents Dorina and Viorel-Aurel Ioniță that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the death of their four-year-old son following routine surgery, in alleged violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention (right to life).

On 7 November 2005 the child underwent polyp-removal surgery at Brăila Emergency Hospital under general anaesthetic with tracheal intubation, performed by surgeon Dr C.B. and anaesthetist Dr P.A. (assisted by nurse P.V.I.). Ten minutes after transfer to intensive care the child became cyanotic and pulseless; blood flooded his lungs. Resuscitation failed and he was pronounced dead two hours after the operation.

An autopsy the next day attributed death to acute respiratory failure caused by blood blocking the airways and lungs; it also recorded pre-existing congenital conditions (myocardia, hepatic dystrophy, inter-atrial septum aneurysm). Subsequent reviews by the Iaşi Forensic Institute (May 2006) and the national Mina Minovici Institute (October 2006) confirmed a causal link between post-operative care and death, identifying possible deflation of the intubation-catheter balloon as the mechanism that allowed blood to enter the lungs.

Disciplinary proceedings initiated by the father produced mixed findings. The local College of Doctors (July 2007) classified the death as “sudden” and found no direct link to medical conduct, merely reprimanding the doctors for inadequate pre-operative tests and failure to obtain informed consent. The National College (June 2008) quashed that decision, fined both doctors, held that pre-surgical examination had been “very superficial,” noted that statements claiming the balloon had remained leak-proof were irreconcilable with the presence of blood in the lungs, and again recorded the absence of informed consent.

A criminal complaint lodged the same day as the death alleged negligent treatment. Dr P.A. was formally charged in 2007. Nurse P.V.I., who had monitored the child in intensive care, left the hospital in January 2006, could not be located, and later proved to be in Italy; she was never questioned despite repeated summonses. Conflicting forensic opinions emerged: official reports pointed to the balloon, while an extra-judicial report commissioned by Dr P.A. blamed the child’s pre-existing conditions. Prosecutors discontinued the case in 2008 for lack of criminal negligence. Courts repeatedly quashed and remitted the file (2009, 2011) because, inter alia, the parents’ claim that they had never given informed consent had not been examined and because the adequacy of post-operative monitoring remained unresolved. Ultimately Dr P.A. was acquitted (final decision May 2012); the courts found neither a proven causal link to any omission by him nor a legal basis to extend the investigation to the missing nurse.

Separate civil proceedings against the hospital and both doctors were stayed pending the criminal outcome and later abandoned by the applicants.

These facts disclose a seven-year investigation marked by an untraceable key witness, unresolved contradictions between official and extra-judicial expert reports, repeated remittals for failure to address central issues (informed consent and post-operative vigilance), and a final acquittal that left the precise cause of the fatal haemorrhage unexplained. The applicants therefore alleged that the investigation had been neither thorough nor effective.

The applicants, Dorina and Viorel-Aurel Ioniță, complained under the Convention of an ineffective investigation into their son's death after surgery. On 7 November 2005 their son (aged 4 years 9 months) underwent polyp-removal surgery at Brăila Emergency Hospital by Dr C.B. under general anaesthesia with tracheal intubation administered by Dr P.A., assisted by nurse P.V.I. Shortly after transfer to intensive care the child became cyanotic with no pulse; haemorrhage flooded his lungs. Resuscitation failed and he was declared dead two hours after the operation.

An autopsy attributed death to acute respiratory failure from blood blocking the airways and lungs, noting congenital conditions (myocardial and hepatic dystrophy plus inter-atrial septum aneurysms) that may have contributed. Higher forensic commissions confirmed a causal link to post-operative care and identified possible deflation of the intubation-catheter balloon as allowing blood to enter the lungs.

Disciplinary proceedings before the College of Doctors initially found no direct causal link to the doctors' conduct (classifying the death as sudden, given pre-existing conditions) but reprimanded them for inadequate pre-surgical tests and failure to obtain informed consent. The superior committee later fined both doctors, holding that pre-operative examinations had been insufficient to avoid predictable complications, that statements claiming the catheter balloon remained leak-proof were inconsistent with the cause of death, and that informed consent had not been obtained.

A criminal investigation was opened the same day. The applicants joined as civil parties, alleging that flawed surgical and post-surgical treatment caused the death. Proceedings focused on Dr P.A.; nurse P.V.I. (who had monitored the child in intensive care) could not be questioned after she left her post and moved to Italy, and no effective steps were taken to locate her. Conflicting forensic material emerged: official reports pointed to post-operative catheter failure, while an extrajudicial report commissioned by Dr P.A. blamed only the child's pre-existing conditions. Prosecutors discontinued the case in 2008, finding no criminal negligence. Courts later quashed that decision, remitting the file because the parents' consent complaint and the adequacy of post-operative monitoring had not been examined.

After further hearings the District Court acquitted Dr P.A. in 2011, holding that lack of informed consent was not causally linked to the death and that negligence regarding the catheter could not be proved beyond reasonable doubt; a request to extend the investigation to the nurse was refused because only the prosecutor could do so. The Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal in 2012 and dismissed the civil claims. Separate civil proceedings against the hospital and doctors were stayed pending the criminal outcome and were later abandoned by the applicants.

These facts reveal a six-year process marked by incomplete witness examination, unresolved contradictions among forensic opinions, a narrow focus that excluded other staff, and courts' inability to address all aspects of alleged medical failings, forming the core of the claimed breach of the State's procedural obligation to investigate the death effectively.

The case of Ioniță v. Romania (Application no. 81270/12) concerns an application by Romanian nationals Dorina and Viorel-Aurel Ioniță, parents of a child who died after surgery, alleging a violation of their Convention rights due to the lack of an effective investigation into the death.

On 7 November 2005, the applicants' son (aged four years and nine months) underwent surgery at Brăila Emergency Hospital to remove polyps. Surgeon Dr C.B. performed the procedure under general anaesthetic with tracheal intubation, administered by Dr P.A. and assisted by nurse P.V.I. The child was transferred immediately to intensive care. Ten minutes later, P.V.I. reported that he was cyanotic and pulseless. He suffered a haemorrhage that flooded his lungs; resuscitation efforts failed, and he was declared dead two hours after the operation.

A criminal investigation began the same day. An autopsy by the Brăila Forensic Service (8 November 2005) attributed death to acute respiratory failure from blood blocking the airways and lungs, noting the child's congenital conditions (myocardia, hepatic dystrophy, interatrial septum aneurysms) as possible contributing factors. The Iași Forensic Institute's commission (5 May 2006) confirmed a causal link between post-operative treatment and death, identifying possible deflation of the intubation catheter balloon (intended to prevent blood ingress) as a factor. The Mina Minovici Forensic Institute approved these findings (12 October 2006).

Disciplinary proceedings followed the father's complaint. The Brăila College of Doctors (9 July 2007) found no direct link to the doctors' conduct, classifying the death as possibly sudden given the child's conditions, but reprimanded both doctors for inadequate pre-surgical tests and failure to obtain informed consent. On appeal, the National College of Doctors (6 June 2008) quashed this, fining each doctor approximately EUR 220. It held that pre-surgical examinations had been insufficient (lacking radioscopy, EKG and coagulation tests) and that the doctors had treated the surgery as "minor" despite the child's deficiencies, breaching deontological rules. It also noted unexplained blood in the airways (contradicting staff statements that the balloon had been leak-proof) and absence of parental informed consent.

Criminal proceedings, initiated by the applicants' complaint, targeted Dr P.A. The hospital identified Dr P.A. as responsible during surgery/transfer and P.V.I. in intensive care. P.V.I. was interviewed initially but could not later be questioned after leaving her job (January 2006) and the country. Other staff were interviewed. Requests for a new forensic report were refused for lack of new evidence. An extrajudicial report submitted by Dr P.A. blamed the child's pre-existing conditions rather than monitoring failures. Prosecutors discontinued proceedings against Dr P.A. (30 September 2008, upheld 10 November 2008), finding no criminal negligence.

The Brăila District Court quashed this (25 February 2009), citing the disciplinary findings on blood in the airways and the need to assess post-operative monitoring. After further hearings (staff maintaining the balloon had remained tight; blood possibly from resuscitation), the court acquitted Dr P.A. (1 October 2010), relying on the extrajudicial report. The County Court upheld the acquittal (21 December 2010) but rejected the extrajudicial report, concluding blood caused death yet timing of balloon deflation and P.V.I.'s supervision precluded Dr P.A.'s responsibility.

The Court of Appeal quashed this (15 April 2011) for failure to address lack of informed consent and remitted the case. On remittal, the District Court again acquitted Dr P.A. (22 December 2011), finding no causal link between omitted consent and death, and insufficient proof of negligence regarding the balloon. It refused to extend the investigation to P.V.I., as only the prosecutor could do so. The Court of Appeal confirmed this finally (22 May 2012). Separate civil proceedings against the hospital and doctors were stayed pending the criminal outcome and later abandoned by the applicants.

These facts highlight the alleged investigative deficiencies, including unresolved contradictions on the cause of haemorrhage, failure to question a key witness (P.V.I.), refusal of further forensic analysis, and inability to extend proceedings to all potentially responsible parties.
001-170837:
**CASE OF IGBO AND OTHERS v. GREECE (Application no. 60042/13, ECtHR, 9 February 2017)**

Fourteen applicants (Greek, Turkish, Nigerian and Senegalese nationals) lodged an application against Greece alleging detention in inhuman and degrading conditions at Chios Prison, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, and a lack of effective domestic remedies (likely under Article 13). They were represented by lawyers from Thessaloniki. Some were in pre-trial detention; others were serving sentences. The first to fifth, tenth and thirteenth applicants were held in cell no. 9; the sixth to ninth, eleventh and twelfth in cell no. 5; and the fourteenth in cell no. 3. The fifth applicant was transferred to Korydallos Prison on 10 September 2013; the seventh was released on 29 October 2013 and the ninth on 4 September 2013.

The applicants described severe overcrowding, with each inmate allocated roughly 2 sq m of personal space. The prison had six cells with 15 beds plus five floor mattresses and three cells with 10 beds. Cell no. 3 measured 10 sq m and held six detainees; cell no. 5 measured 40 sq m and held 20; cell no. 9 measured 20 sq m and held 10. The sixth, eighth and ninth applicants (and others) slept on the floor. Toilets were unpartitioned from living areas, and there was no hot water. Cells were filthy; combined with overcrowding, this exposed inmates to contagious diseases and caused psychological problems for which no medical treatment was provided. Dental care was inadequate. Inmates were not separated by health status or by pre-trial versus convicted status, contrary to the Penal Code. They were confined to cells for 16–17 hours daily with no recreational or educational activities. Meals were insufficient, of poor quality, served in cells and eaten on beds. On 29 August 2013 the applicants complained to the Prison Board about these conditions but received no reply.

The Government stated that Chios Prison had nine cells, each with a table, stools, fridge, cooking stoves, wardrobes and television. Cells were well-ventilated, heated, had adequate natural light, and were regularly cleaned and disinfected. At the time of the application the prison held 142 inmates, slightly above its capacity of 120. Detainees had access to a prison doctor; emergencies were referred to Chios General Hospital or Korydallos Prison Hospital. Those with contagious diseases were isolated or transferred. Some applicants had received medical consultations. Fifty work places were available, and educational or recreational programmes were offered periodically; most applicants participated. A sample weekly menu was provided to show varied meals.

A March 2011 report by the UN Special Rapporteur on torture (based on an October 2010 visit) described Chios Prison as consisting of six chambers with 18 beds and two mattresses each, plus three with 10 beds, plus small cells for the elderly/sick and solitary confinement. Capacity was 120 but 163 persons were held (52 pre-trial, 105 foreign nationals). Severe overcrowding had increased drug problems and inter-prisoner violence. Cells were very small and overcrowded; some had cockroaches. Prisoners complained of diet and hygiene. Recreational activities were limited (only 41 could work). Health care was inadequate (inexperienced doctor visiting three days a week). Conjugal visits were forbidden and other visits restricted. Detainees found it difficult to complain of arbitrary treatment. Overall conditions were fairly poor compared with other Greek prisons.

Relevant domestic law on prison conditions and remedies is set out in prior ECtHR cases (Kanakis v. Greece (no. 2) and Chatzivasiliadis v. Greece). The Court communicated the application to the Greek Government on 4 November 2013; both sides filed observations. The Turkish Government did not intervene.

These facts centre on the competing accounts of physical space, sanitation, medical care, regime, food and complaint procedures at Chios Prison, which form the core of the alleged Article 3 and related remedy violations. The judgment (final on 9 May 2017) assessed these claims but the provided text covers only the facts and procedure.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Igbo and Others v. Greece (Application no. 60042/13, judgment of 9 February 2017) involved 14 applicants of Greek, Turkish, Nigerian and Senegalese nationality detained in Chios Prison (some in pre-trial detention, others serving sentences). They alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, plus a lack of effective domestic remedies under Article 13. The applicants occupied cells 3, 5 and 9. Cell 3 (10 sq m) held six people; cell 5 (40 sq m) held 20; cell 9 (20 sq m) held 10. This produced roughly 2 sq m of personal space per inmate. The prison contained six cells with 15 beds plus five floor mattresses each, and three cells with 10 beds. Several applicants (and others) slept on the floor as a matter of routine.

Applicants described unpartitioned toilets inside the cells, no hot water, pervasive filth exposing inmates to contagious diseases, and resulting psychological problems for which no treatment was given. Dental care was inadequate. Prisoners were not segregated by health status or by whether they were on remand or convicted, contrary to the Penal Code. They were locked in cells 16–17 hours a day with no recreational or educational programmes. Meals were insufficient and of poor quality, served and eaten on the beds. On 29 August 2013 the applicants complained to the Prison Board about these conditions but received no reply. Some applicants were later transferred or released.

The Greek Government maintained that the nine cells were properly equipped (tables, stools, fridges, stoves, wardrobes, televisions), ventilated, heated, naturally lit, and regularly cleaned and disinfected. At the relevant time the prison held 142 inmates against an official capacity of 120—only a modest overcrowding. A prison doctor provided medical care; emergencies were referred to Chios General Hospital or Korydallos Prison Hospital. Detainees with contagious diseases were isolated or transferred. Records showed that several applicants had consulted doctors. Fifty work places existed and educational or recreational activities were offered; most applicants participated. A sample weekly menu was produced to show that meals were varied.

A March 2011 report by the UN Special Rapporteur on torture, following an October 2010 visit, recorded 163 inmates against a capacity of 120. Cells were small and overcrowded; some had cockroaches. Hygiene and diet were poor, recreational opportunities limited (only 41 inmates could work), and health care inadequate (the doctor was young and inexperienced). Visits were restricted and complaints difficult to pursue. Overall conditions were described as fairly poor compared with other Greek prisons.

These facts—severe overcrowding well below 3 sq m per person, unsanitary and unpartitioned sanitation, prolonged lock-up without activities, inadequate healthcare and nutrition, mixing of categories of prisoners, and the absence of any response to the Prison Board complaint—form the core of the alleged Article 3 and 13 violations. Domestic law and practice on prison conditions and remedies were the same as those already examined by the Court in earlier Greek cases such as Kanakis v. Greece (no. 2).

The case of Igbo and Others v. Greece (Application no. 60042/13) concerns 14 applicants (of Greek, Turkish, Nigerian and Senegalese nationality) who were or remained detained in Chios Prison, either on remand or serving sentences. They alleged that the conditions of their detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment and that they had no effective domestic remedies. The first to fifth, tenth and thirteenth applicants were held in cell no. 9; the sixth to ninth, eleventh and twelfth in cell no. 5; and the fourteenth in cell no. 3. Several were later transferred or released.

The applicants described severe overcrowding that left each inmate with roughly 2 m^{2} of personal space. The prison comprised six cells containing 15 beds plus five floor mattresses and three cells containing ten beds. Cell no. 3 measured 10 m^{2} and held six people; cell no. 5 measured 40 m^{2} and held 20; cell no. 9 measured 20 m^{2} and held ten. Several applicants (and other inmates) slept on the floor. Sanitary facilities were not partitioned from the living area and there was no hot water. Filth combined with overcrowding exposed inmates to contagious diseases and caused psychological problems for which no treatment was provided; dental care was also inadequate. Prisoners were not separated according to health status or according to whether they were on remand or convicted, contrary to the Penal Code. They were locked in their cells for 16–17 hours a day with no recreational or educational activities. Meals were insufficient and of poor quality and were eaten on the beds. A complaint lodged with the Prison Board on 29 August 2013 received no reply.

The Government stated that the nine cells were furnished with tables, stools, refrigerators, cooking stoves, wardrobes and televisions, were adequately ventilated and heated, received natural light and were regularly cleaned and disinfected. At the relevant time the prison held 142 inmates against an official capacity of 120. Medical care was available from the prison doctor; emergencies were referred to Chios General Hospital or Korydallos Prison Hospital, and those with contagious diseases were isolated or transferred. Some applicants had in fact seen doctors. Fifty work places existed and educational or recreational programmes were offered from time to time; most applicants participated. A randomly selected weekly menu was produced to show that meals were varied.

A 2010 visit report by the UN Special Rapporteur on torture recorded that Chios Prison (capacity 120) then held 163 inmates, that cells were very small and overcrowded, that hygiene and diet were poor, that healthcare was inadequate and that recreational opportunities were limited. These facts formed the core of the applicants’ complaints concerning the conditions of detention and the absence of an effective remedy.
