The case of Kirins v. Latvia originated in an application by Andrejs Kirins, a Latvian national born in 1971, alleging that he had not received adequate compensation for injuries inflicted by a police officer, in violation of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention, and that the related civil damages proceedings were unfair and excessively lengthy under Article 6.

On 16 January 1995, Daugavpils City Police Inspector S.K. arrested Kirins, who suffered from category 2 visual disability and offered no resistance. S.K. then repeatedly struck him on the head near the eyes and kicked him in the chest after he fell. The assault accelerated Kirins’ pre-existing myopia, causing retinal detachments. Despite several operations in Latvia and Moscow in 1995–1996, he became completely blind and received category 1 disability status in April 1996.

Criminal proceedings against S.K. opened on 30 January 1995; Kirins joined as a civil party. An initial forensic report classified the injuries as moderate, causing long-term health impairment and at least one-third loss of working capacity. Later reports in 1999 and 2002 reclassified them as minor and found no direct causal link to the blindness, attributing the outcome to progressive myopia that could have produced the same result without trauma. S.K. absconded, first remaining at large and later leaving Latvia, generating substantial delays. Additional postponements arose from difficulties obtaining Russian medical records and the need to summon experts. On 27 February 2003 the Daugavpils Court convicted S.K. in absentia of violent abuse of official power and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. It recognised Kirins’ right to State compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage but remitted quantification to the civil courts because supporting documents were incomplete or in foreign languages.

In April 2004 Kirins sued the Ministry of the Interior and State Police under sections 2347 and 2349 of the Civil Law and the Law on Police, seeking LVL 197 624 for medical costs, lost earnings, mutilation and disfigurement. On 2 February 2006 the Riga Regional Court awarded LVL 90 000 in non-pecuniary damages (finding the beating had likely worsened the myopia) plus LVL 4 502 for proven expenses. On 27 September 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the non-pecuniary award, holding that the injuries did not amount to mutilation or disfigurement and that no sufficient causal link existed; it reduced pecuniary damages slightly to LVL 4 427. A further appeal on points of law was dismissed in February 2007.

A subsequent Supreme Court letter confirmed that the 2006 amendment introducing a general right to moral damages (section 1635) lacked retroactive effect and that the medical evidence precluded an award under the earlier special provisions. It nevertheless indicated that a claim under Article 92 of the Constitution remained possible, citing later case-law awarding compensation for human-rights violations. The entire sequence—from the 1995 assault through final dismissal of the civil claim—lasted more than twelve years.

The case of Kirins v. Latvia (Application no. 34140/07) concerns complaints by a Latvian national, Andrejs Kirins, under Articles 3, 13 and 6 of the Convention. He alleged that he received inadequate compensation for injuries inflicted by a police officer and that related damages proceedings were unfair and excessively lengthy.

On 16 January 1995, Daugavpils police inspector S.K. arrested the applicant—who had pre-existing category 2 visual disability and offered no resistance—and beat him with multiple blows to the head near the eyes. When the applicant fell, S.K. kicked him at least once in the chest. The trauma accelerated the applicant’s existing myopia, causing retinal detachments. Despite several operations in Latvia and Moscow in 1995–1996, his vision deteriorated completely. In April 1996 he was granted category 1 disability status for total blindness.

Criminal proceedings against S.K. opened on 30 January 1995; the applicant joined as a civil party. An initial forensic report classified the injuries as moderate, causing long-term health impairment and at least one-third permanent loss of working capacity. S.K. absconded after charges were brought, prompting an arrest warrant that was never executed (he later left Latvia). Multiple hearings were delayed by missing original medical records from Russia, non-attendance of experts and doctors, and requests for additional forensic examinations. Reports issued in 1999 and 2002 reclassified the injuries as minor and found no direct causal link between the 1995 blows and the subsequent total loss of sight, attributing the outcome primarily to progressive pre-existing myopia (though acknowledging that the head trauma had worsened the condition). On 27 February 2003 the Daugavpils Court convicted S.K. in absentia of violent abuse of official power and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. It recognised the applicant’s right to State compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage but, citing insufficient supporting evidence (including foreign-language documents), remitted quantification of the award to the civil courts.

Civil proceedings against the Ministry of the Interior and State Police were registered in April 2004. The applicant claimed LVL 197 624 (approximately EUR 282 000) under Civil Law sections 2347 and 2349 (medical expenses, lost earnings, mutilation and disfigurement) and the Law on Police. On 2 February 2006 the Riga Regional Court awarded LVL 90 000 (EUR 128 500) in non-pecuniary damages and LVL 4 503 in pecuniary damages, finding that the beating might have precipitated the rapid worsening of the applicant’s sight. On 27 September 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the non-pecuniary award, holding that the injuries did not constitute “mutilation or disfigurement” because no direct causal link to blindness had been established, and slightly reduced the pecuniary sum. An appeal on points of law was dismissed in February 2007.

Under then-applicable Latvian law, tort liability required proof of an unlawful act, damage, causation and fault. Section 2349 provided non-pecuniary compensation only for mutilation/disfigurement; a general provision for moral harm (section 1635) entered into force in 2006 and was not retroactive. The Law on Police obliged the authorities to redress rights violations, and Article 92 of the Constitution guaranteed compensation for unlawful State action. Subsequent Supreme Court correspondence indicated that a further claim under Article 92 might still be possible, citing later domestic case-law that had awarded non-pecuniary damages for pre-2006 events on the basis of constitutional and Convention principles.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the State had failed to provide an effective remedy or adequate redress for ill-treatment contrary to Article 3, and that the overall length and conduct of the proceedings (spanning more than a decade) violated Article 6.

The case of Kirins v. Latvia (Application no. 34140/07) concerns complaints by a Latvian national, Andrejs Kirins (born 1971), under Articles 3, 13 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He alleged that he received inadequate compensation for serious injuries inflicted by a police officer, amounting to a failure to provide an effective remedy for ill-treatment, and that the related civil proceedings for damages were unfair and excessively lengthy.

On 16 January 1995, Inspector S.K. of the Daugavpils City Police arrested Kirins, who had pre-existing category 2 visual disability (myopia) and offered no resistance. S.K. then beat him, delivering multiple blows to the head near the eyes; after Kirins fell, S.K. kicked him at least once in the chest. The assault accelerated deterioration of Kirins’s eyesight, causing retinal detachments. He underwent several operations in 1995–1996, including three in Moscow, but the condition progressed. By April 1996 he was granted category 1 disability status for total blindness.

Criminal proceedings against S.K. began on 30 January 1995; Kirins was joined as a civil party. An initial forensic report classified the injuries as moderate, causing long-term health impairment and at least one-third reduction in work capacity. S.K. was charged in March 1995. Proceedings were delayed for years: S.K. absconded (a warrant was issued but never executed; he later left Latvia), multiple further forensic examinations were ordered (including because of Kirins’s worsening sight), original medical records from Russia could not be obtained, and hearings were repeatedly postponed due to non-attendance of experts and doctors (some delays requested by the applicant). Later reports (1999 and 2002) reclassified the injuries as minor and found no direct causal link between the 1995 trauma and the complete loss of vision, attributing the latter primarily to the pre-existing progressive myopia (worsening of a pre-existing condition does not itself reclassify injury severity under domestic law).

On 27 February 2003 the Daugavpils Court convicted S.K. in absentia of violent abuse of official power and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. It recognised Kirins’s right to State compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage but remitted quantification to civil proceedings, citing insufficient evidence (foreign-language documents, lack of allocation of expenses to the injuries).

Kirins then sued the Ministry of the Interior and State Police in civil proceedings, claiming approximately EUR 282,000 under Civil Law provisions (including ss. 2347 and 2349 for medical costs, lost income, and mutilation/disfigurement) plus the Law on Police. On 2 February 2006 the Riga Regional Court awarded LVL 90,000 (EUR 128,500) non-pecuniary damages (finding the injuries may have precipitated rapid visual decline) and LVL 4,502 (EUR 6,433) for proven medical expenses. On 27 September 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the non-pecuniary award, holding that the injuries did not constitute “mutilation or disfigurement” under s. 2349 and that no direct causal link existed with the blindness (which resulted from co-existing circumstances). Pecuniary damages were slightly reduced. An appeal on points of law was dismissed in February 2007.

The Supreme Court later confirmed that general non-pecuniary damages under the amended Civil Law s. 1635 (effective 1 March 2006) could not be applied retroactively, and that the specific statutory conditions for compensation had not been met. It noted, however, that a ten-year limitation period (from the 2003 criminal judgment becoming final) remained open for a claim under Article 92 of the Constitution.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the established police ill-treatment, the contested causal link to total blindness, the lengthy and incomplete compensation process, and the domestic courts’ refusal to award non-pecuniary damages for the health consequences.
001-170358:
The case of Zybertowicz v. Poland (no. 59138/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, Andrzej Zybertowicz (born 1954), is a Polish publicist and sociology professor living in Toruń.

On 13 March 2007, during a telephone interview with journalist M.Z. of the national daily Rzeczpospolita on the publicly debated topic of journalists’ lustration, the applicant made comments later published (after his minor corrections) on 14 March 2007 in a “polemic/discussion/analysis” column titled “Journalists under autohypnosis.” The relevant passage stated: “Some people easily reach for personal arguments. The Gazeta Wyborcza journalist S.B., in a conversation with me stated: professor Zybertowicz speaks now, although during the communist times he was quiet. This is classic. A.M. repeatedly said: I spent so many years in prison, so now I am right. Unfortunately, moral integrity in one situation does not automatically indicate a complete cognitive judgment in another situation.” A.M. was editor-in-chief of Gazeta Wyborcza.

A.M.’s lawyer demanded an apology on 26–27 March 2007, referring specifically to the attributed statement. The applicant refused and published the demand letter in Rzeczpospolita on 10 April 2007.

On 30 April 2007 A.M. sued in the Warsaw Regional Court for protection of personal rights (Civil Code Arts. 23–24 and 448), seeking an apology and 15,000 PLN (approx. EUR 3,570) payable to charity. On 17 December 2007 the court upheld the claim. It treated the phrase “A.M. repeatedly said: I spent so many years in prison, so now I am right” as a statement of fact (owing to the colon, which a 1996 Polish dictionary indicated introduced a direct quotation). Because A.M. had never used those exact words, the statement was untrue and infringed his personal rights (reputation, credibility and good name). The court rejected the applicant’s characterisation of the words as a permissible journalistic paraphrase or reconstruction of A.M.’s publicly expressed mindset (illustrated by numerous 1982–2007 statements in which A.M. invoked his communist-era imprisonment). It held that a set of moral views could not be paraphrased and that the applicant had not shown he acted within the law. The court disregarded two private linguistic expert reports (neither party having requested a court-appointed expert or examination of the authors) and ordered a 10 \times 15 cm apology on the first, second or third page of Rzeczpospolita, payment of 10,000 PLN (EUR 2,380) to charity, and costs.

The Warsaw Court of Appeal confirmed the judgment on 15 October 2008, adding further costs. It agreed the colon rendered the words factual, not a paraphrase, and that an average reader needed no linguistic expertise. Review of A.M.’s public statements showed he had never used the exact phrasing; the remark therefore portrayed him as petty-minded, damaged his professional standing as editor-in-chief of a major daily and impeded his work.

The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal (which invoked Article 10 and the lack of a linguistic expert) on 25 February 2010. Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Code permitted a court to gather evidence of its own motion only exceptionally; here the decisive criterion was the understanding of an average reader of a widely circulated newspaper. Context (public debate on lustration) and column placement did not alter the informative character of the words chosen.

The applicant paid the sums and published the apology (costing an additional approx. EUR 900). Public letters both defended his freedom of expression and insisted that untrue statements exceeded its limits.

These facts—the classification of the remark as a false statement of fact rather than protected commentary, the rejection of paraphrase, the refusal of linguistic evidence, and the resulting civil sanctions—underlie the alleged Article 10 violation.

The case of Zybertowicz v. Poland (Application no. 59138/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). The applicant, Andrzej Zybertowicz, a Polish sociology professor and publicist born in 1954 and living in Toruń, lodged the application on 25 August 2010. He was represented by counsel, while the Polish Government was represented by its agent from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court communicated the Article 10 complaint on 1 September 2014, declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

On 13 March 2007, during a period of intense public debate on the lustration of journalists, the applicant gave a telephone interview to a journalist from the national daily Rzeczpospolita. He reviewed and made minor corrections to the transcript. The interview appeared the next day under the title “Journalists under autohypnosis” in a polemic/discussion/analysis column. It contained this passage: “Some people easily reach for personal arguments. The Gazeta Wyborcza journalist S.B., in a conversation with me stated: professor Zybertowicz speaks now, although during the communist times he was quiet. This is classic. A.M. repeatedly said: I spent so many years in prison, so now I am right. Unfortunately, moral integrity in one situation does not automatically indicate a complete cognitive judgment in another situation.”

A.M., editor-in-chief of Gazeta Wyborcza, regarded the reference to him as false. His lawyer wrote to the applicant on 26–27 March 2007 demanding an apology as a condition for amicable settlement. The applicant refused and published the letter in Rzeczpospolita on 10 April 2007.

On 30 April 2007 A.M. brought a civil action in the Warsaw Regional Court for protection of personal rights under Articles 23, 24 and 448 of the Civil Code. He sought an apology and 15,000 PLN (approximately EUR 3,570) payable to a charity. After hearing the parties and the interviewing journalist (but declining to consider private linguistic expert reports or to appoint its own expert), the court on 17 December 2007 upheld the claim. It characterised the words “A.M. repeatedly said: \ldots” as a statement of fact because a colon, according to a 1996 Polish dictionary, introduces a direct quotation. Since A.M. had never uttered those exact words, the information was untrue and infringed his reputation. The court rejected the applicant’s argument that the phrase was a permissible journalistic paraphrase or summary of A.M.’s publicly expressed views (supported by numerous statements from 1982–2007 in which A.M. referred to his communist-era imprisonment). It ordered a published apology of specified size and placement in Rzeczpospolita, payment of 10,000 PLN (approximately EUR 2,380) to charity, and court costs of 1,500 PLN.

The Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 15 October 2008, confirming the first-instance reasoning and adding further costs of 1,170 PLN. It held that the colon rendered the statement factual rather than a paraphrase, that it portrayed A.M. as petty-minded, and that it damaged his credibility, reputation and ability to practise his profession.

The applicant’s cassation appeal to the Supreme Court invoked Article 10 and criticised the failure to obtain a linguistics expert. On 25 February 2010 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that an expert was unnecessary because the decisive criterion was the understanding of an average reader of a mass-circulation newspaper. The phrase remained informative about A.M.’s personality even in the context of a public debate and could not be recast as mere value judgment by reason of the column in which it appeared. Additional costs of 270 PLN were imposed.

The applicant complied by paying the 10,000 PLN award in October 2008 and arranging publication of the apology at a cost of approximately 3,500 PLN. Public petitions both defending the applicant’s right to comment on participants in the lustration debate and asserting that untrue statements enjoy no protection followed the domestic proceedings.

These events—the characterisation of a critical remark made in a public debate as a false statement of fact, the rejection of the applicant’s paraphrase defence, the absence of linguistic expertise, and the resulting orders to apologise and pay damages—constitute the core facts relevant to the alleged interference with freedom of expression.

The case of Zybertowicz v. Poland (ECHR Application no. 59138/10) arose from a civil judgment against the applicant for statements made in a newspaper interview, which he alleged violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

Andrzej Zybertowicz, a sociology professor and publicist, was interviewed by telephone on 13 March 2007 by a journalist from the national daily Rzeczpospolita about the then-current public debate on the lustration of journalists. After reviewing a transcript and making minor corrections, the interview appeared on 14 March 2007 under the headline “Journalists under autohypnosis.” In a paragraph criticising the use of personal arguments, Zybertowicz wrote: “Some people easily reach for personal arguments. The Gazeta Wyborcza journalist S.B., in a conversation with me stated: professor Zybertowicz speaks now, although during the communist times he was quiet. This is classic. A.M. repeatedly said: I spent so many years in prison, so now I am right. Unfortunately, moral integrity in one situation does not automatically indicate a complete cognitive judgment in another situation.” A.M. was editor-in-chief of Gazeta Wyborcza.

A.M.’s lawyer demanded an apology. Zybertowicz refused and instead published the demand letter. On 30 April 2007 A.M. sued in the Warsaw Regional Court for infringement of personal rights under Articles 23, 24 and 448 of the Civil Code, seeking a published apology and PLN 15,000 (approx. EUR 3,570) for charity.

On 17 December 2007 the Regional Court upheld the claim. It treated the phrase after the colon as a direct quotation of fact that A.M. had never uttered. The court rejected Zybertowicz’s argument that the words were a journalistic paraphrase or reconstruction of A.M.’s frequently expressed views (he had supplied numerous public statements in which A.M. referred to his communist-era imprisonment). Referring to a Polish dictionary, the court held that a colon introduced a quotation and that a set of moral views could not be paraphrased. It therefore found the statement untrue and damaging to A.M.’s reputation. The court declined to appoint a linguistic expert of its own motion (Article 232 of the Code of Civil Procedure) because the parties had not formally requested one. Zybertowicz was ordered to publish a precisely sized apology on an early page of Rzeczpospolita and to pay PLN 10,000 to charity plus costs.

The Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed Zybertowicz’s appeal on 15 October 2008, endorsing the first-instance reasoning. It confirmed that the colon rendered the words a statement of fact, not a paraphrase, and that the statement portrayed A.M. as petty-minded, thereby harming his credibility, good name and professional standing as editor of a major newspaper. Again no linguistic expert was obtained.

The Supreme Court rejected Zybertowicz’s cassation appeal (which invoked Article 10) on 25 February 2010. It held that interpretation must be based on the understanding of an average reader of a widely circulated newspaper; no expert was required. The political context of a public debate on lustration did not transform the statement into protected comment. Zybertowicz paid the sums and published the apology.

The domestic courts thus classified the impugned words as a false factual assertion rather than value-laden opinion or permissible journalistic summary, imposing civil sanctions that Zybertowicz contended unduly restricted debate on a matter of public interest.
001-170593:
The European Court of Human Rights examined three applications by Russian nationals Florid Vakhitov, Maksim Bogdashkin and Karnik Aslanyan alleging, principally, that after arrest they were not brought promptly before a judge, contrary to Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. Additional complaints by Bogdashkin (Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4) and Aslanyan (Article 6 § 2) were also communicated.

Vakhitov had been convicted of drug trafficking in 2009, but the conviction was quashed and the case remitted. The Sovetskiy District Court scheduled a hearing for 4 March 2010 and sent notifications by ordinary post on 26 February; Vakhitov and his lawyer claimed they never received them. When he failed to appear, the court ordered compulsory attendance. A further letter to bailiffs was delayed. On 19 March 2010 the court, again in his absence and without notification according to the applicant, remanded him in custody in absentia. Vakhitov was arrested at work on 15 April 2010, held in a temporary detention centre and transferred to Ufa that day, with the judge being informed. His lawyer immediately appealed the 19 March order, citing lack of notice of the hearings. On 28 April the same judge ordered continued detention at a hearing of which neither Vakhitov nor his lawyer was notified or present. Vakhitov was released on 25 May 2010 against an undertaking to remain at his residence. The district-court president later confirmed that the file contained no proof the summonses had been received. An appeal court nevertheless upheld the in-absentia detention order, finding that Vakhitov had been duly notified at his registered address. He was later reconvicted and immediately remanded.

Bogdashkin’s trial for attempted murder was postponed on 28 September 2010 because of his unexplained absence; he claimed he had not been informed. On 11 October the justice of the peace suspended the proceedings, ordered a search and directed that he be remanded in custody upon arrest. His name was placed on the wanted list. He was arrested on 4 March 2011 and placed in a temporary detention centre. On 11 March he complained to the regional prosecutor that he had never been given a copy of the 11 October detention order and that even after transfer on 7 March he still had not been told the reasons for his arrest. He was convicted and sentenced on 12 April 2011.

Aslanyan was indicted for murder in April 2013. An in-absentia detention order was issued on 14 May after he fled, and an international search warrant followed. He was arrested on 11 July 2013. His detention was extended on 4 September 2013 at a hearing at which he was present; the court stated that his guilt was confirmed by his own statements and other evidence. He appealed, invoking both the two-month delay in being brought before a judge after arrest (Article 5 § 3) and the wording of the extension order as violating the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2). The regional court upheld the order without addressing those arguments.

Under the Russian Code of Criminal Procedure a court may order detention in a defendant’s absence only when an international arrest warrant exists; extensions likewise require the accused’s presence except in narrowly defined circumstances, and defence counsel must then be present. The Constitutional Court has held that every decision depriving a person of liberty must be taken at a hearing at which the detainee can be heard.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ claims that they had been deprived of a prompt judicial appearance after arrest and, in two cases, of related guarantees concerning lawfulness, information and the presumption of innocence.

The case of Vakhitov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 18232/11, 42945/11 and 31596/14) was decided by a Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights on 31 January 2017. The three Russian applicants alleged, principally, that after their arrests they had not been brought promptly before a judge, contrary to Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. Additional complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4 (Bogdashkin) and Article 6 § 2 (Aslanyan) were also communicated.

Mr Vakhitov’s 2009 conviction for drug trafficking was quashed on 2 February 2010 and the case remitted for retrial. A hearing was fixed for 4 March 2010; notification was sent by ordinary post on 26 February, but the applicant and his lawyer claimed they never received it. After he failed to appear, the trial court ordered his compulsory attendance. On 19 March 2010, again in his absence and without (he claimed) prior notification, the court issued a detention order in absentia. He was arrested on 15 April 2010 at his workplace, held briefly in a temporary facility and transferred the same day to Ufa, where the trial judge was informed. His lawyer immediately appealed the in-absentia order. On 28 April 2010 the same judge confirmed continued detention at a hearing of which neither the applicant nor counsel were notified or present. Vakhitov was released on 25 May 2010 subject to an undertaking to remain at his registered address. The appellate court later upheld the 19 March order, finding that he had been duly notified at his place of residence. He was ultimately convicted on 15 March 2011 and taken into custody in court.

Mr Bogdashkin failed to appear at a hearing on 28 September 2010 of which he claimed he had not been informed. On 11 October 2010 the justice of the peace suspended the proceedings, placed him on a wanted list and directed that he be remanded in custody upon arrest. He was arrested on 4 March 2011 and held in a temporary detention centre. On 11 March he complained to the regional prosecutor that he had never been given a copy of the 11 October order, had not been told the reasons for his arrest, and remained uninformed even after transfer on 7 March. He was convicted of attempted murder on 12 April 2011 and sentenced to one year and nine months’ imprisonment.

Mr Aslanyan was charged with murder on 25 April 2013. On 14 May 2013 the district court issued a detention order in absentia; his name was placed on an international wanted list shortly afterwards. He was arrested on 11 July 2013. His detention was extended on 4 September 2013 at a hearing at which he was present; the court stated that “the applicant’s guilt was confirmed” by his own statements and other evidence. He appealed, relying on Article 5 § 3 (failure to bring him promptly before a judge after arrest) and Article 6 § 2 (the wording of the extension order breached the presumption of innocence). The regional court dismissed the appeal on 16 October 2013 without addressing those arguments.

Under the Russian Code of Criminal Procedure a court may order detention in the accused’s absence only if an international arrest warrant has been issued; extensions in the accused’s absence are permitted only in narrowly defined circumstances and require the presence of counsel. The Constitutional Court has held that any deprivation of liberty must result from a hearing at which the detainee can present arguments, and that this requirement applies equally to initial orders and to subsequent confirmations or extensions.

The ECtHR case of Vakhitov and Others v. Russia (apps. nos. 18232/11, 42945/11, 31596/14) concerns three Russian applicants’ allegations that, after arrest, they were not brought promptly before a judge, contrary to Article 5 § 3 ECHR. Additional claims under Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4 (Bogdashkin) and Article 6 § 2 (Aslanyan) were also raised.

Vakhitov’s 2009 drug-trafficking conviction was quashed in February 2010 and remitted for retrial. A 4 March 2010 hearing was fixed; a summons was sent by ordinary post on 26 February, but he and his lawyer claimed never to have received it. After he failed to appear, the court ordered compulsory attendance. A further non-appearance on 19 March led the court to remand him in custody in absentia; again he asserted lack of notification. He was arrested on 15 April 2010 at work in Tuymazy, held in a temporary centre and transferred the same day to Ufa. His lawyer appealed the in-absentia order on 19 April, citing the notification failures. On 28 April the trial judge, without notifying or hearing Vakhitov or counsel, confirmed continued detention. Vakhitov was released on 25 May on an undertaking to remain at his address. The regional supreme court later upheld the 19 March order, finding he had been duly summoned at his residence. He was reconvicted in March 2011 and immediately remanded.

Bogdashkin’s case was adjourned on 28 September 2010 because of his unexplained absence; he claimed he had not been told of the hearing. On 11 October the justice of the peace suspended the proceedings, ordered a search and directed that, once found, he be placed in custody. His name was added to the search list. Arrested on 4 March 2011 and held in a temporary centre, he complained to the regional prosecutor on 11 March that he had been given neither the reasons for arrest nor a copy of the 11 October order and that he remained uninformed even after transfer on 7 March. He was convicted of attempted murder on 12 April 2011 and sentenced to imprisonment.

Aslanyan was charged with murder on 25 April 2013. After he left his residence his name was placed on the international wanted list (30 May). An in-absentia detention order was issued on 14 May. He was arrested on 11 July 2013. Detention was extended on 4 September at a hearing he attended; the court stated that “the applicant’s guilt was confirmed” by his own statements and other evidence. He appealed, invoking Article 5 § 3 (delay between arrest and first judicial appearance) and Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence). The regional court dismissed the appeal on 16 October without addressing those arguments.

Russian criminal-procedure rules permit an in-absentia custody order only when an international arrest warrant has been issued, and generally require the accused’s presence for any extension of detention. The Constitutional Court has likewise held that a detainee must be given an opportunity to be heard before any judicial decision imposing or confirming deprivation of liberty.
001-170839:
The case concerns six accredited journalists (the applicants) who were forcibly removed from the parliamentary gallery while reporting on events of significant public interest. On 24 December 2012, they were stationed in the gallery overlooking the chamber during a tense plenary session on the 2013 Budget Act. Opposition MPs approached the Speaker, created noise (including slapping his table), insulted and threatened him, damaged equipment, and blocked access to the podium. Security officers then entered the chamber, extracted the Speaker, and forcibly ejected opposition MPs.

At the same time, other officers entered the gallery and ordered journalists to leave “for security reasons.” Some complied, but the applicants refused, as events in the chamber were escalating and they believed the public had a right to contemporaneous information. They were physically removed. The Government claimed officers explained the security rationale, that the first applicant tore off an officer’s badge and injured him, and that journalists could follow a live feed from the press room. The applicants disputed these points, denying any injury occurred, noting the absence of supporting official records, and asserting that cameras were turned toward the walls so that no live images of the ejections were available.

The Speaker later stated that, in light of announced protests, he had invoked section 43 of the Parliament Act to request security measures and that the gallery (part of the plenary hall) was vacated to avert a larger incident. An internal Ministry inquiry (DCPS) concluded that journalists were asked to withdraw because of the chamber disturbance, the possible presence of unauthorized persons in the gallery, and the risk that external protests would breach police lines; most left, but a minority (including the applicants) resisted, injuring an officer. The force used was found proportionate. An ad-hoc commission of inquiry, however, later found that the absence of guidelines on media handling in crises had resulted in a violation of journalists’ rights to public information and of the principle of publicity of parliamentary work.

The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that their forcible removal breached Article 10 of the Convention. They argued that section 43 neither authorised nor foreseeably permitted the physical ejection of passive journalists who had no contact with MPs or the Speaker, and that the measure was unnecessary because they posed no security threat. They expressly requested a public oral hearing under the Constitutional Court’s own rules. The Court sat in the parties’ absence, accepted that an interference with journalistic reporting of a matter of high public interest had occurred, but held it lawful under section 43 and necessary to protect journalists from objects thrown toward the gallery and from external unrest. It noted that the applicants had been allowed into the building earlier, could watch the subsequent live broadcast from the press centre, and published reports the same evening. A dissenting judge criticised the majority for relying on an incomplete factual record, for contradictory reasoning, and for failing to explain why journalists seated at a physical distance from the disturbance needed to be removed “for their own safety.”

These events form the factual core of the applicants’ complaints: under Article 10, that the State unjustifiably prevented on-the-spot reporting of parliamentary proceedings of intense public interest; and under Article 6, that the Constitutional Court decided the case without the oral hearing they had requested and that the Court’s rules normally require.

The case of Selmani and Others v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 67259/14) concerns six accredited journalists (Naser Selmani, Toni Angelovski, Biljana Dameska, Frosina Fakova, Snežana Lupevska and Nataša Stojanovska) who alleged violations of Article 6 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from events in the national Parliament on 24 December 2012 and subsequent domestic proceedings.

On that date, Parliament debated the 2013 Budget Act amid intense public and media interest generated by a bitter dispute between opposition and ruling-party MPs over whether statutory procedure had been observed. The applicants were reporting from the gallery overlooking the chamber. Opposition MPs surrounded the Speaker, created a commotion (including slapping his table) and damaged equipment. Parliamentary security officers entered the chamber, extracted the Speaker and began forcibly ejecting the opposition MPs. Simultaneously, other officers entered the gallery and ordered journalists to leave for security reasons. Most complied, but the applicants refused, believing the public had a right to be informed of the unfolding events. They were then physically removed. The Government claimed the first applicant had assaulted an officer (tearing off his badge and causing chest and leg injuries) and that live broadcasts remained available in the press room; the applicants denied any assault and asserted that cameras had been turned away. Protests occurred outside Parliament, resulting in injuries.

The Speaker later stated that, anticipating opposition obstruction and protests, he had invoked section 43 of the Parliament Act to request security measures; the security service independently decided to clear the gallery to prevent a larger incident, a step he regretted. The Ministry of the Interior’s Department for Control and Professional Standards concluded that journalists had been asked to withdraw because of the risk posed by MPs in the gallery, possible protest escalation and the need to restore order; force used was not excessive. An ad hoc commission of inquiry (including EU observers) found that the absence of media-handling guidelines in a crisis had led to the journalists’ removal, thereby violating freedom of public information and the publicity of parliamentary work.

The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that their forcible removal from a vantage point during an event of high public interest was neither prescribed by law (section 43 neither authorised nor foreseeably permitted such action against journalists who had no contact with MPs) nor necessary in a democratic society. They requested an oral hearing under the Constitutional Court’s rules. On 16 April 2014 the Court sat in the parties’ absence, accepted that an interference with journalistic freedom had occurred, but held it lawful under section 43 and necessary to protect those present, restore order and enable the debate to continue. The journalists had been allowed to remain in the building, follow a live broadcast and publish reports the same evening; there had been no pre-planned exclusion. A dissenting judge criticised the decision as factually unsupported, noting that the journalists had been passive observers physically isolated from the disorder, had posed no threat and had themselves felt no need for “protection.”

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the physical expulsion of accredited journalists from the gallery during a politically charged session (Article 10) and the Constitutional Court’s refusal to hold the requested public hearing despite the disputed circumstances and the applicants’ request (Article 6).

**Case of Selmani and Others v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (App. no. 67259/14, ECtHR 2017)** involved six accredited journalists who alleged violations of Article 10 (freedom of expression) due to their forcible removal from the parliamentary gallery while reporting a high-profile session, and of Article 6 (fair hearing) due to the Constitutional Court’s failure to hold an oral hearing.

On 24 December 2012, Parliament debated the 2013 Budget Act amid intense public and media interest and sharp conflict between opposition and ruling MPs over procedural regularity. The applicants reported from the gallery overlooking the chamber. Opposition MPs approached the Speaker, created noise (including slapping his table), surrounded him, insulted and threatened him, and damaged equipment. Security officers extracted the Speaker and began forcibly removing opposition MPs. Concurrently, officers entered the gallery and ordered journalists to leave for security reasons (Government account; applicants denied any explanation). Most journalists complied, but the applicants refused, arguing the public had a right to information as events escalated. Officers then forcibly ejected them. The Government claimed the first applicant injured an officer (denied by applicants, with no supporting official records provided) and that journalists could follow a live broadcast from the press room (applicants contested any live feed, alleging cameras were turned to walls). Simultaneous protests outside injured several people.

The Speaker later stated he had invoked section 43 of the Parliament Act (authorizing security measures for order, after consultation) to vacate the gallery and avert a larger incident, while expressing regret. The Ministry of Interior’s Department for Control and Professional Standards found MPs had created a security risk, journalists were asked to relocate pending restoration of order, some (including applicants) resisted, an officer was injured, and force used was not excessive. An ad hoc commission of inquiry (including two MPs and two EU-appointed observers) concluded that the removal, due to absent guidelines and media-crisis strategy, violated journalists’ rights to freedom of public information and the publicity of parliamentary work.

The applicants complained to the Constitutional Court of an Article 10 (and constitutional Article 16) violation. They argued the removal was not “prescribed by law” (section 43 did not clearly authorize ejecting passive journalists from the isolated gallery, or was insufficiently foreseeable) and was not necessary in a democratic society (they had no contact with MPs or the Speaker, contributed nothing to the disturbance, and the public interest in the events was high). They requested a public hearing under the Court’s rules (Article 55, providing that human-rights cases are as a rule decided after a public hearing, with parties summoned).

The Constitutional Court, sitting without the parties, dismissed the complaint. It accepted an interference with the applicants’ professional function of informing the public on a matter of significant interest. However, it found a legal basis in section 43 (Speaker’s responsibility for order, including measures against MPs or other participants) and necessity arising from the chamber chaos (assaults, damage, objects thrown toward the gallery) plus external protests. Removal protected journalists and restored order rather than restricting expression; they later published reports and could have watched the live parliamentary broadcast (also televised nationally and streamed) from other premises. There was no premeditated exclusion. A dissenting judge criticized the decision as based on insufficient and contradictory evidence, noting the journalists were passive, isolated observers who neither contributed to nor felt threatened by the distant chamber incidents.

These facts framed the alleged Article 10 interference (forcible exclusion of journalists from witnessing and reporting live a matter of public interest inside Parliament) and the Article 6 claim (denial of an oral hearing despite the request and applicable rule). The ECtHR later examined whether the interference was lawful and necessary and whether the Constitutional Court’s procedure satisfied fairness requirements.
001-171781:
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered its judgment on 7 March 2017 (final on 7 June 2017) in Stanka Mirković and Others v. Montenegro (applications nos. 33781/15, 33785/15, 34369/15 and 34371/15). The four applicants—Montenegrin nationals Stanka Mirković and Oliver Mirković, and Serbian nationals Darinka Marjanović and Igor Mirković—complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention about the excessive overall length of administrative proceedings concerning restitution and compensation for expropriated property, delayed by repeated remittals, and the absence of an effective remedy.

On 3 December 2004 the third and fourth applicants requested compensation from the Restitution and Compensation Commission for land expropriated from their legal predecessor in 1946. Between July and August 2005 the first and second applicants waived their rights in favour of the third and fourth. On 28 August 2005 the Commission ruled in favour of the third and fourth applicants. The Ministry of Finance quashed that decision on 14 October 2005 following an appeal by the Supreme State Prosecutor. On 17 April 2006 the Commission issued a fresh decision awarding compensation to all four applicants as heirs, holding that the 2005 waivers could be validly made only in non-contentious court proceedings under the Restitution Act.

From 12 June 2006 to 27 March 2014 the second-instance administrative body (initially the Ministry of Finance, later the Appeals Commission) and the Administrative Court issued sixteen decisions (eight each). The second-instance body decided appeals within periods ranging from 14 to 132 days. The Administrative Court took between 3 months 23 days and 1 year 8 months 17 days. On at least four occasions the applicants expressly invoked sections 37 and 58 of the Administrative Disputes Act, urging the Administrative Court to decide the merits of the original compensation claim. The Court never did so; it repeatedly quashed or upheld the quashing of the Commission’s first-instance decisions and remitted the case. Its last ruling, on 27 March 2014, again remitted the matter to the Commission.

On 27 June 2014 the Supreme Court upheld the Administrative Court’s decision; that ruling was served on 8 July 2014. On 25 July 2014 the applicants lodged constitutional appeals (and, according to the Government, additional appeals against the Administrative Court’s March 2014 decision) invoking, inter alia, Articles 6 and 13. On 28 October 2014 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeals against the Supreme Court’s decision as premature because the Commission was still seised of the compensation request. A further Constitutional Court decision of 28 December 2015 dismissed the appeals, referring throughout to the “impugned judgments” of the Administrative Court and Supreme Court. On 31 March 2016 the Commission adjourned the proceedings at the applicants’ request pending the Strasbourg Court’s ruling.

The relevant domestic legislation (Restitution Act, General Administrative Proceedings Act, Administrative Disputes Act and Right to a Trial within a Reasonable Time Act) prescribed relatively short time-limits for administrative decisions and, in principle, empowered the Administrative Court to decide the merits after repeated remittals. The applicants’ core complaint was that these safeguards had proved ineffective: more than a decade of ping-pong between administrative bodies and courts, with no final determination of the 2004 claim and no adequate domestic remedy for the delay.

**Case of Stanka Mirković and Others v. Montenegro (Apps. nos. 33781/15 et al.)**

This ECtHR case (Second Section judgment of 7 March 2017, final 7 June 2017) arose from four applications by Montenegrin nationals Stanka and Oliver Mirković and Serbian nationals Darinka Marjanović and Igor Mirković. They alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention due to the excessive overall length of administrative restitution/compensation proceedings (delayed by repeated remittals without a merits decision) and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

On 3 December 2004 the third and fourth applicants applied to the Restitution and Compensation Commission for compensation in respect of land expropriated from their legal predecessor in 1946. Between July and August 2005 the first and second applicants waived their inheritance rights in favour of the third and fourth. The Commission initially granted the request on 28 August 2005, but the Ministry of Finance quashed that ruling on 14 October 2005 following an appeal by the Supreme State Prosecutor representing the State.

On 17 April 2006 the Commission issued a fresh decision awarding compensation to all four applicants as heirs. It examined the 2005 waivers but held them invalid under section 40 of the Restitution of Expropriated Property Rights and Compensation Act, which required such issues to be resolved in non-contentious court proceedings.

From 12 June 2006 until 27 March 2014 the second-instance administrative body (initially the Ministry of Finance, later the Appeals Commission) and the Administrative Court (first seised in 2006) together issued sixteen decisions (eight each). Decision times at second instance ranged from 14 to 132 days; the Administrative Court’s ranged from roughly 4 months to 1 year 8 months. On at least four occasions the applicants, invoking sections 37 and/or 58 of the Administrative Disputes Act, expressly asked the Administrative Court to decide the merits of the original compensation claim (the Act permits or, after a prior quashing, requires the court to do so when the administrative body has failed to follow the court’s earlier judgment). The Administrative Court never ruled on the merits; it repeatedly quashed or confirmed the quashing of Commission decisions and, in its last ruling of 27 March 2014, remitted the case yet again.

The Supreme Court upheld the Administrative Court’s decision on 27 June 2014 (served 8 July 2014). On 25 July 2014 the applicants lodged constitutional appeals against the Supreme Court judgment, relying inter alia on Articles 6 and 13; they also apparently filed further appeals against the Administrative Court’s 27 March 2014 decision. On 28 October 2014 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeals against the Supreme Court as premature because the Commission was still seised. On 28 December 2015 it dismissed the constitutional appeals (referring to both the Administrative Court and Supreme Court judgments). On 31 March 2016 the Commission adjourned the matter at the applicants’ request pending the Strasbourg Court’s ruling.

Domestic legislation prescribed short time-limits for administrative decisions (originally one or two months, later reduced) and allowed a party to treat silence as a refusal and to bring an administrative dispute. The Administrative Disputes Act empowered (and in cases of repeated remittal required) the court to decide the merits. A 2007 statute on the right to a trial within a reasonable time provided a request-for-review remedy to accelerate proceedings, including in administrative disputes.

The core facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the more-than-decade-long duration from the 2004 request, the cycle of sixteen decisions and repeated remittals without any court ever examining the substance despite explicit statutory invitations to do so, the Constitutional Court’s successive findings of prematurity and then dismissal, and the continued pendency of the compensation claim before the Commission in 2016. These circumstances underpinned the complaints of unreasonable delay attributable to the authorities and of the ineffectiveness of available remedies (constitutional appeals, the reasonable-time statute, and administrative-silence mechanisms).

The ECtHR case Stanka Mirković and Others v. Montenegro (apps. nos. 33781/15 et al., judgment 7 March 2017) concerned four applicants (two Montenegrin, two Serbian nationals) who complained of the excessive length of restitution/compensation proceedings, caused by repeated remittals, and the lack of an effective remedy, under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention.

On 3 December 2004 the third and fourth applicants applied to the Restitution and Compensation Commission for compensation for land expropriated from their predecessor in 1946. In 2005 the first and second applicants waived their rights in the others’ favour. The Commission granted the claim on 28 August 2005, but the Ministry of Finance quashed the decision on 14 October 2005 after an appeal by the State Prosecutor.

On 17 April 2006 the Commission awarded compensation to all four applicants as heirs, holding the waivers invalid because inheritance questions had to be resolved in non-contentious court proceedings (s. 40 of the Restitution Act).

From June 2006 to March 2014 the case generated 16 decisions—eight by the second-instance administrative body (Ministry of Finance, later Appeals Commission) and eight by the Administrative Court. Second-instance rulings were issued within 14–132 days; Administrative Court rulings took 3 months 23 days to 1 year 8 months 17 days. On at least four occasions the applicants expressly invoked ss. 37 and 58 of the Administrative Disputes Act and asked the Administrative Court to decide the merits itself. The Court never did so; it repeatedly quashed or confirmed the quashing of the Commission’s decisions and, on 27 March 2014, remitted the matter once more.

The Supreme Court upheld the last remittal on 27 June 2014 (served 8 July 2014). Constitutional appeals lodged on 25 July 2014 citing Articles 6 and 13 were rejected as premature on 28 October 2014 because the Commission was still seized, and were later dismissed on 28 December 2015. On 31 March 2016 the Commission adjourned its hearing at the applicants’ request pending the ECtHR’s ruling.

These facts show proceedings that remained unresolved more than eleven years after they began, cycling between administrative bodies and courts without a merits determination despite statutory power for the Administrative Court to end the loop. Constitutional complaints were treated as premature while the case continued, illustrating the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy for the delay.
001-171099:
The case of Pendiuc v. Romania (no. 17605/15) concerns Article 3 complaints by applicant Emanuela Elena Pendiuc (born 1981) over her treatment as a suspect on 6 November 2014. She was pregnant and taking prescribed Utrogestan twice daily to help maintain the pregnancy (first prescribed 4 September 2014; later records confirmed 13 weeks’ gestation as of 19 January 2015).

A warrant to appear was issued at 4 a.m. that day in corruption proceedings involving her father (then mayor of Pitești). Officers collected her from home at 11.30 a.m.; she signed a report confirming she did not object and accompanied them to National Anticorruption Department (DNA) offices. She alleged she was left standing in a corridor for eight hours without food, water or a seat, becoming unwell from her medication and its side-effects, despite the prosecutor knowing of her pregnancy. She claimed aggressive interviewing techniques were used.

Official records show: from 12.50–1.10 p.m. she was informed, in the presence of two chosen lawyers, that she was suspected of complicity in bribe-taking and money-laundering; she was interviewed as a suspect from 1.15–2.45 p.m. (statement recorded). At 6 p.m. she was formally charged; she was informed of the charges (6.05–6.10 p.m.) and interviewed as a charged person (6.15–6.20 p.m.), again with lawyers present and the statement recorded. She and her lawyers signed all documents without written objections. The DNA later stated that water dispensers and cups were available in corridors and offices, a canteen was accessible to all (including the 11 other suspects processed similarly that day), and seating was available during proceedings.

At 7.07 p.m. the prosecutor ordered 24-hour police custody; she was informed at 7.12 p.m. (one lawyer present) and transferred to the Bucharest Police Detention Centre (arrival recorded at 8.20 p.m.). She arrived with a bottle of water and vitamins (the latter confiscated). She signed a medical statement recording that she had been monitored for endometrial hyperplasia, that the recorded information was complete and accurate, and that she had no Utrogestan with her (she would supply documents if detained pending trial). The medical report noted these points and that she was a non-smoker.

She alleged she informed staff of her pregnancy and requested her medication that evening and the next morning, but received none (risking miscarriage); she received no food or water until morning (the meal was unsavoury); she was held in a 5 m² cell with three smokers (despite being a non-smoker and smoke being harmful in her condition), four bunk beds, no bedding except a mattress, a cold temperature, a curtained squat toilet (with a plastic rat-guard and a shower used for flushing), no warm water and contaminated sink water unfit to drink. Outdoor exercise lasted 30 minutes in a 6–7 m² yard with 3 m walls and a metal grill, shared with the smokers.

The detention centre later stated dinner was served 5.30–6 p.m. with no written procedure for later arrivals (she made no request); there was no clear smoker/non-smoker allocation procedure and no record that she had declared non-smoker status, so she was assigned randomly to a smokers’ cell; cold running water was available and the cell was heated.

She was released the next evening after the Bucharest County Court refused a 30-day pre-trial detention request (noting her background as a former television presenter and film producer) and imposed a travel ban instead. These events formed the basis of her complaints of inhuman or degrading treatment through the conditions at the DNA, the physical conditions of her brief detention, and the alleged lack of medical care.

The case of Pendiuc v. Romania concerns Article 3 complaints by a pregnant Romanian national regarding her treatment at the DNA anticorruption offices on 6 November 2014 and subsequent 24-hour police custody.

The applicant had been prescribed Utrogestan twice daily from September 2014 to maintain her pregnancy. On 31 October she was summoned as a witness in a corruption probe involving her father (Pitești’s mayor). Feeling unwell, she obtained a GP referral and uterine ultrasound at hospital; she later claimed this confirmed pregnancy with stress-related complications (though the scan itself contained no report). Police then enforced a warrant and took her for interview; she informed the prosecutor of her condition and submitted medical papers, which a report recorded as “health problems.”

On 6 November a fresh warrant was issued at 04:00. Officers collected her at 11:30 without recorded objection. She alleged she was then left standing in a corridor for eight hours with no food, water or seat, becoming unwell from medication side-effects. Official records show she was informed she was a suspect (complicity in bribery and money-laundering) between 12:50 and 13:10 in the presence of her two lawyers, interviewed 13:15–14:45, charged at 18:00, re-informed 18:05–18:10 and re-interviewed 18:15–18:20. She and her lawyers signed every document without written protest. The DNA later stated that water dispensers, a canteen and seating were available to all eleven suspects processed that day.

At 19:07 she was placed in 24-hour custody and arrived at Bucharest Police Detention Centre around 19:30–20:20 carrying only water and vitamins (confiscated). A medical note recorded her statement of endometrial hyperplasia, that she had no Utrogestan, and that she was a non-smoker; she signed confirming the information was complete. She claimed she also disclosed her pregnancy and requested her medication (never supplied, risking miscarriage), received neither food nor water until morning, and was held in a 5 m² cell with three smokers, four bunks, no linen, a curtain-screened squat toilet doubling as a cold shower, undrinkable tap water, and only 30 minutes’ exercise in a tiny, smoke-filled, high-walled yard.

The authorities replied that dinner finished at 18:00, she arrived late and made no request; non-smoker status was not documented so she was randomly allocated; tap water was potable and the cell heated. She was released the next evening after a court refused pre-trial detention. Later records confirmed she was 13 weeks pregnant on 19 January 2015.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 violations (inhuman waiting conditions, unsanitary detention and withheld pregnancy care).

The case of *Pendiuc v. Romania* (Application no. 17605/15) concerns complaints under Article 3 of the Convention by Romanian national Emanuela Elena Pendiuc, born in 1981. She alleged inhuman and degrading treatment due to the lack of access to water, food or seating during her time at the National Anticorruption Department (DNA) offices on 6 November 2014 before police custody; poor physical conditions at the Bucharest Police Detention Centre; and inadequate medical care for her condition while in custody.

The applicant was prescribed Utrogestan twice daily from 4 September 2014 to support her pregnancy and prevent miscarriage. The medication could cause drowsiness or dizziness if overdosed, but stopping it had no listed effects. Her father, then mayor of Pitești, was under investigation for corruption. On 29 October 2014 she was summoned as a witness. Feeling unwell on 31 October, she obtained a general practitioner's urgent hospital referral for uterine inflammation and an ultrasound at a Bucharest hospital. She claimed the scan confirmed pregnancy with stress- and medication-related complications (though it did not confirm foetal viability) and that she was advised to rest and continue treatment. Police then executed a warrant to bring her to the DNA after she missed the summons. She stated that she informed officers and prosecutor M.N. of her pregnancy and illness, presented medical documents, and was interviewed aggressively while unwell; she signed a report noting health problems and submitted documents without objection. A later check-up on 19 January 2015 recorded her as 13 weeks pregnant. A further prescription for Utrogestan was issued on 25 February 2015.

On 6 November 2014, police executed another warrant at 11.30 a.m. and took her to the DNA. She claimed she was left standing for eight hours in a corridor with no food or water, becoming unwell from her treatment, before a statement was taken. Official records show she was informed of suspicion of complicity in bribe-taking and money-laundering (12.50–1.10 p.m.), interviewed as a suspect (1.15–2.45 p.m.), charged at 6 p.m., and further interviewed (6.15–6.20 p.m.), all in the presence of her lawyers. She and her lawyers signed all documents without written objection. The DNA later stated that water dispensers, a canteen and seating were available, and similar measures were taken against 11 other suspects that day.

She was placed in 24-hour police custody at 7.07 p.m. and arrived at the detention centre around 7.30–8.20 p.m. with only water and vitamins (which were confiscated). A medical report recorded her statement of endometrial hyperplasia, lack of Utrogestan, and intention to provide documents if further detained; it noted she was a non-smoker. She claimed she informed staff of her pregnancy and requested medication but received none, risking miscarriage; she had no food or water until the next morning (unsavoury food that cellmates warned against); she was held in a cold 5 m² cell with three smokers, four bunks, a mattress but no linen, a curtained squat toilet (used also as a shower, with a rat barrier), contaminated undrinkable sink water and no hot water; and she received only 30 minutes of outdoor exercise in a small, enclosed, smoky yard. The centre stated she arrived after dinner hours (5.30–6 p.m.), made no meal request, was randomly assigned to a smokers' cell (no documented non-smoker declaration), had drinkable cold water and heating, and that no written late-arrival meal procedure existed.

The Bucharest County Court released her on 7 November 2014, refusing 30-day pre-trial detention and noting her background as a former television presenter and film producer. Relevant domestic law included Article 106 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, requiring interviews to stop if an interviewee showed excessive fatigue or illness affecting participation, with medical examination if needed.
001-171526:
The case of Ovakimyan v. Russia (Application no. 52796/08) concerns a Russian national born in 1981 who alleged that police unlawfully detained him on 7 September 2007, subjected him to ill-treatment to extract a confession to murder, and that authorities failed to investigate those claims effectively. The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered its judgment on 21 February 2017 (final 21 May 2017).

A.K. was reported missing on 29 August 2007 after intending to sell his car; the vehicle was found on Yoshkar-Ola’s outskirts and a murder investigation opened. On 7 September, police operatives D.K., O. and S. claimed they received information implicating the applicant, invited him (with consent) from his home around 5–6 p.m. to the Yoshkar-Ola Central police station, where he confessed to strangling A.K. to steal the car and offered to show the body’s location. Around 6–7 p.m. they took him there; investigator A. examined the site and recovered the body. Official records, however, show arrest only at 8.55 p.m. as a suspect, followed by a 9.15–9.35 p.m. examination (with State-appointed lawyer V.K.) during which the applicant invoked his right to silence.

The applicant’s account differed sharply. He said three plain-clothes men seized him at 3 p.m. in the street while with his girlfriend, pushed him to the ground, handcuffed him, placed a plastic bag over his head and drove him to a forest. There they punched his forehead, kicked him after he fell, and applied electric shocks to his thumbs, demanding he “cooperate.” He agreed and was taken to investigator G. At 10.45 p.m. the temporary detention facility (IVS) recorded injuries: swelling and haematoma on the left forehead, haematomas on the right chest, shoulder and shoulder-blade, plus waist abrasions.

On 8 September the applicant was taken from the IVS for two confrontations (3.30–5.25 p.m.) and again refused to speak. Investigator G. recorded a “statement of surrender and confession” at 7 p.m. (no lawyer present) in which the applicant admitted participating in a conspiracy to murder A.K. (who, he said, was strangled by co-accused R.K. and M.Ts.) and steal the car. The applicant later claimed that after 9 p.m. G. summoned three men who drove him out of town, beat and strangled him, threatened him with a revolver, bound him with a tow-rope, threw him into a pit and threatened to bury him alive until he signed the confession. He also alleged the signature was forged. IVS records show he was not returned until 3.20 a.m.

On 9 September he was charged with murder and robbery and questioned as an accused (again with V.K.). The record states he confirmed the confession was voluntary. He later claimed that signature too was forged. The Town Court ordered pre-trial detention. Upon admission to SIZO IZ-12/1 a medical assistant noted an 8 cm bruise on the neck, a 2 cm chest bruise and a 3 cm lumbar abrasion.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint on 17 October 2007. Five successive refusals to open proceedings (lack of a crime) were issued between November 2007 and June 2008; several were quashed by the Yoshkar-Ola Town Court as unlawful and unreasoned. A forensic report of December 2007 found the SIZO injuries consistent with blunt trauma but could not date them. The last refusal (9 March 2011) attributed some injuries to a pre-murder fight with A.K. (per co-accused R.K.) and the neck bruise possibly to self-infliction. Domestic courts upheld that decision, though a prosecutor later criticised the inquiry as incomplete.

At trial the Mariy El Supreme Court convicted the applicant of murder and robbery (16 years) on the basis of co-accused statements. It declined to examine the ill-treatment allegations because no challenged evidence whose admissibility they would affect had been used, and the applicant had withdrawn exclusion requests. The Russian Supreme Court (5 February 2009) noted the arrest record was drawn up more than three hours after the actual 3 p.m. arrest, in breach of domestic law, but held the time had been credited against the sentence.
