The case originated in an application by Russian national Suren Avetikovich Ovakimyan (born 1981) alleging unlawful deprivation of liberty, police ill-treatment to extract a confession, and an ineffective investigation into that treatment.

On 29 August 2007, A.K. was reported missing after leaving home to sell his car, which was later found on Yoshkar-Ola’s outskirts. Criminal proceedings for his alleged murder were opened.

On 7 September 2007, according to police operatives, they invited the applicant from his home around 5–6 p.m. to the Yoshkar-Ola Central police station. He allegedly confessed to strangling A.K. to steal the car and showed the body’s location around 6–7 p.m. Official records, however, documented his arrest as a suspect only at 8.55 p.m., followed by a brief examination (9.15–9.35 p.m.) in the presence of a lawyer, during which he refused to make statements, invoking the privilege against self-incrimination.

The applicant’s account differed sharply: around 3 p.m., three plain-clothes men seized him in the street, pushed him down, handcuffed him, placed a plastic bag over his head, and took him to a forest. There they punched him (including on the forehead), kicked him after he fell, and applied electric shocks to his thumbs until he agreed to cooperate. He was then taken to investigator G. Upon admission to the IVS at 10.45 p.m., recorded injuries included swelling and a haematoma on the left forehead, haematomas on the right chest, shoulder and shoulder blade, and abrasions on the lower back.

On 8 September the applicant was taken from the IVS for confrontations (3.30–5.25 p.m.), again refusing to give statements. Investigator G. recorded a “statement of surrender and confession” at 7 p.m. in the absence of a lawyer, in which the applicant admitted participating in a conspiracy to murder A.K. and steal the car, attributing the strangling to co-accused R.K. and M.Ts. The applicant later alleged that after 9 p.m. he was driven out of town, beaten, strangled, threatened with a revolver, bound with a tow-rope, thrown into a pit and threatened with being buried alive until he signed the confession. He subsequently claimed his signature had been forged. Upon transfer to SIZO IZ-12/1 on 9 September, further injuries were noted: an 8 cm bruise on the front of the neck, a 2 cm bruise on the right chest and a 3 cm abrasion near the first lumbar vertebra.

On 9 September he was charged with murder and robbery and questioned as an accused in the presence of a lawyer; the record stated that his confession had been voluntary. He later disputed the signatures on that record as well. The Yoshkar-Ola Town Court ordered his detention on remand.

The applicant lodged a complaint of ill-treatment. Multiple inquiries under Article 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure produced five refusals to open criminal proceedings, each subsequently annulled as unlawful and unfounded. A forensic report found the injuries consistent with blunt objects but could not determine their timing or whether they constituted lasting health damage. The last refusal (9 March 2011) attributed some injuries to a fight with A.K. on 28 August (per co-accused R.K.) and suggested the neck bruise might have been self-inflicted. Domestic courts initially upheld this decision, but the first deputy prosecutor later quashed it, citing an incomplete inquiry that failed to refute the allegations, verify the electric-shock claim, assess the pit, examine IVS records of the applicant’s absences, or establish a full chronology from the actual 3 p.m. arrest.

At trial the Mariy El Supreme Court convicted the applicant of murder and robbery, sentencing him to 16 years. It could not determine how the injuries occurred and declined to examine the ill-treatment allegations because no evidence whose admissibility would have been affected was used. The applicant’s alleged pointing-out of the body was treated as a mitigating factor for the robbery count. On appeal the Russian Supreme Court noted that the arrest record had been drawn up more than three hours after the actual 3 p.m. arrest (in breach of procedural rules) but held that the time spent in detention had been correctly credited toward the sentence. Evidence obtained during the period of alleged ill-treatment was not relied upon given the disputed origin of the injuries.

The case of Ovakimyan v. Russia (Application no. 52796/08) concerns allegations by a Russian national that he was unlawfully arrested, ill-treated by police to extract a confession to murder and robbery, and that no effective investigation followed.

On 29 August 2007, A.K. disappeared after leaving home to sell his car; the vehicle was found abandoned, and murder proceedings were opened. On 7 September 2007, A.K.’s body was located. Official records show the applicant was arrested as a suspect at 8.55 p.m. that evening by investigator G., after which he was examined in the presence of a lawyer and invoked his right to silence. Police officers D.K., O. and S. claimed they had collected him earlier (around 5–6 p.m.) with his consent, that he confessed during an interview to strangling A.K. in order to steal the car, and that he then led them to the body around 6–7 p.m.

The applicant’s account differed sharply. He stated that at 3 p.m., while with his girlfriend, three unidentified men in civilian clothes seized him in the street, forced him to the ground, handcuffed him, placed a plastic bag over his head and drove him to a forest. There he was punched (including on the forehead), kicked while on the ground and given electric shocks via wires attached to his thumbs until he agreed to cooperate. He was then taken to investigator G. He denied ever showing the investigators the location of the body, attributing that act to his co-accused R.K.

Upon arrival at the IVS detention facility at 10.45 p.m., staff recorded a swelling and haematoma on the left forehead, haematomas on the right chest, right shoulder and right shoulder-blade, and abrasions on the lower back.

On 8 September the applicant was taken from the IVS for confrontations (again remaining silent with a lawyer present). Investigator G. later recorded a “statement of surrender and confession” at 7 p.m. in the absence of counsel, in which the applicant admitted participating in a conspiracy to murder A.K. (strangled by co-accused R.K. and M.Ts.) and to steal the car. The applicant claimed that after 9 p.m. three men again took him out of town, beat and strangled him, threatened him with a revolver, bound him with a tow-rope, threw him into a pit and threatened to bury him alive until he signed the confession. He later alleged that both the confession signature and a subsequent questioning record of 9 September (in which he purportedly confirmed the confession was voluntary) had been forged; handwriting expertise proved inconclusive.

On 9 September he was formally charged and placed in pre-trial detention. Admission examination at SIZO IZ-12/1 recorded an 8 cm bruise on the front of the neck, a 2 cm bruise on the right chest and a 3 cm abrasion near the first lumbar vertebra.

The applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment prompted five successive refusals by investigators to open a criminal inquiry (November 2007–June 2008), each later quashed as unlawful by superior prosecutors or the Yoshkar-Ola Town Court. A forensic report of December 2007 confirmed the injuries could have been caused by blunt objects but could not date them. The most recent refusal (9 March 2011) attributed some injuries to a pre-murder fight with A.K. (per co-accused R.K.) and treated the neck bruise as possibly self-inflicted; it was itself later annulled by a deputy prosecutor for incomplete investigation (failure to verify the pit, electric-shock claims, IVS movement records, or the applicant’s actual 3 p.m. arrest). Domestic courts reviewing the refusals under Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure ultimately found the inquiries inadequate.

At trial before the Mariy El Supreme Court the applicant pleaded not guilty, denied pointing out the body or signing the confession, and sought (then withdrew) exclusion of certain evidence. The court heard the investigators and officers, who denied ill-treatment, and noted it could not establish the origin of the injuries; it treated that question as one for a separate inquiry. It convicted the applicant of murder and robbery, sentencing him to 16 years, relying inter alia on co-accused statements and treating the (disputed) pointing-out of the body as a mitigating factor for the robbery. The Russian Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 5 February 2009, acknowledging that the arrest record had been drawn up more than three hours after the actual 3 p.m. detention (a breach of domestic law) but holding that the trial court had remedied it by crediting the extra time against the sentence. It also noted that disputed evidence obtained around the time of the alleged ill-treatment had not been used.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims of unlawful deprivation of liberty (discrepancy in arrest time and circumstances), ill-treatment (documented injuries, consistent allegations of beatings, shocks and threats coinciding with periods outside official records), and an ineffective investigation (repeated, incomplete refusals despite medical evidence and court quashals).
001-171777:
The case of Cerovšek and Božičnik v. Slovenia (Applications nos. 68939/12 and 68949/12) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned two Slovenian nationals, Silvo Cerovšek (born 1962) and Štefan Božičnik (born 1946). They alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention, as the written reasons for their criminal convictions were provided by judges other than the one who had conducted the trials and pronounced the oral verdicts.

The applicants were charged in 2005 and 2006 with theft for cutting down and appropriating trees from forests belonging to others. They were tried separately by professional judge A.K. sitting as a single judge. In Cerovšek’s trial, A.K. heard witnesses, inspected the site, reviewed documents including land-register maps, and appointed an expert who valued the wood at EUR 2,028. No witness directly observed him cutting trees on the injured party’s land, but testimony covered circumstantial matters such as similar cutting methods, transport traces, his wood sales, and observations of him and another person transporting timber across the land. Cerovšek claimed he had only cut marked or beetle-infested trees on his own property.

Božičnik faced two counts. A.K. heard witnesses and reviewed maps and other documents; an expert valued the wood at EUR 457 and EUR 440. For the first count, Božičnik claimed a mistaken belief that the land was his, based on information from former owners who testified. Witnesses, including the injured party’s husband, reported seeing him in the forest, transport of the wood, and an admission of error without agreement on compensation. For the second count, he claimed an agreement to cut trees in exchange for wine, which the owner denied.

On 21 June 2007 A.K. orally pronounced Cerovšek guilty, imposing a six-month suspended prison sentence and compensation (or equivalent wood). On 2 July 2007 she similarly found Božičnik guilty of both counts, imposing a seven-month suspended sentence and compensation. The applicants immediately gave notice of appeal, triggering the statutory duty to prepare written grounds.

A.K. later retired and the case files were lost. In 2010 the local court reconstituted them from available records. Different judges then issued the written grounds: D.K.M. for Cerovšek (served August 2010) and M.B. for Božičnik (served June 2010). Both relied on the restored files, hearing records, and documents. They rejected the applicants’ accounts, assessed witness credibility (finding some biased or unpersuasive), and relied on circumstantial evidence, expert reports, and maps.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the written reasons should have come from the trial judge and that the judgments should be set aside and remitted; they also challenged factual findings and witness assessments. The Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed the appeals in 2010, holding that the delay and change of judge did not render the judgments unlawful. It noted that A.K. had conducted the adversarial hearings, heard the evidence, and pronounced the verdicts, while the later written grounds clearly explained the evidence and credibility assessments. The court itself reassessed evidence in Cerovšek’s case and confirmed the facts and intent in Božičnik’s.

The Supreme Court dismissed further applications for protection of legality in 2011. It held that only the operative verdict (not the written reasons) affected rights; another judge could supply written grounds in cases of prolonged absence or retirement, as writing was not strictly part of the trial. Immediacy required the trial judge to give the verdict, but unconvincing written reasons would simply strengthen an appeal. The Constitutional Court refused to admit the complaints in 2012, finding neither a serious human-rights violation nor an important constitutional issue.

Domestic law (Criminal Procedure Act) required the trial judge to pronounce the verdict orally with brief reasons and, upon appeal notice, to provide full written grounds within 30 days, setting out proven facts, evidence assessment, and legal reasoning. A 2006 Constitutional Court decision had emphasised that the principle of immediacy demands that the judges who hear the evidence and form impressions of credibility also issue the decision.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Cerovšek and Božičnik v. Slovenia (applications nos. 68939/12 and 68949/12) involved two Slovenian nationals convicted of theft who alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicants, Silvo Cerovšek (born 1962) and Štefan Božičnik (born 1946), claimed that the reasons for their guilty verdicts were not given by the judge who had reached them, undermining the fairness of the trial.

The applicants were charged in 2005 and 2006, respectively, with cutting down and appropriating trees from forests belonging to others. They were tried by professional Judge A.K. sitting as a single judge. In Cerovšek’s case, A.K. heard multiple witnesses (none of whom saw him cutting trees on the injured party’s land), inspected the site, reviewed documents including a land register map, and received an expert valuation of stolen wood at EUR 2,028. Circumstantial evidence included similarities in cutting methods, transport traces, and sales of wood. Cerovšek claimed he had only cut marked or beetle-infested trees on his own land. In Božičnik’s case, involving two counts, A.K. similarly heard witnesses and reviewed maps and documents, with an expert valuing the wood at EUR 457 and EUR 440. Božičnik claimed a mistaken belief about land borders (shown by former owners) or an agreement with one owner to cut trees in exchange for wine; witnesses and the injured parties contradicted this.

On 21 June 2007, A.K. orally pronounced Cerovšek guilty of unlawful appropriation, imposing a six-month prison sentence suspended for three years and ordering compensation of EUR 2,028 (or equivalent wood). On 2 July 2007, she similarly convicted Božičnik, imposing a seven-month suspended sentence and compensations of EUR 457 and EUR 440. Hearing records contained no indication of any oral summary of reasons, though the Government asserted one was given. Both applicants promptly notified their intent to appeal, triggering an obligation under the Criminal Procedure Act for written grounds.

A.K. later retired (date unspecified), and the case files were lost. The files were reconstituted in 2010. Different judges then issued the written grounds based solely on the restored documents: D.K.M. for Cerovšek (served 17 August 2010), who disbelieved his version, dismissed a key witness as biased, and relied on unprofessional cutting and transport evidence; and M.B. for Božičnik (served 17 June 2010), who found his defences unconvincing, preferring statements of injured parties, supporting witnesses, maps, and expert evidence.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the judgments should be set aside and remitted because another judge had supplied the reasons, and they challenged the factual findings and credibility assessments. The Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed the appeals (26 August and 25 November 2010), holding that the delay was not unlawful, the oral verdicts had been given by A.K. after adversarial hearings, and the written grounds clearly explained the evidence assessment. The Supreme Court dismissed applications for protection of legality (6 January and 1 September 2011), reasoning that only the operative verdict (not the written grounds) affected rights; another judge could write reasons in cases of long absence or death, as writing was not strictly part of the trial, and unconvincing reasons would aid appeals. The Constitutional Court refused to admit the complaints (3 April 2012), finding no serious human-rights violation or important constitutional question.

Under the Criminal Procedure Act, the presiding judge must orally pronounce the verdict with a brief statement of grounds, and provide full written grounds (in accord with the oral judgment, detailing proven facts, credibility assessments, and legal reasons) within 30 days if appealed. A 2006 Constitutional Court decision (Up-309/04) held that the principle of immediacy requires the decision to be issued by judges who directly participated in the hearing and evidence examination, enabling them to form subjective opinions on credibility through their own senses.

The case of Cerovšek and Božičnik v. Slovenia concerned two applications to the European Court of Human Rights by Slovenian nationals Silvo Cerovšek and Štefan Božičnik. They alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) because the written reasons supporting their criminal convictions had not been prepared by the judge who had heard the evidence and pronounced the oral verdicts.

The applicants were charged separately in 2005 and 2006 with theft, specifically cutting down and removing trees from forests belonging to others and appropriating the wood. Each was tried by professional Judge A.K. sitting as a single judge. In Cerovšek’s case the judge heard multiple witnesses (none of whom had seen him cutting trees on the injured party’s land), inspected the site, reviewed documents including land-register maps, and received an expert valuation of the wood at €2,028. Cerovšek claimed he had only felled marked or beetle-infested trees on his own land. Božičnik faced two counts; he maintained he had either mistaken the boundary of his land or had an agreement with one owner to fell trees in exchange for wine. The judge again heard witnesses, examined maps and other documents, and obtained expert valuations (€457 and €440).

On 21 June 2007 Judge A.K. convicted Cerovšek and imposed a six-month prison sentence suspended for three years, plus restitution or compensation. On 2 July 2007 she convicted Božičnik and imposed a seven-month sentence likewise suspended, plus compensation. Both verdicts were pronounced orally. The Government later asserted that a brief oral summary of reasons had been given, but the hearing records contained no indication of this. Because each applicant immediately announced an intention to appeal, Slovenian law required the trial judge to produce full written reasons.

Judge A.K. subsequently retired and the case files were lost. The files were reconstituted in 2010. Different judges then prepared the written judgments solely on the basis of the restored documents: Judge D.K.M. for Cerovšek (served 17 August 2010) and Judge M.B. for Božičnik (served 17 June 2010). These reasons rejected the applicants’ versions of events, assessed witness credibility and relied on circumstantial evidence such as cutting methods, transport traces and land-register maps.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the written reasons had to be given by the judge who had conducted the trial and that the judgments should therefore be quashed and remitted. The Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed the appeals, holding that the delay and change of judge did not render the judgments unlawful. It emphasised that the oral verdicts had been delivered by the judge who had heard the evidence in adversarial proceedings and that the later written reasons were clear, logical and based on the file. The Supreme Court likewise rejected applications for the protection of legality. It distinguished the oral verdict (which engaged the principle of immediacy) from the subsequent written reasoning (whose purpose was to enable appellate review). In exceptional circumstances such as a judge’s prolonged absence or death, another judge could lawfully draft the reasons from the file. The Constitutional Court declined to admit the applicants’ complaints.

Domestic law (Criminal Procedure Act) required the trial judge to pronounce the verdict orally, to give a brief oral statement of reasons, and thereafter to produce a written judgment containing a full statement of the facts found, the assessment of evidence and the legal reasoning. A 2006 Constitutional Court decision had underscored that the principle of immediacy demanded that the same judges who perceived the evidence directly should also decide the case.

The case of Orlov and Others v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 5632/10, judgment 14 March 2017) concerned four Russian applicants—Oleg Orlov (Memorial NGO chairman), Artem Vysotskiy (REN TV reporter), Stanislav Goryachikh (cameraman) and Karen Sakhinov (assistant cameraman)—who alleged abduction and ill-treatment by State agents in Ingushetia on 23 November 2007, plus an ineffective investigation, in violation of Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Following the death of a child during a counter-terrorist operation, a protest was planned in Nazran for 24 November 2007. The REN TV team was sent to cover it; Orlov was already there monitoring human rights. All four were staying at the Hotel Assa.

Around 11:30 p.m. on 23 November, armed men in balaclavas and camouflage burst into the applicants’ rooms without identifying themselves or showing documents. They questioned Orlov about his presence, collected belongings and equipment, kicked and beat the men (including with rifle butts), placed black plastic bags over their heads, and forced them—wearing only light indoor clothing and slippers—into an unmarked white Gazel minibus. One abductor told Vysotskiy they were from the Ministry of Interior. The group drove for about an hour through Nazran then to a snow-covered field, where the applicants were beaten, threatened with execution (silencers were sought), and abandoned after warnings not to return. They walked in freezing conditions to Nesterovskaya, obtained help, and were taken to police for medical aid. Forensic reports later documented bruises, hematomas and (for Vysotskiy) concussion.

Hotel staff and security confirmed that 10–15 armed men arrived around 11:30 p.m., claimed to be conducting an anti-terrorist identity check, held staff at gunpoint, removed phone batteries and SIM cards, and departed with four bagged men. Police officers regularly assigned to guard the hotel (which housed two Deputy Interior Ministers) had been recalled at about 9 p.m. by Deputy Minister A. Kh. on purported Ministry-security grounds—an unprecedented step. The abductors behaved professionally, used unaccented Russian, operated under a chain of command, and targeted only the applicants despite the presence of high-ranking officials. The minibus passed through lit streets without being stopped at checkpoints.

A criminal investigation was opened the next day (case no. 07560126) for privacy violation, obstruction of journalists’ work and robbery. Victim status was granted and stolen items (including professional equipment valued at hundreds of thousands of roubles) were listed. Numerous witnesses were interviewed, fingerprints collected (later found unusable), and vehicle logs examined (no Gazel recorded). No working CCTV existed. The first applicant repeatedly asked investigators to reclassify the offences as abuse of official powers (Criminal Code Art. 286) and to pursue the State-agent theory, citing the police recall, professional conduct, selective targeting and delayed police response. These requests were rejected for lack of evidence of State involvement. The investigation was suspended and resumed several times for failure to identify perpetrators; access to the full file was denied. It remained pending without results.

The Government did not dispute the events but maintained that the perpetrators were unidentified and not shown to be State agents.

Following the death of a child during a counter-terrorist operation, a protest was planned in Nazran for 24 November 2007. The three journalists were sent by REN TV to cover it; Orlov was already in the region monitoring human rights. All four were staying at the Hotel Assa.

They pointed weapons, ordered the men to the floor, collected personal belongings, cash, documents, passports, credit cards, professional equipment (valued at tens of thousands of euros) and mobile phones, beat them with rifle butts and kicks, and pulled black plastic bags over their heads. One abductor claimed to be from the Ministry of the Interior. The applicants, wearing only indoor clothing and slippers, were taken to an unmarked white Gazel minibus. Hotel staff were held at gunpoint; their phones were confiscated. Police security officers who normally guarded the hotel (due to high-ranking Interior Ministry officials staying there) had been ordered away around 9 p.m. by Deputy Minister A.Kh. because of an alleged threat to the Ministry building.

The applicants were beaten unconscious in some cases, threatened with execution, and abandoned in the freezing night. They walked for an hour to Nesterovskaya, obtained help, and were taken to a police station for medical treatment. Forensic reports documented bruises, hematomas and (for Vysotskiy) cerebral concussion.

Numerous witnesses (hotel staff, police, residents) described the abductors as a professional, well-organised special-forces-style group speaking unaccented Russian who identified themselves as an anti-terrorist unit. They had gone straight to the applicants after checking the guest log and showed no interest in the Interior Ministry officials present. Checkpoints recorded no relevant vehicle. Fingerprints and CCTV inquiries yielded nothing.

They requested reclassification as “exceeding official powers.” Investigators rejected this, citing insufficient evidence of State involvement, and granted only limited file access. The investigation was suspended several times for failure to identify perpetrators (2008, 2011), despite later instructions and criticism of police inaction. It remained pending. The Court received the 1,182-page file, which omitted certain applicant statements stressing State-agent involvement.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Convention violations: abduction amounting to unlawful deprivation of liberty and ill-treatment by (allegedly) State agents, destruction or theft of property, and an ineffective investigation that failed to pursue the State-agent theory or produce results.

The case of Orlov and Others v. Russia concerns the November 2007 abduction and ill-treatment of four applicants in Ingushetia, allegedly by State agents, and the authorities’ failure to investigate effectively. The applicants were Oleg Orlov (Memorial NGO chairman), REN TV reporter Artem Vysotskiy, and camera operators Stanislav Goryachikh and Karen Sakhinov. They were in Nazran covering a planned protest against security-force abuses after a child’s death in a counter-terrorist operation, staying at the Hotel Assa.

On 23 November 2007 around 11:30 p.m., armed men in balaclavas and camouflage uniforms burst into the applicants’ rooms. Police security, present because senior Interior Ministry officials resided there, had been ordered off duty around 9 p.m. by a Deputy Minister. The intruders identified themselves as police or anti-terrorist officers, spoke unaccented Russian, searched the rooms, seized belongings and equipment (including cash, documents, phones, a laptop and cameras), beat the applicants, bagged their heads, and forced them into an unmarked white Gazel minibus. Hotel staff confirmed a coordinated operation: the men communicated by gestures, held staff at gunpoint, and took the four men away.

The vehicle drove through Nazran then to a snow-covered field, where the applicants were beaten with kicks and rifle butts, threatened with execution, and abandoned in light clothing and slippers. After walking an hour in the cold they reached Nesterovskaya village; a resident summoned police. Medical examinations documented bruises, hematomas and, for Vysotskiy, cerebral concussion.

A criminal investigation opened the next day under articles covering privacy violation, obstruction of journalists and robbery (not exceeding official powers). Applicants received victim status. Witnesses, including hotel staff and recalled police officers, corroborated the events and the security withdrawal. Investigators examined the scene (unusable fingerprints), seized the guest log, and questioned dozens of people, including Interior Ministry deputies who claimed ignorance. Checkpoints recorded no minibus; the hotel denied working CCTV.

The inquiry was repeatedly suspended (2008, 2011) for failure to identify perpetrators and resumed after complaints, remaining pending years later. Requests to reclassify the offences as committed by State agents—citing the timed security recall, targeting of journalists rather than officials, professional conduct, unstopped passage through lit streets and checkpoints, and delayed police response—were rejected for lack of evidence. Applicants obtained only partial file access. The Government accepted the abduction and ill-treatment but maintained the perpetrators were unidentified private actors, not State agents.

These facts underpin the complaints of inhuman treatment, unlawful deprivation of liberty, ineffective investigation and unlawful interference with possessions.
001-172458:
The case of Milisavljević v. Serbia (Application no. 50123/06) concerns a journalist’s conviction for criminal insult arising from a newspaper article, which she claimed violated her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Ljiljana Milisavljević (born 1966), worked as a journalist for the major Serbian daily Politika. In September 2003 her editors assigned her to write a profile of Nataša Kandić, a prominent human-rights activist known for investigating war crimes committed during the Yugoslav conflicts (including those by Serbian forces) and for advocating full Serbian cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY). At the time, between 40 % and 64 % of Serbs viewed the ICTY as a security threat, 54 % opposed cooperation (including the arrest and transfer of suspects), and official cooperation was assessed as neither full nor proactive. The March 2003 assassination of Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić, a key pro-cooperation figure, had further strained relations. Kandić herself faced hostility from parts of the political elite and public, resulting in several incidents.

The article, titled “The Hague Investigator,” appeared on 7 September 2003. It reported Kandić’s background, her founding of the Humanitarian Law Centre, her work documenting crimes against non-Serbs, an incident in which she slapped a participant at a commemoration for missing persons (prompting a police request for prosecution and a civil suit seeking 30 million dinars), Western awards she had received, and public perceptions of her. One sentence stated: “Although she has been called a witch and a prostitute and is permanently under threat \ldots she says: ‘This is simply part of this job.’” The piece also quoted Kandić’s remark that even her son accused her of protecting everyone except Serbs, described her as a “lonely voice of reason” or a “Soros mercenary,” and noted that she was accused of pursuing only crimes committed by Serbs.

On 10 November 2003 Kandić lodged a private criminal prosecution. She alleged that the entire article was written with intent to belittle her, portray her as a traitor and a paid foreign servant or prostitute, and that it contained malicious misrepresentations, untruths and blatant insults. She sought no civil damages.

In her defence the applicant stated that she had expressed no personal opinion, had not intended to insult Kandić, and had drawn the entire piece from previously published material. She had used quotation marks for direct citations and omitted them only when paraphrasing. She identified the specific earlier article that contained the “witch and prostitute” phrase.

On 1 September 2005 the First Municipal Court in Belgrade convicted the applicant of insult solely in respect of the unquoted phrase “although she has been called a witch and a prostitute.” Although the court accepted that the words had originated in another publication, it held that the absence of quotation marks meant the applicant had adopted them as her own opinion and thereby intended to insult. In view of her clean record, employment and mature age, the court imposed only a judicial warning (a measure that still records the person as an offender). No prison term or fine was ordered.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the words were another author’s view, that reporting negative public attitudes could not render a journalist criminally liable, and that the conviction threatened press freedom. On 5 July 2006 the Belgrade District Court dismissed the appeal, endorsing the first-instance reasoning. In separate proceedings the applicant was ordered to pay Kandić approximately €386 in costs; she did not appeal that order. She later stated that she had been dismissed from Politika and that the conviction appeared to have been the cause.

Under the then-applicable Criminal Code, insult carried a fine or up to three months’ imprisonment (six months if committed through the press). An exception existed for statements made in the discharge of journalistic duties provided there was no intent to defame. A judicial warning could be issued for minor offences committed under especially mitigating circumstances.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that her criminal conviction for a journalistic report on a matter of public interest constituted an unjustified interference with freedom of expression.

The case of Milisavljević v. Serbia (Application no. 50123/06) concerns a journalist's conviction for criminal insult under Serbian law following publication of a newspaper article, which she alleged violated her right to freedom of expression.

The applicant, Ljiljana Milisavljević, a Serbian national born in 1966 and residing in Belgrade, worked as a journalist for Politika, a major daily newspaper. At the time, a substantial portion of the Serbian public (40-64%) viewed the ICTY as a security threat, with 54% opposing cooperation (including arrests and transfers of suspects). Cooperation was assessed as neither full nor proactive, and it deteriorated further after the assassination of Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić, a pro-cooperation figure. Kandić faced widespread hostility from political elites and the public, including threats and incidents.

The applicant's article, titled “The Hague Investigator,” appeared in Politika on 7 September 2003. It described Kandić's background, her founding of the Humanitarian Law Centre, her awards (none from Serbia), and her role as an ICTY “investigator” focused on Serbian crimes. It noted public contempt in Serbia for her alleged anti-Serbian stance and exclusive focus on crimes by Serbs. The piece included the statement that, although called a witch and a prostitute and permanently under threat (including a bomb threat that year), Kandić viewed this as part of her job. Other details covered her family, education, career, and travels.

On 10 November 2003, Kandić initiated a private prosecution, arguing that the entire article aimed to belittle her as a traitor, a paid servant of foreign interests, and a prostitute who sold herself for money. She claimed malicious misrepresentation, untruths, and blatant insults, but she declined to seek civil compensation.

In her defence, the applicant stated that she had not expressed her personal opinion or intended to insult Kandić. The article drew from documentation in other magazines; she used quotation marks for direct citations and paraphrased other material without them. She identified the specific sources for various phrases, including the “witch and prostitute” description.

On 1 September 2005, after remittal, the First Municipal Court in Belgrade convicted the applicant of criminal insult solely for the phrase “although she has been called a witch and a prostitute.” Although the court confirmed that this wording had previously appeared in another author's article in a different magazine, it held that the applicant's failure to use quotation marks indicated her agreement with the statement, thereby expressing her own opinion and demonstrating intent to insult. Citing no aggravating circumstances and several mitigating factors (clean record, employment, and mature age), the court issued only a judicial warning under Articles 41 and 59 of the General Criminal Code. No prison sentence or fine was imposed.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the words reflected another author's view rather than her own and that reporting negative public attitudes toward Kandić could not render her criminally liable. She warned of broader implications for press freedom. On 5 July 2006, the Belgrade District Court upheld the conviction, endorsing the lower court's reasoning.

In separate proceedings, on 2 October 2006 the First Municipal Court ordered the applicant to pay Kandić RSD 33,125 (approximately EUR 386) in costs; she did not appeal. The applicant later stated that she had been discharged from Politika and that the conviction appeared to have caused this.

Relevant domestic law at the time (Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Serbia 1977, in force until 2006) defined insult as punishable by a fine or up to three months' imprisonment (up to six months if committed through the press). Article 96 provided that no punishment applied for insults made in the discharge of journalistic duties if there was no intention to defame. The General Criminal Code allowed a judicial warning for minor offences committed under particularly mitigating circumstances, taking into account the perpetrator's personality, prior life, subsequent behaviour, and degree of liability. A person receiving such a warning is treated as an offender and could be considered a repeat offender for any future crime.

These facts form the basis of the alleged interference with the applicant's freedom of expression through her criminal conviction and its consequences.

001-173089:
The case of Asatryan v. Armenia (Application no. 3571/09) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. Silva Asatryan, an Armenian national born in 1960, was convicted of instigating the attempted murder of M.G., a businessman and former parliamentarian, by planting a bomb under his car. The bomb detonated on 29 December 2001 when M.G. started the engine, but he survived with minor injuries. M.G. immediately identified the applicant’s ex-husband, A.G., as the likely perpetrator due to business disputes. A.G. denied involvement, providing an alibi involving their son V.G., whose charges were later dropped. Early 2002 interviews with family and acquaintances (including daughter L.G., friend A.At., and neighbours A.A. and A.B.) described the applicant’s strained views of M.G. and ongoing family ties despite a 1999 divorce.

In September 2005, family friend Y.W. was arrested for possessing firearms and explosives. He confessed to the bombing, claiming it was on the applicant’s orders. The applicant was arrested and charged with instigating attempted murder and property damage. The case proceeded to trial before the Avan and Nor-Nork District Court of Yerevan. At trial, Y.W. retracted his confession, alleging duress. The applicant denied any role, asserting she had lived separately from A.G. since their divorce and had no interest in his affairs (though she had signed one related document). Her lawyer successfully requested that L.G. be removed from the witness list due to testimonial privilege as a close relative; L.G. invoked this right. The District Court convicted the applicant on 12 October 2007, sentencing her to nine years’ imprisonment (with Y.W. also convicted). It relied primarily on trial testimony from Y.W.’s spouse S.A. and former colleague L.C., plus evidence of the applicant’s court disputes with M.G. over property, to establish motive linked to A.G.’s conflicts.

The applicant appealed, maintaining her innocence and lack of motive given the separation. Before the Criminal Court of Appeal, Y.W. reversed again, stating he had acted on the applicant’s request but only to frighten M.G., not kill him. On 18 June 2008, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and sentence. To find that the applicant had maintained a “family-like relationship” with A.G. despite the divorce and had expressed annoyance at M.G. to others (supporting motive), it expressly relied on the unread 2002 pre-trial statements of L.G., A.At., A.A., and A.B. These witnesses had not been called or examined at either instance; L.G. had invoked privilege, and the others were never listed. The statements were not read out in court.

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the Court of Appeal’s conclusions rested on unexamined pre-trial statements she had no opportunity to challenge, in breach of fair-trial guarantees. The Court of Cassation declared it inadmissible. After a successful Constitutional Court challenge to related procedural rules, the Cassation Court reopened the appeal but again found it without merit, noting the statements of L.G. and A.A. among the supporting evidence.

Domestic law (CCP Articles 20, 86, 105, 339, 342, 358, 393) requires adversarial proceedings, prohibits using statements obtained in breach of a witness’s right to refuse testimony against next of kin, limits reading of pre-trial statements to cases of genuine unavailability, and mandates that judgments rest only on evidence examined at trial. The applicant’s core complaint was that the Court of Appeal’s uncritical use of these untested, unread statements—without any opportunity for confrontation—denied her a fair hearing, particularly as they were decisive to establishing her continued ties to A.G. and thus motive.

In September 2005 Y.W., a family friend, was arrested after firearms and explosives were found at his home. He confessed that he had planted the bomb on the applicant's orders. The applicant was arrested on 23 September 2005 and charged with instigation of attempted murder and property damage. At the first-instance trial before the Avan and Nor-Nork District Court, Y.W. retracted his confession, alleging duress. The applicant denied any role, asserting that she had divorced A.G. in 1999, lived separately with L.G., and had only minimal contact with A.G. Her lawyer successfully applied to exclude L.G. from the witness list after L.G. invoked testimonial privilege. On 12 October 2007 the District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced her to nine years' imprisonment, relying primarily on the testimony of Y.W.'s wife and a former colleague, together with evidence of the applicant's own civil disputes with M.G.

On appeal the applicant reiterated that she had lived apart from A.G. since 1999 and therefore had no motive. Y.W. again changed his account, now claiming he had acted at the applicant's request but only to frighten M.G. On 18 June 2008 the Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. It found that, despite the divorce, the applicant had maintained a “family-like” relationship with A.G. and had voiced annoyance at M.G. in the presence of others. In support it expressly cited the unread 2002 pre-trial statements of L.G., A.At., A.A. and A.B.—none of whom had testified at either the first-instance or appellate hearings. The applicant's subsequent cassation appeal argued that these statements had never been read out or examined in court and that she had been denied the chance to question the witnesses. The Court of Cassation twice declared the appeal inadmissible (15 December 2008 and, after a constitutional challenge, 25 September 2009), on the second occasion again referring to the statements of L.G. and A.A.

The applicant maintained before the European Court that the appellate court's untested reliance on these statements rendered the proceedings unfair.

The case of Asatryan v. Armenia (Application no. 3571/09) concerns the applicant Silva Asatryan’s conviction for instigating the attempted murder of businessman M.G. via a car bomb on 29 December 2001. M.G. survived with minor injuries. Police initially focused on her ex-husband A.G. due to business disputes, but charges against him and their son were dropped. In 2002, several individuals gave pre-trial statements: A.At. (A.G.’s friend) noted the applicant’s opposition to A.G.’s dealings with M.G., whom she viewed as a “scammer”; neighbour A.A. recalled her complaints about money owed by M.G.; neighbour A.B. described knowing the family; and daughter L.G. stated the parents had divorced years earlier but maintained close, daily contact, with the applicant often staying at A.G.’s apartment.

In 2005, family friend Y.W. was arrested with firearms and explosives; he confessed to planting the bomb on the applicant’s orders. She was charged with instigation of attempted murder. At first-instance trial before the Avan and Nor-Nork District Court, Y.W. recanted, alleging duress. The applicant denied involvement, claiming a 1999 divorce and separate living arrangements with no interest in A.G.’s business, though she had signed related documents. Her lawyer successfully excluded L.G. from testifying after the daughter invoked testimonial privilege. On 12 October 2007 the District Court convicted the applicant (nine years’ imprisonment) based primarily on trial testimony from Y.W.’s spouse and a former colleague, plus evidence of her own property disputes with M.G. The 2002 statements of L.G., A.At., A.A. and A.B. were not relied upon or read out.

On appeal, Y.W. again changed his account, claiming he acted at the applicant’s request but only to frighten M.G. The Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 18 June 2008 and upheld the conviction. It found that, despite the divorce, she had maintained family-like relations with A.G. and expressed annoyance at M.G. before others. This finding rested explicitly on the unread 2002 pre-trial statements of L.G., A.At., A.A. and A.B. Those witnesses were never called or examined at trial or on appeal (L.G. having been excluded; the others not listed). The applicant had no opportunity to confront them.

She appealed on points of law, arguing the Court of Appeal had used unexamined, unread statements in violation of fair-trial rights. The Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible (15 December 2008). After a Constitutional Court ruling on related procedural issues, proceedings were reopened but again declared inadmissible (25 September 2009), with the Cassation Court citing the same statements (particularly L.G. and A.A.) as supporting guilt.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Court of Appeal’s reliance on these untested pre-trial statements, without reading them in court or allowing her to examine the witnesses, denied her a fair trial. Domestic law (CCP Articles 20, 86, 105, 332, 339, 342, 358, 393) addresses witness privileges, the requirement that judgments be based on evidence examined in court, and limited circumstances for reading prior statements (e.g., witness absence). The core alleged violation centres on the use of these statements as a basis for upholding her conviction without the safeguards of confrontation or publicity.

**Case summary: Karajanov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 2229/15), ECHR judgment of 6 April 2017**

Petar Karajanov (born 1936), a former high-ranking communist-era official who held no public office and was not a candidate at the relevant time, was the subject of lustration proceedings under the 2012 Lustration Act. On 27 May 2013 the Fact Verification (Lustration) Commission, acting on a third-party request and of its own motion, found that he had collaborated with State security bodies. Relying on two State Archives files, it concluded he had provided information “in a conscious, secret, organised and continuous manner as a secret collaborator,” thereby meeting the statutory criterion for restricting his eligibility for or exercise of public office. File no. 6825 recorded that in 1963, after a visit to his brother in Sweden, he had supplied information about his brother, sister-in-law and others, and that the services intended to continue the relationship; a 1964 note mentioned him sharing impressions with his father. File no. 2599 recorded that, as a newspaper editor-in-chief from 1962, he had informed on a colleague’s articles and contacts. The Commission published its decision (containing his place of birth, personal identification number and former posts) on its website on 30 May 2013 and served it on him on 4 June 2013.

Karajanov challenged the decision before the Administrative Court on 11 June 2013. He produced documentary evidence of mistaken identity regarding file no. 6825: his birth certificate showed a different date of birth; a notarised inheritance decision established he had a sister, not a brother; his military card placed him in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout 1963; his father’s death certificate showed death in 1962; and he had lived in Skopje since 1955 and never visited Sweden. He also contested the authenticity and legal sufficiency of file no. 2599 (unsigned documents that failed to meet the Act’s definition of conscious, secret, organised and continuous collaboration for material benefit or career favours) and complained that publication of his father’s name (not authorised by the Act) had damaged his reputation, dignity and personal integrity.

On 29 January 2014 the Administrative Court dismissed the claim after a private hearing. It held that the Commission had correctly established the facts from the archival documents, that the applicant’s identity was confirmed by the personal details cited, and that the documents had been drawn up according to the security services’ own rules. It stated that any doubts about authenticity should have been litigated before the Commission’s decision and that the applicant had produced no evidence altering the facts. On 7 March 2014 Karajanov appealed to the Higher Administrative Court, repeating his identity evidence, lack of adversarial examination, absence of an oral hearing, failure to address the private-life complaint, and the fact that he had been unaware of the files until after the Commission’s decision. On 12 June 2014 the Higher Administrative Court dismissed the appeal, endorsing the lower court’s findings and noting that the Commission merely verified the existence of archival documents, which were treated as facts, without adversarial proceedings.

The applicant alleged that these proceedings had been unfair and had violated the presumption of innocence, and that the publication and findings had breached his right to respect for private life. The 2012 Lustration Act (later repealed in 2015) required immediate website publication of collaboration findings and personal data; domestic courts treated the secret-service files as conclusive without independent scrutiny or an opportunity for the applicant to confront the evidence. A 2010 Constitutional Court ruling had already invalidated similar publication provisions in the predecessor 2008 Act as disproportionate to the aim of barring former collaborators from office. Council of Europe materials, including a 2012 Venice Commission opinion, likewise criticised pre-final-judgment publication as damaging reputation without an effective remedy.

The case concerns lustration proceedings against Petar Karajanov (born 1936), a former high-ranking communist-era official who held no public office and was not seeking any at the relevant time. On 27 May 2013, acting on a third-party request and its own motion, the Fact Verification (Lustration) Commission found that Karajanov had collaborated with State security bodies. Relying on two State Archive files, it concluded that he had provided information about individuals in a conscious, secret, organised and continuous manner as a secret collaborator, thereby meeting the statutory criterion under the 2012 Lustration Act for restricting access to public office.

File no. 6825 recorded that in 1963, after visiting his brother in Sweden, Karajanov had supplied information about his brother, sister-in-law and others, and had been engaged by the services beforehand. File no. 2599 recorded that while editor-in-chief of a newspaper in 1962 he had informed on a colleague’s articles and contacts. The Commission’s decision, containing his full name, personal identification number, date and place of birth, positions held and the supporting documents, was published on its website on 30 May 2013 (as required by sections 29 and 31 of the Act) and served on him on 4 June 2013.

Karajanov sought judicial review in the Administrative Court, arguing mistaken identity in file 6825. He produced a birth certificate showing a different date of birth, a notarised inheritance decision confirming he had a sister rather than a brother, a military card proving he was serving in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1963, and a death certificate showing his father had died in 1962. He stated he had never visited Sweden and had lived in Skopje since 1955. He denied any collaboration recorded in file 2599, noting the absence of any signature by him and arguing that the documents did not satisfy the statutory definition of collaboration (section 18). He further complained that publication of the decision, including his father’s name (not required by the Act), damaged his reputation, dignity and private life.

On 29 January 2014 the Administrative Court dismissed the claim after a private hearing, holding that the Commission had correctly established the facts and applied the law. It treated the archive documents as reliable because they had been drawn up according to security-service rules and observed that Karajanov could have challenged their authenticity in separate proceedings before the Commission’s decision. It found no need for an oral hearing.

Karajanov appealed to the Higher Administrative Court, reiterating the identity error, the lack of adversarial examination of the documents, the absence of reasoning on the “conscious, secret, organised and continuous” criteria, the impossibility of requesting an oral hearing, and the unaddressed privacy complaint. On 12 June 2014 the Higher Administrative Court upheld the lower decision, noting that the Commission’s procedure was non-adversarial and that security-service documents were regarded as established facts.

The 2012 Lustration Act (later repealed in 2015) required immediate publication of findings of collaboration. The Constitutional Court had earlier invalidated a comparable publication provision in the predecessor 2008 Act as disproportionate. The Venice Commission had likewise criticised pre-judicial publication as incompatible with Article 8.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints that the lustration proceedings were unfair (no oral hearing, no proper scrutiny of evidence or authenticity, non-adversarial process), violated the presumption of innocence, and interfered with his private life through premature public stigmatisation.

**Case Summary: Karajanov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (ECHR, Application no. 2229/15)**

Petar Karajanov, a Macedonian national born in 1936 and a former high-ranking communist-era official (holding no public office at the relevant time), was subjected to lustration proceedings. On 27 May 2013, the Fact Verification Commission, acting on a third-party request and its own motion, found that he had collaborated with State security bodies. Relying on two State Archives files, it concluded he had provided information about individuals “in a conscious, secret, organised and continuous manner as a secret collaborator,” thereby meeting the 2012 Lustration Act criteria for restricting his eligibility for public office.

File no. 6825 recorded that after a 1963 visit to his brother in Sweden, the applicant supplied information about his brother, his brother’s wife and others, having been engaged by security services beforehand; he later shared impressions with his father. File no. 2599 indicated that, as a newspaper editor-in-chief in 1962 and afterwards, he informed services about a colleague’s articles and relationships. The Commission’s decision, containing the applicant’s place of birth, personal identification number and former positions, was published on its website on 30 May 2013 (pursuant to sections 29 and 31 of the Act) and served on him on 4 June 2013.

On 11 June 2013 the applicant sought judicial review in the Administrative Court. He argued mistaken identity regarding file 6825, submitting a birth certificate (different date), an inheritance decision (showing a sister, not a brother), his military card (confirming 1963 service in Bosnia and Herzegovina), and his father’s 1962 death certificate; he had never visited Sweden and had lived in Skopje since 1955. He challenged the authenticity of file 2599 documents (none signed by him) and denied any collaboration meeting the Act’s criteria of conscious, secret, organised and continuous cooperation involving human-rights violations for personal benefit. He also complained that website publication, including his father’s name (not required by the Act), damaged his reputation, dignity and personal integrity.

On 29 January 2014 the Administrative Court, sitting in private, dismissed the claim. It held that the Commission had correctly established the facts from archival documents confirming collaboration and favours received, using the applicant’s identification number, birthplace and offices. It stated he could have accessed the documents and initiated separate proceedings to contest their veracity before the decision, and that they were drawn up according to security-service rules. A private hearing sufficed because the facts derived from written material and no contradictory evidence had been adduced.

The applicant appealed to the Higher Administrative Court on 7 March 2014, repeating his identity and authenticity arguments, noting the lower court’s failure to address the private-life complaint or analyse evidence adversarially, the absence of any explanation why the statutory collaboration criteria were met, the lack of a right to request an oral hearing, and that he had been unaware of the documents until served with the decision. On 12 June 2014 the Higher Court dismissed the appeal, endorsing the lower findings and observing that the Commission merely verified collaboration without adversarial proceedings, treating security-service documents as established facts.

These proceedings formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints of unfairness (including the presumption of innocence) and violation of private life under the European Convention on Human Rights. The 2012 Act (repealed in 2015) mandated immediate website publication of collaboration findings, including personal data, while defining collaboration as requiring written consent and specific elements that the applicant contested had not been proven. A prior Constitutional Court ruling had already invalidated similar publication provisions in the 2008 Act as disproportionate to lustration aims.

The applicant, a German national residing in Hamburg, married A.S. in 1970. The couple lived in Hamburg from 1980 and acquired a rented apartment there. In 1992 they moved to Riga, where they purchased an apartment that became the applicant’s registered Latvian address, while retaining their Hamburg residence. Around 1999–2000 the applicant returned to the Hamburg apartment; the couple remained in telephone and postal contact and signed a 2000 agreement regulating their separated lives. Her Latvian residence permit expired in 2002 or 2003.

On 5 December 2003 A.S. petitioned the Riga City Ziemeļu District Court for divorce. He stated that he had last seen the applicant in 2000, that the marriage was irretrievably broken, that he had telephoned her to announce the intended proceedings and invite any property claims (which she declined to discuss), and that her last known address was the Riga apartment. Because of their disagreements he claimed he could not discover her current whereabouts and therefore requested service by Official Gazette.

The court first sent a summons to the Riga apartment; postal authorities reported she no longer lived there. It then published notices in the Official Gazette summoning her to hearings on 1 March and (after postponement) 6 April 2004. At the April hearing the court found service lawful under the Civil Procedure Law, proceeded in her absence, heard two witnesses (one of whom later married A.S.) who confirmed they had not seen her since 2000, and granted the divorce. The judgment became final on 27 April 2004. A.S. married one of the witnesses the next day and died on 30 April. The applicant first learned of the divorce when she travelled to Riga for the funeral.

A German authority subsequently refused to recognise the Latvian judgment, finding that A.S. had known the applicant’s Hamburg address (evidenced by correspondence and pension payments) and that she had been denied an opportunity to be heard.

On the applicant’s request the President of the Latvian Supreme Court lodged a supervisory-review protest, arguing that the first-instance court had overlooked evidence of her Hamburg domicile, had failed to use alternative notification methods permitted by law (publication in a Hamburg newspaper or service via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), and had thereby violated Article 6. On 16 March 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the protest. It held that the court had complied with the Civil Procedure Law because the claim itself contained no Hamburg address; publication in a foreign newspaper was merely optional for the plaintiff; and a reference to Article 6 could not justify setting the judgment aside once A.S. had died (rendering further proceedings impossible) and had contracted a new marriage that could not be annulled.

The parties disputed whether A.S. had actually known the Hamburg address and whether the applicant had been informed of the proceedings by telephone. Subsequent property proceedings brought by the applicant against A.S.’s widow remain incompletely documented.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints under Article 6: that defective service deprived her of access to court, of a fair hearing, of public pronouncement of the judgment and of equality of arms.

The case of Schmidt v. Latvia (Application no. 22493/05) involves a German applicant, Heide Lydia Friedel Schmidt (born 1938, resident in Hamburg), who alleged violations of her Article 6 rights (access to court, fair hearing, judgment pronouncement, and equality of arms) arising from Latvian divorce proceedings conducted without her participation.

The applicant married A.S. in 1970. The couple lived in Hamburg from 1980 (renting an apartment from 1986) before relocating to Riga in 1992 while retaining the Hamburg address. They acquired a Riga apartment (the applicant's then-registered Latvian address). Around 1999–2000 the applicant returned to Hamburg; contact continued by telephone and post. On 15 December 2000 they signed an agreement “with a view to regulating their separated life.” The applicant’s Latvian residence permit expired in 2002 or 2003.

On 5 December 2003 A.S. filed for divorce in the Riga City Ziemeļu District Court. He stated he had last seen the applicant in 2000, the marriage was effectively over, he had telephoned her about his intention and invited written property claims (which she refused), and her last known address was the Riga apartment. Because of disagreements he could not obtain a current address and requested summons by Official Gazette notice.

The court first posted a summons to the Riga apartment. After postal confirmation that she no longer lived there, notices were published in the Official Gazette for a 1 March 2004 hearing (postponed at A.S.’s request) and a 6 April 2004 hearing. At the latter the court held that statutory summons requirements had been met, proceeded in the applicant’s absence, heard two witnesses (who had not seen her since 2000), and granted the divorce. No appeal was lodged; the judgment became final on 27 April 2004.

A.S. married one of the witnesses (A.A.) the next day and died the day after. The applicant first learned of the divorce when she travelled to Riga for the funeral.

German authorities refused recognition of the Latvian judgment on 27 July 2004, finding the applicant had not been afforded an opportunity to present her case. They noted A.S. knew her Hamburg address from ongoing correspondence and pension/insurance transfers.

On 8 November 2004 the President of the Latvian Supreme Court applied for supervisory review, arguing the first-instance court had overlooked evidence of the Hamburg domicile and had misapplied summons rules (publication in a Hamburg newspaper or service via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was required). The application invoked Article 6. On 16 March 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the protest. It held that the claim contained no address, so Gazette service complied with the Civil Procedure Law; extra publication was merely a plaintiff’s optional right. Article 6 could not justify quashing. Moreover A.S.’s death precluded fresh proceedings, and his subsequent marriage could not be annulled even if the divorce were set aside.

The parties disputed whether A.S. actually knew the Hamburg address (applicant pointed to telephone use, pensions and a shared bank account; the Government relied on A.S.’s court statements) and whether the applicant knew of the proceedings themselves (the Government cited A.A.’s later testimony of a telephone warning; the applicant said she knew only of A.S.’s wish to divorce). In 2005 the applicant sued A.A. for half the marital property and won at first instance; the appeal outcome is unknown.

These facts—particularly the method of service, the court’s knowledge (or lack thereof) of the Hamburg address, the impossibility of later challenge after A.S.’s death and remarriage, and the German non-recognition—underpin the alleged Article 6 violations.

The case of Schmidt v. Latvia (Application no. 22493/05) concerns a German national, Heide Lydia Friedel Schmidt (born 1938, residing in Hamburg), who alleged that Latvian courts violated her rights under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, she claimed infringements of her rights of access to a court, to a fair hearing, to the pronouncement of a judgment, and to equality of arms in divorce proceedings initiated by her husband, A.S.

The couple married in 1970 and lived in Hamburg from 1980, later acquiring a rented apartment there. In 1992 they moved to Riga, where they purchased an apartment that became the applicant’s registered Latvian address, while retaining their Hamburg residence. Around 1999–2000 the applicant returned to Hamburg; the couple remained in contact by telephone and post. A document signed by both on 15 December 2000 referred to regulating their “separated life,” though its contents are unknown. The applicant’s Latvian residence permit expired in 2002 or 2003.

On 5 December 2003 A.S. filed for divorce in the Riga City Ziemeļu District Court. He stated that he had last seen the applicant in 2000, that the marriage had effectively ended, and that he had informed her by telephone of his intention to divorce (though she refused to discuss property claims). He listed her last known address as the Riga apartment and, citing disagreements, claimed he could not determine where to send summonses, requesting instead that she be summoned by notice in the Official Gazette.

The court first sent a summons to the Riga apartment. After postal authorities confirmed she no longer lived there, it published notices in the Official Gazette summoning her to hearings on 1 March 2004 (later postponed) and 6 April 2004. At the latter hearing the court, satisfied that service complied with the Civil Procedure Law, proceeded in her absence. After hearing two witnesses (including A.A.) who said they had not seen the applicant since 2000, it granted the divorce. The judgment became final on 27 April 2004, no appeal having been lodged. A.S. married A.A. the next day and died on 30 April 2004. The applicant learned of the divorce only upon attending his funeral.

German authorities later refused to recognise the Latvian judgment, finding that A.S. had known the applicant’s Hamburg address (evidenced by correspondence and pension transfers) and that she had been denied an opportunity to present her case.

The President of the Latvian Supreme Court subsequently sought supervisory review, arguing that the first-instance court had overlooked evidence of the applicant’s Hamburg domicile and had failed to apply proper service rules (including possible publication in a Hamburg newspaper or service via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs). On 16 March 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the application. It held that, because A.S.’s claim had not indicated any Hamburg address, the first-instance court had been unaware of her whereabouts and had complied with the Civil Procedure Law. Fresh adjudication was in any event impossible: A.S. had died, and his subsequent marriage to A.A. could not be annulled even if the divorce were set aside.

The parties disputed whether A.S. actually knew the applicant’s Hamburg address (she pointed to their shared telephone line, bank account and pension payments) and whether she had been informed of the proceedings themselves (she maintained she learned of them only after A.S.’s death). Subsequent civil proceedings she brought against A.A. concerning marital property were granted at first instance; their further outcome is unknown.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that she had been deprived of any real opportunity to participate in the divorce proceedings that dissolved her marriage and affected her property rights.
