The case of V.K. v. Russia originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 February 2008 by a Russian national born in 1946 and resident in St Petersburg. He alleged that his involuntary admission to a psychiatric hospital violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention because the authorities failed to satisfy the provision’s substantive requirements, and Article 5 § 4 because of procedural defects in the judicial authorisation of that admission.

The applicant’s medical history recorded mental-health problems since 1979, including organic, psychiatric and personality disorders (psychosis and paranoia), alcohol abuse, suicide attempts, threats of violence against neighbours and medical staff, and repeated involuntary hospitalisations. Between 1998 and 2007 he was admitted at least six times after suicide attempts, alcohol-induced paranoia, unfounded reports of murder threats or planted explosives, and a threat to explode a petrol canister.

In March 2007 the local ambulance service recorded twelve emergency calls from his home (five on a single day), none of which disclosed any medical emergency. He behaved aggressively toward staff, made sexual advances to female doctors and consumed alcohol in their presence; the service therefore requested police escorts and noted that such visits delayed genuine life-saving work. A police report of 2 April 2007 recorded three further false alerts in two days (attacks by nomadic tribes, an unexploded wartime shell and explosives at an industrial site), all of which were investigated and found baseless.

On 3 April 2007 the applicant was admitted without his consent to St Petersburg Psychiatric Hospital No. 3. The stated grounds were the repeated groundless reports of explosives, the sexual propositions and threats directed at ambulance personnel, and his refusal of voluntary treatment. The same day a panel of resident psychiatrists examined him and his records, diagnosed an organic mental disorder combined with a psychiatric and paranoid personality disorder, and concluded that he was a danger to himself and others and that, without inpatient care, his condition was likely to deteriorate significantly. They relied on sections 29(a) and (c) of the 1992 Psychiatric Assistance Act. The panel noted his long-standing uncritical attitude, delusional ideas of personal importance and persecution, and history of involuntary admissions.

On 4 April the hospital applied to the Primorskiy District Court for an order authorising continued involuntary placement. On 9 April the court granted the application after a hearing attended by the applicant, a court-appointed lawyer (Mrs L.), the psychiatrists and the prosecutor. The court reviewed the medical history and heard testimony concerning alcohol abuse, erratic behaviour, frivolous police calls and threats to staff. The applicant insisted that reporting explosives was a civic duty and complained about hospital conditions. The court accepted the panel’s unchallenged conclusions that a severe psychiatric disorder created a risk of significant health damage in the absence of treatment and found no contrary evidence.

The applicant was discharged on 20 April 2007 after clinical improvement. On 25 April, now represented by a privately retained lawyer, he appealed, arguing that the legal-aid lawyer had failed to perform her functions. The St Petersburg City Court dismissed the appeal on 2 August 2007 in a brief decision that upheld the lower court’s reliance on the psychiatrists’ report and held that any shortcomings of the appointed lawyer could not invalidate an order that was lawful on the merits.

Nothing in the case file indicated that the applicant had ever been deprived of legal capacity or placed under guardianship. These facts formed the basis of his complaints that the substantive criteria for deprivation of liberty under Article 5 § 1 had not been met and that the judicial procedure under Article 5 § 4 had been defective.

The case of V.K. v. Russia (Application no. 9139/08) concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights by a Russian national born in 1946, alleging that his involuntary admission to a psychiatric hospital in St Petersburg violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty) because the authorities failed to meet its substantive requirements, and Article 5 § 4 (right to a speedy court review of detention) due to procedural flaws in the judicial authorisation process.

The applicant had a documented history of mental health issues dating to 1979, including organic, psychiatric and personality disorders, psychosis, paranoia, alcohol abuse, suicide attempts, and threats of violence toward neighbours and medical staff. He had been hospitalised at least six times between 1998 and 2007 following such incidents, including claims of murder threats, planted explosives, and threats to detonate a petrol canister.

In March 2007 the applicant made twelve emergency ambulance calls (five on a single day), all without apparent medical need. He behaved aggressively toward staff, made sexual advances to female doctors, and drank alcohol in their presence. The ambulance service requested police escorts for future visits, citing delays to genuine emergencies and risks to personnel. On 2 April 2007 he contacted police three times in two days with unfounded reports of attacks by nomadic tribes, an unexploded wartime shell, and explosives at an industrial site; all alerts proved baseless.

On 3 April 2007 he was admitted without consent to St Petersburg Psychiatric Hospital no. 3. Grounds included the repeated false police reports, ambulance calls involving sexual offers, and threats of violence. A same-day panel of hospital psychiatrists examined him and his records, diagnosing an organic mental disorder with paranoid personality features. They concluded he posed a danger to himself and others and risked significant health deterioration without treatment, citing his lack of insight, ideas of grandeur and persecution, history of aggression and self-harm, and recent inappropriate conduct. The panel invoked sections 29(a) and (c) of the 1992 Psychiatric Assistance Act.

The hospital applied for a court order the next day. On 9 April 2007 the Primorskiy District Court granted involuntary hospitalisation after a hearing attended by the applicant, a court-appointed lawyer (Mrs L.), the psychiatrists and a prosecutor. The court reviewed the medical history and heard the doctors describe severe alcohol abuse, erratic behaviour, frivolous police calls and threats. The applicant insisted the police reports were a civic duty, complained about hospital conditions, and mentioned media connections. The court accepted the panel’s findings of a severe disorder risking health damage without treatment and found the application well-founded; it noted no contrary evidence and recorded that the lawyer considered inpatient treatment reasonable.

The applicant was discharged on 20 April 2007 after improvement. On 25 April he appealed, now represented by a new lawyer, arguing among other points that Mrs L. had failed to discharge her duties properly. The St Petersburg City Court dismissed the appeal on 2 August 2007 in a brief decision, holding that the first-instance order was lawful on the merits and that any alleged shortcomings by the legal-aid lawyer did not warrant annulment. The applicant had never been deprived of legal capacity or assigned a guardian.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: whether the medical and behavioural evidence satisfied the Convention’s substantive criteria for deprivation of liberty on grounds of unsound mind, and whether the judicial proceedings (including the quality of legal representation and the appeal) afforded an adequate and effective review of the detention’s lawfulness.

The case of V.K. v. Russia (Application no. 9139/08) concerned a Russian national born in 1946 who alleged that his involuntary psychiatric hospitalization in April 2007 violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (unlawful detention due to failure to satisfy substantive requirements for confinement of persons of unsound mind) and Article 5 § 4 (procedural defects in the judicial review of that detention).

The applicant had a documented history of mental disorders dating to 1979, including organic, psychiatric and personality disorders, psychosis and paranoia, together with alcohol abuse, suicide attempts and threats of violence. Between 1998 and 2007 he had been hospitalized at least six times after suicide attempts, alcohol-induced paranoia, and unfounded claims of murder threats, planted explosives and plans to detonate a petrol canister.

In March 2007 the applicant made twelve groundless emergency-ambulance calls, five of them on a single day. He behaved aggressively toward staff, made sexual advances to female doctors and consumed alcohol in their presence; the ambulance service therefore requested a police escort, citing delays to genuine emergencies and danger to personnel. On 2 April 2007 he contacted the police three times in two days, alleging attacks by nomadic tribes, discovery of an unexploded wartime shell and explosives at an industrial site; all reports proved false.

On 3 April 2007 he was admitted, without consent, to St Petersburg Psychiatric Hospital No. 3. The stated grounds were the repeated false bomb reports, the ambulance calls accompanied by sexual propositions, and threats of violence against medical staff. A hospital psychiatric panel examined him the same day, diagnosed an organic mental disorder with a paranoid personality disorder, and concluded that he posed a danger to himself and others and risked significant deterioration of his health without treatment. The panel noted his lack of insight, uncorrected ideas of persecution and self-importance, and history of involuntary admissions.

The hospital applied the following day for a court order under section 29(a) and (c) of the 1992 Psychiatric Assistance Act. On 9 April 2007 the Primorskiy District Court, after a hearing attended by the applicant, a court-appointed lawyer (Mrs L.), the psychiatrists and a prosecutor, granted the application. It relied on the panel report, the psychiatrists’ testimony concerning alcohol abuse, erratic conduct and threats, and the absence of contrary evidence. The St Petersburg City Court dismissed the appeal on 2 August 2007 in a brief decision, holding that the first-instance order was lawful on the merits because the psychiatric evidence established a severe disorder carrying a risk of health damage; the complaint about legal representation did not warrant annulment. The applicant had never been deprived of legal capacity or placed under guardianship.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: whether the medical and behavioural evidence reliably established that the applicant was of unsound mind and that detention was necessary to prevent danger or deterioration (Article 5 § 1), and whether the judicial proceedings—particularly the quality of appointed counsel and the appellate court’s reasoning—afforded an effective review of the lawfulness of the detention (Article 5 § 4).
001-173098:
The applicant company, publisher of the Moscow housing-market newspaper Kvartirnyy Ryad, faced civil defamation liability after printing a 20 May 2004 article by journalist G. entitled “So sorry for the bird. The blue one.” The piece described resident complaints, sent to courts, prosecutors, city officials and even President Putin, about alleged misuse of common areas (especially attics) in eight blocks of flats belonging to the Bluebird commonhold association. It portrayed T.—simultaneously the association’s head and deputy head of a Moscow district council—as having launched an “indecently hasty business activity spitting in the face of the association’s Charter and a number of regional and federal laws.” Additional passages asserted that T. had rejected an elected commission, appointed his own (thereby securing a third term), and concluded a contract despite lacking majority support. The article closed with a rhetorical question whether a State official could lawfully combine public office with commercial activity. T. had declined pre-publication comment.

T. sued the company and G. on 28 May 2004 under Article 152 of the Civil Code, claiming the statements harmed his honour, dignity and business reputation. On 8 December 2004 the Presnenskiy District Court partially upheld the claim. It ordered retraction solely of the “indecently hasty \ldots laws” passage because the defendants had not proved T.’s conduct unlawful. Although witnesses described an attic lease as irregular, the court noted the absence of conclusive proof of illegality and relied on a 19 May 2004 Zyuzinskiy District Court ruling that the association’s actions (headed by T.) complied with law. The remaining statements were held non-defamatory or purely rhetorical. Non-pecuniary damages of 10 000 RUB were awarded against the company and 8 000 RUB against G.

The Moscow City Court affirmed on 4 May 2005, reiterating that the defendants bore the burden of proving the contested statement true and that the Zyuzinskiy judgment confirmed legality. Supervisory-review leave was refused on 25 July 2005; enforcement was completed by 13 October 2005.

Domestic law (Constitution Art. 29; Civil Code Art. 152; Supreme Court Resolutions 11/1992 and 3/2005) treated untrue allegations of legal or ethical breach as actionable, placed the proof burden on the publisher, and (after 2005) distinguished facts from value judgments. The Committee of Ministers’ 2004 Declaration on political debate underscored that public officials must tolerate robust media scrutiny of their official conduct. These events constitute the interference with the applicant’s Article 10 rights that formed the core of the Strasbourg complaint.

The case of OOO Izdatelskiy Tsentr Kvartirnyy Ryad v. Russia (Application no. 39748/05) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by a Moscow-based publishing company, the publisher of the newspaper Kvartirnyy Ryad, which specialized in reporting on the local housing market. The applicant alleged a violation of its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention arising from domestic defamation proceedings.

On 20 May 2004 the newspaper published an article by journalist G. entitled “So sorry for the bird. The blue one.” The piece concerned a dispute within the large commonhold association Bluebird, comprising eight blocks of flats in south-west Moscow. It reported that numerous residents had written to courts, prosecutors, the city administration and even the President complaining about T., the association’s head (who was also deputy head of a local district council). The article asserted that T. had “developed an indecently hasty business activity spitting in the face of the association’s Charter and a number of regional and federal laws,” in particular by unlawfully leasing common areas such as attics. It further claimed that T. had distrusted and bypassed a commission elected by the general meeting, instead appointing his own commission, thereby securing a third term; that he had concluded a contract despite lacking a majority of votes; and it posed a rhetorical question whether a State official could properly combine official duties with commercial activity. T. had declined to comment before publication.

On 28 May 2004 T. instituted defamation proceedings against the applicant company and G. under Article 152 of the Civil Code, claiming the statements damaged his honour, dignity and business reputation. On 8 December 2004 the Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow partially upheld the claim. It held that the defendants had failed to prove the truth of the assertion that T.’s actions were unlawful, noting that a contemporaneous judgment of the Zyuzinskiy District Court of 19 May 2004 had found the association’s (and thus T.’s) actions lawful. The court therefore ordered the applicant company to publish a retraction of the impugned statement and awarded T. 10 000 roubles in non-pecuniary damages from the company (and a further 8 000 roubles from G.). Other passages—concerning the appointment of the commission and the rhetorical question—were found not to be defamatory.

The Moscow City Court dismissed the appeal on 4 May 2005, confirming that the defendants had not established the veracity of the contested statement and relying again on the Zyuzinskiy judgment. A request for supervisory review was rejected, and the judgment was fully enforced.

Relevant domestic law placed the burden of proving the truth of disseminated statements on the defendant. A later Supreme Court resolution distinguished statements of fact (actionable if untrue) from value judgments (not actionable). Council of Europe materials stressed that public officials must accept close scrutiny and robust criticism concerning the exercise of their functions.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic courts’ findings and sanctions constituted an unjustified interference with press freedom on a matter of public interest involving a public official.

The case of OOO Izdatelskiy Tsentr Kvartirnyy Ryad v. Russia (application no. 39748/05) was brought to the European Court of Human Rights by a Moscow-based publishing company, alleging a violation of its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant published the newspaper Kvartirnyy Ryad, which specialized in the Moscow-area housing market.

On 20 May 2004 the newspaper ran an article by journalist G. titled “So sorry for the bird. The blue one.” It described a conflict in the large Bluebird commonhold association, which managed eight apartment blocks in southwest Moscow. The piece claimed that residents had been harmed by the alleged misuse of common areas, especially attics, and identified T.—the association’s head and also deputy head of a Moscow district council—as responsible. T. had declined to comment before publication. The article accused T. of having “developed an indecently hasty business activity spitting in the face of the association’s Charter and a number of regional and federal laws.” It further stated that T. had appointed his own commission rather than allowing an elected one, thereby securing a third term and concluding a contract despite lacking a majority of votes. It ended with a rhetorical question: whether a state official could combine official functions with commercial activity.

On 28 May 2004 T. sued the applicant company and G. for defamation in the Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow, claiming the statements damaged his honour, dignity and business reputation. On 8 December 2004 the court partially allowed the claim under Article 152 of the Civil Code. It ordered retraction of the passage alleging unlawful business activity, because the defendants had not proved that T.’s actions violated the Charter or any laws. Although witnesses spoke of an unlawful attic lease, the court noted that the Zyuzinskiy District Court had already ruled on 19 May 2004 that the association’s actions under T. were lawful. The remaining statements—about the commission and the rhetorical question—were held not to be damaging or to constitute non-actionable opinion. The applicant was ordered to pay T. 10 000 roubles (about €270) in non-pecuniary damages and G. 8 000 roubles.

The Moscow City Court upheld the judgment in full on 4 May 2005, confirming that the defendants had failed to prove the veracity of the contested statement and relying on the earlier Zyuzinskiy ruling. A request for supervisory review was rejected and the judgment was enforced.

Article 29 of the Russian Constitution guarantees freedom of expression and of the media. Article 152 of the Civil Code places the burden on the publisher to prove the truth of any statement alleged to be damaging. Supreme Court resolutions in force at the time required courts to distinguish verifiable statements of fact from value judgments, the latter not being actionable.

These events formed the factual basis of the alleged Article 10 violation: a civil sanction imposed on a specialist newspaper for reporting on a matter of public concern—the management of common property and the conduct of a dual-role public official—after the domestic courts treated the core accusation as an unproven fact rather than protected journalistic comment.
001-173351:
The case of Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania (applications nos. 61467/12, 39516/13, 48231/13 and 68191/13) concerns four Romanian nationals who alleged violations of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to inhuman and degrading conditions of detention in various prisons and police facilities. The applicants—Daniel Arpad Rezmiveș (born 1970), Laviniu Moşmonea (born 1966), Marius-Gheorghiţă Mavroian (born 1976), and Iosif Gazsi (born 1972)—lodged their complaints between September 2012 and October 2013. Three remained detained at the time of the judgment (in Timişoara, Pelendava, and Baia Mare prisons), while Mavroian was released in January 2015.

Rezmiveș was held in Gherla Prison from April 2011 to March 2012, then Aiud and Oradea prisons until December 2012, before transfer to Timişoara. He cited overcrowding (1.60–2.22 m² per prisoner), insufficient natural light, brief daily exercise, and absent recreational activities.

Moşmonea entered pre-trial detention in Craiova Prison in February 2008, remaining there post-conviction until May 2012, followed by Târgu-Jiu and then Pelendava prisons. He complained of poor conditions across all three facilities, consistent with systemic issues of space shortages and inadequate amenities.

Mavroian was admitted to Rahova Prison in December 2009, with subsequent transfers to Tulcea, Iași, and Vaslui prisons. His complaints focused on Rahova, including overcrowding, poor ventilation, wall mould, low-quality food, and bedbugs.

Gazsi spent March–May 2012 in Baia Mare police detention (lacking toilets, running water, natural light, ventilation; infested with rats; limited showers) before Gherla Prison, where he alleged overcrowding, inadequate ventilation, poor food served in rusty containers, and one bathroom (two toilets, no hot water, cleaned monthly) for 27 inmates.

The Court identified these as raising a structural problem of overcrowding and deficient material conditions across Romania’s prison system, prompting consideration of the pilot-judgment procedure. National statistics from the National Prison Administration showed chronic overcrowding: 33,434 inmates in December 2013 against 18,820 capacity, with occupancy rates of 149–154% (calculated at 4 m² per detainee under Order no. 433/2010). Actual space often fell far below this, as confirmed by People’s Advocate inspections (e.g., 1 m² at Miercurea-Ciuc; 1.21–2.52 m² at Târgu-Jiu; infestations, unfit water, and unsanitary facilities at multiple sites).

Domestic law (Law no. 254/2013, replacing earlier legislation) allowed complaints to post-sentencing judges for non-compliance with accommodation standards, with appeal to district courts. New 2014 Criminal and Procedure Codes introduced alternatives like house arrest, judicial supervision, and sentence waivers or suspensions, alongside probation reforms. A 2016 bill proposed sentence remissions (three days per 30 days in overcrowded cells) as compensation.

Council of Europe materials underscored the issues. Committee of Ministers recommendations (R(99)22, Rec(2006)2) stressed deprivation of liberty as a last resort, community sanctions, and minimum standards for space, light, ventilation, and hygiene. CPT reports from visits (1995–2014) documented persistent overcrowding (often under 3–4 m²), dilapidated cells, poor sanitation, inadequate food, limited out-of-cell time, and unsuitable police facilities for prolonged detention. A 2016 White Paper on prison overcrowding advocated decriminalization, alternatives to custody, and early release to address root causes.

These facts formed the basis for alleged Article 3 violations, highlighting both individual hardships and a systemic failure to meet Convention standards. The judgment became final on 25 July 2017.

The European Court of Human Rights examined four applications by Romanian nationals Daniel Arpad Rezmiveș, Laviniu Moşmonea, Marius-Gheorghiţă Mavroian and Iosif Gazsi alleging that their detention conditions in Romanian prisons and police facilities violated Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment).

Rezmiveș (detained 2011–2013 in Gherla, Aiud and Oradea prisons) reported living space of only 1.60–2.22 m² per person, insufficient natural light, brief outdoor exercise and no recreational activities. Moşmonea (held from 2008 in Craiova, Târgu-Jiu and Pelendava prisons) complained of similar shortcomings across those establishments. Mavroian (detained 2009–2015 in Rahova, Tulcea, Iași and Vaslui prisons) described overcrowding, unventilated cells, mould, poor food and bedbugs, especially in Rahova. Gazsi (held March–May 2012 in Baia Mare police cells, then Gherla prison) cited absent toilets, running water, light and ventilation, rat infestation and limited showers in the police facility, plus overcrowding, poor ventilation, rusty food containers and one bathroom (two toilets, no hot water, cleaned monthly) shared by 27 inmates in Gherla.

These accounts reflected a systemic crisis. National Prison Administration figures showed occupancy of approximately 150 % (28 000 prisoners in 18 820 places) when calculated against the official 4 m² standard; actual space frequently fell to 1–2.5 m². The People’s Advocate documented comparable problems—overcrowding, infestations, inadequate sanitation, lighting and furniture—in numerous other prisons.

Council of Europe bodies had long recorded the same failings. CPT visits (1995–2014) found police cells (often basement locations) and prisons overcrowded, dilapidated, poorly lit and ventilated, with unpartitioned toilets, insufficient hygiene products, inadequate food and almost no out-of-cell activity. The Committee of Ministers, supervising earlier judgments, described the situation as giving rise to “serious concerns” and noted that 2014 legislative reforms (new Criminal and Procedure Codes introducing house arrest, judicial supervision and expanded parole; Law 254/2013 allowing complaints to post-sentencing judges) had not produced a lasting reduction in the prison population or effective remedies. A 2016 draft law offering sentence remissions for time spent in overcrowded cells remained pending.

The Court therefore treated the applications as raising a structural problem and applied the pilot-judgment procedure.

The case of Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania (applications nos. 61467/12, 39516/13, 48231/13 and 68191/13) concerns four Romanian nationals—Daniel Arpad Rezmiveș (b. 1970), Laviniu Moşmonea (b. 1966), Marius-Gheorghiţă Mavroian (b. 1976) and Iosif Gazsi (b. 1972)—who complained under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights of inhuman and degrading conditions during their detention in various Romanian prisons and police facilities. The Court identified a structural problem of overcrowding and poor material conditions across the Romanian prison system and applied the pilot-judgment procedure.

Rezmiveș was held from April 2011 in Gherla Prison (until March 2012), then Aiud, Oradea (April–December 2012) and Timişoara Prisons. He alleged living space of only 1.60–2.22 m² per prisoner, insufficient natural light, brief daily exercise and a lack of recreational activities. Moşmonea was placed in pre-trial detention in Craiova Prison in February 2008, remaining there after conviction until May 2012, then transferring to Târgu-Jiu and Pelendava Prisons; he complained of inadequate conditions in all three. Mavroian entered Rahova Prison in December 2009 and was later transferred to Tulcea, Iași and Vaslui Prisons. He cited overcrowding, poor ventilation, mould, low-quality food and bedbugs, especially at Rahova. Gazsi was held in the Baia Mare police detention facility from March to May 2012 before transfer to Gherla Prison. In the police facility he reported no toilet or running water, lack of natural light and ventilation, rats and insufficient showers; in Gherla he alleged overcrowding, poor ventilation, inadequate and poorly presented food, and one bathroom (two toilets, no hot water, cleaned monthly) shared by 27 detainees.

National Prison Administration statistics confirmed systemic overcrowding: 33,434 detainees on 31 December 2013 against a capacity of 18,820 places (occupancy rates remaining around 149–154 % through 2016, calculated on a 4 m² standard). The People’s Advocate documented comparable deficiencies—living space as low as 1 m², infestations, insufficient furniture, unsanitary washrooms and unfit water—in multiple prisons including Miercurea-Ciuc, Târgu-Jiu, Jilava, Galaţi, Botoşani and Pelendava.

Domestic law provided a complaint mechanism to a post-sentencing judge (Law no. 254/2013) and civil-liability actions, together with new alternatives to imprisonment under the 2014 Criminal Code and Code of Criminal Procedure. Council of Europe bodies, however, found these measures inadequate. The Committee of Ministers, reviewing the Bragadireanu group of cases, described prison overcrowding and police-cell conditions (basement locations, poor ventilation and light, limited out-of-cell time) as giving rise to “serious concerns.” CPT reports from 2010 and 2014 recorded cells below 3–4 m², dilapidated sanitary facilities, vermin, inadequate food, and almost no activities; police facilities were deemed unsuitable for prolonged detention. A 2016 White Paper on Prison Overcrowding and Committee of Ministers recommendations emphasised the need for reduced reliance on custody, better community sanctions and effective remedies.

These facts underpinned the applicants’ claims that their detention conditions reached the Article 3 threshold of severity. The Court treated the applications as representative of a widespread structural deficiency requiring general measures.

001-173251:
The case of Olisov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 10825/09, 12412/14 and 35192/14) involves three Russian applicants who alleged that police subjected them to ill-treatment after arrest to extract confessions, with no effective investigation of their complaints.

Mr Olisov was detained at about 2 a.m. on 17 May 2006 following a UBOP sting operation in which informants (acting under police instruction) claimed they had killed a target on his orders and demanded payment. At the UBOP office he was interrogated for hours by several officers demanding a confession. He alleged they handcuffed him, punched him, nearly suffocated him with a plastic bag (causing repeated fainting), forced his legs apart, lifted him by shackled hands, tied him in a painful position, dropped him onto his coccyx and stepped on his head. He later signed an “explanation”. No arrest record was drawn up. Hospital records the next day showed multiple bruises; subsequent examinations confirmed two vertebral fractures. Forensic reports found the injuries consistent with his account of blunt-force trauma around the time alleged, though one later opinion held the fractures could not have resulted from the specific acts described.

A pre-investigation inquiry refused to open a criminal case, citing police denials, statements from others present who heard nothing, and Olisov’s temporary mental-health diagnosis; injuries were attributed to possible accident or self-infliction. Subsequent refusals were issued and some annulled as incomplete. Courts upheld the refusals, noting the time elapsed made examination of the premises pointless. Olisov was convicted of attempted murder. In 2015 a refusal was annulled for incompleteness.

Mr Danishkin’s flat was searched on 25 December 2010; explosives were found and he was taken to the Centre for Combating Extremism. After an initial witness interview (no visible injuries noted), officers demanded a confession to preparing a terrorist act. He alleged they punched and kicked him, bound him with rope so that knots pressed on his neck (causing suffocation), lifted and dropped him, and punched his face until it bled. Injuries (facial bruises/abrasions, abdominal and axillary bruises) were recorded at hospital and detention facilities. Police claimed they used force only to stop an escape attempt, causing him to fall.

Forensic reports indicated the injuries could have resulted from either beating or the force described by officers and were reachable by the applicant himself. Six refusals to open a case (several revoked as incomplete) accepted the police version of lawful force. Courts upheld the last refusal. In 2015 it was annulled because the applicant’s contrary account had not been investigated. He was convicted of illegal explosives storage.

Mr Zontov was arrested on 27 August 2011 for robbery after fleeing plain-clothes officers. At the station he alleged officers punched him, beat his feet and torso with a truncheon for about 40 minutes while pinning him down, stepped on his feet and suffocated him with a plastic bag for hours until he signed a confession. Injuries (chest bruises, facial/waist abrasions, wrist injuries) were recorded on admission to detention. Relatives confirmed he had none beforehand. He later retracted the confession, citing ill-treatment.

Over 14 refusals attributed the injuries to falls during flight and lawful handcuffing/force during resistance. Forensic reports found the injuries consistent with his account and unexplained by the police version (especially chest and foot bruises). One investigator opened a case in 2014; a prosecutor annulled it. Later refusals followed. A 2015 prosecutor noted four years of incomplete inquiries violating reasonable-time requirements. Zontov was convicted of robbery; the court admitted the confession and dismissed the ill-treatment claim. A psychologist later diagnosed PTSD.

The facts centre on alleged police violence to obtain confessions, documented injuries whose timing and nature supported the applicants’ accounts, and protracted domestic inquiries that repeatedly accepted officers’ denials without thorough investigation.

The case of Olisov and Others v. Russia concerns three applications (nos. 10825/09, 12412/14 and 35192/14) by Russian nationals Aleksandr Olisov, Nikita Danishkin and Yuriy Zontov. Each alleged that, after arrest on suspicion of crimes, police subjected them to ill-treatment to extract confessions, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, and that the ensuing investigations were ineffective.

Olisov was taken to the Orenburg UBOP at about 2 a.m. on 17 May 2006 following a sting operation in which he paid supposed hitmen who had shown him staged photographs of a victim’s “death.” He claimed officers (including M., G. and O.) handcuffed him, punched him, nearly suffocated him with a plastic bag (causing him to faint repeatedly), forced his legs apart, bound him in a painful “knees-to-neck” position, lifted and dropped him onto his coccyx, and stepped on his head. He later signed an “explanation.” Released without an arrest record, he was hospitalised the next day with extensive bruises and, subsequently, fractures of two vertebrae (including the seventh thoracic vertebra, causing medium-gravity harm). Forensic reports confirmed injuries consistent with blunt trauma at the time and in the manner he described; a later report noted that the spinal fracture could result from axial force along the spine. Multiple pre-investigation inquiries produced refusals to open a criminal case, relying on officers’ denials, the absence of eyewitnesses, and Olisov’s temporary mental-health diagnosis. Some refusals were annulled as incomplete, but a 2008 refusal was ultimately upheld. Olisov was convicted of attempted murder and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment; an additional inquiry was ordered in 2015.

Danishkin’s flat was searched on 25 December 2010; explosives were found and he was taken to the Nizhniy Novgorod Centre for Combating Extremism. After initial questioning as a witness (when no injuries were noted), officers (T., K., A., S., Sh. and later others) allegedly beat him, bound him with rope so that his legs were pressed to his torso, lifted him (causing near-suffocation), dropped him, and punched him in the face. He was then formally arrested. Officers claimed they had used force only to prevent an escape attempt, tripping him and causing abrasions. Injuries (bruises and abrasions to the face, neck, abdomen and elsewhere) were recorded at hospital, the IVS and SIZO. Forensic reports indicated the injuries could have been caused by punches/kicks or by the officers’ described use of force, and that some were within the applicant’s reach. Six refusals to investigate (most later revoked as incomplete) accepted the officers’ account of lawful force. Danishkin was convicted of illegal possession of explosives. A 2012 refusal was annulled in 2015 for failure to examine his version of events.

Zontov was apprehended on 27 August 2011 by plain-clothes officers for a robbery; he fled, believing they were not police. At the station he alleged officers (including O. and A.) punched him, beat his feet with a truncheon for about 40 minutes while pinning him down, struck his torso, stepped on his feet and suffocated him with a plastic bag for hours (causing repeated fainting). He signed a confession and “explanation.” Injuries (bruises to the chest and feet, abrasions to the face, waist and wrists) were recorded at the IVS, traumatology centre and SIZO. Relatives confirmed he had been uninjured beforehand. He later retracted the confession. Forensic reports found the injuries consistent with his account of blunt trauma (including a limited-contact surface on the wrists); while some abrasions could have resulted from a fall or handcuffs, bruises on the chest and feet remained unexplained by the officers’ version. Numerous refusals to open a case accepted that force and handcuffs had been used lawfully during resistance to arrest. An investigator’s 2014 decision to open proceedings under Article 286 of the Criminal Code was quashed by a prosecutor. Zontov was convicted of robbery; the confession was treated as a mitigating factor. Subsequent inquiries noted years of delay and a psychologist diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder.

In all three cases the domestic authorities repeatedly declined to open full criminal investigations, relying primarily on the officers’ denials and offering incomplete or implausible alternative explanations for medically documented injuries.

The case of Olisov and Others v. Russia concerns three applications to the European Court of Human Rights by Russian nationals Aleksandr Olisov, Nikita Danishkin and Yuriy Zontov. They alleged that, after being taken into police custody on suspicion of crimes, they were subjected to ill-treatment aimed at extracting confessions, and that domestic authorities failed to conduct effective investigations into their complaints.

Olisov was taken to the Orenburg UBOP office at around 2 a.m. on 17 May 2006 following a staged operation in which he paid individuals who claimed to have murdered a man at his behest. He alleged that officers, including M., G. and O., interviewed him until 7.30 a.m., demanding a confession. They handcuffed him, punched him, placed a plastic bag over his head causing repeated fainting, forced his legs apart, lifted him by shackled hands, tied him in a position pressing his knees to his neck, dropped him onto his coccyx and stepped on his head. No arrest record was drawn up. He was released later that day after signing an “explanation.” The following day hospital records documented extensive bruises to his head, neck, abdomen and lumbar region. A forensic examination confirmed bruises and abrasions inflicted by hard blunt objects consistent with the timing of his account. He was later diagnosed with fractures of two vertebrae, including the seventh thoracic vertebra causing medium-gravity harm. Subsequent expert opinion indicated the spinal injury resulted from axial force rather than punches or kicking. Pre-investigation inquiries produced multiple refusals to open a criminal case, citing officers’ denials of violence, statements from others present who saw or heard nothing, and Olisov’s temporary mental-health diagnosis. These refusals were repeatedly annulled as incomplete. Olisov was convicted of attempted murder in October 2008; his entrapment claim was rejected. A 2008 refusal to investigate was upheld by courts, though later annulled in 2015 for incompleteness.

Danishkin’s flat in Nizhniy Novgorod was searched on 25 December 2010, yielding explosives. After being taken to the Centre for Combating Extremism and questioned as a witness (with no visible injuries noted), he alleged that officers T., K., A., S. and Sh. beat, punched and kicked him, bound him with rope so that his legs were pressed to his torso, lifted him causing neck constriction and suffocation, then dropped him. Two further officers joined; one punched his face, splitting his lip. The episode lasted until around 8 p.m. He was formally arrested later that night. Officers claimed any injuries arose from lawful force used when he tried to flee. Hospital and detention-facility records documented facial contusions, bruises and abrasions on the face, neck, abdomen and axillary region. Forensic reports classified the injuries as blunt trauma possibly inflicted by punches or kicks, or alternatively by the force described by officers; some injuries were reachable by the applicant’s own hands. Multiple refusals to open a criminal investigation, later revoked as incomplete, ultimately attributed the injuries to lawful restraint during an escape attempt. Courts rejected Danishkin’s challenge. He was convicted of illegal explosives storage. A 2015 prosecutorial decision again found the inquiry incomplete.

Zontov was apprehended on 27 August 2011 on suspicion of street robbery. He alleged that, at the Orenburg police station, officer O. and others punched his chest, struck his feet for forty minutes with a rubber truncheon while pinning him, then applied a plastic bag causing repeated fainting over several hours until he signed a confession. Detention records and hospital notes documented bruises to the chest, face, waist, wrists and feet. Relatives and an acquaintance confirmed he had been uninjured beforehand. He promptly retracted his statements, attributing them to ill-treatment. Officers maintained that injuries resulted from falls while fleeing and lawful use of handcuffs. Numerous refusals to investigate were annulled as incomplete. Forensic reports in 2013–2014 found the injuries consistent with the applicant’s account of blunt-force trauma and unexplained by the officers’ version as regards chest and foot bruises. An investigator opened a case in 2014, but a prosecutor immediately quashed the decision. Subsequent refusals were again annulled. Zontov was convicted of robbery; the trial court relied on an un-annulled refusal and treated his confession as a mitigating factor. A 2015 psychologist’s report diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder linked to the alleged events and lack of redress. A prosecutor later criticised the four-year delay as a flagrant violation.

001-173490:
The case of Bože v. Latvia (Application no. 40927/05) concerns a Latvian national, Valdis Bože (born 1958, resident in Riga), who alleged that an unauthorised search of his apartment on 11 June 2004, together with the seizure of personal belongings, violated Article 8 of the Convention. He further claimed a lack of effective remedies under Article 13.

In May 2004 the Ministry of Health informed the State police that Bože was selling unlicensed pharmaceutical products online, advertised as treatments for HIV, hepatitis C and cancer. After an initial refusal to investigate (on the basis that samples contained no narcotics), officers of the economic-crime department conducted an undercover test purchase on 11 June 2004. They bought ten bottles from Bože at a nearby pizzeria and immediately recorded that, because his apartment was also the registered address of his company Baltijas elektronikas izstrādes, he “voluntarily agreed” to an inspection and to show the equipment used to manufacture the products.

The same officers then entered the three-room apartment. Additional personnel from the organised-crime department, an expert and press officers later joined them. The inspection lasted five hours. Bože stated that he had produced the products at home since early 2004 after pharmaceutical companies declined to cooperate; he admitted selling about fifty packs and knowing that a licence was required. Officers seized a computer, a hard drive and production materials (chemicals, bottles, labels). The entire operation was video-recorded and photographed. The inspection record, drawn up on a standard criminal-procedure form citing Articles 179–183 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, catalogued the layout of the apartment and the contents of shelves, boxes and the refrigerator.

A subsequent forensic examination found no narcotics but established that the computer contained extensive data on production, distribution and client correspondence. Two sets of administrative-offence proceedings were opened: one for unlicensed business activity (remitted to the State Revenue Service) and one for selling unlicensed pharmaceuticals (remitted to the State Pharmacy Inspectorate).

Bože lodged numerous complaints with the police Internal Security Office, prosecutors and later the administrative courts, asserting that the operation had been an unlawful search without judicial authorisation. An internal police inquiry concluded there had been no violation; the officers had merely inspected company premises with the owner’s consent under section 12(1)(23) of the Law on the Police and had seized items that were in plain view. Prosecutors initially expressed doubts: one supervising prosecutor noted that the Code of Administrative Offences provided no legal basis for an inspection of a private dwelling and that several provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure had been breached. Later decisions of the Prosecutor General’s Office, however, upheld the police action, citing either the inspection provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code or the Police Law. Bože’s requests to institute criminal proceedings against the officers were refused; statutory time-limits for disciplinary action had expired. Claims for compensation were likewise dismissed, with the applicant being directed to civil courts.

In the administrative proceedings Bože was fined LVL 200 for unlicensed manufacturing; the seized production materials were confiscated and destroyed. After a brief interlude of criminal proceedings (later discontinued for lack of evidence), the Revenue Service reimposed an identical administrative sanction. The administrative courts ultimately confirmed the lawfulness of the police entry, holding that officers had acted under the Police Law to inspect company premises and to prevent administrative offences. A separate fine of LVL 500 for selling unlicensed products was also upheld.

The computer was retained in the criminal file; the hard drive was later offered for return. Bože’s numerous subsequent complaints to prosecutors (sixty-two in total) were largely unsuccessful.

The case of *Bože v. Latvia* (Application no. 40927/05) concerned a Latvian national, Valdis Bože (born 1958, resident in Riga), who alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He complained of an unauthorised search of his apartment and seizure of personal belongings on 11 June 2004, with no effective domestic remedies available.

In May 2004, a Ministry of Health official informed State police that the applicant was selling unlicensed pharmaceutical products (advertised as treatments for HIV, hepatitis C and cancer) via the internet. Other police departments had declined to investigate after a sample showed no narcotic or dangerous substances. On 11 June 2004, economic crime police officers conducted an undercover test purchase: they contacted the applicant via the advertised email address, met him at a pizzeria near his home, and bought ten bottles for 50 Latvian lati (about EUR 70). A record of the operation, signed by four officers and the applicant, stated that he had voluntarily agreed to an inspection of his apartment (also the registered address of his company, Baltijas elektronikas izstrādes) to show the tools used to fabricate the medicaments.

Immediately afterwards, the same officers (later joined by organised crime officers, an expert and press officers) inspected the applicant’s three-room apartment for five hours. The applicant explained that he had produced the products at home since early 2004 after pharmaceutical companies refused to cooperate, had sold about fifty packs, and knew a licence was required but could not afford one. Officers seized a computer, hard drive, chemical substances, spare bottles and labels; they video-recorded the inspection, took photographs, packed and sealed the items, and compiled a detailed record listing the apartment’s layout, contents of shelves, boxes and fridge. The record used a standard form citing Articles 179–183 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (governing inspections of crime scenes, premises, objects or documents, which could occur even before criminal proceedings were instituted).

A forensic examination found no narcotics or psychotropics but confirmed the computer contained extensive data on production, distribution and client emails. Police then instituted two sets of administrative offence proceedings: one for unlicensed business operations (remitted to the State Revenue Service, VID) and one for selling unlicensed pharmaceuticals (remitted to the State Pharmacy Inspectorate). The VID initially fined the applicant LVL 200 (about EUR 300) and confiscated/destroyed items; after criminal proceedings were opened then terminated for lack of evidence, the VID reimposed an identical fine. Administrative courts upheld this, finding the applicant had engaged in unlicensed manufacturing for profit. The Pharmacy Inspectorate separately fined him LVL 500 (about EUR 700), a decision upheld through three levels of jurisdiction.

The applicant lodged numerous complaints alleging an unlawful search without judicial authorisation. An internal police inquiry (July 2004) and subsequent decisions found no violations, classifying the action as a voluntary inspection of company premises under section 12(1)(23) of the Law on the Police (allowing visits to private company premises to prevent economic crime, inspect facilities and take samples) or sections 10(1)(6)–(7) and 12(1)(4),(24) (duties to prevent administrative offences and rights to seize prohibited items). Prosecutors issued mixed views: one (April 2005) found no legal basis under the Code of Administrative Offences and breaches of the Code of Criminal Procedure; later decisions (2009) upheld the inspection under the Police Law or Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 179 and 183, noting the seized items were visible and no search had occurred. Criminal proceedings against officers were refused; statutory deadlines for disciplinary action expired. Administrative courts declined competence over the pre-proceedings police actions but confirmed their lawfulness. Claims for compensation were dismissed, with civil proceedings suggested but their outcome unknown.

Relevant domestic law distinguished searches (requiring a reasoned decision and judicial authorisation under Code of Criminal Procedure Article 168, except in urgent cases) from inspections (Article 179) and from police powers over company premises. Entry to residential premises generally required judicial authorisation except in specified emergencies (Police Law section 12(1)(16)). The Code of Administrative Offences allowed police examination of persons and objects with a record, but not home inspections as such.

The case originated in an application by Valdis Bože, a Latvian national living in Riga, alleging an unauthorised search of his apartment and seizure of belongings on 11 June 2004, in breach of Article 8 ECHR, and a lack of effective remedies under Article 13.

In May 2004 the Ministry of Health informed police that the applicant was selling unlicensed pharmaceuticals online, advertised as treatments for HIV, hepatitis C and cancer. After other police units declined to investigate (no narcotics detected), officers from the economic crime department made a test purchase on 11 June 2004, buying ten bottles from him at a nearby pizzeria for 50 LVL. A record signed by the officers and the applicant stated that, because his company Baltijas elektronikas izstrādes was registered at his home address, he “voluntarily agreed” to an inspection of the apartment to show the tools used to fabricate the products.

Immediately afterwards the same officers, later joined by organised-crime officers, an expert and press-centre staff, inspected the three-room apartment for five hours. The applicant stated he had produced the products at home since early 2004 after pharmaceutical companies refused to cooperate, had sold about fifty packs, and knew a licence was required. Police seized a computer, hard drive, chemical substances, spare bottles and labels. The operation was video-recorded and photographed; the inspection record (drawn on a Code of Criminal Procedure form citing Articles 179-183) listed the apartment’s layout and the detailed contents of shelves, boxes and the fridge.

Forensic examination found no narcotics but extensive production-related files and client emails on the computer. Two sets of administrative-offence proceedings followed: unlicensed business operations (remitted to the State Revenue Service) and sale of unlicensed pharmaceuticals (remitted to the State Pharmacy Inspectorate).

The applicant lodged repeated complaints asserting that the “search” lacked judicial authorisation. An internal police inquiry concluded there had been no violation: officers had merely verified facts after the test purchase and, with consent, inspected company premises under section 12(1)(23) of the Law on the Police; seized items were in plain view, so the Criminal Procedure Code had not been breached. The applicant did not appeal those decisions internally. Prosecutors’ replies were inconsistent. One noted that the Administrative Offences Code provided no basis for an inspection and that Criminal Procedure Code rules had been breached. Later decisions held the measures lawful under sections 10 and 12 of the Law on the Police (prevention of administrative offences and inspection/seizure of company premises). Requests to prosecute the officers were refused; the disciplinary time-limit had expired. Compensation claims to the Prosecutor General were dismissed, the applicant being told to bring a civil action.

The Revenue Service first fined the applicant 200 LVL and confiscated/destroyed the items. A prosecutor then instituted criminal proceedings (unlicensed business), the administrative decision was revoked, but the criminal case was later terminated for lack of evidence and remitted. An identical administrative decision was issued; appeals were dismissed. The District Administrative Court treated the 2004 actions as occurring in criminal proceedings (outside its competence) but found no unlawfulness. The Regional Administrative Court (final 2010) held that officers had acted under the Law on the Police to inspect company premises and prevent administrative offences; the evidence was therefore lawful. It confirmed unlicensed manufacturing aimed at profit (website, emails, pricing) and imposed the lowest possible fine. A separate 500 LVL fine for selling unlicensed products was upheld through three administrative-court instances.

The applicant complained to prosecutors on 62 occasions, mostly about the administrative or criminal files. These facts centre on the disputed character of the apartment entry (alleged consent versus a warrantless search of the home), the scale of the intrusion and seizures, the shifting legal justifications offered by the authorities, and the applicant’s unsuccessful attempts to obtain redress.
001-173778:
The case of Kość v. Poland (Application no. 34598/12) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. Mr Jarosław Kość, a Polish national born in 1942 and resident in Tomaszów Mazowiecki, was held civilly liable for statements contained in a petition he sent to a district official concerning the financial management of a former village mayor.

On 29 September 2010 a village meeting in Jadwigów voted by a majority of fifteen residents to hold the previous local mayor, Z.M., to account for his handling of public funds. The residents appointed the applicant to pursue the matter. On 7 October 2010 the applicant forwarded a document entitled “Petition” to the mayor of the Tomaszów Mazowiecki District. The petition, co-signed by three other residents, asserted that Z.M. had received commune grants and lease payments from the village shop, had managed those funds arbitrarily without consulting residents or the local council, had used the money for renovation of the community hall, had never disclosed accounts, and had kept the hall inaccessible to villagers and their children for ten years. The applicant alluded to unspecified rumours but declined to repeat them out of respect for the addressee’s office. He requested a full explanation.

The petition was dispatched shortly before local elections held on 21 November 2010, in which both the applicant and Z.M. stood as candidates (neither was elected). An audit committee of the Tomaszów Mazowiecki Commune Council subsequently examined the document and concluded that there were no grounds for alleging mismanagement of funds.

Z.M. instituted civil proceedings in the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court for infringement of his personal rights, seeking a published apology and payment of PLN 4 000 to the Voluntary Fire Brigade. On 31 May 2011 the Regional Court found that the petition contained untrue statements that damaged Z.M.’s reputation. It established that any lease payments had been received by Z.M. in his capacity as chairman of the Fire Brigade (the owner of the building that housed both the shop and the hall), not as local mayor; that the hall had in fact been open for public use; that renovation costs had been met directly by the commune rather than from village funds; and that no cash payments had been made to Z.M. or anyone else. Because the applicant had failed to prove the truth of his accusations, the court held that he had unlawfully infringed Z.M.’s personal rights and ordered him to send a written apology by post to the district mayor, the commune office and Z.M.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the petition constituted an expression of legitimate public-interest concerns. On 4 November 2011 the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It characterised the statements as false assertions of fact rather than mere expressions of doubt and attached decisive weight to their timing: they had been made almost three years after Z.M.’s term had ended and during an election campaign in which the applicant himself was a candidate. The appellate court therefore concluded that the petition had not been motivated by the public interest but by electoral considerations.

A writ of enforcement was issued in March 2012. The applicant’s subsequent attempts to have the enforcement order set aside on the ground that the matter was pending before the Strasbourg Court were unsuccessful. On 21 January 2011 the applicant himself was elected local mayor of Jadwigów.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the civil judgment and the order to apologise constituted an unjustified interference with his right to freedom of expression.

The case of Kość v. Poland (Application no. 34598/12) originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Polish national Jarosław Kość, alleging a violation of his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant, born in 1942 and resident in Tomaszów Mazowiecki, was represented by a Warsaw lawyer; the Polish Government was represented by an agent from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court communicated the Article 10 complaint on 19 January 2015 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

On 29 September 2010, a village meeting in Jadwigów saw fifteen residents vote to hold the former local mayor, Z.M., accountable for his management of public funds. They appointed the applicant to pursue the matter. On 7 October 2010, the applicant submitted a signed “Petition” (co-signed by three other residents) to the district mayor. The document stated that Z.M. had received commune grants and village-shop lease payments during his term, managed the funds arbitrarily without consulting residents or the local council, and used them for community-hall renovations. It alleged he had never disclosed accounts and that the hall had been inaccessible to residents and children for ten years. The applicant indicated he had already raised the issues with the current local mayor and commune mayor, and he requested a full explanation. The petition was sent shortly before local elections on 21 November 2010, in which both the applicant and Z.M. stood (unsuccessfully) as candidates.

An audit committee of the Tomaszów Mazowiecki Commune Council later found no grounds to allege mismanagement of funds. On 14 December 2010 Z.M. brought a civil action against the applicant in the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court for infringement of personal rights, seeking a published apology and payment of 4,000 PLN to the Voluntary Fire Brigade (VFB). On 31 May 2011 the Regional Court found a violation and ordered the applicant to send a written apology to the district mayor, the commune office and Z.M., retracting the allegations that Z.M. had arbitrarily managed village funds, taken shop-lease payments in his capacity as mayor, and that the hall had been unavailable for ten years.

In its fact-finding the court established that any lease payments had been received by Z.M. as VFB chairman (the shop and hall being located in a VFB-owned building), that rent was paid to the VFB via its treasurer, and that Z.M. merely set the annual amount. The hall had been open for public use (contrary to some witness testimony), building works had occurred without cash payments to any individual including Z.M., the village had received no direct commune funds, and the commune itself had financed the renovations. Because the applicant had failed to prove the truth of his statements, which had an adverse effect, a violation of personal rights was made out.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the petition served the public interest. On 4 November 2011 the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the publication of false information necessarily violated personal rights. It rejected the characterisation of the text as mere expressions of doubt and found that the timing—nearly three years after Z.M.’s term and during an electoral campaign in which Z.M. had been unsuccessful—demonstrated that the action was motivated by the applicant’s desire to win office rather than by genuine public interest. Enforcement proceedings followed; attempts by the applicant to have the enforcement order quashed on the ground of a pending Strasbourg application were unsuccessful. The applicant was himself elected local mayor of Jadwigów on 21 January 2011.

The interference with the applicant’s expression consisted of the civil finding of liability and the ordered apology for statements contained in a petition addressed to a public authority concerning the conduct of a former local official. Domestic courts treated the statements as statements of fact that had been shown to be untrue and that lacked a sufficient public-interest justification given their timing and alleged electoral motive. These facts formed the core of the Article 10 complaint.

The case of Kość v. Poland (ECtHR Application no. 34598/12) concerns a complaint by Jarosław Kość, a Polish national born in 1942 and residing in Tomaszów Mazowiecki, alleging a violation of his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The application was lodged on 28 May 2012; only the Article 10 complaint was communicated to the Government.

On 29 September 2010, a village meeting in Jadwigów saw 15 residents vote to hold former local mayor Z.M. accountable for public-fund management. They appointed the applicant to pursue the matter. On 7 October 2010—before 21 November local elections in which both men were unsuccessful candidates—the applicant sent a signed “Petition” (also endorsed by three residents) to the Tomaszów Mazowiecki district mayor. The document recounted the meeting and alleged that Z.M., while in office, had received commune grants and village-shop lease payments, managed the money arbitrarily without consulting residents or the council, spent it on community-hall renovations, never produced accounts, and kept the hall inaccessible to residents and children for ten years. Rumours were alluded to but not specified. A request for a full official explanation was made.

A commune audit committee later found no grounds for alleging mismanagement. On 14 December 2010 Z.M. sued the applicant in the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court for infringement of personal rights, seeking a newspaper apology and PLN 4,000 for the Voluntary Fire Brigade (VFB).

On 31 May 2011 the Regional Court held that the petition contained false statements that damaged Z.M.’s reputation. It ordered the applicant to post a written apology to the district mayor, the commune office and Z.M., retracting the claims that Z.M. had arbitrarily managed village funds, taken lease payments in his mayoral capacity, and kept the hall closed for ten years. The court established that lease payments went to the VFB (of which Z.M. was chairman and merely set the annual rent); the shop and hall occupied a VFB-owned building; the hall had in fact been open (contrary witness evidence being rejected); no cash had been received for works; and the village itself had received no direct commune funds (the commune having paid for the renovations). The applicant had not proved the truth of the accusations, whose adverse effect therefore constituted a civil wrong.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the petition served the public interest. On 4 November 2011 the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that dissemination of false information violates personal rights and that the petition was not a mere expression of doubt. Timing—concerns raised almost three years after Z.M.’s term ended and during an electoral campaign—showed the motive was electoral advantage, not public interest.

A writ of enforcement issued on 1 March 2012; the applicant’s subsequent attempts to have it quashed because of the pending Strasbourg application were unsuccessful. The applicant himself was elected village mayor on 21 January 2011.

These facts—the content and timing of the petition, the domestic courts’ findings of factual inaccuracy, and the civil order to retract—constitute the interference complained of under Article 10.
