The case of Ónodi v. Hungary (no. 38647/09) involved a Hungarian father's complaint that authorities failed to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his daughter, breaching Article 8 of the Convention.

Gábor Ónodi married N.R. in 1990; their daughter R.Ó. was born in 1994. They divorced in March 2006 under a Szolnok District Court-approved agreement placing the child with the mother and granting the applicant contact every other weekend, holidays (including Easter, Whit Monday, post-Christmas, and three summer weeks). He paid child support of at least HUF 20,000 monthly. The mother relocated to Budapest.

Contact occurred only on 25-26 June and 24 July 2006. The 12-year-old daughter was reluctant, preferring grandparents. The mother viewed visits as the child's choice. The applicant sought enforcement from the Szolnok County Guardianship Authority, which on 11 September 2006 ordered compliance, warning of fines and travel-cost reimbursement. Strained relations prompted child-protection proceedings on 27 December 2006. The mother was repeatedly fined. Contact resumed from July 2007 to November 2008.

In 2007 the mother sued to restrict contact and raise support; the applicant counterclaimed for custody and filed a child-endangerment complaint. Stabilization efforts failed, so meetings were ordered at a child-protection centre.

On 10 June 2008 the District Court reduced contact to the first and third Saturdays (09:00-18:00), citing implementation difficulties, an expert's view that an adaptation period was needed, and the 14-year-old's wishes; custody was refused. On 19 November 2008 the Regional Court adjusted this to every other Saturday (09:00-16:00) until 31 May 2009, then full weekends every other weekend.

In 2009 the applicant missed many visits and was fined HUF 10,000. On 29 January 2010 the District Court recorded no contact since November 2008; the guardianship authority had declined enforcement because the applicant had not addressed the daughter's request to travel by public transport rather than car. No circumstances warranted change.

On 15 April 2010 the Regional Court allowed every-other-weekend contact, with the now-16-year-old travelling independently; a support reduction was refused. The Supreme Court dismissed review on 8 February 2011. Meetings were sporadic in 2010 and absent in 2011 despite repeated enforcement applications.

In 2011 the applicant alleged bias; the Budapest Regional Guardianship Authority reassigned the case to another district body, noting eight pending requests dating to January 2010. Support liability later ended (2012-2013), but earlier payments were not reimbursed.

These events—initial non-compliance, repeated fines without lasting effect, successive court modifications that still went unenforced, multi-year delays, and authorities' inaction despite numerous requests—underpinned the Article 8 claim of ineffective protection of family life.

The case of Ónodi v. Hungary (ECHR Application no. 38647/09) concerns a Hungarian father's complaint that national authorities failed to take effective measures to enforce his court-approved contact rights with his daughter, in alleged breach of Article 8 of the Convention (respect for family life).

The applicant married in 1990; the couple's daughter was born in 1994. They divorced in March 2006 pursuant to a court-approved agreement placing the child with the mother and granting the father contact every other weekend, on specified holidays, and for three weeks in summer, plus an obligation to pay child support. The mother relocated from the family home to Budapest.

The father exercised contact on a few dates in June–July 2006, but the daughter (then 12) proved reluctant, preferring time with grandparents. Further visits failed because the mother took the view that the child herself should decide whether to see her father. The father applied to the Szolnok County Guardianship Authority, which in September 2006 ordered the mother to comply and warned of fines and cost-reimbursement. Child-protection proceedings were later opened. The mother was fined on several occasions. Contact in fact occurred between July 2007 and November 2008.

Parallel litigation followed. In 2007 the mother sought to reduce contact and increase support; the father counter-claimed for custody and filed a criminal complaint of child endangerment. A court directed that meetings take place at a child-protection centre. In June 2008 the Szolnok District Court, relying on an expert report that an adaptation period was needed, reduced contact to every first and third Saturday (9 a.m.–6 p.m.) and dismissed the custody claim, citing the child's age (14) and wishes. On appeal the Regional Court further adjusted the timetable (every other Saturday until May 2009, then full weekends thereafter).

In 2009 the father himself missed numerous scheduled visits and was fined. Subsequent proceedings in 2010 recorded that no contact had taken place since the November 2008 judgment; the guardianship authority had taken no enforcement steps because the father had not addressed the child's request to travel by public transport rather than in his car. The courts again refused to alter the contact regime, finding no significant change in circumstances, and in April 2010 granted weekend visits only on condition that the now-16-year-old daughter travel independently. A Supreme Court review petition was dismissed in 2011.

Thereafter contact remained sporadic in 2010 and ceased entirely in 2011 despite repeated enforcement applications. In December 2011, after the father sought the exclusion of local authorities for bias, the case was transferred to a Budapest guardianship office, which noted eight pending enforcement requests, the oldest dating from January 2010. Later proceedings (2012–13) terminated the father's support obligation but refused reimbursement of sums already paid.

These facts illustrate successive reductions in contact, the child's growing autonomy being given increasing weight, the father's own non-attendance, and, above all, protracted delays and limited practical effect of guardianship enforcement measures despite statutory powers to impose fines, involve mediation or child-welfare services, and even seek a change of residence or criminal proceedings. The complaint therefore centred on whether the State had fulfilled its positive obligation under Article 8 to take effective, timely steps to facilitate the father's relationship with his daughter.

The case of Ónodi v. Hungary (Application no. 38647/09) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention due to Hungarian authorities’ failure to effectively enforce the applicant’s contact rights with his daughter.

Gábor Ónodi married N.R. in 1990; their daughter R.Ó. was born in 1994. They divorced in March 2006. The Szolnok District Court approved an agreement placing the child with the mother and granting the applicant contact every other weekend, on specified holidays, and three weeks in summer, plus child support payments of at least HUF 20,000 monthly.

After the mother relocated to Budapest, the applicant had limited contact in June–July 2006. Subsequent attempts failed, as the mother deferred to the child’s wishes. The applicant sought enforcement from the Szolnok County Guardianship Authority, which on 11 September 2006 ordered compliance and warned of fines plus reimbursement of travel costs. Child protection proceedings began in December 2006; the mother was fined repeatedly. Contact occurred from July 2007 to November 2008.

In 2007 the mother sued to restrict contact and increase support; the applicant counterclaimed for custody and lodged a criminal complaint for child endangerment. Court-ordered meetings at a child-protection centre failed to improve relations. On 10 June 2008 the District Court reduced contact to two Saturdays monthly (9 a.m.–6 p.m.), relying on expert evidence that the 14-year-old child’s wishes should be heeded and that prior arrangements were unworkable. The Regional Court on 19 November 2008 adjusted this to every other Saturday until May 2009, thereafter full weekends.

In 2009 the applicant missed numerous visits and was fined HUF 10,000. In January 2010 the District Court dismissed his requests to reduce support and revise contact, noting that no meetings had occurred since November 2008 and that the guardianship authority had declined enforcement because the applicant had not addressed conflicts (e.g., the child’s preference for public transport). A April 2010 Regional Court judgment granted every-other-weekend contact, allowing the now-16-year-old daughter to travel independently; the Supreme Court rejected review in February 2011.

Contact remained sporadic in 2010 and ceased entirely in 2011 despite repeated enforcement applications. In December 2011, citing alleged bias, the Budapest XV District Guardianship Authority was appointed to handle eight pending requests dating from January 2010. The applicant’s support obligation was later terminated (2012–2013), but reimbursement of prior payments was refused.

Domestic law (Government Decree 149/1997) required guardianship authorities to issue enforcement orders within 30 days, impose costs, warn of sanctions, and, for persistent non-compliance, initiate mediation, child-protection measures, or even custody-change proceedings or criminal complaints. The facts show prolonged non-compliance by the mother, successive judicial reductions of contact, the applicant’s own absences in 2009, and delayed or ineffective administrative enforcement despite multiple pending requests.
001-173619:
The case of Bălșan v. Romania (Application no. 49645/09) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Romanian woman's allegations that her husband subjected her to repeated domestic violence and that state authorities failed to prevent or stop it, in breach of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment). The Court later invited observations on a possible violation of Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) read with Article 3, on grounds of gender-based discrimination in the handling of domestic-violence cases.

The applicant, born in 1957, married N.C. in 1979 and had four children. She claimed N.C. had been violent toward her and the children throughout the marriage. The violence intensified in 2007 amid divorce proceedings, which concluded in December 2008. On 24 June, 3 September and 8 September 2007, N.C. physically assaulted and threatened her. Forensic certificates documented bruises, scratches, facial trauma and a nasal contusion requiring between two and ten days of medical care. Police attended each incident, recorded a “domestic dispute,” noted that N.C. had locked her out of their home on one occasion, and merely informed her that she could file a formal complaint.

She lodged criminal complaints in August and October 2007, attaching the medical reports, and wrote to senior police officials seeking protection. Statements from her mother and brother corroborated frequent beatings, threats and lock-outs. Two adult daughters initially told investigators that the applicant drank and became aggressive and that their father had not hit her; N.C. denied assault, suggested she had fallen or forged certificates, and later admitted he “did not hit her so hard as to cause injury.” In December 2007 the prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges, imposing only a 200-lei administrative fine (approximately €50). He found that the applicant had provoked the incidents through alcohol consumption, that N.C. posed no danger to society, and that the threats were unproved.

The applicant appealed unsuccessfully to a superior prosecutor and then to the Petroșani District Court, seeking a conviction, damages and protective measures (including a ban on N.C. entering the apartment or approaching her). She requested legal aid, which was refused. One daughter recanted her earlier statement, testifying that N.C. had beaten the applicant and the children and that she had previously lied under threat. In February 2009 the court acquitted N.C., disregarded the recantation without explanation, attributed the violence to the applicant’s drinking and poor childcare, imposed a 500-lei fine, and dismissed her claim for damages. No ruling was given on the requested protective measures. The Hunedoara County Court upheld the acquittal in May 2009, holding that the violence had been provoked and lacked the gravity of a criminal offence.

Between February and April 2008 the applicant made five further complaints of assault and threats, again supported by medical evidence, and twice asked police to take measures to stop the ongoing violence, stating that she feared for her life. The prosecutor again declined to prosecute, imposing a 100-lei fine, and treated one of her letters as insufficiently specific to constitute a complaint. She did not appeal that decision.

Romanian law at the time (Criminal Code Articles 180 and 193; Law 217/2003) criminalised bodily harm against family members with increased penalties, allowed prosecutions of the authorities’ own motion, and authorised courts to order psychiatric treatment or a ban from the family home. Protection orders became available only in 2012. Official statistics cited in later government documents showed high rates of domestic violence, widespread social acceptance of it as “normal” or “justified,” and very low rates of criminal investigation.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: repeated, medically documented ill-treatment; persistent official minimisation of the violence, victim-blaming, imposition of purely administrative sanctions, refusal to grant protection despite explicit requests and available legal tools, and a broader pattern suggesting that domestic-violence complaints by women were systematically treated as private or insufficiently serious.

The case of Bălșan v. Romania (Application no. 49645/09) concerns a Romanian national, Angelica Camelia Bălşan (born 1957), who alleged that her husband, N.C., subjected her to repeated domestic violence throughout their marriage (from 1979, with four children), which intensified amid 2007 divorce proceedings (finalized 6 December 2008). She claimed Romanian authorities failed to prevent or stop the abuse, violating Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights, the latter due to gender-based bias in handling domestic violence against women.

Key incidents occurred on 24 June, 3 September and 8 September 2007. On 24 June, N.C. punched the applicant in the face and head, threatened to kill her and locked her out of their home. A forensic certificate documented bruises requiring 5–6 days' medical care. On 3 September, further assaults caused ear scratches and bruises needing 2–3 days' care. On 8 September, after another attack, police called an ambulance; she suffered open facial trauma and nasal contusion requiring 9–10 days' care. Police reports noted injuries from a "domestic dispute" and advised her to lodge complaints, but took no further protective steps.

The applicant filed criminal complaints on 3 August and 2 October 2007, attaching medical evidence, and wrote to county police describing repeated violence in front of their children, including lockouts, seeking intervention. Her mother and brother corroborated frequent complaints of beatings and threats. Initially, her adult daughters claimed she drank and became aggressive (one later retracted this, stating N.C. had hit the applicant and children over money issues and that her prior statement was given under his threats; she added the applicant had stopped drinking by 2007). N.C. denied hitting her, attributing injuries to her falling or self-infliction, alleging she drank, neglected the home and children, and that certificates were forged (though he admitted not hitting "so hard as to cause injury").

On 19 December 2007, the prosecutor declined criminal charges for bodily harm, imposing only a 200 RON (~€50) administrative fine. He found the applicant had provoked incidents through alcohol, citing N.C. and the daughters, and deemed the acts insufficiently dangerous to society (N.C. had no record and was retired). Threats were unproven. A superior prosecutor upheld this. The applicant appealed to the Petroșani District Court on 21 April 2008, seeking conviction, damages, and protection (banning N.C. from the apartment or approaching her); she also reported post-decision assaults and submitted a recording (excluded as irrelevant). Denied a court-appointed lawyer, she testified alongside N.C. (who claimed self-defence after she threatened him with a knife while drunk). On 17 February 2009, the court acquitted N.C., imposing a 500 RON fine. It disregarded the daughter's retraction without reasons, held assaults unproven or provoked by the applicant's drinking and childcare failures (thus not socially dangerous), dismissed damages without explanation, and ignored her protection request.

The Hunedoara County Court dismissed her 12 May 2009 appeal, ruling the violence provoked and below the threshold for bodily harm (or damages). Meanwhile, between February and April 2008, the applicant filed five more complaints of assaults/threats (with medical reports) and twice requested police measures, stressing her life was in danger. On 29 September 2008, the prosecutor again declined charges (100 RON fine), treating a general protection request as non-specific. She did not appeal further.

These facts highlight authorities' repeated minimization of documented violence (despite family-aggravated penalties under the Criminal Code and Law 217/2003 on domestic violence, which allowed shelters or home bans but no protection orders until 2012), victim-blaming, failure to investigate thoroughly or provide protection, and persistence of abuse, amid Romania's high unreported domestic violence rates and gender stereotypes.

The case of Bălșan v. Romania (Application no. 49645/09) concerns allegations by Angelica Camelia Bălșan, a Romanian national born in 1957 and resident in Petroșani, that her husband N.C. subjected her to repeated domestic violence and that State authorities failed to prevent it, stop it, or provide effective remedies. The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint primarily under Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), later also considering Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3 on grounds of gender-based discrimination in the handling of domestic violence cases.

The couple married in 1979 and had four children (born 1980, 1988, 1992 and 1999). According to the applicant, N.C. was violent toward her and the children throughout the marriage. Violence intensified in 2007 amid divorce proceedings, which concluded on 6 December 2008.

On 24 June 2007 N.C. punched the applicant in the face and head and threatened to kill her; he later locked her out of their shared apartment. A forensic certificate recorded numerous bruises on her face, arms, back and thorax requiring 5–6 days of medical care. On 3 September 2007 further assaults produced scratches on her ear and bruises on her arm and thighs requiring 2–3 days of care. On 8 September 2007 she suffered an open facial trauma and nasal contusion (9–10 days of care) and was taken to hospital by ambulance after police arrived. Police reports noted injuries from a “domestic dispute” and merely advised her of the possibility of lodging complaints; they recorded that she had been locked out on 24 June.

The applicant filed criminal complaints in August and October 2007, attaching medical certificates, and wrote to the county police chief describing repeated assaults (often in front of the children) and lock-outs. She gave a detailed statement. Her mother and brother confirmed that she frequently sought refuge after beatings, threats or lock-outs. Two adult daughters initially claimed their mother drank and became aggressive and that their father had not hit her. N.C. denied significant violence, suggested she might have fallen, and alleged forged certificates. In December 2007 the prosecutor declined to press charges, imposing only a 200 RON administrative fine (approx. €50). The decision cited the daughters’ statements, attributed the incidents to the applicant’s alcohol consumption and “provocation,” found the threats unproved, and concluded the acts posed no social danger because N.C. had been provoked, had no prior record and was retired. A superior prosecutor upheld the decision.

The applicant challenged the decision in court, seeking conviction, non-pecuniary damages and protective measures (including a ban on N.C. entering the apartment or approaching her). She offered a recording as evidence. The court refused a court-appointed lawyer, excluded the recording and, in February 2009, acquitted N.C. It disregarded one daughter’s later recantation (in which she testified that N.C. regularly beat the applicant and the children, and that her earlier statement had been given under threat). The court again blamed the applicant’s drinking and inadequate childcare, held the acts insufficiently dangerous to constitute crimes, imposed a 500 RON fine and dismissed damages without reasons. It ignored the protection request. An appeal was dismissed on similar grounds of provocation and insufficient severity.

Between February and April 2008 the applicant lodged five further complaints of assaults and threats, supported by medical reports, and twice asked police to take statutory measures because she feared for her life. In September 2008 the prosecutor again declined to prosecute, imposing a 100 RON fine and treating one general request for protection as non-formal because it did not specify a single incident.

At the relevant time Romanian law (Criminal Code Arts. 180 and 193; Law 217/2003) treated violence against family members more seriously, allowed authorities to initiate proceedings of their own motion and provided for protective measures such as shelter, psychiatric detention or a ban from the family home. Protection orders became available only in 2012. Official statistics and reports indicated high prevalence of domestic violence, widespread social tolerance of it, low prosecution rates and inadequate shelters. The applicant’s repeated, medically documented complaints and explicit requests for protection were met with victim-blaming, administrative fines of negligible deterrent value, disregard of recanted testimony and complete failure to apply available protective mechanisms.
001-173621:
The case of Paluda v. Slovakia (Application no. 33392/12) concerns Peter Paluda, a Supreme Court judge, who alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because Slovak courts refused to review the Judicial Council’s decision to suspend him from office.

On 8 September 2009 the Judicial Council—the judiciary’s highest governing body, then chaired by the Supreme Court President—filed disciplinary charges against Paluda for a “serious disciplinary offence.” The charges arose from two acts: Paluda’s criminal complaint accusing the Supreme Court President of abuse of authority, and Paluda’s public statement that case-assignment rules at the Supreme Court had been altered to let the President influence outcomes. The Council proposed revocation of Paluda’s judicial post. On the same day it also suspended him immediately under the Judges and Assessor Judges Act. The suspension, limited to two years, cut Paluda’s salary by 50 per cent and barred him from the workplace except for necessary personnel matters. Restoration of the withheld pay depended on the outcome of the disciplinary case.

Paluda immediately challenged the suspension. He lodged an internal “appeal” with the Council, an administrative-law action, and a constitutional complaint. The Constitutional Court declared the latter inadmissible on 25 November 2009 as premature. The Council’s President later replied that the law provided no internal appeal and that administrative courts could review Council decisions.

The Bratislava Regional Court nevertheless discontinued the administrative action on 13 May 2010; the Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 23 February 2011. Both courts held that the suspension was a merely “preliminary” measure that did not finally determine Paluda’s rights and therefore fell outside judicial review under Article 248(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure (which excludes preliminary or procedural decisions). Paluda then filed a second constitutional complaint alleging that this refusal of review breached Article 6 § 1. On 7 December 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed it as manifestly ill-founded, finding the Supreme Court’s reasoning neither arbitrary nor unsound.

Paluda never invoked the specific statutory remedy that allowed a suspended judge to ask the Council itself to lift the suspension (section 22(5) of the Act), a request the Council would have been obliged to decide within sixty days.

Meanwhile the disciplinary proceedings themselves ended after a 1 May 2011 legislative change made the Minister of Justice a party. The Minister withdrew the charges on 9 May 2011; the Supreme Court, sitting as disciplinary tribunal, discontinued the case on 13 May 2011. Paluda appealed but later withdrew the appeal, so the discontinuation became final on 27 September 2011. The withheld salary was repaid in July 2012.

The central facts for the alleged Article 6 violation are therefore the Council’s power to impose an immediately effective, financially and professionally damaging suspension without any subsequent judicial examination of that measure, the ordinary courts’ classification of the suspension as non-reviewable, and the Constitutional Court’s confirmation of that classification.

The case of Paluda v. Slovakia originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 May 2012 by Peter Paluda, a serving judge of the Slovak Supreme Court. He alleged a violation of his right to a fair hearing by a tribunal under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arising from the refusal of the domestic courts to examine his challenge to a decision suspending him from judicial office.

The Judicial Council of the Slovak Republic, the highest governing body of the judiciary, comprises 18 members. At the relevant time, the President of the Supreme Court automatically served as its President; the remaining members included eight elected by judges and three each appointed by the National Council, the President of the Republic and the Government. On 8 September 2009 the Council, sitting in this composition, decided both to bring disciplinary charges against Paluda and to suspend him from office with immediate effect under the Judges and Assessor Judges Act.

The charges classified Paluda’s conduct as a “serious disciplinary offence” consisting of failure to refrain from behaviour that might cast doubt on the dignity of judicial office, to observe judicial ethics or to uphold the reputation of the judiciary. The Council specifically cited two acts: Paluda’s filing of a criminal complaint accusing the President of the Supreme Court of abuse of authority, and his public statement that case allocation at the Supreme Court had been altered to enable the President to influence outcomes. The Council proposed revocation of Paluda’s judicial office as the sanction.

The suspension automatically reduced Paluda’s salary by 50 per cent for the duration of the disciplinary proceedings (capped at two years) and prohibited him from attending the workplace except for the purpose of asserting personnel rights. Restoration of the withheld salary depended on the final outcome of the proceedings.

Paluda sought to challenge the suspension by an internal appeal to the Judicial Council (29 October 2009), an administrative-law action lodged the same day, and a constitutional complaint (2 November 2009). The Constitutional Court declared the first complaint inadmissible on 25 November 2009 as premature, because the other remedies remained pending. The President of the Judicial Council subsequently informed Paluda that the Council’s decisions were not subject to internal appeal but were reviewable by the administrative courts.

On 13 May 2010 the Bratislava Regional Court discontinued the administrative action. The Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 23 February 2011, holding that the suspension was a merely preliminary measure that did not finally determine Paluda’s rights or affect his fundamental freedoms and was therefore excluded from judicial review under Article 248(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Paluda then lodged a fresh constitutional complaint alleging a breach of Article 6 § 1. On 7 December 2011 the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, finding that the Supreme Court had given adequate, non-arbitrary reasons. Paluda never applied to the Judicial Council itself for the lifting of the suspension, a possibility expressly provided by the Judges Act.

The disciplinary proceedings themselves were discontinued on 13 May 2011 after a legislative amendment made the Minister of Justice a party and the Minister withdrew the charges. Paluda initially appealed but later withdrew the appeal; the discontinuance became final on 27 September 2011. The withheld portion of his salary was restored in July 2012.

These facts formed the basis of Paluda’s claim that he had been denied access to a court in respect of a measure that immediately and substantially affected his professional status, remuneration and ability to perform judicial functions.

The case of Paluda v. Slovakia originated in an application by Peter Paluda, a Slovak Supreme Court judge, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing by a tribunal). This arose from domestic courts' refusal to review a decision suspending him from judicial office.

On 8 September 2009, the Judicial Council of the Slovak Republic—the judiciary's supreme governing body—decided to suspend Paluda immediately from his functions and to file disciplinary charges against him. The Council, then chaired by the Supreme Court President, accused Paluda of a “serious disciplinary offence” for failing to abstain from conduct casting doubt on the respectability of his office, abide by judicial ethics, and uphold the judiciary’s reputation. Specifically, Paluda had filed a criminal complaint accusing the Supreme Court President of abuse of authority and had publicly stated that case distribution at the Supreme Court had been altered to enable the President to influence outcomes. The proposed sanction was revocation of Paluda’s judicial post.

The suspension, pursuant to the Judges and Assessor Judges Act, immediately reduced Paluda’s salary by 50 percent for the duration of the disciplinary proceedings, barred him from the workplace except as needed to assert human-resources rights, and could last a maximum of two years. Restoration of the withheld salary depended on the proceedings’ outcome.

Paluda challenged the suspension on 29 October 2009 via an appeal to the Judicial Council and an administrative-law action, followed by a constitutional complaint on 2 November 2009. The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 25 November 2009 as premature under the subsidiarity principle, given the pending applications. The Judicial Council President later informed Paluda that Council decisions could not be appealed internally and were instead reviewable by administrative tribunals.

On 13 May 2010 the Bratislava Regional Court discontinued the administrative action. The Supreme Court upheld this on 23 February 2011, holding that the suspension was of a preliminary nature, did not finally determine Paluda’s rights, and thus had no bearing on his fundamental rights and freedoms. It was therefore excluded from judicial review under Article 248(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, which barred administrative tribunals from reviewing preliminary administrative decisions.

Paluda lodged a fresh constitutional complaint on 17 June 2011, claiming that the ordinary courts’ refusals breached Article 6 § 1. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 7 December 2011, finding the Supreme Court’s reasoning sound, non-arbitrary, and compatible with the right to a fair hearing.

Meanwhile, a 2011 legislative amendment made the Minister of Justice a party to the pending disciplinary proceedings. The Minister withdrew the disciplinary application on 9 May 2011, prompting the Supreme Court (sitting as disciplinary tribunal) to discontinue the proceedings on 13 May 2011. Paluda appealed but later withdrew the appeal, rendering the decision final on 27 September 2011. The withheld salary was restored in July 2012. Paluda never formally applied to the Judicial Council under section 22(5) of the Act to lift the suspension.

These facts center on the alleged denial of access to a court to challenge a suspension that significantly affected Paluda’s professional status, salary, and reputation, despite its temporary character.
001-174060:
The ECtHR case of Urukov v. Russia (no. 20489/07) concerns a Russian national’s complaints of being denied personal participation in civil paternity proceedings while detained, an unauthorised police entry into his home, and refusal of compensation for a period of detention later found unjustified.

The applicant, born in 1959, was a former university civil-law department head in Cheboksary. In February 2004 a child, V., was born; her mother H. sued to establish the applicant’s paternity and obtain alimony. Genetic testing confirmed paternity, though a medical report stated the pregnancy “could not have occurred naturally.” After an initial 2004 district-court rejection of H.’s claim (quashed on appeal) and a 2005 judgment in H.’s favour (quashed because the parties had not been notified of an expert-hearing date), the case remained pending when the applicant was arrested in March 2007 on suspicion of large-scale bribery and placed in remand prison IZ-21/1.

The district court then sent a letter of request to the prison director seeking the applicant’s position and whether he consented to examination in his absence or wished to appoint a representative. Interviewed on 20 March 2007, the applicant insisted on appearing in person and stated he possessed new evidence. On 26 March the court refused leave, holding that the Code of Civil Procedure contained no provision for transporting detainees. The 4 April 2007 hearing therefore took place with H. and two representatives for the applicant; judgment was given in H.’s favour, noting the applicant’s detention, his non-recognition of paternity and his earlier testimony. The Supreme Court of the Chuvashiya Republic dismissed the appeal on 16 May 2007, reasoning that representation plus prior testimony meant his absence caused no rights violation.

Released on bail in June 2007, the applicant was later found (in his absence) to have breached bail by pressuring witnesses. On 27 March 2008 a detention order was issued and he was listed as a fugitive. At approximately 11 p.m. on 8 April 2008 three officers arrived at his residence after a tip that he was present (he was in fact in hospital). His daughter initially refused entry; officers banged on the door and threatened to force it. Once inside they inspected rooms, opened closets and boxes, and lifted furniture. The applicant was arrested the next day. On 24 April 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the detention order as unjustified, because the lower court had given decisive weight to witness statements that mentioned no actual threats.

A prosecutorial complaint about the entry was refused on 16 May 2009 (no offence). The applicant then sued the Ministry of Finance for compensation, alleging an unauthorised search. Witness testimony conflicted on duration and extent of the inspection. The Leninskiy District Court rejected the claim on 29 October 2009, citing ss. 11 of the Police Act and 8 of the Operational-Search Activities Act: officers had acted on the still-valid detention order and information that the applicant might be at home, so the entry was lawful; compensation was available only for unlawful acts. The judgment was upheld on 9 December 2009.

In April 2009 the applicant was convicted of forcing students to pay bribes for grades and received a custodial sentence (upheld July 2009). He then sought compensation for the 9–24 April 2008 detention. The same district court dismissed the claim on 27 November 2009: the applicant had been convicted, and the Supreme Court had characterised the order as “unjustified” rather than “unlawful,” so no right to compensation existed. The appeal was rejected on 11 January 2010.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Convention violations relating to access to court, respect for the home, and the right to compensation for detention.

The case of Urukov v. Russia (Application no. 20489/07) concerns a Russian national born in 1959, a former university law department head living in Cheboksary. He complained of being denied participation in paternity proceedings, an unlawful police entry into his home, and refusal of compensation for a period of detention.

In the paternity dispute, baby V. was born on 28 February 2004. Her mother, H., sued the applicant one month later to establish paternity and obtain alimony. A genetic study confirmed his paternity, though a medical study indicated the pregnancy could not have occurred naturally. On 7 December 2004 the Moskovskiy District Court in Cheboksary, with both parties present, rejected H.’s claim. The Supreme Court of the Chuvashiya Republic quashed this on 31 January 2005 and remitted the case. A 17 October 2005 District Court judgment in H.’s favour was quashed on 14 December 2005 because the parties had not been informed of a hearing at which genetics experts were cross-examined.

The applicant was arrested in March 2007 on suspicion of large-scale bribery and held in remand prison IZ-21/1. On 15 March 2007 the District Court sent a letter of request to the prison director seeking the applicant’s position and whether he wished to attend or appoint a representative. Interviewed on 20 March, he asked to participate in person and submit new evidence. On 26 March the court refused, citing the absence of any provision in the Code of Civil Procedure for bringing detainees to civil hearings. The 4 April 2007 hearing proceeded with H. and two representatives for the applicant; the court found against him, noting his detention, denial of paternity and prior similar testimony. On 16 May 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, holding that representation and earlier testimony sufficed.

Released on bail on 9 June 2007, the applicant was the subject of a 27 March 2008 District Court detention order (issued in his absence) after he was found to have pressured witnesses; he was listed as a fugitive. Around 11 p.m. on 8 April 2008 three officers arrived at his residence, having been informed he might be there. He was in fact receiving hospital treatment; his daughter was inside. She initially refused entry, stating he was hospitalised. Officers banged on the door and threatened to force it. She opened; they entered, inspected rooms, opened closets and boxes, and lifted furniture before leaving. He was arrested the next day.

On 24 April 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the detention order as unjustified (witnesses had mentioned no actual threats) and ordered his release. A prosecutor’s inquiry into the 8 April entry found no criminal offence. The applicant sued the Ministry of Finance for compensation for an unauthorised search. Witnesses gave conflicting accounts of duration and whether a search occurred. On 29 October 2009 the Leninskiy District Court rejected the claim, holding that officers had acted lawfully under the Police Act and Operational-Search Activities Act on the basis of the (later-quashed) detention order and information that the applicant might be present. The Supreme Court upheld this on 9 December 2009.

Convicted on 17 April 2009 of forcing students to pay bribes and given a custodial sentence (upheld 2 July 2009), the applicant sought compensation for detention from 9 to 24 April 2008. The Leninskiy District Court rejected the claim on 27 November 2009 because he had been convicted and sentenced to custody, and the Supreme Court had characterised the earlier order as “unjustified” rather than “unlawful.” The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 11 January 2010.

These facts underpin the complaints of interference with the right to a fair hearing, respect for home, and an effective remedy regarding detention.

The case of Urukov v. Russia (no. 20489/07) involved a Russian national born in 1959, a former university law department head, who alleged that he had been denied the opportunity to participate in person in civil paternity proceedings while in detention, that police had unlawfully entered his home, and that he had been refused compensation for a period of detention later found unjustified.

In February 2004 a child, V., was born. Her mother, H., sued the applicant to establish paternity and obtain alimony. Genetic testing confirmed his paternity, though a medical examination indicated the pregnancy could not have occurred naturally. After an initial 2004 rejection of the claim (with the applicant present) was quashed and remitted, a 2005 judgment in H.’s favour was itself quashed because the parties had not been notified of a hearing at which genetics experts were examined.

By March 2007 the applicant had been arrested on suspicion of large-scale bribery and was held in a remand prison. The district court sent a letter of request to the prison director asking whether the applicant wished to appear in person, appoint a representative, or have the case heard in his absence. The applicant stated that he wished to attend and to submit new evidence. The court nevertheless refused leave, citing the absence of any provision in the Code of Civil Procedure for transporting detainees to civil hearings. On 4 April 2007 the court heard H. and two representatives appointed for the applicant and found against him, noting his detention, his denial of paternity and earlier testimony. The regional supreme court dismissed his appeal, holding that representation and prior statements were sufficient.

Released on bail in June 2007, the applicant was the subject of a new detention order issued in his absence on 27 March 2008 after the district court found he had pressured witnesses. Late on 8 April three officers arrived at his flat, having received a tip that he was there (he was in fact in hospital). After banging on the door and threatening to force entry, they entered with the consent of his daughter, inspected rooms, opened closets and boxes and lifted furniture. He was arrested the next day. On 24 April the regional supreme court quashed the detention order as unjustified, finding that the lower court had given undue weight to unparticularised witness statements, and ordered his release.

A prosecutor later refused to open a criminal investigation into the police entry. The applicant’s subsequent claim for compensation for an unauthorised search was dismissed on the ground that the officers had acted lawfully on the basis of the (later-quashed) detention order and information that he might be present; the judgment was upheld on appeal.

After the applicant was convicted in April 2009 of accepting bribes from students (sentence upheld on appeal), he sought compensation for the 9–24 April 2008 detention. Domestic courts rejected the claim, observing that he had ultimately received a custodial sentence and that the detention order had been characterised as “unjustified” rather than “unlawful,” so that no right to compensation arose.
001-174381:
The applicant, Inna Ivanovna Cheltsova (born 1947), is a retired Russian journalist and editor-in-chief of the independent weekly newspaper *Fryazinets* (circulation 2,000–5,000) in Fryazino. On a modest monthly pension of approximately 2,440–2,600 RUB, she alleged that three sets of domestic defamation judgments violated her Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

In April 2005 the Shchelkovo prosecutor opened a criminal investigation against municipal employee S.P. for abuse of office (Criminal Code Art. 201). The newspaper published the official announcement, then an article (“Reporting the details”) identifying S.P. as a Public Reception Office civil servant who unlawfully combined that post with paid roles at two housing cooperatives (Strela ZhSK and Strela-3 ZhSK), behaved rudely toward visitors, and permitted financial irregularities that prompted civil suits. S.P. sued. On 14 September 2005 the Shchelkovo Town Court, without distinguishing statements of fact from value judgments, held the impugned passages untrue, ordered a retraction and awarded S.P. 10,000 RUB in non-pecuniary damages. The court rejected payroll and audit evidence, found no employment contracts, and treated “financial irregularities” as unproven. The Moscow Regional Court upheld the judgment on 22 March 2006 without examining the applicant’s arguments on evidence or the disproportionality of the award relative to her pension. (The criminal case against S.P. was later resumed.)

In January 2005 the newspaper published an interview with mayoral candidate N. reporting a residents’ complaint that L.K.—head of the Fryazino Technical Inventory Bureau and wife of the incumbent mayor—had committed forgery by substituting a land-use plan. L.K. sued. On 11 May 2006 the Town Court classified the passage as an unproven statement of criminal fact rather than a value judgment or report of a pending inquiry, held the applicant liable for failing to verify it, ordered a retraction and awarded L.K. 15,000 RUB against the applicant. The Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 20 July 2006 in a brief ruling that declined to re-assess the evidence or consider public-interest or journalist-liability factors.

During the September 2005 mayoral campaign, N. paid from his election fund for an “open letter” to President Putin that the newspaper published as campaign material. The text accused rival candidate G.A. of paying a $1 million bribe to terminate a criminal case against the mayor, of controlling judges and prosecutors, of threatening N.’s life, and of links to a recent shooting. G.A. sued. On 16 May 2006 the Town Court again omitted any fact/opinion analysis or public-interest balancing, found the statements untrue and damaging, ordered a retraction and awarded G.A. 10,000 RUB against the applicant. The Regional Court confirmed the judgment on 2 August 2006, noting only that the defendants had not proved truthfulness and that the article’s election-campaign context afforded no defence.

In each case the domestic courts applied Civil Code Art. 152 (requiring the publisher to prove the truth of damaging “statements”) without applying the Supreme Court’s 2005 guidance that value judgments are not actionable. The cumulative awards (35,000 RUB) and retraction orders formed the interference whose necessity and proportionality the applicant challenged before the European Court.

The case of Cheltsova v. Russia (application no. 44294/06) concerns alleged violations of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). The applicant, Inna Ivanovna Cheltsova, a retired journalist born in 1947 living in Fryazino, Moscow Region, founded and edited the independent weekly newspaper Fryazinets (circulation 2,000–5,000). At the relevant time her monthly pension was approximately 2,440–2,600 Russian roubles (RUB). She complained that three sets of domestic defamation proceedings, resulting in orders to publish retractions and pay damages, unjustifiably interfered with her journalistic activity.

In April 2005 the Shchelkovo prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation against S.P., an employee of the Fryazino town administration’s Public Reception Office, for alleged abuse of powers (Article 201 § 1 of the Criminal Code) involving fraudulent receipt of petty cash from a housing association (ZhSK). The newspaper first published the official statement announcing the investigation. After receiving residents’ complaints about S.P.’s conduct, the applicant published an article on 27 April–3 May 2005 stating that S.P., as a municipal civil servant prohibited from holding a second job, simultaneously served as accountant and head of two ZhSK entities; that she had been rude and raised her voice to visitors (for which she had been reprimanded); that as ZhSK head she had permitted financial irregularities; and that association members had brought civil proceedings against her.

S.P. sued for defamation. On 14 September 2005 the Shchelkovo Town Court, sitting without the applicant, examined witnesses and documents (payroll records, an auditor’s certificate). It made no distinction between statements of fact and value judgments. It held the remarks untrue because no employment contracts or salaries had been proved (volunteer work was alleged), rudeness was unproven, and “financial irregularities” (undefined by law) had not been established. It ordered a retraction of the impugned passages and awarded S.P. 10,000 RUB non-pecuniary damages, noting the particular sensitivity of a civil servant to unverified allegations. The Moscow Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 22 March 2006 without addressing her arguments on evidence or the disproportionate size of the award relative to her pension. The criminal investigation against S.P. was later resumed.

In January 2005 the newspaper published an interview with N., a businessman standing for mayor. N. stated that L.K. (head of the Fryazino Technical Inventory Bureau and wife of the incumbent mayor) had, according to a residents’ complaint to the prosecutor, abused her position by stealing and replacing a land-use plan—an act of forgery. L.K. sued. On 11 May 2006 the Town Court treated the remark as a precise, unproven allegation of crime rather than a value judgment, held that the applicant had failed to verify it or produce criminal-procedure documents, and ordered a retraction plus 15,000 RUB damages from the applicant. It gave no reasons for imposing liability on the journalist, nor did it consider public interest or L.K.’s status as a public official. The Regional Court upheld the judgment on 20 July 2006 in a brief decision rejecting the appeal as a mere re-assessment of evidence.

In August 2005, during the mayoral campaign, N. paid for an open appeal to President Putin that the newspaper published as election material. The article accused rival candidate G.A. (a local entrepreneur linked to the mayor) of paying one million US dollars to corrupt police to terminate a criminal case against the mayor, of having judges, prosecutors and tax officials “in his pay,” of intending to divert municipal funds to his companies, of physically assaulting and threatening to kill N., and of involvement in a subsequent fatal shooting of another businessman. A territorial electoral commission’s challenge failed. G.A. then sued for defamation. On 16 May 2006 the Town Court, again without distinguishing facts from opinions or explaining the journalist’s liability, found the statements untrue and damaging and awarded G.A. 10,000 RUB from the applicant plus a retraction. The Regional Court confirmed the decision on 2 August 2006, rejecting the election-campaign context as a defence and noting the newspaper’s circulation of 3,000 copies.

Russian law (Civil Code Article 152) required the publisher to prove the truth of damaging statements. A 2005 Supreme Court Plenum resolution obliged courts to distinguish verifiable facts from non-actionable value judgments, yet the domestic courts consistently failed to do so, ignored the public-interest character of reporting on official misconduct and elections, and imposed awards that were substantial relative to the applicant’s pension.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 10 violations: interferences with press freedom on matters of legitimate public concern, absence of a fair balance between reputation and expression, and a potential chilling effect on local journalism.

The case of Cheltsova v. Russia (application no. 44294/06) concerns a journalist’s complaint of a violation of her Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The applicant, Inna Ivanovna Cheltsova (born 1947), is a pensioner living in Fryazino, Moscow Region, on a monthly pension of approximately 2,440 RUB. She is the founder and editor-in-chief of Fryazinets, an independent weekly newspaper with a circulation of 2,000–5,000 copies.

The alleged violation arises from three sets of domestic defamation proceedings brought against her and the newspaper under Article 152 of the Russian Civil Code, which requires a defendant to prove the truth of damaging statements or face retraction and damages. A 2005 Supreme Court resolution directed courts to distinguish verifiable statements of fact from non-actionable value judgments, but the applicant contended that the Russian courts failed to do so, imposed liability without adequate regard to public interest or her role as a journalist, and awarded disproportionate sums given her limited means.

In April 2005 the newspaper published a Shchelkovo town deputy prosecutor’s statement announcing the opening of a criminal investigation against S.P., a municipal civil servant in the mayor’s Public Reception Office, for abuse of powers. After receiving complaints from residents about S.P.’s alleged rudeness, the applicant published a follow-up article identifying S.P., noting that municipal servants were forbidden from holding second jobs, describing her concurrent unpaid roles at two housing cooperatives (Strela ZhSK and Strela-3 ZhSK), reporting that she raised her voice and was rude to visitors, and stating that she had allowed financial irregularities that prompted civil proceedings by cooperative members. S.P. sued. On 14 September 2005 the Shchelkovo Town Court, sitting in the applicant’s absence, treated all the statements as untrue facts that tarnished S.P.’s honour and business reputation. It rejected documentary and witness evidence of salary payments and irregularities, held that volunteer work did not constitute prohibited “combining of employment,” found the allegations of rudeness and financial misconduct unproven, and ordered a retraction plus 10,000 RUB in non-pecuniary damages. The Moscow Regional Court upheld the judgment on 22 March 2006 without addressing the applicant’s arguments concerning evidence or the size of the award relative to her pension. The criminal investigation against S.P. was later resumed.

In January 2005 the newspaper published an interview with N., a candidate for mayor, who stated that L.K. (head of the Fryazino Technical Inventory Bureau and wife of the incumbent mayor) had, according to a residents’ complaint to the prosecutor, committed forgery by replacing a land-use plan. L.K. sued. On 11 May 2006 the Town Court classified the remarks as a statement of fact that a crime had been committed, required official criminal-procedure documents to prove it, rejected the defence that the remarks were a value judgment or a fair report of a complaint, and held the applicant liable for failing to verify the allegation before publication. It awarded L.K. 15,000 RUB against the applicant plus a retraction. The Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 20 July 2006 in a brief judgment that did not examine public-interest or journalistic-privilege arguments.

During the August 2005 mayoral campaign the newspaper published a paid appeal by N. accusing another candidate, G.A., of paying one million U.S. dollars to corrupt police to have a criminal case against the incumbent mayor dropped, of having judges and prosecutors “in his pay,” of intending to divert municipal funds to his own companies, of physically assaulting and threatening N., and of being linked to a fatal shooting. An electoral-commission challenge was rejected on the ground that the piece was lawful campaign material. G.A. nevertheless sued for defamation. On 16 May 2006 the Town Court found the statements untrue and damaging, without distinguishing fact from comment or considering the election context, and awarded 10,000 RUB against the applicant plus a retraction. The Regional Court upheld the decision on 2 August 2006, emphasising that the statements should have been verified and that campaign rules did not exempt the defendants from civil liability.

These three judgments, imposing financial liability and retraction orders on a small independent newspaper for publications concerning the conduct of public officials and electoral candidates, form the factual basis of the applicant’s Article 10 complaint.
001-174402:
The applicant, R.M. (born 1988), a dual Uzbek-Turkish national, fled Uzbekistan in September 2007 amid a criminal investigation he claimed was politically motivated and due to fears of ill-treatment. Uzbek authorities issued an international arrest warrant in December 2007. He arrived in Turkey and was arrested on 9 September 2009 on Interpol grounds. The next day, the Bakırköy Magistrates’ Court ordered 45 days’ provisional detention under a bilateral treaty. His appeal was dismissed. He applied to UNHCR and the Turkish Interior Ministry for refugee status. A formal Uzbek extradition request followed on 15 October 2009.

On 23 October 2009 the Bakırköy Assize Court declared extradition admissible and ordered continued detention under Article 18 § 7 of the Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed this on 16 April 2010 for multiple procedural defects, including failure to obtain a photograph, to record a hearing, to inform the applicant of his rights, to take final defence submissions, to enquire whether a conviction or pending case existed in Uzbekistan, and to limit itself to declaring the request admissible (extradition being a Cabinet decision). After receiving the quashing decision, the Assize Court on 7 June 2010 annulled the prior detention order and re-detained the applicant under Articles 100 and 101 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing the nature of the alleged offences, the evidence, a strong suspicion of guilt and flight risk.

The court then sought information from Uzbekistan, which arrived in December 2010 and confirmed neither a conviction nor a pending case. Multiple adjournments followed. Meanwhile UNHCR, on 23 December 2010, refused refugee status but advised the Turkish authorities to grant subsidiary protection and not to extradite or deport the applicant, invoking non-refoulement and Article 3 of the Convention. The Assize Court initially waited for the outcome of the applicant’s appeal against that refusal, then proceeded. On 1 June 2011 the Interior Ministry granted subsidiary protection and a temporary residence permit for Sakarya, expressly instructing other authorities to prevent extradition. The letter was placed before the Assize Court.

Nevertheless, on 20 June 2011 the Assize Court again found the extradition request admissible, stating that an investigation was ongoing in Uzbekistan for non-political, non-military offences (establishing a criminal organisation and causing bodily harm) and ordering detention under Article 18 § 7. The applicant immediately sought release, stressing his new protection status and proposing alternatives (travel ban, bail or reporting), but was refused. He appealed the admissibility ruling on the same grounds. The Cassation prosecutor recommended quashing for lack of any Article 3 examination; the Court of Cassation nevertheless upheld the ruling on 8 March 2012.

On 4 May 2012 the Justice Ministry informed the prosecutor that extradition was now impossible because of the protection status and that detention must be reviewed. The Assize Court ordered release from prison on 9 May 2012; the applicant was then held for one day in a foreigners’ removal centre before being freed on 10 May pursuant to his residence permit. He acquired Turkish nationality on 10 September 2012.

Throughout the period from June 2010 to May 2011 the Assize Court repeatedly extended detention on the grounds of the seriousness of the offences, the state of the evidence and the applicant’s lack of permanent residence. From June 2011 onward the applicant consistently invoked his subsidiary protection as rendering extradition legally impossible and requested release or alternatives; those applications and appeals were rejected. No independent, thorough judicial assessment of the alleged Article 3 risk in Uzbekistan was ever conducted, even after the UNHCR letter and the grant of protection. After release from prison the one-day placement in the removal centre occurred despite the residence permit already in force. Domestic law provided for compensation (Article 141 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) for unlawful detention, but the applicant maintained that no effective remedy existed to challenge the lawfulness of either form of detention or to obtain redress.

Throughout the two-and-a-half-year detention he had no effective opportunity to challenge its lawfulness once the legal basis shifted or to obtain compensation.

The case originated in an application by R.M., an Uzbek-Turkish national born in 1988 and residing in Istanbul, lodged on 5 October 2012. The communicated complaints concerned the risk of ill-treatment if extradited to Uzbekistan, the lack of a thorough judicial examination of that risk, the alleged unlawfulness of his detention pending extradition (and briefly thereafter in a removal centre), and the absence of effective remedies to challenge the detention or obtain compensation.

The applicant left Uzbekistan on 19 September 2007, fearing ill-treatment in a politically motivated criminal investigation. An Interpol arrest warrant followed on 13 December 2007. He was arrested in Turkey on 9 September 2009. The next day the Bakırköy Magistrates’ Court ordered 45 days’ provisional detention under the Turkey-Uzbekistan mutual-assistance treaty; an appeal was dismissed. He immediately applied to the UNHCR and the Ministry of the Interior for refugee status.

A formal Uzbek extradition request arrived on 15 October 2009. On 23 October the Bakırköy Assize Court declared the request admissible and ordered continued detention under Article 18 § 7 of the Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed that judgment on 16 April 2010 for multiple procedural defects (absence of a photograph, incomplete records, failure to inform the applicant of his rights or to take final submissions, no inquiry into any Uzbek conviction or pending case, and an erroneous order of extradition rather than a mere declaration of admissibility, implementation being reserved to the Cabinet). Detention was nevertheless reimposed on 7 June 2010 under Articles 100 and 101 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing the nature of the offences, the evidence, a strong suspicion of guilt and a risk of absconding.

The assize court then requested information from Uzbekistan. Documents received in December 2010 showed neither a conviction nor a pending case. Meanwhile, on 23 December 2010 the UNHCR advised that the applicant, although not a Convention refugee, should be granted subsidiary protection and must not be removed, in view of the principle of non-refoulement and Article 3 of the Convention. The court adjourned repeatedly while awaiting further UNHCR material and the outcome of the applicant’s appeal against the refugee-status refusal.

On 1 June 2011 the Ministry of the Interior granted subsidiary protection and a temporary residence permit, expressly requesting that extradition be prevented. Despite this, on 20 June the assize court again found the extradition request admissible, holding that an investigation was still under way in Uzbekistan for forming a criminal organisation and causing bodily harm (offences it deemed neither political nor military) and re-ordered detention under Article 18 § 7. Subsequent applications for release or alternative measures, which invoked the protection status, were rejected. The Court of Cassation, although invited by its own prosecutor to quash the decision for want of any Article 3 assessment, upheld it on 8 March 2012.

Only after a further Ministry of Justice letter of 4 May 2012 confirming that extradition was now impossible did the assize court order release from prison on 9 May. The applicant was then held for one day in a foreigners’ removal centre before being freed on the strength of his residence permit. He acquired Turkish nationality on 10 September 2012.

Throughout the period of detention (September 2009–May 2012) the applicant repeatedly challenged its lawfulness, especially after June 2011 when subsidiary protection rendered extradition legally barred. Domestic law (Constitution Article 38, Criminal Code Article 18 and Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 100–101 and 141) prohibits the extradition of citizens, requires refusal of extradition where there is a real risk of torture or politically motivated prosecution, permits detention pending an admissible request, and provides a theoretical right to compensation for unlawful preventive detention.
001-174442:
The case of S.M.M. v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 77450/12) concerns an alleged violation of Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention arising from the applicant’s immigration detention from 28 November 2008 to 15 September 2011.

The applicant, a Zimbabwean national born in 1982, entered the United Kingdom in May 2001 as a visitor. From around 2003 he suffered mental illness, including auditory hallucinations and two suicide attempts. He incurred non-custodial convictions for driving offences in 2004–2005. His first asylum claim, made in April 2005, was refused in June 2005 for non-compliance after he failed to attend interview; he was served with notice of liability to removal as an overstayer, did not appeal, and later absconded after failing to report.

In August 2007 he was convicted of possessing Class A drugs with intent to supply and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. While serving the sentence he received antipsychotic medication for the first time. In March 2008 he lodged a second asylum claim describing two 2000 incidents in Zimbabwe: an attack by Zanu-PF supporters while protesting gay rights and a subsequent police-station beating. He was interviewed on the claim in October 2008. On 14 November 2008 he was served with notice of liability to automatic deportation. Upon completing his sentence on 28 November 2008 he remained detained under immigration powers.

During detention his mental health deteriorated; he was admitted to hospital and sectioned for six days in February 2009. Further asylum interviews occurred in May 2009, with additional evidence submitted. Attempts to obtain a travel document in October 2009 and June 2010 failed because he refused to provide bio-data without consulting solicitors. In November 2009 representatives sought extra time for medical evidence. A December 2009 bail application was refused on absconding-risk grounds.

In June–July 2010 representatives wrote asserting that detention was unlawful, citing his medical conditions and the Secretary of State’s policy against detaining those with serious mental illness. The Secretary of State replied that detention was justified by the seriousness of the offence, public-harm and absconding risks, lack of ties, previous non-compliance and absconding, deception, lack of identity evidence, and public-good considerations.

Dr S examined the applicant in August 2010; her October 2010 report (submitted November 2010) recorded scars consistent with the claimed Zanu-PF assault, a psychotic illness with first-rank schizophrenia symptoms, ongoing auditory hallucinations, and PTSD features. Detention-centre staff raised mental-health concerns in November 2010, but assessments concluded he was not unsuitable for detention under the Mental Health Act and did not require compulsory treatment.

In January 2011 the applicant sought judicial review of continuing detention, alleging breach of the Secretary of State’s policies on mentally ill persons and torture victims and of the Hardial Singh principles, and claiming damages. A fresh medical report was submitted. On 8 February 2011 the second asylum claim was refused and a deportation order made; appeals were dismissed by April–May 2011.

Permission for judicial review was refused on paper in June 2011 (mental illness insufficiently severe or unmanageable; eleven-year-old alleged torture irrelevant; Hardial Singh principles satisfied given real absconding/reoffending risks, a non-open-ended period after October 2010, and no lack of expedition) and again after oral hearing in October 2011 (no evidence the illness could not be managed in detention; scarring consistent only with assault, not torture, and no scarring matching the police-station claim; removal prospects not nil). The Court of Appeal refused permission in February 2012.

The applicant was granted bail and released on 15 September 2011. Separately, the February 2011 asylum refusal was later conceded as flawed and remitted; in November 2012 the Upper Tribunal allowed the claim on human-rights grounds. The deportation order was revoked in January 2013 and discretionary leave granted.

Relevant background included a moratorium on enforced removals to Zimbabwe until 14 October 2010 (thereafter pending country-guidance litigation) and the Secretary of State’s policy that detention of those with serious mental illness or independent evidence of torture should be exceptional.

The applicant, a Zimbabwean national born in 1982, arrived in the UK in May 2001 on a six-month visitor visa. From around 2003 he experienced mental illness, including auditory hallucinations and two suicide attempts. In 2004–2005 he received non-custodial convictions for driving offences, obstructing police and failing to surrender. His April 2005 asylum claim was refused in June 2005 for non-attendance at interview; he was treated as an overstayer and later an absconder after failing to report. In August 2007 he was convicted of possessing Class A drugs with intent to supply and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment (his first psychiatric treatment occurred in prison). A second asylum claim in March 2008 alleged 2000 attacks by Zanu-PF supporters and police beatings. Upon completing his sentence on 28 November 2008 he was detained under immigration powers following a notice of liability to automatic deportation.

Detention continued until 15 September 2011 (almost 34 months). Key events included a February 2009 hospital admission and six-day sectioning; further asylum interviews and evidence in 2009; a October 2009 travel-document interview at which he refused bio-data; December 2009 bail refusal for absconding risk; 2010 letters from representatives seeking release on mental-health and policy grounds (rejected by the Secretary of State citing absconding/reoffending risks, prior non-compliance and public-good grounds); an October 2010 psychiatric report diagnosing schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis plus PTSD, with scarring consistent with the Zanu-PF assault; November 2010 assessments finding him unsuitable for Mental Health Act detention but not requiring compulsory treatment; a January 2011 judicial-review claim alleging breaches of the mental-health and torture concessions plus Hardial Singh principles; February 2011 asylum refusal and deportation order (appeal dismissed April 2011); June and October 2011 High Court refusals of permission (finding the illness manageable in detention, no independent torture evidence, and no Hardial Singh breach given real absconding/reoffending risks and adequate expedition); and February 2012 Court of Appeal refusal. He was released on Upper Tribunal bail. (His asylum appeal later succeeded on human-rights grounds in November 2012, leading to revocation of the deportation order.)

Domestic law permitted detention pending deportation (Immigration Act 1971 Sch. 3). Chapter 55.10 of the Enforcement Instructions treated detention as exceptional for those with serious mental illness or independent evidence of torture. Hardial Singh required an intention to deport, detention only for a reasonable period, release if deportation could not occur within that period, and due expedition. Enforced removals to Zimbabwe were under moratorium until 14 October 2010 (thereafter suspended pending country-guidance litigation). The applicant alleged that the entire period of immigration detention violated Article 5 § 1(f).
