001-174420:
The ECtHR case of Bogomolova v. Russia (Appl. no. 13812/09) concerned an alleged failure by Russian courts to protect the private and family life of the applicant, a single mother and PE teacher, and her young son. In November 2007 the applicant discovered that a photograph of her then six-year-old son’s face had been printed, without her knowledge or consent, on the cover of a six-page booklet entitled “Children need a family.” The booklet, produced by a district psychological-support centre and printed in 200 copies, promoted various forms of substitute family care for orphans and ended with an appeal to “save a child from loneliness.” It was distributed in libraries, hospitals and police stations in the applicant’s town and district.

The photograph had been taken openly in 2004 by a photographer known to the applicant; electronic copies later reached a layout artist who selected the image because it “fitted the booklet well,” without knowing the child’s identity. No parental authorisation was ever sought. After publication, acquaintances, neighbours and parents of the applicant’s pupils concluded that she had abandoned her son or lost parental rights. The boy was mocked in kindergarten as a “little vagrant” and “poor orphan”; the applicant felt obliged to resign from her teaching post.

She first requested a criminal investigation, which was refused. In March 2008 she brought civil proceedings against the centre (later redirected against the publishing company and the layout artist), claiming damage to honour, dignity and professional reputation under Civil Code Arts. 151–152 and seeking non-pecuniary damages plus a public apology. The defendants argued that consent was unnecessary because the booklet served “social and public interests.” The District Court dismissed the claim in June 2008, finding no defamatory content, no proven hostility from witnesses, and no restriction placed by the applicant on later use of the 2004 photographs. The Regional Court upheld the judgment in August 2008, noting that the applicant had pleaded only defamation, not the separate right of image under Art. 152.1 (which generally requires consent). She was subsequently ordered to reimburse the centre’s legal costs.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic courts had afforded insufficient protection to her and her son’s right to respect for private and family life.

The case of Bogomolova v. Russia (Application no. 13812/09) was brought by Tatyana Bogomolova, a Russian national and single mother of a son born in 2001, alleging that Russian courts failed to protect their Article 8 rights to private and family life after unauthorized use of the child’s photograph.

In November 2007 Bogomolova, then a physical-education teacher, discovered her son’s identifiable facial photograph occupying most of the cover of a 200-copy booklet titled “Children need a family.” Produced by a municipal Centre for Psychological, Medical and Social Support, the six-page publication promoted adoption, fostering and other substitute-family arrangements for orphans. The cover slogan “Children need a family” appeared directly above the boy’s image, with the Centre’s name below. The applicant had never been informed or asked for consent.

The photograph had been taken in 2004 by a tourist photographer, Mr Sh., with the applicant’s knowledge but without written permission or any restriction on later use. Electronic copies later reached Mr P., a freelance layout artist hired by the publishing company. Searching his files for suitable images, P. selected the boy’s picture because it “fitted” the orphan theme; he did not know the child’s identity. The Centre itself had not approved that particular photograph.

Bogomolova first requested a criminal investigation. Police and the prosecutor declined, noting that the image had been found on the internet and advising a civil claim. In March 2008 she sued the Centre (later substituted by the publisher and P., with the Centre as third party) under Articles 151–152 of the Civil Code, seeking non-pecuniary damages and a public apology. She asserted that the booklet’s context led colleagues, neighbours and parents of her pupils to conclude she had abandoned her son or lost parental rights. The boy was mocked in kindergarten as a “little vagrant” and “poor orphan.” Her professional standing as a teacher suffered; she resigned in June 2008.

The Usolskiy District Court dismissed the action on 20 June 2008. It held that the booklet contained no defamatory statements, that witnesses reported no hostility toward the applicant, and that the publication pursued a socially useful purpose. The court observed that the applicant had allowed the 2004 photographs without conditions and had herself shown the booklet to others. The Perm Regional Court upheld the judgment on 19 August 2008, ruling that the first-instance court had correctly decided the claim as framed (honour and reputation) and had not been obliged to apply Article 152.1 (protection of a citizen’s image) of its own motion. The applicant was later ordered to reimburse the Centre’s legal costs.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: an identifiable photograph of a minor, used without parental consent in a context that publicly implied the child was available for adoption, produced social stigma and interference with family life that the domestic courts, by treating the matter solely as a defamation claim, left unremedied.

The ECHR case of Bogomolova v. Russia (Application no. 13812/09, judgment of 20 June 2017) concerned a complaint by Tatyana Sergeyevna Bogomolova, a Russian national and single mother of a son born in 2001, that domestic courts failed to protect her and her son's right to respect for private and family life. The applicant, a physical-education teacher in Berezniki, Perm region, alleged an interference arising from the unauthorized publication of her son's photograph.

In November 2007 she discovered the photograph on the cover of a six-page booklet titled “Children need a family,” produced by the Centre for Psychological, Medical and Social Support of the Usolskiy District. The boy's face occupied most of the cover beneath the slogan “Children need a family.” Interior pages described forms of substitute family care (adoption, fostering, etc.) and the Centre's work with orphans; the last page invited readers to “save a child from loneliness.” Two hundred copies were distributed in local libraries, hospitals and police stations. The applicant had neither been informed nor given consent.

The image originated in 2004, when photographer Mr Sh. photographed tourists, including the applicant's son, during a trip with layout designer Mr P. Sh. later e-mailed the files to P. In 2007 P., contracted by the publishing company to prepare the booklet, selected the photograph from his computer without knowing the child's identity.

The applicant first sought a criminal investigation; the authorities declined, stating that P. had taken the image from the internet and advising civil proceedings. In March 2008 she sued the Centre (later replaced by the publishing company and P.) under Civil Code Articles 151 and 152, claiming damage to honour, dignity and reputation. She asserted that people believed she had abandoned her son, that kindergarten children called him “little vagrant” and “poor orphan,” and that parental comments forced her to resign. She sought non-pecuniary damages and a public apology.

The defendants argued that consent was unnecessary because the booklet served public interests (an exception under Article 152.1) and that the company was not liable for its contractor. Witnesses for the Centre confirmed that callers had asked whether the depicted child was available for adoption.

On 20 June 2008 the Usolskiy District Court dismissed the claim. It found no defamation: the booklet was informational and positive, witnesses reported no hostility, and the applicant had imposed no restrictions when the photographs were taken and had herself shown the booklet around. The court did not apply Article 152.1 (protection of a citizen's image, which requires consent except in defined public-interest or public-event cases).

On appeal the applicant stressed the absence of parental consent under Article 152.1 and Article 8 of the Convention, together with the social harm (job loss, mockery). The Regional Court upheld the judgment on 19 August 2008, holding that the lower court had correctly confined itself to the defamation claims actually pleaded. The applicant was later ordered to pay the Centre's costs.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation: publication of a child's identifiable image in an adoption context without consent, and the courts' refusal to examine the image-protection rules that would have required such consent.
001-174626:
The case of Bigashev v. Russia (Application no. 71444/13) was brought by Mr Rifkat Maksumovich Bigashev, a Russian national born in 1927 and residing in Izhevsk. A World War II veteran with category 2 disability, he owned two-thirds of a house, outbuildings and adjacent land near a public highway. He and his wife (who died in 2011) had lived there since 1958 and cultivated a garden.

Between 2000 and 2002 municipal authorities repaired the highway and raised its surface. Thereafter the applicant’s property was flooded annually by meltwater and groundwater, causing serious damage that he claimed rendered the house uninhabitable.

In 2004 he sued the authorities, alleging that a drainage pipe had been installed without project documentation or proper supervision, contrary to technical standards, resulting in flooding from May 2002. On 19 March 2007 the Industrialnyy District Court found no sufficient proof of damage or causal link to award compensation, but held that a malfunctioning drainage pipe under the road obliged the authorities to arrange wastewater-collection works. On 5 July 2007 the Supreme Court of Udmurtiya awarded 68 900 RUB (approximately EUR 1 000) for pecuniary damage and otherwise upheld the judgment.

Enforcement began on 12 May 2009. The pipe was unclogged by July 2009 and proceedings were terminated on 23 November 2009; the applicant did not appeal.

Flooding recurred in April 2007. In a second action the Oktyabrskiy District Court, on 30 October 2008, awarded a further 132 017 RUB (approximately EUR 2 000) for pecuniary damage, finding that non-enforcement of the 2007 judgment and inadequate road maintenance were responsible. The decision was upheld on 21 January 2009.

A third action, lodged in September 2010, complained that flooding had continued after the 2007 judgment, leaving the house almost destroyed and living conditions unsanitary. An expert report of 9 January 2013 confirmed that the ordered drainage system had never been installed, that the road lacked a properly designed gradient and pipe, and that flooding persisted. On 21 January 2013 the same court ordered the authorities to commission a specialist project and complete drainage works by 1 July 2013; it dismissed damage claims for want of a causal link. The judgment was upheld on 22 April 2013.

A writ was issued on 16 August 2013 and enforcement began on 4 September 2013. After three formal demands and an administrative fine of 5 000 RUB in February 2014, contracts were signed in September 2014 and works finished in October 2014 (following yet another flood that spring). The bailiff terminated proceedings on 5 November 2014, but the applicant successfully appealed; the Supreme Court on 29 April 2015 held the termination unlawful and ordered reopening. On 8 July 2015 the district court awarded the applicant 10 000 RUB (approximately EUR 160) for non-pecuniary damage caused by delay, noting that flooding had ceased. Enforcement was finally terminated on 20 October 2015 after written acknowledgment of completion.

Separately, in 2013 the applicant sought a declaration that the house was unfit for habitation. The inter-departmental commission found it repairable by the owner; courts later dismissed his challenge. An application for social housing lodged in 2011 remained unmet.

These facts underpin the communicated complaints of non-enforcement of final judgments within a reasonable time and of the authorities’ failure to protect the applicant’s home and property from recurrent inundation.

The case of Bigashev v. Russia (Application no. 71444/13) concerns a retired World War II veteran and disabled Russian national, born in 1927, who has owned two-thirds of a house, outbuildings and adjoining land in Izhevsk since 1958. He and his late wife (who died in 2011) used the property as their home and cultivated a garden. Between 2000 and 2002 the municipal authorities repaired and raised a nearby public highway, installing a drainage pipe without proper project documentation or supervision.

From 2002 the house and land were flooded annually by meltwater and groundwater. The applicant alleged the works caused the inundation, rendering the house seriously damaged and uninhabitable. In 2004 he sued the municipality and the repair company, seeking compensation and an order to install a compliant drainage system. On 19 March 2007 the Industrialnyy District Court found that flooding resulted from a malfunctioning pipe and required the authorities to arrange wastewater-collection works, but rejected damages for lack of proven causal link. On 5 July 2007 the Udmurtiya Supreme Court awarded him 68 900 RUB (approximately EUR 1 000) for pecuniary damage caused by regular flooding since 2000 due to poor road maintenance, while upholding the rest of the first-instance judgment.

Enforcement began in May 2009. The pipe was unclogged by July 2009 and proceedings were terminated in November 2009 without appeal. Flooding nevertheless continued. After a further inundation in April 2007 the applicant sued again. In October 2008 the Oktyabrskiy District Court awarded 132 017 RUB (approximately EUR 2 000) for pecuniary damage, holding that the authorities had failed both to maintain the road and to enforce the 2007 judgment; the award was upheld in January 2009.

A third action was brought in September 2010. An expert report of January 2013 confirmed that the ordered drainage system had never been installed, that flooding had persisted since 2009, and that the road lacked proper gradient, pipe diameter and calculations. On 21 January 2013 the Oktyabrskiy District Court ordered the municipality to commission a specialist project and complete construction by 1 July 2013, but again refused damages. The order was upheld in April 2013. A writ of execution was issued in August 2013; after repeated non-compliance a fine was imposed in February 2014. The house flooded once more in spring 2014. Works were finally completed in October 2014. Enforcement proceedings were terminated in November 2014, reopened after a successful appeal in 2015, and closed again in October 2015 once a representative confirmed that flooding had ceased. In July 2015 the applicant was awarded 10 000 RUB (approximately EUR 160) for non-pecuniary damage caused by the delay.

Separately, in 2013 a commission found the house repairable by its owner rather than unfit for habitation; the applicant’s challenge failed. An application for social housing lodged in 2011 remained unanswered. The applicant complained that the 2007 and 2013 judgments had not been enforced within a reasonable time and that the authorities had failed to protect his home and property from recurrent flooding.

The applicant, a disabled WWII veteran born in 1927, owned two-thirds of a house, outbuildings and adjoining land in Izhevsk near a public highway, where he and his late wife had lived since 1958 and grown food. Between 2000 and 2002 municipal authorities repaired the highway, raising its surface and installing a drainage pipe without project documentation or proper supervision. Thereafter the property flooded annually with meltwater and groundwater, causing serious structural damage that the applicant claimed rendered the house uninhabitable.

Bailiffs opened enforcement in May 2009; a pipe-unclogging operation was completed in July 2009 and proceedings were terminated in November 2009 without appeal.

Further flooding in April 2007 prompted a second action. On 30 October 2008 the Oktyabrskiy District Court held the authorities liable for failing to maintain the road and to enforce the 2007 judgment, awarding 132 017 RUB in pecuniary damages (upheld January 2009). Continued inundation after 2009 led to a third action in September 2010. An expert report of January 2013 confirmed that the 2007 drainage works had never been performed, that the road remained essentially level, and that unauthorized surface changes had altered water flow. On 21 January 2013 the Oktyabrskiy court (upheld April 2013) ordered the authorities to commission a specialist project and complete construction of a drainage pipe by 1 July 2013; damages claims were dismissed.

A writ issued in August 2013; after repeated non-compliance the authorities were fined in February 2014. The house flooded again that spring. Contracts for anti-flood works were signed only in September 2014 and completed in October 2014. Bailiffs terminated enforcement in November 2014, but the Supreme Court later quashed the termination as unlawful and ordered reopening. In July 2015 a court awarded the applicant 10 000 RUB for non-pecuniary damage caused by delay, noting that flooding had ceased. Enforcement was finally closed in October 2015 after the applicant’s representative confirmed compliance.

Separately, an interdepartmental commission in 2013 found the house needed structural repairs (to be performed by the owner) but was not unfit for habitation; the applicant’s challenge failed. A 2011 request for social housing remained unmet.

These facts underpin the complaints of unreasonably delayed enforcement of binding judgments and of the authorities’ failure to protect the applicant’s home and property from recurrent flooding.
001-174615:
**Case Summary: Krndija and Others v. Serbia (ECtHR, 27 June 2017)**

This case joined four applications by Serbian nationals (Neđo Krndija, Enita Mavrić, Predrag Vukosavljević and Bora Jovanović) alleging that Serbian authorities failed to enforce final domestic court judgments in their favour (primarily concerning unfair dismissals by socially or State-owned companies) and that no effective remedy existed. The companies were registered as fully or predominantly socially/State-owned throughout the relevant periods. The applicants obtained judgments ordering reinstatement and/or payment of salary arrears, social contributions and costs; these remained wholly or largely unenforced, often due to insolvency, liquidation or restructuring of the debtor companies.

The first applicant was dismissed in May 2004 by DP Udarnik (later in liquidation). A December 2006 first-instance judgment (upheld July 2008, enforceable December 2008) declared the dismissal void, ordered reinstatement within eight days and awarded costs of RSD 49,500. Temporary insolvency proceedings in 2007 were stayed. The applicant sought enforcement in January 2009 (including unpaid salaries pending reinstatement). The enforcement court rejected the request in October 2009 on the erroneous ground that insolvency remained pending. Fresh insolvency proceedings opened in December 2011 and were still ongoing; after a property division the applicant recovered only 2.89% of his costs claim. Repeated complaints about delays were unsuccessful.

The second applicant, employed 1990–2007 by a Raška Holding subsidiary and placed on compulsory paid leave, received a 1991 dismissal notice only in 2007. A July 2007 judgment (final September 2007) declared it void, ordered reinstatement, arrears from 1990–2007, contributions from 1994–2007 and costs. She was made redundant in October 2007. A further May 2008 judgment (final January 2009) awarded later contributions and costs; enforcement was initially refused but ordered in 2011 after a Supreme Court instruction. A 2013 retrial awarded additional salary for the leave period (proceedings pending). The company entered restructuring in 2006; insolvency opened in 2013. Her claim was admitted in 2015 but remained unpaid, with insolvency ongoing.

The third applicant obtained a June 2010 court-approved settlement with Livnica Ralja AD declaring his 2002 dismissal void, ordering reinstatement and payment of approximately RSD 2 million in arrears/contributions for 2002–2010. An enforcement order issued immediately. No movable assets were found; an order against immovables followed. Preliminary insolvency opened in February 2011 and was terminated in April 2011 with liquidation (no successor, no claims deposited or registered). The company was struck off the register in June 2011 and its assets became State property. Enforcement was suspended in October 2011 and terminated in November 2011 for lack of assets.

The fourth applicant obtained a December 2004 judgment against DP Galpres ordering reinstatement, arrears, contributions and costs (reinstatement/contributions final and enforceable by March 2005; salary part later re-awarded in November 2006). Enforcement orders issued in 2005 and 2007. After the Government submitted observations in 2015 the applicant failed to respond despite reminders, raising the possibility of striking-out.

Relevant domestic law (Insolvency Procedure Act, Enforcement Procedure Act 2004) allowed termination of employment contracts upon insolvency and permitted combined reinstatement/salary claims, but provided no effective mechanism to compel enforcement against insolvent socially/State-owned debtors. The facts highlight prolonged non-enforcement, official errors, and the companies’ public ownership as central to the alleged breaches of the right to enforcement of judgments and an effective remedy.

The European Court of Human Rights examined four applications (nos. 30723/09, 9370/13, 32658/12 and 2632/09) brought by Serbian nationals Neđo Krndija, Enita Mavrić, Predrag Vukosavljević and Bora Jovanović against Serbia. The applicants alleged that the authorities had failed to enforce final domestic court decisions in their favour and that they lacked an effective remedy for this failure.

All four applicants had been dismissed by fully or predominantly socially or State-owned companies. They successfully challenged those dismissals in civil proceedings, obtaining final and enforceable judgments (or court-approved settlements) ordering reinstatement to suitable posts together with payment of salary arrears, pension and social-security contributions, and legal costs. Those decisions have remained unenforced.

Krndija was dismissed in May 2004 by DP Udarnik. On 20 December 2006 the Third Belgrade Municipal Court declared the dismissal void, ordered reinstatement within eight days and awarded costs of RSD 49 500; the judgment became final on 26 December 2008. His January 2009 enforcement request was rejected in October 2009 on the erroneous ground that insolvency proceedings were pending (they had in fact been stayed in 2007). A fresh insolvency was opened in December 2011 and is still pending; after partial distribution he recovered only 2.89 per cent of his costs claim.

Mavrić, employed by a subsidiary of Raška Holding AD, was placed on compulsory paid leave and later treated as dismissed by a 1991 decision served in 2007. On 9 July 2007 the Novi Pazar Municipal Court ordered reinstatement, payment of minimum-salary arrears from 1990 to March 2007 plus interest, social-security contributions from 1994, and costs. Further judgments in 2008 and 2013 awarded additional contributions and salary for a later period. Although an enforcement order was issued in 2011, the company entered restructuring in 2006 and insolvency in 2013; her registered claim remains unpaid.

Vukosavljević concluded a court-approved settlement on 25 June 2010 with Livnica Ralja AD providing for reinstatement and payment of more than RSD 2 million in arrears and contributions. An enforcement order followed immediately, but the company entered insolvency in February 2011, was liquidated in April 2011 (no successor, no registered claims) and was struck off the register. All remaining assets passed to the State; enforcement was terminated in November 2011.

Jovanović obtained judgments in 2004–2006 against DP Galpres ordering reinstatement, salary arrears for 2003–2006, contributions and costs. Enforcement orders were issued in 2005 and 2007, but the applicant thereafter failed to pursue the case before the Court.

In each instance the debtor companies remained socially or State-owned throughout the relevant enforcement and insolvency proceedings. Domestic legislation permitted insolvency to affect employment contracts and required creditors to register claims, yet the applicants’ final judicial titles were never fully executed. The Court gave the applications priority and communicated them to the Government in April 2015.

**Case Summary: Krndija and Others v. Serbia (ECtHR, 27 June 2017)**

This case involved four applications (nos. 30723/09, 9370/13, 32658/12 and 2632/09) by Serbian nationals Neđo Krndija, Enita Mavrić, Predrag Vukosavljević and Bora Jovanović against Serbia. The applicants complained under the Convention that domestic authorities failed to enforce final court judgments in their favour (primarily concerning reinstatement after unlawful dismissal and related pecuniary awards) and that they lacked an effective remedy. The companies involved were socially or State-owned (or predominantly so) both before and during relevant enforcement and insolvency proceedings. All judgments remained largely unenforced.

The first applicant was dismissed on 26 May 2004 by DP Udarnik (later in liquidation). His June 2004 civil action led to a 20 December 2006 Third Belgrade Municipal Court judgment declaring the dismissal void, ordering reinstatement within eight days and awarding RSD 49,500 in costs (he had withdrawn a salary claim). This was upheld on 10 July 2008 and became enforceable on 26 December 2008. Insolvency proceedings against the company (19 March–14 May 2007) were stayed, allowing it to resume operations. The applicant sought enforcement on 21 January 2009 (amended 6 March 2009), including salaries until reinstatement. The enforcement court delayed, incorrectly rejected the request on 13 October 2009 (citing pending insolvency), and ignored repeated complaints. Liquidation attempts failed (2009–2011). Fresh insolvency opened on 19 December 2011 (still pending); the applicant recovered only 2.89% of his costs claim after property division.

The second applicant worked for Raška Holding AD – Pamučna predionica DOO (Novi Pazar) from 1990–2007 and was placed on compulsory paid leave (with reduced pay and social contributions). In 2007 she received a 1991 dismissal decision. A 9 July 2007 Novi Pazar Municipal Court judgment (final 5 September 2007) voided the dismissal, ordered reinstatement to a suitable post, payment of minimum salary arrears (8 November 1990–16 March 2007) plus interest, pension/disability contributions (1 January 1994–16 March 2007) and RSD 11,700 costs. Enforcement was ordered on 3 December 2007, but she was made redundant on 22 October 2007. A further 6 May 2008 judgment (final 22 January 2009) awarded later contributions and costs (salary claim rejected initially); enforcement was delayed until a 2011 Supreme Court instruction and 7 July 2011 order. After retrial, an 18 October 2013 judgment added salary for the paid-leave period (proceedings pending). The company entered restructuring (from 2004/2006); preliminary insolvency opened in 2013, restructuring ended, and full insolvency began 25 October 2013 (ongoing). Her claim was admitted on 26 January 2015 but unpaid.

The third applicant reached a 25 June 2010 court-approved settlement with Livnica Ralja AD declaring his 2002 dismissal void, ordering reinstatement and payment of RSD 1,544,783 plus RSD 484,810.65 in salary arrears/social contributions (11 March 2002–31 May 2010) plus stamp duties. It was immediately final and enforceable. An enforcement order issued on 29 June 2010. Bailiffs found no movable assets (March/June 2011); an immovable-asset order followed in May 2011. Preliminary insolvency opened 9 February 2011; proceedings opened and terminated on 18 April 2011 due to bankruptcy with no successor or registered claims (none of the creditors paid the deposit). The company was struck off registers on 28 June 2011, its property becoming State assets. Enforcement was suspended (18 October 2011, no assets) then terminated (25 November 2011) due to liquidation.

The fourth applicant obtained a 9 December 2004 Leskovac Municipal Court judgment ordering reinstatement, salary arrears, pension/disability contributions and costs against DP Galpres. Reinstatement/contributions parts became final (16 February 2005) and enforceable (19 March 2005); arrears were remitted then awarded on 13 November 2006 (with related sums). Enforcement orders issued on 20 May 2005 and 24 April 2007. After the Government’s observations, the applicant failed to respond to the Court’s requests (despite reminders and Article 37 § 1(a) warnings), suggesting possible striking-out.

Relevant domestic law included insolvency and enforcement statutes (e.g., termination of contracts possible upon insolvency; creditors could claim salaries until reinstatement). Prior ECtHR cases on Serbian socially-owned companies, delayed enforcement and Constitutional Court practice were referenced. The core issue was State responsibility for non-enforcement against such entities amid insolvency/liquidation, despite final judgments.
001-174992:
The case of Kącki v. Poland originated in an application (no. 10947/11) lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Polish journalist Marcin Kącki against Poland, alleging a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant claimed that his criminal conviction for defamation of a politician interfered with his rights as a journalist.

In 2006, A.R., associated with the political party Self-Defence of the Republic of Poland (Samoobrona), emailed Gazeta Wyborcza about an alleged “sex scandal” involving party activists offering or accepting sexual favours in connection with public functions. The applicant, a journalist, telephoned A.R., recorded the conversation after informing her, and published an interview with her on 6 December 2006 titled “Payment for sex, the choice is yours.” A.R. stated that she had begun unpaid work with the party through A.K. When she demanded payment, activist K.Z. allegedly told her he would pay if she slept with him. She further claimed that at a July 2004 party organised by A.K., prominent activist B.S. offered to arrange a post for her in the office of parliamentary deputy R.C. (later identified in proceedings as relating to MEP M.C.) in return for sexual favours. B.S. was so insistent that A.R. sought help from K.S., who called a taxi. When the applicant asked if she obtained the job, A.R. replied that it went to M.C.’s daughter. The newspaper published denials on the same page from K.Z., B.S. and K.S., as well as a short interview with A.K. denying knowledge of any such scandal or having recommended A.R. for work.

On 30 November 2007, M.C., a Member of the European Parliament, lodged a private bill of indictment against the applicant for defamation under Article 212 of the Polish Criminal Code. M.C. argued that the interview suggested his involvement in the sex scandal and that A.R.’s statement about employing his daughter constituted an accusation of nepotism.

On 16 March 2010, the Warsaw District Court found the indictment partially accurate. It held the applicant guilty of defamation solely in respect of the nepotism allegation, ruling that he had neglected professional obligations by failing to verify whether M.C. had a daughter (which he did not). The court rejected the applicant’s defence that he had acted diligently by sending the text to A.R. for authorisation (autoryzacja), which she approved without comment. It discontinued the proceedings subject to a one-year probationary term, ordered the applicant to pay 1,000 PLN (approximately EUR 232) to charity and to cover costs. The court did not find defamation regarding implied involvement in the sex scandal, as the applicant had published B.S.’s denial, meaning an average reader would not conclude M.C. was involved.

Both parties appealed. On 18 June 2010, the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the judgment, emphasising that journalists’ right to publish critical comments must be balanced against individuals’ rights to protection of reputation. The applicant’s lawyer requested the Ombudsman to lodge a cassation appeal, but this was declined on 6 May 2011 for lack of grounds.

Relevant domestic law included constitutional guarantees of press freedom (Article 14), freedom of expression (Article 54 § 1) and the principle of proportionality in limitations on rights (Article 31 § 3). Article 212 of the Criminal Code criminalises defamation that lowers a person in public opinion or undermines confidence in their professional capacity, with higher penalties if committed via mass media, and allows private prosecution. Article 213 provides defences if allegations are true and concern public functions or a justifiable public interest. On 30 October 2006, the Constitutional Court upheld the compatibility of Article 212 with the Constitution, finding that criminal sanctions for defamation could be necessary to protect dignity, reputation and privacy, and that civil remedies alone might be insufficient (with three dissenting opinions).

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the conviction, based on insufficient verification of a statement in an authorised interview about a matter of public interest involving a politician, unjustifiably interfered with journalistic freedom of expression.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered its judgment in Kącki v. Poland (Application no. 10947/11) on 4 July 2017 (final 4 October 2017). The applicant, Polish journalist Marcin Kącki (born 1976, resident in Poznań), alleged that his criminal conviction for defamation interfered with his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. Represented by counsel, he lodged the application on 5 February 2011. The Court communicated the Article 10 complaint on 27 August 2014 and declared the remainder inadmissible.

In late 2006, A.R., a member of the Self-Defence of the Republic of Poland (Samoobrona) party, emailed Gazeta Wyborcza alleging a “sex scandal” in which party activists offered or accepted sexual favours in connection with public functions. The applicant telephoned A.R., recorded the conversation after informing her, and obtained her subsequent authorisation of the transcript (autoryzacja). On 6 December 2006 the newspaper published the interview under the headline “Payment for sex, the choice is yours.” A.R. stated that activist K.Z. had told her he would pay her only if she slept with him, and that prominent activist B.S. had offered to arrange a post in the office of Member of the European Parliament M.C. in return for sexual favours; she claimed she had to enlist another activist’s help to have B.S. removed. When the applicant asked whether she obtained the job, A.R. replied that it had been given to M.C.’s daughter. On the same page the newspaper printed denials from K.Z., B.S., K.S. and A.K., all of whom rejected the sexual-proposition claims and any knowledge of the scandal.

On 30 November 2007 M.C. lodged a private indictment under Article 212 of the Criminal Code, asserting that the interview implied his involvement in the sex scandal and accused him of nepotism. On 16 March 2010 the Warsaw District Court found the applicant guilty solely of the nepotism allegation. It held that he had failed to verify the statement that M.C. had employed his daughter; evidence at trial established that M.C. had no daughter, so the information was false. The court rejected the argument that A.R.’s authorisation of the text discharged the journalist’s duty of verification. It acquitted him of the sex-scandal implication because the published denials meant an average reader would not conclude M.C. was involved. Proceedings were discontinued subject to a one-year probationary period; the applicant was ordered to pay PLN 1 000 to charity and the costs of the case.

Both parties appealed. On 18 June 2010 the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the judgment, reiterating that a journalist’s right of criticism must be balanced against an individual’s right to protection of reputation. The applicant’s request that the Ombudsman lodge a cassation appeal was refused on 6 May 2011.

Relevant domestic provisions include Constitutional Articles 14, 31 § 3 and 54 § 1 (freedom of the press and expression, subject to proportionate statutory limitations) and Criminal Code Articles 212–214 (defamation, aggravated when committed via mass media, with limited truth defences for public-interest statements about persons exercising public functions). On 30 October 2006 the Constitutional Court had declared Article 212 compatible with the Constitution, holding that criminal-law protection of reputation may sometimes prevail over freedom of expression and that civil remedies alone would be insufficient.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 10 violation: a journalist was held criminally liable for publishing an unverified (and false) statement by a source concerning a public figure, notwithstanding source authorisation and the simultaneous publication of contrary statements.

The case of Kącki v. Poland originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by journalist Marcin Kącki, alleging that his criminal conviction for defamation of a politician violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression).

In late 2006, A.R., associated with the Samoobrona political party, emailed Gazeta Wyborcza about an alleged “sex scandal” involving party activists offering jobs for sexual favours. The applicant, a journalist, spoke with A.R. by telephone (which he recorded) and on 6 December 2006 published an interview with her titled “Payment for sex, the choice is yours.” A.R. described how activist K.Z. had offered payment for sex and how prominent activist B.S. had offered to arrange a post for her in the parliamentary office of deputy R.C. (M.C., a Member of the European Parliament) in return for sexual favours. When the applicant asked whether she obtained the job, A.R. replied that it had been given to M.C.’s daughter. The same page carried denials from K.Z., B.S. and K.S., plus a short interview with A.K. denying knowledge of any scandal.

On 30 November 2007 M.C. lodged a private indictment charging the applicant with defamation under Article 212 of the Criminal Code. He claimed the interview implied his involvement in the sex scandal and accused him of nepotism by employing his own daughter.

On 16 March 2010 the Warsaw District Court found the applicant guilty only of the nepotism allegation. It held that he had failed to verify the statement (M.C. in fact had no daughter) and that sending the text to A.R. for authorisation did not constitute due diligence. The court acquitted him of implying involvement in the scandal because the published denials meant an average reader would not conclude M.C. had participated. Proceedings were discontinued subject to a one-year probationary period; the applicant was ordered to pay PLN 1,000 to charity plus costs.

Both parties appealed. On 18 June 2010 the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the judgment, emphasising the need to balance a journalist’s right of criticism against an individual’s right to reputation. The applicant’s request that the Ombudsman lodge a cassation appeal was refused.

Polish constitutional provisions (Articles 14, 31 § 3 and 54) protect press freedom and expression subject to proportionate limitations. Article 212 of the Criminal Code criminalises defamation (especially via mass media) and allows a private prosecution; Article 213 provides a defence of truth for statements concerning public functions or a justifiable public interest. In 2006 the Constitutional Court upheld the compatibility of Article 212 with the Constitution, finding that criminal-law protection of reputation can in some circumstances take precedence over freedom of expression.

The applicant argued that the finding of criminal liability, even though the penalty was modest, constituted an unjustified interference with his Article 10 rights as a journalist reporting on a matter of public interest involving a politician.
001-175143:
The case of T.G. v. Croatia (Application no. 39701/14) originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by a Croatian national born in 1974. He complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention that his firearms licence for hunting was not renewed on the basis of police reports that were not fully disclosed to him or his lawyer.

In February 2011, after holding a firearms licence and hunting permit for about ten years, the applicant (who lived abroad but hunted during holidays in Croatia) requested renewal from the S. Police Department. He submitted a Ministry of Health certificate confirming he was healthy and capable of carrying firearms. A police background check produced a 22 February 2011 report finding that he had often been under the influence of alcohol when visiting Croatia. Summoned on 18 August 2011, he denied alcohol abuse and offered to undergo tests. In further statements, he described hunting as a hobby tied to his social status and argued there was no justification for refusal.

On 23 August 2011 the police dismissed the request and ordered surrender of his weapons, citing an inquiry showing alcohol abuse. He challenged this before the Ministry of the Interior, claiming false accusations by neighbours without evidence. On 11 October 2011 the Ministry ordered a new assessment because the original report lacked substantiation. A 9 November 2011 report gave further details of alleged abuse confirmed by neighbours, but classified the sources as confidential. The Ministry dismissed his complaints on 12 December 2011, relying on case-file documents suggesting an alcohol problem.

The applicant lodged an administrative action in the Administrative Court on 6 February 2012, arguing the refusal rested on mere insinuations and gossip, as he had never been registered for alcohol issues or convicted of related offences. He requested disclosure of the reports, identities of sources, dates and places; this was refused as confidential. At a 26 April 2012 hearing the Ministry invoked the Confidentiality of Information Act. The court later inspected the confidential police file in the parties’ absence on 17 May 2012. The applicant’s representative reiterated there was no drinking problem but sought no further evidence.

On 23 May 2012 the Administrative Court dismissed the action, satisfied from the confidential reports that the police findings of common and excessive alcohol abuse (indicating possible weapons abuse) were well-founded under the Weapons Act. The medical certificate was only one element and did not override the general requirement of no circumstances suggesting abuse. The applicant then complained to the Constitutional Court that denial of access to the evidence left him unable to challenge the allegations (Article 6) and that the unjustified refusal interfered with private life by preventing hunting, his means of contact with friends (Article 8). He submitted neighbour signatures and a medical certificate denying any alcohol problem.

On 6 February 2014 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as unfounded. It held that the applicant had had access to the (non-source) police reports containing the reasons for refusal, so non-disclosure of further personal details of informants did not infringe his rights. The Court did not examine alleged errors of fact or law unless they violated constitutional rights.

These facts focus on the use of undisclosed confidential sources in the background checks that led to non-renewal of the licence, the limited opportunity to contest them, and the asserted impact on the applicant’s long-standing hunting hobby and social relations.

The case of T.G. v. Croatia (Application no. 39701/14) concerns an applicant (a Croatian national born in 1974, granted anonymity) who complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. He alleged that the refusal to renew his firearms licence (held for about 10 years, along with a hunting permit) was based on undisclosed police reports of alcohol abuse, denying him a fair opportunity to challenge the evidence and interfering with his private life (hunting as a long-standing hobby tied to social contacts during holidays in Croatia, where he did not reside).

In February 2011, the applicant applied to the S. Police Department to renew the licence for hunting, submitting a Ministry of Health certificate confirming his medical fitness to carry firearms. Police background checks produced a 22 February 2011 report finding he was often under the influence of alcohol when visiting Croatia. Summoned on 18 August 2011, he denied any abuse, offered to undergo tests, and emphasised hunting's role in his social life. On 23 August 2011, police refused renewal and ordered surrender of weapons, citing the inquiry. The applicant appealed to the Ministry of the Interior, claiming false neighbour accusations and lack of evidence.

The Ministry ordered a new assessment (11 October 2011) as the initial report lacked substantiation. A 9 November 2011 police report provided further neighbour-confirmed details of alleged abuse but classified sources as confidential under domestic law. The Ministry dismissed the appeal on 12 December 2011. The applicant brought an administrative action in the Administrative Court (6 February 2012), arguing the refusal rested on unsubstantiated gossip, with no record of alcohol-related convictions or registrations. He requested disclosure of reports, witness identities, dates and places (14 April 2012); police refused on confidentiality grounds.

At a 26 April 2012 hearing, the applicant's lawyer stressed the absence of credible evidence. The Ministry cited the Confidentiality of Information Act. The court later ordered production of the confidential file for judges' inspection only (not added to the case file). On 17 May 2012, the court examined it ex parte, then heard the applicant's reiteration of denials (no further evidence proposed). On 23 May 2012, it dismissed the action, finding the confidential reports well-founded (indicating frequent excessive alcohol use suggesting possible weapons abuse) per the Weapons Act and police by-law; the medical certificate was merely one (special) requirement, outweighed by the general condition of no abuse risk.

The applicant appealed to the Constitutional Court, complaining of denied access to evidence (preventing challenge) and an unjustified Article 8 interference (hunting as social contact). He submitted neighbours' statements and a medical certificate denying alcohol issues. On 6 February 2014, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint: it does not review factual/legal errors absent rights violations, and the applicant had access to the (non-source) reports.

Domestic law (Weapons Act s.10; police by-law) required checks for circumstances like alcohol abuse indicating weapons risk, with reports omitting sources (classified "restricted" under the Confidentiality of Information Act, accessible to judges via clearance or confidentiality statements). Administrative procedure allowed free evidence assessment but required judgments based on facts/evidence on which parties could comment. Relevant EU firearms Directive permitted licences only for those not posing danger to self/public safety.

These facts centre on the non-disclosure of confidential sources/details underpinning the licence refusal, the ex parte court review, and the resulting inability to contest specific allegations, as well as the impact on the applicant's hunting-related private/social life.

The case of T.G. v. Croatia (Application no. 39701/14) concerns a Croatian national born in 1974 who had held a firearms licence and hunting permit for approximately ten years. In February 2011 he applied to the S. Police Department to renew the licence solely for hunting purposes during holidays in Croatia. He supported the request with a Ministry of Health certificate confirming medical fitness to carry firearms.

A police background check produced a 22 February 2011 report concluding that the applicant was frequently under the influence of alcohol while visiting Croatia. After he was summoned and denied any drinking problem, the police on 23 August 2011 refused renewal and ordered surrender of his weapons on the basis of that finding. The applicant appealed to the Ministry of the Interior, asserting that the allegations originated from false neighbour gossip and that no objective evidence existed.

The Ministry directed a fresh assessment because the first report lacked substantiation. The resulting 9 November 2011 report supplied additional particulars of alleged alcohol abuse, sourced from neighbours, but classified all identifying details as confidential. The Ministry dismissed the appeal on 12 December 2011, relying on the file as a whole.

The applicant then brought an administrative action before the Administrative Court, arguing that the refusal rested on unsubstantiated insinuations rather than any official record of alcohol-related offences or medical diagnosis. He requested disclosure of the underlying reports, including the identities of informants and the dates and places of the alleged incidents; the police refused, citing the Confidentiality of Information Act and the relevant by-law, which required that sources remain undisclosed even to the applicant.

At a 26 April 2012 hearing the Ministry confirmed that informant identities were confidential. The court subsequently inspected the classified police file in the parties’ absence, then resumed the hearing and, on 23 May 2012, dismissed the action. It held that the confidential material established that the applicant was prone to frequent and excessive alcohol abuse, creating a risk of weapons misuse, and that the medical certificate addressed only one statutory requirement, not the general condition of absence of circumstances suggesting possible abuse.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, claiming he had been denied any effective opportunity to challenge the secret evidence, thereby violating his right to a fair hearing, and that the unjustified denial of the licence interfered with his private life by preventing him from hunting, an activity that enabled him to maintain social contacts. He submitted neighbour signatures and a further medical certificate attesting to the absence of an alcohol problem.

On 6 February 2014 the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint. It found that the applicant had been given the non-confidential versions of the police reports and that the withholding of further particulars, including personal data of informants, did not infringe his rights, because those details were lawfully classified.

The applicant’s complaints before the European Court of Human Rights therefore centred on Article 6 (fair-trial guarantees, in particular equality of arms and the right to contest evidence) and Article 8 (respect for private life) arising from the use of undisclosed police reports to refuse renewal of his long-held hunting licence.
001-179819:
**CASE OF BRITANIŠKINA v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 67412/14)**

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 October 2014 by Lithuanian national Ms Libė Britaniškina (born 1930, residing in Vilnius), represented by lawyer M. Kazlauskas. The Lithuanian Government was represented by Agent K. Bubnytė. On 13 September 2016, the Court communicated the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning failure to provide a new plot of land of equal value and overall delays in the restitution process; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

On 29 December 2001, the applicant’s husband requested restoration of property rights to a house and plot of land in Vilnius previously owned by his grandfather before nationalisation. On 28 February 2002, he specified a preference for restoration in natura if possible, or an equivalent plot in Vilnius. Property rights to some premises (a storehouse) were restored in 2003, with monetary compensation for remaining premises.

On 10 April 2003, Vilnius County Administration informed the Municipality that rights would be restored to 0.1638 hectares for residential purposes. In June 2003, a 0.1007-hectare plot was formed near buildings owned by the husband. In November 2003, a court established as fact that the grandmother had owned 362 square fathoms of land. Further notices in 2004 confirmed the husband as a candidate for 0.1638 hectares in natura.

In August 2006, authorities explained that the 0.1007-hectare plot would be divided among co-owners, with remaining land restored by chosen means. The husband died on 16 May 2007; the applicant became his heir. In March 2009, her son (as representative) requested restoration of 0.1171 hectares via compensation in securities.

On 9 April 2009, rights were restored in natura to 0.0467 hectares, with approximately EUR 1,642 in securities for 0.1181 hectares. This was amended on 24 July 2009 to 0.0362 hectares in natura and approximately EUR 1,788 in securities for 0.1286 hectares. In October 2009, the applicant complained to Vilnius Regional Administrative Court that the securities compensation was unjust, seeking recalculation of the 0.1286-hectare plot’s value. In February 2010, she sought suspension and referral to the Constitutional Court.

On 10 February 2010, the court noted that County Administration calculations followed Government methodology, but municipal and Register Centre market valuations were approximately EUR 786,029 and EUR 750,313—327.5 times higher. Uniform calculation for city-centre and outlying plots failed the equal-value principle. Proceedings were suspended and referred to the Constitutional Court.

In April 2013, the National Land Service informed the applicant of law changes allowing alternative restoration forms (new equivalent plot, voiding State liabilities, plot for individual construction, or monetary compensation) instead of securities; she did not reply. On 30 September 2013, she was placed on the list for a plot for individual-house construction.

Following the Constitutional Court’s 11 September 2013 ruling upholding the methodology, Vilnius Regional Administrative Court rejected the claim on 4 November 2013. It noted the Law on Restoration had changed, ending securities compensation (replaced by monetary compensation if no alternative chosen). Authorities had offered other options, and the applicant was listed for a construction plot, rendering the securities decision legally irrelevant.

The applicant appealed. On 29 May 2014, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the decision, citing Constitutional Court reasoning that compensation need not reflect current market value but could consider nationalisation-era value, quality changes, and societal balance under restricted restitution (not restitutio in integrum). It found proceedings length (complaint 4 November 2009; referral February 2010; Constitutional Court ruling September 2013; decision November 2013) reasonable given complexity.

On 11 November 2014, the National Land Service offered restoration via an equal-value forest plot (deadline 1 March 2015); the applicant did not reply.

Domestic law included Constitution Article 23 (property inviolable, just compensation for expropriation) and the 1997 Law on Restoration of Citizens’ Ownership Rights, providing in natura restoration of unoccupied urban land or equal-value compensation (initially including securities, later cash or alternatives). Government methodology (1999, amended) valued urban land at a low per-hectare rate multiplied for Vilnius/Kaunas, based on nationalisation-era averages rather than current market prices. The Constitutional Court confirmed this as constitutional, emphasising restricted restitution to avoid undue burden on society.

The alleged violations centred on the protracted restitution process (from 2001 onward, still unresolved by 2014) and failure to provide a plot of equivalent value, with compensation deemed grossly inadequate relative to market valuations.

The case concerns Lithuanian national Libė Britaniškina’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 regarding restoration of her late husband’s property rights to a nationalized house and land plot in Vilnius, originally belonging to his grandfather. The alleged violations center on failure to provide a replacement plot of equivalent value and excessive delays in completing restitution.

On 29 December 2001 the husband requested restoration, later specifying return of the land in natura if possible or another Vilnius plot. In 2003 some premises (a storehouse) were restored in kind, with monetary compensation for the remainder. Authorities confirmed rights to 0.1638 ha of residential land. The Vilnius Municipality formed a 0.1007 ha plot near the buildings. A 2003 court ruling established that the grandmother had owned 362 square fathoms.

In 2004 authorities reiterated the husband’s entitlement to 0.1638 ha. A 2006 explanation indicated the 0.1007 ha plot would be divided among co-owners, with remaining land restored by his chosen method. The husband died on 16 May 2007; the applicant inherited the claim.

In March 2009 her son requested restoration of 0.1171 ha via securities compensation. Decisions of April and July 2009 restored only 0.0362 ha in natura and offered securities worth approximately EUR 1,788 for 0.1286 ha. The applicant challenged this in the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court as unjust, seeking recalculation. The court noted a massive discrepancy: municipal and register valuations placed market value at EUR 750,000–786,000 (327 times higher). It also observed that the Government methodology applied identical rates regardless of location (city centre versus outskirts). Proceedings were suspended in February 2010 and referred to the Constitutional Court.

While the referral was pending, restitution legislation changed. From 2012 securities compensation was abolished; claimants could switch (by July 2013) to alternatives including an equivalent-value plot, a construction plot, monetary compensation, or voiding of State liabilities. In April 2013 the National Land Service informed the applicant of these options; she did not reply. In September 2013 she was placed on the waiting list for an individual-house construction plot.

The Constitutional Court ruled on 11 September 2013 that the methodology complied with the Constitution and the Law on Restitution. Lithuania had adopted restricted (not full) restitution; compensation could take account of historical nationalization-era values, subsequent changes in quality, and the need to balance individual rights against societal and fiscal burdens. Pure market value was not required.

On 4 November 2013 the administrative court dismissed the claim. The securities decision had become legally irrelevant after the legislative amendments; the applicant now had other restoration options and had been listed for a construction plot. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this on 29 May 2014, also finding the overall length of proceedings (from November 2009) compatible with the reasonable-time requirement given the case’s complexity and the 2010–2013 Constitutional Court referral.

In November 2014 the applicant was offered (deadline March 2015) restoration via an equivalent-value forest plot; she again did not reply. Restitution begun in 2001 thus remained incomplete more than a decade later, with the original in-natura plot never fully formed, the securities compensation amounting to a tiny fraction of market value, and subsequent offers of equivalent land unused. These facts underpin the complaint that the State failed to provide a plot of equal value and subjected the process to unjustified delays.

The case of Britaniškina v. Lithuania (ECtHR Application no. 67412/14) concerns a Lithuanian applicant's complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that she was not provided with a new plot of land of equal value during property restitution and that the process suffered overall delays.

The applicant's husband initiated restitution proceedings on 29 December 2001, seeking restoration of property rights to a house and plot of land in Vilnius that had belonged to his grandfather prior to nationalisation. He specified on 28 February 2002 that the plot should be restored in natura if possible, or that he should receive another plot in Vilnius. In 2003, rights to some premises (a storehouse) were restored, with monetary compensation for remaining unrestored premises. On 10 April 2003 the Vilnius County Administration informed the Municipality that rights would be restored to 0.1638 hectares of residential land. The Municipality formed a 0.1007-hectare plot near the husband's buildings in June 2003. A November 2003 court decision established that the grandmother had owned 362 square fathoms of land. Further notifications in 2004 confirmed the husband as a candidate for the 0.1638-hectare plot.

In August 2006 the authorities explained that the 0.1007-hectare plot would be divided among co-owners, with the remainder returned according to the husband's choice. The husband died on 16 May 2007 and the applicant inherited his claim. On 27 March 2009 her son requested restoration of rights to 0.1171 hectares via compensation in securities. Decisions of 9 April and 24 July 2009 restored 0.0362–0.0467 hectares in natura and awarded compensation in securities of approximately EUR 1,642–1,788 for the remaining 0.1181–0.1286 hectares.

In October 2009 the applicant challenged the compensation as unjust before the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court and sought recalculation of the 0.1286-hectare plot's value. Proceedings were suspended in February 2010 pending a Constitutional Court ruling on the Government-approved methodology, which valued urban land at 6,000 LTL per hectare (multiplied by eight for Vilnius), producing a figure 327.5 times lower than contemporaneous market valuations of EUR 750,000–786,000. The Constitutional Court ruled on 11 September 2013 that the methodology complied with the Constitution and the Law on Restitution, as Lithuania had adopted restricted restitution (not restitutio in integrum). Compensation could take account of original nationalisation-era values, subsequent quality changes and the need to balance individual rights against societal and fiscal interests.

After the Constitutional Court decision, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's claim on 4 November 2013, noting legislative amendments that had abolished securities compensation and introduced alternatives (a new equivalent-value plot, a construction plot, monetary compensation or forest land). The applicant had been offered these options in April 2013 (without reply) and was placed on a waiting list for an individual-house construction plot in September 2013. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the dismissal on 29 May 2014, also finding that the length of proceedings (initiated 2009, interrupted by the Constitutional Court reference 2010–2013) was justified by complexity. A further November 2014 offer of equivalent forest land likewise went unanswered.

Domestic law (Articles 23 and 102 of the Constitution, the Law on Restitution as amended 1997–2014, and the 1999 Methodology) provided for in-natura restoration where possible, otherwise compensation calculated by the approved method, later expanded to cash, equivalent plots or forest. The applicant's complaint focused on the disparity between official compensation and market value together with the protracted administrative and judicial process that left her without an equivalent-value plot.
001-179884:
The case of Bartkus and Kulikauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 80208/13) concerns two Lithuanian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) arising from protracted eviction proceedings that prevented them from using a house they owned.

In December 2010 the first applicant purchased a house at a state auction held to recover a debt owed by the previous owner, Z.B. Ownership was registered, but Z.B. and his wife G.B. remained in occupation. In January 2011 the first applicant brought court proceedings seeking their eviction and compensation for pecuniary damage. On 21 December 2011 the Šiauliai District Court confirmed him as lawful owner, found the occupation unlawful, ordered eviction, and awarded 1,000 LTL (approximately EUR 289) per month from 28 December 2010 until the occupants left. A writ of execution was issued on 4 April 2012 and received by the bailiff the following day. The bailiff notified Z.B. and G.B. to vacate; they received the notice on 13 April 2012.

Thereafter the occupants lodged a series of complaints and requests that repeatedly delayed enforcement. G.B. challenged the bailiff’s actions (dismissed in June and September 2012). In October 2012 the first applicant asked the bailiff and police to assist with eviction, including handling a dog and verifying claims that Z.B.’s minor granddaughter lived in the house; inquiries established that the granddaughter resided in Vilnius. The bailiff scheduled eviction for 23 November 2012 but postponed it after receiving medical evidence of G.B.’s illness. Z.B. then obtained an interim court order suspending eviction pending examination of his complaint against the bailiff. That complaint was dismissed on 19 December 2012, the interim measures were lifted, and a further appeal by Z.B. was rejected on 28 March 2013. The bailiff rescheduled eviction for 16 April 2013. On that date Z.B. asserted that his mother (not named in the writ) was living in the house; the bailiff suspended the eviction.

The first applicant complained of the bailiff’s inactivity. On 14 June 2013 he sold the house to the second applicant, who was substituted as creditor. On 16 August 2013 the district court upheld the complaint, holding that the bailiff had improperly delayed execution: only persons listed in the writ could be evicted, others present were merely temporary occupants required to leave immediately, and only a court (not the bailiff) could postpone eviction. The bailiff’s suspension orders were annulled. Forced eviction finally occurred on 18 November 2013 in the presence of the bailiff, a locksmith and police. Z.B. and G.B. were absent; their furniture and belongings remained. The second applicant was appointed property manager of the seized goods.

Subsequent attempts to have the occupants collect or sell the leftover property produced further complaints, a property-seizure order, unsuccessful applications for interim measures, and court proceedings that continued into 2015. In parallel, G.B. applied (unsuccessfully) for interim measures to prohibit use of the house and to annul the original auction. By May 2017 approximately EUR 5,013 of the awarded compensation had been recovered, with EUR 5,070 still outstanding.

The applicants maintained that these successive delays and residual occupation of the premises by the former owners’ property deprived them of the use of their house both during the lengthy enforcement process and after physical eviction.

The ECHR case of Bartkus and Kulikauskas v. Lithuania (App. No. 80208/13) concerned two Lithuanian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The first applicant, Vytautas Bartkus, purchased a house at a state auction in December 2010 (arising from the debtor Z.B.’s unpaid debts) and registered title. The former owners, Z.B. and his wife G.B., remained in occupation.

In January 2011 Bartkus sued for eviction and damages. On 21 December 2011 the Šiauliai District Court confirmed his lawful ownership, ordered eviction of Z.B. and G.B. as unlawful occupants, and awarded Bartkus 1,000 LTL (approx. EUR 289) per month from 28 December 2010 until eviction. A writ of execution issued on 4 April 2012 and reached the bailiff the next day. The bailiff notified the occupants to vacate; they received the notice on 13 April 2012.

Enforcement was repeatedly delayed. G.B. challenged the bailiff in May 2012 (dismissed June and September 2012). Bartkus requested police presence, dog removal and confirmation that no minor granddaughter lived there; authorities (and Z.B.’s daughter) confirmed the granddaughter resided in Vilnius. After a November 2012 eviction notice, Z.B. cited G.B.’s illness; the bailiff initially refused postponement but later granted it until 14 December 2012 upon medical evidence. Z.B. then obtained court interim measures suspending eviction pending his bailiff complaint. The complaint was dismissed in December 2012 (interim measures lifted), but Z.B.’s further appeal led the Regional Court in January 2013 to uphold the illness-based suspension. A March 2013 Regional Court ruling confirmed no minors resided in the house and no grounds existed to suspend execution.

A new eviction date of 16 April 2013 was set. Z.B. claimed his (unlisted) mother lived there, prompting the bailiff to suspend action. Bartkus complained of bailiff inactivity; the bailiff declined to evict unlisted persons and suggested expanding the writ. On 14 June 2013 Bartkus sold the house to the second applicant, Stanislovas Kulikauskas. The District Court substituted Kulikauskas as claimant. On 16 August 2013 that court found the bailiff had improperly delayed, ruled that only listed persons could be evicted (others must leave immediately) and that only a court (not the bailiff) could postpone eviction, and annulled the April 2013 suspension. The Regional Court dismissed Z.B.’s appeal in October 2013.

Forced eviction occurred on 18 November 2013 (bailiff, locksmith and police present). The occupants were absent but left all furniture and belongings. Kulikauskas was appointed property manager of the seized goods. Subsequent bailiff orders required collection of unsold items by February 2014; when ignored, a March 2014 seizure order authorised sale. Occupants’ challenges were dismissed (May 2014 District Court; later rejections of further complaints and auction challenges). Auctions of the goods were advertised in October 2014; related interim-measure applications by Z.B. were eventually annulled for non-payment of fees.

Separate proceedings by G.B. seeking to annul the original auction and prohibit house use were dismissed by the Panevėžys Regional Court and Court of Appeal in 2013. By May 2017 some EUR 5,013 in court-awarded monthly damages had been recovered (EUR 5,070 remaining). The applicants’ core complaint was that protracted enforcement (from 2012 until November 2013) and leftover belongings thereafter prevented them from using their property.

The case originated from an application by two Lithuanian nationals, Vytautas Bartkus and Stanislovas Kulikauskas, alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to their inability to use a house they successively owned amid protracted eviction proceedings against the former occupants.

In December 2010, Bartkus purchased the house at a state auction held to satisfy a debt of former owner Z.B. Z.B. and his wife G.B. remained in occupation. In January 2011 Bartkus sued for eviction and damages. On 21 December 2011 the Šiauliai District Court declared him the lawful owner, ordered eviction, and awarded 1,000 Lithuanian litai (approximately EUR 289) per month from 28 December 2010 until the occupants left. By May 2017 EUR 5,013 had been recovered, with EUR 5,070 outstanding.

A writ of execution issued on 4 April 2012 reached the bailiff the next day. The bailiff demanded vacation; Z.B. received the notice on 13 April. G.B.’s subsequent complaints against the bailiff were dismissed in June and September 2012. In October 2012 Bartkus sought police assistance, citing a dog and Z.B.’s claim that a minor granddaughter lived there. Authorities confirmed the child resided in Vilnius.

Eviction scheduled for 23 November 2012 was postponed after G.B. produced medical evidence of illness. Z.B. then obtained interim measures suspending proceedings pending his complaint against the bailiff. That complaint was dismissed on 19 December 2012, but a further appeal delayed matters until March 2013. A new attempt on 16 April 2013 failed when Z.B. asserted that his (unlisted) mother occupied the premises; the bailiff suspended action. Bartkus complained of inactivity; the bailiff replied that only persons named in the writ could be evicted and suggested Bartkus apply to enlarge the list.

On 14 June 2013 Bartkus sold the house to Kulikauskas, who was substituted as creditor. On 16 August 2013 the District Court held that the bailiff had unlawfully delayed execution, that only listed persons could be evicted, and that any others present had to leave immediately; it annulled the suspension orders. The Regional Court upheld this on 31 October.

Forced eviction took place on 18 November 2013 in the presence of a locksmith and two police officers. Z.B. and G.B. were absent; all furniture and belongings remained. Kulikauskas was appointed property manager of the seized goods. An order requiring collection by 17 February 2014 went unheeded, prompting a seizure order in March 2014 aimed at sale. Courts repeatedly dismissed the occupants’ challenges, holding that the three-month statutory period for retrieval had expired and that sale was therefore lawful. Further complaints and unsuccessful bids for interim measures continued into 2015.

Parallel applications by G.B. seeking to annul the original auction and to prohibit use of the house were dismissed in 2013. Throughout, the occupants’ successive objections—illness, an alleged minor, an unlisted relative, and leftover property—combined with judicial reviews of the bailiff’s conduct to keep the applicants from occupying or freely using the house for years after title had passed.
