The case of Ciocodeică v. Romania (no. 27413/09) arose from an application lodged on 30 April 2009 by Romanian national Maria Ciocodeică, born in 1969 and resident in Timișoara. She alleged that the State had failed to assist effectively in enforcing a final judgment awarding her salary entitlements against her private employer, in violation of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She further claimed she lacked an effective remedy to obtain enforcement.

In 2004 the applicant brought a labour-law action against her former employer, private company C.G.H.T., seeking revocation of its 17 October 2003 dismissal decision and payment of salary entitlements. The Timiș County Court dismissed the claim on 29 April 2004, but the Timișoara Court of Appeal allowed her appeal in a final judgment of 29 September 2004. It ordered the company to revoke the dismissal and to pay all salary entitlements from 17 October 2003 until the date of the judgment, updated and index-linked, together with costs.

The judgment was validated for enforcement on 15 November 2004. The applicant commenced enforcement proceedings on 21 January 2005 through a bailiff, who issued a payment notice on 26 January 2005. After a visit to the company’s premises on 11 February 2005, the bailiff granted a further five days for voluntary compliance. The company refused and, under Article 399 of the then-applicable Romanian Code of Civil Procedure, sought annulment of the enforcement. On 24 February 2005 the Timișoara District Court suspended the enforcement pending a final decision on the complaint, subject to a modest deposit of approximately EUR 90. The applicant’s urgent application of 16 May 2005 to lift the suspension was dismissed on 18 May 2005 for lack of proof of imminent damage.

On 2 June 2005 the District Court allowed the company’s complaint on the ground that the bailiff had not served a copy of the enforceable judgment; the applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed as unfounded on 6 October 2005. A related restriction on the company’s bank accounts was likewise annulled. The bailiff issued a fresh payment notice on 29 June 2005, which was posted at the company’s premises on 4 July 2005. In November 2005 the applicant inquired about compliance and received a negative reply. On 28 May 2007 the bailiff recorded that the enforcement had become time-barred under Article 389 of the Code because six months had elapsed since the last act without activity by the creditor.

The applicant pursued additional avenues. On 5 May 2005 she applied under Article 580³ of the Code for a coercive daily fine; this was granted but overturned on appeal on 16 December 2005 on the ground that a monetary debt could be enforced by a bailiff without such a measure. A complaint to the Minister of Justice concerning the June 2005 judgment was rejected because the decision was final. Criminal complaints lodged in 2005 against the company’s administrator for non-execution led to an investigation that was discontinued on 4 February 2008 with an administrative fine of approximately EUR 250; the acts were held not to constitute a criminal offence. Subsequent appeals by the applicant were dismissed, the last of them becoming final on 28 January 2009.

In August 2014 the company’s two shareholders decided on its liquidation. After publication of the decision, an accounting report of 30 August 2014 recorded that the only creditors were the shareholders themselves. On 10 October 2014 the company was struck off the register. No opposition was lodged.

These events formed the factual basis of the applicant’s complaints of prolonged non-enforcement of a final judgment against a private debtor, successive procedural obstacles, unsuccessful attempts to accelerate or sanction non-compliance, and the eventual disappearance of the debtor without payment.

The case of Ciocodeică v. Romania (Application no. 27413/09) concerns alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, arising from the State's failure to assist effectively in enforcing a final domestic judgment awarding salary entitlements against a private employer, and the lack of an effective remedy to obtain enforcement.

In 2004 the applicant, Maria Ciocodeică, brought proceedings under the Labour Code against her private employer, company C.G.H.T., seeking revocation of its 17 October 2003 dismissal decision and payment of salary entitlements. On 29 April 2004 the Timiș County Court dismissed the action as ill-founded. On appeal, the Timișoara Court of Appeal, in a final judgment of 29 September 2004, allowed the claim. It ordered the company to revoke the dismissal and to pay all salary entitlements from 17 October 2003 until the date of the judgment (updated and index-linked), together with costs.

On 15 November 2004 the Timiș County Court validated the judgment as enforceable. The applicant commenced enforcement proceedings with a bailiff on 21 January 2005. A payment notice was served on 26 January 2005. After a visit to the company's premises, the company refused to comply and applied to have the enforcement annulled. On 24 February 2005 the Timișoara District Court suspended enforcement pending a final decision on the complaint, subject to a modest deposit. The applicant's urgent request of 16 May 2005 to lift the suspension (citing her need to support herself and her infant) was dismissed on 18 May 2005 for lack of proof of imminent damage.

On 2 June 2005 the District Court allowed the company's complaint and annulled the enforcement because the bailiff had not served a copy of the enforceable judgment. The applicant's appeal on points of law was dismissed as unfounded on 6 October 2005. A related restriction on the company's bank accounts was also set aside as having been imposed after the suspension. The bailiff issued a further payment notice on 29 June 2005, which was posted at the company's premises together with the judgment. In November 2005 the applicant enquired about compliance and was told none had occurred. On 28 May 2007 the bailiff recorded that the enforcement had become time-barred under Article 389 of the Code of Civil Procedure because more than six months had elapsed since the last act and the creditor had remained passive.

The applicant pursued additional avenues. On 5 May 2005 she applied under Article 5803 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a court order of immediate enforcement. The District Court granted a coercive daily fine of ROL 500,000, but on 16 December 2005 the County Court allowed the company's appeal, holding that such a fine applied only to personal obligations that could not be enforced by a bailiff and that a monetary debt could be recovered through ordinary enforcement. A complaint to the Minister of Justice in July 2005 produced no result, the courts noting that the underlying proceedings had already terminated in a final judgment.

In 2005 the applicant also lodged criminal complaints against the company's administrator for failure to execute the judgment, relying on provisions of the Labour Code and Law no. 168/1999. An investigation begun in December 2006 was discontinued in February 2008; the administrator was merely fined administratively because his conduct did not constitute an offence. Subsequent complaints and appeals by the applicant were dismissed, the last of them finally on 28 January 2009.

The company was later liquidated by its shareholders in August 2014 and struck off the register in October 2014. An accounting report recorded only the shareholders as creditors; no opposition was lodged.

These events form the factual basis of the applicant's complaints that the authorities failed over a prolonged period to take effective steps to secure enforcement of a final judgment against a private debtor and that no effective remedy existed to compel such enforcement.

The case of Ciocodeică v. Romania (Application no. 27413/09) concerns the non-enforcement of a final 2004 labour-court judgment in favour of the applicant, Maria Ciocodeică (born 1969, resident in Timișoara). She alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, claiming that the State had failed to assist her effectively in recovering salary entitlements from her private employer and that she lacked an effective remedy.

In 2004 the applicant sued her former employer, the private company C.G.H.T., seeking revocation of her October 2003 dismissal and payment of salary arrears. The Timiș County Court dismissed the claim, but on 29 September 2004 the Timișoara Court of Appeal quashed that decision in a final judgment. It ordered the company to revoke the dismissal, to pay all salary entitlements from 17 October 2003 until the date of the appellate judgment (updated and index-linked), and to cover costs.

The judgment was validated for enforcement on 15 November 2004. The applicant instructed a bailiff on 21 January 2005. A payment notice was served, but a visit to the company’s premises produced no compliance. The company then applied to have the enforcement annulled and, on 24 February 2005, obtained a stay of execution (subject to a modest deposit) pending resolution of its complaint. The applicant’s urgent application to lift the stay, citing her need to support herself and an infant, was refused for want of proof of imminent damage. On 2 June 2005 the District Court annulled the enforcement for a procedural defect (failure to serve a copy of the judgment); the applicant’s further appeal was dismissed in October 2005.

A subsequent payment notice posted at the company’s premises likewise produced no result. After the applicant’s last enquiry in November 2005 went unanswered, the bailiff declared the enforcement time-barred in May 2007 for creditor inactivity.

Parallel attempts to accelerate enforcement also failed. A request for a daily coercive fine against the company was granted at first instance but overturned on appeal on the ground that a money judgment could be executed by ordinary bailiff measures. A complaint to the Ministry of Justice was rejected because the underlying decision was final. Criminal complaints under the Labour Code against the company’s administrator resulted only in a modest administrative fine; prosecutors and courts held that the non-execution did not constitute a criminal offence.

001-179825:
The case of Palevičiūtė and Dzidzevičienė v. Lithuania (no. 32997/14) involved two sisters who alleged a violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 after being deprived of 0.4863 hectares of inherited land without receiving an equivalent plot.

In May 1996, authorities restored their late father’s ownership of 9.87 hectares. After his death, the sisters inherited the land equally and received two plots (8.93 ha and 0.94 ha) in kind. A house belonging to a third party stood on the larger plot but was omitted from the 1995 survey plan.

In 2001 J.P. bought the house and storehouse; the land under them measured 0.5204 ha and was classified as residential. In 2005 his mother’s restored 0.51 ha rights were transferred to that location, creating an overlap. The Alytus County Administration later recognised that the 1996 restoration decision had unlawfully included land under third-party buildings. The sisters rejected a 2007 proposal to amend the borders amicably.

A prosecutor therefore sued in 2008 to annul the relevant part of the 1996 decision. After remittals for fuller examination of the necessary plot size, the Varėna District Court held in February 2012 that 0.4863 ha had to be taken from the sisters (the remainder of the overlap being unused by J.P.) so that he could lawfully occupy the land under his residential buildings. Their rights were to be protected by an equivalent plot elsewhere. Subsequent appeals were dismissed by the Vilnius Regional Court (2013) and the Supreme Court (multiple rulings in 2013).

In January 2014 the National Land Service notified the sisters that registration of the 0.4863 ha had been cancelled and invited them to choose another form of restoration; in-kind return was impossible. They insisted on the original plot and claimed J.P. occupied it unlawfully. The Service repeatedly explained that monetary compensation was the only remaining option (preliminary value EUR 217, later indexed to EUR 433.60). After the sisters failed to lodge a formal request and delayed meetings, the Service issued a decision on 25 July 2017 awarding that sum; one applicant collected it in September 2017 and it was not appealed.

Parallel proceedings initiated by the sisters—criminal complaints against J.P., requests for interim injunctions, challenges to cadastral data, and an attempt to reclassify his house as non-residential—were all unsuccessful. J.P. ultimately purchased the 0.5082 ha plot from the State in 2015.

The core facts thus concern an administrative error in the original restitution, subsequent judicial correction that stripped the applicants of 0.4863 ha, and the authorities’ later offer of modest monetary compensation in lieu of an equivalent plot, which the applicants initially rejected.

The applicants, Lithuanian sisters Birutė Palevičiūtė and Ona Dzidzevičienė, alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention arising from the deprivation of 0.4863 hectares of inherited land without receipt of an equivalent plot.

In May 1996, authorities restored their late father’s ownership rights to 9.87 hectares. Following his death, the sisters inherited equally and received two plots in kind (8.93 ha and 0.94 ha). The larger plot’s survey, however, failed to mark a house and storehouse that did not belong to the family.

In 2001 J.P. purchased those buildings (cadastral measurements from 1992 classified the house as residential) and continued to use the 0.5204 ha of land beneath them. In 2005 his mother’s restored rights to 0.51 ha were transferred to the same location, creating an overlap with the applicants’ holding. National Land Service and county authorities later determined that restoration of land lying under third-party buildings was unlawful.

When the applicants refused an administrative amendment of the 1996 decision, a prosecutor brought proceedings in 2008 to annul the restoration insofar as it concerned the overlapping 0.4863 ha. The Varėna District Court granted the claim in 2009, holding that J.P. was entitled to a 0.51 ha residential plot and that the applicants’ rights would be protected by an equivalent plot elsewhere. After successive appeals, remittals and further fact-finding, the same court in 2012 confirmed the overlap (0.5019 ha in total, of which only 0.4863 ha was claimed), attributed the original surveying error to the engineer who had prepared the applicants’ plan, and again ordered an equivalent plot. The Vilnius Regional Court and Supreme Court upheld those findings in 2013, noting that the buildings had been registered as residential since 1992 and that restoration of land under another person’s structures was prohibited.

The National Land Service thereafter invited the applicants to elect a form of restoration; they insisted on return in kind, which the Service stated was impossible. Subsequent administrative and civil actions by the applicants (seeking criminal investigation of J.P., interim measures, re-measurement of cadastral data, and reclassification of the house as non-residential) were all dismissed. In 2015 J.P. purchased the 0.5082 ha plot from the State.

After the applicants failed to request monetary compensation, the Service calculated the value of the 0.4863 ha at EUR 217 (later adjusted for inflation to EUR 433.60) and, on 25 July 2017, issued a decision awarding that sum. One applicant collected the decision; it was not appealed.

The applicants maintained throughout that they had been deprived of land that had been lawfully restored to their father and that no equivalent plot had ever been provided.

The applicants, Lithuanian sisters born in 1949 and 1950, inherited equal shares of their late father's land after his death in December 1995. In May 1996 the authorities restored his ownership rights over 9.87 hectares; two plots (8.93 ha and 0.94 ha) were returned in kind and registered. The larger plot contained a house that did not belong to the family, but the 1995 survey failed to mark the building or identify its owner.

In 2001 J.P. purchased the house (classified as residential since 1992 cadastral measurements) together with a storehouse. He used the 0.5204-hectare plot beneath it without buying the land. In 2005 his mother had her own rights restored to 0.51 ha and transferred that plot to the site of the house; registration in J.P.'s name was refused because it overlapped the applicants' land.

In 2007 the Alytus County Administration and National Land Service concluded that the 1996 restoration had unlawfully included land under third-party buildings. The applicants rejected an amicable adjustment of boundaries. A prosecutor therefore sued in 2008 to annul the portion of the 1996 decision covering 0.4863 ha and the corresponding part of the inheritance certificate.

After remittals, the Varėna District Court (February 2012) and Vilnius Regional Court (July 2013) held that the restoration had been illegal: domestic restitution law barred return of land under buildings belonging to others. The surveyor's omission of the house constituted the decisive error. Although 0.5019 ha actually overlapped, only the 0.4863 ha claimed by J.P. was to be excised. The applicants' property rights were to be satisfied by an equivalent plot elsewhere. Repeated appeals on points of law (time-limits, building classification, necessity of the plot size) were dismissed by the Supreme Court in 2013 as raising no important legal issues.

In January 2014 the National Land Service notified the applicants that the 0.4863 ha registration had been cancelled and invited them to choose an alternative form of restoration; return in kind was impossible. The applicants insisted on the original plot, alleged unlawful occupation by J.P., and sought damages, an easement and a right to repurchase. All such requests were rejected. J.P. was later allowed to buy 0.5082 ha in 2015.

Parallel actions initiated by the applicants—a criminal complaint against J.P., applications for interim injunctions, a challenge to cadastral measurements and a claim that the house remained a former school with communal rather than residential status—were all unsuccessful.

Between 2014 and 2017 the authorities repeatedly informed the applicants that monetary compensation was the only remaining option (preliminary value €217, later indexed to €433.60). The applicants never lodged a formal request. In July 2017 the National Land Service issued a decision awarding €433.60; one applicant collected it and no appeal was filed.

The applicants complained that they had been deprived of 0.4863 ha without receiving an equivalent plot, engaging Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The relevant Lithuanian provisions treat restitution and land reform as interrelated public processes that must balance former owners against current users of residential plots. Land under third-party buildings is State-redeemable and cannot be restored in kind; if the preferred form of restitution is unavailable, monetary compensation follows. Property rights are not absolute and may be limited for public-interest reasons provided just compensation is paid.

The case of Milić and Others v. Croatia concerns the applicants’ allegations that Croatia failed to meet its procedural obligations under Article 2 of the Convention (and related complaints under Article 14) in investigating the 1995 killing of their relative P.M.

P.M. (born 1942), husband of one applicant and father of the others, lived with the family in Razbojište, near Krupa, in the Krajina region then under Serbian paramilitary control. On the night of 4–5 August 1995, during Croatian Operation Storm (4–7 August 1995) to recapture the area, the family (except P.M.) fled. P.M. was killed on 5 August 1995. The applicants maintained he was an unarmed civilian shot in his courtyard. The Government maintained he was armed and died in an exchange of fire with Croatian Army forces in the broader Krupa area. The nearby villages of Razbojište, Krupa and Žegar (including the Milići settlement) were involved.

On 11 October 1995 police found unidentified remains in Razbojište; they were buried as body 434 at Gračac Cemetery. In June 2002, exhumations under the ICTY and Zadar County State Attorney’s Office recovered the body, which contained P.M.’s identity card. An October 2002 autopsy at Zagreb’s Institute for Forensic Medicine concluded death resulted from three shell wounds. The third applicant identified the remains as P.M.’s on 24 November 2003.

No investigation into the death occurred until after the applicants filed a damages claim with the State Attorney’s Office on 5 September 2005. Police then interviewed Ž.M. (October 2005), who stated P.M. had joined a village guard unit but did not know the killer.

In August 2015 an anonymous letter alleged that two men (V.G. and M.B.) had killed 12 elderly people in the “Milića” cave near Krupa on 10 August 1995. Police interviewed local residents O.M. and S.M. O.M. reported that five people from Milići (including P.M.) had been killed during Operation Storm; all were armed members of Serbian paramilitary forces who perished in rocky areas, though he lacked details of cause or manner. S.M. had no relevant information. On 26 August 2015 police informed the Zadar County State Attorney’s Office of the five deaths, including P.M.’s on 5 August 1995.

V.G. (a Croatian Army captain commanding a military-police company) and M.B. (a soldier in the same battalion) were interviewed in September 2015. Both denied ever being in Žegar, knowledge of any killings there, or crimes by their unit; they had been stationed tens of kilometres away. The investigation closed on 1 October 2015. In January 2016 the Zadar County State Attorney’s Office informed counterparts that the anonymous letter’s claims could not be confirmed (no evidence of 12 killings in the cave) and that five paramilitary members, including P.M., had died in combat during the operation; the letter was therefore unreliable.

In parallel civil proceedings, the applicants’ 2005 damages claim against the State was refused. Their 2006 court action was dismissed at first instance (March 2010) because the manner of death was unproven, it had not been shown to constitute a terrorist act engaging State liability, and it had not been established that Croatian army or police killed P.M. outside combat operations. Ministry of Defence archives indicated Croatian forces entered the area only on 6 August 1995, after the death, and a witness stated Žegar was shelled on 5 August. The claim was also held statute-barred. Appeals were unsuccessful (County Court 2010; Supreme Court 2014 on limitation grounds; Constitutional Court 2015).

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the investigation was inadequate, delayed and ineffective.

001-180316:
The case of Bikas v. Germany (Application no. 76607/13) concerned an alleged violation of the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Konstantinos Bikas (a Greek national born in 1958), claimed that German courts, in sentencing him for four sexual offences, improperly treated as an aggravating factor at least 50 further comparable offences of which he had not been convicted.

On 30 October 2009 the Munich II Public Prosecution Office charged Bikas with coercion to engage in sexual activity in at least 300 cases and sexual coercion in 18 further cases. After 17 days of hearings the Munich II Regional Court, on 20 July 2012, limited the prosecution to four incidents that occurred between 19 and 25 August 2007. It provisionally discontinued the remaining charges pursuant to Article 154 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (which permits termination of proceedings where any additional penalty would be insignificant compared with that expected for other offences). The court expressly warned Bikas that, if convicted, it could still take findings relating to the discontinued incidents into account when determining sentence.

That same day the Regional Court convicted Bikas of four counts of coercion to engage in sexual activity and imposed a six-year prison term. In its findings of fact the court accepted the testimony of the victim P. (then aged 29–35, suffering from a moderate mental disorder, autism and a speech impairment). It found that between January 2001 and October 2007 Bikas had forced P., by threats that she would otherwise be returned to a home for the disabled, to satisfy him sexually on at least 50 additional occasions (in the house they shared or in his car). P.’s account of the pattern, location and manner of the acts was corroborated by other witnesses and by three psychological expert reports confirming her credibility and capacity to testify. The court explained that it had been impossible to particularise the exact dates and places of these further incidents because of P.’s speech disorder; it therefore restricted the formal conviction to the four August 2007 events. Nevertheless, after applying generous deductions in Bikas’s favour, it remained “convinced” that at least 50 comparable acts had occurred.

In the sentencing remarks the Regional Court treated those 50 incidents as an aggravating circumstance. It stated that a conviction for them had been precluded solely by the victim’s inability to identify them as discrete procedural offences, and that it would therefore proceed on the basis of 50 further cases of forced manual satisfaction.

Bikas appealed on points of law to the Federal Court of Justice, arguing that reliance on 50 unproven offences as an aggravating factor violated the presumption of innocence. The Federal Public Prosecutor countered that the incidents formed part of the offender’s “previous history” (Article 46 § 2 of the Criminal Code) and that the Regional Court had made sufficiently precise findings to establish a minimum level of guilt. On 6 February 2013 the Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal without giving reasons. The Federal Constitutional Court, on 16 May 2013, likewise declined to entertain a constitutional complaint raising the same issue.

Domestic law and case-law relevant to the complaint include Article 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (allowing partial discontinuation to streamline proceedings) and Article 46 of the Criminal Code (requiring courts to weigh an offender’s previous history). Settled Federal Court of Justice jurisprudence permits discontinued offences to be taken into account at sentencing provided they have been established at trial to a sufficient degree of certainty—not mere suspicion—so that their gravity can be assessed. The Federal Constitutional Court has held that the presumption of innocence is not breached once an accused has been “properly proved guilty” of the acts in question after a trial that reached the stage at which a verdict could be delivered and in which defence rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 were respected, even if formal conviction was impossible. After a 1994 leading decision, serial sexual offences can no longer be treated as a single continuous crime; each act must be individually established, although a court may find a minimum number of offences within a defined period.

These facts formed the basis of Bikas’s complaint that the sentencing process had treated him as guilty of offences that had never been the subject of a formal conviction.

In Bikas v. Germany (no. 76607/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 ECHR was violated when German courts, sentencing the applicant for four sexual coercion offences, considered at least 50 additional similar incidents as aggravating factors, despite discontinuing proceedings for those charges.

The applicant, Konstantinos Bikas (born 1958), was charged on 30 October 2009 by the Munich II Public Prosecution Office with at least 300 counts of coercion to engage in sexual activity and 18 of sexual coercion. The victim, P., had moderate mental, autistic, and speech disorders.

Following 17 hearing days, on 20 July 2012 the Munich II Regional Court limited the case to four incidents from 19-25 August 2007 and provisionally discontinued the rest under Article 154 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, given the likely penalty for the four. It notified the applicant that findings on discontinued incidents could influence sentencing if convicted.

That day, the court convicted him of four counts and imposed six years' imprisonment. It found that from January 2001 to October 2007 the applicant forced P. to perform manual or oral satisfaction on at least 50 more occasions, typically in their shared house or his car when family was absent. He would isolate her, undress, instruct her (sometimes with pornography), and threaten return to a disabled home if she refused. P.'s consistent accounts were corroborated by witnesses and three psychological experts on her credibility.

The court discontinued other charges because P.'s speech disorder prevented specifying exact times and places, making them undefinable as separate procedural offences. Nonetheless, it was convinced of at least 50 comparable cases, calculating conservatively (excluding some years, assuming monthly frequency, applying safety margin).

In sentencing, these 50 incidents (assumed as manual satisfaction, as oral/manual distinction was unclear) were treated as aggravating. Conviction was impossible only due to lack of precise details.

The applicant appealed to the Federal Court of Justice, claiming this breached Article 6 § 2 by treating unproven offences (proceedings discontinued) as proven for harsher sentencing. The prosecutor argued it was valid consideration of previous history under Article 46 § 2 Criminal Code, with sufficient findings of minimum guilt.

The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 6 February 2013 without reasons. The Federal Constitutional Court declined the subsequent complaint on 16 May 2013, also without reasons.

These proceedings highlight the tension between using established but unconvicted conduct in sentencing and the presumption of innocence.

The case of Bikas v. Germany (no. 76607/13) concerns an alleged breach of the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2 ECHR). The applicant, a Greek national born in 1958 and living in Leipzig, was charged on 30 October 2009 by the Munich II Public Prosecution Office with coercing P. (a woman aged 29–35 with a moderate mental disorder, autism and speech disorder) into sexual activity in at least 300 cases, plus sexual coercion in 18 further cases.

After 17 days of hearings, the Munich II Regional Court on 20 July 2012 limited the prosecution to four incidents between 19 and 25 August 2007. It provisionally discontinued all other charges under Article 154 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, given the penalty expected for the remaining four. The applicant was warned that findings on the discontinued incidents could still be considered at sentencing.

The same day the court convicted the applicant of four counts of coercion to engage in sexual activity and imposed six years’ imprisonment. In its factual findings it accepted P.’s detailed, consistent account—corroborated by witnesses and three psychological experts—that between January 2001 and October 2007 the applicant had forced her, by threats of institutionalisation, to satisfy him manually or orally on at least 50 further occasions (in their shared house or his car, often while playing pornography). Exact dates and locations could not be established because of P.’s speech disorder, so those acts could not be treated as separately chargeable “procedural offences.”

When fixing sentence the court expressly treated the 50 additional incidents as an aggravating factor. It stated that it was “convinced” they had occurred and that conviction had been impossible solely because of the victim’s inability to particularise them; it therefore proceeded on the basis of 50 further cases of manual satisfaction.

The applicant appealed to the Federal Court of Justice, arguing that reliance on 50 unconvicted (and formally discontinued) offences as an aggravating circumstance violated the presumption of innocence. The Federal Public Prosecutor replied that the incidents formed part of the applicant’s “previous history” under Article 46 § 2 of the Criminal Code and that the Regional Court had made sufficiently precise findings to establish a minimum level of guilt. On 6 February 2013 the Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal as ill-founded without giving reasons. The Federal Constitutional Court likewise declined, without reasons, to entertain a constitutional complaint (decision of 16 May 2013).

Domestic law and case-law permit this practice. Article 154 CCP allows discontinuance of offences whose additional penalty would be insignificant. Article 46 CC requires courts to consider an offender’s previous history when sentencing. The Federal Court of Justice has long held that discontinued offences may be used as aggravating circumstances provided their existence is established at trial to a degree that permits assessment of gravity (not mere suspicion). The Federal Constitutional Court, referring to Strasbourg case-law, considers the presumption of innocence rebutted once guilt has been properly proved in proceedings that have reached the stage of a possible verdict, even if no formal conviction follows, provided the accused’s Article 6 defence rights were respected.

A 1994 leading decision of the Federal Court of Justice further requires that serial sexual offences be treated as individual acts; a court may nevertheless find a minimum number of such acts within a given period if it is so convinced. These are the facts on which the alleged violation of Article 6 § 2 rests.
001-180555:
**CASE OF KRISTIANA LTD. v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 36184/13)**

The applicant, a Lithuanian company, alleged that it was prevented from using buildings it owned that had been designated for demolition, without any compensation mechanism or time-limits being set, in violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Related complaints concerned the fairness of proceedings and lack of an effective remedy.

In 1994 the Government adopted a development plan for the Curonian Spit National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage site). It required former military buildings in the dunes to be removed and the natural environment restored. In 1998 the State decided to privatise those buildings (two barracks, a canteen, a storehouse and two sheds) in Juodkrantė without the land. The applicant was the sole bidder at a 1999 public auction and purchased them in February 2000 for LTL 226,000 (approximately EUR 65,454). The contract obliged it to lease the associated land.

The company repeatedly sought to change the land-use designation to recreational so that it could renovate the buildings or construct new ones. In 2001–2003 the municipality prepared a detailed plan, but environmental authorities rejected it. Administrative courts (2003–2004) dismissed the company’s challenge, holding that new recreational buildings were prohibited in the park and that the proposal conflicted with the 1994 plan.

The company paid land tax but could not obtain a lease because no detailed plan existed. Courts (2004) confirmed the tax liability on the basis that it was using the land. From 2006 onwards it asked for the land to be included in a recreational zone or for a compensation mechanism. Authorities consistently replied that the 1994 plan required demolition; any compensation decision lay with the Government. A 2012 working group was formed to examine legal grounds for expropriation, but no concrete mechanism or timetable emerged.

In 2010 the company applied for planning permission for major repairs to the canteen. Permission was refused for lack of a land-lease agreement. First-instance courts granted the claim (2010) because the company paid land tax, but the Supreme Administrative Court reversed the decision (2011), finding no proof of land ownership. Reopening was refused.

On 6 June 2012 the Government approved a new Management Plan that still designated the buildings for demolition (“redevelopment”). It reserved nearby land in Juodkrantė to compensate lawful owners of buildings slated for removal. The company challenged the plan in the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, seeking revocation of the demolition designation and an order to include compensation and time-limits. The court refused to examine the claim (July 2012), holding that the lawfulness of a Government resolution implementing State power fell exclusively within the Constitutional Court’s jurisdiction. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this (November 2012), describing the Management Plan as a normative act; any challenge had to arise in the context of an individual implementing decision, at which point a referral to the Constitutional Court could be requested. Reopening was refused (2013).

In 2013 the municipality found the buildings dilapidated and ordered their maintenance and renovation. The park authority then refused planning permission for major repairs as contrary to the 2012 Management Plan. The company sued, seeking an order to issue permission and compensation of EUR 48,489 for taxes paid since 2000. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed the claim (November 2016), finding the refusal lawful, that no compensation mechanism was required by law (though reserved land existed), and that the company, as a diligent purchaser, should have known of the demolition designation at the time of purchase. It refused a Constitutional Court referral. An appeal remained pending.

Further proposals to amend the Management Plan (2015–2016) were rejected as outside the amendment’s scope. Administrative complaints were dismissed on competence grounds; related court proceedings remained pending.

Throughout, the buildings remained standing, unused for their intended purpose, while the company continued to pay taxes and faced ongoing uncertainty about demolition, renovation and any compensation. The Court communicated the complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, Article 6 and Article 13.

The case of Kristiana Ltd. v. Lithuania (Application no. 36184/13) concerns a Lithuanian company’s complaint that it was unable to use buildings it owned, which were designated for demolition without any set timeline or compensation mechanism. This was alleged to violate Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). Related complaints about the fairness of domestic proceedings and lack of an effective remedy were also raised.

In 1994 the Lithuanian Government approved a Development Plan for the Curonian Spit National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage site of high environmental value). The plan required the removal of former Soviet military buildings located in the dunes near Juodkrantė and full restoration of the natural environment. In 1998–2000 the State privatised those buildings (two barracks, a canteen, a storehouse and sheds) without the underlying land, which remained State-owned. The applicant company was the sole bidder at auction and purchased the buildings in February 2000 for approximately EUR 65,454. The purchase contract required it to lease the assigned land plot.

From 2001 the company repeatedly sought to regularise and use the property. It proposed a detailed plan to rezone the land for recreational use and to renovate or replace the buildings. Environmental and park authorities rejected the plan as incompatible with the 1994 Development Plan, which prohibited new recreational construction. Domestic courts upheld the refusals in 2003–2004. The company could not obtain a land-lease agreement because no detailed plan existed, yet it was required to pay land tax (a liability confirmed by courts in 2004). Between 2006 and 2012 it asked that the land be included in a recreational zone or that a compensation scheme be established if demolition proceeded. Authorities consistently referred back to the 1994 plan and later indicated that any decision on compensation lay with the Government.

In 2010 the company applied for planning permission to carry out major repairs on the canteen. Permission was refused because it could not produce a land-lease contract. After conflicting lower-court rulings the Supreme Administrative Court ultimately sided with the authorities in 2011. A further request for renovation permission in late 2013 was refused on the ground that it would contradict the newly adopted Management Plan.

On 6 June 2012 the Government approved the Curonian Spit National Park Management Plan (replacing the 1994 plan). The applicant’s buildings remained marked for demolition. A “reserve territory” in Juodkrantė was designated to compensate possible losses of lawful owners, and a working group was created to examine legal bases for expropriation, but no concrete compensation mechanism, valuation method or demolition timetable was fixed. The company challenged the relevant part of the Management Plan before the administrative courts, seeking its annulment and an order to amend the plan. Both the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (July 2012) and the Supreme Administrative Court (November 2012) declined jurisdiction, holding that approval of the Management Plan was an exercise of State power by the Government as a collegial body and therefore fell exclusively within the competence of the Constitutional Court. The company could only raise constitutionality issues indirectly, by challenging a subsequent individual implementing act and requesting a referral. An application to reopen the proceedings was rejected.

In 2013 the Neringa Municipality inspected the buildings, found them dilapidated, and ordered the company to appoint a maintenance officer, remove damaged parts and complete renovation by May 2014. Permission for those works was nevertheless refused. In subsequent proceedings the company sought an order compelling the park authority to issue the permission and claimed EUR 48,489 for land and property taxes paid since 2000. In November 2016 the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed the claim, holding that the refusal was lawful, that the Management Plan already contemplated possible compensation via the reserve land, that the company (as a diligent purchaser) had known or should have known of the demolition designation since 1994/2000, and that no expropriation had occurred. A request to refer the Management Plan to the Constitutional Court was refused. The company’s appeal remained pending.

A 2015 Government resolution launched an amendment of the Management Plan. The company’s proposals (to rezone its land or to insert clear demolition and compensation rules) were rejected because the site was said to be unaffected by the amendment. Related complaints before the administrative disputes commission and courts were either dismissed on procedural grounds or still pending. Throughout the period the company continued to pay taxes while being unable to renovate, lease the land or obtain any concrete compensation or timetable. Attempts at friendly settlement proposing alternative land with building rights were refused as contrary to imperative domestic law.

These facts form the core of the alleged interferences with the company’s property rights and the related procedural complaints.

**Summary of CASE OF KRISTIANA LTD. v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 36184/13)**

The applicant, Kristiana Ltd., a Lithuanian company, purchased former Soviet military buildings (two barracks, a canteen, a storehouse and two sheds) in Juodkrantė within the Curonian Spit National Park at a 1999 public auction for approximately EUR 65,454. The 2000 purchase agreement required the company to lease the assigned State-owned land. A 1994 Government development plan for the park, whose main objectives were published, required removal of former military buildings in the dunes and full restoration of the natural environment. The Curonian Spit is a UNESCO World Heritage site subject to strict protection.

From 2001 the company sought a detailed plan to designate nearby land for renovation or new recreational buildings and later requested inclusion of the site in a landscape-management recreational zone. Authorities rejected these on the ground that they conflicted with the 1994 plan, which prohibited new construction in the park except in limited cases. Courts in 2003–2004 upheld the refusals. The company was required to pay land tax (and later property tax) as a user of the land, even though no lease was granted because no detailed plan existed. Between 2000 and 2014 it paid substantial sums in these taxes.

Requests for planning permission for major repairs (including of the canteen in 2010 and other buildings later) were refused, initially for lack of a land-lease document and subsequently as contrary to the 2012 Management Plan. The Supreme Administrative Court in 2011 confirmed that ownership or a lease of the land was required. A 2013 municipal inspection found the buildings in disrepair and ordered maintenance and renovation by mid-2014, yet permission was again denied.

On 6 June 2012 the Government approved a Management Plan (replacing the 1994 plan) that designated the applicant’s buildings for demolition/re-cultivation. It allocated a reserve area in Juodkrantė to compensate possible losses of lawful owners of buildings to be removed, but contained no specific compensation mechanism, valuation method or demolition timetable. A working group was formed to examine legal grounds for expropriation, yet no concrete scheme emerged during the relevant period. The company challenged the relevant parts of the 2012 resolution, arguing that it interfered with its property without compensation or time-limits and frustrated legitimate expectations of continued use or reconstruction without increasing height. Administrative courts declined jurisdiction, holding that the Management Plan was a normative act of State power whose constitutionality fell to the Constitutional Court; the company could raise the issue only in proceedings against an individual implementing act and request a referral. Reopening was refused. Later amendment proceedings (2015 onward) likewise left the company’s land unaffected; its proposals for zoning changes or explicit compensation/timelines were rejected, and related complaints were dismissed or remained pending.

The company proposed a friendly settlement (State compensation via lease of alternative land with construction rights) that was refused as contrary to law. It claimed pecuniary damage for taxes paid and sought an order compelling renovation permission. First-instance courts rejected these claims, noting that demolition had been foreseeable at purchase, that the Management Plan provided a compensatory opportunity via the reserve area, and that no taking for public needs had yet occurred. Appeals, including requests to refer constitutional questions, were ongoing at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

The applicant alleged that the prolonged inability to use or renovate its property, the absence of any concrete compensation mechanism or demolition timetable, and the resulting uncertainty and tax burden violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It further complained of lack of access to court and of an effective remedy in respect of the planning acts and refusals.
001-181177:
The applicant, a Nigerian national born in 1975, first entered Germany in 1997 and applied unsuccessfully for asylum under a false identity. After periods in Italy and Spain, he re-entered Germany in October 2000. His daughter, a German national, was born on 21 October 2000 from a relationship with a German woman. The couple lived together in 2000–2001 and have always held joint custody. In December 2000 the applicant received a residence permit based on family ties, valid until December 2001.

In July 2001 he was arrested. In May 2002 the Munich Regional Court sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment for large-scale drug trafficking. He had recruited the child’s mother (then an adolescent) as a drugs courier for two cocaine consignments from South America. The court noted aggravating factors (professional organisation, exploitation of young women, quantities involved) but also mitigating ones (first conviction, one failed delivery, time already spent in pre-trial detention). The applicant served the full sentence and was released in July 2009, remaining under supervision of conduct until 2013.

From 2001 the daughter visited him in prison; from 2008 regular supervised visits occurred every four weeks. After release the applicant never cohabited with the mother and daughter. They live 30–70 km apart. He sees the child every other weekend; a social worker described him as an important figure in her life. Both the daughter and her mother explicitly wish the contact to continue. Since release the applicant has completed occupational retraining but has not been permitted to work. He has three further minor convictions (fraud 2011, theft 2015 and 2016) resulting in day-fines, plus an ongoing offence of remaining without a passport (prosecution discontinued as of minor gravity).

In March 2003 the Munich authorities refused to renew his residence permit and ordered expulsion. The order was mandatory under the Aliens Act because of the narcotics conviction of more than three years. The authorities considered that the State’s interest in removal outweighed family life: the child had already experienced separation, contact could be maintained by letter, telephone or short visits, and the expulsion complied with Article 8 § 2. The decision, which included an unlimited re-entry ban, became final in August 2003.

A second asylum claim lodged in 2007 was rejected as manifestly ill-founded in 2008; the Federal Office found no impediments to return to Nigeria. In September 2009 the applicant applied for a residence permit on family-reunion grounds. The authorities refused in February 2010, citing the final expulsion order; they reduced the re-entry ban to five years and allowed two short annual visits after one year. The Munich Administrative Court quashed that decision in April 2010, holding that the applicant was entitled to a humanitarian residence permit under Section 25 § 5 of the Residence Act because departure was legally impossible owing to family life protected by Article 8. The child’s best interests and the quality of the father–daughter relationship outweighed the public interest in expulsion, especially as the offences predated the birth, the child had already lost years of contact, and relocation to Nigeria was not feasible.

The Bavarian Administrative Court of Appeal reversed in June 2011. Because the asylum claim had been dismissed as manifestly ill-founded, Section 10 § 3 of the Residence Act barred any residence permit before the applicant left Germany. The statutory exception did not apply: a family-reunion permit was precluded by the expulsion order (Section 11), and a humanitarian permit was unavailable because the applicant lacked a passport (a general requirement from which only a discretionary waiver could be granted). The Federal Administrative Court refused leave to appeal in February 2012; the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider a subsequent complaint.

The applicant has since been granted successive exceptional leaves to remain (Duldung) because he has no valid passport, rendering deportation factually impossible. An August 2012 agreement to leave by November 2012 (with a shortened re-entry ban and a promise of later family-reunion consideration) lapsed when the Nigerian embassy refused to issue a passport while Strasbourg proceedings were pending and the applicant declined to depart.

The alleged violation of Article 8 centres on the refusal of a residence permit that would allow the applicant to remain in Germany and maintain his established family life with his German daughter.

The case of T.C.E. v. Germany (no. 58681/12) concerns a Nigerian national's claim that Germany's refusal to grant him a residence permit after a final expulsion order violated Article 8 of the Convention by interfering with his family life with his German daughter.

The applicant, born in 1975, completed schooling in Nigeria and worked there before living in Spain (1994–1997). He entered Germany in 1997, applying for asylum under a false identity; this was rejected in 1998. He left with a German partner, lived in Italy and Spain (working in restaurants), and re-entered Germany in October 2000. Their daughter, a German national, was born on 21 October 2000. The couple lived together in 2000–2001 with joint custody from the outset. In December 2000, Munich authorities issued a family-based residence permit valid until December 2001.

In July 2001, the applicant was arrested for a narcotics offence. In May 2002, the Munich Regional Court sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment for large-scale drug trafficking. He had recruited his partner (then young and naïve) and another adolescent as cocaine runners for consignments from South America (one failed, one involving 4 kg). The court noted this as a first conviction, remand detention, professionalism, and exploitation of the women, but could not convict on a third instance due to undetermined quantities.

The applicant served the full term, released in July 2009 under conduct supervision until 2013. He received Duldung (exceptional leave to remain) as expulsion could not be executed without a valid passport; this was renewed (most recently to July 2017). Post-release, he completed marketing retraining (2010–2012) but was barred from employment. He has not cohabited with his daughter and her mother since release; they live 30–70 km apart. He maintains close, regular contact (every other weekend), becoming an important figure per a social worker. Both the daughter and mother explicitly support continuation. Subsequent minor convictions (fraud 2011, theft 2015/2016: day-fines) occurred; an ongoing Residence Act offence (no passport) was discontinued as minor/not in the public interest.

In March 2003, authorities refused permit renewal and ordered expulsion (mandatory under the Aliens/Residence Act for the narcotics sentence of at least three years or any non-probation term). They found the State's interest outweighed family life, given short cohabitation, the child's experience of separation, and offence gravity; contact via letters/phone/occasional visits (Betretenserlaubnis) sufficed. This included an unlimited re-entry ban and became final in August 2003. A 2007 asylum application was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded (2008/2009), with expulsion ordered (no ties considered in that procedure).

In September 2009, the applicant sought a family-based permit. Rejected in February 2010 due to the 2003 order (purpose unachieved; long-distance relationship already established). The re-entry ban was reduced to five years, with possible short visits after one year. The Munich Administrative Court (April 2010) quashed this, ordering a humanitarian permit (Section 25(5) Residence Act; discretion reduced to zero). Family life (Article 8) made departure legally impossible; despite offences, child's best interests and the applicant's efforts (staying to serve sentence for contact rather than early expulsion; post-2007 relationship developments) prevailed. Offences predated the birth; expulsion plus ban would end a normal father-daughter relationship for her childhood.

The Bavarian Administrative Court of Appeal (June 2011) reversed: the manifestly ill-founded asylum rejection barred any permit until departure (Section 10(3) Residence Act). Exceptions inapplicable, as family permit was precluded by the expulsion (Section 11), and humanitarian permit required a passport (discretionary waiver not a "claim"). Impediments to return were also rejected. The Federal Administrative Court (February 2012) and Constitutional Court (July 2012, no reasons) upheld this.

In 2012, an agreement limited the ban to 2.5 years post-departure, with future family permit (or discretion if no joint custody) if no further offences, and a November 2012 departure deadline. This voided when the applicant did not leave (Nigerian embassy refused a passport pending ECHR proceedings). He remains on Duldung.

These facts highlight the core tension: established, mutually desired father-daughter ties versus the expulsion's effects amid the applicant's criminal history, lack of passport, and asylum abuse.

**Case Summary: T.C.E. v. Germany (ECtHR, Application no. 58681/12, Judgment of 1 March 2018)**

The applicant, a Nigerian national born in 1975, alleged that German authorities’ refusal of a residence permit violated his Article 8 right to family life with his German-national daughter. He arrived in Germany in 1997, applied for asylum under a false identity (rejected in 1998), left, and re-entered in October 2000. His daughter was born on 21 October 2000; he and the German mother shared joint custody and cohabited briefly in 2000–2001. A residence permit based on family ties was issued until December 2001.

In July 2001 the applicant was arrested. In May 2002 the Munich Regional Court sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment for large-scale drug trafficking. He had recruited the child’s mother (then an adolescent) as a courier for cocaine consignments from South America in 1998 and 1999/2000, exploiting her naivety in a professional operation involving kilograms of cocaine. Mitigating factors included it being his first conviction and remand time served; aggravating factors included the scale, professionalism, and risk to young women.

The applicant maintained contact with his daughter: prison visits occurred until 2003, a 2006 court agreement provided for supervised contact post-release, and from January 2008 she visited every four weeks. He was released in July 2009 after serving the full sentence (under supervision until 2013) and received exceptional leave to remain (*Duldung*) under the Residence Act because he lacked a valid passport, rendering expulsion unenforceable. He completed occupational retraining but was barred from employment. He and the child lived apart (30–70 km distant); she spent every other weekend with him. A social worker confirmed he was an important figure, and both mother and daughter wished contact to continue. Post-release he incurred minor convictions (fraud 2011; theft 2015–2016) and an ongoing Residence Act offence for lacking a passport (prosecution discontinued as minor).

In March 2003 authorities refused to renew his permit and ordered expulsion (mandatory under then-Aliens Act s. 47/Residence Act s. 53 for a narcotics conviction of that length). They held the child’s brief cohabitation and the seriousness of the offences outweighed family-life interests; contact could continue by letter/telephone or limited visits. A 2007 asylum application was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded (2008, confirmed 2009).

In September 2009 the applicant sought a family-ties residence permit. Authorities refused (February 2010), citing the final 2003 expulsion order. The Munich Administrative Court (April 2010) ordered a humanitarian permit under Residence Act s. 25(5): family life constituted an insurmountable legal impediment to departure, the child’s best interests and the father’s efforts (including remaining in Germany rather than seeking early release/expulsion) outweighed public-order concerns, and enforcement plus a re-entry ban would irreparably harm the relationship.

The Bavarian Administrative Court of Appeal (June 2011) reversed. Because the asylum claim had been rejected as manifestly ill-founded, Residence Act s. 10(3) barred any permit until the applicant left Germany. Exceptions did not apply: a family-ties permit was precluded by the expulsion order (s. 11); a humanitarian permit required a passport (a general s. 5 condition waivable only discretionarily, so no “claim” existed). Impediments to return had already been rejected in asylum proceedings. The Federal Administrative Court (February 2012) and Federal Constitutional Court (July 2012) upheld this.

Subsequent attempts to obtain a Nigerian passport failed; a 2012 court agreement (limited re-entry ban, future visa/permit if no further offences) lapsed when the applicant refused to leave. He remained in Germany on renewed *Duldung*.

These facts centre on whether the statutory bars (prior expulsion, manifestly unfounded asylum claim, and lack of passport) and the refusal of a residence permit constituted a disproportionate interference with established family life, given the child’s German nationality, joint custody, regular contact, the father’s post-conviction efforts, and the practical impossibility of family life in Nigeria.
001-181372:
**Case of Cernea v. Romania (Application no. 43609/10, ECtHR, 27 February 2018)**

This case originated in an application lodged on 13 July 2010 by Romanian national Remus Florinel Cernea (born 1974, resident in Bucharest), who alleged a violation of his right to stand for election without discrimination in parliamentary by-elections held on 17 January 2010. At the time, the applicant served as Executive Chair of Partidul Verde (the Green Party), an ecological movement affiliated with the European Green Party. The party had fielded candidates in the 2008 general elections but won no seats. In 2009, the applicant ran as the party's presidential candidate, receiving approximately 60,000 votes (0.6% of valid votes).

The 2008 general elections were governed by Law no. 35/2008 on elections to the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. In 2009, Parliament amended this law via Law no. 323/2009 (approving an earlier emergency ordinance). The amendment introduced a provision (new section 48(17)) restricting parliamentary by-elections exclusively to political parties and national minority organizations that had passed the electoral threshold in the preceding general elections. This barred unrepresented parties and independent candidates from participating.

Parliamentary by-elections were called for 17 January 2010 to fill a vacant seat in a Bucharest constituency (vacant since October 2009). Partidul Verde submitted the applicant's candidacy. On 29 December 2009, the Electoral Board rejected it solely because the party was not represented in Parliament. The party (represented by the applicant) challenged the rejection before Bucharest County Court and raised an objection of unconstitutionality. It argued that the ban infringed the right to free elections and constituted unjustified discrimination vis-à-vis parliamentary parties. It further noted that, contrary to Venice Commission recommendations, the electoral law had been amended less than one year before the by-elections.

On 30 December 2009, the County Court deferred its decision pending Constitutional Court review. In Decision no. 61/2010 of 14 January 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed the objection. It held that by-elections serve to fill vacancies while preserving Parliament's political structure as determined by the general elections and the electorate's expressed will. Allowing unrepresented parties to contest by-elections would alter that structure through "devious means" and undermine sovereignty. The Court viewed the Venice Commission guidance (discouraging changes to fundamental electoral rules within one year of an election, unless at constitutional or higher-than-ordinary-law level) with reservations, finding compliance because the amendment occurred via organic law (enacted by a higher majority than ordinary laws and covering electoral matters).

On 30 March 2010, the County Court dismissed the challenge, endorsing the Constitutional Court's reasoning: as the Green Party had not met the general-election threshold, it could not field candidates. The court also noted the elections had already taken place, rendering the challenge moot.

(Subsequent 25 April 2010 by-elections saw the applicant attempt an independent candidacy, which was rejected; the Constitutional Court later declared the independent-candidate ban unconstitutional in Decision no. 503/2010, distinguishing it from the treatment of unrepresented parties. The applicant later won a Chamber of Deputies seat in the 2012 general elections. Law no. 35/2008 remained in force until 2015.)

The core alleged violation concerned the 2009 amendment's exclusion of the applicant and his unrepresented party from the January 2010 by-elections, raising issues under the right to free elections (Article 3 of Protocol No. 1) and non-discrimination. Domestic authorities consistently applied the restriction to maintain the parliamentary composition established in 2008, despite the applicant's arguments on timing, discrimination, and international electoral standards.

The case of Cernea v. Romania concerns the applicant’s alleged inability to stand, without discrimination, in a parliamentary by-election. Remus Florinel Cernea, a Romanian national born in 1974 and living in Bucharest, served as Executive Chair of Partidul Verde, a small ecological party affiliated with the European Green Party. The party fielded candidates in the 2008 general elections but won no parliamentary seats. In 2009 the applicant ran as its presidential candidate and obtained roughly 0.6 percent of valid votes.

The 2008 elections were conducted under Law no. 35/2008. In October 2009 Parliament adopted Law no. 323/2009 (an organic law) amending that statute. The amendment inserted section 48(17), which limited participation in parliamentary by-elections to political parties and national-minority organisations that had crossed the electoral threshold in the preceding general elections. Unrepresented parties and independent candidates were thereby excluded.

A by-election was called for 17 January 2010 to fill a Bucharest constituency seat that had fallen vacant in October 2009. Partidul Verde nominated the applicant. On 29 December 2009 the Electoral Board rejected the candidacy solely because the party held no parliamentary seats.

The party, represented by the applicant, challenged the rejection before the Bucharest County Court and raised a constitutional objection. It argued that the ban violated the right to free elections, constituted unjustified discrimination vis-à-vis represented parties, and had been enacted less than one year before the poll, contrary to Venice Commission guidelines.

The County Court stayed the proceedings and referred the objection to the Constitutional Court. In Decision no. 61/2010 of 14 January 2010 the Constitutional Court dismissed the objection. It held that by-elections exist only to fill vacancies while preserving the political composition of Parliament as determined by the general elections, which express popular sovereignty. Permitting unrepresented parties to compete would improperly alter that composition. The Court treated the Venice Commission’s one-year rule “with reservations,” noting that the amendment had been made by organic law, a rank higher than ordinary legislation, and therefore satisfied the guideline.

On 30 March 2010, after the by-election had already taken place, the County Court dismissed the challenge as moot, adopting the Constitutional Court’s reasoning.

A further by-election was held in April 2010. The applicant then sought to stand as an independent; his candidacy was again rejected under the same provision. In Decision no. 503/2010 the Constitutional Court later declared the exclusion of independents unconstitutional, finding that it wholly negated their right to be elected (unlike the situation of unrepresented parties, whose exclusion the Court had already upheld). The applicant subsequently won a seat in the 2012 general elections.

The Venice Commission’s Code of Good Practice in Electoral Matters recommends that fundamental electoral rules not be changed within one year of an election unless they are entrenched at constitutional or supra-statutory level. These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaint that the 2009 amendment, applied to the January 2010 by-election, denied him an equal opportunity to stand for Parliament.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Cernea v. Romania (Application no. 43609/10) arose from a 2010 application by Romanian national Remus Florinel Cernea, then Executive Chair of the unrepresented ecological party Partidul Verde. The party had fielded candidates in the 2008 parliamentary elections without winning seats; Cernea himself received about 0.6% of the vote in the 2009 presidential contest. Those 2008 elections were governed by organic Law no. 35/2008. In October 2009 Parliament adopted Law no. 323/2009, inserting a new rule (section 48(17)) that confined parliamentary by-elections exclusively to parties and national-minority organisations that had crossed the 5% national threshold (plus ward-minimum requirements) in the preceding general election. Unrepresented parties and independents were thereby barred.

A by-election was called for 17 January 2010 to fill a Bucharest seat that had become vacant in October 2009. Partidul Verde nominated Cernea. On 29 December 2009 the Electoral Board rejected the nomination solely because the party sat outside Parliament. The party, represented by Cernea, challenged the rejection in Bucharest County Court and simultaneously raised an objection of unconstitutionality. It argued that the restriction violated the right to free elections, constituted unjustified discrimination vis-à-vis parliamentary parties, and had been enacted less than a year before the poll in breach of Venice Commission guidelines on the stability of electoral law.

The County Court stayed proceedings. On 14 January 2010 the Constitutional Court (Decision no. 61/2010) dismissed the objection. It held that by-elections exist only to replace a vacant seat while preserving the political composition produced by the last general election; allowing unrepresented parties would alter that composition “by the ‘devious means’ of a by-election” and undermine the electorate’s expressed will and the sovereignty principle. On the Venice Commission point the Court noted that the amendment had been effected by organic law, a rank higher than ordinary statute, and therefore satisfied the recommended standard. On 30 March 2010 the County Court, following the Constitutional Court’s reasoning and noting that the election had already occurred, dismissed the challenge as moot.

A second Bucharest by-election was scheduled for April 2010. Cernea then stood as an independent; that candidacy was likewise rejected. A fresh constitutional challenge succeeded: Decision no. 503/2010 of 20 April 2010 struck down the ban on independents as an unconstitutional annihilation of the right to be elected, while leaving the ban on unrepresented parties intact. Cernea later won a Chamber of Deputies seat in the 2012 general election.

The facts thus centre on a last-minute legislative change that excluded an unrepresented party from a by-election, the domestic courts’ defence of that exclusion as necessary to freeze the parliamentary arithmetic of the preceding general election, and the differential constitutional treatment later accorded to independents. These elements formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that he had been prevented, in a discriminatory manner, from standing for election.
001-181211:
The case concerns Lithuanian writer V.P., who in September 2003 published a satirical memoir entitled “The Ship of Idiots.” Several passages referred to the late V.L.-Ž., a minister in Lithuania’s short-lived 1941 Provisional Government, and to his son V.L., a prominent politician. The disputed statements alleged that V.L.-Ž. had collaborated with the KGB, been a Soviet spy returned by Moscow, been a friend of Hitler, copied strategic maps, been recruited by the Bolsheviks in 1918, and later evicted pharmacists and sued them over a wooden bench. The book’s copyright page stated that the author assumed full responsibility for the truth of the facts presented.

V.L. immediately lodged a criminal complaint for defamation. Archives, the State Security Department and other official bodies reported that they possessed no material confirming any of the allegations; witnesses named in the book likewise could not corroborate them. In 2005 a district court acquitted V.P. on the ground that defamation could be committed only against a living person. The prosecutor later discontinued a possible charge of contempt for the memory of the dead because the limitation period had expired.

In June 2007 V.L. brought a civil action seeking retraction of the statements and substantial non-pecuniary damages. V.P. argued that the book was a work of literary creativity written in figurative language, that the passages were value judgments based on his own memories and various historical sources, and that both V.L.-Ž. and V.L. were public figures who had to tolerate a higher degree of criticism. V.P. died in December 2008. His three children, including the applicant, accepted the inheritance (which included copyright and royalty rights in the book) and were substituted as defendants. They repeated their father’s arguments and added that any civil liability for a literary work was strictly personal and therefore non-transferable.

The Vilnius Regional Court (December 2009) held that the four passages constituted statements of fact, not value judgments, because they asserted that concrete events had actually occurred. None of the sources relied upon by V.P., nor the material gathered in the criminal investigation, established those events on the balance of probabilities. In the historical context of Lithuania the allegations of Soviet collaboration, Nazi sympathy and petty vindictiveness were insulting both to the deceased and to his surviving family. Because V.L. now sought only a judicial declaration that the statements were erroneous and insulting (rather than an order of personal retraction), the obligation was not strictly personal and could pass to the heirs. The claim for damages was dismissed as time-barred.

The Court of Appeal (August 2010) and the Supreme Court (March 2011) upheld that reasoning. They emphasised that an average reader would understand the passages as assertions of fact, that even public figures are protected against demonstrably false and insulting statements, and that the heirs, having accepted the inheritance, were obliged to prevent further dissemination of the impugned passages.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights complaining that the domestic courts’ findings and the transfer of liability to the heirs constituted an unjustified interference with freedom of expression.

The case of Petkevičiūtė v. Lithuania arose from an application lodged on 2 September 2011 by Lithuanian national Liudmila Petkevičiūtė (born 1956), represented by a Moscow lawyer. It concerned the aftermath of her late father V.P.’s 2003 satirical memoir The Ship of Idiots, which discussed historical Lithuanian events and contained four passages about the deceased V.L.-Ž. (a minister in the 1941 Provisional Government and father of prominent politician V.L.). The passages alleged that V.L.-Ž. had collaborated with the KGB as a spy (later returned by Moscow), been Hitler’s friend and a copier of strategic maps, been recruited by Bolsheviks after a 1918 arrest, and evicted pharmacists over a missing pre-war bench. The book expressly stated that the author assumed full responsibility for the facts presented.

V.L. complained to the Prosecutor General, prompting a 2003 pre-trial investigation into defamation. Inquiries to state archives, the Genocide and Resistance Research Centre, the National Library, and the State Security Department, plus interviews with individuals cited by V.P., yielded no corroboration of the allegations. In October 2005 the Vilnius City First District Court acquitted V.P., holding that defamation required a living victim; it noted that contempt for a deceased person’s memory might have been charged but was not. After appeals, the Vilnius Regional Court quashed the acquittal on procedural grounds in January 2006. In August 2006 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding sufficient evidence for a contempt charge but concluding that it was time-barred.

In June 2007 V.L. brought a civil claim against V.P. seeking public retraction of the statements and approximately EUR 29,000 in non-pecuniary damages, arguing they were false and insulted both his late father’s and his own honour and dignity. V.P. countered that the book was literary creativity based on subjective memories, written in figurative language, and thus consisted of value judgments rather than facts; he listed historical sources and personal experiences as support and stressed that public figures must tolerate greater criticism. V.P. died in December 2008. His three children, including the applicant, accepted the inheritance in equal shares in May 2009 and were substituted as defendants. V.L. then amended the claim to seek a declaration that the statements were erroneous and insulting, plus a symbolic EUR 0.29 in damages.

On 23 December 2009 the Vilnius Regional Court found for V.L. It classified the passages as statements of fact implying that specific events had occurred, which therefore required a sufficient factual basis. After reviewing the criminal-investigation materials and V.P.’s cited sources, it held that none met the civil standard of proof. In Lithuania’s historical context the collaboration and Nazi-support allegations, as well as the bench anecdote (portraying low moral standards), were insulting to both V.L.-Ž. and his family, including V.L. The court rejected the heirs’ argument that liability was purely personal: while an order to retract would have been non-transferable, a mere judicial declaration of falsity and insult was an objective assessment that survived the author’s death. The damages claim was dismissed as time-barred.

The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in August 2010. It confirmed that an average reader would perceive the passages as facts, not opinions, even in context. Although public figures must accept wider criticism, this did not extend to unproven, honour-damaging falsehoods. The heirs, having inherited reprint and royalty rights, could themselves adduce evidence of accuracy and were therefore properly liable; otherwise V.L. would have been left without any remedy. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal in March 2011, reiterating that freedom of expression does not protect the deliberate dissemination of humiliating falsehoods, even about public figures, and that the heirs, as successors to the book’s rights, were obliged to prevent further dissemination of the impugned statements.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the civil courts’ findings and the transfer of liability to the heirs constituted an unjustified interference with freedom of expression.
