The case originated from a 2011 application by Lithuanian national Liudmila Petkevičiūtė, born in 1956 and living in Vilnius, alleging violations arising from domestic civil proceedings that imposed liability on her as heir for statements in her late father’s book.

In September 2003, the applicant’s father V.P., a well-known Lithuanian writer, published “The Ship of Idiots,” satirical memoirs of Lithuanian history. Four passages (the “disputed statements”) concerned V.L.-Ž. (already deceased), a minister in Lithuania’s short-lived 1941 Provisional Government and father of prominent politician V.L. The statements alleged that V.L.-Ž. had long collaborated with the KGB as a spy later returned by Moscow; that he was Hitler’s friend, a spy and copier of strategic maps; that he and others had been arrested, interrogated and recruited by Bolsheviks while fleeing in 1918; and that he had evicted pharmacists onto the streets and sued them over a missing six-metre oak bench left before the war. The book’s fourth page recorded that the author assumed full responsibility for the truth of the facts presented.

V.L. lodged a criminal complaint for defamation of his late father. A prosecutor opened a pre-trial investigation in October 2003 and consulted archives, libraries, the Genocide and Resistance Research Centre, the State Security Department and persons cited as sources; none confirmed any part of the disputed statements. In October 2005 a first-instance court acquitted V.P. because the offence of defamation could be committed only against a living person. The regional court quashed that decision on procedural grounds. In August 2006 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding sufficient evidence for the time-barred offence of contempt for a deceased person’s memory.

In June 2007 V.L. brought a civil claim against V.P. seeking public retraction of the statements and LTL 100 100 (approximately EUR 29 000) in non-pecuniary damages, arguing that the statements were false and insulted both his own and his late father’s honour and dignity. V.P. contended that the passages were literary value judgments written in figurative language, based on historical sources, witness accounts and personal recollection, and that both V.L.-Ž. and V.L., as public figures, had to tolerate greater criticism.

V.P. died in December 2008. In May 2009 the applicant and her two brothers accepted the inheritance in equal shares (including reprint rights and royalties) and were substituted as defendants. V.L. then amended his claim, seeking only a judicial declaration that the statements were erroneous and insulting plus a symbolic LTL 1 in damages.

On 23 December 2009 the Vilnius Regional Court granted the declaration. It classified the statements as assertions of fact (implying that recruitment, collaboration, Nazi sympathy and the pharmacy incident had actually occurred) that therefore required a sufficient factual basis. After examining the criminal-investigation materials and the sources V.P. himself had listed, the court found none capable of confirming the statements to the civil standard of proof. The allegations of Soviet or Nazi collaboration were, in Lithuania’s historical context, clearly insulting to V.L.-Ž. and his family (including the politician V.L.); the bench episode portrayed V.L.-Ž. as lacking moral standards. Because the claim sought an objective judicial assessment rather than a personal retraction by the author, liability could pass to the heirs. The damages claim was time-barred.

The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 13 August 2010. An average reader would perceive the passages as facts, not opinions. Public-figure status required greater tolerance of criticism but did not excuse demonstrably false and insulting statements. The heirs, having inherited rights in the book, could themselves have adduced proof and could not leave the claimant without a remedy.

On 14 March 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal. Freedom of expression did not extend to the deliberate dissemination of falsehoods intended to humiliate, even when directed at public figures. Once the statements had been declared erroneous and insulting, the author’s successors who had accepted the inheritance were obliged to prevent their further dissemination.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the domestic courts’ classification of the statements, their assessment of the evidence and, above all, the transfer of civil liability to her as heir constituted an unjustified interference with her rights.
001-181273:
The case of Libert v. France (Application no. 588/13) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life). The applicant, Eric Libert, a French national born in 1958, was employed by the SNCF (French national railway company) since 1976, most recently as Deputy Head of the Amiens Regional Surveillance Unit.

In 2007, after complaining about a subordinate's conduct, the applicant faced a counter-complaint and was charged with making false accusations. He was suspended from duty. The charges were later discontinued, and he sought reinstatement to his original post. Upon returning on 17 March 2008, he discovered that his work computer had been seized. On 5 April 2008, superiors informed him that analysis of the hard disk had revealed "address change certificates" drawn up for third parties and bearing official logos (including those of the Lille General Security Service and the Ministry of Justice), as well as a large volume of pornographic images and films. These had been discovered by his temporary replacement, who alerted management in 2007 and 2008.

The applicant explained that he had transferred files from a USB key after issues with his personal computer in 2006, and that the pornographic material had been sent unsolicited via the SNCF Intranet. A disciplinary hearing followed, and on 17 July 2008 he was dismissed for breaching obligations of exemplary conduct, SNCF internal rules (including the user's charter on information systems), and provisions of the Criminal Code relating to forgery.

The applicant challenged the dismissal before the Amiens Industrial Tribunal, which rejected his claim in May 2010. The Amiens Court of Appeal upheld this in December 2010. It held that documents on company computers are presumed professional unless clearly identified as personal, allowing the employer access in the employee's absence. The hard disk was labelled “D:/personal data” (a default designation for work files) and contained a folder named “fun” with the pornography, plus other work-related files. These labels did not suffice to mark the contents as private, contrary to the SNCF user's charter, which required explicit identification (e.g., a “private” folder or Outlook option). Occasional private use of equipment was tolerated but the applicant's actions constituted a massive breach, including forgery, and were especially serious given his surveillance role. Dismissal was not disproportionate.

The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal in July 2012. It confirmed that files created with employer-provided equipment are presumed professional unless identified as personal; labelling an entire hard disk “personal data” does not confer privacy on all contents. The files had not been marked “private” as required by the IT charter, so the employer could lawfully open them in the applicant's absence. The volume of material (1,562 pornographic files totalling 787 MB over four years) and the forgeries amounted to a contractual breach justifying dismissal.

Relevant domestic law included Labour Code Articles L. 1121-1 and L. 1321-3, prohibiting unjustified or disproportionate restrictions on individual rights and liberties. Court of Cassation case law established that employees retain privacy rights at work (including confidentiality of communications), that personal messages cannot be read even if non-professional use is prohibited, and that files identified as personal may generally be opened only in the employee's presence (absent serious risk). Unmarked files created on work equipment are presumed professional and accessible in the employee's absence.

The SNCF user's charter restricted equipment to professional use (with limited, clearly identified personal use tolerated) and required private information and media to be explicitly marked as such.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant's complaint that the employer's unilateral access to his computer files, without his presence, interfered with his private life.

The case of Libert v. France (Application no. 588/13) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private life) arising from the SNCF’s examination of files stored on the applicant’s work computer in his absence. Eric Libert, a French national employed by the SNCF since 1976 and serving as Deputy Head of the Amiens Regional Surveillance Unit, was suspended in 2007 after a subordinate whom he had reported for abusive language lodged a complaint of false accusation against him. Criminal proceedings were later discontinued. Upon requesting reinstatement, Libert was invited to consider another post but insisted on returning to his former role.

On the day of his reinstatement (17 March 2008) the computer assigned to him was seized. On 5 April 2008 he was informed that its hard disk had been analysed and found to contain two change-of-address certificates bearing official logos (one of the Lille General Security Service and one of the Ministry of Justice) that had been used to obtain housing or other advantages for third parties, draft financial documents in another person’s name, and a large volume of pornographic images and films (including zoophilia and scatophilia). The analysis had been prompted by alerts from the employee who had temporarily replaced Libert, who reported discovering the material in March 2007 and January 2008.

Libert explained that he had transferred the contents of a personal USB key to the work computer in 2006 after problems with his home computer and that the pornographic files had been sent unsolicited via the SNCF intranet. A disciplinary hearing followed. On 17 July 2008 the SNCF regional director dismissed him, citing breach of the company’s codes of conduct, information-systems security policy and professional-ethics rules, as well as Article 441-1 of the Criminal Code (forgery). The dismissal letter emphasised that, given his senior surveillance functions, an exemplary standard of conduct was required.

Libert challenged the dismissal before the Amiens Industrial Tribunal, which in May 2010 held that it was justified. The Amiens Court of Appeal upheld that ruling in December 2010. It recalled that documents stored on company equipment are presumed professional unless clearly identified as personal, so that the employer may open them in the employee’s absence. The hard disk had been labelled “D:/personal data”, but that was the default name of the “D” drive used for work files; the generic label could not render an entire professional storage volume private. A folder named “fun” that contained the pornography was likewise not unambiguously personal. The SNCF user’s charter required private material to be marked “private” (for example by using the Outlook “private” option or a dedicated “private” folder). The certificates were stored under ordinary names and were therefore also accessible. The Court of Appeal further found the dismissal proportionate: Libert had committed a “massive breach” by using work tools to produce forged documents and by storing 1 562 pornographic files (787 MB) over four years.

The Court of Cassation dismissed Libert’s appeal on points of law in July 2012. It confirmed that files created with employer-provided equipment are presumed professional unless identified as personal in accordance with the IT charter; merely labelling the hard disk itself “personal data” does not confer privacy on its contents. The Court of Cassation also endorsed the finding of serious contractual breach.

Domestic labour-law provisions (Articles L. 1121-1 and L. 1321-3 of the Labour Code) prohibit restrictions on individual liberties that are neither justified by the nature of the work nor proportionate. Earlier Court of Cassation case-law established that an employer may not read personal e-mails even if private use of the computer is forbidden, and that files expressly marked personal may be opened only in the employee’s presence or after due notice, save in cases of serious risk. The SNCF user’s charter itself authorised only occasional, clearly identified private use of the information system. These facts form the core of the privacy complaint subsequently examined by the European Court of Human Rights.

**Case summary: Libert v. France (ECtHR, 22 February 2018)**

Eric Libert, a French SNCF employee since 1976 (last as Deputy Head of the Amiens Regional Surveillance Unit), complained in 2007 about a subordinate’s conduct. The subordinate accused Libert of false accusations; Libert was charged and suspended. After the criminal proceedings were discontinued, Libert sought reinstatement. On 17 March 2008 his work computer was seized. On 5 April 2008 superiors informed him that analysis of the hard disk had revealed forged “address change certificates” (bearing official logos and used to shorten notice periods or certify transfers/financial situations) plus a large volume of pornographic images and films (including zoophilia and scatophilia). A colleague who had replaced him had earlier flagged the material.

Libert explained that he had transferred files from a USB stick after personal-computer problems and that unknown persons had sent the pornography via the SNCF Intranet. After a written explanation request, disciplinary hearing and board, he was dismissed on 17 July 2008 for breach of the SNCF’s code of professional conduct, information-systems charter and Article 441-1 of the Criminal Code (forgery). The dismissal letter stressed his duty of exemplary conduct given his former general-surveillance role.

Libert sued for unfair dismissal. The Amiens Industrial Tribunal rejected the claim (10 May 2010). The Amiens Court of Appeal (15 December 2010) upheld the dismissal as justified and not disproportionate. It held that documents on company computers are presumed professional unless identified as personal, so the employer may access them in the employee’s absence. The pornographic material was stored in a folder named “fun” on a drive labelled “D:/personal data”. The court accepted the SNCF’s unchallenged evidence that the “D” drive defaulted to “D:/data” and was used for work files; an employee could not claim an entire work drive as private. The generic label “personal data” could equally cover work documents personally processed by the employee (and the disk in fact contained work files such as “LGV photos”). The term “fun” did not clearly signal private content. The SNCF user’s charter required private items to be marked with the Outlook “private” option and stored in a “Private” folder; these files were not so identified. The same applied to the certificate files. The Court of Appeal also found a “massive breach” of rules limiting computers to professional use (occasional private use being only tolerated) and noted the particular gravity of forgery by a surveillance official.

The Court of Cassation (Social Division, 4 July 2012) dismissed Libert’s appeal, which had invoked Article 8 ECHR. It confirmed that files created on employer-supplied computers are presumed professional and may be opened in the employee’s absence unless identified as personal. Labelling the hard disk itself “D:/personal data” could not render all its contents private. The files had not been identified as “private” in accordance with the IT charter. Storing 1,562 pornographic files (787 MB) over four years and using the computer to produce forgeries constituted a contractual breach.

Relevant domestic law (Labour Code Arts. L. 1121-1 and L. 1321-3) prohibits restrictions on individual liberties that are unjustified by the nature of the task or disproportionate. Court of Cassation case-law (2001–2006) recognises an employee’s right to privacy even at work, including confidentiality of communications, and requires that files identified as personal be opened only in the employee’s presence (or after due summons) except in cases of serious risk. Unidentified files remain accessible. The SNCF user’s charter confined resources to professional use, tolerated only occasional reasonable private e-mail/Internet use, and required clear “private” marking of both information and storage media.

The application to the ECtHR alleged a violation of Article 8 arising from the opening of the files in Libert’s absence. (The Chamber adjourned the case pending the Grand Chamber judgment in Bărbulescu v. Romania.)
001-181383:
The case of Royer v. Hungary concerns a French applicant’s complaint that Hungarian authorities violated Article 8 of the ECHR by failing to secure the return of his infant son, L., following the child’s wrongful removal from France.

The applicant and K.B.V. (a Hungarian national) began cohabiting in France in 2009. Their son L. was born there on 18 October 2013. On 4 January 2014, without the applicant’s knowledge or consent, K.B.V. took the two-and-a-half-month-old child to Hungary, where they have since lived with her parents. She immediately instituted custody proceedings in Szombathely.

French courts responded swiftly. On 24 March 2014 the Thonon-les-Bains tribunal de grande instance declared the removal unlawful, awarded the applicant sole custody and ordered L.’s return (judgment declared provisionally enforceable). On appeal the Chambéry Court of Appeal, while awarding joint custody, restricted the mother’s contact to two hours every fortnight and otherwise upheld the first-instance decision. A certificate of enforceability under the Brussels IIa Regulation was issued. The French Court of Cassation later quashed the appeal judgment, remitting the case.

In December 2014 the applicant sought L.’s return in Hungary under the 1980 Hague Convention and Brussels IIa. After several hearings the Pest Central District Court, on 12 February 2015, accepted that an abduction had occurred but refused return under Article 13(b) Hague. It found a grave risk of harm: L. was still being breast-fed, the applicant worked 7 a.m.–10 p.m. and proposed that his sister care for the child, maternal contact would be minimal, and the applicant had had virtually no contact with L. for almost a year. The Budapest High Court and the Kúria (6 October 2015) confirmed the refusal, emphasising the child’s very young age, the lengthy interruption of paternal contact (partly attributable to the applicant’s refusal of supervised meetings), the absence of protective measures in France, and the psychological harm of placing a toddler in an unfamiliar environment with a part-time carer.

Parallel Hungarian custody proceedings produced similar results. The Szombathely courts declined to recognise the French judgments, initially citing fair-trial concerns and later public-policy grounds (Article 23 Brussels IIa). They held that the French orders, by virtually eliminating the mother’s role while leaving the child in the care of the applicant’s sister, disregarded L.’s best interests and would constitute “institutional abuse” (forensic-psychiatric evidence). Habitual residence was found to have shifted to Hungary. Interim measures therefore placed L. with the mother.

The applicant twice attempted to take the child himself (April and December 2015), injuring the mother on the second occasion; L. was recovered and returned to Hungary. Supervised contact was subsequently ordered. Enforcement of the French judgments was also refused on public-policy grounds.

These successive Hungarian decisions—refusing Hague return, denying recognition and enforcement of the French custody orders, and awarding de-facto custody to the abducting parent—form the factual core of the Article 8 complaint that the authorities failed to take adequate and timely steps to restore the applicant’s family life with his son.

The case originated in an application by French national Patrick Royer against Hungary, alleging that the authorities' failure to return his son L. to France violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life.

Royer met Hungarian national K.B.V. in 2003. She relocated to France in 2009 and the couple cohabited in Gaillard. Their son L. was born there on 18 October 2013. After Christmas 2013 with Royer's family, K.B.V. complained to French police of his hostility and aggression. On 4 January 2014 she removed L. to Hungary without Royer's knowledge or consent; they have since resided with her parents in Szombathely. She commenced Hungarian custody proceedings on 9 January 2014.

Royer initiated French proceedings. On 24 March 2014 the Thonon-les-Bains tribunal found the removal wrongful, awarded him sole custody, placed L. with him and ordered provisional execution. On appeal the Chambéry Court of Appeal (22 July 2014) substituted joint custody and granted K.B.V. supervised contact every other Saturday for two hours, otherwise upholding the first-instance ruling. A Brussels IIa certificate of enforceability followed. The Cour de cassation later quashed the appellate judgment and remitted the matter.

In Hungary Royer applied on 10 December 2014 for L.'s return under the Hague Convention and Brussels IIa. After hearings the Pest Central District Court dismissed the request on 12 February 2015. It accepted that K.B.V. had abducted L. from his French habitual residence (where the parents held joint custody) but invoked Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention: return would expose the still-breastfed infant to grave risk of psychological harm because of uncertain living arrangements (Royer worked 7 a.m.–10 p.m. and proposed that his sister care for the child), extremely limited maternal contact, Royer's year-long delay and absence of contact. The Budapest High Court confirmed this on 28 April 2015, stressing L.'s age (then 18 months), the complete loss of maternal care and the lack of protective measures; Brussels IIa Article 11(4) was therefore inapplicable. The Kúria dismissed Royer's review petition on 6 October 2015. While agreeing that age or maternal attachment alone could not justify refusal, it held that the lengthy interruption of contact (attributable in part to Royer's refusal of supervised visits), the planned substitution of the sister as carer, the French courts' severe restriction of maternal contact and the absence of any safeguarding arrangements would cause serious psychological harm to a child under two placed in an unknown environment.

Parallel Hungarian custody proceedings resulted in non-recognition of the French judgments (public-policy exception under Brussels IIa Article 23, based on the child's best interests, limited maternal contact amounting to “institutional abuse” according to forensic psychiatric evidence, and lack of protective measures). Interim orders placed L. with his mother. Royer's subsequent application to enforce the French rulings was likewise refused.

These successive refusals to order return, grounded in Article 13(b) and public-policy considerations, constitute the core facts underlying the alleged Article 8 violation.

The case of Royer v. Hungary (Application no. 9114/16) concerns a French applicant’s complaint that Hungarian authorities failed to return his young son to France after the child’s wrongful removal by the mother, thereby violating the applicant’s right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Patrick Royer, a French national born in 1969 and living in Gaillard, France, began a relationship with K.B.V., a Hungarian national, in 2003. She moved to France in 2009, and they cohabited in his flat. Their son L. was born in France on 18 October 2013. After spending Christmas 2013 with the applicant’s family, K.B.V. filed a complaint against him in France on 28 December 2013, alleging hostility and aggression that endangered her and the child. On 4 January 2014 she took L. to Hungary without the applicant’s knowledge or consent and settled with her parents in Szombathely. She immediately commenced custody proceedings there.

French courts, seised by the applicant, found the removal unlawful. On 24 March 2014 the Thonon-les-Bains tribunal de grande instance awarded him sole custody, ordered the child’s placement with him and declared the decision provisionally enforceable. On appeal the Chambéry Court of Appeal on 22 July 2014 granted joint custody but restricted the mother’s contact to two hours of supervised access every other Saturday; the remainder of the first-instance ruling was upheld. A certificate of enforceability under the Brussels IIa Regulation was issued in January 2015, although the French Court of Cassation later quashed the appellate judgment and remitted the case.

The applicant then sought L.’s return under the 1980 Hague Convention and Brussels IIa. The Pest Central District Court dismissed the application on 12 February 2015, accepting that an abduction had occurred but finding a grave risk of harm under Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention: L. was still being breast-fed, the applicant worked long hours and proposed that his sister care for the child, contact with the mother would be extremely limited, the request had been delayed, and the applicant had had no contact with L. despite visiting Hungary. The Budapest High Court and the Kúria upheld this reasoning, emphasising the child’s age (under two), the lengthy period without paternal contact (partly attributed to the applicant’s refusal of supervised visits), the absence of protective measures in France, and the psychological harm of returning the child to an unfamiliar environment.

Parallel Hungarian custody proceedings resulted in non-recognition of the French judgments, initially on fair-trial grounds and later on public-policy grounds under Article 23 of Brussels IIa. Hungarian courts held that the French orders, by severely restricting maternal contact and placing the infant in the care of the applicant’s sister, failed to respect the child’s best interests and would constitute “institutional abuse.” Interim custody was therefore awarded to the mother. Enforcement of the French decisions was likewise refused.

Tensions escalated: the applicant attempted to seize L. in April 2015 and succeeded in abducting him in December 2015, inflicting grievous bodily harm on K.B.V. A European arrest warrant followed; L. was returned to Hungary after a brief stay in French care. Subsequent Hungarian and French interim orders confirmed the child’s placement with the mother, granting the applicant only supervised access.

The applicant complained that these refusals prevented the child’s return to his habitual residence in France and thereby interfered with his family life. The Hungarian courts consistently prioritised the infant’s young age, need for maternal care, lack of established paternal contact, and perceived risks of the French custody arrangements over the prompt-return principle of the Hague Convention and Brussels IIa.
001-181393:
The case concerns an application by Latvian national R.Š. (born 1983) to the European Court of Human Rights alleging violations of Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention. He claimed he could not obtain compensation for serious harm from a 2008 aircraft accident and that Latvia bore responsibility for regulatory shortcomings in private flight safety.

In 2008, the applicant, who held a pilot licence and was in aviation training, used the services of company KD.C. (solely owned and directed by D.K.). The company organised private flights and pilot training courses under a Civil Aviation Agency registration but was uncertified for commercial operations, falling outside relevant regulations.

On 16 August 2008, KD.C. arranged a private multi-engine Piper PA-31 flight (maximum mass 2,900 kg) from Riga to Tukums. The applicant and six others boarded as passengers; the applicant sat next to pilot G.V. and handled radio communications. G.V. lost control in cloudy conditions, and the aircraft crashed, killing G.V. and seriously injuring all passengers. The applicant suffered life-threatening injuries, including permanent loss of vision in his right eye and other lasting health damage requiring treatment in Latvia and abroad. Post-rehabilitation, he continued as an aviation specialist but with restrictions: he could not operate aircraft independently and faced more frequent medical checks.

The Transport Accident and Incident Investigation Bureau (TAIIB) investigated. Its 27 June 2009 report identified the primary cause as “human error”: G.V. lacked sufficient skills and experience for the aircraft under instrument flight rules, had not completed differences training started on 1 August 2008, and lacked Civil Aviation Agency authorisation. Contributing factors included poor visibility and the Agency’s “unsafe supervision” of aviation rules. KD.C. had not monitored G.V.’s training, checked his documents, or properly authorised the flight. TAIIB issued eight safety recommendations to the Agency, including requiring aircraft owners to implement handover procedures ensuring pilots held valid licences and qualifications.

Criminal proceedings followed. Evidence showed G.V. flew despite lacking qualifications. Proceedings against him ended due to his death. D.K. was indicted under Criminal Law sections 197 (negligence in professional duties) and 257(2) (air traffic safety violations) for handing over the aircraft knowing of G.V.’s deficiencies. The first-instance court convicted him in 2012, imposing a suspended five-year sentence and ordering EUR 29,000 compensation to the applicant. The appellate court acquitted D.K. in 2013, finding no specific neglected professional duties (he was not an aviation specialist or “special subject”) and that section 257 required a transport employee, which D.K. was not. It noted no precise regulations were violated. The Supreme Court Senate upheld the acquittal in December 2013, emphasising that relevant laws (Commercial Law, Civil Law, Law on Aviation, Chicago Convention) concerned civil, not criminal, liability. At the time, no legislation mandated aircraft handover procedures, verification of pilots’ training, or owner responsibility for qualifications; the Chicago Convention then imposed duties only on the pilot (owner liability applied from November 2010). Section 91 of the Law on Aviation, prohibiting handover to unqualified persons, was added only in 2013.

The applicant sued KD.C., D.K., and the insurer in civil proceedings (August 2010) under Civil Law sections on dangerous activities, employer liability, and compensation for injury. KD.C. was declared bankrupt (effective from December 2008). Courts dismissed the claims: first instance (2013) found no unlawful acts by D.K. (who had authorised training with an instructor, not independent flight with passengers) and noted the applicant, as a pilot, could have declined to fly in bad weather. The appellate court (2015) terminated proceedings against the defunct company (no successor); held D.K. not liable (no causal link, no unlawful activity, not the owner, pilot not an employee); rejected board-member liability (no company losses); and denied insurance cover (policy excluded unqualified pilots). The Senate dismissed a further appeal in 2016.

A Civil Aviation Agency letter confirmed that, at the material time, owners were responsible only for airworthiness, not in-flight safety (the pilot’s duty). These facts underscored regulatory gaps in general (non-commercial) aviation, unlike commercial operations, contributing to the accident and the applicant’s unsuccessful compensation efforts.

The European Court of Human Rights case of R.Š. v. Latvia (Application no. 44154/14) arose from an aircraft accident on 16 August 2008. The applicant, a Latvian national born in 1983 who held a pilot licence and was undergoing aviation training, boarded a Piper PA-31 multi-engine aircraft (maximum mass 2,900 kg) as a passenger on a private flight organised by KD.C. from Riga to Tukums. The company, wholly owned and managed by D.K., provided private flights and training but was uncertified for commercial operations and thus outside certain regulatory requirements. The applicant sat beside the pilot, G.V., and handled radio communications. G.V. lost control in cloudy conditions, the aircraft crashed and caught fire, killing G.V. and seriously injuring all passengers. The applicant suffered life-threatening injuries, permanently losing vision in his right eye plus other lasting damage; post-rehabilitation, he worked as an aviation specialist only with restrictions (no independent operation, frequent medical checks).

The Transport Accident and Incident Investigation Bureau (TAIIB) report of 27 June 2009 identified the primary cause as G.V.’s “human error”: insufficient skills and experience for independent multi-engine instrument flight, particularly on the Piper PA-31. G.V. had begun but not completed differences training and lacked Civil Aviation Agency (CAA) authorisation. Contributing factors included poor weather/visibility and the CAA’s “unsafe supervision” of aviation legislation and visual flight rules. KD.C. had failed to monitor the training, check documents, or verify qualifications before verbally authorising the flight. At the time, Latvian law lacked procedures for aircraft handover in general (non-commercial) aviation or for owners to confirm pilot qualifications. TAIIB issued recommendations, including that owners establish handover procedures requiring CAA-confirmed qualifications.

Criminal proceedings against D.K. for professional negligence (Criminal Law s. 197) and air-traffic safety violations (s. 257(2)) led to a first-instance conviction and an order to pay the applicant ~€29,000 in non-pecuniary damages. The appellate court acquitted him, finding no neglected professional duties (D.K. was not an aviation specialist or “transport employee”) and no proven regulatory breach. The Supreme Court Senate confirmed the absence of actus reus, noting that relevant Aviation Law, Commercial Law and Chicago Convention provisions imposed civil (not criminal) liability on owners and that, pre-2010, the Convention placed operational responsibility solely on the pilot. Only in 2013 did Aviation Law s. 91 prohibit owners from handing aircraft to unqualified, uninsured persons. The Senate observed that the applicant could pursue civil remedies.

The applicant’s 2010 civil claim against KD.C., D.K. and the insurer (invoking Civil Law ss. 1782, 2347 and 2349 on employee selection, dangerous activities and bodily injury) was dismissed. KD.C. was already bankrupt and later dissolved without successor. Courts found no unlawful act by D.K.: the pilot’s error was primary; D.K. had not authorised an unaccompanied flight (an instructor was expected); no causal link existed; D.K. was neither owner nor employer of G.V.; and insurance excluded coverage for an unlicensed pilot. The Supreme Court rejected a further appeal. A CAA letter confirmed that owners were responsible only for airworthiness, not in-flight safety (the pilot’s duty).

The applicant alleged that these outcomes left him without compensation for the harm and that Latvia bore responsibility for inadequate legal regulation of private-flight safety, engaging Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention.

The ECHR case R.Š. v. Latvia (no. 44154/14) arose from a 16 August 2008 private aircraft crash in Latvia. The applicant, a licensed pilot in training born in 1983, boarded a Piper PA-31 (max. 2,900 kg) as a passenger (front seat, handling radio) with six others on a flight from Riga to Tukums organised by KD.C., a non-commercial private flight and training company solely owned and managed by D.K. (who lacked aviation experience). The company held CAA registration for training but fell outside commercial certification rules.

Pilot G.V. lost control in cloudy weather with poor visibility, executing chaotic manoeuvres; the aircraft crashed ~30-50 m from the ground, caught fire, killing G.V. and seriously injuring all passengers. Forensic examination confirmed the applicant's life-threatening injuries, including permanent loss of vision in his right eye and other lasting health damage. After rehabilitation in Latvia and abroad, he resumed limited aviation work (no independent flying; frequent medical checks).

TAIIB investigation (final report 27 June 2009) found the primary cause as G.V.'s "human error": insufficient skills/experience for multi-engine IFR operations, especially this aircraft type. He lacked CAA authorisation, having started (but not completed) differences training on 1 August 2008. KD.C. failed to monitor training, check documents, or properly handover the aircraft (verbally authorising an unqualified pilot). Contributing factors included weather and CAA's "unsafe supervision" of aviation legislation/VFR compliance. No domestic procedure then existed for general-aviation aircraft handover or owner verification of pilot qualifications/skills (unlike commercial aviation). TAIIB recommended CAA impose such owner duties. A 20 October 2009 TAIIB letter and official statements confirmed the regulatory gap for general aviation.

Criminal proceedings opened immediately. D.K. (witness) claimed he believed G.V. qualified and expected instructor accompaniment; later inconsistencies were attributed to language issues. Proceedings against G.V. ended with his death. D.K. was indicted (24 May 2011) under Criminal Law ss. 197 (professional negligence) and 257(2) (air-traffic violation) for knowingly handing over the aircraft. First-instance court (22 October 2012) convicted him (suspended 5-year sentence) and awarded the applicant ~EUR 29,000 non-pecuniary damages. Appellate court (15 May 2013) acquitted: no specific neglected duties shown; D.K. was neither a "special subject" nor transport employee; no precise regulations violated. Supreme Court Senate (9 December 2013) confirmed: relevant provisions (Aviation Law s. 34, Chicago Convention Annex 6) bound the pilot, not D.K.; owner/pilot liability rules applied only later (2010/2013); no then-existing handover/verification procedure.

Civil claims (13 August 2010) against KD.C., D.K., and the insurer invoked Civil Law ss. 1782, 2347, 2349 (injury, dangerous activity, employee selection). KD.C. was bankrupt (proceedings from 31 December 2008) and dissolved (26 May 2015, no successor). First-instance (14 May 2013) and appellate (24 September 2015) courts dismissed all claims: no evidence D.K. authorised independent flight (planned with absent instructor due to weather); primary cause was pilot error with no causal link to D.K.; D.K. was not owner (company was) or liable under Aviation Law/Chicago Convention (then inapplicable to owners); no unlawful/liable act (pilot's action arbitrary); insurance excluded unlicensed-pilot accidents. Applicant (himself a pilot, aware of weather) possibly contributed. Supreme Court Senate dismissed further appeal (5 May 2016).

At the material time, Aviation Law placed operational safety on the pilot-in-command and airworthiness on the owner (confirmed by 2015 CAA letter and Chicago Annex 6 Part II). A 2013 amendment (s. 91) later banned handover to unqualified persons. The applicant alleged (Arts. 2/8) inability to obtain compensation and State responsibility for private-flight safety regulatory shortcomings.
001-181583:
**Case of Wetjen and Others v. Germany (ECtHR, 2018)**

The applicants—members of the Twelve Tribes Church (Zwölf Stämme) living in a community of about 100 people in Klosterzimmern, Germany—were two families: the Wetjens (parents and their son, born 2011) and the Schotts (parents and three daughters, born 1999, 2002 and 2004). They alleged violations of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for private and family life) due to the withdrawal of parts of their parental authority and the children’s placement into care, which they claimed was disproportionate. Additional complaints under Articles 6, 9 and 14 ECHR (and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1) concerned the fairness and length of family-court proceedings, insufficient factual basis, reliance on general views of their community, interference with raising children according to their religious beliefs, and alleged stigmatisation.

In 2012 press reports highlighted the community’s acceptance of corporal punishment, particularly caning. Former members described practices including tight swaddling of infants (from birth until around age 3) to restrict movement and caning of children (from about age 3 until 12), often administered by supervising adults rather than parents, under community pressure. The local youth office visited and discussed corporal punishment and compulsory schooling with community spokespersons.

On 16 August 2013 the youth office and Nördlingen Family Court received hidden-camera video footage showing ten instances of caning of children aged 3–12 (none involving the applicants; most not by parents). On 21 August the court heard six former members who confirmed the practices. On 1 September 2013, on the youth office’s application, the Family Court issued an interlocutory order withdrawing the parents’ rights to determine the children’s residence, health care, schooling and training, transferring those rights to the youth office. It found a reasonable likelihood of corporal punishment and authorised police assistance and entry to community premises.

On 5 September 2013 the youth office, supported by around 100 police officers, took the children into care during a search that seized seven wooden rods. Medical examinations of the applicant children revealed no physical signs of abuse or beating. The Wetjen son (then 2 years 5 months and still breastfed) was initially housed with his mother under supervision; after she refused an order to wean him, he was forcibly removed on 9 December 2013 and placed in foster care. The Schott daughters went to a children’s home.

The Family Court examined the parents and children. The Wetjen parents admitted swaddling but denied it constituted abuse; they refused to answer questions about caning and cited Bible passages. The Schott daughters wished to return home; the two younger ones declined to discuss discipline, while the oldest confirmed prior caning of her sisters and herself (which she said had stopped after her Bat Mitzvah). Parents generally confirmed “disciplining” but denied beating or abuse.

On 29–30 November 2013 the Family Court largely upheld the orders (revoking them only for the oldest Schott daughter, who was returned in December 2013 as no longer at risk due to her age). It found a high probability that remaining in or returning to the community would expose the children to corporal punishment, violating their dignity, physical integrity and personality development under the German Basic Law, and teaching unconditional obedience. The decisions relied on parents’ statements, video footage, former members’ testimony, other children’s statements, and community teachings (including a leaflet “Our teachings on child training”). Separation was deemed the least-restrictive measure because parents showed no willingness to cease the practices and youth-office support could not guarantee safety at all times (other adults might still cane children). Religion did not justify the methods. Main custody proceedings and psychological expert reports were initiated.

The Munich Court of Appeal upheld the substance of the orders on 5 March 2014 (reversing only schooling/training withdrawals as unnecessary at the interim stage given the children’s ages). It confirmed caning had occurred and would likely resume, based on the same evidence, and held children’s wishes (especially those of the 9- and 12-year-olds) insufficient without the forthcoming expert opinion. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaints on 5 May 2014.

Appeals against the execution of the orders (police involvement) were dismissed as belated or unfounded. German law (Civil Code Arts. 1631, 1666, 1666a) prohibits physical punishment and authorises family-court intervention, including partial removal of parental authority and separation, only when a child’s best interests are endangered and less-intrusive measures fail. UN CRC provisions similarly prioritise the child’s best interests, protection from all violence (including corporal punishment, deemed invariably degrading), and family unity except as a last resort.

The applicants, two families belonging to the Twelve Tribes Church community in Klosterzimmern, Germany, alleged violations of Article 8 ECHR arising from the withdrawal of aspects of their parental authority and the taking of their children into public care. The Wetjen family comprised parents and their son (born 2011); the Schott family comprised parents and three daughters (born 1999, 2002 and 2004). Press reports in 2012 highlighted the community’s endorsement of corporal punishment, including caning, corroborated by a former member. Youth-office visits and ministerial discussions followed, addressing both punishment and compulsory schooling.

On 16 August 2013 the Nördlingen Family Court received hidden-camera footage showing ten instances of caning of children aged 3–12 (none of them the applicants’ children, and often administered by non-parents). The court heard six former community members who confirmed systematic practices: tight swaddling of infants until age three and caning from ages three to twelve by whichever adult was supervising, with communal pressure on parents to conform. On 1 September 2013 the court issued an interlocutory order withdrawing the parents’ rights to determine residence, health care, schooling and vocational training and transferring those rights to the youth office. It found a reasonable likelihood of corporal punishment and authorised police assistance and searches.

On 5 September 2013 approximately 100 officers took the children into care and seized seven wooden rods. Medical examinations revealed no physical signs of abuse. The infant Wetjen (still breast-fed) was initially housed with his mother under supervision; after she refused a weaning order he was forcibly removed to a foster family on 9 December 2013. The Schott daughters were placed in a children’s home; the eldest was returned to her parents in December 2013 once the court found she was no longer at risk of caning.

In subsequent hearings the parents admitted swaddling but refused to discuss caning, citing biblical passages. The Family Court (November 2013) and Munich Court of Appeal (March 2014) upheld the orders (save for schooling rights of the youngest children). They relied on parental statements, witness testimony, the video evidence and community teaching materials to conclude there was a high probability that the younger children would again be subjected to corporal punishment, which German law (Civil Code § 1631(2)) prohibits as contrary to human dignity and personality development. Religious freedom did not justify the practice. Less intrusive measures were unavailable because the parents showed no willingness to refrain and could not guarantee that other community members would not cane the children. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaints.

The applicants contended that the interference with family life was disproportionate, that the decisions rested on generalisations about the community rather than individual evidence, that the proceedings were excessively lengthy and unfair, and that they had been prevented from raising their children according to their religious convictions. The Court communicated the applications solely under Article 8.

The case Wetjen and Others v. Germany (ECtHR applications 68125/14 and 72204/14) concerned eight members of the Twelve Tribes Church (Zwölf Stämme) living in Bavarian communities. Parents and children alleged that German family-court measures withdrawing parental rights and separating families violated Article 8 (private/family life). They further claimed under Articles 6 and 8 that proceedings were excessively long, unfair and based on general religious considerations rather than individual facts; under Articles 9 and 14 with Article 8, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, that the measures prevented religious upbringing and stigmatised the community.

In 2012 press reports and a former member described the community’s use of corporal punishment (caning) and related practices. The youth office visited and discussed the issues with community representatives and the Bavarian Ministry of Education.

On 16 August 2013 a television reporter supplied hidden-camera footage of ten caning incidents involving children aged 3–12 (none involving the applicant families; the punisher was often not a parent). The Nördlingen Family Court heard six former members who confirmed: tight swaddling of infants until age three to suppress movement; caning from ages three to twelve by whichever adult was supervising; and community pressure on parents to conform.

On 1 September 2013, on the youth office’s application, the court issued an interlocutory order withdrawing the parents’ rights to determine residence, health care, schooling and vocational training and transferring those rights to the youth office. The court found a reasonable likelihood of corporal punishment. It authorised police assistance and entry onto community premises.

On 5 September 2013 the children were taken into care by approximately 100 police officers who simultaneously searched the premises and seized seven wooden rods. Subsequent medical examinations revealed no physical signs of beating.

The Wetjen child (then aged 2 years 5 months and still breastfed) was initially housed with his mother under supervision; after she refused to wean him he was forcibly removed and placed with a foster family. The three Schott daughters were placed in a children’s home; the oldest was later returned.

The parents were heard. The Wetjens admitted swaddling but refused to answer questions about caning, citing biblical passages. The Schotts admitted “disciplining” but denied beating. The oldest Schott daughter confirmed that her younger sisters (and she herself when younger) had been caned; the younger girls refused to discuss it and all three wished to return home.

The Family Court upheld the orders (except for the oldest Schott daughter, whom it found no longer at risk because of her age). It relied on the parents’ statements, the video, former members’ testimony and community guidelines, finding a high probability that the remaining children would be caned, infringing their dignity and free personality development. No less-restrictive measure could guarantee safety, because parents could not prevent other community members from punishing the children. Main custody proceedings and a psychological report were ordered.

The Munich Court of Appeal essentially confirmed the decisions (lifting the schooling/vocational aspects as unnecessary at the interlocutory stage). It held that caning formed part of the parents’ religious upbringing methods, was not protected by religious freedom, and that the children’s wishes (aged 9 and 12) could not yet be given decisive weight. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaints.

The facts thus centre on the evidence of systematic corporal punishment, the emergency removal of the children, the partial withdrawal of parental authority, and the domestic courts’ findings that the measures were necessary to protect the children from a continuing risk of violence.

The European Court of Human Rights case Tlapak and Others v. Germany (applications nos. 11308/16 and 11344/16) concerned two families belonging to the Twelve Tribes Church community in Wörnitz, Germany. The Tlapak applicants were parents of a son born in 2012; the Pingen applicants were parents of twin daughters born in 2009 and a son born in 2013. Both families lived in a small community whose members practised corporal punishment, including caning with rods, as a religiously based child-rearing method. A larger sister community existed nearby.

In 2012–2013 media reports and statements by former members highlighted the community’s use of caning. In August 2013 a television reporter supplied hidden-camera footage showing ten instances of children aged 3–12 being caned, often by non-parents. On 3 September 2013 the Ansbach Family Court, acting on a youth-office application, issued an interlocutory order withdrawing the applicants’ rights to determine their children’s residence, health care, schooling and vocational training and transferring those rights to the youth office. The court relied on the footage, the reporter’s testimony and accounts from six former members, finding a reasonable likelihood of continued caning and “restraining.” Police assisted the youth office in taking the children into care on 5 September 2013; a wooden rod was seized. Medical examinations revealed no physical injuries.

The Tlapak son was placed in foster care (with daily breastfeeding visits permitted). The Pingen daughters were placed first with a foster family and later with an aunt; their infant son remained with his mother in a foster placement. In interim appeals the Nuremberg Court of Appeal largely upheld the orders, though it restored the Tlapak parents’ schooling rights (given the child’s age) and the Pingen parents’ residence right over their infant son.

Main proceedings followed. Court-appointed experts interviewed the parents, observed parent–child contact and, in the Pingen case, spoke to the daughters. The experts concluded that the parents regarded corporal punishment with objects as appropriate and necessary from age three, that there was a near-certainty of its continued use, and that this would cause psychological harm. Because the practice was rooted in religious conviction, the parents were unwilling to abandon it or to cooperate fully with authorities; milder measures were therefore insufficient. The parents later withdrew consent to the assessments and submitted a private expert report criticising the court expert’s methodology; the courts held the original reports admissible.

In October 2014 the Family Court confirmed the withdrawal of residence, health and schooling rights. It found a high, concrete risk of systematic, degrading caning—explicitly prohibited by German civil-law provisions guaranteeing a non-violent upbringing and requiring intervention when a child’s welfare is endangered. The interference with family life was justified because unannounced visits could not reliably detect the short-lived physical marks or later psychological effects, and the parents had not credibly distanced themselves from the practice. Settlement talks failed over the parents’ refusal to accept state schooling, play therapy and ongoing supervision; the courts also noted the families’ intention to leave Germany, which would render monitoring impossible. The Pingen infant was ordered returned to care, though enforcement was later suspended on age grounds.

Appeals were dismissed in detailed 2015 judgments. The Court of Appeal emphasised that not every isolated breach of the non-violence rule warranted removal, but systematic caning amounting to abuse did. The daughters had described daily caning; the parents had confirmed “disciplining” with a rod and continued to view it as legitimate. Recent statements accepting a non-violent upbringing were regarded as tactical rather than genuine. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaints.

The applicants alleged that the decisions violated Article 8 (family life) by being disproportionate, based on insufficient evidence and reached in overly lengthy, unfair proceedings; they also invoked Articles 6, 9 and Protocol No. 1 Article 2, claiming the measures targeted their religious beliefs and prevented them from raising their children accordingly. Only the Article 8 complaints were communicated to the Government.

001-182171:
**Case of Goran Kovačević v. Croatia (Application no. 34804/14)**

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Croatian national Goran Kovačević that police ill-treated him at a Dubrovnik station after his 21 October 2010 arrest on drug-abuse suspicion, that authorities failed to investigate effectively (Article 3), and that he was denied a lawyer and coerced into incriminating a co-accused (Article 6).

Police arrested the applicant at 4:40 p.m. Government accounts stated he resisted, requiring wrist- and elbow-lock techniques; all three officers and the applicant fell, after which he was handcuffed. Minor injuries (excoriations) resulted for both the applicant (left elbow, chest, behind left ear) and officer S.D. (knee and elbow). A doctor examined them at 9:40 p.m.; both attributed injuries to falling. Police reports, signed by the applicant without objection, detailed the force used during extraction from a vehicle, restraint in the police car, and a further fall at the station. A shift manager and later the county police chief deemed the measures necessary, justified and lawful.

The applicant was informed of his rights to silence, a lawyer of choice and notification of a third party; he declined counsel and asked that his father be told (contacted at 6:20 p.m.). He signed the relevant report. The following morning he was questioned by police (9:45–11:10 a.m.), again waived a lawyer, and stated he had twice acted as an amphetamine intermediary in August 2010 and had bought cocaine from D.Š. between 2008 and 2010. At noon he appeared before an investigating judge (with a prosecutor present), received the same rights advice twice, again declined counsel, repeated the statements, and said that apart from force used during arrest he had no complaints about police conduct. He was released.

An investigation opened on 29 October 2010 and was later extended; the applicant hired counsel on 3 December 2010. Indicted with D.Š. and V.V., he initially pleaded not guilty at trial but later reiterated the intermediary confession while retracting the cocaine purchases. He alleged that once at the station he had immediately confessed the intermediary role, asked for a lawyer when questioned about D.Š., been beaten by officers L.D., S.D. and I.R., and been told that lawyer D.H. (engaged by his sister) had been refused entry. He claimed fear of the same officers who escorted him to the investigating judge, plus seeing his father in distress, led him to incriminate D.Š.

The trial court convicted all three defendants (applicant: two years, later reduced on appeal to one year). It relied in part on the investigating-judge statement to convict D.Š., rejected the ill-treatment claim as an attempt to assist the co-accused, noted the applicant had spoken freely after rights warnings and without officers present, and dismissed proposed evidence (sister’s testimony, D.H., further medical records) as irrelevant. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court upheld the conviction, finding the retraction implausible given the applicant’s own assertion that he had confessed immediately and therefore had no reason to be pressured.

These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 3 ill-treatment (timing and cause of injuries, use of force reports versus later claims of beating and coercion) and the alleged Article 6 violations (documented waivers of counsel versus later assertions of denial and pressure). The Court later assessed whether the domestic response and trial use of the statements complied with Convention standards.

The case of Goran Kovačević v. Croatia (Application no. 34804/14) arose from the applicant’s arrest and detention in relation to suspected drug offences. On 21 October 2010 at 4:40 p.m., Croatian police arrested Kovačević in Dubrovnik on suspicion of drug abuse. The Government maintained that he actively resisted, necessitating the use of force (including wrist-lock and elbow-lock techniques) by officers S.D., L.D. and I.R. Both the applicant and officer S.D. sustained minor injuries (excoriations). The applicant denied any resistance and asserted that the injuries were inflicted later inside the police station as a means of coercing him into making incriminating statements against his co-accused, D.Š.

Immediately after arrest he was taken to the station. At 9:40 p.m. a doctor recorded minor abrasions on his left elbow, left chest and behind his left ear; S.D. had corresponding abrasions. Both men told the doctor they had fallen. Contemporary police reports described the applicant’s continued resistance during transport and upon arrival, after which force ceased. The applicant signed these reports without objection. He was informed of his rights (including the right to remain silent and to a lawyer) and declined legal assistance; his father was notified at 6:20 p.m.

The following morning the applicant was questioned by police. He again waived counsel and gave a statement admitting that he had acted as an intermediary in two amphetamine sales in August 2010 and had purchased cocaine from D.Š. on several occasions between 2008 and 2010. Shortly afterwards he appeared before an investigating judge, was twice advised of his rights, again declined a lawyer, repeated the same admissions, and expressly stated that the only force used had occurred during the arrest itself. He was then released.

An investigation was opened and later extended; the applicant was indicted together with D.Š. and a third person. He retained counsel only in December 2010. At trial in June–July 2011 he initially reserved his defence, then, when giving evidence, confirmed the amphetamine admissions but retracted the statements concerning cocaine purchases from D.Š. He alleged that, once inside the station, he had been physically and psychologically ill-treated by the same three officers in order to extract those statements, that he had requested a lawyer when questioning turned to D.Š., and that a lawyer hired by his sister (D.H.) had been refused entry. He claimed he had made the incriminating remarks before the investigating judge only because the same officers who had beaten him were present and because he had seen his father in distress. The trial court rejected these claims, noting that the applicant had never raised them contemporaneously, had spoken freely and without interruption before the investigating judge, and had told that judge that force had been used only at the moment of arrest. The court viewed the late change of account as an attempt to assist D.Š. It convicted the applicant and, relying in part on his retracted statement, also convicted D.Š. A sentence of two years’ imprisonment was imposed.

On appeal the Supreme Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year, agreeing that the applicant’s late allegations of ill-treatment and denial of counsel lacked credibility. A subsequent constitutional complaint repeating the same complaints was dismissed as unfounded. The applicant thereafter brought the matter before the European Court of Human Rights, complaining of police ill-treatment, an inadequate official response to that ill-treatment, denial of access to a lawyer, and the use of allegedly coerced statements.

The case of Goran Kovačević v. Croatia concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging police ill-treatment during detention on 21-22 October 2010, lack of an effective official response, denial of access to a lawyer, and pressure to make incriminating statements against a co-accused.

The applicant was arrested at 4:40 p.m. in Dubrovnik on suspicion of drug offences. The Government maintained that he resisted, requiring officers S.D., L.D. and I.R. to apply force (wrist- and elbow-locks, grounding and handcuffing), during which both he and officer S.D. suffered minor injuries. The applicant denied any resistance or arrest-related injuries, asserting that the police later ill-treated him at the station specifically to extract statements against co-accused D.Š.

Taken immediately to the station, the applicant was medically examined at 9:40 p.m. The doctor recorded minor abrasions on his left elbow, left chest and behind the left ear; S.D. had similar abrasions on his right knee and elbow. Both men told the doctor the injuries resulted from a fall. Contemporaneous police reports described the applicant’s active resistance and the techniques used, noting that force ceased once he was seated and compliant. The applicant signed the reports without objection. A shift manager and, later, the police chief reviewed the use of force and found it necessary, justified and lawful.

Upon arrival the applicant was informed of his rights (silence, counsel of choice, notification of a person). He declined a lawyer and asked only that his father be contacted (done at 6:20 p.m.). The following morning, 22 October, police questioned him from 9:45 to 11:10 a.m. He again waived counsel and admitted acting twice as an intermediary in amphetamine sales and having bought cocaine from D.Š. on several occasions between 2008 and 2010.

At noon he was brought before an investigating judge (a prosecutor also present). Twice advised of his rights, he again declined a lawyer and repeated the same admissions. He stated that force had been used only during the arrest and raised no complaint about treatment at the station. He signed the record and was released.

An investigation was opened and he was later indicted together with D.Š. and a third person. At trial in June-July 2011, now represented, the applicant maintained the amphetamine admissions but retracted the cocaine-buying statements. He claimed that after arrival at the station he had immediately confessed the amphetamine offences, requested a lawyer, and been beaten and psychologically pressured by the same three officers to incriminate D.Š.; his sister had allegedly instructed lawyer D.H., who was refused entry. He said fear of the officers who escorted him to the judge explained his failure to complain at that hearing.

The trial court convicted him (two years, later reduced on appeal to one year) and used his original statement to convict D.Š. It rejected the ill-treatment account as inconsistent with his contemporaneous statements to the judge and as an attempt to assist D.Š. Proposed evidence (sister’s testimony, D.H., additional medical records) was dismissed as irrelevant or unnecessary. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court likewise found no violation of his rights.

The facts thus centre on the conflicting accounts of when and why injuries occurred, the applicant’s repeated, documented waivers of counsel and absence of contemporaneous complaint, and the domestic courts’ subsequent rejection of his recantation without an independent inquiry into possible coercion or denial of legal assistance.
001-182847:
The case of Sancaklı v. Turkey (Application no. 1385/07) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 December 2006 by Rıfat Sancaklı, a Turkish national born in 1955 and resident in Istanbul. Represented by lawyer İ. Mendeşağu, the applicant alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. Specifically, he complained that domestic courts imposed an administrative fine on him without holding an oral hearing in the criminal proceedings.

On 2 October 2004, the Büyükçekmece Magistrates’ Court issued a search warrant for public places and suspected persons. That night, gendarmerie officers searched the Sancak Hotel, owned by the applicant. Records indicated that a man, M.Ş., approached plain-clothes officers outside the hotel claiming to have a girl inside; he was identified as a trafficker of women. He and a woman from the hotel were detained. Search records, signed by the hotel manager hours later, noted that five women of foreign nationalities had been staying at the hotel with men and were taken to gendarmerie headquarters.

On 3 October 2004, gendarmerie questioned several men as suspects and the five women as victims. All confirmed they had stayed at the hotel for prostitution. Some women denied any complicity between traffickers and hotel management. The applicant was arrested that day on suspicion of facilitating prostitution. On 4 October 2004, he gave statements denying that he provided premises for prostitution, stating he did not allow procurers into the hotel and had never seen M.Ş. The hotel manager similarly asserted that both he and the applicant strictly excluded procurers.

On 30 May 2005, the Büyükçekmece Public Prosecutor indicted the applicant and three others under Article 526 § 1 of the former Criminal Code (Law no. 765) for failing to obey an official order by providing hotel premises for prostitution. On 1 June 2005, the Misdemeanours Act (Law no. 5326) and new Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) entered into force. On 10 June 2005, the Büyükçekmece Magistrates’ Court, without holding a hearing, found that the accused had provided premises for prostitution, held that the applicant had failed to obey official orders, and imposed an administrative fine of 100 Turkish liras under Section 32 of the Misdemeanours Act.

The applicant objected, arguing that his defence rights had been restricted because the court relied solely on prior police statements without hearing him in person. He maintained that he accepted clients in compliance with regulations and could not be expected to refuse accommodation to foreign nationals or inquire into their motives. On 3 February 2006, the Bakırköy Assize Court examined the objection on the basis of the case file alone (without a hearing) and upheld the Magistrates’ Court’s decision, which became final.

Issues arose regarding notification of the final decision for the purposes of the six-month time-limit. An envelope dated 24 May 2006 invited the applicant to a hearing on 10 July 2006, but there was no confirmation of service. The applicant’s lawyer claimed receipt of the decision on 11 July 2006. A 2009 public prosecutor’s report asserted service on 26 May 2006. Despite requests from the Court in 2014 and 2017, neither party provided supporting documents, and the Government stated they could not locate them.

Relevant domestic law included Article 526 § 1 of the former Criminal Code (punishing failure to obey official orders with imprisonment and a fine), provisions of the Misdemeanours Act (allowing courts to impose administrative sanctions for misdemeanours, with objections examined without hearings and decisions served on parties), and the Code of Criminal Procedure (permitting decisions on objections without hearings unless necessary). Administrative fines were not registered in criminal records.

The core facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation centre on the absence of any oral hearing at either instance, despite the proceedings originating as a criminal charge for facilitating prostitution, the applicant’s personal denial of involvement, and his objection that he had not been heard and that evidence consisted only of police statements. The case thus raised questions about whether the lack of a hearing, combined with the nature of the offence and penalty, complied with fair-trial requirements.
