A public prosecutor later asserted that the decision had been served on 26 May 2006, but supporting documents could not be located despite Court requests. These facts underpinned the applicant’s claim that the absence of an oral hearing in the proceedings leading to the administrative sanction violated his right to a fair trial.

The case of Sancaklı v. Turkey (Application no. 1385/07), decided by the ECHR Second Section on 15 May 2018, concerns applicant Rıfat Sancaklı (born 1955, Istanbul hotel owner). He alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) because domestic courts imposed an administrative fine without holding any hearing.

On 2 October 2004, a magistrates’ court issued a search warrant. That night, gendarmerie searched the applicant’s Sancak Hotel. Records showed that a man (M.Ş.) approached officers and indicated he had a girl inside; he was identified as a trafficker. Five foreign women staying with men were taken into custody. All confirmed they were at the hotel for prostitution. When asked, some women denied any complicity by hotel management.

The applicant was arrested on 3 October 2004 on suspicion of facilitating prostitution. On 4 October he denied the allegation to gendarmerie, stating he barred procurers and had never seen M.Ş. The hotel manager similarly claimed they strictly excluded procurers.

On 30 May 2005 the public prosecutor indicted the applicant (and others) under Article 526 §1 of the former Criminal Code for failing to obey an official order by providing premises for prostitution.

New legislation (Misdemeanours Act and Code of Criminal Procedure) entered into force on 1 June 2005. On 10 June 2005 the Büyükçekmece Magistrates’ Court, without a hearing, found the applicant had provided premises for prostitution, constituting failure to obey an official order, and imposed a 100 TRY administrative fine under Section 32 of the Misdemeanours Act.

The applicant objected that his defence rights had been restricted: the court had relied solely on prior police statements without hearing him. He argued he accepted guests in accordance with regulations and could not refuse foreign nationals or interrogate their motives.

On 3 February 2006 the Bakırköy Assize Court, examining the file only (no hearing), upheld the decision. It became final.

Later disputes arose over service of the final decision (relevant to the six-month time-limit). An envelope dated 24 May 2006 referred to a 10 July 2006 hearing, but service was unconfirmed. The applicant’s lawyer claimed personal receipt of the decision on 11 July 2006 (supported by a certified note). A 2009 prosecutor’s report asserted service on 26 May 2006. The Court requested supporting documents in 2014 and 2017, but none were produced.

Relevant domestic law: former Criminal Code Article 526 §1 (prison and fine for disobeying official orders protecting public order/security/health). Misdemeanours Act Section 24 (courts impose administrative sanctions when an offence is a misdemeanour); Section 29 (objections to magistrates’ decisions heard by assize courts on the file only, without hearing; final decisions served on parties); Section 32 (100 TRY fine for disobeying official orders; former Article 526 references now point here). New CCP Articles 270–271 (objections generally decided without hearing, though prosecutor/defendant may be heard if necessary; such decisions are final). Administrative-fine decisions are not entered in criminal records.

These facts centre on the absence of any oral hearing at either instance, the recharacterisation of the charge as a misdemeanour after legislative change, and the applicant’s inability to contest the evidence in person.
001-182213:
The case of Leonov v. Russia (Application no. 77180/11) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 December 2011 by Sergey Aleksandrovich Leonov, a Russian national born in 1983 and living in Moscow. He alleged that the domestic courts’ refusal to issue a residence order in his favour regarding his son, A., born on 21 August 2007, together with an interim prohibition on contact pending those proceedings, violated his right to respect for family life, the principle of equality of spouses, and amounted to sex discrimination.

Leonov and his then-wife, Ch., lived with A. in Leonov’s Moscow flat, where the child was registered, received paediatric care and attended a local nursery. In November 2009 Ch. left, taking A. to live with her parents; A. has resided with her ever since. On 9 March 2010 Leonov applied for a residence order in his favour. The case was transferred to the Timiryazevskiy District Court of Moscow.

On 26 April 2010 Ch. filed a counterclaim seeking residence with her and an interim measure, alleging a risk that Leonov might abduct A. to Belarus. The same day the District Court granted the interim measure, forbidding Leonov from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s permission. It reasoned that the child already lived with the mother and that the measure was proportionate to prevent complications in enforcing any future judgment. Leonov learned of the order on 30 April 2010 when nursery staff refused him access.

Childcare inspections in April–May 2010 found both parents’ homes suitable. The Lyublino childcare authority reported on 22 June 2010 that A. should live with his mother because of his young age; maternal care until five or six was deemed essential to avoid negative character traits. An expert psychological examination ordered on 29 June 2010 (upheld on appeal) concluded on 11 November 2010 that A. was equally attached to both parents, both of whom were equally capable of raising him, although the parental conflict risked harming his development. A second childcare report of 23 December 2010 likewise favoured the mother, citing A.’s established life with her and attendance at a nearby nursery.

Leonov’s attempts to obtain contact were refused by the childcare authority because of the interim order. On 17 September 2010 Ch. was convicted of assaulting Leonov in A.’s presence (conviction later confirmed). Leonov objected to the trial judge, alleging a systematic preference for mothers; the objection was dismissed. The interim measure was quashed on 8 February 2011 by the Moscow City Court as unconnected to the claim, disproportionate and amounting to prejudgment; a fresh request was rejected on 1 April 2011.

On 12 April 2011 the District Court awarded residence to Ch. It acknowledged both parents’ capabilities and A.’s equal attachment, but held that a change of residence would harm a child not yet four who already had an established life with his mother. Environmental drawbacks of Ch.’s district, family smoking, Leonov’s superior housing and income, and Ch.’s (then non-final) conviction were all deemed non-decisive. The childcare authorities’ unanimous view and the “premature” nature of Leonov’s claim were cited; he could reapply later. The Moscow City Court upheld the judgment on 30 June 2011.

A subsequent contact schedule was granted to Leonov and his family in December 2011. The proceedings thus featured an 11-month interim ban on paternal contact and a residence decision that placed decisive weight on the child’s young age and existing maternal household despite findings of equal parental competence.

The case of Leonov v. Russia (Application no. 77180/11) concerns a Russian father’s complaints to the European Court of Human Rights that domestic courts’ refusal of a residence order in his favour for his young son, together with an interim no-contact measure imposed during the proceedings, violated his right to respect for family life, the principle of equality of spouses, and amounted to sex discrimination.

Sergey Aleksandrovich Leonov, born in 1983 and living in Moscow, was married to Ch. Their son A. was born on 21 August 2007. The family resided in Leonov’s flat, where A. was registered, received paediatric care and attended a local nursery. In November 2009 Ch. left the marital home, taking A. to live with her parents; A. has remained with her since. On 9 March 2010 Leonov applied for a residence order that A. live with him. The case was transferred to the Timiryazevskiy District Court of Moscow.

On 26 April 2010 Ch. lodged a counterclaim seeking residence with her and an interim measure, alleging a risk that Leonov would abduct A. to Belarus. The same day the District Court granted the interim order, prohibiting Leonov from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s permission, on the ground that the child was already living with the mother and that failure to act might impede execution of any future judgment. Leonov first learned of the order on 30 April 2010 when nursery staff refused him access. He later appealed, arguing the measure was unjustified, based on a stereotypical preference for maternal care, contrary to A.’s best interests (risking psychological harm, estrangement and bias in future assessments) and a breach of his contact rights. The appeal was not examined until September 2010 and was ultimately successful: on 8 February 2011 the Moscow City Court quashed the interim order as unconnected to the claim, disproportionate and as having prejudged the merits. On remittal the District Court rejected the request on 1 April 2011.

Meanwhile both parents’ flats were inspected and found suitable. A June 2010 childcare report recommended residence with the mother because of A.’s age (under five or six), stressing the importance of maternal care during typical developmental crises. An expert psychological report of November 2010 found A. equally attached to both parents, both equally capable of raising him, and the parental conflict potentially harmful. A second childcare report in December 2010 again favoured the mother, citing A.’s age, established life with her and local nursery attendance. In September 2010 Ch. was convicted (later upheld) of assaulting Leonov after he hugged A. at a beach; she had also been convicted of a traffic offence. Leonov presented evidence of his comfortable, safe neighbourhood, flexible self-employment, financial stability, close family ties and positive character references, contrasting these with Ch.’s allegedly aggressive behaviour, her mother’s smoking and alcohol use, and the polluted, unsafe district where she lived.

On 12 April 2011 the District Court granted residence to Ch. and dismissed Leonov’s application. It accepted that both parents were capable and A. equally attached, that conflict created a tense atmosphere, and that Ch.’s (then non-final) conviction arose from the residence dispute. Nevertheless it held that A., not yet four, had an established way of life with his mother; a change of residence would harm him. Environmental, smoking and financial arguments were deemed non-decisive. Both childcare authorities favoured the mother. The court added that Leonov’s request was premature and could be revisited when A. reached a more conscious age. The Moscow City Court upheld the judgment on 30 June 2011.

A subsequent December 2011 judgment established that Ch. had been obstructing contact and set a detailed access schedule for Leonov and the paternal family. Domestic law (Family Code Arts. 55, 57, 65–66) required courts to determine residence according to the child’s best interests, attachment, age, parental qualities and material conditions, and guaranteed the non-resident parent’s contact rights and the child’s right to maintain relations with both parents. Interim measures under the Code of Civil Procedure had to be proportionate and necessary to secure execution of judgment.

These facts formed the basis of Leonov’s complaints that the interim ban and the residence decision reflected a gender stereotype favouring mothers, disregarded his equal parental rights and the expert findings of equal attachment, and thereby interfered with his family life.

**Case of Leonov v. Russia (Application no. 77180/11), ECtHR (Third Section), judgment of 10 April 2018 (final 10 July 2018).**

The applicant, Sergey Aleksandrovich Leonov (born 1983), a Russian national living in Moscow, complained that the domestic courts’ refusal of a residence order in his favour for his young son A. (born 21 August 2007) and an interim no-contact measure pending those proceedings violated his right to respect for family life (Article 8 ECHR), the principle of equality of spouses, and amounted to sex discrimination (Article 14).

The family lived in the applicant’s Moscow flat, where A. was registered, received paediatric care, and attended a local nursery. In November 2009 the applicant’s wife Ch. left, taking A. to live with her parents; A. has resided with her since. On 9 March 2010 the applicant applied to the Justice of the Peace for a residence order placing A. with him. The case was transferred to the Timiryazevskiy District Court of Moscow. On 26 April 2010 Ch. lodged a counterclaim seeking residence with her plus an interim measure, alleging a risk that the applicant would abduct A. to Belarus (where his stepfather had a house) and citing a prior attempt to collect A. from nursery.

That same day the District Court granted the interim measure, forbidding the applicant from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s prior permission. It reasoned that the child was living with the mother and that the measure was proportionate to prevent complications in executing a future judgment. The applicant learned of the order on 30 April 2010 when nursery staff refused him access. Childcare authorities inspected both homes and found them suitable. A June 2010 Lyublino childcare report recommended residence with the mother until age 5–6, citing the importance of maternal care during early behavioural crises to avoid negative traits. An expert psychological examination (ordered June 2010, reported November 2010) found A. equally attached to both parents, both equally capable of raising him, but noted that the parents’ serious conflict risked harming A.’s development.

The applicant unsuccessfully sought a contact order from childcare authorities (they cited the interim measure). On 17 September 2010 a justice of the peace convicted Ch. of assault and battery after she snatched A. away and struck the applicant at least twice when he hugged his son at a beach. The Moscow City Court later quashed the interim measure (8 February 2011) as unconnected to the claim, disproportionate, lacking evidence of execution risk, and prejudging the merits; the District Court then rejected a fresh request as unsubstantiated. Childcare authorities instructed Ch. to cease obstructing contact with the paternal family.

In the resumed residence proceedings the applicant emphasised his comfortable, safe flat and countryside home, flexible self-employment allowing time for A., payment of maintenance, strong attachment (including to paternal relatives), and positive character. He contrasted this with Ch.’s alleged aggression, her (then non-final) conviction, an administrative driving offence, residence in a polluted/unsafe area near an oil refinery and prison, and her mother’s smoking/alcohol use. Ch. countered that the applicant was too busy (business, studies, building plans) and that character allegations came only from his relatives. Nursery staff described the applicant becoming agitated when refused access in April 2010.

On 12 April 2011 the District Court awarded residence to Ch. and dismissed the applicant’s claim. It found both parents capable and A. equally attached, but stressed A.’s age (not yet four), established life with the mother and local nursery, and the likely negative impact of a change of residence. The father’s better housing/finances and the (non-final) charges against Ch. were not decisive. Unanimous childcare recommendations favoured the mother; the father’s request was deemed “premature” and could be reconsidered when A. reached a more conscious age. The Moscow City Court upheld the judgment on 30 June 2011 as lawful and well-reasoned.

A later (December 2011) judgment established a contact schedule for the applicant (weekends and holiday periods) and paternal relatives after finding Ch. had obstructed access. Ch.’s assault conviction became final in February 2012.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the interim ban severed contact without justification (risking estrangement of a very young child) and that the residence decision rested on a stereotypical maternal preference rather than an individualised assessment of A.’s best interests or equal parental capabilities.
001-182454:
The applicant, İlkay Baydar (dual Dutch-Turkish national), was convicted by the Zutphen Regional Court on 29 October 2008 of transporting 2,800 grams of heroin and seven counts of people trafficking under Article 197a of the Dutch Criminal Code. He received a partially suspended 40-month prison sentence. Both parties appealed.

On 19 July 2011 the Arnhem Court of Appeal upheld the heroin conviction and four trafficking counts (acquitting three), finding that Baydar and co-perpetrators had, for financial gain, facilitated the unauthorised residence of 20 Iraqi migrants in the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark between November 2006 and January 2007. He was sentenced to 40 months’ imprisonment (less pre-trial detention).

Baydar lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (limited to points of law and procedure). In grounds filed on 8 August 2013 he challenged the four trafficking convictions, arguing that the Court of Appeal had applied Article 197a § 2 (facilitation of unauthorised “residence”) even though the evidence showed only brief, intercepted transit through the Netherlands and Germany en route to Denmark (which the migrants never entered). He contended that “residence” required a long-term stay, distinct from “entry” or “transit” under the newly added § 1, and invoked EU Council Directive 2002/90/EC and Framework Decision 2002/946/JHA (which Article 197a implemented). No preliminary-ruling request was included at this stage.

The Advocate General advised on 10 December 2013 that the appeal should be dismissed except for the length of the cassation proceedings (a reasonable-time violation warranting a sentence reduction). On the “residence” point he favoured a broad interpretation of Article 197a § 2 that encompassed transit, consistent with pre-implementation case-law; the Directive’s implementation had been intended to widen, not narrow, the provision.

In a 24 December 2013 “Borgers letter” Baydar tentatively requested that, if the Supreme Court agreed with the Advocate General, questions be referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on the meaning of “residence”, “entry” and “transit” under the Directive and whether the Directive set minimum rules or a general framework.

On 4 March 2014 the Supreme Court reduced the sentence to 34 months for the reasonable-time violation. It dismissed the remaining grounds under section 81(1) of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act, stating only that they “cannot lead to cassation” and required no further reasoning because they raised no legal issues needing determination in the interests of uniformity or legal development. No further appeal was possible.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that this unreasoned refusal to refer a preliminary question to the CJEU (or to explain why referral was unnecessary) violated his Article 6 § 1 right to a fair trial, given the Supreme Court’s status as a court of last instance under Article 267 TFEU and the CILFIT criteria.

The case of Baydar v. the Netherlands (Application no. 55385/14) originated in a complaint by İlkay Baydar, a dual Dutch-Turkish national born in 1968 and residing in Apeldoorn, alleging a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Specifically, he contended that the Dutch Supreme Court (Hoge Raad) had refused to refer questions he raised for a preliminary ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and had failed to provide adequate reasons for that refusal.

The underlying criminal proceedings began with the applicant’s conviction by the Zutphen Regional Court on 29 October 2008 of transporting 2,800 grams of heroin and seven counts of people trafficking (mensensmokkel) contrary to Article 197a of the Criminal Code, committed jointly with others. He received a partly suspended sentence of 40 months’ imprisonment. Both sides appealed. On 19 July 2011 the Arnhem Court of Appeal upheld the heroin conviction and four trafficking counts (acquitting him of the remaining three). It found that, for financial gain between 10 November 2006 and 17 January 2007, the applicant and co-perpetrators had facilitated the unauthorised residence of 20 Iraqi migrants in the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. The sentence remained 40 months less time already served.

The applicant lodged an appeal in cassation, limited to points of law and procedure. In written grounds of 8 August 2013 he challenged the four trafficking convictions. He argued that the Court of Appeal had convicted him of facilitating unauthorised “residence” under Article 197a § 2, yet the evidence showed only that he had organised and financed the migrants’ transportation toward Denmark via the Netherlands and Germany; the journeys had been intercepted in Germany, the stays had been brief and transitory, and the migrants had never entered Denmark. Consequently there was no “residence.” He invoked Council Directive 2002/90/EC (defining facilitation of unauthorised entry, transit and residence) and Council Framework Decision 2002/946/JHA, noting that Article 197a had been amended to implement the Directive. He maintained that “residence” in § 2 must be understood as a long-term stay, distinct from the “transit” or “entry” separately penalised in the newly added § 1. The grounds contained no request for a preliminary ruling.

In an advisory opinion of 10 December 2013 the Advocate General recommended that the appeal be dismissed except as regards the length of the cassation proceedings, which had exceeded a reasonable time and warranted a sentence reduction. On the “residence” point he considered that Article 197a § 2 retained its pre-implementation broad meaning, which encompassed transit; the Directive had been intended to widen the provision’s scope, and the new § 1 did not narrow § 2.

On 24 December 2013 the applicant submitted a written reply (Borgers letter) in which, should the Supreme Court agree with the Advocate General, he tentatively requested that questions be referred to the CJEU concerning the interpretation of “residence,” “entry” and “transit” under the Directive and whether the Directive laid down minimum rules or a general framework.

On 4 March 2014 the Supreme Court reduced the sentence to 34 months because of the delay but otherwise dismissed the appeal. Citing section 81(1) of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act, it stated that the remaining grievances “cannot lead to cassation” and “do not give rise to the need for a determination of legal issues in the interests of legal uniformity or legal development.” The judgment made no reference to EU law, the Directive, or the request for a preliminary ruling. No further domestic appeal lay.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the Supreme Court’s summary dismissal, without addressing or reasoning its implicit refusal to seek a preliminary ruling from the CJEU, breached Article 6 § 1.

In Baydar v. the Netherlands (Application no. 55385/14), the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) because the Dutch Supreme Court refused to refer questions of EU law interpretation to the CJEU for a preliminary ruling and provided no adequate reasons for that refusal.

He received 40 months’ imprisonment (less pre-trial detention).

He argued that “residence” in § 2 therefore required a long-term stay, distinct from the newly added “transit” and “entry” in § 1. The grounds contained no request for a CJEU preliminary ruling.

On 4 March 2014 the Supreme Court reduced the sentence to 34 months for the delay but dismissed the remaining grounds under section 81(1) of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act. It stated that the grievances “cannot lead to cassation” and required “no further reasoning” because they raised no legal issues requiring determination “in the interests of legal uniformity or legal development.” The judgment annexed the cassation grounds and noted the reply but neither mentioned nor ruled on the request for a preliminary ruling. No further appeal was possible.

These facts—particularly the late, tentative nature of the referral request, the Supreme Court’s use of abridged reasoning under section 81, and the complete silence on the CJEU request—formed the core of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation. (Word count: 512)
001-182867:
The case concerns Norwegian lawyer Steingrim Wolland, who alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life, home and correspondence). On 9 March 2010 he was charged with aiding and abetting art-sale fraud, bank-loan fraud and related forgery. The next day the Oslo City Court, finding reasonable grounds for suspicion, authorised a search of his home and office; he did not appeal.

On 23 March 2010 police executed the search in the presence of a third-party lawyer. Because of the presumption of legal professional privilege (LPP) attaching to a lawyer’s files, paper documents were placed in sealed bags rather than examined on site. A hard disk and laptop were also taken; mirror copies were made and the originals returned two days later. In May 2010 Wolland sorted the papers and identified those he claimed were privileged; they were stored separately under seal.

In January 2011 the prosecution asked the City Court to review the papers and to allow an Økokrim computer specialist to examine the mirror copies, after which a further application for seizure of specific items would be made. Keyword searches of the copies later identified 2 309 files, which were submitted to the court in May 2011.

On 16 February 2011 Wolland’s lawyer challenged the lawfulness of what he termed a “seizure,” arguing that reasonable suspicion no longer existed and demanding return of all material. The City Court replied (letters of 11 May and 22 July 2011) that no formal seizure decision had yet been taken; it was merely performing the preliminary LPP-filtering task required by Supreme Court precedent (Rt. 2011 p. 296). Consequently there was no occasion for a hearing on discontinuation or return, nor for a fresh examination of the original suspicion. Its eventual ruling on what could be released to the prosecution would be appealable.

Wolland appealed the 22 July decision. The Borgarting High Court (9 November 2011) and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee (20 December 2011) dismissed the appeals. They held that the search authorisation of 10 March 2010 had become final, that no seizure had yet occurred, and that Norwegian law (and the Convention) conferred no additional right of judicial review of suspicion or of an “ongoing search” at the filtering stage.

A hearing on the papers took place on 25 January 2012. On 11 May 2012 the City Court released 1 264 electronic documents (and some papers) to the prosecution. Further appeals produced mixed results: after a Supreme Court remittal the High Court ultimately authorised only 36 of the remaining disputed files (May 2013).

Wolland separately sought return of the mirror copies in June 2012. The City Court refused. The High Court (January 2013) ordered their return unless the prosecution promptly applied for court examination. The Supreme Court (June 2013) found the prosecution’s earlier keyword searches unlawful (the copies should have been sealed and sent to the court unused) but remitted the question whether they should nevertheless remain with the court. The copies were transferred to the City Court in September 2013. After the criminal charges were resolved, the prosecution lifted the “seizure” on 28 May 2014 and the High Court dismissed the return application as moot (August 2014).

The underlying criminal case ended with Wolland’s acquittal on one count, a conviction for gross negligence on another, and the dropping of the remaining charges (final in October 2013). Throughout the more than four-year period the authorities retained a large volume of his professional and private material without a formal seizure order and without affording him a judicial opportunity to challenge either the continued existence of reasonable suspicion or the evidentiary relevance of the collected items.

The case of Wolland v. Norway (no. 39731/12) arose from an application by Norwegian lawyer Steingrim Wolland alleging a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. He complained that prosecutors and Oslo City Court had collected and retained, for a lengthy period, numerous paper documents plus mirror copies of his computer and hard disk without any formal seizure decision. Pending such a decision he had no access to judicial review of whether reasonable suspicion still existed or whether the material remained relevant as evidence.

On 9 March 2010 Økokrim charged Wolland with aiding and abetting art-sale fraud, loan fraud and related forgery. The following day Oslo City Court, finding reasonable grounds for suspicion, authorised a search of his home and office. Wolland did not appeal. The search took place on 23 March 2010 in the presence of a third-party lawyer. Because of the presumption of legal professional privilege, papers were placed in sealed bags rather than examined on the spot; a hard disk and laptop were also taken. Mirror copies were made and the originals returned two days later.

On 3 May 2010 Wolland attended prosecutors’ offices, identified the privileged papers and had them separately sealed. In January 2011 prosecutors asked the City Court to review the papers and to allow a computer specialist to examine the mirror copies (keyword searches later identified 2 309 files). Those files were submitted to the court in May 2011.

In February 2011 Wolland’s lawyer challenged the lawfulness of what he termed a “seizure”, arguing that suspicion no longer existed, and sought return of everything. The City Court replied (May and July 2011) that no seizure had yet been ordered; following Supreme Court precedent (Rt. 2011 p. 296) it was simply filtering the material to decide what could be released to prosecutors. A hearing would precede any formal, appealable decision. The court declined to re-examine suspicion or to return the sealed material.

Wolland appealed the July 2011 decision. Borgarting High Court dismissed the appeal on 9 November 2011, holding that the statutory procedure had been followed, that the original search warrant had not been challenged, and that Articles 6, 8, 10 and 13 of the Convention conferred no additional right of interim review. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee rejected a further appeal on 20 December 2011.

Later rulings on the substance of privilege followed. In May 2012 the City Court authorised handover of 1 264 digital documents; after successive appeals (including a Supreme Court quashing for an unduly narrow view of “lawyer’s work”) the High Court ultimately released only 36 of the disputed items. As regards the mirror copies themselves, Wolland applied in June 2012 for their return. The Supreme Court later held (June 2013) that prosecutors’ keyword searches had been unlawful and that the copies should have been sealed and sent immediately to the City Court; they were transferred in September 2013. The seizure was formally lifted in May 2014 and the related proceedings dismissed.

In the underlying criminal case Wolland was acquitted of loan fraud but convicted of gross negligence (final October 2013); the remaining charges were dropped.

The lengthy retention of both paper and digital material without a formal seizure order or any opportunity for contemporaneous judicial review of suspicion or relevance constituted the core of the Article 8 complaint.

The case of Wolland v. Norway (Application no. 39731/12) concerned alleged violations of Article 8 of the ECHR (right to respect for private life, home and correspondence). The applicant, Norwegian lawyer Steingrim Wolland (born 1961), operated a law firm in Oslo until his practising licence was suspended following personal bankruptcy proceedings in April 2009.

On 9 March 2010, Norway’s National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime (Økokrim) charged the applicant with aiding and abetting art-sale fraud, bank-loan fraud and related document forgery. The following day the Oslo City Court, finding reasonable grounds for suspicion, authorised a search of his home and office. The applicant did not appeal.

On 23 March 2010 police executed the search in the presence of a third-party lawyer. Because some material was presumed protected by legal professional privilege (LPP) and therefore exempt from seizure under Article 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, paper documents were placed in sealed bags rather than examined on site. A laptop and hard disk were also taken; mirror copies were made and the originals returned two days later.

On 3 May 2010 the applicant attended Økokrim’s offices and identified papers he considered privileged; those items were stored separately under seal. On 5 January 2011 the prosecution asked the City Court to review the paper documents and release those that could lawfully be seized. For the digital copies it proposed that an Økokrim computer specialist first examine the material, after which a further application would be made concerning any remaining LPP claims. The City Court approved the procedure. Keyword searches subsequently identified 2 309 files.

By letter of 16 February 2011 the applicant’s lawyer challenged the lawfulness of what he termed an unlawful “seizure,” arguing that reasonable suspicion no longer existed and demanding immediate return of all material. On 6 May 2011 the 2 309 files were submitted to the City Court. In decisions of 11 May and 22 July 2011 the City Court held that no formal seizure had yet occurred; it was merely performing the preliminary filtering of potentially privileged material required by Supreme Court practice (Rt. 2011 p. 296). Consequently there was no occasion for a hearing on discontinuation of seizure or return of the items, nor any duty to re-examine the original grounds for suspicion.

The applicant appealed. The Borgarting High Court dismissed the appeal on 9 November 2011, confirming that the statutory scheme afforded no right to judicial review of suspicion or of the material’s evidential relevance at the filtering stage, and that Articles 6, 8, 10 and 13 of the Convention added no further entitlement. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee rejected a further appeal on 20 December 2011.

Subsequent litigation on the merits of individual documents continued into 2013. In June 2013 the Supreme Court held that the prosecution’s own keyword searches of the unsealed digital copies had been unlawful; the copies should have been placed under seal and transferred directly to the City Court. The copies were finally lodged with the court in September 2013. Meanwhile the underlying criminal proceedings concluded: the applicant was acquitted of one fraud count, convicted of gross negligence on the loan application, and the remaining charges were dropped. On 28 May 2014 the prosecution formally lifted the seizure. The High Court therefore dismissed the outstanding application for return of the copies on 22 August 2014.

The applicant complained that, throughout the lengthy period between collection of the material and any formal seizure decision, he had been denied access to any judicial procedure capable of examining whether reasonable suspicion persisted or whether the documents were relevant as evidence.
001-183118:
**Case of Jureša v. Croatia (ECtHR, Application no. 24079/11, Judgment of 22 May 2018)**

The applicant, Ivana Jureša (born 1977, residing in Osijek), alleged that she was deprived of access to Croatia’s Supreme Court, in violation of her right to a fair hearing (Article 6 of the Convention / equivalent constitutional protections). The case arose from a property dispute over an unregistered house inherited after her grandmother’s death.

On 6 November 2000, the Zabok Municipal Court declared the applicant’s relative M.J. and her father as beneficiaries of the house. On 18 October 2007, M.J. sued the applicant in the same court, seeking recognition of his half-share ownership and an order (clausula intabulandi) compelling her to allow registration of that ownership in the land register. He valued the dispute at HRK 110,000. The applicant initially contested this figure (proposing HRK 300,000) but withdrew her objection at a 23 January 2008 hearing and accepted the stated value.

The Municipal Court ruled for M.J. on 25 April 2008. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed as unfounded by the Zlatar County Court on 16 September 2009. She then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court on 24 November 2009.

On 27 May 2010, the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible *ratione valoris*. It treated M.J.’s action as two distinct claims arising from different factual and legal bases: (1) a property-rights claim for recognition of ownership and (2) an obligations-law claim for the clausula intabulandi. Applying section 37(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, it divided the HRK 110,000 value equally. Each resulting figure fell below the HRK 100,001 threshold required under section 382 for an appeal on points of law. The Court noted that section 37(1) would have required summing values only if claims shared the same basis.

The applicant filed a constitutional complaint, arguing the two aspects of the action were inseparable, that the Supreme Court’s splitting of the value was arbitrary, and that this denied her access to the highest court (violating Article 29 of the Constitution). On 17 February 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, finding that she had not shown arbitrary application of the law or any constitutional issue. The decision was served on 3 March 2011.

Domestic law (Civil Procedure Act sections 35, 37, 40 and 382) determines dispute value primarily from the principal claim as indicated by the claimant, with special rules for multiple claims or parties. Supreme Court case-law on whether ownership-recognition plus clausula intabulandi constitute one claim or two was inconsistent: numerous decisions treated them as a single claim (or divided value only by number of parties), while others (including the present case and several from 2010–2011) treated them as two claims from varied grounds and halved (or further divided) the value, often rendering appeals inadmissible.

The Constitutional Court had previously upheld similar Supreme Court divisions of value in other cases, requiring complainants to provide “serious, relevant and sufficient” reasons to overcome established (if sometimes varying) case-law. These facts—particularly the value-setting process, the Supreme Court’s splitting of an originally unified claim, the resulting inadmissibility, and the inconsistency in national jurisprudence—form the core of the alleged denial of access to the Supreme Court.

The case of Jureša v. Croatia (Application no. 24079/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of the applicant’s right of access to a court (the Croatian Supreme Court) under Article 6 of the Convention. Ivana Jureša, a Croatian national born in 1977 and living in Osijek, complained that the Supreme Court’s declaration of her appeal on points of law as inadmissible ratione valoris arbitrarily deprived her of that access.

The relevant facts originated in inheritance proceedings after the death of the applicant’s grandmother. On 6 November 2000 the Zabok Municipal Court declared the applicant’s relative M.J. and her father beneficiaries of an unregistered house. On 18 October 2007 M.J. brought a civil action against the applicant in the same court seeking (i) recognition of his ownership of a half-share of the inherited property and (ii) an order (clausula intabulandi) compelling the applicant to permit registration of that ownership in the land register. He valued the dispute at HRK 110,000.

The applicant initially contested the valuation and proposed HRK 300,000, but at the 23 January 2008 hearing she withdrew the objection and expressly agreed to the claimant’s figure. On 25 April 2008 the Municipal Court upheld M.J.’s claim. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed as ill-founded by the Zlatar County Court on 16 September 2009.

She then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court on 24 November 2009. On 27 May 2010 that court declared the appeal inadmissible ratione valoris. It characterised M.J.’s action as two separate claims arising from different legal bases—one in rem (recognition of ownership) and one in personam (issuance of the clausula intabulandi). Applying section 37(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, it halved the indicated value of HRK 110,000, producing HRK 55,000 per claim—below the statutory threshold of HRK 100,001 required by section 382 for an appeal on points of law.

The applicant filed a constitutional complaint arguing that the two aspects of the action were legally inseparable, that the Supreme Court’s splitting of the claims was arbitrary, and that it thereby violated her constitutional right to a fair hearing (Article 29), in particular her right of access to the Supreme Court. On 17 February 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, holding that the applicant had not shown arbitrary application of the law and that the case raised no constitutional issue.

Domestic law (Civil Procedure Act, sections 35, 37, 40 and 382) provided that only the principal claim’s value counted, that claims from different grounds were to be valued separately, and that non-monetary claims used the value indicated by the claimant. The Supreme Court’s own prior case-law was inconsistent: numerous decisions had treated a claim for ownership recognition together with a clausula intabulandi as a single claim (dividing value only by the number of parties), while later decisions (including several in 2010) treated them as two distinct claims. The Constitutional Court had previously upheld the Supreme Court’s practice of dividing value by the number of claimants, requiring “serious, relevant and sufficient” reasons to depart from that established case-law.

These facts formed the core of the alleged violation: the Supreme Court’s re-characterisation of an agreed valuation of HRK 110,000 as two sub-threshold claims, against a background of fluctuating jurisprudence, had the effect of denying the applicant access to the highest ordinary court.

The ECtHR case of Jureša v. Croatia (no. 24079/11) arose from the applicant’s complaint that she had been denied access to Croatia’s Supreme Court in civil proceedings over inherited property. The applicant, Ivana Jureša, a Croatian national born in 1977 and living in Osijek, was represented by counsel. After her grandmother’s death, the Zabok Municipal Court on 6 November 2000 declared the applicant’s relative M.J. and her father beneficiaries of an unregistered house.

On 18 October 2007 M.J. sued the applicant in the same court, seeking recognition of his half-ownership and an order (clausula intabulandi) enabling land-register inscription. He valued the dispute at HRK 110,000. The applicant initially proposed HRK 300,000 but, at a 23 January 2008 hearing, withdrew the objection and accepted the plaintiff’s figure. The Municipal Court granted M.J.’s claim on 25 April 2008. The Zlatar County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 16 September 2009.

On 24 November 2009 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 27 May 2010 that court declared the appeal inadmissible ratione valoris. It treated the action as two legally distinct claims—one in rem for ownership recognition and one in personam for the clausula intabulandi—arising from different factual and legal bases. Applying section 37(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, it halved the agreed value, producing HRK 55,000 per claim, below the HRK 100,001 threshold of section 382(1).

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that the two aspects of the action were inseparable, that the Supreme Court’s characterisation was arbitrary, and that it violated her constitutional right of access to court. On 17 February 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, holding that the applicant had not shown arbitrary application of the law and that no constitutional issue arose.

The alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 ECHR (access to a court) centres on this valuation ruling. The Civil Procedure Act requires the value of a single-basis action to be the sum of all claims (s. 37(1)) but the value of each claim separately when claims rest on “a variety of grounds” (s. 37(2)). The Supreme Court’s own jurisprudence on whether an ownership-plus-clausula action constitutes one claim or two was inconsistent: numerous earlier decisions treated the pair as a single claim whose value was not divided, while later decisions (including the applicant’s) treated them as two claims whose values had to be split. The applicant had accepted a unique value of HRK 110,000 precisely to meet the Supreme Court threshold; the subsequent re-characterisation therefore determined whether she could obtain a final ruling on the merits.

These facts—the agreed unique valuation, the Supreme Court’s late reclassification of the claims, the resulting inadmissibility, the Constitutional Court’s refusal to intervene, and the documented divergence in Supreme Court case-law—form the core of the access-to-court complaint.
001-183124:
**Case of Svetina v. Slovenia (ECtHR, 22 May 2018, App. no. 38059/13)**

The applicant, Matjaž Svetina, a Slovenian national, alleged violations of Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention arising from police examinations of two mobile telephones during a murder investigation. The core facts concern the timing, legal basis, and use of data from the victim’s (X’s) phone and the applicant’s own phone, which formed the basis for identifying, arresting, and convicting him.

On 4 November 2007 X disappeared. He was found dead the next morning near Komen, having been repeatedly stabbed and cut, then run over by a car. Police, the district prosecutor, and the duty investigating judge attended the scene. X’s mobile phone was found in his car. Officers immediately checked its incoming/outgoing calls and text messages without a prior court order. The records showed that on 4 November X had communicated solely with one number, from which an explicitly sexual message had also been sent. A telephone directory check linked the number to the applicant’s grandmother, with whom official records showed he lived. The prosecutor then asked the investigating judge to order the network operator (S company) to produce X’s traffic data. Later that day the judge issued a search warrant for X’s home and the data-production order; S company supplied a disk the same day.

On 6 November police stopped the applicant’s car, conducted a “security check,” and found a knife (with possible blood traces) and a mobile phone in his pocket. They examined the phone without a court order, confirmed it used the number that had contacted X, seized the items, and arrested him. The investigating judge then issued search warrants for the applicant’s home and cars, and later ordered the applicant’s network operator (M company) to supply his traffic data.

A judicial investigation for aggravated murder followed. The applicant was heard, detained on remand, and later admitted running X over but claimed it was accidental. He was indicted. After a first conviction and a successful appeal (the higher court found the first-instance court had failed to clarify possible third-party involvement), a retrial occurred. The applicant applied to exclude all evidence from the crime-scene investigation onward, arguing that the warrantless examinations of both phones violated Article 37 of the Slovenian Constitution (privacy of correspondence and other means of communication) and that the court orders had been issued too late. He also sought examination of the arresting officers and access to police notes of his phone examination. Both requests were refused.

On 4 September 2009 the Koper District Court convicted him of murder (running X over while X was still alive) and sentenced him to 12 years. It found insufficient proof that he had inflicted the stab wounds but held that forensic, biological, and scene evidence (including a rubber fragment from his car, mutual biological traces, and reconstructions) proved he had been present and had deliberately run X over. The court used telephone records (together with medical evidence and a petrol bill) to fix the time of death after the last recorded missed call. It refused exclusion of evidence, holding that examination of X’s phone had not interfered with the applicant’s constitutional rights and that examination of the applicant’s own phone, though unconstitutional, carried no evidentiary weight because the police already possessed the necessary information from X’s phone; the results of the latter examination had not been placed on the file or relied upon.

The Koper Higher Court reduced the sentence to nine years (finding the act did not meet the legal criteria for aggravated murder) but dismissed the remainder of the appeal, including the phone-examination complaints. It held that the examination of X’s phone had been an urgent step, that a court order had been obtained before the applicant was identified, and that it had not violated privacy of communication. The examination of the applicant’s phone was unconstitutional but evidentially insignificant. The Supreme Court likewise dismissed a further appeal, noting that the applicant had not claimed a direct privacy violation from X’s phone (personality rights ceased at death), that the examination had not revealed his identity, and that a court order preceded his arrest. Regarding his own phone, it accepted the unconstitutionality but applied an inevitable-discovery analysis: the same information would have been obtained by a simple call, SIM-card check (no warrant required), or the later court order. The Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint.

These facts—the warrantless on-scene check of X’s phone, the warrantless examination of the applicant’s phone during the security stop, the subsequent court orders, the domestic courts’ refusal to exclude the resulting identification evidence, and their reasoning on privacy, causation, and inevitable discovery—formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 8 (privacy of correspondence) and Article 6 (fair-trial/use of unlawfully obtained evidence) complaints.

**CASE OF SVETINA v. SLOVENIA (Application no. 38059/13, ECHR Fourth Section, judgment 22 May 2018, final 22 August 2018)**

The applicant, Matjaž Svetina (born 1982), a Slovenian national living in Koper, alleged breaches of Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention arising from police examinations of two mobile telephones during criminal proceedings against him for the killing of X.

On 4 November 2007 X went missing. He was found dead the next morning near the Komen-Branik road, having been repeatedly stabbed and cut with a knife then run over by a car. Police, the district prosecutor and duty investigating judge attended the scene. X’s mobile telephone was found in his car. Officers examined its call and text records on site and established that on 4 November X had communicated solely with one number, from which an explicitly sexual message had also been sent. Directory checks linked the number to the applicant’s grandmother, with whom he lived. The prosecutor requested, and the investigating judge issued, an order requiring the network operator (S company) to produce X’s traffic data; the data were supplied the same day. A search of X’s home was also ordered.

On 6 November 2007 police stopped the applicant’s car and conducted a security check, finding a knife (apparently blood-stained) and a mobile telephone in his pocket. They examined the telephone, confirmed it used the number that had contacted X, seized the items and arrested the applicant. Relying largely on the telephone data, the investigating judge then ordered searches of the applicant’s home and vehicles and the production of his traffic data from another operator (M company). The applicant was later heard (with counsel) and remanded in custody. A judicial investigation for aggravated murder followed; further traffic data were ordered, together with forensic, medical, psychiatric and reconstruction evidence.

The applicant was indicted on 24 December 2007. After an unsuccessful objection he stood trial. He was first convicted of aggravated murder and sentenced to 13 years (June 2008). The conviction was quashed on appeal because of unresolved questions about a possible shoe imprint suggesting a third person, and the case was remitted.

In the retrial the applicant applied to exclude all evidence from the crime-scene investigation onwards, arguing that the examinations of both telephones (his and X’s) had been conducted without timely court orders, violating constitutional privacy of communications (Article 37 of the Slovenian Constitution) and tainting subsequent evidence. He also sought examination of the arresting officers and disclosure of police notes of his telephone examination. Both requests were refused.

On 4 September 2009 the Koper District Court convicted him of aggravated murder solely on the basis of having intentionally run X over (finding insufficient proof that he had stabbed X) and sentenced him to 12 years (later reduced to 9 years on appeal). The court held that X had still been alive when run over and that forensic, biological and vehicle-science evidence placed the applicant at the scene and excluded accident. It used telephone records (together with medical evidence and a petrol bill) to time the death as occurring after the last recorded call from X’s phone. It refused exclusion of evidence, stating that examination of X’s telephone had not interfered with the applicant’s constitutional rights and that examination of the applicant’s telephone, while a violation, had no evidentiary weight because the police already possessed the key information from X’s telephone; the results of the applicant’s telephone examination were not in the file and were not relied upon.

On appeal the Higher Court (January 2010) reduced the sentence but dismissed the remainder of the complaints. It held that examination of X’s telephone had been an urgent police step and that a court order for traffic data had been obtained before the applicant was identified, so there was no privacy violation. Examination of the applicant’s telephone was unconstitutional but evidentially insignificant. The Supreme Court (December 2011) similarly found no interference with the applicant’s privacy from examination of X’s telephone (personality rights cease at death; the applicant’s identity was not revealed; a court order preceded arrest). Information identifying the applicant’s number as the source of the sexual message would have been discovered inevitably (by a simple call, SIM-card check or later court order). The Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint (January 2013).

The applicant complained that the warrantless examinations of the two telephones violated Articles 6 and 8 and that all subsequent evidence should have been excluded under the strict domestic exclusionary rule. The remainder of his application was declared inadmissible.

The ECHR case of Svetina v. Slovenia (App. no. 38059/13) arose from criminal proceedings against the applicant for the 2007 killing of X, who was found stabbed, cut and run over. The applicant alleged that police examinations of X’s and his own mobile phones without prior court orders violated Article 8 (privacy of communications) and Article 6 (fair trial), tainting all subsequent evidence so that it should have been excluded under domestic law.

Police examining the crime scene found X’s phone in his car and immediately reviewed its call/text logs (no court order). These showed contact solely with a number registered to the applicant’s grandmother (with whom he lived), including a sexually explicit message. The prosecutor then obtained a judicial order for the operator to produce X’s full records, which were supplied the same day. The next day police stopped the applicant, conducted a security search, found a knife and his phone, examined the phone (again without an order) and confirmed it as the source of the communications with X. They seized the items and arrested him. Judicial orders for searches of his home/cars and for his own telephone records followed promptly.

A judicial investigation for aggravated murder was opened. The applicant later admitted running X over but claimed it was accidental. After an initial conviction was quashed on appeal (unresolved possible third-party involvement), a retrial ensued. The applicant sought exclusion of all evidence from the crime-scene inquiry onward as fruit of the unlawful phone examinations (violating constitutional privacy of communications) and requested testimony from the officers who searched him. Both requests were refused.

He was convicted of intentionally running X over (the stabbings unproven) and sentenced to 12 years (later reduced to 9). The trial court relied on forensic, biological-trace, reconstruction and other evidence to place him at the scene and disprove accident; it used telephone data only to confirm the pair knew each other and to fix time of death (last missed call). It held that X’s phone examination had not interfered with the applicant’s own privacy rights and that his phone examination, though unconstitutional, carried no weight because its results were never placed on file or relied upon.

On appeal the applicant argued the examinations were unlawful ab initio, that X’s data (especially the sexual message) had been obtained without an order and that his arrest had depended on the subsequent examination of his own phone, so every piece of evidence should have been excluded. The higher court rejected this: an order for X’s records existed before the applicant was identified, the examination was an urgent police step, and no privacy-of-communications violation had occurred; the applicant’s phone examination, though unconstitutional, was evidentially insignificant. The Supreme Court added that X’s examination had not revealed the applicant’s identity (personality rights cease at death) and was not causal to the incriminating evidence; information linking the applicant’s number to the message would have been discovered inevitably (by simply calling the number, inspecting the SIM, or the later court order), so it was not inadmissible. A constitutional complaint repeating the same arguments was not accepted for consideration.
