001-183122:
The case of Bikić v. Croatia originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Ivanka Bikić, a Croatian national born in 1954 and resident in Zagreb. She alleged that the authorities’ refusal of her request to purchase the socially owned flat she had occupied since 1988 violated her right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

Under the former Yugoslav socialist system, employees of socially owned companies contributed a percentage of their salaries to housing funds used to construct or acquire flats. These were allocated as specially protected tenancies, which met the housing needs of the recipient and removed him or her from waiting lists. The applicant was employed by company S. and paid the required 3 per cent contribution. On 31 October 1988 the company granted her a specially protected tenancy of a 65.08 m² flat in the Zagreb suburbs for occupation with her husband and two daughters. Because the decision was not yet final, an agreement of 7 December 1988 permitted the family to move in and care for the premises. They have lived there continuously ever since.

The 1988 allocation was challenged by three co-workers and quashed by the Zagreb Basic Court of Associated Labour. On 27 March 1990 the company’s housing committee placed the applicant first on a new priority list for flat distribution; the workers’ council approved the list on 23 April 1990, entitling her to an allocation decision. Two other employees immediately challenged the list in court. After competence passed to the Zagreb Municipal Court, the claims were dismissed on the merits in 1999 (later amended to inadmissibility in 2004) on the ground that a priority list, unlike an allocation decision, was not open to judicial challenge.

Meanwhile, on 3 June 1991 Parliament enacted the Protected Tenancies (Sale to Occupier) Act, which abolished specially protected tenancies and entitled their holders to purchase the flats under favourable conditions. On 27 April 1992 the flats of company S. were transferred to the management of Zagreb Municipality (later the City of Zagreb). On 29 November 1995 the applicant applied to the municipality to buy the flat; no decision was issued within the statutory sixty-day period. She reapplied in 2005 and was refused on 6 July 2005 because she had never been formally granted a specially protected tenancy.

She then brought a civil action seeking a judgment in lieu of a sale contract. The Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed the claim on 18 June 2007, holding that a priority list did not constitute an allocation decision under the Housing Act. The Zagreb County Court upheld that reasoning on 8 April 2008, stressing the absence of a final allocation decision. The applicant’s subsequent constitutional complaint argued that she had been first on the approved list, that the only obstacles had been the co-workers’ challenge and the ensuing court delays, and that once those proceedings ended all conditions for recognition of her tenancy had been met. She also invoked Constitutional Court decisions protecting similarly situated occupants. On 11 May 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, confirming that she had never acquired a specially protected tenancy and distinguishing the earlier cases as concerning persons who had held and later lost such tenancies.

Domestic law provided that a specially protected tenancy was acquired upon moving in pursuant to a final allocation decision or other valid legal basis (Housing Act, s. 59). Supreme Court practice recognised de-facto holders who occupied premises for years with the provider’s knowledge and fulfilled all tenant obligations, even without a written title. Constitutional Court jurisprudence emphasised the Sale to Occupier Act’s purpose of facilitating purchase by lawful long-term occupants and required interpretation in light of social justice and the inviolability of property, rather than mechanical application of formal requirements.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that she possessed a legitimate expectation amounting to a “possession” that the domestic authorities had arbitrarily denied.

The case of Bikić v. Croatia (Application no. 50101/12) concerns Croatian national Ivanka Bikić (born 1954), who alleged that the authorities’ refusal to allow her to purchase the socially owned flat she had occupied since 1988 violated her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

Under the former Yugoslav socialist system, employees contributed a portion of their salaries (3% in the applicant’s case) to housing funds used to construct and allocate flats. Recipients obtained specially protected tenancies (SPTs), after which their names were removed from allocation lists as their housing needs were deemed met. The applicant, employed by socially owned company S., was granted an SPT on 31 October 1988 for a 65.08 m² Zagreb suburban flat, to be occupied with her husband and two daughters. As the grant was not yet final, company S. entered a 7 December 1988 agreement permitting her family to move in and maintain the flat. She has resided there continuously since.

The 1988 grant was challenged by three co-workers and quashed. On 27 March 1990 company S.’s housing committee placed the applicant first on a new priority list for flat distribution; the workers’ council approved it on 23 April 1990, entitling her to an allocation decision. Two other employees challenged the list in May 1990. After competence transferred to the Zagreb Municipal Court, that court dismissed the actions on 3 February 1999 (holding that a priority list, unlike an allocation decision, could not be challenged). The Zagreb County Court amended the ruling on 23 June 2004 to declare the actions inadmissible on the same ground. Meanwhile, the company’s flats were transferred to Zagreb Municipality management on 27 April 1992.

On 3 June 1991 Parliament enacted the Protected Tenancies (Sale to Occupier) Act, abolishing SPTs and entitling holders of SPTs over socially owned flats to purchase them on favourable terms. Applications had to be submitted by 31 December 1995; owners were obliged to conclude sale contracts within 60 days, failing which tenants could seek a court judgment in lieu of contract.

The applicant applied to purchase on 29 November 1995; the Municipality issued no decision. She reapplied in 2005 and was refused on 6 July 2005 for lack of an SPT. She sued the City of Zagreb (now owner) on 26 September 2005 for a judgment substituting a sale contract. The Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed the claim on 18 June 2007, finding that the priority list was not a “final decision allocating the flat” or other valid legal basis under section 59 of the Housing Act, so no SPT had been acquired upon moving in. The Zagreb County Court upheld this on 8 April 2008, stressing the absence of a final allocation decision.

In her constitutional complaint the applicant invoked equality before the law, the right of appeal and fair trial. She argued that, as first on the 1990 list, she would have received a formal SPT but for co-workers’ challenges and the ensuing decade-long court delay. Once those proceedings ended, all conditions were fulfilled; the list’s one-year validity ran from its judicial confirmation. Denial of purchase rights under favourable conditions therefore violated her rights. She cited Constitutional Court decisions protecting similarly situated persons.

On 11 May 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, confirming that no SPT had been acquired and distinguishing the cited cases (which involved persons who had held, then lost, SPTs).

Relevant domestic law included Housing Act section 59 (SPT arises on moving in pursuant to a final allocation or other valid basis); the Sale to Occupier Act (obliging sale to SPT holders); and the 1996 Lease of Flats Act (abolishing remaining SPTs while preserving certain pending purchase rights). Supreme Court case-law treated long-term occupancy with the provider’s knowledge and fulfilment of tenant obligations as conferring SPT status even without a written title. Constitutional Court jurisprudence emphasised the Sale Act’s purpose of enabling lawful occupants to acquire ownership, requiring interpretation in light of social justice, human rights and inviolability of property rather than purely mechanical application of the old Housing Act, especially where delays were not the occupant’s fault.

The case of Bikić v. Croatia (application no. 50101/12) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Ivanka Bikić, a Croatian national born in 1954 and resident in Zagreb, complained that the domestic authorities’ refusal to allow her to purchase the socially owned flat she had occupied since 1988 deprived her of a legitimate expectation to acquire ownership on favourable terms.

Under the former Yugoslav socialist housing system, employees of publicly owned companies contributed a portion of their salaries (in the applicant’s case, 3 per cent) to housing funds used to construct or allocate flats. Recipients obtained “specially protected tenancies” (SPTs), which conferred strong occupancy rights and, after 1991, a statutory entitlement to buy the flat at a discount. On 31 October 1988 the applicant’s employer, company S., issued a decision granting her an SPT over a 65.08 m² suburban Zagreb flat for herself, her husband and two daughters. Because the decision was not yet final, an interim agreement of 7 December 1988 authorised her to move in and maintain the premises. She has resided there continuously ever since.

Three co-workers successfully challenged the 1988 allocation; it was quashed. In March–April 1990 the company’s housing committee and workers’ council adopted a new priority list on which the applicant ranked first, thereby entitling her to a formal allocation decision. Two further employees then sued to annul the list. After competence was transferred to the Zagreb Municipal Court, those actions were dismissed on the merits in 1999 and declared inadmissible in 2004 on the ground that a priority list, unlike an allocation decision, was not judicially reviewable. Meanwhile, on 27 April 1992 the flats were transferred to Zagreb Municipality (later the City of Zagreb).

The Protected Tenancies (Sale to Occupier) Act of 3 June 1991 abolished SPTs and conferred on existing SPT holders an enforceable right to purchase their flats. On 29 November 1995 the applicant applied to buy the flat; the municipality failed to respond within the statutory 60-day period. A renewed application in 2005 was rejected because she lacked a final SPT decision. She then brought a civil action seeking a court judgment in lieu of a sale contract. The Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed the claim on 18 June 2007, holding that a priority list did not constitute the “final decision allocating the flat” required by section 59 of the Housing Act. The Zagreb County Court upheld that reasoning on 8 April 2008. The Constitutional Court rejected her complaint on 11 May 2012, confirming that she had never acquired an SPT and distinguishing earlier cases in which occupants had already held, then lost, such tenancies.

The applicant maintained that the only reason she never received a formal allocation was the protracted, ultimately unsuccessful challenges by co-workers and the courts’ delay. Once those proceedings ended, all conditions for an SPT were fulfilled; the one-year validity of the priority list should run from the date of judicial confirmation. She relied on Supreme Court case-law treating long-term occupiers who fulfil tenant obligations as de-facto SPT holders even without written title, and on Constitutional Court rulings emphasising the Sale Act’s purpose of enabling lawful users to acquire ownership in light of social justice and transitional difficulties rather than mechanical application of formal requirements.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference: the applicant’s long, unchallenged occupation, her first-place ranking on an officially approved list, her financial contributions, and the legislative scheme that converted SPTs into purchase rights, all of which she argued generated a legitimate expectation that was frustrated by the authorities’ insistence on a missing formal decision whose absence was not attributable to her.
001-183788:
The case of Dimitrov and Momin v. Bulgaria (no. 35132/08) arose from an application by two Bulgarian nationals, Dimitar Angelov Dimitrov (born 1965) and Ventseslav Tobiev Momin (born 1964), both residing in Plovdiv. They alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention, claiming they had been convicted of abducting, falsely imprisoning and raping S.D. solely or primarily on the basis of her statements, without ever having the opportunity to examine her.

On 14 March 1998 S.D., aged 26, reported to Plovdiv police that the applicants had abducted her the previous day, held her captive in premises being refurbished in the city centre, ill-treated her and raped her. A medical examination the same day recorded bruises on her head, neck, arms and knees but found no conclusive physical or biological evidence of sexual intercourse. Questioned by an investigator, S.D. repeated her account of being forced into the premises and raped. On 18 March 1998 she withdrew the statement, citing a desire for peace, ill-health and personal problems. The applicants were then questioned as witnesses: Momin denied any sexual contact and said they had merely accompanied S.D. to a café and then home; Dimitrov admitted consensual sex with her while Momin fetched coffee, after which they all left by taxi.

In January 1999 S.D. again described the encounter as consensual, explaining that she had originally complained under family pressure and out of revenge after Dimitrov admitted he was married. In April 2000, while undergoing chemotherapy, she wrote to prosecutor I.P. reiterating her wish to withdraw the complaint. Nevertheless I.P. formally charged Dimitrov with rape in May 2000. On 19 December 2000 a judge of the Plovdiv District Court, acting under Article 210a of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure (which permitted judicial questioning of a witness of special importance who might be unable to attend trial because of serious illness), heard S.D. in the prosecutor’s presence. Dimitrov had been notified by letter from the police but did not attend; Momin had not yet been charged. S.D. now reverted to her original version of abduction, blows, a hypoglycaemic episode and non-consensual sex with both men. She attributed her earlier retractions to threats from Dimitrov and persons close to the applicants, including a lawyer who had induced her to sign a withdrawal letter.

Both applicants were charged in April 2001 with abduction, false imprisonment, death threats and rape. Their counsel’s request for individual confrontations with S.D. was refused as unnecessary. S.D. died of cancer on 25 June 2001.

At the first-instance trial (2004–2007) the District Court admitted and read out the 19 December 2000 record. It heard the applicants, police officers who had received the initial complaint, relatives and other witnesses, together with medical expert evidence. It convicted only Dimitrov of rape (three-year suspended sentence) and acquitted him of the remaining charges and Momin of all charges. The court found that non-consensual intercourse with Dimitrov was the only fact reliably established; it rejected the rest of S.D.’s account because it had been unable to examine her, her story had changed, two years had elapsed, and the statement contradicted other evidence and the medical findings.

On appeal the Regional Court (June–July 2007) reversed the acquittals, convicted both men of all offences and imposed sentences of six and five-and-a-half years. In a lengthy judgment it accepted S.D.’s 19 December 2000 statement in its entirety as coherent, detailed and consistent with the police officers’ observations of her condition, the medical and site-inspection evidence, and other supporting material. It attributed her changing accounts to pressure from the applicants and rejected defence attempts to portray her as morally unreliable. The Supreme Court of Cassation (January 2008) upheld the convictions (reducing the sentences to five and four years). It held that Dimitrov’s right to participate in the 2000 questioning had not been violated because he had been informed, while Momin, still uncharged, had had no such right. The Regional Court had properly tested the statement’s credibility against the remainder of the evidence; the statement was “an important element, but not the only element” against Dimitrov and “the main evidence” against Momin.

Article 210a required the investigator or prosecutor to enable the accused and counsel to take part in such judicial questioning; Article 279 permitted a deceased witness’s earlier judicial statement to be read at trial. These provisions formed the domestic legal framework against which the applicants’ inability to examine S.D. fell to be assessed.

The case originated in an application lodged on 4 July 2008 by two Bulgarian nationals, Dimitar Angelov Dimitrov (born 1965) and Ventseslav Tobiev Momin (born 1964), both resident in Plovdiv. Represented by counsel, they complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that their convictions rested on statements of the alleged victim, S.D., whom they had never been able to examine.

On 14 March 1998 S.D., aged 26, reported to Plovdiv police that the applicants had abducted, confined and raped her the previous day. A medical examination the same day recorded bruises on her head, neck, arms and knees but no conclusive biological evidence of intercourse. When first questioned she described being forced into premises in the city centre and assaulted. Four days later she withdrew the complaint, citing personal problems. The applicants, questioned as witnesses, denied any rape: Dimitrov admitted consensual sex while Momin was absent buying coffee; Momin denied sexual contact altogether.

In January 1999 S.D. repeated that the encounter had been consensual and that she had complained only under family pressure and out of revenge after learning Dimitrov was married. The investigator recommended discontinuance, but further inquiries were ordered. In April 2000 S.D., then undergoing chemotherapy, wrote to the prosecutor reiterating her withdrawal. Dimitrov was nevertheless charged with rape in May 2000.

On 18 December 2000 the prosecutor applied under Article 210a of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure for a judge to question S.D., whose evidence was of special importance and who risked being unable to attend trial because of serious illness. The following morning a district-court judge heard her in the prosecutor’s presence. Dimitrov had been notified by a police letter; Momin had not yet been charged and therefore had no right to attend. S.D. now reverted to her original account of abduction, blows, hypoglycaemia and non-consensual intercourse with both men. She explained her earlier retractions as the result of threats from the applicants and their associates, including a visit by a lawyer who induced her to sign a withdrawal letter.

Both applicants were charged in April 2001 with abduction, false imprisonment, death threats and rape. Their lawyer’s request for confrontations with S.D. was refused as unnecessary. S.D. died of cancer on 25 June 2001.

At first-instance trial (2004–2007) the 19 December 2000 record was read out. The District Court convicted only Dimitrov of rape (three-year suspended sentence) and acquitted Momin, noting that it had never seen S.D., that her accounts had fluctuated, and that other evidence was inconsistent with parts of her testimony.

On appeal the Regional Court, after commissioning further medical expertise, convicted both men of all charges (six and five-and-a-half years respectively). It accepted S.D.’s 19 December statement in full as coherent, detailed and corroborated by police officers who had seen her the day after the events, by medical findings and by the crime-scene inspection. It attributed her earlier changes of story to intimidation and rejected defence attacks on her character.

The Supreme Court of Cassation (January 2008) upheld the convictions (reducing the sentences to five and four years). It held that Dimitrov, though still without counsel, had been notified and could have attended the 2000 hearing, while Momin had no standing because he was not yet an accused. The statement, though “the main evidence” against Momin and an “important element” against Dimitrov, had been tested against the remainder of the file and was therefore admissible.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ complaint that they were denied an effective opportunity to examine the sole or decisive witness against them.

The case of Dimitrov and Momin v. Bulgaria (Application no. 35132/08) originated in a complaint lodged on 4 July 2008 by two Bulgarian nationals, Dimitar Angelov Dimitrov (born 1965) and Ventseslav Tobiev Momin (born 1964), both residing in Plovdiv. Represented by lawyer Y. Vandova, they alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights, claiming conviction based on statements from the victim, S.D., whom they never had the opportunity to examine.

On 14 March 1998, 26-year-old S.D. reported to Plovdiv police that the applicants had abducted, imprisoned, and raped her the previous day. A medical examination revealed bruises on her head, neck, arms, and knees but no conclusive evidence of sexual intercourse. S.D. initially described being forced into premises in Plovdiv city centre, ill-treated, and raped. On 18 March 1998, she withdrew her statement, citing a desire for peace, illness, and personal problems. The applicants, questioned as witnesses, denied rape: Momin stated they had coffee together and returned S.D. home; Dimitrov admitted consensual sex with S.D. (with whom he had a prior intimate relationship) while Momin fetched coffee.

In January 1999, S.D. recanted further, claiming consensual sex with Dimitrov and that she filed the complaint under family pressure for revenge after learning he was married. The investigator recommended discontinuing proceedings, but further inquiries followed. In April 2000, S.D. wrote to prosecutor I.P., reiterating her withdrawal, requesting discontinuation, and noting her cancer and chemotherapy. Dimitrov was charged with rape in May 2000.

On 19 December 2000, pursuant to Article 210a § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (allowing judicial questioning of a witness at risk of non-appearance due to serious illness, with provision for the accused's participation), a Plovdiv District Court judge questioned S.D. in the prosecutor's presence. Dimitrov was notified via a police letter. S.D. reverted to her original account: Dimitrov forcibly took her from home into a taxi with the intoxicated Momin; they entered refurbished premises, where Dimitrov assaulted her, causing hypoglycaemia treated with sugar; she was then raped twice by Dimitrov and once by Momin. She attributed her withdrawals to threats from Dimitrov and associates, including a lawyer who induced her to sign a retraction letter. She confirmed feeling well despite cancer.

Both applicants were charged on 20 April 2001 with abduction, false imprisonment, death threats, and rape. Their counsel's request for confrontations with S.D. was rejected on 2 July 2001 as unnecessary. S.D. died of cancer on 25 June 2001.

The Plovdiv District Court (2004–2007) admitted and read S.D.'s 19 December 2000 statement. It convicted Dimitrov of rape (suspended three-year sentence) but acquitted him of other charges and fully acquitted Momin, relying only partly on S.D.'s evidence due to inconsistencies, her unavailability for examination, delayed statement, and contradictions with medical findings and other witnesses.

On appeal, the Plovdiv Regional Court (June–July 2007) convicted both of all charges (six and 5.5 years' imprisonment), fully accepting S.D.'s statement as coherent, logical, detailed, and consistent with police observations, medical evidence, site inspections, and other testimony. It attributed recantations to threats and rejected defence efforts to discredit S.D.

The Supreme Court of Cassation (7 January 2008) upheld the convictions (reducing sentences to five and four years), finding no breach of confrontation rights: Dimitrov, though unrepresented, had been notified and could participate; Momin, uncharged then, had no such right. It deemed the statement important (but not sole) evidence against Dimitrov and main evidence against Momin, its credibility verified against other materials. Domestic law (Articles 210a and 279) permitted reading such statements if the witness later died.

The case of Niță v. Romania (Application no. 30305/16) concerns a father’s unsuccessful attempts to enforce court-ordered contact with his daughter after divorce. The applicant, Ion Niță (born 1970), married N.E.C. in 1993; their daughter M.A. was born in 2001. After the 2007 divorce, the mother received physical custody. The parents initially agreed on contact, so visiting rights were not litigated. Until December 2009 the applicant enjoyed unrestricted telephone contact and visits. Thereafter the mother ceased answering calls, leaving only chance encounters outside school.

In July 2011 the applicant commenced contact proceedings. A December 2011 visiting schedule was later modified by parental agreement. In May 2012 the County Court interviewed the then-eleven-year-old child, who stated that her mother had recently forbidden telephone contact and that she did not wish to visit her father because it would upset her mother; she also recounted negative stories her mother had told about the applicant’s business rivalry. The June 2012 contact order, upheld by the Court of Appeal in November 2012, directed that visits take place at the father’s home, finding this necessary to counteract possible alienation and to preserve the child’s psychological development.

Enforcement began in March 2013 through a bailiff. Repeated summonses and home visits (April–June 2013 and March 2014), conducted with police and child-protection officials, found no one present despite prior notice. The mother consistently refused to produce the child, citing the child’s alleged refusal. In June 2013 the District Court imposed a daily penalty of RON 500 (approx. EUR 115) on the mother, holding her solely responsible and finding no evidence of absolute refusal by the child. An additional fine for obstructing enforcement followed in August 2013. In August 2014 the bailiff terminated proceedings as “objectively impossible” and lodged a criminal complaint. The applicant’s objections were dismissed; courts held that the bailiff had correctly stayed enforcement once the prosecutor took over. A 2014 damages award of RON 9 200 against the mother remained uncollectible after she disposed of her assets.

Requests to the child-protection authority for psychological counselling of the daughter (January 2015) were refused because the bailiff had not recorded “absolute opposition.” Subsequent monitoring visits were blocked by the mother, who would not allow officials to speak with the child. The authority advised gradual re-contact and improved parental communication, noting the mother’s opposition.

The criminal investigation, reclassified as breach of custody measures, included a January 2016 interview of the child (in her mother’s lawyer’s presence) in which she again refused contact, attributing the father’s actions to a desire to harm her mother. A April 2016 psychological assessment concluded that counselling the child would not help and recommended support only for the parents. The prosecutor discontinued the case in February 2017, finding the child’s unequivocal will, not proven maternal obstruction, to be the cause. After the applicant’s complaint, a District Court in October 2017 quashed that decision and ordered further inquiry into possible parental-alienation syndrome.

Further private attempts at contact in 2016–2017 likewise failed. Domestic law provided a graduated enforcement regime (daily penalties, possible criminal prosecution, limited counselling) but no physical coercion of the child. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the authorities had failed to take effective measures to secure his parental rights.

The case of Niță v. Romania (Application no. 30305/16) concerns a Romanian father's unsuccessful efforts to maintain contact with his daughter after divorce. The applicant, Ion Niță (born 1970), married N.E.C. in 1993; their daughter M.A. was born in 2001. After the couple divorced in February 2007, the mother obtained physical custody. An informal agreement initially permitted the applicant unhindered telephone contact and visits. From December 2009, however, the mother ceased answering calls, leaving the applicant able to see the child only outside her school.

In July 2011 the applicant brought contact proceedings. A first-instance visiting schedule was set in December 2011. On appeal the parties reached an agreement. After interviewing the then 11-year-old child in May 2012 (who stated that her mother no longer allowed telephone contact and that she herself did not wish to visit her father for fear of upsetting her mother), the County Court issued a contact order on 15 June 2012 providing for visits at the father's home. The Court of Appeal upheld the order in November 2012, stressing the need to consolidate the father-child relationship and to prevent the inculcation of hostility.

When the mother continued to obstruct contact, the applicant initiated enforcement through a bailiff in March 2013. The competent court authorised enforcement. Repeated summonses, home visits (accompanied by police and child-protection officials) and notifications produced no result; the mother and child were consistently absent. In June 2013 the court imposed a daily penalty of 500 RON (approximately EUR 115) for non-compliance and later a further small fine for obstruction. In August 2014 the bailiff terminated enforcement as “objectively impossible” and lodged a criminal complaint against the mother. Domestic courts subsequently dismissed the applicant’s objections, holding that enforcement had become impossible and that the stay pending criminal proceedings was lawful. A later quantification of pecuniary penalties (RON 9 200) proved unenforceable because the mother had disposed of her assets.

The applicant also asked the child-protection authority to seek court-ordered psychological counselling for the child and to monitor the family. The authority declined, citing the absence of an “absolute refusal” by the child in the bailiff’s reports, and later reported that the mother had refused even to allow officials to speak with the child. It recommended gradual re-engagement and improved parental communication rather than further litigation.

A criminal investigation opened in 2014 for failure to respect a court judgment (later reclassified as breach of custody measures). In 2016 the child, interviewed in the presence of the mother’s lawyer and a psychologist, reiterated her refusal to see her father, attributing his actions to a desire to harm her mother because of business disputes. Psychologists likewise recorded the child’s disappointment with the father’s use of official channels and recommended counselling for the parents rather than the child. In February 2017 the prosecutor discontinued the case, finding that the child’s own wishes, rather than proven parental obstruction, explained the lack of contact. After the applicant’s complaint, a district court in October 2017 quashed that decision and remitted the file for further psychological examination of possible parental-alienation syndrome.

Further attempts by a new bailiff in 2016–2017 likewise failed. Throughout, the domestic authorities imposed limited financial sanctions, conducted several unsuccessful enforcement visits and interviews, yet never secured actual contact or addressed the mother’s influence over the child. These protracted, ineffective measures form the core factual basis of the applicant’s complaint that the State failed to take adequate and timely steps to protect his right to family life.

The case of Niță v. Romania (Application no. 30305/16) concerns a father’s unsuccessful attempts to enforce court-ordered contact with his daughter after divorce, implicating Romania’s positive obligations under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life).

Applicant Ion Niță (born 1970) married N.E.C. in 1993; their daughter M.A. was born in 2001. The couple divorced on 28 February 2007, with the mother granted physical custody. An informal agreement allowed the applicant unhindered telephone contact and visits until December 2009, after which the mother ceased responding and restricted access to encounters outside the child’s school.

On 7 July 2011 the applicant sought a formal visiting schedule. The Râmnicu-Vâlcea District Court established one on 16 December 2011. After the mother’s appeal, the parties reached an agreement; on 15 June 2012 the County Court (the “contact order”) endorsed visits at the applicant’s home as beneficial to the child. The Pitești Court of Appeal upheld this on 19 November 2012, noting the child’s prior visits and the risk that maternal influence might instil hatred toward the father, contrary to the child’s psychological development. An interview with M.A. (then aged about 11) revealed she had stopped answering calls because her mother forbade it, viewed her father negatively based on maternal accounts of business disputes, and refused visits to avoid upsetting her mother.

Enforcement began on 13 March 2013 via a bailiff after the mother continued to obstruct contact. The Brezoi District Court authorised enforcement on 23 March 2013. Repeated attempts (5 April, 3 May, 7 June 2013 and 7 March 2014) failed: the mother ignored invitations, and visits to her home with police and child-protection officials found no one present. On 20 June 2013 the court imposed a daily penalty of 500 RON (approx. EUR 115) for non-compliance, attributing the failure solely to the mother rather than any absolute refusal by the child. A further fine of 100 RON was imposed on 21 August 2013 for obstructing proceedings.

On 18 August 2014 the bailiff terminated enforcement as “objectively impossible” and lodged a criminal complaint. The applicant’s objections were dismissed (22 May 2015 and 22 March 2016) on the ground that the child’s opposition rendered execution impossible. A damages award of 9,200 RON (approx. EUR 2,100) under Article 905 CCP proved unenforceable after the mother disposed of her assets.

Requests to the child-protection authority in January 2015 for three months of psychological counselling and monitoring were refused because the bailiff had not recorded “absolute” opposition by the child (Article 912 CCP). Inspectors met the mother four times but were denied access to the child; they advised gradual reconnection while noting the mother’s refusal to cooperate.

Criminal proceedings for non-compliance with a court order (later reclassified as breach of custody measures) included a 4 January 2016 interview in which M.A. (now 14–15) refused contact, attributing her father’s actions to a desire to harm her mother over work disputes. A 22 April 2016 psychological assessment found the child disappointed by the applicant’s use of authorities and recommended counselling for the parents rather than the child. The prosecutor terminated the investigation on 24 February 2017, citing the child’s unequivocal will. On 3 October 2017 the District Court quashed that decision, finding possible parental-alienation syndrome amounting to psychological abuse and ordering further psychological inquiry.

Further informal attempts in 2016–2017 via a new bailiff likewise failed. The facts thus centre on prolonged, unsuccessful enforcement of a final contact order amid maternal obstruction and the child’s progressive alienation, raising questions as to the adequacy of the domestic authorities’ measures.
001-184058:
The case of Telbis and Viziteu v. Romania (Application no. 47911/15) concerns three Romanian applicants—Luminița Telbis (S.T.’s wife), Laura Andreea Telbis (his daughter) and Maria Agata Viziteu (his niece)—who complained that domestic confiscation proceedings were unfair and unlawfully deprived them of property, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

On 13 March 2014 a criminal investigation was opened against S.T., a State pension-office doctor, for bribe-taking. A search of the family home (conducted in the first applicant’s presence) led to the seizure of documents, cash (including EUR 107 915) and other assets. By decision of 17 March 2014 the prosecutor ordered preventive seizure, under Article 249 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, of movable and immovable property belonging to S.T. and the first applicant, as well as items belonging to the second applicant, with a view to possible special or extended confiscation under Articles 112 and 112¹ of the Criminal Code. The second applicant, represented by lawyers, unsuccessfully challenged the seizure before the Caraş-Severin County Court, which held that the measure could be applied to third-party assets and that she had failed to prove independent lawful income.

S.T. was indicted on 291 counts of bribe-taking committed between February and March 2014. He admitted guilt and was convicted by the Arad County Court on 6 November 2014 to the minimum sentence of three years’ imprisonment. The court ordered special confiscation of the bribes themselves and, applying the extended-confiscation provisions of Article 112¹, confiscation of further assets (cash equivalent to EUR 124 000, a dental practice, a flat and a vehicle owned jointly with the first applicant, plus a flat and two vehicles registered to the second applicant). It reasoned that the family’s declared lawful income (approximately EUR 35 000 per year) could not explain assets worth some EUR 300 000 acquired in the preceding five years. Assets acquired before April 2012 were excluded in accordance with Constitutional Court Decision no. 356/2014.

All three applicants appealed. They submitted an accountant’s report showing net family income of EUR 281 071 between 1991 and 2014, sale contracts and a relative’s written statement that money had been lent to the second applicant. The third applicant claimed that EUR 40 400 found in cash belonged to her from the 2013 sale of a jointly owned flat that she had asked S.T. to hold. At the 16 March 2015 hearing their lawyer requested a further witness and a new forensic accountant’s report to quantify the precise discrepancy after family expenses; both requests were refused on the ground that the existing file already permitted an accurate calculation and that the applicants had had sufficient time to prepare their defence. Written pleadings also complained that the second applicant had never been summoned at first instance.

On 24 March 2015 the Timişoara Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals. It inferred from the large number of proven bribes that S.T. had long engaged in the same conduct, noted a “considerable discrepancy” between lawful income and accumulated assets, and held that the applicants had failed to prove lawful origin. The second applicant, a student with no proven income, was found to have acquired her property with parental funds derived from crime. The third applicant’s claim was rejected for lack of supporting evidence. The court considered that the first-instance judgment had correctly applied the statutory criteria and had already lifted the seizure on pre-2012 assets.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints that they were denied a fair opportunity to contest the confiscation of assets they claimed to have acquired lawfully and that the resulting deprivation of property was therefore unlawful.

**Case Summary: Telbis and Viziteu v. Romania (Application no. 47911/15), ECtHR Fourth Section, Judgment of 26 June 2018 (final 26 September 2018)**

The three applicants—Luminița Telbis (wife of S.T.), Laura Andreea Telbis (his daughter), and Maria Agata Viziteu (his niece)—alleged that Romanian court proceedings leading to confiscation of their property were unfair (Article 6 § 1 of the Convention) and that they were unlawfully deprived of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1). S.T., a public pension-office doctor, was investigated from 13 March 2014 for bribe-taking. A search of the shared home of S.T. and the first applicant (in her presence with a lawyer) led to seizure of documents, cash (including EUR 107,915), and items belonging to the second applicant. On 17 March 2014 the prosecutor ordered seizure of movable and immovable assets of S.T. and the first applicant (and some of the second applicant) under Criminal Procedure Code Article 249 for later special/extended confiscation, citing the nature of the offences, damage recovery, and possible money-laundering.

The second applicant challenged the seizure, arguing it applied only to a suspect/accused and that her flats, garages and cars were lawfully bought with family loans. The Caraş-Severin County Court (10 April 2014) upheld the measure: Article 249 § 4 permitted seizure of assets held by any person, she had not proved independent income or purchase with her own funds, and money-laundering suspicions existed. S.T. was later indicted on 291 counts of bribe-taking (February–March 2014).

At first instance the Arad County Court (6 November 2014) accepted S.T.’s guilty plea, imposed a three-year sentence, and confiscated the actual bribes plus, under Criminal Code Article 112^{1} (extended confiscation for corruption offences capable of generating gain), further assets jointly owned by S.T. and the first applicant (cash equivalent to EUR 124,000, a dental practice, a flat and a vehicle) and assets of the second applicant (a flat and two vehicles). The court found the family’s lawful income (circa EUR 35,000 per year) could not explain assets worth the equivalent of EUR 300,000 plus multiple properties acquired in the preceding five years; the second applicant, a student, had no income. Following Constitutional Court Decision no. 356/2014, confiscation was limited to post-April 2012 acquisitions and some earlier seizures were lifted. S.T. had argued family assets came from 2007/2013 real-estate deals (including a EUR 40,400 flat sale involving the third applicant) and that the prosecution had not proved illicit origin.

All applicants appealed. The third applicant claimed the EUR 40,400 cash found in the search belonged to her (proceeds of her 2013 flat sale, entrusted to S.T.). They submitted an accountant’s report calculating the couple’s 1991–2014 salary income at EUR 281,071, sale contracts and a family-loan statement. At the 16 March 2015 hearing their lawyer sought a further witness (another alleged lender) and a new accountant’s report comparing income, expenses and confiscated-property value. The Timişoara Court of Appeal refused both requests, holding that the file already permitted exact calculation of income and assets and that the applicants had had sufficient time to prepare. It dismissed the appeals on 24 March 2015. The court inferred from the scale of S.T.’s admitted offences that bribe-taking was habitual and pre-dated the investigation period; the family’s recent accumulation of assets far exceeded documented lawful income (even allowing for the first applicant’s salary and real-estate earnings); the second applicant had never shown any income or proven family donations; and no evidence established that the EUR 40,400 belonged to the third applicant. Extended confiscation was therefore lawful. The applicants complained they had not been summoned at first instance, had been denied adequate opportunity to prove lawful origin, and that the measure was disproportionate.
