The case of Telbis and Viziteu v. Romania (Application no. 47911/15) involves three Romanian applicants—Luminița Telbis (first applicant, wife of S.T.), Laura Andreea Telbis (second applicant, daughter of S.T.), and Maria Agata Viziteu (third applicant, niece of S.T.)—who alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) arising from confiscation proceedings linked to S.T.’s criminal conviction.

On 13 March 2014, prosecutors opened a bribe-taking investigation against S.T., a state pension office doctor. A search of the shared residence of S.T. and the first applicant (conducted in her and her lawyer’s presence) led to seizure of documents, cash (including EUR 107,915 plus other currencies), and items belonging to the second applicant. The first applicant objected on-site that some assets were unrelated to the probe. On 17 March 2014, the prosecutor formally seized these and other movable/immovable assets of S.T. and the first applicant (plus the second applicant’s property) under Article 249 of the Criminal Procedure Code, pending special or extended confiscation under Criminal Code Articles 112 and 112^{1}. The decision cited the nature of the suspected offences, the need to recover damages, and possible money-laundering.

S.T. received the seizure decision on 19 March without objection. The second applicant, informed on 20 March, challenged it on 25 March before the Caraș-Severin County Court, arguing that seizure for confiscation could apply only to a suspect’s assets and that her two flats, two garages and two cars had been lawfully purchased with family loans (supported by contracts and a family statement). On 10 April 2014 the court rejected the complaint with final effect, holding that Article 249 § 4 expressly permitted seizure of assets held by any person, that the second applicant had not proved personal income or independent purchase, and that money-laundering suspicions justified the measure.

S.T. was indicted on 26 May 2014 on 291 counts of bribe-taking committed between 3 February and 13 March 2014. He admitted guilt before the Arad County Court and received a three-year prison sentence (the minimum). The court confiscated the bribes themselves under Article 289 § 3 of the Criminal Code. Invoking Article 112^{1} (extended confiscation for corruption offences generating financial gain), it also confiscated additional assets acquired as a result of S.T.’s criminal activity: cash equivalent to EUR 124,000, a dental practice, a flat and a vehicle owned jointly by S.T. and the first applicant, plus a flat and two vehicles belonging to the second applicant. The court found that the family’s total assets (approximately EUR 300,000 in cash/bank accounts, 15 flats/plots, five garages and four vehicles) grossly exceeded their combined lawful annual income of about EUR 35,000 over the preceding five years. Following Constitutional Court Decision no. 356/2014 (non-retroactivity), confiscation was limited to assets acquired after April 2012; earlier seizures were lifted. The second applicant, a student with no income, was held to have acquired her property through her parents.

All applicants and S.T. appealed to the Timișoara Court of Appeal. They filed an accountant’s report calculating EUR 281,071 net family income from 1991–2014, numerous sale contracts, and a family loan statement. The third applicant asserted that EUR 40,400 found during the search (from the 2013 sale of a jointly owned flat) belonged to her and had been entrusted to S.T. At the 16 March 2015 hearing the applicants’ lawyer sought a further witness on a loan to the second applicant and an additional accounting report incorporating family expenses; both requests were refused because the file already contained sufficient material and the applicants had had adequate time to prepare. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals on 24 March 2015. It inferred from the volume of S.T.’s offences that bribe-taking had been habitual and possibly longer-standing. A National Integrity Agency report confirmed a large income-asset discrepancy. The court held that S.T. and the applicants had failed to prove lawful acquisition; the first applicant’s salary and any real-estate earnings were insufficient, the second applicant had no income and her donation claims were unproven, and the third applicant had produced no evidence that the EUR 40,400 was hers.

The applicants contended that the confiscation proceedings were unfair (they were not accused of any crime, the second applicant had not been summoned at first instance, and their evidence requests were rejected) and that they had been unlawfully deprived of lawfully acquired property.
001-183127:
The case of Devinar v. Slovenia (Application no. 28621/15) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 ECHR (right to a fair trial) arising from Slovenian social-security proceedings. The applicant, Verena Devinar (born 1959), a former cleaning lady, developed serious left-wrist complications that surgery only partly resolved. Overuse of her right arm produced further medical problems. In 2006 she was declared incapable of work and granted partial-disability status.

On 30 December 2011 she applied to the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute for a disability allowance in respect of physical impairment (defined by statute as loss, severe injury or significant incapacity of organs that inhibits normal bodily function and requires greater effort for vital tasks). Entitlement turns on whether the condition appears on an official List of Physical Impairments originally adopted in 1983 and last amended in 1989.

The Institute’s first-instance disability commission (an occupational-medicine specialist, an orthopaedic specialist and a rehabilitation physician) examined the applicant’s records and conducted a clinical examination. It reported that she suffered none of the listed impairments. The Institute rejected the claim on 15 March 2012. On appeal a second-instance commission (occupational-medicine and orthopaedic specialists) reviewed the file and reached the same conclusion; the Institute dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2012.

The applicant then brought a full-jurisdiction action before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court. She contended that the facts had been wrongly established and that her bilateral arm incapacity, together with psychological illness and headaches, inhibited normal functioning. She requested appointment of an independent medical expert, arguing that only such an expert could determine the precise degree of impairment (which she estimated at least 50 %). On 6 September 2013 a single judge dismissed the action. The court held that its role was merely to verify whether the administrative decisions complied with procedural rules, correctly established the facts and correctly applied the law. Relying on the two commission reports and its own observation of the applicant at the hearing, it found no qualifying physical impairment and refused the expert as unnecessary.

The Higher Labour and Social Court upheld the judgment on 6 February 2014. It considered the commissions’ opinions sufficiently convincing, given the medical documentation and examination reports, so that an independent expert was not required. Physical impairment, it emphasised, is legally distinct from recognised disability and must correspond exactly to the (outdated) List; mere functional difficulties without listed joint inflexibility do not suffice.

Leave to appeal on points of law was refused by the Supreme Court (10 June 2014). A constitutional complaint invoking equal protection of rights and the right to judicial protection was not accepted for consideration (10 December 2014).

The commissions are expert bodies of the Institute itself: their members are appointed by the Institute’s management board, some are Institute employees, and they operate under Institute rules and guidelines. Domestic case-law (including a 2006 Supreme Court decision) had already indicated that such opinions cannot be treated as impartial expert evidence once the Institute becomes a party to court proceedings. The applicant’s central complaint is therefore that the courts’ refusal to appoint an independent medical expert, while treating the Institute’s own commissions as decisive, deprived her of any effective means of challenging the crucial medical findings and thereby violated equality of arms and the adversarial principle under Article 6.

The case of Devinar v. Slovenia (Application no. 28621/15) before the ECHR concerns the applicant’s claim that her right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention was violated. Ms Verena Devinar, a Slovenian national born in 1959 and living in Nova Gorica, worked as a cleaning lady. She developed serious complications in her left wrist that surgery only partly addressed. Overuse of her right arm then caused further medical problems. In 2006 she was found incapable of further work and recognised as having a partial disability.

On 30 December 2011 she applied to the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute for a disability allowance in respect of physical impairment. Under the Pensions and Invalidity Insurance Act, “physical impairment” means loss, severe injury or significant incapacity of organs that inhibits normal body function and requires greater effort for vital tasks. Entitlement also depends on the degree of severity. Qualifying impairments are listed in the Self-Management Agreement on the List of Physical Impairments (first adopted 1983, last amended 1989), which remains in force pending a new ministerial list. The List’s Chapter IV specifies certain functional disorders of the shoulder and wrist.

The Institute’s first-instance disability commission (an occupational-medicine specialist, an orthopaedic specialist and a physical-medicine physician) examined the applicant’s records and conducted a clinical examination. On 12 March 2012 it reported that she suffered from none of the impairments on the List. Relying on that opinion, the Institute’s Nova Gorica unit dismissed the application on 15 March 2012. The applicant appealed. The second-instance commission (an occupational-medicine specialist and an orthopaedic specialist) reviewed the file and reached the same conclusion. The Institute’s Central Office dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2012.

On 12 July 2012 the applicant sued the Institute before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court, seeking annulment of the decisions. She contended that the facts had been wrongly established and the procedure improperly conducted. Because of the incapacity of both arms, she said, her body’s functioning was inhibited and she needed greater effort for daily tasks. She claimed at least 50 % incapacity, a degree that only a medical expert could determine, and therefore asked the court to appoint one.

Sitting as a single judge, the court dismissed the claim on 6 September 2013. It described its role as checking whether the administrative decisions complied with procedural rules, correctly established the facts and correctly applied the law. After reviewing the file and hearing the applicant, it found the Institute’s fact-finding correct. Relying on the commissions’ reports and its own observation of the applicant, it concluded that her health problems did not amount to a statutory physical impairment. It therefore refused the request for an expert as unnecessary.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the List was outdated, that the court should not have relied on the disputed commission opinions or on its own non-medical assessment, that she could not have explained all her problems at the hearing, and that the court could not assess the flexibility of her arms. An independent expert was, in her view, the only effective way to challenge the Institute.

The Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal on 6 February 2014. It held that the facts had been sufficiently established and the law correctly applied. Appointing an expert would not have changed the result, because the commissions’ opinions were convincing in the light of the medical documentation and examination. Physical impairments could be recognised only if they appeared on the List; a recognised disability without the specified functional problems (such as joint inflexibility) was insufficient. The court was not obliged to appoint an independent expert when the commissions’ assessments already showed the Institute’s decisions to be well-founded.

The applicant sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, repeating that refusal of an expert and the court’s self-assessment without medical knowledge had denied her a fair trial and her only means of challenging the Institute. She noted that independent experts had frequently contradicted commission findings in other cases. The Supreme Court refused leave on 10 June 2014, finding no grounds for an appeal on points of law.

On 21 July 2014 she lodged a constitutional complaint. She criticised the Supreme Court’s lack of reasoning, reiterated that she could not fully explain her condition or have her arms properly assessed, and insisted that only an independent expert could have given her an effective defence. She invoked Articles 22 (equal protection of rights) and 23 (right to judicial protection) of the Constitution and again attacked reliance on the outdated List. On 10 December 2014 the Constitutional Court declined to accept the complaint, holding that it raised no important constitutional question and disclosed no human-rights violation with serious consequences for the applicant.

Disability commissions are expert bodies of the Institute that issue opinions on medical questions relevant to pension and disability rights. Their members are appointed by the Institute’s management board. Domestic case-law (Supreme Court 2006; Constitutional Court 2017) has treated such opinions as partisan rather than impartial once proceedings reach court, because the commissions belong to one of the parties. The applicant’s core complaint was therefore that the courts’ refusal to appoint an independent medical expert, while treating the Institute’s own experts as decisive, deprived her of equality of arms and an effective opportunity to contest the decisive medical findings.

The case of Devinar v. Slovenia (Application no. 28621/15) was brought by Verena Devinar, a Slovenian national born in 1959 and living in Nova Gorica, who alleged a violation of her right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant had worked as a cleaning lady and developed serious medical complications in her left wrist that surgery only partly addressed. This led her to overuse her right arm, causing further problems. In 2006 she was officially recognised as having a partial disability and found incapable of further work.

On 30 December 2011 she applied to the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute for a disability allowance in respect of physical impairment. The Institute’s first-instance disability commission (an occupational-medicine specialist, an orthopaedic specialist and a physical-medicine physician) examined her medical records and conducted a clinical examination. It reported that she did not suffer from any physical impairment listed in the Self-Management Agreement on the List of Physical Impairments (an instrument dating from 1983 and last amended in 1989). Relying on that opinion, the Institute dismissed the application on 15 March 2012. The applicant appealed. The second-instance commission (an occupational-medicine specialist and an orthopaedic specialist) reviewed the file and reached the same conclusion. The Institute’s Central Office dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2012.

On 12 July 2012 the applicant brought proceedings in the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court seeking annulment of the Institute’s decisions. She argued that the facts had been wrongly established, that the procedure had been improper, that the functioning of her body was inhibited by the incapacity of both arms, and that greater efforts were required for daily needs. She claimed at least 50 % incapacity and requested the appointment of a medical expert. On 6 September 2013 the court, sitting as a single judge, dismissed the claim. It held that its role was to verify compliance with procedural rules, proper establishment of fact and correct application of law. After reviewing the file and hearing the applicant, it found that the Institute had correctly established the facts, relying on the commissions’ opinions and its own observation of the applicant. It refused the request for an expert as unnecessary.

The applicant appealed, contending that the List was outdated, that the court should not have relied on the commissions’ opinions (which she disputed), that it lacked the medical knowledge to assess her condition, and that an independent expert was required. On 6 February 2014 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal. It held that the facts had been sufficiently established, that the commissions’ opinions were convincing in the light of the medical documentation, and that an expert was unnecessary because the outcome would not have differed. Physical impairment had to correspond to the List; a recognised disability did not automatically constitute physical impairment without functional joint problems.

The applicant sought leave to appeal on points of law, arguing that refusal of an expert and the court’s own medical assessment without expertise deprived her of any effective means of challenging the Institute, especially since independent experts had frequently contradicted the commissions. The Supreme Court dismissed the application on 10 June 2014. A constitutional complaint repeating these arguments and invoking Articles 22 and 23 of the Constitution was not accepted by the Constitutional Court on 10 December 2014.

The core of the alleged violation was the courts’ exclusive reliance on the opinions of the Institute’s own disability commissions (expert bodies of one party to the proceedings) and their refusal to appoint an independent medical expert, despite the applicant’s explicit request and the courts’ lack of specialised medical knowledge. Domestic law defined physical impairment as loss, severe injury or significant incapacity of organs inhibiting normal functioning and requiring greater effort for vital tasks; entitlement depended on the degree of severity matching the old List. Commissions operated under Institute rules, with some members employed by the Institute. Earlier Supreme Court jurisprudence had already indicated that such opinions were not impartial expert evidence in judicial proceedings and that an independent expert should be appointed when requested.
001-183565:
The case of Rungainis v. Latvia originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Ģirts Rungainis, a Latvian national and chairman of the supervisory board of Latvijas Krājbanka (a bank 32.12% state-owned). He alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) arising from domestic civil liability imposed on him for statements to journalists.

In September 2002 the applicant prepared an internal report on the bank’s 2001–mid-2002 advertising and marketing expenditure. It indicated that substantial sums had been transferred to an advertising agency (Z.) without supporting documentation, raising suspicions of misappropriation. The bank’s former president, A.L. (who had resigned in January 2002 and was later elected to parliament for the newly formed Latvia’s First Party, which also used agency Z.), featured in subsequent press coverage. The supervisory board ordered internal and then external audits. These ultimately found no undocumented or excess payments; higher spending was attributable to a corporate rebranding exercise, all contracts had been properly approved, and no personal links or coercion existed. Criminal proceedings requested by A.L. against the applicant for intentional dissemination of false information were refused for lack of intent, though the initial report was acknowledged as erroneous.

NRA, a major daily newspaper, published numerous articles on the 2002 parliamentary elections. Nine articles appearing between 3 and 23 October 2002 were based on information the applicant supplied to its journalists (the parties disputed whether this occurred once by telephone as unverified opinion or repeatedly as statements of fact). The articles reported that LVL 522,000 had been transferred without documentation, described the funds as “stolen from the shareholders,” suggested they financed the party’s campaign, and linked A.L. to possible fraud and other irregularities. The applicant later admitted in court that the figures and implications were incorrect and unfounded.

In July 2003 A.L. brought a defamation action against the applicant and the newspaper’s publishers, seeking retraction and damages in respect of 31 articles, including the nine based on the applicant’s comments. The Riga Regional Court dismissed the claims against the applicant, characterising the statements as non-defamatory personal opinion. On appeal the Civil Cases Chamber of the Supreme Court reversed this finding. It held that the applicant had disseminated false information of fact (which he had admitted) specifically targeting A.L., that his position as supervisory-board chairman created a legitimate expectation of accuracy so that journalists had no duty to verify, and that the allegations of unlawful conduct offended A.L.’s honour and dignity even allowing for a wider margin of criticism of a parliamentarian. The applicant was ordered to pay LVL 10,000 (approximately EUR 14,229) plus statutory interest and to retract the statements. The Senate of the Supreme Court upheld the judgment, confirming that the information concerned A.L. personally rather than the bank’s management generally.

The applicant argued before the Court that his comments had been value judgments or unverified hypotheses about bank management as a whole, that he had not named A.L., and that any defamatory presentation was the journalists’ responsibility. The domestic courts’ imposition of liability and the retraction order formed the basis of the Article 10 complaint.

The case of Rungainis v. Latvia (Application no. 40597/08) originated in a complaint by Ģirts Rungainis, a Latvian national and chairman of the supervisory board of Latvijas Krājbanka (a bank in which the State held 32.12% of shares). He alleged a violation of his Article 10 right to freedom of expression arising from civil liability imposed for statements he made to journalists. Those statements concerned suspected financial irregularities at the bank during the tenure of its former president, A.L.

A.L. had stepped down as bank president in January 2002 and was elected to parliament in November 2002 as a representative of the newly formed Latvia’s First Party. An advertising agency, Z., provided services to both the bank and the party. On 30 September 2002 the applicant prepared an internal report, based on information from bank departments, indicating that substantial advertising and marketing payments (including large sums to Z.) lacked supporting documentation. This raised suspicions of misappropriation of bank funds. The supervisory board commissioned an internal audit, which concluded (in reports of 16 and 30 October 2002) that no undocumented expenses had occurred, although some supporting materials (such as copies of advertisements) were no longer available. An external audit completed in May 2003 confirmed that higher expenditure in 2001–2002 was attributable to a corporate rebranding exercise. All contracts with Z. had been properly approved; there was no evidence of payments for unreceived services, overpayments, or personal links between A.L. (or bank staff) and the agency.

Shortly after a 2 October 2002 board meeting, NRA journalists contacted the applicant. Nine articles published between 3 and 23 October 2002 attributed to him statements that LVL 522,000 had been transferred without documentation “in an unknown direction,” that this constituted destruction of bank assets or theft from shareholders, that more than LVL 200,000 had gone to Z. as an uncertified advance, and that the money may have funded the party’s election campaign. The articles also referred to other alleged procedural breaches under A.L.’s management. The applicant later maintained that he had given only a brief telephone comment expressing an unverified personal opinion about overall management practices and that he had not named A.L. The Government contended that he had supplied concrete, verifiable factual assertions on several occasions.

A.L. brought defamation proceedings against the applicant and the newspaper publishers. At first instance the applicant acknowledged that the information had proved unfounded and apologised for numerical inaccuracies, while insisting he had not targeted A.L. personally. The Riga Regional Court (2005) dismissed the claim against him, characterising the statements as non-defamatory opinion. On appeal the Civil Cases Chamber of the Supreme Court (2007) reversed that finding. It held that the applicant had disseminated specific false factual information about A.L.’s conduct, that his senior position created a legitimate expectation of accuracy so that journalists had no duty to verify, and that the allegations of unlawful activity damaged A.L.’s honour even taking account of the wider margin of criticism applicable to a parliamentary candidate. The applicant was ordered to pay LVL 10,000 (approximately EUR 14,229) plus interest in damages and to retract the relevant passages. The Senate of the Supreme Court (2008) upheld the judgment, confirming that the information related specifically to A.L. rather than to bank management in general and that the applicant, as disseminator, bore responsibility under section 2352a of the Civil Law.

The interference therefore consisted of a civil judgment holding the applicant liable for statements made to the press on a matter of public interest (possible misuse of funds in a partly state-owned bank during an election campaign). The domestic courts treated the statements as assertions of fact rather than value judgments, placed decisive weight on the applicant’s institutional position, and imposed both financial and retractive sanctions after independent audits had disproved the original suspicions.

The European Court of Human Rights case of *Rungainis v. Latvia* (Application no. 40597/08, judgment of 14 June 2018) originated from a complaint by Latvian national Ģirts Rungainis under Article 10 of the Convention, alleging that domestic civil defamation proceedings had unlawfully interfered with his freedom of expression. At the relevant time, the applicant chaired the supervisory board of Latvijas Krājbanka (a bank in which the State held a 32.12% stake). A.L., a shareholder and the bank’s president until he stepped down in January 2002, was elected to parliament later that year as a representative of the newly formed Latvia’s First Party. An advertising agency, Z., provided services to both the bank and the party.

On 30 September 2002 the applicant submitted a report to the bank’s supervisory board concerning advertising and marketing expenditure in 2001 and the first seven months of 2002. Drawing on information from the bank’s marketing and economics departments, the report identified substantial transfers to Z. and other entities for which supporting documentation (contracts, delivery notes, etc.) was lacking. This raised suspicions of misappropriation. An extraordinary board meeting on 2 October 2002 ordered an internal audit. Preliminary findings on 16 October indicated that no undocumented expenses had occurred in 2002; a final internal report of 30 October 2002 reached the same conclusion for 2001, although some supporting materials (press advertisements, posters) were no longer available. An external audit completed in May 2003 attributed the higher-than-usual expenditure to a corporate-identity overhaul, confirmed that all contracts with Z. had been properly authorised by senior management, and found no evidence of payments for undelivered services or of personal links between A.L. (or bank staff) and the agencies.

A.L. sought criminal proceedings against the applicant for intentional dissemination of false information; the prosecution declined on 13 August 2003, noting that the applicant’s initial findings had been erroneous but not deliberately false, and advised A.L. of his civil remedies.

Between 3 and 23 October 2002 the daily newspaper *Neatkarīgā Rīta Avīze* published nine articles that the parties later agreed were based on information supplied by the applicant (the precise manner and extent of that contact being disputed). The articles reported that LVL 522,000 had been transferred without documentation, that more than LVL 200,000 had gone to Z. as an undocumented advance shortly before A.L. left the bank, that the funds may have financed the party’s election campaign, and that the money had been “stolen from the shareholders.” They also alluded to other alleged irregularities during A.L.’s presidency.

On 28 July 2003 A.L. brought a civil defamation action against the applicant and the newspaper’s publishers, seeking retraction and damages in respect of 31 articles, including the nine mentioned above. At first instance the Riga Regional Court (3 October 2005) dismissed the claim against the applicant, characterising the statements as non-defamatory personal opinion about bank management. On appeal the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court (28 May 2007) reversed that finding. It held that the applicant had supplied concrete, verifiable assertions of fact (specific sums and alleged misconduct) that he himself later admitted were incorrect; that his position as supervisory-board chairman created a legitimate expectation of accuracy, so the journalists had no duty to verify; and that the false allegations of unlawful conduct had damaged A.L.’s honour despite the wider margin of criticism applicable to a politician. The applicant was ordered to pay LVL 10,000 (approximately EUR 14,229) plus statutory interest. The Senate of the Supreme Court (30 January 2008) upheld the judgment, confirming that the information targeted A.L. personally rather than the bank as an institution, and additionally directed the applicant to retract the impugned passages.

The applicant argued throughout that he had merely expressed a provisional opinion requiring audit confirmation, that he had not named A.L., and that any defamatory linkage had been introduced by the journalists. Domestic law (Civil Law s. 2352a and the Law on the Press) placed the burden of proving truth on the disseminator of information alleged to offend honour and dignity and imposed liability for untrue statements. These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 10 violation: the imposition of civil liability, damages and a retraction order for information later shown to be inaccurate.
001-184475:
The case of Kamenova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 62784/09) concerns the applicant’s complaint that she was denied access to a court to obtain compensation for the death of her daughter. On 20 August 1997 the applicant’s daughter was killed in a road-traffic accident caused by the negligence of lorry driver H.H.; several other persons were also killed or injured. Criminal proceedings were instituted against H.H. In 1998 he was indicted. At the first-instance hearing the relatives of the other victims joined civil claims against H.H. and his employer; the applicant did not. On 30 June 1999 the Vidin Regional Court convicted H.H. and allowed the civil claims. That judgment was quashed on 19 April 2000 by the Sofia Court of Appeal for serious procedural irregularities and the case was remitted to the prosecution for a fresh investigation.

A new indictment was filed and, at the first hearing of the reopened proceedings on 30 March 2001, the Regional Court accepted a civil claim lodged by the applicant and recognised her as a civil party. On 18 September 2002 the Regional Court again convicted H.H. and awarded damages to the other civil parties but omitted any ruling on the applicant’s claim. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction (which became final in 2003) but remitted the civil claims because of the failure to decide the applicant’s action. On 6 April 2004 the Regional Court, examining only the civil claims, awarded the applicant BGN 10 000 plus default interest. On 8 March 2006 the Court of Appeal quashed that award and discontinued the applicant’s claim as inadmissible: Article 61 § 4 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure required a civil claim to be filed before the first-instance court began examining the case; the applicant had filed hers only after remittal. The Supreme Court of Cassation confirmed this ruling on 4 March 2007.

On 22 August 2007 the applicant brought a fresh tort action in the civil courts seeking the same sum plus interest from the date of the accident. The Sofia District Court dismissed the action as time-barred. The five-year limitation period under the Obligations and Contracts Act had begun to run in 1997, when the identity of the person responsible was known. The applicant’s earlier civil-party claim could not interrupt the period because it had been declared inadmissible; even if interruption had occurred, it was retrospectively nullified by the 2006 discontinuation. The Regional Court had, moreover, failed to transfer the claim to a civil court as required when a tribunal lacks jurisdiction. The Sofia City Court upheld the dismissal on 13 March 2009, adding that the applicant had to bear the consequences of having filed her claim in the criminal proceedings in breach of the applicable rules, even though the Regional Court had initially accepted it. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal on 9 July 2009.

Under the relevant Bulgarian law a civil claim may be joined to criminal proceedings only before the first-instance court commences its examination; after remittal such a claim is generally barred. Limitation is interrupted by the bringing of a claim, but if the claim is not allowed the interruption is treated as never having occurred. The running of time is also suspended during the pendency of judicial proceedings relating to the claim, yet the courts held that this rule did not assist the applicant because her criminal-court claim had been inadmissible. The combination of these procedural and limitation rules left the applicant without any effective judicial determination of her claim for compensation arising from her daughter’s death.

The case of Kamenova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 62784/09) concerns the applicant’s complaint that she was denied access to a court, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, when seeking compensation for the death of her daughter.

On 20 August 1997 the applicant’s daughter was killed in a traffic accident caused by H.H., a lorry driver. Criminal proceedings were opened against H.H. Other victims’ relatives joined as civil parties at the first hearing and obtained awards when the Vidin Regional Court convicted H.H. in June 1999. The applicant did not then submit a civil claim. The Sofia Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in April 2000 for serious procedural breaches and remitted the case to the investigation stage.

A fresh indictment followed. At the first hearing on 30 March 2001 the Regional Court accepted the applicant’s civil claim against H.H. and his employer and recognised her as a civil party. In September 2002 the court convicted H.H. but omitted any ruling on her claim. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction (which became final in October 2003) but remitted the civil claims, citing among other defects the failure to decide the applicant’s claim.

On 6 April 2004 the Regional Court, examining only the civil aspects, awarded the applicant BGN 10 000 plus default interest. In March 2006 the Court of Appeal quashed that award and discontinued her claim as inadmissible. It held that Article 61 § 4 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure required a civil claim to be lodged before the commencement of the first-instance examination; a claim filed after remittal from a higher court was out of time. The Supreme Court of Cassation confirmed this interpretation on 4 March 2007.

On 22 August 2007 the applicant brought a separate tort action in the civil courts, claiming the same sum plus interest from the date of the accident. The Sofia District Court dismissed the action in July 2008 as time-barred. The five-year limitation period under the Obligations and Contracts Act had begun in 1997 once H.H.’s identity was known. The earlier criminal-court claim had not validly interrupted the period because it had been held inadmissible; any interruption was retroactively nullified. The court added that the criminal court, lacking jurisdiction, should have transferred the claim to the competent civil court but had not done so.

The Sofia City Court upheld the dismissal in March 2009, accepting that the claim was well-founded on the merits yet time-barred. It emphasised that only an admissible and successful claim could interrupt limitation; once the criminal proceedings on the claim were discontinued, the period was treated as never having been interrupted. The applicant had to bear the consequences of having filed her claim contrary to the procedural rules, even though the Regional Court had initially accepted it. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal on points of law on 9 July 2009.

Domestic law thus combined a strict, non-extendable time-limit for joining a civil claim to criminal proceedings (interpreted as referring only to the original first-instance examination) with a five-year limitation period that ran from knowledge of the tortfeasor and that was not interrupted by an ultimately inadmissible claim. The applicant’s successive attempts to obtain a ruling on the merits of her compensation claim were therefore rejected on purely procedural grounds.

The case of Kamenova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 62784/09) concerns the applicant's complaint of being denied access to a court to seek compensation for her daughter's death.

Yordanka Eftimova Kamenova (born 1942, resident in Montana) lost her daughter in a traffic accident on 20 August 1997 caused by lorry driver H.H., which also killed and injured others.

Criminal proceedings against H.H. began promptly. He was first convicted by the Vidin Regional Court on 30 June 1999, which also granted damages to other victims' relatives who had joined as civil parties (the applicant had not). This judgment was quashed by the Sofia Court of Appeal on 19 April 2000 for serious procedural breaches and remitted for a fresh preliminary investigation.

A new indictment followed. At the first hearing on 30 March 2001 the applicant submitted a civil claim against H.H. and his employer; it was accepted and she was recognised as a civil party. The Regional Court convicted H.H. again on 18 September 2002 but made no ruling on her claim. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction (finalised 8 October 2003) but remitted the civil claims because of the omission.

On 6 April 2004 the Regional Court awarded the applicant BGN 10 000 (approximately EUR 5 100) plus default interest. On 8 March 2006 the Court of Appeal quashed that award and discontinued her claim as inadmissible. Article 61 § 4 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure required a civil claim to be lodged before the start of first-instance examination; the courts interpreted this as referring only to the initial first-instance stage, not after remittal. The Supreme Court of Cassation confirmed the ruling on 4 March 2007.

The applicant then brought a separate tort action in the civil courts on 22 August 2007, claiming the same sum plus interest from the date of the accident. The Sofia District Court dismissed it on 17 July 2008 as time-barred. The five-year limitation period under the Obligations and Contracts Act had begun in 1997 (when H.H.'s identity was known). Her earlier criminal-court claim had not interrupted the period because it was later held inadmissible; any interruption was in any event retroactively invalidated by the 2006 discontinuation. The court observed that the criminal court, lacking jurisdiction, should have transferred the claim to a competent civil court but had not done so.

The Sofia City Court dismissed the appeal on 13 March 2009, agreeing the claim was time-barred. Interruption of limitation occurs only if the claim is ultimately allowed; after discontinuation there had been no valid interruption. The applicant had to bear the consequences of having filed her claim in the criminal proceedings in breach of the rules, even though the Regional Court had initially accepted it in error. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused cassation review on 9 July 2009.

The applicant therefore never obtained a judicial examination of her compensation claim on the merits. The combination of the strict time-limit for joining a civil claim in criminal proceedings, the effects of remittal, the non-interruption of limitation by an ultimately inadmissible claim, and the civil courts' refusal to treat the earlier filing as having preserved her rights left her without any effective access to a court more than a decade after the accident.
001-184524:
The case of *X v. the Netherlands* (ECHR Application no. 14319/17) concerns a Moroccan national (born 1988) who alleged that his expulsion to Morocco would violate Article 3 ECHR due to a real risk of torture or inhuman treatment as a suspected terrorist.

The applicant entered the Netherlands in July 2012 on a tourist visa, overstayed, and lived with family in Amsterdam. In September 2014, the Dutch AIVD intelligence service reported that he had sworn allegiance to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi and was seeking a firearm to attack Dutch police. He was arrested on 15 October 2014. A search of his residence yielded notes with IED-making instructions, a written ISIS pledge, and Facebook chats in which he inquired about explosives, presented himself as an ISIS supporter, and expressed a desire to join the jihad in Syria.

Dutch authorities sent mutual legal assistance requests to Morocco in November 2014 and April 2015, sharing the applicant’s national identity card number and detailing suspicions of (preparation of) terrorist murder, participation in a terrorist organisation, and terrorism financing.

The Rotterdam Regional Court acquitted him in September 2015, viewing the chats as bravado. The Court of Appeal of The Hague convicted him in June 2016 under Article 134a of the Criminal Code of acquiring information and know-how to commit a terrorist offence, imposing a 12-month sentence based on the systematic, radical nature of the messages over a prolonged period. The Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal in March 2017.

Around April 2015, media reports (in Dutch, Arabic and English) described the dismantling of a terrorist cell in the applicant’s hometown of Salouin. Some articles mentioned a Moroccan living in the Netherlands who had been arrested for planning attacks and had links to the cell, with information from Morocco’s DGST intelligence service having prompted the Dutch arrest.

After his criminal detention ended, the applicant applied for asylum on 28 August 2015, claiming that Moroccan authorities viewed him as a terrorist and that he faced arrest, inhumane detention and torture. He cited the media reports, arrests of two acquaintances (A.M. and B.M.) from his birthplace, and later a Moroccan police report identifying him as having been radicalised by B.B. (a cell member) and expressing interest in firearms and explosives.

A December 2015 person-specific official report by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the applicant’s last known Moroccan address, that the Salouin cell members were arrested on 13 April 2015 and remained detained on charges of forming a jihadist criminal organisation planning assassinations, that neither the applicant nor the exact named acquaintances appeared in the group or media reports (which mentioned only an unnamed Moroccan arrested in the Netherlands), and that the applicant was not being sought or charged in Morocco.

The Deputy Minister rejected asylum on 21 July 2016 and imposed a 20-year Schengen-wide entry ban, finding the applicant a threat to public safety due to his conviction and AIVD information. No Article 3 risk was established: the MFA report showed he was not wanted, and similar Moroccan men convicted of terrorism-related offences in the Netherlands (including Hofstad group members) had been returned without encountering relevant problems.

The Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the appeal on 14 February 2017. It accepted the MFA report as reliable expert evidence (despite a procedural shortcoming in not using a local trusted advisor, which did not prejudice the applicant given existing media awareness). The applicant had not shown he would be arrested or prosecuted; general reports on Moroccan treatment of terror suspects were insufficient without a personal risk, and past return cases supported the authorities’ position. The Council of State rejected a further appeal on 28 February 2017 without additional reasoning.

The applicant later submitted a December 2016 Moroccan judgment convicting B.B. and others of establishing an ISIS-loyal terrorist group; it named the applicant as someone B.B. had been warned to avoid due to terrorist links. A separate Moroccan appellate judgment involving another individual (G.H., represented by the same lawyer) applied *ne bis in idem* to acquit on charges overlapping a prior French conviction.

UN reports (Working Group on Arbitrary Detention 2014; Human Rights Committee 2016) noted Moroccan progress on human rights but documented a pattern, in terrorism/national-security cases, of prolonged incommunicado detention (up to 12 days), restricted lawyer access, reliance on coerced confessions obtained through torture by DST agents, and inadequate investigations of ill-treatment allegations.

The ECHR indicated interim measures under Rule 39 on 3 March 2017 (later extended), preventing expulsion pending the proceedings. The Government confirmed information-sharing with Morocco via the legal-assistance requests, that no extradition had been sought, and that no special diplomatic assurances were obtained.

**Summary of X v. the Netherlands (ECtHR, Application no. 14319/17, 10 July 2018)**

The applicant, a Moroccan national born in 1988, left Salouin, Morocco, in July 2012 to visit family in the Netherlands and overstayed his tourist visa. He lived with his brother in Amsterdam. In September 2014, the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) reported that a Moroccan national (identified as the applicant) had sworn allegiance to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi and was seeking a firearm to attack Dutch police. He was arrested on 15 October 2014 on suspicion of preparing terrorist offences. A search of his residence yielded notes with instructions for making an improvised explosive device (IED), a written pledge to ISIS, and computer evidence of Facebook conversations in which he inquired about making IEDs, expressed support for ISIS, and stated a desire to join jihad in Syria.

Dutch authorities issued mutual legal assistance requests to Morocco in November 2014 and April 2015, providing the applicant’s identity card details and specifying suspicions of preparing murder with a terrorist motive, participating in a terrorist organization, preparing a terrorist offence, and financing terrorism. In April 2015, media reports (in Dutch, Arabic, and English) described the dismantling of a terrorist cell in Selwane (the applicant’s former area) and mentioned the arrest in the Netherlands of a Moroccan linked to the cell who planned attacks there; some reports attributed the Dutch arrest to information from Morocco’s DGST intelligence service.

The applicant was acquitted by the Rotterdam Regional Court in September 2015 (his chats were deemed mere “showing off”), but the Court of Appeal of The Hague convicted him in June 2016 under Article 134a of the Criminal Code of acquiring information and know-how for a terrorist offence, based on the systematic nature of his communications, and sentenced him to 12 months’ imprisonment. His cassation appeal was declared inadmissible in March 2017.

After his remand ended in August 2015, he was placed in immigration detention and applied for asylum, claiming that return to Morocco would expose him to arrest by the secret service, inhuman detention, and torture because Moroccan authorities viewed him as a terrorist. He cited the media reports linking him to the dismantled cell, arrests of two acquaintances (A.M. and B.M.) in 2014, and later documents including a Moroccan police report on B.B. (linked to the cell) that described the applicant as having been radicalized by B.B. and as having discussed buying a firearm and making explosives. A subsequent Moroccan judgment convicting B.B. and others of forming an ISIS-loyal terrorist group referred to B.B.’s connections with the applicant in the Netherlands. The applicant also submitted an email from his Moroccan lawyer warning of prosecution (possibly despite the Dutch conviction) and information on another individual (G.H.) prosecuted in both France and Morocco.

A Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs person-specific official report (December 2015, with January 2016 clarification) confirmed the applicant’s last known Moroccan address but found he was not named in media reports on the cell, was not being sought in connection with that investigation or other offences, and faced no charges. The Deputy Minister rejected asylum in July 2016 (imposing a 20-year entry ban on national-security grounds), finding no real, personal risk under Article 3; similar returnees from Dutch terrorism cases (e.g., Hofstad group members) had encountered no relevant problems. The Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the appeal in February 2017, upholding reliance on the official report (despite a procedural shortcoming in its preparation) and holding that general country information on torture of terrorism suspects was irrelevant absent a showing that the applicant himself would be arrested or prosecuted. The Administrative Jurisdiction Division rejected a further appeal in February 2017 without additional reasoning.

The Government confirmed that Moroccan authorities were aware of the Dutch proceedings via the legal-assistance requests and had not sought extradition. The applicant was to be returned on his valid Moroccan ID card, accompanied by Dutch officers and handed over at the airport, without special procedures or guarantees. Country reports (UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention 2014; UN Human Rights Committee 2016) noted Morocco’s human-rights reforms but documented patterns of torture, prolonged incommunicado detention, and reliance on coerced confessions in terrorism/national-security cases, with vague anti-terrorism laws and limited safeguards.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claim that expulsion would violate Article 3 due to a real risk of torture or inhuman treatment as a perceived terrorist.

The case concerns a Moroccan national (applicant X, born 1988) who travelled to the Netherlands in July 2012 on a tourist visa that he overstayed. He lived with family in Amsterdam. In September 2014, the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) received information that a Moroccan resident had sworn allegiance to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi and was seeking a firearm to attack Dutch police. Investigation identified the applicant, who lacked a residence permit.

On 15 October 2014 he was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist offences. A search of his residence yielded handwritten notes with IED-making instructions and an ISIS pledge, plus a computer containing Facebook conversations in which he enquired about explosives, expressed ISIS support and a desire to join the Syrian jihad. Dutch authorities sent mutual legal assistance requests to Morocco (November 2014 and April 2015) disclosing his identity-card number and the nature of the suspicions (preparation of murder with terrorist motive, participation in a terrorist organisation, financing of terrorism).

In April 2015 Moroccan and international media reported the dismantling of a terrorist cell in Salouin (the applicant’s last Moroccan address). Several articles referred to the arrest in the Netherlands of a Moroccan linked to the cell who had been planning attacks there; some stated that Moroccan intelligence (DGST) had supplied the information that led to the Dutch arrest. The applicant denied any connection with the cell but feared association with it.

The Rotterdam Regional Court acquitted him in September 2015, accepting that his online messages were boastful. The Hague Court of Appeal reversed the acquittal in June 2016, convicting him under Article 134a of the Criminal Code of acquiring information and know-how for a terrorist offence and imposing a 12-month sentence. The Supreme Court declared his cassation appeal inadmissible.

Upon release from remand in August 2015 the applicant was placed in immigration detention and claimed asylum. He argued that Moroccan authorities regarded him as a terrorist, that media coverage and the legal-assistance requests had identified him, and that two acquaintances from his birthplace had been arrested in 2014. He therefore faced a real risk of arbitrary arrest, incommunicado detention, torture and unfair trial if returned.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs produced a person-specific official report (December 2015, later clarified) confirming his last Moroccan address, noting that the Salouin cell members had all been arrested on 13 April 2015 and remained in detention on jihadist-organisation charges, but establishing that the applicant was neither named in the media, wanted, nor charged in Morocco. The Deputy Minister rejected asylum on 21 July 2016, imposed a 20-year Schengen entry ban on national-security grounds, and found no individualised Article 3 risk, citing the official report and the uneventful returns of other Moroccan men previously tried in the Netherlands for terrorism-related offences.

The Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the appeal in February 2017. It held that the applicant had not made a plausible case that he would be arrested or prosecuted; the official report was reliable; general country information on torture of terrorism suspects was relevant only if detention were likely; and a Moroccan police report mentioning him in connection with another suspect (B.B.) did not show that proceedings had been opened against him. The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State rejected a further appeal without additional reasoning.

The applicant later produced a 2016 Moroccan judgment convicting B.B. and others of forming an ISIS-loyal terrorist group; the judgment referred to B.B.’s contacts with the applicant in the Netherlands and a warning that he should break those contacts. A subsequent Moroccan appellate judgment applying the ne-bis-in-idem principle to another dual-jurisdiction terrorism suspect was also submitted.

Interim measures under Rule 39 of the Court’s Rules have prevented the applicant’s removal pending the Strasbourg proceedings. The application alleges that expulsion would expose him to treatment contrary to Article 3.
001-184670:
The case of Petrović and Others v. Montenegro (no. 18116/15) involves four Montenegrin nationals who claimed that two plots of coastal-zone land, historically owned by their predecessor, had been de facto expropriated by the State without compensation. They further alleged that the domestic courts’ rulings denying their ownership claims were arbitrary, engaging Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 of the Convention.

In September 2009 the first two applicants and the father of the third and fourth applicants sued the State, asserting that the land had been lawfully owned by their father (or grandfather) yet had been registered as State property without legal basis. They sought recognition as owners in their capacity as legal successors. In March 2010 the Real Estate Administration divided an adjacent coastal-zone forest plot, registering one portion to the applicants’ predecessor, thereby illustrating that private title in the same zone was possible.

The Kotor Court of First Instance dismissed the claim in November 2011. It accepted historical family ownership but held that the applicants had not proved they inherited the land when the last predecessor died in 1997. Because the plots lay in the coastal zone they constituted State property under section 4 of the 1992 Coastal Zone Act and section 13 of the State Property Act; private claims were therefore precluded. Nationalisation records cited by the State could not be located, and the 2010 adjacent-plot decision was deemed irrelevant.

On appeal the applicants emphasised that the land’s absence from the estate was precisely why they had sued. They invoked section 30 of the Coastal Zone Act (entitling pre-1992 lawful owners to compensation upon expropriation) and noted that neither the Coastal Zone Act nor the 2009 Property Act barred private coastal-zone ownership. They pointed to their own adjacent privately registered plot as evidence of inconsistent treatment.

The High Court (April 2012) and Supreme Court (October 2012) upheld the dismissal. Both characterised the land as a State-owned common resource; even if private title had once existed it had been extinguished by operation of law. Section 30 was read as confirming automatic transfer to the State, with compensation available only in the event of formal expropriation. The 2009 Property Act’s exceptional private-ownership clause was held non-retroactive. Neither court addressed the adjacent plot.

A constitutional appeal stressing legal certainty and the existence of privately owned coastal land was dismissed in July 2014. The Constitutional Court found the lower courts’ application of substantive law constitutionally acceptable and, because the claim had been rejected, concluded that no “possession” capable of engaging Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 existed.

The predecessor died in December 2014; the third and fourth applicants succeeded him. In May 2015 the Supreme Court itself issued a general legal opinion acknowledging that the relevant statutes were imprecise, that exceptional private ownership of coastal-zone land was theoretically possible yet undefined, and that lawfully acquired rights were not clearly regulated—even though section 30 itself recognised such rights.

These facts—the uncompensated transfer of historically private land into State ownership, the courts’ refusal to apply section 30, the disregard of an identically situated adjacent plot, and subsequent judicial recognition of legislative inconsistency—underpin the applicants’ complaints of de facto expropriation and arbitrary adjudication.

The four Montenegrin applicants alleged de facto expropriation of family land in the coastal zone without compensation, plus arbitrary domestic court rulings denying their ownership claims (invoking Convention rights to property and a fair trial).

On 1 September 2009 the first two applicants and the father of the third and fourth applicants sued the State, seeking to be declared owners of two coastal-zone plots. They asserted that the land had been lawfully owned by their predecessor (father/grandfather) but had been registered as State property without legal basis; they claimed it as legal successors.

On 2 March 2010 the Real Estate Administration divided an adjacent coastal-zone forest plot (then municipally registered) and registered one part in the predecessor’s name, demonstrating that private ownership of such land was possible.

The Kotor Court of First Instance dismissed the claim on 21 November 2011. It accepted that the plots had belonged to the predecessors but held that inheritance after the last predecessor’s 1997 death had not been proved. The land lay in the coastal zone and was therefore State property under s. 4 of the 1992 Coastal Zone Act and the 2009 State Property Act; private ownership could not be claimed. Nationalisation files cited by the State could not be located. The 2010 adjacent-plot decision was irrelevant because it concerned different land.

On appeal the claimants confirmed that the plots had been omitted from the estate (the very reason for the action). They argued that s. 30 of the Coastal Zone Act—entitling pre-1992 lawful owners of registered coastal-zone land to expropriation compensation—had never been applied despite undisputed prior ownership. They contended that the legislation did not prohibit private ownership (citing s. 4 of the Coastal Zone Act and s. 20 of the 2009 Property Act) and that the privately owned adjacent plot created legal uncertainty by treating identical land inconsistently.

The High Court upheld the dismissal on 6 April 2012. The plots were State property under the State Property Act; any prior ownership had been lost by operation of that Act and the Coastal Zone Act. Section 30 itself confirmed that the land had become State property by law, with compensation payable only upon expropriation. The adjacent-plot decision was ignored.

The Supreme Court confirmed on 11 October 2012. Coastal-zone land was a common resource that could not be privately owned. Section 30 showed that pre-existing private title had been extinguished by law (leaving only a compensation claim upon expropriation). The 2009 Property Act’s exceptional allowance of private coastal-zone ownership was not retroactive.

A constitutional appeal stressed that private coastal-zone ownership existed in practice (including the applicants’ adjacent plot) and invoked fair-trial, property and legal-certainty rights. The Constitutional Court dismissed it on 23 July 2014, finding the lower courts’ application of law constitutionally acceptable and holding that a dismissed claim was not a “possession.”

The predecessor died in December 2014; the third and fourth applicants succeeded him. A May 2015 Supreme Court legal opinion later acknowledged that the statutes on private ownership of coastal-zone land were inconsistent and imprecise, leaving lawfully acquired rights unregulated even though s. 30 recognised their existence.

These facts underpin the complaints of uncompensated de facto expropriation (title extinguished by statute without any expropriation procedure or payment) and of arbitrary adjudication (inconsistent treatment of identical adjacent land and unreasoned application of contradictory legislation).

The case of Petrović and Others v. Montenegro (Application no. 18116/15) concerns four Montenegrin nationals who alleged that two plots of forest land in the coastal zone (morsko dobro) had been de facto expropriated by the State without compensation. They further claimed that the domestic courts’ decisions dismissing their ownership claims were arbitrary and inconsistent with legal certainty, contrary to their property rights.

The applicants (or their predecessor) initiated civil proceedings against the State on 1 September 2009. They asserted that the land had been lawfully owned by their father (grandfather of the third and fourth applicants) and earlier predecessors, but that the State had been registered as owner in the Real Estate Registry without any legal basis. They sought recognition as owners in their capacity as legal successors. The last predecessor had died in 1997, and the land had not formed part of his estate, which was the reason the proceedings were brought.

On 2 March 2010 the Real Estate Administration, acting on a request by the first applicant, divided an adjacent forest plot in the same coastal zone (then registered to the Municipality). One part remained municipal; the other was registered in the name of the applicants’ predecessor. The applicants later relied on this decision to demonstrate that private ownership of coastal-zone forest was possible and had in fact been recognised in respect of neighbouring land.

The Court of First Instance in Kotor, after a remittal, dismissed the claim on 21 November 2011. It accepted that the land had historically belonged to the family but held that the claimants had not proved they inherited it upon the 1997 death. More fundamentally, the court characterised the land as coastal-zone forest and therefore State property under section 4 of the 1992 Coastal Zone Act and section 13 of the State Property Act. Private ownership claims were therefore excluded. The court made no reference to section 30 of the Coastal Zone Act (which provided compensation for owners who had lawfully acquired and registered coastal-zone land before the Act’s entry into force). Nationalisation decisions invoked by the State could not be located in the archives. The 2010 Real Estate Administration decision was dismissed as irrelevant because it concerned a different plot.

On appeal the applicants stressed that section 30 had never been applied despite the predecessor’s lawful title, that domestic law did not prohibit private ownership of coastal-zone land, and that the adjacent plot was already registered to them. They argued that treating identical legal issues differently created legal uncertainty. The High Court upheld the dismissal on 6 April 2012, confirming that the land was State property. Even if ownership had existed, it had been lost by operation of the State Property Act and Coastal Zone Act; section 30 merely entitled former owners to compensation upon expropriation, implying that title had already passed to the State. No mention was made of the adjacent plot.

The Supreme Court confirmed the outcome on 11 October 2012. It held that coastal-zone land was a common resource belonging exclusively to the State and could not be privately owned. Section 30 did not preserve private title; it merely provided for compensation if expropriation occurred. Section 20(2) of the 2009 Property Act (which exceptionally permitted private ownership of coastal-zone land) could not apply retroactively.

A constitutional appeal invoking the right to a fair trial, the right to property and legal certainty was dismissed on 23 July 2014. The Constitutional Court found the lower courts’ interpretation of substantive law constitutionally acceptable. A claim rejected for failure to meet statutory conditions did not constitute a “possession.” The father of the third and fourth applicants died in December 2014; they succeeded to his claim.

In May 2015 the Supreme Court issued a general legal opinion noting internal inconsistencies in the legislation: while section 20(2) of the 2009 Property Act contemplated exceptional private ownership of coastal-zone land, other provisions appeared to exclude it, and the conditions for such ownership remained undefined. The opinion acknowledged that lawfully acquired rights existed (as evidenced by section 30) but were not regulated with precision.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the State had, through legislative characterisation and judicial interpretation, taken their land without compensation and that the courts had applied the law arbitrarily, particularly given the contrasting treatment of the adjacent plot.
