The case of Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta (Applications nos. 25218/15 and 25251/15) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) in a judgment of 17 July 2018 (final on 17 October 2018). The two applicants, Gerardo Jose Ruiz Pena (a Venezuelan national born in 1964) and Richard Andrews Perez Oberght (a Dominican Republic national born in 1973), alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention on account of the conditions of their detention at Corradino Correctional Facility in Paola, Malta.

The first applicant has been held at the facility since September 2009 and is serving a ten-year sentence imposed in March 2012. He has occupied cell 148 in Division 3 since January 2013. He declined a possible transfer that would have provided an automated flushing system, as it would have required moving from a single cell to a dormitory and thus reduced his privacy. His cell has a single high-set window that can be opened or closed only by climbing onto the sink, together with a dirt-clogged air vent. Ventilation is therefore inadequate. Summer temperatures of 35–40 °C render the two fans he purchased ineffective, as they merely circulate hot air; winter temperatures are correspondingly low and no heater was supplied despite requests, leaving him with one official blanket plus others obtained from NGOs. The toilet must be flushed with buckets because of low water pressure; filling even one bucket takes time and more than one is often required, a situation described as especially deplorable in summer. Dust continually falls from the 150-year-old ceiling and is claimed to harm his lungs. Tap water is rusty and undrinkable, forcing him to buy bottled water. His prison job pays EUR 0.60 per day; in summer he consumes three six-packs weekly. The Government stated that he received EUR 34.77 every four weeks from gratuity and work-pay schemes and that a six-pack cost EUR 2.24.

The second applicant has been detained at the same facility since November 2009 and is serving a nine-year sentence imposed in October 2012. He has occupied cell 155 in Division 3 since January 2012 (apart from one day in Division 6) and also declined a transfer. His window, more than two metres high and fitted with metal bars, is difficult and dangerous to open and admits little natural light. One of two ventilation openings is blocked. Tap water is again undrinkable, requiring purchases; he received EUR 41.58 every four weeks. Ceiling dust aggravates his asthma; the Government maintained that the quantity was normal for Maltese stone and that he had never requested paint. Humidity and the absence of a heater cause frequent winter flu; the Government attributed the humidity to a towel he placed over the vent and to his failure to maintain the cell. Lighting is poor both inside and outside the cell, hampering reading, although he has a ceiling light, a wall-mounted light and a portable lamp, with additional illumination from skylights and 400 W lamps. He further complained that the spiral staircase would impede emergency evacuation (a stretcher could not be carried down it and two persons could not descend simultaneously); the Government pointed to alternative routes such as the inter-division walkway.

These factual allegations concerning ventilation, temperature extremes, sanitation, water quality, dust, lighting and emergency access formed the basis of the Article 3 complaint. Relevant domestic law and comparative material were drawn from earlier Maltese prison-conditions cases.

The ECtHR case of Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta (applications 25218/15 and 25251/15) concerns two foreign nationals detained at Corradino Correctional Facility who alleged that their prison conditions violated Article 3 ECHR (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment). The first applicant, Venezuelan national Gerardo Jose Ruiz Pena (born 1964), has been held since September 2009 and is serving a 10-year sentence imposed in March 2012. He has occupied Division 3, cell 148 since January 2013 and declined transfer (despite potential automated flushing) to retain an individual cell rather than move to a dormitory.

His cell has one high window (requiring him to climb the sink to operate it) and a dirt-clogged air vent, yielding inadequate ventilation. Summer temperatures of 35–40°C render his two personal fans ineffective, as they merely circulate hot air. In winter, authorities provided no heater (requests were refused) and only one blanket; additional blankets and clothes came from NGOs. The toilet must be flushed manually with buckets due to low water pressure, often requiring multiple fills and becoming especially unsanitary in summer. Dust falling from the 150-year-old ceiling allegedly harms his lungs. Tap water is rusty and filthy, forcing him to buy bottled water. His prison work pays €0.60 per day; he consumes three six-packs weekly in summer. The Government stated he received €34.77 every four weeks via gratuity and work schemes, with a six-pack costing €2.24.

The second applicant, Dominican national Richard Andrews Perez Oberght (born 1973), has been detained since November 2009 and is serving a 9-year sentence from October 2012. He has been in Division 3, cell 155 since January 2012 (except one day elsewhere) and also refused a post-communication transfer offer.

His window exceeds two metres in height, is difficult and dangerous to open, and has metal bars that restrict natural light. One of two ventilation openings is blocked, producing insufficient airflow. Water is undrinkable, requiring purchases; he received €41.58 every four weeks. Ceiling dust aggravates his asthma; the Government described it as normal emanation from Maltese stone and noted he never requested paint. Humidity plus lack of a heater cause frequent winter flu; the Government attributed humidity to the applicant blocking the vent with a towel and failing to maintain the cell. Lighting (inside and outside) is poor and hinders reading, though he has a ceiling light, wall-mounted light, portable lamp, three skylights and 400 W lamps. He claimed the spiral staircase was unsuitable for emergencies (preventing stretcher use or two-at-a-time evacuation); the Government cited alternative walkways between divisions.

These facts—poor ventilation and temperature control, unsanitary toilet flushing, contaminated/undrinkable water, dust exposure affecting health, inadequate lighting and emergency access—underpin the Article 3 complaints. Domestic law and CPT-type material are referenced via prior Maltese cases (Story and Yanez Pinon). The Court communicated only the Article 3 detention-conditions complaints.

The case of Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta (Applications nos. 25218/15 and 25251/15) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) on 17 July 2018 (final on 17 October 2018). The two applicants alleged a violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights on account of the conditions of their detention at Corradino Correctional Facility in Paola, Malta.

Mr Gerardo Jose Ruiz Pena, a Venezuelan national born in 1964, has been detained at the facility since September 2009 and is serving a ten-year sentence imposed on 21 March 2012. Since 10 January 2013 he has occupied an individual cell (no. 148) in Division 3. He declined a possible transfer to a division with automated flushing because it would have required him to share a dormitory and lose privacy. His cell has a single high window that can be opened or closed only by climbing onto the sink, plus one air vent that is clogged with dirt. Ventilation is inadequate, producing extreme temperatures: 35–40 °C in summer (two privately purchased fans merely circulate hot air) and cold in winter (authorities supplied only one blanket; additional bedding and clothing came from NGOs, and heater requests were refused). The toilet must be flushed with a bucket because of low water pressure; filling the bucket is time-consuming and often requires more than one bucket, especially in summer. The 150-year-old building sheds dust from the ceiling that the applicant considers harmful to his lungs. Tap water is rusty and undrinkable, forcing him to buy bottled water. His prison job pays €0.60 per day; in summer he consumes three six-packs of water per week. The Government stated that he received €34.77 every four weeks from gratuity and a work-and-pay scheme (started in 2015) and that a six-pack cost €2.24 at the prison shop.

Mr Richard Andrews Perez Oberght, a Dominican national born in 1973, has been detained since 24 November 2009 and is serving a nine-year sentence imposed on 15 October 2012. Since 27 January 2012 he has occupied cell no. 155 in Division 3 (except for one day in Division 6). After the application was communicated he also declined a transfer. His window is more than two metres high, difficult and dangerous to open, and fitted with metal bars that obstruct natural light. Of two ventilation openings one is blocked, leaving ventilation insufficient. Tap water is undrinkable, so he must purchase bottled water; he received €41.58 every four weeks from gratuity and work-and-pay schemes. Ceiling dust (which the Government described as normal for Maltese limestone and which he never sought to paint over) aggravates his asthma. Humidity, combined with the absence of a heater, causes frequent winter flu; the Government attributed the humidity to the applicant blocking the vent with a towel and failing to maintain the cell. Lighting is poor for reading; the Government noted a ceiling light, a wall-mounted light, a privately acquired portable lamp, three skylights and 400-watt bell lamps. The applicant also complained that the spiral staircase would impede emergency evacuation (a stretcher could not be carried down it and two persons could not descend simultaneously); the Government pointed to alternative routes such as the walkway between divisions.

The applicants relied on the same domestic legal framework and international materials previously examined by the Court in Story and Others v. Malta and Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta. These facts formed the core of the Article 3 complaints concerning inadequate ventilation, extreme temperatures, unsanitary toilet and water facilities, dust, lighting and emergency access.
001-185229:
The case of N.K. v. Germany (Application no. 59549/12) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that his trial for violent offences against his wife, R.K., was unfair because neither he nor defence counsel had any opportunity to examine her as the sole direct witness.

In early August 2009, preliminary proceedings began on suspicion of violent acts by the applicant against R.K. On 6 August 2009, at the prosecutor’s request, investigating judge W. examined R.K. for approximately two hours. The judge excluded the applicant (then unrepresented) pursuant to Article 168c § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing a risk that R.K. would not testify or would not tell the truth in his presence. R.K. described an escalation of domestic violence over the weekend of 31 July–2 August 2009, including repeated beatings with fists, a wooden hiking pole, shoes and a thin rope, cigarette burns, choking, and coerced sexual acts, all linked to the applicant’s demand that she write a letter confessing adultery to a former lover’s wife. She maintained eye contact, gave consistent and detailed accounts, and explained that she had not previously reported the violence because she loved the applicant.

An arrest warrant issued the next day. The applicant was arrested on 25 September 2009 and counsel of his choice was assigned on 15 October 2009. At the opening of the main trial before the Arnsberg Regional Court on 3 May 2010, R.K. (who had been summoned) invoked her statutory privilege as the accused’s spouse and refused to give evidence. She later formally withheld consent to the use of her earlier statements.

At the hearing of 28 May 2010 the investigating judge testified in detail to R.K.’s 6 August account. Police officers Ra. and Rü. described finding R.K. in a state of shock on 2 August, bleeding from the head, and hearing her spontaneous statement that “her husband had beaten her.” Additional witnesses (neighbours S., Ke., M. and the Sch. family, R.K.’s son Re.K., and women’s-shelter counsellor N.) described R.K. fleeing the marital home in panic, shouting that her husband was going to kill her, seeking refuge, and displaying bleeding head wounds, facial bruising, burn marks on her breast and neck, and weals on her back. A handwritten draft of the demanded confession letter (given by R.K. to the police) and a later letter she wrote to the applicant recounting the assaults were admitted. R.K. had briefly recanted her accusations in December 2009 and April 2010, claiming a third party had injured her, but she withdrew those recantations before trial.

The Regional Court convicted the applicant on 28 June 2010 of multiple counts of dangerous assault, coercion and related offences, imposing six years and six months’ imprisonment plus subsequent preventive detention. It acknowledged that the applicant’s exclusion from R.K.’s examination, without counsel being present, had violated his confrontation rights, but held that the conviction could still rest on the investigating judge’s report because that evidence was corroborated by independent factors: the two letters, the injuries observed by N. and the police, the neighbours’ accounts of R.K.’s flight and the applicant’s immediate departure, and Re.K.’s hearing of an argument. The court treated R.K.’s initial remarks to the officers as a spontaneous utterance admissible despite her later silence, while discarding later police statements whose timing relative to the caution was unclear.

The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law (16 December 2010), finding no legal error. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit his constitutional complaint (4 April 2012). The applicant’s central contention remained that the untested testimony of the sole direct witness had been decisive and that no subsequent counterbalancing measures could cure the initial denial of confrontation.

The case of N.K. v. Germany (Application no. 59549/12) concerns a complaint by a German national, detained after conviction, that his trial was unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the ECHR. He alleged that neither he nor defence counsel had been able to examine R.K., his spouse and the sole direct witness to the offences of which the Arnsberg Regional Court convicted him.

Preliminary proceedings began in early August 2009 on suspicion of violent acts against R.K. On 6 August 2009 the investigating judge examined R.K. at the prosecutor’s request and excluded the applicant (under Article 168c § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) because of the risk that she would not testify truthfully in his presence. The applicant was arrested on 25 September 2009; counsel was assigned. When the Regional Court opened the main hearing in May 2010, R.K. refused to give evidence. The investigating judge then testified about her two-hour statement of 6 August 2009, in which she had given a detailed, consistent account of escalating domestic violence culminating in specific assaults between 31 July and 2 August 2009 (beatings with fists, a hiking pole, shoes and a rope; cigarette burns; forced writing of a letter confessing adultery; coerced sexual acts; choking). Police officers Ra. and Rü. also testified about her immediate statements to them upon their arrival at a neighbour’s house on 2 August. R.K. later withheld consent to the use of any of her prior statements or medical findings.

On 28 June 2010 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of four counts of dangerous assault (one concurrent with coercion), malicious infliction of bodily injury concurrent with attempted coercion, coercion, and driving without a licence. It imposed six years and six months’ imprisonment plus subsequent preventive detention. The court accepted that counsel should have been appointed for the 6 August examination, but held that the resulting limitation of confrontation rights did not automatically render the trial unfair. Conviction could rest on the untested evidence provided it was corroborated by independent significant factors. The court found such corroboration in: (i) a handwritten draft letter (which R.K. had given police) matching her description of the document the applicant had forced her to write; (ii) a 26 September 2009 letter from R.K. to the applicant recounting the same assaults; (iii) testimony of the women’s-shelter counsellor N., who on 2 August observed bleeding head wounds, burn marks on the breast and neck, bruises and weals, and heard a consistent account naming the applicant; (iv) the son Re.K.’s evidence that he had heard an argument and screaming; (v) independent witnesses (S., M. family, Sch. family) who saw R.K. flee in panic, bleeding from the head, shouting that her husband was trying to kill her, while the applicant drove away; and (vi) the officers’ account of her spontaneous utterance that her husband had beaten her (additional police statements were excluded because it was unclear when she had been cautioned). R.K.’s later retractions (claiming a third party had injured her) were rejected as untruthful.

The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law, finding no legal error. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit his constitutional complaint.

The applicant maintained that evidence obtained in breach of the confrontation right could never be used, irrespective of corroboration or the care taken in assessing it, and that the officers’ testimony was likewise inadmissible. The Government argued that independent corroboration and the Regional Court’s cautious evaluation of the untested evidence had preserved overall fairness.

The case of N.K. v. Germany concerns the applicant’s complaint that his criminal trial violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention because neither he nor counsel could examine R.K., his spouse and the sole direct witness to the alleged offences.

In early August 2009, preliminary proceedings began against N.K. for violent acts against R.K. On 6 August 2009, investigating judge W. examined R.K. at the prosecutor’s request, excluding N.K. under Article 168c § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure due to the risk that R.K. would not testify (or would not testify truthfully) in his presence. An arrest warrant issued the next day; counsel was assigned only after N.K.’s arrest on 25 September 2009. The Arnsberg Regional Court opened the main trial on 3 May 2010. R.K., summoned as a witness, invoked her statutory right as a spouse not to give evidence.

At the 28 May 2010 hearing the investigating judge recounted R.K.’s two-hour statement of 6 August 2009. She had described escalating domestic violence culminating in a weekend of beatings (with fists, a hiking pole, shoes and a rope), cigarette burns, choking and forced sexual acts, all linked to the applicant’s demand that she write a letter confessing adultery to a former lover’s wife. Defence counsel objected that the judge’s testimony could not be used because N.K. had been denied confrontation. The court held that admissibility would be decided only at judgment, depending on whether the account was corroborated by independent evidence.

Further evidence included:
- Police officers Ra. and Rü., who found R.K. bleeding and in shock on 2 August 2009; they reported her immediate statement that her husband had beaten her (admitted as a “spontaneous utterance”) but discarded later details because it was unclear when she had been cautioned.
- Neighbours S., M., the Sch. family and R.K.’s son, who described R.K. fleeing the house screaming for help, bleeding from the head, while the applicant drove away.
- Women’s-shelter counsellor N., who observed head wounds, burns on the breast and neck, bruises and weals, and heard a consistent account from R.K. naming the applicant.
- Two letters by R.K.: a draft confession recovered from the marital home and a later letter to the applicant detailing the assaults.

R.K. later made (and then retracted) voluntary disclosures claiming a third party had injured her and that the applicant had been absent.

On 28 June 2010 the Regional Court convicted N.K. of four counts of dangerous assault (one concurrent with coercion), malicious infliction of bodily injury concurrent with attempted coercion, coercion and driving without a licence. It imposed six years and six months’ imprisonment plus preventive detention. The court accepted that excluding both the applicant and counsel from R.K.’s judicial examination breached the confrontation right. It nevertheless admitted the investigating judge’s account because other independent evidence corroborated it: the letters, the injuries seen by N., the son’s account of an argument, and the neighbours’ observations of R.K.’s flight and the applicant’s departure. R.K.’s subsequent recantations were rejected as untruthful.

The Federal Court of Justice dismissed N.K.’s appeal on points of law (16 December 2010), holding that the trial remained fair because the untested evidence was corroborated and had been assessed with particular care. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit a constitutional complaint (4 April 2012).

N.K. maintained before the European Court that untested testimony obtained in breach of Article 6 § 3(d) could never be used, that the police statements were not spontaneous, and that the domestic courts’ “corroboration” test was insufficient.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Yordan Ivanov and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 70502/13) concerns nine Bulgarian nationals who were board members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden (UMO Ilinden), an association based in the Pirin region of southwest Bulgaria (also known as Pirin Macedonia). The first two applicants served as chairman and deputy chairman. They alleged that Bulgarian courts’ refusal to register Ilinden violated their right to freedom of association under the European Convention on Human Rights. They further claimed the refusal was discriminatory, stemming from the Bulgarian state’s policy of denying the existence of a Macedonian minority.

This refusal formed part of a long history of similar denials. Multiple prior ECHR judgments (including Stankov and UMO Ilinden v. Bulgaria (2001), UMO Ilinden and Ivanov v. Bulgaria (2005), UMO Ilinden-PIRIN and Others v. Bulgaria (2005), and later 2011 cases) had already found violations of Article 11 (freedom of assembly and association) due to repeated registration refusals and restrictions on Ilinden’s activities. Those cases established that Ilinden sought to promote Macedonian identity, cultural autonomy, and protection against alleged assimilation, using peaceful means.

In September 2010, 98 members held a founding meeting, adopted articles of association, elected bodies, and applied for registration as a non-profit association with the Blagoevgrad Regional Court. The court repeatedly requested corrections for deficiencies in the papers. In a February 2012 decision, it refused registration. It cited unresolved issues, such as unclear competences of bodies and inconsistencies among submitted versions of the articles. More substantively, it found Ilinden’s aims contravened Article 44 of the Bulgarian Constitution, which prohibits organisations directed against sovereignty, territorial integrity, national unity, or those stirring racial, national, ethnic or religious hatred, or violating others’ rights. Although Ilinden intended peaceful methods, the court held its goals—demanding that Bulgaria cease “assimilating Macedonians,” halt “nationalist propaganda” sowing hostility, stop blocking peaceful rallies, and end discrimination—threatened state security and would foster hostility between “discriminated Macedonians” and other citizens.

The applicants appealed, arguing the court misconstrued the articles (which did not seek to stir hatred) and that the true motive was disagreement with their views, contrary to official positions. Formal requirements were met.

In April 2012, the Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the refusal. It classified Ilinden’s aims as political, impermissible for associations under the Non-Profit Legal Persons Act 2000 and Article 12 of the Constitution (which reserves political activities forming citizens’ political will, such as elections, to parties). Specific clauses proclaimed Ilinden as successor to the “national liberation struggle of the Macedonian nation,” sought to protect Macedonians’ civic, political, national, social and economic rights, demanded cultural autonomy for Pirin Macedonia, an end to alleged ethnocide and assimilation, protection of Macedonian identity/language/traditions, and the outlawing of “Bulgarian racism.” These pitted groups against each other, engendered national/ethnic hatred, and undermined national unity, violating Article 44 § 2.

The applicants sought cassation review, reiterating arguments of breaches of freedom of conscience and association, and punishment for minority views. In April 2013, a Supreme Court of Cassation panel refused, holding that under the 2007 Code of Civil Procedure (unlike the prior 1952 Code, interpreted in 2001 to allow such appeals), no points-of-law appeal lay against appellate decisions in NGO registration cases. A further procedural appeal was dismissed in July 2013 as unfounded.

Domestic law underpins these decisions: associations cannot pursue party-like political goals; organisations threatening sovereignty/unity or stirring hatred are banned. The Committee of Ministers, supervising earlier judgments, expressed regret and deep concern over continued refusals on criticised grounds, placing execution under enhanced supervision.

These facts centre on the 2010–2013 registration process, where courts invoked constitutional prohibitions on political aims and hatred-stirring despite Ilinden’s peaceful stance and prior ECHR findings, alongside procedural barriers to further review.

The case of Yordan Ivanov and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 70502/13) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by nine Bulgarian nationals who formed the board of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden (“Ilinden”). Ilinden is based in Bulgaria’s Pirin region (also known as Pirin Macedonia). The applicants alleged that Bulgarian courts’ refusal to register Ilinden as a non-profit association violated their right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention. They further claimed the refusal was discriminatory under Article 14, reflecting an official policy of denying the existence of a Macedonian minority in Bulgaria.

This application followed a long series of earlier ECHR cases involving Ilinden, in which the Court had repeatedly found violations arising from refusals to register the organisation or restrictions on its activities. In September 2010, 98 members held a founding meeting, adopted articles of association, and elected governing bodies. On 27 September 2010 they applied to the Blagoevgrad Regional Court for registration.

The Regional Court repeatedly requested corrections to formal deficiencies in the papers. On 3 February 2012 it refused registration. It held that remaining defects (unclear competences of the organisation’s bodies and inconsistencies among submitted versions of the articles) had not been adequately remedied. More fundamentally, it found that Ilinden’s stated aims contravened Article 44 of the Bulgarian Constitution, which prohibits organisations whose activities are directed against the State’s sovereignty, territorial integrity or national unity, or which seek to stir up racial, national or ethnic hatred. Although the organisation intended to pursue its goals peacefully, the court considered the aims themselves—demanding an end to alleged assimilation of Macedonians, cessation of “nationalist propaganda,” cultural autonomy for Pirin Macedonia, and protection against “ethnocide”—to threaten State security and to foment hostility between “discriminated Macedonians” and other citizens.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the refusal on 23 April 2012. It characterised Ilinden’s aims as political and therefore impermissible for an association under the Non-Profit Legal Persons Act 2000 (Article 12 § 2 of the Constitution bars associations from pursuing political goals reserved to parties). Clauses in the articles proclaiming Ilinden as successor to a “national liberation struggle,” seeking to protect Macedonians’ political and national rights, and accusing the Bulgarian State of racism and assimilation were held to pit one group of citizens against another, thereby endangering national unity and generating ethnic hatred contrary to Article 44 § 2.

A three-judge panel refused to admit the appeal on 30 April 2013, holding that, under the 2007 Code of Civil Procedure (unlike the 1952 Code), appellate decisions upholding registration refusals were not subject to cassation. A further procedural appeal was dismissed on 15 July 2013.

Domestic law thus combined a constitutional prohibition on associations pursuing political or nationally divisive aims with a procedural bar on further judicial review. The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, supervising execution of earlier Ilinden judgments, expressed concern that the 2012–2013 refusals repeated grounds already criticised by the Court and placed those cases under enhanced supervision.

The case of X v. Sweden (Application no. 36417/16) was decided by a Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights on 9 January 2018 (final on 9 April 2018). The applicant, a Moroccan national identified only as X, alleged that his expulsion from Sweden to Morocco would violate Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) due to a real risk of ill-treatment as a suspected terrorist. An Article 8 complaint (right to respect for private and family life) was declared inadmissible. The Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 staying expulsion pending its examination.

The applicant obtained a temporary Swedish residence permit in 2005, made permanent in 2007, on the basis of family ties; he was never granted citizenship. In 2009 he married a non-Swedish national holding a permanent residence permit. In March 2016 the Swedish Security Service requested his expulsion under the Special Controls of Aliens Act, citing national-security concerns and a fear that he would commit or participate in a terrorist offence. During the ensuing examination the applicant applied for asylum, arguing that the Security Service’s branding of him as a terrorist would expose him to torture, forced confession and at least ten years’ imprisonment in Morocco. He described a visit to his parents in Morocco a few years earlier during which police officers told him they were monitoring him and advised him to “listen to our friends in Sweden or stay away from Morocco forever.” He acknowledged, however, that he had left Morocco legally on his own passport, was not wanted there, faced no pending proceedings, had never published on religion or politics, and that neither he nor his parents had been contacted by Moroccan authorities. He feared that Swedish or other sources would nevertheless inform Morocco of the expulsion grounds.

The Migration Agency granted the expulsion request on 22 April 2016, revoked the applicant’s residence permit, imposed a lifelong re-entry ban and rejected asylum. It noted significant improvements in Morocco’s human-rights situation, including reduced violence in detention and public statements that counter-terrorism must respect rights. Medical examinations of terror suspects before and after interrogation were now required. The Agency found the applicant lacked credibility because his account contradicted Security Service information. It stressed that he had lived inconspicuously in Sweden for a decade, had left Morocco legally after his last visit, had travelled internationally without incident as late as late 2015, and that no objective evidence showed Moroccan interest in him. The Agency also held that Swedish legislation was designed to avoid labelling risks and that no information indicated Morocco was aware of the Swedish proceedings.

The applicant appealed, complaining that the Agency had accepted the Security Service assessment without proper scrutiny. The Migration Court of Appeal, after an oral hearing, recommended that the Government uphold the decision, finding nothing to show the applicant was known to or of interest to Moroccan authorities. On 8 September 2016 the Government confirmed the expulsion, accepting the Security Service’s assessment of the applicant’s background and concluding that there were reasonable grounds to fear terrorist activity. Enforcement was subsequently stayed following the Court’s interim measure.

Domestic law (Aliens Act and Special Controls of Aliens Act) permits expulsion of aliens who pose a national-security threat or who may commit terrorist offences, subject to an absolute bar on removal where there are substantial grounds for believing the person would face torture or inhuman treatment. Appeals in security cases go to the Government after an opinion from the Migration Court of Appeal on any enforcement impediment.

Country material before the Court (UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention 2014, UN Human Rights Committee 2016, US State Department 2016) acknowledged Morocco’s constitutional and institutional reforms and a reduction in torture overall, but recorded a persistent pattern of torture, incommunicado detention, coerced confessions and lengthy sentences in terrorism and national-security cases, together with a vague anti-terrorism law and restricted access to lawyers.

These facts formed the core of the Article 3 claim: whether the applicant’s identification by Swedish security authorities as a terrorism risk, combined with Morocco’s documented practices toward such suspects, created a real risk of ill-treatment upon return.

**CASE OF X v. SWEDEN (Application no. 36417/16), ECtHR (Third Section), Judgment of 9 January 2018 (final 9 April 2018)**

The applicant, a Moroccan national (anonymised), had lived in Sweden since receiving a temporary residence permit in 2005 (made permanent in 2007) on family-tie grounds; he was not granted citizenship. In 2009 he married a non-Swedish holder of a permanent Swedish residence permit. In March 2016 the Swedish Security Service applied to the Migration Agency for his expulsion under the Special Controls of Aliens Act, citing national-security concerns and a fear that he would commit or participate in terrorist offences.

The applicant sought asylum, arguing that the Security Service’s branding of him as a terrorist would expose him in Morocco to torture, a forced false confession and at least ten years’ imprisonment. He described an earlier visit to his parents in Morocco during which police told him they were monitoring him and advised him to “listen to our friends in Sweden or stay away from Morocco forever.” He acknowledged leaving Morocco legally on his own passport, never having been wanted or subject to proceedings there, never having published on religion or politics, and that neither his parents nor the Moroccan authorities had ever contacted him in Sweden. He relied on country reports of ill-treatment, arbitrary detention and tortured confessions of suspected terrorists, as well as the Court’s case-law.

On 22 April 2016 the Migration Agency granted the expulsion request, rejected asylum, revoked the residence permit and imposed a lifelong re-entry ban. It found Morocco’s human-rights situation much improved, with reduced police/prison violence, legal prohibition of torture and medical examinations of terror suspects before and after interrogation. The applicant lacked credibility (his account contradicted Security Service information) and had not shown any prior Moroccan interest: he had lived inconspicuously in Sweden for a decade, left Morocco legally, travelled internationally in late 2015 without incident, and neither he nor his parents had been approached. No objective evidence indicated Moroccan awareness of the Swedish proceedings; Swedish law was designed to avoid the risks of a “terrorist” label.

The applicant appealed, complaining that the Agency had uncritically accepted the Security Service assessment, rendering the process unfair, and reiterating the prevalence of torture of suspected terrorists. After an oral hearing the Migration Court of Appeal recommended that the Government uphold the decision, finding nothing to show the applicant was known to or of interest to the Moroccan authorities. On 8 September 2016 the Government confirmed the expulsion, accepting the Security Service’s information on the applicant’s background and concluding that there were reasonable grounds to fear he would commit or participate in a terrorist offence.

Following the Court’s indication under Rule 39, the Government stayed enforcement. Relevant Swedish law (Aliens Act and Special Controls of Aliens Act) permits expulsion on national-security or terrorism-risk grounds but prohibits removal where there is a real risk of torture or inhuman treatment; security cases follow a special procedure culminating in a Government decision after an opinion from the Migration Court of Appeal.

Contemporary UN and US reports acknowledged Moroccan reforms (2011 Constitution, National Human Rights Council, reduced overall torture, training of officials) but documented persistent problems in terrorism/national-security cases: vague anti-terror legislation, prolonged incommunicado detention (up to 12 days), delayed access to counsel, a pattern of torture and ill-treatment to extract confessions that were then used as virtually the sole evidence, and incomplete implementation of medical-examination and investigation safeguards.

(The Article 8 complaint was declared inadmissible; only the Article 3 expulsion complaint was communicated.)

The facts centre on whether the Swedish authorities’ risk assessment adequately addressed the specific danger that a person publicly identified by a Western security service as a terrorism suspect would face upon return to Morocco.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of X, a Moroccan national residing in Sweden, who alleged that his expulsion to Morocco would expose him to a real risk of torture or inhuman treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention (the Article 8 complaint having been declared inadmissible). X had obtained a temporary residence permit in Sweden in 2005, converted to permanent status in 2007 on family grounds, and later married a person holding a Swedish permanent residence permit. He was never granted citizenship.

In March 2016 the Swedish Security Service requested his expulsion on national-security grounds under the Special Controls of Aliens Act, asserting that his background and connections gave rise to a reasonable fear that he would commit or participate in a terrorist offence. During the ensuing proceedings X applied for asylum. He claimed that the Security Service’s “terrorist” branding would become known to the Moroccan authorities, exposing him to torture, a forced confession and at least ten years’ imprisonment. He described a visit to his parents in Morocco a few years earlier during which police officers told him they were monitoring him and warned him to heed “our friends in Sweden or stay away from Morocco forever.” He acknowledged, however, that he had left Morocco legally on his own passport, was not wanted there, faced no pending proceedings, had never published political or religious material, and that neither he nor his parents had been contacted by the Moroccan authorities after his departure. He relied on general country reports of torture and lengthy detention of suspected terrorists.

On 22 April 2016 the Migration Agency granted the expulsion request, revoked the residence permit, imposed a lifelong re-entry ban and rejected asylum. It accepted the Security Service’s assessment, found X’s account of his background inconsistent and lacking credibility, and noted that he had lived an inconspicuous life in Sweden for a decade without political or religious activity. There was no evidence that the Moroccan authorities were aware of or interested in him: he had travelled internationally on his passport as recently as late 2015 without incident, his parents had not been approached, and no extradition request had ever been made. The Agency observed that Morocco’s human-rights situation had improved, torture was illegal, and medical examinations were now required before and after interrogation in terrorism cases.

X appealed, arguing that the Agency had uncritically adopted the Security Service’s secret assessment and that torture remained frequent in Moroccan terrorism investigations. The Migration Court of Appeal, after an oral hearing, shared the Agency’s reasoning and recommended that the Government uphold the decision. On 8 September 2016 the Government did so, concluding that X’s known activities justified a fear of terrorist involvement and that no impediment to expulsion existed. Following the Court’s indication of an interim measure under Rule 39, enforcement was stayed.

Swedish law channels “security cases” through a special procedure: the Migration Agency’s decision is appealed directly to the Government, which receives a non-binding but influential opinion from the Migration Court of Appeal on whether Chapter 12 of the Aliens Act (prohibition of expulsion to a country where there is a real risk of capital punishment, torture or persecution) is engaged. The Security Service may withhold sources and methods on confidentiality grounds.

Country material before the Court presented a mixed picture. The 2011 Constitution and the creation of the National Human Rights Council were welcomed, and reports noted a reduction in routine police violence. Nevertheless, UN bodies (Working Group on Arbitrary Detention 2014; Human Rights Committee 2016) and the U.S. State Department (2016) documented a continuing pattern of incommunicado detention of up to 12 days, restricted access to counsel, coerced confessions and ill-treatment specifically in terrorism and national-security cases, with convictions often based solely on such confessions. These were the facts against which the alleged Article 3 risk had to be assessed.

The applicant, Anita Oller Kamińska (a Polish national living in Ireland), and her husband M.K. had a daughter, A, born in Poland in March 2000. The family relocated to Ireland in 2006 but separated in January 2009, after which M.K. returned to Poland. In June 2009 M.K. took A to Poland for the summer holidays, promising to return her by 15 August. The applicant, fearing non-return, obtained an Irish Ennis District Court interim order on 2 July 2009 confirming A’s habitual residence in Ireland and permitting the visit until 15 August, with a certificate of enforceability under the Brussels II bis Regulation. M.K. did not return A.

On 15 September 2009 the Ennis court granted the applicant sole custody, ordered A’s return, and issued another Brussels II bis certificate. M.K.’s appeal was dismissed in December 2009. The Irish High Court later issued a superseding judgment on 9 September 2011 granting joint custody but still ordering A’s return to Ireland by 2 November 2011 (with A to finish the Irish school year before starting school in Poland from September 2012). M.K. unsuccessfully appealed that order.

Meanwhile, in Poland the applicant sought A’s return under the 1980 Hague Convention. The Malbork District Court rejected the application on 18 December 2009 under Article 13, citing expert reports that A (then aged 9) wished to remain in Poland, was closer to her father, and would face psychological harm if returned. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in May 2010.

The applicant also sought enforcement of the September 2009 Irish order. The Gdańsk Regional Court declared it enforceable in December 2009, but the Court of Appeal quashed that decision in June 2010, holding it irreconcilable with the Hague refusal. The Supreme Court quashed the latter ruling in August 2011, clarifying that a Hague Article 13 refusal does not constitute a custody determination and thus cannot block Brussels II bis enforcement; it remitted the case. The Court of Appeal then refused enforcement in February 2012 because of the new 2011 Irish judgment.

Enforcement of the 2011 Irish order was requested in October 2011. After delays in transmission between central authorities and a May 2012 hearing (at which M.K. cited A’s psychological state), the Malbork District Court ordered A’s immediate removal by a guardian on 28 June 2012. Three attempts in July 2012 failed because the home was empty; police intervention was sought. On 7 September 2012 the court discontinued proceedings, wrongly treating the return obligation as expired once the Polish school year began. That decision was later quashed. On 26 September 2012 the applicant collected A from school and took her to Ireland.

Contact between the applicant and A had been minimal after August 2009 (none for three months, thereafter only brief or supervised meetings). Parallel Polish divorce proceedings produced an interim order in July 2011 placing A with M.K. After A’s return, Irish proceedings produced a June 2013 agreement giving the applicant sole custody for a year with defined access for M.K.; the Polish divorce court later declined to rule on custody in light of that agreement. M.K. also unsuccessfully sought A’s return to Poland.

These events spanned more than three years of overlapping, delayed Polish proceedings that failed to secure prompt enforcement of the Irish return orders.

The case of Oller Kamińska v. Poland (Application no. 28481/12) was brought by Anita Oller Kamińska, a Polish national residing in Ireland, against Poland under the European Convention on Human Rights. She alleged violations of Articles 6 (fair trial) and 8 (respect for family life) due to the Polish authorities' failure to promptly enforce Irish court orders reuniting her with her daughter A after abduction by the child's father, M.K.

A was born in Poland on 27 March 2000 to the applicant and M.K., to whom she was married. The family, including the applicant's son B from a prior relationship, relocated to Ireland in 2006. The couple separated in January 2009, with M.K. returning to Poland. In June 2009, M.K. took A to Poland for summer holidays but failed to return her by 15 August 2009, as required.

The Ennis District Court in Ireland issued a 2 July 2009 consent order confirming A's habitual residence in Ireland and permitting the visit until 15 August. On 15 September 2009, it granted the applicant sole custody, ordered A's residence in Ireland, and directed her return, with a certificate of enforceability under the Brussels II bis Regulation. M.K.'s appeal was dismissed in December 2009.

The applicant sought A's return via Poland's Central Authority under the 1980 Hague Convention on International Child Abduction. On 18 December 2009, the Malbork District Court refused, invoking Article 13 (grave risk of harm or intolerable situation), based on expert reports from the Regional Family Consultation Centre indicating A's preference to stay in Poland (where she was nine and deemed mature), M.K.'s closer bond, and the applicant's actions causing discomfort. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 18 May 2010, emphasizing A's wishes.

Concurrently, the applicant applied on 15 October 2009 to enforce the Irish order. The Gdańsk Regional Court granted this on 4 December 2009, but the Court of Appeal quashed it on 22 June 2010, finding it irreconcilable with the Polish Hague refusal. The Supreme Court quashed that ruling on 24 August 2011, remitting the case: it held that Hague non-return decisions under Articles 12/13/20 do not determine custody (per Article 10 Hague and Article 23(e) Brussels II bis) and that EU rules apply directly. On 28 February 2012, the Court of Appeal refused enforcement due to a superseding Irish High Court judgment of 9 September 2011.

That Irish High Court decision granted joint custody but ordered A's return by 2 November 2011, with her finishing the school year in Ireland before starting in Poland from September 2012, plus specified holiday access. M.K.'s appeals failed.

Enforcement of the 2011 order in Poland, lodged in October 2011, involved delays, including Central Authority correspondence and a 4 May 2012 guardian interview where A (now on antidepressants due to parental conflict) wished to remain in Poland with Skype contact. On 28 June 2012, the Malbork District Court ordered immediate removal by a guardian under Article 598§6 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Three July attempts failed as the home was empty; police intervention was sought. On 7 September 2012, the court discontinued proceedings, holding the return obligation expired on 31 August 2012 (as A was to start Polish school). This was quashed on 12 November 2012.

The applicant independently retrieved A from school on 26 September 2012 and returned to Ireland. Post-return Irish proceedings led to a June 2013 agreement granting her sole custody for a year with limited access for M.K.

Parallel Polish proceedings included M.K.'s 2009 divorce action (stayed initially) and a 4 July 2011 interim order awarding him custody, citing A's settlement in Poland, school performance, and uncertainty from dual proceedings. The 30 October 2013 divorce decree (mutual fault) deferred custody/access to the Irish agreement.

After the August 2009 abduction, the applicant had no contact for three months, then limited supervised or sporadic visits (e.g., court interviews, a May 2010 trip, 2011 birthday). A has lived with her in Ireland since September 2012.

These events—Hague refusals treating non-return as custody, conflicting rulings, delayed enforcement of Brussels II bis orders, failed removals, and over three years of separation with restricted contact—form the core of the alleged Article 8 violation (ineffective family reunification) and Article 6 claims (procedural delays/inefficiency).

A psychological report in August 2011 noted both parents’ capabilities but recommended considering A.’s wish to attend school in Poland. On 9 September 2011, the High Court granted joint custody but ordered A.’s return to Ireland by 2 November 2011, with her to complete the school year there before starting in Poland from September 2012. M.K.’s appeal failed.

The applicant sought enforcement of this order in Poland. After correspondence between central authorities, Malbork District Court on 28 June 2012 ordered A.’s immediate removal by a guardian. Attempts on 6, 9, and 13 July 2012 failed as the home was empty; police intervention was requested. On 7 September 2012, the court discontinued proceedings, holding the return right had expired on 31 August 2012 since A. was to start school in Poland. Gdańsk Regional Court quashed this on 12 November 2012. On 26 September 2012, the applicant collected A. herself and returned to Ireland.

Subsequent Polish proceedings included M.K.’s unsuccessful bid for A.’s return (with jurisdictional disputes) and divorce, in which an interim custody order favoured M.K. in 2011; the 2013 divorce judgment deferred to an Irish agreement. After the 2009 abduction, the applicant had no contact for three months, followed by limited visits. A. has lived with the applicant in Ireland since September 2012.

These facts highlight prolonged Polish delays in Hague and enforcement proceedings, unsuccessful removal attempts, and conflicting rulings that prevented swift reunion despite Irish orders.

The applicant, Miguel Cuenca Zarzoso (born 1930), has resided in Valencia’s San José district since 1962. From 1974, the City Council licensed numerous bars, pubs and discotheques nearby. A 1983 resolution to halt further licences was never implemented. A 1993 municipal study confirmed weekend night-time noise far exceeded legal limits.

As president of the neighbourhood association from 1994, the applicant repeatedly complained and sought licence withdrawals. The Council replied that some premises were inactive, others (e.g., bakeries) were not noisy, and many licences had expired. In 1996 it adopted a Noise and Vibrations Ordinance and designated the area an “acoustically saturated zone.” A pub in the applicant’s building basement was later required to install a limiter, yet noise persisted. The applicant installed double glazing and air-conditioning.

In 1999 he filed a State-liability claim citing constitutional rights to physical integrity and inviolability of the home, seeking compensation for expenses and damage. After administrative silence, he sued in the Valencia High Court (2001). He submitted municipal reports (1998, 2000) showing night-time levels still exceeded the Ordinance even after designation; an expert estimated indoor bedroom noise at 50–60 dBA against the Council’s 30 dBA night-time recommendation; and a medical report linking his anxiety to the noise. A court-appointed expert confirmed sleep disturbance causing an “anxious-depressive syndrome.”

The Council argued that indoor levels had not been measured in the applicant’s fourth-floor flat and that it actively enforced noise rules. The High Court dismissed the claim in 2003, finding no proven causal link because the applicant had not commissioned an indoor measurement as the Ordinance required and noise would be weaker on an upper floor.

An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was initially rejected (2004). After the European Court’s Moreno Gómez v. Spain judgment (identical neighbouring facts, Art. 8 violation), the public prosecutor successfully sought admission. In 2011 the Constitutional Court (by majority) rejected the appeal, distinguishing the cases, noting the absence of indoor measurements, crediting the Council’s remedial steps, and finding no proven health causation. Three dissenters argued that, after Moreno Gómez, proof of street-level saturation plus health effects sufficed.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 8 violation: prolonged, officially acknowledged night-time noise from licensed premises that the authorities failed to abate, forcing the applicant to live with windows sealed and causing documented sleep disruption and psychiatric harm.

The case of *Cuenca Zarzoso v. Spain* (Application no. 23383/12) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life and home). The applicant, Miguel Cuenca Zarzoso (born 1930), a resident of Valencia’s San José district since 1962, claimed that excessive night-time noise from nearby licensed premises (bars, pubs and discotheques) interfered with his home life and health. Valencia City Council had permitted such establishments in the area since 1974. A 1983 Council resolution to halt further licences was never implemented. A 1993 municipal study confirmed night-time weekend noise levels significantly exceeded legal norms.

In 1994 the applicant, as neighbourhood association president, lodged complaints seeking licence withdrawals. The Council responded that some premises were inactive, others (e.g., bakeries) were not noisy, and many licences had expired. In June 1996 the Council adopted an Ordinance on noise and vibrations setting night-time limits of 45 dB(A) externally for residential areas. In December 1996 the applicant’s neighbourhood was designated an “acoustically saturated zone.” In 2000, at his request, a basement pub in his building was required to install a noise limiter. Persistent noise led the applicant to install double glazing and air-conditioning.

On 14 June 1999 he filed a preliminary State-liability claim with the Council, invoking constitutional rights to life/physical integrity and inviolability of the home, seeking compensation for expenses plus pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. After administrative silence, he applied to the Valencia High Court of Justice in December 2001. Supporting evidence included municipal reports (April 1998 and March 2000) showing night-time levels still exceeded 65 dB (and Ordinance limits) even after the saturated-zone declaration; an expert physics report estimating street noise at ~70 dB, indoor bedroom levels of 50–60 dBA against a recommended 30 dBA night-time maximum; a medical report linking the applicant’s anxiety to indoor noise; and a court-appointed medical expert confirming sleep disturbance causing an “anxious-depressive syndrome.”

The Council argued that indoor levels in the applicant’s fourth-floor flat had not been specifically measured and that it actively enforced noise rules. On 20 June 2003 the High Court dismissed the claim, finding no proven causal link or evidence that limits were exceeded inside the particular flat (the applicant having failed to request an indoor measurement under the Ordinance).

Following the ECHR’s November 2004 *Moreno Gómez v. Spain* judgment (a neighbour’s similar noise case finding an Article 8 violation), the public prosecutor successfully sought reconsideration. The Constitutional Court, however, dismissed the appeal on 29 September 2011 (served 19 October 2011). It held the cases distinguishable, that indoor exceedance and a direct causal health link remained unproven, and that the Council had taken remedial measures. Three dissenting judges argued that *Moreno Gómez* established that location in a notoriously noisy area plus proof of street-level exceedance sufficed, that indoor measurements were unnecessary, and that expert evidence confirmed health effects from avoidable, prolonged noise that prevented normal life.

The applicant then applied to the ECHR on 13 April 2012, alleging an Article 8 breach through the authorities’ failure to protect his home from persistent, officially acknowledged noise pollution.

The case of Cuenca Zarzoso v. Spain (no. 23383/12) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for the home) arising from prolonged nighttime noise pollution in a Valencia residential area.

The applicant, born in 1930, has lived in the San José district since 1962. From 1974 the City Council licensed bars, pubs and discotheques nearby. A 1983 resolution barring further licences was never implemented. A 1993 official study confirmed weekend night-time levels far above legal limits.

In 1996 it adopted a Noise Ordinance (night-time residential limit 45 dB(A)) and designated the district an “acoustically saturated zone.” In 2000 a pub in the applicant’s basement was ordered to fit a limiter.

Noise persisted, so the applicant installed double glazing and air-conditioning. In 1999 he filed a State-liability claim invoking constitutional rights to physical integrity and inviolability of the home, seeking compensation. After silence he sued in the Valencia High Court (2001).

He produced municipal reports (1998, 2000) showing night-time levels still exceeding 65 dB and Ordinance limits after the designation; an expert report estimating 70 dB in the street and 50–60 dBA inside bedrooms (versus a 30 dBA recommendation); a medical report linking his anxiety to the noise; and a court-appointed expert confirming sleep disruption that produced an anxious-depressive syndrome.

The Council denied that noise inside the applicant’s fourth-floor flat had been proved and pointed to enforcement efforts. The High Court dismissed the claim on 20 June 2003 for lack of indoor measurements and of a causal link.

An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was initially rejected but later admitted after the ECHR’s 2004 Moreno Gómez judgment (identical neighbouring facts, Article 8 violation). These facts—official recognition of saturation, repeated documented exceedances, limited and ineffective measures, and unsuccessful domestic remedies—form the basis of the alleged Article 8 breach.
