The case of Andrey Smirnov v. Russia (no. 43149/10) was brought by a Russian national born in 1992 who alleged that his pre-trial detention lacked relevant and sufficient justification and that parental visits were excessively restricted in frequency and manner.

On 7 May 2009 the applicant (then aged 16–17) and a classmate were arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm on another schoolboy. They confessed but retracted the following day. The applicant was released under parental supervision. After the charges were reclassified as a more serious offence, the Zavolzhskiy District Court on 16 November 2009 ordered his detention, citing the gravity of the charges and the recantation as evidencing a risk of obstructing justice. The Tver Regional Court upheld the order on 11 December 2009, holding that the applicant’s permanent residence, family life, schooling and clean record did not outweigh the extreme gravity of the charges.

Detention was extended on 12 January 2010 because the applicant had shifted from acknowledgement to denial, implying a risk of interference, and to secure any eventual conviction; the Regional Court confirmed this on 3 February 2010. Further extensions on 3 February and 11 March 2010 relied solely on the gravity of the charges against both co-defendants and contained no individualised assessment.

On 20 January 2010 the investigator refused the parents’ request for a visit, asserting that the father (appointed legal representative) was obstructing the investigation by ignoring summonses and causing delays, which could negatively influence the applicant. The supervising prosecutor rejected the father’s complaint, noting that visits were discretionary and the refusal well-founded.

The applicant was convicted of attempted murder on 25 March 2010 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment (upheld by the Supreme Court on 9 June 2010). Between November 2009 and July 2010 his parents visited him 16 times; every visit occurred under warden supervision and behind a glass partition.

Domestic law (s. 18 of the Pre-trial Detention Act) permits a maximum of two supervised visits per month, each of up to three hours, subject to written authorisation. Internal prison rules require purpose-built rooms with partitions that prevent physical contact while allowing visual and oral communication via intercom, which may be monitored. The Constitutional Court has characterised such limitations as inevitable consequences of custody, provided refusals are reasoned and subject to challenge.

International standards applicable to juveniles (UN Rules for the Protection of Juveniles Deprived of their Liberty and the European Rules for juvenile offenders) stress the importance of regular, frequent family contact (in principle weekly) in conditions that respect privacy and unrestricted communication, with any restrictions remaining compatible with an acceptable minimum level of contact.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that his detention violated Article 5 and that the visit regime violated Article 8 of the Convention.

The case of Andrey Smirnov v. Russia (Application no. 43149/10) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 13 February 2018 (final 13 May 2018). The applicant, a Russian national born in 1992 and resident in Tver, alleged violations of the Convention arising from his pre-trial detention (lacking relevant and sufficient reasons) and excessive restrictions on the frequency and conditions of visits by his parents.

On 7 May 2009, the applicant (then a minor) and classmate A. were arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm to a schoolboy. Both initially confessed; the applicant was released under parental supervision while A. was detained. They retracted their statements the next day. After reclassification of the offence as more serious, the Zavolzhskiy District Court in Tver on 16 November 2009 ordered the applicant's detention, citing the gravity of the charges and his recantation (viewed as indicating a risk of obstructing justice). The Tver Regional Court upheld this on 11 December 2009, holding that the applicant's stable residence, family life, schooling, and lack of criminal record did not outweigh the charges' gravity.

Further extensions followed. On 12 January 2010 the District Court prolonged detention, noting the applicant's shift from confession to denial as implying a risk of interference with justice and the need to secure eventual enforcement of any conviction; this was upheld on appeal on 3 February 2010. Additional extensions on 3 February and 11 March 2010 again relied primarily on the seriousness of the charges (the latter without distinguishing the co-defendants' situations). The applicant was convicted on 25 March 2010 of attempted murder and sentenced to five years' imprisonment (upheld by the Supreme Court on 9 June 2010).

Regarding family contact, the investigator on 20 January 2010 refused the parents' request for a visit. He reasoned that the father (appointed legal representative) had vested interests, ignored summonses, caused delays, and risked negatively influencing the applicant or obstructing the truth. A prosecutor rejected the father's complaint, treating visits as discretionary and the refusal as justified. Between November 2009 and July 2010 the parents made 16 supervised visits, each conducted with a glass partition and warden present (no physical contact).

Domestic law (Pre-trial Detention Act, section 18, and remand-prison rules) limited visits to two per month of up to three hours, requiring written authorisation valid for one visit, restricting visitors to two adults, and mandating partitions or separators, intercom communication, and possible monitoring. The Constitutional Court regarded such limits as inherent to custody, provided refusals were reasoned and reviewable. International standards for juveniles (UN Rules and Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2008)11) emphasise frequent, regular, private family contact (ideally weekly, at least monthly) to maintain relationships and prepare for reintegration, subject only to necessary, proportionate restrictions that preserve an acceptable minimum of contact.

These facts formed the basis of the communicated complaints concerning the lawfulness and justification of the applicant's pre-trial detention and the compatibility of the visit regime with respect for family life. The remainder of the original application was declared inadmissible.

The case of Andrey Smirnov v. Russia (Application no. 43149/10) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Russian national born in 1992. The applicant alleged that his pre-trial detention lacked relevant and sufficient reasons and that restrictions on the frequency and conditions of visits from his parents were excessive.

On 7 May 2009 the applicant, then a minor, and a classmate were arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily injuries on a schoolboy. They initially confessed; the applicant was released under parental supervision while his co-suspect was remanded. Both retracted their confessions the following day. After the investigator reclassified the acts as a more serious offence, the Zavolzhskiy District Court on 16 November 2009 ordered the applicant’s detention. The court relied on the gravity of the charges and the recantation, which it treated as evidence of a risk that the applicant would obstruct justice. The Tver Regional Court upheld the order on 11 December 2009, stating that the applicant’s stable residence, family ties, schooling and lack of a criminal record did not outweigh the extreme gravity of the charges.

On 12 January 2010 the District Court extended detention, noting that the applicant had shifted from “outright acknowledgement” to “downright denial” and inferring a risk of interference with the investigation; it also cited the need “to secure the enforcement of the conviction.” The Regional Court confirmed this reasoning on 3 February 2010. A further extension on 3 February 2010 again invoked the particularly serious nature of the offence and the persistence of the original grounds; it was upheld on 19 February. The last pre-trial extension, issued on 11 March 2010, referred only to the gravity of the charges against both co-defendants without differentiating their situations.

On 25 March 2010 the Regional Court convicted both defendants of attempted murder and sentenced each to five years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court of the Russian Federation dismissed their appeals on 9 June 2010.

Regarding family contact, the investigator refused the parents’ request for a visit on 20 January 2010. The decision stated that the applicant’s father, appointed as legal representative, had used “all means to interfere” with the proceedings, ignored summonses, caused delays and might exert a negative influence capable of obstructing the establishment of the truth. The supervising prosecutor dismissed a complaint, observing that visits were discretionary and that the investigator’s reasons were persuasive. Between November 2009 and July 2010 the parents were nevertheless allowed sixteen visits, all conducted under warden supervision and through a glass partition.

Domestic law (section 18 of the 1995 Pre-trial Detention Act and the 2005 Internal Rules) limited pre-trial detainees to two authorised visits per month of up to three hours, required written permission valid for a single visit, and mandated physical separation and monitoring. The Constitutional Court had held such restrictions to be inevitable consequences of custody, provided refusals were reasoned and subject to review. International instruments applicable to juveniles (UN Rules for the Protection of Juveniles Deprived of their Liberty and Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2008)11) emphasised the need for frequent, regular and private family contact as essential to humane treatment and reintegration, permitting only narrowly justified limitations that still guaranteed an acceptable minimum of contact.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints that the detention orders failed to rest on concrete, individualised grounds and that the visit regime was both quantitatively and qualitatively disproportionate for a juvenile detainee.
001-180506:
**CASE OF SEKMADIENIS LTD. v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 69317/14)**

In September–October 2012, Lithuanian clothing company Sekmadienis Ltd. ran a two-week advertising campaign for designer R.K.’s clothing line. Three visual advertisements appeared on 20 public hoardings in Vilnius and the designer’s website. The first depicted a long-haired young man with a headband, halo and tattoos wearing jeans, captioned “Jesus, what trousers!” The second showed a young woman in a white dress and flowered headdress with a halo, holding beads, captioned “Dear Mary, what a dress!” The third featured both figures together (man reclining, woman’s hands on him), captioned “Jesus [and] Mary, what are you wearing!”

The State Consumer Rights Protection Authority (SCRPA) received four telephone complaints that the ads were unethical and offensive to religious people, plus a law-firm complaint that they degraded religious symbols, offended believers and threatened society’s sense of sacredness. The Lithuanian Advertising Agency (a self-regulatory body) found by 5–2 that the ads breached its ethics code on decency and religion, as they could humiliate people of faith; humour had “gone too far.” The State Inspectorate of Non-Food Products notified the company of a possible breach of Article 4 § 2(1) of the Law on Advertising (banning ads contrary to public morals), citing disrespectful use of religious symbols.

The company argued that “Jesus,” “Mary” and “Jesus [and] Mary” were common Lithuanian emotional interjections that had lost exclusive religious meaning; the figures were not unambiguous religious depictions and were aesthetically presented; Lithuania had no state religion, so Catholic interests could not be equated with society’s; and the Advertising Agency’s view was emotional, not factual. Holding otherwise would harm freedom of expression.

The Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference (consulted by SCRPA) stated that the ads referenced sacred objects (rosary, names of Jesus and Mary, Pietà-like pose). Christ and Mary embodied Christian ethical values; their inappropriate (tattooed, commercial) depiction encouraged a frivolous attitude, degraded sacred symbols, offended believers and was contrary to public morals.

On 21 March 2013 SCRPA found a violation. It held that the combined elements would make an average consumer associate the images with religious symbols. Religious people react sensitively to such use (especially tattoos); using God’s name commercially exceeded tolerance; the depiction encouraged a lifestyle incompatible with religious principles and actually offended (complaints plus ~100 letters to the Bishops). Respect for religion was a moral value. A fine of LTL 2,000 (~EUR 580) was imposed—near the legal minimum—after considering public display, limited duration/location, the company’s cooperation, prompt removal and lack of prior violations.

The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed the company’s challenge, holding that the ads distorted the purpose of respected religious symbols. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this, finding the ads “clearly contrary to public morals” because religion shapes societal morals and inappropriate commercial use of its symbols demeans them. A letter from nearly 100 people confirmed offence. The company had cited other ads using religious imagery that were not banned and argued the ads used wordplay without hatred or direct degradation.

The President of the Supreme Administrative Court sought reopening to examine whether freedom of expression (Constitution and ECHR) had been properly balanced for necessity and proportionality. A different panel refused, finding no manifest error: the restriction balanced expression against public morals (the latter prevailing), the fine was modest, the ads were purely commercial (not contributing to public debate on religion), a margin of appreciation applied given Catholicism’s prevalence, and the distorted symbols had offended believers.

The company applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging an Article 10 violation through the fine for ads deemed contrary to public morals. (Word count: 512)

**Sekmadienis Ltd. v. Lithuania (ECHR, 2018) concerned a Lithuanian clothing company's fine for advertisements using imagery and language evoking Christian figures, alleged to violate Article 10 (freedom of expression).**

In September–October 2012, Sekmadienis Ltd. ran a two-week campaign for designer R.K.'s clothing line. Three visual ads appeared on 20 public hoardings in Vilnius and a website. The first showed a long-haired young man with a headband, halo and tattoos wearing jeans, captioned “Jesus, what trousers!” The second depicted a young woman in a white dress and floral headdress with a halo, holding beads, captioned “Dear Mary, what a dress!” The third showed both figures together in a pose resembling the Pietà, captioned “Jesus [and] Mary, what are you wearing!”

The State Consumer Rights Protection Authority (SCRPA) received telephone complaints that the ads were unethical and offensive to religious people, plus a written complaint from a Kaunas law firm claiming they degraded religious symbols, risked eroding respect for spirituality, and violated public order and morals. The Lithuanian Advertising Agency (a self-regulatory body) opined by majority that the ads breached its ethics code on decency and religion, potentially humiliating people of faith and going “too far”; it recommended changing the characters.

The State Inspectorate of Non-Food Products notified the company of a possible breach of Article 4 § 2(1) of the Law on Advertising (banning ads contrary to public morals), citing disrespectful use of religious symbols. The company responded that “Jesus” functioned as a common Lithuanian emotional interjection (like “oh my God”), that the figures were not unambiguously religious or disrespectful (unlike kitschy market items), that Lithuania has no state religion so Catholic interests could not be equated with society’s, and that the agency opinion was emotional rather than factual. It invoked constitutional freedom of expression.

The Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference (Roman Catholic territorial authority) stated that the ads referenced sacred objects (rosary, names of Jesus and Mary, Pietà), degraded Christ and Mary as ethical symbols, encouraged a frivolous attitude incompatible with religious principles, and offended the faithful—especially for commercial gain—thus violating public morals. It cited nearly 100 complaints.

After a hearing, the SCRPA found a violation. It held that the combined elements created an impression of religious symbols for the average consumer; religious people react sensitively (especially to tattoos on the figures); commercial use exceeded tolerance; the depiction degraded sacred Christian symbols and actually offended complainants. Respect for religion was a moral value. The company received a fine of 2,000 LTL (≈€580), near the statutory minimum, after considering the ads’ limited duration/location, the company’s prompt cessation and cooperation, and first-time nature.

The company challenged the decision in the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, arguing the figures and poses differed from religious art, the captions were everyday interjections used for wordplay, the law did not ban all religious-symbol use (only offensive or hateful use), a hundred complaints did not prove majority offense, and the ads were protected artistic expression. The court dismissed the claim, holding the ads distorted the purpose of respected religious symbols.

On appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the finding that the ads were “clearly contrary to public morals.” Religion shaped societal morals; inappropriate use of significant spiritual symbols demeaned them and breached ethical norms. The complaints demonstrated actual offense. A later request by the court’s president to reopen (to better assess necessity/proportionality of the restriction and ECHR case-law) was refused by another panel: there was no manifest legal error; the courts had balanced expression against morals (prioritizing the latter given Catholicism’s prevalence); the small fine was not disproportionate; and the purely commercial ads did not contribute to public debate. A margin of appreciation applied.

(The Law on Advertising was later amended to explicitly ban contempt for registered religious communities’ symbols. Lithuania’s Constitution protects expression but permits limits for morals; it recognizes no state religion.)

**Case Summary: Sekmadienis Ltd. v. Lithuania (ECtHR, Application no. 69317/14)**

Sekmadienis Ltd., a Lithuanian clothing company, alleged a violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression) after being fined for advertisements deemed contrary to public morals.

In September–October 2012, the company ran a two-week campaign for designer R.K.’s clothing line, featuring three visual advertisements on 20 public hoardings in Vilnius and the designer’s website. The first depicted a young man with long hair, a headband, halo, tattoos, and jeans, captioned “Jesus, what trousers!” The second showed a young woman in a white dress with a floral headdress, halo, and beads, captioned “Dear Mary, what a dress!” The third portrayed both figures together (the man reclining, the woman with a hand on his head and shoulder), captioned “Jesus [and] Mary, what are you wearing!”

The State Consumer Rights Protection Authority (SCRPA) received complaints that the ads were unethical and offensive to religious people. It consulted the Lithuanian Advertising Agency (a self-regulatory body), whose commission found (by 5–2) a breach of the Code of Advertising Ethics (decency and religion provisions). The ads risked humiliating people of faith and went “too far” with humour; it recommended avoiding offence to religious dignity and changing the characters.

The State Inspectorate of Non-Food Products notified the company of a possible violation of Article 4 § 2(1) of the Law on Advertising (banning ads contrary to public morals). The company argued that “Jesus” and “Mary” were common Lithuanian emotional interjections (akin to “oh my God”), not religious addresses; the figures were not unambiguously religious and were aesthetically depicted; Lithuania has no state religion, so Catholic sensitivities could not represent society; and the Agency’s view was emotional, not factual. Restricting the ads would harm constitutional freedom of expression.

The Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference (Roman Catholic territorial authority) opined that the ads referenced sacred objects (rosary, names of Jesus and Mary, Pietà symbolism). Christ and Mary embody ethical perfection for the faithful; their inappropriate, commercial depiction encouraged frivolity toward Christian values, degraded sacred symbols, and offended believers, violating public morals.

After a hearing, SCRPA found a violation on 21 March 2013. It held that public morals require respect for others’ rights; ads must meet high moral standards and not degrade people by faith. Combined elements created an impression of religious symbols; religious people react sensitively (especially to tattoos on Jesus/Mary); commercial use of God’s name exceeded tolerance and encouraged a lifestyle incompatible with religious principles. Complaints (including ~100 to the Bishops’ Conference) showed actual offence. Respect for religion is a moral value, so disrespect breaches public morals. A fine of 2,000 LTL (~EUR 580) was imposed, near the minimum, considering the ads’ public reach and complaints, but also their short duration, limited location, the company’s prompt cessation and cooperation, and it being a first offence.

The company appealed to the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, arguing the figures and captions were not religious references but wordplay; the Law on Advertising bans only offensive or hateful use of symbols (not all use); ~100 complaints did not prove widespread offence; and the ads were artistic expression. The court dismissed the claim on 12 November 2013, finding the ads distorted religious symbols’ purpose of referring to the sacred.

The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 25 April 2014. The ads were clearly contrary to public morals: religion shapes societal morals; religious symbols hold spiritual value; their inappropriate use demeans them and breaches ethical norms. Complaints refuted claims of no offence.

The court’s President sought reopening to assess whether freedom of expression (constitutional and international) had been properly balanced for necessity and proportionality, per ECtHR case-law. A different panel refused on 20 November 2014. Restrictions on expression are permitted (including under the Law on Advertising); the prior decision balanced expression against public morals (giving the latter priority) without denying the right’s essence or being disproportionate (fine near minimum). Citing ECtHR cases (Müller v. Switzerland; Otto-Preminger-Institut v. Austria), it noted no uniform European view of religion’s societal role, warranting a margin of appreciation. The ads were purely commercial, not contributing to public debate; Catholicism is the majority faith, and distorting its key symbols offended believers.

These facts underpin the Article 10 claim: an interference via the fine and domestic findings that the ads (using religious imagery/interjections in commercial fashion ads) violated public morals by offending religious feelings and degrading sacred symbols.
001-180310:
The case of Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt v. Hungary (Application no. 201/17) originated from a complaint by the Hungarian political party Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt alleging a violation of its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The party had been fined by domestic authorities for developing and operating a mobile telephone application that enabled voters to anonymously upload, share, and comment on photographs of their (typically invalid) ballot papers during a national referendum.

The referendum took place on 2 October 2016 and was initiated by the Hungarian government. It posed the question whether the European Union should be entitled to mandate the settlement of non-Hungarian citizens in Hungary without the consent of Parliament. Several opposition parties campaigned for a boycott or the casting of invalid ballots, which would not count toward the official result but could symbolically reject the referendum itself. On 29 September 2016, the applicant party released the “cast-an-invalid-vote app,” which allowed users to post photographs of their ballots (or of alternative activities if they abstained) together with comments explaining their choices. All postings were anonymous. The application received coverage in major online media.

A private individual immediately complained to the National Election Commission. On 30 September 2016 the Commission ruled that the application infringed three statutory principles of electoral procedure: fairness of elections, secrecy of the vote, and the proper (purpose-compliant and good-faith) exercise of rights. Relying on its own 2014 guidelines, the Commission held that ballot papers are official documents, not voters’ property; photographing them or removing them from the polling station could facilitate electoral fraud (for example, chain voting) and undermined secrecy, which requires voters’ cooperation. The party was ordered to cease the activity.

The party sought judicial review. On 10 October 2016 the Kúria (Hungary’s highest ordinary court) upheld only the finding that the application violated the proper-exercise-of-rights principle: the sole lawful purpose of a ballot paper is to record a vote on the referendum question, and any other use (including photography and public sharing) is therefore improper. It rejected the secrecy and fairness findings, noting the absence of any legal prohibition on photographing ballots inside the booth and the impossibility of identifying voters through the anonymous application.

After the application was activated on referendum day itself, a second complaint was lodged. On 7 October 2016 the Commission reiterated its earlier conclusions, added that encouraging invalid votes constituted unlawful campaigning capable of influencing voters, and imposed a fine of HUF 832 500 (approximately EUR 2 700). On 18 October 2016 the Kúria again confirmed only the proper-exercise violation, emphasised that the party’s conduct had not affected the referendum’s fairness or secrecy, and reduced the fine to HUF 100 000 (approximately EUR 330).

The party then filed constitutional complaints, arguing that both the Kúria’s legal interpretation and the fine restricted its own freedom of expression (as well as that of voters) without a legitimate constitutional basis. It stressed that the application merely provided an anonymous digital forum for political speech on a matter of public interest and that the Kúria itself had found no actual interference with secrecy or fairness. On 24 October 2016 the Constitutional Court declared the complaints inadmissible. It held that the party had not itself expressed an opinion but had merely offered a platform; consequently it was not personally affected in its own freedom of expression and lacked standing.

Domestic law relevant to the alleged violation includes Article 2 of the Fundamental Law (secret, free elections), the principles of fairness and purpose-compliant rights exercise contained in the Electoral Procedure Act, and the 2014 Commission guidelines that treat ballots as official instruments whose unauthorised use risks fraud. These facts formed the basis of the party’s claim that the fine and associated restrictions constituted an unjustified interference with political expression protected by Article 10.

The case of Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt v. Hungary (Application no. 201/17) concerns an alleged breach of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, a registered Hungarian political party, claimed that a fine imposed for launching a mobile application violated its rights. The application was lodged on 16 December 2016.

A government-initiated referendum took place on 2 October 2016 on the question: “Do you want the European Union to be entitled to order the mandatory settlement of non-Hungarian citizens in Hungary without Parliament’s consent?” Opposition parties urged voters to boycott it or cast invalid ballots as a form of protest. On 29 September 2016, the applicant released a “cast-an-invalid-vote” mobile app enabling voters to anonymously upload, share, and comment on photographs of their ballots (or of activities substituting for voting). The app received coverage in major online media.

A private complainant promptly notified the National Election Commission (NEC). On 30 September 2016 the NEC held that the app infringed the statutory principles of electoral fairness, voting secrecy and the proper (purpose-bound) exercise of rights. It ordered the party to cease the activity, reasoning that ballot papers are official documents, not voters’ property, that photographing them risked fraud (“chain voting”), and that the app could discredit official tallying. The applicant sought judicial review.

On 10 October 2016 the Kúria upheld only the finding of improper exercise of rights: the sole lawful purpose of a ballot is to record an opinion on the referendum question; any other use (photographing and public posting) violates that purpose. It found no separate interference with voters’ freedom of expression, because they remained free to vote and to discuss their choices. The Kúria quashed the secrecy and “discrediting” findings, noting the absence of any statutory ban on photographing ballots and the anonymity of the app.

After the app was activated on polling day, a second complaint produced an NEC decision of 7 October 2016 that reiterated the earlier conclusions, added that encouraging invalid votes constituted unlawful campaigning, and imposed a fine of HUF 832 500 (approximately EUR 2 700). On 18 October 2016 the Kúria again confirmed the improper-exercise violation but rejected claims of unfairness or secrecy breach, holding that voter identities were never revealed and that the app had no impact on the referendum’s integrity. It reduced the fine to HUF 100 000 (approximately EUR 330).

The applicant then lodged constitutional complaints arguing that the Kúria’s interpretation restricted its own freedom of expression (and that of voters) under Article IX of the Fundamental Law. It stressed that the app merely created an anonymous forum for public discussion of a matter of general interest and that the Kúria itself had found no threat to secrecy or fairness. On 24 October 2016 the Constitutional Court declared both complaints inadmissible: the applicant had not itself expressed an opinion but had only provided a technical platform; consequently it lacked personal standing to invoke freedom of expression.

These successive domestic rulings—finding an unlawful use of official ballots, imposing and then reducing a fine, and denying the applicant victim status—constitute the factual core of the alleged Article 10 violation.

The case of Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt v. Hungary (Application no. 201/17) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). The applicant, a Hungarian political party, was fined after developing and operating a mobile application that allowed voters to anonymously upload and share photographs of invalid ballot papers during a 2016 referendum.

On 2 October 2016, Hungary held a government-initiated referendum posing the question: “Do you want the European Union to be entitled to order the mandatory settlement of non-Hungarian citizens in Hungary without Parliament’s consent?” Opposition parties urged a boycott or the casting of invalid ballots (which would not count toward official results but could be seen as rejecting the referendum). On 29 September 2016 the applicant released the “cast-an-invalid-vote app,” enabling anonymous posting of ballot photographs (or images of alternative activities if abstaining) plus comments on voting choices. The app received coverage in major online outlets.

A private individual promptly complained to the National Election Commission. On 30 September 2016 the Commission found the app breached principles of electoral fairness, voting secrecy, and proper exercise of rights under the Electoral Procedure Act and Fundamental Law. It held that ballot papers are official documents, not voters’ property, so photographing them risked fraud; it ordered the party to stop.

The applicant sought review. On 10 October 2016 the Kúria (supreme court) upheld the “proper exercise of rights” finding: ballots exist solely to record opinions on the referendum question, and photographing/publishing them exceeded that purpose. It reversed the secrecy and “discrediting of electoral bodies” findings, noting no statutory ban on booth photographs and that the app kept voters anonymous.

The party nonetheless activated the app on referendum day. A fresh complaint produced a 7 October 2016 Commission decision repeating the earlier violations, adding that encouraging invalid votes amounted to unlawful campaigning, and imposing a fine of HUF 832,500 (approx. €2,700).

On further review the Kúria, on 18 October 2016, again confirmed only the improper-exercise violation, found no impact on fairness or secrecy (identities unrevealed), and reduced the fine to HUF 100,000 (approx. €330).

The applicant lodged constitutional complaints, asserting that the rulings violated its own freedom of expression (Article IX of the Fundamental Law). It argued the app merely offered an anonymous public forum for discussing a matter of general interest—the most protected form of expression—and that neither secrecy nor fairness had actually been compromised, rendering any restriction disproportionate.

The Constitutional Court declared both complaints inadmissible on 24 October 2016. It reasoned that the applicant had not itself expressed an opinion but had only provided a platform; therefore it was not personally affected in its own expression rights. The case concerned voters’ expression, which the Kúria had already found uninfringed.

Domestic law (Fundamental Law Article 2 and Electoral Procedure Act section 2) requires fairness and bona-fide exercise of rights. 2014 Election Commission guidelines explicitly treat ballots as non-property official documents whose photographing can facilitate fraud and breach secrecy. International soft-law instruments (Council of Europe recommendations) encourage ICT use for democratic debate yet require any restriction on online platforms to meet legality, legitimacy and proportionality tests.

These facts raise the question whether sanctioning a political party for facilitating anonymous, non-identifying sharing of ballot images during a highly politicized referendum constituted an unjustified interference with political expression, given judicial findings that the app neither revealed voter identities nor affected referendum integrity.
001-181594:
The case of Igranov and Others v. Russia (ECHR, 20 March 2018) joined nine applications by Russian nationals detained in penal facilities. Each applicant had initiated separate civil proceedings, typically seeking damages for poor detention conditions, unlawful prosecution or inadequate medical care while imprisoned.

None of the applicants was permitted to attend the hearings that decided their claims. Courts at first instance and on appeal uniformly refused to secure their personal presence. They relied on the absence of any domestic legal basis for transporting detainees to civil hearings, citing Article 77.1 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences together with provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. The courts observed that the applicants remained free to lodge written pleadings and to instruct counsel.

All claims were dismissed at both levels of jurisdiction. Final domestic judgments were delivered on dates recorded in the appendix to the Court’s judgment.

The applicants complained that the refusals violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention by denying them an effective opportunity to participate in person in proceedings to which they were parties. The facts relevant to that complaint are therefore the applicants’ status as prisoners, the personal and fact-sensitive character of their claims, the blanket character of the courts’ refusals, and the asserted adequacy of written submissions or legal representation as substitutes for oral presence.

The Court noted the close similarity of the facts to those examined in Yevdokimov and Others v. Russia (2016) and related cases, in which it had already held that such systematic exclusion of detained litigants from civil hearings breached Article 6 § 1.

Domestic law (Article 392 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as interpreted by Supreme Court rulings of 2012 and 2013) permits reopening of final judgments on the basis of an ECHR finding of a Convention violation, provided the violation is of a procedural nature that calls the outcome into question and the applicant continues to suffer its consequences. Subsequent Russian practice has been inconsistent: some courts have reopened proceedings following analogous ECHR judgments, while others have refused, citing destroyed case files or the purely procedural character of the violation already compensated by the Strasbourg Court.

These circumstances—detention, personal claims, unreasoned exclusion from hearings, and limited alternative means of participation—form the factual core of the alleged Article 6 violation.

The case of Igranov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 42399/13 and 8 others) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by nine Russian nationals, all of whom were detained in penal facilities at the material time. Each applicant had initiated separate civil proceedings as a claimant. In the majority of instances, these claims sought compensation related to aspects of their conditions of detention, alleged unlawful criminal prosecution, or inadequate medical care while incarcerated.

The core of the alleged violation centered on the applicants’ complete exclusion from the oral hearings at which their civil claims were examined. None of the nine applicants was permitted to appear in person before the domestic courts at either first instance or on appeal. The courts uniformly refused requests for personal attendance, holding that Russian law contained no provision authorizing the transport of convicted prisoners to court for civil matters. In support of this position they relied on Article 77.1 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences together with the relevant articles of the Code of Civil Procedure. The courts further observed that the applicants had been able to submit written pleadings and to instruct counsel to represent them, and therefore considered that their procedural rights had been adequately protected.

All of the claims were dismissed after examination at two levels of jurisdiction. The applicants contended that this systematic denial of the opportunity to appear in person deprived them of an effective opportunity to present their cases, to comment on evidence, and to participate in the determination of their civil rights, thereby violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The Court communicated the complaint concerning the applicants’ absence from the hearings to the Russian Government and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible. It also invited observations on whether the case was suitable for a pilot-judgment procedure, given the apparently widespread and structural character of the problem already identified in earlier judgments such as Yevdokimov and Others v. Russia.

Domestic law and practice relevant to the alleged violation include the rules of civil procedure governing a party’s right to be present, as well as the provisions of Article 392 of the Code of Civil Procedure that allow re-examination of final judgments in the light of a finding by the Strasbourg Court of a Convention violation of a procedural nature that calls into question the outcome of the original proceedings. Subsequent Russian case-law, however, has produced inconsistent results on whether such a finding automatically warrants reopening.

These facts form the factual matrix of the alleged breach of the right to a fair hearing.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 20 March 2018 in Igranov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 42399/13 and eight others). The case involved nine Russian nationals, all detained in penal facilities at the relevant time, who lodged applications under Article 34 of the Convention. They alleged a violation of their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 because they had been denied the opportunity to appear in person in civil proceedings to which they were parties.

The applicants were claimants in separate civil actions. Most sought compensation for aspects of their detention conditions, unlawful criminal prosecution, or inadequate medical care. None were able to attend the hearings at which their claims were examined. Domestic courts at first instance and on appeal uniformly refused to secure their presence. The courts held that no provision of Russian law required or permitted the escort of detainees to civil hearings, relying on Article 77.1 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences and the relevant rules of the Code of Civil Procedure. They further observed that the applicants had been able to file written submissions and to instruct counsel. All claims were dismissed at both levels of jurisdiction.

The Court had previously examined the same issue in Yevdokimov and Others v. Russia and related cases. Those judgments established that the systematic exclusion of detained litigants from civil hearings, without any individualised assessment of the need for their personal participation, breached Article 6 § 1. The present applications were therefore communicated solely on that complaint; remaining grievances were declared inadmissible. The Court also invited observations on the possible application of the pilot-judgment procedure, given the apparently widespread and structural character of the problem.

Domestic law on the reopening of civil proceedings after a Strasbourg finding of a violation was also relevant. Article 392 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits re-examination of a final judgment on the ground of “new circumstances,” including an ECtHR finding of a Convention violation that is of substantial importance to the correct resolution of the case. Subsequent Plenary Supreme Court rulings confirmed that a procedural violation capable of affecting the outcome of the proceedings could justify reopening, provided the applicant continued to suffer the negative consequences of the original decision. Subsequent practice, however, was inconsistent: some regional courts reopened proceedings on the basis of the Court’s earlier judgments, while others refused, citing the absence of a merits judgment in the particular case or the destruction of the original case file.

The core facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore straightforward and uniform across the nine applications: the applicants, as detained claimants, were excluded as a matter of course from the oral hearings of their civil claims, without any assessment of whether their personal presence was necessary for the fair determination of the dispute, and the exclusion was justified solely by the lack of a statutory mechanism for bringing prisoners to court. Those facts formed the basis of the Court’s examination of whether the applicants had received a fair hearing.
001-180843:
The applicants, six Maltese nationals, have since 2002 held the utile dominium (via sub-emphyteusis expiring in 2047) of land in Zabbar, Malta, inherited from ancestors who acquired it from a prior holder under a 150-year temporary sub-emphyteusis. The State is the directum dominus. The land included a shop rented to third parties as a snack bar.

On 7 May 1965 a Governor’s declaration under the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance (Chapter 88) stated that 80 m² of the property (including the approximately 50 m² shop), plus other land, was required for a public purpose. The Government took possession of the declared land, demolished the shop and began constructing a local civic centre and service roads.

In 1972 the development plan was altered and the intended road was repositioned. A new, larger shop was therefore built, largely on the applicants’ land and at public expense, to serve the civic centre, government offices, square and a bus terminus. The civic centre then housed the local council, social-security office, police station, post office and several commercial premises. The new shop was leased to the original tenant as a snack bar. A small unused portion of the applicants’ land was returned only in 1988.

Extra-judicial requests for return of the land occupied by the snack bar were unsuccessful. While constitutional proceedings were pending, the Commissioner of Land on 13 April 2010 extended the third-party lease until 31 January 2020 at a rent of approximately EUR 2,100 per year. On 6 October 2010 a President’s declaration offered EUR 13,000 compensation, based on a 1 January 2005 architect’s valuation (pursuant to Article 9 of the Ordinance and Act I of 2006). By 2010 the bus terminus had been relocated and eleven take-away food outlets operated within 300 m of the civic centre.

On 2 March 2010 the applicants instituted constitutional redress proceedings, alleging a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (taking not in the public interest and without compensation) and of Article 6 (inability to access a court to pursue their claims), together with corresponding constitutional provisions. They sought annulment of the 1965 declaration, restoration of possession and adequate redress.

The Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction, by judgment of 26 June 2012, upheld the claims. It noted that, under the Ordinance as originally in force, only the Commissioner could make an offer and, if refused, initiate proceedings before the Land Arbitration Board (LAB); even after later amendments, 45 years had elapsed without any offer, leaving the applicants without ordinary remedies. The 2009 amendment permitting a 21-day challenge to public purpose was of no practical assistance. On the merits the court found no public interest: the land had been used for a purely commercial snack bar serving private interests. No compensation had been paid for 45 years and the 2010 offer (based on a 2005 valuation) was far below the capitalised rental value of approximately EUR 60,000. The absence of procedural safeguards also denied access to court under Article 6. The court annulled both the 1965 and 2010 declarations, ordered vacant restitution and awarded EUR 40,000 covering pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage.

On appeal the Constitutional Court, by judgment of 26 April 2013, allowed the appeal in part. It held that the original taking had been in the public interest (road construction) and that the subsequent change of use (snack bar serving the civic centre, offices and terminus) had not extinguished that interest. A violation of property rights nevertheless existed because no compensation had been paid for decades (23 years for the unused land eventually returned, and still none for the remainder). The first-instance court ought not to have awarded pecuniary damage, which remained available under Article 12 § 3 of the Ordinance (5 % interest). The Constitutional Court therefore awarded only EUR 10,000 non-pecuniary damage, declined to order restitution, and left statutory pecuniary claims intact.

After the application was communicated, the applicants refused the Constitutional Court’s award; the Commissioner deposited it in court in January 2014. In September 2015 the Government requested evidence of title in connection with the 2010 declaration.

Relevant provisions of the (now repealed) Ordinance included: the President’s declaration as conclusive proof of public purpose (subject after 2009 to a 21-day LAB challenge that did not stay expropriation); valuation frozen at 1 January 2005 for certain pre-2003 acquisitions still pending; and procedures for offer, bank deposit, owner-initiated LAB proceedings and withdrawal of the deposited sum without prejudice to further claims.

The case of *Galea and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 68980/13) concerns six Maltese nationals who inherited the *utile dominium* (a 150-year sub-emphyteusis expiring in 2047) of land in Zabbar. The State is the *directum dominus*. A shop on the land had long been leased as a snack bar.

On 7 May 1965 a Governor’s declaration (published 14 May 1965) expropriated 80 m² of the land, including the shop, under the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance for a civic centre and service roads. The authorities took possession, demolished the shop and later, after 1972 plan changes that repositioned a road, constructed a larger replacement shop mostly on the applicants’ land. The new shop was leased to the same tenant and served the civic centre, government offices and a bus terminus. A small unused portion of land was returned only in 1988. Extra-judicial requests for the return of the shop plot failed.

No compensation offer was made for 45 years. In 2010, after constitutional proceedings had begun, the Commissioner of Land offered €13,000 based on a 1 January 2005 valuation and simultaneously extended the commercial lease until 2020 at approximately €2,100 per year. By then the bus terminus had been relocated and numerous competing food outlets existed nearby.

The applicants instituted constitutional redress proceedings on 2 March 2010, alleging that the taking was not in the public interest (the land was used for private commercial purposes) and that they had been denied access to court to claim compensation, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 of the Convention.

On 26 June 2012 the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction found violations. Under the original Ordinance only the Commissioner could initiate compensation proceedings before the Land Arbitration Board; the owners had no standing. Even after later amendments, a 45-year delay left them without ordinary remedies. The court held the current use served purely private commercial interests, that the 2010 offer (five times lower than a capitalised rental value of some €60,000) was inadequate, and that the absence of procedural safeguards also breached Article 6. It annulled the 1965 and 2010 declarations, ordered vacant possession and awarded €40,000 covering both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage.

On 26 April 2013 the Constitutional Court partly allowed the State’s appeal. It accepted that the original 1965 taking for roads was in the public interest and that the subsequent snack-bar use continued to serve the civic centre and public. Nevertheless a violation of property rights had occurred because the applicants received no compensation for decades (including 23 years for the unused plot later returned). The court quashed the return order, awarded only €10,000 in non-pecuniary damages (taking the 2005 valuation of €13,000 into account) and left pecuniary compensation, plus 5 % statutory interest, to be pursued under the Ordinance.

The applicants refused the award, which the Commissioner deposited in court in January 2014. The facts therefore centre on an expropriation whose public-interest character became disputed after a change of use, combined with an extraordinary delay in offering any compensation and the owners’ inability, for decades, to institute proceedings themselves.

The case Galea and Others v. Malta (ECtHR Application no. 68980/13) involved six Maltese applicants who inherited the utile dominium (temporary sub-emphyteusis until 2047) of land in Zabbar, including a shop rented as a snack bar; the State held the directum dominium. In a 7 May 1965 Governor’s declaration under the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance, 80 sq m of the land (including the ~50 sq m shop) was expropriated for public purposes. The authorities took possession, demolished the shop, and planned a civic centre with service roads.

In 1972 the development plan changed: the road was repositioned and a larger shop was built mostly on the applicants’ land. It was leased to the same third party as a snack bar to serve the civic centre, government offices and a bus terminus. A small unused portion of the land was returned only in 1988. Extra-judicial requests for return of the shop premises failed. In 2010 the Commissioner of Land extended the commercial lease until 2020 at ~€2,100 per year. After 45 years, a 6 October 2010 President’s declaration offered €13,000 compensation based on a 2005 architect’s valuation.

On 2 March 2010 the applicants brought constitutional proceedings alleging a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property taken without public interest and without compensation) and Article 6 (no access to court to challenge the taking or claim compensation). The Civil Court (First Hall) on 26 June 2012 upheld the claims. It found that, under the Ordinance as originally in force, only the Commissioner could initiate compensation proceedings before the Land Arbitration Board; the 45-year delay therefore left the applicants without any ordinary remedy. Even after 2009 amendments allowing a 21-day challenge to public purpose, the court considered such a challenge impracticable. The taking was not in the public interest because the land was used for private commercial purposes. No compensation had been paid for 45 years and the 2010 offer was far below the court’s capitalised-rent valuation of ~€60,000. The court annulled both declarations, ordered vacant return of the property and awarded €40,000 covering pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage.

The Constitutional Court on 26 April 2013 allowed the State’s appeal in part. It held that the original 1965 taking (for roads) was in the public interest and that the 1972 change of use still served a public purpose (needs of the civic centre, offices and terminus) despite the commercial lease. A violation of property rights nevertheless existed because of the prolonged absence of any compensation (23 years for the unused portion returned in 1988 and still none for the remainder). It quashed the return order, awarded only €10,000 non-pecuniary damages (taking the €13,000 valuation into account) and left pecuniary compensation, including 5 % statutory interest, to be claimed under the Ordinance. The applicants refused the award, which the Commissioner later deposited in court.

The facts thus centre on a 1965 expropriation whose public-interest justification was later contested after a change to commercial use, a 45-year delay before any compensation offer, the applicants’ initial inability to institute proceedings, and the domestic courts’ divergent assessments of public interest and of the adequacy of redress.
001-181203:
The case of *Guja v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2)* (application no. 1085/10) was brought by Iacob Guja, a Moldovan journalist previously employed as Head of the Press Department at the Prosecutor General’s Office. He alleged a fresh violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) arising from his second dismissal after the European Court of Human Rights had already found his first dismissal unlawful.

In the original case (*Guja v. Moldova* [GC], no. 14277/04, 12 February 2008), Guja had, in January 2003, sent two letters to a newspaper. The letters revealed political pressure exerted on the Prosecutor General’s Office by a high-ranking politician unhappy that police officers were being prosecuted for ill-treating and unlawfully detaining suspects. One letter also noted that one of the officers had a prior conviction for similar offences yet had been re-employed. The newspaper published an article based on the letters. Guja was dismissed for breaching internal confidentiality rules. Domestic courts upheld the dismissal. The Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 10: the interference, though prescribed by law and pursuing a legitimate aim, was not necessary in a democratic society. The disclosed information concerned matters of major public interest (separation of powers, political interference and official attitudes to police brutality). Guja had acted in good faith, had no effective internal channels available, and the public interest in disclosure outweighed any damage to the office’s reputation. The harshest possible sanction had been imposed. Moldova was ordered to pay €10,000 in damages and €8,413 in costs.

Following that judgment Guja applied to have the domestic dismissal decisions set aside. On 28 May 2008 the Supreme Court of Justice ordered his reinstatement. He immediately requested reinstatement. On 29 May he met the Prosecutor General, who allegedly asked him to resign and, when he refused, said he had “enough wits to force him” to do so (disputed by the Government). On 5 June an order formally reinstated him and awarded salary arrears. The same day the Prosecutor General sought, and the next day obtained, trade-union consent to dismiss him under section 14(8) of the Public Service Act. That provision allows the newly appointed head of a public authority to terminate the contracts of certain cabinet-level staff (counsellors, aides, press attachés, secretaries). A new Prosecutor General had been appointed in 2007.

On 6 June Guja was shown the reinstatement order but, according to him, was given neither an office nor an access badge, was frequently locked out of the press department, and was assigned no work (also disputed). On 16 June he was dismissed with effect from 10 June, the stated reason being the 2007 change of Prosecutor General.

Guja challenged the second dismissal before the Chișinău Court of Appeal on 10 July 2008. He relied on the 29 May conversation, the conditions of his brief re-employment, the fact that section 14(8) had never previously been used against anyone in his position (which he argued did not form part of the Prosecutor General’s personal cabinet), and the State’s failure to execute the 2008 Strasbourg judgment. The Prosecutor General’s Office did not contest the factual allegations, merely asserting that labour-law formalities had been observed. On 17 December 2008 the Court of Appeal rejected the claim, holding the dismissal lawful under section 14(8) and considering the earlier Strasbourg judgment already executed by the quashing of the 2003 decisions. It did not address Guja’s account of events. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on points of law on 29 April 2009, likewise ignoring the allegations of simulated reinstatement and bad faith and concluding that the 2008 judgment had been implemented once Guja had been formally reinstated.

Guja notified the Committee of Ministers that the second dismissal constituted non-execution of the original judgment. The Government maintained that the judgment had been fully executed and requested closure of supervision, which nevertheless remained open at the time of the present judgment.

The relevant domestic provision is section 14(8) of the Public Service Act. Council of Europe materials (Recommendation Rec(2000)2 and related reports) emphasise the need, where possible, for *restitutio in integrum* after a finding of violation.

Iacob Guja, a journalist employed as Head of the Press Department at Moldova’s Prosecutor General’s Office, leaked two 2003 letters to a newspaper. These revealed a high-ranking politician’s pressure on prosecutors regarding police officers accused of ill-treating and unlawfully detaining suspects (one officer having a prior similar conviction yet being re-employed). A newspaper article followed. Guja was dismissed for breaching internal confidentiality rules. He sued for reinstatement, arguing good-faith disclosure to combat corruption and influence-peddling, and that the letters were not secret. Domestic courts upheld the dismissal.

In its 12 February 2008 Grand Chamber judgment (Guja v. Moldova, no. 14277/04), the ECHR found an Article 10 violation. The interference was prescribed by law and pursued a legitimate aim but was not necessary in a democratic society: Guja lacked internal reporting channels, the information concerned matters of major public interest (separation of powers, political interference, and official attitudes to police brutality), and this interest outweighed any harm to the Office’s reputation. Guja had acted in good faith, yet received the harshest sanction. Moldova was ordered to pay damages.

Guja then obtained a 28 May 2008 Supreme Court order setting aside the prior domestic judgments and directing reinstatement. He immediately applied to the Office. He alleged that on 29 May the Prosecutor General demanded his resignation and, upon refusal, threatened to force him out; the Government disputed this. On 5 June an order formally reinstated him and awarded salary arrears. The same day, however, the Prosecutor General sought (and the next day obtained) trade-union consent to dismiss him under section 14(8) of the Public Service Act, citing a 2007 change in Prosecutor General.

On 6 June Guja was shown the reinstatement order but, he claimed, received neither an office nor an access badge, was given no duties, and was frequently locked out or made to wait outside. The Government again disputed these assertions. On 16 June he was dismissed (effective 10 June) on the basis of the new appointment and union approval.

Guja challenged the second dismissal before the Chișinău Court of Appeal, contending that section 14(8) did not apply (his post was not part of the Prosecutor General’s personal cabinet), that it had never previously been used despite two intervening changes of Prosecutor General, that the reinstatement was simulated, and that the Office had acted in bad faith to circumvent the 2008 ECHR judgment. He repeated his account of the 29 May meeting and subsequent treatment. The Office did not contest these factual claims, arguing only that labour-law formalities had been observed.

On 17 December 2008 the Court of Appeal rejected the claim, holding the dismissal lawful because of the 2007 appointment and that the 2008 ECHR judgment had been fully executed once the earlier domestic decisions were quashed. It ignored Guja’s allegations of bad faith and mistreatment. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law on 29 April 2009 on identical grounds, again without examining those allegations.

Guja informed the Committee of Ministers that the second dismissal and the domestic courts’ reasoning constituted a failure to execute the 2008 judgment. The Government maintained that execution was complete upon the 2008 review and brief reinstatement. Supervision remained pending. Section 14(8) permitted certain political or personal staff (including press attachés) to be dismissed upon a change of head of authority. These events formed the basis of Guja’s complaint of a fresh Article 10 violation.

**Case of Guja v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2) (Application no. 1085/10), ECtHR Second Section, 27 February 2018 (final 27 May 2018)**

This case concerns Iacob Guja, a Moldovan journalist and former Head of the Press Department at the Prosecutor General’s Office. It follows the Grand Chamber’s 12 February 2008 judgment in Guja v. Moldova (no. 14277/04), which found a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). In 2003, Guja had disclosed to a newspaper two letters revealing political pressure on prosecutors regarding the prosecution of police officers for ill-treatment and unlawful detention of suspects, including one officer previously convicted of similar offences but re-employed. He was dismissed for breaching internal confidentiality rules. Domestic courts upheld the dismissal. The Grand Chamber held the interference was not necessary in a democratic society: the information was of major public interest (separation of powers, political interference, police brutality); Guja acted in good faith with no viable internal alternatives; the public interest outweighed harm to the institution’s reputation; and dismissal was the harshest possible sanction. Moldova was ordered to pay €10,000 for damage and €8,413 for costs.

After the 2008 judgment, Guja successfully applied to have the domestic dismissal rulings set aside. On 28 May 2008 the Supreme Court of Justice ordered his reinstatement. He immediately requested reinstatement from the Prosecutor General’s Office. According to Guja (disputed by the Government), he met the Prosecutor General on 29 May 2008, who demanded his resignation and threatened to force him out. On 5 June 2008 an order reinstated him as Head of the Press Department and directed payment of salary arrears. The same day, the Prosecutor General sought (and the next day obtained) trade-union approval to dismiss him under section 14(8) of the Public Service Act, which allowed termination of certain staff (counsellors, aides, press attachés) upon appointment of a new head of authority. A new Prosecutor General had been appointed in 2007.

On 6 June 2008 Guja was presented with the reinstatement order. He alleged he received no office, no access badge, no duties, and restricted building access: he waited outside daily, used the library or press office only when permitted, and was locked out when others left because superiors barred him from sensitive information. The Government disputed these claims. On 16 June 2008 a dismissal order (effective 10 June) was issued, citing the 2007 change in Prosecutor General and union consent.

Guja challenged the dismissal before the Chișinău Court of Appeal, seeking reinstatement. He detailed the 29 May meeting, the lack of office/badge/tasks, and the same-day request for union approval of dismissal. He argued section 14(8) did not apply (his post was not part of the Prosecutor General’s personal cabinet), he was the first such dismissal since 2003 despite two prior changes of Prosecutor General, the reinstatement was simulated (“so-called”), and the State had acted in bad faith to remove an “inconvenient employee,” thereby failing to execute the 2008 ECtHR judgment. The Prosecutor General’s Office did not contest the factual allegations about treatment or the meeting, asserting only that labour-law formalities were observed.

On 17 December 2008 the Court of Appeal dismissed the claim, holding the dismissal lawful under section 14(8) because of the 2007 appointment and that the 2008 ECtHR judgment had been executed by the review and quashing of the original dismissal rulings. It ignored Guja’s allegations about the meeting and working conditions. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on points of law on 29 April 2009, similarly finding the 2008 judgment executed upon review and brief reinstatement, without assessing the allegations of bad-faith treatment or simulated reinstatement.

Guja informed the Council of Europe’s Department for the Execution of Judgments of these events, claiming the second dismissal and unsuccessful reinstatement proceedings constituted non-compliance with the 2008 judgment. The Committee of Ministers’ supervision of that judgment remained ongoing at the time of the present ruling. The present application alleged that the renewed dismissal after the finding of an Article 10 violation itself constituted a fresh breach of freedom of expression.

The case of Danilczuk v. Cyprus (Application no. 21318/12) concerns a Polish national’s complaint under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding conditions of detention at Nicosia Central Prisons from 14 September 2010 to 18 May 2012. The applicant was initially held on remand, then convicted of burglary, theft and other offences and sentenced to concurrent terms of up to two years. He was released early pursuant to a presidential decree.

The applicant alleged severe overcrowding, with personal space of only 0.5–1.7 m² per detainee. Cells were cold and poorly lit, lacked in-cell toilets, and required waits of two to three hours for access. During lock-up he was forced to urinate into bottles and defecate into bags.

The Government supplied occupancy records and block-specific details but no cell-level data. From 14 September 2010 to 24 January 2011 the applicant was in Block 5 (remand wing), comprising 34 double cells of 6.21 m² each (approximately 3.10 m² personal space if shared) plus 8 toilets and 8 showers. From 24 January to 5 October 2011 he was in unrenovated Block 2B (sentenced prisoners). That block contained 26 double cells of 9.98 m² (4.99 m² personal space), two larger cells of 19.55 m² holding 5–7 men (2.8–3.9 m²) and a 90 m² dormitory holding 20–50 men (1.8–4.5 m²). Daily occupancy ranged from 80 to 124. Six toilets and six showers served the block. From 5 October 2011 until release the applicant occupied renovated Block 2A, consisting of 41 double cells of 9.80 m² (4.9 m² personal space) with 6 toilets, 6 showers and 3 urinals.

The prison had central heating, corridor air-conditioning, cell fans and insulated windows providing natural light and ventilation. Detainees could leave cells from 06:00 until 17:00 or 18:00 and move freely inside their blocks until 21:00 or 22:00. Following a 2008 CPT visit the authorities issued Order 32/2008 requiring staff to keep call bells operational so that prisoners could request toilet access; violation of the order was a disciplinary offence. Night-time toilet visits (21:00–06:00) were limited to three per detainee, but no records of such openings were kept.

Contemporary independent reports corroborated the applicant’s account. The CPT’s 2012 report (based on a May 2008 visit) documented occupancy well above official capacity, cells without windows, dilapidated sanitary facilities and the systematic switching-off of cell bells at night, forcing prisoners to use improvised receptacles—a practice the Committee described as degrading. The Cypriot Ombudsman’s September 2011 report, issued while the applicant was still detained, likewise found overcrowding, insufficient toilets and showers, deactivated night bells and the use of bottles and bags, which it characterised as extremely degrading and unhygienic. Later CPT findings (2014 report on a 2013 visit) noted subsequent renovations in Block 2 but confirmed that overcrowding and delayed night-time toilet access persisted.

These facts—personal space frequently falling below 4 m², absence of in-cell sanitation, restricted night-time access and the resulting unsanitary practices—form the core of the alleged Article 3 violation. Domestic law (Article 8 of the Constitution and the 2005 Detention Rights Law) and the Ombudsman’s mandate as national preventive mechanism provided theoretical remedies, yet the contemporaneous reports indicate that the conditions described by the applicant were systemic at the relevant time.

001-182208:
The case of Elita Magomadova v. Russia (no. 77546/14) concerns the applicant’s complaint that Russian courts’ refusal to grant her a residence order for her infant son I. violated her Article 8 right to respect for family life.

The applicant, born in 1974 and living in Moscow, gave birth to I. on 10 November 2009 with her partner E. After their November 2010 separation they agreed I. would reside with her, E. visiting regularly. On 22 October 2013 E. removed I. to Grozny, Chechnya. The applicant followed but E. barred all contact.

On 18 February 2014 she applied to the Leninskiy District Court of Grozny for a residence order, stressing that I. had lived with her from birth, they were closely attached, she had stable income, a suitable Moscow flat and good character references, and could meet all his needs. She also complained of E.’s obstruction. A Moscow childcare inspection confirmed her living conditions were suitable. E. was separately convicted of assaulting her in August 2013.

A Grozny childcare visit found E.’s flat (shared with his mother A. and I.) equally suitable. Its 15 April 2014 report recommended residence with E.: the child had lived with the father “for a long time,” the mother in Moscow “did not participate in upbringing,” I. was attached to E., and contact with the mother would not be hindered. At the hearing E. claimed I. was unattached to the applicant, whom he accused of an improper lifestyle.

On 17 April 2014 the District Court dismissed the application and, acting of its own motion, awarded residence to E. (who had never requested it). Citing the child’s best interests and Article 65 of the Family Code, it noted both parents had suitable housing, employment and character. It nevertheless found the applicant, a working single mother of a teenage daughter, unable to provide proper care: she had placed I. (who had a congenital neural condition) in nursery and allegedly lacked time. E., by contrast, held a managerial post, lived with his supportive mother and enjoyed the child’s attachment. The court held the applicant had failed to discharge her burden of proof.

On appeal the applicant argued that the court had improperly granted an unrequested order, that her daughter was self-reliant, that nursery attendance was educationally appropriate, that neither parent’s work schedule had been examined, and that I. could not have become more attached to E. in the short period after removal. She also reiterated E.’s continuing refusal of contact. The Chechen Supreme Court upheld the judgment on 3 July 2014 as lawful and in the child’s best interests.

A subsequent letter from Grozny authorities confirmed E. would allow no maternal contact. An internal inquiry later established that the April 2014 report contained unverified and incomplete information (E.’s income unconfirmed, non-participation unproved, periods of residence unascertained, the half-sister ignored); the official was disciplined for violating the applicant’s rights. Cassation was nonetheless refused in November 2014, the judge still relying on the flawed report.

(E. died in a car accident on 5 December 2014; I. remained with A. After further litigation the child was eventually returned to the applicant in April 2016, but those events post-date the impugned residence decision.)

The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the courts’ reliance on an incomplete and inaccurate childcare report, their failure to examine the child’s long prior residence and attachment to the mother, their treatment of the applicant’s employment and family situation as disqualifying, and their disregard of E.’s proven obstruction of contact—all while acting beyond the parties’ pleadings to award residence to the father.

The case of Elita Magomadova v. Russia (Application no. 77546/14) concerns the applicant’s allegation that Russian courts’ refusal to grant her a residence order for her young son I. violated her right to respect for family life.
