After the couple separated in November 2010, they agreed that I. would live with the applicant, with E. visiting regularly. On 22 October 2013 E. took I. to Grozny, Chechnya. The applicant followed but E. prevented her from seeing the child.

On 18 February 2014 the applicant applied to the Leninskiy District Court of Grozny for a residence order in her favour. She emphasised that I. had lived with her since birth, they were closely attached, she had a stable income and a suitable Moscow flat (confirmed suitable by a 19 March 2014 inspection), and she could meet all his needs. She also documented E.’s obstruction of contact. Separately, on 19 March 2014 a Moscow court convicted E. of assaulting the applicant in August 2013.

A Grozny childcare inspection of E.’s flat on 9 April 2014 found it suitable. Its 15 April 2014 report recommended residence with E., asserting that I. had lived with him “for a long time,” that the applicant (living in Moscow) did not participate in upbringing, that I. was strongly attached to E., and that E. had a good income; contact with the mother would not be hindered.

At the hearing E. claimed I. was unattached to the applicant and that she led an “improper” life. On 17 April 2014 the District Court dismissed the applicant’s claim and, of its own motion, awarded residence to E. It invoked the child’s best interests, the Grozny report, and comparable parental conditions, but concluded that the applicant—a working single mother with a teenage daughter—could not provide proper care, especially after placing I. (who had a congenital neural anomaly) in nursery. It found E. better placed (managerial job, grandmotherly help) and I. attached to him, while asserting that E. had not blocked contact and that the applicant had failed to prove her case.

The applicant appealed, arguing the court had granted unrequested relief, that she was fully capable (her daughter being self-reliant and helpful), that nursery served educational purposes, that no evidence supported findings about her time constraints or I.’s sudden attachment shift after the removal, and that E. in fact obstructed contact (as confirmed at the hearing). On 3 July 2014 the Supreme Court of the Chechen Republic upheld the judgment as lawful and in I.’s best interests.

Later official correspondence confirmed E.’s refusal of contact. On 12 September 2014 the Grozny childcare authority itself admitted that its April report was based on incorrect and incomplete information (unverified income, unproven non-participation by the mother, unestablished periods of residence, ignored half-sister) and had violated the applicant’s rights; the authoring official was disciplined. The applicant’s cassation appeal citing this admission was refused on 27 November 2014, the judge still relying on the flawed report.

E. died in a car accident on 5 December 2014; I. remained with his paternal grandmother. The applicant later obtained a return order (31 July 2015, upheld on appeal), but enforcement was delayed until police recovered I. on 28 April 2016.

These facts centre on the courts’ decision-making, their reliance on an inaccurate report, their discounting of the mother’s long-term primary-care role, the father’s unilateral removal of the child, and the obstruction of contact—all directly relevant to the alleged Article 8 violation.

The case of Elita Magomadova v. Russia (Application no. 77546/14) concerns the applicant’s complaint that Russian courts’ refusal to grant her a residence order for her young son violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1974 and resident in Moscow, gave birth to her son I. on 10 November 2009. The father was her partner E. After their separation in November 2010, they agreed that I. would live with the applicant while E. visited regularly. On 22 October 2013 E. took I. to Grozny in Chechnya. The applicant followed but was prevented by E. from seeing the child.

On 18 February 2014 the applicant applied to the Leninskiy District Court of Grozny for a residence order in her favour. She emphasised that I. had lived with her from birth until his removal, that they were closely attached, and that she had a stable income, a spacious Moscow flat, good character references and the capacity to meet all of I.’s needs. Moscow childcare authorities inspected her flat on 19 March 2014 and found it suitable. Separately, a Moscow justice of the peace convicted E. of assaulting the applicant in August 2013.

Grozny childcare authorities inspected E.’s flat on 9 April 2014 (where he lived with his mother A. and I.) and found the conditions suitable. Their 15 April 2014 report stated that I. had lived with his father “for a long time,” that the mother (resident in Moscow) did not participate in his upbringing, that the boy was strongly attached to E., and that a residence order for the father would serve the child’s best interests without hindering contact with the mother. At the hearing E. claimed I. was unattached to the applicant, whom he accused of “not leading the right kind of life.”

On 17 April 2014 the District Court dismissed the applicant’s claim and, of its own motion, granted a residence order to E. (who had not requested one). Relying on Article 65 of the Family Code and a 1998 Supreme Court Plenary Ruling, the court held that the child’s best interests required this outcome. It noted both parents’ good references, employment and suitable housing, but treated the applicant’s higher income and Moscow property as non-decisive. It criticised her as a working single mother of a teenage daughter (born 1997) from a previous marriage who had placed I. (who had a congenital neural anomaly) in nursery school, concluding she lacked time to raise the children properly. By contrast, E. held a managerial post, lived with his helpful mother, and enjoyed I.’s attachment. The court found the applicant had failed to prove her case and that E. had not hindered contact.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the court had exceeded the parties’ claims, that her daughter was self-reliant and helpful, that nursery attendance aided I.’s development, that neither parent’s work schedule had been examined, that I.’s sudden attachment to E. after a short period was unexplained, and that E. was in fact blocking contact (as later confirmed by a Grozny official). On 3 July 2014 the Supreme Court of the Chechen Republic upheld the judgment as lawful and in the child’s best interests, citing his age, attachment to the father and the latter’s capacity to provide.

A 7 August 2014 letter from a Grozny deputy mayor recorded E.’s refusal to allow contact. On 12 September 2014 the head of Grozny childcare informed the applicant that the official who produced the 15 April report had been disciplined: the report contained unchecked claims about E.’s income, unsubstantiated assertions that the applicant had not participated in upbringing, no verification of the time I. had spent with each parent, and no mention of I.’s half-sister. The applicant’s cassation appeal citing this letter was refused on 27 November 2014; the judge again relied on the flawed report.

E. died in a car accident on 5 December 2014; I. remained with grandmother A. The applicant then obtained a 31 July 2015 order from the Shali Town Court (upheld on appeal) that I. be returned to her. Enforcement was obstructed when A. hid the child; I. was finally returned by police on 28 April 2016.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation arising from the initial residence decision.
001-182226:
The case of Tsukanov and Torchinskiy v. Russia originated in two applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 May 2013 by Russian nationals Filipp Igorevich Tsukanov (born 1984) and Artem Aleksandrovich Torchinskiy (born 1979), both residing in Moscow. Represented by Moscow lawyer K. Terekhov, they complained against the Russian Federation. The applications were communicated to the Government on 24 March 2014.

On 14 December 2012 the State Duma adopted at first reading a draft law prohibiting adoption of Russian children by United States citizens. On 17 December the official newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta announced that the second reading would take place on 19 December 2012. The applicants learned via social networks that numerous individuals planned to stage solo pickets that day in front of the State Duma to oppose the measure. They chose this format because the statutory three-day notification period for group public events could not be observed.

Around 9 a.m. on 19 December 2012 the applicants positioned themselves holding banners in the vicinity of the State Duma, at a distance from other protesters. Police arrested them within minutes and transported them to a station. Official records of administrative escorting and arrest, drawn up at 10.30 a.m., stated that they had arrived then; the applicants, however, annotated the documents to record actual apprehension at 9.20 a.m. (Tsukanov) and 9.30 a.m. (Torchinskiy). They were charged under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences with organising and holding a group public event without prior notification. The offence records listed the time of commission as 10 a.m. Tsukanov noted that he had arrived at 9 a.m. and been arrested at 9.20 a.m. Both were released after roughly four hours (Tsukanov at 1.20 p.m., Torchinskiy at 1.10 p.m.).

On 15 January 2013 a justice of the peace convicted Torchinskiy and imposed a fine of 20 000 roubles (approximately 495 euros). Relying on police records and officers’ testimony, the court found that he had taken part in an unnotified picket involving fifty people, had waved a banner that attracted passers-by and journalists, and had failed to comply with a police order to stop. On 6 February 2013 the same court convicted Tsukanov on identical reasoning and imposed the same fine.

Both applicants appealed, maintaining that each had conducted a solitary demonstration requiring no prior notification; Tsukanov additionally contested the recorded time of arrest. The Tverskoy District Court dismissed the appeals on 13 February and 11 March 2013. Torchinskiy then sought supervisory review. On 28 June 2013 the Deputy President of the Moscow City Court reclassified the offence as a participant’s breach of procedure under Article 20.2 § 5 and reduced the fine to 10 000 roubles (approximately 233 euros).

These events raise issues concerning the lawfulness and duration of the applicants’ deprivation of liberty and the characterisation of their individual, spatially separated protests as a single unauthorised group assembly. Domestic legislation at the relevant time required prior notification for most public events; a subsequent Moscow City law (in force from 6 January 2013) prescribed a fifty-metre separation between simultaneous solo demonstrations and treated them as individual if they lacked a common organiser or goal. The applicants’ convictions and the short but unacknowledged period of detention therefore form the core factual basis for alleged interferences with freedom of expression and assembly and with personal liberty.

Russia (applications nos. 35000/13 and 35010/13) involves two Russian nationals, Filipp Igorevich Tsukanov (born 1984) and Artem Aleksandrovich Torchinskiy (born 1979), both residing in Moscow. They lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 May 2013, alleging violations arising from their arrest and administrative punishment for public protest activities.

Solo pickets were selected because there was insufficient time to comply with the three-day prior notification requirement under the Public Events Act for group events.

**Case of Zabelos and Others v. Greece (ECtHR, 17 May 2018, App. no. 1167/15)**

Eighteen applicants of various nationalities (listed in the annex) lodged this application against Greece on 24 December 2014. Represented by Thessaloniki lawyers, they alleged that conditions of detention in Korydallos Prison Hospital violated Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment). All but the third applicant (who had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) were HIV-positive. The Greek Government was represented by State Legal Council delegates. The Albanian and Georgian Governments did not intervene.

The applicants were detained (or remained detained) in the Prison Hospital for periods spanning 2010–2016, with some still held when observations were submitted. The case of Sergey Ivanov v. Russia (Application no. 14416/06) concerns allegations by a Russian national of police ill-treatment, ineffective investigation thereof, and the use of resulting coerced confessions in his conviction for robbery and related crimes.

On 24 April 2004 a robbery occurred in Nizhniy Novgorod. Operational-search activities identified the applicant as a suspect. On 8 June 2004 officers searched his flat and took him to the ORB police unit. The applicant alleged that, after his request for a lawyer was ignored, officers (including K., Pr. and S.) punched and kicked him, blocked his airway with a rag, and bound him in a painful position: seated cross-legged on the floor, hands cuffed behind his back, a bag over his head, and a rope linking his feet to his neck and handcuffs. Officers pulled the rope, sat and jumped on his back, and poured water on him when he lost consciousness, while telling one another not to leave marks. The investigator repeatedly demanded a confession. After several hours the applicant signed a “statement of surrender and confession” recorded at 9.30 a.m. Official records listed the statement as voluntary and timed his formal arrest at 9.40 a.m. Later that day, with an appointed lawyer present, he refused to make statements. On 9 June he complained of ill-treatment to the remand judge, who took no action. He was then held in temporary detention before transfer to SIZO-1.

On 22 June officers (Ch., K., P. and Pr.) again took him from SIZO-1 to the police station and subjected him to further violence to obtain statements. On 24 June he lodged detailed complaints with prison, prosecutorial and presidential authorities, naming officers and asserting that the confession had been dictated to him.

On 28 June the same officers punched, kicked and bound him (legs pulled apart) at the police station; no investigative acts occurred. The following day a remand-centre doctor recorded circular abrasions on both shins inflicted the previous day. The applicant complained of chest contusions and abrasions, requested a full examination and an investigation, and asked that future questioning take place at the remand centre in his lawyer’s presence.

On 13–14 July 2004, citing an alleged risk that the applicant would intimidate co-accused, investigator S. ordered his transfer to a remand unit inside correctional colony IK-14. The applicant alleged that he spent 18 days in a punishment cell, where convicted prisoners, acting on police instructions and with colony-administration connivance, beat him unconscious (punches, kicks, rubber truncheon, hanging upside-down). Thereafter he was held with convicts and repeatedly visited by officers Ch. and P., who beat him and instructed convicts (S.P., A.V., Z.) to do likewise or to threaten sexual violence. Medical staff allegedly refused treatment. Under this pressure he signed six further “statements of surrender and confession.” On 3 November he repeated the statements in the presence of S. and a lawyer. He was returned to SIZO-1 on 2 December.

Witness statements later recorded by an NGO (from fellow prisoner I.K., prisoner G., the applicant’s wife and son) described visible injuries, police visits followed by fresh bruising and immobility, and overheard threats. Contemporary medical records were sparse and inconsistent (a 9 June form noted only a headache and “clean” skin; later records recorded shin abrasions and a period of inpatient neurological treatment).

Prosecutors conducted successive pre-investigation inquiries. Decisions of July–August 2004 and April 2005 refusing to open criminal cases (citing officers’ denials and lack of corroboration) were later revoked as incomplete, yet fresh refusals followed. No criminal proceedings were ever instituted.

At a 2005–2006 jury trial the applicant sought exclusion of the confession records as obtained under duress. The court heard I.K. and the applicant’s son but dismissed their evidence, attributing symptoms to pre-existing conditions, relying on the prosecutors’ refusal decisions and noting the presence of a lawyer. The statements were admitted and treated as mitigating circumstances. The applicant was convicted of multiple robberies and sentenced to 19 years (later reduced on appeal and by legislative amendment). Appeals reiterating the ill-treatment claims were rejected.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.

The ECHR case of Gafà v. Malta (App. No. 54335/14, judgment 22 May 2018) concerns applicant Kenneth Gafà (Maltese, b. 1972), who alleged a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention arising from excessive bail conditions that prolonged his pre-trial detention despite a legal entitlement to release.

Gafà was arrested on 11 December 2010 on suspicion of murdering his former partner and charged with wilful homicide on 13 December 2010. He was remanded in custody. Over the ensuing period until August 2012 he lodged ten unsuccessful bail applications (after oral hearings). Numerous other hearings took place, with evidence from many witnesses and some adjournments. In April 2012 Gafà brought constitutional proceedings complaining that detention exceeding 15 months breached Article 5 § 3; these were rejected by the Civil Court (First Hall) in June 2012 and the Constitutional Court in November 2012.

Under Article 575(6)(a)(iii) of the Maltese Criminal Code, a person accused of a crime punishable by nine years’ imprisonment or more must be granted bail after 20 months’ detention. Following Gafà’s request of 17 August 2012, the Court of Magistrates granted bail on 22 August 2012 subject to conditions including attendance at hearings, a prohibition on absconding or contacting prosecution witnesses, daily reporting to police between 08:00 and 20:00, a curfew from 22:00 to 06:00, notification of any address change, a cash deposit of EUR 15,000, and a personal guarantee of EUR 25,000 (EUR 40,000 to be forfeited on any breach).

The Attorney General appealed, seeking a higher deposit and a ban on Gafà entering the victim’s locality. Gafà objected that he could not meet the financial conditions (he had been unemployed during 20 months’ detention and produced evidence of modest unemployment benefits plus 12 years of tax assessments) and sought a reduction. On 7 September 2012 the Criminal Court added the locality restriction but refused both to raise and to lower the deposit. Subsequent reduction requests (October 2012, December 2012 and January/February 2013) were likewise refused, the court citing the seriousness of the offence and the need to balance potential punishment against the risk of non-compliance.

On 22 July 2013 Gafà proposed his mother (and relatives) as sureties over inherited property valued at EUR 95,000. After documentary evidence was supplied, the court accepted a hypothec on the property on 2 August 2013. Gafà was released on 6 August 2013 (after 32 months in custody) upon signing the personal guarantee.

In February 2013 Gafà commenced a second set of constitutional proceedings complaining that the “exorbitant” deposit prevented him from effectively enjoying the bail to which he was entitled. The Civil Court (July 2013) and Constitutional Court (January 2014) rejected the claim. They held that the applicant bore the onus of furnishing verifiable information about his means, assets and inability to obtain a surety; he had supplied only tax forms, had not earlier proposed the available family property, and the EUR 15,000 deposit was proportionate when all statutory factors (Article 576: the accused’s situation, nature of the offence and applicable punishment) were considered together.

(Later events: Gafà’s bail was revoked in April 2014 for breach of conditions; after indictment in January 2015 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced in July 2015 to 35 years’ imprisonment.)

Kenneth Gafà, a Maltese national, was arrested on 11 December 2010 on suspicion of murdering his former partner and charged on 13 December 2010 with wilful homicide. He was remanded in custody. Between arraignment and August 2012 he filed ten bail applications, all rejected after hearings at which witnesses were examined.

After 20 months’ detention—the statutory maximum under Article 575(6)(a)(iii) of the Criminal Code for offences carrying nine years’ imprisonment or more—he became entitled to bail. On 22 August 2012 the Court of Magistrates granted it subject to conditions: attendance at hearings, a travel ban, non-contact with prosecution witnesses, a daily police-station reporting requirement, a 22:00–06:00 curfew, notification of any address change, a cash deposit of €15,000 and a personal guarantee of €25,000 (totalling €40,000, forfeitable on any breach).

The Attorney General immediately appealed, arguing the financial conditions were too lenient. Gafà, now unemployed after prolonged detention, applied for a reduction, producing unemployment-benefit records (€1,262 in 2009 and €1,573 in 2010) and twelve years of tax assessments. On 7 September 2012 the Criminal Court added a geographical restriction but refused both to increase and to reduce the deposit.

Three further applications (October and December 2012, January 2013) seeking a lower deposit were likewise rejected. The courts consistently cited the gravity of the charge, the likely sentence and the continuing risk of interference with evidence. Gafà remained in custody solely because he could not raise the cash.

On 22 July 2013 he proposed his mother as surety, offering an inherited property valued at €95,000. After production of title documents the court accepted a hypothec on 2 August 2013. Gafà was released on 6 August 2013—almost a year after bail had first been granted and 32 months after arrest—having signed the personal guarantee.

They emphasised that the onus lay on the accused to furnish verifiable financial information and to explore all available guarantees.

Committal proceedings continued throughout; the prosecution closed its evidence on 31 July 2013. (Bail was later revoked in April 2014 for breach of conditions; Gafà was ultimately convicted in 2015 after a plea bargain and sentenced to 35 years’ imprisonment.)

The facts relevant to the alleged Article 5 § 3 violation are therefore the continued detention for nearly twelve months after statutory entitlement to bail, caused exclusively by an unaffordable cash deposit that the courts repeatedly declined to moderate despite evidence of indigence, until a property surety was belatedly accepted.

**Case summary: Gafà v. Malta (ECtHR, Application no. 54335/14, judgment 22 May 2018)**

Kenneth Gafà, a Maltese national born in 1972, was arrested on 11 December 2010 on suspicion of murdering his former partner. He was charged on 13 December 2010 with wilful homicide (among other offences) before the Court of Magistrates as a Court of Criminal Inquiry and remanded in custody. From arraignment until August 2012 he filed ten bail requests, all rejected after hearings; numerous other hearings occurred, including some where evidence was taken.

After the statutory maximum pre-trial detention of 20 months for offences punishable by nine years or more (Criminal Code Article 575(6)(a)(iii)), Gafà became entitled to bail. On 22 August 2012 the Court of Magistrates granted it subject to conditions: attendance at hearings; no absconding or leaving Malta; no contact with prosecution witnesses; no further voluntary crimes; daily reporting to police between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; a curfew (home by 10 p.m., not leaving before 6 a.m.); notification of address changes; a €15,000 cash deposit; and a €25,000 personal guarantee. Any breach would forfeit the full €40,000.

Gafà could not pay the deposit. Unemployed after prolonged detention, he had previously received modest unemployment benefits (around €1,262–€1,573 in 2009–2010) and submitted tax assessments. The Attorney General appealed the conditions as too lenient given the offence’s gravity, seeking a higher deposit and a ban on entering the locality where the victim’s family lived. On 7 September 2012 the Criminal Court rejected an increase in the deposit but added the locality restriction and refused Gafà’s reduction request.

Gafà filed further unsuccessful applications (October 2012, December 2012, January/February 2013) to reduce the deposit, citing 22–27 months’ total detention, inability to pay, and that main witnesses had already been heard. Courts consistently rejected them, balancing the crime’s seriousness and potential punishment against the need for compliance guarantees. In July 2013 he offered his mother (and relatives) as surety via hypothec on inherited property valued at €95,000. On 2 August 2013 this was accepted. After signing the personal guarantee and completing the hypothec, he was released on 6 August 2013 after 32 months’ detention.

In parallel, Gafà brought two sets of constitutional proceedings claiming Article 5 § 3 violations. The first (April 2012, concerning the initial 15+ months) was rejected by the Civil Court (First Hall) in June 2012 and the Constitutional Court in November 2012. The second (February 2013) challenged the “exorbitant” deposit that prevented effective enjoyment of bail. The Civil Court (July 2013) and Constitutional Court (January 2014) dismissed it. They held that an accused must furnish checkable information on income, savings, assets and surety possibilities (citing *Iwanczuk v. Poland*). Gafà had provided only tax forms, not a full asset list or proof of objective inability to raise funds or find sureties earlier; the €15,000 deposit was justified by the offence’s gravity, possible life sentence, risk of evidence tampering, and Article 576 factors (including means, considered together with other circumstances). He later offered surety, which the courts viewed as available earlier.

A bill of indictment followed; Gafà later admitted the charges, was convicted in July 2015 and sentenced to 35 years’ imprisonment. (He had also had bail revoked in April 2014 for a breach.) The ECtHR later examined the Article 5 § 3 complaint concerning the post-bail-grant detention caused by the conditions.

The case of Boyan Gospodinov v. Bulgaria originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically that the applicant’s second set of criminal proceedings had not been determined by an impartial tribunal.

The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1983 and living in Stara Zagora, was first prosecuted after a police search of his home on 18 August 2002 uncovered cannabis. He was placed in pre-trial detention on 30 August 2002. On 22 May 2003 the Stara Zagora Regional Court convicted him of unlawful possession of 14.44 grams of cannabis and sentenced him to three-and-a-half years’ imprisonment, deducting time already spent in detention. The Plovdiv Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to one year on 13 October 2003. The Supreme Court of Cassation replaced the detention measure with judicial supervision on 6 April 2004 and the applicant was released the next day, having spent one year, seven months and eight days in custody. The cassation court later upheld the reduced sentence.

On 23 September 2004 the applicant brought a civil action for damages under the Law on State Responsibility for Damages against the Stara Zagora Regional Court, the Plovdiv Court of Appeal, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the prosecutor’s office. He claimed that his pre-trial detention had exceeded the sentence ultimately imposed and sought compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary harm. An initial hearing took place before the Sofia City Court.

While that action was pending, on 14 October 2004 the Stara Zagora regional prosecutor’s office indicted the applicant for narcotics trafficking between March 2000 and March 2002 and committed him for trial before the same Regional Court that was a defendant in the civil claim. At the first hearing on 18 October 2004 defence counsel requested transfer of the case to another regional court, arguing that the judges could not be impartial because their court faced potential liability. The request was refused on the grounds that formal civil proceedings had not yet commenced and that none of the sitting judges (who had not sat in the first case) showed personal bias. The presiding judge nevertheless recused himself because he had participated in the earlier conviction.

The applicant renewed his applications for collective recusal of all Regional Court judges and transfer of the case, asserting that the judges had a direct interest in imposing a substantial prison sentence so as to prevent a finding of State liability that would affect their court’s budget. These applications were rejected: no statutory ground of withdrawal under Article 25 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was made out, no concrete evidence of bias existed, the civil claim was pending before a different court, and an appeal would lie against any conviction.

The Regional Court heard evidence between January and October 2005 and, on 3 October 2005, convicted the applicant of purchasing, possessing and selling cannabis, sentencing him to sixteen years’ imprisonment. It combined this sentence with the earlier one-year term and deducted the period of pre-trial detention already served. On appeal the Plovdiv Court of Appeal, after a hearing at which the defence again raised the issue of first-instance bias, quashed the judgment, excluded certain evidence obtained in breach of defence rights, but nevertheless convicted the applicant on the remaining evidence and reduced the sentence to ten years, confirming the combination and deduction. The Supreme Court of Cassation further reduced the sentence to three years on 16 November 2006, again combining the terms and deducting prior detention, so that the applicant had only seventeen months left to serve.

The civil damages claim, which had been adjourned pending the outcome of the second criminal case, was ultimately dismissed by the Sofia courts on the basis that the combined sentences meant detention had not exceeded the total term imposed.

Domestic law provided that a judge must withdraw in any circumstance liable to jeopardise impartiality and that a case could be transferred if an entire bench recused itself. Courts managed their own budgets and any damages awards would be paid from those appropriations. These facts formed the core of the impartiality complaint.

Bulgaria (Application no. 28417/07) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the applicant’s claim that his second set of criminal proceedings was not determined by an impartial tribunal. The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1983 and resident in Stara Zagora, faced two related sets of criminal proceedings for drug offences, alongside a civil action for damages against the courts involved in the first proceedings.

In August 2002 police searched the applicant’s home and discovered cannabis. He was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention on 30 August 2002. On 22 May 2003 the Stara Zagora Regional Court convicted him of unlawful possession of 14.44 grams of cannabis and sentenced him to three-and-a-half years’ imprisonment, deducting time already spent in detention. The Plovdiv Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to one year on 13 October 2003. The Supreme Court of Cassation ordered his release on 6 April 2004 (effective the following day) after he had spent one year, seven months and eight days in detention; it later upheld the one-year sentence on 25 May 2004.

On 23 September 2004 the applicant brought a civil action for damages in the Sofia City Court against the Stara Zagora Regional Court, the Plovdiv Court of Appeal, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the prosecutor’s office. Relying on section 2(6) of the Law on State Responsibility for Damages, he claimed that his detention had exceeded the sentence ultimately imposed and sought 11 500 Bulgarian leva for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The civil proceedings were later adjourned at the request of a representative of the Plovdiv Court of Appeal (who produced the second criminal judgment) because the outcome of the new criminal case might determine liability.

Meanwhile, on 14 October 2004 the Stara Zagora regional prosecutor indicted the applicant before the same Regional Court for narcotics trafficking between March 2000 and March 2002. At the first hearing on 18 October 2004 defence counsel sought transfer of the case, arguing that the Regional Court judges could not be impartial because their court was a defendant in the pending damages action. The request was refused on the grounds that civil proceedings had not yet been formally commenced, that the sitting judges had not participated in the first criminal case, and that no personal bias had been shown. The trial president nevertheless withdrew because he had sat in the earlier trial. The applicant renewed the recusal request in writing and at subsequent hearings, asserting that the judges had a collective interest in imposing a prison sentence so that, when combined with the first sentence, the prior detention would no longer exceed the total term and the court would avoid financial liability. All requests were dismissed: no statutory ground for recusal under Article 25 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure existed, no evidence of bias had been adduced, the civil action was pending before a different court that the Regional Court could not influence, and an appeal would remain available.

The Regional Court convicted the applicant on 3 October 2005 of purchasing, possessing and selling cannabis and imposed a sixteen-year sentence, combining it with the earlier one-year term and deducting the period of pre-trial detention. The Plovdiv Court of Appeal (before which recusal of the Regional Court judges was again raised) quashed the first-instance judgment on 25 January 2006, excluded certain evidence obtained in breach of defence rights, but re-convicted the applicant and reduced the sentence to ten years, again combining the sentences and deducting detention. The Supreme Court of Cassation further reduced the sentence to three years on 16 November 2006; after combination and deduction the applicant had only seventeen months left to serve. The civil claim was ultimately dismissed in 2007 precisely because the combined sentence meant that detention had not exceeded the term imposed.

Domestic law provided for recusal of judges where impartiality might be jeopardised (Article 25 § 9 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) and for transfer of a case if an entire court recused itself (Article 36). Sentences for concurrent offences were combined under Article 23 of the Penal Code and pre-trial detention was deducted under Article 59. Courts managed their own budgets, from which any damages awarded against them would be paid.

These facts form the core of the impartiality complaint: the same court that stood to incur financial liability in the civil action sat as the trial court in the second criminal case and had a direct interest in producing a conviction and sentence that would extinguish that liability.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Boyan Gospodinov v. Bulgaria (application no. 28417/07) originated from an application lodged on 3 May 2007 by a Bulgarian national alleging, inter alia, a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention on the ground that his second set of criminal proceedings had not been determined by an impartial tribunal.

The applicant was born in 1983 and lives in Stara Zagora. In August 2002 police searched his home and found cannabis. He was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention from 30 August 2002. On 22 May 2003 the Stara Zagora Regional Court convicted him of unlawful possession of 14.44 grams of cannabis and sentenced him to three-and-a-half years’ imprisonment, deducting time already spent in detention. The Plovdiv Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to one year on 13 October 2003. The Supreme Court of Cassation upheld that judgment on 25 May 2004. The applicant had already been released on 7 April 2004 after serving one year, seven months and eight days in pre-trial detention—exceeding the final one-year sentence.

On 23 September 2004 the applicant brought a civil action for damages before the Sofia City Court against the Stara Zagora Regional Court, the Plovdiv Court of Appeal, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the public prosecutor’s office. Relying on section 2(6) of the Law on State Responsibility for Damages, he claimed 11,500 Bulgarian levs for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage arising from the fact that his pre-trial detention had lasted longer than the sentence ultimately imposed.

On 14 October 2004 the Stara Zagora regional prosecutor’s office indicted the applicant before the same Stara Zagora Regional Court for narcotics trafficking committed between March 2000 and March 2002. At the first hearing on 18 October 2004 the applicant’s lawyer sought transfer of the case to another regional court, arguing that the Stara Zagora judges could not be impartial because their court was a respondent in the pending civil damages action. The request was dismissed: the civil proceedings had only recently been instituted and there was no indication of personal bias on the part of the professional or lay judges, none of whom had sat in the first criminal case. The president of the trial court nevertheless recused himself because he had participated in the earlier conviction. The applicant reiterated his request for collective recusal of all regional-court judges and transfer of the case, asserting that the judges had a financial and institutional interest in imposing a lengthy prison sentence so that, when combined with the first sentence and after deduction of the earlier detention period, the civil claim would be defeated. These applications were rejected on 10 January 2005. The court held that none of the statutory grounds for recusal under Article 25 of the 1974 Code of Criminal Procedure existed, that no actual bias had been shown, that the civil action was pending before a different court, and that an appeal would in any event lie against the forthcoming judgment.

Between January and October 2005 the Stara Zagora Regional Court heard evidence and, on 3 October 2005, convicted the applicant of unlawful purchase, possession and sale of cannabis, imposing a sixteen-year sentence. It combined that sentence with the earlier one-year term and deducted the 2002–2004 detention period. The applicant appealed, repeating his complaint of first-instance bias. The Plovdiv Court of Appeal (before which no recusal request was made) quashed the judgment on 25 January 2006, excluded certain evidence, but re-convicted the applicant and reduced the sentence to ten years while upholding the combination and deduction of sentences. On 16 November 2006 the Supreme Court of Cassation further reduced the sentence to three years, again combining the two terms and deducting the earlier detention, so that the applicant had only seventeen months left to serve.

Meanwhile the Sofia City Court had adjourned the civil action at the request of a representative of the Stara Zagora Regional Court, who produced the new conviction and argued that it would determine the compensation claim. After the criminal proceedings ended, both the Sofia City Court and the Sofia Court of Appeal dismissed the damages action on the ground that the combined sentence now exceeded the time spent in detention.

These overlapping proceedings form the core of the alleged impartiality complaint: the same court that stood to incur liability if the detention were found to have been excessive was simultaneously trying the applicant on a new charge whose outcome could, and ultimately did, extinguish that liability through sentence combination.

The case of Dornean v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 27810/07) was brought by Moldovan national Leonid Dornean (born 1951), who lived in Trinca. After divorcing his wife, he continued residing in an annex of the same house as her and their children (some adult), amid a hostile relationship with them and his former in-laws. He alleged that Moldovan authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into repeated claims of ill-treatment by his ex-wife and children, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention. The Court communicated this complaint in 2015 (other claims were declared inadmissible).

Dornean had a history of unheeded complaints. On 30 May 2005 he wrote to the Prosecutor General listing prior reports to police and others of beatings, property destruction, and police inaction; a local prosecutor’s refusal to investigate was later annulled and the matter sent for re-examination. Medical experts examined him on 31 March 2006 (excoriation on the right hand, attributed to a blow from his son D.V.) and 15 May 2006 (three loose teeth and a finger contusion, again blamed on D.V.). On 26 June 2006 prosecutors declined to open an investigation. Further complaints of attacks, death threats, and property damage followed on 31 August and 19 September 2006, again without investigation. In December 2006 police merely held a “cautionary discussion” with the ex-wife and formally warned her.

The core incident occurred on 27 December 2006, when Dornean claimed his ex-wife and children assaulted him at home, breaking his left elbow. He said police immediately refused to act. The next day a local doctor referred him for X-rays at Edineț Polyclinic; on 29 December a forensic expert confirmed a fracture of the upper third of the left radial bone (medium severity, requiring over 21 days’ treatment, caused by a blunt object consistent with his account). He received ongoing treatment through March 2007.

On 5 January 2007 he formally complained of ill-treatment by his ex-wife and three children (including D.V.). Police initially declined to investigate; an investigating judge later noted an inquiry was underway. A prosecutor opened a criminal investigation on 2 February 2007 and recognised Dornean as the victim on 1 March. A second forensic report that month confirmed the injury. However, witnesses later claimed they saw him cutting wood on 12 January 2007 with no sign of injury or pain. Doctor T. (who saw him on 28 December) reported only bruising, disputed the X-ray findings, and said he saw no fracture.

Prosecutors repeatedly sought further medical reports, including from a commission, but Dornean initially refused to supply the 28 December X-rays out of distrust of police; the commission therefore could not examine them. The investigation was discontinued on 19 March 2008 (applicant allegedly provoked quarrels; family denied assault; delayed expert visit; possible self-infliction; X-rays withheld). A higher prosecutor annulled this as premature. Identical discontinuations followed on 17 May and 21 November 2008; both were quashed by an investigating judge or higher prosecutor for superficial, unilateral, and incomplete work (failure to interview all doctors or the radiologist; ignoring prior instructions; denying the victim input on expert questions; not informing him he could send X-rays directly to the commission). After Dornean submitted the films in March 2009, a 9 December 2009 commission report confirmed a radial-bone fracture that could have occurred as he described or been self-inflicted (the films being of poor quality). The investigation was finally discontinued on 30 June 2010 (upheld 17 December 2010 and by an investigating judge in 2011) on essentially the same grounds, plus the self-infliction possibility and contradictory witness statements.

Separate medical reports from August–November 2007 documented additional bruises, excoriations, and pain that Dornean attributed to further beatings by his ex-wife and children. These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 3 violation concerning the investigation’s effectiveness.

The case of Dornean v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 27810/07) concerns applicant Leonid Dornean (born 1951), a Moldovan national living in Trinca. He alleged a violation of Article 3 ECHR arising from the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into repeated ill-treatment by his ex-wife and children. After divorcing, the applicant lived in an annex of the family home amid ongoing hostility with his former wife, adult children (including D.V.), and in-laws. From 2005 he lodged multiple complaints with prosecutors and police about assaults, property destruction and police inaction. A 2005 prosecutorial refusal to investigate was later annulled. Medical examinations in March and May 2006 recorded an excoriation, loose teeth and a finger contusion that the applicant attributed to attacks by his son; prosecutors declined to open a case.

The principal incident occurred on 27 December 2006, when the applicant claimed his ex-wife and children assaulted him, fracturing his left elbow. He said police refused to attend when called. An X-ray the next day and a forensic report of 29 December 2006 confirmed a medium-severity fracture of the upper third of the radial bone (requiring more than 21 days’ treatment) consistent with a blunt-object blow as he described. Follow-up medical visits continued into March 2007.

A police complaint on 5 January 2007 initially produced a refusal to investigate, but a prosecutor opened a criminal case on 2 February 2007 and recognised the applicant as victim. Subsequent forensic reports reiterated the fracture. Witnesses, however, stated they had seen the applicant cutting wood on 12 January 2007 without visible injury or pain. Doctor T., who examined him on 28 December, reported only contusions and disputed the X-ray description of a fracture. The applicant initially refused to surrender the original X-rays, citing distrust of the police.

The investigation was discontinued four times (March, May and November 2008; June 2010). Each discontinuation cited the applicant’s alleged provocation of quarrels, denials by family members (interviewed as witnesses), delayed forensic examination, and the possibility of self-infliction. Higher prosecutors and investigating judges repeatedly quashed these decisions as premature, superficial, tendentious and incomplete: relevant doctors (including the radiologist) had not been properly interviewed, the victim’s rights regarding expert questions had been ignored, and he had not been told he could submit X-rays directly to the forensic centre.

In 2009 the applicant provided the X-rays; they were of poor quality, so a new examination was performed. A December 2009 commission report confirmed the fracture, which “could have been caused in the manner described \ldots but could also have been self-inflicted.” The final discontinuation was upheld in July 2011 on the ground that all possible steps had been taken and that witnesses contradicted the applicant’s account.

Additional medical reports from August–November 2007 documented further bruises and excoriations that the applicant again attributed to beatings by his ex-wife and daughter; these incidents were not the subject of a separate effective inquiry. The pattern of delays, incomplete witness and medical inquiries, and repeated annulled discontinuations formed the factual basis of the Article 3 complaint concerning the State’s procedural duty to investigate alleged ill-treatment.

**Case Summary: Dornean v. the Republic of Moldova (App. No. 27810/07)**

Leonid Dornean, a Moldovan national born in 1951 and residing in Trinca, alleged a violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into repeated claims of ill-treatment by his ex-wife and children.

Following his divorce, Dornean lived in an annex to the family house occupied by his ex-wife, their children (some adults), and former in-laws amid ongoing hostility. From at least 2005 he lodged numerous complaints with police, prosecutors and other bodies about physical assaults, property destruction and police inaction. A May 2005 letter to the Prosecutor General prompted annulment of an earlier refusal to investigate and ordered re-examination.

Medical evidence in 2006 recorded injuries the applicant attributed to his son D.V.: an excoriation on his right hand (March) and loose teeth plus a finger contusion (May). Prosecutors declined to open a criminal investigation. Further complaints in August and September 2006 of attacks, death threats and property damage similarly produced no proceedings. In December 2006 police merely held a cautionary discussion with the ex-wife.

The central incident occurred on 27 December 2006, when the applicant claimed his ex-wife and children assaulted him, fracturing his left elbow. He said police refused to attend. The next day a local doctor referred him for X-ray examination; a 29 December 2006 forensic report confirmed a medium-severity fracture of the upper third of the radial bone (requiring more than 21 days’ treatment) caused by a blunt object, consistent with the applicant’s account. He received subsequent medical treatment.

A police complaint on 5 January 2007 was initially rejected. After an investigating judge’s intervention a prosecutor opened a criminal investigation on 2 February 2007 and recognised Dornean as a victim. Additional medical reports corroborated the fracture. However, witnesses stated they had seen the applicant cutting wood on 12 January 2007 without visible injury or pain. Doctor T., who examined him on 28 December, reported only bruises and denied seeing a fracture on the X-ray.

Repeated discontinuations followed (March, May and November 2008; June 2010). Prosecutors cited the applicant’s alleged provocation of quarrels, family denials, delayed forensic examination, possible self-infliction and contradictory witness evidence. Higher prosecutors and investigating judges repeatedly quashed these decisions as premature, extremely superficial, tendentious and unilateral. They criticised the failure to interview key doctors, to respect the victim’s rights when commissioning expert reports, and to establish the injury’s origin.

After the applicant eventually supplied the X-rays, a 2009 medical commission confirmed fracture signs that could have been inflicted as described or self-inflicted. The investigation was finally closed in 2010–2011; an investigating judge upheld the decision, finding all possible measures had been taken and that witnesses contradicted the applicant.

Further forensic reports from August to November 2007 documented additional bruises, excoriations and pain that the applicant again attributed to beatings by his ex-wife and children. These facts formed the core of the complaint of an ineffective investigation into domestic ill-treatment.

The case of Fatih Çakır and Merve Nisa Çakır v. Turkey (App. no. 54558/11) arose from an application lodged on 8 July 2011 with the European Court of Human Rights. The applicants, Turkish nationals Fatih Çakır (born 1979) and his daughter Merve Nisa Çakır (born 2007), both residing in İzmir, alleged violations of Article 2 of the Convention due to the State authorities’ failure to implement necessary road safety measures, which they claimed caused the death of Yeşim Çakır (Fatih’s wife and Merve’s mother). They further alleged under Articles 6 and 13 that the subsequent judicial proceedings were inadequate to establish any State responsibility for the death.

On 25 October 2008, Fatih Çakır was driving in İzmir with his wife and infant daughter in the rear seats when he lost control of the vehicle at a sharp bend. The car struck a metal crash barrier and plunged into an empty concrete canal five to six metres below the road level. Yeşim Çakır died at the scene; the daughter sustained slight injuries. The same-day traffic police report, based on on-site findings and Fatih’s statement, recorded that the vehicle first hit the barrier (already damaged before the accident) and then fell over it into the canal. A warning sign for the sharp bend was in place.

Fatih told police that the car had skidded left for unknown reasons (possibly sand on a dry road) as he approached the bend; noticing another vehicle approaching from behind on his left, he braked and swerved right, losing control and hitting the damaged barrier, which failed to contain the vehicle. An eyewitness, M.S., confirmed seeing the car suddenly swerve right, strike the barrier and drop. The İzmir public prosecutor later took Fatih’s statement, in which he admitted losing control on the bend. On 28 October 2008 the prosecutor indicted Fatih for negligently causing death and injury. At the 15 December 2008 hearing before the İzmir Assize Court, Fatih repeated that the car had skidded left at normal speed; he had swerved right to avoid an oncoming vehicle. He did not request further investigation but noted the barrier’s pre-existing damage. The court found him negligent yet imposed no penalty, holding that he had been sufficiently aggrieved by his wife’s death under Article 22 § 6 of the Criminal Code. The judgment became final on 23 December 2008 without appeal.

On 17 November 2008 Fatih applied to the İzmir Magistrates’ Court for a declaratory judgment on the barrier’s contribution to the accident, whether it had been repaired afterwards, and any structural road defects such as unusual sloping. The 5 December 2008 expert report found the barrier damaged before the accident and still unrepaired, plus a slight dent near it, but no slope problems.

On 2 March 2009 Fatih sought compensation from the General Directorate of Highways and the İzmir Municipality, arguing that the pre-damaged barrier (evidencing prior accidents at the same spot) had greatly worsened the outcome; a repaired barrier would likely have prevented the drop into the canal. Both authorities denied maintenance responsibility. On 20 May 2009 the applicants sued the Municipality alone in the İzmir Administrative Court, submitting the expert report and alleging failure to repair the barrier promptly plus possible road defects. The Municipality again denied responsibility and attributed the accident solely to Fatih despite the warning sign.

In an 18 February 2010 interim decision the court obtained the criminal file and information showing the Municipality was responsible for barrier repairs. The applicants repeatedly requested an expert examination of possible structural problems and data on prior accidents at the site; these were not obtained. On 27 May 2010 the Administrative Court, relying mainly on the accident report and Fatih’s statements, held him solely responsible for losing control despite the warning sign and dismissed the claim. The applicants appealed, arguing that a technical expert opinion was needed on possible road anomalies and that the court had ignored the barrier’s total loss of protective function. On 25 January 2011 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment.

Domestic law (General Directorate of Highways Act, Road Traffic Act and related regulations) imposed on the Directorate and municipalities duties to ensure road safety through construction, maintenance, accident analysis, markings and preventive technical measures.

The case of Fatih Çakır and Merve Nisa Çakır v. Turkey (Application no. 54558/11) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 8 July 2011 by two Turkish nationals living in İzmir. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 2 of the Convention, claiming that the relevant State authorities' failure to take necessary road safety measures caused the death of Yeşim Çakır (the first applicant's wife and the second applicant's mother). They further alleged, under Articles 6 and 13, that the subsequent judicial proceedings were inadequate to determine whether State authorities bore any responsibility for the death.

On 25 October 2008, the first applicant was driving in İzmir with his wife and one-year-old daughter in the back seat. He lost control of the vehicle at a sharp bend, causing it to crash into a metal barrier along the roadside and fall into an empty concrete canal 5–6 metres below. Yeşim Çakır died at the scene, while the daughter sustained slight injuries. The traffic police accident report, based on on-site findings and the first applicant's statements, noted that the vehicle first hit the barrier (which had been damaged prior to the accident) before falling over it into the canal. A warning sign for the sharp bend was in place.

In criminal proceedings, the first applicant was taken to a police station, where he explained that his car had skidded left for an unknown reason as he approached the bend (possibly due to a slippery substance like sand, though the road was not wet). Noticing another vehicle approaching from behind on the left, he braked and swerved right, losing control and hitting the already-damaged barrier, which failed to stop the vehicle from falling. An eyewitness confirmed seeing the sudden swerve, impact, and fall. The İzmir public prosecutor charged the first applicant with causing death and bodily injury by negligence. At the first hearing before the İzmir Assize Court on 15 December 2008, he reiterated his account, noting the barrier's pre-existing damage. The court found his negligence established but imposed no penalty, accepting that he had been sufficiently aggrieved by his wife's death under Article 22 § 6 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The judgment became final on 23 December 2008 without appeal.

Separately, on 17 November 2008, the first applicant applied to the İzmir Magistrates' Court for a declaratory judgment on the barrier's contribution to the accident (and whether it had been repaired) and any structural road issues, such as unusual sloping. An expert report dated 5 December 2008 found that the barrier had been damaged before the accident and remained unrepaired afterwards, with only a slight dent in the adjacent road surface and no slope problems.

On 2 March 2009, the first applicant sought compensation from the General Directorate of Highways and the İzmir Municipality, arguing that the unrepaired barrier (evidencing prior accidents at the spot) had greatly aggravated the outcome, as a functional barrier would likely have prevented the fall into the canal. Both authorities denied responsibility for the barrier's maintenance. The applicants then sued the Municipality alone in the İzmir Administrative Court on 20 May 2009, submitting the expert report and alleging failure to repair the barrier timely, plus possible road structural defects. The Municipality reiterated denial of responsibility and attributed sole fault to the first applicant, who lost control despite the warning sign.

The Administrative Court obtained information confirming the Municipality's repair duty and a copy of the criminal file. The applicants repeatedly requested an expert examination of the road for structural issues and data on prior accidents at the site, but these were not obtained. On 27 May 2010, relying mainly on the accident report and the first applicant's statements, the court held that he bore sole responsibility for losing control despite the warning sign and rejected the claims. On appeal, the applicants argued that the decision ignored the need for technical expertise on possible road anomalies and the barrier's complete loss of protective function. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment on 25 January 2011.

The ECHR case of Fatih Çakır and Merve Nisa Çakır v. Turkey (no. 54558/11, judgment 5 June 2018) concerned two Turkish nationals from İzmir who alleged that the death of Yeşim Çakır (first applicant’s wife and second applicant’s mother) stemmed from State authorities’ failure to ensure road safety, in violation of Article 2 of the Convention. They further claimed under Articles 6 and 13 that subsequent proceedings failed to adequately establish any State responsibility for the death.

On 25 October 2008 the first applicant was driving in İzmir with his wife and one-year-old daughter when he lost control on a sharp bend. The car struck a metal crash barrier, then plunged into an empty concrete canal 5–6 metres below the road. Yeşim Çakır died at the scene; the child was slightly injured. The same-day police accident report, based on on-site findings and the first applicant’s statements, recorded that the barrier had already been damaged before the crash and that a warning sign for the bend was present.

The first applicant told police and the İzmir public prosecutor that the car had skidded left (possibly due to sand on a dry road), that he had braked and swerved right to avoid another vehicle, and that the damaged barrier had failed to stop the car. An eyewitness confirmed the sudden rightward swerve, impact and fall. On 28 October 2008 the prosecutor indicted the first applicant for causing death and injury by negligence. At the first Assize Court hearing he reiterated that the damaged barrier had been decisive. The court accepted that his negligence was established but, applying Article 22 § 6 of the Criminal Code, imposed no penalty because he had already been sufficiently aggrieved by his wife’s death. The judgment became final without appeal.

Meanwhile the first applicant obtained a declaratory judgment from the İzmir Magistrates’ Court. An expert report of 5 December 2008 confirmed the barrier had been damaged beforehand and remained unrepaired, and noted a slight dent beside it but no structural slope defect.

In March 2009 the applicants sought compensation from both the General Directorate of Highways and İzmir Municipality, arguing that the unrepaired barrier had aggravated the outcome of an accident occurring within the speed limit and that earlier accidents at the same spot indicated a possible road defect. Both authorities denied responsibility for the barrier. The applicants then sued only the Municipality in the İzmir Administrative Court, relying on the expert report. The Municipality again denied liability and blamed the driver despite the warning sign. After an interim request for files, it emerged that barrier repair fell to the Municipality. The applicants repeatedly asked for an expert examination of possible structural problems and data on prior accidents; these requests were not granted. On 27 May 2010 the Administrative Court, relying mainly on the police report and the first applicant’s statements, held that he bore sole responsibility for losing control despite the warning sign and dismissed the claim. The applicants appealed, stressing the absence of technical expertise on possible road anomalies and the court’s failure to consider the barrier’s complete loss of protective function. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment on 25 January 2011.

Relevant domestic legislation (General Directorate of Highways Act, Road Traffic Act and associated regulations) imposed on both the Directorate and municipalities duties to maintain roads, install safety measures, analyse accident causes and take preventive technical action.

The applicants therefore contended that the authorities had failed in their positive obligation under Article 2 to protect life through adequate road-safety measures, and that the administrative courts had not properly investigated or determined State responsibility.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Botnari v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 74441/14) concerns complaints by Viorica Botnari, a Moldovan national born in 1972, of inhuman and degrading detention conditions and inadequate medical care (Article 3 of the Convention) together with the absence of an effective domestic remedy (Article 13). The applicant, represented by counsel, lodged her application on 20 November 2014. She had been arrested on 17 March 2010 on charges of fraud and document forgery and placed in the underground cells of the General Directorate for Fighting Organised Crime. She alleged that those cells offered wholly substandard conditions. On 29 March 2010 she was transferred to Prison no. 13 in Chișinău, where she claimed she was held in a cell with sixteen other inmates, subjected to passive smoking, denied bedding, unable to sleep, exposed to vermin infestation and given food of very poor quality.

The Government stated that the applicant was released to house arrest on 30 March 2011, re-arrested on 26 January 2012 and returned to Prison no. 13, released again on 19 September 2012, and re-detained on 5 June 2013. On 10 June 2013 she was convicted and sentenced to thirteen years and six months’ imprisonment. After June 2013 she occupied cells 108 and 110 (each designed for eight detainees and measuring 18 m²) and cell 109 (designed for six detainees, also 18 m²). The Government asserted that cell 109 had a 100-watt bulb, a window, a tap and a partitioned toilet and that all cells were regularly disinfected.

The applicant had been diagnosed in 2003 with non-Hodgkin lymphoma affecting the spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes, as well as chronic hepatitis. She alleged that treatment was interrupted in the initial detention facility, that transfer to a civilian hospital was refused, and that Prison no. 13 provided no oncologist or chemotherapy. Her last chemotherapy session occurred in April 2013 while she was under house arrest. She claimed her health thereafter deteriorated. Extracts from her prison medical records dated June 2014 and July 2015, signed by senior prison doctors, recorded that she required specialist treatment at the Institute of Oncology and that her condition was of medium seriousness. The Prisons Authority had informed her lawyer in February 2014 that she had been registered as an oncology patient since June 2013 and was receiving treatment consistent with her diagnosis.

The Government countered that between April 2010 and July 2012 the applicant repeatedly refused hospitalisation in the prison hospital, the Prison no. 13 medical unit and, on two occasions, the Institute of Oncology. She had nevertheless been examined by a therapist and a haematologist and given medication. The Prisons Authority maintained an annual service contract worth approximately EUR 1 555 with the Institute of Oncology covering chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Independent reports corroborated systemic problems. The Moldovan Human Rights Centre (Ombudsman) recorded serious overcrowding, inadequate food, ventilation and daylight in Prison no. 13 in its 2013–2015 reports and recommended the prison’s closure or urgent renovation. The CPT’s 2015 visit found the prison (official capacity 1 000, holding 1 186) to be one of the oldest in the country, with living space far below the 4 m² national standard, high prisoner turnover, and female prisoners confined for 22 hours a day in similarly deficient conditions, with limited access to hygiene products and showers.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that her prolonged detention in overcrowded, unsanitary cells and the interruption or inadequacy of specialised oncology care reached the Article 3 threshold, and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address those complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Viorica Botnari, a Moldovan national born in 1972, against the Republic of Moldova (application no. 74441/14). She alleged that her detention involved inhuman and degrading conditions and inadequate medical care, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, and that she lacked an effective domestic remedy, in breach of Article 13. The application was lodged on 20 November 2014 and communicated to the Government on 27 January 2015. The Court, sitting as a Committee, delivered its judgment on 5 June 2018 (later revised).

Botnari was arrested on 17 March 2010 on charges of fraud and forgery of official documents and initially held in an underground cell at the General Directorate for Fighting Organised Crime detention centre, which she described as offering substandard conditions. She was transferred to Prison no. 13 on 29 March 2010. According to the Government, she was released into house arrest on 30 March 2011, re-arrested on 26 January 2012 and returned to Prison no. 13, released again into house arrest on 19 September 2012, and re-detained there on 5 June 2013. On 10 June 2013 the Centru District Court convicted her and imposed a sentence of 13 years and 6 months’ imprisonment; the appeal was still pending when observations were filed. After 5 June 2013 she was held in cells 108 and 110 (each 18 m², designed for eight inmates) and cell 109 (18 m², designed for six). The Government stated that cell 109 had a 100-watt bulb, a window, a tap and a partitioned toilet, and that all cells were regularly disinfected.

Botnari claimed that in Prison no. 13 she shared a cell with 16 other inmates, was exposed to passive smoking, received no bedding, could not sleep properly, lived in vermin-infested conditions and was given very poor-quality food. The Government disputed the overcrowding figures for the later period.

In 2003 Botnari had been diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma affecting her spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes, together with chronic hepatitis. She asserted that treatment was interrupted at the first detention centre and that the administration refused hospital transfer; after her move to Prison no. 13 she received no specialist oncological care or chemotherapy. Her last chemotherapy session occurred in April 2013 while she was under house arrest. The Prisons Authority confirmed she had been registered as an oncology patient since 5 June 2013 and claimed she had received treatment consistent with her diagnosis. The CPT, after its September 2015 visit, described Prison no. 13 as an ageing remand facility with high turnover, official capacity of 1 000 but 1 186 inmates, and living space well below the national 4 m² standard. The case of Botnari v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 74441/14) concerns Viorica Botnari (born 1972), a Moldovan national detained in Chișinău. She alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions and inadequate medical care contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, plus the absence of an effective remedy under Article 13.

Arrested on 17 March 2010 and charged with fraud and document forgery, the applicant was first held in the underground cells of the General Directorate for Fighting Organised Crime (GDFOC). She described these as substandard. On 29 March 2010 she was moved to Prison no. 13. There she claimed to share a cell with 16 other inmates, endure passive smoking, lack bedding (preventing normal sleep), live amid vermin infestation and receive very poor food.

The Government recorded successive periods of detention and release: transfer to Prison no. 13 on 29 March 2010; release to house arrest on 30 March 2011; re-arrest and return to Prison no. 13 on 26 January 2012; release to house arrest on 19 September 2012; and re-detention in Prison no. 13 from 5 June 2013. On 10 June 2013 she was convicted and sentenced to 13 years and 6 months’ imprisonment (appeal pending). After June 2013 she occupied cells 108 and 110 (each 18 m², designed for eight inmates) and cell 109 (18 m², designed for six). Cell 109 had a 100-W bulb, a window, a tap and a partitioned toilet; all cells were regularly disinfected.

The applicant had been diagnosed in 2003 with non-Hodgkin lymphoma affecting the spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes, together with chronic hepatitis. She asserted that treatment was interrupted at the GDFOC (hospital transfer refused) and that Prison no. 13 provided no oncologist or chemotherapy. Her last chemotherapy session occurred in April 2013 while under house arrest; her health thereafter deteriorated. Extracts from her prison medical file (June 2014 and July 2015) recorded a need for specialist treatment at the Institute of Oncology and classified her condition as of medium seriousness. A December 2013 enquiry by her lawyer elicited a February 2014 reply that she had been registered as an oncology patient since 5 June 2013 and treated in accordance with her diagnosis.

The Government replied that between April 2010 and July 2012 the applicant repeatedly refused hospitalisation in the prison hospital, the medical unit of Prison no. 13 or the Institute of Oncology. She was nevertheless examined by a therapist and a haematologist and given treatment. An annual contract (budget approximately €1,555) with the Institute of Oncology made chemotherapy and radiotherapy available.

Independent reports corroborated systemic problems. The Moldovan Ombudsman (2013–2015) documented overcrowding, poor food, inadequate ventilation and insufficient daylight in Prison no. 13 and recommended its closure or urgent improvement. The CPT (2015 visit) noted the prison’s age, high turnover, severe overcrowding (for example eight women in 20 m²), 22-hour daily cell confinement, only two hours’ outdoor exercise, limited natural light, dilapidated fabric and inadequate hygiene products and shower access (once weekly).

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims of Article 3 violations arising from both the physical conditions of detention and the alleged failure to furnish appropriate medical care for a serious oncological illness, together with the asserted lack of any effective domestic remedy.
