The case of Amerkhanov v. Turkey (Application no. 16026/12) concerns a Kazakhstani national, Samat Amerkhanov (born 1989), who alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his detention in Turkey and subsequent deportation to Kazakhstan.

Amerkhanov claimed that in 2010, while living in Atyrau, Kazakhstan, he faced repeated police harassment, beatings in custody, and false accusations of rape and forcing a girl to worship, which he attributed to his status as a practising Muslim who wore a beard. He left Kazakhstan in November 2010, transited through Syria and Georgia, and re-entered Turkey on a tourist visa on 21 May 2011. On 9 June 2011, while applying for a residence permit at Istanbul police headquarters, he was arrested pursuant to an entry ban issued on national security grounds and transferred to the Kumkapı Foreigners’ Removal Centre, where he remained until 13 September 2011.

He applied for asylum and received a UNHCR asylum-seeker certificate, but Turkish authorities rejected his claim after interviews in which he described prior ill-treatment and a real risk of death or duress if returned. His lawyer submitted evidence of a Kazakhstan arrest warrant for “hooliganism” under Article 257 § 3 of the Criminal Code. Amerkhanov was released on 13 September 2011, required to reside in Sakarya, and granted a residence permit until May 2012. Interpol inquiries later confirmed Kazakhstan’s interest in him for an alleged offence; Turkish authorities requested that no information be shared with Kazakhstan to protect him and his family.

On 15 March 2012 he was notified that his asylum and subsidiary-protection claims had been rejected, subjected to an entry ban, and re-detained. Despite last-minute applications for release and a Rule 39 request to the Court (submitted too late for consideration), he was deported to Kazakhstan on 19 March 2012. His lawyer later reported that he was immediately taken into custody by Kazakhstani security forces and remanded in Atyrau Prison, though no documentary evidence of subsequent ill-treatment was available.

Amerkhanov challenged the asylum rejection and deportation decision before the Ankara Administrative Court, which refused a stay of execution and, in February 2013, dismissed the application. The court relied on National Intelligence Organisation information that he was involved in international terrorism and had conducted terrorist activities in Turkey, concluding that there was no well-founded fear of persecution. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this ruling in 2016.

Regarding conditions at Kumkapı, Amerkhanov alleged overcrowding, denial of outdoor exercise or social activities, hygiene deficiencies, and inadequate food. The Government stated that the centre (capacity 300) held 100–150 persons at the relevant time, with specified dormitory sizes, bunk beds, showers, toilets, a cafeteria, weekly medical visits, and cleaning staff; outdoor exercise was available when staffing and conditions permitted.

International materials submitted included UN Committee against Torture concluding observations (2008, 2014), the 2009 report of the Special Rapporteur on torture, UN Human Rights Committee findings, U.S. State Department reports (2011–2012), and Amnesty International reports, all documenting widespread torture and ill-treatment by Kazakhstani law-enforcement and security services—particularly in pre-trial detention, to extract confessions, and in anti-terrorism operations targeting suspected Islamists or religious groups—with inadequate investigations and impunity.

These facts underpin the communicated complaints concerning the risk of ill-treatment upon return, the conditions and lawfulness of detention, the absence of reasons for detention, and the lack of effective remedies.

The case of Amerkhanov v. Turkey (Application no. 16026/12) concerns a Kazakhstani national born in 1989 who fled his country amid alleged police harassment, custody and ill-treatment in 2010. He attributed this to his status as a practising Muslim who wore a beard, and faced accusations including of rape and forcing worship. After leaving Kazakhstan in November 2010 and travelling via Turkey, Syria and Georgia, he re-entered Turkey on a tourist visa on 21 May 2011.

On 9 June 2011, while seeking a residence permit at Istanbul police headquarters, he was arrested. The authorities issued an entry ban on national security grounds and detained him pending deportation, transferring him that day to the Kumkapı Foreigners’ Removal Centre. He applied for asylum to the Turkish authorities and UNHCR. A first interview occurred on 15 June; his application was rejected on 28 June, though UNHCR issued an asylum-seeker certificate the next day. His lawyer objected, sought a second interview and applied to the Istanbul Magistrates’ Court for release while highlighting poor detention conditions, receiving no response. A second interview on 16 August recorded his claim of a real risk of death or duress by Kazakh police if returned, based on prior ill-treatment and targeting of religious persons. Further petitions enclosed documents showing he was wanted in Atyrau for “hooliganism” under Article 257 § 3 of the Kazakh Criminal Code, plus a newspaper report of an arrest warrant. He was released on 13 September 2011 and directed to reside in Sakarya, where he obtained a residence permit valid until May 2012.

Turkish authorities later noted Kazakhstan’s Interpol request for him over the offence but asked that no information be shared with Kazakh authorities to protect the applicant and his family. On 15 March 2012 he was notified that his asylum claim (and request for subsidiary protection) had been rejected on 2 March, that he was banned from Turkey and would be deported if he re-entered; he was detained the same day. His lawyer urgently sought release, citing the risk of torture. He was deported to Kazakhstan on 19 March 2012. Subsequent information indicated transfer to Kazakh security forces and remand in Atyrau Prison, though no documentary evidence of subsequent ill-treatment was available.

After deportation, an application to the Ankara Administrative Court for annulment of the asylum rejection and deportation decision, plus a stay of execution, was rejected (the stay on 11 May 2012; the merits on 13 February 2013). The court cited National Intelligence Organisation information that the applicant had engaged in international terrorism in Turkey and found no well-founded fear of persecution. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this in 2016.

Regarding Kumkapı detention (9 June–13 September 2011), the applicant alleged overcrowding, no outdoor exercise or activities, hygiene problems and inadequate food. The Government stated the centre’s 300-person capacity was not exceeded (100–150 held), described room sizes, bunk beds, natural light, sanitation facilities, a cafeteria, possible outdoor exercise depending on conditions, weekly doctor visits and full-time cleaning staff.

International materials before the Court (UN CAT observations 2008/2014, Special Rapporteur Nowak’s 2009 report, UN HRC 2011, US State Department 2011/2012 reports and Amnesty International 2010/2011) documented persistent torture and ill-treatment in Kazakhstan, especially to extract confessions in pre-trial facilities, targeting of Islamic groups, asylum-seekers and those perceived as security threats, with impunity and use of such evidence in trials. A prior ECHR judgment had found a real risk of Article 3 violation in extraditions to Kazakhstan.

These facts underpin the communicated complaints of a real risk of ill-treatment upon deportation (and lack of effective remedy), poor conditions at Kumkapı (and lack of remedy), unlawful detention there, failure to inform him of reasons, and absence of an effective challenge or compensation mechanism.

The case concerns Kazakhstani national Samat Amerkhanov (b. 1989), who alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention arising from his detention in Turkey and subsequent deportation to Kazakhstan.

Amerkhanov claimed that, while living in Atyrau, he was repeatedly harassed, detained and ill-treated by Kazakh police in 2010 on account of his Islamic faith and appearance (including wearing a beard). He was accused of forcing a girl to worship and of rape, then released. Fearing further persecution of religious persons on fabricated charges, he left Kazakhstan on 27 November 2010, travelled via Syria and Georgia, and re-entered Turkey on a tourist visa on 21 May 2011.

On 9 June 2011 he attended Istanbul police headquarters to apply for a residence permit and was arrested. The authorities had issued an entry ban on national-security grounds. He was transferred the same day to the Kumkapı Foreigners’ Removal Centre pending deportation. He applied for asylum (interviewed 15 June 2011) and to UNHCR (which issued an asylum-seeker certificate on 29 June). His asylum claim was rejected on 28 June. His lawyer lodged objections, requested a second interview, and applied unsuccessfully for release, citing both the risk of persecution and poor detention conditions. A second interview took place on 16 August 2011, during which Amerkhanov reiterated that he faced death or ill-treatment by Kazakh police if returned. Further release applications (22 and 25 August) enclosed documents showing he was wanted in Atyrau for “hooliganism” (Article 257 § 3 of the Kazakh Criminal Code) and that an arrest warrant had been published.

He was released on 13 September 2011 and ordered to reside in Sakarya, where he was granted a residence permit valid until 20 May 2012. In late 2011 Interpol informed Turkish authorities that Kazakhstan sought him for an offence; Turkey asked Interpol not to notify the Kazakh authorities, citing risks to Amerkhanov and his family.

On 15 March 2012 he was notified that his asylum and subsidiary-protection claims had been rejected on 2 March, that he was banned from re-entering Turkey, and that he would be deported. He was re-detained and, despite urgent lawyer applications, deported to Kazakhstan on 19 March 2012. He was subsequently remanded in Atyrau Prison; no documentary evidence of post-return ill-treatment was supplied.

An administrative challenge to the rejection and deportation decisions, lodged on 22 March 2012 with supporting warrant documentation, was unsuccessful. The Ankara Administrative Court (13 February 2013, upheld on appeal 27 April 2016) relied on National Intelligence Organisation information that Amerkhanov had engaged in international terrorism and terrorist activities in Turkey, and found no well-founded fear of persecution.

Amerkhanov was held at Kumkapı from 9 June to 13 September 2011. He alleged overcrowding, denial of outdoor exercise or any social activity, hygiene deficiencies and insufficient food. The Government stated that occupancy (100–150 persons) was well below the 300-person capacity, described the physical layout (dormitories with natural light, bunk beds, showers, toilets and a cafeteria), weekly doctor visits, emergency medical access and full-time cleaning staff, and said outdoor exercise was permitted when staffing and conditions allowed.

International materials cited in the case (UN CAT observations 2008/2014, UN Special Rapporteur on Torture 2009, US State Department reports 2011–2012 and Amnesty International reports 2010–2011) documented persistent, non-isolated use of torture and ill-treatment by Kazakh law-enforcement and security services—particularly in pre-trial detention and in the context of counter-terrorism and operations targeting religious or Islamist groups—to extract confessions, together with impunity and inadequate investigations.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: risk of Article 3 ill-treatment upon return (past mistreatment, outstanding warrant, religious profile and country reports); inadequate procedural safeguards and remedies against deportation; alleged Article 3 conditions at Kumkapı; and Article 5 complaints concerning the lawfulness of the two periods of detention, lack of information on the reasons for detention, and absence of an effective remedy to challenge detention or obtain compensation.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Novotný v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 16314/13, judgment of 7 June 2018) concerns allegations by František Novotný (born 1942) of violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. These arose from his inability to challenge a final 1970 judicial declaration of paternity despite later DNA proof that he was not the biological father.

In 1965 the applicant had a sexual relationship with a woman who gave birth to daughter Z. on 2 March 1966. He denied paternity, prompting Z.’s legal guardian to bring proceedings in the Jihlava District Court. The mother married another man after the birth but before the proceedings. On 23 April 1970 the District Court declared the applicant Z.’s father and ordered maintenance. It relied on witness evidence, documents and a “bio-hereditary” blood test. It found he had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before birth, triggering a presumption of paternity under Article 54 of the Family Code (rebuttable only by clear contrary grounds). Another man who had intercourse in the relevant period was excluded by the blood test.

The applicant appealed to the Brno Regional Court and sought a further expert opinion, which was refused as the facts were sufficiently established. The judgment was upheld on 2 June 1970 and became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to challenge paternity under Article 62 of the Family Code. This was refused on 21 June 2011: Z. (now adult) did not wish to challenge it, it was not in her interests, and no credible expert evidence disproving paternity had been produced.

On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent DNA testing. The report of 19 April 2012 confirmed unequivocally that he was not her father. A fresh request to the Prosecutor General on 9 May 2012 was refused on 12 September 2012. Paternity had been established by a final judicial declaration under Article 54; the law provided no mechanism to challenge it. The Prosecutor’s power under Articles 62/62a applied only to statutory presumptions under Articles 51 and 52, not court determinations.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s decision, relying on Article 6 § 1, asserting he had proved non-paternity, and arguing that Articles 61 and 62 were unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court dismissed it on 13 December 2012, holding that a final judicial decision existed and that the Prosecutor’s competence required fulfilment of all statutory conditions, which were absent.

Domestic law (Family Code, in force until 2013) distinguished paternity by marital presumption (Art. 51), parental acknowledgment (Art. 52), or court declaration with an intercourse-based presumption (Art. 54). Challenges were subject to short time-limits; the Prosecutor could intervene in limited circumstances (child’s interests or apparent non-paternity after time-limits expired) but not against a final Art. 54 judgment. The 2014 Civil Code contained analogous rules. Constitutional Court case-law required domestic authorities to apply the Convention (including Paulík v. Slovakia) and had previously found access-to-court and private-life violations where time-limits barred paternity challenges.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the absence of any procedure to reopen or reverse the 1970 status in light of conclusive scientific evidence, affecting private/family life and access to court, potentially on a discriminatory basis compared with other paternity regimes.

The case of Novotný v. the Czech Republic originated in an application by František Novotný (born 1942) alleging violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. In 1965 the applicant had a sexual relationship with a woman who gave birth to a daughter, Z., on 2 March 1966. He denied paternity. After the birth (but before proceedings began) the mother married another man. Z.’s legal guardian then brought an action in the Jihlava District Court seeking a declaration of paternity.

On 23 April 1970 the District Court held that the applicant was Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. The court relied on witness evidence, documents and a “bio-hereditary” blood test. It found that the applicant had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before the birth, giving rise to a statutory presumption of paternity under Article 54 of the Family Code unless clearly rebutted. Another man who had also had intercourse with the mother at the relevant time was excluded by the blood test. The applicant appealed to the Brno Regional Court and requested a further expert opinion. The Regional Court refused, holding the facts already sufficiently proved, and upheld the first-instance judgment on 2 June 1970. The decision became final on 10 June 1970.

More than forty years later the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to bring proceedings to challenge the paternity finding. On 21 June 2011 the Prosecutor General refused, stating that the conditions of Article 62 of the Family Code were not met: Z. (now an adult) did not wish to contest paternity, it was not in her interests, and no expert evidence credibly disproving paternity had been produced.

On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent DNA testing. The report of 19 April 2012 unequivocally established that the applicant was not Z.’s biological father. He therefore renewed his request to the Prosecutor General on 9 May 2012. On 12 September 2012 the Prosecutor General again refused, explaining that paternity had been judicially determined under Article 54 rather than under the statutory presumptions of Articles 51 or 52. Once a judicial declaration under Article 54 had become final, Czech law provided no mechanism for the Prosecutor General (or anyone else) to reopen it.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, invoking Article 6 § 1, asking the Constitutional Court to order the Prosecutor General to act and arguing that Articles 61 and 62 of the Family Code were unconstitutional. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, observing that paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General’s competence arose only when all statutory requirements were fulfilled—which they were not.

The applicant’s complaints therefore centred on the impossibility, even after conclusive DNA evidence, of obtaining a judicial re-examination of the 1970 paternity declaration, with consequent effects on his private life, access to court and alleged discrimination.

The case of Novotný v. the Czech Republic (no. 16314/13) concerns František Novotný (born 1942), who alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention arising from his inability to challenge a decades-old judicial finding of paternity despite conclusive DNA evidence that he was not the biological father.

In 1965 the applicant had a sexual relationship with a woman who gave birth to daughter Z. on 2 March 1966. He denied paternity. After the birth (but before proceedings began) the mother married another man. Z.’s legal guardian brought an action in the Jihlava District Court seeking a declaration of paternity. On 23 April 1970 that court found the applicant to be Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. The finding rested on witness evidence, documents, a “bio-hereditary” blood test, and the statutory presumption in Article 54 of the Family Code (then in force) that a man who had intercourse with the mother between 180 and 300 days before birth is the father unless serious grounds exist to exclude him. Another man who had also had intercourse at the relevant time was excluded by the blood test. An appeal to the Brno Regional Court was dismissed on 2 June 1970; the judgment became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to institute proceedings to contest paternity under Article 62 of the Family Code. The request was refused because Z. (by then an adult) did not wish to challenge the finding, it was not in her interests, and no expert evidence disproving paternity had been produced. On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent DNA testing; the 19 April 2012 report unequivocally established that he was not her biological father. A fresh request to the Prosecutor General on 9 May 2012 was rejected on 12 September 2012. The Prosecutor General explained that paternity had been determined by a court under Article 54 (not by the marital or acknowledgment presumptions in Articles 51–52), so the prosecution service lacked competence under Articles 62 and 62a. Once a judgment establishing paternity under Article 54 had become final, Czech law afforded no mechanism to challenge it.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint invoking Article 6 § 1, asking the Constitutional Court to order the Prosecutor General to act and arguing that Articles 61 and 62 of the Family Code were unconstitutional. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, holding that paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General’s limited statutory powers did not apply.

The relevant domestic framework (Family Code until 31 December 2013, Code of Civil Procedure Articles 159 and 159a on res judicata, and Constitutional provisions incorporating the Convention) thus left the applicant without any legal avenue to reopen the 1970 determination despite irrefutable scientific evidence. These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: denial of access to a court to correct an erroneous status (Article 6), interference with private and family life through the continued legal attribution of biological parentage that scientific proof had disproved (Article 8), and possible discrimination in the availability of challenge procedures depending on the original method of establishing paternity (Article 14).

The applicant, Euromak Metal Doo, was a limited-liability scrap-metal trading company established in Skopje in 1998 by its sole shareholders, Ms Zhaneta Pavlovska and Mr Rasko Pavlovski. It purchased waste aluminium, copper, iron and other metals, processed them and resold the products. Registered for value-added tax (VAT), the company declared VAT on all outgoing and incoming invoices and periodically claimed deductions under the national “tax-credit” system. Until 2009 its regular VAT returns were processed without objection.

On 22 September 2009 the Internal Revenue Office (IRO) ordered a VAT audit covering 1 January 2005 to 30 June 2009. The audit established that certain suppliers, although VAT-registered, had neither declared nor paid the VAT shown on invoices issued to the applicant; some invoices also lacked supplier addresses. The applicant itself had paid every invoice in full and had correctly declared VAT on its own sales. On that basis the IRO concluded that the statutory conditions for deduction had not been met. On 20 November 2009 it issued two assessment decisions requiring payment of an additional MKD 3 827 546 (approximately EUR 62 000) in VAT for 2005–07. The decisions were immediately enforceable.

The company appealed to the Minister of Finance, arguing that it had fulfilled all of its own VAT obligations and could not be held responsible for its suppliers’ failures. The appeal was dismissed on 8 February 2010. A subsequent written demand raised the total (including interest) to MKD 6 059 124 (approximately EUR 100 000). The IRO blocked the company’s bank account on 29 April 2010. After a first-instance administrative-court decision remitted the case because the ministerial decision had been signed by an unauthorised official, the Ministry again rejected the appeal on 26 May 2011. The Administrative Court dismissed the subsequent action on 1 March 2013, holding that the cumulative statutory conditions (sections 33 and 34 of the VAT Act) were unsatisfied because the applicant’s income derived from taxpayers who had not themselves paid VAT; every taxpayer, the court added, had an interest in knowing with whom it did business. The Higher Administrative Court upheld that reasoning on 13 March 2014.

Meanwhile, in December 2011 several individuals connected with some (but not all) of the suppliers were indicted for organised crime, abuse of office and tax evasion arising from the issuance of fictitious invoices. They were convicted in 2013; the supplier companies themselves were not charged.

The applicant company was struck off the commercial register on 2 February 2017 for failure to file its 2014 annual accounts. Its bank account remained frozen until it was closed on 10 April 2017; the IRO recovered nothing. The former shareholders continued the Strasbourg application in the company’s name, complaining that the State’s refusal to honour VAT deductions that the company had legitimately expected, on account of circumstances entirely outside its control, violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 68039/14) concerned an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant company, a limited-liability scrap-metal trader established in 1998 and wholly owned by two individuals, was registered for VAT. It declared VAT on all incoming and outgoing invoices and regularly claimed deductions under the tax-credit system. Until 2009 its returns were processed without objection.

In September 2009 the Internal Revenues Office (IRO) ordered a VAT audit covering January 2005–June 2009. The audit established that certain suppliers, although VAT-registered, had neither declared nor paid the VAT shown on invoices issued to the applicant (findings drawn from earlier, unspecified audits of those suppliers). Some invoices also lacked supplier addresses. The applicant had nevertheless paid every invoice in full and had itself declared VAT on all its own invoices. On that basis the IRO concluded that the statutory conditions for deduction had not been met.

On 20 November 2009 the IRO issued two assessments requiring payment of an additional MKD 3 827 546 (approximately EUR 62 000) for the years 2005–07. Appeals had no suspensive effect. The Minister of Finance dismissed the appeal in February 2010, repeating the audit reasoning. A subsequent reprimand raised the total (including interest) to approximately EUR 100 000. The IRO blocked the company’s bank account on 29 April 2010.

The Administrative Court first remitted the matter because the ministerial decision had been signed by an unauthorised official, then dismissed the action in March 2013. It held that the cumulative conditions of sections 33 and 34 of the VAT Act were unsatisfied because the applicant’s income derived from taxpayers who had failed their own VAT obligations, and that every trader has an interest in knowing its counterparties. The Higher Administrative Court upheld that judgment in March 2014.

The company was struck from the commercial register in February 2017 for failing to file its 2014 annual accounts and thereby ceased to exist; its two shareholders continued the Strasbourg application. The blocked account was closed in April 2017 with no funds having been recovered.

Separately, in 2011 prosecutors charged several individuals (but not the supplier companies themselves) connected with some of the applicant’s suppliers with organised crime, abuse of office and tax evasion arising from fictitious invoices. Convictions became final in January 2014.

Under the VAT Act a taxable person may deduct input VAT only if it holds a properly issued invoice and all other statutory conditions are fulfilled. The applicant’s complaint was that the State had thereby frustrated its legitimate expectation of VAT deductions for reasons wholly outside its control.

The case of Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 68039/14) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Relying on those findings, the IRO issued two decisions on 20 November 2009 requiring payment of an additional MKD 3,827,546 (approx. EUR 62,000) for “unlawful” deductions in 2005–07. Appeals to the Minister of Finance were dismissed (February 2010 and, after remittal for a procedural defect, May 2011). A March 2010 reprimand raised the total, with interest, to MKD 6,059,124 (approx. EUR 100,000). The company’s bank account was blocked in April 2010.

Administrative actions followed. The Administrative Court dismissed the claim on 1 March 2013, holding that the cumulative conditions of sections 33 and 34 of the VAT Act were unmet because the applicant’s income derived from firms that had failed their own VAT obligations; every taxpayer, the court said, has an interest in knowing its business partners. The Higher Administrative Court upheld that reasoning on 13 March 2014.

The company was struck from the register on 2 February 2017 for failing to file its 2014 financial statement and thereby ceased to exist; its sole shareholders continued the Strasbourg application. The blocked account was closed in April 2017 with no funds collected.

Separately, in December 2011 prosecutors charged individuals linked to some (but not all) of the suppliers with organised crime, abuse of office and tax evasion involving fictitious invoices. Those individuals were convicted in 2013 (final 2014). The supplier companies themselves were not indicted.

Section 33 of the VAT Act entitles a taxpayer to deduct input VAT already paid in the supply chain; section 34 conditions the right on possession of a compliant invoice (or customs declaration) and fulfilment of all section-33 requirements.

These facts underpin the complaint that denial of the deductions constituted an unjustified interference with the company’s possessions.

The case of S.Z. v. Greece (Application no. 66702/13) concerns a Syrian national born in 1984 who alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his administrative detention in Greece in 2013, specifically regarding the conditions of his detention (Article 3), its lawfulness (Article 5 § 1), and the effectiveness of proceedings to challenge it (Article 5 § 4).

On 21 September 2013 the applicant was arrested in Athens for possessing a fake French passport and taken before a prosecutor. On 24 September he was convicted by the Athens Court of First Instance of using a false instrument, giving false unsworn testimony and illegal entry, receiving a ten-month sentence whose execution was suspended pending appeal. The next day he was re-arrested and placed in administrative detention pending expulsion (decision of the Director of the Aliens Subdivision of Attica). On 28 September an expulsion order was issued on the grounds of illegal entry, lack of a residence permit, danger to public order (stemming from the conviction) and possession of false documents; no period for voluntary departure was granted and detention of up to six months was authorised.

The applicant maintained that he had faxed objections (including an asylum request) on 27 September that were never registered and that he was only informed of the decisions on 30 September. On 4 October he appealed the expulsion order and formally requested international protection; the request was forwarded to the Asylum Department on 7 October and the appeal was dismissed the following day. On 8 October he lodged his first set of objections before the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance, arguing that expulsion to Syria was impossible given the ongoing conflict (citing Tabesh v. Greece), that he was an asylum-seeker, and that conditions at Zografou police station were poor. The objections were rejected on 10 October: it was unclear whether earlier objections had been filed, he had produced no proof of Syrian nationality, he could request asylum at the police station, and conditions were “tolerable” given Greece’s financial difficulties and the short period of detention.

On 18 October the applicant reiterated his asylum claim before the Attica Regional Asylum Service. The same day the legal basis of detention was altered to danger to public order/national security and the need for a speedy asylum determination; the expulsion order was suspended. A third set of objections (8 November), citing deteriorating health, a police circular of 9 April 2013 that automatically suspended detention of identified Syrians because expulsion was impossible, and the disputed date of the modified detention order, was rejected on 13 November. The Government countered that the station comprised three 12 m² dormitories (capacity three each) plus an extra space with toilet and 24-hour hot shower; mattresses and blankets were provided, lighting, ventilation and heating were adequate, occupancy never exceeded nine, cleaning occurred daily and disinfection monthly, food was supplied three times daily, and visits, television and telephones were available. The European Court of Human Rights case of S.Z. v. On 4 October he appealed the expulsion order and formally requested international protection; the appeal was dismissed on 8 October. That same day he lodged objections to detention before the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance, arguing that expulsion to war-torn Syria was impossible, that he was an asylum-seeker, and that conditions at Zografou police station were poor. The objections were rejected on 10 October, the court noting the absence of proof of Syrian nationality at that stage and considering the conditions tolerable.

The legal basis of his detention was then altered to danger to public order or national security and the need for speedy determination of the asylum application; the expulsion order was suspended.
