001-183382:
The applicant, a Macedonian national born in 1968, had been held in pre-trial detention since 21 October 2008 in connection with one set of criminal proceedings (КОК бр. 3/09) on suspicion of criminal conspiracy and abuse of office. On 26 December 2009 an investigating judge of the Skopje Court of First Instance opened a separate investigation (КОК бр. 17/10) against him and fourteen others for criminal conspiracy, abuse of office and extortion linked to alleged money-laundering and unlawful property acquisition. The same judge immediately ordered the applicant’s detention for thirty days from 25 December 2009 on all three statutory grounds: risk of absconding, risk of reoffending and risk of interfering with the investigation. The order cited the gravity of the charges, the likely sentence, the circumstances of the alleged offences, the suspects’ interconnections and the fact that numerous investigative steps (including witness examinations) remained outstanding.

The applicant appealed, stressing that he was already detained in the earlier proceedings and that the reasons given were neither relevant nor sufficient. A three-judge panel dismissed the appeal on 30 December 2009, adding his prior “conflict with the law,” the existence of parallel proceedings for similar offences, and the insufficiency of his family ties (a wife and three minor children) as guarantees of appearance. Subsequent thirty-day extensions were ordered on 21 January, 22 February and 24 March 2010, repeating the same grounds and reasoning.

An indictment was filed on 23 March 2010 (later amended by withdrawal of the abuse-of-office charge and re-characterisation of extortion as violence). Thereafter the courts dropped the interference ground because the investigation had closed, but they continued to rely on the risks of flight and reoffending. On 12 April 2010 the Court of Appeal itself excluded the reoffending ground, noting that the accused were already in custody, yet it upheld detention solely on the flight risk, again citing the gravity of the charges and the potential penalty.

From April 2010 until January 2011 three-judge panels issued ten further extension orders, each employing virtually identical language: the nature, character and type of the offences, their gravity, the expected sentence, the applicant’s financial means and his history of conflict with the law demonstrated a real risk of absconding; family ties and immovable property were expressly declared insufficient guarantees. The applicant repeatedly challenged these decisions, arguing that the courts had failed to give concrete, individualised reasons and had not explained why his family situation and property holdings could not secure his presence. He also sought substitution of detention by house arrest. All appeals were rejected; the Court of Appeal consistently held that the first-instance reasoning was adequate and that only prison custody could eliminate the flight risk at that stage of the proceedings.

The applicant lodged three unsuccessful applications for release on bail, offering successively larger securities (immovable property valued at up to EUR 1.23 million plus cash deposits of EUR 100 000–110 000) and, on one occasion, his passport. The courts refused each request, again invoking the gravity of the charges, the likely sentence, the complexity of the multi-defendant case, his prior conviction (still under appeal) in the parallel proceedings, and the inadequacy of the proposed guarantees. On 6 December 2010 the Court of Appeal granted bail and house arrest, but the Supreme Court, acting on a prosecutor’s request for protection of legality, promptly quashed that decision as procedurally inadmissible because the Criminal Proceedings Act barred appeals against a panel’s refusal of release.

On 26 January 2011 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment; detention was ordered to continue until the judgment became final. The conviction was later upheld on appeal. Throughout the relevant period the domestic courts therefore maintained the applicant’s detention for more than thirteen months after the second investigation had been opened, relying almost exclusively on stereotyped references to the seriousness of the charges and the possible penalty, without any evolving, individualised assessment of the actual risk of flight or of the sufficiency of the concrete alternatives he had offered.

The case of Sejdiji v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 8784/11) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that domestic courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for his prolonged pre-trial detention.

The applicant, Bajruš Sejdiji, a Macedonian national born in 1968, had already been held in pre-trial detention since 21 October 2008 in separate proceedings (КОК бр. 3/09) on charges of criminal conspiracy and abuse of office. On 26 December 2009 an investigating judge of the Skopje Court of First Instance opened a fresh investigation (КОК бр. 17/10) against him and fourteen others for criminal conspiracy, abuse of office and extortion linked to alleged money laundering and unlawful acquisition of property. The same day the judge ordered the applicant’s detention for thirty days from 25 December 2009, relying on all three statutory grounds: risk of absconding, risk of reoffending and risk of interfering with the investigation. The order cited the gravity of the charges, the potential penalty, the circumstances of the alleged offences and the suspects’ interconnections; interference was said to be likely because the investigation had only just begun and numerous investigative steps, including witness examinations, remained outstanding.

The applicant appealed, arguing that he was already detained in the earlier proceedings and that the reasons given were neither relevant nor sufficient. A three-judge panel dismissed the appeal on 30 December 2009, adding that the applicant had previously been “in conflict with the law” and faced parallel proceedings for similar offences; his family ties and three minor children were deemed inadequate guarantees. The panel treated the two sets of proceedings as wholly independent. Further thirty-day extensions followed on 21 January and 22 February 2010, repeating the same grounds and additionally referring to the applicant’s possessions in the respondent State. The Skopje Court of Appeal upheld these decisions, emphasising the organised nature of the alleged group, the severity of the possible sentence and the fact that some witnesses and suspects remained at large.

On 23 March 2010 the applicant was indicted (later amended by the withdrawal of the abuse-of-office charge and the recasting of extortion as violence). A subsequent extension order dropped the interference ground because the investigation had closed, but retained the risks of flight and reoffending. On 12 April 2010 the Court of Appeal eliminated the reoffending ground on the basis that the applicant was already in custody, yet confirmed the flight risk solely by reference to the gravity of the charges and the potential penalty. Thereafter, three-judge panels issued ten further monthly extensions (April 2010–January 2011). Each decision used virtually identical language: the evidence corroborated a reasonable suspicion; the nature, character and gravity of the offences together with the possible sentence created a real risk of flight; the applicant’s financial situation and prior “conflict with the law” reinforced that risk; and family ties plus immovable property were insufficient guarantees.

The applicant repeatedly appealed, complaining that the courts had relied only on the abstract gravity of the charges and had failed to explain why his personal circumstances did not suffice. The Court of Appeal consistently rejected these arguments, holding that prison custody was the only effective means of preventing absconding. Concurrent bail applications offering third-party property valued at up to EUR 1.23 million plus cash deposits of EUR 100 000–110 000 were likewise refused, the courts citing the same factors plus a first-instance conviction (still under appeal) in the parallel proceedings. A December 2010 Court of Appeal decision granting bail and substituting house arrest was quashed by the Supreme Court on a prosecutorial request for protection of legality, on the ground that no appeal lay against a panel’s refusal of release.

On 26 January 2011 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment; he remained in detention pending the finality of the judgment, which was later upheld on appeal. The period of detention at issue therefore ran from 25 December 2009 until the first-instance conviction.

The case of Sejdiji v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (application no. 8784/11) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that the domestic courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for his prolonged pre-trial detention.

The applicant, a Macedonian national born in 1968, had already been held in pre-trial detention since 21 October 2008 in connection with separate proceedings for criminal conspiracy and abuse of office. On 26 December 2009 an investigating judge of the Skopje Court of First Instance opened a new investigation against him and fourteen others on suspicion of criminal conspiracy, abuse of office and extortion linked to money-laundering and unlawful acquisition of property. Simultaneously the judge ordered the applicant’s detention for thirty days from 25 December 2009 (together with thirteen co-suspects) on all three statutory grounds: risk of absconding, risk of reoffending and risk of interfering with the investigation. The order cited the gravity of the charges, the potential penalty, the circumstances of the alleged offences, the links among the suspects, and the fact that the investigation had only just begun with numerous actions still pending, including witness examinations.

The applicant appealed, arguing that he was already detained in the parallel proceedings and that the reasons given were neither relevant nor sufficient. A three-judge panel dismissed the appeal on 30 December 2009, adding that the applicant had a prior history of “conflict with the law,” that parallel proceedings for similar offences were pending, and that his family ties (a wife and three minor children) were an insufficient guarantee of appearance. A further thirty-day extension was ordered on 21 January 2010 on the same grounds, now also referring to the applicant’s possessions in the country. The Skopje Court of Appeal upheld this order on 8 February 2010, emphasising the organised nature of the alleged group and the fact that some witnesses and suspects remained at large.

After the applicant and co-accused were indicted on 23 March 2010 (charges later amended by withdrawal of abuse of office and substitution of violence for extortion), the interference-with-investigation ground was dropped. Subsequent monthly extensions through January 2011 continued to rest solely on the risks of absconding and (initially) reoffending. From April 2010 the Court of Appeal itself excluded the reoffending risk on the ground that the accused were already detained, yet consistently upheld detention on the flight risk, repeating stereotyped references to the nature and gravity of the charges, the potential sentence, the applicant’s criminal history and financial situation, and the insufficiency of family and property ties. The applicant repeatedly argued that these recitals failed to explain why his personal circumstances did not guarantee appearance and sought replacement of detention by house arrest or other milder measures; all such requests were rejected.

Three applications for release on bail (offering third-party immovable property valued first at approximately EUR 860 000 and later at EUR 1.23 million, plus cash deposits of up to EUR 110 000 and surrender of his passport) were likewise refused by first-instance panels and the Court of Appeal, again on the basis of the gravity of the charges, the complexity of the multi-accused case and the applicant’s prior conviction (then still under appeal) in the parallel proceedings. On 6 December 2010 the Court of Appeal granted one such application and ordered house arrest once the security was deposited, but the Supreme Court quashed that decision the following day on the prosecutor’s request for protection of legality, holding that the Criminal Procedure Act expressly barred appeals against refusals of release.

On 26 January 2011 the trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment, directing that he remain in custody pending finality of the judgment (later upheld on appeal). The period of detention under challenge thus ran from late December 2009 until the first-instance conviction, overlapping with the earlier detention and characterised throughout by formulaic reasoning that never examined the applicant’s individual situation in any depth or seriously considered alternatives to imprisonment.
001-184060:
The case of Lakatos v. Hungary (ECHR, Application no. 21786/15, judgment of 26 June 2018) concerned a complaint by Hungarian national Péter Lakatos (born 1986) under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention on suspicion of aggravated murder had lasted unreasonably long.

On 26 February 2011 the Pest Central District Court remanded the applicant in custody. It found a reasonable suspicion that he had poisoned the victim on 8 April 2010, based on police reports, an autopsy, medical documents, exhibits and witness statements. Detention was justified by a risk of collusion (he had previously threatened witnesses) and a risk of absconding (unclear finances and the severity of the possible sentence). The court gave no consideration to an application for house arrest. An appeal was dismissed on 3 March 2011.

Detention was extended repeatedly. On 21 March 2011 it was prolonged until 26 May 2011, citing the severity of the possible punishment, lack of a permanent address or regular income, and a risk of interfering with the investigation. The applicant appealed, stressing his family ties (common-law wife, two children, parents and brother’s family), lack of criminal record, cooperation with authorities, and request for house arrest; the Budapest Regional Court upheld the decision on 15 April 2011, holding that the public interest outweighed his right to liberty.

Further extensions followed on similar grounds: 23 May 2011 (until 26 August), 24 August 2011 (until 26 November, still relying on risk of absconding despite a known temporary residence and no criminal record, plus possible further witness questioning), 23 November 2011 (until 26 February 2012, noting failure to provide a hosting declaration and financial-capacity statement for house arrest, and lingering witness-intimidation risk), 24 February 2012, 25 April 2012 (risk of collusion no longer substantiated as remaining witnesses were unreachable), 22 June 2012, 21 August 2012, 24 October 2012 (High Court expressed doubts about the strength of the suspicion and reduced risk of flight given the children and lack of record, but the Court of Appeal extended detention by two months), and 21 December 2012.

On 22 February 2013 the Budapest High Court released the applicant on bail under house arrest, finding that gravity of the offence alone could not justify continued detention. The Court of Appeal reversed this on 28 March 2013. A further High Court decision of 23 April 2013 (release on an undertaking not to leave his residence, citing ECHR case-law that detention must be a last resort) was overturned on 26 April 2013.

A bill of indictment was preferred on 17 June 2013. Detention was then extended until first-instance judgment (25 June 2013) and subsequent review applications were refused (including on 18 February 2014, 8 April 2014, 16 July 2014 and 24 September 2014 by the Kúria), the courts citing gravity of the offence, lack of financial resources or essential ties, and late notification of residence. The applicant was convicted of aggravated murder and sentenced to 18 years’ imprisonment on 29 October 2014. Pre-trial detention thus lasted from 26 February 2011 until conviction, a period of more than three years and eight months.

Throughout, domestic courts repeatedly invoked the risk of absconding (unstable finances, temporary work, address issues, severe possible sentence) despite family ties and children, and initially a risk of collusion. Less restrictive measures were consistently rejected, even after most evidence had been gathered and some lower courts had expressed doubts.

The case of *Lakatos v. Hungary* (no. 21786/15) arose from a complaint by Péter Lakatos (born 1986) under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention had been unreasonably prolonged.

On 26 February 2011 the Pest Central District Court remanded the applicant in custody on suspicion of aggravated murder by poisoning (Criminal Code Art. 166 § 1) committed on 8 April 2010. It relied on police reports, an autopsy, medical records, exhibits and witness statements as establishing reasonable suspicion. Detention was justified by a risk of evidence-tampering (the applicant had previously threatened witnesses) and a risk of absconding (unclear finances and the gravity of the potential sentence). An application for house arrest was ignored. Appeals were dismissed.

Detention was thereafter extended repeatedly (to May, August and November 2011, then February, June and August 2012, and beyond) by successive courts, always citing the same two grounds under Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 129 § 2(b) and (c). Courts repeatedly pointed to the severity of the possible punishment, the applicant’s lack of declared employment or stable income, and his initial unavailability at his registered address. Risk of collusion continued to be invoked even after most witnesses had been heard and more than a year (later two years) had elapsed since the alleged offence.

The applicant consistently contested both risks. He emphasised his family ties (common-law wife, two minor children, parents and brother’s family with whom he lived), absence of a criminal record, cooperation with investigators and a known temporary address. He repeatedly sought house arrest or a residence restriction and submitted hosting declarations; these were routinely rejected for want of additional financial-capacity proofs or because they were deemed insufficient to offset the gravity of the charges.

Later first-instance decisions showed growing hesitation: in April 2012 the collusion risk was found unsubstantiated; in October 2012 doubts were expressed about the strength of the suspicion itself and the absconding risk (given the children and clean record); in February and April 2013 the applicant was briefly released to house arrest or a residence undertaking. All such releases were reversed on appeal, the higher courts treating the seriousness of the offence as decisive regardless of family ties or the passage of time.

A bill of indictment was filed only on 17 June 2013. Detention continued until the Budapest High Court convicted the applicant on 29 October 2014 and imposed an 18-year sentence. The total period of remand thus exceeded three years and eight months.

Domestic law authorised detention only as a last resort and required courts to give individualised, fact-based reasons and to consider less restrictive alternatives (house arrest, territorial restriction). Supreme Court opinions and a 2017 Kúria report criticised the practice of relying solely on offence gravity, of failing to assess alternatives properly, and of inadequate engagement with defence submissions. Official statistics confirmed the overwhelming predominance of remand over alternatives. Council of Europe instruments likewise stressed that remand must remain exceptional, regularly reviewed and used only when no milder measure can secure the proceedings.

These facts formed the basis of the complaint that the successive, stereotyped extensions, the delayed indictment and the systematic rejection of alternatives rendered the detention incompatible with Article 5 § 3.

**CASE OF LAKATOS v. HUNGARY (Application no. 21786/15)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined a complaint by Péter Lakatos, a Hungarian national born in 1986 and residing in Gyál, that his pre-trial detention had lasted an unreasonably long time, in alleged violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention.

On 26 February 2011 the Pest Central District Court remanded the applicant in custody on suspicion of aggravated murder (poisoning a victim on 8 April 2010). It found a reasonable suspicion based on police reports, an autopsy, medical documents, exhibits and witness statements. Detention was justified by a risk of evidence-tampering (he had previously threatened witnesses) and a risk of absconding arising from his “unclear” financial situation and the severity of the possible sentence. The court gave no consideration to a request for house arrest. An appeal was dismissed on 3 March 2011.

Detention was thereafter extended repeatedly by the Buda Central District Court, Budapest Regional Court, Budapest High Court and other courts (until 26 May, 26 August and 26 November 2011; then February, June and August 2012; and thereafter). The courts consistently invoked the risk of absconding, citing the applicant’s lack of a permanent address or regular income at the time of arrest, unstable finances, temporary jobs, and the gravity of the offence and potential punishment. They also relied (at least initially) on a risk of collusion by influencing remaining witnesses or destroying evidence, even after most witnesses had been heard. Later decisions sometimes dropped the collusion ground once investigative measures were largely complete.

The applicant repeatedly appealed and applied for release or less restrictive measures (house arrest or an undertaking not to leave his residence). He emphasised his family ties (he lived with his common-law wife, two minor children, parents and brother’s family), lack of a criminal record, cooperation with investigators, known temporary residence, and the considerable time that had elapsed since the alleged offence (over a year, later two years). He submitted hosting declarations, but these were often rejected for lacking proof of the host’s financial capacity or as insufficient to offset the risk of flight given the potential sentence. Courts frequently held that public interest in detention outweighed his liberty, that family ties did not counterbalance the risk, and that no less restrictive measure would suffice.

In February 2013 the Budapest High Court released him on bail under house arrest, finding that the risk of absconding alone could no longer justify detention after such a lengthy period. The Budapest Court of Appeal reversed this, citing the seriousness of the offence irrespective of family ties. A similar release with an undertaking not to leave his residence in April 2013 was likewise overturned. After a bill of indictment was preferred on 17 June 2013, detention was extended until the first-instance judgment. Subsequent release applications (2013–2014) were dismissed for lack of new circumstances, the gravity and complexity of the case, and insufficient financial or “essential” ties. Reviews by the Budapest Court of Appeal and the Kúria in 2014 upheld detention as necessary and proportionate.

On 29 October 2014 the Budapest High Court convicted the applicant of aggravated murder and sentenced him to 18 years’ imprisonment. Pre-trial detention had lasted from 26 February 2011 until conviction—more than three years and eight months.

The facts centre on the successive justifications for, and the overall duration of, the applicant’s remand in custody despite evolving circumstances and repeated requests for alternatives.
001-183817:
The applicant company, Aviso Zeta AG (a Viennese bank, later placed in liquidation), purchased and held IF company shares in deposit for third parties. It had close professional ties to both IF (shared management and staff) and the A. company (a key distribution partner and investment advisor). After IF shares lost substantial value from mid-2007 onward, multiple civil claims were brought against the applicant.

In the proceedings at issue, F.M. and H.H. had acquired IF shares between 2006 and 2008 on A. company’s advice. They sued the applicant in 2009 to unwind the purchases; IF intervened on the applicant’s side. The Vienna Commercial Court allowed the claim on 6 April 2012, holding the applicant liable for A. company’s inadequate risk warnings because of the companies’ close ties. The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed that ruling on 20 September 2012, finding the advice could not be attributed to the applicant. The plaintiffs then lodged an ordinary appeal on points of law.

On 17 June 2013 a five-judge panel of the Supreme Court (Second Section) allowed the appeal and reinstated the Commercial Court’s judgment. It reasoned that the applicant’s interest in selling IF shares had led it to supply A. company staff with inadequate information material, rendering the applicant liable.

The applicant subsequently learned of the panel’s composition only when the judgment was served. It then filed an action for nullity under section 529 of the Code of Civil Procedure, asserting that Judge N. (one of the five judges) had been biased. Judge N. had himself bought IF shares on A. company’s advice; those shares had also declined in value. He had previously recused himself from at least two comparable IF-share cases (decisions of 14 May 2010 and 26 November 2012), having even contemplated suing the applicant and others for his losses via a litigation funder. After the funder terminated the arrangement, Judge N. decided not to pursue claims and no longer recused himself. The applicant argued this constituted both subjective and objective bias under section 19 § 2 of the Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction and a breach of Article 6 § 1. Because the panel’s identity had been unknown beforehand, a timely challenge had been impossible.

The Supreme Court (Seventh Section) excluded Judge N. from the nullity proceedings. On 27 November 2013 the Second Section rejected the nullity action. It confirmed Judge N.’s share purchase and earlier recusals but held that mere bias is not a nullity ground under section 529; only statutory exclusion from office (section 20 of the Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction) suffices. The circumstances did not amount to a “particularly grave” case comparable to such exclusion. No Article 6 issue was found.

In a parallel set of IF-share proceedings against the applicant, the same company successfully challenged Judge N. On 13 November 2013 the Seventh Section declared him biased: his earlier voluntary recusals in analogous cases created objectively justified doubts about impartiality, even though he no longer intended to sue.

Domestic law (Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction, sections 19–22) permits challenge for legal exclusion or legitimate doubts as to impartiality; judges must report such grounds. An action for nullity after a decision becomes final is available only for statutory exclusion, not bias, and is barred if the ground could have been raised earlier. Supreme Court case-law consistently treats bias as insufficient for nullity except in exceptional circumstances approaching statutory exclusion.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaint that Judge N.’s participation violated the impartiality requirement of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria (Application no. 5734/14) concerns an alleged violation of the right to an impartial tribunal under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, an Austrian bank (in liquidation since 2016), purchased and held shares—primarily in the IF company—for third-party clients. The applicant and IF shared overlapping management and staff, while the A. company served as a key distribution partner. From late 2007, IF shares suffered major successive losses, prompting numerous lawsuits against the applicant.

In the proceedings at issue, clients F.M. and H.H. (acting on A. company advice) instructed the applicant between 2006 and 2008 to buy and hold IF shares. In 2009 they sued to annul the purchases. IF intervened on the applicant’s side. On 6 April 2012 the Vienna Commercial Court upheld the claim, finding the applicant liable for A. company’s inadequate risk disclosures due to the companies’ close professional ties. The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed this on 20 September 2012, holding that A. company’s advice could not be attributed to the applicant.

F.M. and H.H. lodged an ordinary appeal on points of law. On 17 June 2013 a five-judge panel of the Supreme Court’s Second Section (including Judge N.) allowed the appeal and reinstated the first-instance judgment. It reasoned that the applicant’s interest in selling IF shares, combined with the close ties, meant it had supplied A. company employees with inadequate information and was therefore liable.

The applicant then filed an action for nullity under section 529 of the Code of Civil Procedure, asserting that Judge N. had been biased. Judge N. had himself purchased IF shares (on A. company advice) whose value later collapsed. He had previously recused himself from comparable IF-share cases after considering (and even offering shares to a litigation funder for) possible claims against IF or related entities, potentially including the applicant. The Supreme Court had accepted those recusals. The applicant learned of Judge N.’s participation only when the 17 June 2013 judgment was served, precluding an earlier challenge.

The Supreme Court (Seventh Section) excluded Judge N. from the nullity proceedings. On 27 November 2013 the Second Section dismissed the nullity action. It accepted the facts of Judge N.’s share purchase and earlier recusals but held that mere bias (as opposed to statutory exclusion under section 20 of the Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction) is not a ground for nullity of a final judgment. Only exceptionally grave circumstances approaching a statutory exclusion could suffice; Judge N.’s prior consideration of claims did not meet that threshold. No Article 6 issue arose.

In a parallel set of proceedings against the applicant (different claimant, same IF-share context), the applicant successfully challenged Judge N. On 13 November 2013 the Seventh Section declared him biased: his earlier self-recusals from analogous cases created objectively justified doubts about impartiality, even though he no longer intended to sue and did not feel personally biased.

Austrian law (sections 19–21 of the Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction and section 529 of the Code of Civil Procedure) distinguishes statutory exclusion of a judge from mere appearance of bias. The latter may be raised by challenge if known in time, but does not normally permit nullity of a final decision. The applicant’s complaint therefore centred on whether Judge N.’s participation, given his personal financial stake, prior recusals and the late disclosure of the panel’s composition, breached the Convention’s impartiality requirement.

The case of Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria (Application no. 5734/14) arose from civil proceedings in Austria concerning the sale of shares and alleged lack of impartiality by a Supreme Court judge, claimed to violate Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Aviso Zeta AG, a Vienna-based bank (later in liquidation), purchased and held shares in the related IF company on behalf of third-party clients. The two entities shared some management personnel and staff, and the A. company served as a key distribution partner for the applicant. Starting in late 2007, IF shares suffered successive significant losses in value, prompting numerous lawsuits against the applicant.

In the proceedings at issue, clients F.M. and H.H., after consulting the A. company, instructed the applicant between 2006 and 2008 to buy and deposit IF shares. In 2009 they sued the applicant to annul the purchases and recover their investments. IF joined as an intervening party supporting the applicant. On 6 April 2012 the Vienna Commercial Court upheld the claim, finding that the A. company had failed to adequately inform the clients of the risks and that this failure was attributable to the applicant given the close professional ties between the firms.

The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed that decision on 20 September 2012, holding that any inadequate advice by A. company employees could not be attributed to the applicant. The clients then lodged an ordinary appeal on points of law. On 17 June 2013 a five-judge panel of the Supreme Court (Second Section) allowed the appeal and reinstated the first-instance judgment. It reasoned that the applicant had a strong commercial interest in selling IF shares and had therefore supplied the A. company with inadequate information material, rendering the applicant liable for the defective advice.

The applicant subsequently filed an action for nullity of the Supreme Court judgment under section 529 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It argued that Judge N., a member of the deciding panel, was biased. Judge N. had himself purchased IF shares (whose value later collapsed) on the advice of the A. company. He had previously recused himself from comparable cases involving IF shares; the Supreme Court had accepted those withdrawals. At one point he had even contemplated bringing his own action for losses, potentially against the applicant. The applicant learned of Judge N.’s participation only when the judgment was served and therefore could not have challenged him earlier.

On 4 September 2013 the Supreme Court (Seventh Section) excluded Judge N. from sitting on the nullity application. On 27 November 2013 the Second Section rejected the nullity action. It confirmed that Judge N. had bought the shares, had offered them to a litigation funder in 2009 with a view to possible claims against IF or related parties, and had withdrawn from at least two similar cases in 2010 and 2012. After the funder terminated the arrangement he decided not to pursue claims and no longer recused himself. The court held that mere bias (as opposed to statutory exclusion from office under section 20 of the Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction) is not a ground for nullity. The circumstances did not amount to a particularly grave case comparable to a statutory exclusion, and no issue arose under Article 6.

In a parallel set of proceedings against the applicant involving other IF-share purchasers, the applicant successfully challenged Judge N. On 13 November 2013 the Seventh Section declared him biased, finding that his earlier voluntary recusals from comparable cases objectively justified doubts about his impartiality even though he no longer intended to sue.

Austrian law distinguishes between statutory exclusion of a judge (section 20 of the Act on Exercise of Jurisdiction) and challenge for legitimate doubts as to impartiality (section 19). An action for nullity of a final judgment is available only for statutory exclusion, not for bias, except in exceptionally grave situations. Parties may challenge a judge only if they know the judge’s identity; constructive knowledge is insufficient. Judges must report possible grounds for exclusion or bias so that a decision can be taken.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaint that the Supreme Court panel that decided against it was not impartial.
001-184066:
The applicants, Montenegrin company KIPS DOO (founded 1990) and its 99% owner Risto Drekalović, lodged an ECHR application in 2006 alleging excessive length of administrative/enforcement proceedings, lack of effective domestic remedies, and violation of property rights over planned land development in Podgorica.

In 1998 the company contracted with a municipal fund for use of four plots totaling 11,443 m² to build a shopping centre and office building, plus communal infrastructure charges. The plots were later consolidated as cadastral plot 2090/1036; under 2009 property legislation the company became owner in December 2011. Further cadastral splits occurred in 2005 and 2016.

The company’s 2004 development plan was registered in the Detailed Urbanistic Plan (DUP). December 2004 DUP amendments joined the plot with an adjacent 1,557 m² municipal plot into one urban plot. Mid-2005 municipal decisions imposed construction bans of up to one year (except for holders of prior building permits) pending DUP revision; a January 2006 decision confirmed this. A July 2006 DUP detached most of the added land (part becoming a traffic route) and planned two buildings instead of the shopping centre. Further DUP changes followed in 2010 and 2013 (the latter closer to the original scheme). The DUP for the area had already been amended multiple times since 1990, with changing designated uses.

From January 2005 the company repeatedly sought to “complete” the urban plot by purchasing the adjacent municipal land, as required by January 2005 Urban Technical Conditions (incorporated into a February 2005 ministerial location grant). The Secretariat refused, citing ongoing DUP revisions. After at least seven remittals by the municipal Chief Administrator or Administrative Court, the request was again dismissed in 2017 on the ground that later planning changes made completion impossible; an administrative-court challenge remained pending.

In July 2005 the company asked the successor Agency to calculate final communal charges. The Agency refused (citing the construction ban and later the lack of a building permit). A self-assessed payment of €131,325 was returned as “without cause.” After further refusals the company sued in the Commercial Court, which in April 2006 ordered the calculation, observing that no ban applied at the relevant request dates and that charges are a precondition for a permit. Higher courts upheld the judgment in 2008. The Agency then calculated a remaining €269,310 and proposed a new contract. An enforcement order followed; the company objected that the documents failed to specify the applicable DUP, while the Agency asserted compliance.

A July 2005 building-permit application was dismissed in September 2005 for non-payment of charges and non-completion of the plot. The Administrative Court and Supreme Court upheld the refusal in 2005–2006 without addressing the company’s arguments that the requirements were unlawful or that state bodies had obstructed compliance. A fresh 2014 permit application (after the 2013 DUP change) was still pending in 2017 after five remittals.

Constitutional-court motions challenging the 2005–2006 DUP-change decisions were discontinued or rejected. Meanwhile the company rapidly obtained all consents, a 2006 contract and a 2007 building permit for a warehouse on another Podgorica site, completing construction that year. A 2006 ministerial circular criticised municipalities for misapplying construction-ban provisions so as to block permits where locations had already been granted.

These facts—repeated DUP alterations, construction bans, multi-year administrative loops with remittals, judicial enforcement difficulties and refusal of a permit—form the core of the alleged delays, ineffective remedies and interference with the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

**Case summary: KIPS DOO and Drekalović v. Montenegro (ECHR, App. No. 28766/06, 26 June 2018)**

The applicants were KIPS DOO, a Montenegrin company founded in 1990, and its majority owner and executive director Risto Drekalović. In 1998 the company contracted with a municipal development fund for the right to use four plots of land (later consolidated as cadastral plot 2090/1036, totalling about 11,443 m²) in Podgorica to build a shopping centre and office building, plus payment of communal infrastructure charges. By 2011 the company became the landowner under later property legislation. Its construction plan was registered in the 2004 Detailed Urbanistic Plan (DUP).

From late 2004 the DUP underwent repeated revisions. In December 2004 the applicants’ plot was merged with an adjacent 1,557 m² municipal plot into one urban plot. Municipal decisions of June, October 2005 and January 2006 imposed successive construction bans (lasting up to one year) pending further DUP changes, except for investors already holding building permits. A July 2006 DUP split the adjacent land, reallocated parts, and provided for two buildings instead of the planned shopping centre. Further DUP amendments occurred in 2010 and 2013 (the latter appearing closer to the original plans). The land’s designated use also shifted over time.

In January 2005 the company sought to “complete” the urban plot by acquiring the adjacent municipal land, as required by January 2005 Urban Technical Conditions attached to a March 2005 ministerial location grant. The Property Secretariat repeatedly refused, citing ongoing DUP revisions. After at least seven remittals by the Chief Administrator or Administrative Court, the request was again dismissed in 2017 on the ground that later planning changes made completion impossible. Related administrative-court proceedings remained pending as of mid-2017.

Separately, in July 2005 the company asked the successor Agency to calculate final communal charges. The Agency refused multiple times, citing the construction bans and lack of a building permit. The company self-assessed and paid €131,325, which was refunded. After the Agency treated the matter as non-administrative, the company sued in the Commercial Court. That court ruled in April 2006 (upheld by the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court in 2008) that the Agency had been obliged to calculate the charges during periods when no ban applied and that a building permit was not a prerequisite. The Agency produced a calculation in August 2008 requiring a further €269,310 and a new contract. Enforcement proceedings followed; the company objected that the documents did not specify the applicable DUP and declined to sign. The Agency asserted compliance.

The company applied for a building permit in July 2005. The Ministry dismissed the request in September 2005 for unpaid charges and incomplete plot. The Administrative Court (December 2005) and Supreme Court (March 2006) upheld the refusal, holding that required documents were missing, without addressing claims that the conditions were unlawful or that official obstruction had occurred. A second permit application after the 2013 DUP change remained pending in 2017 after five remittals.

The company lodged unsuccessful Constitutional Court challenges to the 2005–2006 DUP-change decisions. It obtained various technical consents in 2005 and successfully built a warehouse on a different site in 2006–2007. Other investors seeking similar plot completions were likewise refused during the DUP revisions. A 2006 Ministry circular criticised municipal over-interpretation of construction-ban powers.

The applicants alleged excessive length of the administrative and enforcement proceedings (spanning 2005–2017 with repeated remittals), absence of an effective domestic remedy for delay, and interference with property rights through obstruction of construction. (Word count: 512)

The applicants, Montenegrin company KIPS DOO and its majority owner/director Risto Drekalović, lodged an application in 2006 complaining of excessively lengthy administrative and enforcement proceedings (Article 6), lack of an effective remedy (Article 13), and interference with property rights (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1). These arose from obstacles to constructing a planned shopping centre and office building.

In 1998 the company contracted to use four plots totalling 11,443 m² (later consolidated as cadastral plot 2090/1036). It became owner in 2011 under the 2009 Property Act. Its 2004 building plan was incorporated into the Detailed Urbanistic Plan (DUP). From December 2004 the DUP was repeatedly revised. Adjacent municipal land of 1,557 m² was added to form one urban plot; construction bans of 90 days (June 2005) then up to one year (October 2005 and January 2006) were imposed, except for holders of existing permits. A July 2006 DUP detached most of the adjacent land and envisaged different buildings. Further revisions occurred in 2010 and 2013 (the latter closer to the original plan).

In January 2005 the company sought to “complete” the urban plot by purchasing the added municipal land, as required by January 2005 Urban Technical Conditions attached to a February 2005 location grant. Repeated requests met refusals citing ongoing DUP revision. After at least seven remittals, the request was dismissed in 2017 on the ground that planning changes made completion impossible; an administrative-court challenge remained pending.

In July 2005 the company asked the successor Agency to calculate the communal infrastructure charges required for a building permit. The Agency refused, invoking the construction ban and the absence of a permit. The company’s self-calculated payment of €131,325 was returned. After four refusals it sued. In April 2006 the Commercial Court ordered the calculation, holding that no ban existed at the relevant dates and that charges precede a permit. The ruling was upheld in 2008. The Agency then produced a calculation requiring an additional €269,310, but the company objected that the documents failed to specify the applicable DUP. Enforcement proceedings followed; the Agency claimed compliance, while the company maintained the judgment remained unenforced.

A July 2005 building-permit application was refused for unpaid charges and an incomplete plot; the Administrative Court and Supreme Court upheld the refusal in 2005–2006 without addressing the alleged unlawfulness of those preconditions. A fresh 2014 application (after the 2013 DUP change) was still pending after five remittals in 2017.

Constitutional-court challenges to the 2005–2006 DUP-change decisions were discontinued or rejected. By contrast, the company obtained all necessary consents and a building permit for a warehouse on another site within months in 2006–2007. A 2006 Ministry circular confirmed that a prior location grant obliged the authorities to issue a permit even during a ban, provided statutory conditions were met.

These facts—repeated planning revisions, construction bans, successive refusals, multi-year court battles with remittals, and proceedings still unresolved more than a decade later—underpin the alleged delays, absence of effective redress, and prolonged frustration of the applicants’ ability to develop their land.
001-184276:
The ECHR case Voynov v. Russia (no. 39747/10) arose from a Russian national’s allocation to a remote prison far from his family, which he claimed breached Article 8 (respect for family life) and Article 13 (effective remedy).

Timur Voynov (born 1985) lived in Oryol with his partner and mother when charged with drug offences. On 2 December 2009 the federal FSIN instructed the Oryol regional FSIN to send up to 40 newly sentenced strict-regime prisoners each month to Krasnoyarsk Region because local facilities were overcrowded; the order remained in force indefinitely. On 7 December 2009 the Sovetskiy District Court sentenced Voynov to twelve years’ imprisonment in a strict-regime colony; the Oryol Regional Court upheld the conviction on 2 February 2010.

Acting on the federal instruction and citing overcrowding, the Oryol FSIN left the precise placement to the Krasnoyarsk FSIN, which assigned Voynov to colony IK-7 in Areyskoye, approximately 4 200 km from Oryol. He arrived on 20 April 2010 and has remained there.

Voynov repeatedly asked penal authorities at every level to transfer him closer to Oryol so that he could maintain family ties. On 12 November 2010 the federal FSIN refused, invoking Article 81 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences (CES): a prisoner must serve the entire sentence in the same facility unless exceptional circumstances exist, none of which were found. The FSIN added that statutory rights to visits, parcels, letters and telephone calls did not depend on geography.

Voynov then sued the Oryol FSIN for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, arguing that the transfer violated Article 73 § 1 CES (the general rule that a prisoner serves his sentence in his home region) and thereby impaired family contact. On 3 August 2012 the Zavodskoy District Court dismissed the claim. It held the allocation lawful under Article 73 § 2 CES and a Constitutional Court ruling because the Oryol facilities had been overcrowded and the local FSIN had simply followed the federal instruction. The court did not examine the practical effect on family life. Voynov did not appeal.

Despite the distance, Voynov’s partner made six long-term visits between July 2011 and October 2013; their daughter was born in 2014. He also received parcels and telephone calls from his mother and partner.

Domestic law (CES Arts. 73 and 81, the Ministry of Justice allocation instruction, and Constitutional Court Ruling No. 599-O of 28 March 2017) permits departure from the home-region rule for operational reasons such as overcrowding and treats the resulting restrictions on family life as inherent in imprisonment. The Constitutional Court regarded the provisions as consistent with the Constitution and with the non-binding European Prison Rules, which merely recommend proximity to home “where possible” and subject to available resources. No domestic procedure allowed a court to weigh the individual impact on family life against the administrative decision to send a prisoner thousands of kilometres away.

**Case of Voynov v. Russia (Application no. 39747/10), European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), judgment of 3 July 2018 (final 3 October 2018)**

The applicant, Timur Vladislavovich Voynov (born 1985), a Russian national from Oryol, alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for family life) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He complained that Russian authorities allocated him to a distant post-conviction prison, impairing his family ties, and that no effective domestic remedies existed.

At the time of his charges for drug-related offences, the applicant lived in Oryol with his partner and mother. On 2 December 2009, the Federal Penal Authority (FSIN) instructed the Oryol regional FSIN department to transfer up to 40 prisoners monthly from local remand prisons to strict-regime facilities in the Krasnoyarsk Region, an order effective from 1 December 2009 due to overcrowding. On 7 December 2009, the Sovetskiy District Court of Oryol convicted him and sentenced him to 12 years’ imprisonment in a strict-regime facility; the Oryol Regional Court upheld this on 2 February 2010.

Citing overcrowding in Oryol facilities and the FSIN instruction, the Oryol FSIN referred allocation to the Krasnoyarsk FSIN, which assigned him to IK-7 in Areyskoye village (approximately 4,200 km from Oryol). He has been held there since 20 April 2010.

The applicant repeatedly requested transfer to a facility nearer Oryol to maintain family ties. On 12 November 2010, the central FSIN refused, invoking Article 81 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences (CES): absent exceptional circumstances (none found here), prisoners serve their full term in one facility. It stated that rights to visits, parcels, correspondence, and calls were available regardless of location.

He then sued the Oryol FSIN in civil proceedings for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, arguing the allocation breached Article 73 § 1 CES (right to serve in the home region) and hindered family/social ties. On 3 August 2012, the Zavodskoy District Court of Oryol dismissed the claim, relying on Article 73 § 2 CES and a Constitutional Court ruling. It found the decision lawful given December 2009–February 2010 overcrowding and compliance with FSIN instructions. The court did not address the family-ties argument. The applicant did not appeal.

Despite the distance, his partner made six long-term visits to IK-7 between July 2011 and October 2013. Their daughter was born in 2014. He received parcels and phone calls from his mother and partner.

Relevant domestic law includes CES Articles 73 and 81 on prisoner allocation and transfers, plus Constitutional Court practice (e.g., Ruling No. 1700-O-O and later Ruling No. 599-O of 28 March 2017). The latter rejected a similar challenge, holding that allocation rules pursue legitimate aims (punishment individualisation, security) and do not arbitrarily determine location; international standards (e.g., European Prison Rules) are recommendatory and subject to resources. Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure (repealed 2015) provided for challenging official actions.

These facts centre on the remote allocation (driven by overcrowding and a standing FSIN order rather than individual assessment), unsuccessful transfer requests and civil challenge (which ignored family-life arguments), and limited but existing family contacts, forming the basis of the Article 8 and 13 complaints. The Court later found a violation of Article 8 due to the lack of individualised consideration of family ties in allocation decisions, with Article 13 also implicated by ineffective remedies.

The case of Voynov v. Russia (Application no. 39747/10) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 June 2010 by Timur Vladislavovich Voynov, a Russian national born in 1985 and resident in Oryol. Represented by lawyer E. Markov, the applicant alleged that Russian authorities violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life by allocating him to a distant post-conviction detention facility, and that he lacked effective domestic remedies under Article 13. The Third Section communicated these complaints on 15 April 2015 after declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicant, his partner and his mother all lived in Oryol when he was charged with drug-related offences. On 2 December 2009 the Federal Penal Authority (FSIN) instructed the Oryol regional FSIN department to transfer up to 40 prisoners per month from local remand prisons to the Krasnoyarsk Region; the instruction remained in force until further notice. On 7 December 2009 the Sovetskiy District Court of Oryol convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment in a strict-regime facility; the Oryol Regional Court upheld the conviction on 2 February 2010.

Acting on the FSIN instruction and citing overcrowding in Oryol-region facilities, the Oryol FSIN left the choice of specific prison to the Krasnoyarsk FSIN. The latter assigned the applicant to IK-7, a strict-regime colony in the village of Areyskoye, Krasnoyarsk Region, some 4 200 km from Oryol. He has been detained there since 20 April 2010.

The applicant repeatedly asked penal authorities at every level to move him closer to Oryol so that he could maintain family ties. On 12 November 2010 the central FSIN refused, relying on Article 81 of the Code on the Execution of Sentences (CES): in the absence of exceptional circumstances a prisoner must serve the entire sentence in the same facility, and no such circumstances existed. The authority added that rights to visits, parcels, correspondence and telephone calls “do not depend on the place in which he is serving the sentence.”

The applicant then brought civil proceedings against the Oryol FSIN, seeking damages for the alleged breach of Article 73 § 1 CES (the right to serve the sentence in the home region) and for the consequent impairment of family and social ties. On 3 August 2012 the Zavodskoy District Court of Oryol dismissed the claim. It cited Article 73 § 2 CES and Constitutional Court Ruling No. 1700-O-O, held that the transfer had been lawful because Oryol facilities were overcrowded between December 2009 and February 2010, and noted that the defendant had merely followed superior instructions. The court did not examine the applicant’s argument concerning the practical difficulty of maintaining family contact. The applicant did not appeal.

Despite the distance, the applicant’s partner made six long-term family visits to IK-7 between July 2011 and October 2013; their daughter was born in 2014. He also received parcels and telephone calls from both his mother and his partner.

Domestic law (Articles 73 and 81 CES, Ministry of Justice allocation instructions and several Constitutional Court rulings) permits assignment outside the home region when local prisons are overcrowded or for other administrative reasons. The Constitutional Court has held that these provisions pursue legitimate aims of individualisation of punishment and are compatible with the Constitution; it regards the European Prison Rules as merely recommendatory and subject to available resources. Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure (repealed in 2015) provided the procedural vehicle for the applicant’s unsuccessful damages claim.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference with family life and the asserted absence of an effective remedy capable of examining the proportionality of sending a prisoner 4 200 km from his family.
001-184485:
**Case of Daoukopoulos v. Greece (Application no. 44711/16), ECtHR judgment of 12 July 2018**

The applicant, Miltiadis Daoukopoulos (born 1971), a Greek national serving a life sentence for drug dealing, alleged that his detention conditions in Diavata Prison from 9 May 2016 to 20 December 2016 amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13. He had been held in Diavata from October 2014 to November 2015, transferred to Malandrino Prison, returned to Diavata on 9 May 2016, and transferred back to Malandrino on 20 December 2016. Only the post-9 May 2016 Diavata period and related remedy complaint were examined.

The applicant stated he was first placed in cell B14 (9 m², four occupants, under 3 m² personal space). From 7 August 2016 he occupied cell GR 2 (24 m², ten occupants, again under 3 m²). Overcrowding caused exposure to infectious diseases and passive smoking, with cramped space and low bunks that prevented sitting upright. Natural light and ventilation were inadequate. Sanitary facilities were old, broken and insufficient for hygiene. Heating operated only one hour daily (21:00–22:00); hot water was available two hours daily in winter and proved inadequate, forcing washing from buckets due to poor shower pressure. Cells contained bunks, stools and a small table but no lockable storage. Mattresses were old, mouldy and odorous; no sheets or towels were supplied. Cultural, recreational and sports activities were lacking, increasing isolation (newspapers obtained only via visitors). Corridor time coincided with meals, visits and calls; the yard had a football field but no balls or other facilities. Food was repetitive and of low nutritional value. These conditions allegedly triggered several cardiac arrests.

The Government, relying on prison records, reported official capacity of 358 (based on 4 m² per person per CPT standards) but occupancy of 460–500. The applicant occupied a 24 m² cell (including a 2 m² toilet) originally for ten but, after an April 2015 overcrowding-relief law, shared with four to six others, yielding 3.14–4.4 m² personal space. The facility had central heating plus electric devices, large windows, regular hot water, hygiene products and disinfection. Weekly menus showed dietary variety. The applicant’s medical file showed pre-existing cardiac problems; needs were met by prison doctors and hospital transfers. He received 15 days’ leave for examinations.

CPT reports (2014, following a 2013 visit; 2016, following a 2015 visit) independently confirmed persistent severe overcrowding at Diavata (capacity 250 holding 590 inmates in 2013; capacity later raised to 370 but still holding 588 in 2015). 24 m² dormitories held up to ten inmates in cramped bunk-bed conditions; light and ventilation were adequate but lockable storage was absent and sanitary annexes were rudimentary.

Relevant Greek law and practice on detention conditions and remedies were as previously described in *Chatzivasiliadis v. Greece*. The parties’ accounts thus diverged sharply on personal space, amenities, hygiene, heating, food and medical causation, while official capacity figures and CPT findings established chronic overcrowding exceeding CPT minimums during the relevant period.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Miltiadis Daoukopoulos, a Greek national born in 1971 serving a life sentence for drug offences, against Greece (no. 44711/16). The applicant complained of inhuman and degrading detention conditions in Diavata Prison from 9 May 2016 to 20 December 2016, together with the absence of an effective domestic remedy. He had previously been held in the same prison from October 2014 to November 2015 before transfers to and from Malandrino Prison.

According to the applicant, he was first placed in cell B14 (9 m², four inmates), then from 7 August 2016 in cell GR2 (24 m², ten inmates). In both cells personal space fell below 3 m². Overcrowding, low bunk beds and restricted movement exposed him to infectious diseases and passive smoking. Natural light and ventilation were inadequate. Sanitary installations were old, broken and insufficient; heating operated only one hour daily and hot water two hours daily in winter, with low shower pressure forcing inmates to wash from buckets. Cells contained only basic furniture (bunk beds, stools, a small table) without lockable storage. Mattresses were mouldy and smelly; no sheets or towels were supplied. Out-of-cell time in corridors was limited and coincided with meals, visits and telephone calls. The exercise yard contained a football pitch but no balls or other recreational facilities. Food was repetitive and of poor nutritional value. The applicant attributed several cardiac arrests to these conditions.

The Government, relying on prison records, stated that Diavata Prison’s official capacity was 358 places (calculated at 4 m² per inmate) but held 460–500 prisoners during the relevant period. The applicant occupied a 24 m² cell (including a 2 m² toilet) originally designed for ten inmates. After a 2015 law reducing overcrowding he shared it with four to six others, yielding 3.14–4.4 m² of living space. The prison had a central heating system supplemented by electric heaters in cells, large windows, regular hot-water supply, hygiene products and disinfection. Menus showed dietary variety. Medical records demonstrated that the applicant already suffered from cardiac problems before incarceration; his needs were met by prison doctors and hospital transfers, and he was granted 15 days’ leave to sit examinations.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) documented persistent overcrowding. Its 2014 report (2013 visit) recorded 590 inmates against a capacity of 250: 24 m² dormitories held up to ten prisoners and 11 m² cells held four, with floor-level toilets also used for washing. Access to light and ventilation was adequate but lockable storage was absent. A 2016 report (2015 visit) found the situation essentially unchanged: 588 inmates against a re-designated capacity of 370, still resulting in cramped conditions.

These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 3 and Article 13 violations. The Court had previously described the relevant Greek prison legislation and remedies in Chatzivasiliadis v. Greece.

**CASE OF DAOUKOPOULOS v. GREECE (Application no. 44711/16), ECtHR judgment of 12 July 2018**

The applicant, a Greek national born in 1971 and serving a life sentence for drug dealing, complained under the Convention about the conditions of his detention in Diavata Prison from 9 May 2016 (after a transfer from Malandrino Prison) until his transfer back on 20 December 2016, as well as the lack of an effective domestic remedy. He had previously been held there from October 2014 to November 2015. The Court communicated these complaints (remainder of the application declared inadmissible) and examined them as a Committee.

According to the applicant, he was first held in cell B 14 (9 sq m, four detainees), then from 7 August 2016 in cell GR 2 on the ground floor (24 sq m, ten detainees). In both cases personal space was under 3 sq m. Overcrowding exposed him to infectious diseases and passive smoking. Movement was severely restricted; bunk beds were too low to sit up comfortably. Access to natural light and ventilation was inadequate. Sanitary facilities were old, broken and insufficient for hygiene. Heating operated only one hour daily (9–10 p.m.); hot water in winter lasted two hours and was inadequate, forcing detainees to wash from buckets because of poor shower pressure. Furniture was minimal (bunk beds, stools, a small table and side tables) with no lockable storage. Mattresses were old, mouldy and smelly; no sheets or towels were supplied. There was virtually no access to cultural, recreational or sports activities. Time in corridors coincided with meals, visits and phone calls, leaving little free movement. The yard had a football field but no balls and offered no meaningful activity. Food was repetitive and nutritionally poor. The applicant claimed these conditions caused several cardiac arrests.

The Government, relying on prison records, stated Diavata had a theoretical capacity of 358 detainees (based on 4 sq m per person, CPT minimum). Actual occupancy was 460–500. The applicant was held in cell 11 (first floor, 24 sq m including a 2 sq m toilet). Although designed for ten, post-2015 overcrowding-relief measures meant he shared it with four to six others, yielding 3.14–4.4 sq m of personal space. The prison had central heating plus electric devices in cells; large windows provided light and ventilation. Hot water and hygiene products were regularly supplied; cells were disinfected. Weekly menus showed varied meals. The applicant’s medical file indicated pre-existing cardiac problems; his needs were met through prison doctors and hospital transfers. He also received 15 days’ leave for exams.

CPT reports (2014 visit of April 2013 and 2016 report of April 2015 visit) confirmed chronic overcrowding at Diavata (capacity 250/370 but holding 590/588). Dormitories of 24 sq m held up to ten inmates; smaller cells of 11 sq m held four. Conditions were cramped, with limited furniture, no lockable storage, and sanitary annexes used also for washing clothes and dishes (though partitioned). Official capacity had been inflated by re-designating rooms.

Domestic law and practice on detention conditions and remedies were as described in Chatzivasiliadis v. Greece (no. 51618/12). These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 3 (inhuman/degrading treatment via overcrowding and poor conditions) and Article 13 (absence of effective remedy) violations. The Court later found a violation of Article 3 on account of the conditions and of Article 13 due to the lack of an effective remedy, awarding just satisfaction.
001-184653:
The European Court of Human Rights case of Yordanova and Others v. Bulgaria (applications nos. 61432/11 and 64318/11) arose from complaints by three Bulgarian nationals—Ms Violeta Aleksandrova Yordanova, Ms Timka Aleksandrova Rusamanova (deceased in 2013, succeeded by her daughter Ms Svetla Velichkova Gogova), and Ms Rumyana Strashimirova Telyatinova—against the Bulgarian authorities’ prolonged failure to deliver compensation for their fathers’ nationalized printing houses.

The applicants’ fathers owned printing businesses in Sofia that the Communist authorities nationalized in 1949–1950. The assets were absorbed by a state printing enterprise later re-registered as the state-owned company ‘Obrazovanie i nauka’ EAD, managed by the Minister of Education and tasked with producing school textbooks.

After the fall of communism, Parliament enacted the 1997 Compensation of Owners of Nationalised Real Property Act. Where restitution in kind was impossible, former owners or heirs could choose compensation in the form of shares in the successor company or compensation bonds (tradable instruments usable in privatizations, typically sold at a discount).

In 1998 the first and second applicants (together with their mother) and the third applicant (together with her mother and sister) applied under the Act, electing shares in ‘Obrazovanie i nauka’ EAD. The Minister of Education initially granted the requests (June 1999 for the first group; December 1998 for the third). Valuations later confirmed entitlements of 57,932 BGN (approximately 29,630 EUR, or 579 shares) for the first group and 26,309 BGN (approximately 13,460 EUR, or 263 shares) for the third applicant’s family; these valuations were approved in June 2003.

Nevertheless, in August 2003 the Minister issued fresh decisions substituting compensation bonds, relying on a 2002 Privatisation Act provision that confined compensation for certain listed state entities to bonds. Both decisions were quashed by the Supreme Administrative Court (2004 judgments) as unlawful modifications of earlier final rulings; the court held the Privatisation Act provision inapplicable to pending compensation proceedings.

Despite the judicial confirmations, the Ministry took no further steps to transfer the shares. In 2006 the first group of applicants lodged complaints with state bodies; official replies referred to a search for a “lawful solution” that would not harm the public interest or breach the Privatisation Act. Family members died in the interim, leaving the applicants as sole heirs.

In 2008 the Privatisation Agency authorized the share transfers, yet the Ministry still failed to implement them. In 2011 the third applicant wrote to the company seeking registration of her shareholding and copies of post-2003 general-meeting decisions; she received no reply. In 2013 the Council of Ministers authorized the company to sell real properties. The applicants challenged that decision, arguing it affected their rights as putative shareholders. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the challenge in 2015, observing that the compensation procedures had never been completed and the applicants therefore held no shares.

These facts—repeated administrative reversals, ignored court judgments, unused 2008 authorization, and continued inaction spanning more than a decade—underlie the applicants’ complaint that the authorities failed to provide the compensation to which they were entitled, thereby violating their property rights.

The case of Yordanova and Others v. Bulgaria (applications nos. 61432/11 and 64318/11) concerns three Bulgarian applicants whose fathers owned printing houses in Sofia that were nationalised by the communist authorities in 1949–1950. The assets were absorbed into a state-owned printing enterprise that later became the company ‘Obrazovanie i nauka’ EAD, managed by the Minister of Education and responsible for printing school textbooks.

Following the 1997 Compensation of Owners of Nationalised Real Property Act, which allowed former owners or heirs to choose compensation either as shares in the successor companies or as compensation bonds, the applicants (together with other family members) applied in 1998 for shares in ‘Obrazovanie i nauka’ EAD.

For the first and second applicants (and their mother), the Minister of Education initially granted the request in June 1999. A subsequent 2000 refusal was quashed by the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) in 2002 as an unlawful modification of a final decision. A 2003 valuation confirmed entitlement to 579 shares (valued at BGN 57,932). The Minister then purported to substitute bonds, citing the company’s inclusion on a list under section 11 of the concluding provisions of the 2002 Privatisation and Post-Privatisation Control Act (which restricted compensation for certain state-owned entities to bonds only). The SAC quashed this decision in October 2004, holding that the provision could not override earlier final awards of shares. Family complaints to the authorities in 2006 yielded only vague assurances of a “lawful solution.”

The third applicant (with her mother and sister) received an initial grant of her request in December 1998. A 2003 valuation confirmed entitlement to 263 shares (BGN 26,309). An identical 2003 ministerial attempt to award bonds instead was quashed by the SAC in March 2004 on the same grounds. Subsequent deaths of co-heirs left the third applicant as sole successor.

In 2007 the Ministry of Education sought and, in April 2008, obtained Privatisation Agency authorisation to transfer the relevant shares to the applicants. No further steps were taken to effect the transfers. In 2011 the third applicant’s request to the company for registration of her shareholding went unanswered. In 2013 the Council of Ministers authorised the company to sell certain real properties; the applicants’ challenge, based on their claimed shareholder status, was dismissed by the SAC in 2015 on the ground that the compensation procedures had never been completed by actual share transfers.

The applicants complained of the authorities’ prolonged failure to implement the final decisions awarding them shares as compensation for the nationalised property. The second applicant died in 2013; her daughter continued the application.
