The case of Yordanova and Others v. Bulgaria originated in two applications to the European Court of Human Rights by three Bulgarian nationals whose fathers had owned printing houses in Sofia. These businesses were nationalized by the communist authorities in 1949 and 1950, after which their assets were absorbed into a state-owned printing enterprise later registered as ‘Obrazovanie i nauka’ EAD, a company managed by the Minister of Education and tasked with printing school textbooks.

Following the fall of the communist regime, Parliament enacted the 1997 Compensation of Owners of Nationalised Real Property Act. This legislation provided for compensation (rather than restitution in kind) of former owners or their heirs when physical return of nationalized assets was impossible. Compensation could take the form of shares in the successor companies or compensation bonds usable in privatization tenders.

In 1998 the applicants (and, initially, other family members) applied under the Act, expressing a preference for shares in ‘Obrazovanie i nauka’ EAD. The Minister of Education granted the requests in 1998–1999, stating that the precise number of shares would be fixed after valuation. Expert valuations later confirmed entitlements of 579 shares (face value BGN 57 932) for the first two applicants and their mother, and 263 shares (BGN 26 309) for the third applicant and her relatives. These valuations were approved by the Minister in June 2003.

Nevertheless, in August 2003 the Minister issued new decisions substituting compensation bonds for shares. He relied on section 11 of the concluding provisions of the 2002 Privatisation and Post-Privatisation Control Act, which listed certain wholly state-owned companies (including public-interest entities) for which only bonds could be awarded. The Supreme Administrative Court quashed both 2003 decisions (final judgments of 2004), holding that they unlawfully modified earlier final administrative acts awarding shares and that section 11 did not apply to pending compensation proceedings.

Despite these rulings, the Ministry took no steps to transfer the shares. In 2006 the first two applicants lodged complaints with various state bodies; replies indicated that the authorities were seeking a solution that would not conflict with the Privatisation Act or the public interest. After further family deaths, the surviving applicants remained the sole heirs.

In April 2008 the Privatisation Agency authorized the transfer of shares to the applicants. The Ministry nonetheless failed to complete the transfers or enter the applicants as shareholders. In 2011 the third applicant wrote unsuccessfully to the company seeking registration of her holding. In 2013 the Council of Ministers authorized the company to sell certain real properties. The applicants challenged the authorization, arguing it affected their rights as shareholders; the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the claim in 2015, observing that the compensation procedures had never been finalized by an actual transfer of shares, so the applicants were not yet shareholders.

The applicants complained that the prolonged failure of the authorities to implement the final decisions entitling them to shares in the successor company violated their rights. The Court communicated the complaints concerning the non-provision of compensation and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible. The second applicant died in 2013 and her daughter continued the proceedings in her place.
001-184476:
The applicant, Grozdana Mateljan (born 1935), was awarded a specially protected tenancy of a 37 m² socially owned flat in Gajeva Street, Split, in 1961 by her employer (later the Croatian Pension Fund). In 1969 she married M.M. and moved into his flat. In 1972 her husband (a serviceman) was allocated a 62 m² socially owned flat in Šimićeva Street to meet the housing needs of himself, the applicant and their two infant sons. The family moved there in 1973; under then-applicable law the applicant automatically became co-holder of that tenancy. Her brother occupied the Gajeva Street flat until 1982.

The applicant claimed that in May 1982 she returned to the Gajeva Street flat to care for her elderly mother. She applied to the Pension Fund for permission to exchange the two flats for a single larger one (a possibility under the 1974 Housing Act if neither flat alone met household needs). The Fund refused consent, holding that she had been using two socially owned flats contrary to law, and sought her eviction from Gajeva Street.

Joined administrative proceedings ensued. First-instance housing authorities repeatedly dismissed the exchange request and ordered eviction, finding that the applicant had permanently left Gajeva Street in 1969 (thereby losing that tenancy) and that the Šimićeva Street flat fully met the family's needs. Higher administrative authorities, the Administrative Court and the Supreme Court repeatedly quashed and remitted the case (in 1983, 1985, 1988, 1996 and 2004). Disputes centred on: whether the applicant had retained the Gajeva tenancy; whether military or general housing standards applied to the Šimićeva flat (allocated by the army); and whether later changes in circumstances were relevant.

In 1992 the applicant divorced M.M. and withdrew her exchange application, citing changed circumstances. Authorities nevertheless ordered her to vacate Gajeva Street, holding that the Šimićeva flat had satisfied housing needs when the family moved there in 1973 and that subsequent events (including the divorce) were irrelevant. After further unsuccessful judicial review, a 1999 first-instance decision became final. The applicant’s 2006 constitutional complaint (alleging unfair procedure and failure to consider her divorce and sole occupation of Gajeva Street) was dismissed in 2011; an interim measure had temporarily stayed enforcement.

Enforcement was ordered in 2003. After postponements (including for medical reasons), the applicant was evicted on 16 May 2012. In parallel, a 1992 uncontested civil judgment (based solely on M.M.’s admission) declared her sole holder of the Gajeva tenancy. In 1995–96 M.M. purchased the Šimićeva flat after the couple agreed he was its sole tenant; an inspection had listed the applicant as an unregistered household member. Post-eviction her domicile was registered at the Šimićeva address. She co-owns several other properties.

The protracted eviction proceedings (spanning 1982–2012) and the authorities’ refusal to re-examine her tenancy status or later circumstances form the core factual matrix relevant to the alleged Convention violations (principally interference with home and/or possessions).

The applicant, Grozdana Mateljan (born 1935), a Croatian national living in Split, was awarded a specially protected tenancy of a 37 m² socially owned flat in Gajeva Street in 1961 by her employer (later the Croatian Pension Fund). She married M.M. in 1969 and moved into his flat. In 1972 the Yugoslav People’s Army awarded M.M. a 62 m² socially owned flat in Šimićeva Street to meet the housing needs of the family (the applicant and their two infant sons). The family moved there in 1973, at which point the applicant automatically became a co-holder of that tenancy. Her brother occupied the Gajeva Street flat until 1982.

The applicant claimed she returned to the Gajeva Street flat in May 1982 to care for her elderly mother and remained there until her eviction on 16 May 2012. In June 1982 she applied to the Pension Fund for permission to exchange the two flats for a single larger one (permitted under the 1974 Housing Act if neither flat alone met household needs). The Fund refused and ordered her to vacate Gajeva Street, asserting she had been unlawfully occupying two socially owned flats.

Joined administrative proceedings followed. A first-instance housing authority in December 1982 dismissed the exchange request and ordered eviction, holding that the applicant had lost her Gajeva tenancy by leaving in 1969 and had not reacquired it. On appeal the second-instance authority quashed this in May 1983, finding she retained the tenancy and directing an examination of whether the flats met family housing needs. Subsequent first-instance decisions (1984, 1987) again found the Šimićeva flat sufficient and ordered eviction; these were upheld on appeal but repeatedly quashed by the Administrative Court (1985, 1988) for incomplete facts or incorrect application of housing standards (military versus general).

In 1992 the applicant withdrew her exchange application, citing the passage of time and her recent divorce. The first-instance authority discontinued that part of the case but again ordered eviction, a decision upheld on appeal and by the Administrative Court in 1993. The Supreme Court quashed the latter judgment in 1996 on a legality request, ruling that needs must be assessed as of 1973 (when the family moved into Šimićeva Street) and that later changes were irrelevant. After further first- and second-instance decisions (1999–2000) confirming eviction, the Administrative Court dismissed a fourth judicial-review action in 2003. The Supreme Court again quashed this in 2004, now holding that general (not military) standards applied. The Administrative Court dismissed the action once more in 2005.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint in 2006 alleging unfair procedure, including failure to consider her divorce, non-use of two flats, and household composition (she lived with her son and his family). The Constitutional Court issued an interim measure postponing enforcement but dismissed the complaint in July 2011. Enforcement proceedings begun in 2003 were repeatedly postponed; an attempted eviction in 2006 was deferred on health grounds. The applicant was evicted on 16 May 2012.

Separately, a 1992 court judgment (based solely on M.M.’s admission) declared the applicant sole holder of the Gajeva tenancy. In 1995 the couple agreed that M.M. was sole holder of the Šimićeva tenancy; he purchased that flat from the State in 1996. A 1995 inspection recorded the applicant as an unregistered occupant there. After eviction she registered her domicile at the Šimićeva address (owned by her former husband). The Government also showed she co-owned several properties, including two houses.

Under successive Housing Acts a tenant could not occupy two flats and had to choose one and vacate the other within a short statutory period; an exchange for a larger flat was possible only if neither existing flat met household needs. Spouse co-tenancy arose automatically upon moving in.

The case of Mateljan v. Croatia (Application no. 64855/11) concerns a Croatian national born in 1935 and her occupancy of a socially owned flat. In 1961 the Municipal Institute for Social Insurance (later the Croatian Pension Fund) awarded her a specially protected tenancy of a 37 m² flat in Gajeva Street, Split. She married in 1969 and moved into her husband’s flat. In 1972 the Yugoslav People’s Army allocated her husband, a serviceman, a 62 m² socially owned flat in Šimićeva Street to meet the housing needs of the couple and their two infant sons. The family moved there in 1973, automatically making the applicant a co-holder of that tenancy under the applicable housing legislation. Her brother then occupied the Gajeva Street flat with his family until 1982.

The applicant asserted that she returned to the Gajeva Street flat in May 1982 to care for her elderly mother and remained there until her eviction thirty years later. In June 1982 she applied to the Pension Fund for permission to exchange the two flats for one larger dwelling, a possibility then available under section 49(3) of the 1974 Housing Act when neither flat alone met household needs. The Fund refused and ordered her to vacate Gajeva Street on the ground that she had been using two socially owned flats, which successive Housing Acts (1962, 1974 and 1985) expressly prohibited. She instituted administrative proceedings seeking the exchange; the Fund simultaneously sought her eviction. The proceedings were joined.

Over the following decades the case generated repeated first- and second-instance administrative decisions, four actions for judicial review before the Administrative Court, two successful requests for the protection of legality before the Supreme Court, and a constitutional complaint. Early decisions held that she had lost her Gajeva tenancy by leaving in 1969 and that the Šimićeva flat fully met family needs. Subsequent remittals required examination of whether she retained the tenancy, whether military or general housing standards applied, and whether sufficiency of accommodation should be assessed as of 1973 (when she moved into Šimićeva Street) rather than in light of later events. In 1992, after her divorce, she withdrew the exchange application; the authorities nevertheless continued to order her eviction, treating subsequent changes in family circumstances as irrelevant. The Constitutional Court issued an interim stay of enforcement in 2006 but dismissed her complaint of unfair procedure in 2011.

An enforcement order was issued in 2003. Eviction attempts were postponed, including one in 2006 on account of the applicant’s health. She was finally evicted on 16 May 2012. Parallel civil proceedings produced a 1992 declaratory judgment (based solely on her former husband’s admission) naming her sole holder of the Gajeva tenancy. In 1995 the couple agreed that he was sole holder of the Šimićeva tenancy; he purchased that flat from the State in 1996. A 1995 inspection recorded her as an unregistered occupant of Šimićeva Street. After eviction her registered domicile was transferred there. She was also co-owner of several other properties, including two houses.

The relevant housing legislation required a tenant who acquired a second habitable flat to notify the authorities and, within a short statutory period, to choose one tenancy and vacate the other, unless an exchange for a single larger flat was authorised. These protracted proceedings and the circumstances of the applicant’s long-term occupancy formed the factual matrix of the case before the European Court.
001-184816:
The case of Dridi v. Germany (Application no. 35778/11) arose from criminal proceedings in which the applicant, a German national, alleged violations of his rights to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) and (c) of the Convention, specifically concerning inadequate time and facilities to prepare his defence and the effective exercise of his right to legal assistance.

On 2 March 2009 the Hamburg District Court convicted the applicant of assault and imposed a sentence of 40 day-fines of EUR 25 each, payable in instalments. At the applicant’s request the court had authorised Mr Arif (then a law student) to act as defence counsel. Both the applicant and the public prosecutor appealed; the latter challenged only the sentence. The applicant thereafter moved to Spain for work and notified the court of his new address.

On 24 April 2009 the Hamburg Regional Court withdrew Mr Arif’s authorisation and simultaneously refused the applicant’s request to be excused from personal appearance at the appeal hearing. That decision was served on the applicant in Spain. The same day the Regional Court listed the appeal hearing for 9.10 a.m. on 13 May 2009 and, because the applicant had left Germany, ordered service of the summons by public notification. The summons was displayed on the court noticeboard from 27 April to 12 May 2009.

On 12 May 2009 Mr Arif learned by telephone that the Court of Appeal had that day restored his authorisation and that the hearing was scheduled for the following morning. He immediately applied by fax for an adjournment, stating that he would be out of town, and requested copies of the file, in particular the prosecutor’s appeal. Transmission of the documents proved impossible because the lawyer’s fax machine lacked a receiving function. The court offered file inspection at 8 a.m. the next day; the lawyer declined.

On 13 May 2009 the Regional Court refused the adjournment, holding that the lawyer had waived the statutory one-week summons period by learning of the date the previous day and that the applicant, who had been properly summoned by public notification, had failed to appear without excuse. It then dismissed the applicant’s appeal without examining the merits, pursuant to Article 329 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on the ground that neither the applicant nor a duly authorised representative had appeared.

Subsequent applications to restore the status quo ante were rejected. The Regional Court and Court of Appeal considered that the statutory conditions for public notification had been met once the first-instance summons had been served in Germany; there was no duty to attempt service at the applicant’s Spanish address or to notify him there of the public display. The lawyer had not been expressly authorised to receive summonses, and no affidavit had been supplied to substantiate the claim that the applicant had been advised he need not attend. An appeal on points of law and a constitutional complaint were likewise unsuccessful.

The Government later offered a unilateral declaration acknowledging violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) and (c) together with compensation. The applicant rejected the offer, insisting that only a judgment of the Court finding a violation would enable reopening of the domestic proceedings under Article 359 no. 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a point on which no domestic case-law existed.

These facts centred on the last-minute restoration of counsel, the absence of any genuine opportunity to obtain the file or prepare, the refusal of an adjournment, and the summary dismissal of the appeal without a hearing on the merits.

The case of Dridi v. Germany (no. 35778/11) concerns alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1, 3(b) and 3(c) ECHR arising from the dismissal of the applicant’s criminal appeal without a merits hearing.

On 2 March 2009 the Hamburg District Court convicted the applicant of assault and imposed a sentence of 40 day-fines. At his request it had authorised Mr Arif (then a law student) to act as defence counsel. Both the applicant and the prosecutor appealed (the latter only against sentence). The applicant thereafter moved to Spain, notifying the court of his new address.

On 24 April 2009 the Regional Court withdrew Mr Arif’s authorisation, refused to dispense the applicant from personal appearance, and served that decision on him in Spain. The same day it listed the appeal hearing for 13 May 2009 at 09:10 and, because the applicant had left Germany, ordered service of the summons by public notification. The summons was displayed on the court notice-board from 27 April to 12 May 2009.

On 12 May 2009 Mr Arif learned (by telephone) that the Court of Appeal had that day reinstated his authorisation and that the hearing was the following morning. He immediately faxed an adjournment request, citing his absence from town, and asked for the case file (in particular the prosecutor’s appeal). The court attempted to fax the documents but the lawyer’s machine could not receive; an offer of file inspection at 08:00 the next day was declined.

On 13 May 2009 the Regional Court refused the adjournment, holding that the lawyer had waived his right to timely summons by already knowing the date and that the (properly summoned) applicant had failed to appear without excuse. It then dismissed the appeal without examining the merits under Article 329 CCP, because neither the applicant nor a permitted representative had appeared.

The applicant’s subsequent application for restoration of the status quo ante was refused by the Regional Court (10 March 2010) and the Court of Appeal (15 April 2010). Both courts held that the statutory conditions for public notification had been met, that the applicant bore responsibility for remaining reachable in Germany, that no prior attempt at service abroad was required, that the lawyer had not been authorised to receive summonses, and that no adequate proof of absence through no fault of his own had been supplied.

The Court of Appeal later rejected an appeal on points of law (16 July 2010) and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint (16 November 2010).

The applicant complained that the combination of public notification, last-minute notice to counsel, refusal of an adjournment and automatic dismissal of the appeal deprived him of a fair hearing, of adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence, and of effective legal assistance. After communication of the case the Government offered a unilateral declaration acknowledging the Article 6 violations and proposing compensation; the applicant rejected it, insisting that only a Court judgment finding a violation would permit reopening of the domestic proceedings.

The case of Dridi v. Germany (App. no. 35778/11) concerns alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b)–(c) ECHR (fair trial, including adequate time/facilities to prepare a defence and the right to legal assistance) arising from the manner in which an appeal against a criminal conviction was handled in the applicant’s absence.

On 2 March 2009 the Hamburg District Court convicted the applicant of assault and imposed a sentence of 40 day-fines of EUR 25 each (payable in instalments). At his request it authorised Mr Arif (then a law student) as defence counsel under CCP Art. 138 § 2. Both parties appealed; the prosecutor challenged only the sentence. The applicant then moved to Spain for work and notified the court of his new address.

On 24 April 2009 the Hamburg Regional Court withdrew Arif’s authorisation and refused to dispense the applicant from personal appearance. The same day it listed the appeal hearing for 13 May 2009 at 09:10 and ordered service of the summons by public notification (displayed on the court noticeboard 27 April–12 May 2009) because the applicant had left Germany.

On 12 May 2009 Arif learned by telephone that the Court of Appeal had reinstated his authorisation and that the hearing would take place the following morning. He immediately applied by fax for an adjournment (he would be out of town) and requested the case file, in particular the prosecutor’s appeal. Copies could not be faxed (his machine had no receive function); he was offered inspection at 08:00 the next day, which he declined.

On 13 May the Regional Court refused the adjournment, holding that Arif had waived the statutory summons period by knowing the date and that the applicant (deemed duly summoned) had failed to appear without excuse. It therefore dismissed the applicant’s appeal without examining the merits, pursuant to CCP Art. 329.

Subsequent applications to restore the status quo ante were rejected (Regional Court 10 March 2010; Court of Appeal 15 April 2010). The courts held that public notification was lawful under CCP Art. 40 §§ 2–3 because the first-instance summons had been served at the applicant’s last German address and he had himself appealed; there was no duty to attempt service (or even notification) at the known Spanish address. The applicant had not proved, by affidavit or otherwise, that he was prevented from attending through no fault of his own. Further remedies (appeal on points of law and constitutional complaint) failed.

After communication of the application the Government offered a unilateral declaration acknowledging violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and/or 3(c) and of Article 6 § 3(b)–(c) together with compensation, and requested strike-out. The applicant refused: he sought a finding of violation that would permit reopening under CCP Art. 359 no. 6 (domestic courts having construed that provision narrowly and having no settled case-law on unilateral declarations). The Government confirmed that the question remained open.

The facts therefore centre on (i) public notification of the appeal summons despite a known foreign address, (ii) the resulting extremely short notice to newly re-authorised counsel, (iii) refusal of an adjournment, and (iv) dismissal of the appeal without a hearing on the merits, followed by unsuccessful attempts to obtain restoration of the proceedings.
001-184654:
The case concerns two sets of criminal defamation proceedings against Jani Makraduli, then vice-president of the opposition SDSM party and a member of parliament. Both were initiated by private prosecution from S.M., a senior figure in the ruling party who simultaneously headed the Security and Counter Intelligence Agency (accountable to the Government). The convictions, which the applicant alleged violated Article 10 of the Convention, arose from remarks he made at SDSM press conferences that were broadcast on television.

In the first matter (application no. 64659/11), on 14 December 2007 the applicant asked at a nationally televised press conference whether S.M. had abused his position (described as de facto head of the police) to obtain inside information via police wiretapping equipment for personal profit on the Stock Exchange. The broadcast also referenced S.M.’s asset declaration showing shares worth EUR 300,000 and noted SDSM queries about whether this wealth had been acquired while in office. S.M. denied the claims, attributing the funds to a lawful foreign business. S.M. sued under Article 172 of the Criminal Code (dissemination of false allegations harmful to reputation). The applicant, represented by counsel, did not attend any of the 12 scheduled hearings (some adjourned due to parliamentary duties) and submitted no evidence. The trial court (single judge) convicted him in November 2009, imposing a EUR 1,500 fine (75 days’ imprisonment in default), costs, and an order to publish the judgment. It held that the remarks, though phrased as questions, amounted to unproven factual assertions capable of damaging S.M.’s reputation; the accused bore the burden of proving truth or reasonable grounds for belief, which he had not discharged. Political status conferred no licence to make unfounded allegations. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision. The Constitutional Court dismissed a subsequent appeal in February 2011, finding the statements an abuse of freedom of expression that targeted a public official’s dignity without any attempt to verify them. (A later civil claim by S.M. resulted in an award of non-pecuniary damages against the applicant.)

In the second matter (application no. 24133/13), on 9 September 2007 the applicant alleged at another press conference that State-owned land in central Skopje earmarked for a hotel had been awarded, after a “megascandal,” to a company linked to O. Holding (sharing an address and personnel) and ultimately to persons with “close family or party ties” to the Prime Minister. He asked whether an “Academy Award for the most corrupt politician” should go to the Prime Minister or his cousins. Although S.M. was not named, the trial court later found the remarks referred to him because the applicant had previously called S.M. the Prime Minister’s cousin and a news presenter identified him by surname. S.M. denied any involvement in the sale. The applicant again failed to attend any of 17 hearings and submitted no evidence (including material he had sent to the public prosecutor requesting an investigation). In February 2011 the trial court convicted him of defamation, imposing a EUR 1,000 fine (100 days’ imprisonment in default) plus costs. It treated the remarks as untrue factual assertions harmful to a public official’s reputation; S.M., as Agency head, had no competence over land sales and no proof of private involvement had been offered. The Court of Appeal confirmed the conviction, reiterating that the statutory presumption of falsity placed the burden of proof on the accused. The Constitutional Court dismissed an appeal in September 2012, acknowledging the public-interest context of a political debate but holding that the unverified statements nevertheless unjustifiably interfered with S.M.’s reputation.

Both fines were later stayed after legislative repeal of the relevant Criminal Code provisions (November 2012), which converted defamation into a purely civil matter. The applicant paid costs in both cases. A related earlier conviction (May 2008) for similar remarks accusing the Transport Minister of abuse of office in the same land sale was not itself before the Court. The proceedings thus turned on the characterisation of the applicant’s politically motivated, interrogative remarks as unprotected false assertions rather than contributions to public debate about a high official’s conduct.

The case of Makraduli v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (applications nos. 64659/11 and 24133/13) concerns Jani Makraduli, vice-president of the SDSM opposition party and a member of parliament. He alleged that two criminal convictions for defamation of Mr S.M.—a senior ruling-party member and head of the Security and Counter Intelligence Agency—violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The statements were made at SDSM press conferences.

In the first matter, on 14 December 2007 the applicant asked publicly (broadcast nationally) whether S.M. had abused his position to obtain timely Stock Exchange information via police wiretapping equipment, citing rumours and S.M.’s asset declaration of shares worth EUR 300,000. S.M. brought a private libel prosecution under Article 172 of the Criminal Code. The applicant did not attend the twelve scheduled hearings. On 3 November 2009 the Skopje Court of First Instance convicted him, holding that the remarks were false factual assertions (despite interrogatory form) that damaged S.M.’s reputation and that the applicant had failed to prove their truth, as required. He was fined EUR 1,500 (75 days’ imprisonment in default), ordered to pay costs and to publish the judgment. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 11 May 2010. The Constitutional Court dismissed a further appeal on 23 February 2011, finding an abuse of expression that harmed the official’s dignity. Civil proceedings later resulted in an order that the applicant pay 550,000 MKD plus costs for non-pecuniary damage.

In the second matter, on 9 September 2007 the applicant alleged that State-owned land had been sold to a company linked to O. Holding and to persons with family or party ties to the Prime Minister, asking whether the “Academy Award for the most corrupt politician” should go to the Prime Minister or his cousins. S.M. claimed the remarks referred to him (he was frequently called the Prime Minister’s cousin) and denied any involvement. After seventeen hearings (again unattended by the applicant and without defence evidence), the trial court convicted him on 23 February 2011. It found the statement identified S.M. and contained an unsubstantiated false assertion capable of harming his reputation. He was fined EUR 1,000 (100 days’ imprisonment in default) plus costs. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 18 May 2011. The Constitutional Court rejected a constitutional complaint on 12 September 2012, stressing the absence of proof of truth despite the public-interest context.

At the material time, Article 172 criminalised dissemination of false allegations (punishable by fine or imprisonment); the accused bore the burden of proving truth or reasonable grounds. Article 176 offered a limited defence for political activity if intent was lacking. Criminal defamation provisions were repealed in November 2012 and the fines were stayed. The applicant had earlier been convicted (2008) of defaming the Transport Minister over the same land sale. These facts—opposition political speech on possible official misconduct, criminal sanctions, and a reverse burden of proof—form the core of the alleged Article 10 violation.

The case of *Makraduli v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (apps. 64659/11 and 24133/13) involved Jani Makraduli, then SDSM opposition vice-president and MP, who alleged that two criminal defamation convictions violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The private prosecutions were brought by S.M., a ruling-party official and head of the Security and Counter-Intelligence Agency (accountable to the government).

On 14 December 2007, at an SDSM press conference broadcast nationally on A1 TV, the applicant asked whether S.M. had abused his powers (and police wiretaps) to profit from stock-exchange trading, citing rumours and S.M.’s asset declaration listing EUR 300,000 in shares. S.M. denied this, attributing the funds to lawful foreign business. S.M. sued under Criminal Code Art. 172 (disseminating false allegations damaging reputation). The applicant, represented but absent from hearings, submitted no evidence. On 3 November 2009 the Skopje first-instance court convicted him, holding the remarks were false factual assertions (not mere questions) that an ordinary viewer would take as true. It rejected defences based on political role, interrogatory form or Art. 176 (no liability for political speech lacking defamatory intent). He was fined EUR 1,500 (75 days’ default imprisonment), ordered to pay costs and to publish the judgment. The Court of Appeal upheld the ruling on 11 May 2010. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal (23 February 2011), finding an abuse of expression that harmed S.M.’s dignity. The fine was later stayed after 2012 decriminalisation. In subsequent civil proceedings the applicant was ordered to pay MKD 550,000 plus costs for non-pecuniary damage.

On 9 September 2007, at another SDSM press conference (broadcast locally), the applicant criticised a public sale of central Skopje land for a hotel. He alleged the winning company was linked to O. Holding and that the deal favoured persons with “close family or party ties” to the Prime Minister, asking whether the PM or “his cousins” deserved an “Academy Award for the most corrupt politician.” S.M. (widely identified as the PM’s cousin) sued, denying any involvement. Again the applicant did not attend or adduce evidence (including material sent to the prosecutor). On 23 February 2011 the trial court convicted him, ruling that the unnamed reference was clearly to S.M. and contained unsubstantiated, reputation-damaging assertions. He was fined EUR 1,000 (100 days’ default) plus costs. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 18 May 2011. The Constitutional Court rejected his complaint (12 September 2012), stressing that even political speech on matters of public interest required proof of veracity, which was absent. The fine was stayed; no civil claim followed.

Domestic law placed the burden of proving truth or reasonable grounds on the accused; the political-activity exception was not applied. Defamation was later moved to civil law.

**Prunea v. Romania (ECtHR, App. no. 47881/11, 8 Jan. 2019)** concerns an alleged Article 10 ECHR violation of freedom of expression arising from civil defamation liability imposed on a journalist-academic for an election-period article criticizing a parliamentary candidate.

Petru Prunea (b. 1945), a Cluj-Napoca university professor and frequent contributor to economic/financial publications (over 180 articles), published a front-page piece in newspaper *F.* on 6 November 2008, shortly before November 2008 parliamentary elections. Headlined “Attention! He also wants [to be] in Parliament,” it discussed public disillusionment with politicians (low confidence in Parliament; candidates seeking privileges, informal benefits, or shielding of criminal records) and targeted M.I.-I., a Democratic Party of Cluj candidate and former public-company manager. It alleged M.I.-I. had borrowed 15 billion lei (12-month term ending 31 Oct. 2008) to invest on the stock market, failed to generate hoped-for profits, then refused repayment despite contractual obligation, pleaded for mercy/postponement, and sued in a court lacking jurisdiction while hoping to invoke future parliamentary immunity (likened to a prior politician who allegedly cost Romania its maritime fleet). It portrayed him as an “impostor” whose “moral profile” showed he would accept any compromise for money, switch parties, sell his electoral district, or even relocate to Tiraspol; voters should therefore scrutinize his promises. A similar article appeared on 21 January 2009; leaflets reproducing the November piece were distributed in public places, bus stations, and mailboxes.

On 9 April 2009 M.I.-I. sued Prunea in civil proceedings for €25,000 non-pecuniary damage, claiming the materials (especially the November article) seriously harmed his reputation and caused him to lose the election by ~100 votes. Prunea admitted authorship, maintained the statements were true (supported by Cluj Chamber of Commerce Arbitration Tribunal documents from a commercial dispute with his brokerage firm), and denied involvement with the later article or leaflets.

On 20 July 2009 the Cluj-Napoca Court of First Instance found the November article defamatory. Prunea had not proved the statements’ truth; the arbitration (partially granting M.I.-I.’s claims, with repayment due 30 April 2010) concerned a private commercial matter unsuitable for media publication. Even if true, the statements should not have been aired. A causal link existed to the leaflets (which amplified harm), as the original article enabled them. Language calling M.I.-I. an impostor (absent any fraud complaints) and implying betrayal of electorate/party/country for money exceeded admissible criticism and disparaged him. Liability of €20,000 plus RON 3,291 costs was imposed.

Prunea appealed, arguing the article served a public-interest role of informing voters about a prospective MP in good faith during an election campaign (where criticism limits are wider) and that damages were disproportionate/punitive.

On 21 January 2010 the Cluj County Court (final) upheld the core finding. Prunea had failed to exercise the “highest rigour and special caution” required by the seriousness of the allegations; he had not complied with Article 10 § 2 duties of good faith and journalistic ethics to ensure trustworthy information (even allowing for exaggeration). Unilateral press exposure of private commercial litigation between two parties could not be justified, despite the electoral context and public-interest element of criticizing a potential MP; reputation, rights of others, and the presumption of innocence imposed limits. Damages were reduced to €5,000 as more proportionate.

These facts—publication of unverified/private-commercial allegations of untrustworthiness against an election candidate, domestic courts’ rejection of public-interest/good-faith justification, and imposition of (reduced) damages—underpin the Article 10 complaint that the interference was not necessary in a democratic society.

In Prunea v. Romania (App. no. 47881/11), a university professor and prolific journalist (over 180 published articles) alleged that Romanian courts had violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression by holding him liable for an article criticising a parliamentary candidate.

Shortly before the November 2008 elections, the applicant published a front-page piece in newspaper F. headlined “Attention! He also wants [to be] in Parliament”. It argued that many candidates sought office for personal privileges or to obtain immunity from past misconduct. Focusing on candidate M.I.-I., it stated that he had borrowed 15 billion lei to invest on the stock market but then refused to repay, imploring the creditor for mercy and hoping to invoke parliamentary immunity if elected. The piece labelled him an “impostor” whose “moral profile” had been revealed, suggested he would switch parties or even sell his electoral district for gain, and urged voters to be wary of his promises.

M.I.-I. sued in April 2009 for EUR 25,000 in non-pecuniary damages, claiming the article (plus a later similar piece and election leaflets reproducing its content) had damaged his reputation and cost him the election by roughly 100 votes. The applicant admitted authorship of the November article but maintained that its contents were true, citing pending commercial arbitration between M.I.-I. and the applicant’s own brokerage firm; he denied involvement with the leaflets or the later article.

On 20 July 2009 the Cluj-Napoca Court of First Instance found the article defamatory. It held that the applicant had not proved the statements true (the arbitration had only partially succeeded for M.I.-I. and set a later repayment date). Even if true, a private commercial dispute should not have been publicised. A causal link existed with the leaflets, which amplified reputational harm. The language—especially calling M.I.-I. an impostor and implying he would betray voters, party and country for money—exceeded acceptable criticism and lacked factual basis (no fraud complaints existed). The court awarded EUR 20,000 plus costs.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the piece served a public-interest purpose during an election campaign, that criticism of political candidates enjoys wider latitude, and that the damages were punitive and disproportionate. In a final judgment of 21 January 2010 the Cluj County Court essentially confirmed the first-instance reasoning. It stressed that the gravity of the allegations required the highest journalistic caution; exposing private commercial litigation in the press could not justify insult or defamation even in an electoral context. The applicant had failed to act in good faith or to ensure the information was trustworthy, thereby exceeding Article 10 § 2 limits. The court nevertheless reduced damages to EUR 5,000 as more proportionate.

These findings formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic courts had failed to strike a proper balance between reputation and political speech of public interest.

The case of Prunea v. Romania (Application no. 47881/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, Petru Prunea (born 1945), a university professor and journalist from Cluj-Napoca who had published over 180 articles, wrote a piece published on 6 November 2008 on the front page of newspaper F. titled “Attention! He also wants [to be] in Parliament.” This occurred just before Romania’s parliamentary elections.

The article broadly criticized political candidates as often lacking merit and seeking office for personal privileges or to evade past wrongdoing. It specifically targeted M.I.-I., a Democratic Party candidate and former manager at a public company. It stated that M.I.-I. had borrowed 15 billion Romanian lei (until 31 October 2008) to invest on the stock market but, after insufficient profits, refused to repay despite a valid contract, instead seeking delays and hoping to invoke future parliamentary immunity. The piece called him an “impostor,” warned he might deny statements, switch parties for gain, sell his electoral district, or flee, and urged caution about his promises.

On 9 April 2009, M.I.-I. sued the applicant civilly for 25,000 euros in non-pecuniary damages, claiming the article (plus a similar January 2009 piece and distributed leaflets reproducing the original) damaged his reputation and caused him to lose the election by about 100 votes.

The applicant admitted writing the article, asserting its truth based on documents from a Cluj Chamber of Commerce Arbitration Tribunal commercial dispute (where M.I.-I.’s claims were later partially granted with a 2010 repayment deadline). He denied involvement with other materials.

On 20 July 2009, the Cluj-Napoca Court of First Instance found the article defamatory. It held the applicant had not proven his statements true; even if accurate, they concerned private commercial matters unsuitable for public media. A causal link existed to the leaflets’ harm. Terms like “impostor” (absent any fraud complaints) and implications of betrayal for money were insulting and exceeded admissible criticism. It awarded 20,000 euros plus costs.

The applicant appealed, arguing the piece served public interest by informing voters about a candidate during elections (where criticism limits are wider) and that damages were punitive/disproportionate.

On 21 January 2010, the Cluj County Court largely upheld the lower court. It found the applicant had not shown the required journalistic caution, good faith, or ethics; his serious allegations demanded rigor. Insulting someone over private litigation could not be justified, even regarding a potential parliamentarian of public interest. Limits under Article 10 § 2 protected reputation and the presumption of innocence. Damages were reduced to 5,000 euros as more proportionate.

These rulings, holding the applicant liable for the article, formed the core of his Article 10 complaint to the Court.

The applicants, Dirk and Petra Wunderlich, are German parents of four children born between 1999 and 2005. They reject compulsory state schooling and seek to homeschool their children. From 2005, when their eldest reached school age, they refused to register her (and later the others) at any school, incurring administrative fines and criminal proceedings, which they paid without altering their conduct. After living abroad from 2008 to 2011, they returned to Germany but still declined to enrol the children.

In July 2012 the State Education Authority notified the family court of the applicants’ persistent non-compliance, listing prior sanctions (including an investigation into the father striking a daughter) and asserting that the children inhabited a “parallel world” isolated from peers and communal life. The youth office endorsed the request for measures under Article 1666 of the Civil Code, citing endangerment of the children’s best interests.

On 6 September 2012 the Darmstadt Family Court, after hearing the parents, children and a guardian ad litem, withdrew the applicants’ rights to determine the children’s residence, decide school matters and represent them vis-à-vis authorities, transferring those rights to the youth office. It ordered handover of the children and authorised the use of force. The court held that the refusal constituted an abuse of parental authority that risked long-term harm by denying the children socialisation, tolerance and the ability to assert their views against majority opinion; five hours of concurrent homeschooling (including lunch) for four children of different ages was inadequate, and no milder measure would suffice given the parents’ stated determination to continue homeschooling.

The Frankfurt Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 25 April 2013 (while restoring the residence right during school holidays). It confirmed a concrete danger arising from a “symbiotic” family system that isolated the children, taught them that community rules could be ignored, and failed to provide age-appropriate education or extracurricular activities. Subsequent attempts by the youth office to conduct learning assessments in late 2012 and early 2013 were blocked by the parents and children.

On 29 August 2013, after a meeting in which the applicants reiterated their principled refusal and the father described children as parental “property,” police officers forcibly removed the four children from the family home, carrying them out individually when they would not leave voluntarily. The children were placed in a children’s home. Two ninety-minute knowledge assessments followed in mid-September. After the applicants declared their willingness to send the children to school, the children were returned on 19 September 2013, having spent three weeks in care. They attended school for the remainder of the 2013–14 year before being withdrawn again in June 2014, prompting a fresh criminal complaint.

In parallel proceedings the Court of Appeal restored the residence right on 15 August 2014, finding that earlier risk factors (possible physical harm, total isolation, resistance to assessment) had receded and that permanent removal would now be disproportionate, although homeschooling remained unlawful. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the applicants’ constitutional complaint in October 2014.

These facts constitute the interference complained of under Article 8: the judicial withdrawal of core parental rights and the subsequent forcible removal and three-week placement of the children in public care.

The applicants, German nationals Dirk and Petra Wunderlich, are the parents of four children born between 1999 and 2005. They reject Germany’s compulsory State schooling system and seek to homeschool their children. From 2005, when their eldest child reached school age, they refused to register her (and later the others) at any school. This led to multiple administrative fines and criminal proceedings for non-compliance with compulsory attendance rules, including one investigation involving alleged physical punishment of a daughter. The applicants paid the fines but persisted in their refusal. After living abroad from 2008 to 2011, they returned to Germany and again declined to enroll the children in school.

In July 2012 the State Education Authority notified the competent family court of the applicants’ deliberate and ongoing non-compliance, listing the sanctions and describing the children as growing up in a “parallel world” isolated from peers and community life. The youth office supported the request for measures under Article 1666 of the Civil Code on the ground that the children’s best interests were endangered. The Darmstadt Family Court heard the applicants, the children, the youth office and a guardian ad litem. The applicants confirmed they would continue homeschooling and stated that the authorities would have to remove the children entirely if they were ever to attend a State school. The children described a daily routine of maternal instruction from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. including a lunch break.

On 6 September 2012 the Family Court withdrew the applicants’ rights to determine the children’s residence, to decide school matters and to act on the children’s behalf before the authorities, transferring those rights to the youth office. It ordered the children to be handed over so that compulsory attendance could be enforced and authorised the use of force if necessary. The court held that persistent refusal constituted an abuse of parental authority that risked long-term harm: even if academic knowledge were adequate, the children were being denied socialisation, tolerance and the ability to assert themselves outside the family. No milder measures would suffice given the parents’ intransigence.

The applicants appealed. Attempts by the youth office to conduct a learning assessment failed because the children and parents refused cooperation. On 25 April 2013 the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal (while restoring residence rights during school holidays). It found a concrete danger arising from a “symbiotic” family system, an educational programme of only five concurrent hours that could not meet age-appropriate standards, the absence of any extra-curricular activities, and the lesson that community rules need not be obeyed. Less intrusive orders had already proved ineffective.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear a constitutional complaint. Meanwhile, after a further meeting in which the applicants restated their principled refusal and the father described children as parental “property,” the children were forcibly removed from the family home on 29 August 2013 by police officers who carried them out individually after they refused to leave voluntarily. They were placed in a children’s home. Two short learning assessments were conducted in mid-September. Once the applicants agreed (in other proceedings) that the children would attend school, the children were returned on 19 September 2013 after a hearing. They attended school for the 2013-14 year but were withdrawn again in June 2014. In August 2014 the Court of Appeal restored the applicants’ residence rights, noting that the earlier risks (possible physical harm, total isolation, resistance to assessment) had receded and that permanent removal would now be disproportionate, while emphasising that homeschooling remained unlawful.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the partial withdrawal of parental authority and the three-week forcible removal and placement of the children violated Article 8 of the Convention.

**Case of Wunderlich v. Germany (Application no. 18925/15), ECtHR Fifth Section judgment of 10 January 2019 (final 24 June 2019)**

Dirk and Petra Wunderlich, a married German couple, are the parents of four children born between 1999 and 2005. They reject the state school system and compulsory attendance, preferring to homeschool. From 2005, when their eldest reached school age, they refused registration, incurring administrative fines and criminal proceedings (including one involving alleged hitting of a daughter). They paid fines but persisted. After living abroad from 2008 to 2011, they returned to Germany without registering the children.

In July 2012 the Hesse State Education Authority notified the family court of the parents’ persistent refusal, listing prior sanctions and incidents. It argued the children lived in a “parallel world” without peer contact or participation in communal life, endangering their best interests under Article 1666 of the German Civil Code. The youth office supported the request.

After hearings involving the parents, children, youth office and a guardian ad litem, the Darmstadt Family Court on 6 September 2012 withdrew the parents’ rights to determine the children’s residence, decide school matters and apply to authorities on their behalf, transferring these to the youth office. It ordered handover of the children to enforce school attendance and authorised force if needed. The court found the refusal an abuse of parental authority risking long-term harm: even if homeschooling imparted knowledge, it prevented acquisition of social skills (tolerance, assertiveness) and integration into society. No milder measures sufficed given the parents’ explicit stance that children would attend state school only if forcibly removed.

The parents appealed. Attempts by the youth office in November 2012–January 2013 to assess the children’s knowledge failed due to resistance; the father asserted sole authority over schooling. On 25 April 2013 the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal (clarifying holiday residence rights remained with the parents). It held that persistent non-attendance created a concrete danger: a “symbiotic” family system denied recognised educational standards essential for societal life. Concurrent five-hour homeschooling of all four children (including lunch) was inadequate; the children belonged to no clubs or similar activities. The parents’ conduct taught non-compliance with community rules. Instructions would be ineffective.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the parents’ complaint in October 2014.

On 26 August 2013 the parents reiterated their principled refusal of external schooling; the father described children as parental “property.” On 29 August 2013 police and a bailiff forcibly removed the children (who had to be carried out) and placed them in a children’s home. Knowledge assessments occurred on 12 and 16 September. After the parents agreed to school attendance, the children were returned on 19 September 2013 following a family-court hearing.

The children attended school in 2013–14. The parents later withdrew them again, prompting a criminal complaint. In August 2014, in parallel proceedings, the Court of Appeal restored the residence-determination right to the parents. It noted that circumstances had changed (no remaining physical-integrity risk, non-alarming knowledge levels, children not kept from school against their will). Permanent removal was no longer proportionate, though the decision was not permission to homeschool; criminal proceedings remained possible.

The applicants complained under Article 8 ECHR that withdrawal of parts of parental authority (including residence determination) and the three-week forced placement in public care violated their right to respect for family life. (Other complaints were declared inadmissible.) German law (Basic Law Art. 6, Civil Code Arts. 1666/1666a/1696, Hesse School Act) permits such measures only to avert concrete endangerment of a child’s best interests when milder steps fail, and treats persistent school refusal as potential abuse of parental authority.

The case of Demjanjuk v. Germany (App. no. 24247/15) was lodged with the ECHR by Vera Demjanjuk (widow) and John Demjanjuk (son), both U.S. nationals, concerning the late John Demjanjuk. They alleged that the Munich Regional Court II’s 5 April 2012 decision not to reimburse his necessary expenses after discontinuing criminal proceedings due to his death violated the presumption of innocence (Art. 6 § 2 ECHR). They further claimed that the Munich Court of Appeal’s 4 October 2012 dismissal of their appeals as inadmissible for lack of standing violated their right of access to a court (Art. 6 § 1).

On 12 May 2011, after a 91-day trial, the Munich Regional Court II convicted Demjanjuk on 16 counts of accessory to the murder of at least 28,060 people. It found he had, as a Sobibór extermination camp guard, aided the systematic killing of deportees in 16 convoys from 27 March to September 1943. He received a five-year sentence; the 220-page judgment followed a thorough evidentiary and legal review. Both Demjanjuk and the prosecutor appealed on points of law. Defence counsel filed grounds in November 2011 plus four further briefs (last received 12 January 2012). On 24 February 2012 the prosecutor directed transfer of the file (plus responses) to the Federal Court of Justice.

Demjanjuk died on 17 March 2012, before the Federal Court received the file. On 5 April 2012 the Regional Court discontinued the proceedings under Art. 206a § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure owing to his death. Relying on Art. 467 § 3 (second sentence, no. 2), it refused to charge his necessary expenses to the treasury. It reasoned that, although the conviction was not yet final, a comprehensive trial had established guilt; the procedural impediment arose only after judgment. Trial length (nearly 18 months) was largely attributable to the defence’s strategy: excessive, repetitive statements under Art. 257 § 2; some 500 evidence applications (many targeting already-taken or unobtainable evidence, such as deceased witnesses); and over 20 bias complaints against each professional judge, often reiterating rejected arguments. A targeted defence approach could have produced a final verdict during Demjanjuk’s lifetime. Reimbursement was therefore inequitable despite the absence of a conclusive guilt finding.

Counsel immediately appealed, later lodging powers of attorney from the applicants. On 4 October 2012 the Munich Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as inadmissible for lack of standing: accused status is personal and non-transferable (including by inheritance) and ceased on death. It added that the appeal was ill-founded; Art. 6 § 2 was not breached because the decision contained no finding of guilt (explicitly so stating). Given the trial court’s establishment of guilt, a continuing state of suspicion justified applying Art. 467 § 3. A subsequent complaint to be heard was dismissed as ill-founded on 15 November 2012. On 18 December 2014 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicants’ constitutional complaint without reasons.

Under German law, an accused’s death is a procedural impediment requiring discontinuation (with a costs ruling) under Art. 206a. Art. 467 § 1 normally requires the treasury to bear costs and expenses upon discontinuation, but the court may refuse reimbursement of the accused’s necessary expenses where conviction failed solely because of an impediment, provided there is at least a significant state of suspicion and additional equitable factors (e.g., the impediment arising after trial opening). The court must exercise discretion and word the decision so as to assess suspicion rather than allocate guilt. Once the appeal court is seized of the file, the appeal’s prospects become relevant to the equities of reimbursement.

**Summary of CASE OF DEMJANJUK v. GERMANY (Application no. 24247/15)**

John Demjanjuk, a former Sobibór camp guard, was convicted on 12 May 2011 by Munich Regional Court II after a 91-day trial on 16 counts of accessory to murder of at least 28,060 people deported in 16 convoys between March and September 1943. He received a five-year sentence. Both he and the prosecutor appealed on points of law. Defence counsel filed grounds in November 2011 plus four further briefs (last received 12 January 2012). On 24 February 2012 the prosecutor directed transfer of the file to the Federal Court of Justice. Demjanjuk died on 17 March 2012 before the file arrived.

On 5 April 2012 the Regional Court discontinued the proceedings under Article 206a § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because of the accused’s death. Relying on Article 467 § 3, second sentence, number 2, it refused to order the treasury to reimburse his necessary expenses. It reasoned that the conviction followed a thorough examination of facts and law after a long trial whose duration was significantly attributable to the defence’s strategy: excessive use of the right to make statements (often repeating arguments), around 500 evidence applications (many targeting already-taken or impossible evidence, including deceased witnesses), and more than twenty bias complaints against each professional judge (again often repetitive). The trial could have concluded with a final verdict during the accused’s lifetime had the defence exercised rights in a targeted manner. Even without a conclusive finding of guilt it was therefore inequitable to reimburse expenses.

Counsel immediately appealed, arguing that the refusal and its reasoning breached the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. Powers of attorney from Demjanjuk’s widow and son (the applicants) were later filed. On 4 October 2012 the Munich Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as inadmissible for lack of standing: the status of accused is personal and non-transferable, including by inheritance, and had ended with death. It added that the appeal was also ill-founded. Article 6 § 2 had not been violated; the decision contained no finding of guilt (as it itself stated). Referring to Nölkenbockhoff v. Germany, it held that the trial court’s establishment of guilt permitted a finding of continued suspicion, justifying application of Article 467 § 3. A subsequent complaint was dismissed as ill-founded. On 18 December 2014 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicants’ constitutional complaint without reasons.

Under German law, death is a procedural impediment requiring discontinuation under Article 206a, with a ruling on costs. Article 467 § 1 generally charges the treasury with costs and necessary expenses upon discontinuation, but the court may refuse reimbursement of the accused’s expenses where conviction failed only because of an impediment, provided there is at least a significant state of suspicion and additional equitable factors (such as the impediment arising after the trial opened). Discretion must be exercised properly. Once the appellate court is seized, the appeal’s prospects become relevant. The wording of any refusal must make clear that it describes a state of suspicion rather than allocating guilt.

The applicants alleged that the refusal to reimburse expenses, and its reasoning, violated the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2), and that dismissal of the appeal for lack of standing violated their right of access to a court (Article 6 § 1). The Court communicated those two complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

001-188997:
The case of Berardi and Mularoni v. San Marino (applications nos. 24705/16 and 24818/16) involves two San Marino nationals, Paolo Berardi (born 1963) and Davide Mularoni (born 1965), who served as public officials responsible for supervising construction-site safety. They alleged a violation of Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights, claiming that criminal law had been applied retroactively to their disadvantage. Specifically, they were convicted of bribery under a provision whose wording was not in force at the time of some of the relevant facts.

In 2011, San Marino’s parliament established a commission to investigate organised crime, including possible collusion between politicians and a fiduciary company (F.) linked to B., a notary. The commission’s report identified a pattern in which representatives of certain construction companies bribed safety officials to skip compulsory inspections on sites connected to F.

On 12 December 2012 the applicants were charged with the continuing offence of bribery (Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the Criminal Code). They were accused of regularly accepting cash payments in exchange for omitting safety inspections and sanctions at construction sites of companies de facto controlled by B. The charges covered events up to 1 January 2010.

On 19 September 2014 the first-instance court convicted them of “direct bribery” under Article 373 § 1. The judge found that they had exercised discretionary powers contrary to their official duties. They were sentenced to five years and six months’ imprisonment, a four-year ban on holding public office or exercising political rights, and a fine of €25,000. Evidence included matching bank deposits during a construction boom, witness statements, and testimony that the applicants made brief visits to the office of one of B.’s formal administrators.

The applicants appealed on 13 February 2015. They argued that, before Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008 entered into force, “bribery inducing omission” (payment to omit or delay a legitimate official act) was not criminalised, or at most constituted the lighter offence of “indirect bribery” under the old Article 373 § 2. They claimed they had been convicted of conduct that either was not an offence or carried a lighter penalty at the time it occurred.

On 12 January 2016 the Criminal Appeals Judge upheld the convictions but reduced the sentences to five years’ imprisonment, a four-and-a-half-year ban, and a €20,000 fine. The court characterised the conduct as a single continuing offence arising from an initial “corrupt pact” that was renewed with each payment. Because all elements of the offence persisted throughout the period, an intervening legislative change applied to the entire course of conduct. The court further held that the applicants had not merely omitted inspections; they had also performed acts contrary to their duties by systematically favouring B.’s companies (incomplete checks, ignored irregularities). Consequently the facts already fell within the old Article 373 § 1. The 2008 amendment merely made explicit, and reclassified more severely, conduct that was already criminal; it did not create a new offence.

Relevant domestic provisions included Article 15 of San Marino’s Charter of Fundamental Rights (non-retroactivity except for more favourable laws) and Article 3 of the Criminal Code (same principle). The pre-2008 Article 373 punished receipt of an undue advantage for performing an act contrary to official duties (heavier penalty) or an act falling within official functions (one degree lighter). The 2008 amendment (effective three months after publication) expanded the heavier paragraph to cover explicitly the omission or delay of official duties as well as the performance of contrary acts. Domestic literature suggested that omissions had already been covered by the old § 1. Case-law treated a continuing offence as a single unit for certain purposes, including the application of intervening law.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ Article 7 complaint: that they were convicted and sentenced under a more severe legal classification (or an expressly broader provision) that did not exist when part of the alleged conduct occurred.

The case of Berardi and Mularoni v. San Marino (applications nos. 24705/16 and 24818/16) concerns two San Marino nationals, Paolo Berardi (born 1963) and Davide Mularoni (born 1965), who served as public officials responsible for supervising construction-site safety. They alleged a violation of Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights, claiming that domestic courts applied a criminal provision retroactively to their detriment by convicting them of bribery under wording that was not in force at the time of the relevant facts.

A 2011 parliamentary commission investigating organised crime identified a pattern of collusion: representatives of construction companies linked to a fiduciary firm (company F., controlled by B., a notary) regularly paid officials such as the applicants to omit mandatory safety inspections and refrain from sanctioning irregularities. On 12 December 2012 the applicants were charged with the continuing offence of bribery (Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the Criminal Code) for periodically accepting cash payments up to 1 January 2010 in exchange for failing to inspect sites of companies de facto controlled by B. and for ignoring violations.

On 19 September 2014 the first-instance judge convicted them of continuing direct bribery (corruzione propria) under Article 373 § 1, sentencing each to five years and six months’ imprisonment, a four-year ban on public office and political rights, and a €25 000 fine. The court found that the applicants had exercised discretionary powers in a manner contrary to their official duties, treating this as an act “contrary to the duties arising from [their] functions.” Evidence included bank deposits correlating with the construction boom and subsequent decline, witness testimony of brief meetings with company administrators, and B.’s role as the de-facto controller who directed the payments.

The applicants appealed, arguing that Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008 (in force three months after publication) had, for the first time, expressly criminalised “bribery inducing omission” (receiving payment to omit or delay an official act). Before that amendment, they contended, such conduct amounted at most to the lesser offence of indirect bribery (Article 373 § 2, carrying a one-degree lighter penalty). They therefore claimed that classifying their pre-2008 conduct as direct bribery constituted an impermissible retroactive application of a more severe law.

On 12 January 2016 the Judge of Criminal Appeals largely upheld the convictions, reducing the sentences to five years’ imprisonment, a four-and-a-half-year ban and a €20 000 fine (and declining to apply an aggravation for a continuing offence because the first-instance court had not quantified it). The appellate court characterised the conduct as a single, prolonged pact (patto corruttivo) of favouritism toward B.’s companies, renewed by each successive payment. Because the offence was continuing, an intervening legislative change applied to the entire period. Alternatively, even under the pre-2008 wording the facts constituted direct bribery: the applicants had not merely omitted inspections but had systematically favoured the companies by performing fewer checks than required or by ignoring irregularities, thereby carrying out acts contrary to their duties.

Relevant domestic provisions include Article 3 of the Criminal Code (non-retroactivity) and Article 15 of the San Marino Charter of Rights (punishments only on the basis of non-retroactive laws, except when more favourable). Article 373 § 1 originally punished receipt of an undue advantage “in order to carry out an act contrary to the duties arising from [the official’s] functions”; the 2008 amendment added the alternatives of omitting or delaying an official act. Domestic literature and earlier case-law treated omission as already covered by the original text of § 1, while regarding § 2 as limited to non-discretionary acts performed within official functions. The appellate court therefore held that the 2008 change merely reclassified conduct that was already criminal, rendering the temporal issue irrelevant.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) examined two joined applications by San Marino nationals Paolo Berardi and Davide Mularoni, officials responsible for construction-site safety supervision. They alleged a violation of Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (no punishment without law), claiming that San Marino courts had retroactively applied a 2008 amendment to the Criminal Code to convict them of a more serious form of bribery for conduct predating the change.

In 2011 a parliamentary commission investigating organised crime identified a pattern of payments from companies linked to notary B. (and his fiduciary company F.) to safety officials, including the applicants, in exchange for omitted or inadequate inspections and non-enforcement of irregularities. On 12 December 2012 the applicants were charged with the continuing offence of bribery under Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the Criminal Code for periodically receiving cash payments up to 1 January 2010 so that they would refrain from inspecting B.-controlled sites and from imposing sanctions.

On 19 September 2014 the first-instance court convicted them of “direct bribery” (corruzione propria) under the then-current Article 373 § 1. It found that they had exercised official discretion in a manner contrary to their duties, sentenced them to five years and six months’ imprisonment plus ancillary penalties, and treated the conduct as a single continuing offence. The applicants appealed, arguing that before Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008 (in force from September 2008) San Marino law contained no offence of “bribery inducing omission.” At most they could have been convicted of the lesser “indirect bribery” under the old Article 373 § 2, which carried a one-degree reduction in penalty. They contended that the post-2008 wording, which expressly criminalised payment to omit or delay official acts as the graver form of bribery, had been applied retroactively to pre-2008 facts.

On 12 January 2016 the Criminal Appeals Judge upheld the conviction (reducing the sentence slightly) and rejected the Article 7 complaint. The court characterised the facts as a single “corrupt pact” (patto corruttivo) lasting from the initial agreement through each successive payment, constituting one continuing offence. It held that the 2008 amendment did not create a new crime but merely reclassified already-criminal conduct more severely. Even under the pre-2008 text the applicants had not merely omitted duties; they had also performed acts contrary to those duties (selective or perfunctory inspections and ignored irregularities) in exchange for money, conduct already covered by the old Article 373 § 1. Consequently the lex mitior principle did not apply and the later, harsher classification could be used for the entire continuing offence.

San Marino’s Constitution and Criminal Code both prohibit retroactive application of harsher criminal law (Article 15 of the 1974 Charter; Article 3 of the Code). Article 55 of the Code, interpreted by domestic courts as also governing the temporal application of substantive criminal provisions, treats a continuing offence as committed on the date of its last act. Pre-2008 legal commentary and later case-law on continuing offences were cited to support the view that the applicants’ conduct remained punishable under the earlier wording.

The ECtHR therefore had to determine whether the domestic courts’ characterisation of the facts as a single continuing offence already criminalised under the old Article 373 § 1, and their consequent application of the post-2008 classification, complied with the Convention’s requirements of foreseeability and non-retroactivity.
