The case concerns the death of the applicant’s son, M.P., while in police custody at Biržai police station and the subsequent investigation. On 11 April 2008 M.P. was arrested on suspicion of burglary and theft of a laptop. A search of his home the next day also uncovered cannabis. On 13 April a court ordered 18 days’ pre-trial detention, citing a risk of flight; M.P. (who had no prior convictions) was present with counsel and confessed only to the drug offence. Because of his clean record he was held alone in cell no. 1. He met his lawyer and an investigator on 14 April, remaining calm and without complaint.

At approximately 08:00 on 15 April 2008 M.P. was found dead, standing with a blanket looped tightly around his neck and attached to the metal bar of the upper bunk. An ambulance arrived within minutes; paramedics observed no vital signs, dilated unreactive pupils, strangulation marks, post-mortem lividity and rigor mortis, concluding he had died one or two hours earlier. No other injuries, handcuff marks or signs of a struggle were noted. A suicide note addressed “To Mother,” written in charcoal from matches, was found in the cell.

An autopsy on 16 April attributed death to mechanical asphyxia from a noose; light facial scratches were unrelated. At the applicant’s request a second autopsy on 18 April confirmed the same cause, noting neck marks consistent with a bed-sheet ligature minutes before death and back bruising attributable to convulsions against the bunk frame; there were no signs of manual strangulation or third-party force. A later 2014 forensic review of the entire file reached identical conclusions, explaining wrist marks as post-mortem binding for burial and ruling out peri-orbital bruising. Handwriting analysis established that M.P. had written the note; video footage showed no one entered the cell between 17:00 on 14 April and discovery of the body; reconstructions demonstrated that hanging in the observed position was physically possible; other detainees heard nothing suspicious.

The applicant, granted victim status, repeatedly challenged the prosecutors’ decisions to discontinue the investigation for lack of a crime. Domestic courts quashed those decisions on six occasions (2009–2013), ordering further steps: additional witness interviews, video-forensic examination (which found no tampering), reconstructions, and supplementary medical reports. An internal police inquiry found no evidence of abuse but identified a disciplinary failure by one guard to maintain constant visual supervision; the officer received a reprimand. Courts consistently held that, because M.P. had shown no suicidal indicators, the officers could not have foreseen or prevented the rapid asphyxia.

On 27 April 2015 the Panevėžys Regional Court finally upheld discontinuation, finding that all reasonable investigative measures had been exhausted and that the evidence—medical, forensic, video and testimonial—uniformly supported suicide with no indication of criminal third-party involvement. The applicant maintained that contradictions remained and that her son had been a victim of police violence.

The case of Vorienė v. Lithuania concerns the death in police custody of the applicant’s son, M.P., and the ensuing investigation. M.P. was arrested on 11 April 2008 on suspicion of burglary involving theft of a laptop. A subsequent search of his home uncovered cannabis. On 13 April a court ordered 18 days’ pre-trial detention, citing a flight risk because he had previously worked in Norway. He confessed to drug possession but initially denied theft; he had no prior convictions and was therefore held alone in cell no. 1 at Biržai police station.

On the morning of 15 April 2008, during a shift change, officers found M.P. dead. He was standing with his feet on the ground, a blanket looped tightly around his neck and attached to a metal bar of the bunk bed. An officer immediately removed him from the noose. An ambulance arrived within minutes; paramedics recorded no pulse or breathing, dilated pupils, strangulation marks, post-mortem lividity and rigor mortis, concluding that death had occurred one to two hours earlier. No other injuries, signs of restraint or handcuffing were observed. A suicide note addressed “To Mother,” written in charcoal from matches, was found in the cell; an empty matchbox was also present.

Autopsies (16 and 18 April 2008) established mechanical asphyxiation from constriction by a noose. Light facial scratches were attributed to acne; back bruising was consistent with convulsions against the bunk-bed frame. Later expert examination confirmed that wrist marks appeared only after death, during preparation of the body for burial. Handwriting analysis established that M.P. had written the note, most probably with burned matches.

The applicant, granted victim status, alleged that her son had been murdered or subjected to police violence. Prosecutors repeatedly discontinued the investigation, concluding suicide on the basis of the note, video recordings showing no unauthorised entry into the cell between 17.00 on 14 April and 08.04 on 15 April, and the absence of third-party injuries. Domestic courts quashed these decisions seven times, citing incomplete inquiries into possible injuries, the bed-sheet/noose, missing matches, video gaps, and contradictions in officers’ statements. Additional steps included reconstructions of the hanging, confrontations, interviews with other detainees (none of whom heard anything suspicious), and forensic examinations of videos (which showed no tampering) and of the death mechanism (which confirmed that self-strangulation in the observed position was possible). An internal police inquiry found that one guard had failed to maintain constant visual supervision and had given false testimony; he received a reprimand. No disciplinary action was taken against a second officer who had monitored cameras.

On 19 December 2014 the prosecutor again discontinued the case, finding suicide and no causal link between any supervisory lapses and the death, because M.P. had displayed no suicidal tendencies. The Panevėžys Regional Court upheld this conclusion on 27 April 2015, holding that all legally required investigative measures had been exhausted and that no evidence of a crime existed.

The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention that the authorities had failed both to protect her son’s life while he was in custody and to conduct an effective investigation into his death.

The case of Vorienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 39423/15) arose from the death of the applicant’s son, M.P., in police custody at Biržai police station and the ensuing investigation. On 11 April 2008 M.P. was arrested on suspicion of burglary involving a stolen laptop. A search of his home the next day uncovered cannabis, prompting additional charges of drug possession. On 13 April a court authorised 18 days’ pre-trial detention, citing a flight risk due to M.P.’s prior work and connections in Norway. M.P., who had no criminal record, was held alone in cell no. 1 to keep him separate from convicted detainees. While in custody he met his lawyer and an investigator; he confessed to drug possession but initially denied theft, later admitting it. His lawyer described him as calm and without complaints.

On the morning of 15 April 2008, during a shift change, M.P. was found dead, standing with a blanket looped tightly around his neck and attached to the metal bar of his bunk bed. Paramedics arrived within minutes, observed no vital signs, strangulation marks, post-mortem discoloration and rigor mortis, and concluded he had died 1–2 hours earlier. A suicide note addressed “To Mother,” written in charcoal from used matches, was found in the cell. Autopsies (including additional ones requested by the applicant) established death by mechanical asphyxiation from the noose. Light facial scratches were attributed to acne; back bruising to convulsions against the bunk-bed frame. Later expert reports (including after reconstructions) confirmed M.P. could have hanged himself in the observed manner using his own body weight; alleged wrist injuries were post-mortem from body preparation for burial, and there were no signs of third-party violence or handcuffing.

The applicant, granted victim status and represented by counsel, suspected police violence or murder rather than suicide. A pre-trial investigation into the death, opened immediately, spanned seven rounds over more than seven years. Prosecutors repeatedly discontinued it, concluding suicide on the basis of the note (handwriting analysis confirmed it was M.P.’s), video recordings (showing no one entered the cell from 5 p.m. on 14 April until discovery, with no tampering), other detainees hearing nothing, M.P.’s calm demeanour, and expert reconstructions and medical reports. Courts, however, repeatedly quashed these decisions on the applicant’s appeals, ordering further steps: additional autopsies, handwriting and forensic examinations, scene reconstructions (in which the applicant participated), confrontations, questioning of co-detainees and officers, video-authenticity checks, and supplementary medical evaluations of injuries and the hanging mechanism.

An internal police inquiry found no evidence of abuse but identified a disciplinary offence by one guard (D.M.) for failing to maintain constant supervision of detainees as required; he received a reprimand. No criminal liability arose under Article 229 of the Criminal Code (failure to perform official duties), as M.P. had shown no suicidal indicators, was introverted and problem-free, and death would have occurred within minutes. The investigation concluded on 27 April 2015 when the Panevėžys Regional Court upheld discontinuation, finding all legally required actions performed, the evidence comprehensively analysed, suicide established, and no crime proven. These facts concern the State’s obligations under Article 2 of the Convention regarding protection of life in custody and an effective investigation into a custodial death.

The case of Johanna Fröhlich v. Germany (Application no. 16741/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant’s complaint that civil proceedings in Germany had lasted an unreasonably long time, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1976, purchased a residential unit in a four-unit complex in 2003 and moved in with her family. In January 2005 she and the other owners commenced independent evidentiary proceedings against the developers over alleged construction defects, chiefly in the water-drainage system. Expert H.K. was appointed, produced a report dated 16 July 2005 and gave evidence, last appearing on 30 March 2007.

On 23 June 2007 the applicant instituted the main compensation action against the developer, claiming roughly EUR 17 000 for drainage defects and consequent damp and mould. The Regional Court processed pleadings, accepted three neighbours as interveners (who themselves claimed EUR 8 000), held a hearing and proposed settlement. After the applicant rejected settlement, the court on 17 March 2008 ordered a further expert report from H.K. The applicant immediately challenged his impartiality. Site inspections occurred on 28 August and 22 October 2008. In January–February 2009 H.K. reported serious illness requiring surgery and a further six-month delay; the court dismissed him on 23 February 2009. Replacement-expert suggestions were obtained from the Chamber of Commerce; after objections and fee-advance disputes, G.K. was appointed on 25 September 2009. Four months of wrangling over additional court-fee advances followed. In August 2010 G.K. declared himself overloaded and suggested reverting to H.K.; the parties agreed and the court so ordered on 21 September 2010.

A further site visit, repeatedly postponed because of the parties’ unavailability, finally took place on 17 January 2011. H.K. delivered his written opinion only on 5 August 2011. The applicant then contested the expert’s fee calculation; the Court of Appeal later annulled the fee decision (12 March 2012). H.K. fell ill again in May 2012. An oral hearing on 12 October 2012 produced a friendly settlement, ending the first-instance proceedings after five years and almost four months.

On 23 July 2012 the applicant lodged a separate claim under s. 198 of the Courts Constitution Act for compensation for excessive length. The Court of Appeal dismissed it on 30 January 2013. Applying the statutory criteria (complexity, importance of the stake, conduct of the parties and third persons) and Article 6 case-law, it found only one period of court delay (summer 2010, when the expert was insufficiently supervised). All other intervals were attributed to the technical complexity of the defects, the three interveners’ participation, and the applicant’s own repeated applications, objections and appeals. The Federal Court of Justice rejected her appeal on points of law (5 December 2013); the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit her constitutional complaint (3 February 2016).

The applicant then turned to Strasbourg, maintaining that the overall duration of the compensation action had violated her right to a hearing within a reasonable time.

The case of Johanna Fröhlich v. Germany (Application no. 16741/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the right to a hearing within a reasonable time in civil proceedings. The German applicant, born in 1976 and residing in Buseck, purchased a residential unit in a shared complex in 2003. In January 2005, she and the other three unit owners initiated independent evidentiary proceedings in the Regional Court against the property developers over alleged defects, particularly in the water drainage system. Expert H.K. produced a report in July 2005 and presented findings through a hearing in March 2007.

On 23 June 2007, the applicant commenced compensation proceedings against the developer, claiming approximately EUR 17,000 for drainage defects and related issues causing damp and mold. The Regional Court processed the claim, forwarded pleadings, extended deadlines, held an oral hearing to discuss the case and propose a friendly settlement, and handled interventions by the applicant’s neighbors seeking EUR 8,000 in damages. After the applicant rejected a settlement proposal, the court ordered an expert opinion from H.K. on 17 March 2008. The applicant challenged H.K.’s impartiality. Further settlement discussions occurred, followed by onsite visits in August and October 2008.

Delays mounted in 2009 when H.K. required urgent surgery and then faced a six-month illness-related postponement; the court dismissed him and sought replacements via the Chamber of Commerce. After disputes over suggested experts and advance fee payments, the court appointed G.K. in September 2009. Fee disputes with G.K. persisted into January 2010. When G.K. reported an excessive workload in August 2010 and recommended reverting to H.K., the court did so in September 2010. An onsite visit scheduled for October 2010 was postponed multiple times (once by the defendants and three times by the applicant) until January 2011. H.K. submitted his opinion in August 2011 after progress inquiries.

The applicant then objected to the expert’s fee calculation and requested deadline extensions. The Regional Court dismissed the objection in December 2011; the applicant appealed, and the Court of Appeal annulled the fee decision in March 2012. H.K. fell ill again in May 2012. An oral hearing on 12 October 2012 resulted in a friendly settlement, concluding the main proceedings after more than five years.

On 23 July 2012, the applicant sought compensation under section 198 of the Courts Constitution Act for the allegedly excessive length of the proceedings. The Court of Appeal rejected the claim on 30 January 2013, holding that the Regional Court had generally conducted the case expeditiously. It identified only one attributable delay in summer 2010 (failure to supervise the expert promptly, which delayed recognition of G.K.’s workload). The court emphasized the proceedings’ complexity (factual issues and evidence-gathering), contributions by three intervening parties, and the applicant’s repeated applications, objections, and appeals. It also noted the case’s importance to the applicant for financial and health reasons but concluded that the overall duration was not unreasonable under both domestic law and Article 6 § 1. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed a further appeal in December 2013, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear a constitutional complaint in February 2016.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint to the ECHR regarding the reasonableness of the proceedings’ length, taking into account complexity, the parties’ conduct, and what was at stake.

**CASE OF HØINESS v. NORWAY (Application no. 43624/14), ECtHR (Second Section), Judgment of 19 March 2019 (final 19 June 2019)**

The applicant, Mona Høiness (born 1958), a well-known Norwegian lawyer specializing in criminal and child-custody matters, former talk-show host, and public commentator, alleged a violation of her Article 8 right to respect for private life. Norwegian courts declined to hold Hegnar Media AS (operator of the Hegnar Online internet portal) and its editor liable in damages for failing to prevent or promptly remove three sexually explicit, anonymous user comments about her on an unmoderated debate forum.

In late summer 2010 Hegnar-owned publications (Kapital, Finansavisen and Hegnar Online) ran extensive coverage of the applicant’s relationship with a wealthy elderly widow whose will named the applicant as heir. Relatives later challenged the will (proceedings the applicant ultimately won). Hegnar Online maintained a high-volume, purely user-generated forum (more than 200 000 posts monthly) accessible via the news site, divided into sub-forums, allowing anonymous posting without registration or pre-publication editorial control.

On 5 November 2010 a thread entitled “Mona Høiness – the case is growing” appeared. Two comments of particular complaint were posted:
- Comment 1 (6 November): an anonymous user claimed to “know someone who \ldots had been lucky to have shagged” the applicant.
- Comment 2 (8 November): another anonymous post described her as “dirt-ugly – looks like a whore” and stated that any sexual encounter would require a blindfold.

A print-out showing Comment 1 had been viewed 176 times and Comment 2 12 times was attached to a letter the applicant’s counsel sent the Press Complaints Commission on 8 November (in existing complaints against Kapital/Finansavisen). The letter was not treated as a request to Hegnar Online to delete the posts. On 17 November counsel emailed Hegnar Online editors; the comments were removed within 13 minutes.

A second thread (“Mona Høiness vs Trygve Hegnar”) started 28 November. Comment 3 (30 November) asked whether the applicant was “still shagging” a person nicknamed “trønderbjørn”. A radio editor alerted counsel on 3 December; by then a Hegnar moderator had already deleted the comment (viewed 115 times). Hegnar’s system featured “warning buttons” beside each post (1 800–2 000 monthly deletions) plus staff monitoring.

On 7 January 2011 the applicant complained to the Press Complaints Commission about both threads. The Commission held that sexually charged remarks and accusations of unethical conduct in the inheritance matter breached journalistic codes and should have been removed immediately.

In April 2011 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against Hegnar Media AS and the editor, claiming the three comments constituted unlawful defamation (Penal Code Arts 246–247) or privacy/personality-right infringements (Art 390a and unwritten principles) and seeking non-pecuniary damages under the Compensation Act s 3-6 (alternatively Gender Equality Act). Defendants relied on the E-Commerce Act s 18 (hosting-provider liability only for intent or gross negligence, and exemption upon prompt removal once aware) and argued they lacked knowledge until notified.

Oslo City Court (4 January 2012) found the comments tasteless and vulgar but incapable of harming honour or reputation; they were unserious, anonymous, posted in a marginal forum, and did not amount to defamation. The applicant was ordered to pay costs.

Borgarting High Court (24 October 2013) agreed the remarks were sexually loaded and that the Press Commission’s finding of delayed removal was justified, but held that compensation required sufficient culpability. The forum’s real-time, user-generated nature made prior censorship impossible; subsequent monitoring (warning buttons plus moderators) was adequate. Comments 1 and 2 were deleted minutes after specific notice; Comment 3 had already been removed on the moderator’s initiative. The 8 November letter was not a deletion request. Costs were again awarded against the applicant.

The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 February 2014.

The applicant complained that the domestic courts’ refusal to impose liability left her without an effective remedy for the interference with her private life caused by the sexually harassing comments.

The case of *Høiness v. Norway* (no. 43624/14) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for private life). The applicant, Mona Høiness (born 1958), a well-known Oslo lawyer specialising in criminal and child-custody matters (and former talk-show host), claimed Norwegian courts failed to hold Hegnar Media AS and its editor liable in damages for insufficiently preventing or promptly removing anonymous, sexually vulgar comments about her on the Hegnar Online debate forum.

From late summer 2010 Hegnar-owned outlets (Kapital, Finansavisen and Hegnar Online) extensively covered an inheritance dispute involving the applicant and a wealthy elderly widow, implying exploitation. Hegnar Online hosted a large, unmoderated-in-advance, user-generated forum (200 000+ anonymous comments monthly) accessible via the news site. Two threads, started 5 and 28 November 2010, contained three impugned posts:

- Comment 1 (6 November): an anonymous claim that someone had “shagged” her.  
- Comment 2 (8 November): an anonymous remark that she was “dirt-ugly” and looked “like a whore,” adding that any sexual encounter would require a blindfold.  
- Comment 3 (30 November): an anonymous query whether she was “still shagging” a nicknamed individual (“trønderbjørn”).

Print-outs showed limited views (176, 12 and 115 respectively). On 8 November the applicant’s counsel mentioned comments 1–2 in a letter to the Press Complaints Commission relating to a separate Kapital complaint, without requesting deletion. An 17 November e-mail to Hegnar staff produced removal within 13 minutes. Comment 3 was already gone when notified on 3 December (deleted by a moderator after a radio-station tip). The Commission later held the comments breached the journalistic code of conduct and should have been removed immediately.

In May 2011 the applicant sued Hegnar Media AS and the editor under Penal Code Articles 246–247 (defamation) and 390a (privacy) plus Compensation Act s. 3-6, arguing the posts constituted unprotected sexual harassment. Defendants invoked E-Commerce Act s. 18 (hosting exemption unless intent or gross negligence) and their warning-button plus moderator system (1 800–2 000 monthly deletions).

Oslo City Court (4 January 2012) found the comments tasteless but not capable of harming honour or reputation: they were anonymous, unserious and posted on a marginal forum; they expressed no accusation of immorality. Costs of NOK 225 480 were awarded against the applicant.

Borgarting High Court (24 October 2013) accepted the comments were sexually loaded and exceeded what the applicant had to tolerate, but held liability required sufficient culpability in failing to discover and remove them. Real-time posting precluded prior censorship; the existing warning and moderator systems were adequate. Comments 1–2 were deleted promptly once the 17 November e-mail arrived; the 8 November letter was treated as relating only to the Kapital complaint. Comment 3 had already been removed. No negligence (let alone gross negligence) was established. Costs of NOK 183 380 were awarded on appeal.

The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 February 2014. These facts framed the Strasbourg complaint that the domestic courts’ refusal to impose liability failed to protect the applicant’s private life.

The ECHR case Høiness v. Norway (App. no. 43624/14) arose from the applicant’s claim of an Article 8 violation. In late 2010 Hegnar-owned outlets (Kapital, Finansavisen and Hegnar Online) extensively covered Høiness’s relationship with a wealthy elderly widow, implying exploitation; after the widow’s 2011 death relatives challenged her will (Høiness ultimately prevailed). Hegnar Online hosted a large, anonymous, unregistered forum (over 200 000 comments monthly) with no prior editorial control.

On 5 November 2010 a “Theme of the day” thread about Høiness generated two vulgar posts: Comment 1 (6 Nov.) stated someone had “shagged” her; Comment 2 (8 Nov.) called her “dirt-ugly” and looking like a “whore.” By 7.26 p.m. on 8 November they had been viewed 176 and 12 times respectively. Counsel mentioned the posts that day in a letter to the Press Complaints Commission concerning a separate Kapital complaint, attaching a print-out but expressly not lodging a new complaint against Hegnar Online. Comments 1 and 2 remained until counsel e-mailed on 17 November; they were deleted 13 minutes later.

A second thread begun 28 November produced Comment 3 (30 Nov.) asking whether Høiness was “still shagging” a nicknamed person. A radio editor alerted counsel on 3 December; by then a moderator had already removed it.

In February 2011 the Press Complaints Commission held that the sexual remarks and accusations of unethical conduct violated journalistic ethics and should have been deleted immediately.

Høiness sued in May 2011 for defamation under the Penal Code and Compensation Act, seeking NOK 250 000 from the company and NOK 25 000 from the editor. Hegnar Media pointed to its “warning-button” system (1 800–2 000 monthly deletions) plus in-house moderators, apologised, and offered NOK 10 000 (refused).

Oslo City Court (Jan. 2012) found the comments tasteless but not capable of harming honour or reputation, given their anonymous, unserious character on a marginal forum; Høiness was ordered to pay costs of NOK 225 480.

Borgarting High Court (Oct. 2013) likewise rejected liability. It stressed the impossibility of prior censorship of real-time user content and the adequacy of subsequent monitoring. The 8 November letter was treated as belonging to the Kapital complaint and contained no deletion request. Comments 1–2 were removed minutes after the 17 November e-mail; Comment 3 had already been deleted by staff. Costs of NOK 183 380 were awarded against Høiness.

The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave to appeal in February 2014.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 8 complaint that the courts had not sufficiently protected the applicant’s private life by imposing liability on the forum operator and editor.
001-189641:
The case of Mifsud v. Malta (Application no. 62257/15) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from Maltese law requiring the applicant to provide a genetic sample in paternity proceedings against his will. The applicant, Francesco Saverio Mifsud (born 1925), a British national living in Dublin, died in December 2017; his widow continued the application.

In December 2012, X (then about 55) brought proceedings before Malta’s Civil Court (Family Section) seeking a declaration that the applicant was her biological father and an order amending her birth certificate (which recorded the father as unknown). The Public Registry Director requested genetic testing under Article 100A of the Civil Code, which incorporates Article 70A. That provision requires the Civil Court, on application, to substitute consent and order a genetic sample (normally a buccal swab) unless the person whose parentage is to be clarified is a minor and testing would unreasonably harm the child’s best interests. Article 86A permits a child born out of wedlock (or the mother) to seek a judicial declaration of paternity at any time.

The applicant denied paternity, invoking the defence of several lovers, and objected that a mandatory test would violate Article 8. He stressed X’s 53-year delay, his advanced age (88), possible medical risks, the lack of any prior supporting evidence, and the disruption a positive result would cause to his established family life. He asked for the constitutional issue to be referred.

X and her mother Y filed affidavits. X described an alleged long-term relationship, meetings in Malta, the applicant acting as godfather to her daughter, and later financial disputes after she was evicted from one of his properties. Y claimed she had worked for the applicant, become pregnant by him, and later left because of his alleged criminal activities and pressure. The applicant cross-examined Y but submitted no evidence of his own.

The Civil Court referred the Article 8 complaint to the constitutional jurisdictions. In October 2014 the Civil Court (First Hall), sitting constitutionally, held that an order to undergo testing would not violate Article 8. It treated the legislation as fulfilling the State’s positive obligation to enable persons to establish their parentage. Relying on Strasbourg case-law (Pascaud v. France; Jäggi v. Switzerland), it found X’s interest in knowing her origins and correcting her birth certificate outweighed the applicant’s objections; her age and the lapse of time were irrelevant given earlier contact.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in June 2015. It accepted that Article 70A(2) left the first-instance judge no discretion, but held that, on the concrete facts, a fair balance had been struck. X had a compelling interest in establishing her identity, ending the humiliation of an “unknown father” entry, and protecting potential inheritance rights. The applicant had identified only the minor inconvenience of a non-invasive swab and possible family disruption; these did not outweigh X’s rights. The court noted that the same test was available to both parties, so equality of arms was not impaired.

After the constitutional rulings, the Family Court ordered the test. The applicant, living abroad, delayed but eventually submitted a sample. The expert report of February 2017 gave a 99.9998 % probability of paternity. In June 2017 the Family Court declared X the applicant’s biological daughter, relying on the unrebutted affidavits and the DNA result, and ordered the registry amendment.

The applicant’s central complaint before the European Court was that the automatic, non-discretionary character of Articles 70A and 100A prevented any judicial balancing of the competing private-life interests and imposed an excessive burden on a putative father who had no real opportunity to contest the claim.

The case of Mifsud v. Malta (Application no. 62257/15) concerned a complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that Maltese law mandating a genetic sample in paternity proceedings, against the putative father's will, breached his right to respect for private and family life.

The applicant, Francesco Saverio Mifsud (British national, born 1925, resident in Dublin), faced proceedings instituted on 20 December 2012 by X (then aged around 55) before Malta's Civil Court (Family Section). X sought a declaration that the applicant was her biological father, with corresponding amendments to her birth certificate (which listed the father as unknown). The Director of the Public Registry, as co-defendant, requested an order under Article 100A of the Civil Code for genetic testing of the parties. The applicant denied paternity and raised the exceptio plurium concubentium, alleging X's mother (Y) had multiple partners.

X and Y submitted affidavits. X described being told from childhood that the applicant was her father; she contacted him unsuccessfully at age 16, later met him in Malta (noting a resemblance to one of his daughters), developed a relationship involving visits, cohabitation in his properties, and his role as godparent to her daughter. Contact continued until around 1985, deteriorating after her 1998 eviction from one property (leading to successful recovery proceedings against him). Y attested to a relationship with the applicant (her employer), a pregnancy he allegedly sought to terminate, subsequent births, and eventual flight from him due to fear and alleged criminal involvement.

On 13 May 2013, X formally requested tests under Article 100A (cross-referencing Article 70A). The applicant objected on 22 May 2013, arguing the mandatory nature of the provision (applicable unless a minor's best interests were at stake) violated Article 8, given the 53-year delay, his advanced age (88), potential medical risks, and lack of initial evidence. He sought referral to the constitutional courts, which occurred on 23 October 2013.

In constitutional proceedings, the applicant contended that the law pursued no legitimate aim under Article 8(2), failed to balance competing interests, imposed an excessive burden by preventing effective contestation (anyone could initiate proceedings without evidence, forcing submission even if paternity was impossible), and would disrupt his established family life. The Civil Court (First Hall, constitutional competence) held on 30 October 2014 that an order to undergo testing would not violate Article 8. It emphasised the State's positive obligation to facilitate knowledge of parentage (citing Pascaud v. France), noting X's long-standing efforts and prior involvement of the applicant in her life; her age was irrelevant, and the putative father's interest alone could not override the right to identity. A particularly rigorous scrutiny applied, but no disproportionality arose here.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 26 June 2015, confirming the first-instance ruling. It identified X's compelling interests in personal identity, correcting a humiliating birth certificate, and potential patrimonial claims. The applicant's objections (age, minor humiliation of a non-invasive buccal swab, possible family disruption) were insufficient. Article 8(2) expressly permitted interference to protect others' rights. While the law's mandatory character (Article 70A(2)) might theoretically unbalance interests in other cases, it did not here. An equality-of-arms complaint was dismissed as frivolous, the test being available to both sides.

Civil proceedings resumed. On 18 October 2015 the Family Court ordered the test. The applicant (who later died on 3 December 2017, with his wife continuing the application) underwent it; a 21 February 2017 report showed 99.9998% probability of paternity. On 21 June 2017 the court declared X his biological daughter, ordering registry amendments. It relied on the unrebutted affidavits (the applicant submitted no testimony) and DNA results.

Relevant domestic law (Civil Code Articles 70A, 86A, 100 and 100A) entitles a child to require genetic testing and obliges the court to substitute consent and order a sample if withheld (save for unreasonable harm to a minor). Article 562 places the burden of proof on the alleging party, though testing provides conclusive evidence.

These facts highlight the core of the alleged violation: the automatic judicial compulsion of a DNA sample in long-delayed adult paternity proceedings, without judicial discretion to weigh the putative father's Article 8 interests against those of the claimant.

The case of Mifsud v. Malta (Application no. 62257/15) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 December 2015 by Francesco Saverio Mifsud, a British national born in 1925 and resident in Dublin. He alleged that Maltese law mandating provision of a genetic sample in paternity proceedings, against his will, violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life). The applicant died on 3 December 2017; his widow and heir, Margaret Mifsud, continued the proceedings.

On 20 December 2012, X (then around 55) brought proceedings in the Civil Court (Family Section) seeking a declaration that the applicant was her biological father and corresponding amendment of her birth certificate (which listed the father as unknown). The Director of the Public Registry, also a defendant, requested that the parties undergo genetic testing under Article 100A of the Civil Code (which incorporated Article 70A, requiring consent to a genetic paternity test and sample-taking, with the court substituting consent if withheld, except where contrary to a minor’s best interests).

The applicant denied paternity and invoked the exceptio plurium concubentium, alleging X’s mother Y had had multiple partners. X and Y submitted sworn affidavits detailing a long-term relationship between Y and the applicant (for whom Y had worked), including an earlier miscarriage after the applicant allegedly sought to terminate the pregnancy, X’s birth, subsequent meetings in Malta (including at the airport and with lawyers), the applicant’s role as godparent to X’s daughter, provision of housing, and later deterioration of relations culminating in eviction proceedings in which X obtained a money judgment against him. X claimed she had always been told the applicant was her father and had attempted contact since age 16.

On 13 May 2013 X formally requested genetic tests. The applicant objected on 22 May 2013, arguing that a mandatory order under Articles 100A and 70A would breach Article 8, given the 53-year delay since X’s birth, his advanced age (then 88), and possible medical risks. He sought referral to the constitutional courts.

The Civil Court referred the constitutional complaint. At first instance, the Civil Court (First Hall) held on 30 October 2014 that an order to undergo testing would not violate Article 8. It emphasised the State’s positive obligation to facilitate knowledge of parentage, citing that a putative father’s interests alone could not override those of a person seeking to establish paternity. X’s age was irrelevant; she had pursued the matter for years and the applicant had previously formed part of her life. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 26 June 2015. It found X’s interests (establishing personal identity, correcting her birth certificate to avoid humiliation, and asserting possible patrimonial claims) compelling. The applicant’s objections (age, humiliation of a non-invasive buccal swab, and potential disruption to his family life) did not outweigh them. While the mandatory nature of Article 70A(2) might conceivably produce disproportionality in other cases, it did not do so on these facts. An equality-of-arms complaint was rejected as the test was available to both sides and conclusive evidence is not inherently unfair.

Thereafter the Civil Court ordered the test. The applicant complied. A 21 February 2017 expert report showed a 99.9998% probability of paternity. On 21 June 2017 the court declared X the applicant’s biological child and directed amendment of her birth certificate, relying on the unrebutted affidavits and DNA evidence.

The mandatory character of the testing regime, the long delay, the applicant’s age and objections, and the constitutional courts’ assessment of competing interests under Article 8 formed the core factual matrix of the alleged violation.
001-189351:
**Case of X and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 22457/16)**

Three minor Bulgarian-born siblings (X, born 2000; Y, born 2002; Z, born 2003) lived in a state orphanage in Strahilovo until their 2012 adoption by an Italian couple, after which they moved to Italy. In October 2012, following an argument, Z accused her brother of sexual abuse. The adoptive parents consulted child-abuse specialists. Psychologist reports (based on recorded “therapy sessions,” not verbatim transcripts) recorded that X described an older boy, D., entering a younger children’s dormitory at night, sexually touching some children, placing his penis in their mouths, forcing others to watch, and hitting children. X said he reported this to the orphanage director (identified as E.), who promised to involve police if it recurred. Y viewed events as a “game” and mentioned sexual acts among children (including with her brother). Z described being taken to a “discotheque” where men “played” with the children; she resisted one assailant. In a later session, X added that men at the “discotheque” engaged in sexual games and filmed the children. The children later refused to discuss the events further.

The parents emailed Bulgaria’s State Agency for Child Protection in November 2012 seeking to complain of abuse, but correspondence stalled after a language barrier. They alerted the Italian adoption association and Intercountry Adoption Commission, naming seven men and four women (staff and outsiders, including N.) as perpetrators. They alleged unsupervised nights at the orphanage allowed older children to repeat abuse on younger ones, and that groups were taken “on holiday” to a village “discotheque” for daily assaults (X forced to watch his sisters being raped). They lodged a criminal complaint with Italian police in December 2012. An Italian journalist published an article in *L’Espresso* (January 2013) describing systematic abuse, an organized network, masked men, weapons, and filming; he visited the sites (which matched descriptions) and informally contacted Bulgarian police, who were later instructed not to pursue it. The Italian prosecutor forwarded materials to the Bulgarian embassy, deeming investigation a Bulgarian matter.

Bulgarian authorities conducted inspections and three overlapping preliminary investigations. A January 2013 Agency inspection of the orphanage (staff interviews, questionnaires of 13 remaining children aged 8–13, psychologist input) found no unsupervised periods, checked visitor access, CCTV, age/gender-separated dormitories preventing unseen movement, and no mentions of sexual abuse (only peer arguments or hitting, which staff addressed). The applicants’ former psychologist reported no prior signs or complaints. A follow-up psychologist team found nothing alarming. The Agency concluded no evidence supporting the press reports but referred the file to prosecutors given the allegations’ gravity. The Veliko Tarnovo district prosecutor opened a preliminary investigation but discontinued it in November 2013, finding no sufficient evidence of a criminal offence.

A second investigation (February 2013) followed a report from the Italian association SOS Telefono Azzuro (including names, descriptions, and psychologist reports). Police, healthcare, social-welfare, and child-protection officials inspected records (including medical files showing no assault signs), interviewed staff (director, psychologist, supervisors, driver, caretaker, heating technician), occasional workers (photographer, electrician N.), and four children. Reports noted three male staff barred from dormitories unaccompanied, weekly police visits, complaints mechanisms unused for such incidents, regular medical checks, and no prior sexual-abuse reports (only unrelated past incidents). Children were supervised at night and on excursions; the only dancing event was a supervised holiday-camp party with a DJ. No director named E. existed; D. had been adopted earlier. The prosecutor discontinued proceedings in June 2013, finding allegations uncorroborated and no unaccompanied male access or outside contact.

After an official Italian Ministry of Justice request (January 2014) transmitting further materials, a third preliminary investigation opened. Proceedings were joined; the June 2013 discontinuance was set aside, but the November 2013 order stood. Later parental challenges prompted a prosecutor recusal. The regional prosecutor (September 2016) and appellate prosecutor (November 2016) upheld discontinuance, citing comprehensive staff/child/outsider interviews, security/supervision measures, absence of named individuals or a “discotheque,” and no added value from later Italian documents. A Supreme Court prosecutor’s own-motion review (January 2017) deemed the investigation thorough, noted inconsistencies between the children’s psychologist statements and later Italian questioning, and suggested they may have witnessed and imitated peer sexual touching then fabricated adult-perpetrator stories to avoid upsetting their adoptive parents.

Italian proceedings included applicant interviews (records not provided to the Court) and an expert finding their accounts sufficiently credible, but the Youth Court declined further questioning as contrary to the children’s interests and found no need for protective measures. The orphanage closed in 2015 under deinstitutionalization. Separate 2013 complaints of physical abuse (stick-hitting) and other regulatory issues were investigated and discontinued for insufficient evidence.

The applicants alleged sexual abuse amounting to ill-treatment while in State care and an ineffective investigation. (The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber.)

The three minor applicants (X, born 2000; Y, born 2002; Z, born 2003) were Bulgarian-born siblings who resided in a state orphanage in Strahilovo until their adoption by an Italian couple in June 2012 (then aged 12, 10 and 9). Shortly after arriving in Italy, Z accused her brother of sexual abuse during an argument. Disturbed by this and by Z’s subsequent distressed behaviour, the adoptive parents arranged for the children to be examined by specialist psychologists in October 2012.

The psychologists’ report recorded that X described an older boy, D., entering the younger children’s dormitory at night, sexually abusing some children (touching genitals and oral penetration) while forcing others to watch, and physically assaulting them. X said he had reported this to the orphanage director, “E.”, who promised to involve police if it recurred but took no action. Y and Z, interviewed together, referred to witnessing sexual acts among children (which Y described as a “game”) and to being taken to a “discotheque” where men arrived and “played” with them; Z said she was the only one who resisted, screaming and hitting an assailant. In a later session X added that men had engaged in sexual games with the children and filmed them. The children later became reluctant to discuss the events.

The parents reported the allegations to the Bulgarian State Agency for Child Protection (receiving only a request for more details in Bulgarian), to Italian adoption bodies and to Italian police (December 2012). They also contacted a journalist; an article in L’Espresso (January 2013) alleged systematic abuse by staff and outsiders, including organised paedophile activity, threats with weapons and filming, at a holiday-village discotheque, plus intra-child abuse after nights left unsupervised. The Italian prosecutor transmitted the material to the Bulgarian embassy, considering investigation a Bulgarian responsibility.

Bulgarian authorities conducted inspections and three sets of preliminary investigations. An Agency inspection (January 2013) interviewed staff and 13 children, used anonymous questionnaires and found no reports of sexual abuse, only ordinary arguments and occasional hitting among children; CCTV, visitor controls and staff supervision were described as adequate, and the orphanage psychologist recalled no prior signs from the applicants. The file was sent to prosecutors, who discontinued proceedings in November 2013 for lack of evidence of any crime.

A second investigation (February 2013), prompted by an Italian child-protection association’s report enclosing the psychologists’ notes and naming alleged perpetrators (including staff and outsiders such as an electrician “N.”), involved further interviews with staff, a few children, a photographer and the electrician. Police reports found no corroboration: there was no director named E., male staff (only three, none allowed unsupervised access to dormitories) had not had isolated contact with children, there had been no discotheque visits (only a supervised summer-camp party with a DJ), and no prior complaints of sexual abuse despite regular medical checks, a complaints box and a child helpline. Proceedings were discontinued in June 2013.

After official Italian requests, the cases were joined. Discontinuance of the first investigation was ultimately upheld through all prosecutorial levels (to January 2017). Reviewing prosecutors noted inconsistencies in the children’s accounts, the absence of supporting evidence from staff/children still at the orphanage, and the possibility that the applicants had witnessed or imitated sexual touching among children and then fabricated an adult-perpetrator narrative to avoid disappointing their new parents. The children themselves were never interviewed by Bulgarian authorities. The orphanage closed in 2015 as part of deinstitutionalisation.

Italian proceedings included recorded interviews with the children (April 2013) and a neuropsychiatric expert assessment finding their allegations sufficiently credible, but the Youth Court declined further questioning as contrary to the children’s interests and criticised the parents for approaching a journalist rather than the court immediately.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: the children’s exposure to (and the state’s failure to prevent) sexual abuse while in institutional care, and the subsequent failure to conduct an effective official investigation capable of establishing the facts and identifying those responsible.

**Case of X and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 22457/16)**

This ECtHR Chamber judgment (17 January 2019; later referred to the Grand Chamber) concerns three Bulgarian-born minors (X, born 2000; Y, 2002; Z, 2003) adopted in June 2012 by an Italian couple after living in a state orphanage in Strahilovo, Bulgaria. The applicants alleged sexual abuse there and an ineffective investigation by Bulgarian authorities, engaging the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3 ECHR.

In October 2012, after a sibling argument, Z accused her brother of sexual abuse. The adoptive parents consulted psychologists specialising in child abuse. In recorded sessions (initially with translation help, as the children spoke little Italian), X described an older orphanage boy, D., entering the youngest children’s dormitory at night, sexually abusing some (touching intimate parts and oral sex) while forcing others to watch, and hitting children. X said he reported this to director “E.,” who promised to call police if it recurred. The sisters spoke together: Y described seeing others “doing sex” (viewing it as a game) and participating with her brother; both noted X was hit more. Z mentioned being taken to a “discotheque” where men “played” with the children; she said she struggled and cried out. Later, X alleged men filmed sexual acts there. The children thereafter refused to discuss events further, saying they were “sick of Bulgaria.” They indicated body parts on dolls.

The parents emailed Bulgaria’s State Agency for Child Protection in November 2012 but correspondence stalled over language. They notified Italian adoption bodies, listing names of seven men and four women (staff and outsiders, including “N.”) as perpetrators. They alleged groups of children were taken “on holiday” to a village discotheque for daily touching and assault by outsiders; X was forced to watch his sisters raped; unsupervised children later repeated the abuse on younger ones. A December 2012 Italian police complaint followed. A January 2013 *L’Espresso* article (“Bulgaria, in the paedophiles’ den”) detailed systematic abuse, an organised network, masked men with weapons, and videos; the journalist claimed sites matched descriptions and informal police contact was blocked by superiors.

Italian authorities forwarded materials to Bulgaria. Three Bulgarian investigations ensued. After the article, the Agency inspected the orphanage (January 2013), interviewing staff and 13 children (aged 8–13) via questionnaires. It found constant supervision, CCTV, age/gender-separated dorms preventing unsupervised movement, no abuse reports (only arguments or peer hitting), and no signs noted by the orphanage psychologist. A psychologist team found no issues. Prosecutors opened a preliminary investigation but discontinued it (November 2013) for lack of criminal evidence.

A second investigation (February 2013) followed an Italian association report with psychologist notes and names. Police and officials interviewed staff (director, psychologist, supervisors, driver, caretaker, heating technician), occasional workers (photographer, electrician “N.”), and some children; they reviewed medical files (no assault signs) and noted unused complaint mechanisms. Only three male staff existed, barred from dorms without female accompaniment. No prior sexual-abuse reports existed; children attended a supervised holiday camp with a DJ-only party. A named child, B., was questioned. Prosecutors discontinued (June 2013): allegations unconfirmed; no unsupervised male/outsider access; no matching “E.” director or discotheque.

After official Italian requests (2014), proceedings were joined but the first discontinuance stood. Further reviews (2015–2017) by regional, appellate, and Supreme Court prosecutors upheld it. They cited consistent findings of supervision, no matching names/details (N. was an occasional electrician; no director E.), no independent corroboration, and inconsistencies in the children’s accounts (possibly witnessing/repeating peer sexual touching, then fabricating an adult-abuse story to avoid upsetting adoptive parents). Italian Youth Court proceedings (2013–2014) found the children’s testimony sufficiently credible via expert review but declined further questioning as contrary to their interests and criticised the parents for approaching a journalist first.

The orphanage closed in 2015 under deinstitutionalisation. Separate 2013 checks (including one over alleged staff hitting of other children) found no sexual abuse and limited other issues. The facts centre on the children’s post-adoption disclosures of intra-orphanage and “holiday”/outsider sexual abuse (including by older children, staff, and men, with filming and violence) versus Bulgarian authorities’ inspections, interviews, and structural findings of adequate supervision and no corroboration, leading to repeated discontinuances without interviewing the applicants in Bulgaria.
001-192767:
The case of Repcevirág Szövetkezet v. Hungary (Application no. 70750/14) originated in an application by a Hungarian agricultural cooperative alleging a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). The applicant claimed that domestic courts had arbitrarily rejected its repeated requests to refer questions of EU law to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) for a preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU.

The applicant cooperative purchased expensive agricultural machines and lent them free of charge to its members, who paid regular contribution fees. It deducted input VAT on the machines on the basis that the lending constituted an economic activity. In 2008 the Hungarian Tax Authority fined the applicant, finding that free lending was not an “economic activity” under the VAT Act and that deduction was therefore unavailable.

In the first set of proceedings the applicant challenged the fine in the administrative courts, relying on domestic law and the contribution fees. The Baranya County Court upheld the tax decision on 17 February 2009. The Supreme Court confirmed that judgment on 26 November 2009, citing the CJEU’s Aardappelenbewaarplaats ruling (that services lacking a definite subjective consideration are not supplied “against payment”).

On 9 December 2010 the applicant began a second set of proceedings, suing the Supreme Court for damages under the Hungarian Civil Code. It alleged that the 2009 judgment had violated EU law by failing to apply Article 17 of the Sixth VAT Directive of its own motion and by mischaracterising the activity. Distinguishing Aardappelenbewaarplaats (which concerned a different directive provision) and relying on the CJEU’s Köbler judgment on State liability for judicial breaches of EU law, the applicant asked the Budapest Regional Court to seek a preliminary ruling on the compatibility of the 2009 judgment with EU law and on the conditions for liability.

The Regional Court dismissed the claim on 31 May 2011 without a referral. It held that the Supreme Court had been bound by the applicant’s original pleadings (which had not invoked EU law) and that Köbler was inapplicable because the suit was directed against the court rather than the State. The Budapest Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal on 28 August 2012, again without a referral, emphasising that the applicant’s failure to plead EU law in the first proceedings rendered the damages claim unfounded.

The applicant then sought review by the Kúria and proposed four questions for a preliminary ruling concerning the applicability of EU law to a damages action against the Supreme Court, the interpretation of Article 17 of the Sixth Directive, the duty of national courts to apply EU law of their own motion, and the seriousness of any infringement. On 2 October 2013 the Kúria refused the referral in a procedural order, finding the first question undisputed and the remaining questions either outside the scope of the damages action or matters of national law. No appeal lay against that order. On 11 December 2013 the Kúria confirmed the Court of Appeal’s judgment, reiterating that the applicant’s earlier omission had prevented the Supreme Court from examining EU-law arguments.

On 13 March 2014 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that the Kúria’s refusal had been arbitrary and contrary to the Cilfit criteria, thereby denying access to a “lawful judge” (the CJEU). It also asked the Constitutional Court itself to refer questions to the CJEU about whether such a refusal could violate Article 47 of the EU Charter. On 19 May 2014 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible, holding that it lacked jurisdiction to review ordinary courts’ decisions on referrals and that a complaint under section 27 of the Constitutional Court Act could not include a request for a preliminary ruling.

These successive refusals, without reasons meeting the Cilfit standard, formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that it had been denied a fair hearing.

The applicant, a Hungarian agricultural cooperative, purchased expensive machinery and lent it free of charge to members (who paid regular contribution fees). It deducted input VAT on the purchases as part of its claimed economic activity. In 2008 the Tax Authority fined it, holding that free lending was not an “economic activity” under the 1992 VAT Act, so no deduction was allowed.

In the first (administrative) proceedings the applicant argued under domestic law that the fees constituted consideration, making the activity economic. The Baranya County Court upheld the fine (17 February 2009). The Supreme Court confirmed this on 26 November 2009, citing the CJEU’s Aardappelenbewaarplaats judgment (no definite subjective consideration means the service is not “against payment”).

In December 2010 the applicant brought a second set of proceedings, suing the Supreme Court for damages under the Civil Code for judicial malpractice. It alleged the 2009 judgment violated EU law by failing to apply Article 17 of the Sixth VAT Directive (on input-VAT deduction) of the court’s own motion and by wrongly classifying the activity. It distinguished Aardappelenbewaarplaats (turnover tax on free storage) from VAT deductibility and invoked Köbler on State liability for last-instance court errors. It asked the Budapest Regional Court to seek a CJEU preliminary ruling on EU-law compatibility and liability conditions.

The Regional Court dismissed the claim (31 May 2011) without a reference. It held the Supreme Court had been bound by the applicant’s original (consideration-based) claim and had examined relevant EU law of its own motion; Köbler was inapplicable because the suit targeted the court rather than the State.

On appeal the applicant also sought a reference on whether Köbler applied to claims against the Supreme Court itself. The Budapest Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal (28 August 2012) without referring, finding the claim unfounded because the applicant had not invoked EU law in the 2009 proceedings.

The applicant then sought Kúria review and proposed four questions for a preliminary ruling: (1) whether a Civil-Code damages claim against the Supreme Court for an EU-law breach in prior administrative proceedings falls within EU law; (2) whether Article 17(2)(a) of the Sixth Directive precludes denying VAT deduction merely because machinery was lent free to members; (3) whether last-instance liability is excluded solely because the party did not explicitly plead a specific EU provision, or whether courts must apply such provisions of their own motion; (4) whether the infringement is “sufficiently serious” if the Supreme Court denied deduction without analysing the EU provision or referring, relying instead on a CJEU judgment on a different issue.

The Kúria refused the reference (2 October 2013): the first question was undisputed and the others fell outside the damages action; the consequences of the applicant’s failure to plead EU law were a matter of national procedural law. No appeal lay against that refusal. On 11 December 2013 the Kúria confirmed the Court of Appeal’s judgment, holding that the applicant’s failure to raise the Sixth Directive in 2009 had barred the Supreme Court from examining those arguments, so no liability arose.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (13 March 2014) alleging that the Kúria’s refusal of a reference was arbitrary and violated the right to a fair trial (and access to a “lawful judge,” the CJEU). It asked the Constitutional Court itself to refer questions on whether an arbitrary last-instance refusal of a reference violates Article 47 of the EU Charter. The Constitutional Court rejected the complaint as inadmissible (19 May 2014), stating it lacked jurisdiction to review ordinary courts’ decisions on whether to refer and that constitutional-complaint procedure under section 27 of the Constitutional Court Act did not permit preliminary-ruling requests.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the successive refusals to refer questions to the CJEU (especially the Kúria’s) were arbitrary and breached Article 6 of the Convention.

The applicant, a Hungarian agricultural cooperative, purchased machinery which it lent to its members free of charge in return for regular contribution fees. It deducted the VAT paid on the machinery as an input tax. In 2008 the tax authority fined the applicant, holding that the lending was not an “economic activity” and that no deduction was therefore permitted.

The applicant challenged that decision. The Baranya County Court dismissed the challenge in 2009 and the Supreme Court upheld the dismissal later that year. The Supreme Court relied on the CJEU’s Aardappelenbewaarplaats judgment to conclude that services supplied without definite consideration were not supplied “against payment.”

In December 2010 the applicant brought a fresh action for damages against the Supreme Court itself before the Budapest Regional Court. It alleged that the 2009 judgment had infringed EU law (in particular Article 17 of the Sixth VAT Directive) by failing to treat the activity as taxable and by misapplying Aardappelenbewaarplaats. Relying on the CJEU’s Köbler case-law, the applicant also sought a preliminary ruling on whether the Supreme Court could be held liable for that infringement.

The Regional Court rejected the claim in May 2011 without making a reference. It considered that the Supreme Court had been bound by the way the original claim had been framed, that it had in any event examined the relevant EU law of its own motion, and that Köbler was inapplicable because the action had been brought against the court rather than the State. On appeal the Budapest Court of Appeal likewise refused a reference and dismissed the claim in August 2012, holding that the applicant’s failure to invoke EU law in the original proceedings rendered the damages action unfounded.

The applicant then sought review by the Kúria and again requested a preliminary ruling. It proposed four questions covering the applicability of Köbler principles to an action against the Supreme Court, the correct interpretation of the Sixth Directive, whether a last-instance court must raise EU-law points of its own motion, and whether a sufficiently serious breach had occurred. In a procedural order of 2 October 2013 the Kúria declined to refer, stating that the first question was undisputed and that the remaining questions fell outside the scope of a damages action. A further request was rejected in December 2013. In its final judgment of 11 December 2013 the Kúria confirmed that, because the applicant had not raised the EU-law arguments in 2009, procedural rules had prevented the Supreme Court from examining them; the Supreme Court therefore bore no liability.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing that the Kúria’s refusal to refer was arbitrary and therefore violated the right to a fair trial. It also asked the Constitutional Court itself to make a reference to the CJEU on whether an arbitrary refusal by a last-instance court could breach Article 47 of the Charter. On 19 May 2014 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible, holding that it had no jurisdiction to review decisions on whether to refer and that a constitutional complaint under the relevant statutory provision could not be used to obtain a preliminary ruling.

These successive refusals to refer, and the reasons given for them, form the core of the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 of the Convention that it was denied a fair hearing.

The case of Taziyeva and Others v. Russia (application no. 32394/11) concerns eight related Russian nationals (three adult siblings, plus one sibling’s wife and three minor children) who lived together at a family compound at 35 Yuzhnaya Street, Nasyr-Kort, Nazran, Ingushetia. They alleged that on 3 March 2011 State servicemen carried out an unlawful search of their home and deliberately caused an explosion that destroyed the property, in violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicants’ brother, Ali T. (“Magas”), had long been suspected of leading illegal armed groups and organising terrorist attacks. He was arrested in June 2010 and later convicted of terrorism offences. The applicants claimed they had had no contact with him since 1998; the Government cited (but did not produce) witness statements indicating otherwise, including that his wife had lived at the address. The same house had been searched without a warrant in December 2005 as part of an operation targeting Ali T.; the Court had already found a violation of Article 8 in that earlier case (Taziyeva and Others v. Russia, no. 50757/06).

On 21 February 2011 an investigator sought, and on 22 February the Lefortovskiy District Court of Moscow granted, a warrant under the Code of Criminal Procedure to search the address (Ali T.’s registered residence) for documents, weapons, ammunition or explosives linked to the ongoing investigation of the terrorist organisation Imarat Kavkaz. On 3 March 2011 armed personnel using an armoured personnel carrier surrounded the compound, entered and searched it. The third applicant signed the warrant at 2 p.m. Occupants and neighbours were then moved a safe distance away; an explosion followed.

Official reports recorded that an improvised explosive device (a 125 mm artillery shell with detonator) had been found in a basement. After evacuation, a bomb-disposal expert attempted deactivation with a water cannon; the attempt failed, the device exploded and a second, previously undetected device also detonated. One dwelling was completely destroyed, another was rendered uninhabitable, two cars were wrecked and a storage building was looted. The applicants produced a video of the aftermath. They denied any explosives had been present, alleged the search had been conducted without proper documentation or attesting witnesses, and claimed they had been threatened, interrogated about Ali T. and forced to sign papers. They asserted the servicemen had announced an intention to blow the house up and had then done so, destroying or stealing household goods.

A military investigator initially refused to open a criminal inquiry into abuse of power or theft. After further steps (questioning of the bomb expert, FSB officers, attesting witnesses and the third applicant), a 22 November 2011 decision again refused to investigate, finding the search lawfully authorised, conducted with witnesses and without violence or threats. The explosion was held to be an unavoidable consequence of a justified attempt to neutralise a genuine IED discovered at the address of a known terrorist; no time had existed to remove belongings. The applicants did not appeal that decision. A separate judicial complaint about investigative delay was dismissed as premature because an inquiry was then still under way.

These facts form the core of the dispute: whether the search and subsequent destruction of the applicants’ home and property were lawful and necessary, or instead constituted an arbitrary intrusion, inhuman treatment and unjustified interference with possessions.

The applicants, eight related Russian nationals (siblings, a spouse and children) living at 35 Yuzhnaya Street in Nasyr-Kort, Ingushetia, alleged that on 3 March 2011 State servicemen unlawfully searched their home and then destroyed it and their property via a deliberate explosion. They claimed violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment via threats and intimidation), Article 8 (unlawful search and interference with home) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (destruction of property). They are siblings or close relatives of Ali T. (“Magas”), a convicted terrorist leader of the “Imarat Kavkaz” group who was arrested in 2010 and later sentenced to life imprisonment. The applicants said they had had no contact with him since 1998; the Government pointed to evidence of later contact and his registered residence at the address (though one applicant was recorded elsewhere).

A 2013 ECHR judgment (no. 50757/06) had already found an Article 8 violation for a 2005 warrantless search of the same house linked to Ali T.

On 21 February 2011 an investigator sought a search warrant as part of the terrorism investigation, citing the possibility that weapons, ammunition or explosives were stored at Ali T.’s registered address. The Lefortovskiy District Court in Moscow authorised the search the next day under Articles 165 and 182 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, noting the case’s complexity and secrecy.

On 3 March servicemen arrived with an armoured personnel carrier and other vehicles, surrounded the area and searched the courtyard and two dwellings. The third applicant signed the warrant at 2 p.m. The family, neighbours and vehicles were then moved away; an explosion followed. One newly finished house (with basement and garage) was completely destroyed along with two cars; the second house was badly damaged and rendered uninhabitable. Technical buildings were looted or damaged. A video clip showed the aftermath.

The applicants said no proper warrant or attesting witnesses were produced, they were threatened and interrogated about Ali T., forced to sign documents, and that a superior officer had radioed that nothing had been found before the house was deliberately blown up. They denied any explosives had ever been present and claimed valuables were stolen.

The Government maintained that the warrant was shown and signed, the search conducted with two attesting witnesses, and that an improvised explosive device (a 125 mm artillery shell with detonator) was found in a basement. Everyone was evacuated; a bomb-disposal expert’s attempt to deactivate it with a water cannon failed, causing an explosion that also detonated a second, previously undetected device. The resulting destruction was therefore an unintended consequence of lawful safety measures. Official reports recorded one IED, the failed deactivation, the explosion(s) and the damage; identity documents and photographs were recovered from the debris. Local police later issued a press release describing two IEDs destroyed by controlled blasts.

The third applicant immediately complained to prosecutors and police, denying any IEDs and alleging a set-up. Neighbours confirmed the evacuation and two explosions. A military investigation ultimately refused, on 22 November 2011, to open a criminal case for abuse of power or theft. It found the search lawful, the IED genuine, no threats or violence, and the deactivation attempt justified to protect lives. The applicants did not appeal that decision. An earlier Article 125 CCrP court complaint about investigative inaction was dismissed because an inquiry was still under way.

These facts—disputed authorisation and conduct of the search, the presence or planting of explosives, the circumstances of the explosion, alleged intimidation, and the resulting total or partial destruction of the family home and belongings—form the core of the alleged Convention violations.

The case of Harisch v. Germany (Application no. 50053/16), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 11 April 2019 (final on 9 September 2019), concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). The German applicant, Klaus Harisch, claimed that domestic courts refused to refer questions of EU law to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) for a preliminary ruling and failed to give adequate reasons for that refusal.

Harisch and a co-founder established T.AG, a directory enquiries company that purchased subscriber data from Deutsche Telekom AG (DTAG) for a fee. In 2007–2008 DTAG was ordered to refund part of those fees as excessive. In 2005 Harisch sued DTAG in the Regional Court, alleging that the overcharging had forced him and his co-founder to dilute their shareholdings ahead of T.AG’s stock-market launch and had lowered the company’s valuation, thereby causing him personal loss. The Regional Court dismissed the action on 28 May 2013.

On appeal Harisch discussed the interpretation of EU competition law (then Article 86 TEC, now Article 102 TFEU) by the CJEU and the Federal Court of Justice, but did not initially request a reference. At the oral hearing the Court of Appeal indicated that the relevant CJEU case-law was clear and that EU law did not apply. Harisch then asked for the proceedings to be stayed and for a preliminary ruling; after the hearing he submitted a proposed question asking whether Article 86 TEC precluded national rules that categorically excluded a dominant undertaking’s liability for losses suffered by founding shareholders who had been forced to dilute their holdings in order to avert the bankruptcy of the damaged company.

On 2 July 2014 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that Harisch fell outside the protective purpose of the EU provisions and therefore could not claim damages under them. The court examined the CJEU’s case-law in detail, concluded that it did not support Harisch’s reading, and found no uncertainty requiring a reference. It also refused leave to appeal on points of law, stating that the legal question lacked fundamental significance and that there were “no doubts concerning the scope and interpretation” of the relevant provisions.

Harisch lodged a complaint against the refusal of leave, repeating his request for a CJEU reference and proposing two slightly refined questions. On 14 April 2015 the Federal Court of Justice dismissed the complaint without giving detailed reasons (as permitted by Article 544 of the Code of Civil Procedure), holding that the case was not of fundamental significance, that procedural complaints were unconvincing, and that neither the development of the law nor the need for uniform adjudication required a decision by the court of last instance.

Harisch then filed an Anhörungsrüge (complaint of a violation of the right to be heard), arguing that the Federal Court of Justice had not adequately explained why a reference was unnecessary. On 18 May 2015 that court rejected the complaint, stating that it had considered the submissions but found them unpersuasive and that a last-instance court was not obliged to give more extensive reasons. On 25 February 2016 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain Harisch’s constitutional complaint, again without reasons.

These successive refusals, and the varying degrees of reasoning supplied for them, form the factual core of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation.
