The case of Aboya Boa Jean v. Malta concerns the detention of Serge Aboya Boa Jean, an Ivorian national born in 1978, from 10 September to 8 November 2016. He arrived in Malta by plane from Russia on 10 September 2016, presenting a national passport while claiming prior refugee status in Armenia after fleeing war in Ivory Coast years earlier. He immediately told authorities of his background, his time in Armenia (which he left due to racial insecurity and fear of return to Ivory Coast), and his wish to seek asylum in Malta. Authorities found him carrying false Italian identification documents and a ticket to Italy; he reportedly said he obtained the documents from a friend and intended to transit Malta en route to Italy.

He was denied entry for lacking proper documentation, questioned further (providing consistent details of his history), and had his documents confiscated. That same day the police issued a detention order under the Immigration Act and Reception of Asylum Seekers Regulations. The stated grounds were that the elements of his international-protection claim could not be established without detention, particularly given a risk of absconding. He was told of his right to appeal to the Immigration Appeals Board within three days, of automatic Board review within seven working days (extendable by seven), of further reviews every two months, and of free legal aid. He was taken to Safi Barracks detention centre. On 20 September 2016 he formally registered as an asylum-seeker.

A possible Board hearing on 30 September 2016 was postponed to 5 October (the applicant disputes that the first sitting occurred and notes the absence of his legal-aid lawyer). At the 5 October review the Board, sitting with the applicant, his lawyers and an interpreter, openly admitted it had missed the statutory seven-day deadline because one member was at an overseas conference and because its part-time members met only weekly, lacked administrative support and handled a heavy caseload. Police and the Board chair identified “fear of absconding” as the main justification. The applicant’s lawyers argued that he had from the outset given consistent, unconcealed information about his identity, nationality, itinerary, prior status and reasons for flight, so that all relevant elements were already known; detention was therefore neither provided by law nor necessary or proportionate. The Board rejected the challenge, holding that the asylum claim remained undetermined, that departure would prevent the Refugee Commissioner from obtaining further information, that the Italy ticket showed an intention not to remain in Malta, and that possession of a forged document indicated a continuing absconding risk. It asked the Principal Immigration Officer to verify whether all elements had been transmitted and to consider alternatives if detention continued solely because of ongoing asylum proceedings.

On 21 October 2016 the applicant applied to the Court of Magistrates under Article 409A of the Criminal Code, repeating that there had been no individualised assessment, that it was unclear what further elements were required, and that a risk of absconding could not justify detention throughout the entire asylum process. The court, on the same day, upheld the detention, observing that the same arguments had already been decided by the Board, that further verification (specifically of Armenian refugee status) was still needed, and that the absconding risk made determination of the claim impossible without detention.

The applicant was released on 8 November 2016 subject to daily police reporting. These events form the factual basis of his complaints that the detention itself was unlawful and arbitrary and that the available review procedures were neither speedy nor effective.

The case of Aboya Boa Jean v. Malta (Application no. 62676/16) concerns allegations by an Ivorian national that his immigration detention in Malta was unlawful and arbitrary (Article 5 § 1 ECHR) and that available remedies to challenge it were neither speedy nor effective (Article 5 § 4).

The applicant, Serge Aboya Boa Jean (born 1978), arrived in Malta by plane from Russia on 10 September 2016. He presented a national passport but carried false Italian identity documents and a ticket to Italy. He immediately informed authorities he was a refugee from Ivory Coast (having fled war years earlier) who had obtained asylum in Armenia, which he left due to racial discrimination and insecurity. He expressed intent to seek asylum in Malta, fearing return to Ivory Coast.

Denied entry for insufficient documentation, he was questioned that day at police headquarters. A detention order was issued under the Immigration Act and Reception of Asylum Seekers Regulations on the ground that elements of his asylum claim could not be determined without detention, particularly given a risk of absconding. He was told of the right to appeal to the Immigration Appeals Board (IAB) within three days, of automatic IAB review within seven working days (extendable by seven), of further reviews every two months if detention continued, and of free legal aid. He was taken to Safi Barracks detention centre. He formally applied for asylum on 20 September 2016 and was registered as an asylum-seeker.

The first IAB review of detention lawfulness (required within seven working days of the order) was delayed. A possible 30 September hearing was adjourned to 5 October (applicant contests its occurrence and notes his legal-aid lawyer’s absence). On 5 October the applicant appeared with lawyers and an interpreter. The Board explained the delay: a member had been at an overseas conference, and the part-time Board (meeting weekly, lacking administrative support) could not meet statutory deadlines. Police and the Board cited “fear of absconding.” The applicant argued he had from first contact consistently and honestly disclosed his identity, nationality, itinerary, prior refugee status, flight reasons and asylum intent, so the statutory ground was inapplicable; detention was neither necessary nor proportionate, as police had not shown any elements could not be obtained without it.

The IAB confirmed detention the same day: refugee-status elements remained undetermined; departure would prevent the applicant from supplying information to the refugee commissioner; the Italy ticket showed he did not intend to stay; and the forged document indicated absconding risk. It directed the Principal Immigration Officer to verify whether all elements had been passed to the commissioner and to consider alternatives (e.g., reporting or residence conditions) if detention continued.

On 21 October 2016 the applicant applied to the Court of Magistrates under Criminal Code Article 409A, arguing absence of individualised assessment, unclear remaining “elements,” and that risk of absconding could not be treated in isolation or justify detention throughout asylum proceedings. Police stated they still required documentary confirmation of Armenian refugee status. The court rejected the application the same day, holding the issues had already been decided by the IAB and that further verifications plus absconding risk rendered detention lawful.

The applicant was released on 8 November 2016 subject to daily police reporting. (He later pleaded guilty to using a false passport and received a three-year conditional discharge; his asylum claim was rejected in March 2017 and he appealed.)

These facts—detention from 10 September to 8 November 2016 on the stated ground, the delayed first review, the IAB and magistrates’ decisions, and the applicant’s consistent disclosures—form the core of the alleged Article 5 violations.

The case of Kosaitė-Čypienė and Others v. Lithuania (Application no. 69489/12) concerned four Lithuanian women who alleged that domestic law effectively prevented healthcare professionals from assisting planned home births, thereby violating their rights under Article 8 of the Convention (respect for private and family life). The applicants, all of reproductive age and residing in Vilnius, had previously given birth at home with the help of an unlicensed doula, J.I.Š., whose activities later became the subject of criminal proceedings.

The first applicant (born 1983, three children) had a negative hospital birth experience in 2009, followed by an uncomplicated home birth in 2011 assisted by J.I.Š. During her third pregnancy in 2012, after J.I.Š. faced charges, she requested assistance from two public hospitals for a planned home birth. Both refused, citing Medical Regulation MN 40:2006, which barred midwives from assisting “regular” births at home. She then asked the Ministry of Health either to guarantee professional assistance or to amend secondary legislation. The Ministry refused on 5 July 2012, relying on unanimous specialist advice that even low-risk births were safest in hospital (owing to unforeseeable complications requiring immediate specialist care), Lithuania’s success in reducing maternal and neonatal mortality through hospital-based services, and the need to balance individual rights against public-health interests. She gave birth at home on 11 July 2012 without qualified assistance, claiming she thereby risked her own and the baby’s life.

The second applicant (born 1979, three children) had three successful home births with J.I.Š. (2006–2011). Pregnant again in 2012, she received identical hospital and Ministry refusals. She stated she was “firmly resolved” to give birth at home regardless of professional assistance (due date November 2012).

The third applicant (born 1982) had two uncomplicated home births with J.I.Š. (2009–2010). After becoming active in the home-birth NGO gimimas.lt, she requested hospital assistance in September 2012 (three Vilnius hospitals refused) and then petitioned the Ministry. The Ministry again refused (16 October 2012), reiterating safety concerns and noting that the Court’s Ternovszky v. Hungary judgment did not impose a general obligation to permit home-birth assistance. She was due in March 2013 and likewise resolved to give birth at home. She later challenged the Ministry’s refusal in administrative courts, which dismissed her claim: the Supreme Administrative Court held that existing law (which confined qualified perinatal care to licensed hospitals) struck a fair balance between privacy and health protection, and that she remained free to choose a hospital offering privacy-enhancing conditions.

The fourth applicant (born 1975) had three home births with J.I.Š. (2001–2011). She stated she dared not become pregnant again while home birth remained unregulated, given the pending charges against J.I.Š.

Context included the 2012 founding of gimimas.lt, professional bodies’ opposition to home-birth midwifery, and criminal proceedings against J.I.Š. for unauthorised economic activity (Criminal Code Art. 202). She was ultimately acquitted by the Supreme Court in 2018 on the grounds that home-birth assistance was neither criminalised nor forbidden, although her conduct had been unlawful; the indictment also failed to prove entrepreneurial income.

At the relevant time Lithuanian law (Laws on Medical Practice, Nursing and Midwifery Practice, and Health-Care System, plus Ministerial regulations) required doctors and midwives to practise only in licensed healthcare institutions and explicitly prohibited midwives from assisting normal births at home. Home birth itself was not banned, but professional assistance was unavailable. (Legislation later authorised regulated home births from 2019, after the facts of the case.)

These circumstances formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the legal framework deterred qualified assistance and thereby interfered with their choice of the circumstances of childbirth.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Kosaitė-Čypienė and Others v. Lithuania (Application no. 69489/12) concerned four Lithuanian women who alleged that the absence of a legal framework permitting qualified healthcare professionals to assist at planned home births violated their right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention. They argued that Lithuanian law effectively dissuaded midwives and doctors from providing such assistance, forcing them either to risk unassisted home births or to give birth in hospitals against their wishes.

The first applicant (born 1983) had a negative hospital experience in 2009, describing staff as rude. She subsequently had a successful unassisted home birth in 2011 with an unlicensed doula. During her third pregnancy in 2012 she requested two public hospitals to provide medical support for a planned home birth; both refused, citing Medical Regulation MN 40:2006, which confined midwives to licensed healthcare institutions and prohibited them from attending normal births at home. The Ministry of Health likewise declined to guarantee assistance or amend the rules, stressing that even low-risk births could involve unforeseeable complications requiring hospital facilities, that Lithuania had achieved low maternal and neonatal mortality through hospital-based care, and that shifting liability onto individual practitioners was unacceptable. She gave birth at home on 11 July 2012 without qualified help, thereby, in her view, endangering herself and the child.

The second applicant (born 1979) had three prior successful home births with the same doula. In April 2012, after the doula faced criminal charges, she made identical requests to hospitals and the Ministry, which were refused on the same grounds. She remained “firmly resolved” to give birth at home regardless of professional assistance (due date November 2012).

The third applicant (born 1982) likewise had two uneventful home births with the doula. After becoming active in a home-birth advocacy NGO, she requested three Vilnius hospitals and the Ministry to allow professional attendance at her third birth; all refused. She also brought unsuccessful administrative-court proceedings. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court and the Supreme Administrative Court held that the existing regulations governed only hospital births and did not expressly prohibit home births; they considered that the State had struck a fair balance by offering well-equipped maternity wards (including family presence and “newborn-friendly” environments) that protected both maternal privacy and health. She too declared her intention to give birth at home irrespective of medical support (due March 2013).

The fourth applicant (born 1975) had three previous home births with the doula and stated that she would not risk a further pregnancy until the legal position of home births was clarified.

All four applicants had previously relied on the unlicensed doula J.I.Š., who between 1999 and 2011 attended 36 home births. After a neonatal death in 2011, prosecutors charged her with unauthorised professional activity. She was ultimately acquitted by the Supreme Court in 2018 on the ground that home births themselves were neither criminalised nor forbidden, although her lack of medical qualification rendered her actions unlawful.

At the material time Lithuanian law required doctors and midwives to practise only in licensed institutions; Medical Regulation MN 40:2006 explicitly barred midwives from attending regular home births. The Ministry of Health and professional associations (midwives, obstetricians, doctors) uniformly opposed home-birth assistance on safety grounds. Subsequent legislative amendments (2019) later authorised midwives to attend low-risk home births under strict conditions, but those changes post-dated the applicants’ complaints.

The applicants contended that this regulatory vacuum, combined with the criminal investigation of the doula, created a chilling effect that prevented them from obtaining professional help for a private, intimate choice—home birth—thereby interfering with their Article 8 rights.

The case of Kosaitė-Čypienė and Others v. Lithuania (Application no. 69489/12) concerned four Lithuanian women who alleged that domestic law violated their rights under Article 8 of the Convention by deterring healthcare professionals from assisting planned home births. The applicants, all of reproductive age and with prior experience of childbirth, sought professional medical support at home for subsequent deliveries but faced refusals grounded in Lithuanian regulations that confined births to licensed hospital settings.

The first applicant had a distressing hospital birth in 2009, followed by an unassisted home birth in 2011 with unlicensed doula J.I.Š. For her third pregnancy in 2012 she requested assistance from two public hospitals, both of which declined, citing Medical Regulation MN 40:2006, which barred midwives from attending regular births outside healthcare institutions. The Ministry of Health likewise refused to amend the rules or guarantee assistance, emphasizing that even low-risk births could require emergency hospital facilities unavailable at home. She ultimately delivered at home without qualified help.

The second applicant had three prior home births with J.I.Š. For her fourth pregnancy she received identical hospital and ministerial refusals. She remained determined to deliver at home regardless of professional support.

The third applicant, having had two successful home births with J.I.Š., joined the advocacy group gimimas.lt. Three Vilnius hospitals refused her 2012 requests for home assistance, stating no legal basis existed. The Ministry of Health repeated its safety-based objections. She later brought administrative proceedings; both the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court and the Supreme Administrative Court rejected her claims, holding that the regulations governed only hospital births and that the absence of home-birth rules did not prohibit them. The courts stressed a constitutional balance between privacy and the protection of maternal and neonatal health, noting that women could choose equipped maternity wards and have family present.

The fourth applicant, who had three prior home births with J.I.Š., refrained from a further pregnancy because of the legal uncertainty and pending criminal proceedings against the doula.

Criminal investigations into unlicensed home-birth assistance, including charges against J.I.Š. under Article 202 of the Criminal Code (unauthorized economic activity), formed the backdrop. J.I.Š. was eventually acquitted by the Supreme Court in 2018, which found that home births themselves were neither criminalized nor forbidden, though her unlicensed medical acts were unlawful.

At the material time, Lithuanian law required obstetric and midwifery care to be provided only in licensed Level II or III hospitals equipped for 24-hour specialist coverage. Midwives could visit homes for certain services but were expressly prohibited from attending normal deliveries there. Healthcare professionals practising outside licensed institutions risked disciplinary or criminal liability. No statutory framework existed for planned home births, and medical associations uniformly opposed them on safety grounds. The State maintained that hospital births, with modern equipment and family presence, best protected health, while shifting liability to individual practitioners was unacceptable. Subsequent 2018–2019 legislative amendments permitting low-risk home births under strict conditions post-dated the facts giving rise to the complaint.

The applicants argued that the legal vacuum and associated deterrents left them no realistic option of a professionally attended home birth, thereby interfering with their private-life choices regarding the circumstances of childbirth.

The case of Chiarello v. Germany (Application no. 497/17) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 December 2016 by a German national, Gaetano Chiarello (born 1977), a former prison officer at Saarbrücken prison. He alleged that criminal proceedings against him were unfair and excessively long, in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that his automatic dismissal from civil service violated Article 7. On 8 January 2018, the Court gave notice only of the length-of-proceedings complaint; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

In April 2007, prison authorities discovered a mobile phone smuggled into the prison in December 2006. An investigation opened against the applicant in May 2007; telephone surveillance and other measures were ordered in October 2007. He was questioned in January 2008. On 13 May 2008 the public prosecutor indicted him (together with seven co-accused) for accepting a €200 bribe and smuggling the phone to an inmate. Counsel were appointed and given file access, including surveillance recordings; an interlocutory appeal on counsel appointment was decided in April 2009.

Main proceedings were instituted on 8 January 2010. After fourteen hearings beginning 3 May 2010, the District Court convicted the applicant on 23 September 2010 of taking a bribe and imposed a suspended sentence of one year and four months. He was immediately suspended from duty with a 25 % salary reduction. He and several co-accused (plus the prosecutor) appealed.

After a change of counsel in September 2011, the Regional Court held seven hearings between 25 October and 18 November 2011 and acquitted all defendants (written judgment 23 December 2011). The prosecutor immediately appealed on points of law. On 21 January 2013 the Court of Appeal quashed the acquittal and remitted the case.

Fresh appeal hearings began only on 11 February 2015 and concluded on 2 April 2015. The Regional Court convicted the applicant, imposing an eight-month suspended sentence and declaring three months already served as compensation for delay. It expressly took into account the eight-year lapse since the 2006 offence, the investigation ongoing since 2007, and the applicant’s lengthy suspension on reduced pay. It rejected discontinuation as disproportionate. The applicant’s further appeal on points of law was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded on 29 April 2016; the conviction became final on 12 May 2016.

A constitutional complaint lodged on 2 June 2016 was not admitted (4 July 2016). Upon the judgment becoming final, the applicant automatically lost civil-servant status under s. 24 of the Status of Civil Servants Act because the sentence exceeded six months for an official bribery offence. Interim-relief applications seeking continuation of pay and status were rejected by the Administrative Court (12 July 2016) and the Court of Appeal (6 October 2016).

The overall proceedings thus lasted from the opening of the investigation in May 2007 until May 2016—approximately nine years—punctuated by a particularly lengthy period of inactivity (January 2013–February 2015) after remittal. Domestic courts applied the “execution approach” (declaring part of the sentence already served) rather than reducing the penalty itself, in line with Federal Court of Justice case-law designed to preserve the sentence’s collateral effects (including loss of civil-service status).

The case of Chiarello v. Germany (Application no. 497/17) originated in a complaint lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 December 2016 by a German national and former prison officer, Gaetano Chiarello. He alleged that criminal proceedings against him had been unfair and excessively lengthy, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that his automatic dismissal from civil service following conviction violated Article 7. On 8 January 2018 the Court communicated only the length-of-proceedings complaint to the German Government; all other complaints were declared inadmissible.

The underlying events began in December 2006 when a mobile telephone was smuggled into Saarbrücken prison. An investigation against the applicant was opened in May 2007. Telephone surveillance and other measures were authorised in October 2007; he was questioned in January 2008. A bill of indictment charging him with taking a bribe of €200 and supplying the telephone to an inmate was filed on 13 May 2008, together with charges against seven co-accused.

After appointment of defence counsel and an interlocutory appeal concerning one co-accused that was resolved in April 2009, the District Court opened the main trial on 8 January 2010. Fourteen hearings culminated in a conviction on 23 September 2010: one year and four months’ imprisonment, suspended. The applicant was immediately suspended from duty and his salary reduced by 25 per cent. He and several co-accused appealed.

Following a change of counsel, the Regional Court held seven hearings between 25 October and 18 November 2011 and acquitted all defendants. The public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law the same day. On 21 January 2013 the Court of Appeal quashed the acquittal and remitted the case.

New appeal proceedings did not begin until 11 February 2015. After further hearings the Regional Court, on 2 April 2015, convicted the applicant of taking a bribe and imposed eight months’ imprisonment, suspended, declaring three of those months already served as compensation for delay. The court expressly took into account that more than eight years had elapsed since the offence, that the applicant had been under investigation since 2007 and that he had suffered salary reductions after his first-instance conviction. It rejected a request to discontinue the proceedings, holding that the delay, though excessive, did not outweigh the need for punishment.

An appeal on points of law was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded on 29 April 2016; the conviction became final on 12 May 2016. A subsequent constitutional complaint was not admitted. By operation of section 24 of the Status of Civil Servants Act the final sentence of at least six months for an official act of bribery automatically terminated the applicant’s civil-service status. Applications for interim relief to preserve his salary and status were unsuccessful.

The relevant period therefore ran from the opening of the investigation in May 2007 until the proceedings became final in May 2016—almost nine years. The most conspicuous period of inactivity occurred after remittal (January 2013–February 2015). Domestic law provided two complementary remedies: the “execution approach” developed by the Federal Court of Justice, under which a portion of the sentence is declared already served, and a separate claim for monetary compensation under sections 198–199 of the Courts Act. The Regional Court applied the former by treating three months as served. The Government later argued that this, together with the possibility of a compensation action, afforded sufficient redress.

The case of Chiarello v. Germany originated in an application by Gaetano Chiarello, a German prison officer born in 1977, who alleged that criminal proceedings against him were unfair and excessively lengthy (Article 6 § 1 of the Convention) and that his automatic dismissal from public service violated Article 7. Only the length complaint was communicated to the Government.

In December 2006 a mobile phone was smuggled into Saarbrücken prison, where the applicant worked. The prison authorities discovered this in April 2007 and opened an investigation against him in May 2007. Telephone surveillance and other measures were authorised in October 2007. He was summoned and interviewed by police in January 2008. On 13 May 2008 the public prosecutor filed an indictment charging him (together with seven co-accused) with accepting a €200 bribe and smuggling the phone to an inmate.

Appointment of defence counsel and sequential access to voluminous files (including surveillance recordings) caused further delay; an appeal concerning counsel for one co-accused was not resolved until April 2009. Main proceedings were instituted on 8 January 2010 and the first of fourteen District Court hearings took place on 3 May 2010. On 23 September 2010 the court convicted the applicant of taking a bribe and imposed a suspended sentence of one year and four months. He was immediately suspended from duty and his salary reduced by 25 per cent.

Appeals by the applicant, four co-accused and the prosecutor followed. After a change of counsel in September 2011 the Regional Court held seven hearings between 25 October and 18 November 2011 and acquitted all defendants. The prosecutor’s appeal on points of law led the Court of Appeal, on 21 January 2013, to quash the acquittals and remit the case.

A two-year delay then occurred because the remitted case could not be scheduled until February 2015. After hearings ending on 2 April 2015 the Regional Court convicted the applicant and imposed an eight-month suspended prison sentence, declaring three months already served as compensation for the excessive length. The court expressly took into account that the offence dated from 2006, that the applicant had been under investigation since 2007, and that he had suffered prolonged professional and financial detriment. It refused to discontinue the proceedings, holding that the prejudice did not outweigh the need for punishment. The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded on 29 April 2016; the judgment became final on 12 May 2016. A constitutional complaint was not admitted.

Under section 24 of the Status of Civil Servants Act the final conviction automatically terminated the applicant’s civil-servant status (a sentence of at least six months for an official bribery offence). Administrative courts rejected his applications for interim relief preserving his status and salary.

The overall proceedings thus lasted from May 2007 until May 2016—almost nine years—with a particularly unexplained two-year gap after remittal. Domestic courts applied the “execution approach” developed by the Federal Court of Justice, first fixing the sentence according to guilt and then declaring part of it served to compensate for state-caused delay. The applicant maintained that this compensation was inadequate and that the automatic loss of office constituted an additional, unforeseeable penalty.

The case of Kurt v. Austria (Application no. 62903/15) was brought by Senay Kurt against Austria under Article 34 of the Convention. She alleged that the authorities failed to protect her and her two children from her violent husband E., resulting in him murdering their son A. (born 2004). Complaints under Articles 2, 3 and 8 were communicated; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The couple married in 2003 and also had a daughter B. (born 2005). On 10 July 2010 the applicant reported that E. had beaten her for years; police noted injuries and issued a 14-day barring order under s. 38a of the Security Police Act requiring him to stay away from the family home, her parents’ apartment and surrounding areas. He complied. Criminal charges followed. In January 2011 he was convicted of bodily harm and dangerous threatening (pushing and slapping the applicant, plus threats to relatives) and received a three-month suspended sentence. The applicant refused to testify.

On 22 May 2012 the applicant, accompanied by a counsellor from a violence-protection centre, filed for divorce, citing continuous threats and violence. That afternoon she reported E. to police for rape and dangerous threats. She described an escalation on 19 May during a discussion of separation: E. choked her, pushed her onto a couch, told her she was obliged to have sex as his wife, and raped her (she did not resist out of fear). He had been violent from the start of the marriage. After the 2010 incident he had sought treatment for gambling addiction and mental-health issues; she had given him another chance. Violence and daily threats (“I will kill you”, “I will kill our children in front of you”, “I will hang myself in front of your parents’ door”) had resumed since February/March 2012. He regularly beat her and sometimes slapped the children, confiscated her phone and locked her in. Police photographed haematoma and scratches; a medical examination found no typical rape injuries. Children confirmed the beatings when interviewed by a specially trained officer.

A new 14-day barring order was issued the same day, removing E. from the home and barring him from it, surrounding areas and the parents’ apartment. He was described as mildly agitated but cooperative; he denied violence and rape (claiming sex occurred after he “convinced” her) but later admitted occasional “educational” slaps of the children. Criminal proceedings for rape, bodily harm and dangerous threats were opened. The barring order was reviewed and confirmed lawful on 23 May. On 24 May E. attended a police station of his own accord to ask about contacting the children and was re-questioned.

On 25 May E. entered the children’s school, asked a teacher (unaware of family problems) to speak privately with A., then shot the boy in the head in the basement (B. witnessed it). An arrest warrant issued immediately. A. died two days later. E. was found dead by suicide in his car; a note dated 24 May showed he had planned to kill both children and himself because he “could not live without them”. Witnesses described E. as friendly and calm that morning.

In 2014 the applicant brought official-liability proceedings, arguing the prosecutor should have sought pre-trial detention on 22 May because a real and immediate risk existed, the barring order could not cover the school, and separation-phase statistics plus specific threats demonstrated heightened danger. The Regional Court dismissed the claim: on the information then available there was no immediate risk to A.’s life. E. had never been publicly aggressive, had not acted on years of threats, had complied with the 2010 order, showed no possession of a weapon, and appeared cooperative after the new order, suggesting reduced tension. Detention was a last resort under Article 5; the barring order was a proportionate less-intrusive measure. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld this assessment, emphasising that general knowledge of homicide risks during separation could not substitute for specific facts indicating a real individual risk of serious further offences.

The case of Kurt v. Austria (Application no. 62903/15) concerns an alleged failure by Austrian authorities to protect the applicant, Senay Kurt, and her children from domestic violence by her husband E., culminating in the murder of their son.

The applicant married E. in 2003; they had two children, A. (born 2004) and B. (born 2005). On 10 July 2010, she reported that E. had beaten her for years, with the situation worsening due to his gambling addiction, debts and job loss. Police observed injuries (haematomas) and issued a 14-day barring order under section 38a of the Security Police Act, requiring E. to stay away from the family home, the applicant’s parents’ home and surrounding areas. They provided a leaflet on seeking a longer temporary restraining order. E. complied. He was later convicted of bodily harm and dangerous threats (against the applicant, his brother and nephew) and received a three-month suspended sentence. The applicant refused to testify.

On 22 May 2012, the applicant filed for divorce, citing ongoing threats and violence, including injuries from an escalation the previous Saturday. That afternoon she reported E. to police for rape and dangerous threats. She described how, on 19 May, during an argument about possible separation, E. had choked her, pushed her, raped her (she did not resist out of fear) and made repeated threats including “I will kill you”, “I will kill our children in front of you”, and suicide threats. Violence had occurred throughout the marriage; daily threats had resumed since March 2012 after E.’s gambling restarted. He sometimes slapped the children and confined her. Police photographed her injuries (neck haematoma, chin scratches) but a medical exam found no typical rape injuries. A female officer accompanied her home, issued another barring order (covering the same locations) after interviewing E. (who denied violence but admitted sex) and the children (who confirmed beatings). E. was cooperative and mildly agitated. The prosecutor opened proceedings for rape, bodily harm and threats, and ordered child interviews (which confirmed the beatings). The barring order was later confirmed as lawful.

On 24 May E. visited the police station unprompted, inquiring about seeing the children; he admitted occasional “educational” slaps (not to the face) and said the children were “his everything.” On 25 May he entered the children’s school, asked to speak privately to A., then shot him in the head in the basement (B. witnessed this). An arrest warrant issued; E. was found dead by suicide in his car later that morning. His note (dated 24 May) revealed plans to kill both children and himself, stating he could not live without his family. A. died on 27 May. Witnesses described E. as friendly and calm that morning; the applicant had seen him near the school and planned to warn the teacher the next day. She noted E. had called repeatedly after the barring order, wanting to see the family.

The applicant later brought official-liability proceedings, arguing the prosecutor should have sought E.’s pre-trial detention on 22 May given a real, immediate risk (especially amid separation, specific death threats to the children, and the barring order’s inability to cover the school). Domestic courts (Regional Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court) dismissed the claim, finding no immediate risk to A.’s life based on information then available: E. had complied with the 2010 order, shown no public aggression or gun possession, cooperated after the new order, and a less intrusive measure (barring order) had been used. Pre-trial detention was an ultima ratio, and general statistics on separation-related homicides were insufficient without case-specific indicators.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 3 and 8 of the Convention due to inadequate protective measures. (The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber.)

The case of Kurt v. Austria (Application no. 62903/15) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 December 2015 by Senay Kurt, an Austrian national born in 1978. She alleged that Austrian authorities failed to protect her and her two children from her violent husband E., resulting in the murder of their son A. Police noted injuries and issued a 14-day barring order under section 38a of the Security Police Act, excluding E. from the family home, her parents’ apartment and surrounding areas. He complied. Criminal charges followed; on 10 January 2011 the Graz Regional Criminal Court convicted him of bodily harm and dangerous threats, imposing a three-month suspended sentence. The applicant refused to testify.

On 22 May 2012 the applicant, accompanied by a counsellor from the Centre for Protection from Violence, filed for divorce at the St. Pölten District Court, citing continuous threats and violence, including injuries from an escalation on 19 May. Police issued another barring order requiring E. to leave the marital home and stay away from it, the applicant’s parents’ apartment and surrounding areas; his keys were confiscated. The applicant received a victim information leaflet. E. denied violence and rape but admitted sexual intercourse, claiming she initially refused then consented. The public prosecutor instituted proceedings for rape, bodily harm and dangerous threats and ordered further child interviews (which corroborated the beatings). On 23 May the Federal Police Department confirmed the barring order’s lawfulness. On 24 May E. voluntarily visited the police station, inquired about seeing the children, admitted occasional “educational” slapping (not to the face), and described the children as “his everything.”

On 25 May 2012 E. went to the children’s school, obtained permission to speak privately with A., then shot him in the head in the basement (witnessed by B., who was uninjured). Witnesses described E. as outwardly friendly and calm that morning. The applicant later stated she had seen him near the school and planned to inform teachers of family problems the next day; she feared he would kill the children in front of her.

In February 2014 the applicant brought official liability proceedings, claiming the prosecutor should have sought pre-trial detention on 22 May given a real and immediate risk of further violence (especially during separation, per statistics) and that the barring order could not cover the school. On 14 November 2014 the St. Pölten Regional Court dismissed the claim, finding no immediate risk to A.’s life based on information available: E. had complied with the 2010 order, shown no public aggression or weapons, cooperated after the 2012 order, and never acted on prior threats. Detention was an ultima ratio; a less intrusive barring order sufficed. The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 30 January 2015, stressing the prosecutor’s discretion and the lack of specific grounds for a real individual risk (particularly in public). The Supreme Court rejected an extraordinary appeal on 23 April 2015.

These facts form the core of the alleged failures to protect life, prevent ill-treatment and safeguard private/family life. (Word count: 512)

The case of Stoian v. Romania (Application no. 289/14) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Ștefan-Moshe Stoian (born 2001) and his mother Luminiţa Stoian (born 1967), Romanian nationals living in Bucharest. The first applicant has spastic quadriplegia, a condition impairing limb function without affecting intellect; he has been registered as severely disabled since infancy, requiring a personal assistant, ongoing surgeries, physiotherapy, and assistive devices. After 2011 surgery, he became fully wheelchair-bound. Authorities consistently recommended mainstream schooling.

The applicants alleged that the first applicant lacked access to his physical environment, particularly school premises, with no reasonable accommodations despite his disability; both claimed they suffered ill-treatment without an effective domestic remedy. The first applicant attended multiple schools. After a brief, unsuccessful nursery placement in 2004, he enrolled at mainstream School no. 131 (2007–April 2013), 60 metres from home. The applicants described no initial ramps, inaccessible toilets (an improvised cubicle later upgraded but still requiring assistance), unadapted sports facilities, and upper-floor rooms (doctor’s office, labs, after-school care) reachable only by the mother carrying him and his devices. She also handled toileting, feeding, exercises, and carrying items, with occasional help from classmates or staff. He was excluded from outings without alternatives. These issues allegedly worsened his condition, increased dependence, and caused tensions with staff, pupils, and parents. The Government countered that adaptations were made from enrolment, including a 2008 funding request, 2012–2013 works (ramp, alarm-equipped toilet, asphalted yard, ground-floor nurse’s office, adapted desks, air-conditioning) funded by the school, and staff assistance with care. The child left after 3 April 2013 and received treatment elsewhere without notice to the school.

In 2013/14 he attended School no. 148 (conditions described as acceptable). From October 2015 to 2017 he was at Mihai Eminescu High School, which the applicants said remained largely inaccessible; the mother carried him daily to upper floors (labs, gym), and the school provided no personal care, feeding, or mobility support, sometimes leaving him unattended. No individualised educational plan was implemented; some teachers refused adaptations or suggested special school, with administrative tolerance. The Government noted partial accessibility (ramps, ground-floor classrooms, reserved parking, adapted desk) and requests for further works (accessible toilet, lift, adapted computer, ground-floor facilities). A stairlift was installed in November 2016 after the mother rejected other options. On occasions she brought him without a wheelchair or refused to leave him without an assistant.

Educational support included a 2007 recommendation for a support teacher (reiterated 2011). School no. 131 adapted timetables, allowed extra exam time, partial exemption, and Skype lessons. At Mihai Eminescu, support teachers drafted intervention plans (2015–2016), but the mother obstructed work, dictated subjects, and refused communication. Post-2016 court order, child-protection professionals were assigned but faced the mother’s refusals and verbal abuse. Long absences (for treatment or other schools) hindered progress. Therapy recommendations emphasised physiotherapy and position changes. Limited school sessions occurred, but the mother withheld medical details, refused non-gym locations, or withheld consent. Psychological counselling was arranged but not pursued.

A personal assistant was requested from 2011 (the mother could not serve as she worked). Courts in 2011–2012 ordered recruitment and funding after finding an inadequate rehabilitation plan. Hiring attempts (2011–2016) failed due to resignations over the mother’s extra-task demands or other issues; part-time appointments were short-lived.

The applicants filed numerous complaints with administrative bodies, the National Council against Discrimination (at least six cases), courts (at least five), and prosecutors (at least sixteen), mainly alleging inadequate services, infrastructure, and support. In a 2014 performance-order action against multiple authorities, the Bucharest County Court (10 June 2016, amended on appeal 7 February 2018) partly granted relief, ordering a new intervention plan, curriculum adaptation, continued psycho-educational support, in-school assistance/safety (via staff, assistant, or caregiver), and accessibility works (adapted desks, upper-floor access, obstacle removal, adapted gym, computer). A 2016 interim injunction required an assistant pending finality; enforcement disputes led to daily-penalty orders (2018) after findings of incomplete compliance amid bureaucratic issues and poor cooperation. A related discrimination claim yielded 7,500 lei non-pecuniary damages (2018). On 3 April 2013 the mother was forcibly removed by police from a classroom after refusing to leave during a lesson; she received a warning. A criminal complaint was closed in 2017 (upheld on appeal), finding proportionate force against her disruptive behaviour.

Third-party interventions (Council of Europe Commissioner, UN Special Rapporteur, NGOs) addressed disability rights and inclusive education. The first applicant later moved to a private school (2017–at least 2018).

Support teachers and adapted testing/Skype classes were provided, but the mother's non-cooperation (e.g., refusing plans or meetings) hindered progress. Physiotherapy and therapy were arranged in schools but often declined or unused due to her conditions. A personal assistant was requested in 2011; courts ordered hiring in 2011–2012, but delays arose from recruitment issues and her demands, leading to resignations.

The applicants lodged numerous complaints with authorities, the National Council against Discrimination, courts, and prosecutors. A 2016 County Court decision (upheld 2018) ordered curriculum adaptations, support personnel, accessibility measures (e.g., lifts, adapted facilities), and assistants. Enforcement faced delays, with fines imposed, though authorities cited partial compliance and cooperation issues.

On 3 April 2013, police forcibly removed the mother from a classroom after a dispute; her complaint was dismissed as the force was proportionate. These facts underpin claims of inadequate accommodations and remedies. (Word count: 498)

The case of Stoian v. Romania (Application no. 289/14) was brought by a mother and her son (born 2001), who has spastic quadriplegia. The condition impairs limb function but not intellect; after 2011 surgery he became wheelchair-bound and requires ongoing physiotherapy, assistive devices, a personal assistant and reasonable accommodations. The applicants alleged that the son was denied access to his physical environment (especially school buildings), that no adequate reasonable accommodations were provided, that both suffered ill-treatment, and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy.

The son was repeatedly assessed as suitable for mainstream schooling. After being rejected by a nursery, he attended School No. 131 (2007–April 2013). The applicants claimed the building lacked ramps, accessible toilets, adapted sports facilities or lifts; the mother had to carry her son, his devices and belongings between floors and assist with toileting and exercise; extracurricular activities were inaccessible; and the absence of proper medical support caused his condition to deteriorate. Tensions arose with staff, pupils and parents. The Government maintained that adaptations were made from the school’s budget (access ramp, alarm-equipped toilet, asphalted yard, ground-floor nurse’s office, adapted desks and air-conditioning) and that staff assisted with personal care.

He later attended M.E. High School (2015–2017). The applicants said the premises remained largely inaccessible, the mother continued to carry him, basic care was not provided, no individualised educational plan was implemented and some teachers refused adaptations. The Government stated that ramps, reserved parking, a ground-floor classroom and an adapted desk existed from the outset; a stair-lift was installed in November 2016 after the mother rejected earlier options; and the school sought further improvements.

Educational support consisted of a recommended support teacher, extra examination time, timetable adjustments and Skype lessons during medical absences. Later support teachers prepared individualised plans, but the mother frequently refused cooperation, dictated curriculum changes or withheld the child. Physiotherapy and speech-therapy sessions were arranged on school premises, yet the mother often declined them or failed to supply medical records. A 2011 court order required the authorities to hire a personal assistant; successive appointments were made from 2014 onward but ended in resignations, which the authorities attributed to the mother’s demands that assistants perform domestic tasks outside their job description.

The applicants lodged numerous administrative, anti-discrimination, civil and criminal complaints. In the principal civil action the Bucharest County Court (June 2016) found that existing measures were insufficient and ordered the relevant authorities to produce a new individualised plan, adapt the curriculum (because a full school day conflicted with medical needs), ensure continuity of specialist support, provide a personal assistant or qualified caregiver for mobility, toileting, note-taking and safety, and render the buildings fully wheelchair-accessible (including upper floors, laboratories, sports facilities and adapted software). Non-pecuniary damages of RON 7 500 were later awarded. An interim injunction required an assistant pending finality. Enforcement proceedings followed, with daily penalty payments imposed after the authorities were found not to have fully complied.

On 3 April 2013 police forcibly removed the mother from a classroom after she refused to leave during a lesson; she received a formal warning. Her subsequent criminal complaint was closed on the ground that the force used had been necessary and proportionate. The son thereafter attended a private school.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ claims concerning inaccessible education, failure to provide reasonable accommodation, alleged ill-treatment and the absence of an effective remedy.

The ECHR case *Rook v. Germany* (no. 1586/15) arose from an application by Michael Rook, a former managing director of a major consumer-electronics retailer, alleging that he and his counsel lacked sufficient access to seized audio recordings, text messages and electronic files during criminal proceedings against him for taking bribes in commercial practice. He invoked Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) of the Convention (fair trial and adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence).

An investigation opened on 7 February 2011. Rook was detained on remand from 9 November 2011 and instructed three lawyers (one based in Augsburg). Authorities conducted wide-ranging telecommunication surveillance, storing some 44,970 telephone calls and 34,000 other data sets (including texts and system files) in a police database. Only 28 conversations deemed relevant were transcribed and placed in the paper investigation file. Parallel searches of Rook’s home and other premises between July 2011 and February 2012 yielded approximately 14 million electronic files (emails and documents). These were imaged, then imported into a specialised forensic-analysis programme that could be read only with proprietary software costing €4,031.72; about 1,100 files were printed and added to the paper file.

From 10 November 2011 the Augsburg lawyer received the paper file (and subsequent updates). On 30 November he requested to examine the audio files and obtain copies. The prosecutor granted supervised inspection at police premises during limited weekday hours but refused copies. Appointments followed, with police retrieving files according to defence-specified parameters; a printed spreadsheet of metadata (dates, times, lines, relevance assessments) was later supplied. In March 2012 the lawyer applied to the Regional Court for read-only copies of the audio material. The court refused, treating the files as evidence that could not be given into defence possession, citing the presence of highly personal data of third parties and the prosecution’s deletion obligations. Access was later extended by depositing a notebook containing the data at the prison for supervised listening during visiting hours, but the lawyer never used this facility and continued examinations at police premises (a total of 20 visits, the last on 31 October 2012). Appeals for unrestricted copies and comprehensive lists were dismissed by the Regional Court and Court of Appeal.

In April 2012 the lawyer sought copies of the 14 million electronic files. Technical processing initially prevented immediate production; a hard-disk copy requiring the proprietary software was supplied in May. The court refused to order the State to purchase a licence or bear the cost, noting that Rook could afford three counsel. After a further request, the data were exported back into a freely readable image format and delivered on 4 September 2012.

Twenty-two hearing days ran from June to December 2012. Applications to stay the trial so that the defence could review the material more thoroughly were rejected, the court observing that the lawyer had under-used available opportunities (including prison access and judicial-staff assistance) and that the other two counsel had never inspected anything. Rook was convicted on 63 counts and sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. The Federal Court of Justice quashed three counts but otherwise dismissed the appeal, holding that adequate access and time had been granted and that the defence had simply failed to exploit them. The applicant, Agro Frigo OOD, a Bulgarian company, applied in 2006 for a SAPARD subsidy (covering half the cost of constructing an agricultural market in Nova Zagora). The State Fund “Agriculture” (the Fund) rejected the application on 18 August 2006, citing missing documents and ineligibility because the project included sale of grapevine seedlings (SAPARD financing being limited to markets for fruit, vegetables, flowers and fish).

The company obtained judicial review. The Sofia City Court quashed the refusal on 31 March 2008 and remitted the matter; the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) upheld this on 29 December 2008, holding that all documents had been submitted and that grapevine seedlings were agricultural products eligible for sale at such a market.

Re-examination proved impossible. Contracting under SAPARD had ceased in October 2007 after Bulgaria’s EU accession on 1 January 2007. The Fund so informed the company on 10 December 2009.

In early 2010 the company sued the Fund in tort under the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act, claiming BGN 5,587,998 (approximately EUR 2.85 million) as the subsidy it would have received, plus interest. The Sofia Administrative Court dismissed the claim on 15 November 2010, finding no causal link. On 15 April 2011 the SAC reversed, holding that the 2009 refusal was null and void because it contradicted the earlier final judgments establishing eligibility. The Fund’s own earlier refusal had prevented timely contracting, so the company had suffered the loss of the subsidy (whose amount was established by expert evidence and supporting contracts). The SAC awarded the full sum plus BGN 717,811 in interest. The judgment was final; the company obtained a writ of execution on 17 May 2011.

In June 2011 the Minister of Finance, acting for the State, applied to set the SAC judgment aside and reopen the proceedings under Articles 245 et seq. of the Code of Administrative Procedure. He argued that SAPARD payments having ended, compensation would now come from the State budget, so the State was directly affected yet had not been summoned. He also contested the merits (new facts, unaddressed challenges to the contracts, the Fund’s exclusive competence, and the company’s failure to prove it could finance the project itself).

The SAC stayed execution on 6 October 2011. After a hearing, it allowed the application on 20 December 2011, set aside its earlier judgment, reopened the case and remitted it. It reasoned that after 21 December 2009 the Fund, acting as SAPARD Agency, lacked standing to be sued alone; any award would be paid from the State budget (whose revenues and expenditures were approved by the Council of Ministers in coordination with the Minister of Finance); the judgment therefore adversely affected the State, satisfying the conditions of Article 246.

On remittal the tort claim was re-examined and finally dismissed by the SAC on 11 December 2014. The courts found no direct causal link: subsidy payment required prior completion of the investment by the company itself, which had not occurred; some supporting documents were also found forged or void.

(The alleged violations concern the reopening and quashing of the final 15 April 2011 judgment awarding damages.)

The case of Agro Frigo OOD v. Bulgaria originated in an application by a Bulgarian limited-liability company alleging that the quashing of a final judgment awarding it damages against the State violated its rights to a fair trial (Article 6 of the Convention) and to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

In 2006 the company applied to the State Fund “Agriculture” (the Fund), the body administering the EU’s SAPARD programme in Bulgaria, for a subsidy covering half the cost of an agricultural market in Nova Zagora. The Fund rejected the application, finding that the necessary documents were missing and that the project contemplated the sale of grapevine seedlings, products not among those (fruit, vegetables, flowers and fish) for which SAPARD financing was available.

The company obtained judicial review. In 2008 the Sofia City Court, whose judgment was upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC), quashed the rejection. The courts held that all required documents had been submitted and that grapevine seedlings were agricultural products that could lawfully be sold at such a market.

By the time the Fund was required to re-examine the application, SAPARD contracting had already ceased (October 2007) because Bulgaria had acceded to the EU. In December 2009 the Fund therefore informed the company that no further contracts could be concluded.

In 2010 the company brought a tort action against the Fund under the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act, claiming BGN 5 587 998 (approximately EUR 2.85 million) – the amount of the subsidy it would have received – plus interest. The Sofia Administrative Court dismissed the claim, finding no causal link between the 2009 refusal and any damage. On appeal the SAC, in a final judgment of 15 April 2011, reversed that decision. It held that the 2009 refusal was null and void because it contradicted the binding 2008 judgments; the Fund’s own earlier unlawful refusal had prevented timely contracting; and the quantum of the subsidy had been established by expert evidence and contracts. The company was awarded the full principal plus interest and obtained a writ of execution.

In June 2011 the Minister of Finance, acting for the State, applied under Article 246 of the Code of Administrative Procedure for the 2011 judgment to be set aside and the proceedings reopened. He argued that, SAPARD funds having expired, any payment would come from the State budget, so the State was directly and adversely affected yet had not been summoned. He also contested the merits, asserting new facts, that the Fund’s challenges to the supporting contracts had been ignored, that only the Fund could assess project viability, and that the company had not proved it possessed the resources to complete the investment itself.

The SAC stayed execution and, on 20 December 2011, allowed the application, set aside its earlier judgment and remitted the case. It reasoned that after 21 December 2009 the Fund, acting as SAPARD Agency, no longer had standing to defend the action alone; any award would be financed from the State budget and therefore affected the State unfavourably.

On remittal the claim was ultimately dismissed by a final SAC judgment of 11 December 2014. The courts found no direct causal link because a subsidy could be paid only after the company had itself made the envisaged investment (which it had not) and because some of the documents originally submitted were forged or invalid.

Domestic law permitted reopening of administrative proceedings, including State-liability claims, at the instance of a third party whose rights were adversely affected and who had not participated, provided that party’s right of participation was guaranteed by law. The Fund is a legal person financed by the State budget that functions as SAPARD Agency. In comparable cases against specialised agencies the Minister of Finance had not previously been summoned, although one later SAC decision (2015) adopted similar reasoning to the present reopening.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations of legal certainty, fair trial and property rights arising from the quashing of a final, enforceable judgment.

The Sofia Administrative Court dismissed the claim on 15 November 2010 for lack of causal link. On 15 April 2011 the Supreme Administrative Court reversed, holding the 2009 refusal void because it contradicted the binding 2008 judgments that the application met the criteria. The Fund’s inability to contract was its own fault; had it contracted promptly, the subsidy would have been paid. The court awarded the full sum plus BGN 717,811 interest. The judgment was final; a writ of execution issued on 17 May 2011.

The Fund itself possessed legal personality and was financed from the State budget.

**Case Summary: Pastörs v. Germany (ECHR, 2019)**

Udo Pastörs, a German national born in 1952 and NPD chairperson in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania Land Parliament, boycotted a 27 January 2010 Holocaust Remembrance Day event. The next day, during a parliamentary speech on commemorating Wilhelm Gustloff sinking victims, he stated that few truly engaged with the “theatrical display of concern” because people sensed the “so-called Holocaust” served “political and commercial purposes.” Germans had faced an “endless barrage of criticism and propagandistic lies” since WWII, cultivated dishonestly by “so-called democratic parties.” The prior event imposed “Auschwitz projections” onto Germans “in a manner that is both cunning and brutal,” hoping for “the triumph of lies over truth.”

Parliament revoked his inviolability from prosecution in February 2012. On 16 August 2012, the Schwerin District Court (presiding professional judge Y plus two lay judges) convicted him of defamation (Criminal Code Art. 187) and violating the memory of the dead (Art. 189), imposing an eight-month suspended prison sentence. The court viewed the remarks as a qualified Auschwitz denial.

Pastörs appealed. The Schwerin Regional Court, after a 25 March 2013 hearing (where he did not testify), dismissed the appeal. It quoted the full speech but focused on the excerpts, interpreting them objectively as asserting that Jewish extermination at Auschwitz “had not taken place, or at least not in the way reported by historians,” that associated atrocities were “a lie and a projection,” and that “Auschwitz lies” served political/economic ends. Linguistically, “lie,” “projection,” “propagandistic lies,” and “Auschwitz projection” were linked, echoing terms like “Auschwitz lie” or “Auschwitz myth” used in Holocaust denial. Motives invoked suppression/exploitation of Germany (for Jews’ benefit), constituting qualified denial that courts had previously deemed criminal. The statements could not be misunderstood.

The Regional Court noted most of the speech (on German WWII victims, other historical massacres, or criticism of “guilt cult” remembrance using terms like “theatrical display”) raised no criminal issues and was protected as parliamentary speech, even if absurd. However, these could not “mitigate or whitewash” the denial, which Pastörs had “inserted... as if inserting poison into a glass of water.” He intended the message as perceived, aiming to question Auschwitz’s accepted truth and “sneak” it into Parliament undetected. The denial defamed Jewish victims (persecuted for religion/ethnicity, many murdered) by treating their documented fate as untruth, attacking their dignity. It also denigrated the memory of Auschwitz’s murdered Jews. The speech, given in Parliament and internet-broadcast, was intentional. Holocaust denial fell outside freedom of expression. Parliamentary non-liability (Land Constitution Art. 24 and Criminal Code Art. 36) did not apply to defamatory insults; inviolability had been revoked. Any error on immunity’s scope did not affect liability.

Pastörs appealed on points of law to the Rostock Court of Appeal. Learning that one of three judges (X) was husband of District Court judge Y, he lodged a 5 August 2013 bias complaint. X stated his wife had informed him of District Court proceedings amid media coverage, but they otherwise did not discuss the case; he was unbiased, as the Court of Appeal reviewed the Regional Court judgment, not the District Court’s. On 16 August 2013, the Court of Appeal (with X participating) dismissed the complaint as inadmissible under Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 26a (challenge “completely ill-suited”). Marriage alone created no bias fear; the Regional Court had conducted a de novo hearing, not reviewing the District Court. The appeal was also dismissed as ill-founded.

Pastörs filed a motion to be heard (claiming unaddressed arguments) plus bias complaints against the three judges (alleging they ignored his points, assigned X as rapporteur, and arbitrarily used Art. 26a). On 11 November 2013, a different three-judge bench found the later complaint admissible due to the mixed decision but ill-founded: a reasonable defendant would not fear bias from prior involvement or disagreement with reasoning, absent specific evidence of grossly flawed/arbitrary decisions. The Court of Appeal later rejected the hearing motion. The Federal Constitutional Court declined the constitutional complaint without reasons (2014).

Pastörs alleged before the ECHR that his conviction breached Article 10 (freedom of expression) and that judge X’s involvement (and related handling) breached Article 6 § 1 (impartial tribunal). Domestic law excluded marriage from automatic judicial disqualification (Art. 22) but allowed bias challenges (Art. 24); Art. 26a permitted challenged-judge participation for “completely ill-suited” claims, interpreted narrowly.

The applicant, Udo Pastörs, was a German national, NPD chairperson and Member of Parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. On Holocaust Remembrance Day (27 January 2010), he and his parliamentary group boycotted a memorial event in the Land Parliament. The next day he delivered a speech commemorating victims of the Wilhelm Gustloff sinking. In it he stated that the “so-called Holocaust” was being used for political and commercial purposes; that Germans had been subjected since 1945 to a barrage of criticism and “propagandistic lies” cultivated dishonestly by so-called democratic parties; and that the previous day’s event amounted to imposing “Auschwitz projections” on the German people in a cunning and brutal manner, in the hope that lies would triumph over truth.

The Land Parliament later revoked his inviolability from prosecution. On 16 August 2012 the Schwerin District Court convicted him of intentional defamation (Criminal Code Art. 187) and violating the memory of the dead (Art. 189), imposing an eight-month suspended prison sentence. He appealed on fact and law. After a full hearing at which he remained silent, the Schwerin Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 25 March 2013. It quoted the entire speech, highlighting the passages above, and held that they objectively amounted to a “qualified Auschwitz denial”: an assertion that the racially motivated mass extermination of Jews at Auschwitz had not occurred (or not as historically established), that the atrocities were a lie and a projection, and that the “Auschwitz lie” had been exploited for political and economic ends. The court found the statements could not reasonably be misunderstood, had been deliberately inserted to evade parliamentary sanctions, and constituted untruths capable of defaming the Jewish victims’ persecution (an aspect of their dignity) while also denigrating the memory of those murdered at Auschwitz. Parliamentary non-liability did not apply to defamatory insults, and the revocation of inviolability permitted prosecution.

Pastörs then appealed on points of law to the Rostock Court of Appeal. Upon learning that one of the three judges (X) was married to the District Court judge (Y) who had first convicted him, he lodged a bias complaint on 5 August 2013. Judge X stated that his wife had informed him of the first-instance proceedings because of media coverage, but that they had not otherwise discussed the case and that he was not biased; the Court of Appeal was reviewing only the Regional Court’s judgment. On 16 August 2013 the Court of Appeal, with X participating, dismissed the bias complaint as inadmissible under Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 26a (the ground being “completely ill-suited”) because marriage alone did not create a fear of bias when the court was examining a later, independent judgment. It simultaneously dismissed the appeal on points of law as ill-founded.

Pastörs then filed a motion alleging a violation of his right to be heard and a further bias complaint against all three judges. On 11 November 2013 a differently composed bench found the second complaint admissible but ill-founded: prior involvement or disagreement with a party’s submissions did not, without more, justify a fear of bias from a reasonable observer’s standpoint. The motion to be heard was later rejected. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept a constitutional complaint.

Pastörs applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the conviction violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) and that the Court of Appeal’s composition, given the marital link and handling of the bias complaints, violated Article 6 § 1 (impartial tribunal).

The case of Pastörs v. Germany (Application no. 55225/14) originated from an application by Udo Pastörs, a German national and former Member of Parliament who chaired the National Democratic Party of Germany (NPD) faction in the Land Parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. On 27 January 2010 (Holocaust Remembrance Day), a memorial event took place in the parliament; Pastörs and his NPD colleagues did not attend. The following day, during a parliamentary debate commemorating victims of the 1945 sinking of the military transport ship Wilhelm Gustloff, Pastörs delivered a speech containing the following statements: that few people were genuinely participating in the “theatrical display of concern”; that “the so-called Holocaust is being used for political and commercial purposes”; that Germans had been subjected since World War II to an “endless barrage of criticism and propagandistic lies” cultivated dishonestly by so-called democratic parties; and that the previous day’s memorial event amounted to “imposing your Auschwitz projections onto the German people in a manner that is both cunning and brutal,” with the speakers hoping for “the triumph of lies over truth.”

The Land Parliament revoked Pastörs’ inviolability from prosecution in February 2012. In August 2012 the Schwerin District Court convicted him of intentional defamation (Article 187 of the Criminal Code) and violating the memory of the dead (Article 189), imposing an eight-month suspended prison sentence. The court found that the statements constituted a “qualified Auschwitz denial”—an assertion that the systematic, racially motivated mass murder of Jews at Auschwitz had not occurred (or not as historically documented) and that related “lies” served political and economic ends.

Pastörs appealed. In March 2013 the Schwerin Regional Court, after a full rehearing, dismissed the appeal. It held that the utterances, viewed objectively, denied the Holocaust, invoked well-known revisionist tropes (“Auschwitz lie,” “Auschwitz projection”), and were capable of defaming Jewish victims of Nazi persecution (an attack on their personal dignity) while also desecrating the memory of those murdered at Auschwitz. The court ruled that parliamentary non-liability (Indemnität) did not cover defamatory insults and that the prior revocation of inviolability permitted prosecution. The applicant’s remaining speech criticising remembrance culture was protected as political expression, but could not “whitewash” the denial, which had been “inserted like poison into a glass of water.”

Pastörs then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Rostock Court of Appeal. Upon learning that one of the three judges (X) was the husband of the District Court judge (Y) who had convicted him at first instance, he filed a bias complaint. Judge X stated that his wife had informed him only of the general course of the first-instance proceedings amid media coverage, but that they had not discussed the merits. On 16 August 2013 the Court of Appeal, with X participating, dismissed the bias complaint as “completely ill-suited” (Article 26a of the Code of Criminal Procedure) because the appeal concerned only the Regional Court’s independent judgment, not the District Court’s, and marriage alone did not raise a fear of bias. The same decision dismissed the appeal on points of law as ill-founded.

Pastörs then filed a motion alleging a breach of his right to be heard and a further bias complaint against all three judges who had sat on 16 August. A differently composed bench of the Court of Appeal later held the second bias complaint admissible but unfounded: prior involvement or disagreement with a party’s arguments does not, without specific evidence of arbitrariness, justify a fear of partiality from the standpoint of a reasonable observer. Subsequent constitutional proceedings were unsuccessful.

These facts form the basis of Pastörs’ complaints under Article 10 (that the conviction unjustifiably interfered with parliamentary freedom of expression) and Article 6 § 1 (that the Court of Appeal lacked impartiality owing to judge X’s participation).
