The case of Fleischner v. Germany (Application no. 61985/12) concerns complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a German national born in 1942, alleged that civil courts violated his rights to a fair hearing and the presumption of innocence by holding him liable for damages on the basis of findings from discontinued criminal proceedings.

The applicant and four co-accused, including his wife, had invested money in the United States through financial adviser A. After A allegedly failed to pay interest or refund the capital, two co-accused kidnapped A and held him captive in Germany. At a meeting also attended by the applicant and his wife, A was forced by threats (including to report him to US police) to sign debt acknowledgements. A then transferred EUR 75,000 to one co-accused’s account before being rescued by police.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 3 February 2010 (preliminarily) and 29 August 2011 (finally) under Article 206a of the Code of Criminal Procedure because he was unfit to stand trial. In the trial of the remaining co-accused, A testified that the applicant had drafted the acknowledgements and insisted A would be released only after payment of the EUR 75,000. On 23 March 2010 the Traunstein Regional Court convicted the co-accused (including the applicant’s wife) of blackmail. Its 16-page factual account, based on A’s testimony, the co-accused’s statements and other evidence, described the applicant’s actions in detail.

Independently, A recovered the EUR 75,000 through a lawyer’s demand letter (without court proceedings) and then sought reimbursement of the lawyer’s fees (EUR 1,880.20) from the applicant and co-accused, who refused. A therefore brought a civil claim against them as joint debtors.

The Speyer District Court served the claim on 25 May 2011 and set deadlines for defence. The applicant indicated an intention to defend but filed no statement of defence. After the court stated on 5 September 2011 that the claim appeared well-founded and that the criminal judgment constituted sufficient documentary evidence, the applicant’s wife filed a defence denying the offences and requesting the criminal file and further testimony. The applicant later submitted a medical report claiming unfitness to stand trial; the court replied that this did not excuse him from the civil proceedings and that he could send a representative. His wife then submitted the applicant’s sworn statement denying prior knowledge of the kidnapping and asserting that he and his wife learned of it only after the meeting. The applicant himself argued there was no evidence of his participation in any unlawful act.

At the 7 November 2011 hearing the applicant was represented by his daughter, who sought dismissal; no evidence was taken. On 2 December 2011 the District Court held the defendants jointly liable under Article 823 § 2 of the Civil Code (read with Articles 239 and 240 of the Criminal Code). It found they had jointly fulfilled the constitutive elements of deprivation of liberty and coercion. Regarding the applicant specifically, it referred to his wife’s statements in the criminal proceedings (that they had failed to end the deprivation despite knowledge of the circumstances) and to A’s testimony that the applicant had prepared documents A was forced to sign, thereby actively participating in the coercion. Undisputed facts were taken from A’s civil submissions; disputed facts were taken from the criminal judgment.

The applicant appealed, arguing the District Court had wrongly treated the criminal judgment as establishing his liability. On 10 April 2012 the Frankenthal Regional Court rejected the appeal without a hearing, holding that it had no prospect of success and relying on the first-instance facts (which the applicant had not sought to rectify). The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his subsequent complaint.

The civil courts thus imposed liability for the lawyer’s fees by treating the applicant as having committed the relevant criminal acts, even though criminal proceedings against him had been discontinued without any finding of guilt.

**Case Summary: Fleischner v. Germany (Application no. 61985/12)**

The applicant, Gerhard Fleischner (born 1942), alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) and Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He claimed that German civil courts ordered him to pay compensation to the victim despite the discontinuation of related criminal proceedings against him on grounds of unfitness to stand trial.

The case arose from events involving the applicant, his wife, and three co-accused. They had made financial investments in the United States through adviser A. When A allegedly failed to pay interest or refund the capital, two co-accused kidnapped A and held him captive in Germany. At a meeting attended by the applicant and his wife, A was compelled—through threats including informing US police—to sign acknowledgements of debt. A then transferred €75,000 to one co-accused’s account before being rescued by police.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued preliminarily on 3 February 2010 and finally on 29 August 2011 under Article 206a of the Code of Criminal Procedure due to his unfitness to stand trial. The remaining co-accused, including the applicant’s wife, were convicted by the Traunstein Regional Court on 23 March 2010 of offences including blackmail. The conviction relied on A’s testimony (that the applicant drafted the documents and insisted on release only after receipt of the €75,000) and statements from the co-accused. The 16-page judgment detailed the actions of all involved, including the applicant.

Independently, A recovered the €75,000 extra-judicially and then sought reimbursement of his lawyer’s fees (€1,880.20 plus interest) from the applicant and co-accused, who refused. A brought a civil claim against them as joint debtors.

In the Speyer District Court proceedings, the applicant indicated an intention to defend but submitted no statement of defence. He later provided a medical report claiming unfitness and a sworn statement denying prior knowledge of the kidnapping or involvement in coercion, asserting that A appeared to be staying voluntarily. His wife similarly denied the offences and requested evidence including files, testimony from A and the applicant, and the criminal judgment. The court informed the applicant that health issues did not excuse him from the civil case (he could send a representative) and considered the criminal judgment sufficient documentary proof.

At the 7 November 2011 hearing, the applicant was represented by his daughter; no evidence was taken. On 2 December 2011 the District Court awarded A the claimed sum. It held the defendants jointly liable under Article 823 § 2 of the Civil Code (in conjunction with Articles 239 and 240 of the Criminal Code) for fulfilling the constitutive elements of deprivation of liberty and coercion. It relied on undisputed parts of A’s civil submissions and, for disputed facts, on the Traunstein criminal judgment’s findings (including co-accused statements and A’s testimony describing the applicant’s role in preparing documents and failing to end the deprivation of liberty despite knowledge of the circumstances). The court addressed causation, the amount of damage, and rejected any set-off for failed investments.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the criminal judgment had not established his liability. The Frankenthal Regional Court rejected the appeal without an oral hearing on 10 April 2012 under Article 522 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, finding no prospect of success. It adopted the first-instance facts (Articles 314 and 529) and declined further fact-finding because the applicant had not requested rectification under Article 320. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his complaint on 11 July 2012.

Under German law, civil liability under Article 823 § 2 requires proof that the defendant fulfilled the objective and subjective elements of a protective criminal statute (here, Articles 239 and 240), plus causation and damage; it does not require a finding of criminal guilt. Civil proceedings rely on party-presented evidence with differing burdens of proof from criminal law (no *in dubio pro reo*). The civil courts’ use of the discontinued criminal case’s findings to establish the applicant’s commission of the offences formed the core of the alleged Convention violations.

The case Balsamo v. San Marino (applications nos. 20319/17 and 21414/17) was brought by two Italian sisters, Valentina Balsamo (born 1986) and Angela Balsamo (born 1985), living in Brescia. They alleged that San Marino's confiscation of their assets after acquittal on money-laundering charges violated Articles 6 § 2 and 7 of the Convention (alone and with Article 13) as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, being neither lawful nor proportionate.

A 2011 investigation targeted their father B. and the applicants for laundering assets worth EUR 2.15 million that B. had obtained through crimes in Italy. On 28 July 2011 the investigating judge seized a current account, a bonds account and a safe-deposit box held in Valentina’s name (with mandates later held by B. and then Angela), totalling EUR 1 920 785.50. Large cash deposits had been made: EUR 500 000 by Valentina on opening the account at age 18, further sums of EUR 150 000 and EUR 400 000 by her, EUR 950 000 by B. and EUR 150 000 by Angela.

Italian judicial cooperation produced a 2008 Brescia Court of Appeal judgment convicting B. of theft and receiving stolen goods whose proceeds were only EUR 750 000, together with evidence of his extensive criminal record (theft, receiving, drug dealing, weapons offences and unexplained wealth).

Proceedings against B. were later archived. In November 2014 the first-instance judge convicted both daughters of money laundering (Articles 50, 73 and 199 bis of the Criminal Code). He held that proof of a specific predicate offence or its perpetrator was unnecessary; logical evidence of illicit origin sufficed. B.’s Italian conviction, his broader criminal career, the family’s disproportionate wealth, contradictory and unevidenced explanations of legitimate sources (family business, property sales) and the decision to bank the funds abroad all established that origin. Despite their youth the applicants knew of it. They received prison terms (two years six months and one year), fines and disqualifications. The seized sums were confiscated under Article 147 § 3; an additional EUR 499 000 previously withdrawn by Valentina was confiscated by equivalent means.

On 10 October 2016 the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted them for lack of proof of mens rea, citing their age. He nevertheless confirmed the funds’ criminal origin: no credible licit explanation existed, fiscal controls of the era did not prove legality, and the transfer to San Marino was an attempt to conceal the source. The confiscation of the seized assets was therefore upheld.

In January 2017 the applicants sought revision before the judge for extraordinary remedies, invoking the same Convention rights and arguing that no other domestic remedy existed. That judge asserted competence (relying on a 2007 constitutional ruling and Article 13) and, in May 2017, rejected the request on the merits. He characterised the confiscation as purely preventive, aimed at keeping illicit proceeds out of circulation independently of any finding of personal guilt or dangerousness. It was lawful under Article 147 (even if interpreted extensively), foreseeable in the light of domestic and international anti-money-laundering standards (including MONEYVAL recommendations and the Strasbourg and Warsaw Conventions), and proportionate given the societal harm of circulating dirty money.

The key facts for the alleged violations are therefore the post-acquittal confiscation of assets whose illicit origin had been established in the same criminal proceedings, the legal basis invoked (Article 147 §§ 2–3), the preventive rather than punitive characterisation given by the domestic courts, and the applicants’ unsuccessful attempt to obtain revision on Convention grounds.

They alleged violations of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 7 § 1 (no punishment without law), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

A 2011 criminal investigation targeted the applicants and their father, B., for laundering €2.15 million in assets that B. had allegedly obtained through offences in Italy. On 28 July 2011 an investigating judge seized a current account, bonds account and safe-deposit box registered in Valentina’s name (with mandates later held by B. and then Angela). The seized assets totalled €1,920,785.50. Valentina, then 18, had opened the account in December 2004 with a €500,000 cash deposit; further large cash deposits followed in 2005–2008, including €950,000 by B. himself. Italian authorities supplied a 2008 Brescia Court of Appeal judgment convicting B. of theft and receiving stolen goods, whose proceeds were only €750,000, plus records of B.’s extensive prior convictions.

Proceedings against B. were archived. In November 2014 a first-instance judge convicted both applicants of money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code. Sentences included imprisonment, fines and a ban on public office. Relying on Article 147 § 3, the court confiscated the seized sums and ordered an additional equivalent-value confiscation of €499,000 that Valentina had withdrawn. It held that a specific predicate conviction was unnecessary; “logical proof” of illicit origin sufficed. That origin was established by B.’s Italian conviction, his long criminal record, the mismatch between the family’s legitimate income and the assets, the applicants’ unsubstantiated and contradictory explanations of licit sources, and the decision to deposit funds in a distant San Marino bank.

On 10 October 2016 the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted both applicants, finding the subjective element (knowledge of illicit origin) unproven beyond reasonable doubt, given their youth. The court nevertheless confirmed the confiscation. It ruled that the funds themselves had a criminal origin: the applicants had offered no credible licit explanation, and the San Marino transfers were designed to obscure that origin.

In January 2017 the applicants sought revision before the judge for extraordinary remedies, invoking the same Convention provisions. That judge asserted competence under Article 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (interpreted in light of a 2007 constitutional ruling and Article 13 of the Convention) and, in May 2017, rejected the request on the merits. He characterised the confiscation as purely preventive, not punitive, applying independently of any conviction once the illicit character of the property was established in a fair trial. The measure was lawful under Article 147 (whether § 2 or § 3), foreseeable in light of domestic and international anti-money-laundering standards (including MONEYVAL recommendations and the Council of Europe Conventions of 1990 and 2005), and proportionate given the need to prevent recirculation of tainted assets.

Domestic law (Article 147) provides for mandatory confiscation of instrumentalities, proceeds and equivalent value upon conviction for money laundering, and also, “regardless of conviction,” of items whose mere possession or transfer constitutes an offence. The applicants argued that the post-acquittal confiscation lacked a sufficient legal basis, was unforeseeable, punitive in substance, and disproportionate, thereby violating the presumption of innocence and the right to property, with no effective domestic remedy.

The case of Balsamo v. San Marino (applications nos. 20319/17 and 21414/17) was brought by two Italian sisters, Valentina and Angela Balsamo, against San Marino. They alleged that the confiscation of assets following their acquittal of money-laundering charges violated Articles 6 § 2 and 7 of the Convention (alone and with Article 13) as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, on the grounds that the measure was unlawful and disproportionate.

A criminal investigation was opened against the applicants and their father, B., for ongoing money laundering of assets allegedly obtained by B. through offences committed in Italy, with a total value of approximately €2.15 million. In July 2011 the investigating judge seized a current account, a securities account and the contents of a safe-deposit box registered in the first applicant’s name (over which B. and later the second applicant held mandates). The seized assets totalled €1,920,785.50. The first applicant, then aged 18, had opened the account in 2004 and made large cash deposits; further cash deposits were made by her, by B. and by the second applicant between 2005 and 2008.

Italian authorities supplied documents pursuant to a letter of request, including a 2008 Brescia Court of Appeal judgment convicting B. of theft and receiving stolen goods with proceeds of €750,000. Proceedings against B. were later archived; the applicants were indicted.

In November 2014 the first-instance criminal judge convicted both applicants of money laundering. The first applicant received two years and six months’ imprisonment and the second one year, together with fines and disqualifications. Relying on Article 147 § 3 of the Criminal Code, the judge confiscated the seized sums and, in respect of the first applicant, ordered confiscation by equivalent of an additional €499,000 that she had withdrawn before the seizure. The judge held that a predicate-offence conviction was unnecessary; reasonable evidence of criminal origin sufficed. Such origin was established by B.’s Italian conviction, his extensive criminal record, the disproportion between the family’s legitimate income and the assets, the applicants’ unsubstantiated and contradictory explanations of licit sources, and the decision to deposit the funds in a foreign bank far from the family’s business interests. The applicants, despite their youth, were found to have been aware of the illicit origin.

On appeal in October 2016 the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted both applicants for lack of proof of mens rea, citing their young age and the absence of evidence beyond reasonable doubt that they knew of the criminal origin. The court nevertheless confirmed that the deposited sums were of criminal origin, given the lack of any credible licit explanation and the transfers’ evident purpose of rendering the money untraceable. The confiscation of the seized assets was therefore upheld.

Unbeknown to the Strasbourg Court at the time of lodging, the applicants had in January 2017 sought revision of the appeal judgment before the judge for extraordinary remedies, alleging the same Convention violations. That judge accepted competence, rejected a request to suspend proceedings pending the Strasbourg case, and in May 2017 dismissed the revision application on the merits. He characterised the confiscation as a purely preventive measure (not punitive) aimed at preventing recirculation of funds whose illicit origin had been established in fair proceedings, found it lawful under Article 147 (independently of conviction or the possessor’s liability), foreseeable in the light of domestic and international standards, and proportionate.

Domestic law provided for money-laundering offences under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code and for various forms of confiscation under Article 147, including mandatory confiscation upon conviction for money laundering and confiscation “regardless of conviction” in certain circumstances. San Marino had ratified the relevant Council of Europe conventions on laundering and confiscation.

The case of Yașar v. Romania (Application no. 64863/13) concerns the confiscation of a vessel owned by Turkish national Erol Yaşar. On 2 April 2010, Kadır Dıkmen (K.D.) and his crew were sailing the vessel—rented from Yaşar and flying a Romanian flag—in the Black Sea when Romanian coastguards intercepted it approximately 42 nautical miles from Sf. Gheorghe. A search revealed no fish but unauthorised fishing equipment showing recent use. The vessel lacked authorisation to fish in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, K.D. had no fishing permit, and there was no fishing journal. The crew were charged with offences under the fishing regime. The vessel (valued by Yaşar at EUR 800,000) and equipment were seized and taken to Constanţa harbour.

K.D. was indicted on 9 June 2010 under Government Emergency Ordinance no. 23/2008 (GEO 23/2008). He acknowledged guilt under a simplified procedure. He testified that he used the vessel under a verbal rental agreement with Yaşar, did not always notify him of departures from Turkish waters, but informed him of fishing locations upon return; Yaşar was reportedly upset yet still paid bonuses. Yaşar submitted a notarised statement claiming the vessel had entered Romanian waters without his knowledge, requesting return of the vessel and equipment, and undertaking not to violate Romanian law. He also provided title documents and a Turkish fishing permit.

On 13 July 2011 the Constanţa District Court sentenced K.D. to two years’ imprisonment (suspended), seized the equipment, and ordered the vessel’s return, finding insufficient evidence that K.D. had used it with Yaşar’s knowledge. The prosecutor appealed, seeking confiscation of the vessel under Article 66 of GEO 23/2008. On 30 March 2012 the Constanţa Court of Appeal remitted the confiscation issue for re-examination after proper summons of Yaşar, whose property rights were at stake.

In the second set of proceedings Yaşar was summoned but neither he nor K.D. attended hearings (both were represented by the same lawyer). On 8 April 2013 the District Court ordered confiscation, holding that the vessel had been essential to the illegal fishing (evidenced by the length of nets deployed) and that Article 66 of GEO 23/2008—as a special norm—did not require proof of the owner’s knowledge or intent.

Yaşar and K.D. appealed, arguing lack of Romanian jurisdiction (disputed exclusive economic zone), that Article 118 of the Criminal Code protected goods used for a profession or subsistence (Yaşar’s sole income derived from the vessel), that confiscation was disproportionate given the vessel’s high value and absence of proven damage or civil claimants, and that any measure should take the form of a EUR 10,000 monetary equivalent. On 26 June 2013 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It applied GEO 23/2008 as lex specialis, rendering confiscation mandatory, but still examined good faith under Article 118. It found Yaşar’s bad faith indicated by the presence of specialised illegal-fishing equipment and the absence of any permit or authorisation. His notarised statement was uncorroborated. Confiscation was held proportionate to the offence’s gravity and potential economic and ecological harm (including damage to protected fish stocks and frequent injuries to dolphins). Later valuation showed 81 % depreciation; the vessel was auctioned in 2016 for approximately EUR 1,900.

These facts underpin the alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, namely whether the confiscation of a third-party owner’s vessel constituted an unlawful or disproportionate interference with peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The case of Yașar v. Romania concerned the confiscation of a fishing vessel owned by Turkish national Erol Yaşar, which he alleged violated his right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 2 April 2010, the vessel—rented verbally by Yaşar to fellow Turkish national K.D. and flying a Romanian flag—was intercepted by Romanian coastguards in the Black Sea, roughly 42 nautical miles from the coast. A search uncovered recently used unauthorized fishing equipment but no fish. The vessel lacked authorization to operate in Romania’s exclusive economic zone; K.D. had no fishing permit and no fishing journal existed. The vessel, which Yaşar valued at EUR 800,000 due to its new engines and advanced electronics, was seized and taken to Constanţa harbour.

K.D. was charged under Government Emergency Ordinance no. 23/2008 (GEO 23/2008) with illegal fishing offences. He admitted guilt under a simplified procedure. In court he stated that the applicant was informed of fishing locations upon the vessel’s return from foreign waters and, though sometimes upset, still paid bonuses. Yaşar submitted a 2011 notarial statement asserting the vessel had entered Romanian waters without his knowledge, requesting return of the vessel and equipment, and undertaking never to violate Romanian law. He also produced title documents and a Turkish fishing permit.

The Constanţa District Court convicted K.D. of two years’ imprisonment (suspended) and seized the equipment but ordered the vessel’s return, finding no clear evidence that Yaşar knew of its illegal use. The prosecutor appealed, seeking confiscation under Article 66 of GEO 23/2008, which mandates seizure of vessels used to commit such offences. The Court of Appeal remitted the confiscation issue for re-examination, requiring Yaşar to be summoned because the measure could substantially affect his property rights.

In the new proceedings Yaşar was summoned but neither he nor K.D. appeared (both were represented by the same lawyer). The District Court ordered confiscation, holding that Article 66, as a special provision, applied irrespective of the owner’s knowledge, departing from the general rule in Article 118 of the Criminal Code (which required a third-party owner’s awareness of illegal use). On appeal the Court of Appeal upheld the order. While applying GEO 23/2008 as lex specialis, it also examined Yaşar’s good faith under Article 118. It found bad faith indicated by the presence of specialized illegal-fishing gear and the complete absence of permits. Yaşar’s uncorroborated notarial statement was insufficient to establish innocence. The court rejected a monetary equivalent (permitted under Article 118 § 2 where confiscation would be disproportionate), considering the measure proportionate to the offence’s gravity and the potential economic and ecological harm—including damage to protected Black Sea fish stocks and frequent injuries to dolphins. It noted the prevalence of similar offences by Turkish-flagged vessels and practices of registering vessels in third-party names to evade confiscation.

A 2013 valuation found the vessel 81 % depreciated; it was later sold at auction for approximately EUR 1,900. These facts formed the basis of Yaşar’s complaint that the confiscation imposed an unjustified and disproportionate interference with his possessions. The domestic courts had established his bad faith in adversarial proceedings and concluded that the measure did not impose an excessive burden.

The case of Yașar v. Romania concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from the confiscation of the applicant’s vessel after its use by a third party for illegal fishing.

The applicant, a Turkish national, owned a vessel (claimed value €800,000) which he rented verbally to K.D. On 2 April 2010 the vessel, flying a Romanian flag, was intercepted by the Romanian coastguard approximately 42 nautical miles offshore. A search revealed no fish but unauthorised, recently used fishing equipment. The vessel lacked authorisation to fish in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, K.D. had no permit and there was no fishing journal. The vessel was seized.

K.D. was convicted under a simplified procedure of illegal-fishing offences and sentenced to a two-year suspended term. He stated that he informed the applicant of fishing in foreign waters and received bonuses. The applicant submitted a notarised declaration that the vessel had been used without his knowledge and requested its return.

The first-instance court initially ordered the vessel’s return for lack of proof of the applicant’s knowledge. On the prosecutor’s appeal the Court of Appeal remitted the confiscation issue, directing that the applicant be summoned.

In the fresh proceedings (neither the applicant nor K.D. appeared) the district court ordered confiscation under Article 66 of GEO 23/2008, holding the measure mandatory irrespective of the owner’s knowledge because the vessel was indispensable to the offence.

On appeal the applicant argued lack of jurisdiction, that the vessel was his sole means of livelihood (protected by Article 118 of the Criminal Code), that confiscation was disproportionate given the absence of proven damage, and that any forfeiture should be limited to a monetary equivalent of €10,000. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. Applying the special fishing legislation as lex specialis, it nevertheless examined good faith and found the applicant had not established innocence: the presence of specialised illegal-fishing gear, the absence of permits and the nature of the activity indicated awareness; his uncorroborated statement was insufficient. Confiscation was held proportionate in view of the gravity of the offence and the potential economic and ecological harm (including injury to protected species). The vessel, later assessed as 81 % depreciated, was sold at auction in 2016 for approximately €1,900.

The European Court of Human Rights concluded that the domestic courts had established the applicant’s bad faith in adversarial proceedings and that the confiscation did not impose an excessive burden, disclosing no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Denis and Irvine v. Belgium (ECtHR Fourth Section, 8 October 2019; later referred to the Grand Chamber) concerns two applications (nos. 62819/17 and 63921/17) alleging that the applicants’ continued compulsory confinement after a change in Belgian law violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (lawfulness of detention) and that they lacked an effective remedy under Articles 5 § 4 and 13.

Jimmy Denis (Belgian, b. 1984) was placed in compulsory confinement on 18 June 2007 by the Turnhout Criminal Court for theft under section 7 of the 1930 Social Protection Act. A January 2007 psychiatric report described a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, severe mental disturbance rendering him incapable of controlling his actions, and danger to society and himself. Multiple conditional discharges were revoked for non-compliance, and confinement was regularly extended.

The Compulsory Confinement Act of 5 May 2014 entered into force on 1 October 2016, replacing the 1930 Act. It restricted confinement to offences harming or capable of harming another’s physical or mental integrity, combined with a mental disorder destroying or seriously reducing discernment or control, plus a risk of reoffending. Denis requested final discharge, arguing that theft no longer justified confinement under the new Act, rendering his detention neither “lawful” nor “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law” under Article 5 § 1(e). He also claimed his disorder was no longer sufficiently serious.

A November 2016 psychosocial report noted he no longer used drugs, was more stable, and supported conditional discharge with inpatient reclassification. The Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court (CPS) granted this on 15 November 2016. He was rearrested on 27 December 2016 for non-compliance. On 25 January 2017 the CPS revoked the discharge, dismissed the final-discharge request, and returned him to the Merksplas Prison social-protection unit. It held that final discharge under section 66 of the 2014 Act required a three-year probationary period and sufficient mental-health stability; the legislature had not intended retrospective application of the “more lenient” law. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 21 February 2017, ruling that Article 7 applied only to penalties (not preventive measures), that Article 5 § 1 did not invalidate a final confinement order merely because later legislation would not have permitted it, and that risk assessment considered current factors rather than solely the original offence. The three-year condition did not deny access to a court. Denis received a further conditional discharge to a psychiatric hospital on 18 July 2017.

Derek Irvine (British, b. 1964) was confined on 14 November 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary under the 1930 Act. A 2002 report identified a serious personality disorder and psychotic disorder rendering him incapable of controlling his actions. Conditional discharge to a Scottish hospital in 2003 ended when he escaped; he was arrested in Belgium in December 2010 and returned to prison. Placement in a forensic centre proved impossible. He requested final discharge on the same legal grounds as Denis. A December 2016 psychosocial report and psychiatric opinion confirmed ongoing schizophrenic symptoms requiring forensic-centre placement. On 25 January 2017 the CPS continued confinement in Turnhout Prison pending a forensic bed and dismissed the request on identical reasoning. Cassation was dismissed the same day on the same grounds. He was later transferred to the Antwerp forensic psychiatry centre in 2018.

Domestic law (as set out in Rooman v. Belgium) confirms the 1930 Act permitted confinement for serious crimes accompanied by mental disorder. The 2014 Act introduced a higher threshold; parliamentary history stated it was not a criminal-law provision and thus not retrospectively applicable. Final discharge under the new Act normally required three years’ probation plus stabilisation eliminating danger of integrity-harming offences. (Subsequent 2019 Cassation rulings, post-dating the applicants’ decisions, held that discharge must occur immediately if the person is no longer mentally ill or dangerous, otherwise Article 5 would be breached.)

The applicants’ core complaint was that the legislative change rendered their detention unlawful and that the three-year probation rule denied an effective judicial remedy capable of ordering immediate release.

The case of Denis and Irvine v. Belgium (ECtHR Fourth Section, 8 October 2019; referred to Grand Chamber) concerns two applications alleging that the applicants’ continued compulsory confinement violated Article 5 § 1 ECHR (unlawful detention) and that they lacked an effective remedy under Articles 5 § 4 and 13. Both men had been confined under Belgium’s 1930 Social Protection Act for offences that, after the 2014 Compulsory Confinement Act entered into force on 1 October 2016, could no longer justify an initial placement.

Jimmy Denis (b. 1984) was confined in 2007 by the Turnhout Criminal Court for theft. A January 2007 psychiatric report diagnosed a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, and a severe mental disturbance rendering him incapable of controlling his actions; he posed a danger to himself and society. Multiple conditional discharges were revoked for non-compliance, and confinement in Merksplas Prison’s social-protection unit was repeatedly extended. After the 2016 Act, Denis applied for final discharge, arguing that theft no longer met the new statutory threshold (an offence harming or capable of harming another’s physical or mental integrity, plus a mental disorder destroying or seriously impairing discernment/control and a risk of similar reoffending). He claimed the detention therefore ceased to be “lawful” or “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law” and that his disorder was no longer sufficiently serious.

A November 2016 psychosocial report noted he had stopped using drugs, was more stable, and recommended reclassification as a psychiatric in-patient. The Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court’s Social Protection Division (CPS) granted conditional discharge but revoked it in January 2017 after further non-compliance. The CPS refused final discharge, holding that the new Act required both sufficient mental-health stability and completion of a three-year probationary period; parliamentary history showed the legislature had not intended retrospective application of the narrower criteria. The Court of Cassation dismissed Denis’s appeal (21 February 2017), ruling that Article 7 ECHR applies only to penalties, not preventive measures; that Article 5 § 1 does not render a final confinement order unlawful merely because the law later changed; and that current risk assessment (not solely the original offence) governs continued detention. The three-year rule did not deny access to a court. Denis was later conditionally discharged to a psychiatric hospital.

Derek Irvine (b. 1964), a British national, was confined in 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary. A 2002 report diagnosed a serious personality disorder and psychotic disorder rendering him incapable of controlling his actions. Conditional discharge to a Scottish hospital ended when he escaped; he was arrested in Belgium in 2010 and returned to prison. Placement in Scotland proved impossible; he remained in Turnhout Prison pending a forensic-psychiatric bed. In December 2016 he sought final discharge on the same legal grounds as Denis. A December 2016 report recorded ongoing schizophrenic symptoms treated by depot medication and recommended a forensic centre. The CPS and Court of Cassation rejected his application on identical reasoning (January–February 2017). He was later transferred to the Antwerp forensic-psychiatric centre.

Under the 1930 Act, confinement was available for any “serious crime” if the offender suffered a mental disorder making him incapable of controlling his actions. The 2014 Act introduced a higher threshold limited to offences affecting another’s integrity, a qualifying disorder, and a specific risk of reoffending. Final discharge now required a three-year probationary period plus sufficient stabilisation so that no reasonable fear of further integrity-harming offences remained. Later 2019 Court of Cassation rulings held that an individual who is no longer mentally ill or dangerous must be released even before the three years expire, otherwise Article 5 would be breached. The applicants’ core complaint was that the legislative change rendered their ongoing detention unlawful and that the statutory conditions for release deprived them of a speedy judicial remedy capable of ordering immediate liberty.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined two applications by Jimmy Denis (a Belgian national, born 1984) and Derek Irvine (a British national, born 1964) against Belgium. Both men were held under compulsory confinement orders imposed for offences committed while they suffered from serious mental disorders. They alleged that their continued detention after a 2016 legislative change violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (right to liberty) because the original offences no longer justified confinement under the new law, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Articles 5 § 4 and 13 because final discharge required a three-year probationary period.

Denis was placed in confinement on 18 June 2007 by the Turnhout Criminal Court for theft, pursuant to section 7 of the 1930 Social Protection Act. A January 2007 psychiatric report described a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, and a severe mental disturbance rendering him incapable of controlling his actions and posing a danger to himself and society. He received several conditional discharges that were later revoked for non-compliance; his confinement in the Merksplas Prison social-protection unit was periodically extended.

The 2014 Compulsory Confinement Act entered into force on 1 October 2016, replacing the 1930 Act. It restricted confinement to offences that had harmed or could harm another person’s physical or mental integrity, combined with a mental disorder destroying or seriously reducing discernment or control and a risk of further such offences. Denis immediately sought final discharge, arguing that theft no longer qualified and that his detention was therefore neither lawful nor “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law” under Article 5 § 1 (e). He also claimed that the new, narrower criteria implied his disorder was no longer sufficiently serious.

A 27 October 2016 psychosocial report noted improved stability (he had stopped using drugs) and recommended reclassification as a psychiatric-hospital in-patient. The Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court’s Social Protection Division granted conditional discharge on 15 November 2016, but Denis was re-arrested on 27 December 2016 for breaching conditions. On 25 January 2017 the Division revoked the discharge, refused final release, and returned him to prison. It held that the 2014 Act required both sufficient mental-health stability and completion of a three-year probationary period; the legislature had not intended retrospective application of the more lenient criteria. Denis’s current condition and incomplete probation justified continued detention.

The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 21 February 2017. Article 7 of the Convention applied only to penalties, not preventive measures. Article 5 § 1 did not require that a confinement order already possessing legal force become unlawful merely because the law later changed; risk assessment considered current mental state and multiple factors, not solely the original offence. The three-year rule did not deny access to a court. Denis later obtained another conditional discharge to a hospital on 18 July 2017.

Irvine was confined on 14 November 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary. A 2002 psychiatric report identified a serious personality disorder and psychotic illness. After a 2003 conditional discharge to a Scottish hospital he escaped, was recaptured in Belgium in 2010, and was returned to prison. Efforts to place him in Scotland failed; in June 2016 the Social Protection Committee ordered priority transfer to a forensic psychiatry centre, but he remained in Turnhout Prison pending a bed.

On 6 December 2016 he sought final discharge on the same Convention grounds as Denis. A December 2016 report recorded ongoing schizophrenia treated by depot medication and recommended a forensic centre. On 25 January 2017 the Post-Sentencing Court continued his prison placement and refused final discharge for the same reasons given in Denis’s case. The Court of Cassation rejected his appeal on identical grounds on 21 February 2017. He was eventually transferred to the Antwerp forensic centre in 2018.

Under the 1930 Act, confinement could follow any “serious crime” committed by a person whose mental disorder rendered him incapable of controlling his actions. The 2014 Act introduced a harm-to-integrity threshold and an explicit reoffending-risk requirement; parliamentary records confirm that the change was not intended to operate retrospectively. Conditional discharge remained available at any time, but final discharge was, in principle, possible only after three years of successful probation if the disorder had stabilised and the risk of harmful reoffending had disappeared. (Later 2019 Court of Cassation rulings, post-dating the applicants’ appeals, held that an individual who is no longer mentally ill or dangerous must be released even before three years have elapsed, in order to comply with Article 5.)

The applicants thus remained detained on the basis of pre-2016 orders whose original offences (theft and attempted burglary) might not satisfy the new statutory threshold, while domestic courts declined to treat the legislative change as automatically rendering those orders unlawful or to dispense with the three-year probationary requirement.

The case of Paunović v. Serbia (application no. 54574/07) originated from a complaint lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 December 2007 by Dragoslav Paunović, a Serbian national born in 1956 and resident in Soko Banja. Represented by lawyer I. Pavlović, the applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) on the ground that the Niš District Court lacked impartiality when it heard his appeal.

On 2 August 2006, deputy municipal public prosecutor I.S. of the Aleksinac Municipal Public Prosecutor’s Office indicted the applicant for causing bodily harm and death by dangerous driving. At the first main hearing before the Aleksinac Municipal Court on 24 October 2006 and at subsequent hearings, the prosecution was represented by deputy prosecutors S.S. and I.S. On 12 December 2006 the Municipal Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to six months’ imprisonment. Both the applicant and I.S. appealed.

On 17 April 2007 a three-judge bench of the Niš District Court (President N.S., rapporteur B.K. and S.M.) dismissed the appeals and upheld the conviction. B.K. had been elected a District Court judge on 15 August 2006. The applicant then filed an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court of Serbia, arguing that B.K.’s participation as rapporteur rendered the appeal court partial. He stressed that B.K. had still been a deputy municipal public prosecutor in Aleksinac throughout the first-instance proceedings and that the Aleksinac prosecutor’s office had represented the public interest against him. He invoked incompatibility of the offices of judge and prosecutor.

On 23 October 2007 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal. It held that B.K. had neither acted as prosecutor in the applicant’s case nor taken part in the investigation, so that mere occupancy of the prosecutorial post in Aleksinac during the first-instance stage did not require his recusal. The applicant served four months of the sentence and was released on 11 June 2008.

Additional background facts relevant to possible bias included the applicant’s employment as a tax inspector. In 2005, while reviewing a company’s affairs, he initiated misdemeanour proceedings against the company and its responsible person, V.K., who is B.K.’s brother. Following the criminal conviction, the Ministry of Finance dismissed the applicant from the civil service on 20 March 2008 pursuant to the State Administration Act.

Domestic law (Article 40 of the 2001 Code of Criminal Procedure) mandated recusal of a judge who had previously acted as prosecutor in the same case, had conducted investigative acts, or whose impartiality was otherwise open to doubt. The Public Prosecutor’s Office Act further provided that deputies performed all functions of the office and were hierarchically subordinate to the public prosecutor.

The alleged violation therefore centred on whether B.K.’s former status as deputy prosecutor in the very office that had indicted and prosecuted the applicant, combined with the family link arising from the applicant’s earlier professional action against B.K.’s brother, objectively or subjectively undermined the impartiality of the appeal bench that confirmed the conviction. The Court ultimately found no dual role or personal involvement by B.K. in the preparatory stages or the drafting of the indictment.

The case of Paunović v. Serbia (Application no. 54574/07) arose from criminal proceedings against the applicant, Dragoslav Paunović, a Serbian national born in 1956 and residing in Soko Banja. On 2 August 2006, deputy prosecutor I.S. of the Aleksinac Municipal Public Prosecutor’s Office indicted him for causing bodily harm and death by dangerous driving. During the subsequent first-instance proceedings before the Aleksinac Municipal Court, the prosecution was represented at hearings by deputy prosecutors S.S. and I.S. On 12 December 2006 the Municipal Court convicted the applicant and imposed a six-month prison sentence. Both the applicant and prosecutor I.S. lodged appeals.

The appeals were heard by a three-judge bench of the Niš District Court on 17 April 2007. The bench comprised Judge N.S. as president, Judge B.K. as rapporteur, and Judge S.M. The District Court upheld the conviction. Judge B.K. had been elected to the District Court only on 15 August 2006; thus, at the moment the indictment was issued (2 August 2006) he still occupied the post of deputy municipal public prosecutor in Aleksinac.

The applicant challenged the District Court’s judgment by way of an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court of Serbia. He specifically complained that Judge B.K.’s participation violated the guarantee of impartiality. He emphasised that B.K. had held the office of deputy prosecutor in Aleksinac throughout the first-instance proceedings, that the same prosecutor’s office had represented the public interest against him, and that the dual roles of prosecutor and judge were incompatible. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 23 October 2007. It held that Judge B.K. had neither participated in the investigation nor acted as prosecutor in the applicant’s case, and therefore no automatic recusal was required merely because he had previously served in the Aleksinac prosecutor’s office.

The applicant served four months of his sentence before being released on 11 June 2008. In a related factual context, the applicant, then employed as a tax inspector, had in 2005 initiated misdemeanour proceedings against a company and its responsible person, V.K., who was the brother of Judge B.K. Following the criminal conviction the Ministry of Finance dismissed the applicant from the civil service.

Domestic law in force at the time (Article 40 of the 2001 Code of Criminal Procedure) listed mandatory grounds for a judge’s exclusion, including prior participation in the same case as prosecutor or the existence of other circumstances capable of casting doubt on impartiality. The Public Prosecutor’s Office Act further provided that deputy prosecutors act under the authority of the public prosecutor and may perform any prosecutorial function. These facts—particularly Judge B.K.’s contemporaneous service in the very prosecutor’s office that indicted the applicant, his subsequent appearance on the appellate bench, and the additional family connection—constituted the core of the alleged breach of the right to an independent and impartial tribunal under Article 6 of the Convention.

The case of Paunović v. Serbia (Application no. 54574/07) arose from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 December 2007 by Serbian national Dragoslav Paunović, born in 1956 and resident in Soko Banja. He alleged a breach of Article 6 of the Convention on account of the Niš District Court’s lack of impartiality in criminal appeal proceedings against him.

On 2 August 2006, deputy municipal public prosecutor I.S. of the Aleksinac Municipal Public Prosecutor’s Office indicted the applicant for the offence of causing bodily harm and death by dangerous driving. On 12 December 2006 that court convicted the applicant and imposed a six-month prison sentence. Both the applicant and prosecutor I.S. appealed.

The appeal was decided on 17 April 2007 by a three-judge bench of the Niš District Court, comprising Judges N.S. (president), B.K. (rapporteur) and S.M. The bench upheld the conviction and sentence. Judge B.K. had been elected to the District Court only on 15 August 2006 and had therefore still occupied the post of deputy municipal public prosecutor in Aleksinac at the date of the indictment.

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court of Serbia. He complained specifically that Judge B.K.’s presence on the appeal bench violated the requirement of impartiality, because B.K. had held office as deputy prosecutor in Aleksinac throughout the first-instance proceedings and the Aleksinac Prosecutor’s Office had represented the public interest in the case. He invoked the incompatibility of the offices of judge and prosecutor. On 23 October 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that B.K. had neither participated in the investigation nor appeared as prosecutor in the applicant’s case and therefore did not have to recuse himself merely because he had previously occupied that post in Aleksinac.

In a related but separate context, the applicant, then a tax inspector, had in 2005 initiated misdemeanour proceedings against a company and its responsible person V.K., who is Judge B.K.’s brother. Following the criminal conviction the applicant was dismissed from the civil service.

The Public Prosecutor’s Office Act provided that deputies act under the hierarchical authority of the public prosecutor and may perform any prosecutorial function.

The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 6, noting that Judge B.K. had not been involved in the preparatory stages of the proceedings or in the drafting of the indictment and that no dual role had therefore arisen.

The case of Makeyan and Others v. Armenia (Application no. 46435/09) arose from events on 19 February 2008, during Armenia’s presidential election. The three applicants—Petros Makeyan (head of a regional electoral headquarters), Shota Saghatelyan (municipal headquarters head), and Ashot Zakaryan—acted as proxies for opposition candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan. They visited polling station no. 34/06 in Gyumri separately that day. Authorities alleged they argued with and threatened electoral commission members over passport-stamping procedures, obstructing voting for about 30 minutes. The applicants maintained they had only raised concerns about irregularities such as ballot-box stuffing and incorrect stamping.

Criminal proceedings began on 21 February 2008. The applicants were arrested between 25 and 26 February, charged under Article 149 § 2 of the Criminal Code (obstructing electoral-commission work, committed by a group and accompanied by threats of violence), and detained. During the investigation, eleven witnesses—commission chairperson S.H., deputy K.H., members including L.M., S.V., L.Mel., V.G., N.H., H.K. and L.S., plus proxies G.G. and S.P.—gave consistent statements that the applicants had appeared in turn, shouted, argued and threatened commission members, thereby disrupting proceedings. Confrontations with some witnesses confirmed those accounts.

The case proceeded to trial before the Shirak Regional Court. Most witnesses were summoned. Several (N.H., S.V., L.M., L.S.) initially sought leave not to attend, citing fear of pressure, insults or harassment from the applicants’ supporters; L.Mel. cited health reasons. All nonetheless appeared. At the 7 May 2008 hearing, seven witnesses (K.H., L.M., S.V., L.Mel., N.H., H.K. and L.S.) retracted their pre-trial statements, claiming they had been guided or dictated by the investigator and that no incident had occurred. S.H. saw no difference between her pre-trial and trial accounts; V.G. denied dictation, though his statements contained some inconsistencies.

On 13 June 2008 the Regional Court convicted the applicants (Makeyan received three years’ imprisonment, Zakaryan two-and-a-half years, Saghatelyan a suspended two-and-a-half-year term). It relied on the eleven pre-trial statements and polling-station records that showed no ballot-box stuffing. The court rejected the retractions as incredible: they were unsupported by other evidence; some witnesses had earlier asked not to testify in a crowded courtroom for fear of psychological pressure; and the changes appeared motivated by a desire to help the applicants avoid liability. The pre-trial statements were therefore accepted as credible.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the unexplained preference for retracted statements violated their Article 6 fair-trial rights. The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the convictions on 20 August 2008 on identical reasoning. The Court of Cassation declared a further appeal inadmissible on 27 February 2009. Makeyan and Zakaryan were released under amnesty on 22 June 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights the applicants complained that their convictions, based on pre-trial statements later retracted in court, denied them a fair hearing. The Court held that the domestic courts had given sufficient, specific reasons for preferring those statements, finding no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Makeyan and Others v. Armenia (Application no. 46435/09) arose from events during Armenia’s 19 February 2008 presidential election. The three applicants—Petros Makeyan, Shota Saghatelyan and Ashot Zakaryan—were opposition supporters of Levon Ter-Petrosyan and served as his proxies. They were accused of successively visiting polling station no. 34/06 in Gyumri, arguing with and threatening members of the electoral commission about passport-stamping procedures, and thereby obstructing voting for approximately thirty minutes.

Criminal proceedings were opened on 21 February 2008. The applicants were arrested between 25 and 26 February, charged under Article 149 § 2 of the Criminal Code with group obstruction of an electoral commission accompanied by threats of violence, and placed in pre-trial detention. During the investigation eleven witnesses—commission members and other proxies—gave consistent statements describing the applicants’ sequential appearances, shouting, threats and disruption of the commission’s work. Confrontations between certain witnesses and applicants confirmed those accounts.

At trial before the Shirak Regional Court most of the summoned witnesses retracted their pre-trial statements. They claimed the statements had been dictated or guided by the investigator and that no incident had occurred. Two witnesses did not fully recant. Several had earlier asked to be excused from appearing, citing fear of pressure or harassment from the applicants’ supporters.

On 13 June 2008 the Regional Court convicted all three applicants. It relied principally on the pre-trial statements and polling-station records that showed no ballot-box stuffing. The court rejected the retractions as incredible, finding they were motivated by external influence and an intention to shield the applicants. It noted that some witnesses had previously affirmed their original statements and sought to avoid courtroom testimony precisely because of anticipated intimidation. The applicants were found to have acted as a pre-planned group. Sentences of three years, two-and-a-half years and a suspended two-and-a-half-year term were imposed.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the trial court had given no adequate reasons for preferring retracted out-of-court statements and had thereby denied them a fair hearing. The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the convictions on identical reasoning. The Court of Cassation later declared the cassation appeal inadmissible for lack of merit. Two applicants were released under an amnesty in June 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights the applicants alleged that the use of the retracted pre-trial statements violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court examined whether the domestic courts had supplied sufficient and relevant reasons for attaching greater weight to the investigation-stage evidence than to the witnesses’ live testimony. It concluded that the Regional Court’s analysis of the circumstances surrounding the retractions—particularly the earlier applications citing fear of pressure—constituted an adequate justification, so that the overall fairness of the proceedings was not undermined.

The judgment of 5 December 2019 (final 5 March 2020) therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Makeyan and Others v. Armenia (application no. 46435/09) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by three Armenian nationals—Petros Makeyan, Shota Saghatelyan and Ashot Zakaryan—who alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing in criminal proceedings). The complaint centred on their convictions for obstructing an electoral commission, which rested on pre-trial witness statements later retracted in court.

The applicants had been active in the 19 February 2008 presidential election as regional and municipal campaign heads and as proxies for opposition candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan. On election day they visited polling station 34/06 in Gyumri. The prosecution alleged that they successively confronted the commission chair and members, argued over passport-stamping procedures, issued threats and thereby halted voting for approximately thirty minutes. The applicants maintained that they had merely reported irregularities (including alleged ballot-box stuffing) and left without incident.

Criminal proceedings were opened on 21 February 2008. The applicants were arrested between 25 and 26 February, charged under Article 149 § 2 of the Criminal Code (obstruction of an electoral commission by a group using threats) and remanded in custody. Eleven witnesses—commission members and candidate proxies—gave consistent pre-trial statements describing the applicants’ shouting, arguments and threats. Confrontations between certain witnesses and the applicants confirmed those accounts.

At trial before the Shirak Regional Court most of the witnesses attended, despite earlier written requests from several (citing fear of harassment by the applicants’ supporters) to be excused. On 7 May 2008 seven witnesses retracted their statements, claiming they had been dictated or guided by the investigator and that no obstruction had occurred. Two others (the commission chair and one member) did not retract.

On 13 June 2008 the Regional Court convicted the applicants, sentencing Makeyan to three years’ imprisonment, Zakaryan to two-and-a-half years and Saghatelyan to a suspended term of the same length. The court treated the pre-trial statements as credible and reliable, noting that they were corroborated by polling-station records that disproved ballot stuffing. It rejected the retractions as implausible, observing that they were unsupported by other evidence, that several witnesses had previously sought to avoid testifying in a crowded courtroom out of fear, and that the change of testimony appeared motivated by a desire to assist the applicants. The court therefore attributed the retractions to external pressure rather than genuine recantation.

The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 20 August 2008, adopting the same reasoning. The Court of Cassation declared the subsequent points-of-law appeals inadmissible on 27 February 2009. Makeyan and Zakaryan were released under an amnesty in June 2009.

The applicants argued before the Strasbourg Court that the domestic courts’ preference for the retracted out-of-court statements, without adequate justification, denied them a fair hearing. The European Court, in its judgment of 5 December 2019 (final 5 March 2020), examined whether sufficient reasons had been given for attaching greater weight to the pre-trial evidence. It concluded that the Armenian courts had provided such reasons, and therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Zinovyeva v. Russia (application no. 69272/13) concerns events surrounding an authorised public demonstration known as the “March of Millions” held in central Moscow on 6 May 2012 to protest alleged electoral fraud. The event, approved as a march followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square ending at 7.30 p.m., proceeded peacefully until participants reached the square. Police barriers had narrowed the allocated space, a cordon was used to contain the crowd, clashes ensued, and at 5.30 p.m. the police terminated the meeting early and dispersed protesters over approximately two hours.

The applicant, Kristina Nikolayevna Zinovyeva (born 1988), participated in the demonstration. She maintained that she conducted herself peacefully and committed no violence. She was arrested at 6 p.m. at Bolotnaya Square and taken to Taganskiy district police station (arriving around 7.20–9 p.m. according to differing accounts). The Government asserted that she had been participating in breaking the police cordon. The official arrest record, drawn up at 8.45 p.m. at the station, contained no release details and recorded that she had not requested notification of anyone. She was charged under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences with disobeying lawful police orders. The charge relied on identical template reports from two arresting officers stating that, as part of a group of 1,500, she had breached public-event rules by breaking the cordon and thereby hindered police duties. Her own explanatory note stated that she had been in the middle of the crowd, which had pulled her toward officers, and that she had not chanted slogans.

At the station the applicant, mother of a 15-month-old child left at home with a babysitter, was denied a telephone call and any opportunity to notify her family despite insistent requests. She was held overnight in a small, overcrowded cell lacking sanitary facilities, sleeping places or bedding, without access to drinking water or food. She appeared before a justice of the peace around 6 p.m. on 7 May 2012, but the case was not heard; she was returned to the station and released at approximately 10 p.m. after signing an undertaking to attend court.

On 8 May 2012 the justice of the peace convicted her on the basis of the police reports, dismissing her account, but exempted her from liability under Article 2.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences because the offence was minor, had produced no serious consequences, and she had a young child. A warning was issued; she did not appeal. (Article 3.9 § 2 of the same Code prohibits administrative detention of women with children under 14.)

On 26 July 2012 the applicant lodged a civil complaint under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure challenging the arrest, overnight detention, early termination of the rally and detention conditions. On 3 September 2012 the Dorogomilovskiy District Court declined to examine the arrest and related acts on the ground that they formed part of the administrative proceedings and could not be challenged separately; it also failed to address conditions. The Moscow City Court on 20 May 2013 quashed the conditions-related refusal but otherwise upheld the decision. On 23 October 2013 the District Court dismissed the conditions complaint as unsubstantiated; this was confirmed on 28 February 2014.

These facts underpin the complaints of unlawful and disproportionate measures against demonstration participants, inadequate detention conditions at the police station, and the absence of effective domestic remedies.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Kristina Nikolayevna Zinovyeva, a Russian national born in 1988 and resident in Moscow, concerning events surrounding a public demonstration on 6 May 2012. The “March of Millions” had been authorised by Moscow authorities as a march through the city centre followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square that was scheduled to end at 7.30 p.m. The march itself proceeded peacefully. Upon arrival at the square, however, police-installed barriers had narrowed the entrance, and a police cordon confined the crowd. Clashes occurred. At 5.30 p.m. the police ordered the meeting to terminate early and began dispersing participants, a process that lasted approximately two hours.

The applicant, who maintained that she had behaved peacefully and had not engaged in violence, was arrested at the square at 6 p.m. Government records indicated she was transferred to Taganskiy district police station at 7.20 p.m.; the applicant stated she arrived around 9 p.m. The official record of administrative arrest listed the time of arrest as 8.45 p.m. at the station itself and contained no details of her later release. She was charged under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences with disobeying lawful police orders by allegedly breaking the cordon as part of a group of some 1,500 people, thereby obstructing officers in the performance of their duties. The charge rested on identical template reports from the two arresting officers that supplied no individualised facts beyond names.

At the station the applicant was held overnight in a small, overcrowded cell lacking sanitary facilities, a sleeping place or bedding. She was given neither food nor drinking water. Despite repeated requests she was denied a telephone call. She informed officers that she was the mother of a fifteen-month-old child left at home with a babysitter and asked that her family be notified; the request was refused. Her passport contained no record of the child. She was produced before a justice of the peace around 6 p.m. on 7 May, but the hearing could not proceed and she was returned to the station. According to her account she was released at about 10 p.m. that evening after signing an undertaking to appear in court.

On 8 May 2012 the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District found that she had committed the offence but, noting that it had produced no serious consequences and that she had a young child, discontinued the proceedings and issued a warning. She did not appeal.

In July 2012 the applicant brought a civil complaint under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure challenging the lawfulness of her arrest and overnight detention, the early termination of the rally, and the conditions of her detention. The first-instance court declined to examine the arrest and detention claims, holding that they formed part of the administrative proceedings and could not be reviewed separately; it also left the conditions complaint unexamined. The Moscow City Court later quashed the refusal to consider detention conditions but upheld the remainder of the decision. In October 2013 the district court dismissed the conditions complaint as unsubstantiated; that ruling was confirmed on appeal in February 2014.

The facts therefore centre on the applicant’s arrest and overnight detention during the dispersal of an authorised demonstration, the conditions in which she was held, the denial of contact with her family despite her status as mother of an infant, and the subsequent domestic courts’ treatment of her attempts to obtain a review of those measures.

The case of Zinovyeva v. Russia (no. 69272/13) arose from the applicant’s participation in the 6 May 2012 “March of Millions” protest in Moscow against allegedly rigged presidential elections. The event had been authorised as a march followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square due to end at 7.30 p.m. The march itself passed without incident, but upon arrival at the square police barriers had narrowed the entrance, creating crowding. A police cordon was formed; clashes ensued. At 5.30 p.m. the authorities ordered the meeting to terminate early and spent approximately two hours dispersing participants.

The applicant, born in 1988, maintained that she behaved peacefully and committed no violence. She was arrested at about 6 p.m. at the square and taken to Taganskiy district police station (the Government placing her arrival at 7.20 p.m.; the arrest record stating 8.45 p.m.). She was charged under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences with disobeying lawful police orders. The charge rested on identically worded reports from two officers asserting that she, as part of a group of 1 500 people, had broken the cordon and thereby obstructed police duties. An explanatory note she provided stated that she had merely been carried by the crowd toward the officers and had not chanted slogans.

At the station the applicant was denied a telephone call despite repeated requests, including a plea that her family be informed because she had left a 15-month-old child with a babysitter (her passport contained no record of the child). She spent the night in a small, overcrowded cell lacking sanitary facilities, a sleeping place, bedding, drinking water or food. After an abortive court appearance on 7 May she was released around 10 p.m., having signed an undertaking to attend a later hearing.

On 8 May 2012 a justice of the peace found her guilty on the basis of the police reports, rejecting her account. Because the offence had produced no serious consequences and she had a young child, the court discontinued the proceedings and issued only a warning. She did not appeal.

She later brought a complaint under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure challenging the arrest, overnight detention, early termination of the rally and the conditions of detention. The district court declined to examine the first three complaints, holding that they were inseparable from the administrative case. The Moscow City Court subsequently permitted examination of the conditions complaint, which was dismissed as unsubstantiated in 2013–2014.

Domestic law (Article 3.9 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences) forbids administrative detention of women with children under 14; Article 2.9 permits exemption from liability for minor offences. Supreme Court guidance indicated that, once administrative proceedings have been discontinued, related police measures may be challenged separately under Chapter 25 if they interfere with rights.

These facts underpin the complaints that were communicated: that the arrest and dispersal measures were unlawful and disproportionate (implicating Articles 5 and 11), that the overnight detention conditions were degrading (Article 3), and that no effective domestic remedy existed (Article 13). The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
