The case of Zakharchuk v. Russia (Application no. 2967/12) concerns a Polish national born in 1980 in Leningrad (now St Petersburg) to a Soviet mother and Polish father. His parents selected Polish nationality for him shortly after birth. He resided primarily in Russia with his mother on successive residence permits, apart from a period in Poland as a young child (1985–1988) and a six-month visit there in 1994–1995, after which he lost contact with his father. He obtained a Polish passport in 1991 and a further five-year Russian residence permit in 2003 (valid until 2008). After graduating from a St Petersburg university in 2004 he worked as a physical-education teacher. He claimed no knowledge of Polish, no family or social ties in Poland and no recent visits there; the Russian authorities noted at least one border crossing into Poland in 2004.

In 1999 he received a suspended sentence for aggravated theft (later expunged). On 22 December 2004 the St Petersburg Military Garrison Court convicted him under Article 111 § 3 of the Criminal Code of causing grievous bodily harm in a drunken group assault on a shop owner (fractured skull base, concussion and broken jaw). He received a six-year sentence in a strict-regime colony. He was released on parole on 4 May 2010 after serving more than two-thirds of the term, on conditions that included finding employment and reporting to a parole officer until 21 December 2010.

On 11 August 2010 the Ministry of Justice issued an exclusion order (valid until 21 December 2018) on the ground that the particularly serious crime demonstrated a threat to public order. The applicant was notified in November 2010 and ordered to leave within three days in March 2011. He appealed, arguing that expulsion would violate Article 8 of the Convention: he had lived his entire life in Russia, his only relative (his mother) lived there, he had no ties to Poland, parole required his continued presence, the order constituted an unlawful additional punishment, and he posed no ongoing threat.

The Kirov District Court dismissed the appeal on 12 April 2011, holding that the applicant remained a Polish national who had never obtained Russian citizenship, that the unexpunged conviction for a premeditated particularly serious offence created a real threat to public order, that parole, positive prison references, his mother’s residence and delayed nationality application were insufficient to outweigh that threat, and that he had failed to obtain employment as required by parole. The St Petersburg City Court upheld this reasoning on 20 June 2011, adding that the applicant had always acted as a foreigner by repeatedly seeking residence permits rather than citizenship.

On 26 July 2011 the applicant married a Russian national. He was deported to Poland three days later. The eight-year exclusion expired on 21 December 2018.

Under Russian law an unexpunged conviction for a particularly serious offence or a finding that a foreigner’s presence constitutes a threat to public order justifies an exclusion order and subsequent re-entry ban. The applicant’s criminal record for the 2004 offence remained unexpunged for eight years after sentence completion.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation arising from the expulsion of a long-term resident following a serious criminal conviction.

The case of Zakharchuk v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 2967/12) concerns a Polish national’s complaint that an eight-year exclusion order from Russia, issued after his criminal conviction, violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life).

Yan Zakharchuk was born in February 1980 in Leningrad (now St Petersburg) to a Soviet-citizen mother and Polish father. His parents selected Polish nationality for him shortly after birth. He lived in the USSR with his mother, spent time in Poland from 1985, and returned in 1988 (the year his parents divorced). He obtained a Polish passport in 1991 but continued residing in Russia with his mother under successive five-year residence permits as a foreign national. He spent six months in Poland in 1994–1995 visiting his father, after which he lost contact with him and returned to St Petersburg. He claimed no knowledge of Polish, no family or social ties there, and no recent visits, though records showed a 2004 border crossing.

A 1999 conviction for aggravated theft (suspended four-year sentence) was later expunged. In 2003 he received a residence permit valid to 2008. He graduated from a St Petersburg university in 2004 and began work as a physical-education teacher.

On 22 December 2004 the St Petersburg Military Garrison Court convicted him under Article 111 § 3 of the Criminal Code of causing grievous bodily harm during a drunken group attack on a shop owner (a military officer). The victim suffered a fractured skull base, brain concussion and a broken jaw. Zakharchuk received a six-year sentence in a strict-regime colony. The sentencing court recorded no prior criminal record.

He was released on parole on 4 May 2010 after serving more than two-thirds of the term (about 7.5 months early), subject to finding employment and reporting to a parole officer until December 2010. In March 2011 he renewed his Polish passport. In April 2011 he applied for recognition of Russian nationality by birth; the claim was rejected in October 2011 because he had never been a Soviet citizen.

On 11 August 2010 the Ministry of Justice issued an exclusion order declaring his presence undesirable until 21 December 2018, citing his conviction for a particularly serious crime and the resulting threat to public order. He was notified in November 2010 and ordered in March 2011 to leave within three days.

He appealed, arguing that exclusion would disrupt his private and family life: he had lived in Russia virtually all his life with his mother (his only relative), had no Polish ties, and parole conditions required him to remain. He also described the order as an additional, unauthorised punishment. The Kirov District Court dismissed the appeal in April 2011, holding that the premeditated serious offence demonstrated a continuing threat to public order outweighing parole, his mother’s residence, and delayed attempts to obtain nationality or employment. The St Petersburg City Court upheld this in June 2011, confirming the decision was lawful, taken to protect state security, and that he had always acted as a foreign national.

He married a Russian citizen on 26 July 2011 and was deported to Poland three days later. The exclusion expired on 21 December 2018. Domestic law permitted exclusion of foreigners whose residence posed a real threat to public order, particularly those with unexpunged convictions for particularly grave crimes (expungement occurring eight years after sentence completion).

**Case Summary: Zakharchuk v. Russia (Application no. 2967/12)**

The applicant, Yan Zakharchuk, a Polish national born in February 1980 in Leningrad (now St Petersburg) to a Soviet-citizen mother and Polish father, had Polish nationality chosen for him by his parents in May 1980. He resided primarily in the USSR/Russia with his mother after their 1988 divorce, obtaining a Polish passport in 1991 while living there as a foreign national on regularly extended five-year residence permits. He spent limited periods in Poland as a child (including 1985–1988 and six months in 1994–1995) and later claimed no Polish language skills, family, or social ties there, though records showed a 2004 border crossing. A 1999 conviction for aggravated theft (suspended four-year sentence) was later expunged. In 2003 he received a residence permit valid until May 2008; he graduated university in St Petersburg in 2004 and began working as a physical education teacher.

On 22 December 2004 the St Petersburg Military Garrison Court convicted him under Article 111 § 3 of the Criminal Code of causing grievous bodily harm (including skull fracture, concussion, and jaw break) during a drunken group attack on a shop owner (a military officer). He received a six-year sentence in a strict-regime colony. The 1999 record was not treated as extant at sentencing. He was released on parole on 12 May 2010 after serving over two-thirds of the term (Tosnenskiy Town Court, 4 May 2010), with conditions including employment and regular reporting until December 2010.

On 11 August 2010 the Ministry of Justice issued an exclusion order (decision no. 6204-p) declaring his presence undesirable until 21 December 2018, citing the conviction for a particularly serious premeditated crime as a threat to public order. He was informed on 30 November 2010 and told on 9 March 2011 to leave within three days or face deportation.

He appealed on 17 February 2011 to the Kirov District Court, arguing the order violated Article 8 by disrupting his lifelong private and family life in Russia (residence with his only relative, his mother; no Polish ties or residence; parole conditions requiring stay in Russia). He described the exclusion as an additional unauthorised punishment and denied posing a public-order threat. On 12 April 2011 the court dismissed the appeal, noting his Polish nationality, failure to obtain Russian citizenship despite eligibility as a USSR-born person, a 2004 Poland visit, the unexpunged serious conviction, parole not outweighing the threat, delayed 2011 citizenship application, and failure to find employment post-release. Positive prison references and parole were deemed insufficient to negate the public-order risk. The St Petersburg City Court upheld this on 20 June 2011, confirming the order was lawful, competence-based, and justified by state safety; it rejected citizenship claims as his parents’ Polish choice had extinguished any Soviet citizenship, and he had lived as a foreigner seeking residence permits.

On 11 April 2011 he separately sought recognition of Russian nationality by birth; the Dzerzhinsky District Court rejected this on 12 October 2011 as he had never been a Soviet citizen. He married a Russian national on 26 July 2011 and was deported to Poland on 29 July 2011. The exclusion expired on 21 December 2018.

These facts concern the alleged Article 8 interference: an eight-year exclusion of a long-term resident after a serious criminal conviction, involving established Russian ties (residence, education, work, maternal family) versus public-order interests. The applicant later obtained a Polish passport in 2011 valid until 2021. (Word count: 512)

The applicant, Dragan Čutura (born 1980), was indicted in 2013 before the Ivanić-Grad Municipal Court for uttering serious threats against neighbours. An expert report established that he had committed the acts while in a state of mental derangement caused by long-standing paranoid schizophrenia. The Municipal Court therefore ordered his pre-trial detention on 26 November 2013 on the ground of risk of reoffending; he was detained on 30 November and transferred to Zagreb Prison Hospital on 2 December. Appeals against the detention orders were dismissed by panels of the Velika Gorica County Court on which Judge LJ.B. sat (12 December 2013 and 13 January 2014).

On 14 January 2014 the Municipal Court found that the applicant had committed the offence in a state of mental derangement, that he posed a danger to others, and ordered his internment in a psychiatric hospital under the Protection of Individuals with Mental Disorders Act, with detention continuing until the judgment became final. Appeals against both the internment order and the continued detention were dismissed by County Court panels that again included Judge LJ.B. (23 January and 3 March 2014). Subsequent extraordinary-review and constitutional complaints alleging lack of impartiality because of Judge LJ.B.’s earlier involvement in the detention decisions were rejected by the Supreme Court (4 June 2014) and the Constitutional Court (20 May 2015).

Once the criminal judgment became final, the file was transmitted on 19 March 2014 to the Zagreb County Court, the court competent to implement the internment. That court opened the civil-committal proceedings, first noting and then formally appointing a legal-aid lawyer (T.Ž.) because the applicant had not chosen counsel. On 10 April 2014 it ordered six months’ confinement in Vrapče Psychiatric Hospital starting 3 May 2014. On 28 July the hospital requested a one-year extension, citing incomplete treatment. New proceedings were opened and T.Ž. was re-appointed. The investigating judge visited the applicant on 30 July; T.Ž. attended but asked no questions. An independent psychiatrist recommended short therapeutic leave.

At a hearing on 27 August 2014 attended by hospital staff, the State Attorney and T.Ž., all present (including T.Ž.) agreed to the extension; T.Ž. made no other submissions. The court ordered a further year of confinement and granted four days’ leave. The applicant’s father, learning of the extension only by chance, appealed, complaining that the family had never been notified and that legal representation had been ineffective. The County Court’s three-judge panel dismissed the appeal on 19 December 2014 solely because a lawyer had been appointed; the Constitutional Court upheld that reasoning on 3 June 2015. The applicant was conditionally released on 24 August 2015 after a later request by privately retained counsel.

These facts form the basis of the complaints of insufficient substantive and procedural safeguards (including ineffective legal aid, absence of family involvement and limited personal participation) surrounding the initial and extended involuntary hospitalisation, and of the alleged lack of impartiality of Judge LJ.B. in the related criminal proceedings.

**Case Summary: Čutura v. Croatia (Application no. 55942/15)**

The applicant, Dragan Čutura (born 1980), a Croatian national, alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (right to liberty) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights. These concerned insufficient substantive and procedural safeguards in his involuntary psychiatric confinement proceedings and a lack of impartiality by an appeal court judge.

In 2013, the applicant was indicted before the Ivanić-Grand Municipal Court for uttering serious threats against neighbours. An expert report established that he had long suffered from paranoid schizophrenia and committed the acts in a state of mental derangement. The State Attorney amended the indictment to seek his placement in a psychiatric hospital under the Protection of Individuals with Mental Disorders Act. On 26 November 2013, the Municipal Court ordered pre-trial detention due to a risk of reoffending; the applicant was detained from 30 November 2013 and transferred to Zagreb Prison Hospital on 2 December 2013. Detention was extended multiple times. Appeals against these orders were dismissed by the Velika Gorica County Court, with Judge LJ.B. participating in the panels on 12 December 2013 and 13 January 2014.

On 14 January 2014, the Municipal Court found that the applicant had committed the offence while mentally deranged and posed a threat to others, ordering his internment in a psychiatric institution. He was to remain detained until the judgment became final. The applicant appealed both the internment order and continued detention. On 23 January 2014, a Velika Gorica County Court panel including Judge LJ.B. dismissed the detention appeal. On 3 March 2014, another panel including Judge LJ.B. dismissed the appeal against the judgment, rendering it final. The applicant’s subsequent requests for extraordinary review (alleging Judge LJ.B.’s lack of impartiality due to prior involvement) were dismissed by the Supreme Court on 4 June 2014 and by the Constitutional Court on 20 May 2015.

After the judgment became final, the file was forwarded on 19 March 2014 to the Zagreb County Court, competent for the confinement procedure. The applicant remained in the prison hospital. The County Court opened proceedings and, noting he had no lawyer, appointed legal aid lawyer T.Ž. On 10 April 2014, it committed him to Vrapče Psychiatric Hospital for six months starting 3 May 2014.

On 28 July 2014, the hospital requested a one-year extension, citing positive but incomplete treatment results. The County Court reopened proceedings and reappointed T.Ž. On 30 July 2014, the judge visited the applicant at the hospital; a note recorded that communication was possible, he participated in therapy, his mother visited, and he sought therapeutic leave. T.Ž. attended but asked no questions. An independent expert later supported short-term leave.

A hearing on 27 August 2014 was attended by hospital representatives, the State Attorney’s Office, and T.Ž. (the applicant was absent). All, including T.Ž. (who made no other submissions), agreed to the extension. The court ordered a further one-year hospitalisation, referencing the visit note and lack of opposition, while granting leave from 28–31 August 2014. The applicant’s father (acting on his behalf) appealed, arguing the family had never been informed of the extension (learning of it only by inspecting the file) and that representation was ineffective. A County Court panel dismissed the appeal on 19 December 2014, noting that a lawyer had been appointed. The Constitutional Court dismissed a further complaint on 3 June 2015.

Meanwhile, the applicant’s chosen lawyer from the criminal proceedings (F.Ž.) had unsuccessfully sought information from the hospital. On 22 May 2015, the applicant (via F.Ž.) requested release. After further review, the County Court ordered conditional release on 24 August 2015.

These facts highlight issues with the judge’s repeated involvement across detention and internment appeals (relevant to impartiality under Article 6 § 1) and deficiencies in the confinement proceedings, including passive legal aid representation, the applicant’s absence from the extension hearing, lack of family notification, and reliance on limited evidence (relevant to safeguards under Article 5 § 1). The Court communicated these complaints in 2016.

001-189163:
The case of Grech and Others v. Malta (Application no. 69287/14) concerns four Maltese part-owners of a twentieth-century corner townhouse of approximately 135 square metres known as “Assunta” in Paola. The first applicant held a one-seventh undivided share, the second and third applicants one twenty-eighth share each, and the fourth applicant one twenty-first share.

In 1962 the applicants’ ancestor granted the property on temporary emphyteusis for seventeen years at an annual ground rent of MTL 45 (approximately EUR 105). In 1971 a sub-emphyteusis was granted to C.C. When the temporary title expired in 1979, Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta converted it into a statutory lease at MTL 86.54 (approximately EUR 200) per year. In April 1986 the State requisitioned the property; C.C. was rehoused and surrendered the keys. In October 1986 the Housing Department allocated the premises to D.L. (recently arrived from the United Kingdom with her employed husband) at an unchanged rent of MTL 86. The owners refused the rent, did not recognise the occupants as tenants, and the latter paid the Department directly. The occupants also took possession of an adjacent room belonging to the owners that was not covered by the requisition order; the authorities took no action despite being notified.

After D.L.’s death the owners sought the property’s return and offered alternative accommodation, without success. Following the husband’s death their son L.L. applied in 2002 to be recognised as tenant and was so recognised in 2003 over the owners’ objections. The same low rent continued. An ombudsman report of October 2003 found that the authorities had given insufficient attention to the owners’ complaints. L.L. later obtained a planning permit (over the owners’ 2007 objection) for structural alterations that included the extra room and that the owners contended damaged the property’s character and value.

In May 2007 the owners commenced constitutional proceedings alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, seeking annulment of the requisition, return of the property and compensation. The property was de-requisitioned in February 2010, but the Government did not recover the keys until August 2014. An April 2010 government offer of EUR 4,507 for twenty-four years’ occupation was refused as inadequate. In April 2011 the Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation, held that the requisition had been lawful and pursued a legitimate aim but had failed to strike a fair balance given the unvaried low rent, and awarded EUR 7,535 (calculated by reference to the statutory increases that would have applied under Chapter 158). It ordered return of the already de-requisitioned property. On appeal the Constitutional Court (April 2014) set aside the return order, characterised the first-instance sum as merely the legal rent rather than just satisfaction for the violation, and awarded an additional EUR 5,000 non-pecuniary damage, making a total of EUR 12,535 (costs to be shared). Material-damage claims were left open.

When the keys were finally returned the property was found abandoned mid-refurbishment, uninhabitable and suffering severe water damage. A 2014 valuation put its vacant-possession market value at EUR 145,000 (EUR 175,000 if completed) and its annual rental value at EUR 7,980, with interpolated historic rents far exceeding the sums actually received. The applicants maintained that the requisition lacked pressing social need, that the State had failed to prevent unauthorised occupation and deterioration, and that the domestic compensation was inadequate.

The applicants, four Maltese co-owners of a 135 m² three-storey townhouse in Paola, inherited shares in a property originally granted by their ancestor on 17-year temporary emphyteusis in 1962. When that arrangement expired in 1979, Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta automatically converted it into a statutory lease at a controlled annual rent of roughly EUR 200. In April 1986 the Housing Department requisitioned the house and allocated it to a British couple who had arrived only three months earlier and who were not shown to be homeless, elderly or otherwise in urgent need; the requisition order itself recorded no exceptional social-need grounds. The owners refused to recognise the occupants or accept rent, so payments were made to the Department. The occupants also occupied an adjacent room belonging to the applicants that lay outside the requisition, yet the authorities took no enforcement action.

After both original occupants died, their adult son was recognised as tenant in 2003 over the owners’ formal objection. An ombudsman later found that the authorities had given insufficient attention to the owners’ repeated complaints. In 2007 the tenant obtained planning permission for structural alterations that, according to the owners, permanently altered the building’s character and value. Constitutional proceedings were then instituted alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The property was formally de-requisitioned in February 2010, but the keys were not recovered from the former tenant until August 2014. A government offer of EUR 4 507 for 24 years’ occupation was rejected as derisory.

The first-instance constitutional court held that the requisition, although lawful and in principle pursuing a social aim, had failed to strike a fair balance because the rent had remained frozen at a fraction of market value for a quarter-century. It awarded EUR 7 535 (calculated solely on the statutory increments that would have applied under Chapter 158) and ordered restitution. The Constitutional Court, ruling in April 2014, confirmed the violation but noted that restitution was no longer possible; it added EUR 5 000 non-pecuniary damage, producing a total of EUR 12 535, while observing that the sum still reflected only the legal rent rather than genuine compensation for the interference.

When the keys were finally handed over the house was found abandoned mid-refurbishment, uninhabitable, and suffering severe water damage. An independent valuation placed its 2014 vacant-possession value at EUR 145 000 (EUR 175 000 if completed) and its annual rental value at almost EUR 8 000—many times the controlled rent actually received. These facts form the core of the applicants’ complaint that the prolonged, low-rent occupation, the unauthorised extra-room use, the permitted structural works, the delay in recovering possession and the inadequate domestic award together constituted a disproportionate interference with their property rights for which they had received no effective redress.

The case of Grech and Others v. Malta (Application no. 69287/14) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property) arising from the long-term requisition of a family-owned townhouse in Paola, Malta, under domestic housing legislation. The four applicants (Mary Grech, Christopher Mintoff, Stephanie Mintoff and Lilian Wismayer) hold undivided shares in the property “Assunta,” a three-storey, 135-square-metre corner house. Their ancestor L.M. had granted it on temporary emphyteusis in 1962 for 17 years at an annual ground rent of MTL 45 (approximately EUR 105). In 1971 a sub-emphyteusis was created in favour of C.C. When the temporary title expired in 1979, Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta automatically converted the arrangement into a statutory lease at MTL 86.54 (approximately EUR 200) per year.

In April 1986 the Housing Authority requisitioned the premises and allocated them to D.L., a recent arrival from the United Kingdom who had previously occupied another house in Senglea that was neither at risk of requisition nor allocated on grounds of age or homelessness. The owners refused to recognise D.L. as tenant and declined the rent; the occupants therefore paid the Housing Department directly. They also occupied an adjacent room belonging to the same owners that fell outside the requisition order; the authorities took no action despite being notified. After D.L.’s death the owners offered the remaining occupant a smaller nearby property in an unsuccessful attempt to regain possession. In 2003 the authorities recognised D.L.’s son L.L. as tenant over the owners’ objections. Rent remained frozen at the 1986 level. L.L. later obtained planning permission (despite the owners’ objection) to carry out structural alterations, including to the unauthorised extra room; these works altered the building’s character.

In May 2007 the owners instituted constitutional proceedings seeking annulment of the requisition, restitution of the property and compensation. The property was de-requisitioned in February 2010, but the keys were not immediately recovered. The Government offered EUR 4 507 as rent for the entire 24-year period; the owners rejected the sum as grossly inadequate. In 2011 the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, holding that although the requisition pursued a legitimate social aim it failed to strike a fair balance. Compensation of EUR 7 535 was calculated solely by applying the statutory rent-increase formula of Chapter 158. On appeal the Constitutional Court (28 April 2014) confirmed that restitution could no longer be ordered and increased the award by EUR 5 000 for non-pecuniary damage, producing a total of EUR 12 535 (costs split equally). It left open any claim for physical damage.

Keys were finally returned in August 2014. An architect’s report of the same month described the property as abandoned mid-refurbishment, uninhabitable, unfinished and severely damaged by water ingress. Its vacant-possession market value was EUR 145 000 (EUR 175 000 if completed); contemporaneous rental value was EUR 7 980 per year, far exceeding the controlled rent that had been paid throughout. Interpolated historic rental figures similarly demonstrated a widening gap. The applicants contended that the combination of requisition, frozen low rent, unauthorised occupation of extra space, structural alterations and delayed, inadequate redress constituted a disproportionate interference with their property rights that was not justified by any pressing social need.

001-189164:
The applicants, Maltese nationals Edward and Cynthia Zammit Maempel, each own a half-undivided share of a residential property in Qormi. In 1986 they granted it on 21-year emphyteusis to third parties at an annual rent of approximately €230. On 31 December 1992 the Director of Social Housing issued requisition order RO53704 (no reasons stated) and allocated the property to Mr and Ms A. In 1997 the Housing Authority arranged transfer of the remaining emphyteutical title to the same occupants. When the grant expired in 2007, Article 12A of the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance automatically converted it into a statutory lease. The occupants thereafter paid only €279.52 per year under rent-control legislation; the applicants rejected this sum as far below market value, so it was deposited in court. The 2010 rent-increase amendments did not apply because the figure already exceeded the statutory threshold of €185.

In March 2009 the applicants commenced constitutional proceedings, alleging that the requisition, the inadequate rent and the authorities’ failure to maintain the property violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. A court-appointed architect later valued the property (2010 figures) at €139,800 for sale and €4,893 annual rental, and estimated €58,234 would be needed to render it habitable again. The Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation in March 2013: the occupants had abandoned the premises, which had fallen into serious disrepair, so the public-interest purpose of providing housing was no longer served. The court declared the requisition null, ordered vacant possession and eviction within one month, and awarded €50,000 compensation.

On appeal the Constitutional Court, in July 2014, confirmed the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 violation, accepting that the requisition imposed a disproportionate burden, that the property had been neglected, and that the Housing Authority had shown no willingness to remedy the damage. It nevertheless revoked both the annulment of the requisition and the eviction order, reduced compensation to €12,000 (non-pecuniary only) and attributed one-fifth of appeal costs to the applicants. It reasoned that constitutional jurisdiction should not replace ordinary remedies: the applicants could still seek judicial review of the requisition under Article 469A of the Code of Organisation and Civil Procedure and pursue material damages and eviction in the ordinary courts. It also noted that the applicants had waited 17 years before instituting proceedings.

Although the Housing Authority formally derequisitioned the property on 5 August 2014, vacant possession was not restored. No keys were delivered and the applicants could not take physical control. They requested a joint condition report to document the extensive damage for which the State is liable under section 5 of the Housing Act; the Authority did not reply. In 2015 the Authority offered the keys; the applicants declined them without a joint report. The Authority then deposited the keys in court in September 2016 and maintained that any claim for dilapidation had to be pursued in ordinary proceedings.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints: a continuing interference with their property rights through a requisition that long outlived any housing need, produced only a peppercorn rent, caused substantial physical deterioration, and left them unable to recover possession or obtain full redress; and the absence of an effective domestic remedy, given the Constitutional Court’s refusal to annul the order, its reduction of compensation, and its insistence that ordinary courts (subject to time-bars and other limitations) remained available.

The applicants, Maltese nationals Edward and Cynthia Zammit Maempel (born 1968), each own a half-share of a residential property in Qormi. In 1986 they granted a 21-year emphyteusis over it to third parties at an annual ground rent of roughly €230. On 31 December 1992 the Director of Social Housing issued a requisition order (RO53704) that contained no statement of reasons and allocated the premises to Mr and Ms A. In 1997 the Housing Authority caused the remaining term of the emphyteusis to be transferred to the same occupants. When the grant expired in 2007, Article 12A of the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance automatically converted the occupation into a statutory lease. The occupants thereafter paid a controlled rent of €279.52 per year—an amount the applicants refused as derisory. The rent was deposited in court and never revised, because it already exceeded the statutory threshold of €185.

A court-appointed architect later valued the property (2010 figures) at a capital value of €139,800 and an open-market rental of €4,893 per annum; he also estimated that €58,234 would be required merely to render the neglected building habitable again. The applicants therefore complained that the requisition, the controlled rent and the authorities’ failure to maintain the premises imposed an excessive and disproportionate burden contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They further alleged that they lacked an effective domestic remedy (Article 13), particularly after the Constitutional Court granted only limited redress.

On 9 March 2009 they instituted constitutional proceedings. The Civil Court (First Hall) held on 26 March 2013 that the requisition violated A1P1: the occupants had abandoned the property, the Housing Authority had done nothing to prevent its deterioration, and the owners had been forced to bear virtually the entire social cost of housing provision. The court declared the requisition null, ordered vacant possession and eviction within one month, and awarded €50,000 compensation.

The Attorney General and Housing Authority appealed. On 18 July 2014 the Constitutional Court confirmed the finding of a violation, accepting that the property had been left uninhabitable and that the requisition therefore served no legitimate housing purpose. It nevertheless revoked both the annulment of the requisition and the eviction order, reduced the award to €12,000 non-pecuniary damages, and held that the applicants’ 17-year delay in suing, together with the availability of ordinary remedies (judicial review under Article 469A of the Code of Organisation and Civil Procedure and ordinary civil actions for eviction and damages), justified the more limited relief.

Although the Housing Authority formally derequisitioned the property on 5 August 2014, the keys were not returned and no condition report was prepared. The applicants refused to collect the keys without such a report, which they needed in order to pursue compensation for the extensive damage under section 5 of the Housing Act. The authorities declined to co-operate; the keys were eventually deposited in court in September 2016. The occupants remained in occupation and the applicants were still unable to regain possession.

These facts—the unexplained 1992 requisition, the conversion into a low-rent statutory tenancy, the long-term neglect of the building, the Constitutional Court’s refusal to restore possession or award adequate compensation, and the subsequent administrative obstruction—constitute the core of the alleged violations of A1P1 and Article 13.

The case of Ragnar Thorisson v. Iceland (Application no. 52623/14) concerns proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights arising from parallel tax and criminal processes in Iceland. The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1971 and living in Reykjavík, lodged his application on 9 July 2014, represented by counsel. The Government was represented by the State Attorney General. Notice of the application was given on 13 June 2017, and the Court (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 12 February 2019 after deliberations on 22 January 2019.

The relevant facts begin with tax proceedings. On 21 October 2010 the Directorate of Tax Investigation opened an audit of the applicant’s 2006 income-tax return. He was interviewed on 5 November 2010. A concluding report was issued on 13 January 2011. The following day the Directorate informed the applicant that the file would be sent to the Directorate of Internal Revenue for tax reassessment and that a decision on possible criminal proceedings was pending; he was given 30 days to comment. On 18 February 2011 (five days after the deadline) the applicant asked that the matter be concluded by a fine or referred to the State Internal Revenue Board.

On 23 November 2011 the Directorate of Internal Revenue, relying on the investigation report, determined that the applicant had failed to declare substantial capital gains received in 2006. It increased the declared capital-gains figure, reassessed the tax and imposed a 25 % surcharge under Section 108 of the Income Tax Act. The applicant paid the additional tax and surcharge. He did not appeal to the State Internal Revenue Board; the decision therefore became final in February 2012 upon expiry of the three-month time-limit.

Criminal proceedings followed. On 28 March 2012 the Directorate of Tax Investigation reported the case to the Special Prosecutor and notified the applicant. He was first interviewed by police on 14 September 2012. On 10 October 2012 the Special Prosecutor indicted him for aggravated tax offences, specifically under-declaration of income in the 2007 tax return, including the 2006 capital gains already the subject of the surcharge.

On 16 May 2013 the District Court found that the applicant had acted with gross negligence (sufficient for criminal liability under the tax legislation) and convicted him. It imposed a three-month prison sentence suspended for two years, a fine of ISK 24 006 000 (approximately EUR 152 000) and legal costs of ISK 878 500 plus VAT.

The applicant appealed. On 22 May 2014 the Supreme Court rejected his request that the case be dismissed on the basis of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention (ne bis in idem). It upheld the conviction and the suspended prison sentence but reduced the fine to ISK 21 000 000 (approximately EUR 136 000), expressly taking the earlier surcharge into account, and awarded further legal costs of ISK 1 286 614.

Domestic law of particular relevance comprises Sections 108–110 of the Income Tax Act No. 90/2003 (surcharges of up to 25 % for incorrect returns; administrative or criminal fines of up to ten times the evaded tax, never less than double, for intentional or grossly negligent false statements or non-filing; procedures for fines, settlements and referral to police) and Article 262 of the Penal Code No. 19/1940 (imprisonment of up to six years for major tax offences involving significant amounts or committed in a particularly flagrant manner). These provisions formed the legal basis for both the administrative surcharge and the subsequent criminal conviction arising from the same undeclared 2006 capital gains.

The dual proceedings—final administrative imposition of a 25 % surcharge followed by a criminal indictment, conviction, suspended imprisonment and (adjusted) fine for identical conduct—constitute the core factual matrix of the alleged violation.

The ECHR case of Levon Alikhanyan v. Armenia (no. 6818/10, judgment of 14 February 2019) concerns an Armenian farmer from Shnogh village whose eight agricultural plots (totalling 6.428 ha, used for crops, gardening, beekeeping and livestock) were expropriated for a copper-molybdenum mining project. In the 1970s the Teghout deposit was identified nearby. In 2001 Armenian Copper Programme CJSC received a 25-year mining licence. Government Decree no. 1279-N of 1 November 2007 designated large tracts of Shnogh and Teghout land as expropriation zones for “State needs,” changing their agricultural classification so that the company (or its subsidiary Teghout CJSC) could acquire them. The Decree asserted that economic development, infrastructure, production and export interests prevailed over private ownership.

Teghout CJSC offered the applicant AMD 3 439 650 (approximately EUR 7 478), being the market value plus the statutory 15 % extra, based on reports prepared by its chosen valuer, Oliver Group LLC. The applicant refused, considering the figures inadequate. He tried but failed to obtain an independent valuation, claiming no other licensed firm would assess the land. On 13 May 2008 the company sued in the Lori Regional Court to compel signature of the transfer agreement, relying on the same Oliver Group reports. The applicant argued that the valuations ignored his original purchase prices and subsequent investments, that the land had been undervalued, and that the taking served private profit rather than genuine public interest.

During the hearing the company produced “corrected” reports that slightly altered some figures. It asked the court to apply the higher of the original or revised amounts (plus 15 %). On 7 November 2008 the Regional Court ordered expropriation and awarded compensation on that basis (individual plot awards ranging from AMD 223 100 to AMD 638 250). The applicant appealed, invoking Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 18 March 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, stating that market value had been properly established from the corrected reports. The Court of Cassation declared the further appeal inadmissible on 18 June 2009.

Domestic law required expropriation only for overriding public interest (including mining of State significance), prior equivalent compensation (market value + 15 %), and an obligatory independent valuation. The Civil Procedure Code guaranteed equality of arms and empowered the court to appoint its own forensic expert, yet none was appointed. These facts form the core of the alleged violations of the right to property and the right to a fair trial: the applicant was deprived of his livelihood land by a private mining company acting under a Government decree, compensation was fixed solely by the acquirer’s valuer, the courts accepted those figures without independent verification, and the applicant was unable to obtain a competing expert opinion.

The case of Parsadanyan v. Armenia (no. 5444/10) concerns three family members from Teghout village who jointly owned 0.430 ha of arable land used for subsistence crops, gardening and livestock. In 2001 a private firm obtained a 25-year mining licence for the nearby Teghout copper-molybdenum deposit. Government Decree 1279-N of 1 November 2007 designated large tracts, including the applicants’ plot, as expropriation zones “for State needs” so that Teghout CJSC (a vehicle of the licence-holder) could acquire the land for a mining plant. The Decree invoked the prevailing public interest in economic development, production and exports.

Teghout CJSC offered AMD 265 650 (market value of AMD 231 000 plus the statutory 15 %). The applicants rejected the figure as inadequate; they could not obtain an independent valuation because no other licensed valuer would assess the land. The company then sued in the Lori Regional Court to compel a sale, relying on an Oliver Group LLC report that valued the plot at AMD 231 000. The applicants contested the methodology (lowest comparable prices, omission of fruit trees, erroneous statement that the land lacked water). After an initial judgment was quashed for defective notification, a corrected Oliver report raised the market value to AMD 262 000 (total compensation AMD 301 300). On 2 June 2009 the Regional Court accepted that report as the sole lawful evidence, refused the applicants’ request for a forensic valuation by the State Expertise Centre (holding that each party must produce its own proof) and ordered expropriation.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the compensation was not equivalent, that the court had uncritically adopted the opponent’s valuation and that it should have used its statutory power to order an expert examination once it became clear they could not obtain an alternative report. The Civil Court of Appeal heard the case on 24 July 2009 in their absence (notifications had been sent) and on 7 August upheld the Regional Court, finding no necessity for a forensic report. The applicants’ counsel claimed the decision was never served on him. After obtaining a copy on 1 October he lodged a cassation appeal on 9 October, seeking restoration of the time-limit. On 28 October 2009 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time, stating that the applicants themselves had been served in due course.

These facts engage Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (whether the compensation, based exclusively on the expropriator’s valuation and without independent verification, amounted to the “prior equivalent compensation” required by the Constitution and the 2006 Alienation Law) and Article 6 (whether the refusal to appoint an expert created an inequality of arms and whether defective notification of the appeal judgment denied access to the Court of Cassation). Domestic law characterises mining projects of State significance as a prevailing public interest and defines adequate compensation as market value plus 15 %, while the Code of Civil Procedure allows a court to order a forensic examination of its own motion when specialised knowledge is required.

The case originated in an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Emanuel Ciantar (a Maltese national) and Maxkim Ltd (a company he owned and controlled). It concerned two sets of criminal proceedings against Ciantar’s son M., who lived with him, and the resulting interference with the applicants’ vehicles.

M. was not a company employee. The Court of Criminal Appeal confirmed the confiscation in October 2011. By the time the authorities took physical possession the van had already been returned to the importer under a hire-purchase arrangement; the Government later contended that Maxkim therefore no longer had a “possession.”

The case of O’Leary v. Ireland (Application no. 45580/16) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Alan O’Leary, an Irish national born in 1986 who lives in Cork and suffers from severe brain damage. He lacks legal capacity and was represented by his sister and guardian. His condition was alleged to have been caused by a measles vaccination given in 1988, when he was 15 months old. In November 2002 his mother instituted High Court proceedings on his behalf against the local health authority, the State, the Attorney General and the doctor who administered the vaccine.

The complaints communicated to the Government concerned the length of the civil proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy, engaging Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention. The remaining complaints were declared inadmissible.

On 5 August 2003 the High Court made a limited discovery order against the health authority, requiring production within eight weeks of all relevant records relating to the applicant, the vaccine, any contemporaneous adverse effects, the obtaining of consent and the health of family members. The authority complied only in June 2008, more than four and a half years late. The applicant appealed the scope of that order, obtaining a further limited discovery order against all four defendants on 30 January 2004. A further appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court in July 2006, subject only to a minor amendment.

The applicant’s mother, described as a vital witness, died in December 2007. In June 2008 the applicant’s solicitor wrote to the health authority complaining that the delays had caused grave prejudice through the loss of essential evidence and proposed settlement, which was not accepted. An application made in May 2008 to have the State defendants’ defence set aside was refused by the High Court on 12 March 2010.

The High Court trial occupied ten hearing days. The applicant called no factual evidence; independent medical witnesses who had reviewed the medical records and the discovered documents gave evidence. On the eleventh day, 19 July 2011, the judge granted the defendants’ application to strike the action out for failure to establish a prima facie case. He noted that the applicant accepted there was insufficient evidence of negligence by the doctor and held that no evidence had been adduced capable of supporting any of the grounds against the State defendants. High Court proceedings formally terminated on 19 December 2011.

The applicant filed a notice of appeal containing 30 grounds. After the Court of Appeal was established in October 2014 the case was transferred to it. Written submissions were lodged in 2015. On 10 February 2016 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the trial judge had correctly taken the applicant’s case at its highest and that there was no basis for overturning the High Court decision. It also observed the many legal hurdles that would have had to be overcome. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 10 May 2016, bringing the proceedings to an end after approximately 13 years and six months.

Irish law, as later clarified by the Supreme Court in Nash v. DPP (2016), recognises a constitutional right to a timely trial and the possibility of damages for its breach, as well as a claim under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 where no other remedy exists. The applicant maintained that no effective remedy had been available in respect of the delay that occurred in his case.

The chronology reveals prolonged periods of inactivity, most notably the four-and-a-half-year failure to comply with the 2003 discovery order, successive appeals on discovery that lasted until 2006, the interval between the mother’s death and the trial, and the subsequent appellate stages that continued until 2016. These delays coincided with the irretrievable loss of the principal witness.

**CASE OF O’LEARY v. IRELAND (Application no. 45580/16)**

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Irish national Alan O’Leary (born 1986, resident in Cork) concerning the length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective remedy. Lacking legal capacity due to severe brain damage (asserted to have resulted from a measles vaccination administered in 1988 at 15 months of age), he was represented by his sister and guardian. Proceedings were instituted in November 2002 by his mother against the local health authority, the State, the Attorney General (collectively the State defendants), and the administering doctor (H).

A High Court discovery order of 5 August 2003 required the local health authority to produce relevant records, vaccine information, adverse-effects data, consent details, and family health information within eight weeks. Compliance occurred only in June 2008—a delay exceeding four and a half years. The applicant appealed the order’s scope, resulting in a further limited discovery order of 30 January 2004 against all defendants. A subsequent appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court in July 2006 with only a minor amendment.

The applicant’s mother, described as a vital witness, died in December 2007. In June 2008 counsel wrote to the health authority highlighting grave prejudice from the delays and the loss of essential evidence, proposing (but not securing) settlement of the substantive claim. An application in May 2008 to set aside the State defendants’ defence was refused by the High Court on 12 March 2010.

The High Court trial occupied ten hearing days. No factual evidence was adduced on the applicant’s behalf; independent medical witnesses testified solely on the basis of records and discovered documents. On the eleventh day (19 July 2011) the judge granted the defendants’ application to strike out the action for failure to establish a prima facie case. The claim against doctor H was dismissed on the applicant’s concession that there was insufficient evidence of negligence in administration. No supporting evidence was found for the grounds advanced against the State defendants. High Court proceedings formally terminated on 19 December 2011.

A notice of appeal raising 30 grounds was lodged. Following creation of the Court of Appeal in October 2014 the case was transferred there. Written submissions were filed in February and September 2015. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 10 February 2016, holding that the trial judge had correctly taken the case at its highest and that the applicant faced multiple legal hurdles with no basis for overturning the High Court decision. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 10 May 2016, bringing the proceedings to an end.

The overall duration from institution of the action in November 2002 until final disposal in May 2016 was approximately thirteen and a half years. Significant periods of inactivity or delay were attributable to the authorities, particularly the health authority’s protracted non-compliance with discovery, successive interlocutory appeals, and the time taken to list and determine the substantive trial and subsequent appeals. The death of the applicant’s mother during the currency of the delays was said to have caused irremediable prejudice through the loss of key testimony.

Domestic law at the relevant time, as later clarified by the Supreme Court in Nash v. D.P.P. (2016), recognised a constitutional right to a timely trial and the theoretical availability of damages for its breach (or under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 where no other remedy existed). The precise circumstances in which such damages would be awarded remained subject to further judicial development.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints under Article 6 § 1 (reasonable-time requirement) and Article 13 (effective remedy) that were communicated to the Irish Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case of *Shamsudinova and Others v. Russia* (applications nos. 4635/08, 14202/08 and 21432/12) concerns three incidents in Chechnya in which applicants’ relatives were killed by Russian federal forces or police, with subsequent investigations allegedly ineffective, engaging Articles 2, 5 and 13 of the Convention.

In the first application, on 27 December 2001 approximately 20 federal servicemen in APCs and UAZ vehicles surrounded the applicant’s house in Urus-Martan, forcibly entered and abducted her son Alvi Bugayev from his bed, taking him undressed along with a family car and documents. He was held for 15 days at the Urus-Martan VOVD. On 12 January 2002, after notification of his release, he drove out of the station followed by military vehicles. Near his sister’s house 200 metres away, four armed servicemen shot him dead in front of his wife and children during curfew. Witnesses identified the perpetrators as the same servicemen who had threatened him. The investigation opened that day collected Kalashnikov cartridges and statements (including an operational report that servicemen killed him as a “traitor”). It was suspended in March 2002 without identifying anyone and without notifying the family. After complaints it was briefly resumed in 2007 (when the applicant finally received victim status) but suspended again. A 2007 court complaint of ineffectiveness was dismissed. No perpetrators were identified.

In the second application, on the night of 29–30 December 2001 a BRDM belonging to the Leninskiy district military prosecutor’s office opened unprovoked fire on a Ministry of Emergency Situations vehicle. On 4 January 2002 the same vehicle was recognised at MES premises. When officers tried to detain it, Deputy Minister Colonel Ruslan Yunusov jumped onto the hull to stop it. The BRDM fired, broke through gates and drove to the nearby military commander’s office, where servicemen shot Yunusov; he died of his wounds. Ballistic evidence established the fatal bullet came from the Kalashnikov of police officer A.L., temporarily deployed from Vologda. Numerous witnesses confirmed the sequence. The investigation was suspended and resumed at least seven times between 2002 and 2008. Repeated superior orders to locate and question A.L. and to take other steps were ignored. Applicants were denied meaningful access to the file until court rulings in 2007. Supervisors repeatedly criticised premature suspensions. No one was prosecuted.

In the third application, on 26 January 2005 the third applicant and two teenage relatives (Dzhabrail Abiyev and Alkhazur Atabayev) were driving near a “West” battalion checkpoint in Grozny when three unregistered UAZ vehicles opened unprovoked machine-gun and grenade-launcher fire, killing the two teenagers and wounding the third. The attackers then passed unhindered through the checkpoint after interacting with its personnel. State television reported the incident as the “liquidation” of illegal fighters. Extensive ballistic evidence (Kalashnikov, TIS and TT cartridges plus grenades) was collected. Witnesses named possible perpetrators including officers Vakha T. and Adlan G. from the battalion or other law-enforcement bodies. The investigation was suspended more than a dozen times between 2005 and 2014; each suspension was later ruled premature, yet orders to question the named individuals were never implemented. Applicants alleged evidence had been planted. No identifications or prosecutions occurred.

These facts demonstrate direct state-agent involvement in the killings and a pattern of investigative inertia, ignored leads, repeated unlawful suspensions and exclusion of the victims’ families.

The case of Shamsudinova and Others v. Russia comprises three applications to the European Court of Human Rights alleging that Russian state agents killed the applicants’ relatives in Chechnya between 2001 and 2005, with authorities failing to conduct effective investigations, in breach of Articles 2, 5 and 13 of the Convention.

In the first application, federal servicemen surrounded the home of Alvi Bugayev on 27 December 2001, forcibly detained him without clothing or shoes, and seized a vehicle and documents. He was held for 15 days at the Urus-Martan temporary police facility. On 12 January 2002, after officials announced his release, military vehicles pursued him as he drove away during curfew. Four servicemen then shot him dead in front of his wife and children near his sister’s house, 200 metres from the facility. His wife reported that the killers were the same men who had threatened him as a “traitor.” An investigation was opened the same day (case no. 61000). Ballistics confirmed Kalashnikov fire; an operational officer and eyewitness corroborated state involvement. Investigators requested but never received identities of the detaining officers. The probe was suspended in March 2002 without notice to the family, then repeatedly resumed and suspended after complaints. Victim status was granted only in 2007; a court later dismissed a challenge to investigative failings. No perpetrators were identified.

In the second application, Colonel Ruslan Yunusov, Deputy Minister for Emergency Situations, was killed on 4 January 2002. After a military reconnaissance vehicle (BRDM) from the Leninskiy district military prosecutor’s office had earlier fired on an Emergency Situations vehicle, the same BRDM appeared at ministry premises for repairs. When officers sought to detain it, the crew fled. Yunusov jumped onto the hull to halt it; the vehicle fired, smashed through gates, and drove to a nearby military checkpoint, where servicemen (including police officer A.L. from Vologda) opened fire, fatally wounding him. Ballistics linked the fatal bullet to A.L.’s Kalashnikov. Case no. 54001 was opened immediately. Multiple witnesses confirmed the sequence. The investigation was suspended and resumed at least seven times between 2002 and 2006, with applicants rarely informed. Repeated prosecutorial orders to locate and question A.L. and other implicated officers produced only formal inquiries, never executed. Courts initially rejected, then in 2007 granted, the family’s request for file access and a thorough probe. A 2015 civil claim for damages was dismissed on procedural grounds. The case stagnated after 2008.

In the third application, on 26 January 2005 two 15-year-old relatives and a third applicant were fired upon without provocation by armed men in three unregistered UAZ vehicles that had just passed a federal “West” battalion checkpoint. The two teenagers died instantly; the third applicant was wounded. Checkpoint personnel allowed the attackers to leave unhindered. State television immediately labelled the victims “illegal fighters.” Case no. 43015 collected over 50 cartridges (including specialised silent-weapon types), grenades and bullets. Applicants and witnesses identified two alleged perpetrators (Vakha T. and Adlan G.) from the same unit; forensic evidence suggested some items may have been planted. Investigators pursued neither these leads nor the source of the television report, nor did they question checkpoint personnel despite multiple orders. The case was suspended more than a dozen times between 2005 and 2011 (and again in 2014), each time overruled as premature and unlawful; ordered steps were ignored. Blood-feud and special-operation theories were noted but never seriously examined. Applicants received scant information and repeatedly complained of a cover-up.

Across all three cases the investigations displayed the same defects: unexplained delays, unlawful suspensions, failure to identify or question named state agents, withheld information from victims, and non-compliance with supervisory orders. No one has been prosecuted.

**Summary of Shamsudinova and Others v. Russia (ECtHR, 5 February 2019)**

The case was transferred/resumed/suspended repeatedly (at least seven times 2002–2006, mostly unnotified). Repeated orders to locate and question A.L. and obtain officer details were ignored beyond formal requests. Applicants (granted victim status in 2002) repeatedly sought information and access; partial file access followed 2007 court orders. A 2008 resumption for locating A.L. was followed by suspension; a 2015 civil compensation claim was dismissed procedurally. No further progress.

In *Atabayeva and Others* (no. 21432/12), on 26 January 2005 the third applicant drove two teenage relatives (Dzhabrail Abiyev and Alkhazur Atabayev, both b. 1989) near a “West” battalion checkpoint. Unprovoked machine-gun and grenade-launcher fire from three unregistered UAZ vehicles (which had just passed the checkpoint unhindered) killed the two relatives instantly and wounded the third applicant in the legs. Federal TV later described it as “liquidation” of illegal fighters. Case no. 43015 opened the same day. The probe was suspended/resumed more than a dozen times (2005–2014), each suspension later ruled premature/unlawful, yet orders to question named suspects, verify theories (blood feud vs. special operation) or identify shooters were ignored beyond formal letters. Applicants repeatedly complained of stalling and cover-up. A 2014 resumption yielded no reported progress.

Across the cases, facts show direct state-agent involvement (servicemen, identifiable vehicles/units, checkpoints, post-incident media) plus systemic investigative failures: premature unnotified suspensions, ignored orders to identify/question suspects, withheld information, and inaction spanning years—relevant to substantive/procedural Article 2 breaches and related claims. The case of Mher Alikhanyan v. Armenia (Application no. 4413/10) concerns an Armenian national from Shnogh village who alleged violations of his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions and to a fair trial arising from the expropriation of his agricultural land.

In the 1970s a copper-molybdenum deposit was identified near the villages of Teghout and Shnogh. In 2001 a private company received a 25-year mining licence. On 1 November 2007 the Government adopted Decree no. 1279-N designating expropriation zones within the two villages for “State needs” connected with the mining project and changing the land-use category. The decree identified Armenian Copper Programme CJSC or its subsidiary Teghout CJSC as the entities authorised to acquire the listed parcels. The applicant’s 0.186-hectare plot of arable land, used for crop-growing, livestock fodder and beekeeping, fell inside the designated zone.

Teghout CJSC offered the applicant AMD 134 000 (approximately EUR 290) plus the statutory 15 per cent supplement. Dissatisfied with the figure, the applicant declined. He attempted to obtain an independent market valuation but asserts that no other licensed valuer was willing to act. On 13 May 2008 the company brought proceedings to compel him to sign a transfer agreement, relying on an evaluation prepared by Oliver Group LLC that placed the market value at AMD 134 000. In the Lori Regional Court the applicant argued that the valuation ignored fruit trees, their productivity, a fence and a water pipeline. He repeated that he could not produce a competing report.

During the hearing the company submitted a “corrected” Oliver Group report raising the market value to AMD 137 000; with the 15 per cent supplement the total compensation became AMD 157 550 (approximately EUR 343). On 28 November 2008 the Regional Court ordered the transfer and awarded that sum. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 19 March 2009, holding that the corrected valuation had been properly accepted. The Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s further appeal inadmissible for lack of merit on 17 June 2009.

The applicant invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that he had been deprived of his property without adequate compensation, and Article 6 of the Convention, alleging that the courts had failed to ensure equality of arms by relying exclusively on the expropriating company’s valuation and by not appointing an independent expert.

Domestic law required that expropriation occur only in exceptional cases of paramount public interest, pursuant to a prescribed procedure and against prior equivalent compensation (Constitution, Art. 31; Law on Alienation of Property, ss. 3–4, 11). Mining projects of State or community importance were recognised as capable of constituting such an interest, provided the aim was not merely to increase budgetary revenue. Market value plus 15 per cent was defined as adequate compensation, to be determined according to the Law on Real Estate Evaluation Activity, which made valuation obligatory and allowed licensed valuers to employ independent methods. The Code of Civil Procedure obliged courts to treat no evidence as pre-established and empowered them to appoint forensic experts of their own motion or on a party’s application.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints communicated to the Government: whether the expropriation pursued a genuine public interest, whether the compensation awarded reflected genuine market value, and whether the applicant had a fair opportunity to challenge the sole valuation relied upon by the domestic courts.

The case of Mher Alikhanyan v. Armenia concerns the forced expropriation of the applicant’s small agricultural plot for a large-scale mining project and the fairness of the domestic court proceedings that approved the taking and the compensation awarded.

The applicant, an Armenian national living in Shnogh village in the Lori Region, derived his livelihood from farming. He owned a 0.186-hectare plot of arable land that he used to grow crops for his family, feed livestock and keep bees. In the 1970s a copper-molybdenum deposit (Teghout) had been discovered a few kilometres from Shnogh. In 2001 a private company, Armenian Copper Programme CJSC, obtained a 25-year mining licence. On 1 November 2007 the Government issued Decree No. 1279-N designating extensive agricultural lands within the administrative boundaries of Shnogh and Teghout, including the applicant’s plot, as expropriation zones required for the construction and operation of a mining plant. The decree invoked a prevailing public interest in economic development, infrastructure, increased production and exports.

Teghout CJSC (the project company) offered the applicant AMD 134 000 (approximately EUR 290) plus the statutory 15 per cent increment. The offer rested on a valuation prepared by Oliver Group LLC, a licensed evaluator commissioned by the company. The applicant rejected the sum as inadequate, complaining that the valuation ignored fruit trees, their profitability, an existing fence and a water pipeline. He was unable to obtain an independent market-value assessment because other licensed firms refused to evaluate land earmarked for the mining project.

In May 2008 the company brought court proceedings to compel the applicant to conclude the expropriation agreement. The case of Negura and Others v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 16602/06) concerns 87 Moldovan entrepreneurs who held licences (patenta) to sell goods at a privately owned marketplace (L.) in central Leova, authorised by local authorities since 1996 to operate Monday to Saturday. A state-owned marketplace (U.), located far from the town centre and offering poorer conditions, operated on Sundays. The applicants viewed Sunday as the most profitable trading day and repeatedly sought permission to operate L. on Sundays (resting Mondays), as was common elsewhere. Local authorities rejected these requests on grounds of traffic, public order, sanitation and disturbance to nearby residents, a school and a hospital. The applicants contended that the true motive was to protect U.’s commercial interests, forcing many of them to incur extra costs by also trading at U.

On 31 January 2005 a general meeting of entrepreneurs (including the applicants) resolved to request the schedule change. L.’s owners forwarded the request to the mayor on 8 February 2005. On 2 March 2005 the Leova city council adopted decision no. 2.2 rejecting the requests; the decision appeared on mayoral stationery and was stamped by the mayor’s office on 29 March 2005. On 4 April 2005 the entrepreneurs (191 in total) declared a strike, submitted a request to the Leova regional council seeking annulment of decision 2.2, and lodged a preliminary request with the Leova Mayoralty seeking the same relief, citing inadequate conditions at U.

On 6 April 2005 the city council considered the matter, heard L.’s director, and adopted decision no. 3.1 confirming that L. must continue to operate in accordance with decision 2.2. On 12 May 2005 the mayor replied that the city council had already answered via decision 3.1.

On 28 May 2005 the 191 entrepreneurs, including the applicants, brought administrative-court proceedings seeking annulment of the 2 March 2005 decision. They argued that it unlawfully protected U. and annexed their 4 April preliminary request, the regional-council complaint and the mayor’s 12 May reply. On 5 July 2005 the Leova District Court upheld the claim, finding no sanitation, traffic or other problems with Sunday trading at L. and holding decision 2.2 contrary to anti-monopoly legislation; it also awarded the applicants their full legal costs of 15 000 lei. The city council appealed.

By final decision of 20 October 2005 the Cahul Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and struck the action out. It held that the entrepreneurs had addressed their preliminary complaint to the mayor rather than to the city council that had adopted the impugned act, thereby failing to comply with Article 14 of the Law on Administrative Proceedings. Consequently they had lost the right to challenge the 2 March 2005 decision.

Domestic law required a preliminary request to the adopting authority (or, at the applicant’s choice, a hierarchically superior body) within 30 days, after which a court action could be lodged within a further 30 days. The Code of Civil Procedure permitted striking-out for non-observance of that extrajudicial procedure. The Law on Petitions obliged an authority receiving a misdirected petition to forward it to the competent body within five days. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints to the European Court of Human Rights concerning access to court and related rights.

The case of Šaranović v. Montenegro concerns complaints under Article 5 of the Convention regarding the lawfulness and duration of the applicant’s pre-trial detention, as well as the alleged lack of reasoning in domestic court decisions extending that detention.

The applicant, born in 1938, was suspected of arranging the April 2013 murder of X in Belgrade as revenge for his own brother’s 2009 killing. Serbian authorities opened an investigation against him in July 2013. He was arrested in Montenegro, but extradition was refused in January 2014 and he was released. On 4 April 2014 Montenegro authorised his domestic prosecution.

He was re-arrested on 8 April 2014. An investigation was ordered the next day for aggravated murder by incitement. On 10 April an investigating judge placed him in detention for one month on the basis of reasonable suspicion, the risk that he would influence witnesses, the gravity of the offence (punishable by at least ten years), its revenge motive, and the risk that his release would disturb public order given media coverage. Subsequent monthly extensions through 5 September 2014 repeated essentially the same grounds. Appeals were dismissed.

An indictment for murder and criminal association was issued on 7 October 2014 (within six months of the investigation’s start) but was returned on 22 October for further investigation. Detention was then extended “until a further court decision.” The Court of Appeal later held that the six-month statutory limit had been respected and that the return of the indictment was irrelevant.

On 15 December 2014 the applicant asked to be released, arguing that detention had become unlawful on 15 November because the court had failed to review it within the 30-day period required by Article 179 § 2 of the Criminal Procedure Code before an indictment enters into force. The same day the High Court, acting of its own motion, extended detention again on the original grounds, noting that the investigation remained incomplete. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, ruling that a missed review deadline did not terminate detention and that the indictment had been issued in time.

A constitutional appeal complained that the courts had ignored the 30-day review duty, that detention had already exceeded six months without an indictment in force, and that the extension decisions merely copied earlier reasoning without examining changed circumstances, the overall length of detention, or the applicant’s age, health, family situation or clean record. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal in May 2015, finding the decisions sufficiently reasoned and free of arbitrariness.

Detention continued to be extended on identical grounds until 9 December 2016, when it was revoked because of its length, the repeated return of the indictment, and uncertainty about when (if ever) it would take effect. The applicant was murdered on 11 March 2017; the criminal proceedings were terminated without any indictment ever entering into force.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: a period of detention (15 November–15 December 2014) said to be unlawful for want of timely review, detention exceeding the six-month limit without a valid indictment, and stereotyped, unreasoned extension decisions that failed to address the passage of time or the applicant’s personal situation.
