The case of *Kobiashvili v. Georgia* (Application no. 36416/06) concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Georgian national Archil Kobiashvili, who alleged that criminal proceedings against him were unfair under Article 6 of the Convention because his conviction for drug offences rested on planted evidence obtained through an unlawful personal search.

On 4 July 2004, the head of a Tbilisi district police investigation unit ordered an urgent personal search of the applicant (then 31 and previously convicted of public-order offences) on suspicion of possessing narcotics. The decision used pre-typed wording with the applicant’s details added by hand and cited provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) permitting warrantless searches in urgent cases. According to the official account, two officers (Sh.Sh. and N.O.) stopped the applicant outside a billiards hall at 5.20 p.m. as he arrived with two friends. Without a judicial warrant they searched him in the presence of two attesting witnesses (U.K. and L.Ts.). The search report recorded that the applicant indicated a trouser pocket containing a yellow powder later identified as 0.059 g of heroin; he refused to sign the report. He was formally arrested at 6 p.m. on suspicion of unlawful possession and use of heroin.

The same day the police notified the district prosecutor and requested post-facto judicial authorisation. The prosecutor’s application to the Gldani-Nadzaladevi District Court relied on brief handwritten notes from the officers and witnesses but omitted the original search order, the inquiry file and the search report itself. On 5 July the court, sitting without the applicant or any oral hearing, declared the search lawful under CCP Articles 290 and 293; the decision was unappealable. The applicant was charged under Article 260 § 2(a) of the Criminal Code with buying and possessing a large quantity of drugs. A later forensic test confirmed the heroin; a narcotics examination found he was not addicted.

During the investigation the applicant remained silent. At his December 2004 trial he denied any on-the-spot search, claimed the drugs had been planted and asserted that police had forcibly injected him with opium at the station. Witness U.K. recanted, stating he had been taken to the station hours later, threatened and forced to sign a dictated statement. Officer Sh.Sh. maintained the official version based on unspecified “operational information” that someone nearby was under the influence of drugs. Officer N.O. gave a similar account but conceded he was unsure whether the applicant appeared intoxicated. The applicant’s two friends testified that no search occurred at the scene. L.Ts. failed to appear. On 18 April 2005 the trial court convicted the applicant, relying on the officers’ testimony and the search report while discounting U.K.’s recantation as inconclusive and the friends’ evidence as biased; he received six years’ imprisonment plus six months from a prior sentence.

On appeal the defence sought exclusion of the search report under CCP Article 111, citing the absence of a properly issued warrant, the recantation, evidence that L.Ts. was a former Interior Ministry employee, and the friends’ consistent accounts. The Court of Appeal heard L.Ts., who confirmed the official version and denied police ties; U.K. again alleged coercion and said he had reported the matter to the Public Defender. On 21 February 2006 the court upheld the conviction, finding U.K. incredible and influenced by the applicant’s family, accepting L.Ts.’s evidence and rejecting the friends’ testimony. The Supreme Court declared the subsequent cassation appeal inadmissible. The applicant was released in January 2011 after serving his sentence.

The alleged violations centred on the use of evidence obtained through a warrantless search whose urgency and lawfulness were never subjected to genuine adversarial scrutiny, coupled with the domestic courts’ unexplained preference for police testimony over recanting and corroborating civilian witnesses.

**CASE OF KOBIASHVILI v. GEORGIA (Application no. 36416/06)**

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Georgian national Archil Kobiashvili that criminal proceedings against him were unfair, as his conviction for drug offences rested on planted evidence obtained through an irregular personal search.

On 4 July 2004, the head of a Tbilisi district police criminal investigation unit ordered an urgent personal search of the applicant (then 31) on suspicion of possessing and using narcotics. The decision used mainly pre-typed phrases with the applicant’s details added by hand and cited relevant Code of Criminal Procedure provisions. It lacked a prior judicial warrant.

According to the official account, at around 5.20 p.m. that day, as the applicant approached a billiards hall with two friends, two police officers in a nearby vehicle summoned him. They searched him on the spot (lasting until 5.45 p.m.). The subsequent police report stated there were grounds to believe he would destroy evidence (heroin). Before the search he was asked to indicate where he kept the heroin and pointed to a trouser pocket, from which a yellow powder wrapped in paper was recovered. Two attesting witnesses (U.K. and L.Ts.) and officer Sh.Sh. signed the report; the applicant refused. He was formally arrested at 6 p.m. on suspicion of unlawful heroin use and possession and again refused to sign the record.

The same day, police informed the district prosecutor of the warrantless search conducted before criminal proceedings were opened and sought post-factum court legalisation. The prosecutor’s application to the Gldani-Nadzaladevi District Court referenced “operational information,” attached short handwritten notes from Sh.Sh. and the two witnesses, but omitted the original search order, the inquiry file, and the search report itself. On 5 July 2004 the court, sitting in writing without hearing the applicant, declared the search lawful under the Code of Criminal Procedure. No appeal was available.

The applicant was later charged under Article 260 § 2(a) of the Criminal Code with buying and possessing a large quantity of drugs. Forensic analysis confirmed 0.059 grams of heroin. A narcotics test showed he was not an addict but required preventive treatment. He remained silent during the investigation.

At trial he pleaded not guilty, claiming he had never been searched at the scene and that police had planted the substance, taken him to the station, forcibly injected him with opium, and then sent him for testing. Witness U.K. recanted in court, stating he had not attended any search but had been taken from a construction site around 10 p.m., dictated a statement at the station, and signed papers under pressure and threats. Officer Sh.Sh. and colleague N.O. maintained they acted on operational information that someone near the hall was under the influence of drugs and that the search occurred immediately in the presence of the two witnesses. The applicant’s two friends testified that police took him away without any on-the-spot search. The second witness, L.Ts., did not appear at first instance (citing travel plans). Defence counsel argued the search report should be excluded for multiple procedural defects, including that L.Ts. was a former police officer who frequently acted as an attesting witness.

On 18 April 2005 the District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment plus six months from a prior suspended sentence. It relied on the officers’ statements and the search results, declining to accept U.K.’s recantation as unequivocal and dismissing the friends’ evidence as biased.

On appeal the applicant repeated his claims of planted evidence and requested exclusion of the search report and re-examination of witnesses. L.Ts. now testified, confirming he had witnessed the street search and denying any police affiliation. U.K. reiterated his recantation, alleging psychological and physical pressure and stating he had later approached the applicant’s family and the Public Defender. The friends confirmed their earlier account. Defence counsel again sought exclusion of the search evidence, citing the unsigned/undated aspects of the original order, failure to read it to the applicant, U.K.’s recantation, L.Ts.’s prior Ministry of Interior employment (supported by a letter), and the friends’ consistent statements.

The Court of Appeal rejected the exclusion request and, on 21 February 2006, upheld the conviction. It found U.K.’s recantation illogical and influenced by the applicant’s family, accepted L.Ts.’s account, and again dismissed the friends as unreliable. The Supreme Court later declared the applicant’s points-of-law appeal inadmissible. He was released in January 2011 after serving the sentence.

The proceedings therefore turned on the contested circumstances of the warrantless search, the reliability of the attesting witnesses (one of whom recanted and alleged coercion), the absence of any contemporaneous recording or independent verification, and the courts’ treatment of the conflicting evidence. These facts formed the core of the applicant’s claim that the conviction was based on planted and procedurally tainted evidence, rendering the trial unfair.

The case of Kobiashvili v. Georgia (Application no. 36416/06) concerns Archil Kobiashvili, a Georgian national born in 1973, who alleged that his 2005 conviction for drug possession violated Article 6 of the Convention because it rested on planted evidence obtained through an unfair process.

On 4 July 2004, a senior police officer at the Gldani-Nadzaladevi district department issued a decision authorising an urgent personal search of the applicant, who was suspected of possessing narcotics. The decision used mostly pre-typed wording and was not based on a judicial warrant. According to official records, around 5:20 p.m. two officers stopped the applicant outside a billiards hall, searched him in the presence of two attesting witnesses (U.K. and L.Ts.), and recovered a yellowish powder later identified as 0.059 g of heroin from his trouser pocket. The applicant was arrested at 6 p.m. He refused to sign either the search report or the arrest record. The prosecutor subsequently applied to the district court for post-facto legalisation of the search. The court granted the request the next day in a purely written procedure; the applicant was not heard and no appeal was permitted. He was charged with buying and possessing a large quantity of drugs.

The applicant’s account differed sharply. He claimed he had never been searched at the scene, had been taken to the police station, forcibly injected with opium, and that the heroin had been planted. He remained silent during the investigation.

At first-instance trial the applicant pleaded not guilty. U.K. recanted, stating he had not witnessed the search but had been collected later from a construction site, taken to the station and compelled under threats and swearing to sign documents whose contents he did not understand. L.Ts. confirmed the official version. Two friends who had been with the applicant testified that no search occurred on the spot. Police officers maintained they had acted on “operational information” that an unidentified person at the location was under the influence of drugs.

On 18 April 2005 the district court convicted the applicant and imposed a six-year sentence (plus six months from a prior suspended term). It relied on the officers’ testimony and the search report, treated U.K.’s recantation as inconclusive, and dismissed the friends’ evidence as biased.

On appeal the defence sought exclusion of the search report under Article 111 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing multiple irregularities: the authorising decision contained details (the applicant’s identity and the type of drug) that could have been known only after the search, lacked a proper senior signature and time, and had not been read to the applicant; U.K. had recanted; and L.Ts. had previously worked for the Ministry of the Interior (a fact he denied). The Court of Appeal rejected the exclusion request, upheld the conviction on 21 February 2006, found U.K.’s testimony “illogical” and family-influenced, accepted L.Ts.’s evidence, and again discarded the friends’ statements. The Supreme Court declared the subsequent points-of-law appeal inadmissible on 12 June 2006. The applicant served his sentence until 3 January 2011.

These facts—warrantless search, non-adversarial legalisation, recanting witness, disputed reliability of the remaining witness, and refusal to exclude the contested evidence—underpin the complaint that the conviction was based on planted and unlawfully obtained material, rendering the trial unfair.
001-191737:
The case of Prebil v. Slovenia (no. 29278/16) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 ECHR, as the applicant (Andrej Prebil, a Slovenian national born in 1974) was unable to participate in non-litigious court proceedings that dismissed him from the supervisory board of company A.

Prebil was appointed to company A’s supervisory board on 11 November 2013 for a four-year term. After the chairman’s resignation on 12 March 2014, the board had only three of the required six members. On 20 March 2014, the Ljubljana District Court initiated “preventive restructuring” of company A to avert insolvency. At a 13 May 2014 board session, member T.H. proposed adding dismissal of the management board chair to the agenda. Alleged physical violence ensued, with some members preventing another from leaving to preserve quorum; a dismissal resolution was passed. On 15 May 2014, a claim to annul that resolution was filed; company A consented and the court granted annulment.

On 29 May 2014, majority shareholder company P (91.42% of shares) moved the District Court to deprive Prebil and T.H. of board membership and appoint provisionals, citing s. 276(2) of the Companies Act (court dismissal for “good reasons”) and their alleged unacceptable conduct in the 13 May incident. P sought an immediate decision without notifying the opponents or holding a hearing, citing urgency from restructuring deadlines, management uncertainty, inability to convene a prompt shareholders’ meeting, and the need for a functional board to avoid insolvency.

On 4 June 2014 the District Court granted the motion without hearing Prebil, relying on P’s submissions and the related nullity file. It found Prebil had cooperated in the incident (harmful given the company’s situation), that board members must act diligently, and that urgency justified immediate effect (appeals possible within eight days but non-suspensive). Prebil learned of the decision via a journalist on 5 June and received a copy days later.

On 24 June 2014 Prebil appealed, invoking s. 4 of the Non-Litigious Civil Procedure Act (right to comment on allegations and participate in evidence-taking unless law provides otherwise). He disputed P’s account of the incident, denied grounds for dismissal, and stressed reputational harm. P replied that the decision resembled an interim injunction and that adversarial principles could be secured on appeal; it later noted that on 4 August 2014 company A’s assembly had appointed replacements, extinguishing Prebil’s interest. Prebil argued judicial (reason-based) dismissal differed from assembly dismissal (no reasons required).

On 21 January 2015 the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal for lack of legal interest: the assembly had already replaced Prebil and T.H., and it could dismiss board members at any time without reasons, so even success on appeal could not restore him. Prebil’s constitutional complaint (Articles 6 and 13 ECHR) was not accepted for consideration by the Constitutional Court on 10 November 2015 (s. 55b(2) Constitutional Court Act). Media reported the dismissal and its factual basis.

These facts centre on the applicant’s exclusion from the initial (urgent, non-adversarial) proceedings that terminated his board membership, the subsequent finding of no remaining interest on appeal, and the resulting inability to contest the allegations or evidence.

The case of Prebil v. Slovenia (Application no. 29278/16) concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the applicant, Andrej Prebil, was unable to participate in non-contentious court proceedings that resulted in his judicial removal from the supervisory board of a company.

Prebil, a Slovenian national born in 1974, was appointed in November 2013 to a four-year term as a member of the supervisory board of company A. In March 2014 the company’s chairman of the supervisory board resigned, leaving the board with only three of the six members required by statute. Shortly afterwards the Ljubljana District Court opened preventive-restructuring proceedings in respect of company A.

On 13 May 2014 a supervisory-board meeting took place at which one member proposed adding an item to the agenda concerning the dismissal of the chairman of the management board. Physical confrontation allegedly ensued when some members prevented another member from leaving in order to preserve a quorum. A resolution dismissing the management-board chairman was apparently adopted. Two days later a claim seeking a declaration of nullity of that resolution was filed; company A consented and the court subsequently annulled the resolution.

On 29 May 2014 company P, which held 91.42 per cent of the shares in company A, applied to the Ljubljana District Court for an order removing Prebil and another board member, T.H., and appointing provisional replacements. The application was directed against Prebil and T.H. as opposing parties. Company P invoked, among other provisions, section 276(2) of the Companies Act (which permits a court, for good reason, to dismiss a supervisory-board member at the request of shareholders holding at least 10 per cent of the capital). It relied principally on the 13 May incident, describing the two members’ conduct as unacceptable and harmful to the company, especially given the ongoing restructuring and the need for a functioning board. Company P asked the court to decide the matter without delay, without notifying the opposing parties and without a hearing, arguing that a general meeting of shareholders could not be convened promptly enough because of uncertainty over who was the company’s manager and because of statutory deadlines in the restructuring process.

On 4 June 2014 the District Court granted the application. Drawing on company P’s submissions and the file of the related nullity proceedings, it found that Prebil had permitted, agreed with and fully cooperated in T.H.’s conduct, which had prevented a board member from leaving the meeting. It held that the two members had failed to act with the diligence required of supervisory-board members and that their continued presence endangered the company’s functioning during restructuring. The court characterised the matter as urgent, declared its decision immediately effective (an appeal would not stay execution) and noted that an appeal could be lodged within eight days.

Prebil learned of the decision first from a journalist and received a copy only days later. On 24 June 2014 he appealed, arguing that he had been unlawfully denied the opportunity to participate, contrary to section 4 of the Non-Litigious Civil Procedure Act (which requires courts, unless otherwise provided, to allow participants to comment on the other side’s allegations and to take part in the taking of evidence). He disputed the account of the 13 May incident, contended that no well-founded reasons for dismissal had been shown, and emphasised that his reputation required that he be able to submit evidence.

Company P replied that the proceedings were of an urgent, interim-injunction character and that the adversarial principle could be satisfied on appeal. On 4 August 2014 a general meeting of company A appointed two new members in place of Prebil and T.H. Company P then invited the court to reject the appeal for lack of legal interest. Prebil responded that a shareholders’ dismissal (possible at any time without reasons) could not be equated with a judicial dismissal, which required well-founded reasons that had never been established after he had been heard.

On 21 January 2015 the Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed the appeal. It held that Prebil no longer had a legal interest because the general meeting had already replaced him; even a successful appeal could not restore him to office, given the assembly’s unrestricted power to dismiss supervisory-board members. Prebil lodged a constitutional complaint invoking Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, arguing that an opportunity to reply to company P’s allegations would have produced a different outcome. On 10 November 2015 the Constitutional Court declined to accept the complaint for consideration. A major financial newspaper reported the judicial dismissal and the underlying allegations.

The complaint communicated to the Government was confined to the applicant’s inability to participate in the first-instance proceedings that led to his removal.

The case of Prebil v. Slovenia (Application no. 29278/16) originated from an application lodged on 10 May 2016 by Slovenian national Andrej Prebil (born 1974, resident in Ljubljana) against Slovenia under Article 34 of the Convention. Represented by lawyer M. Šušmelj, the applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1 due to his inability to participate in court proceedings that resulted in his removal from a company supervisory board. Notice of these complaints was given to the Government on 14 January 2018, with other aspects of the application declared inadmissible.

The applicant had been appointed as a member of the supervisory board of Company A on 11 November 2013 for a four-year term. On 12 March 2014, the board's chairman resigned, reducing membership to three (below the statutory six). On 20 March 2014, the Ljubljana District Court initiated "preventive restructuring" of Company A to avert insolvency. At a board session on 13 May 2014, member T.H. proposed dismissing the management board chair. Alleged physical violence ensued, as some members prevented another from leaving to preserve quorum, and a dismissal resolution was passed. On 15 May 2014, a claim sought to nullify this resolution; Company A consented, and the court annulled it.

On 29 May 2014, Company P (holding 91.42% of Company A's shares) filed a motion under section 276(2) of the Companies Act to deprive the applicant and T.H. of their board membership and appoint provisional replacements. The motion named them as opposing parties and cited their "unacceptable personal qualities," particularly their conduct in the 13 May incident. Company P requested an urgent, ex parte decision without notifying the opposing parties or holding a hearing, arguing that the applicant and T.H. should not complete their terms, that well-founded reasons existed for immediate termination, that the board could not function lawfully, that a general shareholders' meeting could not be convened promptly due to managerial uncertainty, and that restructuring deadlines required swift court intervention.

On 4 June 2014, the Ljubljana District Court granted the motion, relying on Company P's submissions and the file from the related nullity proceedings. It found that one board member had not been voluntarily present on 13 May due to the conduct of the remaining two, that the applicant had allowed, agreed with, and fully cooperated in T.H.'s actions, and that this violated the duty of diligence and responsibility under the Companies Act—especially critical during restructuring. The court deemed the matter urgent, as Company A faced risk and the board (with the applicant and T.H.) could not function until a general meeting. The decision took immediate effect (appeals would not stay execution) and allowed an appeal within eight days.

The applicant learned of the decision from a journalist on 5 June 2014 and received a copy days later. On 24 June 2014, he appealed, arguing unlawful denial of participation (citing section 4 of the Non-Litigious Civil Procedure Act, which generally requires an opportunity to comment on allegations and participate in evidence-taking unless otherwise provided). He disputed the 13 May incident allegations, offered his version of events, contended that court intervention was unnecessary and no well-founded reasons existed for dismissal, and stressed the need to protect his reputation through involvement and evidence submission.

Company P replied on 3 July 2014 that the case was urgent to avoid insolvency losses, analogizing the decision to an interim injunction where adversarial rights could be ensured on appeal. On 4 August 2014, Company A's assembly appointed two new members to replace the applicant and T.H. Company P informed the court on 5 August and sought rejection of the appeal for lack of legal interest. The applicant replied on 25 August 2014 that judicial termination (requiring well-founded reasons) differed from assembly dismissal. On 3 November 2014, he submitted domestic case-law examples showing a requirement for participation.

On 21 January 2015, the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal, holding that the applicant lacked legal interest because the assembly had already appointed replacements. Appointment and dismissal of supervisory board members (who represent shareholder interests) fell within the assembly's discretion; it could dismiss them at any time without reasons. Even a successful appeal would not lead to reinstatement.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, complaining of inability to participate and arguing that a reply to Company P's allegations would have produced a different outcome. On 10 November 2015 (served 13 November), the Constitutional Court declined to consider it under section 55b(2) of the Constitutional Court Act (no serious human-rights consequences or important constitutional question exceeding the case). A major newspaper, Finance, reported the judicial dismissal and its factual basis.

Relevant domestic law included Companies Act provisions on court appointment/dismissal of board members in non-litigious proceedings (sections 50, 256, 276), duties of diligence (section 263), assembly election/dismissal (sections 274-275), the Non-Litigious Civil Procedure Act's participation requirement (section 4), the Financial Operations Act's emphasis on promptness in restructuring, and Constitutional Court Act filtering of complaints.
001-191548:
The case of Kangers v. Latvia (Application no. 35726/10) originated in an application lodged on 2 June 2010 by Latvian national Jānis Kangers with the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention (presumption of innocence), claiming that a domestic judgment had found him guilty of a repeat administrative offence while his appeal against the initial offence remained pending.

The relevant events began with a first set of administrative proceedings. On 20 November 2008 police reported that the applicant had driven with a blood-alcohol concentration exceeding 1.5 permilles, contrary to Article 14915(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences. The Jūrmala City Court terminated the proceedings on 1 December 2008 for lack of corpus delicti; that decision took effect on 5 January 2009 and the applicant’s driving licence was returned. On 10 February 2009 a prosecutor lodged an appeal (for which domestic law prescribed no time-limit). The Riga Regional Court, sitting in the applicant’s absence after refusing an adjournment, quashed the termination on 27 February 2009, convicted the applicant and imposed fifteen days’ detention, a fine of LVL 500 and a two-year driving ban. The judgment became final on 6 March 2009.

A second set of proceedings followed. On 31 July 2009 police reported that the applicant had driven while disqualified (Article 1494(6)). A fine of LVL 250 was imposed on 1 September 2009 and upheld by the State Police on 7 October 2009. The applicant appealed to the administrative courts, arguing that the original termination decision of 1 December 2008 had become final and could not lawfully be quashed. Those appeal proceedings remained pending throughout the subsequent events. The Administrative District Court dismissed the appeal on 20 December 2010 and the Administrative Regional Court confirmed that dismissal on 24 April 2012, holding that the 27 February 2009 judgment was binding and that the prosecutor’s appeal right was unlimited.

The third set of proceedings, which gave rise to the Article 6 § 2 complaint, commenced on 23 September 2009 when police reported that the applicant had again driven while disqualified, this time “repeatedly within a year” (Article 1494(7)). On 6 November 2009 the Riga City Zemgale District Court convicted him of the repeat offence, relying on the 27 February 2009 driving-ban judgment and the 31 July 2009 report, and imposed five days’ detention plus a fine of LVL 400. The applicant appealed, contending that the 27 February judgment was unlawful and that the repeated character of the offence could not be established while the appeal against the 31 July offence was still pending; he asked that the proceedings be terminated or stayed. On 26 February 2010 the Riga Regional Court, by a final judgment, upheld the conviction. It reasoned that the mere pendency of an appeal did not prevent a finding of repetition; the sole relevant criterion was whether the decision on the initial offence had been set aside or its legal effect suspended. Article 283 of the Code provided that an appeal against a driving disqualification did not suspend enforcement. Consequently the 31 July decision remained legally binding and could be used to classify the later offence as a repeat offence.

By the date of his application to the Court the applicant had already served the five-day detention and paid the fine. Domestic law and Supreme Court case-law treated an administrative-penalty decision as effective once served, even if appealed; an appeal suspended only enforcement, not the legal consequences of the decision, unless the decision itself was later quashed. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic courts had treated him as already guilty of the initial offence, contrary to the presumption of innocence, while that offence remained under appeal.

The case of *Kangers v. Latvia* (Application no. 35726/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (presumption of innocence). The applicant, Jānis Kangers, a Latvian national, complained that domestic courts found him guilty of a repeat administrative driving offence while his appeal against conviction for the initial offence remained pending.

On 20 November 2008 police issued a report charging the applicant with driving under the influence of alcohol (blood-alcohol concentration exceeding 1.5‰) contrary to Article 14915(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences. The Jūrmala City Court terminated the proceedings on 1 December 2008 for lack of *corpus delicti*. That decision became final on 5 January 2009 and the applicant’s driving licence was returned. On 10 February 2009 a prosecutor lodged an appeal (permitted without time-limit under the Code). On 27 February 2009 the Riga Regional Court, sitting in the applicant’s absence after refusing an adjournment, quashed the termination, convicted him and imposed 15 days’ detention, a fine of LVL 500, a two-year driving ban and a two-year ban on obtaining a recreational-craft licence. The judgment became final on 6 March 2009.

On 31 July 2009 police reported the applicant for driving while disqualified, contrary to Article 1494(6) (“the initial offence”). A fine of LVL 250 was imposed on 1 September 2009 and upheld by the State Police. The applicant appealed to the administrative courts on 19 October 2009, arguing that the 1 December 2008 termination had been final and that his licence had been restored. Those appeal proceedings remained pending when the events giving rise to the Article 6 § 2 complaint occurred; they were ultimately dismissed in 2010–2012 on the ground that the 27 February 2009 judgment was binding.

On 23 September 2009 police issued a further report charging the applicant with the same offence committed repeatedly within one year, contrary to Article 1494(7) (“the repeat offence”). On 6 November 2009 the Riga City Zemgale District Court convicted him, relying on the 27 February 2009 driving ban and the 31 July 2009 report, and imposed five days’ detention plus a fine of LVL 400. The applicant appealed, contending that the 27 February 2009 judgment was unlawful and that the repeated character of the offence could not be established while the appeal against the 31 July 2009 decision was still pending; he sought termination or stay of the proceedings. On 26 February 2010 the Riga Regional Court dismissed the appeal. It held that an appeal against an administrative decision does not prevent a finding of a repeat offence unless the earlier decision has been set aside or its legal effect suspended. Article 283 of the Code provides that an appeal does not suspend a driving ban. Consequently the 31 July 2009 decision remained legally binding and could be used to classify the September 2009 incident as a repeat offence. By June 2010 the applicant had served the five-day sentence and paid the fine.

Domestic law and Supreme Court case-law treat an administrative penalty as taking effect upon service; an appeal suspends only enforcement (not legal effect) except where *lex specialis* provides otherwise. A later decision classifying an offence as repeated is therefore valid unless the first decision is subsequently quashed, in which event remedies exist to reopen the second case. The applicant maintained that this approach treated him as already guilty of the initial offence while that conviction was under appeal, contrary to the presumption of innocence.

**CASE OF KANGERS v. LATVIA (Application no. 35726/10)**

The applicant, a Latvian national, alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention (presumption of innocence). He claimed that domestic courts found him guilty of a repeat administrative offence of driving while disqualified while his appeal against the initial such offence remained pending. The complaint under Article 6 § 2 was communicated; other parts of the application were declared inadmissible.

The case involved three sets of administrative offence proceedings under Latvia’s Code of Administrative Offences.

In the first set, police on 20 November 2008 reported the applicant for driving with a blood-alcohol concentration exceeding 1.5 permille. The Jūrmala City Court terminated the proceedings on 1 December 2008 for lack of corpus delicti; the decision took effect on 5 January 2009 and his driving licence was returned. A prosecutor lodged an appeal on 10 February 2009 (no statutory time-limit applied to prosecutors). After denying the applicant’s request to postpone the hearing, the Riga Regional Court on 27 February 2009 quashed the termination, convicted him and imposed 15 days’ administrative detention, a fine of LVL 500, a two-year driving ban and a related ban on operating recreational craft. The judgment became final on 6 March 2009. The applicant’s later request to suspend execution was refused.

In the second set, police on 31 July 2009 reported the applicant for driving while disqualified (the “initial offence”). A fine of LVL 250 was imposed and upheld. The applicant appealed to the administrative courts on 19 October 2009, arguing that the original 1 December 2008 decision had become final and could not be quashed. The Administrative District Court dismissed the appeal on 20 December 2010, holding that the 27 February 2009 judgment had taken effect and was binding, so the applicant had driven while his licence was revoked. The Administrative Regional Court upheld this on 24 April 2012, confirming that prosecutors faced no appeal time-limit, that the 27 February 2009 judgment was final and legally binding, and that its legality could not be re-examined in the present proceedings. There was no indication the applicant had been unaware of the revocation.

In the third set, police on 23 September 2009 reported the applicant for driving while disqualified repeatedly within a year (the “repeat offence”). On 6 November 2009 the Riga City Zemgale District Court convicted him under the relevant provision, relying on the 27 February 2009 judgment and the 31 July 2009 report, and imposed five days’ detention plus a LVL 400 fine. The applicant appealed, contending that the 27 February 2009 judgment was unlawful and that the repeated character of the offence could not be established while his appeal against the 31 July 2009 decision remained pending; he asked for the proceedings to be terminated or suspended. On 26 February 2010 the Riga Regional Court upheld the conviction by a final judgment. It held that a person could be found guilty of a repeat offence even while the decision on the initial offence was under appeal. The sole relevant criterion was whether the initial decision had been set aside or its legal effect suspended when the repeat-offence decision was taken. Absent such circumstances the initial findings remained legally binding. An appeal against a driving-disqualification decision did not suspend its enforcement. Consequently the pending appeal did not prevent classification of the later driving as a repeat offence or conclusion of those proceedings.

By the time the applicant lodged his application with the Court on 2 June 2010 he had already served the five-day detention and paid the fine imposed in the third set of proceedings.

Relevant domestic law treated an administrative penalty as imposed once the decision took effect (upon service). Appeals generally suspended execution but, by lex specialis, not the legal effect of driving-disqualification decisions. Supreme Court case-law confirmed that a pending appeal against an initial penalty did not, of itself, preclude reliance on that penalty to establish the repeated nature of a later offence, provided the initial decision remained in force and unsuspended; courts could, however, stay the later proceedings if necessary for a fair outcome.

The applicants, four members of a family residing in Shnogh village in Armenia’s Lori Region, jointly owned two plots of arable land (0.373 ha and 0.448 ha) together with a 69.4 m² beekeeper’s house standing on the second plot. They derived their livelihood from agriculture and apiculture on this land. In the 1970s a copper-molybdenum deposit had been discovered nearby. In 2001 a private company, Armenian Copper Programme CJSC, obtained a 25-year mining licence. On 1 November 2007 the Government adopted Decree No. 1279-N designating large tracts of agricultural land, including the applicants’ plots, as expropriation zones for “State needs” in connection with the Teghout mining project. The decree authorised the licensee or its subsidiary Teghout CJSC to acquire the listed parcels, asserting that economic-development and infrastructure interests outweighed private property rights.

Teghout CJSC subsequently offered the applicants AMD 183 000 (plus the statutory 15 per cent) for the first plot and AMD 304 000 (plus 15 per cent) for the second, figures taken from valuations prepared at the company’s request by Oliver Group LLC. The applicants rejected the offer as inadequate. They were unable to obtain an independent market-value assessment; they claimed no other licensed valuer was willing to act.

On 12 May 2008 Teghout CJSC sued to compel the applicants to execute an expropriation agreement on the basis of the Oliver Group reports. The case of Adamkowski v. Poland (Application no. 57814/12) was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Polish national Mr J. Adamkowski on 31 August 2012. He alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention arising from overcrowded and inadequate prison conditions, as well as a violation of Article 6 § 1 arising from the domestic courts’ rejection of his appeal on formal grounds that he regarded as excessively formalistic and as denying him access to a court.

The applicant, born in 1983, was held in Płock Prison from 26 March to 29 August 2009 (five months and four days). During that period he was placed in cells 400 and 402, which the parties and domestic records confirmed were overcrowded. Ventilation and sanitary facilities were inadequate; the applicant received one shower per week and one hour of outdoor exercise per day.

On 17 January 2011 he brought a civil action against the prison authorities for infringement of his personal rights, claiming PLN 10 000 (approximately EUR 2 500) in compensation. He was granted exemption from court fees but did not at first request legal aid. The Płock District Court repeatedly instructed him that pleadings and requests for evidence had to be filed in two copies. He was not transported to a hearing on 23 March 2011 and was later required to clarify the precise period of detention, again in two copies. Part of the claim was subsequently rejected on res judicata grounds.

On 2 February 2012 the applicant applied for legal aid; the request was refused on 14 February 2012 because the court considered him capable of representing himself, having examined the case file and given evidence. On 28 May 2012 the District Court dismissed the action on the merits. It accepted that the cells had been overcrowded for approximately five months but held that the applicant had failed to prove that the authorities’ conduct was unlawful; remaining allegations concerning material conditions were found unsubstantiated.

The applicant was served with the judgment and a standard notice of appeal rights. He lodged an appeal on 22 June 2012. The court then ordered him to supply two additional copies. On 9 July 2012 he submitted a handwritten document entitled “appeal” (in two copies) whose content was similar but not identical to the original, because he had added references to Supreme Court case-law. On 17 July 2012 the court rejected the appeal, ruling that a “copy” must be an exact reproduction and that the added arguments constituted a change of the original submissions.

The applicant’s subsequent interlocutory appeals against the rejection were themselves rejected for failure to furnish identical extra copies. In one of those appeals he explained that he was a layperson without legal training, that legal aid had been denied, that he could not reproduce from memory a pleading written a month earlier, and that the court had never returned the original so that he could photocopy it.

These facts—the five-month period of overcrowding together with the chain of formal rejections of the appeal and interlocutory appeals—constitute the core of the two complaints examined by the Court.

The case of Meshengov v. Russia (ECtHR, 26 March 2019) concerned a Russian national, Yevgeniy Meshengov (born 1976), who alleged ill-treatment by police after his arrest on suspicion of the aggravated murder of A.S. in Irkutsk, as well as the authorities’ failure to investigate those claims effectively.

Meshengov was arrested by traffic police in Ussuriysk around 9 a.m. on 8 April 2007, held overnight in a temporary detention cell, and flown to Irkutsk the next day. Four arresting officers later stated that he had not resisted and that no force or handcuffs had been used. Around 11 p.m. on 9 April he was taken to the Sverdlovskiy district police department. According to the applicant, seven officers shackled him to a chair and beat him throughout the night: they placed a gas mask over his head and restricted airflow, kicked him in the chest, punched his ears and administered electric shocks, causing him to lose consciousness repeatedly. He signed papers they presented in order to stop the assault.

An arrest record drawn up at 12.30 a.m. on 10 April (without a lawyer) recorded the arrest as having occurred at 10 p.m. on 9 April. From 10.30 a.m. to 2.20 p.m. that morning an investigator questioned him as a suspect in the presence of a State-appointed lawyer. The record stated that he had given statements voluntarily, that wrist injuries resulted from resistance to handcuffs, and that he had not been subjected to violence; he made self-incriminating admissions concerning A.S. Meshengov later claimed the lawyer had not actually been present during questioning. He was placed in a temporary detention facility (IVS) that evening and remanded in custody on 11 April, after which he was transferred to pre-trial detention facility IZ 38/1/2.

Medical evidence recorded on 11 April showed extensive injuries. An IVS doctor noted bruises on the left collarbone, shoulder and lumbar region plus abrasions on the elbows, hands and wrists (attributed without explanation to a “home accident”). A forensic examination the same day documented ten bruises (chest, left shoulder, iliac bone, forearms, elbows, lower spine and left ear) caused by hard blunt objects and eleven stripe-like abrasions on the wrists caused by objects with a limited surface area; the injuries were approximately two days old, not self-inflicted, and classified as not occasioning actual bodily harm. Facility records on arrival confirmed a right-elbow contusion and wrist abrasions.

Meshengov promptly complained of ill-treatment. Materials concerning his injuries were sent to Ussuriysk police, who refused to open a criminal case for lack of the elements of a crime. On 12 March 2008 the Irkutsk regional investigative committee likewise refused, attributing wrist injuries to justified use of handcuffs and treating remaining injuries as a private-prosecution matter for which no complaint had been lodged. Subsequent refusals by the Sverdlovskiy district committee (2009–2011) were issued on similar grounds; some were later annulled and additional inquiries ordered, yet further refusals followed. Domestic courts upheld the refusals as lawful.

At trial Meshengov alleged that a gas mask, electric shocks and prolonged questioning had been used to extract his confession. The Irkutsk Regional Court convicted him on 24 June 2008 (19 years’ imprisonment) relying inter alia on the self-incriminating statements, dismissing the ill-treatment claim because he had not identified the officers or explained why violence continued after he confessed. The Supreme Court reduced the sentence slightly in December 2008, endorsing the trial court’s findings and the 2008 refusal to investigate. Supervisory-review requests were rejected.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints of a substantive and procedural violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

The case of Meshengov v. The record stated that statements were voluntary, wrist injuries resulted from resistance to handcuffs, and no violence occurred; Meshengov made self-incriminating statements. He was placed in a temporary detention facility that evening and remanded in custody the next day.

Detention-facility records confirmed a right-elbow contusion and wrist abrasions.

Appeals and supervisory review endorsed this. The facts show injuries consistent with the applicant’s detailed account of beatings and asphyxiation, unexplained by arrest circumstances or official records, together with a series of superficial, delayed and repeatedly terminated inquiries that never identified officers or examined relevant offences.

The case of Bjarni Ármannsson v. Iceland (Application no. 72098/14) concerned an alleged violation of the ne bis in idem principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, an Icelandic national and former CEO of Glitnir bank from 1997 until April 2007, claimed he had been punished twice for the same undeclared capital income.

On 30 July 2009 the Directorate of Tax Investigation opened an audit of the applicant’s tax returns, initially focused on whether he had declared profits from shares received on leaving Glitnir. He was interviewed in August and October 2009. The investigation ended with a report dated 5 October 2010. The Directorate then referred the file to the Directorate of Internal Revenue for possible tax reassessment and informed the applicant that a decision on criminal proceedings would follow.

By letter of 2 May 2011 the Directorate of Internal Revenue notified the applicant of a proposed reassessment of his 2007–2009 taxes. After objections, an amended notification was issued on 16 January 2012; the share-profit element was dropped. On 15 May 2012 the Directorate ruled that the applicant had failed to declare substantial capital income (property-sale profits, dividends, interest and foreign-exchange gains) received between 2006 and 2008. It therefore increased the capital declared in his 2007–2009 returns and imposed a 25 per cent surcharge. The applicant paid both the additional tax and the surcharge and did not appeal; the decision became final in August 2012.

Meanwhile, on 1 March 2012—before the tax decision was final—the Directorate of Tax Investigation sent the entire file, including the later-dropped share-profit issue, to the Special Prosecutor. The applicant’s lawyer protested that the referral was premature. The Special Prosecutor interviewed the applicant on 26 September 2012, limiting the investigation to the facts retained by the tax authorities. On 17 December 2012 the applicant was indicted for aggravated tax offences under the Income Tax Act and the Penal Code, namely the same failure to declare the 2006–2008 capital income in his 2007–2009 returns.

The applicant sought dismissal of the indictment on ne bis in idem grounds. The District Court rejected the plea on 23 April 2013. On 28 June 2013 it convicted him of acting with gross negligence, imposing a six-month prison sentence (suspended for two years) and a fine of ISK 38 850 000 (approximately EUR 241 000). In fixing the fine the court took account of the surcharge already paid. The Supreme Court, on 15 May 2014, likewise dismissed the ne bis in idem argument, upheld the conviction and increased the prison term to eight months (still suspended), while confirming the fine.

Thus the same factual omissions that had already given rise to a final administrative surcharge became the basis of a subsequent criminal conviction and additional sanctions. The domestic courts held that the two sets of proceedings were sufficiently independent and that the surcharge could be deducted from the criminal fine, thereby avoiding double punishment. These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.

Iceland (Application no. 72098/14) concerns an alleged violation of the ne bis in idem principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The Supreme Court, by judgment of 15 May 2014, likewise rejected the ne bis in idem plea, upheld the conviction and the fine, and increased the prison term to eight months, still suspended for two years.

The two sets of proceedings therefore concerned identical facts—the failure to declare the same capital income—and both resulted in punitive sanctions (the 25 per cent surcharge and the subsequent criminal fine and suspended imprisonment). The tax decision became final in August 2012, after the criminal investigation had already begun but before indictment and conviction. These circumstances form the factual core of the alleged double-jeopardy violation.

The case of Bjarni Ármannsson v. Iceland (Application no. 72098/14) concerns an alleged violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights (the ne bis in idem principle prohibiting double jeopardy). The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1968 and living in Denmark, served as CEO of Glitnir, one of Iceland’s largest banks, from September 1997 until the end of April 2007.

On 30 July 2009, the Directorate of Tax Investigation initiated an audit of the applicant’s tax returns to examine whether he had declared profits from selling shares received upon stepping down as CEO. He was questioned on 17 August and 2 October 2009. The investigation concluded with a report on 5 October 2010. The Directorate informed the applicant on 6 October 2010 of its findings, referral of the case to the Directorate of Internal Revenue for possible tax reassessment, and an upcoming decision on possible criminal proceedings, giving him 30 days to comment. A decision on criminal proceedings was postponed pending the Internal Revenue notification.

On 2 May 2011, the Directorate of Internal Revenue notified the applicant of a re-assessment of his taxes for 2007–2009. After objections, an amended notification was issued on 16 January 2012, cancelling the re-assessment relating to share-sale profits. On 15 May 2012, based on the investigation report and objections, the Directorate found that the applicant had failed to declare significant capital income received from 2006 to 2008. It revised his tax returns for 2007–2009 upwards, re-assessed the taxes, and imposed a 25% surcharge. The applicant paid the amounts due. He did not appeal to the State Internal Revenue Board, so the decision became final in August 2012 upon expiry of the three-month time-limit.

Separately, on 1 March 2012 (before the administrative decision became final), the Directorate of Tax Investigation reported the full matter—including the share-sale profits—to the Special Prosecutor and forwarded its report. The applicant was informed the same day. His lawyer protested, arguing that the objection deadline had not expired and requesting withdrawal of the referral. The Directorate replied on 5 March 2012 that the deadline had expired with the 16 January 2012 notification and that the Special Prosecutor would independently assess the case.

The applicant was interviewed by the Special Prosecutor on 26 September 2012 and informed that the investigation concerned the matter as concluded by the Directorate of Internal Revenue (certain reported aspects having been dropped). On 17 December 2012, the Special Prosecutor indicted him for aggravated tax offences under the Income Tax Act for failing to declare income in his 2007–2009 tax returns. This encompassed undeclared capital income (property-sale profits, dividends, interest, and foreign-exchange gains) received from 2006 to 2008.

The applicant sought dismissal of the indictment under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The District Court rejected this on 23 April 2013. On 28 June 2013, it convicted him of acting with gross negligence (sufficient for criminal liability), imposing a six-month prison sentence suspended for two years and a fine of ISK 38,850,000 (approximately EUR 241,000). In setting the fine, the court had regard to the tax surcharges already imposed. The applicant appealed. On 15 May 2014, the Supreme Court rejected the ne bis in idem claim, upheld the conviction and fine, but increased the sentence to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for two years.

The relevant domestic provisions are Sections 108–110 of the Income Tax Act No. 90/2003 (governing tax surcharges up to 25% for faulty returns and fines/imprisonment for intentional or grossly negligent false statements or non-filing, with deduction of surcharge tax from criminal fines) and Article 262 of the Penal Code (up to six years’ imprisonment for major tax violations involving significant amounts or flagrant circumstances). The administrative surcharge and subsequent criminal conviction and fine thus arose from the same undeclared capital-income facts spanning 2006–2008.
001-192210:
The case of Altay v. Turkey (No. 2) (Application no. 11236/09) was brought by Mehmet Aytunç Altay, a Turkish national born in 1956 and serving a life sentence without parole in Edirne F-type prison for attempting to undermine the constitutional order. He was represented by lawyer Ms G. Tuncer. The applicant alleged that the restriction of privacy in his consultations with his lawyer violated Article 8 of the Convention, and that the related domestic proceedings failed to comply with Article 6 § 1.

On an unspecified date the lawyer sent a postal package to the applicant containing the book Globalisation and Imperialism, the magazine Rootless Anational Publication, and the newspaper Express International Sha la la. Prison authorities considered the contents suspect and, on 12 August 2005, asked the public prosecutor to apply to an enforcement court to determine whether the items related to the defence or contained objectionable material that should be withheld.

On 25 August 2005 the Edirne Enforcement Court examined the package and held that the items did not relate to defence rights, so they should not be handed over under section 5 of Law no. 5351. The applicant objected on 16 September 2005, stating that he had simply wanted to read the materials (which were not illegal) and that the prison administration itself had told the lawyer they could not be brought in person and must be posted. On 30 September 2005 the Edirne Assize Court dismissed the objection on the case file, finding the lower court’s decision lawful.

Meanwhile, on 16 September 2005 the prison administration requested that section 5 of Law no. 5351 be applied so that an official would be present during consultations, arguing that the lawyer’s conduct was incompatible with her professional duties. On 23 September 2005, without a hearing and without seeking submissions from the applicant or his lawyer, the Enforcement Court granted the request (referring to its earlier decision) and ordered an official’s presence during consultations. The order specified no duration. A separate decision on document exchanges could be made if requested.

The applicant objected on 24 October 2005, arguing that the decision failed to explain why the restriction was necessary, that the legal threshold (evidence that lawyer visits were being used for communication with a terrorist or criminal organisation) had not been met, and that exchanging non-illegal publications was not prohibited. He did not request a hearing. On 27 October 2005 the Assize Court dismissed the objection on the case file without a hearing and without addressing his arguments, holding only that the lower-court decision complied with law and procedure.

The restriction remained in force at the time of the Court’s 2019 judgment. Later applications to lift it (2008, 2010 and 2013) were rejected on the grounds that the 2005 decision was final, circumstances had not changed, and a risk still existed because of earlier decisions and the lawyer’s conduct. (A related complaint about the withheld publications was later found by the Compensation Commission to have violated Article 10 for lack of relevant and sufficient reasons.)

These facts concern the imposition of an indefinite monitoring measure on lawyer consultations, the absence of oral hearings or meaningful participation by the applicant, the lack of detailed justification or temporal limit, and the measure’s continued application without fresh assessment of necessity.

**CASE OF ALTAY v. TURKEY (No. 2) (Application no. 11236/09), ECtHR (Second Section), 9 April 2019 (final 9 July 2019)**

The applicant, Mehmet Aytunç Altay (born 1956), a Turkish national serving a life sentence without parole for attempting to undermine the constitutional order in Edirne F-type prison, alleged violations of Article 8 (respect for private life/correspondence, specifically privacy of lawyer consultations) and Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) of the ECHR. He was represented by the same lawyer in multiple Court applications.

On an unspecified date, the lawyer posted a package containing a book (*Globalisation and Imperialism*), a magazine (*Rootless Anational Publication*), and a newspaper (*Express International Sha la la*). Prison authorities deemed the contents suspect and, on 12 August 2005, asked the prosecutor to seek an enforcement court ruling on whether the items related to the applicant’s defence or contained objectionable material.

On 25 August 2005 the Edirne Enforcement Court examined the package and held that the items did not concern defence rights, so they should not be handed over under section 5 of Law no. 5351. The applicant objected on 16 September 2005 to the Edirne Assize Court, arguing he merely wished to read the materials (which the prison had instructed the lawyer to send by post rather than bring in person); they were not illegal and there was no basis to withhold them solely because they arrived via the lawyer. On 30 September 2005 the Assize Court dismissed the objection on the case file, finding the decision lawful.

Meanwhile, on 16 September 2005 the prison administration requested application of section 5 of Law no. 5351 (presence of an official during consultations) because the lawyer’s conduct was incompatible with her duties. On 23 September 2005, referring to its earlier decision and without a hearing or submissions from the applicant or lawyer, the Enforcement Court ordered an official to be present during consultations (no duration specified). It noted a separate decision could later address document exchanges.

The applicant objected on 24 October 2005, arguing the decision failed to explain the necessity of the restriction. Under the law, such a measure required evidence that lawyer visits served as communication within a criminal/terrorist organisation; no such evidence existed and none had been examined. There was also no prohibition on exchanging non-illegal publications. He did not request a hearing. On 27 October 2005 the Assize Court dismissed the objection on the case file without a hearing or addressing his arguments, simply finding the decision lawful.

The restriction remained in force at the time of the 2019 judgment. Later applications to lift it (2008, 2010, 2013) were dismissed on the case file as the 2005 decision was final, with no change in circumstances (including perceived ongoing risk from prior decisions and the lawyer’s conduct). A 2010 request for a hearing under procedural amendments was refused because the restriction was not a disciplinary sanction.

A related 2006 Court application concerning the withheld publications was declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion; a Compensation Commission later found an Article 10 violation, as the interference lacked relevant and sufficient reasons regarding prison security.

Domestic law (Law no. 5275, s. 59(4) as amended by Law no. 5351) permitted an official’s presence, document verification or confiscation only if documents/evidence showed lawyer visits to those convicted of certain organised-crime or terrorism offences served as organisational communication, crime commission or a prison-security threat. Enforcement-court proceedings were generally on the case file without hearing; objections to assize courts were similarly paper-based. The relevant provision was later repealed (2018). International standards (European Prison Rules, UN Body of Principles, Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers) emphasise confidential lawyer-prisoner communications, restrictable only in exceptional, specified circumstances to prevent serious crime or major security breaches.

On 23 September 2005, without a hearing or submissions from the applicant or lawyer, the Enforcement Court granted the request, imposing an official’s presence during consultations. The order cited the 25 August decision, set no time-limit, and reserved a possible further ruling on document exchanges.

The applicant objected on 24 October 2005, arguing that the law permitted such a restriction only where documents or other evidence showed that visits served as a channel of communication with a terrorist organisation, to commit crime or to endanger prison security; no such evidence existed and the court had conducted no examination. He did not request an oral hearing. On 27 October 2005 the Assize Court dismissed the objection on the papers, without addressing his arguments.

Requests for hearings were refused because the measure was not a disciplinary sanction.

A related complaint about the withheld publications was later found by the Compensation Commission to violate Article 10 for lack of relevant and sufficient reasons. Domestic law (section 59 of Law no. 5275) normally guarantees confidential lawyer-client consultations; an official’s presence may be ordered only in the exceptional circumstances described above.
001-192205:
The case of A.V. v. Slovenia concerned a father's complaints under Articles 6 and 8 ECHR regarding Slovenian courts' decisions to discontinue his contact with his three children. The applicant (born 1961) and M. had triplets in 1996. Their marriage was dissolved in January 2003, with sole custody awarded to M. A November 2002 agreement provided for contact twice weekly plus holidays. Contact initially proceeded without issue, but from 2004 the children expressed reluctance; it ceased entirely between July 2006 and November 2008 after M. reported their distress. The applicant attributed this to M.'s alleged manipulation and claimed the Kranj Social Work Centre was biased.

In July 2006 the applicant sought a court order formalising contact three times weekly. Psychiatrist Dr T. reported in November 2006 that the children feared the applicant due to past yelling, physical punishment and negative remarks about M.; they found sessions unpleasant and refused them. She recommended limited contact in the presence of a trusted person, plus parental counselling. The Kranj District Court granted weekly (later potentially weekend) contact in April 2008. On appeal, the Ljubljana Higher Court in October 2008 ordered biweekly 90-minute sessions from November 2008, supervised by a Centre expert to rebuild trust, with M. required to ensure attendance. It found the children's refusal stemmed from genuine past experiences rather than manipulation, but held that the absence of prior expert-assisted contact did not justify total discontinuation.

Supervised sessions from November 2008 lasted only minutes, as the children repeatedly stated they did not wish to see the applicant and left. The Centre cancelled remaining sessions in April 2009, citing a serious psychological burden (Family Act s.119). The applicant repeatedly complained that the Centre failed to implement the order actively (e.g., by providing counselling, involving a trusted school psychologist, or using informal settings) and was biased toward M.

In January 2009 the Centre applied to suspend contact or require family therapy, arguing sessions were unsuccessful and psychologically harmful. Interim orders followed, including a April 2009 temporary suspension. Dr T.'s October 2010 update confirmed the children's resentment arose from early lack of emotional connection and past negatives, not manipulation; she saw no benefit to forced contact given their age but recommended parental therapy (80% success chance if both participated). The District Court discontinued contact on 21 June 2011 (Family Act s.106(5)), holding that the now-almost-15-year-olds' categorical refusal, unsuccessful supervision, and resulting distress meant further attempts would not serve their interests and risked irreparable harm. It refused to compel family therapy, as M. declined and the children were distressed. The Higher Court upheld this in January 2012, finding the applicant's characteristics and M.'s passivity key factors but no legal basis to force therapy; the Constitutional Court declined review in June 2012.

A 2011 Inspectorate audit found the Centre had violated statutes by failing to address parental conflict, treat parents equally, offer available services, assess the situation properly or prepare the children, and by incorrectly concluding discontinuation was warranted. It stressed parental responsibility for the impasse but required remedial measures, which the Centre later implemented.

These facts—concerning the courts' and Centre's handling of contact implementation, children's views, expert evidence, alleged bias/inaction, refusal to order therapy, and procedural fairness—underpin the alleged violations of the right to respect for family life and to a fair hearing.

The case of A.V. v. Slovenia (Application no. 878/13) concerns a Slovenian father’s complaint that domestic courts violated his rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by discontinuing all contact with his three children (triplets born in 1996). The applicant and his former wife M. divorced in January 2003, with M. receiving sole custody. An informal 2002 agreement had provided for contact twice weekly plus holidays. Contact initially proceeded without issue but broke down by 2004–2006, as the children expressed distress and refusal, which the applicant attributed to M.’s alleged manipulation and the Kranj Social Work Centre’s bias. No contact occurred from July 2006 until late 2008.

In July 2006 the applicant sought court-ordered contact. A court-appointed psychiatrist, Dr T., found that the children feared the applicant due to past yelling, physical punishment and negative remarks about M.; she recommended limited, supervised contact plus parental counselling. In April 2008 the Kranj District Court granted weekly contact (later weekends) with school-psychologist support. On appeal the Ljubljana Higher Court, relying on Dr T., reduced this in October 2008 to fortnightly 90-minute sessions at the Centre under expert supervision, stressing that the children’s refusal (rooted in past experiences rather than manipulation) did not yet justify ending contact.

Supervised sessions began in November 2008. The children repeatedly stated they did not wish to see their father and left after minutes; the Centre cancelled remaining sessions in April 2009 as a “serious psychological burden.” The applicant repeatedly complained that the Centre failed to implement the 2008 order, offered no meaningful expert help, was biased toward M., and should have arranged informal settings or independent experts. In January 2009 the Centre applied to suspend contact or confine it to family therapy, arguing that sessions were harming the children and that only joint parental change could restore a relationship.

After an interim suspension in April 2009, Dr T. re-examined the family in 2010. She confirmed the children’s enduring resentment, lack of early emotional bond and view of contact as forced; she saw no benefit in continued sessions but estimated an 80 % chance of success for parental therapy aimed at improving communication. M. refused any therapy. In June 2011 the District Court, citing section 106(5) of the Marriage and Family Relations Act, permanently discontinued contact. It held that the now-15-year-old children categorically refused contact, that sessions caused mental distress, and that the applicant bore partial responsibility through impatience and inability to connect. Family therapy was refused because M. objected and the children were distressed. Appeals were dismissed by the Higher Court (January 2012) and the Constitutional Court declined to hear the case (June 2012).

An Inspectorate audit later identified multiple failings by the Centre: it had not addressed parental conflict, treated the parents unequally, failed to prepare the children or offer home support, and incorrectly assessed past “harm.” The Inspectorate nevertheless concluded that only the parents themselves could resolve the situation. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the authorities had neither taken adequate positive measures to restore contact nor conducted a sufficiently thorough and impartial process before extinguishing his family-life rights.

**The applicant, a Slovenian national born in 1961, and his former wife M. had triplets born in October 1996. Their marriage was dissolved in January 2003, with sole custody awarded to M. A 2002 agreement provided for the applicant's contact twice weekly plus holidays. Contact initially proceeded but deteriorated; by 2004 the children expressed reluctance, and from July 2006 to November 2008 there was none. The parents' relationship had become highly conflicted, preventing agreements.**

In July 2006 the applicant sought a court order for regular contact, alleging M. restricted access and manipulated the children, and that the Kranj Social Work Centre was biased. M. countered that the children feared the applicant's anger and criticism from past incidents (yelling, physical punishment, negative remarks about her). A court-appointed psychiatrist, Dr T., found the children reluctant due to these experiences; she recommended limited supervised contact and parental counselling, noting M. had not actively blocked visits but had ceased encouraging them.

In 2008 the courts ordered contact every other Wednesday (initially weekly, later adjusted) at or near the Centre, supervised by experts to rebuild trust. The first sessions from November 2008 lasted minutes: the children repeatedly stated they did not want to see the applicant and left. The Centre cancelled further sessions in April 2009, citing serious psychological burden under domestic law. The applicant repeatedly complained that the Centre failed to implement the order properly, offered no meaningful expert help, treated him unequally (knowing M. personally), and was working toward suspension rather than facilitation. He suggested involving the children's trusted school psychologist and more informal settings.

In January 2009 the Centre applied to suspend contact or require family therapy (initially parents only), arguing sessions were traumatic, amounted to psychological abuse, and showed no prospect of improvement. It also sought an interim suspension. After initial dismissal, courts issued an interim suspension in April 2009. Dr T.'s 2010 update confirmed the children's resentment stemmed from early negative experiences and lack of emotional bond, not proven manipulation by M.; they viewed contact as forced. She recommended parental therapy (80% success chance if both participated) to build trust, noting the applicant was motivated but the children (then ~14) should not be forced. M. refused any family therapy.

In June 2011 the District Court discontinued contact, finding the now-nearly-15-year-old children categorically refused it due to past experiences, that sessions caused distress and were contrary to their interests, and that reasons for refusal were no longer decisive. It declined to order therapy (M. refused; children distressed) and attributed some failure to the applicant's impatience. The Higher Court upheld this in January 2012, citing the applicant's characteristics and M.'s passivity; it found no legal basis to force M. into therapy and insufficient conviction that the applicant would overcome personal barriers. The Constitutional Court declined review in June 2012.

An Inspectorate audit (finalised 2011 after delay) found the Centre violated multiple provisions: it failed to identify/address parental conflict (especially M.'s non-cooperation), treat parents equally, offer available services, assess the situation properly, or follow the court order to re-establish contact. It had aligned with M., burdened the children with decisions, and inadequately prepared them. However, it concluded the parents bore primary responsibility and that contact under the circumstances was not in the children's interests. The Centre later implemented recommended measures (new team, action plan, training).

These facts underpin the applicant's complaints under Articles 6 and 8 regarding the discontinuation of contact, including alleged failures in implementation, bias, inadequate consideration of therapy despite expert advice, and balancing of the children's wishes/interests against the father's rights.
