001-192458:
The case of Kamoy Radyo Televizyon Yayıncılık ve Organizasyon A.Ş. v. Turkey concerns a Turkish media company’s claims of violations of its property rights and right to a fair trial. The applicant alleged that legislative interference during pending court proceedings unlawfully restricted use of its registered trademark.

On 5 November 1998 an affiliated company registered the trademark “Özlenen Gazete Vatan, Günlük Siyasi Gazete” with the Turkish Patent Institute for ten years. It briefly published a newspaper under that name in early 1999 before stopping for financial reasons. In September 2002 another media company, Bağımsız Gazetecilik, began publishing a newspaper called Vatan. In October 2002 the affiliated company sued Bağımsız Gazetecilik in the Istanbul Intellectual Property Court for unfair competition, seeking an order to stop use of the name. It relied on exclusive rights under Legislative Decree no. 556. The trademark was later transferred to the applicant, which joined the proceedings.

An August 2003 expert report observed that although the applicant held the registration, Bağımsız Gazetecilik possessed a 1974 official declaration of intent to publish a periodical and that Vatan had been a recognisable newspaper name since 1975, well before the 1998 registration. The report concluded that the Patent Institute should have refused registration under Article 7 of the Decree because of prior recognition.

On 27 January 2004 the court dismissed the claim. It accepted that the name had become well-known before registration and that the applicant had not acted in good faith. It also applied section 31(2) of Law no. 5000 (the Turkish Patent Institute Act), which entered into force on 6 November 2003 while the case was pending. That provision stated that persons already publishing periodicals under the Press Act could not be prevented from doing so by the Trademark Decree.

The applicant appealed, arguing that a mere publication declaration could not override a registered trademark, that Turkish law afforded absolute protection to registered marks, and that retrospective application of the new provision lacked a legitimate aim. On 6 May 2005 the Court of Cassation upheld the dismissal solely on the basis of section 31(2). It rejected the first-instance court’s preference for the unregistered but well-known mark, holding that a registered trademark would normally take priority; the new statutory bar nevertheless required dismissal. A rectification request was refused on 28 October 2005. The applicant maintained that the retrospective law had privileged the other party and that a timely judgment would have protected its rights.

In 2008 the Turkish Constitutional Court, examining a different case, annulled section 31(2) as incompatible with the constitutional right to property. It held that a trademark is a possession and that the provision had rendered existing trademark protection inoperative against uses already under way when the law entered into force, thereby protecting unlawful acts without serving the public interest.

In parallel proceedings Bağımsız Gazetecilik applied in 2002 to register Vatan as its own trademark. After an initial refusal it obtained registration in 2005. It also sued to annul the applicant’s mark. On 17 February 2005 the Ankara Intellectual Property Court declared the applicant’s registration void both because of prior well-known status and because of five years of non-use (Article 14 of the Decree). The ruling became final in June 2006. The applicant’s mark was removed from the register in November 2006 and Vatan was registered in Bağımsız Gazetecilik’s name.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: retrospective legislative intervention in ongoing litigation that extinguished the applicant’s ability to enforce its registered trademark, thereby interfering with property rights and compromising the fairness of the proceedings.

The applicant company, a Turkish media firm, alleged violations of its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and its right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. It claimed that a legislative change enacted during pending court proceedings unlawfully restricted its use of a registered trademark.

On 5 November 1998, an affiliated company registered the trademark “Özlenen Gazete Vatan, Günlük Siyasi Gazete” with the Turkish Patent Institute for a ten-year term. The affiliate briefly published a newspaper under that name in early 1999 before ceasing due to financial difficulties. In September 2002, another media company, Bağımsız Gazetecilik, began publishing a newspaper titled Vatan. The applicant (to which the trademark had been transferred) sued Bağımsız Gazetecilik in the Istanbul Intellectual Property Court on 22 October 2002. It sought to halt the defendant’s use of the name, arguing unfair competition and infringement of its exclusive rights under Legislative Decree no. 556 on the Protection of Trademarks.

An expert report noted that a newspaper called Vatan had been published since 1975 (rights later transferred to the defendant) and that the name had become well-known long before the applicant’s 1998 registration. The report concluded that the Patent Institute should have refused registration under Article 7 of the Decree. On 27 January 2004 the court dismissed the claim. It accepted that the name was already well-known and that the applicant had not acted in good faith. Independently, it applied section 31(2) of the Turkish Patent Institute Act (Law no. 5000), which had entered into force on 6 November 2003—after the lawsuit was filed. That provision stated that persons already publishing periodicals in accordance with the Press Act could not be prevented from doing so on the basis of the Trademark Decree.

The Court of Cassation upheld the dismissal on 6 May 2005 solely on the basis of section 31(2). It rejected the first-instance court’s preference for the unregistered but well-known mark, observing that a registered trademark normally takes priority. A subsequent request for rectification was refused on 28 October 2005. The applicant argued that the retrospective application of the new provision privileged the defendant and that, had the first-instance court decided the case within a year, the trademark would have been protected.

In parallel proceedings the Patent Institute ultimately registered “Vatan” in the defendant’s name. On 17 February 2005 the Ankara Intellectual Property Court declared the applicant’s registration void because the mark had become well-known before 1998 and because the applicant had not used it for five consecutive years (Article 14 of the Decree). That decision became final in 2006; the applicant’s mark was cancelled and the defendant’s registration was entered.

On 31 January 2008 the Turkish Constitutional Court annulled section 31(2) as contrary to the constitutional right to property. It held that a registered trademark constitutes a possession, that the Trademark Decree is intended to protect such rights against unlawful use, and that the impugned provision rendered that protection impossible for interferences already under way when the law entered into force. The restriction therefore served no public interest and effectively shielded unlawful acts.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints: the mid-proceedings enactment and retrospective application of section 31(2) deprived it of the practical enjoyment of its registered trademark, while the legislative intervention itself was said to have compromised the fairness of the pending civil proceedings.

The applicant, a Turkish media company, inherited a trademark registered in November 1998 by an affiliate for “Özlenen Gazete Vatan, Günlük Siyasi Gazete.” The affiliate published a newspaper under that name only briefly in early 1999 before ceasing operations for financial reasons. In September 2002 another publisher, Bağımsız Gazetecilik, launched a daily called Vatan. The applicant sued in the Istanbul Intellectual Property Court, alleging trademark infringement and unfair competition under Legislative Decree No. 556, which grants exclusive rights to the registered owner and authorizes courts to halt unauthorized use of an identical sign for identical goods or services.

An expert report found that a newspaper named Vatan had circulated since 1975 and that the name had become well-known long before the 1998 registration; the Patent Institute should therefore have refused the application. On 27 January 2004 the first-instance court dismissed the claim. It accepted the well-known-mark analysis and, more decisively, applied section 31(2) of the newly enacted Turkish Patent Institute Act (Law No. 5000), which entered into force on 6 November 2003—while the case was pending. That provision stated that anyone already publishing a periodical under the Press Act could not be stopped on the basis of Decree No. 556.

The applicant appealed, arguing that a mere “declaration of a periodical” conferred no priority over a registered mark, that Decree No. 556 afforded absolute protection, and that section 31(2) could not be applied retroactively to pending litigation. On 6 May 2005 the Court of Cassation rejected the well-known-mark reasoning (a registered mark would normally prevail) but upheld the dismissal solely on the strength of section 31(2). A rectification request was denied in October 2005.

In parallel proceedings Bağımsız applied to register “Vatan.” After an initial refusal it obtained a provisional restriction on the applicant’s mark and, in February 2005, a decision registering the name in its favour. It also sued to invalidate the applicant’s registration. The Ankara Intellectual Property Court annulled that registration in February 2005 on two grounds: the mark had been well-known before 1998 and the applicant had not used it for five years (Article 14 of Decree No. 556). The Court of Cassation confirmed the invalidation in June 2006; the applicant’s mark was formally cancelled and Bağımsız’s registration was entered.

In January 2008—after the applicant’s proceedings had become final—the Turkish Constitutional Court struck down section 31(2) as unconstitutional. It held that trademarks constitute property, that Decree No. 556 exists to protect registered rights against unlawful use, and that the impugned provision shielded already-commenced infringements, thereby serving no public interest and violating Article 35 of the Constitution.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the legislative intervention, applied mid-proceedings and with retroactive effect, had unlawfully restricted its registered trademark (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) and had compromised the fairness of the trial (Article 6). The subsequent constitutional invalidation of the very provision on which the domestic courts had relied underscored the alleged interference with acquired property rights and with the integrity of pending judicial proceedings.
001-192424:
The case of Ifandiev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 14904/11) arose from a journalist’s book publication that prompted successful defamation proceedings against him in the Bulgarian courts. The applicant, Georgi Menelaev Ifandiev, a writer and journalist born in 1950 and living in Sofia, published The Shadow of Zion in 2003. The book addressed Judaism, Zionism, Freemasonry and their historical influence. On pages 69–70 it compared communists and Nazis to Freemasons and listed various individuals said to have become Freemasons after Bulgaria’s “democratic changes,” among them the “pseudo trade unionist” K.T. A footnote cited a 2002 magazine article. K.T. was a prominent public figure: long-time leader of one of Bulgaria’s largest trade unions (membership around 150,000) and a member of international trade-union bodies.

In September 2005 K.T. brought a civil tort claim, asserting that the statements—that he was a Freemason, a communist linked to the former secret services, and a “pseudo trade unionist”—were false and defamatory. He emphasised that he was a devout Orthodox Christian (incompatible, he said, with Freemasonry), had never belonged to the Communist Party or its youth organisation, and had always opposed the communist regime. He claimed the remarks damaged his honour nationally and internationally and caused him distress that aggravated existing health problems.

Ifandiev denied liability. He said he had relied on earlier published sources (one of which was cited), that K.T. himself had acknowledged membership of the Maltese Order, and that he intended to prove secret-service links by witness evidence. He also argued that the language was not insulting and that K.T. had not demonstrated non-pecuniary harm.

The Sofia City Court found against Ifandiev on 10 July 2008 and awarded K.T. 15,000 BGN (approximately €7,670) plus interest from the date of the claim. The court acknowledged Article 10 of the Convention but held that the applicant had exceeded the bounds of acceptable criticism. It treated the statements as factual assertions that had been disproved: K.T.’s Orthodox faith refuted the Freemason allegation; official archival certificates and unconvincing witness testimony disproved any secret-service connection; and the phrase “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous insult. The court added that insult is a subjective concept, so K.T.’s feeling of offence was sufficient, and that the publication had seriously harmed his reputation both in Bulgaria and abroad, contributing to his hospitalisation.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 23 October 2009, endorsing the lower court’s reasoning and adding that even if K.T. had mentioned the Maltese Order this did not equate to Freemasonry, that repetition of earlier allegations did not make them true or less defamatory, and that K.T.’s public status justified a substantial award. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused to examine Ifandiev’s further appeal on 17 August 2010, confirming that offensiveness is judged by the perception of the addressee and his circle.

Enforcement proceedings followed. By October 2011 the total (principal, interest and costs) stood at 31,549 BGN (approximately €16,100). Only 4.55 BGN was recovered before K.T. abandoned collection in 2016.

After the Strasbourg application was communicated, Ifandiev published a blog post in June 2018 attacking the Government’s observations as lying and defamatory and making personal remarks about Bulgarian judges at the Court. These later statements formed no part of the original domestic proceedings.

The facts therefore centre on a published allegation mixing purported fact and value judgement about a well-known public figure, the national courts’ characterisation of the remarks as untrue and insulting, the size of the award relative to the applicant’s means, and the resulting interference with his journalistic expression.

The case of Ifandiev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 14904/11) arose from a 2003 book published by the applicant, a Bulgarian journalist and writer. Titled “The Shadow of Zion,” the work examined Judaism, Zionism, Freemasonry and their historical effects. On pages 69-70 it compared communists and Nazis to Freemasons and stated that after Bulgaria’s “democratic changes” all those who became Freemasons “were communists and people connected with their gloomy secret services.” The passage named several individuals, including K.T. (described as a “pseudo trade unionist”). K.T. was a prominent public figure who had long led a major Bulgarian trade union (membership around 150,000) and held positions in international labour confederations.

In 2005 K.T. brought a civil tort action against the applicant. He claimed the assertions that he was a Freemason, a communist linked to the former secret services, and a “pseudo trade unionist” were false and defamatory. K.T. emphasised that he was a devout Orthodox Christian (the Church having condemned Freemasonry), had never belonged to the Communist Party or its youth organisation, and had no secret-service ties; on the contrary he had always championed human rights and democracy. He argued that the statements portrayed him as immoral, thereby damaging his national and international standing.

The applicant denied liability. He said the Freemason claim rested on earlier published articles (one cited in a footnote) and on K.T.’s own newspaper remark that he belonged to the Maltese Order. He intended to prove secret-service connections by witness evidence and noted that K.T. had publicly mentioned family links to communist-era figures. He further contended that the language was neither insulting nor defamatory and that K.T. had not proved any non-pecuniary harm.

The Sofia City Court found for K.T. in 2008 and awarded 15,000 BGN (approximately 7,670 EUR) plus default interest for moral damage. While referring to Article 10 of the Convention, the court held that the applicant had exceeded the bounds of acceptable criticism. It found the factual allegations untrue: K.T.’s Christianity refuted the Freemason claim; official archive certificates and unconvincing witnesses disproved any secret-service connection; and the phrase “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous insult. The court treated insult as a subjective matter: it sufficed that K.T. felt offended. It also accepted that the publication had seriously harmed K.T.’s honour both inside Bulgaria’s trade-union community and internationally and had aggravated his health, leading to hospitalisation.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in 2009. It added that membership of the Maltese Order had not been shown to equate to Freemasonry, that repetition of earlier allegations did not make them less defamatory, and that K.T.’s public status justified a substantial award. In 2010 the Supreme Court of Cassation refused to admit a further appeal, confirming that offensiveness is judged by the perception of the person concerned and his social circle, even if that perception diverges from ordinary understanding.

Enforcement proceedings later quantified the total liability (principal, interest and costs) at some 31,549 BGN. Only a token sum was recovered before K.T. abandoned collection in 2016. These domestic decisions, imposing civil liability and a substantial monetary penalty on the applicant for statements about a public figure, formed the core of his complaint that his right to freedom of expression had been violated.

The case of Ifandiev v. Bulgaria (no. 14904/11) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant, a journalist and writer, published a 2003 book titled “The Shadow of Zion.” A paragraph compared communists and Nazis to Freemasons and listed prominent figures who allegedly became Freemasons after Bulgaria’s democratic changes, including K.T. (described as a “pseudo trade unionist”). K.T. was a well-known political figure and long-time leader of Bulgaria’s second-largest trade union (approximately 150,000 members), with roles in international trade union bodies. The list cited a 2002 magazine article in a footnote.

On 28 September 2005, K.T. brought a tort action claiming the statements—that he was a Freemason, a communist linked to former secret services, and a “pseudo trade unionist”—were untrue and defamatory. He asserted he was a devout Orthodox Christian (incompatible with Freemasonry, which the Church condemns), had never belonged to the Communist Party or its youth organization, had no secret-service ties, and had instead advocated for human rights and democracy. He argued the allegations portrayed him as immoral, damaged his national and international prestige, and caused humiliation plus health problems requiring hospitalization.

The applicant denied defamation. He relied on prior publications (including the cited article) and K.T.’s own newspaper interview claiming membership in the Maltese Order. He offered witness evidence on alleged secret-service links and noted K.T.’s boasts of ties to communist-era figures. He contended the remarks were neither offensive nor proven to have caused non-pecuniary harm.

On 10 July 2008 the Sofia City Court found for K.T. and awarded 15,000 BGN (approximately 7,670 EUR) plus default interest for moral damage. While acknowledging Article 10, the court held the applicant had exceeded acceptable criticism. It deemed the allegations untrue: Freemasonry was incompatible with K.T.’s Christianity; official archive attestations and unconvincing witnesses disproved secret-service connections; and “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous insult intended solely to discredit. Insult was treated as subjective—if K.T. felt offended, that sufficed. The publication had seriously harmed K.T.’s honour within Bulgaria’s trade-union community and internationally, aggravating his health.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 23 October 2009. It added that Maltese Order membership was not shown to equal Freemasonry, that earlier publications did not render the statements true or less defamatory, and that K.T.’s public status justified a higher award. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused to examine a further appeal on 17 August 2010, confirming that offensiveness depends on the addressee’s (and his circle’s) perception even if it diverges from common understanding.

Enforcement proceedings later quantified the total (principal, interest, and costs) at 31,549 BGN (approximately 16,100 EUR). Only a negligible sum was recovered before K.T. abandoned collection in 2016.

After the Government’s observations were communicated, the applicant published a June 2018 blog post criticizing them as containing lies, insults, and “primitive tricks,” and attacking Bulgarian ECHR judges as communists or former-security-service agents. These facts form the core of the interference with the applicant’s journalistic expression on a public figure.

The case of Lingurar v. Romania (no. 48474/14) involves four Roma applicants from Vâlcele: Aron Lingurar (b. 1949), Ana Maria Lingurar, Aron Lingurar (b. 1985) and Elena Lingurar. They alleged police ill-treatment during a 15 December 2011 dawn raid on their home, together with an inadequate and ethnically biased investigation, in possible violation of Articles 3 and 14 of the Convention.

According to the applicants, officers, gendarmes and a forest ranger (wearing balaclavas and intervention gear) broke into the house after claiming to be neighbours. They dragged the second and fourth applicants from bed, striking the latter on the collarbone with a truncheon and hitting the former in the mouth (then forcing her to wash away blood). The first and third applicants were kicked, abused, taken outdoors unclothed, beaten further and driven to a police station where the violence continued; they were later fined and released. The women were prevented from bringing them clothes.

The Government maintained that the raid followed a forest ranger’s report of illegal timber-cutting by the first applicant, who had become aggressive after his son (the third applicant) was earlier fined. An intervention plan, targeting a Roma-majority municipality of 4,300 inhabitants (2,902 Roma), described high rates of parole, criminal records and violent crime (80 % of 2011 offences attributed to Roma) and listed several criminal groups. Fifty-three officers and 30 gendarmes searched 140 vehicles, conducted 190 identity checks, issued fines, confiscated timber and took 64 people for questioning. Officers approached after 6 a.m., asked the women to summon the third applicant (wanted for questioning), and used force only after he and then the first applicant became physically violent and abusive. The women allegedly injured themselves by pulling their hair, slapping their faces and hitting the gate in an attempt to intimidate police.

Forensic reports of 15–21 December 2011 recorded: dried blood on the second applicant’s lips and cheek (trauma not excluded); two chest bruises on the first applicant (1–2 days’ care, consistent with a hard object); bruises to the third applicant’s eye, chest and arm (4–5 days’ care, consistent with a baseball-bat blow); and a lower-chest bruise on the fourth applicant (1–2 days’ care).

The applicants lodged a criminal complaint in February 2012. Prosecutors (supervised by the Brașov Court of Appeal prosecutor’s office) interviewed the parties and neighbours, inspected the damaged door and, on 11 March 2013, declined to prosecute, finding the raid lawful, force justified by the applicants’ aggression and the ranger uninvolved. The applicants objected, alleging uncritical reliance on police accounts, unexplained injuries and a pattern of unjustified attacks on Roma. The objection was dismissed.

The Court of Appeal remitted the case in May 2013, criticising the failure to explain injuries (especially those of the unarrested women), to identify who ordered immobilisation, and to establish lawfulness (no prior investigation or arrest warrants). A fresh investigation again found force necessary; a July 2013 police report attributed the women’s injuries to “behaviour specific to Roma”. The prosecutor cited widespread Roma criminality and recent attacks on officers, then closed the file in August 2013. Further objections were rejected.

On 16 January 2014 the Court of Appeal finally dismissed the complaint, holding that the additional evidence did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that officers had caused the injuries, that force had not been excessive, that the applicants themselves should have identified the perpetrators, and that ethnicity had played no role.

These facts—conflicting accounts of a large-scale raid planned with explicit ethnic crime statistics, medically documented injuries left unexplained, and an investigation that repeatedly invoked Roma stereotypes—form the core of the alleged Convention violations.

The ECHR case Lingurar v. Romania (App. no. 48474/14) involved four Roma applicants from Vâlcele who alleged Convention violations arising from a 15 December 2011 police/gendarmerie raid on their home and the subsequent investigation.

Applicants claimed that around 5 a.m., officers in special gear (some wearing balaclavas) and a forest ranger knocked, then forced entry by breaking the door. They dragged the second and fourth applicants (women) from bed and beat them (truncheon blow to the fourth applicant’s collarbone; blow to the second applicant’s mouth, after which she was forced to wash off blood). They then beat the first and third applicants (father and son), dragged the men outside half-dressed, continued striking them, and took them to a police station (where they were fined and released). A baby was present.

The Government stated the raid followed a forest ranger’s report that the first applicant had stolen timber and acted aggressively. An intervention plan (covering a Roma-majority area with high recorded crime, 80% of 2011 offences attributed to Roma, and identified criminal groups) deployed over 80 officers and gendarmes to check identities, recover stolen goods, and question suspects. Officers approached after 6 a.m., sought the third applicant for questioning; he and the first applicant allegedly became abusive and violent, necessitating immobilisation and handcuffing. Women’s injuries were attributed to their own actions (hair-pulling, self-slapping, gate-hitting) to intimidate police.

Forensic reports documented injuries consistent with blows from hard objects: blood on the second applicant’s face (trauma not excluded); chest bruises on the first applicant (1–2 days’ care); bruises to the third applicant’s eye, chest and arm (4–5 days’ care); and a chest bruise on the fourth applicant (1–2 days’ care).

Applicants lodged a criminal complaint for violence. Prosecutors (supervised by the Brașov Court of Appeal prosecutor’s office) interviewed parties and neighbours, inspected the damaged door (timing of damage unclear), and twice discontinued proceedings. They accepted the raid as lawful, force as necessary due to applicants’ aggression, and used ethnic stereotypes (women exhibited “behaviour specific to Roma”). Identities of gendarmes who immobilised the men were withheld for “protection.” The prosecutor cited broader Roma-related disorder and the applicants’ family history of investigations.

The Brașov Court of Appeal initially remitted the case, finding the investigation incomplete: unexplained injuries (especially to the women, who were never arrested); unidentified officers who ordered/carried out immobilisation; no prior criminal proceedings or summons against the applicants; and failure to hear additional witnesses or clarify home entry. After further inquiries, prosecutors again discontinued, repeating earlier conclusions plus recent incidents of police injury during Roma-related operations. The Court of Appeal ultimately upheld discontinuation, finding applicants’ statements plus medical reports insufficient, police explanations plausible, no excessive force proven, and no ethnic bias.

These facts underpin alleged Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation) and Article 14 (discriminatory stereotyping of Roma in the raid planning and probe) complaints.

The case of Lingurar v. Romania (ECHR Application no. 48474/14) involves four Roma applicants from Vâlcele who alleged police ill-treatment during a 15 December 2011 raid on their home, along with racial discrimination. The applicants were Aron Lingurar (b. 1949), Ana Maria Lingurar, Aron Lingurar (b. 1985) and Elena Lingurar.

Around 5-6 a.m., 53 police officers and 30 gendarmes, some in special gear and balaclavas, plus a forest ranger, approached the home as part of a large operation. The raid followed a forest ranger's report that the first applicant had taken illegally cut timber and become aggressive; the ranger described him as a negative influence as a perceived Roma leader. The IPJ intervention plan stereotyped the village: of 4,300 residents, 2,902 were Roma, most without steady income, living off benefits, stolen timber and crime (80% of 2011 offences by Roma). It noted high parole, criminal records and violent crimes among residents, identifying other Roma families as criminal groups (applicants' family not listed).

Applicants stated officers claimed to be neighbours, then broke the unlocked door. They dragged the second and fourth applicants (women, one with a baby present) from bed and beat them; the fourth was struck on the collarbone with a truncheon, the second hit in the mouth (forced to wash away blood). The men were pulled from bed, kicked, abused, taken outside undressed, beaten further and driven to the station (violence continuing), where they were fined. The women were not allowed to approach.

The Government claimed officers knocked after 6 a.m., asked for the third applicant (wanted for questioning). He emerged shouting abuse and became violent, leading to immobilisation and handcuffing; the first applicant then emerged similarly and was also restrained. The women allegedly injured themselves (pulling hair, slapping faces, hitting the gate) to intimidate officers.

Forensic reports confirmed injuries: first applicant (bruises on chest, 1-2 days' care, possible hard-object trauma); third (bruises on eye, chest and arm, 4-5 days' care, possible baseball-bat blow); fourth (chest bruise, 1-2 days' care); second (blood on lips/cheek, possible aggression, no further exam). A door examination showed damage of unknown date.

Applicants complained of beating. Prosecutors (supervised by Brașov Court of Appeal office) interviewed parties and neighbours but twice declined to prosecute (March/August 2013), citing a lawful raid, necessary force due to applicants' aggression, and injuries from immobilisation or "Roma-specific" self-harm. They noted later police-Roma clashes and community law-breaking. Gendarmes who immobilised the men remained unnamed for protection. The court once remitted for more inquiry (May 2013), criticising unexplained injuries, unidentified order-givers, lack of prior investigation against applicants, and incomplete identification of participants. A January 2014 final court ruling upheld dismissal, finding insufficient proof police caused injuries, plausible official explanations, no excessive force, and no ethnic bias; applicants had to name perpetrators.

These facts underpin alleged Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation) and Article 14 (discrimination) violations, given the stereotyped planning, force used, injuries, and investigation relying on ethnic tropes without identifying actors or justifying proportionality.
001-192543:
The case of G.S. v. Bulgaria (Application no. 36538/17) concerns a Georgian national born in 1951 who alleged that Bulgaria’s decision to extradite him to Iran would expose him to corporal punishment (flogging) in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, detained in Sofia Prison, was arrested on 17 December 2016 at Sofia Airport pursuant to an Interpol red notice issued by Iran on 14 September 2016. The notice alleged that on 24 June 2016 he and an accomplice had stolen €50,000 by trickery from a Tehran foreign-exchange office; the accomplice was arrested while the applicant fled. It identified the offence as falling under Article 656 of the Iranian Penal Code, with a maximum penalty of three years’ imprisonment.

Iranian authorities confirmed the notice and provided an arrest warrant. Bulgarian prosecutors detained the applicant and, after a 21 December 2016 hearing at which he protested that Iranian “laws” were arbitrary and would not protect him, the Sofia City Court ordered custody pending a formal extradition request. In January 2017 Iran submitted that request, citing Article 656 § 4 (six months to three years’ imprisonment) and giving assurances that the applicant would not face torture or inhuman treatment. On that basis the Bulgarian Minister of Justice found de facto reciprocity.

Extradition proceedings opened on 29 January 2017. The applicant, represented by counsel of his choice, received the request and supporting documents. His defence focused on discrepancies in the alleged date and time of the offence (initially 24 June, later clarified by Iran as 23 June 2016 at 13:40) and on the absence of an extradition treaty. He argued that the request failed formal requirements and that the evidence did not establish his guilt. The Sofia City Court, exercising its power under section 17(3) of the 2005 Extradition and European Arrest Warrant Act to seek additional information, obtained the date clarification but did not inquire further into Iranian law. On 12 April 2017 it authorised extradition, holding that the request met all formalities, that Iranian law envisaged only imprisonment, that the assurances dissipated any risk of ill-treatment, and that the court could not examine the merits of the underlying charge. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 9 May 2017 on essentially the same grounds and ordered continued detention.

Bulgarian law (section 7 of the 2005 Act) prohibits extradition where there is a risk of violence, torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. The courts, however, relied solely on the Iranian request’s description of the penalty. Independent translations of Article 656 § 4 of the Iranian Penal Code—published by the Iran Human Rights Documentation Center, the Iranian legislature and the Tehran judiciary—show that the offence also carries up to 74 lashes. United Nations reports (Human Rights Committee 2011, successive Special Rapporteurs, Secretary-General 2017–18) and NGO documentation (Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, Abdorrahman Boroumand Center) record that flogging remains a routine judicial punishment for theft in Iran, with hundreds of sentences imposed annually, some carried out publicly. Iran has neither signed the UN Convention against Torture nor accepted recommendations to abolish corporal punishment, citing Islamic principles.

The Court indicated under Rule 39 that the applicant should not be extradited pending the Strasbourg proceedings. The Georgian Government declined to intervene. These facts form the core of the alleged Article 3 violation: the Bulgarian courts authorised extradition without verifying that the offence in fact carried a sentence of flogging, a punishment the Court has consistently treated as inherently inhuman.

The case of G.S. v. Bulgaria (Application no. 36538/17) concerns a Georgian national arrested in Bulgaria on an Iranian Interpol red notice and facing extradition for alleged theft, with the core complaint being a real risk of corporal punishment (flogging) in Iran contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1951, arrived in Sofia from Georgia on 17 December 2016 and was arrested at passport control pursuant to a red notice issued by Iran on 14 September 2016. The notice alleged that on 24 June 2016 he and an accomplice had stolen €50,000 by trickery from a Tehran foreign-exchange office; the accomplice was arrested while the applicant fled the same day. It identified the offence as falling under Article 656 of the Iranian Penal Code, with a maximum penalty of three years’ imprisonment. Iran confirmed the warrant the next day. Bulgarian prosecutors detained the applicant for 72 hours and then sought up to 40 days’ detention pending a formal request. The Sofia City Court granted this, noting it was not yet deciding extradition itself. The applicant protested that Iranian “laws” were arbitrary and that he would not survive.

In January 2017 Iran submitted a formal extradition request specifying Article 656 § 4 (theft by two or more persons) and stating that the penalty was six months to three years’ imprisonment. Iran gave assurances that the applicant would not face torture or inhuman treatment and indicated willingness to honour Bulgarian requests; on that basis the Bulgarian Minister of Justice confirmed de facto reciprocity. Extradition proceedings opened in the Sofia City Court on 29 January 2017. The applicant, now with chosen counsel and a Russian interpreter, received the request and supporting documents. The court kept him in detention.

Hearings took place in February–April 2017. Defence counsel highlighted inconsistencies in the date and time of the alleged offence and argued the applicant had already left Tehran; the court requested clarification from Iran, which replied that the theft occurred at 1.40 p.m. on 23 June 2016. In closing submissions counsel also pointed to remaining doubts about the evidence, formal deficiencies in the request, and the absence of an extradition treaty with Iran. On 12 April 2017 the Sofia City Court authorised extradition. It found the request formally compliant, reciprocity established, and no real risk of ill-treatment because Iran had given assurances and Iranian law envisaged only imprisonment for the offence. The court declined to examine the merits of the underlying charge. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 9 May 2017 for the same reasons, again noting that the possible penalty was imprisonment, and ordered continued detention pending surrender.

The alleged Article 3 violation arises from the fact that the actual text of Article 656 § 4 (published in Persian official sources and English translations) additionally prescribes up to 74 lashes. UN bodies (Human Rights Committee, Special Rapporteurs, Secretary-General) and NGOs (Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, Abdorrahman Boroumand Center) document that flogging remains a routine, often public, punishment in Iran for theft and numerous other offences, with hundreds of sentences implemented annually. Iran has not signed the UN Convention against Torture, has rejected recommendations to abolish corporal punishment, and defends flogging as a lawful, deterrent and even preferred alternative to imprisonment. Bulgarian courts in this case relied solely on the request’s description of the penalty and the diplomatic assurances, without investigating the lashes provision or the well-documented practice. (The Court had indicated under Rule 39 that the applicant not be extradited pending its proceedings.)

The case of G.S. v. Bulgaria (no. 36538/17) concerns a Georgian national’s claim that Bulgaria’s decision to extradite him to Iran would expose him to flogging, in violation of Article 3 ECHR.

G.S. was arrested at Sofia Airport on 17 December 2016 under an Iranian Interpol red notice accusing him of stealing €50,000 by trickery from a Tehran foreign-exchange office on 24 June 2016 (with an accomplice). The notice cited Iranian Penal Code Article 656 and a maximum three-year prison term. Iranian authorities later confirmed the warrant. After initial detention, Iran issued a formal extradition request in January 2017 specifying Article 656 § 4 (six months to three years’ imprisonment) and giving assurances against torture or inhuman treatment. Bulgaria proceeded on the basis of de facto reciprocity, there being no extradition treaty.

In Sofia City Court proceedings (with counsel and an interpreter), G.S. highlighted inconsistencies in the offence date/time (later clarified by Iran as 23 June 2016 at 1:40 p.m.) and claimed he had already left Tehran. He also noted the absence of a treaty. On 12 April 2017 the City Court granted extradition, finding the request formally compliant, reciprocity established, and no real risk of ill-treatment (relying on the assurances and the stated prison penalty). It declined to examine the underlying charges. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld this on 9 May 2017, again noting only imprisonment as the possible penalty, and ordered continued detention. The ECtHR indicated under Rule 39 that extradition should not proceed pending the case.

Central to the Article 3 complaint is that the Iranian request and Bulgarian courts omitted the full penalty under Article 656 § 4. Official Iranian texts (in Persian and English translations) prescribe imprisonment plus up to 74 lashes for such non-hadd (ta’zir) theft involving two or more persons. UN bodies (Human Rights Committee, Special Rapporteurs, Secretary-General) and NGOs (Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, Abdorrahman Boroumand Center) document flogging as a routine, legally prescribed punishment in Iran for theft and over 100 other offences, with hundreds of sentences annually (some public). Iran has not signed the UN Convention against Torture; its Guardian Council blocked ratification as conflicting with Islamic law, and it has rejected UN recommendations to ban corporal punishment. UN General Assembly resolutions (supported by Bulgaria) have repeatedly condemned Iranian flogging. CAT Article 3 and related comments prohibit removal where substantial grounds exist for fearing torture, including corporal punishment.

These facts show the Bulgarian courts failed to identify or assess the real risk of flogging.
001-192467:
The case of Baltic Master Ltd. v. Lithuania (Application no. 55092/16) concerns a Lithuanian company's complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The applicant, a Vilnius-registered firm supplying heating, cooling, ventilation and air-conditioning equipment, challenged customs assessments on goods imported between July 2009 and August 2012 from a United States seller. It claimed the purchases were made on the basis of orders rather than formal contracts.

In 2013 the Vilnius territorial customs office audited the declarations. It found that the declared values in 23 import declarations were three to four times lower than those of similar goods imported by others, that the invoices contained no payment information, and that the companies were related because two of the seller’s logistics managers also worked for the applicant. The office initially assessed EUR 618,083 in customs duty, VAT, late-payment interest and a fine. After the applicant complained, the Customs Department in June 2014 annulled part of the report and ordered a further investigation. It noted that the office had not specified which provisions of Article 143 of Commission Regulation (EEC) No. 2454/93 had been breached and that mere relatedness plus a low declared value did not automatically justify recalculation.

The December 2013 supplementary investigation concluded that the parties were related because the applicant had produced no evidence to the contrary. The office rejected the 23 declarations, determined the customs value under Council Regulation (EEC) No. 2913/92 (the Community Customs Code) and assessed approximately EUR 646,361. The Customs Department confirmed the assessment in March 2014. The Tax Disputes Commission in July 2014 found the data incomplete but waived a small portion of the interest (approximately EUR 7,854).

The applicant appealed to the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, arguing that the relatedness finding was unclear under Article 143, that the transaction-value method had been rejected without reasons, and that a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) was required. On 22 January 2015 the court dismissed the claim, stating that the file contained sufficient material and that no question of interpretation of EU customs law had arisen.

On appeal the applicant submitted that the first-instance court had misapplied Articles 29–31 of the Community Customs Code and Regulation No. 2454/93, that its reasoning was inadequate, and that CJEU case-law on those provisions was inconsistent. It formulated six concrete questions covering, inter alia, whether an outstanding buyer-seller debt constituted a circumstance whose effect could not be quantified under Article 29(1)(b); whether a price discrepancy with customs comparatives independently justified rejection of the transaction value; whether the seller’s authorisation of the buyer’s staff to handle transport and customs formalities created a relationship under Article 29(1)(d); whether Article 31 could be applied without first exhausting Articles 29 and 30; the relevant comparison period and geographic scope of data; and whether unit-price-per-kilogram comparisons were permissible.

On 22 March 2016 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the first-instance judgment. Citing the Court’s own case-law (Hiro Balani, Ruiz Torija, Suominen), it held that Article 6 does not require a detailed answer to every argument and that the extent of the duty to give reasons varies with the nature of the decision. The lower court’s reasoning was adequate. A party’s request for a preliminary ruling is not binding when the application of EU law is so obvious that no reasonable doubt exists; mere disagreement with a court’s interpretation does not render the law unclear. In the present case the court perceived no uncertainty concerning Articles 29–31 and therefore refused the request. A later application to reopen the proceedings was dismissed in April 2017.

These facts form the core of the two alleged violations: the imposition of substantial fiscal charges following a contested valuation methodology, and the final national court’s refusal to refer the applicant’s detailed questions to the CJEU without, in the applicant’s view, supplying adequate reasons.

The case of Baltic Master Ltd. v. Lithuania (Application no. 55092/16) concerns a Lithuanian company's challenges to customs tax assessments on imported goods and the domestic courts' refusal to seek a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). The applicant, a Vilnius-registered limited liability company supplying heating, cooling, ventilation and air-conditioning equipment, alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) arising from the Supreme Administrative Court's failure to provide adequate reasons for declining a CJEU referral, and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) arising from the taxes imposed.

In 2013 the Vilnius territorial customs office audited the company's imports from July 2009 to August 2012. The goods, purchased from a United States seller on the basis of orders rather than formal contracts, had been declared as air-conditioning units and parts. Customs found that the values stated in 23 import declarations were three to four times lower than those of comparable goods imported by others. The invoices contained no payment information, and the companies were treated as related because two of the seller's logistics managers were also employed by the applicant. An initial demand of approximately EUR 618,083 was issued for customs duty, value-added tax, late-payment interest and a fine.

Following a complaint, the Customs Department ordered a further investigation, noting that the original report had not identified the precise legal provisions breached or the specific ground of relatedness under Article 143 of Commission Regulation (EEC) No. 2454/93. It also observed that relatedness plus a low declared value did not automatically justify recalculation. In December 2013 the customs office, relying on the absence of evidence disproving the dual employment of the managers, again treated the parties as related, rejected the transaction-value method under the Community Customs Code (Council Regulation (EEC) No. 2913/92) and recalculated the goods' value, producing a revised liability of approximately EUR 646,361.

The company appealed, supplying documents from the seller stating that none of its employees worked for the applicant and contesting both the finding of relatedness and the refusal to accept the declared transaction values. It also objected to the interest as inflated by investigative delay. The Customs Department upheld the assessment; the Tax Disputes Commission granted only a modest reduction of interest. The company then applied to the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, arguing that the relatedness conclusion lacked a clear statutory basis and that the transaction-value method had been discarded without reasons. It requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU on six questions concerning the interpretation of Articles 29–31 of the Customs Code, including whether an outstanding buyer–seller debt or a price discrepancy with customs comparables could independently exclude the transaction-value method, whether authorisation of the buyer's staff for transport and customs formalities constituted a “relationship”, whether Article 31 could be applied without first exhausting Articles 29 and 30, the temporal and geographic scope of comparable data, and the permissibility of using price-per-kilogram comparisons.

On 22 January 2015 the Regional Court dismissed the complaint, holding that the file contained sufficient material and that no question of EU-law interpretation had arisen. The Supreme Administrative Court, on 22 March 2016, upheld that judgment. Citing the Court's own case-law (Hiro Balani, Ruiz Torija and Suominen), it stated that Article 6 § 1 does not require a detailed answer to every argument and that the duty to give reasons varies with the circumstances. It observed that a party's request for a preliminary ruling is not binding where the application of EU law is so obvious that no reasonable doubt exists (acte clair). Mere disagreement with a lower court's interpretation does not render the law unclear. The court found the relevant provisions of the Customs Code sufficiently clear and therefore refused the referral. A subsequent application to reopen the proceedings was rejected in April 2017.

These facts form the basis of the two alleged Convention violations: the asserted inadequacy of the reasons given for declining a mandatory last-instance referral under Article 267 TFEU, and the interference with property constituted by the additional tax, interest and fine.

The case concerns Baltic Master Ltd., a Lithuanian company importing and selling heating, cooling, ventilation and air-conditioning equipment. It alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention (fair hearing) because the Supreme Administrative Court refused its request for a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) without adequate reasons, and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) arising from the customs taxes, VAT, interest and fine imposed on it.

In 2013 the Vilnius territorial customs office audited the company’s imports from July 2009 to August 2012. The company had declared certain goods bought from a United States seller as air-conditioning units and parts, relying on orders rather than formal purchase contracts. Customs found the declared values three to four times lower than those of comparable imports, noted that invoices contained no payment details, and concluded that the two companies were related because two of the seller’s logistics managers also worked for the applicant. It therefore refused the transaction-value method and recalculated the customs value under the Community Customs Code, initially assessing approximately EUR 618 000 in duties, VAT, late-payment interest and a fine.

The Customs Department partly annulled that finding, holding that customs had failed to specify the precise legal grounds (especially under Article 143 of Regulation No. 2454/93) for treating the companies as related and that mere relatedness plus a low declared value did not justify rejecting the transaction value. After a further investigation, customs again found the companies related (on the basis that the applicant had not disproved overlapping employment), rejected 23 import declarations and assessed a total of approximately EUR 646 000. The Customs Department upheld this decision. The Tax Disputes Commission accepted that the applicant’s data were incomplete but reduced the late-payment interest by a modest amount.

The applicant then brought judicial proceedings before the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court. It argued that customs had not identified which of the statutory grounds for relatedness applied, that employee involvement in transport or customs formalities did not constitute a business partnership, and that the transaction-value method had been rejected without reasons. It expressly asked the court to refer questions of interpretation of Articles 29–31 of the Community Customs Code to the CJEU. In January 2015 the court dismissed the claim, stating that the file contained sufficient facts and that no interpretative issue of EU law had arisen.

On appeal the applicant submitted six detailed questions concerning, inter alia, whether an outstanding debt between buyer and seller, a discrepancy with customs’ comparative-price lists, or authorisation of the buyer’s employees to handle logistics could preclude the transaction-value method; whether customs could apply the fallback method of Article 31 independently of Articles 29 and 30; the relevant temporal and geographic scope of comparable data; and whether a national database could be used in preference to Community-wide information. In March 2016 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the first-instance judgment. Citing the Court’s case-law (Hiro Balani, Ruiz Torija, Suominen), it recalled that Article 6 does not require a detailed answer to every argument. It held that a party’s request for a preliminary ruling is not binding when the application of EU law is acte clair, that mere disagreement with a lower court’s interpretation does not demonstrate uncertainty, and that in the present case the relevant provisions of the Customs Code raised no interpretative doubts. A subsequent request to reopen the proceedings was refused.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s complaints: the national courts’ treatment of the relatedness finding and valuation methods, the specificity of the questions it posed, and the Supreme Administrative Court’s stated reasons for declining to refer those questions to the CJEU, together with the financial burden ultimately imposed.

The case of Adžić v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 19601/16) was brought by Miomir Adžić, a US national residing in North Carolina, against Croatia. It concerns non-contentious proceedings initiated on 13 October 2011 for the return of his son under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The child’s mother, a Croatian national and the applicant’s former wife, had wrongfully retained the boy in Croatia in August 2011.

On 15 March 2012 the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court dismissed the return request without holding any hearing. On appeal, the Zagreb County Court quashed that decision on 2 July 2012 and remitted the case, expressly instructing the first-instance court to schedule a hearing so that the applicant could comment on the opposing party’s arguments and evidence.

In the remitted proceedings the Municipal Court obtained a forensic psychiatrist’s opinion on whether return would expose the child to psychological harm under Article 13(1)(b) of the Hague Convention. The applicant was neither informed of the expert’s appointment nor invited to participate in the assessment, despite having offered to make himself available. On 21 May 2014 the Municipal Court again dismissed the request without a hearing, stating that oral testimony from the parties would unduly prolong the case and would lack objectivity because of their personal interest. The County Court upheld this decision on 22 October 2014.

These same return proceedings had already been examined by the European Court of Human Rights in Adžić v. Croatia (no. 22643/14, 12 March 2015). That judgment found a violation of Article 8 on account of the authorities’ failure to act expeditiously; at the time of the Court’s deliberation the case was still pending before the Croatian Constitutional Court.

In his constitutional complaint the applicant alleged a breach of the right to a fair procedure (in particular the right to an oral hearing, equality of arms and the adversarial principle) as well as a violation of his right to respect for family life arising from the refusal to order the child’s return. The Constitutional Court, by decision of 28 October 2015 (served on 4 December 2015), examined only the fair-procedure complaints and dismissed them. It declined to address the family-life complaint on the ground that it had already been resolved by the European Court in the first Adžić judgment.

The applicant therefore complained to Strasbourg that the complete absence of any hearing throughout the return proceedings, the failure to involve him in the expert assessment, and the ultimate refusal to order the child’s return violated his Convention rights.

The case of Adžić v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 19601/16) concerns an American applicant, Miomir Adžić, who alleged violations of his Convention rights arising from Croatian court proceedings under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The applicant’s former wife, a Croatian national, wrongfully retained their son in Croatia in August 2011. On 13 October 2011 the applicant sought the child’s return to the United States. Those “non-contentious” family proceedings formed the core of the complaint.

On 15 March 2012 the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court dismissed the return request without holding any hearing. After the applicant appealed, the Zagreb County Court on 2 July 2012 quashed the decision and remitted the case, expressly instructing the first-instance court to schedule a hearing so that the parties could comment on evidence and examine the circumstances (relying on Family Act s. 309(5) and Civil Procedure Act ss. 297-298). In the remitted proceedings the Municipal Court obtained a psychiatric expert opinion on whether return would expose the child to grave psychological harm under Article 13(1)(b) of the Hague Convention. It did not notify the applicant of the decision to appoint the expert, did not allow him to object to the choice of expert, and did not involve him in the assessment despite his earlier offer to participate. On 21 May 2014 the court again dismissed the request without a hearing, justifying the omission on the ground that hearing the parties would unduly prolong the case and that their testimony would be inherently biased. The County Court upheld that decision on 22 October 2014.

These same return proceedings had already been examined by the European Court in Adžić v. Croatia (no. 22643/14, 12 March 2015). That judgment found a violation of Article 8 solely on account of the authorities’ failure to act expeditiously; at the date of that judgment a constitutional complaint by the applicant was still pending.

In the constitutional complaint the applicant alleged a breach of his right to a fair procedure (Article 6), specifically the absence of any oral hearing, the violation of equality of arms and the adversarial principle, and the failure to involve him in the expert assessment. He also complained that the refusal to order return itself violated his right to respect for family life (Article 8). On 28 October 2015 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, examining only the fairness arguments and holding that the family-life complaint had already been determined by the European Court. The decision was served on 4 December 2015, prompting the present application.

Relevant domestic law permitted decisions without a hearing in non-contentious family matters unless there was a dispute over decisive facts (Family Act s. 309). Expert evidence was governed by the Civil Procedure Act, which normally required consultation of the parties before appointment and allowed oral presentation or written reports. The 1934 Judicial Non-contentious Procedure Act likewise contemplated written or non-public oral statements. International instruments (the Hague Convention Guide to Good Practice and Brussels IIa Regulation Art. 11(5)) emphasised expedition and limited oral evidence, yet also required that a requesting parent be given an opportunity to be heard before a non-return order could be made.

The applicant therefore contended that the complete absence of a hearing, the lack of notification and participation concerning the expert, and the ultimate refusal of return, taken together, breached Articles 6 and 8.

The case of Adžić v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 19601/16) concerns proceedings under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction for the return of the applicant’s son from Croatia to the United States. The applicant, Miomir Adžić (born 1968), is a US national living in Charlotte, North Carolina. His former wife, a Croatian national, wrongfully retained their son in Croatia in August 2011. The applicant instituted non-contentious return proceedings before the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court on 13 October 2011.

On 15 March 2012 the Municipal Court dismissed the return request without holding any hearing. On appeal the Zagreb County Court quashed that decision on 2 July 2012 and remitted the case, expressly instructing the first-instance court to schedule a hearing so that the applicant could comment on the mother’s evidence and the court could examine the circumstances together with the parties.

In the fresh proceedings the Municipal Court commissioned a forensic psychiatric expert to assess whether return would expose the child to a grave risk of psychological harm under Article 13(1)(b) of the Hague Convention. The applicant was neither notified of the expert’s appointment nor invited to participate in the assessment, despite having previously offered to make himself available. On 21 May 2014 the Municipal Court again dismissed the request without a hearing. It justified the omission by stating that hearing the parties would unduly delay the case and that their testimony would lack objectivity. The County Court upheld the decision on 22 October 2014.

These same return proceedings had already been examined by the European Court of Human Rights in Adžić v. Croatia (no. 22643/14, 12 March 2015). In that judgment the Court found a violation of Article 8 of the Convention because the Croatian authorities had failed to act expeditiously. At the time of that judgment the applicant’s constitutional complaint was still pending.

In his constitutional complaint the applicant alleged a breach of fair-procedure rights, specifically the right to an oral hearing, equality of arms and the adversarial principle. He also complained that the refusal to order return violated his right to respect for family life. The Constitutional Court, by decision of 28 October 2015 (served 4 December 2015), examined only the fair-procedure complaints and dismissed them, holding that the family-life issue had already been resolved by the Strasbourg Court.

Relevant domestic law included the 2003 Family Act, which permitted decisions without a hearing unless there was a dispute on decisive facts (section 309), and the Civil Procedure Act provisions on the appointment and use of experts. The Hague Convention itself and the associated Guide to Good Practice emphasise expedition and the possibility of deciding return applications primarily on written evidence, while Brussels II bis Regulation (applicable by analogy in spirit) requires that the requesting parent be given an opportunity to be heard before a non-return order is made.

The applicant therefore complained to the European Court that the complete absence of any hearing throughout the return proceedings, the failure to involve him in the expert assessment, and the ultimate refusal to order his son’s return violated his rights under the Convention.

The case of Ter-Petrosyan v. Armenia (Application no. 36469/08) concerns events following Armenia’s 19 February 2008 presidential election. Levon Ter-Petrosyan, a former president (1991–1998) and the main opposition candidate, challenged the results after the Central Election Commission declared Prime Minister Serzh Sargsyan the winner with approximately 52% of the vote (Ter-Petrosyan received about 21%). Ter-Petrosyan alleged widespread irregularities and called on supporters to protest at Freedom Square in central Yerevan. From 20 February onward, daily rallies drew tens of thousands, with several hundred camping overnight. Ter-Petrosyan addressed crowds two or three times daily, remaining at the square nearly around the clock.

On 29 February he applied to the Constitutional Court to annul the results. The next morning (1 March, around 6–7 a.m.), police surrounded the encampment. According to Ter-Petrosyan, officers attacked without warning or dispersal order, beating sleeping protesters with batons, destroying tents, and chasing people from the square. He was approached by the Head of the State Protection Department (SPD) and officers, forcibly removed from a platform, and taken to his Yerevan home. There, roads were blocked by special forces, vehicles and visitors were searched, and entry/exit required permission from unidentified superiors. He claimed this constituted de facto house arrest lasting until at least 20 March, preventing him from joining subsequent protests or freely attending court except for one hour on 5 March. A state of emergency was declared that day after clashes elsewhere in Yerevan left ten dead (including eight civilians) and many injured; it banned public assemblies for 20 days.

The Government contested this account. It stated that police arrived to search for weapons after receiving intelligence of planned mass disorder. Protesters attacked officers with bats, rods, and stones, prompting clearance of the square. Because Ter-Petrosyan (as a former president entitled to lifetime state protection) was at risk, SPD officers surrounded him and later escorted him home in a car after he declined advice to leave voluntarily. Additional security was posted near his residence amid city-wide violence; visitors were searched but not barred, and he was told he could leave (though SPD would not accompany him to unsafe protest sites). He attended the Constitutional Court hearing when he requested and did not seek to leave home thereafter. Special reinforcements were withdrawn on 16 March. The Constitutional Court dismissed his election challenge on 8 March.

Ter-Petrosyan alleged that the 1 March operation unlawfully dispersed a peaceful assembly in which he was participating as organizer and speaker, and that subsequent restrictions (including the emergency ban) violated his Article 11 right to freedom of assembly. He further claimed the house arrest interfered with that right and amounted to arbitrary detention, that no effective domestic remedy existed (Article 13), and that he was discriminated against as an opposition leader (Article 14). Domestic law cited included the Assemblies Act (allowing police termination of events posing real risks after warning) and the State Protection Act (imposing lifetime security on former presidents, including access-control measures at protected sites). Council of Europe and Human Rights Watch reports contemporaneously described the applicant’s situation as de facto house arrest. The European Court communicated the complaints concerning house arrest, assembly interference, lack of remedy, and discrimination.

The case of Ter-Petrosyan v. Armenia (Application no. 36469/08) before the European Court of Human Rights arose from events following Armenia’s 19 February 2008 presidential election. The applicant, Levon Ter-Petrosyan, a former president (1991–1998) and the main opposition candidate, alleged that the authorities violated his right to freedom of peaceful assembly (and related rights to liberty, an effective remedy, and non-discrimination). He claimed the police violently dispersed a protest he led and then placed him under de facto house arrest, preventing further participation in assemblies.

After preliminary results indicated victory for Prime Minister Serzh Sargsyan (approximately 52 percent of votes versus the applicant’s 21 percent), Ter-Petrosyan called supporters to Freedom Square in Yerevan to protest alleged electoral irregularities. From 20 February onward, daily rallies occurred there, drawing tens of thousands during the day and hundreds who camped overnight. The applicant addressed the crowds multiple times daily on political issues, urged continuation of the protests, and remained at the square almost continuously.

On 29 February he challenged the results before the Constitutional Court. Early on 1 March, police surrounded the encampment. According to the applicant, officers created panic by banging batons on shields, then—without warning or dispersal order—attacked sleeping protesters with rubber batons, destroyed the camp, and chased people from the square. State Protection Department (SPD) officers (responsible for the security of former presidents) surrounded Ter-Petrosyan on a platform, moved him to a bench, and later forced him into a vehicle to his home. There, special forces blocked roads, established checkpoints, searched all visitors and vehicles, and effectively confined him; he alleged this house arrest lasted until at least 20 March, interrupted only by a one-hour Constitutional Court appearance on 5 March.

The Government contested this account. They stated that police arrived around 7 a.m. on 1 March to investigate intelligence that weapons would be distributed to incite disorder. Demonstrators allegedly attacked officers with bats, rods, and stones. SPD officers then moved the applicant a short distance for his safety and later transported him home at his implicit consent. Additional security was posted because of city-wide violence, but he was never forbidden from leaving; he was merely warned that SPD could not guarantee his safety at an “unlawful demonstration.” He declined to leave without protection, received numerous visitors (journalists, diplomats), attended the Constitutional Court hearing when he wished, and made no further requests to depart until the state of emergency ended.

After the square was cleared, remaining protesters relocated near the French Embassy and were joined by thousands more. Clashes ensued, resulting in ten deaths (eight civilians), many injuries, and a 20-day state of emergency that banned further rallies. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s election challenge on 8 March. International observers, including Council of Europe bodies and Human Rights Watch, described the applicant’s situation as de facto house arrest.

The applicant argued that the unannounced, violent dispersal of a peaceful assembly and his subsequent confinement (justified by the authorities under the Act on Ensuring the Security of Persons Subject to Special State Protection) unlawfully interfered with his Article 11 rights, that no effective domestic remedy existed, and that the measures were discriminatory given his status as opposition leader. The Government maintained that the operation responded to an imminent threat of violence, that the applicant’s removal and security arrangements were lawful protective measures, and that he remained free to move. These contested facts formed the core of the alleged Convention violations communicated to the Government.

The case concerns events after Armenia’s 19 February 2008 presidential election. Applicant Levon Ter-Petrosyan, president from 1991-1998, was the main opposition candidate against Prime Minister Serzh Sargsyan (ruling-party ally of outgoing President Robert Kocharyan). After preliminary results, Ter-Petrosyan alleged electoral irregularities, called the vote neither free nor fair, and urged supporters to protest at Yerevan’s Freedom Square.

From 20 February, daily nationwide rallies occurred, centred on Freedom Square and its park. Daytime and nighttime gatherings drew tens of thousands; several hundred camped around the clock. As opposition leader and candidate, the applicant spoke two or three times daily on political issues and called for continued protests. He remained at the square almost continuously, leaving only briefly.

On 24 February the Central Election Commission announced Sargsyan the winner (approximately 52% of votes) and the applicant the runner-up (approximately 21%). On 29 February, after international observers had departed, the applicant challenged the results before the Constitutional Court, seeking annulment.

On 1 March 2008 at around 6-7 a.m. police arrived at Freedom Square. The applicant’s account states that he was asleep in his car; most campers were also asleep. Police encircled the few hundred remaining demonstrators, banged batons on shields, and—without warning or dispersal order—attacked with rubber batons, destroying the camp and chasing, beating and kicking people of all ages and genders. The applicant addressed the crowd from a platform, urging them to stay peaceful and keep distance. State Protection Department (SPD) officers (responsible for the former president’s lifelong security) then surrounded him, forced him to a bench, and, after he refused to leave voluntarily, placed him in a car and took him to his Yerevan home. There, special police, SPD and traffic units blocked roads, set up checkpoints, searched all visitors and vehicles, and prevented anyone from entering or leaving without superior approval. The applicant claimed this de-facto house arrest continued without interruption until at least 20 March (except a one-hour appearance at the Constitutional Court on 5 March after that court intervened).

The Government disputed these claims. It stated that police had information that weapons would be distributed to incite disorder. Officers arrived to verify this but were attacked with wooden bats, metal rods and stones. For the applicant’s safety amid erupting violence, SPD officers surrounded him on the platform and moved him a short distance; a journalist interviewed him freely. After he refused advice to go home, he entered an SPD car voluntarily and was driven to his house. Extra security was posted later that day as a general measure for all protected persons amid city-wide unrest that caused ten deaths (eight civilians) and prompted a 20-day state of emergency banning assemblies. Officers searched visitors but never prohibited entry or exit; the applicant was told he was free to leave but would not be accompanied to unsafe locations such as the French Embassy area. He expressed a wish to join demonstrators only once and declined to go unprotected. He attended the Constitutional Court hearing after requesting to do so, then asked to return home and made no further requests to leave. Reinforcements were withdrawn on 16 March.

The SPD publicly stated it had removed the applicant under the 2004 State Protection Act to ensure his safety and had warned him not to leave, as it could not protect him at an “unlawful” demonstration. The Constitutional Court, after the applicant’s representatives claimed he was detained, ordered the Prosecutor’s Office to clarify his status and facilitate attendance if he wished. The Prosecutor replied there was no deprivation of liberty or house-arrest concept under Armenian law and that attendance was the applicant’s own responsibility. On 8 March the Constitutional Court dismissed the election challenge.

International reports (Council of Europe Monitoring Committee, Commissioner for Human Rights, Human Rights Watch) described a violent, unannounced police dispersal and characterised the applicant’s subsequent confinement as de-facto house arrest. These events form the factual basis of the alleged violations of freedom of assembly, liberty, effective remedy and non-discrimination.
