The case of Tasev v. North Macedonia (Application no. 9825/13) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 16 May 2019 (final on 16 August 2019). The applicant, Slavčo Tasev, a judge at the Štip Court of Appeal born in 1959, alleged a violation of his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention. This stemmed from the authorities’ refusal to update his self-declared ethnicity (from Bulgarian to Macedonian) in the official electoral roll of judges. He also complained of unfairness in the related administrative proceedings.

On 21 September 2012, a vacancy notice was issued for five positions on the State Judicial Council (SJC), to be filled by sitting judges elected by their peers. Ethnicity was not listed as a formal requirement. Under the State Judicial Council Act, the SJC comprises 15 members, eight of whom are judges elected from among their peers (three of those from ethnic-minority communities). Candidates apply to specific lists: general lists drawn from judges in particular courts (including one for the Štip Court of Appeal’s jurisdiction) or a single list for ethnic-minority judges. All registered judges vote on the minority list. The Ministry of Justice maintains the electoral roll, which records personal details including ethnicity. After an election announcement, the roll is available for inspection, and judges have a short window to request rectification of their own entries.

On 28 September 2012 the applicant asked the Ministry to change his ethnicity entry from Bulgarian to Macedonian. The roll was published for inspection on 15 October 2012 without the change, prompting a second request that same day. On 18 October 2012 the Ministry refused, stating that the request had been made after the election announcement and was intended to secure an electoral advantage, which would disadvantage other judges. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court, arguing that no statute barred a change during an ongoing election, that ethnic self-identification was a personal right, and that the “disadvantage” finding was unsubstantiated.

On 26 October 2012 the Administrative Court upheld the refusal. It noted that the applicant had been recorded as Bulgarian in the 2006, 2008 and 2010 rolls and had previously exercised rights as such. The request was not a mere rectification of an obvious error (as contemplated by the General Administrative Procedure Act) but an attempt to obtain an electoral benefit after the announcement, placing other judges at a disadvantage. The applicant had not been given an opportunity to comment on the earlier rolls submitted by the Ministry.

The applicant’s further appeal to the Higher Administrative Court was dismissed on 5 November 2012. That court repeated that a post-announcement change would disadvantage other candidates and that the refusal did not restrict his right to assert ethnic identity, given the timing. Meanwhile, on 5 October 2012 the applicant had applied for an SJC seat on the general (Štip) list, affirming Macedonian ethnicity. On 3 December 2012 the SJC removed him from that list because his declared ethnicity did not match official records (Bulgarian since 1995) and because of the outcome of the rectification proceedings. The SJC noted it had no competence over roll entries.

Domestically, the Constitution treats free expression of national identity as a fundamental value. Internationally, Article 3 of the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities guarantees the right freely to choose to be treated (or not) as belonging to a national minority, without disadvantage. The Court notified the Government of the Article 8 complaint (ethnic identity forming part of private life) together with the fairness complaint concerning the administrative proceedings; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case of Tasev v. North Macedonia (Application no. 9825/13) originated in a 2013 application by Slavčo Tasev, a judge at the Štip Court of Appeal born in 1959. He alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life) arising from the authorities’ refusal to register his self-declared ethnicity (Macedonian rather than Bulgarian) in the electoral roll of judges. Notice was also given of a complaint concerning the alleged unfairness of the ensuing administrative proceedings.

In September 2012 a vacancy notice was published for five seats on the State Judicial Council (SJC) to be filled by sitting judges elected by their peers. Ethnicity was not among the stated eligibility criteria. On 28 September the applicant asked the Ministry of Justice to amend the electoral roll so that his ethnicity entry would read “Macedonian” instead of “Bulgarian.” When the roll was opened for inspection on 15 October and the change had not been made, he lodged a fresh request, relying on the rectification procedure in the State Judicial Council Act.

The Ministry rejected the request on 18 October. It held that the application had been submitted after the election announcement and was intended to secure an electoral advantage; granting it would place other judges at a disadvantage. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court, arguing that no statutory provision barred a change of ethnicity during an ongoing election, that ethnic self-identification was a personal right, and that the “disadvantage” reasoning was unsubstantiated. The Administrative Court upheld the Ministry on 26 October. It added that earlier rolls (2006, 2008 and 2010) had recorded the applicant as Bulgarian, that he had therefore already enjoyed the electoral rights attached to that status, and that the requested alteration was not a mere correction of an obvious error.

In a further appeal the applicant contested those findings as unreasonable and legally baseless, asserted that past declarations were irrelevant to his present right of self-identification, and complained that he had been given no opportunity to comment on the earlier rolls that the Ministry had produced. The Higher Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 5 November, repeating that a post-announcement change would disadvantage other candidates and that the refusal did not restrict the applicant’s freedom to assert his ethnic identity.

Meanwhile the applicant had put himself forward as a candidate on the general (non-minority) list, submitting a written statement that he was of Macedonian ethnicity. On 3 December the SJC struck his name from that list because the declaration did not correspond to official records that had listed him as Bulgarian since 1995 and because the rectification proceedings had already failed.

The Constitution proclaims the free expression of national identity as a fundamental value. The SJC Act requires that three of the eight judicial members of the Council belong to ethnic-minority communities and establishes separate candidate lists, one of which is reserved for minority judges. The electoral roll, administered by the Ministry of Justice, records each judge’s ethnicity; a short window for rectification exists after an election is announced. The Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities (Article 3) guarantees the right freely to choose whether to be treated as belonging to a national minority, provided the choice is not arbitrary and is linked to objective identity criteria, and that no disadvantage shall result from that choice.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference with the applicant’s private-life interest in ethnic self-identification and of the procedural complaints relating to the administrative courts’ handling of the evidence and the timing of the requests.

The case of Tasev v. North Macedonia (Application no. 9825/13) originated in an application lodged on 30 January 2013 by Slavčo Tasev, a judge at the Štip Court of Appeal born in 1959. He alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life) arising from the authorities’ refusal to register his self-declared ethnicity in the electoral roll of judges. He also complained of unfairness in the related administrative proceedings.

On 21 September 2012 a vacancy notice was issued for five posts on the State Judicial Council (SJC) to be filled by sitting judges elected by their peers. Ethnicity was not listed as a requirement. On 28 September the applicant asked the Ministry of Justice to change his recorded ethnicity from Bulgarian to Macedonian. When the electoral roll was opened for inspection on 15 October and the change had not been made, he submitted a further request under section 17 of the State Judicial Council Act.

By decision of 18 October 2012 the Ministry refused the request. It held that the application had been lodged after the election announcement and was intended solely to secure an electoral right, thereby placing other judges at a disadvantage. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court, arguing that no statutory provision barred a change of ethnicity during an ongoing election, that the determination of ethnicity was a personal right, and that the Ministry’s reasoning was unsubstantiated.

The Ministry produced extracts from the 2006, 2008 and 2010 electoral rolls, all of which recorded the applicant as Bulgarian. On 26 October the Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It characterised the request as an attempt to obtain an electoral advantage rather than a rectification of an obvious error, noted that the applicant had previously enjoyed rights as a person of Bulgarian ethnicity, and concluded that there had been no interference with his right to declare his identity.

The applicant appealed to the Higher Administrative Court. He maintained that the alleged disadvantage to other judges lacked any legal basis, that the timing of his request was irrelevant, that earlier declarations of ethnicity were immaterial, and that he had been denied an opportunity to comment on the historic rolls. On 5 November 2012 the Higher Administrative Court upheld the lower court’s decision, repeating that a change sought after the announcement would disadvantage other candidates and that the refusal did not restrict the applicant’s right to assert his ethnic identity.

Meanwhile, on 5 October 2012 the applicant had submitted his candidacy for the SJC, attaching a written statement that he was of Macedonian ethnicity and applying for inclusion on the general list of judges from the Štip Court of Appeal. By letter of 3 December 2012 the SJC struck his name from that list because his declared ethnicity did not correspond with official records (which had listed him as Bulgarian since 1995) and because the rectification proceedings had already been concluded unfavourably.

The relevant domestic law includes Article 8 of the Constitution (free expression of national identity as a fundamental value), the State Judicial Council Act (composition of the SJC, reserved seats for ethnic-minority judges, administration of the electoral roll by the Ministry of Justice, and a short time-limit for seeking rectification after an election announcement), and the General Administrative Procedure Act (rectification of obvious errors). The Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities, Article 3, guarantees the right freely to choose whether or not to be treated as belonging to a national minority, subject to objective criteria and without disadvantage resulting from that choice.

These facts form the core of the complaints concerning both the refusal to register the applicant’s self-identified ethnicity and the fairness of the administrative process that led to that refusal.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Elvira Dmitriyeva v. Russia (applications nos. 60921/17 and 7202/18) arose from two applications lodged by a Russian national living in Kazan. The applicant alleged violations of her rights to freedom of expression and assembly, the absence of an effective domestic remedy, her unlawful arrest, and the lack of a prosecuting party in the administrative-offence proceedings brought against her.

The events followed a 2 March 2017 YouTube documentary by Aleksey Navalnyy alleging corruption by Prime Minister Medvedev and calling for nationwide protests on 26 March 2017. On 14 March 2017 the applicant notified the Kazan Town Administration of her plan to hold a meeting that day from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., expecting 150 participants, to protest corruption and demand Medvedev’s resignation. She proposed three sites, including a specially designated public-event area in Krylya Sovetov Park. The administration refused approval on 16 March, citing unspecified other events at the same locations and times. The applicant immediately challenged the refusal in the Vakhitovskiy District Court.

On 17 March she submitted a further notification for a “picket” at four alternative sites. This was also refused on 21 March, although an alternative venue was offered and accepted by the applicant. On 23 March she posted a message on the social-network site VKontakte criticising the 16 March refusal as unlawful (because no alternative locations or times had been proposed and because the park was a designated site large enough for simultaneous events), noting that judicial review was pending, and announcing that a meeting would nevertheless take place at 2 p.m. on 26 March in Krylya Sovetov Park.

On 24 March the District Court found the administration’s failure to propose reasoned alternatives unlawful. The same day the police formally warned the applicant that she would be held liable if she proceeded at any unapproved location. On 26 March she held the meeting in the park (attended, according to varying estimates, by 400–1,500 people and lasting approximately 80 minutes). A police officer ordered her to stop the event; she refused, citing the court ruling. No further police action was taken until after the meeting ended.

At about 4.20 p.m., while returning home, the applicant was arrested and taken to a police station. Reports were drawn up charging her with organising an unauthorised public event (Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences) and disobeying a lawful police order (Article 19.3). She was released at 8.35 p.m. The following day the Aviastroitelnyy District Court convicted her of both offences, imposing a 1,000-rouble fine and 20 hours of community work. Her appeal, which argued that the 24 March court decision rendered the meeting authorised and the police order unlawful, was dismissed by the Supreme Court of the Tatarstan Republic on 17 May 2017. That court held that the judicial finding of administrative unlawfulness did not convert the event into an authorised one and that the police order had been lawful.

On 12 July 2017 the same District Court convicted the applicant of a further offence under Article 20.2 § 1 (campaigning for an event before it had been approved), fining her 10,000 roubles. The conviction, based on the 23 March VKontakte post, was upheld on appeal on 9 August 2017. A subsequent civil claim for non-pecuniary damage arising from the administration’s original failure to propose alternatives was dismissed on the ground that she had not proved such damage and that an alternative venue had later been offered.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the refusals, warnings, arrest, and successive convictions interfered with her rights of expression and peaceful assembly, that no effective remedy existed, that the arrest itself was unlawful, and that the administrative proceedings lacked a prosecuting party.

**Case Summary: Elvira Dmitriyeva v. Russia (ECHR, Apps. nos. 60921/17 and 7202/18)**

Elvira Dmitriyeva, a Russian national living in Kazan, lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights complaining of violations of her rights to freedom of expression and assembly (Articles 10 and 11), lack of an effective remedy (Article 13), unlawful arrest (Article 5), and procedural defects in administrative-offence proceedings (Article 6, including the absence of a prosecuting party).

The case arose from nationwide anti-corruption protests called by Alexey Navalny for 26 March 2017 after he published a documentary alleging corruption by Prime Minister Medvedev. Many local authorities refused notifications for assemblies. Dmitriyeva notified the Kazan Town Administration on 14 March 2017 of her plan to hold a meeting (expected attendance 150) from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. on 26 March at one of three proposed sites, including a designated public-event location in Krylya Sovetov Park, to protest corruption and demand Medvedev’s resignation. The administration refused on 16 March, citing unspecified other events at the sites. She challenged the refusal in court.

On 17 March she and another person notified a “picket” at four alternative sites. The administration refused on 21 March (again citing other events) and proposed a different venue, which she accepted on 22 March. On 23 March she posted on VKontakte criticizing the 16 March refusal as unlawful (no alternatives offered; the park was a designated site with space for multiple events) and announcing a meeting at the park at 2 p.m. on 26 March, inviting others to attend. On 24 March the Vakhitovskiy District Court partly upheld her challenge, finding the administration had failed to propose reasoned alternatives despite prior notifications by the United Russia party occupying the sites; this failure was unlawful. The same day police warned her of liability if she held an event at unapproved locations.

On 26 March Dmitriyeva held the meeting at the park (lasting about 80 minutes; attendance estimates ranged from 400 to 1,500). Police ordered her to stop the event as unauthorized; she refused, citing the court decision. No further police action occurred during the event. She was arrested around 4:20 p.m. while walking home, taken to a police station “for examination” of administrative offences, and held until 8:35 p.m. Reports charged her under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (organizing an unauthorized public event, including via the VKontakte post) and Article 19.3 (disobeying a lawful police order).

On 27 March the Aviastroitelnyy District Court convicted her on both counts, imposing a 1,000-rouble fine and 20 hours’ community work. It held she had organized an unapproved event and disobeyed police despite the warning and alternative venue; it did not address her argument that the 24 March court ruling (immediately enforceable) rendered the meeting authorized. The Tatarstan Supreme Court upheld the convictions on 17 May 2017, ruling that the judicial finding of administrative failure did not authorize the event or excuse non-compliance with the Public Events Act; the police order was lawful to maintain order; and her campaigning indicated a different aim.

On 12 July 2017 she was separately convicted under Article 20.2 § 1 for campaigning (via the 23 March post) before approval, fined 10,000 roubles. This was upheld on 9 August 2017, as the Public Events Act prohibited such campaigning. A later civil claim for non-pecuniary damage from the administration’s failure was dismissed for lack of proof of harm.

These facts formed the basis of her complaints that the refusals, convictions, arrest, and lack of effective review interfered with peaceful assembly and expression without adequate justification or remedies, and that the administrative proceedings were unfair. The Court notified the Government of these complaints (declaring the remainder inadmissible). The judgment later found violations of Articles 5, 6, 10, 11 and 13.

The case of Elvira Dmitriyeva v. Russia arose from anti-corruption protests called by Aleksey Navalnyy after his 2 March 2017 documentary accusing Prime Minister Medvedev of corruption. On 14 March 2017, the applicant notified Kazan’s town administration of a planned meeting on 26 March (11 a.m.–4 p.m., ~150 attendees) against corruption and for Medvedev’s resignation, proposing three sites including the designated Krylya Sovetov Park. The administration refused on 16 March, citing unspecified other events at those sites. She challenged the refusal in court.

This too was refused on 21 March (other events cited), though an alternative venue was proposed; she accepted it on 22 March. On 23 March she posted on VKontakte criticizing the 16 March refusal as unlawful (no alternatives offered; park was designated and large enough for multiple events; court challenge pending) and announcing the meeting would proceed at 2 p.m. in the park, inviting others to join.

On 24 March the Vakhitovskiy District Court partly allowed her challenge, finding the administration had received an earlier notification from United Russia for events at all her proposed sites (and two others) that day, so it was required to offer reasoned alternative locations or times—which it had not. The same day police warned her of liability if she held an event at any unapproved location from her notifications.

On 26 March she held the meeting in the park (~400–1,500 attendees, lasting ~80 minutes). On 27 March the Aviastroitelnyy District Court convicted her of both offences (fine of 1,000 RUB plus 20 hours’ community work), holding the event unauthorized and the order lawful. It ignored her argument that the 24 March ruling (immediately enforceable) rendered the meeting authorized and the order unlawful. On 17 May the Tatarstan Supreme Court upheld the convictions, ruling that the judicial finding of administrative inaction did not approve the location/time or waive statutory procedures; the event thus remained unauthorized. Police had acted lawfully to protect public order. It also found the notified aim differed from the “real” aim as promoted.

Her later civil claim for non-pecuniary damage from the administration’s unlawful failure to propose alternatives was dismissed (no proven harm; an alternative had later been offered for the picket).

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of interference with freedoms of expression and assembly (refusals, warnings, convictions for holding/campaigning for the event), lack of an effective remedy, unlawful arrest/detention, and procedural defects (no prosecuting party) in the administrative proceedings.

The case of Kaynar and Others v. Turkey (applications nos. 21104/06, 51103/06 and 18809/07) concerns three Turkish nationals who purchased unregistered land classified as a “category-3 natural site” on Gökçeada island in 1993 and 1995. In 1996, during a cadastral review, the land was registered in the Treasury’s name. The applicants applied that year to the Gökçeada Land Tribunal, seeking registration in their names on the basis of purchase and adverse possession under Turkish civil law (continuous, peaceful possession as de facto owners for over 20 years, with the possibility of combining periods with predecessors).

Expert reports (1997 and 1999) established that the land had been used as farmland, later left fallow for cattle grazing without being abandoned, with unchanged boundaries and no cultural or natural assets requiring special protection. Local witnesses confirmed that predecessors had possessed the plots as de facto owners since at least 1945 (or earlier), transferring them to the applicants, who continued using them. Cumulative possession exceeded 45 years.

On 7 October 1999, after site visits, witness hearings, and expert evidence, the Tribunal granted the claims. It found the land was not grazing pasture ineligible for adverse possession, that possession had been peaceful and continuous, and that its natural-site classification did not bar acquisition given the absence of protected assets. It ordered registration in the applicants’ names.

The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on 12 October 2001, requiring further inquiry into whether the land was used for grazing and whether the applicants had abandoned it. Additional evidence (witnesses, experts, maps) reaffirmed the original findings: the land was not pasture, and the applicants had not abandoned it.

Meanwhile, on 27 July 2004 (effective around mid-July), section 11 of the Cultural and Natural Heritage (Protection) Act (Law no. 2863) was amended. Previously, only “cultural and natural assets the protection of which is necessary” and their surrounding protected areas were ineligible for adverse possession. The amendment extended this bar to all “natural sites,” including category-3 sites like the applicants’ land. (A 2007 amendment later reversed this for category-3 sites.)

On 9 June 2005, the Tribunal rejected the applicants’ claims and ordered registration in the Treasury’s name. It applied the 2004 amendment retrospectively, holding that public-policy considerations overrode the principle of non-retroactivity of legislation, consistent with Court of Cassation case-law that ownership by adverse possession arises only upon a final court decision (not merely when conditions are met). The Court of Cassation upheld this on 31 October 2005 and dismissed a rectification request on 6 June 2006 (notified around 26 June 2006).

The applicants alleged that the legislative change, applied mid-proceedings to defeat their near-complete adverse-possession claims (supported by extensive evidence and an initial favourable judgment), constituted an unjustified interference with their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Two applicants further complained under Article 6 of the Convention of the excessive length of proceedings (approximately 10 years from 1996 to 2006, involving multiple Tribunal hearings, expert reports, and Cassation reviews) and insufficient reasoning in the domestic decisions.

These facts highlight a situation in which applicants had a strong claim to title based on long-standing possession and purchase, only for a statutory amendment—enacted after they had obtained a first-instance victory and while proceedings remained pending—to be applied retroactively, transferring the land to the State without compensation. The timing of the 2004 amendment, the public-policy justification for retrospectivity, the subsequent 2007 reversal, and the overall duration of the cadastral litigation form the core factual matrix for the alleged violations.

The case of Kanciał v. Poland (Application no. 37023/13) concerns allegations of ill-treatment by police and an ineffective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Polish national born in 1985, was arrested on 16 June 2011 during an investigation into the kidnapping of J.R. the previous day, which involved a €1 million ransom demand. Phone records linked the applicant (among others, including friends and employees of the victim’s family) as a possible suspect. The Gdańsk Appellate Prosecutor ordered the arrests; the applicant was detained from 16 to 18 June 2011 by an anti-terrorist police squad of eight officers (equipped with rifles, helmets, balaclavas and vests) assisted by seven Central Bureau of Investigation officers. They forced entry into a friend’s flat in Tczew using a stun grenade. The actual kidnappers were later arrested, and proceedings against the applicant were discontinued in April 2012 as the evidence available at the time of arrest had justified it.

On admission to detention, police recorded bruising to the applicant’s left cheek and abrasions on his arms and back. Medical examinations on 17 June 2011 at a hospital and a Ministry of Internal Affairs health centre documented tenderness of the left temple, significant swelling and bruising of the left face (including the eye socket), tenderness and minor swelling of the right wrist/arm, and a diagnosis of facial and wrist bruising. No fractures were found. The applicant complained of injuries to his head, face and right arm sustained during arrest.

On 27 June 2011 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint alleging abuse of power. He claimed that masked, armed officers stormed the flat; he and others complied with orders to lie on the floor; he was kicked in the face, hit on the head, back and legs, and an electrical discharge weapon (EDW/Taser) was applied to his back, buttocks, genitals and ears; his face was pressed into a pool of another arrestee’s blood; he was suffocated while being taken to a car (where the EDW was used continuously); and at the station he was made to kneel facing a wall while being questioned about the ransom. He alleged resulting bruises, sprained thumbs and EDW burns. Photographs and medical records were attached. Other arrestees (his girlfriend, Ł.W. and D.W.) gave consistent accounts of violence, including an officer hitting Ł.W. with a rifle, kicks to the applicant, EDW use, blood on the floor, and visible injuries (swollen face, black eye, scabs) afterwards. They stated no resistance had been offered.

A 2012 forensic opinion, based on medical records and photographs, confirmed the documented injuries plus bruising to the left arm, torso and abdomen, and knee abrasions. Bruising was consistent with blunt impact or a fall (possibly kicks, though military boots would more likely have caused abrasions); wrist abrasions with handcuffs; and angular back abrasions with EDW use. Health impairment lasted no more than seven days.

Police officers testified that the special squad was used due to the kidnapping’s brutality and possible weapons. Officer R. (who arrested the applicant) sat on him as he lay with hands under his body; the applicant refused orders to raise his arms for handcuffing and tried to dislodge the officer. Fearing a firearm, R. applied the EDW to the applicant’s back (possibly multiple short discharges to different areas) to overcome resistance while another officer handcuffed him. Officers denied other force and stated only justified measures were used. The prosecutor noted a technical error prevented review of some CCTV footage.

On 26 July 2012 the Bydgoszcz Regional Prosecutor discontinued the investigation for insufficient evidence of an offence under Article 231 of the Criminal Code. Officers had given detailed, consistent accounts of justified coercive measures under the Police Act 1990 (s. 16) and 1990 Ordinance (physical force and EDW permitted after non-compliance or without warning if delay risked danger; EDW for overcoming active resistance or effecting arrest of a suspect, with care due to health risks). The confined space, stun grenade and need for swift action could explain unintended injuries. The applicant had not objected in the arrest record, and a court had later upheld the arrest’s lawfulness. Conflicting versions existed, but medical evidence did not prove officers caused the injuries; in dubio pro reo applied.

The Gdańsk-Północ District Court upheld this on 18 March 2013, finding the evidence assessment correct, no need for further inquiries, and no unequivocal proof of abuse. Actions were conditioned by the need for effective arrest in a kidnapping case.

Domestic law required coercive measures to be necessary, proportionate and the least harmful. Council of Europe materials (CPT 2010 General Report and 2017 Poland visit report) stressed that EDWs must be strictly limited to situations of real/immediate threat to life or serious injury, not mere non-compliance; contact/drive-stun mode is particularly problematic; use requires detailed reporting, recording devices, debriefing and independent monitoring.

The case of Kanciał v. Poland (Application no. 37023/13) concerns alleged ill-treatment of the applicant, Maciej Kanciał, by Polish police during his arrest and detention on 16-18 June 2011, as well as the authorities’ subsequent investigation, claimed to breach Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant was arrested as a suspect in a kidnapping investigation opened on 9 June 2011 by the Gdańsk Appellate Prosecutor and delegated to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). Phone records linked him to the case; a prosecutor ordered his arrest on 16 June. Anti-terrorist squad officers (eight, armed, masked, with helmets and vests), assisted by seven CBI officers, stormed a small flat in Tczew at 7.40 p.m. after forcing the door and deploying a stun grenade. Five people were present, including the applicant, his girlfriend and two others (later arrested only for drugs). The applicant was taken to CBI headquarters then a Gdynia detention facility.

Police records noted bruising to the applicant’s left cheek and abrasions on his arms and back upon admission. Medical examinations on 17 June (hospital and Ministry health centre) documented tenderness of the left temple, significant swelling and bruising of the left face (including eye socket), tenderness/swelling of the right wrist/arm, and a diagnosis of facial and wrist bruising. No fractures were found. He was released on 18 June. A 2012 forensic opinion, based on records, certificates and photographs, confirmed these plus bruising to the left arm, torso and abdomen, and abrasions on wrists, knees and back (the latter angular marks consistent with an electrical discharge weapon, or EDW/Taser). Injuries were deemed to have impaired health for under seven days; bruising could stem from blunt force or kicks (though military boots might typically cause more severe wounds), wrist marks from handcuffs, and arm marks from restraint.

The applicant complained on 27 June 2011 of ill-treatment, attaching medical evidence and photos. He described officers kicking him in the face, striking his head, back and legs, handcuffing him, then applying an EDW to his back, buttocks, genitals and ears; pressing his face into blood from another arrestee (Ł.W., allegedly rifle-butted); and continuing EDW use in a police car until he suffocated. At a station he was forced to kneel facing a wall for 30 minutes, questioned about ransom money, and made to sign an unread document. Co-arrestees largely corroborated storming, a stun grenade, screams, blood, kicks/hits, and EDW use on the applicant; his girlfriend later observed his swollen face, black eye and EDW scabs.

Police evidence (from officer R., who arrested the applicant, and others) stated the applicant lay with hands under his body, resisted handcuffing by trying to dislodge the officer sitting on him, and posed a possible firearm risk, justifying EDW discharges (a few seconds each, aimed at the back only) to overcome resistance. Officers denied kicks, rifle strikes or other force, attributing any injuries to the chaotic, confined operation (at least eight people in one room) and stun grenade. The Bydgoszcz prosecutor opened an abuse-of-power investigation (Criminal Code Article 231) but discontinued it on 26 July 2012 for insufficient evidence of an offence. Officers’ accounts were consistent and measures deemed procedurally justified (including EDW per Ordinance rules for overcoming resistance during arrest of a kidnapping suspect). Unintended injuries from the grenade or rapid action could not be excluded; the applicant recorded no objections at the time, and a court later upheld the arrest as lawful. Conflicting versions and medical evidence did not prove criminality (in dubio pro reo). The Gdańsk-Północ District Court confirmed this on 18 March 2013.

Domestic law (Police Act s.16 and 1990 Ordinance) permitted coercive measures, including EDW, only if necessary, proportionate, after a warning (unless delay endangered life/health/property), causing minimal harm, and discontinued upon compliance. EDW use required danger to life/health/property or ineffectiveness of other means, with care due to its risks; striking was generally forbidden except in self-defence. CPT materials (2010 General Report and 2017 Poland visit) criticised broad EDW use, especially contact mode or for mere non-compliance rather than imminent serious threat, urging recording devices, detailed reports, debriefings and investigations of misuse. Poland’s Ombudsman later echoed concerns over EDW reporting. The kidnapping probe against the applicant was discontinued in April 2012 for lack of evidence.

The case of Zammit and Vassallo v. Malta concerns seven Maltese applicants who inherited a property at 8, Flat 1, Old Prison Street, Senglea. The property had been granted to third parties under a temporary emphyteusis expiring in 1990 at an annual ground rent of MTL 40 (approximately EUR 98).

On 1 September 1986 the Government issued a requisition order. It derequisitioned the property in October 1988 and returned the keys. On 15 April 1989 the Commissioner of Land occupied the site. Between March and September 1989 the property was demolished as part of a slum-clearance project to enable social-housing development. The applicants learned of the demolition in spring or summer 1989. A presidential declaration of 27 October 1989 then formally took the already-demolished property under a title of possession and use. A further declaration of 4 October 1991 converted that title into public tenure, a perpetual interest carrying an unalterable recognition rent.

In March 1999 the Commissioner offered a recognition rent of MTL 15.62 (approximately EUR 36.39) per year, far below the previous ground rent and based solely on internal Land Valuation Office policies. The owners refused. In May 2000 the Commissioner commenced proceedings before the Land Arbitration Board (LAB) seeking transfer of the property and assessment of compensation. Expert evidence placed the 1986 capital value at MTL 1,000 (approximately EUR 2,320). An applicants’ architect later valued the (demolished) apartment at a 2005 rental of EUR 229.64 per year and a sale price of EUR 17,470; LAB experts in 2011 assessed rental value at EUR 158.40 and capital value at EUR 10,575.

On 7 March 2012 the LAB acknowledged that demolition had preceded any formal taking and considered outright purchase the appropriate route, yet it fixed the recognition rent at EUR 158.40 per year pursuant to the public-tenure provisions of the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance.

The applicants instituted constitutional proceedings in April 2012, alleging that the demolition constituted an illegal de facto expropriation contrary to the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that the relevant statutory provisions were incompatible with those instruments, and that they were entitled to damages and other redress. The first-instance constitutional court (partial judgment of 12 February 2014) found a violation on the ground that the unalterable recognition rent was disproportionately low. In its final judgment of 27 May 2015 it awarded EUR 15,000 non-pecuniary damage, noting that no compensation had ever been paid, that the applicants would never recover the property, and that the rent would never increase.

On appeal the Constitutional Court (18 February 2016) held that the demolition had occurred while the State had no title and was therefore unlawful; even if the property had still been held under possession and use, demolition would have exceeded the limited rights attaching to that title. The subsequent conversion to public tenure, however, regularised the situation and pursued the legitimate aims of slum clearance and social housing. On 2 September 2010, the Senate's Director General confirmed receipt of the resignation and provided details on her severance payment.

She argued that significant pressure and threats of complaints damaging her non-political career during the 31 August meeting vitiated her consent under Article 1109 of the Civil Code, rendering the resignation null and void. She accused P. of using his presidential powers to advance party interests at W.'s instruction. A follow-up letter on 14 September reiterated the coercion claim (psychological duress) and noted an erroneous agenda reference to her resignation for the 12 October plenary session. The Senate acknowledged the letters on 16 September, stating that no reply to the first letter implied no agreement and that the plenary Senate would decide when examining her successor's credentials.

Senate legal department opinions (15 and 21 September) held that the resignation took effect immediately upon delivery, without needing plenary approval, and was irrevocable. The Senate alone would assess validity (tacitly or otherwise) when ratifying a successor, as Article 48 of the Constitution gave it exclusive power over members' credentials. Courts might later award compensation but could not dictate seating.

The case of Bileski v. North Macedonia (Application no. 78392/14) concerns a former trial court judge, Dragi Bileski (born 1951), who alleged that lustration proceedings against him were unfair, violated his Article 8 rights to private life and reputation, and lacked an effective remedy. In February 2010, under the 2008 Lustration Act, he submitted a required statement denying any post-1944 collaboration with State security bodies. The Lustration Commission confirmed in September 2011 that he met the conditions to serve as a judge.

In November 2012, the Commission reopened the case at its chairman's request, citing “new facts and evidence” from three security files (one involving a third party, Z.T.). These unsigned notes, dating to the 1970s when the applicant was a law student, described him as an “operational liaison” who met a handler, expressed willingness to collaborate, and provided information about individuals of interest. The Commission, applying the replacement 2012 Lustration Act, found that he had collaborated as a secret informant/operational liaison in a conscious, secret, organised and continuous manner, in return for career favours, thereby violating others’ rights and freedoms on political or ideological grounds. It published the decision and redacted notes on its website. The applicant obtained only redacted copies (withholding handler and third-party identities) and was denied unredacted originals.

He submitted a November 2012 notarised statement from handler P.K., who said he had drafted the notes without the applicant’s knowledge or request, based on spontaneous conversations and his own interpretation; the applicant had never been registered as a collaborator, informant or liaison, and the records were untruthful and did not reflect organised collaboration. The Intelligence Service later confirmed that the applicant was unregistered in its records and that the documents did not originate from its archives.

In November 2012 the applicant challenged the Commission’s decision before the Administrative Court, complaining of the absence of an oral hearing, insufficient reasoning (especially as to the statutory criteria of conscious/organised/continuous collaboration and any quid pro quo), the unreliability and inauthenticity of the unsigned copy documents lacking stamps, and the lack of evidence that anyone’s rights had actually been violated. He requested a public hearing to examine P.K. and an expert (a former intelligence officer) on the documents’ reliability and the legal distinction between an informant and a collaborator.

In December 2013 the Administrative Court dismissed the claim after a private hearing held in the parties’ absence. It treated the documents as truthful after comparing copies with originals, confirmed collaboration as an operational liaison that had violated others’ rights irrespective of prosecution, rejected P.K.’s statement, and held that written material sufficed so no oral evidence was needed.

The applicant appealed, reiterating the same points and again seeking an oral hearing. In June 2014 the Higher Administrative Court, likewise sitting privately without the parties or proposed witnesses, dismissed the appeal after verifying that the copies matched State Archives originals. It treated handler reports as established facts and confirmed that the applicant’s conduct had violated others’ human rights.

As a result, the State Judicial Council terminated his judicial office in July 2014. In 2015 the applicant submitted audio recordings (later made public by the opposition) of conversations between the Commission chairman and a ruling-party MP discussing the material supplied by Z.T. and urging expedition of the case.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the reopening and publication of the lustration finding, exclusive reliance on contested documentary material, denial of any oral hearing or opportunity to examine witnesses, and the consequent loss of judicial office.

North Macedonia (Application no. 78392/14) concerns complaints by Dragi Bileski, a serving trial-court judge, about the fairness of domestic lustration proceedings that found him to have collaborated with communist-era security services. Those proceedings led to the termination of his judicial office and were alleged to have violated his rights under Article 8 of the Convention (respect for private and professional life) as well as the right to an effective remedy.

In February 2010 the applicant filed the statutory declaration required of public officials under the 2008 Lustration Act, denying any post-1944 collaboration. The Lustration Commission accepted the declaration and, by decision of 12 September 2011, confirmed that he satisfied the additional condition for holding judicial office.

On 16 November 2012 the same Commission, acting on a request from its chairman that cited information supplied by a third party (Z.T.), reopened the case. It relied on three internal security-service files from the 1970s in which the applicant, then a law student, was described as an “operational liaison.” Extracts recorded two meetings at which he had expressed a wish to cooperate and later conversations in which he had passed on information about named individuals. On that basis the Commission, now applying the 2012 Lustration Act, concluded that the applicant had collaborated “in a conscious, secret, organised and continuous manner” as a secret informant or operational liaison, thereby violating others’ rights on political or ideological grounds. The decision and the supporting notes were published on the Commission’s website. The applicant obtained only redacted copies that concealed the identities of handlers and of the persons about whom he was said to have informed.

A former handler, P.K., subsequently swore an affidavit stating that the notes had been drafted without the applicant’s knowledge or consent, that the applicant had never been registered as a collaborator, and that the contents were not truthful. The applicant lodged an administrative-court challenge, complaining of the absence of an oral hearing, insufficient reasoning on the statutory criteria of collaboration, and the unreliability and lack of authenticity of the unsigned copy documents. He asked the court to hear P.K. and an expert on intelligence practices and submitted a letter from the Intelligence Service confirming that he did not appear in its records and that the documents did not originate from its archives.

The Administrative Court sat in private, without the parties, and dismissed the claim on 20 December 2013. It treated the security-service notes as truthful after comparing copies with originals and rejected P.K.’s affidavit. The Higher Administrative Court likewise sat in private, refused to hear the proposed witnesses, and on 12 June 2014 upheld the finding that the applicant’s conduct had violated others’ rights. Shortly afterwards the State Judicial Council terminated his judgeship.

In 2015 the applicant produced audio recordings, later made public by the political opposition, of conversations between the Commission’s chairman and a ruling-party parliamentarian discussing the material supplied by Z.T. and urging expedition of the case.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the lustration process had been procedurally unfair, that the published findings had damaged his reputation and ended his career, and that no effective domestic remedy had been available.

**CASE OF YAM v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (Application no. 31295/11)**

Mr Wang Yam, a UK national, was charged in connection with the May 2006 murder of Mr A.C., whose body was found on 14 June 2006 after suspicious bank activity. The victim had reported post theft from his home. A postman later described being approached in mid-May by a man claiming to be the victim’s nephew; the postman’s later identification of the applicant was qualified and recorded as less than positive. Extensive identity and bank-account misuse occurred between mid-May and mid-June, facilitated by the stolen post.

The applicant faced counts of murder, burglary, theft, handling stolen goods and two frauds. The prosecution alleged he acted alone: he stole the post, committed the frauds and killed the victim upon unexpected encounter at the house. Evidence showed the applicant’s involvement in using the victim’s cheques and credit card and attempting to handle a post-death electricity bill (suggested as a delay tactic). The murder case was purely circumstantial. The applicant admitted certain cheque and card transactions but claimed he obtained the items from named “gangsters” while gathering evidence to report them; he denied all other fraud, any meeting with the victim or the murder.

Before trial the prosecution applied for part of the defence to be heard in camera. After a mixed open/private hearing at which the applicant’s counsel cross-examined supporting witnesses, the trial judge (15 January 2008) ordered that the applicant’s explanation for the admitted acts be heard in camera, citing national security and witness-protection interests. He held that the inherent power to sit in camera existed where justice required it, but only if the trial remained fair; public attendance would create serious risks that might lead the prosecution to drop the case. The Court of Appeal upheld the order (open and closed judgments).

The first trial (January–April 2008) ultimately heard all of the applicant’s evidence in camera because he could not separate sensitive from non-sensitive parts. Four prosecution rebuttal witnesses were also heard in camera. The applicant and counsel were present throughout; counsel’s speeches on non-sensitive matters remained public. The jury convicted on the two specific frauds, hung on murder/burglary/theft, and (erroneously) convicted on handling stolen goods.

A retrial (October 2008–January 2009) followed. An abuse-of-process argument based on the handling conviction was rejected. The applicant was convicted of murder and burglary and sentenced to life with a 20-year minimum term. Appeals in 2010 and (after a CCRC reference and fresh evidence of other local mail thefts) 2017 were dismissed; the Court of Appeal found the “unique connection” between the applicant’s fraudulent activities and the murder compelling and the new evidence incapable of disturbing it.

Meanwhile the applicant sought variation of the 2008 in-camera order so that the closed material could be placed before the European Court. The trial judge, High Court and Supreme Court all refused, citing continuing national-security interests confirmed by a Public Interest Immunity certificate (with closed schedule). They held that the Strasbourg Court could decide the Article 6 complaint without the material and that independent domestic scrutiny had already occurred.

A postman’s qualified identification was also adduced. After a mixed open/closed hearing at which defence counsel cross-examined supporting witnesses, the trial judge granted the order on 15 January 2008, citing national-security and witness-protection risks; he stressed that the prosecution might otherwise drop the case and that a fair trial remained possible. The Court of Appeal upheld the order. In the event the applicant’s entire evidence (and four rebuttal witnesses) was heard in camera because he could not keep sensitive and non-sensitive material distinct. He and his lawyers were present throughout; other prosecution evidence and counsel’s speeches on non-sensitive parts remained public. The first jury convicted on the specific frauds and (erroneously) handling stolen goods but hung on murder, burglary and theft. The courts held that the handling conviction did not render the retrial an abuse, that the in-camera restriction had not deprived the applicant of a fair hearing (most of the trial was public, the gangsters were named in open court, additional witnesses were speculative and character evidence had been fully deployed), that the postman’s evidence had been properly directed and that the circumstantial web uniquely linking the applicant to both the frauds and the murder was overwhelming.

The applicant later sought variation of the in-camera order so that the closed material could be placed before the Strasbourg Court. The trial judge, High Court and Supreme Court refused, relying on a continuing public-interest-immunity certificate and independent judicial scrutiny; they considered that the Convention organs would take account of that scrutiny and that disclosure was not essential to determine the Article 6 complaint. The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) that the closed proceedings had rendered his trial unfair (publicity might have produced exculpatory witnesses; closed evidence acquired extra weight) and under Article 34 that non-disclosure hindered his application.

The case of Yam v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 31295/11) concerns an applicant's complaints under Article 6 of the Convention that his murder trial was unfair due to parts being held in camera, and under Article 34 that non-disclosure of in camera material hindered his right of application.

Police discovered the body of Mr A.C. on 14 June 2006, murdered around 8 May. Ongoing post theft from his home had enabled identity and bank account misuse. The prosecution case was circumstantial: the applicant alone stole the post, committed the frauds and killed the victim upon unexpected encounter. Evidence included his use of the victim's cheques, credit card and accounts (some admitted), CCTV footage, an attempt to delay discovery of the body via an electricity bill, and a qualified postman identification.

After a mixed open/private hearing at which the applicant's counsel cross-examined prosecution witnesses, the trial judge on 15 January 2008 ordered that the applicant's explanation for the admitted acts be heard in camera. He held that public hearings risked the prosecution dropping the case, but in camera proceedings would permit a fair trial. The Court of Appeal upheld the order.

At the January–April 2008 trial, all of the applicant's evidence (and that of four rebuttal prosecution witnesses) was heard in camera because he could not separate sensitive from non-sensitive matters. The jury convicted on two fraud counts, hung on murder/burglary/theft and (erroneously) convicted on handling stolen goods.

The 2010 Court of Appeal appeal (and a 2017 appeal after CCRC referral of new evidence suggesting alternative perpetrators) was dismissed. In 2013 the applicant applied to vary the in camera order to allow submission of the material to the European Court. Supported by a Public Interest Immunity certificate, the trial judge refused, applying a Janowiec-style balance: without the order there might have been no trial of a grave charge. He prohibited disclosure to the Court. Judicial review and a Supreme Court appeal failed; the courts noted repeated independent domestic scrutiny of the national-security claim and that the European Court might not require the material.

The European Court later found no Article 6 violation (the in camera order received rigorous independent review with the applicant's full participation and did not impair cross-examination) and no Article 34 hindrance (no request for the material had been made by the Court, and meaningful independent scrutiny had occurred).

The case of Clasens v. Belgium (Application no. 26564/16) concerns a Belgian national, John Clasens, who alleged that his detention conditions at Ittre Prison during a staff strike from 25 April to 22 June 2016 violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment). He also claimed a lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. Clasens, born in 1983 and serving a final sentence, was held in a facility with 386 inmates (capacity 420), mostly in 9 m² single cells equipped with washbasins and toilets.

The strike, affecting Brussels and Wallonia prisons, arose due to the absence of any guaranteed minimum service, suspending the ordinary regime to varying degrees. On 2 May 2016, Clasens and other prisoners filed an urgent application under Article 584 of the Judicial Code with the President of the Walloon Brabant Court of First Instance, seeking immediate reinstatement of the normal regime under the 2005 Prison Administration Act and citing Article 3 violations from the resulting inhuman conditions.

On 3 May 2016, the President described conditions since 26 April as including sporadic telephone access (26, 29, 30 April, 1 May), showers (27, 29 April, 1 May), exercise (28, 30 April), normal healthcare but no family visits, and potential food shortages from blocked deliveries. The court ordered the State to provide three daily meals (one hot), showers and telephone access every other day, two weekly family visits, and days for lawyers and the Supervisory Board, under a €10,000 daily fine per infringement. The State later obtained orders prohibiting entrance blockades (including at Ittre on 6 May) and mobilized police, civil protection, Red Cross, and army personnel.

A CPT ad hoc visit from 7–9 May 2016 found prisoners confined 24 hours daily with limited showers (once or twice weekly), weekly yard access, interrupted canteen supplies, no hygiene products or visits, and insufficient staff for phones or medicines. The strike ended on 22 June 2016. A 23 June Supervisory Board report confirmed no lawyer visits before 16 June, family visits only on two weekends, one daily meal, telephone calls every three days, confinement with yard/shower access only every three days until mid-June, inability of the Board to conduct confidential interviews, and no other activities. A 25 May unannounced CFI visit, based on the prison director’s information, noted staff numbers of 4–20 (versus 45 needed normally), with police providing security but not inmate services, locked doors, and confrontations at pickets causing staff absences.

Enforcement of the 3 May order proved difficult; Clasens and others issued a 23 May payment demand for fines, appealed by the State on 3 June 2016, with proceedings delayed (oral submissions reportedly in February 2018). On 26 April 2017, the Brussels Court of Appeal largely upheld the order (reducing fines to €250 daily), finding the conditions—confinement without activities, limited family/lawyer contact, irregular exercise and healthcare, and uncertainty over the strike’s duration—amounted to degrading treatment exceeding inherent imprisonment suffering, even with radio/TV, emergency care, or cell fixtures. It referenced Vasilescu v. Belgium and Muršić v. Croatia principles.

At the time, no law guaranteed prison services during strikes, though a 2019 Act (effective July 2019) later introduced minimum service mechanisms, advisory plans, and requisition powers. CPT reports since 2005, including a 2017 public statement, criticized Belgium’s unique strike impacts—prolonged confinement, hygiene deterioration, cancelled exercise, restricted healthcare and contacts—as risking Article 3 violations, with 2016 action crossing a “red line” by leaving prisons under-resourced despite management efforts. These facts underscored the alleged Article 3 breach from systemic disruptions and the Article 13 claim from ineffective urgent remedies amid ongoing enforcement issues.

Most cells were single-occupancy units of 9 m² equipped with washbasins and partitioned toilets. Healthcare continued normally, but family visits had ceased and food deliveries were blocked by pickets, raising the risk of shortages by 5 May. The CFI ordered the State to supply three daily meals (one hot), showers and telephone access every other day, two weekly family visits, and dedicated days for lawyers and the Supervisory Board, subject to a €10,000 daily fine per breach.

The authorities responded by obtaining an order (6 May) prohibiting entrance blockades, and by deploying local and federal police, prison directors, civil-protection units, the Red Cross and the army. Staff numbers fluctuated between 4 and 20, supplemented by police who performed only security functions. A night regime confined inmates to cells; doors remained locked.

The CPT conducted an ad-hoc visit from 7 to 9 May 2016. Its report recorded 24-hour cell confinement, yard access only once a week, showers once or twice weekly, interrupted canteen and hygiene supplies, no family visits since the strike began, and insufficient staff to recharge telephone accounts. Medicines for anxiety were available, but overall conditions had deteriorated sharply.

The strike ended on 22 June. The Ittre Supervisory Board’s 23 June report confirmed: only one meal per day; confinement to cells with exits only every three days (until 16 June) for showers or exercise; virtually no lawyer visits before 16 June and family visits limited to two weekends; telephone contact every three days; and the Board’s inability to conduct confidential interviews. An unannounced CFI inspection on 25 May corroborated these findings and noted that police reinforcements did not compensate for the absence of trained prison staff.

Enforcement of the 3 May order proved difficult. Clasens demanded payment of accrued fines on 23 May; the State appealed. On 26 April 2017 the Brussels Court of Appeal largely upheld the order (reducing the daily fine to a maximum of €250) and held that the conditions constituted degrading treatment under Article 3. Drawing on Vasilescu v. Belgium and Muršić v. Croatia, the court emphasised prolonged cell confinement without activities, irregular meals and hygiene, severed family and legal contacts, and uncertainty about the strike’s duration.

The CPT had repeatedly criticised this legislative vacuum since 2005 and, after the 2016 strikes, issued a public statement concluding that inmates had been exposed to conditions capable of amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment.

These facts formed the core of Clasens’s complaints that the strike-induced regime crossed the Article 3 threshold and that existing urgent-procedure remedies were ineffective in practice.

The President of the Walloon Brabant Court of First Instance, acting in urgent proceedings, issued an order the next day based on hearing evidence. Nevertheless, the strike continued.

Legislation introducing a minimum-service regime was enacted only in March 2019, entering force on 1 July 2019. These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaints that the prolonged, strike-induced deterioration of conditions attained the Article 3 threshold of severity and that existing judicial avenues had been ineffective in practice.

The ECtHR case Paunoski v. North Macedonia (no. 18669/08) concerns Article 6 complaints by former Defence Minister Ljuben Paunoski of unfair and lengthy criminal proceedings for abuse of office.

Paunoski (minister July 2000–May 2001) and undersecretary K.Gj. were convicted over two December 2000 Ministry contracts (food supplies; army housing construction) awarded to company HS, then owned by Z.S. and wife M.S. In February 2001 the company was acquired by Paunoski’s father-in-law Lj.P. and brother-in-law V.T. (also charged). An armed conflict began in spring 2001.

Investigation opened in 2001. On 26 October 2001 Z.S. testified solely before the investigating judge and prosecutor. He denied knowing Paunoski, said Lj.P. had solicited a food bid, claimed V.T. signed the contracts without authorisation, and alleged subsequent threats after discovering Ministry transfers.

Indictment issued 23 November 2001 (confirmed March 2002), proposing that Z.S. be summoned. At first-instance trial Paunoski denied any involvement or knowledge of relatives’ ownership; K.Gj. claimed he had acted on Paunoski’s orders. On 11 September 2003, over defence objection, the court read Z.S.’s pre-trial statement after police confirmed he had left for the United States. Conviction followed on 3 November 2003 but was quashed by the Court of Appeal on 2 March 2004 for insufficient efforts to hear Z.S. (key evidence) and other gaps.

Retrial began 13 September 2005 with numerous hearings, witnesses and expert reports. On 27 April 2006 the court admitted Z.S.’s written statement under Criminal Procedure Act s. 351(2), citing extreme difficulty in securing his US attendance and the existence of sufficient other evidence. Defence objected that his address was known, diplomatic channels could be used, and live examination was needed on authorisation and use of funds. Further defence applications—to examine Ministry letter signatories, admit the complete procurement file, and introduce army reports, government transcripts and media articles on the conflict (to show urgency, a security exception and execution difficulties)—were refused as redundant or intended to delay.

Conviction on 29 December 2006 (3 years 6 months) relied on Ministry officials’ testimony, documents, expert evidence, K.Gj., K.K. and Z.S.’s statement; the contracts were held non-compliant with procurement rules, with no valid urgency or security justification, and Paunoski’s involvement established. Appeals were dismissed by the Court of Appeal (September 2007 public hearing) and Supreme Court (May 2008), which found facts correctly established, refused evidence irrelevant or unnecessary, and no violation of defence rights.

Paunoski complained to the ECtHR that inability to confront Z.S. and refusal of defence evidence breached equality of arms, rendering the trial unfair, and that the proceedings were excessively long.

The case of Paunoski v. North Macedonia originated in an application by Ljuben Paunoski, a former Minister of Defence (July 2000–May 2001), alleging that criminal proceedings against him violated Article 6 of the Convention due to unfairness and excessive length. He specifically complained that he could not cross-examine key witness Z.S. at trial and that the courts refused defence evidence, breaching equality of arms.

The applicant and co-defendants K.Gj. (Ministry undersecretary), Lj.P. (applicant’s father-in-law) and V.T. (brother-in-law) were charged with abuse of office over two December 2000 Ministry procurement contracts (food supplies and construction of army housing) awarded to a company then owned by Z.S. and his wife M.S. The company was later acquired by Lj.P. and V.T. An armed conflict erupted in the country in spring 2001.

An investigating judge opened an inquiry in 2001. On 26 October 2001, Z.S. was examined solely in the prosecutor’s presence. He denied knowing the applicant, stated that Lj.P. had solicited a food-supply bid, that V.T. had signed contracts without authorisation, and that Lj.P. and V.T. had later threatened him after learning of Ministry payments. The November 2001 indictment requested that Z.S. be summoned.

At the first-instance trial, the court on 11 September 2003 read out Z.S.’s pre-trial statement (over defence objections) after police confirmed he had left for the United States. M.S. testified that neither she nor Z.S. had authorised V.T. to sign and that she had signed takeover documents because her husband was scared. The applicant and K.Gj. were convicted in November 2003. The Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in March 2004, holding that insufficient efforts had been made to hear Z.S. (whose evidence it described as key, particularly regarding V.T.’s role and use of transferred funds), that Ministry officials involved in procurement should be examined, and that all facts concerning contract execution (including objective difficulties) needed establishment.

In the retrial (first hearing September 2005), the court heard additional witnesses (including Ministry officials and K.K., who confirmed the applicant’s insistence on urgent signature of the construction contract) and admitted expert reports. On 27 April 2006 it admitted Z.S.’s written statement under s. 351(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act because securing his attendance from California would be extremely difficult and risk delaying the trial, and because other evidence already addressed the relevant facts. The defence objected that Z.S.’s address was known and he could be summoned diplomatically, and that live examination was needed on authorisation and use of company funds.

The same hearing and later hearings in November 2006 saw the court refuse defence requests to examine the signatories of Ministry letters (whose authenticity was challenged) and to admit further documents (army reports, government transcripts, media articles on the armed conflict) intended to prove urgency of the food contract, a security/defence exemption for the construction contract, execution difficulties caused by the conflict, and Z.S.’s role. The court held that sufficient evidence already existed, there was no reason to doubt the letters, and further requests served only to prolong the trial.

On 29 December 2006 the court convicted all defendants, sentencing the applicant to three years and six months’ imprisonment and ordering joint compensation. It relied on Ministry officials’ testimony, documents, expert reports, K.Gj.’s and K.K.’s statements, and a written order signed by the applicant to find that procurement rules had been circumvented and that the applicant had been involved. It used Z.S.’s and M.S.’s statements to reject the claim of a mutually agreed company takeover and to find that threats had been used.

The applicant’s appeal argued that refused evidence would have shown the security situation justified urgency and impeded execution, that construction fell under a statutory exemption, that Z.S. should have been heard pursuant to the Court of Appeal’s earlier instructions, and that evidence to contradict Z.S. had been blocked. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals in September 2007, finding all relevant facts established, its instructions followed, and the refused evidence (chiefly concerning execution) irrelevant; it referred to Z.S.’s and M.S.’s statements without addressing Z.S.’s absence. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions in May 2008, concluding that the security situation had not affected the events, that necessary evidence from both sides had been admitted, and that further refusals had neither violated defence rights nor affected the outcome.

Under the applicable Criminal Procedure Act, a witness statement could be read if the witness could not be found or attendance was considerably impaired for important reasons. The proceedings ran from the 2001 investigation to the 2008 Supreme Court decision, with some adjournments for defendants’ health.

The case of Paunoski v. North Macedonia (no. 18669/08) involves complaints under Article 6 ECHR by former Defence Minister Ljuben Paunoski (2000–2001) that his criminal trial for abuse of office was unfair (inability to cross-examine key witness Z.S.; refusal of defence evidence, breaching equality of arms) and excessively lengthy.

(applicant’s father- and brother-in-law) over two December 2000 Ministry procurement contracts (food supplies and construction of army housing) awarded to company HS, then owned by Z.S. and wife M.S. The company was acquired by Lj.P. and V.T. in February 2001. An armed conflict erupted in spring 2001. Pre-trial, Z.S. was examined on 26 October 2001 solely in the prosecutor’s presence. He denied knowing the applicant, said Lj.P. had requested a food bid, claimed V.T. signed the contracts without authorisation, and alleged later threats by Lj.P. and V.T. after Ministry payments. The applicant denied involvement, asserting lawful processes handled by Ministry administration of which he was unaware in detail and that he did not know of his relatives’ ownership. K.Gj. claimed he acted on the applicant’s orders.

The 23 November 2001 indictment charged the applicant and K.Gj. with abuse of office (applicant also with ordering irregular contracts) and the others with incitement. After first-instance conviction on 3 November 2003 (Z.S.’s statement having been read on 11 September 2003 after police confirmation he had left for the United States), the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 2 March 2004. It held that insufficient efforts had been made to hear Z.S., whose evidence was “key” concerning V.T.’s role and use of transferred funds; more Ministry officials involved in procurement needed to be examined; and all facts about contract execution (including any objective difficulties) required establishment.

In the retrial (first hearing 13 September 2005), numerous witnesses, documents and two expert reports were admitted. On 27 April 2006 the court admitted Z.S.’s pre-trial statement under Criminal Procedure Act s. 351(2), finding attendance “extremely difficult” given confirmed US residence and that sufficient other evidence existed on the relevant facts. The defence objected that Z.S.’s known US address permitted diplomatic summons and that live testimony was essential to test authorisation and fund use. Repeated defence applications to examine Ministry-letter signatories and to admit further material (full Ministry files, army reports, government transcripts, media articles on the conflict) aimed at proving urgency/security exceptions to procurement rules and impediments to execution were refused. The court saw no reason to doubt the letters’ veracity, held all relevant documents already produced, and viewed further requests as delay tactics or unnecessary given existing evidence.

On 29 December 2006 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to three years six months’ imprisonment (jointly liable for damages). The court relied on K.Gj. and official K.K.’s evidence of the applicant’s involvement, a signed order requiring notification of procurement, Ministry officials’ testimony, experts, and Z.S./M.S. statements showing a threatened takeover for unlawful gain. Contract-award irregularities were found (no urgency for food; no legal framework/plan for the construction site, suggesting circumvention of rules; company unregistered for construction). Execution difficulties were deemed irrelevant. Appeals failed: the Court of Appeal (September 2007) held facts correctly established, its earlier instructions followed and refused evidence (mostly on execution) irrelevant; the Supreme Court (20 May 2008) confirmed the contracts’ unlawfulness, that the security situation had not affected events, that necessary evidence from both sides had been admitted and that refusal of further material neither breached defence rights nor affected the outcome. The overall proceedings lasted from 2001 until May 2008.
