The case of Stephens v. Malta (No. 3) (Application no. 35989/14) concerns a complaint by British national Mark Charles Kenneth Stephens under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He alleged that his criminal trial for drug trafficking conspiracy was unfair because statements given by an accomplice, G.R.E., to the police without legal assistance were admitted as evidence against him.

Police investigations began after G.R.E. and his partner were stopped at Malta International Airport on 11 August 2003 and found with nearly 3 kg of cocaine and 7,151 ecstasy pills. G.R.E. was questioned without a lawyer on 11–12 August 2003. His first statement claimed fear of naming the instructor (described as Russian). His second statement identified “Mark Stephens” (Maltese, with family including a brother running a private school in Malta) as the person who delivered the drugs and arranged a prior money collection involving V.S. On 13 August 2003, G.R.E. confirmed the second statement on oath before an inquiring magistrate (with conflicting accounts as to whether a lawyer was present).

The applicant was arrested in Spain in November 2004 pursuant to a Maltese warrant and extradited in September 2005. He gave two statements to police on 10–11 September 2005 without a lawyer present, confirming he knew G.R.E. from his Zaragoza bar (“Mountain Side Inn”), that A.W. had supplied the drugs, and details of his family in Malta. He was charged with conspiracy to traffic cocaine and ecstasy.

During committal proceedings, G.R.E. recanted, claiming his police statements were fabricated under threat of a 30-year sentence and that the “Mark Stephens” he knew (owner of the “Mountain Side” restaurant) was not the applicant. V.S. testified, identifying the applicant as “Mark Stephens” and confirming related events including handing money to G.R.E. At the 2008 jury trial, G.R.E. again recanted, attributing the name to A.W. The trial judge directed that the prosecution could rely on G.R.E.’s sworn pre-trial statement if the jury accepted it as true. The applicant challenged the statements’ admissibility but did not object to their distribution to jurors; he cross-examined G.R.E., V.S., and others. He was convicted on 5 November 2008 and sentenced to 25 years’ imprisonment plus a €60,000 fine.

The Court of Criminal Appeal dismissed the appeal in 2010, finding the conviction supported by G.R.E.’s second and sworn statements (admissible under s. 30A of the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance if voluntary), consistencies with the applicant’s own statements (family details, bar ownership), and V.S.’s identification and testimony. It held the evidence established the conspiracy beyond reasonable doubt.

In 2012 constitutional proceedings, the applicant alleged unfairness from the use of G.R.E.’s uncounselled statements (claiming G.R.E. suffered withdrawal symptoms) and inadequate jury directions. Domestic courts rejected the claims. They found the applicant had consulted a lawyer before his own questioning, had no standing to exclude a third party’s statements (a right belonging to G.R.E., whose separate challenge was dismissed), ample opportunity to cross-examine G.R.E. at trial, and no proof of unfitness or duress (the magistrate’s involvement supporting voluntariness). The judge’s directions were lawful, and factual issues of credibility had been for the criminal courts.

At the relevant time, Maltese law provided no right to a lawyer during police questioning (introduced only in 2010). Article 661 of the Criminal Code generally limited confessions to the maker, but s. 30A permitted use of a co-accused’s sworn statement against others if voluntary. The European Court held that admission of G.R.E.’s statements did not impair the overall fairness of the trial.

The case of Stephens v. Malta (No. 3) concerns a British national’s complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) ECHR that his trial for drug-trafficking conspiracy was unfair because the courts admitted an accomplice’s police statements given without a lawyer.

On 11 August 2003 G.R.E. and his partner were stopped at Malta airport with nearly 3 kg of cocaine and over 7,000 ecstasy tablets. Questioned without counsel on 11–12 August, G.R.E. first claimed a Russian had instructed him; the next day he named “Mark Stephens,” a Maltese man whose mother and two brothers (one running a private school) lived in Malta. He added that Stephens had earlier sent him to collect money and that he had met V.S., who confirmed a long-standing relationship and a planned Spanish business partnership. On 13 August G.R.E. confirmed the second statement on oath before an inquiring magistrate; whether a lawyer was present is disputed.

The applicant was arrested in Spain in November 2004 and extradited in September 2005. Interviewed without a lawyer (though he had consulted one the previous day and during earlier extradition proceedings), he confirmed knowing G.R.E., leasing the “Mountain Side Inn” in Zaragoza, and having a brother who ran a school and a mother living in Malta; he denied supplying the drugs and blamed another man, A.W. He was charged with conspiracy.

At committal G.R.E. recanted, claiming police pressure and that the Stephens he knew was not in court. V.S., however, identified the applicant as the person who had asked him to collect G.R.E. and to whom money had been handed. At the 2008 jury trial G.R.E. again denied that the applicant was “Mark Stephens.” The trial judge directed the jury that they could legally convict on the sworn statement if they accepted it as true. The applicant challenged admissibility and credibility but did not object when the sworn statement was distributed to the jurors; he cross-examined G.R.E. and V.S. The jury convicted him of conspiracy; he received 25 years’ imprisonment and a €60,000 fine.

The Court of Criminal Appeal upheld the verdict, noting that G.R.E.’s second statement and oath were admissible under s. 30A of the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance provided they were voluntary. It found ample corroboration: the applicant’s own admissions matching G.R.E.’s description, V.S.’s identification, and the family and business details.

In 2012 constitutional proceedings the applicant argued that both his own uncounselled statements and G.R.E.’s should have been excluded, that G.R.E. had been suffering withdrawal, and that the judge had misdirected the jury. The Civil Court (constitutional jurisdiction) rejected the claims: the applicant had had prior access to a lawyer and had not confessed; Salduz rights belonged only to the person questioned; G.R.E.’s own constitutional challenge had failed; withdrawal symptoms were unproven and should have been raised at trial; the applicant had fully cross-examined G.R.E. and had not objected to the statement’s distribution. The Constitutional Court affirmed, adding that confirmation before an independent magistrate showed voluntariness and that the trial judge had correctly left the factual assessment to the jury.

(The European Court later held that, in the light of the overall fairness of the proceedings, no violation of Article 6 had occurred.)

**Case Summary: Studio Monitori and Others v. Georgia (Applications nos. 44920/09 and 8942/10)**

This European Court of Human Rights case (Fifth Section, judgment of 30 January 2020, final 30 May 2020) involved two applications against Georgia alleging violations of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom to receive and impart information). The applicants claimed domestic courts unlawfully denied them access to information they considered of public interest. The Court ultimately found no violation, as the unmotivated requests for unrelated third-party criminal files were not instrumental to exercising freedom of expression and failed a public-interest test. Key facts center on the requests, lack of justification, and courts' reasoned denials based on classified material, personal data, and statutory limits.

The first application was lodged by Studio Monitori, a Georgian NGO founded in 2005 to conduct journalistic investigations into public-interest matters, and Nino Zuriashvili, a journalist and founding member born in 1968. In 2007, Zuriashvili (acting for the NGO) requested the Khashuri District Court registry grant her access to the complete case file of an unrelated concluded criminal case against T.E., including permission to photocopy and photograph archived materials. She provided no reasons or specifics about the documents sought or any intended purpose.

The registry refused on 3 August 2007, inviting her to specify the exact information/documents and purpose. It noted that the file contained classified investigative material whose public disclosure was prohibited under section 5(1) and (2) of the Special Investigative Activities Act 1999 (covering covert/overt activities by authorized agencies to protect rights, security, and prevent crime; disclosure of related documents risked criminal prosecution as State secrets). The file also held personal data of T.E. and other parties, disclosable only with their explicit consent under Article 37 § 2 of the General Administrative Code 1999. Zuriashvili provided no further details. Instead, on 14 September 2007 she sued in Borjomi District Court to annul the decision, claiming it restricted her right to public information under Article 37 § 1 of the Code, without explaining her purpose.

At a 12 December 2007 hearing, she vaguely mentioned needing the file for a "journalistic investigation project" but gave no details, arguing solely that access to public information should be unlimited and that the registry had misinterpreted the laws. The court dismissed the action, upholding the refusal as legitimate under the cited provisions. On appeal, Zuriashvili again omitted any specifics on purpose, focusing on unfettered access. At a 12 June 2008 Tbilisi Court of Appeal hearing, she stated she no longer needed the material (the investigation had ended and been published) but sought a precedent affirming unlimited access to criminal files as public information. The appeal was dismissed on 19 June 2008; the Supreme Court rejected a further appeal as inadmissible on 16 February 2009.

The second application was by Mamuka Nozadze, a Georgian lawyer born in 1974, convicted in 2006 of fraud (stealing client funds intended for bail) and sentenced to 3.5 years' imprisonment. While incarcerated, on 11 October 2007 he requested the Tbilisi City Court registry send him full copies of all court orders imposing pre-trial preventive measures in six distinct, unrelated (and then-ongoing) criminal cases. He gave no reasons for the request.

The registry provided only the operative parts of the orders on 10 October 2007, citing Article 140 § 20 of the then-applicable Code of Criminal Procedure (limiting disclosure of detention orders). Nozadze sued on 1 November 2007, alleging infringement of his unfettered right to public information under Article 37 § 1 of the General Administrative Code. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 19 December 2008, holding that Chapter III of the Code (including Article 37) applied to the judiciary only for purely administrative/organizational functions, not the administration of justice (per Article 3 §§ 2–3); the ongoing nature of the cases was significant. The Supreme Court rejected his points-of-law appeal on 27 July 2009 (decision served 30 October 2009).

Relevant domestic law underscored the denials. The Special Investigative Activities Act classified related documents and prohibited disclosure. The General Administrative Code defined "public information" narrowly (excluding classified personal data, commercial/State secrets, or investigative material); Article 3 limited its application to the judiciary (excluding justice administration and executive criminal investigations/prosecutions); Articles 10, 28, and 37 granted access to non-classified public information but required written requests and third-party consent for personal data.

These facts—unspecified, unmotivated requests for sensitive third-party criminal materials, applicants' failure to demonstrate public-interest or expression-related necessity, and courts' reliance on statutory protections—formed the core of the alleged Article 10 breaches. The first applicants invoked journalistic purposes only vaguely and after the fact; the third applicant offered none. Domestic proceedings consistently prioritized privacy, secrecy, and jurisdictional limits over blanket access claims.

He specified no reason for the request.

The registry supplied only the operative parts of the orders on 10 October 2007, citing Article 140 § 20 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (then in force), which limited disclosure of detention orders to their operative parts. On 1 November 2007 Nozadze brought an action claiming the refusal infringed his right under Article 37 § 1 of the General Administrative Code to unfettered access to public information. All three levels of the Georgian judiciary rejected the action, holding that the registry’s refusal was required by the protective provisions of domestic law.

The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal.

In both cases, therefore, the applicants sought, without any stated purpose or public-interest justification, full access to criminal files concerning third parties who were strangers to them. The domestic courts treated the requests as falling outside the scope of the general right of access to public information and as being barred by specific statutory protections for investigative secrecy, personal data and the integrity of ongoing judicial proceedings.

The case of Lobarev and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 10355/09 and five others) concerns six Russian nationals convicted between 2008 and 2014 in unrelated criminal proceedings. Five were found guilty of drug-related offences and one (Dumler) of fraud; all received prison sentences. The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention because trial courts read out the pre-trial statements of certain prosecution witnesses who failed to appear, thereby restricting the applicants’ right to examine those witnesses in court.

The witnesses in question were themselves suspects or accused in other criminal proceedings. The trial courts admitted their statements under Article 281(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which permits reading out testimony in “exceptional circumstances” that preclude appearance. In Lobarev’s case the decision rested on a police officer’s information that the witness was on a national wanted list; in Shkarin’s case an investigator reported that the witness had been wanted and searched for months. Dumler’s court noted that the witness had gone into hiding; information from the Federal Security Service indicated he was evading the authorities, though Dumler later complained that the information lacked details about the competent authorities, any inquiry, or an instituted criminal case. In Kazakovskiy’s, Kosov’s and Novgorodov’s cases the courts gave more explicit reasons: an investigator’s decision to place the witness on a wanted list (Kazakovskiy), another court’s decision to do so (Kosov), and confirmation that the witness was on a national wanted list (Novgorodov). In the last of these, a second district court examining a case against the same witness had itself placed him on the list for evading justice and suspended proceedings; Novgorodov supported an official request for confirmation, which was obtained and shown to the parties.

The convictions rested on a substantial body of other evidence. This included the applicants’ own statements given at the pre-trial stage and at trial in the presence of lawyers; testimony from police officers who had conducted undercover operations; statements of attesting witnesses and other prosecution witnesses, some of whom were cross-examined in court; physical exhibits (varying quantities of seized drugs, almost one kilogram in Novgorodov’s case, scales and more than two hundred plastic bags in Kosov’s case, and second-hand equipment in Dumler’s fraud case); documentary records of investigative actions and forensic reports; telephone transcripts of conversations with buyers or suppliers (Lobarev, Kazakovskiy, Novgorodov); a video recording of a test purchase (Lobarev); and records of a pre-trial confrontation (Shkarin). Defence witnesses, including spouses, relatives and friends, were examined at trial. The courts did not attach any special weight to the absent witnesses’ statements; they analysed them, cross-referenced them with the remaining evidence, and found them coherent and consistent.

On appeal the applicants argued that the trial courts had not made sufficient efforts to secure the witnesses’ attendance. The convictions were nevertheless upheld. Domestic law provided for compulsory summonses enforceable by bailiffs and a specific search regime for suspects or accused persons who go into hiding, including investigator instructions to inquiry agencies, operational-search measures, and police searches.

The case of Franz v. Germany (Application no. 29295/16) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Friedrich-Carl Franz (born 1955), a German lawyer admitted in 1986, was appointed notary in 1997 by the President of the Celle Court of Appeal. On 9 August 2012, that President provisionally suspended him from office. On 12 February 2013, the President (via Vice-President H. as representative) definitively removed him under section 50(1) point 8 of the Federal Notary Act, which requires removal if a notary’s economic circumstances, business administration or depository conduct jeopardise users of legal services.

The applicant sought annulment of the removal before the Celle Court of Appeal (ordinary-court branch) on 15 March 2013. The case was assigned to that court’s notary senate (composed of a presiding judge of at least Court-of-Appeal rank, an associate professional judge and a notary judge). He objected to the court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the challenged decision had been issued by the President of the same court and that the matter belonged in the administrative courts. On 22 May 2013 the senate confirmed its own jurisdiction under section 111 of the Federal Notary Act (as implemented by Lower Saxony regulations that channelled all such cases to Celle).

The applicant then lodged multiple bias complaints against the senate’s ordinary members and their substitutes. He relied on the President’s close personal and professional ties with the judges, the President’s role as their disciplinary superior, and the President’s influence (as chairman of the court’s executive committee) over the five-year appointments of the professional judges and over the annual allocation of cases. On 8 November 2013 a differently composed panel (including one previously challenged substitute, Judge K.) dismissed the complaints as inadmissible: they were unsubstantiated and merely structural, not personal to any individual judge, and therefore abusive, so the challenged judge could participate.

After a hearing, the original notary senate dismissed the annulment application on 3 March 2014. It held that forty-six enforcement measures against the applicant over roughly ten years (twenty-six of them in the four years preceding removal), mostly for modest sums but one for a large amount, created an impression of untrustworthiness sufficient to justify removal; fault or a concrete past breach of a depository duty was unnecessary, and an abstract risk to clients sufficed.

The applicant sought leave to appeal to the Federal Court of Justice, invoking inter alia his constitutional right to a lawful judge (Article 101 of the Basic Law). On 24 November 2014 the Federal Court of Justice refused leave. It found the statutory assignment of such disputes to the Court of Appeal generally compatible with impartiality guarantees, noted that judges of the notary senate were appointed for fixed five-year terms (so the President could not readily replace them), and saw no serious doubts about the correctness of the first-instance judgment. A subsequent complaint of violation of the right to be heard was dismissed. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear a constitutional complaint on 17 November 2015, without reasons.

Under domestic law, Presidents of Courts of Appeal exercise both the removal power (delegated by Lower Saxony) and limited administrative supervision of the judges who sit in the notary senate; they also chair the executive committee that appoints those judges and draw up appraisal reports used for promotions. Supervision and appraisals are legally constrained so as not to interfere with judicial independence, and both are subject to judicial review. Bias complaints are the exclusive means of challenging a specific composition; they are decided by substitutes unless the complaint is abusive.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s claim that the Celle Court of Appeal’s notary senate lacked the independence and impartiality required by Article 6 § 1.

The case of Franz v. Germany (Application no. 29295/16) concerns a complaint by German notary Friedrich-Carl Franz under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Celle Court of Appeal, which reviewed the revocation of his notarial office, lacked independence and impartiality.

Franz, born in 1955, was admitted as a lawyer in 1986. In 1997 the President of the Celle Court of Appeal conferred upon him the office of notary. On 9 August 2012 that same President preliminarily suspended Franz. After unsuccessful challenges, on 12 February 2013 the President (acting through Vice-President H.) definitively removed Franz from office under section 50(1) point 8 of the Federal Notary Act. That provision requires removal if a notary’s economic circumstances, business administration or handling of deposits jeopardise the interests of users of legal services; no fault or specific past violation is required, only an appearance of untrustworthiness (for instance, repeated enforcement measures against the notary).

Franz lodged an application for annulment with the Celle Court of Appeal on 15 March 2013. Jurisdiction over public-law disputes under the Federal Notary Act lies with the ordinary courts of appeal as first-instance courts, and Lower Saxony had concentrated all such cases in the Celle Court’s specialised “notary senate.” Franz objected that the same court whose President had issued the contested decision should not sit, arguing that administrative courts would be more appropriate. The notary senate confirmed its own jurisdiction.

Franz then filed multiple complaints of bias against the ordinary members of the notary senate (presiding judge, associate judge and notary-judge) and against their substitutes. He relied on the President’s close personal and professional ties with the judges, the President’s status as their disciplinary superior, and the President’s role in appraisals and promotions. On 8 November 2013 a differently composed panel (including one previously challenged substitute) rejected the complaints as inadmissible: they were general and structural rather than specific to any individual judge and therefore abusive.

On 3 March 2014 the original notary senate, after a hearing, dismissed Franz’s challenge on the merits. It found that Franz had been the subject of 46 enforcement measures over approximately ten years (26 of them in the last four years), mostly for modest sums but once for a large amount. This pattern created a sufficient risk to clients, rendering removal proportionate.

Franz sought leave to appeal to the Federal Court of Justice, invoking his constitutional right to a “lawful judge” (Article 101 of the Basic Law) and contesting both jurisdiction and the impartiality of the senate. He did not deny the existence of the enforcement measures but argued they were old, ultimately paid, or legally defective, and that they did not demonstrate a real risk. On 24 November 2014 the Federal Court of Justice refused leave. It held that assigning such disputes to the same Court of Appeal was constitutionally permissible, that senate members were appointed for five-year terms (so the President could not easily replace them), and that there were no serious doubts as to the correctness of the judgment. It added that Franz had also failed to meet tax obligations and that an abstract risk sufficed. Subsequent applications (including a constitutional complaint) were rejected without reasons.

The notary senate comprises a presiding judge (at least a Court of Appeal presiding judge), a permanent associate judge and a notary, all appointed for five years. Professional judges are selected by the court’s executive committee, chaired by the President. The President also exercises limited administrative supervision over the judges and prepares their appraisal reports, which form the basis for promotions decided by the Land Ministry of Justice. Franz contended that these structural links rendered the tribunal neither independent nor impartial vis-à-vis the President who had issued the removal decision.

The case of Franz v. Germany (Application no. 29295/16) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the right to an independent and impartial tribunal, in proceedings that revoked the applicant’s office as a notary.

The applicant, a lawyer since 1986, was appointed a notary in 1997 by the President of the Celle Court of Appeal. On 9 August 2012 that President preliminarily suspended him; the suspension was upheld on challenge. On 12 February 2013 the President (acting through the Vice-President) definitively removed him from office under section 50(1) point 8 of the Federal Notary Act. The provision requires removal where a notary’s economic circumstances, business administration or handling of deposits jeopardises the interests of users of legal services. The decision rested on 46 enforcement measures taken against the applicant over roughly ten years, mostly for modest sums but once for a large amount.

The applicant sought annulment before the Celle Court of Appeal, the first-instance court designated by federal and Land law for such public-law disputes under the Notary Act. The case was assigned to that court’s notary senate (a specialised panel of a presiding judge of at least court-of-appeal rank, a permanent associate judge and a notary). He first objected to the ordinary courts’ jurisdiction, arguing that an administrative court should hear a dispute between a private individual and an administrative decision-maker; the senate rejected the objection by reference to section 111 of the Notary Act.

He then lodged successive bias complaints against every ordinary member of the senate and all their designated substitutes. He relied on the close personal and professional links between those judges and the defendant President, and on the President’s role as their disciplinary superior, as creating structural doubts about independence and impartiality. On 8 November 2013 a differently composed panel (including one previously challenged judge) dismissed the complaints as inadmissible: they were purely general and structural, not specific to any individual judge, and therefore abusive. The original senate then heard the merits and, on 3 March 2014, dismissed the action. It held that the statutory provision was sufficiently precise, required neither fault nor a proven past breach, and was satisfied by the mere existence of repeated enforcement measures that created an impression of untrustworthiness.

The applicant sought leave to appeal to the Federal Court of Justice, invoking inter alia the constitutional right to a lawful judge (Article 101 of the Basic Law) and contesting both the composition of the senate and the proportionality of removal. On 24 November 2014 the Federal Court of Justice refused leave. It found that assigning such disputes to the same Court of Appeal whose President had taken the impugned decision was constitutionally acceptable, that the five-year appointment of senate members limited the President’s ability to manipulate composition, and that no serious doubts existed as to the correctness of the first-instance judgment. A subsequent complaint of a violation of the right to be heard was dismissed; the Federal Constitutional Court declined to entertain a constitutional complaint.

The institutional setting is central to the impartiality complaint. The President of the Court of Appeal is the authority that both removes notaries and chairs the court’s executive committee (himself plus ten elected judges). That committee appoints the professional judges of the notary senate for five-year terms and adopts the annual allocation-of-business plan that determines which of them sit on any given case. The President also exercises limited administrative supervision over the judges, prepares appraisal reports used in promotion decisions, and is their disciplinary superior. Although supervision and appraisal are legally barred from interfering with judicial independence and are themselves subject to judicial review, the applicant maintained that these overlapping functions created an appearance of dependence. Bias recusal is available under the Code of Civil Procedure, but a complaint that is merely structural and unsubstantiated may be rejected even by a panel that includes a challenged judge. Leave to appeal to the Federal Court of Justice is granted only on limited grounds and is decided on the papers without a hearing.

These facts—the identity of decision-maker and reviewing court, the President’s role in composition, discipline and promotion, the unsuccessful bias challenges, and the limited nature of subsequent review—form the core of the alleged violation of the right to an independent and impartial tribunal.

**CASE OF BASTYS v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 80749/17)**

Mindaugas Bastys, a Lithuanian national and former Seimas (parliament) member, was re-elected in October 2016 and chosen as Deputy Speaker in December 2016. The Speaker requested the State Security Department (SSD) to assess his eligibility for security clearance to access classified information, including State secrets. Bastys consented, completed an SSD questionnaire, and was interviewed twice.

On 8 March 2017, the SSD issued a note to the Speaker and Bastys recommending against clearance. It cited doubts about his trustworthiness based on relationships with individuals linked to Russia (including a former KGB employee) whose activities conflicted with Lithuanian national security, as well as persons accused or convicted of crimes. The SSD alleged Bastys maintained personal ties, fulfilled their requests, acknowledged potential pressure from some of them, failed to disclose certain connections in his questionnaire, and later claimed to have forgotten meetings. The note opposed granting clearance.

On 9 March 2017, the Speaker informed Bastys orally that clearance would be refused and requested his resignation as Deputy Speaker. Bastys resigned in writing the next day; the Seimas approved it immediately. He remained an MP. The SSD note’s contents were reported in the media, and the Speaker made public comments.

Bastys requested the underlying information from the SSD on 14 March 2017 to challenge the note in court. The SSD refused on 28 March, citing classified information (to which he had no access) and describing the note as an uncontestable interim document. He also asked the Speaker (on 14 and 31 March) for a written decision refusing clearance so he could contest it. The Speaker replied on 4 April that no such decision could be adopted, as Bastys no longer held an office requiring clearance.

On 6 April 2017, Bastys sued the Seimas and SSD in the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court. He argued the SSD note’s conclusions were unfounded, disputed the nature of the relationships, complained that the Speaker had not issued a written refusal, and claimed the Speaker’s public disclosure of the note had severely damaged his political reputation. He sought annulment of the note and an order for the Speaker to grant clearance.

On 13 April 2017, the court refused to examine the complaint. It held the SSD note was merely an interim document creating no legal consequences (the Speaker, not the SSD, made the final decision) and thus uncontestable; arguments against it could be raised only when challenging a final refusal. As Bastys had resigned and not sought clearance on other grounds, the Speaker’s position also created no contestable consequences.

Bastys appealed, arguing the note contained a decision (not merely interim advice), that refusal denied access to court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that he lacked an effective remedy against possible SSD abuse. On 14 June 2017, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It confirmed the note’s interim nature and lack of legal consequences. Regarding the Speaker, it held administrative courts could review only public-administration acts; Bastys had not sought annulment of a refusal but an order to grant clearance, which fell outside that scope.

These facts formed the core of Bastys’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights: that he had no opportunity to defend himself against the SSD note’s allegations, violating Article 13 (effective remedy) taken with Article 8 (right to respect for private life, including reputation). Subsequent Seimas inquiry, impeachment proceedings, and Constitutional Court findings of constitutional violation (failure to disclose relationships and bad-faith attempt to obtain clearance) occurred after the application but stemmed from the same events. Bastys later resigned as an MP after the Seimas declined to revoke his mandate. 

The domestic courts’ view—that an interim SSD note could not be challenged independently, but its findings could be contested via a final Speaker decision on clearance—was central, as was Bastys’s decision to resign before any such decision issued.

The case of Bastys v. Lithuania (Application no. 80749/17) concerned a Lithuanian politician’s complaint that he had no effective means of challenging damaging allegations in a State Security Department (SSD) intelligence note, in violation of Article 13 of the Convention taken together with Article 8.

Mindaugas Bastys, a long-serving member of the Seimas, was elected Deputy Speaker in December 2016. The Speaker requested an SSD assessment of his suitability for security clearance granting access to classified information, including state secrets. Bastys consented, completed a questionnaire and was interviewed twice.

On 8 March 2017 the SSD sent a note to the Speaker (copied to Bastys) advising against clearance. It cited his relationships with individuals linked to Russian intelligence (including a former KGB officer) whose activities were deemed contrary to Lithuanian national security, as well as persons accused or convicted of serious crimes. The SSD stated that Bastys had maintained personal contacts, fulfilled requests from these individuals, and himself acknowledged that some might exert pressure on him. It further alleged that he had omitted certain connections and meetings from his questionnaire, later claiming forgetfulness.

The following day the Speaker informed Bastys orally that clearance would be refused and asked him to resign. Bastys submitted his written resignation on 10 March, which the Seimas immediately approved. He remained an ordinary member of parliament. The contents of the SSD note were widely reported in the media and the Speaker made public comments about it.

Bastys requested the underlying information from the SSD so that he could challenge the note in court. The SSD refused on 28 March, stating that the note was based in part on classified material to which he had no right of access and that it was merely an interim document that could not itself be contested. He also asked the Speaker for a formal written decision refusing clearance. The Speaker replied that, because Bastys no longer held an office requiring clearance, no such decision would be adopted.

On 6 April 2017 Bastys brought proceedings in the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court against the Seimas and the SSD. He argued that the note’s conclusions were unfounded, that the Speaker had failed to issue a written decision, and that public disclosure of the note had seriously damaged his reputation. He sought annulment of the note and an order that the Speaker grant him clearance. The court declined to examine the complaint, holding that the note created no legal consequences and was therefore not justiciable; any challenge to its contents could be raised only against a final decision by the Speaker. Since Bastys had already resigned, that decision no longer produced legal effects either.

The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his appeal on 14 June 2017. It confirmed that the note was an unappealable interim document and added that Bastys’s request for an order compelling the Speaker to grant clearance did not concern an act of public administration and therefore fell outside the administrative courts’ jurisdiction.

(Subsequent impeachment proceedings initiated by the Seimas and a finding by the Constitutional Court that Bastys had breached his oath by failing to disclose relationships are noted only insofar as they followed from the same facts; they did not form the basis of the Article 13 complaint before the European Court.)

The applicant’s central grievance was thus that he had been left without any judicial avenue to contest the SSD’s allegations once they had been made public, thereby denying him an effective remedy for the interference with his reputation.

The case of Bastys v. Lithuania (no. 80749/17) concerned a Lithuanian MP’s complaint that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13 ECHR, read with Article 8, to challenge damaging allegations contained in a State Security Department (SSD) intelligence note.

Mindaugas Bastys had served several parliamentary terms. After re-election in October 2016 he was chosen Deputy Speaker. The Speaker of the Seimas then requested the SSD to assess his suitability for the highest level of security clearance. The applicant consented, completed a questionnaire and was interviewed twice. On 8 March 2017 the SSD sent a classified note to both the Speaker and the applicant advising against clearance. The note cited personal ties to several individuals linked to Russian intelligence (including a former KGB officer) whose activities were deemed contrary to Lithuanian national-security interests, as well as to persons accused or convicted of serious crimes. It recorded that the applicant had fulfilled requests from these persons, had himself acknowledged that some of them might exert pressure on him, and had omitted several of the relationships and meetings from his questionnaire (later claiming forgetfulness).

The following day the Speaker informed the applicant orally that clearance would be refused and asked him to resign. The applicant submitted a written resignation on 10 March, which the Seimas accepted the same day; he remained an ordinary MP. The contents of the SSD note were immediately reported in the media and the Speaker commented publicly, causing what the applicant regarded as serious damage to his political reputation.

The applicant then sought the underlying material from the SSD so that he could challenge the note in court. The SSD refused, stating that the information was classified and that the note was merely an interim document not itself open to judicial review. He also asked the Speaker for a formal written decision refusing clearance. The Speaker replied that, because the applicant no longer held an office requiring clearance, no such decision could or would be taken.

On 6 April 2017 the applicant lodged an administrative action against the Seimas and the SSD, attacking the factual conclusions of the note, the absence of a written refusal, and the public disclosure that had harmed his reputation. He asked the court to annul the note and to order the Speaker to grant him clearance. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court declined jurisdiction: the SSD note created no independent legal effects and therefore could not be challenged in isolation; once the applicant had resigned, no contestable decision of the Speaker existed either. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that ruling, adding that a request to compel the issuance of clearance did not concern an act of public administration and therefore lay outside the administrative courts’ competence.

Subsequent parliamentary inquiries led to impeachment proceedings. The Constitutional Court later found that the applicant had failed to disclose relevant relationships and had sought clearance in bad faith, thereby breaching his oath and the Constitution. The Seimas ultimately declined to strip him of his mandate, but he resigned as an MP in March 2018.

Domestic law provided that a final decision refusing security clearance could be challenged in the administrative courts, at which stage the applicant could have contested the reliability of the SSD’s findings (including, if necessary, classified material). Civil-law remedies also existed for the retraction of untrue statements that damaged honour and dignity. The applicant did not pursue either avenue, having chosen to resign immediately rather than await a formal refusal that he could then have litigated.

The European Court of Human Rights case Šeiko v. Lithuania (Application no. 82968/17) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention regarding the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicant, Galina Šeiko, a Lithuanian national born in 1950 and residing in Kretinga, alleged that the recovery of court-awarded damages by deducting 20 percent of her monthly old-age pension was unlawful and imposed insurmountable hardship, leaving her without adequate means of subsistence.

On 31 December 2014, the Kretinga Region District Court convicted the applicant, then an old-age pensioner, under Articles 138 §§ 2(5) and 5 and 145 § 2 of the Criminal Code of causing minor psychological injury and terrorising a neighbouring family living in the apartment above hers. Over a period of one year and one month she had made dozens of false reports to the police, municipal authorities and child-care services. These actions caused one neighbour to experience fear and post-traumatic stress disorder that developed into medium-severity and then severe depression; a minor member of the same family also suffered post-traumatic stress disorder. The court imposed a sentence of two years and six months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years, together with a prohibition on approaching the victims. It also partly granted a civil claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, awarding EUR 5,908. Appeals against the conviction and award were dismissed by the appellate court in 2015 and the cassation court in 2016.

A writ of execution was issued on 24 November 2016. After the applicant failed to pay, the bailiff seized a 0.06-hectare plot of land belonging to her. On 22 December 2016 the bailiff wrote to the Kretinga division of the State Social Insurance Fund Board (SODRA) requesting that 20 percent of the applicant’s monthly old-age pension be deducted in order to recover the outstanding sum.

Between 20 January 2017 and 13 March 2019 a total of EUR 2,019 was recovered through monthly deductions ranging from EUR 20.24 to EUR 24.64. At the time of the parties’ observations in 2019 the applicant received a monthly old-age pension of EUR 123.21. From 2019 she also received a monthly allowance of EUR 60.47 from which no deductions were made. Since 1993 she had been provided with municipal housing by the Kretinga regional authorities and, as of December 2016, paid EUR 11.02 per month for it.

In addition to the pension she received limited further social assistance: a monthly social-welfare allowance of EUR 5 (January 2018–March 2019), a monthly social-security pension of EUR 2.59 (December 2016 and January 2018–March 2019), and one-off lump sums of EUR 76 (January 2018) and EUR 114 (January 2019). In 2017 these supplementary benefits were not paid because the difference between her actual income and the State-supported income level was not sufficiently significant.

Under the Code of Civil Procedure, deductions of up to 20 percent may be made from a pension for ordinary recoveries (or up to 50 percent for compensation arising from criminal acts); Article 737 expressly extends salary-deduction rules to pensions. Article 668 prohibits seizure of property indispensable for subsistence or of sums not exceeding the minimum monthly salary, while Article 739 excludes certain social allowances from recovery. Supreme Court case-law characterises the minimum-salary protection as a one-time restriction, after which future income such as a pension may be subject to ongoing percentage deductions. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the continuing 20-percent deductions from her modest pension constituted an excessive interference with her possessions.

The court partly granted a civil claim by one victim and awarded EUR 5,908 in compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. Appeals were dismissed by the appellate court in 2015 and the cassation court in 2016.

On 24 November 2016 a writ of execution was issued. After the applicant failed to pay within the prescribed time, the bailiff seized a 0.06-hectare plot of land belonging to her. On 22 December 2016 the bailiff also requested the Kretinga division of the State Social Insurance Fund Board (SODRA) to recover the debt by deducting 20 per cent of her monthly old-age pension. Between 20 January 2017 and 13 March 2019 a total of EUR 2,019 was recovered, with monthly deductions ranging from EUR 20.24 to EUR 24.64.

At the time of the parties’ 2019 observations the applicant received a monthly old-age pension of EUR 123.21. From 2019 she also received an additional monthly allowance of EUR 60.47 (from which no recovery was made). Since 1993 she has occupied municipal housing provided by the Kretinga region authorities; as of December 2016 her monthly rent was EUR 11.02. She received further modest social assistance: a monthly social-welfare allowance of EUR 5 (January 2018–March 2019), a monthly social-security pension of EUR 2.59 (December 2016 and January 2018–March 2019), and one-off lump sums of EUR 76 (January 2018) and EUR 114 (January 2019). In 2017 the difference between her actual income and the State-supported income level was not large enough to trigger additional benefits.

Lithuanian law (Code of Civil Procedure, Articles 663, 668, 736, 737 and 739) permits deductions from pensions of up to 20 per cent (or, in some cases, 50 per cent) of amounts not exceeding the minimum monthly salary, while protecting property indispensable for subsistence and sums below one minimum monthly salary (a one-time restriction). The applicant maintained that the deductions left her without adequate means of subsistence; the Government stressed that she retained the bulk of her pension, additional allowances, municipal housing and other social payments, and that the recovery served the legitimate aim of compensating the victims of her crime.

Pensions were treated analogously to salary (Article 737). Article 668 prohibited seizure of property indispensable for subsistence or of sums not exceeding the minimum monthly salary, while Article 739 protected certain social allowances. Article 663 allowed recovery from income if the debt could be cleared within six months via such deductions. Supreme Court rulings (2017–2018) confirmed that subsistence protections were “one-time” restrictions and that future income, including analogous payments, remained subject to percentage-based recovery to balance creditor and debtor interests.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s claim that the deductions interfered with her possessions, were not prescribed by law in a manner that respected her subsistence needs, and lacked proportionality given her limited income and additional (non-deducted) benefits. The Court ultimately found no violation, holding that the measure pursued the legitimate aim of protecting crime victims and did not leave the applicant devoid of all means of subsistence.

The case Atamanchuk v. Russia (no. 4493/11) arose from the 2010 criminal conviction of Vladimir Atamanchuk, a Sochi-based entrepreneur, local Democratic Party of Russia branch leader, newspaper founder and occasional freelance journalist, for two publications of an article containing statements about ethnic groups.

On 1 March 2008 Lazarevskaya Panorama (circulation 10,000) published his front-page article “Why I will not vote in these elections.” The piece criticised the impending presidential election as a farce orchestrated by political gangs that produced corruption, state-controlled propaganda and violence. It then contrasted “Russian people” with non-Russian ethnic groups historically labelled “non-Russians.” The applicant asserted that these groups, after leaving their homelands, had come to Russia and now posed as builders or entrepreneurs solely to exploit others. He described them as crowds staring greedily, holding closed-language meetings in which they declared they would defeat “Kuban people,” and ultimately intending to “burn, slaughter, rape, rob and enslave” Russians “in line with their barbaric ideas, as it was in Chechnya.” He accused them of participating in the country’s destruction and criticised official honours awarded to alleged slave traffickers. The same text was reprinted on 25 December 2009 in the applicant’s own free newspaper Sochi–Drugoy Vzglyad (circulation 8,000), distributed in letterboxes in Sochi and Lazarevskoye, together with material about the ensuing prosecution.

A pre-investigation inquiry was opened on suspicion of inciting hatred and enmity and debasing dignity on grounds of ethnicity, language, origin and religion (Article 282 § 1 of the Criminal Code). Linguistic and psychological expert reports (November 2009 and January 2010) found that the text employed “hate speech,” created an enemy image of non-Slavic groups (implicitly those from Central Asia, the North Caucasus and Transcaucasia, including Armenians), attributed criminal propensities and conspiracies to them as a whole, and could incite readers to hatred, although it contained no explicit calls to violence. A philologist’s report identified implicit incitement to violent acts. The applicant was charged for both publications.

At trial he denied guilt, describing the text as personal opinion and claiming no responsibility for the 2009 reprint. The Lazarevskiy District Court of Sochi examined the expert reports and defence witnesses but declined to summon the philologist. On 19 July 2010 it convicted him, holding that the statements were intentionally provocative, portrayed non-Russians as inherently ignorant, cruel and criminal, asserted unverifiable future violence and a conspiracy against Russians in the multi-ethnic Krasnodar Region, and thereby incited hatred. It imposed a fine of 200 000 roubles (approximately €5 086) for each publication (the first sentence being unenforceable because of the limitation period) plus a two-year ban on journalistic or publishing activity. The court noted the offences were of minor gravity, the applicant’s first, his care for an elderly mother and his status as a self-employed entrepreneur. The Krasnodar Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 8 September 2010, relying on the experts and making no finding on the unused witness. Because the remaining fine went unpaid it was later converted into 200 hours of community work.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 10 (freedom of expression) concerning the conviction, fine and activity ban, and under Article 6 (fair trial) concerning the refusal to hear the philologist.

The case of Atamanchuk v. Russia (Application no. 4493/11) originated in a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights by Russian national Vladimir Leonidovich Atamanchuk, born in 1951 and resident in Sochi. At the relevant time he led the local branch of the Democratic Party of Russia and founded the free local newspaper Sochi–Drugoy Vzglyad (circulation 8,000); he also published occasionally as a freelancer. On 1 March 2008 the local newspaper Lazarevskaya Panorama (circulation 10,000) printed his article “Why I will not vote in these elections” on its front page, alongside pro-voting statements. The piece criticised the forthcoming presidential election as a farce organised by “political gangs,” condemned state-controlled media, corruption and violence, and then turned to ethnicity. It asserted that in fifteen years of “new-style” democracy no ethnic Russian had seen any benefit and had been reduced to serving “small ethnic groupings.” Non-Russians, the author claimed, had abandoned their homelands after criminal activity, herding or prayer and now posed as builders or entrepreneurs in order to exploit others. He described “crowds of them staring at you greedily,” quoted them as plotting to “be victorious over you all” and to “hold all these Kuban people,” and predicted that once they had “paralysed our will” they would “burn, slaughter, rape, rob and enslave” as in Chechnya. The article was illustrated with the applicant’s photograph and political affiliation.

The same text was reprinted on 25 December 2009 in Sochi–Drugoy Vzglyad, which the applicant founded, paid to print and distributed free of charge in letter-boxes in the Sochi area, including Lazarevskoye. That issue also carried commentary on the ensuing criminal investigation.

A pre-investigation inquiry was opened for incitement of hatred and enmity and for degrading the dignity of a person or group on grounds of ethnicity, language, origin or religion (Article 282 § 1 of the Criminal Code). Linguistic and psychological experts (reports of November 2009 and January 2010) found that the text expressed a negative attitude toward non-Slavic groups (principally from Central Asia, the North Caucasus and Transcaucasia, including Armenians), attributed collective negative traits, employed hate speech and created an “enemy image,” but contained no explicit calls to violence. A further specialist report detected implicit incitement to violence. The applicant was charged in respect of both publications.

At trial before the Lazarevskiy District Court of Sochi the applicant pleaded not guilty, insisting the text reflected personal opinion and denying involvement in the 2009 reprint. The court refused to summon one defence specialist for oral examination. On 19 July 2010 it convicted him, holding that he had deliberately opposed ethnic Russians to other groups, attributed criminal propensities and secret plans of violence to non-Russians, and thereby incited hatred in a multi-ethnic region. It imposed a fine of RUB 200,000 (approximately EUR 5,086) for each count plus a two-year ban on journalistic or publishing activity. Because the limitation period had expired for the 2008 article, that fine and ban were not to be enforced. The Krasnodar Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 8 September 2010. After the applicant failed to pay the remaining fine it was converted in 2011 into 200 hours of community work.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention concerning the fairness of the criminal proceedings and the alleged violation of freedom of expression by the conviction, fine and professional ban.

The case of Atamanchuk v. Russia (no. 4493/11) concerns complaints under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention arising from the applicant’s criminal conviction for hate speech.

The applicant, a Sochi-based entrepreneur born in 1951, led the local Democratic Party of Russia branch, founded the newspaper Sochi–Drugoy Vzglyad (circulation 8,000) and occasionally published elsewhere as a freelancer. On 1 March 2008 Lazarevskaya Panorama (circulation 10,000) printed his front-page article “Why I will not vote in these elections,” placed opposite pro-voting statements under a large “Time to vote” headline. The piece criticised the presidential election as a “farce” staged by “political gangs,” denounced state- and oligarch-controlled media for promoting “platitudes, depravity and aggressive propaganda,” and then contrasted the plight of the “Russian person” with “small ethnic groupings.” It asserted that people whose “ethnic characteristics” disposed them to crime, herding or prayer had abandoned their homelands, entered Russia as purported builders or entrepreneurs “to get their hands into others’ pockets,” stared “greedily” from every corner, held secret meetings declaring they would “be victorious over you all” and the “Kuban people,” and would later “burn, slaughter, rape, rob and enslave” in the manner of Chechnya. The author claimed these groups were destroying the country while the President decorated “slave traffickers.” His photograph and party title appeared with the text. The identical article was reprinted on 25 December 2009 in Sochi–Drugoy Vzglyad, which also reported the applicant’s prosecution, carried comments (including a lawyer’s view that the piece contained no call to violence and an Armenian community statement) and the applicant’s reply. Both papers were distributed free of charge into letter-boxes in several Sochi streets, including Lazarevskoye.

A criminal inquiry was opened under Article 282 § 1 of the Criminal Code (incitement of hatred or enmity and humiliation of dignity on grounds of ethnicity, language, origin or religion). Linguistic and psychological experts concluded that the text displayed a negative attitude toward a non-Slavic social group (implicitly including Armenians and peoples of Central Asia, the North Caucasus and Transcaucasia), generalised negative traits, employed “hate speech” that created an enemy image, and could incite readers to hatred, yet contained no explicit calls for violence. One philologist found an implicit incitement to violence. The applicant was charged in respect of each publication.

At trial he pleaded not guilty, describing the article as personal opinion and denying responsibility for the reprint; the court found he had founded the paper, paid for the issue and distributed it. The District Court refused to summon the philologist. On 19 July 2010 it convicted him on both counts, holding that he had deliberately opposed “the Russian people” to other ethnicities, attributed criminal propensities and a conspiracy against Kuban residents, portrayed non-Russians as inherently cruel and aggressive, and thereby incited hatred in a multi-ethnic region. It imposed a fine of RUB 200,000 (approximately EUR 5,000) for each publication and a two-year ban on journalistic or publishing activity; enforcement of the first sentence was barred by limitation. The court treated the offences as of minor gravity, noted the applicant’s first-offender status, neighbourly reviews, care for an elderly mother and main occupation as entrepreneur, and justified the activity ban solely because the offences involved journalism. The Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 8 September 2010, relying on the expert reports and making no finding on the refusal to hear the philologist. The unpaid fine was later converted into 200 hours of community work.

These facts form the basis of the alleged interferences with freedom of expression and the right to a fair trial.

The case of Alexandru Marian Iancu v. Romania (Application no. 60858/15) originated in an application lodged on 4 December 2015 with the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1965 and detained in Rahova Prison, alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman detention conditions) and Article 6 § 1 (right to an impartial tribunal) of the Convention. Notice of these complaints was given to the Romanian Government on 4 May 2017; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant faced two related but distinct sets of criminal proceedings arising from economic crimes committed between 2000 and 2003 while acting as manager or director of private companies dealing in oil products and related activities. In the first set (file no. 171/P/2003), a prosecutor’s decision of 29 September 2005 sent him to trial for continuous tax evasion and conspiracy to commit money laundering, together with eight co-defendants. The charges involved falsifying accounting records to introduce illegal oil products onto the market and evade taxes. Additional acts involving other companies and a privatisation were separated into file no. 692/P/2005. On 28 November 2011 the Bucharest County Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment, taking into account specific invoices and bank transfers. On appeal, a two-judge panel of the Bucharest Court of Appeal (judges C.B. and M.A.M.) examined the case. The applicant sought acquittal and asked for consideration of evidence (police reports, tax documents and telephone transcripts) that had become the focus of the second file. After a 275-page judgment of 14 October 2014, the same panel convicted him of continuous tax evasion, conspiracy and continuous money laundering and increased the sentence to twelve years. Accusations against one co-defendant had been disjoined to the second file.

In the second set (file no. 692/P/2005), a prosecutor’s decision of 24 August 2006 sent the applicant to trial for being an accessory to fraud, two counts of incitement to abuse of office, two counts of instigation of an organised criminal group and two counts of money laundering. These charges concerned damage to the state budget arising from the privatisation of a state-owned synthetic-rubber company and involved additional companies. On 16 December 2014 the Bucharest County Court convicted him and imposed a sentence of thirteen years and eight months. The appeal began before a two-judge panel (D.D. and C.B.). At the first hearing on 11 May 2015 the prosecution successfully requested that the first-set file be attached because of overlapping civil aspects. A co-defendant then challenged both judges for bias, citing C.B.’s prior involvement in the connected first-set judgment and D.D.’s alleged prejudgment. On 20 May 2015 another panel allowed the challenge, recusing both judges on the grounds of the manner in which hearings had been conducted (short adjournments, unconsulted measures, a remark about impending time-bars) and C.B.’s implicit recognition of a strong connection between the files, including shared evidence such as an expert report. The case was reassigned to judges M.A.M. and T.G.

M.A.M. immediately applied to withdraw, noting his participation in the 14 October 2014 conviction even though the offences differed. On 2 June 2015 a different panel dismissed the request in a ten-page decision, holding that the cases involved distinct offences and (save for two defendants) different accused, that M.A.M. had expressed no opinion on guilt in the second set, and that common evidence had to be assessed separately. Subsequent recusal applications by the applicant and co-defendants, alleging contradictory rulings and the same grounds that had led to C.B.’s recusal, were rejected as raising already-examined facts or as inadmissible under the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 8 June 2015 the panel of M.A.M. and T.G. convicted the applicant with final effect of the second-set offences and sentenced him to fourteen years, relying on a different set of contracts, invoices and transfers.

Later attempts to change venue and a complaint to the Superior Council of Magistracy were unsuccessful; the Council found that recusal and withdrawal procedures had been followed and that the conviction was thoroughly reasoned. During the 4 June 2015 hearing the applicant, having persisted in challenging M.A.M. and disobeyed an order to remain silent, was found in contempt and removed. He alleged that he was then held for hours in an unsanitary, unventilated, bug-infested cell of just over two metres in height, without furniture, water or food. The Government produced evidence that the Court’s detention facilities consisted of cells equipped with toilets, sinks, running water, ventilation, heating, lighting and benches, cleaned daily; the applicant occupied a 5 m² cell alone for approximately seven hours, having breakfasted and being permitted to bring food.

These facts formed the basis of the impartiality complaint (overlap of the same appeal judge in two related proceedings whose files had originally been joined then severed, together with shared companies and some evidence) and of the Article 3 complaint concerning the one-day detention conditions. Domestic courts had rejected the bias allegations in reasoned decisions emphasising the distinct nature of the offences and the absence of any prejudgment.

These acts involved companies A, B, E, F and G and caused damage to the state budget during the privatisation of state-owned company D (synthetic-rubber production). On 16 December 2014 the County Court convicted him and imposed a sentence of 13 years and 8 months. The appeal began before a panel of judges D.D. and C.B. On 3 and 4 June 2015 the applicant’s lawyer repeatedly challenged the panel, arguing inconsistency with C.B.’s recusal and that the same judges should not have decided the withdrawal request. The challenges were rejected as already examined or inadmissible under Article 67 of the Code. Subsequent requests to change venue and a complaint to the Superior Council of Magistracy were rejected; the latter found random allocation, recusal/withdrawal procedures and reasoning fully compliant with law.

Separately, during the 4 June 2015 hearing the applicant was removed for contempt. He alleged detention for hours in an unventilated, insect-infested, windowless cell without water or food. The Government produced evidence that he was held alone for approximately seven hours in a 5 m² cell equipped with toilet, sink, running water, ventilation, lighting and benches, cleaned daily; he had breakfast and could have taken food from prison but did not request it.

The case of Alexandru Marian Iancu v. Romania (ECHR Application no. 60858/15) arose from an application lodged on 4 December 2015 by a Romanian national born in 1965, then detained in Rahova Prison. He alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman detention conditions) and Article 6 § 1 (lack of an impartial tribunal) of the Convention. Notice of these complaints was given to the Romanian Government on 4 May 2017; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant faced two related sets of criminal proceedings for financial offences committed between 2000 and 2003 in his capacity as manager or director of several private companies. In the first set (file 171/P/2003), the prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice sent him to trial on 29 September 2005 for continuous tax evasion and conspiracy to commit money laundering, together with eight co-accused (some of them foreign nationals). The charges concerned falsified accounting records relating to oil-product acquisitions, intended both to place illegal products on the market and to evade taxes. Additional alleged acts involving other suspects were disjoined into a separate file (692/P/2005). On 28 November 2011 the Bucharest County Court convicted the applicant and imposed a ten-year prison sentence. All parties appealed. A two-judge panel of the Bucharest Court of Appeal (judges C.B. and M.A.M.) examined the appeal. After considering the evidence (including material originally collected for the disjoined file) and hearing all defendants, witnesses and injured parties, the panel delivered a 275-page judgment on 14 October 2014 convicting the applicant of continuous tax evasion, conspiracy and continuous money laundering and increasing the sentence to twelve years.

In the second set (file 692/P/2005) the applicant was sent to trial on 24 August 2006 for being an accessory to fraud, two counts of incitement to abuse of office, two counts of instigation of an organised criminal group and two counts of money laundering. These charges related to significant damage caused to the State budget during the privatisation of a State-owned synthetic-rubber company and involved five co-accused. The Bucharest County Court convicted him on 16 December 2014 and imposed a sentence of thirteen years and eight months. Appeals were lodged. The first appeal hearings took place before a two-judge panel comprising D.D. and C.B. At the prosecution’s request the first-set file was attached because of perceived connections (common evidence such as expert reports and company financial documents).

On 15 May 2015 a co-defendant challenged both judges for bias, citing C.B.’s prior participation in the first-set appeal and alleged prejudgment by D.D. On 20 May 2015 another two-judge panel, after a hearing in chambers, allowed the challenge. It referred extensively to Strasbourg case-law and found a reasonable suspicion of bias arising from: the manner in which the first two hearings had been conducted (short adjournments, measures ordered without discussion, the president’s remarks about statute-barred acts); C.B.’s implicit acceptance of a strong connection when she joined the files; and the existence of overlapping evidence. Both judges were disqualified under Article 64(1)(f) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the case was randomly reassigned.

The new panel consisted of M.A.M. and T.G. On 2 June 2015 M.A.M. requested withdrawal, noting that he had sat on the 14 October 2014 panel that had convicted the applicant. A two-judge panel (T.G. and a duty judge) dismissed the request the same day in a ten-page reasoned decision. It emphasised the principles of reasonable time, random case allocation and continuity of the bench. The two sets of proceedings concerned different offences and (apart from the applicant and one co-accused) different defendants; M.A.M. had expressed no opinion on the guilt of the persons then on trial; and the possible use of overlapping evidence did not constitute prejudgment.

Subsequent recusal applications by the applicant and co-defendants, repeating the same arguments, were rejected as already examined or as inadmissible under the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 8 June 2015 the panel of M.A.M. and T.G. convicted the applicant with final effect of the charges in the second set and imposed a fourteen-year sentence. The specific contracts, invoices and transfers relied upon were different from those underpinning the first-set convictions.

Later requests by co-defendants for a change of venue, based on lingering impartiality concerns, were rejected by the High Court of Cassation and Justice. A complaint lodged by the applicant with the Superior Council of Magistracy was likewise unsuccessful: the Judicial Inspection Department found that random allocation, formation of benches and examination of recusal/withdrawal requests had complied with the law and that the relevant decisions were thoroughly reasoned.

Separately, on 4 June 2015 the applicant was found in contempt and removed from the courtroom. He alleged that he was then held for several hours in an unsanitary, insect-infested, unventilated cell of little more than two metres in height, without furniture, water or food. The Government produced evidence that the court’s detention facilities consisted of cells equipped with toilets, running water, ventilation, heating, lighting and benches, cleaned daily. The applicant had been held alone for approximately seven hours in a cell of about 5 m²; he had breakfasted before leaving prison and could have taken food with him.

Domestic law (Articles 64, 66–68 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) provides for disqualification on grounds of reasonable suspicion of bias, obligatory withdrawal, and recusal examined by another panel, with no further appeal against such interlocutory decisions. A 2012 High Court decision in the interests of the law confirmed that prior participation in connected proceedings does not automatically create incompatibility unless an opinion on the remaining accused’s guilt has been expressed.

The case of Marilena-Carmen Popa v. Romania (Application no. 1814/11) concerns the applicant’s complaints of an unfair criminal trial under Article 6 of the Convention and an unlawfully heavy penalty under Article 7. The applicant, a notary public, authenticated a land-sale contract on 28 November 2003 between two companies. In July 2005 she was indicted for continuous acts of forgery on the ground that, between January 2003 and February 2004, she had authenticated several contracts, including the November 2003 instrument, in the absence of the signatory parties.

At first instance the Bucharest Court of Appeal heard the applicant (who was legally represented) and 39 witnesses, among them E.C., the purported representative of the seller company. E.C. testified that she had never been present at the notary’s office, that the signature on the contract was not hers and that she had no connection with the company. A forensic report of 28 June 2005 confirmed that the signatures were not E.C.’s. On 9 July 2008 the Court of Appeal acquitted the applicant. It accepted that the expert report supported E.C.’s account but held that the report was not corroborated by other evidence capable of rebutting the applicant’s assertion that E.C. had in fact attended; consequently the material element of the offence had not been established.

The prosecutor appealed to the High Court of Cassation and Justice. At a hearing on 28 May 2010 the applicant’s lawyer made oral submissions and filed additional documents but neither objected nor requested further evidence. The High Court heard the applicant, who repeated that all the contracts had been signed in her presence. No witnesses were reheard. On 29 June 2010 the High Court quashed the acquittal, re-examined the merits and reclassified the charge as a single act of forgery relating solely to the November 2003 contract. It convicted the applicant, attaching decisive weight to E.C.’s testimony and the forensic report, which it described as “scientific” evidence that “erased any doubt.” The court imposed a six-month prison sentence, conditionally stayed, together with a three-year probation period.

The applicant lodged an extraordinary application for annulment, complaining that she had not been given an opportunity to comment on the reclassification, that she had not been properly heard, and that the three-year probation exceeded the statutory maximum of two years and six months (the length of the sentence plus two years). A differently constituted formation of the High Court dismissed the application as inadmissible on 16 November 2010, observing that the applicant had been heard and that her lawyer had submitted evidence; it did not examine the length of the probation period.

These facts underpin the applicant’s allegations that the final court overturned her acquittal without a direct assessment of the key witness evidence, that she was deprived of a proper opportunity to address the reclassified charge, and that the probation period constituted a heavier penalty than that prescribed by law.

The case of Marilena-Carmen Popa v. Romania (Application no. 1814/11) concerns a Romanian notary public convicted of forgery after an initial acquittal was overturned. Born in 1960 and practising in Bucharest until her 2010 removal from the notaries’ register, the applicant authenticated a land-sale contract on 28 November 2003 between S.C. V. S.R.L. (represented by E.C.) and S.C. O.E. S.R.L. On 1 July 2005 the prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice indicted her for continuous acts of forgery, alleging that between 31 January 2003 and 9 February 2004 she had authenticated several contracts, including the November 2003 instrument, in the absence of the signatory parties.

The Bucharest Court of Appeal, sitting as first-instance court, heard the applicant (assisted by counsel) and 39 witnesses, among them E.C. E.C. testified that she had never been present at the notary’s office, that the signature on the contract was not hers, and that she had no knowledge of or connection to S.C. V. S.R.L. A forensic expert report of 28 June 2005 confirmed that the signatures were not E.C.’s. On 9 July 2008 the Court of Appeal acquitted the applicant. It reasoned that the forensic conclusion had not been corroborated by other evidence capable of rebutting the applicant’s assertion that E.C. had in fact been present; consequently the material element of the offence was lacking.

The prosecutor appealed on points of fact and law. At a hearing on 28 May 2010 before the High Court of Cassation and Justice the applicant’s lawyer made oral submissions and filed additional documents but raised no preliminary objections and requested no further evidence. The applicant herself was heard and reiterated that all contracting parties had signed in her presence. No witnesses were reheard. In a final judgment of 29 June 2010 the High Court quashed the acquittal, re-examined the merits, reclassified the charge as a single act of forgery relating solely to the 28 November 2003 contract, and convicted the applicant. It relied principally on E.C.’s statement and the forensic report, describing the latter as “an aspect of scientific order which erases any doubt.” The court imposed a six-month prison sentence whose execution was conditionally stayed, together with a three-year probation period.

An interlocutory decision of 15 July 2010 corrected certain clerical errors but left the probation term unchanged. On 2 July 2010 the applicant lodged an extraordinary application for annulment, complaining that she had not been given an opportunity to address the reclassification, that the High Court had not heard her properly, and that the three-year probation exceeded the statutory maximum (sentence plus two years). A differently constituted High Court rejected the application as inadmissible on 16 November 2010, noting that the applicant had been heard and that her lawyer had confined himself to documentary submissions; it did not address the probation issue.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 that the High Court had overturned her acquittal without rehearing the decisive witness E.C. and without allowing her to comment on the reclassification, and under Article 7 that the three-year probation constituted a heavier penalty than the law permitted. These complaints were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
