In July 2005 the prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice indicted her for continuous acts of forgery, asserting that between January 2003 and February 2004 she had authenticated several contracts, including the November 2003 contract, in the absence of the contracting parties.

The Bucharest Court of Appeal, sitting as first-instance court, heard the applicant (assisted by counsel) and 39 witnesses, among them E.C., the purported representative of the seller company. E.C. testified that she had not been present at the notary’s office, that the signature on the contract was not hers, and that she had no connection with the company. A forensic expert report of 28 June 2005 confirmed that the signatures were not E.C.’s. On 9 July 2008 the Court of Appeal acquitted the applicant. It reasoned that the forensic conclusions had not been corroborated by other evidence capable of rebutting the applicant’s assertion that E.C. had in fact been present and signed the document; consequently the material element of the offence had not been established.

The prosecutor appealed on points of fact and law. At a hearing on 28 May 2010 the High Court of Cassation and Justice heard oral argument from the applicant (who repeated that all parties had signed in her presence) and received additional documents from her lawyer; no preliminary objections were raised and no request was made to adduce further evidence. No witnesses were reheard. By final judgment of 29 June 2010 the High Court quashed the acquittal, re-examined the merits, reclassified the charge as a single act of forgery relating solely to the November 2003 contract, convicted the applicant and imposed a six-month prison sentence whose execution was conditionally stayed, together with a three-year probation period. The High Court treated E.C.’s statement, corroborated by the forensic report, as scientifically decisive and as eliminating any remaining doubt.

An interlocutory decision of 15 July 2010 corrected certain clerical errors but left the probation period unchanged. The applicant’s subsequent extraordinary application for annulment (contestaţie în anulare) argued that she had not been properly heard, that she had been denied the opportunity to comment on the reclassification, and that the three-year probation exceeded the statutory maximum of two years and six months (the term of the sentence plus two years under Article 82 of the former Criminal Code). On 16 November 2010 a differently composed High Court panel declared the application inadmissible, holding that the applicant had been heard and that her lawyer had submitted only documentary evidence. Following the conviction the Ministry of Justice struck the applicant from the register of notaries public.

These facts form the basis of the complaints: that the final-instance court overturned an acquittal without directly assessing the decisive witness evidence and without allowing adequate comment on the reclassification (Article 6), and that the probation period imposed a heavier penalty than that prescribed by law (Article 7).

**Case Summary: Jidic v. Romania (Application no. 45776/16)**

The applicant, Stelian Jidic (born 1964), a professional driver living in Bucharest, was involved in an incident on 16 July 2012 while driving a company car with a friend. After a heated verbal dispute with occupants of another vehicle, the friend alighted to intervene. The applicant then engaged the gear, causing the car to move and slightly injure the friend. Police administered a breathalyser test showing a blood-alcohol concentration exceeding the legal limit of 0.8 g/l. The applicant’s driving licence was immediately withheld and he was suspended from driving. A subsequent forensic toxicology report (28 December 2012, confirmed 2 July 2014) verified the excess alcohol.

Criminal proceedings were instituted of the authorities’ own motion only on 22 November 2013 (more than 16 months after the incident) under Article 87 § 1 of Government Ordinance no. 195/2002 (old law), which punished the offence solely by imprisonment of one to five years. The new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 February 2014. Article 336 § 1 thereof provided the same offence with alternative penalties of imprisonment (one to five years) or a fine. Article 5 required application of the more lenient law. The legal classification was accordingly changed to the new Code (30 April 2014) and the applicant was charged under it (5 August 2014). He consistently admitted the essential facts, requested expedition because the driving suspension had cost him his livelihood (he sold his apartment and could not retrain at his age), and sought a summary procedure.

At first instance the Bucharest District Court (8 October 2015) applied the new Code. It found the conditions for postponement of sentence met (no prior convictions, admission of guilt, social integration, modest seriousness of the offence committed on a quiet road) and imposed a ten-month prison term whose execution was postponed for two years, without a driving ban. The court considered the new law more lenient because postponement or waiver would avoid automatic licence revocation under residual provisions of the Ordinance.

The prosecutor appealed, arguing that the offence was too serious (very high alcohol level, injury caused, initial denial, heated dispute) to justify postponement and that the old law was in fact more favourable because it permitted suspension of a sentence of less than four years with automatic rehabilitation after a supervision period. On 2 February 2016 the Bucharest Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment, applied the old law, convicted the applicant of the Ordinance offence, sentenced him to three years and four months’ imprisonment (reduced by one-third for the guilty plea) plus accessory penalties, and suspended both the sentence and accessories for seven years subject to conditions that included a driving ban. It held that the old law’s suspension regime was more lenient in concreto for the applicant.

The applicant complained under Articles 6 and 13 that the proceedings (incident July 2012, investigation delayed until late 2013, forensic reports slow, trial 2015, final judgment February 2016) were excessively lengthy and that no effective remedy existed, during which time the driving suspension had ruined him financially. Under Article 7 he alleged that the appellate court’s retrospective application of the old law violated the principle that the more lenient criminal law must be applied. He maintained that the new Code, by permitting postponement or waiver (and thereby avoiding licence revocation), was the milder law. The Government contended that leniency had to be assessed in the concrete circumstances of the case, including the manner of serving the sentence, and that the old-law suspension regime with automatic rehabilitation was more favourable.

The ECHR case of Jidic v. Romania (application no. 45776/16, judgment of 18 February 2020) concerned alleged violations of Articles 6, 13 and 7 of the Convention. The applicant, a Romanian professional driver born in 1964, was involved in an incident on 16 July 2012. While driving his company car with a friend during a heated verbal dispute with occupants of another vehicle, the applicant shifted into gear after his friend exited the car, causing a slight injury. Police breathalyser and subsequent forensic tests confirmed his blood alcohol level exceeded the 0.8 g/l legal limit. His driving licence was immediately withheld and he was suspended from driving, preventing him from working in his profession.

Criminal proceedings were instituted on 22 November 2013 by the Bucharest traffic police (confirmed by prosecutors) under Article 87 § 1 of Government Ordinance no. 195/2002 (old law), which punished driving with excess alcohol solely by 1–5 years’ imprisonment. After the new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 February 2014, the legal classification was changed in April 2014 to Article 336 § 1 of the new Code (imprisonment of 1–5 years or a fine), invoking Article 5 of the new Code requiring application of the more lenient law. The applicant was charged under the new provision in August 2014. Despite his March 2015 request to expedite (citing inability to work, financial hardship, sale of his apartment, health issues and a simple, admitted case), the case reached trial in April 2015.

At the Bucharest District Court, the applicant admitted the offence and requested a summary procedure (entitling him to a one-third penalty reduction). Prosecutors sought reclassification to the old law as more lenient for individualisation and urged a suspended sentence. The applicant argued the new law was more lenient, as it permitted postponement or waiver of sentence (avoiding licence revocation under remaining Ordinance provisions) given his clean record, remorse, social integration, non-busy road and the already-served punitive effect of lengthy suspension. On 8 October 2015 the District Court applied the new law, convicted him, imposed a 10-month prison sentence (reduced by one-third) whose imposition was postponed for two years’ probation without a driving ban.

Prosecutors appealed, contending the sentence was inadequate given the high alcohol level, injury risk and applicant’s conduct, and that the old law was more favourable for suspended sentences (automatic rehabilitation if no reoffending). On 2 February 2016 the Bucharest Court of Appeal quashed the judgment, applied the old law as more lenient in concreto (considering conditions for suspending service), convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 3 years and 4 months’ imprisonment (within reduced limits), plus additional penalties (loss of voting/electoral rights and ban on public-office posts). It suspended both the prison term and additional penalties for seven years, imposing conditions including a driving ban.

The applicant alleged excessively lengthy proceedings (from 2012 incident to 2016 final judgment, with delays in investigation and forensics in a straightforward case) without an effective domestic remedy (Articles 6 and 13), and that applying the old law (rather than the allegedly more lenient new law allowing postponement/waiver and avoiding licence revocation) breached the principle of retrospective application of the more lenient criminal law (Article 7). The Court examined these complaints, emphasising that leniency assessment must be in concreto (including manner of sentence service) rather than abstracto.

**CASE OF JIDIC v. ROMANIA (Application no. 45776/16)**

The applicant, a Romanian professional driver born in 1964, was involved in an incident on 16 July 2012. While driving his company car during a verbal dispute with occupants of another vehicle, he accidentally shifted into gear after his passenger (a friend) exited, causing the car to bump into and slightly injure the friend. Police administered a breathalyser test showing a blood-alcohol level exceeding the 0.8 g/l legal limit, withheld his licence, suspended him from driving, and arranged forensic blood testing. A December 2012 toxicology report confirmed the excess alcohol.

Criminal proceedings began on 22 November 2013 under Article 87 § 1 of Government Ordinance no. 195/2002 (old law), which punished driving with excess blood alcohol solely by 1–5 years’ imprisonment. The applicant admitted the facts but claimed the car had been parked and the contact accidental. After the new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 February 2014, investigators reclassified the offence under its Article 336 § 1 (punishable by 1–5 years’ imprisonment or a fine). Article 5 of the new Code required application of the more lenient law where successive laws applied. The applicant was charged under the new provision in August 2014. He repeatedly requested expedition, stressing that licence suspension had prevented him from working, exhausted his resources, forced him to sell his apartment, and caused health problems; at his age retraining was impractical. The case reached trial in 2015.

At first instance the Bucharest District Court (October 2015) applied the new Code as more lenient. It convicted the applicant under a summary procedure (one-third penalty reduction for admission of guilt), imposed a 10-month prison term but postponed its imposition for two years’ probation, and imposed no driving ban. The court cited the offence’s limited seriousness (not on a busy road), the applicant’s clean record, remorse, social integration and employment history, concluding that postponement sufficed for rehabilitation.

The prosecutor appealed, arguing the offence was grave (high alcohol level, injury risk, initial denial, verbal dispute) and that the old law was more favourable because it permitted suspension of sentence with automatic rehabilitation after a supervision period. On 2 February 2016 the Bucharest Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, applied the old law as more lenient “in concreto,” convicted the applicant of a 3-year-4-month prison term (reduced by one-third), suspended its serving (and additional penalties such as loss of civic rights) for seven years’ supervision, and imposed a driving ban during that period. The court emphasised general and special prevention, the alcohol level, post-offence conduct and the need for a penalty within statutory limits.

The applicant complained under Article 7 that the appeal court had wrongly applied the old law, denying him the new Code’s more lenient options (fine, waiver or postponement of sentence). Under the new Code those options would have avoided licence revocation under the still-applicable Ordinance provisions, enabling him to resume driving and work. He also alleged (Articles 6 and 13) that the proceedings from 2012–2016 were excessively long, leaving him unable to work, and that no effective domestic remedy existed.

(The ECtHR later held that leniency must be assessed in concreto, including the manner of serving any sentence, and that the new law’s theoretically milder options had not been found applicable on the facts.)
001-201331:
The case of Abukauskai v. Lithuania (Application no. 72065/17) concerned three Lithuanian applicants (a married couple and their son) who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the State's failure to conduct an effective criminal investigation into the arson of the couple's house.

On 30 May 2013, the first and second applicants' house was deliberately set on fire in the early morning. They escaped through a window and suspected their neighbour P.K., with whom they had an ongoing conflict. Police immediately opened a pre-trial investigation under Article 187 § 2 of the Criminal Code (destruction of property in a manner dangerous to people). That day, officers inspected the scene, collected fire debris and footprints (the latter lacking identifiable characteristics), and deployed a police dog. The dog tracked a scent from rear footprints to P.K.'s yard but stopped amid loose cattle; the handler then checked the back of P.K.'s house without reaction. P.K. was arrested, swabbed, and notified as a suspect; he denied involvement, claiming he had been asleep and routinely passed the applicants' house to reach his pasture. A search of his house occurred about ten hours later and yielded no flammable liquids, related clothing, or other evidence. P.K. later provided the clothes and shoes he claimed to have worn.

Subsequent steps included soil sampling (an expert found no match between soil on P.K.'s shoes and samples from the applicants' property), forensic examination of debris, P.K.'s clothing/shoes, and hand swabs (traces of machine oil appeared on the clothing but none of any flammable liquid on the debris or swabs; the expert noted the volatility of such liquids and that P.K.'s items had been wrapped in non-hermetic paper rather than sealed containers), review of P.K.'s phone records (unhelpful), and interviews of neighbours, the applicants, P.K., and the dog handler (neighbours provided no information). The applicants were granted victim and civil-claimant status.

In January 2014 the prosecutor discontinued proceedings against P.K. for lack of direct evidence (no forensic links, no witnesses, P.K.'s denial, and the applicants' statements deemed unreliable due to the conflict) and suspended the investigation as the perpetrator could not be identified. The applicants did not appeal.

In March 2014 they complained to the prosecutor of incompetent and delayed measures that may have lost evidence, claiming approximately LTL 500,000 (EUR 144,810) in property damage. A disciplinary inquiry found irregularities: the dog handler should have had the cattle removed to continue tracking to P.K.'s front door; the search was delayed, failed to verify or seize P.K.'s actual clothing at arrest, did not seize potentially relevant items, and was conducted while P.K. was outside; and evidence packaging breached regulations requiring hermetic sealing. The prosecutor concluded the errors had not necessarily affected the outcome and imposed no penalties (time-barred). The applicants did not appeal.

In March 2015 they sued the State under Article 6.272 of the Civil Code for pecuniary damage (the destroyed property's value) and non-pecuniary damage, arguing the police errors had irreversibly prevented identification of the arsonist. The Panevėžys District Court dismissed the claim, finding the dog handler had acted reasonably (the dog lost the trail and did not bark, indicating the footprint-leaver was absent), the packaging issue immaterial (no flammable liquid identified on debris anyway), the search adequate (based on officer and P.K. testimony that the same clothes were later provided and no relevant items or odours were present), and other measures prompt; non-identification alone did not prove lack of diligence.

The Panevėžys Regional Court partially allowed the appeal, endorsing the disciplinary findings of insufficient diligence and holding that proper action might have clarified more circumstances. It awarded modest non-pecuniary damages (EUR 900 each to the first two applicants, EUR 200 to the third) but rejected pecuniary claims for lack of direct causal link between the errors and the fire damage.

The Supreme Court reversed, upholding the first-instance dismissal. Citing Blumberga v. Latvia, it held that the State's investigative obligation for property crimes is less stringent than for violent crimes and is breached only by "flagrant and serious" deficiencies. It found none here: the handler's decision around the cattle was rational, and even identified P.K. footprints would prove only proximity, not arson; because no accelerant was identified on the debris, proper search or packaging could not have linked P.K. to the fire. Thus there was no causal connection between any shortcomings and the failure to identify a perpetrator. (The applicants had not raised risks to life or health before domestic courts.)

The case of Abukauskai v. Lithuania involved three Lithuanian nationals—Feliksas Augėnius Abukauskas, his wife Vladislava Abukauskienė, and their son Gintaras Abukauskas—who alleged that Lithuanian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the arson of their home, violating the State's positive obligations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (protection of property).

On 30 May 2013, the first and second applicants' house caught fire in the early morning. Firefighters determined the blaze was started deliberately. The couple escaped through a window and suspected their neighbor P.K., with whom they had an ongoing conflict. Police immediately opened a pre-trial investigation into the destruction of property in a dangerous manner (Criminal Code Article 187 § 2). That day, officers inspected the site, collected fire debris, and noted footprints lacking distinctive features. A police dog tracked a scent from the rear of the house to P.K.'s yard but stopped there (later disputed as due to loose cattle or a lost trail). P.K. was arrested, denied involvement (claiming he was asleep and regularly walked past the house), and provided hand swabs. A search of his home about 10 hours later yielded no flammable liquids or related items. The next day, he provided the clothes and shoes he said he had worn.

Subsequent forensics showed that soil on P.K.'s shoes did not match samples from the applicants' property. Examination of the debris (packaged in sealed plastic) found no flammable liquids, while P.K.'s items (wrapped in unsealed paper) showed machine oil traces but no accelerants; experts noted that volatile liquids might have evaporated or burned away. Phone records, neighbor interviews, and questioning of the applicants, P.K., and the dog handler produced no useful leads. The applicants were granted victim and civil claimant status.

In January 2014, the prosecutor discontinued the case against P.K. for lack of direct evidence, forensic links, or witnesses, viewing the applicants' statements as unreliable given the conflict, and suspended the investigation as the perpetrator remained unidentified. The applicants did not appeal. In March 2014, they complained of an incompetent and delayed investigation that risked losing evidence, citing roughly €144,810 in damage. A disciplinary inquiry identified irregularities: incomplete dog tracking (the handler should have continued after removing cattle), a delayed search that failed to seize P.K.'s worn clothing and occurred while he was outside, and non-hermetic packaging contrary to regulations. The prosecutor found these errors had “not necessarily affected” the outcome and imposed no sanctions due to time limits. The applicants did not appeal.

In 2015, they sued the State civilly, arguing the flaws caused irreversible loss of evidence that prevented identifying the arsonist. They claimed pecuniary damages for destroyed property (€31,400 jointly for the first two applicants, €2,600 for the third) and €3,000 each in non-pecuniary damages. The Panevėžys District Court dismissed the claim in March 2016, holding that the dog handler had acted reasonably (the trail was lost and the dog did not indicate P.K.'s presence; P.K. had already been arrested), that packaging was immaterial because no accelerant was identified on the debris (so traces on clothing could not have linked P.K.), and that the search was adequate (P.K. was present, wore the same clothes, and no items or tampering risk existed). Other steps were prompt, and non-identification did not prove lack of diligence.

The Panevėžys Regional Court partially allowed an appeal in September 2016, finding diligence failures that could have clarified more circumstances. It awarded non-pecuniary damages (€900 each to the first two applicants, €200 to the third) but rejected pecuniary claims for lack of a direct causal link. The Supreme Court reversed this in April 2017, restoring the dismissal. Citing Blumberga v. Latvia, it held that while the State has a positive duty to protect property rights, the investigative obligation is less stringent for property crimes than for violent ones and is breached only by “flagrant and serious” deficiencies. The errors here were neither significant nor decisive: even proper tracking would have shown only that P.K. walked past the house, not that he committed arson; unidentified accelerant meant even a timely, sealed search could not have linked him. Thus, no causal connection existed between the shortcomings and the unidentified perpetrator.

These events formed the core of the applicants' claim that the investigation's deficiencies breached the State's duties under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case Summary: Abukauskai v. Lithuania (ECHR, Application no. 72065/17)**

On 30 May 2013, the house of the first and second applicants (husband and wife) in Lithuania caught fire around 3:15 a.m.; firefighters determined it was arson. The applicants escaped through a window and suspected their neighbor P.K., with whom they had a long-standing conflict. Their son (third applicant) was not present. Police immediately opened a pre-trial investigation under Article 187 § 2 of the Criminal Code for destruction of property in a manner dangerous to people.

Investigators inspected the scene, collected fire debris, and noted footprints lacking distinctive features. A police dog tracked a scent from rear footprints toward P.K.’s property but stopped in his yard amid loose cattle; the handler circled the house without further reaction or barking. P.K. was arrested the same day, denied involvement (claiming he was asleep and regularly passed the house to tend cattle), and provided hand swabs. A search of his home occurred about 10 hours later, yielding no flammable liquids or related items; he was outside milking cows at the time. P.K. later supplied the clothes and shoes he said he had worn. Soil samples from near both properties did not match traces on P.K.’s shoes. Forensic examination (October 2013) found machine oil on P.K.’s clothes and shoes but no flammable liquids on the debris or swabs. Samples of clothes, shoes, and swabs had been wrapped in non-hermetic paper (contrary to rules requiring sealed plastic, glass, or metal containers for volatile substances), while debris was properly packaged; experts noted that liquids could have evaporated, burned away, or been washed out. Telephone records, neighbor interviews, and questioning of the parties produced no useful evidence. Applicants were granted victim and civil claimant status.

In January 2014 the prosecutor discontinued proceedings against P.K. for lack of direct, indisputable evidence (no forensic link, no witnesses, P.K.’s denial, and applicants’ statements deemed unreliable due to the conflict) and suspended the investigation as the perpetrator remained unidentified. Applicants did not appeal. They later complained to the prosecutor of incompetent and delayed measures that may have lost evidence; a 2014 disciplinary inquiry identified procedural errors (dog handler should have removed cattle and continued tracking; delayed/incomplete search without seizing arrest-day clothes or ensuring P.K.’s presence; improper packaging) but found they “had not necessarily affected” the outcome. No sanctions were imposed due to the one-year time bar. Applicants did not appeal.

In 2015 applicants sued the State under Civil Code Article 6.272 for pecuniary damage (destroyed/damaged property, ~EUR 34,000 total) and non-pecuniary damage, arguing police errors made identification of the perpetrator impossible. The Panevėžys District Court dismissed the claim, finding the dog handler acted rationally (trail lost, no barking indicating P.K.’s presence), packaging was immaterial (no accelerant identified on debris), search testimony was credible, and other steps were prompt; absence of an identified perpetrator did not prove lack of diligence. The Regional Court reversed in part, finding insufficient diligence that might have clarified more facts, awarding modest non-pecuniary damages (EUR 900 each to the first two applicants, EUR 200 to the third) but rejecting pecuniary claims for lack of direct causal link. The Supreme Court (2017) quashed the Regional decision and restored the District Court’s dismissal. Citing Blumberga v. Latvia, it held that the State’s positive obligation to investigate property crimes is less stringent than for violent offenses and is breached only by “flagrant and serious” deficiencies. The alleged errors were neither significant nor decisive: even successful tracking would not prove arson; unidentified accelerant meant proper packaging or an earlier search could not have linked P.K. to the fire. Thus there was no causal connection to the failure to identify the perpetrator. Applicants had not raised risks to life or health in domestic proceedings.

The ECHR application alleged that the inconclusive investigation violated the State’s positive obligations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court declared other complaints inadmissible and examined only this issue.
001-201649:
The case of Dyagilev v. Russia (Application no. 49972/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a complaint under Article 9 of the Convention (freedom of thought, conscience and religion). The applicant, Maksim Andreyevich Dyagilev (born 1990, resident in St Petersburg), alleged that Russian authorities unlawfully dismissed his request to replace compulsory military service with alternative civilian service on grounds of pacifist conscientious objection.

After graduating in 2014 with a master’s degree in philosophy, Dyagilev became liable for conscription. In late August 2014 he attended a legal seminar organised by the Committee of Soldiers’ Mothers, which he later described as having crystallised his pacifist views (though he initially characterised the seminar as a means of finding a “lawful way to avoid military service”). On 4 September 2014 he applied to the local military commissariat for civilian service, attaching only his curriculum vitae and a workplace recommendation letter. The application was examined by a seven-member military recruitment commission (comprising a district administration deputy head as president, military commissariat officials, a medical officer, a police representative, an education official and an employment-office deputy head). On 25 November 2014 the commission dismissed the request, finding the submitted materials insufficiently persuasive to establish genuine pacifism.

Dyagilev immediately challenged the decision in court. While those proceedings were pending he lodged a second, identical application (9 February 2015), which was rejected as repetitive. On 25 February 2015 the Frunzenskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed his complaint. The court observed that neither the CV nor the recommendation mentioned humanist or pacifist convictions, that such views ought to have formed over time rather than crystallising spontaneously after a single seminar, and that the evidence as a whole failed to prove the claimed beliefs.

On 12 August 2015 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It stressed that the constitutional right to alternative service does not confer an unconditional choice between military and civilian service, nor does a mere negative attitude toward the army suffice. Drawing on ECHR case-law, the court held that only a serious and insurmountable conflict between the duty to serve and deeply held convictions attracts Article 9 protection. An applicant must therefore substantiate the claim by stating reasons and circumstances, listing supporting facts and adducing evidence. Dyagilev’s CV referred to philosophical influences, his brother’s army stories and the seminar; the workplace reference listed mixed personal qualities. Neither document demonstrated deep convictions incompatible with military service, and he submitted no further material at any stage. He therefore failed to prove the requisite conflict. Subsequent cassation appeals were rejected (November 2015 and March 2016).

Russian law (Constitution Art. 59; Civilian Service Act) entitles a citizen to alternative service where convictions or religious beliefs conflict with military duty. Applications must be lodged within statutory time-limits, accompanied by a CV, a reference and any other supporting documents, and must explain the reasons for the request. The recruitment commission examines the application in the applicant’s presence, considers oral statements and documents, and issues a reasoned decision that may be challenged in the ordinary courts (with automatic suspensive effect). The courts conduct a full review of lawfulness, including whether the applicant’s rights were breached and whether procedural requirements were observed.

The applicant contended that the dismissal of his request, and the manner in which it was examined, violated his Article 9 rights. The Court ultimately found no violation, holding that he had failed to substantiate a genuine conscientious objection and that an effective, independent procedure with judicial review had been available.

**Case Summary: Dyagilev v. Russia (Application no. 49972/16, ECtHR, 10 March 2020)**

The applicant, Maksim Andreyevich Dyagilev (born 1990, resident in St Petersburg), a Russian national, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 August 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention. Represented by lawyers from St Petersburg, he complained primarily under Article 9 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion) that Russian authorities dismissed his request to replace compulsory military service with alternative civilian service, despite his claimed pacifist convictions. The Government of the Russian Federation contested the claim. The Movement of Conscientious Objectors was granted leave to intervene as a third party. Notice of the complaint was given on 29 June 2017, with the remainder of the application declared inadmissible.

In 2014, after obtaining a master’s degree in philosophy from Herzen State Pedagogical University, Dyagilev became liable for conscription. In late August 2014, seeking a “lawful way to avoid military service,” he attended a legal seminar organised by the Committee of Soldiers’ Mothers in St Petersburg. He later claimed this event allowed him to understand and crystallise his adherence to pacifist philosophy. On 4 September 2014, he applied to the Frunzenskiy district military commissariat for assignment to civilian service, attaching his curriculum vitae and a letter of recommendation from his workplace.

The application was examined by a seven-member military recruitment commission. Members included the deputy head of the Frunzenskiy district administration (as president), the head of the local military commissariat, a commissariat secretary, a medical officer for conscript certification, a deputy head of neighbourhood and juvenile police, a head of the district educational department, and a deputy head of the employment office. On 25 November 2014, the commission dismissed the request, finding the submitted documents and information insufficiently persuasive to establish that Dyagilev was a genuine pacifist.

The next day, Dyagilev initiated court proceedings challenging the decision, again submitting his CV and recommendation. While those proceedings were pending, he lodged a second identical application on 9 February 2015, which was rejected as repetitive without merits examination. On 25 February 2015, the Frunzenskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed his complaint. It held that humanist or pacifist convictions were not mentioned in his CV or recommendation letter; such views must form over a period of time rather than crystallising spontaneously; and the circumstances he relied upon were unproven considering the intertwined evidence.

On 12 August 2015, the St Petersburg City Court upheld the first-instance judgment on appeal. Dyagilev did not attend the hearing or submit new evidence. The appeal court emphasised that the right to alternative service is not an unconditional choice and that a mere negative attitude toward military service is insufficient. Citing ECtHR case-law, it stated that only a serious and insurmountable conflict between military obligations and deeply held beliefs attracts Article 9 protection. Applicants must substantiate reasons, circumstances, facts confirming deep convictions, and relevant evidence. Dyagilev’s CV referred to philosophical influences, his brother’s army stories, and the seminar as the point of crystallisation, while the employer reference listed mixed qualities but no evidence of convictions preventing military service. He provided no further information to the commission or courts and thus failed to prove the required conflict. Subsequent cassation appeals were dismissed by the St Petersburg City Court (3 November 2015) and the Supreme Court (24 March 2016), fully endorsing the appeal court’s reasoning.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 9 violation: the rejection of his conscientious objection claim despite the constitutional right (Article 59) to alternative civilian service where convictions preclude military service, as implemented by the Civilian Service Act (requiring substantiation of conflicting beliefs, examination by a mixed commission, reasoned decisions, and court review with automatic suspension of the disputed decision). The ECtHR ultimately found no violation, citing the applicant’s failure to substantiate the seriousness of his objection and the existence of an effective, accessible procedure with sufficient guarantees, independence, and judicial review.

The case of Dyagilev v. Russia (Application no. 49972/16), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 10 March 2020, concerns an alleged violation of Article 9 of the Convention (freedom of conscience). The applicant, Maksim Andreyevich Dyagilev, a Russian national born in 1990 and living in St Petersburg, complained that his request to replace compulsory military service with alternative civilian service as a conscientious objector was wrongly dismissed.

Dyagilev obtained a master’s degree in philosophy from Herzen State Pedagogical University in 2014, after which he became liable for conscription. In late August 2014 he attended a legal seminar organised by the Committee of Soldiers’ Mothers in St Petersburg. He later described this as allowing him to understand his pacifist philosophy and as a “lawful way to avoid military service.”

On 4 September 2014 he applied to the Frunzenskiy district military commissariat for assignment to alternative civilian service. He attached only his curriculum vitae (listing education and stating that his views had been shaped by philosophers and his brother’s accounts of army life) and a work recommendation letter. The application was examined by a seven-member military recruitment commission chaired by a deputy head of the district administration and including the head of the local military commissariat, a commissariat secretary, a medical officer, a police representative, an education-department head and an employment-office deputy head.

On 25 November 2014 the commission dismissed the application, finding the materials insufficiently persuasive that Dyagilev was a genuine pacifist. He immediately challenged the decision in court. A second identical application lodged while the first challenge was pending was rejected as repetitive.

On 25 February 2015 the Frunzenskiy District Court dismissed his complaint. It observed that neither the CV nor the recommendation mentioned humanist or pacifist convictions and that such beliefs could not arise spontaneously; they had to form over time. The court held that the circumstances relied upon were unproven.

On 12 August 2015 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment. It recalled that the constitutional right to alternative service is not an unconditional choice and requires proof of a serious, insurmountable conflict between military duty and deeply held beliefs (citing ECHR case-law). Dyagilev’s evidence—philosophers’ influence, his brother’s stories and the seminar—was inadequate; the recommendation listed both positive and negative traits but said nothing about convictions. He had supplied no further documents, witnesses or information at any stage. Subsequent cassation appeals to the City Court and the Supreme Court were dismissed on the same reasoning.

Russian law (Constitution Article 59(3) and the Civilian Service Act) permits replacement of military service where personal convictions or religious beliefs conflict with it. An application must set out reasons, be accompanied by a CV and personal reference, and may include other documents or named witnesses. The mixed commission examines the request in the applicant’s presence, may gather additional material, and decides by simple majority; two-thirds attendance constitutes a quorum. Dismissal is possible if the materials fail to prove a genuine conflict. Decisions are automatically suspended and fully reviewable by courts of general jurisdiction, which assess lawfulness, procedural compliance and any breach of rights.

The alleged Article 9 violation therefore turned on whether the commission and courts had properly examined the sincerity and cogency of Dyagilev’s claimed conscientious objection, whether the procedure afforded sufficient guarantees of independence and impartiality, and whether the applicant had been given a genuine opportunity to substantiate his beliefs.
001-202119:
The case of Mraović v. Croatia (Application no. 30373/13) concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that the applicant, Josip Mraović, was denied a public hearing in criminal proceedings against him for rape.

On 14 April 2005, I.J., a professional basketball player, reported to police that Mraović had sexually assaulted her. He was arrested the same day. The next day, local police issued a detailed media statement disclosing I.J.’s identity and personal details. This prompted a successful damages action by I.J. against the State for the privacy breach.

Mraović was indicted on 30 June 2005 in the Gospić County Court. At his request, those proceedings were closed to protect the private lives of both him and the victim. He was acquitted on 1 December 2005. On appeal by the State Attorney, the Supreme Court (sitting in private, with OSCE observers admitted under a confidentiality instruction) quashed the acquittal on 14 December 2006 and remitted the case.

The retrial was transferred to the Rijeka County Court. At the first hearing on 13 September 2007, Mraović applied for an open trial. He argued that OSCE representatives had already attended the Supreme Court sitting, that I.J. had given multiple media interviews about the case, and that closed proceedings had allowed the media to stigmatise him without objective reporting of the evidence. The prosecution opposed, stating that the reasons for exclusion persisted. After hearing both sides, the court excluded the public throughout to protect the victim’s private life (and, incidentally, the applicant’s) under the Criminal Procedure Act. The decision was pronounced publicly.

Mraović repeated the request on 3 December 2007, citing four further interviews in which I.J. had disclosed private details and parts of her investigative statement. The court again refused. I.J. testified the next day (appearing distressed while the applicant reportedly grinned). Media coverage of her evidence continued. Mraović later complained that I.J.’s lawyer had breached confidentiality by speaking to the press.

On 7 February 2008 the Rijeka County Court convicted Mraović of rape and imposed a three-year sentence. The pronouncement of judgment was public and televised.

On appeal, Mraović argued that the exclusion of the public had been unjustified. After a closed hearing, the Supreme Court on 8 June 2009 upheld the conviction (reducing the sentence to two years). It held that exclusion was lawful to protect the victim given the intimate nature of the offence; the defence’s change of position from the first trial did not alter this. Minor procedural irregularities (failure to supply a written decision) did not affect the outcome. The Constitutional Court dismissed a further complaint on 8 November 2012.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation: the wholesale exclusion of the public from the retrial (despite the victim’s own media statements, the initial police leak of her identity, and the applicant’s request for publicity to counter stigma), the courts’ repeated refusals, and the subsequent domestic review finding no breach. The conviction itself was pronounced publicly.

The case of Mraović v. Croatia concerned an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a public hearing) arising from the exclusion of the public from the entirety of the applicant’s retrial on rape charges.

On 14 April 2005 I.J., a professional basketball player, reported to police that the applicant had sexually assaulted her. He was arrested the same day. The following day the local police issued a detailed media statement that disclosed the victim’s identity and personal details; she later obtained damages from the State for this breach of privacy. The applicant was indicted on 30 June 2005. At his request the first-instance trial in Gospić County Court was held in camera to protect the private lives of both parties. He was acquitted on 1 December 2005.

The State Attorney appealed. At a closed sitting on 14 December 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the acquittal and remitted the case, again excluding the public at the applicant’s request (OSCE observers were permitted to attend on condition of confidentiality). The retrial was transferred to Rijeka County Court.

At the first retrial hearing on 13 September 2007 the applicant reversed his position and applied for the proceedings to be held in public. He argued that the victim had already given multiple media interviews, that OSCE observers had attended the Supreme Court sitting, and that the closed nature of the trial had allowed the media to stigmatise him without access to the evidence. The prosecution opposed the application, maintaining that protection of the victim’s private life remained necessary. After hearing both parties the court excluded the public from the entire main hearing under section 293(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, reasoning that facts disclosed at trial could harm the private and family lives of both the victim and the accused. The decision was pronounced publicly. Recusal applications by the applicant were dismissed.

On 13 November 2007 a newspaper published an exclusive interview with I.J. in which she discussed the impact of the case on her private life. At the next hearing on 3 December 2007 the applicant renewed his request for a public trial, citing four media interviews in which the victim had disclosed intimate details, including parts of her statement to the investigating judge. The prosecution again objected, noting that cross-examination might elicit still more intimate information. The court reiterated its earlier ruling.

I.J. testified on 4 December 2007. The following day a newspaper published comments by her and her lawyer about the examination. The applicant complained of a breach of confidentiality. After closing submissions the court convicted him of rape on 7 February 2008 and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. The pronouncement of the judgment was public and broadcast on three television channels.

On appeal the applicant argued that the exclusion of the public had been unjustified. Following a closed hearing the Supreme Court, on 8 June 2009, dismissed the appeal (reducing the sentence to two years). It held that the trial court had lawfully excluded the public to protect the victim’s private life, that the decision had been publicly announced, and that any procedural irregularity in failing to provide a written copy of the oral ruling had not affected the outcome. The Constitutional Court dismissed a subsequent constitutional complaint on 8 November 2012, finding no violation of the applicant’s rights.

The applicant complained to the Court that the complete exclusion of the public from his retrial, despite the victim’s own media statements and the earlier police disclosure of her identity, had breached his right to a public hearing. The Chamber noted that the State retained a positive obligation to protect the victim from secondary victimisation and that a still higher degree of protection was required given the initial unlawful police disclosure; it further observed that intimate information could emerge at any stage of the trial, rendering partial closure insufficient. The judgment against the applicant had been pronounced publicly and the closure decision had been reviewed by the Supreme Court, which found no breach.

The court again excluded the public, repeating that disclosure of hearing contents could harm the private lives of both victim and accused.

I.J. testified on 4 December 2007. The following day a newspaper reported statements by her and her lawyer about the examination. Mraović complained that confidentiality had been breached. Closing arguments were heard in camera on 29 January 2008. On 7 February 2008 the court convicted Mraović of rape and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. The judgment was pronounced publicly and broadcast on three television channels.

Mraović appealed, arguing that closure of the trial had been unjustified. After a closed hearing the Supreme Court, on 8 June 2009, upheld the conviction (reducing the sentence to two years). It held that the first-instance court had lawfully excluded the public to protect the victim’s private and family life given the intimate nature of the charge; any procedural irregularity in recording the decision had not affected the outcome. The Constitutional Court dismissed Mraović’s complaint on 8 November 2012.

The Chamber noted that the victim’s media statements did not relieve the State of its positive obligation to protect her privacy and to prevent secondary victimisation. An even higher degree of protection was required because of the police’s earlier unlawful disclosure of her identity. Partial closure would have been insufficient, as intimate information could emerge at any stage of the trial. The public pronouncement of the conviction and the Supreme Court’s review of the closure decision were also taken into account.

The case of Vardosanidze v. Georgia (Application no. 43881/10) concerned the death of the applicant’s son, G.K., from carbon monoxide poisoning in a rented Tbilisi apartment on 30 April 2008. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 2 of the Convention, claiming the Georgian authorities failed in their positive obligation to protect life by inadequately regulating and supervising the safe use of gas-operated household devices, and that the subsequent investigation was ineffective.

G.K. and his grandmother had rented the ground-floor apartment in an eight-storey building since December 2006. The owner had purchased and installed a gas-operated water heater in 2005 with assistance from a shop technician, without notifying the licensed gas distributor, Kaztransgaz-Tbilisi, or obtaining required documentation. On 1 June 2007, during a routine safety inspection, gas company technicians discovered the heater was improperly installed. They disconnected it from the gas pipe, wrapped the meter in cellophane, provided verbal instructions to the grandmother (who signed the inspection record), and noted the actions taken. The record did not specify the violation or why disconnection occurred. Technicians later explained that such heaters were prohibited in buildings of five or more storeys due to the absence of proper chimney and ventilation systems, creating a risk of incomplete combustion and carbon monoxide buildup; they were not required under then-applicable internal rules to seal the faucet, allowing potential reconnection.

On 30 April 2008, G.K. was found dead. Autopsy confirmed death by asphyxiation from carbon monoxide poisoning (60% carboxyhaemoglobin). The heater had been reconnected and was operational. A criminal investigation was opened, initially for incitement to suicide, then reclassified under Article 240(1) of the Criminal Code as a safety violation causing death. Forensic reports established the heater itself was technically sound and legally manufactured, but its use with closed windows/doors (or even a small open window, plus possible dampness in the apartment) could cause incomplete combustion. Experts noted residents bore primary responsibility for safe use of household devices, while the gas company supervised pipes and installations. The owner confirmed prior dampness issues requiring renovations but denied knowledge of the 2007 inspection or installation problems.

The investigation closed in October 2009 for lack of a crime, concluding G.K.’s death was an accident caused by the family’s careless reconnection despite the warning. The applicant appealed, arguing technicians failed to properly disconnect or document the issue, the owner violated installation rules by using an unlicensed technician, and her son could not have avoided the accident given the open window. Domestic courts upheld the closure, finding reconnection by the users caused the fatality.

Domestic regulations at the time placed responsibility for safe use of installed devices on inhabitants, required licensed installation with ventilation checks and registration, and mandated disconnection (including capping) of unsafe equipment with written records. Annual inspections were required, and heaters exhausting fumes indoors were banned without adequate ventilation. A 2002 presidential decree highlighted rising accidents and called for stricter enforcement. Statistics showed thousands of carbon monoxide incidents in Tbilisi around that period.

The Court ultimately found no Article 2 violation regarding positive obligations, as the gas company had identified and disconnected the heater before the death; any regulatory gaps did not suffice to attribute responsibility to the State given the family’s unforeseeable reconnection. The investigation was deemed adequate. The State also complied with its Article 38 duty to provide information.

The case of Vardosanidze v. Georgia (ECtHR, Application no. 43881/10, judgment of 7 May 2020) concerns the death of the applicant’s son from carbon monoxide poisoning and alleged failures by the Georgian authorities under Article 2 of the Convention.

The applicant, Lali Vardosanidze, complained that the State failed to protect her son G.K.’s life through inadequate regulation and supervision of gas-operated household devices, and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective. G.K. and his grandmother P.A. had rented a ground-floor apartment in an eight-storey Tbilisi building since December 2006. The apartment contained a gas-operated water heater installed by the owner in 2005 with a private technician; the owner had not notified the licensed gas distributor, Kaztransgaz-Tbilisi.

On 1 June 2007, company technicians conducting a routine safety inspection found the heater improperly installed. Inspection record no. 171786 recorded that they disconnected it from the gas pipe, sealed the meter in cellophane, and gave instructions to P.A., who signed the document. The record did not specify the precise violation. Technicians later testified that installation was prohibited in buildings of five or more storeys lacking proper chimney and ventilation systems; they had issued a verbal warning against reconnection. Sealing the faucet itself fell outside their then-applicable internal instructions.

On 30 April 2008 G.K. was found dead. A forensic report established death by asphyxiation from carbon monoxide (60 % carboxyhaemoglobin). A subsequent technical examination concluded that the heater itself was in satisfactory condition and of a type permitted in Georgia if correctly used, but that it had probably been operated in violation of safety rules. Incomplete combustion could occur if doors and windows were closed; even an open window might not suffice if the apartment was damp (a recurring problem noted by the owner). Responsibility for safe household use rested with residents, while supervision of pipes and devices lay with the gas company. A friend who discovered the body reported that a small upper window had been open.

A criminal investigation was opened, initially for incitement to suicide and later reclassified under Article 240(1) § 2 of the Criminal Code (breach of safety regulations causing death). The applicant and P.A. maintained that the technicians had neither disconnected the heater nor given proper warnings. The prosecutor closed the case on 16 October 2009, finding no crime: the family had carelessly reconnected the device despite the 2007 warning; residents bore primary responsibility; and G.K. could have avoided the accident by adequate ventilation. Domestic courts upheld the termination, accepting that reconnection by the occupants had caused the death.

The applicant argued that the technicians had failed to lock the faucet or compile a sufficiently detailed record, that the owner should have used a licensed installer, and that the gas company and State supervisory bodies had not adequately enforced existing rules (including a 2002 ban on certain heaters in poorly ventilated multi-storey buildings and requirements for licensed installation). Between 2007 and 2015 thousands of carbon-monoxide incidents were recorded in Tbilisi.

The Court ultimately held that, although dangerous activities engaged the State’s positive obligations, the identified regulatory and supervisory shortcomings were not sufficient to attribute responsibility to Georgia. The violation had been discovered and the heater disconnected well before the death; the family’s subsequent decision to reconnect the device constituted an unpredictable and unreasonable risk that the authorities could not reasonably have been expected to prevent. The investigation, while not flawless, met the requirements of Article 2. The Court also found that Georgia had complied with its Article 38 duty to furnish necessary information. No violation of Article 2 was therefore established.

The case of Vardosanidze v. Georgia concerned the death of the applicant’s son, G.K., from carbon monoxide poisoning on 30 April 2008 in a rented one-bedroom apartment in an eight-storey Tbilisi building. G.K. and his grandmother had occupied the apartment since December 2006. The owner had purchased and installed a gas-operated water heater in 2005 with the assistance of a shop technician, without notifying the licensed gas distributor or obtaining verification of compliance with technical requirements.

On 1 June 2007, technicians from the sole licensed gas company, Kaztransgaz-Tbilisi, conducted an annual safety inspection. They found the heater improperly installed, disconnected it from the gas pipe, sealed the meter in cellophane, issued verbal instructions, and completed an inspection record signed by the grandmother. The record did not specify the violation. Subsequent technician statements clarified that installation of such heaters was prohibited in buildings of more than five storeys owing to the absence of chimney and adequate ventilation systems, creating an inherent risk of incomplete combustion and carbon monoxide accumulation. Sealing the faucet was not required under the company’s internal instructions at the time, leaving open the possibility of reconnection. The owner was never informed of the inspection or the irregularity.

On 30 April 2008 a friend found G.K. unresponsive through a ground-floor window and summoned police and an ambulance, who forced entry. A small upper window was open. Autopsy and biochemical analysis established death by asphyxiation from carbon monoxide (60 per cent carboxyhaemoglobin). The heater was removed for examination.

A criminal investigation was opened, initially for incitement to suicide and later reclassified under Article 240(1) § 2 of the Criminal Code (breach of safety regulations causing death). A technical expert concluded that the industrially manufactured heater was in satisfactory condition and its use was not prohibited when correctly installed, but that it had been operated in violation of safety rules. Closed doors and windows would have restricted air circulation, producing incomplete combustion. Responsibility for safe household use lay with residents; the gas company was responsible for supervising pipes and devices. G.K. could have avoided the accident by ensuring ventilation, although the expert later noted that dampness (a recurring problem that had prompted prior renovations) could have intensified incomplete combustion even with a window open.

The investigation was terminated in October 2009 for absence of a crime. Prosecutors found that the family had carelessly reconnected the heater despite the 2007 warning and disconnection, and that residents bore primary responsibility for safe use. The applicant’s appeals were dismissed by the Tbilisi City Court and Court of Appeal, which accepted that the fatal reconnection, not any criminal act, had caused the death.

Domestic instruments in force at the time assigned inhabitants responsibility for the safe operation of household gas devices, required the gas company to disconnect leaking, unauthorised or unsafe equipment and to compile inspection records, and prohibited such heaters in high-rise buildings lacking proper exhaust systems. The National Inspectorate for Technical Supervision exercised limited oversight of gas enterprises. Statistics recorded 16 538 carbon-monoxide incidents in Tbilisi between 2007 and 2015.

The applicant alleged that these facts demonstrated a failure by the State to fulfil its positive obligation under Article 2 of the Convention to regulate and supervise the inherently dangerous activity of household gas use, and that the ensuing investigation had been ineffective.

**Case of Asady and Others v. Slovakia (Application no. 24917/15)**

On 17 November 2014 at 1:30 a.m., Slovak Border and Foreigners Police apprehended 19 Afghan nationals (the applicants) and others near the Ukrainian border. The group was hidden in a truck whose driver fled after ignoring warning signs; none carried identity documents. Thirty-two persons were taken to the Petrovce border police station. Ten officers handled identity checks and documentation; a Persian interpreter was present from 9 a.m. for 24 hours. Twelve others (five men, five women, two children) who requested asylum were transferred to a reception centre at 2 a.m. on 18 November.

The Government produced documents dated 17 November 2014 (mostly signed by applicants and the interpreter) showing: official notes on identity checks; 10-minute oral explanations in which all applicants denied persecution in Afghanistan, stated they left for economic reasons, and said they wished to go to Germany and did not seek asylum in Slovakia; notifications of expulsion proceedings and legal-aid rights; interviews as parties to those proceedings repeating the lack of persecution or death-sentence risk; opportunities to comment on files (unused); individual but identically worded expulsion decisions under the Aliens Act (ss. 77(1), 82(1)(a)) imposing a three-year re-entry ban, with no voluntary-departure period and no suspensive effect of appeal on grounds of urgent public interest; notifications of data registration (including EURODAC and SIS) and voluntary-return options; and simplified readmission requests to Ukraine. The applicants were handed over to Ukrainian authorities at 10:30 p.m. the same day. Interview times overlapped (e.g., two officers and one interpreter recorded at three interviews simultaneously), questions were standardised, and answers were largely identical except for sums of money possessed.

The applicants maintained that police failed to identify them all properly, interviewed only a few, and had them sign unknown Slovak-language documents after being told the papers concerned asylum claims and that they would be transferred to a reception centre. They received no information on the asylum procedure, their requests for asylum and legal assistance were ignored (unlike the other 12), and the interpreter was present only a few hours (interviews listed between 9:10 a.m. and 12:30 p.m.). They obtained copies of the decisions only later, after authorising their representative to inspect files. The decisions themselves recorded consideration of the applicants’ economic situation, lack of Slovak family ties, and absence of obstacles under Aliens Act s. 81 and Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention; the applicants had not alleged risks in Ukraine or of onward refoulement to Afghanistan (Ukraine having ratified the Convention).

In Ukraine the applicants were detained (initially in Chop, later Zhuravychi). From 18 November they told NGO staff they had requested asylum in Slovakia, did not understand their removal (unlike the other 12), and believed the interpretation inaccurate. On 25 November four applicants appealed, alleging that only one person had been questioned, others had signed unread documents, asylum requests and legal-aid requests had been ignored, decisions had not been served, no effective remedy existed, and the process amounted to collective expulsion. The border-police directorate dismissed the appeals on 7 January 2015, citing the file, interpretation throughout, signed statements declining asylum, individual decisions, and absence of expulsion obstacles.

Domestic law (Aliens Act s. 77(2)) prohibits collective expulsion by a single decision. Obstacles to expulsion include risks of persecution, torture, or death penalty, or chain-refoulement (s. 81). Asylum is initiated by a declaration to a competent police office (Asylum Act s. 3). Appeals against expulsion normally have suspensive effect unless urgent public interest requires otherwise (Administrative Proceedings Act s. 55(2)). A 2010 Human Rights Watch report documented similar summary returns from Slovakia to Ukraine, ignored asylum claims, and lack of information or legal access.

The applicants complained of collective expulsion contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 and lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. (Word count: 512)

The case of Asady and Others v. Slovakia involves 19 Afghan nationals who alleged that their removal from Slovakia to Ukraine on 17 November 2014 amounted to a prohibited collective expulsion under Article 4 of Protocol No. 4, and that they had no effective remedy under Article 13 of the Convention. They claimed a lack of individual assessment, denial of access to the asylum procedure, and inadequate information or legal assistance.

The 19 applicants and other Afghan nationals were found hidden inside without identity documents. According to the Government, 32 people in total were taken to the Petrovce police station. Twelve others (including women and children) who requested asylum were transferred to a reception centre the following night. The applicants, by contrast, were processed for administrative expulsion.

Some recorded times overlapped, meaning the same officers and interpreter were listed as present at multiple interviews simultaneously. Applicants were given the chance to comment on their files or add evidence but did not. Individual expulsion decisions (identically worded) were issued the same day under the Aliens Act for irregular border crossing. These imposed a three-year re-entry ban, set no period for voluntary departure, and excluded suspensive effect of any appeal on grounds of urgent public interest. The applicants disputed this account. They said not all were properly identified, only a few were actually interviewed, and they were made to sign Slovak-language papers whose content they did not understand after being told the documents concerned asylum requests and transfer to a reception centre. The interpreter was present only a few hours, as shown by the interview transcripts covering 9:10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. They received no copies of the decisions while still in Slovakia.

In Ukraine they were detained, first in Chop and later in Zhuravychi. From 18 November they told Ukrainian NGO staff they had sought asylum in Slovakia, did not understand why they (unlike the others) had been removed, and believed the interpreter had mistranslated. Four applicants later instructed a lawyer and appealed, alleging ignored asylum requests, lack of individual examination, no legal aid, and collective expulsion. The appeals were dismissed on 7 January 2015 on the basis that interpretation had been provided, the applicants had signed documents declining asylum, and individual decisions had been issued with no obstacles to return.

The case of Gheorghe Cobzaru v. Romania (no. 21171/16) before the ECHR concerns the alleged continued ineffectiveness of the official investigation into the 2006 police shooting death of the applicant’s son, following a 2013 ECHR judgment that had already found violations of Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) in both its substantive and procedural aspects.

On the night of 18 September 2006, the applicant’s son—suspected of theft from a truck and fleeing in a stolen vehicle—was pursued by police. Officer A.S. fired a shot that struck the son in the throat; he died from the wound. The applicant claimed the killing amounted to murder and that no effective investigation followed.

In its 25 June 2013 principal judgment (no. 6978/08), the Court held that the use of lethal force had not been shown to be “absolutely necessary.” The shooting occurred at night without sufficient prior precautions, against an inadequate legislative and regulatory framework for police firearms use. Procedurally, the investigation (still pending years later) suffered from excessive delay, flawed evidence-gathering (including an inadequate ballistics report), and insufficient public scrutiny or protection of the applicant’s interests. A 2012 Bucharest County Court decision had already remitted the file to prosecutors for these same shortcomings. The Court awarded the applicant €30,000 for non-pecuniary damage.

The investigation was then reopened. On 4 June 2015 the prosecutor closed the case, finding A.S.’s actions justified under Article 21 § 1 of the Criminal Code as the lawful exercise of police duties. A.S. had acted on reasonable suspicion of a crime in progress, issued a verbal warning plus three vertical warning shots, and fired only then; the fatal shot complied with applicable firearms rules. Supporting material included statements from A.S., the applicant and witnesses; 2013 and 2015 ballistics/trace reports addressing trajectory, distance, direction and relative positions; medical records; and a reconstruction of events. A clothing-sample forensic examination proved impossible because flood damage in 2012 had rendered the items unusable; autopsy tissue samples had likewise deteriorated after laboratory testing, with no long-term reserves remaining. Prosecutors recorded that evidence steps followed the applicant’s requests, that he and his lawyer participated in the reconstruction and expert reports (with rights to file submissions and challenge conclusions), and that they had full file access.

The Bucharest County Court upheld the closure on 14 October 2015. It confirmed A.S. had been performing his public-safety and crime-prevention duties. Ballistics established the impact was indirect: the victim was struck by a fragment that had ricocheted off concrete pavement.

In September 2017 the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers, reviewing execution of the 2013 judgment, noted the additional investigative steps taken after that ruling and the subsequent domestic termination on grounds of legal justification. It concluded that no further individual measures remained possible in the applicant’s case, while general measures (including 2016 legislative tightening of police firearms rules) remained under supervision.

These post-2013 facts—irreversible loss of physical evidence, reliance on later ballistics concluding a ricochet, and a final finding of justification despite the earlier ECHR finding that force had not been shown to be absolutely necessary—form the core of the applicant’s complaint that the reopened investigation still failed to meet Article 2’s procedural requirements of effectiveness, thoroughness and adequate protection of the next-of-kin’s interests.

The case of Gheorghe Cobzaru v. Romania (Application no. 21171/16) concerns the alleged failure of Romanian authorities to conduct an effective investigation into the 2006 killing of the applicant’s son by a police officer, following an earlier finding of violation by the European Court of Human Rights.

On 4 June 2015, the prosecutor’s office attached to the Bucharest County Court closed the case against A.S., finding that he had acted with justifiable cause under Article 21 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The officer, patrolling the area, had a reasonable suspicion of a crime in progress. He issued a verbal warning and fired three vertical warning shots before the fatal (indirect) shot, which ricocheted from concrete pavement and struck the victim with a fragment. This was held to comply with firearms regulations. The decision relied on statements from A.S., the applicant, and applicant-called witnesses; ballistic and trace analyses from March 2013 and March 2015 establishing trajectory, distance, and positions; medical records; and an on-site reconstruction.

Certain forensic examinations could not be performed: clothing samples from A.S. and the victim had been damaged in a 2012 flood, and autopsy tissue samples had deteriorated during laboratory tests, with no long-term conservation samples available. The prosecutor noted that evidence-gathering followed the applicant’s and his lawyer’s requests. They participated in the reconstruction and ballistics/forensic processes, submitted challenges, and had full access to the case file.

The Bucharest County Court upheld the closure on 14 October 2015, confirming that A.S. had acted in the exercise of his duties to ensure public safety and prevent street crime, consistent with the ballistic findings of an indirect ricochet impact.

In September 2017, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe examined execution of the 2013 judgment. It noted that further individual measures were no longer possible after the investigation’s termination and court confirmation that the officer had complied with the then-applicable legal framework. Supervision of general measures (including 2016 legislative amendments tightening police firearms rules and instructions on operational planning) remained ongoing.

The present application, lodged on 1 April 2016, specifically complained of the continued ineffectiveness of the post-2013 investigation into the death. The Court communicated this complaint to the Government.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined Gheorghe Cobzaru v. Romania (Application no. 21171/16) in a 7 May 2020 judgment. The case alleged an ineffective official investigation into the 18 September 2006 death of the applicant’s son, continuing after the Court’s 25 June 2013 principal judgment (no. 6978/08) that had already found Article 2 violations (substantive and procedural).

On 4 June 2015 the prosecutor’s office attached to the Bucharest County Court closed the case against A.S. under Article 21 § 1 of the Criminal Code (justifiable cause: exercising a legal right or fulfilling a legal obligation). It found A.S. had acted in the line of duty while patrolling, on reasonable suspicion of a crime; he issued a verbal warning, fired three vertical warning shots, and then an indirect fatal shot, all in compliance with firearm-use rules. Evidence included statements from A.S., the applicant and his witnesses; 28 March 2013 and 2 March 2015 ballistics/trace reports on shot direction, distance, trajectory and relative positions; medical records; and a reconstruction. A forensic examination of clothing samples could not be performed because flood damage in 2012 had rendered the items unusable; autopsy tissue samples had also deteriorated and no long-term-conservation samples existed.

The prosecutor stated that evidence-taking followed the applicant’s and his lawyer’s requests. They participated in the reconstruction and ballistics/forensic work, filed challenges, and had full file access. On 14 October 2015 the Bucharest County Court upheld the closure, confirming that A.S. had been fulfilling public-safety and crime-prevention duties. Ballistics showed the impact was indirect: a bullet fragment ricocheted off the courtyard pavement.

On 21 September 2017 the Committee of Ministers, reviewing execution of the 2013 judgment, noted the additional steps (new ballistics, reconstruction, hearings) and the 2015 termination on the ground that the officer had complied with then-applicable law. It recorded that no further individual measures were possible. General measures (2016 legislative tightening of police firearm rules, 2009 special-units regulation) were noted as ongoing; supervision under Article 46 § 2 remains open for similar cases.

Domestic law includes Article 21 of the Criminal Code and the firearm/police-organisation provisions described in the 2013 judgment. These facts form the core of the alleged continuing failure to conduct an effective Article 2 investigation.
