The case of Georgouleas and Nestoras v. Greece (applications nos. 44612/13 and 45831/13) concerned administrative fines imposed in 2007 by the Hellenic Capital Market Commission on two Greek nationals for alleged market manipulation involving shares of company D.K. listed on the Athens stock exchange. The applicants argued that the sanctions, treated as criminal in nature, violated Article 7 of the Convention because the offence was not foreseeable.

The Commission investigated trading from January 2003 to October 2004 and found that persons linked to company G. had conducted organised transactions to artificially set the price and marketability of D.K. shares. This created misleading data published in official stock-exchange lists and records, thereby disseminating inaccurate information to investors. The first applicant (majority shareholder, president and CEO of G.) coordinated the scheme with the second applicant (a G. employee). They executed trades on their own account and for clients, including pre-arranged matched orders through multiple brokers (often with co-participants as counterparties), recommendations of artificial pricing confirmed by telephone records, and substantial end-of-day trading (some internal to the group) to fix closing prices.

On 2 October 2007 the Commission fined the first applicant €100,000 and the second €60,000 under the first sentence of Article 72 § 2 of Law no. 1969/1991. That provision authorised fines on anyone who “publish[ed] or disseminate[d] in any way inaccurate or misleading information” concerning listed securities that could affect their price. A second sentence excluded professional facilitators unless they knew or should have known the transactions were intended to disseminate false information.

The Athens Administrative Court of Appeal annulled the fines in 2008, holding that mere transactions did not constitute “dissemination” under the first sentence (the second sentence being limited to professionals). The Commission appealed. In 2013 the Supreme Administrative Court (enlarged panel) reversed, ruling that the provision’s purpose—to protect market integrity and investors—did not restrict methods of dissemination. Transactions that generated artificial published data therefore amounted to dissemination of misleading information. A later statute (Law no. 3340/2005 implementing EU Directive 2003/6/EC) that separately listed transactions and information dissemination as forms of market abuse merely clarified, and did not alter, the earlier rule. The interpretation was foreseeable to diligent market professionals; the applicants had not cited contrary higher-court authority. Two dissenting judges insisted the literal wording excluded transactions.

The cases were remitted; the appellate court later confirmed the first fine and reduced the second to €20,000. Separately, the first applicant was acquitted of criminal charges under an older fraud statute.

Earlier first-instance judgments (2002–2003) had already treated manipulative trades as dissemination, although a 2006 Supreme Administrative Court decision had held the opposite. The applicants maintained that this judicial expansion rendered the offence unforeseeable under Article 7.

The Court accepted that Article 7 applied to the punitive administrative fines. It found, however, that the statutory language (“in any way”) was sufficiently precise at the material time. The domestic courts’ reading remained compatible with the essence of the offence, was supported by pre-existing lower-court precedents, and was reasonably foreseeable to professionals expected to exercise special care. Subsequent legislative rewording was irrelevant.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Georgouleas and Nestoras v. Greece (applications nos. 44612/13 and 45831/13) concerned two Greek nationals, Ilias Georgouleas (born 1965) and Spyridon Nestoras (born 1974), who were fined by the Hellenic Capital Market Commission for alleged market manipulation involving shares of the listed company D.K. The Commission, an independent administrative body overseeing stock exchange compliance, investigated trading in D.K. shares across periods in 2003 and 2004. It found that individuals linked to company G. had conducted organized transactions to artificially inflate the shares' value and marketability, thereby disseminating inaccurate and misleading information to investors. This was based on transaction volumes, timing, and the identities of participants, particularly during price-rise periods from January to July 2003 and October 2003 to April 2004.

Georgouleas, majority shareholder, president, and CEO of G., coordinated with Nestoras, a company employee. They traded on their own behalf and for clients, engaging in pre-arranged purchases and sales through the same or multiple brokers (often with scheme participants as counterparties), placing matched orders, recommending artificial price-fixing (evidenced by telephone records), and conducting substantial end-of-day trading among implicated parties to manipulate closing prices and marketability.

On 2 October 2007, the Commission convicted both under the first sentence of Article 72 § 2 of Law no. 1969/1991 (as amended), imposing fines of EUR 100,000 on Georgouleas and EUR 60,000 on Nestoras. The provision prohibited publishing or disseminating "in any way" inaccurate or misleading information about listed securities that could affect their price or dealings, with a limited exception for professional facilitators unaware of manipulative intent.

The applicants appealed to the Athens Administrative Court of Appeal, which in 2008 overturned the fines (decisions nos. 3289/2008 and 3290/2008). It held that entering into transactions did not constitute dissemination of information under the first sentence, even if intended to manipulate prices; such conduct fell only under the second sentence, limited to professionals.

The Commission appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court. After a 2012 referral due to conflicting lower-court case-law, the Court in 2013 (judgments nos. 109/2013 and 111/2013) quashed the appellate decisions. It interpreted the provision as covering transactions performed with intent to create false price and marketability data, which—once published in official daily lists and electronic records—misled investors. This aligned with the law's purpose of protecting market integrity. A subsequent law (no. 3340/2005, transposing EU Directive 2003/6/EC) distinguishing transactions from information dissemination merely specified existing rules and did not alter prior meaning. The Court found the interpretation foreseeable to diligent market professionals, as earlier first-instance judgments (2002–2003) had treated pre-arranged trading as dissemination. A two-judge minority dissented, arguing the literal text excluded transactions and that the later law's distinction confirmed this.

The cases were remitted; the Court of Appeal upheld Georgouleas's fine and reduced Nestoras's to EUR 20,000. Separately, Georgouleas was acquitted in 2007 of related criminal charges under Law no. 3632/1928 for lack of fraudulent intent and because share prices had fallen 46%.

The applicants complained to the ECHR that the fines, amounting to criminal sanctions under Article 7, lacked foreseeability. The law's wording ("in any way") and evolving interpretations—initial first-instance support for including transactions, a 2006 Supreme Court ruling excluding them, and the 2013 reversal—rendered the offence unpredictable, especially given the later law's clarifications. The Court ultimately found Article 7 applicable but no violation, as the interpretation matched the offence's essence, was supported by pre-existing precedents, and professionals should have anticipated it.

The applicants, Ilias Georgouleas (majority shareholder, president and CEO of company “G.”) and Spyridon Nestoras (an employee of that company), were investigated by the Hellenic Capital Market Commission for trading in shares of listed company D.K. during periods in 2003–2004. The Commission found that persons linked to “G.” had conducted organised, pre-arranged transactions (including matched orders placed through the same or multiple brokers, often with counterparties also involved in the scheme, and substantial trading at market close) aimed at artificially inflating the price and marketability of D.K. shares. These trades, published in the official daily list and electronic transaction record, were held to disseminate inaccurate or misleading information to investors.

In October 2007 the Commission fined the first applicant €100,000 and the second applicant €60,000 for breach of the first sentence of Article 72 § 2 of Law 1969/1991 (as amended). That provision imposed administrative fines on anyone who “publish[es] or disseminate[s] in any way inaccurate or misleading information regarding securities \ldots that by its nature may affect the price of or dealings in those securities.” A second sentence exempted professional intermediaries unless they knew or ought to have known they were assisting such dissemination.

The applicants appealed. The Athens Administrative Court of Appeal quashed the fines in 2008, ruling that mere entry into transactions could not constitute “publication or diffusion” under the first sentence (the second sentence being limited to professional facilitators). The Commission appealed on points of law. In 2013 a seven-judge panel of the Supreme Administrative Court allowed the appeals, holding that the provision’s purpose (market integrity and investor protection) did not confine “dissemination in any way” to verbal or written statements. Transactions executed with the intent of creating false price and volume signals, once published by law, themselves constituted dissemination of misleading information. The later, more detailed Law 3340/2005 (transposing the EU Market Abuse Directive) merely clarified rather than altered the earlier offence. The court remitted the cases; the fines were ultimately confirmed (the second reduced to €20,000). A minority of two judges dissented, arguing that the literal wording excluded transactions and that the later statute’s distinction between trading and dissemination confirmed this.

Separately, the first applicant was acquitted in 2007 of a related criminal charge under Law 3632/1928 (use of fraudulent means to affect share prices), the indictment division finding insufficient evidence of fraudulent intent and noting that the shares had in fact fallen 46 % over the relevant period.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the fines were criminal in nature and that the Supreme Administrative Court’s interpretation of Article 72 § 2 was unforeseeable, violating Article 7 of the Convention. They relied on the Court of Appeal’s initial reading, the subsequent statutory distinction between transactions and information dissemination, and the absence of Supreme Court precedent at the time of the trades. The Government maintained that the wording “in any way,” the provision’s protective purpose, earlier first-instance case-law treating organised trading as dissemination, and the professional context rendered the interpretation reasonably foreseeable.
001-202621:
The applicants, a couple who had worked for senior official C, became witnesses in a widely publicised 2012 anti-corruption investigation into C and D. Interviewed between February and August 2015, they were declared “threatened witnesses” by prosecutor’s order of 28 August 2015 under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Immediate measures included police surveillance of their home and a constant escort by the Special Actions Service. The order cited a reasonable suspicion of risk to their lives or physical integrity arising from their statements.

They were proposed for the National Office for Witness Protection programme. After meetings explaining the conditions (relocation, limited family contact, possible unemployment), they consented on 9 December 2015. Transfer of responsibility was delayed: the Directorate General of Police reported non-cooperation (unaccompanied departures, no notice of movements) and the absence of specific regulations until July 2016. Protocols detailing officers’ duties and the applicants’ obligations (no compromising actions, no disclosure of status) were presented in March and July 2016; the applicants refused to sign, claiming the terms were overly restrictive. They later accepted them verbally but expressed distrust of the officers.

The High Court of Cassation and Justice assumed responsibility once the trial opened in September 2015. In August 2016 it rejected a prosecutorial request to lift protection, holding that the original risk persisted while evidence was still being heard, attributing protocol delays to the authorities, yet stressing that the measures inherently limited freedom and were not negotiable. Formal inclusion in the programme occurred on 5 January 2017, with measures of enhanced home protection, court-travel escorts, employment assistance and monthly financial support equivalent to the minimum wage. Requests for new identities and relocation abroad were refused because the applicants’ testimony remained necessary and temporary identity documents prevented border crossing.

Implementation produced conflicting accounts. The applicants alleged unprepared officers who slept in cars, drank on duty, left posts, lost a liaison file containing photographs and confidential data, imposed rigid travel hours, and displayed weapons conspicuously, thereby revealing their status. They claimed they were sometimes left unprotected or forcibly detained. They also reported unidentified followers, slashed tyres and two bullets left on their doorstep; they refused to surrender the bullets or lodge a formal complaint. The authorities documented repeated refusals of escorts, verbal abuse, traffic violations to evade officers, and fines for disorderly conduct. Periodic assessments found no independent evidence of external threats and recorded the applicants’ systematic non-cooperation.

The applicants maintained a public Facebook page under their real names, posted video confrontations with officers, and appeared on television, thereby disclosing their protected status and case details. After leaving Romania in October 2017 they continued to receive financial support and remained in contact with their liaison officer. C was ultimately convicted in June 2018.

These facts underpin the complaint that the authorities failed in their positive obligation under Article 2 to provide effective protection once a risk to life had been identified, owing to delays, inadequate instructions, insufficient resources and failure to investigate concrete threats.

**CASE OF A AND B v. ROMANIA (Apps. nos. 48442/16 & 48831/16, ECtHR 2 June 2020)**

The applicants, a couple (A, born 1981; B, born 1978), were former employees of senior official C. They became witnesses in a high-profile 2012 corruption investigation (widely publicised) into C and another official D, interviewed February–August 2015 about alleged transactions.

On 28 August 2015, prosecutors declared them “threatened witnesses” under the Code of Criminal Procedure due to a reasonable suspicion of risk to life/physical integrity from their statements. Immediate measures included police home surveillance/protection and constant escort (via Special Actions Service teams). An internal action plan existed but was not disclosed (containing officer data). They met the National Office for Witness Protection (NOWP) to discuss inclusion in the full programme (relocation, identity change, contact cuts, asset sales), initially delaying a decision.

They agreed to the programme on 9 December 2015, but NOWP later reported no consensus (applicants sought unattainable high-comfort relocation). Directorate General of Police (DGP) protocols detailing officer duties and witness obligations (e.g., no compromising actions, inform of changes, no status disclosure) were presented; applicants refused to sign in March and July 2016, claiming rights restrictions and distrusting officers (alleging abuse like unaccompanied-travel blocks). DGP adopted specific witness-protection regulations in June 2016.

Prosecutors sought to lift measures in June 2016 (no specific threats identified; non-cooperation; refused protocols). High Court of Cassation and Justice (HCCJ) rejected this on 25 August 2016, noting ongoing trial evidence and authority delays in protocols, but confirming protocols were non-negotiable and imposed limited restrictions.

Applicants testified October 2016. HCCJ ordered programme inclusion on 5 January 2017 (home protection, court-travel escorts, employment aid, financial support equivalent to minimum wage, later raised). They signed protocols/framework on 17 January 2017 (no compromising activities/recordings; programme-end grounds per Witness Protection Act). Protection transferred from DGP.

Implementation complaints (applicants’ account): Officers uninstructed (first such mission), slept/drank on duty, guarded wrong building, unarmed, lost liaison file (photos/data, 9 February 2016), left them unprotected or blocked exits, limited travel (7 a.m.–10 p.m., town-only, wait for escorts), conspicuous/unconcealed weapons revealing status, filmed them. They missed family events. B faced arguments/fines (offending officers, blocking access, social-media posts). They alleged officer threats and harassment to withdraw statements.

Government documents showed 24-hour home shifts and travel teams. Periodic assessments noted applicants’ refusals, escapes (own cars, traffic violations), abuse of officers, filming encounters, and demands to stop following. A May 2017 NOWP letter (disputed by Government; investigation ongoing) admitted ineffective camera surveillance, social-media leaks by officers, refused relocation/identity change (HCCJ-dismissed as applicants needed for trial; temporary IDs barred border-crossing), and employment issues (applicants rejected qualified offers).

Alleged threats: Staking-out, car tampering (2015; DGP remedied), unidentified followers/slashed tyres (2017; unconfirmed), bullets on doorstep (September 2017; applicants refused handover/complaint). Complaints of officer misconduct/abuse were mostly dismissed (officers acted lawfully); some officers investigated administratively/criminally (e.g., lost file—applicants took it).

Applicants compromised security via Facebook page (thousands of followers, posts on their story/police interactions, DGP/prosecutor letters, bullet photos), B’s live videos/emergency calls about officers, media interviews/articles naming B, and a January 2018 TV appearance (labelled “protected witness”). NOWP warned this rendered measures ineffective.

HCCJ dismissed further requests (March 2017: refused jobs/relocation). Applicants left Romania October 2017 (informed NOWP/liaison; sought work) but received continued financial support. They testified in another C case; C was convicted June 2018. Later complaints (uninvestigated threats, programme issues) yielded no recorded outcome. Protection persisted despite their unilateral move.

**CASE OF A AND B v. ROMANIA (ECtHR, 2 June 2020)**

Applicants A (born 1981) and B (born 1978), a couple, were interviewed as witnesses in 2015 by Romania’s anti-corruption prosecutor in a high-profile investigation into alleged corruption by senior officials C and D (their former employer). Their statements were deemed potentially decisive.

On 28 August 2015 the prosecutor declared them “threatened witnesses” under the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing a reasonable suspicion of risk to their life or physical integrity. Immediate measures were ordered: police surveillance and protection of their home plus a constant escort. The Special Actions Service (SAS) began protection that day; a second team was added in February 2016. An internal action plan existed but was not disclosed to them because it contained officers’ personal data.

The applicants viewed the order as temporary pending inclusion in the National Office for Witness Protection (NOWP) programme. After being informed of the programme’s requirements (relocation, severance of contacts, sale of possessions, limited employment prospects), they consented on 9 December 2015. The Directorate General of Police (DGP) later reported their refusal to cooperate (leaving home unaccompanied). The NOWP stated in February 2016 that agreement on the scope of protection could not be reached because the applicants demanded an unattainably high standard of comfort.

They were invited to sign detailed protection protocols in March 2016 (obliging them to cooperate, report changes and not disclose their status) but refused a similar set in July 2016, claiming the measures were abusive and unduly restrictive. New DGP regulations on threatened-witness protection entered force on 1 July 2016. In June 2016 the prosecutor sought to lift the measures, arguing the applicants could identify no concrete threat and were uncooperative. The High Court of Cassation and Justice (HCCJ) rejected the request in August 2016, holding that the original risk persisted while evidence was still being heard and attributing protocol delays to the authorities. Protection therefore continued under the 2015 order, though the court noted that protocols imposed legitimate limitations.

After giving evidence in October 2016, the applicants were formally included in the NOWP programme by HCCJ order of 5 January 2017 (increased home protection, escort to court, employment assistance and financial support). They signed a framework agreement and protocols on 17 January 2017. Their request for new identities and relocation abroad was refused because their presence was still required for the investigation and they could not travel on temporary identity documents. They rejected all employment offers matching their qualifications. Monthly financial support equivalent to the minimum wage (later raised to approximately €500) was provided and continued after they left Romania.

Implementation was imperfect. Officers initially lacked clear instructions (the assignment being novel) and some incidents occurred: an officer left a post and mislaid a liaison file containing photographs and confidential data (9 February 2016); officers were sometimes unarmed, conspicuous or unavailable, restricting movement; the applicants alleged they were prevented from attending family events. Administrative and criminal inquiries followed; some officers were investigated and the file-loss case was closed after it was found the applicants themselves had taken the file. The authorities promptly issued clearer instructions, adopted regulations and reminded the applicants that cooperation was essential.

The applicants repeatedly refused escorts, fled protection teams, verbally abused officers (leading to fines, some later cancelled), filmed encounters and posted their status and complaints on a public Facebook page (thousands of followers) and appeared on television in January 2018, naming themselves as protected witnesses. They alleged unidentified surveillance, slashed tyres and two bullets left on their doorstep (2017), but refused to surrender the bullets or file a complaint; police found no corroboration. They left Romania in October 2017 after notifying the NOWP and remaining in contact with their liaison officer. Financial support continued. The main trial ended with C’s conviction in June 2018.

The applicants lodged numerous complaints of abuse, negligence and threats; most were dismissed after investigation as unfounded or as officers acting within their powers. A disputed May 2017 letter purporting to be from the NOWP director (later the subject of a criminal inquiry) admitted shortcomings and advised against litigation. Protection and support were maintained despite the applicants’ unilateral departure and public disclosures that compromised secrecy.

The applicant, a Sudanese national born in 1993, entered the Netherlands on 14 May 2010 and claimed asylum, asserting birth in a village near Nyala in South Darfur and membership of the non-Arab Tunjur ethnic group. He stated that his Chadian mother had arranged his departure after his father sought to force him to fight the Janjaweed militia, and that return would expose him to killing by his father or ethnic group. A language analysis identified him as originating from Sudan, with a likely Darfur childhood but significant time spent in the Khartoum region (or outside Darfur), and as belonging to a non-Arab group. Security-camera footage showed him arriving from Istanbul on an authentic Chadian passport; he claimed the facilitator had given him the document only at checkpoints. Authorities rejected his first asylum claim in 2011, finding that use of the genuine Chadian passport undermined his asserted Sudanese identity and nationality, so the merits were not examined. Appeals failed.

A second claim in October 2014, after his arrest for assault, added documents (a Sudanese residence declaration and embassy confirmation of Sudanese origin) and repeated fears of forced recruitment by either the military or his ethnic group. The Deputy Minister rejected it for lack of new facts. The Regional Court initially required examination of the merits, but the Council of State in February 2015 held that the documents and a prior detention decision accepting Sudanese nationality did not disprove Chadian nationality or constitute new circumstances warranting re-examination.

On 9 October 2015 the applicant was notified of imminent removal to Sudan. He objected, arguing that as a non-Arab Darfuri he would attract adverse attention at Khartoum airport and that the absence of an automatic-suspensive remedy violated Articles 3 and 13. The provisional-measures judge refused a stay, relying on the earlier finding that identity and nationality had not been established. The Court granted an interim measure that day.

A third claim followed in January 2016. After an additional interview addressing the applicant’s participation in a Sudanese-opposition demonstration in The Hague in January 2016, the Deputy Minister again rejected the claim: even assuming Sudanese nationality, the applicant’s statements about Darfur were vague, contradictory and inconsistent with the language analysis, so Darfur could not be treated as his region of origin and no Article 3 risk (including from the demonstration or forced conscription) was established. After the Regional Court identified insufficient reasoning, additional expert comments confirmed that the applicant’s Arabic pointed to long-term residence in the Khartoum region and made early childhood in Darfur or Chad unlikely; his claimed Tunjur origin could not be verified. In December 2017 the Regional Court accepted Khartoum as the region of origin and found no real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment there. A further appeal was dismissed in September 2018.

The applicant also relied on the general situation in Darfur, forced-recruitment risk and the humanitarian consequences of the conflict. Subsequent events included the April 2019 ouster of President Al-Bashir, the formation of a Transitional Military Council and, later, a Sovereignty Council, together with country reports indicating that non-Arab Darfuris were not generally at risk in Khartoum solely on ethnic grounds and that failed asylum-seekers without a political profile faced no systematic mistreatment on return.

The applicant, a Sudanese national born in 1993 claiming non-Arab Tunjur ethnicity from Nyala in South Darfur, entered the Netherlands on 14 May 2010 using an authentic Chadian passport (which he said was not his own and had been provided only at checkpoints). He immediately applied for asylum, stating that his father had sought to force him to fight against Janjaweed militias and that his mother had arranged his departure to prevent this. He feared being killed by his father or ethnic group members upon return, as well as forced recruitment and the general situation arising from the Darfur conflict.

A language analysis identified him as originating from Sudan with a likely Darfur background and non-Arab affiliation, but his Arabic showed strong Khartoum-region influences, indicating he had spent a significant part of his life outside Darfur. His first asylum claim was rejected in 2011 solely because his entry on a genuine Chadian passport undermined his claimed Sudanese nationality; no merits assessment occurred. Appeals failed.

A second claim in 2014, after his arrest, reiterated his Darfur origin and fears of forced fighting for either side. He submitted a Sudanese residence declaration and embassy confirmation of Sudanese nationality, plus evidence that the Chadian embassy had refused to confirm he lacked that nationality. The authorities again found no new facts capable of altering the prior nationality finding. The Council of State upheld the rejection.

In October 2015 the Sudanese embassy issued a laissez-passer and removal to Sudan was scheduled. The applicant objected, arguing that as a non-Arab Darfuri he would immediately attract adverse official attention at Khartoum airport and that no proper Article 3 risk assessment had been conducted. A domestic request for a stay was refused on the ground that identity and nationality remained unestablished. The European Court indicated an interim measure staying removal.

A third asylum application followed. After an additional interview that addressed his participation in a January 2016 Sudanese opposition demonstration in The Hague, the authorities accepted Sudanese nationality but rejected his claimed Darfur origin as vague, contradictory and inconsistent with the language analysis (he could not name nearby places, knew little of Nyala, and displayed an unexpectedly large vocabulary). They treated Khartoum as his region of origin and found no real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment there from ethnicity alone, the single demonstration, or forced conscription. The Regional Court, after requiring supplementary reasoning, accepted the appeal but left the legal consequences intact, confirming Khartoum as the relevant region and the absence of established risk. A further appeal was dismissed.

Subsequent country information showed that, after the 2019 ouster of President Al-Bashir and the establishment of a transitional government, the general situation in Sudan no longer itself entailed an Article 3 risk. Non-Arab Darfuris in Khartoum faced discrimination and possible heightened scrutiny if they possessed a political or rebel-linked profile, but ethnicity alone did not generate a real risk of persecution or serious harm. Failed asylum-seekers and holders of emergency documents were questioned on arrival but not systematically ill-treated unless they fell into additional risk categories. No evidence established forced recruitment of returnees in Khartoum.

The applicant alleged that expulsion would expose him to treatment contrary to Article 3 on account of his origins, ethnicity, risk of forced recruitment and the humanitarian situation, and that he had lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

He stated that his divorced father had tried to force him to fight with their ethnic group against the Janjaweed, prompting his Chadian mother and her new husband to arrange his departure; he feared being killed by his father or group members, or forcibly recruited by either side, upon return. A 2011 language analysis confirmed Sudanese origin with a plausible Darfur (non-Arab) background but significant time spent in the Khartoum region (or outside Darfur), plus command of a Chadian tribal language (Gorane/Tubu) learned from his mother.

His first asylum claim was rejected in October 2011 (upheld on appeal through August 2013) because use of the genuine Chadian passport undermined his claimed identity and Sudanese nationality, so the merits were not assessed. A second claim in October 2014 (after an assault arrest), supported by a Sudanese residence declaration, origin statement, and Sudanese embassy confirmation of nationality (the Chadian embassy having refused to confirm non-nationality), was rejected as lacking new facts or circumstances; the Council of State held in February 2015 that he had not disproved Chadian nationality and that no special circumstances warranted merits review.

001-202757:
The European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Croatian national Dušan Vujnović alleging that Croatia had failed to comply with its procedural obligation under Article 2 of the Convention to investigate the 1993 killings of his parents by Croatian Army soldiers, and that the Supreme Court’s calculation of the statutory limitation period for his related civil claim for damages had been inconsistent with its own case-law, thereby violating his right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1.

The applicant’s parents were killed on 9 September 1993 during Croatian Army Operation Pocket-93, which recaptured the Medak Pocket from Serbian forces. Fifty-one bodies were recovered, examined, and handed over to Serbian authorities. A 2002–2003 Croatian police investigation and ICTY materials identified the parents among the victims. ICTY indictments against Croatian generals R.A. (2001, amended 2001) and M.N. (2004) listed the parents as victims of unlawful killings. The ICTY transferred the case to Croatia in 2005. In 2006 the Zagreb County State Attorney’s Office indicted the generals for war crimes, specifying that unknown subordinates of R.A. had killed the parents on 9 September 1993.

The Zagreb County Court acquitted R.A. in 2008 and acquitted M.N. of the 9 September killings (convicting him of later war crimes). It found the applicant’s father (an armed civilian) had been killed while fleeing Croatian soldiers and that his mother (an unarmed civilian, initially misidentified) had also been killed by them. The Supreme Court upheld the judgment in 2009. Subsequent Croatian proceedings did not address the parents’ killings. A 2015 criminal complaint listing them among victims remains under investigation.

On 6 December 2007 the applicant sought an amicable settlement from the State Attorney’s Office. After refusal he sued the State on 6 March 2008 for HRK 520 000 in damages, asserting that Croatian soldiers had unlawfully killed his civilian parents. Civil proceedings were stayed pending the criminal trial and resumed in 2010. The Zagreb Municipal Civil Court in 2012 awarded damages for the mother’s death (a non-time-barred war crime) but dismissed the claim for the father (not established as an unlawful killing). The Zagreb County Court reversed in 2012, holding the entire claim statute-barred under section 376 of the Civil Obligations Act: the damage occurred in 1993, so the objective five-year period expired in 1998. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law in 2015. It characterised the deaths as non-war damage for which the State was liable, but held that unknown perpetrators precluded application of the longer criminal-law limitation under section 377. The objective five-year period therefore applied and, given the 2001 ICTY indictment listing the parents, the applicant had had an objective possibility of learning of the damage by then; the claim lodged in 2008 was out of time. The Constitutional Court rejected a subsequent complaint in 2015.

Separately, the applicant obtained final court decisions in 2012 and 2013 declaring his parents dead (deaths dated 9–10 September 1993).

Domestic law provides a three-year subjective limitation running from knowledge of the damage and perpetrator and an absolute five-year objective period from occurrence of the damage. Supreme Court practice uniformly treats the objective period as decisive even if the subjective period has not begun. In some cases involving delayed discovery of a relative’s death the Court has started the objective period from the date of knowledge; in missing-person cases it has started it from the date a declaration of death became final. The applicant contended that the Supreme Court had departed from this latter line of authority by not calculating the period from the 2012–2013 declarations of death.

The case of Vujnović v. Croatia (Application no. 32349/16) concerned an applicant whose parents were killed by Croatian Army soldiers on 9 September 1993 during Operation Pocket-93 in the Medak Pocket. The applicant alleged violations of Article 2 (procedural obligation to investigate) and Article 6 § 1 (access to court and legal certainty) of the Convention, the latter arising from how Croatian courts calculated the statutory limitation period for his civil damages claim against the State.

The applicant’s parents, A.V. and M.V., were among those killed when Croatian forces recaptured the area. Fifty-one bodies were recovered and later handed to Serbian authorities; identifications (some initially mistaken) occurred in late 1993 records obtained years later. An ICTY indictment of 21 May 2001 (amended 26 November 2001) against General R.A. listed the parents among unlawful killings. Domestic investigations began in 2002–2003. In 2006 an indictment was filed in Zagreb against Generals R.A. and M.N. for war crimes, specifying the parents’ deaths on 9 September 1993. The 2008 first-instance judgment acquitted R.A. entirely and M.N. of the 9 September killings (while convicting him of later acts); the Supreme Court largely upheld this in 2009. Later proceedings did not target the parents’ deaths. The applicant, who had served in the Croatian Army and received no Red Cross information, stated he first learned the details via media in 2006 when the Zagreb proceedings began.

He requested a friendly settlement in December 2007 and sued the State on 6 March 2008, claiming 520,000 HRK. The first-instance court awarded damages for the mother’s death (deemed a war crime against an unarmed civilian) but dismissed the claim for the father (an armed civilian). Both sides appealed. The Zagreb County Court reversed in 2012, dismissing the entire claim as time-barred under section 376 of the Civil Obligations Act: the objective five-year period ran from the 1993 deaths and expired in 1998. The longer period under section 377 did not apply because the perpetrators remained unknown. The Supreme Court confirmed this in 2015, holding that the damage occurred in 1993 (or at latest by the 2001 ICTY indictment listing the parents) and that the objective five-year limit barred the 2008 claim regardless of when the applicant subjectively learned of it. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint in 2015.

The applicant had also obtained court decisions declaring his parents dead in 2011–2013 (final in 2012–2013). He argued the limitation period should run from 2006 (when he learned of the killings) or from those declarations, citing Supreme Court practice in missing-persons cases. The Government pointed to earlier identifications and public ICTY material.

The ECtHR examined the Article 6 complaint (the Article 2 complaint having been notified but the judgment focusing on access to court). It found the Supreme Court’s application of the objective five-year period from 1993/2001 consistent with its case-law (which distinguishes cases of subsequent learning of death from true missing-persons cases ending in declarations of death) and not a disproportionate restriction. No violation of Article 6 § 1 was found. The judgment became final on 11 September 2020.

The case of Vujnović v. Croatia (no. 32349/16) originated in an application lodged on 2 June 2016 by Dušan Vujnović, a Croatian national born in 1963. He alleged a failure to comply with the procedural obligation under Article 2 of the Convention regarding the investigation of his parents’ deaths, as well as a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to inconsistent Supreme Court practice on calculating the statutory limitation period for a civil damages claim, which he claimed denied him access to a court.

The applicant’s parents, A.V. and M.V., were killed on 9 September 1993 by unidentified Croatian Army soldiers during Operation Pocket-93, a military action to recapture the Medak Pocket from Serbian forces amid Croatia’s war of independence. Fifty-one bodies were recovered, examined, and handed over to Serbian authorities, with some identifications recorded (the applicant’s father as a soldier, his mother initially misidentified). The applicant, then serving in the Croatian Army, received no information about their fate despite contacting the Red Cross.

A police working group began investigating the events in late 2002, interviewing witnesses and collecting documents, including a 2001 ICTY indictment against Croatian generals that listed the parents among 29 civilian victims. The ICTY transferred related cases to Croatia in 2005. In 2006, the Zagreb County State Attorney’s Office indicted generals R.A. and M.N. for war crimes, including the killings of the applicant’s parents by subordinates. In a 2008 judgment (upheld in 2009, with a sentence amendment), the Zagreb County Court acquitted R.A. entirely and M.N. of the 9 September killings, while convicting M.N. of later war crimes. The court established that the parents died on 9 September 1993: the mother as an unarmed civilian, the father (armed by locals for home defence) while fleeing with others. Subsequent proceedings against others did not address these deaths. A 2015 criminal complaint listing the parents remains under investigation.

On 6 March 2008 (after a failed 2007 settlement request), the applicant sued the State for damages of HRK 520,000, arguing the killings were war crimes (not war damage) and that he first learned of them in 2006 via media coverage of the criminal case. Civil proceedings were suspended pending the criminal judgment, then resumed. In 2012, the first-instance court awarded damages for the mother’s death (as a non-time-barred war crime) but dismissed the claim for the father (as an armed civilian). On appeal, the Zagreb County Court dismissed the entire claim as statute-barred under section 376 of the Civil Obligations Act (three-year subjective period from knowledge of damage and perpetrator; five-year objective period from occurrence). The Supreme Court (24 March 2015) upheld this: the State was liable under the 2003 Liability Act, but the perpetrator remaining unknown precluded the longer period under section 377. Damage occurred in 1993, yet the objective period started in 2001 (when the ICTY indictment listed the parents, giving an “objective possibility” to learn of their fate); the 2008 claim thus fell outside five years. The subjective period was inapplicable as it would exceed the objective one. The Constitutional Court dismissed a related complaint in 2015.

Separately, the applicant obtained decisions declaring his parents dead (final in 2012–2013). He maintained he could not have known earlier due to wartime circumstances. **Case Summary: Azerkane v. the Netherlands (ECHR, Application no. 3138/16, Judgment 2 June 2020)**

The applicant, Khalid Azerkane (born 1993), a Moroccan national, was born and has lived his entire life in the Netherlands with his parents and seven siblings. His parents and five siblings hold Dutch nationality; all family members reside lawfully there. He held a temporary renewable residence permit for family reunion (from birth or December 2000), which expired in January 2005 with a brief unextended gap until mid-February 2005, after which it was renewed until December 2014. He has a mild intellectual disability and received some vocational training, though he left school after a 2009 family car accident in Spain that killed a sister and uncle.

The applicant has a significant criminal record starting in adolescence. In 2006, he was convicted of street muggings and received 150 days’ juvenile detention (82 suspended) plus a training order. In 2007, he performed community service for setting off fireworks. In 2009, he was convicted of two house burglaries and received 42 days’ juvenile detention. In 2011, he was convicted of assault, theft with violence against his father, domestic violence, and criminal damage, receiving 60 days’ juvenile detention. Later that year (age 18), he committed an armed robbery, for which he received a three-year prison sentence in 2012 (with possible clinical treatment recommended due to his disability). Treatment in a forensic psychiatric facility was terminated early for lack of motivation, and he served the remainder in prison. Subsequent convictions after the impugned measures (firearms possession, threats) are noted but post-date the core decisions.

On 22 October 2013, the Deputy Minister of Security and Justice revoked the residence permit (retroactively from the 2011 robbery date) and imposed a 10-year entry ban, requiring immediate departure. This was based on section 3.86 of the Aliens Decree 2000’s sliding-scale system: 41 months of unsuspended custodial sentences against 6–7 years of continuous lawful residence (the 2005 gap interrupting continuity), exceeding thresholds for public-order threats (including five or more serious offences). The authorities accepted this interfered with Article 8 family/private life but found it justified. They weighed the persistent, serious, violent nature of the offences (especially the armed robbery and recidivism as an adult), the threat to public order, the applicant’s failure to reform despite opportunities, his majority/adulthood, limited evidence of exceptional ties beyond normal family bonds, some Moroccan connections (parental origins, a 2009 visit, some Berber language knowledge, family there), and the family’s ability to visit/support him. No objective impediment to settlement in Morocco was established; he was deemed capable of managing independently.

The applicant objected, arguing the 2005 gap was not his fault (he was a minor), his full life-long residence and strong post-accident family ties should prevail, the offences (mostly as a minor) were not sufficiently grave, his disability and lack of Arabic/Moroccan ties/network made settlement impossible, and he needed continued treatment in the Netherlands. The objection was rejected in June 2014 after a hearing. The Regional Court of The Hague dismissed his appeal in October 2014, upholding the residence calculation, finding insufficient substantiation of special family/social/cultural ties or impossibility of managing in Morocco, and confirming the public-interest outweighing. The Council of State dismissed further appeal in July 2015 without additional reasoning.

The ECHR found no violation of Article 8. The measures were “in accordance with the law” and pursued legitimate aims of public safety/crime prevention. A fair balance was struck: the persistent/serious offending constituted a real threat; there was no evidence of exceptional difficulty settling in Morocco; the ban was time-limited; and while the impact on the applicant’s long-established Netherlands life was serious, the authorities’ assessment was not unreasonable.

The case of Azerkane v. the Netherlands (Application no. 3138/16) concerns a Moroccan national, Khalid Azerkane (born 1993 in the Netherlands), who alleged that the revocation of his residence permit and imposition of a 10-year entry ban violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He had lived his entire life in the Netherlands with his parents and seven siblings (most of whom hold Dutch nationality or lawful residence). He held successive temporary residence permits for family reunification, though a brief 2005 gap (due to a late extension application by his father, when he was 12) interrupted continuity.

Azerkane accumulated a substantial criminal record starting as a juvenile. In 2006 he was convicted of street muggings and sentenced to 150 days' juvenile detention (partly suspended). Further convictions followed for burglary (2009, 42 days' detention), assault, theft with violence against his father, domestic violence and criminal damage (2011, 60 days' detention). In October 2011, at age 18, he committed armed robbery and received a three-year prison sentence. A psychiatrist noted a mild intellectual disability; attempted clinical treatment in a forensic psychiatric facility was terminated early due to lack of motivation. A 2009 family car accident in Spain (killing a sister and uncle) had already disrupted his vocational training and family life.

On 22 October 2013 the Deputy Minister of Security and Justice revoked the permit (retroactively effective from the 2011 robbery) under section 3.86 of the Aliens Decree 2000. The total unsuspended custodial sentences (41 months) far exceeded the applicable sliding-scale threshold for someone with 6–7 years of continuous lawful residence. A 10-year entry ban was also imposed because Azerkane posed a serious threat to public order. Switzerland and Üner v. the Netherlands, concluded that public-order interests prevailed. They cited the persistent and serious nature of the offences (especially the armed robbery), recidivism after majority, limited substantiated social/cultural ties, and the absence of objective obstacles to settlement in Morocco (he had visited once, spoke some Berber, and had family origins there). He argued that, as a young adult, he should be given time to reform and complete treatment. Domestic remedies failed: the objection was rejected, the Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the appeal (finding insufficient evidence of more than normal emotional family ties or inability to manage in Morocco), and the Council of State upheld that ruling.

Subsequent events included further convictions (2016: 12 months for possessing a loaded automatic firearm and related items; 2018: additional sentences for firearms offences and threatening police). Moroccan authorities had not yet issued a travel document by early 2019, despite repeated Dutch requests.

The case of Zirnīte v. Latvia (ECHR Application no. 69019/11, judgment of 11 June 2020) concerns allegations of unfair criminal proceedings and disproportionate confiscation of property.

The applicant, Ilona Zirnīte, was sole owner of SIA Raiņa bulvāra nams, whose sole asset was an apartment building in central Riga. In 2005 she negotiated its sale to M.R. via transfer of the company. She sought a short-term EUR 210,000 bank loan to purchase property in France; the bank lent the sum to the company instead, conditional on an escrow agreement for the sale. On 3 October 2005 an additional audit was performed at M.R.’s request. The parties disputed whether the purchase price was increased from EUR 5.2 million to EUR 5.4 million to account for the loan.

That evening the applicant, still representing the company, requested transfer of EUR 208,000 from its (then empty) account to her private account, without informing M.R. or the auditors. On 4 October the escrow was signed, the company sold, and the EUR 5.4 million purchase price paid into escrow. The bank then transferred EUR 210,000 to the company; immediately thereafter it executed the applicant’s request, sending EUR 208,000 to her private account. She used the funds to purchase a Deutsche Bank cheque with which she later bought French property. After sale formalities on 17 October, the remaining purchase price (minus the loan) was paid to her.

In 2006 the company sued her civilly for repayment of EUR 208,000. She counterclaimed that she had repaid the loan. A final 2008 judgment upheld the company’s claim; she repaid the sum plus costs.

Criminal proceedings were opened in March 2006. In 2007 the applicant was charged with large-scale misappropriation of funds and large-scale money laundering. Two of her properties, including the Bramberģes pils manor, were seized.

The Riga Regional Court (first instance) heard the applicant and eleven witnesses, including M.R. (cross-examined by defence counsel) and her husband V.R., who had taken part in all negotiations. Both M.R. and V.R. testified that the price had been raised to leave EUR 210,000 in the company after sale and that they had not been told of the transfer request. The court acquitted the applicant on 19 August 2009: the facts were established, but mens rea could not be proved beyond reasonable doubt because she had acted on bank advice.

The prosecutor and victim company appealed. The Supreme Court Criminal Chamber held an oral hearing at which the applicant, her lawyer and V.R. appeared. V.R. was examined and cross-examined; the applicant answered questions but gave no further statement. The court reviewed first-instance testimony of M.R. and others, the pre-trial confrontation minutes, and other materials. During closing submissions the defence lawyer sought to rely on M.R.’s pre-trial statements (not reviewed by the appellate court) and requested that the investigation be reopened and three witnesses, including M.R., be summoned. He argued that the victim had relied on those statements and that M.R. had said pre-trial she did not need the loan.

The court refused, finding no doubt about the completeness of the first-instance examination, noting that the parties had not earlier requested review of the pre-trial statements, and recording that the victim had withdrawn the relevant part of its appeal. On 26 November 2010 it quashed the acquittal and convicted the applicant on both charges. It relied on consistent testimony from M.R., V.R., the victim’s lawyer and bank employees (supported by documents) that the price had been increased on the understanding that EUR 210,000 would remain in the company. The applicant had admitted failing to inform M.R. of the transfer. Intent was inferred from the timing of her request (ensuring execution after she no longer represented the company), its contravention of loan conditions, and her failure to notify M.R. or the auditor. Use of the funds to buy the cheque constituted money laundering.

A suspended six-year prison sentence was imposed together with confiscation of the already-seized manor, the court citing the fact that damage had been repaired and that the applicant had two minor children. Cassation was dismissed on 10 May 2011.

The applicant alleged that the appellate court’s refusal to summon M.R. (whom she regarded as the principal witness) and the consequent inability to rely on her pre-trial testimony violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) by rendering the reversal of her acquittal unfair. She further complained that confiscation of legally acquired property, after she had already repaid the civil claim, violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 as disproportionate.

The case of P.N. v. Germany (Application no. 74440/17) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life). The applicant, a German national born in 1961 and living in Dresden, challenged a police order for the collection and five-year retention of his identification data: photographs of his face and body (including tattoos), fingerprints, palm prints, and a physical description.

On 18 August 2011, Dresden police issued the order under Article 81b (second alternative) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. This followed the opening of proceedings against him in June 2011 for receiving stolen goods after he purchased a nearly new bicycle for €29 at a flea market. The police classified him as a recidivist likely to reoffend or be suspected of similar property crimes, arguing the data would aid future investigations by confirming or excluding him as a perpetrator. His record included a 2010 fine for casting false suspicion; 2009 proceedings for assault and property damage (discontinued after payment); 2004 fraud proceedings (discontinued as minor); a 2001 prison sentence for fraud and a false declaration; a 2000 fraud fine; and other discontinued cases from 1999–2000 for withholding wages and property damage. Broader history from 1986–2001 comprised 13 convictions for traffic offences, intoxication, theft, fraud and insolvency crimes, with five prison terms (two months to 2.5 years) and various fines.

The applicant appealed administratively on 24 August 2011, claiming disproportionality given only three petty, dated convictions. Police dismissed the appeal on 16 May 2012, holding that discontinued proceedings (absent proven innocence) could be considered, albeit to a lesser degree, when assessing future risk. The 2011 stolen-goods case was discontinued on 4 June 2012 for insufficient evidence that he knew the bicycle was stolen.

He then sued in the Dresden Administrative Court. On 16 March 2015 the court dismissed the action, finding the statutory requirements met: he had been a suspect when the order issued (subsequent discontinuance being irrelevant). Measures were necessary for police records if criminological evidence suggested he might reasonably be suspected of future crimes, considering offence nature/severity, manner of commission, personality and time since last notice. Despite a drop in frequency after 2001, later events (2010 false-suspicion conviction, 2007 discontinued fraud cases, and a 2013 insult conviction during the proceedings) supported the assessment. Discontinued cases remained relevant unless innocence was established. His rheumatoid arthritis did not eliminate risk, as prior offences required little mobility. The interference was proportionate given 25 years of investigations; deletion remained possible if future conduct showed the data were no longer needed.

The Saxony Administrative Court of Appeal refused to admit his appeal on 7 October 2016. His 17 November 2016 constitutional complaint (alleging violation of personality rights and human dignity) was declined without reasons by the Federal Constitutional Court on 10 May 2017. Data were collected on 30 March 2017.

Domestic law (Saxony Police Act and related directive) permits storage of such data for crime prevention, limited to what is strictly necessary, with review deadlines of generally five years for adults (two years for minor cases) and judicial review of deletion refusals. The Court ultimately held there was no Article 8 violation, given the individualized risk assessment, less-intrusive nature of the data (compared with DNA), safeguards, review possibility, limited duration and modest daily-life impact.

Suspicion existed when the order issued (subsequent discontinuance being immaterial). It noted thirteen convictions between 1986 and 2001 (traffic offences, intoxication, theft, fraud and insolvency offences), resulting in prison terms of two months to two-and-a-half years on five occasions and fines otherwise. Although the frequency of proceedings had declined, a 2010 conviction for false suspicion was not petty; 2007 fraud proceedings had been discontinued; and the applicant had been convicted of insult in 2013 during the present litigation. His rheumatoid arthritis did not eliminate risk, as his prior offences required little physical activity. The interference was therefore proportionate; the applicant could later seek deletion if his conduct showed the data were no longer needed.

The Saxony Administrative Court of Appeal refused to admit an appeal in October 2016. A constitutional complaint to the Federal Constitutional Court was declined without reasons in May 2017. Identification data were collected on 30 March 2017. The case of Ilya Lyapin v. Russia (Application no. 70879/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the deprivation of the applicant’s parental authority over his biological son, alleged to constitute an unjustified interference with his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicant married A.K. in April 2000. Their son V. was born on 3 January 2001. The couple divorced by mutual consent on 15 April 2003. From 2004 A.K. lived with M.K., whom she married in 2005; the couple later had a son, Ye. V. grew up in this household and regarded M.K. as his father.

On 23 March 2011 A.K. applied to the Oktyabrskiy District Court of Arkhangelsk to divest the applicant of parental authority. She asserted that the applicant had never taken part in V.’s upbringing or provided meaningful financial support, had lived separately since the child’s birth, and had had no contact with V. after the divorce. V. barely remembered him. Since 2004 V. had been fully integrated into A.K.’s new family, was deeply attached to M.K. and Ye., identified himself as a member of that family, and was distressed that his surname and patronymic differed from Ye.’s. M.K. intended to adopt V.

The applicant lodged a counter-claim seeking defined access (fortnightly visits and annual holidays). He maintained that he loved V., had accepted that the child should remain with A.K. after the divorce, and had later orally agreed with A.K. not to intervene so that V. could adapt to the new family. He claimed that strained relations with A.K. had prevented any informal arrangement.

The District Court ordered a psychological assessment of the parent-child relationship. The applicant did not attend, citing illness; the assessment proceeded without him. V. told the experts that he lived with his “mum”, “dad” (M.K.) and brother Ye., knew of an “other dad” but did not remember him and did not want contact. A single meeting in April 2011 had left V. fearful of being kidnapped.

Witnesses confirmed the applicant’s absence from V.’s life. The kindergarten teacher had never seen him; V. treated M.K. as his father. The school teacher likewise had never encountered the applicant, whereas A.K. and M.K. were actively involved; V. spoke of M.K. as his father and wished to take his surname. The paediatrician reported that the applicant had never attended medical appointments. An acquaintance described a 2011 supermarket encounter in which V. failed to recognise the applicant until told who he was.

On 6 May 2011 the District Court granted A.K.’s application. It found that, since 2003, the applicant had provided only token support (small transfers in 2005 and 2011, one gift and a birthday greeting) and had taken no part in upbringing from 2004 onwards. A.K. had not obstructed contact and the applicant had never sought official assistance. Family ties had therefore been extinguished; V. perceived M.K. as his father. Deprivation of parental authority was a measure of last resort justified by the child’s best interests in health, personality development, education and emotional stability. The applicant’s access claim was dismissed and he was ordered to pay maintenance.

The Arkhangelsk Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 27 June 2011. Supervisory-review attempts failed. In January 2012 M.K. adopted V., thereby extinguishing the applicant’s remaining legal ties and maintenance obligation.

These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that the national courts had severed his residual family relationship with V. without sufficient justification.

The case of Ilya Lyapin v. Russia (Application no. 70879/11) concerned the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Russian courts had unlawfully deprived him of parental authority over his biological son, V. The applicant, born in 1980 and resident in Arkhangelsk, married A.K. in April 2000. Their son V. was born on 3 January 2001. The couple divorced by mutual consent on 15 April 2003, after which V. remained with his mother.

In 2004 A.K. began a relationship with M.K.; they married in 2005 and had a son, Ye. On 23 March 2011 A.K. brought proceedings in the Oktyabrskiy District Court of Arkhangelsk seeking to strip the applicant of parental authority. She asserted that he had never taken part in V.’s upbringing or provided meaningful financial support, had lived apart from them since the boy’s birth, and had had no contact with V. after the divorce. V., she said, scarcely remembered the applicant, regarded M.K. as his father, was deeply attached to M.K. and Ye., and felt distressed by having a different surname and patronymic. M.K. intended to adopt V.

The applicant lodged a counter-claim on 8 April 2011, insisting that he loved his son and wished to be involved in his upbringing. He claimed that after the divorce he had accepted that V. should stay with the mother in the child’s best interests and that, following A.K.’s remarriage, he had orally agreed not to interfere so as not to traumatise the boy. He complained that relations with A.K. were strained and that he had been unable to secure access; he therefore asked the court to grant him fortnightly weekend visits and the right to spend his annual leave with V.

The District Court ordered a psychological assessment of the parent-child relationship. The applicant sought a postponement on grounds of illness; the request was refused and the assessment proceeded in his absence. V. told the psychologists that he lived with his “mum,” his “dad” (M.K.) and his brother Ye., knew of his “other dad” but did not remember him and did not want contact. A single meeting in April 2011 had left him fearing abduction.

At the hearing on 6 May 2011 the court heard the parties and several witnesses. V.’s kindergarten teacher, class teacher and paediatrician all confirmed that they had never seen the applicant and that A.K. and M.K. were the adults actively involved in the child’s daily life and education. An acquaintance of the applicant described a chance supermarket encounter in which V. did not recognise the applicant until told who he was. Documentary evidence showed only token financial contributions (1,000 roubles in 2005, 1,500 roubles in 2011, one delivery of gifts, a birthday greeting and the opening of a small bank account). Photographs produced by the applicant depicted contact only before 2004.

In its judgment of 6 May 2011 the District Court held that the applicant had, without objective justification, failed since 2004 to participate in V.’s upbringing or to show any genuine interest in his life. Family ties had been extinguished; V. perceived M.K. as his father. Deprivation of parental authority was therefore a necessary last-resort measure in the child’s best interests. The applicant’s request for access was rejected and he was ordered to pay monthly child maintenance. The Arkhangelsk Regional Court upheld the judgment on 27 June 2011. Subsequent supervisory-review applications failed. On 24 January 2012 M.K. was granted a full adoption of V., thereby terminating the applicant’s maintenance obligation.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s allegation that the removal of his residual legal link with V. constituted an unjustified interference with his right to respect for family life.

The case of Ilya Lyapin v. Russia concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that Russian courts unlawfully deprived him of parental authority over his biological son, V. (born 3 January 2001), thereby interfering with his right to respect for family life.

The applicant married A.K. in April 2000. The couple divorced by mutual consent on 15 April 2003. Thereafter A.K. formed a relationship with M.K.; they married in 2005 and had a son, Ye. From 2004 onward V. lived with A.K. and M.K. as a family unit. On 23 March 2011 A.K. applied to the Oktyabrskiy District Court of Arkhangelsk to have the applicant stripped of parental authority. She asserted that the applicant had never participated in V.’s upbringing or provided meaningful financial support, had lived separately from the child since birth, and after the divorce had never seen V. or shown any interest in him. V. barely remembered his biological father, regarded M.K. as his dad, was deeply attached to M.K. and Ye., and was distressed that his surname and patronymic differed from those of his half-brother. M.K. intended to adopt V.

The applicant filed a counter-claim seeking access (fortnightly visits plus annual holiday). He claimed he had accepted that V. should remain with A.K., had orally agreed after her remarriage not to “intervene” so as not to traumatise the child, and that strained relations with A.K. had prevented him from arranging contact. He produced photographs showing pre-2004 contact and asserted informal cash payments, but adduced no corroborating evidence.

The court commissioned a psychological assessment of the parent-child relationship. The applicant sought postponement on medical grounds; the assessment nevertheless proceeded in his absence. V. told the experts he lived with his “mum,” “dad” (M.K.) and “brother Ye.,” knew of an “other dad” but did not remember him and did not wish contact. A single April 2011 encounter had left V. fearing abduction. Witnesses (kindergarten teacher, class teacher, paediatrician) confirmed that only A.K. and M.K. had ever been involved in V.’s daily life, schooling and healthcare; the applicant had never appeared. A further witness described a supermarket meeting in which V. failed to recognise the applicant until the latter identified himself, after which the boy immediately wanted to leave.

On 6 May 2011 the District Court granted A.K.’s claim and dismissed the access application. Applying Article 69 of the Family Code and Supreme Court guidance, it found that deprivation of parental authority is a last-resort measure justified only by deliberate avoidance of parental duties. The applicant had lived apart from V. since 2003, provided only token financial support (1 000 RUB in 2005, 1 500 RUB in 2011, one gift parcel, a birthday greeting and a 1 000-RUB bank deposit), and had never sought access or official assistance before A.K. instituted proceedings. Family ties had been extinguished; V. perceived M.K. as his father. The measure was therefore necessary to protect V.’s rights to health, education and proper development. Monthly child support was ordered. The Arkhangelsk Regional Court upheld the judgment on 27 June 2011. Subsequent supervisory-review attempts failed. On 24 January 2012 M.K. adopted V., terminating the applicant’s support obligation.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 8 complaint that the deprivation lacked relevant and sufficient reasons and ignored his genuine wish to restore contact.

The case of Ghoumid and Others v. France concerned five dual nationals (four Moroccan, one Turkish) who acquired French nationality between 1991 and 2001—some by birth in France and declaration upon majority, others via parental naturalisation or their own declarations. In a 11 July 2007 Paris Criminal Court judgment (upheld on appeal for two applicants in 2008), they were convicted of participating in a criminal conspiracy to commit terrorist acts spanning 1995–2004. They had provided financial and logistical support to the Moroccan Islamist Combatant Group (GICM), linked to the Salafiya Jihadia organisation responsible for the May 2003 Casablanca bombings. Their actions included operating businesses that funded GICM activities, clandestinely harbouring its members (except for one applicant), and procuring passports later falsified to facilitate GICM travel. Sentences ranged from six to eight years’ imprisonment with lengthy minimum terms; all were released in 2009 or 2010.

In April 2015 the Interior Minister notified the applicants of proceedings to deprive them of French nationality under Articles 25 and 25-1 of the Civil Code, citing the 2007 terrorism convictions. After they submitted observations and the Conseil d’État assented, the Prime Minister issued deprivation orders on 7 October 2015. The applicants sought urgent suspension and judicial review before the Conseil d’État. Suspensions were refused in November 2015. On 8 June 2016 the Conseil d’État dismissed the merits challenges. It held that deprivation of nationality was an administrative (not criminal) sanction, so Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (ne bis in idem) was inapplicable. It also ruled that a 2006 legislative extension of the applicable time-limit from ten to fifteen years could be applied, as the original period had not yet expired when the law entered force. On the substance, the court accepted that the measure engaged the right to respect for private life (as nationality forms part of personal identity) but found it proportionate to the gravity of the terrorist offences and the applicants’ subsequent conduct. It saw no interference with family life, because deprivation itself produced no automatic effect on residence rights or family relationships.

Two applicants later appeared before a deportation board; favourable opinions were issued but no deportation orders were served. The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the 2015 deprivation constituted a second punishment contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 and a disproportionate interference with their private and family life under Article 8. The Court declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible and examined only those two complaints.

The Court held that Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 did not apply: applying the Engel criteria, deprivation of nationality is not a “criminal” sanction. On Article 8 it found no interference with family life, as the measure did not entail deportation. Private life was engaged because of the impact on personal identity, but the measure was not arbitrary. The eight-year interval between conviction and deprivation was explained by the authorities’ response to the marked rise in terrorist violence around 2015. Adequate procedural safeguards existed (prior notification, opportunity to make representations, Conseil d’État assent and subsequent judicial review). The consequences were not disproportionate: the applicants had participated for a decade in a terrorist conspiracy posing a grave threat to democracy and human rights; they did not become stateless; and loss of nationality did not automatically extinguish their right to reside in France. The Court therefore found no violation.

**CASE OF GHOUMID AND OTHERS v. FRANCE (ECtHR, 25 June 2020)**

Five dual-national applicants (four Moroccan, one Turkish) who had acquired French nationality between 1991 and 2001 challenged Prime Ministerial orders of 7 October 2015 stripping them of French citizenship. All had been convicted on 11 July 2007 by the Paris Criminal Court (upheld on appeal for two) of participating in a criminal conspiracy to commit terrorist acts between 1995 and 2004. They provided financial and logistical support to the Moroccan Islamist Combatant Group (GICM), linked to the Salafiya Jihadia organisation responsible for the 16 May 2003 Casablanca bombings. Support included working in businesses aiding GICM, clandestinely harbouring members (except one applicant), and obtaining passports for falsification to facilitate GICM movement. Sentences ranged from six to eight years’ imprisonment (with security periods); they were released in 2009–2010.

In April 2015 the Interior Minister notified them of proceedings under Articles 25 and 25-1 of the Civil Code (as amended in 2006 to extend the relevant time-limit from 10 to 15 years for terrorism-related convictions). After the Conseil d’État’s assent, the Prime Minister issued the deprivation orders, citing the 2007 convictions. Urgent applications to suspend the orders were rejected in November 2015. In June 2016 the Conseil d’État dismissed judicial-review actions. It held that deprivation was an administrative (not criminal) sanction, so Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (ne bis in idem) did not apply; the 2006 time-limit extension was valid because the original 10-year period had not expired by the law’s entry into force. On Article 8, it found no interference with family life (the measure itself had no automatic effect on residence or family ties) but recognised an impact on private life/identity. Given the gravity of the terrorism-related acts, subsequent conduct, and the measure’s preventive purpose, the interference was not disproportionate. Two applicants later faced deportation-board hearings, but no orders were notified.

The applicants complained to the ECtHR under Article 8 (private and family life) and Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The Court declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible. Applying the Engel criteria, it held that nationality deprivation was not a “criminal” sanction: it pursued a preventive/public-order aim rather than punishment, was classified as administrative under French law, and did not involve the severity or stigma of a criminal penalty. Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 was therefore inapplicable. On Article 8, there was no interference with family life because the orders did not entail deportation. There was an interference with private life (impact on personal identity and social ties), but it was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim (prevention of terrorism), and was not arbitrary. The eight-year gap between conviction and deprivation was explained by the authorities’ response to a surge in terrorist violence around 2015. Procedural safeguards existed (prior notice, opportunity to comment, Conseil d’État assent, and full judicial review). The measure was not disproportionate: the applicants had been convicted of sustained, serious support for a terrorist conspiracy over a decade; they retained their other nationalities (no statelessness); and loss of French nationality did not automatically extinguish their right to reside in France. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8.
