The case of Ghoumid and Others v. France (ECtHR, 25 June 2020) concerned five dual nationals (four Moroccan, one Turkish) convicted in 2007 of participating in a criminal conspiracy to commit terrorist acts between 1995 and 2004. They had provided financial and logistical support to the Moroccan Islamist Combatant Group (GICM), including through businesses, harbouring members and obtaining falsified passports. Sentences ranged from six to eight years’ imprisonment; they were released in 2009–2010. All had acquired French nationality by declaration or naturalisation between 1991 and 2001 (two having been born in France).

In April 2015 the Minister of the Interior initiated deprivation-of-nationality proceedings under Articles 25 and 25-1 of the Civil Code (as amended in 2006 to extend the relevant time-limits from 10 to 15 years for terrorist offences). After inviting observations and obtaining the assent of the Conseil d’État, the Prime Minister issued orders on 7 October 2015 stripping the applicants of French nationality. The Conseil d’État dismissed their challenges in June 2016, holding that the measure was an administrative (not criminal) sanction, that the 2006 amendment applied because the original time-limit had not expired, and that the orders were proportionate given the gravity of the acts. Two applicants later faced deportation proceedings, but no orders were served.

The applicants complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (ne bis in idem) that deprivation of nationality constituted a second punishment for the same terrorist offences, and under Article 8 that it arbitrarily interfered with their private and family life, identity and residence rights.

The Court first examined Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. Applying the Engel criteria, it held that deprivation of nationality was not a “criminal” sanction: it was classified as administrative under domestic law, pursued the preventive aim of protecting the Nation rather than punishment, and, while severe, did not entail the stigmatic or punitive consequences typical of a criminal penalty. The provision was therefore inapplicable.

Turning to Article 8, the Court found no interference with family life, because the measure itself did not entail deportation or automatic loss of residence rights. It did, however, affect private life by altering a core element of personal identity. The interference was lawful (based on precise statutory grounds) and pursued the legitimate aims of national security and public safety. It was not arbitrary: the eight-year gap between conviction and deprivation was explained by the sharp rise in terrorist violence in 2015; the applicants had been given notice, an opportunity to comment, and full judicial review; and they did not become stateless. Balancing the seriousness of participation over a decade in a conspiracy linked to deadly attacks against the applicants’ long-standing ties to France, the Court concluded that the consequences were not disproportionate. Subsequent conduct did not alter that assessment.

The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8 and no applicability of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The judgment underscores that, while nationality forms part of identity, States retain a wide margin in withdrawing it from dual nationals convicted of terrorism, provided procedural safeguards exist and statelessness is avoided.

The case of Voica v. Romania (Application no. 9256/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The applicant, a dual French-Romanian national living in Bucharest, complained that Romanian courts ordered the return of her two young sons to France (their prior habitual residence, where their father still lived). She argued that the courts failed to give due weight to French decisions establishing the children’s residence with her and ignored the grave risk of harm from the father’s alleged past violence toward her.

The applicant cohabited with Mr. X (a French national) in France from 2009. Their sons, Y (born 2012) and Z (born 2015), were raised bilingually and regularly visited Romania. The couple separated in April 2016; X moved out, while the applicant and children remained together. On 2 September 2016, the Bobigny tribunal de grande instance granted joint parental authority, set the children’s residence with the mother in France, and awarded X contact rights. Both parents had to inform each other of any residence change. Both appealed.

The applicant alleged psychological pressure throughout the relationship, which became verbal and physical after separation. On 2 December 2016, X violently attempted to take the children (who were present), breaking the applicant’s finger. A restraining order followed. X was convicted of domestic violence and given a suspended fine, but the conviction was later quashed on appeal in 2019 (the applicant said she was not informed or able to participate). She obtained support from a French domestic-violence organisation.

In June 2017 the applicant accepted a three-year job in Romania starting 1 September. She informed X on 3 July of her intention to take the children; he did not reply. She moved, notified the new address on 19 August, and enrolled the children in a French school in Bucharest.

On 21 November 2017 the Paris Court of Appeal dismissed X’s interim request for the children’s return (noting he had not yet invoked the Hague Convention) and the applicant’s request for exclusive parental authority and approval of the move. It left the 2016 arrangements in place.

X then applied under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. On 30 April 2018 the Bucharest County Court ordered the children’s return to France. It found the removal wrongful: habitual residence had been France, parental authority was joint, and the move occurred without X’s consent or a final French court authorisation. The court examined the 2 December 2016 incident and other evidence but held that X had not been shown to be violent, abusive or neglectful toward the children themselves; thus Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention (grave risk of physical or psychological harm or an intolerable situation) was not met. Even if a risk existed, international cooperation under the Brussels II bis Regulation could protect the children after return. The children (then very young) were not interviewed. Although they had integrated in Romania, the court considered that legalising the mother’s unilateral, unlawful change of residence would not serve their best interests. The Bucharest Court of Appeal upheld the order on 9 August 2018.

Enforcement proved difficult. The children refused to leave Romania with X. Incidents of alleged verbal abuse, threats and property damage by X occurred during attempted visits. Psychological counselling was ordered and the applicant’s objection to enforcement was dismissed. Meanwhile, on 22 October 2019 the Paris Court of Appeal, in the still-pending French custody proceedings, rejected the applicant’s allegations of abuse as unsubstantiated, criticised her unilateral relocation and obstruction of contact, and transferred the children’s residence to the father in France (the applicant receiving contact rights only in France).

The applicant contended that these Romanian decisions violated Article 8 by failing to take full account of the French residence orders and the risk posed by the father’s violence. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found that the domestic courts had adequately examined the family context, the violence allegations, the children’s best interests and their integration, and that their application of the Hague Convention and Brussels II bis Regulation satisfied the guarantees of Article 8.

The case of Voica v. Romania (Application no. 9256/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The applicant, a dual French-Romanian national, claimed that Romanian courts unlawfully ordered the return of her two young sons to France, where they had lived with their French father before she moved them to Romania. She argued that the courts failed to give due weight to French custody decisions favouring her or to the grave risk of harm from the father's alleged past violence.

The applicant and Mr X began cohabiting in France in 2009 and had two sons, born in 2012 and 2015. The children were raised bilingually and regularly visited Romania. The couple separated in April 2016, after which the applicant and children remained in the family home. In September 2016 the Bobigny tribunal de grande instance awarded the parents joint parental authority, set the children's residence with the mother in France, and granted the father contact rights. Both parents were required to notify each other of any change of residence and to consult on the children's welfare. Both appealed.

The applicant alleged ongoing psychological pressure by X and, after separation, verbal and physical abuse. She described a December 2016 incident in which X, attempting to take the children, became violent in their presence and broke her finger. A restraining order was issued and X was convicted of domestic violence (later quashed on appeal in 2019, without the applicant's participation). She obtained support from a specialist organisation.

In June 2017 the applicant accepted a three-year job in Romania. She informed X of her intention to move with the children; he did not reply. She relocated in August 2017, notified him of the new address, and enrolled the children in a French school in Bucharest. In November 2017 the Paris Court of Appeal rejected both X's interim request for the children's return and the applicant's request for exclusive parental authority and approval of the move, maintaining the 2016 arrangements. It noted that X had not sought residence with himself or initiated Hague Convention proceedings.

In February 2018 X applied under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction for the children's return. The Bucharest County Court granted the application in April 2018. It found the removal wrongful: at the time of the move the children's habitual residence was France, parental authority was joint, and French law required mutual consent or court authorisation for a change of residence—neither of which existed. The court examined the 2016 and 2017 French decisions. It rejected the applicant's “grave risk” defence under Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention, holding that the evidence (including the 2016 incident) did not establish that X had been violent, abusive or neglectful toward the children. Any residual risk could be managed through cooperation with French authorities under the Brussels II bis Regulation. The children were too young to be interviewed. Although they had integrated in Romania, the court held that this could not legalise a unilateral, unlawful change of residence contrary to their best interests. The Bucharest Court of Appeal upheld the order in August 2018.

Subsequent enforcement attempts met resistance. The children refused to return; the applicant alleged further verbal abuse and threats by X. Psychological counselling was ordered and an objection to enforcement was dismissed. In October 2019 the Paris Court of Appeal, in the final custody ruling, transferred the children's residence to the father in France, finding that the applicant's unilateral relocation and obstruction of contact had violated the children's right to maintain relations with both parents. Contact was granted to the mother only in France.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the Romanian courts' interpretation and application of the Hague Convention and Brussels II bis Regulation adequately protected Article 8 rights. They had examined the full family context, including the violence allegations, identified the children's best interests, and given no decisive weight to their Romanian integration given the unlawful removal and maintained links to France. The children's young age justified not hearing them. No violation was found.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Popović and Others v. Serbia (applications nos. 26944/13, 14616/16, 14619/16 and 22233/16) concerns four Serbian nationals who alleged discrimination in the provision of disability benefits. All four applicants suffer from paraplegia that left them unable to use their legs and dependent on wheelchairs. They were each classified by the authorities as 100% disabled. Their injuries arose from civilian incidents rather than military service: the first applicant (Dejan Popović) fell from a height of about five metres in 2005; the second (Josip Vlček) and third (Miroslav Homa) were injured in traffic accidents in 1970 and 1986 respectively; and the fourth (Zvonko Nikolić) was injured in a shooting in 1994.

Under the 1991 Social Welfare Act (repealed in 2011), persons in the applicants’ position were entitled to an assisted living allowance (and an increased version thereof for those classified as 100% disabled). The increased allowance equalled 70% of the average net salary, adjusted twice yearly for the cost of living. The applicants received this benefit but were not entitled to a personal disability allowance or an orthopaedic allowance.

By contrast, the Veterans’ Entitlements Act granted disabled war veterans classified as 100% disabled a personal disability allowance equal to the average net salary increased by 80%, an assisted living allowance in the same amount, and an orthopaedic allowance amounting to 29% of the average net salary increased by 80%. Additional healthcare, nutritional, mobility and orthopaedic entitlements were also available to veterans. The applicants therefore received fewer categories of benefit and substantially lower overall amounts than veterans with identical paraplegic disabilities.

The applicants brought civil discrimination claims against the Ministry responsible for labour and social policy, seeking damages for mental anguish caused by the disparity. They argued that the difference in treatment, despite identical disabilities and needs, violated domestic anti-discrimination provisions, constitutional equality principles and Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The first applicant’s claim was dismissed at first instance in 2009, on appeal in 2011, by the Supreme Court of Cassation in 2011 and by the Constitutional Court in 2012. The remaining three applicants initially succeeded at first instance in 2008 (each being awarded 500,000 dinars plus costs) but lost on the State’s appeal in 2010; the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Constitutional Court (2015) upheld the dismissal.

Domestic courts acknowledged that civilian disabled persons were placed in a less favourable position but held that the difference did not constitute discrimination. They emphasised the State’s wide margin of appreciation in social-policy matters, the legitimacy of positive discrimination or affirmative action in favour of war veterans (who were regarded as being in a fundamentally different situation), and the fact that any differentiation arose from the applicable legislation itself rather than from arbitrary application of that legislation. The Constitutional Court additionally noted that the applicants had not properly raised a challenge to the constitutionality of the statutes themselves.

The relevant legal framework included Article 21 of the Serbian Constitution (prohibiting discrimination on grounds including disability while permitting special measures to achieve substantive equality) and Article 69 (affording special protection to disabled persons, war veterans and war victims). The 2020 legislation that later replaced the Veterans’ Entitlements Act explicitly based veterans’ benefits on “the principle of national recognition.” International materials cited in the case, including concluding observations of the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, criticised distinctions in social entitlements based on the cause of impairment.

The applicants contended that the statutory scheme treated persons with the same disability and the same practical needs differently solely because of the civilian versus military origin of their injuries, thereby violating the prohibition on discrimination in the enjoyment of property rights (the benefits constituting possessions). The Government maintained that the difference pursued the legitimate aim of recognising the special contribution and sacrifice of war veterans and fell within the State’s margin of appreciation in allocating limited social-security resources.

The case of Popović and Others v. Serbia concerns four Serbian nationals with identical paraplegic disabilities who alleged discrimination in state disability benefits. The first applicant, Dejan Popović, became paraplegic and wheelchair-dependent after a 2005 fall of approximately five metres. He was assessed as 100% disabled in 2006 and granted an increased assisted living allowance (for constant care by another person). The remaining applicants—Josip Vlček (injured in a 1970 traffic accident), Miroslav Homa (1986 traffic accident) and Zvonko Nikolić (1994 shooting)—likewise sustained complete paraplegia, were classified as 100% disabled between 1987 and 2007, and received the same increased civilian allowance. All four became active in disability-rights organisations.

Under the 1991 Social Welfare Act then in force, civilian beneficiaries classified as 100% disabled received only an increased assisted-living allowance equal to 70% of the average net salary (adjusted twice yearly for living costs). By contrast, the Veterans’ Entitlements Act entitled war veterans with the identical 100% paraplegia to three separate monthly cash benefits: a personal disability allowance of 180% of average net salary, an assisted-living allowance of the same amount, and an orthopaedic allowance of 29% of that elevated base, together with additional healthcare, mobility and prosthetic entitlements. The applicants therefore received both fewer categories of benefit and substantially lower total sums, despite having the same functional impairment and the same daily care needs.

In 2007–2008 the applicants brought civil discrimination actions against the Ministry of Labour seeking damages for the mental anguish caused by this disparity. They argued that the sole differentiating factor was the civilian versus military origin of their injuries and that the resulting treatment violated domestic anti-discrimination rules as well as Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (the benefits constituting “possessions”). The first applicant’s claim was dismissed at every level. The Novi Sad Municipal Court accepted that civilians were placed in a less favourable position but held that the administrative authorities had merely applied binding legislation. The Court of Appeal added that the State enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation in social-policy matters, that the difference constituted legitimate positive discrimination for a group in a fundamentally different situation, and that discrimination could arise only if identically situated persons were treated differently in the application of the same law. The Supreme Court of Cassation endorsed this reasoning and noted that constitutional review of legislation lay exclusively with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court rejected the subsequent constitutional appeal on the ground that the applicant had invoked only accessory constitutional principles rather than specific rights.

The other three applicants initially succeeded at first instance (each awarded RSD 500 000 plus costs), the Municipal Court focusing on the unequal assisted-living amounts for persons with identical needs. The Court of Appeal reversed, repeating the margin-of-appreciation and positive-discrimination analysis and citing European Court of Human Rights case-law. The Supreme Court of Cassation upheld the reversal. The Constitutional Court dismissed their 2012 appeals in 2015, holding that it could not act as a fourth-instance court absent manifest arbitrariness, that the applicants’ arguments were sometimes contradictory, and that any challenge to the constitutionality of the statutes themselves required separate abstract-review proceedings.

The applicants then lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that the statutory scheme systematically discriminated against civilian disabled persons in the enjoyment of property rights. The Court ultimately found the difference in treatment objectively and reasonably justified by the distinct social purpose of veterans’ benefits (recognition of service and sacrifice) and by the State’s wide margin in the allocation of scarce social-security resources.

The case of Popović and Others v. Serbia (ECtHR, 2020) concerns four Serbian civilians with identical 100% paraplegic disabilities who alleged discrimination in state disability benefits compared to war veterans.

Applicant Dejan Popović became paraplegic and wheelchair-dependent after a 5-metre fall in July 2005. The others (Josip Vlček, Miroslav Homa and Zvonko Nikolić) suffered the same outcome from traffic accidents (1970 and 1986) and a 1994 shooting. All were officially assessed as 100% disabled between 1987 and 2007 and received an increased assisted-living allowance (for needing another person’s constant help) under the 1991 Social Welfare Act. That allowance equalled 70% of the average net salary, adjusted twice yearly for living costs. They were ineligible for two further monthly payments available only to disabled war veterans under the Veterans’ Entitlements Act: a personal disability allowance (average net salary plus 80%) and an orthopaedic allowance (29% of that enhanced salary figure). Veterans also received an assisted-living allowance at the higher personal-disability rate.

The applicants argued that the statutory scheme treated them less favourably than veterans who had exactly the same physical impairment and the same practical needs. They claimed this difference constituted discrimination on the ground of “other status” (civilian versus military origin of the disability) in the enjoyment of property rights (social-security entitlements), contrary to Article 14 of the Convention read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They sought compensation for the resulting mental anguish.

Popović sued the Ministry of Labour in 2008. The Novi Sad Municipal Court dismissed the claim in 2009, holding that any disparity followed directly from the applicable statutes, which the administration was bound to apply. The Court of Appeal (2011) and Supreme Court of Cassation (2011) affirmed, emphasising the State’s wide margin of appreciation in social-policy matters and characterising the veterans’ extra benefits as legitimate positive discrimination for a group in a fundamentally different situation (wartime service and sacrifice). Discrimination, they said, could arise only if identically situated persons were treated differently. The Constitutional Court rejected Popović’s 2011 appeal in 2012, finding that he had invoked only accessory constitutional principles rather than a specific constitutional right.

The remaining three applicants brought a joint claim in 2007. The Municipal Court initially awarded each of them RSD 500 000 (then ≈ €6 440) plus costs, focusing on the lower assisted-living payments. The Court of Appeal reversed in 2010, repeating the margin-of-appreciation and positive-discrimination reasoning and adding that persons excluded from affirmative-action measures cannot claim a violation merely by that exclusion. The Supreme Court of Cassation upheld that judgment in 2011. The Constitutional Court dismissed their 2012 appeal in 2015, declining to act as a fourth-instance court in the absence of manifest arbitrariness, describing the pleadings as sometimes contradictory, and noting that a challenge to the constitutionality of the underlying statutes should have been brought in separate abstract-review proceedings.

Domestic law (Constitution Articles 21, 69 and 168–170; Social Welfare Act Articles 9–11, 23 and 25; Veterans’ Entitlements Act Articles 21, 28–29, 39–40 and 43–44) explicitly distinguishes the two categories and permits special measures for veterans. UN CRPD concluding observations on Serbia and neighbouring States have criticised distinctions based on the cause of impairment and recommended equal benefits regardless of origin. The applicants maintained that these facts demonstrated an unjustified difference in treatment of persons in analogous situations.

The ECHR case of Kaminskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 44817/18) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for home) arising from a court-ordered demolition of the applicant’s house, built unlawfully on forest land.

A three-month extension was granted, but a further request was refused. In September 2013 the Inspectorate sued for non-compliance. The applicant did not contest the unlawfulness but sought to reclassify the relevant portion of the land (arguing it was treeless) so that the buildings could be legalised ex post facto. He emphasised his personal circumstances and lack of alternative housing.

Repeated requests in 2013–2014 to forest authorities to redraw the forest boundaries were refused: the plot had met the statutory definition of forest land since 2004, as shown by contemporaneous photographs, and unlawful building was not a ground for reclassification. Related administrative complaints were dismissed by the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (March 2015) and the Supreme Administrative Court (March 2016); age and income, the courts held, did not excuse compliance with the law.

The applicant had built on forest land without the required permit or status change; subsequent legalisation efforts had failed. The Kaunas Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 9 February 2018, stressing that the applicant had knowingly built without a permit and that personal hardship did not override the statutory duty to remove unlawful structures. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on points of law (27 April 2018).

Enforcement continued: in September 2019 the applicant was fined €80 for non-compliance; the amount reflected his age, health, income and first-time status, but the fine did not extinguish the demolition obligation. The fine was upheld on appeal. As of February 2020 the house remained standing.

Domestic courts had in fact considered the applicant’s personal situation (age, health, income, sole home) even though Lithuanian law did not require it. Substantial time—more than a year of extensions and adjournments—had been afforded so that legalisation could be attempted. Given the applicant’s conscious defiance of known building restrictions on protected forest land, preference for environmental protection did not exceed the State’s margin of appreciation. An abstract review of the legislation was not the Court’s role.

It noted that the proceedings pursued complementary aims (addressing ordinary traffic violations versus particularly serious consequences), were foreseeable, involved adequate interaction between the courts, and produced combined penalties that did not exceed what was strictly necessary given the gravity of the offences. The case of Pormes v. the Netherlands (ECHR Application no. 25402/14) concerns an Indonesian national's claim that Dutch authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by refusing him a residence permit after he had lived in the Netherlands since early childhood. Hein Pormes was born in Indonesia in 1987. His Indonesian mother died in January 1991. In April 1991, at nearly age four, he entered the Netherlands on an Indonesian passport with a tourist visa, accompanied by his presumed Dutch father. The visa was extended until 1 August 1991 but he remained thereafter. His presumed father returned frequently to Indonesia, leaving the applicant in the care of a Dutch paternal uncle and aunt (his foster parents), with whose four children he grew up. The presumed father died in April 1999.

The applicant attended Dutch primary and secondary schools, completing pre-vocational education in metalworks in 2002/03 and later enrolling in culinary training. In 2004 he accepted an out-of-court settlement (10 hours' community service) for an assault. That year a truant officer's inquiry revealed he was unregistered in municipal records. His Indonesian 1991 passport was located, confirming his lack of legal status. Distressed, he used drugs briefly and abandoned his studies.

In August 2006 he was convicted of indecent assault (Criminal Code Art. 246) and four counts of attempted indecent assault (September–October 2005), receiving 240 hours' community service, a training order and a six-month suspended prison sentence. Four offences involved following female cyclists to force them to stop or fall so he could commit lewd acts. In September 2006 he applied for a temporary residence permit for extended family reunion with his foster father, asserting he had always believed himself Dutch. The Deputy Minister rejected the application in December 2007: the offences made him a threat to public order (Aliens Act s. 16(1)(d) and Aliens Decree s. 3.77); he had never been lawfully resident, so refusal did not interfere with existing family life and created no positive obligation under Article 8.

A further objection was rejected in July 2008 after a June 2008 conviction for two counts of indecent assault and three attempted offences (May–December 2007), resulting in 15 months' imprisonment (five months suspended) plus execution of the earlier suspended term. Authorities again stressed the seriousness and repetition of the crimes, his adulthood, the absence of more-than-normal dependence on his foster parents, and his capacity to live independently in Indonesia (where contact could continue via visits).

The applicant appealed. A separate 2008–2011 application to confirm Dutch nationality from birth failed: his parents had never married and he was not recorded as the presumed father's child. The Regional Court of The Hague (Zwolle) initially allowed the residence-permit appeal in January 2012, finding the authorities had not transparently weighed his long integration, schooling and social ties. The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State reversed this in November 2013. It held that, although the applicant had very strong Dutch ties, his foster parents had known or ought to have known of his precarious status from the outset; the offences were serious, committed as an adult and as a recidivist after he knew he lacked status; he was an adult without exceptional family dependence; and he could manage in Indonesia despite language and family-absence difficulties. There was therefore no positive Article 8 obligation.

In August 2016 the applicant departed for Indonesia with IOM assistance. The alleged Article 8 violation centres on the refusal, after 15-plus years of de-facto residence from age four, of a permit that would have regularised his private and family life with his foster family, despite his integration and the late discovery of his status.

**Case of Pormes v. the Netherlands (App. no. 25402/14, ECtHR, 28 July 2020)**

Indonesian national Hein Pormes (born 1987) alleged that Dutch authorities’ refusal of a residence permit violated his Article 8 rights to respect for private and family life. He had lived in the Netherlands from early childhood without lawful status.

Born in Indonesia to an Indonesian mother who died in January 1991, he travelled to the Netherlands on 13 April 1991 (nearly age 4) with his presumed Dutch father on an Indonesian passport and tourist visa. The visa was extended to 1 August 1991, but he overstayed. His presumed father (who died in April 1999) frequently returned to Indonesia, leaving him in the care of a Dutch paternal uncle and aunt (his foster parents) and their four children. He attended Dutch primary and secondary school, completing pre-vocational education in metalwork around 2002/03, and later enrolled in culinary training.

In 2004, a local truant officer inquiry revealed he was unregistered in the municipal database. His Indonesian passport from 1991 was located among his presumed father’s effects, confirming his lack of legal status. He experienced stress, used drugs, and abandoned his studies. That year he accepted an out-of-court settlement (10 hours’ community service) for assault.

On 1 August 2006 he was convicted of indecent assault (Criminal Code Art. 246) and four counts of attempted indecent assault (September–October 2005), receiving 240 hours’ community service, a training order, and a six-month suspended prison sentence. The offences involved following young women cyclists to stop or unseat them for lewd acts. On 28 September 2006 he applied for a temporary residence permit for extended family reunion with his foster father, claiming he had always assumed Dutch nationality.

The Deputy Minister of Justice rejected the application on 18 December 2007. He was an alien posing a public-order threat due to the offences (Aliens Act 2000 s. 16(1)(d); Aliens Decree 2000). Any family life with his uncle did not create a positive Article 8 obligation to admit him, as he had never held a residence permit; long unlawful stay conferred no rights. An objection was lodged.

On 27 June 2008 he was convicted of two indecent assaults and three attempts (May, November, December 2007), receiving 15 months’ imprisonment (five months suspended) plus execution of the prior sentence. Offences were similar. The objection was rejected on 17 July 2008: the convictions confirmed the public-order ground; he had never been lawfully resident; his presumed father or foster parents should have regularised his status (they had applied for a tourist visa); he was an adult with only ordinary emotional ties to foster parents and could manage in Indonesia (no family or language knowledge there was an acceptable adjustment difficulty). Family life could continue via visits.

He appealed to the Regional Court of The Hague (Zwolle). He also sought confirmation of Dutch nationality from birth (Kingdom Act on Netherlands Nationality); this was rejected on 14 February 2011 because his parents were unmarried, his presumed father later married another woman, and he was not registered as the father’s child.

The Regional Court allowed his appeal on 30 January 2012, finding family life existed and that the authorities had not transparently balanced his long residence, schooling, and social/cultural/family ties against the public-order interest.

The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State allowed the Minister’s further appeal on 13 November 2013, quashing the Regional Court and dismissing the applicant’s appeal. Very strong Dutch ties existed due to age of arrival and length of stay, but Article 8 imposed no positive obligation. Private and family life arose when foster parents knew or ought to have known his status was precarious (identifying children with parents’ conduct). Great weight attached to the offences’ nature, seriousness, and repetition (adult recidivist aware of unlawful status). He was an adult without more-than-normal ties to foster parents; no objective bar existed to family life in Indonesia, and he could manage independently despite adjustment problems.

On 1 August 2016 he departed for Indonesia with IOM assistance, signing a declaration discontinuing residence-permit proceedings.

His presumed father travelled frequently to Indonesia, leaving the applicant in the care of a Dutch uncle and aunt (whom he regarded as foster parents) and their four children. The presumed father died in 1999. The applicant attended Dutch schools and completed pre-vocational secondary education in metalworking around 2002/03; he later began culinary training.

In 2004 an out-of-court settlement (10 hours’ community service) resolved a suspicion of assault. That year a truant officer revealed that the applicant was not registered in the municipal database. His 1991 Indonesian passport was located, confirming his illegal status. He had always assumed Dutch nationality. The discovery caused stress, temporary drug use and discontinuation of his studies.

On 1 August 2006 he was convicted of indecent assault and four attempted indecent assaults (September–October 2005). The offences involved following young women cyclists in order to stop them and commit lewd acts. He received 240 hours’ community service, a training order and a six-month prison sentence suspended for two years.

On 28 September 2006 he applied for a temporary residence permit for extended family reunion with his foster father, stating that he had believed himself Dutch. The application was refused on 18 December 2007 (notified 28 December) on the ground that the offences rendered him a danger to public order. The authorities found no positive Article 8 obligation, noting that family life had never been based on a residence permit and that the period of unlawful stay conferred no rights.

On 27 June 2008 he was convicted of two further indecent assaults and three attempts (May–December 2007) of the same nature, receiving 15 months’ imprisonment (five months suspended) plus activation of the earlier sentence. His objection to the residence refusal was dismissed on 17 July 2008. The authorities emphasised that the applicant had never been lawfully resident, that his carers ought to have known his status was precarious, that he was an adult recidivist who had offended after learning of his illegal position, that there were no more than normal emotional ties with his foster parents, and that he could manage in Indonesia (where family life could continue by visits).

An application for confirmation of Dutch nationality by descent was rejected in 2011 because his parents had never married and he had not been registered as his presumed father’s child. The Regional Court of The Hague (sitting in Zwolle) allowed his appeal against the residence refusal on 30 January 2012, finding that the authorities had failed to conduct a sufficiently transparent balancing of his long-term Dutch ties against public-order concerns. The Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State reversed that ruling on 13 November 2013, holding that the balancing had been adequate: the applicant’s private and family life had been created while his immigration status was known (or ought to have been known) to be precarious; he had offended as an adult after becoming aware of that status; he remained capable of living independently in Indonesia; and strong immigration-control interests therefore prevailed.

The applicant departed voluntarily for Indonesia in August 2016 with IOM assistance. The ECtHR later found no Article 8 violation, concluding that the domestic authorities had struck a fair balance.

**Case Summary: Stoyan Krastev v. Bulgaria (Application no. 1009/12)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered its judgment on 6 October 2020 (final 8 March 2021) in this case, which concerned a complaint under Article 5 § 5 of the Convention about the applicant’s inability to obtain compensation for 14 days of unlawful confinement in a prison disciplinary isolation cell.

The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1966, began serving a three-year prison sentence in April 2008 under the general prison regime. He initially resided in an open-type prison hostel, working as a driver on an external site and sleeping away from the hostel. After 25 February 2009, external work was revoked due to frequent absences. In 2009, prison authorities learned of alleged threats by the applicant against the warden and his encouragement of other inmates to submit complaints. On 6 August 2009, he was involved in a brawl with another prisoner.

On 12 August 2009, the director of the Chief Directorate for the Execution of Sentences ordered the applicant’s placement in a disciplinary isolation cell for 14 days as punishment for arrogant behaviour and threats toward fellow detainees and staff. The order also cited the need to ensure the applicant’s physical safety and overall prison security, and directed his transfer to Bobov Dol Prison due to psychological tension and incompatibility with other inmates. The applicant was transferred on 13 August 2009 and held in isolation until 30 August 2009 (except for 17–19 August, when he was taken to Sofia Prison for investigative measures). Isolation entailed restrictions including no visits or food parcels, no telephone use, limited personal items, meals in the cell, showers twice weekly, and isolated outdoor exercise.

On 17 August 2009, the applicant challenged the order in court, arguing it harmed his health and well-being. The Sofia District Court, treating it as an individual administrative act, declared the challenge admissible regarding the punishment and set it aside as unlawful in a final decision of 3 September 2009. The court found the 6 August incident had risked unrest and compromised safety, but the order breached substantive and procedural rules: it lacked a title, failed to indicate the appeal authority or timeframe, did not specify the offence type (depriving the applicant of the chance to repent or appeal), and erroneously treated his (and others’) complaints against the administration as a disciplinary breach, despite prisoners’ rights to complain.

The applicant then sought damages under section 1(1) of the State and Municipalities’ Responsibility for Damage Act, claiming lasting distress, severe psychological disturbance, and physical suffering (worsened lower back pain) from the isolation. Administrative courts at two instances dismissed the claim on the merits. They accepted that an unlawful administrative act had occurred but held that the applicant failed to prove sufficiently intense or prolonged non-pecuniary damage (no documentary evidence of lasting stress during or after isolation) and found no causal link to his back pain. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this in a final decision of 13 June 2011.

The European Court examined whether Article 5 § 5 applied, which requires a right to compensation for detention in contravention of Article 5. It distinguished the case from prior rulings involving a significant change in detention implementation. Here, there was no modification of the legal grounds for the applicant’s deprivation of liberty (he remained a sentenced prisoner). Isolation aimed at ensuring safety of all detainees. The Court did not accept claims of disturbance and distress, noting no major difference between the isolation regime/conditions and the general prison regime. Thus, there was no further “deprivation of liberty” within the meaning of Article 5 § 1, rendering Article 5 inapplicable. The complaint was therefore outside the Court’s competence ratione materiae.

Isolation entailed no visits, parcels, telephone use or personal money; cells were in a high-security wing; meals were taken in-cell; showers were twice weekly; and exercise was taken separately. On 3 September 2009 the Sofia District Court, treating the order as an individual administrative act, set it aside as unlawful. The court found both substantive and procedural defects: the order lacked a title and any indication of the competent review body or time-limit; it failed to specify the offence committed, thereby denying the applicant the chance to repent or contest it; and it wrongly treated the writing (or prompting) of complaint letters as a disciplinary breach, which prisoners are entitled to do.

The applicant then sought damages under section 1(1) of the State and Municipalities’ Responsibility for Damage Act, claiming lasting distress, severe psychological disturbance and aggravated lower-back pain. Administrative courts at two levels dismissed the claim. They accepted that an unlawful administrative act had occurred, but held that the applicant had not proved sufficiently intense or prolonged non-pecuniary harm; no documentary evidence supported his assertions of lasting stress, and no causal link existed with his pre-existing back condition. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this reasoning on 13 June 2011.

The Court recalled that isolation is a statutory disciplinary sanction subject to prompt judicial review. It found Article 5 inapplicable: the isolation did not constitute a further “deprivation of liberty” within the meaning of Article 5 § 1. Unlike earlier cases involving a fundamental change in the legal basis or manner of detention, the measure here merely implemented the existing sentence, served security purposes, and produced no major difference in regime or conditions. The applicant’s claimed distress was not accepted as establishing a distinct deprivation. Consequently Article 5 § 5 did not arise.

Although isolation entailed additional restrictions (no visits, parcels or telephone, meals taken in the cell, limited personal items and separated exercise), these did not amount to a qualitatively different regime from ordinary prison conditions under the general regime. Consequently there was no further deprivation of liberty, Article 5 was inapplicable, and the complaint under Article 5 § 5 failed.

The case of Bilal Akyıldız v. Turkey (ECHR Application no. 36897/07, Second Section judgment of 15 September 2020) involves a Turkish national's arrest and 27-day pre-trial detention in late 2002 on suspicion of attempted child abductions linked to a series of sexual assaults, followed by his acquittal. The applicant primarily alleged a violation of Article 5 of the Convention (right to liberty and security), arguing there was no reasonable suspicion he committed an offence and that his remand followed an irregular investigation. The Court also notified the Government of complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2002, multiple children in Ümraniye, Istanbul, suffered sexual assaults by one perpetrator. Two attempted child abductions also occurred in nearby Samandıra on 25 October and 6 November. On 16 November 2002, an anonymous caller reported a man resembling the photofit of the assailant. Gendarmes arrested the applicant there on suspicion of attempted child abduction; he was notified of his rights and signed the report, which incorrectly noted he had a criminal record. A separate handwritten report by three gendarmes claimed the arrest occurred during a routine patrol because he failed to produce identification.

An identification parade that day involved two child victims and a child witness. The witness identified the applicant with certainty as the attempted abductor; the victims stated he strongly resembled the perpetrator. DNA testing while in custody excluded the applicant from the sexual assaults.

Questioned on 18 November about the abductions, the applicant acknowledged his resemblance to the photofit but denied involvement, citing the DNA results. Records confirmed he had no criminal record. After being informed of his right to counsel, he declined a lawyer. The gendarmerie commander forwarded the file to the Kartal public prosecutor, noting the identification parade (applicant presented with two civilians) and DNA exclusion, and expressing the view that the identifications likely resulted from media coverage of the “Ümraniye pervert” plus physical resemblance.

The same day a Kartal Criminal Court judge ordered pre-trial detention, citing the investigation evidence and the offences’ nature and gravity. On 20 November the applicant’s lawyer objected, highlighting the negative DNA, contradictions in victim accounts, an irregular parade (applicant’s partially burned face versus unremarkable stand-ins; identifications not certain), the commander’s doubts, and an alibi (the applicant had been working far from the scenes). The objection was rejected on 21 November.

The applicant was charged on 22 November with attempted abduction of minors. On 11 December one victim’s father petitioned that the family had recanted: after seeing the actual sexual-assault suspect on television, they believed media influence had caused the earlier identification and that the applicant was innocent. At a 13 December hearing the victims unequivocally stated the applicant was not the perpetrator. The Assize Court of Kartal acquitted him, finding he had not committed the acts.

Subsequent domestic investigations into alleged irregularities (wrongful jurisdiction, inaccurate reports, denial of rights in custody, flawed parade, public exposure) ended in decisions not to prosecute officers, though three gendarmes were charged with abuse of authority over the handwritten report (proceedings later time-barred). The applicant obtained modest compensation under repealed Act No. 466 for the 27-day detention and, after administrative proceedings, a larger award for non-pecuniary damage arising from breach of investigation confidentiality through press disclosures. 

These circumstances underpin the Article 5 complaint that the arrest and detention lacked reasonable suspicion at the relevant time.

The case of Ahmadov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 32538/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (respect for private life) arising from the Azerbaijani authorities’ arbitrary refusal to issue the applicant an identity card, thereby denying recognition of his citizenship.

The applicant, of Azerbaijani ethnicity, was born in 1973 in Marneuli, Georgia. He received a Soviet passport from Georgian SSR authorities in 1990. After finishing secondary school, he moved to Baku in 1991 to study at the Azerbaijan Oil and Chemistry Institute and was registered at its dormitory on 9 October 1991. From 1 February 1999 he was registered at his sister’s address in Baku.

On 22 September 1998 the Nasimi District Police Office inserted a photograph into his Soviet passport, sealed it, and stamped it to confirm he was a “citizen of the Republic of Azerbaijan.” He was listed as an Azerbaijani citizen and Baku resident on his son’s 2002 Georgian birth certificate. He had been on the Azerbaijani electoral roll as a citizen since 1991, received polling cards, and voted in the 2008 presidential election and 2009 referendum. A 2008 military identity card recorded him as a reserve lieutenant (rank awarded in 1996).

In 2008 he applied to the Sabunchu District Police Office for an identity card. On 26 September 2008 it refused, citing Article 5 of the 1998 Law on Citizenship (in force 7 October 1998). That provision treated as citizens those resident in Azerbaijan before the law’s entry into force, evidenced by registration; the police classified his student registration as merely temporary. The State Migration Service confirmed on 22 December 2008 that he was not a citizen.

On 19 February 2009 the applicant sued both bodies, arguing continuous residence since 1991, official treatment as a citizen (passport stamp, military status, voting), and that the Citizenship Law and the 1996 Law on Registration at Place of Residence and Stay drew no distinction between temporary and permanent registration (dormitories being recognised places of residence).

On 1 April 2009 the Sabunchu District Court upheld the claim and ordered issuance of an identity card. It found uncontested continuous residence since 1991, applied the pre-24 June 2008 wording of Article 5, held that the quality-of-law requirement (accessibility and foreseeability) was unmet by the authorities’ interpretation, noted that registration law made no temporary/permanent distinction, and emphasised the applicant’s citizen-like relations with the State (voting, military registration, passport stamp). Until February 1999 a stamped Soviet passport had been accepted as an identity document.

The State Migration Service appealed, arguing the provision required permanent registration and noting the applicant’s 2002 use of a Georgian passport to cross the border. On 27 July 2009 the Baku Court of Appeal quashed the judgment. It held that the applicant lacked permanent registration when the Citizenship Law entered into force and that voting, property ownership, and the birth-certificate entry were insufficient to establish citizenship. It was silent on the passport stamp and military status.

The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 15 December 2009, interpreting Article 5 (in both original and amended versions) as applying only to those who already held Azerbaijani citizenship and were registered before the law’s entry into force; the applicant had not previously held such citizenship.

(A later 2013 action briefly produced an identity card in 2014, later invalidated on res judicata grounds.)

These facts—long-term residence and registration, official acts treating the applicant as a citizen, and the subsequent refusals based on a disputed interpretation of Article 5 that ignored contrary evidence and the absence of any temporary/permanent distinction in registration law—underpinned the Article 8 complaint of an arbitrary interference with private life through denial of an identity document confirming citizenship.

The authorities classified his student registration as merely temporary. The State Migration Service confirmed the refusal in December 2008.
