The case of Banzhayev v. Russia (Application no. 21129/09) concerns complaints under Articles 2 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Shaaman Banzhayev (born 1966), alleged that Russian authorities were responsible for the 2001 killing of his wife, Malika Vanayeva (born 1975), during artillery shelling and the 2002 abduction of his brother Shamkhan Banzhayev (born 1969, then village administrator), as well as for failing to investigate these events effectively or provide remedies.

In August 2001, during Russia’s counter-terrorist operation in Chechnya, the applicant, his wife and their four young children lived in the tiny village of Gezenchu (Vedeno district), home to fewer than a dozen families. The village had already been shelled several times. On 24 August Shamkhan and other residents visited the nearby federal military unit at Engenoy, explaining that the settlement was too small to conceal fighters and asking that it not be targeted. Officers said orders came from Khankala headquarters but promised to take the request into account.

The next day, 25 August, at about 3–4 p.m., artillery fire resumed from the direction of Engenoy. Bombs struck the courtyard of the applicant’s brother’s house and nearby. The applicant, going to help, was shot in the left leg; a subsequent bomb exploding in a tree killed his wife and a relative instantly and wounded his youngest son and others. The applicant and the injured were treated first at Sayasan Hospital and later elsewhere. Vanayeva’s death certificate, issued years later, recorded multiple shrapnel wounds to the head and chest.

Shamkhan immediately lodged detailed complaints with Chechen civilian and military prosecutors, the republican administration and the Vedeno district prosecutor, enclosing medical certificates and demanding identification and prosecution of the servicemen responsible. An interim military commander acknowledged an inquiry in November 2001, but no criminal case was opened. After Shamkhan’s later disappearance the family, fearing for their safety, largely ceased pressing the matter. Only in 2007 did the applicant complain again; criminal case no. 23031 was then opened under the negligent-homicide provision. The applicant was granted victim status, yet the investigation was repeatedly suspended (September 2007, December 2007) with few of the ordered steps ever taken. It remained formally pending. In November 2008 the applicant challenged the investigators’ inaction before the Shali District Court, which granted him limited access to the file but did not compel further investigative measures.

On 15 November 2002 Shamkhan was abducted at approximately 3 p.m. while leaving the Vedeno military commander’s office. Armed men in camouflage and balaclavas forced him into an unmarked UAZ minibus; he has not been seen since. The applicant, who did not witness the event, attributes it to servicemen seeking to halt Shamkhan’s pursuit of the shelling investigation. Eyewitnesses (a bodyguard and a friend) later confirmed that 10–15 armed men seized him without explanation.

The applicant reported the abduction on 26 November 2002; no reply followed. A police search file was opened only in July 2003. A criminal case (no. 53028) was instituted in June 2005 after prosecutors noticed the earlier omission. The applicant received victim status in August 2005. Witnesses were questioned and the scene examined, but the investigation was suspended repeatedly (August 2005, February 2006, November 2006, October 2017) and remains unfinished. Supervisors periodically ordered additional steps—questioning of military personnel, relatives and former bodyguards—yet these produced no identification of the perpetrators.

The facts therefore centre on two violent incidents implicating federal forces, the authorities’ years-long delay in opening investigations, repeated suspensions without meaningful progress, and the absence of any effective domestic remedy.

The case of Banzhayev v. Russia (Application no. 21129/09) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Shaaman Banzhayev, a Russian national born in 1966. He alleged violations of Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention arising from the killing of his wife, Malika Vanayeva (born 1975), during Russian military shelling in Chechnya and the subsequent abduction of his brother, Shamkhan Banzhayev (born 1969), together with the authorities’ failure to conduct effective investigations or provide remedies.

In August 2001, during the counter-terrorist operation, the applicant, his wife and their four children lived in the small village of Gezenchu in Vedeno district. On 25 August 2001, while they were at home, explosions occurred in a nearby forest. The applicant’s wife noted that their children were playing at his brother’s house. A bomb then exploded in that courtyard, followed by others. The children fled home. The applicant ran to offer help, was shot in the left leg from the direction of Engenoy village, and saw relatives wounded by a further explosion. Renewed shelling killed his wife and a relative (R.G.) when a bomb caught in a tree detonated; his young son and another relative were wounded by shrapnel. The wounded were taken to hospital. Vanayeva’s death certificate recorded multiple shrapnel wounds to the head and chest. Uniformed officials later questioned some of the injured. Frequent shelling led residents to abandon the village in 2002.

Shamkhan Banzhayev, then village administration head, immediately complained to Chechen and military prosecutors and commanders, stating that an unprovoked attack by a military unit near Engenoy had launched 12–15 bombs, killing two people, wounding six and destroying houses. He noted that on 24 August he and other villagers had visited the unit, been told orders came from Khankala headquarters, and received a promise that Gezenchu would not be bombed. Further complaints followed in September and November 2001. A military commander later indicated that an inquiry was under way. After Shamkhan’s disappearance, the applicant and family feared for their safety and largely ceased pressing the matter until 2007.

On 23 July 2007 the Vedeno prosecutor opened criminal case no. 23031 under Article 109(3) of the Criminal Code (negligent causing of death to two or more persons) against unidentified servicemen. The applicant was granted victim status and interviewed. The investigation was repeatedly suspended for failure to identify perpetrators (September and December 2007) despite a supervisory order to take further steps; those steps were not implemented and the applicant was not always notified. The investigation remained pending years later. In November 2008 the applicant complained to the Shali District Court of ineffectiveness and possible cover-up; the court ordered investigators to consider his requests and grant limited file access.

On 15 November 2002, around 3–4 p.m., Shamkhan Banzhayev was abducted by armed men in military uniforms and balaclavas as he left the Vedeno military commander’s office checkpoint. He was forced into an unregistered UAZ minibus and driven away; he has not been seen since. The applicant did not witness the event but later statements by two companions (a bodyguard and a friend) confirmed that 10–15 camouflaged, masked men surrounded him and took him away, one saying they were going to another commander’s office. The applicant attributed the abduction to an attempt to halt his brother’s campaign for prosecution of those responsible for the 2001 shelling.

The applicant complained to the Vedeno prosecutor on 26 November 2002 and to the police in June 2003; a search file was opened but no criminal case followed until June 2005 (case no. 53028), after an inspection revealed the omission. He received victim status in August 2005. Witnesses were interviewed, the crime scene examined (yielding no evidence) and some military and local officials questioned, yet the investigation was suspended multiple times (2005, 2006, 2017) with only intermittent supervisory overrides. Limited additional steps were taken; the case remained open as of 2018. The applicant was often not promptly informed of suspensions.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that the State had failed to protect life, to investigate the killing and enforced disappearance adequately, and to provide an effective domestic remedy.

The case of Banzhayev v. Russia (Application no. 21129/09) concerns complaints under Articles 2 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights relating to the 2001 killing of the applicant’s wife during artillery shelling of a Chechen village and the 2002 abduction and disappearance of his brother, as well as the alleged ineffectiveness of the ensuing investigations and lack of remedies.

The applicant, Shaaman Banzhayev (born 1966), lived with his wife Malika Vanayeva (born 1975) and their four minor children in the small village of Gezenchu in Chechnya’s Vedeno district during the 2001 counter-terrorist operation. On 25 August 2001, while the couple were at home, they heard explosions from a nearby forest. Vanayeva noted that their children were playing at the house of the applicant’s brother Shirvani. A bomb then exploded in that courtyard, followed by others. The children fled home; the applicant instructed his wife to hide them in the basement and ran to help. En route he was shot in the left leg from the direction of Engenoy village; a subsequent bomb wounded relatives nearby. A further explosion, from a bomb caught in a tree, killed Vanayeva and relative R.G. instantly from shrapnel wounds to the head and chest; the applicant’s young son and another relative were also wounded. The survivors received emergency treatment. A death certificate later confirmed Vanayeva’s death that day. The village was abandoned in 2002 owing to repeated shelling.

The applicant’s brother Shamkhan Banzhayev (born 1969), then village-administration head, promptly complained to Chechen prosecutors, the military commander and other officials. He described unprovoked shelling by a federal military unit stationed near Engenoy (12–15 bombs destroying four households, killing two and wounding six). On 24 August 2001 local representatives, including teachers, had visited the unit and been assured it would not bomb Gezenchu, yet the attack occurred the next day. He requested identification and prosecution of those responsible. An interim military commander later stated that an inquiry was under way. Shamkhan continued pressing authorities through 2001–2002.

On 15 November 2002, around 3 p.m., Shamkhan was abducted by armed, camouflaged men in balaclavas as he left the Vedeno military commander’s office checkpoint. They forced him into an unregistered UAZ minibus and drove away; he has not been seen since. The applicant, who did not witness the event, alleged the abduction was intended to halt Shamkhan’s pursuit of the shelling perpetrators. Two companions later confirmed seeing armed men surround and take him.

The applicant reported the abduction to the Vedeno prosecutor on 26 November 2002 (no reply) and to police in June 2003 (a search file was opened). A criminal case (no. 53028) was instituted only in June 2005 after an inspection revealed the omission. The applicant was granted victim status in August 2005; witnesses were interviewed and the crime scene examined, but the investigation was repeatedly suspended (2005, 2006, 2017) and resumed on orders of supervising prosecutors, remaining pending.

Regarding the killing, a criminal case (no. 23031) under the provision on negligent homicide was opened only in July 2007 after the applicant renewed complaints. He was granted victim status and described the events, including his brother’s prior negotiations with the military. The investigation was suspended in September and December 2007 without completing ordered steps and appears still pending. In November 2008 the applicant challenged its ineffectiveness before the Shali District Court, which in December 2008 partly granted the complaint by ordering limited access to the case file.

The Government did not contest the facts as submitted. The Court later examined the complaints concerning the killing, abduction, investigative failings and absence of remedies.
001-200450:
The case concerns six Maltese applicants (or their predecessors) who, together with two other parties, acquired perpetual emphyteusis over a 23,606 sq.m. plot known as “Tal-Ħriereb” in 1960. In 1961 the Governor declared 7,531 sq.m. of that land required for a public purpose and subject to outright purchase; the applicants held one-third of the affected interest.

A 1964 Notice to Treat offered the emphyteutae and the owners of the direct dominium a joint sum of approximately EUR 1,470. They refused. The Land Arbitration Board (LAB) fixed compensation at approximately EUR 2,704 in 1978 and, after correcting a measurement error in 1981, left the figure unchanged. It declined to apportion the award between the two classes of owners, leaving that question to the ordinary courts. Because the parties could not agree on shares, the deed was never published and no payment was made.

Constitutional proceedings alleging inadequate compensation and excessive length of the LAB process ended in 2005 with a finding against the applicants. In its 2008 judgment the European Court held that the length of the LAB proceedings had violated Article 6 § 1 in respect of those applicants who had been parties, but declared the property complaints inadmissible: the claim of inadequate quantum had not been exhausted and non-payment was attributable to the applicants’ own failure to seek apportionment.

Following that judgment the applicants (or their heirs) instituted fresh constitutional proceedings in 2011, again attacking the quantum of the 1978/1981 award under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They relied on an expert valuation placing the land’s 1964 market value at approximately EUR 17,319 and its 2006 development value at more than EUR 8.8 million, and they sought reimbursement of ground rent paid in the interim.

The Civil Court (First Hall) rejected the claim in 2014. It noted that the applicants had paid the equivalent of EUR 0.08 per sq.m. when they acquired the emphyteusis and had been awarded EUR 0.41 per sq.m.; the land had been agricultural at the date of taking and the applicants’ valuations ignored both that character and the public purpose of the expropriation. The Constitutional Court confirmed the decision in 2015. It emphasised that the applicants themselves had caused the decades-long delay by failing to have the shares determined, that ground rents had already been repaid, and that a fair balance had been struck given the legality of the measure and the public interest involved.

The present application, lodged in 2015, therefore challenges the Constitutional Court’s conclusion that the historic compensation remained Convention-compliant despite the passage of time and the applicants’ continued non-receipt of any sum.

**Case Summary: Bezzina Wettinger and Others v. Malta (Application no. 52673/15)**

This ECtHR case (Third Section judgment of 21 January 2020) concerns six Maltese applicants’ complaints arising from the long-running expropriation of land in which they held emphyteutic rights. The core alleged violations relate to the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (primarily the adequacy and non-payment of compensation) and, by reference to earlier proceedings, Article 6 § 1 (length of proceedings). The facts focus on the taking, valuation disputes, delays attributable to the parties, and successive domestic and Strasbourg challenges.

In August 1960 the applicants (and/or their predecessors), together with two other parties, acquired equal shares of perpetual emphyteusis over approximately 23,606 m² of land known as “Tal-Ħriereb” lying between Birkirkara and Msida. In August 1961 the Governor declared that 7,531 m² of this land was required for a public purpose and would be acquired by outright purchase. The applicants jointly held one-third of the affected portion.

A 1964 Notice to Treat offered the emphyteutae (together with the dominus) approximately £631 (EUR 1,470). The offer was refused. The matter was referred to the Land Arbitration Board (LAB). In February 1978 the LAB fixed compensation at MTL 1,161 (approximately EUR 2,704) and set a date for the deed of transfer, but did not apportion the sum between the interested parties. A 1981 rectification corrected an error in the land measurement but left the compensation figure unchanged; the LAB declined to determine respective shares, leaving that issue to the ordinary courts.

The parties never agreed on apportionment, so the compensation remained unpaid. Constitutional proceedings alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (taking without compensation) and Article 6 § 1 (unreasonable delay before the LAB) were dismissed by the Constitutional Court in October 2005. In a 2008 ECtHR judgment in related proceedings the Court found an Article 6 violation in respect of the LAB proceedings (which had ended in 1981) for those applicants who had been parties, but declared the inadequacy-of-compensation claim inadmissible for non-exhaustion and the non-payment complaint manifestly ill-founded, because the applicants themselves had failed to take the necessary steps to divide the award.

After that judgment, in October 2011 several of the present applicants (together with co-owners) instituted fresh constitutional proceedings confined to the quantum of the LAB award. They argued that the sum was inadequate, sought annulment of the LAB decision, an award of market-value compensation, reimbursement of ground rent paid in the interim, and other damages. Their architect valued the 7,530 m² plot at approximately EUR 8.8 million on the 2006 open market (treating most of it as development land), EUR 17,319 in 1964 and EUR 121,210 in 1978.

The Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction dismissed the claim in October 2014. It observed that the applicants were not attacking the statutory rule that compensation is assessed at the date of the Notice to Treat. The applicants had originally paid the equivalent of 0.08 euro cents per m²; the LAB award equated to 0.41 euro cents per m². Government valuation evidence treated the land as agricultural (outside a development zone) and produced a figure of approximately EUR 3,610. The court held that the applicants’ higher valuation ignored the public purpose and actual use of the land.

On appeal the Constitutional Court confirmed the dismissal in April 2015. It noted that the applicants had limited their challenge to the amount of compensation. Non-payment resulted from their own failure to determine the parties’ shares and to pursue ordinary proceedings—an omission already recorded by the ECtHR in 2008. Ground rents had been repaid. The land had been agricultural at the time of taking and had to be valued as such, not as development land. Even allowing for the measurement error, a fair balance had been struck given the lawfulness of the measure and the public interest.

These facts—the 1961 taking, the modest 1978/1981 award, the applicants’ successive failures to resolve apportionment, the competing valuations, and the domestic courts’ conclusions that compensation was adequate and that delays were largely self-inflicted—form the factual matrix of the alleged Article 1 Protocol No. 1 (and related Article 6) violations examined in the 2020 judgment.

The case of Bezzina Wettinger and Others v. Malta (Application no. 52673/15) concerns six Maltese applicants who, together with others, acquired perpetual emphyteusis in 1960 over approximately 23,606 sq.m of land known as “Tal-Ħriereb” near Birkirkara and Msida. In 1961 the Governor declared that 7,531 sq.m of this land was required for a public purpose and would be acquired by outright purchase. The applicants held a one-third share (in unequal portions) of the emphyteutical interest in the affected land.

A 1964 Notice to Treat offered the emphyteutae and the owners of the direct dominium a joint sum of approximately EUR 1,470, which they refused. The matter was referred to the Land Arbitration Board (LAB). In February 1978 the LAB fixed compensation at MTL 1,161 (approximately EUR 2,704) and set a date for the transfer deed, but it did not allocate the sum among the interested parties. A 1981 rectification corrected an error in the land measurement yet left the award unchanged and declined to determine the respective shares, leaving that question to the ordinary courts.

Disagreement between the emphyteutae and the dominus over apportionment meant that no compensation was ever paid. The applicants and co-owners therefore brought constitutional proceedings alleging a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (inadequate and unpaid compensation) and of Article 6 § 1 (excessive length of the LAB proceedings). The Constitutional Court dismissed the claims in 2005.

In a 2008 judgment the European Court found a violation of Article 6 in respect of the length of the LAB proceedings (which had ended in 1981) for those applicants who had been parties to the domestic proceedings. It rejected the remaining complaints: the adequacy of the quantum was inadmissible for non-exhaustion of ordinary remedies, while the non-payment complaint was manifestly ill-founded because the applicants themselves had failed to take the necessary steps to divide the awarded sum.

Following that judgment, in October 2011 the applicants (together with the remaining co-owners) instituted a fresh set of constitutional proceedings confined to the quantum of compensation. They contended that the LAB award was inadequate and therefore violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They sought annulment of the award, payment of market-value compensation, reimbursement of ground rents paid in the interim, and other damages. An architect instructed by them valued the land at approximately EUR 17,319 in 1964, EUR 121,210 in 1978 and EUR 8.8 million in 2006 (treating most of it as development land).

The Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence dismissed the claim in October 2014. It observed that the applicants were not challenging the governing legislation (which required valuation as at the date of the Notice to Treat). The compensation of EUR 2,786 for 6,774.54 sq.m equated to 0.41 euro cents per square metre, a figure well above the 0.08 cents the emphyteutae had themselves paid in 1960 and closer to the Government’s valuation of agricultural land (0.36 cents) than to the applicants’ open-market figure. The court held that the land’s actual use and the public purpose of the taking had to be taken into account.

On appeal the Constitutional Court confirmed the first-instance judgment in April 2015. It noted that the applicants had limited their challenge to the amount of compensation and that any delay in payment was attributable to their own failure to resolve the shares among the interested parties—a finding already endorsed by the European Court in 2008. Ground rents had been repaid. Because the land had been agricultural at the time of taking, it had to be valued as such, not as building land. Even allowing for the measurement error, a fair balance had been struck given the legality of the expropriation and the public interest involved.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ renewed complaint that the compensation awarded and upheld domestically was so low, and so long delayed, as to constitute a disproportionate interference with their property rights.
001-200451:
The case of Idrisova v. Russia (Application no. 19/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the disappearance of the applicant’s husband, Mukhumad Magomadov (born 1990), in Chechnya on 6 December 2014 and the subsequent domestic investigation. The applicant, Markha Idrisova (born 1993), alleged facts pointing to possible State responsibility for the abduction and a failure to conduct an effective inquiry.

Mukhumad Magomadov’s brother Alik had been a member of an illegal armed group and was killed in 2009. On the night of 3–4 December 2014, members of such a group attacked a Grozny police station, killing officers, and occupied buildings in the city centre. In response, Chechen President Ramzan Kadyrov publicly stated that families of illegal armed group members would be expelled from Chechnya and their houses demolished.

On the evening of 6 December 2014, around 10 p.m., a group of men arrived at the Magomadov family home in Sadovoye in a white Lada Priora car whose registration number included the digits 646 95. Mukhumad, wearing only indoor clothing and flip-flops, opened the door and was immediately forced into the vehicle and driven away. His mother and brother were present; the applicant was also at the house. Subsequent attempts to reach him by mobile phone failed; the phone was later switched off, briefly reactivated, and then remained unanswered.

The family reported the incident to police the next day. Officers examined the scene but collected no physical evidence. Witnesses, including a neighbour, confirmed seeing the white Lada Priora heading toward the house. Investigators identified two possible owners of similar vehicles: a civilian (R.S.) and police officer R.T. of the Chechen Ministry of the Interior’s security service. R.T. stated he had been on continuous duty at his workplace due to the 4 December events and had not lent his car. No further questions were put to him at that stage.

Investigators initially refused to open a criminal case on 18 January 2015, citing lack of evidence of a crime. This decision, and two subsequent refusals, were repeatedly overruled by superiors for incompleteness (failure to question additional witnesses, obtain telephone data, verify R.T.’s alibi, search the vehicles, or check detainee records). A criminal case for aggravated abduction (Article 126 § 2 of the Criminal Code) was finally opened only on 20 April 2017. Thereafter, steps included re-examination of the scene, DNA sampling, obtaining Mukhumad’s photograph and call records, granting victim status, and interviewing neighbours, officials and both car owners. R.S. produced photographs showing his vehicle was not entirely white. R.T. reiterated his alibi and refused a lie-detector test; an internal inquiry into his conduct yielded no known result. Police suggested Mukhumad might have joined an illegal armed group in Syria, citing a 2013 visit to Turkey and “non-traditional” religious views; family members rejected this, noting he had returned home and had no intention of leaving. No matching unidentified bodies were found. The investigation was suspended in June and July 2017 for failure to identify perpetrators and appears to have remained open at the time of the Court’s judgment. Domestic court challenges to the initial refusals were dismissed on procedural grounds.

These facts formed the basis of complaints concerning the abduction itself (possible involvement of State agents) and the prolonged, incomplete investigation.

The case of Idrisova v. Russia concerns the abduction of the applicant’s husband, Mukhumad Magomadov (born 1990), from the family home in Sadovoye, Grozny district of Chechnya, on 6 December 2014, and the subsequent investigation. Magomadov’s brother Alik had been a member of an illegal armed group and was killed in 2009. On the night of 3–4 December 2014, militants attacked a Grozny police station, killing officers and occupying buildings; a large-scale counter-terrorist operation followed. Chechen President Ramzan Kadyrov then publicly stated that families of illegal armed group members would be expelled from Chechnya and their houses demolished.

Around 10 p.m. on 6 December 2014, a group of men in a white Lada Priora (registration containing the digits 646 95) arrived at the Magomadov house. Magomadov, wearing only indoor clothing and flip-flops, opened the door and was immediately forced into the car and driven away. The applicant, Magomadov’s mother Z.M., and brother I.M. were present. Subsequent calls to Magomadov’s mobile went unanswered; the phone was later switched off, then briefly reactivated without response.

On 7 December 2014 I.M. reported the abduction to Grozny district police, describing the events and noting Magomadov had been taken in winter without proper clothing. Police examined the scene but collected no evidence. They questioned the applicant, Z.M., and neighbour K.U., who (with acquaintance I.A.) had seen the matching car heading toward the house. The inquiry was transferred to the Grozny inter-district investigative committee. Further interviews confirmed the family’s account. Traffic police identified two matching Lada Priora owners: Chechen Interior Ministry security officer R.T. and private citizen R.S.

On 18 January 2015 R.T. was questioned. He confirmed ownership of a white Lada Priora with the relevant digits, stated he had been on continuous 24-hour duty at work because of the 4 December events and had not left or lent the car, and offered no further details. Investigators asked no additional questions about that night. That same day they refused to open a criminal case for lack of evidence of a crime. The applicant’s subsequent court challenges to the refusal were dismissed on procedural grounds or because superiors later overruled the decision.

Superiors repeatedly quashed refusals (in November 2015, March 2016 and April 2017) for investigative shortcomings, including failure to question I.A. and R.S., obtain telephone data, search the cars, take DNA samples, examine the scene with GPS or photography, or verify R.T.’s alibi. Limited additional steps followed: a second scene examination with photographs, DNA sampling from Z.M., requests to law-enforcement bodies (which yielded no location information), and neighbour interviews (none of whom witnessed the abduction). In April 2016 investigators again refused to open a case.

A criminal investigation for aggravated abduction (Article 126 § 2 of the Criminal Code) was finally opened on 20 April 2017 (case no. 11702960008000021). The applicant was granted victim status. Further inquiries included a third scene examination, Magomadov’s photograph, mobile-phone records, and questioning of neighbours, friends, colleagues, local officials (who described him as uninvolved in illegal groups) and R.S. (whose car had a black roof and bonnet and who claimed an alibi). Police suggested Magomadov might have joined an illegal armed group in Syria, citing a 2013 visit to Turkey and “non-traditional Islam”; I.M. explained the trip as an unsuccessful attempt to study Islam. R.T. was re-interviewed, confirmed his earlier statement, and refused a lie-detector test on health grounds; an internal inquiry was requested but its outcome is unknown. Investigators also checked detainee logs, unidentified-body databases (no DNA match), and travel records (none found).

The investigation was suspended for failure to identify perpetrators on 20 June 2017, briefly resumed, and suspended again on 30 July 2017; it appears to remain pending. These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints regarding the abduction (allegedly by or with the involvement of state agents) and the investigation’s effectiveness.

Russia concerns the disappearance of the applicant’s husband, Mukhumad Magomadov (born 1990), from the family home in Sadovoye settlement, Grozny district, Chechnya, on 6 December 2014, and the ensuing investigation. On 7 December I.M. reported the disappearance to Grozny district police, describing the events and the car. The crime scene was examined (no traces collected). The applicant, Z.M., neighbour K.U. and later I.A. gave consistent accounts of the car’s presence. The investigation was transferred to the Grozny inter-district investigative committee. (whose car had a black roof and bonnet). R.T. refused a lie-detector test; an internal inquiry into that refusal had no recorded outcome. The investigation was suspended in June 2017 for failure to identify perpetrators, briefly resumed, then suspended again in July 2017 and remains unresolved. These facts—abduction by unidentified men in a vehicle linked to a security officer, occurring immediately after official threats against families of former militants, Magomadov’s winter clothing, and a years-long investigation marked by repeated unlawful refusals, incomplete inquiries and untested alibis—form the core of the alleged violations.
001-200553:
The case of Atayev v. Russia (application no. 39070/08) concerns a Russian national, Anatoliy Atabayevich Atayev (born 1970), who was convicted of fraud on 11 June 2008 by the Leninskiy District Court of Krasnodar and sentenced to five years and one month’s imprisonment (running from his arrest on 4 November 2005). He was held in prison IZ-23/1 in Krasnodar.

In July 2008 his representative applied for conditional release. On 5 August 2008 the Oktyabrskiy District Court granted the application. The operative part of the decision stated that it took effect immediately upon pronouncement and could be appealed to the Krasnodar Regional Court within ten days. Prison management was notified the same day but refused to release the applicant, citing “doubts” about the decision’s form and lawfulness, and returned it for clarification.

On 6 August 2008 the District Court’s vice-president confirmed in writing that the release order had to be enforced immediately. Russian criminal procedure treated decisions on release from detention or exemption from serving a sentence as exceptions to the general rule that first-instance decisions enter into force only after the appeal period; the right of appeal did not suspend the obligation to release. The prison received this letter the same day but still refused to act.

On 7 August 2008 the prosecutor’s office lodged an appeal that did not address the question of immediate effect. On 14 August 2008 the prison governor wrote that execution of a doubtful release decision could be suspended pending verification and that the statutory exceptions for immediate release did not apply to conditional release; the pending appeal therefore prevented enforcement.

On 10 September 2008 the Regional Court quashed the 5 August decision, disagreeing with the first-instance finding that the applicant had mended his ways (citing, inter alia, attempts to discredit the Federal Security Service and the Prosecutor’s Office during the original criminal proceedings). It remitted the matter for fresh examination but did not rule on the lawfulness of the applicant’s continued detention between 5 August and 10 September or on the wording of the original operative part. On 1 October 2008 the applicant withdrew the application, believing it had no prospect of success; the District Court terminated the proceedings on 9 October 2008.

Throughout his time in IZ-23/1 the applicant was held in overcrowded cells. He suffered from chronic hepatitis, a duodenal ulcer, gastritis and chronic pancreatitis (documented in 2004–2005) and required a special diet and treatment. On 14 August 2008 he began a hunger strike in protest at the refusal to release him, ending it on 23 August. He claimed he received no medical attention during the strike. The Government stated that a doctor examined him on 20, 21 and 22 August 2008, found his condition satisfactory and recorded no complaints, so no treatment was required.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints of unlawful detention after a binding release order and of inadequate detention conditions, including medical care.

The ECtHR case Atayev v. Russia (no. 39070/08) arose from events after the applicant’s 11 June 2008 fraud conviction by the Leninskiy District Court of Krasnodar, which imposed a sentence of five years and one month running from his 4 November 2005 arrest.

Throughout his stay in IZ-23/1 the applicant was held in overcrowded cells. Medical records from 2004–2005 established that he suffered from chronic hepatitis, a duodenal ulcer, gastritis and chronic pancreatitis requiring a special diet and ongoing treatment. On 14 August 2008 he began a hunger strike in protest at his continued detention, claiming he received no medical attention. The Government stated that doctors examined him on 20–22 August, found his condition satisfactory and recorded no complaints, so no treatment was given. The strike ended on 23 August.

These facts concern the lawfulness of detention after a court order of release, prison overcrowding, and the medical response to a hunger strike by a prisoner with documented chronic illnesses.

The case of Atayev v. Russia (no. 39070/08) involves Russian national Anatoliy Atabayevich Atayev (born 1970, resident in Krasnodar). On 11 June 2008 the Leninskiy District Court convicted him of fraud and imposed a sentence of five years and one month’s imprisonment, running from his arrest on 4 November 2005.

In July 2008 his representative applied for conditional release. On 5 August 2008 the Oktyabrskiy District Court granted the application. Its operative part stated that the decision took effect immediately upon pronouncement and could be appealed to the Krasnodar Regional Court within ten days.

The administration of remand prison IZ-23/1 was notified the same day but refused to release the applicant, citing “doubts” about the decision’s form and lawfulness. The prison governor returned the decision to the District Court seeking clarification on when it entered into force.

On 6 August 2008 the vice-president of the District Court wrote to the governor confirming that the decision was immediately enforceable as regards release. He explained that, under the Code of Criminal Procedure, decisions ordering release from detention or exemption from serving a sentence constitute an exception to the general rule on entry into force and must be executed at once; the existence of a right of appeal did not suspend that obligation.

The prison received the letter the same day yet still declined to release the applicant. On 7 August the prosecutor’s office lodged an appeal that did not address the question of immediate effect.

On 14 August the prison governor informed the applicant’s representative that a release order giving rise to doubts could be suspended pending verification. He maintained that the statutory exceptions to delayed entry into force did not apply to conditional-release decisions and that, in any event, the prosecutor’s appeal prevented enforcement of the immediate-release clause.

On 10 September 2008 the Regional Court quashed the 5 August decision. It rejected the first-instance finding that the applicant had reformed, noting that during the criminal proceedings he had sought, among other things, to discredit the Federal Security Service and the Prosecutor’s Office. The case was remitted for fresh examination. The Regional Court did not consider the lawfulness of the applicant’s detention between 5 August and 10 September or the validity of the original operative part.

On 1 October 2008 the applicant’s representative withdrew the release application, concluding that it had no prospect of success after the appeal judgment. The District Court accepted the withdrawal and terminated the proceedings on 9 October 2008.

Throughout his detention in IZ-23/1 the applicant was held in overcrowded cells. Medical records from 2004–2005 showed that he suffered from chronic hepatitis, a duodenal ulcer, gastritis and chronic pancreatitis and required a special diet and ongoing treatment.

On 14 August 2008 he announced a hunger strike until his release. He alleged that he received no medical attention during the strike. The Government stated that a doctor examined him on 20, 21 and 22 August, found his condition satisfactory and recorded no complaints, so no treatment was required. The hunger strike ended on 23 August 2008.

These facts form the basis of the complaints concerning the lawfulness of the applicant’s continued detention after 5 August 2008, the conditions of his confinement and the medical care afforded during the hunger strike.
001-200556:
**CASE OF A.P. v. SLOVAKIA (Application no. 10465/17), ECHR (Third Section), 28 January 2020 (final 28 May 2020)**

The applicant, A.P., a Slovak national of Roma origin born in 1999, was 16 at the time of the events. He alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) due to ill-treatment by municipal police officers during an arrest and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. Racial motivation was also raised but formed part of the Article 3 complaints.

On 10 February 2015, the father of 15-year-old Roma boy M.Č. reported that M.Č. had been beaten by a group of boys. The matter was treated as a suspected minor offence. The next morning, 11 February 2015, police and M.Č. attempted identifications outside a local school. M.Č. identified the applicant and another Roma boy, A.T., as among the attackers. Officers E.P. and R.M. then intervened.

According to the applicant, at about 7.45 a.m. one officer grabbed him by the hood, leaned him against a car and punched him in the face several times before placing him and A.T. in a police car, where punching continued. At the Rudňany police station the officers allegedly put on white gloves, punched him further in the face and pressured him to confess to attacking M.Č. Official records stated he was taken to the station at 7.50 a.m., released at 8.10 a.m. and had no injuries.

After release the applicant, accompanied by his mother, sought hospital treatment. A surgeon recorded nose oedema and pain “allegedly during police intervention.” An otolaryngologist noted treatment after injury caused during a police intervention, with nose bleeding and upper-lip swelling. That evening another doctor confirmed a superficial nasal injury and that the applicant had been beaten around 7.15 a.m.

Police records on the use of coercive measures stated that R.M. grasped the applicant’s elbow to prevent him leaving; the applicant pulled away, spat on the officer, said he was not afraid and swung his arm, after which R.M. grasped and hit him. No injuries were recorded. The Prosecutor General later described an elbow-lock grip followed by a slap after the applicant spat; the applicant then calmed down. The applicant maintained he had complied voluntarily and offered no active resistance.

On 11 February 2015 the applicant (represented by his mother) lodged a criminal complaint, later amended. On 13 March the investigator dismissed it after hearing the officers and M.Č.’s father, who gave consistent accounts of the applicant’s disrespect, verbal aggression and spitting. R.M. admitted an elbow-lock grip and a slap. The applicant appealed, arguing failure to hear independent witnesses, ignore medical reports, consider racial motive, or note the absence of a required report on coercive measures.

On 9 April and 6 May 2015 the investigator instituted proceedings against the officers for suspected abuse of power. He heard the applicant, his mother, the officers (who admitted an open-hand slap while getting the applicant into the car), A.T. (who saw the applicant already in the car with a bleeding nose but denied later beatings), and M.Č. and his father (who had not witnessed the entire incident). An expert opinion of 16 June 2015 found minor injuries consistent with mild blunt-force trauma to the face, possibly from a slap or striking the car; a fist was excluded.

On 27 July 2015 the investigator discontinued the proceedings, concluding the officers had acted lawfully and that the injuries could not have resulted from fists as alleged. The applicant’s appeals were dismissed by the district and regional public prosecutor’s offices and the Prosecutor General. On 8 June 2016 the Constitutional Court rejected a complaint alleging violations of Articles 3, 13 and 14 (and domestic equivalents) as manifestly ill-founded, finding the applicant had not substantiated claims of disproportionate or unlawful force.

Relevant domestic law (Municipal Police Act) permits coercive measures, including grips, grabs and blows, only against active resistance, requires prior warning except in limited circumstances, and obliges reporting of such measures. International reports cited by the Court noted concerns about police ill-treatment of Roma in Slovakia and the need for effective investigations of racial incidents.

The case of A.P. v. Slovakia (Application no. 10465/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned alleged violations of Article 3 of the Convention arising from the treatment of a 16-year-old Roma boy by municipal police officers during an arrest on 11 February 2015 and the subsequent investigation.

On 10 February 2015, the father of 15-year-old M.Č. reported that his son had been beaten by a group of boys. The next morning, police accompanied M.Č. to a school in Rudňany to identify the perpetrators. M.Č. pointed out the applicant (A.P.) and another Roma boy, A.T. Officers E.P. and R.M. intervened. According to the applicant, one officer grabbed him by the hood, leaned him against a car and punched him in the face several times before placing him in a police vehicle, where the punching continued. At the station, both officers allegedly donned white gloves, punched him again and pressured him to confess to attacking M.Č. The boys were held briefly (from 7.50 a.m. to 8.10 a.m.) and released. Official records noted no injuries.

The applicant sought medical treatment the same day. Hospital records documented nasal oedema, pain, bleeding from the nose and swelling of the upper lip, attributed to a police intervention. A later examination confirmed a superficial nasal injury from being beaten around 7.15 a.m.

Police accounts differed. A record of coercive measures stated that R.M. grasped the applicant’s elbow to prevent him leaving; the applicant pulled away, spat, expressed no fear and swung his arm, prompting R.M. to grasp and hit him. No injuries were recorded. A later prosecutorial report described an elbow-lock grip followed by a slap after the applicant spat, after which he calmed down. The applicant maintained he had complied voluntarily without resistance.

The applicant (represented by his mother) filed a criminal complaint on 11 February 2015, later amended. An investigator initially dismissed it on 13 March 2015 after hearing the officers and M.Č.’s father, who described verbal aggression and spitting by the applicant; R.M. admitted an elbow-lock grip and a slap. Following the applicant’s appeal citing unheard independent witnesses, ignored medical reports, possible racial motive and failure to report coercive measures, proceedings were instituted on 9 April/6 May 2015 for suspected abuse of power.

Further hearings occurred. Officers admitted the open-hand slap while placing the applicant in the car. A.T. recalled the applicant already in the car with a bleeding nose but denied beatings in the car or station. M.Č. and his father had not witnessed the entire incident. An expert opinion of 16 June 2015 found minor facial injuries from mild blunt force, consistent with a slap or impact against the car but excluding a fist.

On 27 July 2015 the investigator discontinued proceedings, finding the officers had acted lawfully: injuries could not have resulted from fists as alleged, and a slap had been used to overcome resistance. The applicant appealed, arguing reliance solely on officers’ accounts, biased witnesses, failure to hear other bystanders, inadequate scrutiny of lawfulness/proportionality of force (including lack of warning and reporting), and unexamined racial motive. The district public prosecutor dismissed the appeal on 7 September 2015, holding that the applicant (suspected of a minor offence) had ignored orders and resisted, justifying coercive measures under the Municipal Police Act; the light injury was consistent with a slap or car impact. Higher prosecutors and the Prosecutor General upheld this. A constitutional complaint alleging disproportionate force, ineffective investigation and unexamined racial motive was rejected on 8 June 2016 as manifestly ill-founded.

Relevant domestic law (Municipal Police Act) permitted coercive measures, including grips and blows, against active resistance after warning (waivable in urgent cases), required reporting, and mandated investigation if injury resulted. International reports noted concerns over anti-Roma violence and police ill-treatment in Slovakia. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 3 on both substantive (unnecessary force against a minor) and procedural (ineffective investigation) limbs.

The case of A.P. v. Slovakia concerns a 16-year-old Roma boy’s allegations of police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation under Article 3 of the Convention.

On 10 February 2015, the father of 15-year-old M.Č. (also Roma) reported that his son had been beaten by a group of boys. The next morning, in front of a school, M.Č. identified the applicant and another Roma boy, A.T., as among the attackers. Municipal police officers E.P. and R.M. then intervened. According to the applicant, one officer grabbed him by the hood, forced him against a car and punched him repeatedly in the face before placing him in a police vehicle, where the blows continued. At the station, both officers donned white gloves, punched him further and pressed him to confess.

Official records stated that the applicant was detained from 7.50 a.m. to 8.10 a.m. with no injuries. Later that day, however, medical examinations recorded nose oedema, pain, bleeding and swelling of the upper lip, attributed to an injury during the police action. A police report on the use of force claimed that R.M. grasped the applicant’s elbow after he pulled away, spat and swung his arm; the officer then slapped him. The applicant denied any resistance.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint alleging ill-treatment, including a possible racial motive. An investigator initially dismissed it after hearing only the officers and M.Č.’s father, who described verbal aggression and spitting. Following an appeal, proceedings were opened against the officers for abuse of power. The officers admitted an open-hand slap in front of the school. A.T. confirmed the applicant’s bleeding nose but denied further beatings. An expert found minor facial injuries consistent with a slap or accidental contact with the car, but not fists.

The investigator discontinued the case, holding that the officers had acted lawfully against active resistance and that the injuries did not match the applicant’s account of punches. Prosecutorial appeals were rejected on similar grounds: the force was deemed proportionate, the injury light, and no racial motive established. The Constitutional Court dismissed a subsequent complaint as manifestly ill-founded for lack of concrete substantiation.

The applicant maintained that the slap (and alleged punches) on a minor was not strictly necessary, constituted degrading treatment, and that the investigation was deficient: it relied mainly on the officers’ statements, failed to hear independent school witnesses, overlooked the absence of a prior warning or timely reporting of force, and ignored possible racial bias. These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 3 violations.

The case of Vatsayeva and Others v. Russia (application no. 44658/12) concerns the abduction, alleged detention, ill-treatment and killing of Khalid Dushayev (born 1951) in Chechnya in 2011, together with two other men, and the subsequent ineffective investigation. The first applicant is Dushayev’s widow (and sister of another man previously killed by State agents); the second and third applicants are his children. All three applicants are Russian nationals.

In 2009 Dushayev had been convicted of running an illegal armed group. While imprisoned he met A.A. and I.A., who had similar convictions. All three were released by 2011. On the evening of 24 June 2011 the three men were walking in Gudermes when two officers of the Chechen President’s security service stopped them, checked their mobile phones and then left. Minutes later a group of 10–15 armed men in camouflage uniforms intercepted them near a petrol station, saying they had arrested a “shaitan” (illegal-armed-group member). After a telephone call to a known officer, I.A. was released; Dushayev and A.A. were taken to Tsentaroy district police station.

The next day I.A. informed the first applicant of the arrests. That same day two armed men in a Lada (registration containing “130 TT 95”) abducted I.A. himself. Relatives immediately sought information at Tsentaroy but were turned away at a checkpoint and advised not to complain “for Dushayev’s safety.” Formal abduction complaints were lodged on 25 June and 5 July 2011. Separate criminal cases were opened in July and joined in August (case no. 53047) under Article 126 of the Criminal Code.

Investigators examined the two crime scenes but collected no physical evidence and took no photographs. They granted victim status to relatives, questioned several family members and the petrol-station attendant (who later recanted his initial statement that the abductors had called one of the men a “shaitan”), authorised two-month telephone intercepts, and later identified (but did not pursue) the owners of two cars bearing similar plates. The investigation was repeatedly suspended for “failure to identify perpetrators” (September and December 2011, February and December 2012) and equally often resumed after prosecutors ruled the suspensions premature and unlawful, citing superficial interviews, unanalysed telephone data and unfollowed leads about a possible neighbour-perpetrator.

In January 2012 the authorities announced that several alleged illegal-armed-group members, including Dushayev, A.A. and I.A., had been killed in an exchange of fire on 8 January. The bodies shown to relatives were abnormally pale and emaciated, with long hair and beards, and were dressed in summer uniforms despite the winter date. Dushayev’s body displayed missing front teeth, electric-shock and cigarette burns, a broken right leg and, according to those who prepared it for burial, gunshot wounds inflicted after death. Relatives were charged 5 000 roubles for the body’s release and instructed to bury it immediately, away from Dushayev’s home village. Family members consistently rejected the official version that the three men had voluntarily joined an illegal group and staged their own abductions; they maintained that the men had been secretly detained, tortured and extra-judicially executed, after which the scene of the “exchange of fire” had been fabricated.

The investigation remained open but inactive at the time of the application. These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints under Articles 2 (right to life – both the killing itself and the lack of an effective investigation), 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment of the deceased and of the relatives), 5 (unlawful detention) and 13 (lack of an effective remedy) of the Convention.

The case of Vatsayeva and Others v. Russia (application no. 44658/12) concerns the abduction, alleged torture, and killing of Khalid Dushayev (born 1951) by State agents in Chechnya, along with deficiencies in the subsequent investigation. The applicants are Dushayev’s widow (first applicant) and two of his children. Dushayev had previously been convicted of running an illegal armed group and released by 2011; he associated with A.A. and I.A., who had similar convictions.

On the evening of 24 June 2011, Dushayev, A.A., and I.A. were walking in Gudermes when two officers from the Chechen President’s security service stopped them, checked their (absent) identity documents and mobile phones, and departed. Minutes later, 10–15 armed men in camouflage uniforms intercepted the trio near the “Leader” petrol station. The station attendant, Ab.Ats., witnessed the event and was told the men had arrested a “shaitan” (illegal armed group member). After I.A. requested a call to a known security-service officer (which one of the armed men placed), I.A. was released; Dushayev and A.A. were taken to Tsentaroy district police station.

The next day I.A. informed the first applicant of the arrests. Later on 25 June 2011, two similarly armed men in a Lada (registration containing 130 TT 95) abducted I.A. himself. In early January 2012 investigators told the families that several illegal-armed-group members, allegedly including the three men, had been killed in an 8 January 2012 exchange of fire in Vedeno district. On 10 January the bodies were shown to relatives for identification. They were abnormally pale and emaciated, with unusually long hair and beards, and dressed in summer uniforms (despite winter conditions). Dushayev’s body displayed missing upper front teeth, electric and cigarette burns, and a broken right leg; those preparing it for burial observed gunshot wounds inflicted after death. The body was released a week later upon payment of RUB 5,000, with instructions to bury it immediately rather than transport it home. The applicants supplied photographs of Dushayev before and after death.

Relatives attempted to visit Tsentaroy police station on 24–25 June 2011 but were turned back at a checkpoint and advised not to complain “for Dushayev’s safety.” Formal complaints followed on 25 June and 5 July 2011. Separate investigations into the abductions of I.A. and Dushayev were opened in July 2011 under Article 126 of the Criminal Code (abduction) and joined in August. Crime-scene examinations yielded no evidence or photographs. Ab.Ats. initially corroborated the “shaitan” remark but later recanted, claiming misunderstanding and inability to identify anyone. Victim status was granted to several relatives, whose consistent accounts of the arrests were recorded. Court-authorised telephone intercepts were obtained but never analysed. Vehicle-registration leads (the Lada plate) were pursued only superficially; owners had sold the cars without timely re-registration.

The investigation was repeatedly suspended (September 2011, December 2011, February 2012, December 2012) and resumed only after prosecutors ruled the suspensions premature and unlawful, citing failure to analyse telephone data, follow the vehicle lead, or properly question witnesses (including possible pressure on Ab.Ats.). After the bodies were identified, investigators asked relatives whether the men might have staged their own abductions to join insurgents; all rejected this, insisting the men had been secretly detained, tortured, killed, and their bodies planted to simulate combat deaths. As of the Court’s judgment the investigation remained formally open but inactive.

These facts underpin alleged violations of the right to life (substantive and procedural aspects), prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment (both of the victim and of relatives through prolonged uncertainty and the condition of the body), unlawful detention, and lack of an effective domestic remedy.

The case concerns the abduction, alleged secret detention, torture and killing of Khalid Dushayev (born 1951) by Russian/Chechen State agents in 2011, together with two associates, and the subsequent ineffective investigation. The applicants are Dushayev’s widow (also sister of another man previously abducted and killed by State agents) and two of his sons. Dushayev had been convicted in 2009 of running an illegal armed group; after release he associated with two other former convicts, A.A. and I.A.

On the evening of 24 June 2011 the three men were walking in Gudermes when two officers of the Chechen President’s security service stopped them, checked their (absent) identity documents and telephones, then left. Minutes later 10–15 armed men in camouflage seized them near a petrol station. The attendant later stated that the men described their captives as members of an illegal armed group. After one of the armed men telephoned a known security-service officer, I.A. was released; Dushayev and A.A. were driven to the Tsentaroy district police station. The next day armed men in a Lada (partial plate 130 TT 95) abducted I.A. as well.

Relatives who tried to reach the police station were turned back at a checkpoint and warned not to complain “for Dushayev’s safety.” Formal abduction complaints were nevertheless lodged. Investigations were opened in July 2011 (later joined) but were repeatedly suspended for failure to identify perpetrators. Prosecutors twice quashed the suspensions as premature, criticising the investigators for superficial witness interviews, failure to photograph the crime scene, failure to analyse intercepted telephone data, and failure to trace the vehicle plate. A key witness later recanted his original account that the abductors had identified their prisoners as militants. Owners of similarly plated cars said they had sold the vehicles to unregistered third parties. Relatives were granted victim status and consistently denied any suggestion that the three men had voluntarily joined an illegal armed group.

In January 2012 investigators announced that several militants, allegedly including the three missing men, had been killed in a firefight on 8 January. The bodies shown to relatives were emaciated, pale, with unnaturally long hair and beards, dressed in summer clothing despite the winter date. Dushayev’s corpse displayed missing front teeth, electric and cigarette burns, a broken leg and (according to those who prepared it for burial) gunshot wounds inflicted after death. The family paid 5 000 roubles to recover the body and were instructed to bury it immediately, away from the home village.

The applicants submitted contemporaneous photographs showing the contrast between Dushayev’s appearance before abduction and after death. They maintained that the men had been held in dark cells, tortured and then executed, their bodies planted at a staged shoot-out. The criminal investigation remained pending, having been suspended and resumed several more times without any identified suspects or meaningful progress.

These facts form the basis of complaints that State agents abducted the three men, subjected Dushayev to unacknowledged detention and torture, and killed him, while the ensuing investigation was structurally inadequate and repeatedly obstructed.
001-200719:
The case of Kruglov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 11264/04 and 15 others) involved 25 Russian nationals, mostly practising lawyers (Bar members except for a few like Fedorov, Silivanov and Mezentsev, plus some clients). They complained of police searches of their homes and offices, plus seizures and prolonged retention of electronic data-storage devices (computers, hard drives, phones), alleging interferences with Article 8 rights to respect for home and correspondence (including professional secrecy) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (control of property use). Domestic challenges failed.

Searches occurred amid criminal probes (e.g., libel, theft, drug dealing, fraud, tax evasion, illegal transfers), often targeting clients, associates or the lawyers themselves. Courts issued warrants under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP) or Operational-Search Activities Act, typically citing “sufficient grounds” that evidence might be found, without detailed necessity or proportionality assessment. Some used “urgent” procedures or “crime-scene examinations”/“inspections” avoiding full warrants.

Key incidents included: Kruglov’s parents’ flat searched under warrant, then his actual home without one; Buraga’s home searched (husband suspected of theft), with computers, phones and documents seized (partially returned later); Belinskaya’s home searched (co-resident suspected of drugs); Fedorov’s (non-Bar) home searched for stolen goods (warrant later quashed, items returned); Fast’s law firm office searched in a fraud probe, computers seized (returned after case closure); Balyan, Sokolov and Solovyev’s law firm offices searched, computers/hard drives/safe seized (some returned, others not); Silivanov’s (non-Bar) home searched over a client’s real-estate case; Belinskaya’s office searched (suspected in forging a medical report for client Makovoz), computers/hard drive seized (one returned); Bulycheva’s office searched (linked to employer’s alleged illegal transfers); Moiseyeva’s home and office searched (suspected of stealing case files); Mezentsev’s (non-Bar) office “examined” without warrant, hard drive seized (used in tax cases, later returned); Lazutkin’s home/office searched via operational activities, notebooks/computers seized (retained as evidence); Parnachev et al.’s advocate association premises searched extensively over misappropriation claims, all computers seized (not returned); Ponyayeva’s (Yeliseyeva) rented office and flat searched (client suspected of fraud); Levchenko’s shared arbitral/advocate office searched, notebooks seized (returned after 15 months); Pashkina et al.’s office searched over bankruptcy probe, case files and computer data seized.

Seizures often captured potentially privileged lawyer-client material. Domestic reviews (appeals, Article 125 CCrP complaints) were dismissed: courts upheld warrants as formally valid, noted no comments on lawyer status or privileged items in records, and found no irregularities. Some warrants were later quashed or amended for lack of specificity, but seizures/retention continued. Non-Bar lawyers received no special protections. Devices were retained for months or years, even if unrelated or after case closures, contrary to later CCrP rules requiring prompt decisions and returns.

Domestic law required court warrants for advocates’ premises and barred use of privileged material, but lacked robust safeguards (e.g., no mandatory Bar representative presence until 2017 amendments). Other legal advisers had none. International standards stressed confidentiality of lawyer-client communications.

**CASE OF KRUGLOV AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA (Applications nos. 11264/04 and 15 others)**

This case joined 16 applications by 25 Russian nationals, mostly practising lawyers (the majority Bar members/advocates, with exceptions including non-Bar legal advisers Fedorov, Silivanov and Mezentsev, plus some clients). They alleged violations of Article 8 (respect for home and correspondence) arising from police searches of their homes and/or offices and seizures of electronic data-storage devices, and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to lengthy retention of seized items. They also claimed a lack of effective domestic remedies.

The searches typically occurred in the context of criminal investigations targeting the lawyers themselves, their clients, family members, associates or related companies (e.g., suspicions of libel, theft, drug dealing, fraud, tax evasion, illegal money transfers or bankruptcy). Courts issued search warrants under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP) or Operational-Search Activities Act, often on applications stating that relevant objects/documents “might be located” at the premises. Warrants were frequently broad, failing to specify particular items or to address the lawyers’ professional status. Some searches used “urgent procedure” without a warrant for the actual premises (Kruglov) or took the form of a “crime-scene examination” without judicial authorisation (Mezentsev, a non-Bar lawyer). Shared or adjacent premises (law firms, companies, arbitral tribunals) led to searches of individual lawyers’ offices or workspaces not individually authorised.

Seizures commonly included computers, hard drives, CPUs, mobile phones, notebooks and documents. These devices contained or potentially contained client files and legally privileged material. In several instances, police continued searches after being informed of the lawyer’s advocate status or privilege claims. Seized items were sometimes examined by experts and, in at least one case, used by tax authorities in unrelated disputes involving other clients (Mezentsev). Retention periods were often lengthy: devices were held for months or years, even after being deemed unrelated to the investigation, after cases were closed for lack of corpus delicti, or after warrants were later quashed. Some items were never returned (e.g., hard drives in Balyan and others; computers and phones in Parnachev and others; notebooks and computers in Lazutkin).

Applicants challenged the warrants and the manner of searches/seizures via appeals and Article 125 CCrP complaints. Domestic courts generally dismissed these, finding the searches lawful because they were based on valid warrants, the lawyers had not recorded privilege objections in search records, no privileged material had been proved to have been seized, or the premises belonged to a third party under investigation. Courts frequently did not assess necessity or proportionality, did not permit lawyers to participate meaningfully in warrant hearings, and treated Bar members and non-Bar legal advisers differently. Non-Bar lawyers had no special procedural protections under domestic law. Later amendments (e.g., CCrP Article 450.1 from 2017) introduced limited extra safeguards only for advocates who were themselves suspects, and only after the events in these cases.

These facts underpinned the complaints of unjustified interferences with homes, correspondence and professional secrecy (including a complete absence of safeguards for non-Bar legal advisers) and of disproportionate control over property through prolonged retention of electronic devices.

The ECHR case Kruglov and Others v. Russia (applications 11264/04 and 15 others) concerns 25 Russian applicants, mostly practising lawyers (Bar members except Fedorov, Silivanov, Mezentsev and certain clients). They alleged Article 8 violations from searches of homes/offices and seizures of electronic devices, plus Article 1 Protocol 1 violations from lengthy unjustified retention of those devices, and lack of effective remedies.

Police searched applicants' premises amid criminal probes typically targeting others (spouses, clients or associates), though some lawyers faced suspicion of involvement. Courts issued warrants citing “sufficient grounds” that instruments of crime, documents or valuables might be present, without examining necessity, proportionality or the risk to lawyer-client confidentiality. Warrants were often broad, omitting specific items or documents and ignoring applicants' professional status.

Illustrative facts include: Kruglov's actual flat searched under “urgent procedure” after a warrant for his parents' home; Buraga's computers, phones and documents seized despite her advocate role; Belinskaya's home and office searched (computers later partly returned); Fedorov's (non-Bar) flat searched for stolen goods, items returned only after the warrant was quashed for insufficient grounds; Fast's office computers seized in a later-closed fraud inquiry; Balyan, Sokolov and Solovyev's law-firm offices searched, a computer, hard drives and a safe seized (safe returned but devices retained after the warrant was quashed for lack of specificity); Silivanov's (non-Bar) home searched; Belinskaya's office computers seized over an alleged forged report; Bulycheva's office searched; Moiseyeva's home and office searched for stolen case files; Mezentsev's (non-Bar) office “crime-scene examined” without a warrant, a hard drive containing multiple clients' tax data seized and later used against them; Lazutkin's home, office and workplace inspected, notebooks and computers seized and retained as evidence; the NTAA premises (housing several advocates) searched over two days, all computers and hard drives seized under a warrant later amended for greater specificity; Ponyayeva's rented office space and flat searched; Levchenko's shared arbitral/advocates' office searched, notebooks seized for over a year; and Pashkina, Privalov and Levin's office searched, litigation files and computer databases seized.

Seizures routinely included computers, hard drives and phones likely holding privileged communications. Domestic law required court warrants for Bar members' premises (Advocates Act s. 8(3)) but supplied no effective safeguards such as independent observers, sifting of privileged material or limits on electronic searches. Non-Bar legal advisers enjoyed no special protections whatsoever; a mere “crime-scene examination” sufficed. Later amendments (CCrP Art. 450.1 from 2017) improved some rules but post-dated the events.

Applicants challenged warrants and search conduct via appeals or CCrP Art. 125 proceedings. Domestic courts uniformly dismissed the complaints, reciting formal compliance, the existence of a warrant, the absence of advocate-status remarks in search records, or a lack of proof that privileged items had been taken. They never assessed whether the measures were necessary or proportionate, nor whether professional secrecy had been adequately protected. Some warrants were subsequently quashed for inadequate reasoning or over-breadth, yet seized items often remained withheld.

Devices were retained for months or years even after investigations closed, items were found unrelated, or warrants were invalidated. No timely decisions on retention as evidence were issued (later CCrP Art. 81.1 time-limits were not yet in force), impairing applicants' professional work and property rights.

These facts illustrate systemic failures: courts' refusal to scrutinise necessity and proportionality, domestic law's inadequate safeguards for professional secrecy, and the complete absence of protection for non-Bar legal advisers, all contrary to international standards requiring confidentiality of lawyer-client communications.

The case of Özgüç v. Turkey (Application no. 3094/09) concerns a Turkish national, Kadriye Özgüç (born 1985), arrested on 8 March 2007 and placed in pre-trial detention on 10 March 2007. She faced charges of PKK membership, possessing explosives, damaging public property, and violating demonstration laws, stemming from a 15 February 2007 Istanbul protest against Abdullah Öcalan’s arrest (during which a bus was damaged by stones and Molotov cocktails) and a related 2006 incident.

An informant and an anonymous witness (whose identity was kept confidential) identified the applicant (known as Kader) and co-accused S.S. as participants who threw Molotov cocktails at the bus, with the applicant allegedly leading the group. The anonymous witness, known from DTP youth activities, repeated this to police and the prosecutor, claiming the pair had invited him to the event. The applicant admitted attending the demonstration but denied any involvement in the violence or explosives, challenging the anonymous statements.

An indictment followed on 26 March 2007. At trial, the defence argued the case rested solely on the anonymous witness, breaching equality of arms, and sought to examine the bus driver (who testified that stones were thrown but could not identify anyone) and the anonymous witness himself. Initial requests to hear the latter were refused. A further identification by R.S. (described as a PKK member) occurred in May 2008.

On 13 June 2008, the court agreed to hear the anonymous witness in a closed session (due to security concerns and lack of technical facilities under Article 58 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). The accused were invited to submit questions in advance, based on the known content of prior statements; the applicant submitted none. The witness was heard on 2 September 2008 in the parties’ absence. His identity was sealed. He confirmed seeing the applicant (face partially covered) holding Molotov cocktails, leading the group that threw stones and cocktails at the bus (windows broken, no fire). He identified her from photos and answered the co-accused’s questions, citing personal security for anonymity. Statements were later read out and contested by the defence as contradictory and obtained without direct confrontation.

On 12 June 2009, the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant, relying on the scene-of-incident report (confirming a Molotov explosion), the anonymous witness’s consistent statements, R.S.’s identification, police evidence, and the bus driver’s account (discrepancies attributed to the chaos). She received sentences including 7 years 6 months for explosives possession, 5 years for property damage, and 6 years 3 months for PKK membership. The Court of Cassation (10 May 2011) upheld the 2007-related convictions and membership finding (reducing one sentence) but quashed the 2006 charges for insufficient evidence; the applicant was later acquitted of those.

Regarding detention, reviews (including objections on 18 June 2008 to continued remand) were decided on the case file in the prosecutor’s presence, without serving his written opinions on the applicant or lawyer, and without a hearing.
