The case of Gaughran v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 45245/15) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR arising from the indefinite retention of biometric data of a person convicted of a minor recordable offence. The applicant, Fergus Gaughran (born 1972), was arrested on 14 October 2008 for driving with excess alcohol (65 mg/100 ml breath, 30 mg over the limit), a recordable offence under Northern Ireland law. Police took his fingerprints, photograph and a DNA sample (via buccal swab), from which a DNA profile was generated.

On 5 November 2008 he pleaded guilty at Newry Magistrates’ Court, receiving a £50 fine and 12-month driving disqualification but no custodial sentence. The conviction became spent after five years (by 5 November 2013). He had one prior conviction (disorderly behaviour at age 17 in 1990). In January 2009 his solicitor requested destruction of the data, citing S. and Marper v. UK. PSNI refused, stating it would follow any legislative changes. The DNA sample itself was destroyed in 2015, but the profile, fingerprints and photograph continue to be retained indefinitely.

Gaughran sought judicial review. The Northern Ireland High Court (2012) accepted an Article 8 interference but held it justified and proportionate. It cited the value of a convicted-persons database for crime detection (larger databases being more effective), the different rights of convicted versus unconvicted persons, the limited identifying nature of the data, statutory restrictions on use, an exceptional-case deletion procedure, administrative complexity of further differentiation, the policy’s distinction between recordable and non-recordable offences, the offence’s seriousness (anti-social and life-endangering), the arbitrariness of time limits, and a deterrent effect against reoffending.

The UK Supreme Court (2015) dismissed the appeal by majority. Lord Clarke observed that S. and Marper concerned only unconvicted persons; the interference here was low-level. Recordable offences provided a rational, proportionate threshold. Comparative data showed many Council of Europe states retain data for long periods or until death, with few review mechanisms. The photograph database was standalone and lacked facial-recognition matching at the time. Lord Kerr dissented, arguing the policy was not the least restrictive means: a more tailored scheme with offence-based time limits, periodic review (e.g., for exemplary post-conviction conduct) and regard to spent convictions was feasible and required.

Northern Ireland law remained unchanged after S. and Marper, unlike England and Wales (Protection of Freedoms Act 2012), which introduced time-limited retention for unconvicted persons and certain minor/juvenile cases plus a Biometrics Commissioner. PSNI still applies a rarely used exceptional-case procedure. Photographs were later subject to a 2017 Custody Image Review recommending deletion applications after six years for non-serious offences, with presumptions in some cases. Rehabilitation legislation treats spent convictions as non-disclosable.

Council of Europe recommendations (R(87)15 and R(92)1) require storage limited to necessity, taking account of rehabilitation, spent convictions and seriousness. Comparative surveys showed only a handful of states (including Ireland) retain DNA/fingerprints/photographs indefinitely after minor convictions; most impose time limits (some linked to death), periodic assessments or judicial/administrative review.

These facts—the blanket, indefinite, indiscriminate retention of all three data types after a spent minor conviction, without reference to seriousness, without review and without the safeguards later adopted in England and Wales—form the core of the alleged disproportionate interference with private life.

The case of Gaughran v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 45245/15) concerned a British national, Fergus Gaughran (born 1972, resident in Newry), who alleged a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The claim centred on the indefinite retention by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) of his DNA profile, fingerprints and photograph following conviction for a minor recordable offence.

On 14 October 2008, Gaughran was stopped at a police checkpoint and arrested for driving with excess alcohol contrary to the Road Traffic (Northern Ireland) Order 1995, an offence punishable by imprisonment. Breath samples showed 65 milligrams of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath (30 milligrams over the limit). At the station, police took his fingerprints, a photograph and a non-intimate DNA sample by buccal swab; a DNA profile was later extracted. On 5 November 2008 he pleaded guilty at Newry Magistrates’ Court, receiving a £50 fine and a 12-month driving disqualification with no custodial sentence. The conviction became spent after five years (5 November 2013). His only prior conviction, from 1990 when he was 17, was for disorderly behaviour, attracting a £25 fine.

In January 2009 his solicitor requested destruction of the biometric data, citing the Grand Chamber judgment in S. and Marper v. the United Kingdom. The PSNI refused, stating that any legal changes would be implemented in due course. The DNA sample itself was destroyed in 2015, but the PSNI has retained, and intends to retain indefinitely, the DNA profile, fingerprints and photograph.

Gaughran sought judicial review in the High Court of Northern Ireland, seeking a declaration that the indefinite retention was an unjustifiable interference with his Article 8 right to respect for private life and an order prohibiting further use of the data. In November 2012 the High Court accepted that retention interfered with Article 8 but held it justified and proportionate. It listed eleven reasons, including the value of a convicted-persons database for crime detection, the lesser privacy expectations of convicted persons, the restricted uses of the data, an exceptional-case deletion procedure, administrative difficulties of further differentiation, the seriousness of drink-driving, the arbitrary nature of time limits, and a deterrent effect.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in May 2015 by a majority. Lord Clarke emphasised that S. and Marper concerned only unconvicted persons; the interference here was of a low level; and the choice of “recordable offences” as the retention threshold struck a fair balance. Comparative material showed many Council of Europe States retained data until death or for very long periods, with few providing review. Lord Kerr dissented, finding the policy neither the least intrusive means nor a fair balance: it lacked any consideration of offence seriousness, contained no periodic review, and failed to examine whether indefinite retention of all recordable-offence data was necessary.

The alleged Article 8 violation therefore rested on the blanket, indiscriminate character of the Northern Irish scheme: biometric data of every adult convicted of any recordable offence (however minor) was retained indefinitely, without reference to the nature or gravity of the offence, without any possibility of review, and without taking into account that the conviction had become spent. The DNA sample had been destroyed, but the digital profile, fingerprints and photograph remained on PSNI databases, capable of being used for identification and, in the case of the photograph, potentially for facial-recognition matching.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Gaughran v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 45245/15, judgment of 13 February 2020) concerned the indefinite retention of biometric data belonging to a person convicted of a minor offence, alleged to violate Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life).

Fergus Gaughran, a British national born in 1972, was stopped at a police checkpoint in Newry, Northern Ireland, on 14 October 2008 and arrested for the recordable offence (punishable by imprisonment) of driving with excess alcohol. Breath samples showed 65 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of breath, exceeding the limit by 30 mg. At the police station, officers took his fingerprints, a photograph, and a non-intimate DNA sample via buccal swab, from which a DNA profile was later extracted. On 5 November 2008 he pleaded guilty at Newry Magistrates’ Court, receiving a £50 fine and a 12-month driving ban with no custodial sentence. The conviction became spent after five years (by November 2013). His only prior conviction was for disorderly behaviour in 1990, when he was 17, for which he was fined £25.

In January 2009 Gaughran’s solicitor requested destruction or return of the data, citing the Court’s earlier ruling in S. and Marper v. the United Kingdom. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) refused, stating that any legislative changes would be followed. The DNA sample itself was destroyed in 2015, but the PSNI continues to retain the DNA profile, fingerprints and photograph indefinitely.

Gaughran sought judicial review, seeking a declaration that indefinite retention was an unjustifiable interference with Article 8 and an order prohibiting further use of the data. The High Court of Justice of Northern Ireland dismissed the claim in 2012, holding that while there was an interference it was justified. It listed eleven factors: the proven value of a convicted-persons database for crime detection; the differing expectations of convicted versus unconvicted persons; the objective, non-intimate nature of the data; statutory restrictions on its use; its potential exculpatory value; an exceptional-case deletion procedure; the administrative complexity of further differentiation; the policy’s distinction between recordable and non-recordable offences; the seriousness of drink-driving as an offence endangering life; the arbitrariness of time limits; and the deterrent effect of permanent retention.

The UK Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in 2015 by majority. Lord Clarke stressed that S. and Marper concerned only unconvicted persons, that the interference here was of a low level, and that the choice of “recordable offence” as the retention threshold was a proportionate exercise of the state’s margin of appreciation. He noted comparative practice across Council of Europe states, many of which retain data until death or for decades, and observed that few operate review mechanisms. Lord Kerr dissented, arguing that the policy was not the least restrictive means of achieving crime-prevention aims, that no evidence showed indefinite retention of all such data was necessary, and that a more nuanced scheme (time limits linked to offence gravity, periodic review, or deletion after exemplary behaviour) was feasible.

Northern Ireland law, unlike the post-2012 Protection of Freedoms Act regime in England and Wales, continued to permit indefinite retention of DNA profiles, fingerprints and photographs of anyone convicted of a recordable offence, subject only to a rarely invoked exceptional-case procedure. Photographs were held on a database without facial-recognition matching at the relevant time. Rehabilitation legislation treated spent convictions as non-disclosable in certain contexts but did not require deletion of biometric data.

Council of Europe Recommendations R(87)15 and R(92)1 emphasise that police data should be stored only as long as necessary, taking account of rehabilitation, spent convictions and the seriousness of the offence. Comparative surveys of 31 member states showed that the great majority impose time-limited retention (often linked to the offender’s death) and provide for administrative or judicial review; only a handful, including Northern Ireland, retain indefinitely without such safeguards.

These facts formed the core of the alleged Article 8 violation: a blanket, indiscriminate power to retain biometric data indefinitely after conviction for even a minor recordable offence, without reference to the gravity of the offence, the spent status of the conviction, or any realistic possibility of review.

The European Court of Human Rights examined nine joined applications from Russian nationals arrested between 2005 and 2015 on suspicion of crimes in various regions. The applicants alleged police ill-treatment (beatings, electric shocks, strangulation, and threats) often aimed at extracting confessions, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, along with ineffective investigations into those claims.

In Botov, the applicant was taken to a Moscow police station on 11 December 2005 after a street attack. He claimed officers beat him and threatened relatives. A 12 December medical certificate recorded facial/chest scratches, bruises, and shoulder injuries. He was charged the next day. A January 2006 prosecutor complaint led to a January 2007 refusal to open a case (injuries attributed to the original fight, based on officers’ statements); a district court dismissed his appeal in July 2007. He remained in pre-trial detention until conviction in October 2006.

Bayramkulov, already serving a sentence, was transferred and taken on 1 November 2010 to an anti-extremism centre where officers allegedly applied electric shocks for five hours. Records showed hand abrasions and a temple wound. A similar incident occurred on 23 March 2011; a later forensic exam found no shock-related injuries. Investigators issued over 21 refusals (2011–2014), repeatedly quashed for incompleteness; a 2013 prosecutor report noted delays. The latest 2014 refusal (relying on officers’ denials) was upheld by courts.

Rasputin, arrested in May 2009, alleged kicks and punches by officers visiting his detention facility on 20 August 2009. An ambulance certificate recorded concussion, hematoma, and facial bruises; forensic reports confirmed blunt-object injuries (possibly 3–6 days prior, inconsistent with a fall). Three 2009 refusals (two quashed) culminated in a March 2010 decision citing officers’ denials and the applicant’s retracted “fall from bed” account (allegedly given under fear). Courts dismissed his appeal in 2012.

Fedorov was stopped on 10 April 2012 and allegedly kicked in the chest at a station. Ambulance and X-ray evidence showed a chest bruise and three fractured ribs. Multiple refusals (2012–2015) cited officers’ denials and a prior fall explanation; some were quashed. A 2014 court noted failures to question a forensic expert or clarify the arrest, but later refusals were also quashed or not examined.

Pushnin was arrested on 24 February 2009 and alleged prolonged beatings plus electric shocks (and later pistol blows). Forensics noted arm bruises; a hospital recorded a forehead wound. On 27 August 2009, after complaining in court, detention officers allegedly beat, strangled, and suspended him; medical records showed eye contusion, facial/body bruises, and a rib fracture. Refusals (2009–2013) attributed injuries to self-infliction, resistance, or unrelated events; courts dismissed appeals.

Krivonogov alleged punches after a 18 October 2011 flat search. Hospital records showed facial/head bruises. An initial 2011 refusal cited a drunken home fall; later refusals (at least five, most quashed) relied on officers’ claims the injuries predated arrest.

Bogdanov, arrested 22 October 2011 on murder suspicion, alleged kicks, punches, bag-strangulation, and rape threats. Forensics recorded hematomas and bruises consistent with the timeframe. A 2012 trial court attributed injuries to the murder night. At least six refusals cited self-injury while intoxicated; courts declined review citing the trial findings.

Kalinin, arrested 2 March 2012, alleged kicks and punches (including groin). Medical records showed a swollen cheek plus facial/limb/groin bruises from a blunt object. Refusals cited pre- or during-arrest causation (one quashed); a case opened against one officer only for unlawful detention, not ill-treatment.

Forensics recorded bruises, abrasions, and eye haemorrhage (later excluding shocks). Multiple 2015–2016 refusals (most quashed) relied solely on officers’ denials; courts dismissed the appeal.

Domestic rules required reporting of visible injuries upon police intake and proper examination of torture complaints.

The case of Botov and Others v. Russia comprises nine applications by Russian nationals alleging police ill-treatment (in violation of Article 3 ECHR) after arrests on suspicion of various crimes between 2005 and 2015. Applicants claimed officers beat, kicked, punched, applied electric shocks, strangled them with bags, and issued threats (including of rape or harm to relatives) to extract confessions while in police stations or related facilities.

Medical records corroborated injuries consistent with the allegations and timing. Botov (arrested December 2005) had facial/chest scratches, bruises, and contusions. Bayramkulov (2010) showed hand abrasions and a temple wound after alleged shocks. Rasputin (August 2009) had concussion, head hematoma, facial bruises, and lip injury; forensics indicated blunt-object blows. Fedorov (April 2012) had chest bruises and multiple rib fractures. Pushnin (February 2009, plus August 2009 incident) had arm bruises, a forehead wound, eye hematoma/contusion, and a rib fracture. Krivonogov (October 2011) had facial/head bruises. Bogdanov (October 2011) had lip/eye/ear/limb hematomas and bruises. Kalinin (March 2012) had a swollen cheek plus face/limb/groin bruises. Father and son Onipenko (September 2015) had body/limb bruises, neck/body abrasions, and an eye haemorrhage; forensics attributed these to blunt objects (excluding shocks in one report).

Applicants promptly complained to investigators or prosecutors. Inquiries proved ineffective, featuring repeated refusals to open criminal cases (often 5–21+ per applicant). Refusals relied mainly on officers’ denials of force, attributing injuries instead to pre-arrest fights/falls (sometimes while intoxicated), self-infliction, resistance, or unrelated events. Many refusals were quashed by superiors as incomplete, premature, or deficient, prompting similar new refusals. Courts typically dismissed applicants’ appeals, endorsing investigators’ reasoning (e.g., Botov in 2007; others through 2017). Occasional court findings of shortcomings (e.g., Fedorov: failure to query experts on injury causation or clarify arrest reasons) were not fully remedied. In Bogdanov, a trial court in related criminal proceedings deemed injuries insignificant and pre-arrest. In Kalinin, a case opened against one officer only for unlawful detention, not ill-treatment. Some applicants retracted complaints (citing fear), which investigators cited.

Domestic law prohibits torture/ill-treatment and requires prompt, effective complaint investigations; police rules mandate reporting detainees’ visible injuries. The facts show a pattern of custody violence for confessions, backed by medical evidence, met by superficial probes that privileged police accounts over forensic/other data.

The joined applications in Avdyukov and Others v. Russia concern multiple Russian nationals arrested between 2005 and 2015 on suspicion of various crimes (robbery, murder, and others) in different regions. They alleged police ill-treatment, primarily beatings to extract confessions, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture/inhuman treatment), including both the acts themselves and ineffective subsequent investigations. One applicant also raised an unrecorded detention issue.

Avdyukov was arrested on 29 November 2005 in Yekaterinburg, allegedly beaten and suffocated with a gas mask overnight; he attempted suicide by jumping from a window. A doctor recorded a head bruise and forearm cuts. On 18 May 2006, he was again arrested, allegedly beaten, given electric shocks, suffocated, and burned on the palms; he again tried to jump from a window. Hospital examination showed facial hematomas and eyelid swelling. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal cases, attributing injuries to suicide attempts or resistance and concluding no force was used. Courts upheld these refusals. A prosecutor separately found 13 hours of unrecorded detention unlawful; the sentencing court noted the arrest-record breach.

Zakalyayev was arrested on 1 August 2008 in the Rostov Region. On 3 August, during questioning, officers allegedly punched his ribs and beat his head with a water-filled bottle, causing a fractured seventh rib diagnosed on 5 August. Investigators refused to open a case, citing officers’ denials and claiming pre-arrest injuries from a fight. The trial court (convicting him) and appeal courts dismissed the claims.

Garmashov was arrested on 19 December 2007 in Novorossiysk at a flat and allegedly beaten at the station. He requested an ambulance on 22 December, diagnosed with craniocerebral injury, concussion, and cheekbone contusion. A forensic exam on 24 December found bruises on face, body, and hands consistent with blunt trauma 6–8 days earlier. Multiple refusals to investigate cited his statement (allegedly coerced) that injuries predated arrest. The convicting court found witness evidence of no pre-arrest injuries unreliable.

Kolykhalov, aged 17, was arrested on 9 October 2007 in Kemerovo, allegedly beaten with a stick and threatened with rape overnight. A forensic exam on 11 October recorded extensive bruises (face, head, limbs, buttocks) and kidney contusion from blunt trauma. Investigators issued repeated refusals (some quashed as incomplete), claiming lawful force due to resistance. Courts dismissed appeals. He was later detained on remand from 2008 until acquittal in 2013; a 2015 civil judgment awarded compensation for unlawful prosecution and poor detention conditions.

Fomin’s flat was searched on 17 December 2010 in Moscow; officers allegedly handcuffed and beat him, continuing in a car and at a detention facility. A remand-prison exam showed scapular bruises and a dislocated right shoulder. Forensic analysis confirmed blunt-trauma bruises. Investigators refused to open a case, citing resistance; courts (including at conviction) upheld this.

Yepifanov was arrested on 15 March 2012 near his home by drug-control officers who allegedly kicked and punched him (no resistance claimed); further punches occurred at the station. Hospital exam showed a right-eye hematoma and chest contusion. A criminal inquiry into abuse of power was opened then terminated, citing officers’ resistance reports and concluding the applicant sought to evade responsibility. Courts dismissed appeals.

The Tyurin brothers were arrested on 28 January 2013 in Astrakhan by a rapid-response unit and allegedly beaten for confessions. Medical exams recorded closed craniocerebral injuries, concussion, a jaw fracture (one brother), and multiple bruises/abrasions from blunt trauma. Investigators refused a case, finding force lawful due to resistance; courts agreed.

Shcherbakov was arrested on 8 February 2015 in Primorskiy Region and allegedly ill-treated at the station. A 10 February forensic exam found facial/ear/knee abrasions (recent) and chest abrasions/shoulder bruises (up to four days old) from blunt objects. Investigators refused a case, attributing injuries to a pre-arrest fight; the convicting court agreed.

Prisyazhnyy alleged beatings, plastic-bag suffocation, and arm-twisting on 14 January 2014 in Primorskiy Region, then further beating by convoy officers on 26 February (while taken from remand prison for questioning). Hospital exam showed concussion, nasal fracture, and contusions. Repeated refusals cited officers’ denials or claimed self-inflicted injuries (hitting a wall while attempting escape) and proportional force. Courts largely upheld the refusals.

Across the cases, medical records often aligned temporally with detention, yet inquiries relied on officers’ accounts, attributed injuries elsewhere, and were frequently incomplete. Domestic courts routinely dismissed the allegations, often in conjunction with criminal convictions.

The European Court of Human Rights case Avdyukov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 33373/07 and 9 others) involves ten Russian nationals arrested between 2005 and 2015 on suspicion of various crimes in different regions. They alleged police ill-treatment (beatings, suffocation, electric shocks, burns, and threats) during arrest, transport, questioning, or detention, often to extract confessions, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. Medical records consistently documented injuries consistent with blunt trauma shortly after the events.

Avdyukov was arrested in Yekaterinburg on 29 November 2005, beaten and suffocated with a gas mask overnight; he attempted suicide by jumping from a window. A doctor recorded a head bruise and forearm cuts. On 18 May 2006 he was again arrested, beaten, electrocuted, suffocated, and burned with a cigarette; he again tried to jump from a window. Hospital records showed facial hematomas and eyelid swelling. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal cases, attributing injuries to self-inflicted attempts to evade responsibility or resistance; courts upheld the refusals. Unrecorded detention of 13 hours was also noted.

Zakalyayev was arrested in the Rostov Region on 1 August 2008. During questioning on 3 August he was punched in the ribs and beaten with a water-filled bottle, resulting in a seventh-rib fracture confirmed on 5 August. Investigators refused to open a case, citing a pre-arrest fight; the trial court dismissed the allegations.

Garmashov was arrested on 19 December 2007 in Novorossiysk. He alleged beatings at the station to obtain a confession. On 22 December he was diagnosed with a craniocerebral injury, concussion and cheekbone contusion; a forensic report recorded bruises inflicted 6–8 days earlier. Investigators issued multiple refusals relying on his earlier statement that injuries predated arrest; courts rejected appeals.

Kolykhalov, then 17, was arrested on 9 October 2007 in Kemerovo. Officers allegedly beat him with a wooden stick and threatened rape until morning. A forensic report of 11 October documented extensive bruises on face, body and limbs plus kidney contusion. Investigators issued eight refusals, claiming lawful use of force against resistance; courts dismissed appeals. He later received civil compensation for unlawful prosecution and poor detention conditions after acquittal.

Fomin’s Moscow flat was searched on 17 December 2010; officers allegedly beat him while handcuffed, continuing in the car and at a detention facility. Remand-prison records showed scapular bruises and a dislocated shoulder. Investigators refused to open a case, citing resistance; courts convicted him, rejecting the ill-treatment claim.

Yepifanov was arrested on 15 March 2012 in Mari El. He claimed he did not resist yet was kicked and punched; at the station he was punched at least 15 times. Hospital records showed a right-eye hematoma and chest contusion. A criminal inquiry into abuse of power was opened then terminated; investigators attributed injuries to lawful force against resistance. Courts upheld the termination.

The Tyurin brothers were arrested by a special rapid-response unit in Astrakhan on 28 January 2013 and allegedly beaten to obtain confessions. Medical cards recorded closed craniocerebral injuries and concussions; forensic reports documented bruises, abrasions and a jaw fracture. Investigators refused to open a case, finding lawful force against resistance; courts dismissed appeals.

Shcherbakov was arrested in the Primorskiy Region on 8 February 2015. A forensic report of 10 February recorded facial, ear, knee and chest abrasions plus shoulder bruises inflicted by a blunt object. Investigators attributed injuries to a pre-arrest fight; the trial court rejected the allegations.

Prisyazhnyy was arrested on 14 January 2014 in the Primorskiy Region, allegedly beaten, suffocated with a plastic bag and had his arms twisted. On 26 February 2014 convoy officers allegedly beat him again. Hospital records showed concussion, nasal fracture and contusions. Multiple refusals followed, citing no force used or proportional force after an escape attempt; courts dismissed appeals.

In all cases domestic inquiries were incomplete or one-sided, relying primarily on police statements while medical evidence of injuries coinciding with police custody was disregarded. The pattern of repeated refusals, often quashed then reissued on the same grounds, formed the core of the alleged investigative failures.

The case of Avdyukov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 33373/07 and nine others) concerns complaints by Russian nationals of police ill-treatment upon arrest (and ineffective investigations thereof) between 2005 and 2015, primarily under Article 3 of the Convention. The applicants were arrested on suspicion of various crimes (including robbery and murder) in different regions and taken to police stations.

Medical examination recorded a head bruise and forearm cuts. On 18 May 2006 he was again arrested, allegedly beaten, given electric shocks, suffocated, and burned on the palms (again attempting to jump from a window). Examination showed facial hematomas and eyelid swelling. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal cases, attributing injuries to suicide attempts or resistance; courts upheld these. A prosecutor later found his 29 November detention unrecorded for 13 hours.

Zakalyayev, arrested on 1 August 2008, alleged being punched in the ribs and beaten with a water-filled bottle during questioning on 3 August, resulting in a fractured seventh rib. Investigators refused to open a case, citing a pre-arrest fight; courts upheld this.

Garmashov, arrested on 19 December 2007, alleged beatings to extract a confession. He was diagnosed with craniocerebral injury, concussion and cheekbone contusion, plus bruises. Multiple refusals to open a case (later quashed as incomplete) relied on his forensic statement of a pre-arrest fight (which he claimed was coerced); courts dismissed his complaints.

Kolykhalov (then 17), arrested on 9 October 2007, alleged beatings with a wooden stick and rape threats overnight. Forensic examination showed extensive bruises and kidney contusion. Investigators issued (and courts largely upheld) repeated refusals, citing resistance during arrest. He was later detained on remand until acquittal in 2013, with subsequent civil compensation for unlawful prosecution and poor conditions.

Fomin alleged beatings during a 17 December 2010 flat search, in a car and at a detention facility, causing scapular bruises and a dislocated shoulder. Investigators refused to open a case (once quashed), citing resistance; a trial court dismissed the allegations.

Yepifanov, arrested on 15 March 2012, alleged kicks and punches despite no resistance, producing an eye hematoma and chest contusion. A criminal case for abuse of power was opened then terminated, citing resistance; courts upheld this.

The Tyurin brothers, arrested on 28 January 2013, alleged beatings for a confession, causing concussion (and a jaw fracture for one). Investigators refused to open a case, citing lawful force against resistance; courts dismissed appeals.

Shcherbakov, arrested on 8 February 2015, alleged station ill-treatment producing abrasions and bruises. Investigators concluded injuries predated arrest in a fight; a trial court dismissed the claim.

Prisyazhnyy alleged beatings, plastic-bag suffocation and arm-twisting on 14 January 2014, plus further beatings by convoy officers on 26 February (causing concussion, nasal fracture and contusions). Investigators issued multiple refusals (some quashed), citing no force or self-inflicted/proportional injuries from escape attempts.

In all cases, domestic inquiries relied on officers’ denials or resistance claims, without thorough investigation, despite medical evidence of injuries consistent with the allegations. (Word count: 512)

The case of Krebs v. Germany (Application no. 68556/13) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the presumption of innocence. The applicant, Reiner Krebs (born 1979), a German national, was convicted on 9 August 2010 by the Weiden District Court of 25 counts of fraud in conjunction with 22 counts of forgery of data. He had ordered documents and services online under a false name, using another person’s bank details. He received a global sentence of 10 months’ imprisonment, which was not suspended on probation owing to an unfavourable prognosis of reoffending, based on his prior similar convictions and the fact that the offences occurred while he was already on probation. Both the applicant and the public prosecutor appealed, later limiting the appeals to the sentence only.

In February and April 2011, new criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant following further complaints of fraud. On 17 June 2011 police searched his home and seized evidence. During oral hearings before the Weiden Regional Court on 7 and 21 June 2011, police officer P., who was investigating the new allegations, testified that items ordered fraudulently online using a fake identity had been delivered to and seized at the applicant’s address. The applicant, through counsel, declined to comment, stating he could not remember the events.

On 21 June 2011 the Regional Court dismissed the appeals. In its sentencing assessment it declared that it had “no doubt” the applicant had committed further fraud offences after the first-instance conviction. It relied on P.’s “credible” and “objective” testimony and treated the seizure of the goods at the applicant’s property as proof that he was “once more guilty of several offences of fraud.” The court therefore refused to suspend the 10-month term, citing the applicant’s reoffending during psychotherapy and while the appeal was pending as evidence of “a high degree of obstinacy.”

The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that these statements breached the presumption of innocence because he had not been finally convicted of the later offences and had denied them. The public prosecutor countered that domestic law permitted a court to consider subsequent offences if it had heard evidence and was itself convinced of guilt. On 11 January 2012 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal; a subsequent complaint of a violation of the right to be heard was also rejected. The 10-month sentence became final.

The applicant was formally indicted for the further frauds on 20 February 2012. On 16 August 2012 the Weiden District Court convicted him of, inter alia, 10 counts of fraud and 5 counts of forgery (including the offences mentioned by the Regional Court). After hearing witnesses he confessed. A new global sentence of 18 months’ imprisonment was imposed, incorporating the earlier 10-month term; it was not suspended because of his criminal record. The applicant withdrew his appeal and the judgment became final on 18 December 2012. A constitutional complaint against the original 10-month sentence was declined without reasons by the Federal Constitutional Court on 31 July 2013.

The core of the alleged violation lay in the Regional Court’s unambiguous declarations of guilt concerning offences that remained the subject of separate, pending proceedings. Those statements, made while the applicant remained silent on the new charges, were used to refuse suspension of the first sentence. Subsequent observance of due-process formalities in the later trial could not, in the applicant’s view, retroactively cure the earlier infringement of the presumption of innocence.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered its judgment in Krebs v. Germany (application no. 68556/13) on 20 February 2020 (final on 20 June 2020). The German applicant, Reiner Krebs (born 1979), alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention (fair trial and presumption of innocence). The core issue was the Weiden Regional Court’s unambiguous statements, during sentencing on appeal from an earlier conviction, declaring him guilty of further untried fraud offences then pending in separate proceedings.

On 9 August 2010 the Weiden District Court convicted Krebs of 25 counts of fraud combined with 22 counts of forgery of data. He had ordered goods and services online under a false name, using another person’s bank details. He received a global sentence of 10 months’ imprisonment. The court declined to suspend the sentence on probation, citing an unfavourable prognosis of reoffending based on his prior similar convictions and the fact that he had committed the offences while already on probation. Both Krebs and the prosecutor appealed, later restricting the appeals to the sentence alone.

In February and April 2011 new investigations were opened after additional complaints of fraud. On 17 June 2011 police searched Krebs’s home and seized items ordered online under a false identity. At the Regional Court’s appeal hearings on 7 and 21 June 2011, police officer P. (leading the new inquiry) testified about the fresh accusations and the seized items. Krebs, through counsel, declined to comment, stating he could not remember the events.

On 21 June 2011 the Regional Court dismissed the appeals and confirmed the 10-month sentence. In assessing whether to suspend it, the court stated it had “no doubt” that Krebs had committed further frauds after the first-instance conviction. It relied on P.’s “credible” testimony, found “no doubt” that Krebs was responsible, and declared that delivery and seizure of the fraudulently ordered goods at his address “proved” he was “once more guilty of several offences of fraud.” The court further remarked that Krebs had “reoffended” while in psychotherapy and shortly before the appeal hearing, demonstrating “a high degree of obstinacy.” These findings formed the basis for the unfavourable prognosis and the refusal of probation.

Krebs appealed on points of law, arguing that the statements breached the presumption of innocence because the further offences remained unadjudicated and he had denied them. The public prosecutor countered that domestic law permitted a court to take subsequent offences into account for sentencing if it heard evidence and was itself convinced of guilt. On 11 January 2012 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal rejected the appeal; a subsequent hearing complaint was also dismissed. The sentence became final.

Krebs was formally indicted on the new charges on 20 February 2012. On 16 August 2012 the Weiden District Court convicted him of 10 counts of fraud (plus related forgeries), including the offences referred to by the Regional Court. He confessed after witnesses testified. A new global sentence of 18 months (incorporating the earlier individual sentences) was imposed and not suspended. That judgment became final in December 2012. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear a constitutional complaint against the original 10-month sentence.

The Court of Human Rights later held that the Regional Court’s categorical declarations of guilt concerning pending charges, made while deciding on probation, violated the presumption of innocence. Krebs’s decision not to comment and the Regional Court’s observance of certain procedural formalities could not cure the breach.

The case of Krebs v. Germany (Application no. 68556/13) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by German national Reiner Krebs on 15 October 2013. Krebs alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention, specifically the presumption of innocence, arising from statements made by a German criminal court during sentencing in one set of proceedings that declared him guilty of further offences still pending in separate proceedings.

On 9 August 2010, the Weiden District Court convicted Krebs of 25 counts of fraud in conjunction with 22 counts of forgery of data. He had ordered documents and services online under a false name while providing another person's bank details for payment. The court imposed a global sentence of 10 months' imprisonment, which it declined to suspend on probation. This decision rested on an unfavourable prognosis regarding the risk of reoffending, taking into account Krebs's prior convictions for similar offences and the fact that he had committed the frauds while already on probation. Both Krebs and the public prosecutor appealed, later limiting the appeals to the question of sentence.

In February and April 2011, new criminal investigations were opened against Krebs following additional complaints of fraudulent behaviour. On 17 June 2011 police searched his home and seized items linked to the new accusations. During oral hearings before the Weiden Regional Court on 7 and 21 June 2011, police officer P., who was leading the new investigations, testified that items ordered online under a fake identity had been delivered to Krebs's address and seized there. Krebs, through his lawyer, declined to comment on the new charges, stating that he could not remember anything.

In its judgment of 21 June 2011 the Regional Court dismissed the appeals and confirmed the 10-month sentence. When assessing whether the sentence could be suspended, the court stated that it had “no doubt” Krebs had committed further frauds after the first-instance conviction, relying on P.'s “credible” testimony. It declared that “it has been proven that the accused is once more guilty of several offences of fraud.” The court further observed that Krebs had reoffended while undergoing psychotherapy and despite the impending appeal hearing, describing this as evidence of “a high degree of obstinacy.” These findings were decisive in refusing suspension.

Krebs appealed on points of law, arguing that the Regional Court's unambiguous declarations of guilt in respect of unconvicted offences breached the presumption of innocence. The public prosecutor countered that domestic law permitted a court to consider subsequent offences if it had heard evidence and was itself convinced of guilt. On 11 January 2012 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, endorsing the prosecutor's position; the 10-month sentence thereby became final.

Krebs was formally indicted for the additional frauds on 20 February 2012. On 16 August 2012 the Weiden District Court convicted him of, inter alia, 10 counts of fraud (including those previously referred to by the Regional Court) after he confessed following witness testimony. A new global sentence of 18 months' imprisonment was imposed, incorporating the earlier 10-month term; suspension was again refused on the basis of his overall criminal record. Krebs withdrew his appeal and the judgment became final on 18 December 2012. On 31 July 2013 the Federal Constitutional Court declined, without reasons, to consider his constitutional complaint against the original 10-month sentence.

The core of the alleged violation thus lay in the Regional Court's explicit findings of guilt concerning pending charges—findings that were not merely incidental but directly motivated the refusal to suspend the sentence—while those charges remained the subject of separate, unfinished proceedings in which Krebs had exercised his right to silence.
001-201648:
The applicant, a Swedish national born in 1961, and his Romanian wife have three sons: A (born 2000), B (born 2005) and C (born 2007). The family moved to Norway in 2013. On 4 November 2013, child welfare services issued emergency care orders for all three children under section 4-6 of the Child Welfare Act, following reports from health personnel, school services and social insurance authorities. Concerns centred on A's health (possible Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or EDS), the children's isolation, lack of social stimulation and pathologisation of their conditions. The children were placed in emergency foster homes that day (B and C together). Interim contact was set at twice monthly for one supervised hour.

The parents' appeals were dismissed. On 16 December 2013, services applied to the County Social Welfare Board for care orders, undisclosed foster placements, removal of parental responsibilities and supervised contact. After a February 2014 hearing, the Board (24 February 2014) issued care orders for all three children, with contact four times yearly for 1.5 hours (supervised). Parental responsibilities were retained and foster-home locations disclosed.

The Board found serious neglect stemming from the parents' (especially the mother's) excessive focus on illness. This inflicted psychosomatic problems and anxiety on A, whose life centred on pain, rest and passivity, rendering him "heavily disabled" beyond any EDS effects; he lacked social interaction and held mother-derived beliefs (e.g., he could die or could not attend school). B and C showed unusual attitudes to illness/pain, language/pronunciation difficulties, poor self-care routines, academic/social shortcomings and claims of EDS symptoms, though they interacted well with the applicant. The applicant could provide practical care but failed to recognise the burden of the family's lifestyle or set boundaries. Assistance measures were impossible due to parents' distrust of services, lack of insight and rejection of differing medical views. Care-order criteria (section 4-12) were met, with placements expected to be prolonged.

The District Court (3 July 2014) upheld the orders after hearings, reducing A's contact to twice yearly. It confirmed A's abnormal development and preoccupation with illness (regardless of EDS), and B/C's pre-care deficits versus post-placement progress (no illness issues, better hygiene/self-care).

On appeal, a court-appointed psychologist reported (31 May 2015) that all children had significant unmet needs from prior inadequate care and parents' insistence that problems were solely somatic or placement-related. Assistance was unfeasible; contact should be rare and controlled. A needed psychiatric assessment in a challenging, trusting environment. B showed physical/emotional/language/self-assertion issues linked to early care. C (least affected) had language/emotional-regulation difficulties possibly tied to placement uncertainty.

The High Court (2 July 2015; three judges, psychologist, layperson) heard evidence including the children, experts and witnesses. It found (with doubt) that section 4-12 criteria were unmet: parental capacity was hard to assess after prolonged separation; no expert had examined the original home situation; a Swedish court had earlier found no harm to A. A's challenging health (now including wheelchair use and possible psychiatric issues) and parents' possible over-focus were understandable given services' disagreement on EDS/Munchausen suspicions. For A, care was unnecessary; home assistance (now feasible with clarified diagnoses and parental cooperation) plus his wish to return would be in his interests. For B and C (now 10 and 8), however, nearly a year in a joint foster home (after emergency placement) created attachment; their representative and expert noted they were happy, secure and progressing socially/academically/hygienically. Return risked serious long-term harm. Parents would be overburdened caring for A. Children's views carried limited weight given their vulnerability. Placement continued (per section 4-21 logic); contact was six times yearly for six supervised hours (to preserve biological ties, with possible later expansion). The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal (15 September 2015).

These facts underpin the Article 8 complaint concerning long-term foster care of B and C with limited contact.

The case of Hernehult v. Norway (Application no. 14652/16) concerned a Swedish national’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that Norwegian child-welfare authorities had violated his right to respect for family life by placing two of his three sons in long-term foster care and severely restricting contact.

The applicant (born 1961) and his Romanian wife had three sons: A (born 2000), B (born 2005) and C (born 2007). The family relocated to Norway in 2013. On 4 November 2013 the child-welfare service issued emergency care orders for all three children after reports from health, school and social-insurance services raised concerns about A’s health (possible Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) and the parents’ overall care. The children were described as isolated, under-stimulated and subject to “pathologisation.” They were placed in emergency foster homes (B and C together). Supervised contact was initially set at two hours per month.

The County Social Welfare Board, after a hearing in February 2014, issued care orders for all three children under section 4-12 of the Child Welfare Act. It found serious neglect stemming from the parents’ (especially the mother’s) intense focus on illness, which had inflicted psychosomatic problems and abnormal development on A and, indirectly, on B and C. The applicant was judged incapable of setting boundaries or recognising the harm caused by the family’s lifestyle. Assistance measures in the home were deemed unfeasible because of the parents’ distrust of services and lack of insight. Contact was reduced to four sessions of 1½ hours per year, supervised. Parental responsibility was not removed and the foster homes’ locations were disclosed.

The District Court upheld the care orders in July 2014, further restricting contact with A to twice yearly. A court-appointed psychologist’s 2015 report concluded that all three boys had significant unmet needs arising from prior inadequate care and the parents’ insistence that problems were solely somatic. Contact, she recommended, should remain infrequent and tightly controlled.

On appeal the High Court (July 2015) found, albeit with doubt, that the statutory criteria for a care order under section 4-12 had not been proved. No expert had examined the original home situation, the family had previously lived in Sweden where a court had found no harm to A, and assistance measures had never been properly tried before the emergency orders. For A the High Court considered a care order unnecessary; with diagnoses now clearer, extensive home-based assistance was feasible, A was unhappy in institutional care and wished to return, and reunification was in his best interests.

For B and C, however, the High Court refused to discontinue care. By then they had lived nearly a year in the same foster home, showed positive development in schooling, hygiene and social skills, and appeared settled. Returning them would create a real risk of long-term harm. The parents would already face a heavy burden caring for A. Contact with B and C was fixed at six supervised six-hour sessions per year, intended merely to preserve knowledge of biological roots. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee refused leave to appeal.

The European Court later held that these procedures contained insufficiencies that called into question the justification for the original placement of B and C, that the subsequent decisions had served only to strengthen their attachment to the foster home, and that the authorities had failed to make genuine efforts to keep the family together or to consider reunification.

The case of Hernehult v. Norway (Application no. 14652/16) concerns a Swedish national, Dan Mikael Hernehult (born 1961), who, with his Romanian wife, had three sons: A (born 2000), B (born 2005) and C (born 2007). The family relocated to Norway in 2013. On 4 November 2013 the child welfare service issued emergency care orders for all three boys under section 4-6 of the Child Welfare Act, following reports from health personnel, school services and social insurance authorities. The reports highlighted serious concerns over A’s health (his mother’s preoccupation with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome/EDS, pathologisation, isolation and lack of social stimuli) and the parents’ general care of the children. B and C were placed together in an emergency foster home; A was later moved to an institution. Supervised contact was initially set at twice monthly for one hour. Appeals were dismissed.

On 24 February 2014 the County Social Welfare Board issued full care orders. It found serious neglect arising from the parents’ intense focus on illness (especially the mother’s impact on A, who displayed abnormal psychological development, anxiety and severely reduced functioning). The applicant was judged unable to recognise the burden this imposed or to set boundaries. Assistance measures in the home were deemed unfeasible because of the parents’ distrust of services and lack of insight. Contact was reduced to four times a year for 1.5 hours, supervised. Parental responsibilities were not stripped. The District Court upheld the orders in July 2014.

An expert psychologist appointed for the High Court appeal reported in May 2015 that all three boys had significant, unmet care needs linked to prior unsatisfactory parenting, isolation and pathologisation; the parents lacked insight and insisted problems were purely somatic or caused by the placements themselves. Contact should therefore be infrequent and tightly controlled.

In its 2 July 2015 judgment the High Court (sitting with an expert lay judge) expressed doubt that the original statutory criteria for care orders (section 4-12) had been met. No expert assessment of the pre-placement home situation existed; a Swedish court had earlier found no harm to A; and no in-home assistance measures had been tried before the emergency orders. For A the Court ordered return with extensive support, noting his unhappiness in care and wish to go home. For B (then 10) and C (then 8), however, who had lived together in a foster home for nearly a year after emergency placement, the Court held that they had formed a strong attachment. Return would risk serious long-term harm (section 4-21). Their positive development in foster care (schooling, social skills, daily routines) weighed against reunification. The parents’ anticipated burden of caring for A rendered caring for all three unfeasible. Placement was therefore expected to be long-term. Contact was set at six times a year for six hours, supervised, solely to preserve biological roots and possible later attachment, taking account of the brothers’ mutual longing. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 8 violation: emergency removal without prior less-intrusive measures, procedural shortcomings that prevented proper assessment of the original family situation, and subsequent decisions that entrenched the children’s attachment to foster carers, thereby rendering reunification impossible and converting a temporary protective measure into de facto permanent separation with only token contact. The authorities thereby failed to take reasonable steps to keep the family together or to keep open the possibility of reunion.
001-201890:
The case of Pendov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 44229/11) concerned the seizure and prolonged retention of a computer server belonging to Bulgarian national Lazar Milkov Pendov. The facts relevant to the alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights arose in the context of a copyright-infringement investigation against third parties.

In 2010 a publishing house complained to police that one of its books had been uploaded online without authorisation, an offence under Article 172a of the Criminal Code. Inquiries established that the infringing site was partially hosted on a server owned by the applicant. That server also hosted several other sites, including a Japanese-anime website that the applicant himself owned and administered. The anime site had been operating for more than four years and attracted 500–600 daily visitors; it offered a forum, chat service and image-hosting facilities.

On 18 June 2010 a Sofia District Court judge issued a search warrant after finding sufficient grounds that evidence relevant to the investigation would be found at the premises where the server was kept. Police executed the warrant on 21 June 2010, seizing the server. The applicant was not present and received neither a copy of the warrant nor the search-and-seizure record. He was interviewed two days later.

From 23 July 2010 onwards the applicant repeatedly asked the Sofia district prosecutor’s office to return the server, invoking Article 111 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He argued that any data needed for the investigation of third parties could be copied, after which the hardware should be released. He stressed that his own site had gone offline, damaging his reputation among users and colleagues, causing financial loss and wasting years of personal and financial investment. Later submissions added that the server stored users’ private correspondence and copyrighted material, and that its continued detention therefore also interfered with privacy and copyright interests. Similar letters were sent to the Chief Public Prosecutor.

An expert examination was commissioned on 29 June 2010 to determine whether the server had hosted the infringing site and, if so, to copy the relevant files. The examination never took place. On 6 August 2010 the Sofia proceedings were discontinued after it emerged that a parallel investigation into the same facts had already been opened in Troyan. The Sofia decision merely noted that the physical evidence would be placed at the disposal of the Troyan prosecutor. Subsequent correspondence revealed that neither office knew the server’s whereabouts.

On 27 July he launched a “minimal” version assembled from old archives; the substitute server had “very limited capacity,” so the forum, chat and image-hosting functions were unavailable. Full functionality was restored only after the original server was returned, but the site never regained its former popularity and its chat service was later abandoned.

Bulgaria (ECtHR, Application no. 44229/11, judgment of 26 March 2020) concerned the seizure and prolonged retention of a computer server belonging to the applicant, Lazar Milkov Pendov, a Bulgarian national. The case originated in an application by two Bulgarian nationals, Krastyo Chorbadzhiyski and his daughter Desislava Krasteva, concerning excessive court fees imposed after they succeeded in part of a damages claim against the State. The first applicant later died, and the second continued the proceedings on her own behalf and as his heir.

On 29 August 1998, the first applicant’s wife (the second applicant’s mother) died when a tree branch fell during a storm. In August 2003 the applicants sued the State, Plovdiv Municipality and two private individuals under the State Liability for Damage Caused to Citizens Act 1988. They claimed BGN 2 million (approximately EUR 1.02 million) in non-pecuniary damages and BGN 200,000 in pecuniary damages. Under the 1988 Act no court fees were payable in advance; fees were levied only on any dismissed portion of a claim and calculated as a percentage of that portion.

The Plovdiv Regional Court dismissed the claims in 2004 and ordered the applicants to pay BGN 88,000 in fees (4 % of the total sum claimed). On appeal the Plovdiv Court of Appeal re-characterised the claim against the municipality as an ordinary tort action under the Obligations and Contracts Act 1951 rather than a claim under the 1988 Act, discontinued proceedings against the State, and remitted the case. After further appeals, the Plovdiv Court of Appeal in 2008 awarded each applicant BGN 50,000 (total BGN 100,000) plus interest for non-pecuniary damage, holding that the original claims had been excessive. Because fees had not been paid in advance, it then ordered the applicants jointly to pay BGN 126,000 in court fees (4 % of the dismissed amount at first instance plus 2 % on appeal). The Supreme Court of Cassation upheld the award of damages in 2010.

The applicants sought to have the fee order varied, relying on the Court’s earlier judgment in Stankov v. Bulgaria, which had led to a 2008 amendment of the 1988 Act replacing percentage-based fees with modest flat fees and requiring the State to bear costs when a claim succeeded in whole or in part. Domestic courts refused, holding that the claim had been re-characterised as an ordinary tort action, that statutory percentage fees were mandatory and not subject to judicial discretion, and that the special procedure for amending costs orders did not apply to court fees. After the municipality paid the compensation plus interest, the applicants were compelled to pay the fees plus interest, leaving them with a net recovery of approximately BGN 121,126.

The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the fees, which exceeded half the compensation awarded, impaired their right of access to court. They also invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13. The Court examined the complaints primarily under Article 6 § 1, focusing on the lack of foreseeability of the fees (arising from the unexpected re-characterisation of the claim), the automatic application of rigid percentage rules without regard to the Stankov judgment or to the modest amounts actually awarded, the absence of any effective domestic safeguard or exemption, and the striking disparity between the fees payable in ordinary tort proceedings and those payable under the amended 1988 Act for identical services. These features rendered the fees disproportionate and unforeseeable, thereby violating the right of access to a court.

The applicants then paid the fees plus interest (approximately BGN 73,000 / EUR 37,500 each). After these payments their net recovery was BGN 121,125.64 (EUR 61,931), or BGN 60,562.82 (EUR 30,966) each—less than half the compensation awarded.

The applicants, Bulgarian nationals Krastyo Chorbadzhiyski and his daughter Desislava Krasteva, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention of a violation of their right of access to court due to excessive court fees imposed after a partially successful damages claim against the State.

In 1998, Chorbadzhiyski’s wife (Krasteva’s mother) died when a tree branch fell on her during a storm. In 2003, the applicants sued the State, Plovdiv Municipality and two individuals under the 1988 State Liability for Damage Caused to Citizens Act, claiming BGN 2 million in non-pecuniary damages and BGN 200,000 in pecuniary damages. The first-instance court dismissed the claims in 2004 as the death was accidental and the amounts excessive, ordering the applicants to pay BGN 88,000 in court fees (4% of the total claimed).

On appeal in 2006, the Plovdiv Court of Appeal discontinued proceedings against the State (which lacked standing), dismissed the claim against the individuals, recharacterised the claim against the municipality as one under general tort law (as tree maintenance was not administrative activity under the 1988 Act), remitted the case and quashed the fees order. The Supreme Court of Cassation in 2007 directed the appeal court to examine the claims itself rather than remitting them.

In 2008 the Plovdiv Court of Appeal awarded each applicant BGN 50,000 (total BGN 100,000) plus interest for non-pecuniary damage, finding the remainder of the claims excessive. It ordered the applicants to pay BGN 126,000 jointly in court fees (4% of the dismissed BGN 2.1 million at first instance plus 2% on appeal), as the statutory fees had not been paid upfront. The applicants’ cassation appeal was time-barred. The municipality’s cassation appeal was admitted only on the merits; the Supreme Court of Cassation in 2010 upheld the award, noting that the fees issue (raised as a procedural question) would not alter the outcome because the dismissal of most of the claim was already final.

The applicants then sought to vary the fees order under Article 248 of the 2007 Code of Civil Procedure, relying on Stankov v. Bulgaria (2007), after which the 1988 Act had been amended to impose only modest flat fees (payable upfront) and to require the defendant to reimburse fees and costs if a claim succeeded even in part. Two successive three-judge panels of the Supreme Court of Cassation refused in 2010–2011. They held that Article 248 applied only to expenses (not statutory court fees, which courts had no discretion to reduce) and that the claim had been recharacterised as an ordinary tort action, to which the 1988 Act’s special regime did not apply. The rejection of most of the claim was also final.

A writ of execution issued for the BGN 126,000 fees. The municipality paid the applicants a total of BGN 267,869 (awards plus interest from 1998). The applicants then paid the State approximately BGN 146,743 in fees plus interest. Their net recovery was thus BGN 121,126 (about BGN 60,563 each).

Under ordinary civil procedure, claimants must pay court fees of 4% (first instance) and 2% (appeal) of the sum claimed upfront, with reimbursement proportional to success. The original 1988 Act required no upfront fees but, if a claim failed in whole or in part, required the claimant to pay fees calculated on the dismissed portion—even where liability was established—without judicial discretion. After Stankov the 1988 Act was changed to small flat fees and reimbursement by the defendant on partial success. Means-tested exemptions existed under both regimes.

The applicants argued that the fees exceeded half the award, were unforeseeable (because of the recharacterisation and collection only at the end rather than upfront), were applied automatically despite Stankov, and differed markedly from the fees payable for equivalent claims remaining under the 1988 Act, thereby impairing access to court.
001-202116:
**Case of Mazahir Jafarov v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, Application no. 39331/09, judgment of 2 April 2020)**

The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1959, lived in Baku. In 1991 he, his wife, son and daughter occupied a State-owned three-room flat under an occupancy voucher issued by his State-employer. In 1994 he privatised the flat and became sole owner after his then-adult wife waived any ownership claim. All family members nevertheless retained a statutory “right of use” (residence right).

After the couple’s 2007 divorce, relations deteriorated into frequent conflicts; the applicant alleged he was sometimes locked out or insulted and eventually left the flat. In 2008 the former wife sued for a three-quarters ownership share. The applicant counter-claimed under Article 228.2 of the Civil Code for termination of the family’s right of use upon payment of AZN 6 000 to each of the three family members (AZN 18 000 total), asserting that sum would cover comparable alternative accommodation for at least five years.

On 24 July 2008 the Narimanov District Court dismissed both claims. It held the flat was not marital property because it had been allocated from the State housing fund and privatised free of charge. On the counter-claim it cited Article 228.2 and a 2007 Constitutional Court ruling that compensation must enable former family members to obtain “suitable alternative accommodation on a continuous basis and for a certain period of time.” It then simply declared the offered sum “does not correspond to a real market value and is contrary to the mentioned legal acts,” without stating what amount would suffice or examining any market data. Relying on the parties’ alleged failure to produce “reliable evidence,” it rejected the counter-claim as unsubstantiated.

The applicant appealed, complaining that the court had given no reasoned assessment of an adequate figure, had ignored his arguments and evidence, and had failed to appoint an expert. He also submitted a letter from the NGO “Property Market Participants” valuing the monthly rent of two rooms at USD 230 (approximately AZN 187). On 14 October 2008 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, repeating that the proposed compensation was insufficient and adding that the flat had originally been allocated to a family of four, that the occupants had lived there since 1991 and that they had no other housing. It did not mention the NGO letter or explain why the offered sum was inadequate.

The applicant’s cassation appeal repeated that the lower courts had given no reasons for finding the compensation insufficient and had failed to assess the new evidence. On 24 February 2009 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in brief terms, restating that the sum was insufficient and adding—contrary to the text of Article 228.2—that termination was possible only with the users’ agreement.

The applicant alleged that the unreasoned refusals violated Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The domestic courts never quantified an adequate market-based compensation, never explained why AZN 18 000 was inadequate, never addressed the rent valuation he had produced, and never considered appointing an expert, thereby leaving his property-related claim unresolved without a properly reasoned judicial decision.
