The ECHR case Mazahir Jafarov v. Azerbaijan (no. 39331/09) alleges violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property rights) due to unreasoned domestic court refusals to terminate former family members’ residence rights in the applicant’s flat in exchange for compensation.

In 1991 the applicant, his wife, son and daughter occupied a State-owned three-room Baku flat under an employer occupancy voucher. In 1994 he privatised it as sole owner after his adult wife waived any ownership claim; all retained rights of use. After their 2007 divorce, conflicts forced the applicant to leave.

In 2008 the former wife claimed three-quarters ownership. The applicant counterclaimed for termination of the family’s use rights against AZN 6 000 each (AZN 18 000 total), sufficient for five years of comparable rented accommodation.

On 24 July 2008 the Narimanov District Court dismissed both claims. The flat was not marital property (privatised free of charge). Citing Civil Code Art. 228.2 and a 2007 Constitutional Court ruling that compensation must enable “suitable alternative accommodation on a continuous basis and for a certain period,” it held the offered sum did not reflect market value and was contrary to law, without quantifying an adequate figure or examining evidence. Both claims were unsubstantiated for lack of reliable proof.

The applicant appealed, complaining of failure to assess adequate compensation, absence of reasons why his figure was insufficient, and breaches of the right to a reasoned decision and of property rights; he proposed an expert valuation. He later filed an NGO letter estimating monthly rent for two rooms at USD 230.

On 14 October 2008 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, repeating that the sum was inadequate for continuous suitable housing and adding that the flat had been allocated to a family of four, the defendants had lived there since allocation and had no other home. It was silent on the NGO evidence.

The applicant’s cassation appeal reiterated the lack of reasoning and the failure to consider his evidence. On 24 February 2009 the Supreme Court confirmed the lower rulings, adding that, because the family had originally shared housing rights and had consented to privatisation while retaining use, termination required their agreement.

Domestic law (1982 Housing Code Art. 123; 2000 Civil Code Art. 228.2; 2009 Housing Code Art. 30.4) and Constitutional Court decisions (2001, 2007, 2013, 2016) establish that use rights persist after family breakdown unless terminated by court order with market-value compensation sufficient for alternative accommodation of similar standard for a reasonable period. Courts must themselves determine that amount, strike a fair balance between ownership and use, and give reasons.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the courts never calculated an adequate compensation figure, offered no substantiated reasons for rejecting the applicant’s proposal or his evidence (prima facie relevant to market value and duration), and thereby failed to deliver a reasoned, evidence-based decision on a claim that directly affected his property rights.

The case of Mazahir Jafarov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 39331/09) concerned alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1959 and living in Baku, complained of unreasoned domestic court decisions rejecting his request to terminate his former family members’ residence rights in his flat in exchange for compensation.

In 1991, the applicant, his wife, son and daughter took up residence in a State-owned three-room flat allocated via an occupancy voucher from his State-owned employer. In 1994 he privatised the flat and became sole owner after his wife (then the only other adult) waived any ownership claims. All family members nevertheless retained a “right of use” (residence rights). After the couple divorced in 2007, domestic conflicts arose; the applicant was sometimes denied entry or insulted and eventually moved out.

In 2008 the former wife sued in the Narimanov District Court claiming three-quarters ownership of the flat. The applicant lodged a counterclaim seeking termination of the family’s right of use upon payment of AZN 6 000 to each of the three members (AZN 18 000 total), asserting that this sum would suffice for comparable alternative accommodation for at least five years.

On 24 July 2008 the District Court dismissed both claims. It held that the flat was not marital property (having been allocated from the State housing fund and privatised free of charge) and that the wife had voluntarily waived any share. As to the counterclaim it cited Article 228.2 of the Civil Code (allowing judicial termination of a right of use subject to “appropriate compensation at the market price”) and a 2007 Constitutional Court ruling requiring compensation sufficient for “suitable alternative accommodation on a continuous basis and for a certain period of time.” The court then stated, without further analysis or indication of a sufficient figure, that the proposed amount “does not correspond to a real market value and is contrary to the mentioned legal acts.” Invoking provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure on substantiation and evidence, it concluded that neither party had presented reliable evidence and rejected both claims as unsubstantiated.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the court had failed to assess an adequate compensation sum, had given no reasons for deeming his offer insufficient (in breach of domestic law and Article 6), and should have appointed an expert if market-value evidence was lacking. Before the Baku Court of Appeal he submitted a letter from an NGO assessing the monthly market rent for two rooms of the flat at approximately AZN 187.

On 14 October 2008 the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, repeating that the proposed compensation did not reflect real market value and was insufficient for continuous alternative accommodation. It added that the flat had originally been allocated to a family of four, that the defendants had lived there since 1991 and currently had no other housing, but it remained silent on the NGO evidence.

The applicant’s cassation appeal to the Supreme Court reiterated that the lower courts had given no reasons for finding the compensation inadequate and that the appellate court had ignored his evidence without explanation. He again maintained that his offer would cover five years of comparable housing. On 24 February 2009 the Supreme Court upheld the judgments, briefly repeating the finding of insufficiency. It referred to Article 228.2 and the 2007 Constitutional Court decision, then added that, because the family members had retained their rights of use upon consenting to privatisation, termination was possible only with their agreement.

The applicant alleged that the courts’ unreasoned refusal to terminate the right of use, their failure to assess an adequate compensation amount having regard to relevant factors, and their disregard of prima-facie relevant arguments and evidence breached his right to a fair hearing and his property rights.
001-201865:
The case of Cantaragiu v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 13013/11) was brought by Vasile Cantaragiu, a Moldovan national born in 1986, who alleged violations of Articles 2, 3 and 13 of the Convention arising from ill-treatment he and his brother suffered in detention (leading to the brother’s death) and the absence of effective investigations. The applicant, granted legal aid and represented by counsel, lodged the application on 15 February 2011; the Court later accepted his standing to pursue claims on behalf of his deceased brother given the circumstances allegedly engaging State responsibility.

On 29 April 2005 the applicant and his 21-year-old brother (a former junior judo champion) were arrested on suspicion of murder; their father was arrested the following month. All three were held in detention pending trial. On 1 November 2005 the applicant was hospitalised with “decompensated post-contusion syndrome” and subsequently complained of police ill-treatment. A prosecutor declined to open a criminal investigation on 17 May 2007, concluding that no offence had occurred. A “verification file” opened on 10 May 2007 was destroyed in September 2013 after the statutory five-year period.

Meanwhile the brother reported headaches and epigastric pain on 30 October 2005. He received repeated emergency treatment overnight. At approximately 5 a.m. on 1 November an ambulance transferred him, already comatose, to hospital, where he died on 3 November. An autopsy established abdominal trauma causing rupture of the duodenum. On 29 November 2005 prosecutors opened an investigation into possible medical malpractice. They interviewed prison and hospital staff, the emergency doctors (who observed no visible signs of ill-treatment) and co-detainees; no evidence of assault was found. On 25 September 2008 the investigation was suspended because the origin of the rupture could not be established; medical negligence, ill-treatment, self-harm and accident were all deemed unsupported. Subsequent challenges by the father (rejected 2011–2012) and by the applicant (rejected October 2011) failed.

In the parallel murder proceedings the three men were convicted in December 2006 (the brother’s case being discontinued on account of his death). After an extraordinary appeal the Supreme Court of Justice, in December 2010, remitted the case, holding that the applicant, his brother and their father had been ill-treated in detention. The court applied the strong presumption that unexplained injuries to a detainee result from ill-treatment and found that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation, rendering any evidence obtained thereby unusable under Article 6. On rehearing the Chișinău Court of Appeal again convicted the applicant in June 2012, dismissing the ill-treatment claims by reference to the 2008 suspension decision. The Supreme Court’s final judgment of 9 April 2013 upheld the conviction but reiterated that the case file demonstrated ill-treatment of all three men and the absence of an effective investigation, so that self-incriminating statements could not be relied upon.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints that a young, previously healthy detainee died from injuries consistent with ill-treatment for which the State bore responsibility (Article 2 substantive limb), that no adequate investigation into that death was carried out (Article 2 procedural limb), that the applicant himself suffered inhuman and degrading treatment (Article 3 substantive limb), and that the national finding of an Article 3 breach was not followed by any investigation (Article 3 procedural limb).

The case of Cantaragiu v. the Republic of Moldova concerns allegations that the applicant, Vasile Cantaragiu, and his brother suffered ill-treatment in detention, that this caused the brother’s death, and that the authorities failed to investigate effectively. On 29 April 2005 the applicant and his brother were arrested on suspicion of murder; their father was arrested shortly afterwards. While in detention the applicant was admitted to hospital on 1 November 2005 with a diagnosis of decompensated post-contusion syndrome and later complained that the police had ill-treated him. On 17 May 2007 a prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, finding that no offence had been committed. A verification file opened around the same time was destroyed in 2013 after the statutory five-year retention period.

The applicant’s brother, a healthy 21-year-old former junior judo champion, complained on 30 October 2005 of headaches and epigastric pain. He received repeated urgent medical attention overnight. At approximately 5 a.m. on 1 November an emergency team transferred him to hospital in a comatose state; he died there on 3 November. An autopsy established abdominal trauma that had ruptured the duodenum.

On 29 November 2005 prosecutors opened an investigation into possible medical malpractice. They interviewed prison and hospital staff, the emergency-team doctors (who reported seeing no signs of ill-treatment) and co-detainees. The inquiry produced no evidence of ill-treatment. On 25 September 2008 the investigation was suspended because the origin of the duodenal rupture could not be established; medical error, ill-treatment, self-mutilation and accident were all deemed unsupported by the evidence. Subsequent complaints by the applicant’s father were rejected by a superior prosecutor and an investigating judge; the applicant’s own complaint was rejected on 26 October 2011.

In parallel criminal proceedings the three men were convicted of murder in December 2006 (the brother’s case being discontinued on account of his death). After an extraordinary appeal the Supreme Court of Justice, on 14 December 2010, quashed the convictions. It held that the applicant, his brother and their father had been ill-treated in detention, applying the presumption that unexplained injuries suffered by detainees are attributable to the authorities, and that no effective investigation of those allegations had taken place. Evidence obtained through such treatment was therefore inadmissible.

On retrial the Chișinău Court of Appeal reconvicted the applicant (to twelve years’ imprisonment) and discontinued the case against his brother, dismissing the ill-treatment claims by reference to the earlier investigation. In its final judgment of 9 April 2013 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the convictions but expressly confirmed that the case file demonstrated that all three men had been ill-treated and that no effective investigation had been conducted, rendering their self-incriminating statements unusable.

These events form the factual basis of the complaints under Articles 2, 3 and 13 concerning the brother’s death, the applicant’s own ill-treatment, the absence of effective investigations, and the applicant’s standing to pursue the application on his deceased brother’s behalf.

The case of Cantaragiu v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 13013/11) arose from events following the 29 April 2005 arrest of the applicant Vasile Cantaragiu and his 21-year-old brother (a former junior judo champion) on suspicion of murder; their father was arrested the following month. Both brothers later alleged police ill-treatment in detention. On 1 November 2005 the applicant was hospitalised with “decompensated post-contusion syndrome” and subsequently complained of beatings. A prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation on 17 May 2007, concluding that no offence had occurred. A related “verification file” created that month was destroyed in 2013 after five years, pursuant to domestic rules.

The brother first reported severe headaches and epigastric pain on 30 October 2005. Prison staff administered urgent treatment overnight. Around 05:00 on 1 November an emergency team transferred him, already comatose, to hospital, where he died on 3 November. Autopsy established abdominal trauma that had ruptured the duodenum. A criminal inquiry into possible medical malpractice was opened on 29 November 2005. Prosecutors interviewed prison and hospital staff (including the emergency doctors, who reported seeing no signs of violence) and co-detainees; they found no evidence of ill-treatment. The investigation was suspended on 25 September 2008 because the precise cause of the rupture—malpractice, ill-treatment, self-mutilation or accident—could not be established. Challenges by the father and later the applicant were rejected by higher prosecutors and an investigating judge.

In the underlying murder proceedings the three men were convicted in 2006 (the brother’s case being discontinued on account of his death). After an extraordinary appeal, the Supreme Court of Justice in December 2010 quashed the conviction. It held that the applicant, his brother and their father had been subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 while in detention, that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation, and that any evidence obtained through that treatment was inadmissible under Article 6. On rehearing the Chișinău Court of Appeal in June 2012 again convicted the applicant (sentencing him to twelve years) and dismissed the ill-treatment allegations by reference to the suspended 2008 inquiry. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in April 2013 but reiterated that the case file proved the trio had been ill-treated and that no effective investigation had taken place, so their self-incriminating statements could not be relied upon.

The applicant complained under Articles 2 and 3 (substantive and procedural limbs) that his healthy young brother had died from injuries inflicted in detention and that both men had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment, none of which had been properly investigated. He also invoked Article 13. Because the brother had died before the application was lodged, the Court first examined the applicant’s standing under Article 34 to pursue the claims on the deceased’s behalf. The facts thus centred on unexplained abdominal trauma suffered in State custody, a national finding of Article 3 ill-treatment that produced no further inquiry, and the repeated judicial acknowledgements of investigative failings.

The case of Madžarović and Others v. Montenegro (Applications nos. 54839/17 and 71093/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned alleged violations of the right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and unlawful deprivation of property. The applicants were Mihailo Madžarović (a Slovenian national) and two Montenegrin companies he solely founded, owned, and directed (Zetmont d.o.o. and Bermont d.o.o.). These companies were the sole shareholders of company T (the debtor), of which Madžarović was also the legal representative.

In 2006, T borrowed €7.5 million from an Austrian bank, secured by pledges of T's shares in an investment fund. After T defaulted, the bank applied to Montenegro's Commercial Court. In October and November 2013, the court found the pledges valid and T in default (outstanding debt around €3.46 million in one instance), ordering seizure and transfer of the specified shares to the bank under section 20 of the Pledge Act. Appeals did not have suspensive effect. T, represented by Madžarović, appealed the original and rectified decisions, arguing inter alia that the court had relied solely on the Pledge Act (not the Enforcement Act), had not reviewed original pledge contracts, and that the debt (especially interest) remained legally undefined.

The bank sold the shares to company O.B. on 9 January 2014. On 16 January 2014, T's new Board appointed I.P. as executive director (replacing Madžarović); this was registered by the Tax Administration on 20 January 2014. The applicants immediately appealed the registration. On 5 February 2014, I.P. withdrew T's pending appeals and revoked the lawyer's power of attorney (granted by Madžarović). The applicants promptly notified the Commercial Court and Court of Appeal of their appeal against I.P.'s registration (which, under the then-applicable General Administrative Procedure Act, had suspensive effect) and that I.P. lacked standing to withdraw the appeals. They urged examination of the appeals on the merits.

On 18 February 2014, the Court of Appeal dismissed certain appeals on the merits, holding the pledges lawful and registered, T's default undisputed (T had sought more time rather than denying the debt), and the exact debt amount irrelevant at that enforcement stage. Other appeals were rejected as withdrawn. In March 2014, the Ministry of Finance annulled I.P.'s registration because the applicants had been denied participation; related proceedings were later terminated. Madžarović lodged constitutional appeals on T's behalf, complaining of lack of access to court (due to the unauthorised withdrawal), ineffective remedies, and property deprivation through court-enabled abuses. The Constitutional Court dismissed them in November 2016, finding the withdrawal valid, remedies used, and proceedings overall fair (without addressing property rights).

Related events included a stay order on share processing that arrived too late, temporary restrictions on O.B. (which had unlawfully acquired over 10% of shares without prior consent), and unsuccessful further domestic challenges (including on points of law, barred in enforcement proceedings).

The ECHR held the applicants had victim status (as sole shareholders of T, with no risk of diverging views) and found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The domestic courts' acceptance of the withdrawal by a director whose appointment was known to be challenged (and later annulled) caused the applicants to lose a remedy they reasonably believed available, amounting to a disproportionate hindrance to access to court.

The ECHR case Madžarović and Others v. Montenegro (apps. 54839/17 and 71093/17) was brought by Mihailo Madžarović (a Slovenian national) and two Montenegrin companies he solely owned and directed, Zetmont d.o.o. and Bermont d.o.o. In 2010 and 2011 T, represented by Madžarović, pledged specified shares it held in an investment fund to the bank.

After T defaulted, the bank applied to the Podgorica Commercial Court. In October and November 2013 that court, relying on the Pledge Act, found the pledges valid and T in default, and ordered seizure and transfer of the shares to the bank. T (still represented by Madžarović) appealed, arguing that the court had ignored the Enforcement Act, had not examined original documents, and had left the exact debt (especially interest) legally undefined. Rectification decisions were also appealed.

On 9 January 2014 the bank sold the transferred shares to company O.B. On 16 January T’s new board appointed I.P. as executive director in Madžarović’s place; the change was registered by the Companies Registry on 20 January. The applicants immediately appealed that registration, which (under the then-applicable General Administrative Procedure Act) had automatic suspensive effect.

On 5 February 2014 I.P. withdrew T’s pending appeals and cancelled the lawyer’s power of attorney. The applicants repeatedly notified both the Commercial Court and the Court of Appeal that I.P. lacked standing because of the unresolved challenge to his appointment, and they urged examination of the appeals on the merits.

On 18 February 2014 the Court of Appeal dismissed one set of appeals on the merits (finding the pledges lawful and default undisputed) and rejected the other set as withdrawn. Identical rulings were given in the parallel proceedings. The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaints in 2016, holding that the appeals had been validly withdrawn, that available remedies had been used, and that the proceedings as a whole had been fair; it did not address the property claim.

Separately, a court order staying the share transfer reached the Central Depository only after the shares had already been transferred. The Securities Commission later found that O.B. had acquired more than 10 % of the fund without the required prior consent and ordered it to dispose of the excess.

These events form the factual core of the applicants’ complaints under Article 6 § 1 (access to court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The Court later found a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the appellate court had accepted the withdrawal by a director whose appointment was known to be under challenge and was subsequently quashed, thereby extinguishing a remedy the applicants had reasonably expected to remain available.

The case of Madžarović and Others v. Montenegro (applications nos. 54839/17 and 71093/17) concerns complaints by Mr Mihailo Madžarović (a Slovenian national and sole founder, owner and executive director of two Montenegrin companies, Zetmont d.o.o. and Bermont d.o.o.) and those companies themselves. The two companies were the sole shareholders of company T (the “debtor”), of which Madžarović was also the legal representative.

In 2006 the debtor obtained a €7.5 million loan from an Austrian bank. The loan was secured by contracts of pledge over the debtor’s shares in the Joint Investment Fund “Trend”. Following default, the Commercial Court in Podgorica, on the bank’s applications, issued decisions in October and November 2013 ordering seizure and transfer of the pledged shares to the bank under the Pledge Act. The court recorded that the debtor’s representative had acknowledged payment delays but disputed interest calculations. Appeals against such orders have no suspensive effect.

The debtor appealed both decisions in December 2013, contesting reliance solely on the Pledge Act, the absence of original documents and the legally undefined debt amount (particularly interest). On 9 January 2014 the bank sold the transferred shares to company O.B.

On 16 January 2014 a new board appointed I.P. as the debtor’s executive director in place of Madžarović; the Companies Central Registry registered the change on 20 January 2014. The applicants immediately appealed that registration. On 5 February 2014 I.P. withdrew the debtor’s pending appeals and revoked the prior power of attorney. Between 5 and 18 February the applicants repeatedly informed the Commercial Court and Court of Appeal that the registration decision was under appeal (which, under the General Administrative Procedure Act, had suspensive effect) and that I.P. therefore lacked standing; they urged the courts to examine the appeals on the merits.

On 18 February 2014 the Court of Appeal dismissed one appeal on the merits (finding the pledges valid and default established, and treating the precise debt figure as irrelevant at that stage) and rejected the others as withdrawn. On 7 March 2014 the Ministry of Finance annulled I.P.’s registration because the applicants had been denied participation; related proceedings were later terminated.

Madžarović lodged constitutional appeals on the debtor’s behalf, alleging denial of access to court through an unauthorised withdrawal, lack of an effective remedy and unlawful deprivation of property. The Constitutional Court dismissed them in November 2016, holding that the withdrawal had been valid, available remedies had been used and the proceedings as a whole had been fair; it did not address property rights.

Additional facts include the bank’s unilateral cancellation of the loan in 2013, later findings that O.B. had acquired the shares without required regulatory consent, unsuccessful attempts to stay the transfers or rectify irregularities, and the Supreme Court’s rejection of appeals on points of law (unavailable in enforcement proceedings). Subsequent disputes over other director registrations remained unresolved for years.

The applicants complained of a breach of their right of access to court (Article 6 § 1) because an individual whose appointment was under challenge and later annulled had been allowed to withdraw meritorious appeals they reasonably believed to be available, and of an unlawful deprivation of property. The Court examined victim status (finding the sole shareholders could claim it despite not being parties) and held that acceptance of the withdrawal constituted a disproportionate hindrance to access to court.
001-202416:
The applicant, a Russian national born in 1976, cohabited with Ms O.M. from 1994 and they had five children (born 1997–2009). He was not named as father on their birth certificates, as he then resided in Russia illegally without identification documents; the certificates listed only the mother, with a dash for the father (though the children’s patronymics reflected his first name). The family lived together.

In January 2011 the applicant was placed in pre-trial detention on theft charges. While he was in custody, Ms O.M. died on 4 February 2011. The children were taken into public care around March 2011: the four older children went to a boarding school for orphans, while 14-month-old D. (born November 2009) was placed in a children’s home on 9 March 2011 because of her age. The same day, a childcare authority referred D. to Ms N.S., a prospective adoptive parent unrelated to the family. On 18 March 2011 Ms N.S. was appointed D.’s legal guardian and took her to live with her and her husband (Mr S.S.) in Morshansk; D. has resided there since. In May 2011 Ms O.M.’s sister was appointed guardian of the four older children.

The applicant learned of the death in March 2011 (while still detained) and began seeking recognition of paternity for all five children. His initial applications were returned for lack of jurisdiction. On 8 September 2011 the Morshanskiy District Court granted Ms N.S. and Mr S.S. a full adoption of D., changing her name, surname and place of birth. The childcare authority supported this, stating that D. had no father (her mother having died), that relatives had neither visited her nor sought guardianship, and that she had four siblings in another foster family. The court found the applicants suitable and the child left without parental care; the judgment became final without appeal.

In December 2011 the applicant refiled his paternity claim in a court of proper jurisdiction; the claim concerning D. was severed. In April 2012 that court recognised his paternity of the four older children (who were returned to him in June 2012). Meanwhile a prosecutor (acting in D.’s interests) sought revocation of her adoption; the applicant, joined as a third party, learned of the adoption order in March 2012 and added a revocation request to his paternity claim.

At the October 2012 hearing, the applicant (supported by witnesses, including his eldest son, plus childcare and human-rights representatives) argued that he was D.’s biological father, had cohabited with and supported the family, and had collected mother and child from the maternity hospital; that the adoption unlawfully separated siblings and proceeded without parental consent despite authorities knowing of the father and siblings; and that revocation was required in D.’s and the siblings’ best interests. The first-instance court accepted that D. was the applicant’s biological child but refused both paternity recognition and revocation. It held that recognition would be pointless without statutory grounds for revocation (Family Code Art. 141), which required adoptive-parent fault or (per Supreme Court guidance) an unsuitable family environment; neither applied, given the adoptive parents’ resources, living conditions and the close bond formed over 18 months. Alleged procedural defects in the original adoption were deemed irrelevant to revocation. The appellate court (November 2012) and subsequent cassation courts upheld this, noting that the law did not treat established biological paternity as a revocation ground and that sibling-separation and the applicant’s willingness to raise D. could not override the finding that revocation would not serve D.’s interests.

(The case thus concerns the alleged Art. 8 violation arising from the refusal to restore the applicant’s parental rights after a deficient adoption process that ignored known relatives.)

The ECtHR case of Uzbyakov v. Russia (App. no. 71160/13) concerned a biological father’s unsuccessful efforts to establish paternity of, and revoke the adoption of, his youngest daughter after her mother’s death, raising issues under Article 8 ECHR (family life and positive obligations).

Sergey Uzbyakov (born 1976) cohabited with O.M. from 1994 and fathered five children (S. 1997, R. 2002, Ser. 2003, V. 2007, D. 29 November 2009). As an initially undocumented migrant, he was not registered as father; birth certificates listed only O.M. as mother, with dashes for the father (though patronymics reflected his name). The family lived together. He obtained a residence permit in 2010 and nationality in 2013.

On 21 January 2011, Uzbyakov was detained on theft charges (discontinued on 20 April 2011, leading to his release). O.M. died on 4 February 2011 while he was in custody. The children entered public care around March 2011: the four older ones went to a boarding school (later placed with O.M.’s sister O.E. as guardian from 16 May 2011), while 14-month-old D. entered a children’s home on 9 March 2011.

That same day, childcare authorities referred D. to N.S., a prospective adoptive parent on their list. On 18 March 2011, N.S. was appointed D.’s guardian and took her to live with N.S. and husband S.S. in Morshansk, where she has remained. Uzbyakov, learning of O.M.’s death in March 2011 while detained, immediately sought to establish paternity of all five children.

On an unspecified date, N.S. and S.S. applied to adopt D. On 8 September 2011, the Morshanskiy District Court granted a full adoption order, changing D.’s name, surname and birthplace. The childcare authority supported this, stating D. had “no father,” her mother had died, and “relatives had not visited her” during her brief stay in the home (9–18 March). The court noted D.’s four siblings in another foster family but found N.S./S.S. met all statutory criteria with good conditions and care; the order was unappealed and became final.

Uzbyakov’s initial paternity claims (March–April 2011) were rejected for lack of jurisdiction or form. He refiled on 15 December 2011 in the competent Kamenka Town Court (which severed D.’s claim). On 16 April 2012, paternity was established for the four older children, who returned to him on 9 June 2012. A prosecutor then sought to revoke D.’s adoption (Uzbyakov joined as third party and learned of the 8 September 2011 order around 22 March 2012); those proceedings were later discontinued.

Uzbyakov amended his claim to seek both paternity recognition for D. and revocation of her adoption. He argued the adoption violated law (no parental consent, sibling separation forbidden except in the children’s interests, and authorities knew of him and the siblings). Witnesses (including son S.) confirmed he was D.’s biological father, had cohabited with O.M., collected D. from hospital, and supported the family. Childcare and human-rights representatives supported him, citing procedural deficiencies (no hearing of relatives or grandfather, sibling split, and no transfer to O.E. like the others).

On 1 October 2012, the Kamenka Town Court accepted that D. was Uzbyakov’s biological child (from the relationship with O.M.) but refused recognition and revocation. It held recognition pointless without revocation grounds under Family Code Article 141 (limited to adopters’ guilty conduct, such as abuse or neglect, or unsuitable conditions). None existed: N.S./S.S. provided financial security, jobs, housing, and (after 1.5 years) close bonds and beneficial development; revocation was not in D.’s interests. Alleged adoption-stage breaches were deemed irrelevant to revocation.

The Penza Regional Court upheld this on 13 November 2012, noting domestic law did not treat paternity establishment as a revocation ground. Uzbyakov’s willingness/ability to raise D., and the siblings’ suffering from separation, were irrelevant as they did not alter the finding that revocation was contrary to D.’s interests. Cassation appeals were dismissed in 2013.

These facts underpin the Article 8 complaint: a deficient adoption process (failure to hear relatives despite knowledge of the father and siblings) and inadequate later examination of all interests, with rigid application of formal revocation grounds insufficient to justify refusal.

The case of Uzbyakov v. Russia concerns a biological father’s unsuccessful efforts to have his paternity recognised and his infant daughter’s adoption revoked after her mother’s death, raising issues under Article 8 of the Convention regarding family life and positive obligations.

The applicant cohabited with Ms O.M. from 1994 and they had five children together: S. (born 1997), R. (2002), Ser. (2003), V. (2007) and D. (born 29 November 2009). He was not registered as their father because he was residing illegally in Russia without identification documents. The children’s birth certificates therefore named only their mother, with a dash in the father’s section; their patronymics derived from the applicant’s first name and they took their mother’s surname. The family lived together.

On 21 January 2011 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of theft and placed in pre-trial detention. Ms O.M. died on 4 February 2011. Around March 2011 the children were taken into public care: the four older children went to a boarding school, while D. (then 14 months old) was placed in a children’s home because of her age.

The applicant learned of the death while still detained and began attempting to establish paternity. On 9 March 2011 D. entered the children’s home; the same day a local authority referred a prospective adoptive parent, Ms N.S., to visit her. On 18 March 2011 Ms N.S. was appointed D.’s legal guardian and took the child to live with her and her husband. On 16 May 2011 the mother’s sister was appointed guardian of the four older children.

Ms N.S. and her husband later applied to adopt D. On 8 September 2011 the Morshanskiy District Court granted a full adoption order, changing the child’s name, surname and place of birth. The court recorded that the mother had died, no father was registered, and relatives had neither visited nor sought guardianship, although it noted that D. had four siblings living with another foster family. The judgment was not appealed and became final.

The applicant’s initial paternity claims were returned on jurisdictional and formal grounds. On 15 December 2011 he refiled in a competent court. On 16 April 2012 that court established his paternity of the four older children, who were returned to him on 9 June 2012.

In March 2012, while participating as a third party in prosecutor-initiated proceedings seeking revocation of the adoption, the applicant learned of the September 2011 order. He then sought both recognition of paternity of D. and revocation of the adoption. He argued that the adoption had violated domestic law by separating siblings without parental consent and that the authorities had known of his existence and of the siblings. Witnesses, including his eldest son, confirmed that he was D.’s biological father, had cohabited with the mother and had raised the children. Certain guardianship authorities supported his claim.

On 1 October 2012 the first-instance court accepted that D. had been born of the applicant’s relationship with Ms O.M. but refused both paternity recognition and revocation. It held that Article 141 of the Family Code permitted revocation only for adoptive parents’ misconduct or, exceptionally, where conditions in the adoptive family were unsuitable; neither applied. The adoptive parents provided good care, had formed close bonds with D. over 18 months, and revocation would not serve the child’s interests. Alleged procedural irregularities in the original adoption were considered irrelevant to the revocation question. Appeals and cassation applications were dismissed on similar reasoning: establishment of biological paternity did not constitute a statutory ground for revocation, and the child’s established ties with her adoptive family prevailed.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation: the adoption court failed to hear any relatives despite being informed of the siblings and biological father, and later courts declined to examine all relevant interests in depth when refusing revocation.
001-202419:
The European Court of Human Rights examined Megrelishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 30364/09), concerning the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings against Merab Megrelishvili arising from the manner in which key evidence was obtained and used. The applicant, a Georgian national born in 1961, was detained in Tbilisi. On 3 July 2007, the Special Operations Department (SOD) of the Ministry of the Interior received operational information that G.V. regularly purchased drugs from the applicant. The report indicated that G.V. would have drugs at home that morning and that the applicant would be driving a vehicle containing drugs. Proceedings were initiated against the applicant and others under Article 260 § 1 of the Criminal Code for unlawful purchase, storage and sale of drugs.

That day, SOD officers stopped the applicant while he was driving in Tbilisi. He was handcuffed and subjected to a body search between 10.40 and 10.50 a.m. by investigator R.M. and two officers, without attesting witnesses. The police report cited urgent circumstances under Article 102 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP), claiming a risk that the applicant would hide or destroy drugs. Two Subutex pills were found in one jeans pocket and two-and-a-half in another. The applicant refused to sign the report, denying ownership. He was formally arrested at 11.00 a.m. His car was then searched at 11.05 a.m. under identical conditions, yielding more hidden pills; he again refused to sign.

SOD officers also searched the applicant’s apartment (11.15 a.m.–1.30 p.m.) and garage (2.25–2.55 p.m.). Drugs were recovered from the balcony and garage. The applicant’s wife, who was present for part of the apartment search along with their children and mother-in-law, requested attesting witnesses; this was refused on urgency grounds (risk of concealment or destruction). Family members later stated that officers entered the apartment before the wife returned (remaining alone with the children for about 30 minutes), that more than three officers participated and moved freely, that the garage door was already open, and that the searches were video-recorded. The investigator later denied any recording existed, rejected claims of extra officers, and deemed family statements unreliable.

A total of 62 pills, 24 split pills and powder containing 0.5562 grams of buprenorphine were seized. The applicant tested positive for drugs. G.V. was also arrested with drugs but admitted only personal use and denied purchasing from the applicant. On 4 July 2007 the applicant was charged with aggravated offences under Article 260 § 3(a). A prosecutor sought court validation of the four searches as urgent. The Tbilisi District Court approved them in writing the same day without hearing the applicant or reviewing the operational report or search-ordering decisions. The summary rulings cited no facts or reasons and allowed a 72-hour appeal, which the applicant did not pursue.

At trial the Tbilisi City Court convicted the applicant on 31 March 2008 of unlawful possession of a large quantity of drugs (Article 260 § 3), imposing 12 years’ imprisonment (sale charges were dropped for lack of evidence). The conviction rested on the search reports and testimony from the five SOD officers. The court rejected the applicant’s repeated requests to exclude the evidence as illegally obtained, noting that the CCP permitted searches without witnesses in urgent cases, deeming family statements unreliable, accepting officers’ testimony of urgency, and observing that the searches had been validated without appeal.

On appeal the Tbilisi Court of Appeal (16 July 2008) upheld the conviction, finding no procedural violations, that officers had no motive to plant evidence, and that family evidence was subjective. The applicant’s further appeal on points of law, reiterating the absence of independent witnesses, the implausibility of destruction risk given that he was handcuffed, and officers’ interest in the outcome, was declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 19 November 2008.

Relevant CCP provisions at the time required judicial authorisation for searches except in urgent necessity, after which a judge had to assess lawfulness and evidence admissibility within 24 hours. Attesting witnesses were normally required for searches, but could be omitted only when there was a real risk of evidence being damaged, destroyed or concealed; the right to call witnesses revived once that risk ceased. Evidence obtained in violation of the law was inadmissible. These facts formed the core of the applicant’s complaint that the principal evidence had been obtained and used in a manner rendering the proceedings unfair.

The case of Megrelishvili v. Georgia concerns the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings against the applicant arising from the manner in which key evidence of drug possession was obtained during warrantless searches and subsequently used to convict him.

On 3 July 2007, police received operational information that the applicant was selling drugs to G.V. and that both would be found with narcotics that morning. Proceedings were opened against the applicant under Article 260 of the Criminal Code. While driving in Tbilisi he was stopped, immediately handcuffed and subjected to a body search (10.40–10.50 a.m.) by investigator R.M. and two officers. Invoking “urgent circumstances” under Article 102 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (risk of concealment or destruction of evidence), the officers refused his request to invite independent attesting witnesses. Two Subutex pills were recovered from one pocket and two-and-a-half from another. After the search he was permitted to call witnesses but declined; he also refused to sign the report, denying ownership of the pills. He was formally arrested at 11 a.m.

A search of his vehicle immediately followed, again without witnesses and on the same urgency grounds, yielding further pills hidden in the front seat. Concurrently, a second team searched his apartment (11.15 a.m.–1.30 p.m.) and garage (2.25–2.55 p.m.). The applicant’s wife’s request for neighbours to attend was refused on identical urgency grounds. Drugs were found on the balcony and in the garage. In total 0.5562 g of buprenorphine (62 whole pills, 24 split pills and powder) was seized; the applicant was found to be under the influence of drugs. G.V. was also arrested with drugs but denied purchasing them from the applicant.

The following day the applicant was charged with aggravated possession. A prosecutor sought court validation of the four searches as urgent. The Tbilisi District Court granted the requests in writing, without the applicant’s participation or sight of the operational report or the investigators’ urgency decisions. The rulings were summary, contained no factual reasoning and afforded a 72-hour appeal window that the applicant did not use.

Subsequent statements by the applicant’s wife, mother-in-law and daughter contradicted the official reports: officers had entered the apartment while the children were alone (after posing as cable technicians), remained there for 15–30 minutes before the wife returned, numbered at least four to six (with others entering and leaving), had already opened the garage, and had video-recorded the search. The investigator later denied any recording existed, asserted that only three officers had been present, and dismissed the family’s accounts as unreliable.

At trial the applicant repeatedly sought exclusion of the seized drugs, arguing that the searches had been unlawful: he had been handcuffed and therefore unable to interfere with evidence; no genuine urgency existed; independent witnesses had been arbitrarily excluded; and the officers had had both opportunity and motive to plant the drugs. The Tbilisi City Court rejected these claims on 31 March 2008, relying exclusively on the police reports and the testimony of the five participating officers. It held that the law permitted witness-less searches in urgency, that the family’s evidence was unreliable, and that the searches had already been judicially validated. The applicant was convicted of possession of a large quantity of drugs and sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment; sale charges were dropped for lack of evidence.

The Court of Appeal heard the daughter’s testimony confirming delayed entry, multiple officers, a refused witness request and video-recording, yet on 16 July 2008 it upheld the conviction in summary terms, finding the officers unbiased and the family’s evidence “subjective.” The Supreme Court declared the subsequent appeal on points of law inadmissible on 19 November 2008.

These facts form the core of the complaint that the proceedings were unfair because the decisive evidence was obtained in violation of domestic safeguards, without independent verification, and without adequate judicial scrutiny of either the urgency claims or the contradictory accounts.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Megrelishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 30364/09, judgment of 7 May 2020) concerns an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. The complaint focused on the manner in which the principal evidence—narcotic substances recovered during multiple searches—was obtained and subsequently used to convict him.

Criminal proceedings were immediately opened against the applicant for unlawful purchase, storage and sale of drugs. While driving in Tbilisi, the applicant was stopped, immediately handcuffed and subjected to a body search between 10.40 and 10.50 a.m. Two Subutex pills were found in one pocket and two-and-a-half pills in another. The search was conducted without attesting witnesses on the ground of “urgent circumstances” under Article 102 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP), the investigator citing a risk that the applicant would hide or destroy evidence. The applicant refused to sign the report, denying ownership of the pills. He was formally arrested at 11.00 a.m.

A search of his vehicle followed at 11.05 a.m., again without witnesses and on the same urgency grounds; more Subutex pills were recovered from the front seat. Concurrently, other SOD officers searched the applicant’s apartment (11.15 a.m.–1.30 p.m.) and garage (2.25–2.55 p.m.). Additional drugs were found on the balcony and in the garage. The applicant’s wife, who was present for part of the apartment search, requested that neighbours attend as attesting witnesses; the request was refused. Family members later stated that officers entered the apartment while only the children were present, that more officers participated than the three recorded in the official reports, and that the searches were video-recorded. The investigator later denied that any recording existed and dismissed the family’s account as unreliable.

A total of 62 pills, 24 split pills and powder containing 0.5562 g of buprenorphine were seized. The applicant tested positive for drugs. G.V. was also arrested and admitted personal use but denied buying from the applicant.

On 4 July 2007 the applicant was charged with aggravated drug offences. A prosecutor applied to the Tbilisi District Court for validation of the four searches. The written applications contained no copy of the original operational report and no detailed justification of urgency. The court approved the searches the same day without hearing the applicant, issuing brief decisions that merely recited the existence of urgency and compliance with the CCP. The applicant did not appeal those decisions within the 72-hour time-limit.

At trial the Tbilisi City Court convicted the applicant on 31 March 2008 of unlawful possession of a large quantity of drugs and sentenced him to 12 years’ imprisonment (sale charges were dropped). The court relied exclusively on the search reports and the testimony of the five participating SOD officers. It rejected the applicant’s repeated applications to exclude the evidence, holding that the CCP permitted searches without witnesses in urgent cases, that the officers had no motive to plant drugs, and that the family’s evidence was unreliable. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 16 July 2008, again preferring the officers’ evidence and characterising the family’s testimony as subjective. The Supreme Court declared the applicant’s points-of-law appeal inadmissible on 19 November 2008.

The applicant maintained throughout that no genuine urgency existed (he had been immediately restrained), that the absence of independent witnesses rendered the searches unlawful, that the drugs had been planted, and that the courts had failed to scrutinise these allegations or the discrepancies in the official record. These facts formed the basis of his complaint that the proceedings as a whole were unfair.

The case of Romić and Others v. Croatia comprises seven applications by eight individuals (seven Croatian nationals and one from Bosnia and Herzegovina) alleging breaches of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention. The complaints centre on criminal appeal proceedings in which reasoned opinions or submissions by the competent State Attorney’s Office were never served on the defence, and/or sessions of the appeal courts were held without notifying or inviting the applicants or their lawyers, even where attendance had been expressly requested. This, they argued, violated equality of arms, the adversarial principle and the right to defend oneself in person.

The first and second applicants (Romić application) were indicted in 2004 for economic crime. The Zagreb County Court convicted them in June 2010 and imposed prison terms. They appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging both facts and law. The file was sent to the State Attorney’s Office, whose Deputy submitted a reasoned opinion in December 2010 urging dismissal of the appeals; the opinion was never forwarded to the defence. A January 2011 session took place in the presence of the applicants’ lawyers and the Deputy State Attorney, who simply confirmed his written opinion. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions. Constitutional complaints that the defence had never seen the prosecutor’s submissions were dismissed in 2012 on the ground that domestic law imposed no duty to serve them.

The third applicant (Vlaškalić) was indicted in 2001 for armed robbery. After several remittals he was convicted in April 2012 by the Osijek Municipal Court and given a suspended sentence. He appealed and specifically requested that he and his lawyer be invited to the appeal-session. The Osijek County Court sat on 30 May 2012 in the presence only of the Deputy County State Attorney, without informing the defence, and dismissed the appeal the same day. His constitutional complaint was rejected as unfounded.

The fourth applicant (Radonić) was convicted in 2010 of damaging State property and merely reprimanded. Both he and the prosecution appealed. The Zagreb County State Attorney’s Office filed a reasoned opinion that was never served on the defence. Despite the applicant’s request to attend, the County Court held its January 2011 session without him or his lawyer and dismissed both appeals. The Constitutional Court rejected his complaint in 2013.

The fifth applicant (Dumančić) was initially acquitted in 2008 of a fatal public-safety offence. On the prosecution’s appeal the Supreme Court reversed the acquittal in July 2011 and imposed a four-and-a-half-year sentence. He appealed to a five-judge panel. The State Attorney’s Office submitted a written opinion in December 2011 seeking dismissal; it was not forwarded. At the March 2012 session (attended by the applicant’s lawyer) the Deputy State Attorney merely restated the written opinion. The appeal was dismissed. The Constitutional Court held that oral restatement had given the lawyer an adequate opportunity to comment.

The sixth applicant (Severec) was convicted of fraud in 2010 and given a suspended sentence. He appealed and asked that his lawyer be invited. The Pula County State Attorney’s Office filed an opinion that was never served. The April 2012 appeal session took place in the absence of both the applicant and his lawyer; the conviction was upheld. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint in 2014.

The seventh applicant (Topalović) was convicted in 2010 of attempted murder and related offences and sentenced to five-and-a-half years. He appealed and requested attendance. The State Attorney’s Office submitted an opinion in September 2010 that was never served. The November 2010 Supreme Court session was attended by his lawyer but not by him (the court considering his presence unnecessary). The conviction was confirmed. The Constitutional Court again relied on the lawyer’s opportunity to comment orally.

The eighth applicant (Domazet) was convicted in 2014 of causing a road accident and given a suspended sentence. He appealed and asked to attend the session. The municipal State Attorney’s reply proposing dismissal was never served. The May 2014 County Court session proceeded in his absence and the appeal was rejected. His constitutional complaint was dismissed.

In each instance the Constitutional Court either held that Croatian law imposed no obligation to serve prosecutorial opinions or considered that oral confirmation at a hearing (when a lawyer was present) cured the omission. These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 6 violations concerning equality of arms and the right to be present and to defend oneself in person.

Despite his request, neither he nor his lawyer was invited to the 18 April 2012 session; the conviction was upheld. His 2014 constitutional complaint was rejected.

001-202440:
The ECHR case Kostov and Others v. Bulgaria (apps. 66581/12 and 25054/15, judgment 14 May 2020) involved three Bulgarian nationals whose agricultural land on Sofia’s outskirts was expropriated for road projects. They alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the compensation awarded was disproportionately low and unrelated to market value.

The first applicant bought three plots (totalling ~23,830 m²) in 2008 after restitution. One plot (19,187 m²) was eighth-category marshland (tax value BGN 671.50); the others (4,643 m²) were tenth-category agricultural land, partly former gravel ponds (tax value BGN 41.80). In September 2011 the Council of Ministers expropriated 21,323 m² for a motorway junction, awarding BGN 1,748 (~EUR 894, or BGN 0.08/m²) under the 1998 Regulation on agricultural land values.

He sought judicial review, citing 2007 awards of BGN 55–101/m² for similar nearby land expropriated for the same project. An expert found no comparable sales meeting the 1996 State Property Act’s strict criteria (same village territory, transactions in the prior year involving a commercial entity) and therefore applied the Regulation, valuing the land at BGN 4,779 (~EUR 2,445). After considering the applicant’s documents the expert identified one qualifying sale at ~BGN 225/m² (implying a value of over BGN 4.8 million). The Supreme Administrative Court held that a single comparable was insufficient to establish an average market value and confirmed the Regulation figure.

The second and third applicants owned a 6,101 m² fourth-category field (tax value BGN 1,141.20), restituted in 1999 and rented for grain. In December 2013 it was expropriated for Sofia’s ring road; they received BGN 5,116 (~EUR 2,616, or BGN 0.84/m²). An expert listed several area transactions and proposed values ranging from BGN 21.5 to 104/m² depending on which plots counted as comparable. The Supreme Administrative Court found only one qualifying sale (BGN 25/m²); others failed the criteria (different zone, joint mortgages without individual values, or unregistered capital contributions). It therefore upheld the Regulation award. In early 2015 the government settled analogous cases arising from the same expropriation decision at BGN 20.05/m² to unblock construction.

Bulgarian law requires “equivalent” (i.e., market-value) compensation. A 2006 amendment to the 1996 Act defined market value by reference to comparable nearby transactions (same zone/village, preceding year, at least one commercial party). Where insufficient comparables exist, valuation reverts to the Regulation, whose 1998 rental-based formulae (BGN 0.04–0.63/m² basic, plus adjustments) have never been updated. The Constitutional Court upheld the scheme as supplying objective criteria, though four judges dissented that it systematically produced “evidently and dramatically lower” figures.

These facts—strict statutory filters that frequently left only one or zero comparables, refusal to consider other same-project expropriations or broader market evidence, and consequent reliance on an obsolete low-value formula—produced awards far below contemporaneous transaction prices and later settlements for similar land.

**Case of Kostov and Others v. Bulgaria (ECtHR, 14 May 2020)**

The applicants (Bulgarian nationals living in Sofia) complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that they received disproportionately low compensation after the State expropriated their agricultural land for road construction (a motorway junction and Sofia ring-road section). Compensation was calculated under Bulgaria’s 1996 State Property Act, which required “equivalent” compensation based on the market value of comparable nearby properties (defined strictly: same village territory/zone, transactions in the prior year involving a commercial entity, later requiring at least two comparables). If none existed, outdated 1998 formulae in a Regulation (25 times annual rent by land category, plus limited adjustments) applied, yielding very low values (BGN 0.04–0.63/sq m).

**First applicant (Kostov):** In 2008 he bought three plots (totalling ~23,830 sq m of 8th- and 10th-category marshland/other agricultural land on Sofia’s outskirts) for BGN 4,000 (EUR 2,046); tax valuations were only BGN 713. In September 2011 the Council of Ministers expropriated 21,323 sq m for a motorway junction (land previously not privately owned, so missed in 2007 expropriations). Compensation: BGN 1,748 (EUR 894), or BGN 0.08/sq m under the Regulation.

He sought judicial review, citing much higher awards (BGN 55–101/sq m) for 2007 expropriations of similar land in the same village area. A court-appointed expert found no plots meeting the Act’s strict comparability criteria and valued the land at BGN 4,779 (BGN 0.22/sq m) via the Regulation. Kostov produced sale deeds (one at ~BGN 6/sq m just outside the one-year window; another at BGN 225/sq m that did qualify). The expert noted most others were ineligible (different village, urban/non-agricultural, or wrong timing). The Supreme Administrative Court held that a single comparable was insufficient to establish an “average” market value, so applied the Regulation and awarded BGN 4,779.

**Second and third applicants (Popova and Velichkov):** They owned a 6,101 sq m 4th-category field (tax value BGN 1,141) via 1999 restitution, rented as agricultural land. In December 2013 it was expropriated for the Sofia ring road; compensation was BGN 5,116 (EUR 2,616), or BGN 0.84/sq m under the Regulation.

They challenged this as unrelated to market value. An expert listed area contracts and proposed valuations of BGN 21.5–104/sq m depending on which plots counted as comparable. The Supreme Administrative Court found only one qualifying plot (sold 2012 for BGN 25/sq m); others failed (different zone, joint mortgages without individual values, or non-registerable transactions such as contribution to company capital). It therefore applied the Regulation and upheld the original award.

In early 2015 the government settled several similar pending cases (same expropriation decision, same zone, unspecified-category agricultural land) at BGN 20.05/sq m to unblock construction, noting this matched awards in a neighbouring zone based on sufficient comparables.

The applicants alleged the strict statutory criteria created an artificial shortage of comparables, forcing use of the low, unupdated Regulation values. This ignored values of other plots expropriated for the same projects and produced major discrepancies with market indications, so compensation bore no reasonable relation to the land’s value and imposed an excessive individual burden. (The Court later found a violation of Article 1 Protocol 1 on these grounds; reopening of domestic proceedings was deemed an appropriate just-satisfaction remedy.)

The ECtHR case of Kostov and Others v. Bulgaria (apps. 66581/12 and 25054/15) concerns three Bulgarian nationals whose agricultural land on Sofia’s outskirts was expropriated for road projects. They alleged that the compensation awarded was disproportionately low and unrelated to market value, in violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The first applicant bought three restituted plots (totalling ~23,830 m²) in 2008 for BGN 4,000. These comprised eighth-category marshland (19,187 m², tax value BGN 671.50) and tenth-category agricultural land (4,643 m², tax value BGN 41.80), some of which had contained ponds from prior gravel extraction. In September 2011 the Council of Ministers expropriated 21,323 m² of this land for a Sofia–Varna motorway junction, awarding BGN 1,748 (~BGN 0.08/m²) under the 1998 Regulation on agricultural land values. He sought judicial review, citing 2007 expropriations of similar land in the same village that had produced awards of BGN 55–101/m². A court-appointed expert found no sufficient comparable transactions meeting the 1996 State Property Act’s strict criteria (sales in the preceding year, same village territory, at least one commercial party, registered). One possible sale (August 2010, ~BGN 225/m²) was deemed inadequate to establish an average. The Supreme Administrative Court therefore applied the Regulation (basic values of BGN 0.04–0.63/m², unupdated since 1998, adjusted for location/quality) and awarded BGN 4,779 (~BGN 0.22/m²).

The second and third applicants owned a restituted 6,101 m² fourth-category field (tax value BGN 1,141.20). In December 2013 it was expropriated for Sofia’s ring road with compensation of BGN 5,116 (~BGN 0.84/m²) under the Regulation. They challenged this. An expert identified several nearby 2012–2013 transactions yielding possible values of BGN 21.5–104/m². The Supreme Administrative Court accepted only one as comparable (BGN 25/m²), found it insufficient for an average, and upheld the original award. In early 2015 the Government settled other pending cases involving unspecified-category land in the same zone (expropriated under the same 2013 decision) at BGN 20.05/m², citing the need to unblock construction and similar awards in a neighbouring zone.

The 1996 Act (as amended 2006) requires “equivalent” compensation based on the market value of comparable nearby properties (defined as registered transactions for valuable consideration in the prior year involving a commercial entity, in the same zone/village). Where no such properties exist, section 32(3) mandates use of the Regulation’s formulae. The Constitutional Court upheld the scheme as filling a lacuna and ensuring objective, equal treatment, but stressed that the formula method is an exceptional last resort. Subsequent 2014 legislation explicitly required at least two comparables. The applicants argued that the rigid criteria produced a shortage of comparables, ignored higher values paid for other plots taken for the same infrastructure, and generated major discrepancies with indicative market prices, so that the awards bore no reasonable relationship to their land’s value and imposed an excessive individual burden.

The case of Farzaliyev v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, 28 May 2020) concerned an Azerbaijani national who alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention (fair trial and presumption of innocence) in civil compensation proceedings linked to a discontinued criminal investigation.

The applicant served as Prime Minister of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic (NAR) in the early 1990s but had lived in Turkey since 1993 without holding public office. In November 2005, the Nakhchivan prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into alleged embezzlement of NAR public funds in 1991–1992. The probe centred on contracts for the purchase of helicopters that were never delivered; instead, funds were said to have been diverted. The applicant was identified as having abused his authority to authorise transfers totalling SUR 11,750,000 to a private company. Investigators questioned others and reviewed documents and an expert report but could not question the applicant (who was abroad) even as a witness. The investigation concluded that SUR 7,450,000 had been returned by wire transfer, while SUR 4,300,000 given in cash to persons allegedly sent by the applicant was never recovered.

On 21 January 2006 the proceedings were discontinued under the 12-year limitation period without anyone being formally charged. The decision stated that the applicant “ought to be charged” as an accused but was “absolved” of liability; similar language applied to two co-suspects. The applicant remained unaware of both the investigation and its discontinuation until a civil claim was later filed.

On 16 February 2006 the same prosecutor’s office lodged a civil claim against the applicant and the two others under the Code of Criminal Procedure provisions governing claims “within the framework of criminal proceedings.” It asserted that embezzlement had been “proved” by the investigation material, that the defendants had been “absolved” only because of limitation, and that they still owed compensation for “the crime.” The claim relied on the criminal-file evidence and invoked a provision excluding ordinary civil limitation periods.

The Nasimi District Court, sitting in the applicant’s absence (though his lawyers attended), examined the criminal-file documents, witness statements containing inconsistencies about who initiated the contracts and how cash was returned, and an expert valuation. On 8 May 2006 it held the applicant and one co-defendant jointly liable for AZN 2,327,059 (then about EUR 2 million) as compensation for “the damage caused as a result of the criminal offence of embezzlement,” while dismissing the claim against the third person. The court repeated that the defendants had been “absolved” of criminal liability yet the damage remained uncompensated.

In appeals the applicant argued that the civil court had improperly treated the prosecution’s untested version of events as proved, that no criminal conviction existed, that the special criminal-procedure claim was unavailable once proceedings had been discontinued, and that ordinary civil limitation had long expired. He also highlighted factual inconsistencies and his lack of involvement after leaving office in February 1992. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the judgment, essentially repeating the first-instance reasoning without addressing these arguments. Subsequent attempts at reopening failed.

The ECtHR held that the civil proceedings were a “direct consequence” of the discontinued criminal investigation. Given the temporal proximity, the prosecuting authorities’ role, the language used, and the applicant’s status as primary suspect, he had been “substantially affected.” Article 6 § 2 therefore applied and was violated. Article 6 § 1 was also breached because the domestic courts failed to give a specific, express reply to potentially decisive arguments concerning the legal basis of the claim and the use of untested criminal-file material.

The case of Farzaliyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 29620/07) concerns alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights in civil compensation proceedings linked to a discontinued criminal investigation. The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1946 and living in Turkey since 1993, had served as Prime Minister of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic (NAR) in the early 1990s but held no public office thereafter.

Contracts were signed by former Health Minister F.J. and businessman A.M. for delivery of helicopters; based on the applicant’s ministerial orders, SUR 11,750,000 was transferred to A.M.’s company. Helicopters were never delivered. SUR 7,450,000 was later returned by wire transfer, but the remaining SUR 4,300,000 was allegedly handed in cash in February 1992 to unidentified persons sent by the applicant and never recovered. The investigation named the applicant as having abused his authority to embezzle funds. Authorities questioned several witnesses (including F.J. and A.M.) and reviewed documents and an expert report but could not question the applicant, who was abroad.

On 21 January 2006, the proceedings were discontinued under Article 75.1.3 of the Criminal Code due to expiry of the 12-year limitation period for serious crimes. The decision stated that the applicant “ought to be charged” as an accused for embezzlement and abuse of power but, along with F.J. and A.M., was “absolved of criminal liability.” No one had been formally charged. The applicant first learned of the investigation and discontinuation between February and May 2006, during subsequent civil proceedings; he later unsuccessfully challenged the discontinuation on grounds including lack of notice and absence of corpus delicti.

On 16 February 2006, the prosecutor’s office lodged a civil claim against the applicant, F.J., and A.M. under Articles 179–183 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP), which permit civil claims “within the framework of criminal proceedings.” The claim asserted that embezzlement had been “proved” by investigation evidence but that the defendants, though absolved due to limitation, remained obliged to compensate the State for “the crime.” Civil-law limitation periods were said not to apply. Supporting materials from the criminal file were submitted.

The Nasimi District Court examined documents (contracts, transfer orders, payment records, expert valuation), defendants’ statements, and witness evidence. The applicant (via lawyers) argued inconsistencies in F.J.’s and A.M.’s accounts, that his orders fulfilled official duties based on contracts they initiated, and that he had left office by February 1992 and had no involvement in the cash return. On 8 May 2006 the court allowed the claim against the applicant and A.M. (dismissing it against F.J.), finding SUR 4,300,000 (equivalent to AZN 2,327,059, or approximately EUR 2 million) “embezzled.” It held that, despite discontinuation, “the damage caused as a result of the criminal offence has not been compensated” and ordered joint payment.

In appeals, the applicant disputed the facts, argued that evidence from discontinued criminal proceedings should not have been used, and contended that a civil court could not find liability for a crime absent a criminal conviction. He further submitted that the CCrP civil-claim procedure was inapplicable after discontinuation and that ordinary civil-law limitation periods (long expired) should have applied; the 2005 investigation had been opened belatedly solely to revive an otherwise time-barred claim. The Court of Appeal (21 July 2006) and Supreme Court (13 December 2006) upheld the judgment, essentially repeating the first-instance reasoning without addressing these arguments. Subsequent attempts to reopen the case failed.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the civil proceedings treated him as guilty of an uncharged, unconvicted offence (presumption of innocence) and that the courts failed to give a reasoned response to potentially decisive arguments (fair hearing).

The applicant appealed, arguing that (i) the civil court had treated the prosecutor’s factual narrative as proved despite the absence of any criminal conviction; (ii) evidence from a discontinued criminal file should not have been used; (iii) the claim was inadmissible because the criminal proceedings had already ended and all civil limitation periods had long expired; and (iv) the 2005 investigation had been opened solely to revive an otherwise time-barred civil claim. Neither the Court of Appeal nor the Supreme Court addressed these arguments; both simply repeated the first-instance reasoning. Subsequent attempts to obtain plenary or constitutional review failed.

The European Court later found that the civil proceedings were a direct consequence of the discontinued investigation, that the applicant had been “substantially affected” by the authorities’ conduct, and that Article 6 § 2 therefore applied.
