**CASE OF GREMINA v. RUSSIA (Application no. 17054/08), ECtHR (Third Section), 26 May 2020**

The applicant, Liliya Mikhaylovna Gremina (born 1937), a 70-year-old resident of Nizhniy Novgorod, intended to join the unauthorised “Dissenters’ March” rally at Gorkiy Square on 24 March 2007. She carried a rolled-up poster in a plastic bag bearing an anti-government slogan targeting the United Russia party. City authorities had refused authorisation for the event, a decision later upheld by a district court, but the applicant was unaware of this and never reached the square.

En route, police stopped her, inquired about her destination, inspected her bag, unrolled the poster, and filmed the encounter. Officers ordered her onto a nearby bus to establish her identity. She refused, produced her pensioner’s certificate, and sat on the ground to resist what she viewed as unlawful action and to draw public attention. Three officers then lifted her by the arms and elbows, dragged her several metres to a patrol car, lifted her legs, and pushed her inside from behind, twisting her arms; she felt a blow to her lower back and attempted limited resistance by bracing a foot against the car. She was transferred to a bus holding other civilians, then to Avtozavodskiy district police station around 3–4 p.m. There she was held standing in a basement corridor, denied the chance to sit or walk, and later questioned without any arrest or escort records being drawn up. Around 5 p.m. she suffered a hypertensive crisis (headache, dizziness, nausea, breathing difficulty); an ambulance treated her and took her to hospital, which she declined.

Medical records confirmed a hypertensive crisis at the station (treated at 4.57 p.m.) and, two days later, two bruises (2.7 \times 2 cm and 3.2 \times 1.8 cm) on her inner right shoulder consistent with blunt trauma on 24 March. A later medical opinion linked the crisis to psycho-emotional stress, noting her chronic hypertension and age made it dangerous.

Police video footage (examined in later inquiries) showed officers surrounding her, examining the poster, warning of force, lifting her after she sat down, and placing her in the car with no visible special restraints or strikes, though she offered some resistance near the vehicle. A second angle from a nearby building confirmed multiple uniformed officers present.

The applicant complained to prosecutors on 11 May 2007 of unlawful arrest, use of force amounting to degrading treatment, and health damage. Pre-investigation inquiries (including a video transcript) produced two refusals to open a criminal case under Article 286 of the Criminal Code (abuse of office). Investigators accepted police statements that she had been lawfully apprehended around 11.30 a.m. for an administrative offence under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (participation in an unauthorised rally) or Article 19.3 (disobeying lawful orders), that force was a proportionate response to resistance, and that bruises could have resulted from her own struggles. No officers were identified despite the video and the large-scale police deployment that day. Domestic courts upheld the refusals.

In 2009–2011 civil proceedings the applicant sought compensation. A district court found the arrest (lasting over five hours, far exceeding the three-hour statutory limit) unlawful: although officers had a basis to prevent an administrative offence, they breached procedural requirements (no escort/arrest records, no subsequent proceedings) and acted disproportionately. It awarded 30,000 roubles for non-pecuniary damage arising from the deprivation of liberty and associated mental/physical suffering (including the crisis). The regional court reduced this to 10,000 roubles, confirming the unlawfulness of the detention but finding no causal link to later cardiac treatment. Officers remained unidentified.

These facts underpin the Court’s later findings of violations of Article 5 § 1 (arbitrary detention lacking a proper factual or legal basis and procedural safeguards) and Article 3 (unjustified force causing injury and a deficient investigation that failed to identify the officers involved).

The case of Gremina v. Russia (no. 17054/08) concerns the 24 March 2007 arrest of 70-year-old Liliya Gremina by police in Nizhniy Novgorod, who used force to prevent her from attending the unauthorized “Dissenters’ March.” She alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (arbitrary/unlawful arrest and detention) and Article 3 (degrading treatment via unjustified force harming her health, plus ineffective investigation).

Unaware the rally had been banned, Gremina carried a rolled-up anti-government poster in a bag. Near Gorkiy Square, officers stopped her, inspected the bag, unrolled the poster on camera, and ordered her onto a bus. She refused, sat on the ground in protest, and was lifted by three officers who twisted her arms, dragged her to a car, pushed her inside (striking her back), and transferred her to a bus. Held there until about 3 p.m., she was taken to Avtozavodskiy police station around 3:30–4 p.m., made to stand in a basement corridor, and suffered a hypertensive crisis. An ambulance treated her at 4:57 p.m.; she declined hospital admission.

Medical records confirmed a hypertensive crisis (linked to her chronic condition, age, and psycho-emotional stress) and two bruises on her right shoulder from blunt trauma, consistent with being dragged. Police video (corroborated by a bystander recording) showed officers surrounding her, extracting the poster, and using force after she sat down, with little visible resistance as they lifted her legs into the car.

The Government claimed lawful apprehension at 11:30 a.m. for displaying a poster and resisting orders, with minimal force used and video-recorded; no administrative case proceeded due to her illness.

Gremina’s 11 May 2007 criminal complaint alleged unlawful arrest, excessive force, and degrading treatment. Investigators repeatedly refused to open proceedings (21 May 2007 and 23 January 2009), finding officers acted to prevent an administrative offence (CAO Articles 20.2, 19.3) with justified “non-aggressive” force under the Police Act; bruises were attributed to her resistance. Courts upheld the refusals. Despite video, no officers were identified, and no documents (escort/arrest records) were drawn up. Detention lasted over five hours, exceeding the three-hour CAO limit.

In 2009–2011 civil proceedings, the District Court found the detention unlawful (disproportionate, undocumented, exceeding time limits) despite a possible preventive purpose, awarding 30,000 RUB non-pecuniary damages. The Regional Court reduced this to 10,000 RUB, acknowledging mental/physical suffering from the liberty restriction but deeming the original sum excessive. Pecuniary claims for later heart treatment were dismissed for lack of causal link.

The ECHR held the arrest arbitrary and unlawful under Article 5 § 1, lacking factual basis or grounds for escort to the station. Unjustified force constituted degrading treatment under Article 3, damaging her health. The investigation was ineffective, as authorities made no effort to identify officers despite video evidence.

**CASE OF GREMINA v. RUSSIA (Application no. 17054/08), ECtHR, 26 May 2020 (final 26 August 2020)**

She alleged a blow to the lower back during this process. An ambulance was called at approximately 4:42 p.m.; she received treatment but declined hospital admission.

Pre-investigation inquiries (including review of the police video) repeatedly concluded that officers had acted lawfully to prevent an administrative offence under the Code of Administrative Offences (participation in an unauthorised rally or failure to obey a lawful order). The court awarded RUB 30 000 for non-pecuniary damage arising from mental and physical suffering (including the hypertensive crisis). The Regional Court (24 May 2011) reduced the award to RUB 10 000, while confirming the unlawfulness of the detention. Claims for pecuniary damage related to later cardiac treatment were dismissed for lack of causation.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints of arbitrary arrest and detention (Article 5 § 1), unjustified use of force amounting to degrading treatment (Article 3 substantive) and an ineffective investigation that failed to identify the officers involved despite video evidence (Article 3 procedural).

The case of P.T. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 1122/12) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the right to respect for private life, arising from the unnecessary disclosure of the applicant’s sensitive medical information. The applicant, a Moldovan national born in 1978 and residing in Sângera, is HIV-positive. In 2011 he attended a medical examination at the Chișinău Military Centre for the purpose of obtaining a military service record book. After disclosing his condition, which the doctors confirmed, he received on 11 July 2011 an exemption certificate in lieu of the record book. The certificate stated that he was exempted from military service under Section 5 of the Medical Standards contained in Defence Ministry order no. 177 of 2003. It was issued in accordance with the model prescribed by Government Decision no. 864 of 17 August 2005, which required the certificate to identify the precise section of the Medical Standards as the ground for exemption.

Section 5 of those Standards addresses immunodeficiency disorders of congenital or acquired origin that are accompanied by pathological changes in the haematopoietic system or other organs; fitness for service is assessed according to the degree of functional impairment of the affected organ or system. Because both the Medical Standards and the Defence Ministry order had been published in the Official Gazette and were expressly identified by number and date on the certificate, any person examining the document could readily determine that the exemption related to an immunodeficiency condition, thereby revealing the applicant’s HIV status.

Domestic law made production of the military record book or exemption certificate obligatory in a wide range of everyday situations. All citizens aged 16 and over must hold a national identity card; the competent authorities could issue identity cards, passports or register a change of residence for persons of military age only after military registration or official exemption. The applicant therefore had to present the exemption certificate when he renewed his identity card in August 2011. The same document was also required when concluding employment contracts and in other circumstances provided by law, including requests by private companies.

A comparable challenge brought by another HIV-positive individual, B., who sought a certificate omitting any reference to Section 5, was rejected by the Supreme Court of Justice on 15 April 2010. The court held that the certificate did not identify a specific illness (Section 5 covering several conditions) and was intended only for a limited circle of state authorities, so no disclosure of confidential information had occurred. Subsequent complaints by B. were likewise dismissed.

Individual litigants lacked standing to seize the Constitutional Court. In November 2012, however, that court, acting on an application by the Ombudsman, declared the requirement to indicate the specific section of the Medical Standards unconstitutional. It observed that the published nature of the Standards rendered the intended “coding” ineffective and that the obligatory production of the certificate to both public and private bodies constituted a disproportionate interference with private life. The Government subsequently amended Decision no. 864 in February 2013, removing the requirement to state the ground for exemption.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: the inclusion, in a widely circulated official document, of information that, although coded, was readily decipherable and thereby disclosed the applicant’s HIV-positive status in circumstances where such disclosure was neither necessary nor justified by a legitimate aim.

The Government thereafter amended the decision (February 2013) so that exemption certificates no longer had to state the ground of exemption.

These facts underpin the complaint that the inclusion of identifiable medical data in a document required for routine official and private transactions amounted to an unnecessary and disproportionate interference with the applicant’s private life that pursued no legitimate aim.

The applicant, a Bosnian national born in 1962, faced criminal charges after a 5 April 2004 incident in which he allegedly damaged a neighbour’s house, then spat on and assaulted one police officer and verbally abused another. He was briefly arrested and released the next day. On 4 May 2004 the prosecutor ordered a psychiatric examination, which the applicant did not attend. He was indicted on 16 July 2004 for damaging another’s property and for assaulting an official in the performance of security duties.

Proceedings were repeatedly delayed. The applicant obtained court-appointed counsel (later replaced by counsel of his choice). In 2007 he missed a hearing, citing the need to attend a mental-health centre. The Municipal Court then ordered psychiatric examinations in 2007 and 2008; none took place until November 2010, when the applicant was forcibly taken after failing to appear voluntarily. The expert concluded that chronic psychological distress had produced symptoms approaching psychosis, rendering him incapable of participating in the proceedings, and recommended compulsory psychiatric treatment in an institution.

On 4 March 2011 the property-damage charge was terminated as time-barred. On 8 April 2011 the Municipal Court accepted the expert findings, adjourned the remaining assault charge until the applicant’s health improved sufficiently for him to stand trial, and referred him to the Social Work Centre. The Cantonal Court dismissed his appeal in June 2011.

The Social Work Centre then applied in non-contentious proceedings for mandatory institutional treatment. In November 2012 the Municipal Court dismissed that application, holding that only a criminal court could impose such a measure and that the applicant did not meet the statutory definition of a person with a mental disorder. It stated that criminal proceedings would resume once the decision became final. The applicant appealed in February 2013 (within the statutory time-limit); the appeal was rejected as inadmissible only in December 2015.

Meanwhile, without a prosecutor’s request to resume the adjourned criminal proceedings, the Municipal Court issued successive orders (December 2012, January, March, May and June 2013) requiring the applicant to undergo further psychiatric and psychological examinations, with judicial police to forcibly escort him if he refused. He was taken by force on 5 February, 8 May, 6 June and 19 June 2013. On 6 June four officers entered his home (owned by his father), informed him of the order, and, after he refused to accompany them and turned toward a staircase, handcuffed him in the presence of his family and transported him to hospital. An emergency report recorded three-to-four 1 cm haematoma on his right upper arm and noted his complaint of mental injury and anxiety. The officers’ report described the handcuffing as a “binding measure” applied without other coercion; a confirmation of the home search was left unsigned by the father.

The applicant lodged an objection with the judicial police on 10 June 2013, alleging unnecessary handcuffing in front of his ailing parents. After a conversation he accepted an informal resolution on condition that the officers be reprimanded. In July 2013 the Municipal Court again adjourned the criminal case on fresh expert evidence that the applicant suffered a permanent chronic psychological illness and remained incapable of participating. The Cantonal Court quashed that decision in April 2014, holding that the 2011 adjournment remained in force and that the prosecutor had never requested resumption; further examinations and a new adjournment were therefore meaningless. The prosecutor later withdrew the indictment, and the proceedings were terminated in October 2016.

The Constitutional Court had already found the original criminal proceedings excessively lengthy (February 2013) but later rejected the applicant’s Article 3 complaint concerning the 2013 escorts as manifestly ill-founded (July 2015). The applicant complained to the European Court that the repeated forcible escorts under orders issued after the criminal proceedings had been unlawfully continued violated Article 8, and that the 6 June 2013 handcuffing in front of his family constituted degrading treatment contrary to Article 3.

The case of Pranjić-M-Lukić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina concerns an applicant’s complaints of violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention arising from repeated forcible escorts (one involving handcuffing) to involuntary psychiatric and psychological examinations ordered in the course of criminal proceedings that had been adjourned.

In April 2004 the applicant allegedly damaged a neighbour’s property and assaulted police officers. He was indicted for those offences. From an early stage the authorities noted his mental-health problems. After he failed to appear at trial in 2007 citing the need to attend a mental-health centre, the Mostar Municipal Court ordered a psychiatric examination. A 2010 expert report concluded that chronic psychological distress rendered him unable to participate in the proceedings and recommended compulsory treatment. In April 2011 the Municipal Court terminated the property-damage charge as time-barred and adjourned the remaining assault charge until the applicant’s health improved, referring him to social-welfare authorities. The adjournment was upheld on appeal.

Despite the adjournment, and without any prosecutor’s request to resume the proceedings as required by the accusatory principle in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Municipal Court in December 2012 issued fresh orders for psychiatric and psychological examinations to determine the applicant’s fitness to stand trial and his mental state at the time of the alleged offence. The applicant objected that the proceedings remained adjourned and that related non-contentious proceedings were still pending; he refused to attend. The court nevertheless issued successive arrest warrants under Article 139 of the Code, resulting in the applicant being forcibly taken by judicial police to hospital on 5 February, 8 May, 6 June and 19 June 2013. Examinations either did not take place because of his requests for the experts to be recused or were conducted against his will.

On 6 June 2013 four judicial police officers entered the applicant’s home. After he refused to accompany them, stating that he had already been examined, they handcuffed him (despite no physical resistance) in the presence of his family and transported him to hospital. A subsequent medical report recorded small haematoma on his arm and his complaint of psychological injury. The officers’ reports stated that no other coercive measures had been used and that the examination itself passed without incident. The applicant lodged an objection with the judicial-police department alleging unnecessary handcuffing; the matter was resolved informally after he accepted an explanation of the officers’ conduct.

In July 2013 the Municipal Court again adjourned the criminal proceedings on the basis of new expert evidence confirming the applicant’s chronic incapacity. The Cantonal Court quashed that decision in 2014, holding that the entire continuation of the proceedings (and therefore the examinations) had been unlawful because the prosecutor had never requested resumption. The criminal case was finally terminated in 2016 after the prosecutor withdrew the indictment.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint under Article 3 was rejected as manifestly ill-founded. These facts form the basis of the Court’s findings that the court orders for the examinations were not “in accordance with the law” (Article 8) because the underlying criminal proceedings had not been lawfully resumed, and that the 6 June 2013 handcuffing constituted degrading treatment (Article 3) because it was not strictly necessary, the applicant was outnumbered and mentally vulnerable, and no waiver of the right not to be subjected to such treatment could be accepted.

The applicant company, a Moldovan quarry operator extracting limestone, gravel and sand since 2000, held a five-year licence issued on 27 December 2010. In March 2012 the Prosecutor General’s Office commissioned an expert report from the National Institute of Judicial Expertise on possible extractions outside the licensed area, volumes, values, unpaid taxes and environmental damage. The 1 June 2012 report found no extraction beyond the allocated surface yet stated that 1,400 cubic metres of minerals had been extracted unlawfully, valued the gravel and sand at 175,812 MDL, and provided no methodology or site visit details.

On 19 June 2012 the Prosecutor’s Office informed the Licensing Chamber of the alleged unlawful extraction of 1,400 cubic metres of undeclared sand, non-completion of tax forms and breaches of Article 39(b), (c) and (g) of the Mining Code, claiming 175,560 MDL State damage and noting an opened criminal investigation. The Licensing Chamber issued two successive one-month official warnings (2 July and 2 August 2012) requiring the company to remedy the unspecified breaches. The company received neither the prosecutor’s letter, the expert report nor any explanation of the accusations; it protested that the warnings were incomprehensible, challenged them in court (outcome unknown) and later produced evidence that it had declared all extracted minerals and submitted the required forms (initially without mineral-type distinction, as then permitted).

On 7 September 2012 the licence was revoked; the Licensing Chamber sought court confirmation. The company argued that the warnings remained vague, the experts lacked mining qualifications and had never visited the site or obtained company documents, any pre-2009 conduct should have been judged under the old Mining Code, only the Mining Authority (not the prosecutor) was competent, and all declarations and tax forms had in fact been filed. On 6 December 2012 the Centru District Court dismissed the revocation action: the expert report had not been produced by the competent Mining Authority, the experts’ conclusions were internally contradictory, and Mining Authority records confirmed full declarations.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal reversed on 28 February 2013, holding that the company had failed to comply with the two warnings and, for the first time, relying on an unmentioned 3 September 2012 expert report that allegedly showed extraction beyond the licensed area. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the company’s appeal on points of law on 26 June 2013 without addressing its arguments. On 16 April 2013 (communicated 17 July) the criminal investigation was discontinued after the prosecutor found that all minerals had been declared and the required forms completed. A subsequent revision request based on that discontinuation was rejected by the Supreme Court on 4 December 2013.

The company complained that the licence withdrawal interfered with its possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The European Court held that the interference lacked lawfulness because the warnings were so unclear that even specialist advice could not identify the alleged breaches, no expert report or further explanation was supplied, and the appellate judgment quashing the first-instance finding in the company’s favour contained insufficient reasoning. Proportionality was likewise not shown. A violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was therefore found.

Only the Mining Authority, it argued, was competent to initiate licence proceedings; the experts lacked qualifications.

On 7 September 2012 the Chamber revoked the licence and sought court confirmation. On 6 December 2012 the Centru District Court dismissed the action: the experts were incompetent (only the Mining Authority may conduct mining expertise), had not inspected the site, and produced internally contradictory findings, while the Mining Authority confirmed all quantities had been declared and forms submitted.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal reversed this on 28 February 2013, citing non-compliance with the warnings and, for the first time, a 3 September 2012 report alleging extra-area exploitation. It gave no reasons for rejecting the company’s arguments. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed an appeal on points of law on 26 June 2013.

On 16 April 2013 (served 17 July) the criminal investigation was discontinued after finding that the company had in fact declared all extracted minerals and completed the required forms. A revision request based on this decision was rejected on 4 December 2013.

Under Article 21 of the Licensing Law a licence may be withdrawn for failure to heed two warnings. The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the opacity of the warnings (even specialist advice could not clarify the accusations), the unexplained contradiction in the first expert report, the Court of Appeal’s reliance on new evidence and failure to address the company’s submissions, and the subsequent official finding that no undeclared extraction had occurred. These elements undermined both the lawfulness and the proportionality of the licence withdrawal.

The applicant company operated a limestone, gravel and sand quarry in Moldova since 2000 under a five-year licence issued on 27 December 2010. It claimed 1,400 m³ of undeclared sand extraction causing 175,560 MDL damage and noted a criminal investigation had begun, attaching the expert report. The company stated it could not understand the accusations, had declared all extractions and submitted the required forms to the Mining Authority (noting that earlier forms did not distinguish mineral types), and challenged the warnings in court (outcome unknown). It also argued that only the Mining Authority, not the Prosecutor, was competent to initiate such action.

The licence was revoked on 7 September 2012. The Chamber sought court confirmation on 11 September. The applicant contested the action as based on unclear or possibly inapplicable old-Code provisions, unnotified investigation documents, unqualified experts who had neither visited the site nor obtained company records, vague warnings, and its actual compliance with declarations and tax forms.

It held that the Mining Authority alone was competent to conduct mining expertise, the experts had not visited or obtained documents, their conclusions were contradictory (no extra area yet 1,400 m³ unlawful without explanation), and the Mining Authority confirmed that all quantities had been declared and all forms submitted. The Court of Appeal reversed this on 28 February 2013, finding non-compliance with the warnings and, for the first time, relying on a 3 September 2012 expert report alleging extra-area exploitation. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 26 June 2013, without addressing its arguments.

On 17 July 2013 the company’s head received the 16 April 2013 decision discontinuing the criminal investigation, which found that all extracted minerals had in fact been declared (albeit without type distinction) and the required forms completed. A subsequent revision request based on this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 4 December 2013.

These events form the basis of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the licence withdrawal interfered with peaceful enjoyment of possessions without fulfilling the requirements of lawfulness (unclear warnings lacking the expert report or any explanation, rendering them incomprehensible even with specialist advice) or proportionality (the first-instance judgment in the applicant’s favour being quashed without sufficient reasoning).

The applicant, Mihai Aftanache, a Romanian national born in 1982, has been insulin-dependent with type-1 diabetes since 1996 and receives disability benefits. On 30 March 2017, while unwell with a lingering cold, he visited a nearby pharmacy on his diabetologist’s advice. Feeling weak, he sat down; the pharmacist summoned an ambulance.

The ambulance arrived around noon with two nurses (M.G. and M.E.), a volunteer student and a driver. A paramedic suspected drug use despite the applicant’s denials and explanation of his diabetes. A blood test confirmed glucose imbalance, but no insulin was available. The applicant requested assistance to walk home for his prescribed treatment. The team refused, insisting on hospital transport first to test for prohibited substances. He was restrained on a stretcher inside the ambulance after declining transport. Police were called; two officers arrived, rejected his request to retrieve insulin from home (200 metres away) and escorted the ambulance to Timișoara Municipal Hospital (TMH).

At TMH, doctor O.T. was told by paramedics that the applicant was on drugs. Despite the applicant’s requests, insulin was withheld pending a drug test, which he refused. O.T. deemed the case non-emergency and directed transfer to Timișoara Psychiatric Hospital (TPH) under the same ambulance and police escort. At TPH the applicant was again restrained; staff attempted to administer calming injections, which he refused. He contacted his diabetologist, who could not speak with staff and instead sent a nurse. The applicant’s wife arrived and, with the nurse, opposed planned transfer to another psychiatric facility for supposed drug addiction. The applicant eventually agreed to testing and was returned to TMH. A drug test proved negative; insulin (in a non-prescribed dose) was then given. Severe anaemia was also noted. He declined further ambulance transport, collected his own insulin at home and proceeded to an infectious-diseases hospital.

TMH records listed hypothermia, headache, asthma, anaemia and insulin dependence. TPH records noted psychomotor agitation and “hetero-aggressive” behaviour, after which he was sent back for blood-sugar rebalancing. The applicant remained under police escort for approximately six hours.

On 4 April 2017 he filed a criminal complaint against the ambulance team for withholding treatment and thereby endangering his life. A police officer allegedly pressured him to withdraw it. The prosecutor interviewed the team (who described the applicant as aggressive and uncooperative), the police officer and obtained hospital and police records, but did not interview the diabetologist whose out-of-court statement detailed the applicant’s history and the events. On 22 May 2018 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation for lack of supporting evidence; the decision was upheld internally. Domestic courts confirmed the discontinuance, imposing costs on the applicant. A parallel administrative complaint to the public-health directorate was likewise unsuccessful after he could not afford expert fees.

The Mental Health Act permits non-voluntary psychiatric admission only on certified medical grounds and at the request of specified persons (including police); the Police Act authorises escort of persons posing danger or whose identity cannot be verified. No such certification or necessity assessment occurred.

At TMH, doctor O.T. likewise refused insulin pending a drug test, which the applicant declined. He contacted C.H., who was unable to speak with staff but dispatched a nurse colleague. The applicant’s wife also arrived and, with the nurse, emphasised that his condition stemmed from diabetes, not addiction. After several hours he consented to testing and was returned to TMH. Results were negative for drugs; insulin was administered (in a dose differing from his prescription). Tests also revealed severe anaemia, hypothermia, headache, bronchial asthma and fever. He declined further ambulance transport, collected his own insulin at home, and proceeded independently to an infectious-diseases hospital. Police custody lasted approximately six hours. Hospital records noted psychomotor agitation, hetero-aggressive behaviour and oppositional conduct at TPH.

C.H.’s detailed out-of-court statement on the applicant’s medical history and the day’s events was disregarded. On 22 May 2018 the prosecutor closed the investigation for lack of supporting evidence; this was upheld by the chief prosecutor and, on 23 August 2018, by the Timişoara District Court, which ordered the applicant to pay costs and the accused persons’ lawyers’ fees. An appeal was declared inadmissible. A parallel complaint to the Directorate for Public Health yielded no confirmation of misconduct; an expert examination required an unaffordable fee of 9 000 lei (his monthly disability income being 375 lei).

The applicant alleged violations of Article 2 (life endangered by refusal of insulin and lack of effective investigation) and Article 5 § 1 (arbitrary six-hour confinement). The Court found Article 2 applicable given the illness’s nature and absence of conclusive evidence that life was not at risk, and held that the investigation had been inadequate. It further found the confinement arbitrary, unlawful, outside any authorised exception, unnecessary, and the result of medical professionals’ failure to consider the applicant’s personal circumstances.

**Case of Aftanache v. Romania (App. no. 999/19)**

The applicant, Mihai Aftanache (born 1982), has been insulin-dependent with type-1 diabetes since 1996 and receives disability benefits. On 30 March 2017 he felt unwell after a 10-day cold. His diabetologist advised pharmacy medication. Around 11 a.m. he walked 200 metres to a pharmacy but sat down due to weakness; the pharmacist called an ambulance.

The ambulance arrived around noon with two nurses (M.G. and M.E.), a volunteer student, and a driver. Staff suspected drug use and confronted him. He denied this, explained his diabetes, and a blood test confirmed glucose imbalance. With no insulin available, he asked to be helped home for his treatment. They refused, stating they would first take him to hospital to check for prohibited drugs. He called emergency services again but was refused help as an ambulance was already present. He declined hospital transport. Staff closed the ambulance, restrained him on a stretcher, and called police. He alerted his wife amid the commotion.

Two police officers arrived. He explained his need for home insulin and denied drug use, requesting they accompany him home. They refused, assuring hospital insulin, and escorted the ambulance to Timişoara Municipal Hospital (TMH). There, doctor O.T. heard his diabetes explanation but was told by paramedics he was on drugs. O.T. refused insulin pending a drug blood test, which he declined. Finding no emergency, O.T. sent him to Timişoara Psychiatric Hospital (TPH) by the same ambulance and police.

At TPH he was again restrained; staff tried to inject calming medication, which he refused, untying himself. He called his diabetologist, who could not speak to staff and contacted a known nurse to explain his unbalanced diabetes. His wife arrived and, with the nurse, insisted the issue was his chronic disease, not addiction. Staff planned transfer to another psychiatric hospital for supposed drug treatment. He eventually agreed to testing and was returned to TMH under escort.

Tests at TMH showed no drugs but severe anaemia, hypothermia, headache, asthma, and insulin dependence. He received a non-prescribed insulin dose, then left with his wife (after taking his own insulin at home) for an infectious-diseases hospital. TPH records noted agitation, aggression, and opposition; TMH noted his conditions. He remained in police custody for about six hours.

On 4 April 2017 he lodged a criminal complaint against the ambulance team for withholding treatment and endangering his life, detailing events. A police officer allegedly urged withdrawal, claiming no crime and insufficient evidence; he refused. He was fined for verbal abuse (annulled by court in October 2017 as unproven). His complaint about the officer was joined to the main one.

The prosecutor interviewed him, the officer, ambulance staff (who described him as aggressive, uncooperative, and refusing identity/treatment, necessitating handcuffs and planned confinement), and reviewed records. His diabetologist’s statement (describing his history, awareness of imbalances, the day’s events, and staff refusal to speak) was allegedly ignored. On 22 May 2018 the prosecutor closed the case, finding no supporting evidence. This was upheld by the prosecutor-in-chief (with costs) and, after complaint, by the Timişoara District Court (23 August 2018) and Court of Appeal (29 November 2018, inadmissible; further costs and fees awarded against him).

He also complained to the Directorate for Public Health (May 2017) of misconduct. It found records unsupportive and referred negligence to a commission, which required an unaffordable expert fee (RON 9,000 vs. his RON 375 monthly benefits).

These facts underpin alleged Article 2 failures (no effective investigation of life-endangering insulin refusal given his illness) and Article 5 §1 (arbitrary six-hour hospital confinement not justified as necessary or falling under authorised exceptions, ignoring his circumstances).

The case of Tolmachev v. Russia (Application no. 42182/11) concerns a journalist's unsuccessful defence of two sets of civil defamation claims in Russian courts arising from newspaper articles criticising two judges. The applicant, Aleksandr Tolmachev, owned and edited Argumenty Nedeli Yug through his company IPT. He alleged that the domestic courts had failed to apply Article 10 Convention standards on freedom of expression.

In May 2010 the newspaper published an editorial, “An Incident Involving the Judiciary,” following earlier reports that Ms M., president of the S. District Court, had unlawfully appropriated communal space in her apartment block. The article described her as a “lawless person in a judge’s robe,” referred to her “unlawful position” and “tainted honour,” and asserted that she and similar judges used their powers for personal gain and should not hold office. A July 2010 article repeated that she had “usurped communal space.” Ms M. sued for defamation. The Oktyabrskiy District Court treated most passages as unproven statements of fact rather than value judgments. It rejected the applicant’s supporting document (which did not name Ms M.) and a neighbour’s testimony (deemed unreliable because of prior complaints). The court awarded Ms M. RUB 500 000 from the applicant and the same sum from IPT, plus costs, stressing that allegations against a sitting judge were especially cynical. It did not examine the applicant’s means. The Rostov Regional Court reduced each non-pecuniary award to RUB 100 000 (total liability for the applicant, as IPT’s sole owner, approximately RUB 215 000) on proportionality grounds but left the factual characterisation intact.

Separately, in 2008 the newspaper reported that former L. District Court judge Ms A. had been “caught taking a bribe” around the time of her resignation and a pre-investigation inquiry. A later article described bribe-taking as “standard practice.” Ms A. sued, then withdrew the claim; proceedings were discontinued. After a 2010 article again labelled her a “bribe-taker,” she sued once more but died. Her minor son then brought a fresh claim in his own name, arguing that the three articles had defamed his mother and thereby himself. The District Court refused the applicant’s request to adjourn and heard the case in his absence. It held that the son had standing because untruths about a deceased parent also injured the child, classified every contested statement as an unproven fact, and made no reference to the applicant’s journalistic status or the public-interest context of judicial integrity. It awarded the son RUB 500 000 from the applicant, RUB 500 000 from IPT and RUB 250 000 from the publisher, citing the boy’s distress and school-related stigma but giving no calculation method or detailed financial analysis of the defendants. The Regional Court upheld the judgment verbatim.

The European Court found that both sets of proceedings violated Article 10. The domestic courts had omitted essential elements of the Convention analysis: they had not carefully distinguished value judgments (opinions on judicial fitness) from statements of fact, had failed to weigh the public interest in scrutinising judges against reputation, and had imposed very substantial damages without demonstrating a reasonable relationship of proportionality to any injury suffered. The reasons given were relevant but insufficient.

The applicant, a journalist and sole owner of the legal entity IPT (which edited the local newspaper Argumenty Nedeli Yug), faced two sets of successful civil defamation claims in Russian courts over articles criticizing two district court judges in Rostov-on-Don. He alleged that the courts failed to apply ECHR Article 10 standards on freedom of expression.

In the first proceedings, the newspaper published an editorial on 27 May 2010 titled “An Incident Involving the Judiciary.” It followed earlier articles alleging that Ms M. (president of the S. District Court) had unlawfully appropriated communal space in her apartment building. The piece described her as a “lawless person in a judge’s robe,” referred to her “unlawful position,” claimed she had “disgraced herself,” and asserted that people like her “should not be vested with judicial powers” because they used those powers for personal gain and disgraced the judiciary. A further article on 15 July 2010 stated that another official had “covered up” for Ms M., who had “usurped communal space.”

Ms M. sued for defamation. On 4 October 2010 the Oktyabrskiy District Court allowed the claim in part. It treated most of the impugned passages as unproven statements of fact (rather than value judgments), rejecting the applicant’s supporting official document (which did not name Ms M.) and a witness (deemed unreliable). It ordered retractions and awarded Ms M. RUB 500,000 in non-pecuniary damages from each of the applicant and IPT, plus fees, for a total of approximately EUR 24,360. The court highlighted the particular cynicism of allegations against a sitting judge but did not assess the applicant’s financial means. On appeal the Rostov Regional Court reduced the damages to RUB 100,000 each (total liability for the applicant of approximately EUR 5,250), citing the need for proportionality so as not to impose an excessive burden on the media.

In the second set of proceedings, articles published in 2008 and 2010 referred to former L. District Court judge Ms A. as having been “caught taking a bribe” and as a “bribe-taker,” describing such conduct as long-standing judicial practice. Ms A. initially sued but later withdrew the claim; the proceedings were discontinued. After a decision not to open a criminal case against her and her subsequent death, her minor son (Mr A.) brought a fresh claim in November 2010, asserting that the articles had caused his mother immense suffering and had also harmed him.

On 28 February 2011 the District Court, sitting in the applicant’s absence after rejecting his adjournment request, found for the claimant. It held that the son had standing because the statements defamed him as well, classified the passages as unproven statements of fact rather than value judgments, and made no reference to the applicant’s status as a journalist or the public-interest context of judicial accountability. It ordered retractions and awarded RUB 500,000 each from the applicant and IPT (plus RUB 250,000 from the publisher), totalling approximately EUR 31,250. The court alluded vaguely to the defendants’ financial situations and to the son’s distress and schoolyard repercussions. The Regional Court upheld the judgment in full.

Both awards greatly exceeded the then-applicable monthly minimum wage of RUB 4,330. The domestic courts’ treatment of the statements, their failure to weigh competing interests, and the size of the awards formed the core of the alleged Article 10 violations.

The case of Tolmachev v. Russia (Application no. 42182/11) concerns a journalist's complaints that Russian courts violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression in two sets of defamation proceedings. The applicant, Aleksandr Mikhaylovich Tolmachev (born 1955), was a journalist and sole owner of Informatsionno-pravovoy Tsentr Aleksandra Tolmacheva (IPT), which edited the local newspaper Argumenty Nedeli Yug in Rostov-on-Don.

The first proceedings arose from an editorial published on 27 May 2010 entitled “An Incident Involving the Judiciary.” It criticised Ms M., President of the S. District Court, for allegedly usurping communal space in her apartment block to the detriment of neighbours and using her position and colleagues to protect her “tainted honour.” The article described her as a “lawless person in a judge’s robe,” referred to her “unlawful position,” stated that she had “disgraced herself,” and asserted that people like her “should not be vested with judicial powers” as they used them “for their personal gain.” A further article on 15 July 2010 accused her of usurping communal space. Ms M. sued the applicant, IPT and others for defamation, seeking retraction of the extracts.

On 4 October 2010 the Oktyabrskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don upheld most of the claim. It treated the statements as unproven allegations of unlawful and immoral conduct (statements of fact) rather than value judgments, despite the applicant’s reliance on an official document about partitions and a witness’s testimony. It dismissed the document as not naming Ms M. and the witness as unreliable. The court ordered retractions and awarded Ms M. 500,000 roubles (RUB) in non-pecuniary damages from each of the applicant and IPT, plus costs, totalling approximately 24,360 euros (EUR). It described the allegations as “particularly cynical” given Ms M.’s judicial office but did not assess the applicant’s finances. On 13 December 2010 the Rostov Regional Court reduced the damages to 100,000 RUB each (applicant’s total liability approximately 5,250 EUR, against a monthly minimum wage of 4,330 RUB) on proportionality grounds, while leaving costs unchanged. There was no indication the judgment was enforced.

The second proceedings concerned articles about Ms A., a former L. District Court judge. A 31 July 2008 article stated she “was caught taking a bribe” and that a criminal case would be opened after her resignation. A September 2008 article referred to her as having been “caught taking bribes,” describing this as “standard practice.” After an initial claim that she later withdrew, a 10 June 2010 article called her a “bribe-taker.” Ms A. died on 13 July 2010. Her minor son (born 1995) then sued in his own name on 9 November 2010, claiming the articles had caused his mother and him immense suffering.

On 28 February 2011, after refusing the applicant’s postponement request, the District Court examined the case in his absence. It held that the son had standing because defamation of the deceased also affected him, treated the statements as unproven facts rather than opinions, and made no reference to journalistic context or public interest. It ordered retractions and awarded 500,000 RUB each from the applicant and IPT (approximately 25,000 EUR total) plus 250,000 RUB from the publisher, vaguely citing the defendants’ finances and the son’s distress at school. On 5 May 2011 the Regional Court upheld the judgment in full. Again, enforcement was not confirmed.

The applicant alleged that the courts failed to apply Convention standards: they omitted to distinguish value judgments from facts, ignored the public-interest context of criticism of judges, failed to balance freedom of expression against reputation, and imposed disproportionate awards without adequate reasoning. The European Court of Human Rights later found a violation of Article 10 on these grounds.

**CASE OF NEŠIĆ v. MONTENEGRO (Application no. 12131/18)**

The applicant, Ilija Nešić (born 1931, resident in Tivat), lawfully purchased two plots of land (originally nos. 697/1 and 698/1) from a private seller on 21 October 1980 and was registered as owner in the Real Estate Register the following day. Over time the plots were subdivided and renumbered; the disputed portions became plots 955/3 and 955/4. These plots lie on the seashore and form part of a concrete beach and marina.

On 17 October 2006 the State brought civil proceedings seeking a declaration that it was the owner of the two plots. On 1 October 2014 the Kotor Court of First Instance inspected the site and confirmed the land’s location on the seacoast. On 19 December 2014 that court ruled for the State. It accepted that the applicant had acquired title lawfully in 1980 but held that the land formed part of the coastal zone (specifically the seacoast itself). Under sections 2 and 4 of the 1992 Coastal Zone Act and sections 11 and 13 of the 2009 State Property Act, such land is State property and a common resource that cannot be privately possessed. The applicant’s rights therefore terminated automatically upon the entry into force of those statutes (the Coastal Zone Act on 11 April 1992). The court added that the plots had become State property by operation of law.

The High Court (25 September 2015) and Supreme Court (16 December 2015) upheld the judgment, the High Court specifying that the applicant retained a right of use “until dispossession.” The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s subsequent constitutional complaint on 23 October 2017, finding no breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because any restriction or deprivation had a statutory basis.

Separately, on 14 October 2016 the applicant sued to be registered as user of the plots until dispossession. The first-instance court granted that claim on 13 April 2017, noting his pre-emptive right of use and, with reference to section 30 of the Coastal Zone Act, his entitlement to compensation under the expropriation legislation. The High Court and Supreme Court confirmed the decision in 2018. As of June 2019 the Real Estate Register recorded the State as sole owner and the applicant as user.

Relevant domestic law (1992 and 2007 Constitutions, 1980 and 2009 Property Acts, Coastal Zone Act, State Property Act and 2000 Expropriation Act) recognises lawful private acquisition, permits deprivation or restriction of property only in the public interest and on a statutory basis, and, for former owners of coastal-zone land acquired before 1992, expressly provides for compensation according to expropriation rules together with a pre-emptive right of use. No individual expropriation decision identifying a beneficiary, defining public interest or fixing compensation was ever issued in respect of the applicant’s land, and no compensation has been paid.

The application alleges a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from the automatic transfer of title to the State by operation of the coastal-zone legislation, without any prior individual decision and without the compensation that the same legislation itself contemplates.

The case of Nešić v. Montenegro (Application no. 12131/18) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the alleged unlawful deprivation of the applicant’s property. The applicant, Ilija Nešić, a Serbian national born in 1931 and residing in Tivat, purchased two plots of land (registered as nos. 697/1 and 698/1) from a private seller on 21 October 1980. He was registered as their owner in the Real Estate Register the following day. Over subsequent years the plots were subdivided and renumbered, eventually including plots 955/3 and 955/4.

On 17 October 2006 the Montenegrin State commenced civil proceedings against the applicant seeking a declaration that it owned these plots. During the proceedings the Court of First Instance in Kotor inspected the site on 1 October 2014 and established that the land lay on the seashore. On 19 December 2014 the court found for the State. It accepted that the applicant had lawfully acquired title in 1980 but held that the land formed part of the coastal zone (specifically the seacoast itself), comprising a concrete beach and marina. Under sections 2 and 4 of the 1992 Coastal Zone Act and sections 11 and 13 of the 2009 State Property Act such land constitutes State property and a common resource that no private person may possess. The applicant’s ownership therefore ceased automatically upon the entry into force of those statutes and the delimitation of the coastal zone.

The High Court in Podgorica dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 25 September 2015, confirming the first-instance reasoning and adding that he retained a right of use “until dispossession.” The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 16 December 2015. On 23 October 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a constitutional complaint, holding that any restriction of property rights was based on law and therefore compatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In parallel, the applicant instituted separate proceedings in October 2016 seeking registration as the user of the plots until dispossession. The Court of First Instance granted that request on 13 April 2017, recognising a pre-emptive right of use and noting that former lawful owners were entitled to compensation under the expropriation provisions (section 30 of the Coastal Zone Act). Higher courts confirmed the judgment in 2018. By June 2019 the Real Estate Register recorded the State as sole owner and the applicant as user.

The relevant domestic framework includes Article 45 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 58 of the 2007 Constitution, both of which protect property and permit deprivation only in the public interest and against just compensation. The 1992 Coastal Zone Act defines the coastal zone (including a seacoast strip at least six metres wide) as State property, while granting pre-1992 lawful owners a right to compensation upon dispossession in accordance with expropriation law and a pre-emptive right of use. The 2009 State Property Act reaffirms that the coastal zone consists of common resources that cannot be privately owned. The 2000 Expropriation Act sets out the procedure for establishing public interest, identifying beneficiaries and determining compensation.

The alleged violation centres on the automatic legislative transfer of ownership without any individual expropriation decision served on the applicant and without any award of the compensation that the same legislation expressly contemplated, together with the lack of clarity as to the precise moment and legal mechanism of the deprivation.

The case of Nešić v. Montenegro (Application no. 12131/18) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that the applicant, a Serbian national residing in Tivat, was deprived of lawfully acquired land without any individual decision or compensation.

In October 1980 the applicant purchased two plots of land (originally registered as nos. 697/1 and 698/1) from a private individual and was entered as owner in the Real Estate Register the following day. Over subsequent years the plots were subdivided and re-numbered; the parcels ultimately in dispute became nos. 955/3 and 955/4.

In October 2006 the State brought a civil action seeking a declaration that it was the owner of these two plots. During a site visit in October 2014 the first-instance court established that the land lay on the seashore itself and formed part of a concrete beach and marina. In December 2014 that court held that, although the applicant had acquired title lawfully in 1980, the land fell within the coastal zone as defined by the 1992 Coastal Zone Act and the 2009 State Property Act. Those statutes declared the seacoast and coastal zone to be State property and a common resource that no private person could possess. Consequently the applicant’s ownership had ceased automatically upon the entry into force of the relevant legislation. The High Court and Supreme Court confirmed this reasoning in 2015, adding that the applicant would remain entitled to use the land “until dispossession.” A constitutional appeal was dismissed in 2017.

Separately, in 2016 the applicant sued to be registered as user of the plots pending dispossession. The courts granted that request in 2017–2018, noting that former lawful owners enjoyed a pre-emptive right of use and were entitled to compensation under the expropriation legislation. The Real Estate Register now records the State as sole owner and the applicant as user.

The applicable domestic framework includes constitutional guarantees that property may be taken only in the public interest and against just compensation. The 1992 Coastal Zone Act (in force from April 1992) defined the seacoast as a strip reaching at least six metres beyond the highest storm-wave line and declared it State property, while section 30 expressly preserved a right to expropriation-style compensation and a pre-emptive right of use for owners who had acquired title lawfully before the Act. The 2009 State Property Act reaffirmed that the coastal zone constitutes a common resource incapable of private ownership. The Expropriation Act sets out a detailed administrative procedure requiring an express finding of public interest, identification of the beneficiary, and assessment of compensation before title can pass.

The applicant’s complaint is that these statutes effected an automatic transfer of title without any individual expropriation decision, without payment of the compensation the same statutes purported to confer, and amid legal uncertainty as to when and how dispossession would occur. The facts therefore centre on the contrast between the applicant’s undisputed 1980 acquisition, the subsequent legislative characterisation of the land as inalienable State property, the complete absence of any compensatory award, and the courts’ recognition that compensation and continued use were in principle available yet never implemented through the expropriation mechanism.
