The European Court of Human Rights case of Kandarakis v. Greece (applications nos. 48345/12, 48348/12 and 67463/12) arose from complaints by two Athens Bar Association lawyers, Alexandros Kandarakis and Michail Kandarakis. They alleged that Greek courts denied them access to court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (and related property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) by refusing locus standi to claim lawyers’ fees awarded in expropriation proceedings.

Under the Expropriation Code (Law no. 2882/2001, Articles 8 and 18) and related provisions of the Lawyers’ Code, amounts awarded for court costs and lawyers’ fees in expropriation cases must be deposited by the liable party (typically a public entity or company such as ERGOSE AE) into the Consignment Deposits and Loans Fund for the benefit of the bar association with which the expropriated party’s lawyers are registered. The bar association then withholds a statutory percentage and remits the balance to the lawyer. Fees form the bulk of awarded costs but are treated as belonging initially to the bar association rather than the individual lawyer.

In the first two applications the applicants, though registered in Athens, had been authorised by local-bar lawyers to appear in expropriation proceedings before the Kalavryta and Korinthos first-instance courts. Those courts fixed substantial fees (EUR 54,387.75 plus EUR 320 costs; EUR 18,405 plus EUR 120 costs). The liable company deposited the sums for the benefit of the local (Kalavryta and Korinthos) bar associations. The applicants applied to the Athens first-instance court seeking an order that the deposits be made instead for the Athens Bar Association, arguing they had performed the actual work. Both applications were dismissed for lack of locus standi: only the relevant bar association was the statutory beneficiary and could initiate proceedings. The applicants could at most bring a subrogation action under Article 72 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but only after pleading that the Athens Bar had neglected or refused to act. Appeals and cassation appeals (judgments nos. 5140/2010 and 694/2012; 5139/2010 and 693/2012) confirmed this reasoning.

In the third application the proceedings had taken place in Athens itself and the Ministry deposited EUR 40,683.91 for the Athens Bar Association; the Fund nevertheless refused to transfer the money. The applicant’s own application seeking an order against the Fund succeeded at first instance and on appeal, but the Court of Cassation (judgment no. 1922/2008) reversed, holding that only the bar association itself could sue.

Subsequent attempts by the Athens Bar Association itself produced mixed and delayed results. In the Kalavryta matter the bar’s application was initially rejected; an appeal was allowed and the case remained pending before the Patras Court of Appeal. In the Korinthos matter half the fees had already been transferred by the local bar, but the remainder was held time-barred (31 December 2012). Only in the third case did the bar obtain a final order; the Fund then paid the sum, the bar withheld its percentage and remitted the balance to the applicant.

The Court later found that the applicants had been left without a clear, practical and effective opportunity to assert their claims, that later payments (where they occurred) did not deprive them of victim status, and that the restriction on access to court was disproportionate.

The case of Kandarakis v. Greece (applications nos. 48345/12, 48348/12 and 67463/12) was brought by two Greek lawyers, Alexandros Kandarakis (born 1938) and Michail Kandarakis (born 1979), both registered with the Athens Bar Association and living in Athens. They complained of a denial of access to court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (and related property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) after Greek courts refused them standing to recover lawyers’ fees awarded in expropriation proceedings.

Under Greek expropriation law (principally Articles 8 and 18 of Law no. 2882/2001 and Article 9 of Law no. 1093/1980), the party liable for compensation must deposit court costs and lawyers’ fees into the Consignment Deposits and Loans Fund for the benefit of the bar association with which the expropriated party’s lawyers are registered. The bar association withholds a statutory percentage before remitting the balance to the lawyers. The applicants had represented clients in three sets of expropriation proceedings (sometimes after authorisation by a locally registered lawyer) and sought to have the deposited sums redirected to the Athens Bar Association.

In the first set of proceedings, the Kalavryta first-instance court (judgment 56/2007) awarded EUR 54,387.75 in fees (plus EUR 320 costs). The sums were deposited for the Kalavryta Bar Association. The applicants applied to the Athens first-instance court for redirection to their own association, arguing they had performed the actual representation. That court (judgment 119/2009), the Athens Court of Appeal (5140/2010) and the Court of Cassation (694/2012) all held they lacked locus standi: only the relevant bar association could claim the funds; the lawyers could at most bring a subrogation action (Article 72 of the Code of Civil Procedure) if they pleaded that their own association had neglected or refused to act. The Athens Bar Association later brought its own claim; at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings the matter remained pending before the Patras Court of Appeal.

In the second set, the Korinthos court (judgment 54/2007) awarded EUR 18,405 in fees (plus EUR 120 costs), deposited for the Korinthos Bar Association. Identical applications by the lawyers were dismissed on the same standing grounds (Athens first-instance judgment 118/2009, appeal 5139/2010, Cassation 693/2012). A subsequent Athens Bar Association claim was also dismissed, the Court of Appeal noting that part of the fees had already been transferred and that the remainder of the lawyers’ claim had become time-barred.

In the third set, the Athens Court of Appeal (judgment 4531/2002) awarded EUR 40,683.91, deposited for the Athens Bar Association, but the Fund refused to release the money. The applicant’s personal application was ultimately rejected by the Court of Cassation (1922/2008) on the same standing ground. Only after the Athens Bar Association itself sued in 2013 did the courts order payment; the Fund complied, the association deducted its percentage and remitted the balance to the applicant.

The applicants argued that the rigid requirement of bar-association action, coupled with the impracticality of the subrogation remedy, left them without a clear, practical and effective means of asserting their claim to fees that had already been judicially quantified. They maintained they remained victims even after later payments obtained through the associations. The Government contended that the legislative scheme pursued the legitimate aim of protecting both lawyers and bar associations and that alternative procedures existed.

The ECHR case of Kandarakis v. Greece (applications 48345/12, 48348/12 and 67463/12) concerned two Athens Bar Association lawyers (Alexandros and Michail Kandarakis) who represented clients in three sets of expropriation proceedings. Courts awarded costs and lawyers’ fees, which were deposited in the Consignment Deposits and Loans Fund to the benefit of the relevant bar association under the Expropriation Code (Law 2882/2001, Arts. 8 and 18). The applicants were denied locus standi when they sought to have the sums transferred to the Athens Bar (with which they were registered), as domestic courts held that only the bar association itself could initiate such proceedings. Lawyers could at most bring a subrogation action if the bar neglected or refused to act. They complained of a violation of Article 6 § 1 (access to court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In application 48345/12, the applicants (authorised by a Kalavryta Bar lawyer) obtained a 2007 Kalavryta court judgment awarding EUR 320 in costs and EUR 54,387.75 in fees. ERGOSE AE deposited these sums for the Kalavryta Bar. The applicants applied to the Athens first-instance court to redirect them to the Athens Bar, arguing they alone had represented the clients. The court dismissed for lack of locus standi (judgment 119/2009), a ruling upheld on appeal (5140/2010) and by the Court of Cassation (694/2012). The Athens Bar later applied in 2013; after mixed first-instance and appellate outcomes, the matter remained pending before the Patras Court of Appeal at the time of the ECHR proceedings.

In application 48348/12, similar facts arose from a 2007 Korinthos judgment awarding EUR 120 in costs and EUR 18,405 in fees, deposited for the Korinthos Bar. The applicants’ identical application was dismissed on the same locus-standi grounds plus a failure to plead finality of the judgment (118/2009), with appeals rejected (5139/2010 and Cassation 693/2012). The Athens Bar’s 2013 application was later dismissed on appeal (1624/2018) after partial payment had occurred and the remaining claim had become time-barred.

In application 67463/12, the first applicant obtained a 2002 Athens Court of Appeal award of EUR 40,683.91 in costs and fees. The Ministry deposited this for the Athens Bar, but the Fund refused to transfer it. The applicant’s application to compel payment was rejected at first instance (1635/2005), allowed on appeal (5162/2005), but reversed by the Court of Cassation (1922/2008) on the ground that only the bar association could sue. The Athens Bar’s 2013 application succeeded through all instances, after which the Fund paid the sum; the Bar withheld its statutory percentage and remitted the balance to the applicant.

Domestic law (including the Lawyers’ Code) treated the bar association as the formal beneficiary to protect fee collection and enable a statutory withholding, with lawyers’ fees conceptually distinct from party costs. Subrogation (Code of Civil Procedure Art. 72) or a separate fee-recovery action remained theoretically available, but the applicants’ direct attempts were uniformly rejected. Even after eventual payment in the third case, the applicants retained victim status. The ECHR found the restriction on access to court disproportionate, as no clear, practical and effective means existed to assert the claim.
001-202755:
The case of Sļadzevskis v. Latvia (ECHR, Application no. 32003/13) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention due to the excessive length of civil proceedings involving divorce, child custody, contact rights, and support. The applicant, a Latvian national residing in London since at least early 2005, initiated the case. He married V.S. in 1994; their son N.S. was born in 1995 and their daughter E.S. in 2002. N.S. lived with the applicant in the UK from March 2006. On 20 December 2006, Latvian authorities viewed an incident as the applicant’s attempted forcible removal of E.S. to the UK, leading to temporary suspension of his care rights over her; E.S. remained with V.S.

On 11 March 2005 the applicant applied to the Riga Regional Court for divorce, requesting that both children reside with him and that V.S. pay child support. Proceedings began on 13 April 2005. V.S. counterclaimed on 24 August 2005 for sole custody of both children, support from the applicant, and determination of his contact rights. Both parties later submitted addenda on property division, contact, and support. The first-instance court delivered judgment on 12 May 2008, dissolving the marriage, granting shared custody of N.S. and sole custody of E.S. to V.S., and rejecting the applicant’s request for contact with E.S. as well as V.S.’s request for contact with N.S. Both parties appealed.

Ten hearings were scheduled at first instance. Two were adjourned for the applicant’s illness and one for V.S.’s illness (approximately nine months’ delay). Two further hearings were adjourned at the applicant’s request because he and N.S. (then aged 11–12) lived in London and N.S. attended school, producing about one year’s delay. Another hearing was adjourned pending an opinion from the Rīga City Bāriņtiesa (municipal guardianship authority).

The Bāriņtiesa was asked for an opinion on 15 April 2005. It repeatedly reported that it could not assess the situation because the applicant failed to attend meetings, cooperate, or ensure N.S. attended. Its first opinion (8 February 2007) recommended sole custody of both children for V.S. with contact for the applicant. A second opinion (5 March 2008) recommended shared custody of N.S., sole custody of E.S. for V.S., and psychological recommendations for the applicant regarding contact with E.S. Later, during the appeal, the Bāriņtiesa sought UK judicial assistance but was informed that the applicant had not responded to interview invitations and could not be met at home.

The appellate court received the file on 24 July 2008 but initiated proceedings only on 2 July 2009, scheduling the first hearing for 1 June 2010. The applicant did not attend (claiming non-receipt of the summons, though he possessed a plane ticket and later cited a delayed flight). The court postponed pronouncement and, after further adjournment because of the applicant’s UK residence, held a hearing on 27 April 2011 at which he appeared and asked that a Latvian contact address be used. He missed the next hearing on 6 December 2011, citing late notice and finances; the court proceeded. Judgment was delivered on 20 December 2011: the marriage was dissolved, V.S. received sole custody of E.S., the applicant’s contact application was dismissed because of the 2006 incident (though a fresh application remained possible), shared custody of N.S. stood unappealed, and V.S. was granted contact with N.S. The court recorded that the applicant had intentionally delayed the proceedings. Divorce became enforceable on 7 February 2012; the applicant’s cassation appeal on remaining issues was dismissed by the Senate of the Supreme Court on 24 January 2013 as raising no relevant legal questions.

Between August 2007 and September 2011 seven ancillary applications concerning interim measures and contact produced seven hearings and eight decisions; the applicant was repeatedly denied contact with E.S. because he failed to cooperate with a psychologist working with the child. The overall proceedings thus lasted from April 2005 until January 2013.

The case of *Sļadzevskis v. Latvia* (Application no. 32003/13) was brought by Sergejs Sļadzevskis, a Latvian national residing in London, alleging that the length of his divorce, custody, and related proceedings violated Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant married V.S. in 1994; their son N.S. was born in 1995 and daughter E.S. in 2002. The applicant lived in London from at least early 2005, with N.S. joining him in March 2006. On 20 December 2006 an incident occurred that Latvian authorities treated as an attempt by the applicant to remove E.S. forcibly to the United Kingdom; his right to care for her was temporarily suspended and she remained with V.S.

Proceedings began when the applicant filed for divorce at the Riga Regional Court on 11 March 2005. They were initiated on 13 April 2005 after he submitted an addendum seeking residence of both children with him and child-support payments from V.S. V.S. filed a counterclaim on 24 August 2005 seeking sole custody of both children, support from the applicant, and determination of his contact rights. Both parties later filed further addendums on property division, contact, and support.

Of ten hearings scheduled at first instance, two were adjourned because the applicant was ill and one because V.S. was ill, causing roughly nine months’ delay. Two more were adjourned at the applicant’s request because he and school-age N.S. lived in London and he could not leave the child unattended, causing about one year’s delay. Another hearing was adjourned to obtain an opinion from the Rīga City Bāriņtiesa (the municipal guardianship authority). The Bāriņtiesa had been asked for an opinion on 15 April 2005 but repeatedly reported that it could not assess the situation because the applicant failed to attend meetings or ensure N.S.’s attendance. It issued a first opinion on 8 February 2007 recommending sole custody of both children for V.S. and contact rights only for the applicant, then a second opinion on 5 March 2008 recommending shared custody of N.S., sole custody of E.S. for V.S., and psychological recommendations before any contact with E.S. The first-instance court delivered judgment on 12 May 2008, dissolving the marriage, granting shared custody of N.S. and sole custody of E.S. to V.S., and rejecting both parties’ contact applications and the applicant’s support claim. Both appealed.

The Civil Division of the Supreme Court received the file on 24 July 2008 but initiated appellate proceedings only on 2 July 2009, listing the first hearing for 1 June 2010. The applicant did not attend (he later claimed he had not received the summons, though he also cited a delayed flight; a plane ticket for that date was produced). The court examined the case anyway and listed judgment for 15 June 2010, but then postponed it because it could not decide without him. Subsequent hearings were delayed by difficulties serving the applicant at his London address (he later said a Latvian contact address should be used). He appeared on 27 April 2011 but missed the 6 December 2011 hearing, citing late notice and financial hardship; the court proceeded. Judgment was delivered on 20 December 2011: the marriage was dissolved (enforceable 7 February 2012), V.S. received sole custody of E.S., the applicant’s contact application was dismissed because of the 2006 incident (though a fresh application remained possible), shared custody of N.S. was left undisturbed, and V.S. was granted contact with N.S. The court recorded that the applicant had intentionally delayed the proceedings. His subsequent appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Senate of the Supreme Court on 24 January 2013 as raising no relevant legal issues.

Between August 2007 and September 2011 the courts also examined seven ancillary applications concerning interim measures and contact, resulting in seven hearings and eight decisions. The applicant was consistently denied contact with E.S. because he failed to cooperate with the psychologist working with her. The Bāriņtiesa’s later attempt to obtain assistance from the UK Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service also failed because the applicant could not be contacted.

The overall proceedings thus lasted from April 2005 until January 2013. Delays arose from parties’ absences and non-cooperation (especially the applicant’s), court scheduling, the need for expert opinions, and cross-border service difficulties.

The case of Sļadzevskis v. Latvia (no. 32003/13) concerned the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that civil proceedings relating to his divorce, child custody, contact rights and maintenance had lasted an unreasonably long time. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant, a Latvian national born in 1970, had lived in London since at least early 2005. He married V.S. in 1994; their son N.S. (born 1995) joined him in London in 2006, while their daughter E.S. (born 2002) remained in Latvia. On 20 December 2006 an incident occurred that the Latvian authorities treated as an attempt by the applicant to remove E.S. forcibly to the United Kingdom; his rights of care in respect of E.S. were therefore temporarily suspended and she stayed with V.S.

On 11 March 2005 the applicant lodged a divorce petition with the Riga Regional Court; after an addendum the proceedings were formally opened on 13 April 2005. He sought residence of both children with him and maintenance from V.S. V.S. counter-claimed for sole custody of both children, maintenance from the applicant and determination of contact. Further pleadings addressed property division. Ten hearings were listed. Two were adjourned because of the applicant’s illness and one because of V.S.’s illness (approximately nine months’ delay). Two further hearings were adjourned at the applicant’s request because he and the school-age N.S. were in London (approximately one year’s delay). One hearing was adjourned to obtain an opinion from the municipal guardianship authority (Bāriņtiesa). Judgment was delivered on 12 May 2008: the marriage was dissolved, shared custody of N.S. and sole custody of E.S. were granted to V.S., and the parties’ respective contact and maintenance claims were rejected. Both sides appealed.

The Bāriņtiesa, asked for an opinion as early as April 2005, repeatedly reported that the applicant failed to attend meetings or to produce N.S. Its first opinion (February 2007) favoured sole custody of both children for V.S.; a later opinion (March 2008) recommended shared custody of N.S. and sole custody of E.S. for V.S., with the applicant requiring psychological input before contact with E.S. Subsequent attempts by the Bāriņtiesa and by a UK authority to interview the applicant and N.S. also failed because of non-cooperation.

The file reached the Civil Division of the Supreme Court on 24 July 2008; appellate proceedings were opened only on 2 July 2009 and the first hearing was fixed for 1 June 2010. The applicant did not appear, later claiming he had not received the summons (although he held a plane ticket for that date). The court adjourned, then encountered difficulties serving him in London; he appeared on 27 April 2011 and indicated a Latvian contact address. He missed the 6 December 2011 hearing, citing late notice and lack of funds. Judgment was given on 20 December 2011: the marriage was confirmed dissolved, V.S. received sole custody of E.S., the applicant’s contact application was refused because of the 2006 incident, V.S. was granted contact with N.S., and the court expressly recorded that the applicant had delayed the case. The divorce became enforceable on 7 February 2012. The Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s points-of-law appeal on 24 January 2013.

Between August 2007 and September 2011 seven ancillary applications concerning interim contact and security of claims generated seven hearings and eight decisions; the applicant was consistently denied contact with E.S. because he failed to co-operate with a psychologist.

The overall proceedings therefore lasted from April 2005 until January 2013—almost eight years across three instances—against a background of the applicant’s residence abroad, repeated non-cooperation with the guardianship authorities, multiple adjournments attributable to him, and parallel interim proceedings.
001-203153:
The case of Kasmi v. Albania (Application no. 1175/06) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applicant, Gëzim Kasmi (born 1942), claimed he was unable to recover possession of a house in Tirana for over 13 years due to occupation by tenants protected under post-communist housing laws.

During Albania’s communist era, privately owned properties were nationalized and allocated to tenants via State Housing Company agreements. After 1992, the Privatisation Act allowed tenants of purely State-owned dwellings to purchase them, but excluded former private properties. The 1993 Property Restitution and Compensation Act enabled former owners (or heirs) to reclaim expropriated properties, yet existing tenancies persisted. The State was obliged to house displaced tenants via loans, allowances, or new construction (e.g., sections 16 and 25 of the Privatisation Act; later the 1995 Contribution to Homeless Households Act and 2004 Social Programmes Act). Rents for such properties remained frozen at 1993 levels (or indexed only minimally after later amendments), with tenants paying a fraction and the State theoretically covering the rest. Constitutional Court rulings (e.g., nos. 5/1997, 26/2005, 11/2007) repeatedly struck down provisions accelerating evictions or liberalizing rents, citing tenants’ housing rights, legal certainty, and financial hardship (many being pensioners). A 2012 Normative Act later facilitated evictions but post-dated the main events.

The applicant’s father owned two four-room houses (plus courtyards) nationalized in the 1950s and tenanted. After the 1993 Act, he claimed restitution; the Tirana Commission recognized his rights on 27 September 1995. Following his death, the applicant and siblings registered title on 15 August 1997. Unable to regain one house (occupied by tenants J.D., B.S., M.S., and F.S.), the applicant sued for eviction, arguing the tenants lacked property rights, paid no rent, and were not legally homeless.

On 17 March 2003, the Tirana District Court ordered vacation: J.D. had no lawful occupancy authorization; B.S. and M.S. had lived abroad for years; F.S. had received State housing. The Court of Appeal (23 April 2004) partially quashed this, upholding only F.S.’s eviction. It found J.D., B.S., and M.S. had occupied since the 1980s; J.D. was legally homeless with a 1993 tenancy right; B.S. and M.S. had not abandoned the dwelling despite temporary emigration. The Supreme Court (19 July 2005) upheld this, affirming the applicant’s ownership but confirming the tenants’ lawful status under the Property Act (section 14) and noting parties could “regulate their relationship.” It treated B.S. and M.S. as homeless despite emigration.

No alternative housing was provided by the State despite statutory duties and priority for such tenants. Rents stayed low and non-indexed to inflation, with no time-limited tenancies or effective termination mechanisms. The applicant reported in 2010 that the remaining tenants had died, allowing him to take possession—after more than 13 years of exclusion (from restitution circa 1995–1997).

The Court examined this as a “control of use” of property amid Albania’s complex post-communist transition. Key relevant facts included the imposed, indefinite tenancies; frozen rents failing to cover maintenance or inflation; absent State measures for alternative housing; and the prolonged uncertainty placing a disproportionate social burden on the individual owner rather than society.

The case of *Kasmi v. Albania* (Application no. 1175/06) concerned an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the ECHR. The applicant, Gëzim Kasmi, claimed he was unable to recover possession of a restituted family house in Tirana that remained occupied by tenants for over 13 years.

During Albania’s communist era, households typically occupied State-owned dwellings under tenancy agreements with the Housing Company. Privately owned properties nationalized by the State were allocated similarly. The applicant’s father owned two four-room houses with courtyards in Tirana, which were nationalized in the 1950s and subsequently tenanted.

Following the end of communist rule, the 1992 Privatisation Act enabled tenants of State-owned dwellings (excluding formerly private properties) to purchase them. The 1993 Property Restitution and Compensation Act allowed former owners or heirs to claim restitution of nationalized properties or compensation. However, existing tenancies were preserved, and section 14 provided that relations between restituted owners and tenants would be governed by the Privatisation Act. The State was obliged to resolve tenants’ housing needs, prioritizing those of limited means. If an owner provided equivalent alternative housing, tenants had to vacate.

The applicant’s father claimed restitution around 1994–1995. On 27 September 1995 the Tirana Commission recognized his title. After his death, the applicant and siblings registered ownership on 15 August 1997. Unable to regain possession of one house, the applicant sued the occupying tenants (J.D., B.S., M.S. and F.S.) for eviction. He argued they lacked property rights, paid no rent and were not legally homeless, thereby infringing his constitutional and Convention property rights.

On 17 March 2003 the Tirana District Court ordered eviction. It found J.D. lacked a lawful occupancy authorization; B.S. and M.S. had lived abroad for at least five years; and F.S. had received State housing.

The tenants appealed. On 23 April 2004 the Court of Appeal partially quashed the judgment. It held that J.D., B.S. and M.S. had occupied the house since the 1980s. J.D. was legally homeless and entitled to tenancy since 1993; B.S. and M.S., as economic migrants without permanent foreign residence, had not abandoned their Albanian dwelling. Eviction of F.S. was upheld.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, contesting J.D.’s authorization and asserting that B.S. and M.S. had lived abroad for ten years. On 19 July 2005 the Supreme Court upheld the appellate ruling. It confirmed the applicant’s undisputed ownership but found J.D. lawfully occupied pursuant to a 1986 authorization and an unenforced 1993 court decision; B.S. and M.S. remained legally homeless. It noted that section 14 of the 1993 Property Act left the parties legal space to regulate their relationship.

Subsequent legislation (1995 Contribution to Homeless Households Act; 2004 Social Programmes Act; 2004 and 2006 Property Acts) sought to address tenant housing via allowances, loans and social programmes, designating tenants of restituted properties a priority. Rents were initially to be liberalized but remained frozen at 1993 levels after Constitutional Court rulings (1997, 2005, 2007) struck down provisions that would have raised rents, imposed eviction deadlines or liberalized the market, citing legal certainty and tenants’ housing rights. No effective, time-limited mechanism existed for owners to terminate the imposed tenancies, and the State took no concrete steps to rehouse the occupants.

In May 2010 the applicant informed the Court that the tenants had died and he had recovered possession. The interference thus lasted from recognition of title until 2010. The Court later held that this prolonged inability to enjoy the property, against a background of low unindexed rents and State inaction, imposed an excessive individual burden.

The case of Kasmi v. Albania (Application no. 1175/06) was brought by Gëzim Kasmi, an Albanian national born in 1942 and residing in Tirana, alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. He claimed that he had been unable to recover possession of a house restituted to his family, which remained occupied by tenants for more than 13 years.

During Albania’s communist period, privately owned dwellings were typically nationalized and allocated to households via tenancy agreements with the State-owned Housing Maintenance Company. The applicant’s father owned two houses in Tirana (each comprising four rooms, a dining room and courtyard), which were nationalized in the 1950s and subsequently tenanted. After the end of communist rule, the 1992 Privatisation Act enabled privatization of most State-owned dwellings, while the 1993 Property Restitution and Compensation Act permitted former owners or heirs to reclaim expropriated or nationalized properties (or receive compensation). However, restitution decisions did not automatically terminate existing tenancies.

The applicant’s father lodged a restitution claim around 1994–1995. On 27 September 1995 the Tirana Commission on Property Restitution and Compensation recognized his ownership. After his death, the applicant and his siblings registered title on 15 August 1997. One house remained occupied by tenants who paid no rent to the applicant. He therefore brought eviction proceedings, arguing that the occupants held no property rights, were not legally homeless, and that their presence violated his constitutionally and Convention-protected property rights.

On 17 March 2003 the Tirana District Court granted eviction. It found that tenant J.D. lacked a lawful occupancy authorization, that B.S. and M.S. had lived abroad for at least five years, and that F.S. had already received State housing. The Tirana Court of Appeal partially quashed this judgment on 23 April 2004. It noted that the tenants had occupied the property since the 1980s; J.D. was legally homeless and held a tenancy right dating from 1993; and B.S. and M.S., though economic migrants abroad for two years, had not abandoned their Albanian dwelling. Only F.S. was ordered to vacate one room. On 19 July 2005 the Supreme Court upheld the appellate decision. It confirmed the applicant’s undisputed ownership but held that J.D. lawfully occupied the premises pursuant to a 1986 authorization and an unenforced 1993 court order, while B.S. and M.S. retained homeless status. The court observed that section 14 of the 1993 Property Act left scope for the parties to regulate their relationship.

Domestic legislation (the Privatisation Act, the 1995 Contribution to Homeless Households Act and later Social Programmes Acts) imposed continuing tenancies on restituted properties, fixed rents at 1993 levels without inflation indexation, and assigned the State primary responsibility for providing alternative housing to affected tenants (via allowances, loans or new social rental units). These arrangements were intended to be temporary. Successive Constitutional Court rulings (1997, 2005, 2007) struck down attempts to liberalize rents or impose fixed eviction deadlines, citing tenants’ acquired rights, legal certainty and the absence of an overriding public interest sufficient to override housing protections. No effective statutory mechanism existed allowing owners to terminate the imposed tenancies, and the authorities took no concrete steps to rehouse the occupants of the applicant’s property.

The resulting interference lasted from at least 1997 until May 2010, when the remaining tenants died and the applicant recovered possession. Throughout this period the applicant bore the full social and economic burden of a complex post-communist housing crisis that the State had failed to resolve.

001-207132:
**Case of L.B. v. Hungary (ECHR Fourth Section, Application no. 36345/16, Chamber judgment 12 January 2021; later referred to Grand Chamber)**

The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1966 and resident in Budapest, alleged that the publication of his personal data by the National Tax and Customs Authority violated his rights under Articles 8 (respect for private life) and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core facts centre on the tax authority’s mandatory online publication of identifying information about major tax defaulters, which the applicant claimed constituted an unjustified interference with his private life, including through subsequent media use of the data.

On 27 January 2016 the tax authority published the applicant’s name, home address, tax identification number and the amount of his tax arrears on a public list of “major tax defaulters” on its website. This was required by section 55(3) of Act no. XCII of 2003 on Tax Administration, which mandated publication, within 30 days of the end of each quarter, of details of taxpayers (private individuals) against whom a final decision had established tax arrears exceeding 10 million Hungarian forints (HUF) for the previous quarter, together with the legal consequences of non-payment. A decision was not treated as final if the time-limit for judicial review had not expired or if court proceedings were pending.

On 16 February 2016 an online media outlet used the published data to create an interactive “national map of tax defaulters.” The applicant’s home address (and those of others) appeared as a red dot; clicking the dot displayed his name and address to any reader. Subsequently the applicant also appeared on a second public list of “major tax evaders” under section 55(5) of the same Act. This list, published quarterly, named private individuals who had owed tax debts exceeding 10 million HUF (net of overpayments) for more than 180 consecutive days, again including names, home addresses, tax identification numbers and related details. The applicant’s data were later removed from the tax authority’s website.

The legislative purpose, as explained in the Act’s notes, was to enhance the clarity and reliability of economic relations, encourage tax compliance, and inform potential contractual parties about a taxpayer’s solvency. Publication was presented as a tool to “whiten” the economy by isolating non-compliant actors. The case of L.B. v. On 27 January 2016 the Tax Authority published the applicant’s name, home address, tax identification number and the amount of his tax arrears on its list of “major tax defaulters.” The measure was required by section 55(3) of Act no. XCII of 2003 on Tax Administration, which mandated quarterly publication of data concerning any individual against whom a final Tax Authority decision had established arrears exceeding 10 million Hungarian forints (HUF). Shortly afterwards, on 16 February 2016, an online media outlet used the published addresses to produce an interactive “national map of tax defaulters.” The applicant’s home address appeared as a red dot; clicking it displayed his name and address to any internet user.

The applicant was later included on a second list, that of “major tax evaders,” published under section 55(5) of the same Act. That provision required quarterly publication of the names, home addresses and tax identification numbers of persons who had owed the Tax Authority more than 10 million HUF for longer than 180 consecutive days. The applicant’s data were subsequently removed from the Tax Authority website.

The legislative purpose, as stated in the explanatory note to section 55(5), was to enhance the transparency and reliability of economic relations, to encourage compliance, and to alert contractual partners to a taxpayer’s possible insolvency. A 2004 Constitutional Court decision had already held that comparable publications of identifying data did not, in themselves, breach the constitutional right to data protection, because they served the public interest of protecting compliant taxpayers and “whitening” the economy. By contrast, a 2012 circular of the National Authority for Data Protection and Freedom of Information criticised the online publication of local tax-debtors’ names and addresses, arguing that internet dissemination went beyond the legislature’s intended local publicity (for example, a notice-board) and therefore exceeded the statutory aim.

The applicant complained that the combination of official listing and subsequent media mapping made his home address globally accessible, thereby constituting an unjustified interference with his private life. The Chamber examined the interference under Article 8, noting that the publication pursued the legitimate aims of protecting the integrity of the tax system and the rights of third parties. Given the wide margin of appreciation accorded to States in matters of economic and social strategy, the Court found that the statutory scheme was sufficiently circumscribed: only taxpayers with very large, finally assessed arrears or long-standing debts were named, the data were limited to identifiers necessary for public information, and the interference with the applicant’s private life was limited. Consequently the Chamber held that the publication did not violate Article 8.

The case of Svilengaćanin and Others v. Serbia concerns 11 Serbian nationals (active, former or retired professional or civilian officers of the former Yugoslav Army or the Army of Serbia and Montenegro). They alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention arising from the Supreme Court of Serbia’s lack of impartiality in their civil proceedings for unpaid military salary arrears, as well as from inconsistent domestic case-law on the jurisdiction of civil courts over such claims.

Military salaries were calculated by multiplying a base amount (fixed by the Federal Government according to rank, position and other factors) by a coefficient set monthly by the Minister of Defence within the defence budget approved by the Federal Assembly and published in the Official Military Gazette. The applicants claimed that the Minister had failed to determine and publish the coefficient properly and regularly. Confidential Ministry reports and a Ministry of Finance statement indicated that allocated salary funds had been diverted to pensions and other unexpected expenses, resulting in salaries below the statutory minimum.

The applicants first lodged administrative claims with military units seeking proper calculation and payment. Those units declined jurisdiction, characterising the dispute as civil rather than administrative because no separate administrative decisions on salaries had been issued. The Supreme Military Court confirmed this view in two judicial-review cases, holding that the matter concerned damages caused by payment of salaries below the statutory minimum and therefore belonged in the civil courts. The applicants accordingly abandoned the administrative route.

Between 2003 and 2007 they brought separate civil actions against the State for pecuniary damage caused by the Minister’s improper and malfeasant acts, relying on Article 172 of the Obligations Act. First-instance municipal courts largely found in their favour between 2005 and 2009, holding that sufficient budgetary resources had existed and that the State was liable. Approximately 910 similar first-instance judgments were delivered for other military personnel. Appellate outcomes were mixed.

Faced with a large volume of identical cases and inconsistent lower-court practice, first-instance courts sought guidance from the Supreme Court under the Civil Procedure Act. On 31 May 2005 the Supreme Court’s Civil Division issued a legal opinion distinguishing two situations: challenges to the legality of an administrative act determining a salary or pension must be pursued through administrative proceedings and judicial review; civil courts retain jurisdiction only over claims for damages caused by subsequent malfeasance (non-payment, under-payment or selective payment) once a final administrative decision exists. In the applicants’ subsequent appeals on points of law (2007–2010) the Supreme Court applied this reasoning, concluding that the disputes were public-law matters concerning the calculation of salaries determined by military decisions and therefore fell outside the ratione materiae competence of the civil courts. All applicants ultimately lost.

A central factual element of the impartiality complaint is a 2004 meeting, disclosed by a Ministry of Defence representative in unrelated proceedings. The then President of the Supreme Court, the President of its Civil Division and a first-instance court president met the Head of the Ministry’s Department for Property and Legal Affairs to discuss the influx of salary cases overburdening the courts and military bodies. They agreed in principle that first-instance courts would issue partial decisions on the legal basis of the claims; the Supreme Court would then rule on the merits; and, if the claims were accepted, the Ministry would settle remaining cases out of court. In one applicant’s case the Ministry later wrote to the Supreme Court requesting priority treatment of three appeals in order to avert “irreparable damage” to the military budget and asked to be served directly with the judgment.

By 2012 all applicants had lodged constitutional appeals alleging, inter alia, that the Supreme Court’s judgments were the product of the 2004 agreement and therefore lacked impartiality. The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaints as unsubstantiated subjective impressions, finding that the Supreme Court had been lawfully composed, had correctly established the facts and had given constitutionally acceptable reasons; it also characterised the underlying dispute as administrative rather than civil.

This coefficient, multiplied by a base salary set according to rank, position and other factors, determined monthly pay within the overall defence budget allocated by the Federal Assembly. As a result, they received significantly lower salaries than legally mandated for years. Internal Ministry reports from 2003 and 2006 confirmed that funds allocated for salaries had been diverted to other expenses, and coefficients had not been regularly adapted or published.

The units declined jurisdiction, classifying the matter as civil rather than administrative, as no separate decisions on salaries had been issued. The Supreme Military Court upheld this, stating that claims concerned damages from underpayment below statutory minima and thus fell under civil jurisdiction. It did not demonstrate that the Supreme Court altered its legal interpretation due to the meeting or that professional, tenured judges of last resort were influenced by extraneous considerations. No appearance of bias arose sufficient to undermine objective impartiality.

The case of Fariz Ahmadov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 40321/07) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. It concerned alleged unfairness in criminal proceedings against the applicant for illegal drug sales, specifically that his conviction relied on inadmissible evidence obtained in violation of his right to legal assistance under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c).

The applicant, an Azerbaijani waiter born in 1971, was arrested on 8 March 2005 after R.S. was found with 0.24 grams of marijuana on 7 March and claimed to have obtained it from A.S., who in turn named the applicant as the source. The arrest record noted that the applicant was informed of his rights, including the right to a lawyer, and he signed a handwritten waiver choosing to defend himself. On 10 March he was charged under Article 234.2 of the Criminal Code (illegal preparation, possession, purchase, transportation or sale of drugs) and ordered detained. Before questioning that day, he again signed a handwritten waiver after being informed of his rights. A report on his procedural rights was signed by the investigation officer, the applicant and a State-funded lawyer (though the applicant later disputed the timing of the lawyer’s signature). Questioning proceeded without a lawyer present; the applicant stated that A.S. had asked him for marijuana at his workplace, that he had refused, and that he had instead given A.S. a cigarette containing animal manure without receiving payment. A face-to-face confrontation with A.S. followed immediately, also without a lawyer: A.S. claimed he had paid the applicant 10,000 Azerbaijani manats for a marijuana-filled cigarette, while the applicant denied receiving money and insisted he had given only manure.

On 5 April 2005 the applicant appointed his own lawyer. A further confrontation on 5 August 2005, this time with the lawyer present, saw A.S. reverse his account and confirm that he had received only manure and paid nothing. Later that day, however, A.S. privately told investigators that he had recanted out of fear of the applicant and that he had in fact purchased marijuana. A.S. died before trial. In November 2005 a preliminary hearing at the Goranboy District Court remitted the case for fresh investigation, finding that it had not been established beyond reasonable doubt that the applicant’s right to legal assistance had been respected, because his handwritten waiver bore only his signature and a copy of the 10 March report lacked the State-funded lawyer’s signature.

A new indictment was nevertheless issued in December 2005. At trial the court read out one of A.S.’s pre-trial statements (affirming the purchase of drugs) and heard R.S., who testified that he had given A.S. money to buy drugs from the applicant. On 30 May 2006 the Goranboy District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to three and a half years’ imprisonment. The conviction rested on A.S.’s statements (including the 10 March confrontation record), R.S.’s testimony, a crime-scene reconstruction, an expert report confirming the substance as marijuana, and other witnesses. The applicant appealed, arguing that the 10 March confrontation was inadmissible because it had been conducted without proper legal assistance (contrary to Article 92.12 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which required a waiver to be given in the presence of counsel) and should have been excluded after the remittal. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, holding that the evidence was lawfully obtained and that neither the applicant nor A.S. had complained of pressure during the investigation. The applicant died in 2015; his mother continued the proceedings.

In those proceedings the applicant stated that he had given A.S. a cigarette containing animal manure rather than drugs and had received no payment; A.S. claimed he had paid 10,000 AZM for a cigarette of marijuana.

In a separate statement given the same day without the applicant or his lawyer, A.S. reverted to his original account, explaining that he had been afraid of the applicant.

The applicant stated that A.S. had asked him for marijuana at the tearoom; he refused but later placed animal manure in a cigarette and gave it to A.S. without receiving payment. A face-to-face confrontation with A.S. followed the same day, again without a lawyer. A.S. claimed he had paid 10,000 AZM (approximately EUR 1.5) for a marijuana-filled cigarette; the applicant denied receiving money and insisted he had given only manure.

In a subsequent unaccompanied statement to police, however, A.S. reverted to his original account, explaining that he had recanted out of fear of the applicant.

The core allegations centred on whether the waiver of legal assistance—executed in the absence of a lawyer and in breach of domestic procedural rules—rendered the subsequent statements and the resulting conviction unfair, particularly given the later recantation and the trial court’s reliance on the uncounselled confrontation.

The applicants, Croatian nationals Đurđica Grozdanić and her daughter Vedrana Gršković-Grozdanić, alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) and Article 6 (access to court) arising from the invalidation of a 2002 contract by which the first applicant and her late husband had purchased a socially owned flat in Osijek of which they had previously held a specially protected tenancy.

In 1983 the first applicant’s husband was awarded a specially protected tenancy of a 90 m² socially owned flat; the first applicant automatically became a co-holder. The 1991 Sale to Occupier Act entitled such tenants to buy their flats on favourable terms. The couple applied to purchase in January 1992. Shortly afterwards they left Osijek for work, first to Rijeka and then permanently to Pula (where both obtained jobs in 1996). Their children joined them later that year. The provider company then allocated the flat to a third party, J.P., for temporary use. The couple wrote to J.P. in 1993 asking him to leave, but took no formal steps to recover possession until 2003. In 1999 they bought land in Pula on which they later built a house.

The company’s 1992 action to terminate the tenancy was withdrawn in 2002 after the courts held the company no longer had standing. The couple then reapplied to the local authority (now the owner) and, on 26 November 2002, signed a sale contract at a discounted price of HRK 63,251. The State Attorney’s Office immediately issued a negative opinion, citing their prolonged absence and lack of registered domicile. A notary nevertheless certified the contract and the couple were entered as owners in the land register.

In November 2003 the State Attorney sued to have the contract declared null and void. The Osijek courts ultimately granted the claim in 2008. They found that the couple had not used the flat for more than six months without justification (Housing Act s. 99) and had taken no timely steps against the occupier; their tenancy had therefore already ended before the sale. Consequently they had lacked the statutory entitlement to purchase and the contract was contrary to mandatory rules. Earlier Supreme Court case-law had required a prior court judgment to terminate a tenancy; the courts now treated the existence of grounds for termination as a preliminary question they could decide themselves. The purchase price was refunded. Parallel eviction proceedings against J.P. were dismissed on the same ground.

The couple’s appeal on points of law (value of claim HRK 79,064) was declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court in 2010 because it fell below the HRK 100,000 statutory threshold. Although the Constitutional Court had earlier struck down that threshold, it had deferred the effects of its decision until 1 October 2008; the appeal had been lodged in the intervening period. The Constitutional Court later rejected the applicants’ complaint, holding that no legal gap had existed.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints that the reversal of case-law three years after the Housing Act’s repeal rendered the deprivation of property unforeseeable and that the refusal to examine the appeal on points of law denied access to court.

Shortly thereafter they left Osijek for work, relocating first to Rijeka and then to Pula (where they obtained permanent jobs by February 1996); their children, including the second applicant, joined them later that year. IPK then allocated the flat temporarily to J.P.

IPK sued to terminate the tenancy but later withdrew the action after management rights passed to the Municipality of Osijek (later Osijek Township). In 2002 the applicants resubmitted their purchase request to the local authorities. Although the State Attorney’s Office issued a negative opinion citing their long absence and lack of registered domicile at the flat, a notary certified the signatures and the Land Registry recorded them as owners.
