Their subsequent constitutional complaint was dismissed. In 2010 the authorities refunded the purchase price. Meanwhile the applicants had bought land in Pula in 1999 and built a house there around 2005; after M.G.’s death in 2009 only the first applicant inherited the Osijek flat.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints that the unexpected reversal of case-law three years after repeal of the Housing Act arbitrarily deprived them of property and that the Supreme Court’s refusal to hear the appeal denied access to court.

The case concerns two Croatian nationals, Đurđica Grozdanić (born 1949) and her daughter Vedrana Gršković-Grozdanić (born 1982), who alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) and Article 6 (access to court) of the European Convention on Human Rights following the invalidation of a 2002 contract under which they (and the first applicant’s late husband) purchased a socially owned flat in Osijek.

In 1983 the first applicant’s husband was awarded a specially protected tenancy of the 90 m² flat; the first applicant automatically became a co-holder. The 1991 Sale to Occupier Act allowed such tenants to buy their flats on favourable terms. In January 1992 the couple applied to purchase the flat. Shortly afterwards they moved first to Rijeka and then to Pula for work; their children (including the second applicant) joined them later that year. Both obtained permanent employment in Pula by February 1996. The provider company immediately allocated the flat to a third party, J.P., for temporary use.

The couple’s purchase request was put on hold while the company unsuccessfully sought termination of the tenancy (proceedings later withdrawn). After the local authority succeeded to the company’s rights, the couple renewed their purchase application in 2002, obtained a certificate confirming they met the statutory conditions, and signed a sale contract on 26 November 2002 for HRK 63,251 (a 20 % cash-payment discount). Their signatures were notarised and they were registered as owners. The State Attorney’s Office, however, issued a negative opinion on the ground that they had not lived in the flat for a prolonged period and had not been registered there.

In November 2003 the State Attorney sued to have the contract declared null and void. The Osijek Municipal Court (and later the County Court) held that the tenancy had already terminated because the couple had not used the flat for more than six months without a justified reason (Housing Act, s. 99). They had taken no steps to recover possession from J.P. until June 2003—well after the six-month statutory period. Consequently they no longer held the tenancy required by the Sale to Occupier Act, rendering the contract contrary to mandatory law and therefore void (Obligations Act, s. 103). The courts treated the existence of grounds for termination as a preliminary question that could be examined even without a prior court judgment terminating the tenancy—an approach endorsed by a 2007 Constitutional Court decision that departed from earlier Supreme Court case-law requiring a formal termination judgment.

An appeal on points of law was declared inadmissible because the value of the dispute (HRK 79,064) fell below the statutory threshold of HRK 100,000. The Constitutional Court dismissed the subsequent constitutional complaint, finding no violation of the right to a fair trial.

Parallel eviction proceedings against J.P. were dismissed on the same ground: the applicants had lost the tenancy through prolonged absence. The purchase price was later refunded.

The applicants complained that the unexpected reversal of case-law three years after the Housing Act’s repeal, and the refusal to hear their appeal on points of law, arbitrarily deprived them of their property and of access to the Supreme Court.
001-208245:
The case of Pavel Shishkov v. Russia (Application no. 78754/13) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Russian authorities refused to transfer his young daughter, V., into his care. The applicant, a Moscow resident born in 1989, had an unmarried relationship from 2006 with Ms Ye. of Orel (approximately 360 km away). Their son K. was born in 2007 and daughter V. in 2008. The children’s birth certificates listed only Ye. as parent (with dashes for the father), as she sought single-mother social benefits; the children used her surname and the applicant’s patronymic. The applicant claimed regular visits and involvement in upbringing until the relationship ended in 2009, after which he had no regular contact.

In February 2010, police removed the children from Ye. due to her drunkenness and neglect, placing them in hospital and then public care (an infant home for V.; later a children’s home for K.). Ye. made limited visits and, by 2011, was deprived of parental authority over both children by the Sovetskiy District Court of Orel (in July for K. and November for V.), on grounds of prolonged non-involvement. The court did not pursue Ye.’s mention of a father in Moscow. In December 2011–January 2012, V. (then aged 3) was transferred to a foster family (Ms L.P. and Mr Yu.P.) with the infant home’s consent, as she had formed a bond with them; the foster parents declined also taking K. due to his reported disability. The applicant was neither notified nor consulted.

The applicant later claimed he learned of the 2010 removal around March 2010 and proposed paternity recognition, but Ye. ignored him or falsely said she had retrieved the children. He formally sought paternity recognition and transfer of both children in May 2012, after learning of the parental-authority deprivation. DNA testing confirmed he was V.’s father; paternity was legally recognized in August 2012, with new birth certificates issued. K. was transferred to the applicant in September 2012, as he and his mother had visited regularly, the boy had a good relationship with them, and the applicant’s circumstances were deemed adequate.

V.’s transfer was refused by the District Court on 21 February 2013. The court found the applicant had known of the placement since early 2010 yet delayed action for over two years, demonstrating indifference; he had not visited or contacted V. Reports showed V. was well-integrated with her foster parents (whom she called “mum” and “dad”), attended nursery, and had a strong emotional attachment to them with no other significant adult bonds. Expert evidence indicated transfer would be highly stressful, risking loss of trust in adults given her age and prior trauma; she did not know her biological father. The applicant’s Moscow flat lacked space for V., was untidy, and his son K. (already with him) lacked insurance and nursery attendance. A Moscow childcare report noted the applicant’s limited emotional attachment even to K. and vagueness about plans for V. Witnesses (psychologist, nursery staff) corroborated V.’s anxiety about removal from the foster family. Higher courts (Orel Regional Court in May 2013; cassation refusals later) upheld the decision as in V.’s best interests, noting the applicant retained parental rights and could reapply if circumstances changed. A 2013 court-approved contact agreement allowed limited visits, but actual contact was infrequent amid disputes.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation, centering on the authorities’ refusal to reunite V. with her biological father after her mother’s rights were terminated and she was placed in foster care without his involvement. The Court ultimately found no violation, holding the refusal proportionate to V.’s best interests.

The case of Pavel Shishkov v. Russia (Application no. 78754/13) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the Russian authorities’ refusal to transfer his young daughter into his care after her mother was deprived of parental authority.

The applicant, a Moscow resident, began a relationship in 2006 with Ms Ye., who lived in Orel (approximately 360 km away). They never married. Their son K. was born in 2007 and daughter V. in 2008. The children’s birth certificates listed only the mother, with a dash for the father, as Ms Ye. wished to qualify as a single parent for social benefits. The applicant claimed he visited regularly and participated in the children’s upbringing until the relationship ended in 2009, after which he had no regular contact.

In February 2010, police removed the children from Ms Ye. due to neglect and alcohol abuse and placed them in hospital. In April 2010 they were transferred to a municipal infant home. K. later moved to a children’s home upon turning three. Ms Ye. visited infrequently and made no serious effort to resume care. In 2011 courts deprived her of parental authority over both children. During the proceedings concerning V., Ms Ye. mentioned that the girl’s father and grandmother lived in Moscow and that she intended to take V. there, but the court did not investigate this information.

In January 2012, without the applicant’s knowledge or consent, V. (then aged three) was placed with a foster family, Ms L.P. and Mr Yu.P., with whom she developed a close emotional bond.

The applicant learned of the children’s removal in 2010 but did not immediately seek legal recognition of paternity. He later claimed Ms Ye. had concealed developments and ignored his requests. In April 2012 he applied to the childcare authorities and in May 2012 lodged a court claim seeking recognition of paternity and transfer of both children to his care. DNA testing confirmed he was V.’s biological father. In August 2012 the court recognised his paternity of both children and new birth certificates were issued. In September 2012 the court ordered K.’s transfer to the applicant, noting the applicant’s regular visits, good contact with the boy, and suitable living conditions.

The claim concerning V. was heard separately in February 2013. The District Court dismissed it, finding that the applicant had known of the children’s removal since early 2010 yet waited more than two years to act, demonstrating indifference. V. had lived with her foster parents since January 2012, was well-integrated, called them “mum” and “dad,” and showed strong attachment. Psychological evidence indicated that sudden separation would cause her severe distress, given her young age and prior trauma. Reports on the applicant’s home noted inadequate space for V., an untidy kitchen, and lack of medical insurance or nursery attendance for K. Experts concluded the applicant could not adequately assess the psychological consequences of transferring a child who had not seen him for four years. Witnesses confirmed V.’s anxiety after encountering her biological relatives during DNA testing.

Appeals were unsuccessful. Higher courts endorsed the first-instance findings and noted that the applicant retained parental rights and could reapply if circumstances changed. Subsequent court-approved contact arrangements were poorly utilised: the Government reported the applicant attended only two sessions and showed little engagement, while the applicant claimed he attended when possible and blamed hostility from the foster parents.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 8 complaint that the authorities had failed in their positive obligation to reunite him with his daughter.

The case of Pavel Shishkov v. Russia (Application no. 78754/13) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the Russian authorities’ refusal to transfer the applicant’s daughter, V. (born 2008), into his care after her mother’s parental rights were withdrawn and V. was placed in foster care without his knowledge or consent. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life).

The applicant, a Moscow resident, had a relationship with Ms Ye. of Orel (360 km away) but they never married. Their children—son K. (born 2007) and daughter V.—were registered with no father listed, as Ms Ye. wished to claim single-mother benefits. The applicant visited regularly until the relationship ended in 2009, after which contact ceased.

In February 2010 police removed both children from Ms Ye. following reports of neglect and alcohol abuse, placing them first in hospital and then in municipal care (an infant home for V.). Ms Ye. visited infrequently and was deprived of parental authority over K. in July 2011 and over V. in November 2011. On 30 December 2011 the Mayor of Orel ordered V.’s transfer to a foster family (Ms L.P. and Mr Yu.P.); she moved there on 12 January 2012 and has remained since. The foster parents declined to take K. because of his reported disability. The applicant was not notified or consulted at any stage.

The applicant learned of the children’s removal around March 2010 but did not act immediately. He later claimed Ms Ye. had misled him about their whereabouts. In April 2012 he wrote to the childcare authority seeking consent to recognise paternity. In May 2012 he sued for paternity recognition and transfer of both children. DNA testing confirmed he was V.’s father; paternity of both children was judicially recognised in August 2012 and new birth certificates issued.

K. was ordered returned to the applicant in September 2012 after evidence of regular visits, good contact and suitable living conditions. The claim regarding V. was heard separately. On 21 February 2013 the Sovetskiy District Court of Orel dismissed it. The court found the applicant had known of V.’s removal from the outset yet waited more than two years to act, demonstrating indifference. V., then aged four, had formed a strong attachment to her foster parents (whom she called “mum” and “dad”), was well-integrated, attended nursery and showed no bond with the applicant, whom she did not know. Expert reports indicated transfer would cause severe trauma; the applicant’s Moscow flat was assessed as inadequate (no dedicated space for V., untidy, no nursery place for K.) and his attitude as emotionally detached. Higher courts upheld the decision in 2013–2014, noting that changed circumstances could later justify a fresh application and that foster placement did not extinguish parental rights.

A 2013 court-approved settlement provided for contact (initially twice monthly, then weekly). The applicant attended only sporadically; the foster parents were described as uncooperative. The applicant retained parental authority and could seek V.’s transfer if circumstances evolved.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 8 complaint: the unconsulted foster placement and subsequent refusal to reunite father and daughter despite recognised paternity.
001-207538:
The case of Mihail Mihăilescu v. Romania (Application no. 3795/15) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that pre-trial judge proceedings confirming the discontinuation of a criminal investigation were unfair. The proceedings occurred in chambers without the parties present, without disclosure of opposing submissions, and without an opportunity for the applicant to rebut the alleged perpetrator’s arguments.

The applicant, a Romanian police officer born in 1971, was divorced from his wife by a Bucharest District Court judgment of 19 March 2009. The court attributed sole responsibility for the breakdown of the marriage to him and ordered him to pay child maintenance. The judgment relied in part on a 19 February 2009 statement by his former mother-in-law alleging inappropriate behaviour towards his wife. The applicant did not attend the divorce hearings.

On 1 March 2013 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against his former mother-in-law for perjury, alleging that her statement was false. He joined the proceedings as a civil party and claimed RON 20,000 (approximately EUR 4,600) in non-pecuniary damages for harm to his honour, dignity and professional standing. His employer had been notified of the statement and subjected him to psychological and professional scrutiny.

On 24 October 2013 police proposed discontinuing the prosecution and imposing an administrative penalty, citing three witnesses (a neighbour, an acquaintance and the applicant’s underage daughter) who denied witnessing violence or threats. On 27 January 2014 a prosecutor discontinued the case and fined the mother-in-law, finding her conduct insufficiently serious. She challenged the decision.

On 25 August 2014 a senior prosecutor quashed the earlier decision and closed the proceedings. She found the investigation inadequate to establish guilt, discounted the witnesses’ testimony on procedural and reliability grounds, and noted that the limitation period had expired.

The applicant appealed to the District Court on 13 October 2014, arguing that the senior prosecutor had mis-assessed the evidence and ignored readily remediable procedural defects. He stressed that a finding of perjury was professionally vital. On 22 October 2014 the court, sitting as a pre-trial judge, notified him of the hearing date and invited written observations; he made no further submissions.

By an unappealable interlocutory judgment of 3 November 2014, delivered in chambers and in the parties’ absence, the pre-trial judge dismissed the appeal. The judge held that the witnesses had not seen arguments and that the mother-in-law, given her close relationship, was better placed to know of them. The daughter’s evidence was discounted because of her living arrangements. The original divorce court had relied on additional factors, including the applicant’s non-cooperation and medical records (submitted by the mother-in-law) showing he had been hospitalised in 2008 for erratic behaviour.

Separately, on 9 May 2014 the applicant brought ordinary tort proceedings against his former mother-in-law seeking damages; their outcome is unknown.

The relevant domestic provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Articles 341 and related texts) required the pre-trial judge to examine such complaints in chambers without the parties. Subsequent Constitutional Court decisions of October and November 2014 declared aspects of this written, non-adversarial procedure unconstitutional for failing to guarantee orality, equality of arms and the right to rebut submissions. The Strasbourg Court ultimately found that, although Article 6 § 1 applied to the civil limb of the proceedings, the pre-trial phase had not rendered the applicant’s subsequent civil claim unfair from the outset.

The case of Mihail Mihăilescu v. Romania (Application no. 3795/15) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) in its civil limb. The applicant, a Romanian national and police officer born in 1971, complained that proceedings before a pre-trial judge confirming a prosecutor’s decision to discontinue a criminal investigation were unfair. These took place in chambers without the parties present or aware of each other’s submissions, denying him the chance to rebut the alleged perpetrator’s arguments. This, he argued, prejudiced his civil claim for damages attached to the criminal complaint.

In March 2009, a Bucharest court granted the applicant’s wife a divorce, holding him solely responsible and ordering child maintenance. The judgment relied in part on a February 2009 statement by his former mother-in-law alleging his inappropriate behaviour toward his wife. On 1 March 2013, the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against her for perjury, joining as a civil party and claiming RON 20,000 (about EUR 4,600) in non-pecuniary damages for harm to his image, honour and dignity. He noted that the statement had been notified to his employer, triggering intense professional and psychological scrutiny.

Police recommended discontinuation in October 2013, proposing only an administrative penalty as the act lacked sufficient gravity. Three witnesses (a neighbour, an acquaintance and the applicant’s minor daughter) stated they had neither seen nor heard violence or coercion. A prosecutor discontinued the case in January 2014 and imposed a fine, citing the offender’s lack of record, reduced social impact and the applicant’s non-attendance at the divorce hearings. The mother-in-law successfully challenged this; a senior prosecutor closed the proceedings in August 2014. She found the investigation inadequate to establish guilt, discarded the witnesses’ evidence (the acquaintance had not been questioned on key family matters, the neighbour had known the applicant only post-divorce, and the daughter lived with the applicant, was a minor and had not been informed of her right not to testify against her grandmother) and noted expiry of the limitation period.

The applicant appealed to the District Court on 13 October 2014, contesting the assessment of evidence and stressing the professional repercussions. The court, sitting as a pre-trial judge, informed him of the date and invited written observations. On 3 November 2014 it dismissed the appeal in chambers without the parties present. The judge found no proof of perjury, reasoning that the mother-in-law was better placed to observe family tensions, the witnesses might simply have missed them, the daughter’s evidence was potentially influenced by her living arrangements, the divorce court had also relied on the applicant’s non-cooperation, and medical records of his 2008 hospitalisation for erratic behaviour corroborated the allegations.

Separately, in May 2014 the applicant brought ordinary tort proceedings against his former mother-in-law for the same damage, relying on the (later-overruled) first prosecutor’s finding; the outcome is unknown.

At the material time the Code of Criminal Procedure authorised a pre-trial judge to review non-prosecution decisions solely on written submissions, in chambers and without the parties. Although later Constitutional Court rulings (October–November 2014) declared aspects of this procedure unconstitutional for lacking orality, adversarial argument and equality of arms, those rulings post-dated the impugned decision. The applicant maintained that the closed, non-adversarial process fatally undermined the fairness of any subsequent determination of his civil claim.

**Summary of Mihail Mihăilescu v. Romania (ECtHR, Appl. no. 3795/15, 12 January 2021)**

The applicant, a Romanian police officer, alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (civil limb: right to a fair hearing) arising from pre-trial judge proceedings that confirmed a prosecutor’s decision to discontinue a criminal investigation for perjury against his former mother-in-law. He claimed the closed, non-adversarial, written-only procedure (in chambers, without parties present or able to see/rebut each other’s submissions) unfairly prejudiced his position regarding related civil claims for damage to his honour, dignity and professional standing.

In March 2009 a Bucharest court granted the applicant’s wife a divorce, holding him solely at fault on the basis (among other things) of a February 2009 statement by his former mother-in-law alleging his inappropriate and violent behaviour towards his family. The applicant had not attended the hearings. On 1 March 2013 he lodged a criminal complaint for perjury and joined as a civil party, seeking approximately €4,600 in non-pecuniary damages. He stressed that the statement had been notified to his employer, triggering intensive psychological and professional scrutiny that delayed his return to work.

The police and a first-instance prosecutor initially proposed discontinuing the prosecution (with an administrative fine) on the ground that the conduct lacked the requisite gravity. Three witnesses (a neighbour, an acquaintance and the applicant’s under-age daughter living with him) had not observed violence. A more senior prosecutor, however, closed the file on 25 August 2014, finding the investigation insufficient to establish guilt, the witnesses unreliable or improperly heard, and the limitation period expired.

The applicant appealed to the District Court (sitting as pre-trial judge). On 22 October 2014 he was notified of the date and invited to file written observations on admissibility and merits; he made no further submissions beyond his original appeal. On 3 November 2014 the pre-trial judge, sitting in chambers without the parties, dismissed the appeal in a final interlocutory judgment. The judge found no proof of perjury, held that the mother-in-law had been better placed than the witnesses to observe family tensions, discounted the daughter’s evidence as potentially influenced, noted that the divorce court had relied on additional factors (including the applicant’s non-cooperation), and took into account (though not examined by prosecutors) medical records showing the applicant’s 2008 hospitalisation for erratic behaviour after police intervention requested by his wife.

Separately, in May 2014 the applicant had already instituted ordinary tort proceedings against his former mother-in-law relying in part on the first prosecutor’s finding of guilt; the outcome of those proceedings is unknown. Under the then-applicable Code of Criminal Procedure, pre-trial judges examined complaints against decisions not to prosecute exclusively on the papers, in the parties’ absence. Subsequent Constitutional Court rulings (October–November 2014) later declared aspects of this written, non-oral, non-adversarial procedure unconstitutional, but they post-dated the applicant’s case.

The key facts relevant to the fairness complaint are therefore the exclusively written, closed character of the 3 November 2014 hearing, the applicant’s inability to know or rebut the alleged perpetrator’s or prosecutor’s arguments (or the extra medical material), the pre-trial judge’s reliance on that material, and the potential res judicata or persuasive effect of the discontinuation decision on any subsequent civil claim for the same facts.
001-208278:
The applicants—a foundation owning an estate and study centre in Wapenveld, plus three local residents—live near a motocross track in Heerde (Gelderland Province) operating since 1987 under a permit limiting hours to Wednesday/Saturday afternoons (plus two extra weekdays April–October). The track and applicants’ land lie partly in a Natura 2000 area; applicants claim they hear the bikes.

On 27 September 2013 the operator sought a new permit under the 1998 Nature Conservation Act for more bikes and longer hours. On 4 December 2013 the Provincial Executive posted a website notice of its draft decision to grant the permit. The draft and documents were available for inspection (physically and online) from 9 December 2013 to 20 January 2014; “interested parties” (those whose own, personal, current and objectively determinable interests were directly affected) could submit views by the latter date. The draft itself stated that only those who had submitted views could later appeal the final decision.

No views arrived. The permit was issued on 27 January 2014. Notification appeared solely on the provincial website, with documents inspectable (again physically and online) from 30 January to 13 March 2014; appeals had to be lodged by the latter date. Chapter 3.4 of the General Administrative Law Act (public-participation procedure) applied.

Applicants first learned of the decision on 4 November 2014 and appealed to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State on 12 November 2014, after the statutory deadline. They contended that website-only publication did not constitute notification “in some other suitable manner” under s. 3:12(1) of the General Administrative Law Act (or the analogous provision of the Nature Conservation Act). Citizens could not reasonably be expected to monitor every local-authority website; the notifications might never have been posted at all. Consequently their Article 6 right of access to court had been violated.

The Province produced archive screenshots confirming publication and invoked the 2012 Gelderland Electronic Notification Ordinance, which expressly authorised sole electronic publication of such notices (a practice already used since October 2011 and advertised in local newspapers). Internet access in the Netherlands was high, rendering electronic notification at least as effective as traditional newspaper publication.

On 7 September 2016 the Administrative Jurisdiction Division dismissed the appeal as out of time. It recalled its earlier case-law that internet notification is “suitable” but that, absent a specific statutory exception, a non-electronic channel is also required. The 2012 Ordinance supplied that exception. Article 6 does not confer an absolute right of access; States enjoy a margin of appreciation provided the very essence of the right is not impaired, a legitimate aim is pursued and the means are proportionate. Sole electronic publication pursued the legitimate aim of faster, more accessible administration and did not impair the essence of the right. The notifications had been published; applicants were therefore at fault for missing both the views stage and the appeal deadline. Section 6:13 of the General Administrative Law Act accordingly barred their appeal.

(The applicants also invoked Articles 8 and 13, but the central complaint—and the focus of the subsequent Strasbourg proceedings—was the alleged denial of access to court caused by exclusively electronic notification.)

The applicants—a foundation owning a study-centre estate and three residents of Wapenveld (municipality of Heerde, Gelderland)—lived near a motocross track (partly in a Natura 2000 site) whose 1987 permit limited operations to specific weekday/Saturday hours. They could hear the bikes from their land.

On 27 September 2013 the operator applied under the 1998 Nature Conservation Act for a new permit allowing more bikes and longer hours. On 4 December 2013 the Provincial Executive posted notice solely on its website that the draft decision and documents would be available for inspection (physically and online) from 9 December 2013 to 20 January 2014; interested parties (those whose interests were directly affected) could submit views by the latter date. The draft itself stated that only such parties who had submitted views could later appeal the final decision.

No views arrived. The permit was issued on 27 January 2014; notification again appeared solely on the provincial website, with inspection from 30 January to 13 March 2014 and an appeal deadline of 13 March. Chapter 3.4 of the General Administrative Law Act (public-participation rules) applied.

The applicants first learned of the decision on 4 November 2014 and appealed to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State on 12 November, arguing that electronic-only publication might never have occurred and, in any event, was not a “suitable manner” of notification under s. 3:12(1) of the Act. Citizens could not be expected to monitor every government website. They claimed this denied them access to court (Art. 6) and also invoked Arts. 8 and 13.

The Province produced archive screenshots proving the notices had been posted and relied on the 2012 Gelderland Electronic Notification Ordinance, which expressly authorised sole electronic publication of such announcements. The Ordinance had merely codified a practice begun in October 2011 that had been advertised in local newspapers; computer ownership in the Netherlands was high, so electronic reach was expected to exceed that of free local papers.

On 7 September 2016 the Administrative Jurisdiction Division declared the appeal out of time and therefore inadmissible. Internet notification was a “suitable manner”; the Ordinance supplied the statutory exception (required by s. 2:14(2) of the Act) that permitted purely electronic communication of non-personalised notices. Exclusive electronic notification pursued the legitimate aims of faster, cheaper and more accessible administration and did not impair the very essence of the right of access to a court. The applicants had failed to show the archive was unreliable and were reasonably at fault for missing both the view-submission and appeal deadlines. Under s. 6:13, failure to submit views (absent excuse) bars a later court challenge; under s. 6:11 a late appeal is admissible only if the appellant is not at fault.

Thus the alleged Art. 6 violation rested on the claim that website-only notice of a decision affecting nearby landowners, coupled with the statutory bar on appeals by those who had not first commented, had in practice closed the courts to them.

The case concerns whether solely electronic publication of notifications for a draft administrative decision and the final permit granting extended operations at a nearby motocross track violated the applicants’ right of access to court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (they also invoked Articles 8 and 13). The applicants are a foundation owning an estate and study centre in Wapenveld (municipality of Heerde, Province of Gelderland) plus three residents there. A motocross track, operated since 1987 under a permit limiting hours, lies close by (partly in a Natura 2000 area); the applicants hear the bikes from their premises.

In September 2013 the operator applied for a new Nature Conservation Act permit allowing more bikes and longer hours. On 4 December 2013 the Provincial Executive posted a website notice that the draft decision (and documents) could be inspected from 9 December 2013 to 20 January 2014 at the provincial offices and online. Interested parties (those whose interests are directly affected) could submit views orally or in writing by 20 January. The draft itself stated that only those who had submitted views and qualified as interested parties could later appeal the final decision. No views were received.

The permit issued on 27 January 2014. Notification appeared solely on the provincial website, stating the decision could be inspected from 30 January to 13 March 2014 (offices and online) and that appeals had to be lodged by 13 March. The decision noted that the public-participation rules of the General Administrative Law Act applied.

The applicants first learned of the permit on 4 November 2014 and appealed to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State on 12 November 2014. They questioned whether the notices had actually been published and argued that website-only notification was not “some other suitable manner” under the General Administrative Law Act. Dutch citizens could not reasonably be expected to monitor every local and regional authority website. Their failure to comment on the draft and their late appeal were therefore excusable, and their Article 6 access to court had been breached.

The Provincial Executive produced archive-website screenshots confirming publication and relied on the 2012 Gelderland Electronic Notification Ordinance (in force since 2011 and publicly advertised), which expressly authorised sole electronic publication of such notices. High internet penetration made electronic notice at least as effective as traditional newspaper publication; Article 6 was not violated.

In its 7 September 2016 judgment the Division declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time. Earlier case-law accepted internet notification as “suitable” but required at least one non-electronic method unless a statute provided otherwise. The 2012 Ordinance supplied that statutory basis and predated the decision. Article 6 does not confer an absolute right of access; limitations are permissible if they pursue a legitimate aim and remain proportionate. Facilitating faster, more accessible communication between citizens and authorities was a legitimate aim. Solely electronic notification did not impair the very essence of the right. The applicants had not shown the archive site was unreliable, so they were at fault for missing both the comment period and the appeal deadline.

Domestic law (General Administrative Law Act ss. 1:2, 2:14, 3:11–3:15, 6:13; Nature Conservation Act s. 42(3)) generally requires newspaper or other suitable notice and, absent contrary statutory provision, forbids solely electronic communication of non-personal notices. The Gelderland Ordinance, whose adoption was itself published in official gazettes and the provincial bulletin, created the required exception. The Court later examined whether this coherent system struck a fair balance, given high Dutch internet usage, prior public advertisement of the practice, and the clear opportunity it afforded to comment and appeal.
001-207134:
The case concerns Iraqi national Marsel Munir Johana (born 1994), who entered Denmark aged 4 in 1999 and obtained permanent residence in 2004. From age 16 he built a criminal record of violent and drug offences, receiving two suspended expulsion orders. In December 2011 he was convicted of two violent offences and given a 30-day suspended sentence with supervision. In March 2014 he was convicted of another violent offence (60 days’ imprisonment plus a two-year suspended expulsion). In November 2015 he was convicted of possessing 93 g of cocaine for resale (six months’ imprisonment, initially partly suspended but served in full after he failed community-service conditions, plus a further two-year suspended expulsion). He was later fined for insulting a prison officer.

The index offence occurred on 18 September 2016, during the currency of the latest suspended expulsion. Together with three accomplices the applicant committed an aggravated assault: the group repeatedly punched two victims in the head; after one victim fell the applicant kicked him in the head, causing facial bruising and a broken ankle. He was charged under Penal Code Articles 245 and 247.

A police interview recorded that the applicant had completed lower-secondary school, begun but not finished a mechanic’s apprenticeship, taken some higher-preparatory courses and held a part-time job. His immediate family lived in Denmark (with relatives also in Sweden, Canada and Australia); he had no family or other ties in Iraq, which his Christian family had fled, and he claimed he would be killed if returned. He had no partner or children.

The Immigration Service, noting some 13 months of prior imprisonment, supported the prosecutor’s request for expulsion. The Viborg District Court convicted him in August 2017, imposed four months’ imprisonment and ordered expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban, holding that the seriousness of the offence outweighed his limited Iraqi ties and fear of return and that expulsion was not contrary to Denmark’s international obligations. The Western High Court (October 2017) upheld the conviction, increased the sentence to six months and confirmed the expulsion, emphasising his 15-plus years of lawful residence, family presence in Denmark, lack of education or stable employment, and the two prior warnings.

The Supreme Court (19 September 2018) likewise upheld the sentence and the six-year ban. Applying the Maslov criteria it found a significant risk of further violent or drug offending. Although the applicant had spent most of his life in Denmark, lived with his mother and had close family there, he remained poorly integrated (no completed education or labour-market attachment, reliance on benefits). Ties to Iraq were weak—he had never returned, spoke Assyrian (used in parts of Iraq) and some Arabic, and possessed only family-transmitted cultural knowledge—but he was not wholly incapable of establishing a life there. The latest aggravated offence, committed during the probation period of a previous expulsion warning, together with his adult criminal record, supplied “very compelling reasons” that outweighed the interference with his private life. The limited duration of the ban and the possibility of remote family contact were also taken into account. A later minor conviction for personal-use cocaine did not alter the assessment.

The European Court of Human Rights subsequently held that the domestic courts had duly applied its case-law, that no minimum sentence threshold exists for expulsion of a settled migrant, and that the combination of the aggravated violent offence, the prior serious criminality and the two unused warnings justified the measure. Article 8 was therefore not violated.

The case of Munir Johana v. Denmark (Application no. 56803/18) concerns an Iraqi national’s complaint that a Danish expulsion order, combined with a six-year re-entry ban, violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant was born in Iraq in 1994 and entered Denmark in 1999 at age four. He received residence permission in 2000 and permanent residence in 2004. His parents and siblings live in Denmark; remaining relatives are in Sweden, Canada and Australia. He has no family in Iraq (his family fled as Christians), has never returned there, speaks Assyrian (with limited Arabic comprehension reported by his father) and possesses only residual knowledge of Iraqi culture through relatives. He is unmarried with no partner or children, completed lower-secondary education but not an apprenticeship or further training, and has only modest, intermittent employment, relying mainly on state grants or benefits.

From age 16 the applicant accrued a substantial criminal record. In December 2011 he received a 30-day suspended sentence for two violent offences. In March 2014 he was sentenced to 60 days’ imprisonment for a further violent offence and given a two-year suspended expulsion order. In November 2015 he was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment (four months initially suspended for community service, later served in full after non-compliance) for possessing 93 grams of cocaine with intent to resell, together with another two-year suspended expulsion order. In October 2016 he was fined for insulting a prison officer. A later 2018 conviction for possessing 0.1 grams of cocaine for personal use resulted in a fine.

The index offence occurred on 18 September 2016, during the probation period of the most recent suspended expulsion. Together with three others the applicant repeatedly punched two victims in the head; after one victim fell he kicked him in the head, causing facial bruises and a broken ankle. The offence was charged as aggravated, particularly aggressive and repetitive violence (Penal Code Arts. 245 and 247).

After a police interview and an Immigration Service report confirming prior imprisonment totalling approximately 13 months and supporting expulsion, the Viborg District Court convicted the applicant in August 2017, imposing four months’ imprisonment and a six-year re-entry ban. It found no particular reasons rendering expulsion contrary to international obligations, given the offence’s seriousness and the applicant’s limited Iraqi ties. The Western High Court increased the sentence to six months in October 2017 and upheld expulsion, emphasising the violence, 15-plus years’ residence, family presence in Denmark, absence of an independent family unit or stable education/employment, and two prior suspended expulsion orders. The Supreme Court, on 19 September 2018, confirmed both the sentence and the expulsion. Applying the Maslov criteria, it required “very compelling reasons” to expel a settled migrant who had spent most of his life in Denmark. It identified a significant risk of further violent or drug-related offending, noted that the aggravated assault occurred while a suspended expulsion was still in force, and concluded that the public-interest considerations outweighed the applicant’s strong Danish ties and weak Iraqi connections. The six-year (rather than permanent) ban and the possibility of remote family contact were treated as relevant to proportionality.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the domestic courts had duly applied its case-law: there is no minimum sentence threshold for expulsion of a settled migrant, and the combination of an aggravated violent offence, a history of serious criminality and two prior warnings justified the measure. No violation of Article 8 was found.

The case of Munir Johana v. Denmark (Application no. 56803/18) involves an Iraqi national born in 1994 who entered Denmark in 1999 at age four, obtaining residence in 2000 and permanent residence in 2004. He alleged that a 2018 expulsion order with a six-year re-entry ban, imposed after conviction for an aggravated violent offence, violated Article 8 of the Convention by interfering disproportionately with his private life as a settled migrant who had spent most of his life in Denmark.

From age 16, the applicant built a criminal record. In December 2011, the District Court convicted him of two violent offences (committed September–October 2011) and imposed a suspended 30-day prison sentence with supervision. In March 2014, he was convicted of a further violent offence (October 2013, committed with another) and received 60 days’ imprisonment plus a suspended expulsion order (two-year probation). In November 2015, he was convicted of possessing 93 grams of cocaine for resale, sentenced to six months’ imprisonment (four months initially suspended for community service, later served in full after non-compliance), and issued a second suspended expulsion (probation until November 2017). He was later fined for insulting a prison officer (October 2016) and for possessing 0.1 grams of cocaine (January 2018).

The decisive offence occurred on 18 September 2016, during the latest probation period. Aged 21, the applicant and three accomplices punched one victim repeatedly in the head and assaulted another similarly; the applicant then kicked the fallen victim in the head, causing facial bruises and a broken ankle. Charged with particularly aggressive, brutal or dangerous violence as a repeat offender (Penal Code Arts. 245(1) and 247(1)), he was convicted by the Viborg District Court in August 2017 (four months’ imprisonment plus expulsion and six-year ban). The Western High Court (October 2017) upheld the conviction and expulsion, increasing the sentence to six months. The Supreme Court (19 September 2018) confirmed both.

Personal circumstances, assessed via a 2016 police interview and Immigration Service reports, showed the applicant had completed 10th grade, begun (but not finished) a mechanic apprenticeship, taken preparatory courses and held part-time work. He lived with his mother and stepfather; his parents and siblings resided in Denmark, with other relatives in Sweden, Canada and Australia. He had never visited Iraq, claimed no ties there (family had fled as Christians, and he feared death if returned), spoke Assyrian (used in parts of Iraq) and some Arabic, and had no partner or children. He possessed only modest education and labour-market links, relying on grants or benefits after age 18.

Danish courts applied Aliens Act provisions (ss. 22, 24a–b, 26, 32) and Maslov v. Austria criteria. They weighed the offence’s gravity (senseless group violence causing injury), the applicant’s prior convictions (including after majority), two explicit warnings via suspended expulsions, commission during probation, and assessed reoffending risk. Against this they balanced 17 years’ lawful residence from early childhood, strong Danish family/social ties versus weak Iraqi ones (no family there, never visited, but some linguistic/cultural knowledge via family). The limited six-year ban and possibility of remote family contact were noted. The Supreme Court concluded the interference was necessary for crime prevention and proportionate under Article 8 § 2, as compelling public-interest reasons outweighed private-life considerations.

The case of Gawlik v. Liechtenstein (App. no. 23922/19) involved a German doctor, Lothar Gawlik, who alleged a violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression) after his summary dismissal from the Liechtenstein National Hospital. Employed from June 2013 as deputy chief physician in internal medicine under an indefinite contract terminable on six months’ notice, Gawlik reported to Dr H., the department’s chief physician.

On 9 September 2014, while examining electronic patient files, Gawlik identified four deaths shortly after morphine administration and inferred that Dr H. had practised active euthanasia. That day, at a meeting initiated by the President of Parliament’s Control Committee (prompted by anonymous quality complaints), Gawlik voiced these suspicions. On 11 September, he lodged a criminal complaint with the Public Prosecutor, who opened investigations for killing on request and assisting suicide. On 19 September, after further electronic-file review, he reported six additional cases, citing deaths soon after morphine (sometimes without documented pain), “supportive therapy” notations, and the drugs used. He stressed his aim was to protect patients.

The hospital maintained a Critical Incident Reporting System for anonymous internal alerts, recently handled by a three-person group excluding Dr H.; Gawlik did not use it or consult paper files (known to be more complete and to which he had access). Hospital vice-president reports (19–24 September) and a Swiss palliative-care expert (October) examined the paper files and interviewed Dr H., concluding all ten patients were in WHO-standard palliative situations; morphine treated pain or dyspnoea, not to cause death; and no errors or active euthanasia occurred. An Austrian court-appointed expert later confirmed this. Gawlik was suspended on 26 September. In a 2 October statement he maintained the treatments were not lege artis, invoked ethical duties and the Physicians’ Act notification obligation, and explained he had gone straight to prosecutors because of urgency and distrust of internal investigation.

On 17 October the hospital director dismissed him without notice, citing irretrievable loss of trust: he had not first raised concerns internally (with Dr H., the director or the foundation board) and his allegations were “clearly unfounded.” Media coverage followed. Criminal proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014; those against Gawlik for false accusation ended in 2016.

Gawlik sued for roughly CHF 600,000 in lost salary and damages, arguing the complaint was justified given the suspected offence’s gravity. The Regional Court upheld the dismissal under Civil Code Article 1173a § 53 (important reason: continuation of employment no longer reasonably expected). The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that reporting to confidential external bodies was proportionate and that internal reporting to Dr H. was unsuitable; it awarded CHF 125,000 in arrears. The Supreme Court quashed that ruling: as a senior doctor Gawlik knew electronic files were incomplete yet failed to check paper files, which would have instantly shown the suspicions unfounded; this constituted a serious, unjustified breach of loyalty. The Constitutional Court dismissed his Article 10 complaint (indirect Drittwirkung in a private-law employment relationship). Applying the Court’s whistle-blower criteria (Heinisch v. Germany), it accepted public interest in proper hospital care and Gawlik’s lack of improper motive, but found he had acted irresponsibly by not verifying incomplete electronic data before making grave, publicly damaging accusations.

The Strasbourg Court unanimously found no Article 10 violation. The dismissal was an interference prescribed by law and pursuing legitimate aims (protection of reputation and rights of others). Domestic courts had struck a fair balance: the public interest in unverified information did not outweigh the detriment to the hospital and Dr H. Gawlik, acting in good faith, had nevertheless failed to verify his suspicions to the extent circumstances permitted.

The case of Gawlik v. Liechtenstein (Application no. 23922/19) concerned the dismissal without notice of the applicant, a German doctor employed since June 2013 as deputy chief physician in the internal medicine department of Liechtenstein’s only public hospital. His superior was Dr H., the department’s chief physician. On 9 September 2014 the applicant reviewed electronic medical files and concluded that four patients had died after receiving morphine in circumstances suggesting active euthanasia by Dr H. That same day he reported his suspicions to the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee (who had contacted him about anonymous quality complaints). On 11 September, on that official’s advice, he lodged a criminal complaint with the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which opened proceedings against Dr H. for suspected killing on request and related offences. After further electronic-file research he added suspicions concerning six more patients, citing rapid deaths after morphine administration, absence of documented pain, and labels such as “supportive therapy.”

The hospital maintained an anonymous internal reporting system (CIRS). Although its composition had recently changed, the applicant did not use it, later citing urgency, his ethical and statutory duties under the Physicians’ Act to notify authorities of suspected criminal deaths, and distrust of internal investigation. Hospital inquiries—including reports by the foundation-board vice-president and a Swiss palliative-care expert who examined paper files and interviewed Dr H.—concluded that all ten patients had been in a recognised palliative situation, that morphine had been given for pain and dyspnoea rather than to hasten death, and that the applicant would have seen this immediately had he consulted the complete paper records to which he had access. An Austrian expert commissioned in the criminal investigation reached the same conclusion. Proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014; later proceedings against the applicant for making false accusations were also discontinued.

The applicant was suspended on 26 September and dismissed without notice on 17 October 2014. The hospital stated that the relationship of trust had been irretrievably destroyed because he had gone public with grave, unverified accusations instead of first informing Dr H., the hospital director or the foundation board.

He sued for salary and damages, arguing the dismissal violated his freedom of expression as a whistle-blower. The Regional Court dismissed the claim, holding that his failure to check the paper files and to report internally constituted an important reason for summary dismissal. The Court of Appeal reversed, finding the suspicions not wholly unfounded (the prosecutor had opened a file) and external reporting proportionate given the seriousness of the alleged offence. The Supreme Court restored the dismissal, emphasising that a senior physician who knew the electronic files were incomplete had acted irresponsibly by not consulting the paper records. The Constitutional Court, applying the Court’s Heinisch criteria, accepted a public interest in lawful hospital treatment and the absence of personal motive, but held that the applicant’s failure to verify incomplete data before making public accusations of homicide rendered his conduct irresponsible; the interference with Article 10 was therefore justified.

The European Court of Human Rights likewise found no violation of Article 10. The dismissal interfered with the applicant’s freedom of expression but was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aims of protecting the reputation and rights of others and the hospital’s operational interests. Although the applicant acted in good faith and the subject-matter was of public concern, the information remained unverified and was later shown to be unfounded. He could readily have consulted the paper files. The resulting harm to the hospital (media coverage, official investigations) and to Dr H. outweighed any public interest in the unconfirmed allegations. The domestic courts had struck a fair balance in accordance with the Court’s case-law.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) case of Gawlik v. Liechtenstein (Application no. 23922/19, judgment of 16 February 2021) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression) arising from the applicant’s dismissal without notice. The applicant, a German doctor specialised in internal medicine, had been employed since June 2013 as deputy chief physician in the internal medicine department of Liechtenstein’s only public hospital, under an indefinite contract terminable on six months’ notice. His superior was the department’s chief physician, Dr H.

On 9 September 2014 the applicant examined the hospital’s electronic medical records and identified four patients who had died after receiving morphine. Interpreting the notes as indicating active euthanasia by Dr H., he immediately informed the President of Parliament’s Control Committee (who had approached him about quality concerns) of his suspicions. On 11 September, on that official’s advice, he lodged a criminal complaint with the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which opened an investigation for possible killing on request and assisting suicide. After further electronic-file research he reported six additional cases on 19 September, emphasising that his aim was to protect patients. He did not consult the hospital’s internal Critical Incident Reporting System (which by then was handled by a three-person group excluding Dr H.) or raise the matter with Dr H., the hospital director or the foundation board.

Police seized the corresponding paper files and questioned Dr H. Hospital-commissioned internal reports and an external Swiss palliative-care expert subsequently concluded that all ten patients had been in a recognised end-of-life palliative situation; morphine had been administered solely to relieve pain or dyspnoea and had not caused death. An Austrian expert later reached the same conclusion for the investigating judge. The applicant was suspended on 26 September and dismissed without notice on 17 October. The hospital cited an irretrievable breakdown of trust: the applicant had failed to verify the (incomplete) electronic data against the readily available paper files, which would have immediately shown the suspicions to be unfounded, and had gone public without first using internal channels.

Criminal proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014; proceedings against the applicant for false accusation were discontinued in 2016. The applicant sued the hospital for roughly CHF 600 000 in lost salary and damages. The Regional Court upheld the dismissal as justified under Article 1173a of the Civil Code. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that the disclosure was protected expression and that the suspicions had not been wholly unfounded. The Supreme Court reinstated the dismissal, stressing that a senior physician who knew the electronic records were incomplete had an obligation to check the paper files before making grave, public accusations. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint, applying the ECtHR’s whistle-blowing criteria (notably Heinisch v. Germany). It accepted a public interest in lawful medical practice and that the applicant had acted in good faith, but found he had behaved irresponsibly by omitting an elementary verification that would have dispelled the allegations. The resulting harm to the hospital’s and Dr H.’s reputations therefore outweighed any public-interest value of the unverified information. The ECtHR later endorsed this balancing, finding no violation of Article 10.

The case of Gilligan v. Ireland (Application no. 55276/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned civil proceedings under Ireland’s Proceeds of Crime Act 1996 (“the Act”) initiated against four family members—John Gilligan, his wife Geraldine, and their children Treacy and Darren. The applicants alleged that the overall length of the proceedings violated their right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court communicated only this complaint, declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

On 21 November 1996 the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) obtained an interim High Court freezing order under s. 2 of the Act over the applicants’ houses, land and vehicles, followed on 5 and 19 December 1996 by temporary “interlocutory” orders under s. 3. A further s. 3 order was made on 16 July 1997. Although later treated by the Irish courts as a final freezing order that would remain in force for seven years unless discharged, the applicants consistently maintained that they had understood it to be merely provisional and that they had not been afforded a proper adversarial hearing at that stage.

Parallel constitutional proceedings challenging the Act itself were dismissed by the High Court in June 1997 and by the Supreme Court in October 2001. Throughout 1997–2008 the applicants lodged a series of motions seeking to strike out the proceedings, to vary or discharge the 1997 order under s. 3(3), to extend time for appealing that order, and to argue procedural unfairness. Most were unsuccessful. The Supreme Court in April 2005 and again in December 2008 confirmed that the July 1997 order was final, that s. 3(3) provided an effective subsequent remedy, and that the applicants’ legal advisers had been aware of the statutory scheme since at least May 1997.

CAB applied for a disposal (confiscation) order under s. 4 in December 2004, once the statutory seven-year period had elapsed. That application was held in abeyance while the applicants’ s. 3(3) challenges were determined. Those applications were finally issued in early 2009, heard over several days in 2010, and rejected by a 90-page High Court judgment of 27 January 2011 that found the properties to be the proceeds of crime (save for a modest portion of one house). Further High Court rulings of 20 December 2011 dismissed Convention-based objections and granted the s. 4 disposal orders, subject to short stays in respect of certain family homes.

The applicants appealed all three 2011 judgments. Case-management delays, requests for new evidence, adjournments sought by the applicants and a “Greendale” motion to reopen the 2008 Supreme Court ruling postponed the hearing until June 2016. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals on 1 February 2017, observing that the applicants had “slept on their rights” and had repeatedly re-litigated the same points. The properties were confiscated in June 2017.

Thus the proceedings, which began in November 1996 and ended with a final Supreme Court judgment more than twenty years later, were marked by successive, often overlapping challenges by the applicants, many of which the domestic courts characterised as misconceived or vexatious. The Irish courts repeatedly emphasised that an effective statutory remedy under s. 3(3) had been available from 1997 onwards and that the applicants themselves had chosen not to invoke it promptly.

The case of Arewa v. Lithuania (Application no. 16031/18) concerns a Nigerian national, Mr Olusegun Bamise Arewa (born 1989, resident in Vilnius), who alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a trial within a reasonable time) and Article 8 (right to respect for family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from protracted criminal proceedings and their effects.

On 7 July 2014, a Lithuanian bank received a transfer of USD 1,853,800 to the account of Jammo (a Vilnius-registered company in which the applicant had been a shareholder since February 2012) from Sinowide Energy Limited (Hong Kong). Attempts to withdraw EUR 100,000 in cash and transfer the remainder to Italy prompted the bank to freeze the funds and notify the Financial Crimes Investigation Service (FCIS) of suspected money laundering. On 11 July 2014 prosecutors froze the applicant’s and Jammo’s accounts (the former lifted only on 21 January 2018). On 15 July 2014 the applicant was formally suspected of money laundering (Criminal Code Article 216 § 1) and document forgery causing major damage (Article 300 § 3). Investigators alleged Jammo was a shell company acquired to conceal criminal proceeds; a forged contract purporting to cover wood, metal and mineral sales was used to justify the transfer. The applicant, then legally represented, refused to sign the suspicion notice or to testify.

On 18 July 2014 the Vilnius City District Court ordered two months’ pre-trial detention, citing flight risk: the applicant was a Nigerian citizen with no close Lithuanian ties or marriage, suspected of serious offences punishable by over one year’s imprisonment, and Lithuania lacked close legal cooperation with Nigeria. The measure was replaced on 16 September 2014 by weekly police registration and a written undertaking not to leave Vilnius.

The ensuing investigation required extensive international mutual legal assistance. Requests were sent to Spain and Hong Kong (October 2014), with later requests to the United States, Hungary and Denmark. Hong Kong replies arrived only in June 2017 (after supplementary requests in 2015–2016) and proved incomplete, necessitating further requests in October 2017. Additional delays arose from translations, Interpol inquiries, specialist examinations of accounts and documents, and the need to establish the funds’ origin amid a suspected large-scale international scheme. A chronological table showed virtually no domestic investigative acts between September 2014 and January 2017 while authorities awaited foreign responses. The applicant refused to testify on 16 July and 11 August 2014; he first gave a statement only on 12 July 2017. He repeatedly complained (February 2015, July 2016, November 2017, May/October 2018, April 2019) that the investigation was unreasonably delayed, that a seized computer remained unexamined for years, and that the proceedings prevented economic activity, residence-permit renewal and marriage. All complaints were dismissed by the Vilnius City District Court and Regional Court, which emphasised the case’s complexity, international character, Lithuania’s treaty obligations on money-laundering, the applicant’s non-cooperation, and the public interest in thorough investigation.

The applicant’s one-year temporary residence permit (issued November 2013 on the basis of lawful economic activity) expired on 15 November 2014. His October 2014 extension request was refused on 14 November 2014 because the pending suspicions constituted a real threat to public order (Law on the Legal Status of Aliens, Article 35 § 1(1)). Administrative appeals failed; the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (19 October 2015) upheld the refusal, noting the applicant’s purely economic (not family) ties and the seriousness of the charges. On 30 August 2015 a son was born to the applicant and Lithuanian national E.M. A November 2015 family-reunification application was rejected by reference to the earlier decision. In 2016 the civil registry refused to register their marriage because the applicant lacked a valid visa or residence permit and was therefore unlawfully present. Subsequent complaints linking these family-life restrictions to investigative delay were likewise rejected.

By October 2019 the proceedings remained ongoing, having lasted more than five years. The applicant sought (unsuccessfully at first instance) the lifting of remaining restrictive measures, citing the duration’s burden.
