**Case Summary: Arewa v. Lithuania (ECtHR, Application no. 16031/18)**

The applicant, a Nigerian national born in 1989 and resident in Vilnius, alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a trial within a reasonable time) due to the length of criminal proceedings against him, and of Article 8 (right to respect for family life) due to the proceedings' impact on his ability to reside, work, and marry in Lithuania. Notice of the application was given solely on these complaints.

In July 2014, a Lithuanian bank received a transfer of USD 1,853,800 to the account of Jammo (a Vilnius-registered company in which the applicant had been a shareholder since February 2012) from a Hong Kong company, Sinowide Energy Limited. Suspicious attempts to withdraw or transfer the funds led the bank to freeze the sum and notify the Financial Crimes Investigation Service (FCIS). On 11 July 2014, prosecutors temporarily froze funds in the applicant's and Jammo's accounts (the applicant's freeze was lifted in January 2018). On 15 July 2014, the applicant was notified that he was suspected of money laundering (Criminal Code Article 216 § 1) and document forgery causing major damage (Article 300 § 3). Investigators alleged that Jammo had no real activity and had been acquired to conceal crime; the applicant and director A.L.C. (also Nigerian) had forged documents purporting to evidence a sale of wood, metal and minerals to justify the transfer.

On 18 July 2014, the Vilnius City District Court ordered two months' pre-trial detention, citing evidence (bank records, search materials, emails and A.L.C.'s statement), the applicant's foreign nationality, lack of family or social ties in Lithuania, risk of flight, and limited legal cooperation with Nigeria. An appeal was dismissed on 5 August 2014; the applicant did not then invoke family ties. On 16 September 2014, detention was replaced by weekly police registration and a written undertaking not to leave Vilnius.

The applicant, represented by counsel, repeatedly complained of delays in the pre-trial investigation (e.g., February 2015, July 2016, and subsequently through 2019). He argued that necessary steps had already been taken, that he had not signed company documents or initiated transfers, and that the proceedings had prevented extension of his residence permit, economic activity, marriage and family life (a son, D.A., was born on 30 August 2015 to Lithuanian citizen E.M.). He also criticised a four-year delay in examining a seized computer, loss of his passport and inability to leave Lithuania. Domestic courts consistently rejected the complaints. They emphasised the case's complexity (international financial crime of particularly large scale), the need for mutual legal assistance from Hong Kong, Spain, the USA, Hungary and Denmark (requests sent from September 2014 onward, with follow-ups and translations causing delays; some replies incomplete), the applicant's initial refusal to testify, and Lithuania's obligations under money-laundering instruments (EU Directive 2005/60/EC, the 1990 Strasbourg Convention and the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime). Courts held that investigative actions were timely, that inconvenience to the applicant was a natural consequence of his suspect status, and that society's interest in uncovering the funds' origin prevailed. A chronological table showed limited domestic activity between September 2014 and January 2017 while awaiting foreign replies. As of October 2019 the investigation remained ongoing; the applicant requested lifting of the registration obligation while accepting the residence restriction.

Separately, the applicant's temporary residence permit (issued November 2013 on the basis of lawful economic activity and valid until November 2014) was refused extension in November 2014 because he was a suspect in a serious intentional crime posing a threat to public order. An administrative appeal was dismissed in October 2015; no further appeal was lodged. A November 2015 application to change the permit on family grounds (cohabitation and the child) was rejected by reference to the earlier decision. In 2016 the civil registry refused to register the applicant's marriage to E.M. because he lacked a valid visa or residence permit and was therefore unlawfully present; no appeal followed.

The ECtHR ultimately found the proceedings (lasting over five years) sufficiently expeditious given their particularly complex international and financial character and the lack of tangible practical consequences for the applicant.

The case of Arewa v. Lithuania (Application no. 16031/18) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns complaints by Nigerian national Olusegun Bamise Arewa under Article 6 § 1 (right to a trial within a reasonable time) and Article 8 (right to respect for family life) of the Convention. The alleged violations stem from the duration of pre-trial criminal proceedings against him and their effects on his residence status, ability to marry, and family life in Lithuania.

On 7 July 2014, a Lithuanian bank received a transfer of USD 1,853,800 from Sinowide Energy Limited (Hong Kong) to the account of Jammo, a Vilnius-registered company. Attempts to withdraw EUR 100,000 in cash and transfer the remainder to unidentified Italian recipients prompted the bank to freeze the funds and notify the Financial Crimes Investigation Service (FCIS) of suspected criminal activity. On 11 July 2014, prosecutors temporarily froze funds in the applicant’s and Jammo’s accounts (the former measure lifted on 21 January 2018). On 15 July 2014, the FCIS formally notified the applicant that he was suspected of money laundering (Criminal Code Article 216 § 1) and document forgery causing major damage (Article 300 § 3). The FCIS found that the applicant, a Jammo shareholder since February 2012, directed its director (fellow Nigerian A.L.C.) and that both knew the company conducted no real activity but existed to conceal crime and launder proceeds. They had forged a document purporting to show Jammo selling wood, metal and minerals to Sinowide to justify the transfer.

On 18 July 2014 the Vilnius City District Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand for two months, citing evidence from bank documents, a search, his email account and A.L.C.’s statement, plus a risk of flight given the seriousness of the offences, his foreign nationality (Nigeria having no close legal cooperation with Lithuania) and lack of family or firm social ties in Lithuania. An appeal was dismissed on 5 August 2014. On 16 September 2014 the measure was replaced by weekly police registration and a written undertaking not to leave his Vilnius residence.

The applicant, represented by counsel, repeatedly complained to the courts that the pre-trial investigation was protracted, preventing extension of his residence permit, economic activity, marriage and family life, and leaving him unable to leave Lithuania. All complaints (February 2015, July 2016, November 2017, May/October 2018 and April 2019) were dismissed. Domestic courts emphasised the case’s complexity: an international financial crime of particularly large scale requiring mutual legal assistance (MLA) from Hong Kong (request sent September 2014; incomplete replies in 2015–2016 necessitating follow-ups; full reply June 2017, translated September 2017; further request October 2017), Spain, the USA, Hungary, Denmark and Interpol. Additional delays arose from translations, specialist examinations of accounts and documents, searches for possible forgers of company records, and the need to establish the funds’ criminal origin in compliance with Lithuania’s obligations under the 1990 Council of Europe Convention on Laundering, the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime and EU Directive 2005/60/EC. Courts noted that the applicant had initially refused to testify (July/August 2014), giving a statement only in July 2017, and that his later complaints about seized computer examination and other steps were unfounded given ongoing necessary actions. Periods of apparent inactivity (e.g., September 2014–January 2017) were attributed to waiting for foreign replies. Courts held that any inconvenience to the applicant’s social and economic rights was a natural, proportionate consequence of his suspect status and that society’s interest in thoroughly investigating money-laundering outweighed his right to expeditious proceedings.

Separately, the applicant’s one-year temporary residence permit (issued November 2013 on the basis of lawful economic activity via Jammo) expired in November 2014. The Migration Department refused renewal on 14 November 2014 under Article 35 § 1(1) of the Law on the Legal Status of Aliens, finding that his status as a suspect in a serious intentional crime posed a real threat to public order (supported by Schengen Convention Article 96). The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court upheld this on 19 October 2015 after a hearing, noting the applicant’s purely economic (not family) ties to Lithuania at that stage and the prior remand detention; the applicant did not appeal. A son, D.A., was born to the applicant and Lithuanian citizen E.M. on 30 August 2015. In November 2015 they applied to change the permit on family-reunification grounds; this was rejected in December 2015 by reference to the earlier decision. In May 2016 E.M. sought to register their marriage, but the civil registry refused in July 2016 because the Migration Department had confirmed the applicant lacked a valid visa or residence permit and was therefore staying unlawfully. Neither the applicant nor E.M. appealed these decisions. The applicant remained subject to the movement restriction and weekly registration into at least October 2019, when he unsuccessfully sought their lifting.

The proceedings remained at the pre-trial stage more than five years after their commencement, with the applicant arguing that the resulting inability to regularise his stay, marry the mother of his child or pursue economic activity constituted an unjustified interference with family life.
001-208751:
The applicants—a Moroccan couple and their two young sons—complained that Spanish authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by evicting them from and demolishing their only home, which they had built illegally on public land. The first applicant arrived in Spain in the late 1990s and registered in Madrid from 2001; his wife registered from 2003. Around late 2004 or early 2005 they began constructing a dwelling without permission on a plot in the Cañada Real Galiana, a historic livestock route classified as protected public-domain land that could not be developed. They registered it as their residence in April 2005, when their first child was an infant; a second son was born in 2007. At the time of the application they were unemployed and surviving by collecting scrap.

The Cañada Real settlement had grown since the 1960s despite its legal status. By 2011 more than 5,000 people, many in vulnerable circumstances, lived in the Madrid section. Authorities long tolerated the occupation but from 2005 systematically pursued unauthorised buildings, citing public-order, safety, health and social problems.

In March 2005 municipal police issued a formal warning. An April 2005 order required work to stop immediately. A May 2005 decision declared the construction illegal and incapable of regularisation, giving 15 days for comments. A June 2005 demolition order followed, personally served in July. The applicants neither complied nor used the available administrative or judicial remedies. Enforcement proceedings began in 2006. After they rebuilt an extension, a court in September 2007 authorised entry, noting the limited scope of such proceedings (prima-facie legality and necessity of entry) and the applicants’ failure to contest the underlying orders. They were evicted and the house demolished on 18 October 2007 amid serious disturbances.

They immediately began reconstruction. Police warnings were ignored. An April 2008 decision, issued within the original proceedings, required them to vacate and demolish the rebuild within 15 days; it was treated as non-appealable. After service difficulties and a struck-out court application, a fresh request for judicial authorisation was filed in 2010. The first applicant argued that a new demolition order was required, that the 2011 Cañada Real Galiana Act (which reclassified the land as private-domain property of the region and envisaged a social-framework agreement) rendered individual demolitions unlawful and discriminatory, and that eviction would harm the children’s schooling. In April 2011 the court authorised entry only after the school year ended, holding that the 2005 order remained valid, the Act did not legalise existing buildings, and entry was the sole means of enforcement. The applicants appealed, reiterating these points.

Eviction and demolition occurred at 05:00 on 6 September 2011 without prior notice of the exact time, to avoid a repeat of 2007 incidents. Emergency services offered temporary accommodation and support, which the family refused, saying they would stay with relatives. The High Court of Justice dismissed the appeal in March 2012, finding the Act did not suspend planning enforcement and describing the first applicant’s conduct as an abuse of rights. The Constitutional Court rejected an amparo appeal in November 2013, stressing that the applicants had never challenged the original administrative decisions on the merits and that the courts had balanced the interests involved, including the children’s education. Two judges dissented, criticising procedural shortcuts and insufficient proportionality assessment given the settlement’s long tolerance and the new Act.

The applicants also applied unsuccessfully for social housing in 2007 and 2011. The 2011 Act and subsequent 2014 and 2017 agreements sought a comprehensive solution for registered residents but expressly did not regularise prior illegal constructions. The family later faced a bill of some €10,767 for both demolitions.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 8 complaint: whether the successive evictions and demolitions of the family’s sole home, after decades of official tolerance and amid a legislative process addressing the wider settlement, were necessary and proportionate.

The applicants—Moroccan nationals Abdelilah Ghailan, Fatima Zahra Alami Wahabi and their two young sons—unlawfully constructed a dwelling on public-domain livestock-route land (Cañada Real Galiana) in Madrid, a protected non-developable area where private building was forbidden. They began work in late 2004/early 2005, registered the site as their residence in April 2005, and later rebuilt after the first demolition. The informal settlement of several thousand (including many in extreme vulnerability) had been long tolerated, but from 2005 the municipality systematically pursued illegal constructions for reasons of public order, safety, health and planning.

On 17 March 2005 police recorded the unauthorised works. The first applicant received a personal warning, an immediate suspension order (April 2005) and, after he ignored a 15-day comment period, a demolition order (23 June 2005) served on 5 July 2005. He used none of the administrative or judicial remedies. Enforcement proceedings followed; he again failed to comment. After he enlarged the house, the municipality obtained judicial authorisation to enter (Madrid Administrative Court no. 7, September 2007). The court limited its review to prima-facie legality and necessity of entry, noting the applicants’ non-participation. Eviction and demolition occurred on 18 October 2007 amid violence; costs were later charged to the applicants.

They immediately rebuilt. Police issued a fresh warning. In April 2008 the municipality, relying on the already-final 2005 order, again required vacation and demolition within 15 days. Service difficulties led to publication; the applicants still did not challenge it. A second judicial-authorisation request was struck out on a technicality (2009). After personal service in November 2009 the first applicant appointed a lawyer and later argued, inter alia, that a new demolition order was required, that the 2011 Cañada Real Galiana Act (which reclassified the land as private-domain property of the region and contemplated a future social-framework agreement) rendered individual demolitions unlawful, and that the children’s schooling would be disrupted.

Madrid Administrative Court no. 30 authorised entry on 20 April 2011, again stressing the limited scope of the proceedings, the finality of the 2005 order, the applicants’ persistent defiance, and the Act’s failure to legalise existing constructions. It postponed enforcement until the school year ended. The applicants were evicted without prior notice of the exact hour (to avoid a repeat of 2007 disturbances) on 6 September 2011; emergency services offered short-term accommodation and support, which they declined, citing family networks. The High Court of Justice dismissed their appeal (March 2012), characterising their conduct as an abuse of rights. The Constitutional Court (November 2013) likewise rejected an amparo claim, reiterating that the courts’ role had been confined to verifying appearance of legality and necessity of entry; any fuller proportionality review should have been sought by timely judicial review of the original demolition order, which the applicants had never done. Two dissenting judges considered that the authorities and courts had failed to weigh the settlement’s long tolerance, the new Act and possible alternatives.

The applicants’ two social-housing applications (2007 and 2011) were unsuccessful—one apparently refused, the second left incomplete. Municipal social services had been alerted before both evictions.

These facts form the core of the Article 8 complaint: whether the successive evictions and demolitions of the family’s only home were necessary and proportionate, and whether domestic courts adequately examined that issue.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Ghailan and Others v. Spain (Application no. 36366/14) involved four Moroccan nationals—a couple and their two minor sons—who alleged that the demolition of their only home and their eviction violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for home). The key issue was whether this interference was necessary in a democratic society and proportionate to legitimate aims.

The first applicant arrived in Spain in the late 1990s; he and the second applicant married in Morocco in 2001 and registered as residents in Madrid from 2001 and 2003 respectively. Around late 2004 or early 2005, they began unlawfully constructing a house on public land in the Cañada Real Galiana (Madrid section), a former livestock route classified as non-developable public-domain land where private construction was forbidden. They registered it as their residence in April 2005, along with their elder son (born 2004); a younger son was born in 2007. Informal settlements had proliferated there since the 1960s, housing over 5,000 people (many of Roma or Moroccan origin) with high unemployment and vulnerability. Authorities had long tolerated this but, from 2005, began systematic enforcement against illegal builds due to public-order, safety, health and social problems.

On 17 March 2005, police issued a warning during an inspection. The Municipality ordered work to stop (April 2005) and issued a demolition order (June 2005), noting the construction could not be legalised. Multiple notices were served personally, informing of remedies, but the applicants submitted no comments and lodged no appeals. They continued building, adding a floor. Enforcement proceedings followed; after they refused to leave, judicial authorisation to enter was granted (September 2007) following limited review of legality and necessity. They were evicted and the house demolished on 18 October 2007 amid disturbances. They immediately rebuilt, ignoring further warnings.

Authorities issued a further leave-and-demolish order (April 2008) within the original proceedings, later personally served. After failed attempts and a struck-out authorisation application, they reapplied. In 2011 observations, the first applicant argued the original order had already been enforced, a new one was needed, the 2011 Cañada Real Galiana Act (which reclassified the land as private-domain property of the region but explicitly did not legalise existing constructions or grant building rights, pending a social-framework agreement) rendered individual demolitions unlawful or discriminatory, and eviction would harm the children's education. The Administrative Court authorised entry (April 2011) but delayed it until after the school year, finding the (final) demolition order lawful and entry the only enforcement means, given the applicants' disregard for prior decisions. They were evicted and the house demolished on 6 September 2011 without prior notice of the exact time (to avoid incidents); emergency social services offered short-term aid and support, which they refused, citing family help. Costs were later claimed from them.

Appeals to the High Court of Justice (2012) and Constitutional Court (amparo, 2013) failed. Courts emphasised the limited scope of entry-authorisation proceedings (prima-facie legality and necessity, not full merits review of final administrative decisions, which should have been challenged earlier via judicial review). They held the Cañada Real Act did not suspend planning rules or legalise the build, the measure protected urban order, and delays had protected the children's schooling. A dissent argued for greater scrutiny of proportionality, given long-term tolerance of the settlement and the new Act. Separate social-housing applications (2007 and 2011) were unsuccessful or incomplete.

The Court found any shortcomings in proportionality review attributable to the applicants' unexplained failure to use available domestic remedies at earlier stages.
001-209992:
The case of Valdís Fjölnisdóttir and Others v. Iceland concerns three Icelandic nationals: a former married couple (the first and second applicants) and a child (the third applicant) born in February 2013 via gestational surrogacy in California. The intended parents engaged a US surrogacy agency and obtained a Californian birth certificate and US passport listing them as the child’s parents. The child was conceived through IVF using donor gametes and has no biological connection to either intended parent. The surrogate mother waived any parental claim.

Three weeks after the birth the applicants returned to Iceland and applied to Registers Iceland to record the child in the national register as an Icelandic national born abroad. After learning of the surrogacy, Registers Iceland refused on 18 June 2013, holding that Icelandic parentage rules treat the woman who gives birth as the mother; the child therefore had no automatic claim to Icelandic citizenship and was a foreign unaccompanied minor. The Ministry of the Interior confirmed the refusal on 27 March 2014. Meanwhile the municipal child-protection committee assumed legal custody, appointed a guardian and placed the child in temporary foster care with the intended parents so that the existing de-facto bond could be preserved.

The applicants sought judicial review, seeking both annulment of the refusal and a declaration that they must be registered as the child’s parents. While the case was pending the Icelandic Parliament enacted special legislation granting the child citizenship (effective 31 December 2015). He was thereafter entered in the register as an Icelandic citizen, but the intended parents were still not recorded as his legal parents. The couple divorced in May 2015; the foster-care arrangement was thereafter adjusted so that the child lived alternately with each intended parent and her new spouse, and since December 2019 he has been in permanent foster care with the first applicant while retaining equal access to the second applicant. An earlier adoption application was withdrawn after the divorce.

The District Court of Reykjavík dismissed the claims in March 2016. It accepted that family life existed among the three applicants and that the refusal to recognise parentage interfered with that life, but held the interference justified by Iceland’s statutory ban on surrogacy (punishable by fine or imprisonment) and by the need to protect women from exploitation and children from being denied knowledge of their origins. The court emphasised that the authorities had mitigated the interference by granting citizenship and by maintaining the foster-care relationship. The Supreme Court of Iceland upheld the result in March 2017 but reasoned differently: at the moment of the original refusal no legally protected family life existed, because neither intended parent had given birth to the child or had a biological link with him, both of which are prerequisites under Icelandic law. Only the later foster-care orders created a protected family relationship.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the continuing non-recognition of a legal parent-child relationship violated their right to respect for private and family life (Article 8) and constituted discrimination (Article 14). The Court examined whether a fair balance had been struck between the applicants’ family life (now formally recognised through foster care) and the general interests served by Iceland’s prohibition of surrogacy.

The case concerns three Icelandic applicants: a former married couple (first and second applicants) and their intended son (third applicant, born 2013). The couple engaged a paid US gestational surrogacy agency; the child was conceived via IVF using donor gametes and thus shared no biological link with either intended parent. A California birth certificate and US passport named the couple as parents after the surrogate waived all claims.

Three weeks after the birth the family returned to Iceland and applied to Registers Iceland to enter the child in the national register as an Icelandic citizen born abroad. The application was refused on 18 June 2013 (confirmed by the Ministry of the Interior on 27 March 2014). Icelandic law treats the woman who gives birth as the legal mother irrespective of genetic contribution (Children Act s. 6) and expressly prohibits surrogacy (Artificial Fertilisation Act s. 5). Consequently the child was regarded as a US national with no automatic entitlement to Icelandic citizenship. He was treated as an unaccompanied foreign minor; a child-protection committee assumed legal custody, appointed a guardian (Ms M.) and placed him with the couple under successive temporary foster-care agreements.

While judicial review of the registration refusal was pending, Parliament granted the child citizenship by special statute (Act 128/2015). He was entered in the national register as an Icelandic citizen but still not as the couple’s son. The couple divorced in May 2015, rendering the existing foster arrangement void. New sequential one-year placements followed; since December 2019 the child has been permanently fostered by the first applicant and her new spouse while enjoying equal access to the second applicant. An earlier joint adoption application was first suspended and later withdrawn after the authorities indicated that the surrogate (and possibly her husband) would have to consent and that any payment connected with consent would bar adoption.

The Reykjavík District Court (2 March 2016) accepted that “family life” existed among the three applicants and that non-recognition of parentage interfered with Article 8 rights. It held the interference justified by the legitimate aim of upholding the surrogacy ban (protection of women from exploitation and of children’s right to know their origins) and sufficiently mitigated by foster care, a residence permit and eventual citizenship. The Supreme Court (30 March 2017) upheld the outcome but on different reasoning: relying on Paradiso and Campanelli v. Italy, it found that no protected family life existed at the moment of the 2013–14 decisions because the parent–child link had not been established in accordance with Icelandic law (neither applicant had given birth and neither had a biological connection). The child’s best interests, though paramount, could not override those fundamental principles.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the persistent refusal to recognise a legal parent–child relationship violated their rights to respect for private and family life (Article 8) and amounted to discrimination (Article 14). At the date of the Court’s judgment the child remains an Icelandic citizen under permanent foster care with the first applicant, Ms M. still acting as legal guardian.

The couple travelled to California and used a paid gestational-surrogacy agency. The child was conceived by IVF with donor gametes and therefore has no genetic link to either intended parent. The applicants withdrew the application after their divorce.

The District Court (March 2016) accepted that de-facto family life existed but held that non-recognition was justified by the public-policy ban on surrogacy, the need to prevent exploitation of women and the child’s interest in knowing its origins. Mitigating measures (foster placement and later citizenship) were deemed sufficient. The Supreme Court (March 2017) upheld the refusal. Relying on Paradiso and Campanelli v. Italy, it found that, at the moment of the 2013–14 administrative decisions, no legally recognised family life existed because the parental link had been created in a manner contrary to fundamental Icelandic rules (neither applicant had given birth and there was no genetic tie). Subsequent foster care created protected family life, but that later development could not retroactively invalidate the earlier refusal.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ complaints under Article 8 (non-recognition of parentage despite an established social bond, uncertainty of legal status, and obstacles to adoption) and Article 14 (alleged difference in treatment compared with families possessing a biological link).
001-209358:
**The case of Omdahl v. Norway (Application no. 46371/18) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to the excessive length of proceedings for administering and dividing a deceased person’s estate.**

The applicant, Olav Omdahl (born 1951), was a grandson and heir of O.A. Knutsen, who died on 24 April 1993 at age 94. Knutsen had built substantial wealth through shipping, property, and industrial activities, though the family had lost control of the shipping company in the 1980s due to financial difficulties. At death, the estate was valued at approximately 100 million Norwegian kroner (NOK), with about 10 million NOK in debts. Assets included a large property portfolio, shares in wholly and partly owned companies, securities, and moveable property. Initial heirs were three children and two grandchildren. The applicant’s mother (one of the children) and another child died before final distribution.

Public administration of the estate began on 5 May 1993 before the Probate Court (later reorganized as a District Court), with an advocate appointed as administrator. Accounts were kept and audited by a public accountant, and numerous in- and out-of-court meetings occurred throughout. Some small properties were converted to cash early on, but legal proceedings over heirs’ rights to in-kind distribution of assets (per the deceased’s will and a codicil) tied up proceeds until late 2005/early 2006. Parallel Probate Court decisions aiming to convert more assets to cash were frequently quashed or amended on appeal by the High Court, preventing distributions.

A trust established by the deceased in the Bahamas (managed by a London bank) came to light only after the applicant’s mother’s death in 2002. In December 2005, each of the deceased’s children and grandchildren received 5.5 million NOK from it. This sparked disputes over whether certain funds belonged to the estate, plus complex tax issues for the estate and heirs. Correspondence between the Probate Court and tax authorities from 2006 onward resolved these by winter 2010. Tax uncertainties had blocked a proposed 2007 interim distribution.

An interim distribution occurred on 1 July 2010, giving each lineal branch 10 million NOK. Heirs appealed; the High Court dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2011, and the Supreme Court refused leave on 1 November 2011. Concurrent disputes arose over selling estate shares (District Court decision 11 June 2010, finally settled 25 March 2011 after appeal), other inter-heir lawsuits, a motion to disqualify a judge for alleged partiality, and sales of shares in a property company and a fish oil factory. Those proceedings ended in 2012; most sales completed in the first half of 2013, and remaining limited-liability companies were wound up in December 2013. The financial crisis of autumn 2008 and difficulties selling a large volume of property in a limited area added delays.

The Probate Court ordered final distribution on 1 August 2014. The High Court dismissed an appeal on 27 November 2014, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 April 2015. Funds were disbursed on 16 April 2015 (approximately 18.9 million NOK per family branch). A further distribution of later-recovered assets was decided on 10 August 2015 (no payments to heirs) and became final in September 2015. The entire public administration thus lasted 22 years and 4 months.

On 9 March 2016, the applicant sued the Norwegian Government in Oslo City Court, seeking a declaration that the length violated Article 6 § 1’s “reasonable time” requirement and claiming compensation. The City Court (15 September 2016) found no violation, emphasizing the estate’s size and complexity, numerous difficult legal/factual issues, the fact that other heirs (not primarily the applicant or his predecessor) initiated many proceedings (including those blocking property sales for ~12 years), absence of proven inactivity, and lack of evidence that courts or authorities could have acted differently. The applicant had no separate interest in a mere declaratory judgment.

The High Court (judgment 22 March 2018, after a hearing with witnesses) similarly found no violation, though it noted the duration far exceeded the normal 1–3 years for such administrations and was “very long.” It conducted a detailed phase-by-phase review and found no periods of inactivity. Disputes (many complex, reaching two or three court levels) continually arose, often triggered by prior decisions, making greater parallelism impractical. A 1997 High Court ruling (not appealed by the applicant’s predecessor) had been criticized by the applicant as blocking progress, but it had become final. The court referenced ECtHR case-law (including lengthy Polish estate cases and others) but distinguished them due to this estate’s exceptional scale, asset realization needs, volume of disputes, trust/tax complications, and sale difficulties. Interim distributions and other court measures (e.g., refusing leave to appeal) mitigated delays. The State could not legally have accelerated matters further without impairing other parties’ rights; some heirs were more litigious, and several of their actions succeeded. No resource shortages or organizational shortcomings were shown. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave to appeal on 21 June 2018.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, judgment 22 April 2021, final 6 September 2021) held Article 6 § 1 applicable, as the administration mixed contentious and non-contentious elements under domestic law (then the 1930 Administration of Estates Act). It found the length not excessive given the exceptional complexity, numerous disputes, absence of legal/procedural framework shortcomings, and mitigation via interim distributions. The State was not responsible for delays attributable to the parties’ litigation.

The case of Omdahl v. Norway (no. 46371/18) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 ECHR (reasonable time) arising from public administration of the estate of O.A. Knutsen, who died on 24 April 1993. Administration began on 5 May 1993 before the Probate Court and concluded only in September 2015, lasting 22 years and 4 months. Heirs were three children and two grandchildren (including the applicant); two children died before final distribution.

An advocate-administrator was appointed. Early cash conversions of minor properties were blocked by successive disputes over heirs’ rights to in-kind distribution under the will and a codicil; proceeds remained tied up until late 2005. Parallel Probate Court orders to realise further assets were repeatedly quashed or varied on appeal, preventing any distribution. A Bahamas trust (discovered after 2002) generated additional litigation over ownership of funds and complex tax questions for the estate and heirs; those issues were resolved only in winter 2010. Each lineal branch then received an interim NOK 10 million in July 2010 (appeals dismissed by 2011). Further contests over the method of selling company shares, a property company and a fish-oil factory occupied the courts until 2012–13; remaining companies were wound up in December 2013. Final distribution (NOK 18.9 million per branch) was ordered in August 2014, upheld on appeal, and paid in April 2015; residual assets were dealt with by September 2015.

The applicant sued the State in 2016 seeking a declaration of breach and compensation. The Oslo City Court (September 2016) and Borgarting High Court (March 2018) both held that Article 6 applied to the mixed contentious/non-contentious probate process but that the length was not excessive. They stressed the estate’s exceptional size and legal/factual complexity, the large number of sequential disputes (many reaching the Supreme Court), the absence of any proven periods of inactivity, and the fact that delays were attributable to the heirs’ own litigation rather than to the authorities. Interim distributions had mitigated prejudice; courts had refused leave to appeal where possible. No alternative procedural steps were identified that the State could lawfully have taken without impairing other parties’ rights. The Supreme Court refused leave in June 2018.

The European Court likewise found no violation. The proceedings, though far longer than the normal one-to-three years, were “exceptionally complex” and formed a framework for numerous inter-related disputes. Continuous activity, interim payments and the lack of any systemic or organisational shortcoming meant the overall duration remained compatible with Article 6 § 1.

**The ECHR case of Omdahl v. Norway (Application no. 46371/18, judgment of 22 April 2021) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention due to the excessive length of public administration of a deceased person’s estate, lasting 22 years and 4 months.**

Heirs at death were three children and two grandchildren; two children (including the applicant’s mother) died before final distribution.

Public administration began on 5 May 1993 in the Probate Court, with an appointed administrator. Meetings, accounts, and audits occurred throughout. Early sales of small properties generated cash, but multiple legal proceedings over heirs’ rights to in-kind distribution (per the will and a codicil) tied up proceeds until late 2005/early 2006. Parallel Probate Court decisions to convert more assets to cash were quashed or amended on High Court appeal, blocking distributions.

A Bahamas trust (managed from London) emerged after the applicant’s mother’s 2002 death. Each heir received NOK 5.5 million from it in December 2005. This sparked disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and complex tax issues for the estate and heirs. Correspondence with tax authorities from 2006 led to clarification only in winter 2010. These issues delayed a 2007 proposed interim distribution.

On 1 July 2010, an interim distribution of NOK 10 million per family branch occurred. Heirs appealed; the High Court dismissed this on 7 June 2011, and the Supreme Court refused leave on 1 November 2011. Concurrent disputes arose over selling estate shares. A District Court decision of 11 June 2010 was appealed and finalized only on 25 March 2011. Further actions included a motion to disqualify a judge for partiality, plus disputes over shares in a property company and a fish oil factory. These ended in 2012; most share sales completed by mid-2013, and remaining companies were wound up in December 2013.

The Probate Court ordered final distribution on 1 August 2014. The High Court dismissed an appeal on 27 November 2014; the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 April 2015. Disbursement occurred on 16 April 2015 (approximately NOK 18.9 million per branch). A later recovery of additional assets (no payments to heirs) became final in September 2015, ending administration after 22 years and 4 months.

In March 2016, the applicant sued the Norwegian Government in Oslo City Court for a declaration of an Article 6 § 1 violation (unreasonable delay) and compensation. The City Court (15 September 2016) acknowledged the exceptional length but found no violation, citing the estate’s size and complexity, numerous factual/legal issues, other heirs’ litigation (e.g., codicil suits blocking property sales for ~12 years), absence of proven inactivity, and no blame attributable to authorities.

The High Court (judgment 22 March 2018, after a hearing with witnesses) agreed Article 6 applied but that the case did not require special expedition. It reviewed all phases, finding no inactivity: early disputes (from September 1993) reached the Supreme Court by December 1995, with further appellate decisions through 2006; later disputes (post-2005/06) were similarly active. New disputes often followed earlier rulings, limiting parallel handling. A 1997 High Court ruling (unappealed by the applicant’s predecessor) had delayed progress but was legally binding. The process was extraordinary due to asset scale, numerous heir actions, delayed property realization until January 2007, a difficult market (including the 2008 financial crisis), trust/tax complications, and complex legal questions. Interim distributions mitigated harm; courts refused some appeals to speed matters. The State could not legally accelerate further without infringing other parties’ rights. The High Court (with some doubt) held the length justified by complexity and sufficient progress. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 21 June 2018.

The ECHR held Article 6 applicable to this mixed contentious/non-contentious estate administration. The length was not excessive given exceptional complexity, multiple disputes, lack of inactivity or systemic shortcomings, and mitigation via interim payments. No violation was found.

The case of M.C. v. the United Kingdom (App. no. 51220/13) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for private life) arising from the mandatory disclosure of the applicant’s criminal conviction on an enhanced criminal record certificate (ECRC).

The applicant, a British national born in 1955 and residing in Solihull, was convicted in August 2007 of failing to stop after a road traffic accident. She was fined and received five penalty points on her driving licence. This was her only conviction and did not result in a custodial sentence.

Years later, in connection with a teaching job in China, she applied for an ECRC. Under the pre-2013 legislative regime (Police Act 1997, s. 113B, and Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 Exceptions Order 1975), all previous convictions—spent or unspent—were subject to mandatory disclosure on ECRCs for roles involving children or vulnerable adults. An ECRC dated 9 January 2013 accordingly revealed the 2007 conviction. The applicant initially claimed this caused her to be refused the post, but later clarified that she had already secured a teaching position in China in December 2012, which she held until summer 2014.

She also complained to the Independent Police Complaints Commission about the original police investigation, seeking to have the conviction expunged. The West Midlands Police Professional Standards Department refused, stating she had pleaded guilty. The applicant disputed that she had entered a guilty plea and requested supporting evidence.

Amendments to the disclosure regime took effect on 29 May 2013 (following an independent review, Court of Appeal findings of incompatibility, and parliamentary approval). Under the revised rules, a conviction is filtered from ECRCs if: (i) 11 years have elapsed since conviction for adults (“currency rule”); (ii) it is the person’s only offence (“multiple conviction rule”); (iii) it did not result in a custodial sentence; and (iv) it is not a specified offence (primarily violence, sexual, or safeguarding-related offences). Equivalent shorter periods apply to cautions. The individual disclosure obligation under the 1974 Act was aligned with these ECRC rules. The former requirement to send a copy of the ECRC to the prospective employer was later repealed.

Because the applicant’s conviction satisfied the other three filtering conditions, it remained subject to mandatory disclosure solely by operation of the currency rule until 31 August 2018 (11 years after the August 2007 conviction). Thereafter it ceased to be disclosable.

The applicant’s complaint therefore encompassed both the 2013 disclosure under the old, blanket-disclosure regime and the continued mandatory disclosure of her spent, minor traffic conviction under the amended regime until 2018. The Court examined whether the post-2013 framework (particularly the currency rule) was “in accordance with the law” and proportionate, having regard to the competing interests of offender rehabilitation and public protection in sensitive occupations. Approximately four million ECRC applications are made annually in England and Wales. The Supreme Court had previously upheld the amended scheme as a whole (subject to two limited exceptions not relevant here), emphasising its prescriptive, category-based nature, the absence of unfettered discretion, and the State’s margin of appreciation in drawing bright-line rules after extensive consultation.

The Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 allowed convictions to become “spent” after a rehabilitation period, after which a person could generally deny them. However, the 1975 Exceptions Order required disclosure of even spent convictions for work involving children or vulnerable adults. At the time of the 2013 ECRC, all spent convictions had to be disclosed where the exception applied.

The individual duty to disclose spent convictions was aligned with the ECRC rules, and the requirement to send a copy of the certificate to the prospective employer was later repealed.

The applicant’s 2007 traffic conviction was therefore still mandatorily disclosed on any ECRC issued between May 2013 and August 2018. The Court examined both the historic disclosure under the old, wholly unfiltered regime and the continued operation of the currency rule under the amended scheme. It found the new, highly prescriptive rules to be “in accordance with the law” and the currency rule itself to be a proportionate, category-based measure falling within the State’s margin of appreciation.

The case of Milosavljević v. Serbia concerns journalist Ranko Milosavljević’s Article 10 complaint over a civil defamation award for articles on an alleged sexual assault.

Milosavljević (born 1960) was journalist and editor-in-chief of Svetlost magazine in Kragujevac. On 3 June 2010 it published two pieces on a late-April incident involving Mr B, head of a municipal branch office. Milosavljević’s article “Shame through Silence” stated that Mr B impersonated a market inspector, lured an underage Romani street vendor into his car on a pretext, and attempted rape (thwarted by her resistance). Arrested the next day, he was charged with impersonation, unlawful deprivation of liberty and attempted rape. The piece criticised silence by police, prosecutors, NGOs and city officials, implying a cover-up linked to the girl’s ethnicity or a possible payoff to withdraw the complaint, and questioned protection of a municipal employee.

A second article by colleague Ms A, titled “The false inspector \ldots attempted to rape an underaged girl,” recounted (citing police) the girl’s complaint: Mr B locked her in his car, drove off, touched and kissed her, tore her clothing, then arranged a meeting at which police arrested him. Police had issued no standard release until requested.

Criminal proceedings were pending at publication. Mr B was charged in July 2010 only with unlawful deprivation of liberty and illicit sexual acts (not attempted rape). The alleged victim recanted in September 2010. He was acquitted in December 2012 (after remittal) and the judgment became final in December 2013.

In July 2010 Mr B sued civilly for defamation. In December 2010 the High Court found Milosavljević and the magazine liable (Ms A not), awarding 100,000 RSD for mental anguish plus costs and ordering publication of the judgment. It held that the first article presented unproven pending charges (including an untrue attempted-rape allegation, as police had not so charged) as established fact, breaching the presumption of innocence. Ms A’s text was accurate per police information.

In April 2011 the Appeals Court held all three jointly liable for 50,000 RSD (c. €485) plus costs, upholding publication. It reduced the sum given public interest in the incident (though reported inappropriately), noted Ms A’s title inaccurately stated attempted rape, and held Mr B was not a public figure (a mere municipal employee, not an official) required to tolerate greater criticism.

Domestic courts relied on the Obligations Act (compensation for honour/reputation harm) and 2003 Public Information Act (duty to verify information, prohibition on pronouncing guilt without a final decision, editor liability). Milosavljević’s constitutional appeal was dismissed in December 2013; the Constitutional Court found a proper balance struck, as even accurate reporting of a pending criminal case or breach of the presumption of innocence was unlawful.

Enforcement began in 2014 but remained unexecuted as of 2020 (Milosavljević unemployed since 2013, owning only a family flat). He had offered Mr B space to reply (refused); Mr B sought psychiatric help after publication.

These facts underlie the alleged interference with journalistic expression.

The ECtHR case Milosavljević v. Serbia (Appl. no. 57574/14) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) arising from a Serbian civil defamation judgment against journalist and editor Ranko Milosavljević.

On 3 June 2010, Milosavljević’s weekly Svetlost published two articles about an incident involving Mr B, head of a municipal branch office in a village near Kragujevac. The first article, written by the applicant and titled “Shame through Silence,” stated as fact that in late April 2010 Mr B had impersonated a market inspector, lured an underage Romani street vendor into his car, driven her away, and attempted to rape her. It reported that her screams thwarted him, that he was later arrested after arranging a further meeting, detained 48 hours, and charged with false impersonation, unlawful deprivation of liberty and attempted rape. The piece criticised police, prosecutors, NGOs and city authorities for remaining silent, asking whether the cover-up occurred because the victim was Romani or to protect a municipal employee so he could “buy off the Gypsies.” The second article, by another journalist but edited under the applicant’s responsibility, gave a more detailed account of the same events (impersonation, abduction, groping, tearing of clothing) drawn from police information and the criminal complaint; its title nonetheless asserted that Mr B had “attempted to rape an underaged girl.”

At the time of publication, criminal proceedings against Mr B were still at an early stage. He was later charged only with unlawful deprivation of liberty and illicit sexual acts (not attempted rape or false impersonation). The alleged victim and her mother recanted their accusations in September 2010. After two trials, Mr B was finally acquitted in December 2013.

In July 2010 Mr B brought a civil defamation action. The Kragujevac High Court (December 2010) held the applicant and Svetlost jointly liable, awarding 100,000 RSD for mental anguish plus costs and ordering publication of the judgment. It found that the first article presented unproven criminal accusations as established facts while proceedings were pending, thereby violating the presumption of innocence, and that the claim of attempted rape was factually untrue because police had never charged that offence. The Appeals Court (April 2011) reduced the award to 50,000 RSD (approximately EUR 485) payable jointly by the applicant, the second journalist and the magazine, again ordering publication. It confirmed the inaccuracies and the breach of the presumption of innocence, added that the second article’s headline was itself defamatory, and held that Mr B was not a public figure: as a mere municipal employee performing administrative tasks, his private conduct attracted no higher duty of tolerance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in December 2013, finding that the ordinary courts had struck a proper balance between expression and reputation.

Enforcement of the modest award remained pending years later; the applicant, by then unemployed, owned only the family flat. These facts formed the basis of the Article 10 complaint: that the domestic courts had disproportionately sanctioned journalistic reporting on a matter of public interest involving an official and an alleged serious crime against a vulnerable minor.

The case of Milosavljević v. Serbia (App. no. 57574/14) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression) arising from a civil defamation judgment against journalist Ranko Milosavljević, editor-in-chief of the Kragujevac weekly Svetlost.

On 3 June 2010, while criminal proceedings were pending, Svetlost published two articles about an alleged April 2010 incident involving Mr B, head of a municipal branch office. The applicant's article "Shame through Silence" stated as fact that Mr B had impersonated a market inspector, lured an underage Romani street vendor into his car, and attempted to rape her; she resisted, he obtained her number, and police arrested him the next day after he called her. It reported charges of false impersonation, unlawful deprivation of liberty and attempted rape, criticised the silence of police, NGOs and city authorities (suggesting a possible cover-up due to the girl's ethnicity or to protect a publicly paid official), and posed rhetorical questions implying official intervention to buy time for a deal with the victim's family.

A second article by journalist Ms A, titled "The false inspector from [D] near Kragujevac attempted to rape an underaged girl", detailed the girl's complaint (impersonation, abduction, touching, kissing, tearing of clothing, loud music to drown screams, warning not to tell anyone) and noted police confirmation of charges of unlawful deprivation of liberty and illicit sexual acts, plus delayed public information.

Mr B was charged on 21 July 2010 with the latter two offences. The victim and her mother recanted in certified statements of 16 September 2010. After hearings, the Kragujevac Court of First Instance acquitted him on 25 December 2012 and again (after remittal) on 17 June 2013; the acquittal became final on 30 December 2013.

In July 2010 Mr B sued the applicant, Ms A and Svetlost for defamation. On 23 December 2010 the High Court found the applicant and magazine jointly liable for 100,000 RSD (mental anguish from honour/reputation breach) plus costs, and ordered publication of the judgment. It held that the first article presented pending charges (including uncharged attempted rape) as proven facts, violating the presumption of innocence; the second article was accurate based on police information, so Ms A was not liable. Recantation post-dated publication and was irrelevant.

On 4 April 2011 the Appeals Court reduced the award to 50,000 RSD (approx. €485) jointly against all three respondents (plus costs), upholding publication. It found Ms A also liable for her title stating attempted rape as fact, held Mr B was not a public figure (mere municipal employee, not a local official, so entitled only to private-person tolerance), and considered public interest in reporting but required more appropriate presentation. Statutory interest ran from the first-instance date.

The applicant's 20 May 2011 constitutional appeal was dismissed on 3 December 2013 (served 6 February 2014). The Constitutional Court held that even accurate information on pending criminal cases could not be published if it breached the presumption of innocence, and that the civil courts had struck a proper balance between expression and reputation.

Enforcement proceedings began in 2014 but remained unenforced as of 2020; the applicant (unemployed since 2013, owning a family flat) faced potential seizure. Mr B had refused an offer of space to reply and sought psychiatric care for distress.

Domestic law (Obligations Act; 2003 Public Information Act) required verification of information, prohibited pronouncing guilt without a final decision, limited privacy protection for officials only where relevant to functions, and imposed joint editor/founder liability for unverified or inadmissible publications. Municipal branch heads performed administrative tasks (records, certificates) but were not high officials. Average local salaries were far below the award.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 10 complaint that the defamation ruling, holding journalists to private-person standards and finding a failure of responsible journalism, disproportionately interfered with reporting on a matter of public concern.

**CASE OF HALET v. LUXEMBOURG (Application no. 21884/18), ECtHR Third Section, 11 May 2021 (later referred to Grand Chamber)**

Raphaël Halet, a French national employed by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in Luxembourg, was convicted in the “Luxleaks” affair. PwC prepared tax declarations and obtained Advance Tax Agreements (“tax rescripts”) from Luxembourg authorities on behalf of multinational clients. Between 2012 and 2014, media outlets published hundreds of these documents, exposing highly advantageous tax arrangements from 2002–2012.

An internal PwC investigation identified auditor A.D., who on 13 October 2010 (the day before resigning) copied some 45,000 pages, including 20,000 pages of tax documents covering 538 tax-rescript folders, and later gave them to journalist E.P. A second investigation identified Halet. After the first media reports, Halet contacted E.P. in May 2012 and between October and December 2012 supplied 16 further documents (14 tax declarations plus two covering letters). Some featured in a June 2013 television programme; all were published online by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists in November 2014 as “Luxleaks.” PwC suffered reputational harm but later reported increased turnover and staffing.

On PwC’s complaint, Halet, A.D. and E.P. were prosecuted. On 29 June 2016 the Luxembourg District Court convicted Halet of theft from his employer, fraudulent access to a data-processing system, betrayal of commercial secrets, breach of professional secrecy and related laundering/possession offences. He received a nine-month suspended prison sentence and a €1,000 fine, plus a symbolic €1 in civil damages to PwC. E.P. was acquitted.

The Court of Appeal (15 March 2017) confirmed the core convictions against Halet. Applying the six *Guja v. Moldova* criteria for whistle-blower protection under Article 10, it found the revelations served the public interest (sparking European debate on corporate taxation, tax rulings and fairness), the information was authentic, disclosure to the media was a last resort, and Halet acted in good faith. However, the fifth criterion (balancing public interest against harm to the employer) was not met. Unlike A.D.’s tax rescripts, Halet’s documents were ordinary tax returns—unilateral taxpayer statements that revealed nothing new about the authorities’ practice or optimisation techniques. They had been chosen merely because the companies were well-known, added no essential information after A.D.’s disclosures, and merely illustrated already-known tax-evasion examples. PwC therefore suffered greater reputational and confidentiality harm than any incremental public benefit justified. Halet therefore could not invoke the whistle-blower defence. Taking his honourable, disinterested motive as an extenuating circumstance, the court imposed only the €1,000 fine (no prison term). The Court of Cassation (11 January 2018) rejected Halet’s appeal, holding that the appellate courts’ factual assessment of the documents’ limited relevance was neither insufficient nor contradictory.

Halet complained to the ECtHR that his conviction violated Article 10. The Chamber held that he was *a priori* a whistle-blower, but that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance: the specific documents lacked sufficient public-interest value to outweigh the harm, and the modest penalty was proportionate.

The case of Amaghlobeli and Others v. Georgia (no. 41192/11) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) arising from administrative fines imposed on two journalists for news-gathering in a restricted customs zone.

In 2009 the Batumelebi newspaper received reports of arbitrary customs practices at the Sarpi checkpoint on the Georgia-Turkey border. On 15 August 2009 journalists Mzia Amaghlobeli and Eter Turadze crossed into Turkey and returned. After passport control they entered the fenced customs-control zone (clearly marked by warning signs) although they had nothing to declare. Turadze began interviewing travellers who were completing declarations; Amaghlobeli photographed the scene. After they had recorded interviews with everyone present, a customs officer told them they were obstructing operations and must leave. They refused, citing journalistic freedom, and persisted even after the chief officer repeated the order. Each was fined 1 000 GEL (approximately €320) under Article 245 § 1 of the Customs Code for disobeying a lawful order and was escorted out. Their equipment and recordings were not seized.

The following week Batumelebi published a detailed article that incorporated the interviews obtained inside the zone.

The journalists sought annulment of the fines, arguing that their conduct had not been disruptive, that the legal basis was unforeseeable, and that the sanction interfered with their professional freedom to investigate a matter of public interest. On 4 February 2010 the Tbilisi City Court rejected the claim. It found that the journalists’ questions had provoked disputes between travellers and officers, thereby disrupting procedures. Their unauthorised presence breached Article 20 § 4 of the Customs Code and the implementing ministerial order. The fine was therefore lawful and proportionate. Journalists enjoyed no immunity from generally applicable rules; they could have sought prior authorisation or interviewed travellers after they had left the restricted area.

The Tbilisi Court of Appeal confirmed the judgment on 22 June 2010, stressing that the applicants had entered as ordinary passengers and were bound by the same rules as everyone else. The relevant provisions were sufficiently clear, and less intrusive alternatives had been available. The Supreme Court declared an appeal on points of law inadmissible on 29 December 2010.

The European Court of Human Rights noted that the journalists’ activities concerned a matter of public interest. Nevertheless, doubts existed as to whether they had acted in good faith and in accordance with the duties of responsible journalism. They had been able to use all the recorded material and to publish their article. The fine was not excessive. The domestic courts had struck a fair balance, applying the criteria developed in the Court’s case-law. There had therefore been no violation of Article 10.

The case of Amaghlobeli and Others v. Georgia (no. 41192/11) involves an alleged violation of Article 10 of the ECHR (freedom of expression). The applicants are journalists Mzia Amaghlobeli (managing director) and Eter Turadze (editor-in-chief) of a weekly newspaper published by the third applicant, the Batumelebi publishing house.

On 15 August 2009, they crossed into Turkey and returned. After passport control, having nothing to declare, they entered the fenced-off restricted customs control zone (marked with warning signs), where passengers completed declarations and paid duties on imported goods.

Turadze interviewed travelers declaring goods, while Amaghlobeli photographed the scene. They recorded interviews with all present travelers. A customs officer warned that they were hindering operations and must leave the zone. They refused, invoking their journalistic profession. They persisted after repeated orders from the chief customs officer. They were each fined 1,000 GEL (approximately €320) under Article 245 § 1 of the Customs Code for disobeying lawful orders, then escorted out. Their equipment and recordings were not confiscated.

The following week, Batumelebi published a comprehensive article on the customs procedures, incorporating all findings from the investigation, including the interviews recorded in the restricted zone.

On 4 February 2010, the court dismissed the action. It found their interviews had prompted importers to argue with officers over duty amounts, disrupting procedures. They had entered without prior authorization, breaching Article 20 § 4 of the Customs Code (requiring official authorization and supervision for movement in the zone) and Articles 2 and 3 of Ministerial Order no. 1766 (designating areas with declarable goods as restricted by default). The fine was lawful and proportionate. Journalists were not immune from general rules; they could have obtained prior authorization or interviewed travelers after they exited the checkpoint.

The case of Busuttil v. Malta (Application no. 48431/18) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (presumption of innocence) arising from criminal proceedings in which the applicant, a former company director, was convicted of failing to pay tax dues through the application of legal presumptions under Maltese fiscal law.

The applicant, Antonio Busuttil, served as a co-director (holding 25% of shares) of company M. from 2001 until his voluntary resignation in 2006. Between 2003 and 2006 the company failed to submit required tax forms or remit provisional tax and national insurance contributions on behalf of employees. After his departure the company became bankrupt. In 2011 the tax authorities demanded that the applicant personally pay approximately EUR 323,500 in outstanding dues. When he did not pay, criminal proceedings were brought against him under Section 23 of the Income Tax Management Act (Chapter 372) and related rules for failing to submit the forms and remittances.

The applicant’s defence was that he had been unaware of the defaults because his role was limited to sales, that he had no involvement in administration, and that he had insisted on the appointment of a financial controller. The Court of Magistrates convicted him on 23 March 2012, imposing a EUR 400 fine. It rejected the defences of lack of knowledge and due diligence, finding that he had shown no interest whatever in the company’s fiscal obligations. The Court of Appeal confirmed the conviction on 6 December 2012 and added a daily fine of EUR 4 until the full sum was paid. It held that the offence was of a continuing (permanent) nature so that liability persisted until payment was made, irrespective of whether the applicant remained a director. His resignation was treated as a self-inflicted impossibility that did not extinguish responsibility. Section 13 of the Interpretation Act (which would have allowed a director to escape liability by proving lack of knowledge plus due diligence) was held inapplicable because the offence arose under a special fiscal statute. The court further noted that, during protracted negotiations preceding his resignation, the applicant had had ample opportunity to enquire about the company’s tax position but had failed to do so.

The applicant then sought constitutional redress, arguing that the statutory scheme and its application after he ceased to be a director reversed the burden of proof and thereby breached the presumption of innocence. Both the Civil Court (First Hall) and the Constitutional Court dismissed the claim. They emphasised that the prosecution had proved the two essential facts—that the applicant had been a director and that the company had failed to comply with its tax obligations. Directors, including non-executive or minority directors, bear a legal duty to inform themselves of and to discharge all statutory fiscal duties; ignorance, lack of competence or reliance on others does not excuse them. Witness evidence (unchallenged by the applicant) established that he had in fact received copies of relevant documents and had attended meetings at which the company’s liquidity problems and unpaid tax were discussed. Any reverse onus under the legislation applied only to the quantification of the amounts due, which the applicant had never contested.

The two remaining directors of the company were later convicted of the same offences. Domestic case-law confirms that the offences are continuing and that a former director remains liable unless genuine impossibility is proved.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the legal presumptions and the continuing nature of the offence after resignation had deprived him of the benefit of the presumption of innocence.

The applicant, Antonio Busuttil, a Maltese national born in 1947, served as a co-director (holding 25% of the shares) of company M. from 2001 until his resignation in 2006, having been invited to the role by the two other directors. His responsibilities were limited to sales, a role he had held since joining the company as an employee in 1996; he claimed no involvement in administration and had insisted on the appointment of a financial controller, which eventually occurred. Between 2003 and 2006, the company failed to submit required tax forms and to pay provisional tax and national insurance contributions on behalf of its employees. After the applicant's departure, the company, under the remaining directors, became bankrupt.

The applicant maintained that he had been unaware of the defaults, that they had never been discussed at company meetings, and that his own contributions appeared to have been paid, giving him no reason to suspect otherwise. He also invoked Section 13 of the Interpretation Act, arguing that the offence occurred without his knowledge and that he had exercised all due diligence.

On 23 March 2012, the Court of Magistrates convicted him, imposing a €400 fine (but no daily fine, as he no longer represented the company). It rejected his defences, finding from his own testimony that he had taken no interest whatsoever in the company's fiscal obligations and had left them entirely to third parties. Both the applicant and the Attorney General appealed. On 6 December 2012, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and added a daily fine of €4 until the €323,500 was paid. It held that the applicant's status as director made him responsible for the unfulfilled obligations, irrespective of internal company arrangements or his sales-focused role. The offence was of a permanent nature, so time-barring commenced only upon payment, not upon his resignation. His claimed impossibility of compliance (no longer being a director) was self-inflicted, as he had left voluntarily during prolonged negotiations over shares and directorship while the company faced financial difficulties; he had had ample opportunity to inquire about tax compliance but failed to do so. Section 13 of the Interpretation Act was inapplicable, as the special fiscal legislation governed directors' duties exclusively.

The applicant then sought constitutional redress, alleging a breach of the presumption of innocence. On 26 April 2017, the Civil Court (First Hall) dismissed the claim, holding that Section 23 imposed legal obligations on directors rather than creating a presumption, and that the prosecution had proved the company's failings. On 13 April 2018, the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal. It emphasised that directors (including non-executive or minority ones) bear equal responsibility and must inform themselves of all duties; ignorance, incompetence or reliance on others is no defence. Witness evidence (unchallenged) showed the applicant had received relevant documents and attended meetings discussing liquidity problems and unpaid taxes. The prosecution had proved the failure to fulfil statutory duties; any reverse presumption applied only to the uncontested quantum of tax due. The other two directors were later convicted on the same charges.

Relevant domestic law included Section 23 of Chapter 372 (creating personal liability for non-remittance and treating unchallenged demand notices as evidence of amounts due) and the Final Settlement System Rules (imposing joint and several obligations on payers, with managers personally answerable). Domestic case-law confirmed the permanent nature of such offences and directors' continuing responsibility, while allowing a defence of genuine impossibility. Malta's reservation to Article 6 § 2 permitted laws imposing a burden of proving particular facts.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered its judgment in Dijkhuizen v. the Netherlands (Application no. 61591/16) on 8 June 2021 (final 8 September 2021). The applicant, a Netherlands national born in 1966 and detained in Peru, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention that he had been denied a fair hearing because he could not attend his criminal appeal in person or by videoconference, thereby impairing his defence rights.

The applicant imported tinned vegetables from Peru. Arrested on 12 November 2005, he was charged with others in a complex multi-defendant case involving the importation of large quantities of cocaine concealed in tins. Tried in person at first instance, he was convicted by the Rotterdam Regional Court on 13 March 2008 of importing 1,623 kg of cocaine and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment (acquitted of other counts). Both he and the prosecution appealed; six co-accused also appealed.

A preparatory appeal hearing occurred on 20 October 2008 before The Hague Court of Appeal, with the applicant present. His remand detention was later suspended subject to conditions (passport surrender, remaining in the Netherlands, and appearing when summoned). These were gradually relaxed, allowing EU travel and then unrestricted travel; his passport was returned in December 2009 and he went to Peru.

Further preparatory hearings proceeded without him. The merits hearing was listed for 25 November–6 December 2013. En route back via Ecuador, he was arrested by Peruvian authorities on money-laundering charges related to narcotics and detained. At the 25 November 2013 hearing his counsel sought an adjournment and extradition (despite no treaty), stating the applicant refused videoconference or letters rogatory, wished to be heard in person, and would say nothing while detained in Peru. The hearing was adjourned sine die. Counsel later confirmed the wish to appear in person as both accused and witness and requested a formal extradition request. The Advocate General replied that Peruvian law barred transfer of suspects in ongoing Peruvian proceedings (information obtained via the Netherlands liaison officer). A formal request was refused on that ground.

On 16 October 2014, days before the rescheduled hearing, counsel informed the court that the applicant was now willing to be heard as a witness by videoconference from Castro Castro prison (where facilities existed). The merits hearing resumed on 20 October 2014 without the applicant or any video link. Counsel conducted the defence, requested adjournment for personal attendance, and later sought a declaration of prosecutorial inadmissibility (gross defence-rights violation) or reopening for extradition/temporary surrender or videoconference.

In its 21 November 2014 judgment the Court of Appeal rejected these requests. It noted the applicant’s earlier unambiguous refusal of videoconference (25 November 2013) and that the first indication of willingness came too late (16 October 2014) to arrange international legal assistance. Balancing the applicant’s interest in making a statement against the need for an effective, speedy trial of a 2005 case, the interests of co-accused, and society, it proceeded. It reduced the nine-year sentence by 15 % for delay, imposing seven years and six months. The Supreme Court dismissed the points-of-law appeal on 19 April 2016.

(The ECtHR ultimately held that physical presence was impossible, that substitution by videoconference was permissible in the circumstances, and that the applicant’s repeated, unambiguous refusals constituted a waiver of the right to participate.)

Subsequent inquiries established that Peruvian law prohibited the temporary transfer of a person who was himself a suspect in pending Peruvian proceedings.
