The case of Ballıktaş Bingöllü v. Turkey (no. 76730/12) involved a Turkish applicant's complaint that domestic courts' dismissal of her request to lift statutory restrictions arising from a past conviction denied her a fair hearing and interfered with her private and professional life.

Born in 1978, the applicant was arrested in March 2000 and convicted in October 2001 by the Istanbul State Security Court of membership of an illegal organisation. She received a sentence of 12 years and 6 months' imprisonment plus a permanent ban on holding civil-service posts. The conviction became final in 2002. (A prior ECHR application had already found violations of Articles 3 and 6 § 1 concerning her custody and trial.) A 2002 writ of execution treated her sentence as having begun on 9 March 2000, with conditional release scheduled for 3 September 2007 and full expiry on 2 September 2012.

After publication of a more lenient new Criminal Code in 2004, the applicant sought revision of her release date. On 5 November 2004 the Istanbul Assize Court suspended execution of the sentence (she had already served 1 705 days, corresponding to the period required for conditional release under the forthcoming Code) and she was released. The new Code entered into force in June 2005. In June 2008, in adaptation proceedings, the same court reduced her sentence to 6 years and 3 months and applied Article 53 of the new Code (which imposes temporary deprivations of certain rights, including civil-service employment, until the sentence is fully served). That decision became final in October 2011.

Having graduated from university in 2010, the applicant passed a competitive examination for a research-assistant post at a public university. In October 2011 the university refused her appointment under section 48 of the Law on Civil Servants because of her conviction for an offence against the constitutional order.

The parties disputed the circumstances of a brief second period of imprisonment. The applicant stated that, when she attended court in December 2011 to obtain a copy of the writ of execution, officials told her an earlier calculation error meant she still had five days to serve; she was immediately detained from 13 to 18 December 2011. The Government maintained that the 2004 release had merely been a suspension pending the new Code; once the 2008 adaptation decision became final a fresh writ was issued, requiring her to serve those five remaining days to become eligible for conditional release. The second writ therefore recorded 18 December 2011 as the conditional-release date and 11 July 2013 as the date of full execution.

On 16 February 2012 the applicant applied to the Ankara Assize Court under section 13/A of Law no. 5352 for restoration of her civil rights. She argued that any calculation error should not be remedied at her expense and that the relevant date remained 5 November 2004. The court dismissed the request on 19 March 2012, holding that the sentence had not yet been fully executed and relying on the later dates in the second writ. An objection was rejected on 9 April 2012; identical applications to the Istanbul Assize Court were likewise dismissed.

The applicant complained that the courts' excessively formalistic approach had denied her effective access to court (Article 6 § 1) and had prolonged restrictions that severely affected her private and professional life (Article 8), in particular her prospects of civil-service employment. Subsequent administrative-court challenges to the university's refusal were unsuccessful, and the Constitutional Court declared an individual application inadmissible. In May 2014, after the sentence had expired, the Istanbul Assize Court granted restoration of her rights.

The case of Anghel v. Romania (Application no. 76328/16) concerns alleged violations of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the use of force by police against the applicant, Alexandru Anghel (born 1939), on 12 June 2015 in Bucharest, and the subsequent investigation. The applicant died in 2017, and the case was pursued by his heirs.

On the morning of 12 June 2015, protester C.-C.A. climbed onto the roof of Casa Radio, waving a flag in protest. Police officers S.I. and D.T. attended, along with a medical unit. After several hours in the sun (and claiming a hunger strike), C.-C.A. descended and was assessed as needing transfer to Obregia Psychiatry Hospital. While a fine was being prepared for disturbing public order, the applicant (accompanied by M.M.) approached, identifying himself as a friend and seeking to prevent the hospitalisation, offering to care for C.-C.A. himself.

The applicant refused repeated police requests to produce identification, asserting that no justification existed and claiming knowledge of his rights as a former judge. According to the applicant, officers then attacked him: punching him in the eye, slamming a police car door on his legs, pulling at his genitals (thwarted by tight jeans), and subjecting him to verbal abuse both in the car (where he hid between seats) and at the station. He was taken to the police station, identified, and fined approximately €700 for obstructing police duties and refusing to identify himself. He did not sign the report, citing Parkinson’s disease.

A police report of 16 June 2015 stated that the applicant had pushed officer D.T. and blocked him from assisting the medical team. After further refusals, reinforcements (officers B.M. and L.B.) immobilised the applicant by the hands and forced him into the car because he resisted by stiffening his body and grabbing the vehicle. Officer D.T. later noted a minor bruise on the applicant’s forearm at the station and offered medical help, which was refused. Video footage submitted to the Court showed officers calmly requesting identification, the applicant refusing and raising his voice, attempting to flee, being restrained by one arm, and being taken to the car; the footage then became unusable.

A forensic examination on 13 June 2015 documented bruises consistent with being struck by a hard object and scratches (dating to 12 June): a violet bruise near the right eye, bruises on the chin, arms, elbow, both legs, and a superficial bruise on the scrotum, requiring four to five days’ care.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint in August 2015 accusing unidentified officers of abusive behaviour, ill-treatment, threats, and unlawful detention, requesting that C.-C.A. and M.M. be heard. A supplementary complaint targeted senior officers. The prosecutor opened an in rem investigation, hearing witnesses. C.-C.A. confirmed the applicant’s intervention and refusals but saw no later events after being placed in the ambulance. M.M. described the applicant being pushed into the car, the door slammed, and later seeing the applicant with a swollen eye and bleeding legs; he heard the applicant yell “Don’t kill me” and reported the applicant’s account of further beatings. Police officers denied any assault, attributing bruises to the applicant’s resistance during lawful immobilisation under Law no. 218/2002 (Articles 31 and 34, permitting force to escort individuals posing a danger or whose identity cannot be verified, using means not endangering life). Other officers present saw no injuries on the applicant. The prosecutor terminated proceedings in January 2016, finding no intent to harm and lawful use of force. Challenges were rejected by the chief prosecutor (March 2016) and Bucharest District Court (June 2016), which held that the applicant’s account lacked corroboration, bruises were consistent with resistance, and any doubt favoured the officers (in dubio pro reo). The court noted photographs confirmed the injuries but attributed them to the applicant’s vehement resistance.

These facts form the basis of the alleged substantive violation (excessive force causing injury) and procedural violation (inadequate investigation failing to explain all injuries or hear all requested witnesses).

The case of Anghel v. Romania (no. 76328/16) concerns complaints under Article 3 ECHR of police ill-treatment through excessive force and an ineffective investigation. Applicant Alexandru Anghel (b. 1939) died in 2017; his wife and daughters continued the proceedings.

On 12 June 2015, police and medical personnel responded to C.-C.A. protesting on the roof of Bucharest’s Casa Radio. After descending, C.-C.A. received aid (having been in the sun and on hunger strike) and was recommended for psychiatric hospitalisation; he was also fined for public-order disturbance. The applicant and M.M. approached, with the applicant claiming friendship and seeking to prevent what he viewed as unlawful forced hospitalisation.

The applicant alleged that, after repeatedly refusing to show identity papers (asserting no legal basis existed), officers punched him in the eye, slammed a police-car door on his legs, pulled his genitals while he hid between seats, and verbally abused him en route to and at the station. He was fined ~€700 for obstructing police and refusing identification.

Police reports stated the applicant pushed officer D.T. and blocked efforts to place C.-C.A. in an ambulance. He refused identification despite warnings that this and his interference constituted offences. Reinforcements arrived; officers immobilised him by the hands and forced him into the car amid resistance (he grabbed the vehicle and stiffened his legs). At the station a minor forearm bruise was noted; he refused an ambulance and left unsigned the fine report (citing Parkinson’s). Officers later attributed any injuries to the struggle during lawful immobilisation and denied seeing facial bruises initially.

Video footage showed officers calmly requesting identification, the applicant refusing and raising his voice, then attempting to flee before being caught and taken to the car; the recording then became unusable.

A 13 June 2015 forensic certificate recorded a violet bruise near the right eye, chin bruises, multiple arm and leg bruises, and a scrotal bruise, requiring 4–5 days’ care and consistent with hard-object impact and scratching on 12 June.

On 15 August 2015 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint of abusive behaviour and ill-treatment, requesting that C.-C.A. and M.M. be heard. The prosecutor opened an in rem investigation. C.-C.A. confirmed the applicant’s attempt to block hospitalisation and the ID dispute but saw nothing after being placed in the ambulance. M.M. described the applicant being forced into the car (door slammed) and later emerging with bleeding legs and a swollen eye, claiming beatings. Officers described only necessary force against resistance and lawful action under Law 218/2002 (escort of unidentified or obstructive persons; restraint means for aggressive behaviour). Other witnesses added little.

On 8 January 2016 the prosecutor terminated proceedings, finding no intent to injure and lawful immobilisation. The applicant’s challenge (seeking further witnesses) was dismissed by the chief prosecutor (24 March 2016) without new evidence. On 6 June 2016 the Bucharest District Court upheld the decisions: bruises were consistent with resistance to lawful force; the applicant’s account lacked corroboration; any residual doubt favoured the accused (in dubio pro reo). These facts underpin the Article 3 complaints of disproportionate force and an investigation that failed to hear all requested witnesses or fully account for the injuries.

The case of *Anghel v. Romania* (Application no. 76328/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns allegations under Article 3 of the Convention of excessive police force against Alexandru Anghel (born 1939, deceased 10 February 2017; case pursued by his heirs) and an ineffective investigation. On 12 June 2015, police attended Casa Radio in Bucharest after C.-C.A. climbed onto the roof in protest. After hours in the sun (and an alleged hunger strike), C.-C.A. descended; medics recommended transfer to a psychiatric hospital, and he was fined for disturbing public order.

The applicant and M.M. approached as C.-C.A.’s friends, seeking to stop the hospitalisation (claiming they could care for him). The applicant repeatedly refused police requests to identify himself, arguing lack of justification and (as a former judge) knowledge of his rights. According to the applicant, officers then punched him in the eye, slammed a car door on his legs, pulled his genitals (while he hid between seats), and verbally abused him; he was taken to the station and fined ~€700 for obstruction and non-identification (which he did not sign, citing Parkinson’s). Police reports stated the applicant had pushed officer D.T. (blocking aid to medics) and resisted identification; reinforcements immobilised him and forced him into a car due to struggling (he grabbed the vehicle and stiffened his legs). A minor forearm bruise was noted at the station; he refused an ambulance.

Video footage showed calm repeated ID requests, the applicant’s rising voice and failed escape attempt, then seizure and movement to a car (footage ended amid ambulance-related screaming). A forensic exam the next day recorded bruises (violet near the right eye; red on chin; violet/red on arms/elbow; vertical on left leg; brownish on right leg; superficial on scrotum), consistent with being struck by a hard object or scratched on 12 June, requiring 4–5 days’ care.

The applicant’s August 2015 criminal complaint (against unnamed officers for abuse, threats, and unlawful detention; later expanded to superiors) alleged unjustified force after ID refusal. The prosecutor opened an *in rem* investigation in October 2015. C.-C.A. confirmed the applicant’s intervention and ID refusal but saw no later violence (he was hospitalised). M.M. described force, a slammed door, the applicant’s screams, and later visible injuries (bleeding legs, swollen eye) plus the applicant’s account of beatings. Officers (D.T., S.I., L.B., B.M., and others) denied assault, attributing injuries to lawful resistance during immobilisation; they reported no facial bruises at the scene or station. A nurse confirmed the hospital decision was medical, with police support only. Some witnesses saw nothing relevant.

On 8 January 2016, the prosecutor terminated proceedings, finding no intent to harm and bruises from lawful immobilisation under Law no. 218/2002 (Articles 31(1)(b) and 34(1), permitting escort of those endangering order or unidentifiable, plus restraint means not endangering life). Challenges (seeking more witnesses) were dismissed by the chief prosecutor (24 March 2016) and Bucharest District Court (6 June 2016), which held the applicant’s account uncorroborated; bruises were consistent with resistance to lawful force, applying *in dubio pro reo*. The Civil Code (Article 1349) addresses general liability for damage.
001-210496:
The applicant, Jana Hasáliková (born 1972), was convicted in Slovakia of “particularly serious” murder committed jointly with J.O. on 23 October 2009 and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. She alleged that the criminal proceedings were unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention because authorities failed to make adjustments for her slight intellectual disability (rendering her particularly vulnerable), she had insufficient time to choose counsel, and her later-retracted police confession formed the basis of conviction. She also raised an Article 5 § 2 complaint concerning the timing and circumstances of her arrest/notification.

Prosecution opened on 24 October 2009 against an unknown perpetrator. J.O. was arrested that evening. The next day (25 October), both were charged. Because of the offence’s gravity, legal representation was mandatory from the outset; they had 30 minutes to choose counsel or have one court-appointed. An investigator promptly requested appointments for both (the applicant later disputed that her position was known). J.O. was interviewed that morning in the presence of the two appointed lawyers and implicated the applicant.

The applicant voluntarily attended the police station around 3 p.m. on 25 October, was notified of the charges, and was interviewed from 3:20–5:25 p.m. with the appointed lawyers present. Records show she was informed of her rights (including silence and counsel), confirmed she understood the charges and information, signed the record, and stated she had consulted counsel beforehand. She mentioned annual psychiatric visits and an invalidity pension (spinal disorder) but waived further explanation. She initially denied participation then confessed in detail that J.O. stabbed the victim first, passed her the knife, and the victim died after she stabbed her. She was arrested at 5:30 p.m. as a flight risk. (She later claimed arrest actually occurred a day earlier, on 24 October, after she was taken from another town; two witnesses placed her in a pub at the time of the murder, and no victim blood was found on her clothes handed over by her sister early on 25 October.)

On 26 October a privately chosen lawyer (appointed by her sister) took over. On 28 October a pre-trial judge re-interviewed her (substitute counsel present); she retracted, claiming the confession was untrue and given out of fear, though she admitted stabbing under threat while asserting J.O. delivered the fatal injury. Detention was ordered (later upheld). A January 2010 psychiatric/psychological expert report, based on multiple tests, found slight intellectual disability (IQ 64–69), naivety, emotional immaturity and suggestibility. She could recognise the social dangerousness of her acts but had limited self-control owing to distress, reduced capacity and alcohol. Experts noted her insincerity, changing accounts and feigned memory issues during examination.

J.O. later pleaded guilty via a plea bargain (22.5-year sentence) of which the applicant’s counsel was not notified in advance; the court approved it, finding no substantial breach of her rights. At trial the applicant denied involvement, attributing her confession to fear and coaching during an alleged earlier undocumented detention. A psychologist once rephrased a prosecutor’s question for her. After J.O. died, his earlier statements (given with counsel present) were read. The first-instance court convicted her on 11 January 2011, relying primarily on J.O.’s consistent implication of her, her own detailed and largely matching pre-trial confessions (which she could not explain away except by unsubstantiated fear), telephone recordings and other circumstantial evidence. It held her disability did not diminish responsibility.

Appeals were dismissed. The regional court found the evidence sufficient and lawfully obtained (all interviews with counsel present; no violence or threat alleged), the timeline did not exclude her presence, and counsel’s absence from the plea-bargain talks was not a decisive violation. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rejected further challenges concerning factual findings, the reliability of her confession in light of her disability, the alleged earlier arrest, and the lack of expert assistance at interviews, noting counsel never requested such assistance and the conviction rested on multiple sources, not the confession alone.

The case of Hasáliková v. Slovakia (no. 39654/15) involved complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 ECHR that criminal proceedings leading to the applicant’s conviction for particularly serious murder and a 15-year prison sentence were unfair. The applicant, Jana Hasáliková (born 1972), alleged that authorities made no reasonable adjustments for her slight intellectual disability, that she lacked sufficient time to choose a lawyer, and that her retracted police confession improperly formed the basis of her conviction.

A murder occurred on 23 October 2009. On 25 October both the applicant and co-accused J.O. were charged. Mandatory legal representation applied from the pre-trial stage. After they failed to select counsel within 30 minutes, the investigator obtained court-appointed lawyers. The applicant arrived voluntarily at Žilina police station around 3 p.m. that day. She was notified of the charges and interviewed from 3:20–5:25 p.m. in the lawyers’ presence. She signed acknowledgments that her rights (including silence and counsel of choice) had been explained and understood, mentioned annual psychiatric visits and an invalidity pension for a spinal condition, confirmed she understood the charges, waived further explanation, and accepted the appointed lawyer for financial reasons. She had time to consult counsel beforehand. She first claimed presence without participation, then admitted stabbing the victim after J.O. handed her the knife. She was arrested at 5:30 p.m. as a flight risk. Two witnesses later placed her elsewhere at the relevant time.

On 26 October her sister appointed a lawyer who consulted the file. On 28 October a pre-trial judge interviewed her (with substitute counsel); she retracted the confession as fear-induced but admitted stabbing under threat (asserting J.O. inflicted the fatal wound). Detention was ordered. A January 2010 expert psychiatric-psychological report (using multiple tests) found slight intellectual disability (IQ 64–69), naivety, emotional immaturity, simplistic thinking and easy influence. She could recognise the social danger of her acts and foresee consequences but had limited self-control owing to distress, reduced capacity and alcohol. During examination she initially denied then confessed, was insincere, repeatedly changed accounts and naively feigned memory problems.

A May 2010 confrontation with J.O. saw her deny presence; she later claimed her detailed earlier confession merely repeated the charges. She and counsel reviewed the full file on 4 June 2010 without requesting repetition of prior acts. She was indicted on 17 June 2010. J.O. entered a plea bargain (approved despite her counsel’s objection that he had not been informed) and later died. Trial hearings (September 2010–January 2011) heard numerous witnesses and experts. The applicant denied guilt, attributing her confession to fear; a psychologist occasionally rephrased questions. On 11 January 2011 she was convicted, the court relying primarily on J.O.’s statements (read after his death) and her detailed, largely consistent pre-trial confessions (to investigator, judge and expert), plus telephone records and other evidence. Her later denials were rejected as unexplained except by unsubstantiated fear. The disability did not establish diminished responsibility.

Appeals were dismissed. The Regional Court held the first-instance assessment neither unfounded nor arbitrary, noting all interviews occurred with counsel present and no violence was alleged. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rejected further challenges, including that her disability required expert assistance during interviews, that she had been arrested a day earlier than recorded, and that counsel’s exclusion from J.O.’s plea-bargain talks violated defence rights. The courts stressed the verdict rested on multiple sources, not solely the confession, and that counsel had never requested an expert on mental-state grounds.

These facts framed the Court’s examination of whether the authorities had sufficient indications of particular vulnerability requiring adjustments, whether defence rights were irretrievably prejudiced, and whether the trial as a whole remained fair.

The applicant, Jana Hasáliková, a Slovak national born in 1972 with a slight intellectual disability, was convicted of particularly serious murder (committed jointly with co-accused J.O.) and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. She alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention, claiming that the authorities failed to make reasonable adjustments for her disability (rendering the trial unfair and her defence rights ineffective), that she had insufficient time to choose a lawyer, and that her retracted police confession formed the improper basis of her conviction.

A prosecution for the 23 October 2009 murder opened the next day. On 25 October 2009 both the applicant and J.O. were charged. Because of the offence’s gravity, legal representation was mandatory from the pre-trial stage. The charging decision notified them that if they (or authorised persons) did not select counsel within 30 minutes, the court would appoint one. The investigator requested court-appointed lawyers after J.O. indicated he lacked funds; the applicant later asserted this was done without ascertaining her position. She arrived voluntarily at the police station around 3 p.m., was notified of the charges, and was interviewed from 3.20–5.25 p.m. in the presence of the two appointed lawyers (one for each accused). The record contained printed information on her rights to choose counsel, remain silent and not be forced to confess; she signed that these had been adequately explained and that she understood them and the charges. She mentioned annual psychiatric visits and an invalidity pension for a spinal disorder, waived any challenge to the charges, confirmed she had not chosen a lawyer for financial reasons, consented to the appointed counsel, and stated she had been given time to consult him. She first denied participation, then confessed that J.O. had stabbed the victim and handed her the knife, after which she stabbed the victim (who died). She answered questions from both lawyers. She was arrested at 5.30 p.m. as a flight risk.

On 26 October a privately chosen lawyer (engaged by her sister) took over; he consulted the file and authorised a substitute. On 28 October a pre-trial judge interviewed her (with the substitute present), again informing her of her rights. She retracted the confession as untrue and made out of fear, while admitting she had stabbed the victim under threat (claiming J.O. inflicted the fatal wound). Detention was ordered (upheld on appeal). A January 2010 psychiatric-psychological expert report (using multiple tests) found a slight intellectual disability (IQ 64–69), infantile/naïve features, emotional immaturity and susceptibility to influence. She could recognise the social dangerousness of her acts and foresee their consequences, but her self-control was limited by distress, reduced capacity and alcohol. During examination she first denied then confessed the events, was insincere, changed accounts and naively feigned memory issues.

Further pre-trial steps included a confrontation with J.O. (both counsel present), in which she denied presence at the scene and claimed her detailed confession merely repeated the charges. Her counsel later inspected the full file and raised no request to repeat earlier acts. She was indicted in June 2010. J.O. entered a plea bargain (approved despite her counsel’s complaint that he had not been notified of negotiations). At trial the applicant again denied guilt, attributing her confession to fear. An expert psychologist present at one hearing rephrased a prosecutor’s question she did not understand. J.O. died before trial; his statements (including the confrontation record) were read out without objection. The first-instance court convicted her, relying primarily on J.O.’s consistent pre-trial accounts (no motive for false implication) and her own detailed, largely consistent confessions to the investigator, pre-trial judge and experts (which she could not have invented if absent), plus circumstantial evidence (telephone recordings, some witness statements, expert findings that two persons could have stabbed the victim). It treated her later recantations as unexplained and, relying on the expert report (no mental illness), held that her slight disability did not diminish responsibility.

Appeals were dismissed. The regional court found the verdict based on lawful, sufficient evidence (including counsel-attended interviews with no allegation of violence) and that any omission to summon her counsel to the plea-bargain hearing was not a substantial breach. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rejected further complaints (including alleged earlier unrecorded arrest/coaching and failure to assess her disability’s impact on confession reliability or to provide expert assistance at interviews) as unfounded or insufficiently proven; her counsel had never requested such assistance, and the courts’ reasoning was comprehensive and non-arbitrary.

001-210764:
The case of Lesław Wójcik v. Poland (Application no. 66424/09) concerns a convicted prisoner’s complaints under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding restrictions on unsupervised conjugal visits during his imprisonment.

The applicant, a Polish national, was convicted in January 2007 by the Tarnobrzeg Regional Court of offences including robbery, currency counterfeiting and property destruction, receiving a five-year sentence. In March 2009 the Tarnobrzeg District Court convicted him of robbery and battery, imposing a further three-and-a-half-year term. He served these sentences from September 2009, alternating between Rzeszów Prison, Cracow Remand Centre hospital, Wrocław Prison and other facilities, with periods of temporary leave granted for cardiological problems. In June 2012 he was transferred to an open prison.

In 2008 the applicant married and had a child with his wife. From the start of his post-conviction detention he regularly requested visits from his wife, child, parents, siblings and other relatives. He also sought private conjugal (“intimate”) visits in an unsupervised room. During his first detention period (September 2009–November 2010) he received on average three supervised visits per month (37 in total), seven of them unaccompanied visits from his wife. Similar patterns continued in later periods, with additional supervised family visits granted.

Supervised visits occurred at a table in a common room under a prison officer’s presence; physical contact such as kissing or hugging was prohibited. The applicant argued that these contacts were insufficient to maintain marital bonds or to conceive another child, and that his improving conduct, prison work, religious activities and other contributions merited rewards.

Requests for conjugal visits were refused repeatedly: fourteen times in the first detention period alone, plus further refusals later. The applicant’s own requests (dated, inter alia, September and November 2009, January–July 2010 and January–November 2011) were typically rejected by handwritten notes from prison governors or deputies citing “reprehensible attitude and behaviour.” Supervisors added that the visits were privileges he did not deserve, that educational reasons existed, that exceptional family circumstances were lacking, and that he had already received extra supervised visits. One November 2011 request was refused because his wife’s written consent was missing from his file. His wife’s separate requests received formal written refusals stating that he did not qualify for a reward or motivational measure given his poor conduct.

The applicant’s prison record showed mixed behaviour. He incurred multiple disciplinary sanctions, including fourteen days’ solitary confinement in October 2009 and a fourteen-day ban on visits and calls in January 2010 after asking escorts to release him for payment. He was described as insolent, dismissive and uncooperative (thirteen punishment requests in the first ten months at Rzeszów). Isolated positive actions (cleaning, posters, religious meetings) were noted but deemed insufficiently consistent. Authorities also cited a hostile letter he wrote to his wife as a reason to withhold unsupervised contact.

The applicant challenged several refusals via interlocutory appeals under Article 7 of the Code on the Execution of Criminal Sentences. A penitentiary judge dismissed one such appeal in April 2010, holding that rewards served resocialisation and that the applicant’s insolence and punishments disqualified him; family ties were adequately maintained through supervised visits, correspondence and calls. Similar complaints to prison inspectors, the Minister of Justice and the Ombudsman produced replies that conjugal visits were privileges, not rights, granted only for outstanding conduct or special circumstances, and that the applicant enjoyed sufficient other family contact.

Domestic law treats conjugal visits, extra visits and short leave as discretionary rewards (Articles 137–141 of the Code) for good behaviour or as motivational measures in particularly justified family situations. Standard family visits remain available according to prison type (two per month in closed prisons, more in open ones). International instruments (European Prison Rules, CPT standards, UN Nelson Mandela Rules) emphasise maintaining family ties while permitting privilege systems that incentivise good conduct.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the repeated, inadequately reasoned refusals of unsupervised conjugal visits constituted an unjustified and disproportionate interference with his right to family life.

The case of Lesław Wójcik v. Poland (Application no. 66424/09) concerns alleged violations of Article 8 ECHR arising from repeated refusals of unsupervised conjugal visits during the applicant’s post-conviction detention.

The applicant, a Polish national, was convicted in January 2007 of robbery, currency counterfeiting and property destruction and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. In March 2009 he received a further sentence of three years and six months for robbery and battery. He served his sentences (with interruptions for medical leave on cardiological grounds) in Rzeszów Prison, Cracow Remand Centre hospital, Wrocław Prison and other establishments between September 2009 and June 2012, later being transferred to an open prison.

He married in 2008 and had one child. Throughout detention he received frequent supervised family visits (“visits at the table”) in a common room in the presence of a guard; physical contact with his wife was prohibited. In the first period (September 2009–November 2010) he received 37 such visits, including seven unaccompanied visits from his wife. Similar numbers of supervised visits were granted in later periods.

He and his wife lodged numerous written requests for unsupervised conjugal (“intimate”) visits in a private room without a guard, arguing that these were essential to maintain their marriage, conceive another child, and reward his alleged good conduct (prison work, cleaning, religious meetings, preparation of information materials). Fourteen such requests were refused in the first period alone, with further refusals later. Refusals were typically recorded by brief handwritten notes on the requests (“refused”) citing the applicant’s “reprehensible attitude and behaviour,” lack of consolidated good conduct, or absence of exceptional family circumstances. One request was refused because the applicant’s wife had not submitted a written consent. Supervisors’ notes sometimes added that the applicant did not deserve a reward, that a hierarchy of rewards existed, or that he had already received extra supervised visits. The applicant claimed reasoning was often only oral.

His wife’s separate requests were refused by formal letters stating that he did not qualify for a reward, that his behaviour remained highly reprehensible despite motivational attempts (such as extra sibling visits), and that numerous disciplinary reports had been filed.

The applicant’s prison record showed mixed but predominantly poor conduct: thirteen requests for disciplinary punishment in the first ten months, fourteen days’ solitary confinement, an attempt to bribe hospital escorts, and unauthorised family contact. Some positive actions were acknowledged but deemed insufficient to warrant the privilege sought.

He lodged interlocutory appeals to penitentiary judges under Article 7 of the Code on the Execution of Criminal Sentences. These were dismissed on the ground that conjugal visits are discretionary rewards intended to promote resocialisation and may be granted only for consistently outstanding behaviour or in particularly justified family circumstances; the applicant’s insolence and repeated infractions disqualified him. Supervised visits, correspondence and telephone calls were held to suffice for family contact.

Further complaints to prison governors, the Regional Inspectorate, the Minister of Justice and the Ombudsman were rejected on the same basis: conjugal visits are a privilege, not a right, and the authorities retain discretion even after isolated positive actions.

Under Polish law, convicted prisoners have a statutory right to a limited number of supervised family visits (two per month in closed prisons, more in semi-open or open prisons). Unsupervised conjugal visits, extra or longer visits, and short leaves are classified as rewards (Articles 137–141 of the Code) granted by the prison governor for distinguished good behaviour or as a motivational measure in exceptional personal or family circumstances. They may also be withheld as a disciplinary sanction.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaint that the refusals constituted an unjustified and disproportionate interference with his right to respect for family life.

**Case of Lesław Wójcik v. Poland (ECHR, Application no. 66424/09)**

The applicant, a Polish national convicted in 2007 and 2009 of offences including robbery, currency counterfeiting, property destruction and battery, received prison sentences totalling over eight years. He served these intermittently from 2009 to 2012 in closed and other facilities (Rzeszów Prison, Cracow Remand Centre, Wrocław Prison and others), with temporary licences for cardiological treatment. He married in 2008 and had a child; from the start of post-conviction detention he regularly sought visits from his wife, child, parents and siblings.

He received frequent supervised “visits at the table” in a common room (typically with a guard present, no kissing or hugging permitted): an average of three per month in his first detention period (37 visits total, including seven unaccompanied from his wife), 13 in the second period (three unaccompanied from his wife), and 13 in the third (three unaccompanied from his wife). Additional family visits were sometimes authorised. However, he and his wife repeatedly requested unsupervised conjugal (“intimate”) visits in a private room without a guard. These were refused at least 14 times in the first period, plus further refusals later (some granted in the third period according to the government). The applicant argued such visits were essential to maintain marital bonds and conceive another child, as supervised contact was too limited; he also cited his rehabilitation efforts (prison work, posters, cleaning, religious meetings) as meriting a reward.

Refusals were recorded as handwritten notes on his written requests (or letters to his wife), citing his “reprehensible attitude and behaviour” based on staff reports of insolence, uncooperativeness and disciplinary infractions (13 punishment requests in the first 10 months at Rzeszów alone). Infractions included placement in solitary confinement, a 14-day ban on visits/calls after asking escorts to release him for payment, and unauthorised family contact. Some notes mentioned a lack of consolidated good conduct, a hierarchy of rewards, or (once) absence of his wife’s written consent. Supervisors sometimes recommended refusals for “educational reasons” or because he had already received extra supervised visits. The applicant claimed reasoning was inadequate and often only oral.

He lodged interlocutory appeals to a penitentiary judge of the Rzeszów Regional Court (under Article 7 of the Code on the Execution of Criminal Sentences) against at least two refusals, invoking Article 8 of the Convention and arguing he deserved the visits. These were dismissed: rewards/motivational measures (including conjugal visits under Articles 137, 138 and 141 of the Code) aimed at resocialisation for those showing consistent good behaviour or special family circumstances, not occasional compliance; his insolence and punishments disqualified him; family ties were maintained via supervised visits, correspondence and calls. He also complained to prison authorities, the regional inspectorate, the Minister of Justice and the Ombudsman, who confirmed conjugal visits were privileges (not rights) granted exceptionally as rewards, that the authorities had discretion, and that basic family contact via supervised visits sufficed.

Under Polish law, sentenced prisoners in closed facilities are entitled to two monitored visits per month (more in semi-open/open prisons). Conjugal visits, extra/longer visits and similar measures are rewards for prisoners standing out by good behaviour or, exceptionally, as motivation for family/personal reasons. Disciplinary breaches can restrict visits. The applicant alleged the refusals unjustifiably and disproportionately interfered with his family life under Article 8.

The case of Chizhov v. Russia (ECtHR, Application no. 11536/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life) arising from Russian courts’ restriction of the applicant’s contact with his son Yu.

Applicant Aleksey Yuryevich Chizhov (born 1968) cohabited with E.Ch. in St. Petersburg from 2004. Their son Yu. was born on 15 July 2008. **CASE OF NORMAN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (ECHR, Application no. 41387/17, judgment 6 July 2021)**

Robert Norman, a prison officer at high-security HM Prison Belmarsh (housing notorious inmates), supplied information obtained in his duties to a tabloid journalist on around 40 occasions between May 2006 and April 2011. He received payments totalling £10,684, often via cheques made out to his son to conceal the arrangement. The information underpinned numerous articles in the Daily Mirror and News of the World, ranging from anonymous general reports to stories naming or identifying prisoners and staff.

In 2011, public revelations of journalistic misconduct (including phone hacking and payments to officials) prompted the Leveson Inquiry and Operation Elveden, a police investigation into such payments. In July 2012, police sought details of paid public officials from Mirror Group Newspapers (MGN) under a Memorandum of Understanding allowing voluntary disclosure. MGN could withhold “excluded material” (including confidential journalistic sources) if not in the public interest, considering CPS guidance, press codes, and a balance of freedom of expression against wrongdoing. After an internal search overseen by counsel, MGN identified and disclosed Norman’s name to police in early 2013. There was no police compulsion, threat, or promise regarding prosecutions of MGN or its executives; MGN, a large entity with legal advice, acted independently amid public scrutiny.

Norman was arrested in June 2013 and charged with the common-law offence of misconduct in public office. The offence requires a public officer wilfully neglecting duty or misconducting himself to a degree amounting to abuse of public trust, without reasonable excuse or justification (elements confirmed in Attorney General’s Reference (No. 3 of 2003) and R v. Chapman). He admitted the payments and disclosures but claimed justification (public-interest concerns about prison management) and insufficient seriousness for criminal liability, arguing any sanction should be disciplinary.

At trial (May 2015), he applied to stay the indictment as an abuse of process, alleging Article 10 ECHR breaches: MGN’s disclosure was not truly voluntary (it hoped to avoid corporate prosecution) and lacked Article 10 safeguards (no independent scrutiny or opportunity for representations; MoU omitted explicit Article 10 reference). The judge refused, finding the MoU captured Article 10’s essence, disclosure was justified under Article 10(2) given the flagrant, long-term breach of employment rules (Prison Rule 67.1 and Civil Service Code), and journalistic privilege did not bar voluntary source identification. A no-case-to-answer submission was also rejected: evidence (including concealment of payments) allowed a jury to find all elements proved, including the high “seriousness” threshold of harm to the public interest (undermining prison integrity, staff/prisoner trust and morale, and innocent colleagues).

A jury convicted him on 1 June 2015; he received 20 months’ imprisonment. The judge accepted some genuine concerns as a partial motive but found money and personal dislike of the governor predominated. Many disclosures lacked public-interest justification; Norman (a union representative) ignored official channels. Harm included suspicion falling on other staff, demonisation of prisoners (risking inmate enmity), and eroded trust.

The Court of Appeal (2016) dismissed his appeal. Disclosure was “truly voluntary” with no improper police pressure. Even assuming Article 10 applied to source protection (doubted, as it is a journalist’s moral/professional obligation, not an absolute right imposing duties on newspapers), prosecution was necessary and proportionate under Article 10(2). There was a strong public interest in maintaining prison-service integrity, efficacy, and public confidence. Most disclosed information lacked public interest; Norman was not a whistle-blower. The seriousness test was met by the scale, duration, and corrupt nature of the conduct. Article 7 was satisfied: the offence (including seriousness, requiring harm to the public interest) was sufficiently foreseeable following recent Court of Appeal clarification, enabling a person (with legal advice if needed) to regulate their conduct.

The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The ECHR later held the prosecution and conviction justified under Article 10 and the offence sufficiently foreseeable under Article 7. (Word count: 612)

**CASE OF NORMAN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (Application no. 41387/17)**

Robert Norman, a prison officer at high-security HMP Belmarsh, provided information about the prison to a tabloid journalist on around 40 occasions between May 2006 and April 2011. He received payments totalling £10,684. The information underpinned articles in the Daily Mirror and News of the World, ranging from general pieces (with anonymous individuals) to specific stories identifying prisoners or staff.

In 2011, revelations of journalistic misconduct—including unlawful payments to public officials—sparked public concern, parliamentary inquiries, the Leveson Inquiry, and a police investigation (Operation Elveden). In July 2012, police sought details from Mirror Group Newspapers (MGN) of officials paid for information. A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) framed voluntary disclosure, allowing MGN to withhold or redact “Excluded Material” (including confidential journalistic sources) if, in its judgment and balancing factors such as CPS guidance and public interest in expression versus wrongdoing, disclosure was not warranted. In 2013, MGN’s records search (overseen by counsel) identified Norman as a payee; his name was disclosed to police.

Norman was arrested in June 2013 and charged with the common-law offence of misconduct in public office: a public officer, acting as such, wilfully neglecting duty or misconducting himself to a degree amounting to an abuse of public trust, without reasonable excuse or justification. He admitted providing the information and receiving payment but argued justification and insufficient seriousness. He applied to stay the indictment as an abuse of process, claiming an Article 10 violation. He contended disclosure was not voluntary (MGN was a corporate suspect hoping to avoid higher-level prosecutions), the MoU lacked source-protection safeguards (independent scrutiny, representations, explicit Article 10 reference), and police received the material without a lawful process.

The trial judge refused the stay in May 2015, inferring MGN acted in hope of leniency but finding no Article 10 breach. The MoU embodied Article 10’s essence; disclosure was justified under Article 10 § 2 given prima facie evidence of repeated, paid breaches of confidentiality and employment terms. Journalistic privilege did not bar voluntary source identification. A later no-case-to-answer application was also refused: evidence (including cheques made out to Norman’s son) supported all offence elements, including knowledge of wrongdoing, lack of excuse (no official channels used despite claimed public-interest motives), and seriousness (long-term paid relationship harming public interest).

A jury convicted Norman on 1 June 2015; he received 20 months’ imprisonment. Sentencing remarks accepted some genuine concerns about prison management as a partial motive but emphasised money, personal dislike of the governor, non-public-interest disclosures, unused official (including union) channels, harm to innocent staff (suspicion), demonised prisoners (risk of inmate enmity), eroded trust, and flagrant, knowing, prolonged rule-breaking.

The Court of Appeal dismissed his 2016 appeal. Disclosure was truly voluntary: no police threats, promises, or improper pressure; MGN (a large, legally advised entity) retained Article 10 refusal rights under the MoU and decided independently amid public scrutiny. Even assuming Article 10 source-anonymity rights applied, prosecution was compatible with Article 10 § 2. The conduct—prolonged corrupt paid disclosure of confidential information by a public official—constituted serious misconduct in public office; revealing it served the compelling public interest in prison-service integrity, efficacy, and public confidence. Most information lacked public interest; Norman was no whistle-blower. The seriousness threshold was met by the scale (£10,000+ over five years), harm to confidence, morale, trust, and reporting. Article 7 was satisfied: the offence, including its seriousness element (harm to public interest, per recent case law such as *Attorney General’s Reference (No 3 of 2003)* and *R v Chapman*), was sufficiently foreseeable.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused. Norman applied to the ECtHR alleging Article 10 (unjustified prosecution and source disclosure) and Article 7 (unforeseeable offence) violations. The Court later held the prosecution justified (strong public interest; no whistle-blower claim) and the offence sufficiently foreseeable; source disclosure was not attributable to the State absent police compulsion.

The case of Milachikj v. North Macedonia (Application no. 44773/16) concerned an alleged violation of the applicant’s right to the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The applicant, a Macedonian national born in 1955, claimed that language used by domestic appellate courts in related civil compensation proceedings imputed criminal liability to him after earlier misdemeanour proceedings for a customs offence had been discontinued as time-barred.

On 13 January 2006, police impounded a car the applicant was driving (acquired from a foreign national and bearing foreign plates) on suspicion of a forged registration certificate and fake plates. They reported the matter to the Customs Authority, suspecting unpaid taxes and customs duties, an offence under section 206 of the Customs Act. In June 2006 the Authority instituted misdemeanour proceedings under sections 206 and 207, alleging the applicant ought to have known the car had not been declared and duties unpaid, and sought mandatory confiscation under section 208.

After jurisdictional issues, the Misdemeanour Commission within the Customs Authority found the applicant liable on 10 December 2009 and imposed a fine. The Administrative Court quashed that decision on 13 December 2010 for errors of law. On 6 April 2011 the Commission discontinued the proceedings due to expiry of the five-year limitation period and ordered the car’s return under section 268. The Agency for Confiscated Property returned the vehicle in October 2011.

In February 2012 the applicant brought civil proceedings against the Customs Authority under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for the car’s loss of value. He argued that no responsibility had been established against him and that the vehicle had been impounded without legal basis. On 25 April 2014 the Ohrid Court of First Instance upheld the claim, awarding the equivalent of €10,660 (the car’s value at impoundment, as assessed by an expert). It held that the Authority’s actions had been lawful but that it had not acted diligently, allowing the limitation period to expire and thereby causing the delay and depreciation. The court rejected any attribution of liability to the applicant, noting that the misdemeanour proceedings had been discontinued without a finding of guilt.

On 6 October 2014 the Bitola Court of Appeal reversed the judgment and dismissed the claim. It stated that the proceedings had not been discontinued because the offence had not been committed, but solely because of the time-bar. There had been no unlawful conduct or impoundment without legal basis. The court added that the applicant “was required to declare the car to the Customs Office and he knew that he had been driving it with fake number plates, which was the basis for the proceedings against him.”

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the Court of Appeal had violated the presumption of innocence by assessing his conduct in civil proceedings after the misdemeanour case had ended without a finding of liability. On 3 February 2016 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It held that the Authority had been legally obliged to report the offence and institute proceedings against “the perpetrator, now the plaintiff.” The proceedings had not been discontinued because the offence had not been established, but because of the time-bar. The Supreme Court also noted that the Commission had found the applicant liable in 2009 and that any delay had not been caused by the Authority.

The applicant complained that the higher courts’ language, including references to him as a “perpetrator” and assertions about his knowledge and duty to declare the car, amounted to an affirmation of criminal liability despite the discontinuation of the misdemeanour proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether that language, viewed in the context of the civil compensation claim (which was heard by different courts of different composition and under different rules on the burden of proof), could reasonably be read as imputing criminal liability.

The case of Milosavljević v. Serbia (No. 2) concerns an application by Ranko Milosavljević, a Serbian journalist and editor-in-chief of the weekly magazine Svetlost, alleging a violation of his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application stemmed from a civil defamation judgment against him following the publication of an article criticizing the director of a State-run public utility company.

On 6 August 2009, Svetlost published an article titled “The City’s Chief Undertaker (CCU): [Mr A] From a Smuggler to a Rich Man.” Written by journalist Ms B, it accused Mr A, director of Kragujevac’s public burial company, of misconduct. It alleged he had been a cigarette smuggler who amassed unofficial wealth, issued bizarre threats, was professionally and personally unfit, wore expensive Gianfranco Ferré shoes while profiting from rising burial costs, improperly facilitated cemetery plot sales, and obtained diplomas opportunistically. A photograph of Mr A from a public book presentation accompanied the piece.

Mr A sued the applicant, Ms B and Svetlost for defamation. On 13 September 2010 the Kragujevac High Court partially found in his favour, awarding 100,000 RSD (approx. EUR 955) for mental anguish from the breach of honour and reputation, 50,000 RSD (approx. EUR 477) for privacy violation via the photograph, plus costs. It held there was no public interest in details of Mr A’s private life (such as clothing), that he had sold cigarettes but never wore Italian shoes and had obtained his diplomas properly, and that other allegations (including those about company operations) remained unverified despite the respondents’ references to a 2006 press conference and former employees. Witnesses, including the Mayor, contradicted the claims. The article mixed value judgments with unsubstantiated facts, intending to belittle Mr A and breaching journalistic ethics. Friends, colleagues and the Mayor had contacted Mr A after publication, causing him distress. Consent for the photograph had not been obtained.

The case of Milosavljević v. Serbia (No. 2) (Application no. 47274/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, Ranko Milosavljević (born 1960), was at the relevant time editor-in-chief of Svetlost, a weekly news magazine based in Kragujevac, Serbia.

On 6 August 2009, Svetlost published an article by journalist Ms B entitled “The City’s Chief Undertaker (CCU): ... [Mr A] ... From a Smuggler to a Rich Man.” A subtitle suggested that in Kragujevac only the privileged had the right to die, implying one should first consult the CCU. The article, accompanied by a photograph of Mr A (taken at a public presentation of a book on graveyards and identifying him by name), criticised Mr A, director of the city’s State-run public burial company. It referred to an earlier controversy over a local businessman (the “Pharaoh”) allegedly building a family crypt in the cemetery centre by digging up existing graves, which Mr A had described as lawful and market-based. The piece accused Mr A of enforcing debts against the dead and living via bizarre threats, of being personally and professionally unfit for office (and thus needing immediate removal in a rule-of-law society), of leading the company while wearing luxury “Gianfranco Ferré” shoes, of rapidly rising from a “transitional loser,” ordinary worker and street cigarette smuggler to a high-income director (official and unofficial/under-the-counter), of building his career by raising prices of death and human tragedy, of switching political parties at a superior’s order to sell cemetery land to the “Pharaoh,” and of securing two diplomas “just in case.”

In August 2009 Mr A brought a civil defamation action against the applicant, Ms B and the magazine. On 13 September 2010 the Kragujevac High Court partially upheld the claim, jointly ordering the respondents to pay Mr A RSD 100,000 (then approx. EUR 955) for mental anguish from breach of honour and reputation, RSD 50,000 (approx. EUR 477) for privacy violation, and RSD 47,025 (approx. EUR 449) in costs, all plus interest. It found no justified public interest in details of Mr A’s private life (including dress), accepted his testimony that he had never worn Italian shoes and had properly obtained his diplomas (while confirming he had sold cigarettes), and held that the respondents had failed to verify other allegations (e.g., company functioning claims were unsupported by a 2006 press conference or former employees’ statements; witnesses including the Mayor contradicted them). Post-publication inquiries from friends, colleagues, partners and the Mayor had caused Mr A anguish. No consent had been obtained for the photograph. The title, subtitle and remaining text mixed value judgments with unverified facts intended to belittle Mr A, breaching journalistic ethics.

On 23 December 2010 the Kragujevac Appeals Court upheld the honour/reputation award but rejected the privacy claim entirely (Mr A was a public official; the photograph depicted a public event tied to his duties, so consent was unnecessary) and reduced costs to RSD 30,621 (approx. EUR 286). The rulings invoked the Obligations Act and 2003 Public Information Act (requiring journalists/editors to verify origin, veracity and completeness of information with due diligence; limiting privacy rights of public officials proportionately to public interest; imposing joint liability on editors for damage from unverified or private information).

The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal on 9 February 2011. On 25 February 2014 the Constitutional Court dismissed it, endorsing the Appeals Court’s reasoning. The decision was served on 27 February 2014.

Mr A initiated enforcement in March 2011 (order issued same day, upheld on appeal). In May 2013, during related criminal proceedings he had brought against Ms B (which he then dropped), Mr A withdrew the enforcement request against all respondents and renounced any right to reinstitute it. Enforcement proceedings were discontinued in February 2018 after inactivity.

The applicant complained that the civil judgment interfered with his editorial freedom of expression concerning the public utility company’s operations and alleged malfeasance/corruption by its director. The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 21 September 2021 (final 21 December 2021), holding that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance between the competing interests and that the applicant had failed to observe the tenets of responsible journalism. There was accordingly no violation of Article 10.

The case of Milosavljević v. Serbia (No. 2) concerns an Article 10 complaint by Ranko Milosavljević, editor-in-chief of the Kragujevac weekly Svetlost. On 6 August 2009 the magazine published an article by journalist Ms B entitled “The City’s Chief Undertaker (CCU): [Mr A] From a Smuggler to a Rich Man.” Its subtitle advised readers to consult the CCU before dying, “since in Kragujevac only the privileged have this right.” The piece portrayed Mr A, director of the municipal burial company, as a former cigarette smuggler who had rapidly become wealthy through official and unofficial income. It accused him of issuing “bizarre” threats over unpaid cemetery debts, of facilitating the unlawful sale of a prime cemetery plot to a local businessman (the “Pharaoh”), of inflating burial prices for personal gain, of obtaining diplomas merely for show, and of being professionally and personally unfit for office. A photograph of Mr A, taken at a public book launch on cemeteries, accompanied the text.

Mr A sued Milosavljević, Ms B and Svetlost for defamation. On 13 September 2010 the Kragujevac High Court awarded him RSD 100 000 (approximately EUR 955) for mental anguish caused by the attack on his honour and reputation, RSD 50 000 (approximately EUR 477) for the privacy violation inherent in the photograph, and costs. The court held that the public had no legitimate interest in details of Mr A’s private life (including his alleged taste in shoes), that he had never worn Italian footwear and had obtained his diplomas properly, and that the remaining allegations—though mixed with value judgments—had not been verified. Witnesses, including the mayor, contradicted the respondents’ claim that the accusations rested on a 2006 press conference or statements by former employees. After publication, colleagues and the mayor had contacted Mr A to enquire about the article’s accuracy, causing him distress. Consent for the photograph had not been obtained.

The Kragujevac Appeals Court, on 23 December 2010, upheld the award for damage to honour and reputation but dismissed the privacy claim, noting that Mr A was a public official and the photograph depicted a public event connected with his duties. Costs were reduced. The courts relied on the Obligations Act (compensation for non-pecuniary harm) and the 2003 Public Information Act (duties of verification, limited privacy protection for public officials, and joint liability of editor-in-chief and publisher).

Milosavljević’s constitutional appeal was dismissed on 25 February 2014; the Constitutional Court endorsed the appellate reasoning. Enforcement proceedings begun by Mr A in 2011 were later withdrawn by him in 2013 and formally discontinued in 2018. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the civil judgment interfered with editorial freedom concerning alleged malfeasance in a state-run utility. It concluded that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance: the article failed the standards of responsible journalism because its factual assertions remained unverified and were presented in a manner intended to belittle rather than inform.

The case of Ali Riza v. Switzerland (Application no. 74989/11) concerned a professional footballer’s claim that Swiss authorities denied him access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant, a dual British-Turkish national born in 1979, signed a fixed-term employment contract in January 2006 with Trabzonspor, a Turkish club affiliated with the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) and FIFA. The English-language contract included an arbitration clause favouring FIFA and specified his salary.

In January 2008 the applicant left the club, citing repeated failures to pay his salary (delays exceeding four months). The club imposed fines for unauthorised departure and missed training. He initially referred the matter to FIFA’s Dispute Resolution Chamber, alleging unpaid wages. FIFA declined jurisdiction in February 2008, stating it could not intervene in disputes between parties of the same nationality and directing him to the TFF. In April 2008 he formally terminated the contract over unpaid March salary.

The club then initiated proceedings before the TFF Dispute Resolution Committee, seeking damages for wrongful termination, payment of the fines, and a transfer ban. In December 2008 the Committee ruled against the applicant, awarding compensation and a four-month suspension. His appeal to the TFF Arbitration Committee was largely unsuccessful in April 2009 (the sanction was lifted and the sum reduced). Under then-applicable Turkish law, Arbitration Committee decisions were final and not subject to ordinary judicial review.

The applicant lodged a parallel application against Turkey with the European Court of Human Rights, which in 2020 found a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the TFF Arbitration Committee lacked independence and impartiality (Ali Rıza and Others v. Turkey).

Meanwhile, in November 2009 he appealed the TFF decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Lausanne. The CAS first examined its own jurisdiction under the Swiss Private International Law Act (PILA) and the CAS Code. After written submissions (the applicant having requested but not obtained a hearing), the CAS declared the appeal inadmissible on 10 June 2010. It found no contractual arbitration clause or subsequent agreement conferring jurisdiction. FIFA statutes and regulations were inapplicable because the dispute lacked an “international dimension.” Article 14 of the TFF Arbitration Committee Regulations permitted a CAS appeal only where a dispute possessed an international element; the CAS held that the purely contractual wage dispute between a Turkish club and a player registered and treated as Turkish (despite dual nationality) contained none. FIFA’s earlier refusal to intervene was noted as consistent.

The applicant challenged the CAS ruling before the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, invoking PILA grounds (erroneous jurisdiction and violation of the right to be heard), constitutional access-to-court guarantees, and Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention. He also requested a public hearing. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 19 April 2011. It refused a public hearing, held that only exhaustively listed PILA grounds were admissible, and found the applicant had failed to substantiate his Convention and constitutional complaints sufficiently. It endorsed the CAS’s conclusion that no international element existed and confirmed that neither a hearing nor particular reasoning was required.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the combined effect of the CAS’s jurisdictional refusal and the Federal Supreme Court’s confirmation left him without access to an independent court for his civil claim, given the earlier finding against the TFF bodies. He further alleged breaches of the rights to a public hearing and equality of arms. The Court ultimately found Article 6 applicable to the contractual economic rights but held that the Swiss decisions were neither arbitrary nor unreasonable, given the extremely tenuous connection of the purely Turkish dispute to Switzerland and the specialised nature of CAS and Federal Supreme Court review.

The applicant, Ömer Kerim Ali Rıza (a dual British-Turkish national and professional footballer), signed a 2006 fixed-term employment contract with Turkish club Trabzonspor (a TFF member affiliated to FIFA). The English-language contract specified salary terms and an arbitration clause favouring FIFA. In January 2008 he left the club, alleging repeated unpaid or delayed salaries, and later formally terminated the contract. The club imposed fines for unauthorised absence.

FIFA declined jurisdiction on the ground that both parties shared Turkish nationality and referred the matter to the TFF. The club then brought proceedings before the TFF Dispute Resolution Committee, which in December 2008 found against the applicant, awarding the club compensation for wrongful termination, upholding a fine and imposing a four-month transfer ban. The TFF Arbitration Committee (April 2009) confirmed the finding of wrongful termination but reduced the monetary award and lifted the ban. Under then-applicable Turkish law these decisions were final, binding and immune from ordinary judicial review.

The applicant separately complained to the ECHR about the TFF system; in Ali Rıza and Others v. Turkey (2020) the Court later held that the Arbitration Committee lacked structural independence and impartiality, violating Article 6 § 1.

Meanwhile, in November 2009 the applicant appealed the TFF Arbitration Committee decision to the CAS in Lausanne. After written exchanges on jurisdiction, the CAS (June 2010) declared the appeal inadmissible without a hearing (despite the applicant’s request). Applying Swiss private-international-law rules, it found no contractual or subsequent arbitration agreement conferring jurisdiction. FIFA statutes and regulations were inapplicable because the dispute lacked an international dimension. Article 14 of the TFF Arbitration Committee Regulations permitted a CAS appeal only for disputes possessing an “international element”; the CAS held that this element was absent. The dispute concerned purely domestic salary arrears and contract termination between a Turkish club and a player whose closest ties (registration, residence, dual-nationality analysis) were with Turkey; no foreign club or transfer was involved. FIFA had already reached the same conclusion.

The applicant challenged the CAS ruling before the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, seeking recognition of CAS jurisdiction, a public hearing, and annulment on grounds of erroneous denial of jurisdiction and breach of the right to be heard (including the failure to hold a hearing). He invoked, inter alia, Swiss constitutional guarantees and Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, arguing that the CAS refusal left him without access to any independent and impartial tribunal.

The Federal Supreme Court (April 2011) dismissed the appeal. It refused a public hearing, holding that none was required in limited-review proceedings against international arbitral awards. Only the exhaustive grounds listed in the Private International Law Act (erroneous jurisdiction, violation of the right to be heard, public-policy incompatibility) were available; Convention and constitutional arguments could be considered solely insofar as they supported those grounds and had been properly particularised. The applicant’s submissions on access to court and the right to be heard were found insufficiently substantiated. On the merits the Court upheld the CAS finding of no international element and therefore no jurisdiction. It also confirmed that Swiss arbitration law conferred no right to an oral hearing or to any particular form of reasoning.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints that the Swiss authorities (CAS and Federal Supreme Court) denied him access to a court, a public hearing and equality of arms under Article 6 § 1, leaving a contractual dispute of economic significance without independent judicial determination.

The case of Ali Riza v. Switzerland (App. no. 74989/11) arose from an employment dispute between the applicant, a dual British-Turkish professional footballer, and his former club Trabzonspor. In January 2006 he signed a fixed-term contract (to June 2008) containing an arbitration clause in favour of FIFA. In January 2008 he left the club, alleging repeated non-payment of salary, and later formally terminated the contract. FIFA declined jurisdiction on the ground that both parties were Turkish nationals and directed him to the Turkish Football Federation (TFF).

The TFF Dispute Resolution Committee found against him in December 2008, ordering compensation for wrongful termination plus a fine and a four-month transfer ban. On appeal the TFF Arbitration Committee upheld the finding of wrongful termination but reduced the financial award and lifted the sporting sanction. Under then-applicable Turkish law the Arbitration Committee’s decisions were final, binding and not subject to ordinary judicial review.

In November 2009 the applicant appealed that decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Lausanne. After written submissions on jurisdiction, and without holding the hearing the applicant had requested, the CAS declared the appeal inadmissible in June 2010. It held that neither the contract nor any subsequent agreement conferred jurisdiction, that FIFA statutes and regulations did not apply, and that Article 14 of the TFF Arbitration Committee Regulations permitted a CAS appeal only where the dispute contained an “international element.” The CAS found none: the dispute concerned salary arrears under a contract between a Turkish club and a player registered and treated as Turkish; no foreign club or transfer was involved; dual nationality was insufficient to create an international dimension; and FIFA itself had already reached the same conclusion.

The applicant challenged the CAS ruling before the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, seeking recognition of CAS jurisdiction (or remittal) and alleging, inter alia, that the refusal left him without access to an independent tribunal (given the later-established structural deficiencies of the TFF bodies), that the CAS had failed to give adequate reasons and had breached his right to be heard by omitting a hearing. He also requested a public hearing before the Supreme Court.

In April 2011 the Federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It refused a public hearing, holding that none was required under the Federal Supreme Court Act for challenges to international arbitral awards. It recalled that review of such awards is strictly limited to the exhaustive grounds in Article 190(2) of the Private International Law Act (PILA) and that constitutional or Convention arguments could be considered only insofar as they supported those grounds and had been properly particularised. The applicant had not met that requirement. On the merits the Court agreed with the CAS that no international element existed, so CAS lacked jurisdiction. It further confirmed that neither a hearing nor detailed reasoning is guaranteed under the relevant PILA provision.

These Swiss decisions form the core of the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 that he was denied access to a court, as well as related claims concerning the absence of a public hearing and equality of arms. (The European Court later found a violation of Article 6 by Turkey in respect of the TFF Arbitration Committee’s lack of independence, but that finding post-dated the Swiss proceedings.) The Court of Human Rights ultimately held that the Swiss bodies’ conclusions were neither arbitrary nor unreasonable, given the extremely tenuous connection of the purely Turkish dispute to Switzerland and the specialised nature of CAS and Federal Supreme Court review of international arbitration.
