The case of Staniszewski v. Poland (ECtHR, 2021) arose from sanctions imposed on a journalist for publications during a local election campaign. The applicant, Jan Staniszewski, edited a free monthly newsletter distributed in the Municipality of Bulkowo since 2010. The September and October 2014 editions (2,000 copies each) criticised the incumbent mayor, G.G., who was seeking re-election. The September issue suggested G.G. had selected a harvest-festival venue to boost his candidacy, attributed a controversial wind-farm project solely to him despite its earlier origins, highlighted a charity in which G.G.’s wife served as treasurer, criticised disparities in councillor/mayor allowances, and noted a municipal loan of over PLN 2.6 million. The October issue claimed municipal debt had reached PLN 10 million (implying tax hikes), stated G.G. owned more than 40 hectares of farmland, and alleged he earned extra income “on the side.”

The official campaign period began on 27 August 2014. G.G. was registered as a mayoral candidate on 7 October. The applicant served on the municipal electoral commission. On 21 October, G.G. filed a claim under Article 111 § 1 of the Election Code, seeking to halt dissemination of allegedly untrue campaign material, confiscate the newsletters, require public and handwritten apologies, and impose a PLN 10,000 payment to charity plus costs. The applicant received notice that afternoon of a hearing the next morning; he later claimed this left insufficient time to instruct counsel.

On 22 October the Płock Regional Court granted nearly all of G.G.’s requests. It classified the newsletters as campaign material because they focused on electoral issues and G.G. personally, constituting a “negative campaign” of gossip, insinuations and sensationalist claims that manipulated readers’ emotions and lacked sources. G.G. had supplied evidence showing the statements of fact were inaccurate: the festival location was traditional; the wind farm predated G.G.’s term; he had no role in setting allowances; debt was approximately PLN 7.8 million with no planned 80 % tax rise; he owned 19 hectares, not 40; and he engaged in no extra paid work. The court ordered the applicant and the newsletter’s publisher to cease dissemination, seize remaining copies, publish a correction and apology in a regional weekly by 28 October, provide a handwritten apology, pay PLN 10,000 to charity and cover costs.

The applicant appealed, arguing the newsletters were not campaign material (especially the September issue, published before G.G.’s formal candidacy) and did not support any candidate. On 27 October the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that Article 111 covered all speech linked to the campaign, including negative agitation, regardless of origin or the precise date of candidacy registration. The applicant had not challenged the finding that the statements were untrue. The court also noted that the applicant’s campaign involvement breached the ban on electoral-commission members campaigning. The local elections proceeded on 16 November; G.G. was re-elected. The applicant later paid the remaining charity sum in instalments.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s complaints of a violation of freedom of expression (Article 10) through the sanctions and of a fair trial through the extremely rapid summary procedure.

The case of Staniszewski v. Poland concerned a journalist sanctioned under Poland’s Election Code for publishing allegedly untrue statements about a mayoral candidate. Jan Staniszewski, born in 1956 and residing in Bulkowo, had since 2010 solely edited a free monthly newsletter, “The Voice of the Municipality of Bulkowo.” Distributed in shops and public places (2,000 copies per edition), it covered local issues and scrutinized Mayor G.G.

In edition 9/2014 (10 September 2014), Staniszewski suggested G.G. selected Blichów for a traditional harvest festival to boost his re-election chances. He reported on a wind-farm project, highlighting health risks to residents and falling land prices, while attributing implementation solely to G.G. and current councillors (despite its origins under a prior mayor). He also covered a charity where G.G.’s wife served as treasurer, alleged G.G. caused unfair disparities in allowances favoring councillors over mayors, and noted a PLN 2,622,466 municipal loan.

Edition 10/2014 (10 October 2014) claimed municipal debt had reached PLN 10 million (implying tax and charge hikes), that G.G. owned over 40 hectares of farmland, and that G.G. had earned extra money “on the side” during his term.

The local election campaign began on 27 August 2014. On 22 September, Staniszewski joined the Municipality of Bulkowo’s Electoral Commission. Both G.G. and rival S.S. registered as mayoral candidates on 7 October.

On 21 October, G.G. (via lawyer) filed a claim under Article 111 § 1 of the Election Code against Staniszewski and the newsletter’s publisher (a trade union). He sought a ban on disseminating the untrue information, confiscation of the editions, publication of a correction and apology in a regional weekly, a handwritten apology, PLN 10,000 to charity, and costs. G.G. submitted evidence that the statements were false: the festival was a longstanding tradition unrelated to elections; the wind farm predated G.G.’s term; allowances were set by the council, not the mayor; actual debt was about PLN 7.8 million with no planned 80% tax rise (debts would be repaid from improved collections); G.G. owned 19 hectares, not 40; he had no extra paid work; and the charity (operating since 2001) had no campaign ties. G.G. argued the sensationalist content tarnished his reputation during the campaign.

Staniszewski was notified of the claim and a 9 a.m. hearing the next day at 10:45 a.m. on 21 October; the claim arrived by email at 12:09 p.m. He claimed this left insufficient time to appoint a lawyer. At the hearing he argued the newsletters were not campaign material and thus fell outside Article 111, noting earlier criticisms of G.G. (deemed irrelevant by the court) and that the content drew on documents plus his conclusions.

On 22 October the Płock Regional Court largely granted the claim, ordering a dissemination ban, seizure of the editions, a published correction/apology, a handwritten apology, joint payment of PLN 10,000 to charity, and costs. It held the editions (almost wholly dedicated to election issues and G.G.’s activities) constituted campaign material, triggering the Code’s 24-hour summary procedure to protect electoral fairness. The press must report fact-based information; the newsletters amounted to a negative campaign of gossip, insinuations, and speculative claims that manipulated readers’ emotions and lacked sources, violating journalistic standards and G.G.’s personal rights. G.G. had proven the factual inaccuracies.

Staniszewski appealed, arguing the newsletters predated G.G.’s candidacy (September edition) and supported no candidate. On 27 October the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, noting Staniszewski had not challenged the finding of untruth. Article 111 covered all election-linked speech (not just from campaign committees) during the campaign period, which began in August; the editions agitated against G.G. As an electoral-commission member, Staniszewski was also barred from campaigning. G.G. was re-elected on 16 November 2014. Staniszewski later paid the remaining charity sum in instalments.

These facts underpinned complaints of disproportionate interference with freedom of expression (via sanctions for political speech in an election context) and unfair summary proceedings (short notice, limited time to prepare).

The ECtHR case of Staniszewski v. Poland (App. no. 20422/15) involved journalist Jan Staniszewski, editor of the free local newsletter The Voice of the Municipality of Bulkowo, which he distributed publicly and used to scrutinise the incumbent mayor, G.G. In its September and October 2014 editions (around 2,000 copies each), the applicant made several statements about G.G., who was standing for re-election. These included claims that G.G. had chosen a harvest-festival venue to boost his campaign; that he alone was responsible for a controversial wind-farm project with alleged health and land-value impacts; that he had set councillor/mayor allowances unfavourably; that municipal debt had reached PLN 10 million (necessitating tax rises); that G.G. owned over 40 hectares of farmland; that he earned extra income “on the side”; and references to a charity involving G.G.’s wife.

The local-election campaign began on 27 August 2014. The applicant sat on the municipal electoral commission (which prohibited members from campaigning). G.G. was registered as a candidate on 7 October. On 21 October G.G. sued the applicant and the newsletter’s publisher under Article 111 of the Election Code, seeking an injunction against further dissemination of untrue information, seizure of the two editions, a published correction and apology, a handwritten apology, and payment of PLN 10,000 to charity. G.G. submitted documentary evidence that the statements were factually false (e.g., the festival was traditional, the wind-farm decision pre-dated G.G.’s term, the council not the mayor set allowances, actual debt was lower, no tax-rise plan existed, G.G. owned only 19 hectares, and he had no extra paid activity).

The applicant was notified of the claim and next-day hearing at 10.45 a.m. on 21 October; papers were emailed at 12.09 p.m. He later said he opened the email too late to instruct a lawyer. At the 22 October hearing he argued the newsletters were not campaign material (one edition pre-dated G.G.’s formal candidacy and neither supported any candidate) and therefore fell outside the Election Code. The Płock Regional Court nevertheless treated both editions as “campaign material” constituting a “negative campaign” of gossip, insinuation and sensationalist speculation. It found the statements of fact untrue, held that they violated journalistic standards and G.G.’s personal rights, and granted almost all the relief sought (except the charity-related complaint). A 24-hour appeal to the Łódź Court of Appeal was dismissed on 27 October; the appellate court confirmed that Article 111 covered any untrue election-related statements made during the campaign period, that the newsletters agitated against G.G., and that the applicant’s commission membership independently barred him from campaigning. G.G. was re-elected on 16 November 2014.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the summary Election-Code procedure and the resulting sanctions (injunction, seizure, forced apologies and financial penalty) violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression, and that the extreme haste of the proceedings (24-hour deadlines, delayed receipt of papers) also breached Article 6 fair-trial guarantees. The Court examined whether a fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s expression rights and the need to protect electoral fairness and G.G.’s reputation during a campaign.
001-212368:
The case of Spinelli v. Russia concerns Italian national Carlo Spinelli’s complaints under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. He alleged that Russian authorities failed to assist in reuniting him with his son after the child’s mother wrongfully retained the boy in Russia, and that he had no effective domestic remedy.

Spinelli married Russian national A.Sh. in 2009; they lived in Italy. Their son A., holding dual Italian-Russian nationality, was born in Russia in January 2012. The family promptly returned to Italy. In late December 2014 they travelled to Moscow to visit A.Sh.’s parents. Spinelli flew back to Italy on 1 January 2015 under an agreement that A.Sh. and A. would follow three days later. On 2 January A.Sh. telephoned to say she had decided to remain in Russia. Spinelli made three unsuccessful trips to Moscow that month to persuade her to return. He last saw his son in April 2015. Between May and July 2015 he repeatedly petitioned Moscow childcare authorities for assistance in securing contact, without success.

In Italy, Spinelli commenced judicial-separation proceedings in January 2015, seeking sole custody and a residence order. The Monza District Court granted those claims in January 2016, awarding A.Sh. only supervised contact; the Milan Court of Appeal upheld the decision and it became final in September 2016. In January 2017 the same Italian court convicted A.Sh. in absentia of child abduction, imposed a four-year sentence and terminated her parental rights.

Meanwhile A.Sh. filed for divorce in Moscow in February 2015 and sought a residence order plus child maintenance. Spinelli objected, citing the pending Italian proceedings and the 1979 Italy-USSR Bilateral Convention on Legal Assistance. The Gagarinskiy District Court initially declined jurisdiction, but the Moscow City Court reversed that ruling in December 2015, holding that the child (a Russian national registered and living with his mother in the Moscow region) fell within Russian competence. On 17 February 2016 the District Court dissolved the marriage, fixed A.’s residence with A.Sh. and ordered Spinelli to pay maintenance. It relied on the child’s tender age, attachment to his mother, established life in Russia (kindergarten, medical care, suitable housing) and Principle 6 of the 1959 UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child. The City Court dismissed Spinelli’s appeal in July 2016, emphasising A.Sh.’s habitual residence in Moscow when she instituted proceedings, the child’s settlement in Russia for more than a year, and the absence of any Hague return application (the 1980 Hague Convention entered into force between the two States only in July 2016). Cassation appeals were rejected.

Spinelli then sought recognition and enforcement of the Italian custody judgment. The Moscow City Court refused in October 2016 because a final Russian judgment already existed on the same parties, subject-matter and grounds, invoking the Bilateral Convention and the Russian Code of Civil Procedure. Subsequent appeals failed.

These facts formed the basis of Spinelli’s complaints that Russian courts had failed to restore his family life with A. and had provided no effective remedy against the child’s retention.

The case of Spinelli v. Russia (ECtHR, Application no. 57777/17) concerns complaints under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention by Italian national Carlo Spinelli. He alleged that Russian authorities failed to help reunite him with his son after the child's mother retained the boy in Russia, and that no effective remedy existed.

Spinelli married Russian national A.Sh. in 2009; they lived in Italy. Their son A., holding dual nationality, was born in Russia in January 2012. The family returned to Italy shortly thereafter. In late December 2014 they travelled to Moscow to visit A.Sh.'s parents. Spinelli returned to Italy on 1 January 2015, expecting his wife and son to follow on 4 January. He last saw his son in April 2015. Between May and July 2015 he applied to Moscow childcare authorities for assistance in securing contact.

In Italy, Spinelli instituted judicial-separation proceedings on 29 January 2015, seeking sole care of A. and a residence order. On 21 January 2016 the Monza District Court granted these claims, giving Spinelli exclusive decision-making authority over the child's upbringing and residence and awarding A.Sh. supervised contact. The Milan Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 4 May 2016; it became final on 16 September 2016. Spinelli objected, citing the pending Italian case and the 1979 USSR–Italy Bilateral Convention on Legal Assistance. The Gagarinskiy District Court initially declined jurisdiction, but the Moscow City Court reversed that decision on 2 December 2015, holding that the child's Russian nationality, Moscow registration and residence with his mother conferred competence on the Russian courts. It relied on the child's tender age and attachment to A.Sh., her provision of suitable living conditions in Moscow Region, medical and kindergarten records, witness statements and Principle 6 of the 1959 UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child. The City Court dismissed Spinelli's appeal on 22 July 2016, confirming the child's habitual residence in Russia, noting that he had been settled there for more than a year and that no Hague-return application had been filed. The case of Kupás v. Hungary (ECtHR, 28 October 2021) concerns an alleged breach of the applicant’s Article 8 right to respect for family life. The applicant, a Hungarian-Romanian national residing in Basel, Switzerland, married Sz.I. in May 2014. Their son Z.A. was born in Switzerland in January 2015. In May 2015 the family travelled to Budapest. The applicant returned to Switzerland after one week, expecting his wife and infant son to follow once the child’s travel documents were issued. Those documents were issued on 26 May 2015, but Sz.I. remained in Hungary, initiated divorce and custody proceedings, and informed the applicant of her decision. The applicant thereafter had no contact with Z.A. until October 2015 despite regular visits to Hungary. The child was deregistered from the Swiss population register at the mother’s request (the applicant disputed that he had consented).

Hungarian courts initially questioned their jurisdiction over custody because the child’s habitual residence had been Switzerland, but the Budapest High Court ultimately accepted jurisdiction on the basis of the pending divorce proceedings. At a hearing on 6 October 2015 the applicant’s lawyer stated that the applicant sought an amicable settlement, had not commenced Hague Convention proceedings and did not intend to remove the child from the mother’s custody; he merely wished to exercise contact in Hungary every second weekend. An interim contact order was made accordingly (later modified to unsupervised contact at the applicant’s Budapest flat).

In April 2016 the applicant applied under the 1980 Hague Convention for Z.A.’s summary return to Switzerland, alleging wrongful retention. Sz.I. conceded that the child’s habitual residence had been Switzerland and that she had misled the applicant, but invoked Article 13(a) (subsequent acquiescence) and Article 13(b) (grave risk). On 9 June 2016 the Pest Central District Court ordered return, holding that the October 2015 statement and the interim contact arrangements did not constitute consent. The Budapest High Court reversed that order on 6 September 2016. It accepted that retention after 26 May 2015 had been wrongful but found that the applicant’s statement, his delay in invoking the Hague Convention, his request for and acceptance of contact rights in Hungary, and his provision of a Hungarian flat demonstrated subsequent acquiescence within the meaning of Article 13(a). The Kúria dismissed the applicant’s review petition on 10 January 2017, endorsing that interpretation and emphasising that the applicant had waited almost a year—until Sz.I. sought to restrict contact—before seeking return.

The applicant complained that the refusal to order return violated his Article 8 rights by failing to protect his family life with his son and by misapplying the Hague Convention’s exceptions. The Court examined whether the domestic courts had fulfilled their positive obligation to secure the child’s prompt return while striking a fair balance between the competing interests, taking into account the child’s best interests as a primary consideration. The key factual matrix relevant to that assessment comprised the initial wrongful retention, the applicant’s contemporaneous statements and conduct in the Hungarian divorce proceedings, the lengthy delay before the Hague application, and the child’s integration in Hungary during that period.

The case of Kupás v. Hungary (Application no. 24720/17) involves the applicant's complaint that Hungarian courts breached his Article 8 right to respect for family life by dismissing his request for the summary return of his infant son to Switzerland under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction.

The applicant, a dual Hungarian-Romanian national resident in Basel, married Sz.I. in May 2014 after the couple had begun living together in Switzerland. Their son Z.A. was born there on 9 January 2015. In early May 2015 the family travelled to Budapest on a short visit, for which a temporary passport was issued for the child. The applicant returned to Switzerland after one week, expecting Sz.I. and Z.A. to follow once the child's permanent documents (issued on 26 May 2015) were ready. Instead Sz.I. remained in Hungary, initiated divorce, custody and maintenance proceedings before the Pest Central District Court, and informed the applicant that she would not return. The child was deregistered from the Swiss residents' register at Sz.I.'s request; she claimed (but the applicant denied) that he had consented.

Between May and October 2015 the applicant had no contact with Z.A. despite travelling to Hungary every fortnight. His application to place the child under protective measures was discontinued after child-welfare services found Z.A. to be well cared for. Hungarian courts initially declined jurisdiction over custody but later accepted it on the basis that the divorce proceedings themselves conferred competence.

At a hearing on 6 October 2015 the applicant's lawyer stated that he wished a friendly settlement, had not commenced Hague Convention proceedings and did not intend to remove the child from the mother's custody. Interim contact orders were made: first, supervised contact every other weekend; later, unsupervised contact at the applicant's Budapest flat. Both parents subsequently applied to vary those arrangements.

Only in April 2016, after Sz.I. sought to restrict contact, did the applicant apply under the Hague Convention for Z.A.'s return, alleging wrongful retention. Sz.I. conceded that she had misled the applicant and that Switzerland had been the child's habitual residence, but invoked Article 13 exceptions (acquiescence and grave risk of harm). While confirming that the retention had been wrongful, it found that the applicant's express willingness to exercise contact rights in Hungary, his delay of almost a year in seeking return, and his request that meetings take place at his own Hungarian flat constituted subsequent acquiescence under Article 13(a). The Kúria dismissed the applicant's review petition on 10 January 2017, endorsing that interpretation and stressing that the applicant had prioritised contact arrangements over prompt return until Sz.I. attempted to limit those rights.

The applicant complained to the European Court that these rulings failed to secure the child's prompt return and thereby violated his Article 8 rights. The Court later held the domestic decisions to be proportionate.

The case of Kupás v. Hungary (Application no. 24720/17) arose from the Hungarian courts’ refusal to order the summary return of the applicant’s infant son from Hungary to Switzerland under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The applicant, a dual Hungarian-Romanian national living in Basel, alleged that this refusal violated his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant married Sz.I. in May 2014 after the couple had already begun living together in Switzerland. Their son, Z.A., was born there in January 2015. In early May 2015 the family travelled to Budapest for a short visit, for which a temporary passport was obtained for the child. The applicant returned to Switzerland after one week, believing that his wife and son would follow once the child’s permanent documents were issued on 26 May 2015. Instead, Sz.I. remained in Hungary, commenced divorce, custody and maintenance proceedings before the Pest Central District Court, and notified the applicant that she would not return. She also arranged the child’s deregistration from the Swiss residents’ register, claiming the applicant had consented.

The applicant had no contact with his son between May and October 2015 despite travelling to Hungary every second weekend. He applied unsuccessfully to the local guardianship authority for protective measures; the authority found the child to be well cared for and discontinued the case. In the divorce proceedings the Budapest High Court confirmed Hungarian jurisdiction on the basis that the child’s habitual residence was now in Hungary or, alternatively, because the custody claim was ancillary to the divorce action.

At a hearing on 6 October 2015 the applicant’s lawyer stated that he wished to reach an amicable settlement, had not initiated Hague Convention proceedings and did not intend to remove the child from the mother’s custody. He merely sought regular contact during his visits. The court granted an interim contact order (every second weekend, initially in the presence of the mother at a relative’s flat). The arrangement was later varied, at the applicant’s request, to unsupervised contact at his own Budapest flat. Only in April 2016, after the mother applied to restrict and supervise contact, did the applicant lodge a Hague Convention return application.

Sz.I. conceded that the child’s habitual residence had been Switzerland and that she had misled the applicant, but invoked Article 13 of the Hague Convention, arguing both subsequent acquiescence and a grave risk of harm. The first-instance court ordered return, holding that neither the October 2015 statement nor the request for contact constituted consent or acquiescence. The Budapest High Court reversed that order in September 2016. It accepted that the retention had been wrongful but found that the applicant’s explicit statement that he would not seek return, his participation in Hungarian contact proceedings and his provision of a local flat amounted to acquiescence under Article 13(a). The Kúria dismissed the applicant’s review petition in January 2017, emphasising that he had waited nearly eleven months—until contact was threatened—before invoking the Hague Convention and that his conduct demonstrated acceptance of the child’s new habitual residence in Hungary.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic courts had failed to fulfil their positive obligation under Article 8 to secure the prompt return of his child and thereby protect his family life.

The case of Kindlhofer v. Austria (Application no. 20962/15) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which guarantees the right of a person convicted of a criminal offence by a tribunal to have the conviction or sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal (subject to exceptions for offences of a minor character). The applicant, Manfred Kindlhofer, an Austrian national, also raised related arguments concerning equality of arms under Article 6.

On 20 November 2012 the Styria Regional Police Directorate issued a penalty notice finding that the applicant had breached section 4(5) of the Road Traffic Act. He had been driving a vehicle involved in a traffic accident that caused only material damage and had failed to inform the nearest police station of the incident without undue delay. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 200 plus EUR 20 in costs, with four days’ imprisonment in default of payment. The statutory maximum for the offence was a fine of EUR 726 or, if irrecoverable, imprisonment of up to two weeks.

The applicant appealed to the Styria Regional Administrative Court, denying that he had been the driver at the relevant time. He stated that he had consumed alcohol that evening and had therefore not driven the borrowed vehicle home; he could not identify the actual driver. He also challenged the assessment of the evidence. After an oral hearing the Regional Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 5 February 2014. It confirmed the fine of EUR 200 (plus EUR 40 appeal costs) and the four-day default term of imprisonment. The court relied on witness statements, physical traces from the vehicle found at the scene, and the applicant’s admission that he had driven the car earlier that evening. It rejected his defence that the true driver would have sustained head injuries from a cracked windscreen and declined to commission a technical expert report. In its information on further remedies the court stated that an appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court was excluded by section 25a(4) of the Administrative Court Act, which bars such appeals where a fine of no more than EUR 400 has been imposed and no custodial sentence (other than in default) could have been imposed.

On 31 March 2014 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court. He argued that section 25a(4) was unconstitutional because it deprived him of a review by a higher tribunal contrary to Article 2 of Protocol No. 7. Both the abstract penalty range and the sanction actually imposed included imprisonment in default of payment. He further contended that the provision breached equality of arms under Article 6, since the original authority and the competent federal minister retained an unrestricted right of appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court regardless of the amount of the fine. On 25 September 2014 the Constitutional Court declined to examine the complaint for lack of prospects of success, holding that its existing case-law disclosed no appearance of a violation of a constitutionally guaranteed right.

Under Austrian law an appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court is generally available only if the decision turns on a question of law of fundamental importance. Federal law may exclude such appeals in cases involving small fines. Imprisonment in default of payment of an administrative fine must be fixed at the same time as the fine, but its enforcement is subject to strict safeguards: the authority must first attempt recovery through ordinary enforcement proceedings or establish, on the basis of recent and comprehensive enquiries into the debtor’s financial situation, that the fine is irrecoverable; a formal notice to serve the sentence must be issued; and payment at any time prevents imprisonment. These procedural requirements formed part of the factual matrix against which the alleged denial of a higher-court review was assessed.

The case of Kindlhofer v. Austria (Application no. 20962/15) concerns an Austrian national’s complaint that he was denied access to a higher tribunal to review an administrative criminal conviction, in alleged breach of Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Manfred Kindlhofer, was also represented in proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights.

On 20 November 2012 the Styria Regional Police Directorate issued a penalty notice against the applicant for an offence under section 4(5) of the Road Traffic Act. He had been involved in a traffic accident causing only material damage and had failed to notify the nearest police station without delay. A fine of EUR 200 plus EUR 20 costs was imposed, together with four days’ imprisonment in default of payment.

The applicant appealed to the Styria Regional Administrative Court, denying that he had been driving the vehicle at the relevant time and criticising the assessment of the evidence. After an oral hearing the court dismissed the appeal on 5 February 2014, confirming the fine (now plus EUR 40 costs) and the default prison term. It accepted the police assessment of witness statements, physical evidence from the scene and the applicant’s own admission that he had driven the car earlier that evening. It rejected his request for a technical expert report. The court’s information note stated that an appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court was barred by section 25a(4) of the Administrative Court Act because the fine imposed did not exceed EUR 400.

On 31 March 2014 the applicant complained to the Constitutional Court. He argued that the statutory bar on further appeal violated Article 2 of Protocol No. 7, since both the abstract penalty range (fine up to EUR 726 or two weeks’ imprisonment in default) and the concrete sanction included the possibility of imprisonment. He further alleged a breach of equality of arms under Article 6, because the prosecuting authority and the competent federal minister retained an unrestricted right of appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court. On 25 September 2014 the Constitutional Court declined to examine the complaint for lack of prospects of success, finding no indication of a constitutionally guaranteed right having been violated.

Under Austrian law, Article 133 of the Federal Constitution Act permits federal legislation to exclude appeals in cases involving only a “small fine.” Section 25a(4) of the Administrative Court Act implements this by rendering an appeal inadmissible where a fine of no more than EUR 400 has been imposed and no prison sentence (as a primary penalty) could have been imposed. Although imprisonment in default of payment is mandatory under section 16 of the Administrative Offences Act, its enforcement is subject to strict procedural safeguards: the authority must first attempt recovery or establish that the fine is irrecoverable, serve a notice requiring the person to begin serving the sentence, and grant payment extensions or instalments where financial hardship is shown. Domestic case-law confirms that enforcement without these steps is unlawful.

The applicant’s essential grievance was therefore that an offence carrying a default prison term could not be regarded as “minor” for the purpose of the exception in Article 2 § 2 of Protocol No. 7, and that the absence of any possibility of review by the Supreme Administrative Court left him without an effective remedy against the Regional Administrative Court’s decision.

The case of Kindlhofer v. Austria (Application no. 20962/15) concerns an alleged violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the right to have a conviction or sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal. The applicant, Manfred Kindlhofer, an Austrian national born in 1963 and residing in Graz, challenged the lack of access to further judicial review of an administrative criminal penalty.

On 20 November 2012, the Styria Regional Police Directorate issued a penalty notice against Kindlhofer for violating section 4(5) of the Road Traffic Act. This provision requires persons involved in a traffic accident causing only material damage to inform the nearest police station without undue delay (unless names and addresses are exchanged). The Directorate found that Kindlhofer had driven a borrowed vehicle involved in such an accident and failed to report it. He was fined EUR 200 plus EUR 20 in costs, with four days’ imprisonment in default of payment. Under section 99(3) of the Road Traffic Act, the offence carried a maximum fine of EUR 726, or up to two weeks’ imprisonment if the fine proved irrecoverable.

Kindlhofer appealed to the Styria Regional Administrative Court on 19 December 2012. He denied driving the vehicle at the relevant time, claiming he had consumed alcohol in bars and left the car with an unidentified person. He also contested the evidence assessment. After an oral hearing, the Regional Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 5 February 2014. It upheld the EUR 200 fine (plus EUR 40 appeal costs) and four days’ default imprisonment. The court relied on witness statements, debris from the vehicle found at the scene, and Kindlhofer’s admission that he had driven the car earlier that evening. It rejected his defence regarding possible head injuries from a cracked windscreen and declined to commission a technical expert report, finding it unnecessary. The decision explicitly stated that an appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court was inadmissible under section 25a(4) of the Administrative Court Act, which bars such appeals in administrative criminal matters where the maximum possible fine is EUR 750 (with no primary prison sentence) and the fine actually imposed does not exceed EUR 400.

On 31 March 2014, Kindlhofer lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court. He argued that section 25a(4) was unconstitutional as it violated Article 2 of Protocol No. 7. Both the abstract penalty range (including default imprisonment of up to two weeks) and the sanction applied to him included a custodial element. He further claimed a breach of equality of arms under Article 6 of the Convention, noting that the imposing authority and the competent federal minister could appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court regardless of the fine amount, whereas he could not.

The Constitutional Court declined to examine the complaint on 25 September 2014, citing lack of prospects of success. It found no indication of a violation of a constitutionally guaranteed right or of another right arising from an unconstitutional law, and held that the issues did not require specific constitutional scrutiny. Under Austrian law (Articles 133 and 144 of the Federal Constitution Act, section 25a of the Administrative Court Act, and related provisions of the Administrative Offences Act), default imprisonment is mandatory to specify but can be enforced only after unsuccessful recovery attempts, recent comprehensive enquiries into the debtor’s finances, and service of a notice to serve the sentence. Enforcement is not automatic or discretionary.

These facts form the core of the alleged deprivation of a higher-tribunal review of both conviction and sentence in an administrative offence treated as criminal for Convention purposes.

The case of *Vig v. Hungary* (Application no. 59648/13) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the Hungarian police’s statutory powers to conduct identity checks and personal searches during “enhanced checks.” The applicant, Mr Dávid Vig, alleged that these powers and their application to him violated Articles 5 (liberty and security), 8 (respect for private life) and 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention.

On 16 January 2013 the National Police Commissioner, acting under section 26 of the Police Service Regulation, issued a nationwide authorisation for enhanced checks running until 31 March 2013. The stated purpose was to monitor illegal-migration routes into the European Union and to operate a screening network against illegal immigration.

A cultural festival was held at the Sirály Community Centre in Budapest on 29–30 March 2013. On 29 March the Budapest VI District Police Department adopted an operational plan that invoked the national authorisation. Although the plan cited the migration-control notice, its concrete aims were to check visitors’ identities, look for wanted persons and prevent the centre’s alleged irregular operation (lack of authorisation and fire-safety measures).

Around midnight on 30 March police officers entered the centre. An employee announced that everyone would be checked and that those who wished to leave could do so. Half an hour later all persons were required to leave; only those who submitted to the check would be allowed to return. When the applicant asked for the legal basis he received inconsistent answers: a “night check,” a search for a missing person, or an “enhanced check.” He handed over his identity card but was then ordered outside. Surrounded by officers and feeling intimidated, he complied; one officer pushed him. His outer clothing was searched, nothing incriminating was found, and he was released.

The applicant challenged the measures at every available level. A constitutional complaint attacking sections 30(1)–(3) and 31 of the Police Act and section 26 of the Service Regulation was declared time-barred. The Independent Police Complaints Board held the identity check and search lawful and compatible with private life, but found that the search had a repressive purpose (violating fair-trial rights) and that the officers’ manner had violated human dignity. The Budapest police dismissed all other complaints. On judicial review the Administrative and Labour Court ruled that it had no competence to examine either the national authorisation or the operational plan; it could review only the individual measures, which it found to be in accordance with both the legislation and the plan. No further appeal was pursued.

These facts illustrate the alleged violations. The Police Act permitted an officer to check identity and search clothing or vehicles in any “public place” or “certain location” designated by a police chief, for the purpose of preventing endangerment of public security or illegal conduct at an event. The Service Regulation defined an enhanced check as the sealing of an area and the systematic checking of everyone present; such an operation could be ordered for an entire country or region by senior officials with virtually no temporal, geographic or purpose-related restrictions and with no independent prior or subsequent review. In the applicant’s case the nationwide migration-control notice was used to justify a local operation whose stated aims were unrelated to migration. Reasons given on the spot were inconsistent, no individualised suspicion was required, and domestic courts expressly declined to scrutinise the underlying authorisation. The combination of an extremely broad, unreviewable executive power and the absence of effective judicial control formed the core of the complaint that the legal framework itself was incompatible with the Convention.

The case of Vig v. Hungary concerns a Hungarian national, Dávid Vig, who alleged that police identity checks and a personal search during an “enhanced check” violated his rights under Articles 5, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 16 January 2013 the National Police Commissioner, relying on section 26 of the 2011 Police Service Regulation, authorised enhanced checks across the entire territory of Hungary until 31 March 2013. The stated purpose was to monitor illegal-migration routes into the European Union and to operate a screening network against illegal migration. On 29 March 2013 the Budapest VI District Police Department, acting under that nationwide authorisation, drew up an operational plan targeting the Sirály Community Centre, where a cultural festival was taking place. The plan cited earlier information from municipal authorities that the centre operated without proper authorisation and fire-safety measures; it instructed officers to check visitors’ identities and look for wanted persons in order to prevent irregular operation and related illegal activity.

Around midnight on 30 March 2013 officers entered the centre. Patrons were told they could leave immediately or remain and submit to checks; later everyone was required to exit and only those who had been checked were permitted to re-enter. When Vig asked the legal basis he received inconsistent answers—“night check,” search for a missing person, or “enhanced check.” He handed over his identity card and, feeling intimidated by surrounding officers (one of whom pushed him), followed them outside. His outer clothing was searched; nothing incriminating was found and he was allowed to leave.

Vig first lodged a constitutional complaint challenging sections 30(1)–(3) and 31 of the 1994 Police Act and section 26 of the Service Regulation. A single judge of the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as time-barred (the 180-day limit ran from the provisions’ entry into force in 1994). He then complained to the Independent Police Complaints Board, arguing that the statutory scheme conferred unfettered power to stop and search anyone without requiring specific grounds, making effective challenge virtually impossible, and that the officers had failed to identify themselves, state reasons, inform him of remedies, or treat him with dignity. The Board found the identity check and search formally lawful and not an interference with private life or data protection, yet held that the search had a repressive character (violating fair-trial rights) and that the officers’ manner had violated dignity.

A subsequent complaint to the Budapest Main Police Department was dismissed except as regards the manner of execution. On judicial review the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court held that it lacked competence to examine either the nationwide authorisation or the operational plan; it could review only the individual measures, which it found to have complied with the applicable legislation and plan. The court did not address Vig’s request that it refer the statutory provisions to the Constitutional Court. Vig did not seek review by the Kúria.

The relevant domestic law (Police Act ss. 30–31 and Service Regulation s. 26) permits senior officers to designate public places or events for identity checks and clothing/vehicle searches “to prevent or hinder an activity endangering public security” or “to prevent illegal conduct endangering \ldots public order.” No prior judicial authorisation, temporal or spatial limitation beyond the discretion of the issuing officer, or subsequent independent review of the authorisation itself is required. Failure to obey a lawful order constitutes a minor offence.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: the identity check and search as interferences with private life and liberty, and the absence of adequate safeguards or effective remedies against the underlying authorisations.

Hungary (Application no. 59648/13) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant, Hungarian national Mr Dávid Vig, who alleged that police identity checks and personal searches conducted during “enhanced checks” under Hungarian law violated his rights under Articles 5 (liberty and security), 8 (private life) and 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention.

On 16 January 2013 the National Police Commissioner, relying on section 26 of the 2011 Police Service Regulation, issued a nationwide authorisation for enhanced checks lasting until 31 March 2013. The stated purpose was to monitor illegal-migration routes into the European Union and to operate a screening network against illegal migration. On 29 March 2013 the Budapest VI District Police Department, citing both that authorisation and information from local authorities that the Sirály Community Centre was operating irregularly and lacked fire-safety authorisation, prepared an operational plan to conduct an enhanced check at a cultural festival being held there. The plan authorised officers to monitor visitors, verify identities and look for wanted persons, with the additional aim of preventing irregular operation of the venue.

When the applicant asked the legal basis for the operation he received inconsistent answers: first that it was a “night check,” then that officers were searching for a missing person; other attendees were told it formed part of the nationwide enhanced-check programme. The applicant surrendered his identity card. Although he saw no reason to remain once his identity had been verified, he felt intimidated by the surrounding officers and complied with an order to step outside. One officer pushed him. His outer clothing was searched; nothing incriminating was found and he was released.

A single judge of the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as time-barred (the 180-day period having begun when the provisions entered into force in 1994). He next complained to the Independent Police Complaints Board, arguing that the statutory scheme conferred unfettered power to stop and search anyone without requiring specific grounds, thereby rendering effective challenge virtually impossible, and that the officers had failed to identify themselves, state reasons, inform him of remedies or treat him with dignity. On judicial review the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court held on 28 April 2016 that it lacked competence to examine either the nationwide authorisation or the operational plan; it could review only the individual measures, which it found to have complied with the plan and the Police Act. The court did not address the applicant’s request that it refer the statutory provisions to the Constitutional Court. No further appeal was pursued to the Kúria.

These facts illustrate the core of the alleged violations: the absence of any meaningful statutory restrictions on, or independent review of, the executive’s decision to authorise wide-area enhanced checks, and the consequent inability of individuals subjected to identity checks and searches to know or contest the true legal basis or necessity of the measures.

The ECHR case of Buliga v. Romania (no. 22003/12) involves applicant Ionel Petrică Buliga (born 1984, resident of Giera) alleging unfair criminal proceedings under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. The complaint centres on his conviction for a minor theft offence based on decisive witness statements from individuals he could not question, in circumstances lacking sufficient counterbalancing factors for the defence. Fair-trial guarantees under Article 6 apply to all criminal proceedings regardless of offence gravity.

On 31 March 2010, the prosecutor’s office attached to Deta District Court opened proceedings against the applicant for several acts of theft of a metal fence (a continuous offence under then-applicable Articles 208 § 1, 209 § 1(g) and 41 § 2 of the Criminal Code). On 18 June 2010 the prosecutor discontinued the case, finding the acts insufficiently serious to constitute a criminal offence and imposing an administrative fine of 350 Romanian lei (approximately €85). The applicant’s challenge was rejected by the chief prosecutor on 16 July 2010.

On 6 August 2010 the applicant challenged the decisions before Deta District Court under Article 278¹ of the Code of Criminal Procedure, offering additional evidence and requesting that witnesses be heard in court to prove his innocence. In a final decision of 21 October 2010 the court dismissed the request to hear witnesses, holding that it lacked power to do so, but found the existing evidence insufficient and referred the case back with instructions to continue the investigation and hear the applicant plus his proposed witnesses.

The applicant was summoned on 8 March 2011, informed of the charges and interviewed; he denied the theft, proposed witnesses and requested two expert examinations to show that the fence on his property differed from the stolen one. Several witnesses (including some he had proposed) were interviewed and his purchase documentation was examined. On 27 April 2011 the prosecutor rejected the expert requests, citing sufficient existing evidence (chiefly witness statements) and the lapse of time. All statements were taken in the applicant’s absence and without a lawyer present.

On 9 June 2011 the prosecutor again discontinued the prosecution and imposed a higher administrative fine of 800 lei (approximately €190); this was upheld on 29 June 2011. The applicant objected, arguing that his evidence offers had been rejected and that certain witness statements had been obtained under duress.

In a final decision of 23 August 2011 the District Court dismissed the objection. It refused the expert examination because it did not constitute “new documents,” the only additional evidence the court could consider under Article 278¹ § 7 CCP. The court noted that the original two witnesses had been re-interviewed and that seven new witnesses (some proposed by the applicant) had given statements, concluding that the evidence had been correctly gathered and interpreted and that the applicant had stolen the metal fence.

The decisive evidence consisted of these untested witness statements. The domestic court’s inability to hear the witnesses itself was not a good reason for their non-attendance, and no adequate counterbalancing measures (such as the applicant’s presence during interviews or alternative confrontation) were afforded to the defence. These facts formed the basis of the Court’s finding of a violation of Article 6.

The case of Buliga v. Romania (ECtHR, Application no. 22003/12) concerns allegations of unfair criminal proceedings under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. The applicant, Ionel Petrică Buliga (born 1984), was prosecuted for theft of a metal fence, classified as a continuous aggravated offence under the Criminal Code then in force.

On 31 March 2010 the prosecutor’s office attached to the Deta District Court opened an investigation. On 18 June 2010 it discontinued the criminal prosecution, finding that the acts lacked the requisite social danger to constitute a criminal offence and instead imposed an administrative fine of 350 RON. The applicant challenged this outcome. On 21 October 2010 the District Court, acting under Article 2781 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, referred the case back with instructions to interview the applicant and the witnesses he proposed, while noting that it itself lacked power to hear witnesses.

Further investigation followed. On 8 March 2011 the applicant was interviewed, denied the theft and requested expert examinations (later refused on the ground that existing evidence, principally witness statements, sufficed and that the passage of time rendered expert analysis useless). Several witnesses, including some nominated by the applicant, were interviewed; all statements were taken in the absence of the applicant or any lawyer. On 9 June 2011 the prosecutor again discontinued the prosecution and imposed a higher administrative fine of 800 RON. The applicant objected, arguing that his evidence had been rejected and that certain witness statements had been obtained under duress.

On 23 August 2011 the District Court dismissed the objection in a final decision. It refused the request for expert evidence because Article 2781 § 7 limited it to “new documents” only. The court observed that two original witnesses had been re-interviewed and seven additional witnesses (some proposed by the applicant) had given statements, and it concluded that the prosecutor had correctly determined that the applicant had stolen the fence. The administrative sanction was therefore upheld.

The applicant complained that the proceedings were unfair because the court had based its finding of guilt on witness statements that he had never been able to challenge. The procedure under Article 2781 CCP, as interpreted by the Constitutional Court, confined judicial review to the existing file and new documents, preventing the court from hearing the witnesses itself. The Government later accepted that Article 6 applied to the proceedings notwithstanding their classification as “administrative,” given the nature of the offence and the possible consequences.

The Court subsequently found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d). It held that the general guarantees of fairness apply irrespective of the minor character of the offence; that the domestic court’s statutory inability to hear the witnesses did not constitute a good reason for their non-attendance; and that no sufficient counterbalancing factors (such as the possibility of confronting the witnesses at any stage, video recordings, or other safeguards) had been provided to compensate for the handicap thereby created for the defence. The statements in question were decisive. The most appropriate redress was therefore reopening of the domestic proceedings together with an award of non-pecuniary damages for distress.

The case of Buliga v. Romania (Application no. 22003/12) concerned allegations of unfair criminal proceedings under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the ECHR. The applicant, Ionel Petrică Buliga, a Romanian national born in 1984 and living in Giera, claimed that a domestic court had convicted him of minor offences based on decisive evidence from witnesses he had been unable to question.

On 31 March 2010, the prosecutor’s office attached to the Deta District Court opened criminal proceedings against the applicant for theft of a metal fence (under Criminal Code Articles 208 § 1, 209 § 1(g) and 41 § 2, as a continuous offence). On 18 June 2010 the prosecutor discontinued the proceedings, finding the acts insufficiently serious to constitute a criminal offence under Article 181 of the Criminal Code, and imposed an administrative fine of 350 RON (approximately EUR 85). The applicant challenged this, but the decision was upheld by the chief prosecutor on 16 July 2010.

On 6 August 2010 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Deta District Court under Article 2781 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, offering additional evidence and requesting that witnesses be heard to prove his innocence. In a final decision of 21 October 2010 the court dismissed the request to hear witnesses (on the ground that it lacked power to do so in this procedure) but found the prosecutor’s evidence insufficient. It referred the case back, instructing the prosecutor to continue the investigation and hear the applicant and his proposed witnesses.

The applicant was summoned on 8 March 2011, informed of the charges and interviewed; he denied the theft, proposed witnesses and requested two expert examinations to show that the fence on his property differed from the stolen one. Several witnesses (including some proposed by him) were interviewed and documents concerning the fence’s purchase were examined. All statements were taken in the applicant’s absence (and without a lawyer). On 27 April 2011 the chief prosecutor dismissed the expert requests, stating that existing witness statements sufficed and that the passage of time rendered an examination useless. This was upheld on appeal.

On 9 June 2011 the prosecutor again discontinued the prosecution and imposed a higher administrative fine of 800 RON (approximately EUR 190); this was upheld on 29 June 2011. The applicant objected to the District Court, arguing that his evidence offers had been rejected and that some witness statements had been obtained under duress.

In a final decision of 23 August 2011 the District Court dismissed the objection. It refused an expert examination because such evidence did not constitute “new documents” (the only additional material it could consider under Article 2781 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). It noted that two original witnesses had been re-interviewed and seven new witnesses (some proposed by the applicant) had given statements. Finding the evidence correctly gathered and interpreted, the court concluded that the prosecutor had rightly determined that the applicant had stolen the metal fence.

The applicant alleged that these proceedings were unfair because the court had relied on untested witness statements as decisive evidence of guilt, without any opportunity for him (or the court) to examine the witnesses. The procedure under Article 2781 limited the court to reviewing the prosecutor’s file and any new documents, precluding the hearing of witnesses. Although the resulting administrative sanction was classified as non-criminal under domestic law, the applicant maintained that Article 6 guarantees applied in full. The European Court of Human Rights later held that they did, that the court’s inability to hear the witnesses was not a good reason for their absence, and that no sufficient counterbalancing factors compensated for the resulting handicap to the defence.
001-208015:
The case of Mtchedlishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 894/12) concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the Kutaisi Court of Appeal dispensed with an oral hearing in criminal proceedings against the applicant, Ms Vera Mtchedlishvili, without reasons and despite issues requiring in-person assessment of evidence.

On 18 March 2010 police received anonymous information that the applicant was illicitly transporting narcotic and psychotropic medication from Turkey. She was stopped and searched at the Sarpi border checkpoint, where 15,410 pills (later recounted as 15,761) were seized. Some were in 310 blister packs labelled “Stablon”; the rest were in an unlabelled bag. She was arrested as a suspect for purchasing and storing narcotics. An expert examination the next day found no narcotic or psychotropic substances, so she was released. The National Forensic Bureau later valued the pills at GEL 15,655.89 (approximately EUR 6,586).

On 30 July 2010 further anonymous information led to an investigation of the applicant and A.M. for the same offence. A search of the applicant in Batumi and of her home yielded nothing. A search of a garden belonging to G.Ch. (A.M.’s mother-in-law) uncovered a plastic bag containing 10,956 unidentified pills and 710 blister packs of “Stablon”. G.Ch. said A.M. had asked her to store a bag whose contents she did not know. The pills were valued at GEL 22,427.47 (approximately EUR 9,392). The applicant and A.M. were arrested the following day.

On 27 August 2010 the applicant was charged with two counts of violating customs regulations under Article 214 § 1 of the Criminal Code (carrying goods of large quantity—value exceeding GEL 15,000—across the border by bypassing inspection). A.M. was charged only in respect of the second incident.

At trial the applicant admitted importing the “Stablon” pills on 18 March 2010 (her second such trip) with the intention of opening a pharmacy. She claimed their value was below the GEL 15,000 threshold, so her actions were not criminal, and she denied any connection to the second incident, asserting that A.M. had incriminated her to avoid liability. She knew A.M. as a taxi driver and had stayed at his home after returning from Turkey on 29 July 2010, leaving belongings there. A.M. stated that the applicant had left bags at his home and later asked him to hide one containing painkillers. Investigators testified that A.M. had told them the pills belonged to the applicant (which he denied). G.Ch. confirmed hiding the bag on A.M.’s instruction but did not know its origin.

On 14 February 2011 the trial court convicted both defendants. The applicant received nine years’ imprisonment (four and a half years per count) plus a GEL 25,000 fine. It held that the first-incident valuation used a standard method and that the evidence as a whole (A.M.’s indication, border records showing both had crossed into Turkey and back on 29 July 2010, and officers’ testimony) proved the applicant’s guilt on the second count.

The applicant appealed on 14 March 2011. For the first incident she accepted the facts but disputed the valuation method, requesting that the original expert and an alternative expert she had commissioned be questioned. For the second incident she maintained she had no involvement, that A.M. had implicated her, and that even if his account were true it did not prove importation from Turkey (no illicit items having been found on her at the border). She expressly requested an oral hearing. The prosecutor filed no observations.

On 31 March 2011 the Kutaisi Court of Appeal dispensed with an oral hearing without explanation and upheld the conviction in full. It treated the first-incident facts as uncontested and accepted the customs-value method. For the second incident it found the applicant’s and A.M.’s accounts unconvincing and contradictory, relying on officers’ statements, G.Ch.’s evidence, the search report, the valuation, and border records to conclude they had jointly imported the medication by circumventing inspection.

The applicant’s subsequent appeal on points of law, which included a complaint about the lack of an oral hearing, was rejected as inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 22 June 2011. She was released in January 2013 under an amnesty. The Court later found a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the unreasoned decision to forgo a hearing left unaddressed questions that, as a matter of fair trial, required direct personal assessment of the evidence.

The case of Mtchedlishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 894/12) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Kutaisi Court of Appeal dispensed with an oral hearing in her criminal appeal, despite issues requiring in-person assessment of evidence.

Vera Mtchedlishvili, a Georgian national born in 1959, faced two sets of charges relating to the alleged illicit transport of pills from Turkey into Georgia. On 18 March 2010, following anonymous information, police stopped and searched her at the Sarpi border checkpoint, seizing 15,410 pills (later recounted as 15,761), some in “Stablon” blister packs and others unlabeled. She was arrested on suspicion of purchasing and storing narcotics. An expert examination the next day found no narcotic or psychotropic substances, leading to her release. The pills’ value was later assessed at GEL 15,655.89 (approximately EUR 6,586).

On 30 July 2010, further anonymous information prompted a search of the applicant in Batumi and her home, both yielding nothing. A search of a garden belonging to G.Ch. (mother-in-law of co-accused A.M.) recovered a bag containing 10,956 unidentified pills and 710 “Stablon” blister packs, valued at GEL 22,427.47 (approximately EUR 9,392). The applicant and A.M. were arrested the next day. On 27 August 2010, she was charged with two counts of violating customs regulations under Article 214 § 1 of the Criminal Code (transporting goods exceeding GEL 15,000 in value by bypassing inspections). A.M. was charged only in respect of the second incident.

At trial, the applicant admitted importing the first batch of Stablon pills (her second such import) intending to open a pharmacy. She argued they were neither narcotic nor psychotropic and that their true value fell below the GEL 15,000 threshold, rendering her actions non-criminal. She denied any involvement in the second incident, claiming A.M. (whom she knew as a taxi driver) had implicated her to evade liability. She explained staying overnight at his home after returning from Turkey on 29 July 2010 and leaving belongings there. A.M. testified that she left bags, later instructing him via message to hide the medication bag (described as painkillers). Investigators stated A.M. had told them the pills belonged to the applicant (which he denied). G.Ch. confirmed receiving a request from A.M. to dispose of the bag, which she threw into her garden, but she did not know its origin or the applicant personally. The trial court dismissed as untimely the applicant’s request to question the valuation expert.

On 14 February 2011, the applicant was convicted on both counts and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment (four and a half years per count) plus a GEL 25,000 fine. The court accepted the expert valuation for the first incident and found the overall evidence (including A.M.’s statements, border-crossing records showing both had entered Turkey and returned around the same times on 29 July, and officers’ testimony) established her guilt in the second.

She appealed on 14 March 2011, requesting an oral hearing. She reiterated her admission regarding the first incident but disputed the valuation method, seeking to question both the state expert and an alternative expert she had commissioned. For the second incident, she maintained her lack of involvement and A.M.’s self-serving implication. Even accepting his account, she argued, it did not prove the pills originated in Turkey rather than being acquired domestically, especially as none were found on her at the border and A.M. claimed ignorance of their source.

The prosecutor submitted no observations. On 31 March 2011, the Court of Appeal dispensed with an oral hearing without explanation and upheld the conviction in full. It treated the first incident’s facts as uncontested except for the valuation method (always based on customs value). For the second, it dismissed the accounts of the applicant and A.M. as unconvincing and contradictory, relying instead on officers’ statements that the pills belonged to her, G.Ch.’s testimony about A.M.’s instructions, the search report, the valuation, and border records indicating joint circumvention of customs on 29 July 2010.

The applicant’s subsequent appeal on points of law (including the lack of an oral hearing) was rejected as inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 22 June 2011. She was released on 24 January 2013 under an amnesty. Under the applicable Code of Criminal Procedure, the appellate court could re-examine facts and law but was permitted a written procedure in certain “less serious” cases.

The case of Mtchedlishvili v. Georgia (no. 894/12) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that the Kutaisi Court of Appeal’s unreasoned decision to dispense with an oral hearing in her criminal appeal denied her a fair trial, as certain issues required in-person assessment of evidence and witness credibility.

On 18 March 2010, acting on anonymous information, police searched the applicant at the Georgia-Turkey border and seized 15,410 pills (some in “Stablon” blister packs). An expert found no narcotics, so she was released, but the pills were later valued at GEL 15,655.89 (above the GEL 15,000 “large quantity” threshold for a customs offence). On 30 July 2010, further anonymous information led to searches of the applicant (nothing found) and of a garden belonging to G.Ch. (mother-in-law of co-accused taxi driver A.M.), yielding 10,956 pills and 710 Stablon packs valued at GEL 22,427.47. Both were arrested.

The applicant was charged with two counts of violating customs regulations (Article 214 § 1 Criminal Code) for transporting goods of large value across the border by concealing them from inspection. At trial she admitted importing the March pills (intending to open a pharmacy) but disputed the valuation method, claiming the true value fell below the criminal threshold. She denied any link to the July pills, asserting A.M. had implicated her to evade his own liability. A.M. claimed she had left bags at his home and later instructed him (via message) to hide the medication. Investigators testified that A.M. had told them the pills belonged to the applicant; G.Ch. said A.M. had asked her to conceal a bag. Border records showed the pair had crossed into and out of Turkey on 29 July within short intervals of each other.

On 14 February 2011 the trial court convicted both, sentencing the applicant to nine years’ imprisonment (4½ years per count) plus a GEL 25,000 fine. It accepted the expert valuations and found the combined evidence (A.M.’s statements, officers’ testimony, G.Ch.’s account, search reports and border records) proved joint importation.

The applicant appealed, requesting an oral hearing. She sought to examine the State expert and her own alternative expert on valuation methodology for the first count. For the second she argued that even if A.M.’s account were accepted it did not prove the pills had been brought from Turkey (none were found on her at the border and A.M. himself claimed ignorance of their origin). On 31 March 2011 the Court of Appeal dispensed with a hearing without giving reasons and upheld the conviction in full. It treated the March facts as uncontested and the valuation method as standard; for July it dismissed the appellants’ accounts as unconvincing and held that the same body of evidence demonstrated joint, concealed importation.

The Supreme Court later declared her points-of-law appeal (which included the hearing complaint) inadmissible. The applicant was released under a 2012 amnesty. Under the then-applicable Code of Criminal Procedure an appellate court could retry both facts and law but was permitted to use a purely written procedure for “less serious” offences.

These facts underscore that the appeal raised live issues of expert methodology and witness credibility that, as a matter of fair trial, required direct oral assessment.
001-207414:
The case of Velesco v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 53918/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the alleged failure of Moldovan authorities to conduct an effective investigation into the death of the applicant’s son, V., raising issues under the procedural obligations of Article 2 of the Convention.

On 20 January 2009, V. was found hanged in the garden of his parents’ summer house. An initial forensic examination occurred the next day at the request of the Buiucani police, but the request lacked a registration number and the expert was not formally warned of criminal liability for false statements. On 10 February 2009 the General Police Department criticised the investigation for incomplete steps, including failure to locate two cigarette ends precisely, examine the memory of V.’s mobile phone, interview contacts or nearby residents, or explore any link between V.’s death and an ongoing fraud investigation against him.

The applicant complained on 12 February 2009 that she had received no information about the circumstances or investigative measures. She specifically asked whether a criminal inquiry into possible coercion or incitement to suicide had been opened and whether toxicological tests had been performed, noting that V. had felt unwell shortly before his death. A criminal investigation was formally opened on 2 March 2009. The investigator recorded that V. had been accused of large-scale fraud and that relatives claimed he had been pressured by individuals linked to the company to repay twice the alleged losses, which might have driven him to suicide. A further expert examination of the body was ordered to determine the exact cause of death and whether it had preceded the hanging.

The applicant was interviewed as a witness on 9 March 2009. An autopsy was ordered on 25 May 2009 (this time with a registered request and a warning to the expert) but was delayed when the responsible expert fell ill; it was completed only on 20 October 2009. On 16 June 2009 the applicant was recognised as successor of the injured party and informed of her rights, including the right to question or challenge the expert. Investigative time-limits were repeatedly extended because of the unfinished expert report and the need to examine possible pressure from V.’s former company.

After studying the first autopsy report the applicant complained that it was superficial and had not addressed whether V. had been hanged after death. A second autopsy with additional questions was ordered on 27 November 2009 and completed on 23 April 2010. Both autopsies found no injuries other than rope marks, concluded that death resulted from strangulation by hanging with no signs of struggle or prior death, and detected no alcohol or drugs. The applicant separately commissioned and paid for a histopathology examination whose completion remains unclear.

On 30 July 2010 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, holding that V. had committed suicide because of financial difficulties and that no evidence of persecution existed. The applicant challenged the decision. On 17 December 2010 the Buiucani investigating judge quashed it, finding that the histopathology report had not been obtained, that the applicant had been treated only as a witness rather than as the victim’s representative (thereby denying her full access to the file), that the last persons to see V. alive had not been identified, and that the suicide hypothesis appeared to have been given priority from the outset.

According to the Government the investigation was again discontinued on 9 August 2011 on the ground that no crime had been committed; the applicant did not appeal. The applicant stated that she was re-interviewed once and that no further investigative steps were taken.

These facts—delays, omitted examinations, limited participation rights for the next of kin, and an apparent early commitment to the suicide theory—constitute the core of the complaint that the investigation into V.’s death was ineffective.

The case of Velesco v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 53918/11) concerns an alleged failure by Moldovan authorities to conduct an effective investigation into the death of the applicant’s son, V., raising issues under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Moldovan national born in 1956 and resident in Chișinău, lodged her application on 15 August 2011.

On 20 January 2009, V. was discovered hanging in the garden of his parents’ summer house. An initial forensic examination the following day contained irregularities: the police request lacked a registration number, and the expert had not been warned of criminal liability for false statements. On 10 February 2009 the General Police Department criticised the Buiucani investigating authority for incomplete steps, including uncertainty over the location of two cigarette ends and failure to examine the memory of the mobile telephone found on V. The investigator was instructed to re-register the case, analyse the telephone, interview persons who had last seen V., identify nearby residents, explore any link with a pending fraud investigation against V., and question the applicant about her suspicion that V. had been poisoned (he had felt unwell days earlier).

The applicant complained on 12 February 2009 that she had received no information and asked whether an inquiry into possible incitement to suicide or a toxicological analysis had been opened. The investigator noted that V. had been accused of large-scale fraud at a private company and that relatives alleged he had been pressured to repay double the losses, possibly prompting suicide. A fresh expert examination was ordered to determine the precise cause of death and whether it preceded hanging.

The applicant was heard as a witness on 9 March 2009 but not granted full victim status until 16 June 2009, when her rights were explained and she was informed of the pending expert report. Time-limits for the investigation were repeatedly extended (June, August and October 2009) because of the need to verify alleged pressure from the company and because the autopsy report remained unfinished. An autopsy ordered on 25 May 2009 was delayed by the expert’s illness and completed only on 20 October 2009. Informed of the results on 23 October, the applicant criticised the report as superficial, noting it failed to address whether V. had been hanged after death, and requested a new examination.

Both autopsies found only rope marks, concluded death by strangulation without signs of struggle or ante-mortem hanging, and detected no alcohol or drugs. The applicant successfully challenged the decision. On 17 December 2010 an investigating judge quashed it, finding that the paid histopathology report had never been performed, that the applicant had been treated merely as a witness and thereby denied full access to the file and other victim rights, that the last persons to see V. alive had not been identified, and that the suicide hypothesis had been prematurely privileged.
