The applicant stated that she was re-interviewed once and the case then closed without further investigative steps. These successive shortcomings—delays, incomplete forensic and witness inquiries, inadequate victim participation, and failure to exhaust alternative hypotheses—form the core of the complaint that the investigation into V.’s death was ineffective.

The case of Velesco v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 53918/11) concerns the applicant Tatiana Velesco’s complaint under the European Convention on Human Rights that Moldovan authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the death of her son, V. The applicant, a Moldovan national born in 1956 and residing in Chișinău, lodged her application on 15 August 2011. The alleged violation centres on the procedural obligation to investigate deaths thoroughly, independently and promptly, particularly given suspicions of possible homicide, coercion or incitement to suicide rather than a straightforward suicide.

On 20 January 2009, V. was found hanging in the garden of his parents’ summer house. An initial forensic examination took place the following day pursuant to a request from the Buiucani Police that lacked a registration number; the expert was not warned of criminal liability for false statements. On 10 February 2009 the General Police Department criticised the investigating authority for incomplete steps, including failure to record precisely where two cigarette ends had been found, to examine the memory of the mobile phone discovered in V.’s pocket, to interview persons who had last had contact with V., to identify nearby residents, to explore any link between V.’s death and an ongoing criminal investigation against him for large-scale fraud at a private company, and to interview the applicant about her suspicion that V. had been poisoned after feeling unwell days earlier.

The applicant herself complained on 12 February 2009 that she had received no information and asked whether an investigation into possible coercion or incitement to suicide had been opened and whether a toxicological analysis had been performed. A formal criminal investigation was instituted only on 2 March 2009. The investigator noted that relatives alleged V. had been persecuted by individuals acting for the company in order to extract repayment of twice the alleged losses, which might have driven him to suicide; a fresh expert examination of the body was ordered to determine the precise cause of death and whether it had preceded hanging. The applicant was heard as a witness on 9 March 2009 but was not immediately granted full status as successor of the injured party (that occurred only on 16 June 2009, when her procedural rights were explained).

An autopsy was ordered by the prosecutor on 25 May 2009 and completed on 20 October 2009 after delay caused by the expert’s illness. The applicant, informed of the results on 23 October, criticised the report as superficial and as failing to answer whether V. had hanged himself or been hanged after death; she requested a new examination. A second autopsy, ordered on 27 November 2009 with additional questions, ran from 14 December 2009 to 23 April 2010. Both autopsies found only rope marks, death by strangulation/suffocation, no signs of a struggle or of death prior to hanging, and no alcohol or drugs. The applicant privately commissioned a histopathology examination starting 14 December 2009; it is unclear whether it was ever completed.

On 30 July 2010 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, concluding that V. had committed suicide owing to financial difficulties and that there was no evidence of persecution. The applicant challenged the decision. On 17 December 2010 the investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court quashed it, criticising the failure to carry out the paid-for histopathology report, the fact that the applicant had been treated only as a witness rather than afforded full victim-representative rights (including access to the file), the omission to identify those who last saw V. alive, and the autopsy expert’s apparent assumption from the outset that death had occurred by hanging.

According to the Government the investigation was discontinued again on 9 August 2011 on the ground that no crime had been committed; the applicant did not appeal. The applicant states that after the court’s ruling she was interviewed once more and the case was then closed without further investigative steps. These events—procedural irregularities in the initial forensic work, prolonged delays, incomplete inquiries into alternative hypotheses, limited participation rights for the next of kin, and repeated discontinuances without addressing the court’s criticisms—form the core of the alleged violation of the duty to investigate V.’s death effectively.
001-207410:
The case arose amid post-election unrest in Moldova. After the 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections, which the ruling Communist Party narrowly won, protests erupted in Chișinău on 6–7 April over alleged fraud. Initially peaceful gatherings of several thousand, mostly young people, turned violent after poorly planned police interventions. Protesters stormed and looted the Presidential Palace and Parliament, setting fires. From 1 a.m. on 8 April, police and special forces conducted mass arrests using excessive force, detaining anyone present regardless of involvement; arrests and beatings continued for days.

Applicant Iurie Muradu (born 1986) was arrested around 4:15 p.m. on 7 April and taken to Centru police station. He was not informed of the reasons, nor permitted to contact his parents or choose a lawyer. The 11 p.m. arrest report cited suspicion of robbery (Criminal Code s. 187) but omitted the arrest time and specific acts. At the station he was forced to pose for photographs holding a riot shield with a black T-shirt masking his face; officers hit him, verbally abused him and burned him with cigarettes. He spent nine hours in an unfurnished cell without food, water, toilet access or rest. Around 1 a.m. on 8 April a state-appointed lawyer was assigned; his request for his own counsel was rejected. He was compelled to sign unread documents, being struck whenever he tried to read them. Ill-treatment continued, including in the investigator’s presence; the investigator threatened torture unless he cooperated. After seeing severely injured detainees, he signed everything.

A 9 April police medical examination recorded only a forehead bruise. Upon release on 16 April, examination at the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre (an IRCT member) found three cigarette-burn scars on his left hand, sequelae of head trauma (intracranial hypertension, PTSD, ear damage) and psychological evidence consistent with his account; PTSD persisted in 2019.

Detention conditions were harsh. On 8 April he shared a 12 m² cell with 24–25 others, lacking furniture, ventilation or a toilet (access often refused) and receiving no food; his pre-existing stomach condition worsened and he could not rest. On 10 April he was moved to a similar 12 m² cell with nine others, no beds, an unscreened tap-hole serving as a toilet and constant artificial light. On 11 April he entered Prison no. 13, where seven inmates shared six beds. Official correspondence confirmed Centru station was not a designated detention facility and therefore provided neither beds nor food.

On 8 April the state lawyer merely attended and signed papers without consulting him. On 9 April he appeared before an investigating judge at the station, uninformed of the hearing’s purpose and without copies of the prosecutor’s detention request or the file. The five-minute hearing consisted of one question about stone-throwing (while viewing the posed photographs). Twenty days’ detention was ordered, citing reasonable suspicion of robbery and hooliganism (ss. 187(2b), 287(2b)), collusion risk and the need to protect public order amid societal “shock.” He received neither the decision nor file access. His mother was repeatedly denied information or contact. On 11 April his parents retained lawyer V. Gașițoi, who was refused any information about his whereabouts despite telegrams demanding her presence. On 13 April she obtained the file and lodged a habeas-corpus application alleging ill-treatment, inhuman conditions, denial of chosen counsel, lack of time and facilities to prepare a defence, and an unreasoned detention order. The Chișinău Court of Appeal ordered his immediate release on 16 April (subject to an undertaking to remain in the city), citing his lack of record, good character, residence, employment and citizenship, but awarded no compensation.

On 25 May 2010 he admitted finding and intending to take a discarded riot shield. Hooliganism and group-robbery charges were dropped; he was charged with simple robbery. A 31 May settlement with the Interior Ministry (shield returned, no further claims) led to discontinuation of proceedings.

Complaints of ill-treatment began immediately. On 13 April he described events to the Prosecutor General but stated he had “no complaints” against officers; a 21 April statement added details of ranks, uniforms, locations and perpetrators. His lawyer’s 14 April complaint seeking identification and prosecution went unanswered. Officers interviewed in April–June 2009 denied everything. On 22 June 2009 a prosecutor refused to open an investigation, citing the single forehead bruise (incompatible with claimed multiple blows), denials and the possibility a stone had caused the injury. The decision was quashed in December 2011 and an investigation opened, but it was suspended in August 2012 after the applicant (who had left Moldova in 2010) failed to appear and all officers again denied involvement. Reopened in 2018, it was suspended once more in March 2019 and remains unresolved.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 3 (substantive ill-treatment and inadequate investigation) and Article 5 (unreasoned detention, lack of information and access to a lawyer of choice and to the case file).

The case of Muradu v. the Republic of Moldova arose from events following the 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections, in which the ruling Communist Party narrowly prevailed amid allegations of fraud. Protests began on 6 April and intensified on 7 April, with several thousand participants initially peaceful before some became violent, leading to the occupation and looting of the Presidential Palace and Parliament building. Police subsequently conducted mass arrests, including of non-violent individuals, with reports of beatings by officers.

The applicant, Iurie Muradu, was arrested around 4:15 p.m. on 7 April 2009 near the protests and taken to Chișinău’s Centru police station. He was not informed of the reasons for arrest, denied the chance to contact his parents or choose his own lawyer, and the arrest report (drawn at 11 p.m.) vaguely cited suspected robbery without specifics. At the station, officers forced him to pose for photographs holding a riot shield with a black T-shirt over his head; they beat him, verbally abused him, and burned him with cigarettes. He spent nine hours in a bare cell (except for a chair) without food, water, toilet access, or rest. Around 1 a.m. on 8 April, he appeared before a prosecutor with a state-appointed lawyer (V.R.), whose request to contact family or hire private counsel was rejected. Officers compelled him to sign unread documents, striking him if he attempted to read them. Ill-treatment continued regularly, including in the investigator’s presence, who threatened torture unless the applicant cooperated; seeing severely injured detainees, he signed everything.

A 9 April police doctor noted only a forehead bruise. Upon release on 16 April, the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre documented three cigarette burns on his left hand, head-injury sequelae (including intracranial hypertension, PTSD, and ear damage), concluding the findings corroborated his ill-treatment account. PTSD persisted as of 2019.

Detention conditions were harsh: on 8–10 April at Centru station (not a designated facility), he shared a 12 m² cell with 24–25 others, lacking furniture, ventilation, a toilet (access often denied), food, or rest, aggravating his stomach condition. At police headquarters (10 April), a similar cell held 10 people with an unseparated tap-toilet and constant lighting. At Prison no. 13 (from 11 April), seven detainees shared six beds.

On 8 April, the appointed lawyer merely signed documents without consultation or defense. At a 9 April detention hearing (held at the station, lasting ~5 minutes), the applicant received no prosecutor’s request, case documents, or decision copy, and was uninformed of the hearing’s nature. The judge asked one question about stone-throwing while viewing the posed photos, then ordered 20 days’ pre-trial detention citing robbery/hooliganism charges, reasonable suspicion, collusion risk, and public-order needs due to societal shock. Minutes recorded a guilt acknowledgment. The applicant’s mother searched unsuccessfully for him. A privately hired lawyer (from 11 April) was repeatedly denied information or access despite telegrams requesting her presence at all acts. On 13 April she obtained the file, filed habeas corpus (alleging ill-treatment, inhuman conditions, defense-rights breaches including lack of documents/time to prepare, unreasoned decision, and no compensation), and complained formally of access denial.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal released him on 16 April on an undertaking not to leave the city, citing his clean record, character, residence, job, and citizenship, but awarded no compensation.

Criminal charges were later reduced; the applicant admitted picking up a found riot shield intending to keep it. Proceedings discontinued in May 2010 after a settlement returning the shield.

The applicant detailed his ill-treatment (including officer descriptions and locations) in statements on 13 and 21 April 2009 (initially noting no complaints against officers). His lawyer’s 14 April complaint seeking identification and prosecution of perpetrators went unanswered. Officers interviewed in 2009 all denied involvement. A 22 June 2009 decision declined to investigate, citing the single bruise (deemed incompatible with alleged multiple blows, possibly from a protest stone), denials, and the applicant’s own account. This was annulled in 2011, an investigation opened (applicant, now abroad, did not appear), and suspended in 2012. It was reopened in 2018 but suspended again in 2019, remaining pending. The case of Jurčić v. Croatia (Application no. 54711/15) involves Croatian national Kristina Jurčić (born 1975), who alleged discrimination on the basis of sex and her method of becoming pregnant. She had been employed since 1993 (with brief interruptions), most recently until 31 October 2009, after which she was unemployed.

On 17 November 2009, the applicant underwent in vitro fertilisation (IVF); her doctor recommended rest. Ten days later, on 27 November 2009, she signed a full-time employment contract with a company headquartered near Split (about 360 km from her home in Rijeka) to perform administrative tasks there for a monthly salary of approximately 600 euros. She applied to register with the Croatian Health Insurance Fund on 11 December 2009 and was initially registered as an insured employee.

On 14 December 2009 she felt nauseous. Her doctor confirmed the IVF had succeeded and prescribed sick leave for pregnancy-related complications. An ultrasound on 17 December confirmed a twin pregnancy. On 28 December she requested compensation for lost salary during this sick leave (a benefit available under compulsory health insurance for pregnancy-related illness).

On 5 January 2010 the Fund independently initiated a review of her insurance status. On 16 February 2010 it reopened the matter and rejected both her registration as an insured employee and her compensation request. Relying on an in-house expert report, it concluded that she had been medically unfit for employment on 27 November 2009 due to the recent IVF and that the contract was therefore fictitious, entered solely to obtain employment-related pecuniary advantages (including sick-leave compensation).

The applicant appealed, arguing she had felt well after the IVF, could not have known whether implantation would succeed, and thus had no reason to decline the job. She submitted a specialist gynaecology report confirming she had been healthy and awaiting results on the date of the contract, with neither she nor her doctor able to predict the outcome.

The Fund’s Central Office obtained further information from the employer (noting that some tasks could be done remotely from home, though the role also required travel) and another in-house expert report. The latter stressed that rest had been recommended immediately after IVF (including avoidance of travel and stress, which could harm implantation) and that she should have rested until a pregnancy test on 3 December. On 30 March 2010 the Central Office dismissed her appeal, holding that while pregnancy alone could not bar employment, the circumstances indicated a fictitious contract aimed only at obtaining benefits.

The applicant challenged this before the High Administrative Court, expressly alleging sex discrimination contrary to the Prevention of Discrimination Act and the Convention, and noting her plans to relocate near Split (where her husband was registered) plus the company’s compatibility with remote work. On 5 December 2012 the court dismissed her action, finding that post-IVF she had been unfit for distant work requiring travel during a sensitive phase of (possible) twin pregnancy. It therefore viewed the contract as entered solely for social-security benefits rather than genuine mutual obligations. It rejected the discrimination claim, stating that pregnancy itself is no bar to employment or related rights, but that her specific unfitness due to recent IVF justified the refusal.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint reiterating her discrimination arguments. Meanwhile she complained to the Gender Equality Ombudsperson, who in December 2010 issued a warning to the Fund that its decision violated the prohibition of less favourable treatment on grounds of pregnancy (constituting sex discrimination). The Ombudsperson criticised the stereotypical premise that every woman post-IVF (or facing high-risk pregnancy) is physically unfit for any work and would not be genuinely employed, and later annual reports highlighted the Fund’s long-standing practice of targeting pregnant women (especially those employed late in pregnancy or by family members) for “fictitious employment” findings.

On 22 April 2015 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as unfounded, upholding the lower findings and noting that the 360 km distance and limited remote-work possibilities justified the authorities’ scrutiny of whether the contract was genuine or merely a vehicle for insurance benefits. (The applicant’s insurance with the company was terminated with effect from 13 December 2009.)

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaint of unjustified direct sex discrimination in the refusal of an employment-related benefit to a woman who had undergone IVF shortly before taking up the post.

In Jurčić v. Croatia the applicant, unemployed since late 2009 after years of work, underwent IVF on 17 November 2009; rest was advised. Ten days later she signed a full-time administrative contract with a firm 360 km from her home, starting immediately at a modest salary, and registered as an employed person with the Health Insurance Fund.

Pregnancy (twins) was confirmed in mid-December; complications prompted sick leave and a claim for salary-replacement benefits. The Fund then reopened her file of its own motion. In-house medical opinions declared her unfit for work (and especially for travel) on the date of hiring because of the recent embryo transfer; the employment was therefore labelled fictitious and designed solely to obtain social-security payments. Her registration and benefit claim were rejected.

She appealed, producing an independent gynaecological report that she had been healthy, that implantation success could not have been known, and that rest recommendations were not an absolute bar to employment. The Central Office and High Administrative Court upheld the Fund, stressing the distance, the need to avoid mechanical stress after IVF, and the inference that the contract had no genuine purpose. The Constitutional Court likewise found the scrutiny justified. The Gender Equality Ombudsperson, however, formally warned the Fund that its premise—that any woman who had undergone IVF or was pregnant was presumptively unemployable—constituted sex discrimination.

The applicant complained that the refusal of an employment-related benefit solely because she had become pregnant via IVF amounted to direct sex discrimination contrary to Article 14 taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court agreed. It held that the financial burden pregnancy may impose on the State cannot justify differential treatment based on sex; that verification practices systematically targeting women who enter employment late in pregnancy or after fertility treatment are themselves suspect; that maternity-protection rules cannot be made to depend on whether a woman’s presence at work is “essential” or on a temporary inability to perform tasks; and that treating IVF itself as rendering a woman medically unfit for any employment discourages women from seeking work because of possible pregnancy and rests on gender stereotypes forbidden by both Croatian and international law. The domestic authorities’ conclusion therefore constituted unjustified direct discrimination.

The case of Jurčić v. Croatia (Application no. 54711/15) involves Croatian national Kristina Jurčić, born in 1975 and living in Rijeka. She alleged discrimination on the basis of her sex and the manner of her pregnancy (via IVF), contrary to Article 14 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, after authorities refused her employment-related health insurance benefits.

The applicant had worked intermittently since 1993, with her most recent job ending on 31 October 2009, after which she was unemployed. On 17 November 2009 she underwent IVF; her doctor recommended rest. Ten days later, on 27 November 2009, she signed an employment contract with a company headquartered near Split (about 360 km from Rijeka). The contract required full-time administrative duties in Split from that date, at a salary of roughly 600 euros per month. The employer later stated that some tasks could be done remotely from home, though the role involved travel within and outside Croatia.

On 11 December 2009 the applicant registered with the Croatian Health Insurance Fund as an insured employee. On 14 December she reported nausea; a doctor confirmed the IVF had succeeded and prescribed sick leave for pregnancy-related complications. An ultrasound on 17 December verified a twin pregnancy. On 28 December she applied for salary-loss compensation during the sick leave.

On 5 January 2010 the Fund, acting of its own motion, reviewed her insurance status. On 16 February 2010 it reopened the file and rejected both her registration as an employed insured person and her compensation claim. Relying on an in-house expert report, it found her medically unfit for work on 27 November because of the recent IVF and the recommended rest; the employment was therefore deemed fictitious and intended solely to obtain benefits such as sick-leave pay.

The applicant appealed, asserting she had felt well after the procedure and could not have known whether implantation would succeed. A gynaecological expert report she submitted confirmed she was healthy on the date of hiring and awaiting test results. The Fund’s Central Office obtained further information from the employer about travel requirements and a second in-house report stressing that rest (including avoidance of travel) is standard after IVF until a pregnancy test. On 30 March 2010 it dismissed the appeal, concluding that the particular circumstances showed the contract was fictitious and aimed only at securing statutory benefits.

The applicant then brought an administrative action before the High Administrative Court, expressly invoking the Prevention of Discrimination Act and the Convention and arguing that she had been treated less favourably as a woman who had undergone IVF. On 5 December 2012 the court dismissed the action. It held that, given the IVF ten days earlier, she had been unfit to perform distant, travel-intensive work in the “most sensitive phase” of a twin pregnancy; the contract therefore lacked genuine mutual obligations and could not found insurance status. The discrimination claim was rejected because pregnancy itself is not a bar to employment, but her specific post-IVF unfitness was.

A subsequent constitutional complaint was dismissed on 22 April 2015. The Constitutional Court found it legitimate for the authorities to verify whether the contract had been concluded merely to obtain insurance benefits, citing the 360 km distance and the employer’s single-employee status.

Separately, the Gender Equality Ombudsperson, responding to the applicant’s complaint, warned the Fund that its decision constituted sex discrimination based on pregnancy. The warning criticised the Fund’s stereotypical premise that any woman who had recently undergone IVF (or who was pregnant) was automatically unfit for work and that such employment must be fictitious. The Ombudsperson recommended that the Fund abandon this interpretation.

The Fund later terminated the applicant’s insurance with effect from 13 December 2009. These events form the core facts of the alleged violation: the denial of an employment-related benefit to a woman who had undergone IVF immediately before starting work, on the ground that the employment was fictitious because of her medical condition.

The case concerns two Azerbaijani students and NIDA civic movement members—Mammad Azizov (first applicant) and Shahin Novruzlu (second applicant, a minor)—who alleged unjustified pre-trial detention (Article 5 § 3 ECHR) and its use for ulterior political purposes (Article 18 + Article 5 § 3). NIDA, founded in 2011, pursued non-violent advocacy for liberty, justice and change.

From January to March 2013, protests in Baku highlighted non-combat deaths of Azerbaijani soldiers. Organized via social media with NIDA’s central role, the demonstrations were peaceful yet dispersed by police, with multiple arrests. A further protest was scheduled for 10 March 2013; both applicants participated actively.

On 7 March 2013 both were arrested by the Ministry of National Security and Prosecutor General’s Office. Searches of their flats allegedly yielded 174.54 g of narcotics plus 28 “democracy urgently needed” leaflets (Azizov) and 252.27 g of narcotics plus three Molotov cocktails (Novruzlu). Search records were never supplied to the Court. On 9 March Azizov was charged under Criminal Code Article 234.1 (illegal narcotics possession) and remanded for two months; Novruzlu was charged under Articles 228.3 (illegal weapons possession by an organised group) and 234.1 and remanded for three months. Both orders cited only the gravity of the charges and generic risks of absconding or obstructing the investigation. Neither applicant appealed the initial orders.

The following day the Prosecutor General and Ministry issued a joint press statement branding the applicants (and another NIDA member) as “radical destructive forces” who, being drug-addicted NIDA activists, had prepared Molotov cocktails to incite violence and unrest at the 10 March protest. NIDA publicly denounced the arrests as politically motivated intimidation intended to deter the demonstration. Four of NIDA’s seven board members were later arrested in the same proceedings.

Detention was repeatedly extended. Azizov’s March request for house arrest was rejected. On 2 May 2013 his detention was prolonged by two months on grounds of case complexity, absconding risk, need for further investigation, “way of life” and foreign links; a further house-arrest request was denied. Appeals were dismissed. Identical grounds were used for extensions on 2 July and 29 August. Novruzlu’s detention was extended on 30 May 2013 by three months for the same generic reasons. His appeal, stressing his minority, clean record and fixed residence, was rejected without addressing those points. Subsequent house-arrest requests and a further three-month extension in August were likewise dismissed, even though he remained a minor.

In September 2013 both faced additional charges of preparing a crime and mass disorder (plus organised-group weapons possession for Azizov). On 6 May 2014 they were convicted on all counts and sentenced to 7½ and 6 years respectively; the convictions were upheld on appeal. Presidential pardons led to Novruzlu’s release in October 2014 and Azizov’s in March 2016. Separate applications challenging the fairness of the trial remain pending.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: the domestic courts’ stereotyped, unsubstantiated justifications for successive extensions of pre-trial detention, and the surrounding circumstances indicating that the measure’s predominant purpose was to punish and silence opposition activists rather than to serve any legitimate aim of criminal procedure.

The European Court of Human Rights examined applications by two Azerbaijani student members of the non-violent civic group NIDA, which advocated liberty, justice and change. In early 2013, NIDA helped organise peaceful Baku demonstrations protesting non-combat deaths of soldiers; the applicants took an active part. A further demonstration was planned for 10 March 2013.

On 7 March both men were arrested by the Ministry of National Security and the Prosecutor General’s Office. Searches of their flats (records of which the Government never produced) allegedly yielded 174 g of narcotics plus 28 leaflets reading “democracy urgently needed” at the first applicant’s home, and 252 g of narcotics plus three Molotov cocktails at the second applicant’s home. The latter was still a minor. They were charged the same day with illegal possession of narcotics (and, for the second applicant, organised illegal possession of weapons). District-court detention orders of 9 March cited only the gravity of the charges and a risk of absconding or obstructing the investigation; neither applicant appealed those initial orders.

The next day the prosecuting authorities issued a joint public statement claiming the arrests targeted “radical destructive forces” planning violence at the 10 March demonstration and asserting that the applicants, as NIDA members addicted to drugs, had prepared the Molotov cocktails. NIDA immediately denounced the arrests as politically motivated intimidation.

Detention was repeatedly extended. For the first applicant, courts invoked complexity of the case, further investigative needs, a risk of flight, his “way of life” and unspecified foreign links; a request for house arrest was rejected without reasoning. For the second applicant the same formulaic grounds were used, even though he was a minor with no prior record and a fixed residence; statutory and international standards requiring detention of children only as a last resort and for the shortest possible time were ignored. Appeals were dismissed in equally stereotyped terms that never addressed the applicants’ specific arguments.

Additional charges of preparing mass disorder and organised weapons offences were later added. In May 2014 both were convicted and sentenced to lengthy prison terms; they were subsequently pardoned. Parallel applications concerning the fairness of the trial remain pending.

These facts formed the basis of the Court’s findings that the domestic courts had failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for continued pre-trial detention (Article 5 § 3) and that the detention had been imposed predominantly to punish and silence opposition activists for their role in anti-government protests (Article 18 taken together with Article 5 § 3).

The applicants, Azerbaijani students Mammad Azizov and Shahin Novruzlu (a minor), were members of NIDA, a non-violent civic group seeking political change. In early 2013, they actively joined peaceful Baku demonstrations—organized largely by NIDA via social media—protesting non-combat soldier deaths and criticizing the government. A further protest was set for 10 March 2013.

On 7 March, both were arrested by security and prosecutorial officers. Same-day home searches allegedly found 174.54 g of narcotics plus 28 “democracy urgently needed” leaflets at Azizov’s flat, and 252.27 g of narcotics plus three Molotov cocktails at Novruzlu’s. The Government never produced the search records despite the Court’s request. On 9 March Azizov was charged with illegal narcotics possession (Criminal Code Art. 234.1) and remanded for two months; Novruzlu was charged with the same offence plus organised-group weapons possession (Art. 228.3) and remanded for three months. The Nasimi District Court cited only the gravity of the charges and generic risks of absconding or obstructing justice; neither applicant appealed the initial orders.

The next day the Prosecutor-General and Ministry of National Security issued a joint press statement accusing “radical destructive forces” of threatening stability and claiming the applicants (together with another NIDA member) had planned to incite violence at the 10 March rally, were drug addicts who had joined NIDA online, and had themselves prepared the Molotov cocktails. NIDA immediately denounced the arrests as politically motivated intimidation ahead of the protest. Four further NIDA board members were later detained in the same investigation.

Requests to replace custody with house arrest were rejected without individualised reasoning. Detention was repeatedly extended (Azizov: 2 May, 2 July and 29 August 2013; Novruzlu: 30 May and 29 August 2013) on formulaic grounds—case complexity, need for further investigation, risk of flight, and, for Azizov, “lifestyle” and foreign links. Appeals were dismissed in equally stereotyped terms that ignored the applicants’ concrete arguments: permanent residence, student status, lack of prior convictions and, crucially, Novruzlu’s minority (domestic law permits pre-trial detention of minors only as an exceptional, short-term measure for the most serious offences). Additional charges of preparing mass disorder (and, for Azizov, organised weapons possession) were added in September 2013.

The applicants were convicted in May 2014 and sentenced to 7½ and 6 years respectively; they were later pardoned. These facts underpin the complaints that the courts never supplied relevant and sufficient reasons for prolonged pre-trial detention (Art. 5 § 3) and that the measure was in reality used to punish and silence opposition activists (Art. 18 taken with Art. 5 § 3).

The case of Dabić v. Croatia (Application no. 49001/14) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention regarding the State's failure to compensate the applicant for damage to and plundering of his sequestered house by a temporary occupant (a refugee), which the Court held amounted to a failure to discharge positive obligations.

The applicant, a Croatian national of Serbian origin born in 1949, owned a house in Sunja. He fled Croatia on 4 August 1995, the day before Operation Storm. On 27 September 1995 the Temporary Takeover and Administration of Certain Property Act ("Sequestration Act") entered into force, providing for State sequestration of property belonging to persons who had left after 17 October 1990 and empowering local sequestration commissions to accommodate others therein.

On 23 March 1996 the Sunja Municipality Sequestration Commission allocated the house to D.V. (a refugee from Bosnia and Herzegovina) and his family, who moved in. The Act on the Termination of the Sequestration Act of 5 August 1998 required owners to apply to housing commissions for recovery. The applicant returned in 1999 and applied on 17 August 2000.

On 25 April 2001 the Housing Commission set aside the 1996 allocation, ordered D.V. to vacate within 15 days of receiving State alternative accommodation, and inspected the house, finding it undamaged. D.V.'s house in Bosnia was returned in June 2002, extinguishing Croatia's alternative-accommodation obligation. D.V. vacated on 21 March 2003; the applicant repossessed on 24 March 2003. Ministry officials completed standardised handover records on both dates but left the "state of the property" section blank.

The applicant found the house almost empty, with most movables (plus vehicles and livestock) missing or destroyed and parts of the structure damaged. A neighbour's handwritten record (drawn up the same day in the presence of two witnesses, without authorities or the applicant) listed the damage and items. The Government maintained that the applicant had not notified the authorities of the damage or missing items.

On 17 July 2003 the applicant sued the State, Sunja Municipality and D.V. in the Sisak Municipal Court for HRK 224,400 (damage/theft) and HRK 48,000 (loss of use from 1 September 2000 to repossession). He relied on the neighbour's record. After D.V. died, the applicant withdrew the claim against him. At a 27 February 2006 hearing the applicant testified that police had refused to attend the handover, advising him only to take photographs.

On 20 February 2008 the Municipal Court dismissed the action. The Sisak County Court upheld dismissal of the damage claim on 23 October 2008 but quashed the loss-of-use part; the applicant was later awarded HRK 18,905.12 for the latter. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law on 31 August 2011, holding that neither the State nor local authorities were liable (vicariously or otherwise) for damage inflicted by third persons, including temporary occupants. The Sequestration Act imposed a "prudent administrator" duty on occupants and allowed revocation for non-compliance, but created no State tort liability. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's complaint (invoking, inter alia, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) on 9 January 2014.

The case of *Dabić v. Croatia* (Application no. 49001/14) concerns the State's positive obligations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The applicant, Nikola Dabić (born 1949), a Croatian national of Serbian origin, owned a house in Sunja, Croatia, where he lived until 4 August 1995. He left the country the day before Operation Storm, a Croatian military operation.

On 27 September 1995, the Temporary Takeover and Administration of Certain Property Act (Sequestration Act) entered into force. It provided that property of persons who had left Croatia after 17 October 1990 would be sequestered (taken into State care and control). Local sequestration commissions were entitled to temporarily accommodate other persons in such property. On 23 March 1996, the Sunja Municipality Sequestration Commission allocated the applicant's house to D.V. (a refugee from Bosnia and Herzegovina) and his family. D.V., his wife, six children and sister moved in shortly afterwards; the children later moved out but remained in Croatia, while D.V., his wife and sister continued occupying the house.

On 5 August 1998, the Act on the Termination of the Sequestration Act repealed the earlier law and required owners whose property had been sequestered and used to house others to apply to local housing commissions for recovery. The applicant returned to Croatia in 1999 and applied on 17 August 2000. On 25 April 2001, the Housing Commission set aside the 1996 allocation decision and ordered D.V. to vacate within 15 days of receiving alternative State accommodation. An on-site inspection that day found the house undamaged.

In June 2002, D.V.'s house in Bosnia and Herzegovina was returned to him, extinguishing Croatia's obligation to provide alternative accommodation. D.V. and his family vacated on 21 March 2003; the applicant repossessed the house on 24 March 2003. Handover records signed on both dates (using a standardised form) left the section on the property's state of repair blank. Upon repossession, the applicant found the house almost completely empty: nearly all movable property, vehicles and livestock were missing or destroyed, and parts of the house were damaged. A neighbour, in the presence of two witnesses, later prepared a handwritten record listing the damage and missing items (neither officials nor the applicant were present). The Government contended that the applicant had not notified the authorities of the damage or losses.

On 17 July 2003, the applicant (represented by a lawyer) brought a civil action in the Sisak Municipal Court against the State, Sunja Municipality and D.V., seeking 224,400 Croatian kunas (HRK) for stolen, destroyed or damaged property and HRK 48,000 for inability to use the house from 1 September 2000 until repossession. He argued joint and several liability and proposed evidence including the neighbour's record. After D.V. died, the proceedings were stayed; the applicant withdrew the claim against D.V. on 12 May 2005.

At a 27 February 2006 hearing, the applicant testified that police had declined to attend his move-in (claiming they lacked authorisation) and advised him to photograph the house, which he did. On 20 February 2008, the Municipal Court dismissed the action. The Sisak County Court (23 October 2008) upheld the dismissal of the property-damage claim but quashed the judgment on lost-use compensation; in resumed proceedings, the applicant was awarded HRK 18,905.12 after withdrawing part of that claim.

The Supreme Court (31 August 2011) dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law. It held that neither the State nor local authorities could be liable for damage inflicted on sequestered property by third persons (including occupants). Occupants had a statutory duty to use property with the care of a prudent administrator, and commissions could revoke allocations for non-compliance, but no legislation imposed vicarious State liability for occupants' actions. The mere fact of sequestration (intended to protect abandoned property) did not render the State liable.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint on 30 April 2012, relying inter alia on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Constitutional Court dismissed it on 9 January 2014 (served 29 January 2016). The applicant complained to the European Court that the State had failed to compensate him for damage and plundering by the refugee occupant whom it had placed in his sequestered house, thereby not discharging its positive obligations.

The case of Dabić v. Croatia (Application no. 49001/14) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicant, Nikola Dabić, a Croatian national of Serbian origin born in 1949, owned a house in Sunja where he lived until 4 August 1995. He left Croatia the day before Operation Storm.

On 27 September 1995, the Temporary Takeover and Administration of Certain Property Act (Sequestration Act) entered into force. It provided for State sequestration of property belonging to persons who had left Croatia after 17 October 1990, allowing local sequestration commissions to accommodate others in such properties. On 23 March 1996, the Sunja Municipality Sequestration Commission allocated the applicant’s house to D.V., a refugee from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and his family (wife, six children, and sister). They moved in shortly thereafter.

The Act on the Termination of the Sequestration Act entered into force on 5 August 1998, requiring former owners to apply to housing commissions for recovery of sequestered property. The applicant returned to Croatia in 1999 and applied on 17 August 2000. On 25 April 2001, the Housing Commission set aside the 1996 allocation decision and ordered D.V. to vacate within 15 days of receiving State-provided alternative accommodation. An on-site inspection that day found the house undamaged.

In June 2002, Bosnian authorities returned D.V.’s own house, extinguishing Croatia’s obligation to provide alternative accommodation. D.V. and his remaining family moved out on 21 March 2003; the applicant repossessed the house on 24 March 2003. Handover records signed on both dates (using standardised Ministry forms) left blank the sections on the property’s state of repair. The applicant found the house nearly empty, with most movable property, vehicles, and livestock missing or destroyed, and parts of the house damaged. The Government maintained that he did not notify the authorities of the damage or missing items. A neighbour later prepared a handwritten record (in the presence of two witnesses but without the applicant or officials) listing the damage and missing items.

On 17 July 2003, the applicant sued the State, Sunja Municipality, and D.V. in the Sisak Municipal Court for HRK 224,400 in compensation for stolen, destroyed, or damaged property and HRK 48,000 for inability to use the house from 1 September 2000 until repossession. He argued joint and several liability and proposed evidence including the neighbour’s record. After D.V. died, the applicant withdrew the claim against him. The first-instance court dismissed the action in 2008. The Sisak County Court upheld the dismissal regarding property damage but quashed and later awarded (after partial withdrawal) HRK 18,905.12 for inability to use the house. In 2011, the Supreme Court dismissed an appeal on points of law, holding that neither the State nor local authorities were liable under domestic law for damage inflicted by third parties (including temporary occupants) on sequestered property; the Sequestration Act imposed a duty of care on occupants but created no vicarious State liability. The Constitutional Court dismissed a complaint in 2014.

Relevant domestic law included Sequestration Act sections requiring occupants to act as prudent administrators and allowing revocation for non-compliance, as well as criminal provisions on theft and property damage. International standards such as the Pinheiro Principles emphasised measures to prevent destruction or looting of abandoned property and to inventory contents.

These facts underpin the alleged violation: the State’s sequestration and allocation of the house to a refugee occupant, followed by its return in a looted and damaged condition without adequate inventory, supervision, or subsequent compensation from the State.
001-208413:
The case of Schrade v. Georgia (Application no. 15016/07) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned alleged delays in two sets of Georgian civil proceedings brought by the applicant over unauthorized use of his photographs, together with the claimed lack of an effective domestic remedy for those delays. The applicant, a photographer born in 1934 and resident in Germany, invoked Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2005 Global Access Georgia Ltd published a tourist booklet that reproduced the applicant’s photograph of Gurjaani Church without permission. On 7 September 2005 he sued in the Tbilisi City Court for damages for infringement of his intellectual-property rights. The claim was rejected as inadmissible on 9 September 2005 for want of standing. An appeal filed on 22 November 2005 was refused on 15 December 2005 for non-payment of court fees. After the applicant reapplied on 12 January 2006, arguing that intellectual-property disputes were exempt from fees, the Tbilisi Court of Appeal on 22 March 2006 accepted that he had standing and remitted the case for examination on the merits. The applicant maintained that the matter then remained pending; the Government produced a further first-instance decision of 18 April 2006 dismissing the claim because it had been lodged by an unauthorized representative.

The second and more protracted set of proceedings concerned 57 photographs reproduced by Artanuji Publishing House in school history textbooks. On 24 January 2005 the applicant claimed GEL 171 680 (then approximately EUR 85 000) in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages from the company and its chief executive. After several hearings in spring 2005 the Tbilisi Regional Court ordered an expert examination by the National Forensic Bureau (NFB). Following a change in court jurisdiction the file was transferred to the Tbilisi City Court on 15 July 2005. The expert examination never took place: the NFB informed the court on 18 August 2005 that it had no art expert and lacked funds to outsource the work, yet the file was not returned until 14 March 2007. Throughout this period the applicant’s representatives repeatedly sought information from the NFB and the courts; most of their letters went unanswered. Proceedings resumed on 14 June 2007 and the claim was dismissed as unsubstantiated on 31 July 2007.

The applicant appealed on 14 September 2007. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal held numerous hearings between 2008 and 2010, many of which were adjourned—some at the applicant’s request for additional expert examinations in Germany, others at the respondent’s request with the applicant’s consent. On 26 July 2010 the appellate court found 152 instances of infringement of the 57 photographs and awarded the applicant GEL 3 090 (approximately EUR 1 500) plus modest costs. Both parties’ further appeals were declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 10 February 2011.

Georgian law at the relevant time treated unreasonable delay as a disciplinary offence for judges. Any interested person could request the initiation of disciplinary proceedings, but the decision whether to open them lay with designated judicial officials and was not subject to appeal. No other compensatory or acceleratory remedy for delay in civil cases was identified.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the length of both sets of proceedings had been excessive and that no effective domestic remedy had been available.

The case of Schrade v. Georgia (no. 15016/07) concerns a German photographer’s complaints of excessive delays in two Georgian civil actions he brought to enforce his intellectual-property rights, together with the alleged absence of any effective domestic remedy for those delays. The applicant invoked Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2005 Global Access Georgia Ltd reproduced, without authorisation, a photograph the applicant had published in Germany in 1986. On 7 September 2005 he sued in the Tbilisi City Court. The claim was rejected as inadmissible two days later for lack of standing. An appeal was initially refused for non-payment of court fees (15 December 2005). After the applicant demonstrated that fees were inapplicable to intellectual-property disputes, the Court of Appeal on 22 March 2006 remitted the case for examination on the merits. The applicant maintained that the action then remained dormant; the Government produced a later first-instance decision of 18 April 2006 dismissing the claim on the ground that it had been lodged by an unauthorised representative.

The second and far longer set of proceedings began when the applicant discovered, in late 2004, that Artanuji Publishing House had reproduced 57 of his copyrighted photographs in Georgian school textbooks. On 24 January 2005 he claimed GEL 171 680 in damages before the Tbilisi Regional Court. After several hearings the court ordered a forensic examination of the photographs (29 June 2005). Jurisdictional reforms then transferred the file to the Tbilisi City Court (15 July 2005). The National Forensic Bureau, lacking both an art expert and funds to outsource the work, returned the file on 18 August 2005; it was not received by the court until 14 March 2007. Throughout 2005–2006 the applicant’s lawyers repeatedly wrote to the Bureau, the City Court and the president of the Court of Appeal seeking information or a hearing date; most letters went unanswered. Proceedings resumed only on 14 June 2007 and the claim was dismissed on 31 July 2007.

An appeal lodged on 14 September 2007 generated more than twenty hearings between 2008 and 2010. Many were adjourned—some at the applicant’s request so that a technical examination could be organised in Germany (a two-month stay was granted in February 2009), others at the defendant’s request with the applicant’s consent. On 26 July 2010 the Court of Appeal found 152 infringements and awarded GEL 3 090 plus modest costs. Both parties’ cassation appeals were declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 10 February 2011.

The only theoretical remedy for judicial delay was a request for disciplinary proceedings under the 2000 Disciplinary Liability of Judges Act. Any interested person could lodge such a request, but initiation lay entirely within the discretion of court presidents or the High Council of Justice; a decision not to proceed was unappealable. No other compensatory or acceleratory mechanism existed.

The chronology therefore reveals a first action that never reached a merits decision and a second action that lasted more than six years, including a two-year period of complete inactivity caused by the forensic-examination impasse. These facts form the core of the alleged violations of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time and of the right to an effective remedy.

The case of Schrade v. Georgia (Application no. 15016/07), decided by the ECtHR on 11 March 2021, concerns alleged excessive delays in two sets of Georgian civil proceedings initiated by the applicant (born 1934, resident in Germany) over unauthorized use of his copyrighted photographs, together with the claimed absence of an effective domestic remedy. He invoked Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In the first set of proceedings, a 2005 tourist booklet published by Global Access Georgia Ltd reproduced the applicant’s photograph without permission. On 7 September 2005 he claimed damages in the Tbilisi City Court. The claim was rejected as inadmissible on 9 September 2005 for lack of standing. His 22 November 2005 appeal was refused on 15 December 2005 for unpaid court fees. After he reapplied on 12 January 2006 arguing that intellectual-property disputes were fee-exempt, the Tbilisi Court of Appeal on 22 March 2006 allowed the appeal, recognized standing and remitted the case for examination on the merits. The applicant maintained that the matter thereafter remained pending; the Government produced an 18 April 2006 first-instance decision rejecting the claim because it had been lodged by an unauthorized representative.

The second, lengthier set of proceedings arose after the applicant discovered in late 2004 that Artanuji Publishing House had reproduced 57 of his photographs in secondary-school history textbooks. On 24 January 2005 he sued the company and its CEO in the Tbilisi Regional Court for approximately EUR 85 000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. After several hearings between March and June 2005 an expert examination was ordered on 29 June 2005. Following a jurisdictional change the file was transferred to the Tbilisi City Court in July 2005. Repeated inquiries by the applicant’s representatives (December 2005–March 2006) about the stalled expert report elicited no substantive response. A letter dated 18 August 2005 from the National Forensic Bureau stated that it lacked an art expert and funds to outsource the examination and had returned the file; the court received it only on 14 March 2007. Proceedings resumed on 14 June 2007 and the claim was dismissed as unsubstantiated on 31 July 2007.

The applicant appealed on 14 September 2007. At least twenty hearings took place between 2008 and 2010, interrupted by multiple adjournments (a further technical expert examination ordered in June 2008; a two-month stay granted in February 2009 at the applicant’s request so that an examination could be arranged in Germany; and further postponements in 2010, some requested by the applicant and others by the respondent with the applicant’s consent). On 26 July 2010 the Court of Appeal found 152 infringements and awarded approximately EUR 1 500 plus costs. Both parties’ appeals on points of law were declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court on 10 February 2011.

The relevant domestic framework (Disciplinary Liability of Judges Act) treated unreasonable delay as a disciplinary offence, allowed any interested person to request proceedings, and left initiation to the discretion of senior judicial officials; a decision to terminate such proceedings was not open to appeal.

These facts centre on multi-year periods of inactivity (especially 2005–2007) and overall duration (2005–2011), which formed the basis of the complaints of a violation of the reasonable-time requirement and of the lack of an effective remedy.
