001-208764:
The applicant, Catherine Cauchi (born 1941), owns a property in Ħal Għaxaq, Malta. In February 1967 she granted a 17-year temporary emphyteusis at 25 Maltese liras (c. €58) per year. The interest was successively sub-granted; by expiry in February 1984 the occupants (couple A.) used the premises as their sole ordinary residence and had carried out substantial works (with later improvements) to render it habitable.

Couple A. then invoked Act XXIII of 1979 (amending the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, Cap. 158) to convert the arrangement into a statutory lease. Rent was thereafter subject to inflation-linked increases capped at double the original figure until 1999, after which it was to become MTL 100 (c. €116) annually; in practice the couple continued to pay MTL 50 because the applicant never demanded the increase. From 2010, following Act X of 2009, the rent rose to €185, then €197.31 (2013) and €200 (from 2017). The tenants owned no other property; Mr A. had a low wage, periods of unemployment and later a pension of €515 per month.

In 2017 the applicant brought constitutional proceedings claiming that Article 12 of the Ordinance had imposed an involuntary, indefinite lease at a rent that was neither fair nor adequate, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She sought compensation from 1984 and eviction, noting that she had originally granted the emphyteusis only to avoid requisition. Court-appointed and Government experts valued the refurbished property in 2017 at €165 000–€174 000; corresponding annual market rents were estimated at €4 785–€5 775, with historical figures ranging from €701 (1984) to €5 775 (2017).

On 31 October 2018 the Civil Court (First Hall), sitting in its constitutional competence, found a violation. It described the discrepancy between controlled and market rents as “enormous if not shocking”, noted the 34-year duration of the imposed tenancy, the absence of procedural safeguards and the State’s failure to legislate effectively. It awarded €20 000 (covering both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage) but declined to order eviction, holding that it was not the proper forum; instead it merely declared that the tenants could no longer rely on Article 12. The applicant was ordered to pay one-third of the costs. She did not appeal, regarding Constitutional Court review as ineffective because that court systematically reduced first-instance awards.

Act XXVII of 2018 (in force 1 August 2018) inserted Article 12B into the Ordinance. Even after a favourable constitutional judgment an owner could not seek eviction without first applying to the Rent Regulation Board for a rent revision (capped at 2 % of current market value, subject to a tenant means test, possible gradual increases and a six-year revision cycle). The applicant lodged such an application in 2019; the proceedings remained pending in May 2020.

These facts form the basis of the complaints: that the statutory rent-control regime imposed a disproportionate burden on the owner by denying her a fair return for an indefinitely prolonged occupation, and that the aggregate of available remedies (constitutional compensation, the 2018 RRB procedure and the inability to recover possession) was ineffective to redress the continuing interference.

The case of Cauchi v. Malta (ECHR Application no. 14013/19) concerns Ms Catherine Cauchi, a Maltese owner of a dwelling at 19 Dar il-Bebbux Street, Ħal Għaxaq. In February 1967 she granted a 17-year temporary emphyteusis at MTL 25 (approximately EUR 58) per year. After successive sub-emphyteuses the property was occupied, by the 1984 expiry, by couple A as their sole residence. They had carried out substantial works to make it habitable, a condition of the original grant, and continued improvements with the applicant’s consent.

Act XXIII of 1979, amending the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance (Chapter 158), converted the expired emphyteusis into a statutory lease. Rent was capped at inflation-linked increases not exceeding double the original amount until 1999, then MTL 100 (EUR 116) annually. The tenants in fact paid only MTL 50 until later statutory uplifts: EUR 185 from 2010, EUR 197.31 from 2013 and EUR 200 from 2017. Couple A owned no other property; Mr A was on a low wage, intermittently unemployed and later received a EUR 515 monthly pension.

In 2017 the applicant brought constitutional proceedings alleging that Article 12 of the Ordinance imposed an involuntary, indefinite lease at a rent so low as to violate Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She sought compensation from 1984 and eviction. Court-appointed and Government experts valued the refurbished property in 2017 at EUR 165 000–174 000. Annual market rents were estimated at EUR 701 (1984) rising to EUR 5 775 (2017), against the EUR 200 actually received.

On 31 October 2018 the Civil Court (First Hall), exercising constitutional jurisdiction, found a violation. It described the rent gap as “enormous if not shocking”, noted the 34-year duration of the imposed relationship, the absence of procedural safeguards and the State’s failure to balance social-housing aims without placing a disproportionate burden on owners. It awarded EUR 20 000 for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage but refused eviction, holding itself not the proper forum; it merely barred the tenants from relying on the Ordinance in any future eviction action. One-third of costs were borne by the applicant because not all claims succeeded.

The applicant did not appeal, regarding the Constitutional Court’s systematic reduction of first-instance awards as rendering the remedy ineffective. Act XXVII of 2018 (in force 1 August 2018) then inserted Article 12B, requiring any owner holding a favourable judgment first to apply to the Rent Regulation Board for a rent revision (capped at 2 % of 1 January market value) before seeking eviction. The Board must conduct a means test of the tenant; if the tenant qualifies, rent is set with regard to the tenant’s means and age and any special burden on the landlord, and may be increased only gradually. Even after a proportionality finding, eviction remained unlawful without exhausting this procedure.

In 2019 the applicant lodged an Article 12B application with the Board; it was still pending in May 2020. The complaints before the ECHR were that the persistently inadequate statutory rent, coupled with the inability to recover possession, continued to impose a disproportionate burden contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and that the aggregate of domestic remedies (constitutional award plus the 2018 RRB mechanism) was ineffective under Article 13.

The case of Cauchi v. Malta concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) due to a legally imposed, indefinitely prolonged lease at a rent far below market value, as well as a related claim under Article 13 that available domestic remedies were ineffective.

The applicant, born in 1941, owns a house at 19 Dar il-Bebbux Street, Ħal Għaxaq. In February 1967 she granted it under temporary emphyteusis for 17 years at 25 Maltese liras (approximately €58) per year. Sub-emphyteutae, a couple who used the property as their only residence, carried out substantial works to make it habitable. When the original title expired in February 1984 they invoked Act XXIII of 1979 (amending the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance) to convert the arrangement into a statutory lease. Rent remained tightly controlled: it doubled by 1999 but was not collected at the higher rate; later statutory uplifts produced only €185 in 2010, €197 in 2013 and €200 from 2017. Throughout, the tenants owned no other property; the husband earned a low wage, was at times unemployed, and later received a pension of €515 a month.

In 2017 the applicant brought constitutional proceedings. She argued that the Ordinance, as amended, had unilaterally imposed a perpetual lease without fair compensation, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Expert evidence valued the refurbished property at €165,000–€174,000 in 2017; corresponding annual market rents ranged from €701 in 1984 to €5,775 in 2017. The Civil Court (First Hall), sitting in its constitutional jurisdiction, found a violation on 31 October 2018. It held that the 34-year discrepancy between the statutory rent and market value was “enormous if not shocking,” that the interference had been imposed rather than freely agreed, and that the law lacked procedural safeguards. Compensation of €20,000 was awarded for both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, taking into account the legitimate social-housing aim, the applicant’s delay in suing, and the State’s legislative inertia. Eviction was refused; the court merely declared that the tenants could no longer rely on the Ordinance in future proceedings.

The applicant did not appeal, citing the Constitutional Court’s established practice of reducing first-instance awards. Shortly afterwards Act XXVII of 2018 inserted Article 12B into the Ordinance. Even after a favourable judgment, an owner could not seek eviction without first applying to the Rent Regulation Board. The Board could raise rent only to a maximum of 2 per cent of the property’s open-market value, after a means test of the tenant and having regard to the tenant’s age and means and any disproportionate burden on the landlord. Increases could be made gradual and would last six years. If the tenant failed the means test, five years’ notice to quit could be given, during which double the previous controlled rent would be payable. In 2019 the applicant applied to the Board; the proceedings remained pending in May 2020.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: a decades-long, state-imposed restriction that left the owner with a derisory return, combined with domestic redress that neither restored possession nor provided adequate compensation, and that was further constrained by the 2018 amendments.
001-209029:
The case of Olga Kudrina v. Russia (Application no. 34313/06) involved a Russian national associated with the National Bolshevik Party (NBP). It arose from two 2004–2005 protests against government policies, leading to her conviction for hooliganism (a gross breach of public order by an organised group using weapons) and intentional property damage under Articles 213(2) and 167(2) of the Criminal Code. The alleged violations concerned the fairness of her trial (Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d)) due to the refusal to summon defence witnesses, and interference with her freedom of expression (Article 10) via an allegedly disproportionate sentence.

On 2 August 2004, around 30 NBP members, dressed in emergency-service uniforms, protested at the Ministry of Health and Social Development against a draft law converting in-kind social benefits (for pensioners, veterans, disabled persons and others, covering about 27% of the population) into modest cash payments. They forced entry past a security guard, occupied offices on the second and third floors, told staff to leave for “training exercises,” nailed doors shut and barricaded them with furniture. They displayed NBP flags from windows, threw leaflets, chanted for the Health Minister’s resignation, set off firecrackers and threw a portrait of President Putin. After about an hour, police broke in and arrested them. The applicant denied any involvement. Seven other participants were later convicted of the same offences and sentenced to 2.5–5 years’ imprisonment (some commuted on appeal).

On 4 May 2005, the applicant and L. used rock-climbing equipment to exit a window at Moscow’s Rossiya Hotel, hanging an 11-metre “Go away Putin” poster. They waved signal flares and threw leaflets demanding dissolution of the State Duma for free elections, investigation of various crimes and tragedies, release of political prisoners, abolition of the benefits law, and an end to TV censorship. Police arrested them after 40 minutes without resistance.

The applicant was charged in May 2005 for both incidents. At trial in the Tverskoy District Court, evidence on the Ministry protest included statements from a frightened security guard, Ministry employees (some of whom reported no aggression, fear or injuries, and none identified the applicant) and police. A police report recorded her arrest that day based on passports; she claimed someone else used hers. Participant G.-M.’s pre-trial statement implicated her, but he retracted it in court, alleging FSB duress, falsification and that she had not participated. The court also admitted the prior convictions of the other seven.

On 14 April 2006, defence counsel requested summons of those seven (G., K., B., Ye., T. and Kl.) as eyewitnesses/participants. The court refused, holding that the defence must secure their attendance itself and that the prosecution need not present them. They did not appear on 3 May, and no further request was made.

Hotel employees testified to seeing the pair from below (fearing a fall) and concern over flares near flammable items; damage was fully compensated, with no injuries reported.

On 10 May 2006 the court convicted the applicant, relying on G.-M.’s original statement to find her participation in the Ministry action. It held that nail guns, firecrackers and flares constituted weapons; the acts (anti-government slogans, occupying offices, hanging the poster, using flares) showed organised contempt for society, disrupted operations (including near Victory Day commemorations) and risked harm. Mitigating factors included her being a first-time offender with positive references who had compensated hotel damage. She received 3 years and 6 months’ imprisonment.

The applicant fled to Ukraine (granted refugee status in 2008) and did not attend sentencing. Her appeal, arguing unproven participation in the Ministry protest, the need to examine the refused witnesses, that the acts were peaceful political expression without violence or real weapons, insignificant damage (partly caused by police) and an excessive sentence, was dismissed by the Moscow City Court on 19 June 2006 as lawful and justified, with no serious procedural flaws.

These facts underpinned the claims that the witness refusal (despite their potential to corroborate or refute her presence) undermined trial fairness, and that prosecuting/convicting her for political protest with a severe prison term disproportionately interfered with expression.

The European Court of Human Rights case of Olga Kudrina v. Russia concerned a Russian national born in 1985 who alleged breaches of her fair trial rights and freedom of expression after conviction for anti-government protests. On 2 August 2004, around 30 National Bolshevik Party members protested at the Ministry of Health and Social Development against a draft law converting in-kind social benefits for pensioners, veterans, the disabled and others (covering about 27% of the population) into modest monthly cash payments. Dressed in emergency-service uniforms, they forced entry past a security guard, occupied offices on the second and third floors, ordered staff to leave, nailed doors shut and blocked them with furniture. They waved party flags, threw leaflets, chanted for the health minister’s resignation, set off firecrackers and threw a presidential portrait from a window. They remained for about an hour until police arrested them. The applicant denied any participation. Seven co-participants were later convicted of group hooliganism involving weapons and public-property damage, receiving sentences later reduced on appeal to between 2.5 and 3 years.

On 4 May 2005 the applicant and another person used climbing gear to exit a Rossiya Hotel window in Moscow, hung an 11-metre “Go away Putin” banner, waved signal flares and scattered leaflets demanding dissolution of parliament, investigation of political crimes and tragedies, prisoner amnesties, repeal of the benefits law and an end to television censorship. Police arrested them after 40 minutes without resistance.

The applicant was charged under Criminal Code Articles 213 § 2 (group hooliganism with weapons) and 167 § 2 (significant public-property damage committed dangerously) for both events. At trial the Tverskoy District Court heard Ministry employees and police; none identified the applicant or reported injuries, though one mentioned fright from shooting sounds and the guard described initial fear of an armed siege. Damage had been fully compensated. A co-participant’s pre-trial statement placing the applicant at the Ministry was read; at trial he retracted it, alleging FSB duress and fabrication. A police report recorded the applicant’s arrest that day, identities having been checked from passports. The defence unsuccessfully sought to exclude the retracted statement and claimed another person had used her passport.

On 14 April 2006 counsel requested summons of six convicted co-participants as eyewitnesses. The court refused, stating that the defence must itself secure attendance and that the prosecution need not call them. They did not appear. Hotel employees described seeing the protesters and fearing a fall or fire risk from flares; none reported injury and damage was compensated.

On 10 May 2006 the court convicted both defendants, relying on the retracted statement for the Ministry incident. It held they had destabilised ministry and hotel operations, shown contempt for authority by anti-government slogans and a presidential insult, used nail-guns, firecrackers and flares as weapons, and acted as a structured organised group, causing significant damage on the eve of Victory Day commemorations. Mitigating factors (first offences, compensation, good character) produced a sentence of three years and six months’ imprisonment. The applicant fled to Ukraine and later obtained refugee status. An appeal arguing lack of proof of her Ministry presence, the importance of the uncalled witnesses, the peaceful nature of the hotel action, absence of real weapons or violence, and sentence severity was dismissed by the Moscow City Court on 19 June 2006.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints that the refusal to hear defence witnesses rendered the trial unfair and that the prosecution and heavy sentence for expressive protest were disproportionate.

The case of Olga Kudrina v. Russia concerns two anti-government protests by National Bolshevik Party members in 2004–2005, leading to the applicant’s conviction for hooliganism (gross breach of public order by an organised group using “weapons”) and intentional property damage under Articles 213 § 2 and 167 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

On 2 August 2004, about 30 activists in emergency uniforms forced entry into the Ministry of Health and Social Development, occupied offices, nailed doors shut with nail guns, blocked them with furniture, waved flags, threw leaflets, chanted for the minister’s resignation, set off firecrackers and threw out a portrait of the President. They remained for about an hour until arrested. The applicant denied participating. Seven others were convicted in December 2004 and given prison sentences later reduced on appeal.

On 4 May 2005 the applicant and another person (L.) used climbing equipment to hang an 11-metre “Go away Putin” poster on the Rossiya Hotel, waved signal flares and threw leaflets listing political demands (including free elections, investigations of crimes, release of political prisoners, repeal of a social-benefits law and an end to censorship). They were arrested after 40 minutes without resistance.

The applicant was charged in connection with both events. At trial the court heard Ministry employees and police who described the occupation but did not identify the applicant or report injuries; some said they had not been frightened. A co-participant’s pre-trial statement placing her at the Ministry was read out; he recanted in court, alleging FSB duress and stating she had not taken part. A police report recorded her arrest that day. Hotel staff described fear that the climbers or flares might cause harm; property damage had been fully compensated.

Defence counsel requested that six previously convicted co-participants—identified by the prosecution as eyewitnesses—be summoned. The court refused, holding that the defence must itself secure attendance and that the prosecution had already presented sufficient evidence. The witnesses did not appear. The court relied on the recanted pre-trial statement to find the applicant had participated in the Ministry action, treated nail guns, firecrackers and flares as “weapons,” and characterised both protests as organised criminal acts that destabilised public institutions and showed contempt for society and the State. Mitigating factors (first offence, positive character, compensation) were noted, but she was sentenced to three years and six months’ imprisonment. She fled to Ukraine, where she later obtained refugee status.

On appeal counsel argued that participation in the Ministry protest had not been proved, that the refusal to hear the six eyewitnesses violated the right to examine witnesses, that the actions were peaceful political protest without violence or significant damage, and that the penalty was excessive. The Moscow City Court upheld the conviction as lawful and the sentence as justified.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints that the refusal to summon relevant defence witnesses undermined the fairness of the trial and that the conviction and exceptionally severe sentence constituted a disproportionate interference with freedom of expression.
001-208763:
The case of *Matalas v. Greece* (Application no. 1864/18) concerns the criminal conviction of Theodoros Matalas, appointed CEO of AGROGI A.E. in November 2007, for slanderous defamation of the company's former legal advisor, Ms L.P. This arose from statements in an official letter dated 4 February 2008, which Matalas alleged violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

Upon taking office, Matalas requested full information from staff, including L.P., on outstanding matters. She provided an oral briefing and a brief six-line report on 23 November 2007, which he considered incomplete and inaccurate, as it generally stated there were no pending cases. Matalas terminated her contract and sent several official documents in December 2007 and January 2008 demanding the return of files and payment of compensation. L.P. handed over files on 24 January 2008 in his absence, with the receiving employee signing without comment.

Matalas then sent the 4 February letter, served on 6 February, condemning her "unprofessional and contrary to ethics" conduct. He accused her of persistently failing to provide complete information on pending cases despite repeated requests, attributing this to "malicious intention" to harm the company in revenge for her dismissal, and of supplying incomplete and erroneous details.

L.P. filed a criminal complaint on 22 April 2008. The Athens first-instance court convicted Matalas in November 2014 of slanderous defamation (Articles 362-363 of the Criminal Code), imposing a 10-month suspended prison sentence. He denied any intent to harm her reputation. On appeal in October 2015, the court upheld the conviction (8 months suspended), finding the statements unnecessary for protecting company interests, false (as L.P. had fully informed him), and known by him to be false. It rejected evidence such as the new advisor's testimony and the unmarked handover record. The court held the allegations were "facts" disseminated to third parties, including the drafting lawyer, the process server, and building residents (the letter having been posted on L.P.'s door in her absence).

On remittal (4 October 2017) the appellate court imposed a five-month suspended sentence.

The interference stemmed from statements contained in private official correspondence arising from an internal commercial dispute that never reached the public. Domestic courts treated the remarks as knowingly false slanderous defamation, rejected any legitimate-interest defence, and regarded limited third-party awareness (arising from formal service) as sufficient dissemination. The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered judgment on 30 March 2021 in D.S. v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 70988/12). The applicant, a British national born in 1964 and living in Croydon, alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life) arising from the disclosure of her old criminal record data under the pre-2013 regime in England and Wales.

In May 1990 the applicant received a six-month conditional discharge for a property-damage offence. A police officer advised her that the matter would be deleted from her record after six months. In January 2010 her then-employer required her to obtain an Enhanced Criminal Record Certificate (ECRC). Under the Police Act 1997 (s. 113B) as it then stood, every previous conviction had to be disclosed automatically; there was no filtering mechanism. The July 2010 ECRC therefore recorded the 1990 discharge. The applicant was later made redundant (April 2012) but did not claim the disclosure caused that loss. In July 2012 she asked the Metropolitan Police to destroy her fingerprints, DNA sample and the corresponding Police National Computer (PNC) entry; the request was refused. After she obtained new employment the same information reappeared on an August 2012 ECRC. She made no allegation that either disclosure affected her job prospects.

A subsequent subject-access request under the Data Protection Act 1998 confirmed that the PNC still held both the formal record of the discharge and a description of the underlying facts.

The old statutory scheme required an ECRC to contain every conviction plus any “soft intelligence” the police considered relevant, and a copy had to be sent to the prospective employer. The Court had already held in M.M. v. the United Kingdom (2012) that this blanket, exception-free system lacked the legal safeguards necessary to ensure that any interference with private life was both necessary and proportionate; it was therefore not “in accordance with the law.” The United Kingdom Supreme Court reached the same conclusion in R (T) v. Secretary of State for the Home Department (2014).

Amendments that took effect on 29 May 2013 introduced filtering rules: an adult conviction is no longer disclosed if eleven years have elapsed, it is the person’s only offence, it did not attract a custodial sentence and it is not a specified (generally violent or sexual) offence. The applicant’s 1990 discharge therefore ceased to be disclosable and did not appear on a June 2015 ECRC. A later Supreme Court decision (In re Gallagher, 2019) accepted that the revised, highly prescriptive scheme was in principle “in accordance with the law” and proportionate, subject to two discrete incompatibilities (multiple convictions and youth cautions) that were subsequently removed by further amendment. An independent monitor for reviewing soft intelligence had also been created in 2012.

The Court confined its examination to the disclosures that actually occurred under the unreformed regime. Those disclosures—of a single, minor, twenty-year-old matter that the applicant had been told would be spent—were effected by a system that afforded no opportunity for an individualised assessment of relevance or proportionality. Consequently the interference with the applicant’s private life was not “in accordance with the law” and constituted a violation of Article 8.

The case of Liebscher v. Austria (Application no. 5434/17) concerns complaints under Article 8 of the Convention (respect for private life and personal data), Article 13 (effective remedy) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of property). The applicant, an Austrian national born in 1957 and living in Vienna, challenged a legal requirement that forced disclosure of sensitive personal information as a condition for transferring real-estate title after divorce.

On 21 May 2013 the applicant and his wife obtained a consensual divorce before the Döbling District Court. They signed a comprehensive court settlement under section 55a(2) of the Marriage Act covering division of assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, alimony, and an overview of the applicant’s assets and income.

On 13 December 2015 the applicant applied to the same court, now sitting as land-register court, to record the transfer of his half-share of their jointly owned property to his former wife. He submitted only a certified excerpt of the settlement, limited to the “real-estate” chapter and bearing a judicial note that it contained “all agreements pertaining to the real estate property.” Austrian land-register law (sections 7, 87 and 94 of the 1955 Land Register Act) makes the register and its document archive publicly accessible and requires that applications be accompanied by the “original” complete document so that the court can verify the absence of any conditions or facts that might affect title.

On 25 February 2016 the land-register court rejected the application, holding that a partial excerpt is not an “original” and that only the full settlement would enable the mandatory comprehensive examination. The applicant appealed, arguing that the excerpt already certified by the same judge satisfied the statutory formalities and that forcing disclosure of the entire settlement would place highly sensitive data—children’s names and addresses, custody arrangements and alimony figures—into a publicly searchable archive, in breach of Article 8, the Austrian Data Protection Act and Article 52 of the EU Charter. He maintained that no legitimate public interest outweighed his privacy.

The Vienna Regional Civil Court dismissed the appeal on 25 April 2016, confirming that an excerpt cannot be an original and citing Supreme Court precedent. It found no Article 8 violation because a statutory basis existed. The applicant then lodged an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court, repeating the data-protection arguments and seeking referrals to the CJEU and the Constitutional Court. On 11 July 2016 the Supreme Court refused the appeal. It reiterated that the family court’s note was not binding on the land-register court, that only a complete original permitted the required examination, and that the examination served the protection of registered property rights; the subsequent inclusion of the document in the public archive was not before the court.

These successive refusals left the applicant unable to complete the property transfer without placing the entire divorce settlement, containing intimate family and financial details, into a publicly accessible register. The domestic courts treated the formal requirement as absolute and declined to weigh it against the applicant’s concrete privacy interests or to consider less intrusive alternatives.

The case concerns the Bulgarian authorities’ refusal to register the applicant church, an Old Calendarist Eastern Orthodox community, and related complaints by the church and five individual members (its hierarch, secretary, deacon, nun and council member) under Articles 9, 11, 13 and 14 of the Convention.

A minority of clergy and faithful, objecting on calendrical, doctrinal and autonomy grounds, disaffiliated and formed the Old Calendarist community. After establishing links with Greek Old Calendarists, the second applicant was ordained (1988) and consecrated bishop (1993); the Greek and Romanian Old Calendarist Churches recognised the group as autocephalous. A 1993 registration request to the Religious Denominations Directorate received no formal reply.

By 2013 the community had grown to 24 priests and some 2 000 adherents. Lacking legal personality it could not itself own property, so its cathedral, 15 churches, four chapels and monastery were registered in the names of individual clerics or believers. Two buildings were lost when their owners left; the church could obtain no tax exemptions, receive donations, formally employ clergy or conduct related commercial activity.

In November 2011 the church applied to the Sofia City Court for registration, enclosing a certificate that its proposed name did not coincide with that of any existing legal entity. The court invited comments from the Directorate, which in turn sought and enclosed the opinion of the BOC Holy Synod. The Synod asserted that only the BOC could represent Eastern Orthodoxy or use the word “Orthodox,” that the applicant church was identical to it, and that registration should be refused (or permitted only under the name “Bulgarian Old Calendar Church”).

Relying on paragraph 3 of the transitional provisions of the 2002 Religious Denominations Act (persons who had seceded from a registered institution in breach of its internal rules may not use its name or assets) read with section 15(2) (no two denominations may share the same name), the court held that the applicant church had seceded from the BOC in 1993, that the names were identical, and that registration was therefore barred. It disregarded the Synod’s submissions as procedurally irrelevant.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the refusal on 23 April 2012, adding that Eastern Orthodoxy’s traditional status and the official church’s role as its embodiment, together with the Act’s rule that only one denomination may bear a given name, precluded registration. The Supreme Court of Cassation declined on 29 March 2013 to admit a further appeal, treating the legal-interpretation issues as going to the merits and the name-identity question as factual.

The 2002 Act (enacted to end a schism within the official church) grants that church legal personality automatically while requiring all others to register. It characterises each denomination by name and beliefs, forbids more than one denomination of the same name, and bars pre-Act seceders from using the original name or assets. Domestic courts have treated even slight verbal or word-order differences as insufficient to distinguish names, consistently refusing “Orthodox”-containing titles as identical to the official church’s. (By contrast, multiple Protestant churches with similar names had been registered.) The Constitution proclaims religious freedom and the traditional status of Eastern Orthodoxy; the official church’s privileged position and the name ban were criticised by the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly as potentially blocking breakaway groups.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged interferences with religious manifestation, possible discrimination, and absence of an effective remedy against the registration refusal.

The case of Alimpiev v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 48802/08) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 27 April 2021. It concerns complaints by the applicant, Mr Alexandru Alimpiev (a Russian national born in 1950 and residing in Tiraspol), of inhuman detention conditions, inadequate observance of his rights during pre-trial detention, and censorship of his prison correspondence. The applicant, former president of the Tiraspol People’s Court in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”), alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 §§ 3 and 4, 6 § 1, 8 and 13 of the Convention. Notice of these complaints was given to the respondent Governments on 2 November 2017 (the remainder of the application having been declared inadmissible).

On 31 August 2006 the “MRT” prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into corruption allegations against the applicant. He was arrested and formally charged on 17 May 2007. He remained in pre-trial detention until his conviction by the “MRT” Supreme Court on 25 December 2008 (seven years’ imprisonment). That judgment was upheld on 18 March 2009; in extraordinary proceedings on 24 July 2009 the sentence was reduced to five years and he was released under an amnesty.

Throughout the pre-trial period the prosecutor periodically sought (and obtained) extensions of detention. The applicant and his lawyer were unable to obtain copies of any such decisions. Requests for copies or to photocopy parts of the criminal file were refused on the ground that “MRT” law conferred no such right on the defence. The lawyer (who had not been involved at the pre-trial stage) argued that he needed the documents to prepare an effective defence and invoked Article 34 of the Convention. Applications to replace detention with a less restrictive measure cited Articles 3, 5, 6, 8 and 13, noting that the “MRT” courts had merely recited the statutory grounds (risk of absconding, reoffending or interfering with the investigation) without referring to any specific evidence, and describing the applicant’s deteriorating health and detention conditions. On 11 November 2008 the lawyer issued a press release about the case.

The applicant described conditions in the Tiraspol temporary detention facility (IVS) and prison UIN-3 as follows: no separate toilet or shower, no hygiene products or bed linen, parasite infestation, poor-quality tap water, a small window admitting damp and cold air, and only very brief daily walks. A 30 kg monthly limit on parcels (including bottled water), combined with inedible prison food, allegedly caused hunger. During trial he was held in a metal cage; on 6 August 2008 his lawyer unsuccessfully requested that he be allowed to sit beside counsel and that courtroom cages be declared unlawful.

A medical certificate recorded that an emergency team attended the applicant on 23 June 2008, diagnosing respiratory problems and moderate persistent asthma and prescribing medication. As a non-smoker he was subjected to heavy passive smoking by cellmates.

The applicant alleged systematic censorship of correspondence. He produced an envelope from his lawyer bearing an official stamp “Verified. Censor (signature), 8/09/2008”.

The relevant domestic and international legal framework is summarised in the Grand Chamber judgment in Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia.

The case of Batrakov v. Russia (Application no. 9519/10) concerns allegations of police ill-treatment, an ineffective investigation, and the use of a coerced confession in criminal proceedings. The applicant, a Russian national born in 1990, was identified on 28 August 2008 as a suspect in a physical assault following operational-search activities by the Zheleznodorozhniy district police in Ulyanovsk. He was arrested around 2:30 p.m. near his home, allegedly pushed to the ground, handcuffed, and punched in the head before being taken to the police station.

According to the applicant, two officers at the station covered his head with a sweatshirt, pushed him to the floor, and beat him for about two hours on the lumbar region and legs, including with a heavy object resembling a thick rope. He then wrote a “surrender and confession” statement as dictated by the officers. He later gave self-incriminating statements to an investigator while one of the officers remained present and threatened further violence if he complained. When his mother was allowed to see him, he denied ill-treatment and did not fully undress; she later observed bruises on his legs and handcuff marks on his wrists after they left around 11 p.m.

Police records indicate the confession was given at 6 p.m. An investigator questioned him as a witness from 8:30 to 9:30 p.m. in the presence of a duty lawyer, N.Ya. On 29 August 2008, a traumatology examination diagnosed contusions of both hips, the lower left leg, and the lumbar region, which the applicant attributed to police assault. A forensic medical examination that afternoon documented two bruises on the right hip, one on the left hip, two abrasions on the lower left leg, another bruise on the left hip, hyperaemia of both wrists, and pain in the parietal region. These injuries were caused by a hard, blunt object, consistent with the applicant’s account of events on 28 August. A follow-up examination in April 2009 confirmed at least six blows, possibly from kicks or a rope-like object.

On 29 September 2008, the regional FSB found that two identified officers had beaten the applicant to force a confession, constituting abuse of power under Article 286 of the Criminal Code. The applicant and his mother complained of ill-treatment. Investigators conducted a pre-investigation inquiry and issued nine refusals to open criminal proceedings (between 22 September 2008 and 15 May 2009), repeatedly overruled by higher authorities as unsubstantiated or unlawful. The regional prosecutor’s office criticised the inquiry as stalled and incomplete, noting failure to follow up on FSB findings. Police officers denied any violence. The investigator and lawyer N.Ya. claimed they saw no injuries and received no complaints. N.Ya. was later reprimanded by the regional bar association for providing poor legal assistance (failing to consult the applicant beforehand) and for giving statements that supported the refusals. The final refusal concluded that the injuries were unrelated to police actions.

On 9 July 2009, the Zheleznodorozhniy District Court convicted the applicant of assault and sentenced him to five and a half years’ imprisonment, relying on his confession despite his claims that it was dictated under duress. The court dismissed ill-treatment allegations based on officers’ denials. It also rejected claims that two witnesses’ incriminating statements (one supported by a medical record of a genital burn) were extracted by electric shocks. One witness testified to seeing the applicant beaten. The Ulyanovsk Regional Court upheld the conviction on 19 August 2009.

At the police station, two officers allegedly covered his head with a sweatshirt, forced him to the floor, and beat him for about two hours on the lumbar region and legs, including with a thick rope. Under this duress, he wrote a dictated “surrender and confession” statement. He then gave self-incriminating statements to an investigator while a threatening officer remained present, initially denying ill-treatment to his visiting mother (who saw no upper-body injuries as he kept his pants on). In May 2009, the Ulyanovsk Regional Bar Association reprimanded N.Ya. for inadequate assistance (no pre-interrogation meeting or advice) and unethical statements used to reject Batrakov’s claims and undermine his later retraction. The final 15 May 2009 refusal found allegations unconfirmed and injuries unrelated to police actions.

It relied on his confession despite his trial testimony of coercion and his lawyer’s inadmissibility argument. Police denials led the court to reject ill-treatment claims. Two witnesses alleged their incriminating statements were obtained via police electric shocks (one with a 23 December 2008 medical record of a genital burn); one also claimed to have seen Batrakov’s beating. The court dismissed these, citing police testimony. Batrakov’s appeal, reiterating inadmissibility of the confession and witness statements, was largely upheld by the Ulyanovsk Regional Court on 19 August 2009, endorsing the trial findings.

The case of Abdullayev and Others v. Azerbaijan involves 13 applications by Azerbaijani nationals who founded NGOs as associations. They alleged that the Ministry of Justice's refusals to register those associations as legal entities violated Article 11 of the Convention (freedom of association).

The applicants established their associations (on various dates) and adopted charters. They applied to the Ministry of Justice for state registration, submitting the required documents. The Ministry repeatedly issued letters citing alleged deficiencies in the documents and returned them unexecuted (or simply returned), invoking Article 11.3.1 of the Law on State Registration. After the applicants corrected the documents and resubmitted, the Ministry identified further deficiencies and returned the papers again. In several cases this cycle repeated multiple times.

The applicants then sued the Ministry in the Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1. They argued that the cited deficiencies in already-rectified documents were unfounded or unlawful, and that the Ministry had breached Article 8 of the Law on State Registration by failing to identify all alleged defects at once (so they could be corrected together). They asked the courts to order registration, claiming a violation of their freedom of association.

The first-instance court dismissed the claims, finding the Ministry's reasons lawful and its actions a proper exercise of power under Article 11.3.1. Appellate and cassation courts upheld those judgments. In one application the Supreme Court characterised the Ministry's steps as mere returns for rectification rather than outright refusals.

These repeated returns, the alleged failure to list all defects simultaneously, and the domestic courts' endorsement of the Ministry's conduct form the core facts underlying the Article 11 complaints. (The remainder of the applications, save one, were declared inadmissible at the communication stage.)

The ECHR Fifth Section Committee judgment of 20 May 2021 in Abdullayev and Others v. Azerbaijan joined 13 applications by Azerbaijani NGO founders alleging Article 11 violations from Ministry of Justice refusals to register their associations as legal entities.

Applicants established associations, adopted charters, and submitted registration requests with documents to the Ministry. It repeatedly returned documents under Article 11.3.1 of the Law on State Registration, citing alleged deficiencies (detailed in an appended table) and stating they were “returned” or “returned unexecuted.” Applicants rectified issues and resubmitted, but the Ministry identified further deficiencies, repeating the cycle multiple times in several cases.

After two or more such letters, applicants sued in Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1, arguing the post-rectification deficiency findings were unlawful and that the Ministry breached Article 8 of the Law by failing to identify all issues at once for simultaneous correction. They claimed this violated freedom of association and sought registration orders.

The first-instance court dismissed the claims, finding the Ministry’s actions and reasons lawful under its Article 11.3.1 power to refuse registration. Appellate and cassation courts upheld these rulings. In application no. 22809/15, the Supreme Court treated the actions as returns for rectification, not refusals.

Relevant law includes Azerbaijan’s 1995 Constitution, 2000 Law on NGOs, and 2003 Law on State Registration (as described in Jafarov and Others v. Azerbaijan). These facts of prolonged, piecemeal registration delays form the core of the alleged Article 11 breaches.

The case of Trafik Oil-1 EOOD v. Bulgaria (Application no. 67437/17), decided by the ECtHR on 18 May 2021, concerns complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant company alleged that its diesel fuel was confiscated in administrative-penal proceedings against a third-party supplier in which it had no opportunity to participate.

In September 2014, customs authorities inspected a petrol station operated by the applicant and found 26,504 litres of diesel lacking required excise-duty documents. The fuel was seized in October 2014. On 24 April 2015 the authorities issued penal order no. 896 against the applicant under section 126 of the Excise Duties and Tax Warehouses Act (EDTWA). The order imposed a financial sanction, confiscated the fuel pursuant to section 124(1) EDTWA (which permits confiscation of goods that are the subject of certain offences “regardless of their ownership”), and suspended the company’s operations for one month.

The applicant sought judicial review. After the Sandanski District Court upheld the order, the Blagoevgrad Administrative Court quashed it on 7 April 2016. The court held that the applicant, as final recipient, could possess only the documents supplied by its vendor, Petrol Company EOOD, which had issued a valid invoice.

In parallel, on 10 July 2015 the same authorities issued penal order no. 613 against Petrol Company EOOD for selling the identical fuel without proof that excise duty had been paid. That order likewise confiscated 30,023 litres of diesel. Because the supplier did not appeal, the order became final on 11 September 2015.

Once its own penal order had been quashed, the applicant requested return of the fuel or its monetary equivalent. Customs refused on 4 May 2016, relying exclusively on the now-final order no. 613. Judicial review followed. The Blagoevgrad Administrative Court annulled the refusal, reasoning that the quashing of order no. 896 removed any legal basis for retention. The Supreme Administrative Court reversed that decision on 14 June 2017. It held that a valid penal order establishing a breach of section 126 EDTWA rendered confiscation lawful irrespective of ownership and irrespective of the subsequent transfer of title. Only the simultaneous quashing of both orders would have eliminated the grounds for confiscation.

The applicant was never a party to the proceedings that produced order no. 613 and therefore had no opportunity to contest the factual or legal basis for the confiscation of property that it owned. Section 124(1) EDTWA expressly authorises such confiscation even when the owner is not the offender. These facts formed the core of the alleged violations of the right of access to court and of the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The case of Trafik Oil - 1 EOOD v. Bulgaria (Application no. 67437/17) concerns the confiscation of diesel fuel owned by the applicant company, a Bulgarian firm registered in 2013 that operated a petrol station, through administrative-penal proceedings against a third-party supplier in which the company had no right to participate. These events formed the basis of complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

In September 2014 customs officials inspected the applicant’s petrol station and found 26,504 litres of diesel for which the company could not produce the required excise-duty documents. The fuel was seized the following month. On 24 April 2015 the customs authorities issued penal order no. 896 against the applicant company under section 126 of the Excise Duties and Tax Warehouses Act (EDTWA). The order imposed a fine, confiscated the fuel pursuant to section 124(1) of the same Act, and suspended the company’s right to operate the station for one month.

The applicant sought judicial review. During the first-instance hearings the authorities produced a later penal order (no. 613) issued against the supplier; the Sandanski District Court nevertheless upheld order no. 896 on 3 December 2015. On appeal the Blagoevgrad Administrative Court, in a final judgment of 7 April 2016, quashed the order. It held that the applicant, as end recipient, could possess only the documents supplied by its seller, Petrol Company EOOD, which had issued a valid invoice.

Meanwhile, on 10 July 2015 the same authorities had issued penal order no. 613 against Petrol Company EOOD for selling the fuel without an excise document. That order also confiscated 30,023 litres of diesel and became final on 11 September 2015 because the supplier did not contest it.

After its own penal order was quashed, the applicant asked customs on 21 April 2016 to return the fuel or pay its value. The request was refused on 4 May 2016 on the ground that the fuel had already been confiscated under the now-final order no. 613. The applicant challenged the refusal. The Blagoevgrad Administrative Court quashed it on 14 July 2016, finding no remaining legal basis for retention. The Supreme Administrative Court, however, reversed that decision in a final judgment of 14 June 2017. It ruled that section 124(1) of the EDTWA authorises confiscation of goods that are the subject of a section 126 offence “regardless of their ownership.” The unpaid duty and the existence of a valid penal order against the supplier therefore justified continued confiscation even though the applicant’s own order had been set aside and even though the applicant had never been a party to the supplier’s proceedings.

The applicant company thus lost its property through proceedings to which it was a stranger and from which it was legally excluded. Later legislative amendments (not applicable at the time) would have allowed an owner who is not the offender to receive a copy of the penal order and to appeal, underscoring the procedural gap that existed when the confiscation occurred. These facts underpin the alleged violations of the right of access to court and of the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

Bulgaria (Application no. 67437/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the confiscation of diesel fuel owned by the applicant company following administrative-penal proceedings against a third-party supplier in which the company had no opportunity to participate. In September 2014, customs authorities inspected the applicant’s petrol station and found 26,504 litres of diesel fuel for which the company could not produce the required excise-duty documents. The fuel was seized in October 2014. On 24 April 2015 the authorities issued penal order no. 896 against the applicant under section 126 of the Excise Duties and Tax Warehouses Act (EDTWA). The order imposed a financial penalty, confiscated the fuel pursuant to section 124(1) EDTWA (which permits confiscation of goods that are the subject of an offence “regardless of their ownership”), and suspended the company’s operating licence for one month.

The applicant sought judicial review. During the first-instance hearing the Sandanski District Court admitted as evidence a later penal order (no. 613) issued against the supplier. That court upheld the confiscation. On appeal, however, the Blagoevgrad Administrative Court, in a final judgment of 7 April 2016, quashed penal order no. 896. It held that the applicant, as the end purchaser, had received a valid invoice from its supplier, Petrol Company EOOD, and therefore could not be held liable for the missing excise documents.

Meanwhile, on 10 July 2015 the same customs authorities had issued penal order no. 613 against Petrol Company EOOD for selling the fuel without proof of paid excise duty. That order also confiscated 30,023 litres of diesel. Because the supplier did not appeal, the order became final on 11 September 2015.

After the quashing of order no. 896 the applicant requested the return of the fuel (or its monetary equivalent). The customs authorities refused, citing the now-final confiscation under order no. 613. The Blagoevgrad Administrative Court initially set aside the refusal, but the Supreme Administrative Court, in a final judgment of 14 June 2017, reinstated it. The SAC reasoned that a valid penal order establishing a breach of section 126 EDTWA rendered confiscation lawful irrespective of who owned the fuel; the subsequent sale to the applicant and the later annulment of the order issued against the applicant were legally irrelevant.

The applicant therefore lost its property on the basis of an uncontested administrative decision rendered in proceedings to which it was a stranger and in which it had no right to be heard or to present evidence. National law at the time provided no mechanism for a non-offender owner to challenge such a confiscation. (Subsequent legislative amendments, not applicable to the present case, later introduced such a right.)

These facts formed the core of the complaints: the company was deprived of its possessions without any effective opportunity to contest the measure that directly affected its title, and the domestic courts treated ownership as irrelevant once a third-party offence had been recorded.

The case of F.O. v. Croatia (Application no. 29555/13) involves a Croatian pupil (born 1993) who alleged verbal abuse by his mathematics teacher, R.V., at a State secondary school between 2008 and 2012, together with the authorities’ failure to respond adequately.

On 19 September 2011, after the applicant and classmates arrived late, R.V. shouted that the applicant was “a moron, an idiot, a fool, hillbilly, [and] a stupid cop” (referring to the applicant’s policeman father). The following day, after the incident was reported to the headteacher, R.V. remarked in class that calling a fool a fool should not be insulting and that the pupils would learn what real insults were. On 28 September R.V. again called the applicant a fool for turning to the wrong page, adding that he had not intended an insult because the applicant would tell his father.

The applicant received psychological treatment on two occasions. His general practitioner recorded a working diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder linked to the harassment; a hospital psychologist diagnosed acute anxiety disorder and recommended extra school support. The applicant, otherwise a good student from a functional family, later claimed the conflict (and R.V.’s involvement in his final mathematics examination) caused him to miss his chosen university place. An official report, however, stated that the examination was anonymised and that the applicant had simply failed to follow the instructions.

The applicant’s father immediately complained to the school, the Ombudsperson for Children, the education inspectorate, the police and the State Attorney’s Office. The school psychologist interviewed R.V., who admitted most of the words used on 19 September but denied targeting the applicant personally and promised to stop. The applicant told the psychologist he felt stressed and wanted to change class or school or have the teacher removed. The Ministry of Education referred the matter to the Education Agency, which in November 2011 interviewed staff, pupils and the applicant and conducted a pupil survey. It concluded that R.V. was a highly regarded, award-winning teacher whose pupils were generally satisfied; the conflict had nevertheless harmed the applicant’s progress. After a December meeting the father informed the school that the relationship had been restored.

A criminal complaint lodged by the applicant in November 2011 produced witness statements that R.V. regularly used insulting language, especially towards weaker mathematics students; some pupils treated it as commonplace or joking, while one former pupil mentioned sexual remarks and another said classmates had been afraid to answer official questionnaires honestly. On 18 June 2012 the State Attorney dismissed the complaint, holding that the remarks lacked the intensity, recurrence and malicious intent required for the offence of harassment and had not caused severe psychological harm.

In August 2012 the applicant applied to the Constitutional Court, challenging both the harassment and the authorities’ response (as well as the examination result). The Court declared the complaints inadmissible on 18 October 2012 on the ground that neither the prosecutor’s decision nor the examination result constituted a determination of rights on the merits.

These events formed the factual basis of the alleged violations of Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the Convention, in particular the State’s positive obligation under Article 8 to protect a pupil’s private life from a teacher’s verbal abuse.

The case of F.O. v. Croatia (Application no. 29555/13) involves a Croatian national born in November 1993 who attended a State secondary school from 2008 to 2012. He alleged verbal harassment by his mathematics teacher, R.V., and an inadequate response by the authorities, invoking Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

On 19 September 2011 the applicant and several classmates arrived late to class. R.V. shouted at the applicant, calling him “a moron, an idiot, a fool, hillbilly [and] a stupid cop” (referring to the applicant’s father, a policeman). The following day, after the incident was reported, R.V. told the class that calling a fool a fool should not constitute an insult and that they would learn what real insults were. On 28 September R.V. approached the applicant, called him a fool for turning to the wrong page in a textbook, and added that he had not meant to insult him because he knew the applicant would “call [his] dad.”

The applicant received psychological treatment. His general practitioner recorded a working diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder linked to the harassment, while a hospital psychologist diagnosed an acute anxiety disorder and recommended greater support at school. The applicant later claimed the conflict and R.V.’s involvement in his final mathematics examination contributed to his poor results and failure to enter his chosen university course; an official report, however, attributed the examination outcome to his failure to follow instructions in an anonymised process.

The applicant’s father immediately notified the school, the Ombudsperson for Children, the education inspectorate, the police and the State Attorney’s Office, repeating the complaints a week later. The school psychologist interviewed R.V., who admitted most of the words used on 19 September but denied addressing the applicant personally and promised to refrain from further insults. The applicant told the psychologist he felt stressed and wished to change class or school; he did not take up the suggestion of a direct conversation with R.V. The Ministry of Education referred the matter to the Education Agency, which in November 2011 interviewed the teacher, staff, the applicant and classmates and conducted a pupil survey. The Agency concluded that R.V. was a highly regarded teacher whose pupils were largely satisfied; it recommended a meeting between the school and the father and noted that the conflict had harmed the applicant’s progress. After a subsequent meeting the father informed the school that the relationship had been settled.

On 4 November 2011 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint of harassment. Witnesses confirmed that R.V. regularly used insulting language, particularly towards weaker pupils; some regarded it as joking, while others spoke of fear of retaliation when completing official questionnaires. The State Attorney dismissed the complaint in June 2012, holding that the remarks lacked the intensity, recurrence and malicious intent required for the offence of harassment and had not caused sufficiently severe psychological harm. The Constitutional Court later declared the applicant’s constitutional complaints inadmissible.

These facts formed the basis of the Court’s finding of a violation of Article 8: the teacher’s particularly disrespectful insults, delivered in a position of trust and in front of other pupils, caused the applicant emotional distress, and the domestic authorities’ responses were inadequate. There is no room for tolerating any form of violence, including verbal abuse, by a teacher towards a pupil.

The ECtHR case F.O. v. Croatia (Appl. no. 29555/13) concerns a Croatian pupil's allegations of verbal harassment by his state-school mathematics teacher and the authorities' inadequate response, engaging Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

F.O., born November 1993, attended a Croatian state secondary school from 2008 to 2012. On 19 September 2011 he and classmates arrived late to class. Teacher R.V. shouted insults at him personally: “a moron, an idiot, a fool, hillbilly, [and] a stupid cop” (alluding to the applicant’s policeman father). The next day R.V. told the class that calling a fool a fool was not an insult and that pupils would “see what the insults are.” On 28 September R.V. again called him a fool for turning to the wrong page, adding he had not meant to insult because he knew the applicant would tell his father.

The incidents caused documented distress. Between September and December 2011 the applicant received psychological treatment. His GP recorded a working diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder linked to the harassment; a hospital psychologist diagnosed an acute anxiety disorder attributable to psychological harassment at school and recommended extra support. The applicant, otherwise from a functional family and academically successful, claimed the conflict plus R.V.’s role in his final mathematics examination produced poor results that blocked his chosen university course. A later official report attributed the exam outcome to failure to follow anonymised instructions.

The applicant’s father immediately notified the school, the Ombudsperson for Children, the education inspectorate, the police and the State Attorney’s Office, seeking protection. The school psychologist interviewed R.V., who admitted most of the words but denied they were personal or that he had used “stupid cop”; she reproached him and he undertook to stop. The applicant told her he felt stressed during mathematics lessons and wanted to change class, school or teacher.

The Ministry forwarded the complaint to the Education Agency, which in November 2011 interviewed R.V., staff, the applicant and classmates and conducted a pupil survey. It found R.V. an award-winning teacher whose pupils were generally satisfied; only two wanted a change. The Agency concluded the conflict had damaged the applicant’s progress and recommended a meeting. A December 2011 school meeting recorded the father as saying the matter was settled.

On 4 November 2011 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint of harassment. Police and prosecutorial interviews of pupils revealed that R.V. regularly used terms such as “fools,” “idiots” and “idlers,” that some regarded this as joking while others said they had stopped noticing, and that pupils had feared answering an earlier questionnaire honestly after R.V. had reacted angrily. One former pupil reported sexual comments. On 18 June 2012 the State Attorney dismissed the complaint, holding that the insults lacked the intensity, recurrence or cruel intent required for the offence of psychological harassment of a minor and had not produced sufficiently severe health damage.

In August 2012 the applicant applied to the Constitutional Court, alleging both the harassment and the inadequacy of the school, Agency and prosecutorial responses. The Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 18 October 2012 because the challenged decisions had not determined any of his rights on the merits.

These facts—repeated public insults by a teacher in a position of trust, resulting in medically attested emotional harm, together with investigative findings that minimised the conduct and produced no meaningful sanction or protective measure—constitute the core of the alleged violations.
