**Case Summary: Investigative Journalists v. Armenia (ECtHR, Application no. 64023/11, 18 May 2021)**

The applicant, Investigative Journalists, is an Armenian NGO based in Yerevan that promotes investigative journalism through a news website (operating since 2001) and by commissioning articles. The case arose from defamation proceedings initiated over two articles it published, raising an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression).

On 20 May 2008, the NGO published an article titled “Who Is Pocketing Money from the Sand Mine?” as an insert in *Azg* newspaper (later posted on its website on 26 May 2008). The piece described the White Water reservoir near Ijevan, noting sand and pebble accumulation from river flooding (estimated at two million cubic metres) and visible extraction by excavators and cranes amid a local construction boom. It reported a driver paying 8,000–20,000 AMD per lorry-load and questioned who received “large illegal and untaxed profits” under the pretext of lake cleansing. It stated that, “according to our knowledge,” the business was under the control of Ijevan Mayor V.N. The journalist described sending inquiries to the Tavush Regional Prosecutor’s Office (which replied that only mud was being used for park levelling and no sand was extracted) and to other authorities, including the Mayor, Regional Governor, and environmental inspectorate, who largely failed to respond. It highlighted discrepancies in official claims about park work, noted extraction from the river banks, and alleged that a prior environmental inspection had imposed a fine that was later invalidated due to procedural issues involving acting mayors. The article criticised authorities for ignoring open “plundering” despite rhetoric on the rule of law and the shadow economy.

A follow-up article on 9 July 2008, “Will the Three Commissions ‘Notice’ the Illegal Use of the Reservoir Sand?”, also published in *Azg* and online, reported a regional commission’s examination. It quoted an environmental official stating that sand extraction was illegal because no Ministry of Environment study or authorisation existed, questioned the dumping of extracted material, and noted four to five years of extraction under a “cleansing” pretext via allegedly unlawful contracts. It criticised the local council’s allocation of over USD 3,000 from a tight community budget for the lawsuit against the NGO, suggesting it could have been used for road repairs instead.

On 19 June 2008, the Ijevan Mayor’s Office filed a civil claim under Article 19 of the Civil Code, seeking retraction of the 20 and 26 May publications and pecuniary damages. It alleged untrue information damaging its work and tarnishing the Mayor’s honour, dignity, and business reputation. The court later recognised Mayor V.N. personally as a plaintiff regarding his reputation.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan dismissed the claim on 7 July 2009, finding the Mayor’s Office was not a legal person entitled to protection under Article 19, that the articles posed questions rather than alleging proven facts of illegal extraction by the Mayor’s Office itself, and that statements about the Mayor’s control were not presented as established facts. It cited the Constitution and Article 10. On appeal, the Civil Court of Appeal remitted the case on 13 November 2009, holding the Mayor’s Office was a legal person and that the lower court had not properly verified the information’s veracity or examined the articles in full.

On rehearing, the District Court allowed the claim on 9 July 2010. It found the articles tarnished the Mayor’s Office’s business reputation and the Mayor’s honour and dignity, and that the NGO had not proved the information corresponded to reality (thus treating it as fictitious). The court noted the Mayor had complained to authorities about third-party extraction. It ordered retraction in *Azg* and online plus AMD 952,600 in costs. The Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the NGO’s appeal on 27 December 2010 (reducing costs to AMD 472,600), stressing protection of honour and reputation as a high societal value and finding the articles tarnished the Mayor and, by extension, the community/Mayor’s Office. The Court of Cassation declared the NGO’s further appeal inadmissible on 2 March 2011. The pecuniary award was never paid, as enforcement was not pursued.

These proceedings formed the interference with the NGO’s journalistic expression on a matter of alleged public-resource misuse and official accountability. (Word count: 612)

The European Court of Human Rights case of Investigative Journalists v. Armenia (Application no. 64023/11) arose from defamation proceedings against an Armenian NGO that publishes investigative journalism. The applicant organisation, based in Yerevan, aims to promote investigative reporting and operates a news website. It commissioned and published articles alleging possible official involvement in illegal sand extraction.

On 20 May 2008 an article titled “Who Is Pocketing Money from the Sand Mine?” appeared as a newspaper insert and was later posted on the organisation’s website. It described large-scale sand and pebble extraction from the White Water reservoir near Ijevan, an activity visible to the public and occurring amid a local construction boom. The piece reported that a lorry of sand sold for thousands of drams, generating substantial untaxed profits. It stated that, according to the author’s knowledge, the business was controlled by Ijevan’s Mayor, V.N. The journalist had sent inquiries to the regional prosecutor’s office, the Mayor, the regional governor and environmental authorities. Official replies claimed only mud was being used for park landscaping and that no sand extraction by the Mayor’s Office was occurring. The article highlighted contradictions in those replies, noted the absence of responses from several officials, and referred to an environmental inspectorate inspection that had allegedly resulted in a fine later invalidated on procedural grounds. It concluded by criticising the apparent plunder of public resources in plain view.

A follow-up article published on 9 July 2008 reiterated that extraction was illegal, cited an environmental official’s view that contracts for “cleansing” the lake lacked proper authorisation, and questioned the Mayor’s Office’s expenditure of community funds on litigation against the journalists rather than on local infrastructure.

On 19 June 2008 the Ijevan Mayor’s Office brought a civil claim seeking retraction of the statements and pecuniary damages. It argued that the articles contained untrue information damaging the Office’s work and tarnishing the Mayor’s honour, dignity and business reputation, relying on Article 19 of the Civil Code. The courts later joined the Mayor personally as a co-plaintiff.

The first-instance court initially dismissed the claim in July 2009, holding that the Mayor’s Office was not a legal person entitled to the relevant protection, that the articles posed questions rather than asserting proven facts, and that no tarnishing conclusions had been drawn. It referred to constitutional free-speech guarantees and Article 10 of the Convention. The Civil Court of Appeal reversed this in November 2009, finding the Office to be a legal person and criticising the lower court for failing to require the journalists to prove the veracity of the statements.

On remittal the district court, in July 2010, upheld the claim. It classified the information as tarnishing and fictitious because the applicant had not proved its accuracy, noting that the Mayor himself had complained of extraction by third parties. It ordered publication of a retraction and payment of costs (later reduced on appeal to AMD 472,600). The Court of Appeal dismissed the journalists’ appeal in December 2010, emphasising the high value of reputation protection. The Court of Cassation declared the subsequent appeal on points of law inadmissible in March 2011. The costs award was never enforced.

The applicant organisation complained that the domestic decisions interfered with its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The publications concerned a matter of public interest—possible illegal exploitation of natural resources and the role of a public official—and the journalist had attempted to verify the information through official channels. The courts’ approach, which treated the statements as unproven facts of a defamatory character and placed the full burden of proof on the publisher, formed the core of the alleged violation.

The case of Investigative Journalists v. Armenia (ECtHR Application no. 64023/11, judgment of 18 May 2021) concerns civil defamation proceedings brought against an Armenian NGO over two investigative articles, alleged to violate Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression).

The applicant organisation, a Yerevan-based non-profit promoting investigative journalism via a news website and commissioned articles, published “Who Is Pocketing Money from the Sand Mine?” on 20 May 2008 as an insert in Azg newspaper (reposted on its website on 26 May). The piece described large-scale sand and pebble extraction from the White Water reservoir near Ijevan, a publicly visible activity amid a construction boom. It questioned who was profiting illegally and untaxed, stating that “according to our knowledge, this business is under the control of the Mayor of Ijevan, [V.N.]”. The journalist had sent inquiries to the Tavush Regional Prosecutor’s Office (which accepted the Mayor’s Office’s denial of sand use), the Mayor, the Regional Governor and environmental authorities, receiving no or inadequate replies. The article highlighted discrepancies in official park-levelling claims, noted extraction also from the river banks, and cited an unnamed official on a fine later dismissed in court due to procedural issues. It criticised authorities for failing to act against obvious “plundering”.

A follow-up article on 9 July 2008, “Will the Three Commissions ‘Notice’ the Illegal Use of the Reservoir Sand?”, reported that a regional commission was examining the earlier claims and that the head of the local environmental inspectorate considered the Mayor’s Office’s “cleansing” contracts illegal for lack of ministry authorisation. It questioned the dumping of extracted material and the lawfulness of spending community funds (over USD 3,000) on a lawsuit against the applicant rather than local needs.

On 19 June 2008 the Ijevan Mayor’s Office sued the applicant under Article 19 of the Civil Code, seeking retraction of the publications and damages. It alleged untrue statements damaging its work and tarnishing the Mayor’s honour, dignity and business reputation. The court later joined Mayor V.N. as plaintiff.

The first-instance court dismissed the claim on 7 July 2009, holding that the Mayor’s Office was not a legal person entitled to protection, that the articles posed questions rather than asserting proven facts, and that no tarnishing conclusions were drawn; it cited the Constitution and Article 10. The Court of Appeal reversed this on 13 November 2009, finding the Mayor’s Office a legal person and remitting the case because the lower court had not verified whether the information corresponded to reality (the burden lying on the publisher).

On retrial the District Court allowed the claim on 9 July 2010. It held that the articles tarnished the Mayor’s Office’s business reputation and the Mayor’s honour and dignity, and that the applicant had failed to prove the information true, rendering it fictitious (supported by the Mayor’s complaints about third-party extraction). It ordered retraction in Azg and on the website plus AMD 952,600 in costs. The applicant’s appeal, arguing an unjustified interference with freedom of expression, was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 27 December 2010 (costs reduced to AMD 472,600); the Court of Cassation declared the further appeal inadmissible on 2 March 2011. The costs award was never enforced.

Armenian law (Civil Code Article 19, Mass Media Act Section 8) required the media defendant to prove the truth of tarnishing statements or retract them. The applicant contended that the courts’ approach failed to give due weight to journalistic reporting on a matter of public interest involving a public official, thereby disproportionately interfering with Article 10.
001-210039:
The case of Dareskizb Ltd v. Armenia (Application no. 64004/11) concerns civil defamation proceedings brought against the applicant, a private company that published the opposition daily Haykakan Zhamanak. It raises issues under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression).

On 14 October 2010 the newspaper published an article headed “Seven out of Eight are in the List.” It stated that Russian law-enforcement agencies investigating drug trafficking, human trafficking and money-laundering had identified involvement by Armenian officials and had compiled a list of 32 names of officials linked to Russian criminal gangs. The list had been unofficially shared with Armenia’s Prosecutor General and National Security Service chief. The first seven names included three members of parliament—Ruben Hayrapetyan, Levon Sargsyan and Samvel Aleksanyan—together with other high-ranking figures; President Serzh Sargsyan’s name had been omitted. The article asserted that Armenian authorities had declined to act, claiming they lacked power.

On 26 October the three MPs demanded a full retraction, asserting that the information was untrue and unverified. The editor refused on 1 November, noting that the MPs had not identified specific inaccuracies and that the claims had been confirmed by S.K., president of the Moscow-based Armenian National Club, who had seen the list. On 2 November the paper published a follow-up interview with S.K. elaborating on the Club’s anti-corruption work and consultations with Russian agencies about pending cases involving the officials.

The three MPs sued on 8 November 2010, seeking retraction and damages for statements that allegedly did not correspond to reality, tarnished their honour and dignity, and had been published without verification. On 7 February 2011 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court upheld the claim. Applying Article 1087.1 of the Civil Code, it held the statements defamatory: they publicly attributed serious crimes (which inherently tarnish honour, especially of elected officials) and the applicant had failed to discharge the burden of proving their truth. A letter from the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office of 19 October 2010 confirmed that no material existed linking the plaintiffs to the alleged offences. The court ordered publication of a court-approved retraction and awarded each plaintiff the statutory maximum of AMD 2 million in non-pecuniary damages plus costs, citing the MPs’ public status and the articles’ wide circulation.

The Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal (which invoked Article 10) on 9 June 2011; the Court of Cassation declared a further appeal inadmissible on 3 August 2011. The company, whose monthly income was approximately AMD 1.8 million, had to raise more than AMD 6 million from readers to satisfy the judgment.

Domestic law (Article 1087.1) treats public statements of fact as defamatory if they are untrue and tarnish honour, with the burden of proof on the defendant (subject to limited exceptions for statements pursuing a paramount public interest that have been reasonably verified in good faith). The court-ordered retraction and the size of the award constitute the impugned interference with the newspaper’s freedom of expression.

The case of Dareskizb Ltd v. Armenia (Application no. 64004/11), decided by a Committee of the ECtHR’s Fourth Section on 18 May 2021, concerns civil defamation proceedings brought against an Armenian opposition newspaper publisher and the resulting interference with its Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

Dareskizb Ltd published the daily Haykakan Zhamanak. On 14 October 2010 it ran a front-page article headed “Seven out of Eight are in the List.” The piece stated that Russian law-enforcement bodies investigating drug trafficking, human trafficking and money-laundering had compiled a list of 32 Armenian officials with links to Russian criminal groups. The first seven names included three members of parliament (Ruben Hayrapetyan, Levon Sargsyan and Samvel Aleksanyan), the President’s brother (also an MP), the head of the State Revenue Committee, the Speaker of Parliament and the leader of a parliamentary faction. The article added that the Russian authorities had unofficially shared the list with Armenia’s Prosecutor General and National Security Service chief and had sought accountability, but the Armenian officials had claimed they lacked power to act. The President himself was said to have been omitted because the Russians considered him beyond reach.

The three named MPs immediately demanded a full retraction, asserting that the information was false and unverified. The editor refused, maintaining that the MPs had not identified specific inaccuracies and that the allegations had been confirmed by S.K., president of the Moscow-based Armenian National Club Miabanutyun, who had seen the list and discussed it with Russian investigators. On 2 November 2010 the newspaper published a second article, “Moscow is after the ‘Serzhs’,” containing an interview with S.K. in which he repeated and elaborated the claims, adding that an anti-corruption centre run by the Club had been consulted by Russian agencies and that the list had grown to 36 names. He noted that much of the information was confidential.

On 8 November 2010 the three MPs sued the company for retraction and non-pecuniary damages, arguing that the statements were untrue, unsubstantiated and damaging to their honour. The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan upheld the claim on 7 February 2011. Applying Article 1087.1 of the Civil Code, it held that the statements were defamatory because they publicly attributed serious crimes, tarnished the reputation of elected officials and had not been proved true. The burden of proof lay on the defendant, which produced no supporting evidence. A letter from the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office confirmed that no materials existed linking the plaintiffs to the alleged offences. The court therefore ordered publication of a court-drafted retraction and awarded each plaintiff the statutory maximum of AMD 2 000 000 (plus court fees), citing the plaintiffs’ high public standing and the wide circulation of the newspaper.

The Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the company’s appeal on 9 June 2011; the Court of Cassation declared a further appeal inadmissible on 3 August 2011. The total sum payable (approximately AMD 6.38 million) exceeded three times the company’s monthly income, forcing it to solicit donations from readers.

Domestic law defines defamation as a public statement of fact that is untrue and injures honour, dignity or business reputation. The defendant bears the burden of proof unless that burden is unreasonable. Liability may be avoided if the statements pursue a paramount public interest, the publisher took all reasonable verification steps and acted in good faith and in a balanced manner, or if the statements merely reproduce information from another source with attribution.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 10 violation: the imposition of a mandatory retraction and substantial damages for reporting allegations of official corruption that the newspaper claimed were based on information received from a named source with access to Russian investigators.

The case of Dareskizb Ltd v. Armenia (Application no. 64004/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged violations of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) arising from civil defamation proceedings in Armenia against the applicant, a private company publishing the opposition daily newspaper Haykakan Zhamanak.

On 14 October 2010 the newspaper published an article titled “Seven out of Eight are in the List.” It reported that Russian law-enforcement bodies, investigating drug trafficking, human trafficking and money laundering, had compiled a list of 32 Armenian officials with ties to Russian criminal gangs. The article stated that the list had been unofficially shared with Armenia’s Prosecutor General and National Security Service chief, who claimed they lacked power to act. It named seven officials at the top of the list, including three members of parliament (MPs): Ruben Hayrapetyan, Levon Sargsyan and Samvel Aleksanyan. The article claimed President Serzh Sargsyan’s name was omitted because holding him accountable was never considered.

On 26 October 2010 the three MPs wrote to the newspaper demanding a full retraction, asserting the information was unverified and untrue. They attached a proposed retraction text. The editor-in-chief refused on 1 November 2010, arguing that the MPs had not identified specific inaccuracies and that the information had been confirmed by S.K., president of the Moscow-based Armenian National Club Miabanutyun. S.K. had reportedly seen the list after discussions with Russian officers.

On 2 November 2010 the newspaper published a second article, “Moscow is after the ‘Serzhs’,” featuring an interview with S.K. He described the Club’s anti-corruption work, consultations with Russian agencies about pending cases involving Armenian officials, a confidentiality undertaking, and an expanded list of 36 names.

On 8 November 2010 the three MPs sued the company in the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan. They claimed the articles contained untrue statements that tarnished their honour and dignity, sought a court-ordered retraction of the specified text, and claimed damages. The company contested the claim.

On 7 February 2011 the District Court upheld the claim. Applying Article 1087.1 of the Civil Code, it found the statements defamatory because they were public, tarnished honour (by alleging serious crimes especially damaging to elected officials), and were untrue. The burden of proving truth lay on the defendant, which produced no supporting evidence. A letter from Russia’s General Prosecutor’s Office (19 October 2010) confirmed no material linking the plaintiffs to such crimes in Russia. The court ordered publication of a retraction stating that the 14 October article’s claims “do not correspond to reality and were presented without checking their veracity.” It awarded each plaintiff the statutory maximum of AMD 2,000,000 in non-pecuniary damages plus AMD 44,000 in fees, citing the MPs’ expected impeccable standing and the wide audience reached.

The company appealed, invoking Article 10 principles. The Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 9 June 2011. The Court of Cassation declared the further appeal inadmissible on 3 August 2011.

The company later stated that the total award (over AMD 6 million, more than three times its monthly income of about AMD 1.8 million) forced it to solicit reader donations; it paid AMD 6,381,288 on 28 October 2011.

Domestic law (Civil Code Article 1087.1) defines defamation as public untrue statements of fact that tarnish honour, dignity or reputation, with the burden of proof on the defendant (shifting only in limited circumstances). Liability is excluded if statements pursue a paramount public interest, the publisher took all reasonable verification steps, and the statements were balanced and made in good faith, or if they reproduce information from identified sources. These facts formed the basis of the company’s complaint that the domestic proceedings and sanctions disproportionately interfered with its journalistic freedom of expression on a matter of public interest involving high officials.
001-210041:
The applicant, a Russian limited-liability company, founded and operated an unregistered information agency via its registered electronic periodical website (www.taminfo.ru). During the 2011 State Duma election campaign (officially launched in August, with the media “pre-election campaigning” period beginning 5 November), the site published two October articles by A. criticising United Russia, A Just Russia and a candidate, plus a November online poll and an accompanying article by editor T. assessing its results.

Domestic authorities treated the A. articles as “pre-election campaigning” under the 2005 State Duma Deputies Election Act (negative comments about one party/candidate, inciting a negative voter attitude). The company was convicted twice: first under CAO Art. 5.12 § 1 (2 December 2011) for omitting mandatory “campaigning-material” particulars (print-run, date, funding source, producer details) required by s. 61(4) of the Act, receiving the statutory-minimum fine of RUB 50 000; second under CAO Art. 5.5 § 1 (18 May 2012) for publishing the material before the official campaigning window, receiving a further RUB 30 000 fine. Both convictions were upheld on appeal. Courts rejected arguments that the company (as founder) was not liable for the editor’s decisions, that the agency was not a company unit, and that Art. 5.12 applied only to printed matter; they held that an internet site constituted a “complex multitude of objects” capable of audio-visual dissemination and that a founder could be held separately liable. By contrast, A. himself was acquitted on appeal: the texts contained no direct calls to vote and were not shown to pursue a campaigning aim.

Separately, the website hosted a static online poll (“What party will you vote for \ldots?”) created by a third-party institute; users could vote but not view cumulative results. T.’s 8 November article presented the (then 2 000-vote) results, noting no clear United Russia majority and a rising protest vote. The company was convicted under CAO Art. 5.5 (2 December 2011) for disseminating poll results without the information mandated by s. 53 of the Act (organiser, dates, sample size, methodology, region, exact wording, margin of error, commissioner and funder). The RUB 30 000 fine was upheld despite the institute’s confirmation that results were never publicly accessible via the poll itself. The company paid the three fines (totalling RUB 103 000) in instalments.

The applicant maintained throughout that the publications formed part of ordinary journalistic activity (analytical commentary and voter information), not campaigning, that only the editor (not the founder) could be liable, and that internet dissemination fell outside the print/audio-visual rules then in force. These facts formed the basis of the subsequent Article 10 complaint alleging unjustified interference with the freedom to impart information during an election period.

The applicant, OOO Informatsionnoye Agentstvo Tambov-Inform, is a Russian limited-liability company that founded and operated an information agency of the same name via the website www.taminfo.ru (registered as an electronic periodical). Its main activities included radio/television broadcasting and online news. In the run-up to the 4 December 2011 State Duma elections (campaign formally launched in August; official “pre-election campaigning” period on media commencing 5 November), the website published two articles by journalist A. (3 and 12 October 2011). These contained critical remarks about a candidate, the United Russia party and the A Just Russia party (e.g., accusations of empty promises, lack of genuine opposition activity, and that “what United Russia have been doing deserves nothing more than laughter”).

The Tambov Regional Electoral Committee initiated administrative prosecutions. On 2 December 2011 a justice of the peace convicted the company under Article 5.12 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for disseminating “campaigning material” that omitted mandatory details (print-run, publication date, electoral-fund payment, and producer identities) required by section 61 of the 2005 State Duma Deputies Election Act. The company was fined the statutory minimum of RUB 50,000. The court rejected the defence that the company, as mere founder, bore no liability for editorial content: the agency lacked separate legal personality, the editor was a company employee, and the company itself had previously described its activities as including election coverage. The conviction was upheld on appeal (22 December 2011) and further review (16 April 2012). In separate proceedings the same articles led to a second conviction, on 18 May 2012, under Article 5.5 § 1 CAO for publishing campaigning material before the official 28-day media campaigning window. The company received another minimum fine of RUB 30,000 (upheld on 27 June 2012). The company argued that the texts formed part of ordinary analytical journalism, contained no direct calls to vote, and pursued no campaigning intent; it also noted that A. himself had been acquitted of identical charges on the ground that the articles did not constitute campaigning.

Independently, an online poll (“What party will you vote for \ldots?”) created by a third-party institute was hosted on the site. On 8 November 2011 the editor-in-chief published an article analysing the (then 2,000-response) results, noting the absence of a clear United Russia majority and a surge in protest voting. The company was prosecuted under Article 5.5 CAO and section 53 of the Election Act for disseminating poll results without the required methodological data (organiser, dates, sample size, method, region, exact question, margin of error, and commissioning/payment details). On 2 December 2011 it was fined RUB 30,000 (upheld on appeal and further review). The company maintained that users could not see cumulative results and that the article was legitimate voter information rather than campaigning.

The company paid the three fines (totalling RUB 103,000) in instalments between 2012 and 2014. These prosecutions and convictions form the basis of the Article 10 complaints.

The applicant, a limited-liability company, founded an unregistered information agency that operated solely via the website www.taminfo.ru (registered as an electronic periodical). Its activities included radio/television broadcasting and online news.

Ahead of the 4 December 2011 State Duma elections (campaign launched August 2011; official media “pre-election campaigning” period 5 November–3 December), the site published two October 2011 articles by A. These contained critical remarks about candidate B., United Russia and A Just Russia, e.g., that the parties “kept their distance from actual opposition activities,” that United Russia members were “the best” at empty promises, and that their actions “deserve nothing more than laughter.”

The regional Electoral Committee classified the texts as “pre-election campaigning” under s. 55 of the 2005 State Duma Election Act (negative commentary predominantly about one party/candidate). In December 2011 a justice of the peace convicted the company under Art. 5.12 § 1 CAO for omitting mandatory particulars required of printed/audio-visual campaigning material (print-run, publication date, electoral-fund payer, producer details) and imposed the statutory minimum fine of RUB 50 000. The company was held liable as founder because the agency lacked separate legal personality and the editor was its employee. An appeal court confirmed that an internet site constituted a “complex multitude of objects” subject to the same rules and that a founder could be held responsible for an editor’s compliance with election law.

In separate May 2012 proceedings the same articles led to a further conviction under Art. 5.5 § 1 CAO (violation of media-participation rules) for publication before the official campaigning window, plus a RUB 30 000 fine. Domestic courts again treated the company as the responsible media entity. Meanwhile, author A. was acquitted on appeal: the texts contained no direct voting calls, evinced no intent to influence the result, and therefore did not constitute campaigning.

Independently, the site hosted an online poll (“What party will you vote for \ldots?”) created by a third-party institute; users could vote but (according to the institute) could not see results. On 8 November editor T. published an article analysing the 2 000 responses, noting the absence of a United Russia majority and a “surging protest vote.” The company was convicted under Art. 5.5 CAO for disseminating poll results without the data required by s. 53 of the Election Act (pollster, dates, sample size, methodology, region, exact wording, margin of error, commissioner/payer). A further RUB 30 000 fine was imposed; higher courts upheld the finding that both the poll interface and T.’s article constituted unlawful dissemination.

The company paid the three fines (total RUB 103 000) in instalments. It argued throughout that the publications were ordinary journalistic/analytical output, not campaigning; that a founder is not liable for editorial content; that internet material fell outside the printed-media rules; and that the poll results had not been publicly accessible. All domestic courts rejected these submissions.

These prosecutions formed the factual basis of the alleged Art. 10 violations (unjustified interference with the freedom to impart information during an election).
001-210256:
**Case of Mihu and Oprea v. Romania (ECtHR, 8 June 2021)**

The applicants, Monica-Angela Mihu (born 1963) and Victoriţa Oprea (born 1974), Romanian nationals living in Bucharest, were insolvency and bankruptcy practitioners sharing an office. They alleged under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that they were unlawfully deprived of liberty from 8.30 a.m. on 6 April 2016 until 3 a.m. on 7 April 2016 (Mihu) and from 8 a.m. on 6 April 2016 until 4.55 a.m. on 7 April 2016 (Oprea).

In September 2015 the Caraș-Severin prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into several individuals, including Mihu, on suspicion of forming an organised criminal group, embezzlement, fraud by false representation, bankruptcy fraud, abuse of office and money laundering linked to her work as a bankruptcy practitioner. In January 2016 the investigation was extended to Oprea’s similar activities.

On 5 April 2016, on the basis of evidence gathered, the prosecutor ordered simultaneous investigatory measures for 6 April 2016, including searches and seizures at multiple locations, questioning of 21 suspects (including the applicants), witness interviews and an order for the handing over of relevant documents. Separate orders to appear were issued that day requiring police to bring each applicant to the Caraș-Severin prosecutor’s office in Reșița for questioning. The orders cited the accusations, the relevant Criminal Code provisions and Article 265 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP), justifying the measure as necessary “for the purpose of the investigation.” Enforcement was to follow Article 266 CCP.

On the morning of 6 April 2016 Mihu received a police telephone call asking her to meet officers at the office; Oprea was visited at home, shown the order and asked to accompany officers there. Both contacted their lawyer, I.M.P., and arrived at the office. Between six and eight police officers were present. From 9 a.m. until 2 p.m. (officially; 2.30 p.m. according to the applicants) the applicants, their lawyer and staff were required to hand over documents relating to a specific insolvency case. The documents were inventoried in a report signed without objection. The applicants and I.M.P. later stated (I.M.P. confirming this before a notary in 2019) that they were forbidden to leave the premises or make telephone calls during the operation.

Afterwards the applicants were taken in police cars to a Bucharest police station; I.M.P. followed. There they were told they would be transported to Reșița (approximately 500 km away). At 3.30 p.m. they and two other suspects were driven by four gendarmes in a minivan. I.M.P. travelled separately after buying them water and food. They arrived after midnight on 7 April 2016. They were informed of the accusations, interviewed first as suspects and then as accused persons in their lawyer’s presence, and remained accompanied/guarded by police, needing permission to use the toilet.

Mihu was questioned from 12.10 a.m. to 2.30 a.m. and briefly thereafter; she was arrested for 24 hours at 3 a.m. Oprea was questioned from 3.45 a.m. to 4.50 a.m. and arrested at 4.55 a.m. Later that day the prosecutor applied for pre-trial detention. The Caraș-Severin County Court ordered 30-day pre-trial detention for each, dismissing defence complaints of unjustified physical constraints from the previous morning onward on the ground that no nullity of the acts or breach of procedural rules had been shown. On 15 April 2016 the Timișoara Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeals after examining the lawfulness of the earlier measures and the necessity of detention.

The applicants contended that the entire period from their initial contacts with police until formal arrest constituted an unlawful deprivation of liberty not justified under the CCP provisions governing orders to appear or police custody.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) considered the applications of Monica-Angela Mihu and Victoriţa Oprea, two Romanian insolvency and bankruptcy practitioners based in Bucharest, who alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. They claimed they were unlawfully deprived of their liberty from the morning of 6 April 2016 until the early hours of 7 April 2016, when they were formally arrested.

Criminal investigations into organized crime, embezzlement, fraud, bankruptcy offences, abuse of office and money laundering began in September 2015 against several persons, including the first applicant, in connection with her work as a bankruptcy practitioner. The inquiry was extended to the second applicant in January 2016. On 5 April 2016 the Caraș-Severin prosecutor’s office decided to carry out coordinated investigative steps the following day, including searches, seizures, the questioning of 21 suspects (the applicants among them) and the collection of documents.

The prosecutor issued orders to appear under Article 265 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, directing the police to bring the applicants to the prosecutor’s office in Reșița for questioning because their presence was considered necessary for the investigation. The orders set out the accusations and authorised the police to use the powers provided by Article 266.

On the morning of 6 April the police contacted the applicants (by telephone for the first applicant and by a visit to her home for the second). Both went to their shared Bucharest office, where they were joined by their lawyer. Between approximately 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. (or 2.30 p.m.) six to eight officers conducted a search and seizure of documents relating to a particular insolvency file. The applicants and their lawyer later stated that they were forbidden to leave the premises or to make telephone calls during this operation. All requested documents were produced, inventoried and recorded in a report signed without objection.

Immediately afterwards the applicants were taken by police car to a Bucharest police station. At 3.30 p.m. they and two other suspects were transported by gendarmes in a minivan some 500 km to Reșița, arriving after midnight. Their lawyer followed independently. Upon arrival they were informed of the accusations, interviewed first as suspects and then as accused persons in their lawyer’s presence, and remained under constant police guard; they had to request permission even to use the toilet.

The first applicant was questioned between 12.10 a.m. and 2.50 a.m. and was placed in 24-hour police custody at 3 a.m. The second applicant was questioned between 3.45 a.m. and 4.50 a.m. and arrested at 4.55 a.m. Later that day the prosecutor applied for, and the Caraș-Severin County Court granted, 30-day pre-trial detention. Defence complaints about the physical constraints imposed from the previous morning were dismissed; an appeal raising the same points was also rejected.

The applicants argued that the entire period from the start of the office operation until their formal arrests constituted an unlawful deprivation of liberty, because the order-to-appear procedure permitted detention only for the time strictly necessary for questioning (normally no more than eight hours) and because they had been subjected to continuous physical control, a lengthy forced journey and restrictions on movement and communication well before any questioning occurred.

The ECtHR case of Mihu and Oprea v. Romania (applications nos. 54983/16 and 59295/16) concerns allegations under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention by two Romanian insolvency practitioners, Ms Monica-Angela Mihu (born 1963) and Ms Victoriţa Oprea (born 1974), both based in Bucharest, that they were unlawfully deprived of liberty from the morning of 6 April 2016 until their formal 24-hour arrests in the early hours of 7 April 2016.

In September 2015 the Caraș-Severin prosecutor’s office opened an investigation into several persons, including the first applicant, on suspicion of forming an organised criminal group, embezzlement, fraud, bankruptcy fraud, abuse of office and money-laundering connected with her professional activities. The investigation was extended to the second applicant in January 2016.

On 5 April 2016, on the basis of evidence already gathered, the prosecutor ordered simultaneous investigative measures for the following day: searches and seizures at multiple locations, questioning of 21 suspects (including both applicants), witness interviews and production of documents. The same day the prosecutor issued individual “orders to appear” requiring the police to bring each applicant to the Caraș-Severin prosecutor’s office in Reșița (approximately 500 km from Bucharest) for questioning. The orders recited the accusations, cited the relevant Criminal Code provisions and invoked Articles 265 §§ 2, 3 and 10 and 266 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stating that the applicants’ presence was “necessary for the purpose of the investigation.”

On the morning of 6 April the first applicant received a telephone call at 8 a.m. instructing her to meet police officers at the applicants’ office; the second applicant was visited at home, shown the order to appear and asked to go to the office. Both arrived shortly afterwards, together with their lawyer. Between 9 a.m. and approximately 2 p.m. six to eight police officers required them to produce documents relating to a particular insolvency file. The documents were handed over, inventoried and recorded in a report signed by the applicants and their lawyer without objection. According to the applicants (later corroborated by a notarised statement of their lawyer), they were forbidden to leave the premises or to make telephone calls during the operation.

After the search they were taken in police vehicles to a Bucharest police station and then, at 3.30 p.m., transported in a gendarmerie minivan with two other suspects to Reșița. Their lawyer followed by car. They arrived after midnight on 7 April. They were informed of the accusations and questioned in their lawyer’s presence, first as suspects and then as accused persons, while remaining under constant police guard and required to seek permission to use the toilet. The first applicant was questioned between 12.10 a.m. and 2.50 a.m. and arrested at 3 a.m. The second applicant was questioned between 3.45 a.m. and 4.50 a.m. and arrested at 4.55 a.m.

Later the same day the prosecutor applied for pre-trial detention. The Caraș-Severin County Court ordered 30-day detention, rejecting defence complaints that the applicants had been subjected to unjustified physical constraint from the early hours of 6 April onward. The court found no indication of a breach of the statutory rules governing hearings, searches, production of documents, orders to appear, police custody or defence rights. On 15 April 2016 the Timișoara Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeals after examining both the lawfulness of the preceding measures and the necessity of detention.

These events form the factual basis of the applicants’ claim that they were deprived of liberty for a period exceeding that permitted by the orders to appear and without a valid legal basis until the prosecutor’s 24-hour arrest orders were issued.
001-210045:
**Case Summary: Lapshin v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, 2021)**

Alexander Valeryevich Lapshin, a blogger and traveler holding Israeli, Russian, and Ukrainian nationality, was detained in Azerbaijan after traveling to the Nagorno-Karabakh region in 2011 and 2012 in a manner Azerbaijan deemed unlawful, prompting an international arrest warrant. Arrested in Belarus in December 2016 and extradited in February 2017, he was held in Kurdakhany prison. Convicted on 20 July 2017 under Article 318.2 of the Criminal Code for illegally crossing the border, he received a three-year sentence plus expulsion. He sought transfer to Israel to serve the sentence. On 11 September 2017, he was pardoned by the Azerbaijani President and expelled to Israel on 14 September 2017 immediately after hospital discharge. The Government submitted purported handwritten thank-you letters from Lapshin dated around the pardon, which he denied writing.

The alleged violations under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life, both procedural and substantive aspects) center on a 10 September 2017 prison incident that placed Lapshin’s life at serious risk, requiring urgent medical intervention, leaving him in critical condition with ongoing treatment needs. Lapshin claimed that around midnight, while isolated in his cell, masked men entered, restrained him, covered his face, strangled him, and beat him, causing unconsciousness. He awoke after about two days in intensive care unable to speak, feeling numbness on the right side of his face, with mobility, hearing, and coordination impairments.

The Government maintained it was a suicide attempt. Lapshin, held in the medical unit and expecting a family visit, learned on 9 September that his child was ill in Georgia, becoming depressed; officers placed him under watch. Around 10:05–10:12 a.m. on 10 September, a guard found him unresponsive in the cell’s sanitary facility, hanged by a shoulder strap/belt on a wall hook/nail (about 1.90 m high). Guards cut him down, administered artificial respiration, and called emergency teams; he was transferred to Merkezi Clinic in Baku around 1:05 p.m.

Clinic records described him arriving unconscious with a red throat mark, hyoid bone fracture, rapid breathing, and other issues; he was intubated, sedated, and later showed dysphonia, swallowing difficulties, and tongue injuries (attributed by some to biting). He was discharged on 14 September against further treatment and flown to Israel. Israeli examinations noted strangulation signs, multiple bruises, hematomas, and a possible blunt throat trauma. Psychiatric evaluation found no suicidal ideation or psychosis; Lapshin alleged an attack.

Lapshin’s privately commissioned experts (Russian doctors and a Croatian forensic specialist) concluded the injuries (including hyoid fracture, laryngeal issues, and bruises on face, arms, and body) indicated third-party manual strangulation and blunt-force trauma, consistent with attempted murder, not hanging (missing typical hanging signs like certain fractures or incontinence in some accounts). They highlighted inconsistencies, such as initial Azerbaijani records omitting bruises later documented in Israel. The Government’s experts, reviewing similar records, supported hanging, attributing injuries to convulsions, medical interventions (e.g., injections), or amnesia-related confabulation, and noted urinary incontinence in initial aid.

A prompt inquiry by a Sabuncu District Prosecutor’s investigator inspected the tidy cell (no fight signs, surveillance in corridor, peephole), found a looped 0.9 m belt, and took statements from guards (Z.I., A.A., T.A.) and medical staff aligning with the hanging account around 10:12–10:15 a.m., linking it to family distress. On 4 October 2017, the investigator refused a criminal case, finding a suicide attempt with no criminal elements; the decision was not served on Lapshin. Later, the applicant emailed and posted (from Latvia) complaints in February 2018 to Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prosecutor General alleging attempted murder and seeking investigation details (citing media interviews), providing proof of dispatch and delivery; no reply came. Authorities claimed the letter was lost by a postman due to health/workload issues.

Additional materials included phone recordings (8 September family call about the child’s illness and transfer; 11 September wife’s inquiry post-pardon) and Israeli consular notes of Azerbaijani threats to renew proceedings over media statements. These facts highlight discrepancies in timing (midnight vs. morning), injury descriptions, witness accounts, scene evidence, and inquiry thoroughness, relevant to claims of an attack on life and an ineffective investigation failing to resolve contradictions or notify the victim.

**CASE OF LAPSHIN v. AZERBAIJAN (Application no. 13527/18), ECtHR Fifth Section, Judgment of 20 May 2021 (final 11 October 2021)**

The applicant, Alexander Valeryevich Lapshin (born 1976), an Israeli/Russian/Ukrainian national and blogger, was extradited to Azerbaijan in February 2017 on an international arrest warrant related to his 2011–2012 travels to Nagorno-Karabakh, deemed unlawful under Azerbaijani law. He was held in Kurdakhany prison (isolated from other inmates), convicted on 20 July 2017 under Article 318.2 of the Criminal Code (illegal border crossing) and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment plus expulsion. He was pardoned by the President on 11 September 2017 and expelled to Israel on 14 September 2017 immediately after hospital discharge. The Government produced two purported handwritten letters from him dated 11 September 2017 thanking the President and prison staff; he denied writing them.

The core incident occurred on 10 September 2017. The applicant alleged that around midnight, masked men entered his cell, restrained him, covered his face, beat him and strangled him until he lost consciousness. He awoke after about two days in intensive care with no voice, facial/tongue numbness, right-side motor difficulties, hearing impairment and coordination problems.

The Government’s account was that the applicant, held in the medical unit, became depressed after learning (via phone calls on 8–9 September) that his wife and child could not visit because the child fell ill in Tbilisi. At 10:05 a.m. on 10 September a guard saw him enter the in-cell sanitary facility. After he failed to respond to calls, guards entered around 10:12 a.m. and found him hanged by a bag-strap loop on a 1.90 m wall hook/nail. They cut him down, performed artificial respiration and summoned medical teams; he was transferred to Merkezi Clinic at 1:05 p.m.

A 14 September 2017 Merkezi Clinic epicrisis recorded him arriving unconscious with a red mark on the throat, hyoid-bone fracture, rapid breathing and crepitation; he was intubated, later showed dysphonia, swallowing difficulties and tongue-biting marks, and was discharged against medical advice. Israeli records (Chaim Sheba Medical Centre, 14 September onward) noted strangulation signs, multiple bruises, possible acute stress disorder, and the applicant’s denial of suicidal intent plus claim of attempted murder. Later Israeli reports confirmed lingering speech/swallowing issues and throat trauma. Applicant-commissioned experts (Russian team and Croatian forensic expert) concluded the injuries (blunt-force trauma to face/body/arms, hyoid fracture, laryngeal oedema, tongue haemorrhage) indicated third-party manual strangulation and beating, not hanging/suicide, and amounted to attempted murder; they highlighted missing hanging indicators and inconsistencies in Azerbaijani records.

Government-commissioned Azerbaijani forensic experts (April 2019) accepted the hanging-suicide version, attributing injuries to the act itself, convulsions, wall contact or medical interventions (e.g., IV sites), and attributing the applicant’s inconsistent accounts to hanging-induced amnesia. They cited first-aid findings of a neck mark and urinary incontinence.

An inquiry by the Sabuncu District Prosecutor’s Office began immediately. The 10 September scene protocol described a tidy cell with no signs of struggle, a looped belt, and a surveillance camera in the corridor. Undated guard statements (Z.I., A.A., T.A.) uniformly described discovering and rescuing the hanging applicant; they noted his low mood over the family but no prior suicide attempts. On 4 October 2017 the investigator refused to open a criminal case, finding a suicide attempt with no criminal elements, citing the protocol, guard/medical statements and prison files. The decision was not shown to have been served on the applicant.

The applicant emailed and posted complaints to the Deputy Prosecutor General in February 2018 alleging attempted murder (supported by media interviews). The Government stated the letter was lost by a postman and never received; an internal inquiry confirmed this. He supplied phone-call recordings from 8 and 11 September 2017 and an Israeli consular note warning of possible renewed proceedings.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s Article 2 complaints of an attempt on his life in detention and an ineffective investigation, with the Court later finding Article 2 applicable due to the life-threatening nature of the incident, the need for urgent intervention, and his critical subsequent condition.

The case of Lapshin v. Azerbaijan (no. 13527/18) before the ECHR concerned an alleged life-threatening attack on the applicant in prison and the authorities’ failure to investigate it effectively, engaging Article 2 of the Convention (right to life).

Applicant Alexander Lapshin, a blogger of Israeli, Russian and Ukrainian nationality, had entered Nagorno-Karabakh in 2011 and 2012 in a manner Azerbaijan deemed illegal. An international arrest warrant led to his arrest in Belarus and extradition to Azerbaijan in February 2017. He was held in Kurdakhany prison, convicted in July 2017 under Article 318.2 of the Criminal Code, and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment plus expulsion. On 11 September 2017 he was pardoned by the President and expelled to Israel on 14 September after hospital discharge.

The core incident occurred on 10 September 2017. The applicant stated that around midnight, while isolated in his cell, masked men entered, restrained him, covered his face, strangled him and beat him; he lost consciousness and awoke two days later in intensive care, voiceless, with facial numbness, impaired mobility, hearing problems and coordination difficulties. The Government’s account was that, after becoming depressed over news that his child’s illness had prevented a family visit, the applicant hanged himself with a bag strap from a towel-rack nail in the cell’s sanitary facility at about 10.05 a.m. Guards found him, performed resuscitation and transferred him to hospital.

Azerbaijani medical records (Merkezi Clinic) recorded him arriving unconscious with a throat mark, hyoid-bone fracture, breathing difficulties and later swallowing/voice problems; he was intubated and sedated. Israeli examinations upon arrival noted strangulation traces, multiple bruises, hematomas and neurological deficits; psychiatrists found no suicidal ideation. Private experts instructed by the applicant (Russian team and Croatian forensic specialist) concluded the injuries—blunt-force trauma, hyoid fracture, tongue bite, laryngeal oedema—were inflicted by third parties via manual strangulation, not hanging, and were incompatible with suicide. Government experts, reviewing the same materials plus prison first-aid notes, maintained the hanging account, attributing extra injuries to convulsions, wall impacts or medical interventions and dismissing Israeli photos as artefacts.

A prosecutor’s inquiry, based solely on a scene protocol (tidy cell, belt with loop found), undated statements from three guards and medical staff, and prison files, decided on 4 October 2017 that it was a non-criminal suicide attempt linked to family distress; no criminal case was opened. The applicant was never served the decision. He later emailed and posted complaints of attempted murder to the Prosecutor General; the Government claimed the letter was lost by a postman.

The Court held Article 2 applicable because of the serious, imminent risk to life, survival only through urgent intervention, and ensuing critical condition. Procedurally, the investigation was ineffective: unexplained discrepancies (time of discovery, who entered first, location of the belt, camera unused), no applicant interview, no forensic tests, no notification, and no response to later complaints. Substantively, the State failed its burden to give a satisfactory explanation; medical evidence of extra injuries, inconsistencies in official statements, and the applicant’s consistent account made the suicide version unconvincing. Violations of both the procedural and substantive limbs of Article 2 were therefore found.

001-210259:
The case of Palfreeman v. Bulgaria (Application no. 840/18) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned allegations by Australian national Jock Anthony Palfreeman of a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. Palfreeman, serving a sentence in Sofia Prison from 2011 to 2019 in a unit for foreign prisoners, claimed that prison guards subjected him and his cellmates to unjustified physical ill-treatment on 17 October 2013 and that the subsequent investigation was neither independent nor thorough.

On the morning of the incident, two guards entered the applicant’s cell (shared with ten other foreign inmates, most of whom spoke no Bulgarian) and ordered the prisoners to line up in the corridor for a routine roll-call. The parties disputed what followed. According to the applicant, the inmates did not understand the order; after the guards locked the wing, a larger group of officers entered, handcuffed the prisoners, led them into the corridor and repeatedly struck them (including with truncheons), kicked them and pushed them against walls. The prisoners were returned to the cell, after which they gathered at the locked wing door demanding access to exercise or classes. Guards later forced entry (after breaking a padlock), lined the men up again and repeated the beatings and kicks. The applicant was then isolated for several hours. He immediately telephoned his lawyer, the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee (BHC) and Australia’s honorary consul.

The Government maintained that the inmates deliberately ignored repeated orders and uttered threats. After the first two guards left and locked the wing, the applicant kicked the cell door open and made his calls; his cellmates then entered the corridor. An intervention team used only “leading techniques” (gripping by the back and neck) to extract the prisoners, applied handcuffs solely to prevent escalation, searched the cell and released the men. No truncheons, kicks or punches were used.

A BHC staffer who visited later that morning observed bruises consistent with truncheon blows on the backs and feet of all but one inmate. The prison doctor recorded three small bruises under the applicant’s right shoulder and noted complaints of head and neck pain without further visible injuries. Most cellmates’ contemporaneous handwritten statements alleged beatings (some written with assistance). Guards reported only the use of authorised “leading techniques.” The Ombudsman’s staff, visiting the next day, confirmed bruises indicating force; while some force might have been justified by disobedience, continued use after extraction or the use of truncheons (absent active resistance) would have been disproportionate. The wing had no cameras.

A preliminary police investigation was assigned to an officer stationed inside Sofia Prison. Later printed statements by the remaining cellmates (taken with unofficial inmate interpreters) denied any beating. Guard statements were largely identical and denied extra force. The officer and successive prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings, citing insufficient evidence. Higher prosecutors quashed several refusals, noting discrepancies between the inmates’ initial handwritten accounts and later statements, the need for sworn translators, and the requirement to clarify the origin of the injuries. Subsequent inquiries by the same officer produced no new material of substance; most cellmates had been released or extradited, and the Ministry of Interior had no sworn translators. All further appeals, including to the Supreme Cassation Prosecutor’s Office, were dismissed.

CPT reports from 2014 and 2015 documented numerous allegations of deliberate ill-treatment of prisoners (especially foreigners) by Sofia Prison staff, including mass beatings with truncheons. The facts as presented thus centred on a contested episode of force against foreign inmates and a protracted, internally delegated inquiry that failed to resolve key contradictions or secure independent evidence.

**Case Summary: Palfreeman v. Bulgaria (ECHR, Application no. 840/18, 8 June 2021)**

The European Court of Human Rights examined allegations under Article 3 of the Convention by Australian national Jock Anthony Palfreeman, who served a sentence in Sofia Prison from 2011 to 2019. He claimed prison guards unjustifiably assaulted him and fellow foreign inmates on 17 October 2013, and that the subsequent investigation lacked independence and thoroughness. His case drew public attention; he was housed in a unit for foreign prisoners.

The incident began around 8:30 a.m. when two guards entered the applicant’s cell (shared with ten other non-Bulgarian-speaking inmates from Iraq, Iran, and Palestine) for a routine roll-call. Accounts diverge. The applicant stated that his cellmates did not understand the order (which he himself was ready to obey). The Government, relying on later investigation materials, claimed the inmates ignored repeated orders and issued threats. The guards locked the cell and wing, reporting to the chief guard.

The applicant alleged that a large group of guards then entered, handcuffed the inmates, led them into the corridor, and repeatedly hit them (including with truncheons), kicked them, and pushed them against walls. After returning them to the cell and locking the wing, inmates gathered at the door, shouting to attend exercise or language classes. One inmate padlocked the door from inside; the applicant telephoned his lawyer, the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee (BHC), and Australia’s honorary consul to report the assault and feared further violence. Guards later broke the lock with help from another prisoner, lined the group against a wall, and again beat and kicked them. The applicant was then isolated for hours.

The Government maintained that the applicant himself kicked the cell door open to make calls, after which cellmates followed. An intervention team used only “leading techniques” (gripping by back and neck) after warnings, without hitting, kicking, pushing, or truncheons. Prisoners were handcuffed briefly for a cell search, then released.

A BHC staffer visiting around midday observed bruises consistent with truncheon blows on the backs and feet of nearly all inmates. The prison doctor that afternoon recorded three 2-by-0.5 cm bruises under the applicant’s right shoulder plus complaints of head and neck pain (without visible injuries there). Same-day handwritten cellmate statements (some assisted by another inmate) largely alleged beatings; later printed statements (via fellow-prisoner interpreters) recanted this. Guards reported only lawful “leading techniques.” The applicant received disciplinary sanctions for disobedience and leaving the cell.

The next day the BHC requested an Ombudsman investigation. Staff interviewed inmates and reviewed reports; the wing lacked cameras. The Ombudsman’s November 2013 report found bruises indicating force, some of which may have been justified by disobedience but potentially disproportionate if continued after extraction from the cell; truncheons were unlawful absent active resistance.

On 22–23 October 2013 the BHC, applicant, and two cellmates complained to prosecutors alleging assault. A “preliminary investigation” was assigned to a police officer stationed inside Sofia Prison. He collected later cellmate statements denying beatings, identical guard statements claiming only lawful measures, and the doctor’s note. His January 2014 report recommended against criminal proceedings, dismissing bruise evidence and BHC observations; the Sofia district prosecutor’s office refused to open a case, largely copying the report.

Multiple appeals followed under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Higher prosecutors twice quashed refusals, citing unaddressed discrepancies between contemporaneous handwritten statements and later recantations, the need for sworn translators, and clarification of injuries. The same prison-based officer handled all additional inquiries (2014–2016). Further cellmate interviews were limited because most had been released or extradited; no sworn translators were used (budget reasons cited). Four refusals occurred, each essentially repeating prior findings. Higher offices (including the Supreme Cassation Prosecutor’s Office in 2017) ultimately upheld the last refusal, finding no confirmation of ill-treatment. No judicial review of refusals was available.

CPT reports from 2014–2015 visits documented numerous allegations of deliberate staff ill-treatment in Sofia Prison, especially of foreign inmates, including mass beatings.

These facts underpin the dual Article 3 claims of unjustified force and an investigation that was neither independent (conducted by a prison-based officer whose reports prosecutors copied uncritically) nor thorough (failing to resolve contradictory evidence or use proper interpreters).

**CASE OF PALFREEMAN v. BULGARIA (Application no. 840/18, ECtHR, 8 June 2021)**

This ECtHR case concerns an Australian national, Jock Anthony Palfreeman, who alleged violations of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from an incident in Sofia Prison on 17 October 2013. He claimed prison guards unjustifiably hit him (including with truncheons), kicked him and pushed him, and that the subsequent investigation lacked independence and thoroughness. Palfreeman, born in 1986, served a sentence in Sofia Prison from August 2011 to September 2019 in a unit for foreign prisoners; his case had drawn significant public and media attention. He was represented by a lawyer from the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee (BHC).

On the morning of the incident, two guards entered Palfreeman’s cell, which he shared with ten other foreign prisoners (mostly Iraqi, Iranian and Palestinian, few of whom spoke Bulgarian). They ordered the inmates to line up in the corridor for a routine roll-call. Accounts diverge. Palfreeman stated that his cellmates did not understand the order (which he himself was ready to obey). The Government, relying on later investigation materials, claimed the prisoners deliberately ignored repeated orders and issued threats. The guards locked the cell and wing door and reported the matter.

Palfreeman alleged that a large group of guards then entered, handcuffed the prisoners, led them into the corridor and repeatedly struck them with truncheons, kicked them and pushed them against walls. After returning them to the cell, the prisoners gathered at the locked wing door, shouting to be allowed out for exercise or language classes. Palfreeman telephoned his lawyer, the BHC and Australia’s honorary consul. Guards later broke a padlock placed on the door (with help from another prisoner), lined the group against a wall and again assaulted them before isolating Palfreeman. The Government maintained that Palfreeman himself kicked the cell door open and made calls; an intervention team then used only “leading techniques” (gripping by the back and neck) after warnings, without blows, kicks, pushing or truncheons. Prisoners were briefly handcuffed during a cell search.

A BHC staffer and lawyer visited around midday and observed bruises consistent with truncheon blows on most cellmates. The prison doctor later recorded three 2 cm by 0.5 cm bruises under Palfreeman’s right shoulder plus complaints of head and neck pain (no other visible injuries). Same-day handwritten statements by cellmates (some drafted with assistance) alleged beatings. Guards reported using “leading techniques” and “auxiliary means.” The prison governor later imposed disciplinary sanctions on Palfreeman for disobeying the roll-call order and leaving his cell.

The Ombudsman’s staff visited on 23 October 2013. The Ombudsman’s report noted bruises indicating force, which may have been initially justified by non-compliance but became disproportionate if continued after removal from the cell; truncheon use was unlawful absent active resistance. The wing lacked cameras.

A BHC complaint prompted a “preliminary investigation” by a police officer stationed inside Sofia Prison. Later printed statements from cellmates (obtained via prisoner interpreters) recanted beating allegations, claiming only lawful physical contact. Guards uniformly denied unlawful force. The officer recommended no criminal proceedings, citing lack of corroboration and asserting the bruises were inconsistent with truncheons (none of which existed in the prison). The Sofia district prosecutor refused to open a case in January 2014, copying the officer’s reasoning.

Appeals highlighted discrepancies between initial handwritten and later statements, the investigator’s lack of independence, and failure to address the Ombudsman’s findings. Higher prosecutors repeatedly quashed refusals and ordered further steps (e.g., sworn translators, clarification of injuries, statements from remaining witnesses). Yet the same in-prison officer conducted three additional inquiries, largely repeating prior reports. Many cellmates had been released or extradited; translators were unavailable. Prosecutors issued three further refusals (2014–2016), each copying the officer’s text, with higher offices ultimately upholding them by 2017, finding no evidence of ill-treatment and noting compliance with prior instructions.

CPT reports from 2014–2015 documented numerous allegations of deliberate ill-treatment of prisoners (especially foreigners) by staff in Sofia Prison, including mass beatings with truncheons and inadequate medical recording of injuries.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 3 claims regarding both the alleged ill-treatment and the investigation’s independence and effectiveness.

**CASE OF IMERI v. CROATIA (Application no. 77668/14), ECtHR (First Section), judgment of 24 June 2021 (final 24 September 2021)**

The case concerned the confiscation of undeclared cash from Norwegian national Ardian Imeri (born 1980) at the Croatia-Slovenia border, alleged to violate Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) as a disproportionate control of the use of property. The Court also addressed just satisfaction under Article 41.

On 13 March 2011, customs stopped Imeri and found he was carrying EUR 43,500 and NOK 730,000 without the required declaration for sums exceeding EUR 10,000. The entire amount was temporarily seized under the Foreign Currency Act and Administrative Offences Act. A drug-detection device indicated traces on Imeri’s hands, phone, banknotes and vehicle seat, but a search found no drugs. Administrative-offence proceedings were opened for the undeclared cash (an offence under the Foreign Currency Act and Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism Act).

Imeri claimed the money represented joint earnings and savings of himself, his brother and his brother’s wife, intended to buy land in Kosovo. He produced company documents, tax declarations, bank records and a preliminary purchase agreement (sale price EUR 150,000). The Ministry of Finance requested Norwegian police information; Interpol later reported Imeri was known in connection with property fraud, though he and his brother had no criminal record and related 2008/2011 theft proceedings had been discontinued for lack of evidence.

On 25 October 2011 the Ministry convicted Imeri, imposed a HRK 5,000 fine and confiscated the full sum as a protective measure. After Imeri’s appeal, the High Court for Administrative Offences quashed the decision and remitted the case. On 5 September 2013 the Ministry again convicted him and fined him HRK 5,000 but confiscated only NOK 530,000, returning EUR 43,500 plus NOK 200,000. It held Imeri must have known of the EU-wide declaration duty. On confiscation it found he had not proved the lawful origin and intended use of the entire sum: the Kosovo land price far exceeded the cash carried; documents showed some savings were possible after 13 years’ work in Norway but not the full amount given living costs. Partial return was justified by evidence of some lawful earnings and the death of Imeri’s child during proceedings. The High Court upheld this on 4 December 2013. Imeri’s constitutional complaint (citing the Court’s Gabrić v. Croatia judgment) was dismissed on 17 June 2014 because, unlike Gabrić, he had not proved lawful origin.

Subsequent information (not before the domestic courts at the time) showed a Norwegian money-laundering investigation, charges in 2016 and a 2017 conviction with imprisonment plus confiscation of other assets; those proceedings concerned later transfers (2013–2014).

The Court treated the whole undeclared sum as Imeri’s “possession” because neither he nor the domestic courts specified his exact share of the co-owned funds. It found the confiscation (in addition to the modest fine) substantially disproportionate to the mere declaration offence. The measure went beyond what was necessary to ensure compliance or pursue legitimate aims of preventing undeclared cash movements and possible money laundering, especially as the authorities had not established the money was proceeds of crime. Later Constitutional Court decisions in similar cases and EU law (including CJEU rulings on the Cash Control Regulation) confirmed that full or near-full confiscation plus a fine for non-declaration is generally disproportionate. Reopening of the domestic proceedings was the most appropriate form of redress for pecuniary damage.
