The case of Imeri v. Croatia concerns the confiscation of undeclared cash by Croatian customs, alleged to violate the applicant’s property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (control of the use of property). The applicant, a Norwegian national, was stopped on 13 March 2011 while crossing from Slovenia into Croatia carrying €43,500 and NOK 730,000. He had not declared the sums, contrary to Croatian law (which implements EU cash-control rules requiring declaration of amounts exceeding €10,000). The entire amount was temporarily seized. A drugs-detection device indicated traces on the applicant’s hands, phone, banknotes and car seat, but a vehicle search found no narcotics.

Administrative-offence proceedings were opened for the non-declaration. The applicant stated that the money represented joint savings and earnings of himself, his brother and his brother’s wife, accumulated over 13 years of work in Norway and intended for the purchase of land in Kosovo. He produced company documents, tax returns, bank-transaction records and a preliminary sale agreement (price €150,000). Croatian authorities sought information from Norway; Interpol initially described the applicant as known for property fraud, but later confirmed he had no criminal record and that earlier theft proceedings had been discontinued for lack of evidence.

In October 2011 the Ministry of Finance found him guilty, imposed the statutory minimum fine of HRK 5,000 and confiscated the whole sum as a protective measure. The High Administrative Offences Court quashed the decision. On remittal, in September 2013 the Ministry again convicted the applicant and imposed the same fine, but confiscated only NOK 530,000, returning the remainder. It accepted that some savings were possible yet held that the applicant had not proved the lawful origin and intended use of the entire amount (the land price exceeded the cash carried and Norwegian living costs made full accumulation implausible). The child’s death during the proceedings was treated as a mitigating factor. The High Court upheld the decision in December 2013. The Constitutional Court dismissed a subsequent complaint in June 2014, distinguishing the case from Gabrić v. Croatia on the ground that lawful origin had not been established.

(The Croatian Government later informed the Court that Norwegian authorities had, after the application was lodged, investigated and convicted the applicant of money-laundering, imposing imprisonment and further confiscation; those proceedings post-dated the Croatian measures and were not decisive.)

The European Court treated the whole undeclared sum as the applicant’s “possession” because neither he nor the domestic courts had specified his exact share. It found that the confiscation of NOK 530,000, in addition to a modest fine, was substantially disproportionate to the mere administrative offence of non-declaration. Domestic authorities had not adequately balanced the general interest in preventing undeclared cash movements against the applicant’s property rights, particularly given the documentary evidence of possible legitimate earnings. A violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was therefore established. The Court indicated that reopening of the domestic proceedings would be the most appropriate form of just satisfaction for pecuniary damage.

The case of Imeri v. Croatia (Application no. 77668/14) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (protection of property) arising from the confiscation of undeclared foreign currency at the Croatian-Slovenian border. The applicant, Ardian Imeri, a Norwegian national born in 1980 and residing in Ski, Norway, was represented by a Zagreb lawyer. The Croatian Government was represented by its Agent.

On 13 March 2011, while crossing from Slovenia into Croatia, customs authorities stopped Imeri and discovered he was carrying EUR 43,500 and NOK 730,000 in cash, which he had not declared as required for sums exceeding EUR 10,000. The entire amount was temporarily seized under the Foreign Currency Act and Administrative Offences Act. A specialised customs official used a drug-detection device, which indicated traces of drugs on Imeri’s hands, mobile phone, the banknotes, and the passenger seat. His vehicle was searched, but no drugs were found.

That same day, the authorities initiated administrative-offence proceedings against Imeri for failing to declare the cash, an offence under the Foreign Currency Act and the Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism Act. In his defence, Imeri stated that the money represented the joint earnings and savings of himself, his brother, and his brother’s wife, intended for purchasing a plot of land in Kosovo. He submitted supporting documents, including tax declarations and business records of companies in which he and his brother held shares and were employed, bank-account transaction reports, and a preliminary agreement for the real-estate purchase (priced at EUR 150,000).

The Ministry of Finance sought information from Norwegian authorities. Interpol Oslo initially reported that Imeri was known to police in connection with property fraud, but later clarified that he and his brother had no criminal record; related theft proceedings from 2008 and 2011 had been discontinued for lack of evidence.

On 25 October 2011, the Ministry found Imeri guilty, imposed a fine of HRK 5,000, and confiscated the entire undeclared sum as a protective measure. Imeri appealed. On 4 July 2012, the High Court for Administrative Offences quashed the decision and remitted the case.

On 5 September 2013, the Ministry again found Imeri guilty and fined him HRK 5,000. It confiscated only NOK 530,000, returning EUR 43,500 and NOK 200,000. The Ministry held that Imeri should have known of the declaration obligation, as it applied in all EU states he transited. Regarding confiscation, it concluded he had not proven the lawful origin or intended use of the full amount: although some savings were possible after 13 years of work in Norway, the high cost of living there made accumulation of the entire sum implausible, and the carried amount was insufficient for the EUR 150,000 purchase. Partial legitimacy was accepted on the basis of the submitted documents, and Imeri’s child’s death during the proceedings was treated as a mitigating factor.

The High Court upheld the decision on 4 December 2013. Imeri lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging a violation of his right to property and citing the Court’s judgment in Gabrić v. Croatia. On 17 June 2014 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, distinguishing the case on the ground that Imeri had not established the money’s lawful origin.

The European Court treated the entire undeclared sum as Imeri’s “possession,” given that neither he nor the domestic courts had specified his exact ownership share. It found the confiscated NOK 530,000 substantially disproportionate to the administrative offence of non-declaration (punished by the statutory minimum fine). For just satisfaction, reopening of the domestic proceedings was identified as the most appropriate remedy for pecuniary damage.

(The Government later submitted information on Norwegian money-laundering proceedings against Imeri concerning transactions in 2013–2014, culminating in a 2017 conviction and additional confiscations; these events post-dated the Croatian confiscation at issue.)
001-210752:
The case of Kirakosyan v. Armenia concerns the prolonged and allegedly incomplete enforcement of a 2005 final judgment requiring a private neighbour (the debtor) to demolish unauthorised constructions (a structure, stairs and fence) that impeded the applicant’s enjoyment of her ground-floor property in a jointly owned two-storey house in Yerevan. The constructions reduced natural light, caused humidity rendering a bedroom unusable and compromised earthquake resistance.

The Arabkir and Kanaker-Zeytun District Court granted the applicant’s demolition claim on 15 November 2004. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld this on 3 March 2005, noting that bailiffs of the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts (DEJA) would execute the order at the debtor’s expense if he failed to comply voluntarily. The Court of Cassation confirmed the judgment on 5 May 2005, rendering it final.

Enforcement proceedings began on 1 June 2005 after a writ issued on 30 May. The debtor ignored a 10 June 2005 order to demolish by 30 June. DEJA initiated, suspended and discontinued proceedings repeatedly in 2005–2006. On 10 May 2006 it discontinued them, asserting full demolition. On 13 July 2006 the Civil Court of Appeal, on the applicant’s challenge, found DEJA had failed to enforce the judgment (citing procedural omissions) and ordered it to do so, without determining whether demolition had in fact occurred. This became final on 28 July 2006.

A second writ issued on 30 August 2006. After an on-site inspection on 25 September 2006, DEJA again discontinued, claiming compliance. The applicant challenged this. A 6 April 2007 District Court inspection saw her identify remaining elements (part of a top-floor structure and metal pillars). The State Real Estate Registry could not furnish confirmatory plans because the debtor obstructed access. The District Court rejected her claim on 10 July 2007, but the Civil Court of Appeal quashed this on 4 October 2007, holding that the 13 July 2006 order remained unenforced and citing a Registry letter confirming unauthorised structures.

A third writ issued on 8 October 2007. DEJA resumed proceedings, conducted another inspection on 22 February 2008 concluding that nothing remained to demolish, and discontinued on 22 and 25 February 2008. The Administrative Court quashed the 22 February decision on 17 December 2009 (upheld by the Court of Cassation on 24 February 2010), finding the inspection record unreliable without expert evidence, and ordered enforcement of the 4 October 2007 judgment.

A fourth writ issued on 23 April 2010. After a 4 June 2010 inspection with municipal specialists reporting full demolition, DEJA discontinued on 18 June 2010. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s challenge on 2 August 2011, placing the burden of proving incompleteness on her and noting she had not rebutted the inspection record or consented to a further visit. Appeals failed in December 2011 and February 2012.

In 2016 the applicant sued the debtor’s heirs, producing a 4 October 2016 expert report identifying remaining metal pillars, wall components and a steel-concrete shelter. The Court of General Jurisdiction ordered their demolition on 30 March 2018 (upheld on appeal and by the Court of Cassation in 2018), finding the remnants still breached her property rights. On 23 June 2020, however, bailiffs discontinued enforcement after expertise showed further demolition would collapse the neighbours’ toilet. The applicant’s appeal against that decision remained pending as of 1 October 2020.

These successive, contradictory enforcement cycles, repeated discontinuations despite judicial findings of non-compliance, shifting evidential burdens and the ultimate physical impossibility of complete demolition form the factual core of the alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to effective enforcement of a final judgment) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

The case of Kirakosyan v. Armenia concerns the incomplete and unduly delayed enforcement of a 2005 judgment requiring a private neighbour (the debtor) to demolish unauthorised constructions that interfered with the applicant’s property rights. The applicant owned the ground floor of a two-storey house on land jointly owned with neighbours occupying the upper floor. She sued the debtor to remove an unlawful structure, access stairs and fence that reduced natural light, caused excessive humidity (rendering a bedroom unusable) and weakened the building’s earthquake resistance.

On 15 November 2004 the District Court ordered demolition. This was upheld by the Civil Court of Appeal on 3 March 2005 (which also directed bailiffs to execute the order at the debtor’s expense if necessary) and became final after the Court of Cassation’s decision of 5 May 2005.

Enforcement proved protracted and ineffective. The first set of proceedings, begun in June 2005, was discontinued in May 2006 on the ground that demolition had been completed. The Civil Court of Appeal quashed that decision in July 2006, finding the judgment unenforced, and ordered the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts (DEJA) to proceed. A second set of proceedings followed; after an on-site inspection the bailiffs again discontinued enforcement in September 2006. The District Court rejected the applicant’s challenge, but the Civil Court of Appeal reversed that ruling in October 2007, holding that earlier final judgments established non-enforcement and that a State Real Estate Registry letter confirmed remaining unauthorised structures.

A third set of proceedings was discontinued in February 2008 after another inspection. The Administrative Court, in a final December 2009/February 2010 judgment, annulled the discontinuation because the inspection report lacked expert evidence on whether demolition had actually occurred and ordered enforcement of the October 2007 decision. A fourth set of proceedings ended in June 2010 after an inspection involving municipal specialists concluded that all structures had been removed. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s subsequent action in August 2011 (upheld on appeal and cassation in 2011–2012), placing the burden of proof on her and accepting the inspection record as sufficient evidence of completion.

In 2016 the applicant sued the debtor’s heirs, relying on a fresh expert report that identified remaining metal pillars, wall fragments and part of a steel-and-concrete shelter. The first-instance court found in her favour in March 2018, a ruling confirmed on appeal and becoming final in December 2018. Enforcement of this new judgment was itself discontinued in June 2020 after expert evidence indicated that further demolition would collapse the neighbours’ toilet; the applicant’s challenge remained pending in October 2020.

The sequence of contradictory administrative decisions, repeated discontinuations without adequate expert verification, shifting burdens of proof and the continued presence of remnants more than fifteen years after the original judgment form the factual core of the alleged breaches of the right to a fair hearing (Article 6 § 1) and the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

The case of Kirakosyan v. Armenia concerns the incomplete enforcement of a 2005 court judgment requiring demolition of unlawful constructions on shared property, raising issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing, including effective enforcement of judgments) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

The applicant, Emma Kirakosyan, owns the lower floor of a two-storey house in Yerevan on a jointly owned plot; her neighbours own the upper floor. She sued her neighbour (the debtor) for demolition of unauthorised constructions—an added structure, stairs to the upper floor, and a fence—that obstructed her property. On 15 November 2004 the District Court ordered demolition. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld this on 3 March 2005, finding that the constructions reduced natural light, caused excessive humidity (rendering the bedroom unusable) and weakened the building’s earthquake resistance. It directed that if the debtor did not comply voluntarily, the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts (DEJA) must execute the order at the debtor’s expense. The Court of Cassation confirmed the ruling on 5 May 2005, making it final.

Enforcement began in June 2005. After the debtor failed to act, DEJA initiated, suspended and discontinued proceedings multiple times. In May 2006 it discontinued the first set, claiming full demolition. On the applicant’s appeal the Civil Court of Appeal ruled in July 2006 that DEJA had not properly enforced the judgment (failing to set a compliance deadline or compel action) and ordered it to do so.

A second set of proceedings followed. An on-site inspection in September 2006 again asserted demolition, leading to discontinuation. The applicant challenged this. After a further inspection and a State Real Estate Registry letter noting incomplete information due to the debtor’s obstruction, the District Court initially upheld DEJA. The Civil Court of Appeal reversed this in October 2007, holding that the 2005 judgment remained unenforced.

Proceedings resumed. A February 2008 inspection again claimed no remaining structures, prompting discontinuation. The Administrative Court quashed this in December 2009 (upheld by the Court of Cassation in February 2010), finding the inspection record unreliable without expert construction evidence, and ordered enforcement of the prior appellate ruling.

A fourth set began. A June 2010 inspection with municipal specialists concluded that demolition was complete, and DEJA discontinued proceedings. The applicant’s challenge failed: the Administrative Court (August 2011, upheld on appeal) placed the burden on her to prove incompleteness and found she had not done so or contested the inspection record.

In 2016 the applicant sued the debtor’s heirs, submitting a private expert report identifying remaining metal pillars, wall components and part of a steel-and-concrete shelter. In March 2018 the Court of General Jurisdiction ordered the heirs to demolish the remnants, citing the expert evidence of ongoing interference with the applicant’s rights. This was upheld on appeal. However, in June 2020 DEJA discontinued enforcement, citing a new expert finding that further demolition would collapse the neighbours’ toilet. The applicant’s appeal against that decision remained pending as of October 2020.

The facts thus show a 15-year history of repeated DEJA discontinuations based on contested inspections, successive court findings of non-enforcement, and later judicial confirmation of remaining structures, followed by a new practical obstacle. These circumstances underpin the alleged violations of the applicant’s rights to effective judicial protection and undisturbed property use.

The case of Memedov v. North Macedonia (Application no. 31016/17) concerns an applicant of Roma ethnic origin who alleged racially motivated police brutality during an incident on 5 May 2013 in the Roma neighbourhood of Topaana, Skopje, and the authorities’ failure to investigate possible racist motives. He invoked Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 3, and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

Police officers from the “Alfa” unit attended the area that evening to arrest a convicted fugitive suspected of a knife assault. After the arrest, a crowd of local residents gathered around the police vehicle, some attempting to extract the suspect, using offensive language and throwing stones and other objects. Reinforcements arrived; officers ordered the crowd to disperse and pushed non-compliant individuals toward nearby shops. Five people, including the applicant, were arrested inside the shops. Two officers were injured and a police car damaged.

The applicant’s account differed: officers entered the shop, insulted those present and physically attacked them, punching and striking them with batons on the head and body. One officer allegedly told him, “Shut up, you Gypsy motherfucker!” He protested, stating he was in the army, but neither resisted nor attacked the officers. He was taken into custody at 10.30 p.m.; police records noted visible injuries to his arms, neck and back. He appeared before an investigating judge the next day and was released early on 7 May 2013.

Medical certificates of 7 and 9 May 2013 recorded bruises on his upper right chest (11-12 cm), left shoulder (22-23 cm, consistent with a truncheon), head, neck and chest, plus head pain. Later records diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder. Photographs confirmed the bruises.

Internal Ministry reports confirmed the crowd’s actions and use of proportionate force against several persons but contained no specific details of force used against the applicant. The Sector for Internal Control similarly found the force lawful and proportionate, providing details only for three others.

The Ministry charged the applicant and four others with assaulting police officers by throwing objects. An investigating judge stayed the investigation after the prosecutor withdrew the charges for lack of evidence.

The applicant, via the Helsinki Committee and then personally, complained to the Sector of beatings and verbal abuse in the shop, alleging the reaction was provoked by his Roma origin and constituted discrimination, ill-treatment and torture. The Sector declined further inquiry, citing its earlier findings.

In March 2014 he lodged a criminal complaint against six identified officers for ill-treatment, torture, violence and racial discrimination. He requested examination of the officers and co-accused. The first-instance prosecutor initially rejected it, finding the acts not subject to State prosecution and the intervention lawful. After a higher prosecutor ordered resumption, delays ensued; the applicant, who had left for Germany and sought asylum citing harassment, was not heard until 2019. Officers denied arresting or using force on him. The prosecutor ultimately rejected the complaint in October 2019, finding no evidence of physical force or racial motivation. Injuries were noted but their timing, manner and location could not be established; the applicant could not identify the officers. A higher prosecutor confirmed this in January 2020.

In civil proceedings under the Discrimination Act against the Ministry, the applicant claimed racially motivated abuse. The first-instance court heard officers (who denied force), a co-accused (who confirmed beatings and Roma-related slurs) and the applicant’s father (who confirmed slurs). Video footage showed officers beating a person in the shop, but identity could not be confirmed. The court credited the beating accounts but found no evidence of discrimination based on Roma origin, noting the neighbourhood’s demographics explained why all those arrested were Roma and that officers were not selective. Slur evidence was dismissed as biased. The appeal court upheld this. Separate proceedings against the prosecution office for failing to investigate (unlike other 2014 complaints) were dismissed, as was a Constitutional Court challenge.

International reports on the situation of Roma in North Macedonia were submitted. These facts form the core of the alleged substantive ill-treatment with a racial motive and the procedural investigative shortcomings.

Reinforcements arrived and officers pushed people toward two nearby shops, arresting five persons inside, including the applicant. Two officers were injured and a car damaged. Police records noted the applicant’s visible injuries to his arms, neck and back upon custody at 10.30 p.m.

The applicant’s account differed: several officers entered a shop and insulted and beat those present (including him) with punches and batons to the head and body. One officer allegedly shouted “Shut up, you Gypsy motherfucker!” The applicant protested that he was in the army, neither resisted nor attacked anyone, and was released on 7 May 2013. Medical certificates of 7 and 9 May 2013 recorded bruises consistent with truncheon blows on his chest (11-12 cm), left shoulder (22-23 cm), head, neck and back, plus later post-traumatic stress disorder. Photographs corroborated the injuries. A Ministry report confirmed the applicant had been seen near the police car but gave no specific details of force used against him.

The applicant and four others were charged with assaulting officers by throwing objects, but the investigation was stayed on 10 June 2013 for lack of evidence. The applicant then pursued complaints of ill-treatment and racial discrimination. The Sector for Internal Control found the force used lawful and proportionate and declined further inquiry. On 28 March 2014 he lodged a criminal complaint against six named officers. Prosecutors repeatedly rejected it (November 2014, March 2017, October 2019), citing lawful duty performance, lack of evidence of force or racist motive, and inability to establish how the injuries occurred; higher prosecutors twice ordered resumption for incomplete fact-finding. The applicant was eventually heard in 2019 and described subsequent harassment urging him to withdraw his complaint. A final rejection was upheld in January 2020.

In parallel civil proceedings under the Discrimination Act, the applicant sued the Ministry in 2016. The first-instance court (December 2018) accepted that officers had hit him in the shop (supported by a co-accused and his father, plus video footage of a beating) but found no racial discrimination, attributing arrests to the Roma neighbourhood setting rather than ethnic targeting and dismissing testimony of slurs as biased. The appeal court upheld this in April 2019. A separate claim against the prosecution service for investigative failings was dismissed in 2018-2019 as the inquiry had followed applicable rules. A 2019 constitutional challenge remained unresolved. International reports on the situation of Roma in North Macedonia were submitted in the proceedings.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s claims of racially motivated brutality and inadequate investigation. (Word count: 512)
001-211033:
The applicant, Tofig Yagublu (born 1961), was a prominent opposition figure as deputy chairman of the Musavat Party, a member of the Public Chamber, and a newspaper columnist. He alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention arising from two administrative arrests in May 2012, which he claimed were politically motivated to prevent his participation in unauthorised Public Chamber protests in Baku.

On 24 May 2012, according to the applicant, plain-clothes officers arrested him around 10.30 a.m. near his home and took him first to the Surakhani district police office for “prophylactic conversations” and then to police station no. 31. The Government stated that the arrest occurred around noon near a market. An administrative-offence record charged him under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (failure to obey a lawful police order) on the basis that he had behaved suspiciously, refused to produce identity documents and used offensive language. He was denied a lawyer despite requests. At around 5 p.m. the Surakhani District Court, after hearing only two police officers and without addressing the applicant’s account that he had been framed to stop him attending a protest, convicted him and imposed a 20-manat fine. He was released from the courtroom. His appeal, in which he was represented by counsel of his choice and in which he reiterated that the arrest, more-than-eight-hour detention, denial of family contact and mobile phone, lack of legal assistance and one-sided evidence violated Articles 5 and 6 and amounted to political discrimination, was dismissed by the Baku Court of Appeal on 18 June 2012.

The second arrest occurred on 25 May 2012. The applicant stated that, after leaving a metro station around 5.45 p.m. with his minor son, he was warned not to approach the planned protest site, turned away, and was then seized by four plain-clothes officers and taken to the Sabail district police office, where he remained until noon the following day. The Government asserted that he was arrested at 7.30 p.m. while participating in the unauthorised demonstration. He was again charged under Article 310.1 for failing to stop participating in the protest and was denied a lawyer. He described overcrowded conditions: first a 20 m² walking area holding 63 people until 3 a.m., then a cell designed for eight that held 23 people, with no drinking water supplied. He also complained that his son had been left unattended in the courtyard. The Government maintained that only four persons were held in the facility, that the applicant occupied a 14 m² cell alone, and that he received bedding, water and food. On 26 May the Sabail District Court, after hearing one police officer and ignoring the applicant’s denial of participation, convicted him and imposed another 20-manat fine. His subsequent appeal, raising the same fairness complaints plus Article 3 allegations concerning the detention conditions and uncertainty over his son’s whereabouts, was dismissed on 18 June 2012 without examination of the ill-treatment claims.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that both arrests and detentions were arbitrary, that the administrative proceedings lacked the guarantees of a fair trial, that the second period of detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, and that no effective domestic remedy existed.

**Summary of Yagublu v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, Application no. 69686/12)**

The applicant, Tofig Yagublu (born 1961), was at the material time deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat Party, a member of the Public Chamber political union, and a columnist. The Public Chamber organised two unauthorised protests in Baku on 24 and 25 May 2012 (in front of the public television building and at Seaside Park), both of which were dispersed promptly. Yagublu alleged that his two successive administrative arrests, detentions, and convictions were politically motivated to prevent his participation, and that they violated Articles 5 § 1, 6, 3, and 13 of the Convention.

On 24 May 2012, according to the applicant, he was arrested around 10:30 a.m. near his home in Garachukhur by plain-clothes officers while heading to work, taken to Surakhani district police office for “prophylactic” conversations, and then transferred around 4 p.m. to police station no. 31. He was not allowed a lawyer despite requests and could not contact family. An administrative offence record charged him under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (failure to obey a lawful police order). Police reports claimed he had been behaving suspiciously near a market, refused to produce identity documents, and used offensive language. The Government placed the arrest later (around noon) and at a different location. Around 5 p.m. he appeared before Surakhani District Court, where he represented himself after declaring he would do so. The court heard only the two arresting officers, ignored his account that the arrest was a pretext to block the protest, convicted him, and imposed a 20 AZN fine. He was released from court. His appeal to Baku Court of Appeal (where he had counsel) was dismissed on 18 June 2012 without addressing his arguments on unlawfulness, lack of legal assistance, refusal to hear his witnesses, or political discrimination; the decision was final.

On 25 May 2012 the applicant stated that he and his minor son left Sahil metro station around 5:45 p.m. A uniformed officer told them not to proceed toward Seaside Park; they turned the other way but were immediately arrested by four plain-clothes officers and taken to Sabail district police office, where he was held until around noon on 26 May. His son was left unattended in the courtyard. He received no lawyer despite requests and could not contact family. The offence record again invoked Article 310.1, alleging participation in the unauthorised demonstration and failure to stop. The Government claimed arrest occurred later (around 7:30 p.m.) at the demonstration itself and that he was released at 10 a.m. on 26 May. Detention conditions were sharply disputed: the applicant described being held first in a 20 m² walking area with 63 others until 3 a.m., then in an 8-person cell with 23 others, and being denied drinking water; the Government asserted only four detainees in total, that he occupied a 14 m² cell alone, and that bedding, water and food were provided.

On 26 May he appeared before Sabail District Court, again representing himself after refusing a State-funded lawyer. The court heard only one police officer, disregarded the applicant’s claim that he had been arrested before the demonstration and had not participated, convicted him, and imposed another 20 AZN fine. He was released from court. His appeal (again with counsel) was dismissed on 18 June 2012; the appellate court did not examine his complaints of overcrowding, denial of water, or anxiety over his unattended son. He also alleged discrimination on political grounds.

The facts thus centre on two short but successive periods of administrative detention (over 8 hours then over 19 hours), contested locations and purposes of arrest, denial of legal assistance at the police and first-instance stages, exclusive reliance on police testimony, and disputed conditions of the second detention, all occurring immediately around planned opposition protests.

The case of Yagublu v. Azerbaijan (no. 69686/12) involves Tofig Yagublu, a 1961-born Azerbaijani opposition figure (Musavat Party deputy chairman, Public Chamber member, and newspaper columnist). He alleged that his May 2012 arrests and detentions violated Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (unlawful/arbitrary deprivation of liberty), that related administrative proceedings breached Article 6 (fair trial guarantees), that conditions after his second arrest amounted to Article 3 inhuman/degrading treatment, and that he lacked an effective Article 13 remedy. The Public Chamber had organized two unauthorized Baku protests on 24–25 May 2012 (near a TV building and Seaside park), both quickly dispersed.

On 24 May, Yagublu claimed arrest around 10:30 a.m. by plain-clothes officers ~100–150 metres from his Garachukhur home while heading to work. He was taken to Surakhani district police office for consecutive “prophylactic” conversations with senior officers, then (around 4 p.m.) to station No. 31. Officer Y.M. cited an “order to arrest.” An administrative record charged him under CAO Article 310.1 (disobeying a lawful police order) for “suspicious” behaviour, failing to produce ID, and using offensive language. The Government stated arrest occurred around noon near an Amirjan market, with direct transfer to the station. Yagublu received no lawyer despite requests. At ~5 p.m. he appeared before Surakhani District Court, where he waived counsel and self-represented. Two officers (E.A., Y.M.) repeated the official account; the court ignored Yagublu’s contrary version (different location/circumstances, politically motivated framing to block protest attendance) and convicted him, imposing a 20 AZN fine. He was released from court. His appeal to the Baku Court of Appeal (now with chosen counsel) detailed an 8+ hour detention, family-contact denial, phone seizure, sole reliance on police evidence, refusal of his witnesses, initial lack of counsel, and political discrimination. On 18 June 2012 the appeal was dismissed as correctly decided; no further appeal lay.

On 25 May Yagublu stated that around 5:45 p.m., after exiting Sahil metro with his minor son, an officer ordered them away from Seaside park. They complied but four plain-clothes officers immediately arrested him. Both were taken to Sabail DPO; the son remained unattended in the courtyard while Yagublu was held until ~noon on 26 May. He again received no lawyer. Charged under the same CAO provision for joining the unauthorized protest and ignoring a stop order (per officers F.M. and E.G.). The Government placed arrest at 7:30 p.m. during the protest itself, with detention until 10 a.m. Yagublu described being held until 3 a.m. in a 20 m² walking area with 63 others, then in an 8-person cell with 23 occupants, and denied drinking water. The Government asserted only four detainees total, a 16.3 m² walking area, and sole occupancy of a 14 m² two-person cell supplied with bedding, water and food. On 26 May Sabail District Court heard one officer (F.B.) repeating the official narrative, ignored Yagublu’s account (pre-protest arrest, no participation or disobedience), and again fined him 20 AZN after he refused a state lawyer and self-represented. His identically dated appeal (with chosen counsel) repeated unlawfulness claims (19+ hours), fair-trial defects, political bias, plus Article 3 complaints about overcrowding, water denial and distress over his unattended son. The appeal court upheld the conviction without examining ill-treatment allegations.

These facts centre on disputed arrest circumstances timed to the protests, short but contested detentions, exclusive police evidence, first-instance absence of counsel, and the second episode’s physical conditions and familial impact.
001-210534:
The case of Kurnosova v. Russia (Application no. 36072/07), decided by an ECtHR Committee on 15 June 2021, concerned a fine imposed on the applicant, Olga Vladimirovna Kurnosova (a St Petersburg journalist born in 1961), for publishing an article calling for participation in a public demonstration. The article was written by a regional leader of the National Bolsheviks Party, whose activities had been suspended pending court proceedings to ban it as an extremist organisation. This raised issues of alleged interference with the applicant’s rights under the Convention (primarily freedom of expression and/or assembly) through administrative liability for editorial decisions linked to a public event.

On 2 March 2007 the Moscow City prosecutor applied to court to declare the National Bolsheviks Party extremist and ban it. On 21 March 2007 the acting prosecutor suspended the party’s activities pending those proceedings, pursuant to section 10(1) of the Suppression of Extremism Act. Suspended organisations and their branches were prohibited from, among other things, publishing mass media or organising/holding public events.

On 5 April 2007 a special issue of the Yabloko party newspaper Petersburg Ahead (distributed in St Petersburg) was released. The applicant served as its executive editor. The issue was dedicated to the “March of Dissenters” planned for 15 April 2007 by a coalition of opposition groups. It called for participation, explained the march’s aims and political demands, and included an article by Mr D., leader of the National Bolsheviks of St Petersburg, urging supporters to attend.

On 14 April 2007 police searched the St Petersburg Yabloko office and seized copies of the special issue. The following day the Justice of the Peace of the 201st Court Circuit of St Petersburg convicted the applicant under Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) of a premeditated breach of the established procedure for public events. The court described her as the organiser of the meeting and march who had involved members of the (suspended) National Bolsheviks Party by publishing Mr D.’s article, which called for participation and advocated the party’s ideology. This was held to breach section 16 of the Suppression of Extremism Act (prohibiting involvement of extremist organisations in mass gatherings and imposing responsibility on organisers). The court added that, as a journalist, the applicant had a duty to verify information and should have known of the 21 March suspension; by publishing the calls she had allowed a suspended association to participate in organising the event. She was fined 1,000 Russian roubles (approximately EUR 28.5).

The applicant appealed. She argued she had complied with the Public Events Act, so there was no basis for CAO liability. The article had been written by Mr D. in a private capacity as an ideological supporter rather than as a party member; she had received it on 18 March 2007 (before the 21 March suspension); and the party had not yet been judicially banned as extremist. On 31 May 2007 the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg upheld the conviction. It found a breach of public-event procedure through publication of an article by a member of the suspended party that advocated its ideology. The appellate judgment cited only Article 20.2 § 1 CAO.

The Suppression of Extremism Act defined extremist organisations and authorised pre-ban suspension, with restrictions on media use and event organisation. Section 16 prohibited extremist activities at public events and the involvement of (suspended) extremist organisations, with organisers liable for failures. At the relevant time Article 20.2 CAO punished organisers of public events for procedural breaches with fines of 10–20 minimum wages. These facts formed the core of the alleged Convention violations, centred on whether the fine constituted an unjustified restriction on publishing a call to a demonstration involving a not-yet-banned association.

The case of Kurnosova v. Russia (Application no. 36072/07), decided by an ECtHR Third Section Committee on 15 June 2021, concerned a fine imposed on journalist Olga Vladimirovna Kurnosova for publishing material that called for participation in a public demonstration. The applicant, born in 1961 and living in St Petersburg, served as executive editor of a special issue of the Yabloko party newspaper Petersburg Ahead. The issue, released on 5 April 2007, promoted the March of Dissenters scheduled for 15 April 2007, a protest organised by a coalition of opposition groups. It outlined the event’s aims and political demands and included an article by Mr D., leader of the St Petersburg branch of the National Bolsheviks Party (NBP), urging supporters to attend.

The NBP’s status formed the core of the domestic proceedings. On 2 March 2007 the Moscow City prosecutor had applied to a court seeking a declaration that the NBP was extremist and its ban. On 21 March 2007 the acting Moscow City prosecutor suspended the party’s activities pending those proceedings, pursuant to section 10(1) of the Suppression of Extremism Act. Under that Act a suspended association and its branches were prohibited from publishing media, using state or municipal media, or organising or holding public events.

On 14 April 2007 police searched the St Petersburg Yabloko office and seized copies of the special issue. The next day the Justice of the Peace of the 201st Court Circuit of St Petersburg convicted the applicant of an administrative offence under Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for breaching the established procedure for public events. The court found that, by publishing Mr D.’s article, she had involved members of the already-suspended NBP in the March, thereby violating section 16 of the Suppression of Extremism Act (which forbids involving extremist organisations in mass gatherings and makes organisers responsible for compliance). As a journalist she had a duty to verify published information and therefore should have known of the 21 March suspension. She was fined 1,000 roubles (approximately EUR 28.50).

The applicant appealed. She maintained that she had complied fully with the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004), so liability under the CAO lacked any legal basis. She further argued that Mr D. had written in a purely private capacity as an adherent of National Bolshevik ideology rather than as a party official; that she had received the article on 18 March 2007, before the suspension decision; and that the NBP had not yet been judicially banned as extremist. On 31 May 2007 the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed the appeal, holding that publication of an article by a member of the suspended party that advocated its ideology itself constituted a breach of public-event procedure. The District Court cited only Article 20.2 § 1 CAO.

The Suppression of Extremism Act defined an extremist organisation as one dissolved or banned by a final court decision. Section 10(3) spelled out the consequences of interim suspension, including the media and event-organisation bans later invoked against the applicant. Section 16 placed positive duties on event organisers to prevent extremist participation and provided for liability if they failed. At the relevant time Article 20.2 CAO prescribed fines of ten to twenty minimum wages for organisers who breached event-procedure rules. A 24 July 2007 amendment (after the events) required publication of lists of suspended associations, but no such official list existed when the newspaper appeared.

These facts raised issues of foreseeability and necessity of the interference with the applicant’s journalistic activities in connection with a planned peaceful assembly. The small fine was imposed solely for disseminating a call to a public protest authored by a person associated with an organisation that had been administratively suspended but not yet judicially banned, and in circumstances where the applicant claimed she could not have known of the suspension at the time she accepted the text.

The case of Kurnosova v. Russia (Application no. 36072/07) concerned a fine imposed on journalist Olga Vladimirovna Kurnosova for publishing an article calling for participation in a public event. The article was written by a regional leader of the National Bolsheviks Party, whose activities had been suspended pending court proceedings to ban it as an extremist organisation.

On 2 March 2007 the Moscow City prosecutor applied to have the National Bolsheviks Party declared extremist and banned. On 21 March 2007 the acting Moscow City prosecutor suspended the party’s activities under section 10(1) of the Suppression of Extremism Act pending those proceedings. A suspended association and its branches were barred from publishing mass media or organising or holding public events.

On 5 April 2007 a special issue of the Yabloko party newspaper Petersburg Ahead, of which the applicant was executive editor, appeared in St Petersburg. The issue was devoted to the “March of Dissenters” planned for 15 April 2007 by a coalition of opposition groups. It explained the march’s aims and political demands and called for participation. It also carried an article by Mr D., leader of the St Petersburg National Bolsheviks, urging their supporters to attend the march.

On 14 April 2007 police searched the St Petersburg Yabloko office and seized copies of the special issue. The following day the Justice of the Peace of the 201st Court Circuit of St Petersburg convicted the applicant of a breach of the established procedure for public events under Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The court found that she had committed a premeditated breach by involving members of the suspended National Bolsheviks Party in the event. She had done so by publishing, as executive editor, Mr D.’s article containing calls to participate and advocating the party’s ideology. This violated section 16 of the Suppression of Extremism Act, which prohibits organisers of mass gatherings from involving extremist organisations. As a journalist the applicant had a duty to verify published information and therefore should have known of the 21 March suspension. She was fined 1,000 Russian roubles (approximately EUR 28.50).

The applicant appealed. She maintained that she had complied with the Public Events Act and that her conviction therefore lacked a legal basis. The article had been written by Mr D. in his private capacity as a supporter of National Bolshevik ideology, not as a party official. She had received the text on 18 March 2007, before the suspension took effect, and in any event the party had not yet been banned as extremist when the newspaper was released.

On 31 May 2007 the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. It held that the applicant had breached the procedure for public events by publishing an article by a member of the suspended party that advocated its ideology. The District Court relied only on Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences and cited no other domestic provisions.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that the fine violated her Convention rights, in particular those relating to freedom of expression and the organisation of public events. The domestic courts treated the mere publication of the article as sufficient to constitute “involvement” of a suspended organisation in a public gathering, despite the applicant’s arguments concerning timing, the author’s capacity and the absence of a final ban.
001-211013:
The case of Orazbayev and Others v. Russia concerns four applicants’ allegations of police ill-treatment in Chechnya (2002–2006), mainly at the notorious ORB-2 facility in Grozny, plus ineffective investigations into those claims (and related complaints). CPT statements from 2003 onward singled out ORB-2 for frequent, grave torture allegations corroborated by medical evidence, a climate of fear deterring complaints, and the authorities’ failure to conduct meaningful inquiries.

Orazbayev was arrested in April 2004 for arms possession and later charged with terrorism. Transferred to ORB-2 in November 2004, he alleged officers handcuffed him, beat him with fists/truncheons, applied electric shocks and plastic-bag suffocation over several days (and again in February 2005) to extract confessions. After retracting those statements, he claimed further beating at Shelkovskoy IVS in July 2005. A July 2005 forensic report documented bruises and scars consistent with recent trauma, though remand-prison records noted none. Investigators repeatedly refused to open a case, citing officers’ denials and a claim that injuries came from co-detainees. A cellmate testified at trial to seeing bruises and the applicant’s inability to walk after night-time interrogations. The Chechen Supreme Court convicted him in April 2006, relying on the contested confessions and dismissing the ill-treatment claims; the conviction was upheld on appeal.

Satabayev was arrested in March 2002 during a Grozny operation (found with a gun) and allegedly beaten on arrest, then subjected at ORB-2 to punches, kicks, water-filled bottles, gas-mask suffocation, electric shocks, cigarette burns and hanging by handcuffs until he signed unread papers. Similar treatment occurred during later transfers (Leninskiy VOVD, further ORB-2 visits). An October 2002 medical record and April 2003 forensic report confirmed recent bruises from blunt objects. A 2002 complaint produced a refusal to prosecute. Post-conviction complaints (2007 and 2013, after ECHR notification) likewise failed, with investigators citing officers’ denials, destroyed records and the original conviction. He was convicted in 2003.

Chapanov was seized at home in September 2005 by unidentified armed men and taken to ORB-2, where he alleged overnight beatings with bottles, shocks, gas-mask suffocation and cigarette burns, plus later threats to rape his pregnant wife. Confessions followed. A December 2005 forensic report confirmed multiple cigarette-burn scars. Inquiries were refused on the basis of officers’ denials and a cellmate’s (later recanted) claim of self-infliction; the cellmate testified at trial that police had coerced that statement. The Chechen Supreme Court convicted him in December 2006 on the confessions, finding the injuries self-inflicted; the conviction was upheld.

Zulkarnayev was seized near his Volgograd-region home in April 2006 by officers claiming GRU affiliation, bagged, handcuffed in a stress position and beaten until he signed unread papers; further beating occurred at Volgograd UBOP. After transfer to Chechnya he alleged repeated ill-treatment at ORB-2 and an IVS. Initial medical notes recorded bruises and cuts; cellmates later described a broken arm, wounds and inability to walk. An inquiry was refused because witnesses were unavailable and later records showed only an arrest-related scar. The Chechen Supreme Court convicted him in May 2007 on the (partly retracted) confessions.

These facts underpin the applicants’ claims of torture/inhuman treatment and of wholly inadequate investigations that systematically privileged police denials over medical evidence, witness accounts and the well-documented practices at ORB-2.

The case of Orazbayev and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 15367/07 and three others) concerns four Russian nationals who alleged they suffered ill-treatment while in police custody in Chechnya between 2002 and 2006, primarily at the Operational-Search Bureau (ORB-2) in Grozny, along with ineffective investigations into those claims. The European Court of Human Rights examined these under Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment) and related issues, including the use of allegedly coerced confessions in criminal trials.

Orazbayev was arrested in April 2004 in Stavropol Region on arms charges and later accused of terrorism. Transferred to ORB-2 in November 2004, he alleged officers handcuffed him, beat him with fists, kicks and truncheons, applied electric shocks and suffocated him with a plastic bag over several days, forcing a confession. Further beatings occurred in February 2005 before a verification of statements and in July 2005 at the Shelkovskoy IVS after he retracted his confession. A forensic examination in July 2005 documented bruises and scars consistent with recent trauma. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open a criminal case, citing officers’ denials and a cellmate’s claim of self-inflicted injuries. At trial, the Supreme Court of Chechnya convicted him in 2006 relying on the confession, dismissing a cellmate’s testimony of visible bruises and the applicant’s inability to walk after night-time interrogations as unreliable.

Satabayev was arrested in March 2002 in Grozny during a special operation. He alleged severe beatings during arrest, followed by prolonged ill-treatment at ORB-2 (punches, kicks, water-filled bottles, gas-mask suffocation, electric shocks to ears and fingers, and cigarette burns) through April, May, July, September and October 2002, often after complaints or retractions. Medical records from October 2002 showed multiple large bruises; a 2003 forensic report confirmed they resulted from blunt-force trauma days earlier. Investigators refused to open a case in 2002, 2007 and 2013, relying on destroyed logs, officers’ denials and the trial court’s earlier rejection of the claims. He was convicted in 2003, with the Supreme Court of Russia upholding the judgment.

Chapanov was detained in September 2005 by unidentified armed men and taken to ORB-2. He described beatings with water bottles, electric shocks, gas-mask suffocation and cigarette burns; officers also threatened to rape his pregnant wife. He made multiple confessions. Further burns occurred in November 2005. A December 2005 forensic report identified eight burn scars inflicted one to two months earlier. An investigator refused to open a case, accepting officers’ denials and a cellmate’s (later recanted) statement that the injuries were self-inflicted. The trial court convicted him in 2006 on the basis of the confessions, rejecting the recantation as unreliable.

Zulkarnayev was seized in April 2006 near Volgograd by officers claiming to be from military intelligence, who bagged his head, handcuffed him in a painful position and beat him until he signed unread papers. Further beatings occurred at the Volgograd organised-crime unit and repeatedly at Chechen facilities including ORB-2. Admission records noted bruises and cuts. Cellmates later testified to seeing extensive bruising, a broken arm and the applicant’s inability to walk or eat after overnight absences. A 2007 prosecutorial inquiry refused to open a case, citing missing records, departed officers and denials of force. He was convicted that year, the court relying on the confessions and deeming the allegations unfounded.

Council of Europe CPT public statements from 2003, 2007 and 2013 singled out ORB-2 as a site of systematic, medically corroborated ill-treatment amid a climate of fear that deterred complaints. In each case domestic authorities conducted only pre-investigation inquiries, never full criminal investigations, and trial courts used the resulting confessions while dismissing supporting medical and witness evidence.

The case of Orazbayev and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 15367/07 and three others) concerns four Russian nationals’ complaints of ill-treatment while in police custody in Chechnya between 2002 and 2006, primarily at the Operational-Search Bureau (ORB-2) in Grozny, together with the alleged ineffectiveness of subsequent investigations. The European Court of Human Rights also noted related complaints under well-established case-law, including the use of resulting confessions at trial.

Orazbayev was arrested in April 2004 on arms charges and later transferred to Chechnya on terrorism-related accusations. Held at ORB-2 from 20 November 2004, he alleged that officers handcuffed him, beat him with fists, feet and truncheons, applied electric shocks and suffocated him with a plastic bag until he fainted, continuing until 23 November and again on 27 November to extract a confession. Further beatings occurred at ORB-2 on 10 February 2005 and at the Shelkovskoy IVS in July 2005 after he retracted statements. A July 2005 forensic examination recorded bruises and scars consistent with recent trauma, although remand-prison records noted none. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open a criminal case, citing officers’ denials and a medical assistant’s claim that injuries were inflicted by co-detainees. The Supreme Court of Chechnya convicted him in April 2006, relying on the confession statements and dismissing a cellmate’s testimony of visible injuries and nocturnal interrogations; the conviction was upheld on appeal.

Satabayev was arrested in Grozny in March 2002 during a special operation and allegedly beaten on the spot. At ORB-2 he claimed officers punched and kicked him, used water-filled bottles, induced suffocation with a gas mask, administered electric shocks, burned him with cigarettes and left him hanging by handcuffs, prompting him to sign unread documents. Similar treatment recurred at the Leninskiy VOVD in May and again at ORB-2 in July, September and October 2002, the last episode following a prosecutor’s complaint. An October 2002 medical record documented multiple recent bruises later confirmed by forensic examination as caused by blunt objects. Inquiries in 2002, 2007 and 2013 all refused to open a case, relying on officers’ denials, destroyed records and the applicant’s conviction. He was convicted in 2003; the conviction was upheld.

Chapanov was seized at home in September 2005 by unidentified armed men and taken to ORB-2, where he alleged beatings with water-filled bottles, electric shocks, gas-mask suffocation and cigarette burns, plus threats against his pregnant wife. He confessed to robberies. Further threats and a cigarette burn occurred in November. A December 2005 forensic report recorded eight burn scars. Prosecutors attributed the injuries to self-infliction on the basis of a cellmate’s statement; the cellmate later testified at trial that he had been coerced. The Supreme Court of Chechnya convicted Chapanov in December 2006, relying on the confessions and dismissing both the ill-treatment claim and the cellmate’s recantation; the conviction was upheld.

Zulkarnayev was abducted in April 2006 near Volgograd by officers claiming to belong to military intelligence, hooded, handcuffed in a painful position and beaten until he signed unread papers. After transfer to Chechnya he alleged further ill-treatment at the Nozhay-Yurtovskiy IVS and ORB-2, including overnight sessions that left him unable to walk. Cellmates corroborated bruises, a broken arm and repeated nocturnal removals. Medical records were incomplete or recorded only an arrest-related scar. A 2007 inquiry refused to open a case, citing unavailable witnesses, officers’ denials and the absence of recorded injuries. He was convicted in May 2007 on the basis of the confessions; the conviction was upheld, though the court dated his detention from the unofficial arrest.

Across all applications, prosecutors consistently declined to open criminal investigations, relying on official denials while discounting medical evidence, witness statements and the applicants’ recantations. The case of Azer Ahmadov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 3409/10) concerns the secret interception of telephone conversations of an opposition journalist. The applicant, born in 1962 and living in Baku, served as editor-in-chief of the opposition newspaper Azadlıq. The alleged violations arise primarily under Article 8 (respect for private life and correspondence), with related claims under Articles 6, 10 and 13, stemming from the tapping of his calls in the context of an investigation into an assault on a colleague.

In February 2008, journalist A.K., also employed by Azadlıq, was allegedly beaten by Ministry of National Security (MNS) agents while photographing in Olive Gardens; proceedings into this incident were later discontinued. On 13 March 2008, A.K. was stabbed while returning home. Criminal proceedings followed, with the investigation relying in part on intercepted conversations that ultimately led to the conviction of S.S.

On 14 March 2008, the Sabail District Court granted an application by the First Deputy Prosecutor General authorising operational-search activities for six months in respect of A.K. “and his contacts.” The decision, citing information that the stabbing had been organised by foreign special services to aggravate the socio-political situation, permitted covert interception of telephone and other conversations, audio/video recordings, postal surveillance, inspections of premises and observation of persons. It was based on Articles of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Law on Operational-Search Activities, with execution entrusted to the MNS.

A 10 May 2008 MNS letter to the Prosecutor General’s Office referenced the substance of a 7 May 2008 call from the telephone number used by the applicant to one used by colleague V.M. In that conversation V.M. informed the applicant of an alleged attempt to push A.K. under a train, after which A.K. took the phone and confirmed the information. The applicant learned of the interception in July 2008 when his lawyer, also representing A.K., reviewed the stabbing case file.

On 29 July 2008 the applicant brought civil proceedings against the MNS, arguing that no court decision specifically authorised the tapping of his telephone, that none of the exceptional grounds for interception without prior judicial authorisation applied, and that the measure unlawfully interfered with his privacy and (in general terms) his Article 10 rights as a journalist who received information from sources. He sought a declaration of unlawfulness and compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

Domestic courts initially declared the action inadmissible, holding that lawfulness should be examined under the Code of Criminal Procedure rather than civil law. After a Supreme Court remittal noting that the MNS was not shown to be conducting the criminal proceedings and that the applicant was not a participant therein, the MNS disclosed the 14 March 2008 decision. The Sabail District Court dismissed the claim on 24 June 2009, finding the interception lawful because the applicant was one of A.K.’s contacts and (erroneously, according to the applicant) because they had used the same number. Appeals were unsuccessful.

Separately, the applicant lodged an appeal against the 14 March 2008 decision itself once he obtained a copy in June 2009. Courts rejected it for lack of standing, holding that only the person in respect of whom the measures had been ordered (A.K.) and his lawyer could challenge it.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: an overly broad and imprecise judicial authorisation covering an undefined category of “contacts” of a stabbing victim, applied to intercept conversations of a journalist who was neither a suspect nor a formal participant in the proceedings, without adequate legal precision or an effective domestic avenue for the affected person to contest the measure.

The case of Badalyan v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 51295/11) involves an Armenian national, Artur Badalyan (born 1978), who alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 5 § 1 (right to liberty and security) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from his capture and 22-month detention by Azerbaijani forces.

On 9 May 2009, Badalyan disappeared while picking mushrooms in a forest near the Armenia-Azerbaijan border in the Tavush region, close to Navur village, in the company of unarmed friends. Witnesses reported his sudden disappearance. Armenian police registered him as missing on 11 May 2009, searched the area (finding only mushrooms 5-6 km from the border), interviewed locals, and opened a criminal investigation in July 2009, which was later suspended. His whereabouts remained unknown to family and Armenian authorities until 5 November 2010, when the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) registered him as an Armenian captive in Baku. The ICRC visited him regularly until his release on 17 March 2011 through ICRC-mediated exchange of captives in the Agdam region.

Badalyan, who claimed to have been a healthy civilian with no military role, alleged capture on Armenian territory by four individuals who spoke Armenian then Azerbaijani, bound him, and transferred him across the border. He was held in various undisclosed military facilities for 22 months as a presumed military prisoner. Conditions included insufficient food, denial of toilet access (forcing him to relieve himself in the cell), repeated beatings to the legs causing loss of sensation and mobility, electric shocks via wires attached to his fingers, and metallic objects striking his cell door, resulting in a hearing disorder. He endured harassment to extract information, mental anguish, and was never informed of detention reasons in a language he understood, brought before a judicial authority, or given opportunity to challenge lawfulness. As a civilian, he asserted he should have been released immediately. No health records were kept during captivity.

Upon release, he was hospitalized in Armenia on 18 March 2011 and diagnosed with neurasthenia, depression, fear, stress, anxiety, fatigue, and arm/leg pains. Later examinations at a Yerevan mental health centre (June-July 2011 and subsequent 3-4 week periods through 2015) revealed chronic delusional disorder, protracted reactive paranoia, spinal disc hernia, hallucinations (voices, beliefs of implanted control devices and cameras), insomnia, aggression toward family, and eventually paranoid schizophrenia requiring recommended inpatient care. He received state disability benefits from October 2011 as unfit for work.

Azerbaijan contended that Badalyan illegally crossed the border, initially requested transfer to a third country due to poor conditions in Armenia (prolonging his stay pending ICRC arrangements), then reversed course. He was detained as an Armenian armed forces member and saboteur, treated as a prisoner of war under the 1949 Geneva Convention, and released in a POW exchange. Authorities claimed continuous medical supervision with no ill-treatment; documents showed 2009-2011 examinations (blood/urine tests, dental check, physical assessments finding no issues) and a 7 March 2011 psychiatric note detecting no psychopathological symptoms or mental illness.

Armenia, as third-party intervener, reported that post-release investigation (reopened March 2011) included Badalyan's police statement of kidnapping on Armenian soil and transfer of the case to national security authorities.

These facts underpin the alleged degrading treatment (unexplained serious mental injuries linked to detention conditions and torture) and unlawful, incommunicado detention at an undisclosed site without legal safeguards.

The case of Tabak v. Croatia (Application no. 24315/13) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ivan Tabak, claimed he was denied a fair hearing in Croatian civil proceedings because the courts relied on the opinion of a court-appointed expert, V.B., who had professional ties to the defendant insurance company.

On 8 June 1995, Tabak was injured in a road traffic accident, suffering a knee injury. He was granted a disability pension from 1 January 1999. In May 1999, he sued the insurance company C.O. before the Đurđevac Municipal Court for damages, including non-pecuniary loss, lost income, and a monthly allowance.

The first-instance court obtained several expert reports. In 2000, surgeon D.H. opined that Tabak’s disability retirement stemmed from spinal issues rather than the knee injury. In 2002, traffic expert F.R. attributed the accident equally to both parties’ speeding. In March 2006, following the defendant’s proposal, the court appointed V.B., an occupational medicine specialist and permanent court expert, to assess the link between the knee injury and Tabak’s work capacity. V.B.’s June 2006 report (supplemented in October) concluded that initial sick leave (9 June–26 August 1995) related to the accident, but subsequent leave and reduced capacity were due to pre-existing knee and spinal conditions unrelated to the accident.

The Municipal Court, in its 2 March 2007 judgment, held Tabak 50% responsible (based on F.R.), awarded partial compensation for non-pecuniary damage and lost income up to retirement (drawing on D.H. and V.B.), but dismissed the monthly allowance claim based on V.B.’s findings. After appeals, the Koprivnica County Court quashed and remitted the lost-income portion. Further first-instance judgments in the remitted proceedings (2009–2012) granted only a small sum for the initial sick-leave period and dismissed the rest, again relying on V.B. that later incapacity was unrelated to the accident.

In his March 2012 appeal against the final first-instance dismissal of remaining lost-income claims, Tabak (now with new lawyers) raised for the first time that V.B. lacked impartiality. Publicly available information showed she had served as a medical examiner in C.O.’s directorate general in 1995 and as president of the management board of its subsidiary C.Z.O. from March 2004 (during the period of her expert reports). He argued this required her disqualification under the Civil Procedure Act (sections 71 and 254), as experts could be recused on the same grounds as judges (including employment by a party). He attached her professional biography and claimed her conclusions demonstrated bias by downplaying the injury’s impact.

The County Court dismissed the appeal on 4 September 2012. It held that Tabak was precluded from raising the impartiality objection for the first time on appeal under section 352(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, as such procedural objections (not considered by the first-instance court of its own motion) must be raised earlier. Section 254 required parties to seek disqualification as soon as they learned of grounds, at latest before evidence-taking (or immediately upon later discovery). The court noted V.B. was not employed by C.O. itself at the time of her reports. Tabak’s constitutional complaint, arguing that section 352(1) allowed new facts on serious procedural breaches and that he had raised the issue promptly upon discovery, was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 19 December 2012 as manifestly ill-founded.

These facts formed the basis of Tabak’s Article 6 § 1 complaint that the courts’ reliance on a potentially biased expert, combined with the appellate court’s refusal to examine the issue, denied him a fair hearing on the defendant company’s liability.

The case of Tabak v. Croatia (no. 24315/13) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) in civil proceedings. The applicant, Ivan Tabak, complained that domestic courts had based their decisions on the opinion of an expert, V.B., who had professional ties to the defendant insurance company, rendering the hearing unfair.

On 8 June 1995 the applicant sustained a knee injury in a road traffic accident. He was granted a disability pension from 1 January 1999. In May 1999 he sued insurer C.O. before the Đurđevac Municipal Court for damages, including non-pecuniary loss, lost income and a monthly allowance.

The court commissioned several expert reports. In March 2006, at the defendant’s proposal and with the applicant and his then-lawyer present, it appointed V.B., a permanent court expert in occupational medicine, to assess the link between the accident injury and the applicant’s reduced work capacity. V.B.’s June 2006 report (supplemented in October 2006) concluded that only the initial period of sick leave (9 June–26 August 1995) was attributable to the accident-related knee injury. Subsequent incapacity and the disability retirement itself stemmed from pre-existing knee pathology and spinal/cervical-nerve conditions unrelated to the accident. The applicant challenged V.B.’s conclusions on their merits at a December 2006 hearing and questioned her at a February 2007 hearing, but did not raise any issue of impartiality. He later even relied on parts of her oral evidence to support his claim.

The first-instance court, relying inter alia on V.B., held the applicant 50 % responsible for the accident, awarded limited damages, and dismissed the monthly-allowance claim because the disability pension was not caused by the accident injury. After appeals, remittals and further proceedings (including an unsuccessful appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court), the remaining lost-income claim covering the period after 26 August 1995 was again dismissed in March 2012 solely on the basis of V.B.’s findings.

Only then, in his March 2012 appeal and now represented by new lawyers, did the applicant first object that V.B. should have been disqualified. Publicly available information (her professional biography, attached to the appeal) showed she had served as a medical examiner in the defendant company’s directorate-general in 1995 and as president of the management board of its subsidiary C.Z.O. from March 2004 until an unknown retirement date. He argued this constituted an absolute ground for exclusion under the Civil Procedure Act (ss. 71 and 254) and that her findings themselves demonstrated bias.

The Koprivnica County Court dismissed the appeal in September 2012. It observed that V.B. had not been employed by the defendant itself at the time of her 2006 report. More decisively, the applicant was procedurally barred from raising the impartiality objection for the first time on appeal. Under ss. 254 and 352 of the Civil Procedure Act, a party must request an expert’s disqualification as soon as the ground becomes known and at latest before the expert evidence is taken; if the ground is discovered later, the court treats the objection as if made in time. Because the first-instance court does not examine such matters of its own motion, an untimely objection cannot be introduced on appeal. The applicant’s constitutional complaint reiterating that he had raised the issue immediately upon learning of it was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded by the Constitutional Court in December 2012.

(The European Court of Human Rights later held that the applicant had failed to act with the necessary diligence in using his available procedural rights concerning the expert’s neutrality, so the second-instance court’s inability to examine the complaint was mainly imputable to him.)

In Tabak v. Croatia the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that civil proceedings determining an insurer’s liability for accident-related injury were unfair because the courts relied on an expert with undisclosed ties to the defendant.

On 8 June 1995 Tabak injured his knee in a traffic accident. He received a disability pension from 1 January 1999 and sued insurer C.O. in May 1999 before the Đurđevac Municipal Court. The court commissioned reports from surgeon D.H. (2000) on pain and disability causation and from traffic expert F.R. (2002) on fault; Tabak accepted the latter but disputed D.H.’s view that spinal changes, not the knee injury, caused retirement.

In March 2006 the court, on the defendant’s proposal and after hearing Tabak’s then-lawyer, appointed occupational-medicine specialist V.B. (a permanent court expert) to assess any causal link between the accident and reduced work capacity. V.B.’s June and October 2006 written reports, based solely on medical records, concluded that only a short 1995 sick-leave period was accident-related; later incapacity and retirement stemmed from pre-existing spinal disease and cervical-nerve damage. Tabak challenged the reports; V.B. was examined in February 2007 and Tabak subsequently relied on her oral evidence to support part of his claim.

The first-instance court (2007) found Tabak 50 % at fault (F.R.) and awarded limited non-pecuniary and lost-income damages up to retirement, but dismissed a monthly-allowance claim from 1999 onward, expressly relying on V.B. After remittals confined to the remaining lost-income period, the same court in March 2012 again dismissed that claim on V.B.’s findings.

Only then, in a March 2012 appeal drafted by newly instructed lawyers who had examined the file, did Tabak first allege V.B.’s lack of neutrality. Publicly available data showed she had served as a medical examiner in C.O.’s directorate-general in 1995 and later as president of the management board of its subsidiary C.Z.O. (until an unspecified retirement date). He argued she should have been disqualified under Civil Procedure Act ss. 71 and 254 and that her conclusions themselves evidenced bias. The Koprivnica County Court rejected the appeal (September 2012). It noted that V.B. was not employed by C.O. itself when she reported, and held Tabak procedurally barred: under s. 352(2) an objection the first-instance court does not examine of its own motion cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, and under s. 254 a party must seek an expert’s disqualification as soon as the ground is known (or, if discovered later, immediately upon objecting to the report). The Constitutional Court dismissed the subsequent complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

The Strasbourg Court found no violation. The applicant had failed to act with the diligence required of a party concerning an expert’s neutrality and had not used the available procedural safeguards; the second-instance court’s inability to examine the complaint was therefore a situation mainly and objectively imputable to him.
