The case of Adomaitis v. Lithuania (ECHR, Application no. 14833/18) concerns complaints by former Kybartai prison director Virginijus Adomaitis under Articles 6 § 1, 13 and 8 of the Convention. He alleged that he lacked a fair hearing and effective challenge to the lawfulness of secret interception of his communications during a criminal intelligence investigation, and that use of the resulting material in disciplinary proceedings leading to his dismissal breached his right to respect for private life.

In June 2015 the Internal Affairs Division of the Department of Prisons opened a criminal-intelligence investigation against Adomaitis on suspicion of abuse of office (Criminal Code Art. 228 § 1), namely that he had, for payment, granted inmates better conditions and unwarranted incentives. A prosecutor applied to the Vilnius Regional Court, citing prior unsuccessful conventional measures and the applicant’s sensitive post. On 30 June 2015 the court authorised interception of his telephone and other electronic communications for three months; successive extensions (September 2015, December 2015, March 2016) were granted on the basis of newly obtained transcripts that mentioned payments. Covert listening devices were also installed in his office throughout the same twelve-month period—the statutory maximum.

The criminal investigation was discontinued on 23 June 2016 for lack of evidence sufficient to charge. The prosecutor nevertheless authorised declassification and use of the material in disciplinary proceedings. Adomaitis sought access to the file. In March 2017 the Vilnius Regional Court ordered disclosure of declassified reports (including 54 pages of conversation transcripts) but excluded, pursuant to Art. 19 § 7 of the Law on Criminal Intelligence, details of methods, tactics and the identities of secret participants. He received these documents in 2017 and again during later court proceedings.

He then challenged the lawfulness of the surveillance itself. The Prosecutor General’s Office dismissed the complaint in August 2017, finding the investigation properly opened and conducted. The Vilnius Regional Court, after examining the classified file, upheld that decision in September 2017, holding that the measures had been judicially authorised, that each extension was supported by fresh evidence of possible criminality, and that interception was proportionate given the applicant’s position inside a closed prison and the public interest in preventing corruption that could affect early release of inmates.

Meanwhile the Ministry of Justice, relying on the declassified intelligence, imposed a strict reprimand (September 2016) for improper organisation of internal staff competitions and dismissed Adomaitis (November 2016) for awarding unprocured mobile-telephone contracts to associates and using the prison car for private purposes. Both decisions characterised the conduct as gross disciplinary offences amounting to abuse of office.

Adomaitis contested the penalties before the administrative courts. After a stay pending a Constitutional Court ruling of 18 April 2019 (which confirmed that declassified intelligence relating to corruption-related misconduct could be used in disciplinary proceedings provided courts scrutinise lawfulness, reliability and proportionality), the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed his claims in December 2020. It found the intelligence lawfully obtained and transferred, the offences established by a combination of witness testimony, documents and the intercepts themselves, and dismissal a proportionate sanction for a prison director. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment in April 2021, emphasising that the applicant had been able to contest the evidence and that the use of the material served the legitimate aims of transparency and prevention of corruption in the civil service.

The court granted the request on 30 June 2015 for an initial three-month period and later extended it, on the basis of transcripts of intercepted conversations that mentioned payments, until June 2016. Covert listening devices were also installed in the applicant’s office.

The investigation was discontinued on 23 June 2016 for lack of evidence sufficient to bring criminal charges. The prosecutor nevertheless authorised use of the collected material in disciplinary proceedings. The applicant sought access to the intelligence file. In March 2017 the Vilnius Regional Court ordered disclosure of information that was not restricted under Article 19 § 7 of the Law on Criminal Intelligence. He received declassified reports (including 54 pages of transcripts) together with the court authorisations; information concerning methods, tactics and the identities of secret participants was withheld. He also challenged the lawfulness of the measures. Both the Prosecutor General’s Office and, on appeal, the Vilnius Regional Court (ruling of 25 September 2017) found the investigation lawful and proportionate. They noted that it had lasted the statutory maximum of 12 months, that extensions had been based on newly obtained information, and that the applicant’s position inside a closed institution made interception a necessary and proportionate means of investigating suspected corruption that endangered public safety.

On the strength of the declassified material the Minister of Justice imposed a strict reprimand in September 2016 for unlawful organisation of internal staff competitions and, in November 2016, dismissed the applicant for signing a telecommunications contract without public procurement, using a prison vehicle for private purposes and related abuses of office. The applicant contested both decisions before the administrative courts. After suspensions (including one awaiting a Constitutional Court ruling of 18 April 2019 that permitted declassified intelligence to be used in corruption-related disciplinary cases), the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed the claim in December 2020. It held that the intelligence had been obtained and used lawfully, that the offences were proved by a combination of witness statements, documents and the applicant’s own conversations, and that dismissal was an appropriate penalty for two gross disciplinary offences committed by a senior manager. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment in April 2021, emphasising that the applicant had been given access to the relevant materials, that the use of the intelligence pursued legitimate aims of transparency and prevention of abuse in public service, and that it was proportionate.

The European Court of Human Rights subsequently found no violation of Article 6 § 1 (effective access to court, adversarial proceedings and equality of arms) or of Article 8 (interference necessary in a democratic society and accompanied by adequate safeguards).

The ECHR case of Adomaitis v. Lithuania (no. 14833/18) concerned complaints by Virginijus Adomaitis, former director of Kybartai prison, under Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention. He alleged that he lacked a fair hearing and effective means to challenge the lawfulness of telephone interceptions conducted during a criminal intelligence investigation, as well as the subsequent use of that material in disciplinary proceedings that led to his dismissal, and that this interfered with his right to respect for private life.

On 22 June 2015 the Internal Affairs Division of the Department of Prisons opened a criminal-intelligence investigation into suspected abuse of office (Criminal Code Art. 228 § 1). The suspicion was that the applicant had, for payment, granted inmates better living conditions and unwarranted incentives. On 26 June a prosecutor, citing prior unsuccessful conventional inquiries and the applicant’s senior position, applied to the Vilnius Regional Court for authorisation to intercept his electronic communications. The court granted the request on 30 June for an initial three-month period, relying on intelligence reports. Authorisations were extended three times (until June 2016) on the basis of newly intercepted conversations that mentioned payments. Covert listening devices were also installed in the applicant’s office.

The investigation was discontinued on 23 June 2016 for lack of evidence sufficient to bring criminal charges. The prosecutor nevertheless authorised the declassified material to be used in disciplinary proceedings.

The applicant obtained access to two declassified reports (including 54 pages of conversation transcripts) and, later, to the court authorisations and related prosecutor applications, but certain operational details (methods, identities of covert participants) remained withheld under Art. 19 § 7 of the Law on Criminal Intelligence. He challenged the lawfulness of the measures before the Prosecutor General’s Office (dismissed August 2017) and the Vilnius Regional Court (dismissed September 2017). The latter found the twelve-month interception proportionate, given the applicant’s role in a high-security prison, the corruption-related nature of the suspicions, and the successive emergence of new incriminating information.

Disciplinary action followed. On 26 September 2016 the Minister of Justice imposed a strict reprimand for organising internal competitions so as to favour associates. On 3 November 2016 the applicant was dismissed for, among other things, awarding mobile-telephone contracts without public procurement and using a prison vehicle for private purposes—conduct characterised as gross official misconduct and abuse of office.

He contested both penalties before the administrative courts. After delays linked to related proceedings and a 2019 Constitutional Court ruling on the use of intelligence material, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (December 2020) and the Supreme Administrative Court (April 2021) dismissed his claims. They held that the declassified material had been lawfully obtained and transferred, that the offences were established by a combination of transcripts, witness statements and documents, and that dismissal was a proportionate response to two intentional gross breaches committed by a prison director. The applicant had been able to examine and contest the evidence in adversarial proceedings.

These facts formed the basis of the complaints that the interception and its later disciplinary use had been neither fairly reviewable nor necessary and proportionate.

The case of Kramareva v. Russia (Application no. 4418/18) was brought by Anastasiya Olegovna Kramareva, a Russian national born in 1990 and residing in Lyubertsy, against the Russian Federation under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. At the first-instance hearing the applicant’s representatives, the company’s representatives and a third-party company appeared and made submissions. A prosecutor also attended. At the close of the hearing the prosecutor opined that only the claim for documents should be granted and the remaining claims dismissed. The parties then delivered oral closing arguments. The applicant repeated her request that all claims be allowed, without specifically addressing the prosecutor’s opinion. The company sought full dismissal and objected to the prosecutor’s partial support of the applicant.

At the Moscow City Court hearing she and her representative maintained their claims while the company opposed them. The prosecutor supported the first-instance judgment. Cassation appeals to the Moscow City Court (28 June 2017) and the Supreme Court (25 July 2017) were dismissed.

Constitutional Court rulings confirm that the opinion cannot predetermine the court’s decision, which must rest on a full examination of the parties’ arguments and evidence, and that such participation does not upset adversarial equality.

The case of E.M. and Others v. Norway (ECtHR, Application no. 53471/17, judgment of 20 January 2022) concerns complaints under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life) arising from Norwegian child-protection decisions. Czech national E.M. (born 1976) applied in her own name and on behalf of her sons B (born 2005) and C (born 2008). The Court first held that E.M. lacked standing to represent the children: their interests conflicted with hers because of findings of serious joint parental neglect and a care order based on concerns that she had failed to protect them.

E.M. moved to Norway in 2005 to live with A (also Czech). Their sons were born and raised there. On 20 May 2011 the children were placed in emergency care amid concerns of sexual abuse and violence. The parents separated; E.M. was to have daily care, but the children remained in emergency placement by agreement. Contact (initially weekly, later twice weekly) ceased in August 2011 after further statements prompted a police investigation. E.M. later filed for separation.

On 8 February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board issued a public-care order, finding serious neglect and physical abuse (it declined to assess sexual abuse further). Return to E.M. was highly likely to result in further serious neglect. She was granted supervised contact of two hours four times a year; A received none. The children entered separate foster homes in spring 2012.

The District Court (July 2012) upheld the care order but withdrew E.M.’s contact rights. It found serious care deficiencies, physical punishment, and probable sexual abuse by A of which E.M. had been aware (and had sometimes observed). The children associated her with violence and abuse and displayed fear during sessions. The High Court (March 2013) restored limited contact (two hours twice yearly, supervised). It found insufficient evidence that E.M. had herself abused the children or knowingly failed to intervene, but held she had failed to shield them, had slapped them, and shared responsibility for neglect. Experts indicated she needed to shift focus from herself to the children. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused. An earlier ECtHR application concerning these events was declared inadmissible.

In December 2014 E.M. sought to have the care order lifted. Child-welfare authorities sought its continuation, removal of her parental responsibilities, refusal of contact with B, and authorisation of C’s adoption. After hearings, the Board (September 2015) refused to lift the orders, withdrew parental responsibilities, refused contact with B and authorised C’s adoption, citing E.M.’s extensive media exposure of the case (including children’s photographs and details of alleged sexual abuse) that had distressed B.

The District Court (June 2016), after hearing 18 witnesses, found E.M.’s parenting capacity had improved but that the children still needed specialised care. B had PTSD from complex neglect; his caregivers could not be those who had caused the trauma. He firmly opposed return, citing painful memories and violence, and showed severe physical anxiety (shaking, chest/throat pain) at the mere mention of contact. C, placed at age 2½, had only weak ties to E.M., a strong attachment to his foster family, and likewise opposed return. Media publication of sensitive information (including parts of an expert report) had already harmed B and risked harming C. Return would therefore not be in either child’s best interests. Parental responsibilities were withdrawn for both boys because E.M. had used information obtained through those responsibilities to publicise private details, thereby violating their privacy; she would otherwise retain access to further confidential records. Contact with B was refused on “special and compelling reasons”: forcing it risked his health and contradicted his expressed wishes and best interests. Contact with C was likewise refused because of his serious adverse reactions (agitation, sleeplessness, soiling). Adoption of C was refused, principally to preserve the sibling bond with B.

The High Court refused leave to appeal (November 2016); the Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee dismissed a further appeal (January 2017). The ECtHR later held that the domestic decisions were justified: proceedings had been extensive and accompanied by adequate safeguards; reasons were relevant and sufficient; they were based on the children’s best interests; the measures were neither irreversible nor permanent; and considerable attention had been given to the mother-child relationship. There was accordingly no violation of Article 8.

C was well-adjusted with no comparable difficulties. Both children strongly opposed return: B described constant painful memories of violence; C stated that his parents had “lost all parent points” and that he wished to remain where “nobody is mean.” E.M. had posted sensitive material online (including parts of an expert report on sexual abuse and B’s health information). For C, adoption was refused in order to preserve the sibling bond, but parental responsibilities were likewise withdrawn for privacy reasons (he would soon have internet access). Contact was refused because of his documented pre- and post-visit reactions (agitation, sleep disturbance, soiling). The High Court refused leave to appeal in November 2016; the Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee dismissed the further appeal in January 2017.

These successive decisions, reached after multi-stage proceedings that included expert evidence, the children’s appointed representative and the children’s own expressed views, constitute the impugned interferences with family life.

**Case of Y v. Poland (Application no. 74131/14), ECtHR (First Section), judgment of 17 February 2022 (final 17 May 2022)**

The applicant, a Polish national born in 1969 and living in France, was registered as female at birth. He later underwent gender reassignment. On 6 April 1992 the Warsaw District Court ordered an annotation on his birth certificate recording the change of sex from female to male and of first name from X to Y; the annotation was entered. He married K. in a civil ceremony in 1993. Their daughter A. was born in France in 2001; her French birth certificate lists the applicant as father.

In 2005 the applicant requested the Prudnik Civil Registry Office to remove the 1992 annotation from his birth certificate. The request was refused under section 21 of the 1986 Civil Status Records Act, which required post-birth events affecting a record to be entered as a “marginal annotation.” Subsequent administrative and judicial appeals (Opole Governor, Opole Regional Administrative Court, Supreme Administrative Court) were dismissed; the courts held that only annotations contrary to law or personal rights could be removed, and the gender-change annotation was lawful.

In 2011 the applicant applied to the Warsaw District Court for a new birth certificate, invoking by analogy the 1986 Act provisions (sections 48–49) that permit a fresh certificate (with the original sealed) in cases of full adoption. The District Court, Regional Court and Supreme Court (28 May 2014) rejected the request. They held that new certificates were available only in the specific circumstances listed by statute (adoption); a birth certificate records the situation at birth and later gender reassignment is recorded solely by annotation. Civil-status provisions could not be applied analogically. After annotation a person may obtain a new PESEL number and identity documents reflecting the reassigned gender. A short extract of the birth certificate omits deleted text and, in most official contexts (marriage, identity documents, passports), is sufficient; a full copy (which includes all annotations) is required only in limited situations such as certain adoptions, nationality applications, complex inheritance or criminal proceedings.

The applicant also referred to 2010 French foster-care proceedings in which custody of his wife’s niece was granted to the wife; the child lived with the family. He complained under Article 8 that the continued presence of the original-sex annotation on the full birth certificate violated his right to respect for private life, because it disclosed his transgender history even though short extracts and new identity documents showed only the reassigned gender. He further alleged discrimination under Article 14 taken with Article 8, arguing that he was treated less favourably than adopted children, who receive a new, sealed original certificate.

The Court noted that Polish law provided a judicial route to legal gender recognition (declaratory judgment under Article 189 of the Code of Civil Procedure, followed by annotation) that had been available since at least the early 1990s. The applicant had obtained recognition, a new name, new identity documents and the ability to marry and be registered as father. The Court found he had not demonstrated any sufficiently serious concrete negative consequences or practical difficulties arising from the annotation. Full copies are rarely required. Any potential risk of disclosure was not shown to render the system as a whole deficient. A fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s privacy interest and the public interest in the integrity and historical accuracy of civil-status records; the State had not overstepped its margin of appreciation. The applicant was not in an analogous situation to adopted children, whose original parentage is replaced by a new legal parentage, so no discrimination arose.

The case of Y v. Poland (Application no. 74131/14) concerned a Polish national born female in 1969 who later underwent gender reassignment surgery and obtained legal recognition of his male gender. In 1992, a Warsaw District Court ordered an annotation on his original birth certificate recording the change of sex from female to male and of his name from X to Y. Thereafter he obtained a new PESEL number and identity documents reflecting only his reassigned gender. He married in 1993 and, in 2001, became the father (as recorded on the French birth certificate) of a daughter born in France, where he now lives.

Polish law (the 1986 Civil Status Records Act, later substantially reproduced in the 2014 Act) requires that any post-birth event affecting the content of a civil-status record be entered as a “marginal annotation.” A full extract of the birth certificate reproduces the original text plus all annotations; a short extract incorporates the legal effects of those annotations but omits the original wording. In everyday official dealings (marriage, identity documents, passports) only the short extract is required. A full extract is needed only in limited circumstances such as adoption proceedings, certain nationality or name-change applications, complex inheritance cases, or criminal proceedings if prior convictions are in doubt.

In 2005 the applicant asked the civil-registry office to delete the 1992 annotation. The request was refused on the ground that the annotation was mandatory. Successive administrative and judicial appeals, culminating in a 2008 Supreme Administrative Court judgment, confirmed that the annotation could not be removed because it was neither unlawful nor contrary to personal rights.

In 2011 the applicant applied to the Warsaw District Court for an entirely new birth certificate, invoking by analogy the provisions that allow a new certificate to be drawn up after full adoption (ss. 48–49 of the 1986 Act). Those provisions replace the original parents with the adoptive parents and thereafter withhold the original certificate except in narrowly defined circumstances. Both the District Court and, on appeal, the Regional Court held that the adoption rules were exhaustive and could not be applied analogously; a birth certificate records the facts existing at the moment of birth, and subsequent gender reassignment is properly recorded by annotation. The Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal in May 2014, reiterating that the statutory scheme did not permit a new certificate after gender recognition.

The applicant complained under Article 8 that the continued existence of the annotated full certificate forced him, on the rare occasions when a full extract was demanded, to reveal his transgender history, thereby interfering with his private life. He also invoked Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, arguing that he was treated less favourably than adopted persons who receive a “clean” new certificate.

The Court observed that the applicant had not identified any concrete, sufficiently serious adverse consequences he had actually suffered. He lived and worked in France, where his French documents and his daughter’s birth certificate already recorded him as male; he had not shown that Polish authorities or private parties had required a full Polish extract in circumstances that caused him real difficulty. The theoretical risk that a full extract might one day be needed was insufficient to render the Polish system incompatible with Article 8. The State had struck a fair balance between the applicant’s interest in confidentiality and the public interest in the accuracy and historical integrity of civil-status records. The margin of appreciation had not been overstepped. As regards Article 14, the Court found that the situations of a transgender adult and of an adopted child were not analogous: the latter involves the legal replacement of parental filiation, whereas gender recognition does not alter the biological facts of birth. Consequently neither provision had been violated.

The case of Milanković v. Croatia (Application no. 33351/20) concerned the applicant’s conviction for war crimes against Serb civilians and a prisoner of war, based on command responsibility, and whether this complied with Article 7 of the ECHR (nullum crimen sine lege).

Vladimir Milanković, a Croatian police official born in 1962, served as deputy head of the Sisak-Moslavina Police Department. From 18 July to 1 October 1991 he was also commander of all police forces in the Sisak-Banovina area. The relevant period of alleged offences ran from mid-August 1991 to mid-June 1992. Croatia had declared independence on 25 June 1991 but postponed implementation until 8 October 1991; international recognition followed on 15 January 1992. Consequently the armed conflict was regarded as non-international until at least 8 October 1991.

In June 2011 an investigation was opened into killings and other offences committed against ethnic Serbs in the area. On 16 December 2011 the applicant was indicted (later amended) on 22 counts of war crimes against civilians (18 of them pre-dating 8 October 1991) and one count against a prisoner of war (also pre-dating that date). Five counts alleged personal participation or ordering; the remaining 18 alleged omission—failure to prevent illegal arrests, detentions, ill-treatment and killings by police units under his command.

The charges relied on Articles 120 § 1 and 122 of the 1977 Basic Criminal Code (war crimes against civilians and prisoners of war), read with Article 28 § 2 (offences by omission where a duty to act exists). These “blanket” provisions referred to “rules of international law.” The prosecution invoked customary international humanitarian law on command responsibility together with common Article 3 and other provisions of the 1949 Geneva Conventions and their 1977 Additional Protocols.

The applicant argued that the Code contained no express concept of command responsibility; that Additional Protocol I (Articles 86–87) applied only to international armed conflicts and was therefore inapplicable before 8 October 1991; that Protocol II (non-international conflicts) contained no command-responsibility clause; that he was a police, not military, commander; that the direct perpetrators had not been identified and might have belonged to other units; and that as deputy head he lacked sufficient authority.

On 9 December 2013 the Osijek County Court convicted him on all counts and imposed an eight-year sentence. It found he possessed both formal and de facto command authority, knew or must have known of the crimes, and was therefore liable under the domestic concept of “guarantor liability” derived from international law. The Supreme Court, on 10 June 2014, upheld the conviction, increased the sentence to ten years and confirmed that the perpetrators were members of units under his command. It did not address the international/non-international character of the conflict.

The Constitutional Court, on 10 March 2020, accepted that Protocol I could not apply to pre-8 October 1991 offences. It held, however, that command responsibility for war crimes in non-international armed conflicts had already crystallised as customary international law by 1991, citing ICTY jurisprudence (Hadžihasanović, Delalić, Tadić) and ICTR case-law (Akayesu). Civilian as well as military superiors could incur such liability.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 24 July 2020, complaining that his conviction lacked a sufficiently accessible and foreseeable legal basis, contrary to Article 7.

The case of Milanković v. Vladimir Milanković, a Croatian police official born in 1962, served as deputy head of the Sisak-Moslavina Police Department and, from 18 July to 1 October 1991, as commander of all police forces in the Sisak-Banovina area. Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, but a three-month moratorium delayed full effect until 8 October 1991; international recognition followed on 15 January 1992. Consequently, 18 of the 22 civilian war-crime counts and the single prisoner-of-war count predated 8 October 1991, raising the question whether the conflict was then international or non-international.

The remaining 18 civilian counts and the prisoner-of-war count alleged liability by omission: as commander he had failed to prevent crimes committed by units under his formal and actual control (Articles 120 § 1 and 122 read with Article 28 § 2, which equates omission with commission when a legal duty exists). As a military-academy graduate he could not have been unaware that his inaction was prohibited. It accepted that the conflict was non-international before 8 October 1991, so Articles 86 and 87 of Protocol I could not furnish the legal basis for the pre-October crimes. It nevertheless held that, by 1991, command responsibility for war crimes committed in non-international armed conflicts had already crystallised as customary international law, citing the ICTY’s Hadžihasanović, Čelebići and Tadić jurisprudence and the ICTR’s Akayesu judgment.

**Case of Manannikov v. Russia (ECtHR, Application no. 9157/08, judgment 1 February 2022)**

The applicant, Aleksey Petrovich Manannikov (born 1956, Moscow resident and human-rights activist), alleged a violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression) arising from his administrative conviction and fine for displaying a banner at an approved public gathering.

On 27 October 2007, ahead of Russian legislative and presidential elections, an officially approved pro-Putin rally supporting his economic and political ideas took place in Lenin Square, Novosibirsk, from 12:00 to 12:30. Several thousand people attended, many waving supportive banners; the event drew media coverage. Manannikov and a companion, Mr B., positioned themselves among the participants and displayed a banner reading “Putin is better than Hitler.”

Video footage later reviewed by domestic courts showed two participants objecting to the banner and asking that it be removed; Manannikov and Mr B. continued to display it. Police officers then ordered its removal; they refused and remained at the event holding the banner until it ended. Afterward, three individuals in plain clothes (whom the applicant claimed were undercover officers) seized and tore up the banner. Police later detained Manannikov and Mr B. en route home and prepared an administrative-offence report.

The same day, a justice of the peace of the 1st Circuit of the Tsentralniy District of Novosibirsk convicted Manannikov under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (breach of established rules for public events). Relying on the footage, the court found the banner provocative and contrary to the event’s programme. Participants’ negative reaction created a real threat to public order, health and safety, justifying the police order under the Public Events Act. Manannikov’s refusal constituted the offence. He was fined 500 Russian roubles (approximately €14). On 28 November 2007 the Tsentralniy District Court of Novosibirsk dismissed his appeal, confirming the facts (undisputed by the applicant), the provocative nature of the banner, the threat assessment, the legal classification and the proportionality of the fine.

Relevant domestic law included the 2004 Public Events Act, requiring participants to obey lawful police and organiser instructions, maintain order and follow the event programme (section 6(3)). Police may issue orders to ensure compliance, facilitate the event, protect public order and safety, and (at organisers’ request) remove non-compliant persons; an event may be terminated if it poses a genuine risk to life, health or property (sections 14 and 16). Article 20.2 § 2 CAO (as then in force) punished such breaches with modest fines for participants.

The ECtHR examined the interference with Article 10. It identified the applicant’s location amid the crowd of opponents as a key factor. The police order was triggered by his conduct and the demonstrators’ hostile reaction rather than the banner’s content alone. He was not ejected from the event. Applying Article 11 principles (peaceful assembly) to this Article 10 counter-demonstration context, the Court held there is no absolute right to counter-demonstrate; it must be balanced against the State’s positive obligation to enable a lawful demonstration to proceed peacefully. The small fine was therefore justified and proportionate. No violation of Article 10 was found.

This case concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the applicant’s administrative conviction and fine for refusing a police order to remove a banner at a public event. Several thousand people attended, many waving pro-Putin banners, and it attracted media coverage.

The applicant and companion Mr B. positioned themselves among the participants and unfurled a banner reading “Putin is better than Hitler.” Footage showed two attendees reacting negatively and asking them to remove it; they refused and continued displaying it. Police officers then ordered removal, citing a real threat to public order, health, and participants’ lives. The pair refused and remained at the event holding the banner. At the meeting’s end, three people in plain clothes seized and tore it up (the applicant alleged they were undercover police). Police later detained the applicant and Mr B. at a station to prepare an administrative-offence report.

Negative reactions from participants justified the police order under the Public Events Act; the applicant’s refusal violated section 6(3)(2) of that Act. He was fined 500 Russian roubles (approximately 14 euros). Section 6(3) required participants to comply with lawful instructions from organisers, authorities and police, maintain public order, and follow the event programme. Police could order compliance, remove non-compliant persons at organisers’ request, facilitate the event, and secure public order and safety (section 14); events could be terminated if they created a genuine risk to lives, health or property (section 16(1)). Article 20.2 § 2 CAO (then in force) punished breaches by participants with a fine of 500–1,000 roubles.

Key facts relevant to the alleged Article 10 interference were: the applicant’s status as a counter-demonstrator displaying a provocative banner that distorted the event’s message amid a crowd of opponents, creating a likelihood of unrest; his location among the main participants as a decisive factor; the police order being triggered by his conduct and the demonstrators’ negative reaction rather than the banner’s content alone; the fact that he was not removed from the event; and the modest sanction. The Court held there is no absolute right to counter-demonstration; it must be balanced against the State’s positive obligation to enable lawful demonstrations to proceed peacefully. The interference was found justified and proportionate.

The applicant, Vladimir Šeks, a retired Croatian politician who had held high office (including membership of the Defence and National Security Council), requested access on 5 June 2017 to 56 classified “State secret – strictly confidential” presidential records from 1994–1999 held in the State Archive. He sought the documents to research a documentary history of Croatia’s founding. Because the records remained classified for 30 years, the Archive referred the request to their owner, the Office of the President.

The President consulted the National Security Council, which examined the contents and concluded that disclosure of certain records would still risk irreparable harm to Croatia’s independence, integrity, national security and foreign relations (the values protected under section 6 of the Data Secrecy Act). On 16 August 2017 the President declassified 31 documents but refused to declassify the remaining 25 (transcripts of 1994–95 Council sessions and certain meetings between the then President and senior Croatian and foreign officials). The decision stated that the Council’s non-binding opinion had been considered, that the owner alone decides classification status, and that the protected values outweighed the public interest.

On 7 September 2017 the Archive therefore granted early access only to the declassified material. The applicant appealed to the Information Commissioner, arguing the refusal was arbitrary because access had been given to some transcripts involving the same individuals but not others. After personally inspecting the still-classified documents, the Commissioner dismissed the appeal on 13 July 2018. She accepted that disclosure could harm national security and foreign relations, noted that the applicant had not explained why his interest should prevail, and confirmed that only the owner could alter classification.

The applicant sought judicial review in the High Administrative Court, claiming inadequate reasoning for the selective declassification. The Court dismissed the action on 25 October 2018. It held that the statutory procedure (consultation of the National Security Council followed by the owner’s exclusive decision) had been followed, that the Commissioner had given clear reasons, and that the protection of the listed values outweighed the public interest. The applicant’s complaint of “voluntarism” was unproven.

A constitutional complaint alleging violations of the rights of access to information and to a fair hearing was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 10 March 2020 (12 judges, three dissenting). The majority found an interference with the applicant’s Article 38 right of access (his academic work being of public interest) but held it lawful, pursuing the legitimate aims of national security and foreign relations, and necessary and proportionate. More detailed reasons, it said, would themselves disclose the protected information. Two dissenting judges argued that the President’s decision contained no real proportionality assessment, that the reviewing bodies had confined themselves to formal legality rather than examining the substance of the secrecy claim, and that this deprived the applicant of effective judicial protection of his freedom of expression.

The applicant later completed and published his book without the withheld records, stating he would supplement it if ultimately granted access.

The case of Fischer v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 24314/13) concerned alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right of access to a court) and of the applicant’s property rights. The applicant, a German national and former 100% owner of the Czech joint-stock company Cestovní kancelář FISCHER, a.s., entered a 2003 consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group a.s. (controlled by K.K.). The agreement preserved proportional participation rights in any share-capital increase. He then transferred 75% of his shares to K & K, retaining a 25% minority stake.

On 3 March 2004 the company’s general meeting, controlled by K & K, resolved to increase share capital from CZK 1 million to CZK 11 million and to exclude existing shareholders’ pre-emptive subscription rights so that the new shares could be offered to another K.K.-controlled entity. The applicant voted against the resolution, which reduced his holding from 25% to 2.3%. He immediately applied to the Prague Municipal Court to have the resolution set aside, arguing that it breached Article 204a § 5 of the Commercial Code (requiring a serious company reason for exclusion of pre-emptive rights) and the consortium agreement, and that its sole purpose was to enable K.K. to seize control.

Before that application was decided, a further general-meeting resolution of 17 December 2004 approved a merger with three other companies. The merger was entered in the Commercial Register on 18 March 2005, further diluting the applicant’s stake to 0.07%. On 13 April 2005 the Municipal Court dismissed the set-aside application, holding that the capital-increase resolution complied with the law and that, in any event, Article 131 § 3(c) of the Commercial Code barred annulment once a merger had been registered. The High Court upheld the decision, treating the resolution as lawful. The Supreme Court quashed that ruling in 2008 and remitted the case, finding that Article 204a § 5 had not been observed.

On remittal the High Court in 2009 again refused to set the resolution aside. It now accepted that the resolution had breached the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals and had circumvented the law, but held that Article 131 § 3(b) precluded annulment because the subsequent merger had created bona-fide third-party rights in the new shares that would be substantially impaired. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal in 2010, confirming that interpretation and noting that the applicant remained entitled under Article 131 § 4 to claim damages and just satisfaction for the infringement of his shareholder rights. The Constitutional Court in 2012 rejected a constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded, observing that access to court had been afforded and that ownership of shares does not freeze a shareholder’s percentage or influence; compensation proceedings remained available.

A parallel application to set aside the merger resolution was dismissed in 2012–2013 on the ground that the applicant no longer held a 25% stake (the capital-increase resolution having stood) and that registration of the merger again triggered Article 131 § 3.

The applicant complained that the courts’ refusal to annul the capital-increase resolution, despite finding it unlawful, denied him effective judicial protection of his shareholder rights and thereby also violated his property rights. The domestic courts had instead directed him to a separate compensation claim under Article 131 § 4, whose limitation period ran from the final dismissal of the set-aside proceedings.

On remittal the High Court (2009) accepted that the resolution violated the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals and circumvented the law, yet still refused to set it aside under Article 131 § 3(b) because doing so would substantially interfere with bona-fide third-party rights acquired through the merger. The Supreme Court (2010) endorsed this and noted that the applicant could still claim damages and just satisfaction under Article 131 § 4. The Constitutional Court (2012) rejected a further appeal as manifestly ill-founded, observing that access to court had been provided and that share ownership does not guarantee an unchanging position; compensation proceedings remained available.

The merger challenge was later dismissed on the ground that the earlier capital-increase resolution had not been set aside, so the applicant no longer held 25% at the time of the merger vote. Even if a violation had occurred, Article 131 § 3 would have precluded setting the merger aside after registration.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the courts had denied effective examination of an allegedly unlawful resolution that stripped him of control and value, leaving him without an effective remedy for the interference with his shares.

The ECtHR case Fischer v. the Czech Republic (no. 24314/13, 24 February 2022) concerned a German applicant, Václav Fischer, who alleged a violation of his right of access to court under Article 6 § 1 ECHR (and consequently of his property rights) after Czech courts refused to set aside a company resolution that drastically diluted his shareholding.

Fischer originally held 100% of shares in Cestovní kancelář FISCHER, a.s. In November 2003 he concluded a consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group a.s. (controlled by K.K.), transferring 75% of the shares. The agreement guaranteed both parties the right to participate proportionally in any future share-capital increase.

On 3 March 2004 the general meeting, voting with K & K’s majority, resolved to raise the company’s share capital from CZK 1 million to CZK 11 million and to exclude existing shareholders’ pre-emptive rights so that the new shares could be offered to another K.K.-controlled entity. The stated justification was the company’s negative equity and need for external capital. Fischer objected and voted against the resolution; his stake consequently fell from 25% to 2.3%.

Nine days later he applied to the Prague Municipal Court to have the resolution declared invalid, arguing that it breached Article 204a § 5 of the Commercial Code (which required a “serious reason” for excluding pre-emptive rights) and the consortium agreement, and that its sole purpose was to enable K.K. to seize control.

While that application was pending, a merger with three other companies was approved on 17 December 2004 and entered in the Commercial Register on 18 March 2005. Fischer’s remaining stake was thereby reduced to 0.07%. He also challenged the merger resolution, claiming that it had not been adopted by the required 90% majority calculated on the basis of his original 25% holding.

The Municipal Court dismissed the first application in April 2005, holding the resolution lawful and, in any event, unsettable once the merger had been registered (Commercial Code Art. 131 § 3(c)). After an intervening Supreme Court remittal that found a breach of Art. 204a § 5, the High Court in 2009 again refused to set the resolution aside. It accepted that the resolution violated the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals and circumvented the law, yet concluded that setting it aside would substantially interfere with the bona-fide rights of new shareholders acquired through the merger (Art. 131 § 3(b)). The Supreme Court (2010) and Constitutional Court (2012) confirmed this outcome, stressing that Fischer remained entitled to claim damages and just satisfaction under Art. 131 § 4 even after the resolution had become unassailable. The merger challenge was likewise dismissed in 2012–2013 on the ground that, once the capital-increase resolution stood, the required majority had been obtained.

Article 131 of the Commercial Code permitted a court to refuse to annul a general-meeting resolution where annulment would interfere with third-party rights acquired in good faith or where a merger had already been registered. Article 131 § 4 nevertheless allowed an injured shareholder to seek both pecuniary damages and non-pecuniary just satisfaction, and domestic courts had in comparable cases examined the lawfulness of the underlying resolution as a preliminary question in such compensation proceedings.

These facts formed the core of the alleged violations: the courts had declined to nullify an unlawful resolution for reasons of legal certainty, leaving the applicant with a diluted shareholding and, in his view, without effective judicial protection of his rights as a minority shareholder.
001-216201:
The ECHR case of Normantowicz v. Poland (no. 65196/16) alleged a violation of Article 3 due to inadequate medical care for a special-needs prisoner. The applicant, a habitual reoffender born in 1983, had prior psychiatric treatment for addiction and a 2008–2011 sentence. In 2012 he suffered spinal disc herniation, spondylolisthesis and chronic back pain; a neurosurgeon recommended surgery that never occurred. He held a disability certificate permitting light work. A 2014 duodenal ulcer preceded his 15 September 2014 re-detention after an offence committed on probation.

Held in closed facilities as a repeat offender, he moved between Olsztyn Remand Centre, Kamińsk Prison, Barczewo Prison hospital wing, Gdańsk Remand Centre hospital wing and others. He occupied regular cells (bottom bunk) or hospital wings. On admission he reported epilepsy and orthopaedic problems; authorities supplied painkillers, anti-epileptic drugs, a light diet, crutches and a stair-climbing aid. Multiple specialist examinations (neurology, neurosurgery, gastroenterology, psychiatry), MRI and CT scans followed, some in civilian hospitals. Non-urgent surgery for herniated disc was advised; prison staff repeatedly requested admission at civilian hospitals.

Delays arose from abnormal blood results, urological problems, suspected inflammation and the applicant’s refusals of medication and tests (including a 2016 colonoscopy). The Government suspected he manipulated fasting blood tests. Surgery dates were set for 2016, May 2017 and later 2018, all contingent on satisfactory results. Independent experts (February 2016) confirmed surgery was needed but that continued detention posed no threat to life or health; they recommended a bottom bunk, medication and three months’ post-operative leave for rehabilitation. By 2016 he used a wheelchair; a fellow inmate later assisted with dressing and toileting, though the Government denied dependence. A December 2015 suicide attempt (no injuries, Government-claimed staging) led to monitoring and a suicide-risk warning. He also received psychological and psychiatric care, including anger-management therapy.

In May 2015 he applied for health-based prison leave. Prison transfers caused successive jurisdictional changes among regional courts. After hearings, social enquiries and expert reports, the Olsztyn Regional Court refused leave on 11 May 2016; the Court of Appeal upheld the refusal on 4 July 2016, finding no risk of danger to life or health. A complaint about the year’s delay was dismissed, the court citing hospitalisations, transfers and case complexity. A second leave application was refused in December 2016 and on appeal in February 2017. Parallel civil and disciplinary proceedings against a prison doctor remained pending.

These facts formed the basis for examining whether Polish authorities met their Article 3 positive obligation to provide adequate medical assistance and accommodate special needs.

The ECHR case of Normantowicz v. Poland (no. 65196/16) concerned an alleged violation of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) arising from the Polish authorities’ alleged failure to provide a special-needs prisoner with timely backbone surgery and from delays exceeding one year in processing his health-based application for a licence for prison leave.

The applicant, a repeat offender born in 1983, had a history of psychiatric treatment for substance addiction and, from 2012, suffered spinal disc herniation, spondylolisthesis and chronic back pain. A prison neurosurgeon recommended surgery that year, but it never occurred. He also had a duodenal ulcer (2014) and later developed epilepsy, sciatica, hypertension, gastritis, kidney stones, depression and incontinence. He used crutches upon re-entering detention in September 2014 and was wheelchair-bound by 2016; a 2016 certificate recorded a marked degree of disability requiring long-term care.

He served sentences in closed facilities (with brief semi-open classification), moving frequently among regular cells (bottom bunk assigned) and prison hospital wings in Olsztyn, Kamińsk, Barczewo, Gdańsk, Dubliny and Szczytno. Upon admission he received painkillers, anti-epileptics, a light diet and mobility aids. Prison staff arranged specialist consultations (neurologists, neurosurgeons, internists, psychiatrists), MRI and CT scans (2015), and urological tests. Non-urgent surgery was repeatedly recommended, with requests sent to civilian hospitals; dates were set for 2016–2018 but postponed owing to abnormal blood/urological results, suspected inflammation, the applicant’s refusals of medication or preparatory procedures (e.g., colonoscopy, fasting for tests), and the need for a specialised clinic. Court-appointed experts (February 2016) confirmed the need for surgery yet found continued detention posed no risk to life or health, provided a bottom bunk, medication and post-operative leave. The applicant received physical therapy, anger-management counselling and psychiatric monitoring. A December 2015 suicide attempt (no injuries) led to a monitored cell and a “suicidal prisoner” warning; the Government alleged it was staged. A fellow inmate’s note claimed daily assistance, which the Government denied.

In May 2015 the applicant (and later his lawyer) sought a licence for leave on health grounds, citing inability to walk unaided, incontinence, dependence on inmates, inadequate specialist care and delayed surgery. Proceedings were transferred between Gdańsk and Olsztyn Regional Courts owing to prison moves, requiring health reports, a social enquiry, hearings and a 2016 expert assessment. Both first-instance refusals (May and December 2016) and appellate dismissals held that detention did not endanger life or health and that prison care (including medication) remained adequate pending surgery. A complaint about unreasonable length of the first set of proceedings was dismissed as attributable to hospitalisations, jurisdictional changes and medical complexity. Related civil and disciplinary actions against a prison doctor remained pending.

The Court ultimately found that medical assistance and special-needs accommodation had been adequate, that surgery delays stemmed from medical contraindications and the applicant’s conduct rather than official neglect, and that the advisability of continued detention had been continuously monitored.

The case of Normantowicz v. Poland concerns an alleged Article 3 violation due to inadequate medical care for a special-needs prisoner, including delayed spinal surgery and protracted examination of his health-based prison leave application.

Applicant Rafał Normantowicz (born 1983), a habitual reoffender with prior substance addiction and psychiatric treatment, began serving sentences on 15 September 2014 in closed facilities (with brief semi-open classification). He had a 2012 spinal injury (disc herniation, spondylolisthesis, chronic pain) with a surgery recommendation that went unfulfilled, plus a disability certificate and 2014 duodenal ulcer. He reported epilepsy upon admission.

Held across multiple prisons and hospital wings (Olsztyn, Kamińsk, Barczewo, Gdańsk, Szczytno), he received painkillers, anti-epileptics, a light diet, crutches, a stair aid, and a bottom bunk. Specialists (neurologists, neurosurgeons, gastroenterologists, psychiatrists) examined him, including in civilian hospitals. He had MRI/CT scans in 2015 confirming herniation, plus treatment for infections, hypertension, gastritis, kidney stones, insomnia, anxiety, and depression. He progressed to wheelchair use by 2016 and required inmate assistance for daily tasks (disputed by the Government). A December 2015 suicide attempt (claimed staged by authorities) led to monitoring.

Surgery arrangements began in 2014 but faced delays from needed tests, poor blood/urological results, suspected inflammation, hospital specialisation issues, and the applicant’s refusals of medications/tests (e.g., colonoscopy prep). It was deemed non-urgent; requests went to various hospitals, with scheduling for 2017 then 2018 (conditional on blood results). Experts in 2016 and 2017 confirmed detention posed no life/health risk pending surgery, recommending accommodations, medicines, and post-surgery rehabilitation leave.

On 14 May 2015 he applied for health-based leave, arguing unfitness, dependency, inadequate prison care, and worsening pain. Transfers caused jurisdiction shifts (Gdańsk/Olsztyn courts). Proceedings included prison reports, a social enquiry, hearings, and a February 2016 expert report (neurosurgeon/forensic specialist) finding prison treatment feasible. Refusal came on 11 May 2016 (upheld 4 July 2016), as illness did not endanger life/health. A delay complaint was dismissed due to transfers, hospitalisations, and complexity. A second application (for inflammation treatment to enable surgery) was refused in December 2016 (appeal dismissed February 2017). Civil/disciplinary actions against prison doctors were also started.

These facts underpinned claims of degrading treatment via unsuitability for a disabled inmate, delayed essential surgery, and over-year-long leave proceedings, despite ongoing monitoring and care.
001-216349:
The case of Mickovski v. North Macedonia (applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18) concerns alleged interference with the applicant’s property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant, Vlado Mickovski (born 1964), a registered bailiff since 2006 with a practice in Kichevo, brought the applications in his personal capacity and on behalf of his legal-person bailiff practice.

On 3 February 2011 the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against him for negligence in official duties, specifically alleged double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. On 11 April 2011 the Chamber of Bailiffs imposed a compulsory temporary suspension of his practice pursuant to section 60(2) of the then-applicable Enforcement Act. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff (M.D. from Struga) to handle necessary activities. Income generated by the deputy was credited to the applicant’s practice, minus the deputy’s own fees. The applicant’s Constitutional Court request for abstract review of the suspension provision was rejected on res judicata grounds.

The investigation was terminated on 21 November 2011 for lack of evidence, after which the Chamber lifted the suspension. The measure had thus lasted from 11 April to 21 November 2011. The applicant subsequently sued the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for actual pecuniary damage (approximately EUR 10,418 for partial employee salaries and office-maintenance costs during the relevant period, supported by employment-suspension decisions, bank statements, utility bills and a services agreement), loss of income (approximately EUR 23,845) and non-pecuniary damage for harm to reputation (approximately EUR 15,450).

On 2 March 2016 the Kichevo Court of First Instance awarded the applicant EUR 10,418 against the State for actual loss on the basis of an expert report and the submitted evidence; it found it unnecessary to examine the claim against the Chamber and dismissed the non-pecuniary claim because the applicant had been neither convicted nor fined. On 10 November 2016 the Gostivar Court of Appeal accepted the first-instance factual findings but reversed the outcome, dismissing all claims. It held that the State could not be held liable in the absence of a wrongful conviction or imprisonment, as required by sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 17 May 2018.

The applicant also lodged unsuccessful complaints with the State Judicial Council and the State Public Prosecutor seeking disciplinary proceedings against the investigating prosecutor and judge.

Relevant domestic law included the general compensation principles in the Obligations Act (sections 141, 178 and 189), the limited compensation rights for unjustified detention or conviction in the Criminal Proceedings Act, and the Enforcement Act provisions that conferred public prerogatives on bailiffs, mandated automatic suspension upon the opening of a related criminal investigation, and assigned disciplinary and suspension decisions to the Chamber (which possessed legal personality). Subsequent 2016 amendments restricted suspension to cases in which an indictment had been confirmed. The Court ultimately found that the applicant had failed to demonstrate that the temporary suspension imposed an individual and excessive burden.

The case of Mickovski v. North Macedonia (Applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights regarding alleged interference with property rights. The applicant, Vlado Mickovski (born 1964), a citizen of North Macedonia living in Vraneshtica, registered as a bailiff with the Chamber of Bailiffs in 2006 and established his practice in Kichevo. He lodged the applications both personally and on behalf of his registered bailiff practice.

On 3 February 2011, the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against the applicant for negligence in performing his official duties as a bailiff, specifically alleged double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. Pursuant to section 60(2) of the Enforcement Act then in force, the Chamber of Bailiffs ordered the temporary suspension of his practice on 11 April 2011 as a compulsory measure. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff (M.D. from Struga) to handle necessary activities during the suspension. Income generated by the deputy on behalf of the applicant's practice was credited to it, minus certain fees charged by the deputy. The applicant unsuccessfully requested an abstract constitutionality review of section 60(2) from the Constitutional Court, which rejected it on res judicata grounds on 22 June 2011.

The criminal investigation was terminated on 21 November 2011 for lack of evidence, after which the Chamber lifted the suspension. The relevant period of suspension thus lasted from 11 April to 21 November 2011. The applicant subsequently brought a civil claim against the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for pecuniary damage (actual losses of approximately EUR 10,418 for employee salaries and office maintenance costs, plus loss of income of approximately EUR 23,845) and non-pecuniary damage (approximately EUR 15,450 for harm to reputation). Supporting evidence included employment decisions, bank statements, utility bills, and a services agreement, as well as an expert report.

On 2 March 2016, the Kichevo Court of First Instance awarded the applicant EUR 10,418 against the State for actual losses, based on the evidence, but dismissed the non-pecuniary claim because he had neither been convicted nor fined; it found no need to examine the claim against the Chamber. The Gostivar Court of Appeal overturned this on 10 November 2016, accepting the facts but holding that the State could not be held liable absent a wrongful conviction or imprisonment, as required by sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. The Supreme Court upheld this on 17 May 2018. The applicant also unsuccessfully sought disciplinary proceedings against the investigating prosecutor and judge.

Relevant domestic law included general compensation principles in the Obligations Act (sections 141, 178, and 189) and the Enforcement Act, which conferred public prerogatives on bailiffs and mandated suspension upon the opening of a criminal investigation related to official duties (with later 2016 amendments restricting this to cases of confirmed indictment). The Supreme Court had previously held that mere initiation of criminal proceedings did not entitle compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

The alleged violation centered on the temporary suspension of the bailiff practice—interfering with the applicant's professional activity and income-generating capacity as property—and the domestic courts' subsequent rejection of his compensation claim, which he argued imposed an unjustified burden without adequate remedy, despite the investigation's termination for lack of evidence. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether this constituted a control of the use of property resulting in an individual and excessive burden.

The case of Mickovski v. North Macedonia concerns two applications by Vlado Mickovski (born 1964, residing in Vraneshtica) and his registered bailiff practice against North Macedonia. It alleges a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the temporary suspension of his bailiff practice amid a criminal investigation and the subsequent rejection of his compensation claim.

Mickovski registered with the Chamber of Bailiffs in 2006 and established his practice in Kichevo. On 3 February 2011, the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation into him for alleged negligence in his official duties, specifically the double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. On 11 April 2011, the Chamber of Bailiffs imposed a compulsory suspension of his practice under section 60(2) of the then-applicable Enforcement Act. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff (M.D. from Struga) to perform necessary functions. Income from the deputy’s services was credited to Mickovski’s practice, minus certain fees retained by the deputy.

Mickovski’s request for an abstract constitutionality review of section 60(2) was rejected by the Constitutional Court on 22 June 2011 on res judicata grounds. The investigation was later terminated for lack of evidence, and the Chamber lifted the suspension on 21 November 2011. The measure thus lasted from 11 April to 21 November 2011.

Mickovski then sued the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act for compensation. He claimed approximately EUR 10,418 in actual pecuniary damage (partial employee salaries and office maintenance costs during the suspension), EUR 23,845 in lost income, and EUR 15,450 in non-pecuniary damage for reputational harm. He supported the claim with an expert report, employment suspension decisions, bank statements, utility bills, and a services agreement.

On 2 March 2016, the Kichevo Court of First Instance awarded EUR 10,418 against the State for actual losses (finding no need to examine the claim against the Chamber) but dismissed the non-pecuniary claim because Mickovski had neither been convicted nor fined. On 10 November 2016, the Gostivar Court of Appeal accepted the first-instance factual findings but reversed the outcome and dismissed all claims. It held that the State could not be liable absent a wrongful conviction or imprisonment, as required by sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. The Supreme Court upheld this on 17 May 2018.

Mickovski also unsuccessfully sought to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the investigating prosecutor and judge.

At the relevant time, the Enforcement Act conferred public prerogatives on bailiffs and required automatic suspension of practice upon the opening of a related criminal investigation (a rule later amended in 2016 to apply only after confirmation of an indictment). The Obligations Act generally provided for compensation, including for loss of profit and interference with personal rights, while a 2009 Supreme Court decision and the Criminal Proceedings Act limited State liability in criminal contexts to cases of unjustified detention or conviction. These facts underpin the alleged interference with the applicant’s property rights through control of his professional practice and the denial of redress for the resulting financial burden.
001-216440:
The applicant, Remigijus Laniauskas (born 1972), a Lithuanian national serving a prison sentence until March 2023, alleged that his near-blindness rendered continued detention incompatible with Article 3 ECHR (inhuman/degrading treatment). He was convicted in 2013 and 2015 of serious organised-crime offences involving firearms, explosives and narcotics (committed 2006–2008) and later of inciting a prison officer to smuggle forbidden items.

In 1993 an explosion injured his eyes; vision deteriorated despite surgery, particularly from 2009. By 2014 he had lost 50 % working capacity. In May 2017 an ophthalmologist diagnosed bilateral blindness. A June 2017 medical commission recorded right-eye acuity of 0.01 and left-eye perception of finger movements at 10 cm—classified under Lithuanian law as a serious incurable illness potentially warranting early release.

Kybartai Correctional Facility applied for release in August 2017. The Vilkaviškis District Court granted it in December 2017, citing excessive hardship, more than one-third of the sentence already served, expired disciplinary sanctions and positive behaviour. On prosecutor’s appeal the Kaunas Regional Court reversed the decision in January 2018. It emphasised judicial discretion: a serious incurable illness is not automatically decisive. Staff testimony showed the applicant walked unassisted, read and signed documents, exercised, attended yoga and computer classes, gardened and participated in other activities. He had never complained of self-care difficulties, retained limited vision, had committed grave offences and reoffended in prison, and posed no risk to other inmates. Continued detention was therefore not inhuman.

By August 2018 working capacity had fallen to 90 % and constant care was recorded. A January 2019 commission noted further subjective deterioration (right-eye finger movements at 20 cm, left-eye light perception only) but found no objective cause and recommended continued eye-drop treatment. Subsequent prison applications (March and June 2019) were refused by district and regional courts on essentially the same grounds: no material change, independent self-care, participation in activities, and familiarity with prison surroundings. After transfer to Vilnius Correctional Facility (August 2019)—which the administration later confirmed was unadapted for disabled prisoners—further applications were rejected. The Vilnius Regional Court (November 2019) added that vision loss predated detention, had not worsened in prison, that the applicant had declined earlier offers of hospital placement, and that blindness had neither prevented the original offences nor later acquisition of a professional qualification.

In December 2019 he was transferred, at his request, to the Prison Hospital’s Social Care Department. A 2021 commission found no significant change. The Hospital administration’s June 2021 release application was refused: staff provided regular medical, social and cleaning support; the applicant walked without a cane, used the gym independently, applied to work as a yoga instructor, and had access (via a cooperation agreement) to Braille and audio books. He had never requested extra assistance. Appeals were dismissed.

Domestic law (Criminal Code Art. 76) permits but does not require release for a post-conviction serious incurable illness; courts must weigh offence gravity, character, conduct, illness nature, sentence already served, treatability in prison and risk to others. The applicant’s condition, while severe, was held throughout not to make detention excessively difficult given the assistance and activities available and his demonstrated independence.

The applicant, Remigijus Laniauskas (born 1972), is a Lithuanian national serving a prison sentence until March 2023. In 1993 he suffered eye injuries in an explosion; despite surgery and treatment, his vision deteriorated (especially from 2009), leading to a 50% loss of working capacity by 2014. He was convicted in 2013 and 2015 of firearms, explosives and drugs offences (committed 2006–2008 as part of an organised group) and began serving his sentence at Kybartai Correctional Facility in March 2015. He later incurred a further conviction for inciting a prison officer to supply forbidden items.

By May 2017 an ophthalmologist diagnosed bilateral blindness and prescribed drops. A June 2017 medical commission recorded visual acuity of 0.01 in the right eye and perception of finger movements at 10 cm in the left, classifying the condition as a serious incurable illness under domestic rules. Prison authorities applied for his release under Article 76 of the Criminal Code. In December 2017 a district court granted release, citing the difficulty of serving the sentence, the portion already served, expired disciplinary sanctions and positive behaviour. The regional court reversed this in January 2018, holding that courts were not obliged to release and must weigh additional factors (gravity of offences, personality, prison conduct, nature of illness, time already served). Staff testimony showed the applicant walked independently, read and signed documents, exercised, attended yoga and computer classes, gardened and took part in other activities; he had never complained of inability to care for himself. He retained limited residual vision, had reoffended in prison and posed no risk to others. Detention was therefore not inhuman or degrading.

In August 2018 his working-capacity loss was assessed at 90% with a need for constant care. A January 2019 commission found only light perception in one eye and finger movements at 20 cm in the other, but no objective basis for claimed deterioration. A further release application was refused in April and June 2019 on essentially the same grounds as before: independent self-care, participation in activities and familiarity with surroundings. A third application (June 2019) was likewise dismissed after transfer to Vilnius Correctional Facility (August 2019). Courts noted that vision loss pre-dated detention, had not worsened in prison, that the applicant had declined transfer to the Prison Hospital and had never reported self-care difficulties. His impairment had not prevented offending, sports, social activities or acquisition of a builder/decorator qualification.

In December 2019, at his request, he was moved to the Prison Hospital’s Social Care Department. A 2021 medical review found no significant change. A fourth release application was refused in July–August 2021. Hospital staff confirmed regular medical and social visits, cleaning and food provision; the applicant walked without a cane, used the gym independently, sought permission to teach yoga outside prison and never complained of needing extra help. The hospital had an agreement with a blind-persons’ association offering braille and audio-books. Courts therefore held that continued detention did not constitute inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3.

He complained under Article 3 ECHR that his near-blindness rendered continued detention inhuman and degrading. He was not totally blind, had reoffended in prison and posed no danger to others. Continued detention was therefore compatible with Article 3.

The applicant walked without a cane, used the gym unaided, applied to work as a yoga instructor, and never complained of unmet needs. The hospital had a cooperation agreement with a blind-persons’ association offering Braille and audio books. Domestic courts repeatedly held that, while visual impairment made prison life harder, it did not render detention excessively difficult or Article 3-incompatible, given his demonstrated independence, pre-existing condition, offence gravity, reoffending and available care.
