001-216861:
The case of A.A. and Others v. North Macedonia (ECtHR, 2022) concerned complaints by eight nationals of Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan under Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens) and Article 13 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that they were immediately and collectively returned to Greece after illegally crossing into North Macedonia in March 2016, without individual removal decisions or access to an effective domestic remedy.

Against the backdrop of the 2014–2016 migrant crisis along the Balkan route, North Macedonia initially facilitated transit. Following an EU announcement on 7 March 2016 that irregular flows had ended, a decision took effect the next day barring entry and transit for migrants who did not meet entry requirements or seek asylum. A crisis situation had already been declared in August 2015 around key border points.

On 14 March 2016 the applicants joined the so-called “March of Hope,” a group of around 1,500 people who left the Idomeni camp in Greece, waded across the Suva Reka river and entered North Macedonian territory. They were intercepted near Moin village by North Macedonian soldiers (joined by Czech and Serbian personnel). Hundreds were surrounded. The Syrian family applicants spent the night in the open; the next morning soldiers allegedly threatened violence unless the group returned to Greece, after which they walked back to Idomeni.

Other applicants were ordered onto army trucks and driven to the border. Soldiers separated journalists, activists and volunteers, confiscated cameras and prevented documentation. Some applicants alleged soldiers formed lines and beat refugees with sticks as they were forced to run to a border fence, then crawl through holes or under it into Greece. Police allegedly guarded the fence. All applicants returned to the Idomeni camp, whose conditions were later described as squalid and abysmal.

The Ministry of the Interior confirmed that approximately 1,500 migrants had illegally crossed near Moin and were returned, along with 72 foreign journalists who were processed and sent back. Videos, identity documents and witness statements from volunteers and journalists corroborated parts of the events. Official statistics showed that while hundreds of thousands of transit certificates had been issued in 2015 and early 2016 (mostly to Syrians, Afghans and Iraqis), virtually none were issued after 8 March 2016, and few of those who expressed an intention actually lodged asylum claims or remained for interviews.

Domestic law (Asylum and Temporary Protection Act, Aliens Act and Border Control Act) required entry at official crossings, permitted expression of an asylum intention orally or in writing at the border or inside the territory, prohibited punishment of those coming directly from a risk country who immediately reported themselves, and provided for individual expulsion decisions with appeal rights and non-refoulement protections. Official border crossings existed nearby (Bogorodica, 7.6 km from Idomeni). The applicants did not use them or formally seek asylum.

The complaints centred on the absence of any individual assessment or removal decisions for the large group, the use of threats and force, and the practical impossibility of accessing remedies once they had been returned. The Court later found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 because genuine and effective legal entry procedures had been circumvented without cogent reasons, and no violation of Article 13 because the applicants’ own unlawful conduct had made a challenge unavailable.

The case of A.A. and Others v. North Macedonia (applications nos. 55798/16 and others) involves five Syrian, two Iraqi and one Afghan national who complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens) and Article 13 of the Convention (right to an effective remedy). They alleged that North Macedonia immediately returned them to Greece after they illegally crossed its southern border in a large group on 14 March 2016, without individual removal decisions, and that they had no effective means to challenge this.

A major influx of migrants from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq used the Balkan route through Greece, North Macedonia and Serbia towards the EU in 2014–2015. North Macedonia initially permitted transit. On 8 March 2016, following EU-level decisions to halt irregular flows, the respondent State ceased allowing entry or controlled transit of persons who did not meet entry requirements or did not seek asylum there.

The applicants left the large, overcrowded Idomeni camp in Greece (near the border) and joined approximately 1,500 people in the “March of Hope.” They crossed the Suva Reka river on foot into North Macedonia. One applicant, who used a wheelchair, was carried over difficult terrain. After a short distance they were intercepted by North Macedonian soldiers (with some Czech and Serbian personnel also present). Hundreds of migrants, including a Syrian family from Aleppo, were surrounded and spent a night in the open. At 5 a.m. soldiers allegedly threatened violence unless they returned. Other applicants reached the village of Moin, where soldiers ordered cameras and phones switched off, separated activists, journalists and volunteers (some of whose equipment was confiscated), and placed the migrants on army trucks. Soldiers then formed two lines and ordered them to run between them towards a border fence; some alleged they were beaten with sticks. They were forced to crawl through holes or under the fence back into Greece and returned to Idomeni.

Video footage, identity documents and statements from a volunteer who accompanied the group and from journalists corroborated the events. The Ministry of the Interior publicly confirmed that about 1,500 migrants had crossed illegally near Moin and had been returned, while accompanying journalists were issued travel orders and sent back.

North Macedonia had 19 official border crossings, the nearest (Bogorodica) being a 1.5-hour walk from Idomeni. A crisis situation had been declared at key crossings in 2015. Between August 2015 and March 2016 hundreds of thousands of certificates of intention to seek asylum were issued, but very few people actually lodged applications or remained for processing; most transited onward. After 8 March 2016 no such certificates were issued on 14 March and numbers dropped sharply. Asylum legislation permitted expression of an intention to seek asylum orally or in writing at a border crossing or police station; illegal entrants who immediately sought asylum were not to be punished and were to be escorted to the competent authority. Entry could not be refused, and expulsion was prohibited, for those expressing such an intention. Non-refoulement protections applied.

UNHCR and other reports noted persistent practical obstacles to accessing the asylum procedure (limited identification capacity, interpretation shortages). Conditions in the Idomeni camp were described as squalid. These facts underpin the complaints of collective expulsion of a large group that had circumvented available legal entry points and of the unavailability of a remedy because of the applicants’ own conduct.

The case of A.A. and Others v. North Macedonia (ECtHR, applications nos. 55798/16 and four others, judgment of 5 April 2022) concerns eight applicants (five Syrian nationals, two Iraqi nationals and one Afghan national) who alleged violations of Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens) and Article 13 of the Convention (right to an effective remedy) in connection with their summary return from North Macedonia to Greece.

In 2014–2016 large numbers of migrants, including from Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan, travelled the Balkan route from Turkey via Greece toward EU states. North Macedonia initially applied a “wave-through” policy, issuing hundreds of thousands of certificates of expressed intention to seek asylum while the vast majority of arrivals transited onward without lodging formal claims. On 7–8 March 2016, following EU-level talks, the respondent State closed this route, deciding not to admit or permit transit of persons who failed to meet entry requirements or did not seek asylum.

On 14 March 2016 the applicants left the overcrowded and unsanitary Idomeni camp on the Greek side of the border and joined a group of approximately 1,500 people in the so-called “March of Hope.” They waded across the Suva Reka river and entered North Macedonian territory illegally, avoiding the nearby official Bogorodica crossing (a 7.6 km walk). One applicant, reliant on a wheelchair, was carried over difficult terrain.

The group was intercepted near the village of Moin by North Macedonian soldiers (joined by Czech and Serbian personnel). Applicants were surrounded; soldiers ordered cameras and phones switched off or confiscated them, and separated accompanying journalists, activists and volunteers (who were later fined and banned). Some applicants were made to board army trucks and driven to the border fence. Others were formed into columns and forced to run a gauntlet of soldiers who allegedly beat them with sticks. They were ordered to crawl through holes or under the fence back into Greece. A Syrian family among the applicants spent the night in the open before being threatened with violence unless they returned. All applicants re-entered the Idomeni camp the following day. The Ministry of the Interior publicly confirmed that some 1,500 migrants who had crossed illegally near Moin, together with a further intercepted group of about 600, had been returned, along with 72 journalists.

No individual removal decisions were issued, no asylum claims were recorded that day, and the applicants were given no opportunity to explain their personal circumstances or to challenge the returns. Official statistics showed that certificates of intention to seek asylum, previously issued in large numbers, ceased after 7 March 2016. Domestic law permitted expression of an asylum intention at the border or inside the territory and prohibited expulsion of persons seeking protection, but the applicants had not used official crossings or immediately presented themselves to the authorities.

The applicants complained that they had been subjected to collective expulsion without any examination of their individual situations and that no effective domestic remedy had been available to contest the returns.

The case of Starkevič v. Lithuania concerned a police officer's complaints under Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention regarding the use of covertly obtained criminal-investigation material in subsequent disciplinary proceedings that resulted in his dismissal.

In October 2015 a burglary suspect, V.M., was detained and later released. He reported to police internal affairs that the applicant had approached him in detention and asked him to steal specified goods (handbags, sports shoes and whiskey). Subsequent meetings between V.M., the applicant and two associates (the applicant's wife and another individual) were confirmed by CCTV footage. A pre-trial investigation was opened into abuse of office. Because the applicant, as a serving officer, was familiar with investigative techniques and had confined contact to face-to-face meetings, a prosecutor obtained judicial authorisation under Article 159 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for interception of the applicant's electronic communications, secret surveillance and a limited criminal-conduct-simulation model allowing V.M. to appear to comply with the applicant's requests (no more than twice) so that the exchanges could be recorded.

On 8 January 2016 V.M. delivered a bottle of whiskey; the applicant was arrested in flagrante. He received a notice of suspicion, acknowledged its contents but refused to testify. He was temporarily suspended. Telephone records later found to contain no relevant information were ordered destroyed. On 29 January 2016 a disciplinary investigation was opened on the same factual basis; the applicant was invited to submit an explanation but instead asked the authorities to rely on his (non-existent) criminal-investigation testimony.

In September 2016 the prosecutor discontinued the criminal proceedings, finding that the applicant's conduct lacked the element of significant damage required for the offence of abuse of office. The same conduct nevertheless displayed features of a disciplinary breach incompatible with a police officer's duties. The prosecutor therefore transmitted the file to the police under Article 214 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. With the prosecutor's consent the internal-affairs unit accessed the discontinued file. Its disciplinary report of 26 October 2016 recited the evidence already gathered (V.M.'s statements, CCTV, telephone-location data, the recovered whiskey and the simulation recordings) and concluded that the applicant had used his office for private gain, incited another to commit crime and thereby discredited an officer's name—an independent statutory ground for mandatory dismissal under the Statute of Internal Service. He was dismissed the following day.

The applicant challenged the dismissal in the administrative courts, arguing that he had been denied a proper opportunity to defend himself, that evidence obtained through the simulation model and interceptions could not lawfully be used in disciplinary proceedings, and that the interference with his private life was disproportionate. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court and, on appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the claims. They held that the misconduct notice had been sufficiently specific, that the applicant had chosen not to give an explanation, that the prosecutor's decision constituted admissible evidence under the Law on Administrative Proceedings, and that even if the simulation material were excluded the remaining evidence (consistent witness testimony, CCTV and telephone data) independently established the disciplinary offence. A separate civil claim for salary lost during suspension was likewise dismissed.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant's complaints that the disciplinary proceedings had been unfair and that the use of covertly obtained communications and simulated-conduct material constituted a disproportionate interference with his private life.

The applicant, a Lithuanian police officer born in 1986, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing in civil matters) and Article 8 (respect for private life) concerning the use, in disciplinary proceedings that led to his dismissal, of information obtained via interception of communications and a criminal conduct simulation model during a prior criminal investigation.

In October 2015 V.M. was arrested for burglary and held in a Vilnius police detention facility before release on reporting conditions. On 12 November 2015 V.M. told the Vilnius county police internal affairs division that the applicant had approached him in detention asking him to steal specified goods, and that they (and associates of the applicant) had later met in public. A pre-trial investigation was opened the same day into suspected abuse of office under Article 228 § 2 of the Criminal Code (abuse for personal gain causing significant damage). CCTV footage corroborated one meeting. On 16 November 2015 a court, citing the applicant’s professional knowledge of investigative methods, authorised secret surveillance, interception of his electronic communications, and a criminal-conduct simulation model (under Article 159 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) allowing V.M. to agree to the applicant’s requests on up to two occasions.

The applicant met V.M. at the police station on 7 January 2016 (an unassigned encounter) and again the next day in public, when V.M. delivered a bottle of whiskey. The applicant was arrested in flagrante. He received a notice of suspicion alleging that, between 25 October 2015 and 8 January 2016, he and two others (his wife and another individual) had asked V.M. to obtain handbags, sports shoes and whiskey illegally. He acknowledged the notice but denied the allegations and exercised his right to silence. Telephone records later proved irrelevant and were destroyed. He was temporarily removed from duty.

On 29 January 2016 the internal affairs division opened a disciplinary investigation, notifying the applicant that his alleged conduct had damaged police prestige and possibly discredited an officer’s name; he was invited to explain by 5 February. He asked that his (non-existent) criminal-investigation testimony be used instead. The disciplinary proceedings were then suspended. On 9 September 2016 the prosecutor discontinued the criminal investigation, finding no corpus delicti because the acts had caused no significant damage to the State or police and had provoked little public reaction. The prosecutor nevertheless considered that the conduct contained elements of a disciplinary offence incompatible with police duties and forwarded the file under Article 214 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The evidence relied upon included the simulation, V.M.’s testimony, other witnesses, CCTV, telephone-location data and the recovered whiskey. The applicant did not appeal.

With prosecutorial consent the police accessed the criminal file. A 26 October 2016 disciplinary report concluded that the applicant, whose duty was to prevent crime, had instead used his position for personal gain, encouraged an offence, and thereby breached police ethics, the Law on the Police, the Law on the Civil Service and the Statute of Internal Service. The acts, committed with direct intent, discredited an officer’s name (Article 2 § 5 of the Statute). Under Article 62 § 1 (7) of the Statute, such discredit mandated dismissal regardless of prior record. The applicant was dismissed the following day.

He brought administrative proceedings for reinstatement and unpaid salary, arguing that the criminal and disciplinary grounds differed, that he had been denied a proper opportunity to defend himself, and that evidence obtained by simulation (authorised only for a criminal investigation) was disproportionate and inadmissible. He did not initially raise the presumption of innocence. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (May 2017) and the Supreme Administrative Court (final ruling September 2017) dismissed the claim. They held that the misconduct notice had sufficiently identified the alleged acts and period; that the applicant had understood the accusations yet deliberately declined to explain; that the prosecutor’s discontinuation decision was an official document whose facts could be used as evidence; and that even without the simulation material, corroborated testimony, CCTV and telephone data established the discrediting conduct. Dismissal was the sole statutory sanction. A separate civil claim for salary during suspension was also rejected.

The case of P.D. v. Russia (Application no. 30560/19) concerns a Belgian applicant’s unsuccessful request to Russian courts for the return of his daughter M. to Switzerland under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The applicant alleged that the refusal violated his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant and Russian national E. began cohabiting in Geneva in June 2014. Their daughter M., a dual Belgian-Russian national, was born on 4 June 2014. They signed a joint-custody agreement on 5 May 2015. After their relationship deteriorated in November 2015, the applicant moved to France. M. thereafter lived primarily with E. in Geneva and spent several days each week with the applicant in France. E. also had a son, A., from a prior relationship.

On 5 December 2016, while M. and A. were in the applicant’s care, A. was allegedly sexually abused by the applicant’s close friend S. Swiss authorities arrested S. on 9 December 2016 and charged him with sexual offences and child pornography; he was later released on bail subject to mandatory psychiatric treatment. On the morning of 16 December 2016, E. departed Switzerland with both children for St Petersburg and never returned.

Swiss courts issued a series of interim orders. On 13 December 2016 the Geneva Adult and Child Protection Court stripped the applicant of parental authority over M., barred all contact, and prohibited him from removing her from Switzerland. Later that same day, after E. had already left, the court prohibited E. from changing M.’s residence or taking her abroad. In February 2017 the court restored the applicant’s parental authority and authorised Skype contact. In November 2017 it withdrew E.’s de facto custody, ordered M.’s placement with the applicant, and directed E. to return the child to Switzerland. Criminal kidnapping proceedings were also opened against E. in Switzerland.

On 23 August 2017 the applicant applied to the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg seeking M.’s return under the Hague Convention. E. objected that she had held sole custody at the moment of departure and that return would expose M. to a grave risk of psychological harm because of the pending Swiss criminal case against S., his release, the absence of any contact ban vis-à-vis M., and the risk of further offences. On 11 January 2018 the District Court rejected the application. It held that M.’s habitual residence had been Switzerland but that her removal was not wrongful: at 7.30 a.m. on 16 December 2016 the 13 December interim order remained in force, so E. alone possessed custody rights, including the right to determine residence. The subsequent Swiss order of 16 December 2016 had been issued after E. had already left and did not restore the applicant’s authority. Independently, the court applied the Article 13(b) “grave-risk” exception, citing the sexual-abuse incident involving A., the still-pending Swiss proceedings, S.’s release without a prohibition on contact with M., and the Swiss court’s own finding of a risk of recidivism. Given M.’s age (three) and her attachment to her mother, return was refused.

The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment on 22 March 2018. Cassation appeals were dismissed by a City Court judge on 18 July 2018 and by a Supreme Court judge on 20 November 2018. The final decision was notified to the applicant’s lawyer on 5 December 2018.

These Russian decisions form the core of the alleged Article 8 violation: the courts’ refusal to order return despite the Hague Convention and subsequent Swiss orders placing M. with the applicant.

**P.D. v. Russia (Application no. 30560/19), ECtHR (Third Section), judgment of 3 May 2022 (final 5 September 2022)**

The applicant, a Belgian national born in 1972 and living in France, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that Russian courts had violated his right to family life by refusing to order the return of his daughter M. (a Belgian-Russian dual national born in June 2014) to Switzerland under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The case turned on whether the Russian courts had properly assessed the lawfulness of the child’s removal/retention and the “grave risk” exception in Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention.

The applicant and Russian national E. began cohabiting in Geneva in June 2014. They signed a joint-custody agreement for M. in May 2015. After their relationship deteriorated in November 2015, the applicant moved to France. M. lived primarily with E. in Geneva but spent several days a week with the applicant. On 5 December 2016, while M. and her half-brother A. (E.’s son from a prior relationship) were in the applicant’s care, A. was allegedly sexually abused by the applicant’s close friend S. S. was arrested on 9 December 2016; Swiss criminal proceedings were opened against him for sexual acts, coercion and child pornography. He was later released on bail with mandatory psychiatric treatment. The outcome of those proceedings is unknown.

On 13 December 2016 the Geneva Adult and Child Protection Court, at E.’s request, issued an immediately enforceable interim order stripping the applicant of parental authority over M., banning all contact, and prohibiting him from removing her from Switzerland or changing her residence. At 7.30 a.m. on 16 December 2016 E. left Geneva for St Petersburg with both children and never returned. Later that evening the same Swiss court issued a further interim order (at the applicant’s request) forbidding E. from changing M.’s residence or taking her out of Switzerland. E. learned of this order after her departure.

Swiss proceedings continued. In February 2017 the Geneva court restored the applicant’s parental authority, finding no evidence that contact posed a risk to M., and ordered Skype contact. In July 2017 a Swiss criminal court banned S. from contacting A., the applicant or E. (citing risk of revenge and recidivism from prior offences in France) but imposed no such ban regarding M. In November 2017 the Geneva court withdrew E.’s de-facto custody, ordered M.’s placement with the applicant, directed E. to return the child to Switzerland, and granted E. limited contact rights inside Switzerland. Criminal proceedings were also opened in Switzerland against E. for kidnapping; their outcome is unknown.

On 23 August 2017 the applicant applied to the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg for M.’s return under the Hague Convention (in force between Russia and Switzerland since June 2015). E. argued she had held sole custody at the moment of departure (by virtue of the 13 December 2016 Swiss interim order) so the removal was not “wrongful,” and that return would expose M. to grave risk of psychological harm given the alleged abuse of A., S.’s release, the lack of a contact ban protecting M., and the risk of further offences. She also cited her own potential detention in Switzerland.

On 11 January 2018 the District Court dismissed the application. It accepted that Switzerland had been M.’s habitual residence but held the removal was not wrongful because, at the time E. left, the 13 December interim order had given her sole custody (including the right to determine residence). The later 16 December order had come too late and had not restored the applicant’s authority. Independently, the court found a grave risk under Article 13(b): the alleged abuse of A. while in the applicant’s care, pending Swiss proceedings against S., S.’s release on bail with psychiatric treatment, the absence of a protective contact ban covering M., and the Swiss court’s finding of a risk of revenge/recidivism. Given M.’s age (then three) and need for her mother’s daily care, return was refused in the child’s best interests.

The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment on 22 March 2018, endorsing the same reasoning. Cassation appeals were rejected by a City Court judge (18 July 2018) and a Supreme Court judge (20 November 2018). The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 3 June 2019, arguing that the Russian courts had failed to treat the removal as wrongful and had not adequately assessed or reasoned the grave-risk exception, thereby interfering with his family life.

001-217039:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) case of Lings v. Denmark (Application no. 15136/20) concerned a retired Danish physician, Svend Lings (born 1941), who founded the association “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia.” In support of legalizing euthanasia, he published an online guide titled “Medicines suited for suicide.” This detailed document listed approximately 300 common pharmaceuticals, specified lethal doses and combinations, and advised methods such as combining drugs with a plastic bag over the head secured by a rubber band. Under Danish law, publishing such general information not directed at specific individuals was lawful.

Following a 2017 radio interview in which Lings stated he had helped a terminally ill patient die by administering Fenemal, the Patient Safety Authority reported him to police and revoked his medical license. He was subsequently charged under section 240 of the Danish Penal Code, which criminalizes assisting another person in deliberately ending their life (punishable by fine or up to three years’ imprisonment). Suicide itself and general (non-targeted) suicide advice remain unpunishable.

The District Court convicted him on one count of assisted suicide and one of attempt (40 days’ suspended imprisonment). The High Court convicted him on all three counts (60 days’ suspended). The Supreme Court upheld this by majority on 23 September 2019.

The three counts involved targeted assistance:

- Count 1 (attempt): In March 2017, after telephone and email contact with A (who had neurological diseases and wished to die), Lings arranged for a co-defendant to prescribe Fenemal, knowing A would use it for suicide. The attempt failed; A’s condition later improved with treatment.

- Count 2: In spring 2017, Lings visited B (paralyzed after a stroke and wanting to die after failing to obtain Swiss euthanasia approval). He advised on the guide’s methods and facilitated procurement of pills via a third party. B’s former wife collected and delivered the medication. B died days after a family farewell dinner.

- Count 3: Between July and August 2018, 85-year-old C (with various infirmities but not terminally ill) contacted Lings by email after obtaining pills herself. In at least nine emails, Lings confirmed her medications were “excellent,” directed her to his guide, and specifically endorsed combining them with a plastic bag and rubber band, writing that this would make death “100% certain.” C was found dead with a plastic bag over her head.

The Supreme Court majority held that even the emails in count 3 constituted specific, significant assistance that intensified C’s resolve, going beyond the lawful general guide. A minority would have acquitted on this count, viewing it as mere republication of public information. Aggravating factors included the systematic nature of the acts and the fact that count 3 occurred after Lings had already been charged. Mitigation included his age (nearly 78). The suspended 60-day sentence was confirmed.

Lings complained under Article 10 ECHR that the conviction violated his freedom of expression, as he had only given general advice. The ECtHR (Second Section, judgment of 12 April 2022, final 12 July 2022) found no violation. There was no European consensus on assisted suicide (most Council of Europe states prohibit it). Denmark therefore enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation. The interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aims of protecting health and morals and the rights of others, and was proportionate: the advice was personalized and concrete rather than abstract, and the modest suspended sentence reflected a fair balance.

The Court noted ongoing Danish debate (including reports by the Council of Ethics opposing legalization and limited reforms on refusing life-sustaining treatment) but no parliamentary majority to amend section 240. Comparative material confirmed that targeted assistance remains criminalized in the large majority of member states.

**CASE OF LINGS v. DENMARK (Application no. 15136/20)**

The applicant, Svend Lings, a retired Danish physician born in 1941, founded the association “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia” around 2015 to advocate for legalising euthanasia. He prepared and published online a detailed guide titled “Medicines suited for suicide,” listing approximately 300 common pharmaceuticals, required doses, combinations, procedures, and methods such as combining drugs with a plastic bag over the head secured by a rubber band. Publication of this general guide was lawful under Danish law.

Following a February 2017 radio interview in which Lings stated he had assisted a terminally ill patient by administering Fenemal, the Patient Safety Authority reported him to police and withdrew his medical licence in March 2017, preventing him from prescribing medications. He was subsequently charged under Article 240 of the Danish Penal Code, which criminalises assisting another person in deliberately ending their life (punishable by fine or up to three years’ imprisonment). Suicide itself is not a crime.

The charges involved three specific incidents:

- Count 1 (attempted assisted suicide, 23 March 2017): Lings communicated by telephone and email with A, who had neurological diseases and wished to die. Knowing A intended to use the medication for suicide, Lings arranged for a co-defendant to prescribe Fenemal (as Lings could no longer prescribe). The attempt failed. A later received treatment for pain and anxiety and improved.

- Count 2 (assisted suicide, spring 2017): B, paralysed after a stroke and no longer finding life worth living, had unsuccessfully sought Swiss euthanasia. Lings visited B, advised him on suicide methods consistent with the published guide, and discussed procuring pills with another person. B’s former wife received a supply of medication which she gave to B. After a farewell dinner, B was found unresponsive and died days later.

- Count 3 (assisted suicide, 17 July–6 August 2018): 85-year-old C, suffering from various infirmities but not seriously ill, had obtained pills herself and contacted Lings by email seeking assistance, expressing fear of failure. They exchanged at least nine emails. Lings confirmed her medications were “excellent,” directed her to the general guide, and on 6 August stated that combining them with a plastic bag over the head (secured by a rubber band) would make death “100% certain.” C was found dead with a plastic bag over her head.

The District Court convicted Lings on one count of assisted suicide and one attempt, imposing a 40-day suspended prison sentence. The High Court convicted him on all three counts and increased the sentence to 60 days’ imprisonment, suspended. The Supreme Court upheld this on 23 September 2019. A 3–2 majority held that the specific, targeted advice and practical assistance (including procuring medication and confirming methods in personal communications) constituted punishable “assistance” under Article 240, even if based on the lawful general guide. The majority noted that the tailored advice was more likely to intensify the recipient’s resolve than the published material alone. Two dissenting judges would have acquitted on count 3, viewing the emails as mere transmission of already-public information without encouragement.

Lings maintained he had only given general advice and that the conviction violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The European Court of Human Rights found the conviction and suspended sentence justified and proportionate, given the absence of European consensus on assisted suicide and the wide margin of appreciation afforded to states in this sensitive area.

**CASE OF LINGS v. DENMARK (ECHR, App. No. 15136/20, 12 April 2022)**

The applicant, Svend Lings (born 1941), a retired Danish physician and founder of the association “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia,” challenged his conviction under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). He argued that he had only provided general advice on suicide methods, which Danish law permitted to be published, and that his conviction for assisting specific individuals therefore violated his rights.

Around 2015, Lings published an online guide titled “Medicines suited for suicide.” It listed approximately 300 common pharmaceuticals, detailed dosages and combinations, and described methods to ensure death, including pairing medication with a plastic bag over the head secured by a rubber band. Disseminating this general information was lawful in Denmark. Following a February 2017 radio interview in which Lings stated he had helped a terminally ill patient die using the drug Fenemal, the Patient Safety Authority reported him to police and revoked his medical licence, preventing him from prescribing medication.

He was charged with two counts of assisted suicide and one count of attempted assisted suicide under section 240 of the Danish Penal Code, which criminalises assisting another person to end their life (punishable by a fine or up to three years’ imprisonment). The provision has existed since 1930 and does not cover general, non-targeted encouragement or “suicide recipes.” Suicide itself is not a crime.

The counts were as follows. Count 1 (attempted assisted suicide, March 2017): After multiple telephone and email contacts with A, who suffered from neurological conditions and wished to die, Lings asked a co-defendant (who still held a licence) to prescribe Fenemal for A, knowing it would be used for suicide. The attempt failed; A later improved with pain and anxiety treatment. Count 2 (assisted suicide, spring 2017): B, largely paralysed after a stroke, no longer wished to live. After Lings visited and advised him using the online guide, B’s former wife contacted Lings; he indicated he could arrange for someone to obtain pills. She received a supply, gave it to B, and B died days after a family farewell dinner. Count 3 (assisted suicide, July–August 2018): C, an 85-year-old woman with various infirmities but not seriously ill, had already obtained pills and contacted Lings by email seeking help. They exchanged at least nine emails. Lings confirmed her medications were suitable, directed her to the public guide, and on 6 August wrote that combining them with a plastic bag and rubber band around the neck would make success “100% certain.” C was found dead with a plastic bag over her head.

The District Court convicted Lings on two counts (40-day suspended sentence). The High Court convicted him on all three (60-day suspended sentence). The Supreme Court (23 September 2019) upheld the convictions by a 3–2 majority, finding the acts constituted specific, significant assistance rather than mere repetition of public information. Aggravating factors included a systematic element and the fact that the last offence occurred after Lings had already been charged; his age (nearly 78) was mitigating. Two dissenting judges would have acquitted on count 3, viewing the emails as non-punishable transmission of already-public material and more compatible with Article 10.

Denmark has repeatedly debated but not legalised euthanasia or assisted suicide. The Council of Ethics has consistently opposed legalisation. Comparative material showed no European consensus: most Council of Europe states prohibit assistance to suicide, while a minority permit it under strict conditions.

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) held that the conviction and suspended sentence were justified and proportionate. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in this sensitive area given the lack of consensus, and Denmark had not overstepped it. There was no violation of Article 10.

The case of Mediengruppe Österreich GmbH v. Austria (App. no. 37713/18) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression). The applicant company, publisher of the daily newspaper Österreich, was permanently injuncted from publishing images of H.S. without consent whenever the accompanying text labelled him a “convicted neo-Nazi” or equivalent.

On 20 July 2016, amid intense public interest in Austria’s presidential run-off (the first ballot having been annulled by the Constitutional Court), Österreich reported on a meeting between FPÖ candidate N.H. and journalists from the German newspaper Bild. The article reproduced a 1987 photograph showing N.H.’s office manager R.S., R.S.’s brother H.S., and G.K. at a right-wing gathering; G.K. was giving the Kühnen salute and the men carried batons. The text identified H.S. and G.K. as “convicted neo-Nazis.” H.S. had been convicted in 1995 under the National Socialist Prohibition Act, released on parole in 1999, and his conviction subsequently expunged.

H.S. sued under section 78 of the Copyright Act, seeking both an interim and a permanent injunction. He argued that more than twenty years had passed, he had fully reintegrated (family, regular employment, no further offences), was no longer a public figure, and had a legitimate interest, protected by the Criminal Record Deletion Act, in not being confronted with his spent conviction. He denied any continued involvement in neo-Nazi activity and stated he did not even know N.H.

The applicant company maintained that the statement was true, that H.S. remained a person of contemporary historical significance, and that the public had a strong interest in knowing the political milieu of a presidential candidate’s closest staff. It cited 2009 events (disputed by H.S.) as evidence of continued extremist links.

The Vienna Commercial Court and Court of Appeal initially refused interim relief, holding that the public-interest value of reporting on N.H.’s associations outweighed H.S.’s privacy interest and that the contested statement was factually accurate.

On 30 January 2017 the Supreme Court reversed, issuing the requested prohibition. It recalled its 2007 ruling in a similar case involving the same plaintiff: after a sentence has been served and the offender reintegrated, republication of images that “pillory” him by recalling long-past crimes generally violates legitimate interests unless the accompanying text is both complete and closely connected to the image. Here the 2016 article focused on R.S. and N.H., not on H.S.; mentioning the 1995 conviction therefore lacked objective justification. The absence of any temporal nexus between the 1987 photograph, the 1995 conviction and the 2016 publication confirmed the lack of public-interest necessity.

In the subsequent main proceedings the Commercial Court (21 April 2017) granted a permanent injunction on the same reasoning, finding no need to re-balance interests. The Court of Appeal and, on 21 December 2017, the Supreme Court (citing Österreichischer Rundfunk v. Austria) upheld the order.

The applicant company complained to the European Court that the injunction constituted an unjustified interference with its right to impart information of public interest during an election campaign.

The case concerns an application by Mediengruppe Österreich GmbH, publisher of the Austrian daily newspaper Österreich, alleging a violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). The complaint arose from a 2016 injunction issued by Austrian courts that prohibited the newspaper from publishing photographs of H.S. accompanied by text identifying him as a “convicted neo-Nazi” (or equivalent phrasing).

In July 2016, amid intense public interest in Austria’s presidential election run-off (after the Constitutional Court annulled the initial ballot), Österreich reported on a meeting between Freedom Party candidate N.H. and journalists from the German newspaper Bild. The article, illustrated by a 1987 photograph, described how Bild confronted N.H. with the image showing his office manager R.S. alongside R.S.’s brother H.S. and G.K. at a right-wing event. H.S. and G.K. were identified as convicted neo-Nazis; the photo depicted them holding batons, with G.K. giving a Nazi-style salute. The article noted that R.S. (then under 18) had no criminal record, quoted N.H. defending him as a mere “follower” from 25–30 years earlier, and reported N.H.’s intent to retain R.S. even if elected. The piece highlighted the political context of N.H.’s associations during the campaign.

H.S., convicted in 1995 under Austria’s National Socialist Prohibition Act and released on parole in 1999, sued the publisher under section 78 of the Copyright Act. He sought an injunction against publication of his image if paired with references to his conviction as a neo-Nazi. His conviction had been expunged under the Criminal Record Deletion Act, extinguishing all legal consequences; he claimed full social reintegration (family, regular employment), no ongoing public profile, and no connection to N.H. or the 2016 election. He denied post-release neo-Nazi activity, characterizing 2009 events (cited by the publisher) as non-extremist or misreported.

The publisher countered that the statement was true, H.S. remained a figure of contemporary historical significance due to his past prominence in Austria’s neo-Nazi scene, and there was overriding public interest in the political circles of a presidential candidate (including how the Freedom Party handled right-wing extremism). It cited media reports and a 2009 Wikipedia/Documentation Archive entry alleging H.S.’s continued involvement.

Lower courts initially rejected H.S.’s request for an interim injunction, finding the public interest in election-related reporting and the truth of the statement outweighed his privacy interests. The Supreme Court reversed this in January 2017 (provisional proceedings), issuing the prohibition. It reasoned that the article focused on N.H. and R.S., not H.S., providing no objective justification for referencing the long-past conviction. It invoked its prior 2007 ruling against the same publisher (prohibiting a similar photo of H.S. labeled “neo-Nazi leader” without noting his rehabilitation) and emphasized the lack of temporal connection between the 1987 photo, 1995 conviction, and 2016 article. Subsequent main-proceedings judgments by the Vienna Commercial Court (April 2017), Court of Appeal (September 2017), and Supreme Court (December 2017, rejecting further appeal) confirmed the injunction, holding that no balancing of interests was required given the absence of justification. The courts noted that H.S. had served his sentence, behaved well since, and lost notoriety, entitling him to protection against “pillorying” reminders of old crimes that could hinder reintegration (per section 7a of the Media Act, interpreted alongside the Copyright Act).

The applicant company argued the injunction unduly restricted its right to impart information on a matter of public concern. (The ECtHR later found the domestic courts’ balancing of H.S.’s rehabilitation interests against Article 10 rights consistent with its case-law, such as Österreichischer Rundfunk v. Austria.)

**Summary of Mediengruppe Österreich GmbH v. Austria (ECtHR, Application no. 37713/18)**

The applicant, Mediengruppe Österreich GmbH (publisher of the newspaper *Österreich*), alleged a violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression) after Austrian courts issued an injunction restricting its reporting.

On 20 July 2016, amid a highly publicized Austrian presidential election (following a Constitutional Court annulment of a close run-off between FPÖ candidate N.H. and another contender), *Österreich* published an article on N.H.’s interview with the German paper *Bild*. The piece included a 1987 photograph of N.H.’s office manager R.S. alongside his brother H.S. and G.K. at a right-wing event. The text identified H.S. as a “convicted neo-Nazi,” noting the photo depicted individuals with batons and a Nazi salute (Kühnen salute). N.H. was quoted defending R.S. (then a minor) as having no criminal record and calling the events 25–30 years old.

H.S. had been convicted in 1995 under the National Socialist Prohibition Act and released on parole in 1999. By 2016 the conviction was expunged under the Criminal Record Deletion Act (ss. 1–3), which extinguishes legal negative consequences, deems the person judicially innocent, and imposes no duty to disclose it. H.S. asserted he had reintegrated (family, regular job), committed no further offences, was no longer a public figure, and had no link to N.H. He sued under s. 78 of the Copyright Act (protecting images where “legitimate interests” are harmed) for an injunction barring publication of his image without consent if the accompanying text called him a “convicted neo-Nazi” or equivalent. He invoked the “pillorying effect” on rehabilitation after a spent conviction.

The applicant argued the statement was true; H.S. was a historically significant former neo-Nazi figure; he had allegedly attended 2009 events (disputed by H.S. as non-extremist); and there was overriding public interest in a presidential candidate’s associations, especially regarding right-wing extremism during an election.

Lower courts initially refused an interim injunction, finding public interest and truth outweighed H.S.’s interests. The Supreme Court reversed (30 January 2017, 6 Ob 216/16g), granting the prohibition. It held the article concerned N.H. and R.S., not H.S., so there was no objective justification for referencing the old conviction. There was no temporal link between the 1987 photo, 1995 conviction and 2016 article. Citing prior case-law (including a 2007 decision involving the same parties) and s. 7a of the Media Act (requiring balancing of public interest against harm to a person’s advancement), it stressed former convicts’ strong interest in reintegration once they have served their sentence, lost notoriety and shown no further criminality. The main proceedings confirmed the injunction; the Supreme Court again noted the lack of temporal connection (referencing *Österreichischer Rundfunk v. Austria*).

These facts underpinned the Article 10 complaint: the injunction interfered with imparting information on a matter of public interest (election-related political associations and historical context). (The ECtHR later held the Supreme Court’s balancing of H.S.’s rehabilitation/privacy rights against expression complied with its case-law, finding no violation.)

The case concerns Ms Siremon Roengkasettakorn Eriksson (a Swedish-Thai national born in 1977) and her daughter X (born October 2007). It arose from child-welfare measures taken after X, then two weeks old, was admitted to hospital on 18 October 2007 with multiple fractures (including a complex skull fracture), bruises, retinal haemorrhages and cerebral bleeding. Medical opinion attributed the injuries to repeated blunt-force trauma, possibly including shaking. X and her older brother Y (born 2006) were immediately placed in emergency foster care. Both parents were remanded; the father was later convicted of aggravated assault (sentence increased on appeal to four years), while the applicant was acquitted. A 2007 care order was granted on the basis that an adult in the household had caused the injuries and that the parents had failed to protect X.

Y’s care order was lifted in 2008. X was moved to a long-term foster home in June 2008 (when she was eight months old). Contact between the applicant and X was initially restricted to two supervised hours per month, later increased to two hours every fortnight. After the father’s conviction became final and the parents divorced (2011), the applicant sought termination of the care order, arguing that she now had sole custody and could protect X. Social services refused, citing the applicant’s alleged inability to meet X’s special needs, X’s strong attachment to the foster family, and psychiatric assessments warning of serious harm from a move. The Supreme Administrative Court nevertheless lifted the care order in June 2012, holding that the original grounds (risk of ill-treatment and parental incapacity) no longer existed and that risks of disruption could be addressed by other measures.

Immediately afterwards the authorities imposed a removal prohibition (upheld by the County Administrative Court) and, in December 2012, applied to transfer custody to the foster parents under Chapter 6, section 8 of the Parental Act. They relied on X’s five-year residence in the foster home, her perception of the foster parents as her real parents, her distress at talk of returning to the applicant, and the harm caused by the applicant’s increased (unsupervised) visits after the care order was lifted. In October 2013 the District Court granted the transfer, awarding the applicant fortnightly contact (plus certain holidays). The Court of Appeal upheld the transfer in March 2015 (after an oral hearing at which experts testified), while modestly increasing contact to every second weekend with overnight stays from October 2015. It found that X’s almost lifelong placement, her secure attachment and the experts’ view that even a gradual return would endanger her health outweighed the possibility of reunification. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Meanwhile, new medical evidence (vitamin levels and birth circumstances) led the Supreme Court to reopen the criminal case; the Court of Appeal acquitted the father in 2015, holding that the injuries could not be shown to have been caused by violence. The applicant’s subsequent application to the European Court alleged that the transfer of custody, the limited contact rights and the authorities’ failure to work actively toward reunification while the care order remained in force violated Article 8. The domestic courts had repeatedly cited X’s best interests, the length of the placement and the need for stability as justifying the measures.

The case of Roengkasettakorn Eriksson v. Sweden (Application no. 21574/16) concerns Article 8 complaints by the applicant, a Swedish-Thai national, regarding child-welfare measures taken in respect of her daughter X (born October 2007). On 18 October 2007, two-week-old X was hospitalised with multiple fractures (skull, arm, clavicle, ankles, tibia), bruises, eyelid discolouration, retinal haemorrhage and cerebral bleeding. Medical evidence indicated these resulted from repeated blunt-force trauma or shaking, inflicted on at least two occasions and inconsistent with ordinary care. Social services placed X (and her brother Y, born 2006) in emergency foster care the same day; both parents were briefly remanded. On 12 December 2007 the County Administrative Court issued a care order, finding that an adult in the household had caused X’s injuries (likely in Y’s presence) and that the parents’ failure to protect her demonstrated inadequate parenting skills creating concrete risks to the children’s health.

The applicant was acquitted of criminal charges; X’s father was convicted of aggravated assault and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment (later reopened and resulting in his 2015 acquittal after new medical evidence on vitamin levels and birth circumstances). Contact was initially restricted to two supervised hours per month. Y’s care order was lifted in April 2008. X was moved to a long-term foster home in June 2008. Contact was later increased to two supervised hours fortnightly. In 2010 the applicant, having filed for divorce and obtained sole custody, applied to terminate the care order, arguing she could now protect X. Social-services investigations and psychiatric/psychological reports identified deficiencies in her ability to understand and meet X’s special needs (arising from her injuries and trauma), X’s lack of attachment to her, and X’s strong attachment to and dependence on the foster parents. Removal was assessed as posing a serious risk of harm.

The care order was nevertheless lifted by the Supreme Administrative Court in June 2012, as the original grounds (risk of physical ill-treatment or lack of parenting skills) no longer existed given the father’s imprisonment and the parents’ divorce. Social services then sought a removal prohibition and, in December 2012, a transfer of custody to the foster parents under Chapter 6, section 8 of the Parental Code, citing X’s five-year placement (from age eight months), her perception of the foster family as her own, her distress at the prospect of leaving, and harm caused by the applicant’s subsequent increase in unsupervised visits. An interim removal prohibition was granted; the District Court transferred custody in October 2013, awarding the applicant fortnightly contact (later adjusted by the Court of Appeal in 2015 to include overnight weekend stays after a transition period). The Court of Appeal emphasised X’s virtually lifelong residence with and deep bonds to the foster parents, her limited (supervised, often group) contact with the applicant, the absence of any realistic prospect of reunification without risk to her health and development, and the paramountcy of her need for stability. Leave to appeal was refused by the Supreme Court. The applicant complained that the custody transfer and restricted contact violated her right to respect for family life.

The case of Roengkasettakorn Eriksson v. Sweden (Application no. 21574/16) concerns alleged violations of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding respect for family life. The applicant, a Swedish-Thai national, complained on her own behalf and that of her children X (born 2007) and Y (born 2006) about child-welfare measures applied to X, including the transfer of custody to foster parents and restrictions on contact rights. She also alleged that the authorities failed in their duty to facilitate family reunification while a care order remained in force.

On 18 October 2007, when X was approximately two weeks old, she was taken to hospital by her parents and diagnosed with multiple fractures (including to the skull, arm, clavicle, tibia and ankle), bruises, retinal haemorrhaging and cerebral bleeding. A medical opinion concluded that the injuries resulted from repeated physical violence, likely involving shaking and blunt force, inflicted on at least two occasions and inconsistent with ordinary childcare. Social services immediately placed both X and Y in emergency foster care and obtained care orders. The parents were remanded in custody. The applicant was later acquitted of criminal charges; the father was initially convicted of aggravated assault and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. In 2015, following new medical evidence concerning X’s vitamin levels and birth circumstances, the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction, finding the cause of the injuries unexplained.

Contact between the applicant and X was initially limited to two supervised hours per month. Although the care order for Y was lifted in 2008, the order for X remained. X was moved to a long-term foster home at eight months of age. The applicant divorced the father in 2011 and applied for the care order to be terminated, arguing that she now had sole custody and could protect X. Social services refused, citing her alleged inability to understand X’s special needs arising from the injuries and trauma, her limited attachment to X, and the strong bonds X had formed with her foster parents. Psychiatric assessments indicated that removal from the foster home would seriously risk X’s health and development.

In June 2012 the Supreme Administrative Court lifted the care order, holding that the original grounds (risk of physical ill-treatment or insufficient parenting skills) no longer existed once the parents had divorced and the father was imprisoned. It stressed, however, that any harm from disrupting X’s attachment to her foster family should be addressed by other legal means, such as a transfer of custody or a prohibition on removal. Social services promptly obtained an interim prohibition on removal and, in December 2012, applied for custody to be transferred to the foster parents. The District Court granted the application in October 2013, noting that X (then six) had lived almost her entire life with the foster family, regarded them as her parents, and had reacted negatively to increased contact with the applicant. The Court of Appeal upheld the transfer in 2015 (with modestly increased contact rights of every other weekend plus overnight stays), emphasising X’s need for stability, the limited nature of her prior contact with the applicant, and expert evidence that even a gradual return carried risks to her well-being. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Throughout the care period the authorities maintained that reunification was the ultimate goal but that X’s particular vulnerabilities and the passage of time had made it unrealistic. The applicant contended that these measures, and the authorities’ failure to promote more substantial contact or a phased return, constituted an unjustified interference with family life.

**CASE OF X v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC (Application no. 64886/19)**

The applicant, a Czech national with dual US citizenship, married a US national in 2007. Their daughter was born in the United States in March 2014. The applicant alleged she was the child's primary caregiver. After the father physically attacked her in November 2014, he was arrested and barred from contact; no criminal proceedings followed as she declined to testify. A 2015 US court approved an agreement granting her primary care with the father's visitation rights and travel conditions. The parents later reconciled and exercised joint custody.

In June 2016 the family travelled to the Czech Republic. The applicant claimed this was intended as a long-term relocation due to the child's health issues and US insurance difficulties; the father maintained it was a temporary visit with return tickets for September 2016. He departed alone that autumn. In May 2017 he briefly returned and sought contact facilitation via Czech authorities. In August 2017 he applied to the Brno Municipal Court for the child's return under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, alleging wrongful retention.

The Municipal Court dismissed the application in October 2017. It found the child's habitual residence had been in the US (where the parents held joint custody) and the retention wrongful, but concluded the father had acquiesced under Article 13(a) given his delay and limited contact efforts. It did not examine Article 13(b) grave-risk exceptions.

On appeal, the Brno Regional Court reversed this in January 2018 and ordered the child's return within one month, subject to "soft landing" safeguards: the father must provide separate housing for the applicant and child, purchase tickets, deposit six months' maintenance, and refrain from removing the child from the applicant's care pending US custody rulings. It rejected acquiescence, found no grave risk of harm (noting the child's resolved health issues, comparable US care, existing insurance, and her young age allowing language adaptation), and held Article 12 settlement considerations inapplicable as proceedings began within one year.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal in December 2018 as manifestly ill-founded, confirming wrongful retention, timely application, lack of acquiescence, and no grave risk. Differences in living conditions did not meet the Article 13(b) threshold, and the imposed safeguards were appropriate.

The father sought enforcement in December 2018. The applicant applied to suspend it, citing unfulfilled safeguards and new evidence of risks to the child's mental health and development after years in the Czech Republic. The Municipal Court rejected enforcement in February 2019 due to the father's housing non-compliance. After failed mediation (in which the child's guardian ad litem warned of possible removal and later recommended against enforcement as contrary to the five-year-old's best interests after three years settled in the Czech Republic), the Regional Court in June 2019 reversed this. It accepted the father's rental agreement and six months' rent payment, noted his undertaking not to take the child from the applicant's care, and held that the applicant's non-cooperation justified removal and handover to the father. It declined to re-examine merits or new reports, finding no material change of circumstances and no grounds to discontinue enforcement. The Constitutional Court later upheld this.

On 1 July 2019 the order was enforced by removing the child and handing her to the father (with advice that return with the mother served the child's interests). An incident occurred the next day at the US embassy in Prague. The father and child returned to the US on 4 July; the applicant followed on 10 July, later claiming the promised housing had not been arranged. US courts issued temporary protective orders awarding the father custody (citing the embassy incident as potential mental abuse), later permitting limited supervised contact. Additional criminal proceedings against the applicant (assault and alleged abduction) ensued; she was acquitted of assault in 2021. Custody hearings were repeatedly delayed.

The applicant complained under Article 8 that the Czech authorities' enforcement of the return order (without adequately considering changed circumstances, the child's best interests, or the quality/enforceability of safeguards) violated her right to respect for family life and the State's positive obligations. The Court later held that the domestic courts' examination complied with Article 8's procedural requirements (judgment subsequently revised under Rule 80).

The case of X v. the Czech Republic (no. 64886/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for family life) arising from Czech courts’ enforcement of a Hague Convention return order sending the applicant’s young daughter back to the United States.

The applicant (dual Czech-US national) married a US citizen in 2007; their daughter was born in the US in 2014. After the father physically attacked the applicant in late 2014, a US court approved an agreement giving the applicant primary care with visiting rights for the father; the couple later resumed joint custody. In June 2016 the family travelled to the Czech Republic. The applicant maintained this was intended as a long-term relocation prompted by the child’s health problems and inadequate US medical insurance; the father insisted it was a temporary visit. He returned alone to the US in autumn 2016.

In August 2017 the father applied under the 1980 Hague Convention for the child’s return, alleging wrongful retention. The Brno Municipal Court initially refused the application, finding the father had acquiesced. The Regional Court reversed that ruling in January 2018 and ordered return within one month, subject to “soft-landing” safeguards: the father had to secure and pay for separate housing, buy tickets, deposit six months’ maintenance and refrain from removing the child from the applicant’s care pending US custody proceedings. The court rejected both the acquiescence exception (Article 13(a)) and any grave-risk exception (Article 13(b)), noting the child’s earlier febrile seizures had resolved, comparable paediatric care existed in the US, and the child (then aged four) would adapt linguistically. The Constitutional Court upheld the order in December 2018, stressing that because proceedings had been commenced within one year of the retention, any subsequent settlement of the child in the Czech Republic was irrelevant.

Enforcement proceedings followed immediately. The applicant sought to halt them, arguing that the father had not complied with the housing condition and that new medical and psychological evidence showed the return would now harm the child’s mental health and development after three years in the Czech Republic. The Municipal Court first refused enforcement for lack of adequate housing proof. On appeal the Regional Court (June 2019) reversed, accepting a rental agreement in the father’s name and his oral undertaking not to remove the child from the applicant. It held that enforcement proceedings could not re-examine the merits of the return order or the child’s best interests; they were limited to verifying that the order was final and that the father had met the imposed conditions. New reports did not demonstrate a material change of circumstances. The child’s guardian ad litem opposed enforcement, warning that an unprepared return of a five-year-old after three years in Czechia would be contrary to her best interests and noting the father’s stated intention to file criminal charges against the applicant.

On 1 July 2019 the child was forcibly removed from the applicant and handed to the father. An incident occurred the next day outside the US embassy. Both parents and the child travelled to the United States; the applicant discovered no housing had been arranged for her. A US court immediately issued a temporary protective order awarding custody to the father on the basis of the embassy incident (later characterised as mental abuse of the child). The applicant was thereafter limited to supervised, non-overnight contact. Assault charges arising from a later parental confrontation were eventually dismissed; an abduction complaint was never pursued.

The applicant contended that the Czech courts, by refusing to reassess the child’s current best interests, the adequacy of the father’s compliance, the passage of time and the absence of preparatory measures, had failed to discharge their positive obligation under Article 8 to protect family life. The European Court later held that the domestic courts’ examination had in fact satisfied the procedural requirements of Article 8.

**Case Summary: X v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 64886/19)**

The applicant, a Czech (and dual US) national born in 1980, married a US citizen in 2007. Their daughter was born in the United States in March 2014. The applicant was the primary caregiver. After the unemployed father physically attacked her in November 2014, he was arrested and barred from approaching her and the child; she declined to testify, so no criminal case followed. A March 2015 US court order approved their agreement granting her care of the child with visiting rights for the father and travel conditions. They later resumed cohabitation and joint custody.

In June 2016 the family travelled to the Czech Republic. The applicant claimed a long-term move due to the child’s health issues and US insurance difficulties; the father insisted it was a temporary visit with September 2016 return tickets. He returned to the US alone that autumn. In May 2017 he briefly visited and sought contact assistance from the Czech Office for International Legal Protection of Children.

On 25 August 2017 the father applied to the Brno Municipal Court for the child’s return under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, alleging wrongful retention. On 6 October 2017 the court dismissed the application: the child’s habitual residence had been the US (where parents held joint custody) as of 16 September 2016, making retention wrongful, but the father’s delay and conduct showed acquiescence under Article 13(a). It did not examine grave-risk arguments under Article 13(b).

On 9 January 2018 the Brno Regional Court reversed this, ordering the applicant to return the child within one month provided the father arranged “soft landing” safeguards: separate housing for mother and child, plane tickets, six months’ maintenance deposited in her account, and no removal of the child from her de facto care pending US custody rulings. The court rejected acquiescence (father had attempted contact) and found no grave risk of harm or intolerable situation under Article 13(b), citing resolved health issues, comparable paediatric care, available insurance, the child’s young age (easy language adaptation), and the mother’s expected return with her. Article 12 settlement arguments were inapplicable as proceedings began within one year.

The applicant’s February 2018 constitutional appeal was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded on 11 December 2018 (decision I. ÚS 735/18). The Constitutional Court confirmed wrongful retention, timely filing (requiring return regardless of settlement), no acquiescence, and no grave risk; mere differences in living conditions did not suffice, and the imposed undertakings were beneficial and enforceable.

The return order became enforceable on 13 December 2018. The father applied for enforcement on 20 December 2018. The applicant sought suspension/discontinuance on 15 January 2019, citing unmet safeguards and new evidence of mental-health/developmental harm. On 27 February 2019 the Municipal Court rejected enforcement for the father’s failure to provide suitable housing; both parties appealed.

After hearings, mediation, and a case conference (at which the child’s guardian ad litem opposed return after three years without preparation and noted the father’s possible US criminal complaint against the applicant), the Regional Court on 4 June 2019 allowed the appeal, reversed the lower court, and ordered enforcement. It accepted the father’s rental agreement (as tenant) and six months’ rent payment, plus his in-court declaration not to remove the child from the applicant’s care. Further formalities were unnecessary given her non-cooperation; forced removal and handover to the father were thus required. It declined to re-examine the return order’s merits or new reports (no material change shown) and found no grounds to suspend.

The order was enforced on 1 July 2019 by removing the child and handing her to the father. An incident occurred the next day outside the US embassy (video-recorded). The applicant’s 2 July 2019 constitutional appeal was dismissed on 16 July 2019 (I. ÚS 2160/19) as ill-founded: enforcement proceedings could not review the original decision, safeguards had been met, and prompt return served the child’s interests under the Hague Convention.

Father and child returned to the US on 4 July 2019; the applicant followed on 10 July. US courts later granted the father temporary custody (initially citing the embassy incident as mental abuse), with the applicant receiving only supervised, limited contact. Assault and other charges were filed against her (she was later acquitted of assault). The applicant alleged the Czech enforcement process violated Article 8 by failing adequately to assess current circumstances, the child’s best interests, and the father’s incomplete compliance with safeguards.
