The ECtHR case of Bežanić and Baškarad v. Croatia (applications nos. 16140/15 and 13322/16) concerned complaints by two Croatian nationals that orders requiring them to pay real-estate transfer tax, after initial exemptions, violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

In January 2007 the first applicant bought a flat in Rijeka and immediately registered it as his domicile. He applied for exemption under section 11(9) of the Real Estate Transfer Tax Act (as in force 2003–2011), which relieved first-time buyers of Croatian citizenship of the 5 % tax if the property resolved their housing needs, they registered domicile there, and neither they nor family members already owned suitable housing. The Rijeka Tax Office granted a partial exemption of HRK 23 437 (approx. EUR 3 125) while warning that the sum would be collected if the conditions of section 11(10) were later found unmet. Section 11(10) provided for subsequent collection only if the property was disposed of within five years or if the Tax Administration later established that the original conditions had not been satisfied. In December 2009 the applicant changed his domicile after marrying. In 2010 the Tax Office revoked the exemption, holding that he no longer used the flat for housing needs. His appeals to the Finance Ministry, Rijeka Administrative Court and Constitutional Court failed; the courts interpreted the statute as requiring continued compliance with the housing-purpose condition, including maintenance of domicile, throughout the five-year period. The tax plus interest was enforced in 2011.

The second applicant bought a flat in December 2008, registered it as his domicile and obtained a full exemption of HRK 22 506 (approx. EUR 3 000) under the same provision, again with the section 11(10) warning. He changed domicile in July 2009 to care for his ill mother. In 2012 the Tax Office revoked the exemption on the ground that the flat had not been purchased to resolve housing needs. Parallel appeals were dismissed on identical reasoning. The 2011 amendments later made explicit that changing domicile or ceasing to live at the property triggered collection, but the domestic courts held that this merely clarified an already-existing requirement under the earlier text.

Both applicants argued that the pre-2011 statute mentioned neither change of domicile nor continued residence as grounds for revocation, that they had satisfied all conditions at the moment the tax liability arose, and that the later interpretation was unforeseeable and retroactive. They further invoked section 5 of the General Tax Act, which required application of the law in force when the taxable event occurred. Domestic case-law was mixed: some administrative and Supreme Court decisions treated subsequent change of use or domicile as fatal to the exemption, while one Constitutional Court ruling (in an unrelated case) found such an interpretation of “disposal” arbitrary. Tax-administration manuals issued before 2011 mentioned only disposal or original non-compliance.

The ECtHR ultimately held that the decisions were lawful and proportionate and that the State’s wide margin of appreciation in tax matters had not been exceeded.

The case of Bežanić and Baškarad v. Croatia (applications nos. 16140/15 and 13322/16) concerns two Croatian nationals who alleged that domestic decisions requiring them to pay real estate transfer tax after initially granting exemptions violated their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Aleksandar Bežanić purchased a flat in Rijeka on 26 January 2007 and registered it as his domicile on 15 March 2007. On 20 March 2007 he applied for exemption under section 11(9) of the Real Estate Transfer Tax Act (in force 2003–2011), which exempted first-time buyers of a flat or house to resolve housing needs if they held Croatian citizenship, registered domicile at the property, and neither they nor family members owned other suitable housing. On 28 March 2007 the Rijeka Tax Office found him liable for HRK 28,192.32 (approx. EUR 3,760) but exempted HRK 23,437.63 (approx. EUR 3,125), warning that the exempted sum would be collected if section 11(10) conditions were met. Section 11(10) provided for subsequent collection if the property was disposed of within five years or if the Tax Administration later found the exemption conditions had not been complied with.

Bežanić changed his domicile on 18 December 2009 after marrying and moving to his wife’s flat (having lived in the purchased property for more than two years). On 8 September 2010 the Tax Office annulled the exemption, holding that the domicile change showed he no longer used the flat to resolve housing needs, and ordered payment of the exempted amount. He appealed, arguing that section 11(10) mentioned only disposal or original non-compliance, not a later domicile change. The Finance Ministry dismissed the appeal in 2013. The Rijeka Administrative Court dismissed his action in 2014, finding that changing domicile within five years meant he had ceased to meet the statutory conditions. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint as manifestly ill-founded in December 2014. The tax plus statutory interest (HRK 23,617.43, approx. EUR 3,150) was collected by enforcement in 2011.

Stipica Baškarad purchased a flat on 29 December 2008, registered it as his domicile on 23 January 2009 and applied for exemption the same day. On 13 March 2009 the Tax Office granted full exemption from HRK 22,506 (approx. EUR 3,000) with an identical warning. He changed domicile on 15 July 2009 to live with and care for his mother after her health deteriorated. On 2 February 2012 the Tax Office annulled the exemption, concluding he had not purchased the flat to resolve housing needs, and ordered payment. He appealed on the same grounds as Bežanić, stressing that he had satisfied all conditions at the time of purchase. The Finance Ministry dismissed the appeal in 2013. The Rijeka Administrative Court dismissed his action in 2014, holding that exemption required the property to be used for housing needs throughout the five-year period and that 2011 amendments had merely clarified the existing scheme. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint in July 2015. The tax was collected in 2012.

The 2011 amendments (not applicable at the relevant time) expressly required the buyer and family to register domicile and live at the property and listed changing address as a ground for subsequent collection within three years. Domestic case-law before the amendments was not uniform, but several administrative-court decisions treated a later change of domicile as demonstrating that the property was no longer used to resolve housing needs, thereby triggering section 11(10). These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ claim that the subsequent tax demands were unforeseen, lacked a sufficiently clear legal basis and interfered disproportionately with their possessions.

The ECtHR case of Bežanić and Baškarad v. Croatia (apps. 16140/15 and 13322/16) concerned two Croatian nationals who alleged that domestic decisions requiring them to pay real estate transfer tax, after initially granting exemptions, violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

The first applicant, Aleksandar Bežanić, bought a flat in Rijeka on 26 January 2007 and registered it as his domicile on 15 March 2007. He applied for exemption under section 11(9) of the Real Estate Transfer Tax Act (as in force until February 2011), which exempted Croatian citizens making a first purchase of a flat or house to resolve housing needs, provided they registered their domicile there and met other conditions (e.g., no other suitable property). On 28 March 2007 the Rijeka Tax Office found him liable for HRK 28,192.32 (approx. EUR 3,760) but exempted HRK 23,437.63 (approx. EUR 3,125), warning that the exempted sum would be collected if section 11(10) conditions were met. Section 11(10) provided for subsequent collection if the property was disposed of within five years or if the Tax Administration later found the exemption conditions had not been complied with.

In December 2009, after marrying, Bežanić registered a new domicile at his wife’s flat. In September 2010 the Tax Office annulled the exemption, holding that he no longer used the purchased flat for housing needs, and ordered payment of the exempted amount. He argued on appeal that section 11(10) did not list a change of domicile as a triggering event and that he had lived in the flat for over two years. The Finance Ministry, Rijeka Administrative Court and Constitutional Court all dismissed his challenges (the Administrative Court reasoning that a domicile change within five years meant he had ceased to satisfy the statutory conditions). The tax (plus interest) was enforced in 2011.

The second applicant, Stipica Baškarad, bought a flat on 29 December 2008, registered it as his domicile on 23 January 2009 and obtained a full exemption of HRK 22,506 (approx. EUR 3,000) on 13 March 2009, again with a section 11(10) warning. In July 2009 he changed his domicile to his mother’s address to care for her after her health declined. In February 2012 the Tax Office revoked the exemption, finding the flat had not been purchased to resolve his housing needs. He argued that all conditions had been met at purchase and that a later domicile change was not a ground for revocation under the law then in force. His appeals were likewise dismissed; the Administrative Court added that 2011 amendments (which expressly required continued residence and domicile registration for three years) merely clarified existing requirements. The tax was collected in 2012.

The 2011 amendments replaced the relevant provisions, introducing an explicit three-year residence/domicile condition and reducing the claw-back period. Earlier Tax Administration guidance and domestic case-law had treated continued use for housing needs (including domicile) as implicit in the original scheme, though one 2015 Constitutional Court decision found an interpretation equating “disposal” with a mere domicile change to be arbitrary in different factual circumstances. Both applicants maintained that the revocations were unforeseeable, lacked a sufficient legal basis under the pre-2011 text, and therefore unlawfully interfered with their possessions.
001-217436:
The case of Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland (Application no. 23077/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention arising from the applicant’s inability, as a wheelchair user, to access two local public buildings that hosted cultural and social activities.

The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1976 and living in Reykjanesbær, was left permanently paralysed from the chest down after a 2002 accident and has used a wheelchair ever since. In 2015 he and an association of people with spinal injuries brought civil proceedings against the municipality of Reykjanesbær and its holding company. They sought a declaratory judgment requiring specific accessibility improvements at two municipal buildings, together with compensation of ISK 1 000 000 (approximately EUR 7 300) for non-pecuniary damage.

Duushús, comprising adjoining structures dating from 1877 and 1954–70 and extensively renovated between 2006 and 2014, served as the municipality’s principal arts and cultural centre. The plaintiffs demanded a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps no steeper than 1:20 between ground-floor galleries, and modification of the 51 mm main-entrance threshold. 88 Húsið, originally built in 1963 as an engine house and converted into a municipal youth centre in 2004, required a lift between floors, ramps of 1:20 from the car park and between rooms, and a designated disabled parking space within 25 metres of the entrance.

A court-appointed assessor confirmed the absence of lifts in both buildings, a 1:7 ramp and high threshold at Duushús, a 1:9 ramp and lack of disabled parking at 88 Húsið. The plaintiffs contended that these features breached applicable building regulations, the Icelandic Constitution, the Convention and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). They argued that the inaccessibility prevented the applicant, and other wheelchair users, from participating equally in cultural and social life, thereby interfering with his private life.

The Reykjanes District Court (24 November 2016) accepted that access needed improvement but held that both buildings predated the relevant regulations and therefore complied with them. It recognised the municipality’s statutory duty to enhance wheelchair access to public buildings yet emphasised municipal discretion in prioritising works and the separation of powers, which prevented courts from ordering specific measures.

The Supreme Court (25 October 2018) upheld that judgment. It noted that the CRPD, although ratified, had not been incorporated into domestic law and could not be relied on directly, though statutes had to be interpreted consistently with Iceland’s international obligations. Responsibility for disability matters had been transferred to municipalities in 2010. Reykjanesbær had adopted and begun implementing a strategy for improving public-building accessibility in line with national legislation enacted in light of those obligations. Municipalities enjoyed constitutional autonomy over their affairs and a wide margin of appreciation in allocating limited funds.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the State had failed in its positive obligation to make “necessary and appropriate modifications and adjustments” that did not impose a “disproportionate or undue burden,” thereby discriminating against him in the enjoyment of his right to respect for private life by hindering his participation in important local cultural and social events.

The case of Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland (ECtHR, Application no. 23077/19) concerns a wheelchair-using applicant's claim that inaccessible municipal public buildings violated his rights under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). The applicant, born in 1976 and resident in Reykjanesbær, was left paralysed from the chest down after a 2002 accident and relies on a wheelchair. In 2015, together with a spinal injuries association, he brought civil proceedings against the municipality of Reykjanesbær and its holding company F. (owner of one building). He sought a declaratory order requiring specific accessibility upgrades to two local public buildings that served important cultural and social functions, plus ISK 1,000,000 in non-pecuniary damages.

Duushús, a three-storey arts and cultural centre formed from adjoining 19th- and mid-20th-century buildings and extensively renovated 2006–2014, lacked a lift between floors, had a ground-floor ramp with an incline of approximately 1:7 (steeper than the 1:20 required by later building regulations) and a 51 mm entrance threshold. 88 Húsið, a two-storey 1963 former engine house converted into a municipal youth centre in 2004, similarly lacked a lift, had no ramps between rooms, featured a 1:9 incline from the car park and had no designated disabled parking within 25 metres of the entrance. A court-appointed assessor confirmed these deficiencies.

The applicant argued that the buildings failed to comply with applicable construction regulations and that the resulting inaccessibility prevented him (and other wheelchair users) from participating equally in cultural, recreational and social life, contrary to the Icelandic Constitution, the ECHR and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). The Reykjanes District Court dismissed the claim on 24 November 2016, holding that the buildings predated the relevant regulations, that municipalities enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation in prioritising accessibility works, and that the municipality was already implementing a general improvement programme. The Supreme Court of Iceland upheld this on 25 October 2018, noting that the CRPD had been ratified but not incorporated into domestic law, that municipalities enjoyed constitutional autonomy over their finances and that the municipality had adopted and begun executing a strategy for gradual accessibility improvements consistent with national legislation that itself reflected international obligations.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the continued inaccessibility of two clearly identified public buildings that played a central role in local cultural and social life constituted a failure of the State's positive obligations under Article 8 (respect for private life, encompassing the right to participate in community cultural activities) read with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). He relied on the CRPD concepts of accessibility and “reasonable accommodation” (necessary and appropriate modifications not imposing a disproportionate or undue burden). The Court accepted that the lack of access fell within the ambit of Article 8 but ultimately found no violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8. It held that Iceland had taken considerable measures to achieve universal accessibility gradually and that the remaining barriers in the two specific buildings did not amount to a failure to provide reasonable accommodation or to unjustified discrimination.

The case of Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland (ECtHR, Application no. 23077/19) concerned alleged discrimination against a wheelchair user due to inaccessible public buildings. The applicant, born in 1976 and residing in Reykjanesbær, was left permanently paralysed from the chest down after a 2002 accident and relies on a wheelchair. In 2015, together with a spinal injuries association, he brought civil proceedings against his municipality (Reykjanesbær) and its holding company F. (owner of one building). They sought a declaratory judgment requiring specific accessibility improvements to two municipal buildings that housed arts, cultural and social facilities, plus ISK 1,000,000 (approximately EUR 7,300) in non-pecuniary damages.

The first building, Duushús, consisted of adjoining structures from 1877 and 1954–70, extensively renovated between 2006 and 2014. It served as the municipality’s main arts and cultural centre. The plaintiffs demanded a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps no steeper than 1:20 between ground-floor galleries (per building regulations) and a lowered main-entrance threshold. The second building, 88 Húsið, a two-storey 1963 former engine house converted into a municipal youth centre in 2004, required a lift between floors, 1:20 ramps from the car park and between rooms, plus a disabled parking space within 25 metres of the entrance.

A court-appointed assessor confirmed the deficiencies: Duushús lacked any lift, featured a 1:7 ramp (96–161 cm wide) between ground-floor halls and a 51 mm entrance threshold; 88 Húsið had no lift or internal ramps, a 1:9 car-park ramp and no designated disabled parking. The plaintiffs argued that the buildings failed to meet applicable regulations and that the resulting inaccessibility prevented the applicant (and other wheelchair users) from enjoying private life on an equal basis with others, contrary to the Icelandic Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

The Reykjanes District Court dismissed the claim on 24 November 2016. It accepted that accessibility needed improvement but held that the pre-existing buildings did not violate later-enacted regulations. Municipalities were legally obliged to work toward better wheelchair access to public buildings and services, and Reykjanesbær had launched an improvement initiative. Courts, however, could not dictate specific measures given the authorities’ margin of appreciation and the separation of powers.

The Supreme Court upheld this outcome on 25 October 2018. Although Iceland had ratified the CRPD, it had not incorporated the treaty, so its provisions could not be invoked directly; domestic law nevertheless had to be interpreted consistently with international obligations where possible. The municipality had fulfilled its statutory duty (under the Disabilities Act) to devise and implement an accessibility strategy for public buildings, taking account of international human-rights commitments. Responsibility for disability matters had been transferred to municipalities in 2010; those bodies enjoyed constitutional autonomy over local affairs and the allocation of their funds, and therefore possessed a wide margin of appreciation in prioritising improvements. The Supreme Court did not expressly address the Convention or the equality/non-discrimination arguments.

Domestic law relevant to the complaint included constitutional guarantees of equality (Art. 65), respect for private life (Art. 71) and assistance for persons with disabilities (Art. 76), together with municipal autonomy (Art. 78). The Disabilities Act placed organisation of disability services, including accessibility plans for public buildings, on municipalities. International materials emphasised accessibility as a precondition for equal participation (CRPD Arts. 2, 9 and 30), the distinction between gradual group-oriented accessibility duties and immediate individual reasonable-accommodation duties, and the need to ensure access to cultural and social venues without imposing a disproportionate burden.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the continued inaccessibility of two locally important public buildings hindered his participation in cultural and social life, engaging Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14.
001-217437:
The case of Galeano Peñas v. Spain (ECtHR, 2022) concerns a former Civil Guard officer convicted of forging official records. On 15 July 2013 the Audiencia Provincial of Madrid sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment (a “less severe” penalty under Art. 33 of the Criminal Code), together with a two-year disqualification from public office, electoral suspension and a fine. The judgment became final on 8 January 2014 and execution proceedings were opened. Four days later the applicant applied for a royal pardon; two days after that he sought suspension of the prison sentence pending the pardon decision. On 28 January 2014 the court granted the suspension under Art. 4 § 4 of the Criminal Code.

Spanish law then provided that a pardon request not decided within one year could be treated as rejected (Royal Decree 1879/1994). The Ministry of Justice nevertheless repeatedly informed the court that the request remained pending (July 2017, January 2019). In May 2017 the court first treated the request as rejected and ordered the applicant to prison; after an appeal and further ministerial confirmation that the pardon was still under examination, it re-imposed the stay. Meanwhile the applicant served a three-year disciplinary suspension from the Civil Guard (2015–2018) and paid the criminal fine (January 2017).

By late 2018 the five-year limitation period that, under the version of Art. 134 of the Criminal Code in force at the time of conviction, ran from the date of the final judgment was about to expire. The public prosecutor advised that the successive stays had interrupted the period. On 4 April 2019 the Audiencia Provincial lifted the stay, holding that continued suspension of a three-year sentence was no longer justified. The applicant’s appeals, including a plea of nullity, were dismissed on the ground that the earlier stay decisions had interrupted limitation. He entered prison on 3 June 2019, lost his military status and, after serving part of the sentence in closed then open conditions, was placed on parole; the sentence expired on 1 June 2022.

An amparo application to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible for lack of constitutional significance. The applicant complained to the ECtHR that, because the original wording of Art. 134 did not list suspension as a ground of interruption, the limitation period had expired and his imprisonment therefore violated Art. 5 § 1 (unlawful detention) and Art. 7 (retroactive application of a more severe rule). The Court ultimately found the detention lawful and the interruption reasonably foreseeable, but those conclusions rest on the chronology and domestic procedural steps summarised above.

The case of Galeano Peñas v. Spain concerns a Spanish Civil Guard officer convicted in 2013 of forging facts in a public record after reporting traffic offences against a woman following an off-duty argument. The Audiencia Provincial of Madrid imposed a three-year prison sentence (classified as “less severe”), a two-year disqualification from public office, a fine, and other penalties. The judgment became final on 8 January 2014, when execution proceedings opened and the applicant was ordered to prison.

On 17 January 2014 the applicant requested a royal pardon of the prison term. Two days later he sought suspension of execution pending that request. On 28 January 2014 the Audiencia Provincial granted the suspension under Article 4 § 4 of the Criminal Code, which permits suspension where execution might violate the right to trial without undue delay. Spanish law required the Council of Ministers to decide pardon requests within one year, after which they could be deemed rejected. No express decision was ever issued.

In the intervening years the applicant was suspended from duty (2015–2018) as a disciplinary consequence of the conviction and paid the fine in 2017. On 19 May 2017 the court treated the pardon as rejected by silence and ordered resumption of the sentence. After an appeal and confirmation from the Ministry of Justice that the request remained pending, the court re-suspended execution on 14 September 2017.

By late 2018 the five-year limitation period for enforcing a less-severe sentence (Article 133 Criminal Code), calculated from the final judgment under the then-applicable Article 134, was approaching expiry in January 2019. The Ministry again confirmed the pardon was pending. In March 2019 the public prosecutor advised that the limitation period had been interrupted by the earlier suspension. On 4 April 2019 the Audiencia Provincial lifted the suspension, holding that such measures were exceptional, that the public interest in serving sentences weighed heavily given the three-year term, and that execution must resume. The applicant’s appeal, arguing that the limitation period had expired (or alternatively that suspension should continue), was dismissed on 13 May 2019; the court ruled that its prior suspension decision had interrupted the running of time. A plea of nullity was likewise rejected.

The applicant entered Alcalá de Henares Prison on 3 June 2019. He subsequently lost his military status and pay. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court, invoking the right to liberty and the principle of legality, was declared inadmissible in February 2020 for lack of constitutional relevance.

Under the Criminal Code as it stood at conviction, limitation ran from the final judgment (or from breach if service had begun) and listed no grounds of interruption other than commencement of service. Constitutional Court case-law (e.g., SSTC 192/2013, 87/2013, 12/2016) had repeatedly held that a mere suspension pending pardon did not interrupt limitation and that any contrary interpretation violated the requirement of rigorous reasoning where personal liberty was at stake. A 2015 legislative amendment expressly added suspension as an interrupting event, but the applicant’s conviction and initial execution proceedings predated that change. Supreme Court jurisprudence on intertemporal application of execution rules was mixed.

The applicant served part of the sentence in closed regime, later moved to open conditions and parole, and completed it in June 2022. He alleged before the European Court that enforcement after the five-year period had expired rendered his detention arbitrary (Article 5 § 1) and contrary to the principle of legality (Article 7).

The case of Galeano Peñas v. Spain (Application no. 48784/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged violations of Article 7 and Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant, a Spanish Civil Guard officer born in 1987, claimed that the time-limit for enforcing his three-year prison sentence had expired, rendering his subsequent detention unlawful.

On 17 December 2011, while off duty, the applicant argued with a woman over a traffic incident and later allegedly fabricated two traffic offences against her in official records. On 15 July 2013 the Audiencia Provincial of Madrid convicted him of forgery of facts in a public record committed by a civil servant. The penalties included three years’ imprisonment (classified as a “less severe” sentence under Spanish law), a six-month fine, two years’ disqualification from public office, and other measures. The judgment became final on 8 January 2014 and execution proceedings were opened, ordering the applicant to prison.

On 17 January 2014 the applicant sought a royal pardon for the prison term. Two days later he requested suspension of execution pending the pardon decision. On 28 January 2014 the Audiencia Provincial granted the suspension under Article 4 § 4 of the Criminal Code, which permits suspension where a pardon request is pending and continued execution might breach the right to trial without undue delay. Spanish law required the Council of Ministers to decide pardon requests within one year, after which they could be deemed rejected.

The applicant was separately suspended from his Civil Guard post for three years (February 2015–February 2018) following disciplinary proceedings linked to the conviction. He paid the criminal fine in January 2017.

On 19 May 2017 the Audiencia Provincial treated the pardon as tacitly rejected and ordered resumption of the sentence. After the applicant appealed, the Ministry of Justice confirmed the request remained pending, so suspension was reinstated in September 2017. In November 2018 the court warned the Ministry that the five-year limitation period (Article 133 of the Criminal Code) would expire in January 2019. The Ministry again reported the pardon still pending.

In March 2019 the public prosecutor advised that the limitation period had been interrupted by the successive suspensions. On 4 April 2019 the Audiencia Provincial lifted the suspension, holding that such measures were exceptional, that the three-year term justified prompt enforcement, and that the general interest required the sentence to be served. The applicant’s appeals, including a plea of nullity, were dismissed; the court found the limitation period interrupted by the earlier suspension decisions. He entered Alcalá de Henares Prison on 3 June 2019.

An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible in February 2020 for lack of constitutional relevance. The applicant served the sentence under a closed regime until February 2021, then an open regime, and later on parole, completing it on 1 June 2022. Meanwhile he lost his professional status pursuant to the disqualification penalty.

The legal framework at issue included the original Article 134 of the Criminal Code (limitation calculated from the final judgment or from any subsequent breach of an already-commenced sentence) and its 2015 amendment, which expressly provided that suspension of enforcement interrupts the limitation period. Constitutional Court case-law predating and post-dating the amendment generally treated limitation as an ordinary-law matter requiring rigorous reasoning, and had held that, under the old wording, a pardon-related suspension did not interrupt the period. Supreme Court jurisprudence applied the law in force at the time of execution rather than the date of the offence.

These facts form the core of the applicant’s claims that the limitation period had expired by 2019, that the courts’ contrary interpretation was unforeseeable and contrary to the principle of legality, and that his imprisonment therefore lacked a lawful basis.
001-217616:
The case of Maria Azzopardi v. Malta (no. 22008/20) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from the expropriation of the applicant’s land under Malta’s Building Development Areas Act (BDAA) of 1983 (repealed 1988). The applicant, born in 1943, held bare ownership of approximately 3,193 m² of land in Qormi (usufruct to her father after her mother’s 1975 death). On 4 July 1983 a parliamentary resolution under the BDAA declared the land a Building Development Area, causing the owners to lose possession (father notified 14 January 1985). The land was subdivided and sold to third parties; at least 25 private homes now occupy it. The applicant, already a homeowner, could not use the BDAA provision allowing original owners a preferential plot for personal residence.

In 1992 compensation proceedings began before the Land Arbitration Board (LAB); the applicant joined and continued after her father’s death. On 19 December 2013 the LAB awarded €4,000, treating the land as agricultural under BDAA s. 6. In 2016 the applicant sought constitutional redress, claiming the award was inadequate. She argued the land had been taken specifically for residential development (not agriculture) and that the BDAA itself violated Protocol 1 by ignoring the land’s nature, intended use and development potential. Her architect valued it at €163,000 as a building site in 1985 and €2,283,400 by 2014.

The Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction (12 June 2018) found no violation. Compensation had to reflect the land’s actual status and market value at the moment of taking, not the State’s subsequent use or later market prices. The land had been rural and lacked independent development potential; existing building sites were excluded from BDAA expropriation. The €4,000 restored the applicant to her pre-taking position and produced no economic loss. The Constitutional Court (29 November 2019) confirmed this. The public-interest purpose was unchallenged and unproven to be absent. Any later increase in value accrued to third-party purchasers, not the applicant. Potential arising solely from the expropriation itself could not be claimed as a “windfall.” Delay in the LAB proceedings was irrelevant to the compensation issue.

The European Court of Human Rights (9 June 2022, final 9 September 2022) held that the expropriation pursued a legitimate public-interest aim, that domestic courts had reasonably classified the land as agricultural for valuation purposes, that procedural safeguards existed, and that the wide margin of appreciation had not been exceeded. A fair balance between the applicant’s rights and the general interest had therefore been struck. No violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was found.

The case of Maria Azzopardi v. Malta (Application no. 22008/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, arising from the expropriation of the applicant’s land under Malta’s Building Development Areas Act (BDAA) of 1983 (repealed in 1988).

The applicant, born in 1943, owned a tract of land measuring approximately 3,193 square metres known as Tal-Andar in the limits of Qormi. The land had originally belonged to her mother, who died in 1975, leaving the applicant with bare ownership and her father with usufruct. On 4 July 1983, a parliamentary resolution under the BDAA declared the land a Building Development Area. This resulted in the owners losing possession; the applicant’s father was notified by judicial letter on 14 January 1985. The authorities then divided the land into plots and sold them to third parties, who constructed at least 25 privately owned residential homes that remain on the site. The applicant, already owning other residential property, could not benefit from a BDAA provision allowing original owners to acquire a plot for their own residence.

In 1992 the applicant’s father (with the applicant later joining) initiated proceedings before the Land Arbitration Board (LAB) seeking compensation. After the father’s death, the case continued in the applicant’s name. On 19 December 2013 the LAB awarded €4,000, applying Section 6 of the BDAA, which required land declared a Building Development Area to be valued as agricultural or wasteland for compensation purposes.

Dissatisfied, the applicant brought constitutional redress proceedings in 2016, claiming a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She argued that the compensation was inadequate given that the land had been taken specifically for residential development and sold on to third parties who now owned valuable homes. She submitted an architect’s valuation placing the land’s worth at €163,000 in 1985 if treated as a building site, rising to €2,283,400 by 2014. She further contended that the BDAA itself was incompatible with the Convention because it disregarded the land’s nature, designated use and development potential when fixing compensation.

The Civil Court (First Hall) sitting in its constitutional jurisdiction dismissed the claim on 12 June 2018. It held that compensation must reflect the land’s actual use and situation at the moment of expropriation, not subsequent development or neighbouring values. The land had been agricultural, possessed no inherent development potential (building permits being at the Minister’s discretion before the BDAA), and could not have been included in a development area had it already been a building site. The €4,000 award therefore represented fair value and caused no economic loss.

The Constitutional Court upheld this decision on 29 November 2019. It found no evidence that the expropriation lacked a public-interest purpose or that the land possessed pre-expropriation development potential. Compensation restored the applicant to her pre-taking position; any later increase in value accrued to third parties and did not infringe her rights. Delay in payment was unrelated to the compensation issue.

The Strasbourg Court ultimately found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It accepted that the expropriation pursued a legitimate public-interest aim, that domestic valuations as agricultural land were reasonably founded, that procedural safeguards existed, and that a fair balance had been struck within the State’s wide margin of appreciation. Compensation was therefore adequate.

**Case of Maria Azzopardi v. Malta (App. no. 22008/20, ECHR 9 June 2022, final 9 Sept. 2022)**

The applicant, a Maltese national born in 1943, owned approximately 3,193 m² of land known as Tal-Andar in Qormi (bare ownership inherited from her mother, who died in 1975; her father held the usufruct). In July 1983, pursuant to a House of Representatives resolution under the Building Development Areas Act (BDAA, Act 1 of 1983, repealed 1988), the land was declared a Building Development Area. Possession was lost; her father was notified in January 1985. The authorities divided the land into plots sold to third parties, who built at least 25 privately owned residential homes that remain today and have become highly valuable. The applicant, already housed elsewhere, could not benefit from BDAA s. 12 (preference for original owners to acquire a plot for their own residence).

In 1992 her father (joined later by the applicant) sought compensation before the Land Arbitration Board (LAB). After his death the case continued in her name. In December 2013 the LAB awarded €4,000, applying BDAA s. 6, which required valuation as rural or wasteland. The applicant’s architect valued the land as a building site at €163,000 (1985) and €2,283,400 (2014).

In 2016 she brought constitutional redress proceedings, alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She argued the compensation was inadequate because the land had been taken specifically for development (now generating valuable private assets) rather than agricultural use, and that the BDAA itself was incompatible with the Convention by ignoring the land’s nature, designated use and potential. She also contended there was no genuine social purpose benefiting those in need.

The Civil Court (First Hall, constitutional jurisdiction) found no violation in June 2018. It held that compensation must reflect the land’s actual agricultural character at expropriation (not later development or neighbouring values), that the BDAA took potential into account via s. 7 (higher compensation for bona-fide pre-1983 purchasers at a premium), and that developable land could not be included under the BDAA. The €4,000 restored the applicant to her pre-taking position, so there was no economic loss.

The Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal in November 2019. It confirmed the public-interest purpose (uncontested by the applicant) and the fairness of the award, noting she had produced no evidence of higher pre-BDAA market value or of the plots’ sale conditions. The land was undisputedly agricultural before 1983 and possessed no development potential independent of the expropriation itself; any later increase accrued to third parties after a fair payment had been made. Delay in the LAB proceedings was irrelevant to the constitutional claim.

The ECHR (First Section) likewise found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The expropriation pursued a legitimate public-interest aim (housing development). Domestic courts had reasonably treated the land as agricultural for valuation purposes, consistent with its pre-taking character and the statutory scheme. Procedural safeguards existed (LAB proceedings with appeal, constitutional review). Malta had not exceeded its wide margin of appreciation; a fair balance had been struck between the community’s interest and the applicant’s rights, given the compensation awarded.

The ECHR case Algirdas Butkevičius v. Lithuania (no. 70489/17) concerns the former Lithuanian Prime Minister’s Article 8 complaint that authorities breached his rights to private life and correspondence by disclosing an intercepted telephone conversation to the media.

Butkevičius, a long-serving politician and PM from November 2012 to November 2016, was linked to a 2015 pre-trial investigation (no. 03-7-00012-15) into possible abuse of office (Criminal Code Art. 228 § 2) over Government Resolution no. 1025 of 23 September 2015. The resolution revoked protected “resort” status for certain territories, including areas near Druskininkai, amid allegations of political corruption tied to construction in Vijūnėlė park. The resolution was later annulled.

Investigators, authorised by a court, intercepted calls of R.M., Druskininkai’s mayor and a political ally of the applicant. On 11 August 2015 the applicant and R.M. discussed the resolution’s progress: R.M. noted it had left the Ministry of Justice and awaited Environment Ministry submission, and the applicant agreed to “move things along.” The exchange was purely work-related.

On 29 February 2016 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding no crime, and included conversation transcripts in the decision. The same day, responding to a request from the Seimas Anti-Corruption Commission (conducting a parliamentary inquiry), the prosecutor forwarded the decision without any non-disclosure warning. A copy also went to the Chief Official Ethics Commission.

On 1 March 2016 the Commission held a public hearing attended by some 20 journalists. Members quoted the transcripts. That evening Delfi published an article reproducing extracts of the applicant–R.M. call and others, suggesting government members (including the PM) were influenced by the mayor on business interests. The story was widely republished.

The applicant complained to the Prosecutor General of unlawful disclosure of restricted pre-trial material, arguing it violated correspondence secrecy, caused psychological harm, damaged his reputation and political career, and was politically motivated. He noted the number was his official work mobile and that, as a witness, he had not discussed private matters. R.M. and the Environment Minister filed similar complaints.

A follow-up investigation into unauthorised disclosure (Criminal Code Arts. 247 and 168) was discontinued on 5 October 2016. Prosecutors and courts held the conversation concerned public official duties, not private life; the applicant himself had described it as work-related and denied informal ties with R.M. As prominent public figures, the individuals faced higher scrutiny. Society had a legitimate interest in possible corruption in territorial planning. Commission members were not parties to the original proceedings, had not been warned of criminal liability, and were entitled to the material; the hearing was lawfully public. Higher prosecutors and courts (Vilnius City District Court 10 February 2017; Vilnius Regional Court 20 March 2017) upheld these findings.

The Ethics Commission declined to investigate, noting the resolution was of general application with no proven personal benefit to those involved.

The applicant maintained that the disclosure of intercepted correspondence by state bodies nevertheless interfered with his private life and reputation among colleagues.

001-217715:
The case of Alexandru-Radu Luca v. Romania (Application no. 20837/18) involves a complaint under Article 6 of the Convention that criminal proceedings were unfair due to pre-trial judge proceedings confirming the applicant’s indictment.

The applicant, a Romanian loans broker born in 1978, faced charges after U.Ţ. bank lodged a 2009 criminal complaint (with civil claims) against him, co-defendants I.H., C.M., I.B.C.N., C.Ş., and his company for fraud in obtaining loans. On 7 April 2011 the National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) indicted him for four counts of being an accessory to fraud (and others on related charges), relying on defendant statements, witness testimony, documents and specialist reports. He received notice of the indictment and evidence.

Initial proceedings under the former CCP (in force until 1 February 2014) were public, oral and adversarial. On 22 May 2013 the Bucharest County Court convicted the applicant (and co-defendants), imposing a 10-year sentence and upholding civil claims. On 28 February 2014 the Bucharest Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted for retrial because the bank’s insurer had not been summoned.

After the new CCP entered into force, the County Court (at a public hearing on 5 June 2014) referred the remitted case to a pre-trial judge on 6 June 2014, treating all prior acts as quashed. The pre-trial judge sent the applicant the indictment and invited written comments on the lawfulness of the investigation and evidence-gathering. He objected in writing, arguing the indictment misinterpreted evidence, relied on missing or misread contracts, failed to establish forgeries, and that the County Court lacked competence (a district court being proper under new rules). Co-defendants raised similar points, including DNA’s alleged lack of competence given the damage value and failure to involve the insurer (or appoint a special representative for the company).

The DNA responded in writing. On 20 August 2014 the pre-trial judge, sitting in chambers without the parties, dismissed the objections and sent the case to trial. Competence lay with the DNA and County Court; arguments about evidence sufficiency or completeness of investigation were for the trial court, not the pre-trial review of lawfulness.

The applicant (and co-defendants) challenged this. He indicated he would file arguments later but did not. On 30 October 2014 the Court of Appeal pre-trial judge, again in chambers without the parties, dismissed the challenges as ill-founded.

The applicant’s extraordinary appeal of annulment (claiming he was neither summoned nor notified of the date) was dismissed as inadmissible on 3 December 2014, as such appeals apply only to merits judgments and the closed procedure was then lawful. His appeal to review (invoking Constitutional Court Decision no. 641 of 11 November 2014, which later declared key CCP provisions unconstitutional for lacking oral/adversarial character) was likewise dismissed as inadmissible on 26 June 2015 (and his further appeal withdrawn).

The subsequent trial was fully public, oral and adversarial. The applicant and counsel attended all hearings, contested evidence (including some pre-trial arguments), requested additional documents/experts/testimony, made statements, challenged other parties and questioned witnesses (including those from the investigation). On 24 April 2017 the County Court convicted him of part of the charges and imposed 2 years 6 months’ imprisonment (plus partial civil liability). On 18 December 2017 the Court of Appeal (after appeals by the applicant, most co-defendants and the DNA) confirmed guilt and increased the sentence to 3 years 6 months.

(The Constitutional Court had stressed that pre-trial review of evidence lawfulness can exclude material permanently and thus directly affects trial fairness, requiring oral/adversarial guarantees.)

The applicant, a Romanian national, complained under Article 6 of the Convention that criminal proceedings against him were unfair due to pre-trial judge proceedings that confirmed his indictment in breach of fair-trial guarantees.

In November 2009 a private bank filed a criminal complaint with civil claims against the applicant and several others, alleging fraud in connection with loans the applicant had brokered while employed by the bank. In April 2011 the National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) indicted the applicant for four counts of being an accessory to fraud (and others for related fraud or accessory offences), relying on defendant statements, witness testimony, documents and expert reports. The applicant was notified of the indictment and supporting evidence.

Proceedings initially followed the former Code of Criminal Procedure. In May 2013 the Bucharest County Court convicted the applicant and co-defendants, sentencing him to ten years’ imprisonment and upholding the bank’s civil claims. On appeal the Bucharest Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in February 2014 and remitted the case for retrial, finding that the insurer of the bank had not been summoned.

By then a new Code of Criminal Procedure had entered into force. At a June 2014 hearing the County Court, over the defendants’ objections, referred the remitted case to a pre-trial judge, holding that the remittal had invalidated all prior first-instance acts and that the new procedural rules therefore applied.

The pre-trial judge transmitted the indictment to the applicant and invited written comments on the lawfulness of the investigation and of the evidence-gathering. The applicant objected that the indictment misinterpreted or contradicted the evidence, relied on missing or misread contracts, and failed to establish whether documents had been forged; he also challenged the County Court’s competence under the new rules. Co-defendants raised additional points concerning the DNA’s competence, the insurer’s absence and the lack of a special representative for the corporate defendant. The DNA replied in writing.

Sitting in chambers and without the parties, the pre-trial judge dismissed all objections on 20 August 2014 and sent the case to trial. The judge found that competence issues were properly determined by the DNA and County Court given the alleged damage, that the insurer need not have been summoned at the investigation stage, and that the remaining arguments concerned the sufficiency or completeness of the evidence rather than its lawfulness and therefore belonged to the trial court.

The applicant and co-defendants challenged the decision. The Court of Appeal’s pre-trial judge, again sitting in chambers without the parties, dismissed the challenges on 30 October 2014, largely endorsing the first-instance reasoning. The applicant’s subsequent extraordinary appeals of annulment and review were declared inadmissible; the courts held that those remedies applied only to merits judgments and that the written, non-adversarial procedure then in force had been correctly applied. (A November 2014 Constitutional Court decision later declared key pre-trial-judge provisions unconstitutional for failing to guarantee oral and adversarial proceedings, but that ruling had only prospective effect.)

The subsequent trial was public, oral and adversarial. The applicant and his lawyer attended all hearings, contested the evidence, requested additional documents, experts and witnesses, examined co-defendants and witnesses (including those heard at the investigation stage) and made statements. The County Court convicted him in April 2017 of part of the charges and imposed a sentence of two years and six months. On appeal the Court of Appeal, in a final December 2017 judgment, increased the sentence to three years and six months while confirming guilt on the original charges.

(The ECtHR ultimately found no violation, concluding that the pre-trial stage had not so compromised the applicant’s position as to render the later full trial unfair from the outset.)

**CASE OF ALEXANDRU-RADU LUCA v. ROMANIA (Application no. 20837/18), ECtHR Fourth Section, 14 June 2022 (final 14 September 2022)**

The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1978, alleged that criminal proceedings against him for being an accessory to fraud were unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention. He claimed the pre-trial judge proceedings that confirmed the public prosecutor’s indictment decision breached his fair-trial rights, thereby rendering the subsequent trial unfair from the outset.

In November 2009 a private bank filed a criminal complaint with civil claims against the applicant (then a loans broker), several individuals and a company he managed, alleging fraud in obtaining bank loans. On 7 April 2011 the National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) indicted the applicant and co-defendants on accessory-to-fraud charges, relying on defendants’ statements, witness testimony, documents and specialist reports. The applicant received notice of the indictment and supporting evidence.

Proceedings initially followed the former Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP). On 22 May 2013 the Bucharest County Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment, also allowing the bank’s civil claims. On appeal the Bucharest Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 28 February 2014 and remitted the case for retrial because the bank’s insurer had not been summoned.

After the new CCP entered into force on 1 February 2014, the County Court, at a public hearing on 5 June 2014, referred the case to a pre-trial judge. The applicant and co-defendants had opposed the referral; the DNA supported it. The court reasoned that the remittal had quashed all prior procedural acts, so the new procedure, including the pre-trial stage, applied.

The pre-trial judge sent the applicant a copy of the indictment and invited written comments on the lawfulness of the investigation and evidence-gathering. The applicant objected that the indictment misinterpreted or contradicted the evidence, relied on missing or misread employment contracts, and failed to establish whether documents had been forged; he also argued the County Court lacked competence under the new rules (the case should go to a district court). Co-defendants raised similar points plus claims that the DNA lacked competence given the alleged damage value and that evidence was null because the insurer had not been involved at the investigation stage. The DNA replied in writing.

On 20 August 2014 the pre-trial judge, sitting in chambers without the parties, dismissed all objections and sent the case to trial. The judge held that the DNA and County Court were competent, that the insurer need not have been summoned at the investigation stage, and that remaining arguments concerned the sufficiency or interpretation of evidence rather than its lawfulness and therefore belonged to the trial court.

The applicant and co-defendants challenged the decision. On 30 October 2014 the Court of Appeal’s pre-trial judge, again sitting in chambers without the parties, dismissed the challenges. The applicant had not submitted supporting arguments. Extraordinary appeals of annulment and for review were later rejected as inadmissible.

The subsequent trial was public, oral and adversarial. The applicant and his lawyer attended all hearings, commented on and challenged evidence (including reiterating some pre-trial objections), requested additional documentary, expert and testimonial evidence, made statements, questioned co-defendants and witnesses, and contested other parties’ submissions. On 24 April 2017 the County Court convicted him in part and sentenced him to two years and six months. On 18 December 2017 the Court of Appeal, dismissing his appeal and partly allowing the DNA’s, sentenced him to three years and six months.

A Constitutional Court decision of 11 November 2014 (published 5 December 2014) later declared certain CCP provisions governing the pre-trial judge procedure unconstitutional because they lacked oral, public and adversarial character and thereby violated fair-trial rights. The decision had only ex-nunc effect.

The Court examined whether the closed, written pre-trial confirmation of the indictment had so weakened the applicant’s position that the ensuing trial was unfair from the outset. It noted that the trial itself fully respected the requirements of publicity, orality and adversarial proceedings and that the applicant had been able to contest the evidence and the charges on the merits.
001-218020:
The case of P.W. v. Austria (ECHR Application no. 10425/19) concerns an Austrian woman’s complaints under Articles 5, 6 and 14 of the Convention regarding her compulsory confinement in an institution for mentally ill offenders. The applicant, born in 1964, was involved in an incident on 7 May 2016 when she could not pay a taxi fare. Police were called; she became agitated, shouted and repeatedly struck an officer in the chest without causing injury. She was arrested, examined by a medical officer who noted possible psychotic episodes and a danger to others, and committed to hospital. The arrest was later revoked and charges pressed without continued detention.

From 7 May to 20 June 2016 she was placed in a high-security psychiatric ward under the Hospitalisation Act. Psychiatrist Dr M.F. diagnosed long-standing schizoaffective disorder, lack of insight into her illness, and a risk of aggressive reactions toward third parties, concluding that a voluntary stay was impossible. A second civil placement occurred from 24 November 2016 to 23 January 2017 after neighbours reported ranting, self-talk and paranoid killing fantasies. Dr M.F. now classified the condition as paranoid schizophrenia; because the applicant had begun taking medication, the placement ended.

Criminal proceedings were opened for attempted resistance to State authority (maximum three years’ imprisonment) and fraud. Expert Dr W.S., working from files only, found the applicant criminally liable, the offence not the product of a serious mental disorder, and offered no prognosis of future serious offences. After a further in-person examination, psychiatrist Dr A.K. diagnosed chronic undifferentiated schizophrenia present since 2001, complete lack of insight, repeated non-compliance with medication and, at the time of the offence, a total loss of connection with reality that excluded criminal liability. She assessed a high risk of future serious attacks on random victims (neighbours, caregivers or police) and concluded that the medical criteria for preventive confinement under Article 21 § 1 of the Criminal Code were met because outpatient treatment would be insufficient.

On 19 April 2017 the prosecutor substituted the criminal charges with an application for indefinite preventive detention. The applicant was arrested on 8 May 2017 and placed in provisional detention. On 8 August 2017 the Linz Regional Court, relying principally on Dr A.K.’s report, found that the applicant had committed the offence under the influence of a serious mental disorder that excluded liability and that there was a fear of further offences with serious consequences. It therefore ordered her confinement in an institution for mentally ill offenders.

The applicant lodged a plea of nullity, an appeal, a request for a further psychiatric opinion and a constitutional challenge. The Constitutional Court declined to examine the application. The Supreme Court rejected the nullity plea. The Court of Appeal refused a new expert, obtained a supplementary opinion from Dr A.K. (July 2018) confirming persistent, non-remitted schizophrenia and a continuing high probability of serious future offences, and upheld the confinement. Conditional release with a five-year probation period was ordered only on 15 October 2020, taking effect on 30 October 2020.

The facts thus centre on a three-year deprivation of liberty based on a minor, non-injurious act of resistance, multiple expert assessments of a chronic psychotic disorder, and the domestic courts’ conclusion that the risk of serious future offences justified preventive confinement under Article 21 § 1.

The case of P.W. v. Austria (ECtHR, 21 June 2022) concerned an Austrian applicant’s complaints under Articles 5, 6 and 14 of the Convention regarding her confinement in an institution for mentally ill offenders. The applicant, born in 1964, was arrested on 7 May 2016 after failing to pay a taxi fare. She became agitated, shouted at police officers and attempted to resist arrest by hitting one officer’s chest (causing no injury). A medical officer found her fit for detention but noted possible psychotic episodes and danger to others, leading to hospital committal.

Civil placement proceedings followed. From 7 May to 20 June 2016 she was held in a high-security ward under the Hospitalisation Act. Expert Dr M.F. diagnosed schizoaffective disorder with elements of danger due to psychosis, lack of illness awareness and treatment refusal, ruling out voluntary stay. A second placement occurred from 24 November 2016 to 23 January 2017 after neighbours reported ranting, self-talk and paranoid killing fantasies. Dr M.F. reclassified this as paranoid schizophrenia but noted medication agreement, so the placement ended.

Criminal proceedings began on 11 October 2016 for attempted resistance to State authority (Articles 15 and 269 Criminal Code) and fraud. Expert Dr W.S., reviewing files only (as the applicant missed examination), found schizoaffective disorder; she was closer to lacking than possessing criminal liability at the time but remained liable, with the offence not stemming from serious mental disorder. He offered no future-offence prognosis. Charges were limited to attempted resistance. The defence sought a new expert, citing Dr W.S.’s lack of personal examination and later hospitalisation.

Dr A.K. (a university-qualified forensic psychiatrist) examined the applicant and reported chronic undifferentiated schizophrenia dating to 2001, with delusions, hallucinations, withdrawal, total lack of self-care and no illness insight or treatment adherence. At the offence she had lost all reality-connection, rendering her not criminally liable. She was high-risk for future serious aggression against random victims (neighbours, carers, police) due to untreated symptoms and impulse issues; outpatient care was insufficient, meeting Article 21 § 1 Criminal Code criteria for confinement.

On 19 April 2017 the prosecutor sought preventive confinement instead of charges. The applicant was arrested on 8 May 2017 and provisionally detained. On 8 August 2017 the Linz Regional Court, relying primarily on Dr A.K.’s opinion (deemed conclusive), found she had committed the offence under a disorder excluding liability (Article 11) and feared further serious offences, ordering indefinite confinement under Article 21 § 1. Appeals failed: the Constitutional Court declined review; the Supreme Court rejected a nullity plea; the Court of Appeal dismissed a further-expert request, obtained a July 2018 supplementary opinion from Dr A.K. confirming ongoing high risk and no remission, and upheld the order. Conditional release with five-year probation was granted in October 2020.

The applicant alleged her ~3-year deprivation of liberty was unjustified (particularly given the minor underlying offence) and raised fair-trial and discrimination issues. The Court examined the facts under Article 5 § 1(e), noting objective medical verification of persisting unsound mind and dangerousness.

The case of P.W. v. Austria concerns the applicant’s complaints under Articles 5, 6 and 14 (with Article 5) of the Convention regarding her confinement in an institution for mentally ill offenders. P.W., an Austrian national born in 1964, was involved in an incident on 7 May 2016 when a taxi driver called police after she could not pay her fare. She became agitated, shouted at officers and attempted to resist arrest by hitting one officer’s chest (applying force but causing no injury). A medical officer found her fit for detention but noted psychotic episodes and danger to others during aggression flare-ups, ordering hospital committal. The arrest was revoked, but the prosecutor pressed charges without arrest.

P.W. was placed in a high-security psychiatric ward from 7 May to 20 June 2016 under the Hospitalisation Act. Expert Dr M.F. diagnosed long-standing schizoaffective disorder (first inpatient stay 2006), with psychotic danger to others, lack of awareness of her condition and no possibility of voluntary treatment. A second placement ran from 24 November 2016 to 23 January 2017 after neighbours reported ranting, self-talk, paranoid ideas and killing fantasies. Dr M.F. reclassified the condition as paranoid schizophrenia, but placement ended after she agreed to medication.

On 11 October 2016 the prosecutor opened proceedings for attempted resistance to State authority (Articles 15 and 269 Criminal Code) and fraud (Article 146). Expert Dr W.S. (opinion based on files only, as P.W. did not attend examination) found schizoaffective disorder, criminal liability at the time of the offence (ability to control actions closer to absent than present, but not totally lacking), the offence not resulting from serious mental/emotional disorder, and no possible prognosis of future serious offences.

Charges of attempted resistance followed. P.W.’s lawyer requested a new psychiatric opinion, citing the lack of personal examination and objecting to Dr W.S. The court appointed Dr A.K. (head of a forensic department, with venia docendi), who examined P.W. and issued a 29-page opinion diagnosing chronic undifferentiated schizophrenia since 2001 (bizarre delusions, hallucinations, total lack of motivation/social withdrawal/self-care). She had no insight, repeatedly stopped medication unauthorised, and at the time of the offence had no connection to reality, rendering her unable to assess the situation or decide independently, thus not criminally liable. Dr A.K. classified her as high-risk for future aggression (lack of insight, negative treatment attitude, active symptoms, impulse-control issues, treatment failures), posing danger to neighbours, caregivers and police as random victims of serious attacks. Outpatient treatment was insufficient, meeting medical requirements for confinement under Article 21 § 1 Criminal Code.

On 19 April 2017 the prosecutor replaced charges with a request for preventive confinement. P.W. was arrested on 8 May 2017 and provisionally detained. At the 8 August 2017 trial (where experts were heard), the Linz Regional Court found she had committed the offence under a state of mind excluding liability (Article 11) due to undifferentiated schizophrenia, and that further offences with serious consequences were to be feared. Confinement was ordered, relying principally on Dr A.K.’s conclusive opinion.

P.W. lodged a plea of nullity, appeal and request for a further expert (to prove lack of dangerousness), plus a constitutional challenge. The Constitutional Court declined to hear the latter (finding statutory limits prevented disproportionate confinement). The Supreme Court rejected the nullity plea (arguments went to appeal only; no proper request to question the expert first). The Court of Appeal dismissed the further-expert request (no contradictions or deficiencies requiring it) but obtained a supplementary opinion from Dr A.K. (after re-examination) confirming ongoing undifferentiated schizophrenia, no remission, high probability of future serious offences and thus continuing need for confinement; conditional release was refused.

On 15 October 2020 the Regional Court ordered conditional release by 30 October 2020 with a five-year probation period. The confinement had lasted approximately three years. Key issues for the alleged violations included whether the (minor) nature of the underlying offence (attempted resistance without injury) rendered deprivation of liberty under Article 5 § 1(e) unlawful/disproportionate despite objective medical evidence of persisting unsound mind and dangerousness; whether expert-opinion procedures (conflicting reports, no initial examination by Dr W.S., refusal of a further expert) breached Article 6 fairness; and possible discrimination against mentally ill persons. Domestic law (Articles 11, 21 and 25 Criminal Code) permits indefinite confinement for offences punishable by over one year’s imprisonment if committed under a serious mental disorder excluding liability and if future serious offences are feared, with annual review. Ongoing Austrian reform discussions noted a rise in such confinements, including for lower-risk/minor offences, quality issues with risk prognoses, and proposals to raise the offence threshold (generally over three years, with high-risk exceptions).

The ECtHR case *Naumenko and SIA Rix Shipping v. Latvia* (no. 50805/14) concerns Article 8 complaints that a 2014 Competition Authority “dawn raid” on the applicants’ business premises, plus seizure of large volumes of documents and electronic data, was unlawful, disproportionate and insufficiently safeguarded.

The first applicant, Andrey Naumenko (Russian national, resident in Riga), is sole owner and board member of the second applicant, SIA Rix Shipping (Latvian shipping-agency company established 2008). On 10 May 2013 the Authority opened proceedings against the National Association of Latvian Shipbrokers and Shipping Agents (NALSA) for an alleged prohibited agreement (Competition Law s. 11(1)) consisting of recommended minimum/fixed agency fees.

On 9 January 2014 the Authority sought District Court authorisation to search four entities, including NALSA and the second applicant. It relied on an online NALSA “Recommended scale of agency fees”, one invoice issued by the second applicant that referenced the recommendation, and an NALSA examination question on fee calculation. On 14 January a judge granted the request, finding “reasonable suspicion” of a prohibited agreement and “no other means” of obtaining evidence. The warrant (operative part) authorised unannounced police-accompanied searches of the second applicant’s movable/immovable property, that of its officials/employees, and even unidentified third-party premises if evidence might be stored there. It contained no time-limit, no list of target items and no further reasoning.

On 28 January 2014 officials and a police officer entered the second applicant’s offices at 10 a.m. After the applicants’ lawyer arrived they began the search at 11.10 a.m., examining invoices, accounting records, Naumenko’s office computer and the company server. Naumenko cooperated and successfully requested that original accounting documents not be taken. An IT expert later created forensic images. Two 2012 invoices, 2014 e-mails and 2009/2014 client letters were seized. The computer image initially captured 70.1 GB (including personal e-mails dating to 1993 and e-mail passwords); after Naumenko’s protest 70 GB were deleted and a 25.7 GB image (83 581 e-mails from five named folders) was retained. A 141 MB Outlook image was taken from the server without indexing. Naumenko objected that the material included unrelated personal correspondence (some allegedly from 2003) and risked commercial harm; the Authority granted restricted-access status but did not return the remaining data. The raid ended at 8 p.m.

On 7 February 2014 Naumenko, on the company’s behalf, asked the District Court President to quash the warrant as regards the second applicant. He argued it lacked any specific factual basis linking the company to the alleged cartel (it was not a NALSA member), was drafted in excessively broad terms, conferred unfettered discretion on the Authority, and failed to balance investigative needs against Article 8 rights. On 18 February the President dismissed the complaint as final, holding that the judge had examined the (restricted) file, heard the Authority and issued a proportionate order within the 72-hour statutory period.

On 8 September 2014 the Authority fined NALSA €715.35, relying in part on the invoices and e-mails seized from the second applicant. No proceedings were pursued against the company itself.

At the material time Competition Law ss. 9(5)(4)–(5) and 91 required prior judicial authorisation for such intrusive measures, subsequent records, presence of the target, legal assistance and a limited complaint to the court president. A 2014 Supreme Court analytical report criticised the practice of rubber-stamping equally broad warrants and recommended legislative tightening; the law was amended in 2016 to require judges to specify targets, purpose, items sought and time-limits.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 8 violations: an overly wide warrant, indiscriminate copying of personal and commercial data, and inadequate judicial control both before and after the raid.

These facts form the core of the Article 8 complaint: the breadth of the judicial warrant, the volume and nature of data seized (including potentially private correspondence), the limited contemporaneous review of the copied material, and the subsequent judicial-review decision that did not address the proportionality concerns in detail.
