**Case of Alleleh and Others v. Norway (ECHR, 2022)**

This ECHR case concerned a complaint under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life) arising from the expulsion of the first applicant, a Djiboutian national, and its effects on her family life with her Norwegian husband and their four Norwegian-citizen children.

The first applicant arrived in Norway in September 2001 and applied for asylum, falsely claiming to be Somali and providing a fabricated personal history. Her application was rejected in 2002, and her appeal was dismissed in 2003. She remained in Norway unlawfully. In 2003 she sought revision of the refusal, again providing false information (still claiming Somali origin) and presenting false identity papers; this was refused in 2005. Meanwhile, she met the second applicant (a Norwegian citizen) in 2002 and married him in April 2004, while lacking lawful residence. She then applied for a residence permit on the basis of marriage, repeating the same false information, and was granted a temporary permit in 2005 (renewed in 2006). Their first child was born in 2005. In 2007 she obtained Norwegian citizenship, still claiming Somali nationality and signing a declaration that the information was complete and correct (with revocation possible for falsehoods). Twins were born in 2009 and a fourth child in 2013.

In 2014, during a broader inquiry, police suspected her true Djiboutian nationality. She initially maintained the false account. After a warning of possible citizenship withdrawal and expulsion, she disclosed her true identity in December 2014. Citizenship was withdrawn in June 2015, and she was expelled in November 2015 with a two-year re-entry ban. Administrative appeals were dismissed. The Immigration Appeals Board found that the husband could adequately care for the children in Norway if she left alone, that the family had a network in Djibouti, and that any burden on the children from expulsion did not exceed the ordinary consequences of a parent’s expulsion. Serious, repeated immigration-law breaches over many years, plus general deterrence and respect for the law, outweighed the family’s interests.

Court proceedings followed. The Oslo City Court (after expert psychological evidence) upheld the expulsion in 2017, describing the first applicant’s violations as intentional, serious, and prolonged (false identities, stories, and documents over 13 years). It found no disproportionality: she had family, language, and cultural ties in Djibouti; family life could continue there; the husband was a capable carer; and the children (then aged 12, 7, 7, and 4) had a secure upbringing with both parents, no exceptional prior stresses (unlike in Nunez v. Norway), and would remain in a familiar environment. The Borgarting High Court in 2019 found the decision invalid as disproportionate vis-à-vis the children, emphasizing the mother’s role as primary daily caregiver, the children’s (especially the younger and somewhat vulnerable twins’) emotional and practical needs, and a risk that the father (who worked long hours) could not adequately cope, creating an unusually heavy burden.

The Norwegian Supreme Court in 2019 reversed this, applying the ECHR’s “fair balance” test (Jeunesse v. the Netherlands) and “exceptional circumstances” threshold where family life was established on a precarious immigration basis (Nunez and related cases). It held the breaches very serious (repeated, prolonged falsehoods undermining the immigration system’s trust). Family life was a “fait accompli” created while the first applicant knew her status was unlawful/false; the husband’s later awareness of the deception carried little weight. There were no insurmountable obstacles to the family relocating to Djibouti. The children were generally well-functioning with no prior disruptions comparable to Nunez, Kaplan, or Butt. Any strain (emotional, practical, or financial) from a two-year separation from the primary carer was ordinary, not unusually great. The short ban duration, possibilities of visits/communication, and potential revision of the ban if circumstances worsened were relevant. The child’s best interests were fundamental but not automatically decisive. Expulsion was thus proportionate and valid.

The ECHR (Fifth Section) unanimously found no violation of Article 8. The interference (expulsion with a two-year ban) pursued legitimate aims of immigration control and prevention of disorder. Domestic courts (especially the Supreme Court) had thoroughly assessed proportionality in light of ECHR case-law, including the children’s best interests, the mother’s primary caregiving role, family ties, and lack of insurmountable obstacles to relocation. The two-year ban could be revised or allow brief visits; no “exceptional circumstances” existed to override the State’s margin of appreciation given the serious, long-term immigration breaches. The family-life disruption, while significant, did not render the measure disproportionate.

The case of Alleleh and Others v. Norway (ECtHR, Application no. 569/20) concerned a complaint under Article 8 ECHR regarding the expulsion of the first applicant (a Djiboutian national) from Norway and its impact on her family life with her Norwegian husband and their four Norwegian-citizen children.

The first applicant entered Norway in September 2001 and sought asylum under a false Somali identity and fabricated personal history. Her claim was rejected in 2002 (appeal dismissed 2003). She remained unlawfully, later seeking revision of the refusal with a new false account and forged documents (revision denied 2005). In 2002 she met the second applicant; they married in April 2004 (while she lacked lawful status). She obtained a one-year residence permit in 2005 based on the marriage but restated the same false information. This was renewed in 2006. In 2007 she was granted Norwegian citizenship after again claiming Somali nationality and certifying her information as complete and accurate. The couple’s children were born in 2005, 2009 (twins) and 2013.

A 2014 inquiry into Somali-claim cases prompted suspicion. The first applicant initially persisted with false statements but later admitted her true Djiboutian identity. Her citizenship was withdrawn in June 2015 and she was expelled in November 2015 with a two-year re-entry ban. Administrative appeals were dismissed. The Immigration Appeals Board found the second applicant able to care for the children in Norway and no insurmountable obstacles to the family relocating to Djibouti (where the first applicant had family, language and cultural ties). The children’s best interests did not override the seriousness of the prolonged, repeated immigration-law breaches (which undermined the system’s integrity and general deterrence).

The Oslo City Court (2017) upheld the expulsion after hearing witnesses and a court-appointed psychologist. It characterised the first applicant’s 13-year pattern of false identities, stories and documents as intentional and grave. It saw no disproportionality: the family could live together in Djibouti; the second applicant was a capable carer in a stable environment; the children were generally well-functioning and closely attached to both parents (with no prior disruptions comparable to those in Nunez v. Norway). Any strain from a two-year separation from their primary caregiver was a typical consequence of parental expulsion.

The Borgarting High Court (2019) declared the expulsion invalid as disproportionate to the children. It found them more attached to their mother (the daily caregiver while the father worked long hours), with two twins somewhat vulnerable; expulsion risked extraordinary emotional and practical burdens on four children (three young), potentially overwhelming the father’s care capacity.

The Supreme Court (2019) reversed. The breaches were “very serious.” Family life had been established on a highly precarious (indeed false) basis, constituting a “fait accompli” not warranting strong Article 8 protection. There were no insurmountable obstacles to family life in Djibouti. The children were well-functioning with no unusual prior stress; any burden was not “unusually great” or exceptional (unlike Nunez or Butt). The two-year ban (chosen with the children in mind) could be revised for negative developments and allowed brief visits or remote contact. After a concrete balancing in which the children’s best interests were fundamental but not decisive, the expulsion was proportionate.

The ECtHR found no Article 8 violation. Domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of the Court’s case-law (including the “exceptional circumstances” threshold for precarious family life). The margin of appreciation had not been exceeded: there were no insurmountable obstacles to relocation, the ban was short and revisable, and exceptional circumstances were absent.

The case Alleleh and Others v. Norway (ECtHR, 23 June 2022) concerned a complaint under Article 8 ECHR about the expulsion of the first applicant (a Djiboutian national) from Norway with a two-year re-entry ban, and its effects on family life with her Norwegian husband and their four Norwegian-citizen children.

The first applicant entered Norway in 2001 and sought asylum under a false Somali identity, giving a fabricated personal history. Asylum was refused in 2002 (appeal dismissed 2003). She remained unlawfully and in 2003 sought revision with a further false account and forged documents (refused 2005). She met her future husband (a Norwegian citizen) in 2002 and married him in April 2004 while lacking lawful status. She then applied for residence on the basis of marriage, repeating the false identity and history, and obtained a one-year temporary permit in 2005 (renewed 2006). Their first child was born in 2005. In 2007 she obtained Norwegian citizenship on the same false Somali identity. Twins were born in 2009 and a fourth child in 2013.

A 2014 police inquiry into purported Somali applicants led to questioning; she persisted with the false story until admitting her true Djiboutian identity in late 2014. Citizenship was withdrawn in June 2015 and an expulsion order with a two-year re-entry ban issued in November 2015. Administrative appeals failed. The Immigration Appeals Board held that the husband could adequately care for the children in Norway, that the family could relocate to Djibouti (where the first applicant had relatives, language and cultural familiarity), that any burden on the children would not exceed the ordinary consequences of a parent’s expulsion, and that the gravity of the long-term, repeated immigration fraud (false identity, forged papers, exploitation of the asylum system) plus the need for general deterrence outweighed family interests.

The applicants challenged the expulsion in the Oslo City Court (the other family members lacked standing and appeared as interveners). A court-appointed psychologist examined the children. In 2017 the City Court upheld the order, stressing the intentional, methodical and protracted nature of the fraud over some 13 years. It found the first applicant had ties to Djibouti, that family life could continue there or via visits, that the husband (aware of the irregularities for years) could care for the children in their familiar Norwegian environment, and that the children were generally well-functioning with no exceptional prior disruptions of the kind found in Nunez v. Norway.

The Borgarting High Court in 2019 declared the expulsion invalid as disproportionate to the children. It treated the mother as the primary daily caregiver (the father worked long hours), noted some vulnerability in the twins, and considered that a two-year separation would impose an extraordinary emotional and practical burden, potentially exceeding the father’s capacity and creating a situation unlike that of an ordinary single parent.

The Supreme Court reversed in December 2019, holding the order valid. It characterised the fraud as very serious (repeated false identity and origin, forged documents, citizenship obtained by deception), so that family life had been established on a precarious basis amounting to a fait accompli. There were no insurmountable obstacles to the family moving to Djibouti. The children had developed normally in a stable setting with both parents; any hardship was the ordinary consequence of a parent’s expulsion for a limited period and did not constitute “exceptional circumstances.” The two-year ban (chosen out of regard for the children) could be revised if circumstances deteriorated, brief visits were possible, and contact could be maintained. The child’s best interests were a fundamental but not decisive consideration.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 8. The domestic courts had carried out a thorough, case-specific proportionality assessment in line with Strasbourg case-law (including Jeunesse, Nunez and Antwi). The first applicant’s prolonged and systematic immigration-law breaches were grave. Family life had been created while her status was known (or should have been known) to be precarious. Relocation to Djibouti was feasible; the father could provide adequate care in Norway; the limited-duration ban with possibilities of revision and visits did not impose an unusually great burden. No exceptional circumstances existed. The national authorities had not exceeded their margin of appreciation.
001-218021:
**S.M. v. Russia (Application no. 17219/20), ECHR (Third Section), 21 June 2022 (final 21 September 2022)**

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1982 and living in Voronezh, is the biological mother of two daughters: Ye. (born 2010) and A. (born 2014). She lived with them and her mother. She has suffered from polydrug addiction since 1998. On 21 September 2017 she was convicted of manufacturing and selling narcotic drugs and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment, with the sentence adjourned until her younger child turned 14.

The Federal Service for the Execution of Sentences (FSIN) issued warnings in 2017–2018 that failure to fulfil parental duties could lead to cancellation of the adjournment. In August 2018 FSIN sought cancellation, citing two administrative offences of neglecting parental duties (December 2017 and July 2018). The Sovetskiy District Court dismissed the request on 10 September 2018, noting the applicant had found work, the children attended school/kindergarten regularly, and she participated in their activities. FSIN issued a further warning in October 2018.

Childcare authorities inspected the family home. A 9 June 2018 report described unsatisfactory sanitary conditions (odour, scattered belongings, trash, insufficient food) unsuitable for children. Later reports (30 January and 14 February 2019) found conditions satisfactory after furniture purchases, some repairs, and clean-up, with adequate food, sleeping space, and study areas.

On 17 December 2018 the childcare authority applied to deprive the applicant of parental authority over both daughters (and her former husband over A.) and to order child maintenance. Grounds included her drug conviction, five administrative offences for neglecting parental duties (2016–2018), alcohol/drug abuse in public, registration of the family as dysfunctional since 2016 due to her addiction and non-compliance with parental obligations, lack of treatment until mid-2018, and the June 2018 inspection.

On 27 February 2019 the District Court granted the application, placing the children in public care (to be enforced immediately) and ordering maintenance from 17 December 2018. It relied on inspection reports, the applicant’s unemployment since December 2018, medical notes documenting her appearances in an intoxicated or inadequate state, her long-standing untreated addiction, administrative liabilities, criminal conviction involving drugs stored in the home with children, and FSIN evidence of a socially dangerous situation. Positive school/kindergarten references and some recent improvements (furniture, repairs, care) were noted but attributed to the pressure of pending proceedings rather than genuine earlier change. The court held that she should have altered her conduct at least after the 2017 conviction and that grounds existed under Article 69 of the Family Code (avoidance of parental duties, chronic drug abuse, etc.).

The Voronezh Regional Court upheld the decision on 30 May 2019, emphasising her long-term drug use since age 15, lack of treatment, prolonged neglect despite warnings, and risk to the children’s physical/mental health and moral development. Cassation appeals were dismissed by the Regional Court (31 July 2019) and Supreme Court (12 September 2019). The applicant’s June 2019 application to restore parental authority was dismissed (upheld on appeal and cassation through 2020) as recent lifestyle improvements were insufficient to show persistent change.

The children were removed on 18 June 2019, given a medical check-up, and placed under the temporary then permanent guardianship of Ye.’s paternal grandmother. The applicant did not visit or contact them thereafter. In 2020 the sentence adjournment was cancelled due to the deprivation of parental authority; she began serving her prison term in December 2020.

The complaint alleged a violation of Article 8 (respect for family life) arising from the deprivation of parental authority. (The Court later found the measure proportionate to the children’s best interests after exhaustion of less drastic options, given the history of addiction, neglect, and warnings, with the applicant’s procedural rights adequately protected.)

The case of S.M. v. Russia (Application no. 17219/20) concerns the applicant’s complaint that the deprivation of her parental authority over her two daughters violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention. S.M., born in 1982, is the biological mother of Ye. (born 2010) and A. (born 2014). She lived with the children and her mother in a two-room apartment in Voronezh. The applicant had a documented history of polydrug addiction since 1998 and had been registered as suffering from this condition. In September 2017 she was convicted of manufacturing and selling narcotic drugs and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment; service of the sentence was adjourned until the younger child turned 14.

The Federal Service for the Execution of Sentences issued repeated warnings that failure to fulfil parental duties could lead to cancellation of the adjournment. The applicant was found administratively liable for neglect of parental duties on multiple occasions (October 2016, March and December 2017, July and September 2018) and for public alcohol and drug abuse. In 2016 the family was registered as dysfunctional because of her untreated addiction and non-compliance with parental obligations. Medical records from 2018 noted that she had appeared intoxicated, that the apartment was dirty and malodorous, that she failed to follow medical advice for the children, and that one child had required hospitalisation.

Home inspections by the childcare authority in June 2018 found unsanitary conditions, scattered belongings, insufficient food and an environment unsuitable for children. Later inspections in January and February 2019 recorded improvements, including furniture, appliances, repairs and adequate food. In December 2018 the authority sought deprivation of parental authority, citing the conviction, five neglect offences and the earlier poor living conditions.

On 27 February 2019 the District Court granted the application. It relied on the addiction history, lack of treatment until shortly before the proceedings, repeated official warnings, the presence of drugs in the home shared with the children, medical and inspection evidence of neglect, and the fact that any positive changes appeared only after legal pressure. Although school and kindergarten references noted her interest in the children’s education and some officials acknowledged recent efforts, the court held that Article 69 of the Family Code (avoidance of parental duties and chronic substance abuse) was satisfied. The children were immediately placed in public care and the applicant was ordered to pay maintenance from the date of the claim.

The Regional Court dismissed her appeal in May 2019, stressing the long period of untreated addiction and neglect that endangered the children’s physical, mental and moral development despite official interventions. Cassation appeals were rejected by the Regional Court and the Supreme Court. A subsequent application to restore parental authority under Article 72 of the Family Code was dismissed in August 2019 (upheld on appeal) because the short interval since deprivation did not demonstrate a persistent change of behaviour.

The children were removed in June 2019 and later placed under the guardianship of Ye.’s paternal grandmother. The applicant did not visit or contact them thereafter. The sentence adjournment was subsequently cancelled and she began serving her term in December 2020.

These circumstances—the lengthy record of addiction and neglect, repeated official warnings, the children’s exposure to drugs and inadequate care, and the timing of any improvements—formed the factual core of the alleged Article 8 interference.

The case of S.M. v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 17219/20) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that Russian authorities disproportionately deprived her of parental authority over her two daughters, Ye. (born 2010) and A. (born 2014). The applicant, born in 1982, lived with the children and her mother in Voronezh. She has suffered from polydrug addiction since 1998 and was convicted in September 2017 of manufacturing and selling narcotics, receiving a four-year sentence whose execution was adjourned until A. turned 14.

FSIN authorities repeatedly warned her in 2017–2018 that failure to fulfil parental duties could lift the adjournment. A 2018 request to lift it was dismissed after the District Court noted two administrative convictions for neglect but also that the children attended school/kindergarten, the applicant had employment, and no current failure of duties was proven. Home inspections by childcare authorities found unsanitary, inadequate conditions in June 2018 (dirt, odour, insufficient food) but satisfactory conditions after repairs and furnishings in January–February 2019.

In December 2018 the childcare authority sought deprivation of parental authority (and child maintenance) against the applicant and A.’s father, citing her conviction, five administrative offences for neglect between 2016–2018, alcohol/drug abuse in public, registration of the family as dysfunctional, failure to undergo addiction treatment until mid-2018, and the June 2018 inspection. On 27 February 2019 the District Court granted the claim. It reviewed the inspections, medical notes documenting the children’s vaccinations but also the applicant’s intoxication and the home’s disorder, school references showing her later interest in the children’s education, her unemployment, and witness testimony of recent improvements. The court held that the applicant had long neglected her duties despite warnings, stored drugs in the home, and that positive changes were recent and prompted only by the threat of losing the adjournment or parental rights. Deprivation under Family Code Article 69 (avoidance of duties and chronic drug addiction) served the children’s best interests; they were placed in public care (later with Ye.’s paternal grandmother as guardian) and maintenance was ordered from the date of the claim. Enforcement was immediate.

The applicant appealed, stressing the 2019 inspections, a new job, and positive school references. The Regional Court upheld the judgment on 30 May 2019, emphasising her decades-long untreated addiction, prolonged neglect despite official efforts, and the danger to the children’s physical, mental and moral development. Cassation appeals to the Regional Court and Supreme Court were dismissed. A June 2019 application to restore parental authority under Family Code Article 72 was rejected in August 2019 (and upheld on further appeal) because any behavioural improvement was neither persistent nor sufficient given the time elapsed. The children were removed in June 2019; the applicant did not visit or contact them thereafter. In 2020 the sentence adjournment was cancelled and she began serving her term.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation: that the irreversible measure was not necessary, ignored recent improvements, and was not the result of a fair process that adequately weighed the children’s best interests against the applicant’s family-life rights. (Word count: 512)
001-218118:
The case of Loizides v. Cyprus (Application no. 31029/15) arose from criminal proceedings against Andreas Loizides, a Cypriot national and Chief of the Special Unit for Disaster Response, following a naval-base explosion that killed 13 people and caused numerous casualties. The Attorney General prosecuted six high-ranking officials, including the applicant as sixth defendant, before the Larnaca Assize Court (proceedings no. 4904/2012). On 9 July 2013 the Assize Court convicted the applicant of causing death by a rash, reckless or dangerous act; some co-defendants were acquitted and others convicted. On 2 August 2013 he received a two-year prison sentence, which he served.

On 9 August 2013 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 145/2013), challenging both conviction and sentence. Co-defendants lodged similar appeals (nos. 154/13–156/13) and the Attorney-General filed counter-appeals (nos. 157/13–163/13). All were joined. At the 3 April 2014 hearing the President of the Supreme Court announced that Judge D.H. would not sit because of impending retirement. The remaining twelve judges heard the matter.

On 19 December 2014 the twelve-judge bench delivered three separate judgments on the applicant’s appeal. The introductory statement recorded that the President (M.N.), with whom Judge S.N. agreed, would deliver one judgment; Judges G.E., P.P., A.L. and K.S. would deliver a second (by P.P.) agreeing in result but with different reasoning; and Judges A.P., L.P., D.M., M.C. and Y.Y. would join a third judgment by C.P. Judge C.P.’s opinion (joined by five colleagues) dismissed the appeals against conviction and sentence. The President’s opinion (joined by one colleague) would have allowed the appeal and acquitted the applicant of all charges. Judge P.P.’s opinion (joined by three colleagues) would likewise have allowed the appeal and quashed the conviction, albeit on different reasoning. After the judgments were read in open court, the President announced that the applicant’s appeal was dismissed because of a 6–6 tie and because he had failed to discharge the burden of proving that the first-instance decision and sentence were incorrect. A contemporaneous press release repeated the same formula.

Domestic law relevant to the alleged Article 6 violations includes Article 30 § 2 of the Constitution, which requires a reasoned judgment. The Administration of Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Law 1964 provides that the Supreme Court comprises thirteen equal judges; appellate jurisdiction is normally exercised by at least three or five judges, but the Court remains duly constituted despite vacancies. Section 27(2) of the Courts of Justice Law 1960 states that, when an even-numbered bench reaches a tie, judgment is given against the party bearing the burden of proof. Section 77(3) of the Criminal Procedure Law gives a first-instance president a casting vote on sentence, but no equivalent exists on appeal. Supreme Court case-law places the burden of quashing a conviction on the appellant; the prosecution need only show that any trial error caused no substantial miscarriage of justice. Reasoning must analyse the evidence, make concrete findings and pronounce a clear outcome, though form and extent vary with the case. In a prior constitutional reference that also produced a 5–5 tie, the Court treated the relevant laws as constitutional because the presumption of constitutionality had not been displaced.

The applicant complained that the Supreme Court’s failure to produce a single, sufficiently reasoned and clearly outcome-determinative judgment, given the 6–6 split, violated his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1, the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2, the right to an effective remedy under Article 13, and the right of appeal in criminal matters under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7. The Court communicated those complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered its judgment in Loizides v. Cyprus (Application no. 31029/15) on 5 July 2022 (final on 14 November 2022). The case concerned the fairness of criminal appeal proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the alleged failure of Cyprus’s Supreme Court to issue a sufficiently reasoned judgment with a clear outcome following a tied vote.

The applicant, Andreas Loizides (born 1958, residing in Nicosia), was Chief of Cyprus’s Special Unit for Disaster Response. Following an explosion at a naval base that killed 13 people and caused numerous casualties, the Attorney-General prosecuted six high-ranking officials before the Larnaca Assize Court (proceedings no. 4904/2012). Loizides was the sixth defendant. On 9 July 2013, the Assize Court convicted him of causing death by a rash, reckless or dangerous act; other defendants were variously acquitted or convicted. On 2 August 2013 he received a two-year prison sentence, which he served.

On 9 August 2013 Loizides appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 145/2013), challenging both conviction and sentence. Related appeals by co-defendants and counter-appeals by the Attorney-General were joined. One Supreme Court judge recused himself due to impending retirement. On 19 December 2014 a 12-judge bench issued three separate judgments on Loizides’s appeal. The President (M.N.), joined by one judge, would have allowed the appeal and acquitted him. Four judges (led by P.P.) also favoured allowing the appeal and quashing the conviction, albeit on different reasoning. Six judges (led by C.P.) dismissed the appeals against both conviction and sentence. After the judgments were read in open court, the President announced that the appeal was dismissed because of a 6-6 tie and because Loizides had failed to discharge the burden of proving that the first-instance decision and sentence were incorrect. A similar press release was issued.

Domestic law (section 27(2) of the Courts of Justice Law 1960) provides that, in the event of a tied vote by an even-numbered court, judgment is given against the party bearing the burden of proof. Cypriot case-law places that burden on a criminal appellant seeking to quash a conviction. Article 30 § 2 of the Constitution requires reasoned judgments; domestic jurisprudence interprets this as requiring analysis of the evidence, concrete findings and a clear pronouncement of the outcome. Prior Supreme Court practice in tied-vote cases (including constitutional questions) had similarly upheld the status quo where a presumption had not been displaced.

The applicant complained that the three judgments, the 6-6 split and the summary announcement failed to produce a sufficiently reasoned and unambiguous outcome, thereby violating his right to a fair hearing. Additional complaints under Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 13 (effective remedy) and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 (right of appeal in criminal matters) were communicated to the Government; remaining complaints were declared inadmissible. The Court ultimately held that a tied vote does not per se violate Article 6 and that the dismissal, grounded in the applicant’s failure to discharge the domestic burden of proof, was sufficiently reasoned.

The case of Loizides v. Cyprus (ECHR Application no. 31029/15) arose from criminal proceedings following a naval base explosion in Cyprus that killed 13 people and caused numerous casualties. The applicant, Andreas Loizides (born 1958), then Chief of the Special Unit for Disaster Response, was the sixth of six high-ranking officials prosecuted. On 9 July 2013 the Larnaca Assize Court convicted him of causing death by a rash, reckless or dangerous act. On 2 August 2013 he received a two-year prison sentence, which he served.

He appealed to the Supreme Court on 9 August 2013 against both conviction and sentence (Criminal Appeal no. 145/2013). Related appeals by co-defendants and counter-appeals by the Attorney-General were joined. One Supreme Court judge recused himself due to impending retirement, leaving a 12-judge bench.

On 19 December 2014 the Supreme Court issued three separate judgments on the applicant’s appeal. Judge C.P.’s judgment (joined by five others) dismissed the appeals against conviction and sentence. The President’s judgment (joined by one other judge) would have allowed the appeal and acquitted the applicant. Judge P.P.’s judgment (joined by three others) would also have allowed the appeal and quashed the conviction, albeit on different reasoning. This produced a 6–6 split.

The judgments were read in open court. The President then announced that the appeal was dismissed because of the tie vote and because the applicant had failed to discharge his burden of proving the first-instance decision incorrect. A press release repeated this outcome. Domestic law (section 27(2) of the Courts of Justice Law) provides that a tie among an even number of judges results in judgment against the party bearing the burden of proof; established case-law places that burden on a criminal appellant seeking to quash a conviction. The Constitution (Article 30 § 2) and case-law require judgments to be reasoned, comprising analysis of the evidence, findings and a clear pronouncement of outcome.

The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court’s procedure—multiple judgments followed by a tie-based announcement rather than a single, clear reasoned decision—violated Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing and reasoned judgment), Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 13 (effective remedy) and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 (right of appeal in criminal matters). The ECHR held that the dismissal was sufficiently reasoned by reference to the applicant’s failure to discharge the domestic burden of proof and that a tied vote does not in itself breach Article 6.
001-218132:
**Case summary: Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 8000/21), ECHR, 7 July 2022**

This case concerned the applicant’s claim of a fresh Article 8 violation arising from continued non-enforcement of contact rights with his son after an earlier ECHR finding of a breach. In *Jurišić v. Croatia* (no. 29419/17, 16 January 2020), the Court had found Croatia in violation of Article 8 due to prolonged failure to enforce a 14 May 2010 final decision granting the applicant (Stjepan Jurišić, born 1970) contact with his son I.R. (born 2006) every other weekend and during parts of school holidays. Execution of that judgment remained pending before the Committee of Ministers. The present application, lodged 25 January 2021, alleged that a subsequent domestic decision and ongoing inability to have contact constituted a new breach. The Court confined its examination to the post-2020 period and new decisions.

In the first set of enforcement proceedings concerning the 2010 order, on 20 May 2019 the court heard psychiatrist J.G., who had treated I.R. for four years. J.G. warned that a further expert evaluation (ordered on appeal) or hearing the child in court would cause additional harm and proposed several meetings in his office to build trust. The applicant refused, accusing J.G. of bias and manipulation. On 29 January 2020 the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court terminated enforcement for a second time. It relied on a 6 September 2018 psychologist’s report (prepared for related criminal proceedings) finding that gradual contact would be more appropriate and that coercive enforcement of the outdated 2010 order would further traumatise the child. Because the enforcement court lacked power to amend the 2010 decision and the parties refused agreement, it discontinued proceedings, noting that parallel proceedings to amend contact rights could set precise terms. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 17 June 2020 and a constitutional complaint declared inadmissible on 21 October 2020.

Meanwhile, in fresh contact proceedings instituted by the mother (M.R.) in 2019, a guardian ad litem reported that I.R. (then around 13–14) was willing to give his father “one final chance” at Dr J.G.’s office; the applicant again refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly Friday meetings in a neutral location without the mother. On 2 November 2020 the Municipal Court issued a new order for supervised weekly contact in a neutral setting, progressing to weekends and holidays once trust was established. In extensive reasoning the court found both parents at fault: the mother had obstructed contact, refused professional help, ignored Centre invitations and delayed proceedings; the applicant denied the child’s medical issues, questioned all experts and staff, insisted on his preferred arrangements, involved police during pick-ups, and failed to communicate constructively. Both treated the child as a tool in their conflict rather than prioritising his rights and best interests. The court emphasised that contact is the child’s right, that institutions had taken all necessary protective steps, and that parental obstruction (not institutional inaction) was the cause of failure. The decision became final after the County Court upheld it on 10 May 2021.

Enforcement of the new order also failed. On 2 and 9 January 2021 the applicant and a Centre representative visited the child’s home; no one answered the first time and I.R. refused contact the second. On 25 June 2021 the mother brought I.R. but the parents argued and the child left, stating he was 14 and his opinion mattered. On 2 July they argued again; I.R. protested being forced, the applicant threatened that the mother would go to prison, and the child left. Official reports noted the applicant stood with crossed arms, did not engage the child, and focused on staff to enforce his rights. Subsequent meetings on 7 July, 20 and 27 August 2021 saw the child refuse contact, citing past alleged abuse and declining to explain. The applicant missed the 8 September session.

Criminal proceedings against the mother for obstructing contact resulted in two convictions (suspended sentences of 10 and 9 months for periods in 2015–2016); further complaints covering later periods remained pending.

The facts showed repeated institutional steps—expert hearings, new contact orders tailored to the child’s needs, supervised meetings, guardian involvement, Centre proposals and criminal prosecutions—undermined primarily by both parents’ conduct rather than lack of official diligence. The child, by then a teenager, consistently refused contact amid parental conflict.

Execution of that judgment remains pending before the Committee of Ministers. A guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father “one final chance” at the psychiatrist’s office; the applicant again refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly unsupervised meetings in a neutral location. On 2 November 2020 the Municipal Court issued a new order for supervised weekly contact in a neutral setting, progressing to weekend and holiday contact once trust was established. The lengthy decision criticised both parents: the mother for isolating the child, refusing professional help and delaying proceedings; the applicant for denying I.R.’s medical needs, questioning all experts, calling police during disputes and insisting on contact on his own terms. It emphasised that contact is the child’s right, not the parents’, and that both had used I.R. as a tool in their conflict. The County Court upheld the order on 10 May 2021.

Enforcement of the new order fared no better. In January 2021 the applicant and Centre staff visited I.R.’s home twice; no one answered the first time and I.R. refused contact the second. On 25 June 2021 M.R. brought the child (then 14) to a scheduled meeting; the parents argued and I.R. left, asserting that his opinion mattered. At the 2 July meeting the parents again argued and accused each other of abuse; the applicant told I.R. his mother would go to prison. I.R. left. Official notes recorded that the applicant stood with arms crossed, made no attempt to engage the child and focused solely on asserting his rights vis-à-vis Centre staff. Subsequent meetings in July and August 2021 saw I.R. refuse all contact, citing alleged past abuse; he would not explain further. The applicant failed to attend a 8 September 2021 session.

Criminal proceedings against M.R. continued in parallel. She was convicted in 2020 and 2021 of obstructing contact in 2015–2016 periods and received suspended prison sentences. Three further complaints lodged by the Centre for later periods remain pending.
