**Case Summary: Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 8000/21)**

This ECHR case follows a 2020 judgment finding a violation of Article 8 (family life) due to Croatian authorities' failure to enforce 2010 court decisions granting the applicant, Stjepan Jurišić, contact with his son I.R. (born 2006) every other weekend and during school holidays. Execution of that judgment remains pending. The present application, lodged in 2021, alleges a fresh Article 8 violation from continued non-contact after subsequent domestic decisions.

In the later period, enforcement of the original 2010 order continued. On 20 May 2019, the court heard psychiatrist J.G., who had treated I.R. for four years. J.G. warned that further expert evaluations or court hearings would harm the child and proposed initial meetings in his office to build trust. The applicant refused, claiming J.G. was biased and manipulating the child. The court lacked power to amend the 2010 order.

On 29 January 2020, the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court terminated enforcement (for the second time). It relied on a 2018 psychologist's report (from related criminal proceedings) concluding that gradual contact was appropriate and that coercing the outdated 2010 terms would traumatize I.R. Given the impossibility of enforcement as ordered, the parties' refusal to agree otherwise, and the court's inability to modify the order in enforcement proceedings, it discontinued them. It noted that parallel amendment proceedings could redefine contact terms. The applicant's appeal was dismissed on 17 June 2020; a constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 21 October 2020.

Meanwhile, in 2019 the mother (M.R.) initiated fresh contact proceedings. A guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father "one final chance" at J.G.'s office; the applicant again refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly meetings every Friday in a neutral location without the mother. On 2 November 2020, the Municipal Court issued a new order for supervised weekly contact in a neutral setting, to progress to weekends and holidays once trust was established.

The court's lengthy reasoning found both parents at fault and acting contrary to I.R.'s best interests. The mother had obstructed contact, refused professional help, ignored Centre summonses, delayed proceedings, and sought to isolate the child. The applicant denied I.R.'s medical/psychological issues, questioned all experts and institutions, insisted on contact on his terms, unnecessarily involved police, and failed to engage positively (e.g., jokes perceived as mockery). Parents communicated only through courts, argued and threatened in the child's presence, and treated the dispute as a contest of their own rights rather than the child's. Institutions had taken all possible steps, but parental conduct—not official inaction—prevented contact. I.R. (an excellent student with friends) was caught between loyalty to his mother and a desire for his father. The decision was upheld on appeal on 10 May 2021 and became final.

Enforcement of the new order also failed. In January 2021 the applicant and Centre staff visited I.R.'s home twice; no one answered or the child refused. On 25 June 2021 M.R. brought I.R., but the parents argued and I.R. (then 14) left, asserting his opinion mattered. At July 2021 meetings the parents argued again; the applicant threatened prison for the mother; I.R. protested, accused the father of past abuse, and left. Official reports noted the applicant stood with arms crossed, ignoring the child and focusing on asserting his rights. Subsequent sessions saw I.R. refuse to speak or explain. The applicant missed one appointment. The supervisor suggested I.R. write a letter.

Parallel criminal proceedings convicted M.R. of obstructing contact (suspended sentences of 10 months in 2020 and 9 months in 2021 for earlier periods). The Centre filed three further complaints (2019–2021) still pending.

These facts centre on the authorities' repeated efforts—expert input, new tailored orders prioritizing the child's welfare, social-service involvement, and criminal sanctions—amid persistent parental conflict, the applicant's non-cooperation, the mother's obstruction, and I.R.'s increasing refusal as he matured. The alleged violation concerns whether this constituted a continued failure of positive obligations under Article 8.
001-218116:
The case concerns five applications (nos. 815/18 and others) by three German trade unions—the Association of Civil Servants and Union for Collective Bargaining (dbb), Marburger Bund (physicians), and Trade Union of German Train Drivers (GDL)—plus individual GDL members, alleging that Germany’s 2015 Uniformity of Collective Agreements Act violated Article 11 ECHR (freedom to form and join trade unions).

A company may conclude multiple collective agreements with different unions covering the same business unit (Betrieb). This can produce “conflicting collective agreements” with diverging terms for employees in similar positions. From 1957 the Federal Labour Court applied only the most specifically tailored agreement; in 2010 it reversed course and allowed multiple agreements to apply according to an employee’s union membership.

The 2015 Act (inserting s. 4a into the Collective Agreements Act) reversed that approach. Where agreements overlap in place, time, unit and employee category and differ in content, only the agreement concluded by the union with the largest membership in the unit at the date of the last agreement remains applicable; the minority agreement is rendered inapplicable. The stated aims were to preserve the protective, distributive, pacifying and ordering functions of collective bargaining, prevent employees in key positions from bargaining to the detriment of others, and encourage cooperation rather than fragmentation. Minority unions may subsequently adopt the majority agreement in full (Nachzeichnung). Employers must notify other unions of impending negotiations and hear their demands. Special labour-court proceedings determine which union holds the majority; a notary may certify the fact of majority without disclosing numbers or names.

The applicants lodged constitutional complaints, arguing that the Act impaired their right under Article 9(3) of the Basic Law to form associations for the improvement of working conditions. The Federal Constitutional Court (2017) accepted standing: the mere existence of the rule already forced unions to adjust bargaining strategy and organisational structure. It found a substantial interference: minority agreements become inapplicable, leaving members without a contract; minority unions lose credibility as bargaining partners, reducing their ability to attract members or mobilise for strikes; they may have to reveal membership strength; and they are pressured to alter the professional groups they represent. The right to strike itself was untouched.

The Court held the interference largely justified. Freedom of association may be regulated to secure a functioning system of autonomous collective bargaining. The legislature enjoyed a wide margin. Restrictive interpretation was required: an agreement is inapplicable only while a genuine conflict exists; long-term personal guarantees (pensions, job security) survive unless a comparable benefit appears in the majority agreement; non-compliance with notification rules keeps the minority agreement in force; and adoption rights must be construed broadly. One defect was identified: the statute lacked safeguards ensuring that a majority union seriously considers the interests of professional groups that may be under-represented in its ranks. That proviso was to apply until legislative amendment (enacted 2019). International instruments, including Article 11 ECHR and the European Social Charter, were held not to confer wider protection.

The applicants then turned to Strasbourg, complaining that rendering minority agreements inapplicable, weakening minority unions’ attractiveness and bargaining power, and exposing membership data disproportionately restricted an essential element of trade-union freedom.

The case Association of Civil Servants and Union for Collective Bargaining and Others v. Germany (ECtHR, 5 July 2022) concerned five applications by German trade unions (dbb, a public/private-sector confederation; Marburger Bund, representing physicians; and GDL, representing train drivers) plus individual GDL members. They alleged that the 2015 Uniformity of Collective Agreements Act violated Article 11 ECHR by impairing trade-union freedom of association and collective bargaining.

German companies may negotiate with multiple unions, producing “conflicting collective agreements” that overlap in a business unit (same workplace, time, and employee positions) but contain divergent terms. After a 2010 Federal Labour Court reversal of earlier case-law, such agreements could coexist according to individual membership. The 2015 Act inserted section 4a into the Collective Agreements Act to restore uniformity: only the agreement of the union with the largest membership in the unit remains applicable; minority agreements become inapplicable. Minority unions may “adopt” (Nachzeichnung) the majority terms in full. Employers must notify other unions of bargaining and allow them to present demands. Labour courts determine the majority union (with procedures designed to avoid disclosing exact membership figures). The stated aims were to preserve the protective, distributive, pacifying and ordering functions of collective agreements, prevent key-position employees from bargaining to the detriment of others, foster solidarity, and facilitate overall compromises (especially in crises).

The applicants contended that the rule left minority members without their bargained terms, rendered minority unions unattractive bargaining partners (weakening recruitment and strike mobilisation), forced disclosure of organisational strength, and distorted unions’ choices of whom to represent. They lodged constitutional complaints arguing incompatibility with Article 9(3) of the Basic Law.

In its leading 11 July 2017 judgment (6–2), the Federal Constitutional Court held that the applicants had standing because the Act already affected their bargaining strategy. It accepted that section 4a constituted a considerable interference (loss of bargained terms, reduced attractiveness, possible membership disclosure) but found it largely justified. The measure pursued the legitimate aim of safeguarding autonomous collective bargaining by encouraging cooperation and preventing fragmentation that would undermine solidarity. Restrictive interpretation was required: inapplicability arose only in cases of genuine conflict (overlap plus differing working-condition provisions); long-term personal-planning benefits (pensions, job security) survived unless matched; the right of adoption applied to the entire majority agreement; non-compliance with notification rules prevented inapplicability; and court proceedings should use notarial certification to conceal exact numbers. The sole unconstitutionality was the absence of safeguards ensuring that majority unions seriously considered the interests of under-represented professional groups. The Court therefore kept the provision in force until 31 December 2018 subject to that proviso; the legislature amended the Act accordingly in 2019. The Court found no broader protection under Article 11 ECHR or the European Social Charter.

The ECtHR, after receiving third-party interventions from major German employer and union confederations, likewise examined the Act under Article 11. It concluded that the restriction was limited, did not affect an essential element of trade-union freedom, and pursued the weighty aim of ensuring the proper functioning of collective bargaining in the interests of both employees and employers. The legislation therefore fell within Germany’s margin of appreciation and disclosed no violation.

The case Association of Civil Servants and Union for Collective Bargaining and Others v. Germany (applications nos. 815/18 et al.) concerns complaints by three German trade unions—the Association of Civil Servants and Union for Collective Bargaining (a confederation negotiating for public- and private-sector members), the Marburger Bund (representing employed physicians since 2006), and the Trade Union of German Train Drivers (GDL, representing railway employees)—together with individual GDL members. They alleged that the Uniformity of Collective Agreements Act of 3 July 2015 (in force 10 July 2015) violated Article 11 of the Convention by interfering with their freedom to form and join trade unions and to engage in collective bargaining.

The Act inserted section 4a into the Collective Agreements Act to address “conflicting collective agreements”—situations in which multiple unions have concluded agreements with differing terms that overlap in the same business unit (Betrieb) of a company, covering employees in similar positions. Previously, Federal Labour Court case-law from 1957 had applied only the most specifically tailored agreement; a 2010 reversal permitted concurrent application according to each employee’s union membership. The new provision states that only the agreement of the union with the largest number of members in the unit at the time the last conflicting agreement was concluded remains applicable; the others become inapplicable. The minority union may subsequently adopt the majority agreement in its entirety (Nachzeichnung). Employers must notify other statutory unions of the start of negotiations, and those unions may present their demands. Labour courts have exclusive jurisdiction to determine which agreement applies, with proceedings designed (via notarial certification) to avoid disclosing exact membership figures or names.

The applicants lodged constitutional complaints directly against the Act, claiming it breached Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law (freedom to form associations to safeguard and improve working conditions). In a leading judgment of 11 July 2017 the Federal Constitutional Court held that the provision considerably impaired that freedom: minority agreements resulting from bargaining became inapplicable, leaving members without coverage; minority unions lost credibility as bargaining partners, reducing their ability to attract or mobilise members; they might have to reveal their industrial-action strength; and their representational choices (which professional groups to organise) were affected. The right to strike itself, however, remained intact even if a union knew in advance it was in the minority.

The Constitutional Court found the interference largely justified and within the legislature’s margin of appreciation. The Act pursued the weighty aim of preserving the protective, distributive, pacifying and ordering functions of collective agreements and of securing a functioning system of autonomous collective bargaining. It sought to prevent strategically placed employees from extracting advantages that undermined other workers’ bargaining power and solidarity, and to encourage overall compromises (especially in crises). Restrictive interpretation limited the impact: parties could contract out of inapplicability; only genuinely overlapping, differing provisions on working conditions triggered the rule; long-term personal-planning benefits (pensions, job security) could not be displaced without a comparable majority provision; inapplicability was barred if notification/hearing rules had been ignored; and membership numbers were to be protected. One respect was incompatible: the absence of safeguards ensuring that a majority union seriously and effectively considered the interests of under- or unrepresented professional groups. Until legislative amendment (required by 31 December 2018), inapplicability therefore required substantiation of such consideration. (The 2019 amendment added an explicit proviso to that effect.) Later complaints were dismissed by reference to this judgment.

These facts—the automatic displacement of minority bargaining outcomes, the consequent weakening of minority unions, and the limited procedural safeguards—underpinned the applicants’ claim that the Act disproportionately restricted an essential element of trade-union freedom under Article 11.
001-218427:
The applicant, a Greek judge born in 1970, began a relationship with K.P. in late 2013 and cohabited with her from January 2014. He ended the relationship in June 2014 (a month before their planned wedding) while she was pregnant. Their daughter M. was born on 1 December 2014. Communication thereafter was non-existent. On 26 January 2015 the applicant unilaterally recognised paternity before a notary (without K.P.’s consent).

He immediately sought interim contact and parental-responsibility orders. Provisional applications were rejected because paternity had not been formally established with the mother’s consent. An August 2015 interim judgment granted three hours of supervised Saturday contact at K.P.’s home. In the main first-instance proceedings (judgment of 13 June 2016) the court recognised paternity but refused joint parental responsibility. It found the parents’ relationship “tense” because of the applicant’s selfish, aggressive behaviour (losing his temper, throwing objects, and one incident of physical violence). Contact was limited, for the first year, to four monthly daytime visits (first/third Saturdays and second/fourth Sundays, 12:00–17:00) at the mother’s home in the presence of K.P. and a relative. Overnight stays were excluded. The court relied on the complete absence of any bond (the applicant had met M. only once), the child’s young age and exclusive maternal care, and the lack of suitable facilities at the applicant’s home.

The Athens Court of Appeal (8 June 2017) upheld the refusal of joint parental responsibility (that issue being appealable only on points of law). It reiterated the findings of the applicant’s aggressive conduct and noted that he had not used the interim contact schedule, had visited M. only once (March 2015), had sent critical extrajudicial notices, and had paid no maintenance. Nevertheless, the child’s best interests required gradual contact so that a bond could form. The court therefore imposed an even more restrictive initial regime (first six months: Saturdays 12:00–15:00 and Sundays 12:00–17:00, fully supervised at the mother’s home), followed by modest extensions and the possibility of playground venues, still without overnights in the first year.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation on the contact schedule and parental-responsibility issues. On 23 March 2018 he filed additional grounds in a separate document. The Court of Cassation (13 July 2018) rejected those additional grounds as out of time: under the Code of Civil Procedure they had to be lodged and served at least 30 full days before the hearing. The thirtieth day fell on a Sunday; the statutory extension to the next working day coincided with the hearing date itself, rendering the filing late. On the merits the cassation court held that the lower courts had given adequate reasons, taking into account the mother’s biosocial role with a very young child and the other circumstances already identified.

Later first-instance decisions (2018–2020) gradually liberalised contact, eventually permitting unsupervised weekends, overnight stays and holiday periods, although the applicant claimed K.P. never complied with the final 2020 order.

Separately, K.P.’s lawyer reported the applicant’s conduct in the family proceedings to the Court of Cassation’s inspection council. Disciplinary proceedings for “undignified behaviour” were opened in 2017. Pending those proceedings (and an unrelated delay-in-judgment complaint) the applicant was twice refused promotion; he was later promoted after completing the outstanding decisions. He argued that the involvement of Court of Cassation judges in the disciplinary process compromised the impartiality of the chamber that later dismissed his family-law appeal.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the contact regime violated Article 8 (private/family life) and that the rejection of his additional cassation grounds (and alleged lack of impartiality) violated Article 6.

The case of Katsikeros v. Greece (Application no. 2303/19) concerned a Greek national's complaints under Article 8 (right to respect for private life) that domestic courts imposed an overly restrictive contact schedule with his infant daughter, preventing any meaningful relationship, and under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) that the Court of Cassation rejected additional appeal grounds as out of time on formalistic grounds and that the tribunal lacked impartiality.

The applicant met K.P. in late 2013; they cohabited from January 2014. He ended the relationship in June 2014, one month before their planned wedding and while K.P. was pregnant. Their daughter M. was born on 1 December 2014. Thereafter, communication between the parents was nonexistent. On 26 January 2015 the applicant unilaterally recognized paternity before a notary without K.P.'s consent.

In March 2015 he sought interim measures for joint parental responsibility or contact rights. An August 2015 first-instance judgment granted limited supervised contact (Saturdays, three hours at K.P.'s home in her presence and that of a relative). Provisional-order applications were rejected because paternity had not been judicially or notarially established with the mother's consent. In a June 2016 final first-instance judgment the court recognized paternity but awarded sole parental responsibility to K.P. It cited the applicant's selfish, aggressive conduct (temper outbursts, throwing objects, and one incident of violence against K.P.) and the complete absence of a bond with M., whom he had met only once. Contact was limited, for the first year, to two Saturdays and two Sundays per month (noon–5 p.m.) at K.P.'s residence under supervision, later extended slightly in duration and allowing unsupervised pickup/drop-off. Overnight stays were deferred until a minimum relationship existed, given M.'s young age, exclusive maternal care, and the lack of suitable facilities at the applicant's home.

The Athens Court of Appeal (June 2017) largely upheld these findings, noting that the applicant had ignored the earlier schedule, seen M. only once, sent critical extrajudicial messages, and paid no maintenance; his relatives showed similar disinterest. While affirming that M.'s best interests required gradual contact, the court imposed even more limited initial hours (Saturdays noon–3 p.m. for the first six months) under supervision, later relaxing them modestly, again excluding overnight stays until a genuine bond formed. Both parents were urged not to involve the child in their conflict.

The applicant appealed on points of law, challenging the contact restrictions as contrary to the child's best interests and the rejection of joint responsibility. On 23 March 2018 he filed additional grounds in a separate document. The Court of Cassation (July 2018) dismissed those additional grounds as time-barred: under the Code of Civil Procedure they (and service on the respondent) had to occur at least 30 full days before the hearing. The 30th day fell on a Sunday; the time-limit therefore expired on the Monday of the hearing itself. On the merits the court found the lower courts' reasoning sufficient, including the mother's biosocial advantage with a very young child.

Subsequent interim-measure decisions incrementally expanded contact (removing the relative's presence, adding psychologist-supervised meetings, then overnight stays and holiday periods). The applicant alleged non-compliance by K.P.

Separately, K.P.'s lawyer lodged a disciplinary complaint against the applicant (a sitting judge) for undignified conduct in the family proceedings. Pending disciplinary action contributed to his temporary exclusion from promotion.

The ECtHR held that the intended relationship with the biological child did not attract “family life” protection because the lack of any established bond was attributable to the applicant himself. The contact restrictions were based on relevant and sufficient reasons (child's age, absence of prior contact, parental conflict, and the need for a gradual bond) and remained within Greece's margin of appreciation; there was therefore no Article 8 violation. The rejection of the additional grounds neither impaired the very essence of the right of access to court nor exceeded the national margin of appreciation, so there was no Article 6 violation.

The applicant, a Greek national born in 1970, began a relationship with K.P. in late 2013 and cohabited with her from January 2014. He ended the relationship in June 2014, shortly before their planned wedding and while K.P. was pregnant. Their daughter M. was born on 1 December 2014. Communication between the applicant and K.P. thereafter ceased. On 26 January 2015 the applicant unilaterally recognised paternity before a notary (without K.P.’s consent).

On 18 March 2015 he sought interim measures for joint parental responsibility or contact rights. By judgment of 5 August 2015 he was granted limited supervised contact (three hours every Saturday at K.P.’s home in her presence and that of a relative). Further provisional-order applications were rejected because paternity had not been established with the mother’s consent. In the main proceedings, the first-instance court (judgment of 13 June 2016) recognised paternity but refused joint parental responsibility, citing the applicant’s selfish, aggressive behaviour (including throwing objects and one incident of physical violence against K.P.). Contact was set at four half-days per month (initially 12 noon–5 p.m.) at the mother’s home with supervision, later extended in hours and allowing pick-up/drop-off. The court relied on the child’s young age (ten months), exclusive maternal care, the applicant’s having met M. only once, the lack of an adapted space at his home, and the need for gradual bonding.

The Athens Court of Appeal (judgment of 8 June 2017) upheld the refusal of joint parental responsibility and imposed a still more gradual, initially more restricted schedule (first six months: even shorter hours, fully supervised at the mother’s home; thereafter modest extensions, later pick-up/drop-off). It noted that the applicant had not used the first-instance schedule, had met M. only once (March 2015), had paid no maintenance and had shown no interest; it stressed the risk of harm to the very young child if overnight stays or unsupervised contact occurred before a natural bond formed.

The applicant appealed on points of law against both judgments. Additional grounds filed on 23 March 2018 were rejected by the Court of Cassation (judgment of 13 July 2018) as out of time: they had to be lodged and served at least thirty full days before the hearing; the thirtieth day was a Sunday, so the deadline moved to the Monday of the hearing itself. On the merits the Cassation court found the lower courts’ reasoning sufficient, including the mother’s biosocial advantage in caring for an infant.

Subsequent first-instance decisions (2018–2020) progressively liberalised contact, eventually permitting unsupervised weekends and holiday periods, though the applicant alleged non-compliance by K.P.

Separately, K.P.’s lawyer reported possible disciplinary offences by the applicant (a sitting judge). An investigation led to a disciplinary action for undignified behaviour; this (together with another pending action) caused the applicant’s temporary exclusion from promotion by the Supreme Judicial Council (composed of Court of Cassation judges). He was later promoted.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the contact regime prevented establishment of a relationship with his daughter (Article 8) and that the Cassation court’s rejection of additional grounds and alleged lack of impartiality (linked to the disciplinary proceedings) violated Article 6.
001-214771:
The case of Pertaia v. Georgia (ECtHR, 13 January 2022) concerns complaints by Ruslan Pertaia, a Georgian national, under Article 3 (ill-treatment by police and ineffective investigation) and Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) (fair trial, specifically refusal to hear a defence witness).

On 23 August 2014 at 4 a.m., Pertaia was arrested near a crime scene in Zugdidi on suspicion of aggravated theft. The arrest record noted redness around his left temple. At 10 a.m. he was taken to hospital with headaches, pain in his waist and right palm, bruises on his left temple and cheek, and cuts on his right palm; he was diagnosed with a closed head injury of serious condition. He stated that he had fallen and hit his head on a stone. A detention-centre visual examination confirmed multiple cuts and bruises, with the applicant claiming they predated arrest.

On 25 August he returned to hospital for headaches and nausea; a scan showed no brain damage. That day, in an interview with the Public Defender’s Office, he alleged physical and verbal assault by four officers (including Sh.K.) during arrest and transfer, plus further ill-treatment by L.K. (head of Zugdidi Police) at the station to extract a confession. He said he lost consciousness several times and, fearing retaliation, signed documents attributing injuries to a pre-arrest fall. The interviewer observed cuts and bruises on his tibias, knees, abdomen and arms. Subsequent examinations confirmed the injuries; he later attributed them to the arrest.

Pertaia pleaded not guilty at trial, admitting presence near the scene but denying the theft. On 4 December 2014 the Zugdidi District Court convicted him and imposed five years’ imprisonment.

He appealed, arguing the conviction rested mainly on police evidence while ignoring defence witnesses. On 30 April 2015 his counsel sought to call a new witness, T.Q., who had allegedly confessed to the prosecutor as the true perpetrator; Pertaia claimed he had only recently learned of this. The prosecutor objected that the evidence exceeded the appeal’s scope and might be vexatious (T.Q. had attended the trial without offering to testify). The Kutaisi Court of Appeal dismissed the request under Article 297(e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, holding the evidence fell outside the appeal’s scope. On 21 May 2015 it upheld the conviction.

Pertaia’s points-of-law appeal to the Supreme Court complained that the refusal to hear T.Q. violated defence rights. On 4 June 2016 the Supreme Court reclassified the offence as attempted theft but left the sentence unchanged and did not address the witness issue. A subsequent request to reopen proceedings on the basis of T.Q.’s confession was rejected as inadmissible because the evidence was not “new.”

Regarding the ill-treatment allegations, the Public Defender’s Office notified the Chief Prosecutor on 29 August 2014. An investigation under Article 333 § 3(b) of the Criminal Code (abuse of power) was opened on 4 September 2014. Before that date the same investigator handling the theft case (from the same police department) interviewed the arresting officers (whose statements were virtually identical), detention-centre staff and the examining doctors; all stated the injuries predated arrest or resulted from a fall. A forensic report based solely on medical records (no in-person examination) described the injuries as minor.

The case was later transferred. In October 2014 family members, a villager, the implicated police chief, his deputy and the arresting officers were questioned; the officers denied ill-treatment. Pertaia was interviewed on 28 October and repeated his detailed account. Between 2014 and 2016 he and his lawyers repeatedly sought updates; replies confirmed the investigation remained pending and, as a mere witness, he could not receive details. Requests for victim status in 2018–2019 were refused. The investigation was still pending at the time of the Court’s judgment.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: documented injuries coinciding with arrest, delayed and internally conducted inquiries into police conduct, and the appellate court’s refusal to examine potentially exculpatory witness evidence.

**Case Summary: Pertaia v. Georgia (ECtHR, Application no. 44888/16, 13 January 2022)**

The case concerned alleged ill-treatment of Ruslan Pertaia, a Georgian national born in 1976 and living in Zugdidi, by police officers during and after his arrest, together with a claimed failure to investigate those allegations effectively (Article 3 ECHR). It also involved a complaint that an appellate court refused to examine a new defence witness (Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d)).

On 23 August 2014 at 4 a.m., Pertaia was arrested near a crime scene in Zugdidi on suspicion of aggravated theft. The arrest record noted redness around his left temple. At 10 a.m. he was taken to hospital with headaches, pain in the waist and right palm, bruises on the left temple and cheek, and cuts on the right palm. He was diagnosed with a closed head injury of serious condition. He initially stated that he had fallen and hit his head on a stone. Visual examinations on transfer to detention confirmed multiple cuts and bruises; he reported no complaints and attributed injuries to a pre-arrest incident.

On 25 August he was hospitalised again with headaches and nausea; a tomography scan showed no brain damage. That day he told a Public Defender’s Office representative that four officers (one identified as Sh.K.) had physically and verbally assaulted him during arrest and transfer to the Zugdidi Police Department. Upon arrival, the department head (L.K.) had allegedly ill-treated him to extract a confession; he claimed to have lost consciousness several times. Out of fear he had signed documents stating the injuries predated arrest. The representative observed cuts and bruises on his tibias, knees, abdomen and arms. A 26 August examination upon transfer to pre-trial detention confirmed the injuries; he then attributed them to the arrest.

At trial Pertaia pleaded not guilty, admitting proximity to the scene but denying the theft. On 4 December 2014 the Zugdidi District Court convicted him and imposed five years’ imprisonment.

On appeal he argued the trial court had relied excessively on police statements while ignoring defence evidence. On 30 April 2015 counsel applied to examine a new witness, T.Q., who had confessed to the prosecutor that he had committed the crime; Pertaia said he had only recently learned of the confession. The prosecutor objected that the evidence fell outside the appeal’s scope and might be vexatious, as T.Q. had attended the trial without offering to testify earlier. The Kutaisi Court of Appeal dismissed the application under Article 297(e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, holding it had no jurisdiction because the evidence exceeded the appeal’s scope. On 21 May 2015 it upheld the conviction.

Pertaia’s points-of-law appeal to the Supreme Court complained, inter alia, that refusal to hear T.Q. had denied him an effective defence. On 4 June 2016 the Supreme Court reclassified the offence as attempted theft but left the sentence unchanged and did not address the witness issue. A 27 May 2016 request to reopen proceedings on the basis of T.Q.’s confession was rejected as inadmissible on 27 June 2016 because the evidence was not new and had already been considered (and excluded) at earlier stages.

Regarding the ill-treatment investigation, the Public Defender’s Office wrote to the Chief Prosecutor on 29 August 2014 enclosing Pertaia’s statement. An investigation under Article 333 § 3(b) of the Criminal Code (abuse of power) was opened on 4 September 2014. Before formal opening, on 1 September an investigator from the same department who had handled the theft case interviewed the two arresting officers (statements virtually identical) and detention-centre staff; all said injuries predated arrest. Doctors who examined Pertaia on 23 and 25 August confirmed the injuries and his initial “fall” account. A forensic report based solely on the 23 August medical record (no in-person examination) described the injuries as minor with no health damage and some sources undetermined.

The case was transferred in September 2014. In October the new investigator questioned family members, a villager, L.K., his deputy and the arresting officers (all four officers denied ill-treatment). Pertaia was interviewed on 28 October and gave a detailed account matching his earlier statement. Between 2014 and 2016 Pertaia and representatives made at least six requests for information; replies stated only that the investigation remained pending and that, as a mere witness, he could receive no details. In 2018–2019 lawyers repeatedly sought updates and victim status; all requests were refused. The investigation remained pending at the time of the Court’s judgment.

These facts formed the basis of the Court’s examination of the alleged Article 3 and Article 6 violations.

The case of Pertaia v. Georgia (Application no. 44888/16) concerns two alleged Convention violations arising from events in August 2014.

On 23 August 2014 at 4 a.m., the applicant was arrested in Zugdidi on suspicion of aggravated theft. The arrest record noted redness around his left temple. At 10 a.m. he was taken to hospital with headaches, pain in the waist and right palm, bruises on the left temple and cheek, and cuts on the right palm. He was diagnosed with a closed head injury of serious condition. He told doctors he had fallen and hit his head on a stone. A visual examination at the detention centre confirmed multiple cuts and bruises; the applicant stated the injuries predated arrest and he had no complaints.

On 25 August he was hospitalised again for headaches and nausea. A tomography scan showed no brain damage. That day, in an interview with the Public Defender’s Office, he alleged that four police officers (one identified as Sh.K.) had physically and verbally assaulted him during arrest and transfer, and that L.K., head of the Zugdidi Police Department, had further ill-treated him at the station to extract a confession. He claimed he had lost consciousness several times and had signed documents attributing the injuries to a pre-arrest fall only out of fear of retaliation. The representative observed cuts and bruises on the applicant’s tibias, knees, abdomen and arms. A 26 August examination at a pre-trial detention centre again confirmed the injuries; the applicant now stated they had been received during arrest.

On 29 August the Public Defender’s Office requested information from the Chief Prosecutor’s Office and forwarded the applicant’s statement. An investigation under Article 333 § 3 (b) of the Criminal Code (abuse of power) was opened on 4 September 2014. Prior to that date the same investigator who had handled the theft case interviewed the arresting officers (from the same department); their virtually identical statements claimed the temple redness already existed and that medical care had later been arranged. Detention-centre staff and treating doctors similarly reported that the applicant had attributed the injuries to a fall. A forensic report based solely on the 23 August medical record (no in-person examination) described the injuries as minor and of partly unknown origin. Subsequent interviews of family members, a villager, the implicated police officers and the applicant produced denials from the officers and a detailed reaffirmation by the applicant of his ill-treatment account. From 2014 to 2019 the applicant and his lawyers repeatedly sought updates and victim status; all such requests were refused or met with statements that the investigation remained pending. It was still pending at the time of the Court’s judgment.

Separately, the applicant was convicted of theft by the Zugdidi District Court on 4 December 2014 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. He appealed, arguing that the conviction rested unduly on police testimony. On 30 April 2015 his counsel applied to the Kutaisi Court of Appeal to examine a new witness, T.Q., who had allegedly confessed to the prosecutor that he, not the applicant, had committed the theft. The prosecutor opposed the application as going beyond the scope of the appeal and as possibly vexatious (T.Q. having attended the trial without offering testimony). The Court of Appeal dismissed the application on procedural grounds under Article 297(e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, holding that the evidence exceeded the issues raised in the appeal. It upheld the conviction on 21 May 2015. The Supreme Court, on 4 June 2016, reclassified the offence as attempted theft but left the sentence unchanged and did not address the witness issue. A subsequent request to reopen the proceedings on the basis of T.Q.’s confession was rejected as inadmissible because the evidence was not “new.”

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation (Article 3) and of a denial of the opportunity to examine a defence witness (Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d)).
001-214669:
**Case of Marshalov and Others v. Russia (Applications nos. 49290/06 and 2 others)**

This European Court of Human Rights judgment addresses three applications by Russian nationals alleging ill-treatment by State officials (primarily police) between 2006 and 2008, plus ineffective investigations into those claims. The applications also raise related complaints under the Court’s well-established case-law. The facts, as submitted by the parties, focus on the incidents of alleged abuse, medical evidence of injuries, confessions obtained, and repeated unsuccessful attempts to secure investigations or judicial review.

**Marshalov (no. 49290/06)**  
On 12 July 2006, the applicant was apprehended near his home in Kazan, handcuffed, and taken to the Vysokogorskiy District Police Department. There he was beaten, allegedly in the presence of a senior investigator from the District Prosecutor’s Office and later the District Prosecutor. Officers used gas masks and electric shocks to extract a murder confession. On 14 July he was transported to the Kazan Police Department while lying on the car floor, where officers kicked his back; at the station he was again beaten and electrocuted on his fingers before being returned. A surgeon documented bruises on his forehead and nose. A forensic report recorded a forehead/nose scar, hematomas on shoulders and hips, and abrasions on knees and elbows. He was later taken again to the Kazan station and subjected to similar methods. He confessed on 20 July 2006. A further medical examination on 28 July confirmed the facial bruise.  

He complained of torture to the Vysokogorskiy District Prosecutor’s Office on 19 July 2006; the complaint was summarily rejected, as were later attempts before various authorities. On 28 August 2006 the Vakhitovskiy District Court dismissed his Article 125 Code of Criminal Procedure complaint against the prosecutors’ refusal to open a criminal case. The Supreme Court of Tatarstan upheld this on 22 September 2006, holding that any alleged investigative abuses and the admissibility of evidence obtained thereby should be examined later by the trial court hearing the criminal case against him.

**Yarullin (no. 58179/09)**  
On 29 June 2008 at around 4 a.m., two police officers approached the applicant (who was intoxicated) at a Kazan bus stop and took him to check his identity. Around 6 a.m. he was brought to the sobering-up centre of the Privolzhskiy District Police Department. After officers ignored his requests to telephone his parents, he attempted to leave. One officer grabbed his arm and violently threw him to the ground, fracturing his right shoulder. He was treated at Medical Emergency Centre no. 1 until 2 July; medical records confirmed the fracture.  

On 2 July he requested that criminal proceedings be opened against the officer. An investigator refused on 14 July, citing video footage and finding the force justified by the applicant’s attempt to leave without permission; the decision did not examine proportionality in detail. The applicant challenged this. On 31 October the Deputy Prosecutor of Kazan quashed the refusal of his own motion and remitted the matter; the decision was formally quashed on 6 November with instructions for further steps (consulting registers, ambulance records, and questioning cellmates). The district court then discontinued the judicial challenge as moot. A fresh refusal issued on 15 November was essentially identical to the first. Throughout 2009 the applicant’s court challenges failed because the authorities repeatedly quashed their own decisions before judicial review could occur. A court later found the Investigation Committee’s failure to reply to his lawyer’s request for access to inquiry documents unlawful.

**Kapranov (no. 14043/09)**  
Arrested on 28 December 2006 on suspicion of six serious violent crimes, the applicant was held in remand prison IZ-63/1 in Samara. He alleged that authorities pressured him into confessing, including by having cellmates beat him on investigators’ orders. Medical examinations on 12 January and 6 February 2007 recorded superficial wounds to the forearms and back of the head, a chest bruise, and first-degree facial burns. Under this pressure he confessed to every episode in the presence of a lawyer suggested by the investigation and requested that his own lawyers (hired by his family) be replaced.  

The Samara Regional Prosecutor’s Office refused to open a criminal case on 16 April 2007, relying on statements by the investigator and officers; it claimed the injuries were self-inflicted (falling from bed, sleeping against a hot radiator, cutting himself with a nail) and that his choice of lawyer had been voluntary. A further refusal by the Investigative Committee on 22 February 2008 likewise treated the injuries as self-inflicted. The applicant’s court complaints about these refusals were unsuccessful.  

On 28 April 2008 the Samara Regional Court convicted him of all charges, relying in particular on the self-incriminating statements given with the suggested lawyer; his alibi evidence and ill-treatment claims were summarily dismissed. The Supreme Court of Russia slightly modified the conviction on 8 September 2008 and imposed a 22-year sentence, again dismissing the ill-treatment allegations as unsubstantiated. Separately, on 26 June 2008 the Samara Bar Association reprimanded the suggested lawyer for breaching professional ethics by failing to defend the applicant effectively during the pre-trial investigation. Later complaints about ill-treatment and denial of counsel of choice were also unsuccessful.

These facts form the core of the applicants’ claims of Article 3 violations (substantive ill-treatment and procedural failure to investigate) and related complaints. The Government contested the accounts, but the judgment records the above sequence of events, medical findings, and investigative/judicial responses as submitted.

The ECHR case of Marshalov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 49290/06, 58179/09 and 14043/09) concerns three Russian nationals who alleged ill-treatment by state officials between 2006 and 2008, together with the failure of the authorities to investigate those allegations effectively. The applications also raised additional complaints under the Court’s well-established case-law.

In the first application, Marshalov was apprehended by police near his home in Kazan on 12 July 2006, handcuffed and taken to the Vysokogorskiy District Police Department. He alleged that officers beat him in the presence of a senior investigator and later the District Prosecutor, using a gas mask and electric shocks to extract a confession to murder. On 14 July he was transferred to another police station, kicked while lying on the floor of the vehicle, then beaten and electrocuted on the fingers before being returned. Medical examinations recorded bruises to the face, a scar on the forehead and nose, haematoma on the shoulders and hips, and abrasions. He was subjected to further similar treatment on a later date and confessed on 20 July. Complaints lodged from 19 July onwards were rejected by prosecutors; the courts held that any alleged abuse and the possible exclusion of evidence would be examined only in the subsequent criminal trial.

In the second application, Yarullin, who was intoxicated, was stopped by two officers at a Kazan bus stop in the early hours of 29 June 2008 and taken to a sobering-up centre. When he attempted to leave after being refused permission to telephone his parents, an officer seized his arm and threw him violently to the ground, fracturing his right shoulder. Hospital records confirmed the injury. His request for a criminal investigation was refused on 14 July on the basis of video footage that the investigator considered justified the force used; proportionality was not examined. The decision was later quashed, but a virtually identical refusal was issued. Subsequent court challenges were repeatedly frustrated because the investigative authorities themselves quashed their decisions before judicial review could take place. A lawyer’s request for access to the inquiry file was ignored, a failure later declared unlawful by a district court.

In the third application, Kapranov was arrested on 28 December 2006 on suspicion of six serious violent offences and held in a Samara remand prison. He alleged that investigators applied severe pressure, including arranging for cellmates to beat him, in order to obtain confessions. Medical examinations in January and February 2007 recorded wounds to the forearms and head, a bruise on the chest and first-degree facial burns. He confessed in the presence of a lawyer proposed by the investigation and simultaneously dismissed the lawyers hired by his family. Prosecutors refused to open a criminal investigation, relying on statements by the investigators and officers and on the applicant’s supposed admissions that the injuries were self-inflicted (falling from a bed, sleeping against a radiator, cutting himself with a nail). He was convicted in April 2008 largely on the basis of those statements; the trial court and the Supreme Court of Russia dismissed the ill-treatment claims as unsubstantiated. The Samara Bar Association later reprimanded the assigned lawyer for failing to defend him effectively.

In each instance the applicants’ attempts to obtain an effective investigation into their allegations of ill-treatment were unsuccessful.

The case Marshalov and Others v. Russia (applications 49290/06, 58179/09 and 14043/09) concerns three Russian applicants who alleged they were ill-treated by State officials in 2006–2008 and that subsequent investigations were ineffective, along with related complaints.

Medical examinations the same day and later recorded bruises and a scar on the forehead and nose, hematomas on the shoulders and hips, and abrasions on the knees and elbows. He was subsequently tortured by similar methods at the Kazan station and confessed on 20 July. His 19 July complaint to the prosecutor was rejected; further complaints to various authorities were also unsuccessful. On 28 August 2006 the Vakhitovskiy District Court dismissed his Article 125 CCP challenge to the failure to open a criminal case; the Supreme Court of Tatarstan upheld this on 22 September, holding that any evidence obtained by alleged abuse should be assessed at the applicant’s later criminal trial.

When officers ignored his request to telephone his parents and he tried to leave, one officer seized his arm and violently forced him to the ground, fracturing his right shoulder. He was treated at Medical Emergency Centre No. 1 until 2 July; the fracture was medically confirmed. His 2 July request to open a criminal case was refused on 14 July on the ground that force had been justified by his attempt to leave; proportionality was not examined. After he challenged the decision, a deputy prosecutor acknowledged its unlawfulness and it was quashed, with further steps (register consultation, ambulance records, cell-mate interviews) ordered. A similar refusal followed on 15 November. Throughout 2009 the authorities repeatedly quashed their own decisions before courts could review them. A court later held that the Investigation Committee’s failure to reply to the applicant’s lawyer’s request for access to the inquiry file had been unlawful.

Kapranov was arrested on 28 December 2006 on suspicion of six serious violent offences and held in Samara remand prison IZ-63/1. He alleged that investigators pressured him, including by arranging beatings by cell-mates, to obtain confessions. Examinations on 12 January and 6 February 2007 recorded superficial wounds on the forearms and back of the head, a chest bruise and first-degree facial burns. He then confessed to all charges in the presence of a lawyer suggested by the investigation and asked to dismiss the lawyers his family had hired. On 16 April 2007 the Samara Regional Prosecutor’s Office refused to open a case, citing statements by investigators and officers and claiming the injuries were self-inflicted (falling from a bed, sleeping against a radiator, cutting himself with a nail). A further refusal on 22 February 2008 repeated that the injuries were self-inflicted. The Samara Regional Court convicted him on 28 April 2008 on the basis of the confessions and dismissed his ill-treatment and alibi claims. The Samara Bar Association later reprimanded the assigned lawyer for failing to defend him effectively. The Supreme Court of Russia slightly modified the conviction on 8 September 2008 (22-year sentence) and again dismissed the ill-treatment allegations. Subsequent complaints to prosecutors and courts about the lack of a comprehensive investigation were unsuccessful.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints of ill-treatment and of failures to investigate those allegations effectively.
001-214670:
**CASE OF FREDRIKSEN AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA (ECtHR, 11 January 2022)**

This judgment addresses five joined applications (nos. 15476/08 and others) by eight individuals (mostly Russian nationals, one later obtaining Norwegian citizenship) against Russia. The core allegations involve ill-treatment amounting to torture or inhuman/degrading treatment in police custody at the Operational-Search Bureau (ORB-2) in Grozny, Chechnya, between 2003 and 2007; unrecorded or delayed-recorded detention; ineffective investigations into the complaints; and related issues such as coerced confessions used in criminal proceedings. The Court examined these under Articles 3, 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention, drawing on CPT reports documenting widespread ill-treatment and unlawful detention at ORB-2.

**Fredriksen (formerly Ocherkhadzhiyev, no. 15476/08):** Arrested on 11 May 2005 during a special operation and taken to ORB-2 (arrest recorded only on 13 May). He alleged electric shocks, beatings with wooden sticks, suffocation via gas mask, forced inhalation of ammonia, and cigarette burns to extract a confession to terrorist crimes. A 27 May 2005 remand-prison examination recorded cigarette-burn marks, crusted skin, a haematoma, and a head scar; he complained of widespread pain and vision deterioration. Further alleged beatings occurred in June/December 2005 and January–February 2006. A 26 April 2006 forensic examination confirmed the injuries plus post-traumatic eye contusion and encephalopathy consistent with his account. Complaints from 20 May 2005 onward produced repeated refusals to open a criminal case, relying on ORB-2 officers’ denials. The Chechnya Supreme Court acquitted him in January 2007, citing “physical and psychological impact,” lack of legal assistance, and unrebutted allegations, but Russia’s Supreme Court quashed this. The case was later suspended after he absconded.

**Dzhantemirov, Matsiyev, Salavatov and Khabibulayev (no. 8607/09):** Apprehended in January 2003 (dates of actual arrest preceding official records by 4–5 days) by armed men and held unrecorded at ORB-2 for months (until April or July 2003; official logs later destroyed). They alleged repeated electric shocks, suffocation, rubber-truncheon beatings, and threats of sexual violence to force confessions to terrorism, murder and attacks on law-enforcement officers. Upon transfer to remand prison, doctors noted no fresh injuries; no forensic examinations occurred. May 2003 complaints yielded refusals. A 2005 court-ordered inquiry again refused a criminal case (citing lack of injuries, delayed complaints, and officers’ statements). The applicants were convicted in 2005 (later quashed), then reconvicted in 2008 relying on the confessions; courts dismissed ill-treatment and unrecorded-detention claims. A 2020–21 inquiry also refused to open a case.

**Razhayev (no. 21531/09):** Arrested on 7 August 2007 in Ingushetia, transferred to ORB-2 (recorded 8 August), and held until 17 August. He alleged beatings, electric shocks, suffocation and threats of sexual violence to extract a confession. Admission notes recorded reddened chest/neck, haematomas and bruising. An initial inquiry refused a criminal case. During trial the court ordered a forensic examination (December 2007) confirming injuries timed to custody. A February 2008 refusal again cited officers’ denials. He was convicted in April 2008 on the confession; later refusals (including 2020) were upheld.

**Gairbekov (no. 19278/10):** Arrested by FSB officers in Dagestan on 15 March 2005 and taken to ORB-2 on 22 April. He alleged electric shocks and beatings. On 2 June a doctor recorded a dislocated shoulder and refused prison admission, after which he was returned to ORB-2 and beaten again. He made several confessions in late May–early June. A 3 June forensic examination found no injuries. Convicted in 2009 on the confessions; courts dismissed his May 2005 complaint based on officers’ statements.

**Ganayev (no. 26030/10):** Arrested on 3 January 2006 and held at ORB-2 for several periods until March. He alleged severe beatings and electric shocks. Medical notes recorded extensive thigh haematomas (16 January), facial/thigh bruises (forensic exam 23 January, 3–7 days old) and rib fractures (28 January). Complaints from 25 January 2006 produced refusals citing officers’ denials. Convicted in 2008 after courts dismissed the allegations.

In all cases, investigations consisted of superficial inquiries that uncritically accepted officers’ accounts, failed to interview relevant witnesses or secure evidence, and did not lead to criminal proceedings. Domestic courts generally relied on the resulting refusals to reject ill-treatment claims and admit the confessions. CPT public statements (2003, 2007, 2013, 2019) repeatedly identified ORB-2 as a site of frequent, grave ill-treatment and unofficial detention, noting a climate of fear and the authorities’ failure to conduct independent inquiries.

The case of Fredriksen and Others v. Russia (ECtHR, 11 January 2022) joins five applications by eight individuals (mostly Russian nationals, one later a Norwegian citizen) alleging ill-treatment by Russian security forces at the Operational-Search Bureau (ORB-2) in Grozny, Chechnya, between 2003 and 2007. Complaints centre on torture or inhuman treatment during unrecorded or poorly documented detention, ineffective investigations into those claims, and related use of coerced confessions in terrorism trials (implicating Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention). CPT public statements from 2003–2019 are cited as context, repeatedly identifying ORB-2 as a site of frequent, grave ill-treatment, unlawful prolonged detention, and a climate of fear that deterred complaints.

Applicant Fredriksen (formerly Aslan Ocherkhadzhiyev) was arrested on 11 May 2005 during a special operation and taken to ORB-2. He alleged electric shocks, beatings with wooden sticks, gas-mask suffocation, forced ammonia inhalation and cigarette burns to extract a terrorism confession. His arrest was recorded only on 13 May. A 27 May 2005 remand-prison examination recorded cigarette-burn marks, crusted skin, a haematoma and a head scar; he reported whole-body pain and vision deterioration. A 2006 forensic report confirmed the injuries plus post-traumatic eye contusion and encephalopathy consistent with his account. Further alleged beatings occurred in June and December 2005 and January–February 2006. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open a criminal case, relying solely on ORB-2 officers’ denials. The Chechnya Supreme Court later acquitted him (noting ill-treatment, lack of legal assistance and an unrecorded arrest date), but the Russian Supreme Court quashed the acquittal and remitted the case; proceedings were then suspended after he absconded.

Four co-applicants (Dzhantemirov, Matsiyev, Salavatov and Khabibulayev) were seized in January 2003 by armed men in uniform (witnessed by bystanders or family) and taken to ORB-2; their arrests were recorded days later. They were held unrecorded for months (until April or July 2003). They alleged repeated electric shocks, rubber-truncheon beatings, suffocation and threats of sexual violence until wounds healed, to force confessions to 2000–2002 terrorist attacks. Remand-prison notes recorded no fresh injuries and no forensic examinations were performed. Early complaints were rejected as unsubstantiated. The Chechnya Supreme Court ordered an inquiry in 2005 but investigators again refused to open a case, citing lack of injuries, the applicants’ silence while detained, and officers’ statements (one officer never interviewed). Domestic courts later dismissed challenges, relying on the same refusal. The applicants were convicted in 2005 (quashed on appeal) and reconvicted in 2008–2009 on the basis of the confessions; the courts rejected ill-treatment and unrecorded-detention claims. A 2020–2021 post-notification inquiry produced another identical refusal.

Razhayev was arrested on 7 August 2007 in Ingushetia, transferred to ORB-2 and held until 17 August. He alleged beatings, shocks, suffocation and threats of sexual violence. Admission notes recorded reddened chest and neck, shoulder and shin haematomas and a temple bruise; a forensic report confirmed timing consistent with detention. Investigators refused to open a case, citing officers’ denials. He was convicted in 2008 on his confessions; later challenges failed.

Gairbekov, arrested in Dagestan on 15 March 2005, was taken to ORB-2 on 22 April and allegedly subjected to shocks and beatings. A doctor recorded a dislocated shoulder (refusing prison admission); he was returned and beaten again. He made several May–June confessions. A forensic exam found no injuries. He was convicted in 2009 on the confessions, with ill-treatment claims dismissed on officers’ statements.

Ganayev was arrested on 3 January 2006 and held at ORB-2 in three periods until March. He alleged severe beatings and shocks. Prison notes and a forensic exam recorded extensive thigh haematomas, facial and thigh bruises, and closed fractures of three right ribs. Repeated refusals to open a case cited officers’ denials. He was convicted in 2008; appeals against the refusals were dismissed.

In all instances investigations consisted of officers’ self-serving statements, ignored medical evidence or delayed complaints, and never progressed to a criminal case. Trials routinely admitted the resulting confessions.

The ECHR case of Fredriksen and Others v. Russia (applications 15476/08 et al.) involved eight applicants (mostly Russian nationals; one later obtained Norwegian citizenship) alleging ill-treatment in unrecorded or unofficial detention at ORB-2 (Operative and Search Bureau) in Grozny, Chechnya, between 2003 and 2007. The facility, highlighted in repeated CPT public statements (2003, 2007, 2013, 2019) as a site of frequent severe ill-treatment, unacknowledged lengthy detentions, and climate of fear, was used to extract confessions to terrorism-related crimes. Investigations consisted of repeated refusals to open criminal cases, relying on officers’ denials, lack of contemporaneous injuries in some records, and (later) destruction of logs. Domestic courts often dismissed claims by reference to these refusals while relying on the resulting confessions for convictions. CPT reports noted no meaningful independent inquiry into ORB-2 methods.

Fredriksen (then Ocherkhadzhiyev) was arrested 11 May 2005 (record dated 13 May) and taken to ORB-2. He alleged electric shocks, beatings with sticks, gas-mask suffocation, ammonia inhalation, and cigarette burns to force a confession. A 27 May 2005 remand-prison exam recorded cigarette-burn marks, crusted skin, hematomas, a head scar, body pain, and vision deterioration. Further alleged beatings occurred in June/December 2005 and January–February 2006. A 2006 forensic exam confirmed the injuries plus post-traumatic eye contusion and encephalopathy consistent with his account. Complaints from 20 May 2005 produced multiple refusals (citing officers). Chechnya’s Supreme Court acquitted him in 2007, finding physical/psychological pressure, lack of legal assistance, and unrebutted well-founded allegations (also confirming the 11 May arrest date); Russia’s Supreme Court quashed this, citing the refusals. Proceedings later suspended after he absconded.

The four Dzhantemirov applicants (Dzhantemirov, Matsiyev, Salavatov, Khabibulayev), suspected of 2000–2002 terrorist acts, were seized by armed men in January 2003 (arrests recorded 4–5 days later) and held in ORB-2 for months (until April or July 2003). They alleged electric shocks, suffocation, truncheon beatings, and threats of sexual violence until wounds healed, to extract confessions. Later prison notes recorded no fresh injuries; no forensic exams occurred. Complaints from May 2003 yielded refusals (no injuries noted at the time; officers’ statements; one officer not interviewed). Chechnya’s Supreme Court convicted them in 2005 (noting arrest-date discrepancies) but Russia’s Supreme Court quashed this; they were reconvicted in 2008–2009 on the confessions, with ill-treatment and unrecorded-detention claims dismissed by reference to a 2005 refusal. A 2020–2021 resumed inquiry again refused a case.

Razhayev was arrested 7 August 2007 (record 8 August) in Ingushetia and held at ORB-2 until 17 August, alleging beatings, shocks, suffocation, and sexual-violence threats. Prison notes recorded reddened chest/neck, hematomas, and temple bruising; a December 2007 forensic exam confirmed them (one hematoma possibly 1–2 days pre-17 August). An initial inquiry and later refusals cited officers; courts dismissed challenges by reference to his 2008 conviction (upheld 2008) that relied on the confession.

Gairbekov was arrested 15 March 2005 in Dagestan and taken to ORB-2 on 22 April, alleging shocks and beatings. A 2 June 2005 doctor noted a dislocated shoulder (refusing prison admission); he was returned and allegedly beaten further, making confessions around that time. A 3 June forensic exam found no injuries. Convicted in 2009 (upheld same year) on the confessions, with claims dismissed via FSB officers’ statements.

Ganayev was arrested 3 January 2006 and held in ORB-2 in several periods until March, alleging beatings and shocks. Notes recorded extensive thigh hematomas (16 January), facial/thigh bruises (23 January forensic, 3–7 days old), and closed rib fractures (28 January). Refusals from 2006–2008 cited officers. Convicted in 2008 with claims dismissed; court challenges failed.

These facts underpin alleged Article 3 (substantive ill-treatment and procedural investigative failures) violations, plus related complaints (unrecorded detention, confession use) under well-established case-law.
001-215138:
The case of Pashinyan v. Armenia (Applications nos. 22665/10 and 2305/11) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned Nikol Pashinyan’s conviction for organising mass disorder following Armenia’s disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election, raising issues under Articles 5, 10 and 11 of the Convention. Pashinyan, editor-in-chief of the opposition newspaper Haykakan Zhamanak and an active supporter of opposition candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan, alleged unlawful detention from 12 October 2009 to 19 January 2010, as well as interference with his rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

After preliminary election results indicated victory for then-Prime Minister Serzh Sargsyan of the ruling party, Ter-Petrosyan called supporters to Freedom Square in Yerevan to protest alleged irregularities, claiming the vote was neither free nor fair. Daily nationwide rallies ensued from 20 February 2008, attracting tens of thousands at times, with hundreds camping overnight. Pashinyan attended daily, delivering speeches; he maintained the gatherings were peaceful, aimed at annulling the results and holding a new election. Authorities allegedly harassed opposition figures, dismissing officials suspected of support and arresting leaders.

On 1 March 2008, police dispersed the Freedom Square camp at dawn, prompting demonstrators to flee to the area near the French Embassy, Yerevan Mayor’s Office and Myasnikyan monument. Tensions escalated into violence, with barricades formed from vehicles; Pashinyan claimed he and other leaders urged calm, formed a human chain to prevent clashes, and acted in self-defence after police and military encircled the area, using crowd-control weapons, live ammunition and snipers. This resulted in up to ten deaths and numerous injuries. A state of emergency was declared, and criminal cases were opened against opposition activists. Pashinyan went into hiding around this time.

On 4 March 2008, Pashinyan was charged under Article 225 of the Criminal Code (organising mass disorder) and Article 300 (usurpation of State power), accused of conspiring with Ter-Petrosyan and others to unconstitutionally seize power if the election was lost. The charges alleged he organised unlawful continuous events from 20 February, delivered incendiary speeches inciting civil disobedience and violence, and on 1 March instigated mass disorder involving violence, arson, looting, armed resistance and murders. Article 300 was dropped in March 2009 after legislative amendment.

Pashinyan surrendered on 1 July 2009. On 3 July, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court detained him for two months as a flight risk who could obstruct proceedings, citing a prior search; this was upheld on appeal. Detention was extended on 27 August 2009 on similar grounds. On 12 October 2009, after investigation, the District Court committed the case to trial and maintained detention, noting the seriousness of the charges (four to ten years’ imprisonment possible) and his prior hiding.

On 19 January 2010, the District Court convicted Pashinyan under Article 225 § 1, sentencing him to seven years’ imprisonment. It found he and others organised activities from 20 February to foment discontent, spread false information, distributed weapons, and prepared crowds for violence. On 1 March, after learning of police arrival, he allegedly woke campers, urged them to arm and attack officers, leading to discoveries of weapons. Demonstrators then moved to the Myasnikyan area, blocked streets, attacked police, rejected relocation offers, built barricades, and followed his instructions to arm, assault officers and recruit others. The court held he structured groups, issued orders, encouraged grabbing police equipment, called on security forces to join protesters, and coordinated ongoing disorder involving property destruction and looting.

Pashinyan appealed on 19 February 2010, arguing the conviction violated Articles 10 and 11: the authorities politically repressed Ter-Petrosyan supporters; speeches at Freedom Square involved no incitement to violence or overthrow; the square was a public debate platform stressing rule of law; demonstrators fled police brutality rather than being led by him; actions were not “mass disorder,” and he took no concrete organising steps, with no prior conspiracy among alleged leaders. He denied incitement and claimed self-defence after arriving post-barricading.

The Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 9 March 2010, holding he freely expressed views at the assembly but committed the crime of organising mass disorder during later events; Article 11 rights were limited, and prosecution targeted criminal conduct, not participation or opinion. Weapons found meant neither assembly was peaceful. The Court of Cassation declared his points-of-law appeal inadmissible on 30 April 2010.

These facts underpinned the alleged violations: detention continued without sufficient fresh reasons after the investigation ended, and the conviction punished political expression and assembly rather than proven violent organisation.

The case of Pashinyan v. Armenia concerns the conviction of opposition journalist Nikol Pashinyan for organising mass disorder after Armenia’s disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election, raising issues under Articles 5, 10 and 11 ECHR.

Serzh Sargsyan of the ruling party was declared the winner over opposition candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan, who alleged fraud and called supporters to Freedom Square in Yerevan. Pashinyan, editor-in-chief of the opposition daily Haykakan Zhamanak and an active Ter-Petrosyan campaigner, attended the ensuing daily rallies (which at times drew tens of thousands) and regularly spoke. Several hundred protesters camped overnight. Pashinyan maintained the gatherings were peaceful, aimed at annulling a rigged election, and that the authorities instead persecuted opposition supporters.

In the early hours of 1 March 2008 police broke up the camp. Protesters fled to the area of the French Embassy, Yerevan Mayor’s Office and Myasnikyan monument, where thousands joined them. Tensions escalated into violence involving barricades (using vehicles), attacks on police, property damage, arson, looting and the use of firearms; up to ten people died. A state of emergency was declared and criminal cases opened against opposition figures. Pashinyan went into hiding.

On 4 March 2008 he was charged with organising mass disorder (Article 225 of the Criminal Code) and usurpation of state power (Article 300, later dropped after amendment). The indictment alleged that he had conspired, from election day, to hold unlawful continuous events, give incendiary speeches inciting disobedience, and, on 1 March, instigate mass violence, massacre, arson and armed resistance.

Pashinyan surrendered on 1 July 2009. On 3 July the District Court ordered two months’ detention as a flight risk, given the earlier search; this was extended and upheld on appeal. On 12 October 2009, when setting the case for trial, the court maintained detention, citing the seriousness of the charge (four to ten years’ imprisonment) and the risk of absconding.

On 19 January 2010 the District Court convicted Pashinyan under Article 225 § 1 and sentenced him to seven years. It found that, with co-accused already convicted in separate proceedings, he had from 20 February organised protests to foment discontent, spread false claims of a 500,000-strong authorised rally and Ter-Petrosyan’s 60 % victory, supplied camping equipment and money, and distributed weapons. On 1 March, learning of the police approach, he woke campers and urged them to arm themselves and “give a proper welcome”; the crowd then attacked officers. Protesters (led by him) moved to the Myasnikyan area, blocked streets with trolleybuses, rejected relocation, built barricades, armed themselves with stones and improvised weapons, assaulted police, and looted. Pashinyan circulated among groups, issued orders to split, barricade and seize police equipment, called on security forces to join the protesters, declared areas “captured,” and coordinated with others while violence occurred on nearby streets. The court characterised these events as “mass disorder” falling within Article 225 § 1.

Pashinyan appealed, arguing the conviction violated Articles 10 and 11. He claimed a politically motivated campaign, that speeches at Freedom Square neither incited violence nor a violent overthrow, that protesters had fled police brutality and barricaded for self-defence, that there was no prior conspiracy among alleged organisers, and that the trial court identified no concrete organising acts by him. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that he had freely exercised expression until he organised criminal mass disorder (the assemblies being non-peaceful given the weapons found). The Court of Cassation declared a further appeal inadmissible.
