The case of Pashinyan v. Armenia concerned Nikol Pashinyan, an Armenian journalist and opposition activist, and his conviction arising from the protests that followed the disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election. Pashinyan, then editor-in-chief of an opposition newspaper, was an active supporter of defeated candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan. After preliminary results were announced, Ter-Petrosyan called supporters to Freedom Square in Yerevan to protest alleged electoral irregularities. Daily rallies attracting tens of thousands ensued from 20 February, with several hundred camping round-the-clock. Pashinyan participated daily and gave speeches. He maintained that the gatherings were peaceful and sought only to annul the results and hold a new election.

On 1 March 2008 police dispersed the Freedom Square camp in the early morning. Demonstrators regrouped near the French Embassy, Yerevan Mayor’s Office and Myasnikyan monument. Tensions escalated into violence, a state of emergency was declared, and criminal proceedings were opened against opposition figures. Pashinyan alleged police brutality, the use of live ammunition and military equipment, multiple deaths and injuries, and that he and others had tried to prevent clashes by forming a human chain. Around this time he went into hiding.

On 4 March 2008 he was charged, inter alia, under Article 225 of the Criminal Code (organising mass disorder) and Article 300 (usurpation of State power). The charging decision alleged a conspiracy to destabilise the country, unauthorised continuous events, incendiary speeches calling for civil disobedience, and, on 1 March, instigation of mass violence, arson, looting, armed resistance and murders. The Article 300 charge was later dropped after legislative amendment.

Pashinyan surrendered on 1 July 2009. On 3 July the District Court ordered two months’ detention on the grounds that he was a flight risk and might obstruct proceedings, citing the earlier search. The detention was extended on the same grounds. On 12 October 2009, when the case was set down for trial, the District Court maintained detention because the applicant faced a serious charge carrying four to ten years’ imprisonment, had previously been in hiding, and therefore presented a high risk of absconding if released. He remained in detention until conviction.

On 19 January 2010 the District Court convicted him under Article 225 § 1 and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. It found that after the election he and others had organised activities to foment discontent, spread false information, supplied participants with goods and money, and distributed weapons and ammunition. On 1 March, learning of the impending police operation, he had woken campers and urged them to arm themselves and resist, leading to an attack on officers. The crowd then moved to the Myasnikyan monument area, blocked streets with trolleybuses, rejected relocation offers, built barricades, armed themselves with stones and other objects, and assaulted police. The court held that Pashinyan had given concrete instructions to split into groups, erect barricades, seize police equipment, incite soldiers and officers to mutiny, and coordinate the violence; he had thereby organised and overseen mass disorder.

Pashinyan appealed, arguing that his conviction violated Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention. He contended that the Freedom Square events had been peaceful public debate on a matter of public concern, that speeches had not incited violence, that he had not led the crowd to the later site (they had fled police), that no prior agreement existed among alleged organisers, and that the District Court had failed to identify any concrete acts of organisation of disorder on his part. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that he had been free to express himself until 1 March, that he had thereafter committed the criminal offence of organising mass disorder rather than merely participating in an assembly, and that neither assembly had been peaceful given the weapons recovered. The Court of Cassation declared his further appeal inadmissible.

The complaints notified to the Government concerned the lawfulness of detention from 12 October 2009 to 19 January 2010 and the alleged interference with freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
001-215162:
The case of Faysal Pamuk v. Turkey (Application no. 430/13) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned alleged unfairness in the applicant’s criminal trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention, specifically his inability to confront four witnesses whose incriminating statements formed a key basis for his conviction on terrorism-related charges.

The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1978, surrendered voluntarily to the authorities on 7 December 2009. He admitted having been a PKK member from 1994 to 2005 and using the successive code names “Kendal” and “Avareş-Tekoşin.” He was charged under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code with participation in three armed incidents: an attack on a police checkpoint on 3 September 1997 that killed two soldiers; an assault involving abduction and a rocket-launcher attack on 22 September 1995; and an armed clash on 30 May 1997 that injured two gendarmes.

The charges rested in significant part on earlier statements given by four other alleged PKK members (F.K. in 1995, Y.A. in 1996, S.Y. in 1999 and A.T. in 1999). Those statements, some taken without a lawyer, described a person using the code name “Avareş” (or similar variants) as having taken part in the incidents, offering varying physical descriptions and places of origin.

At trial before the Malatya Specially Authorised Assize Court, the applicant denied any involvement in armed activities and repeatedly requested an in-person confrontation with the four witnesses. Instead of securing their attendance, the court issued letters of request to courts in the witnesses’ places of residence, instructing those courts to take statements, show photographs of the applicant, and notify defence counsel.

Y.A. was examined by the Elbistan Assize Court in the lawyer’s absence; he denied knowing the applicant or the incidents, could not identify him from photographs, and recalled the code name only after being reminded of his 1996 statement. He later failed to appear at a reconvened hearing citing illness. S.Y. was heard by an Istanbul court without the applicant or his lawyer present; she stated that several people used the code name “Avareş” and that she did not know the applicant. A.T. was examined by the Muş Assize Court (counsel having been notified) and likewise denied knowledge of anyone with the relevant code names and failed to identify the photographs. F.K. could not be located despite summonses, telephone calls and police inquiries; the request was ultimately dropped.

The applicant remained in pre-trial detention throughout. On 14 April 2011 the trial court convicted him and imposed a life sentence. It treated the original 1990s statements of the four witnesses (together with those of seven others) as establishing that the applicant had been a PKK “warrior” who participated in the three incidents. The court found the physical description given by A.T. (including facial lines) to match the applicant, regarded the recantations as attempts to protect the organisation, and dismissed any possible confusion of code names. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment in summary fashion on 5 April 2012.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: the trial court relied on the untested written statements of absent witnesses who supplied decisive evidence, without making reasonable efforts to secure their personal attendance or providing adequate counterbalancing safeguards.

The case of Faysal Pamuk v. Turkey (Application no. 430/13) concerned criminal proceedings against the applicant, a Turkish national born in 1978, for membership of the PKK terrorist organisation and participation in armed activities. He surrendered voluntarily on 7 December 2009, admitting 11 years of PKK membership (1994–2005) under code names including “Kendal” (later changed to “Avareş-Tekoşin”). He denied involvement in any armed actions.

On 5 January 2010 the Malatya public prosecutor charged him under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code with secessionist activities, specifically three incidents: (1) an armed attack on a police checkpoint on 3 September 1997 that killed two soldiers and injured another; (2) assaults, an abduction and a rocket-launcher attack on 22 September 1995; and (3) an armed clash on 30 May 1997 that injured two gendarmes. The indictment relied on earlier statements by four co-accused PKK members (F.K., Y.A., S.Y. and A.T.), given between 1995 and 1999 without lawyers present. Those statements described a “warrior” from Diyarbakır using variants of the code name “Avareş” (or “Avreş”) who had taken part in the incidents; physical descriptions varied (height, complexion, facial lines, glasses, origin).

At the first hearing on 18 February 2010 the applicant, still in pre-trial detention, reiterated his admissions of membership but denied the armed acts. His lawyer requested an in-person confrontation with the four witnesses, noting discrepancies in code names and descriptions and that several PKK members had used “Avareş”. The prosecutor opposed confrontation because of the time that had elapsed. The trial court (Erzurum Assize Court with special jurisdiction) instead issued letters of request to the courts of the witnesses’ residences, asking them to take statements, show the applicant’s photographs, and notify defence counsel.

- Y.A. was heard by Elbistan Assize Court on 28 April 2010 (defence counsel absent). He denied knowing the applicant or the incidents, failed to identify him from photographs, and attributed the gap to the 15 years that had passed; he later failed to attend a rescheduled hearing because of illness.
- S.Y. was heard by Istanbul Assize Court on 26 May 2010 (applicant and counsel absent). She said two or three people used the name “Avareş” and she did not know the applicant.
- A.T. was heard by Muş Assize Court on 27 May 2010 (counsel notified but not present). He denied knowing anyone with the relevant code names or recognising the photographs.
- F.K. could not be located despite summonses, police inquiries and telephone attempts; the trial court abandoned efforts on 11 November 2010.

At later hearings the defence repeated that none of the witnesses had identified the applicant and that his code name was “Avareş-Tekoşin”, not simply “Avareş”. On 14 April 2011 the trial court convicted him of all three incidents and sentenced him to life imprisonment. It treated the original written statements of the four witnesses as decisive, holding that their later inability to identify or recall the applicant stemmed from a desire to protect the PKK or fear of reprisals. It found the physical description given by A.T. (facial lines) matched the applicant, that the “Avareş” from Diyarbakır who had acted in Dersim was the applicant, and that PKK naming practices made coincidence with another person of the same name, origin and area of activity improbable. The applicant’s own admissions of presence in the region at the relevant times and of membership were also cited. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction on 5 April 2012 without detailed reasoning.

The applicant complained that he had been unable to confront the four witnesses whose statements formed the core of the case against him.

The case of Faysal Pamuk v. Turkey (Application no. 430/13) concerned the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings against the applicant under Articles 6 § 1 and 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention, specifically his inability to confront four witnesses whose earlier statements incriminated him in terrorist activities as a PKK member.

The applicant, born in 1978, was accused of involvement in three armed incidents in 1995 and 1997 in the Mazgirt area: an attack on a police checkpoint on 3 September 1997 killing two privates (incident 1); an assault, abduction and rocket attack on 22 September 1995 (incident 2); and a clash injuring two gendarmes on 30 May 1997 (incident 3). These accusations stemmed from statements given years earlier by four other alleged PKK members. F.K. (30 October 1995) identified a “warrior” from Diyarbakır with the code name “Avarej” in the Mazgirt attack. Y.A. (12 May 1996, without a lawyer) described “Avareş” (aged about 25, 1.75 m tall, slim, dark-skinned, black wavy hair, wearing glasses, carrying a Kalashnikov) participating in the 22 September 1995 activities under “Navdar”. S.Y. (17 and 21 November 1999) referred to “Avareş”, a warrior from Diyarbakır, in a 1997 clash. A.T. (30 November 1999, without a lawyer) mentioned “Avreş” (short, dark-skinned, lined face, from Ergani or Kulp) in an autumn 1997 clash.

On 7 December 2009 the applicant surrendered, admitting 11 years of PKK membership (1994–2005) but denying armed activities. In police, prosecutor and judge interviews (with a lawyer), he stated his code names were initially “Kendal” then “Avareş-Tekoşin”. He distinguished himself from others named “Avareş” and identified some members from photos, expressing regret and seeking active repentance.

Indicted on 5 January 2010 by the Malatya public prosecutor before the Erzurum Assize Court (specially authorised), he faced charges under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code for secessionist activities.

At hearings from February 2010, the applicant repeated his denials. His lawyer requested in-person examination and confrontation with the four witnesses, noting discrepancies in code names, origins and descriptions, and the existence of several “Avareş” members. The trial court instead issued letters of request to courts in the witnesses’ residences, seeking statements, photo identifications of the applicant, and notification of the lawyer. The applicant remained detained.

Y.A. was heard on 28 April 2010 by Elbistan Assize Court (lawyer absent); he denied knowing the applicant or incidents, failed to identify him from photos, and vaguely recalled “Avareş” from 1996 statements, citing elapsed time. He was unwell for a later hearing. S.Y. was heard on 26 May 2010 by Istanbul Assize Court (applicant and lawyer absent despite notification); she mentioned two or three “Avareş” but denied knowing the applicant. A.T. was heard on 27 May 2010 by Muş Assize Court (lawyer notified); he denied knowing anyone with those code names or recognising photos. F.K. could not be located despite efforts, including summonses and police searches; the trial court revoked the order to hear him.

On 14 April 2011 the trial court convicted the applicant of all charges and imposed life imprisonment. It relied on his admissions of membership and the 1990s statements of the four (plus others), treating later recantations as attempts to protect the PKK or due to fear of reprisals. It found A.T.’s description of lined facial features matched the applicant; combined F.K.’s and Y.A.’s accounts to identify the applicant as the Diyarbakır “Avareş” in incident 2; and linked S.Y.’s account (with others) to incident 3 via command structures. It dismissed code-name confusion, citing PKK practices and the applicant’s presence in the relevant region.

The applicant’s appeal criticised the lack of confrontation, failed identifications, and unaddressed submissions. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction on 5 April 2012.

These facts underpinned the complaint that the conviction rested on untested written statements of absent witnesses who provided decisive evidence, without sufficient efforts to secure their attendance or counterbalancing measures.
001-215166:
The applicant, a Spanish national later convicted of ETA membership and explosives possession, was first arrested in 2010 under a European arrest warrant, remanded on terrorism charges, then released after the investigation was discontinued for lack of evidence. In a second set of proceedings, the Guardia Civil arrested him on 29 September 2010. The investigating judge immediately authorised incommunicado detention (initially 48 hours, later extended) to prevent frustration of the search for explosives depots linked to an ETA cell. This measure, imposed without individualised reasons beyond the general nature of the offences and seized computer material, automatically triggered assignment of a legal-aid lawyer. The applicant was informed of his rights (including silence and non-self-incrimination) but, pursuant to then-applicable Articles 520 and 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, was denied both the right to appoint counsel of his choice and any private consultation with the assigned lawyer before or during police questioning.

On 1 October 2010, in the legal-aid lawyer’s presence, the applicant made a self-incriminating statement admitting ETA cooperation (including planning kidnappings and attacks) and identifying a storage room at his home. A subsequent search recovered 56 kg of potassium chlorate, detonators, firearms-related items, spent cartridges from previous killings, and digital materials containing ETA training handbooks and attack plans. Two days later, despite the lawyer’s explicit opposition to a further interview, the applicant made a second statement revealing additional hidden items (a firearm, ammunition, USB devices with terrorist manuals, and false plates); these were also recovered. Daily forensic-medical examinations recorded no physical ill-treatment, though the applicant later alleged a threat to arrest his girlfriend.

On 4 October 2010 the incommunicado regime was lifted, the applicant appeared before the investigating judge, recanted the police statements as products of isolation, and appointed counsel of his choice. At the 2013 trial the Audiencia Nacional convicted him to 17 years’ imprisonment, relying essentially on the computer files, the explosives and weapons found at the locations he had indicated, co-defendants’ and witnesses’ testimony, and his later silence. The court treated the police confessions as voluntary, citing the forensic reports. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2014, finding no evidence of torture and regarding the recovered material as independently corroborative of both storage of explosives and ETA membership. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the automatic, unreasoned denial of a lawyer of his own choosing and of confidential communication with the assigned lawyer while he was held incommunicado vitiated the initial confessions, which in turn produced the physical evidence used to convict him, thereby rendering the proceedings as a whole unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c).

The ECHR case of Atristain Gorosabel v. Spain (Application no. 15508/15) concerned a Spanish national convicted of ETA terrorist-group membership and explosives possession. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) (fair hearing and right to legal assistance of one’s choosing) because he was held incommunicado, denied a lawyer of his choice, and barred from private consultation with his assigned legal-aid lawyer, prompting self-incriminatory statements that produced the key evidence used to convict him.

In April 2010 the applicant was arrested in France on a European arrest warrant, transferred to Spain and remanded in custody on suspicion of ETA membership. Assisted by a lawyer of his own choosing, he denied the allegation before the investigating judge of the Audiencia Nacional and was released on weekly reporting conditions. The first set of proceedings was discontinued in June 2010 for lack of evidence.

Fresh inquiries produced further material. On 28 September 2010 the Guardia Civil obtained judicial authorisation to search properties linked to an alleged ETA cell that the applicant was said to have organised and used for explosives storage. He was arrested at 09:45 on 29 September. The following day the investigating judge authorised incommunicado detention (under the then-applicable Code of Criminal Procedure) to prevent frustration of the investigation, principally the location of explosives. A search of his home seized computer equipment. Because of the incommunicado regime the applicant was assigned a legal-aid lawyer but was neither permitted to choose his own counsel nor allowed a private meeting with the assigned lawyer before police interviews. He was informed of his rights, including the right to silence.

On 1 October 2010, in the presence of the legal-aid lawyer, the applicant admitted “cooperating” with ETA, described attempted kidnappings, targeting of a businessman and police officers, and indicated a storage room containing explosives. A subsequent search recovered detonators, 56 kg of potassium chlorate, spent cartridges linked to prior murders, training materials and traces of explosives. On 3 October, again despite the lawyer’s recorded opposition, the applicant made a second statement identifying a further hiding place at his home; police found a firearm, ammunition, USB devices containing terrorist training manuals, detonators and false licence plates. Daily forensic-medical examinations recorded no physical ill-treatment, though the applicant later claimed he had been threatened with his girlfriend’s arrest.

Incommunicado detention was lifted on 4 October when the applicant was brought before the investigating judge; he immediately appointed a lawyer of his choice and retracted the police statements as the product of isolation. In April 2013 the Audiencia Nacional convicted him on the basis of the seized computer files, the explosives and weapons found at the locations he had indicated, co-defendants’ statements, witness testimony and his silence at trial. The court, relying on the forensic reports, held the statements to have been given freely. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in March 2014, finding no evidence of physical or psychological torture. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible in November 2014.

The ECHR later found that the systematic denial of a lawyer of choice and of confidential consultation, without individualised justification, rendered the initial confessions unreliable and undermined the overall fairness of the proceedings, in violation of Article 6.

The ECtHR case of *Atristain Gorosabel v. Spain* (Application no. 15508/15) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention. The applicant, a Spanish national, complained that while held incommunicado as a terrorist suspect he was denied a lawyer of his own choosing (and private consultation with the assigned legal-aid lawyer). This led him to make self-incriminatory statements that enabled police to obtain the evidence on which his conviction was based, undermining the overall fairness of the proceedings.

The applicant was first arrested in France under a European arrest warrant and transferred to Spain on suspicion of ETA membership. Assisted by a lawyer of his choice, he denied membership and was later released. New evidence prompted a second investigation. On 29 September 2010 the Guardia Civil arrested him. The next day an investigating judge of the Audiencia Nacional authorised incommunicado detention (lasting five days) to prevent frustration of the inquiry, which was aimed primarily at locating explosives. A home search seized computers. He was assigned a legal-aid lawyer and informed of his rights (including silence and non-self-incrimination) but, due to the incommunicado regime under then-applicable Articles 509, 520, 520 bis and 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, could neither choose his own lawyer nor meet privately with the assigned one before police interviews.

On 1 October 2010, in the legal-aid lawyer’s presence, he admitted cooperating with ETA (including attempted kidnapping and providing information for attacks) and indicated a storage room containing explosives. Both he and the lawyer signed the statement. A search immediately yielded large quantities of explosives, detonators, ammunition, spent cartridges linked to killings, and related items. On 3 October 2010, despite the lawyer’s opposition, he made a further statement revealing a hidden firearm, ammunition, USB keys with terrorism training materials and false plates; these were then found at his home. Daily forensic-medical examinations recorded no physical ill-treatment, though he alleged threats to arrest his girlfriend.

On 4 October 2010 he was brought before the judge, recanted the statements as having been obtained under incommunicado conditions, the restriction was lifted, and he appointed counsel of his choice. In 2013 the Audiencia Nacional convicted him of terrorist-group membership and explosives possession, imposing a 17-year sentence. The conviction rested essentially on computer files linking him to ETA, the explosives and other items located via his statements, co-defendants’ testimony, witnesses, and his trial silence. The court (citing forensic reports) held the statements voluntary and free of coercion. The Supreme Court upheld the judgment in 2014, finding no evidence of torture. An amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible.

The ECtHR found a violation: the blanket denial of a lawyer of choice and of private consultation with the legal-aid lawyer, without individualised justification, together with the use of the resulting confessions that directly produced the key physical evidence, rendered the criminal proceedings as a whole unfair.

The case of Freitas Rangel v. Portugal (no. 78873/13) concerns a journalist’s Article 10 complaint over his criminal conviction and civil sanctions for statements criticising two professional associations during a public parliamentary hearing.

Emídio Arnaldo Freitas Rangel, a prominent Portuguese journalist, was invited by the Socialist Party in February 2010 to testify before the Parliamentary Commission on Ethics, Society and Culture. The open hearing, attended by media, examined conditions for freedom of expression, media ownership and political/economic influence, journalists’ precarious employment, editorial participation, and public-entity influence on the press. More than seventy figures were invited.

On 6 April 2010 Rangel testified that journalistic standards had declined and that political and judicial actors were using the media for partisan ends. He described the Professional Association of Judges (ASJP) and the Professional Association of Public Prosecutors (SMMP) as “two hubs managing information relating to judicial cases” that maintained close ties with journalists, obtained case documents and exchanged them openly in coffee shops, thereby facilitating breaches of judicial confidentiality. He warned that the judiciary’s political involvement would have serious consequences unless rules were restored. Immediately afterwards he told a Público reporter that confidential material could only originate inside the justice system, that the associations engaged in “extensive and broad political intervention” with negative effects, sought to constrain the Attorney-General and public opinion, and periodically passed documents to selected journalists.

The remarks received extensive national media coverage. The same day the ASJP issued a statement calling the allegations false and defamatory, damaging the association’s 35-year record and the honour of its more than 2,050 members; it noted that Rangel had identified no individual perpetrator.

On 23 April and 5 May 2010 the ASJP and SMMP lodged criminal complaints for insulting a legal entity (Criminal Code Art. 187). They joined the prosecution as assistentes and filed civil claims. After a failed request for a judicial investigation, the Lisbon Criminal Court convicted Rangel on 7 May 2012 of two counts. It found the statements unsubstantiated assertions of fact, made with intent to undermine the associations’ prestige in a solemn, widely broadcast parliamentary setting. He was fined €6,000 (or 200 days’ imprisonment) and ordered to pay each association €50,000 plus interest.

The Lisbon Court of Appeal (22 November 2012) upheld the conviction (reclassifying it solely under Art. 183 § 2) but reduced damages to €10,000 each. It accepted that Convention case-law required a restrictive approach to honour-based restrictions and wider criticism of public figures, yet held that attributing serious criminal and ethical breaches to bodies composed of judges and prosecutors, without good-faith grounds, exceeded permissible expression.

The Supreme Court (5 June 2013), on the associations’ appeal, raised each award to €25,000. It stressed the statements’ gravity, their knowing falsehood, the high degree of intent, the media amplification, and the associations’ constitutional role in defending judicial independence and ethics; compensation therefore served a preventive, sanctioning function.

Rangel paid the fine in full. The ASJP recovered its award by seizure; the SMMP received a first instalment before Rangel’s death on 13 August 2014, after which the balance passed to his estate. His daughters continued the application he had lodged with the Court on 5 December 2013.

The applicant argued that the conviction and heavy sanctions, imposed for remarks delivered as an invited expert in Parliament on a matter of public interest, violated Article 10. The Court later found the interference unjustified and disproportionate.

The case of Freitas Rangel v. Portugal (Application no. 78873/13) concerned a journalist’s Article 10 complaint over his conviction for insulting legal entities. Emídio Arnaldo Freitas Rangel, a prominent Portuguese journalist, was invited in February 2010 by the Socialist Party to testify before the public Parliamentary Commission on Ethics, Society and Culture. The hearing addressed freedom of expression and the media, including journalistic standards, media ownership transparency, precarious employment, editorial independence, and public-entity influence.

On 6 April 2010 the applicant testified that political and judicial actors were exploiting journalism. He specifically accused the Professional Association of Judges (ASJP) and the Professional Association of Public Prosecutors (SMMP) of acting as “two hubs managing information relating to judicial cases” through close journalist ties. He claimed they obtained case documents for publication, exchanged them openly in coffee shops, and thereby facilitated breaches of judicial confidentiality (segredo de justiça). Leaving the session he repeated similar remarks to a Público journalist, asserting that material covered by confidentiality originated inside the justice system and that the associations pursued broad political intervention, limited the Attorney-General and cultivated privileged journalist relationships to leak documents.

The statements received extensive media coverage. The same day the ASJP issued a public denial, calling the allegations false, defamatory and insulting to the association and its 2,050 member judges; it noted that no specific individual had been identified.

In April–May 2010 both associations lodged criminal complaints for the offence of insulting a legal entity (ofensa a pessoa colectiva). They were admitted as assistants (assistentes) and filed civil claims. The Lisbon public prosecutor supported private-prosecution submissions alleging two counts of defamation. After the applicant’s request for a judicial investigation was dismissed, the case proceeded to trial. At trial the applicant maintained that he had personally witnessed a journalist (E.D.) exchanging files in a café with an SMMP member; E.D. denied the incident.

On 7 May 2012 the Lisbon Criminal Court convicted the applicant of two counts under Articles 187 and 183 of the Criminal Code. It held that he had made unsubstantiated statements of fact with the intent to diminish the associations’ credibility before Parliament and the public, that E.D.’s denial was credible, and that the solemn parliamentary setting plus the applicant’s prominence amplified the harm. He was fined EUR 6,000 (or 200 days’ imprisonment) and ordered to pay each association EUR 50,000 in non-pecuniary damages plus interest.

The Lisbon Court of Appeal, on 22 November 2012, upheld the conviction (re-classifying it solely under the more serious media-dissemination provision of Article 183 § 2) but reduced damages to EUR 10,000 each. It characterised the remarks as false factual imputations of criminal and ethical breaches rather than value judgments, found no good-faith basis, and emphasised the special duties of judges and prosecutors. A subsequent nullity plea was rejected; no further criminal appeal was available.

On the associations’ appeal concerning quantum, the Supreme Court on 5 June 2013 raised compensation to EUR 25,000 each, stressing the statements’ seriousness, the applicant’s knowledge of their falsity, their wide dissemination, and the need for a deterrent civil sanction to protect the entities’ prestige and public trust.

The applicant paid the fine in full. Enforcement of the ASJP award was completed by seizure; an instalment arrangement with the SMMP was only partly fulfilled before the applicant’s death on 13 August 2014. Remaining liability passed to his estate. His daughters continued the Strasbourg application.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 10 violation: a criminal conviction and substantial financial sanctions imposed on a journalist-expert invited to address Parliament on a matter of public interest concerning the justice system and the media.

The case of Freitas Rangel v. Portugal concerns journalist Emídio Arnaldo Freitas Rangel’s Article 10 complaint over his conviction for insulting legal entities based on statements about two professional associations.

A renowned Portuguese journalist, Rangel was invited in February 2010 by the Socialist Party to testify publicly before the Parliamentary Commission on Ethics, Society and Culture. The hearing examined freedom of expression and the media, covering journalists’ working conditions, media ownership, editorial rights, and public influence on the press.

On 6 April 2010, Rangel criticised falling journalistic standards and accused political and judicial actors of exploiting the media. He described the Professional Association of Judges (ASJP) and Professional Association of Public Prosecutors (SMMP) as “two hubs managing information relating to judicial cases” via close journalist ties. He claimed they obtained case documents for publication, exchanged them openly in coffee shops, breached judicial confidentiality, and pursued political aims, warning of dire consequences without rules separating judiciary from politics.

After the session he repeated the allegations to a Público journalist, questioning the origin of confidential material, accusing the associations of political interference, attempts to constrain the Attorney-General, and privileged leaks to journalists.

The remarks were widely reported by at least ten outlets. The ASJP immediately issued a statement branding them false and defamatory, insisting no member had ever leaked documents and that the claims insulted the association and its 2,050 judge members.

On 23 April and 5 May 2010 the associations filed criminal complaints for insulting a legal entity. The Lisbon prosecutor opened proceedings; the associations joined as civil claimants. After an unsuccessful request for a judicial investigation, the case went to trial. Rangel maintained he had personally seen a journalist exchange files with an SMMP member in a café; the journalist denied this.

On 7 May 2012 the Lisbon Criminal Court convicted him on two counts under Criminal Code Articles 187 and 183. It treated the statements as unsubstantiated facts uttered with intent to damage the associations’ prestige in a solemn, media-accessible parliamentary setting that guaranteed wide and lasting dissemination. He received a €6,000 fine (or 200 days’ imprisonment) plus €50,000 damages to each association.

The Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 22 November 2012 (reclassifying it slightly but leaving the penalty unchanged) while reducing damages to €10,000 each. It accepted that Article 10 required a proportionality exercise and that public-figure criticism enjoys wider latitude, yet held that falsely attributing serious criminal and ethical breaches to bodies whose members are bound by special duties, without any good-faith factual basis, exceeded the limits of free speech.

The associations appealed the award. On 5 June 2013 the Supreme Court raised compensation to €25,000 each, stressing the statements’ gravity, the applicant’s knowing intent, the extensive publicity, and the need for a deterrent civil sanction to protect the associations’ credibility and public trust.

Rangel paid the fine; the ASJP recovered its award by seizure and the SMMP received instalments. He died on 13 August 2014; his daughters continued the application and the remaining debt passed to his estate.

These events—expert testimony invited in a parliamentary debate on media freedom, followed by criminal conviction and heavy civil awards for remarks about influential legal-professional bodies—underpin the alleged violation of freedom of expression.
001-215174:
The case of Salmanov v. Slovakia concerns the applicant’s continued detention on remand after a first-instance bribery conviction and related release proceedings. On 23 April 2013 Salmanov was remanded pending trial under Article 71 § 1 (b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (risk of interfering with justice and of further offences). Only the former ground was later retained. He was indicted before the Specialised Criminal Court (SCC) on 25 September 2013.

On 29 September 2014 he applied for release, citing the length of detention. On 11 November 2014 the SCC ordered his release, but a same-day prosecution appeal prevented the order from becoming final, so detention continued. The SCC adjourned the merits hearing (originally 14 November) to 28 November and 3 December 2014, expecting a judgment on the latter date. The file reached the Supreme Court on 14 November. Prosecution reasons followed on 19–21 November; the applicant responded by 25 November. On 27 November the Supreme Court returned the file to the SCC without deciding the appeal, so as not to disrupt the 28 November hearing, instructing its return immediately after any merits judgment.

The SCC convicted Salmanov on 3 December 2014 and imposed six years’ imprisonment. The file returned to the Supreme Court, which on 10 December 2014 quashed the SCC release order. Although it accepted that the original Article 71 § 1 (b) and (c) grounds had lapsed, it ordered continued detention under Article 71 § 1 (a) (flight risk). It cited the (non-final) conviction, prior convictions and prosecutions, possession of four passports, a forthcoming witness interview in another case, and the potentially severe penalty.

A later Supreme Court formation (5 February 2015) refused a fresh release application. It held that after a first-instance prison sentence detention fell under Article 5 § 1 (a) ECHR, yet remained subject to the Code until finality. A severe sentence (understood as eight years or more, or an applicable scale providing for one) itself created a flight risk; the six-year term was therefore sufficient given the statutory range.

Salmanov lodged two constitutional complaints in March 2015 against the 10 December 2014 decision, alleging violations of personal liberty, fair trial and the presumption of innocence (Article 5 §§ 1 (c), 3 and 4 ECHR and Article 17 of the Constitution). He complained of 105-day delay and an arbitrary flight-risk assessment, seeking quashing, remittal, release and €8 000 just satisfaction. The Constitutional Court admitted only the Article 5 § 4 / Article 17 claims, declaring the remainder inadmissible on the ground that Article 5 §§ 1 (c) and 3 applied solely to initial detention.

On 3 February 2016 it found a violation of Article 17 §§ 1, 2 and 5 arising from the Supreme Court’s delay and decision. Repeated file transfers after 27 November were self-serving; the appeal could have been decided before the 3 December hearing, and the delay allowed the conviction to alter the factual basis to the applicant’s detriment. Severity of sentence alone could not justify detention under Article 71 § 1 (a); the additional reasons given were “tendentious and even illusory.” The Article 5 § 4 complaint was dismissed because, by the time of the constitutional application, a (non-final) conviction existed, so protection should have been sought under Article 5 § 1 (a). The finding of a violation was held sufficient redress; the just-satisfaction claim was unsubstantiated. The Supreme Court later upheld the conviction, which became final on 28 April 2015.

These facts underpin the Strasbourg complaints of arbitrary detention ordered after the first-instance conviction (Article 5 § 1) and the absence of an enforceable right to compensation (Article 5 § 5).

The case concerns Alexander Salmanov, a Slovak national born in 1986, who was remanded in detention on 23 April 2013 pending trial on a bribery charge. Detention was initially based on risks of interfering with justice and further criminal activity under Article 71 § 1 (b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP); the latter ground was later dropped. He was indicted on 25 September 2013 before the Specialised Criminal Court (SCC).

On 25/29 September 2014, Salmanov applied for release, arguing that detention was no longer justified given its length and other factors. On 11 November 2014, the SCC ordered his release. The prosecution immediately lodged an interlocutory appeal, preventing the order from becoming final, so he remained detained. The SCC rescheduled merits hearings for 28 November and 3 December 2014. The file was sent to the Supreme Court on 14 November 2014. Prosecution reasons followed on 19 and 21 November, with defence observations by 25 November.

On 27 November 2014, without ruling on the appeal, the Supreme Court returned the file to the SCC to avoid disrupting the scheduled hearing, instructing its return after any merits judgment. The SCC convicted Salmanov on 3 December 2014 and sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment. The file was then returned to the Supreme Court, which on 10 December 2014 quashed the SCC’s release order. It agreed that the original grounds no longer applied but ordered continued detention under Article 71 § 1 (a) CCP for risk of absconding. Reasons included the (non-final) first-instance conviction, behavioural issues, a prior conviction and administrative offence, possession of four passports, a pending witness interview, and the potentially severe penalty.

In a 5 February 2015 decision on a further release application, a differently composed Supreme Court panel held that post-conviction detention fell under Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention but remained subject to CCP requirements until finality. It treated the applicable penalty scale (providing for at least eight years) as itself creating an absconding risk, rejecting the application.

Salmanov lodged constitutional complaints on 12 and 16 March 2015 against the 10 December 2014 decision, alleging violations of personal liberty, fair trial rights, and the presumption of innocence (relying on Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention and constitutional equivalents). He criticised 105-day delays and an arbitrary absconding assessment, seeking quashing, remittal, release, and EUR 8,000 just satisfaction. On 20 May 2015 the Constitutional Court declared the complaints admissible only under Article 5 § 4 and Article 17 §§ 1, 2 and 5 of the Constitution, finding the other Convention provisions inapplicable to this later detention stage.

On 3 February 2016 the Constitutional Court found a violation of personal liberty under the Constitution due to the Supreme Court’s delays (repeated file transfers were self-serving; it could have ruled before the 3 December conviction, which then prejudiced Salmanov) and arbitrary grounds (severity of sentence alone insufficient; other factors “tendentious and even illusory,” contrary to earlier rulings excluding absconding risk). It quashed the 10 December decision and awarded costs but no remittal (as pre-trial detention had ended) and no just satisfaction beyond the finding of a violation (the claim was insufficiently substantiated). It dismissed the Article 5 § 4 complaint, holding that post-conviction the applicant should have relied on Article 5 § 1 (a).

The conviction became final on 28 April 2015 when the Supreme Court dismissed Salmanov’s appeal. These events formed the basis of alleged Convention violations concerning the lawfulness and arbitrariness of post-conviction remand detention and the absence of an enforceable compensation right.

001-215175:
The case of Edzgveradze v. Georgia (ECtHR, 20 January 2022) centres on the applicant’s complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2 that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into her husband M.M.’s suicide, which occurred one day after he was questioned by police as a witness.

On 5 July 2013 M.M.’s friend G.M. was arrested on suspicion of possessing cannabis after a package was found near G.M.’s car at the garage where M.M. worked. M.M., who was present, accompanied officers to the station and was questioned as a witness for 81 minutes. In his statement he confirmed the package contained cannabis, that G.M. had shown it to him, and that G.M. had intended to give it to him (M.M. admitted occasional cannabis use). A subsequent drug test was negative and M.M. was released.

The following morning M.M. left home, contacted several people, and told a friend he intended to kill himself at Tbilisi Sea. The applicant, a neighbour and others searched the area. Around noon they called emergency services reporting him missing but initially omitted any mention of suicidal intent or the previous day’s questioning. Patrol officers met them, learned of the suicide risk, took the applicant to the station to record a statement (while alerting colleagues to search), and later returned to the scene. At 13:55 a passer-by found M.M. hanging from a tree; the scene inspection revealed no suspicious items.

A criminal investigation into incitement to suicide was opened the same day by the local police. It was promptly reassigned to the Ministry of Interior’s General Inspectorate (the unit overseeing police conduct) and, in September 2013, to the Investigations Department of the Chief Prosecutor’s Office after the family alleged a link between the questioning and the suicide.

Statements collected were contradictory. G.M. said neither he nor M.M. had been physically assaulted, that they had mostly remained visible to each other in an open-plan office, but that M.M. had been taken to a private office for about 40 minutes and had appeared nervous on leaving. The applicant first told investigators that M.M. had reported verbal and physical abuse to force an incriminating statement; she later recanted, saying M.M. had denied “serious violence” and that she had heard of beatings only from his colleagues. Five colleagues described M.M. as anxious that evening, claiming he had been beaten into signing the statement, yet they saw no injuries. One colleague added that on 6 July M.M. had said he “could not live with a disgraced name.” Police officers, station guards and drug-test staff uniformly denied any pressure, physical or psychological; they said M.M. had remained calm, been questioned in the open office, and left without signs of distress. Video of the entrance and forensic reports (including a private expert) found only hanging-related injuries plus a small nostril haemorrhage that an expert attributed to the suicide itself, not prior assault.

No investigative steps occurred between November 2014 and March 2016. On 25 March 2016 a prosecutor discontinued the case, concluding there was no evidence of ill-treatment, threats or degrading treatment capable of causing suicide. The applicant’s appeal was rejected because she had never been granted victim status and therefore lacked standing.

The applicant alleged that the investigation had been neither independent nor thorough: it had initially been conducted by the police themselves, had concentrated almost exclusively on the absence of physical marks while ignoring possible psychological pressure, had suffered lengthy unexplained delays, and had failed to examine the adequacy of the police response to the known suicide risk.

The case of Edzgveradze v. Georgia (Application no. 59333/16) concerned the applicant’s complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention that Georgian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the suicide of her husband, M.M., which occurred the day after police questioned him as a witness.

On 5 July 2013, M.M.’s friend G.M. was arrested on suspicion of possessing cannabis after police found a package near G.M.’s car at the garage where M.M. worked. M.M. was present and accompanied officers to the police station, where he was questioned for 81 minutes as a witness. He stated that the package contained cannabis, which G.M. had shown him before discarding it upon seeing police, and that G.M. had intended to give it to him, as M.M. occasionally used cannabis. M.M. then underwent a negative drug test and was released.

The next day, 6 July 2013, M.M. left home early, contacted the applicant and others, and revealed suicidal intentions at the Tbilisi Sea to a friend. The applicant and others searched the area. Around noon, they called emergency services, reporting him missing (without initially mentioning suicide or the prior questioning). Patrol officers later learned of his suicidal thoughts, took the applicant to a station to record her statement (citing potential crime indications), and arranged a search. At 1:55 p.m., a passer-by found M.M.’s body hanging from a tree near the shore. Scene inspection revealed no suspicious items.

An investigation into suspected incitement to suicide (Criminal Code Article 115) opened that day at the local police station with territorial jurisdiction. The applicant alleged M.M. had told her of verbal and physical abuse at the station to force an incriminating statement, though she later clarified he denied “serious violence” and that she had heard of abuse from colleagues. She stated he had no psychological, material, or other issues that could explain suicide. G.M. (questioned 7 July) reported no physical violence, that M.M. was visible in an open-space office most of the time but taken out for ~40 minutes (G.M. himself for ~20 minutes, during which he was pressured to confess), that M.M. seemed nervous afterward, and that he doubted M.M.’s statement was voluntary.

Forensic reports (9 July private expert; 12 July National Forensic Bureau) found neck injuries consistent with hanging as the cause of death, plus a small left-nostril haemorrhage possibly inflicted hours before or during the act; no other injuries indicating beating. Experts excluded ill-treatment as the cause of the bruise.

On 9 July, the case transferred to the Ministry of Interior’s General Inspectorate (overseeing police lawfulness) due to “circumstances revealed” and the case’s nature, without referencing the prior questioning. Police officers involved (questioned 11–13 July) stated M.M. went voluntarily, remained calm, was questioned in the open-space office with G.M. present, faced no physical or psychological pressure, and left freely. Guards, entrance video, and drug-test personnel confirmed no visible injuries or distress. Colleagues (questioned December 2013) reported M.M. returned anxious, claiming police beat him to force the statement (no visible injuries); one said M.M. could not live with a “disgraced” name after testifying against his friend and had attempted drowning before hanging.

The case of Edzgveradze v. Georgia (Application no. 59333/16) concerns the applicant Zizi Edzgveradze’s complaint under Article 2 of the Convention that Georgian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the suicide of her husband, M.M., on 6 July 2013, the day after he was questioned by police as a witness.

On 5 July 2013, M.M.’s friend G.M. was arrested on suspicion of cannabis possession after police found a package near G.M.’s car at the garage where M.M. worked. M.M., present at the scene, accompanied officers to the police station and was questioned as a witness for 1 hour 21 minutes. He stated that G.M. had shown him the cannabis and discarded it upon seeing police, intending it for M.M. (an occasional user). A subsequent drug test on M.M. was negative, and he was released.

The next morning, M.M. left home early and contacted the applicant and others, revealing suicidal intentions at Tbilisi Sea (an artificial lake). The applicant, a neighbour (M.P.), and friends searched for him. Around noon they called emergency services, initially omitting mention of suicide or the prior police questioning. Patrol officers met them, learned of the suicide risk, took the applicant to the station to record a statement (citing indications of a potential crime), and alerted colleagues to search the area. At 1:55 p.m. a passer-by found M.M.’s body hanging from a tree near the shore. Scene inspection revealed no suspicious items; the body was transferred for forensic examination.

An investigation into suspected incitement to suicide was opened the same day by the territorially competent police station. It was soon reassigned first to the Ministry of Interior’s General Inspectorate (overseeing police lawfulness) and later, in September 2013, to the Chief Prosecutor’s Office Investigations Department after the family alleged a link to the questioning.

Witness statements were mixed. G.M. reported no physical violence; M.M. had been visible in an open-plan office for most of the time but was taken to a private office for about 40 minutes, returning without visible injury though appearing nervous; G.M. later doubted the statement was voluntary. The applicant initially claimed M.M. had reported verbal and physical abuse to force an incriminating statement, but later said he denied “serious violence” and that she had heard of beatings from colleagues. She noted M.M. had no prior psychological or material problems. Colleagues stated M.M. returned anxious on 5 July, claiming he had been beaten into signing against G.M. (no visible injuries); he told one he could not live with a “disgraced” name after betraying a friend and had already attempted drowning. A neighbour reported M.M. said he had given the statement because of covert recordings. Police officers involved in the arrest and questioning uniformly denied any pressure (physical or psychological), stating M.M. remained calm and stayed in the open office (though one officer briefly “talked to” him while documents were drafted). Guards, entrance video, and drug-test personnel confirmed M.M. left calmly without distress or injury. Forensic reports identified neck injuries consistent with hanging and a small nostril haemorrhage (possibly contemporaneous with death, not indicative of beating).

The investigation was inactive from late 2014 until March 2016, when it was closed with a finding of no crime. The prosecutor relied on officers’ and G.M.’s accounts, the absence of physical injuries, and the applicant’s inconsistent statements, concluding there was no ill-treatment, threats, or degrading treatment that could have caused the suicide. Psychological pressure was not separately addressed. The applicant’s appeal against closure was rejected because she held only witness (not victim) status and thus lacked standing.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 2 procedural violation: questions of investigative independence (initial Interior Ministry involvement despite police being implicated), delays, thoroughness (focus on physical rather than psychological factors, unexamined private-office period and statement inconsistencies), family participation, and the police response to the imminent suicide risk on 6 July.

The case of Drača v. Croatia (Application no. 55724/19) concerns a complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Milan Drača, a Croatian national born in 1975, alleged that criminal proceedings against him were unfair because he was not invited to attend the session of the appellate court, thereby denying him the opportunity to present his defence in person.

On 16 May 2014, the Zadar Municipal State Attorney’s Office indicted Drača in the Zadar Municipal Court for threatening a public official under section 139(2) and (3) of the Criminal Code. The charge arose from text messages sent to S.Z., a county prefect, in January 2014. Drača, who had previously worked at a county-owned museum, sent messages seeking reinstatement to his former position. One message, sent on 18 January 2014, stated that he was capable of making S.Z.’s life hell and even of “mercifully and quickly breaking [his] neck.” S.Z. reported the messages to the police, stating they had distressed and scared him.

Drača represented himself throughout. The trial court heard testimony from S.Z. and Drača, examined material evidence (including medical records and mobile phone reports), and obtained a psychiatric expert report. The report concluded that Drača’s ability to understand and control his actions was reduced by a personality disorder and alcohol-related illness, though he was not acutely intoxicated at the time. Drača testified that the message was an ironic, cynical response to S.Z. having reported him to the police the previous day, sent in a private capacity rather than targeting S.Z.’s official role. He argued S.Z. could not have felt intimidated, as no protective measures were taken, and he apologised.

On 13 April 2017, the Zadar Municipal Court convicted Drača and imposed a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years. It found that the message was sent to S.Z. in his official capacity, was objectively capable of causing fear, and that Drača’s claimed lack of intent was legally irrelevant. Mitigating factors included his reduced criminal liability, lack of prior convictions, and apologies.

Drača appealed to the Split County Court on 1 June 2017, denying commission of the offence and arguing that the trial court had incorrectly established the facts and applied the law. He contended the message was sent privately (as shown by its content), so it did not constitute an offence against a public official; that S.Z.’s statement that he did not wish to punish anyone undermined the prosecutor’s standing; that S.Z. reported him only later out of revenge after an inspection at the museum; and that the sentence was excessively severe given the single message, his apology, subsequent good behaviour, cessation of alcohol use, and the lengthy proceedings already endured. He did not request to attend the appeal hearing.

The prosecutor replied on 7 June 2017, seeking dismissal of the appeal. The prosecutor argued that prosecution did not depend on the victim’s wishes, that S.Z. had initially tolerated earlier messages but the later one demonstrated persistent disrespect for his official status, that the psychiatric report confirmed no severe intoxication, and that the sentence was already mild (the legal minimum) with no possibility of forgoing a sanction.

On 16 January 2018, the Split County Court held a session without notifying or inviting the parties and upheld the conviction and sentence. It found the facts correctly established and the offence proven, and deemed the suspended sentence appropriate as the legal minimum, taking account of all mitigating circumstances and serving deterrent purposes. No reasons were given for not inviting Drača.

Drača lodged a constitutional complaint on 13 March 2018, arguing that the appellate court had failed to address his arguments properly and should have invited him so he could respond to the prosecutor’s reply. On 3 April 2019, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, noting that Drača had not requested notification of the session and that the panel could have invited him of its own motion only if his presence was deemed useful.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violation of the right to a fair hearing, specifically the right to defend oneself in person before the appellate court when challenging both the factual and legal basis of the conviction and sentence.

The case of D’Amico v. Italy (Application no. 46586/14) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that Italian legislation enacted during pending court proceedings retrospectively determined the substance of a dispute over a survivor’s pension, thereby violating the applicant’s right to a fair hearing.

The applicant, Immacolata Filomena D’Amico (born 1938), is the widow of A.C., a public-sector employee who retired on 1 January 1990. His pension included a special supplementary allowance (indennità integrativa speciale, or IIS), a cost-of-living adjustment treated as an independent element separate from the core pension. Unlike private-sector pensions, which were calculated on an all-inclusive basis, public-sector pensions consisted of a fixed salary component plus ancillary allowances such as the IIS paid in full. Consequently, a public-sector survivor’s pension was computed as a percentage of only the fixed element, with ancillary allowances remaining intact.

From 1994 the Italian legislature sought to harmonise public- and private-sector pension rules. Law no. 724/1994 introduced an all-inclusive calculation for public-sector pensions that incorporated the IIS, but section 15(5) expressly preserved existing arrangements for pensions already in payment, including A.C.’s. Law no. 335/1995 subsequently extended private-sector survivor-pension rules to the public sector without expressly repealing the 1994 preservation clause.

A.C. died on 1 April 2002. From 1 May 2002 the applicant received a survivor’s pension equal to 60 per cent of her late husband’s overall pension, with the IIS therefore paid only as a percentage rather than in full. On 22 July 2005 she sued the National Public Service Social Security Institute (INPDAP, later absorbed by INPS) before the Basilicata Court of Auditors, arguing that she remained entitled to the full IIS under the 1994 preservation provision.

On 2 April 2007 the Basilicata Court of Auditors upheld her claim. It relied on a 2002 ruling of the Joint Sections of the Court of Auditors (judgment no. 8/QM) which had held that Law no. 335/1995 did not repeal section 15(5) of the 1994 law; the new all-inclusive method therefore applied only to direct pensions commencing after 1 January 1995. Because A.C. had retired in 1990, the applicant was entitled to the full IIS.

While the INPDAP’s appeal was pending before the Central Section of the Court of Auditors, Law no. 296/2006 entered into force on 1 January 2007. Section 1(774) supplied an “authentic interpretation” of the 1995 law, declaring that for any survivor’s pension commencing after that law’s entry into force the IIS must be paid only as a percentage, irrespective of the date the original pension had begun. Section 1(775) excluded from the new interpretation only those pensions already fixed by final judicial decision. On 21 October 2013 the appellate court applied the 2006 law, reversed the first-instance judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim.

The Italian Constitutional Court later upheld the 2006 law as a permissible authentic interpretation that selected one of several possible readings of the 1995 text, pursued legitimate aims of expenditure control and inter-sectoral harmonisation, and did not unreasonably interfere with acquired rights.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s allegation that the legislature intervened directly in pending litigation, substituting its own preferred interpretation for that previously adopted by the courts and thereby depriving her of a fair determination of her civil rights.

The case of Zakharova and Others v. Russia (Application no. 12736/10) concerns three employees of a municipal Youth Creativity Centre in Ostrov, Pskov Region—Yekaterina Zakharova, Lina Krauze and Svetlana Andreyeva—who alleged discrimination on grounds of trade-union membership and activity. The primary union belonged to a district organisation that later clashed with the regional education-and-science trade union. In January 2008 the district union was liquidated by arrangement between the local education department and the regional union, and the primary union was pressured to affiliate directly with the latter.

The applicants instead sought affiliation with an alternative regional culture-workers’ union, which rejected them. On 21 March 2008 they therefore established an independent trade union at the Centre, electing Krauze chair and the other two deputy chairs. The independent union later joined a nationwide association of trade unions (SOCPROF). From early 2008 the Centre began reducing the applicants’ working hours and salaries, citing under-funding. Orders of 19 March and 17 April 2008 (the first later revoked) implemented these cuts. On 26 May 2008 the head of the district education department met Zakharova and Krauze and proposed that they either resign or leave SOCPROF and join the official regional union. The independent union complained to the prosecutor about alleged unlawful liquidation of the former district union, discrimination, labour-rights violations and financial irregularities.

On 1 September 2008 the Centre again reduced their hours and announced that their posts would be abolished on 6 November. The independent union requested revocation of that order. On 5 November 2008, while collective-agreement negotiations were under way, the three applicants were dismissed for staff redundancy. No other employees were dismissed.

On 2 December 2008 they sued the Centre, seeking reinstatement, unpaid wages, non-pecuniary damages and a finding that the employer’s conduct constituted discrimination on account of their union activity. On 26 March 2009 the Ostrov Town Court allowed the claims. It held the November dismissals unlawful because the independent union had not been consulted, awarded back-pay (approximately EUR 600–900 each) and EUR 220 each for non-pecuniary damage, and found the repeated dismissals (two of which had already been quashed) discriminatory, including on grounds of membership of a public association. The court recalled that, under Supreme Court guidance, the employer bore the burden of proving lawful grounds and procedural compliance.

On 7 July 2009 the Pskov Regional Court upheld the finding of procedural unlawfulness and the monetary awards (already enforced) but quashed the discrimination ruling, stating that the case file contained no evidence that union membership had been the reason for dismissal. The applicants were reinstated in March 2009 and thereafter continued working at the Centre; Zakharova later became its director.

The applicants complained to the European Court that the domestic courts had failed to provide effective judicial protection against anti-union discrimination, contrary to Article 14 taken together with Article 11 of the Convention. They argued that they had established a prima-facie case (repeated, targeted dismissals coinciding with union organising, an explicit invitation to leave their union, and the absence of any other redundancies) which should have shifted the burden of proof onto the employer—an obligation the Regional Court had ignored.

The applicants remained employed; Zakharova later became Centre director.

The Strasbourg Court focused on the appeal court’s failure, despite a clear prima facie case (repeated, targeted measures against union leaders alone, timing during negotiations, and an official’s explicit suggestion to leave the union), to shift the burden of proof onto the employer or to examine the discrimination claim with the required rigour. Domestic law prohibited discrimination on union grounds and provided for judicial protection, yet the courts did not apply those guarantees effectively.
001-216352:
**Case Summary: Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 13472/18, ECHR Second Section, 22 March 2022)**

Serghei Cosovan (born 1971), a Moldovan businessman and opposition local councillor, was arrested on 26 September 2017 on suspicion of abuse of office and fraud involving false promises of kiosk ownership in exchange for payments. On 29 September 2017, a court ordered 30 days’ pre-trial detention, citing reasonable suspicion of a particularly serious offence (punishable by up to 15 years), complexity of the investigation, and risks of absconding, reoffending or obstructing justice. Appeals were dismissed on similar grounds. Detention was repeatedly extended using essentially identical reasoning, despite Cosovan’s arguments that he had known of related investigations since 2014, had always appeared when summoned, and posed no proven risks (his passport could be seized).

Cosovan suffered from long-standing hepatitis C leading to decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) with complications including severe hypersplenism, ascites, and oesophageal varices. Diagnosed upon arrest, his condition was confirmed as terminal-stage by multiple medical councils and experts. Prison Hospital No. 16 (where he spent much of his detention) lacked a hepatologist, intensive-care facilities, accreditation as a medical institution, and contracts for specialised transplant care. Treatment fell short of national protocols: prescribed albumin and plasma transfusions were administered only sporadically and late; a hepatologist consultation recommended in March 2018 was delayed; transfer to a civilian hospital for inpatient specialised care was not promptly effected despite recommendations and haemorrhage risks. Efforts to place him on a liver-transplant waiting list stalled over additional tests. Cosovan and his lawyers repeatedly complained of incomplete records, unaddressed refusals of treatment, and lack of specialist oversight (a family doctor managed his care). The Ombudsman, after a 2018 visit, highlighted worsening health and urgent need for specialist intervention. Cosovan underwent emergency surgery in January 2018 for variceal haemorrhage and multiple civilian-hospital transfers, but returned to prison facilities.

On 24 April 2018 an investigating judge replaced detention with house arrest, finding no evidence of flight or interference risks, noting that a long sentence alone could not justify detention, and emphasising the terminal illness as a ground for exemption from sentence (absurd, in the judge’s view, to deny this to a pre-trial detainee). Cosovan was released but immediately re-arrested the same day under a new prosecution (opened 1 March 2018) concerning other alleged victims from the same scheme. A different judge ordered fresh 30-day detention without referring to the house-arrest order, which was later annulled. Detention continued.

In July 2018 Cosovan was convicted of fraud (damage of €8,000) and sentenced to seven years; the conviction was twice quashed and remitted. A 2018 Council for the Prevention and Elimination of Discrimination found that denying seriously ill pre-trial detainees the release available to convicted prisoners constituted discrimination. Prison authorities and an expert later confirmed the illness met statutory criteria for exemption from sentence (decompensated cirrhosis with hypersplenism; progressive deterioration and limited life expectancy). After further delays, a court ordered release on health grounds in November 2019. Cosovan died in a civilian hospital on 25 March 2021.

The alleged violations centre on inadequate medical care amounting to degrading treatment (Article 3) for a terminally ill detainee and the incompatibility of continued detention with that condition, plus insufficiently reasoned and prolonged pre-trial detention (Article 5 § 3) achieved in part by splitting investigations.
