The case of Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 13472/18) concerns alleged violations of Article 3 ECHR (inadequate medical care and detention incompatible with a terminal illness) and Article 5 § 3 (unjustified pre-trial detention). Serghei Cosovan, a businessman and opposition local councillor, was arrested on 26 September 2017 for suspected fraud and abuse of office. On 29 September 2017 the Chișinău Court ordered 30 days’ pre-trial detention, citing reasonable suspicion of a particularly serious offence (up to 15 years’ imprisonment) and risks of absconding, reoffending or obstructing the investigation. Extensions relied on essentially identical generic grounds, despite the applicant’s unchallenged record of appearing when summoned since the investigation began in 2014 and the absence of concrete evidence of any risk.

Cosovan already suffered from chronic hepatitis C that had progressed to decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) with hypersplenism and other complications. Medical councils repeatedly confirmed the diagnosis as terminal, prescribed regular albumin and plasma transfusions, specialist hepatology care and evaluation for liver transplant, and noted a continuously worsening condition with limited life expectancy. Prison Hospital No. 16 lacked a hepatologist, intensive-care facilities, proper accreditation and transplant contracts. Prescribed treatments were administered irregularly or not at all; specialist consultations and the QuantiFERON test needed for the transplant waiting list were delayed for weeks or months. The Ombudsman and the Council for the Prevention of Discrimination documented these shortcomings and found that the legal framework (Criminal Code Art. 95(2) and Ministry of Justice Order 331) discriminated against pre-trial detainees by reserving release on medical grounds exclusively to convicted prisoners.

On 24 April 2018 an investigating judge replaced detention with house arrest, holding that continued imprisonment of a terminally ill person would amount to torture and that the public-order rationale was insufficient. Cosovan was immediately re-arrested on newly severed charges arising from the same events; a fresh detention order was issued without reference to the house-arrest decision, which was later annulled. He was convicted of fraud in July 2018 (seven years) and, after two remittals, again in 2019. Expert reports of 2018–2019 confirmed that his illness featured on the statutory list of conditions warranting exemption from sentence and that his health was deteriorating. The prison administration nevertheless delayed submitting the required release request until July 2019. Although a court ordered release on 18 November 2019, Cosovan remained in a succession of prisons and civilian hospitals until his death on 25 March 2021.

These facts form the basis of the complaints that the authorities failed in their positive obligation to provide equivalent medical care, that detention itself became incompatible with his terminal condition, and that the domestic courts never supplied relevant and sufficient reasons for prolonged pre-trial detention, using an artificial splitting of the investigation to circumvent earlier release decisions.

The applicant, Serghei Cosovan (born 1971, died 25 March 2021), a Moldovan businessman and opposition local councillor, was arrested on 26 September 2017 on suspicion of abuse of office and fraud involving payments for promised metal kiosks. On 29 September 2017 the Chișinău Court ordered 30 days’ pre-trial detention, citing lawful investigation start, reasonable suspicion of a particularly serious offence (up to 15 years’ imprisonment), and risks of absconding, reoffending or obstructing justice. Appeals were dismissed on 16 October 2017; the Court of Appeal repeated these grounds, added case complexity, and asserted that medical treatment was available in detention or via hospital transfer.

Detention was extended repeatedly on essentially identical reasoning. Lawyers noted the applicant had been aware of the probe since 2014 (including a prior 72-hour arrest) yet had always appeared when summoned and had been arrested only after responding to a summons. On 24 April 2018 an investigating judge substituted house arrest, finding no evidence of flight or witness-interference risks, observing that a lengthy sentence alone could not justify detention, and stressing the applicant’s terminal-stage illness (confirmed by the National Prisons Administration as a ground for exemption from sentence). Continued detention would expose him to suffering potentially amounting to torture; public-order concerns (victim protests) were insufficient given his condition.

Upon release the applicant was immediately re-arrested on a newly opened file (1 March 2018) concerning other alleged victims of the same scheme; a fresh 30-day detention order followed on 27 April 2018 without reference to the house-arrest decision, which was later annulled. He was convicted of fraud (EUR 8 000 damage) on 11 July 2018 and sentenced to seven years; the conviction was twice quashed and remitted. On 18 November 2019 a court granted release on health grounds after an expert report confirmed the illness (hepatic cirrhosis) was listed as warranting exemption, was deteriorating, and entailed limited life expectancy. The applicant died in hospital on 25 March 2021.

He suffered from hepatitis-C decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) with hypersplenism and other complications, already present before arrest. Prison doctors confirmed the diagnosis; a 27 March 2018 medical council prescribed albumin and plasma transfusions, hepatologist review and possible liver-transplant assessment. Only partial transfusions were given; specialist consultations and transplant-list inclusion were delayed. Prison hospital no. 16 lacked a hepatologist, resuscitation facilities and medical accreditation. Transfers to civilian hospitals occurred only after complications (oesophageal haemorrhage, January 2018) or complaints; even then, treatment protocols were incompletely followed and refusals of tests or medication were recorded without independent review. The Ombudsman, lawyers and later the Council for the Prevention and Elimination of Discrimination highlighted inadequate, non-equivalent care, delays, and the statutory distinction that barred pre-trial detainees (unlike convicted prisoners) from illness-based release—an inequality later found discriminatory.

These facts underpin the complaints of degrading treatment through inadequate medical care incompatible with a terminal condition and of insufficiently reasoned, repeatedly extended pre-trial detention achieved in part by splitting the investigation.
001-215716:
The case of A and B v. Georgia (Application no. 73975/16) concerns complaints by C’s mother (first applicant) and son (second applicant) that Georgian authorities failed to protect C from gender-based domestic violence culminating in her murder by her partner D, a serving police officer, and failed to investigate the authorities’ inadequate response, in violation of Articles 2 and 14 of the Convention.

In 2011, when C was 17, D (then 22) kidnapped her for marriage. They cohabited from December 2011 until June 2012, when the pregnant C fled his jealousy-driven physical and psychological abuse and returned to her parents. Thereafter D subjected C and her family to regular verbal and physical attacks, repeatedly threatening to kill them and invoking his police status and connections. The family feared reporting most incidents.

In July 2012 C reported a death threat against her mother; police did not respond. On 31 August 2013 D beat C at her parents’ home over child-support payments. Three patrol officers who were D’s colleagues interviewed the visibly injured C in his presence, described wife-beating as commonplace, allowed him to mock and shout at her, and recorded only a “minor family altercation.” They overheard D threaten to kill C if she refused to sign their inaccurate report, then warned her not to contact them again without a “valid reason.” C immediately complained to prosecutors about D’s ongoing violence (including threats to abduct their child) and the officers’ negligence, stressing she could not trust the police because D was one of them. Prosecutors interviewed the parties, accepted D’s denial and a written undertaking that he would cease abuse, and declined to open a criminal investigation.

In July 2014 C reported two further public assaults to the Ministry of Interior’s General Inspectorate. Multiple witnesses had already confirmed to police and prosecutors that, between 2011 and 2014, D had brandished his service pistol at least seven times, threatened false charges against C’s relatives, and boasted that he need not fear the law because he was part of it. D was nevertheless promoted to senior lieutenant on 20 July 2014. On 25 July, immediately after C’s Inspectorate interview in which she reiterated systematic harassment, D stalked her, argued with her in a park and shot her five times in the chest and stomach with his service pistol, killing her instantly.

D was convicted of premeditated murder of a family member and sentenced to 11 years’ imprisonment; the judgment contained no finding of gender-based discrimination. In January 2015 the first applicant requested a criminal investigation into the police officers’ and prosecutors’ failures, alleging possible gender discrimination. An inquiry into the three 2013 officers was opened; they claimed the incident was non-violent. Witnesses contradicted them. No charges were brought and no investigation was opened into the prosecutors. A parallel civil claim resulted in a 2015 Tbilisi City Court judgment (final in 2017) holding that the authorities’ inaction—failure to interview witnesses properly, issue a restraining order, restrict D’s pistol, or investigate the violence—was causally linked to C’s death and breached the duty to combat gender-based discrimination. Partial compensation of approximately €7,000 was awarded.

These facts illustrate the authorities’ passive and even accommodating stance toward a police officer’s protracted, well-documented violence against his former partner, which enabled the murder and left the subsequent investigation of official failings incomplete.

The case of A and B v. Georgia (ECtHR, Application no. 73975/16, judgment of 10 February 2022) concerns the killing of C (born 1994) by her partner D, a police officer and father of the second applicant (B, born 2013). The first applicant (A, C’s mother) and B alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life, substantive and procedural limbs) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the ECHR. They claimed the Georgian authorities failed to protect C from prolonged gender-based domestic violence that culminated in her murder, and then failed to investigate the law-enforcement response adequately. The Court highlighted the authorities’ passive and accommodating attitudes toward violence against women.

In 2011, when C was 17, D (then 22) kidnapped her for marriage. Under threat, she cohabited with him in an unregistered relationship from December 2011 until June 2012, when she returned to her parents’ home two months pregnant, exhausted by D’s physical and psychological abuse driven by jealousy. From late 2011 onward, D regularly subjected C and her family to verbal and physical violence, including death threats, while invoking his police status and connections. The family feared reporting most incidents but did report some of the most serious ones.

In July 2012 C reported D’s threat to kill A; police did not respond. On 31 August 2013 D beat C at her parents’ house over child support. Three patrol officers who were D’s colleagues interviewed her in his presence, minimized the violence as a “minor family altercation,” failed to stop D from mocking and threatening her, and warned her against wasting police time. D forced her to sign their inaccurate report. That same day C lodged a criminal complaint with the public prosecutor against both D and the officers, detailing ongoing harassment, death threats and a threat to abduct their child, and explaining she could not trust the police because D was an officer. Prosecutors interviewed the parties, accepted D’s and one officer’s denials, took a written undertaking from D that he would not reoffend, and declined to open a criminal investigation.

C later complained to the General Inspectorate of the Ministry of the Interior about two public assaults by D in early July 2014. Multiple witnesses confirmed that between 2011 and 2014 D had repeatedly flaunted his service pistol, threatened false charges against C’s relatives, and boasted that he was immune from the law because he was part of it; this information reached both police and prosecutors. D was nevertheless promoted to senior lieutenant on 20 July 2014.

On 25 July 2014, immediately after C told the Inspectorate of systematic abuse (while asking that D not be treated too harshly because he was her child’s father), D stalked her, argued with her in a public park and shot her five times at close range with his service pistol, killing her instantly.

D was convicted in 2015 of the premeditated murder of a family member and sentenced to 11 years’ imprisonment; the judgment made no finding of gender-based discrimination. In parallel, A sought a criminal investigation into the alleged negligence of police and prosecutors, arguing that their inaction was influenced by gender stereotypes. An investigation was opened only into the police officers and remained pending without charges or victim status being granted to A; her complaints against prosecutors went unanswered. In a 2015 civil judgment (final in 2017) a domestic court awarded modest compensation, finding a causal link between the authorities’ inactivity and C’s death, their failure to issue a restraining order or restrict D’s access to his firearm, and their disregard of the obligation to respond effectively to gender-based violence.

These facts formed the core of the applicants’ claims that the State had breached its positive obligations under Article 2, taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14.

The case of A and B v. Georgia (ECtHR, 10 February 2022) concerns the 25 July 2014 murder of C (born 1994) by her former partner D, a police officer and father of the second applicant (B, born 2013). The first applicant (A) is C’s mother. The applicants alleged violations of Article 2 (right to life, substantive and procedural limbs) taken with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention, arguing that the Georgian authorities failed to protect C from gender-based domestic violence despite known risks and failed to investigate that failure adequately, reflecting a pattern of official passivity toward violence against women.

In 2011, when C was 17, D (then 22 and a serving police officer) kidnapped her for marriage. They cohabited from December 2011 until June 2012, when C, two months pregnant, fled to her parents amid physical and psychological abuse driven by D’s jealousy. From late 2011 onward D subjected C and her family to repeated verbal and physical violence, death threats (invoking his police status and connections), and intimidation, including flaunting his service pistol on at least seven occasions and threatening false charges against C’s relatives. Fear of D’s position meant most incidents went unreported, though some were notified to police.

In July 2012 C reported D’s threats to kill A; police did not respond. On 31 August 2013 D beat C at her parents’ home over child-support payments. Three patrol officers—D’s colleagues and acquaintances—attended and interviewed C in D’s presence. One officer remarked that wife-beating was commonplace and unimportant. D interrupted, mocked C and shouted at her without intervention. The officers produced a report that minimised the violence as “a minor family altercation,” which D forced C to sign while threatening to kill her (overheard by the officers). An officer then warned C not to call police again without “valid reason” or face a fine. D left with the officers in the same car.

That same day C lodged a criminal complaint with the public prosecutor against both D (for ongoing abuse, death threats and possible child abduction) and the three officers (for failing to act diligently). She explained she could not trust the police because D was an officer. On 4 September 2013 the prosecutor interviewed C, D and one officer; D and the officer denied any ill-treatment. D gave a written undertaking not to reoffend. Satisfied, the prosecutor declined to open a criminal investigation.

C later reported two further public assaults by D (3 and 5 July 2014) to the Interior Ministry’s General Inspectorate. Witnesses independently confirmed D’s systematic use of his official position. On 20 July 2014 D was promoted to senior lieutenant. On 25 July 2014, immediately after C’s Inspectorate interview (in which she again described systematic harassment but asked that D not be treated too harshly because he was the child’s father), D stalked her, argued with her in a public park and shot her five times at close range with his service pistol, killing her instantly.

D was convicted of premeditated murder of a family member and sentenced to 11 years’ imprisonment; an insanity defence based on “pathological jealousy” was rejected. The judgment made no reference to gender-based discrimination as an aggravating factor (available under the Criminal Code since 2012).

In January 2015 the applicants complained to the Chief Public Prosecutor that police and prosecutors had failed to protect C and that this neglect was influenced by gender discrimination. An investigation into the 31 August 2013 officers was opened; they claimed the incident was non-violent, while multiple witnesses described serious violence. No charges were brought and victim status was refused. No investigation was opened into the prosecutors. A parallel civil claim against the Ministry of the Interior and Prosecutor’s Office succeeded in part: the Tbilisi City Court found a causal link between the authorities’ inaction (failure to interview witnesses, issue a restraining order or restrict D’s access to his pistol) and C’s death, held that the State had breached its duty to respond promptly to discrimination, and awarded modest non-pecuniary damages. The judgment became final in 2017.

These facts establish that, despite repeated, documented complaints spanning years and D’s known status as an armed police officer, the authorities displayed a dismissive and even accommodating attitude, leaving C unprotected and allowing the violence to culminate in her murder. The subsequent investigation into official failings remained incomplete and unaccountable.
001-216356:
The applicant, journalist Ganimat Zayidov (former editor of opposition newspaper Azadlıq), was detained in Baku Detention Facility No. 1 from November 2007 to May 2008 on hooliganism charges, later convicted to four years’ imprisonment (pardoned 2010). While detained, he wrote a 278-page journalistic manuscript reflecting his detention experiences, cellmates’ stories of offences and treatment by authorities, prison life and “criminal world” rules since Soviet times, and criticisms of the political regime (including alleged corruption, based on published sources).

By late April 2008, 203 pages existed. The applicant informed officials of his intent to send it to family for publication; they took the pages, orally promising return to family/lawyer (no seizure record shown to him). Official records instead noted his request to “secretly send” it to Azadlıq, leading to seizure (he refused to sign). Remaining 75 pages (written in May) were found hidden and seized on 22 May 2008 during transfer to prison (again, he refused to sign the record).

Deputy-head reports (8 and 30 May 2008) described the content as containing “indecent and insulting statements about the republic’s leadership [and officials], insulting words directed at staff, and information about the detention facility prohibited from disclosure.” No passages were quoted. On 14 July 2008 the 278 pages were burned pursuant to a decision citing the same (unquoted) findings and Rule 110 of the 2004 Internal Disciplinary Rules (allowing destruction of prisoners’ letters with “indecent content” or undisclosable facility information). The applicant and lawyers learned of the records, reports and destruction only during later proceedings.

On 11 July 2008 (pre-destruction) a lawyer filed a civil claim against the Penal Service and facility seeking a finding of unlawful seizure (breaching freedom of expression) and return of the manuscript. An injunction request to prevent destruction was refused (no evidence of the manuscript’s existence). After destruction, the claim was amended (relying on the Constitution, copyright/intellectual-property law, Article 10 ECHR and Protocol 1 Article 1) to seek damages (ultimately AZN 100,000 pecuniary + AZN 1,000,000 non-pecuniary) for breaches of intellectual-property rights and freedom of (political) expression. The manuscript was a book, not correspondence, and contained no “indecent” statements.

First-instance hearings (Sabail District Court, from August 2008) occurred without the imprisoned applicant’s presence (requests refused without reasons; unclear if he was personally summoned). Requests to call the facility head (who allegedly took the manuscript under false promises) and cellmates (who witnessed writing and knew contents) as witnesses were also refused without reasons. The court heard officials (who reiterated unquoted reports, one adding unquoted claims of “illegal expressions” inciting war), plus the applicant’s wife and Azadlıq’s editor (who confirmed the book’s existence from the applicant’s statements). On 6 October 2008 the claim was dismissed: the manuscript was a “letter” (as the applicant wished to “send” it), seizure/destruction lawful under Rules 110 and 182, no rights violations. Wife/editor testimony was “unreliable” (hearsay).

The applicant appealed, arguing he first learned of records/destruction during first-instance proceedings (hence unsigned them); his personal presence was essential (as author, to contest unquoted “inappropriate” content, as lawyers lacked first-hand knowledge); additional witnesses were needed; and courts failed to require concrete examples of prohibited content. Appeal requests for presence and witnesses were refused without reasons. On 14 January 2009 the Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, reiterating the first-instance reasoning without addressing arguments. Cassation (Supreme Court, 19 June 2009) proceeded without parties (deemed unexplained absences) and upheld the judgments without addressing complaints of absence from hearings, unreasoned witness refusals, or unreasoned decisions.

The case of Zayidov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) involves journalist Ganimat Zayidov, former editor of the opposition newspaper Azadlıq. Arrested in November 2007 on hooliganism charges, he was convicted in March 2008 and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He was held at Baku Detention Facility No. 1 from 12 November 2007 until 22 May 2008, after which he was transferred to prison. A presidential pardon in March 2010 led to his release; he later obtained political asylum in France.

While detained, Zayidov authored a 278-page manuscript in a journalistic style. It covered his detention experiences, political developments, and personal memories. The first chapter recounted cellmates' accounts of their alleged crimes, expected penalties, and treatment by authorities and courts. The second addressed criminal-world rules, prison life, and historical facts since Soviet times. The third criticized the "current political regime," including general and army-related corruption, drawing from published newspaper articles.

By late April 2008, 203 pages existed. On 27 April, Zayidov informed facility officials of the manuscript and his intent to provide it to his family for publication. Officials took the pages, with the facility head orally promising delivery to family or lawyers. Zayidov was not told of any seizure and continued writing. The remaining 75 pages were taken in May 2008 under a similar promise. He claims no seizure records were prepared or shown to him.

Official records differ: they state Zayidov asked an official to secretly send the 203 pages to Azadlıq for publication. This was refused; the pages were seized in officials' presence, and Zayidov allegedly refused to review or sign the record. A similar seizure occurred on 22 May for the remaining pages, found hidden in his belongings. Deputy-head reports of 8 and 30 May 2008 described the content as containing "indecent and insulting statements" about the republic's leadership, government officials, and facility staff, plus "prohibited" information about the facility. No excerpts were quoted. Destruction under Rule 110 of the Internal Disciplinary Rules of Penal Facilities (2004) was proposed.

On 14 July 2008, the full manuscript was burned pursuant to a facility decision citing the same unquoted reasons. Zayidov and his lawyers learned of the records, reports, and destruction decision only during later civil proceedings.

On 11 July 2008 (pre-destruction), a lawyer filed a civil claim in Sabail District Court against the Penal Service of the Ministry of Justice and the detention facility, seeking a declaration that the seizure was unlawful, return of the manuscript, and alleging a breach of freedom of expression. An injunction request to halt destruction was refused on 22 July for lack of evidence of the manuscript's existence. After destruction (confirmed 27 July), the claim was amended on 3 August, invoking constitutional, civil, copyright, and intellectual-property provisions plus Article 10 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It sought AZN 100,000 in pecuniary and AZN 1,000,000 in non-pecuniary damages, arguing the work was a publishable book (not mere correspondence) whose content stayed within permitted expression limits.

Hearings began 3 August 2008. Zayidov, then in Penal Facility No. 17, was not personally summoned. Lawyers' requests for his presence were rejected without reasons, as were requests to call the facility head (to clarify seizure circumstances) and cellmates (who had witnessed writing and knew the content). The court did hear the deputy head, four officials who signed records (repeating the reports), Zayidov's wife, and Azadlıq's then-editor. The deputy head added unquoted claims of "illegal expressions" inciting war over Nagorno-Karabakh but could not cite passages.

On 6 October 2008 the court dismissed the claim, treating the manuscript as an inmate's letter (not a book) containing prohibited information. It accepted the authorities' unquoted assessments at face value and found the seizure and destruction lawful under Rules 110 and 182, with no unjustified interference with expression or property rights. Witness statements from Zayidov's side were deemed unreliable hearsay.

Zayidov appealed, arguing he first learned of the records in court (hence had not refused to sign them), that the facility head must be heard regarding alleged false promises, and that his own presence was essential as author to contest the unspecified "inappropriate" content. Additional witnesses were needed because the four officials had only signed records without reading the manuscript. The first-instance court had failed to require concrete examples of prohibited material.

The Baku Court of Appeal, sitting on 14 January 2009 without Zayidov (his presence and extra-witness requests again rejected without reasons), dismissed the appeal by repeating the lower court's reasoning and ignoring the new arguments. The Supreme Court, examining the cassation appeal on 19 June 2009 without any parties present (claiming they had failed to appear despite notification), upheld the judgments in a brief decision that likewise failed to address complaints about absence, uncalled witnesses, or inadequate reasoning.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 10 (seizure and destruction lacking a sufficiently foreseeable legal basis and safeguards against arbitrariness) and Article 6 § 1 (unfair civil proceedings due to unexamined necessity of the applicant's presence, unreasoned refusals to hear additional witnesses, and inadequately reasoned decisions).

The case of Zayidov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) (Application no. 5386/10) concerns journalist Ganimat Zayidov, former editor of the opposition newspaper Azadlıq. Arrested in November 2007 on hooliganism charges, he was convicted in March 2008 and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment (later pardoned in 2010). From 12 November 2007 to 22 May 2008 he was held in Baku Detention Facility No. 1.

While detained, Zayidov wrote a 278-page manuscript in journalistic style. It described his experiences, cellmates’ accounts of offences and treatment by authorities, the “rules of the criminal world” since Soviet times, and alleged “crimes” of the political regime, including corruption (drawing on published newspaper sources). By late April 2008 he had completed 203 pages; the rest followed in May.

On 27 April 2008 he informed facility officials of the manuscript and his wish to give it to his family for publication. Officials took the 203 pages. Facility records (produced only later in court) stated he had asked an official to “secretly send” them to Azadlıq; the request was refused and the pages seized in the presence of officials. Zayidov was not shown or asked to sign the records at the time and continued writing. On 22 May 2008, during a search before his transfer to prison, the remaining 75 pages were found in his bag and seized under similar records that he allegedly refused to sign.

Handwritten reports by the deputy head (8 and 30 May 2008) described the content as containing “indecent and insulting statements about the republic’s leadership” and “information about the detention facility prohibited from being disclosed.” No passages were quoted. On 14 July 2008 the entire manuscript was burned pursuant to a decision citing Rule 110 of the 2004 Internal Disciplinary Rules of Penal Facilities. That rule forbids sending letters using secret symbols, of “indecent content,” or containing undisclosable facility information; such letters are destroyed after notification. Rule 182 and Annex 30 also prohibit certain documents being taken out of facilities. Zayidov and his lawyers learned of the records, reports and destruction decision only during later civil proceedings.

On 11 July 2008 (before destruction) his lawyers filed a civil claim in the Sabail District Court against the Penal Service and the facility, seeking return of the manuscript as an unlawful seizure violating freedom of expression. An injunction request was refused for lack of evidence of the manuscript’s existence. After destruction the claim was amended to seek damages (initially AZN 100,000, later raised) for breaches of intellectual-property rights, freedom of expression (including political speech) and property rights, relying on the Constitution, domestic law, Article 10 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The manuscript was a book intended for publication, not correspondence, and contained nothing “indecent.”

First-instance hearings occurred without Zayidov’s personal presence (he was then in prison); it is unclear whether he was summoned. Requests for his attendance and to call the facility head and cellmates as witnesses were rejected without reasons. Some officials and Zayidov’s wife and the then Azadlıq editor were heard. On 6 October 2008 the court dismissed the claim, treating the manuscript as inmate correspondence containing prohibited information and finding the seizure and destruction lawful under Rules 110 and 182, with no unjustified interference.

Appeals to the Baku Court of Appeal (14 January 2009) and Supreme Court (19 June 2009) likewise proceeded without Zayidov. Repeated requests for his presence and additional witnesses were rejected without reasons. The higher courts essentially reiterated the first-instance reasoning without addressing his arguments (including that officials could not quote specific prohibited passages and that he had not signed records because he had never seen them). The Code of Civil Procedure granted parties a general right to appear and to request evidence, but contained no specific modalities for detained persons in civil cases; the Code on Execution of Punishments likewise omitted any procedure for escorting convicts to civil hearings.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 10 (unlawful, unforeseeable seizure and destruction lacking safeguards against arbitrariness) and Article 6 § 1 (unfair civil proceedings through failure to consider the applicant’s presence, unreasoned witness refusals and inadequately reasoned decisions).
001-216357:
The case of Wyszyński v. Poland (Application no. 66/12) concerns a complaint by Polish national Antoni Wyszyński under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, born in 1946 and residing in Poznań, owned several flats in a building there, including flat no. 11. This flat had been occupied for years by tenant R.S., who failed to pay rent and service charges.

On 24 August 2007, the Poznań District Court ordered R.S. to vacate the flat and remove his belongings. However, it also granted R.S. the right to social housing from the Municipality of Poznań and suspended his eviction obligation until the municipality provided such housing. The judgment became final on 15 September 2007. R.S. remained in the flat until 22 June 2012, when the municipality finally offered him social housing and he moved out.

On 13 August 2008, the applicant sued the Municipality of Poznań for compensation under section 18(5) of the Act of 21 June 2001 on the protection of tenants' rights and municipal housing resources (the 2001 Act). This provision allows a flat owner to claim compensation from a municipality, via Article 417 of the Civil Code, if the municipality fails to provide social housing as required by a final court judgment, thereby causing damage through an unlawful omission in exercising public authority.

On 16 September 2009, the Poznań District Court partially granted the claim, awarding 21,971 Polish zlotys. It relied on two expert opinions assessing potential market rent: one based on the flat's current condition and another assuming future renovation (which the applicant intended). The court used the higher renovation-based figure. Both parties appealed.

On 11 May 2011, the Poznań Regional Court amended the judgment and dismissed the entire claim. It held that compensation under the relevant provision required the applicant to prove damage, its exact amount, and a causal link to the municipality's failure. Even if R.S. vacated, the applicant had not shown he would find a new tenant or receive rental income. The court noted the flat needed renovation, would not be immediately rentable, and the applicant provided no evidence of renovation duration or readiness for rental. The applicant filed a cassation appeal, citing prior successful similar claims against the same municipality, but the Supreme Court refused to examine it on 3 June 2011 (served 30 June 2011).

Relevant law includes section 18 of the 2001 Act, which requires persons occupying a flat without legal title to pay compensation equivalent to potential market rent (or, for those entitled to social housing with a suspended eviction, the amount payable under the prior legal relationship). A 2006 Supreme Court resolution clarified that such claims against municipalities are compensatory and require the owner to prove actual damage from the unauthorized occupation.

The applicant alleged that the refusal of compensation for the unauthorized occupation constituted an interference with his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The domestic courts' approach imposed requirements that were extremely difficult to meet, such as proving hypothetical future rental success and precise renovation timelines, thereby arbitrarily denying redress for the damage caused by the municipality's prolonged failure to provide social housing. This placed an excessive burden on the applicant, essentially stripping him of any practical right to compensation despite the statutory framework intended to protect property owners in such circumstances. The case highlights tensions between municipal housing obligations, tenant protections, and owners' property rights under Polish law as applied to the Convention.

The case of Wyszyński v. Poland (Application no. 66/12) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, relating to control of the use of property. The applicant, Antoni Wyszyński (born 1946, resident in Poznań), claimed that Polish courts arbitrarily dismissed his compensation claim against the Municipality of Poznań for a tenant occupying his flat without valid legal title. This, he argued, imposed an excessive burden, effectively denying him redress for damage and interfering with his peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The applicant owns several flats in one Poznań building; the dispute involves flat no. 11. Tenant R.S. had occupied it for years without paying rent or service charges. On 24 August 2007, the Poznań District Court ordered R.S. to vacate the flat and remove his belongings. At the same time, it granted R.S. entitlement to social housing from the Municipality of Poznań and suspended the eviction obligation until such housing was provided. The judgment became final on 15 September 2007. R.S. remained in occupation until 22 June 2012, when the municipality finally offered social housing and he moved out.

On 13 August 2008, the applicant sued the Municipality for compensation under section 18(5) of the Act of 21 June 2001 on the protection of tenants’ rights, municipal housing resources and Civil Code amendments. That provision entitles an owner to claim from the municipality (via Article 417 of the Civil Code) if it fails to provide court-ordered social housing. Article 417 makes public authorities liable for damage caused by unlawful acts or omissions in the exercise of public power.

On 16 September 2009 the Poznań District Court partially granted the claim and awarded 21,971 Polish zlotys. It relied on two expert opinions calculating potential open-market rental income: one based on the flat’s existing condition and a second assuming renovation (which the applicant intended to carry out). The court used the higher, renovation-based figure.

Both parties appealed. On 11 May 2011 the Poznań Regional Court reversed the award and dismissed the entire claim. It held that section 18(5) required the applicant to prove actual damage, its exact amount and a causal link. Even after R.S. left, the applicant had not shown he would find a new tenant or receive rental income. The court stressed that the flat needed renovation, would not be immediately lettable, and that the applicant had provided no evidence of renovation duration or when the property would be ready.

The applicant lodged a cassation appeal, noting that courts had previously ruled in his favour in similar proceedings against the same municipality. On 3 June 2011 the Supreme Court refused to examine it (decision served 30 June 2011).

Relevant domestic law includes section 18 of the 2001 Act: occupants without legal title must pay monthly compensation equal to market rent (or, for those awaiting social housing, the former contractual rent). Subsection (5) specifically allows the owner to claim against the municipality for its failure to provide housing. A Supreme Court resolution of 7 April 2006 (III CZP 21/06) confirmed that such claims are compensatory; the municipality is liable only if the owner proves damage resulting from the unauthorised occupation.

The alleged violation arose from the Regional Court’s imposition of proof requirements that were extremely difficult to satisfy. By demanding evidence of immediate re-letting after renovation of unspecified duration, the court effectively deprived the applicant of any realistic prospect of compensation for years of lost use caused by the municipality’s delay, placing an excessive and arbitrary burden on him.

The case of Wyszyński v. Poland (Application no. 66/12) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the Polish authorities' refusal to compensate the applicant for a tenant occupying his flat without valid legal title after a court-ordered eviction was suspended. This was alleged to violate Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, protecting the peaceful enjoyment of possessions, by imposing an excessive burden through arbitrary dismissal of his claim.

The applicant, Antoni Wyszyński (born 1946, resident in Poznań), owns several flats in one building, including flat no. 11. Tenant R.S. had occupied it for years without paying rent or service charges. On 24 August 2007, the Poznań District Court ordered R.S. to vacate the flat and remove his belongings. Simultaneously, it granted R.S. a right to social housing from the Municipality of Poznań and suspended the eviction obligation until that housing was provided. The judgment became final on 15 September 2007. R.S. remained in occupation until 22 June 2012, when the municipality offered social housing and he departed.

On 13 August 2008, the applicant claimed compensation from the Municipality of Poznań under section 18(5) of the 2001 Act on the protection of tenants' rights (and Article 417 of the Civil Code). Section 18 requires persons occupying flats without legal title to pay monthly compensation equivalent to market rent (or, if entitled to social housing with a suspended eviction, the amount they would have paid under the prior legal relationship). Subsection (5) entitles the owner to claim from the municipality if it fails to provide the ordered social housing.

On 16 September 2009, the Poznań District Court partially upheld the claim, awarding 21,971 Polish zlotys. It obtained two expert opinions on potential open-market rental income: one based on the flat's current (unrenovated) state and another assuming renovation (which the applicant intended). The court adopted the higher post-renovation figure.

Both parties appealed. On 11 May 2011, the Poznań Regional Court reversed the award and dismissed the claim entirely. It ruled that compensation under the invoked provision required strict proof of actual damage, its precise quantum, and a causal link to the occupation. Even assuming R.S. vacated, the applicant had not proven he would find a new tenant or receive rental income. The flat required renovation, would not be immediately lettable, and the applicant had not shown how long works would take or when it would be ready. The applicant's cassation appeal (citing inconsistent prior rulings in similar cases against the same municipality) was refused by the Supreme Court on 3 June 2011 (served 30 June 2011).

A 2006 Supreme Court resolution confirmed that such municipal liability claims are compensatory and require the owner to prove damage from the unlawful occupation. The applicant contended that the appellate court's near-impossible evidentiary demands (on hypothetical tenants, renovation timelines, and immediate lettability) arbitrarily denied statutory redress for nearly five years of occupation caused by the municipality's delay, interfering with his property rights and imposing an excessive individual burden.
001-216626:
The case concerns two Moroccan nationals employed as domestic staff at foreign embassies in London whose employment claims were barred by UK state immunity legislation, raising issues of access to court (Article 6) and discrimination (Article 14 + Article 6).

Fatima Benkharbouche (born 1964) worked as housekeeper/cook for the Sudanese ambassador from 2000 (with a break) until her summary dismissal on 27 November 2010. She claimed unpaid National Minimum Wage over nearly six years (£168,761), unfair dismissal (£37,230), wrongful dismissal, failure to provide pay statements or reasons, and breaches of the Working Time Regulations.

Mina Janah (born 1967) arrived in the UK on 2 November 2005 as a domestic worker/nanny in the household of the Libyan Cultural Attaché. She was dismissed by letter dated 24 January 2012. Her claims included unpaid minimum wage over six years (£149,348), unfair dismissal (£72,230), failure to provide written particulars, Working Time breaches, and racial discrimination/harassment.

Both brought claims in the Employment Tribunal. Sudan and Libya successfully invoked immunity under the State Immunity Act 1978. Section 16(1)(a) rendered foreign states immune in claims concerning employment of mission members. For Janah, section 4(2)(b) additionally applied, as she was neither a UK national nor habitually resident in the UK when her contract was made. (Benkharbouche’s habitual residence was not determined.) These provisions blocked jurisdiction despite the private-law character of the employment (domestic service unrelated to sovereign functions).

The Employment Tribunal stayed the claims after finding it could neither “read down” the 1978 Act under the Human Rights Act 1998 nor disapply it for EU-law rights. The Employment Appeal Tribunal identified a breach of Article 6 regarding section 16(1) and assumed one for sections 4(2)(b) and 14; it disapplied the provisions only for EU-derived claims (Working Time Regulations and Janah’s discrimination claim). The Court of Appeal issued a declaration of incompatibility: section 16(1)(a) violated Article 6 in both cases; section 4(2)(b) violated Articles 6 and 14 (nationality discrimination) in Janah’s case. It also disapplied the sections for EU claims pursuant to Article 47 of the EU Charter. The Supreme Court (2017) unanimously upheld the incompatibilities. Customary international law follows a restrictive doctrine of immunity limited to sovereign (iure imperii) acts; it does not require immunity for private-law employment of purely domestic staff. Section 4(2)(b) was additionally unjustifiable nationality discrimination. The cases were remitted for the EU claims, some of which were later settled (Benkharbouche received £10,000 for Working Time; Janah received £1,012 plus costs). The remaining domestic-law claims (minimum wage, unfair/wrongful dismissal) stayed barred. The UK Government later indicated it would make a remedial order.

The applicants lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights in April 2018, complaining of the denial of access to court and (for Janah) discrimination. The UK Government conceded the breaches. The Court accepted the concession, declined to strike the cases from the list (redress via declaration and possible legislative change being inadequate, as it provided no compensation for the barred claims), and awarded just satisfaction without independently examining the merits. The judgment became final on 5 September 2022.

The European Court of Human Rights examined applications by two Moroccan domestic workers employed at foreign embassies in London whose employment claims against Sudan and Libya were blocked by UK state immunity legislation.

Fatima Benkharbouche began work as housekeeper/cook for the Sudanese ambassador in 2000 (with interruptions). Her employment ended summarily on 27 November 2010. She claimed unpaid National Minimum Wage (nearly six years), unfair and wrongful dismissal, failure to provide an itemised pay statement or written reasons for dismissal, and breaches of the Working Time Regulations 1998. A schedule of loss valued the claims at over £210,000 plus an unquantified rest-period claim.

Mina Janah arrived in the United Kingdom on 2 November 2005 to work as a domestic worker and nanny for the Libyan Cultural Attaché. She was dismissed by letter dated 24 January 2012. She claimed unfair dismissal, unpaid minimum wage (six years), failure to provide a written statement of particulars, Working Time Regulation breaches, and race discrimination/harassment. Her claims were valued at over £224,000.

Both employers invoked the State Immunity Act 1978. Section 16(1)(a) excludes employment claims by members of a diplomatic mission from the ordinary employment-contract exception in section 4. Section 4(2)(b) further denies the exception where, at the time of contracting, the employee was neither a UK national nor habitually resident in the United Kingdom. Janah was found not to have been habitually resident when her contract was made; Benkharbouche’s habitual-residence status was not determined.

Employment Tribunals accepted the immunity pleas and stayed the claims. The Employment Appeal Tribunal held that Article 6 ECHR was breached by section 16(1)(a) and assumed breaches of Articles 6 and 14 by section 4(2)(b). It disapplied those provisions only for claims falling within EU law (Working Time and race-discrimination claims). The Court of Appeal (2015) declared both provisions incompatible with the Convention: section 16(1)(a) because customary international law does not require immunity for purely private-law claims by service staff, and section 4(2)(b) because it discriminates on nationality without international-law justification. It also disapplied the provisions for EU-law claims under Article 47 of the EU Charter. The Supreme Court (2017) unanimously dismissed the state’s appeal, confirming that neither provision reflected customary international law (which limits immunity to sovereign acts, not private-law employment of domestic staff) and were therefore incompatible with Article 6 and Article 47. It held the nationality discrimination under section 4(2)(b) equally unjustifiable.

EU-law claims were remitted and later settled for modest sums (£10,000 for Benkharbouche’s Working Time claim; £1,012 plus costs for Janah’s). Janah withdrew her discrimination claim after a later Supreme Court ruling. Domestic-law claims (principally minimum-wage and unfair-dismissal claims) remained barred. The United Kingdom later indicated it would make a remedial order to remove the incompatibility.

The applicants complained to the Strasbourg Court that the statutory bar violated Article 6 (access to court) and, in Janah’s case, Article 14 taken with Article 6. The Government conceded the breaches. The Court accepted the concession, declined to strike the applications out despite later legislative intentions, and proceeded to just satisfaction.

**Case Summary: Benkharbouche and Janah v. the United Kingdom (ECtHR, 2022)**

Two Moroccan nationals, Fatima Benkharbouche and Mina Janah, worked as domestic staff at foreign diplomatic missions in London. Benkharbouche served as housekeeper/cook to the Sudanese ambassador from 2000 (with a break) until summary dismissal on 27 November 2010. Janah worked as a domestic worker/nanny for the Libyan Cultural Attaché from November 2005 until dismissal by letter dated 24 January 2012.

After dismissal, both brought employment claims in UK tribunals. Benkharbouche claimed unpaid National Minimum Wage (nearly six years), unfair and wrongful dismissal, failure to provide an itemised pay statement or written reasons, and Working Time Regulations breaches. Her schedule of loss exceeded £211,000. Janah claimed similar unpaid minimum wage (six years), unfair dismissal, failure to provide employment particulars, Working Time breaches, and race discrimination/harassment. Her claims were valued at over £224,000 plus a discrimination element.

The respondent states (Sudan and Libya) successfully invoked immunity under the State Immunity Act 1978. Section 16(1)(a) excluded employment claims by members of a diplomatic mission from the general exception to immunity in section 4. Section 4(2)(b) further barred claims where, at the time of the contract, the claimant was neither a UK national nor habitually resident in the UK (applied to Janah; Benkharbouche’s residence status was not finally determined). These provisions prevented the tribunals from hearing the claims.

The Employment Tribunal stayed both cases after finding it could not “read down” the 1978 Act under the Human Rights Act 1998 or disapply it for EU-law claims. The Employment Appeal Tribunal found a breach of Article 6 ECHR regarding section 16(1) and assumed one (plus Article 14) for section 4(2)(b). It disapplied the provisions only for claims within EU law (Working Time for both; discrimination for Janah).

The Court of Appeal (2015) held that neither international law (including the 1972 European Convention on State Immunity, the UN Convention, ILC Draft Articles, or State practice) required immunity for purely private-law employment claims by service staff absent special features (e.g., recruitment/reinstatement or security interference). Section 16(1)(a) therefore violated Article 6. Section 4(2)(b) was nationality-discriminatory and also incompatible with Articles 6 and 14, as no such limitation was required by customary international law. A declaration of incompatibility was issued. EU-law claims were again disapplied under Article 47 of the EU Charter.

The Supreme Court (2017) unanimously dismissed the states’ appeal. It confirmed that customary international law follows a restrictive doctrine: immunity covers only sovereign (iure imperii) acts, not private-law (iure gestionis) acts such as employing domestic staff. Neither statutory provision was therefore justified, rendering them incompatible with Article 6 ECHR and Article 47 of the EU Charter. Discrimination under Article 14 added nothing once Article 6 was engaged.

The EU-derived claims (Working Time, and Janah’s withdrawn discrimination claim) were remitted and later settled for modest sums (£10,000 and £1,012 plus costs). Non-EU claims (minimum wage, unfair/wrongful dismissal) remained barred. The UK Government later indicated it would make a remedial order to address the incompatibility.

The applicants then applied to the ECtHR, alleging that the statutory immunities denied them access to court (Article 6) and, in Janah’s case, discriminated on nationality/residence grounds (Article 14 taken with Article 6). The Court noted the Government’s concession of the breaches, declined to strike the cases from the list given inadequate domestic redress, and proceeded to just satisfaction without independently examining the merits.
001-216685:
The case concerns journalist Eynulla Fatullayev, previously convicted in 2007 of defamation and related offences (later found to violate Articles 6 and 10 in Fatullayev v. Azerbaijan, no. 40984/07). While serving that sentence at Penal Facility No. 12, he published articles (via Mediaforum) criticising prison authorities, alleging a 2009 riot cover-up and warning of possible fabricated charges linked to his pending Strasbourg application. He claimed prior attacks, provocations (including a 2008 assault and 2009 riot involvement attempt), questioning about drug use, and threats tied to journalist Elmar Huseynov’s death.

On 28 December 2009, officer K.S. reported “operational information” that Fatullayev and four inmates showed signs of drug use. The governor authorised a personal search (no court warrant required under prison rules) and dormitory search. On 29 December, Fatullayev was searched in K.S.’s office by officers, with inmate and staff witnesses present. Two plastic packages of yellowish powder (later identified as 0.223g homemade heroin) were found in his jacket sleeve and shoe; a similar package was found on another inmate. His request to contact family or have a lawyer present was refused. He was placed in a punishment cell; the dormitory search found nothing.

The packages were sent for initial examination (confirming heroin). Blood/urine samples (30 December) showed traces of morphinan (heroin metabolite), amphetaminil and flunitrazepam via chromatography and other tests (report 18 January 2010). Jacket and shoe traces confirmed heroin (22 January). A narcology examination (19 January) found him psychologically stable, not a drug user, with no administration traces or need for treatment—but, based on blood/urine results, recommended prophylactic registration as a user. A 5ml blood sample given to his lawyer could not be independently tested, as labs refused.

Charged on 31 December 2009 under Criminal Code Article 234.1 (illegal drug possession without intent to sell, exceeding personal-use amount), Fatullayev alleged at trial that drugs were planted due to his journalism, pending ECHR case, and to force cooperation. He argued the “operational information” was fabricated (informants imaginary or complicit); no inquiry into drug sources despite high-security conditions; fingerprint testing would show he never handled the packages; planting was possible (e.g., during showers). He requested joint examination of drug sources (severed into separate proceedings under Article 234.2), informant questioning, fingerprint analysis, re-testing of blood/urine (claiming the 18 January report contradicted the narcology findings and charts showed lethal levels), independent blood testing, and hair/nail analysis (drugs detectable up to two years). All requests were dismissed: sources need not be examined together; informants irrelevant (information not the case basis); fingerprint grounds unclear; 18 January report reliable; hair/nail tests useless (traces last weeks/months, no Azerbaijani facilities) after hearing expert G.H.

Witnesses (officers, governor, inmates) described the search; governor denied riots, attacks or questioning; some inmates claimed it was impossible to plant drugs, though one noted Fatullayev sometimes left clothes outside showers (contradicted by others). One inmate (O.B.) claimed Fatullayev admitted past use and appeared under influence. Experts confirmed reports; G.H. clarified charts showed presence not levels, remaining samples could be retested, and hair detection lasts up to two years (testimony partly disregarded).

On 6 July 2010, Garadagh District Court convicted him, relying on expert reports and most testimony, dismissing planting claims (articles lacked specific threats; governor testimony refuted attacks/riots; Huseynov allegations irrelevant). Sentence: 2.5 years. Appeals (reiterating requests) were dismissed without full investigation (Court of Appeal, 25 January 2011) and as unfounded (Supreme Court, 3 November 2011). Separate source proceedings remained pending. Fatullayev was pardoned and released in May 2011.

On 8–9 August 2014, investigating authorities seized all pending Strasbourg case files (including this one) from representative I. Aliyev’s office during unrelated proceedings against him; some documents were later returned.

The applicant, Azerbaijani journalist Eynulla Fatullayev, founded and edited newspapers known for criticising the government and public officials. He had previously been convicted in 2007 of defamation, threat of terrorism, incitement to ethnic hostility and tax evasion (based on published articles) and sentenced to 8.5 years’ imprisonment. Those convictions formed the subject of the Court’s 2010 judgment in Fatullayev v. Azerbaijan, which found violations of Articles 6 and 10. While serving that sentence at Penal Facility No. 12, the applicant (with third-party assistance) published further articles on an internet outlet, including one in December 2009 referencing his pending Strasbourg case and expressing concern over possible new fabricated charges. He alleged prior attacks by inmates, attempts to implicate him in a 2009 riot, questioning by the prison governor about drug use, and threats from a public official linked to his inquiries into a fellow journalist’s death.

On 28 December 2009 a prison officer reported “operational information” that the applicant and four other inmates had shown signs of drug use. The governor authorised personal searches and dormitory searches. On 29 December the applicant and others were searched by officers in the presence of inmate and staff attesting witnesses. Two plastic packages containing yellowish powder (later confirmed as 0.223 grams of homemade heroin) were found on the applicant (one in a jacket sleeve, one in a shoe). His request to contact family and have a lawyer present was refused. No prohibited items were found in the subsequent dormitory search. The applicant was placed in a punishment cell. Blood and urine samples, plus his jacket and shoe, were later tested, revealing traces of heroin, amphetaminil and a benzodiazepine metabolite. A narcology examination, however, found him psychologically stable, not a drug user, with no health issues or injection traces (though it recommended prophylactic registration based on the blood/urine results). He was charged on 31 December 2009 with illegal possession of narcotics exceeding personal-use quantity (Criminal Code Article 234.1). Separate proceedings were later severed to investigate the drugs’ source.

At trial before the Garadagh District Court the applicant maintained that the drugs had been planted by authorities because of his journalism, pending ECHR application and refusal to cooperate. He submitted his articles and described prior attacks/provocations. He requested that the source of the drugs be examined in the same proceedings, that alleged informants be identified and questioned, that fingerprint analysis of the packaging be ordered, that blood/urine samples (including one given to his lawyer, which laboratories had refused to test independently) be re-examined, and that hair and nail samples be tested for longer-term traces. All requests were refused: the court saw no difficulty from the severed source investigation, deemed informants irrelevant, found no reason to doubt the existing expert reports, and held hair/nail testing untimely and technically unavailable in Azerbaijan. Prison staff testified that planting was impossible and that the applicant’s riot/attack claims were false; some inmates gave conflicting accounts of whether he left clothes unattended. One inmate claimed the applicant had spoken of prior drug use and appeared intoxicated. Experts confirmed their reports (clarifying that charts showed detection, not concentration).

On 6 July 2010 the court convicted the applicant, relying on the search records, expert reports and most witness testimony, while dismissing planting/fabrication claims as unsupported and unrelated to his journalism. He was sentenced to 2.5 years’ imprisonment. Appeals to the Court of Appeal (examined without further investigation) and Supreme Court were dismissed on the same grounds. The applicant was pardoned and released in May 2011; the source investigation remained pending.

Separately, in August 2014 the investigating authorities (in unrelated proceedings against the applicant’s then-representative) seized the entire case file relating to this application from the lawyer’s office, along with other Strasbourg files. Some documents were later returned.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 6 § 1 fair-hearing violation (inability to challenge planted-evidence claims or adduce exculpatory tests) and the Article 34 complaint (interference with the right of petition via seizure of the pending application file).

Eynulla Fatullayev, a prominent Azerbaijani journalist and editor of opposition newspapers known for criticizing government officials, was imprisoned following 2007 convictions for defamation and related offences. The ECHR later found those proceedings violated Articles 6 and 10; the convictions were quashed in 2010. While serving his sentence at Penal Facility No. 12, Fatullayev published online articles alleging a 2009 prison riot (which authorities later denied) and warning of possible new fabricated charges, given prior attacks, provocations (including an official query about drug use), and threats linked to his journalism and a pending ECHR application concerning a colleague’s death.

On 28 December 2009, a prison officer reported “operational information” that Fatullayev and others showed signs of drug use. The next day, without a court warrant and after denying his request to contact family or a lawyer, officers searched him in the presence of mixed inmate/staff witnesses, finding two plastic packages of homemade heroin (0.223 grams total) in his jacket sleeve and shoe. A similar package was found on another inmate. No items were found in a subsequent dormitory search. Initial testing confirmed heroin. Blood and urine samples (taken 30 December) later tested positive for morphinan, amphetaminil and flunitrazepam via chromatography and other methods; traces of heroin were also found on his clothing. However, a narcology committee examination found him psychologically stable, with no health issues, no drug-use traces on his body and no need for treatment—though it still recommended “prophylactic” registration as a user based on the lab results. Fatullayev claimed the samples may have been tampered with and noted contradictions, as the detected substances should have produced visible effects.

Charged on 31 December 2009 with illegal possession of drugs exceeding personal-use amounts (Article 234.1 of the Criminal Code), Fatullayev’s trial began in March 2010. He argued the drugs were planted to punish his journalism and pending Strasbourg case, citing opportunities such as showers or cafeteria visits. He requested: identification and questioning of the (possibly fictitious) informants; fingerprint analysis of the packages (to show he never touched them); inclusion of a severed investigation into the drugs’ source; re-testing of remaining blood/urine samples (claiming annexed charts implied lethal levels, though an expert later clarified they only identified substances); independent testing of a blood sample given to his lawyer (which labs refused); and hair/nail analysis (which can detect use for months/years). All requests were dismissed without adequate reasons: informants were irrelevant; source proceedings created no difficulties; fingerprint grounds were unclear; the 18 January 2010 report was reliable; hair/nail tests were useless after five months (despite UN guidelines and expert testimony indicating longer windows) and technically unavailable in Azerbaijan.

Witnesses—primarily prison staff—described the search as proper and planting as impossible, denying any riot, attacks or provocations. Inmates gave conflicting accounts of whether Fatullayev left clothes unattended. One inmate claimed Fatullayev had spoken of prior drug use and appeared under the influence. Experts confirmed their reports. On 6 July 2010 the Garadagh District Court convicted him, relying on the expert reports and most staff/inmate testimony (disregarding contrary evidence, such as remaining samples or a two-year hair-detection window). It dismissed planting claims, finding his article contained no specific threat and no causal link to other allegations. He was sentenced to 2½ years. Appeals were dismissed without further investigation, upholding the refusals.

Fatullayev was pardoned and released in May 2011. In August 2014, while this application was pending, authorities seized all ECHR-related case files (including this one) from his representative’s office during unrelated proceedings against the lawyer; some documents were later returned. These facts underpin the alleged Article 6 unfairness (inability to challenge planted evidence or adduce favourable proof, with courts relying solely on officials while ignoring his targeting as a journalist) and Article 34 hindrance of petition.
001-216629:
The case concerns the death of 18-year-old conscript V. Muradyan, son of applicant Nana Muradyan, during compulsory military service in unit no. 39318 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. Drafted in November 2009, his body was discovered at around 12.35 a.m. on 15 March 2010 hanging from a metal pole behind the officers’ room of the maintenance company, with a chair nearby. Criminal proceedings were immediately opened under Article 110 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (indirectly or negligently causing suicide by threats, cruel treatment or repeated humiliation).

Scene examination yielded a military belt belonging to fellow serviceman N.G., other clothing items, and a torn cardboard box bearing V.’s name. Forensic medical examination established death by mechanical asphyxia from hanging; a bruise on the left arm and abrasion on the right wrist (inflicted 2–4 days earlier) were unrelated. A post-mortem psychiatric-psychological assessment found no mental disorder but concluded that V. had been in a severely depressed state immediately before death, causally linked to confrontations over a modest debt (AMD 6,000, about €11) owed to N.G. for a mobile telephone. On the evening of 14 March, N.G., A.K., H.H. and junior sergeant K.A. confronted V. about a false promise to repay the money via another soldier; they denied violence but told him to produce the sum by midnight. V. then left and was later marked present at evening roll-call by K.A., who falsely claimed he was in the toilet; the platoon commander did not verify this.

The applicant, recognised as legal heir, insisted her son had been murdered after witnessing fuel theft (which he had mentioned by telephone days earlier). Later questioning revealed a pattern of unofficial hierarchy and violence: contractual serviceman A.G. had earlier slapped and assaulted V. over another unpaid telephone sale; A.K. had struck both K.A. and V. for refusing errands. A.G. was charged with degrading treatment but benefited from an amnesty. No fuel shortage was officially confirmed. Investigators repeatedly stayed the case (January 2011, December 2015, July 2017), citing insufficient evidence of incitement or ill-treatment and the absence of identified perpetrators, despite multiple forensic examinations (including of clothing and the rope, which showed traces of undetermined blood).

The applicant lodged numerous unsuccessful complaints about a preconceived suicide hypothesis, incomplete scene examination (her son’s boots were never seized), failure to notify her of expert examinations, and lack of exploration of alternative theories. Domestic courts initially dismissed her challenges on procedural grounds. In 2017 N.G. and A.K. were charged under Article 359 § 3 (breach of military conduct causing serious consequences) but fled; proceedings were stayed. A 2018 first-instance court ruling later found the investigation formally deficient, unreasonably lengthy and in breach of Article 2, as the applicant had been denied genuine participation. The investigation remained pending as of July 2020.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of a substantive violation of Article 2 (failure of the military authorities to protect a conscript’s life amid known harassment, monetary disputes and a culture that discouraged reporting misconduct) and a procedural violation (ineffective, delayed and one-sided investigation that never identified those responsible or provided a satisfactory explanation). An Article 13 claim of lack of an effective domestic remedy was also raised.

The case of Nana Muradyan v. Armenia concerns the 15 March 2010 death of the applicant’s 18-year-old son, V. Muradyan, a conscript drafted in November 2009 and assigned to military unit no. 39318 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. His body was found hanging from a metal pole behind the officers’ room of the maintenance company. An investigation was promptly opened under Article 110 § 1 of the Criminal Code (inciting suicide by threats, cruel treatment or humiliation).

Scene examination yielded a military belt belonging to fellow serviceman N.G., other clothing items, a chair near the body and remnants of the rope. Forensic medical examination confirmed death by mechanical suffocation from hanging. A bruise on the neck was consistent with the ligature; additional bruises and an abrasion on the arm and wrist, inflicted 2–4 days earlier while alive, were unconnected to the death and possibly work-related. No traces of struggle appeared on clothing, though sparse unidentified blood was later found on the rope. The applicant’s son’s boots were never seized or examined.

Witness statements described a monetary dispute. V. Muradyan owed AMD 6,000 (about EUR 11) for a mobile telephone. On the evening of 14 March he was confronted in an empty office by N.G., A.K., H.H. and junior sergeant K.A. after giving a false assurance that another soldier would lend him money. He appeared upset, said little and was told to produce the sum by midnight. The four servicemen denied any violence that night. Later interviews, however, revealed prior incidents: contractual serviceman A.G. had publicly slapped and assaulted V. Muradyan over an unpaid telephone; A.K. had struck him for refusing a favour; and a culture of impunity prevailed in which even a junior sergeant feared reporting misconduct because it would destroy his standing. Platoon commander A.Ar. failed to verify V. Muradyan’s absence at lights-out after K.A. falsely claimed he was in the toilet.

A forensic psychiatric-psychological assessment found no mental disorder but concluded that V. Muradyan had been in a severely depressed state immediately before death, caused by the money-related confrontations, establishing a causal link with the actions of N.G., A.K. and H.H. The applicant maintained her son had been murdered after witnessing fuel theft; an internal inquiry detected no shortage.

The investigation suffered repeated stays, changes of investigator, incomplete forensic work and a preconceived suicide theory. A.G. was charged with assault but the case was dropped under an amnesty. In 2017 N.G. and A.K. were charged with harassment that negligently caused suicide, yet they absconded and proceedings were stayed. The applicant’s numerous complaints about inadequate measures, lack of genuine participation and excessive length were largely unsuccessful until a 2018 court found formal involvement, unaddressed arguments and unreasonable delay. The investigation remained pending in 2020, more than ten years after the death.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 2 (substantive failure to protect a vulnerable conscript amid known harassment, debts and a climate that discouraged reporting of abuse, and procedural failure to conduct an effective investigation) and Article 13 (absence of an effective domestic remedy).

**Case Summary: Nana Muradyan v. Armenia (ECtHR, Application no. 69517/11, Judgment 5 April 2022)**

The applicant, Nana Muradyan, is the mother of V. Muradyan, an 18-year-old conscript who died on 15 March 2010 during compulsory military service. Drafted in November 2009, he was assigned to military unit no. 39318 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. His body was found hanging from a metal pole behind the officers’ room of the maintenance company around 12:35 a.m.

Criminal proceedings were opened the same day under Article 110 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (indirectly or negligently causing suicide by threats, cruel treatment or humiliation). The scene examination recovered military items, including a belt belonging to fellow serviceman N.G., clothing, and a rope; V. Muradyan’s military boots were later found missing from seized evidence. A forensic medical report confirmed death by mechanical suffocation from hanging, with a ligature mark and unrelated bruises/abrasions inflicted 2–4 days earlier. A psychiatric-psychological assessment found no mental disorder but concluded he was severely depressed immediately before death due to money-related discussions involving N.G., A.K. and H.H., with a causal link requiring legal assessment. Fellow servicemen reported he owed N.G. AMD 6,000 (about EUR 11) for a mobile phone. On 14 March, A.K. and H.H. pressed him over the debt after he allegedly lied about obtaining a loan; he was told to produce the money by midnight. They denied violence. Platoon commander A.Ar. and junior sergeant K.A. failed to account for his absence at evening roll-call; K.A. falsely said he was in the toilet.

The applicant, recognised as legal heir, stated her son had mentioned witnessing fuel theft days earlier and rejected suicide, alleging he was killed. Later questioning revealed a pattern of harassment: in February 2010 contractual serviceman A.G. had assaulted and publicly humiliated V. Muradyan over another unpaid phone sale (A.G. was later charged with a disciplinary breach but amnestied). K.A. described other beatings and forced favours by A.K., which went unreported due to fear of losing respect or retaliation. The unit culture discouraged reporting misconduct.

The investigation was repeatedly stayed (January 2011, December 2015, July 2017) for lack of identified suspects or because N.G. and A.K. (charged in 2017 under Article 359 § 3 for harassment/humiliation leading to suicide) had fled. It was resumed multiple times on prosecutorial or judicial orders. Additional forensics (biological, trace, medical panel) yielded limited results, such as sparse unidentified blood on the rope. Domestic courts, including a 2018 Yerevan Court ruling, found the probe formal, incomplete, excessively lengthy, and failing to involve the applicant properly (e.g., no prior notice of expert examinations). As of July 2020 the investigation remained pending. The applicant’s civil and review claims were largely unsuccessful.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 2 violations (substantive positive obligation to protect life in a military setting known for harassment, debts and non-reporting, plus failure to prevent foreseeable risk) and the procedural obligation (ineffective, delayed, one-sided investigation that did not pursue alternative hypotheses or all leads). Article 13 was also invoked regarding lack of effective remedies. The Court later found both aspects of Article 2 violated.
