001-217259:
The case of L.F. v. Hungary (ECtHR Application no. 621/14, judgment of 19 May 2022) concerns an unannounced inspection of the applicant’s home by municipal officials in Gyöngyöspata. The applicant, a Hungarian national of Roma origin born in 1956, lodged the application on 19 December 2013 alleging violations of Article 8 (right to respect for home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention. He died in April 2015; his wife and children continued the proceedings.

Following anti-Roma demonstrations and paramilitary activity, a politician from the far-right Jobbik party was elected mayor in July 2011. Tensions rose, and the mayor sought to introduce the “Érpatak model,” under which social benefits would be restricted to residents deemed to contribute to the community and respect “law and order,” as opposed to those viewed as “destructive.”

On 13 October 2011 the mayor, the chief councillor and the chief of cabinet, accompanied by police officers who remained outside, entered the applicant’s house without prior notice or explanation of purpose. They inspected and measured every room; the applicant alleged that video recordings were also made of the interior (later contested by the authorities). His wife and children were present. Comparable inspections were carried out on other Roma households in the same period.

The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Rights of National and Ethnic Minorities reported that the practice lacked any legal basis, was experienced as intimidation or reprisal given the local political climate, and recommended a thorough investigation by the Heves County Governmental Office to restore legality.

The applicant filed a criminal complaint of unlawful entry into private property (Criminal Code Article 176). The mayor’s office asserted that the visit was to verify compliance with Government Decree 253/1997 (OTÉK) requiring 15 m³ of air per person per room and, secondarily, to check living conditions because the applicant’s wife received municipal housing benefit. The Gyöngyös police dismissed the complaint on the grounds that the applicant had not asked the officials to leave and that the measure was justified. The public prosecutor upheld the dismissal.

The Heves County Governmental Office subsequently established that no administrative or municipal proceedings were pending on 13 October 2011 that would have authorised entry. Verification of OTÉK standards fell outside local-government competence, and no decision assessing the family’s housing-benefit eligibility had been taken after July 2011. The Office also found that the relevant local social-benefits decree had been applied unlawfully.

A second criminal complaint led to an investigation that was later discontinued. The police and prosecutor relied on a September 2011 amendment to the local decree empowering the mayor to review benefits annually or as needed, and on witness statements that the inspection concerned continued payment rather than a new application. They concluded that, although the visit had not fully complied with administrative-procedure rules, it did not constitute a criminal offence because the officials had believed they were acting lawfully.

These facts form the core of the alleged interference with the applicant’s home: an unannounced, multi-official entry and measurement of private living space without a pending procedure, without a clear statutory mandate, and in a context of heightened anti-Roma tension.

In July 2011 a Jobbik politician, J.J.O., was elected mayor. Tensions between Roma and non-Roma residents rose. The new mayor prepared to introduce the “Érpatak model,” under which social benefits would be paid only to residents deemed to contribute to the community and respect law and order.

The officials entered, inspected and measured every room, and allegedly made video recordings of the interior (later contested). The applicant was given no explanation of the visit’s purpose. His wife and children were present. Similar unannounced inspections were carried out on other Roma families in the same period.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint of unlawful entry onto private property. The mayor’s office claimed the visit verified compliance with Government Decree no. 253/1997 (OTÉK) requiring 15 cubic metres of air per person per room, and secondarily checked living conditions because the applicant’s wife received housing benefit. Police and prosecutors dismissed the complaint, holding that the applicant had not asked the officials to leave and that OTÉK plus the housing-benefit rules supplied a basis.

The applicant requested an examination by the Heves County Governmental Office. In May 2012 that office found that no administrative or municipal procedure had been pending on 13 October 2011 that could have authorised entry. OTÉK verification fell outside local-government competence and could occur only in specific building-control proceedings. No decision assessing the family’s housing-benefit eligibility had been taken after July 2011. The office confirmed these findings in its reply to the Parliamentary Commissioner.

A second criminal complaint alleging a spurious official procedure and a racist motive was likewise dismissed. Police later discontinued an investigation, asserting that the visit related to a housing-benefit application granted in July 2011 and that a local social-benefits decree required on-site inquiry and empowered the mayor to reassess benefits. Prosecutors upheld the discontinuation, citing a September 2011 amendment to the calculation method that supposedly necessitated the inspection, even if the visit had not fully complied with administrative-procedure rules.

The applicant died in 2015; his widow and children pursued the application. The facts establish that municipal officials entered and measured the family’s home without any pending procedure, without statutory authority under OTÉK or the housing-benefit rules, and without informing the occupants of the purpose. The inspections formed part of a pattern directed at Roma households in a climate of heightened ethnic tension.

After his death in 2015, his widow and children continued the application.

They measured every room; video recording of the interior was alleged but later denied by the authorities. The applicant’s wife and children were present. Comparable inspections were carried out on other Roma households receiving housing benefit.

The applicant immediately lodged a criminal complaint for unlawful entry onto private property (Criminal Code Art. 176, which covers entry by force or under the pretence of an official procedure). The municipality initially claimed the visit verified compliance with Government Decree 253/1997 (OTÉK) requiring 15 m³ of air per person per room and, secondarily, checked living conditions linked to the wife’s housing benefit. Police and prosecutors dismissed the complaint, noting that the applicant had not asked the officials to leave and accepting the OTÉK justification.

On 17 May 2012 the Office established that no administrative or municipal procedure was pending on 13 October 2011 that could have authorised entry. Verification of OTÉK standards fell outside local-government competence and could occur only within specific building-control proceedings. No reassessment of the housing benefit (granted on 31 July 2011) had taken place after that date. The Office later confirmed to the Parliamentary Commissioner for National and Ethnic Minorities that OTÉK could not serve as a legal basis and that the last relevant decision predated the inspection.

Police again discontinued proceedings, first acknowledging the absence of any pending file, then (after a new investigation) asserting that an on-site inquiry was required by the local social-benefits decree and that an amendment of 28 September 2011 authorised the mayor to review existing awards. Prosecutors upheld this reasoning, concluding that even if the inspection had not fully complied with administrative-procedure rules it did not constitute a criminal offence because the officials believed they were acting lawfully.

The Commissioner’s December 2011 report described the visits—conducted by a large group of officials plus police—as lacking any clear statutory foundation under either the social-benefits decree or the general administrative-procedure act, and as inherently intimidating in the prevailing climate. The County Office’s supervisory review similarly found the relevant local decree unlawful in several respects (including the delegation of housing-benefit decisions and the linking of benefits to “orderliness” of living conditions) and referred the matter to the Kúria; the municipality subsequently repealed the decree.

001-217387:
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined applications by Turkish nationals Sinan Çetinkaya and Ağyar Çetinkaya alleging a violation of Article 7 of the Convention (nullum crimen sine lege). The applicants claimed that domestic courts failed to apply more lenient criminal provisions retrospectively, resulting in their conviction for embezzlement lacking any legal basis.

In 1999 the applicants, respectively general director and board chairman of an automobile company, were indicted with a Ziraat Bank branch manager for using forged documents to obtain loans from the then state-owned bank for personal purposes. Subsequent legislation altered the applicable framework: the 1999 Banks Act (Law no. 4389) created a specific banking-embezzlement offence; Law no. 4603 of 2000 converted Ziraat Bank into a public limited company, so that its employees ceased to be public officials; a new Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) entered into force in 2005; and the 2005 Banking Activities Act (Law no. 5411) replaced Law no. 4389.

The Istanbul Assize Court first acquitted the applicants of forgery but convicted them of aggravated fraud. After the Court of Cassation remitted the case, the trial court again convicted them of fraud under the new Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation then re-characterised the facts as banking embezzlement under Law no. 4389 (later Law no. 5411), treating the applicants as co-principals who had acted in concert with the bank manager. It considered Law no. 4389 more favourable even though it post-dated the offence. On remittal the trial court convicted the applicants of aggravated banking embezzlement under Law no. 4389 and imposed lengthy prison sentences.

The Court of Cassation again quashed, holding that the offence date was 14 May 1999, so that the acts constituted embezzlement by a public official under Article 202 of the former Criminal Code. Because Law no. 4603 had removed the bank’s public status, however, Law no. 4389 was more favourable. The trial court was instructed to compare that law with later provisions (Law no. 5411 and Article 247 of the new Criminal Code). On the third occasion the trial court convicted the applicants under Article 247 of the new Criminal Code as the most lenient provision, sentencing each to more than ten years’ imprisonment.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the courts had disregarded the principle that only the law may define an offence and that they could not be principals of a “special offence” (embezzlement), which under Turkish law may be committed only by public officials or bank employees. Article 40 § 2 of the new Criminal Code further limited non-qualifying participants to incitement or assistance. The Court of Cassation nevertheless upheld the convictions, noting that the case should have fallen under the later banking statutes but declining to quash because no appeal had been lodged to the applicants’ detriment.

Turkish law required courts to apply the most favourable provision (Article 7 § 2 of the Criminal Code). Embezzlement remained a special offence throughout; under the former Code non-qualified persons could still be treated as co-principals, whereas the new Code precluded that possibility. The sequence of legislative changes and the courts’ successive re-characterisations therefore produced a conviction for a special offence that the applicants, lacking the requisite status, could not lawfully commit as principals.

The case of Sinan Çetinkaya and Ağyar Çetinkaya v. Turkey (ECtHR applications 74536/10 and 75462/10) concerns an alleged violation of Article 7 ECHR (nullum crimen sine lege). The applicants, Turkish nationals born in 1966 and 1964 living in Istanbul, were executives of an automobile company (second applicant as board chairman, first as general director). They were charged with using forged documents of 76 people to obtain loans from Ziraat Bank (then a state-owned public bank) for personal use, to the detriment of victims.

A July 1999 indictment charged them with forgery of official documents and aggravated fraud under Articles 342 and 504 of the former Criminal Code (Law 765). An additional September 1999 indictment added bank manager B.E. for collusion in granting the loans despite knowing of the forgeries. Key legislative changes followed: the Banks Act (Law 4389) entered force on 23 June 1999, creating a banking embezzlement offence for bank officials; Law 4603 of November 2000 converted Ziraat Bank into a public limited company, so its employees were no longer public officials for criminal purposes; a new Criminal Code (Law 5237) entered force on 1 June 2005; and the Banking Activities Act (Law 5411) of November 2005 repealed Law 4389.

In November 2003, the Istanbul 4th Assize Court acquitted the applicants of forgery but convicted them of fraud, sentencing each to over five years’ imprisonment plus a fine. B.E. was convicted of misconduct in public office. The Court of Cassation quashed this in November 2004 for missing documents. In July 2005 the trial court reconvicted the applicants of aggravated fraud under the new Criminal Code (more favourable), with similar sentences for B.E. of misconduct. In June 2006 Cassation quashed again, recharacterising the acts as embezzlement under Law 4389 (later 5411). It held B.E. (now not a public official) committed banking embezzlement by granting unchecked loans knowing they would not be repaid, and the applicants were co-principals sharing joint intent. Law 4389 applied as more favourable despite post-dating the offence.

In April 2007 the trial court convicted all of aggravated banking embezzlement under Law 4389 (more favourable than 5411), imposing over 13 years’ imprisonment each. Cassation quashed in February 2008, fixing the offence date as 14 May 1999 (last harm to the bank). At that time the acts constituted embezzlement under Article 202 of the former Code (public officials). Law 4389 was more favourable due to Law 4603, but the court must compare later provisions (Law 5411 or new Code Article 247). In June 2009 the trial court found banking embezzlement under Laws 4389/5411 but convicted the applicants under Article 247 of the new Code (embezzlement by public officials) as “most favourable” after comparing all texts, imposing nearly 11 years each. B.E. had died, so proceedings against him discontinued.

Applicants appealed, arguing failure to apply the most favourable law (nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege) and that the first applicant could not be a principal in the “special offence” of embezzlement, which required public-official or bank-member status he lacked. In June 2010 Cassation upheld the judgment. It criticised the trial court for not applying post-offence Laws 4389 or 5411 per plenary Cassation decisions, but did not quash as no appeal sought a worse outcome for the applicants.

Embezzlement is a special offence in Turkish law, committable as principal only by those with statutory qualifications (public officials under the Codes, or bank members under banking laws). After the 2005 Code, unqualified persons could only be liable as inciters or assistants (Article 40 § 2), unlike under the former Code. Courts must apply the most favourable provisions (Criminal Code Article 7 § 2). The applicants argued their conviction as principals under Article 247 (which did not apply to them) lacked any legal basis, as more lenient post-offence banking laws were ignored.

The ECHR case of Sinan Çetinkaya and Ağyar Çetinkaya v. Turkey (applications 74536/10 and 75462/10) involved two Turkish nationals convicted of embezzlement. They alleged a breach of Article 7 (nullum crimen sine lege) because domestic courts failed to apply more lenient laws retrospectively, resulting in a conviction without legal basis.

In a 13 July 1999 indictment, the applicants (chairman and general director of an automobile company) were charged with forgery of official documents and aggravated fraud under the former Criminal Code (Law no. 765, Arts. 342 and 504). They had allegedly obtained loans from the then state-owned Ziraat Bank on behalf of 76 people using forged documents, diverting the funds personally. An additional 21 September 1999 indictment charged bank manager B.E. with connivance by granting the loans despite knowing of the forgeries.

The Banks Act (Law no. 4389) entered into force on 23 June 1999. Law no. 4603 (25 November 2000) converted Ziraat Bank to a public limited company, so its employees ceased to be public officials for criminal purposes. A new Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) took effect on 1 June 2005, and the Banking Activities Act (Law no. 5411) replaced Law no. 4389 on 1 November 2005.

On 19 November 2003 the Istanbul 4th Assize Court acquitted the applicants of forgery but convicted them of fraud (five years, eight months and one day’s imprisonment plus a fine each). B.E. was convicted of misconduct in public office (Art. 240 of the former Code). The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment in 2004 for missing documents.

On 8 July 2005 the trial court reconvicted the applicants of aggravated fraud under the new Code (Art. 158 § 1(e) and (j)), deemed more favourable, and B.E. of misconduct (Art. 257). The Court of Cassation quashed again on 15 June 2006, holding that B.E.’s acts constituted banking embezzlement under Law no. 4389 (later Law no. 5411) because bank staff were no longer public officials. The applicants, sharing joint intent and acting in concert, were principal material participants. Law no. 4389 was more favourable despite post-dating the offence.

On 27 April 2007 the trial court convicted all three of aggravated banking embezzlement under section 22(3) of Law no. 4389 (thirteen years, seven months and ten days’ imprisonment plus a fine each), finding it more favourable than Law no. 5411. The Court of Cassation quashed on 14 February 2008, fixing the offence date as 14 May 1999 (last harm to the bank). The acts originally constituted embezzlement under Art. 202 of the former Code, but Law no. 4389 was more favourable after Law no. 4603. The trial court had to compare Law no. 5411 and Art. 247 of the new Code.

On 17 June 2009 the trial court convicted the applicants of embezzlement under Art. 247 of the new Code (most favourable after comparing all relevant provisions), imposing ten years, ten months and twenty-five days’ imprisonment. Proceedings against B.E. were discontinued after his death. The applicants appealed, arguing that the court had ignored more favourable laws and that they could not be principal offenders of a “special offence” (embezzlement) because they were neither public officials nor bank members.

On 16 June 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the convictions, criticising the failure to apply Law no. 4389 or 5411 (post-offence but potentially more favourable per plenary case-law) yet declining to quash because no appeal had been lodged to the applicants’ detriment.

Embezzlement is a special offence requiring specific qualifications (public official or bank member). Under the new Code (Art. 40 § 2), unqualified participants may only be inciters or assistants; the former Code allowed co-principal or principal liability. Article 7 § 2 of the Criminal Code requires application of the most favourable provisions.

The case of Yeğer v. Turkey (Application no. 4099/12) centres on the applicant’s in-absentia conviction and resulting detention. İhya Tamer Yeğer, a Turkish national born in 1958, was convicted on 17 November 2009 by the Istanbul Criminal Court of First Instance of issuing an uncovered cheque under section 16(1) of Law no. 3167 (as then in force). He was sentenced in his absence to a judicial fine of 80,000 Turkish liras (approximately €36,364 at the time).

Throughout the proceedings the trial court could not notify the applicant in person of the indictment, hearings or any decisions. Service was first attempted at the business address listed on the company’s specimen-signature document (where the applicant had been managing director). The documents were returned undelivered. Police inquiries then identified a residential address, which the court thereafter used.

On 31 July 2008 the writ of summons was served, pursuant to section 21 of the Notification Act, on the neighbourhood district chief (muhtar). Postal workers had observed that the applicant was at work, informed a neighbour (F.K.) of the attempted service and posted a notice. On 2 December 2009 the conviction judgment itself was served at the same residential address under section 35 of the Notification Act, a notice being affixed to the building door. The judgment became final on 10 December 2009, no appeal having been lodged.

The unpaid fine was converted into a term of imprisonment by the Istanbul public prosecutor on 12 April 2010. Subsequent police efforts in January 2011 to locate the applicant for execution of sentence produced no trace at the business address (a neighbour of twenty years had never heard of him) and confirmation from the building manager that the applicant had left the residential address three years earlier because of debts.

The applicant was arrested on 30 March 2011 and began serving the prison term. On 25 April 2011 he wrote to the trial court requesting a retrial, asserting that he had been abroad from July 2008 until July 2009 and had therefore received no documents. The court rejected the request on 3 May 2011, holding that both the summons and the judgment had been validly served at his last-known address and that he had simply failed to appear. An objection was dismissed by the Istanbul Assize Court on 6 June 2011 in a summary ruling containing no case-specific reasoning; the applicant’s lawyer was notified on 2 August 2011.

On 30 May 2011 the applicant’s lawyer applied to have the conviction declared void, repeating that the applicant had been unaware of the proceedings because of his prolonged absence abroad. The application was dismissed on 6 October 2011 because the seven-day time-limit for an ordinary appeal under Article 315 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure had expired. No further appeal was lodged.

The applicant was released on 3 February 2012 after legislative amendments removed imprisonment as a penalty for issuing an uncovered cheque.

These facts underpin the complaints that the criminal proceedings were unfair (Article 6 § 1) because the applicant was tried and convicted without personal notification, was denied a fresh determination of the merits once he became aware of the case, and was refused leave to appeal out of time, and that the ensuing detention was therefore unlawful (Article 5 § 1).

The ECtHR case Boboc and Others v. Moldova (no. 44592/16) concerns the death of 24-year-old Valeriu Boboc, beaten by police during the 7-8 April 2009 post-election protests in Chișinău, and the ensuing investigation. After the 5 April 2009 elections (narrowly won by the ruling Communist Party), protests against alleged fraud began on 6 April. On 7 April some 5,000-6,000 people gathered; the initially peaceful demonstration turned violent after poorly planned police interventions. Several hundred protesters occupied lower floors of the Presidential Palace and Parliament, looting and causing fires.

Around 1 a.m. on 8 April, police and special forces (uniformed and plain-clothed) launched a mass operation to restore order. According to a later parliamentary commission, excessive force was used and everyone remaining in the square was arrested irrespective of violent conduct. Arrests and beatings continued for days.

Boboc had been peacefully protesting. Around 00:50 a.m. on 8 April, officers surrounded approximately 50 protesters, ordered them to the ground and beat them. Relatives had no information for days. At 1:30 a.m. his body was found near Chișinău’s emergency hospital. Ambulance staff, directed by a uniformed officer to a Ministry of Interior vehicle, found the body in the boot; when they declared him dead the officer dropped it and left. The body showed visible head injuries.

An initial official conclusion (announced by the Prosecutor General and Health Minister) attributed death to poisoning by an unknown toxic agent. A forensic examination (8 April–14 May 2009) noted sudden death, injuries inflicted 1–2 hours beforehand (including neck and thoracic trauma affecting the vagus nerve and carotid sinus, plus a broken rib with pulmonary contusion), and acute cardiovascular insufficiency from force applied to reflexogenic throat areas. After public, NGO and EU pressure, a second examination (involving British expert Professor Derrick Pounder, certified 9 July 2009) found multiple blunt-force injuries to the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, lower body and limbs, typical of a person lying on the ground being kicked and struck with batons. These injuries, inflicted shortly before death, caused it; no toxins or contributing health problems were present.

Witnesses (including D., R.T. and I.D.) described seeing Boboc beaten by uniformed officers, plain-clothes personnel and special-forces members in balaclavas, with blows continuing after he became unresponsive. One officer (I.P.) was identified from Government-building security footage as the first to strike him. He was charged with causing serious bodily harm resulting in death; his case was separated in May 2010. After an initial acquittal he was convicted in 2015 and sentenced to 10 years, but absconded.

The main investigation into the death remained at the investigative stage and was suspended in 2013. Parallel probes examined high-ranking officials who ordered the operation and (separately) former Interior Minister G.P. and Chișinău police chief V.B. for negligence; both were acquitted in 2015. Applicants (Boboc’s parents and widow) were denied injured-party successor status and file access in all but I.P.’s case; video footage was first examined only in March 2010. The Court held that the force used was not absolutely necessary (substantive Article 2 violation) and that the investigation was ineffective (procedural Article 2 violation).

On 7 April a demonstration of 5,000-6,000 people turned violent after poorly planned police interventions; protesters occupied and looted parts of the Presidential Palace and Parliament buildings.

The applicants stated that Boboc was peacefully protesting when, at approximately 00:50 a.m., officers surrounded about 50 people, ordered them to the ground, and beat them. His family had no news of him for days.

At 1:30 a.m. on 8 April his body was found near a hospital. Ambulance staff reported being stopped by a uniformed officer who directed them to a Ministry of Interior vehicle whose boot contained the body of a man in his thirties with visible head injuries. When told the man was dead, the officer dropped the body and left. An initial official conclusion, publicised by prosecutors and the Health Minister, attributed death to poisoning by an unknown toxin.

A May 2009 forensic report noted sudden death from acute cardiovascular insufficiency caused by force applied to the throat (closed trauma to the neck and thorax, haemorrhages, a broken rib and pulmonary contusion) inflicted 1-2 hours earlier, though it could not fully exclude other factors. After public and international pressure, the body was exhumed. A July 2009 report by Moldovan experts and British professor Derrick Pounder found multiple injuries to the head, neck, chest, abdomen, lower body and limbs caused by blunt objects (kicks and strikes with flexible implements such as batons) while the victim lay on the ground; these were the cause of death. No toxins or relevant pre-existing conditions were present. The applicants obtained the report only in February 2010 after repeated requests.

Witnesses (including D., R.T. and I.D.) described seeing Boboc beaten by several officers (some in black uniforms and balaclavas) with batons, rifle butts and kicks while he lay unresponsive on the ground; an officer later ordered the beatings stopped because “there was already one person dead.” One officer (I.P.) was identified from security-camera footage and charged with causing serious bodily harm resulting in death. After an initial acquittal he was convicted on appeal in 2015 and sentenced to ten years, but absconded. Separate investigations into high-ranking officials who allegedly ordered the operation and into the former Interior Minister and Chișinău police chief for negligence ended in acquittals; the applicants were denied victim-successor status and access to most files. The main investigation remained at the pre-trial stage and was suspended in 2013.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 2 violations: use of lethal force that was not absolutely necessary against a protester, and an ineffective investigation marked by delays, restricted family participation, incomplete identification of perpetrators and failure to examine command responsibility.

The case concerns the death of Valeriu Boboc (aged 24), son of the first two applicants and husband of the third, during post-election protests in Chișinău in April 2009, and the subsequent investigation.

Following 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections, protests against alleged fraud began on 6 April and resumed on 7 April with 5,000–6,000 participants. Initially peaceful, the demonstration turned violent after poorly planned police and fire-service interventions. Around 250 protesters occupied and looted the lower floors of the Presidential Palace and Parliament buildings, setting fires.

At approximately 1 a.m. on 8 April, police and special forces launched a large-scale operation to restore order. Excessive force was used; all remaining persons in the square were arrested regardless of involvement. Media later showed ongoing beatings and arrests by uniformed and plain-clothes officers.

According to the applicants, Boboc was peacefully protesting. At around 00:50 a.m. on 8 April, police surrounded some 50 protesters, ordered them to the ground and beat them. Relatives had no news of him for days.

At 1:30 a.m. his body was found near Chișinău’s Municipal Clinical Emergency Hospital. Ambulance staff testified they had been stopped by a uniformed officer and shown a body in the boot of a Ministry of Interior vehicle. When they confirmed death, the officer dropped the body and left.

An initial official statement claimed death by poisoning with an unknown toxic agent. A subsequent forensic examination (8 April–14 May 2009) found the exact cause undetermined but noted sudden death and life-threatening injuries (closed neck trauma, thoracic haemorrhages affecting the vagus nerve and carotid sinus, broken rib with pulmonary contusion) inflicted 1–2 hours earlier. Death resulted from acute cardiovascular insufficiency caused by force applied to reflexogenic throat areas.

After public pressure, the body was exhumed. A joint Moldovan–British forensic report (certified 9 July 2009) established multiple blunt-force injuries to the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, lower body and limbs, consistent with kicks and baton blows while the victim lay on the ground. The injuries, inflicted shortly before death, were the cause of death. No toxic substances or relevant pre-existing conditions were found.

Witnesses (including D., R.T. and I.D.) described seeing Boboc beaten by several officers—uniformed, plain-clothes and special-forces personnel in balaclavas—who continued striking him even after he ceased reacting. One officer (I.P.) was identified from security-camera footage as the first to hit him.

A criminal investigation into intentional grievous bodily harm resulting in death was opened on 8 April 2009. I.P. was later charged separately, convicted in 2015 of causing the injuries that led to death and sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment, but absconded. Parallel inquiries into high-ranking officials for ordering the operation or for negligence ended in acquittals. The main investigation remained at the pre-trial stage and was suspended in 2013. The applicants were denied victim-successor status and access to most case files.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life): that lethal force used against Boboc was not absolutely necessary, and that the investigation into his death was ineffective.
001-217703:
The applicant, a Russian national of Chechen origin born in 1974, arrived in Lithuania in September 2001 without identity documents. He claimed to have fought alongside Chechen forces in the wars of 1994–1996 and 1999–2001, during which he was injured. In March 2001 Russian federal forces detained, beat and interrogated him; he thereafter went into hiding and fled, discarding a temporary identity certificate en route through Belarus. He applied for asylum, stating that he had never held a Russian passport.

In 2003 the Lithuanian authorities refused refugee status, finding his account of persecution insufficiently consistent, but granted a one-year temporary residence permit on humanitarian grounds because of the ongoing armed conflict in Chechnya and the lack of a safe internal-relocation alternative in Russia. An alien’s passport (a travel document) was issued the same year. Between 2004 and 2008 subsidiary protection and successive one-year residence permits were granted on the same general-risk grounds. A 2005 request for refugee status, based on a Russian newspaper article that listed the applicant among former Chechen fighters, was rejected; the courts held that the article did not establish a personal risk of persecution and noted that subsidiary protection already shielded him from return. In 2008, after five years of lawful residence, he obtained a five-year permanent residence permit, later renewed in 2013 and 2018. Alien’s passports continued to be issued until 2013.

In August 2018 the Migration Department refused a fresh application for an alien’s passport. It observed that the applicant was no longer a beneficiary of subsidiary protection, that his earlier status had been based on generalised violence rather than individual persecution, and that Russian passports could be obtained from the embassy (or online) by submitting an expired or lost passport together with proof of identity. Subsequent requests in 2018–2019 were likewise refused. The applicant argued that any contact with Russian authorities—whether in person or online—would disclose his identity, location and past as a fighter (already publicised in 2005), exposing him to persecution; he also claimed he should be treated as stateless because he had never applied for Russian citizenship. The authorities maintained that he remained a Russian national, that he had not demonstrated an objective impossibility of obtaining a Russian document, and that he must first apply to the embassy and be refused.

The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (January 2020) and the Supreme Administrative Court (February 2020) upheld the refusals. They emphasised that the applicant had not renewed subsidiary protection after 2008, that the 2005 article was outdated and unreliable, that no new evidence of personal risk had been adduced, and that an online application did not require direct contact with the Russian authorities. Domestic law permits an alien’s passport only where a foreign national holding a Lithuanian residence permit cannot, for objective reasons, obtain a travel document from his country of origin. EU law similarly requires Member States to issue travel documents to beneficiaries of subsidiary protection who cannot obtain a national passport.

The applicant complained that the refusal violated Article 8 of the Convention (private and family life) and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom to leave any country), given his long-term residence, family ties (including minor children in the United Kingdom) and occupational need to travel. The Court examined the case primarily under the latter provision.

The case of L.B. v. Lithuania (Application no. 38121/20) concerns a Russian national of Chechen origin, born in 1974 and living in Vilnius, who alleged that Lithuania’s refusal to re-issue him an alien’s passport violated his right to leave the country under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention (and, relatedly, Article 8). The applicant arrived in Lithuania in September 2001 without identity documents after fleeing the Chechen Republic via Belarus. He claimed to have fought in both Chechen wars (1994–1996 and 1999–2001), been injured, arrested, beaten and interrogated by Russian federal forces in March 2001, and then gone into hiding before leaving due to health and safety fears. He had never held a Russian passport, only a temporary identity certificate which he discarded in Belarus.

In 2003 the Migration Department and courts denied refugee status, citing inconsistencies in his account and lack of proof of persecution on Convention grounds, but granted a one-year temporary residence permit on humanitarian grounds because of the ongoing war and absence of internal relocation options in Russia. He received an alien’s passport that year after arguing that Russian authorities routinely refused such documents to Chechens. From 2004 to 2008 he was granted subsidiary protection annually on the same conflict-related grounds and issued successive temporary residence permits. A 2005 bid for refugee status, based on a Komsomolskaya Pravda article naming him as a former fighter, was rejected; the authorities found the article insufficient to establish a personal risk of persecution. In 2008 he obtained a permanent residence permit after five years of lawful stay; it was later renewed. Alien’s passports continued to be issued until 2013.

From August 2018 the Migration Department refused further alien’s passports. It noted that Russian nationals could apply online at the embassy in Lithuania with an expired/lost passport or proof of identity, and that the applicant’s earlier protection had been based on the war rather than persecution by the Russian state. He was no longer a current beneficiary of subsidiary protection (having not reapplied after 2008) and there was no evidence the Russian authorities knew of his prior status. The applicant repeatedly argued that contacting the Russian authorities—whether in person or online—would reveal his identity and location, exposing him to persecution as a publicly identified former fighter; a friend named in the same 2005 article had been convicted upon return. He also claimed he should be treated as stateless because he had never applied for Russian citizenship and supported Chechen independence. The Department rejected these points, noting his prior statements about a temporary certificate and possible lost passport, and later required proof of an actual refusal by the Russian embassy.

The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in January 2020, holding that prior asylum proceedings had already found no personal persecution risk, that he could apply online without direct contact, and that he had not even attempted to obtain Russian documents. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this in February 2020, describing his fears as unfounded and the 2005 article as outdated. The applicant emphasised his long residence (nearly 19 years), work in cargo transport requiring travel, and two minor children in the United Kingdom. Domestic law (Article 37 of the Law on the Legal Status of Aliens) permitted an alien’s passport only where a resident could not obtain a national travel document “for objective reasons.” EU instruments (Qualification Directive, Long-Term Residents Directive, Schengen rules) require travel documents for beneficiaries of subsidiary protection unable to obtain national passports and recognise that international-protection status does not automatically lapse upon grant of permanent residence. The Lithuanian authorities conducted no individualised assessment of the current situation in Russia, the practical accessibility of Russian passports for someone in the applicant’s position, or the proportionality of the restriction on his freedom of movement.

In 2008 the applicant obtained a five-year permanent residence permit on the basis of five years’ lawful stay; it was renewed in 2013 and 2018. Alien’s passports continued to be reissued until 2013. In August 2018, however, the Migration Department refused a further passport. It noted that Russian passports could be obtained from the embassy (or online) upon presentation of an expired or lost passport or other identity proof, and that the applicant’s earlier protection had been based on generalised wartime conditions rather than personal persecution. Subsequent requests in 2018–2019, in which the applicant emphasised his fear that any contact would reveal his location and past to the Russian authorities (citing the 2005 article and the reported fate of a co-listed friend), were likewise refused. The Department also rejected a claim of statelessness, pointing to his consistent treatment as a Russian national and his own earlier statements.

The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (January 2020) and the Supreme Administrative Court (February 2020) upheld the refusals. They observed that subsidiary protection had not been renewed after 2008, that the 2005 article was outdated and already assessed, that online application avoided direct contact, and that the applicant had never attempted to obtain a Russian document. He therefore lacked “objective reasons” for being unable to do so.

The applicant, who works in international cargo transport and has minor children in the United Kingdom, complained that the refusal prevented him from leaving Lithuania (Article 2 of Protocol No. 4) and interfered with his private and family life (Article 8). Lithuanian law prohibits departure without a valid travel document, and an alien’s passport is the only document available to him.

001-217759:
**Case of Ramiz Jafarov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 40424/12), ECtHR (Fifth Section), 16 June 2022 (final 16 September 2022).**

The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1954, graduated from Baku State University’s law faculty in 1977. He served in prosecution roles (investigator, deputy prosecutor, prosecutor) from 1 August 1977 to 1 September 2000 (23 years and 1 month), then as a judge until 28 July 2007. In April 2007, before reaching pensionable age, he applied to the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) for a special pension based on service with the prosecution authorities. The SSPF refused on 22 May 2007, citing failure to meet the 25-year statutory minimum.

On 20 November 2007 the applicant sued the SSPF, arguing that his five years of legal studies (1972–1977) and seven years as a judge should count toward the 25-year requirement. The Yasamal District Court partly allowed the claim on 17 December 2007, holding that judicial service should be included and awarding the pension from 1 January 2006. Appeals followed. On 7 May 2008 the Baku Court of Appeal adjusted the award (50% pension for part of the period, full thereafter). The Supreme Court remitted the case on 26 September 2008 for incorrect application of law.

Subsequent appellate judgments of 14 January 2009 and 26 August 2009 dismissed the claim, finding that studies could not be counted, the applicant had left prosecution service on his own initiative short of 25 years, and judicial service should not be added to prior prosecution service (rather the reverse). The Supreme Court remitted again on 21 April 2009 and 25 December 2009. A 3 February 2010 appellate judgment allowed the claim in full (counting both studies and judicial service, pension from 19 July 2001) and was upheld by the Supreme Court on 27 May 2010. After a cassation appeal by the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Plenum of the Supreme Court remitted on 11 November 2010. A further appellate dismissal occurred on 10 February 2011; the Supreme Court then issued a merits judgment on 8 June 2011 allowing judicial (but not study) years to count.

The Prosecutor General’s Office sought constitutional review. On 18 May 2012 the Constitutional Court held the 8 June 2011 decision contrary to relevant pension and service laws. It noted an unjustified distinction: years of judicial service could be added when transferring *to* prosecution but not vice versa, creating a privileged difference between similarly situated persons that lacked objective justification and engaged Article 14 of the Convention. It recommended legislative improvement of social-protection rules for prosecutors and judges and ordered reconsideration after such improvement. Parliament discussed but did not amend the legislation in 2013.

The Plenum of the Supreme Court remitted the case again on 30 October 2015. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the claim on 28 January 2016 for lack of entitlement under existing law; the Supreme Court upheld this on 6 March 2017.

The applicant alleged that the pension refusal violated his property rights (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) and was discriminatory (Article 14), and that the proceedings (lasting from November 2007 to March 2017) were excessively lengthy (Article 6 § 1). The Court gave notice of these complaints (declaring the remainder inadmissible) and, after considering observations, found a violation of Article 6 § 1 on account of the unreasonable length of the civil proceedings, which involved repeated remittals across multiple levels including the Constitutional Court. The judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention.

The facts highlight the applicant’s service history, the statutory 25-year threshold, courts’ conflicting interpretations of whether studies or subsequent judicial service could be aggregated, the Constitutional Court’s identification of an unrectified legislative disparity, and the protracted domestic litigation spanning nearly a decade with numerous quashings and remittals.

**CASE OF RAMIZ JAFAROV v. AZERBAIJAN (Application no. 40424/12), ECtHR (Fifth Section), Judgment of 16 June 2022 (final 16 September 2022)**

The applicant, Ramiz Jafarov (born 1954, resident in Baku), an Azerbaijani national, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 14 of the Convention that the refusal of a special pension for his service with the prosecution authorities violated his property rights and was discriminatory. He further complained under Article 6 of excessively lengthy domestic proceedings. The Court notified the Government of the length, property and discrimination complaints (declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible).

The applicant graduated from Baku State University’s law faculty in 1977. He held positions as investigator, deputy prosecutor and prosecutor from 1 August 1977 to 1 September 2000 (23 years and 1 month). He then served as a judge from 1 September 2000 to 28 July 2007. In April 2007, before reaching pensionable age (62 for men), he applied to the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) for a special pension based on prosecution service. The SSPF refused on 22 May 2007, stating he had not completed the then-required 25 years with the prosecution authorities.

On 20 November 2007 the applicant sued the SSPF, arguing that his five years of law studies (1972–1977) and seven years as a judge should be counted toward the 25-year threshold. The Yasamal District Court partly allowed the claim on 17 December 2007, holding that judicial service should be included and awarding a pension from 1 January 2006. After appeals, the Baku Court of Appeal on 7 May 2008 adjusted the award (50% pension for part of the period, full thereafter). The Supreme Court allowed the SSPF’s cassation appeal on 26 September 2008 and remitted the case.

Subsequent proceedings involved repeated remittals. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the claim on 14 January 2009 and again on 26 August 2009, finding the applicant had only 23 years and 1 month of prosecution service, had left that service voluntarily to become a judge, that studies could not be counted, and that judicial years could not be added to prior prosecution service (the reverse being possible under the law). The Supreme Court remitted again on 21 April 2009 and 25 December 2009. On 3 February 2010 the Court of Appeal allowed the claim in full (counting studies and judicial service, pension from 19 July 2001); the Supreme Court upheld this on 27 May 2010.

Following an additional cassation by the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Plenum of the Supreme Court quashed those decisions on 11 November 2010 and remitted. The Court of Appeal dismissed again on 10 February 2011. On 8 June 2011 the Supreme Court partly allowed the claim (excluding studies but including judicial service). At the Prosecutor General’s request, the Constitutional Court on 18 May 2012 held that the 8 June 2011 decision conflicted with Article 32.5 of the Law on Service with the Prosecution Authorities and Article 9.4.1 of the Law on Work Pensions. It observed an unjustified distinction: years of judicial service could be added if transferring into the prosecution authorities, but not vice versa, creating a privileged difference without objective justification, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention. It recommended legislative improvement to Parliament (which discussed but did not amend the laws in 2013) and directed reconsideration after such improvement.

The Plenum of the Supreme Court remitted again on 30 October 2015. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the claim on 28 January 2016 (no entitlement under domestic law). The Supreme Court upheld this on 6 March 2017, ending the proceedings.

Relevant law (at the material time) required 25 years of prosecution service for the special old-age pension (Law on Service with the Prosecution Authorities, Art. 32.4; Law on Work Pensions, Art. 9.4.1). Article 32.5 provided for adding prosecution years to subsequent judicial or other service, and (under Prosecutor General procedure) adding incoming service from those bodies to prosecution years, but not the reverse for outgoing prosecutors who became judges. The applicant’s proceedings lasted from November 2007 to March 2017 (over nine years), with multiple remittals, quashings and a Constitutional Court interlude. These facts underpin the complaints of excessive length, denial of a claimed pension as a possession, and discrimination in pension entitlement compared with persons transferring in the opposite direction.

The case of Ramiz Jafarov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 40424/12) was brought by an Azerbaijani national born in 1954. He alleged that the refusal of a special pension for his prosecution service violated his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and was discriminatory under Article 14 of the Convention. He further complained under Article 6 of the excessive length of the related domestic proceedings.

The applicant graduated from Baku State University’s law faculty in 1977. He held investigator, deputy prosecutor and prosecutor posts from 1 August 1977 to 1 September 2000 (23 years and one month). He then served as a judge from 1 September 2000 until 28 July 2007.

In April 2007, before reaching the then-pensionable age of 62, he applied to the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) for a special pension requiring 25 years’ prosecution service. The SSPF refused on 22 May 2007, stating he lacked the statutory minimum.

On 20 November 2007 he sued, arguing that his five years of legal studies (1972–1977) and seven years as a judge should count toward the 25-year threshold. The Yasamal District Court partly allowed the claim on 17 December 2007, holding that judicial service should be included and awarding a pension from 1 January 2006. Both parties appealed. The Baku Court of Appeal on 7 May 2008 confirmed the inclusion of judicial years and awarded 50 % of the pension from 1 August 2002 to 27 June 2007 and the full amount thereafter.

The Supreme Court remitted the case on 26 September 2008. Subsequent appellate judgments in January and August 2009 dismissed the claim, finding that studies could not be counted and that judicial service should not be added to earlier prosecution service; the Supreme Court remitted both times. On 3 February 2010 the Court of Appeal allowed the claim in full, counting both studies and judicial years and awarding a pension from 19 July 2001; this was initially upheld but later quashed by the Plenum of the Supreme Court. Further judgments followed in 2011: an appellate dismissal and a Supreme Court ruling of 8 June 2011 that counted judicial but not study years.

At the Prosecutor General’s request the Constitutional Court, on 18 May 2012, declared the 8 June 2011 decision contrary to the relevant statutes. It observed an unjustified distinction: service years of a former judge joining the prosecution service were counted, whereas the reverse (prosecutor becoming a judge without 25 years) was not. The Court recommended that Parliament amend the social-security legislation for prosecutors and judges in light of Article 14, and ordered reconsideration after such reform.

Parliament discussed the matter in 2013 but made no change. The Plenum of the Supreme Court remitted the case in October 2015. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the claim on 28 January 2016; the Supreme Court upheld that dismissal on 6 March 2017.

The proceedings thus lasted from November 2007 to March 2017—more than nine years—through repeated remittals. Domestic law (Article 32 of the 2001 Law on Service with the Prosecution Authorities and Article 9 of the 2006 Law on Work Pensions) required 25 years’ prosecution service for the special pension and provided for counting of certain transfers, but not in the manner the applicant sought.

The European Court of Human Rights ultimately examined the length complaint under Article 6 § 1, finding the duration excessive.

The case of Haščák v. Slovakia (Applications nos. 58359/12 and 2 others) arose from a 2005–2006 surveillance operation by the Slovak Intelligence Service (SIS), later publicly known as “Gorilla.” The applicant, a prominent Slovak businessman associated with an influential finance group and partner of Zoltán Varga (the subject of a related ECHR judgment), alleged that two warrants issued by the Bratislava Regional Court (BRC) on 23 November 2005 and 18 May 2006 unlawfully interfered with his private life. The first warrant targeted Varga and meetings in his flat; the second appeared to target another person whom the applicant believed to be himself. Implementation involved audio surveillance of the flat, generating primary material (recordings and transcripts) and derivative material (summaries and analytical notes).

Domestic authorities accepted that the SIS destroyed the primary material on 2 April 2008 because it yielded nothing useful to the operation. Derivative material, however, remains archived by the SIS under section 17(6) of the SIS Act “in a way that excluded access to it by anyone except a court,” pursuant to confidential internal rules issued by the SIS Director (section 17(8)). Related BRC files were later destroyed after their statutory archiving period expired. In December 2011 an anonymous online text—purportedly an SIS analytical summary of the recordings—described meetings involving the applicant and others that allegedly coordinated massive corruption in the privatisation of strategic state enterprises. The applicant’s name appeared more than 800 times. In 2018 a digital audio track matching this text was seized in an unrelated search and forwarded to a corruption investigation (“the Gorilla investigation”). A similar recording was posted online in 2019. Authenticity has never been officially confirmed, though the Prosecutor General later indicated grounds to believe the 2018 recording originated from the SIS operation.

The applicant was never charged in the Gorilla investigation (opened January 2012 against persons unknown) but was repeatedly questioned as a witness. He contends the inquiry is in substance directed at him and his companies. Public statements by the Interior Minister and investigators referring to “organised groups” and “finance groups” were, in his view, identifiable as referring to him, violating the presumption of innocence. A 2020 charge of operating a corporate cover-up to compensate a former SIS agent for leaking Gorilla material was quashed in 2021 for lack of evidence; that investigation remains open.

The applicant pursued multiple remedies: requests to the SIS for destruction of all material, complaints to the Government Office and Parliament, administrative-law actions (dismissed because the SIS is not a public-administration body), and constitutional complaints (joined with Varga’s). The Constitutional Court (6 October 2015) held that primary recordings had already been destroyed, that statute did not require destruction of “data extracted from the recordings,” and that such material could not lawfully be used as evidence. It found no jurisdiction to supervise SIS implementation of warrants and rejected remaining claims as moot or res judicata. Parallel civil actions seeking destruction and non-use of the material remain pending, with courts divided on whether the SIS or the State can be ordered to act. The applicant also complained of the length of the Gorilla investigation and the absence of an effective remedy.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 8 (private life) concerning the warrants’ implementation, retention of derivative material under secret internal rules without external control, lack of clarity in jurisdictional rules, and absence of safeguards for persons randomly affected; Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 (reasonable-time requirement and presumption of innocence); and Article 13 (effective remedy).

Derivative material remained archived under section 17(6) of the SIS Act (inaccessible except to a court) pursuant to classified internal rules issued by the SIS Director. Related court files were destroyed in 2016–2017 after the statutory archiving period.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 8 interference (unfettered SIS surveillance powers without adequate safeguards, unclear jurisdictional rules, flawed implementation, and unsupervised retention of derivative material under confidential internal rules, lacking a lawful basis after the warrants’ annulment in related proceedings). The case of Haščák v. Slovakia (ECtHR Applications nos. 58359/12, 27787/16 and 67667/16) arose from a 2005–2006 audio-surveillance operation by the Slovak Intelligence Service (SIS), later known as “Gorilla.” Two warrants issued by the Bratislava Regional Court authorised monitoring of a flat belonging to businessman Zoltán Varga and of meetings held there; the second warrant also targeted another individual whom the applicant, Varga’s business partner and a prominent financier, believed to be himself.

Implementation produced primary recordings (destroyed by the SIS on 2 April 2008 as containing nothing of operational value) and derivative material (summaries and analytical notes). The latter remains archived by the SIS under s. 17(6) of the SIS Act, accessible solely to a court and governed by a classified internal regulation issued by the SIS Director. Related court files were later destroyed after their statutory retention period expired.

In December 2011 an anonymous internet posting purported to be an SIS analytical summary of conversations recorded in the flat. It described alleged large-scale corruption surrounding the privatisation of state assets and mentioned the applicant more than 800 times. In 2018 a digital audio file matching the posted text was seized in an unrelated search and transferred to a corruption investigation (“the Gorilla investigation”). Copies have since circulated in other inquiries. Although official confirmation of authenticity is lacking, the material is widely treated as connected to the operation. The Prosecutor General later indicated grounds for believing the 2018 recording originated from the SIS surveillance.

Three investigations followed: (i) possible SIS failure to transmit intelligence and abuse of authority (no charges outstanding); (ii) the ongoing Gorilla corruption inquiry, in which the applicant has been questioned only as a witness but regards himself as a central suspect; and (iii) alleged slander by the Interior Minister (terminated without charge). Public statements by the Minister and investigators suggested the leaked material had a factual basis and referred to organised crime involving “certain finance groups,” statements the applicant considers identifiable as targeting him.

The applicant sought destruction of all surveillance products through requests to the SIS, complaints to government and parliamentary bodies, administrative-law actions and civil proceedings under the State Liability Act and personal-integrity rules. Most were unsuccessful: courts held they lacked jurisdiction to issue orders to the SIS, and the Constitutional Court (2015) declared the complaints largely moot or res judicata, noting that primary recordings had already been destroyed and that the statute did not require destruction of derivative material, which could never be used officially. Parallel constitutional complaints alleging violation of the presumption of innocence and excessive length of the Gorilla investigation were rejected for lack of standing, the applicant never having been formally charged.

In 2020 the applicant was charged with operating a corporate scheme to compensate a former SIS agent for leaking Gorilla material; those charges were quashed in 2021 by the Prosecutor General for want of supporting evidence. Related proceedings remain pending.

The ECtHR examined complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13 concerning the warrants’ implementation, retention of derivative material, absence of safeguards against abuse, alleged leaks, and lack of effective remedies. It found, in particular, that the SIS had exercised practically unfettered power without adequate legal safeguards, that jurisdictional rules were unclear and poorly applied, that storage of derivative material was subject only to confidential internal rules without external control, and that there was no lawful basis for the implementation of the warrants or the continued retention of the material.

The case of Drousiotis v. Cyprus (Application no. 42315/15) arose from civil defamation proceedings against Cypriot journalist Makarios Drousiotis over a 10 March 2005 article in the newspaper Politis. Drousiotis, who wrote a political commentary column, alleged that the domestic courts’ judgment violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

The background concerned S.P., a high-ranking attorney in the Law Office of the Republic. In 2001, the Public Service Commission ordered his compulsory retirement on the Attorney General’s recommendation. The Supreme Court set this aside in 2003, reinstating S.P. In January 2005 the Council of Ministers extended his service by one year for reasons of public interest, citing the earlier unlawful removal. This decision provoked public controversy. Earlier Politis articles and other media reports highlighted political inconsistency: parties that had previously opposed extensions of retired officials now supported this one. Critics, including politicians and a trade union, described it as a scandal involving clientelism, favouritism and a failure to consult the Attorney General.

Drousiotis’s article, titled “The regime (of the south) promotes paranoia,” criticised the extension as secret, unrequested by S.P.’s superior, and contrary to past practice. It asserted that S.P. had obtained it by “kissing up” to D.C. (President of the House of Representatives), who was preparing him for the Attorney General post as part of a broader political quid pro quo. The piece quoted an excerpt from S.P.’s lengthy book, calling it a “monument of incoherence and turbulent thought,” and implied S.P. was paranoid and unfit for public office. It accused the government of insulting common sense, promoting paranoia, and engaging in favouritism and gerontocracy.

S.P. sued Drousiotis and the publisher on 30 March 2005, claiming the article was written in bad faith to harm his reputation as an attorney, writer and commentator. Drousiotis argued that the piece contributed to a matter of public interest, used strong language to shock readers and criticise governmental inconsistency, and was based on publicly known facts, including S.P.’s own statements and writings.

On 4 May 2011 the Nicosia District Court found the article defamatory. It held that the piece contained factual allegations (not mere comments) implying that S.P. had secured the extension through flattery in a political deal and portraying him as paranoid and unsuited to public office. The court described the tone as aggressive, mocking and ironic, exceeding what was reasonably appropriate. It awarded EUR 25,000 in damages plus costs of EUR 3,472.59 (with interest and VAT), jointly and severally against Drousiotis and the publisher, taking into account S.P.’s serious position, the gravity of the defamation, the absence of an apology and the newspaper’s circulation of 6,697 copies that day.

Drousiotis appealed, reiterating that the article constituted protected political speech on a public-interest matter and that the damages were excessive. On 6 March 2015 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It accepted that S.P. was a public figure who, through his writings, had laid himself open to scrutiny, but found that the article had not merely criticised the book or other politicians; instead it had presented S.P. as paranoid and unfit, using insults and a selective quotation to mock him. The court saw no reason to alter the damages award.

The publisher paid the full sums. Drousiotis maintained that the courts had failed to strike a proper balance, placing excessive weight on the language used while giving insufficient consideration to the public-interest context, and that the unusually large award risked chilling open discussion of matters of public concern.

The case of Drousiotis v. Cyprus concerns a journalist's Article 10 complaint over a civil defamation judgment. Applicant Makarios Drousiotis, a political commentator for the daily newspaper Politis, published an article on 10 March 2005 titled “The regime (of the south) promotes paranoia.” This followed controversy over the Council of Ministers' 20 January 2005 decision to extend by one year the service of S.P., a high-ranking attorney in the Law Office of the Republic, beyond retirement age, citing public interest. S.P. had been compulsorily retired in 2001 on the Attorney General's recommendation, but the Supreme Court set aside that decision in 2003 and reinstated him. The extension occurred amid political debate, including criticism of inconsistency by coalition parties that had previously opposed employing retirees, suggestions of clientelism, and reports that the Attorney General had not been consulted (he was reportedly abroad).

The article accused the government of secrecy and disrespect for institutions, claiming the Attorney General neither requested nor was informed of the extension. It portrayed S.P. as having requested the extension himself on personal fairness grounds (having joined late, at age 33). It alleged the extension occurred because S.P. was “kissing up” to D.C., President of the House of Representatives (who was purportedly preparing S.P. for Attorney General), as part of a “quid pro quo” political deal with President T.P. The piece quoted a short excerpt from S.P.'s 1,482-page book The Falsified Annan Plan and Rosemary’s Baby (presented by D.C.), describing it as a “monument of incoherence and turbulent thought.” It concluded that the “regime” spat on logic, insulted common sense, and promoted paranoia, with S.P. meeting “patriotic criteria” as an opponent of the Annan Plan.

S.P. sued Drousiotis and the publisher in March 2005, claiming the article was written in bad faith to damage his reputation as an attorney, writer, and public commentator, especially given his potential Attorney General candidacy (he later became Deputy Attorney General in 2008). Drousiotis argued the piece contributed to public debate on a matter of political (not merely legal) interest involving a public figure; strong language was intended to shock and highlight governmental inconsistency and institutional disrespect, based on contemporaneous reports and S.P.'s own statements/book. He maintained “kissing up” reflected a close relationship (D.C. presented S.P.'s books, shared political views, and had criticised S.P.'s earlier retirement).

The Nicosia District Court (2011) found the article defamatory. It held that statements were factual allegations, not protected comment: the “kissing up” claim created the impression that S.P. secured the extension through flattery as part of a political bargain, and the book excerpt implied S.P. himself was paranoid and unfit for office. The tone was aggressive, mocking, and ironic, exceeding reasonable criticism of the decision or politicians involved. Damages of €25,000 (plus interest and costs of €3,472.59 plus VAT) were awarded jointly and severally, considering S.P.'s senior position, the defamation's seriousness, lack of apology, circulation (6,697 copies), and absence of aggravating factors.

The Supreme Court (2015) dismissed the appeal, upholding the findings. It recognised S.P. as a public figure through his writings, who had invited scrutiny, but held the article unduly harmed his honour by presenting him as paranoid and unfit rather than merely criticising the book or politicians. References were treated as factual allegations or insults, not value judgments. The damages award was confirmed. The publisher paid all sums.

These facts framed the alleged Article 10 violation: the domestic courts' characterisation of the statements, their balancing of reputation against expression in a political debate, and the size of the award.

The case of Drousiotis v. Cyprus concerned journalist Makarios Drousiotis’s complaint under Article 10 ECHR that a Cypriot defamation judgment against him for a newspaper article violated his freedom of expression.

S.P. was a high-ranking attorney in Cyprus’s Law Office. In 2001 the Public Service Commission compulsorily retired him on the Attorney General’s recommendation. In 2003 the Supreme Court set that decision aside and reinstated him. In January 2005 the Council of Ministers, at S.P.’s request, extended his service by one year on public-interest grounds, citing the period he had been unlawfully removed.

On 9 March 2005 Politis published an article criticising the extension as politically inconsistent: parties now supporting the government (AKEL and DIKO) had previously opposed employing retired officials, viewing it as favouritism. The article called the decision legally valid but politically wrong. S.P. responded that the piece aimed to disrupt his possible appointment as Attorney General. Other reports quoted politicians and a union calling the decision a scandal, clientelistic, and taken without consulting the Attorney General.

The next day Drousiotis published “The regime (of the south) promotes paranoia.” It stated the extension had been approved in secret without the Attorney General’s knowledge or request, showing disrespect for institutions. It called the government the most unreliable Cyprus had known, accused S.P. of “kissing up” to D.C. (President of the House of Representatives) who was grooming him for Attorney General, and portrayed the extension as part of a broader political quid pro quo. It mocked an excerpt from S.P.’s 1,482-page book as a “monument of incoherence and turbulent thought” and concluded that the “regime” spat on logic and promoted paranoia.

S.P. sued Drousiotis and the publisher for defamation, claiming the article was written in bad faith to harm his professional and personal reputation. Drousiotis argued the piece contributed to public debate on a matter of public interest involving a public figure, criticised government inconsistency rather than making factual allegations, and used strong language to shock readers. He said “kissing up” described a close relationship evidenced by D.C. presenting S.P.’s books, shared political views, and S.P.’s praise of D.C.

In May 2011 the Nicosia District Court found the article defamatory. It rejected Drousiotis’s explanations, holding that the piece alleged S.P. had obtained the extension by flattery, portrayed him as paranoid and unfit for public office, and used an aggressive, mocking tone that exceeded reasonable criticism. It awarded €25,000 damages plus costs and interest, considering S.P.’s senior position, the seriousness of the statements, the lack of apology, and circulation of 6,697 copies.

The Supreme Court dismissed Drousiotis’s appeal in March 2015. It accepted S.P. was a public figure open to scrutiny because of his writings, but held the article attacked his honour by presenting him as paranoid rather than merely criticising the book or the politicians involved. The references were treated as factual allegations or insults, not value judgments. The damages award was left unchanged. The publisher paid the sums in full.

(The ECHR later found a violation of Article 10 on the grounds that the domestic courts had given insufficient reasons, over-emphasised the language used without properly balancing competing rights, and awarded an unusually large sum capable of chilling public debate.)

The European Court of Human Rights case A.B. and Others v. Poland (no. 42907/17) involved six Russian nationals of Chechen origin—a married couple (A.B. and A.E.), their three minor children, and A.K. (in a domestic partnership with the couple)—who sought international protection at the Terespol Polish-Belarusian border crossing. Between 21 February and 14 April 2017 they appeared there on 24 occasions, and on eight further dates in April–May 2017 they carried written asylum applications. They told border guards they had fled Chechnya after the first applicant and his father were persecuted by the Kadyrov regime: threats to confiscate the family farm, accusations of supporting terrorism, multiple arrests and torture, and subsequent terrorism charges that forced the father to surrender the farm. They stated they could not remain in Belarus (where genuine protection was unavailable) and risked chain-refoulement to Russia, where they faced torture and inhuman treatment.

Polish Border Guard officers consistently refused to accept the oral or written applications and issued administrative refusal-of-entry decisions. Official notes recorded only economic or personal motives—desire to work in Europe, loss of the family business, lack of jobs in Chechnya, better prospects for the children, and reunion with relatives already in Poland—and asserted that the applicants had never mentioned persecution. The applicants did not appeal these decisions.

On 16 June 2017, while the applicants were again at the border, their lawyer requested an interim measure under Rule 39. The Court indicated that they should not be removed to Belarus until 30 June and notified the Polish Government before the scheduled expulsion. They were nevertheless returned at 11.25 a.m.; the official note again cited only economic reasons. On 19 June they returned with a copy of the Court’s letter and a written application, explicitly requesting protection; their lawyer simultaneously transmitted the documents by e-mail, fax and ePUAP to the Border Guard and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They were again turned back; official notes denied any asylum request.

The Government later asked the Court to lift the measure, claiming the applicants had never sought protection and were abusing the procedure. The Court instead extended it until 21 July, observing that the applicants had tried to lodge a request. After the applicants left the border area and returned to Russia the measure was discontinued.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: repeated refusal to register asylum claims and summary removals exposing the applicants to chain-refoulement and ill-treatment (Article 3), a systemic practice of misrepresenting statements, collective expulsion through a policy of blanket refusal of entry that disregarded protection intentions (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4), absence of an effective domestic remedy (Article 13), and hindrance of the right of individual petition by non-compliance with the interim measure (Article 34).

The case of A.B. and Others v. Poland concerns six Russian nationals of Chechen origin (a married couple, their three minor children, and a woman in a domestic partnership with them) who repeatedly sought to enter Poland from Belarus to apply for international protection. Between 21 February and 14 April 2017 they presented themselves at the Terespol border crossing on 24 occasions.
