They explained they could not remain in Belarus, where they had no realistic prospect of protection and faced onward removal to Russia.

Despite these statements, the Border Guard issued refusal-of-entry decisions on every occasion, recording that the applicants possessed no valid entry documents and had expressed only economic or personal motives (desire to work in Europe, loss of the family business, lack of jobs in Chechnya, a better future for the children, and family already in Poland). Official notes systematically omitted any mention of persecution or asylum. The applicants did not appeal those decisions.

In April–May 2017 they made eight further attempts, this time carrying a written asylum application which they tried to lodge. They were again turned back. On 16 June 2017, while they were at the border, their lawyer requested an interim measure under Rule 39. The Court granted it at 10:48 a.m., instructing Poland not to remove them to Belarus until 30 June because of the risk of chain-refoulement to Chechnya and ill-treatment. The Government was notified before the scheduled expulsion, yet the applicants were returned at 11:25 a.m.; the official note again cited only economic reasons.

On 19 June they returned with a copy of the Court’s letter and a fresh written application, which they handed over while verbally requesting protection. Simultaneously a Polish lawyer transmitted the same application by e-mail, fax and ePUAP to the Terespol Border Guard post, its Warsaw headquarters and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, expressly invoking the interim measure. They were nevertheless refused entry; official notes once more recorded only economic motives. The Government later claimed no asylum request had been made.

On 23 June the Government asked the Court to lift the Rule 39 measure, asserting that the applicants had never sought protection and were abusing the procedure. The Court instead extended the measure until 21 July, noting the documentary evidence of their attempts. The applicants subsequently left the border area and returned to Russia; the measure was discontinued on 19 July.

These events form the factual core of the alleged violations: repeated refusal to register asylum claims, systematic misrepresentation of the applicants’ statements, summary removals exposing them to a real risk of torture or inhuman treatment (Article 3), a wider policy of collective expulsion disregarding individual protection claims (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4), the absence of any effective domestic remedy (Article 13), and non-compliance with the Court’s interim measure that hindered their right of individual petition (Article 34).

The case concerns the death of Ms A.T. (born 1947), who suffered from schizophrenia since 1964 and retained legal capacity despite repeated hospitalisations. Her mother (the applicant) alleged that Russia breached its Article 2 positive obligations through deficient regulation of clinical trials, inadequate informed-consent safeguards for a mentally ill participant, and an insufficient investigation.

In 2004 the Ethics Committee approved a Phase-III double-blind trial (protocol 25517) comparing the experimental antipsychotic asenapine with olanzapine. The patient leaflet warned of unforeseeable side-effects (including possible psychiatric aggravation and, for olanzapine, potentially fatal neuroleptic syndrome), required regular monitoring (weekly then monthly visits, ECGs and blood tests) and stipulated that participants must be in satisfactory general health. A second, longer-term trial (protocol 25520) was approved in 2005 for those who had completed the first year.

On 19 December 2004 A.T.’s treating psychiatrist invited her to join the first trial; she signed a consent form incorporating the leaflet. She began asenapine on 27 December 2004. Documented side-effects included worsening psychosis, agitation, insomnia and weight gain. In May 2005 she was hospitalised after an acute exacerbation. While still an in-patient she signed a second consent form on 26 December 2005. On 10 April 2006 she suffered cardiac and respiratory arrest, remained comatose and died four days later. Autopsy recorded advanced atherosclerosis, cardiosclerosis, acute cardiovascular failure, pneumonia, cerebral oedema and brain herniation.

The St Petersburg Healthcare Committee (September 2006) found the trials compliant, consent freely given and no direct causal link to asenapine; it attributed the coma possibly to pulmonary embolism linked to long-term neuroleptic use and vascular disease.

A criminal inquiry produced three expert reports (January 2007, April and December 2009). They identified multiple breaches of Good Clinical Practice: no recorded monitoring of cardiac or hepatic function despite asenapine’s known cardiotoxicity; only one ECG (taken after collapse); visits every three or four days instead of the required daily observation of a new drug; no pulse, blood-pressure, temperature or laboratory data in the file; and continuation into the second trial despite side-effects that should have prompted exclusion. The experts found an indirect causal contribution of these omissions to the fatal deterioration (undiagnosed pneumonia plus latent heart disease). Intensive-care treatment after collapse was deemed correct.

On 31 December 2009 the investigator refused to open a criminal case, citing A.T.’s written consents, the absence of a direct causal link and proper resuscitation. Domestic courts upheld the refusal.

Domestic law (1998 Medicines Act and 2003 Clinical Practice Rules) required ethics-committee approval, written informed consent after adequate information, free withdrawal, medical supervision, and interruption of a trial if danger to participants emerged. The applicant maintained that these guarantees had not been implemented and that the investigation had been inadequate.

The case of Traskunova v. Russia (Application no. 21648/11) concerned the death of the applicant’s daughter, A.T., during clinical trials of the antipsychotic asenapine and alleged violations of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to life). A.T., born in 1947, had been diagnosed with schizophrenia in 1964. The illness progressed over decades, requiring repeated hospitalizations, though she retained legal capacity. In December 2004 her psychiatrist invited her to join a Phase-III double-blind trial (protocol 25517) comparing asenapine with the established drug olanzapine. She signed a consent form that incorporated a patient information leaflet describing the trial’s purpose, random allocation, monitoring schedule (weekly then monthly visits, periodic ECGs and blood tests) and known risks, including unforeseeable side-effects, possible worsening of psychiatric symptoms, and, for olanzapine, potentially fatal neuroleptic malignant syndrome. The doctor certified that she fully understood the risks.

A.T. began asenapine on 27 December 2004. Documented adverse effects included aggravation of schizophrenia, agitation, insomnia and weight gain. On 18 May 2005 she was hospitalized for acute psychiatric deterioration and remained an in-patient. While still in hospital she signed a second consent form on 26 December 2005 for a continuation trial (protocol 25520) that offered no new risk information and envisaged less frequent monitoring. On 10 April 2006 she suffered cardiac and respiratory arrest, lapsed into a coma and died four days later. Autopsy attributed death to acute cardiovascular failure secondary to advanced atherosclerosis and cardiosclerosis, complicated by pneumonia and cerebral oedema.

Domestic inquiries produced conflicting assessments. A St Petersburg Healthcare Committee found the trials compliant with Good Clinical Practice, the consents valid and no direct causal link to death. Subsequent forensic expert reports commissioned by investigators, however, identified multiple deficiencies: absence of recorded cardiovascular, hepatic or vital-sign monitoring despite asenapine’s known cardiotoxicity; only one ECG (taken after collapse); failure to perform the daily observations required for a new drug; recruitment into the second trial despite first-trial side-effects that should have prompted exclusion; and overlooked pneumonia. Experts concluded that these shortcomings stood in an indirect causal relationship with death by exacerbating latent cardiovascular disease.

The investigator nevertheless refused to open a criminal case, citing the signed consents, the lack of a direct causal link and the correctness of terminal intensive care. Domestic courts upheld the refusal. Russian legislation (Federal Law 86-FZ and the 2003 Rules of Clinical Practice) required free, informed written consent after clear disclosure of risks, ongoing medical supervision, and termination of a trial if danger to participants emerged. The European Court later held that these guarantees had been inadequately implemented, especially given the heightened vulnerability of a person with long-standing mental illness, and that the judicial response had been insufficient to satisfy the procedural limb of Article 2.

The case of Kotlyar v. Russia concerns three applications by Tatyana Kotlyar, a Russian human-rights defender and Obninsk Town Council member who since 2006 has assisted migrants from former Soviet republics, including under a State resettlement programme. In January 2012 then-Prime Minister Vladimir Putin publicly called for harsher penalties, including criminal liability, for breaches of migration and residence-registration rules. Kotlyar responded with an open letter declaring that she had deliberately turned her flat into an “elastic flat” by registering more than a hundred people there and would continue to offer registration to anyone who needed it.

In December 2012 Putin introduced a draft law targeting “fictitious residence registration”—the practice of registering people at addresses where they had no intention of living. An explanatory note cited hundreds of thousands of such registrations that impeded the delivery of official documents and accurate migration statistics. The law, enacted in December 2013 and effective 3 January 2014, inserted Articles 322.2 and 322.3 into the Criminal Code, criminalising fictitious permanent or temporary registration of Russian or foreign nationals (punishable by a fine or up to three years’ imprisonment) and adding a “repentance and cooperation” exemption. “Fictitious registration” was defined as filing an application based on false information or where neither the registrant nor the homeowner intended that the person would actually reside at the address.

Kotlyar was prosecuted three times. In the first set of proceedings she was charged with registering three foreign nationals at her flat between 6 and 10 January 2014 (after the law entered force) and later with identical acts committed between January and December 2013 (before the law). The cases were joined. At trial she argued that prosecution for 2013 conduct violated the prohibition on retroactive criminal law, that she had acted without payment and for compassionate reasons so that the migrants could apply for Russian nationality (which they subsequently obtained), and that the new provisions themselves were unconstitutional. A magistrate convicted her in November 2015 of a single continuous offence covering 91 fictitious registrations of Tajik, Uzbek, Moldovan, Georgian, Kyrgyz, Ukrainian and Armenian nationals between 1 January 2013 and 1 April 2014. The court held that the new articles were merely specialised provisions of the pre-existing offence of organising illegal stay (Article 322.1) and carried lower penalties, so there was no retroactive application. She received a fine but was exempted under a general amnesty. The town court dismissed her appeal, which had reiterated the retroactivity complaint and characterised her conduct as civil disobedience.

In 2017 she was convicted of 167 further counts committed between January and July of that year (nine additional counts were initially acquitted under the repentance clause). The fine was not enforced because the limitation period had expired; the town court later quashed the acquittals but otherwise upheld the judgment. In 2019 police charged her with 292 more counts; proceedings were discontinued under the repentance clause, a decision confirmed on appeal after the prosecutor withdrew his challenge.

Kotlyar maintained throughout that her registrations constituted protest against an overly restrictive registration regime and therefore engaged her right to freedom of expression. The European Court later held that the generally applicable criminal provisions were neither designed to suppress, nor had the effect of interfering with, any communicative activity and therefore fell outside the ambit of Article 10. The remaining complaint under Article 7 (no punishment without law) concerned the alleged retroactive characterisation of pre-2014 conduct.

Since 2006 Kotlyar had advised and assisted migrants from former Soviet republics, including participants in the State Programme for Voluntary Resettlement of Compatriots. In December 2012 President Putin submitted draft legislation creating administrative and criminal liability for “fictitious residence registration”—defined as registering a person who has no intention of living at the address or whom the owner has no intention of accommodating. An explanatory note cited widespread abuse of “elastic flats” that hindered summons, tax collection and migration control. On 9 November 2015 a magistrate convicted her of a single continuous offence of falsely certifying the residence of 91 nationals of Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Moldova, Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Ukraine and Armenia between January 2013 and April 2014, knowing they lived elsewhere. The court held that the new articles were merely special rules carving out lower-penalty subsets of the pre-existing offence of organising illegal stay (Article 322.1) and therefore did not apply retroactively. A fine was again imposed but not collected because the limitation period had expired. In August 2018 the town court quashed the acquittals and discontinued those counts while confirming the rest of the judgment.

Kotlyar appealed, seeking an acquittal rather than discontinuation; the prosecutor withdrew his appeal. The town court upheld the discontinuation in August 2019.

Russia (applications nos. 38825/16, 29722/18 and 12920/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Russian human-rights defender and local councillor, Tatyana Kotlyar, who was prosecuted for fictitious residence registrations of migrants as a form of protest. Kotlyar responded with an open letter on 6 February 2012, announcing she would register anyone needing it at her flat, which she described as an “elastic flat” already housing over 100 people on paper.

It created new Criminal Code offences: Article 322.2 (fictitious permanent registration, punishable by fine or up to three years’ imprisonment) and Article 322.3 (fictitious temporary registration for non-nationals, with similar penalties). Both included a “repentance and cooperation” exemption. These supplemented the existing Article 322.1 on organising illegal migration.

In the first (application 38825/16), she was charged in 2014 under the new articles for registering three foreigners in January 2014 and, later, for 2013 acts. On 9 November 2015, a magistrate convicted her of a single continuous offence of falsely registering 91 nationals of Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Moldova, Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Ukraine and Armenia at her address between 1 January 2013 and 1 April 2014, knowing they lived elsewhere. Kotlyar consistently argued her actions protested Russia’s restrictive registration system, constituted protected expression, and that 2013 convictions applied law retroactively. The alleged violations centred on Article 7 (prohibition of retroactive criminal law) regarding pre-2014 conduct and Article 10 (freedom of expression) concerning her protest-motivated registrations. The Court later held Article 10 inapplicable, as the generally applicable law neither targeted nor interfered with communicative activity.

The case of Y.G. v. Russia (application no. 8647/12) concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the authorities’ failure to protect the confidentiality of the applicant’s sensitive health data and to investigate its public disclosure. The applicant, a Russian national born in 1971 and resident in Moscow, is HIV-positive and suffers from hepatitis; he is registered with the Moscow Centre for the Prevention and Control of AIDS.

In February 2011 an acquaintance informed him that a compact-disc database purchased at Moscow’s Savelovskiy Market contained details of his medical conditions. The applicant bought a copy of the same disc. Its first page bore the inscription “ЗИЦ Москва 02.2007”, which he identified as referring to the Information Centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior and a 2007 compilation date; copyright was attributed to a private company. The database listed personal particulars (names, dates and places of birth, addresses, ethnicities, nicknames, criminal records and organised-crime affiliations) of more than 400,000 persons registered in or living in Moscow, including 281 people recorded as HIV-positive, 30 as having AIDS and 750 as having hepatitis. The applicant’s own entry (no. 308812, dated 26 April 1999) recorded his identity, address, nationality, convictions for hooliganism, theft and unlawful drug possession, and the note that he was “a hooligan, thief and drug addict, was suffering from Aids and hepatitis”. His representative later purchased an identical disc from a vendor at the same market.

On 3 March 2011 the applicant complained to the Information Centre, demanding an explanation for the inclusion of health data, the deletion of the inaccurate AIDS reference and the removal of the hepatitis information given without his consent. The Centre replied that its official database contained no health information about him and that the print-out he had supplied was unrelated to its records.

On 18 April 2011 he lodged a criminal complaint with the Investigative Committee, enclosing the disc, a print-out and a video of the purchase. He alleged that the unhindered sale of a database purporting to belong to the Interior Ministry constituted an unauthorised collection and dissemination of private-life information (Article 137 of the Criminal Code) and an abuse of office (Article 285), made possible by the unlawful transfer of official data. The complaint was successively forwarded to the Prosecutor General, the Moscow city prosecutor and the Tverskoy district prosecutor. The latter declined to open a pre-investigation inquiry, finding no evidence that Interior Ministry officials had committed an offence and noting that the market lay outside his territorial jurisdiction. A subsequent request for clarification was rejected for lack of sufficient indications of a crime. A judicial challenge to the Investigative Committee’s inaction was dismissed by the Moscow City Court on 8 August 2011 on the same ground.

The applicant later purchased a similar 2010-dated database at the same market in July 2013 that still contained the identical health entries. After the Government was notified of the application he discovered that, while he was a suspect in 1999, an investigator had formally requested his medical records from an infectious-diseases hospital, which confirmed his HIV and hepatitis status. Press reports from 2011, uncontested by the Government, described large-scale police and Roskomnadzor raids that seized thousands of illicit databases, including those attributed to the Moscow Information Centre. A 2017 official check of the Ministry’s records revealed only the applicant’s criminal history.

Domestic law at the material time classified medical information as confidential (section 61 of the 1993 Basic Principles of Public Health Law), permitting disclosure without consent only in the context of an investigation or judicial proceedings, and provided criminal and administrative sanctions for unauthorised collection, storage or dissemination of personal data. The Council of Europe Data Protection Convention (which entered into force for Russia in 2013) likewise required special safeguards for health data and effective remedies against unauthorised processing.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the authorities had failed both to safeguard the confidentiality of his health data and to conduct an effective investigation into its disclosure.

The case of Y.G. v. Russia (Application no. 8647/12) concerns alleged violations of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the applicant’s right to respect for private life. Y.G., a Russian national born in 1971 and living in Moscow, is HIV-positive, suffers from hepatitis, and is registered with the Moscow Centre for the Prevention and Control of Aids.

In February 2011, an acquaintance informed Y.G. that a database purchased at Moscow’s Savelovskiy Market revealed his medical conditions. Y.G. then bought a compact disc containing the database, labelled “ЗИЦ Москва 02.2007.” He asserted that “ЗИЦ” referred to the Information Centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior and that the database dated from 2007. The disc’s properties indicated copyright belonging to company C.I. The database comprised a table of personal data on hundreds of thousands of people registered in or living in Moscow, including foreigners, organised by categories such as name, date and place of birth, gender, ethnicity, address, nicknames, organised crime affiliations, criminal records, and preventive measures. It listed 281 people with HIV, 30 with Aids, and 750 with hepatitis. Y.G. appeared as entry 308812, with his name, patronymic, surname, date and place of birth, nationality, residence, and convictions for hooliganism, theft, and unlawful drug possession. The “Notes” section described him as “a hooligan, thief and drug addict, was suffering from Aids and hepatitis,” with an entry date of 26 April 1999.

In March 2011 Y.G.’s representative confirmed that various databases, including one similar to that purchased by Y.G., were openly sold at the market and obtained another copy from a vendor who provided a telephone number for technical support.

On 3 March 2011 Y.G. complained to the Information Centre, enclosing a printout and requesting an explanation for the inclusion of his health data, deletion of the inaccurate Aids reference, and removal of the hepatitis information (to which he had never consented). The Centre replied on 14 March 2011 that its database contained no health information about him and that the printout was unrelated to its records.

On 18 April 2011 Y.G. lodged a complaint with the Investigative Committee, alleging that the sale of a database titled “Database of the Information Centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior” was unlawful under Articles 137 § 2 (breach of privacy by an official) and 285 § 1 (abuse of office) of the Criminal Code and must have resulted from officials transferring or selling the data. He enclosed a printout, the original CD, and a video of the purchase. The complaint was forwarded through the Prosecutor General’s office to the Moscow prosecutor and then to the Tverskoy District prosecutor. On 1 June 2011 the latter stated that there was no evidence of an offence by Interior Ministry officials and therefore no basis for a pre-investigation inquiry; the market also lay outside the district’s territorial jurisdiction. A later request for clarification elicited the response that the complaint lacked sufficient information disclosing elements of a crime. On 8 August 2011 the Moscow City Court dismissed Y.G.’s judicial complaint, confirming that the Investigative Committee had found insufficient indications of a crime by Ministry officials.

Shortly afterwards Y.G.’s representative was contacted by the Security Service of the Moscow Department of the Interior in connection with a media-triggered inquiry into the sales. In July 2013 Y.G. purchased a similar 2010-dated database that still contained the same health information. After the application was communicated to the Government, Y.G. discovered that on 15 March 1999 an investigator had requested (and apparently received) his HIV and hepatitis status from the Hospital for Infectious Diseases while he was a criminal suspect.

Contemporary press reports (uncontested by the Government) described 2011 raids by Roskomnadzor and the Ministry of the Interior at Savelovskiy Market and other Moscow shopping centres, resulting in the confiscation of thousands of CDs containing databases attributed to State agencies, including the Information Centre. A 2017 official check of the Ministry’s database found only Y.G.’s criminal-record information.

Domestic law at the time classified medical information as confidential and prohibited its disclosure except in limited circumstances (including requests by investigating bodies). Unauthorised collection or dissemination of private-life data, especially by officials, was a criminal offence, and breaches of personal-data rules were administrative offences. The Council of Europe Data Protection Convention (which entered into force for Russia only in 2013) likewise required safeguards for health data and security against unauthorised dissemination.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints that the authorities collected, stored and released his sensitive health data without adequate legal basis or consent, failed to prevent its public sale, and failed to conduct an effective investigation into the leak.

The case of Safarov v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, Application no. 885/12, judgment of 1 September 2022) concerns an Azerbaijani author’s claim that the State failed to protect his intellectual property rights after a private NGO published his book online without permission. The applicant, Rafig Safarov (born 1959, resident in Baku), wrote and published in 2009 a historical work entitled “Changes in the ethnic composition of the people of Irevan Governorate in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.” In 2010 the Irali Public Union, a youth NGO, posted a complete digital version of the book on the website of one of its projects (www.history.az). The site recorded 417 downloads. Irali removed the file only after the applicant protested.

On 3 August 2010 Safarov sued Irali in the Sabail District Court. Invoking Articles 14, 15, 30, 31 and 45 of Azerbaijan’s Law on Copyright and Related Rights, he alleged unauthorised reproduction and public communication of his work without payment of royalties. He claimed AZN 50,067 (then about EUR 47,460) for pecuniary loss and AZN 28,800 (about EUR 27,300) for non-pecuniary damage.

On 13 October 2010 the District Court accepted that Irali had published the book but dismissed the action. It relied principally on the chapeau of Article 18.1 of the Copyright Law (reprographic reproduction by libraries, archives and educational institutions for non-commercial purposes). The court added that the file had been taken down and that the applicant had not proved actual damage.

Safarov appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal, arguing that Article 18 applies only to the listed institutions and to the exhaustive purposes set out in its sub-paragraphs, none of which fitted Irali’s conduct. On 24 January 2011 the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment and additionally invoked Article 17.1 (private copying of a lawfully published work). 

The Supreme Court, on 14 June 2011, rejected the cassation appeal. Besides repeating the lower courts’ reasoning it cited Article 14.1(q) (the author’s moral right of communication) and Article 15.3 (exhaustion of distribution rights after first sale). It observed that by publishing and selling physical copies the applicant had already exercised his communication right, and that Irali’s posting under a “library” heading served merely to inform the public about Azerbaijani history.

Safarov then applied to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining under Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) that the domestic courts had failed to protect his copyright against unauthorised digital reproduction and communication. The ECtHR declared the remainder of the application inadmissible and focused on the property complaint. It held that intellectual-property rights constitute “possessions” and that the State has a positive obligation to provide effective judicial protection of those rights vis-à-vis private parties. The national courts’ failure to give relevant and sufficient reasons for dismissing the infringement claim—particularly their misapplication of the limited exceptions in Articles 17 and 18 and their disregard of the author’s exclusive reproduction and making-available rights—breached that obligation. A violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was therefore found.

The case of Safarov v. Azerbaijan (no. 885/12) concerns the applicant’s complaint of the State’s failure to protect his intellectual-property rights. Mr Rafig Safarov, born in 1959 and living in Baku, is the author of the 2009 book “Changes in the ethnic composition of the people of Irevan Governorate in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.”

In 2010 the youth NGO Irali Public Union placed a complete digital copy of the book on its website www.history.az without the author’s consent or payment of royalties. The site recorded 417 downloads. After the applicant protested, Irali removed the file.

On 3 August 2010 the applicant sued Irali in the Sabail District Court, relying on Articles 14, 15, 30, 31 and 45 of the 1996 Law on Copyright and Related Rights. He sought AZN 50 067 (approximately EUR 47 460) for pecuniary loss and AZN 28 800 (approximately EUR 27 300) for non-pecuniary damage, arguing that the unauthorised digital reproduction and making-available of the entire work infringed his exclusive economic rights.

On 13 October 2010 the first-instance court accepted that the book had been published online yet dismissed the claim. It invoked only the opening clause of Article 18.1 (which permits limited reprographic copying by libraries, archives and educational institutions for specified non-commercial purposes) and added that the file had already been taken down and that damage had not been proved.

The applicant appealed, stressing that Article 18’s exhaustive list of purposes had not been applied, that Irali was not a library or educational institution, and that the provision did not cover wholesale digital dissemination of a whole book. On 24 January 2011 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal, repeating the same reasoning and adding a reference to Article 17.1 (private-copy exception). That provision, however, expressly excludes reprographic reproduction of entire books.

The Supreme Court, on 14 June 2011, rejected the cassation appeal. It additionally cited Articles 14.1(q) and 15.3, observing that by publishing and selling physical copies the applicant had already exercised his right of communication, and that Irali’s purpose had been to supply historical information under the website’s “library” heading.

The domestic copyright statute grants authors exclusive rights of reproduction, distribution and communication to the public, together with a right to royalties. Limited exceptions exist for personal use (Art. 17) and for specific library/educational copying (Art. 18), but neither provision, on its face, authorises an NGO to place an entire book on the internet for unrestricted public download. Azerbaijan is also bound by the Berne Convention and the WIPO Copyright Treaty, both of which confirm that the reproduction right applies in the digital environment and that any exception must be confined to special cases that do not conflict with normal exploitation or unreasonably prejudice the author.

The alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 therefore rests on the courts’ failure to give any coherent legal explanation for treating Irali’s conduct as falling within a statutory exception, thereby leaving the applicant’s intellectual-property “possession” unprotected against unauthorised digital exploitation by a private party.

The case of Safarov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 885/12) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an Azerbaijani author's claim that national authorities failed to protect his copyright after a private NGO reproduced and posted his book online without permission or payment. Rafig Safarov, born in 1959 and living in Baku, wrote “Changes in the ethnic composition of the people of Irevan Governorate in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries,” published in 2009. In 2010 the Irali Public Union, a youth NGO, placed a digital copy on its project website history.az. The site recorded 417 downloads. Irali later removed the file at Safarov’s request.

On 3 August 2010 Safarov sued Irali in the Sabail District Court. He invoked Articles 14, 15, 30, 31 and 45 of the Law on Copyright and Related Rights, arguing that the unauthorised reproduction and online publication violated his exclusive rights of reproduction, distribution and communication to the public and his right to royalties. He claimed approximately AZN 50,067 in pecuniary damage and AZN 28,800 in non-pecuniary damage.

On 13 October 2010 the District Court accepted that Irali had published the book but dismissed the action. It relied principally on the opening paragraph of Article 18.1, which permits limited, non-commercial reprographic reproduction by libraries, archives and educational institutions provided the author’s name and source are indicated. The court added that the work had been taken down and that Safarov had not proved actual damage.

Safarov appealed, pointing out that the first-instance judgment had not identified any of the exhaustive purposes listed in Article 18 and that the provision applied only to the institutions named. On 24 January 2011 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal, repeating the lower court’s reasoning and additionally citing Article 17.1 (personal-use copying of a lawfully published work).

The Supreme Court rejected the cassation appeal on 14 June 2011. Besides endorsing the earlier judgments, it referred to Article 14.1(q) (the moral right of communication) and Article 15.3 (exhaustion of the distribution right after first sale). It held that by publishing and selling copies the applicant had already exercised his communication right, and that Irali’s posting under the “library” section of the website pursued the legitimate aim of informing the public about Azerbaijani history.

Safarov complained to the Strasbourg Court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging that the domestic courts had failed to protect his intellectual-property rights by dismissing his claim without adequate reasoning. The European Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the national courts had not properly examined whether Irali’s digital publication fell within any statutory exception, had not addressed the applicant’s arguments about the limited scope of Articles 17 and 18, and had therefore failed in their positive obligation to provide effective protection of copyright as a “possession.” The courts’ cursory and internally inconsistent reasoning left the applicant without a reasoned judicial response to a serious interference with his exclusive rights.

The ECHR case of Z. v. Croatia (Application no. 21347/21) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life). The applicant, a Croatian national, and the children's mother (Ms X) lived as an unmarried couple from 2007 and had four children born in Croatia between 2008 and 2015. All were Croatian nationals. The family led a nomadic lifestyle across several European countries before returning to Croatia in spring 2018. Their relationship ended in October 2018.

On 22 October 2018, the mother provided written consent for the applicant to take the children to Germany and care for them independently. The applicant and children moved there in December 2018, registering residence and enrolling the children in a private school and kindergarten. On 18 July 2019, the mother revoked her consent. She collected the children in Germany on 9 August 2019 and took them to Croatia, refusing to return them after the summer holidays. The applicant then relocated back to Croatia.

The applicant sought a provisional measure in a German family court for sole determination of the children's residence and their handover. The court found it had jurisdiction on residence but advised pursuing handover under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention, as the children were abroad. It later dismissed the request for lack of urgency, noting that under Croatian law (Family Act s. 99(1)) unmarried parents share joint parental responsibility, which persisted after the move to Germany pursuant to Article 16(3) of the 1996 Hague Convention on Jurisdiction, Applicable Law, Recognition, Enforcement and Co-operation in Respect of Parental Responsibility and Measures for the Protection of Children.

Meanwhile, on 9 October 2019, the applicant initiated return proceedings in the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court under the Hague Child Abduction Convention and the Brussels II bis Regulation, arguing wrongful retention in Croatia. The mother claimed an agreement to return permanently. Correspondence from German authorities confirmed that Croatian law on joint custody (acquired at birth) continued to apply in Germany via the Hague Jurisdiction Convention, rendering German custody rules (Civil Code Art. 1626a, granting sole custody to unmarried mothers unless jointly declared or court-ordered) inapplicable.

The Zagreb court dismissed the request on 15 November 2019, holding that the children's habitual residence was in Germany, so German law applied. As the parents were unmarried and no joint-custody declaration or court order existed, the mother had sole parental responsibility; thus, retention was not in breach of the applicant's custody rights and not wrongful under Hague Article 3 or Brussels II bis Article 2(11). The Zagreb County Court upheld this on 15 January 2020, ignoring the applicant's arguments (supported by the German letter and court decision) that Croatian law and Hague Jurisdiction Convention Article 16(3) preserved his joint custody, which could not be lost by relocation. The Croatian Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint on 18 February 2021, endorsing the lower courts and misapplying Hague Jurisdiction Convention Article 7 (on jurisdiction in wrongful-removal cases) to reject the subsistence argument.

Separate Croatian proceedings initiated by the mother resulted in a 2021 first-instance judgment awarding her sole custody and residence of all children (with limited contact for the applicant), pending appeal.

The ECHR found a violation of Article 8. The domestic courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for refusing return by erroneously deeming the Hague Child Abduction Convention inapplicable through misapplication of the relevant international instruments on custody attribution. However, the judgment does not require the children's return at this stage.

The case of Z. v. Croatia (no. 21347/21) concerns Croatian courts’ refusal to order the return of the applicant’s four children to Germany under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention after their mother retained them in Croatia. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8 ECHR (family life) because the courts lacked relevant and sufficient reasons for holding the Convention inapplicable.

The applicant (Croatian national, born 1982) and Ms X (also Croatian) lived unmarried from 2007 and had four children (born 2008–2015 in Croatia). The family relocated frequently (Greece, Slovakia/Hungary, Sweden, France) before returning to Croatia in spring 2018. Their relationship ended in October 2018. They led an unconventional lifestyle, refusing public schooling, resulting in a 2018 Croatian minor-offence conviction.

On 22 October 2018 the mother gave written consent for the applicant to take the children to Germany and care for them independently. They moved, registering residence from 3 December 2018; the children attended private school/kindergarten. On 18 July 2019 the mother revoked consent. On 9 August 2019 she collected the children in Germany and took them to Croatia, refusing to return them after the holidays. The applicant then returned to Croatia.

In Germany the applicant applied on 9 September 2019 to the Singen District Court for a provisional order granting him sole determination of the children’s residence and their handover. The court asserted jurisdiction over residence but advised using the Hague Abduction Convention for handover (the applicant withdrew that part). On 21 November 2019 it dismissed the request for lack of urgency, noting that Croatian Family Act s. 99(1) conferred joint parental responsibility on unmarried parents, which Article 16 § 3 of the 1996 Hague Jurisdiction Convention preserved after the move to Germany.

Meanwhile, on 9 October 2019 the applicant sought the children’s return in Zagreb Municipal Civil Court under the Hague Abduction Convention and Brussels IIa Regulation, alleging wrongful retention. The mother claimed an agreement to remain permanently in Croatia. German authorities confirmed to their Croatian counterparts that German law was inapplicable and that Croatian joint custody continued via the Jurisdiction Convention.

Unaware of (or ignoring) this, the Zagreb court on 15 November 2019 dismissed the request. It held the children had been habitually resident in Germany, so German law governed. Under German Civil Code Art. 1626a, unmarried mothers have sole parental responsibility unless the parents declare joint custody or a court awards it; those conditions were unmet, so the applicant had no custody rights and retention was not wrongful.

The applicant appealed, arguing Croatian law (in force at the children’s births) automatically conferred joint responsibility, which Art. 16 § 3 of the Jurisdiction Convention preserved; he enclosed the German court’s decision and Federal Office of Justice letter. Zagreb County Court dismissed the appeal on 15 January 2020, repeating the German-law analysis and ignoring the Jurisdiction Convention arguments.

A constitutional complaint was dismissed on 18 February 2021. The Constitutional Court endorsed the lower courts and, addressing Art. 16 § 3, instead cited Art. 7 of the Jurisdiction Convention (jurisdiction after wrongful removal), which was irrelevant to the applicable-law question.

Separately, the mother obtained a first-instance judgment (April 2021, appeal pending) awarding her sole parental responsibility, residence of all children with her, and limited professional-supervised contact for the applicant.

The ECtHR held that the Croatian courts’ exclusive reliance on German law, without addressing the preservation of Croatian parental rights under the Jurisdiction Convention, failed to furnish relevant and sufficient reasons, violating Article 8. The judgment does not require the children’s present return.

**Case of Z. v. Croatia (ECtHR, Application no. 21347/21, Judgment of 1 September 2022)**

The applicant, a Croatian national, complained under Article 8 of the ECHR (right to respect for family life) that Croatian courts wrongly refused to order the return of his four children to Germany under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention after their mother retained them in Croatia. The ECtHR found a violation due to the courts’ lack of relevant and sufficient reasons for holding the Convention inapplicable, though it did not require the children’s return now.

The applicant and Ms X (the mother), both Croatian nationals, lived unmarried from 2007 and had four children born in Croatia (2008–2015). The family moved frequently across Europe (Greece, Slovakia, Hungary, Sweden, France) before returning to Croatia in spring 2018. Their relationship ended in October 2018. They had an unconventional lifestyle, including refusing public education, leading to a 2018 minor-offence conviction in Croatia.

On 22 October 2018 the mother gave written consent for the applicant to take the children to Germany and care for them independently. He moved them there (registered residence from 3 December 2018) and enrolled them in a private school and kindergarten. On 18 July 2019 the mother revoked consent. On 9 August 2019 she collected the children in Germany and took them to Croatia; after the summer holidays she refused to return them. The applicant then returned to Croatia.

The applicant sought provisional measures in a German family court (Singen District Court) to determine the children’s residence and obtain their handover. The court confirmed jurisdiction on residence but noted the handover request was inadmissible (children abroad) and advised a Hague Convention application. On 21 November 2019 it dismissed the request for lack of urgency, holding that under Croatian Family Act s. 99(1) unmarried parents have joint parental responsibility, which continued after the move to Germany pursuant to Article 16 § 3 of the 1996 Hague Convention on Jurisdiction, Applicable Law, Recognition, Enforcement and Co-operation in Respect of Parental Responsibility.

Meanwhile, on 9 October 2019 the applicant applied to the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court for the children’s return under the 1980 Hague Convention and Brussels II bis Regulation, arguing wrongful retention after the holidays. The mother claimed an agreement to remain in Croatia. German Central Authority correspondence (30 October 2019) confirmed that Croatian law on joint custody applied and continued under the 1996 Convention; German law was irrelevant.

The Zagreb court (15 November 2019) found the children habitually resident in Germany at the time of the request, so German law governed whether retention breached custody rights. Applying German Civil Code Art. 1626a, it held that the unmarried mother had sole parental responsibility (no joint-custody declaration, marriage or court order). The father therefore had no custody rights, so retention was not wrongful. This was the sole ground for dismissal. The court was unaware of the German correspondence.

On appeal the applicant argued that Croatian law (Family Act ss. 97, 99) automatically conferred joint parental responsibility at birth in Croatia, which could not be lost by the move (contrary to 1996 Convention Art. 16 § 3). He enclosed the German letter and Singen decision. The Zagreb County Court (15 January 2020) dismissed the appeal, repeating that German law applied and only the mother had custody; it ignored the 1996 Convention argument.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint (breach of fair proceedings and family life) was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 18 February 2021. It endorsed the lower courts and rejected the 1996 Convention argument by citing that Convention’s Art. 7 (wrongful removal/retention definition) rather than addressing Art. 16 § 3.

Separately, in April 2021 the Zlatar Municipal Court awarded the mother sole exercise of parental responsibility and residence of all four children (with supervised contact for the father). That judgment is under appeal.

The ECtHR held that the Croatian courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons by erroneously applying German law and disregarding the subsistence of joint Croatian parental responsibility under the 1996 Convention. This violated Article 8. The finding does not require the children’s return given the time elapsed and pending custody proceedings.

The case of Pařízek v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 76286/14) concerns a tenant’s challenge to court-ordered payment of increased rent for a flat originally let under the State rent-control scheme. The applicant, Josef Pařízek, became tenant of the Prague flat on 13 October 1995. The tenancy agreement fixed monthly rent at CZK 297 (then about EUR 11) under the statutory rent-control regime and permitted later adjustment only by valid decrees or in line with service-price rises. The building was sold to a new private landlord in 1999. Controlled rent rose to CZK 900 in July 2002.

On 5 August 2003 the landlord sued, seeking a declaration that the contractual rent clause was void and an order that the applicant pay CZK 4 500 per month from 1 April 2003. An expert report attached to the claim calculated maintenance costs at 1.5 % of the flat’s market value (CZK 801 960), yielding annual costs of CZK 12 029. The first-instance and appellate courts dismissed the claim; the Supreme Court likewise rejected an appeal on points of law.

The Constitutional Court, in its 21 March 2006 judgment (I. ÚS 717/05), quashed the Supreme Court’s decision. It relied on its plenary judgment of 28 February 2006 (Pl. ÚS 20/05), which had held that the legislature’s failure to replace repealed rent-control regulations created an unconstitutional vacuum. Ordinary courts were therefore obliged, by judicial law-making, to set rents according to local conditions so as to avoid discrimination among landlords and tenants. The Supreme Court then remitted the case.

Meanwhile, on 21 December 2006 the applicant purchased the flat for CZK 900 000. The landlord amended the claim to cover only the period 1 April 2003–21 December 2006. The district and regional courts again dismissed it. A further Constitutional Court judgment of 2 March 2011 (II. ÚS 115/08), applying the Court’s plenary opinion of 28 April 2009 (Pl. ÚS-st. 27/09), held that courts could not award rent increases for any period before the action was filed, but could do so from the date of filing until 31 December 2006 (when Act No. 107/2006 on unilateral rent increases entered into force). The regional court therefore remitted the case solely for the interval 6 August 2003–21 December 2006 and directed that an expert determine the “usual” (market) rent.

The landlord revised the claim to the following monthly sums: CZK 4 494 (2003), CZK 5 248 (2004), CZK 5 036 (2005) and CZK 5 543 (2006). On 31 July 2012 the district court, relying on both the landlord’s expert and a court-appointed expert who had used a comparative method (location, size, fittings, heating), granted the claim in full. It rejected the applicant’s request for a further audit and observed that the purchase of the flat in 2006 was a voluntary act undertaken with full knowledge of the pending dispute.

The regional court upheld the judgment. The Supreme Court, on 19 September 2013, dismissed an appeal on points of law, finding that the lower courts had correctly applied Constitutional Court case-law by setting rent at the locally prevailing market level and had given adequate reasons. The applicant’s subsequent constitutional complaint, alleging violations of property rights and of the right to judicial protection, was rejected as manifestly ill-founded on 30 May 2014 (III. ÚS 3772/13).

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the retroactive imposition of market-level rent constituted an unlawful and disproportionate interference with his possessions (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) and that the domestic courts’ successive applications of evolving Constitutional Court jurisprudence had deprived him of a fair hearing (Article 6 § 1).

Ordinary courts were therefore obliged to fill the legislative gap by deciding rent increases according to local conditions so as to avoid discrimination among landlords. The case of Axel Springer SE v. Germany (Application no. 8964/18) before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, a Berlin-registered publishing house that issues the daily newspaper Die Welt, challenged a domestic court order requiring it to publish a rectification of a 4 October 2013 article. The article, headlined “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side,” discussed Ms K., then executive director of the party die Linke (formerly PDS). It referred to her alleged past as a Stasi agent for the GDR Ministry of State Security and linked her to the post-1989 disappearance of vast SED (East German Communist Party) assets, including a business empire, real estate and 6.2 billion East German marks (with possible secret foreign accounts remaining). The piece noted that she sat on the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission; that her name “stands \ldots for a particularly unsavoury chapter” in the handling of those assets; that while there was “currently no evidence” of her involvement in possible criminal activities, documents showed she remained “involved, directly or indirectly,” with companies whose assets originated from the SED/Honecker-party heritage (she held shares privately, though a 1995 court had found two of them managed PDS assets on a fiduciary basis); and that she was honorary chairwoman of the “Association of Friends of the ND,” which had suddenly provided large sums (one to four million Deutschmarks) to rescue the former party newspaper Neues Deutschland in the early 1990s, with the origin of the funds unknown.

Two days before publication the newspaper had sent Ms K. a list of questions, including about her ND association membership; she declined to reply. After publication she demanded a rectification stating, inter alia, that she had not been involved in the disappearance of SED assets. When the publisher refused, she obtained an injunction. The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed her claim, holding that the article had not expressly alleged any such connection and that a possible interpretation to that effect was insufficient. The Court of Appeal, however, granted the injunction under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act (which obliges periodicals to print factual rectifications by persons with a legitimate interest, provided the text is of appropriate length, limited to facts and not a punishable offence). It ordered publication, on page 8, of a reply that corrected three points: Ms K. had not sat on the Arbitration Commission since 1 January 2013; she had “nothing to do with the disappearance of the SED party assets after 1989,” the companies (FEVAC and Vulkan) having been founded in 1992 with PDS money on Treuhandanstalt recommendation and she having become a shareholder only in 1998; and she had joined the ND association only around 2000 (chair since 2002). In subsequent main proceedings the Regional Court again dismissed the claim, but the Court of Appeal reaffirmed the order. It reasoned that an average reader would infer a link between Ms K. and the vanished assets because the article juxtaposed the “no evidence of crime” disclaimer with her continuing ties to SED-derived companies; the reply was confined to what was necessary to refute those implications; her pre-publication silence did not negate a legitimate interest; and the reply’s date (11 October 2013) was not manifestly inaccurate given that the core request had been made then.

The publisher printed the rectification (adding an editorial note that it accepted the information as correct and had no knowledge connecting Ms K. to any asset disappearance). The Federal Constitutional Court declined to examine a constitutional complaint. The ECtHR found the order a justified and proportionate interference with Article 10, the domestic courts having given a well-reasoned assessment that duly considered the Court’s case-law on the right of reply.

The case Axel Springer SE v. Germany (no. 8964/18) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression) arising from a German court order requiring the applicant publishing company (publisher of Die Welt) to print a rectification/reply by political official Ms. K. to a 4 October 2013 article headlined “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side.”

The article, published on page 8, discussed Ms. K. (then executive director of die Linke, formerly PDS) as a former Stasi agent and her links to the post-1989 disappearance of vast SED (East German Communist Party) assets. It noted that even at the end of 1989 the SED held a large business empire, real estate and 6.2 billion East German marks, with possible secret accounts remaining. It stated there was “currently no evidence that K. was involved in possible criminal activities” but that she remained involved with companies whose assets stemmed from SED/Honecker-party heritage (she held shares privately; a 1995 court had found two such companies managed assets for the PDS on a fiduciary basis). It further linked her to the “Association of Friends of the ND” (the party’s former newspaper), of which she was honorary chairwoman, in the context of unexplained large sums promised to rescue the paper in the early 1990s. Two days before publication the newspaper had sent questions (including on her ND association membership) which Ms. K. refused to answer.

Ms. K. requested a rectification denying any involvement in the disappearance of SED assets and correcting details of her roles and timelines. After the newspaper refused, she sought an injunction under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act (which requires publication of a reply to factual allegations by an affected person with a legitimate interest, provided the reply is of appropriate length, limited to facts and not itself unlawful). The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed the application, finding no explicit allegation of involvement in asset concealment. On appeal the Berlin Court of Appeal (18 November 2013, confirmed in main proceedings on 16 January 2014) ordered publication of a specific reply text on page 8. The ordered text corrected three points: (1) Ms. K. had not sat on the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission since 1 January 2013; (2) she had nothing to do with the post-1989 disappearance of SED assets (the two companies, FEVAC and Vulkan, were founded in 1992 with PDS funds on Treuhandanstalt recommendation; she became a FEVAC shareholder only in 1998); and (3) she had been a member of the ND association only since around 2000 and chair since 2002. The Court of Appeal held that an average reader would nonetheless infer involvement in asset concealment from the juxtaposition of the “no evidence” disclaimer with details of ongoing company ties, so a reply was required to rectify the factual implication. It found the reply’s length and content limited to what was necessary, that Ms. K. had a legitimate interest despite having declined pre-publication questions, and that the date on the text was not manifestly incorrect.

The newspaper published the reply on 3 February 2014 together with an editor’s note stating that the information was correct and that the paper had no knowledge connecting Ms. K. to the disappearance of SED assets. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the publisher’s constitutional complaint.

The applicant company complained that the compulsory publication constituted an unjustified interference with its editorial freedom and freedom of expression. The ECtHR (Fourth Section) held that the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting reputation, and was necessary and proportionate in a democratic society. The domestic courts had given a well-reasoned assessment that took due account of the Court’s case-law; the reply was confined to factual correction of inaccuracies or misleading implications and did not impose a disproportionate burden. There was accordingly no violation of Article 10. The judgment became final on 17 April 2023.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined an application by Axel Springer SE, publisher of the newspaper Die Welt, alleging a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The case arose from a German court order requiring the company to publish a reply by Ms K., then executive director of the political party Die Linke (formerly the PDS), to correct factual inaccuracies in a 4 October 2013 article.

The article, headed “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side,” appeared on page 8. It described Ms K. as sitting on the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission and linked her name to the handling of billions in former East German Communist Party (SED) assets after 1989. It noted the SED’s remaining business empire, real estate and cash holdings, possible secret bank accounts, and Ms K.’s continued involvement (directly or indirectly) with companies whose assets originated from the SED, including two firms (FEVAC and Vulkan) found in 1995 to manage PDS assets on a fiduciary basis. It further stated that the PDS had placed “utmost confidence” in her when the party newspaper Neues Deutschland faced financial collapse in the early 1990s; an “Association of Friends of the ND” then promised substantial funds, with Ms K. as honorary chairwoman. The article added that there was no evidence of her involvement in criminal activity.

Two days before publication the newspaper sent Ms K. questions, including about her Association membership; she declined to answer. After publication her lawyer demanded a rectification denying any role in the disappearance of SED assets. When the newspaper refused, Ms K. sought an injunction under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act, which obliges publishers to print a reply by any person affected by a factual allegation, provided the person has a legitimate interest, the reply is of appropriate length and is limited to statements of fact.

The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed the application, holding that the article had not expressly connected Ms K. to asset concealment and that a possible interpretation was insufficient. The Court of Appeal reversed this, finding that an average reader would infer such a connection from the juxtaposition of the “no evidence” disclaimer with details of her ongoing company ties. It approved a three-point reply that (1) corrected her Commission membership (ended 1 January 2013), (2) denied any involvement in asset disappearance and explained that FEVAC and Vulkan were founded in 1992 with PDS funds approved by the Treuhandanstalt, with her becoming a shareholder only in 1998, and (3) stated she had joined the Association only around 2000 and become chair in 2002. The reply was to appear on page 8; a front-page announcement was refused.

In the main proceedings the Regional Court again dismissed the claim, but the Court of Appeal reaffirmed its order. It held that the reply’s length and content were confined to what was necessary to refute the article’s implications, that Ms K. had no duty to answer pre-publication questions, and that the date on the reply (11 October 2013) was not misleading. The newspaper published the text on 3 February 2014 together with an editorial note confirming the reply’s accuracy and stating it had no knowledge linking Ms K. to asset disappearance. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint.

The Strasbourg Court later held that the domestic courts’ assessment was well-reasoned, gave due weight to the Court’s case-law, and that the order was a justified and proportionate interference with freedom of expression. The judgment became final on 17 April 2023.
