001-223107:
The case of G.K. v. Cyprus arose from an application to the European Court of Human Rights alleging a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life). The applicant, a Cypriot national, had moved to New York in 2011 and married a US citizen in 2016. Their son, a US national, was born there later that year. The family resided together in New York, where both parents jointly exercised custody rights under US law.

On 6 October 2017 the applicant lodged a domestic-violence complaint against the father, alleging that he had become possessive, controlling and verbally abusive. She obtained a temporary protection order from the New York Family Court prohibiting contact with her and the child, and the pair moved to a safe house. On 25 October 2017, assisted by the Cypriot authorities (who had granted the child Cypriot nationality and a passport), she took the one-year-old child to Cyprus. The New York court later dismissed her protection petition after she failed to appear.

The father located the child in August 2018 through private investigators. In October 2018 the US Central Authority transmitted a request under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction to the Cypriot Central Authority. On 7 February 2019 that authority applied to the Family Court of Paphos for the child’s return to the United States.

The applicant opposed return. She invoked Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention, asserting a grave risk of physical or psychological harm or an intolerable situation arising from the father’s alleged violence and a prior criminal record in Ohio. She further argued that the child had settled in Cyprus within the meaning of Article 12, citing preschool attendance since December 2017, extra-curricular activities, close ties with extended family and Greek as his mother tongue. She produced a child-psychologist’s report concluding that separation from her and his Cypriot environment would be harmful and recommending only supervised contact with the father.

The first-instance court heard the father’s testimony (finding him credible and consistent) but declined to interview the child on account of his age (then three). It refused the applicant leave to file a late supplementary affidavit containing the psychologist’s report and the father’s criminal record, holding that the material merely repeated earlier claims and that granting the request would unduly prolong proceedings contrary to the Convention’s expedition requirement. In its judgment of 21 January 2021 the court rejected both Hague defences. It found the violence allegations vague, inconsistent with the applicant’s earlier New York filings and unsubstantiated; the protection order had been dismissed for non-appearance. The criminal-record claim was likewise unproven; the father had admitted only minor, decades-old convictions that did not affect his fitness as a parent. No clear evidence of grave risk had been adduced. The settlement argument was equally unsubstantiated given the child’s young age and the availability of US transitional assistance. Return was ordered.

The Family Court of Second Instance dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 19 March 2021, confirming the first-instance findings in full. It observed that the first-instance delay had been lengthy and partly attributable to the applicant’s late procedural manoeuvres, which it characterised as an abuse of process from which she should not benefit. It also clarified that the one-year period under Article 12 ran from the date of wrongful removal to the date proceedings commenced, not to the date of judgment.

After the European Court refused an interim-measure request, the child was handed over to the Cypriot authorities on 29 May 2021 and returned to the United States. The applicant complained that the return order, the refusal to hear the child, the exclusion of additional evidence and the overall delay had disproportionately interfered with her family life.

The case of G.K. v. Cyprus (Application no. 16205/21) concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The Cypriot applicant, G.K., challenged domestic court orders requiring the return of her son to the United States under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction.

The applicant moved to New York in 2011 and married U.S. national C.T.G. in April 2016. Their son, a U.S. citizen, was born there in October 2016. The family lived together in New York, with both parents exercising joint custody under U.S. law. In October 2017 the applicant filed a domestic violence complaint against the father, alleging possessiveness, controlling behaviour, anger outbursts, belittling and humiliation. She and the child moved to a safe house. The New York Family Court issued a temporary order prohibiting the father from contacting them. On 25 October 2017 the applicant and the one-year-old child left the United States for Cyprus with assistance from Cypriot authorities, who granted the child Cypriot nationality and a passport. The New York court later dismissed her family offence petition because she failed to appear, citing illness.

The father learned of the child’s location in August 2018. In September 2018 he requested the child’s return via the U.S. Central Authority. The Cypriot Central Authority applied to the Paphos Family Court on 7 February 2019. The applicant objected, invoking Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention (grave risk of physical or psychological harm or an intolerable situation). She cited the U.S. protection order, the father’s alleged violence and Ohio criminal record, and the child’s integration in Cyprus (preschool since December 2017, riding and art classes, Greek as mother tongue, family ties). She also relied on Article 12, arguing the child was settled in Cyprus. The father denied violence, asserting he had been the family’s sole provider, and offered evidence of his ability to care for the child in the United States (stable job, apartment, health coverage). He submitted a letter from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children offering transition assistance.

The first-instance court allowed the father to file a supplementary affidavit but later refused the applicant’s request to file one containing a May 2019 child-psychologist report (finding the child integrated in Cyprus and predicting psychological harm from separation) and details of the father’s old convictions. The court held that the request lacked good reason, repeated existing claims, and would cause unacceptable delay contrary to the Hague Convention. The child, then aged three, was not interviewed because of his age and the applicant’s preference. After written submissions (proceedings delayed by COVID-19), the court delivered judgment on 21 January 2021. It found the father a credible witness whose evidence was consistent and largely unchallenged, while the applicant’s account was vague, contradictory and failed to meet the high burden of proof. The protection-order allegations were inconsistent with her U.S. affidavit, the petition had been dismissed for her non-appearance, and the criminal record consisted of minor offences from 25 years earlier. No grave risk was established, nor was settlement under Article 12 proven; the child’s young age meant he would readjust quickly with U.S. assistance. Immediate return was ordered.

The applicant appealed. The Family Court of Second Instance stayed execution, then on 19 March 2021 upheld the first-instance judgment in full. It confirmed that the one-year period under Article 12 ran from the date of wrongful removal (25 October 2017) to the date proceedings commenced (7 February 2019). It criticised the lengthy, unjustified first-instance delay (attributable both to court inefficiency and to the applicant’s late, abusive request to file a supplementary affidavit) but held that the applicant should not benefit from it. The psychologist report merely restated obvious bonds. Return was ordered by 29 March 2021.

The applicant sought an interim measure from the European Court of Human Rights, which was refused. The child was handed over to Cypriot authorities and returned to the United States. The Strasbourg Court later found no violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic courts had thoroughly examined the objections (including violence allegations), conducted fair adversarial proceedings, and given due weight to the child’s best interests, with the regrettable delay not amounting to a disproportionate interference.

The case of G.K. v. Cyprus (no. 16205/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that Cypriot courts violated her right to family life by ordering the return of her son to the United States under the 1980 Hague Convention on international child abduction.

The applicant, a Cypriot national born in 1986, moved to New York in 2011. She married C.T.G., a US national, in April 2016; their son (a US citizen) was born there on 15 October 2016. The family lived together in New York, where both parents jointly exercised custody and related rights under US law.

On 6 October 2017 the applicant lodged a domestic-violence complaint against the father, alleging he had become possessive, controlling, prone to angry outbursts and humiliating. She and the child moved to a safe house. On 11 October the New York Family Court issued a temporary protection order barring the father from approaching or contacting them. On 25 October, with assistance from the Cypriot authorities (who granted the child Cypriot nationality and a passport), the applicant and the one-year-old child left the United States for Cyprus. The New York court later dismissed the protection petition on 31 October because the applicant failed to appear, citing illness.

The father located them in August 2018 through private investigators. On 18 September he authorised the US Central Authority to seek the child’s return; the request reached the Cyprus Central Authority on 1 October 2018. On 7 February 2019 that Authority applied to the Family Court of Paphos for the child’s return to his habitual residence in the United States.

The applicant objected on 29 March 2019, invoking Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention (grave risk of physical or psychological harm or an intolerable situation) on the basis of the father’s alleged violence, the protection order and his criminal record, and Article 12 (child settled in the new environment). She submitted that the child had attended preschool since December 2017, formed friendships, taken riding and art classes, spoken Greek as his mother tongue and developed strong ties with her extended family in Cyprus.

The father filed a supplementary affidavit denying violence, stating he had been the family’s sole provider, still had the New York apartment, employment, health cover and a paediatrician, and offering assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children for the child’s transition. The applicant later sought leave to file a further affidavit attaching the father’s Ohio convictions (disorderly conduct and possession of drug paraphernalia) and a May 2019 psychologist’s report concluding that the child was fully integrated in Cyprus, that separation from his mother would cause psychological harm and that any contact with the father should be supervised. The first-instance court refused the request on 10 January 2020, holding that it disclosed no new circumstances, would cause unacceptable delay contrary to the Hague Convention’s expedition requirement, and merely repeated earlier claims; the applicant had already been able to cross-examine the father extensively.

The court declined to hear the child (then aged three) because of his age and the applicant’s wish that he not participate. In its judgment of 21 January 2021 it found the father a credible, consistent witness whose evidence was largely unchallenged, while the applicant’s account was vague, contradictory and unconvincing. She had failed to discharge the high burden of proving either a grave risk under Article 13(b) or that the child had settled under Article 12. The protection-order application had been dismissed for non-appearance and the criminal record consisted of minor offences committed 25 years earlier. The child’s young age meant he would readjust quickly, and US authorities would assist the transition. Immediate return was ordered.

The applicant appealed. On 19 March 2021 the Family Court of Second Instance upheld the decision in full, confirming that the one-year period under Article 12 ran from the wrongful removal (25 October 2017) to the commencement of proceedings (7 February 2019). It described the first-instance delay as lengthy and unjustified but attributable in part to the applicant’s late procedural requests, which it characterised as an abuse of process. A stay of execution had been granted pending appeal; after dismissal the child was to be handed over on 29 March 2021.

On 26 March 2021 the applicant applied to the Strasbourg Court for an interim measure under Rule 39. The request was refused on 29 May 2021; the child was handed over to the Cypriot authorities that day and subsequently returned to the United States.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 8 violation: the return order, made after the mother had removed the child amid unresolved violence allegations, interfered with her family life, raising questions about the thoroughness of the domestic courts’ examination of the risks, the child’s settlement and best interests, the fairness of the procedure (including the refusal to admit further evidence and to hear the child) and the impact of the delay.
001-223271:
The case of Căpăţînă v. Romania (Application no. 911/16) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the temporary seizure of the applicant’s assets during criminal proceedings and the subsequent confiscation of alleged proceeds of crime. The applicant, Daniela Căpăţînă, a Romanian national born in 1968 and living in Rădăuţi, was a border police officer at the Siret customs office on the Ukraine-Romania border. She later resigned. In late January and early February 2011, Romania’s National Anti-corruption Directorate opened investigations against her and over 60 other officers for participation in organised crime and bribe-taking linked to the illegal importation of cigarettes, diesel and alcohol from Ukraine between September 2010 and January 2011.

Prosecutors established that officers checking incoming vehicles accepted bribes of RON 8,000–25,000 (approximately EUR 1,800–5,600) per shift, which they hid and later shared according to each person’s duties. The applicant faced 13 counts of bribe-taking between 17 and 25 December 2010. On 18 April 2011, relying on Articles 163–166 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure, the prosecutor ordered the seizure of EUR 5,530, USD 24 (equivalent to roughly RON 22,192) and a car belonging to the applicant. The measure was intended to cover estimated damage of RON 28,800 (about EUR 7,000). The applicant was present, denied causing any damage and challenged the estimation method.

On 26 April 2011 the prosecutor committed 67 officers, including the applicant, for trial before the Suceava Court of Appeal. Because exact individual amounts could not be determined, the prosecutor proposed calculating confiscation by reference to each officer’s number of shifts, duties and an average sum per shift, arriving at RON 28,800 for the applicant. On 17 October 2011 the applicant applied to lift the seizure, submitting documents (including a letter from the National Integrity Authority and bank contracts) to show the funds were lawfully obtained. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application on 24 November 2011, finding that the applicant had not proved the seized money corresponded to the documented lawful sums and that those sums might already have been spent.

In a judgment of 6 May 2014 the Court of Appeal convicted 63 defendants, including the applicant, of bribe-taking. Video evidence showed that bribe-taking had become institutionalised, occurring openly in the presence of colleagues and superiors. The applicant was convicted only of the six counts visible on video and received a two-year suspended prison sentence. The court accepted the prosecutor’s calculation method but limited confiscation to RON 3,400 (approximately EUR 800), corresponding solely to the six proven counts. It ordered that this sum, plus RON 6,000 in costs, be taken from the seized assets, with any remainder to be returned once the decision became final. The seizure order itself was upheld.

All parties appealed to the High Court of Cassation and Justice. The applicant sought acquittal and the lifting of the seizure, relying on a 2013 Integrity Authority report that her assets were not disproportionate to her income. On 17 March 2015 the High Court dismissed the defendants’ appeals, upheld the prosecutor’s appeal and additionally convicted them of forming an organised criminal group. The applicant’s sentence remained unchanged and she was ordered to pay a further RON 1,000 in costs. The High Court endorsed the calculation method, confirmed that the defendants had failed to prove the lawful origin of the seized assets, and maintained confiscation of only RON 3,400. The remaining seized funds of RON 13,785 (approximately EUR 3,200) were reimbursed on 21 September 2015 after the applicant’s requests.

Under Romanian law, assets obtained through crime are subject to confiscation unless used to compensate damage (Article 112 § 1 (e) of the new Criminal Code and Article 118 § 1 (e) of the old Code). The European Court of Human Rights ultimately held that neither the temporary seizure nor the confiscation was arbitrary, that the amounts were not disproportionate given the calculation method employed, that the proceedings were adversarial and fair, and that a fair balance between the competing interests had not been upset.

The applicant, a Romanian border police officer at the Siret customs crossing, faced criminal investigation from January 2011 alongside over 60 colleagues for organised crime and bribe-taking. The allegations concerned a scheme from September 2010 to January 2011 in which officers accepted bribes (cash or goods) from traffickers to permit illicit imports of cigarettes, diesel and alcohol from Ukraine. Bribes of RON 8,000–25,000 per shift were pooled and shared according to each officer’s duties and shift timing. The applicant faced 13 specific counts of bribe-taking between 17 and 25 December 2010.

On 18 April 2011 the prosecutor, relying on Articles 163–166 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure, ordered precautionary seizure of assets to cover an estimated RON 28,800 in damage. EUR 5,530 plus USD 24 (then worth approximately RON 22,192) and a car remaining in the applicant’s possession were seized. She was present, denied causing damage and contested the estimation method. The prosecutor later committed 67 officers for trial, explaining that exact individual receipts could not be isolated because of the sharing system; he therefore proposed an average-per-shift calculation based on each accused’s number of shifts and role, yielding the same RON 28,800 figure for the applicant.

In October 2011 the applicant applied to the Suceava Court of Appeal to lift the seizure, submitting a National Integrity Authority letter and bank documents to prove lawful origin of the funds. The court dismissed the application on 24 November 2011, finding that she had not shown the seized cash matched the documented sums and that lawful income might have been spent elsewhere.

On 6 May 2014 the Court of Appeal convicted 63 defendants, including the applicant, of bribe-taking. Video evidence showed the practice had become institutionalised. She was convicted only of the six counts visible on recordings and received a two-year suspended sentence. The court accepted the prosecutor’s averaging method but limited confiscation to the shifts corresponding to the proven counts, ordering forfeiture of RON 3,400 as proceeds of crime under both the old and new Criminal Codes. The original seizure remained in force; after deduction of the confiscated sum and RON 6,000 in costs, any remainder was to be returned once the judgment became final.

All parties appealed. The applicant sought acquittal and release of the assets, citing a 2013 Integrity Authority report that her wealth was not disproportionate to income. On 17 March 2015 the High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed the defence appeals, additionally convicted the accused of forming an organised criminal group, and upheld both the RON 3,400 confiscation and the seizure. It confirmed that the defendants had received bribes and had failed to prove lawful origin of the seized property, while endorsing the shift-based averaging method (adjusted downward for the reduced number of counts). An additional RON 1,000 in costs was imposed.

The High Court judgment was served on 16 September 2015. After two requests, the remaining RON 13,785 was reimbursed to the applicant on 21 September 2015. The interference with possessions thus consisted of a four-year temporary seizure of cash and a vehicle, followed by permanent confiscation of a modest sum calculated by an averaging method necessitated by the communal nature of the bribes, all occurring within adversarial criminal proceedings in which the applicant was able to contest both the measure and the calculation.

The case of Căpăţînă v. Romania (Application no. 911/16) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the temporary seizure of the applicant’s assets during criminal proceedings and the subsequent confiscation of alleged proceeds of crime following her conviction.

The applicant, Daniela Căpăţînă, a Romanian national born in 1968, worked as a border police officer at the Siret customs office on the Ukraine-Romania border. In January and February 2011, Romania’s National Anti-corruption Directorate opened investigations against her and more than 60 other border and customs officers for suspected participation in organised crime and bribe-taking linked to the illegal importation of cigarettes, diesel and alcohol from Ukraine between September 2010 and January 2011. Investigators established that officers checking incoming vehicles accepted bribes (cash or goods) from traffickers, hiding the proceeds and sharing them at the end of each shift according to roles, shift timing and other factors. Amounts received per shift ranged from approximately 8,000 to 25,000 Romanian lei (RON).

The applicant was charged with 13 counts of bribe-taking occurring between 17 and 25 December 2010. On 18 April 2011 the prosecutor, acting under Articles 163–166 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure, ordered the seizure of EUR 5,530, USD 24 (together valued at about RON 22,192) and a car belonging to her, to cover estimated damage of RON 28,800 (approximately EUR 7,000). She was present during the seizure and immediately contested both the measure and the estimation method.

On 26 April 2011 the prosecutor committed 67 officers, including the applicant, for trial before the Suceava Court of Appeal. Because exact individual receipts could not be determined, the prosecutor proposed calculating confiscation amounts by reference to each accused’s number of shifts, duties performed and an average per-shift figure. For the applicant this produced the RON 28,800 figure.

In October 2011 the applicant applied to lift the seizure, submitting bank documents and a letter from the National Integrity Authority to prove the lawful origin of the seized funds. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application on 24 November 2011, holding that she had not shown the seized cash corresponded to the documented sums and that lawfully obtained money might already have been spent.

On 6 May 2014 the Court of Appeal convicted 63 defendants, including the applicant, of bribe-taking. Video evidence showed that the practice had become institutionalised; officers took bribes openly in the presence of colleagues and superiors. The applicant was convicted only of the six counts visible on recordings and received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Adopting a refined version of the prosecutor’s method (attributing RON 1,400–300 per relevant shift according to role), the court ordered confiscation of RON 3,400 (approximately EUR 800) as the proceeds of the six proven offences, to be deducted from the already-seized assets, with any remainder returned once the judgment became final. She was also ordered to pay RON 6,000 in costs.

All parties appealed. The applicant sought full acquittal and release of the seized assets, relying on a further Integrity Authority report of April 2013 showing her wealth was not disproportionate to her income. In a final judgment of 17 March 2015 the High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed the defendants’ appeals, allowed the prosecutor’s appeal, added a conviction for forming an organised criminal group (sentence unchanged) and confirmed the RON 3,400 confiscation. It endorsed the calculation method, noted that the defendants had failed to prove lawful origin of the seized assets, and observed that the original RON 28,800 estimate had properly been reduced to reflect only the six counts of which the applicant was convicted. Additional costs of RON 1,000 were imposed.

The remaining balance of RON 13,785 (approximately EUR 3,200) was reimbursed to the applicant on 21 September 2015 after she made two requests.

Domestic law (Articles 112 § 1(e) of the new Criminal Code and 118 § 1(e) of the old Criminal Code) requires confiscation of goods obtained through crime unless used to compensate victims. The European Court of Human Rights later held that the temporary seizure and post-conviction confiscation were not arbitrary, that the amounts were not disproportionate given the calculation method employed, that the proceedings had been adversarial and fair, and that a fair balance between the applicant’s property rights and the public interest had not been upset.
001-223021:
The case of Ibrahimbeyov and Others v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 32380/13) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the annulment of the three applicants’ ownership titles to four small adjacent plots of land in Baku (totalling approximately 0.3585 hectares) without compensation. The applicants alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) due to the deprivation and of Article 6 (fair trial) due to an allegedly unreasoned domestic judgment.

In 1962 the Baku City Council allocated a large area, including the plots, to the Bibiheybat Oil and Gas Exploitation Entity (later a SOCAR subsidiary) for permanent industrial use. A 1999 order returning part of the land to the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) was later quashed. A 2000 BCEA order allocated other land to Sabail Municipality, but the Government maintained this did not include the plots at issue.

In December 2004 the Municipality sold three plots of 0.06 ha, 0.0585 ha and 0.06 ha to N.G., M.M. and the first applicant respectively for AZN 960 each. In October 2006 it sold a fourth plot of 0.18 ha to the first applicant for AZN 7,488. Cadastral plans and State Register of Immovable Property ownership certificates followed in late 2006. In 2009 the second applicant acquired the first plot from N.G. by swapping her 230 m² apartment (each valued at AZN 300,000). The first applicant received the second plot by gift from M.M. and then gifted the third plot to the third applicant. By December 2009 the first applicant held the second and fourth plots, the second applicant the first, and the third applicant the third. The BCEA approved house-construction plans (intended as part of a cinema centre) and work began.

From October 2009 SOCAR representatives occupied the plots and halted construction. In May 2010 the applicants sued SOCAR for unlawful occupation. SOCAR counterclaimed for annulment of the certificates, Municipality orders, related acts, the swap and the gifts, asserting the land remained in lawful permanent use by its subsidiary. The Municipality later confirmed to the court that it neither owned the plots nor possessed allocation documents.

On 31 January 2012 the Sabail District Court dismissed the applicants’ claim and granted the counterclaim. It held that the 1962 allocation remained valid, the land was industrial with no reclassification, and the Municipality had no authority to sell it. All titles, decisions, contracts and plans were declared invalid. The applicants appealed, arguing the 1962 decision conferred no proper title under later Land Codes, the land had been returned to the BCEA and then the Municipality, they were bona fide acquirers, any fault lay with the State, and the court had ignored their unquantified claims for construction expenditure and lost profit (supported by an expert valuation of AZN 4.32 million for the land).

The Baku Court of Appeal (27 July 2012) and Supreme Court (4 December 2012) upheld the first-instance judgment, including dismissal of the damages claim. They added that the gifts of State-owned land produced no legal consequences and that the second applicant could pursue a separate action concerning her apartment. The courts relied on Civil Code provisions allowing invalidation of unlawful State or municipal acts and on the Law on the State Register of Immovable Property.

The applicants maintained that the interference was unlawful, disproportionate and uncompensated, violating their property rights, and that the decisions lacked adequate reasoning.

The case of Ibrahimbeyov and Others v. Azerbaijan (no. 32380/13) was brought by three Azerbaijani nationals whose titles to four plots of land in Baku were annulled by domestic courts without compensation. They alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), as well as a lack of reasoned decisions under Article 6.

In 1962 the Baku City Council allocated a large area of land (including the plots later at issue) to the Bibiheybat Oil and Gas Exploitation Entity for permanent use. That entity later became a subsidiary of the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR). In 1999 the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA) ordered the return of 266.05 ha from the entity, but the order was later quashed. In 2000 the BCEA allocated 198.62 ha to the Sabail Municipality; the Government later maintained that this allocation did not cover the specific plots.

In December 2004 the Municipality sold three small plots (0.06 ha, 0.0585 ha and 0.06 ha) to N.G., M.M. and the first applicant for 960 AZN each. In October 2006 it sold a fourth plot of 0.18 ha to the first applicant for 7 488 AZN. Cadastral plans were issued in November 2006 and ownership certificates followed in December 2006.

In 2009 the plots were transferred among the applicants: the second applicant obtained the first plot from N.G. by a swap agreement in which she transferred a 230 m² flat (each party valuing the exchanged assets at 300 000 AZN); M.M. gifted the second plot to the first applicant; and the first applicant gifted the third plot to the third applicant. Fresh ownership certificates were issued. By December 2009 the first applicant held two plots, the second applicant one plot and the third applicant one plot. The BCEA approved construction plans for houses intended to form part of a cinema centre and work began.

From October 2009 SOCAR representatives entered and occupied the land, stopping the works. In May 2010 the applicants sued SOCAR for unlawful occupation. SOCAR counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the applicants’ certificates and of the Municipality’s allocation decisions, arguing that the land had remained in the lawful permanent use of its subsidiary since 1962. The applicants later added claims for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage (actual expenditure, lost profit and alleged market value of approximately 4.32 million AZN), while hoping the land would be restored to them.

In March 2012 the Municipality informed the court that it did not own the land and possessed no documents of allocation. The Sabail District Court dismissed the applicants’ claims and granted SOCAR’s counterclaim. It held that the 1962 allocation remained valid, the land was industrial and had never been reclassified, and the Municipality therefore had no title to sell. All related certificates, contracts and plans were declared invalid. The Baku Court of Appeal (July 2012) and the Supreme Court (December 2012) upheld that outcome. The appellate court added that the gratuitous gift deeds produced no legal consequences because the land belonged to the State, and that the second applicant could bring a separate claim in respect of the swapped flat. No compensation was awarded.

The applicants maintained that they were bona-fide purchasers, that any defect was attributable to the public authorities, and that the courts had ignored their damage claims and the 1999–2000 reallocations. The European Court later examined whether the annulment pursued a legitimate aim (restoration of legality) and whether a fair balance had been struck, noting that avenues for compensation remained open under domestic law.

The case of Ibrahimbeyov and Others v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 32380/13) concerns three Azerbaijani applicants whose titles to four small plots of land in Baku were annulled by domestic courts without compensation. This raised issues primarily under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), as well as Article 6 (right to a reasoned decision).

In 1962 the Baku City Council allocated a large area of land, including the plots later at issue, to the Bibiheybat Oil and Gas Exploitation Entity (later a subsidiary of the state-owned SOCAR) for permanent industrial use. A 1999 BCEA order purporting to return part of that land was later quashed. In 2000 the BCEA allocated other land to Sabail Municipality; the Government maintained that this allocation did not cover the disputed plots.

Between 2004 and 2006 the Municipality sold the four plots (totalling approximately 0.36 ha) to the first applicant and two other private parties for modest sums. State cadastral plans and ownership certificates were issued. In 2009 the plots were transferred among the three applicants by a swap agreement (in which the second applicant exchanged a large flat valued at AZN 300,000) and two deeds of gift. Fresh certificates of title were registered. The BCEA then approved the applicants’ construction plans for houses forming part of a proposed cinema centre, and building work commenced.

From October 2009 SOCAR personnel occupied the sites and halted construction. The applicants sued SOCAR for unlawful occupation. SOCAR counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the titles and related municipal acts, arguing that the land had remained in its subsidiary’s lawful permanent use since 1962 and had never been reclassified or validly transferred.

In a 13 March 2012 letter the Municipality itself confirmed that it did not own the plots and possessed no allocation documents. On 31 January 2012 the Sabail District Court dismissed the applicants’ claims (including a late request for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages supported by an expert valuation of over AZN 4 million) and declared the certificates, municipal orders, swap and gifts invalid. It held that the 1962 allocation remained effective, the land was still industrial, and the Municipality had never acquired title. The Baku Court of Appeal (27 July 2012) and Supreme Court (4 December 2012) upheld that reasoning. They added that the gratuitous gifts produced no legal effects and that the second applicant could bring a separate action concerning the exchanged flat. No compensation was awarded.

The applicants argued that the 1962 decision conferred no valid title, that the land had been returned to the Municipality, that they were bona fide purchasers who had invested in planning and materials, and that any administrative error was attributable to the State. They also complained that the courts failed to address their damage claims. Domestic law (Civil Code Arts. 19, 149.2, 337.5 and 1100; Law on Administrative Procedure Art. 89; State Register Law) permitted challenges to registrations, restitution of invalid transactions and State liability for unlawful acts. Later Supreme Court practice in similar cases awarded compensation against public authorities.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the 1962 industrial allocation that was never formally revoked, the Municipality’s subsequent sales despite lacking title, the applicants’ acquisition of registered titles and commencement of construction, SOCAR’s occupation, and the courts’ subsequent annulment of those titles without any award of compensation in the same proceedings.

The case of Stoenescu v. Romania (ECtHR, Application no. 14166/19, judgment of 28 February 2023) concerns complaints by a Romanian national, Vlad Stoenescu, under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). These arose from domestic courts’ refusal to reimburse or cancel remaining court fees after his partition action was dismissed as devoid of purpose following an out-of-court settlement, requiring him to pay the fees in full despite the case ending at the first hearing.

After divorcing M.S. in 2012, the couple jointly owned two immovable properties in Bucharest. On 8 September 2017, the applicant filed a partition action in the Bucharest District Court. On 12 September 2017, the court notified him of stamp duty of 42,419.2 RON (approximately €9,220), equalling 5% of the property value under Article 5 of Emergency Government Ordinance no. 80/2013. He requested payment in 20 monthly instalments, which was granted on 2 October 2017, as his income did not qualify him for exemption or reduction.

On 10 October 2017, the parties signed a notarial agreement for voluntary partition of the properties. Notary fees totalled about €120 (including VAT) and land-register taxes about €150. The first hearing was scheduled for 18 January 2018. At that hearing—the only one in the case—the District Court noted the parties’ request to take account of the agreement and dismissed the action as devoid of purpose.

On 16 April 2018 the applicant lodged a separate claim for reimbursement of fees already paid and cancellation of remaining instalments, relying on Article 45 § 1 (c) of EGO no. 80/2013. This provision allows refund (in full, part or proportionally) where an action becomes devoid of purpose “as a result of certain legal provisions.” He argued that the State’s purpose in allowing such refunds was to prevent material harm when actions lose purpose, that legal rules prevented the court from ruling once a notarial settlement existed, and that he had already paid notarial and registration costs. He cited one comparable county-court decision granting reimbursement.

On 23 April 2018 the Bucharest District Court (Third District) dismissed the claim. It held that the listed refund situations were exceptions requiring restrictive interpretation, that judicial expenses are in principle non-refundable, and that the outcome resulted from the parties’ own will rather than legislative interference, so Article 45 § 1 (c) did not apply.

The applicant appealed, contending that “legal provisions” included those obliging the court to acknowledge a notarial agreement (rendering contentious proceedings impossible) and that requiring court fees after notarial costs amounted to double taxation. On 2 October 2018 the Bucharest County Court dismissed the appeal, confirming that termination by out-of-court settlement before the first hearing did not fall within the statutory grounds for reimbursement or cancellation. By September 2021 the applicant had paid the full 42,419.2 RON.

Relevant domestic law included EGO no. 80/2013 (5% stamp duty on partition actions; 50% when a court merely confirms an agreement; refunds under Article 45), the Mediation Act (partial refunds except in property-partition cases), and Civil Code Article 320 (division by agreement or court). Constitutional Court decisions emphasised that reimbursements prevent unjust enrichment of the State but that access to justice is not free of charge; citizens must contribute reasonably to the public costs of administering justice, and the legislature has exclusive power to set payment and refund conditions.

The applicant submitted several domestic judgments in which courts had granted refunds when actions became devoid of purpose (including similar partition or pre-hearing settlement cases). The Government submitted one judgment holding that refunds applied only in cases of legislative interference, independent of the parties’ conduct.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: that the reimbursement proceedings were unfair (owing to allegedly inconsistent interpretation of Article 45 § 1 (c)) and that requiring full payment of substantial fees, despite the action ending immediately after a notarial settlement, disproportionately interfered with the applicant’s property rights.

The case of Stoenescu v. Romania (ECtHR Application no. 14166/19) arose from complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applicant, a Romanian national living in Bucharest, alleged that domestic courts had unfairly required him to pay the full stamp duty on a partition action that was dismissed as devoid of purpose at the first hearing following an out-of-court settlement, imposing a disproportionate financial burden.

The applicant and his former wife M.S. divorced in April 2012 after years of marriage during which they had become joint owners of two immovable properties in Bucharest. On 8 September 2017 he brought an action in the Bucharest District Court seeking judicial partition of those properties. On 12 September 2017 the court notified him of his obligation to pay stamp duty of 42,419.2 RON (approximately EUR 9,220), calculated as 5% of the value of the estate under Article 5 of Emergency Government Ordinance no. 80/2013. He applied to pay in twenty monthly instalments; this was granted on 2 October 2017 because his income did not qualify him for exemption or reduction, only for instalment payments.

On 10 October 2017, before any hearing, the parties signed a notarial agreement effecting voluntary partition of the two properties. Notary fees amounted to RON 565.25 (approximately EUR 120 including VAT) and land-register taxes to RON 677 (approximately EUR 150). The first (and only) hearing was scheduled for 18 January 2018. At that hearing the District Court noted the parties’ request that the voluntary agreement be taken into account and dismissed the action as devoid of purpose.

On 16 April 2018 the applicant lodged a separate claim seeking reimbursement of the stamp duty already paid and cancellation of the remaining instalments, relying on Article 45 § 1 (c) of EGO no. 80/2013. That provision permits refund of stamp duty where an action becomes devoid of purpose “as a result of certain legal provisions.” He argued that the State’s purpose in allowing reimbursement was to prevent material harm once an action lost its object, that his claim had been dismissed because legal rules prevented a court from ruling on partition once it had been settled extra-judicially, and that he had already paid notarial and registration costs for the same transaction. He produced one county-court decision that had granted reimbursement in analogous circumstances.

On 23 April 2018 the Bucharest District Court of the Third District dismissed the reimbursement claim. It held that the statutory grounds for refund were exceptions to the general rule that judicial expenses are non-refundable and must be interpreted restrictively. Because the action had been terminated by the parties’ own agreement rather than by legislative interference, Article 45 § 1 (c) did not apply.

The applicant appealed on 9 May 2018, contending that the phrase “as a result of certain legal provisions” could not be confined to direct legislative intervention. Once a notarial partition had occurred, the law itself obliged the court to take note of it and to dismiss the contentious action; mediation and extra-judicial settlement were actively encouraged by Romanian law. Paying stamp duty in addition to notarial fees amounted to double taxation for the same matter. On 2 October 2018 the Bucharest County Court dismissed the appeal, confirming that an out-of-court settlement reached before the first hearing did not fall within the situations justifying reimbursement or cancellation of court fees. By September 2021 the applicant had paid the entire sum of RON 42,419.2.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the domestic courts had misapplied the stamp-duty legislation, that their interpretation produced an unfair and inconsistent result, and that the obligation to pay the full fee for a case that never proceeded beyond the first hearing constituted an unjustified interference with his property rights.

In Stoenescu v. Romania (no. 14166/19), the applicant, a Romanian national, alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property rights). These arose from domestic courts’ refusal to reimburse or cancel remaining court fees after his partition action was dismissed as devoid of purpose following an out-of-court settlement, despite the case ending at the first hearing.

After divorcing M.S. in 2012, the pair jointly owned two Bucharest properties. On 8 September 2017 the applicant sued in the Bucharest District Court for judicial partition. Under Article 5 of Emergency Government Ordinance no. 80/2013, stamp duty of 42,419.2 RON (approximately €9,220)—5 % of the properties’ value—was required. The court allowed payment in 20 monthly instalments after finding the applicant ineligible for exemption or reduction.

On 10 October 2017, before any hearing, the parties executed a notarial deed of voluntary partition. They paid modest notary fees (€120) and land-registry taxes (€150). At the sole hearing on 18 January 2018 the District Court noted the agreement and dismissed the action as devoid of purpose.

He also claimed the fees amounted to double taxation given the notarial costs already incurred, and he produced one similar decision in which reimbursement had been granted.

On 23 April 2018 the Bucharest District Court (Third District) rejected the claim. By 2021 the applicant had paid the entire stamp duty.

001-223380:
**Z.A. v. Ireland (ECtHR, App. No. 19632/20, 9 March 2023)**

The applicant, a Nigerian national born in 1994, arrived in Ireland in 2001 aged 7 to join his mother (who had arrived in 1999) and siblings. His father was deceased. His mother later obtained Irish citizenship as the parent of an Irish-born child, as did all six of the applicant’s siblings. Until age 16 he held permission to remain as her dependant; thereafter he received successive permissions in his own right (subject to obeying the law and avoiding crime). Permission was not renewed after 2014 amid pending criminal proceedings. By the time of his ECtHR application he was living in Vietnam as a professional footballer.

In 2010, aged 16, he was charged with sexual assault and two counts of attempted defilement of a child under 17 arising from incidents with a 14-year-old girl known to him and other teenage boys. He pleaded guilty at trial in 2014 (aged 20). The Circuit Court imposed a two-year sentence, fully suspended for three years (citing delay), plus 12 months’ probation supervision. The judge described the offences as serious and distressing to the victim, noted a moderate risk of reoffending, and expressed concern that the offenders still failed to grasp the impact on the victim. In July 2014 the applicant was also caught driving on a motorway without a full licence or insurance; he was convicted and fined €300 in February 2015.

A first deportation proposal (February 2015) led to an April 2016 order that was later revoked. A fresh proposal followed. A detailed April 2017 INIS analysis accepted that deportation would interfere with the applicant’s private life (long residence, education at all levels, football career and social ties) and family life (residence with his mother and some siblings/nephews; a relationship with an Irish girlfriend of Nigerian origin). It found, however, that he retained cultural and family ties to Nigeria (formative years there, remaining relatives) and could reintegrate and pursue football there. The sexual offences (treated as very serious despite his age and the absence of a custodial sentence) plus the later traffic offences demonstrated ongoing disregard for Irish law and a threat to public order. No formal rehabilitation had occurred. Applying a balancing exercise (citing A.A. v. UK among other authorities), the analysis concluded that the public interest in preventing crime outweighed the Article 8 rights; family members (including the girlfriend) could relocate or visit. Constitutional rights of the Irish-citizen relatives were likewise outweighed by the State’s interest in immigration control and the common good. The Minister issued a deportation order on 21 April 2017.

The applicant sought judicial review, arguing the decision was a disproportionate interference with Article 8 rights and that the Immigration Act 1999 lacked an independent appeal mechanism, contrary to Article 13. The High Court (30 May 2019) applied the established Meadows/ISOF reasonableness test: whether the Minister’s balancing exercise contained a flaw producing a conclusion that “plainly and unambiguously flies in the face of fundamental reason and common sense.” It found none. The court distinguished A.A. v. UK on the facts (age, post-offence conduct, risk assessment) and held that traffic offences could be considered. Judicial review itself supplied an effective remedy capable of vindicating Convention rights. Leave to appeal was refused (no point of exceptional public importance). The Supreme Court likewise refused leapfrog leave, holding that settled principles had been correctly applied.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR of violations of Article 8 (disproportionate expulsion after 16 years’ lawful residence, family integration and limited post-conviction offending) and Article 13 (absence of a full independent proportionality review). He had by then left Ireland for employment in Vietnam but maintained the challenge.

The case of Z.A. v. Ireland involves a Nigerian national born in 1994 who arrived in Ireland in 2001, aged seven, to join his mother and siblings after his father’s death. His mother had entered Ireland in 1999, obtained leave to remain as the parent of an Irish-citizen child born shortly after her arrival, and later acquired Irish citizenship along with the applicant’s six siblings. The applicant held dependent permission to remain until age 16 (2010), after which he received independent permission for one year and then three years, conditioned on obeying the law and avoiding criminal activity. This was not renewed after 2014, when he applied for naturalisation (then pending).

In March 2010, aged 16, the applicant was charged with one count of sexual assault and two counts of attempted defilement of a child under 17, arising from incidents in February–March 2010 involving a 14-year-old girl known to him and other teenage boys. He pleaded guilty in 2014 (aged 20). On 31 October 2014 the Circuit Court imposed a two-year sentence, suspended for three years due to the delay in proceedings (as a matter of fairness), plus 12 months’ probation supervision. The judge described the offences as serious and concerning, noted the victim’s significant distress, recorded a moderate risk of reoffending, and observed that the offenders (including the applicant) still failed to appreciate the impact on the victim. Separately, in July 2014 the applicant was detected driving on a motorway without a full licence or insurance; he was convicted in February 2015 and fined €300.

On 26 February 2015 the Minister for Justice proposed a deportation order under section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999 on the ground that it would be conducive to the common good. An initial April 2016 order was revoked after judicial-review proceedings. Fresh representations were invited and submitted in December 2016. A detailed 7 April 2017 analysis by the Irish Naturalisation and Immigration Service examined the applicant’s private life (long residence from age 7, education through third level, football achievements and prospects, social ties) and family life (residence with his mother, two brothers, a sister and her children; a four-year relationship with an Irish-national girlfriend of Nigerian origin). It accepted interference with both rights but found remaining cultural ties and relatives in Nigeria, possible football opportunities there, and no insurmountable obstacles to family members relocating or visiting. The analysis treated only the sexual convictions (not other uncharged allegations) as relevant, described them as very serious offences against a minor committed when the applicant was above the age of criminal responsibility, noted the absence of formal rehabilitation, and viewed the subsequent traffic offences as evidence of ongoing disregard for the law. Distinguishing A.A. v. the United Kingdom (where post-offence conduct had been exemplary and risk low), it concluded that the public interest in preventing disorder and crime outweighed the applicant’s Article 8 rights and that no less-restrictive measure existed. Constitutional rights of Irish-citizen family members were likewise held not to prevail. The Minister accepted the recommendation and issued the deportation order on 21 April 2017, requiring departure by 4 June 2017.

The applicant sought judicial review in the High Court, contending that the order was a disproportionate interference with private and family life and that the statutory scheme lacked an independent appeal mechanism, contrary to Article 13. On 30 May 2019 the High Court dismissed the claim. Applying the Meadows/ISOF test, it held that the applicant had not identified any flaw in the Minister’s balancing exercise that produced a conclusion “plainly and unambiguously flying in the face of fundamental reason and common sense.” The court rejected arguments that insufficient weight had been given to the suspended sentence, that rehabilitation could be expected only if ordered, that the traffic offences were irrelevant, or that A.A. was indistinguishable. It noted the Minister’s power to revoke a deportation order at any time, taking all current circumstances (including Convention rights) into account. On Article 13 the court held that judicial review itself supplied an effective remedy, as the High Court could quash a decision shown to violate Convention rights. Leave to appeal was refused by the High Court (11 July 2019) for want of a point of exceptional public importance and by the Supreme Court (13 November 2019) on the ground that settled principles had been correctly applied. By then the applicant had left Ireland to play professional football in Vietnam, but he maintained the challenge.

These facts underpin the complaints that the deportation order violated Article 8 and that Irish law provided no effective remedy under Article 13.

The case of Z.A. v. Ireland (Application no. 19632/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns a Nigerian national born in 1994 who arrived in Ireland in 2001, aged seven, to join his mother and siblings. His father was deceased. The mother had entered Ireland in 1999, obtained leave to remain as the parent of an Irish-citizen child born shortly after her arrival, and later acquired Irish citizenship, as did all six of the applicant’s siblings. The applicant held permission to remain as a dependant until age 16 in 2010, after which he received independent permission (initially for one year, then three years from March 2011) subject to conditions that he obey the law and avoid criminal activity. In June 2014, while criminal proceedings were pending, he applied again for permission (and for naturalisation); it was not renewed.

In March 2010, aged 16, the applicant was charged with one count of sexual assault and two counts of attempted defilement of a child under 17, arising from incidents in February–March 2010 involving a 14-year-old girl known to him and other teenage boys. He pleaded guilty at trial in 2014 (then aged 20). On 31 October 2014 the Circuit Court imposed a two-year sentence, fully suspended for three years as a matter of fairness given the delay, together with 12 months’ probation supervision. The judge described the offences as serious and concerning, noted the victim’s significant distress, recorded a moderate risk of reoffending in the probation report, and observed that even after four years the offenders lacked appreciation of the impact on the victim. Separately, in July 2014 the applicant was caught driving on a motorway without a full licence or insurance; he was convicted in the District Court on 27 February 2015 and fined €300.

A proposal to deport him under s. 3 of the Immigration Act 1999 (on the ground that deportation would be conducive to the common good) was notified in February 2015. An initial April 2016 order was challenged and revoked. Fresh representations were invited and submitted in December 2016. A detailed April 2017 analysis by the Irish Naturalisation and Immigration Service accepted that deportation would interfere with the applicant’s private life (education through third level, football talent and social ties developed since age seven) and family life (residence with his mother, siblings and a claimed four-year relationship with an Irish girlfriend of Nigerian birth). It found, however, that he retained cultural ties and relatives in Nigeria, could pursue football there, and that family members (including the girlfriend) could relocate or visit. Weighing the sexual offences (serious, involving a minor, committed after the age of criminal responsibility), the absence of formal rehabilitation, the victim’s lasting harm, and the subsequent traffic convictions as evidence of ongoing disregard for Irish law, the analysis concluded that the public interest in preventing disorder and crime outweighed the Article 8 rights. The Minister accepted the recommendation and issued a deportation order on 21 April 2017 requiring departure by 4 June 2017.

The applicant sought judicial review in the High Court, contending that the order was a disproportionate interference with private and family life and that the Immigration Act 1999 was incompatible with Article 13 for lack of an independent merits appeal. In a 30 May 2019 judgment the High Court applied the Meadows/ISOF unreasonableness test (whether any flaw in the Minister’s balancing produced a conclusion that plainly flew in the face of fundamental reason and common sense). It rejected arguments that insufficient weight had been given to the suspended sentence, the lack of a court-ordered rehabilitation programme, or the asserted inadequacy of evidence of future risk (distinguishing A.A. v. United Kingdom on the facts of age, post-offence conduct and risk assessment). Traffic offences were held relevant to general propensity and respect for the law. The court also held that High Court judicial review itself constituted an effective remedy under Article 13. Leave to appeal was refused by both the High Court (11 July 2019) and the Supreme Court (13 November 2019) on the ground that no point of exceptional public importance or general public importance arose; the applicant (who had by then left for professional football employment in Vietnam) had not properly raised any claimed tension between domestic and Convention standards at first instance.

The applicant complained to the Court that the deportation decision and the limited scope of domestic review violated Articles 8 and 13.
001-223719:
The case of X v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 64886/19) originated as a complaint under Article 8 ECHR concerning the Czech courts’ enforcement of an order returning the applicant’s young daughter to the United States under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. An original Chamber judgment of 12 May 2022 found no violation. The applicant then sought revision under Rule 80, arguing that Judge Kateřina Šimáčková (elected in respect of the Czech Republic) should have recused herself under Rule 28 because, while a Constitutional Court judge, she had sat on a 7 April 2020 chamber that dismissed a related constitutional appeal. The Court accepted the request, holding that the judge’s prior involvement in closely linked domestic proceedings raised an objective impartiality issue that required the original judgment to be set aside in its entirety, irrespective of whether the applicant had flagged the point earlier.

The underlying facts are as follows. The applicant, a dual Czech–US national, married a US citizen in 2007; their daughter was born in the United States in March 2014. After an alleged incident of domestic violence the couple later resumed cohabitation. In June 2016 the family travelled to the Czech Republic. The applicant claimed they intended to settle there because of the child’s health problems and insurance difficulties; the father maintained it was a short visit. He returned alone to the United States in autumn 2016.

In August 2017 the father applied to the Brno Municipal Court for the child’s return, asserting wrongful retention. That court dismissed the application, finding that the father had acquiesced. On appeal the Regional Court reversed the decision in January 2018 and ordered return within one month, subject to “soft-landing” safeguards (separate housing, air tickets, six months’ maintenance, and an undertaking not to remove the child from the applicant’s care pending US custody proceedings). The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in December 2018, holding that none of the Hague Convention exceptions applied and that the safeguards were adequate.

Enforcement proceedings followed. The father applied in December 2018. After disputes over housing, the Municipal Court initially refused enforcement. On 4 June 2019 the Regional Court allowed the father’s appeal, accepted a rental agreement he had produced, and ordered immediate enforcement, noting the applicant’s non-cooperation. The child was physically removed from the applicant on 1 July 2019 and flown to the United States with the father; the applicant followed days later. Subsequent US proceedings awarded the father temporary custody, citing an incident at the US embassy in Prague.

In the revised judgment the Court examined whether the enforcement proceedings satisfied Article 8’s procedural requirements. It concluded that the domestic courts had given sufficient, relevant reasons, had treated the child’s best interests as paramount, and had struck a fair balance between the competing family-life claims. No violation of Article 8 was found.

**Summary of X v. The Czech Republic (Application no. 64886/19)**

The applicant, a dual Czech-US citizen born in 1980, married a US national in 2007. Their daughter was born in the United States in March 2014. The applicant claimed she was the child’s primary caregiver. In November 2014 the father allegedly assaulted her, leading to his arrest and a prohibition on approaching her and the child (no criminal charges followed as she declined to testify). A US court later approved an agreement giving her primary care and the father visitation rights. The parents subsequently resumed cohabitation and joint custody.

In June 2016 the family travelled to the Czech Republic. The applicant maintained they intended to settle there long-term because of the child’s health issues and difficulties obtaining adequate medical insurance in the United States. The father contended it was a temporary visit, supported by return tickets for September 2016. He returned to the United States alone in autumn 2016. In May 2017 he briefly visited the Czech Republic and sought facilitated contact through the Czech Office for International Legal Protection of Children.

On 25 August 2017 the father commenced Hague Convention return proceedings in the Brno Municipal Court, alleging wrongful retention. On 6 October 2017 the Municipal Court dismissed the application, finding the child’s habitual residence had been in the United States and the retention wrongful, but concluding the father had acquiesced under Article 13(a). On 9 January 2018 the Brno Regional Court reversed this decision and ordered the child’s return within one month, subject to the father’s provision of safeguards: separate housing, plane tickets, six months’ maintenance, and non-removal of the child from the applicant’s de facto care pending US court rulings. The court rejected arguments of grave risk under Article 13(b), citing the child’s resolved health issues, comparable paediatric care, and available insurance, as well as her young age facilitating adaptation. The applicant’s constitutional appeal was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded by the Czech Constitutional Court on 11 December 2018.

The father applied for enforcement on 20 December 2018. The applicant sought suspension, citing non-compliance with safeguards and new evidence of harm to the child’s mental health. On 27 February 2019 the Municipal Court rejected the enforcement application due to inadequate housing. On 4 June 2019 the Regional Court reversed this, accepting a rental agreement and proof of rent payment as sufficient (given the applicant’s non-cooperation), and ordered enforcement. It declined to re-examine the merits of the original return order or commission further expert reports, finding no material change in circumstances. On 1 July 2019 the child was forcibly removed from the applicant and handed to the father, who returned with her to the United States on 4 July 2019. The applicant followed on 10 July. An incident occurred at the US embassy in Prague on 2 July.

In the United States, a temporary protective order awarded the father custody, citing the embassy incident as mental abuse; later orders granted the applicant supervised visits. Criminal charges for assault and related incidents were filed against the applicant (she was later acquitted of assault). Housing for the applicant and child was not provided as ordered, requiring her to arrange it independently. Contact remained limited and supervised.

The applicant alleged that the Czech courts’ enforcement of the return order violated her Article 8 right to respect for family life. (The original ECHR judgment of 12 May 2022 finding no violation was later revised in full after it emerged that Judge Šimáčková, who participated, had previously sat on a closely linked Constitutional Court decision; the revised judgment of 30 March 2023 again found no violation, holding that the domestic courts had complied with Article 8 procedural requirements, given sufficient reasons, and struck a fair balance with the child’s best interests as the primary consideration.)

**Case of X v. The Czech Republic (App. No. 64886/19), ECtHR (former Fifth Section), Judgment (Revision) of 30 March 2023 (final 30 June 2023)**

This ECtHR case (revised after an original 12 May 2022 ruling) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for family life) arising from Czech courts’ enforcement of a return order for the applicant’s young daughter to the United States under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The applicant (born 1980, dual Czech-US citizen) married a US national in 2007; their daughter was born in the US in March 2014. The applicant alleged she was the child’s primary carer. After the father (unemployed) allegedly physically attacked her in November 2014, he was prohibited from approaching them. A 2015 US court order granted her care with the father’s visiting rights and travel conditions. They later resumed cohabitation and joint custody.

In June 2016 the family travelled to the Czech Republic. The applicant claimed a long-term move due to the child’s health issues and US insurance difficulties; the father asserted it was a temporary visit (return tickets booked). He left alone in autumn 2016. In May 2017 he briefly returned and sought contact via the Czech Office for International Legal Protection of Children.

On 25 August 2017 the father applied to the Brno Municipal Court for the child’s return, alleging wrongful retention. On 6 October 2017 that court dismissed the claim, finding US habitual residence and joint custody but concluding the father had acquiesced (Hague Art. 13(a)) due to delay and lack of interest; it did not examine grave-risk (Art. 13(b)). On 9 January 2018 the Brno Regional Court reversed, ordering return within one month if the father provided safeguards (separate housing, tickets, six months’ maintenance, no removal from the applicant’s care pending US custody rulings). It rejected acquiescence (father had attempted contact) and grave risk (child no longer had seizures; comparable US paediatric care/insurance existed; young child would adapt/learn English). Settlement in the Czech Republic did not bar return as proceedings started within one year (Hague Art. 12).

The Constitutional Court (11 December 2018) dismissed the applicant’s appeal as manifestly ill-founded, confirming wrongful retention, timely application, no acquiescence, and no grave risk from mere differences in living conditions; the safeguards were beneficial and not arbitrary.

The father applied for enforcement on 20 December 2018. The applicant sought suspension/discontinuance, citing unmet safeguards and changed circumstances (new evidence on the child’s mental health/development). The Municipal Court (27 February 2019) rejected both applications due to the father’s housing non-compliance. After mediation, the child’s guardian (Children Office) opposed enforcement, citing the father’s possible US criminal complaint against the applicant and the child’s three-year settlement. On 4 June 2019 the Regional Court reversed, ordering enforcement. It accepted the father’s rental agreement and six months’ rent payment (despite no co-tenant designation, as the applicant refused cooperation), found no change in circumstances from original proceedings, declined to re-examine the return order’s merits or order new expert reports, and noted no US abduction charges. It emphasised the child’s best interests in prompt return.

The child was forcibly removed on 1 July 2019 and handed to the father (who returned to the US on 4 July; the applicant followed on 10 July). Incidents occurred at the US embassy. Subsequent US proceedings awarded the father temporary custody (citing embassy events as possible mental abuse), with the applicant granted limited supervised visits; she was later acquitted of assault charges. Czech Constitutional Court decisions (16 July 2019 and 7 April 2020) dismissed further appeals, holding enforcement courts could not review the return order’s substance and that objections had been addressed.

The applicant alleged the enforcement ignored the child’s best interests, new evidence, inadequate/unenforceable safeguards, and parental non-cooperation, breaching Article 8 positive obligations. After revision (due to a Czech ECtHR judge’s prior Constitutional Court role in linked proceedings, raising Rule 28 impartiality issues), the ECtHR found no violation: Czech courts met Article 8 procedural requirements, gave sufficient reasons, and struck a fair balance with the child’s best interests as primary consideration. Enforcement review was properly limited to the order’s finality and compliance, without re-litigating merits.
