001-223649:
The case of Simona Mihaela Dobre v. Romania (Application no. 8361/21) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Romanian courts unlawfully refused permission for her to relocate with her minor son from Bucharest to Canada.

The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1976, and X had a son, Y, born in 2008. They married in 2010 and separated in 2014; Y thereafter lived with the applicant. She also has an older son, E, from a previous relationship. Y has an eating disorder involving sensitivity to food textures and flavours, requiring a carefully managed diet that the applicant has provided since early childhood.

In February 2016 the Bucharest District Court granted a divorce (finalised on appeal in November 2017). The courts approved the parents’ agreement on shared parental authority, assigned Y’s residence to the applicant, and fixed a contact schedule entitling X to every other weekend from Friday to Sunday, portions of Christmas/New Year/Easter, one exclusive summer month, and half of other school holidays. X was required to confirm 48 hours in advance and to pay child support.

In January 2018 the applicant informed X of her intention to move to Canada with Y, where she held a permanent residence permit, had a job offer, sufficient funds, friends, and planned to buy a house near a suitable English-language school that Y (already fluent in English) had seen and liked during a visit. X opposed the move, arguing it would sever Y’s ties with him and the extended family. X then sued for sole custody, claiming the applicant systematically excluded him from decisions. The applicant counterclaimed, seeking either exclusive parental authority (on grounds of X’s limited involvement, neglect of Y’s dietary needs, and failure to attend medical appointments or take overnight care) or, alternatively, court authorisation to relocate despite X’s objections. She argued Canada offered superior economic, social and educational opportunities and proposed maintaining contact through direct flights (which X already used for work) and videoconferencing.

The District Court commissioned a psychological assessment. The psychologist interviewed the family in late 2018 and reported in January 2019 that Y was more emotionally attached to his mother and half-brother E than to X, showed a preference for Canada but might not grasp the consequences, and that any change of residence (to X or to Canada) would not serve Y’s needs. She recommended sensory-integration therapy for Y and counselling to help the applicant foster age-appropriate autonomy, while advising both parents to keep Y out of their conflicts.

The court also heard Y in camera in January 2019. He expressed a wish to live with his mother and to move to Canada, citing enjoyment of a prior holiday there, while confirming he returned home each night after seeing X. A social inquiry into the proposed Canadian accommodation was refused as hypothetical.

On 18 February 2019 the District Court dismissed all claims. It found no serious grounds to revoke X’s parental authority, as there was no evidence of abuse, systematic neglect or non-payment of support. Relocating Y to X would contradict his emotional attachment to the applicant. Moving to Canada would likewise not serve Y’s best interests: given his age and maturity, his stated preference (focused on tourist attractions) carried limited weight; the psychologist’s report indicated he perceived reality through his mother’s attitudes and needed to develop autonomy rather than adapt to a new environment; and the move would deprive him of regular contact with X and with E (who would remain in Romania).

Both parents appealed. The applicant reiterated her Canadian arrangements, Y’s informed visit, and two earlier Romanian decisions permitting relocation to England; she again sought a Canadian social inquiry, which was refused. On 7 August 2020 the Bucharest County Court upheld the first-instance decision for the same reasons, concluding that the applicant had not shown specific circumstances justifying the move at the expense of Y’s development of autonomy and his relationships with his father and brother.

Romanian law (Children’s Act 2004 and Civil Code Article 497) requires that any change of a child’s residence that affects the other parent’s rights be authorised by a court applying the paramount principle of the child’s best interests, taking account of the child’s views (weighted by age and maturity), family attachments, developmental needs, and a psychosocial report. The applicant contended that the refusals interfered with her right to respect for family life by preventing her from offering Y better living conditions and education.

**Case of Simona Mihaela Dobre v. Romania (Application no. 8361/21), ECHR Fourth Section, judgment of 21 March 2023 (final 21 June 2023).**

The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1976 and living in Bucharest, complained under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life) that Romanian courts refused permission for her and her son Y (born 2008) to relocate to Canada without the father’s consent. She argued the move would provide better living conditions and education. The ECHR found no violation, holding that the courts gave relevant and sufficient reasons based on the child’s best interests and struck a fair balance.

The applicant and X married in 2010 after Y’s birth and separated in 2014; Y remained with the applicant, who also has an older son E from a prior relationship. Y has an eating disorder involving sensitivity to food textures and flavours, requiring a carefully managed diet provided by the applicant since early childhood. A 2016 District Court divorce (amended 2017 by the County Court) recorded the parents’ agreement on shared parental authority, Y’s residence with the applicant, child support from X, and a contact schedule: X could have Y every other weekend from Friday to Sunday evening, plus specified holiday periods, subject to 48 hours’ confirmation.

In January 2018 the applicant informed X of her plan to move to Canada with Y. X opposed it, citing loss of contact with him and the extended family, and sued in the Bucharest District Court for custody, alleging the applicant systematically failed to consult him. The applicant denied this, claiming X had been uninvolved, neglected Y’s diet and safety, and rarely exercised contact (supported by emails showing refusals). She counterclaimed for exclusive parental authority or, alternatively, court permission to relocate, asserting she held Canadian permanent residence, a job offer, sufficient funds, friends, a house Y had seen and liked, and a nearby English-language school. She noted direct flights and possible videoconferencing to maintain contact. X admitted limited involvement (never taking Y to school or medical appointments, no overnights or holidays together).

A court-appointed psychologist assessed the family in late 2018. Y showed ambivalence about residence changes but preferred Canada; however, he might not grasp the consequences. He was more emotionally attached to his mother and E than to X. The psychologist advised against any residence change, recommending therapy for Y’s sensory integration and counselling for the applicant to foster Y’s autonomy, plus parental avoidance of conflict. In a January 2019 in-camera hearing, Y (then about 10) told the judge he liked school and friends, preferred living with his mother, wanted to move to Canada after enjoying a holiday there, and believed X (who travelled for work) could visit.

The District Court refused a social inquiry into the proposed Canadian arrangements as irrelevant. On 18 February 2019 it dismissed all claims. It found no grounds to strip X of parental authority (no abuse or financial neglect) and held a move to X’s home contrary to Y’s attachment to his mother. Relocation to Canada would not serve Y’s best interests: his stated reasons (tourism, public transport) reflected immaturity; he perceived reality through his mother’s lens and needed to develop autonomy rather than adapt to a new environment; the move would also sever regular contact with X and E (who would stay in Romania). The County Court upheld this on 7 August 2020 for the same reasons, noting the applicant had not shown specific justification outweighing Y’s developmental needs and family ties. Requests for a Canadian social report were again refused as hypothetical.

Domestic law (Children’s Act and Civil Code) prioritises the child’s best interests, including development, family life, the child’s views (weighted by age/maturity), and maintaining attachments. The ECHR reviewed these facts and the courts’ process, concluding they had properly assessed competing interests.

The case of Simona Mihaela Dobre v. Romania (Application no. 8361/21) concerns the Romanian courts’ refusal to authorise the applicant to relocate with her son Y (born 2008) to Canada without the consent of Y’s father, X. The applicant alleged that this decision violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant and X married in 2010 and separated in 2014. Y remained with his mother; she also has an older son, E, from a prior relationship. Y suffers from an eating disorder requiring a carefully managed diet, which the applicant has provided since early childhood. A 2016 divorce judgment (final in 2017) confirmed shared parental authority, assigned Y’s residence to the applicant, and set a contact schedule entitling X to every other weekend, certain holidays, one exclusive summer month and half of remaining school holidays. X was to confirm visits 48 hours in advance and pay child support.

In January 2018 the applicant notified X of her intention to move to Canada, where she held a permanent residence permit, had a job offer, sufficient financial means, friends and a suitable house and school near which Y (fluent in English) had already visited and expressed liking. X opposed the move, citing loss of contact with himself and the extended family. He then sued for sole custody, claiming the applicant systematically excluded him from decisions about Y. The applicant counterclaimed for exclusive parental authority or, alternatively, court permission to relocate, arguing that Canada offered Y superior economic, social and educational opportunities. She asserted that X had never been involved in Y’s schooling or medical care, had neglected the special diet, had rarely exercised overnight or holiday contact, and that communication between the parents was impossible. She proposed videoconferencing and noted the existence of direct flights.

A court-appointed psychologist interviewed the family in late 2018. Y displayed ambivalence but a preference for Canada, though the psychologist doubted he grasped the consequences. Y was more emotionally attached to his mother and half-brother than to his father; a change of residence (whether to the father or to Canada) was not recommended, as it would disrupt his need to develop autonomy. Counselling for sensory integration and parental support was advised. When interviewed by the District Court judge in January 2019, Y confirmed he wished to move to Canada, liked the places he had seen there, and believed his father could visit. The court refused a social-inquiry report on the Canadian accommodation, deeming it irrelevant.

On 18 February 2019 the Bucharest District Court dismissed both parents’ claims. It found no grounds to strip X of parental authority: although contact was limited, there was no proof of abuse, neglect or financial default. Transferring residence to the father would contradict Y’s emotional needs. Relocation to Canada was equally contrary to Y’s best interests. Despite Y’s stated wish, his reasons (tourism, public-transport etiquette) reflected immaturity; the move would shift his focus from gaining independence to adapting to a new environment and would sever regular contact with his father and with E (who would remain in Romania). The psychologist’s findings were given decisive weight.

Both parents appealed. The applicant reiterated her material circumstances in Canada, Y’s informed preference and two earlier Romanian decisions permitting relocation to England. The County Court refused a Canadian social inquiry as hypothetical and, on 7 August 2020, upheld the first-instance judgment on identical reasoning: the applicant had not demonstrated specific advantages outweighing Y’s need for autonomy and continuity of relationships with his father and half-brother.

The European Court of Human Rights later held that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons centred on the child’s best interests and had struck a fair balance between the competing claims, finding no violation of Article 8.
001-224075:
The applicant, a Moroccan national born in 1978, moved to the Netherlands in 1981 at age three with his mother and siblings to join his father. He obtained lawful residence as a dependent, followed by a temporary permit (1993–2001) and an indefinite-duration residence permit in December 2001. From 2002 he had a relationship with a Dutch national, fathering two sons (born 2008 and 2014, the latter while he was in pre-trial detention). The children, both Dutch nationals, lived with their mother; the applicant acknowledged paternity of only the younger son and never cohabited with the family. He claimed regular access (Wednesday afternoons and alternate weekends) and some financial support, but provided limited documentary proof.

The applicant accumulated multiple criminal convictions, predominantly for hard-drug offences. These included a 2000 possession conviction (community service); three convictions between 2004 and 2012 for possession, assault, property damage and handling stolen goods (short prison terms and community service); a 2014 conviction for complicity in selling and possessing cocaine and heroin (12 months’ imprisonment, two months suspended); and a 2017 conviction for possessing 500 grams of cocaine (five months’ imprisonment plus forfeiture of his vehicle). Total unconditional imprisonment amounted to 16 months. Domestic courts repeatedly emphasised the grave public-health and societal harm caused by hard-drug trafficking.

In June 2017 the Deputy Minister of Justice and Security notified the applicant of an intended revocation of his residence permit, a return decision and a ten-year entry ban, citing the convictions and the “sliding-scale” provisions of the Aliens Decree 2000 (which allow revocation after 15+ years’ lawful residence once the aggregate sentence reaches 14 months). The applicant submitted written comments stressing his 35-year residence, employment, claimed break with crime, and family ties, and attached salary slips plus a brief statement from his former partner describing the access arrangement. He waived an oral hearing.

The November 2017 decision revoked the permit with retroactive effect from October 2016, ordered immediate departure and imposed the ten-year ban. The authorities acknowledged an Article 8 interference with family life but held it justified: the offences were serious and repetitive, the risk of reoffending remained high (especially given recent offending and lack of independent corroboration of reform), long residence and social ties were outweighed by the criminal record, Moroccan cultural and linguistic links (birth, parental origins, a 2016 holiday) were sufficient for resettlement, and contact with the children could continue from abroad. The children’s primary carer was their Dutch mother, who retained custody; no relationship of dependency requiring them to leave the EU was shown.

An objection was dismissed in May 2018 after a hearing. The authorities reiterated doubts about the depth of the applicant’s involvement with his children (no verifiable evidence of regular contact or financial contributions), noted that employment had coexisted with prior offending, and found no objective proof (e.g., a probation report) of reduced recidivism risk. A Regional Court judgment of March 2019 and a Council of State ruling of August 2019 upheld the measures, confirming that a fair balance had been struck under the Boultif/Üner criteria and that public-order interests prevailed.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the revocation and ban constituted a disproportionate interference with his family life under Article 8.

The case of Loukili v. the Netherlands (Application no. 57766/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the revocation of the applicant’s indefinite residence permit and the imposition of a ten-year entry ban. The applicant, a Moroccan national born in 1978, arrived in the Netherlands in 1981 at the age of three or four to join his father and has resided there lawfully ever since, obtaining a residence permit of indefinite duration in December 2001.

He formed a relationship with a Dutch national, resulting in two sons born in August 2008 and February 2014, both of Dutch nationality who live with their mother. The applicant acknowledged paternity of only the younger child and never cohabited with the family. His criminal record includes a 2000 conviction for possession of cocaine and heroin (community service); further convictions between 2004 and 2012 for drug possession, assault, property destruction and handling stolen goods (short prison terms and community service); a February 2014 conviction for complicity in selling and possessing hard drugs (twelve months’ imprisonment, two months suspended); and a January 2017 conviction for possessing 500 grams of cocaine (five months’ imprisonment and forfeiture of his car). The 2014 and 2017 courts emphasised the grave public-health and societal harm caused by hard-drug trafficking.

In June 2017 the Deputy Minister notified the applicant of the intention to revoke his permit, issue a return decision and impose a ten-year ban on public-order grounds under the Aliens Act 2000 and the “sliding-scale” provisions of the Aliens Decree 2000. The applicant submitted that revocation would separate him from his sons, parents and siblings; that he had reformed, obtained employment and maintained regular access (every Wednesday afternoon and every other weekend); and that he had virtually no ties to Morocco beyond a short 2016 holiday. He provided salary statements and a brief note from the children’s mother describing the access arrangement.

By decision of 21 November 2017 the permit was revoked with effect from October 2016, a return decision was issued and a ten-year ban imposed. The authorities accepted that family life existed but considered the interference justified after applying the Boultif and Üner criteria. They highlighted the pattern and gravity of the drug offences, the high risk of reoffending, the limited substantiation of day-to-day involvement with the children (the applicant had been detained for much of the younger son’s life), the applicant’s ability as an adult to rebuild a life in Morocco (where he had been born and to whose culture he remained connected through his parents), and the absence of obstacles to maintaining contact from abroad. The ban’s duration was deemed proportionate to the serious threat posed.

The applicant’s objection was dismissed in May 2018 after a hearing. The Deputy Minister reiterated that family-life evidence remained insufficiently corroborated, that employment had coexisted with earlier offending, and that no independent report (e.g., from probation services) demonstrated a reduced risk. An appeal to the Regional Court of The Hague sitting in Roermond was rejected in March 2019; the court found the authorities’ assessment of a current threat adequate, the evidence of changed conduct inadequate, and the overall balancing exercise compatible with Article 8. A further appeal to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State was dismissed in August 2019 without additional reasoning.

The European Court of Human Rights later held that the domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of its case-law and had not overstepped the margin of appreciation.

The case of Loukili v. the Netherlands (Application no. 57766/19) concerns a Moroccan national’s complaint that the revocation of his long-term residence permit and a 10-year entry ban unjustifiably interfered with his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant was born in Morocco in 1978 and moved to the Netherlands in 1981 at around age three or four to join his father, together with his mother and siblings. He was registered in the municipal database in January 1982 and resided lawfully thereafter, first as a dependent family member, then on a temporary permit from 1993 to 2001, and on an indefinite-duration permit from December 2001. From 2002 he had a relationship with a Dutch national; they had two sons born in 2008 and 2014 (the latter while the applicant was in pre-trial detention). The children, who hold Dutch nationality, live with their mother. The applicant formally acknowledged paternity only of the younger child and never cohabited with the family. He claimed regular access (every Wednesday afternoon and every other weekend) plus financial support, though he provided limited documentary evidence.

The applicant accumulated six final convictions between 2000 and 2017, mostly for drug offences. These included a 2000 conviction for possession of cocaine and heroin (community service); further convictions between 2004 and 2012 for possession of hard drugs, assault, property damage and handling stolen goods (short prison terms and community service); a 2014 conviction for complicity in selling and possessing cocaine and heroin (12 months’ imprisonment, two suspended); and a 2017 conviction for possessing 500 grams of cocaine (five months’ imprisonment plus forfeiture of his car). The total non-suspended prison time was 16 months. Domestic courts emphasised the commercial quantities involved, modifications to the applicant’s vehicle, and the societal harm caused by hard-drug trafficking.

In June 2017 the Deputy Minister of Justice and Security notified the applicant of an intention to revoke the permit, issue an immediate return decision and impose a 10-year entry ban on public-order grounds. After considering the applicant’s written comments (which stressed his long residence, family ties, recent employment and claimed break with crime, plus a short 2016 holiday in Morocco), the Deputy Minister issued the measures in November 2017. The decision applied the “sliding-scale” rule under the Aliens Decree and conducted an Article 8 balancing exercise by reference to the criteria in Boultif v. Switzerland and Üner v. the Netherlands. It found a high risk of reoffending given the pattern and gravity of the offences, attributed limited weight to the applicant’s 35-year stay because of his persistent criminality, considered that he retained sufficient ties to Morocco to rebuild a life there, and held that contact with the children could continue from Morocco or through visits. The entry ban was justified by the serious threat to public order posed by repeated hard-drug offences.

The applicant’s objection, appeal to the Regional Court of The Hague and further appeal to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State were all dismissed. The authorities repeatedly noted the insufficient substantiation of the claimed intensity of family life (a single unauthenticated note from the mother and the applicant’s own statements), the absence of independent evidence of rehabilitation, and the fact that prior employment had not prevented further offences. They concluded that the public-order interest outweighed the applicant’s private interest and that no relationship of dependency existed that would force the children to leave the European Union.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violation of Article 8.
001-224580:
The case of Zaghini v. San Marino (Application no. 3405/21) concerns an Italian national’s unsuccessful attempts to recover approximately EUR 1.89 million confiscated in San Marino following money-laundering proceedings against third parties (not the applicant). The complaint was examined solely under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2003 Italian authorities opened proceedings against the applicant for tax evasion and making unjust profits of around EUR 15 million. Letters rogatory led San Marino judges to investigate accounts linked to the applicant, his father, G.A. and P.A. (the applicant’s former partner). They discovered withdrawals of EUR 939,500 and EUR 1,006,700 in cash from an account in the applicant’s name (executed by his father while the applicant was under house arrest) and a safety-deposit box in G.A.’s name containing EUR 1,892,700. The box was seized. San Marino then instituted money-laundering charges (Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code) against the father, G.A. and P.A. Evidence showed that the father had handed the withdrawn cash to P.A., who arranged for G.A. to deposit it. The applicant had himself admitted depositing around EUR 1.8 million of illicit origin in San Marino.

In November 2005 the first-instance court convicted the three accused, imposed suspended sentences and ordered confiscation of the seized sum under Article 147 of the Criminal Code (mandatory confiscation of the proceeds or instrumentalities of money laundering). On appeal in May 2008 the convictions of the father and P.A. and the confiscation were upheld; proceedings against G.A. were discontinued as time-barred. The appeal court held that Italian evidence sufficed to establish that the funds (or the bulk of them) derived from the crimes for which the applicant was being prosecuted in Italy; a final Italian conviction was unnecessary. Fraud against the State was also an offence in San Marino. The accused had knowingly concealed the money’s illicit origin. An enforcement order of December 2008 confirmed confiscation of EUR 1,892,700 plus interest.

In Italy the applicant’s own trial ended in 2016 with a finding that the charges were time-barred; the Bologna Court of Appeal ordered restitution of any sums still under Italian seizure. The applicant then sought release of the San Marino funds. Three requests to the judge of international cooperation (2017–2018) were refused because the money had already been confiscated in the San Marino money-laundering case; the applicant was not an extraneous third party in good faith, having instigated the transfers. Appeals were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction or on procedural grounds.

In August 2018 the applicant applied to the Enforcement Judge to annul the confiscation, relying on the Italian time-bar decision. The request was rejected: the funds constituted the corpus delicti of money laundering whose illicit origin had been independently established in San Marino; the Italian outcome (limitation, not acquittal) was irrelevant. The applicant was not a bona-fide third party; his own Italian statements showed he knew of and directed the concealment. He had not attempted to prove a licit origin. Subsequent appeals (including to the third-instance judge) confirmed that the Enforcement Judge was competent to hear post-judgment claims of third parties, that the applicant had been afforded an adversarial hearing, and that the confiscation could not be undone without contradicting a final criminal judgment. San Marino procedure did not entitle an uncharged third party to intervene in the original trial.

The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, holding the confiscation proportionate to the fight against money laundering and that the applicant had been given a reasonable opportunity to put his case.

The case of Zaghini v. San Marino concerned an Italian national’s unsuccessful attempts to recover EUR 1,892,700 (plus interest) confiscated in San Marino following money-laundering convictions of third parties. In 2003, Italian authorities opened proceedings against the applicant for tax evasion and unjust profits totalling around EUR 15 million. Via letters rogatory, San Marino judges investigated the applicant’s father, G.A. and P.A. (the applicant’s former partner). They discovered that, while the applicant was under house arrest, his father—acting under a delegation—withdrew EUR 939,500 and EUR 1,006,700 in cash from an account in the applicant’s name. The father then delivered EUR 1,903,700 to P.A., who arranged for G.A. to open a safety-deposit box in his own name and deposit EUR 1,892,700 (the pair retaining small sums). The box was seized on 5 December 2003.

San Marino instituted money-laundering proceedings against the father, G.A. and P.A. under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code. The applicant’s Italian pre-trial statements, in which he admitted depositing approximately EUR 1.8 million of illicit origin in San Marino, formed part of the file. In November 2005 the first-instance court convicted the three accused, imposed suspended prison sentences and ordered confiscation of the seized sum pursuant to Article 147 of the Criminal Code. On appeal in May 2008 the convictions of the father and P.A. and the confiscation were confirmed; proceedings against G.A. were discontinued as time-barred. An enforcement order of December 2008 made the confiscation definitive.

Meanwhile, the applicant’s Italian trial ended in 2016 when the offences were declared time-barred; the Italian court ordered restitution of any preventively seized assets. From 2017 the applicant sought return of the San Marino funds as their legitimate owner. Requests to the international-cooperation judge were rejected on the ground that the money had already been confiscated as the proceeds of money laundering and that the applicant, as perpetrator of the predicate offence, was not an extraneous third party in good faith. Subsequent applications to the Enforcement Judge (under Articles 203 bis et seq. of the Code of Criminal Procedure) seeking annulment of the confiscation in light of the Italian outcome were likewise dismissed. The judges held that the illicit origin of the funds had been independently established by the San Marino courts on the basis of the accused’s statements and the applicant’s own admissions, and that a time-barred Italian prosecution did not alter those findings. The applicant had not demonstrated a licit source. Appeals to the second-instance criminal judge and the third-instance judge were rejected: the Enforcement Judge was competent to hear post-judgment claims of third parties, the applicant had been given a full adversarial hearing, and a final criminal judgment could not be reopened.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the confiscation of property belonging to him, effected without his conviction or participation in the San Marino proceedings, and the subsequent refusal to restore the funds, amounted to an unlawful and disproportionate interference with his possessions.

The case of Zaghini v. San Marino (Application no. 3405/21) concerns the confiscation of approximately EUR 1.89 million following money-laundering proceedings against third parties (not the applicant) and the applicant’s unsuccessful efforts to recover the funds, raising issues under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

In 2003 Italian authorities opened proceedings against Gianluca Zaghini (an Italian national) and others for tax evasion and unjust profits of around EUR 15 million. Via letters rogatory, San Marino investigated linked assets, identifying a bank account in the applicant’s name from which his father withdrew over EUR 1.9 million in cash (while the applicant was under house arrest). A safety-deposit box in G.A.’s name containing EUR 1,892,700 was seized.

San Marino then prosecuted the applicant’s father, G.A., and P.A. (the applicant’s former partner) for money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code. Evidence showed the applicant had deposited some EUR 1.8 million obtained from illegal activity; his father passed the withdrawn cash to P.A., who arranged for G.A. to hide it. The applicant’s own pre-trial statements in Italy admitted the illicit origin.

In November 2005 a first-instance court convicted the three (suspended sentences) and ordered confiscation of the seized sum under Article 147 of the Criminal Code (obligatory confiscation of proceeds/instrumentalities). A 2008 appeal confirmed the convictions of the father and P.A. (G.A.’s case became time-barred) and the confiscation, holding that the money derived from the applicant’s Italian offences even without a final Italian conviction. An execution order of December 2008 confiscated EUR 1,892,700 plus interest.

Separately, Italian proceedings against the applicant were declared time-barred in 2016, with an order for restitution of preventively seized funds. The applicant then sought recovery in San Marino, claiming ownership on the basis of the Italian ruling.

From 2017 he applied to San Marino’s judge for international cooperation for release of the sums. The requests were refused: the money had already been confiscated in the independent San Marino laundering case, and the applicant (author of the predicate offence) could not be treated as a third party in good faith. Appeals failed on jurisdictional or procedural grounds.

In 2018 he applied to the Enforcement Judge to annul the confiscation. This was rejected: the illicit origin had been established independently by San Marino courts (based on the accused’s confessions and the applicant’s own statements) and did not depend on an Italian conviction (the outcome there being a time-bar, not an acquittal). The applicant had instigated the hiding of the funds and had not shown licit origin. Further challenges (including claims of lack of participation in the original proceedings, absence of adversarial process, and incompatibility with G.I.E.M. S.r.l. and Others v. Italy) were dismissed. Domestic courts held the Enforcement Judge competent to hear post-judgment claims by interested third parties, that the applicant had been given a full opportunity (representation, hearings) to present his case, but that the judge could not contradict the final criminal judgment’s findings of illicit origin. Third-instance review confirmed these conclusions.

The facts thus centre on a confiscation measure applied after proceedings to which the applicant was not a party, relying on his earlier statements, and his subsequent inability to recover the money despite the Italian time-bar, against the background of San Marino’s obligations to combat money laundering.
001-224076:
**CASE OF T.H. v. BULGARIA (Application no. 46519/20)**

The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 2004, attended a mainstream municipal primary school in Sofia for years one (2011/12) and two (2012/13). He exhibited behavioural difficulties from an early stage. A March 2011 aptitude test indicated borderline school readiness, with behavioural problems and cognitive issues. His kindergarten history and parental reports confirmed difficulties controlling his behaviour.

In year one, shortly after enrolment, his teacher sought help from the pedagogical advisor due to adaptation problems. Meetings with his parents followed in autumn 2011. The advisor worked with the class monthly. A December 2011 meeting highlighted deteriorating behaviour; parents were advised to consult a family therapist but did not follow up immediately. In March 2012, the school's commission for preventing anti-social behaviour met with parents present. The teacher described the applicant provoking classmates, disrupting lessons (especially English), and preventing others from receiving education. Other parents had unenrolled children upon learning of his attendance. The head teacher warned of possible referral for punishment if behaviour did not improve. Parents cited financial barriers to psychologists.

Incidents ensued: on 19 March 2012, the applicant alleged assault (scratch on forehead); investigations, including by the music teacher and nurse, indicated he had kicked another boy who was responding to systematic harassment (insults, spitting, kicking). A similar 27 March incident was deemed accidental. Multiple parental complaints detailed the applicant's insults, aggression, threats with a screwdriver, cutting hair/supplies, hitting, and theft. Seventeen parents complained of ongoing disruption.

Parents sought child-protection help, leading to six months of Animus foundation counselling. A April 2012 meeting with school staff occurred; Animus opposed transfer. In May 2012, the pedagogical council reviewed 49 documented misbehaviour incidents (January–May). The teacher detailed aggression, rule-breaking, and failed interventions involving a teacher team and advisor. Despite parental opposition, the council recommended (38-0) a deferred warning of transfer, issued by the head teacher. Parents later alleged teacher misconduct (hair-pulling, exclusion without needs, pocket searches); these were denied, with one incident involving the applicant pointing a screwdriver.

In year two, Animus psychologists referred him for assessment. On 27 September 2012, specialists diagnosed hyperkinetic disorder and specific developmental disorder of scholastic skills, recommending an individual plan, resource teacher, and speech therapist. Parents informed the school. A October meeting discussed options; the head teacher rejected class transfer (school policy: one SEN child per class) and proposed individual education with classmate interaction only at breaks, citing psychologist views that behaviour would persist regardless of class. Parents refused, insisting on class integration.

The parents requested, and the head teacher granted, the interruption. The National Ombudsman later criticised the school for insufficient efforts at socialisation.

001-224505:
**CASE OF STRASSENMEYER v. GERMANY (Application no. 57818/18)**

This ECtHR case (judgment 2 May 2023) concerns the applicant Marco Straßenmeyer’s 2016 conviction for murder (life sentence) after a 1994 killing in the Czech Republic. It raises issues under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) ECHR regarding the use of untested pre-trial statements by co-accused who refused to testify at trial, and the police’s failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel.

In September 1994, G. was killed and his body found in woods in the Czech Republic (initially unidentified; G. was declared missing in Germany). G. had run a clothing shop in Erfurt with F., who later died by suicide. In 2012, N. (a former friend of F.) told police that F. had confessed involvement in killing a co-worker in the Czech Republic. In September 2014, police arrested K. (another shop worker). Before questioning, K. was informed in writing of his rights to remain silent and consult a lawyer, but—due to an outdated form not reflecting a 2013 legislative change implementing EU Directive 2012/13/EU—he was not told of his right to court-appointed counsel (applicable given the seriousness of the potential murder charge). K. described a group trip to the Czech Republic on 13 September 1994 involving G., S., M.S. (deceased), V., and the applicant; he claimed he was not present at the killing but was told the applicant had done it. Later, with counsel present, K. said he saw the applicant hit G. with a truncheon.

The applicant was arrested the next day and similarly informed (outdated form). He admitted visiting the shop but denied knowing G. or visiting the Czech Republic. S. (initially a witness) and V. were later arrested and questioned the same way. V. gave a detailed account: F. was angry at G. for financial mismanagement; the group drugged G. with LSD, drove him to the Czech Republic under the pretence of a party, and, after G. threatened to go to police, the applicant punched him. G. was put in a car boot; at a wooded area, the applicant and M.S. beat him. V. handed the applicant a tonfa (truncheon); after G. stopped moving, they decided to burn the body. K. fetched petrol. They discovered G. was still breathing; the applicant threw a rock at his head. V. claimed he later saw G. running as a “burning torch” (an account later contradicted by forensic experts). S. confirmed presence and screams but not seeing the killing; he said his late brother told him the applicant beat G. to death.

At the Erfurt Regional Court trial (starting April 2015), the applicant made only a limited statement about past drug use; the co-accused (V., K., S.) exercised their right to silence. The court heard the interviewing officers as witnesses regarding the pre-trial statements (to which the defence objected). Other evidence included: N.’s account of F.’s confession (drugging, beating, burning, burial); L.’s testimony that, shortly after the killing, K. and the applicant (in L.’s presence) admitted the murder, with the applicant boasting of beating G. “until it was quiet” with a club and “setting the finale”; B.’s confirmation of L. having told him this years later; Czech police and forensic evidence (bloodied rocks near the body, head fractures consistent with a tonfa, burns); and pathology showing it was highly unlikely G. could have moved after being set alight.

The court largely adopted V.’s account as the facts of the crime. It found V.’s statement reliable and corroborated by K.’s accounts (similar details of the trip and beating; no likely collusion as both were surprised by the investigation), L.’s testimony (matching details of beating and location), forensics (injuries and scene), and V.’s self-incrimination. Inconsistencies (G. moving after burning; distance of the body from cars) were explained as possible misperception at night from a moving car or G. briefly fleeing after an initial blow. The court noted the lack of interview recordings and the accused’s trial silence but held there was sufficient other evidence. The information omission was unintentional (not deliberate), the accused knew of the right to a lawyer (V. even insisted on speaking without one and had prior police experience), and there was no evidence of inability to afford counsel. The applicant and K. were convicted of murder and deprivation of liberty resulting in death; V. of murder; S. acquitted.

The applicant appealed, arguing the conviction relied primarily on untested co-accused statements (especially V.’s, of significant weight) that he could never examine, with insufficient counterbalancing factors (including denial of a psychological expert on V.’s veracity), violating fair-trial and defence rights. He also claimed the statements were inadmissible due to the counsel-information failure. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal (noting the State’s strong interest in prosecuting a grave crime, the unintentional error, and no indication of lack of means for a lawyer). The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaint.

The case of Strassenmeyer v. Germany (Application no. 57818/18) concerned the applicant’s 2016 conviction for murder (and related offences) by the Erfurt Regional Court, for which he received a life sentence. The conviction arose from the 1994 killing of G. in the Czech Republic, whose body was found in a wooded area with head injuries consistent with blows from a tonfa-style truncheon and burns. The investigation reopened in 2012 after witness N. reported that F. (G.’s business partner, who later died by suicide) had confessed involvement in drugging, beating, burning and burying a co-worker.

In September–October 2014 the police arrested K., the applicant, S. and V. (all former associates of F. and G.). Before questioning, each was given a written notice of the rights to remain silent and consult a lawyer, but an outdated form omitted the newly enacted right (under Article 136 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, implementing EU Directive 2012/13/EU) to request court-appointed counsel for serious offences. K. first implicated the applicant as the killer; later, with counsel present, he described seeing the applicant strike G. with a truncheon. V. gave a detailed account: the group had drugged G. with LSD, driven him to the Czech Republic, and the applicant had punched him, later beaten him with a tonfa supplied by V., thrown a rock at his head and participated in setting the body alight. S. confirmed presence but denied seeing the fatal acts. The applicant denied any knowledge of G. or travel to the Czech Republic. After questioning, an investigating judge assigned counsel and ordered detention; the accused made no further statements.

At trial the co-accused exercised their right to silence. The Regional Court therefore admitted the police officers’ testimony recounting the pre-trial statements (over defence objection) and heard additional witnesses. N. repeated F.’s confession. L. testified that in September 1994 K. and the applicant had confessed the killing to him in a shop back-room; the applicant had boasted of delivering the “finale” with a club while G. “squealed like a pig.” B. corroborated that L. had recounted the same conversation years earlier. Forensic evidence (bloodied rocks, injury patterns, burn traces) largely matched V.’s narrative, although medical experts considered it highly improbable that G. had risen and run after being set on fire—an inconsistency the court attributed to V.’s nighttime observation from a moving car. The court rejected a defence request for a psychological expert on V.’s credibility, holding that such an assessment was for the judges unless special circumstances (absent here) existed.

The Regional Court found the applicant guilty primarily on the combined force of V.’s detailed, self-incriminating statement (corroborated by K.’s account, L.’s testimony, N.’s report and the physical evidence). It treated the statements as reliable because collusion was implausible, V. had volunteered details only a participant would know, and he had no motive to fabricate a story that implicated himself. The court acknowledged the inability to examine the co-accused, the lack of recordings, and the omitted counsel warning, but regarded the last as an unintentional oversight; V. had expressly wished to speak without a lawyer and had prior police experience. It concluded that sufficient other evidence existed for conviction.

The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law, reiterating the State’s strong interest in prosecuting a grave crime and the absence of any indication that lack of funds had prevented counsel. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the subsequent constitutional complaint.

The applicant complained to the ECHR that his Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) rights had been violated by the use of untested, decisive co-accused statements and by the police failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel.
001-224732:
**Summary of Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. v. the Netherlands (ECHR, Appl. no. 2799/16)**

The applicant, a Dutch company collecting ship waste liquids in Rotterdam, alleged violations of Article 8 (respect for correspondence) and Article 13 (effective remedy) of the ECHR. The core issue was the transmission of lawfully obtained telephone intercepts from a criminal environmental investigation to the competition authority (NMA, later ACM) and their use as evidence in administrative fine proceedings for alleged price-fixing.

In late 2006, the VROM-IOD (a special investigative service under public prosecutor authority) launched the “Toto” criminal investigation into the I. company for illegal disposal of polluted waste. An investigating judge authorized telephone intercepts of I. company employees. These captured conversations between an I. employee and an applicant employee that indicated possible price-fixing.

On 21 April 2008, a VROM-IOD official recorded these indications in an official report with summary transcripts. The public prosecutor approved transmission to the NMA under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG) on 21 October 2008 (handwritten endorsement). Transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further transcripts and audio files were transmitted in 2009–2010 after contacts between the services to select relevant data. NMA inspectors later visited the applicant’s premises, questioned management, and played a recording.

The NMA found that several companies, including the applicant, had coordinated to allocate contracts and restrict price competition in ship waste collection from August 2005 to July 2007, violating section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it imposed an €834,000 fine.

The applicant objected, arguing the intercepts were not “criminal data” under the WJSG (as they were irrelevant to the environmental probe and mere “by-catch”), that transmission lacked prior judicial control, and that they should be excluded. With NMA consent, it appealed directly to the Rotterdam Regional Court (joined with related appeals). On 11 July 2013 the Regional Court quashed the fine, holding that while the data qualified as criminal data, the prosecutor’s unreasoned handwritten and pre-printed approvals showed no reviewable balancing of interests, requiring exclusion of the evidence on which the NMA had mainly relied.

The ACM appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry (CBb). The applicant cross-appealed on the “criminal data” point. On 9 July 2015 the CBb quashed the Regional Court judgment and remitted the case. It held the intercepts were “criminal data” (broadly defined as data obtained in a criminal investigation and processed in a file or automatically; a criminal file need not be limited to prosecuted offences). Transmission served a “compelling general interest” (economic well-being of the country, via competition enforcement) under WJSG s. 39f. Necessity, proportionality and subsidiarity were satisfied: cartels are rarely documented in writing, so intercepts could not reasonably have been obtained less intrusively; the ACM had no tapping powers of its own, but the WJSG expressly permitted transmission of such data. The prosecutor’s power was statutory; written contemporaneous reasoning was not required. Adequate safeguards existed via ex post civil-court review of the factual act of transmission and administrative-court review of the fine (including opportunity to comment on the evidence). Selection of data after consultation did not render transmission unlawful. There was no Article 8 violation.

Relevant WJSG provisions defined criminal data and permitted transmission by the Board of Procurators General (delegable to prosecutors) where necessary for a compelling general interest (including enforcement of legislation) after balancing interests, necessity, proportionality and subsidiarity. Transmission was a factual act, not an administrative decision, so not subject to administrative remedies; the sole prior remedy was a civil tort action. A 2008 Designation Order provided further guidance and a flowchart. Domestic case-law (including the Supreme Court’s Trafigura judgment) confirmed the broad definition of a criminal file and the availability of ex post judicial review of transmissions.

The Chamber found the transmission sufficiently foreseeable under domestic law, that extensive ex post judicial oversight and other safeguards adequately prevented abuse, that Article 8 did not require prior court authorization in this context, and that the interference was necessary and proportionate with relevant and sufficient reasons. It also found an effective remedy under Article 13. (The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber.)

Certain conversations between an I. employee and an employee of the applicant (a competing waste-collector operating in the Rotterdam port) contained indications of price-fixing. On 21 April 2008 a VROM-IOD official recorded those indications in an official report to which summary transcripts were annexed.

On 21 October 2008 the competent public prosecutor endorsed the report “transmission to NMA approved”. The document was sent to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) on 29 June 2009. In 2009–2010 the same prosecutor authorised further transmissions of selected transcripts and audio files after consultations between VROM-IOD and NMA officials on relevance. In June 2010 NMA inspectors visited the applicant’s premises, questioned management under caution and played one of the recordings.

The NMA concluded that between August 2005 and July 2007 several firms, including the applicant, had coordinated contract allocation and price limitation in ship-waste collection, thereby infringing section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it imposed a fine of €834 000.

The applicant objected that the material did not constitute “criminal data” under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG) because it was irrelevant to the environmental investigation, and that transmission lacked prior judicial authorisation. With NMA consent the objection proceeded directly to the Rotterdam Regional Court, which joined it with similar appeals by other fined companies. On 11 July 2013 that court quashed the fine: while the data qualified as criminal data, the prosecutor had recorded no reviewable balancing of interests, so the intercepts had to be excluded.

The Consumer and Market Authority (ACM, NMA’s successor) appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry. The applicant cross-appealed, insisting the intercepts were mere “by-catch” never properly part of any criminal file. On 9 July 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court reversed. It held that “criminal data” is defined broadly (WJSG s. 1(b)) and includes material processed automatically even if not used for prosecution; a criminal file may cover more than the offences ultimately charged. Transmission under WJSG s. 39f served a compelling general interest—the economic well-being of the country—because the ACM enforces the cartel prohibition. The original interceptions had been judicially authorised; transmission is a factual act, not an administrative decision, and is therefore reviewable ex post in the civil courts (lawfulness) and administrative courts (the resulting fine). The ACM had assessed the evidence, the applicant had been heard, and no less-intrusive means existed for uncovering unwritten cartel agreements. Selection of material in consultation with VROM-IOD did not render the transmission unlawful. The case was remitted.

The applicant maintained before the European Court that the transmission had not been foreseeable and that safeguards were inadequate. The Chamber later found the domestic legal framework sufficiently precise, the ex-post judicial oversight extensive, and the balancing of interests adequate; Article 8 therefore required no prior judicial authorisation in this context, and an effective remedy existed under Article 13.

The case concerns Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., a Dutch company collecting waste liquids from ships in the Rotterdam area. It alleges violations of Article 8 of the Convention (respect for correspondence) arising from the transmission and subsequent use in competition proceedings of telephone intercept data originally obtained in a criminal investigation, as well as a related complaint under Article 13 (effective remedy).

An investigating judge authorised the interception of telephone conversations of certain I. employees. Among the recorded calls were exchanges between an I. employee and an employee of the applicant company that contained indications of price-fixing.

On 16 November 2011 the NMA (later succeeded by the ACM) imposed an administrative fine of €834 000, finding that the applicant and several other companies had, between August 2005 and July 2007, coordinated the allocation of contracts and restricted price competition in ship-waste collection, thereby infringing section 6 of the Competition Act.

The court found no Article 8 breach: the original taps had been judicially authorised, the transfer had a statutory basis, adequate judicial oversight existed, the ACM had thoroughly assessed the evidence, the parties had been heard, and no less-intrusive means of uncovering secret cartels were available. The case was remitted.

The applicant then lodged the present application, complaining that the transmission had not been foreseeable under domestic law and that procedural safeguards were insufficient, and that no effective remedy existed.

The ECHR case Janssen de Jong Groep B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands (no. 2800/16) involved three Dutch construction companies. They alleged violations of Article 8 (respect for correspondence) and Article 13 (effective remedy) arising from the transmission of lawfully intercepted telephone data from a criminal investigation to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA, later ACM) and its subsequent use to impose an administrative fine for price-fixing.

Around 2007 the Public Prosecution Service, assisted by the National Police Internal Investigations Department, opened the “Cleveland” investigation into suspected bribery of local officials by contractors seeking infrastructure contracts. The applicant companies were implicated. An investigating judge authorised interception of certain employees’ telephone conversations. Some recordings contained indications of price-fixing.

In July 2008 police officers, on police premises and in strict confidence, gave NMA officials access to selected written reports of the intercepts. The officials were permitted to take notes that had to be left behind. On 19 August 2008 the public prosecutor supplied a CD of selected recordings “for information purposes only.” After the NMA opened a formal investigation on 9 December 2008, the prosecutor granted permission on 16 December 2008 to use the material (approximately 2 % of all intercepts) for Competition Act inquiries. NMA inspectors later visited company premises and questioned employees under caution. The prosecutor informed the companies that the data had been transmitted under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG) and the relevant Designation Order.

The companies brought civil summary proceedings seeking return of the data and an injunction against its use, relying on Article 8. On 26 June 2009 the Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the application, holding that transmission was necessary for the economic well-being of the Netherlands, proportionate, and not obtainable by less intrusive means. No appeal followed.

On 29 October 2010 the NMA imposed a €3 million fine after finding that one of the companies had coordinated bids and exchanged information in 2008, contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. An objection was rejected in 2012. The applicant companies were implicated as suspects. An investigating judge authorised interception of telephone conversations of some of their employees.

In July 2008, police officers provided NMA officials confidential access, on police premises, to selected written reports of the intercepts; officials could take notes but had to leave them behind. On 19 August 2008 the public prosecutor supplied a CD of selected recordings for information purposes only, requiring his permission for any other use. After the NMA opened an official investigation on 9 December 2008, the prosecutor on 16 December 2008 authorised use of the data (approximately 2% of all intercepts) for Competition Act inquiries.

NMA inspectors later visited company premises, accessed records and questioned employees. On 29 October 2010 the NMA fined the companies €3 million for coordinating bids and exchanging information on tenders between March and December 2008, in breach of the cartel prohibition.

The original intercepts had been judicially authorised; the WJSG provided a legal basis; both civil (tort) and administrative review were available; the ACM had thoroughly assessed the evidence and heard the companies; and the information could not reasonably have been obtained by less intrusive means. The case of UAB Braitin v. Lithuania (Application no. 13863/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in administrative proceedings. The applicant, a Lithuanian investment management company (formerly Lewben Investment Management), sought permission from the Commission for Assessment of Compliance of Potential Participants with National Security Interests to acquire UAB Prosperus Real Estate Fund II, a licensed investment firm. Its sole shareholder was R.K.

On 21 September 2017, the Commission refused permission, finding that R.K. had connections with individuals linked to institutions or persons in non-EU/NATO states. This breached Article 7 § 10(3) of the Law on Enterprises and Facilities of Strategic Importance. The decision relied on information from State authorities, including classified material from the State Security Department (SSD). The applicant received only the protocol decision, without supporting evidence or detailed reasoning.

The applicant appealed to the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, arguing the decision lacked evidential basis. The SSD was joined as a third party and supplied the court with classified documents (12 pages marked secret/confidential, later supplemented) plus 59 pages of public material. The latter included press reports on Belarusian businessmen A.O. (arrested in Belarus) and J.Č. (subject to EU sanctions for supporting the Lukashenko regime, with ties to State-linked entities and the President’s Sports Club). The SSD refused to declassify its documents.

The Chancellery (representing the Commission) confirmed reliance on a classified SSD report of 20 September 2017, presented only to Commission members (all security-cleared) in a closed hearing. No applicant representative was invited, as hearings were non-public. Closed oral hearings occurred in 2018 with the applicant’s lawyers present. They examined nine Commission members as witnesses and R.K., who admitted seeing A.O. and J.Č. at a private event outside Lithuania but denied personal connections. The lawyers inferred the classified material concerned links to those individuals (plus others) but argued no clear threat existed, noting some EU sanctions had been lifted. Additional classified material was provided solely to the court panel, refuting R.K.’s testimony.

On 26 April 2018 the court dismissed the appeal. It held the Commission’s decision was supported by both public material (disclosed to the applicant) and classified SSD documents it had reviewed. Sufficient information on R.K.’s connections had been revealed; R.K.’s own testimony and witness statements corroborated the findings. The applicant had opportunities to submit evidence, examine witnesses, and participate. National security prevailed over private interests even at minimal risk; the threat need not be “clear and present.” The decision was not based solely on undisclosed classified information, complying with Article 56 of the Law on Administrative Proceedings and Constitutional Court case-law.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, complaining it could not contest unknown classified facts and that one meeting with third-country nationals did not establish a security threat. It also alleged Article 8 breaches from press leaks about the proceedings. On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the first-instance ruling. Public information independently confirmed the relevant links (R.K. had admitted acquaintance with the Belarusians). Classified material could be used provided the decision was not based exclusively on it, which it was not. The first-instance court had comprehensively assessed all evidence.

The applicant complained to the ECHR that non-disclosure of classified information prevented an effective defence, violating equality of arms and adversarial proceedings under Article 6 § 1. (Press reports on the refusal also formed the basis of a reputation complaint under Article 8, though the judgment’s core analysis concerned the fair-hearing claim.)

The case of Alonso Saura v. Spain (Application no. 18326/19) concerns Spanish judge María Pilar Alonso Saura’s challenge to the appointment of another candidate as President of the Murcia High Court of Justice. She alleged that the authorities failed to provide adequate reasons for selecting a male rival, rendering the process arbitrary and discriminatory on gender grounds, in violation of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing), Article 14 (non-discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

In October 2014 the General Council of the Judiciary launched a public competition for the five-year post, which combined judicial and executive functions. The Council enjoyed wide discretion but had to apply published criteria: length of judicial service, experience in civil and criminal jurisdictions, service in collegiate bodies, quality of judgments, managerial aptitude, participation in governing bodies, knowledge of regional courts, and each candidate’s action plan. Three judges applied, including the applicant (born 1952) and Mr M.P.H.

The applicant’s record comprised 31 years and one month in the judiciary (26 years six months as senior judge), membership of the Murcia Audiencia Provincial since 1991, various presidencies and deanships, and service on the Murcia High Court’s Administration Chamber since 2009, plus academic and training roles. Mr M.P.H. had 22 years 11 months of service (21 years two months as senior judge), 14 years as a criminal first-instance judge, six years as Dean of Murcia courts, membership of the same Administration Chamber, and international and management qualifications.

Both presented recorded oral programmes. The applicant emphasised work-family balance, extra resources for corruption cases, specialisation, mediation and “new judicial office” reforms. Mr M.P.H. offered 62 proposals grouped under governance, public service, efficiency and innovation, highlighting intermediate administrators, transparency offices, specialisation, mediation and expansion of the new judicial office.

On 29 January 2015 the Council appointed Mr M.P.H. The applicant appealed. On 10 May 2016 the Supreme Court quashed the decision for insufficient reasoning on comparative merits and ordered a fresh, more detailed decision.

The third candidate having withdrawn, the Council on 26 May 2016 again appointed Mr M.P.H. It acknowledged the applicant’s superior objective merits (seniority, collegiate experience, mixed civil-criminal practice and volume of judgments) but described Mr M.P.H.’s programme as “indisputably, obviously indisputably, overwhelming even” superior, while hers was “sparse, generic and very trivial.” Particular weight was given to his plans for the new judicial office, mediation and management transparency, plus his regional knowledge, criminal-court experience and quality of decisions. Five of 21 members dissented, stressing the applicant’s greater seniority and broader adjudicative experience.

The applicant appealed once more. On 27 June 2017 the Supreme Court (17–15) upheld the appointment. It held that the Council had complied with the 2016 judgment, exercised its broad discretion (especially for a governmental-judicial post) without bias or misuse of power, and provided adequate, non-arbitrary reasons. The Court reviewed the Council’s comparison of programmes, additional factors such as Mr M.P.H.’s Technical Office service and teaching, and rejected any gender-equality preference because the candidates were not sufficiently similar. Fifteen judges dissented, arguing that the Council had ignored the earlier ruling and that the applicant’s merits remained superior.

The Constitutional Court later declared her amparo appeal inadmissible, finding no constitutional-rights violation.

These facts—the comparative records, the two Council decisions and their reasoning (or alleged lack thereof), the successive Supreme Court judgments (with substantial dissents) and the gender-equality argument—underpin the alleged failures of reasoned decision-making, arbitrariness and discrimination.

Port Invest wholly owned and directed I. company; Burando wholly owned and directed Port Invest. They alleged violations of Articles 8 and 13 ECHR arising from the transmission of lawfully intercepted telephone data from a criminal inquiry to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA, later ACM) and the latter’s use of that material to impose administrative fines for cartel conduct.

In late 2006 the special investigative service VROM-IOD opened a criminal investigation (“Toto”) into I. company for alleged unlawful disposal of polluted waste. An investigating judge authorised telephone intercepts of I. employees. Certain conversations with an employee of another waste-collection firm indicated possible price-fixing. On 21 April 2008 a VROM-IOD official recorded those indications in an official report to which summary transcripts were annexed. On 21 October 2008 the competent public prosecutor endorsed transmission of the report to the NMA under section 39f of the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG); the material was sent on 29 June 2009. Further selections of transcripts and audio files were transmitted, after informal liaison between the two authorities, on dates in 2009–2010, the last approval being given in August 2010. Meanwhile the criminal case against I. company was settled; on 5 July 2010 the Rotterdam Regional Court declared the prosecutor inadmissible.

Relying principally on the intercepted material, the NMA found that I. company and others had allocated contracts and restricted price competition between August 2005 and July 2007, contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it imposed a fine of €1 861 000 on I. company, jointly and severally on Port Invest, and of €621 000 on Burando, attributing decisive influence to the parent companies.

The applicants challenged the fines, arguing that the prosecutor had recorded no reviewable balancing of interests and that transmission had lacked prior judicial authorisation. The Rotterdam Regional Court (2013) accepted the first point, excluded the transcripts and quashed the fines. The ACM appealed. The applicants cross-appealed, contending that the recordings were not “criminal data” under the WJSG and that some transmissions occurred after the criminal proceedings had ended, in breach of the two-month destruction rule in Article 126cc of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry (CBb) (2015) set aside the Regional Court’s judgment. It held that the intercepts constituted “criminal data” (broadly defined and automatically processed). Transmission pursued a compelling general interest—the economic well-being of the country—and served enforcement of legislation. Written contemporaneous reasoning by the prosecutor was not required; lawfulness could be reviewed ex post (civil courts for the transmission itself, administrative courts for the subsequent fine). Original intercepts had been judge-authorised; the ACM had evaluated the material and heard the companies; no less-intrusive means of obtaining evidence of unwritten cartel agreements existed; and all transmissions preceded the statutory destruction deadline. The CBb therefore found no breach of Article 8 or of domestic law.

The applicants maintained before the European Court that the legal framework was insufficiently foreseeable and that procedural safeguards (absence of ex-ante judicial control of transmission and of a recorded balancing exercise) were inadequate. They also alleged the lack of an effective remedy under Article 13.
