The ECHR case of X and Others v. Ireland (Applications nos. 23851/20 and 24360/20) concerned alleged discrimination in the denial of Ireland’s universal child benefit to two mothers who were lawfully present in the State but lacked formal residence rights at the relevant times. The applicants invoked Article 14 of the Convention (prohibition of discrimination) read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 8 (right to respect for family life). Child benefit, governed by the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, is paid to a “qualified person” (typically the parent or guardian with whom a “qualified child” resides) provided that person is habitually resident. Section 246(5) provides that a person without a right to reside cannot be regarded as habitually resident. Direct provision supplied accommodation, meals, healthcare and modest weekly allowances to those awaiting status decisions.

In the first application, X (a Nigerian national) arrived in Ireland in November 2013 and claimed asylum a year later; the claim was rejected in mid-2015. Her daughter E, born on 23 December 2014, acquired Irish citizenship through her Irish father. Both entered direct provision. On 11 September 2015 X applied for residence on the basis of being the mother of an Irish-citizen child and, on 16 October 2015, claimed child benefit. The claim was refused on 2 November 2015 for want of habitual residence. Residence permission was granted on 6 January 2016, after which benefit became payable. The claim before the domestic courts was therefore limited to the roughly twelve-month period from E’s birth until permission was granted.

In the second application, Y (an Afghan national) arrived in 2008 with her husband and first child and claimed asylum. The family spent periods in direct provision. Three further children were born in Ireland, the youngest (M) in April 2013. After an initial false claim of Pakistani nationality was rejected, the family established their true nationality. M was granted refugee status on 9 December 2014 (notified 8 January 2015). The remaining family members immediately sought reunification. Y claimed child benefit on 19 February 2015; it was refused on 2 April 2015 for lack of habitual residence. Reunification was granted on 11 September 2015 and benefit was then paid from that date. The domestic claim covered the intervening eight-month period.

The High Court (2017) held that the statutory right vested in the qualified person, not the child, rejected EU-law arguments based on Ruiz Zambrano and the Qualification Directive, and found the habitual-residence condition neither arbitrary nor discriminatory. Direct provision met the children’s needs and there had been no culpable delay. The Court of Appeal (2018) reversed in part. It treated the benefit as ultimately for the child and held that excluding an Irish-citizen child (E) solely because of her mother’s immigration status lacked objective justification and breached constitutional equality. For M it held that the Qualification Directive required payment from the date of his refugee status. The Supreme Court (2019) restored the High Court’s approach. Benefit was payable to the parent, not the child; the habitual-residence rule applied uniformly and served legitimate immigration-control aims. Once residence rights were granted, the mothers received the benefit on the same terms as everyone else. Zambrano did not apply because there had been no risk of the children being forced to leave the EU, and the Directive created no obligation to back-date payments.

Before the ECHR the applicants argued that the denials constituted unjustified discrimination in the enjoyment of a proprietary interest (the statutory benefit) and of family life. The Court accepted that child benefit constituted a possession within the ambit of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but held that the applicants, given their legal and factual situation at the material time, were not in a relevantly similar position to persons already possessing a right of residence. Consequently there was no discrimination. Applying the Beeler criteria, the Court further held that the benefit’s purpose was not to promote or organise family life; it did not affect key aspects of daily life and, in light of the Supreme Court’s characterisation of its nature and statutory basis, did not constitute a modality of the exercise of Article 8 rights. The complaints under Article 14 taken with Article 8 were therefore incompatible ratione materiae. The applications were dismissed.

The case of X and Others v. Ireland (applications nos. 23851/20 and 24360/20) concerns alleged discrimination in the denial of Ireland’s universal child benefit to two mothers who were lawfully present but lacked a formal right of residence. The applicants invoked Article 14 of the Convention read with Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

X, a Nigerian national, arrived in Ireland in November 2013 and claimed asylum in 2014; the claim was refused in 2015. Her daughter E, born in December 2014 to an Irish-citizen father, is herself an Irish citizen. Mother and child were accommodated in the State’s direct-provision system. In September 2015 X applied for residence on the basis of her relationship with E; while that application was pending she claimed child benefit in October 2015. The claim was refused because she was not “habitually resident,” a statutory condition that requires a right to reside. Residence was granted on 6 January 2016 and benefit thereafter paid. The period in issue was therefore the twelve months from E’s birth until the grant of residence.

Y, an Afghan national, arrived in 2008 with her husband and first child and claimed asylum (initially using false Pakistani documents). Three further children were born in Ireland, including M in April 2013. After the family disclosed their true nationality, M was recognised as a refugee on 8 January 2015. The remaining family members immediately sought family reunification. Y claimed child benefit on 19 February 2015; the claim was refused on the same habitual-residence ground. Reunification was granted on 11 September 2015 and benefit paid from that date. The claim therefore covered the intervening eight months.

Irish law (Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005) pays child benefit to a “qualified person” (the parent with whom a “qualified child” normally resides) provided the parent is habitually resident. Section 246(5) provides that a person without a right to reside cannot be regarded as habitually resident; persons awaiting asylum or family-reunification decisions fall into this category. Once residence is granted, benefit is paid prospectively only. During the waiting periods the families received comprehensive State support through direct provision (accommodation, meals, healthcare, schooling) plus modest weekly cash allowances.

The High Court found no discrimination, noting that the families’ needs were met by direct provision and that the residence condition applied equally to all claimants. The Court of Appeal held that the exclusion of an Irish-citizen child such as E from a universal benefit, solely because of her mother’s immigration status, lacked objective justification and violated constitutional equality; it rejected the claim in respect of M, a non-citizen. The Supreme Court reversed. It held that the benefit belongs to the parent, not the child; the habitual-residence condition is nationality-neutral and rationally linked to immigration control. Once status was granted the mothers were treated identically to every other qualified person. Neither EU law (Zambrano or the Qualification Directive) required back-dating.

Before the European Court the applicants argued that the residence condition produced unjustified discrimination. The Court accepted that child benefit constitutes a proprietary interest within Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but found the applicants not in a relevantly similar situation to persons already holding a right of residence. Applying the Beeler criteria, it further held that the benefit did not fall within the ambit of Article 8, its purpose not being to promote or organise family life. No violation was therefore found.

The case of X and Others v. Ireland (ECtHR, 22 June 2023) concerned two joined applications alleging discrimination in the denial of Ireland’s universal child benefit. The applicants—two mothers lawfully present in the State and their children—complained that they were refused the benefit solely because they had not yet been granted a formal right to reside, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and with Article 8.

X, a Nigerian national, arrived in Ireland in November 2013 and applied for asylum a year later; the claim was rejected in mid-2015. Her daughter E, born on 23 December 2014, is an Irish citizen by virtue of her Irish father. While X’s subsequent application for residence as the parent of an Irish-citizen child remained pending, she applied for child benefit in October 2015. The claim was refused because she did not satisfy the statutory “habitual-residence” condition (Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, s. 246(5)), which requires a right to reside. Residence permission was granted on 6 January 2016 and benefit was paid thereafter. The period in issue was therefore the twelve months from E’s birth until the residence decision.

Y, an Afghan national, arrived in 2008 with her husband and first child and later gave birth to three further children, the youngest being M (born April 2013). After an initial unsuccessful asylum claim the family obtained refugee status for M on 9 December 2014 (communicated 8 January 2015). Y immediately applied for family reunification. Pending that decision she sought child benefit for all four children in February 2015; the claim was refused on habitual-residence grounds. Reunification was granted on 11 September 2015 and benefit commenced from that date. The disputed period was the intervening eight months.

Both families were housed and supported throughout under Ireland’s direct-provision system (accommodation, meals, healthcare, schooling and a modest weekly allowance). Domestic courts ultimately upheld the refusals. The High Court treated the benefit as belonging to the “qualified person” (normally the parent) rather than the child and found the residence condition neither arbitrary nor discriminatory. The Court of Appeal held that exclusion of an Irish-citizen child such as E was unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court reversed, confirming that the payment is made to the parent and that the habitual-residence rule applies equally to all claimants, irrespective of the child’s nationality. It also rejected arguments based on the CJEU’s Zambrano case-law and on Article 28 of the EU Qualification Directive.

Before the ECtHR the applicants argued that they had been treated differently from persons already holding residence permission, without objective justification, and that the denial interfered with family life. The Court accepted that child benefit constitutes a proprietary interest falling within Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held, however, that the applicants were not in a relevantly similar situation to persons possessing a legal right of residence; the distinction therefore disclosed no discrimination. As regards Article 8, the Court applied the Beeler criteria and concluded that the benefit’s statutory purpose was not to promote or organise family life; the payment therefore fell outside the ambit of Article 8. The applications were dismissed.

The case of S.C. Zorina International S.R.L. v. Romania (Application no. 15553/15) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Romanian limited company based in Constanţa and represented by Mr Călin Dumitru, alleged that tax sanctions imposed for failing to issue receipts were disproportionate and interfered with its right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

On 26 March 2013 the Constanţa Finance Inspectorate inspected the applicant’s store. Inspectors found that receipts had not been issued for goods worth RON 179 (approximately EUR 40). The company’s representative, present during the inspection, offered no explanation at the time. Relying on Government Emergency Ordinance no. 28/1999 (GEO 28/1999), the authority imposed a fine of RON 8,000 (approximately EUR 1,900, the statutory minimum), confiscated the RON 179 and ordered a three-month suspension of the company’s activities.

The applicant challenged the report before the Constanţa District Court. It contended that the RON 179 was merely change kept in the till, a claim it said was supported by the cash-register tape (which was nevertheless illegible because the paper had run out and been marked with red ink). It therefore sought annulment of the entire report. In the alternative it argued that the sanctions were excessive given the modest sum involved and the perishable nature of its stock, and asked that the fine be replaced by a warning; the three-month closure, it maintained, already constituted a sufficiently severe penalty.

On 7 October 2013 the District Court dismissed the action. It held that the applicant’s explanation was unproven: the inspection report had been signed without reservation and the till tape was unreadable. Both the fine (being the legal minimum) and the suspension were therefore proportionate, particularly in light of the company’s persistent denial of the offence.

The applicant appealed to the Constanţa County Court, repeating its earlier arguments and adding that the combined sanctions were excessively harsh. It cited domestic decisions in which similar penalties had been reduced. On 24 September 2014 the County Court dismissed the appeal. It emphasised that the sanctions served a preventive and educational purpose rather than a compensatory one. High fines had been deliberately chosen by the legislature because official statistics showed a marked increase in tax offences. The social value protected by the law, not the precise amount unaccounted for, was decisive. Divergent case-law from other courts could not assist the applicant, whose circumstances did not warrant any mitigation.

At the material time GEO 28/1999 classified the failure to issue receipts as a tax offence punishable by a fine of RON 8,000–10,000, confiscation of the unreceipted sum and a mandatory three-month suspension of activity. The general administrative-offences legislation (Government Ordinance no. 2/2001) allowed courts to assess proportionality and, in principle, to substitute a warning for a fine, but the suspension remained compulsory once the offence was established. Subsequent amendments (effective from late 2014 and May 2015) later permitted a mere warning for sums below RON 300 and confined suspension to repeat offenders, but those changes post-dated the events.

Domestic practice confirmed that courts routinely examined proportionality. They could reduce a fine to the statutory minimum or replace it with a warning, yet they generally treated the three-month closure as inseparable from the principal penalty. Isolated decisions, including one relied on by the applicant, had nevertheless set aside the suspension by invoking the Court’s case-law on excessive individual burden.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the cumulative sanctions imposed an excessive and disproportionate interference with its possessions.

The case of S.C. Zorina International S.R.L. v. Romania (no. 15553/15) involves a Romanian company's complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the ECHR that tax sanctions for failing to issue receipts interfered disproportionately with its peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

On 26 March 2013 the Constanţa Finance Inspectorate inspected the applicant company's store and reported that it had not issued receipts for merchandise worth RON 179 (approximately EUR 40). The company's representative, present during the inspection, offered no explanation. Pursuant to Articles 10(b), 11 §§ 1(b) and 3, and 14 § 2 of Government Emergency Ordinance no. 28/1999, the authorities imposed a fine of RON 8,000 (the statutory minimum, approximately EUR 1,900), confiscated the RON 179, and suspended the company's activities for three months.

The company challenged the report before the Constanţa District Court. It contended that the cash-register tape (though blurred by red ink after the paper ran out) showed the money had been kept as change rather than representing unreceipted sales. It sought annulment of the report or, in the alternative, replacement of the fine with a warning, arguing that the combined sanctions—especially the suspension, given the perishable nature of its goods—were excessively harsh relative to the small sum involved.

On 7 October 2013 the District Court dismissed the action. It held that the representative's signature on the report without contemporaneous explanation, together with the illegible tape, disproved the company's account. Both the minimum fine and the suspension were found fair and proportionate, particularly in light of the company's persistent denial of the offence.

The company appealed to the Constanţa County Court, repeating its arguments and citing other domestic decisions that had mitigated similar sanctions. On 24 September 2014 the County Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It emphasised that the sanctions served preventive and educational purposes, not mere reparation, and that the legislature had prescribed high penalties because of a documented surge in tax offences. What mattered was the social value protected by the obligation to issue receipts, not the modest amount involved. The particular circumstances of the case did not justify any reduction.

GEO no. 28/1999 made the fine, confiscation and three-month suspension mandatory for the offence in question. Complementary general rules in Government Ordinance no. 2/2001 authorised courts to examine proportionality and, in principle, to substitute a warning for a fine if the offence was minor. Subsequent legislative amendments (2014–2015) eliminated the warning option for this offence and later restricted suspension to a second offence and a shorter period. Domestic practice varied: most courts treated suspension as obligatory once a fine was confirmed, though a minority, relying on ECHR case-law, had set it aside; the applicant produced one such decision concerning a comparable sum.

The company lodged its application with the ECHR on 23 March 2015. In its judgment of 27 June 2023 (final 27 September 2023) the Court held that the sanctions were lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of securing tax collection and combating a widespread economic problem, and were subject to full judicial review that disclosed no unfairness or arbitrariness. A fair balance had been struck and no excessive individual burden imposed. There was therefore no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of S.C. Zorina International S.R.L. v. Romania (Application no. 15553/15) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) on 27 June 2023 (final 27 September 2023). It concerned a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that Romanian tax authorities imposed disproportionate sanctions on the applicant company for failing to issue receipts, thereby interfering with its right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The applicant, a limited company based in Constanţa, operated a store selling perishable goods such as food. On 26 March 2013, the Constanţa Finance Inspectorate inspected the premises and found that the company had failed to issue receipts for merchandise valued at RON 179 (approximately EUR 40). The company’s representative, present during the inspection, provided no explanation. The tax authority issued a report imposing a fine of RON 8,000 (approximately EUR 1,900), confiscating the RON 179, and suspending the company’s activities for three months. These measures were based on Articles 10(b), 11 §§ 1(b) and 3, and 14 § 2 of Government Emergency Ordinance no. 28/1999 (GEO no. 28/1999), which required traders to use cash registers and issue receipts for all sales, treating non-compliance as a tax offence.

The company challenged the report before the Constanţa District Court. It argued that the RON 179 was cash kept for customer change, not unaccounted sales, as allegedly shown by a blurred cash-register report. It requested that the report and sanctions be declared null and void or, alternatively, that the fine be replaced with a warning due to disproportionality, given the small amount involved and the risk the three-month suspension posed to its perishable-goods business. On 7 October 2013 the District Court dismissed the action. It found the company’s explanation unproven because the representative had signed the tax report without offering any contemporaneous justification and the cash-register paper was illegible. The court held the sanctions fair and proportionate: the fine was the statutory minimum and the company had persistently denied the offence.

The company appealed to the Constanţa County Court, reiterating its arguments and citing domestic case-law in which courts had mitigated similar sanctions. On 24 September 2014 the County Court dismissed the appeal. It emphasised that the sanctions served preventive and educational purposes rather than reparation. High fines were justified by a documented rise in tax offences; the protected social interest, not the modest unaccounted sum, was decisive. Other courts’ more lenient decisions were distinguishable on the facts and could not justify alleviation here.

GEO no. 28/1999, as in force at the time, prescribed a fine of RON 8,000–10,000, confiscation of unreceipted sums, and a mandatory three-month activity suspension for failure to issue receipts. It was complemented by Government Ordinance no. 2/2001, which empowered courts to review the lawfulness, necessity and proportionality of administrative sanctions, including the possibility of substituting a warning for a fine unless the special law excluded that option. At the relevant date the suspension measure remained compulsory once a fine was imposed. Subsequent legislative amendments (effective from late 2014 and 2015) introduced more flexibility, such as warnings for sums under RON 300 and shorter or second-offence-only suspensions, but these changes post-dated the events.

Domestic courts routinely examined proportionality in comparable cases and could reduce fines (though not below the statutory minimum) or replace them with warnings when circumstances warranted, yet they could not generally set aside the linked suspension unless the entire inspection report was quashed as unlawful. The applicant submitted one 2015 decision in which a court had annulled a suspension while retaining a minimum fine, citing ECHR case-law on the need for sanctions to regulate rather than merely punish.

The ECHR ultimately found the sanctions lawful and proportionate, noting that the offence formed part of a recurring national problem that hampered the proper functioning of the economy, that the company had enjoyed access to judicial review, that the domestic decision-making process showed no unfairness or arbitrariness, and that a fair balance had been struck without imposing an excessive burden.

The applicant, Audronė Ispiryan, was appointed principal of Rasa Progymnasium (a public school in Šiauliai) in 2014. In March 2017 she was notified of suspicion of bribery: allegedly accepting monthly payments (via a fictitious employee, the school accountant’s husband) from a cleaning company in return for awarding it a procurement contract. Several others (including the company’s director/employees, the accountant, her husband, and two other school principals) were suspected of related offences. In a separate investigation she was also suspected of misappropriation, document forgery, fraudulent accounting, abuse of office and witness tampering.

The prosecutor obtained a court order suspending her from duty for six months (later repeatedly extended by three-month periods until after the October 2018 indictment). The applicant did not initially object; she later unsuccessfully challenged one extension, arguing the grounds were vague and that any evidence had already been secured. The criminal cases remained pending at first instance as of late 2022.

In August 2018 the school council wrote to the municipal council expressing concern that the prolonged absence of a permanent principal was damaging the school’s environment, future and public image. The municipal administration drafted a decision to remove her under Article 104 of the Labour Code and the school’s articles of association (which permitted removal of the principal for loss of the founder’s confidence). The explanatory note stated that a school could not remain without a permanent head for over 18 months and that the measure was administrative, not a determination of guilt.

In committee and full-council meetings (October 2018) deputy municipal-administration head M.V. noted the bribery suspicion, the lengthy court-ordered suspension, community concerns, and the practical impossibility of appointing an acting or permanent replacement without first removing her. He described the alleged crime as “continuous \ldots over many years or months” and “quite difficult to prove,” stated that an indictment was being prepared so the suspicions had been “confirmed at least in some part,” and emphasised that removal was for loss of confidence irrespective of eventual guilt. Some councillors favoured waiting for the criminal outcome; others (and a parents’ representative) stressed the need for stability. The applicant addressed the council, defending her record. The council voted to remove her with effect from 5 October 2018, awarding one month’s severance pay.

The applicant sued the school and municipality, seeking reinstatement and damages. She argued that public-law entities had narrower discretion than private ones, that the articles of association conflicted with the Law on Budgetary Entities, that no specific loss-of-confidence reasons had been given, that she had been treated less favourably than other suspects (one principal remaining in post, the accountant receiving four months’ pay on mutual termination), and that remarks such as “suspicions confirmed at least in some part” violated the presumption of innocence. She also claimed discrimination arising from her earlier complaints about the deputy principal’s management.

Both the Šiauliai District Court (April 2019) and Regional Court (August 2019) dismissed the claim. They held that Article 104 applied equally to public entities, that the founder’s right to remove a head for loss of confidence was absolute and required no demonstration of fault or specific reasons, and that presumption-of-innocence and discrimination arguments were legally irrelevant. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the removal (and the accompanying statements) breached the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2), was discriminatory (Article 14) and that the domestic courts had failed to address her arguments adequately (Article 6 § 1).

The municipal administration proposed removing the applicant under Article 104 of the Labour Code and the school’s articles of association, which permitted removal for loss of confidence. The accompanying report stressed that the measure was not a determination of guilt but was needed because an institution could not remain without a permanent head for so long.

The proposal was discussed in municipal committees and the council. The deputy head of the administration, M.V., noted the ongoing suspicions, court-ordered suspensions and community concerns. He stated that an indictment was being prepared, so the suspicions had been “confirmed at least in some part,” that the alleged crime had been “continuous and committed over many years,” and that without removal no acting principal could be appointed. He repeatedly emphasised that the council was not judging guilt, that loss of confidence arose from the mere existence of the investigation irrespective of eventual outcome, and that the applicant would receive severance pay. Some councillors favoured waiting for the criminal verdict; others, including a parents’ representative, supported removal to end uncertainty. The applicant spoke in her own defence. On 4 October 2018 the council voted to remove her with effect from the following day, granting one month’s severance.

She argued that public entities lacked the unlimited discretion enjoyed by private employers, that the articles of association conflicted with the Law on Budgetary Entities (which did not list loss of confidence as a ground), that the decision was unreasoned and motivated by her earlier complaints about the deputy principal, and that she had been treated more harshly than other similarly suspected persons (one of whom remained in post, another of whom received a more generous severance). She further claimed that statements made at the municipal meetings (especially M.V.’s remarks that suspicions had been “confirmed at least in some part”) violated the presumption of innocence.

The first-instance court dismissed the claim, holding that the municipality, as founder, possessed an absolute right to remove the principal for loss of confidence and that the reasons given were adequate. The regional court upheld that ruling, finding the 2017 Labour Code authorised such removal without any finding of fault and that, consequently, arguments about presumption of innocence and discrimination were legally irrelevant. The Supreme Court refused to examine her cassation appeal.

The case of Ispiryan v. Lithuania (Application no. 11643/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant’s removal as principal of a public school amid pending criminal proceedings against her. Ms Audronė Ispiryan, a Lithuanian national born in 1978, was appointed principal of Rasa Progymnasium in Šiauliai in August 2014 by the municipal council.

On 14 March 2017, she was notified of suspicion of bribery. Authorities alleged she accepted monthly bribes from a cleaning company—paid as a fictitious salary to the school accountant’s husband—in exchange for awarding the company a procurement tender. She denied the claims. Several others, including two other school principals, were suspected in related offences. The prosecutor sought her six-month suspension from duty on 15 March 2017, arguing her equivalent civil-servant status, alleged influence over subordinates, and risks of evidence tampering, witness interference, or further crimes. She did not object, and the Šiauliai District Court granted the request the next day. The suspension was extended multiple times (September 2017, December 2017, March, June, and September 2018), citing the investigation’s scale and a separate probe alleging witness tampering. She appealed only the first extension, which the Šiauliai Regional Court dismissed, finding reasonable grounds and a risk of interference given her position. An indictment for bribery followed on 24 October 2018; the criminal case remained pending at first instance as of late 2022. A parallel investigation into other alleged offences (misappropriation, forgery, abuse of office, and witness tampering) was also ongoing.

In August 2018, the school council wrote to the municipality expressing concern over the lack of a permanent principal since March 2017, which harmed the school’s environment, future, and image. The municipal administration drafted a removal decision under Article 104 of the Labour Code and the school’s articles of association, which permitted removal for loss of the founder’s (municipal council’s) confidence. The explanatory note stressed that prolonged absence of a permanent head was intolerable; removal aimed solely at ensuring proper school functioning, not determining guilt.

At committee meetings on 1–2 October 2018, deputy administration head M.V. noted the bribery suspicions, repeated suspensions, and school concerns. He stated the council could remove her for loss of confidence due to the suspicions, that the investigation involved a “continuous” crime “committed over many years or months” that was “quite difficult to prove,” and that removal was irrespective of eventual guilt. At the 4 October 2018 council meeting, M.V. added that an indictment was being prepared, so suspicions had been “confirmed at least in some part.” Some members favoured waiting for the criminal outcome; others, including a parents’ representative, urged action due to community frustration. The applicant defended her record and claimed the proposal sought to prejudice her. The council voted to remove her effective 5 October 2018, with one month’s severance pay.

In November 2018, she sued the school and municipality in the Šiauliai District Court, seeking a declaration of unlawfulness, reinstatement, and damages. She argued the Law on Budgetary Entities did not authorise loss-of-confidence removal (making the articles of association invalid), that reasons were inadequate and possibly retaliatory (she had reported the deputy principal’s mismanagement), that she was treated more harshly than similarly suspected others, and that officials’ statements (including that suspicions were “confirmed at least in some part”) breached the presumption of innocence. The defendants maintained the removal was lawful under the Labour Code, based on confidence (not guilt), justified by the long suspension, indictment, and school impact, and that principals must meet high moral standards.

The District Court dismissed her claim on 16 April 2019, holding the removal lawful, the municipality’s right unlimited, and reasons adequate. The Šiauliai Regional Court upheld this on 13 August 2019, finding the Labour Code primary, removal an absolute right not requiring specific reasons or fault, and her innocence/discrimination arguments irrelevant. The Supreme Court refused her points-of-law appeal on 14 November 2019.

She alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 (inadequate judicial reasoning and presumption of innocence) and Article 14 (discrimination). The Court found no breach of Article 6 § 2, as the impugned statements, read in context, did not treat her as guilty.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of A.A., a Libyan national born in 1988, who alleged that his expulsion from Sweden to Libya would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention by exposing him to a real risk of death or ill-treatment.

A.A. entered Spain on a valid visa in July 2012 without seeking asylum. In August 2012 he arrived in Sweden using a false identity and claimed asylum based on threats from the Libyan mafia. Swedish authorities ordered his transfer to Spain under the Dublin Regulation, but he absconded. After that decision lapsed, he reapplied for asylum in Sweden on 7 May 2015, this time asserting a risk of persecution because of his and his father’s links to the Gaddafi regime. He stated that he had worked unpaid as a civilian for the Revolutionary Guards at a Tripoli university from 2006 to 2011. In May 2011 he fled to Tunisia to avoid conscription into the Revolutionary Brigade; he returned to Tripoli in October 2011 after Gaddafi’s fall. An arrest warrant was allegedly issued against him on 15 April 2012 and served on his mother (he produced only a scanned copy). His father, a retired high-ranking officer recalled to service in 2011, was imprisoned on the same date and subsequently disappeared. A.A. obtained a Spanish visa and left Libya in July 2012.

The Migration Agency rejected the claim on 8 June 2017. Country information confirmed an internal armed conflict, yet the level of indiscriminate violence was not such that every returnee faced a real risk. A.A.’s initial use of a false identity undermined his credibility. The arrest warrant was rudimentary, undated, unaddressed and easily forged, and therefore given little weight. His account of Gaddafi-era activities was vague and unsubstantiated. Passport stamps showed multiple lawful entries and exits after the alleged warrant, and he had been issued a visa and an extended passport, indicating he was not wanted by the authorities. Close family members remained in Libya.

The Migration Court dismissed the appeal on 21 November 2019. It noted that A.A. had originally cited only mafia threats, not Gaddafi affiliation. Further arrest-warrant copies remained rudimentary and originals were never produced. His return to Libya in October 2011, when thousands of Gaddafi supporters were detained, and his unhindered stay until July 2012 despite the claimed warrant and his father’s arrest, further damaged credibility. He had not shown a personal, real risk, nor did the general security situation justify protection.

Leave to appeal was refused in January 2020. The Court indicated an interim measure staying removal. Subsequent applications based on an employment offer, marriage (his wife later died) and alleged new impediments were rejected; the authorities found no change in the security situation at his place of origin sufficient to alter the earlier assessment.

The Court ultimately held that expulsion would not breach Articles 2 or 3. The security situation in Libya, while serious, did not create a general need for international protection. The domestic authorities had conducted a thorough, rationally based examination of A.A.’s individual circumstances, and he had failed to substantiate a personal risk of being killed or subjected to ill-treatment upon return.

The case of A.A. v. Sweden concerned a Libyan national (born 1988) who alleged that expulsion to Libya would breach Articles 2 and 3 ECHR (right to life; prohibition of torture/inhuman treatment). He arrived in Spain in July 2012 on a valid visa without seeking asylum, then entered Sweden on 8 August 2012 under a false identity and claimed asylum due to threats from the Libyan mafia. Authorities ordered his return to Spain under the Dublin Regulation, but he absconded.

He reapplied in May 2015 with an expired handwritten passport, now claiming risk of ill-treatment due to his and his father's work for the Gaddafi regime. He said he had served as an unpaid civilian in the Revolutionary Guards at a Tripoli university from 2006–2011. In May 2011 he fled to Tunisia to avoid conscription as a professional soldier in the Revolutionary Brigade, returning to Tripoli in October 2011 once the situation appeared calmer. An arrest warrant was issued against him on 15 April 2012 and served on his mother (he provided a copy). His father, a high-ranking officer who retired in 1997 but was recalled in 2011, was imprisoned the same day and disappeared. The applicant left for Spain around July 2012.

On 8 June 2017 the Migration Agency rejected the claim and ordered deportation with a two-year re-entry ban. It found an internal armed conflict existed in Libya but that indiscriminate violence was not of such intensity that all returnees faced risk. The applicant's initial use of a false identity undermined his credibility. The arrest-warrant copy was rudimentary (no addressee, date or reason) and easily falsifiable, so of low evidential value. Claims of Gaddafi affiliation lacked supporting documents and his oral account was vague and unreliable. Passport stamps showed multiple lawful entries/exits from Libya without incident (including after the alleged warrant), plus a valid Spanish visa. Close family members remained in Libya unharmed.

Later applications (employment-based residence; impediments based on Gaddafi links, security and marriage) were rejected; his wife died in 2021. The case of A.A. v. Sweden (Application no. 4677/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned a Libyan national's claim that his expulsion from Sweden to Libya would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, due to a risk of being killed or subjected to ill-treatment.

Swedish authorities ordered his transfer to Spain under the Dublin Regulation on 12 October 2012, but he absconded and the decision lapsed.

He stated that he had worked unpaid as a civilian for the Revolutionary Guards at a university in Tripoli from 2006 to 2011. In May 2011 he fled to Tunisia to avoid conscription as a professional soldier in the Revolutionary Brigade. He returned to Tripoli in October 2011 after the situation appeared calmer. On 15 April 2012 an arrest warrant was allegedly issued against him and served on his mother; he produced a copy. His father, a high-ranking army officer who had retired in 1997, was summoned back to service in 2011, imprisoned on 15 April 2012 and subsequently disappeared. A.A. obtained a visa and left for Spain a few months later.

The Swedish Migration Agency rejected the claim on 8 June 2017 and ordered his deportation to Libya with a two-year re-entry ban. It accepted that an internal armed conflict existed in Libya but found the level of indiscriminate violence insufficient to place every civilian at risk. The applicant's general credibility was damaged by his use of a false identity. The arrest-warrant copy was rudimentary, lacked identifying details and could easily have been fabricated. His oral account of Gaddafi affiliation was vague and unsupported by documents. Passport stamps showed lawful entries and exits from Libya even after the alleged warrant, and he had been granted a Spanish visa and an extended passport. Close family members remained in Libya.

It was inconsistent with a genuine fear that he had returned to Libya in October 2011, when thousands of Gaddafi supporters were being detained, and that he had stayed until July 2012 after the warrant without incident. An overall assessment showed no real and personal threat, nor a risk from the general security situation. Leave to appeal was refused on 10 January 2020.

Subsequent applications for a residence permit on the basis of an employment offer and later on claimed impediments (Gaddafi affiliation, security conditions and marriage) were rejected. A.A.'s wife died in July 2021.

These facts formed the core of the alleged risk: a personal profile linked to the former regime combined with Libya's volatile security environment. Swedish authorities concluded that neither element had been substantiated.

The case of Paslavičius v. Lithuania (Application no. 15152/18) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that his right of access to a court was impaired by domestic courts ordering him, as the unsuccessful party, to reimburse his former employer’s legal costs in litigation over disciplinary sanctions and his dismissal.

Tadas Paslavičius, a qualified lawyer, began work in June 2013 as a senior legal specialist (grade A10) in the Trakai district municipal administration’s legal and personnel department. After a 2015 reorganisation that created a combined legal, personnel and public-procurement department, he continued in that role. On 14 April 2016 the municipality imposed a strict reprimand for prolonged insulting and harassing behaviour towards a colleague. The applicant challenged the penalty in the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, seeking its annulment and €650 in non-pecuniary damages. Represented by external advocate A.P. (engaged under a 2015 legal-services contract), the municipality defended the action. After a public hearing at which the applicant appeared in person, the court dismissed the claim on 1 February 2017, finding the disciplinary commission’s findings well-founded. An appeal was rejected as out of time.

The municipality then claimed costs of €1,016 (drafting the defence), €381 (court representation) and €398 (response to the Supreme Administrative Court). The applicant objected that the municipality possessed in-house lawyers, the case was simple, and he was unemployed and receiving only modest unemployment benefit. On 16 August 2017 the Regional Court awarded €1,000, noting that the municipality was entitled to choose external counsel in an employee dispute, that the file was voluminous and witnesses had been heard, and that the applicant’s unemployment warranted a reduction on grounds of justice and fairness. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the award on 21 September 2017, emphasising that the applicant (a legally trained former municipal lawyer who had himself represented the municipality) had initiated the proceedings and that equality of arms was not thereby breached. Subsequent claims yielded further awards of €327 and €150.

Separately, on 26 October 2016 the municipality abolished the applicant’s post for operational and budgetary reasons (reduced caseload after legislative changes and under-utilisation of lawyers). He was notified that he would be dismissed on 30 December 2016 unless reassigned; the only vacancies were an A11 post or an A9 post requiring a biomedical degree he lacked. He sued for reinstatement and damages. After an oral hearing the Regional Court dismissed the claim on 12 April 2017. The Supreme Administrative Court, in written proceedings, confirmed on 3 August 2017 that the reorganisation was genuine, that remaining staff could perform his functions, and that statutory guarantees had not been engaged.

The municipality sought €1,694 in costs. The Regional Court awarded €904, citing the volume of pleadings, procedural complexity and the need for effective defence despite in-house capacity. On 18 October 2017 the Supreme Administrative Court reduced the sum to €700, applying the “loser-pays” rule, confirming the legitimacy of external representation in an employment dispute initiated by a legally educated applicant, and taking account of his financial hardship. An unsuccessful request to reopen the dismissal proceedings produced a further modest costs award of €168.

Throughout, the applicant maintained that the costs orders created inequality of arms, given the municipality’s resources and his inability to afford counsel, and that they chilled access to court. Domestic courts repeatedly reduced the sums on fairness grounds while holding that public entities retain discretion to instruct advocates when internal resources or case complexity so require.

**CASE OF PASLAVIČIUS v. LITHUANIA (Application no. 15152/18)**

Tadas Paslavičius, a Lithuanian lawyer born in 1986, began work in June 2013 as a senior legal specialist (grade A10) in the Trakai district municipal administration’s legal and personnel department. After a 2015 reorganisation, he continued in the legal, personnel and public procurement department until his dismissal on 30 December 2016 on redundancy grounds.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violation concerned orders that he, as the unsuccessful party, reimburse the municipality’s legal costs incurred through an external advocate (A.P.) in two sets of administrative proceedings he had initiated.

In April 2016 the municipality imposed a strict reprimand for alleged prolonged insulting and harassment of a colleague. Paslavičius sought annulment (later adding a €650 non-pecuniary claim). After a public hearing with witnesses, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed the claim in February 2017; his appeal was out of time. The municipality then claimed costs of €1,016 (response to the complaint), €381 (court representation) and €398 (response to the Supreme Administrative Court). The first-instance court awarded €1,000 after reductions, noting the municipality’s discretion to instruct an external advocate in an internal employment dispute, the voluminous file, witness testimony from municipal staff, and Paslavičius’s revisions to his claim. It considered his unemployment but observed he was of working age with a law degree. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this, finding no equality-of-arms breach because Paslavičius had initiated the proceedings, possessed legal qualifications, and had himself previously represented the municipality successfully. Subsequent cost awards of €327 and €150 followed for later filings.

Separately, in October 2016 the municipality abolished Paslavičius’s post, citing reduced departmental workload after legislative changes and lower demand for certain legal services; remaining functions could be performed by fewer staff. He was warned of possible dismissal if not reassigned. After dismissal he sought reinstatement plus damages. Both the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court (April 2017, oral hearing) and Supreme Administrative Court (August 2017, written proceedings) rejected the claim, finding the reorganisation genuine and the municipality entitled to optimise resources. Suitable alternative posts were unavailable.

The municipality then claimed €1,694 in costs. The first-instance court awarded €904 after reductions, citing case complexity, voluminous documents, Paslavičius’s multiple revisions and procedural applications, and established case-law. The Supreme Administrative Court further reduced the sum to €700 on grounds of justice, reasonableness, fairness and Paslavičius’s financial hardship. An additional €168 was later awarded for costs of opposing his unsuccessful reopening request.

Paslavičius argued throughout that the municipality possessed in-house lawyers, that the cases were not complex, that he was unemployed or low-paid and unable to match the external advocate’s fees, and that this created inequality of arms. Domestic courts repeatedly held that public entities retain discretion to instruct advocates, that representation was justified by the nature of the employment disputes and the need to protect municipal interests, and that Paslavičius’s own legal training and initiation of the proceedings prevented any unfairness. Amounts were consistently reduced below recommended maxima, taking his circumstances into account.

(The ECtHR later found no violation, holding that access-to-court requirements had been properly applied, that Paslavičius had a reasonable opportunity to present his cases, and that the degree of legal assistance afforded the municipality did not produce unfairness.)

The case of Paslavičius v. Lithuania concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right of access to a court) arising from Lithuanian administrative court orders requiring the applicant to reimburse his former employer’s legal costs after he unsuccessfully challenged a disciplinary penalty and his dismissal.

The applicant, a qualified lawyer, began work in June 2013 as a senior legal specialist (grade A10) in the Trakai district municipal administration. After a departmental reorganisation, he continued in the legal, personnel and public procurement department until his post was abolished on 26 October 2016 and he was dismissed on 30 December 2016 on redundancy grounds. The municipality cited reduced workload following legislative changes, fewer cases and the need to optimise resources; remaining staff could perform his functions. He was offered no suitable alternative post matching his qualifications.

Separately, on 14 April 2016 the municipality imposed a strict reprimand for prolonged insulting and harassing of a colleague (Ms X). The applicant sued to annul the penalty and later claimed €650 for non-pecuniary damage. Represented by external advocate A.P. (under a 2015 legal-services contract), the municipality successfully defended the claim before the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court on 1 February 2017 after a public hearing with witnesses. The applicant’s appeal was time-barred (Supreme Administrative Court, 28 April 2017).

The municipality then sought reimbursement of A.P.’s fees (€1,016 for the response, €381 for court representation and €398 for a further response). The first-instance court awarded €1,000, noting the case’s volume (three volumes, witness testimony including from the applicant’s former head of department), the applicant’s revisions necessitating extra work, and the municipality’s discretion to hire external counsel in an employee-employer dispute despite having in-house lawyers. It reduced the sum for fairness given the applicant’s unemployment (he received only modest benefits) while observing he was of working age with a law degree. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this on 21 September 2017, adding that self-representation by a legally trained applicant who had himself previously represented the municipality did not breach equality of arms. Subsequent costs claims for responses to the applicant’s further complaints yielded reduced awards of €327 and €150.

In parallel, the applicant challenged his dismissal, seeking reinstatement and damages. After an oral hearing, the first-instance court dismissed the claim on 12 April 2017; the Supreme Administrative Court confirmed on 3 August 2017 that the reorganisation was genuine and lawful, the functions were being performed by remaining staff, and no suitable alternative posts existed. The municipality claimed €1,694 in A.P.’s fees. The first-instance court awarded €904 after finding the voluminous, complex employment-related material (including structural-reform documents and multiple revisions/procedural issues) justified external counsel despite in-house capacity. The Supreme Administrative Court further reduced this to €700 on 18 October 2017, applying “loser pays,” justice and the applicant’s financial hardship. A later claim for costs of opposing the applicant’s unsuccessful reopening request yielded €168.

The applicant, who represented himself throughout the main proceedings, argued that the awards were disproportionate, that the municipality’s in-house lawyers should have sufficed, and that the disparity in resources (he was unemployed while the municipality hired a “well-paid advocate”) impaired access to court and equality of arms. Domestic courts applied the Law on Administrative Proceedings and related recommendations, assessing necessity of counsel by reference to case nature, complexity, novelty and the parties’ positions, while reducing sums for the applicant’s circumstances. The European Court found no violation: the applicant, a lawyer who initiated the suits, had a reasonable opportunity to present his cases; the costs regime was applied with due regard to fairness and his situation; and the employer’s representation did not render the proceedings unfair.

The case of Bijan Balahan v. Sweden concerns an Iranian-US dual national (born 1993) who complained that his extradition from Sweden to the United States would violate Article 3 ECHR. He alleged a real risk, if convicted, of an irreducible life sentence without parole (or a de facto equivalent via a 61-year minimum term) or a grossly disproportionate sentence.

In May 2020 the applicant was arrested in Los Angeles after allegedly inflicting around 30 knife wounds on a victim (requiring more than 40 stitches plus chemical burns), transferring USD 2,500 from the victim’s account without consent, and offering a security guard money not to summon emergency services. Released on bail, he left the United States and failed to appear for trial.

On 10 June 2021 the US Department of Justice requested extradition on the basis of a 5 May 2021 arrest warrant charging five counts committed on 18 May 2020: (1) aggravated mayhem, (2) torture, (3) inducing false testimony, (4) dissuading a witness after a prior conviction, and (5) grand theft. The Swedish Supreme Court (23 December 2021) held that extradition was permissible only for torture, grand theft and the disfigurement element of aggravated mayhem; the remaining charges did not correspond to Swedish offences. It found no Convention obstacle. The Swedish Government authorised extradition on those counts on 3 February 2022. Enforcement was later suspended pursuant to an ECHR interim measure. The applicant has been detained in Sweden since 24 May 2021.

The Article 3 claim turned on California sentencing rules. Aggravated mayhem and torture each carry life imprisonment with parole eligibility after a statutory minimum (normally seven years). Grand theft is punishable by 16 months, two or three years. Consecutive sentencing applies. Because of alleged prior serious/violent felony convictions, California’s Three Strikes Law could double or treble terms or impose 25-to-life minima. Consecutive 25-to-life terms plus a doubled grand-theft sentence and a five-year prior-conviction enhancement could produce a 61-year minimum before parole eligibility.

US authorities informed Sweden that life without parole was legally unavailable on the extraditable counts, that courts or prosecutors could dismiss prior-strike allegations “in the furtherance of justice,” and that, absent Three Strikes, the applicant would face life with parole after 17 years. The applicant’s California counsel asserted that Three Strikes would apply, requiring service of 85 percent of the term (approximately 52 years), so parole eligibility only at age 81—beyond average US male life expectancy (73 years)—and that parole is granted in only 16 percent of hearings. A 2022 policy report noted that third-strike enhancements are now rare (0.4 percent of recent admissions) and that prisoners earn 33 percent credits for violent offences. Parole decisions rest with a Board that must grant release unless public safety requires otherwise; reasons, representation and periodic review are provided, and gubernatorial clemency exists.

The Court held that the first stage of the Sanchez-Sanchez test was not met: there was no demonstrated real risk of irreducible life imprisonment (de jure or de facto). The length of any minimum term depended on multiple unknown variables (including judicial discretion to strike priors) and could be substantially shorter than 61 years. A sentence is not grossly disproportionate merely because it is harsher than one that would be imposed in a Convention State; the strict “gross disproportionality” threshold is met only in rare, unique cases. Extradition therefore raised no issue under Article 3.

The case of Bijan Balahan v. Sweden (Application no. 9839/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s claim that extradition from Sweden to the United States would breach Article 3 of the Convention. Born in 1993 and holding dual Iranian and US nationality, the applicant was detained in Sweden at the time of the proceedings.

In May 2020 he was arrested in California over an incident on 18 May 2020 in Los Angeles. He was alleged to have inflicted around thirty knife wounds on a victim, necessitating more than forty stitches and causing chemical burns. He was further accused of transferring USD 2,500 from the victim’s account without authorisation and of offering money to a security guard in exchange for not contacting the emergency services. Released on bail, he left the United States and failed to appear for trial.

On 10 June 2021 the US Department of Justice requested extradition, supported by an arrest warrant charging five counts: aggravated mayhem, torture, inducing false testimony, dissuading a witness after a prior conviction, and grand theft. Sweden’s Supreme Court ruled on 23 December 2021 that extradition was permissible for torture, grand theft and the disfigurement element of aggravated mayhem (but not the permanent-disability element), while the remaining counts lacked equivalents under Swedish law. It found no Convention obstacle. The Swedish Government authorised extradition on 3 February 2022 on those counts; enforcement was later suspended pursuant to an interim measure indicated by the Court. The applicant has been in detention pending extradition since 24 May 2021.

The Article 3 complaint centres on the sentence the applicant would face if convicted. Under California law, aggravated mayhem and torture each carry life imprisonment with parole eligibility after a statutory minimum term (normally seven years). Grand theft is punishable by sixteen months to three years. Sentences are consecutive. California’s Three Strikes Law, however, applies if the applicant has one or more prior serious or violent felony convictions. A single prior doubles the term; two or more priors convert each current serious felony into an indeterminate sentence of twenty-five years to life, plus possible five-year enhancements for each prior, all running consecutively. This could produce a minimum term of sixty-one years before parole eligibility. Courts and prosecutors retain discretion to dismiss prior-strike allegations “in the furtherance of justice.”

US authorities confirmed that life without parole is unavailable for these charges. Absent Three Strikes the minimum would be seventeen years; with it, sixty-one years. After the minimum term the California Board of Parole Hearings must grant parole unless public safety requires further incarceration; hearings consider social history, mental state, criminal record, attitude to the offence and other factors. Inmates may be represented, review documents and receive reasoned decisions; denials trigger future hearings. The Governor may review parole grants and grant clemency. An expert instructed by the applicant maintained that Three Strikes would almost certainly apply, that 85 per cent of the term would have to be served (approximately fifty-two years), and that eligibility at age 81 would exceed US male life expectancy, rendering the sentence de facto irreducible. Parole grant rates were said to be low (around 16 per cent). Sentencing credits of 33 per cent for violent offences and judicial/prosecutorial discretion exist, but their application remains uncertain.

The applicant also argued that any such sentence would be grossly disproportionate to the offence. These facts formed the basis of the alleged risk of treatment contrary to Article 3.

The case of Bijan Balahan v. Sweden (Application no. 9839/22) concerns the proposed extradition of the applicant, a dual Iranian-US national born in 1993, from Sweden to California for prosecution. In May 2020 he was arrested in the US on allegations that he inflicted around 30 knife wounds on a victim (requiring over 40 stitches) together with chemical burns, transferred USD 2,500 from the victim’s account without consent, and offered money to a security guard to refrain from summoning emergency services. Released on bail, he fled and failed to appear for trial.

On 10 June 2021 the US authorities requested extradition pursuant to an arrest warrant charging five counts committed on 18 May 2020: aggravated mayhem, torture, inducing false testimony, dissuading a witness after a prior conviction, and grand theft. The Swedish Supreme Court, applying the 1957 Extradition Act and relevant treaties, held on 23 December 2021 that extradition was permissible on the torture and grand-theft counts and on the disfigurement element of aggravated mayhem, but not on the remaining counts (which lacked dual criminality). It found no Convention obstacle. The Swedish Government accordingly ordered extradition on 3 February 2022. Enforcement was later suspended pursuant to an interim measure indicated by the Court. The applicant has been detained pending extradition since 24 May 2021.

The applicant’s Article 3 complaint centres on the sentence he would face if convicted. California law does not prescribe life without parole for the extraditable offences; a life term carries parole eligibility after a statutory minimum. Because the applicant is alleged to have two prior serious or violent felony convictions, California’s Three Strikes Law could apply. Letters from the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office state that, if the strikes are not dismissed, consecutive terms of 25 years to life for aggravated mayhem and for torture, six years for grand theft and a five-year prior-conviction enhancement would produce a minimum of 61 years before parole eligibility. If the strikes are dismissed, the minimum would be 17 years. Courts and prosecutors retain discretion under Penal Code § 1385 to strike prior convictions “in the furtherance of justice.” Once the minimum term is served, a prisoner is entitled to a hearing before the Board of Parole Hearings, which must grant parole unless public safety requires further incarceration; the prisoner may be represented, present evidence and obtain a reasoned decision, with the possibility of an earlier subsequent hearing.

The applicant’s California counsel asserted that the Three Strikes Law would almost certainly apply, that “violent-strike” credits would require service of at least 85 per cent of the 61-year term (approximately 52 years), and that parole would first become available when the applicant was 81—beyond average male life expectancy of 73. Counsel further noted that only 16 per cent of parole hearings result in a grant. A 2022 California Policy Lab report recorded that third-strike enhancements are now rare (0.4 per cent of recent admissions) and that both judges and prosecutors frequently exercise discretion to avoid them. Credit-earning rates of 33 per cent for violent offences also reduce actual time served.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s claim that extradition would expose him to a real risk of a de jure or de facto irreducible life sentence, or of a grossly disproportionate term, contrary to Article 3.

The case of Ikotity and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 50012/17) concerns three opposition members of the Hungarian Parliament from the Lehet Más a Politika (LMP) party: István Ikotity, Bernadett Szél (the group leader), and Róbert Benedek Sallai. They alleged a violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression) arising from the refusal of permission to display posters during a parliamentary interpellation and the subsequent imposition of financial sanctions for doing so without authorization.

On 1 March 2017 the applicants formally requested permission from the House Committee, pursuant to section 38/A of the Parliament Act, to use eight images of deforestation as visual aids during an interpellation scheduled for 6 March 2017. The interpellation, titled “Do you think it is possible to live without green landscape?”, concerned government development plans for Budapest. The House Committee failed to reach the required consensus. The Speaker of Parliament then refused the request on 6 March, reasoning that the illustrations were unnecessary to understand or expand upon the interpellation, which could be adequately conveyed orally under the Rules of Procedure.

Despite being notified of the refusal, the applicants simultaneously held up three 50 cm by 60 cm posters during their colleague’s speech that same day. Each poster displayed “before and after” photographs of specific Budapest sites (Dagály Strand, Orczy Garden, and Hajógyári Island) accompanied by explanatory text alleging environmental degradation. Photographs of the display were published in the Hungarian press.

The session Chair immediately noted the breach of the prohibition on unauthorized presentation tools. The House Committee again failed to reach consensus on sanctions, so the Speaker, on 16 March 2017, reduced each applicant’s monthly remuneration by 100,000 Hungarian forints (approximately 320 euros). An MP’s basic monthly salary at the time was roughly 747,878 forints; the group leader’s was higher. The applicants challenged the decisions before the Immunity Committee (composed equally of ruling-coalition and opposition members). Szél attended and was heard. The Committee deadlocked 3–3 and therefore did not set aside the Speaker’s decisions. It held that the posters were not required to express the interpellant’s views, served instead as a protest, and that the rules protected Parliament’s orderly functioning and authority.

The applicants then asked Parliament itself to annul the sanctions. On 3 April 2017 Parliament, without debate, upheld the Speaker’s decisions, and the salary reductions took effect.

The relevant domestic framework is contained in the Fundamental Law and the Parliament Act. Article 5 of the Fundamental Law grants the Speaker policing and disciplinary powers to ensure undisturbed operation and dignity. Section 38/A of the Parliament Act generally prohibits objects, images or recordings at sittings, subject to House Committee (or, absent consensus, Speaker) permission limited to what is strictly necessary to elucidate a speaker’s position. Sections 49 and 51/A authorize salary reductions for breaches of those rules, with subsequent review by the Immunity Committee and, ultimately, a vote of Parliament. A later Justice Committee opinion confirmed that visual aids are exceptional and must not be used for protest or publicity.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ claim that the refusal of permission and the fines unjustifiably interfered with their freedom of expression as opposition parliamentarians.

The case of Ikotity and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 50012/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns three opposition members of the Hungarian Parliament from the LMP party—István Ikotity, Bernadett Szél (the group leader), and Róbert Benedek Sallai. They complained of a violation of their freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention arising from the denial of permission to display posters during a parliamentary interpellation and the subsequent imposition of fines for using the posters without authorization.

The Speaker reasoned that the interpellation had been properly submitted and that illustrations were unnecessary to understand or expand its meaning; the speaking member could adequately convey the group’s position through oral communication within the existing procedural rules.

Later that day, after being notified of the refusal, the three applicants simultaneously held up three posters (each measuring 50 cm by 60 cm) during their colleague’s interpellation speech. The posters displayed paired “before and after” photographs of specific Budapest sites—Dagály Strand, Orczy Garden and Hajógyári Island—accompanied by corresponding captions highlighting alleged environmental degradation. Photographs of the incident were published in the Hungarian press.

The Chair presiding over the sitting immediately noted that the posters had been displayed without permission, contrary to the Parliament Act. The House Committee again failed to reach consensus on a sanction. On 16 March 2017 the Speaker therefore imposed a deduction of 100 000 Hungarian forints (approximately 320 euros) from each applicant’s monthly remuneration. At the time an ordinary MP’s basic monthly salary was approximately 747 878 forints (about 2 420 euros); the parliamentary-group leader received a higher amount.

The applicants challenged the Speaker’s decisions before the Committee on Immunities, Conflict of Interest, Discipline and Verification of Credentials. They argued that the display of posters formed part of their freedom of expression, that their conduct had neither disrupted parliamentary business nor impaired the institution’s authority or dignity, and that the visual material was directly relevant to the effective communication of their views. They also criticised the Speaker’s broad discretion and the absence of a remedy against the initial refusal of permission. Ms Szél was heard in person. The Immunity Committee, composed equally of three members from the governing alliance and three from the opposition, deadlocked 3–3 and therefore declined to set the decisions aside. It observed that the statutory scheme generally prohibits visual or material aids unless they are indispensable to elucidating a speaker’s position, a threshold the requested posters had not met; their purpose appeared to be political protest rather than necessary illustration.

The applicants then asked Parliament itself to quash the sanctions. On 3 April 2017 Parliament, sitting without debate, voted to uphold the Speaker’s decisions. The salary reductions were consequently implemented. These successive refusals and disciplinary measures constitute the factual core of the applicants’ Article 10 complaint.

The case of Ikotity and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 50012/17) concerns three opposition members of the Hungarian Parliament (MPs) from the Lehet Más a Politika (LMP) party—István Ikotity, Bernadett Szél (the group leader), and Róbert Benedek Sallai—who alleged a violation of their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The dispute arose from their request to use visual posters during a parliamentary interpellation and the subsequent sanctions imposed after they displayed the posters without permission.

On 1 March 2017, the applicants, acting as MPs, formally requested permission from the Speaker of Parliament (via the House Committee) to use eight images of deforestation as a visual presentation during an upcoming interpellation scheduled for 6 March 2017. The interpellation, submitted by their parliamentary group, addressed the government’s development plans for Budapest and was titled “Do you think it is possible to live without green landscape?” The request cited section 38/A of the 2012 Parliament Act, which generally prohibits the use of objects, images, or audio recordings (“presentation tools”) during sittings unless exceptionally permitted by the House Committee as limited to what is necessary to elucidate a speaker’s position.

The House Committee reviewed the request but failed to reach the required unanimous consensus. The matter was therefore referred to the Speaker, who rejected it on 6 March 2017. The Speaker’s decision stated that no convincing arguments had been made justifying the posters and that they were not necessary to understand or expand upon the interpellation. The MP delivering the speech could adequately convey the group’s views through oral communication within the existing Rules of Procedure.

Despite being notified of the refusal, the applicants proceeded on 6 March 2017 to simultaneously hold up three posters (each 50 cm by 60 cm) during their colleague’s interpellation speech. The posters displayed paired “before and after” photographs of Budapest sites (Dagály Strand, Orczy Garden, and Hajógyári Island) allegedly showing environmental degradation, accompanied by explanatory text. Photographs of the applicants displaying the posters were published in the Hungarian press.

The chair presiding over the session immediately noted that the display violated parliamentary rules on presentation tools. The House Committee considered sanctions but again failed to reach consensus, referring the issue to the Speaker. On 16 March 2017, the Speaker imposed a fine of 100,000 Hungarian forints (approximately €320) on each applicant, to be deducted from their monthly parliamentary salary. At the time, a regular MP’s basic monthly salary was approximately 747,878 forints (€2,420), while the group leader’s was approximately 1,296,321 forints (€4,195). The Speaker relied primarily on the lack of prior permission.

The applicants challenged the fines before the Committee on Immunities, Conflicts of Interest, Discipline and Verification of Credentials (the Immunity Committee), arguing that displaying posters was an exercise of freedom of expression guaranteed by the Constitution. They contended that their conduct had not disrupted parliamentary proceedings, undermined Parliament’s authority or dignity, or been self-serving; rather, the visual aids had persuasive value relevant to influencing a vote. They further criticised the Speaker’s allegedly unlimited discretion to restrict the form of expression and the absence of any remedy against the initial refusal of permission.

The Immunity Committee, composed equally of three ruling-party and three opposition MPs, heard Ms Szél in person on 28 March 2017. By a 3–3 vote, it declined to set aside the Speaker’s decisions. The Committee’s reasoning emphasised that the requested illustrations were not indispensable to understanding the interpellation, which could be fully expressed orally; the posters had instead been used as a tool of protest and political confrontation. It stressed that the relevant statutory provisions protected the orderly functioning and authority of Parliament—a legitimate aim recognised by both the Hungarian Constitutional Court and the European Court of Human Rights. The applicants then asked the full Parliament to overturn the sanctions. On 3 April 2017, Parliament voted without debate to uphold the Speaker’s decisions, and the salary deductions were implemented.

These events formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint that the refusal of permission and the ensuing fines constituted an unjustified interference with their freedom of expression as opposition MPs. The legal framework at issue included Article 5 of Hungary’s Fundamental Law (empowering the Speaker to maintain order and dignity) and sections 38/A, 49 and 51/A of the Parliament Act (regulating presentation tools and disciplinary measures, including the possibility of remuneration reductions of up to one-third of monthly salary, subject to review by the Immunity Committee and Parliament). The applicants also invoked Article 13 of the Convention regarding the lack of an effective remedy against the Speaker’s initial refusal.
