**Case Summary: Gurbanov v. Armenia (Application no. 7432/17)**

This case concerns complaints by an Azerbaijani national, Salman Gurbanov, regarding Armenia’s 38-day delay in returning the body of his son, Chingiz Gurbanov (born 1994), an Azerbaijani soldier killed on 29 December 2016 during border clashes. The body was found near Chinari village in Armenia’s Tavush region. The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman treatment of him and his family), Article 8 (interference with private and family life, including inability to bury the body per religious tradition), Article 13 (lack of effective remedies), and Article 14 (discriminatory motive for the delay).

Facts surrounding the death were disputed. The applicant claimed Armenian forces crossed into Azerbaijan, were ambushed, and that his son’s body was then taken into Armenian territory. The Armenian Government maintained that an Azerbaijani sabotage group, including the applicant’s son, invaded Armenian territory at the Bitlis military base, killing three Armenian soldiers (Shavarsh Melikyan, Edgar Narayan, and Erik Abovyan); the applicant’s son died in the same incident.

A criminal investigation was opened the same day under Armenia’s Code of Criminal Procedure. The crime scene and body were examined immediately, with a forensic doctor and witnesses present; no signs of torture or ill-treatment were recorded. A forensic medical examination was scheduled for 30 December 2016. Armenia invited the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) forensic coordinator to attend, citing humanitarian concerns and potential Azerbaijani allegations of mutilation, but the specialist was absent from Armenia at the time (border records confirmed travel dates). The body was re-examined on 14 January 2017 in the ICRC specialist’s presence; again, no torture signs were found and the body was well-preserved. Additional biological, chemical, and criminological tests (issued 9, 18, and 30 January 2017) found no sexual abuse, alcohol, or drugs. Final forensic conclusions confirming death by gunshot wounds were issued on 22 February 2017.

On 3 February 2017, the National Forensic Medicine Authority informed investigators that examinations were complete and the body was no longer needed. It was transferred to ICRC representatives and repatriated to Azerbaijan on 5 February 2017, then handed to the family.

The OSCE Minsk Group Co-Chairs (9 January 2017) and Council of Europe Secretary General (11 January 2017) publicly urged prompt return of remains per the 2010 Astrakhan Summit agreements, emphasizing the issue’s humanitarian nature amid ceasefire violations and mutual accusations.

Domestic law provided relevant context: Article 102 of the Code of Criminal Procedure required prompt examination of petitions; Article 14 of the Criminal Code established jurisdiction over crimes committed (or continuing) on Armenian territory; and a 2013 Ministry of Health order set forensic examination timelines of up to 30 days (extendable by 20 days).

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the delay was attributed by Armenia to a necessary investigation into a violent incident causing multiple deaths, conducted within legal time limits and with ICRC involvement. The applicant viewed the delay as unjustified, inhumane, obstructive of timely religious burial, without remedies, and discriminatory compared to the handling of deceased Armenian soldiers, in a context of longstanding Armenia-Azerbaijan hostility. The Court later found no violation of Article 8 (or Article 14 with Article 8), holding the period reasonable given the investigative needs, conflict context, and diligent process, with a fair balance struck and no ethnic prejudice shown.

The case of Gurbanov v. Armenia (no. 7432/17) before the ECtHR concerns the 38-day delay by Armenian authorities in repatriating the body of the applicant’s son, Chingiz Gurbanov (born 1994), an Azerbaijani soldier killed on 29 December 2016 during border clashes. The applicant, an Azerbaijani national living in Baku, alleged that this delay constituted inhuman treatment of him and his family under Article 3 of the Convention, breached their Article 8 rights to private and family life (including by preventing timely religious burial), lacked effective domestic remedies (Article 13), and was discriminatory on ethnic grounds (Article 14).

The facts were disputed. The applicant claimed Armenian forces crossed into Azerbaijan, were ambushed, and his son’s body was then taken into Armenian territory near Chinari village in the Tavush region. Azerbaijani authorities, the ICRC, the OSCE Minsk Group, and Azerbaijan’s State Commission on Prisoners of War, Hostages and Missing People pressed for prompt return, but Armenia cited an ongoing investigation.

The Armenian Government maintained that an Azerbaijani sabotage group, of which the applicant’s son was a member, invaded Armenian territory at the Bitlis military base. The clash also killed three Armenian soldiers (Shavarsh Melikyan, Edgar Narayan and Erik Abovyan). A criminal investigation was opened the same day under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The crime scene and body were examined that day by a local forensic doctor and two witnesses; no signs of torture or ill-treatment were found.

A forensic medical examination was scheduled for 30 December 2016. Armenia invited the ICRC’s forensic coordinator, but the specialist (M.V.) was absent from the country (having departed on 17 December 2016). The body was re-examined on 14 January 2017 in M.V.’s presence; the report again found no torture and recorded that the body was well preserved. Further biological, chemical and criminological analyses (issued 9, 18 and 30 January 2017) excluded sexual abuse, alcohol or drug intoxication. Final conclusions confirming death by gunshot wounds were issued on 22 February 2017. On 3 February 2017 the National Forensic Medicine Authority confirmed that retention of the body was no longer required. It was transferred to the ICRC on 5 February 2017 and repatriated the same day.

On 9 January 2017 the OSCE Minsk Group Co-Chairs noted that Armenia still held the body, condemned ceasefire violations, and urged immediate return of remains in accordance with the 2010 Astrakhan Summit agreements, stressing the issue’s exclusively humanitarian character. On 11 January 2017 the Council of Europe Secretary General echoed this call.

Domestic law required prompt examination of petitions (Article 102 CCP), applied Armenian criminal law to offences committed (or completed) on its territory (Article 14 Criminal Code), and set a 30-day limit (extendable by 20 days) for forensic examinations of bodies (2013 Minister of Health Order).

The Fifth Section of the Court (judgment of 5 October 2023, final 5 January 2024) held that the 38-day period pursued the legitimate aim of establishing the circumstances of an incident that had also caused Armenian deaths, in the context of hostile relations between the two States. The forensic steps were diligent, fell within the statutory timeframe, and were not excessive or misplaced. The ICRC had been kept informed throughout. The overall delay was therefore not unreasonable and a fair balance had been struck under Article 8. Different treatment of the applicant’s son’s body compared with those of the Armenian soldiers was objectively justified by the general context of hostility and the need for distinct investigative measures; it was proportionate and showed no ethnic prejudice. No violation of Article 14 taken with Article 8 was found. (The judgment text provided does not recap the Court’s conclusions on Articles 3 and 13.)

The case of Gurbanov v. Armenia (no. 7432/17) arose from the delayed return of the body of the applicant’s son, Chingiz Gurbanov, an Azerbaijani soldier killed during border clashes on 29 December 2016. The body was discovered near Chinari village in Armenia’s Tavush region. International actors, including the OSCE Minsk Group Co-Chairs and the Council of Europe Secretary General, publicly urged Armenia to return the remains promptly on humanitarian grounds, referencing earlier agreements.

The parties disputed the incident’s circumstances. The applicant maintained that Armenian forces had crossed into Azerbaijan, been ambushed, and taken his son’s body into Armenia. Azerbaijani authorities, the ICRC and the OSCE Minsk Group pressed for repatriation, but Armenia cited an ongoing investigation. The body was handed over on 5 February 2017, 38 days after death.

Armenia asserted that an Azerbaijani sabotage group, including the applicant’s son, had invaded the Bitlis military base on Armenian soil, killing three Armenian soldiers. A criminal investigation was opened the same day. Immediate examination of the crime scene and body (conducted with a forensic doctor and witnesses) found no signs of torture or ill-treatment. A full forensic examination was scheduled for 30 December 2016; ICRC forensic specialists were invited, but the relevant coordinator was outside Armenia until early January. A re-examination took place on 14 January 2017 in the ICRC coordinator’s presence; he confirmed the absence of torture and the body’s good condition. Further biological, chemical and criminological tests (completed 9–30 January 2017) excluded sexual abuse, alcohol or drugs. Final conclusions attributing death to gunshot wounds were issued on 22 February 2017. On 3 February the forensic authority stated the body was no longer required; it was transferred to the ICRC the same day for return to Azerbaijan.

The applicant complained that the 38-day delay constituted inhuman treatment of himself and his family (Article 3), interfered with private and family life and prevented timely burial according to religious tradition (Article 8), left them without an effective remedy (Article 13), and was motivated by ethnic/national discrimination (Article 14). Domestic law permitted forensic examinations of up to 30 days (extendable by 20 days) and conferred Armenian jurisdiction over offences occurring on its territory.

The Court examined the delay principally under Article 8. It accepted that the period pursued the legitimate aim of establishing the facts of an incident that had also caused Armenian deaths, in a context of intense interstate hostility. The examinations were conducted diligently, within the statutory timeframe, and with ICRC involvement throughout. The overall 38-day interval was therefore not unreasonable and struck a fair balance with the applicant’s rights. As regards Article 14 taken with Article 8, any difference in the speed of returning the Azerbaijani soldier’s body compared with those of Armenian soldiers was objectively justified by the security and investigative demands of the hostile relationship between the two States; the difference was proportionate and showed no ethnic prejudice.

The case of Internationale Humanitäre Hilfsorganisation e.V. v. Germany (Application no. 11214/19) before the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Germany’s 2010 ban on the applicant association, resulting in its dissolution and asset confiscation, breached Article 11 of the Convention (freedom of association). The association, founded in 1997 as a Frankfurt-based non-profit, had the statutory purpose of delivering worldwide humanitarian aid in disasters and conflicts. Its board members were also staff of Millî Görüş, Germany’s largest Islamic organisation.

Until June 2010 the association collected donations in Germany and transferred them to six organisations in predominantly Muslim countries. Nearly half of its funds—rising to approximately €723,000 out of €1.45 million in 2010—went to two Palestinian “social societies.” The first, the Islamic Society (Al-Yamiya al-Islamiya) based in Jabaliya, Gaza, ran projects for orphans of “martyrs” (Palestinians killed or wounded fighting Israel). After its Jabaliya chairman became Hamas mayor in 2010, the association switched support to the newly created Salam Society, headed by a former Islamic Society official and staffed by former Islamic Society employees who continued identical projects. The courts later found this switch was an attempt to conceal ongoing Hamas funding.

On 23 June 2010 the Federal Ministry of the Interior banned the association under Article 9(2) of the Basic Law and section 3 of the Law on Associations. It held that the long-term, substantial transfers to Hamas-linked charities constituted activity contrary to the constitutional concept of “international understanding between peoples.” Hamas, listed as a terrorist organisation by the EU, denies Israel’s right to exist and carries out attacks; its political, military and social branches form a single entity, with social aid to martyrs’ families used to encourage violence and recruitment. The Ministry concluded that the association’s board knew these facts—given their Islamist affiliations, familiarity with a 2004 Federal Administrative Court judgment identifying the Islamic Society as part of Hamas, and their identification with Hamas—and that no less restrictive measure was possible because the association’s entire object was to channel funds to Hamas-linked bodies.

The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the association’s challenge in April 2012 after oral hearings and extensive evidence. It confirmed the Islamic Society (and later Salam) as integral to Hamas, whose social work boosted popular support and military capacity. The board’s knowledge and the disguise attempt demonstrated identification with Hamas’s aims. A proposed settlement allowing temporary operations outside Palestinian territories was rejected by the Ministry. The court rejected the argument that lawful activities elsewhere could immunise the prohibited support.

The Federal Constitutional Court upheld the ban in July 2018. Although a ban is the most severe interference and requires proportionality, less intrusive alternatives (activity restrictions, measures against individuals, etc.) would have been ineffective: the association had deliberately, over years, funnelled large sums to a terrorist organisation while concealing the link and identifying with Hamas’s illegal objectives. The Court found this compatible with Article 11 of the Convention.

The ECtHR, in its 10 October 2023 judgment, found no violation. The interference pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others by combating international terrorism. Given the weight of that aim, States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation. The ban was a last resort after genuine consideration of milder options. The domestic courts had established, on solid evidence, that the association knowingly supported terrorism under a humanitarian guise, conduct incompatible with the Convention’s core values. Their transparent balancing exercise supplied relevant and sufficient reasons; the margin of appreciation was not exceeded. The interference was therefore necessary in a democratic society.

The case Internationale Humanitäre Hilfsorganisation e.V. v. Germany (no. 11214/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 11 ECHR (freedom of association) arising from the 2010 proscription, dissolution and asset confiscation of the applicant, a Frankfurt-based non-profit founded in 1997. Its statutes mandated worldwide humanitarian aid in disasters and wars. Board members were also staff of Millî Görüş e.V., Germany’s largest Islamic organisation. Until June 2010 the association collected German donations and transferred them to six entities in Muslim-majority countries, including two Palestinian “social societies” operating in Gaza and the West Bank.

One recipient was the Islamic Society (Al-Yamiya al-Islamiya), established in 1979 in Jabaliya, Gaza. It ran projects for orphans of “martyrs”—individuals killed or wounded fighting Israel. In spring 2010 its local chairman became Hamas mayor of Jabaliya. The applicant then redirected funds to the newly formed Salam Society for Relief and Development, created by a former Islamic Society board member who later chaired Salam’s supervisory board. Salam employed former Islamic Society staff and continued identical projects, notably aid to martyrs’ families. From 2006 to 2010 nearly half the applicant’s donations (approximately EUR 1.45 million, of which EUR 723 000 in 2010) went to these two societies.

On 23 June 2010 the Federal Ministry of the Interior declared the association contrary to the constitutional principle of international understanding (Völkerverständigung) and banned it under the Law on Associations. The Ministry found that the Islamic Society formed an integral part of Hamas, a terrorist organisation whose Charter and actions deny Israel’s right to exist and promote violent destruction of the Israeli state. Hamas’s social, political and military wings are inseparable; support for martyrs’ families incentivises further attacks. The applicant’s leaders, given their Islamist affiliations and knowledge of a 2004 Federal Administrative Court ruling that had already identified the Islamic Society as a Hamas component, knowingly channelled substantial long-term funds, thereby indirectly financing terrorism. No milder measure could suffice because the association’s very purpose was to collect and transmit such donations.

The applicant challenged the ban before the Federal Administrative Court, denying any Hamas links. After hearings and a rejected settlement proposal (which would have allowed non-Palestinian activity for three years), the court dismissed the action on 18 April 2012. It confirmed that support for the Islamic Society (and later Salam as a transparent successor) undermined peaceful Israeli-Palestinian coexistence. The 2004 Al-Aqsa judgment had already established the Islamic Society’s Hamas affiliation; the switch to Salam, orchestrated by the same Hamas-linked individuals, was an attempt to conceal continued funding. The association’s leadership knew these facts and identified with Hamas. Diversification of other aid activities could not immunise terrorist financing.

A constitutional complaint was rejected by the Federal Constitutional Court on 13 July 2018. The court held that Article 9 of the Basic Law (and, by reference, Article 11 ECHR) permits prohibition only as a last resort when an association knowingly and substantially supports third-party terrorism in a manner that gravely impairs international relations. Less restrictive alternatives (activity restrictions, individual sanctions) would have been ineffective given the association’s deliberate, disguised and long-term funding of Hamas while identifying with its violent aims.

The Strasbourg Court (Fourth Section, 10 October 2023, final 19 February 2024) found no violation. The interference pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others through the fight against international terrorism and the promotion of international understanding. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation. The ban followed exhaustive consideration of milder options and rested on established facts that the association had knowingly supported terrorism under a humanitarian façade, conduct incompatible with core Convention values. Domestic courts performed a comprehensive, transparent balancing exercise and gave relevant and sufficient reasons. The measure was therefore proportionate and necessary in a democratic society.

Germany (Application no. 11214/19) concerned the 2010 prohibition of a German non-profit association, resulting in its dissolution and asset confiscation, and whether this interfered with its Article 11 right to freedom of association.

Founded in 1997 in Frankfurt am Main, the applicant association’s statutes aimed at providing worldwide humanitarian aid in disasters and conflicts. **Case Summary: Anagnostakis v. Greece (Application no. 26504/20)**

The applicant, a Greek national, alleged a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to the non-enforcement of domestic court decisions granting him contact rights with his son (born 23 September 2014 outside marriage), who remained in the mother’s custody. He claimed the mother had alienated the child from him and that Greek authorities failed to act with sufficient diligence to restore contact, despite his repeated requests. (A prior ECHR judgment in Anagnostakis and Others v. Greece, no. 46075/16, had already found a violation of Article 8 based on delays in the initial proceedings setting the contact schedule.)

The applicant voluntarily recognized the child on 20 October 2014, with the parents initially agreeing to joint parental responsibility. They cohabited briefly until early October 2014, after which the child lived with the mother and the applicant visited daily. Contact deteriorated; from November 2018 the child refused to accompany the applicant, who ceased visits after February 2019 to avoid distress.

Following earlier proceedings (2015–2017) on alimony, contact, and the child’s name, the applicant applied on 16 April 2018 for shared custody (alternating 15-day periods) or a definitive contact schedule. On 10 September 2018 the Athens Court of First Instance rejected shared custody, finding it contrary to the child’s best interests given his adaptation to the mother’s care and the parents’ circumstances. It established a contact schedule of two weekly three-hour visits plus two weekends per month (initially one overnight stay, increasing to two then three), plus alternating holidays. Both parties appealed. On 21 March 2019 the Athens Court of Appeal upheld the no-shared-custody ruling, citing the parents’ tense relationship marked by mistrust and rivalry, reduced alimony, and left the contact schedule unchanged. The Court of Cassation later addressed related points (decision of 11 August 2021); a further application by the applicant remains pending. Criminal proceedings were also pending against the mother (for alleged breach of a court decision, false testimony, and slander) and against the applicant.

The applicant lodged numerous complaints with the Athens public prosecutor (specialized in children’s cases) starting in 2016, alleging the mother impeded contact. The prosecutor opened a social-services file, ordered reports on the child’s living conditions, and facilitated counseling. A 2017 municipal social report on the mother’s household recommended counseling for both parents on interpersonal issues; the prosecutor directed them accordingly. In 2018 the applicant obtained a second report on his own home (positive regarding the child’s needs and family support), which, together with the first report, was transmitted to the courts deciding custody/contact. The prosecutor summoned the mother in November 2018 to urge facilitation of contact and non-interference; she cited the child’s negative views and ongoing specialist consultations (noting the applicant had declined participation). The prosecutor referred both parents to the NGO GONIS for consultations, but these were discontinued after arguments; the applicant alleged bias (including a GONIS volunteer lawyer assisting the mother in court). Further requests by the applicant for additional social reports, on-site psychological observation of refusals, or revocation of referrals were largely refused or redirected to criminal prosecutors for possible breach-of-decision investigations. A psychiatric evaluation of the child (ordered December 2018 at the Hellenic Centre for Mental Health, at the mother’s request) found no mental or behavioral issues; the applicant declined to participate and sought his own evaluation.

The applicant also sought help from the Greek Ombudsman (December 2018), who contacted the mother, emphasized her duty to facilitate contact (noting a young child’s susceptibility to influence), and proposed specialized mental-health interventions after GONIS efforts stalled. Both parents declined further cooperation (the applicant citing repeated expert changes and lack of results), leading the Ombudsman to withdraw. The applicant additionally recorded refusals with police, who transmitted files for criminal investigation but provided no other assistance.

These facts center on the persistent non-exercise of court-ordered contact amid parental conflict, the applicant’s multiple formal requests, and the authorities’ sequential interventions via prosecutors, social services, NGOs, mental-health evaluations, and the Ombudsman.

Greece (Application no. 26504/20) concerns the alleged failure of Greek authorities to enforce judicial decisions granting the applicant contact rights with his young son, in alleged breach of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The applicant, Nikolaos Anagnostakis, and Ms E.K. had a son born out of wedlock on 23 September 2014. The applicant voluntarily recognised paternity on 20 October 2014, with the parents agreeing to joint parental responsibility and that the child would take the applicant’s surname. The couple separated in early October 2014; the child remained with the mother while the applicant initially visited daily. Contact became fraught, and from November 2018 the child refused to go with the applicant. The applicant ceased attempts after February 2019 to avoid distressing the child.

Following earlier proceedings on alimony, contact and the child’s name (2015–2017), the applicant applied on 16 April 2018 for shared custody (15 days each) or a definitive contact schedule. On 10 September 2018 the Athens Court of First Instance (decision 585/2018) awarded the mother monthly alimony of €540, rejected shared custody as contrary to the child’s best interests (the child being well adapted to the mother’s care), and set a detailed contact regime: two three-hour weekday visits plus two weekends per month (initially one overnight stay, increasing to two then three over subsequent months), plus alternating holiday periods. Both parents appealed. On 21 March 2019 the Athens Court of Appeal (decision 1600/2019) reduced alimony to €380, upheld the rejection of shared custody given the parents’ tense, mistrustful relationship, and left the contact schedule unchanged. The Court of Cassation (decision 1020/2021 of 11 August 2021) dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on points of law (the custody ruling having been unappealable). Related criminal proceedings against the mother (for breach of a court decision, false testimony and slander) remain pending, as do unspecified proceedings against the applicant.

From 2016 the applicant repeatedly complained to the Athens public prosecutor for minors that the mother was obstructing contact. The prosecutor opened a social-services file, ordered reports on the child’s living conditions (September 2017: both parents should receive counselling; May 2018: the applicant’s home was suitable), transmitted material to the civil courts, summoned the mother (November 2018) to facilitate contact, and referred both parents to the NGO GONIS for consultation. The applicant discontinued GONIS sessions, alleging bias after a GONIS volunteer lawyer assisted the mother in court and after recommendations he viewed as contrary to the court order. In December 2018 the prosecutor ordered a psychiatric evaluation of the child at the Hellenic Centre for Mental Health; the applicant refused to participate, claiming he had not been consulted and that he had already arranged an alternative assessment. The evaluation (completed September 2019) found no mental or behavioural problems. Multiple further requests by the applicant for additional reports, on-site psychologist attendance, revocation of orders or direct enforcement were variously granted, refused or forwarded for possible criminal investigation under Article 232(a) of the former Criminal Code. Police recorded the child’s refusals and likewise transmitted files to the criminal prosecutor.

In December 2018 the applicant also sought help from the Greek Ombudsman, who contacted the mother, stressed her duty to facilitate contact and noted the risk of influence on a four-year-old. After the mother attributed the refusal to the child himself and both parents declined further specialised intervention (the applicant citing “systematic mishandling” through successive experts), the Ombudsman ceased involvement. A prior ECHR judgment (Anagnostakis and Others v. Greece, 2021) had already found a violation of Article 8 arising from delay in the original contact-schedule proceedings.

The case of Anagnostakis v. Greece (Application no. 26504/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the alleged failure of Greek authorities to enforce court-ordered contact rights between the applicant, Nikolaos Anagnostakis, and his son, in violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life). The applicant claimed that the child's mother, E.K., had alienated the boy from him and that domestic authorities had not acted diligently enough to restore contact, despite his repeated requests.

The couple's son was born out of wedlock on 23 September 2014. The applicant recognised the child shortly afterwards, and the parents initially agreed to joint parental responsibility. They separated in early October 2014, after which the child lived with his mother. The applicant visited daily at first, but contact became irregular. From November 2018 the child refused to go with his father; the applicant ceased visits after February 2019 to spare the boy distress.

Earlier proceedings (2015–2017) had addressed alimony, contact and the child's name. In April 2018 the applicant sought shared custody or a fixed contact schedule. The Athens Court of First Instance (decision 585/2018 of 10 September 2018) rejected shared custody as contrary to the child's best interests, given his adaptation to life with his mother. It set a detailed contact timetable: two three-hour weekday visits, two weekends per month (initially with one overnight stay, later increased), and alternating holiday periods. Both parents appealed. The Athens Court of Appeal (decision 1600/2019 of 21 March 2019) upheld the custody ruling, citing the parents' tense, mistrustful relationship, and left the contact schedule unchanged (while reducing alimony). The Court of Cassation later dismissed most of the applicant's further appeal (decision 1020/2021).

The applicant repeatedly turned to the Athens public prosecutor responsible for children's cases. From 2016 he complained that the mother was obstructing contact. The prosecutor commissioned social-service reports on living conditions in both homes (2017–2018). These found the mother's household adequate and the applicant's suitable, and recommended parental counselling. Reports were forwarded to the courts. In November 2018 the prosecutor summoned the mother and urged her to facilitate contact. Both parents were referred to the NGO GONIS for counselling; sessions broke down after arguments, and the applicant withdrew, alleging bias. Further requests for additional social reports or a psychologist to attend handovers were largely refused, though files were sent to the criminal prosecutor to examine possible offences under former Criminal Code Article 232(a) (breach of a court decision).

At the mother's request the prosecutor ordered a psychiatric evaluation of the child at the Hellenic Centre for Mental Health. The applicant declined to participate, preferring his own arranged assessment; the Centre later reported no mental or behavioural problems. The applicant also lodged complaints with the police (who recorded incidents of refusal but offered no further practical help) and the Greek Ombudsman. The Ombudsman reminded the mother of her duty to encourage contact and proposed specialist public mental-health services, but both parents declined further intervention.

Criminal proceedings against the mother for alleged breach of court decisions, false testimony and slander remain pending, as do unspecified proceedings against the applicant. A related earlier judgment of the Court (Anagnostakis and Others v. Greece, 2021) had already found an Article 8 violation arising from delays in setting the original contact schedule. The present application focuses on subsequent non-enforcement.

The case of Myslihaka and Others v. Albania (applications nos. 68958/17 and five others) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, which guarantees the right to free elections, specifically the right to vote. The six Albanian applicants—Hyqmet Myslihaka, Imer Ruko, Mehmet Rrapaj, Fatmir Bakalli, Rigels Kushe and Blendi Spaho—were all serving prison sentences when Albania held parliamentary elections on 25 June 2017 and were thereby prevented from voting.

Myslihaka had been convicted of murder in 2002 and sentenced to 16 years’ imprisonment (arrested 2007). Ruko was convicted in 2014 of manufacturing and selling narcotic drugs and sentenced to 7 years and 6 months (arrested 2014). Rrapaj was convicted in 2014 of attempted drug trafficking and sentenced to 5 years and 4 months (arrested 2013). Bakalli was convicted in 2015 of participating in an organised criminal group and facilitating illegal border crossing and sentenced to 7 years and 8 months (arrested 2014). Kushe was convicted in 2016 of attempted drug trafficking and sentenced to 5 years (arrested 2015). Spaho was convicted in 2016 of manufacturing and selling narcotic drugs and sentenced to 4 years and 8 months (arrested 2015). All sentences were final.

The ban stemmed from Law no. 138/2015 (the Decriminalisation Act), enacted by a three-fifths parliamentary majority on 17 December 2015 after political consensus and a Venice Commission opinion. The law’s main purpose was to exclude persons convicted of specified serious crimes from public office in order to protect public confidence in institutions. It additionally disenfranchised anyone serving a prison sentence (regardless of length) for offences listed in section 2, including murder, drug manufacture/sale/trafficking, organised-crime participation, crimes against humanity, life or health, sexual offences, terrorism, and certain offences against the State, justice or elections. The restriction ended automatically once the sentence (including any reduction) was served; it did not apply to remand prisoners. Although the convicting judgment was supposed to mention the voting ban, the ban applied even if omitted, and it applied retroactively to persons already convicted. Prison authorities confirmed that none of the six applicants appeared on the 2017 electoral roll. Official figures showed the law affected 923 prisoners out of 5,379 prisoners otherwise eligible to vote.

The applicants did not institute domestic proceedings, asserting that no effective remedy existed. A separate constitutional challenge brought by the Albanian Helsinki Committee was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 5 June 2017. That court held that the law pursued legitimate aims (safeguarding democratic values, crime prevention, civic responsibility and institutional integrity) and was not disproportionate.

The applicants complained that the statutory ban arbitrarily deprived them of the right to vote. The Court examined the facts against the Convention standard: the restriction was prescribed by law, pursued legitimate aims and was not a blanket, automatic or indefinite ban on all prisoners. It applied only to a defined list of grave offences, was temporary and was linked to the nature and gravity of the crimes actually committed. In the applicants’ cases those crimes (homicide, serious drug offences and organised crime) furnished a sufficient and proportionate link to the withdrawal of voting rights. The Court concluded that the Albanian legislature had stayed within its margin of appreciation and that no violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 had occurred.

Rrapaj had been given 5 years 4 months in 2014 for attempted drug trafficking (arrested October 2013). Prison administrations confirmed in writing that none of the six applicants appeared on those rolls.

The ban was neither automatic nor indiscriminate: it was confined to a finite list of grave offences, affected a limited subset of prisoners, was conditioned on the nature and gravity of the crime, and lasted only for the duration of the sentence. The applicant, Frank Stott, a British national detained at HMP Full Sutton, complained to the ECHR that the early-release rules applicable to his extended determinate sentence (EDS) discriminated against him contrary to Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 5.

On 3 May 2013 he was convicted of multiple sexual offences, including eleven counts of rape of a child under 13. On 24 May 2013 the Crown Court imposed an EDS under s. 226A of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 comprising a 21-year custodial term and a 4-year extended licence. Permission to appeal sentence was refused. Under the applicable provisions he becomes eligible for Parole Board consideration only after serving two-thirds of the custodial term; release before the end of that term requires the Board to be satisfied that detention is no longer necessary for public protection.

He argued that a discretionary life sentence would have made him eligible for parole at the halfway point of the equivalent determinate term, and that the later eligibility date for EDS prisoners was therefore discriminatory. Judicial-review proceedings were dismissed by the Administrative Court, which felt bound by the House of Lords decision in *R (Clift)* to hold that sentence type did not constitute “other status.” The court nevertheless examined analogy and justification, concluding that the difference in the punitive element of the sentence lacked rational basis and would have warranted a declaration of incompatibility but for the binding precedent.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by a 3–2 majority. Lady Black (with whom Lords Carnwath and Hodge agreed) accepted that the differential treatment engaged Article 14 on the ground of “other status.” She held, however, that EDS prisoners were not in an analogous position to those serving standard determinate sentences or discretionary life sentences. Each sentencing regime is a self-contained package tailored to a particular combination of offence seriousness and risk; early-release rules form an integral part of that package. The later parole-eligibility date for EDS prisoners pursued the legitimate aim of public protection and, viewed holistically, was a proportionate means of achieving it. Lady Hale and Lord Mance dissented, finding no convincing justification for requiring EDS prisoners to serve a greater proportion of their custodial term than discretionary life prisoners, who are generally more dangerous yet become eligible earlier.

The ECHR unanimously found no violation. Distinguishing *Clift*, it observed that early-release eligibility may legitimately rest on policy as well as purely factual risk assessments. The criteria need not be identical for every prisoner category. Seriousness of offending and degree of dangerousness are plainly relevant. EDS prisoners, who have been found to present a significant risk of serious harm from further specified offences, are not sufficiently similar to prisoners under other regimes that may involve different levels of offending and risk. Different sentencing frameworks pursue the legitimate aim of matching release arrangements to those differing combinations of gravity and danger. The impugned provisions fall within the wide margin of appreciation accorded to States in matters of penal policy and are therefore objectively justified and proportionate.

The applicant, Frank Stott (born 1968), was convicted on 3 May 2013 of multiple sexual offences, including eleven counts of raping a child under 13, having earlier pleaded guilty to other crimes. On 24 May 2013 the Crown Court imposed an extended determinate sentence (EDS) under section 226A of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, consisting of a 21-year custodial term plus a four-year extended licence period. Permission to appeal the sentence was refused. Under the applicable rules (section 246A), he becomes eligible for Parole Board consideration only after serving two-thirds of the custodial term; release may then be directed if continued detention is no longer necessary for public protection. If not released earlier, he must be freed at the end of the 21-year term regardless of residual risk.

Stott challenged the early-release provisions by judicial review, arguing they discriminated against him contrary to Article 14 (taken with Article 5). He compared his position with prisoners serving standard determinate sentences (normally released automatically at the halfway point) and those serving discretionary life sentences (generally eligible for parole after serving a minimum term set at half the notional determinate sentence that would otherwise have been imposed). He also noted the later-introduced special custodial sentence for offenders of particular concern (SOPC), under which eligibility arose at the halfway point of the custodial term.

The Administrative Court, bound by the House of Lords decision in R (Clift), held that the difference did not engage “other status.” Had it been free to decide otherwise, it would have found EDS prisoners analogous to both determinate-sentence and discretionary-life prisoners (all sentences containing a punitive element followed by a risk-based phase) and would have declared the two-thirds rule incompatible: the later eligibility date could not be justified once risk was properly assessed by the Parole Board.

The Supreme Court (majority) accepted that the difference was based on “other status” but dismissed the claim. Each sentencing regime was a distinct statutory package tailored to a particular combination of offence gravity and dangerousness; early-release rules formed an integral part of that package. EDS prisoners were not in an analogous position to those serving ordinary determinate terms (no finding of significant risk required) or discretionary life terms (no guaranteed release date and lifelong licence). Even if analogous, the difference pursued the legitimate aim of public protection and was proportionate. Dissenting justices considered the two-thirds threshold especially hard to justify against discretionary-life prisoners, who are typically more dangerous yet become eligible earlier, while the Parole Board equally protects the public in both cases.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the same comparisons. It emphasised that eligibility for early release is a matter of penal policy as well as fact, unlike the purely factual risk assessment at issue in Clift v. the United Kingdom. Different categories of prisoner are not required to be treated identically; seriousness of offending and assessed dangerousness are plainly relevant. EDS prisoners therefore could not be regarded as sufficiently similar to those sentenced under other regimes. The impugned provisions formed part of a coherent legislative scheme designed to address distinct combinations of offence and risk and fell within the wide margin of appreciation afforded to States in matters of sentencing and prison policy. No violation of Article 14 taken with Article 5 was found.

The applicant, Frank Stott (born 1968), was convicted on 3 May 2013 of multiple sexual offences, including 11 counts of rape of a child under 13, having previously pleaded guilty to others. On 24 May 2013 the Crown Court imposed an extended determinate sentence (EDS) under s.226A of the Criminal Justice Act 2003: a 21-year custodial term plus a four-year extended licence. Permission to appeal sentence was refused.

Under s.246A, an EDS prisoner becomes eligible for parole only after serving two-thirds of the custodial term. The Parole Board may then direct release if continued detention is no longer necessary for public protection; otherwise release is automatic at the end of the custodial term. Stott contended that this regime was discriminatory contrary to Article 14 taken with Article 5. He compared himself with two other groups: standard determinate-sentence prisoners (automatically released at the halfway point) and discretionary life-sentence prisoners (generally eligible for parole after serving half of the notional determinate term that would otherwise have been imposed). He argued that an EDS, like a life sentence, comprises a punitive/deterrent element followed by a risk-based element, so that delaying parole eligibility until the two-thirds point treated him less favourably than similarly situated prisoners solely because of the particular sentencing regime applied to him.

In judicial-review proceedings the Administrative Court, bound by the House of Lords decision in R (Clift), held that Stott did not possess an “other status”. Had it not been so bound, it would have found EDS prisoners analogous to those serving determinate or discretionary-life terms and the difference unjustified, because dangerousness is already addressed by Parole Board review and the later eligibility date arbitrarily inflates the punitive element.

The Supreme Court (3–2) dismissed the appeal. Following the Strasbourg judgment in Clift it accepted that sentence type constituted “other status”. The majority nevertheless held that EDS prisoners were not in an analogous situation to prisoners sentenced under different statutory regimes. Each regime is a complete, tailored package designed for a distinct combination of offence seriousness and risk: an EDS requires a specific finding of significant risk of serious harm and guarantees release at the end of a finite term plus only a limited licence, whereas a discretionary life sentence may entail lifelong detention and lifelong licence and does not invariably require a dangerousness finding. Early-release rules form an integral part of that package and cannot be isolated. Even if the situations were analogous, the difference pursued the legitimate aim of public protection and was a proportionate means of achieving it. Contracting States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in matters of penal policy.

The two dissenting justices considered the later parole threshold for EDS prisoners (especially vis-à-vis more dangerous discretionary lifers) unexplained and disproportionate; public protection is equally secured by Parole Board assessment in both cases.

Before the European Court the Government maintained that the regimes were not comparable and that any difference was justified by the distinct risk profiles they address. The Court agreed. Unlike Clift (which concerned a purely factual risk assessment), eligibility for early release may legitimately incorporate policy as well as factual considerations. The criteria need not be identical across all prisoner categories; seriousness of offending and degree of dangerousness are plainly relevant. EDS prisoners are not sufficiently similar to those sentenced under other regimes that present different combinations of offending and risk. The legislative scheme pursues the legitimate aim of matching sentencing packages to those combinations and remains within the wide margin afforded to States in prisoner and penal policy. The impugned measures were therefore objectively justified and proportionate. There was no violation of Article 14 taken with Article 5.
001-228681:
The case of Toivanen v. Finland (Application no. 46131/19) before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) concerns alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal) in proceedings revoking the applicant's licence to act as trial counsel.

The applicant, a Finnish lawyer licensed on 30 January 2014, sent emails over about ten months in 2014–2015 to judges and authorities, criticising them and seeking action regarding criminal proceedings against him. The Board on Trial Counsel, acting of its own motion, revoked his licence unanimously on 22 October 2015, finding him manifestly unsuited.

He appealed to the Helsinki Court of Appeal. A three-judge bench held an oral hearing on 29 August 2016 and indicated it would rule within 30 days. On 23 November 2016, Judge L. (Acting Chief Justice in the Chief Justice's absence) transferred the case to a seven-judge extended composition under section 8c of the then-applicable Act on Courts of Appeal. This provision allowed the chief justice to transfer cases that might deviate from prior case-law, or that had far-reaching consequences or were otherwise important as a matter of principle; special reasons were required if an oral hearing had been or would be held. No contemporaneous reasons for the transfer were recorded.

The extended bench, chaired by Judge L. (who in 2014 had forwarded one of the applicant's emails to police, perceiving a possible threat to a judge), held a hearing on 2 January 2017. The applicant was summoned but did not attend; the bench heard a recording of his prior testimony. On 17 March 2017, by five votes to two, it dismissed the appeal and upheld the revocation. The two dissenting judges had sat on the original three-judge bench.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing a procedural error: the case had been transferred after the three-judge bench had (he claimed) decided 2–1 in his favour, in order to reverse that outcome. He also alleged bias by Judge L. due to the 2014 email incident, and that there were no legal grounds for revocation. He did not request an oral hearing.

The Supreme Court granted unlimited leave to appeal. In its 28 February 2019 decision, it unanimously found Judge L. unbiased: the email contained no specific threat against or criticism of her, she merely forwarded it as standard practice for security threats, and it formed no part of the case file. On the transfer (by 3–2), the majority held it lawful. The case involved recent legislation with no relevant practice, raising a matter of principle about whether off-duty conduct rendered a person unsuited as trial counsel, requiring a balancing of fundamental rights. It thus met the statutory criteria of far-reaching consequences and importance. Special reasons existed after the hearing: a new hearing would cause no significant inconvenience (only the applicant had testified), and the case's importance favoured an authoritative extended ruling. Transfers commonly occur once an initial composition's views have formed; the provision's purpose would otherwise be undermined. The extended bench was properly constituted (original three judges plus three drawn by lot, chaired by the Acting Chief Justice). Two dissenting Supreme Court justices considered that the overall procedure, given the case's nature, gave the applicant a reasoned, objective ground to doubt fairness and impartiality, warranting quashing.

The ECHR (judgment of 9 November 2023, final 9 February 2024) found no violation. The transfer rule sought a sound, broad basis for important rulings. The applicant suffered no loss of participatory opportunity. Procedural safeguards existed; the Supreme Court had full jurisdiction to quash for unfairness or lack of impartiality and conducted an extensive, non-deficient examination prescribed by law, remedying any appellate defects. The general law was fully accessible, and Judge L.'s detailed reasons (given in a statement) were thoroughly reviewed. There was no reason to doubt the transfer was objectively justified. The proceedings provided sufficient guarantees to exclude any legitimate doubt as to the Court of Appeal's impartiality. The Supreme Court also unanimously upheld the revocation on the merits.

The ECHR case Toivanen v. Finland (no. 46131/19) concerned a Finnish lawyer whose trial-counsel licence was revoked, and his subsequent complaint under Article 6 § 1 of bias and unfairness arising from the transfer of his appeal to an extended Court of Appeal bench.

The applicant received his licence in January 2014. Over the following ten months he sent numerous emails criticising judges and authorities in connection with criminal proceedings against him. Acting of its own motion, the Board on Trial Counsel revoked the licence on 22 October 2015 on the ground that he was manifestly unsuited to the role.

He appealed to the Helsinki Court of Appeal. A three-judge bench heard him orally on 29 August 2016 and indicated that a decision would be given within 30 days. On 23 November 2016 Acting Chief Justice Judge L. (who had, in 2014, forwarded one of the applicant’s emails to the police because she considered it contained a threat) transferred the case to a seven-judge extended composition pursuant to s. 8c of the then Act on Courts of Appeal. That provision permitted transfer of a case of far-reaching consequence or of importance as a matter of principle, but required a “particular reason” once an oral hearing had already taken place. No contemporaneous written reasons for the transfer were recorded.

The extended bench, chaired by Judge L., sat on 2 January 2017. The applicant did not attend; the court therefore replayed the recording of his earlier testimony. On 17 March 2017 it dismissed the appeal by five votes to two (the two dissenting judges having sat on the original bench; Judge L. voted with the majority).

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, alleging that the transfer had been effected after the three-judge bench had already decided (by 2–1) in his favour, solely in order to reverse that outcome, and that Judge L. was biased because of the 2014 email incident. He also challenged the revocation on the merits. Leave to appeal was granted without restriction.

In its judgment of 28 February 2019 the Supreme Court held, by three votes to two, that the transfer was lawful. It found unanimously that Judge L. was not biased: she had merely forwarded the email in accordance with standard security practice; the email formed no part of the file and had not been relied upon. On the transfer itself the majority emphasised the novelty of the trial-counsel legislation, the absence of relevant case-law, and the need to decide whether off-duty conduct could render a person unsuited to the profession—an issue of principle requiring the balancing of fundamental rights. These features made the case far-reaching. A new oral hearing would cause little inconvenience. It was in any event common for transfer decisions to be taken only after the original bench had formed a view. The two dissenting justices accepted that no specific statutory provision had been breached, but considered that the overall procedure, viewed in the light of the subject-matter, gave the applicant an objectively justified reason to doubt the Court of Appeal’s fairness and impartiality.

The ECHR later found no violation of Article 6 § 1. The transfer rule existed to secure a broad and authoritative decision in important cases; the applicant had been able to participate fully; the Supreme Court possessed full jurisdiction, examined the process exhaustively and thereby remedied any possible defect. The criteria for transfer were accessible and the reasons given by Judge L. had been thoroughly scrutinised. There was accordingly no legitimate doubt as to the impartiality of the Court of Appeal.
001-228835:
The case of W.A. and Others v. Italy (Application no. 18787/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns five Sudanese nationals who alleged they formed part of a group of 40 migrants collectively expelled from Turin to Khartoum on 24 August 2016. They claimed this exposed them to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment in Sudan (Article 3), amounted to collective expulsion (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4), involved nationality-based discrimination (Article 14) and lacked an effective remedy (Article 13).

A Memorandum of Understanding signed on 3 August 2016 between the Italian Ministry of the Interior and Sudanese police aimed to improve cooperation on border controls and the removal of irregular Sudanese migrants. The applicants asserted they had arrived irregularly by sea in July–August 2016, been rescued by the Italian Navy, processed at hotspots (photographs and fingerprints taken) without any information on international protection, and later hosted at a Red Cross centre in Ventimiglia. Between 18 and 22 August they were arrested, subjected to coercive identification (including alleged slaps and forced fingerprinting), and detained for two to five days. They stated they had clearly expressed a wish not to return to Sudan because of persecution as non-Arab Darfuris (specifically Zaghawa in one case) amid government-led violence, but communication was impaired by dialect differences with interpreters. No documents, legal advice or opportunity to apply for asylum were provided. They were taken to the Sudanese embassy for nationality confirmation, then transported to Turin and forcibly boarded, physically resisting and being restrained with Velcro straps. A five-year exit ban was later imposed in Sudan. (Some co-nationals who resisted more successfully later received asylum.)

The Italian Government denied the applicants had ever been on Italian territory, producing identity photographs of the 40 removed persons (none of which, they said, matched) and search results from police databases showing no records. Discrepancies in name spellings were attributed by the applicants to Arabic-to-Latin transliteration.

Faced with this factual dispute the Court commissioned an expert facial-comparison report from the Belgian Federal Judicial Police’s Biometric Identification Service (Rule A1 of the Rules of Court). Using specialised software and morphological analysis of facial features, the experts scored matches on a –2 to +2 scale. The first applicant received +2 (strongest support for identity with one removed person, “A.A.”); the second received –2 (exclusion); the third and fourth received +1 (support); no photographs existed for the fifth. The Court therefore declared the complaints of the second to fifth applicants manifestly ill-founded and examined only those of the first applicant, whom it accepted had been among the removed group.

Documents relating to “A.A.” showed that on 22 August 2016 he signed an information sheet at Imperia police headquarters ticking “other reasons” for entry (wish to reach Germany) and “I do not wish to go back to my country of origin,” together with a handwritten statement (Italian and Arabic) “I do not wish to ask for international protection.” The next day the Prefect issued a refusal-of-entry order, which was served on him. At a validation hearing the same day his representative invoked Article 19 of Legislative Decree 286/1998 and Strasbourg case-law on the risk of ill-treatment in Sudan. The Justice of the Peace nonetheless validated the order, noting that A.A. had declared he was merely transiting, had refused protection during an interview conducted with Arabic-speaking mediators, and that the Memorandum of Understanding applied. He was removed the following day.

The first applicant later obtained refugee status in Niger. The Court ultimately found that the domestic procedure had afforded him effective guarantees against arbitrary refoulement.

The case of W.A. and Others v. Italy (Application no. 18787/17) concerns five Sudanese nationals who alleged that they were among a group of 40 migrants forcibly removed from Turin to Khartoum on 24 August 2016. They claimed this exposed them to a real risk of inhuman and degrading treatment in Sudan, in breach of Article 3 of the Convention, due to their membership of non-Arab Darfur tribes facing persecution and genocide. They further alleged a collective expulsion contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 4, nationality-based discrimination under Article 14, and lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. The facts must be read alongside the related judgment in A.E. and Others v. Italy (no. 18911/17), in which some intended deportees successfully resisted removal and later obtained asylum.

A 3 August 2016 Memorandum of Understanding between the Italian and Sudanese police aimed to enhance cooperation against human trafficking and facilitate returns of irregular Sudanese migrants. The applicants described arriving by sea in July–August 2016, being processed at hotspots (where photographs and fingerprints were taken but no information on asylum was provided), travelling north to a Red Cross centre in Ventimiglia, and being arrested in mid-August. They said they were detained for two to five days, subjected to coercive identification (including alleged slapping and forced fingerprinting), and interviewed with inadequate interpretation. They maintained that they had clearly expressed their fear of return to Sudan on account of their ethnicity. They received no written decisions, had no access to lawyers or NGOs, were identified at the Sudanese embassy, and were then transported to Turin, where they physically resisted boarding but were restrained with Velcro straps and expelled. Upon arrival they faced a five-year travel ban. The first applicant later obtained refugee status in Niger.

The Italian Government denied that any of the applicants had ever been present in Italy and produced identity photographs of the 40 deportees whose names and appearances, they said, did not match. The Court therefore commissioned a facial-comparison report from the Belgian Federal Police Biometric Identification Service (Rule A1 of the Rules of Court). Using specialised software and morphological analysis, the experts found “strongest support” (+2) that the first applicant (W.A.) was the deportee known as A.A., “support” (+1) for the third and fourth applicants, “source exclusion” (–2) for the second applicant, and no usable images for the fifth. The Government argued that even a +2 result was insufficient without fingerprints. The Court held that the evidence was sufficient to establish only the first applicant’s presence among the deportees; the remaining applications were therefore declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded.

Documentary evidence relating to A.A. (identified as the first applicant) showed that on 22 August he signed an information sheet stating that he wished to travel to Germany, did not want to return to Sudan, and did not wish to seek international protection. A refusal-of-entry order was issued and served the next day. At a hearing before the Justice of the Peace his representative invoked Article 19 of the Immigration Act and ECHR case-law on the risk of ill-treatment in Sudan. The Justice of the Peace nevertheless validated the order, noting that A.A. had declared he was merely in transit, had refused asylum in an interview conducted with Arabic-speaking mediators, and that the Memorandum of Understanding applied. He was removed on 24 August.

The Court ultimately found that, in respect of the first applicant, the domestic procedure had afforded effective guarantees against arbitrary refoulement.

The case of W.A. and Others v. Italy concerns five Sudanese nationals who alleged they were among a group of forty migrants forcibly removed from Turin to Khartoum on 24 August 2016. They claimed this exposed them to a real risk of inhuman and degrading treatment in Sudan (Article 3), amounted to a collective expulsion (Article 4 of Protocol No. 4), involved nationality-based discrimination (Article 14), and occurred without an effective remedy (Article 13). The events followed a 3 August 2016 Memorandum of Understanding between Italian and Sudanese police authorities aimed at managing irregular Sudanese migration and removals.

The applicants stated they had arrived irregularly by sea in July–August 2016, been rescued by the Italian Navy, and been processed at hotspots (in Crotone or Sicily) where photographs and fingerprints were taken, without receiving information on international protection. They then travelled north to the Red Cross centre in Ventimiglia. Between 18 and 22 August they were arrested near the centre, subjected to further (sometimes coercive) identification procedures, and detained in police stations for two to five days. Some had briefly attempted to enter France and been returned informally.

During detention they asserted that they had expressed a clear wish not to be returned to Sudan, citing persecution and serious human-rights violations faced by the non-Arab population of Darfur, including genocide by government-linked groups. Communication with interpreters speaking a North African variety of Arabic was impaired. They received no written decisions, copies of records or information about asylum procedures, had no access to lawyers or human-rights organisations, and were taken to the Sudanese embassy solely for nationality confirmation. On 24 August they were transported to Turin, physically resisted removal, were restrained with Velcro straps and flown to Khartoum, after which a five-year travel ban was imposed. Other co-nationals who resisted more successfully later obtained asylum in Italy.

The Italian Government denied that any of the applicants had ever been present on Italian territory and supplied identity photographs of the forty persons actually removed, whose names and appearances allegedly did not match. After the parties remained in disagreement, the Court commissioned a facial-comparison expert report from the Belgian Federal Judicial Police’s Biometric Identification Service. Using specialised software and morphological analysis of facial features, the experts assigned the following scores on a –2 to +2 scale: first applicant +2 (strongest support for a common source), second applicant –2 (exclusion), third and fourth applicants +1 (support). No photographs were available for the fifth applicant.

The Government produced the administrative file relating to one removed individual whose photograph received the +2 score. That person had signed an information sheet on 22 August stating he was transiting to Germany, did not wish to return to Sudan and did not wish to apply for international protection. A refusal-of-entry order was issued and served the following day. At the validation hearing before the Justice of the Peace his representative invoked Article 19 of the Immigration Act and prior Court judgments finding that return to Sudan would breach Article 3. The Justice of the Peace nevertheless validated the order, noting the applicant’s stated intention merely to transit and his refusal of protection during an interview conducted with Arabic-speaking cultural mediators. He was removed the next day.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: an asserted failure to assess individual risk of ill-treatment, the simultaneous removal of a large group of Sudanese nationals without individualised examination, the absence of information, legal assistance or suspensive remedies, and the differential treatment of Sudanese migrants under the newly signed memorandum. The case of Minasian and Others v. the Republic of Moldova (App. no. 26879/17) involves four Georgian nationals: Eleonora Minasian (born 1984) and her three children (born 2002, 2009 and 2012). The family had been lawfully present in Moldova, claiming to have fled persecution in Georgia. On 16 February 2017 they illegally crossed into Romania, were detained by Romanian border police and returned to Moldova. Minasian’s husband was separately placed in pre-trial detention and is not an applicant.

On 17 February 2017 the Bureau for Migration and Asylum (BMA) ordered Minasian’s return to Ukraine solely on account of the illegal crossing; the children were not mentioned. The same day the BMA asked a court to place Minasian in public custody “accompanied by” the three minors, observing that they would otherwise be unaccompanied. The Chișinău District Court granted the request, citing the unenforced expulsion order and (repealed) Article 64(4) of Law No. 200 on Foreigners. It thereby authorised the detention of Minasian together with her children.

Minasian’s lawyer appealed, arguing that she had not been given a lawyer within three hours of deprivation of liberty, that the children were left legally defenceless (violating equality of arms), and that Article 64(1) of Law No. 200 permits detention of minors and families with minors only as a last resort and for the shortest possible time. On 20 March 2017 the Court of Appeal reduced the period from 90 to 60 days. It accepted that detention was necessary because of a risk of absconding, lack of means and refusal to leave voluntarily, but acknowledged the last-resort rule. It nevertheless confirmed the joint detention of mother and children and relied also on Article 40 of the Contraventions Code.

The family was held in the Centre for Temporary Placement of Foreigners (CTPF). On 28 March Minasian applied for asylum. Her lawyer sought transfer to the asylum-seekers’ centre, stressing the last-resort requirement and the children’s need for social interaction, outdoor activity and recreation unavailable at the CTPF. The BMA confirmed that the asylum claim was under consideration but did not release them. On 13 April Minasian was convicted of illegal border-crossing (later acquitted) and fined. The BMA obtained a further 30-day extension of her detention “accompanied by” the children, citing the pending criminal case and asylum request. Release was again refused. The family was freed on 11 May 2017; the asylum claim was rejected in September 2017 and they left Moldova in March 2018.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1 and 4. The children were never the subject of any independent expulsion or detention decision; they were detained solely because they accompanied their mother. Domestic courts never examined whether their detention was a measure of last resort or whether the CTPF was suitable for families with minors, despite the explicit statutory requirement. Article 64(4), relied upon by the first-instance court, had already been repealed. The principle of personal responsibility under both the Criminal Code and the Contraventions Code further underscores that the children could not be held liable for their mother’s conduct. Being minors, the children themselves had no opportunity to institute proceedings capable of reviewing the lawfulness of their own detention. A later Ombudsman visit (2020) recorded that the CTPF lacked psychologists, social workers and medical staff, confirming the unsuitability of the facility.

The case of *Minasian and Others v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 26879/17) concerned four Georgian nationals: Eleonora Minasian (born 1984) and her three minor children (born 2002, 2009 and 2012). The mother’s husband was placed in pre-trial detention and was not an applicant.

On 17 February 2017 the Bureau for Migration and Asylum (BMA) ordered the mother’s return to Ukraine for the illegal crossing; the children were not mentioned. The same day the BMA asked a court to place the mother in public custody “accompanied by” the three named minors, noting that they would otherwise be unaccompanied. The Chișinău District Court granted the request, citing an unenforced expulsion order and Article 64(4) of Law No. 200 on Foreigners (a provision already repealed in December 2016 and therefore not in force). The mother and children were detained together in the Centre for Temporary Placement of Foreigners (CTPF).

The mother appealed, arguing that she had been denied a lawyer within three hours of detention and that the children had been left legally defenceless, contrary to equality of arms and Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention. On 20 March 2017 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld the necessity of detention because of the illegal crossing, the mother’s lack of means, her failure to contest expulsion and a risk of absconding. It nevertheless recognised that detention of minors and families is permitted only as a last resort and for the shortest possible time, and reduced the period from 90 to 60 days. The court also invoked Article 40 of the Contraventions Code, which allows detention of foreigners subject to expulsion.

After the family was placed in the CTPF the mother requested asylum on 28 March 2017. Her lawyer sought release to an asylum-seekers’ centre, stressing the children’s need for social interaction and the last-resort rule. The BMA confirmed the asylum application was pending but did not release them. On 13 April the mother was convicted of illegal border-crossing and fined (later acquitted by the Supreme Court in 2018). The same day the BMA obtained a 30-day extension of detention, which the mother supported; the court cited the pending criminal case and asylum claim. Release was again refused on 5 May. The family was freed on 11 May 2017. Asylum was refused in September 2017 and they left Moldova in March 2018.

An Ombudsman visit later recorded that the CTPF lacked psychologists, social workers and medical staff. Domestic law (Article 64 of Law No. 200) permitted detention of foreigners for illegal entry or risk of absconding but expressly limited detention of minors and families to a last-resort, shortest-period measure. Both the Criminal Code and the Contraventions Code embodied the principle of personal responsibility. The children’s detention therefore lacked any independent legal basis, the courts never examined whether it was a last resort or whether the CTPF was suitable for families, and the children themselves had no procedural means to challenge the lawfulness of their detention.
