001-222143:
The European Court of Human Rights examined the application of Anita Potoczká and Branislav Adamčo (partners living together at the relevant time) concerning a 2004 telephone-tapping warrant issued in criminal proceedings against the second applicant for suspected extortion as part of a criminal enterprise. On 11 May 2004 proceedings opened against unknown persons. On 27 May 2004 the Bratislava Regional Court issued a warrant under Article 88 of the 1961 Code of Criminal Procedure, following a 25 May 2004 request from the Public Prosecution Service. The warrant authorised tapping of a mobile line subscribed in the first applicant’s name (but used by the second applicant) from 27 May to 27 November 2004. It contained no reasoning beyond a statement that other means of obtaining evidence were ineffective or impossible, and the written version in the file lacked the court’s official seal and the issuing judge’s signature (showing only a typed name).

The warrant was implemented throughout its validity. A 26 October 2005 police file note recorded that transcripts of eight conversations (to which the second applicant was a party) had been prepared and stored on disc; there was no allegation that the first applicant was involved in or the subject of those conversations. On 28 December 2005 the second applicant was charged, with the indictment relying inter alia on the tapping results and identifying both the warrant and the line. He inspected the investigation file in January 2008 (seeing the transcripts in a confidential enclosure; it is disputed whether the warrant itself was included) and again on 3 September 2013 (when he was shown the warrant but not permitted to copy it). A first indictment filed in February 2008 was rejected in July 2008 for unrelated procedural errors and the case remitted. A 15 October 2015 prosecution letter later confirmed that the warrant had not been submitted with the 2008 indictment because its lack of reasoning was viewed as an obstacle to lawfulness. A fresh indictment of 13 February 2016 again relied on the tapping material. On 12 April 2018 the Michalovce District Court terminated the proceedings on the ground of excessive length, without addressing the warrant.

On 31 October 2013 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 127 of the Constitution, alleging violations of their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The first applicant stated she learned of the tapping on 20 September 2013. The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 23 June 2015 (served 31 July 2015, with no appeal). It held that the first applicant had suffered no interference because the line was used by the second applicant and she had not even claimed otherwise. As regards the second applicant, it found that any violation had occurred at the pre-trial stage and could be raised at trial, so the subsidiarity principle excluded its jurisdiction; it also noted in passing that the complaint might be out of time if he had seen the warrant in 2008.

Domestic law required a written judicial warrant, issued on a prosecution request, specifying the person and a period not exceeding six months, and supported by reasoning. Constitutional Court case-law emphasised that warrants authorising serious interferences with privacy must contain concrete reasoning because the persons concerned normally learn of the measure only after the event and have no direct remedy; ordinary courts are bound by a final warrant and cannot review its justification in, for example, personal-integrity actions. The Constitutional Court had previously reviewed and quashed unreasoned warrants where no other remedy existed, but here it declined jurisdiction on the basis that the matter could be examined at trial.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 8 (the warrant authorising tapping of private correspondence was not in accordance with domestic law owing to the absence of reasoning and formal defects) and of Article 13 taken with Article 8 (no effective remedy, given the Constitutional Court’s refusal to examine the warrant on the merits and the inability of ordinary courts to review its lawfulness independently of any later trial use of the evidence). The first applicant’s standing was also in issue, as subscriber to the line she claimed to have used.

The case of Potoczká and Adamčo v. Slovakia concerns a 2004 court-authorised telephone tap in criminal proceedings against the second applicant, Branislav Adamčo. The first applicant, Anita Potoczká, was the named subscriber of the mobile line, which the authorities said Adamčo used. The couple had been partners since 1999, lived together and had a son. The tap was authorised by the Bratislava Regional Court on 27 May 2004 under Article 88 of the 1961 Code of Criminal Procedure, following a public prosecutor’s request of 25 May 2004, and was valid until 27 November 2004.

The warrant itself (never produced in full to the Strasbourg Court) identified Potoczká as the subscriber and Adamčo as the user. It contained no reasoning beyond a formulaic statement that other investigative means were ineffective or impossible. The written version in the file bore neither the court’s official seal nor the issuing judge’s signature, only the judge’s typed name.

Police implemented the warrant throughout its validity. A 26 October 2005 file note recorded that eight conversations between June and September 2005 had been transcribed and stored on disc; Adamčo was a party to them, and none involved or concerned Potoczká. The transcripts later formed part of the charges brought against Adamčo on 28 December 2005 for extortion as a member of a criminal enterprise.

Adamčo first inspected the investigation file (including the transcripts) in January 2008. A 2008 indictment that relied on the tap was rejected for unrelated procedural errors and the case returned to investigation. In September 2013 Adamčo was shown the warrant itself (but not allowed to copy it). Potoczká learned of the tap during a prison visit later that month. The applicants then complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging that the warrant’s lack of reasoning and formal identifiers violated their rights under Article 8 (and Article 6) of the Convention.

The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 23 June 2015. It held that Potoczká had no standing because the line was used solely by Adamčo and she had not even claimed personal use. As regards Adamčo, it applied the subsidiarity principle: any challenge to the warrant could be raised at trial, so the Constitutional Court lacked jurisdiction. It also noted, as an aside, that he might already have seen the warrant in 2008, rendering the complaint out of time. The decision contained no examination of the warrant’s lawfulness.

A fresh indictment filed in 2016 again relied on the tap. Criminal proceedings were eventually terminated in 2018 solely on grounds of excessive length; the warrant was not addressed. A 2015 letter from the public prosecutor confirmed that the warrant had been withheld from the 2008 indictment precisely because its lack of reasoning was then regarded as rendering the tap unlawful.

The applicants’ core complaints before the European Court therefore centred on (i) an interference with private life and correspondence that was not “in accordance with the law” because the warrant failed to meet the domestic statutory requirements of reasoning and proper authentication, and (ii) the absence of any effective domestic remedy capable of reviewing that deficiency. The first applicant’s standing was also in issue, given the authorities’ assertion that she had never used the line.

The case of Potoczká and Adamčo v. Slovakia concerns a 2004 court-authorised telephone tap in criminal proceedings against the second applicant (Branislav Adamčo), on a mobile line subscribed in the name of the first applicant (Anita Potoczká, his partner). The pair had lived together since 1999 and had a son. The tap was authorised by a Bratislava Regional Court warrant of 27 May 2004 (valid until 27 November 2004), issued under Article 88 of the 1961 Code of Criminal Procedure on a Public Prosecution Service request. The warrant stated that the line was subscribed to the first applicant but used by the second; it contained virtually no reasoning beyond a formulaic assertion that other means of obtaining evidence would be ineffective or impossible. The written version lacked an official court seal and the issuing judge’s signature (only a typed name appeared).

The warrant was implemented in full. A police file note of 26 October 2005 recorded that eight conversations (to which the second applicant was a party) had been transcribed and stored. On 28 December 2005 the second applicant was charged with extortion as a member of a criminal enterprise; the charges expressly relied on the tap. He inspected the investigation file in January 2008 (seeing the transcripts) and again on 3 September 2013 (when he was shown but not allowed to copy the warrant). A first indictment of February 2008 was rejected for unrelated procedural defects and the case remitted. A 2015 prosecution letter later confirmed that the warrant itself had been withheld from the 2008 indictment precisely because it lacked reasoning, then regarded as fatal to lawfulness. A fresh indictment of February 2016 again relied on the tap material. The Michalovce District Court terminated the entire criminal proceedings on 12 April 2018 solely for breach of the reasonable-time requirement; it made no finding on the warrant.

On 31 October 2013 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that the warrant violated Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The first applicant said she had also used the line and learned of the tap only in September 2013. The Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible on 23 June 2015. It held that the first applicant had suffered no interference (the police note stated the line was used by the second applicant and she had not claimed otherwise). As to the second applicant it applied the subsidiarity principle: any defect could be raised at trial. It added, in passing, that he might already have seen the warrant in 2008, rendering the complaint out of time. The decision contained no examination of the warrant’s formal or substantive defects.

Domestic law required a written judicial warrant supported by reasoning that identified the target and the (maximum six-month) period. Constitutional Court case-law established that there is no ordinary-court remedy against a final tapping warrant itself; review is possible only if the product is later tendered as evidence at trial (or, exceptionally, by the Constitutional Court when no other forum exists). In the present case the criminal courts never examined the warrant and the Constitutional Court declined jurisdiction, leaving the applicants without a forum in which to challenge the absence of reasoning or the missing formalities. These facts form the core of the alleged Article 8 violation (interference not “in accordance with the law”) and the connected Article 13 complaint (lack of an effective remedy).
001-229130:
The case of Drago Tadić v. Croatia concerns the applicant’s conviction for conspiring to influence the Croatian Supreme Court, by means of payment, to alter an unfavourable appellate decision in a high-profile war-crimes case against politician B.G. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court (acting as appellate court) lacked objective impartiality under Article 6 § 1 because its president, B.H., had given prosecution testimony about his own alleged role and that a media campaign had also breached his rights to a fair hearing and the presumption of innocence under Articles 6 §§ 1 and 2.

In 2009 B.G. was convicted at first instance and sentenced to ten years. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in June 2010 but reduced the sentence to eight years. The Security Intelligence Agency (SIA) thereafter intercepted the applicant’s telephone conversations (4–20 July 2010) after learning that he and others knew of the decision and were seeking to have the court’s Records Service remit the case to the panel. Those particular recordings were never placed in the criminal file.

An investigating judge authorised further special measures. In March 2011 President B.H. told investigators that, after a 14 July lunch, the applicant had privately raised the B.G. case, claimed knowledge of the decision and of possible remittal, and suggested assignment of the file to a specific judge (A.P.) in the Records Service. B.H. reported the conversation to the State Attorney General the next morning.

The applicant was indicted in July 2011 for conspiracy and illegal intercession. Co-accused entered plea bargains; the trial proceeded against him alone. The Zagreb County Court heard thirty witnesses (including B.H. and the former co-accused), played later lawful surveillance recordings, and examined photographs and videos. B.H. testified that he had asked the head of the Records Service to re-assign the file to Judge A.P. simply to avoid criticism that an adviser rather than a judge would review a sensitive case; A.P. ultimately declined. The court refused the applicant’s request to call that head of service, holding the matter irrelevant. On 27 February 2013 it convicted the applicant and imposed a two-year sentence, relying principally on the undisputed later recordings (which showed coded language, money-raising and attempts to contact judges and officials) and on those parts of witness testimony consistent with them. Differences between the applicant’s and B.H.’s accounts of their conversation were treated as immaterial because it was common ground that the applicant had initiated discussion of the B.G. case.

The applicant appealed, asserting that B.H.’s testimony was the sole incriminating evidence, was internally contradictory (B.H. had himself later assigned the file to A.P.), and served to conceal B.H.’s own involvement. He again complained of the refused witness.

While the appeal was pending, a newspaper published an article (11 December 2016) reproducing the unused July 2010 SIA recordings. The article suggested the lunch had been pre-arranged, quoted post-lunch conversations implying B.H. had promised assistance, and named serving judges and officials. The recordings themselves remained outside the case file.

On 7 February 2017 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the trial court’s factual and legal findings. It held that B.H.’s alleged conduct was not in issue, that the conversation’s initiation by the applicant was undisputed, and that remittal by the Records Service was possible in practice. The court made no reference to the newspaper article. The Constitutional Court later rejected the applicant’s complaints of institutional bias and media influence, stressing that conviction rested on a substantial body of lawful evidence, that B.H.’s actions were extraneous, and that there was no indication the experienced appellate judges had been affected by the publication.

(The ECtHR subsequently found neither complaint well-founded.)

The case of Drago Tadić v. Croatia concerns criminal proceedings in which the applicant, a businessman, was convicted of conspiring with others to influence the Croatian Supreme Court (by paying money) to reverse or alter an unfavourable appellate decision in a war-crimes case against well-known politician B.G. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to an independent and impartial tribunal) because the Supreme Court’s president, B.H., had allegedly been involved in the underlying events and later testified as a prosecution witness in the applicant’s trial. He further alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 (fair hearing and presumption of innocence) arising from the media publication, during the appeal, of unused intelligence recordings of his telephone conversations.

Co-accused later pleaded guilty pursuant to agreements; the trial proceeded against the applicant alone.

He unsuccessfully sought to call the Records-Service head, Judge S.B.K., to clarify B.H.’s reassignment request. On 27 February 2013 the County Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment, relying principally on the undisputed authorised recordings and on those portions of witness testimony consistent with them. It found that the applicant had orchestrated efforts to locate intermediaries who could influence Supreme Court judges and Records-Service staff, had borrowed €50 000 for that purpose, and had spoken in code while later attempting to destroy evidence.

Both the applicant and the prosecution appealed to the Supreme Court. While the appeals were pending, on 11 December 2016 a national newspaper published an article entitled “How the SIA discovered the infiltration of the Supreme Court.” The article reproduced transcripts of the unused July 2010 SIA recordings (still available on the newspaper’s website). Those transcripts suggested the lunch with B.H. had been pre-arranged, that the applicant believed B.H. had promised to intervene, and that various sitting judges and politicians had been mentioned. The article noted that B.H.’s trial testimony appeared to contradict the recordings.

On 7 February 2017 a three-judge Supreme Court panel (assigned automatically under the Court’s annual work schedule) dismissed both appeals and upheld the conviction and sentence. It did not mention the newspaper article or the unused recordings. It held that B.H.’s credibility was irrelevant because it was undisputed that the applicant had initiated the conversation about B.G.’s case and the Records Service; Judge S.B.K.’s evidence was likewise unnecessary. The panel emphasised that the offence displayed disrespect for the highest court and Croatia’s value system.

In constitutional complaints the applicant argued that the Supreme Court lacked objective impartiality because its president had been placed in a position of having to defend himself against public suspicion of involvement and because the Court had erected an “institutional self-protecting shield.” He also claimed the media publication, eight weeks before the Supreme Court decision, constituted a State-sponsored campaign that contaminated the appellate judges and violated the presumption of innocence. On 13 March 2018 the Constitutional Court rejected both complaints. It found B.H.’s testimony neither sole nor decisive (the conviction rested on a large body of lawful recordings) and discerned no link between the article and the Supreme Court’s reasoning.

The applicant later brought a still-pending civil action against the newspaper publisher for violation of personality rights and filed a criminal complaint against journalists and unidentified SIA and prosecutorial officials for leaking the unused recordings. In 2015 the Constitutional Court had separately quashed B.G.’s original conviction; on remittal B.G. was resentenced in 2023 to seven years.

The case concerns the conviction of Croatian businessman Drago Tadić for conspiring (with others) to influence Croatia’s Supreme Court, via payments, to issue a favourable ruling in war-crime proceedings against politician B.G.

In May 2009 a first-instance court convicted B.G. and sentenced him to ten years. On 2 June 2010 the Supreme Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to eight years. The Security Intelligence Agency (SOA) then learned that Tadić and associates had become aware of the (still-unpublished) decision and were taking steps to have it altered. SOA therefore tapped their telephones between 4 and 20 July 2010. Those recordings never formed part of the subsequent criminal file.

On 20 July 2010 a judge authorised official special investigative measures (further tapping and covert surveillance) against Tadić and others. On the basis of the resulting material an indictment was issued in 2011 charging Tadić with conspiracy and instigating illegal intercession. Co-accused pleaded guilty; Tadić denied the charges, claiming he had merely gathered information for a journalist friend of B.G.

At the 2012–13 trial before Zagreb County Court the official recordings were played and thirty witnesses were heard, including Supreme Court President B.H. B.H. testified that, after a lunch on 14 July 2010, Tadić had privately asked him about the B.G. case, indicated knowledge of the already-adopted decision, and suggested that it be assigned in the Records Service to Judge A.P. (who might remit it to the panel). B.H. reported the conversation the next morning. He later asked that A.P. examine the decision “to avoid criticism”, but A.P. declined. Tadić’s version was that he had merely asked how the Records Service worked and that B.H. himself had mentioned A.P. The court refused Tadić’s request to hear Records Service head S.B.K., deeming her evidence irrelevant.

On 27 February 2013 Tadić was convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. The court found that he had organised contacts with judges, politicians and the Records Service, borrowed €50 000 for the purpose, and spoken in code; the plan was aborted only when the group suspected surveillance. Conviction rested principally on the undisputed official recordings, corroborated by other evidence. Differences between Tadić’s and B.H.’s accounts of the 14 July conversation were held immaterial because both agreed the discussion of the B.G. case had been initiated by Tadić.

Appeals were lodged with the Supreme Court. On 11 December 2016, while they were pending, a newspaper published an article reproducing the unused SOA recordings. The article claimed the recordings showed a pre-arranged meeting with B.H., contradicted B.H.’s testimony, and named serving judges and officials. The audio remained available online.

On 7 February 2017 the Supreme Court dismissed both appeals and upheld the conviction and sentence. It did not mention the article. It accepted that the Records Service could remit cases, found S.B.K.’s evidence irrelevant, and treated the credibility of B.H.’s testimony as outside the indictment because the conversation itself was undisputed.

Tadić’s constitutional complaints (lack of impartiality of the Supreme Court because of B.H.’s role and testimony; media pressure violating fairness and the presumption of innocence) were dismissed on 13 March 2018. The Constitutional Court emphasised that conviction rested on a large body of lawful evidence, that B.H.’s alleged conduct was not in issue, and that no link existed between the article and the Supreme Court’s decision.

Tadić also instituted (still-pending) civil and criminal proceedings concerning the leak of the SOA recordings.

These facts underpin the two Article 6 complaints later examined by the European Court: (i) objective impartiality of the Supreme Court given B.H.’s alleged involvement and his appearance as a prosecution witness, and (ii) whether publication of unused recordings eight weeks before the Supreme Court’s ruling exerted undue pressure or breached the presumption of innocence.
001-222409:
The case of Khural and Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) concerns the civil liability imposed on the newspaper Khural and its editor-in-chief Avaz Zeynalov for defamation of Vugar Safarli, executive director of the State Fund for Support of the Media. It arose under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression).

In July 2010 the Press Council and State Media Support Fund commemorated the 135th anniversary of Azerbaijan’s national media by awarding 20,000 AZN (approximately EUR 20,000) to selected journalists and newspapers. Khural was neither invited nor among the recipients. Shortly afterwards Khural published two articles written by Zeynalov. The first, entitled “Isn’t Ilham Aliyev the President of Khural?!”, criticised the awards as discriminatory against independent media. It described Safarli as a “press butcher” heading a “press shop”, accused the organisers of “press dishonour”, “press immorality” and “press rascality”, and likened their conduct to mafia rules. The second article listed the laureates and questioned the independence of most of them, noting that many were state-financed or linked to government officials.

Safarli sued Khural, claiming the statements were false, insulting and damaging to his honour, dignity and reputation. He sought an apology, retraction and 10,000 AZN in non-pecuniary damages. The applicants argued that the language consisted of value judgments possessing a sufficient factual basis: Khural had never received state support, the awards had favoured government-linked or poorly selling outlets, and the newspaper was performing its public-watchdog function on a matter of high public interest. They requested the court to obtain the list of laureates, but this request was not granted.

On 12 October 2010 the Narimanov District Court held four specific expressions to be false and slanderous. It ordered Zeynalov to issue an apology and retraction and Khural to pay 500 AZN in damages, taking into account the newspaper’s financial situation. The court did not examine the remainder of the first article or any part of the second. On 7 February 2011 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the findings but increased the damages to 5,000 AZN. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 17 June 2011, repeating the lower courts’ reasoning.

The applicants neither apologised nor paid. On 19 October 2011 the District Court ordered the seizure of Khural’s assets (computers, printers, etc.). Print publication ceased, although the online edition continued. Non-compliance later formed one ground for Zeynalov’s 2013 criminal conviction for failure to execute a court judgment.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 10. The domestic courts had not applied standards consistent with the Convention, had failed to assess the relevant facts acceptably, had not struck a fair balance between the competing interests, and had given no relevant and sufficient reasons for the interference.

The ECtHR case of Khural and Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) (Application no. 383/12) concerned the civil defamation liability imposed on the Azerbaijani newspaper Khural and its founder and editor-in-chief Avaz Zeynalov for articles criticising Vugar Safarli (V.S.), executive director of the State Media Support Fund. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression).

In July 2010 the Press Council and the State Media Support Fund organised an event marking the 135th anniversary of the national media. Financial awards of 20,000 AZN (approximately EUR 20,000) were distributed to selected journalists and newspapers. Khural was neither invited nor among the recipients.

Shortly afterwards, the 25–31 July 2010 edition of Khural published two articles authored by Zeynalov. The first, entitled “Isn’t Ilham Aliyev the President of Khural?!”, accused the Fund of discrimination against independent outlets lacking political or official connections. It described V.S. as a “press butcher” running a “press shop”, acting according to “mafia rules” and managing the press “like the mafia”. The awards process was labelled “press dishonour”, “press immorality” and “press rascality”. The second article listed recipient newspapers, asserting that most were state-funded, government-linked or otherwise non-independent, and questioned why they received additional public money.

V.S. brought a civil action against Khural, claiming the expressions were false, insulting and damaging to his honour, dignity and reputation. He sought an apology, retraction and 10,000 AZN in non-pecuniary damages. The applicants maintained that the statements were value judgments protected by Article 10, grounded in the newspaper’s independent status, its exclusion from support, and the alleged political bias of the awards. They requested the court to obtain and examine the list of laureates, but this was not done.

On 12 October 2010 the Narimanov District Court found four specific phrases (the “press butcher” characterisations, the mafia comparison, and the “press dishonour/immorality/rascality” labels) to be false and slanderous. It ordered Zeynalov to issue an apology and retraction and Khural to pay 500 AZN in damages. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the finding on 7 February 2011 but increased the award to 5,000 AZN, citing the newspaper’s financial situation. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 17 June 2011, repeating the lower courts’ reasoning.

The applicants neither published an apology nor paid the damages. On 19 October 2011 the District Court ordered seizure of Khural’s assets (computers, printers and other equipment) to enforce payment. Print publication of Khural thereafter ceased, although its online version continued. Zeynalov’s non-compliance later formed one ground for his 2013 criminal conviction under Article 306.2 of the Criminal Code.

The ECtHR held that the domestic courts had failed to apply standards consistent with Article 10. They did not distinguish between statements of fact and value judgments, did not assess the factual basis of the criticism or the public-interest nature of debate about state media funding, and provided no relevant and sufficient reasons. Consequently they struck no fair balance between V.S.’s reputation and the applicants’ freedom of expression as a public watchdog. A violation of Article 10 was therefore found.

The case of Khural and Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) (Application no. 383/12) concerned a complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the civil liability imposed on a newspaper and its editor-in-chief for alleged defamation. Khural, a Baku-based newspaper with legal personality, and Avaz Zeynalov, its founder and editor-in-chief, challenged domestic court findings that articles published in the newspaper in July 2010 constituted slanderous defamation of Vugar Safarli (V.S.), executive director of the State Media Support Fund under the President of Azerbaijan.

In July 2010, the Press Council and the State Media Support Fund organized an event marking the 135th anniversary of the national media, at which various journalists and newspapers received awards of 20,000 Azerbaijani manats (AZN) each. Khural and Zeynalov were not among the recipients. Shortly thereafter, the 25–31 July 2010 edition of Khural published two articles authored or overseen by Zeynalov. The first, titled “Isn’t Ilham Aliyev the President of Khural?!”, criticized the awards process as discriminatory against independent media outlets lacking political or governmental connections. It used vivid, critical language, describing V.S. as a “press butcher” heading a “press shop,” alleging that he and others managed the press like a “mafia,” and labeling the event and its organizers as examples of “press dishonour,” “press immorality,” and “press rascality.” It claimed awards went to poorly selling or government-linked newspapers while excluding more successful independent ones like Khural, which had never received state support. A second article, “Real disgrace in [the field of the] press!!!,” listed numerous award recipients, questioning their independence and linking many to government officials, including V.S. himself (as owner of one newspaper) or figures such as Ali Hasanov.

V.S. initiated civil defamation proceedings against Khural in the Narimanov District Court, arguing that the first article (and others in the edition) contained false, insulting expressions harming his honour, dignity, and reputation. He sought an apology, retraction, and AZN 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages. The applicants contended that the statements were value judgments, not susceptible of proof, but grounded in facts: Khural’s independence and lack of prior support, and alleged discriminatory distribution of awards to less meritorious or loyal outlets. They requested the court to obtain and examine the list of award laureates, but this was not addressed.

On 12 October 2010, the District Court partially upheld the claim, deeming four specific expressions from the first article (“press butcher,” related “butcher Vugar” references, mafia comparisons, and “press dishonour/immorality/rascality”) as false and slanderous. It ordered Zeynalov to apologize and retract them, and Khural to pay AZN 500 in damages, considering the newspaper’s financial situation. The court did not assess the articles’ remaining content or public-interest aspects. The Baku Court of Appeal, on 7 February 2011, upheld the findings but increased damages to AZN 5,000. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 17 June 2011, repeating the lower courts’ reasoning.

The applicants did not comply. Assets of Khural (computers, printers, etc.) were seized in October 2011, leading to cessation of print publication (though the online version continued). Non-compliance later contributed to Zeynalov’s 2013 criminal conviction for failing to obey a court judgment.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 10. Domestic courts failed to apply Convention-compliant standards, did not adequately distinguish facts from value judgments or assess the articles’ factual basis and contribution to debate on a matter of public interest (state media funding and alleged discrimination), and provided no relevant and sufficient reasons. They thus failed to strike a fair balance between V.S.’s reputation and the applicants’ freedom of expression, particularly given the newspaper’s watchdog role. The interference was not necessary in a democratic society.
001-222408:
The case of Zayidov v. Azerbaijan (No. 3) involves journalist Ganimat Zayidov, editor of the pro-opposition newspaper Azadlig and a member of the Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan (PFPA). He alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention, claiming his 2008 conviction for hooliganism and deliberate infliction of moderate harm to health was based on unreliable, fabricated evidence that he could not effectively challenge, with courts failing to investigate his allegations or provide reasoned judgments.

On 7 November 2007, Zayidov approached the Azerbaijan publishing house (where Azadlig had offices). An unknown woman, S.Q., accused him of insulting her. A man, V.H., then joined and physically attacked him, tearing his jacket; Zayidov pushed back, causing V.H. to fall. Bystanders separated them, and the pair left. Zayidov publicly alleged the incident was an authority-orchestrated setup to punish his critical reporting, citing prior attacks on Azadlig staff and politically motivated cases against his brother.

V.H. claimed an unknown man insulted and beat him after he approached S.Q. He received hospital treatment for a nosebleed, facial puffiness, a lip laceration, eardrum hemorrhage, concussion, closed brain injury, and an incomplete right cheekbone fracture (detected via 9 November X-ray, absent on 7 November). These were classified as moderate harm to health (long-term effects). V.H. filed a complaint that day; proceedings began under Article 221.1 (hooliganism) of the Criminal Code, later adding Article 127.2.3 (moderate harm). V.H. identified Zayidov from a newspaper photo.

Investigation included witness statements (S.Q. and two partial eyewitnesses, A.I. and V.R., who described Zayidov punching V.H., causing bleeding), identification parades confirming Zayidov, and medical exams. Expert report 1024 (circa 9-11 November) noted bruises and relied on hospital records for the fracture and moderate harm. Zayidov disputed this, as no independent X-ray was done. A follow-up request for visual exam of V.H. was granted then aborted after V.H. refused. New report 205/2007 (23 November) by three experts found fading injuries (a 3mm lip scar, no visible bruises) but classified the cheekbone bruise and fracture as moderate harm, again relying on the 9 November X-ray (V.H. refused a new one). Zayidov called the reports forged, noting the bruise vanished by 21 November (contradicting 21-day guidelines for moderate harm) and requesting a CT scan or X-ray of V.H., plus production of the original image—which later vanished from the file. Clothes exams confirmed V.H.'s blood. Zayidov had only minor bruises.

Charged on 11 November and detained, Zayidov (and V.H., also charged with hooliganism) went to trial. He argued fabrication: V.H. (ex-police, 2000-2004; former PFPA member who met Zayidov seeking poem publication, later expelled as a suspected spy) and S.Q. (criminal record, later confirmed wanted then arrested) had official leverage; eyewitnesses (one, I.T., later claimed coercion via ill-treatment) were planted. He requested background probes, defence witnesses on V.H./S.Q. ties and crimes, full phone records (1-30 November) of V.H., S.Q., investigator, and police chief, plus doctor F.Z.'s testimony and X-ray review. The court confirmed V.H.'s police history, heard three witnesses on PFPA links, and limited phone checks (no mutual calls found, 1-7 November only). Other requests were refused as irrelevant, without reasons. V.R. did not appear (claiming illness; no confirmation), so his pre-trial statement was used. I.T. testified similarly.

On 7 March 2008, the Yasamal District Court convicted Zayidov to four years' imprisonment, relying on reports 205/2007, 196, 1026, and 206/2007 plus testimonies (V.H., S.Q., A.I., I.T., police, V.H.'s relatives/friends). V.H. received six months. Appeals reiterated challenges (missing X-ray, unexamined fracture, faded injuries, unprobed fabrication). The Court of Appeal (13 May 2008) reviewed only existing files, without new evidence or witnesses, upholding the verdict. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal (26 August 2008). Zayidov was pardoned in 2010.

These facts highlight the alleged unfairness: inability to test key medical/witness evidence or adduce counter-evidence, plus unreasoned refusals and uninvestigated claims of political framing.

The applicant, Ganimat Zayidov, a prominent Azerbaijani journalist, opposition party member and editor of the critical newspaper Azadlig, alleged that his 2008 criminal conviction violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. He claimed he had been framed by the authorities in retaliation for his reporting, convicted on unreliable and fabricated evidence (particularly medical reports and witness statements), denied an effective opportunity to challenge that evidence or adduce favourable evidence, and deprived of a reasoned judgment.

On 7 November 2007, Zayidov was involved in a brief physical altercation outside the Azerbaijan publishing house. According to him, an unknown woman (S.Q.) began shouting accusations and swearing at him; a man (V.H.) then attacked him, tearing his jacket. Zayidov pushed V.H. to the ground in self-defence; bystanders separated them and the pair fled. Zayidov immediately told the press the incident was a staged attack to punish his journalism.

V.H. instead complained to police that an unknown man had insulted S.Q., then slapped, head-butted and punched him, causing bleeding. He identified Zayidov the next day from a newspaper photograph. Both V.H. and S.Q. repeated this account. Two passing motorists (A.I. and V.R.) described seeing a tall, thin, bespectacled older man punch a suited man to the ground. Identification parades confirmed Zayidov as that man. V.H. received hospital treatment; reports recorded facial bruising, a lip injury, eardrum haemorrhage, concussion and (on a 9 November X-ray) an incomplete right-cheekbone fracture. Forensic experts classified the fracture and associated bruise as causing “moderate harm to health” (long-term effects of 21 days or more). Zayidov himself had only minor bruises. Blood matching V.H.’s type was found on his clothes.

Zayidov was charged with hooliganism and deliberate infliction of moderate harm; V.H. was also charged with hooliganism. Throughout the investigation and trial Zayidov maintained he had inflicted no injuries, that the X-ray was forged or belonged to someone else, and that the entire case was fabricated. He pointed to V.H.’s prior PFPA membership, earlier attempts to publish poetry in Azadlig, previous police service and unserved convictions, as well as S.Q.’s criminal record, as evidence the pair had been induced to cooperate. He requested: (i) a fresh X-ray or CT scan of V.H. (refused because V.H. objected); (ii) production and examination of the missing original 9 November X-ray (never produced; it later vanished from the file); (iii) testimony from the treating doctor F.Z.; (iv) a full visual medical examination of V.H. (V.H. refused); (v) defence witnesses on V.H.’s and S.Q.’s backgrounds and possible coercion; (vi) telephone records linking the complainants to investigators; and (vii) consideration of an audio-recorded recantation by a later eyewitness (I.T.) who claimed he had been ill-treated into giving false evidence. The investigator and trial court granted only a few requests (some background witnesses who confirmed V.H.’s earlier party ties, and a narrowly framed telephone check that yielded nothing). Most were refused without reasons or dismissed as “irrelevant.”

At trial the Yasamal District Court heard Zayidov, V.H., S.Q., A.I., I.T. and several police and medical witnesses, but relied on V.R.’s unread pre-trial statement after he failed to appear. It convicted Zayidov of both offences (four years’ imprisonment) solely on the contested expert reports and the prosecution witnesses. The Court of Appeal examined the case “without judicial investigation” and without new evidence; the Supreme Court likewise dismissed the appeal. Both higher courts failed to address Zayidov’s consistent, detailed allegations of fabrication, the disappearance of the key X-ray, the experts’ reliance on an unexamined image, the classification of a bruise that had vanished within days, or the refused investigative steps.
