The case of *Zayidov v. Azerbaijan (No. 3)* (Application no. 60824/08) concerns Azerbaijani journalist Ganimat Zayidov, editor of the pro-opposition newspaper *Azadlig* and a member of the Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan (PFPA). On 7 November 2007, near the newspaper’s offices, Zayidov alleged that an unknown woman (later identified as S.Q.) accosted him with insults; a man (V.H.) then attacked him physically. Zayidov claimed he pushed V.H. in self-defence, after which bystanders intervened and the pair fled. He immediately publicised the incident as an authority-orchestrated provocation to punish his critical reporting.

V.H. instead filed a police complaint that same day, claiming Zayidov had insulted and beaten him, causing a nosebleed and other injuries. V.H. received inpatient treatment (7–10 November 2007) at the Clinical Medical Centre, whose report recorded facial puffiness, a lip laceration, eardrum haemorrhage, concussion and an “incomplete fracture” of the right cheekbone visible only on a 9 November X-ray (a 7 November X-ray having shown none). Criminal proceedings were opened against Zayidov under Criminal Code Articles 221.1 (hooliganism) and 127.2.3 (deliberate infliction of moderate harm to health). V.H. later identified Zayidov from a newspaper photograph.

The investigation included confrontations, identification parades (two passing motorists, A.I. and V.R., identified Zayidov as the aggressor) and successive forensic examinations of V.H. Report no. 1024 (circa 9–11 November) classified the injuries as “moderate harm” on the basis of the hospital records, without a fresh X-ray. After Zayidov objected, a second panel issued report no. 205/2007 (23 November), again relying on the missing 9 November X-ray (V.H. having refused a new scan) and concluding that the cheekbone bruise and alleged fracture constituted moderate harm (long-term effects) while other injuries were minor. Zayidov’s clothes and person showed only superficial bruises. V.H. was also charged with hooliganism.

At trial before the Yasamal District Court, Zayidov maintained that the entire episode had been fabricated, citing V.H.’s prior PFPA membership, unsuccessful attempt to publish poems in *Azadlig*, former police service, and outstanding criminal sentences, as well as S.Q.’s criminal record (later confirmed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs). He requested that the court: (i) examine V.H. and S.Q.’s backgrounds and telephone records for collusion with investigators; (ii) hear defence witnesses on those connections and on S.Q.’s past; (iii) produce and scrutinise the vanished X-ray; (iv) summon treating physician F.Z.; (v) order a contemporaneous X-ray or CT scan of V.H. (arguing even a healed fracture would leave traces); and (vi) consider an *Azadlig* interview in which another purported eyewitness, I.T., alleged he had been coerced into false testimony. The court granted only limited requests (confirmation of V.H.’s police service; three PFPA witnesses who corroborated prior acquaintance; a narrow telephone-check that yielded no relevant calls). It refused the remainder without reasons or by declaring them “irrelevant.” V.R. did not appear; his pre-trial statement was read out. The X-ray image had disappeared from the file before trial.

On 7 March 2008 Zayidov was convicted and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment, the court relying exclusively on reports 205/2007 and 196 (blood on V.H.’s clothes) plus the contested eyewitness and police testimony. V.H. received a concurrent six-month term. The Court of Appeal examined the case “without judicial investigation,” refused to hear additional evidence, and upheld the conviction on 13 May 2008. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 26 August 2008. Zayidov was pardoned and released in March 2010.

These facts underpin Zayidov’s complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) that he was denied an effective opportunity to challenge the reliability of the decisive medical and witness evidence, to adduce exculpatory material, and to obtain a reasoned judicial response to his serious, consistent allegations of fabrication.
001-222651:
The case of Kutayev v. Russia (Application no. 17912/15) concerns Chechen human rights activist Ruslan Kutayev, a former politician who organised a 18 February 2014 conference in Grozny marking the 70th anniversary of Stalin’s 1944 deportation of the Chechen people. This date clashed with President Ramzan Kadyrov’s official 10 May commemoration. Kutayev refused to attend a 19 February meeting with Kadyrov, who publicly rebuked participants.

On 20 February 2014, according to Kutayev, armed men in unmarked vehicles (linked to Kadyrov’s security) abducted him from a relative’s house in Gekhi. He was taken to an undisclosed site, beaten for 30 minutes by Deputy Interior Minister A.A. and presidential administration official M.D., then subjected to electric shocks in a basement while a knife was held to his throat. Fearing death, he signed unread documents. He was then transferred to a Grozny police station, where he signed further papers. He later described ongoing threats, including of sexual violence against him and his family.

The government claimed officers stopped him on the street for “suspicious behaviour,” searched him, and found 3.257 grams of heroin in his pocket. Formal arrest occurred at 1:30 a.m. on 21 February. In initial interviews (with a state-appointed lawyer), Kutayev confirmed the police version and admitted possession. A reconstruction was staged near the house. On 22 February he was charged and remanded in custody (extended until conviction). Detention records noted bruises; photographs from 24–28 February showed extensive marks consistent with beating and electric shocks. In a 24 February written interview with his own lawyer, Kutayev retracted the confession, detailed the torture, and requested medical help.

An inquiry into alleged abuse of power opened after a 1 March 2014 Novaya Gazeta exposé. Investigator Z. obtained statements from officials denying involvement and from Kutayev’s brothers confirming the abduction and political motive. A 14 March forensic examination noted only a minor abrasion and ignored the electric-shock query. On 2 April the investigator refused to open a criminal case, citing official denials, Kutayev’s initial statements, and his alleged attempt to evade responsibility. Domestic courts upheld this, later noting the conviction itself.

At trial Kutayev retracted his confessions, alleging abduction and torture. Defence witnesses (relatives, NGO lawyer Kalyapin, politicians) corroborated the house arrest, pre-arrest calls expressing fear of persecution over the conference, and visible injuries. Police and attesting witnesses supported the street-search version. M.D. denied knowing Kutayev; A.A. was never called. On 7 July 2014 the Urus-Martan District Court convicted him of large-scale drug possession and sentenced him to four years, relying heavily on the initial confessions, police evidence, and the chemical report. It dismissed political-motive and ill-treatment claims. The Chechen Supreme Court upheld the verdict on 31 October, citing the April refusal to investigate.

Kadyrov’s 25 February television remarks explicitly linked the arrest to the conference. International observers (Amnesty International, Memorial, PACE, European Parliament) described Kutayev as a political prisoner; A.A. and M.D. were later sanctioned under the Magnitsky Act. These facts underpin the alleged violations: torture to extract a confession (Art. 3), ineffective investigation (Art. 3), use of coerced statements rendering the trial unfair (Art. 6 § 1), arbitrary detention lacking legitimate purpose (Art. 5 § 1), and an ulterior political motive of punishing conference organisation and refusal to meet Kadyrov (Art. 18 in conjunction with Art. 5).

**CASE OF KUTAYEV v. RUSSIA (Application no. 17912/15, ECtHR Third Section, 24 January 2023)**

Ruslan Kutayev, a Chechen politician and human rights activist born in 1957, headed the Assembly of Peoples of the Caucasus. He had previously served in the Maskhadov government and criticized Russian military actions in Chechnya. On 18 February 2014 he organized a Grozny conference marking the 70th anniversary of the 1944 Stalin-era deportation of Chechens (deemed genocide by the European Parliament). Approximately 100 participants discussed possible legal action against Russia as USSR successor. Chechen authorities, including President Ramzan Kadyrov, preferred commemoration on the official 10 May “Day of Remembrance.” On 19 February Kutayev refused a summons to meet Kadyrov; other participants were admonished.

Fearing reprisals, Kutayev left Grozny and stayed with relative Mr B. in Gekhi. On 20 February around noon he telephoned contacts, including lawyer I. Kalyapin, expressing fears of persecution over the conference. According to Kutayev, at about 2 p.m. armed men in black camouflage arriving in vehicles with Chechen presidential security plates abducted him from B.’s house, covering his head. At an undisclosed site Deputy Interior Minister A.A. and presidential administration official M.D. beat him for 30 minutes (he fainted repeatedly). In a basement an officer used a knife and electric-shock device for 30–40 minutes, forcing him to sign unread documents. He was then taken to Grozny criminal police department no. 2.

The Government claimed officers stopped him on a Gekhi street for “suspicious behaviour,” searched him in the presence of attesting witnesses, and seized a bag of heroin (3.257 g confirmed by expert report). Arrest was recorded at 1.30 a.m. on 21 February. With a state-appointed lawyer he initially confirmed the official account and was charged with large-scale drug possession. On 24 February, in a written lawyer interview, he described beatings by A.A. and M.D., electric shocks, threats (including sexual violence and against family), and stated the injuries were not from a prior fight. Medical records of 21 February noted bruises; later photographs showed dots and purple marks consistent with electric shocks. A 14 March forensic exam found an abrasion but did not address electric-shock injuries.

Detention on remand was ordered on 22 February and extended until conviction. After a 1 March Novaya Gazeta article, an inquiry was opened but on 2 April 2014 the investigator refused a criminal case, citing official denials, Kutayev’s initial silence, and the forensic report; relatives’ statements were discounted. Courts upheld the refusal.

At trial Kutayev retracted his confession, alleging abduction from B.’s house, torture, and forced statements. B. confirmed the house arrest; brothers, Kalyapin, and politicians testified to pre-arrest calls about conference-related threats. Police and attesting witnesses supported the street-search version. A.A. was not called; M.D. denied involvement. On 7 July 2014 the Urus-Martan District Court convicted him (four years’ imprisonment), relying on the initial confessions, police evidence, and reconstruction. It dismissed political-motive and ill-treatment claims. The Supreme Court of Chechnya upheld this on 31 October 2014, referencing the inquiry refusal. Kadyrov publicly linked the arrest to the conference date. Amnesty International later named Kutayev a prisoner of conscience; A.A. and M.D. were added to the US Magnitsky list.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 (torture to extract a confession; ineffective investigation), Article 6 § 1 (unfair use of the confession without independent review), Article 5 § 1 (arbitrary arrest/detention), and Article 18 (ulterior purpose of punishing the conference and refusal to meet Kadyrov).

**Case summary: Kutayev v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 17912/15)**

Ruslan Kutayev, a Chechen politician and human rights activist born in 1957, organized a conference in Grozny on 18 February 2014 to mark the 70th anniversary of the 1944 Stalin-era deportation of the Chechen people. Around 100 participants discussed the events, including possible international legal action against Russia as USSR successor. Chechen President Ramzan Kadyrov had designated 10 May as the official commemoration date. On 19 February, administration head M.D. summoned conference participants to meet Kadyrov; Kutayev refused to attend. Kadyrov later publicly stated that the conference timing prompted Kutayev’s arrest.

Fearing repercussions, Kutayev left Grozny and stayed with relative B. in Gekhi. On 20 February around noon, he telephoned contacts including lawyer Kalyapin, expressing fears of persecution linked to the conference and his refusal to meet Kadyrov. Around 2 p.m., armed men in black camouflage arrived in vehicles bearing plates associated with the presidential security service. According to Kutayev, they hooded him and took him to an undisclosed location where Deputy Interior Minister A.A. and M.D. beat him for about 30 minutes until he fainted repeatedly. He was then moved to a basement, where an officer used a device resembling a remote control to apply electric shocks for 30–40 minutes while holding a knife to his throat, demanding he sign documents. Fearing death, he signed unread papers at criminal police premises. Police remained nearby except A.A. and M.D.

The Government’s account stated police stopped Kutayev on a Gekhi street around 2 p.m. for an identity check due to “suspicious behaviour.” A search in the presence of attesting witnesses recovered a plastic bag of beige powder (later identified as 3.257 grams of heroin) from his jeans pocket. A site report timed the events slightly later. An arrest record was drawn up at 1.30 a.m. on 21 February. Kutayev, with a State-appointed lawyer, initially confirmed the official version and was charged with large-scale drug possession without intent to sell. Detention on remand was ordered on 22 February and later extended.

On 24 February Kutayev met Kalyapin (with A.A. present) and privately told his own lawyer, via written questions due to surveillance fears, that A.A. and M.D. had beaten him, that he had been given electric shocks in Grozny, that threats (including of sexual violence and harm to family) continued, that he needed medical help, and that he did not confess but had been tortured. He asked that the answers serve as an official complaint. Medical notes from 21 February recorded bruises on his right leg/buttock and left hand (which he then attributed to a fall); later photographs showed additional marks, including dotted lesions consistent with possible shocks. A March forensic exam noted only a minor abrasion and did not address electric-shock injuries.

After a 1 March newspaper article publicized the allegations, an inquiry into official abuse of power was opened but closed on 2 April without a criminal case. The investigator relied on denials by police, A.A. and M.D., the limited medical findings, and Kutayev’s initial lack of complaint, concluding he was evading responsibility. Judicial review of the refusal was dismissed.

At trial Kutayev retracted his confession, describing abduction from B.’s house, beatings and shocks to force a confession; he had delayed retraction out of fear. Relatives and friends (including politicians) testified to his telephone warnings of persecution and to inconsistencies in the official arrest account. Police and attesting witnesses supported the street-search version. A.A. was not called. On 7 July 2014 the court convicted him, relying on the confession, police statements, the search report and chemical analysis, and sentenced him to four years. It rejected political-motivation and torture claims. The appeal court upheld the verdict, citing the inquiry refusal. Kadyrov’s 25 February televised remarks explicitly linked the arrest to the conference. Amnesty International later designated Kutayev a prisoner of conscience; U.S. Magnitsky sanctions were imposed on A.A. and M.D.

These facts underpin the complaints of torture to extract a confession, ineffective investigation, unfair trial through use of the contested confession without proper review, arbitrary detention, and detention for an ulterior political purpose.
001-222783:
The ECHR case of Kreyndlin and Others v. Russia (no. 33470/18) arose from a violent attack on 9 September 2016 against nine individual applicants, all personnel of Greenpeace’s Russian branch, and the authorities’ subsequent failure to investigate the incident or its alleged xenophobic motive. The applicants also alleged a violation of Article 38 owing to destruction of the investigation file after the Court was seised.

In early September 2016 the applicants formed a Greenpeace volunteer group that travelled through Krasnodar Region to assist firefighting efforts and raise awareness. They were subjected to repeated police checks. On 7 September unidentified persons demanded they leave a hunting lodge and threatened “adverse consequences”; the lodge director evicted them, citing a request from “influential people.” The next day, while camped near Sadki, several men in Cossack paramilitary uniforms entered the site, displayed hostility, labelled the volunteers “American agents” who had “come from abroad,” and ordered them to leave “their land.” Police summoned by the applicants merely checked the volunteers’ documents and took no action against the visitors, with whom the officers appeared acquainted.

Around 1 a.m. on 9 September approximately six masked assailants armed with batons, knives, pepper spray, lamps, firearms and explosives attacked the camp. They beat four applicants (Kreyndlin, Kuksin, Aksenov and Rebechenko) and threatened the remainder. Kreyndlin was struck repeatedly with a rubber truncheon on the head, chest and legs, losing consciousness; forensic examination recorded scratches, bruises, a facial wound and a possible broken nose. Kuksin, sleeping in a vehicle, was woken by screams, breaking glass and explosions; attackers cut the tyres, threatened him with pistols, kicked him and fired a shot nearby. Aksenov suffered concussion after a pyrotechnic device was thrown through his windscreen. Gas was sprayed into tents occupied by two female applicants; another hid in nearby water. The assailants made explicit xenophobic remarks, describing Greenpeace as a “foreign” (US) organisation, telling the victims to “get back to America” and threatening to bury them if they did not leave immediately. A sign bearing the slur “Pindos” was later found at the site. Tents, telephones, tyres and windscreens were damaged or stolen.

On 9 September police opened three separate files for minor bodily harm, threat of murder and theft. These promptly stalled. In November the applicants sought victim status and recategorisation as hate crimes, citing the verbal abuse and the sign; the request was refused on the ground that suspects first had to be identified. Proceedings were repeatedly suspended for failure to identify perpetrators or to question all witnesses. Two applicants were granted victim status only in February 2017. Courts later dismissed complaints that the events should be treated as a single ideologically motivated offence. In September 2018 the files were closed as time-barred. The investigation file was destroyed in January 2021, after notification of the application to the Government, ostensibly because the statutory storage period had expired. Fresh proceedings under the hooliganism provision were instituted in 2021 but were never communicated to the applicants.

These facts formed the basis of the Court’s findings of violations of Article 3 taken with Article 14 (ineffective investigation of the attack and of its hate motive) and of Article 38 (unjustified destruction of the case file).

The case concerns an attack on nine volunteer members of Greenpeace Russia (Sovet Greenpeace) while they assisted in firefighting in Russia’s Krasnodar Region in September 2016, together with the authorities’ subsequent investigation.

The volunteers, travelling in marked vehicles, were subjected to repeated police checks. On 7 September two unidentified persons approached them at a hunting lodge, demanded that they leave, and threatened “adverse consequences.” The lodge director then evicted them, citing pressure from “influential people.” The next day, while camped near Sadki, several men in Cossack paramilitary uniforms entered the site, blocked the entrance, labelled the volunteers “American agents,” and ordered them off “their land.” Police arrived, checked the applicants’ documents, but took no action against the uniformed men, with whom the officers appeared familiar.

Around 1 a.m. on 9 September approximately six masked assailants armed with batons, knives, pepper spray, lamps, firearms and pyrotechnics attacked the camp. They beat four applicants (one with a rubber truncheon to the head, chest and legs, causing him to lose consciousness; another by kicking him after cutting car tyres and firing a shot nearby; a third by smashing a windscreen and throwing a pyrotechnic device that caused concussion). They cut tents, sprayed gas inside them, threatened the remaining applicants, and stole or damaged equipment. Throughout they uttered xenophobic abuse, calling Greenpeace a “foreign” (US) organisation, repeating earlier demands to leave the region, and threatening to “bury” the volunteers so that “nobody would ever find them.” A sign reading “Pindos” (a slur for Americans) was later found at the site. Forensic examination confirmed bruises, scratches and a facial wound (possibly a broken nose) on the first applicant; the applicants also reported concussion and acute angioedema.

Three separate criminal files were opened the same day—for minor bodily harm, death threats and theft—but the investigation repeatedly stalled. Suspects were never identified. Applications to classify the attack as a hate crime (motivated by ideological hostility toward a “foreign” NGO) were rejected on the ground that such a conclusion could be reached only after perpetrators had been identified and questioned. Proceedings were suspended several times for failure to interview all witnesses or take other basic steps, then discontinued in September 2018 as time-barred. A later judicial complaint seeking a single hate-crime investigation was dismissed. In January 2021 the entire case file was destroyed because the statutory storage period had expired. After the Court notified the application, prosecutors briefly reopened a hooliganism inquiry, but the applicants were neither informed nor granted victim status; the outcome remains unknown. Separate complaints about property damage were rejected as falling below the criminal threshold.

These facts form the basis of the complaints under Article 3 taken with Article 14 (failure to investigate the violent attack and its alleged xenophobic motive) and Article 38 (destruction of the investigative file after the Court had requested it).

**The applicants, nine Greenpeace volunteers and the organization's Russian branch, alleged that Russian authorities failed to effectively investigate a violent attack on their camp in September 2016 and its possible xenophobic motives, in breach of Articles 3 and 14 of the Convention, and later failed to provide the Court with the investigation file (Article 38).**

In early September 2016, the volunteers, who had notified local authorities of their firefighting and awareness-raising activities in the Krasnodar Region, faced escalating hostility. On 7 September they were threatened by unidentified persons and evicted from a hunting lodge at the request of “influential people.” The next day, individuals in Cossack paramilitary uniforms entered their camp near Sadki, called them “American agents” who “came from abroad,” and demanded they leave “their land.” Police arrived, checked the volunteers’ documents, but took no action against the Cossacks, with whom they appeared familiar.

Around 1 a.m. on 9 September, approximately six masked assailants armed with batons, knives, pepper spray, lamps, firearms and explosives attacked the camp. They beat four volunteers (including blows to the head, chest and legs, kicks, and a pyrotechnic device thrown into a vehicle causing concussion), threatened the others with death (“we will bury you and nobody will ever find them”), sprayed gas into tents, and damaged or stole equipment. They made explicit xenophobic remarks linked to Greenpeace’s “foreign”/US character, referred to prior “warnings,” used a local accent matching the previous day’s visitors, and left a sign reading “Pindos” (a slur for Americans). Forensic examination confirmed injuries to the first applicant (scratches, bruises, facial wound, possible broken nose); others reported concussion and acute angioedema.

Police opened three separate cases on 9 September (minor bodily harm, death threats, and theft) but the investigation stalled. Applicants requested victim status and reclassification as a single hate-motivated crime, citing the slurs, threats, and “Pindos” sign. Victim status was later granted to two applicants, but the hate-motive claim was refused pending identification of suspects. Proceedings were repeatedly suspended for failure to identify perpetrators, identify all witnesses, or take basic steps; they were never meaningfully resumed after June 2017. A judicial complaint seeking unified investigation of ideological hatred was dismissed. The cases were discontinued as time-barred in September 2018.

Property-damage complaints were rejected as falling below criminal thresholds (treated as administrative offences). In January 2021—after the Court had given notice of the application—the entire investigation file was destroyed because the domestic storage period had expired. The Government later claimed new hooliganism proceedings were opened in March 2021, but the applicants were never informed or granted victim status and the outcome remains unknown.

These facts underpin the alleged failures: the authorities did not treat the events as a coordinated, ideologically motivated attack despite clear xenophobic language and prior incidents; they omitted essential investigative steps; they allowed the cases to become time-barred; and they destroyed the file after being notified of the Strasbourg proceedings, offering only the expired storage period as explanation. The Court ultimately found violations of Article 3 taken with Article 14 (ineffective investigation of the attack and possible hate motive) and of Article 38 (failure to furnish necessary facilities).
001-222789:
The case of Akshin Garayev v. Azerbaijan concerns an Azerbaijani national (born 1953), sole owner of the company Maksima (established 1997). He alleged that the continuing lengthy retention of 28 gas turbines—owned by Maksima—as physical evidence in long-suspended criminal proceedings violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

In May 1992, pursuant to a Cabinet of Ministers decision, 28 apparently State-owned gas turbines were transferred for sale to the State-owned Azermashavadanliq Union. On 1 September 1992 the Prosecutor General’s Office instituted criminal proceedings under Article 88-1 of the 1960 Criminal Code for large-scale embezzlement of State or public property. The investigation, assigned to the Transport Prosecutor’s Office, concerned unspecified State-owned goods (suspected to include the turbines) that had been unloaded at Azerbaijani stations while being transported by train to Armenia.

In 1997 the Union sold the turbines to private Company B for a very low price (reportedly equivalent to approximately USD 25). Company B then sold them to Maksima under two May 1997 contracts for a total of AZM 196,000,000 (approximately USD 50,000). Maksima took physical possession of six turbines; the remaining 22 stayed with the Union.

On 26 August 1997 the authorities seized all 28 turbines (the six from Maksima and the 22 still with the Union) and transferred them to a Ministry of Defence military unit for safekeeping. On 31 December 1997 a prosecutor recognised the turbines as physical evidence and simultaneously suspended the investigation because requests for information (including to Russian and Ukrainian authorities concerning turbine prices and a key witness) remained unanswered and no person to be charged had been identified.

In December 1999 Maksima brought a civil claim for return of the turbines. The Nasimi District Court allowed it on 19 January 2000, wrongly treating the proceedings as discontinued. The Supreme Court quashed that judgment on 14 June 2000, holding that the proceedings were merely suspended and still pending, so any decision on return of evidence had to be taken under criminal-procedure rules.

The case was later transferred to the Prosecutor General’s Office. Responses eventually received from the Russian and Ukrainian authorities in 2001 were unhelpful (price information was a “State secret”; the witness could not be located). On 17 August 2002 the investigation was again suspended for continued inability to identify a suspect.

In July 2010 the applicant wrote to the Prosecutor General complaining of the lengthy retention, invoking his constitutional and Convention property rights, and requesting either return of the turbines under Article 129.4 of the 2000 Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP) or discontinuance under Article 39 (notably expiry of the limitation period). The Office replied on 7 September 2010 that the still-suspended proceedings precluded return; that question would be decided only upon their conclusion.

On 26 October 2010 the applicant challenged the 2002 suspension decision and sought return of the turbines before the Nasimi District Court under Article 449 CCrP. The court dismissed the complaint on 5 November 2010, finding the suspension and continued retention lawful and noting that the turbines were not among the limited categories of evidence (perishables, everyday items, animals, vehicles) that Article 131 CCrP allowed to be returned before conclusion of proceedings. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 19 November 2010, adding that return could occur only by final court judgment, a discontinuance decision, or (inapplicable here) an Article 131 order, and that no ground existed to resume the proceedings.

As of June 2019 the criminal proceedings remained suspended and the 28 turbines continued to be retained as evidence, more than 25 years after their seizure. The applicant contended that this situation imposed an excessive and unjustified burden on his property rights and that domestic law afforded no effective means of obtaining their release or discontinuance of the case.

The case of Akshin Garayev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 30352/11) concerns complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) and Article 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention. The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1953 and living in Baku, is the sole owner of Maksima, a company established in 1997.

In May 1992, 28 state-owned gas turbines were transferred to the state-owned Azermashavadanliq Union for sale, pursuant to a Cabinet of Ministers decision. On 1 September 1992, the Prosecutor General’s Office instituted criminal proceedings under Article 88-1 of the 1960 Criminal Code for large-scale embezzlement of state or public property. The investigation, assigned to the Transport Prosecutor’s Office, concerned unspecified state-owned goods being transported by train to Armenia that had been unloaded at Azerbaijani stations; the turbines were later suspected to be among them.

In 1997, the Union sold the turbines to private Company B for a nominal sum (approximately USD 25). Company B then sold them to Maksima under two contracts for approximately USD 50,000. Maksima took possession of six turbines; the remaining 22 stayed at the Union. On 26 August 1997, prosecutors seized all 28 turbines (including those already in Maksima’s possession) and placed them with a Ministry of Defence military unit for safekeeping. On 31 December 1997, they were formally recognised as physical evidence in the 1992 proceedings. The same day, the investigation was suspended because requests to domestic and foreign authorities (including Russia and Ukraine) remained unanswered and no suspect could be identified.

Maksima brought a 1999 civil claim for return of the turbines. The Nasimi District Court granted it in January 2000, wrongly treating the proceedings as discontinued. The Supreme Court quashed this in June 2000, holding that the proceedings were merely suspended and still pending, so any decision on evidence had to follow criminal procedure rules.

Responses from Russian and Ukrainian authorities arrived in 2001 (the former treating turbine prices as a state secret; the latter unable to locate a key witness). On 17 August 2002, the Prosecutor General’s Office again suspended the proceedings for inability to identify a suspect. Ownership of the former Union later passed to a privatised entity.

In July 2010 the applicant wrote to the Prosecutor General, arguing that the lengthy retention violated his property rights and requesting return of the turbines under Article 129.4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP) or discontinuance (e.g., on limitation grounds under Article 39 CCrP). The Office replied that return could occur only upon conclusion of the still-pending (suspended) proceedings. A further complaint went unanswered.

On 26 October 2010 the applicant challenged the 2002 suspension and sought return of the turbines under Article 449 CCrP. The Nasimi District Court dismissed the complaint on 5 November 2010, citing Articles 53, 124, 128, 129.4 and 131 CCrP: the suspension remained lawful and the turbines were not among the limited categories (perishables, everyday items, animals, vehicles) that could be returned before conclusion of proceedings. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld this on 19 November 2010, adding that only a final judgment, a discontinuance decision, or an Article 131 exception could authorise early return; the ground for suspension (unidentified suspect) had not ceased.

As of June 2019 the 1992 proceedings remained suspended without a suspect having been identified, and the 28 turbines continued to be retained as evidence. The applicant alleged that this more-than-25-year retention imposed an excessive individual burden incompatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and that no effective domestic remedy existed.

The case of Akshin Garayev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 30352/11) concerns the applicant’s complaint that the prolonged retention of 28 gas turbines—owned by his wholly owned company, Maksima—as physical evidence in criminal proceedings that have remained suspended for over 25 years violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. He also alleged a lack of effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

The turbines, originally State property, were transferred in May 1992 to the State-owned Azermashavadanliq Union for sale. On 1 September 1992, the Prosecutor General’s Office opened criminal proceedings under Article 88-1 of the 1960 Criminal Code for large-scale embezzlement of State property, suspected to include these turbines (among other goods unloaded from trains bound for Armenia). The investigation was assigned to the Transport Prosecutor’s Office.

In 1997, Azermashavadanliq sold the turbines to a private company (“Company B”) for a nominal sum (equivalent to about USD 25). Company B then sold them to Maksima in May 1997 for approximately USD 50,000. Maksima took possession of six turbines; the remaining 22 stayed with Azermashavadanliq.

On 26 August 1997, prosecutors seized all 28 turbines (the six from Maksima and the 22 from Azermashavadanliq) and transferred them to a Ministry of Defence military unit for safekeeping. On 31 December 1997, they were formally recognised as physical evidence, and the investigation was suspended because requests for information (including to Russian and Ukrainian authorities) remained unanswered and no suspect had been identified.

In December 1999, Maksima brought a civil claim for return of the turbines. The Nasimi District Court granted it in January 2000, mistakenly treating the proceedings as discontinued. The Supreme Court quashed this in June 2000, holding that the case was merely suspended and thus still pending; return of evidence required a decision under criminal procedure rules.

Responses from Russian authorities (stating the turbine price was a State secret) and Ukrainian authorities (unable to locate a key witness) arrived in 2001. On 17 August 2002, the Prosecutor General’s Office again suspended the proceedings due to the inability to identify a suspect.

The applicant wrote to the Prosecutor General on 8 July 2010, requesting return of the turbines under Article 129.4 of the 2000 Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP) or discontinuance (e.g., due to expiry of the limitation period under Article 39). The Office replied on 7 September 2010 that the turbines could not be returned while proceedings remained pending.

On 26 October 2010, the applicant challenged the 2002 suspension decision in the Nasimi District Court under Article 449 CCrP, seeking its quashing and return of the property. The court dismissed the complaint on 5 November 2010, citing CCrP Articles 53, 124, 128, 129.4 and 131: the suspension was lawful, and the turbines were not among the limited categories (perishable goods, daily-use items, animals, or vehicles not needed for claims) that could be returned before conclusion of proceedings. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld this on 19 November 2010, adding that return was possible only via a final judgment, a discontinuance decision, or the specific circumstances of Article 131; the ground for suspension (unknown perpetrator) persisted, so proceedings could not resume or conclude.

As of June 2019, the criminal proceedings remained suspended and the turbines continued to be retained as evidence. Domestic law (CCrP Articles 53, 129.4, 131 and 132) generally requires physical evidence to be held until a final decision on the merits or discontinuance, with no provision for periodic review of continued retention in suspended cases or compensation for lengthy deprivation.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that the indefinite retention imposed an excessive individual burden without a fair balance, and that no effective remedy existed to challenge the situation or obtain return/discontinuance.
001-222872:
The case of B v. Russia concerns the secondary victimisation of a highly vulnerable child during Russian criminal proceedings relating to her sexual abuse. The applicant, born in 2007, lost her mother in June 2018 and was placed in an orphanage before being assigned guardians. In February 2019 she disclosed to psychologists that several adult males had sexually abused her between 2014 and 2017. Separate investigations were opened against four suspects under Article 132 § 4(b) of the Criminal Code.

Between February 2019 and September 2020 five different investigators (four of them male) conducted twelve interviews with the applicant, almost all in ordinary offices. The first interview, which covered all four perpetrators and was videotaped, was lost the same day through “technical malfunctions.” She was therefore required to repeat the full account three further times and to give additional focused interviews. On-site verifications of her statements took place in the flats where the abuse had allegedly occurred; one such visit was conducted in the presence of a suspect’s brother. Identification parades were held behind a one-way mirror, yet one suspect accidentally entered the room where the applicant was waiting, causing her acute fright. Confrontations with two suspects obliged her to recount the assaults in their presence and to answer questions from their lawyers. She broke down in tears on both occasions, necessitating breaks; after the second confrontation psychologists certified that she was exhausted and unwell.

Requests by her guardian and lawyer to spare her further participation were granted only belatedly and only in some of the files. An application to join the four cases in order to reduce her involvement was refused. Forensic examinations (medical, psychological and psychiatric) repeatedly documented her growing distress. By January 2020 a commission of experts diagnosed a prolonged depressive reaction caused by the original abuse, family losses and the investigation itself, and advised against any further participation. Later psychological assessments recorded emotional exhaustion, post-traumatic stress, moderate depression and emerging suicidal risk. These opinions were largely disregarded.

At the closed trial of the first accused the court refused to admit a key expert report from another file and rejected applications to read the applicant’s pre-trial statements instead of examining her in person. On 10 June 2020 she was questioned for two hours by the prosecutor, defence counsel and the judge about the details of the abuse; the examination continued even after a psychologist requested an adjournment. Subsequent hearings required her continued presence. Convictions followed, but her condition deteriorated further; by late 2021 she exhibited acute suicidal tendencies and required psychiatric hospitalisation.

The Court found that the manner in which the proceedings were conducted—repeated unrecorded interviews by multiple male investigators, on-site reconstructions, face-to-face confrontations, and an unjustified courtroom examination—ignored the applicant’s extreme vulnerability and the consistent expert warnings. Russian law contained no adequate safeguards to prevent secondary victimisation of child victims of sexual offences. These failings attained the threshold of severity required by Article 3 and constituted a violation of the State’s positive obligation to protect the applicant’s personal integrity.

**Case of B v. Russia (ECtHR, Appl. no. 36328/20, 7 Feb. 2023)**

The applicant, a girl born in 2007, was placed in an orphanage after her mother's death in 2018 and later with guardians. In February 2019, psychologists recorded her account of sexual abuse by several men (2014–2017). Proceedings were opened under Criminal Code Art. 132 § 4(b) against four suspects (A.M., E.T., R.T., Ye.Ch.) in separate cases.

Between February 2019 and September 2020, five investigators (four male) conducted 12 interviews of the applicant (three per case) in ordinary offices, with her guardian, psychologists/educators, and (from April) a lawyer present. The first videotaped interview of 16 February 2019, covering all episodes, was lost the same day due to “technical malfunctions.” She therefore had to repeat her full account three more times and give focused interviews in each case. On-site statement verifications required her to reconstruct events at two flats (19 February 2019); a perpetrator’s brother was present in one. After she objected, photographs were used later. Identification parades (16–18 February) used a one-way mirror, but one perpetrator entered her room by investigator error, terrifying her. Two others were identified by photograph.

Confrontations occurred with A.M. (8 April) and E.T. (26 April). She recounted the abuse in their presence, answered questions from (male) lawyers, and was asked to confirm her statements. She flushed, cried, and needed breaks; psychologists and her guardian requested a halt due to exhaustion. Some later requests to spare her further actions (citing trauma) were granted under the investigator’s general powers (CCP Art. 38); others, including joining the cases to reduce interviews, were refused. Video-recording objections and confrontation refusals were sometimes accepted. Supervisory prosecutors found no violations.

At A.M.’s closed trial, the court rejected requests (supported by prosecutors and experts) to read her prior statements or admit a January 2020 forensic report diagnosing prolonged depressive reaction from the abuse, family losses, and the proceedings themselves, which advised against further participation. On 10 June 2020 she underwent two hours of detailed questioning by the prosecutor, defence lawyer, and judge about the abuse (accused absent), with a psychologist and guardian present; she answered some questions in writing and showed distress, but examination continued after a short break. Further hearings followed. Applications citing Art. 3 ECHR and her hospitalisation for asthenic-neurotic syndrome were unsuccessful. A.M. was convicted (12 years; upheld on appeal/cassation). In the other trials her statements were read out; two convictions followed, with remaining proceedings pending.

Forensic medical examination (19 February 2019) found no injuries. Multiple psychological/psychiatric commissions initially found no disorder but later (2019–2020) diagnosed mental/emotional distress, then prolonged depressive reaction, PTSD, anxiety-depressive disorder, exhaustion, suicide risk, and self-harm, attributing deterioration to the abuse plus repeated interviews, confrontations, and trial participation. Psychologists repeatedly noted typical trauma reactions, recommended avoiding contact with perpetrators and stressful procedures, and certified breakdowns. A 2021 report confirmed lasting harm requiring years of therapy.

Domestic law (CCP Arts. 45, 191, 281, as amended 2013) grants under-16 sexual-abuse victims free legal aid, obligatory psychologist/representative presence, video-recording (absent objection), time limits (1 hour uninterrupted/2 hours daily), and allows reading prior statements at trial without examination unless the court decides otherwise. The Lanzarote Convention (ratified by Russia) and related instruments require child-sensitive procedures, specialised investigators, limited interviews in adapted premises by the same trained persons, video evidence, and avoidance of perpetrator contact unless strictly necessary, all in the child’s best interests and without aggravating trauma.

The Court found a violation of Art. 3 (substantive limb, positive obligations). The applicant was an extremely vulnerable child; the accumulated failures—unrecorded/multiple interviews by changing (mostly male) investigators in ordinary settings, on-site reconstructions, a botched identification, confrontations, and unjustified trial examination despite expert warnings—caused secondary victimisation that attained the Art. 3 threshold. Authorities showed utter disregard for her suffering, which demonstrably worsened her condition. Domestic law lacked adequate specific safeguards for child sexual-abuse victims in criminal proceedings.

**Between February 2019 and September 2020, five investigators (four male) conducted 12 interviews of the applicant in ordinary offices, despite her extreme vulnerability. The first videotaped interview (16 February 2019), covering all episodes, was lost to "technical malfunctions," forcing her to repeat the full account three more times across the other cases. Further interviews focused on individual perpetrators. On-site reconstructions occurred at two crime-scene flats (19 February 2019), one with a perpetrator's relative present; she later objected to returning and used photographs instead. Identification parades used a one-way mirror, but one perpetrator (A.M.) entered her room by mistake, terrifying her. Confrontations with A.M. (8 April 2019) and E.T. (26 April 2019) required her to recount the abuse in the perpetrators' presence and answer questions; she flushed, cried, and needed multiple breaks, after which one confrontation was halted due to her exhaustion. Psychologists present documented typical trauma reactions (shame, fear, overstrain) and later certified her breakdowns. A request to join the cases (to reduce her participation) was refused. Some evidence was later shared across files, but this did not prevent repetition.**

**Investigators occasionally granted limited protections (e.g., ending some actions after a June 2019 lawyer's request citing health damage; rejecting one confrontation). However, they ignored psychologists' early advice to avoid perpetrator contact and did not use specialized child-friendly settings or consistent interviewers. Forensic medical examination (19 February 2019) required her to recount the abuse again. Multiple psychological/psychiatric reports (2019–2020) found no initial mental disorder but noted distress from the events, family loss, and proceedings; a January 2020 commission diagnosed prolonged depressive reaction from the abuse plus the investigation itself, recommending against further participation and requiring treatment. Later reports (May–July 2020) documented deterioration, PTSD, depression, suicide risk, and exhaustion, advising avoidance of all stress.**

**At A.M.'s closed trial, the court rejected requests (supported by the prosecutor and psychologists) to read prior statements instead of examining her, citing insufficient evidence of incapacity. On 10 June 2020 she faced two hours of detailed questioning by the prosecutor, defence, and judge about the abuse (accused absent); records were read due to alleged inconsistencies, and examination continued despite psychologist objections that she was being retraumatised. She was summoned repeatedly. An application to the Supreme Court of Tatarstan highlighting Convention obligations and her prior inpatient treatment for asthenic-neurotic syndrome was ineffective. A.M. was convicted (12 years); other trials used prior statements or remained pending. By December 2021 she had anxiety-depressive disorder/PTSD, suicidal ideation, and self-harm, requiring psychiatric hospitalisation.**

**Domestic law (Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 191 and 281, as amended 2013) mandated psychologist participation, video-recording (unless objected), time limits, and reading of prior statements at trial for child victims under 16, but these were not consistently applied or enforced. International standards (Lanzarote Convention Articles 30–36, ratified by Russia) require child-best-interest proceedings, specialised investigators, limited/same-person interviews in adapted premises, video evidence to avoid repetition, and avoidance of perpetrator contact. The authorities' disregard of expert opinions, repeated unrecorded interviews, confrontations, and trial examination caused secondary victimisation, worsening her condition and attaining the Article 3 severity threshold through failure of positive obligations to protect her integrity.**

The case of Janáček v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 9634/17) arose from the Constitutional Court’s failure to forward to the applicant the written observations of three ordinary courts that had decided his matrimonial-property dispute, thereby depriving him of any opportunity to comment on those observations before the complaint was dismissed.

In December 2013 the Zlín District Court divided the former spouses’ assets and ordered the applicant to pay his ex-wife approximately CZK 2 million. Valuation of the applicant’s business assets proved contentious. After two other experts declined to report promptly, the court appointed expert S., who submitted an opinion in November 2012. When the applicant later produced a competing report by expert M., the presiding judge emailed S. for comments rather than following a formal procedure; S. replied the day before judgment. The court preferred S.’s valuation. On appeal the Brno Regional Court (March 2015) largely confirmed the reliance on S., heard him in person and again rejected a request for a fresh expert. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal as manifestly ill-founded (January 2016). Enforcement followed, culminating in an order for the sale of the applicant’s immovable property.

In April 2016 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He argued that the ordinary courts had based their decisions solely on S.’s reports without adequate justification, that the informal e-mail exchange with S. was irregular, that an alternative expert should have been commissioned, and that the resulting division of property violated his rights under Article 11 of the Czech Charter, Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Constitutional Court invited observations from the District, Regional and Supreme Courts. The Supreme Court judge explained the formal inadmissibility of the points-of-law appeal and recommended rejection of the complaint. The District Court judge addressed the alleged “non-standard relationship” with expert S., stating that he had never previously known the expert and had used e-mail merely to accelerate proceedings. A Regional Court judge supplied a two-page defence of S.’s appointment and methodology. None of these submissions was sent to the applicant.

On 19 July 2016 the Constitutional Court, sitting without an oral hearing, declared the complaint manifestly ill-founded. Its brief reasoning noted only that it had “familiarised itself with” the ordinary courts’ observations. After receiving the decision the applicant inspected the case file, discovered the uncommunicated comments and asked why he had been given no chance to reply. The Constitutional Court answered that the judge-rapporteur had considered the observations to contain no new facts or arguments.

The applicant maintained before the European Court that the failure to communicate the observations, some of which contained factual explanations and legal justifications not previously available to him, breached the principle of adversarial proceedings guaranteed by Article 6 § 1. The Government contested that the observations added nothing material and that the Constitutional Court’s practice, refined after earlier Strasbourg judgments, permitted non-communication in such circumstances.
