The case of Janáček v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 9634/17) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the Czech Constitutional Court’s failure to communicate to the applicant the written observations submitted by the lower courts that had decided his case, thereby depriving him of any opportunity to comment on those observations.

The applicant, a Czech national, was involved in proceedings for the division of matrimonial property following his divorce. On 17 December 2013 the Zlín District Court ordered him to pay his former wife CZK 300 000 within three days and a further CZK 1 759 627 within one year. In valuing the assets the court relied principally on an expert report prepared by expert S., whom it had appointed after other experts indicated they could not begin work for many months. The applicant later submitted a contrary report by expert M.; the presiding judge then emailed S. asking for comments, which S. provided. The District Court accepted S.’s reasoning and rejected M.’s report.

On appeal the Brno Regional Court, on 24 March 2015, increased the applicant’s overall liability to CZK 2 134 878 (CZK 1 million payable within six months and the balance within one year). It admitted a further statement from S., heard him and two other experts, and expressly endorsed S.’s methodology and conclusions, finding that he had convincingly rebutted the parties’ objections. The Supreme Court subsequently dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded.

On 14 April 2016 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He argued that both the District Court and the Regional Court had relied exclusively on S.’s report without adequate justification (explicitly mentioning the informal email exchange), that the Regional Court had refused his request for an alternative expert, and that the courts’ formalistic approach had resulted in an incorrect and unfair division of the property. He invoked the rights to a fair trial and to the protection of property under the Czech Charter and the Convention.

The Constitutional Court invited the three lower courts to submit written observations. The Supreme Court judge (11 May 2016) explained the inadmissibility of the points-of-law appeal and invited the Constitutional Court to reject the complaint. The District Court judge (17 May 2016) addressed the applicant’s allegation of a “non-standard relationship” with expert S., stating that he had approached S. only after other experts were unavailable and that the email request had been made solely to expedite proceedings. A member of the Regional Court chamber (25 May 2016) submitted a two-page commentary focusing on S.’s appointment, valuation method and the reasons for relying on his report.

On 19 July 2016, after a purely written procedure, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded, expressly stating that it had “familiarised itself with [the] contents” of the lower courts’ observations. The applicant first learned of those observations when his lawyer inspected the file on 18 August 2016. In a letter of 19 September 2016 he asked why he had not been given the chance to comment. The Constitutional Court replied on 29 September 2016 that the judge rapporteur had presumably considered the observations to contain no new facts or legal arguments.

Under the Constitutional Court Act the lower courts are joined parties entitled to submit observations, and the judge rapporteur is required to send the complaint to them. The Court’s own evolving internal practice, adopted after earlier Strasbourg judgments, recommended that such observations be forwarded to the applicant whenever they might contain new facts, claims or arguments.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: the Constitutional Court’s decision to take the lower courts’ uncommunicated observations into account without affording the applicant an opportunity to respond.

The case of Janáček v. the Czech Republic (no. 9634/17) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing). The core issue is the Constitutional Court’s failure to communicate to the applicant the written observations submitted by the ordinary courts involved in his case, thereby denying him any opportunity to comment on those observations.

The underlying domestic proceedings concerned the division of matrimonial property after the applicant’s divorce. On 17 December 2013 the Zlín District Court ordered him to pay his former wife CZK 300 000 immediately and a further CZK 1 759 627 within one year. The court relied principally on an expert valuation prepared by expert S., whom it had appointed after other experts indicated they could not begin work for many months. The applicant produced a competing report by expert M.; the presiding judge then obtained S.’s comments on that report by informal e-mail. The court ultimately accepted S.’s valuation and rejected M.’s.

On appeal the Brno Regional Court, by judgment of 24 March 2015, increased the overall sum payable to CZK 2 134 878 and again based its decision exclusively on S.’s opinions, which it described as logically justified and convincing. The applicant’s subsequent appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 12 January 2016 as manifestly ill-founded. Enforcement proceedings were then commenced and an order for the sale of the applicant’s immovable property was issued.

On 14 April 2016 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He argued that the ordinary courts had relied solely on S.’s report without adequate justification, had refused to commission an independent expert, and had thereby violated his rights to a fair trial and to the protection of property (Articles 36 § 1 and 11 of the Czech Charter, Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1).

The Constitutional Court invited the three ordinary courts to submit observations. The Supreme Court (11 May 2016) explained the inadmissibility of the appeal on points of law and recommended dismissal of the complaint. The District Court judge (17 May 2016) defended both the appointment of S. and the informal e-mail exchange as a means of avoiding delay. A member of the Regional Court chamber (25 May 2016) set out in two pages the reasons why S.’s valuation had been preferred. None of these observations was forwarded to the applicant.

On 19 July 2016, after a purely written procedure, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded, expressly noting that it had “familiarised itself with” the courts’ observations. Only after receiving the decision did the applicant’s lawyer inspect the file (18 August 2016) and discover the existence of the observations. In a letter of 19 September 2016 the applicant asked why he had been given no opportunity to reply. The Constitutional Court answered that the judge rapporteur had presumably considered that the observations contained no new facts or legal arguments.

The relevant provisions of the Constitutional Court Act confer on the ordinary courts the status of joined parties with the same procedural rights as the complainant, including the right to submit observations. The Act also requires the complaint to be sent to those parties. Following earlier Strasbourg judgments (notably Milatová), the Constitutional Court had itself adopted internal recommendations that observations should be communicated to the complainant whenever they contained, or might contain, new facts, allegations or lines of argument.

These facts form the exclusive basis of the alleged violation of the principle of adversarial proceedings under Article 6 § 1.
001-222867:
The ECHR case Paun Jovanović v. Serbia (no. 41394/15) concerns alleged discrimination in official language use during criminal proceedings and inadequate reasoning in a related constitutional appeal.

The applicant, Paun Jovanović (b. 1957), is a Serbian lawyer from Bor who uses the Ijekavian variant of Serbian. On 18 February 2013, while acting as defence counsel for a defendant at a hearing before the investigating judge of the Bor Court of First Instance, he put questions directly to a witness. The hearing transcript records that, upon being given the floor, he was “warned to ask questions in the court’s official language.” He requested that the warning be entered in the record and acknowledged that he was an Ijekavian speaker. All participants, including the applicant, signed the transcript without objection.

The applicant maintained that the warning occurred immediately after his first question, which he had posed in Ijekavian (a variant of equal official status to Ekavian). He regarded the recorded wording as a “watered-down” and inaccurate version of events; he had raised the discrepancy orally, but the judge left the transcript unchanged. Throughout the same hearing the lawyer representing the victim—an Ekavian speaker—received no comparable warning. The applicant, of Montenegrin origin, therefore claimed he had been discriminated against on linguistic grounds in violation of constitutional guarantees, Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

On 7 March 2013 he lodged a constitutional appeal (supplemented on 15 November 2013) alleging that the judge’s conduct had denied him the free use of Ijekavian. On 10 February 2015 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal under Article 36 § 1(7) of the Constitutional Court Act. It held that, having regard to the appeal’s reasoning and the “legal nature and substance” of the judge’s conduct as shown in the transcript, there had been no “individual action” within the meaning of Article 170 of the Constitution capable of being challenged before it.

Separately, the applicant complained to the High Judicial Council. The Acting President of the Bor Court, after obtaining the investigating judge’s account, found the complaint unfounded. The judge stated that she had asked the applicant to reformulate only one question because the witness had clearly not understood it; the applicant complied and noted that he was an Ijekavian speaker. After completing his examination he requested that the instruction be recorded; the insertion was worded in accordance with his own proposal and he signed the transcript. The court concluded that the applicant had not been prevented from using Ijekavian but had merely been required to use “the court’s official language” to clarify a question. There was neither unlawfulness nor discrimination, nor any intent to offend; the applicant’s characterisation of the episode as “fascist” was itself inappropriate.

Serbian is the official language of the State and of the courts. It comprises two equal standard variants, Ekavian and Ijekavian. Ekavian predominates in Serbia (including Bor) and is used by the judicial authorities; Ijekavian is the form principally spoken in other former-Yugoslav territories such as Montenegro. The relevant statutes confirm that court proceedings are conducted in Serbian, while other languages may be used officially only under conditions prescribed by law.

The applicant further complained that the Constitutional Court’s rejection decision lacked adequate reasoning, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: unequal treatment of two officially equal language variants in the same hearing, and the subsequent failure of the Constitutional Court to give sufficient reasons for refusing to examine the complaint.

The case concerns alleged discrimination in the official use of Serbian language variants during a criminal hearing and inadequate reasoning by Serbia’s Constitutional Court.

Applicant Paun Jovanović, a lawyer born in 1957 and resident in Bor, speaks the Ijekavian variant of Serbian. On 18 February 2013 he appeared as defence counsel before an investigating judge of the Bor Court of First Instance. According to the official transcript he put questions to a witness and was immediately “warned to ask questions in the court’s official language.” He asked that the warning be recorded and confirmed that he was an Ijekavian speaker. All participants, including the applicant, signed the transcript without objection.

In his subsequent account the applicant stated that the warning followed his first Ijekavian question and that the judge had told him to speak “Serbian,” even though Ijekavian is an equally official variant. He claimed the transcript was a watered-down version of events; he had verbally protested but the judge left the record unchanged. The opposing lawyer, an Ekavian speaker representing the victim, received no similar instruction.

On 7 March 2013 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal alleging that the judge’s conduct deprived him of the right to use Ijekavian and constituted discrimination against him as an Ijekavian speaker of Montenegrin origin, contrary to the Constitution, Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. He supplemented the appeal on 15 November 2013.

On 10 February 2015 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal under Article 36 § 1(7) of the Constitutional Court Act. It held that, having regard to the “reasoning of the constitutional appeal” and the “legal nature and substance” of the judge’s conduct as shown by the transcript, there had been no “individual action” within the meaning of Article 170 of the Constitution capable of being challenged.

A parallel disciplinary complaint forwarded by the High Judicial Council was also dismissed. The Acting President of the Bor court, relying on the investigating judge’s own report, found that the applicant had merely been asked to rephrase one question that the witness had not understood. After he did so and noted that he spoke Ijekavian, the warning was entered exactly as he had requested. He then signed the record without reservation. The President concluded there had been no prohibition of Ijekavian, no unlawfulness and no discriminatory intent.

Standard Serbian comprises two equal variants, Ekavian and Ijekavian, as defined by Matica srpska. Ekavian realises the historical jat vowel as /e/; Ijekavian realises it as /ije/ or /je/. Ekavian predominates in Serbia (including Bor), while Ijekavian is typical of territories of the former Yugoslavia such as Montenegro. The Constitution designates Serbian as the official language; both variants therefore enjoy the same official status. Court legislation likewise requires the use of Serbian but does not distinguish between the two variants.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the investigating judge unjustifiably prevented him from using Ijekavian while permitting unrestricted use of Ekavian, and that the Constitutional Court’s refusal to examine the appeal lacked adequate reasoning.

The case of Paun Jovanović v. Serbia (Application no. 41394/15) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged discrimination arising from the official use of the two equal standard variants of the Serbian language—Ekavian and Ijekavian—during judicial proceedings, as well as a related complaint of inadequate reasoning by the Constitutional Court. The applicant, a practising lawyer born in 1957 and resident in Bor, Serbia, invoked Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention together with Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

On 18 February 2013 the applicant appeared as defence counsel at a hearing before an investigating judge of the Bor Court of First Instance. The official transcript records that he put a series of questions to a witness and that, at the outset of his examination, he was “warned to ask questions in the court’s official language.” He immediately requested that the warning be entered in the record and acknowledged that he was an Ijekavian speaker. The transcript was signed by all participants, including the applicant, without objection. The applicant later maintained that the warning had been issued after his first (perfectly grammatical Ijekavian) question and that the written version of events was a diluted account of what had actually occurred. Throughout the same hearing the lawyer representing the injured party, an Ekavian speaker, received no comparable instruction.

On 7 March 2013 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal. He contended that the investigating judge had deprived him of the right to use the Ijekavian variant, which enjoys the same official status as Ekavian, thereby discriminating against him as an Ijekavian speaker of Montenegrin origin. He supplemented the appeal on 15 November 2013. On 10 February 2015 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal under Article 36 § 1 (7) of the Constitutional Court Act, holding that the judge’s conduct, as evidenced by the transcript, did not constitute an “individual action” capable of being challenged under Article 170 of the Constitution.

In parallel the applicant complained to the High Judicial Council. The Acting President of the Bor court replied on 31 October 2013 that the complaint was unfounded. According to the investigating judge’s account, she had asked the applicant to reformulate only one question because the witness had not understood it; the applicant then identified himself as an Ijekavian speaker, finished his examination, and requested that the instruction be recorded in the wording he himself proposed. He signed the transcript. The judge insisted she had not forbidden Ijekavian but had merely required the use of the court’s official language for the sake of clarity. The Acting President accepted this explanation, found no unlawfulness or discrimination, and characterised the applicant’s description of the episode as “fascist” as itself inappropriate.

The Serbian language comprises two equally recognised variants. Ekavian is the form generally used by the population and by official bodies in Serbia, including in Bor; Ijekavian predominates in other parts of the former Yugoslavia, notably Montenegro. Both variants are standard and enjoy identical official status according to the authoritative pronouncements of Matica srpska.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s allegations that the investigating judge’s conduct constituted unjustified differential treatment on the ground of language (Article 1 of Protocol No. 12) and that the Constitutional Court’s rejection of his appeal lacked adequate reasoning (Article 6 § 1).
001-223104:
The case concerns Azerbaijani civil society activist Ilkin Rustamzade (born 1992), a student and co-founder of the NGO Free Youth. In early 2013, following non-combat deaths of soldiers, protests occurred in Baku criticising the government. These were organised via social media, with the NIDA civic movement playing a central role; the applicant participated actively in them (and their organisation). Separately, on 1 March 2013, the applicant observed (but did not join) acquaintances performing a “Harlem Shake” dance in a Baku seaside park; a short video (including sexually suggestive movements near a statue by one dancer) was later uploaded to YouTube. A TV programme later criticised the dancers as NIDA-linked “drug addicts and anarchists.” The applicant was questioned as a witness in related NIDA criminal proceedings (involving alleged explosives and drugs).

On 30 April 2013, he was administratively arrested and convicted (15 days’ detention) for participating in another gathering (later found by the ECtHR to violate Arts. 6 and 11). On 17 May 2013, after release, he was arrested and charged with group hooliganism (Criminal Code Arts. 221.2.1–2): allegedly video-recording “immoral actions” and “chaotic” movements in the park, resisting officials, and disseminating the video online as disrespect to society. Only one other dancer faced similar charges. On 13 September 2013, additional charges were added (Arts. 28, 220.1, 228.3): preparing mass disorder as part of an “organised group” with NIDA members for a 10 March 2013 demonstration (to disrupt stability, using Molotov cocktails stored by co-accused, social media discussions of violence by others, leaflets, and funds). The bill of indictment (filed October 2013 with the Baku Court of Serious Crimes, covering eight accused, mostly NIDA members) restated the hooliganism charge verbatim and described the new charges in one long, unclear, disconnected sentence.

At trial, the applicant pleaded not guilty, stating the charges were unclear; he had created a social media event for a peaceful protest against soldier deaths (without calling for violence or disorder) and had merely observed (not performed or uploaded) the dance video, which was not criminal. On 6 May 2014, the court convicted him on all counts and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The judgment contained no specific reasoning: it asserted the acts fell under the cited articles based on “reliable and indisputable evidence” but did not link evidence (e.g., Molotovs or messages found with co-accused, or a witness account of NIDA violence discussions) to the applicant, nor explain how the dance video or its upload constituted hooliganism. Co-accused were convicted on overlapping charges with more (though still limited) factual references.

The applicant appealed, arguing innocence, lack of evidence, and no reasoning (citing Arts. 6, 10 and 11 ECHR). The Baku Court of Appeal (16 December 2014) and Supreme Court (15 October 2015) upheld the conviction without further reasoning on guilt. He was pardoned and released in March 2019. Related ECtHR judgments found his (and NIDA members’) pre-trial detention unlawful (no reasonable suspicion; ulterior purpose of silencing protesters, violating Arts. 5 and 18). In 2021, some NIDA convictions were quashed domestically.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the proceedings as a whole lacked fair trial guarantees (esp. a reasoned judgment explaining the characterisation of acts as criminal or the applicant’s involvement); and the conviction lacked a clear, foreseeable domestic-law basis, as specific offence elements (e.g., hooliganism via the video; organised mass disorder/explosives) were not shown to exist, interfering with freedom of expression.

The case of Rustamzade v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) (Application no. 22323/16) involves Ilkin Bakir oglu Rustamzade, a 1992-born Azerbaijani student and civil society activist who co-founded the Free Youth NGO. It concerns his 2014 criminal conviction and 8-year prison sentence, which he alleged violated Articles 6 (fair trial), 7 (no punishment without law), 10 (freedom of expression), and 18 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The ECHR found violations of Article 6 § 1 (proceedings as a whole failed fair trial guarantees, including lack of a reasoned judgment) and Article 10 (conviction lacked a clear, foreseeable legal basis, as offence elements were not shown).

In early 2013, protests erupted in Baku over non-combat deaths of Azerbaijani soldiers. These were organized via social media, with the NIDA civic movement playing a central role. The applicant actively participated in and helped organize the peaceful demonstrations, which police dispersed with arrests. Concurrently, the “Harlem Shake” dance gained popularity. On 1 March 2013, the applicant accompanied acquaintances to a Baku seaside park, where they performed the dance near a bronze statue (one making suggestive movements). He observed but did not dance. A ~1-minute video was uploaded to YouTube as “Harlem Shake – Park Bulvar.” A private TV program later portrayed the dancers as drug-addicted NIDA anarchists, linking them to the soldier-death protests.

Criminal proceedings (case no. 132006017) were opened against NIDA board members for illegal possession of explosives and narcotics. The applicant was questioned twice as a witness. On 30 April 2013, he was arrested at a gathering near the State Oil Academy, convicted administratively under Article 298.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences for assembly violations, and given 15 days’ detention (later found by the ECHR in a related case to violate Articles 11 and 6). Upon release, on 17 May 2013, he was rearrested and charged with hooliganism under Criminal Code Articles 221.2.1 (group commission) and 221.2.2 (resisting officials). The charges—a single lengthy sentence—alleged that, with others including B.G., he breached public order at the park by recording “immoral actions” toward the statue and chaotic movements after stripping to the waist, resisted park security and police, and uploaded the 6.16 MB video widely. Only B.G. among the dancers faced similar charges.

On 13 September 2013, he received additional charges under Articles 28 (crime preparation), 220.1 (mass disorder), and 228.3 (organized-group illegal arms/explosives). These accused him of joining an “organized group” with NIDA members to plan a 10 March 2013 demonstration aiming to disrupt political/social stability, paralyze state functions, and breach order. Specific acts included storing money at co-accused S.N.’s flat to attract “destructive forces,” social-media discussions of Molotov cocktails with B.G., S.N., and M.A., spreading protest calls and making leaflets, and storing Molotovs at co-accused flats. The investigation was joined to the NIDA case. The 10 October 2013 bill of indictment against eight accused (mostly NIDA members) restated the hooliganism charges verbatim and used one unclear, disconnected page-long sentence for the new ones.

At the Baku Court of Serious Crimes trial, the applicant pleaded not guilty, arguing unclear charges, no crimes committed, no violence calls (he had only created a social-media event for the protest), and that observing/recording the dance (which he did not perform or necessarily upload) was not criminal. On 6 May 2014, he was convicted on all counts. The judgment offered no specific reasoning linking evidence (Molotovs found at co-accused flats, their social-media messages, a witness on NIDA violence discussions) to him, nor explained how the dance video constituted hooliganism. The Baku Court of Appeal (16 December 2014) and Supreme Court (15 October 2015) upheld this without further reasoning. He was pardoned and released on 16 March 2019.

Related ECHR judgments found Article 5 violations (unlawful detention without reasonable suspicion) in his pre-trial proceedings and those of NIDA members, plus Article 18 breaches (ulterior purpose of silencing activists). Some NIDA convictions were later quashed domestically. These facts underscore the conviction’s targeting of his protest organization and expressive activity via an unclear, unreasoned process lacking proof of offence elements.

The applicant, Ilkin Rustamzade (born 1992), was an Azerbaijani student and civil-society activist who co-founded the NGO Free Youth. In early 2013 he helped organise and took part in peaceful demonstrations in Baku protesting non-combat deaths of soldiers; the protests were publicised on social media and received wide coverage. NIDA, another youth group, played a leading organisational role. Around the same time a “Harlem Shake” video featuring acquaintances dancing in a Baku park (one dancer making suggestive movements near a statue) was uploaded to YouTube. The applicant did not dance; he merely observed. A television programme later portrayed the dancers as NIDA-linked “drug addicts and anarchists.”

Criminal proceedings were opened against several NIDA members for alleged possession of explosives and narcotics. The applicant was questioned twice as a witness. On 30 April 2013 he was administratively detained for 15 days after attending a gathering (later found to violate Articles 6 and 11). On 17 May 2013 he was re-arrested and charged with hooliganism (Criminal Code Arts. 221.2.1 and 221.2.2) for “blatantly breaching public order” by filming the dance, resisting park-security and police requests to stop, and uploading the video. Only one other dancer was charged.

In September 2013 additional charges of preparing mass disorder and illegal possession of arms/explosives by an organised group (Arts. 28, 220.1, 228.3) were added and joined to the NIDA case. The indictment accused the applicant of forming an organised group with NIDA members to stage a 10 March demonstration that would paralyse state institutions, store money to attract “destructive forces,” discuss Molotov cocktails on social media, produce leaflets, and store the cocktails at co-accused’s flats. The relevant passage consisted of a single, grammatically disconnected page-long sentence.

At trial the applicant denied every charge, stating he had merely created a Facebook event for a peaceful protest and had not danced or called for violence. On 6 May 2014 the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted him on all counts and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The judgment contained no reasoning linking him to the Molotov-cocktail evidence (found at others’ flats), the social-media exchanges (between other accused) or the witness statement about a NIDA meeting; it merely recited the video and concluded that “reliable and indisputable evidence” established guilt. The Court of Appeal (16 December 2014) and Supreme Court (15 October 2015) upheld the conviction without adding any reasoning.

The applicant was pardoned and released in March 2019. Related Strasbourg judgments had already found his pre-trial detention lacked reasonable suspicion (Article 5) and that similar proceedings against NIDA members pursued an ulterior purpose of silencing critics of the army deaths (Article 18). In 2021 the Azerbaijani Supreme Court itself quashed the convictions of four NIDA co-accused for lack of proof.

These facts underpin the complaints that the criminal process, taken as a whole, failed to meet fair-trial standards (absence of a reasoned judgment) and that the convictions themselves lacked any foreseeable legal basis, the specific elements of the offences never having been shown to exist.
001-223106:
The European Court of Human Rights case of Hysa v. Albania (no. 52048/16) concerned the pre-trial detention of Afërdita Hysa, an Albanian tax official born in 1968. At the time she served as director of the Inspection Department in Tirana’s Regional Tax Directorate. On 5 November 2013 the Tirana District Court, acting on a prosecutor’s request and in her absence, ordered her detention on suspicion of abuse of office under Article 248 of the Criminal Code. The court found she had approved unlawful VAT rebates totalling ALL 515 455 275 (approximately EUR 3.7 million) to several companies. It held that the statutory conditions of Articles 228 and 229 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were met, citing the circumstances of the offence, a flight risk, the gravity of the conduct, its serious impact on state finances, the risk the offence posed to society, and the incompatibility of any lesser measure. After Hysa surrendered on 6 November, the same court confirmed the order on 9 November following a hearing at which she was present.

Hysa appealed to the Tirana Court of Appeal on 15 November, arguing that her voluntary surrender, fifteen years of public service, marriage to a police officer and two young children eliminated any flight risk; that her suspension from office and the seizure of the relevant tax files removed any possibility of tampering with evidence; that detention was disproportionate to the charge; and that her poor health warranted a less severe measure. On 27 November the Court of Appeal upheld the detention. It referred to “the circumstances of the commission of the offence and the flight risk of the suspect,” the gravity of the facts, the substantial financial harm to the State, the offence’s danger to society, the statutory penalty, and the existence of aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Detention was deemed the only proportionate and appropriate measure. The applicant surrendered on 6 November 2013. After a further hearing on 9 November at which she was present, the same court confirmed that the conditions for detention remained fulfilled.

On 15 November 2013 the applicant appealed to the Tirana Court of Appeal. She argued that her voluntary surrender, fifteen-year career in the tax authorities, marriage to a police officer and two young children demonstrated the absence of any flight risk; that she could not interfere with evidence because she had been suspended and the relevant files had already been seized; that detention was disproportionate to the charge; and that her poor health warranted a less restrictive measure. On 27 November 2013 the Court of Appeal upheld the detention order. It did not mention flight risk. Instead it stressed the seriousness of the offence (in view of the penalty prescribed by Article 248), its particular danger to society, and the significant economic harm caused by acts committed in the name of a public inspection body. Only detention, the court concluded, could prevent the risk of re-offending or the commission of a more serious offence; any other measure was inappropriate.

A dissenting judge argued that this approach departed from established Constitutional Court case-law (decisions 28/2011 and 40/2012) and that a person whose liberty had been restricted in possible violation of the Constitution suffered prejudice that was not cured by subsequent substitution of a milder measure.

In the interim the applicant had lodged habeas-corpus applications. One was dismissed; another, after the investigation ended and the case was sent for trial, resulted in the District Court ordering house arrest with electronic surveillance on 19 June 2014. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but suspended the sentence (8 April 2015), leading to her release. Subsequent Supreme Court and Constitutional Court proceedings ultimately confirmed that outcome.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the first-instance and appellate courts had not given relevant and sufficient reasons capable of justifying the applicant’s detention and that these deficiencies had not been remedied by the Supreme Court or the Constitutional Court. The case concerns Orkhan Ayyubzade, a young Azerbaijani opposition activist and NIDA civic movement member who posted government criticisms on social media. In December 2013 he organised an unauthorised protest against bureaucratic injustices, receiving 18 days’ administrative detention. He alleged repeated ill-treatment there (handcuffing, beatings), which media reports corroborated. In May 2014, after attending a protest against the conviction of other NIDA members, he received a further 20-day administrative sentence at the same facility.

On 15 May 2014, while still serving that sentence, officers recorded that they handcuffed him for two hours for disciplinary breaches (loud talking, arguing, disobeying orders). The applicant stated he had merely requested a telephone call; officers then took him to an office, stripped him naked, beat him, threatened rape and placed him in solitary confinement while handcuffed. Several detainees allegedly witnessed the events.

His administrative term expired on 26 May 2014. Instead of release he was taken to the prosecutor’s office, arrested as a suspect and charged under Article 315.1 of the Criminal Code (resistance to or violence against a public official not endangering life or health). The decision relied solely on a police report that he had violently resisted three named officers that morning. When questioned he repeated his ill-treatment account, named witnesses, offered torn underwear as evidence and asked for CCTV footage from the detention unit. He also recalled earlier, publicly reported ill-treatment at the same facility.

On 27 May the district court ordered one month’s pre-trial detention, citing the gravity of the charge, the alleged public threat, a risk of obstruction and forensic notes of “non-classifiable” injuries on two officers. The applicant appealed, arguing there was no reasonable suspicion: the only evidence came from the very officers he accused of covering up their own violence, he himself had documented injuries, and CCTV had not been produced. The appeal court upheld detention on similar generic grounds plus a risk of absconding.

The investigator granted a request for the video recordings, but the facility’s chief replied that cameras had been removed for renovation and in any event lacked storage capacity. Detention was extended by one month on 24 June on the same stereotyped reasons; further appeals failed. A July request for house arrest—citing completed investigative steps, police witnesses, the applicant’s student status, family dependence and illness—was refused without addressing those points.

After the extension expired on 26 July the applicant remained in custody without a fresh court order until his trial began in August. Requests to declare that period unlawful and to substitute house arrest were dismissed. He was convicted in October 2014 and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment (later pardoned in March 2015).

These facts—his known opposition role, the immediate conversion of an ending administrative sentence into a criminal charge, exclusive reliance on the implicated officers’ statements, unexamined CCTV, documented injuries on both sides, and formulaic detention justifications—form the core of the alleged Article 5 (and Article 18) violations.

**Case Summary: Georgiou v. Greece (ECHR, Application no. 57378/18, Judgment of 14 March 2023)**

This European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) case concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair hearing in criminal proceedings). The core issue is the Greek Court of Cassation’s failure to examine or give reasons for tacitly refusing the applicant’s request that it seek a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) under Article 267 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). The ECHR also addressed execution of its judgment under Article 46, noting that reopening of domestic proceedings could allow examination of the preliminary reference request if sought.

The applicant, Andreas Georgiou (born 1960, residing in the United States), served as President of the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT) from August 2010 to August 2015. On 10 November 2010, he transmitted revised Greek fiscal deficit data for 2009 to Eurostat without first presenting it to ELSTAT’s seven-member administrative board for approval. He maintained that this complied with the principle of professional independence in the European Statistics Code of Practice (Principle 1.4), which assigns the head of the national statistical institute “sole responsibility” for decisions on statistical methods, standards, procedures, content, and timing of releases. Principle 1.4 states: “The heads of the National Statistical Institutes and of Eurostat and, where appropriate, the heads of other statistical authorities have the sole responsibility for deciding on statistical methods, standards and procedures, and on the content and timing of statistical releases.”

Criminal proceedings were brought against him for breach of official duty. On 6 December 2016, the three-member Athens Criminal Court acquitted him of three charges: (i) continuing to hold a position at the International Monetary Fund while serving at ELSTAT; (ii) failing to convene ELSTAT’s board from November 2010 to September 2011; and (iii) releasing the 2009 deficit data without first communicating it to or obtaining consent from the board, contrary to Article 10 § 2 A of Law no. 3832/2010 (which tasked ELSTAT with compiling and publishing official statistics as the “National Statistical Service” under EU Regulation 223/2009).

The prosecutor appealed. On 1 August 2017, the Athens Court of Appeal convicted him solely on the third charge (judgment nos. 3103/2017 and 4480/2017), finding he had intentionally transmitted the data without board communication or consent in order to gain an “illegal moral benefit” by strengthening his power as president, becoming a “quasi-one-person executive organ,” and usurping the board’s functions. He received a two-year suspended prison sentence.

The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. In a 21 March 2018 memorandum of additional grounds, he explicitly requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU on the interpretation of Principle 1.4 of the European Statistics Code of Practice if any doubt existed as to its meaning. He argued that failure to refer the question would violate his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 of the Convention.

On 7 June 2018, the Court of Cassation rejected the appeal (judgment no. 977/2018) without any reference to the request for a CJEU preliminary ruling. Relevant domestic and EU law, including Article 267 TFEU on preliminary references by national courts of last instance and prior ECHR case law (such as Gorou v. Greece (no. 2), Baydar v. the Netherlands, and Ilias Papageorgiou v. Greece), framed the obligation of highest courts to give reasons when declining to refer questions of EU law interpretation.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation: the Court of Cassation, as a court of last instance, neither examined nor reasoned its implicit refusal of a request that could have clarified a key EU-law provision central to the applicant’s defence (his professional independence and sole responsibility for statistical releases). The conviction rested on a domestic interpretation of ELSTAT’s duties that the applicant contended conflicted with directly applicable EU statistical independence rules. The ECHR’s judgment highlights this procedural omission as the focal point of unfairness, with Article 46 implications for potential reopening of the cassation proceedings to address the unanswered request.

The case of Deltuva v. Lithuania (Application no. 38144/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns restrictions on family visits imposed on a remand prisoner, alleged to violate Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life).

The applicant, Juozas Deltuva, was arrested on 17 November 2019 on suspicion of leading an organised group smuggling large quantities of drugs from the Netherlands to Lithuania and Russia. He was placed in pre-trial detention on 19 November 2019. Detention was repeatedly extended until his release under house arrest and electronic monitoring on 16 November 2020. Courts cited risks of absconding (international ties, prior German conviction, lack of habitual residence or work in Lithuania), interfering with the investigation (unidentified accomplices, coded phones and surveillance equipment found at his home and in his car), and committing further crimes (no lawful income yet substantial assets). While detained, the applicant twice obtained a mobile phone unlawfully.

On 20 November 2019 the prosecutor banned all visits and telephone calls except to the applicant’s lawyer and investigating officers. The decision, later extended, stated that many investigative steps remained, including identification of accomplices, so contact with others risked undermining the inquiry.

On 3 December 2019 the applicant requested a visit from his wife and ten-year-old daughter. The prosecutor refused on 11 December 2019, citing the seriousness of the charges, the organised nature of the alleged offences and the unfinished investigation. Appeals to a senior prosecutor and the Vilnius District Court failed.

A further request on 7 February 2020 enclosed a psychologist’s report: the daughter, who had witnessed the arrest, exhibited severe stress possibly amounting to post-traumatic stress disorder and needed to see her father to restore her sense of security. One visit was authorised on 17 February 2020.

Subsequent requests (28 February, 26 March and 22 May 2020) sought visits, or a visit with the daughter only, in the presence of the applicant’s lawyer. Each was refused. The prosecutor relied on the gravity of the suspected crimes, the courts’ earlier findings of interference risk, the continuing investigation with unidentified suspects, the applicant’s unauthorised acquisition of phones (showing disregard for rules), and the view that a lawyer’s presence would not prevent information transfer. The prosecutor also noted that the applicant had previously spent most of his time abroad and therefore had not seen his daughter regularly; the single granted visit rendered further restrictions proportionate. The applicant’s appeals, arguing lack of evidence of any actual interference, the family’s non-involvement in the case, the possibility of supervised visits, and the child’s best interests, were dismissed, the last decision being issued on 2 July 2020.

On 20 August 2020 the prosecutor, while maintaining that the investigation remained incomplete and the applicant uncooperative, found no information suggesting that visits with his wife and daughter would affect the inquiry. Two monthly contactless visits were therefore permitted. Video calls were later allowed (16 October 2020). The pre-trial investigation concluded in April 2022; proceedings were still pending when observations were filed.

Domestic law authorised prosecutors to prohibit visits if they might prejudice an investigation, while providing for contactless visits in the presence of staff and, under conditions, unsupervised contact visits. The applicant contended that the near-total ban for the first nine months of detention was not “necessary in a democratic society,” that the authorities had not demonstrated a concrete risk of interference through his family, and that they had failed to consider less restrictive alternatives expressly contemplated by Lithuanian law.
