On 17 November 2019, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of leading an organised group smuggling large quantities of drugs from the Netherlands to Lithuania and Russia. He was formally notified of the charges the next day. On 19 November 2019, the Vilnius District Court ordered his remand in detention for three months, a decision upheld on appeal. The courts cited a risk of absconding given the potential lengthy sentence, the applicant’s strong foreign ties (frequent time in the Netherlands, claimed work in Germany, prior German conviction), lack of Lithuanian employment for nine years, and absence of habitual residence there. They also identified a risk of interfering with the investigation, as not all suspects had been identified, numerous measures remained outstanding, and coded communication devices plus surveillance equipment had been found in his home and car. Further, his lack of lawful income despite owning substantial property suggested possible continued criminal activity. Detention was repeatedly extended on similar grounds through August 2020; later decisions also noted that the applicant had twice unlawfully obtained a mobile phone while detained.

On 20 November 2019, the prosecutor banned all visits and telephone calls except those with his lawyer and investigating officers. The stated reason was the ongoing investigation and incomplete identification of accomplices; contact with others risked undermining the probe. This restriction was extended several times.

On 3 December 2019 the applicant requested a visit from his wife and ten-year-old daughter. The prosecutor refused on 11 December, citing the seriousness of the organised-crime allegations and the still-pending investigation. Appeals failed.

A fresh request on 7 February 2020 enclosed a psychologist’s report. The daughter, who had witnessed the arrest, was experiencing severe stress possibly amounting to post-traumatic stress disorder; she described her father as central to her life and said she needed at least brief contact to confirm he was alive. The psychologist urged an immediate visit to restore her sense of security. One visit was granted on 17 February 2020.

Three further requests (28 February, 26 March and 22 May 2020) sought visits with both family members or the daughter alone, in the presence of the applicant’s lawyer. All were refused. The prosecutor reiterated the risk of interference (coordination with suspects, witness tampering or evidence destruction), the incomplete investigation, the two illicit mobile phones, and the view that a lawyer’s presence would not prevent information transfer. He added that the single prior visit already satisfied proportionality and that the applicant’s earlier frequent absences abroad meant contact with his daughter had not been regular. Appeals to a senior prosecutor and the Vilnius District Court were dismissed, the last on 2 July 2020.

The applicant argued there was no evidence he had ever used his family to obstruct the investigation, that his wife and daughter had no connection to the case, that the illicit phones had been used only to speak to his daughter, and that supervised visits (with a lawyer or officer present) were available under domestic law yet had not been considered.

On 20 August 2020 the prosecutor authorised two monthly contactless visits with the wife and daughter, finding no indication those specific visits would harm the investigation, while maintaining the general ban on other contacts. Video calls were later permitted. The applicant was released under electronic monitoring on 16 November 2020; criminal proceedings remained pending as of mid-2022.

Domestic law (Article 22 of the Law on Execution of Pre-trial Detention) permitted visits unless a written prosecutorial or judicial instruction was issued to protect the investigation. Unlimited three-hour visits were the norm, normally supervised and non-contact; monthly family contact visits and, after two weeks, unsupervised overnight visits were also possible.

The Court later found that the near-total restriction during the first nine months of detention—resulting in only one visit—had not been shown to be necessary, as the authorities failed to substantiate any concrete risk arising from contact with the family and did not properly examine less restrictive alternatives.
001-223656:
The ECHR case Rogalski v. Poland (no. 5420/16) concerned disciplinary sanctions imposed on Polish lawyer Rafał Rogalski for lodging a criminal notification accusing a prosecutor of bribery. On 20 January 2011, acting for a client company, the applicant filed a formal notification stating there existed sufficient data to justify suspicion that prosecutor M.P. had accepted a bribe (an offence under Article 228 § 1 of the Criminal Code) from unknown persons, probably employees of a named company. This was linked to an investigation into alleged forging of contracts harming the client. The applicant claimed his evidence requests had not been examined promptly, other shortcomings had occurred, and the investigation had been “prematurely and unjustifiably” discontinued for lack of evidence without any forensic expert reports being obtained. He viewed this “irrational decision” as explainable only by bribery. The notification gave no further details on the alleged bribe-givers.

On 28 January 2011 the Warsaw-Centre District Prosecutor refused to open an inquiry, stating that the applicant had adduced no evidence or factual circumstances substantiating bribery. No appeal followed. On 11 May 2011 the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor notified the Dean of the Warsaw Regional Bar Council to examine possible ethics breaches.

On 23 November 2012 the Bar’s disciplinary officer charged the applicant with failing to act with moderation in making, in a professional capacity, a criminal complaint without “reasonable suspicions.” At a hearing the applicant repeated his claims, adding that his client (convinced of bribery) had requested the filing, and that he had accompanied the client to unspecified meetings in 2009–2010 with Central Anticorruption Bureau (CAB) officers who expressed interest; he provided no dates, names or further particulars.

On 13 November 2013 the Disciplinary Court of the Warsaw Bar Association found the applicant guilty of lodging the complaint without “any evidence whatsoever or any objectively verifiable circumstances” that could justify the suspicion, in breach of section 80 of the Bar Act read with paragraphs 14 and 17 of the Lawyer’s Code of Professional Ethics. It examined the notification’s language, content and context, plus the client’s testimony (which denied any knowledge, discussion or suspicion of a bribe, stated he would never claim M.P. had taken money, and could not recall specifically instructing the filing, though it was not against his will). The applicant’s inability to particularise the CAB meetings was also noted. The court held that a lawyer’s freedom of expression is restricted to protect others from unjustified attacks; lawyers must display moderation, proportionality and caution, avoid unsubstantiated complaints, identify sources and use the conditional tense. The applicant’s language was found contrary to these duties and derogatory to the prosecutor and the prosecution service as a whole.

The applicant was fined the equivalent of twenty basic Bar contributions (2,400 PLN / approx. €535) and banned from acting as a professional tutor for one year. The High Disciplinary Court of the Bar upheld the decision on 27 September 2014, stressing that a lawyer must observe ethics independently of a client’s wishes. The Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded on 8 July 2015. In 2016 the applicant was additionally charged 1,000 PLN in costs.

These events formed the basis of the alleged Article 10 violation (unjustified disciplinary sanctioning of a lawyer’s expression).

The case of Rogalski v. Poland (Application no. 5420/16) concerns disciplinary proceedings against Polish lawyer Rafał Rogalski for filing a criminal complaint against a prosecutor, which he alleged violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

On 20 January 2011, Rogalski, acting for a client company, submitted a formal notification of a crime to prosecutors. It accused prosecutor M.P. of bribery under Article 228 § 1 of the Criminal Code, stating that “data exists to sufficiently justify a suspicion” that M.P. had accepted a bribe from unknown persons, probably employees of a named company. Rogalski linked this to an ongoing investigation into alleged forging of contracts harming his client. He claimed his evidence requests had not been examined promptly, other shortcomings occurred, and the investigation was “prematurely and unjustifiably” discontinued for lack of evidence without obtaining expert reports. He argued the only explanation for this “irrational decision” was that M.P. had been bribed. The notification provided no details of the alleged bribe-givers beyond the company name.

On 28 January 2011 the Warsaw-Centre District Prosecutor refused to open an inquiry, finding that Rogalski had adduced no evidence or factual circumstances supporting bribery. No appeal followed.

On 11 May 2011 the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor informed the Dean of the Warsaw Regional Bar Council of the complaint to determine whether Rogalski had breached professional ethics. On 23 November 2012 the disciplinary officer charged him with failing to act with moderation in lodging a criminal complaint without “reasonable suspicions.”

At a hearing the same day, Rogalski repeated the complaint’s contents and noted that M.P. had closed the forgery investigation without a forensic document examiner’s report. His client’s representative had requested the complaint, convinced M.P. had been bribed. Rogalski mentioned accompanying his client to meetings with Central Anticorruption Bureau (CAB) officers, who expressed interest, but gave no dates (placing them vaguely in 2009–2010), names, or further details.

On 13 November 2013 the Disciplinary Court of the Warsaw Bar Association found Rogalski guilty of filing the complaint without “any evidence whatsoever or any objectively verifiable circumstances” justifying the suspicion, in breach of section 80 of the Bar Act and paragraphs 14 and 17 of the Lawyer’s Code of Professional Ethics. The court examined the complaint’s language, content and context, plus the client’s testimony (who denied seeing or hearing of any bribe, discussing it with CAB, or suspecting money was given to prosecutors, and could not confirm specifically instructing the filing). Rogalski could not specify CAB meeting dates or agent names. The court concluded his account was uncorroborated.

It held that a lawyer’s freedom of expression is limited to protect others from unjustified attacks. Rogalski had a duty to act with moderation, proportionality and caution, avoid unsubstantiated complaints, indicate sources and use the conditional tense. His language violated these rules and was derogatory to M.P. and the prosecutor’s office. He was fined 2,400 PLN (approximately EUR 535, equivalent to 20 basic bar contributions) and banned from acting as a professional tutor for one year.

The High Disciplinary Court of the Bar upheld the decision on 27 September 2014, stressing that lawyers must abide by ethics regardless of client wishes. On 8 July 2015 the Supreme Court’s Criminal Chamber dismissed Rogalski’s cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded. In October 2016 he was ordered to pay PLN 1,000 in proceedings costs.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 10 violation arising from the sanction for the complaint.

The ECHR case Rogalski v. Poland (no. 5420/16) arose from disciplinary sanctions imposed on Polish lawyer Rafał Rogalski for filing a criminal notification against a prosecutor, alleged to breach Article 10 (freedom of expression).

On 20 January 2011, Rogalski notified authorities on behalf of his client that prosecutor M.P. had likely accepted a bribe (Criminal Code Art. 228 § 1) from unknown persons, probably employees of a named company. This related to an investigation of forged contracts harming the client. Rogalski claimed M.P. had discontinued the probe prematurely without expert reports or prompt evidence review, an “irrational” act only explicable by bribery. The notification named no specific bribers or details.

On 28 January 2011 the Warsaw-Centre District Prosecutor refused to open an inquiry, finding no evidence or circumstances supporting the claim. No appeal followed.

On 11 May 2011 the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor referred the matter to the Warsaw Bar Council for possible ethics breaches. On 23 November 2012 the disciplinary officer charged Rogalski with failing to act with moderation (umiar) by lodging a complaint lacking “reasonable suspicions.”

Heard that day, Rogalski repeated his allegations and mentioned accompanying his client to unspecified CAB meetings (circa 2009–2010) where agents showed interest, but gave no dates or names. His client later testified he had neither seen/heard of any bribe nor discussed one with the CAB, did not specifically instruct the filing, and would never accuse M.P. of taking money, though he had not opposed the lawyer’s action.

On 13 November 2013 the Warsaw Bar Association Disciplinary Court found Rogalski guilty of filing a complaint without “any evidence whatsoever or any objectively verifiable circumstances,” breaching Bar Act s. 80 and Lawyer’s Code of Professional Ethics paras. 14 and 17. It analysed the complaint’s language, content and context, noted the client’s denials and Rogalski’s inability to corroborate CAB contacts, and concluded his account was uncorroborated. Lawyers’ expression, the court held, is more restricted than the general constitutional right in order to protect others from unjustified attacks; they must act with moderation, proportionality and caution, avoid unsubstantiated claims, cite sources and use the conditional tense. Rogalski’s language was found contrary to these duties and derogatory to M.P. and the prosecution service.

He was fined 20 basic bar contributions (PLN 2,400 / ≈ EUR 535) and banned from acting as a professional tutor for one year. The High Disciplinary Court of the Bar upheld the decision on 27 September 2014, stressing that lawyers must observe ethics irrespective of client wishes. The Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded on 8 July 2015. Rogalski was later charged PLN 1,000 in costs.

These events underpin the alleged Article 10 violation: an unjustified disciplinary sanction imposed without relevant and sufficient reasons, overstepping the State’s margin of appreciation.
001-223709:
The case of Szolcsán v. Hungary concerns alleged discrimination against a Roma child through his enrollment in a segregated State primary school, violating the right to education. The applicant, Imre Szolcsán (born 2005, of Roma origin, residing in Piliscsaba), enrolled in 2013/14 at Jókai Mór primary school, the sole ordinary-curriculum State school in town and part of the Pilisvörösvár district. It was attended almost exclusively by Roma pupils, though Roma comprised only about 4% of the local population. The applicant alleged a poor curriculum, inadequate resources, and low progression rates: under 10% of completers advanced to secondary grammar school.

Two other local schools offered specialized curricula (Catholic Church-run and German-minority). Until 2013, Jókai Mór fell under the municipality, which acknowledged racial segregation, resolved to desegregate, and imposed an enrollment moratorium for 2012/13. From January 2013, the State-run Klebelsberg Institution Maintenance Centre assumed management; enrollments resumed in 2013/14 with just four first-year pupils.

On 17 July 2014 the applicant sought transfer to Dózsa György school (same district, neighboring town), citing suitability for his mild hearing impairment. It was five minutes away by public transport; 27 Piliscsaba children (about one-quarter of its roll) already attended. The headmaster rejected the request on 6 August 2014 because the applicant lived outside the catchment area.

The applicant appealed to the district authority on 22 August 2014, claiming the refusal stemmed from his Roma origin and denied him inclusive education under s. 8(e) of the 2003 Equal Treatment Act. The appeal was dismissed on 8 September 2014: Jókai Mór was geographically closest and in his best interests; the two other Piliscsaba schools were now alternatives; and its curriculum was adequate.

He sought judicial review on 14 October 2014 before the Budapest Surroundings Administrative and Labour Court, alleging segregation and ethnic discrimination. The court dismissed the claim on 20 January 2015, holding that the headmaster had properly exercised discretion on location grounds.

A petition to the Kúria on 7 April 2015 reiterated discrimination and the best-interest value of inclusive education (ss. 7(3) and 8(e)). It was dismissed on 2 September 2015: the applicant had misconstrued the right to choose a school; headmasters retain discretion over out-of-catchment admissions; daily travel constituted an undue burden; and attendance at the same catchment school as other Roma children did not amount to segregation. The Kúria noted that no complaint had been made to the Equal Treatment Authority.

A constitutional complaint filed on 7 December 2015 (right to education free from discrimination) was refused by the Constitutional Court on 5 July 2016 as raising no constitutional issue.

The Equal Treatment Act prohibits ethnic-origin discrimination and unlawful educational segregation. The National Public Education Act recognizes a student’s right to request transfer and parents’ right to choose a school, subject to headmaster approval of admissions. These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations of Article 14 (non-discrimination) taken with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education).

**Case Summary: Szolcsán v. Hungary (Application no. 24408/16)**

The case concerns alleged racial segregation and discrimination in education against a Roma child in Hungary. The applicant, Imre Szolcsán (born 2005), a Hungarian national of Roma ethnic origin living in Piliscsaba, enrolled in the 2013/14 school year at Jókai Mór primary school. This was the only ordinary-curriculum state school in the town (part of the Pilisvörösvár educational district). Although Roma constituted only about 4% of Piliscsaba’s population, the school was attended almost exclusively by Roma children. The applicant alleged that the school offered a poor curriculum with insufficient material and human resources; 2013 data showed that fewer than 10% of pupils completing eight years there progressed to a secondary grammar school.

Two other schools operated in Piliscsaba with specialised curricula: one run by the Catholic Church and one by the local German minority self-government. Until 2013 the Jókai Mór school fell under municipal authority, which had acknowledged its racial segregation, passed a desegregation resolution and imposed a moratorium on new enrolments for 2012/13. From January 2013 responsibility transferred to the state-run Klebelsberg Institution Maintenance Centre (under the Ministry of Human Resources). Enrolments then resumed, with only four pupils entering year one in 2013/14.

On 17 July 2014 the applicant applied to transfer to Dózsa György school in a neighbouring town within the same educational district, citing a mild hearing impairment that would be better addressed there. Approximately 27 children from Piliscsaba already attended Dózsa György (about one-quarter of its pupils), and the school was only five minutes away by public transport. The headmaster rejected the request on 6 August 2014 solely because the applicant lived outside the school’s catchment area.

The applicant appealed to the Pilisvörösvár educational district, arguing that the refusal constituted ethnic discrimination and denied him racially inclusive education (relying on section 8(e) of the 2003 Equal Treatment Act). The district dismissed the appeal on 8 September 2014, stating that Jókai Mór was geographically closest and thus in his best interest; it noted that the two specialised Piliscsaba schools had since joined the district and that Jókai Mór’s curriculum was adequate.

A request for judicial review before the Budapest Surroundings Administrative and Labour Court was dismissed on 20 January 2015: the headmaster had properly exercised discretion and location was the decisive factor. A further petition to the Kúria (Hungary’s highest court) was dismissed on 2 September 2015. The Kúria held that the right to choose a school did not entitle a pupil to admission at a specific institution; daily travel would impose an inappropriate burden; the applicant belonged to the same catchment area as other Roma children, so the school’s ethnic composition did not amount to segregation; and he had not first complained to the Equal Treatment Authority. A constitutional complaint was refused by the Constitutional Court on 5 July 2016 as raising no issue of constitutionality.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that he had been subjected to de facto racial segregation in a state school, contrary to the prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 of the Convention) taken together with the right to education (Article 2 of Protocol No. 1). He argued that the authorities had failed to take adequate desegregation measures, thereby perpetuating factual inequality. Domestic courts had consistently upheld the catchment-area rule and administrative discretion without addressing the systemic ethnic concentration or the quality of education provided. The European Court later found a violation, holding that the state had not justified the situation and that individual and general measures (including ending segregation at the specific school and developing an anti-segregation education policy) were required under Article 46.

The case of Szolcsán v. Hungary (Application no. 24408/16) concerns a complaint by Imre Szolcsán, a Hungarian national of Roma origin born in 2005 and resident in Piliscsaba. Represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, he alleged discriminatory segregation in education contrary to Article 14 of the Convention (prohibition of discrimination) taken with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education).

In the 2013/14 school year, the applicant enrolled at Jókai Mór primary school, the sole ordinary-curriculum State school in Piliscsaba (part of the Pilisvörösvár educational district). The school was attended almost exclusively by Roma children, despite Roma comprising only about 4% of the town’s population. The applicant described the curriculum as poor and material/human resources as inadequate; 2013 data showed that fewer than 10% of its graduates proceeded to secondary grammar school. Two other local schools offered specialised curricula: one run by the Catholic Church and one by the local German minority self-government.

Until 2013 the school fell under municipal authority, which had itself acknowledged racial segregation, passed a desegregation resolution and imposed a 2012/13 enrolment moratorium. From January 2013 responsibility transferred to the State-run Klebelsberg Institution Maintenance Centre. Enrolments then resumed; only four pupils entered year one in 2013/14.

Citing a mild hearing impairment, the applicant sought transfer in July 2014 to Dózsa György school (same district, five minutes away by public transport). Twenty-seven Piliscsaba children already attended that school. The headmaster refused on 6 August 2014 because the applicant lived outside its catchment area. An appeal to the educational district was dismissed on 8 September 2014: Jókai Mór was geographically closest and therefore in the child’s best interests; the two specialised Piliscsaba schools were now district alternatives; and the curriculum at Jókai Mór was deemed adequate.

Judicial review before the Budapest Surroundings Administrative and Labour Court failed on 20 January 2015 (headmaster’s discretion properly exercised; location decisive). The Kúria dismissed a further petition on 2 September 2015, holding that the right to choose a school did not confer a right of admission to a particular institution, that daily travel constituted an undue burden, and that the school’s Roma majority simply reflected the shared catchment area rather than unlawful segregation. The applicant had not first complained to the Equal Treatment Authority. A subsequent constitutional complaint was refused by the Constitutional Court on 5 July 2016 as raising no constitutional issue.

Domestic law invoked included Act CXXV of 2003 (Equal Treatment Act), which prohibits direct discrimination on grounds of ethnic origin and specifically outlaws unlawful segregation in educational institutions or the maintenance of sub-standard schooling that denies a reasonable chance of preparing for State examinations. Act CXC of 2011 (National Public Education Act) recognises pupils’ right to request transfer and parents’ right to choose a school, while requiring an interoperable school system.

Contextual materials underscored the systemic dimension. ECRI’s 2015 report on Hungary recorded that more than 20% of Roma pupils attended de facto segregated (non-special) schools following a lighter curriculum and providing inferior education; it recommended a national anti-segregation policy. Piliscsaba’s own 2013–18 Equal Opportunities Programme identified several Jókai Mór classes as segregated and proposed eliminating them while better utilising the building’s 230-pupil capacity (then occupied by fewer than 50 children).

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the authorities had failed to correct a situation of ethnic segregation, thereby denying him racially inclusive education of adequate quality. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 14 taken with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 and indicated, under Article 46, both individual measures to end segregation at the specific school and general measures to develop and implement an anti-segregation policy in education.
001-223919:
The case of Radonjić and Romić v. Serbia (Application no. 43674/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns two former Serbian secret police officers arrested on 14 January 2014 on suspicion of murdering journalist Slavko Ćuruvija in 1999. The applicants, Milan Radonjić and Ratko Romić, were held in pre-trial detention until 6 July 2017 (thereafter under house arrest). They alleged violations of Article 5 § 3 (unreasonable length of pre-trial detention without sufficient justification) and Article 5 § 4 (unduly lengthy review of detention lawfulness by the Constitutional Court). They also raised issues under Article 34 regarding victim status, as the Constitutional Court’s acknowledgment of a breach lacked compensation.

Ćuruvija, a critic of Slobodan Milošević, was shot in the back outside his Belgrade home on 11 April 1999 amid state media accusations of supporting NATO. The killing drew international condemnation. Renewed attention followed a 2013 government commission on journalist murders and a public campaign that highlighted forgotten cases.

A pre-trial judge ordered initial 30-day detention citing reasonable suspicion (based on intercepts, witnesses, and evidence), risk of absconding (applicants’ intelligence training in false identities and a co-suspect at large, despite family ties), risk of influencing witnesses (former colleagues), and public-order preservation (intense public and media focus). Extensions followed on similar grounds through mid-2014. After the applicants were charged with aggravated murder on 6 June 2014 and witnesses were interviewed, the Court of Appeal reduced some risks but upheld detention for public order.

Subsequent High Court extensions (initially 30 days, later 60 days) repeatedly invoked public order: the crime’s brutality (a journalist assassinated by high-ranking officers to protect a regime), its ongoing shock to Serbia and its international reputation, and the risk that release would be seen as acquittal, disturbing proceedings. The Court of Appeal frequently quashed these for insufficient concrete evidence of a persisting threat, citing ECHR precedents (Letellier v. France; Tomasi v. France) requiring facts showing actual public-order disturbance rather than abstract gravity. Remittals occurred, but the High Court reissued similar orders, which were sometimes upheld. The indictment was confirmed in March 2015; 83 hearings followed with over 100 witnesses. Applications for release were rejected.

The Constitutional Court, in multiple rulings on the applicants’ 27 appeals, applied ECHR criteria and found the initial detention period (14 January 2014 to 3 April 2015) justified. For the subsequent period (to 6 July 2017), however, it held that courts had failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons. It dismissed non-pecuniary damage claims, ruling that the finding of a violation itself constituted just satisfaction, while noting possible (but unestablished) claims under the Code of Criminal Procedure if conditions were met. Constitutional Court reviews of some appeals lasted over two years.

In April 2019 the applicants were convicted of aggravated murder (sentences of 30 and 20 years). The Court of Appeal quashed this in 2020; a 2021 retrial conviction (same sentences) remained on appeal as of August 2022, with the applicants still under house arrest.

Domestic law included the Civil Obligations Act (state liability for liberty breaches), the Constitutional Court Act (final decisions; damages awards possible since 2012), and the Code of Criminal Procedure (detention grounds including public order for serious offences; compensation for “wrongful” deprivation, interpreted by some as limited to procedural time-limit excesses rather than Convention rights). Constitutional Court practice treated it as having exclusive jurisdiction over damages for rights violations it established. These facts underpinned the alleged failures to justify prolonged detention after April 2015 and to provide speedy review, plus inadequate redress.

The applicants, former Serbian secret police officers Milan Radonjić and Ratko Romić, were arrested on 14 January 2014 on suspicion of involvement (with two co-suspects) in the 11 April 1999 murder of journalist Slavko Ćuruvija, a prominent critic of the Milošević regime whose killing had attracted international condemnation. A 2013 government commission and public-awareness campaign had revived media attention to the unsolved case. On 15 January 2014 a High Court pre-trial judge ordered their detention for 30 days, citing reasonable suspicion (based on intercepts, witnesses and other evidence), a high risk of absconding (as trained intelligence officers able to cross borders under false identities, with one suspect still at large), a risk of influencing former-colleague witnesses, and the need to preserve public order given intense public interest. Appeals chambers repeatedly upheld extensions on these grounds.

The public prosecutor charged them with aggravated murder on 6 June 2014. Thereafter the High Court continued 30-day (later 60-day) extensions, initially retaining all three grounds but, after witnesses had been heard, relying solely on public order. It reasoned that the crime—a daylight assassination of a journalist by secret-police officers to protect the former regime—had shocked Serbia, damaged its international standing and would provoke strong public reaction (equated by some with acquittal) if the applicants were released, thereby prejudicing the administration of justice. The Court of Appeal repeatedly quashed several of these orders as insufficiently reasoned or abstract (failing to show an actual, current threat to public order after many months, contrary to ECHR case-law such as Letellier and Tomasi) and remitted them; the High Court then reissued virtually identical orders, which were eventually upheld. Eighty-three trial hearings were held and more than 100 witnesses heard. Applications for release were rejected. Detention ended on 6 July 2017 when the applicants were placed under house arrest (a decision ultimately upheld after a further remittal). They remained under house arrest at least until August 2022.

The applicants lodged 27 constitutional appeals against the initial detention order and every extension. In a series of decisions the Constitutional Court, applying ECHR criteria, held that detention from 14 January 2014 to 3 April 2015 had been justified, but that from 3 April 2015 until 6 July 2017 (more than two years) the ordinary courts had failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons. It therefore found a violation of the equivalent of Article 5 § 3. It refused to award non-pecuniary damages, stating that the finding itself constituted sufficient just satisfaction and noting (without deciding) that a claim might still be possible under the Code of Criminal Procedure if its conditions were met. One representative constitutional appeal (lodged 28 May 2015) was decided only on 21 December 2017.

In April 2019 the High Court convicted both applicants (and the two co-accused) of aggravated murder and imposed sentences of 30 and 20 years. The Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in July 2020 and ordered a retrial. A fresh conviction with the same sentences was delivered on 2 December 2021; appeals remained pending. Domestic law (Civil Obligations Act, Constitutional Court Act as amended in 2012, and Code of Criminal Procedure) provides for State liability and Constitutional Court awards of damages for human-rights violations, but the Constitutional Court’s own case-law asserts exclusive jurisdiction over such claims once it has found a violation, and legal literature indicates that the Code’s “wrongful deprivation of liberty” provisions do not cover excessive but otherwise lawful pre-trial detention.

These facts underpin the complaints that the overall length of pre-trial detention (particularly the second, insufficiently reasoned period) violated Article 5 § 3, that the Constitutional Court’s review of lawfulness took more than two years in breach of Article 5 § 4, and that the applicants remained victims under Article 34 because the acknowledgment of the Article 5 § 3 breach was unaccompanied by any compensation and no clear, established domestic avenue existed for obtaining adequate redress.

The case concerns two former Serbian secret-service officers, Milan Radonjić and Ratko Romić, arrested on 14 January 2014 on suspicion of involvement in the April 1999 assassination of journalist Slavko Ćuruvija. The killing, widely viewed as politically motivated, generated renewed public attention after a 2013 government commission and media campaign. The applicants remained in pre-trial detention until 6 July 2017, when they were transferred to house arrest; criminal proceedings were still pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

Detention was initially ordered for 30 days by a pre-trial judge of the Belgrade High Court’s Organised-Crime Department. The judge cited three grounds: a high risk of flight (the applicants’ training in clandestine travel and the fact that a co-suspect remained at large), a risk of influencing witnesses (numerous former colleagues had yet to be heard), and the need to preserve public order given the case’s notoriety. Subsequent extensions, first for 30 days and later for 60 days, repeated these justifications, although the flight and witness-interference risks were progressively discounted once statements had been taken and the indictment confirmed in March 2015.

From April 2015 onward the sole remaining ground was public order. The High Court repeatedly asserted that release of former intelligence officers accused of assassinating a prominent critic would provoke public unrest and undermine the administration of justice. The Court of Appeal in Belgrade remitted several of these decisions, finding the reasoning formulaic and insufficiently linked to concrete facts capable of showing that release would actually disturb order. Nevertheless, detention continued to be prolonged on essentially the same language until July 2017.

The applicants lodged 27 constitutional appeals challenging each detention order. In a series of rulings beginning in June 2017 the Constitutional Court accepted that detention had been justified until 3 April 2015 but held that, thereafter, the ordinary courts had failed to supply relevant and sufficient reasons. It refused to award non-pecuniary damages, stating that the mere finding of a violation constituted adequate redress and noting that compensation might theoretically be sought under the Code of Criminal Procedure once the criminal case became final. Domestic law, however, provided no clear, established avenue for such a claim while proceedings remained pending, and later Constitutional Court case-law indicated that only that court itself could award damages for Convention breaches it had itself established.

The applicants also complained that the Constitutional Court’s review of the lawfulness of their detention had itself lasted more than two years. They argued that the combination of an unjustified second period of detention exceeding two years and the absence of compensation rendered them victims of a violation of Article 5 § 3, while the delay in constitutional review violated Article 5 § 4.

001-223982:
The ECHR case Drozd v. Poland (App. no. 15158/19, judgment of 6 April 2023) concerned a one-year ban on two Polish nationals, Paweł Drozd and Dagmara Drozd, members of the informal civic movement Obywatele RP (known for political protests), from entering the Sejm. This arose from their display of a banner during a 22 June 2017 peaceful demonstration against planned judicial reforms, held outside Sejm grounds. The applicants had obtained single-entry passes to observe the parliamentary debate. Upon entering the grounds, they unrolled a banner reading “Defend Independent Courts.” They maintained they posed no traffic danger (no vehicles or pedestrians present) and acted passively solely to convey their message to parliamentarians. The Government contended that the Parliament Security Service instructed them to behave consistently with their visit’s purpose, but they refused, blocking an internal road and creating a hazard.

The applicants were immediately escorted from the grounds and required to return their passes. By letters of 14 July 2017 (received 31 July and 7 August 2017), the Head of the Parliament Security Service informed them of a ban on Sejm entry until 21 June 2018, citing disturbance of public order and non-compliance with security instructions. This measure derived from a 2008 Speaker’s ordinance allowing temporary bans in justified cases to maintain order and security, including for non-observance of regulations, disturbance of peace, or undermining the Sejm’s dignity.

On 30 August 2017, the applicants appealed to the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court, arguing the ordinance lacked foreseeability, clarity, and precision, and that the ban limited their constitutional right of access to public information (Article 61). The applicants, Paweł Drozd and Dagmara Drozd, took part on 22 June 2017 in a peaceful demonstration held outside the Sejm in protest against planned judicial reforms. The Government maintained that the Parliament Security Service had instructed them to act consistently with the purpose of their visit, that they had refused to comply, and that they had blocked an internal road, thereby creating a traffic hazard.

The applicants were immediately escorted from the grounds and required to surrender their passes. By letters dated 14 July 2017 (received on 31 July and 7 August respectively), they were informed that the Head of the Parliament Security Service had imposed a ban on their entry until 21 June 2018. It added that the Rules of Procedure of the Sejm conferred no general right on members of the public to attend sittings; access remained a matter for the competent parliamentary authorities.

**Case Summary: Dursun Aliyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 20216/14)**

The applicant, a former operations officer at the Binagadi District Police Office in Baku, was convicted in 2012 of drug dealing under Article 234.2 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He alleged that the criminal proceedings violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights due to conviction on fabricated or unreliable evidence, denial of an effective opportunity to challenge that evidence or adduce evidence in his favour, and lack of effective legal assistance during initial pre-trial questioning. The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) found a violation of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing).

The applicant claimed a conflict with police chiefs H.H. and A.M., who pressured him to resign after A.M.’s 2010 appointment; he was demoted in 2011. On 5 July 2011, Organised Crime Department (OCD) officer K.A. initiated an operation based on a statement by F.G., a driver with a prior conviction and alleged drug addict. F.G. reported that the applicant had offered to sell him drugs and agreed to act as a police-instructed “buyer.” In the presence of attesting witnesses D.G. and M.A., F.G. received two marked 10 AZN banknotes.

F.G. entered the applicant’s office (where retired officer B.B. was also present). Police, including K.A., later kicked the door open. F.G. handed over a package and a “Winston” cigarette containing marijuana-like substances, claiming he bought them from the applicant for 20 AZN. Officers searched the office, seized marijuana from a desk drawer (later confirmed as 0.7g dried marijuana; F.G.’s items totalled 1.3g, though a later expert report found only tobacco in the cigarette), and recovered the banknotes from the backyard. The applicant allegedly admitted the sale and throwing the notes out the window but refused to sign the search record. He later claimed F.G. was a paid police “agent” who produced the drugs in a setup; police then beat him at the OCD, causing injuries (bruises documented on 9 July 2011 at a detention facility) and forcing partial self-incriminating statements.

The applicant was questioned three times on 5–7 July 2011 without a lawyer of his choosing initially (a state-funded lawyer, Sh.A., later signed records but was inactive and removed). He admitted giving F.G. marijuana free of charge (from prior seizures or a detainee’s cigarette) in exchange for operational help, denying any sale or payment, and alleged ill-treatment. He was charged with drug dealing (and later abuse of authority, of which he was acquitted). Requests for fingerprint analysis of the banknotes and background checks on F.G., D.G., and M.A. (to probe their alleged “agent” status and prior involvement) were denied as irrelevant. A prosecutor refused to open an ill-treatment investigation, citing officer and witness denials plus a later medical report finding no lasting injuries; this was not challenged in time.

At trial in the Binagadi District Court, prosecution witnesses (F.G., D.G., M.A., B.B., and officers) gave inconsistent testimony contradicting pre-trial statements (e.g., on drug packaging, banknote location, F.G.’s presence, and events). M.A. had admitted at a pre-trial confrontation to being a paid “agent” (code-named “Yashar”) but recanted; F.G. used the nickname “Fedya.” The court read out pre-trial statements. Defence requests to exclude unreliable evidence (including self-incriminating statements, citing duress and injuries; original banknotes, which were never produced despite a court order; and attesting witnesses as biased/regular police collaborators) were largely rejected. The court convicted based on expert reports, selected testimonies, pre-trial records, and the applicant’s initial statements, ignoring contradictions and favourable evidence (e.g., B.B. denying seeing any sale).

On appeal, the Baku Court of Appeal reviewed “without judicial investigation” (no rehearing of witnesses or new evidence) and did not address reliability arguments or grant requests, upholding the conviction (later amending to transfer rather than destroy the banknotes). The Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal, including new claims about a discontinued related case involving F.G. and M.A. as “agents.” The ECtHR held that the applicant was deprived of an effective opportunity to challenge key evidence’s reliability, oppose its use, and adduce favourable evidence, with inadequate review of objections and unreasoned procedural decisions preventing higher-court challenges.

The applicant, a former police operations officer in Baku, alleged a longstanding conflict with superiors who pressured him to resign after a 2010 leadership change, leading to his 2011 demotion. On 5 July 2011, Organised Crime Department (OCD) officers, acting on a statement from F.G.—a previously convicted drug addict and purported police informant—conducted a sting. They provided F.G. with two marked 10 AZN banknotes to buy drugs from the applicant. F.G. entered the applicant’s office (where retired officer B.B. was also present). Police then kicked the door open; F.G. produced packages of marijuana (later confirmed as 1.3 g dried cannabis) that he claimed to have purchased for 20 AZN. Officers seized additional marijuana (0.7 g) from the applicant’s desk drawer and recovered the marked notes from the backyard. The applicant refused to sign the search record.

He was arrested, taken to the OCD, and questioned three times that day and the next without effective access to counsel of his choice. A state-appointed lawyer signed one record but was later removed for non-performance. The applicant initially gave partially self-incriminating statements: he admitted knowing F.G. as an informant, having previously given him small amounts of seized marijuana as “rewards,” and having provided F.G. marijuana free of charge that day (from prior seizures) while claiming the desk drugs came from a discarded cigarette. He later retracted these, asserting they were extracted through severe beating at the OCD that caused a tachycardia attack and documented bruises (behind ears, kidney area, ribs, shoulder) noted upon transfer to detention on 9 July 2011. A prosecutor declined to investigate ill-treatment, citing witness denials and a later medical report finding no remaining injuries and insufficient details for timing; the applicant did not challenge this decision in time.

Pre-trial, the applicant requested fingerprint analysis of the notes (denied as they had been handled by multiple people) and background checks on F.G. and attesting witnesses D.G. and M.A. (denied as irrelevant). Confrontations revealed contradictions. At trial, witnesses recanted or altered accounts: F.G. described different packaging and denied seeing notes thrown; D.G. and M.A. (who admitted prior attesting roles and, in M.A.’s case, being a paid agent under a code name) showed inconsistencies on locations of drugs/notes; B.B. denied witnessing any sale or payment; officers contradicted their own records on participation and details. The applicant argued F.G., D.G., and M.A. were paid agents used to frame him (citing M.A.’s statements, F.G.’s nickname “Fedya,” and regular police-office access), that F.G. was not searched beforehand, that originals of the notes were never produced despite court orders, and that his initial statements should be excluded as coerced. The trial court requested but received a denial that the three were registered secret collaborators; it rejected exclusion of statements (citing the unchallenged prosecutor decision) and ignored production of original notes.

On 5 June 2012 the first-instance court convicted the applicant of drug dealing (Article 234.2 Criminal Code), relying on the expert reports, pre-trial witness statements (read out and “confirmed”), officer testimony, B.B.’s partial account, and the applicant’s initial statements; it acquitted him of abuse of office. Appeals reiterated unreliability of evidence, ignored contradictions (e.g., on packaging, presence when notes were found, backyard drugs), and unaddressed requests. The Court of Appeal reviewed without rehearing witnesses or new evidence and upheld the conviction (later amending disposal of the notes). The Supreme Court dismissed cassation, including arguments that a discontinued later case against the applicant for disclosing agent identities supported the framing claim.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 6 violations: conviction on allegedly fabricated/unreliable evidence (unstested notes, unsearched informant, contradictory/agent-linked witnesses, unexcluded coerced statements); denial of effective opportunity to challenge that evidence or adduce favouring material (denied examinations, ignored originals, unread inconsistencies); and initial lack of effective legal assistance, with inadequate higher-court review of objections and unexplained procedural refusals.

**Case Summary: Dursun Aliyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 20216/14)**

The applicant, a former Azerbaijani police operations officer born in 1961, alleged unfair criminal proceedings under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the ECHR. He was convicted of drug dealing (illegal sale of marijuana) in 2012 and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He claimed the case was fabricated due to workplace conflicts with superiors who pressured him to resign after a 2010 leadership change; he was demoted in 2011. Key issues included conviction on unreliable/fabricated evidence, inability to effectively challenge it or adduce favorable evidence, and lack of effective legal assistance during initial pre-trial questioning.

On 5 July 2011, based on a statement from F.G. (a previously convicted driver and alleged paid police “agent” known as “Fedya”), the Organised Crime Department (OCD) conducted a sting. F.G. received two marked AZN 10 banknotes and entered the applicant’s office, where retired officer B.B. was present. Police then burst in, seized marijuana packages (totaling ~2g, confirmed by experts as dried marijuana, though a later report found only tobacco in one cigarette), and recovered the banknotes outside the window. The applicant refused to sign the search/seizure record. He claimed F.G. (whom he knew as a police informant) brought the drugs himself as a setup, that F.G. requested drugs during a conversation, and that police then fabricated the sale. He denied receiving/throwing money.

The applicant was arrested and questioned three times that day without a lawyer of his choice initially (a state-funded lawyer, later removed for inactivity, merely signed a record). He gave partially self-incriminating statements (admitting giving F.G. marijuana from seized drugs as a “reward” for informants, and finding some in a detainee’s cigarette), but later retracted them, alleging severe beating, a tachycardia attack, and coercion at the OCD (bruises documented on 9 July 2011 upon transfer to detention). A prosecutor refused to open an ill-treatment case based on officer/witness denials and a 2011 medical report noting no current injuries and unclear original documentation; the applicant did not timely challenge this.

Investigation requests (e.g., fingerprinting banknotes, checking F.G./attesting witnesses D.G. and M.A.’s backgrounds/prior involvement as “agents”) were denied as irrelevant. Witness statements (F.G., D.G., M.A., B.B., officers) contained inconsistencies on details like drug forms/packages, money handling, presence during seizures, and F.G.’s addiction/prior dealings. F.G. and M.A. (code-named “Yashar”) admitted or were alleged as police collaborators; M.A. made a vengeful remark in court.

At the 2011–2012 trial, witnesses contradicted pre-trial accounts (read out in court), with some claiming memory lapses. The defense argued a frame-up, cited inconsistencies (e.g., F.G. on marijuana packaging/money finding; B.B. denying seeing a sale), F.G.’s un-searched person, and requested: excluding unreliable witness testimony and coerced statements; producing original banknotes (ordered but never provided, as they remained at OCD); examining “agent” status (denied by authorities); and ill-treatment evidence. The court rejected exclusions (citing unchallenged prosecutor decision) and convicted based on experts, pre-trial statements, some testimony, and the applicant’s initial admissions, while acquitting on abuse of authority.

Appeals reiterated requests/arguments, including new details (e.g., D.G.’s other attestations, a discontinued 2012–2013 case against the applicant for disclosing “secrets” about F.G./M.A.). The Court of Appeal reviewed “without judicial investigation” (no new evidence/witnesses) and upheld, later amending banknote disposal. The Supreme Court dismissed as unfounded.

The ECHR found an Article 6 § 1 violation: the applicant lacked an effective opportunity to challenge key evidence reliability/probative value (e.g., banknotes, witnesses, statements), with inadequate judicial review of objections and insufficient reasons for procedural decisions, preventing higher-court challenges. (The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.)
001-224365:
The case of Ohanjanyan v. Armenia (Application no. 70665/11) concerns the death of the applicant’s son, T. Ohanjanyan, on 30 August 2007 during compulsory military service, and the ensuing investigation, engaging Article 2 of the ECHR (right to life) in both its substantive and procedural limbs.

T. Ohanjanyan was drafted in November 2006 and assigned to military unit no. 28418. The official account held that after evening roll-call he left for a nearby unit’s backup checkpoint, accidentally contacted guy-wires of an R-419 radio-relay antenna mast, and was fatally electrocuted. Junior Sergeant A.G. found the body after hearing moans, also received a shock from the wires but survived minor injury. The body was transferred for autopsy. The applicant disputed this version, citing unexplained injuries visible in photographs he took (missing teeth, head, ear, jaw and facial wounds not recorded in the autopsy), prior possible violence (a bloodshot eye, mention of a fight), and inconsistencies in the account of why T. was in the area late at night.

Criminal proceedings were opened the next day under Article 376 § 2 of the Criminal Code (negligence in military duties causing grave consequences). The investigation was marked by serious shortcomings. Night-time scene inspection was incomplete; an initial 180-volt reading on the guy-wires was not replicated the following day. The radio station was dismantled despite preservation orders. The October 2007 autopsy attributed death to electrocution (wounds on neck, wrist, fingers and a pre-existing toe laceration treated as the exit point), but later examinations questioned this: a 2009 court-ordered combined report could neither confirm nor exclude electrocution, citing elapsed time, conflicting data, and inability to establish current path. Biological tests found no traces on the wires or clothing. Witness statements (A.G., fellow soldiers, officers) conflicted on timing, T.’s presence at roll-call (his signature was missing from the register), and his reason for leaving (trainers versus washing feet). An allegation that the unit commander had slapped T. was not substantiated.

Two signal-corps officers were charged with improper installation and lack of earthing but were acquitted in 2010 (upheld on appeal). The courts highlighted unlawfully obtained evidence, inapplicable technical regulations, irreconcilable expert reports (one asserting 180 V, another that the subframe produced only 27 V), and failure to explain why the same current killed one man yet barely harmed another.

After the acquittals the investigation was repeatedly resumed and suspended (2015, 2017 and later) because the original radio station (serial 190913) was never located and circumstances remained unclear. Additional expert commissions largely reiterated earlier findings or proved inconclusive owing to the passage of time. Domestic courts sometimes quashed suspensions, finding the inquiry neither prompt nor diligent and noting failure to address the applicant’s photographs and arguments. The applicant died in 2017; his widow continued the proceedings. As of 2022 the investigation remained open after more than 14 years.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: the State’s failure to furnish a plausible explanation for a death occurring under its exclusive control (substantive Article 2) and the prolonged, flawed investigation that never established the cause or identified those responsible (procedural Article 2).

The case of Ohanjanyan v. Armenia (ECtHR, Application no. 70665/11) concerns the death of the applicant’s son, T. Ohanjanyan, during compulsory military service and the subsequent investigation, raising issues under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life).

T. Ohanjanyan was drafted in November 2006 and assigned in May 2007 to military unit no. 28418 near Kartchaghbyur. According to the official account, on 30 August 2007, after evening roll-call, he left the armoury toward a nearby checkpoint of unit no. 28233. His neck and left wrist allegedly contacted guy-wires of an R-419 radio relay station antenna mast, resulting in fatal electrocution. Junior Sergeant A.G. found the body, received a shock himself upon touching a wire, and summoned help. The body was transferred to hospital and then Yerevan for autopsy.

The investigation began the same night. Military police recorded 180-volt current in a guy-wire but did not inspect the scene due to darkness. Criminal proceedings were opened on 31 August 2007 under Article 376 § 2 of the Criminal Code (negligence causing grave consequences). Autopsy on 8 October 2007 attributed death to electrocution, citing electrical wounds on the neck, left wrist, fingers, and right big toe, plus other abrasions inflicted while alive. However, a contemporaneous Ministry of Defence inspection found no current possible, as the station had no mains connection and insulation prevented transfer. The station was later dismantled despite orders to preserve it.

Witnesses gave inconsistent accounts. T. Ohanjanyan had reportedly gone to fetch trainers, though he owned none; his signature was absent from the roll-call register despite claims of his presence. Friends mentioned prior fights, a bloodshot eye, and a slap by former commander S.S. (denied and unprosecuted). Medical records noted a pre-existing toe laceration on 27 August. The applicant photographed the body, revealing unrecorded injuries including missing teeth, head trauma, and jaw/ear marks, which the autopsy expert later dismissed as poor-quality images.

Multiple forensic examinations conflicted. An initial electrical report (November 2007) blamed poor earthing and insulation, leading to charges against two signal-corps officers (R.A. and K.T.). A 2009 court-ordered combined examination found the station could produce only 27 volts (not 180), insulation issues were possible but unconfirmed, and electrocution could neither be affirmed nor excluded due to evidential gaps and time lapse. The officers were acquitted in January 2010 (upheld on appeal) owing to unlawfully obtained evidence, inapplicable regulations, conflicting reports, and unexplained discrepancies (e.g., A.G.’s mild shock versus fatal outcome; inability of the deceased to moan per autopsy).

The investigation was transferred, resumed, and repeatedly suspended (2015, 2017, 2020) for failure to locate the original station, clarify contact circumstances, or identify the current source. Additional examinations of photographs confirmed their authenticity but yielded no new insights; later tests on a similar station were inconclusive due to elapsed time. Domestic courts twice found the post-2010 investigation ineffective (2016, 2018), citing delays, failure to address photos/injuries, and incomplete measures. The applicant died in 2017; his widow continued as heir. As of 2022 the probe remained open after 15 years, with no plausible explanation for the death established and no one held accountable.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 2 violations: an ineffective, delayed, and incomplete investigation that failed to resolve contradictions or provide a credible account of the death in State custody.

The case concerns the death of conscript T. Ohanjanyan on 30 August 2007 while serving in an Armenian military unit, and the ensuing investigation, under Article 2 ECHR (right to life). Drafted in November 2006 and transferred to unit no. 28418 in May 2007, T. was officially said to have left after evening roll-call to collect trainers from a nearby checkpoint of unit no. 28233. En route, his neck and left wrist allegedly contacted guy-wires of an R-419 radio-relay antenna mast, causing instantaneous fatal electrocution. Junior Sergeant A.G. found the body after hearing moans, himself receiving a shock from a wire. The body reached Vardenis hospital at 23:35; an autopsy followed.

The applicant (T.’s father) contested this account, noting prior indications of a fight (T. mentioned detention risk in August 2007; a visitor observed a bloodshot eye) and a recorded laceration on T.’s right big toe days earlier. Photographs he took of the body before autopsy showed unrecorded injuries: missing teeth, head/ear/jaw wounds, and foot burns. These were later authenticated but not fully reconciled with official findings.

Criminal proceedings began the next day under Criminal Code Article 376 § 2 (negligent performance of military duties causing grave harm). Initial military-police checks (night-time, no witnesses) detected 180 V in the guy-wires; a later prosecutor inspection found none. The station was dismantled contrary to preservation orders and never recovered (serial 190913). Autopsy (8 October 2007) attributed death to electrocution via wounds on neck, left wrist/fingers and right toe, stating T. could not have moved or shouted afterward; additional non-fatal abrasions existed. Subsequent exams conflicted sharply: a November 2007 electrical report blamed missing earthing allowing mains current to reach the wires; a 2009 court-ordered joint exam found the subframe produced only 27 V, an insulator present, and insufficient grounds to confirm or exclude electrocution (noting the toe injury predated death and histopathology did not confirm an exit burn). A 2011 commission endorsed the original autopsy; later electrical commissions highlighted flaws in both reports but agreed the station could not supply 180 V. No skin/blood traces appeared on the seized guy-wire (examined late). Witness accounts clashed on T.’s presence at roll-call (signature missing), purpose of his departure, and incident timing.

Appeals failed. Investigations (transferred among agencies) were suspended repeatedly from 2015 onward because the original station was missing and circumstances of contact unexplained; a similar unit (serial 160913) later showed cable damage, but elapsed time precluded answers. Domestic courts occasionally quashed suspensions as ineffective (e.g., 2016, 2018), criticising delays, unaddressed photographs, and unexplored alternative causes. The applicant died in 2017; his widow continued. As of 2022 the probe remained open.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 2 violations: the State’s failure to furnish a coherent explanation for a death occurring under its exclusive control, and an investigation marred by lost evidence, contradictory forensics, delays, and incomplete inquiry into possible non-accidental injury.
001-224774:
The ECtHR case of Buhuceanu and Others v. Romania (applications nos. 20081/19 and 20 others) was brought by 42 Romanian nationals forming 21 same-sex couples. They alleged that Romania’s complete lack of any legal framework for recognising or protecting their relationships violated Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for private and family life), taken alone or together with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation).

The applicants lived in stable, committed cohabiting relationships of varying lengths. Each couple formally notified their local civil-status registry of their intention to marry. All notices were rejected as contrary to the Civil Code: Article 258 defines the family as based on marriage between a man and a woman; Article 259 and 271 likewise restrict marriage to opposite-sex unions concluded with free consent; and Article 277 expressly prohibits same-sex marriage, refuses recognition of same-sex marriages contracted abroad, and refuses recognition of any registered partnerships (whether same-sex or opposite-sex) contracted abroad. Consequently, the couples possessed no civil status, no access to the legal incidents of marriage (inheritance, next-of-kin rights, tax or social-security benefits, etc.), and no alternative form of registered partnership.

One couple (application no. 20081/19) additionally challenged administrative refusals to grant one partner co-insured status under the other’s health-insurance contract. After jurisdictional disputes the Bucharest Court of Appeal referred questions of constitutionality to the Constitutional Court and stayed the proceedings; they remain pending.

Domestic constitutional provisions protect equality (Art. 16), intimate/family/private life (Art. 26) and the family founded on marriage “between spouses” (Art. 48). Anti-discrimination legislation (Government Ordinance 137/2000) lists sexual orientation among prohibited grounds and includes the right to marry and to choose a partner. Same-sex sexual activity was fully decriminalised only in 2001. A 2018 popular initiative to amend Article 48 so as to define marriage exclusively as a union of a man and a woman failed for lack of the required 30 % turnout. Subsequent parliamentary bills for civil partnership have either been rejected or remain un-debated.

The Constitutional Court has drawn a distinction between the narrower right to marry and the broader right to family life. In 2016 it held that an amendment specifying opposite-sex marriage would not, of itself, restrict the protection of family life under Article 26. In 2018 (decision 534) it declared Article 277 §§ 2 and 4 unconstitutional insofar as they prevented recognition, for EU free-movement purposes, of same-sex marriages validly contracted in another Member State; it also stated that stable same-sex couples enjoy the protection of family life under the Constitution, the ECHR and the EU Charter and are entitled, over time, to legal recognition of the corresponding rights and duties.

Surveys cited in the case indicated that a majority of Romanians (especially those under 34) did not consider legal recognition of same-sex couples a threat to their own lives, while LGBTI respondents reported high rates of concealment and cohabitation without legal status. International bodies (ECRI, FRA) had already called for a legal framework affording same-sex couples recognition and protection without discrimination.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ claim that the total absence of any legal recognition or protection placed them in a legal vacuum incompatible with the State’s positive obligations under Article 8 and constituted unjustified discrimination compared with opposite-sex couples.

**Case Summary: Buhuceanu and Others v. Romania (ECtHR, 2023)**

The applicants, 42 Romanian nationals forming 21 same-sex couples, alleged that Romania’s failure to provide any legal recognition or protection for their committed relationships violated their rights under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken alone or with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). They had lived together for varying periods in stable partnerships.

On various dates, each couple notified local civil registry offices of their intention to marry. All notices were rejected as contrary to the Civil Code: Article 271 requires marriage between a man and a woman with free personal consent, while Article 277 §1 prohibits same-sex marriage. Article 277 §§2–3 further bars recognition of same-sex marriages or registered partnerships contracted abroad.

One couple (application no. 20081/19) also challenged administrative denials of co-insured health status under a partner’s insurance. After jurisdictional disputes, the Bucharest Court of Appeal referred questions on Law no. 95/2006 (health system reform) to the Constitutional Court in 2019 and suspended proceedings, which remained pending.

Romanian law provides no alternative recognition such as registered partnership. The Constitution’s Article 48 founds the family on “freely consensual marriage between spouses,” interpreted via Civil Code Articles 258–259 as a union of man and woman; the State must support marriage and family. Article 26 protects intimate, family, and private life more broadly. Anti-discrimination Ordinance no. 137/2000 lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground and refers to the right to marry and choose a partner, but does not create recognition mechanisms.

Historically, same-sex relations were criminalized until 2001. A 2018 referendum seeking to amend Article 48 to specify marriage “between a man and a woman” failed for insufficient turnout (21% versus the required 30%). Subsequent popular initiatives and several parliamentary bills on civil partnerships (2010–2020) have not been enacted; some remain in committee.

The Constitutional Court, in 2016, distinguished the narrower constitutional “family” (marriage-based) from broader family life under Article 26. In 2018 (decision no. 534), it held Article 277 §§2 and 4 unconstitutional insofar as they denied residence rights to same-sex spouses of EU citizens married abroad, affirming that stable same-sex couples enjoy family life protection equivalent to opposite-sex couples under the Constitution, EU Charter, and Convention, and should receive legal recognition of rights and duties over time.

The Court applied principles from *Fedotova and Others v. Russia* [GC]. It found that the complete absence of any legal framework for same-sex couples interfered with private and family life. Public-interest justifications advanced by the Government did not outweigh the applicants’ interests, and Romania had exceeded its margin of appreciation. A violation of Article 8 was therefore established. (The judgment became final on 25 September 2023.)

The case of Buhuceanu and Others v. Romania (ECtHR Fourth Section, 23 May 2023) involved 21 applications by 42 Romanian nationals comprising 21 same-sex couples. They claimed that Romania’s total lack of legal recognition or protection for their relationships violated Article 8 of the Convention (respect for private and family life), alone or with Article 14 (non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation).

The applicants were in committed, cohabiting same-sex relationships of varying durations. Each couple submitted notices of intent to marry to local civil registry offices (Serviciul de Stare Civilă). All were rejected as contrary to Civil Code Articles 271 and 277 § 1. These provisions, together with Articles 258–259, define marriage exclusively as the freely consented union of a man and a woman, prohibit same-sex marriage, and refuse recognition of same-sex marriages or registered partnerships contracted abroad (subject only to limited EU free-movement exceptions). No alternative form of civil partnership or registered union exists under Romanian law.

In application no. 20081/19, one couple additionally challenged health-insurance authorities’ refusal to grant co-insured status under a partner’s policy. After courts declined jurisdiction, the Bucharest Court of Appeal referred questions of interpretation of the health-system law to the Constitutional Court and stayed proceedings, which remain pending.

Romanian constitutional and statutory law reinforces this exclusion. Constitution Article 48 founds the family on marriage between “spouses,” while Article 26 protects intimate, family and private life more broadly. The Civil Code (in force 2011) reiterates that spouses are a man and a woman and that family is based on such marriage. Homosexuality had been criminalized until 1996 (with residual public-scandal provisions repealed only in 2001). A 2018 popular referendum seeking to amend Article 48 to define family explicitly as marriage “between a man and a woman” failed for lack of the required 30 % turnout (only 21 % voted). Subsequent legislative proposals to amend the Constitution and several parliamentary bills (2010–2020) seeking to introduce civil partnerships were either rejected or never scheduled for debate.

The Constitutional Court has distinguished the right to marry (Article 48) from the broader right to family life (Article 26). In 2018 it held that stable same-sex couples enjoy the protection of family life under the Constitution, Article 8 of the Convention and the EU Charter, and are entitled in principle to legal recognition of corresponding rights and duties. Nevertheless, no legislative framework implementing that recognition has been enacted.

These facts establish that, despite the applicants’ long-term committed relationships and repeated attempts to obtain formal status, Romanian law afforded them no possibility of legal recognition or the attendant protections (inheritance, next-of-kin rights, social-security benefits, etc.). The Court later found this complete absence of any form of recognition to overstep Romania’s margin of appreciation.

The case of Abbasaliyeva v. Azerbaijan (no. 6950/13) was brought by Shahla Abbasaliyeva, an Azerbaijani doctor born in 1959, alleging that domestic courts failed to protect her reputation under Article 8 of the Convention after disparaging newspaper articles about her appointment.

Her brother Elchin Amiraslanov, former head of the Gazakh OMON police unit, had been convicted of participating in the March 1995 attempted coup d’état. Originally sentenced to death, his penalty was commuted to life imprisonment after Azerbaijan abolished capital punishment. On 19 August 2011 the applicant, who had used the married surname Abbasaliyeva for 26 years, was appointed head physician of the outpatient clinic of Gazakh District Central Hospital.

Between 23 August and 10 September 2011 the newspaper Gündəlik Bakı published four articles under headlines such as “Relatives of the government’s enemies appointed to posts,” “The sister of an OMON member has become Gazakh’s head physician,” and “One of the twins serves the State, the other the coup d’état.” The pieces repeatedly identified her as Elchin Amiraslanov’s sister (using her maiden name), described her earlier protests against the authorities after his arrest, and questioned why she had been chosen over eight other candidates, including an experienced doctor. They characterised the appointment, approved by Health Minister O.S. at the request of local official R.H., as a “paradox,” an “undesirable fact,” and a betrayal of state interests that showed a “perfunctory attitude” toward protecting those interests. The articles suggested officials had forgotten or been made to forget her defence of her convicted brother.

On 12 September 2011 R.H. asked her to resign; she refused and was immediately dismissed, reverting to her previous post as a staff physician. She unsuccessfully sued her employer for reinstatement, the courts holding that the appointment had violated labour-law formalities.

She then requested a retraction from the newspaper, which was refused. In October 2011 she sued the editor-in-chief and authors for retraction, an apology to herself and her family, and damages, arguing that the repeated emphasis on her brother’s conviction served only to attack her personally and had caused her dismissal.

The Yasamal District Court dismissed the claim on 8 February 2012. On 25 May 2012 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that decision, finding that three facts were true (her maiden name, her brother’s conviction, and her appointment and later dismissal) and that the remaining statements were value judgments possessing a sufficient factual basis. It held that such judgments were protected by freedom of expression and the right to criticise public officials, including doctors, who must tolerate a higher degree of criticism. The Supreme Court rejected her cassation appeal on 2 October 2012 on the same grounds.

The applicant complained that the articles had exaggerated her appointment into an act of state treason solely because of her brother’s crime and that the courts had failed to protect her private life and reputation.
