The case of Alif Ahmadov and Others v. Azerbaijan (App. no. 22619/14) involves four Azerbaijani nationals—a married couple and their two adult children—who complained to the ECtHR about an unenforced court order for their eviction from, and the demolition of, the Baku house they had long occupied. The claims alleged violations of Article 8 ECHR (respect for home) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property).

In 1963 the Baku City Executive Committee allocated 3.3 ha of State land to Leninneft OGED (later Balakhanineft OGED, part of SOCAR’s Azneft) for oil-and-gas extraction. The applicants’ house, built in 1938 at 2 Stansiyayani cul-de-sac, house 4, stood on that land, 45 m from an oil well (within the 75 m protection zone). A 1963 technical passport issued to the previous occupier E.L. recorded the house (49.9 m² habitable area plus yard) but noted “no documents” of title; plans were added in 1981–82. The first applicant began working for the oil company in 1977 and claimed to have bought the house that year, though no sale contract existed. He and his family were registered there from 1979/1984 onward. Utility contracts were signed in 2011 and 2017. Certificates later showed 12 people registered in a five-room dwelling of 88–108 m². The first applicant said housing applications he made as an oil worker in 1982 and 1992 were refused after local inspections found the existing house adequate; no supporting documents were produced.

In 2012 Azneft sued in the Sabunchu District Court, arguing the house was an unauthorised construction on State land assigned for oil operations and that it interfered with well exploitation. On 25 January 2012 the court, citing Civil Code Art. 180 (unauthorised constructions) and Land Code Art. 111 (squatting), plus letters confirming State ownership and lack of permits, ordered eviction and demolition at the applicants’ expense. It found no proof of the applicants’ rights over the land or house.

The applicants appealed, stressing the house predated the 1967 well, their 1977 purchase, the first applicant’s rejected housing claims, and the risk of homelessness. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the order (10 May 2012). The Supreme Court remitted the case (27 November 2012). An expert report of 29 March 2013 confirmed the well’s proximity. On 19 April 2013 the appeal court again upheld, holding the house breached planning rules, endangered health and property, and hindered operations. The Supreme Court dismissed cassation on 6 September 2013 without addressing the homelessness argument.

As of 2018 the orders remained unenforced and the family continued to occupy the house. The central facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the lengthy, uninterrupted occupation of a dwelling that had never been lawfully authorised on land reserved for oil extraction, the absence of any alternative housing, and the domestic courts’ failure to weigh those personal circumstances when ordering eviction and demolition.

The applicants appealed, arguing the house dated to 1938 (with 1963 passport), the 1977 purchase, the oil well's 1967 excavation far from the house (not obstructing operations), rejected housing applications due to existing occupancy, and lack of alternative housing (risking homelessness). They sought quashing and alternative allocation. Certificates showed 12 people registered there (including relatives), with the first applicant registered since 1979 and others since 1984; house size was listed as 88–108 sq m.

The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the order on 10 May 2012. The Supreme Court remitted the case on 27 November 2012. An expert opinion of 29 March 2013 placed the house 45 m from the well (within the 75 m protection zone). On 19 April 2013 the appellate court reaffirmed the first-instance ruling, finding the house built without permits, in breach of planning rules, posing danger to health/property, and hindering well operations. The applicants were ordered to pay expert costs (~EUR 98). Their cassation appeal (reiterating prior arguments) was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 6 September 2013, without addressing the homelessness claim.

Enforcement without such review would breach Article 8.

Land-reform provisions transferring certain occupied plots to private ownership excluded land used for oil/gas exploitation. **Case Summary: Lalik v. Poland (ECHR, Application no. 47834/19, 11 May 2023)**

The applicant, Przemysław Lalik (born 1995), was convicted in Poland of murder committed with particular cruelty and sentenced to 25 years’ imprisonment. He alleged a violation of Article 6 § 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights, claiming that his conviction rested largely on incriminating statements made during informal police questioning shortly after arrest. He was not adequately informed of his defence rights and had no access to a lawyer at that stage. The statements were recorded only in an official note rather than a formal interrogation record, and the domestic courts relied on them as particularly credible evidence of guilt and motive.

On 26 January 2016, the applicant (intoxicated) encountered T.B. (heavily intoxicated, later found to have 3.79‰ blood alcohol) and another man. After the third man left, the applicant and T.B. went to the basement of the applicant’s building. T.B. collapsed. The applicant allegedly searched T.B.’s pockets for a debt (which he later denied intending as motive), then set fire to T.B.’s winter jacket with a lighter and left. T.B. died from severe burns covering 60% of his body and upper respiratory tract. Neighbours extinguished the fire.

The applicant was arrested at 11:20 p.m. A breathalyser at 11:39 p.m. showed 1.3‰ alcohol. An arrest record was drawn up around 12:20 a.m. on 27 January, and he was given a document informing him of arrestee rights, including the right not to make “statements” and to contact a lawyer (exact content unknown, as copies were not provided). He later claimed he did not recall being informed of his rights or what he said/signed.

At 10:55 a.m. on 27 January (intoxication level not rechecked), three officers informally questioned him for nearly three hours until 1:40 p.m. No formal interrogation record (protokół przesłuchania) was prepared, contrary to domestic law requirements for questioning. Officer P.R. made an official note summarising the applicant’s statements: he was in conflict with T.B. over an unpaid debt, confirmed setting T.B. on fire, could not explain why, and said he wanted to see if he was capable of such an act. The note was signed only by P.R. and added to the file. The applicant asserted he was not informed of his right to refuse explanations or to have a lawyer present. One officer later testified it was a routine “conversation” in which the applicant spoke freely and spontaneously; no documents were given for signature.

Later that day (2:55–3:05 p.m.), the applicant briefly consulted a lawyer appointed by his father, with a police officer present. On 28 January he was formally charged with murder with particular cruelty and questioned as a suspect. Initially without his lawyer (who arrived late), he pleaded guilty “in its entirety,” referencing the debt and inability to explain the fire. After a short consultation with his lawyer, he rectified this: he had no intent to kill and the fire was not motivated by the debt. He then refused further explanations. At a subsequent detention hearing he retracted his earlier statements, claiming fear of the officers.

During investigation and trial, the applicant pleaded not guilty, refused further explanations, and admitted only setting the fire without intent to kill (citing a prior similar “prank”). Other evidence included witnesses, scene findings, and medical/psychiatric assessments.

The Zamość Regional Court convicted him on 27 March 2017, explicitly treating the informal statements as particularly credible because he had “no chance to think about his line of defence.” It found a financial motive (debt, also linked to the 2015 incident) as an aggravating factor, hostility toward T.B., and intent to inflict maximum suffering—all based on the unofficial questioning. The Lublin Court of Appeal upheld this, citing Supreme Court case law that police officers could testify about informal/spontaneous statements (no exclusionary rule applied, unlike for formal interrogations). The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded.

The ECHR found the proceedings as a whole unfair. Existing domestic guarantees (e.g., later rights notifications, formal charging) were insufficient given the circumstances: the applicant’s intoxication, lengthy informal questioning without a lawyer or proper rights advice, use of an unofficial note, and decisive reliance on those statements for findings of intent, motive, and particular cruelty. This compromised the right to legal assistance from the earliest stages.

The case of Lalik v. Poland (Application no. 47834/19) concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 3 (c) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Przemysław Lalik, alleged that his 2017 conviction for murder with particular cruelty (under Article 148 § 2 of the Polish Criminal Code) was unfair because it relied heavily on incriminating statements he made during informal police questioning shortly after his arrest. He claimed he was not adequately informed of his defence rights, including the right to remain silent and to consult a lawyer, and that these statements—recorded only in an unofficial police note—were used against him despite his subsequent recantations.

On 26 January 2016, the applicant (then aged 20 and intoxicated) encountered T.B. (also heavily intoxicated) and M.D. after drinking together. After M.D. departed, the pair entered the basement of the applicant’s building, where T.B. collapsed unconscious. The applicant allegedly searched T.B.’s pockets (claiming a debt owed to him, which he later denied) and set fire to T.B.’s jacket with a lighter before leaving. T.B. died from severe burns covering 60% of his body and respiratory tract; his blood-alcohol level was 3.79 per mille.

The applicant was arrested at 11:20 p.m. A breathalyser test at 11:39 p.m. recorded 1.3 per mille alcohol in his system. An arrest record was prepared at 12:20 a.m. on 27 January, and he was notionally informed of arrestee rights (including the right not to make statements and to contact a lawyer), though no copies of these documents were produced. At 10:55 a.m. that day—without a further intoxication check—three officers informally questioned him (rozpytanie) for nearly three hours. No formal interrogation record (protokół przesłuchania) was made, contrary to Articles 143 and 148 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP). Instead, officer P.R. prepared an official note (notatka urzędowa) stating that the applicant admitted setting T.B. on fire due to a debt dispute and “to see if he was capable” of the act. The applicant later said he was neither informed of his right to refuse explanations (Article 175 CCP) nor offered a lawyer. He briefly consulted a lawyer appointed by his father later that afternoon, but a police officer was present.

On 28 January the applicant was formally charged. Without his lawyer present he initially pleaded guilty in full, repeating the debt motive and inability to explain the fire. After a short consultation with counsel, he recanted, denying intent to kill or any financial motive, and refused further statements. At a remand hearing he claimed fear of the officers had prompted his earlier admissions. He thereafter pleaded not guilty and remained silent.

At trial the applicant admitted starting the fire but insisted it was a “prank” (referring to a similar 2015 incident) with no lethal intent. The Zamość Regional Court convicted him on 27 March 2017 and imposed a 25-year sentence. It treated the informal statements as “particularly credible” because they were made before he could formulate a defence, relied on them to establish both intent and a financial motive as an aggravating factor, and explicitly referenced the officers’ later testimony confirming the unofficial note. The Lublin Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, citing Supreme Court case-law that permitted police officers to testify about spontaneous utterances during informal questioning (as opposed to formal interrogations, which would trigger Article 174 CCP’s exclusionary rule). The Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal as manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant argued that the informal questioning circumvented mandatory recording and rights-notification rules (Articles 244, 300–301 CCP), that he was still intoxicated, and that the domestic courts’ heavy reliance on those uncounselled statements rendered the proceedings as a whole unfair. The Government contended that rights had been notified upon arrest, that informal questioning was a routine, non-coercive “conversation,” and that other evidence supported the conviction. Third-party interveners (Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and Fair Trials) highlighted systemic shortcomings in early-stage access to counsel, inconsistent with EU Directive 2013/48/EU and the Court’s prior judgment in Płonka v. Poland.

The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 3 (c), holding that the applicant had not been sufficiently apprised of his rights, that the informal statements were used to his detriment, and that existing Polish procedural guarantees were inadequate under the circumstances, rendering the trial unfair.

The applicant’s statements from the informal, lawyer-free questioning of an intoxicated arrestee who had not been properly apprised of his rights were used by the domestic courts as a key basis for findings of guilt and motive. This rendered the proceedings as a whole unfair, in violation of Article 6 § 3(c).
001-224775:
The case of Yılmaz Aydemir v. Türkiye (Application no. 61808/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 5 § 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1993, complained that judicial review of his post-conviction detention failed to respect the principles of equality of arms and adversarial proceedings, as he was not provided with the public prosecutor’s written opinion or given an opportunity to comment on it.

On 4 February 2016, Aydemir was taken into police custody on suspicion of drug trafficking after 1.27 grams of heroin were found on him. He denied the accusations and was released the next day. An indictment was filed on 23 February 2016 charging him with production and trade of narcotics under Article 188 of the Criminal Code. Proceedings commenced before the Ankara 8th Assize Court while he remained at liberty.

On 26 April 2016, the trial court convicted him and imposed a sentence of twelve years, six months and five days’ imprisonment, simultaneously ordering his immediate detention. The following day he lodged an objection (itiraz), arguing that the detention order lacked legal and factual grounds, was disproportionate, and was unsupported by evidence of strong suspicion or any risk of absconding, evidence-tampering or witness interference.

The 8th Assize Court dismissed the objection and transmitted the file to the Ankara 9th Assize Court. That court obtained a written opinion from the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor, who concluded that the 26 April detention order complied with procedure and law. The opinion was not communicated to Aydemir or his lawyer. On 2 May 2016 the 9th Assize Court dismissed the objection, expressly stating that it had followed the prosecutor’s opinion.

Aydemir applied to the Turkish Constitutional Court on 20 May 2016, repeating his challenges to the lawfulness and proportionality of the detention and adding that the failure to disclose the prosecutor’s opinion had breached equality of arms. On 10 May 2019 the Constitutional Court declared the lawfulness complaint manifestly ill-founded and the equality-of-arms complaint inadmissible for lack of constitutional and individual importance, finding that Aydemir had suffered no significant disadvantage. His conviction became final on 12 April 2018.

Under Turkish law, Article 19 of the Constitution guarantees a right to judicial review of any deprivation of liberty. The Code of Criminal Procedure (Articles 101, 104, 267–270) permits objections to detention orders and, when an examining court seeks the prosecutor’s written observations, requires those observations to be transmitted to the detainee for comment. Constitutional Court case-law, however, distinguishes “detention after conviction” from pre-trial detention and applies the procedural safeguards of Article 19 § 8 only to the extent compatible with the nature of post-conviction detention. In later decisions the Constitutional Court treated non-disclosure of a prosecutor’s opinion as lacking constitutional importance where the opinion contained no new factual or legal material requiring a response.

The European Court of Human Rights later held that the review proceedings had violated Article 5 § 4 because the applicant was denied any opportunity to comment on the prosecutor’s opinion on which the reviewing court expressly relied, thereby breaching both the adversarial principle and equality of arms.

The case of Yılmaz Aydemir v. Türkiye (Application no. 61808/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1993, complained that judicial proceedings reviewing the lawfulness of his post-conviction detention failed to afford him an opportunity to comment on the public prosecutor’s written opinion, thereby breaching the adversarial principle and equality of arms.

The facts began with a criminal investigation into suspected drug trafficking. On 4 February 2016 the applicant was taken into police custody; a body search revealed 1.27 grams of heroin. He denied the accusations in the presence of his lawyer and was released the following day on the public prosecutor’s instructions. On 23 February 2016 the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office filed an indictment charging him under Article 188 of the Criminal Code with production and trade of narcotics. After the indictment was accepted, proceedings continued before the Ankara 8th Assize Court while the applicant remained at liberty.

On 26 April 2016 the trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twelve years, six months and five days’ imprisonment. It simultaneously ordered his immediate detention. The next day he lodged an objection (itiraz) against that order, arguing that it lacked legal grounds, was disproportionate, and was unsupported by strong suspicion that he had committed an offence or by any risk of absconding, concealing evidence or influencing witnesses. The trial court dismissed the objection and transmitted it to the Ankara 9th Assize Court. Before examining the objection that court obtained a written opinion from the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor, who considered the 26 April detention order fully compliant with procedure and law. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer was given a copy of this opinion or any opportunity to respond to it.

On 2 May 2016 the 9th Assize Court dismissed the objection, expressly stating that it had acted in line with the public prosecutor’s opinion. The applicant then lodged an individual application with the Turkish Constitutional Court on 20 May 2016. He contended that the detention was unlawful because it was not based on reasonable suspicion and lacked relevant and sufficient grounds, that it was disproportionate, and that his right to equality of arms had been violated by the failure to communicate the prosecutor’s opinion, thereby depriving him of the chance to examine and comment on it.

On 10 May 2019 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint concerning the lawfulness of detention inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It declared the equality-of-arms complaint inadmissible for lack of constitutional and individual importance, holding that the applicant had not suffered a significant disadvantage. The applicant’s conviction became final on 12 April 2018.

Under domestic law, Article 19 of the Constitution and Articles 101, 104, 267–270 of the Code of Criminal Procedure confer a right to judicial review of any detention and, when an examining court requests the public prosecutor’s observations, require those observations to be transmitted to the detainee for comment. Constitutional Court case-law distinguishes “detention on remand” from “detention after conviction,” applying only those safeguards compatible with the latter’s nature. In a comparable 2018 admissibility decision the Constitutional Court had likewise found no significant disadvantage where a prosecutor’s opinion contained no new factual or legal grounds and the reviewing court made no substantive reference to its content.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 5 § 4 violation: the reviewing court obtained and relied upon an undisclosed prosecutorial opinion without giving the applicant any opportunity to comment, thereby undermining the adversarial character of the proceedings that determined the lawfulness of his continued detention after conviction.

The case of *Yılmaz Aydemir v. Türkiye* (Application no. 61808/19), decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 23 May 2023 (final on 25 September 2023), concerned an alleged violation of Article 5 § 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Turkish national, complained that judicial review proceedings examining the lawfulness of his post-conviction detention failed to respect the principles of adversarial proceedings and equality of arms, as he was not afforded an opportunity to comment on the public prosecutor’s written opinion submitted to the reviewing court.

The facts began with a criminal investigation into the applicant for suspected drug trafficking. On 4 February 2016 he was taken into police custody, where a search yielded 1.27 grams of heroin. He denied the accusations in the presence of his lawyer and was released the following day on the prosecutor’s instructions. An indictment was filed on 23 February 2016 charging him with production and trade of narcotics under Article 188 of the Criminal Code. The applicant remained at liberty throughout the subsequent trial before the Ankara 8th Assize Court.

On 26 April 2016 the trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twelve years, six months and five days’ imprisonment. It simultaneously ordered his immediate detention. The applicant lodged an objection (*itiraz*) the next day, arguing that the detention order lacked legal grounds, was disproportionate, and was unsupported by strong suspicion of an offence or any risk of absconding, evidence tampering or witness interference. The trial court rejected the objection and transmitted the file to the Ankara 9th Assize Court. Before ruling, that court obtained a written opinion from the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor, who considered the original detention order procedurally and legally compliant. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer received a copy of this opinion.

On 2 May 2016 the 9th Assize Court dismissed the objection, expressly stating that it had followed the prosecutor’s opinion. The applicant then lodged an individual application with the Turkish Constitutional Court, repeating his challenges to the lawfulness and proportionality of the detention and specifically alleging a breach of equality of arms because he had been denied the chance to examine and respond to the prosecutor’s observations.

On 10 May 2019 the Constitutional Court declared the lawfulness complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It also declared the equality-of-arms complaint inadmissible for lack of constitutional and individual importance, holding that the applicant had suffered no significant disadvantage. The applicant’s conviction became final on 12 April 2018.

These facts formed the core of the alleged violation: a post-conviction detention-review procedure in which a decisive prosecutorial opinion was obtained and relied upon without being disclosed to the detained person, thereby undermining the adversarial character of the review and the equality of arms between the parties. The remainder of the original application was declared inadmissible by the Court, which proceeded solely on the Article 5 § 4 complaint.
001-224776:
The case of Irodotou v. Cyprus (Application no. 16783/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention regarding the excessive length of private criminal proceedings against the applicant, which were discontinued by the Attorney General via nolle prosequi, and under Article 13 regarding the lack of an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The applicant, a Cypriot national born in 1964 and resident in Paphos, was subject to a District Court of Paphos judgment of 18 June 2013 in civil case no. 3594/12. This ordered him to pay €300 monthly from 1 September 2013 onward to the Cooperative Credit Company of Geroskipou and East Paphos until a specified debt plus interest was discharged. On 2 March 2015, Paphos Cooperative Savings Bank Ltd initiated private criminal proceedings (case no. 1312/15) against him in the same District Court for failing to pay instalments due between 1 September 2013 and 1 January 2015. He was first notified of the charges on 3 April 2015, entered a not-guilty plea, and the matter was listed for hearing on 5 November 2015.

From 5 November 2015 to 22 March 2017 the hearing was adjourned on four occasions, principally because the District Court lacked time to commence it. On 28 September 2017 the prosecution notified a change of name: the original bank had transferred its assets and liabilities to Cooperative Central Bank Ltd (effective 1 July 2017), which was renamed Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd on 24 July 2017. A further adjournment for lack of court time occurred on 6 November 2017. The hearing was postponed on 29 March 2018 at the applicant’s request for health reasons. On 14 September 2018 another name-change notification recorded that Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd had become Cooperative Asset Management Company Ltd as of 3 September 2018. The hearing was then postponed on 24 September 2018 because a prosecution witness was absent.

On 15 November 2018 the applicant challenged the prosecutor’s standing as a legal entity capable of acting as a credit institution and therefore of instructing counsel or continuing the proceedings. The court granted the prosecution an adjournment to 15 January 2019. Subsequent hearings on 15 January, 26 March and 24 May 2019 were adjourned by consent so that the parties could exchange documents and agree undisputed facts.

By letter of 5 September 2019 the prosecution applied to the Attorney General for discontinuance. It explained that successive mergers had created uncertainty whether a now-non-existent entity could validly prosecute; a similar issue was pending before the Supreme Court; and in another comparable case the defendant had been acquitted at the pre-trial stage. Continuation no longer served any useful purpose and an adverse first-instance ruling might prejudice the successor institution’s future civil or criminal rights in respect of unpaid instalments. The Attorney General granted nolle prosequi on 23 September 2019. On 2 October 2019 the District Court formally discontinued the case and discharged the applicant.

The applicant sought to challenge the decision, complaining that he had not been consulted, that he had himself raised the standing issue as early as 15 November 2018 yet the court had repeatedly adjourned the matter, that he could not recover the losses and expenses incurred over four-and-a-half years (including court-stamp fees), and that he had been treated unfairly. The court held that the Attorney General’s power under Article 113 § 2 of the Constitution was exclusive, discretionary and immune from judicial review, including on costs; the case was therefore closed without any costs order against the applicant.

The overall duration of the criminal proceedings was approximately four years and seven months. Multiple adjournments were attributable to the court’s lack of time, successive corporate reorganisations of the prosecutor, witness absence, and consensual requests by both parties. The proceedings ended without a determination on the merits and without any award of costs or other compensation to the applicant. Domestic law (Criminal Procedure Law, Cap. 155, s. 154(1)) and constitutional practice confirm that nolle prosequi immediately discharges the accused and is not susceptible to review. While Cypriot case-law recognises that excessive delay may lead to acquittal or sentence reduction in continuing prosecutions, and that human-rights violations may sound in damages in civil actions, no such remedy was available or granted once the Attorney General had discontinued the case.

The case of Irodotou v. Cyprus (Application no. 16783/20) concerns complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention regarding the excessive length of private criminal proceedings against the applicant, which ended via a nolle prosequi, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

The applicant, Marios Irodotou, a Cypriot national born in 1964 and resident in Paphos, was the subject of a civil judgment dated 18 June 2013 by the Paphos District Court. That judgment required him to pay EUR 300 monthly from 1 September 2013 onward to the Cooperative Credit Company of Geroskipou and East Paphos until a specified debt plus interest was discharged.

On 2 March 2015 the Paphos Cooperative Savings Bank Ltd instituted a private prosecution (case no. 1312/15) before the same District Court, charging the applicant with failing to pay the ordered instalments between 1 September 2013 and 1 January 2015. He was first notified of the charges on 3 April 2015, entered a not-guilty plea, and a hearing was fixed for 5 November 2015.

Thereafter the proceedings were repeatedly adjourned. Between November 2015 and March 2017 the hearing was postponed on four occasions, principally because the court lacked time. Further adjournments followed on 6 November 2017 (again for lack of judicial time), 29 March 2018 (at the applicant’s request for health reasons), 24 September 2018 (absence of a prosecution witness), 15 November 2018 (after the applicant challenged the prosecutor’s legal capacity following corporate mergers), 15 January 2019 (to exchange documents), 26 March 2019 (to produce a statement of undisputed facts) and 24 May 2019 (unopposed). In the interim the prosecuting entity underwent successive name changes and asset transfers: first to Cooperative Central Bank Ltd (renamed Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd) and later to Cooperative Asset Management Company Ltd. The applicant specifically questioned, on 15 November 2018, whether a non-existent or transformed legal person could maintain the prosecution.

On 5 September 2019 prosecution counsel applied to the Attorney General for discontinuance, citing the unresolved legal status of the prosecutor after the mergers, a pending Supreme Court decision on a similar issue, and an acquittal in a comparable case. The applicant unsuccessfully sought to contest the decision, arguing that he had not been consulted, that he had raised the prosecutor’s standing more than a year earlier, that he could not recover his losses or expenses after four-and-a-half years of appearances, and that he had been required to pay court stamps. The court held that the Attorney General’s constitutional power under Article 113 § 2 of the Constitution was exclusive and not subject to judicial review, including as regards costs.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the overall duration of the private criminal proceedings (approximately four years and seven months from institution to discontinuance) violated the reasonable-time guarantee in Article 6 § 1, and that no effective domestic remedy existed under Article 13 (read with Article 6 § 1) either to accelerate the proceedings, to obtain their dismissal on length grounds, or to recover costs and damages. Relevant domestic provisions included Article 30 § 2 of the Constitution (right to a hearing within a reasonable time) and section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Law (nolle prosequi). Cypriot case-law recognised that excessive delay could, in principle, lead to acquittal or sentence reduction, and that civil actions for compensation for Convention breaches were available, yet none of these mechanisms had been applied or shown to be effective in the circumstances of a discontinued private prosecution.

001-224777:
The case of I.S. v. Greece (ECtHR, Application no. 19165/20) concerns a Greek father’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that domestic authorities failed to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his two daughters or to take effective steps to restore their relationship, despite repeated applications.

The applicant married G.S. in 2007. Their daughters A. and K. were born in 2007 and 2011. The couple separated in January 2012 and divorced in 2013 on grounds attributable to the applicant, who was later convicted of domestic violence against G.S. arising from a 2011 incident. Temporary custody was initially granted to the applicant in 2012 while G.S. received medical treatment; after her recovery, interim custody passed to her in December 2013. Permanent custody was awarded to G.S. in 2017 (upheld on appeal in 2019 and by the Court of Cassation in 2021). The courts found the children had adapted well to living with their mother and were refusing contact with their father; a change of residence was not in their best interests.

Contact rights were first granted to the applicant in 2014 (two to three days per week plus holidays, no overnights). A 2015 interim-measures judgment refined the schedule (Thursday evenings, selected weekends including some overnights in the presence of the paternal grandmother or aunt, plus holiday periods) and designated Kifissia police station as the handover point to reduce parental conflict. From January 2016 onward the children consistently refused to leave with the applicant; police logged each incident. The same pattern continued after G.S. and the children moved to the island of Tinos in July 2019; a 2020 judgment confirmed Tinos police station as the new handover location, noting that the move itself did not prevent contact. The applicant appeared only once and the children again refused.

In 2017 the first-instance court ordered a social-welfare report and a child-psychiatrist evaluation to determine the reasons for the children’s refusal and the suitability of police-station handovers. G.S. repeatedly sought to revoke or replace the experts, refused to cooperate, and failed to produce the children. The child psychiatrist therefore never examined them; her 2018 report, based solely on documents and meetings with the applicant, attributed the refusal to the mother’s influence, criticised police-station handovers as psychologically harmful, and recommended urgent reinstatement of contact plus a psychiatric examination of G.S. Social-welfare reports (Oropos 2019, Tinos 2020) were similarly hampered by G.S.’s non-cooperation and her concealment of the family’s actual address; they noted the children’s distress, the damage to the paternal relationship, and the need for professional supervision of meetings. A 2020 prosecutorial order for psychiatric evaluations of G.S. and the children was never executed because of her continued refusal; it was later withdrawn after a January 2021 judgment that provided for gradual restoration of contact (initially without overnights, later including weekends and holidays) and imposed fines and imprisonment for obstruction. That judgment itself remained unenforced; both parents appealed.

Throughout 2014–2021 the applicant lodged numerous complaints with public prosecutors, police, municipal social services, the Ombudsman and two ministries, seeking enforcement of the contact orders, completion of the outstanding reports, and assistance in locating the children. Prosecutors issued recommendations to G.S. and occasionally ordered counselling, but took no coercive steps; social services were unable to complete their work; and other authorities either declined jurisdiction or referred the applicant back to the courts or prosecutor. Telephone contact attempts after 2020 also failed. The Court later found that the authorities had not taken all necessary measures to enforce the applicant’s right to contact and to rebuild a relationship with his daughters, in particular by failing to follow up on the ordered counselling, evaluations and reports.

**CASE OF I.S. v. GREECE (Application no. 19165/20)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 23 May 2023 (final 23 August 2023) in this Article 8 complaint by a Greek father concerning the authorities’ failure to enforce his court-ordered contact rights with his two daughters and to implement ordered counselling, psychiatric evaluations and social welfare reports.

The applicant married G.S. in 2007. Their daughters were born in 2007 and 2011. The couple separated in January 2012 and divorced in 2013; the applicant was later convicted of domestic violence against G.S. arising from a 2011 incident. Temporary custody was initially granted to the applicant, then transferred to G.S. in December 2013; permanent custody was awarded to her in 2017 (upheld on appeal in 2019). The courts found a change of environment contrary to the children’s best interests given their adaptation to the mother and their refusal to see the father.

Contact rights were granted in 2014 and detailed in a 2015 interim-measures decision: specified weekly, weekend and holiday periods, with overnight stays only in the presence of the applicant’s mother or sister and handover at Kifissia police station to avoid parental conflict. From January 2016 the children consistently refused to go with the applicant; police recorded the incidents. This pattern continued after G.S. moved the children to Tinos in mid-2019. A 2020 court decision confirmed the move (G.S. having the right to determine residence) and designated Tinos police station as the handover point. The applicant appeared only once (October 2019); the children refused. Subsequent telephone contact initiated by the applicant also failed.

In 2017 the applicant sought a definitive contact schedule. The court ordered a social-welfare report and a child-psychiatrist report. G.S. repeatedly obstructed both. She applied (unsuccessfully) to revoke the orders, refused to produce the children, and moved municipalities, causing jurisdictional delays. The child psychiatrist (2018) never met the children because G.S. did not attend any of seven scheduled meetings; she concluded that the mother’s conduct, not the father’s, appeared responsible for the refusal and that contact should be reinstated urgently. Social-welfare reports (Oropos 2019; Tinos 2020) noted parental hostility, the children’s distress, G.S.’s non-cooperation and impediments to private interviews, and recommended professional monitoring and supervised meetings. A prosecutor’s 2020 order for psychological/psychiatric evaluation of G.S. and the children was never executed because of her refusal to cooperate or disclose her address; it was later revoked after a 2021 contact judgment.

That 2021 judgment provided for gradual reinstatement of contact (initially without overnight stays, later weekends and holidays, with telephone contact) and imposed a €250 fine plus one month’s imprisonment for each obstruction by G.S. The applicant asserted it remained unenforced. Appeals were pending.

The applicant lodged repeated complaints with public prosecutors (from 2014 onward), police, ministries, the Ombudsman and municipal social services. Prosecutors issued recommendations to G.S. not to obstruct contact, referred the applicant to counselling, and later ordered a preliminary investigation into possible breach of the 2021 judgment, but took no coercive steps. Police merely logged refusals. Other authorities either declined jurisdiction or advised that enforcement was a matter for the courts or prosecutor. G.S. received counselling privately; no effective follow-up occurred on the court-ordered reports or evaluations.

The Court held that the authorities had failed to take all necessary measures to facilitate contact and rebuild the father-child relationship, in violation of Article 8.

**I.S. v. Greece (ECtHR, Appl. no. 19165/20, 23 May 2023)**

The applicant, a Greek national, married G.S. in 2007; daughters A. (b. 2007) and K. (b. 2011) were born of the marriage. The couple separated in January 2012. The marriage was dissolved in 2013 (upheld on appeal) for reasons attributable to the applicant, who was later convicted of domestic violence against G.S. relating to a 2011 incident.

Temporary custody of the children was initially awarded to the applicant. Following the mother’s recovery from health issues, interim measures transferred custody to her in December 2013; the children have lived with her since. Permanent custody was granted to G.S. in 2017 (upheld on appeal in 2019). Courts found the children well-adapted to their mother and unwilling to see the applicant; a change of environment was not in their best interests.

Contact rights were granted in 2014 and refined in 2015: a detailed schedule (weekdays, weekends including overnights with the applicant’s mother or sister present, plus holidays), with handover at Kifissia police station to reduce parental conflict. From January 2016 the children consistently refused to leave with the applicant; police recorded each incident in the log. The pattern persisted until mid-2019.

In May 2017 the first-instance court ordered a social-welfare report and a child-psychiatrist evaluation to ascertain the children’s psychological state, the reasons for their refusal of contact, and the suitability of police-station handovers. G.S. repeatedly obstructed the process: she sought revocation of the orders (claiming the older child would be re-traumatised), refused to attend sessions or produce the children, moved residences (Kifissia to Oropos then Tinos), and withheld her actual address. The appointed psychiatrist never examined the children; on the basis of documents and meetings with the applicant she concluded that the mother’s non-cooperation and behaviour were the likely cause of the children’s refusal, that police-station handovers were psychologically harmful, and that contact should be reinstated urgently. She recommended psychiatric examination of G.S. Social-welfare reports (2019–2020) were equally delayed and incomplete; they noted intense parental hostility affecting the children, the mother’s lack of cooperation, the need for professional supervision of meetings, and the children’s requirement for mental-health monitoring. A 2020 prosecutorial order for psychiatric evaluation of G.S. and the children was never executed because she continued to refuse cooperation and conceal her address.

In July 2019 G.S. relocated with the children to Tinos. Courts upheld her right to choose residence and designated Tinos police station for handovers. Police logs show G.S. appeared with the children on 14 occasions in late 2019; the applicant appeared once, and the children again refused. Telephone contact arranged by the applicant went unanswered.

The applicant lodged repeated applications with public prosecutors (2014–2021) seeking enforcement of contact orders, investigation of possible parental alienation, and completion of the ordered reports. Prosecutors issued verbal recommendations to G.S., ordered counselling (later revoked or not followed up), and referred the applicant back to the civil courts. After the 2021 first-instance judgment (which set a new graduated contact schedule, imposed a €250 fine plus one month’s imprisonment for each obstruction, and required handover on Tinos), the outstanding evaluation order was revoked. That judgment has not been enforced; appeals remain pending. Complaints to police, ministries, the Ombudsman and municipal social services produced only referrals or statements that the matter was for the courts.

The Court held that the authorities had failed to take all necessary and reasonably prompt measures to enforce the applicant’s contact rights and to facilitate the re-establishment of a relationship with his daughters, in breach of their positive obligations under Article 8. There had been no effective follow-up of the counselling, psychiatric-evaluation and social-welfare orders whose purpose was to identify and address the causes of the children’s refusal.
001-224961:
The case of Stanevi v. Bulgaria (Application no. 56352/14) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns two Bulgarian applicants, Maria Hristova Staneva (born 1963) and her daughter Darina Veselinova Staneva (born 1991). They complained under Article 2 of the Convention that they could not obtain non-pecuniary compensation for the death of Veselin Stanev (Maria’s husband and Darina’s father) in a 2010 car crash caused by a mentally ill driver. This raised issues regarding the State’s positive obligation to maintain an effective legal system providing civil redress for unintentional deaths.

On 21 August 2010, Veselin Stanev died from crash injuries; Maria, a passenger, was also seriously hurt. The crash was caused by H.T., diagnosed in 1999 with bipolar affective disorder. He had managed the condition with medication, completing university and working, with only isolated episodes. In July 2010 his health declined: he became overly excited, smoked and drank coffee excessively, and drove recklessly. A psychiatrist prescribed extra medication, but on holiday H.T. discarded it, ate and slept little, consumed much alcohol and coffee, and behaved erratically. En route home he stopped in Karnobat, brutally killed his grandfather, then caused the fatal crash. He was not intoxicated.

Criminal proceedings confirmed H.T. caused the accident while in a manic psychotic episode with delusions and hallucinations dominating his actions. On 15 June 2011 a prosecutor discontinued the case (and the related grandfather-killing case) because H.T. could not be held criminally liable due to mental illness. The applicants did not appeal. H.T. underwent compulsory treatment until December 2014.

The applicants sued H.T.’s insurer, each claiming 150,000 BGN (about 77,000 EUR) for non-pecuniary damage from Stanev’s death. An expert report based on the criminal file confirmed H.T.’s psychosis. The Sofia City Court (23 July 2012) awarded each 90,000 BGN, analogously applying section 47(2) of the Obligations and Contracts Act to hold the insurer liable despite H.T.’s incapacity. The Sofia Court of Appeal (14 March 2013) reversed, finding H.T. of unsound mind so that he lacked fault; the section 45 fault presumption therefore did not apply, H.T. had no civil liability, and the insurer’s “functional” liability (dependent on the insured’s) likewise failed. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal on 10 March 2014.

In parallel injury proceedings the Supreme Court (15 October 2015) awarded Maria 80,000 BGN after finding the fault presumption unrebutted, as incapacity under section 47(1) had not been proven. It observed obiter that neither insurer nor Guarantee Fund would normally be liable in true incapacity cases and urged legislative reform.

Bulgarian tort law (Obligations and Contracts Act) imposes a general duty to compensate damage caused by fault (section 45, presumed unless rebutted). Section 47 exempts a person “incapable of controlling or understanding his or her actions” unless the incapacity was self-induced; supervisors may then be liable. Compulsory motor-liability insurance (Insurance Code 2005, Art. 226) allows direct claims against the insurer but only when the insured is at fault. A Guarantee Fund covers uninsured, unknown or unlicensed drivers, but not mentally ill drivers.

Domestic case-law was inconsistent: some courts awarded damages by treating mental illness as not automatically rebutting fault or by invoking exceptions; others, as in the present death claim, denied liability once incapacity was established. These facts underpinned the applicants’ complaint that Bulgaria’s legal system afforded no effective civil redress for an unintentional death caused by a mentally ill person.

The ECHR case of Stanevi v. Bulgaria (no. 56352/14) concerns the applicants’ inability to obtain non-pecuniary damages for the death of their close relative in a car crash caused by a mentally ill driver. The applicants, Maria Hristova Staneva (wife) and Darina Veselinova Staneva (daughter), complained under Article 2 (procedural limb) of the Convention of a failure to provide an effective legal system allowing civil redress for unintentional death, as well as under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 regarding the inability to obtain compensation.

On 21 August 2010, Veselin Stanev died from injuries in a car crash; the first applicant, a passenger, was seriously injured. The crash was caused by H.T., who had bipolar affective disorder and was experiencing a manic episode with psychotic symptoms. Diagnosed in 1999, H.T. had been stable on medication until July 2010, when his condition deteriorated: he became overly excited, consumed excessive alcohol and coffee, discarded his medication, and drove recklessly. After brutally killing his grandfather, H.T. caused the fatal accident (he was not intoxicated).

Criminal proceedings against H.T. were discontinued on 15 June 2011, as his mental illness precluded criminal liability. The applicants did not appeal. H.T. was placed in compulsory medical treatment until 2014.

The applicants then sued H.T.’s civil-liability insurer for BGN 150,000 (approx. EUR 77,000) each in non-pecuniary damages. An expert report, based on the criminal investigation, confirmed that H.T.’s actions (including reckless driving) were dominated by delusions and hallucinations, rendering him psychotic and incapable of understanding or controlling his conduct.

The Sofia City Court awarded BGN 90,000 (EUR 46,000) to each applicant. Although H.T. himself could not be held civilly liable due to incapacity under section 47(1) of the Obligations and Contracts Act, the court held the insurer liable by analogy to section 47(2) (liability of persons supervising an incapable person).

The Sofia Court of Appeal reversed this. It accepted that H.T. had caused the accident while of unsound mind, so the statutory presumption of fault under section 45 did not apply and H.T. was not civilly liable. The insurer’s liability was merely “functional” and contingent on the insured’s liability; thus the insurer owed nothing. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal, endorsing the functional-liability analysis.

In parallel proceedings concerning the first applicant’s own injuries, the Supreme Court later (2015) held the insurer liable, finding that the presumption of fault had not been rebutted because incapacity under section 47(1) had not been proven on the evidence.

Bulgarian law (Obligations and Contracts Act) generally imposes liability for fault-based damage (section 45, with a presumption of fault) but exempts persons incapable of controlling or understanding their actions unless they caused the incapacity themselves; supervisors may then be liable (section 47). Under the 2005 Insurance Code, a victim may claim directly from the insurer only if the insured was at fault. The Guarantee Fund covers uninsured, unidentified or unlicensed drivers, but not cases of incapacity of an insured driver. Domestic case-law on mentally ill tortfeasors was inconsistent, with some courts awarding compensation where fault was not rebutted and others dismissing claims against insurers.

The applicants thus obtained no compensation for the death, highlighting a gap in the legal framework for civil redress in cases of death caused unintentionally by an incapable driver.

The ECtHR case Stanevi v. Bulgaria (App. no. 56352/14) arose from the applicants’ inability to obtain non-pecuniary damages for the death of Mr Veselin Stanev (husband of the first applicant and father of the second) in a 21 August 2010 car crash. The first applicant was also seriously injured. The crash was caused by H.T., who suffered from bipolar affective disorder (diagnosed 1999) and was in a manic episode with psychotic symptoms. H.T. had previously been stable on medication and pursued education and work, but his condition worsened in July 2010 (excitement, reckless driving). He consulted a psychiatrist, received extra medication, then went on holiday, stopped taking it, drank heavily, and on the return journey killed his grandfather before causing the fatal crash (he was not intoxicated).

Criminal proceedings established H.T.’s causation but were discontinued on 15 June 2011, as his mental illness meant he could not be held criminally liable. Separate proceedings for the grandfather’s death were likewise discontinued. The applicants, notified of the decision regarding Mr Stanev, did not appeal. H.T. was ordered to undergo compulsory treatment (April 2011–December 2014).

H.T. held valid civil-liability insurance. On 26 June 2011 the applicants sued his insurer, each claiming BGN 150,000 (≈ EUR 77,000) in non-pecuniary damages for the death. An expert report (based on the criminal file) confirmed that on 21 August 2010 H.T. was in a psychotic state whose delusions and hallucinations “dominated” his judgment and reckless driving. The Sofia City Court (23 July 2012) awarded each applicant BGN 90,000, holding that although H.T. himself could not be civilly liable (incapable of understanding his actions), his insurer was liable by analogy to s. 47(2) of the Obligations and Contracts Act (OCA).

The Sofia Court of Appeal (14 March 2013) reversed and dismissed the claims. It accepted that H.T. caused the accident while of unsound mind, so the damage was not “through his fault.” The OCA s. 45 presumption of fault therefore did not apply and H.T. was not civilly liable. Because an insurer’s liability (Insurance Code 2005, Art. 226) is purely “functional”/conditional on the insured’s liability, the insurer owed nothing. The Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal (10 March 2014), endorsing the functional-liability analysis.

In parallel proceedings for the first applicant’s own injuries, lower courts first awarded then dismissed damages. The Supreme Court (15 October 2015) ultimately awarded BGN 80,000, finding on the evidence that the s. 45 presumption of fault had not been rebutted (incapacity under OCA s. 47(1) was not proven). Obiter, it observed that neither the insurer nor the Guarantee Fund (Insurance Code Art. 287–288) was liable when a tortfeasor was truly incapable, and recommended legislative reform.

Relevant domestic law: OCA s. 45 imposes liability for damage caused “through fault” (fault presumed). Section 47(1) excludes liability if the tortfeasor was “incapable of controlling or understanding his or her actions” (unless self-induced); s. 47(2) then imposes liability on supervisors. Insurer liability tracks the insured’s civil liability; the Guarantee Fund covers only enumerated gaps (unknown/uninsured drivers, etc.), not mentally ill insured drivers. Domestic case-law on similar facts was inconsistent: some courts found the fault presumption unrebutted or applied the Guarantee Fund; others (like the courts in the applicants’ death claim) denied all compensation once incapacity was accepted.

These facts underpinned the applicants’ complaint that Bulgaria had failed to provide an effective legal system allowing appropriate civil redress for unintentional death, contrary to the procedural limb of Article 2.

The ECHR case Nepomnyashchiy and Others v. Russia (apps. 39954/09 and 3465/17) involved four Russian LGBTI community members and activists alleging discrimination (Art. 14 + Art. 8) due to homophobic statements by state officials and inadequate domestic responses.

In the first application, three gay men challenged a 16 May 2008 Komsomolskaya Pravda interview with Tambov Governor Betin. Responding to a mayor's arrest over a same-sex relationship, Betin stated he opposed “perversions,” that Orthodox principles must be sacrosanct, and that “Homos must be torn to pieces. And the pieces thrown to the wind!” Applicants filed a criminal complaint under Art. 282 CC (public incitement to hatred/enmity or dignity humiliation on grounds including social group membership). Tambov experts found no insults, foul language, or violence calls, as statements were impersonal and homosexuals were not a “social group” per social science. The Investigations Committee refused to open proceedings. Applicants sought judicial review under Art. 125 CCrP. The Leninskiy District Court denied standing, as their interests were unaffected. The Tambov Regional Court upheld this, holding sexual preferences did not confer distinct social group status under Art. 282.

In the second application, applicant Krikkerik (an LGBTI activist) had been shot in a 3 November 2013 baseball-bat/pneumatic-gun attack on a St Petersburg LGBTI office (another victim lost an eye). A 6 November Fontanka.ru interview with St Petersburg legislator Milonov followed. Milonov called LGBTI people “perverts,” “sickos,” and “foreign agents”; justified “booting” them as any Russian would; compared homosexuality to murder or immorality; claimed public displays insulted children and families; and dismissed attacks as provoked. Applicants alleged Art. 282 violations (calls to violence, incitement, dignity humiliation of LGBTI as a social group).

Pre-investigation experts varied: some identified humiliating/inciting/homophobic content and negative evaluations of homosexuals; others (including sociological reports) held homosexuals were not a “social group.” The Investigations Committee repeatedly refused to open a case (citing lack of social-group status and no proven direct intent, as Milonov was allegedly unwarned of recording/publication), though prosecutors quashed some refusals. A 2014 Constitutional Court ruling had indicated sexual orientation could qualify as social-group membership for anti-discrimination protection, but this was not applied. Under Art. 125 CCrP review, the Kuybyshevskiy District Court and St Petersburg City Court upheld the refusal as lawful and reasoned, finding no private-life breach.

Krikkerik also brought a civil claim (Arts. 150-151 Civil Code) against Milonov for breaches of dignity, private life, and non-discrimination (invoking Constitution Arts. 19, 21, 23 and Convention Arts. 8/14). Relying on expert reports and data on rising homophobic violence, she argued Milonov’s high-profile statements (as a known anti-LGBTI politician) foreseeably harmed the vulnerable LGBTI group, including her as a recent attack victim. The Kirovskiy District Court rejected this, viewing statements as personal opinions expressing reprobation (rude due to Milonov’s personality/manners) but not justifying violence, interfering with private lives, or targeting the applicant. Appeals (City Court, cassation, Supreme Court) were dismissed similarly.

Domestic law (Constitution equality/dignity/private-life guarantees; Art. 282 requiring direct intent; civil remedies for intangible rights) theoretically offered protection, but provisions were not applied. Courts failed to balance Arts. 8/10 in criminal proceedings or engage any balancing in civil ones. International materials (ECRI, UN, HRW) noted rising Russian homophobia, official anti-LGBTI rhetoric, violence, and enforcement gaps (sexual orientation not explicitly listed in Art. 282 despite Constitutional Court guidance).

The ECHR case Nepomnyashchiy and Others v. Russia (apps. 39954/09 and 3465/17) involved complaints by four Russian LGBTI activists of discrimination (Art. 14) in conjunction with the right to private life (Art. 8). They alleged that domestic authorities failed to adequately address homophobic public statements by state officials targeting the LGBTI community.

In the first application, three gay LGBTI activists challenged a 16 May 2008 interview in Komsomolskaya Pravda with Tambov Governor Oleg Betin. Discussing a mayor’s arrest over a same-sex relationship, Betin declared himself “against perversions,” insisted “Orthodox [Christian] principles must be sacrosanct,” called for a “foul den” to be “cleansed,” referred to “queers” in the media, and stated: “Homos must be torn to pieces. And the pieces thrown to the wind!” The applicants filed a criminal complaint under Article 282 of the Criminal Code (incitement to hatred/enmity and humiliation of dignity on grounds including membership of a social group). Commissioned experts found no insults or foul language; homosexuals were not a “social group” under social science; and the remarks contained no calls to violence as they were impersonal and unnamed specific perpetrators or victims. Investigators refused to open proceedings. Courts dismissed the applicants’ challenge for lack of standing, ruling that sexual orientation did not constitute membership of a distinct social group, so their interests were unaffected.

In the second application, the applicant (an LGBTI activist) had been shot in the back during a 3 November 2013 attack on a St Petersburg LGBTI support office. On 6 November 2013, Fontanka.ru published an interview with St Petersburg legislator Vitaly Milonov. He blamed LGBT organisations’ “eccentric escapades” and “provocation” for rising tension, described the office as a “homosexual hellhole,” suggested a victim’s injury was a “planned act of provocation” involving “toy guns,” stated an activist “dancing... with a banner... is asking for it,” admitted he would “boot” someone insulting his family “as any Russian would do,” called LGBTI people “perverts” who “insult our children,” denied they had human rights (terming them “rights of sickos and perverts”), compared homosexual acts to murder, claimed children could be “brainwashed,” “gotten drunk” and “raped or seduced” into becoming gay, and asserted that 99 of 100 people opposed them. The applicant lodged a criminal complaint under Article 282. Experts produced mixed reports: some identified humiliating descriptions, negative evaluations, insults, and statements inciting action or justifying violence against homosexuals; others concluded homosexuals were not (or not “unquestioningly”) a social group, there were no direct violence calls (statements being ambiguous opposition to “negative influence” on youth), and no proof of direct intent because the journalist had not warned Milonov the conversation would be recorded and published verbatim. Investigators issued repeated refusals (some quashed by prosecutors then reissued). Courts upheld the final refusal, citing the lack of a social group and absence of direct intent.

The applicant also brought a civil claim under Articles 150–151 of the Civil Code (protection of dignity, private life, and compensation for non-pecuniary damage), arguing the statements (from a prominent politician) were offensive, foreseeably risked violence given rising homophobic attacks, and violated her rights as an LGBTI person and recent attack victim. Courts rejected it, holding the remarks expressed personal opinion and reprobation of lifestyle rather than interference with private life or negative statements against the community; they were rude due to personality/manners but not insulting or directed at the applicant personally, and expressed compassion for the attack victim.

Domestic law (Constitution Arts. 19, 21, 23; Criminal Code Art. 282; Civil Code Arts. 150–151) theoretically protected dignity, private life, and equality (including, per a 2014 Constitutional Court ruling, sexual orientation as potentially a social group), but was not applied here. The ECHR later found a violation of Art. 14 taken with Art. 8, as authorities failed to respond adequately; courts did not fairly balance Arts. 8 and 10 in criminal proceedings and performed no balancing in civil ones.

The ECtHR case Nepomnyashchiy and Others v. Russia (apps. 39954/09 and 3465/17) involved four LGBTI activists alleging discrimination (Art. 14 + Art. 8) due to homophobic statements by state officials and the authorities’ inadequate response.

In the first application, three gay LGBTI activists challenged a 16 May 2008 Komsomolskaya Pravda interview with Tambov Governor Betin. Discussing the arrest of Tambov’s mayor (suspected of kidnapping his former same-sex lover), Betin declared himself “against perversions,” insisted Orthodox principles and high moral values for politicians were sacrosanct, and stated that the mayor had disgraced the authorities. He added: “This ... foul den must be cleansed” and, when asked about tolerance, “Homos must be torn to pieces. And the pieces thrown to the wind!” The applicants filed a criminal complaint under Criminal Code Art. 282, arguing the remarks called for violence against gay people as a social group.

Experts commissioned by the Tambov Investigations Committee found no insults or foul language. They concluded homosexuals were not a “social group” under social science, and the statements contained no calls to violence (being impersonal, naming neither perpetrators nor victims). On 8 July 2008 the Committee refused to open proceedings. The applicants sought judicial review under Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 125. The Leninskiy District Court held they lacked standing because their interests were unaffected. The Tambov Regional Court upheld this on 13 November 2008, ruling that sexual preferences do not create a distinct social group protected by Art. 282, so the applicants belonged to no such group.

In the second application, the applicant (an LGBTI activist) was shot in the back during a 3 November 2013 baseball-bat and pneumatic-gun attack on a St Petersburg LGBTI support office; another victim lost an eye. That victim publicly blamed politicians, including St Petersburg Legislative Assembly member Milonov, for stirring hatred by calling homosexuals perverts. On 6 November 2013 Fontanka.ru published Milonov’s interview. He described LGBT organisations as tiring, rude and provocative; called homosexuals “perverts,” “sickos” and their acts “as repulsive ... as a murder”; justified “booting” them (as any Russian would) if they insulted families or children; denied they had a right to public assemblies (unacceptable before children); claimed homosexuality could be induced in minors by brainwashing, alcohol and rape/seduction; and stated 99 out of 100 Russians opposed them.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint under Art. 282. Milonov confirmed the statements to investigators but claimed they were metaphorical, out of context, and reflected personal opinion; he had assumed publication. One expert found humiliating, insulting and inciting remarks against homosexuals; another held they were not a “social group.” After prosecutor quashals, the Investigations Committee repeatedly refused to open a case, citing lack of social-group status and absence of proven direct intent (the journalist had not warned of recording/publication). The Kuybyshevskiy District Court and St Petersburg City Court upheld the 11 September 2014 refusal, accepting the investigator’s findings.

The applicant also brought a civil claim against Milonov under Civil Code Arts. 150–151 (dignity, private life, non-discrimination), arguing the high-profile statements stigmatised the entire vulnerable LGBTI community, especially after recent violence, and that the State had a positive obligation to protect private life. The Kirovskiy District Court dismissed the claim, finding no justification of violence, only personal (if rude) opinions about lifestyle that did not interfere with private life or target the applicant specifically. The City Court and Supreme Court upheld this.

These facts illustrate the authorities’ consistent refusal to recognise LGBTI persons as a protected social group and their failure to apply available criminal and civil remedies or to balance competing rights against official homophobic speech.

The case Fragoso Dacosta v. Spain concerns a trade-union representative's criminal conviction for insulting Spain's national flag during a labor protest, alleged to violate Article 10 of the ECHR (freedom of expression).

Applicant Pablo Fragoso Dacosta (born 1986) represented the Galician union Confederación Intersindical Galega. In late 2014, a cleaning company at the Ferrol Military Arsenal faced a dispute over unpaid wages. Its employees struck from October 2014 to March 2015, staging daily protests outside the base coinciding with the solemn flag-raising ceremony (national anthem, guard presenting arms). Protesters shouted wage-related slogans (e.g., “the flag does not pay the bills”) and made noise.

On 28 October 2014 the arsenal's Chief Admiral wrote to the union complaining of disrespect toward the flag. The next day he met the applicant and asked him to “tone down” protests during the ceremony.

At 8 a.m. on 30 October the applicant, among some 30 protesters, used a megaphone to shout two phrases in Galician: “Here you have the silence of the fucking flag” and “The fucking flag must be set on fire.” No other incidents, disturbances or violence occurred. Some fellow protesters immediately objected (“no, not that”).

He was charged under Article 543 of the Criminal Code (public insults to Spain or its symbols). On 22 March 2017 Ferrol Criminal Court no. 1 convicted him, finding the remarks public, made before military personnel with intent to show contempt, and uttered despite the recent request to moderate the protest. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,260 (replaceable by imprisonment if unpaid), noting that judges must apply the law even if scholars favored decriminalization.

The A Coruña Audiencia Provincial dismissed his appeal on 8 February 2018, emphasizing the “intense feeling of humiliation” experienced by military personnel. The applicant paid the fine; criminal liability was extinguished on 1 March 2019.

He lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court alleging violations of freedom of ideology (Article 16) and expression (Article 20). The Court admitted the appeal for its “special constitutional significance.” The public prosecutor supported granting it, arguing the sanction was disproportionate and that lower courts had ignored context and purpose.

On 15 December 2020 the Constitutional Court (6–5) dismissed the appeal. It held that its role was to check whether the judgments had properly balanced freedom of expression against protection of State symbols. The remarks, it found, occurred at the most solemn military ceremony, used the qualifier “fucking” and an incitement to burn the flag, were unnecessary and unconnected to the wage claims, isolated from other slogans, and had been rejected by some protesters. They conveyed intolerance, exclusion and belligerence toward a symbol of national identity rather than contributing to public debate. Unlike prior cases involving political criticism of officials, the statements were objectively offensive and unrelated to the protest's legitimate aim. They therefore fell outside the protection of freedom of expression (and ideology). The minimum fine, calibrated to the applicant's means, was proportionate.

These events—peaceful labor protest, isolated verbal insults during a flag-raising, absence of disorder or incitement to violence, criminal conviction and fine—underpin the alleged Article 10 violation: a disproportionate interference with expression on a matter of public interest (unpaid wages) that did not amount to hate speech.

He was charged under Article 543 of the Spanish Criminal Code (public insults against Spain or its symbols). On 22 March 2017 Ferrol Criminal Court no. 1 convicted him, finding the utterances had been made publicly before the military with the aim of showing contempt. It noted the prior requests to moderate the protests and sentenced him to a fine of EUR 1,260 (replaceable by imprisonment in default of payment). The A Coruña Audiencia Provincial dismissed his appeal on 8 February 2018, emphasising that the military had experienced “an intense feeling of humiliation.” After the fine was paid, criminal liability was extinguished.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, claiming violations of freedom of ideology and expression. The Court accepted the case for its “special constitutional significance.” The public prosecutor supported the appeal, arguing the criminal sanction was disproportionate and that the lower courts had failed to take proper account of context and purpose.

By a 6–5 majority on 15 December 2020 the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal. It held that the statements were unconnected to the unpaid-wages dispute, had been uttered during the most solemn military ceremony, and had been rejected by some fellow protesters who said “no, not that.” The words conveyed intolerance, hostility and a wish to destroy a national symbol, falling outside the protection of freedom of expression. The minimum fine was deemed proportionate.

These facts— the labour-protest setting on a matter of public interest, the applicant’s union role, the isolated use of insulting language after warnings, the absence of disorder or incitement to violence, and the imposition of a criminal (rather than civil) penalty—formed the core of the Article 10 complaint that the domestic courts had failed to strike a fair balance between the applicant’s expression and the protection of state symbols.
