The case of Erik Adamčo v. Slovakia concerns the applicant’s 2017 conviction by the Žilina District Court for two counts of complicity in murder in an organised-crime context, for which he received a 25-year sentence. In 1997, victim A was killed after being driven to a meeting by the applicant, C and another person, at the direction of B. In 1999, victim D was shot dead; the applicant and his brother were alleged to have hired E to carry out the killing, with the applicant assisting. The applicant has always denied any involvement.

The conviction rested to a significant degree on incriminating statements by B, C and E—described as cooperating accused, cooperating witnesses or “penitents”—who testified after agreeing to assist prosecutors in return for immunity or other advantages. B, already serving a life sentence for other murders, confessed in March 2014 that he had ordered A brought to him for killing and named the applicant as one of those who delivered A. C gave a statement in May 2014 confirming his and the applicant’s role. E, remanded in 2013 for an unrelated murder, confessed in October 2013 to killing D and implicated the applicant and his brother; he was released from custody, placed in a witness-protection programme, and had prosecutions for three murders stayed under provisions allowing this for significant contributions to organised-crime investigations. Charges against C were temporarily suspended on similar grounds. No judicial oversight of the advantages appears to have occurred, and details of their precise scope remained unavailable.

At trial (April 2015–March 2017) B, C and E were examined and cross-examined. The applicant pointed to material inconsistencies: B and C disagreed on the number and identity of participants in A’s killing (four of those named had alibis), on motives (none involving the applicant), and on timing (B placed the killing a day earlier than forensic experts). For D’s murder, E claimed he shot from the front, yet the autopsy showed a back wound; his accounts of the scene, escape route, other persons present and a purported pre-murder telephone call by the applicant also conflicted with objective evidence. E had previously been acquitted of D’s murder and a retrial had been refused because of similar inconsistencies. A forensic psychologist noted E’s self-serving motives: to enhance his credibility in his own cases and to obtain immunity that would allow medical treatment.

The District Court nevertheless convicted, stating it had examined the cooperating witnesses’ evidence “particularly carefully” for internal logic and consistency with other material. It treated the advantages as lawful, regarded self-incrimination as a mark of reliability, dismissed inconsistencies as insignificant given the lapse of time, darkness and stress, and suggested D might have turned unnoticed or that unregistered telephones had been used. The Regional Court endorsed this reasoning, holding that a conviction may rest mainly on accomplice evidence provided it is thoroughly scrutinised and assessed freely like any other proof. The Supreme Court declared an appeal on points of law inadmissible, stressing society’s interest in prosecuting serious crime. The Constitutional Court likewise found no violation, concluding the lower courts had considered the evidence in context and had taken possible advantages into account.

The applicant complained under Article 6 that the proceedings were unfair: the courts failed to give individual attention to the nature and extent of the advantages obtained, did not rule out self-serving motives, and relied on the impugned testimony without adequate reasoning or safeguards.

The case of Erik Adamčo v. Slovakia concerns the applicant’s 2017 conviction (25 years’ imprisonment) for two counts of complicity in murder, committed in 1997 and 1999 in an organised-crime setting. The alleged Article 6 violation centres on the domestic courts’ heavy reliance on incriminating testimony from three accomplices (B, C and E) who cooperated with prosecutors in exchange for advantages such as charge suspensions or de facto immunity.

In 1997, victim A was driven by the applicant, C and another person to a meeting with B, who ordered the killing. In 1999, victim D was shot; prosecutors alleged that the applicant and his brother had hired E to carry out the murder and that the applicant had assisted. The applicant has always denied any involvement.

The charges (June 2014) and subsequent indictment rested principally on statements given by B (then serving a life sentence for other murders), C and E. B confessed in March 2014 that the applicant had helped deliver A. C corroborated this in May 2014. E, arrested in 2013 for an unrelated murder, confessed to D’s killing and implicated the applicant. At the 2015–2017 trial the District Court heard the three men (who were examined and cross-examined) plus other witnesses and experts. The applicant pointed to multiple inconsistencies: B and C gave conflicting accounts of the number of participants, their identities (four named persons had alibis) and the motive; B’s claimed time of A’s death differed by at least a day from expert findings; E’s description of shooting D from the front contradicted the autopsy (back wound); E’s account of the crime scene, escape route and a purported telephone call was unsupported by other evidence; and E had previously been acquitted of D’s murder, a retrial having been refused.

The District Court nevertheless convicted, finding that the applicant knew A would be killed and had hired and assisted E. It treated the inconsistencies as insignificant (possible expert error, D turning at the moment of the shot, lapse of time and darkness). It stated that it had examined the cooperating witnesses’ evidence “particularly carefully,” noting that they had also incriminated themselves and that any rehearsal would have eliminated discrepancies. The advantages they received were lawful.

On appeal the applicant argued that the men were perpetrators whose testimony was therefore inadmissible, that they had had access to the investigation file, that the precise advantages and conditions of their cooperation remained undisclosed, and that the de facto immunity granted to them and to numerous other cooperating perpetrators was disproportionate and lacked judicial oversight. The Regional Court dismissed the appeal, endorsing the first-instance reasoning and holding that a conviction may rest to a decisive extent on accomplice evidence provided it is thoroughly scrutinised; such evidence is assessed freely like any other. The Supreme Court declared an appeal on points of law inadmissible, stating that accomplice evidence is evaluated on a case-by-case basis under the free-assessment principle. The Constitutional Court likewise rejected the complaint, finding the lower courts’ assessment compatible with constitutional guarantees.

Documents later showed that C’s charges were temporarily suspended under Article 205 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because of his contribution to an organised-crime investigation, and that E’s prosecutions for three other murders were stayed under Article 228 on the same ground; E was also released from custody and placed in witness protection. An expert report noted that E’s motives included obtaining credibility for his own defence and the possibility of immunity to seek medical treatment. No detailed judicial examination of the precise nature, scope or proportionality of these advantages occurred in the applicant’s trial. These facts formed the core of the complaint that the conviction, based to a significant degree on self-serving accomplice testimony obtained in exchange for substantial benefits, lacked sufficient safeguards and reasoning.

The case of Erik Adamčo v. Slovakia (Application no. 19990/20) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair hearing in criminal proceedings). The applicant, a Slovak national born in 1976 and serving a prison sentence, was convicted of two counts of complicity in murder committed in an organised-crime context. His conviction rested to a significant degree on incriminating testimony from accomplices (B, C and E) who cooperated with prosecutors in exchange for immunity or other advantages. These individuals are known in Slovakia as cooperating accused, cooperating witnesses or “penitents.”

In 1997, victim A was killed near a mountain pass; courts later found that several people led by B carried out the killing after A was driven to the scene by three others, including the applicant and C. In 1999, victim D was killed in front of a hotel; the applicant’s brother and E were initially tried and acquitted for lack of evidence, with the acquittal becoming final in 2010. In 2013, after his arrest for an unrelated murder, E confessed to D’s killing and implicated the applicant and his brother. Prosecutors sought to reopen those proceedings, but courts refused in 2016 because E’s account (claiming he shot D from the front) contradicted forensic evidence that D had been shot in the back.

Meanwhile, in 2014, B (already serving a life sentence for other murders) confessed to ordering A’s killing and named the applicant among those who brought A to him. C also gave evidence implicating himself and the applicant in transporting A. The applicant has always denied any involvement.

In June 2014 the applicant was charged with complicity in both murders on the basis of statements by B, C and E. A bill of indictment followed in 2015. The Žilina District Court heard the case from 2015 to 2017, taking oral evidence (including cross-examination of B, C and E), expert testimony on the deaths and psychological profiles, and other evidence. The applicant highlighted multiple inconsistencies: conflicting accounts by B and C about the number and identities of participants in A’s murder (four people they named had alibis), differing motives none of which involved the applicant, a discrepancy of at least one day between B’s timeline and expert-established time of death, E’s claim of shooting D from the front versus the back wound, inconsistencies about the crime scene, escape route and telephone records, and E’s prior acquittal (with no retrial allowed).

On 2 March 2017 the District Court convicted the applicant and imposed a 25-year sentence. It found he had helped take A to B knowing A would be killed and had hired and assisted E in killing D. The conviction relied mainly on the three cooperating witnesses plus hearsay from others. The court acknowledged inconsistencies but deemed them insignificant given the passage of time, darkness, stress and the “commonplace” nature of such crimes for the witnesses. It claimed to have examined their evidence “particularly carefully,” noting that they had incriminated themselves as well as the applicant (making untruthful testimony illogical) and that any advantages they received were lawful. It treated the evidence under the principle of free assessment like any other evidence.

The Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in 2017, endorsing the first-instance reasoning and stating that a conviction could rest primarily on accomplice evidence provided it was thoroughly scrutinised. The Supreme Court declared an appeal on points of law inadmissible in 2019, holding that such evidence is assessed case-by-case under free assessment of evidence and serves society’s interest in prosecuting serious organised crime. The Constitutional Court rejected a complaint as inadmissible later that year, finding the lower courts’ conclusions compatible with constitutional guarantees.

Regarding the witnesses’ advantages: B was charged separately after confessing, with no further details available. Charges against C were temporarily suspended under Article 205 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because he had significantly contributed to investigating organised crime; proceedings remained at the pre-trial stage years later. E, remanded for another murder, was released and had prosecutions for three murders stayed under Article 228 because of his contributions; an expert noted his motives included securing favourable treatment in his own cases and obtaining medical care. No information confirmed whether charges were ultimately brought against him.

The applicant argued that the witnesses, as perpetrators, could not properly testify, that they had access to the investigation file allowing them to tailor statements, that no details of the advantages or conditions attached to their cooperation were disclosed, and that the advantages (amounting to de facto immunity under prosecutorial rather than judicial control) were disproportionate. Domestic courts gave no discernible individual attention to the scope and nature of those advantages and provided insufficient reasoning for relying on the evidence, without adequate safeguards against self-serving motives.

The case of Pricope v. Romania (no. 60183/17) arose from civil defamation proceedings against Sterian Pricope, a Romanian economist and long-time local media contributor in Câmpulung (to television and the online outlet bitpress.ro). For years he published articles criticising P.V., a prominent local businessman, former manager of the town’s main automobile factory (“the A. factory”), and owner of the newspaper Evenimentul Muscelean. Pricope alleged that P.V.’s business dealings had contributed to the factory’s bankruptcy, which ruined thousands of local jobs.

Between 2011 and 2014 Pricope wrote several pieces. One described a public-procurement contract under which P.V.’s company sold sports equipment to a municipal club at the highest quoted prices as the sole bidder. Another portrayed P.V. as a former factory worker who grew rich after 1989 through “phantom” companies that “sucked money” from the factory via unfavourable swaps of engines for vehicles and spare parts, plus advertising “compensation.” Later articles called P.V. a “racketeer” (căpuşă, “tick”) who had victimised the factory, hypocritically lamented its demise, and ran a newspaper that denied the right of reply while insulting the community. Additional language included “spits at Câmpulung” and a sarcastic remark about the owner’s “intellectual level.” Pricope later explained that he drew on public-auction records and earlier national-press reports (including a 2006 România Liberă article on shell companies).

In June 2014 P.V. sued Pricope and the publishing company for damage to his reputation and business image, attaching the articles. Pricope argued good faith, public-figure status, public-interest subject-matter and an intent merely to intimidate him. The Argeş County Court dismissed the claim in April 2015, holding that the criticism of a well-known public figure (businessman, former factory director, press owner) stayed within permissible limits and concerned widely reported factory-related grievances. The Piteşti Court of Appeal quashed that judgment in December 2015 for incomplete examination and remitted the case.

On remittal the County Court, in April 2016, found selected expressions unlawful and deprecating. It awarded P.V. 5 000 Romanian lei (approximately EUR 1 100) in non-pecuniary damages plus 2 000 lei costs. Pricope paid roughly EUR 770 of the total. The Court of Appeal upheld the ruling in February 2017. It characterised the articles as aimed solely at offending P.V., concluded that Pricope had acted in bad faith, denied him journalistic status because he lacked formal journalism training or ethical-code membership, and held that he had failed to prove a real factual basis or proper verification of sources.

Pricope applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the civil sanction violated Article 10 of the Convention. The Strasbourg Court found a violation: the domestic courts had not given relevant and sufficient reasons, had failed to balance the competing rights properly, and had imposed an award capable of producing a chilling effect. The interference was therefore not “necessary in a democratic society.”

The case of Pricope v. Romania (Application no. 60183/17) before the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). The applicant, Sterian Pricope (born 1962), an economist and long-time contributor to local television and the online outlet bitpress.ro, published articles criticizing P.V., a local businessman, former A. factory manager, and owner of the newspaper Evenimentul Muscelean. The articles alleged that P.V.’s corrupt dealings, via his company A.A.G., helped bankrupt the A. factory (the area’s main industry), harming thousands of residents.

Key articles (2011–2014) highlighted by P.V. included: a 20 September 2011 piece on P.V.’s company winning a high-priced public auction to supply sports equipment to a local club; an 8 November 2011 article describing P.V. as a former factory worker who grew rich post-1989 revolution; a 2 February 2012 article calling P.V. a “racketeer” (“căpuşa”) who benefited from an allegedly pre-arranged illegal tender, referencing his past illicit car-parts trade that contributed to the factory’s collapse (citing national reports of advantageous engine sales and advertisement “compensation” in vehicles); a 13 November 2013 piece accusing P.V. of “racketeering” the factory while hypocritically organizing a commemorative exhibition; a 6 March 2014 article listing P.V. among “honourable businessmen” whose firms “sucked money” from the factory; and a 2 July 2014 article labeling P.V. the “Oltenian who ‘spits’ at Câmpulung,” criticizing his newspaper’s denial of reply rights and lowbrow headlines.

P.V. filed a civil damages action on 13 June 2014 (extended 22 September 2014) against the applicant and bitpress.ro’s owner, claiming the articles tarnished his reputation as a public figure and businessman. The applicant defended on good-faith grounds, citing public sources (auction records, a 2006 România Liberă article on “shell companies”/firme căpuşă, and prior national/local reporting), arguing the pieces addressed P.V. solely as a public figure (not private life), used no truly insulting language, and that the suit aimed to intimidate.

The Argeş County Court dismissed the claim on 21 April 2015, holding the language within broader permissible criticism of public figures (politician, ex-director, businessman, press owner) on a matter of public interest (factory mismanagement, widely covered in the press). No unlawful acts existed for tort liability.

The Piteşti Court of Appeal quashed this on 9 December 2015 for incomplete factual examination and remitted. On rehearing, the County Court on 18 April 2016 found certain phrases unlawful (implying illegal racketeering causing bankruptcy; terms such as “spits at Câmpulung” and intellectually dismissive remarks). These harmed P.V.’s dignity given his local prominence in business, culture, and sport. It awarded 5,000 RON (~EUR 1,100) damages plus 2,000 RON costs (jointly with the company). The applicant paid his share (~EUR 770) in February 2017.

The Court of Appeal upheld this on 8 February 2017. It held the articles aimed to offend P.V.’s honour and image under a pretext of public interest; the applicant acted in bad faith and could not claim journalist protections (as an untrained economist who ignored professional ethics); the pieces lacked a contemporaneous factual basis from national media and failed verification duties.

The applicant alleged these sanctions violated Article 10. (The ECtHR later found a violation, citing insufficient reasons and a chilling-effect award, but this summary focuses on the underlying facts.)

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1970, arrived in Cyprus on 22 October 2018 and was immediately flagged due to an Interpol Red Notice issued in December 2017. The notice related to a Russian investigation into large-scale fraud, based on a 24 August 2017 arrest warrant from the Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow. He was provisionally arrested that evening pursuant to Cyprus’s Extradition Law and the European Convention on Extradition.

Extradition proceedings commenced the following day before the Larnaca District Court. Russia submitted a formal request on 8 November 2018 (received 9 November). After requests for better translations, the Minister of Justice authorised proceedings on 15 November. Multiple hearings followed through April 2019, marked by adjournments: the applicant changed lawyers, requested time to study documents and translations, and sought to call witnesses from Russia; the government sought time for a sick witness, clarifications from Russian authorities on whether proceedings remained active, and rebuttal evidence. The applicant’s repeated bail requests were refused due to flight risk and the seriousness of the charges. On 20 May 2019 the District Court approved extradition, confirming compliance with double criminality, ne bis in idem, and the Convention, and ordered continued detention pending surrender. The applicant was advised of his right to seek habeas corpus within 15 days.

A first habeas corpus application (4 June 2019) was withdrawn on 4 July after the Supreme Court indicated it had been improperly framed as an appeal rather than a challenge to detention lawfulness. A second application was filed on 9 July 2019. After government requests for extra time (including a scheduling error), it was heard on 26 September and dismissed on 3 October 2019 as out of time; the court also examined the merits and found no basis for release under the Extradition Law.

The applicant appealed on 7 October 2019 (initially using an incorrect form and later representing himself before instructing new counsel). Directions on 3 December 2019 allowed 60 days per side for written outlines. Further delays arose from an application to add grounds (granted February 2020). Covid-19 led the Supreme Court to suspend most judicial activity from mid-March to late April 2020, though extradition and habeas matters were excepted. The appeal was next listed on 11 September 2020; the government was given 45 more days for submissions. On 14 September the applicant asked to withdraw the appeal and be extradited immediately. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 16 September 2020.

The Ministry of Justice then prepared a surrender order. On 16 October Russian authorities requested postponement because regular flights had been suspended since March 2020 due to the pandemic, asking that the applicant remain detained “as long as possible.” On 29 October the Minister signed a surrender order but immediately suspended it under Article 18(5) of the Extradition Convention (force majeure), without fixing a new date; the authorities stated they would agree a date once restrictions allowed. The applicant repeatedly sought prompt surrender, citing resumed flights from early November and offering to pay his own fare. After further correspondence, Russia agreed to 6 December 2020, and the applicant was extradited that day.

Detention thus lasted from 22 October 2018 until 6 December 2020. The complaints centred on whether this period remained lawful under Article 5 § 1 (unjustified delays in the habeas corpus and appeal proceedings, plus the open-ended suspension without an agreed surrender date, which removed the Convention’s procedural safeguards) and whether the habeas corpus appeal review met the “speediness” requirement of Article 5 § 4 (proceedings lasting over eleven months, with lengthy extensions persisting after Covid restrictions ended).

The case of Khokhlov v. Cyprus (no. 53114/20) concerns Russian national Iurii Khokhlov’s detention in Cyprus pending extradition to Russia for alleged large-scale fraud. An Interpol Red Notice was issued on 8 December 2017 pursuant to a 24 August 2017 Moscow arrest warrant. Khokhlov arrived in Cyprus on 22 October 2018, was flagged, and provisionally arrested that evening under a warrant issued by the Larnaca District Court. Formal extradition proceedings (application no. 5/2018) began the next day. Detention was extended on 24 October 2018 owing to the seriousness of the offence and flight risk. Russia’s official request arrived on 9 November 2018 and was authorised by the Cypriot Minister of Justice on 15 November.

Multiple hearings ensued between November 2018 and May 2019, featuring adjournments for lawyer changes, document translations, a government witness’s illness, additional Russian evidence, and rebuttal witnesses. On 20 May 2019 the District Court approved extradition as compliant with the European Convention on Extradition (including dual criminality and non-political character) and ordered continued detention pending surrender, informing Khokhlov of his right to seek habeas corpus within 15 days.

Khokhlov lodged habeas corpus application no. 94/2019 on 4 June 2019 but withdrew it on 4 July after the Supreme Court observed that it amounted to an appeal rather than a challenge to detention lawfulness. He filed a fresh application (no. 118/2019) on 9 July 2019. The government obtained successive extensions for its objection. On 3 October 2019 the Supreme Court dismissed the application as out of time (49 days after the 15-day limit) yet examined the merits and found none of the statutory grounds for release under section 10(3) of the Extradition Law satisfied.

Khokhlov appealed on 7 October 2019 (initially in person on the wrong form). After lawyer changes, an amendment application and extensions, written outlines were directed on 3 December 2019 with 60-day deadlines each. On 16 March 2020 the Supreme Court suspended most proceedings until 30 April because of Covid-19, albeit with explicit exceptions for habeas corpus, extradition and urgent appeals. Normal functioning resumed in May, yet the appeal was not listed until 11 September 2020, when a further 45-day extension was granted to the State. On 14 September Khokhlov asked to withdraw the appeal and be extradited immediately; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 16 September 2020.

The Minister signed a surrender order on 29 October 2020 but immediately suspended it indefinitely, citing Russia’s inability to receive him owing to flight cancellations and invoking Article 18 § 5 of the Extradition Convention (force majeure requiring a mutually agreed new date). Khokhlov repeatedly requested prompt surrender, pointing to scheduled flights, but no date was fixed until Russia agreed to 6 December 2020, when extradition finally occurred. The habeas-corpus appeal thus lasted more than eleven months amid repeated extensions, even after Covid restrictions had ended, and the subsequent open-ended suspension occurred without an agreed surrender date.

The case of Tena Arregui v. Spain (Application no. 42541/18) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for private life and correspondence). The applicant, a Spanish national and former member of UPyD’s governing board until March 2015, claimed unlawful interception and disclosure of his emails, plus inadequate judicial protection after Spanish courts dismissed his related criminal complaint.

During UPyD’s 2015 leadership renewal, internal divisions emerged over a possible coalition with rival party Ciudadanos. The applicant and others supported it. In early April 2015, UPyD expelled member Mr. P. on suspicion of negotiating with Ciudadanos. Party leaders then hired a private firm to monitor Mr. P.’s emails on two UPyD-domain accounts from the preceding months.

The monitoring uncovered emails sent by the applicant from his personal (non-UPyD) account to Mr. P. These discussed plans by dissenting members to form a new party facilitating the coalition while retaining an internal faction. Details leaked to the press; newspapers reported the monitoring and named the applicant as involved.

On 3 June 2015, UPyD organizational manager Mr. F. emailed a report reproducing the applicant’s emails to 20 governing-board members and 150 political-council members.

The applicant complained to UPyD’s Dispute Settlement Body, seeking disciplinary proceedings against board members. On 1 July 2015 the Body dismissed the complaint, holding the interception necessary (a response to a serious pre-election threat) and proportionate (limited to a few emails selected by keywords). It found the emails concerned party actions, not private or family life.

On 17 July 2015 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against Mr. F. (later extended to another leader, Mr. H.) for unlawful disclosure of secrets (Criminal Code Art. 197) and breach of privacy (Constitution Art. 18). He argued the emails were private, sent from an external personal account with a legitimate expectation of privacy, and that political strategies plus the right to dissent were protected by Constitution Art. 6 (democratic party structure). He invoked Art. 8’s coverage of professional/business relations.

On 29 February 2016 Madrid Investigating Judge no. 32 opened proceedings, finding prima-facie evidence of an offence. The judge held Constitutional Court case-law on employer monitoring of employee business emails inapplicable, as there was no employment relationship between UPyD and either Mr. P. or the applicant; an extensive interpretation harming the secrecy of communications was impermissible.

On 21 September 2016 the Madrid Audiencia Provincial, allowing the accused’s appeal, provisionally discontinued the case. It found the firm had been commissioned solely to detect internal irregularities via a “blind search” of UPyD mailboxes using terms such as “coalition.” UPyD’s email policy (of which Mr. P. claimed ignorance) forbade personal use, required storage on party systems, permitted monitoring to protect the party’s image/resources, and allowed deactivation and retention of data after a user’s relationship ended. The court saw no evidence of any purpose other than identifying irregularities, nor proof of disclosure to the press. The offence was therefore not sufficiently established. A subsequent nullity request was rejected.

The applicant’s amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court (alleging violations of effective judicial protection, privacy, secrecy of correspondence and freedom of association) was dismissed on 5 March 2018. The Court held the Audiencia Provincial’s reasoning adequate and sufficient; criminal proceedings confer no unconditional right to trial or punishment; other remedies existed; and the Court would not reassess offence elements absent unreasonableness or illegality. Two judges dissented, arguing the reasoning was insufficient (especially regarding consent/knowledge of monitoring rules) and citing Bărbulescu v. Romania.

Workplace-surveillance case-law did not apply, as there was no employment relationship with UPyD, and an extensive interpretation harming the secrecy of communications was impermissible.

The monitoring company had been tasked with detecting internal irregularities via a keyword search of party-owned mailboxes assigned to Mr P. UPyD’s email-use policy forbade personal use, required storage on party systems, permitted monitoring to protect the party’s image and resources, and provided that accounts and data remained at the party’s disposal after a relationship ended. There was insufficient proof of any purpose other than identifying irregularities, or of disclosure to the press. The offence was not duly proved.

The applicant’s request to declare that decision void was rejected on 26 October 2016. He then filed an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of effective judicial protection, privacy, secrecy of correspondence and freedom of association.

On 5 March 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal. The Audiencia Provincial’s reasons were adequate and sufficient; it had placed the facts in context and reasonably excluded criminal-law intervention, without prejudice to other remedies. There is no unconditional right to a trial or to have another person punished. The rights invoked are protected by multiple legal avenues, not solely criminal proceedings. Two judges dissented, arguing the reasoning was insufficient given the constitutional dimension, particularly regarding the user’s knowledge of and consent to the email rules (citing Bărbulescu v. Romania). They viewed the facts as an objective limitation of private-life rights regardless of intent.

The alleged offence was therefore not established.

The applicant's subsequent request for annulment was rejected. His amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was dismissed on 5 March 2018. The Court found the Audiencia Provincial's reasoning adequate and sufficient, stressed that criminal law is an ultima ratio and that other civil remedies remained available, and declined to re-examine the elements of the offence. Two dissenting judges considered that the appellate court had failed to analyse whether Mr P. had been informed of, or had consented to, the monitoring rules, and that the decision therefore provided insufficient protection of the applicant's Article 8 rights.

These events—the targeted interception of personal correspondence, its internal dissemination to a large number of party members, the media leak, and the refusal of the criminal courts to proceed—constitute the factual core of the alleged Article 8 violation.

The case of Wiegandová v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 51391/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the ECHR arising from an unpaid, perpetual statutory easement restricting the applicant’s use of a flat she owned.

In January 2003 the applicant inherited a 691 m² tenement house in Prague. Her partner had obtained it from the State in October 1991 under restitution Law no. 87/1991 after its 1961 expropriation. While the building was State-owned, a construction cooperative had added six loft-conversion flats using 1,219,145 Czechoslovak korunas (of which 766,969 was a government loan). In 1987 a housing cooperative acquired those flats.

On 23 June 1992, statutory measure no. 297/1992 created, ex lege and without compensation, an easement over the six flats in the housing cooperative’s favour. The measure sought a post-communist compromise: it protected original owners/successors while preserving rights of persons who had acquired interests in good faith under the prior regime. The easement applied cooperative-tenancy rules, gave the cooperative landlord rights (including rent collection from its member-tenants), and required tenants to pay service charges to the building owner. The statutory “compensation” was deemed to be the physical improvement of the building.

In June 2009 the applicant recorded 59 separate units (including the six cooperative flats) as her property; the easements remained. Between 2009 and 2019 she sold 58 units (including five of the six cooperative flats to their occupant-members) for approximately CZK 99 million (EUR 3.7 million). She retained one 59.45 m² cooperative flat. The cooperative contributed 15.83–17.86 % of building costs in 2006–2011.

In June 2013, while still owning two cooperative flats, the applicant sued the cooperative for unjust enrichment (CZK 428,054 / EUR 16,700), arguing that members paid rent solely to the cooperative and that she had received no compensation for the unrestricted, unpaid easement. All domestic courts rejected the claim, holding that the 1992 measure treated the improvement itself as compensation and that cooperative-tenancy rules applied. The Supreme Court confirmed that compensation consisted of the increase in the property’s value. The Constitutional Court dismissed her 2015 complaint as manifestly ill-founded, noting that any time-limitation of the easement had to be sought individually.

In November 2016 the applicant sought termination or reduction of the easement over her remaining two flats, citing elapsed time, non-use by members, and alleged non-contribution to services. The District Court refused, stressing that the 1992 measure had been enacted precisely to resolve such post-restitution conflicts and that the cooperative’s repair contributions offset the burden. The Municipal Court added that the mere passage of time could not disturb the legislator’s balance between the owner’s title and the cooperative’s rights over flats it had created. The Supreme Court (March 2018) held that the legislature had not intended a temporal limit, that restitution restored property in its existing encumbered state, and that termination would extinguish valuable, transferable membership shares (functionally equivalent to ownership) of tenants who were not parties to the proceedings—an outcome contrary to Article 11 § 4 of the Czech Charter. The applicant had not shown the flats were vacant. The Constitutional Court (March 2019) again dismissed the complaint, emphasising that each case’s unique circumstances (including the short interval since the prior proceedings) had to be assessed and that time alone did not produce a “gross disproportion.”

These facts—the uncompensated, unlimited statutory easement imposed on restituted property to protect a cooperative’s investment, the applicant’s unsuccessful attempts to obtain monetary compensation or to terminate/reduce the burden, and her continued ownership of one encumbered flat—formed the core of the alleged interference with her property rights.

The ECHR case Wiegandová v. the Czech Republic (no. 51391/19) involves an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from an unpaid, perpetual easement restricting the applicant’s ownership of restituted property. In January 2003 Ms Helena Wiegandová inherited a Prague tenement house of 691 m² that her partner had recovered from the State in 1991 under restitution Law no. 87/1991, after its 1961 expropriation. While the building was State-owned a construction cooperative had added six loft-conversion flats at a cost of 1 219 145 Czechoslovak korunas (partly a government loan). In 1987 those flats passed to a housing cooperative. Statutory measure no. 297/1992, enacted to reconcile competing claims in the post-communist transition, automatically created an easement in the cooperative’s favour. The easement applies cooperative-tenancy rules, entitles the cooperative to collect rent and obliges it only to contribute to building maintenance (its share was 15.83–17.86 % of costs in 2006–11). The increase in the building’s value is treated by law as the sole compensation for the owner’s restricted rights.

In 2009 the applicant divided the house into 59 units of which she became sole owner; the easements remained. Between 2009 and 2019 she sold 58 units (including five of the six cooperative flats) for approximately CZK 99 million (€3.7 million), retaining only a 59.45 m² flat.

She first sued the cooperative in 2013 for unjust enrichment of CZK 428 054 for the two remaining cooperative flats, arguing that she received no rent and no other compensation. All domestic courts, culminating in the Supreme Court (2015) and Constitutional Court (decision I. ÚS 2096/15), dismissed the claim. They held that the statutory compensation consists precisely in the value added by the loft conversions and that the easement therefore does not constitute unjust enrichment.

In 2016 she sought judicial termination or reduction of the remaining easements, citing the passage of more than 25 years, alleged non-use of the flats and insufficient contributions. The District Court, Municipal Court and Supreme Court (2018) rejected the action. They emphasised that the 1992 measure was a deliberate, lasting compromise between the restituted owner’s title and the cooperative’s investment; mere lapse of time does not create a “gross disproportion” under Article 1299 of the Civil Code. Terminating the easement would destroy the tenants’ heritable membership rights (acquired in good faith at market prices) without their participation in the proceedings, violating Article 11 § 4 of the Czech Charter. The Constitutional Court (I. ÚS 2163/18) found no fair-trial or constitutional defect, repeating that any adjustment must be case-specific and that the short interval since the earlier litigation precluded a finding of changed circumstances.

These facts—restitution of a building improved at State expense, the subsequent statutory easement, the applicant’s substantial proceeds from sales, and the repeated domestic findings that the value added constitutes adequate compensation and that time alone cannot extinguish the burden—underpin the claim that the easement imposes an individual and excessive control of the use of property contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case of Wiegandová v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 51391/19) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights arising from an unpaid, perpetual easement encumbering a residential unit owned by the applicant.

The applicant inherited a Prague tenement house in January 2003. Her partner had acquired the building from the State in October 1991 under restitution legislation (Law no. 87/1991), following its expropriation in 1961. While the State owned the building, a construction cooperative had added six loft-conversion flats, investing KČS 1,219,145 (of which KČS 766,969 was a government loan). In 1987 those flats passed to a housing cooperative.

Statutory Measure no. 297/1992, which entered into force on 23 June 1992, created an ex-lege easement over the six flats in favour of the housing cooperative. The measure was designed as a compromise in the transition from the communist regime: original owners (or their successors) would recover title, yet persons who had invested in good faith under the prior legal order would retain use rights. Under the statutory scheme the cooperative (or its successor) enjoys landlord rights, collects rent calculated according to cooperative-housing rules, and must contribute to building maintenance; the improvement of the building itself is deemed compensation for the restriction on the owner’s title. The applicant later made an owner’s declaration converting the building into 59 units, all of which she initially owned. Between 2009 and 2019 she sold 58 units (including five of the six cooperative flats) for approximately CZK 99 million; she retains one 59.45 m² cooperative flat.

In June 2013, while she still owned two cooperative units, the applicant sued the cooperative for unjust enrichment (CZK 428,054), arguing that the unpaid, unlimited easement allowed members to occupy the flats without paying her rent. Domestic courts at all levels, including the Constitutional Court (I. ÚS 2096/15), rejected the claim. They held that the statutory improvement of the property constituted the prescribed compensation and that the cooperative lawfully collected rent.

In November 2016 the applicant sought termination or reduction of the remaining easements, citing the passage of time, non-occupation by some members and alleged non-contribution to service charges. The District Court, Municipal Court and Supreme Court dismissed the action. They reasoned that the legislature had deliberately made the easements imprescriptible, that mere lapse of time did not create a “gross disproportion” between burden and benefit (Article 1299 of the 2012 Civil Code), and that termination would extinguish valuable, heritable membership shares acquired by third parties in good faith, thereby violating those parties’ property rights. A further constitutional complaint (I. ÚS 2163/18) was rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant complained that the unpaid, perpetual easement constituted an unlawful and disproportionate control of her property, imposing an individual and excessive burden without fair compensation.
001-230292:
The case of Dabo v. Sweden (Application no. 12510/18) concerns whether Sweden’s refusal of family reunification for a recognised refugee’s first wife and five children breached Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life). The applicant, a Syrian doctor born in 1961, fled Syria in 2013, arriving in Sweden in December 2014 with his second wife (whom he married in Greece). Both were granted permanent refugee status on 8 March 2016. His first wife and their five children (born 2002–2009) had also left Syria around the same time and remained in Jordan under UNHCR protection. The applicant had last seen them in July 2013 and intended to live with both wives and all children in Sweden (noting that Swedish law does not recognise polygamy).

On 20 July 2016, Sweden’s Temporary Restrictions Act entered into force (until 19 July 2019), responding to a sharp rise in asylum seekers (nearly 163,000 in 2015). It aligned Swedish rules with the EU minimum under the Family Reunification Directive by introducing a “maintenance requirement”: the sponsor in Sweden must demonstrate sufficient income (salary or comparable work-related benefits, excluding certain social benefits) and adequate accommodation (size and standard for the family). An exemption applied if the family applied within three months of the sponsor receiving refugee status. Applications after that period, or those failing the requirement, could still be granted if refusal would violate Sweden’s international obligations.

The family applied at the Swedish Embassy in Amman on 24 November 2016 (eight months after the applicant’s status grant), with supporting documents in April 2017. The Migration Agency rejected the applications on 17 May 2017. The three-month exemption did not apply. The applicant received only “introduction benefits” (not treated as salary) and rented a one-and-a-half-room apartment with kitchenette, deemed insufficient for the family. The decision was found not contrary to Sweden’s convention commitments.

The applicant appealed, arguing that embassy contact in April 2016 (to book an interview) should count as the application date, making the exemption applicable. The Migration Court rejected this on 1 August 2017 for lack of evidence, confirming the November filing date. It accepted the applicant’s good future prospects of meeting the requirement (as a doctor seeking Swedish qualification) but found no current evidence of compliance. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 14 September 2017.

Supporting facts included the applicant’s steps toward fulfilling the requirement: he applied in January 2017 for assessment of his overseas medical qualifications (confirmed comparable in March 2017, but requiring a Swedish-language proficiency test); he completed a specialised Swedish course and a one-year fast-track programme for licensed professions run by the Public Employment Service (aimed at shortening licensing for doctors amid labour shortages); and his landlord offered to arrange larger housing if the family arrived.

The applicant complained under Article 8 that the three-month period was too short and inflexible for refugees, the maintenance rules overly strict given his circumstances and the children’s best interests (under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child), and that no proper individualised assessment occurred. Sweden argued the measures pursued legitimate aims of immigration control, reception capacity, and integration, consistent with EU law, and that the applicant could reapply later.

The Court (First Section, judgment of 18 January 2024, final 18 April 2024) found no violation. Member States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in imposing such conditions. There were no issues with calculating the exemption period or its flexibility. The applicant could lodge a fresh application at any time and had realistic prospects of meeting the requirement. An individualised assessment had been made, later legal changes allowed exemptions on “special grounds,” and a fair balance was struck between family life and the public interest without overstepping the margin.

The case of Dabo v. Sweden (Application no. 12510/18) concerns a Syrian refugee's unsuccessful bid for family reunification with his first wife and five children, which he alleged violated Article 8 of the ECHR (right to respect for family life). The applicant, a doctor born in 1961, fled Syria for Jordan in summer 2013; his first wife and children (born 2002–2009) followed months later and remain there under UNHCR protection. He briefly returned to Syria to work in a hospital before leaving again in November 2013, arriving in Greece in April 2014. There he married a second Syrian wife in November 2014. The couple entered Sweden on 12 December 2014 and claimed asylum. Both received permanent residence permits as refugees on 8 March 2016.

On 20 July 2016 Sweden enacted the Temporary Restrictions Act (in force until 19 July 2019) in response to a surge in asylum applications. The Act limited family reunification rights to immediate family members and introduced a “maintenance requirement”: the sponsor must demonstrate sufficient income (from salary or comparable work-related benefits, after tax, meeting a statutory reserve amount plus family support needs) and adequate housing (owned or rented accommodation of suitable size and standard). An exemption applied only if the application was lodged within three months of the sponsor receiving refugee status.

On 24 November 2016—eight months after the applicant’s status grant—his first wife and children applied for residence permits at the Swedish Embassy in Amman, Jordan (later supplemented in April 2017). The applicant stated he intended to live with both wives and all children, though polygamy is unrecognized in Sweden; he had last seen his first family in July 2013. His second wife had suffered a miscarriage and was pregnant. On 17 May 2017 the Migration Agency rejected the applications. The three-month exemption did not apply, and the applicant failed the maintenance test: he survived on non-comparable “introduction benefits” and occupied a one-and-a-half-room apartment with kitchenette, insufficient for the household. The Agency held that refusal did not breach Sweden’s international obligations.

The applicant appealed, claiming the family had contacted the embassy in April 2016 (within the exemption window) to book an interview, which should count as the application date. On 1 August 2017 the Migration Court dismissed the appeal, finding no evidence of the April contact; the applications were therefore dated 24 November 2016. Although the court accepted the applicant’s good prospects of later securing suitable employment and housing, he did not meet the requirements at the time of assessment. Leave to appeal was refused by the Migration Court of Appeal on 14 September 2017.

Meanwhile the applicant pursued professional integration. On 16 January 2017 he applied to have his Syrian medical qualifications recognized. The National Board of Health and Welfare confirmed they were comparable but required a Swedish-language proficiency test. He completed a one-year Public Employment Service “fast-track” programme for licensed professions (ending 1 February 2017) and obtained a certificate in specialized Swedish. His landlord indicated willingness to provide larger accommodation if the family arrived.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 8 complaint: that the rigid three-month deadline and maintenance conditions, applied without sufficient flexibility to a recently arrived refugee still completing language and licensing requirements, disproportionately interfered with family unity, especially given the children’s best interests and the applicant’s ongoing integration efforts. The applicant lodged his application with the Court on 6 March 2018.

The case of Dabo v. Sweden concerns a Syrian refugee's unsuccessful bid for family reunification with his first wife and five children, which he claimed violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life).

The applicant, a doctor born in 1961, fled Syria for Jordan in summer 2013. His first wife and their five children (born 2002–2009) followed months later and remain in Jordan under UNHCR protection. After briefly returning to Syria to work at a hospital, the applicant left again in November 2013, arriving in Greece via Turkey in April 2014. There he married his second wife (also Syrian) in a religious ceremony in November 2014. The couple entered Sweden on 12 December 2014 and applied for asylum, receiving permanent residence permits as refugees on 8 March 2016.

Sweden's Temporary Restrictions Act entered into force on 20 July 2016 (lasting until July 2019) in response to a record influx of asylum seekers. It introduced a maintenance requirement—sufficient income (from salary or equivalent work-related benefits, after tax, meeting a specified threshold including family support needs) plus adequate housing (owned or rented, of reasonable size and standard, e.g., extra rooms for children)—for family reunification unless the application was filed within three months of the sponsor receiving refugee status. This aligned Swedish rules with the EU Family Reunification Directive's minimum standards and aimed to ease integration pressures. An exemption also existed if refusal would breach international obligations.

On 24 November 2016 (eight months after the applicant's status grant), his first wife and children applied for residence permits at Sweden's embassy in Amman, Jordan (later supplemented in April 2017). The applicant stated he planned to live with both wives and all children; he had last seen his first family in July 2013. His second wife had suffered a miscarriage and was pregnant again. Swedish law does not recognize polygamy, so only one spouse could typically join a sponsor already living with another.

The Migration Agency rejected the applications on 17 May 2017. The late filing triggered the maintenance requirement. The applicant received only introduction benefits (not salary-equivalent) and rented a 1.5-room apartment with kitchenette, deemed too small. The refusal was held compatible with Sweden's international commitments.

On appeal, the applicant claimed his family had contacted the embassy in April 2016 (within the exemption window), constituting a timely application. The Migration Court (1 August 2017) found this unsubstantiated and confirmed the November 2016 filing date. It accepted the applicant's strong future prospects—his medical qualifications were deemed comparable to Swedish standards (pending a Swedish-language proficiency test); he had completed a specialized language course and a fast-track employment program for shortage professions like medicine; and his landlord offered to arrange larger housing—but found no current evidence of meeting the income or accommodation criteria. The court saw no Article 8 breach. The Migration Court of Appeal denied leave to appeal on 14 September 2017.

These facts centered on the application's timing outside the three-month exemption, the applicant's then-unmet maintenance criteria despite integration efforts and professional skills, the children's best interests, the polygamous setup, and the possibility of reapplying later (with later law allowing "special grounds" exemptions). The ECtHR ultimately found no violation, citing states' wide margin of appreciation, individualized review, and a fair balance of interests.

The case of Ismayilzade v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 17780/18) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life). The applicant, Leyla Miryagub gizi Ismayilzade (born 1990, resident in Baku), sought to register an unusual forename for her son born on 25 July 2016.

On 28 September 2016 she applied to the Yasamal District Registration Department (Ministry of Justice) to register the name “Əbülfəzlabbas”. The request was refused on 3 October 2016. A second application on 13 October 2016 for the variant “Əbülfəzl Abbas” was likewise rejected. The authorities invoked Article 21 of the Constitution (Azerbaijani as the state language), Article 26.1 of the Civil Code (every person’s right to a name consisting of forename, patronymic and surname) and Article 8 of the Law on State Language (names in official documents must be written in the state language). They further noted that the proposed name did not appear on the advisory list of recommended names issued by the Azerbaijani National Sciences Academy.

On 31 October 2016 the applicant sued the Registration Department in the Baku Administrative-Economic Court No. 1, seeking an order to register “Əbülfəzlabbas”. She relied on Article 32 of the Constitution (protection of private and family life), Articles 53.1 and 53.2 of the Family Code (child’s right to a name chosen by parental consent), the 2011 Rules on granting and changing names (rules 1.4 and 1.5), and Article 8 of the Convention. She argued that the Academy’s list was merely advisory. The child’s father—a religious leader of an unregistered Shia-related movement who was in pre-trial detention on serious charges including murder and incitement of hostility—wrote to the court consenting to the name “ƏbülfəzlAbbas”.

On 28 March 2017 the first-instance court dismissed the claim. It held that the name (in any spelling) was contrary to the child’s best interests because of its pronunciation, citing Article 26.1 of the Civil Code and rule 1.4 of the Rules (which prohibit names that harm a child’s interests, mismatch gender or expose the child to ridicule).

On 4 May 2017 the applicant applied to register the simpler name “Abbas”; this was granted on 10 May 2017. She nevertheless appealed the March judgment on 26 May 2017, arguing that the refused name fell outside the prohibited categories of rule 1.4 and that the court had failed to explain why its pronunciation was against the child’s interests.

The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 16 August 2017, finding that the Registration Department had acted within its discretion and had given adequate reasons. In a cassation appeal lodged on 22 September 2017 the applicant added that she and her husband followed Shia Islam, that the chosen name referred to a historical Islamic figure and was common in Shia-majority countries, and that it did not conflict with Azerbaijani phonetics, pronunciation or syntax.

On 29 November 2017 the Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal. Because “Abbas” had already been registered at the applicant’s own request, the child’s right to a name (Civil Code Art. 26.1, Family Code Art. 53.1) and the parents’ naming rights (Family Code Arts. 53.2 and 166.2) had been respected. The claim now concerned a change of an already-registered name, which under Family Code Art. 54.1 requires a joint parental request, consent of the custody authority and consideration of the child’s best interests.

The applicant’s Article 8 complaint was therefore that the authorities’ refusal to register the original chosen name interfered with her private and family life. The domestic courts examined the matter at three levels and issued reasoned decisions; the European Court later found that the authorities had enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation and that the inconvenience caused did not amount to a lack of respect for the applicant’s Article 8 rights.

The inconvenience of using a different registered name was insufficient to establish a lack of respect for the applicant’s Article 8 rights. No violation was found.

The case of Maroslavac v. Croatia (Application no. 64806/16) concerns complaints by a Croatian notary public under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant alleged that a tax audit of her financial affairs was procedurally flawed, preventing effective participation, and that she was ordered to pay unpaid profit tax for periods in respect of which the State's collection rights had become time-barred.

In 2001, the applicant purchased business premises for approximately HRK 2,700,000 (EUR 360,000), later valued by experts at HRK 5,000,000 (EUR 660,000). Under domestic law, she was entitled to deduct this value from her profit tax over the following six years.

On 26 June 2007, the Zagreb Office of the Ministry of Finance’s Tax Administration initiated a tax audit covering VAT from 1 January 2003 to 31 May 2007 and profit tax from 1 January 2003 to 31 December 2006. By a determination of 26 October 2007 (notified on 5 November 2007), the audit was extended to income tax for 1 January 2003 to 31 December 2005.

An audit report dated 6 November 2007, served on 7 November 2007, found that the applicant had failed to declare income from the revaluation of her assets in 2001, 2002, and 2003, contrary to law. Consequently, her 2003 profit tax declarations required an increase. The applicant objected, arguing that the audit improperly covered 2001 and 2002 (outside the statutory limitation period) and that late notification of the extension prevented her active participation. The objection was mistakenly sent to the wrong department.

On 28 December 2007, a tax ruling established unpaid profit tax for 2003–2005, VAT for 2003–2007, and capital income tax for 2003–2005, ordering payment of the additional amounts plus default interest. The applicant appealed on 6 February 2008, reiterating the time-bar and participation issues. After the objection reached the correct department on 14 February 2008, a fresh ruling on 20 February 2008 replaced the prior one, with similar findings. It detailed that the applicant had recorded the premises' estimated value in 2001 and claimed amortisation deductions through 2006. Invoking section 100(5) of the General Tax Act, the authorities extended the audit to prior periods due to facts indicating a significant alteration in tax liability. They cited interruption of the three-year relative limitation period (section 91) by official actions and noted the six-year absolute limitation (section 92) had not expired. The ruling stated the applicant had participated by providing records and documents. Undeclared revaluation income of HRK 1,462,084.59 led to an increase in 2003 profit tax (with 20% interest amounting to approximately EUR 68,500 for that year).

The applicant appealed on 31 March 2008, repeating her arguments. The Ministry of Finance dismissed it on 9 July 2008, affirming the assessment, the justification for extension, and her participation. She sought judicial review on 21 October 2008. The Administrative Court dismissed her action on 19 January 2011, holding that she had participated in the audit and had not timely raised the limitation issue with administrative authorities. Her constitutional complaint of 5 May 2011, alleging unfair proceedings and a property rights breach, was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 4 May 2016. It upheld the failure to raise the limitation timely and confirmed the relevant period fell outside the absolute statutory limitation.

Relevant provisions of the General Tax Act (in force 2001–2008) included a three-year limitation for assessing tax liability (starting after the year in question), interruptible by notified official actions, with an absolute six-year bar; taxpayer rights to declare facts before tax orders; and rules allowing audit extensions if significant liability changes were indicated, requiring taxpayer participation via records and documents.

The case of Maroslavac v. Croatia (Application no. 64806/16) concerns complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention relating to a tax audit of the applicant’s financial affairs, which she alleged was procedurally flawed, and to an order that she pay additional taxes (plus default interest) for periods in respect of which the State’s right of collection had allegedly become time-barred.

The applicant, a notary public born in 1958 and resident in Zagreb, purchased business premises in 2001 for approximately HRK 2,700,000 (EUR 360,000). Domestic law entitled her to deduct the purchase value from her profit tax over the ensuing six years. A later expert valuation placed the premises’ worth at HRK 5,000,000 (EUR 660,000).

On 26 June 2007 the Zagreb Office of the Ministry of Finance’s Tax Administration opened a tax audit covering VAT for 1 January 2003–31 May 2007 and profit tax for 1 January 2003–31 December 2006. By a determination of 26 October 2007 (notified to the applicant on 5 November 2007) the audit was extended to income tax for 1 January 2003–31 December 2005. An audit report dated 6 November 2007, served the following day, recorded that the applicant had failed to declare income arising from the revaluation of her assets in 2001, 2002 and 2003, contrary to domestic law; consequently the sums declared in her 2003 profit-tax return required increase.

The applicant lodged an objection, arguing that the audit had improperly covered 2001 and 2002 (periods already outside the three-year relative statutory limitation) and that late service of the extension decision had prevented her effective participation. The objection was mistakenly directed to the wrong department.

On 28 December 2007 the Zagreb Office issued a tax ruling finding under-payment of profit tax for 2003–2005, VAT for 2003–2007 and capital-gains income tax for 2003–2005. The applicant was ordered to pay the additional tax plus 20 % default interest. The ruling attributed the 2003 profit-tax increase of HRK 1,462,084.59 to undeclared revaluation income of the same amount.

The applicant appealed on 6 February 2008, repeating her limitation-period and participation complaints. After the original objection reached the correct department, a fresh ruling of 20 February 2008 replaced the earlier decision and restated essentially the same findings. It explained that section 100(5) of the General Tax Act permitted extension of the audit to earlier years where facts indicated a possible significant alteration of tax liability; the 2001–2002 amortisation calculations were therefore corrected in 2003. Official actions of which the taxpayer had been notified had interrupted the relative three-year limitation period (section 91), while the absolute six-year limitation (section 92) had not expired. The applicant had participated by supplying records and documents.

A further appeal was dismissed by the Ministry of Finance on 9 July 2008. The applicant then brought an action for judicial review, which the Administrative Court rejected on 19 January 2011 on the grounds that she had taken part in the audit and had not raised the limitation objection before the administrative authorities. A constitutional complaint alleging unfair procedure and interference with property rights was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 4 May 2016, which likewise held that the limitation point had not been timely raised and that the absolute limitation period had not expired.

The applicant maintained throughout that the audit procedure had been defective (late notification, inability to participate) and that the 2003 profit-tax assessment effectively recovered tax for 2001–2002 after both the relative and absolute limitation periods had run. The Court ultimately found the tax decision lawful and proportionate.

The case of Maroslavac v. Croatia concerns a Croatian notary public's complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that a tax audit of her affairs was procedurally flawed and that she was ordered to pay taxes for time-barred periods.

In 2001 the applicant purchased business premises for about HRK 2.7 million (later valued at HRK 5 million). Domestic law allowed her to deduct this value from profit tax over the following six years via amortisation.

On 26 June 2007 the Zagreb Tax Administration Office opened a tax audit covering VAT (1 January 2003–31 May 2007) and profit tax (1 January 2003–31 December 2006). On 26 October 2007 the audit was extended to income tax (1 January 2003–31 December 2005); she was notified on 5 November 2007. An audit report of 6 November 2007 (served 7 November) found she had failed to declare income from revaluation of assets in 2001–2003, so her 2003 profit-tax declaration required an increase. She objected that 2001–2002 fell outside the limitation period and that late service of the extension decision prevented effective participation; the objection was sent to the wrong department.

On 28 December 2007 a tax ruling ordered payment of additional profit tax (2003–2005), VAT (2003–2007) and income tax (2003–2005) plus default interest, citing undeclared revaluation income of HRK 1,462,084.59 that increased 2003 profit tax. She appealed on 6 February 2008, repeating the limitation and participation arguments.

After the objection arrived, a replacement ruling of 20 February 2008 reached the same conclusions (including roughly EUR 68,500 interest for 2003). It explained that the audit had been extended under section 100(5) of the General Tax Act because facts indicated a significant alteration of the tax base; amortisation for 2001–2002 had therefore been corrected in 2003. Limitation had been interrupted by notified official actions (section 91) and the six-year absolute period (section 92) had not expired. The applicant had participated by supplying records and documents.

She appealed again. The Ministry of Finance dismissed the appeal on 9 July 2008, upholding the first-instance findings, the justification for extension, and her participation. On 21 October 2008 she brought an action for judicial review. The Administrative Court dismissed it on 19 January 2011, holding that she had taken part in the audit and had failed to raise the limitation complaint in time before the administrative authorities.

She lodged a constitutional complaint on 5 May 2011 alleging unfair proceedings and a breach of property rights. The Constitutional Court dismissed it on 4 May 2016, endorsing the Administrative Court’s reasoning on the untimely complaint and adding that the audit period was not covered by the absolute six-year limitation.

The applicant maintained that the audit had been procedurally defective (late notification of the extension preventing effective participation) and that tax had been assessed for 2001–2002 after the State’s right to collect it had become time-barred, constituting an unlawful and disproportionate interference with her possessions.

The case of Leka v. Albania concerns Durim Leka, a 22-year-old bricklayer at the time of the events, who was convicted in 2005 of serious violent offences arising from a shooting in Shijan, Saranda, and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 23 August 2005 A.S., a foreign-exchange dealer, was shot dead; his brother P.S., who was present, was also fired at but escaped unharmed and immediately reported the incident. Police recovered spent cartridge cases at the scene. The applicant was initially interviewed as a potential witness because a note containing his telephone number had been found on the victim; he denied knowing the brothers.

The following day a covert listening device placed in a police waiting room recorded a conversation in which the applicant told his brother that he had killed A.S. and had disposed of the weapon at sea. He was arrested on 27 August 2005 and questioned by prosecutors. Although informed of his rights to silence and to legal assistance, he elected to speak without a lawyer and gave a detailed confession: he had lured A.S. to the village on the pretence of exchanging a large sum of euros he did not possess, intending to rob him of the Albanian currency A.S. would bring. When the brothers arrived he produced a pistol, shot A.S. dead and fired twice at the fleeing P.S. An identity parade was conducted the same afternoon. The applicant wore a dark long-sleeved shirt while the two foils wore white short-sleeved shirts; after P.S. had first given a detailed physical description, the three men changed positions three times and P.S. identified the applicant on each occasion. The applicant signed the parade record without comment. Subsequent interviews on 14 and 22 September 2005, again conducted without counsel after the applicant waived the right, added details of the weapon’s disposal.

A state-appointed lawyer was assigned only on 4 October 2005. The indictment charged murder of two or more persons in specific circumstances together with illegal possession of a firearm. At trial the applicant recanted, claiming A.S. had owed him money, had arrived armed and that he had seized the gun in a struggle and fired only at A.S. The first-instance court convicted him as charged, relying inter alia on the confession, the covert recording, the identity parade and eyewitness testimony.

On appeal the applicant’s new lawyer argued that the absence of counsel during pre-trial questioning and alleged duress vitiated the confession, and later invited the court to re-characterise the facts as a different offence. The Court of Appeal reclassified the killing as robbery resulting in death and the shots at P.S. as attempted murder committed with intent to commit another crime, while upholding the weapons conviction and the life sentence. It did so on the same factual matrix (the applicant’s ruse to obtain money he never intended to pay, the fatal shooting of A.S. and the unsuccessful shots at P.S.), without referring to the confession or the parade. Subsequent appeals to the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court were dismissed; the latter held that an appellate court may re-characterise facts, even more severely, provided the sentence is not increased.

These events form the basis of the complaints that the identity parade was unfairly suggestive, that the late reclassification of charges deprived the applicant of adequate notice and time to prepare a defence, and that the denial of a lawyer during the first prosecutorial interviews (for which no compelling reason existed) irretrievably prejudiced the overall fairness of the proceedings.

The case of Leka v. Albania (Application no. 60569/09) concerns the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a), (b) and (c) of the Convention. The applicant, Durim Leka (born 1983), was convicted of robbery resulting in death, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and sentenced to life imprisonment.

On 23 August 2005, A.S. was shot dead in Shijan; his brother P.S. was also fired upon but escaped unharmed and reported the incident. Spent cartridge cases were recovered. The applicant, then aged 22 and a bricklayer, was initially interviewed as a potential witness after his telephone number was found on A.S.; he denied knowing the brothers and made no incriminating remarks. Secret surveillance of a police waiting-room conversation with his brother N.L. captured the applicant admitting the killing and disposing of the gun at sea. He was arrested on 27 August 2005 and questioned by prosecutors the same day. Informed of his rights (including silence and legal assistance), he elected to proceed without a lawyer and confessed in detail: he had lured A.S. (a currency dealer) to Shijan on the pretext of exchanging non-existent euros for leks, intending to rob him, then shot A.S. and twice at the fleeing P.S. An identity parade followed immediately. The applicant wore a dark long-sleeved shirt while the two fillers wore white short-sleeved shirts. After P.S. described the shooter, positions were changed three times and P.S. identified the applicant each time. The applicant signed the record without comment. He was questioned twice more in September, again waiving counsel. A State-appointed lawyer was assigned only on 4 October 2005, immediately before the indictment charging murder of two or more persons in specific circumstances (Article 79(dh) Criminal Code) and illegal firearm possession.

At first-instance trial the applicant recanted, claiming A.S. owed him money, arrived armed, and was shot after a struggle; he denied firing at P.S. The District Court convicted him as charged, relying inter alia on the confession, intercept, P.S.’s consistent account, mobile-phone data and forensic evidence that the cartridges came from a TT pistol (never recovered). On appeal the Gjirokastra Court of Appeal reclassified the offences, without altering the facts, as attempted robbery causing death (Articles 141 and 22) and attempted murder of P.S. connected with another crime (Articles 77 and 22), plus the firearm offence. It explained that the applicant’s sole motive had been to steal the leks P.S. was carrying; the original murder characterisation was therefore legally incorrect. The court relied on crime-scene, medical, ballistic and witness evidence but omitted any reference to the confession or identity parade. Subsequent appeals to the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court were dismissed; the latter held that recharacterisation of unchanged facts, even if more serious, was permitted provided the sentence was not increased on the defendant’s sole appeal.

The applicant complained that the identity parade was suggestive, that he had been denied a lawyer during pre-trial questioning (despite purported waiver), and that the appellate reclassification deprived him of adequate notice and time to prepare a defence. The European Court ultimately found the parade compliant, the reclassification foreseeable on the same facts, and the overall fairness of the proceedings not irretrievably prejudiced by the absence of counsel at the initial questioning stage.
