It found the first-instance court had misapplied the law: the applicant’s motive from the outset had been robbery; he had not succeeded because P.S. carried the money and escaped. The identity parade and confession were not mentioned. Subsequent Supreme Court and Constitutional Court appeals were dismissed; the latter held that recharacterisation of unchanged facts was permissible even if more serious.

The applicant alleged that the identity-parade procedure, the unexpected reclassification and the lack of a lawyer during prosecutor questioning (for which no compelling reasons existed) rendered the trial unfair.
001-231959:
The case of Wangthan v. Denmark (Application no. 51301/22) involves a Thai national, Karnchana Wangthan (born 1980), who alleged that her expulsion from Denmark with a six-year re-entry ban violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life). She entered Denmark in June 2017, aged 37, with her two children (then aged 6 and 8). She married a Danish national and received a residence permit on 22 December 2017 based on family reunification. At the relevant time, she had resided lawfully in Denmark for under four years.

On 13 December 2021, the District Court convicted her of attempted aggravated violence (Penal Code Article 245 § 1, read with Article 21) for attempting to stab her husband on 25 October 2021 while threatening to kill him, plus violence against her son (kicking, beating and scratching him repeatedly over two years). She was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The court held that statutory conditions for expulsion under the Aliens Act were satisfied. Applying section 26(2), it found expulsion would not “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8. The applicant (then 41) had limited Danish ties: two years of work, some language classes but needing an interpreter in court, and children without sufficiently independent ties after only four years. She had strong Thai ties (born and raised there, family, language fluency, and access to a house). The offences’ nature and the six-month sentence rendered expulsion proportionate.

On appeal, the High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 22 February 2022. The applicant submitted she had worked three years, spoke some Danish with colleagues and friends (English with her husband, Thai with the children, who replied in Danish), that the children (now 10 and 12) attended Danish school, viewed her husband as their father, and wished to remain (as did she). She referenced mental-health treatment in Denmark (hospitalization for stress/depression; prescribed but unused bipolar medication) and facial paresis, plus uncertainty about the Thai house (owned by her ex-husband). The High Court confirmed lawful residence of approximately three years and ten months and that expulsion interfered with Article 8 rights but was justified under Article 8 § 2. Drawing on criteria from Maslov v. Austria, it found very strong Thai ties (lifelong residence until 2017, university economics degree, language, family, and prior holidays there with her husband and children) versus weaker Danish ties (limited Danish proficiency, short stay, English used with husband). The children understood Thai, had been born there (older child schooled there), and could reintegrate despite some Danish school ties and language skills. The offences were serious (attempted stabbing during an emotional divorce discussion, plus repeated child violence), though she had no prior convictions. Compelling societal interests outweighed private/family-life considerations; the husband could maintain contact via phone/internet or visits to Thailand (where they had met). The six-year ban was therefore not disproportionate.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 5 August 2022. Implementation of the expulsion remains unknown. The European Court held that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had properly assessed proportionality in light of its case-law.

The applicant, a Thai national born in 1980, entered Denmark in June 2017 at age 37 together with her two children (then aged 6 and 8) and married a Danish national. She was granted a residence permit on 22 December 2017 on family-reunification grounds. By December 2021 she had therefore been lawfully resident for just under four years.

On 13 December 2021 the District Court convicted her of attempted aggravated assault (Penal Code Art. 245(1) read with Art. 21) for trying to stab her husband on 25 October 2021 while threatening to kill him, and of repeated violence against her son (kicking, beating and scratching him over a two-year period). She received a six-month prison sentence and an expulsion order accompanied by a six-year re-entry ban. The court held that the statutory conditions for expulsion were met and that, under Aliens Act s. 26(2), expulsion was mandatory unless it would “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8 ECHR.

In assessing proportionality the District Court noted that the applicant had no family in Denmark apart from her (soon-to-be-divorced) husband and the two children, had worked for two years, had attended language classes and spoke some Danish (though she required an interpreter). She had been born and educated in Thailand, retained family there and had a house at her disposal. The children, having lived in Denmark for only four years, had not formed independent ties sufficient to render expulsion “conclusively inappropriate.” The interference was therefore not disproportionate.

The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 22 February 2022. It confirmed that the applicant had been lawfully present for approximately three years and ten months. It characterised her ties to Thailand as “very strong”: she had lived there until age 37, obtained a university degree in economics, spoke the language fluently, maintained family links, had met her husband there and had holidayed there with the children. Ties to Denmark were “considerably weaker”: limited Danish (she spoke English with her husband and Thai to the children), four years’ residence and three years’ employment. The children, now 10 and 12, understood Thai, the older child had attended school in Thailand, and both were young enough to reintegrate; they nevertheless had some Danish-language and school ties that had to be taken into account.

The High Court emphasised the seriousness of the offences—an attempted stabbing accompanied by a death threat (albeit in an emotionally charged marital context) and repeated physical violence against a child—while noting the absence of prior convictions. It concluded that the public-interest considerations in favour of expulsion outweighed the applicant’s private- and family-life interests. Contact with the husband could be maintained by telephone, internet and visits to Thailand (where the couple had originally met). Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 5 August 2022. It is unknown whether the expulsion order has been executed.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the expulsion and six-year ban violated Article 8. The Court found that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had properly applied the Court’s own case-law on proportionality. No violation was established.

The case of Wangthan v. Denmark (no. 51301/22) concerns a Thai national’s complaint under Article 8 ECHR that her expulsion from Denmark, with a six-year re-entry ban, following conviction for violent offences, disproportionately interfered with her private and family life. The applicant, born in 1980, entered Denmark in June 2017 aged 37, together with her two children (then aged 6 and 8). She married a Danish national and obtained a residence permit on 22 December 2017 on family-reunification grounds. She had no prior convictions.

On 13 December 2021 the District Court convicted her of attempted aggravated violence (Penal Code Art. 245 § 1 read with Art. 21) for trying to stab her husband on 25 October 2021 while stating that she would kill him, and of repeated violence against her son (kicking, beating and scratching him over two years). She was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The court held that the statutory conditions for expulsion under the Aliens Act were met. It balanced the six-month sentence and the nature of the violence against her relatively short lawful residence (just under four years), two years of work, limited Danish-language ability (she required an interpreter), strong ties to Thailand (birth, upbringing, schooling, family and a house there) and the children’s correspondingly limited independent ties to Denmark. Expulsion was therefore not “for certain” contrary to Article 8.

On appeal the High Court of Eastern Denmark, in its judgment of 22 February 2022, upheld both the conviction and the expulsion order. It confirmed that expulsion interfered with the applicant’s Article 8 rights but found the interference justified after applying the Court’s criteria (citing Maslov v. Austria). The court emphasised her very strong ties to Thailand (university degree in economics, family, prior holidays there with her Danish husband and children) versus weaker ties to Denmark (three years’ work, some language classes, limited spoken Danish; she communicated with her husband in English and with her children in Thai). The children, born in Thailand and still of an age to reintegrate, understood Thai and would not face serious difficulties on return, even though they spoke Danish and attended school in Denmark. The offences—attempted stabbing of her spouse amid divorce discussions and repeated violence against her son—were serious. Public-order considerations therefore outweighed her private and family life; contact with her husband could continue by telephone, internet or visits to Thailand.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 5 August 2022. It remains unknown whether the expulsion has been implemented. The applicant complained to the Court that the measure violated Article 8. The Chamber found that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had properly assessed proportionality in the light of the Court’s case-law, so there was no violation.

The case of Lazăr v. Romania involved Marius Lazăr (born 1973), a Hells Angels Romania member, regarding his extradition to the US and related detention.

Lazăr was arrested on 19 November 2020. US authorities requested extradition on 14 January 2021 under the 2007 Romania-US Extradition Treaty for: (1) conspiracy to commit racketeering involving money laundering, murder and drug trafficking (max. life imprisonment); (2) conspiracy to import/export cocaine (max. life, min. 10 years); and (3) conspiracy to commit money laundering (max. 20 years). Charges arose from a 2020 undercover DEA operation in which Lazăr and others attempted to buy 400 kg of cocaine (to be smuggled from Peru via Texas to Romania/New Zealand) and he allegedly asked the undercover agent to kill two rival motorcycle club members.

Initial 24-hour prosecutor detention was followed by 30-day provisional arrest by the Bucharest Court of Appeal under Law no. 302/2004 s. 44 (urgent cases pre-request). Detention was regularly reviewed. After the request, it continued under s. 43 pending proceedings (max. 180 days, with periodic review and possible alternatives).

On 1 March 2021 the Court of Appeal granted extradition, finding Treaty and Law requirements met with no bars. It rejected Article 3 arguments (risk of irreducible life imprisonment, citing Trabelsi v. Belgium), holding (per US information) that life sentences were discretionary/reducible (unlike Trabelsi) and not disproportionate given charge seriousness. Fair-trial claims were premature. Detention was maintained until surrender (ss. 52(3), 57). The High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld this on 11 March 2021. Surrender was set for 12 May 2021.

Lazăr applied to the ECHR on 19 April 2021. A Rule 39 interim measure on 5 May 2021 barred extradition pending ECHR proceedings.

On 11 May 2021 the Court of Appeal suspended enforcement (CCP Art. 598 § 1(c)) due to the measure and released Lazăr under 60-day judicial supervision. The High Court reversed this on 17 May 2021 (majority), remanding him: Law 302/2004 mandated post-grant detention with a view to surrender (distinct from pre-grant detention; no 180-day limit/review/alternatives applied); the measure did not affect it, and the 30-day surrender limit (s. 43(7)) had not expired.

On 8 June 2021 the High Court released him under judicial supervision (CCP Art. 215), citing the "wholly particular situation," uncertain surrender date post-measure, and inability to detain indefinitely. Supervision was extended until terminated on 27 September 2022 (no further measures).

The ECHR lifted the measure on 12 December 2022 (post-Sanchez-Sanchez v. UK [GC]). Authorities then sought arrest for surrender (unenforceable without escort, s. 57(4)). On 15 December 2022 the Court of Appeal ordered 30-day detention (s. 43(6), analogizing CCP as lex specialis lacked duration post-amendment), holding prior 180-day detention did not preclude it. Lazăr was arrested 28 December 2022. High Court challenges (no basis; time-limits exhausted; CCP "invention") were dismissed on 13 January 2023: time-limits had not run (no surrender date set due to the measure); detention was proportionate to enforce the final decision. A separate request for supervision was refused (Law 302/2004 required detention until surrender). He was surrendered on 16 January 2023.

A 26 May 2022 Constitutional Court decision (published 4 October 2022) found parts of ss. 52(3)/57(5)-(6) unconstitutional (indefinite detention risk sans clear framework; no periodic review/alternatives post-grant). Amendments effective 20 November 2022 unified concepts (180-day max. until surrender, including force majeure) without transitional provisions, creating a sui generis situation.

The applicant, a Romanian national and Hells Angels member, was arrested on 19 November 2020. The US requested his extradition on 14 January 2021 under the 2007 Extradition Treaty for conspiracy to commit racketeering (involving money laundering, murder and drug trafficking, carrying a possible life sentence), conspiracy to import/export 400 kg of cocaine (possible life sentence with 10-year minimum) and conspiracy to launder money (up to 20 years). The charges stemmed from a 2020 undercover DEA operation in which the applicant and others sought to smuggle cocaine from Peru via Texas to Romania and New Zealand; he had also asked an undercover agent to kill two rival motorcycle-club members.

He was initially held for 24 hours by a prosecutor, after which the Bucharest Court of Appeal ordered 30 days’ provisional arrest under Law 302/2004 (urgent cases pending a formal request). Detention was reviewed regularly. After the request arrived, he was held under the same law pending extradition proceedings. On 1 March 2021 the Court of Appeal granted extradition, finding the US information showed that any life sentence would be discretionary and both de jure and de facto reducible (unlike Trabelsi v. Belgium) and not grossly disproportionate given the gravity of the charges. Fair-trial objections were rejected because the US trial had not yet begun. The High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld the decision on 11 March 2021. Detention was maintained until surrender (initially planned for 12 May 2021).

On 19 April 2021 the applicant applied to the ECtHR, invoking Articles 3 and 5. On 5 May 2021 the Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 prohibiting extradition pending its proceedings. On 11 May the Court of Appeal, citing the measure, released him under 60-day judicial supervision. The High Court reversed this on 17 May, remanding him in custody on the ground that Law 302/2004 made detention mandatory once extradition was granted and that the 30-day post-surrender-date limit had not yet expired. On 8 June 2021, however, the High Court released him again under judicial supervision, noting the indefinite duration caused by the Rule 39 measure. Supervision was extended until 27 September 2022, after which he was free of all preventive measures.

The Constitutional Court, in a 26 May 2022 decision (published October 2022), held that the absence of periodic review and alternative measures after an extradition order was constitutional given short surrender deadlines, but found the “force majeure” exception permitting indefinite detention unconstitutional. The legislature was ordered to create a clear framework. Law 302/2004 was amended with effect from 20 November 2022, capping total detention until actual surrender at 180 days and treating it as a single concept.

On 12 December 2022 the ECtHR lifted the Rule 39 measure following its Grand Chamber judgment in Sanchez-Sanchez v. the United Kingdom. The next day the execution department sought an arrest warrant to enable surrender. On 15 December the Court of Appeal, applying Article 598 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (objection to enforcement) together with Law 302/2004, ordered 30 days’ detention for surrender, distinguishing it from earlier provisional arrest. The applicant was re-arrested on 28 December 2022. Challenges arguing lack of legal basis, exhaustion of all prior measures and unlawfulness after the 180-day cap were dismissed by the High Court on 13 January 2023; it held that the time-limits had never begun because no surrender date had been set during the Rule 39 period, that the situation was sui generis after the law’s amendment without transitional provisions, and that detention was proportionate and Convention-compliant. The applicant was surrendered on 16 January 2023.

He alleged that both detention periods (initial arrest to June 2021 release, and December 2022–January 2023 re-arrest) violated Article 5 § 1 (f) as not “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law,” excessive, lacking due diligence and based on arbitrary interpretation. He further alleged a real risk of irreducible life imprisonment without parole in the US, contrary to Article 3.

On 14 January 2021 the US requested his extradition under the 2007 Treaty for three offences arising from an undercover operation: conspiracy to commit racketeering (including money-laundering, murder of rival gang members and drug trafficking, maximum life imprisonment); conspiracy to import/export 400 kg of cocaine (maximum life, mandatory minimum 10 years); and conspiracy to commit money-laundering (maximum 20 years).

He was first held for 24 hours, then placed in 30-day provisional detention under s. 44 of Law no. 302/2004 (urgent arrest pending a request). Detention was reviewed regularly. After the request arrived, detention continued under s. 43 while extradition proceedings were pending. On 1 March 2021 the Bucharest Court of Appeal granted extradition, finding the Treaty and Law no. 302/2004 requirements met, no bars applicable, a potential life sentence discretionary and de jure/de facto reducible (unlike Trabelsi v. Belgium), and not grossly disproportionate. Detention was maintained until surrender under ss. 52(3) and 57. The High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld the decision on 11 March 2021. A surrender date of 12 May 2021 was agreed.

On 5 May 2021 the European Court indicated a Rule 39 interim measure preventing extradition. On 11 May the Court of Appeal suspended enforcement of the extradition decision (CCP Art. 598 § 1(c)) and released the applicant under 60-day judicial supervision, treating detention as ancillary and noting uncertainty over the Strasbourg proceedings. The High Court, by majority on 17 May, remanded him in custody. It held that Law no. 302/2004 (not the CCP) governed extradition detention, distinguishing “provisional arrest pending proceedings” (s. 43, with 180-day maximum and possible alternatives) from mandatory “detention with a view to surrender” (s. 57) once extradition was granted; the interim measure did not affect the latter, and the 30-day post-surrender-date limit (s. 43(7)) had not started.

The applicant lodged an unsuccessful unconstitutionality challenge and multiple detention appeals. On 8 June 2021 the High Court released him under judicial supervision, citing the “wholly particular situation” created by the interim measure, the absence of a surrender date and the risk of indefinite detention. Supervision was extended until 27 September 2022, after which no preventive measures applied.

The Court lifted the interim measure on 12 December 2022 following Sanchez-Sanchez v. the United Kingdom. On 14 December the authorities applied under CCP Art. 598 § 1(c) and s. 43(6) for an arrest warrant, arguing that surrender required escort (s. 57(4)) and the final extradition decision was otherwise unenforceable. On 15 December the Court of Appeal ordered 30-day detention from 28 December, analogising it to enforcement of a custodial sentence and applying general CCP rules because Law no. 302/2004 (even as amended on 20 November 2022 after Constitutional Court decision no. 359/2022) set no specific duration for post-grant surrender detention. It distinguished the 180-day limit (applicable only to pre-grant arrest). The High Court dismissed the applicant’s challenge on 13 January 2023, holding that time-limits had not begun to run while the interim measure prevented a surrender date and that renewed detention was a proportionate enforcement measure. He was surrendered on 16 January 2023.

The applicant alleged that both periods of detention violated Article 5 § 1(f) as not “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law,” excessive, lacking a proper legal basis after the 180-day limit, and obtained through an invented CCP “objection to enforcement.” He also claimed under Article 3 that extradition exposed him to a real risk of irreducible life imprisonment without parole.
001-230627:
The case of Bernotas v. Lithuania (ECtHR, Application no. 59065/21) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). In January 2010, the applicant, Jurgis Bernotas, accidentally shot Ž.K. while cleaning a rifle after a hunt, causing multiple serious injuries to the abdomen, hip and leg. Charged with negligently causing serious health impairment under the Criminal Code, he fully admitted guilt.

In criminal proceedings, Ž.K. claimed pecuniary damages (medication, treatment and transport) and non-pecuniary damages. The applicant paid LTL 9,000 (approx. EUR 2,607) during the proceedings. In February 2011, the Skuodas Regional Court convicted him, imposing a two-year suspended prison sentence. It noted his lack of prior convictions, admission of guilt and partial compensation, but also the serious consequences (four surgeries, hip replacement, hospitalisation, dismissal from the fire service) and his financial situation as a truck driver. The court found he had fully compensated pecuniary damage and awarded additional non-pecuniary damages of LTL 77,032 (approx. EUR 22,310). On appeal, the Klaipėda Regional Court reduced this to LTL 37,032 (approx. EUR 10,725), citing case-law and the applicant’s modest income and assets. The Supreme Court refused further appeal.

From August 2010, after Ž.K.’s working capacity was assessed as diminished by 60% (later reassessed periodically, settling at 45% until retirement in 2039), the State Social Insurance Fund (SSIF) paid him a lost working capacity pension. Amounts varied with assessments, basic pension rates, his service length and prior salary, totalling thousands of euros over successive periods (e.g., EUR 2,687 from August 2010–October 2011; EUR 6,790 from October 2019–April 2022). Ž.K. remained employed, sometimes with comparable or higher income, and received other social allowances.

Under Civil Code Article 6.290 § 3, the SSIF claimed reimbursement from the applicant as the person who caused the damage, treating the pension as covering lost income and injury-related expenses (medication, care, rehabilitation). From 2011, it issued successive claims. The applicant initially did not object and paid in instalments due to low salary (around EUR 260 monthly) and lack of savings or assets, while also paying court-awarded compensation to Ž.K. Later claims led to default judgments (which he did not challenge) and seizures of his car and bank account, later stayed. He sometimes contested claims, arguing he had already fully compensated Ž.K. in criminal proceedings; that the pension did not reflect actual pecuniary loss (as Ž.K. worked and his income had not fallen); that assessments of working capacity were unreliable; that pension increases (due to rising service length, wages or inflation) should not increase his liability; and that repeated proceedings violated fair-trial rights. He requested forensic examination (which confirmed the 45% diminution as directly caused by the accident) and instalment payments, often granted.

Domestic courts consistently upheld the SSIF’s claims, holding that the pension compensated post-accident damage (diminished earning capacity and extra expenses) distinct from the accident-time harm already compensated. They cited Constitutional Court and Supreme Court case-law allowing full recovery if the payment matched the damage, with the burden on the applicant to prove otherwise. They rejected arguments of overcompensation or unfairness from pension increases, noting economic changes and the dual purpose of the pension. The Supreme Court repeatedly declined to examine appeals as raising no important legal issues. A 2022 claim was adjourned pending the ECtHR application. The applicant’s financial difficulties were accommodated through instalments and deferred fees, though his overall burden remained substantial and long-term.

The case of Bernotas v. Lithuania (ECtHR, Application no. 59065/21) concerns the applicant’s obligation under Lithuanian law to reimburse the State Social Insurance Fund (SSIF) for lost-working-capacity pensions paid to Ž.K., whom the applicant accidentally shot in January 2010 while cleaning a rifle after a hunt. The victim suffered multiple serious abdominal, hip and leg injuries requiring four operations, prolonged hospitalisation and a hip replacement. In February 2011 the Skuodas Regional Court convicted the applicant of negligently causing serious health impairment, imposing a two-year suspended prison sentence. Taking into account his clean record, full admission of guilt, remorse and partial payments already made, the court awarded Ž.K. additional non-pecuniary damages (later reduced on appeal to approximately EUR 10,725). The applicant’s arguments that the award was excessive and that his modest income (approximately EUR 260 per month as a long-haul truck driver, with no real estate or savings) had been misassessed were only partially successful.

From August 2010 the Disability and Capacity for Work Service assessed Ž.K.’s working capacity as reduced by 60 per cent; subsequent periodic reassessments established reductions of 50 per cent, 45 per cent, a disputed 30 per cent (later restored to 45 per cent) and, from 2017, a permanent 45 per cent reduction until retirement in 2039. On that basis the SSIF paid Ž.K. a lost-working-capacity pension calculated by reference to the statutory basic pension, the degree of incapacity, length of service and former salary. The monthly amounts fluctuated and, over successive periods, totalled several thousand euros.

Beginning in November 2011 the SSIF invoked Article 6.290 § 3 of the Civil Code (which entitles social-insurance authorities to recoup allowances paid to an injured person from the person who caused the injury) and issued successive reimbursement claims. The applicant initially accepted liability for the first claim (approximately EUR 2,687) and obtained an instalment arrangement because of his limited means and the existing court-ordered compensation. Later claims (2013, 2015, 2016) were met by default judgments after he failed to contest them; enforcement measures including seizure of his car and bank account followed, but were stayed once he agreed to further instalments. In 2017 he contested a claim of EUR 1,799, questioning both the accuracy of the capacity assessments and whether Ž.K. (who had found new employment and whose earnings had not fallen) had suffered actual pecuniary loss. A forensic examination confirmed the 45 per cent reduction and its causal link to the accident. Domestic courts held that the pension compensated both lost income and additional injury-related expenses, that prior criminal-court payments covered only the immediate consequences of the accident, and that the SSIF was therefore entitled to full recoupment. Subsequent claims in 2019 (EUR 5,597 plus arrears) and 2022 (EUR 6,790) were likewise allowed, the courts rejecting arguments that rising pension amounts (driven by length-of-service increments and general wage inflation) produced unjust enrichment or that repeated proceedings violated Article 6.

Throughout, the applicant emphasised his low and unpredictable income, the impossibility of forecasting future liability, the absence of any deterioration in Ž.K.’s health after the original compensation, and the fact that he had already made substantial payments. Lithuanian law permits courts to reduce compensation where full payment would cause unacceptable hardship (Civil Code Arts. 6.251, 6.282) and allows the SSIF to waive claims on socio-economic grounds; in comparable cases reductions have been granted. The applicant obtained several instalment plans and a temporary stay of enforcement, but no reduction of the principal sums. A 2022 claim was adjourned pending the Strasbourg proceedings.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the successive recoupment orders constituted a disproportionate interference with his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case of Bernotas v. Lithuania (Application no. 59065/21), ECHR (Second Section), 30 January 2024 (final 30 April 2024)**

The applicant, Jurgis Bernotas (born 1957), accidentally shot Ž.K. in January 2010 while cleaning a rifle after a hunt, causing serious abdominal, hip, and leg injuries requiring multiple surgeries, hip replacement, and prolonged hospitalization. Charged with negligently causing serious health damage (Criminal Code Art. 137 § 3), he admitted guilt. In February 2011, the Skuodas Regional Court convicted him and imposed a two-year suspended prison sentence. It awarded Ž.K. additional non-pecuniary damages (later reduced on appeal to ~EUR 10,725) after the applicant had already paid ~EUR 2,607; the courts noted the applicant’s low official salary, lack of assets, and the victim’s severe consequences, including job loss from the fire service and reduced working capacity. The Supreme Court declined further review.

From August 2010, the Disability and Capacity for Work Service assessed Ž.K.’s working capacity as reduced by 60% (later fluctuating between 30–50%, settling at 45% until 2039 retirement). The State Social Insurance Fund (SSIF) paid him a lost working capacity pension calculated from the basic pension, reduction percentage, length of service, and prior salary. Amounts paid included ~EUR 2,687 (2010–2011), ~EUR 2,291 (2011–2013), EUR 3,146 (2013–2015), EUR 1,021 (2015–2016), EUR 1,799 (2016–2017), EUR 5,597 (2017–2019), and EUR 6,790 (2019–2022), with a brief interruption when capacity was assessed at 30%.

Under Civil Code Art. 6.290 § 3, the SSIF repeatedly claimed reimbursement from the applicant as the person who caused the damage, treating the pension as compensable pecuniary loss (lost income plus injury-related expenses). Claims began in 2011. The applicant initially accepted the first amount but requested installments due to low income (~EUR 260/month) and existing compensation obligations; the SSIF agreed. Subsequent claims (2013, 2015) proceeded by default after he failed to respond, without review applications. Later claims (2016, 2017, 2019, 2022) were contested. He argued he had already fully compensated Ž.K. in criminal proceedings; the victim was employed (sometimes at higher pay) so suffered no actual income loss; capacity assessments were unreliable (a 2018 forensic exam confirmed 45% reduction directly caused by the accident); pension increases tied to the victim’s accumulating service or statutory adjustments were unforeseeable and unfair; and repeated proceedings violated fair-trial rights. He also cited his limited means and sought reductions or deferred payments.

Domestic courts consistently granted the SSIF’s claims in full (or residual unpaid balances), holding that the pension compensated both lost earning capacity and ongoing expenses (medication, care, etc.), that this post-accident damage was distinct from the original injury compensation, and that the SSIF could recover the entire amount paid as it did not exceed proven damage (per Constitutional Court 2012 ruling and Supreme Court case-law). They rejected arguments that compensation was capped at 2010 levels or that increases caused unjust enrichment. Some flexibility was shown: installments were repeatedly granted (e.g., over 19 months in 2021); a 2016 seizure of the applicant’s car and account was stayed after he accepted a payment plan; stamp duty was deferred; and the 2022 claim was adjourned pending the ECHR application. Civil Code provisions allowed courts to reduce awards in cases of hardship or unintentional harm, but reductions were not applied here (unlike some other first-instance decisions). The applicant never successfully invoked reduction mechanisms or proved the pension exceeded actual damage.

The applicant lodged his ECHR application in November 2021, alleging that the ongoing, escalating reimbursement obligation interfered with his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, without adequate individual assessment or fair balance given his financial situation, prior payments, and the victim’s continued employment. (He had also invoked Article 6 in domestic proceedings regarding repeated litigation.) The Court examined whether the interference was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim (protecting public funds and ensuring full compensation), and struck a fair balance, noting opportunities to contest amounts, seek reductions, and obtain payment relief.
001-233494:
The ECHR case of Thomaidis v. Greece (Application no. 28345/16) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) arising from a Greek journalist’s civil liability for broadcasting materials on alleged match-fixing.

Applicant Kyriakos Thomaidis presented the live nationwide programme “Trial at SKAI.” In 2011, criminal proceedings began against Greek football stakeholders, including V.M. (a club chairman and Hellenic Football Federation vice-chairman), for match-fixing. On 22 October 2012, during a segment on championship reorganisation, Thomaidis quoted a 2010 witness statement from the investigation file. It described A.M. (another club chairman) approaching an Italian referee, claiming collaboration with V.M., and unsuccessful bribery attempts by both A.M. and V.M. via another referee, after which V.M.’s team lost.

On 8 November 2012, Thomaidis announced that A.K. (a lawyer and rival club chairman) would reveal match-fixing details. V.M. immediately served a legal letter demanding they cease defamatory references and use of unlawful audiovisual material or intercepted evidence. On 12 November 2012, A.K. appeared, calling V.M.’s control a “junta” and “criminal organisation,” stating V.M. and others were “trash” who “should go to jail,” and alleging slander plus a violent incident by V.M.’s supporters. A.K. read lengthy excerpts from unlawfully intercepted conversations (containing vulgar language) indicating V.M.’s referee-bribery attempts. A.M. phoned to protest the reading of illegal intercepts; a guest noted the show had become passive listening. Thomaidis stated he did not condone A.K.’s views or the “unlawful, intercepted transcripts” but did not interrupt A.K. The match-fixing investigation was already public, and A.K. had previously disclosed intercept details.

V.M. sued Thomaidis civilly for €500,000 in non-pecuniary damages for personality-rights infringement. The Piraeus Court of First Instance (2013) found liability and awarded €10,000. It held that broadcasting the investigation-file witness statement (explicitly prohibited by Presidential Decree 77/2003/Code of Press Conduct, Articles 8 and 11) was unnecessary and unrelated to the championship discussion, already public knowledge, and presented in an insulting manner. The second programme likewise failed to inform (allegations already known) and instead gave A.K. a platform for personal insults and illegal intercepts amid their quarrel, with no substantive debate. Thomaidis’s disclaimer did not relieve him as presenter who planned and permitted the content. The national audience amplified reputational harm to V.M.’s professional standing.

The Piraeus Court of Appeal (2014) confirmed, finding the programmes defamatory with intent to insult. Dissemination was illegal, unnecessary (already public, no new information), and irrelevant; Thomaidis designed both shows to attack V.M. despite the prior warning and failed to prevent A.K.’s remarks. The Court of Cassation (2015) dismissed the appeal, holding the decisions complied with Article 10, the Constitution, and Civil Code personality/tort provisions (read with Penal Code insult rules). The broadcasts were not public-interest journalism but targeted insults via prohibited materials, rendering the interference proportionate.

(V.M. was later acquitted in 2021 of match-fixing and criminal-organisation charges.) The ECHR found no Article 10 violation: domestic courts gave relevant, sufficient reasons applying Convention-compliant standards on an acceptable factual assessment. Thomaidis overstepped responsible journalism; the authorities stayed within their margin of appreciation in balancing expression against reputation.

**Case of Thomaidis v. Greece (Application no. 28345/16), ECHR Third Section, Judgment of 7 May 2024 (final 7 August 2024)**

The case concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression) following a finding of civil liability and an award of damages against journalist Kyriakos Thomaidis. He was the main presenter of the live television programme “Trial at SKAI” on the nationwide channel SKAI.

In 2011, criminal proceedings were opened against several figures in Greek professional football over alleged match-fixing. Among those accused was V.M., then chairman of a football club and Vice-Chairman of the Hellenic Football Federation. The investigation attracted significant media attention and some details, including intercepted conversations, were already in the public domain.

On 22 October 2012, during a programme segment on the reorganisation of the national football championships, Thomaidis produced and quoted from a 2010 witness statement that formed part of the official investigation file. The statement described how A.M. (another club chairman) had approached an Italian referee, claimed collaboration with V.M., and unsuccessfully attempted a bribe. V.M. was then alleged to have tried to bribe the same referee through another official, again without success, after which V.M.’s team lost the match.

On 8 November 2012 Thomaidis announced on the programme’s website that A.K., a lawyer and chairman of another club, would make revelations about the scandal. On 12 November 2012 V.M. served a legal letter on the station, Thomaidis and A.K., complaining of repeated defamation through false facts and unlawful audiovisual material and demanding that they cease such references.

That same day A.K. appeared on the programme. He made statements such as “there is literally a junta in Greek football,” “who should go to prison,” “this criminal organisation,” and “the trash of Greek football.” He read lengthy extracts from records of intercepted conversations between A.M. and others that suggested V.M. had attempted to bribe referees and contained vulgar language. A.K. also alleged V.M.’s involvement in a violent incident. A.M. telephoned the programme to protest the reading of unlawfully intercepted material. Thomaidis stated that he did not condone A.K.’s views or the transcripts and described them as “unlawful, intercepted transcripts,” but he did not prevent A.K. from continuing.

V.M. brought a civil action seeking approximately €500,000 in non-pecuniary damages for infringement of his personality rights (honour, reputation and professional standing).

The Piraeus Court of First Instance (judgment no. 2891/2013) found that broadcasting the investigation-file witness statement (expressly prohibited by Article 11 of Presidential Decree 77/2003, the Code of Press Conduct) and allowing A.K. to read unlawfully intercepted conversations accompanied by insulting comments had damaged V.M.’s honour and reputation. The material was irrelevant to the championship-reorganisation discussion, already known to the public, and presented in a manner indicating an intent to insult. The national reach of the channel made the damage significant. The court awarded €10,000.

The Piraeus Court of Appeal (judgment no. 186/2014) upheld the finding, emphasising that the programmes had been constructed to insult V.M., that dissemination of the file document and intercepted conversations was illegal, that the information added nothing new, and that Thomaidis’s disclaimer did not absolve him as presenter.

The Court of Cassation (judgment no. 1158/2015) dismissed Thomaidis’s appeal on points of law. It held that the broadcasts constituted an insult, that the lower courts had correctly applied Articles 57, 59, 914 and 932 of the Civil Code together with the relevant Penal Code provisions, and that the interference was compatible with Article 10 of the Convention and Article 14 of the Greek Constitution. The Court of Cassation noted the prohibition on publishing investigation documents and intercepted material, the absence of any genuine public-interest discussion, and the programmes’ design aimed at attacking V.M.’s reputation. It concluded that the interference was proportionate.

(In 2021 V.M. was acquitted of match-fixing and related charges.)

The European Court of Human Rights later held that the domestic courts had adduced relevant and sufficient reasons, applied standards conforming to Article 10 principles, and based their decisions on an acceptable assessment of the facts. The interference was therefore necessary in a democratic society and the authorities had remained within their margin of appreciation in balancing the competing interests.

In 2011, criminal proceedings began against football stakeholders, including V.M. (a club chairman and Hellenic Football Federation vice-chairman), for match-fixing. (another club chairman) approaching an Italian referee, claiming collaboration with V.M., and attempting a bribe; V.M. then allegedly tried via another referee, D., without success, after which V.M.’s team lost.

V.M. served a legal letter on 12 November 2012 protesting repeated defamation via false facts and unlawful audiovisual material, demanding they cease such references and reserve his rights. That same day, A.K. appeared and made comments such as “a junta in Greek football,” “who should go to prison,” and “this criminal organisation.” He accused V.M. of slander, alleged involvement in a violent incident by fans against A.K., and read lengthy excerpts from intercepted conversations suggesting V.M.’s referee-bribery attempts (including vulgar language). The Piraeus Court of First Instance (judgment no. 2891/2013, 20 May 2013) found liability. The witness-statement publication was prohibited by Presidential Decree 77/2003 (Code of Press Conduct, Articles 8 and 11, banning illegally obtained or investigation-file material), unrelated to the championship discussion, already public, and presented in an insulting manner. The second broadcast provided no new public information but allowed A.K. (amid a personal feud) to insult V.M. via unlawful intercepts, without debate. The applicant’s disclaimer as presenter did not excuse him. Given the channel’s national reach, audience (including professionals and fans), intent, publicity, and impact on V.M.’s position, the court awarded €10,000.

The Piraeus Court of Appeal (judgment no. 186/2014, 6 March 2014) confirmed, holding the programmes defamatory with intent to insult, as dissemination was illegal, unnecessary (already known), and irrelevant, lacking any in-depth discussion. The Court of Cassation (judgment no. 1158/2015, 31 August 2015) dismissed the appeal, finding compliance with Article 10, the Greek Constitution (Article 14), Civil Code personality/tort provisions, and Penal Code insult rules. It rejected a public-interest defence due to the materials’ illegality, prior publicity, absence of discussion, and programmes’ design to attack V.M.’s reputation; the interference was proportionate. V.M. was acquitted of match-fixing and criminal-organisation charges in 2021.

The ECHR found no Article 10 violation. Domestic courts provided relevant and sufficient reasons, applied Convention-compliant standards, and made an acceptable factual assessment. The applicant overstepped responsible journalism by disseminating prohibited investigation material and allowing unlawful intercepts with insults. The interference was necessary in a democratic society; authorities stayed within their margin of appreciation in balancing expression against reputation and personality rights.

001-234125:
The case of Kokëdhima v. Albania concerned the Constitutional Court's termination of Koço Kokëdhima's mandate as a Member of Parliament (MP) on grounds of incompatibility with his business interests. The applicant alleged this breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to stand for election and exercise a parliamentary mandate) and Article 8 (protection of reputation).

The applicant was sole shareholder of Abissnet SHA, a company providing internet and telephony services, from 1999 until he sold his shares on 6 February 2014. Between January and August 2013 the company signed contracts with numerous public authorities.

He stood as a candidate in the 23 June 2013 parliamentary elections. On 25 July 2013 he sought advice from the High Inspectorate for the Declaration and Audit of Assets and Conflicts of Interest about a possible conflict arising from his shareholding if elected. He resigned as company manager on 31 July 2013. His election was certified on 2 August 2013.

The High Inspectorate replied on 7 August 2013 that preventing conflicts was his responsibility and that he could consult Parliament; he would in any event be audited. He then approached the Speaker of Parliament, who on 18 October 2013 referred him to the Human Resources service. That service had not previously handled such cases and directed him back to the High Inspectorate.

In February 2015 the Democratic Party parliamentary group (more than one-tenth of MPs) asked Parliament to refer the incompatibility question to the Constitutional Court under Article 73 of the Constitution. Parliament did so on 10 March 2016.

On 3 June 2016 the Constitutional Court held that the applicant's MP role was incompatible with his position as sole shareholder of a company receiving income from State contracts, in violation of Article 70(3) of the Constitution. It criticised a six-month delay in resolving the conflict. Although no new contracts were concluded after 2 August 2013, the company continued to receive payments under existing contracts. The Court rejected arguments that only new contracts mattered, that the applicant received no dividends (having sold before year-end), that the company was a separate legal person, and that removal would damage his reputation or voters' rights. The mandate began upon certification of election, not the oath. Indirect benefit arose because State payments increased the company's capital and thus the value of the applicant's shares. He had failed to take the necessary steps (such as prompt transfer of shares) to avoid the conflict before exercising his mandate.

The applicant was therefore debarred from remaining an MP. The European Court found the applicable laws and practice accessible, that the applicant had not taken all required measures to end the ongoing conflict upon assuming office, and that the measure was sufficiently foreseeable and not arbitrary.

The case of Kokëdhima v. Albania (Application no. 55159/16) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the termination of the applicant’s mandate as a Member of Parliament (MP). Koço Kokëdhima, an Albanian national born in 1959, was the sole shareholder of Abissnet SHA, a private joint-stock company registered in Tirana, from 29 October 1999 until 6 February 2014, when he sold his shares. Between 3 January and 2 August 2013 the company concluded contracts with numerous public authorities to supply internet and fixed telephony services.

On 23 June 2013 general parliamentary elections were held; the applicant stood as a candidate. On 25 July 2013 he requested advice from the High Inspectorate for the Declaration and Audit of Assets and Conflicts of Interest under section 42(1)(f) of Law no. 9367/2005 on potential conflict of interest arising from his shareholding if elected. He resigned as company manager on 31 July 2013. His election was certified by the Electoral College on 2 August 2013.

On 7 August 2013 the High Inspectorate replied that it was the applicant’s responsibility to prevent any conflict of interest and that he could seek advice from Parliament, which assessed such cases. It added that he would in any event be audited within one year of submitting his declaration of private interests. The applicant later approached the Speaker of Parliament, who on 18 October 2013 directed him to the Human Resources and Management of Members of Parliament Service (which had not previously handled such investigations) and to the Parliamentary Legal Service for guidance on the law, while also repeating that he could consult the High Inspectorate.

The applicant sold his shares on 6 February 2014; the sale was registered the following day. In February 2015 the Democratic Party’s parliamentary group (representing more than one-tenth of MPs) requested Parliament, under Article 73 of the Constitution, to refer to the Constitutional Court the question of whether the applicant’s MP mandate was incompatible with his former shareholding. Parliament referred the case on 10 March 2016.

In judgment no. 32/2016 of 3 June 2016 the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s position as an MP incompatible with his prior status as sole shareholder of Abissnet SHA. It held that he had acted contrary to Article 70(3) of the Constitution, which prohibits MPs from engaging in any profit-making activity that generates income from public assets. The Court criticised the six-month delay in resolving the conflict. Although the company entered no new contracts with public authorities after 2 August 2013, it continued to receive payments under pre-existing contracts while the applicant sat as an MP. The Court rejected arguments that incompatibility turned solely on new contracts, that the applicant received no dividends because he divested before the end of the financial year, that profits accrued only to the distinct legal entity of the company, and that removal would damage his reputation or interfere with voters’ rights. It found that income received by the company increased its capital and thus the value of the applicant’s shares, constituting an indirect benefit. The prohibition applied irrespective of whether the activity was carried on personally or through a company and irrespective of the final destination of the revenue.

The Constitutional Court’s judgment, being final, resulted in the applicant being debarred from remaining an MP. The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the termination of his mandate violated his right under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to carry out his parliamentary role and tarnished his reputation in breach of Article 8 of the Convention.

The case of A.D. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 22283/21) concerns a family of five Albanian nationals—a former police officer (first applicant), his wife (second applicant), and their three children—who claimed that their expulsion from Sweden to Albania would violate Article 3 of the ECHR. They alleged a real risk of ill-treatment by unidentified non-State actors linked to the first applicant’s anti-cannabis police work, combined with the Albanian authorities’ inability or unwillingness to provide effective protection.

The family applied for asylum in Sweden on 6 December 2018, shortly after the first applicant resigned from the police in November 2018. They described several incidents in Albania. On 3 October 2017, three unknown masked men attempted to kidnap the eldest daughter (third applicant), leaving her traumatised and depressed; the attackers made statements perceived as threats referring to the first applicant. Additional events in 2017–2018 included shots fired at the family’s front door and a hand grenade detonating near their home. The first applicant also reported threats from two armed men on 20 August 2017 and anonymous telephone threats. The family did not report most incidents to Albanian police, citing widespread corruption and fear that doing so would increase danger, though the first applicant had informal contact with a senior officer. They submitted supporting documents, including a news article, a prosecutor’s report, and a police record of the kidnapping attempt. They feared being killed upon return, noting similar killings of a former police officer and his wife in their hometown.

The Swedish Migration Agency rejected the claim on 18 January 2019 and ordered deportation. It accepted that the incidents occurred but treated them as criminal acts by unknown perpetrators whose motives and interconnections were unclear. Relying on country-of-origin information (COI), it found that Albania possessed a general capacity and willingness to protect citizens despite corruption problems, which the authorities were actively addressing. The applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not reporting the kidnapping, and any work-related threat to the first applicant should have dissipated after his resignation.

The Migration Court upheld the decision on 28 April 2020. While COI indicated a largely functioning judicial system, it also highlighted residual corruption and police hesitation, so the court assessed the individual circumstances. Given the first applicant’s long police career and documented contacts with police and prosecutors, the evidence did not demonstrate that the authorities lacked the will or ability to act. Leave to appeal was refused on 22 June 2020.

In July 2020 the applicants sought re-examination, citing two new explosions at the family house in Albania (7 January and 12 July 2020). The first explosion injured the first applicant’s mother and was preceded by an anonymous call stating that the first applicant “has nowhere to hide” and “must pay the debts.” Police documents linked both explosions to the 2017 incidents. The Migration Agency and Migration Court treated the events as mere additions to previously assessed facts. Although police reports had now been filed, there was no evidence that the family had exhausted available protection mechanisms. Re-examination was therefore refused and leave to appeal denied.

The European Court later found that the Swedish proceedings contained effective guarantees against arbitrary refoulement and that the applicants had not shown the Albanian authorities to be unable or unwilling to afford appropriate protection against any risk from non-State actors. Removal would therefore not breach Article 3. (Word count: 512)

The case of A.D. and Others v. Sweden (ECHR Application no. 22283/21) concerns a family of five Albanian nationals—a former police officer (first applicant), his wife (second applicant), and their three children—who applied for asylum in Sweden on 6 December 2018. They alleged that their expulsion to Albania would violate Article 3 of the Convention due to a real risk of ill-treatment by non-state actors (criminals linked to cannabis trafficking), against which Albanian authorities were unable or unwilling to provide effective protection.

The first applicant had served as a police officer since 1998, focusing on disrupting cannabis production and trade. He resigned in November 2018, after which the family fled. Their claims centred on several incidents in 2017–2018. On 3 October 2017, three unknown masked men attempted to kidnap the eldest daughter (third applicant), traumatising her and causing depression; the men made statements perceived as threats referencing the first applicant’s work. Other events included shots fired at the family’s front door and a hand-grenade explosion near their home. The first applicant also reported being threatened by two armed men on 20 August 2017 and receiving anonymous threatening calls. The family did not formally report the kidnapping or later attacks to Albanian police, citing widespread corruption, distrust of law enforcement, and fear that reporting would worsen their situation. The first applicant had informal contact with a senior officer and submitted a prosecutor’s report on the August threats plus a police document on the kidnapping attempt. They also provided a news article corroborating some events and claimed others (including a former officer and his wife) had been killed in their hometown. They feared being killed upon return.

In interviews, the Swedish Migration Agency presented country-of-origin information indicating that Albanian authorities possessed the general ability and willingness to protect citizens despite corruption issues. The Agency accepted that the incidents occurred but noted the unknown identities of the perpetrators, unclear motives or connections between events, and the criminal (rather than state-sponsored) nature of the acts. It held that protection against such acts was primarily a matter for Albanian authorities, that the applicants had not exhausted available domestic remedies (particularly by failing to report the kidnapping), and that the first applicant’s resignation likely ended work-related threats. On 18 January 2019 it rejected asylum and ordered deportation.

The Migration Court, after appointing counsel, dismissed the appeal on 28 April 2020 without an oral hearing. It acknowledged Albania’s functioning but imperfect judicial system (corruption and police reluctance in some disputes) and thus required an individualised assessment. Given the first applicant’s long police service, connections within the system, and prior contacts with police and prosecutors, the Court found insufficient evidence that authorities lacked the will or capacity to protect the family.

Leave to appeal was refused on 22 June 2020. The applicants then sought re-examination, citing two new explosions at their Albanian house (7 January and 12 July 2020) that damaged the property and injured/threatened the first applicant’s mother (who remained there). Police documents linked these events to the earlier incidents and recorded an anonymous call demanding payment of “debts.” Photographs, articles and medical certificates were submitted. The Agency (20 July 2020) and Court (10 August 2020) treated the explosions as mere additions to previously assessed circumstances involving unknown actors. They reiterated that state protection existed and had not been exhausted, as the new reports lacked evidence of full legal follow-up or changed country conditions. Final leave to appeal was denied on 21 September 2020.

The Court later indicated an interim measure preventing removal, which Sweden respected. The applicants maintained that Albanian authorities, plagued by corruption and organised-crime influence, could not protect them. Domestic authorities and, ultimately, the Court found the proceedings procedurally sound and that the applicants had not shown Albanian authorities unable or unwilling to provide appropriate protection against any non-state risk.

The applicants—an Albanian family comprising a former police officer (first applicant), his wife, and their three children—entered Sweden and claimed asylum on 6 December 2018. They alleged a well-founded fear of ill-treatment by unidentified non-State actors if returned to Albania, in breach of Article 3 of the Convention, because the Albanian authorities were unable or unwilling to protect them.

The first applicant had served as a police officer since 1998, focusing on cannabis production and trafficking. The family fled after a series of incidents in 2017–2018. On 3 October 2017 three masked men attempted to kidnap the eldest daughter (third applicant), an event that left her traumatised and depressed. Shots were later fired at the family home and a hand grenade exploded nearby. The first applicant had also been threatened by two armed men in August 2017 and received anonymous telephone threats linked to his police work. The family attributed these events to criminal groups angered by the first applicant’s anti-cannabis activities. They reported none of the incidents (except the August 2017 threats) to the Albanian police, citing widespread corruption and a fear that reporting would increase the danger. The first applicant did, however, inform a senior officer informally.

The Swedish Migration Agency interviewed the family (with interpretation) and received supporting documents, including a news article, the first applicant’s statement to a prosecutor, and a police record of the kidnapping attempt. On 18 January 2019 it rejected the claim and ordered deportation. The Agency accepted that the incidents had occurred but regarded them as ordinary crimes by unknown perpetrators. Country information indicated that, despite corruption, Albania possessed a functioning justice system capable of offering protection. The family had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not formally reporting the kidnapping; the first applicant’s resignation from the police was also considered likely to have ended any work-related threat.

The Migration Court upheld the decision on 28 April 2020 after written proceedings (an oral hearing having been refused). It acknowledged deficiencies in the Albanian system but held that an individualised assessment was required. Given the first applicant’s long police career and documented contacts with senior officers and prosecutors, the court found insufficient evidence that the authorities lacked the will or capacity to protect the family.

Leave to appeal was refused by the Migration Court of Appeal on 22 June 2020.

In July 2020 the family applied for a residence permit or re-examination, citing two new explosions at their Albanian home (7 January and 12 July 2020). The first damaged the house and injured the first applicant’s mother; an anonymous caller had warned that the first applicant “must pay the debts he owes us.” Police reports linked both explosions to the earlier incidents. The Migration Agency (20 July 2020) and Migration Court (10 August 2020) treated the new events as mere additions to previously assessed circumstances. The family had still not demonstrated that they had exhausted available Albanian protection. Leave to appeal was again refused.

The European Court of Human Rights later received the application (no. 22283/21) and indicated an interim measure preventing expulsion pending its examination. The applicants maintained that the risk of serious harm from non-State actors, combined with ineffective state protection in Albania, would violate Article 3.

The case of Bechi v. Romania (application no. 45709/20) concerns a Romanian national, Daniel Bechi (born 1982), who tested HIV-positive and began serving a three-year prison sentence on 17 September 2019. He was transferred to Târgu Ocna Prison on 17 January 2020, remaining there until 9 March 2021, after which he was moved to Poarta Albă Prison. He was released on parole on 3 June 2022. Both prisons housed him in dedicated medical/vulnerable-person wings due to his HIV status. The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (alone and with Article 14) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from poor material conditions of detention and discriminatory segregation that prevented contact with other prisoners and any work. He also invoked Article 8 regarding the prisons’ distance from his family home in Reteag, which he claimed hindered family contact. The Court raised an Article 13 issue of its own motion.

At Târgu Ocna the applicant complained of overcrowding, insufficient storage, bedbugs, poor ventilation, sharing a cell with smokers despite his chronic illness, and exclusion from activities or work. The post-sentencing judge dismissed the complaints, noting a 44 m² cell occupied by seven inmates (unlocked under the semi-open regime) with unrestricted outdoor access in a designated area. The judge acknowledged a formal bar on work for HIV-positive inmates, intended as protection. Similar later complaints about sharing with smokers and hepatitis-C sufferers were also dismissed.

At Poarta Albă the applicant alleged overcrowding (cell E6.1), lack of shower privacy, mould, co-detention with hepatitis-C prisoners posing a contamination risk, and the distant transfers. A post-sentencing judge partially upheld the overcrowding claim (less than 4 m² personal space) but recorded recent renovations and found the medical-wing placement protective rather than discriminatory; a medical report confirmed no contagion risk. Subsequent rulings confirmed the legality of the placement while conceding remaining issues (overcrowding, defective bathrooms, dilapidated furniture, mould) and recommending a cell offering at least 4 m². The National Prison Administration (ANP) justified the transfers by reference to the applicant’s medical needs and the facilities’ specialised capacity.

The Government described Târgu Ocna cells as hygienic, with individual beds, adequate furniture, running water, ventilation, lighting and heating, plus bathroom privacy. At Poarta Albă (open regime) personal space ranged from 3.06 m² to 5.86 m² across successive cells; some had been renovated. The applicant enjoyed free courtyard access, educational activities (April–August 2021) and socio-educational programmes. Other HIV-positive inmates who wished to work were permitted to do so; the applicant had expressed no such interest.

Domestic law (Law no. 254/2013 and implementing rules) classifies HIV/AIDS as a vulnerability criterion justifying separate accommodation. ANP decisions authorised specialised HIV wings and allowed transfers for medical or overcrowding reasons. CPT reports on Romanian prisons noted severe overcrowding, poor hygiene and prejudice against HIV-positive inmates, concluding that separate accommodation might be acceptable if it genuinely served health and well-being, despite the absence of a public-health justification for segregation solely on HIV status.

The Court held that the material conditions under semi-open and open regimes did not exceed the unavoidable level of suffering inherent in detention (no Article 3 violation). Placement in prison hospitals was necessitated by the particular circumstances of Romanian prisons; any differential treatment vis-à-vis ordinary detainees was intended to provide better, medically tailored conditions and had an objective and reasonable justification (no Article 3 or 14 violation).

The case of Bechi v. Romania (Application no. 45709/20) concerns a Romanian national, Daniel Bechi (born 1982), who tested HIV-positive and began serving a three-year prison sentence on 17 September 2019. He was transferred on 17 January 2020 to Târgu Ocna Prison (until 9 March 2021) and then to Poarta Albă Prison, from which he was released on parole on 3 June 2022. Both facilities had specialised medical wings for HIV-positive detainees. The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), arising from poor material conditions of detention and his segregation from the general prison population due to his HIV status. He further alleged a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) on account of the prisons’ distance from his family home in Reteag, which hindered contact. The Court also examined of its own motion whether an effective domestic remedy existed under Article 13.

In Târgu Ocna Prison the applicant was held in the medical wing (cells E5.1, E5.3 and E5.7). He complained of overcrowding, insufficient storage space, bedbugs, inadequate ventilation, sharing a cell with smokers despite his non-smoking status and chronic illness, and a complete bar on work or other activities solely because of his HIV status. The cell he occupied measured 44 m² and housed seven detainees; because he was serving under a semi-open regime the cell remained unlocked during the day and he had unrestricted access to a designated outdoor area. Post-sentencing judges dismissed his complaints, confirming that HIV-positive prisoners were formally prohibited from work in order to protect both them and others, and that the arrangement did not infringe their rights. A subsequent complaint about being housed with smokers and hepatitis-C sufferers was likewise rejected, the judge noting that smoking in cells was forbidden.

After transfer to Poarta Albă Prison the applicant was placed in cells E6.1, E6.2 and E6.3 of the medical wing. He alleged overcrowding (personal space below 4 m²), lack of shower privacy, mould, dilapidated furniture, and cohabitation with hepatitis-C prisoners exposing him to contagion. He also reiterated the distance from his family. A post-sentencing judge partially upheld the overcrowding and hygiene complaints, recorded that renovation work had been carried out, and recommended relocation to a cell offering at least 4 m². Later judicial decisions confirmed that placement in the vulnerable-persons section was lawful and protective rather than discriminatory, and a medical report of 24 March 2021 found no risk of contagion from hepatitis C. Space calculations supplied by the Government showed occupancy yielding between 3.06 m² and 5.86 m² per person; the applicant served under an open regime with free access to a courtyard and educational programmes. Other HIV-positive prisoners in the same wing who wished to work were permitted to do so; the applicant expressed no such interest.

The National Prison Administration (ANP) justified the distant placements by reference to the applicant’s medical needs and the existence of dedicated HIV wings at the two prisons. Domestic law (Law no. 254/2013 and its implementing rules) requires the ANP, when assigning prisoners, to consider proximity to home but also regime type, security, social-reintegration needs and medical vulnerability. HIV status is an explicit vulnerability criterion justifying special accommodation. ANP decisions of 2016 and 2020 expressly authorised Târgu Ocna to operate an HIV wing and permitted transfers to more distant facilities in order to relieve overcrowding or for other well-founded reasons.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), in its 2018 report on Romania, noted the systematic segregation of HIV-positive prisoners, their exclusion from work and their separate regime of outdoor access. While stating that there is no public-health justification for such segregation in principle, the CPT accepted that, given severe overcrowding, poor hygiene, lack of medical confidentiality and high levels of prejudice in Romanian prisons, separate accommodation could be tolerated provided it offered conditions conducive to health and well-being.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that the material conditions exceeded the unavoidable suffering inherent in detention, that his isolation and work ban constituted discriminatory treatment lacking objective justification, and that the remote placements disproportionately interfered with family life.

The case of Bechi v. Romania (App. no. 45709/20) before the ECtHR involved a Romanian HIV-positive applicant, Daniel Bechi (born 1982), serving a three-year sentence from 17 September 2019. He was held at Târgu Ocna Prison (17 January 2020–9 March 2021) then Poarta Albă Prison until parole on 3 June 2022. He alleged Article 3 violations from poor detention conditions (overcrowding below 4 m² personal space, bedbugs, poor ventilation, mold, dilapidated furniture, inadequate bathrooms/privacy, sharing with smokers and hepatitis C patients) under semi-open/open regimes. Combined with Article 14, he claimed degrading treatment and discrimination via segregation in HIV-positive/vulnerable wings, isolating him from other prisoners and barring work. Under Article 8, distant transfers from his Reteag family home hindered contact. The Court raised Article 13 proprio motu.

The applicant filed complaints under Law no. 254/2013 with post-sentencing judges. At Târgu Ocna, he cited overcrowding, storage shortages, ventilation issues, smoker cellmates, and activity/work bans. The 3 September 2020 judgment (upheld 30 September 2020) dismissed it, noting a 44 m² cell for seven (over 6 m² each), unlocked under semi-open regime with unlimited outdoor access; HIV status barred work for protection. A 1 October 2020 ruling (upheld) rejected similar claims, confirming no in-cell smoking and protective intent.

At Poarta Albă, his 17 March 2021 complaint alleged overcrowding in cell E6.1, shower privacy lacks, mold, hepatitis C risks, and distant transfers. Partially allowed on 25 March 2021 (challenge rejected 29 April 2021), it noted under 4 m² space but February 2021 renovations; placement protected him, with no contagion risk per 24 March 2021 medical report. A 23 June 2021 judgment confirmed legitimacy of vulnerable-section placement but conceded overcrowding, poor bathrooms/toilets, dilapidated furniture, and mold, recommending at least 4 m² space. An ANP complaint on transfers was rejected on 9 March 2021, citing medical needs and specialized facilities.

Government details: Târgu Ocna medical-wing cells (E5.1, E5.3, E5.7) offered individual beds, adequate furniture/hygiene, bathroom privacy, hot/cold water, and satisfactory ventilation/lighting/heating. At Poarta Albă (from 11 March 2021), space ranged from 3.06 m² (cell E6.1, 19 prisoners in 58.14 m², 11–26 March) to 5.86 m² (cell E6.3, 8 prisoners in 46.89 m², 22 July–20 October), with 4.33 m² (E6.2) and 3.90 m² intervals. A 5 March 2021 judge visit noted recent renovations (windows, bathroom ceiling) despite some damp; further work followed. Open regime allowed courtyard access, educational activities (1 April–31 August 2021), and socio-educational spaces. The applicant showed no work interest; willing HIV-positive inmates in his wing did.

Law no. 254/2013 (Arts. 11, 45, 48, 56) governs transfers (proximity to residence, regime, needs, capacity) and complaints. Methodological rules (Arts. 5, 34, 108, 345) allow special HIV-positive spaces and vulnerability criteria. ANP decisions (704/2016, 360/2020) designated special wings and permitted non-proximity transfers for capacity/medical reasons. CPT reports (2018) noted Romanian prison overcrowding/HIV segregation but deemed it potentially tolerable amid poor conditions if promoting well-being. These facts underpinned assessments of conditions not exceeding inherent detention suffering and justified differential treatment for medical needs.
