The case of Boronyák v. Hungary (Application no. 4110/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an actor’s complaint under Article 10 of the Convention that a contractual penalty imposed for disclosing his fees violated his freedom of expression. The applicant, Gergely Boronyák, signed an indefinite agency contract on 28 November 2011 with private production company M. to play a lead role in the television series Marslakók. The company had been commissioned by the state-owned and state-financed Media Services and Support Trust Fund (MTVA) to co-produce the series, which the contract described as an asset of public-service media. The applicant’s remuneration was set at HUF 28,000 (approximately EUR 70) per episode plus a monthly lump-sum of HUF 600,000 (approximately EUR 1,500).

Section 20 of the contract contained a non-disclosure clause. The applicant undertook not to reveal any confidential business information, including data relating to the principal, its partners, ownership and business connections, media-service activities, programme production, the actors, or any persons who received fees for contributing to the series. Breach of the clause triggered a contractual penalty of HUF 10,000,000 (approximately EUR 26,000) in addition to any damages, unless the company consented to disclosure. The company also reserved a unilateral right of termination.

Production of the series was discontinued in 2012 because of low viewer interest, and the applicant’s contract was terminated on 1 August 2012. Investigative portal atlatszo.hu subsequently brought a freedom-of-information action against MTVA seeking details of production costs and documents concerning the termination. The Budapest High Court ordered disclosure; the Budapest Court of Appeal upheld that order in June 2013.

On 16 January 2014 the applicant gave a video interview to atlatszo.hu in which he stated the fees he had received. The portal published an accompanying article alleging non-payment of severance. Shortly afterwards the applicant testified as a witness in related civil proceedings brought by the production company against the portal. On 17 January 2014 the company demanded payment of the HUF 10 million penalty. When the applicant refused, the company sued him for breach of confidentiality.

The applicant argued that his contractual obligations, including confidentiality, had ceased upon termination and that the information was in any event of public interest because it concerned the expenditure of public funds. The Pest Central District Court found against him on 14 January 2015, holding that the confidentiality clause survived termination and that neither party processed public-interest data under the Data Protection and Information Act. The court ordered payment of the full penalty plus costs. The Budapest High Court confirmed the judgment on 15 September 2015, emphasising that the applicant had expressly agreed to keep the information secret even if he regarded it as public-interest data and that the company had a legitimate interest in protecting commercially sensitive production details. The Kúria dismissed a review request on 30 June 2016, reasoning that although entities managing public funds cannot withhold budgetary information as a business secret, the applicant himself neither managed public funds nor processed public information and therefore could not invoke the relevant provisions of the Civil Code to escape his contractual duty. The Constitutional Court rejected a constitutional complaint on 18 June 2019, holding that the Fundamental Law does not preclude private parties from concluding non-disclosure agreements even when the counterparty would itself be obliged to disclose the same information.

Hungarian law (Articles VI and 39 of the Fundamental Law, Article 81 of the Civil Code and section 27 of the Data Protection and Information Act) classifies data relating to the central budget and the use of public funds as information of public interest that cannot be treated as a business secret. Public entities and persons entering into financial relations with them must disclose such data on request. The National Authority for Data Protection and Freedom of Information has likewise stated that public-interest data cannot be withheld by means of confidentiality agreements. These statutory mechanisms were available independently of the applicant’s contractual clause.

The case of Boronyák v. Hungary (ECtHR Application no. 4110/20) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) arising from a contractual penalty imposed on the applicant, Hungarian actor Gergely Boronyák, for disclosing details of his remuneration under a non-disclosure agreement.

On 28 November 2011 the applicant signed an indefinite agency contract with private production company M. to play a leading role in the television series Marslakók. The contract recorded that M. had been commissioned by the state-owned and state-financed Media Services and Support Trust Fund (MTVA) to co-produce the series, which was designated an asset of public-service media. The applicant’s fees were set at HUF 28 000 (approximately EUR 70) per episode plus a monthly lump sum of HUF 600 000 (approximately EUR 1 500). Clause 20 obliged him not to disclose any “confidential business information,” expressly including data relating to the principal, its partners, ownership structure, programme production or the fees paid to any contributors. Breach attracted a penalty of HUF 10 million (approximately EUR 26 000) in addition to damages; M. also reserved a unilateral right of termination.

Production ceased in 2012 owing to poor ratings and the contract was terminated on 1 August 2012. In 2013 atlatszo.hu, an investigative portal specialising in public-expenditure transparency, obtained a court order (upheld on appeal) requiring MTVA to release information on the series’ production costs and related termination documents. On 16 January 2014 the applicant gave a video interview to the same portal in which he disclosed his contractual fees and complained of unpaid severance. He later testified as a witness in separate proceedings brought by M. against the portal.

M. immediately demanded payment of the HUF 10 million penalty and sued the applicant for breach of confidentiality. The applicant argued that the confidentiality obligation had lapsed on termination of the contract and that the information constituted data of public interest because public funds had been used. The Pest Central District Court (14 January 2015) found against him, holding that the clause survived termination and that neither party processed public-interest data under the Data Protection and Information Act. The Budapest High Court (15 September 2015) and the Kúria (30 June 2016) upheld the judgment. They accepted that public-budget data are not business secrets and that public entities must disclose them, but stressed that the applicant himself neither managed public funds nor processed public information; he therefore remained bound by his private contractual undertaking. The Constitutional Court (18 June 2019) confirmed that the Fundamental Law does not prohibit non-disclosure agreements between private parties even when the counterparty would otherwise be obliged to release public-interest data.

The applicant complained that the penalty interfered with his right to impart information of public concern. The Court examined the existence of alternative legal channels (statutory FOI obligations on bodies managing central-budget funds) and the domestic courts’ reasoning that a private contractor could validly be bound by confidentiality. It concluded that those courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons, had struck a fair balance between the competing interests, and had not overstepped the State’s margin of appreciation. No violation of Article 10 was therefore found.

The case of Boronyák v. Hungary (ECtHR Application no. 4110/20) arose from a complaint under Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression) concerning a contractual penalty imposed on the applicant, actor Gergely Boronyák, for disclosing details of his remuneration under a non-disclosure agreement.

In November 2011 the applicant signed an indefinite agency contract with private production company M. to play a lead role in the television series Marslakók. The contract recorded that M. had been commissioned by the state-owned and state-financed Media Services and Support Trust Fund (MTVA) to co-produce the series, which was expressly described as an asset of public-service media. The applicant’s fees were set at HUF 28,000 (approximately EUR 70) per episode plus a monthly lump sum of HUF 600,000 (approximately EUR 1,500). Section 20 of the contract contained a broad confidentiality clause covering all business information relating to the production, the actors’ fees and any other remuneration paid. Breach triggered a contractual penalty of HUF 10 million (approximately EUR 26,000) in addition to damages; M. also reserved a unilateral right of termination.

Production of the series was discontinued in 2012 because of poor ratings and the applicant’s contract was terminated on 1 August 2012. In the meantime the investigative portal atlatszo.hu obtained a final court order requiring MTVA to disclose the production’s budgetary information on the ground that it constituted data of public interest under Hungarian freedom-of-information legislation.

On 16 January 2014 the applicant gave atlatszo.hu a video interview in which he revealed the precise amounts he had been paid. The portal published an accompanying article focusing on the non-payment of severance. Shortly afterwards the applicant also testified as a witness in related civil proceedings brought by M. against the portal. M. immediately demanded payment of the contractual penalty and, when the applicant refused, sued him for breach of confidentiality.

The applicant argued that the confidentiality obligation had lapsed upon termination of the contract and that, in any event, the information was of public interest because it concerned the expenditure of public funds. All levels of the Hungarian judiciary rejected these defences. The Pest Central District Court (2014), upheld by the Budapest High Court (2015) and the Kúria (2016), held that the non-disclosure clause survived termination and that the applicant, as a private contracting party who neither managed public funds nor processed public-interest data, could not invoke the statutory exceptions that applied to public bodies. The Constitutional Court (2019) confirmed that the Fundamental Law did not prohibit private parties from agreeing to keep confidential information that a public entity would itself have been obliged to disclose.

The applicant was ordered to pay the full HUF 10 million penalty plus costs. He complained to the European Court that the sanction constituted a disproportionate interference with his right to impart information on a matter of public interest. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 10, holding that adequate alternative mechanisms existed for the public to obtain the same information from the public entities concerned and that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance within their margin of appreciation.

The applicant, an Ethiopian national born in 1954, married in Eritrea and had two daughters (born 2004 and 2010). He left for South Sudan around 2011, working as a driver, while his wife and daughters relocated to Uganda in 2013 as UNHCR-protected asylum seekers. He maintained contact and visited them (including in 2014). In early 2017, UNHCR sought his resettlement to Sweden due to an untreated eye condition risking blindness and job loss.

On 27 June 2017, Sweden granted him a permanent residence permit as a recognised refugee. He arrived on 6 September 2017, received introduction benefits, and attended an immigrant course. His family applied for residence permits based on family ties on 21 October 2017 (nearly four months later). Sweden’s Temporary Restrictions Act (in force 2016–2021) generally required sponsors to meet a “maintenance requirement” of sufficient income and adequate housing. Recognised refugees were exempt only if the application was filed within three months of status being granted. The Migration Agency rejected the request on 7 February 2018, finding the exemption inapplicable and that the applicant’s benefits and one-bedroom flat did not satisfy the requirement. It held this consistent with international obligations.

The applicant appealed, citing lack of a personal identity number in his first month, ignorance of Swedish law, brief time in the country, and health issues, invoking Article 8 ECHR. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 15 March 2018, and the Migration Court of Appeal denied leave on 27 April 2018.

A second application was filed on 15 January 2019 after the applicant turned 65, began receiving a guarantee pension and rent subsidy, and was registered with reduced work capacity due to mobility impairment. The Agency rejected it on 21 August 2019, as the pension was not a work-related income. On appeal, citing age (now 66), stress, high blood pressure, and vision impairment, the Migration Court on 18 January 2021 found family ties strong and circumstances difficult but not exceptionally vulnerable, so applying the requirement was not disproportionate given immigration-control interests. Leave to appeal was refused on 4 May 2021.

The Temporary Restrictions Act expired on 20 July 2021. The Aliens Act retained the three-month rule and maintenance requirement for later applications but introduced exemptions for “exceptional reasons” (e.g., retirement or permanent disability making compliance unreasonable). For quota refugees the three-month period was briefly calculated from entry (later repealed). After visiting his family, a third application was filed on 17 February 2022. On 14 July 2022 the Agency granted permits, finding it unreasonable to expect the applicant to meet the income requirement given his age and health. His wife and children (then 17 and 12) arrived in September 2022.

The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 that the refusals violated his right to family life by imposing an unmet maintenance requirement outside the exemption window. (The Court later applied Dabo v. Sweden principles, finding no violation after an individualised assessment.)

The applicant, an Ethiopian national born in 1954, is a recognised refugee living in Sweden. He moved from Ethiopia to Eritrea in 1998, where he married and had two daughters (born 2004 and 2010). In 2010 he left for South Sudan (arriving around 2011) and worked as a driver. In 2013 his wife and daughters relocated to Uganda as UNHCR-protected asylum seekers; he maintained contact and visited them, including in 2014.

Sweden’s Temporary Restrictions Act (in force 20 July 2016–19 July 2021) limited family reunification by imposing a “maintenance requirement”: the sponsor must have sufficient income (typically work-related) and adequate housing. Recognised refugees were exempt if the application was filed within three months of the grant of status.

In early 2017 UNHCR requested the applicant’s resettlement to Sweden due to an untreated eye condition risking blindness and loss of his driving job. On 27 June 2017 he received a permanent residence permit as a refugee; an English-language letter referred him to the Migration Agency website for information. He arrived on 6 September 2017, attended an introduction course and received “introduction benefits.”

On 21 October 2017 (nearly four months after the permit grant) his wife and daughters applied online for residence permits based on family ties. On 7 February 2018 the Migration Agency refused: the three-month exemption no longer applied, the benefits were not salary-equivalent income, and his one-bedroom flat was inadequate. The decision was held compatible with Swedish law and international obligations.

The applicant appealed, citing the lack of a personal identity number in his first month, ignorance of Swedish law, recent arrival, health issues and a desire to become self-supporting; he invoked Article 8 ECHR. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 15 March 2018. Leave to appeal to the Migration Court of Appeal was denied on 27 April 2018.

Meanwhile, in March 2018 the Employment Service noted his reduced work capacity. Upon turning 65 in January 2019 his benefits converted to a guarantee pension plus rent subsidy. A second family-reunification application (15 January 2019) was refused on 21 August 2019 because the pension was not work-related. On appeal he stressed his age, stress, hypertension and impaired vision, arguing he could not meet the requirement. The Migration Court rejected the appeal on 18 January 2021, acknowledging strong family ties and hardship but finding the situation not “particularly vulnerable” and the refusal not disproportionate. Leave to appeal was again refused (4 May 2021).

The Temporary Restrictions Act expired on 20 July 2021; new Aliens Act provisions retained the three-month rule but allowed full or partial exemption for “exceptional reasons” (e.g., retirement or permanent disability making the requirement unreasonable). The applicant visited his family in late 2021–early 2022. A third application (17 February 2022) was granted on 14 July 2022: given his age and health it was neither likely nor reasonable to expect him to obtain sufficient work income, so enforcing the requirement would be unreasonable. His wife and children (then 17 and 12) received permits and arrived in Sweden in September 2022.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR (application lodged 17 October 2018) that the refusals violated his right to family life (Article 8) and amounted to discrimination (Article 14), given his refugee status, health, age and the family’s circumstances.

The case of Okubamichael Debru v. Sweden (no. 49755/18) concerns an Ethiopian refugee’s complaint under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that Sweden’s refusal of family reunification with his wife and two daughters violated his right to family life. The refusals were based on his failure to meet a statutory maintenance requirement after applying outside a three-month exemption window.

The applicant, born in 1954, moved from Ethiopia to Eritrea in 1998, married and had daughters in 2004 and 2010. He later worked as a driver in South Sudan. In 2013 his wife and daughters relocated to Uganda as UNHCR-protected asylum-seekers; he maintained contact and visited them. In early 2017 UNHCR sought his resettlement to Sweden because an untreated eye condition threatened his sight and livelihood. On 27 June 2017 he received a permanent residence permit as a recognised refugee. He arrived in Sweden on 6 September 2017, began an introduction course and received introduction benefits.

On 21 October 2017—almost four months after the permit was granted—his family applied online for residence permits on family-reunification grounds. The Migration Agency rejected the applications on 7 February 2018. Under the Temporary Restrictions Act (in force 2016–2021) a sponsor who had been granted refugee status was exempt from the income-and-accommodation requirement only if the application was lodged within three months of that grant. The applicant lived on non-work-related benefits in a one-bedroom flat, so the requirement applied and was not met. The Agency found the decision compatible with Sweden’s international obligations.

The applicant appealed, citing the absence of a personal identity number in his first month, ignorance of Swedish law, his short stay and health problems, and relying on Article 8. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 15 March 2018; leave to appeal was denied on 27 April 2018.

A second application was filed on 15 January 2019 after the applicant, now 65, received a guarantee pension and rent subsidy. It was rejected on 21 August 2019 because the pension was not regarded as work-related income. Appeals emphasising his age, vision impairment, stress, high blood pressure and reduced working capacity were dismissed by the Migration Court on 18 January 2021: the family’s situation was not particularly vulnerable and the requirement was not disproportionate to the public interest in regulated immigration. Leave to appeal was again refused.

The Temporary Act expired on 20 July 2021. New provisions of the Aliens Act retained the three-month rule but allowed full or partial exemptions for “exceptional reasons,” including age or permanent disability. A third application lodged on 17 February 2022 was granted on 14 July 2022; the Agency considered it unreasonable to expect the applicant, given his age and health, ever to meet the income threshold. His wife and daughters (then 17 and 12) arrived in Sweden in September 2022.

The Court applied the principles set out in Dabo v. Sweden. It found no objectively excusable reasons for missing the three-month period, noted that a fresh application could be (and eventually was) lodged, observed that the authorities had conducted an individualised assessment, and took account of the subsequent legislative possibility of exemptions. A fair balance had been struck between the competing interests and Sweden had not overstepped its wide margin of appreciation. There was therefore no violation of Article 8; the Article 14 complaint was not separately examined.
001-235465:
The case of Namık Yüksel v. Türkiye concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life). The applicant, convicted with his wife of aiding a terrorist organisation and each sentenced to three years and nine months' imprisonment, complained that prison authorities failed to allow him sufficient contact with their four-year-old son, who resided with the wife in the same facility.

The wife began her sentence on 5 January 2009 at Bakırköy Prison and was transferred on 2 March 2009 to Gebze Prison with the son. At her request they were housed in a general 12-person cell rather than one reserved for terrorism-related offenders. The applicant started his sentence the same day at Metris Prison and moved to Amasya Prison on 29 January 2009. He successfully applied for transfer to Gebze Prison to facilitate family contact and arrived on 2 November 2009, placed in a terrorism-offender cell.

On 13 November 2009 the applicant petitioned the Gebze enforcement judge. He noted that he already received weekly non-contact visits from his wife and son plus monthly contact visits, but argued that national rules permitting children under six needing care to stay with imprisoned mothers contained no equivalent provision for fathers. He called this sexist, harmful to the child's psychological well-being, and requested daytime meetings with the son plus regular sessions involving both parents.

The prison observation board (governor, psychologist, doctor and others) examined the request the same day. Citing the regulation that children under six may stay with their mothers, it refused to let the boy reside in the father's cell. On humanitarian grounds it authorised one hour of physical contact during the weekly Thursday non-contact visits and one hour of monthly contact involving both parents and the child.

The enforcement judge dismissed the petition on 4 December 2009 as lawful. The applicant objected to the Gebze Assize Court on 16 December 2009, clarifying that he sought only daytime meetings in visiting or recreation areas, not co-residence. He argued the regulation did not bar paternal contact, suggested using his unused ten weekly hours of open-area socialisation for time with the child, and asked that the child's rights be considered. The Assize Court rejected the objection on 21 December 2009.

The applicant was released on 26 June 2010; his wife remained imprisoned until 17 October 2011. These facts formed the basis of the Article 8 complaint that the limited contact arrangements failed to respect family life.

The case of Namık Yüksel v. Türkiye concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention arising from restrictions on the applicant’s contact with his four-year-old son, who resided with the applicant’s wife in the same prison. Both parents had been convicted in 2006 of aiding a terrorist organisation and each sentenced to three years and nine months’ imprisonment.

The wife began her sentence on 5 January 2009 and was transferred on 2 March 2009 to Gebze Prison together with the child. At her request they were housed in an ordinary twelve-person cell rather than a terrorism-designated unit. The applicant started his sentence the same day, was later moved to Amasya Prison, and successfully applied for transfer to Gebze Prison on 2 November 2009 so that he could see his family more readily. He was placed in the terrorism-related cell B-1.

On 13 November 2009 the applicant petitioned the Gebze enforcement judge. He noted that he already received weekly non-contact visits and a monthly contact visit, but argued that the absence of any provision allowing the child (who needed care and lived with his mother) to spend additional time with his father was sexist, ignored the child’s psychological welfare and prevented the parents from spending time together with their son. He asked the prison administration to create facilities for daytime meetings with the child and for regular sessions involving both parents.

The prison’s administration and observation board examined the request the same day. Relying on Article 70 of the prison regulations (which permits children under six who need care to remain with their mothers), it refused to let the child stay in the father’s cell. On humanitarian grounds, however, it authorised one hour of physical contact during the weekly Thursday non-contact visit and one hour of family contact during the monthly visit.

The enforcement judge dismissed the petition on 4 December 2009, holding the board’s decision lawful. The applicant objected to the Gebze Assize Court, clarifying that he did not seek cohabitation but only extra daytime meetings in visiting or recreation areas. He pointed out that he was entitled to ten hours of weekly open-air association which he could not use because of the prison regime applicable to him, and asked that the child’s rights also be taken into account. The Assize Court dismissed the objection on 21 December 2009.

The applicant was released on 26 June 2010; his wife remained in prison until 17 October 2011.

Domestic law (Constitution Article 41 and Law no. 5275, sections 65 and 83, together with the relevant prison and visit regulations) permits young children to stay with convicted mothers and provides for weekly visits of 30–60 minutes, three of them non-contact and one contact. Prisoners held in the same establishment may visit each other if they are close relatives. International instruments cited by the Court (UNCRC Articles 3, 9 and 18, the Bangkok Rules and Council of Europe recommendations) emphasise the child’s best interests, the right to regular direct contact with both parents and the need for child-friendly visiting arrangements.

These facts constitute the core of the applicant’s complaint that the authorities failed to ensure sufficient family contact.

The case of Namık Yüksel v. Türkiye (Application no. 28791/10) concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding restrictions on the applicant’s family life while he and his wife served prison sentences for aiding a terrorist organisation.

In August 2006 the Istanbul Assize Court sentenced both the applicant (born 1966) and his wife to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. Their four-year-old son had no alternative carer. The wife began her sentence on 5 January 2009 at Bakırköy Prison and was transferred on 2 March 2009 to Gebze Prison, where she and the child were housed, at her request, in a general women’s cell rather than one reserved for terrorism-related convictions. The applicant began his sentence on the same date at Metris Prison, was later moved to Amasya Prison, and, following his own request, was transferred on 2 November 2009 to Gebze Prison so that he could be near his family. He was placed in a cell designated for terrorism convicts.

On 13 November 2009 the applicant petitioned the Gebze enforcement judge. He noted that he already received weekly non-contact visits from his wife and son and one monthly contact visit, but argued that the statutory rule permitting children under six to remain with their imprisoned mothers (and not fathers) was discriminatory and ignored the child’s psychological needs. He requested that the prison create conditions for him to spend daytime hours with his son in visiting or recreation areas and that the family be allowed to meet together regularly.

The prison’s administration and observation board examined the request the same day. Citing the regulation that children under six in need of care may stay only with their mothers, it refused to house the boy with the applicant. On humanitarian grounds, however, it authorised one hour of physical contact between father and son during the existing weekly non-contact visits and one hour of joint contact visits with both parents each month. The enforcement judge upheld this decision as lawful on 4 December 2009. The applicant objected, clarifying that he did not seek to have the child live in his cell but merely wished for additional daytime meetings; he also invoked the child’s independent rights. The Gebze Assize Court dismissed the objection on 21 December 2009.

The applicant was released on 26 June 2010; his wife remained in prison until 17 October 2011. Throughout the relevant period the child stayed exclusively with the mother, and the only additional contact granted to the father was the one-hour weekly physical interaction and the monthly family hour already described.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the authorities had failed to take reasonable steps to facilitate meaningful family contact, thereby violating his right to respect for family life. Domestic law (Law no. 5275 and implementing regulations) expressly limited young children’s residence in prison to the mother’s care and provided only weekly visits (three non-contact and one contact per month). International instruments such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and Council of Europe recommendations emphasise the child’s best interests and the need to maintain regular contact with both parents, but they do not create an automatic right for a child to reside with or spend unrestricted time with an imprisoned father. The Court later held that the limited extra contact authorised by the prison board struck a fair balance in the particular circumstances of the case.

The case of S.F. v. Finland (ECtHR Application no. 35276/20) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life) arising from Finland’s refusal to grant family reunification. The applicant, an Eritrean national granted refugee status in Finland, sought to sponsor her husband (also Eritrean, with refugee status in Uganda) to join her and their three minor children.

The applicant and her children received asylum on 27 October 2016 (notified 8 November 2016) due to a risk of persecution for political opinions. The decision included written information (in Finnish) on family reunification, including a three-month exemption from the statutory maintenance requirement (sufficient financial resources to avoid reliance on social assistance) if the family had been established before the sponsor’s arrival in Finland. The applicant also discussed reunification with a social worker in November 2016 and January 2017, assisted by a Tigrinya interpreter. She was specifically informed of the three-month deadline and its consequences, given application forms, contact details for the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi, and information on online applications.

The husband applied for a residence permit on 30 January 2018 at the Nairobi embassy—nearly 15 months after notification. He had fled Eritrea in 2014 and held a Ugandan refugee status. The Finnish Immigration Service refused the application on 20 February 2019. The family did not meet the maintenance requirement (a monthly income of at least €2,900 was needed, but the applicant relied solely on social benefits). The three-month exemption did not apply due to the late filing. No “exceptionally serious grounds” existed for a derogation: explanations for the delay (attempts at the honorary consulate in Kampala, which lacked authority; passport issues; and later-claimed health problems) were deemed insufficient or implausible. Passport stamps indicated prior travel to Kenya and Eritrea, suggesting he could have applied earlier. The husband was settled in Uganda with a support network. Children’s best interests did not warrant a permit, given their residence with the mother, limited prior contact with the father, and no specific harm shown.

Appeals to the Administrative Court (dismissed 6 September 2019, with a minority dissenting) and Supreme Administrative Court (leave refused 26 February 2020) upheld the refusal. The Administrative Court found the delay not objectively excusable (financial or passport-related reasons), instructions adequate despite being in Finnish, unsubstantiated health claims irrelevant, and no specific child-welfare factors justifying derogation.

The ECtHR applied the principles from Dabo v. Sweden. It held that the applicant received timely, adequate advice on the procedure and deadline. There were no objectively excusable reasons for missing the three-month window. The refusal was not irreversible, as a fresh application could be made invoking exceptional circumstances if new facts arose. A fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s family-life interest and the State’s interest in controlling immigration and public finances. Finland had not overstepped its wide margin of appreciation. No violation of Article 8 was found.

**CASE OF S.F. v. FINLAND (ECtHR, App. no. 35276/20, 8 Oct 2024)**

The case concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for family life) arising from Finland’s refusal of family reunification for an acknowledged refugee who failed to meet a maintenance (income) requirement after missing a three-month statutory exemption period.

The applicant, an Eritrean national born in 1982, was granted asylum in Finland on 27 October 2016 (notified 8 November 2016) together with her three minor children (born 2003, 2008 and 2015) on grounds of feared political persecution. Her husband, also Eritrean and a recognised refugee living in Kampala, Uganda, applied for a residence permit on family-reunification grounds only on 30 January 2018 at the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi—nearly 15 months later.

Finnish law (Aliens Act, ss. 39 and 114) requires sufficient financial resources for family-reunification residence permits unless the application is lodged within three months of the sponsor’s asylum notification (and other conditions, including that the family existed before the sponsor’s arrival, are met). The Immigration Service’s accompanying written information (in Finnish) and two interpreter-assisted meetings with a social worker (November 2016 and January 2017, in Tigrinya) expressly explained the three-month deadline, the exemption from the maintenance test, how and where to apply, and provided forms plus Nairobi Embassy contacts and online-application details.

The Immigration Service refused the husband’s application on 20 February 2019. The family link was accepted, but the late filing meant the maintenance requirement applied: the household needed at least €2,900 per month, yet the applicant lived solely on social-security benefits and could not show continuous income sufficient to prevent the husband becoming a burden on public funds. No “exceptionally serious grounds” justified a derogation. The Service found the husband’s explanations for delay (attempts at the Kampala honorary consulate, which does not process residence permits, and passport difficulties) unconvincing; passport stamps indicated prior travel to Kenya and Eritrea, he was healthy, had refugee status and a support network in Uganda, and had been settled there for years. Children’s best-interests considerations did not require the father’s admission: they lived with their mother, the eldest had never had a relationship with him, the youngest was born after the father left Eritrea, and contact had been limited to telephone.

The Administrative Court dismissed the subsequent appeal (6 September 2019). The late application was undisputed, income was insufficient, and delay reasons (financial/passport-related) plus unsubstantiated later-claimed health problems of the husband did not constitute exceptionally serious grounds. Possible provision of written instructions in Finnish was not decisive given the interpreter-assisted meetings. Children’s best interests required specific circumstances beyond mere interruption of family ties; the children were healthy and cared for by their mother. A minority would have referred the case back, viewing the income threshold as unrealistic given the applicant’s childcare responsibilities. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal (26 February 2020).

Applying the principles in *Dabo v. Sweden*, the ECtHR held there were no objectively excusable reasons for missing the three-month window. The applicant had received timely, adequate advice. The refusal was not irreversible (a fresh application invoking exceptional circumstances remained possible). A fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s family-life interests and the State’s legitimate interest in controlling immigration and public finances; Finland had not overstepped its wide margin of appreciation. No violation of Article 8 was found.

The case of S.F. v. Finland (Application no. 35276/20) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention arising from the Finnish authorities’ refusal of a family-reunification request by an acknowledged refugee. The applicant, an Eritrean national born in 1982, was granted asylum together with her three minor children (born 2003, 2008 and 2015) by decision of 27 October 2016, notified on 8 November 2016. Refugee status was recognised because of a well-founded fear of persecution for political opinions. The decision was accompanied by written information, in Finnish, explaining that a family member could obtain a residence permit without satisfying the statutory maintenance requirement if the application was lodged within three months of notification and the family had been formed before the sponsor’s arrival in Finland (Aliens Act, s. 114(4)).

In November 2016 and January 2017 the applicant discussed family reunification with a social worker, assisted by a Tigrinya interpreter. She was expressly told of the three-month time-limit and the consequences of missing it, and was given application forms, the contact details of the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi and information on on-line filing. Her husband, also Eritrean and a recognised refugee living in Kampala, Uganda, applied for a residence permit only on 30 January 2018 at the Nairobi Embassy—nearly fifteen months after the time-limit had expired. He presented a passport issued on 18 May 2017 and later explained that he had fled Eritrea in 2014 after leaving military service without permission.

By decision of 20 February 2019 the Finnish Immigration Service refused the application. The couple were found to be family members, but the applicant’s only income consisted of social-security benefits; she therefore failed to meet the maintenance requirement of EUR 2 900 per month (s. 39 of the Aliens Act). The three-month exemption did not apply. No derogation was granted: the husband’s difficulties in contacting the honorary consulate in Kampala, the need to travel to Nairobi, alleged financial obstacles and unsubstantiated health complaints (shortness of breath and fainting, first mentioned on appeal) did not constitute “exceptionally serious grounds.” Passport stamps indicated that he had been able to travel to Kenya (and possibly Eritrea) well before January 2018. The children lived with their mother; the eldest had never had a relationship with the father and the youngest had been born after the father’s departure. Telephone contact existed, but the children’s best interests did not require the grant of a permit.

The Administrative Court dismissed the subsequent appeal on 6 September 2019, holding that the delay was considerable, that the applicant had received timely advice (the language of the written information not being decisive) and that neither the husband’s health nor the children’s situation justified a derogation. Leave to appeal was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court on 26 February 2020. The European Court later applied the principles set out in Dabo v. Sweden, finding that the applicant had received adequate advice, that the reasons for the delay were not objectively excusable, that the refusal was not irreversible and that a fair balance had been struck within the State’s wide margin of appreciation.
001-235896:
The case of Melandri v. San Marino (Application no. 25189/21) concerns an Italian national’s complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a)–(b) of the Convention (fair trial rights in criminal proceedings) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) arising from his conviction for money laundering and the confiscation of assets.

In November 2012 the San Marino Financial Intelligence Agency reported suspicious transactions at a local bank. Between September 2009 and March 2010 the applicant deposited approximately €4.87 million in cash and €500,000 in cheques into a personal account. A company linked to him also transferred €310,000 to an account opened by L.C. for a wine firm. Italian press reports and subsequent letters rogatory revealed that the applicant and L.C. were under investigation in Italy (“Operation Baccus”) for organised-crime offences including money laundering, extortion, usury and large-scale tax fraud against the Italian State and the European Union, carried out through fictitious wine-sector invoices. The Italian Court of Appeal (later largely confirmed by the Court of Cassation) convicted the applicant of issuing false invoices and criminal association.

San Marino opened proceedings under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code. In November 2013 an investigating judge charged the applicant and L.C. with money laundering and ordered preventive seizure of a life-insurance policy (then worth some €6.8 million) into which the deposited funds had been channelled, together with other accounts and a safe-deposit box. Formal charges issued in December 2014 and an indictment of April 2015 particularised two counts: (i) transferring and concealing proceeds of false invoicing, tax fraud and EU scams by depositing more than €7.9 million, converting the money into investments and the insurance policy (conduct ending with seizure in December 2013); and (ii) similar transfers of €310,000 together with L.C.

At trial the applicant, represented by counsel, argued that the funds’ illicit origin had not been proved and that “self-laundering” (laundering one’s own proceeds) became an offence only with a 2013 amendment that post-dated his acts. The first-instance court convicted him solely of the post-29 July 2013 conduct, imposing four years and six months’ imprisonment and ordering confiscation of the seized assets and accrued interest under Article 147 of the Criminal Code. It relied on circumstantial evidence: the applicant’s history of economic crime generating millions of euros, the implausibility of a legitimate source for large cash deposits, and the Italian findings of false invoicing.

On appeal the applicant reiterated that the money originated from lawful VAT refunds and that self-laundering was not punishable at the material time. The appeal court upheld the first charge, holding that Law 99/2010 had already removed the self-laundering exemption for the predicate offence of issuing false invoices; the relevant transfers therefore occurred after that law (March–December 2011). It found the funds to be profits of tax fraud and false invoicing, acquitted the applicant of the second charge, reduced the sentence to four years and three months and confirmed confiscation. In December 2020 an enforcement judge transferred the assets (including the insurance policy) to the San Marino treasury.

The complaints therefore centred on alleged defects in the formulation and notification of the charges (particularly the legal characterisation of self-laundering and the applicable dates), the fairness of the assessment of illicit origin, and the proportionality and procedural regularity of the confiscation of several million euros as proceeds of crime.

The case of Melandri v. San Marino (Application no. 25189/21) concerns an Italian national's complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a)–(b) of the ECHR regarding the fairness of San Marino criminal proceedings for money laundering, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 regarding the subsequent confiscation of his assets.

In November 2012, San Marino’s Financial Intelligence Agency (FIA) reported suspicious transactions by the applicant and L.C. at a local bank. Between September 2009 and March 2010 the applicant deposited approximately €4.87 million in cash plus €500,000 in cheques into his personal account. L.C., introduced by the applicant, opened an account for company O. (of which L.C. was sole director) that received €310,000 from the applicant’s company A.G. in late 2010. Italian press reports linked both men to “Operation Baccus,” an investigation by the Bari Anti-Mafia Directorate into a criminal association that used fictitious wine-sector transactions (false invoices for non-existent supplies of must) to launder proceeds, evade Italian taxes and obtain undue EU benefits. The applicant was charged in Italy (proceedings no. 14219/09) with money laundering, extortion, usury and fraud.

San Marino opened proceedings no. 865/2012 and obtained Italian documentation via letters rogatory. The Italian Court of Appeal (later largely confirmed by the Court of Cassation) had convicted the applicant of issuing false invoices and criminal association; other counts were time-barred or unproven. On 22 November 2013 the Investigating Judge charged the applicant and L.C. with money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code and ordered preventive seizure of a single-premium life-insurance policy (then worth roughly €6.8 million) plus other accounts. A safe-deposit box was later seized. Formal charges were notified on 9 December 2014; the applicant was questioned in March 2015. The April 2015 indictment alleged that the applicant, acting continuously, had transferred and concealed proceeds of predicate offences (false invoicing, tax fraud and EU scams) by depositing more than €7.9 million, converting funds into movable property and the insurance policy (last movements December 2011), and that he had jointly transferred €310,000 with L.C.

At trial the applicant, represented by counsel, argued that the funds’ illicit origin was unproven and that self-laundering only became an offence under Law no. 100/2013 (in force 29 July 2013), after the relevant acts. The first-instance judge (10 January 2019) convicted him solely of post-July 2013 conduct, treating the offence as continuous until seizure, and imposed four years and six months’ imprisonment plus mandatory confiscation of the seized assets and accrued interest under Article 147 of the Criminal Code. The court relied on “logical evidence”: the applicant’s long involvement in organised economic crime generating millions, the timing and cash nature of the San Marino deposits (incompatible with lawful activity), and the disproof of his business explanations.

On appeal the applicant again contested the link to Italian predicate offences (claiming the money came from legitimate VAT refunds) and the temporal application of self-laundering. The Judge of Appeal (6 November 2020) upheld conviction on the first charge but recharacterised it as self-laundering already prosecutable under Law no. 99/2010, which had removed the self-laundering exception for false-invoice predicates. The offence was dated from 10 March 2011 (policy opening) to 27 December 2011. The second charge was quashed because the €310,000 constituted means rather than proceeds. The sentence was reduced to four years and three months; confiscation was confirmed. On 10 December 2020 the Enforcement Judge transferred the assets (including the policy) to the State treasury.

Article 147 made confiscation of instrumentalities, proceeds or equivalent value mandatory upon conviction for money laundering, even when mixed with legitimate assets or held through intermediaries. Article 199 bis originally exempted the author of the predicate offence; that exemption was limited by Law no. 99/2010 for false invoicing and wholly removed in 2013.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: the applicant claimed insufficient notice of the precise legal characterisation (self-laundering versus ordinary laundering) and inadequate time to prepare a defence, as well as a disproportionate interference with property through confiscation of sums he could not recover.

The case of Melandri v. San Marino (Application no. 25189/21) arose from criminal proceedings in San Marino against Italian national Vincenzo Secondo Melandri for money laundering, culminating in the confiscation of substantial assets. In late 2012, San Marino’s Financial Intelligence Agency flagged suspicious transactions involving the applicant and associate L.C. at a local bank. Between September 2009 and March 2010, the applicant deposited €4,865,830 in cash plus approximately €500,000 in cheques into his personal account. L.C., introduced by the applicant, opened an account for wine company O. (of which he was sole director), which received €310,000 from company A.G. (traceable to the applicant) in late 2010.

These activities coincided with Italian investigations under “Operation Baccus,” in which the applicant and others faced charges of money laundering, conspiracy to commit extortion, usury, and fraud against Italian tax authorities and the EU through fictitious wine-sector operations. Italian authorities informed San Marino that the deposited sums were incompatible with the applicant’s legitimate savings and stemmed from organised-crime activities, including false invoicing that generated illicit proceeds and undue tax benefits. In 2013, the Bari Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of issuing false invoices and criminal association (largely confirmed by the Court of Cassation).

San Marino opened proceedings (no. 865/2012). In November 2013 the Investigating Judge charged the applicant and L.C. with money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code and ordered preventive seizure of a life-insurance policy (valued at roughly €6.8 million after transfers of securities and cash), a small bank account, and any other assets traceable to the applicant. A later seizure targeted a safe-deposit box. Formal notification of charges occurred in December 2014; questioning followed in March 2015. The April 2015 indictment specified two counts: (i) transferring and concealing proceeds of predicate offences (false invoicing, treasury fraud, and EU scams) via large cash/cheque deposits, subsequent investments, withdrawals, and the insurance policy (conduct ending with the 2013 seizure); and (ii) jointly transferring €310,000 of similarly illicit funds through company O.

At trial the applicant, represented by counsel, contended that the funds’ illicit origin had not been proved and that self-laundering (laundering one’s own proceeds) only became an offence under 2013 legislation enacted after the impugned acts. The first-instance court convicted him in January 2019 of continuous money-laundering offences but limited liability to acts after the 2013 amendment; it imposed a sentence of four years and six months’ imprisonment and ordered confiscation of the seized assets (including accrued interest) pursuant to Article 147 of the Criminal Code. L.C. was acquitted.

On appeal the applicant reiterated that the sums reflected legitimate VAT refunds and business activity, that no link to the Italian offences existed, and that self-laundering had not been criminalised at the relevant time. In November 2020 the Judge of Appeal upheld guilt on the first count, re-characterising the conduct as self-laundering that was already prosecutable under a 2010 law excluding the “participation exception” for false-invoicing predicates. The court found the funds (or most of them) constituted personal profit from the applicant’s role in a criminal association that used false invoices to obtain tax advantages. It acquitted him of the second count (the transferred sums being instrumentalities rather than proceeds) and reduced the sentence to four years and three months. Confiscation was confirmed; an Enforcement Judge subsequently transferred the assets to the State treasury.

These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints of unfair trial (Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a)–(b))—particularly concerning the precision and timing of the charges, the evolving legal characterisation of self-laundering, and his ability to prepare a defence—and of a disproportionate interference with property (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) arising from the confiscation of assets treated as proceeds of crime.
