The case Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2) (Application no. 36013/13) concerns complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention by Moldovan national Serghei Cosovan (who died in 2021; his widow pursued the application). It arose from the special confiscation of money after criminal proceedings against him were discontinued as time-barred.

On 15 January 2007 a criminal investigation began against Cosovan for illegal commercial activity under Article 241 of the Criminal Code. As director of company V.G., he was suspected of operating an unauthorised public car park in Chișinău from April to November 2006 without paying taxes. Tax authorities calculated the proceeds at 116,428 MDL (approximately €7,080). V.G. had submitted no tax returns since December 2004 and was listed as a delinquent entity.

On 27 June 2011, at Cosovan’s request, the prosecutor discontinued the investigation because the limitation period had expired. The decision recited evidence (ten witness statements, site records and tax data) confirming the suspicion and stated that Cosovan had obtained the 116,428 MDL “as a result of the criminal offence” of illegal commercial activity. Invoking Article 285 § 6(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (allowing precautionary measures on discontinuance) and Article 106 of the Criminal Code, the prosecutor ordered special confiscation of an equivalent sum from Cosovan, as the proceeds themselves had not been seized.

Cosovan challenged only the confiscation. He argued he had never admitted guilt, his guilt had never been established by a court, he had received no explanation of the confiscation provision, and the measure could not be applied without a judicial finding of the offence and offender. A hierarchically superior prosecutor dismissed the appeal on 6 April 2012, repeating that the sum represented proceeds of crime. The prosecutor added that a request for discontinuance on limitation grounds constitutes a waiver of the right to have guilt proved and does not entail rehabilitation.

On 19 April 2012 Cosovan complained to the investigating judge, repeating that he had never been formally charged, had not admitted guilt, and that the language of the decisions implied guilt in breach of the presumption of innocence and fair-trial rights. The confiscation had already been enforced.

On 15 January 2013 the Buiucani District Court investigating judge dismissed the complaint. The court held that sufficient evidence existed, that Cosovan had been acknowledged as a suspect on 28 February 2008 (and had declined to make a statement), and that he had requested discontinuance. It reiterated that 116,428 MDL had been obtained “as a result of criminal offences” under Article 241. Cosovan had not contested those factual conclusions. Special confiscation, a precautionary measure under Article 98 of the Criminal Code, could be applied even without a criminal penalty when income derived from an act prohibited by the Criminal Code.

The Government later produced the complete investigation file, which included police reports on illegal car parks, a decision authorising Cosovan to administer V.G., ten witness statements (including staff confirming he collected all income and the company owner describing an informal transfer of control), and Cosovan’s own and his lawyer’s requests for discontinuance.

Under the Criminal Code then in force, special confiscation is classified as a precautionary measure (Article 98) whose purpose is to remove risks arising from prohibited acts. Article 106 permits the uncompensated transfer to the State of proceeds of an act prohibited by the Code (or their equivalent) and expressly provides that the measure “shall be applicable even if no criminal sanction was imposed on the perpetrator.”

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims that the confiscation procedure was unfair (Article 6 § 1) and that the wording of the prosecutorial and judicial decisions constituted an affirmation of guilt after proceedings had ended without conviction, thereby violating the presumption of innocence (Article 6 § 2).

The case of Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2) arose from the special confiscation of 116,428 Moldovan lei (approximately €7,080) from Serghei Cosovan after criminal proceedings against him were discontinued as time-barred. Cosovan, a Moldovan national born in 1971, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights of a breach of his right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. He died in 2021; his widow pursued the application.

On 15 January 2007 a criminal investigation was opened following municipal complaints. Cosovan, as director of company V.G., was suspected of operating an unauthorised public car park in Chișinău from April to November 2006 without State authorisation or tax payments. The tax authorities, relying on seized documents, calculated the park’s income at 116,428 lei. V.G. had submitted no tax returns since December 2004 and had been classified as a “delinquent” entity.

The investigation assembled ten witness statements (including from V.G.’s owner, who described an informal transfer of the company to Cosovan, and from five security staff who said Cosovan collected all receipts), site records, police reports, and tax correspondence. Cosovan was formally acknowledged as a suspect on 28 February 2008 and, in the presence of counsel, declined to make a statement. In October 2009 and June 2011 he (or his lawyer) requested discontinuance on limitation grounds.

On 27 June 2011 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation as time-barred. The decision nevertheless recorded that the 116,428 lei constituted income “obtained \ldots as a result of the criminal offence” of illegal commercial activity under Article 241 § 2 (e) and (f) of the Criminal Code. Invoking Articles 285 § 6(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and 98 and 106 of the Criminal Code, the prosecutor ordered special confiscation of an equivalent sum as a “precautionary measure” because the original cash had not been seized. The order was immediately enforced.

Cosovan challenged only the confiscation, arguing that he had never admitted guilt, that no court had established his guilt, that he had never been formally charged, and that the legal basis for confiscation had never been explained to him. A hierarchically superior prosecutor dismissed the appeal on 6 April 2012, stating that a request for time-bar discontinuance “indicates a waiver of the right to have guilt proved” and that such discontinuance does not confer rehabilitation.

On 19 April 2012 Cosovan complained to the investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court. He maintained that the prosecutor’s language amounted to a finding of guilt, violating the presumption of innocence, and that special confiscation could be imposed only after a judicial determination of both the offence and the offender. On 15 January 2013 the judge rejected the complaint. The court held that ample evidence confirmed the suspicion, that Cosovan had himself sought discontinuance, that he had not contested the factual findings concerning the origin of the money, and that Article 106 of the Criminal Code expressly permitted special confiscation even in the absence of a criminal sanction when assets derived from an act prohibited by the Criminal Code.

Domestic law characterises special confiscation as a precautionary, in-rem measure aimed at preventing the use of assets stemming from unlawful acts; it may be applied after discontinuance on non-rehabilitating grounds such as expiry of the limitation period and does not require a conviction. Cosovan contended that the wording of the prosecutor’s and court’s decisions nevertheless treated him as guilty of a criminal offence, thereby violating Article 6 § 2.

The case of Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2) concerns a Moldovan national, Serghei Cosovan (who died in 2021, with his wife pursuing the application), who alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the special confiscation of funds following the discontinuance of time-barred criminal proceedings against him.

On 15 January 2007, a criminal investigation was opened against the applicant for illegal commercial activity under Article 241 of the Criminal Code. As director of company V.G., he was suspected of operating an unauthorised public car park in Chișinău from April to November 2006 without State authorisation or tax payments. Tax authorities, using seized documents, calculated the park’s income at 116,428 Moldovan lei (approximately €7,080). V.G. had submitted no tax returns since December 2004 and was classified as a “delinquent” entity.

On 27 June 2011, at the applicant’s request, the prosecutor discontinued the investigation as time-barred under Article 275 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The decision recorded “sufficient evidence” of the offence, including ten witness statements, three on-site records of park activity, and tax authority confirmations of the income. It stated that the 116,428 lei constituted proceeds of the criminal offence of illegal commercial activity. Invoking Article 285 § 6(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 106 of the Criminal Code (special confiscation as a precautionary measure), the prosecutor ordered the applicant to pay an equivalent sum to the State, as the original proceeds had not been identified or seized. Special confiscation could apply even without a criminal penalty.

The applicant challenged only the confiscation, arguing that he had never admitted guilt, that no court had established his guilt, that he had not been formally acknowledged as a suspect or charged, and that the legal basis for confiscation had not been explained. A superior prosecutor dismissed the appeal on 6 April 2012, reiterating the evidence and stating that discontinuance on limitation grounds does not rehabilitate the person concerned and that requesting it waives the right to have guilt proved.

On 19 April 2012 the applicant applied to the investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court, alleging breaches of the right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. He contended that special confiscation required judicial establishment of both the offence and the offender, and that the confiscation (already enforced) was therefore unlawful.

On 15 January 2013 the investigating judge dismissed the complaint. The court held that the evidence confirmed the suspicion and that the income had been obtained through the prohibited acts. It noted that the applicant had been formally acknowledged as a suspect on 28 February 2008 (in the presence of a lawyer) and had himself requested discontinuance. Special confiscation, being a precautionary measure directed at property rather than a penalty, could be imposed even without a criminal sanction when income derived from an act prohibited by the Criminal Code. The applicant had not contested the prosecutor’s factual findings.

The criminal file contained additional material, including police and municipal reports on illegal car parks, a company authorisation for the applicant to act as administrator, witness statements (including from the company owner and security staff confirming that the applicant received all income), and the applicant’s own requests for discontinuance.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the authorities’ statements linking him to a criminal offence and its proceeds, despite the absence of a conviction, violated the presumption of innocence and the fairness of proceedings under Article 6.
001-236192:
The case of S.M. v. Italy involves an Italian national (born 1977) with HIV infection and related conditions including Kaposi sarcoma, HIV-related encephalopathy, chronic HCV hepatopathy, and a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. He exhibited progressive neurological deterioration, severe cognitive deficit, impaired mobility, and required assistance for daily tasks. Antiretroviral treatment had been prescribed since 2008, with eventual good compliance and immune response.

Convicted of offenses including theft, fraud, drug trafficking, weapons possession, forgery, and tax evasion (committed 1998–2015), he received a sentence exceeding 11 years and had been detained since 2010. Due to his health, he received multiple grants of house arrest, which were repeatedly suspended or revoked owing to his non-compliance. In 2015, house arrest at a residential unit was revoked after he left without authorization. It was then granted at his sister’s home but later suspended when she withdrew consent. Reinstated at his brother’s residence in 2018, it was again suspended in September 2019 after police found him unlawfully occupying an apartment in poor conditions. House arrest was reinstated in a disability residential unit, but he repeatedly escaped and, in one incident, accosted a woman and kissed a minor on the cheek. The unit withdrew consent, leading to his redetention in Milan’s San Vittore Prison on 22 November 2019.

On 23 December 2019, the Milan Supervisory Court confirmed detention and revoked house arrest. It found that his claimed AIDS diagnosis lacked supporting documentation and that a February 2018 medical report indicated a good immune response, so conditions for compulsory penalty deferral (Article 146 Criminal Code) were unmet. While noting repeated rule breaches and ongoing dangerousness (largely attributable to cognitive deficit), the court requested prison medical services to reassess health compatibility with detention and seek alternative facilities if needed. A 10 January 2020 certificate confirmed the cognitive deficit, limited autonomy (with an assigned carer), regular antiretroviral treatment, virologist monitoring, and scheduled specialist exams.

The COVID-19 pandemic emerged shortly thereafter: WHO declared a public health emergency on 30 January 2020 (pandemic on 11 March), Italy declared a national emergency on 31 January, and cases appeared in Lombardy in February. On 15 March 2020, presidents of Milan and Brescia Supervisory Courts wrote to the Justice Ministry highlighting severe regional prison overcrowding (preventing adequate COVID precautions), recent riots (including at San Vittore), and the need to reduce the prison population.

On 17 March 2020, the applicant urgently requested the Milan Supervisory Judge replace prison detention with house arrest, citing his health and COVID-19 risks (relying on Prison Administration Act provisions or emergency Decree-Law no. 18/2020). This was rejected on 23 March 2020 because he lacked a suitable residence, residential units were not accepting detainees amid the emergency, and release would leave him homeless without medical access. The judge directed the prison administration to seek accommodation and referred the matter to the Supervisory Court. Hearings were postponed due to COVID-related organizational issues.

The applicant also sought an ECHR interim measure on 25 March 2020 for transfer to an appropriate facility (rejected the next day). On 28 July 2020, after accommodation was identified with prison medical support, he renewed his house-arrest request based on severe physical/cognitive issues previously deemed incompatible with detention and his need for constant assistance. This was granted on 29 July 2020, and he was transferred to a Varese residential unit. He completed his sentence on 20 July 2021.

These facts underpin the alleged incompatibility of his health with prison detention (22 November 2019–29 July 2020) and insufficient COVID-19 protections, particularly given his vulnerabilities, prison overcrowding, and delays in domestic proceedings amid the pandemic outbreak.

The case of S.M. v. Italy (Application no. 16310/20) before the European Court of Human Rights addresses the applicant’s complaints under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. These concerned the alleged incompatibility of his serious health conditions with continued detention in prison from 22 November 2019 until 29 July 2020, as well as insufficient protective measures against the risk of contracting COVID-19 during the early stages of the pandemic.

The applicant, an Italian national born in 1977, had longstanding HIV infection with related conditions including Kaposi sarcoma, HIV-related encephalopathy, chronic HCV-related hepatopathy, and a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. He suffered progressive neurological deterioration, severe cognitive deficit, impaired mobility, and required assistance with daily tasks. Antiretroviral treatment, prescribed since 2008, later produced a good immune response after initial poor compliance.

He had been convicted of multiple offences (theft, fraud, drug-related crimes, weapons possession, forgery and tax evasion) committed between 1998 and 2015, resulting in a sentence exceeding 11 years. Although detained since 2010, he received several grants of house arrest due to his health. These measures were repeatedly suspended or revoked after he left authorised locations without permission, occupied an apartment unlawfully in poor sanitary conditions, or engaged in problematic conduct (including escaping a residential unit and accosting a woman and a minor). On 22 November 2019, following withdrawal of consent by a disability residential unit, he was returned to Milan’s San Vittore Prison.

On 23 December 2019 the Milan Supervisory Court confirmed his detention, observing that an AIDS diagnosis lacked supporting documentation and that a 2018 medical report indicated a good immune response, so the conditions for compulsory sentence deferral under Article 146 of the Criminal Code were unmet. It invited prison medical services to reassess compatibility with detention and seek alternative facilities if needed. A 10 January 2020 medical certificate confirmed ongoing cognitive deficits, limited autonomy (with a carer assigned), regular antiretroviral treatment and specialist monitoring.

COVID-19 was declared a public health emergency by the WHO in January 2020 and a pandemic in March; Italy declared a national emergency. Prisons faced overcrowding (121% occupancy in February 2020) and riots, including at San Vittore. On 17 March 2020 the applicant urgently requested replacement of detention with house arrest, citing his health and COVID-19 risks, relying on domestic provisions allowing such measures for serious illness. The Supervisory Judge rejected this on 23 March 2020, noting the absence of a suitable residence (residential units were not accepting detainees) and the risk that release would leave him homeless without medical care. Prison authorities were directed to seek accommodation. The European Court rejected an accompanying Rule 39 interim-measure request. Hearings were postponed due to organisational difficulties.

On 28 July 2020, after suitable accommodation was identified with prison medical support, the applicant renewed his request. It was granted the following day and he was transferred to a residential unit. He completed his sentence in July 2021.

Relevant domestic law permitted compulsory or optional deferral of sentence execution (Articles 146–147 Criminal Code) or substitution with house arrest (section 47 ter of the Prison Administration Act) for serious illness, particularly AIDS or conditions incompatible with detention. Emergency COVID-19 decrees facilitated house arrest for certain detainees with short remaining sentences, but only where suitable housing existed, and imposed prison screening, isolation and contact restrictions.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: that detention of a highly vulnerable, disabled detainee with multiple HIV-related conditions, amid a novel pandemic and overcrowding, without adequate alternatives, constituted inhuman or degrading treatment and insufficient protection of life and health.

The applicant, an Italian national born in 1977, has suffered since at least 2014 from HIV infection and multiple related conditions, including Kaposi sarcoma, HIV-related encephalopathy, chronic HCV-related hepatopathy, and a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. These have caused progressive neurological deterioration, a severe cognitive deficit, impaired mobility, and a need for assistance with daily tasks. He has received antiretroviral treatment since 2008, with initially poor but later improved compliance and a good immune response.

Convicted of various offences (theft, fraud, drug offences, weapons possession, forgery and tax evasion) committed between 1998 and 2015, he received a sentence exceeding 11 years and has been detained since 2010. Owing to his health, the Milan supervisory authorities repeatedly granted house arrest (under Articles 146–148 of the Criminal Code and section 47-ter of the Prison Administration Act), to be served at family members’ homes or residential units for persons with disabilities. These measures were frequently revoked after the applicant absconded, occupied premises unlawfully, lived in unsanitary conditions, or engaged in problematic behaviour (including accosting a woman and a minor). On 22 November 2019, after a residential unit withdrew consent, he was redetained at Milan’s overcrowded San Vittore Prison. On 23 December 2019 the Supervisory Court confirmed detention, observing that an AIDS diagnosis was undocumented, that he had a good immune response (so compulsory deferral was unavailable), and that his conduct remained dangerous albeit largely attributable to cognitive impairment; it invited a medical reassessment and a search for alternative accommodation.

A January 2020 medical certificate confirmed ongoing cognitive and mobility limitations, assignment of a carer, regular antiretroviral treatment and specialist monitoring. After the COVID-19 outbreak (WHO public-health emergency on 30 January 2020, pandemic declaration on 11 March, Italian national emergency from 31 January), the applicant, on 17 March 2020, urgently sought house arrest citing his vulnerability and the virus risk. The Supervisory Judge refused on 23 March because no suitable residence existed and residential units were not accepting detainees; release would leave him homeless and without treatment. The prison administration was instructed to locate accommodation. Hearings before the Supervisory Court were postponed owing to organisational difficulties. An application to the European Court for an interim transfer was refused on 26 March.

A further request of 28 July 2020, after accommodation had been identified, was granted the next day and the applicant was transferred to a Varese residential unit. He completed his sentence on 20 July 2021. Throughout the relevant period he continued to receive antiretroviral therapy, specialist care and daily assistance in prison, with no documented deterioration in his condition.

The complaints (under Articles 2 and 3) alleged that continued detention from 22 November 2019 to 29 July 2020 was incompatible with his health and that insufficient steps were taken to protect him, as a vulnerable disabled detainee, from COVID-19. The Court examined the facts against the background of the novel pandemic, prison overcrowding, and the authorities’ search for alternatives.
001-237295:
**CASE OF CESARANO v. ITALY (Application no. 71250/16, ECtHR, 17 October 2024)**

The applicant, Ferdinando Cesarano (born 1954), an Italian national serving a life sentence, alleged violations of Article 7 (no punishment without law, specifically the principle of the more lenient penalty) and Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core issue was the Italian courts’ refusal to reduce his life sentence to 30 years’ imprisonment despite his later choice of the summary procedure, unlike the situation in *Scoppola v. Italy (no. 2)*.

In 1995, the applicant was committed for trial with co-defendants on charges of mass murder (*strage*) and murder committed in 1983. These offences were then punishable by life imprisonment with daytime isolation. At that time, defendants facing life sentences were ineligible for the summary procedure (a simplified process based on the existing case file, normally reducing any sentence by one-third upon conviction). Law no. 479 of 16 December 1999 (in force from 2 January 2000) reintroduced eligibility for such defendants and amended Article 442 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to replace life imprisonment with 30 years’ imprisonment following a summary-procedure conviction.

A transitional provision (section 4-ter of Decree-Law no. 82/2000, converted into Law no. 144/2000, in force 8 June 2000) allowed eligible defendants in ongoing cases with evidentiary hearings still pending to request the summary procedure at their next hearing. The applicant’s first-instance proceedings were then pending with hearings ongoing, so he could have requested the procedure and potentially obtained a 30-year sentence. He did not do so (unlike some co-defendants). On 24 November 2000, Decree-Law no. 341/2000 entered into force. It “authentically interpreted” the 1999 law so that “life imprisonment” meant life without daytime isolation (eligible for reduction to 30 years), while life *with* daytime isolation (the applicant’s situation) would, after a summary-procedure conviction, become only life without isolation.

The applicant was convicted under the ordinary procedure by the Naples Assize Court on 25 October 2007. While his appeal was pending, the Grand Chamber delivered *Scoppola* (17 September 2009), finding a violation of Articles 7 and 6 § 1 where a defendant who had requested the summary procedure *while the 1999 law was in force* was later given life imprisonment instead of 30 years. On 19 February 2010 the Naples Assize Court of Appeal quashed the applicant’s conviction and remitted the case. He was recommitted for trial in 2012 on the same charges. At a preliminary hearing on 2 October 2012 he requested the summary procedure (now governed by the 2000 Decree-Law).

The Rome preliminary hearings judge convicted him on 26 September 2013 and imposed life imprisonment without daytime isolation, citing aggravating circumstances, the gravity of the offences, and his prior record. The judge rejected a request for reduction to 30 years, distinguishing *Scoppola* because the applicant had neither requested nor been granted the summary procedure while the 1999 law was in force. Subsequent appeals to the Rome Assize Court of Appeal (4 November 2014) and Court of Cassation (judgment of 7 January 2016, deposited 24 June 2016) were unsuccessful. Domestic courts, relying on consistent Court of Cassation case-law (especially the plenary *Giannone* judgment of 2012), held that the relevant period for identifying the *lex mitior* in summary-procedure cases ran from the date of the request (not from the offence to final judgment). The 1999 law’s 30-year reduction therefore did not apply. The Constitutional Court had already declared the 2000 Decree-Law unconstitutional only insofar as it applied retroactively to cases like *Scoppola* (judgment no. 210 of 2013), not to later requests.

The applicant argued that the most lenient law in force between the 1983 offences and his final conviction (the 1999 law) should have been applied, and that he had a legitimate expectation of a 30-year sentence. The domestic courts treated the date of his 2012 request as decisive and found no such entitlement or frustrated expectation. The ECtHR later examined whether this approach complied with Articles 7 and 6 § 1.

The case of Cesarano v. Italy (Application no. 71250/16) concerns an Italian national serving a life sentence who alleged violations of Articles 7 and 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant’s first-instance trial was then pending and he could have requested the summary procedure (as some co-defendants did), but he did not. In February 2010 the Naples Assize Court of Appeal quashed the applicant’s conviction and remitted the case. He was recommitted for trial in May 2012 and, at a preliminary hearing on 2 October 2012, requested the summary procedure.

The Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s further appeal inadmissible on 7 January 2016, confirming that the relevant legal framework was that in force when the request was made (the 2000 Decree-Law) and that the fact that proceedings remained pending was irrelevant.

The applicant argued that Article 7 required application of the most lenient law in force between commission of the offences and final judgment (the 30-year term under the 1999 law) and that Article 6 § 1 had been breached by frustration of a legitimate expectation of that term. Domestic courts, relying on Court of Cassation plenary judgments (notably Giannone, 2012), held that, because the summary procedure depends on the defendant’s request, the relevant period for identifying the lex mitior runs from the date of that request rather than from the date of the offence. **Case Summary: Cesarano v. Italy (Application no. 71250/16)**

This ECHR judgment (17 October 2024, final 17 March 2025) addresses alleged violations of Article 7 (no heavier penalty) and Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) of the Convention. The applicant, Ferdinando Cesarano (born 1954), an Italian serving a life sentence, claimed domestic courts wrongly refused to reduce his sentence from life imprisonment to 30 years after he opted for a summary (abbreviated) trial procedure. Unlike the leading case of *Scoppola v. Italy (no. 2)* (2009), he requested the procedure after a 2000 legislative change that replaced the 30-year option with life imprisonment without daytime isolation for the most serious cases.

The offences—mass murder (*strage*) and murder—occurred in 1983 and were then punishable by life imprisonment *with* daytime isolation. The applicant was committed for trial in 1995 alongside co-defendants. At that time, Italian law barred those facing life sentences from the summary procedure (Articles 438 and 441–443 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). This simplified process allows a case to be decided on the existing file at a private preliminary hearing, with a one-third sentence reduction on conviction (and limited appeal rights). The defendant waives certain ordinary-trial safeguards in exchange for speed and the reduction.

Law no. 479 of 16 December 1999 (in force 2 January 2000) restored access to the summary procedure for life-sentence cases. Article 442 § 2 CCP was amended so that “life imprisonment shall be replaced by thirty years’ imprisonment.” A June 2000 decree further allowed such requests at the next hearing if evidentiary hearings remained ongoing (as they were in the applicant’s first-instance proceedings). Some co-defendants requested and received the procedure; the applicant did not.

Decree-Law no. 341 of 24 November 2000 (converted into law in 2001) then provided an “authentic interpretation”: “life imprisonment” in the 1999 law meant only life *without* daytime isolation. For cases like the applicant’s (life *with* isolation, often due to cumulative or continuous offences), the reduction became merely life imprisonment without isolation. The applicant was convicted in 2007 under the ordinary procedure (exact penalty unclear from the file).

After *Scoppola*—in which the ECHR held that a defendant who requested the summary procedure while the 1999 law was in force was entitled to the 30-year sentence under the principle of the more lenient subsequent law (*lex mitior*), and that frustration of that legitimate expectation also breached Article 6—the applicant’s conviction was quashed in 2010 and the case remitted. He was recommitted for trial in 2012 on the same charges and formally requested the summary procedure on 2 October 2012.

In July 2013 the Italian Constitutional Court (judgment no. 210) declared the 2000 decree unconstitutional insofar as it retrospectively deprived defendants who had already requested the procedure under the 1999 law of the 30-year benefit. It did not, however, invalidate the new regime for later requests. On 26 September 2013 the Rome preliminary-hearings judge convicted the applicant after a summary trial and imposed life imprisonment without daytime isolation. The judge rejected a request for 30 years, holding (in line with Court of Cassation plenary judgment *Giannone*, 2012) that the applicant’s situation was distinguishable from *Scoppola*: he had neither requested nor been granted the procedure while the 1999 law was in force. Aggravating factors (premeditation, multiple victims, the applicant’s extensive prior criminal record including more than 40 murders and mafia offences) were also cited.

The Rome Assize Court of Appeal (2014) and Court of Cassation (judgment no. 26519, 2016) upheld the conviction and sentence. They confirmed that, for summary-procedure cases, the relevant legal framework is that in force when the request is made, not an abstract survey of every law between the offence and final judgment. Because the 2000 decree applied at the time of the 2012 request, the applicant had no entitlement to 30 years and no frustrated legitimate expectation.

The applicant argued that *Scoppola* required application of the single most lenient law in force at any point from 1983 until the final 2016 judgment, and that the courts’ approach violated both the *lex mitior* principle and fair-trial guarantees. The ECHR examined whether the temporal scope of *lex mitior* analysis is abstract or is instead tied to the defendant’s procedural choice and the moment of agreement with the State. The original offences carried the heavier penalty of life with isolation; after the summary procedure the applicant received the comparatively more lenient penalty of life without isolation. The request itself constituted an unequivocal waiver of certain procedural rights in exchange for known advantages under the law then in force. The penalty actually imposed was therefore foreseeable and did not constitute a heavier penalty or an unfair surprise.
001-237706:
The case of Harutyun Karapetyan v. Armenia (ECtHR, 2024) concerns the alleged lack of an effective investigation into the death of the applicant’s wife, T. Simonyan, following surgery, raising issues under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention.

In March 2011, 53-year-old T. Simonyan visited a Yerevan hospital with uterine problems and was diagnosed with a myoma. Doctor G.O. recommended prompt hysterectomy, which she underwent on 22 March 2011. Her prior records noted thrombophlebitis (2007), varicose veins, and venous insufficiency (2010). On 23 March she reported acute pain and died around midday from pulmonary thromboembolism linked to her varicose veins and phlebothrombosis.

Police were notified the same day and ordered an autopsy, performed on 24 March 2011. It confirmed the cause of death but left questions of negligence and the possibility of avoiding the outcome outside its scope. Informal statements were taken from staff. Head of gynaecology S.K. and anaesthetist S.E. both described a pre-operative examination revealing varicose veins, with a decision to apply elastic bandages; S.E. also mentioned a Fraxiparine (anticoagulant) injection. Other staff corroborated prophylaxis and unsuccessful resuscitation. Hospital records contained a Fraxiparine entry in different ink, with no matching prescription note.

An initial expert commission concluded that injections (including Fraxiparine) had been given, the hysterectomy was indicated, varicose veins had been diagnosed pre-operatively without signs of thrombosis, and prophylaxis had been adequate; thromboembolism carried a high mortality risk regardless. The investigator refused to open a case on 5 August 2011.

The applicant appealed. On 6 September 2011 the prosecutor instituted proceedings under former Criminal Code Article 130 § 2 (negligent medical duty causing death), citing incomplete inquiry, conflicting accounts of Fraxiparine, possible later record entries, and unanswered questions about surgical suitability.

The applicant was granted victim status. Further document examinations of records and the anaesthetic register noted possible ink differences and an alteration (figure “1” overwritten as “2”). Re-questioning of nurses and doctors produced consistent accounts that one Fraxiparine dose was given pre-operatively on 22 March and a second on 23 March; discrepancies were explained as reflecting actual use. Additional medical expert reports (including answers to the applicant’s questions) reiterated that prophylaxis had been indicated and implemented, varicose veins did not contraindicate surgery, and thrombosis likely formed intra- or post-operatively. Expert G.B., whose newspaper interview suggested treating varicose veins first, confirmed when questioned that no such complications existed in this case.

The case of Harutyun Karapetyan v. Armenia (Application no. 53081/14) concerns the alleged lack of an effective investigation into the death of the applicant’s wife from medical negligence, raising issues under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention.

Doctor G.O. recommended prompt hysterectomy. Simonyan’s records (provided later) noted 2007 thrombophlebitis, 2010 varicose veins in the lower extremities and Doppler ultrasound evidence of venous insufficiency. Surgery proceeded on 22 March 2011. The following morning she complained of acute pain; she died around midday. Autopsy on 24 March established pulmonary thromboembolism secondary to varicose veins and shank-vessel thrombosis as the cause of death.

The hospital notified police the same day. An inquiry collected informal statements from staff. Gynaecology head S.K. and anaesthetist S.E. described pre-operative examination revealing visible varicosity; they stated legs were wrapped in elastic bandages and (according to S.E.) Fraxiparine anticoagulant was administered. Head of anaesthesia S.Ba. similarly recalled prophylactic measures. Hospital records contained conflicting or later-appearing entries on Fraxiparine prescription and use; the colour of ink differed and the medication register was later altered from “1” to “2” doses.

On 5 August 2011 the investigator refused to open a criminal case, finding no offence. The Yerevan prosecutor’s office quashed that decision on 6 September, citing incomplete examination of contradictions about Fraxiparine administration, possible document falsification, and failure of the first expert commission to address whether hysterectomy was contraindicated given the varicose veins. Proceedings were instituted under Article 130 § 2 of the former Criminal Code (negligent medical performance causing death). The applicant was granted victim-heir status.

Thereafter three forensic-document examinations were ordered. They could not conclusively establish whether Fraxiparine entries were contemporaneous or later additions, though one confirmed an alteration in the anaesthetic-medication register. Three successive expert-commission reports (November 2011, July 2012 and related addenda) concluded that pre-operative assessment had correctly identified thromboembolism risk, that compression and anticoagulant prophylaxis had been indicated and recorded as given, that hysterectomy was justified by age, pain and anaemia, that varicose veins without active phlebothrombosis were not a contraindication, and that thromboembolism carries a high mortality even with prophylaxis. Staff (including nurses who claimed to have injected Fraxiparine on 22 and 23 March) were re-questioned and a confrontation held with an expert. Doctor G.B., who had headed one commission, was examined after a newspaper interview in which he appeared to criticise operating in the presence of varicose veins; he distinguished the general remark from Simonyan’s asymptomatic presentation.

The applicant’s complaint that he had been denied full access to the file and that contradictions (timing of thrombus formation, G.B.’s statements, document alterations) remained unresolved was rejected by the District Court (12 September 2013) and Court of Appeal (11 November 2013). The Court of Cassation declared his further appeal inadmissible on 16 January 2014.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 2 procedural violation: initial inquiry deficiencies, unresolved contradictions in medical records and witness accounts, and the subsequent termination of proceedings without, in the applicant’s view, fully clarifying the events surrounding his wife’s death.

The case of Harutyun Karapetyan v. Armenia (no. 53081/14) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 2 of the Convention of an ineffective investigation into his wife T. Simonyan’s death after hysterectomy, allegedly due to medical negligence.

In March 2011, 53-year-old Simonyan was diagnosed with uterine myoma at a Yerevan hospital. Surgery was recommended as non-complex but urgent. Her records noted 2007 thrombophlebitis and 2010 varicose veins with venous insufficiency. Hysterectomy occurred on 22 March 2011. She died the next day of pulmonary thromboembolism from varicose veins and phlebothrombosis.

Police ordered an autopsy, which confirmed the cause but left negligence questions unaddressed. Informal staff statements revealed discrepancies: some mentioned prophylactic Fraxiparine (anticoagulant) and elastic bandages; others omitted the drug. Records showed possible later entries in different ink, absent from prescriptions.

An August 2011 refusal to open proceedings was overturned in September. Prosecutors cited incomplete inquiry, conflicts over Fraxiparine, and unanswered questions on surgery suitability given varicose veins. Proceedings began under former Criminal Code Article 130 § 2 (negligent medical duties causing death). The applicant was recognised as victim’s heir.

Multiple forensic medical commissions generally found pre-operative exams adequate, surgery indicated, Fraxiparine and compression given (though not guaranteeing safety), no pre-surgery phlebothrombosis (thus no contraindication), and death a high-mortality complication. Document examinations noted possible ink differences and a register alteration (1 to 2 doses). Staff (doctors, nurses) later confirmed administration; one explained the register change as updating actual use. An expert’s newspaper remark implying varicose veins should be treated first was clarified as general and inapplicable here (no complications present). A confrontation addressed thrombus timing as likely intra- or post-operative.

Proceedings terminated in March 2013: no medical errors or record falsification. Domestic courts (District Court September 2013; Court of Appeal November 2013; Cassation January 2014) upheld this, finding expert reports complementary/supplementary, personnel questioned, and issues (including the interview) resolved. The applicant’s access to the file was delayed but not ultimately prejudicial.

The Court held that, despite initial inquiry shortcomings (informal statements, incomplete analysis), authorities later conducted a thorough response with experts, questioning, and forensics that adequately clarified events. No Article 2 procedural violation.

The case of Winther v. Denmark (Application no. 9588/21) concerns a Syrian national’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that a criminal expulsion order with a six-year re-entry ban interfered disproportionately with his private and family life in Denmark.

In November 2018 he committed several offences: jointly with others, he participated in a planned aggravated assault involving beating and kicking a victim (including while the victim was prostrate) with a bat and bottle; blackmail and attempted duress linked to debt collection; possession of cannabis (partly for distribution); and importation of forged banknotes. It balanced the seriousness of the offences against his short residence, limited Danish ties (a Danish girlfriend expecting twins, some language skills, two aunts, and education) and stronger Syrian ties (birth, upbringing, language and family origins). Expulsion was held proportionate for crime prevention and not contrary to Denmark’s international obligations.

By then the applicant’s twins had been born prematurely (one with health issues); after release from remand he lived with his Danish partner and children, completed education and obtained work. The partner and children (Danish nationals) would not relocate to Syria. The High Court found the new family circumstances insufficient to alter the proportionality assessment.

The Supreme Court (August 2020) increased the sentence to eight months but confirmed expulsion. It noted lawful residence of approximately three years and nine months. Applying Article 8 criteria (including Maslov v. Austria), it found strong Syrian ties and only limited Danish ties (short cohabitation with the partner from 2018, young children, modest integration). The offences were planned, joint and serious rather than spontaneous. Although expulsion would separate the applicant from his partner and infant children—an interference with family life—the short duration of that family life, the children’s young age, possibilities of visits/communication and the time-limited ban rendered the measure proportionate. The domestic courts thus examined the nature and gravity of the offences, the length of lawful residence, the applicant’s ties to Denmark and Syria, and the impact on his newly formed family, concluding that the expulsion and six-year ban struck a fair balance under Article 8.

The case of Winther v. Denmark (Application no. 9588/21) concerns a Syrian national’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his expulsion from Denmark, together with a six-year re-entry ban, violated his right to respect for private and family life.

The three offences formed part of planned debt-collection activities on behalf of a third party. He was also convicted of possessing 2.44 g of cannabis for personal use and 5.94 g for distribution, and of importing 91 forged 100-euro notes. He received a seven-month prison sentence and was ordered expelled with a six-year re-entry ban.

It noted that he had arrived as an adult, had only limited residence, spoke some Danish, was attending adult education and had two aunts in Denmark, and that his Danish girlfriend was expecting twins. It also recorded that he had been born and raised in Syria, spoke and wrote Arabic, and that his family had fled that country. The case of Winther v. Denmark (no. 9588/21) concerns a Syrian national’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that an expulsion order with a six-year re-entry ban, imposed after his conviction for serious offences, disproportionately interfered with his private and family life in Denmark.

Born in Syria in 1994, the applicant entered Denmark in September 2014 at age 20 and sought asylum. He received a time-limited refugee residence permit on 6 February 2015 (valid until 6 February 2020). On 1 March 2019 the Aalborg District Court convicted him of aggravated assault (Penal Code Art. 245 § 1) committed jointly with three others by beating and kicking a victim with a bat and bottle, including while the victim lay prostrate; blackmail and attempted duress (offences linked to debt-collection on three dates in November 2018); possession of cannabis for personal use and distribution; and importation of 91 forged 100-euro notes. He received a seven-month prison sentence plus expulsion and a six-year re-entry ban.

The District Court conducted a proportionality assessment under the Aliens Act and Article 8 § 2. It weighed the gravity of the planned, group-committed violence against the applicant’s short lawful residence, limited Danish-language skills, ongoing education, two aunts in Denmark, and a Danish girlfriend then expecting twins, versus his Syrian upbringing, Arabic fluency and remaining ties to that country (despite his family’s flight). Expulsion was held necessary to prevent disorder and crime and not contrary to Denmark’s international obligations.

The High Court of Western Denmark upheld the judgment on 29 January 2020. By then the twins had been born prematurely (one with health problems); after release from remand the applicant had lived with his family, participated in childcare, completed ninth grade and obtained employment. His Danish partner and children would not relocate to Syria. The High Court found these facts did not render expulsion disproportionate.

The Supreme Court, on 14 August 2020, increased the sentence to eight months and confirmed expulsion. It recorded lawful residence of approximately three years and nine months. The applicant retained very strong Syrian ties. Danish ties were relatively limited: cohabitation with his partner only since January 2018, two infant children, modest education and work history. The offences were premeditated, not impulsive, and serious. Family life was of short duration and the children were young, so temporary physical separation (mitigated by possible visits, telephone/internet contact and the six-year limit on the ban) carried less weight. Societal interests in crime prevention therefore prevailed.

After serving the remainder of his sentence the applicant was placed in a deportation centre (not deprived of liberty). On 5 April 2022 the Aliens Appeals Board refused further asylum under s. 7(1) of the Aliens Act but held that the general situation in Syria prevented forced implementation, leaving him on “tolerated stay.” He subsequently failed to comply with reporting obligations, absconded in June 2022, applied for asylum in the Netherlands, disappeared after Denmark accepted readmission, and was re-arrested in Denmark in May 2024. Throughout he had maintained a registered Danish address.

The applicant argued that the expulsion order, given his partner, young children and developing life in Denmark, violated Article 8. The Court examined whether the interference pursued a legitimate aim and was necessary and proportionate in a democratic society.

Domestic courts treated the reduced ban length as decisive to proportionality.

**Case Summary: Al-Habeeb v. Denmark (ECHR, Application no. 14171/23, Judgment of 12 November 2024)**

This case concerned an Iraqi national’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life) regarding a Danish expulsion order with a 12-year re-entry ban imposed after his conviction for a serious violent offence. The applicant, born in 1991, entered Denmark in 1998 aged seven, obtained subsidiary protection status in 1999 and permanent residence in 2002, and had resided lawfully there for more than 21 years. He had strong ties to Denmark, including fluency in Danish, Danish education and employment (including four years as an assistant social educator), and family members (parents and siblings) living there. His ties to Iraq were weak: he had no relatives there, spoke only broken Arabic, and could not read or write it.

The applicant had prior convictions: in 2010 (aged 17) for attempted robbery (eight months’ imprisonment); in 2011 for attempted aggravated violence (three months’ imprisonment); and in 2019 for repeated violence (three months’ imprisonment), at which time he was warned of possible expulsion. Around 2020 he married a Danish national in a Muslim ceremony; their daughter (a Danish national) was born in March 2021. He was arrested in December 2020 in his wife’s apartment in Sweden.

In September 2021 the District Court convicted him of particularly offensive, brutal or dangerous assault (Penal Code Articles 245 § 1 and 247 § 1) committed on 26 July 2020. Acting jointly with three masked co-offenders (some armed with impact weapons), he stabbed the victim five times in the back, groin and lung; the injuries could have been fatal without medical treatment. He received a sentence of two years and three months’ imprisonment plus expulsion with a 12-year re-entry ban.

The court found the statutory conditions for expulsion met (Aliens Act section 22(1)(iii) and (vi)). A permanent ban would normally apply (section 32(4)(vii)), but the court reduced it to 12 years (section 32(5)(i)) because a permanent ban would “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8. It assessed the applicant’s long residence, family life (Danish wife and infant daughter who would remain in Europe), and stronger Danish than Iraqi ties, but held that the gravity of the offence (life-threatening, joint masked attack), prior similar convictions, recent expulsion warning, and significant risk of future serious violent offences outweighed these factors. Contact with family could continue via visits to Iraq and remote communication. The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment in May 2022; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in December 2022. The applicant was expelled to Iraq in July 2022 and later joined his family in Sweden; his wife became pregnant with a second child in 2023.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) found no violation of Article 8. The domestic courts had properly applied the Court’s case-law, treating the reduced 12-year duration of the re-entry ban as the decisive factor that rendered the measure compatible with Article 8. The prospect of the applicant later re-entering Denmark (e.g., via family reunification with his Danish spouse or long-term partner) was not purely theoretical, as shown by available statistics on post-ban residence permits. The courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and conducted a due proportionality assessment balancing the applicant’s private and family life against the public interest in preventing crime. The time-limited nature of the ban distinguished the case from a permanent exclusion. The judgment became final on 17 March 2025.

The case of Savuran v. Denmark (Application no. 3645/23) concerns an expulsion order with a six-year re-entry ban imposed on a settled Turkish migrant following conviction for serious drug offences. The applicant, Ilhan Savuran (now Savran), born in Denmark in 1991, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the measure violated his right to respect for private life. He had lawfully resided in Denmark for around 30 years, was born and raised there, completed training as a car mechanic, lived with his parents (who were employed), and had two adult siblings in Denmark. He had no girlfriend or children. His grandparents in Türkiye had died five or six years earlier, leaving him with no remaining family there. He had holidayed in Türkiye (most recently in 2015 and 2019), spoke some Kurdish (used alongside Danish at home), and had no real property or other substantial ties there.

On 21 October 2021, the District Court convicted him under Article 191 of the Penal Code of possessing 52.25 grams of cocaine for resale and selling 350 grams of cocaine between November 2020 and May 2021 (profit of DKK 128,850, or approximately EUR 17,300). He was also convicted of possessing 16.87 grams of hashish for personal use. He pleaded guilty, describing repeated sales arranged by telephone, deliveries by car, and storage of proceeds at home. He received two years’ imprisonment plus a warning of expulsion (rather than expulsion itself). The court found expulsion conditions met under the Aliens Act but held it would violate Denmark’s international obligations (including Article 14 of the EU-Turkey Association Decision No. 1/80 and Article 8 ECHR). Factors included no prior serious convictions or expulsion warnings, lifelong Danish residence, entire family in Denmark, and lack of real ties to Türkiye, making expulsion a disproportionate interference with private life.

It held that expulsion was required unless it would certainly breach international obligations. The offences were planned and repeated over a long period (many transactions of one-to-two sachets, significant driving and profit), constituting a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental interest of society under Article 14 of the Association Decision (as interpreted in CJEU case-law such as Ziebell). No prior record existed, but the conduct was not random. For Article 8, the High Court applied ECtHR criteria (citing Maslov v. Austria [GC] and others), noting very compelling reasons are needed to expel a settled migrant born in the host country. Ties to Denmark were much stronger, but he had some ties to Türkiye (nationality, language, prior visits) and could cope there. Family contact could continue via visits, telephone, and online. The six-year ban (discretionarily reduced from a potential permanent ban) was not disproportionate.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 7 October 2022. In August 2023, while detained, he was convicted of possessing 19.93 grams of cannabis for personal use (14 days’ imprisonment and a warning). He was released and deported to Türkiye on 28 August 2023.

It characterised the drug offences as serious, planned and prolonged rather than isolated, constituting a genuine and sufficiently serious present threat to a fundamental interest of society. Although the applicant’s ties to Denmark were much stronger than those to Türkiye (where he could nonetheless cope, given his nationality, language skills and holiday visits), the nature and gravity of the crimes outweighed the private-life considerations. Family contact could continue via visits, telephone and online means. The six-year duration of the ban was itself a relevant factor in the proportionality assessment.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in October 2022. While detained the applicant received a further conviction in August 2023 for possessing 19.93 grams of cannabis (two occasions), resulting in fourteen days’ imprisonment and another expulsion warning. He was released and deported to Türkiye on 28 August 2023.

The applicant complained that the expulsion order interfered disproportionately with his right to respect for private life under Article 8. The European Court of Human Rights held that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had duly assessed proportionality in the light of its case-law, finding no violation.

**The case concerns the 10 November 2014 shooting of applicants Kasım Özdemir (son, b. 1984) and Mehmet Özdemir (father, b. 1956) in the legs by gendarmerie officer C.Ç. during a confrontation in Deliosman village, Gaziantep Province, Türkiye. They alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention (right to life and prohibition of ill-treatment), focusing on the shooting itself and the subsequent investigation's ineffectiveness. The ECHR examined the complaints under Article 3 (substantive and procedural aspects).**

Three gendarmerie officers on patrol pursued a vehicle that ignored a stop warning; it entered the village and was found to contain smuggled cigarettes. Villagers gathered, throwing stones that severely damaged the officers' vehicle (broken windows, tyres, radio, dents/holes) and attempting to seize rifles. Officers reported a crowd of 15–60 people blocking escape routes, injuring all three (bruises, hematomas, lesions treated by simple intervention, 10 days' leave). C.Ç. fired multiple warning shots into the air. According to officers, the applicants (and others) continued advancing, grabbing at rifles/belts and threatening to shoot; C.Ç. then fired at their feet from ~3 metres. Forensic analysis confirmed gunshot residue on C.Ç. and the applicants; seven bullets were missing from his rifle; shooting distance was undetermined. Bloodstains were found ~30 metres from the vehicle; 375 cartons of cigarettes were recovered near the first applicant's house. Wiretap transcripts of the vehicle driver's calls showed him urging villagers to mobilise against the officers and later describing an attempted lynching.

Applicants claimed C.Ç. began firing randomly upon arrival. The first applicant said he merely warned against shooting (to avoid scaring children) and was hit in the left leg (tibia/fibula fracture, potential functional loss). The second applicant arrived after hearing shots, yelled at C.Ç., and was also shot (multiple tibia/fibula fractures requiring surgery, seriously affecting daily life). Both injuries were non-life-threatening but required more than simple medical intervention. Villager witnesses largely supported this, stating they found the first applicant already down and saw the second shot while approaching; they alleged C.Ç. threatened those trying to help.

The Kilis public prosecutor immediately opened an investigation, ordering scene reports, forensics, statements, and evidence preservation. Two scene reports and sketches were prepared the same day. Officers and applicants gave statements. On 13 February 2015 the prosecutor declined to prosecute C.Ç. for intentional bodily harm, finding self-defence under Law No. 2559 (police use of force, including firearms when necessary after warnings) and Criminal Code Article 25 (proportionate response to unjust attack). The applicants' objection was dismissed by the magistrate's court as remaining within self-defence. Parallel proceedings convicted the applicants (and others) of resisting officers by force, based on initial witness statements aligning with officers' accounts; sentences of eight months' imprisonment were suspended upon their approval.

The Constitutional Court (2019) found no violation of the prohibition of ill-treatment (Constitution Article 17): the force was necessary and proportionate after ignored warnings amid an assault involving stones and weapon-grabbing attempts; the investigation was independent, prompt, and adequate in evidence collection (applicants had not specifically alleged inclusion/expediency failures). A related fairness complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

The ECHR held there was no Article 3 violation. The investigation was effective (prompt, independent, thorough). Substantively, there was sufficient evidence that C.Ç. acted in self-defence to protect his life/integrity and that of two colleagues against a serious, imminent threat from a violent crowd; the use of force (aimed at legs after warnings) was indispensable and not excessive in the circumstances.

Bloodstains were found 30 metres away; 375 cartons of smuggled cigarettes were located near the first applicant’s house. Seven bullets were missing from C.Ç.’s rifle. They denied any resistance, smuggling involvement or damage to property. Villager witnesses largely supported this version, stating they found the son already wounded and that C.Ç. threatened those trying to help.

The applicants’ objection was dismissed. They were themselves indicted for resisting officers by force. The case concerns Kasım Özdemir and his father Mehmet Özdemir, Turkish nationals who alleged that a gendarmerie officer unlawfully shot them in the legs during an incident in their village on 10 November 2014, inflicting serious injuries, in violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention (right to life and prohibition of ill-treatment). Villagers quickly gathered. According to the officers, the crowd (growing to 50-60 people) threw stones, damaged the gendarmerie vehicle extensively (broken windows, tyres, radio, dents, and holes), blocked escape routes, and tried to seize the officers’ rifles and a belt. When the first applicant and others continued advancing and attempting to grab weapons, C.Ç. shot at their feet from close range. The second applicant then approached shouting and attempting to draw a weapon, prompting a similar shot. The officers fled in a civilian vehicle.

The applicants’ account differed: they claimed C.Ç. fired indiscriminately upon arrival; the first applicant merely warned him not to shoot near children and was then shot in the leg; the second applicant arrived later after learning of the shooting and was also shot without resistance or involvement in smuggling. Witnesses (villagers) largely supported this, stating shots were heard first and C.Ç. threatened those trying to help.

Scene reports and sketches documented damage and bloodstains 30 metres from the vehicle. On 13 February 2015 the prosecutor declined to prosecute C.Ç., finding self-defence under relevant gendarmerie/police laws and the Criminal Code after warnings failed against an imminent attack. Applicants’ objections were dismissed.

Separately, the applicants and others were charged with using force to impede officers. In 2018 they were convicted (eight months and ten days’ imprisonment, suspended) based on officer statements and an initial witness account aligning with them. Their Constitutional Court applications (2015 and 2019) alleging ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, and unfair proceedings were unsuccessful; the Court found the force necessary and proportionate after ignored warnings, and the investigation independent and adequate.

001-238039:
The applicant, a Tunisian national born in 1980, arrived in Switzerland in 1999 after marrying Swiss national M.E. They divorced in 2005, after which he married Tunisian national M.B.B., who joined him at age 28. The couple had three children born in Switzerland (daughter 2006, son 2009, daughter 2015). The applicant resided there for around 20 years. Workplace accidents caused a 2004 thumb-tip amputation and later arm surgeries including a wrist-joint replacement, restricting hand mobility; he received CHF 370 monthly from accident insurance. He held only temporary jobs and, with his wife, received social welfare from April 2005 to April 2017.

In 2013 he was fined (60 daily units of CHF 70, two-year probation) for vehicle theft and unlicensed/unfit driving. On 16 May 2018 the Winterthur District Court convicted him of fraud and unlawfully claiming social-security/welfare benefits (1 May 2005–30 April 2017) plus document falsification. He and his wife had concealed insurance payments, work income and ex-wife support (and a Tunisia house she financed) to obtain excess benefits, causing at least CHF 186,960 public loss. He received 24 months’ imprisonment (suspended) plus 90 daily units of CHF 30, and a five-year expulsion under Criminal Code Article 66a (mandatory for listed offences, including social-benefit fraud, absent personal hardship). The order was not entered in the Schengen system.

The court found poor integration despite long residence: no long-term employment, few social contacts beyond his ex-wife and a Tunisian acquaintance. He retained Tunisian family ties, visited yearly and owned a house there, where work was possible. Children spoke Arabic and knew Tunisia from visits; the ex-wife planned to spend substantial time with them in the Tunisia house. The eldest daughter (then 13) had ADHD, concentration issues, skin conditions and obesity; equivalent multidisciplinary Swiss support might be unavailable in Tunisia, but closer family ties there would help and care would not be insufficient. Public interest outweighed private/family interests.

On appeal the Zurich Cantonal Supreme Court (25 June 2019) held expulsion could rest only on the seven post-1 October 2016 months (when Article 66a entered force), increased the sentence to 30 months (20 suspended) and upheld expulsion. The Federal Supreme Court (4 December 2019) confirmed. It found the youngest child (age 4) would face no special difficulty, the son (age 10) could adapt via social skills, and the eldest’s ADHD (not specialist-diagnosed) did not reach the high health-expulsion threshold; Tunisia guaranteed basic care (per WHO/fact-finding data). Pre-2016 offences could be considered for integration/reoffending/proportionality. Integration remained weak: limited contacts, wife also expelled, ex-wife intending to live in Tunisia, no long-term Swiss employment. Reintegration in Tunisia posed no major obstacle (prior tourism work, language skills acquired in Switzerland). Health operations were complete and basic care available. Long-term fraud against the supporting state showed lack of integration and values.

The wife received an 18-month suspended sentence and identical five-year expulsion; she left for France (near the Swiss border) in March 2020. In 2021 the child-protection authority placed the children with the Swiss ex-wife as foster parent in Switzerland (after consulting the parents). The applicant served the unsuspended term from May 2022; post-release he was ordered to leave immediately, but expulsion remained unenforced as of 2023.

He alleged the expulsion disproportionately interfered with Article 8 family life given his 20-year residence, family ties, children’s Swiss upbringing/integration (especially the eldest’s health, language/education barriers and claimed hymen-related stigma in Tunisia), low reoffending risk, and the offences’ limited economic impact. The Court held that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had properly assessed proportionality in light of its case-law, finding no violation.

The case of I.B.A. v. Switzerland (Application no. 28995/20) concerns a Tunisian national’s claim that a five-year expulsion order from Switzerland, imposed after his conviction for social-benefit fraud, disproportionately interfered with his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1980, entered Switzerland in 1999 upon marrying a Swiss national (M.E.); they divorced in 2005. That year he married a Tunisian woman (M.B.B.) from his hometown, who joined him at age 28. The couple had three children born in Switzerland (2006, 2009 and 2015). Workplace accidents in 2003 and 2013 left the applicant with a partial thumb amputation and restricted wrist mobility, for which he received a monthly CHF 370 insurance payment. He held only temporary jobs and, together with his wife, received social-welfare benefits from April 2005 to April 2017. In 2013 he was fined (suspended) for vehicle theft and related driving offences.

On 16 May 2018 the Winterthur District Court convicted him of fraud and unlawfully claiming social-security or welfare benefits (1 May 2005–30 April 2017) plus document falsification. He and his wife had concealed his insurance payments, work income and support from his ex-wife, and he had submitted falsified documents and failed to declare a house in Tunisia paid for by M.E. The fraud caused losses of at least CHF 186,960. He received a 24-month suspended prison sentence, 90 daily penalty units and a five-year expulsion under Article 66a of the Swiss Criminal Code (mandatory for the listed offences unless “serious personal hardship” existed). The expulsion was not entered in the Schengen Information System.

The District Court found the applicant poorly integrated despite two decades in Switzerland: no long-term employment, few social contacts beyond his ex-wife and one Tunisian acquaintance, annual trips to Tunisia where he owned a house and had family, and realistic prospects of work there. Concerning the children, it noted they spoke Arabic, visited Tunisia yearly and would retain contact with M.E., who planned to spend substantial time there. The eldest daughter (then 13) had ADHD, skin conditions and obesity; while Swiss multidisciplinary support would be less available in Tunisia, the court considered Tunisian family networks and basic care adequate and concluded that public-interest considerations outweighed private interests.

The Cantonal Supreme Court (25 June 2019) limited the expulsion trigger to offences after 1 October 2016 (when Article 66a entered force), raised the sentence to 30 months (10 unsuspended) but upheld the five-year expulsion. The Federal Supreme Court (4 December 2019) confirmed. It assessed the children’s situations separately: the youngest (age 4) would face no particular difficulty; the son (age 10) could adapt thanks to social skills; the eldest daughter’s ADHD diagnosis was not specialist-confirmed and did not meet the high threshold for health-based hardship (basic medical care existed in Tunisia). Arguments about hymen damage and cultural stigma were unsupported and unpersuasive. The applicant’s 20-year residence, limited Swiss social and professional ties, continued links to Tunisia, and the long duration of the fraud (including pre-2016 conduct relevant to integration and proportionality) all supported expulsion. His wife received a similar sentence and expulsion and later moved to France; the children were subsequently placed with M.E. as foster parent in Switzerland. The applicant served the unsuspended term; expulsion had not yet been enforced by 2023.

The applicant contended that the courts undervalued his length of stay, post-conviction conduct, modest scale of the (purely financial) offence relative to a family of five, linguistic difficulties, children’s Swiss upbringing and the eldest daughter’s special needs. Domestic courts held that no “serious personal hardship” existed and that the public interest in expelling a long-term welfare-fraud offender prevailed.

The case of I.B.A. v. Switzerland (Application no. 28995/20) involved a Tunisian national born in 1980 who arrived in Switzerland in 1999 following marriage to a Swiss citizen, M.E. The couple divorced in 2005. That year, the applicant married M.B.B., a Tunisian national from his hometown who joined him in Switzerland. They had three children born in Switzerland: a daughter in 2006, a son in 2009 and a daughter in 2015.

The applicant suffered workplace accidents in 2003 (partial thumb amputation) and 2013 (multiple arm surgeries culminating in wrist replacement with restricted mobility). He received CHF 370 monthly from Swiss accident insurance. He held only temporary jobs. From April 2005 to April 2017, he and his wife received social welfare benefits.

In 2013 he was fined (suspended, with two-year probation) for motor-vehicle theft, unfit driving and driving without a licence.

On 16 May 2018 the Winterthur District Court convicted him of fraud and unlawfully claiming social-security/welfare benefits between 1 May 2005 and 30 April 2017, plus document falsification. The couple had omitted to declare the applicant’s insurance payments, work income and financial support from his ex-wife, and had submitted falsified documents; they also failed to declare a house in Tunisia paid for by the ex-wife. Public funds lost at least CHF 186,960. The court imposed a 24-month suspended prison sentence, daily fines and a five-year expulsion order under Article 66a of the Swiss Criminal Code (in force since 1 October 2016). The expulsion was not entered in the Schengen Information System.

The District Court found the applicant poorly integrated despite two decades in Switzerland: he had never held long-term employment and had few social contacts besides his ex-wife and a Tunisian acquaintance. He retained family ties in Tunisia, visited yearly and owned a house there, so he could work upon return. Concerning the children, the court noted they spoke Arabic, were familiar with Tunisia from annual visits and would remain in contact with the applicant’s ex-wife, who planned to spend substantial time in the Tunisian house. The eldest daughter (then 13) had ADHD, concentration difficulties, skin conditions and obesity. Multidisciplinary support available in Switzerland might be less extensive in Tunisia, but closer family ties there would provide support and care would not be inadequate. Public interest in expulsion therefore outweighed private and family interests.

On appeal the Supreme Court of the Canton of Zurich held that expulsion could rest only on the seven-month period after 1 October 2016. It increased the sentence to 30 months’ imprisonment (20 months suspended) while upholding the expulsion.

The Federal Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 4 December 2019. It considered the children’s ages: the youngest (four) would face no particular difficulty; the son (ten) could adapt thanks to social skills; the eldest daughter’s ADHD had not been diagnosed by a specialist and did not constitute an illness treatable only in Switzerland. Basic medical care existed in Tunisia. Claims that gynaecological surgery damaging her hymen would cause “serious problems” in a traditional Muslim society lacked expert support and did not evidence risk of gender-based violence. The applicant’s social network in Switzerland was limited mainly to his Tunisian friend and Swiss ex-wife (who intended to move to Tunisia); his co-accused wife would also be expelled. He had never achieved stable employment. Reintegration in Tunisia was feasible given prior residence, language skills acquired in Switzerland and earlier tourism-sector work. His health issues had been treated in Switzerland and basic care was available in Tunisia. Long-term offences against the State that had supported his family demonstrated lack of integration and disregard for Swiss values. Previous offences, though not themselves triggering expulsion, could be taken into account when assessing hardship and proportionality.

In parallel proceedings the applicant’s wife received an 18-month suspended sentence and the same five-year expulsion; she left for France in March 2020. In March 2021 the child-protection authority appointed the applicant’s ex-wife as foster parent of the three children in Switzerland. The applicant served the unsuspended ten-month prison term starting in May 2022. The expulsion order had not been enforced by 2023.

The applicant alleged that the five-year expulsion was a disproportionate interference with his right to respect for family life under Article 8. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had duly assessed proportionality in the light of its case-law.
