The case of Sardar Babayev v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR applications 34015/17 and 26896/18) concerns the pre-trial detention and criminal conviction of an Azerbaijani clergyman for conducting Islamic religious rites after receiving his education abroad.

Babayev, born in 1974, studied religion in Iran from 1991 to 2000 before returning to Azerbaijan. From 2009 he regularly preached and led Friday prayers at the Masalli city mosque. In December 2015 Azerbaijan amended its Criminal Code by inserting Article 168-1, which made it an offence for Azerbaijani citizens educated abroad to conduct Islamic rites or rituals. A parallel amendment to the Law on Freedom of Religious Belief imposed the same prohibition. (A later 2017 amendment allowed such activity only with permission from the official Caucasus Muslims Board.)

In October 2016 the mosque building was closed for works, but the community continued to gather in the courtyard. On 4 and 18 November 2016 Babayev led Friday prayers there. The local executive authority reported the 4 November event to the State Security Service. Criminal proceedings were opened on 30 December 2016. On 22 February 2017 Babayev was charged under Article 168-1.3.1 (repeated commission of the offence) and immediately placed in pre-trial detention for one month and seven days. The court cited only the gravity of the charge and a risk of absconding or obstructing the investigation. His appeal was dismissed on 16 March 2017; during that hearing he was held in a metal cage in the courtroom. Detention was later extended twice (to 30 April and then 20 May 2017) on essentially identical grounds; further appeals were rejected.

A private news agency reported on 23 February 2017, citing a senior official of the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations, that Babayev had been detained for “unlawful religious activity” after repeated warnings.

On 3 July 2017 the Masalli District Court convicted Babayev and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. Relying on witness statements and a video of 9 December 2016, it found that he had preached and led prayers on the two November dates and on 9 December, thereby repeatedly violating Article 168-1. Appeals to the Shirvan Court of Appeal (25 September 2017) and the Supreme Court (13 February 2018) were dismissed; the appellate courts did not address his Article 9 argument.

The ECtHR later held that the conviction, based solely on a blanket statutory ban unrelated to any concrete threat to public order or the rights of others, pursued no pressing social need and was therefore not necessary in a democratic society (Article 9). It also found that the metal-cage confinement constituted degrading treatment (Article 3) and that the domestic courts had failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for the lengthy pre-trial detention (Article 5 § 3).

The relevant domestic framework included constitutional guarantees of secularism, equality of religions and freedom of conscience, subject only to public-order and morality limits. Article 21 of the 1992 Law on Freedom of Religious Belief, as amended in 2015, flatly prohibited citizens educated abroad from conducting Islamic rites (a later 2017 amendment allowed such activity only with the consent of the Caucasus Muslims Board). The Venice Commission had already criticised an earlier version of the restriction as discriminatory and incompatible with the right to manifest religion through worship and teaching.

These facts form the core of the complaints under Article 9 (blanket ban on preaching by those educated abroad), Article 3 (confinement in a metal cage) and Article 5 § 3 (insufficient reasons for pre-trial detention).

The case of Giannakopoulos v. Greece (no. 20503/20) concerns a Greek father’s Article 8 complaint that domestic courts arbitrarily declined jurisdiction over his application for custody of his two young children, wrongly concluding that they were habitually resident in Germany under the EU Brussels II bis Regulation.

The applicant married German national E.B. in 2009; they lived in Rhodes and had a daughter (2010) and son (2012). After separation, the Rhodes first-instance court, by decision 590/2013 of 18 October 2013, granted E.B. sole interim custody and the applicant scheduled contact rights. The court recorded E.B.’s explicit assurance that she would remain in Greece and found no evidence of any intention to relocate. E.B. later filed (then withdrew) a custody action. On 11 December 2013 she took the children to Germany, stating it was a Christmas visit ending 13 January 2014; she never returned. She registered the family in Kevelaer, obtained German social-security coverage, began work, and enrolled the children in nursery (from March and August 2014). They rapidly acquired German-language skills, formed social ties and grew close to E.B.’s extended family.

In January 2015 the same Greek court, finding a material change of circumstances (E.B. had misled it and obstructed contact), revoked decision 590/2013 and granted the applicant interim custody (decision 26/2015). Enforceability certificates were issued under Articles 39 and 42 of Brussels II bis. On 29 January 2015 the applicant sought sole custody. The first-instance court (decision 51/2017) dismissed the application as inadmissible for want of jurisdiction: the children had lived more than a year in Germany and were settled there.

The Dodecanese Court of Appeal (decision 302/2017) confirmed the lack of jurisdiction. Applying CJEU case-law (A and Mercredi), it held that habitual residence under Article 8 of the Regulation is the place of the child’s social and family integration. At the moment the Greek court was seised the children had already spent over a year in Germany, attended school, developed relationships and lost virtually all Greek. Because E.B. held sole custody when she moved, the relocation was lawful; Article 10 (wrongful removal) therefore did not apply. Decision 26/2015 was an interim order issued before the German non-return judgment and had never been enforced in Germany, so Article 11(8) was inapplicable. E.B. had never accepted Greek jurisdiction under Article 12 (she withdrew her 2013 action and later contested competence). Continuing the proceedings in Greece would also have been contrary to the children’s best interests given their three-and-a-half-year settlement in Germany.

The Court of Cassation (decision 927/2019, available November 2019) upheld this reasoning in full. Parallel German Hague Convention proceedings initially ordered return (June 2015) but the appeal court reversed that order (November 2015) because the request was lodged after the one-year deadline and the children were settled (Article 12(2) Hague Convention). A later German court, after the Greek cassation ruling, awarded parental responsibility to E.B.

The applicant contended that the Greek courts ignored the breach of his contact rights, E.B.’s fraudulent assurances, the certified but unenforced 2015 custody order, and the children’s brief presence in Germany. The ECtHR, however, found the domestic assessment neither arbitrary nor disproportionate: it weighed all relevant factors in the light of the Regulation and the children’s best interests.

The case concerns the applicant Georgios Giannakopoulos, a Greek national residing in Rhodes, who alleged a violation of Article 8 ECHR (right to respect for family life) arising from Greek courts’ refusal of jurisdiction over his application for custody of his two children.

The applicant married German national E.B. in December 2009. The couple lived in Greece and had a daughter (born 2010) and a son (born 2012). After separating, E.B. applied in July 2013 for interim custody, assuring the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance that she would remain in Rhodes with the children and had no intention of relocating to Germany. The applicant sought custody or shared custody plus contact rights. By decision no. 590/2013 of 18 October 2013 the court awarded sole custody to E.B. and set a contact schedule for the applicant, finding no evidence that she would leave Greece without consent.

On 11 December 2013 E.B. took the children to Germany, stating it was a Christmas visit from which they would return on 13 January 2014. She did not return and settled permanently. The applicant served decision 590/2013 on the German authorities in July 2014. In September 2014 he applied to have that decision set aside. By decision no. 26/2015 of 14 January 2015 the same court granted him interim sole custody, holding that E.B. had misled the court by her earlier assurances and had thereby obstructed the applicant’s contact rights. The applicant obtained Brussels IIbis enforceability certificates and served the new decision in Germany.

On 29 January 2015 the applicant lodged a substantive sole-custody application in Rhodes. Parallel Hague Convention return proceedings were commenced. The Düsseldorf District Court initially ordered return (24 June 2015), but the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal reversed that order on 27 November 2015, applying the one-year time-limit and finding the children well settled in Germany. The Federal Constitutional Court later dismissed the applicant’s constitutional complaint.

Greek courts thereafter declined jurisdiction. The first-instance court (decision 51/2017) held that the children had been living in Germany for more than a year, had adapted, and were therefore habitually resident there. The Dodecanese Court of Appeal (decision 302/2017) confirmed, relying on CJEU case-law (A and Mercredi). It found that by the date the applicant’s custody application was lodged the children had already acquired habitual residence in Germany: they had been registered, insured, attending nursery, developing social and family ties, and speaking German fluently, while retaining almost no Greek. Because E.B. held sole custody at the time of the move she was entitled to determine the children’s residence; the relocation was therefore not “wrongful” under Article 10 Brussels IIbis. Decision 26/2015 had never been enforced in Germany and did not constitute a subsequent return order under Article 11(8). E.B. had not accepted Greek jurisdiction under Article 12, and prorogation would in any event have been contrary to the children’s best interests after more than three years’ settlement. The Court of Cassation (decision 927/2019) upheld these conclusions.

Separately, a Greek criminal court convicted E.B. in absentia of disobeying the two Greek custody orders.

The applicant contended that the courts had misapplied Brussels IIbis by ignoring (a) the breach of his contact rights, (b) E.B.’s deception, (c) the later interim custody award and its certificates, (d) the German courts’ initial return order, and (e) the short duration of the children’s stay in Germany, thereby arbitrarily denying him a forum in which to seek custody of his children.

The case of Giannakopoulos v. Greece (Application no. 20503/20) concerns a Greek father’s complaint under Article 8 of the ECHR that domestic courts violated his right to family life by dismissing his application for custody of his two children (born 2010 and 2012) for lack of jurisdiction. The courts held that the children were habitually resident in Germany, so German courts had competence under the EU Brussels II bis Regulation 2201/2003.

The applicant, a Greek national living in Rhodes, married German national E.B. in 2009; the family resided in Greece. After separation, E.B. sought interim custody in 2013, assuring the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance that she would remain in Greece with the children. Decision no. 590/2013 (18 October 2013) awarded her sole custody and set a contact schedule for the applicant, noting no evidence she would relocate without consent. E.B. later withdrew a related custody action. On 11 December 2013 she took the children to Germany, claiming a Christmas visit with a 13 January 2014 return, but settled there permanently. The applicant served the 2013 decision on German authorities.

In 2014 the applicant applied to set aside the 2013 decision. Decision no. 26/2015 (14 January 2015) granted him interim custody, finding a material change of circumstances: E.B. had misled the court and obstructed contact. He obtained enforceability certificates under Brussels II bis Articles 39 and 42 and served the decision in Germany.

The applicant then sought sole custody. Greek courts (first-instance decision no. 51/2017; Dodecanese Court of Appeal no. 302/2017; Court of Cassation no. 927/2019) rejected the application as inadmissible for want of jurisdiction. They found that, by the time of the applicant’s 2015 application (the relevant date under Brussels II bis Article 8), the children had been in Germany for over a year, were registered and insured there, attended nursery/school, had adapted socially and linguistically (they held German nationality and spoke the language), and had family ties. E.B. had held sole custody under the 2013 decision, so the relocation was lawful; there was no “wrongful removal or retention” triggering residual Greek jurisdiction under Article 10. Decision no. 26/2015 had not been enforced in Germany and was not a subsequent return order under Article 11(8). E.B. had not accepted Greek jurisdiction under Article 12 (she withdrew her earlier action and later contested competence). The courts applied CJEU case-law on “habitual residence” (integration into a social and family environment) and held that the children’s best interests favoured the courts of their current residence.

Parallel German proceedings under the 1980 Hague Convention initially ordered the children’s return (Düsseldorf District Court, June 2015) but the Court of Appeal reversed this (November 2015) because the request was filed after one year and the children were settled (Hague Article 12(2)). A later German court awarded parental responsibility to E.B. after the Greek Cassation ruling.

The applicant argued that the Greek courts misapplied Brussels II bis by ignoring the 2013 decision’s contact rights, E.B.’s alleged deception, the unenforced 2015 interim custody order, certain German rulings, and the relatively short German stay. A Greek criminal court later convicted E.B. (in absentia) of breaching the 2013 and 2015 decisions. The ECtHR ultimately found no Article 8 violation, concluding the domestic assessment was neither arbitrary nor disproportionate and properly weighed the children’s best interests.

The ECHR case Hellgren v. Finland (App. no. 52977/19) concerned a Finnish postal worker’s complaints under Articles 11 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that her employer’s withholding of two days’ wages, following her refusal to perform one of her assigned tasks during a union-led “selective strike,” unlawfully restricted her trade-union rights and constituted discrimination on grounds of union membership and industrial action.

The applicant, Anu Marjaana Hellgren, was employed on a permanent contract by the state-owned postal company Posti Oy. Her core duties were sorting and delivering mail; she also served as an in-company trainer and occasionally provided induction training to new staff. After the applicable collective agreement expired at the end of October 2015, her union (PAU) sought to pressure negotiations. On 1 November 2015 it issued a collective decision, effective the next day, prohibiting overtime and the induction training of externally recruited (agency) workers at sites where such workers were being used.

On 2 November hundreds of agency workers were introduced. On 10 and 11 November the applicant reported for her scheduled mail-delivery shifts at 06:30. Her supervisor instructed her to train an agency worker while performing her delivery round. She refused, citing the union decision, but stated she remained available for her ordinary postal duties. She was sent home at 07:03 on the first day and 09:45 on the second; wages for the remainder of each day were withheld. Identical measures were applied to all employees who refused the training task. A new collective agreement was concluded on 30 November 2015.

The applicant sued for the withheld wages (€142.70) and €5,000 compensation under the Non-Discrimination Act. The District Court (August 2016) awarded €122.70 in wages plus €2,000 compensation, holding that the industrial action was lawful and targeted only part of her duties, that the employer had prevented her from performing the non-targeted work, and that she had been discriminated against for complying with the union decision. The Court of Appeal (November 2017) upheld the finding and increased the wage award to the full amount claimed.

The Supreme Court, by a 3–2 majority (April 2019), reversed. It held that wages are payment for work performed under the employer’s direction. An employer is not obliged to accept a different or partial performance once an employee refuses an assigned task, even if the refusal stems from official industrial action. Training was not a separable minor duty; performing only postal work would not have yielded the same benefit. Consequently the employer bore no responsibility for the resulting non-performance and owed no wages. On discrimination, the majority found no unfavourable treatment relative to employees who, for other reasons within their control, fail to perform assigned work.

The two dissenting justices considered the tasks separable (different pay rates applied), viewed the employer’s assignment of the targeted training duty as an attempt to restrict industrial action, and would have held the employer responsible both for the lost wages and for discrimination.

The ECHR ultimately found that trade-union freedom had been secured and that the domestic authorities, in balancing the competing rights, had remained within their wide margin of appreciation.

The case of Hellgren v. Finland (ECHR Application no. 52977/19) concerned a postal worker's claim that her employer unlawfully withheld two days' wages, thereby restricting her trade-union rights and discriminating against her on grounds of industrial action, in alleged violation of Articles 11 and 14 of the Convention.

Anu Marjaana Hellgren, a Finnish national, held a permanent contract with the State-owned postal company Posti Oy. Her principal duties were sorting and delivering mail; she also occasionally provided in-company induction training to new staff. The relevant collective agreement expired at the end of October 2015. Her union, the Finnish Post and Logistics Union (PAU), then took collective industrial action to pressure negotiations for a new agreement. On 1 November 2015 it declared that no overtime would be worked and that no externally recruited (temporary-agency) employees would receive induction training at workplaces using such workers.

On 2 November the employer brought hundreds of agency workers onto its sites. On 10 and 11 November Hellgren reported for her scheduled mail-delivery shifts. Her supervisor instructed her to give induction training to an agency worker while performing her delivery round. She refused, citing the union decision, but stated she remained available for her ordinary postal work. She was sent home at 07:03 on 10 November and 09:45 on 11 November; wages for the remainder of each day were withheld. Identical measures were applied to all employees who refused the training. A new collective agreement was concluded on 30 November 2015.

Hellgren sued in the District Court for the withheld wages (€142.70) plus €5,000 compensation under the Non-Discrimination Act. The District Court awarded €122.70 in wages and €2,000 compensation, holding that the employer had no right to interrupt her entire working day and that she had been discriminated against for complying with lawful union action. The Court of Appeal confirmed the finding of discrimination and increased the wage award to the full amount claimed.

By a 3–2 majority the Supreme Court reversed. It held that wages are payment for work performed under the employer's direction and supervision. An employer is not obliged to accept an employee's unilateral offer of different or partial performance once the employee has refused an assigned task, even if the refusal stems from official industrial action. Training formed part of Hellgren's contractual duties and, in the circumstances, could not be severed from delivery work; the employer was therefore entitled to withhold pay for the unused hours. There was no discrimination because the proper comparator was another employee who had refused assigned work for reasons within his or her control.

The ECHR (Second Section) ultimately found that trade-union freedom had been generally secured and that the Finnish courts, in balancing the competing interests of the employee, the union and the employer, had remained within their wide margin of appreciation. No violation of Article 11 (or, by implication, Article 14) was established.

The case of Hellgren v. Finland (Application no. 52977/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned alleged violations of Articles 11 and 14 of the Convention arising from the withholding of a postal worker’s wages for two days. The applicant, Anu Marjaana Hellgren, was a permanent employee of the state-owned Posti Oy, working as a postal sorter and distributor in Hämeenlinna under a 2015 contract that also required her occasionally to provide induction training to new employees. She belonged to the Finnish Post and Logistics Union (PAU). After the applicable collective agreement expired at the end of October 2015, PAU launched industrial action to press for a new agreement. On 1 November 2015 the union collectively decided that no overtime would be worked and that no induction training would be given to externally recruited temporary agency workers.

On 2 November hundreds of agency workers were brought onto Posti sites. The applicant reported for her scheduled mail-delivery shifts on 10 and 11 November. Her supervisor instructed her to train an agency worker while performing her ordinary delivery round. She refused the training component, citing the union’s decision, but remained available for her normal postal duties. The supervisor sent her home (at 7.03 a.m. on the first day and 9.45 a.m. on the second) and withheld wages for the remainder of each day. Identical measures were applied to all employees who similarly refused training. A new collective agreement was concluded on 30 November 2015.

Hellgren sued Posti for the withheld wages (EUR 142.70) plus EUR 5 000 discrimination compensation under the Non-Discrimination Act. The District Court and Court of Appeal found in her favour. They characterised the union’s action as a lawful “selective strike” targeting only training, held that the employer had no right to prevent her from performing the unaffected postal work, and concluded that the wage deduction constituted prohibited discrimination on grounds of trade-union activity.

The Supreme Court, by a 3–2 majority, reversed. It recalled that wages are payment for work performed under the employer’s managerial prerogative. An employee who refuses assigned tasks is not entitled to pay, even if the refusal stems from official industrial action. The employer was not obliged to accept a different or partial performance (postal work without simultaneous training). Because the assigned work combined both elements throughout the shift, the applicant’s refusal rendered her wholly unavailable; the employer therefore bore no responsibility for the lost work and owed no wages. On discrimination, the majority held that the proper comparator was not co-workers who performed their full duties but an employee who, for reasons within his or her control, declined assigned work; Hellgren had not been treated less favourably than such a person.

The two dissenting justices viewed the postal and training tasks as separable (they even carried different pay rates). They considered that the employer had deliberately assigned the prohibited training in order to frustrate the strike, had failed to allow the applicant to perform her ordinary work, and had thereby both withheld wages unlawfully and discriminated against her for participating in union action.

Hellgren complained to the Strasbourg Court that the Supreme Court’s ruling restricted her Article 11 right to participate in trade-union industrial action and discriminated against her contrary to Article 14. The Court ultimately found no violation, holding that Finnish authorities had remained within their wide margin of appreciation in balancing the competing interests.

The case of O.R. v. Greece (no. 24650/19) involved an Afghan national born in 2003 who arrived in Greece in November 2018 as an unaccompanied minor seeking international protection. He alleged violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the ECHR arising from his living conditions and the authorities’ failure to appoint a permanent legal guardian for nearly six months.

The applicant’s representative notified the Piraeus Regional Asylum Office, the Athens Public Prosecutor for Minors and EKKA of his status, location in Athens and need for housing as early as 24–29 November 2018. On 19 December 2018 he lodged an asylum application, citing abuse by his drug-addicted father (who had forced him to work and denied him schooling in Afghanistan and later Iran) and seeking family reunification with his mother in Germany. The asylum office immediately requested EKKA to locate accommodation and informed the prosecutor.

Despite these steps, the applicant remained without stable housing until mid-May 2019. He spent nights outdoors on Agios Panteleimonas Square, in overcrowded dwellings with unrelated adult men, and unofficially inside the Malakasa and Skaramagas camps (sleeping on floors reserved for adults or outdoors to avoid detection). Homeless throughout the winter, he lacked reliable access to drinking water, food, heating, sanitation and hygiene facilities; an NGO supplied some clothing and meals. He received no education or recreational activities. A social worker recorded his history of physical violence and exploitation and noted two incidents of sexual harassment by adults in Greece. He developed psychological difficulties but obtained no support. Although the prosecutor acted as temporary guardian, no permanent guardian was appointed and no other protective measures were taken.

A place in a dedicated reception facility for unaccompanied minors was finally reserved on 10 May 2019; the applicant entered it on 16 May. His asylum claim was later declared inadmissible because family-reunification proceedings were under way. He remained in the facility until 25 September 2019, when he left for Germany.

The Government maintained that the authorities had used all available resources, that even unregistered residents of the camps had access to food, health, psychosocial and protection services, and that the applicant enjoyed free public healthcare.

Domestic law then in force (Law 4540/2018 and Presidential Decree 220/2007, transposing relevant EU directives) required the authorities to treat the child’s best interests as a primary consideration, to notify the prosecutor and competent protection service immediately, to appoint a representative without delay, to trace family members and to place unaccompanied minors in suitable accommodation. International monitoring bodies (CPT, European Committee of Social Rights) contemporaneously documented chronic shortages of dedicated shelters in Greece, leaving thousands of unaccompanied children homeless or in insecure conditions and thereby exposing them to violence, exploitation and other grave risks.

The Court held that the applicant, a highly vulnerable unaccompanied minor with a traumatic background, had been left to fend for himself for almost six months in extreme material poverty and an environment wholly unsuited to his safety, hygiene and care needs. The failure to appoint a guardian and to expedite placement in an appropriate structure breached both domestic law and the State’s positive obligation under Article 3 to protect such persons.

The case of O.R. v. Greece involves an Afghan national born in 2003 who arrived in Greece in November 2018 as an unaccompanied minor seeking international protection and family reunification with his mother in Germany. On 24 November 2018, his representative emailed the Piraeus Regional Asylum Office to report his status and location in Athens. The Athens Public Prosecutor for Minors and the National Centre for Social Solidarity (EKKA) were notified days later of the urgent need for accommodation. On 19 December 2018, the applicant formally lodged his asylum claim, explaining that his drug-addicted father had subjected him to physical violence, barred him from school and forced him to work. The asylum office immediately requested EKKA to secure housing and informed the prosecutor of the need to appoint a permanent legal guardian.

Despite these steps, no stable placement materialised for nearly six months. A February 2019 assessment by an ARSIS social worker recorded the applicant’s traumatic history and current homelessness: after sleeping in a church and briefly staying with compatriots, he was again on the streets. A letter of 12 February 2019 alerted authorities that he was unofficially residing in Malakasa camp, where he felt unsafe and had experienced attempted sexual harassment. A 30 April 2019 follow-up attached a psychosocial note confirming two incidents of sexual harassment, continued homelessness and high vulnerability.

The applicant described his living conditions from November 2018 until mid-May 2019 as utterly unsuitable. He spent nights outdoors on Agios Panteleimonas Square, in overcrowded dwellings with adult men, and unofficially inside Skaramagas and Malakasa camps—either on the floor of rooms reserved for adults or outside to evade security. He endured winter cold and rain without reliable access to drinking water, food, heating, hot water or sanitation, preventing basic hygiene. NGO ARSIS supplied limited clothing and food. He had no educational or recreational opportunities, received no psychological support despite emerging mental-health problems linked to past trauma and current insecurity, and was never assigned a permanent guardian; the prosecutor remained only a temporary representative.

A place in a dedicated unaccompanied-minors facility was finally reserved on 10 May 2019 and he entered it on 16 May. His asylum application was later declared inadmissible because family-reunification proceedings with his mother were under way. He remained in the facility until 25 September 2019, when he left for Germany.

The Government maintained that the applicant had access, even as an unregistered resident of the camps, to food, health care, psychosocial support, interpretation and alternative education, and that he enjoyed free public-health services from the outset. These facts form the core of the complaints under Article 3 (inhuman or degrading treatment arising from prolonged homelessness, extreme material poverty, exposure to sexual harassment and failure to appoint a guardian) and Article 8 (interference with private life through the State’s failure to protect a highly vulnerable unaccompanied child in accordance with domestic law).

**CASE OF O.R. v. GREECE (Application no. 24650/19)**

The applicant, an Afghan national born in 2003, arrived in Greece in November 2018 as an unaccompanied minor. His representative notified the Piraeus Regional Asylum Office on 24 November 2018 that he was living in Athens and wished to seek international protection; the Athens Public Prosecutor for Minors and the National Centre for Social Solidarity (EKKA) were informed shortly afterwards of the need for accommodation.

On 19 December 2018 he lodged an asylum application, citing a traumatic family history: his drug-addicted father had subjected him to physical violence, prevented him from attending school and forced him to work. He sought family reunification with his mother in Germany. The same day the asylum office requested EKKA to find him accommodation and informed the prosecutor of the application, the accommodation request and the need for a permanent guardian.

A social worker from the NGO ARSIS recorded in February 2019 that the applicant had not grown up in a safe environment and had again become homeless after brief stays in a church and with fellow Afghans. His representative wrote to the authorities on 12 February 2019 stating that he was living in precarious conditions, including an unauthorised stay at the Malakasa camp where he had suffered attempted sexual harassment and felt unsafe. A follow-up email on 30 April 2019, accompanied by a psychosocial assessment, reiterated that he remained without suitable accommodation, was at high risk and had been sexually harassed twice by adults.

A place in a dedicated reception facility for unaccompanied minors was allocated only on 10 May 2019; he entered it on 16 May 2019. His asylum claim was later declared inadmissible because of the pending family-reunification procedure. He left Greece for Germany in September 2019.

The applicant described almost six months of homelessness or highly insecure housing. He slept outdoors on an Athens square in winter, in overcrowded premises with adult men, and unofficially in the Skaramagas and Malakasa camps (on floors reserved for adults or outside to avoid detection). He lacked reliable access to drinking water, food, heating, hot water or sanitation, could not maintain hygiene, and received only ad-hoc help from ARSIS for clothing and food. He had no access to education or age-appropriate activities, developed psychological problems linked to both past trauma and his reception conditions, and unsuccessfully sought psychological support. Despite the prosecutor acting as temporary guardian, no permanent guardian was appointed and no protective measures were taken in his best interests. He felt afraid, isolated and abandoned.

The Government maintained that the authorities had taken available steps, that unofficial camp residents could still access reception, food, health and psychosocial services, and that the applicant enjoyed free access to public healthcare.

The Court held that the applicant, a highly vulnerable unaccompanied minor with a documented history of abuse, had been left to fend for himself for nearly six months in conditions of extreme material poverty that were totally unsuitable as regards safety, accommodation, hygiene, food and care. The failure to appoint a guardian and to place him promptly in an appropriate facility, contrary to domestic law then in force (Law 4540/2018 and Presidential Decree 220/2007), amounted to a breach of the State’s positive obligation to protect him. This treatment reached the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 of the Convention. (The Article 8 complaint was not separately examined once the Article 3 violation was established.)

The case of Ribár v. Slovakia (no. 56545/21) concerns Martin Ribár, a Slovak practising lawyer born in 1977, who alleged that the conditions of his pre-trial detention violated Article 3 of the Convention. Charged on 28 October 2019 with establishing a criminal enterprise, perjury and extortion (allegedly coordinating a gang’s testimonies under the guise of legal services), he was arrested that day and remanded on 30 October 2019. Detention was ordered both to prevent interference with the course of justice (“kolúzna väzba”) and to stop further offending. The collusion ground was lifted by the Supreme Court on 9 March 2021; the applicant was released on 14 May 2021 after the Constitutional Court quashed a related decision, holding that the grounds had been insufficiently particularised given the length of detention and the gravity of the extortion allegation.

Throughout his 18-month detention the applicant was held in Banská Bystrica Prison under the ordinary regime applicable to collusion-risk remand prisoners. He occupied a double cell of 8.02 m² (plus in-cell sanitary annex) alone, first because no non-smoking cell-mate was available and later at his own request. He was locked in the cell for 23 hours a day (23½ hours during COVID-19 measures from 22 March to 21 April 2021). In-cell time could be spent reading (66 library books were borrowed), writing, watching television or exercising. Daily out-of-cell activity consisted solely of one hour (30 minutes during the COVID period) of solitary exercise in one of nine rooftop yards (9.45–53.5 m²) surrounded by high concrete walls and steel mesh that afforded no horizontal view. Some yards contained basic fitness equipment; the applicant often used a 24 m² yard. He received five gym sessions, weekly chaplain visits, two closed family visits and several short video visits. Telephone contact with close relatives was authorised only after more than a year; incoming and outgoing correspondence was delayed by 17–19 days for prosecutorial inspection. Additional complaints concerned inadequate daylight, intermittent hot water, winter cell temperature, food quality/quantity and hourly nocturnal cell checks that disrupted sleep.

The applicant claimed that the prolonged 23-hour lock-up, limited movement, poor nutrition, lack of daylight and sleep interruption caused post-release health problems (back/knee/tendon pain, varicose veins, osteoarthritis, slipped vertebrae, deteriorated vision, glaucoma and insomnia) that he had not suffered before detention.

A January 2021 letter from his lawyer prompted a Public Prosecution Service inspection. In interviews the applicant expressed satisfaction with staff and cell conditions, mentioning only family separation. A later constitutional complaint (14 July 2021) reiterating the confinement, exercise, lighting, correspondence, contact and sleep issues was declared inadmissible on 30 September 2021 for failure to exhaust ordinary remedies (complaints to the Prison Service under s. 65da of the Prison and Court Guard Service Act and to the prosecution service under the Public Prosecution Service Act and Detention Act).

The Court confined its examination to those aspects of the ordinary-regime regime for which no effective domestic remedy existed. It held that, although the 16-month period of 23-hour cellular confinement with only one hour of solitary rooftop exercise was restrictive, the cumulative conditions—viewed together with the applicant’s contemporaneous statements of contentment, the availability of in-cell activities, the later grant of family contact and the absence of other severe material deficiencies—did not reach the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3.

**Case Summary: Ribár v. Slovakia (Application no. 56545/21)**

Slovak lawyer Martin Ribár (born 1977) was charged on 28 October 2019 with establishing a criminal enterprise, perjury and extortion, allegedly using legal services as a cover to coordinate testimony for a gang and shield its leaders. He was arrested the same day and detained from 30 October 2019 primarily to prevent interference with justice (under Article 71 § 1(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure) and continuation of crime (Article 71 § 1(c)). The first ground was lifted on 9 March 2021, leaving only the second. Detention lasted until his release on 14 May 2021, following a Constitutional Court ruling of 13 May 2021 that quashed a Supreme Court decision upholding detention; that court found the grounds rested solely on the charges’ nature (without sufficient facts), that the extortion allegation was vague yet carried a severe penalty (20–25 years or life, versus 5–10 years for other charges), and that lower courts had inadequately addressed Ribár’s arguments that his actions were legitimate legal practice. Similar findings appeared in later Constitutional Court judgments, one of which also noted a lack of speedy review.

Ribár was held throughout in Banská Bystrica Prison in a single-occupancy double cell of 8.02 m² plus sanitary annex (sink, shower, toilet). Furniture (bunk bed, cupboards, table, chairs, shelf, TV) left roughly 3 m² of free space. He was locked in for 23 hours daily (23.5 hours during COVID measures from 22 March to 21 April 2021). In-cell activities included reading (66 library books), writing, television and exercise. Out-of-cell time was limited to one hour daily (30 minutes during COVID) in one of nine rooftop yards (9.45–53.5 m²) surrounded by high walls and netting that blocked horizontal views; yards had some fitness equipment (pull-up/parallel bars, occasionally balls or ropes) and a canopy but no unobstructed outlook. He used these periods alone. He met a chaplain weekly and attended the gym five times in early 2021. Family contact was restricted: two “closed” in-person visits from his wife (September–October 2020); later regular unsupervised calls to his wife, mother and children (authorised from December 2020/March 2021); several short virtual visits; and correspondence delayed 17–19 days by prosecutorial review. Other complaints concerned cell lighting, hot water, winter temperatures, food quantity/nutrition and hourly nocturnal checks disrupting sleep.

Until 9 March 2021, extra restrictions applied because of the interference-prevention ground (visits/calls required authorisation; post was inspected). A January 2021 letter from Ribár’s lawyer to the Prosecutor General (raising detention justification and the harshness of conditions for such detainees) prompted a February 2021 inspection. In interviews then and later (January and April 2021), Ribár expressed no reservations about conditions, praised staff, and described himself as well and balanced, mentioning only family separation and (jokingly) limited cell space. Prosecutors found no irregularities requiring action, though they noted general detainee complaints about one-hour outdoor time (comparable to life prisoners) and viewless yards (previously criticised by the CPT).

After release, Ribár complained to the Constitutional Court (July 2021) of Article 3 and 8 violations, citing confinement, limited outdoor/out-of-cell activity, lighting, correspondence delays, restricted family contact and sleep disruption. The court declared it inadmissible on 30 September 2021 for non-exhaustion of ordinary remedies (complaints under the Prison and Court Guard Service Act and to the Public Prosecution Service). He later attributed post-release health problems (back/knee/tendon pain, varicose veins, osteoarthritis, slipped vertebrae, vision deterioration, glaucoma, insomnia) to the conditions, contrasting his prior fitness.

The European Court of Human Rights limited its examination to complaints lacking effective domestic remedies. It found that the cumulative conditions—23-hour cell confinement under the ordinary (not mitigated) regime for over 16 months, very limited out-of-cell activity, and Ribár’s specific complaints—did not amount to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3.

The case of Hamzayan v. Armenia (Application no. 43082/14) involves complaints by Marina Hamzayan, an Armenian national and Jehovah’s Witness, under Articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It arose from an administrative penalty imposed by authorities of the unrecognized “Nagorno-Karabakh Republic” (“NKR”) for discussing the Bible in a private home.

At the material time the applicant lived in Stepanakert, NKR. On 23 February 2013 she and her friend A.H. visited N., an elderly woman in Shushi with whom A.H. was acquainted and who had attended a couple of Jehovah’s Witness gatherings, to discuss the Bible. Police soon arrived, searched their belongings and seized religious literature from the applicant’s bag. The two women were taken to the police station, questioned and searched again, remaining there for about four and a half hours.

The applicant was charged under Article 206 § 2 of the NKR Code of Administrative Offences, which punishes breaches of legislation on organising and holding religious gatherings, marches and other rituals of worship. On 2 April 2013 the Administrative Commission of the Stepanakert Mayor’s Office imposed a fine of 1,000 Armenian drams (approximately €2). The hearing record noted testimony from a police officer who had responded to N.’s complaint that Jehovah’s Witnesses had visited her home, disturbed her, invited her to gatherings she had refused, and that she had felt embarrassed into admitting them. The officer added that three complaints had been received from N. The Government later asserted that a local police inspector had received similar complaints from other residents about Jehovah’s Witnesses distributing literature and disturbing the peace, but produced no supporting documents.

The applicant appealed to the NKR Administrative Court, arguing that the Commission’s decision contained no description of the facts, failed to identify any specific wrongdoing and lacked reasons. On 24 June 2013 that court declared the decision null and void as improperly reasoned: it was unclear what action had constituted the offence or which rules on religious gatherings had been violated.

The Stepanakert Mayor’s Office appealed, relying on Article 26 of the NKR Constitution (which guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion but states that the freedom of activity of religious organisations operating in accordance with the law is guaranteed) and sections 6 and 7 of the NKR Freedom of Conscience and Religious Organisations Act. Those provisions recognise the Armenian Apostolic Church and other organisations that operate in accordance with their charters, granting rights only upon registration. The appeal also cited N.’s statement that she was not a Jehovah’s Witness and had been manipulated into attending two gatherings.

On 31 October 2013 the NKR Administrative Court of Appeal quashed the lower court’s judgment and upheld the fine. It held that freedom of religion was guaranteed only to followers of legally registered associations and that only such organisations could carry out religious activity. No certificate of registration for “Jehovah’s Witnesses” existed, so the law did not guarantee their right to operate. The case rested on N.’s complaint to police.

The applicant’s appeal on points of law to the NKR Supreme Court was declared inadmissible on 13 December 2013 for lack of merit.

The applicant complained that the penalty interfered with her freedom of religion and was discriminatory. The European Court of Human Rights held that the interference was not “in accordance with the law” because the legal basis lacked the required clarity and foreseeability.

The case of Hamzayan v. Armenia (Application no. 43082/14) was brought by Marina Hamzayan, an Armenian national and Jehovah’s Witness living in Stepanakert in the unrecognized “Nagorno Karabakh Republic” (“NKR”). It concerned an administrative fine imposed on her by NKR authorities for discussing the Bible privately with a third person in that person’s home, raising issues under Articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 23 February 2013 the applicant and a fellow Jehovah’s Witness, A.H., visited several people in Shushi who had shown interest in Bible discussions. One was an elderly woman, N., who had previously attended a couple of Jehovah’s Witness gatherings. Police soon arrived, searched the pair’s belongings and seized religious literature from the applicant’s bag. The two women were taken to a police station, questioned and held for approximately four and a half hours.

The applicant was subsequently charged under Article 206 § 2 of the NKR Code of Administrative Offences with “breaching the rules set out in the legislation on the organising and holding of religious gatherings, marches and other rituals of worship.” On 2 April 2013 the Administrative Commission of the Stepanakert Mayor’s Office imposed a fine of 1 000 Armenian drams (about €2). The decision relied on a police officer’s account of complaints from N. that Jehovah’s Witnesses had repeatedly visited her home, invited her to gatherings and “disturbed the peace” after she had declined further participation.

The applicant appealed to the NKR Administrative Court, arguing that the Commission’s decision contained no description of the facts, failed to identify any specific wrongdoing and was wholly unreasoned. On 24 June 2013 that court declared the fine null and void, holding that it was impossible to discern which particular legislative rule the applicant had allegedly violated.

The Mayor’s Office appealed, invoking Article 26 of the NKR Constitution (which guarantees freedom of religion only to legally registered religious organisations) and sections 6 and 7 of the NKR Freedom of Conscience and Religious Organisations Act (which confer operational rights solely upon registered entities). The appeal also referred to N.’s statement that she was not a Jehovah’s Witness and had attended gatherings only after being “manipulated.”

On 31 October 2013 the NKR Administrative Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and reinstated the fine. It reasoned that, because Jehovah’s Witnesses were not registered in the NKR, they enjoyed no constitutional or statutory right to conduct any religious activity, including private Bible discussions. The NKR Supreme Court later refused the applicant leave to appeal on points of law.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 9. The fine constituted an interference with the applicant’s right to manifest her religion. That interference was not “prescribed by law” because the relevant NKR provisions lacked the clarity and foreseeability required by the Convention. Nothing in the legislation unambiguously prohibited a private conversation about the Bible inside a private home, and the sudden application of registration requirements to such an activity was unpredictable. The Court therefore held that the penalty was not “in accordance with the law.” Complaints under Article 14 were not separately examined once the Article 9 violation had been established.

The case of J.A. and A.A. v. Türkiye (no. 80206/17) involves two Iraqi Sunni nationals (husband born 1971, wife born 1984) and their four then-minor children, who fled Ninewa governorate in northern Iraq in 2014. Their home was bombed amid conflict with ISIS. They entered Türkiye on 2 March 2014 on tourist visas and applied for residence permits on 27 March 2014.

On 7 July 2014 they were arrested at a permit appointment. Post-arrival entry bans had been issued on grounds of criminal proceedings and a threat to general security. The Istanbul governor ordered deportation under section 54(1)(ı) of Law no. 6458 (entry despite bans) plus administrative detention. The applicants were not notified of the deportation order. They challenged detention; after an initial refusal, the Istanbul 3rd Magistrates’ Court ordered release on 7 August 2014, citing insufficient evidence for detention, the children’s ages, and pending asylum claims. They were given 15 days to leave but remain in Istanbul.

On 19 August 2014 they sought annulment of the deportation order before the Istanbul Administrative Court. They argued a real risk of death or ill-treatment from the conflict, ISIS in their region, and their opposition to ISIS ideology, invoking section 55 of Law no. 6458 (no deportation if serious risk of death penalty, torture or inhuman treatment). They submitted photos of the bombed house and asylum applications.

On 21 January 2015 the court dismissed the action solely on National Intelligence Agency information that the applicants might travel to Syria for terrorist activity. It made no assessment of the alleged risks of death or ill-treatment; the authorities’ late submissions were not admitted or served.

On 4 March 2015 the applicants complained to the Constitutional Court of the failure to examine their risk claims, reiterating flight from ISIS-controlled territory, discord with ISIS and the Iraqi government, and submitting the photos. They sought an interim measure. The Court granted one on 27 March 2015 (later extended), finding an arguable claim of immediate risk given the post-entry ban and ongoing conflict.

In its 1 March 2017 plenary judgment the Constitutional Court declared the application admissible (not manifestly ill-founded) but, by 9–6, found no violation of Article 17 of the Constitution. While accepting that the authorities had failed to assess the risk claims, the majority held that the applicants had not sufficiently particularised their personal circumstances, residence or ownership of the photographed house. It noted ISIS did not control all of Iraq and that unspecified “discord” with the government did not require examination. The dissenters considered the claims (photos, timing of flight amid ISIS advances, general reports) arguable and requiring assessment, finding a procedural breach; they highlighted inconsistency with the earlier admissibility and interim-measure findings.

The European Court indicated under Rule 39 that expulsion should not occur pending its proceedings. Removal without a fresh ex nunc assessment of the claims would breach Articles 2 and 3; the domestic assessments of facts and risks did not meet those provisions’ requirements.

International sources showed ISIS controlled only parts of Iraq, with security elsewhere. Their unspecified “discord” with the Iraqi government did not require examination as it was not claimed to create a real risk.

They criticised the inconsistency between unanimous admissibility (and the interim measure) and the later finding of no arguable claim, and found a procedural violation of Article 17 because authorities had not fulfilled their positive obligation to assess the risk.

The case of Janočková and Kvocera v. Slovakia (Application no. 39980/22) concerns the first applicant, Beáta Janočková (born 1978), and her son, the second applicant Daniel Kvocera (born 2014). The family lived together with the father, D.K., until 2017, after which the parents informally alternated care of the child. On 13 March 2017, D.K. sought court regulation of care, initiating merits proceedings before the Bratislava III District Court (with appeals to the Bratislava Regional Court) and various auxiliary proceedings involving urgent interim measures. The child's interests were represented by a court-appointed guardian.

On 13 September 2017, an urgent interim measure placed the child in D.K.'s sole care pending the merits outcome; the child has lived with D.K. in Bratislava ever since. The first applicant has had no contact with her son since 2 September 2018, save for one meeting on 23 February 2021. Contact was regulated by a series of urgent interim measures, beginning with the 9 October 2018 order providing for unsupervised weekend and holiday contact (the “2018 contact order”). This order remains in force after multiple annulments that were subsequently quashed on appeal. A later “assisted contact order” of 21 April 2021, requiring meetings at a child-protection centre without D.K., is also still in place and under enforcement. A further order for supervised contact in D.K.'s presence was quashed. The Regional Court observed an “alarming” family situation of high conflict that was harming the child; D.K. had failed to produce the child for centre meetings, while the first applicant had sought police assistance and publicity.

Merits proceedings produced a 4 July 2019 judgment (later quashed) and a 21 April 2022 judgment awarding custody to D.K., providing for contact in his presence and allowing both parents to act for the child; that judgment remains under appeal.

On 26 November 2018 the first applicant petitioned for judicial enforcement of the 2018 contact order. Under Slovak law (Code of Civil Non-Contentious Procedure), enforcement of urgent interim measures must be initiated of the court’s own motion. Available tools include requests for compliance, repeated fines of up to EUR 1,000, suspension of parental or child allowances, and, if those fail, direct enforcement. The District Court took none of these steps, repeatedly directing only counselling. On 11 May 2022 it dismissed the petition, citing the child’s dismissive attitude (unattributed to manipulation by D.K.), the parents’ strained relations despite counselling, and an expert opinion that forced contact could worsen the relationship. The Regional Court upheld the dismissal on 29 September 2022 on the erroneous ground that the 2018 order had been annulled. The Supreme Court quashed that decision on 22 June 2023 as arbitrary (the annulment itself having been reversed) and remitted the matter; enforcement proceedings remain pending.

The Constitutional Court examined several related complaints. In a 21 September 2021 judgment it found violations of the applicants’ rights to a hearing within a reasonable time and to respect for family life, noting that the District Court had issued no compliance requests, imposed no fines and suspended no allowances, relying solely on ineffective counselling; it awarded each applicant EUR 7,500 and ordered expedition. A later complaint covering the subsequent period was rejected for lack of new constitutional issues. A 29 June 2022 judgment found similar violations regarding the assisted-contact order, observing that D.K. had repeatedly obstructed meetings and that the District Court had failed to respond.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints that the authorities failed to take adequate and effective measures to enforce the 2018 contact order and thereby facilitate reunion, in breach of the positive obligations inherent in Article 8, and that no effective remedy existed under Article 13.

The mother claims no contact since 2 September 2018, except once on 23 February 2021.

The applicant, Angelica Diaconeasa (born 1953), suffered a 2013 stroke that left her unable to move independently, speak, or manage basic self-care. In 2015 and November 2016 the Hunedoara County Commission for the Protection of Adults with Disabilities certified a severe disability requiring a State-funded personal assistant. A June 2017 neurological evaluation produced an ADL score of 2/8 (independent only in telephone use and medication) and a Barthel score of 45/100 (total dependence for hygiene; needing help to eat, dress, toilet and climb stairs; able to walk only with mechanical aids or another person). A Commission “complex evaluation” of October 2017 noted continued dependence on her two daughters and low frustration tolerance, yet the November 2017 certificate (valid two years) reclassified her as severely disabled but not entitled to an assistant.

She challenged the certificate. The Hunedoara County Court in September 2019 annulled it, finding her condition unchanged since 2016 and that she still required help with hygiene, food preparation, shopping, mobility and transport; the Commission had given no reasons for the downgrade. The Alba Iulia Court of Appeal reversed in June 2020, holding that she could walk with a cane or frame and needed only partial assistance, so she had not lost all self-care capacity and did not require permanent help. The court applied Order 762/1992/2007, which reserves a personal assistant for persons who cannot move even with support (wheelchair- or bed-bound), cannot perform daily activities, and need full or partial third-party support.

A further certificate of November 2019 (now permanent) repeated the same classification. A September 2019 social enquiry recorded comprehensive needs (hygiene, dressing, housework, mobility, transport, shopping, money management) yet noted she could walk with a cane or support and feed herself; her daughters provided all care. A 2020 forensic examination confirmed left-arm paralysis, severe walking difficulty and unchanged dependence since 2016, concluding she required permanent help. A 2019 Barthel score of 30 (attributed to a recent fracture) was later cited. The County Court again annulled the certificate (November 2020), but the Court of Appeal quashed that ruling in April 2021. It treated the Barthel score of 30 as “assisted independence,” stressed that she was not immobile or wheelchair-dependent, and held that only total incapacity plus need for permanent help justified an assistant. The court emphasised that support must rest solely on “objective” statutory criteria, not subjective perceptions of need.

Throughout, medical and social evidence consistently showed profound, stable dependence and family-provided care that the applicant could not replace. Domestic decisions nevertheless focused narrowly on residual mobility (cane or frame) and refused to treat the loss of autonomy as warranting a personal assistant, without assessing alternative practical arrangements or the concrete impact on her private life.

The case of *Diaconeasa v. Romania* (App. no. 53162/21) concerns the withdrawal of State-funded personal assistance from a physically disabled applicant, alleged to violate Article 8 ECHR (right to private life) by causing severe loss of autonomy without adequate assessment or balancing of interests.

Ms Angelica Diaconeasa (b. 1953) suffered a 2013 stroke rendering her unable to move, speak or meet basic needs independently. Certificates issued in 2015 and 2016 classified her as having a severe disability requiring a personal assistant.

In June–October 2017, a neurologist scored her 2/8 on the ADL index (independent only in using a telephone and taking medication) and 45/100 on the Barthel scale (high dependency for hygiene, feeding, dressing, toileting and stairs; walking only with aids or help). The Commission’s complex evaluation noted support from her two daughters (recommended to continue) and low frustration tolerance. On 22 November 2017 it issued a two-year certificate of severe disability *without* entitlement to an assistant.

The applicant challenged this, citing unchanged health. The Hunedoara County Court (26 September 2019) cancelled the certificate: medical, social and psychosocial evidence showed no improvement and ongoing inability to manage hygiene, food preparation, shopping, mobility or transport. The Alba Iulia Court of Appeal (15 June 2020) reversed, holding that she could walk with a cane or frame and needed only partial (not permanent) help, so she had not completely lost self-care capacity. It found the lower court had misapplied the relevant ministerial Order.

A further certificate of 20 November 2019 (condition now deemed permanent, no periodic review) relied on a September 2019 social enquiry: comprehensive help needed for hygiene, dressing, housework, laundry, indoor/outdoor mobility, transport, telephone use, cooking, money management and shopping; complete memory loss and disorientation; daughters provided care and funds. A 2020 forensic examination confirmed inability to use her left arm, walking difficulties making hygiene, dressing and cooking impossible, and unchanged status since 2016 (Barthel score 30 after a fracture). A June 2020 social report repeated these findings.

The County Court (25 November 2020) again cancelled the certificate. The Court of Appeal (12 April 2021) upheld it, applying the Order’s criteria for severe motor impairment: inability to move even with support (wheelchair- or bed-bound), total incapacity for daily living, and need for full or partial third-party support. Because she could walk with a cane/support and her Barthel score indicated only “assisted independence,” she fell outside the category requiring an assistant. Objective legal criteria, not empathy, governed.

Domestic law (Disability Act 448/2006) entitles persons with severe disability to a personal assistant after multi-disciplinary evaluation; ministerial criteria and methodological rules stress a bio-psycho-social assessment serving the person’s interests. Romania has ratified the UN CRPD, which requires support for independent living.

These facts—abrupt withdrawal despite consistent medical evidence of high dependency, family support only, and no exploration of alternatives—underpinned the alleged Article 8 violation. (Word count: 512)

**Case Summary: Diaconeasa v. Romania (ECtHR, Application no. 53162/21, Judgment of 20 February 2024)**

The case concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private life) by Angelica Diaconeasa, a Romanian national born in 1953 and living in Lupeni. She alleged that the Romanian authorities’ withdrawal of a State-funded personal assistant, despite her severe physical disability, caused a severe loss of autonomy without a proper assessment of her needs or alternative support, failing to balance competing interests.

In 2013, Diaconeasa suffered a stroke that left her unable to move independently, speak properly, or manage basic self-care. In 2015 and November 2016, the Hunedoara County Commission for the Protection of Adults with Disabilities issued annual certificates classifying her as having a severe disability requiring a personal assistant, based on medical, social, and psychological evaluations under Law no. 448/2006 (the Disability Act). This law establishes county commissions to assess disability levels (mild, medium, elevated, or severe) using medico-psycho-social criteria, with severe disability entitling individuals to a personal assistant if evaluations confirm the need.

On 22 November 2017, following a neurologist’s assessment (ADL index score of 2/8, indicating inability to shop, cook, clean, do laundry, use transport, or manage money, though able to use a telephone and take medication; Barthel scale score of 45/100, showing total dependence for hygiene, needing help to feed, dress, toilet, and climb stairs, and walking only with aids or assistance), the Commission issued a new two-year certificate. It classified her disability as severe but not requiring a personal assistant, noting support from her two daughters and recommending its continuation. A complex evaluation form recorded her low frustration tolerance but did not detail reasons for the change.

Diaconeasa challenged this in Hunedoara County Court, arguing no improvement in her condition. The court (26 September 2019) cancelled the certificate, citing unchanged needs for help with hygiene, food, shopping, mobility, and transport, plus the lack of reasoning, and ordered a new certificate with assistant provision. The Alba Iulia Court of Appeal (15 June 2020) reversed this, holding she could move with a cane or frame and needed only partial daily assistance, thus not meeting the strict criteria under Order no. 762/1992/2007 for a personal assistant (e.g., inability to move even with support, wheelchair/bedridden status, or total incapacity requiring permanent help).

A 20 November 2019 certificate reiterated the 2017 findings, declaring her condition permanent without further reassessment. A September 2019 social enquiry noted comprehensive needs for hygiene, dressing, cleaning, laundry, mobility (with cane or support), transport, shopping, and money management; she could feed herself but had complete memory loss, disorientation, and no leisure activities. Her daughters provided care. A 2020 forensic exam confirmed unchanged status since 2016: unused left arm, walking difficulties preventing independent hygiene, dressing, or cooking, requiring permanent help. A June 2020 social report echoed prior findings; Barthel score was 30/100 due to a fracture.

Diaconeasa again challenged the certificate. Hunedoara County Court (25 November 2020) cancelled it. The Court of Appeal (12 April 2021, final) upheld the Commission, interpreting the Order’s Chapter 7.III.2 strictly: severe disability with assistant requires total immobility or incapacity, not her “assisted independence.” It dismissed empathy-based arguments, insisting on objective legal criteria, and noted her indoor mobility with cane/support excluded her from the highest support category.

Domestic law (Disability Act Articles 35, 85–88; Methodological Rules) emphasizes complex, continuous bio-psycho-social assessments prioritizing the person’s interests, social inclusion, and choice, not pity. The 2022–2027 National Strategy called for shifting from purely medical models and clarifying individualized support. The UN CRPD (ratified by Romania) and EU law similarly stress independent living.

These facts underpinned the Article 8 claim: the reclassification and assistant withdrawal ignored consistent medical/social evidence of profound dependence, lacked thorough severity assessment or alternatives (e.g., other services), and applied rigid criteria without balancing her autonomy against State resources, resulting in loss of independence despite family support. The Court later found a violation on these grounds. (Word count: 612)

The case of Podchasov v. Russia concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding respect for private life and correspondence. The applicant, Anton Valeryevich Podchasov (born 1981, resident in Barnaul), is a user of Telegram, a free messaging app used by millions in Russia and globally. Telegram employs custom server-client encryption by default in “cloud chats” but permits users to enable end-to-end encryption in “secret chats,” ensuring only the sender and recipient can access message contents.

On 28 June 2017, Telegram Messenger LLP was registered as an “Internet communication organiser” (ICO) under Section 10.1 of the 2006 Information Act (as amended). This imposed obligations to store all users’ communications data (voice, text, visual, sound, video or other electronic messages sent, received, transmitted or processed) for one year and the contents of those communications for six months, on Russian territory. ICOs must also submit stored data to law-enforcement authorities or security services in circumstances specified by law, along with any information needed to decrypt encrypted messages. Additional rules require ICOs providing instant messaging to identify users by mobile telephone numbers and to install government-specified equipment enabling remote, around-the-clock access by security services to stored data, contents and decryption keys.

On 12 July 2017 the Federal Security Service (FSB) issued a disclosure order to Telegram under Section 10.1(4.1) and FSB Order no. 432. Citing six court decisions of 10 July 2017, it demanded technical details—including IP addresses, port numbers and encryption-key material—sufficient to decrypt communications of six Telegram users (identified by mobile numbers) suspected of terrorism-related activities since 12 July 2017. The information was to be supplied by 19 July 2017.

Telegram refused, stating that the targeted users had activated secret chats and that compliance would require creating a backdoor that would weaken end-to-end encryption for all users. Telegram was fined by the Meshchanskiy District Court on 12 December 2017; the Taganskiy District Court later ordered the app blocked in Russia (judgments upheld on appeal). The app nevertheless remains available and functional.

On 12 March 2018 the applicant and 34 other users challenged the FSB order in the Meshchanskiy District Court. They argued that handing over encryption keys would enable decryption of every user’s communications, thereby violating their Article 8 rights, that the Information Act’s scope was excessively broad, and that no adequate safeguards existed against unjustified access. Once keys were obtained, they claimed, the FSB would possess the technical capacity to read all traffic without the judicial authorisation required by Russian law.

The District Court dismissed the complaint as inadmissible on 22 March 2018, holding that the order did not affect the plaintiffs’ rights (no further reasoning given). The Moscow City Court upheld the decision on 22 May 2018. A cassation appeal was refused by a Moscow City Court judge on 10 September 2018 for lack of significant legal violations; a further cassation appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court on 16 January 2019.

These events, together with the statutory retention, access and decryption regime, constitute the factual basis of the alleged Article 8 interference. The legislation imposes an indiscriminate, bulk duty of storage and supplies security services with remote access and decryption capabilities, affecting all Telegram users including the applicant. Subsequent government decrees (e.g., Orders nos. 743, 571 and 1526) detail procedures for remote equipment access and data delivery but do not alter the breadth of the underlying obligations. The applicant’s unsuccessful domestic challenge left him without an effective remedy against the risk that his own encrypted correspondence could be accessed.

The case of Podchasov v. Russia concerns a complaint by Telegram user Anton Valeryevich Podchasov under Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life and correspondence). It challenges Russian legislation imposing retention, access and decryption duties on “Internet communication organisers” (ICOs).

Telegram, used by millions including the applicant, defaults to server-client encryption but permits users to activate end-to-end encrypted “secret chats” readable only by sender and recipient. On 28 June 2017 Telegram was registered as an ICO under section 10.1 of the 2006 Information Act (as amended). This required it to store all user communications data (voice, text, visual, sound, video or other) for one year and contents for six months on Russian territory, to furnish those data to law-enforcement or security services in circumstances specified by law, and to supply any information needed to decrypt encrypted messages. Instant-messaging ICOs must also identify users by mobile number. Government and FSB orders further require ICOs to install equipment giving the FSB round-the-clock remote access, to search and deliver stored data and decryption material automatically or on request, and to respond to requests within three to thirty days using identifiers such as telephone numbers or protocol headers.

On 12 July 2017 the FSB issued a disclosure order citing six Telegram accounts linked to terrorism suspicions and six court decisions. It demanded IP addresses, ports and encryption keys “necessary and sufficient” to decrypt those users’ communications from that date, to be supplied within one week. Telegram refused, stating that the users employed secret chats and that compliance would necessitate a backdoor weakening encryption for all users. Courts subsequently fined Telegram and ordered its blocking in Russia (though the service remains accessible).

On 12 March 2018 the applicant and 34 others challenged the FSB order, arguing that handover of keys would enable decryption of every user’s communications, allowing the FSB to access them without the judicial authorisation otherwise required by Russian law. They highlighted the Act’s extremely broad retention duty and the absence of safeguards against unjustified disclosure. Domestic courts declared the complaint inadmissible on the ground that the order did not affect the plaintiffs’ rights; further appeals and cassation proceedings failed.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 8 violation. The statutory scheme creates an exceptionally wide-ranging and serious interference by mandating indiscriminate, long-term storage of all internet communications and related data. Safeguards governing subsequent access by law-enforcement and security services are inadequate. The additional obligation to decrypt end-to-end encrypted communications is inherently disproportionate, as it cannot be fulfilled without undermining encryption for the entire user base. The impugned legislation therefore exceeds the margin of appreciation and is not necessary in a democratic society.

Citing six court decisions of 10 July 2017, the FSB demanded technical data—including IP addresses, port numbers and encryption keys—sufficient to decrypt communications of six Telegram users suspected of terrorism-related activities, to be supplied by 19 July 2017.
