The case of Vagdalt v. Hungary concerns the applicant’s inability, as a biological father, to contest a competing paternity declaration and establish his own legal paternity over his daughter under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicant, István Vagdalt, had an extramarital relationship with E.R. (married to Cs.H.) between 2000 and 2005. On 27 September 2002 E.R. gave birth to their daughter C. Under the old Family Act’s presumption of paternity, C. was registered as the child of E.R. and her husband Cs.H. The applicant maintained regular contact with C. until the relationship with E.R. ended in 2005.

Lacking standing to sue in his own name, the applicant in May 2006 asked the Guardianship Authority to appoint a guardian ad litem for C. to rebut Cs.H.’s paternity. After initial refusals (on the ground that C.’s status was settled) and Supreme Court remittal, a guardian was appointed in August 2008. Expert psychological evidence showed C.’s emotional attachment to the applicant, her awareness of the disputed origins, and the harm caused by uncertainty; the authorities and courts (up to the Supreme Court in 2010) accepted that clarification served C.’s best interests.

The guardian’s action succeeded: a DNA test confirmed the applicant as biological father. In November 2010 the Sopron District Court annulled Cs.H.’s paternity (upheld on appeal in April 2011) and his name was deleted from the register.

The applicant immediately declared paternity, but without E.R.’s consent it was ineffective. On 3 June 2011 Cs.H., with E.R.’s consent, also declared paternity; the registrar re-entered him as father on 7 July 2011. The applicant had no administrative decision to challenge and his subsequent complaints (including to prosecutors and police alleging forgery) were dismissed.

Further guardianship proceedings followed. After multiple remittals, the Kúria in May 2014 confirmed that clarification remained in C.’s best interests. A guardian was appointed in August 2014 with a mandate to seek both annulment of Cs.H.’s paternity and establishment of the applicant’s. The guardian, however, sued only for establishment of the applicant’s paternity (May 2015). Courts dismissed the claim because paternity was not vacant and the guardian had failed to challenge Cs.H. The Kúria upheld this in January 2017.

A second action by the guardian against Cs.H. (March 2017) was declared time-barred under the new Civil Code (in force March 2014). The one-year limit applicable to the child ran from the 2014 appointment; earlier proceedings on a different subject-matter did not interrupt it. The Constitutional Court declined to examine the applicant’s complaint.

The applicant’s own 2018 civil action against C. and E.R. remained pending as of 2023.

These facts illustrate the alleged Article 8 violation: despite confirmed biological paternity and repeated findings that proceedings served C.’s interests, the applicant was wholly dependent on a State-appointed guardian who failed to pursue the necessary parallel challenge in time; successive delays, remittals and a rigid time-bar extinguished any prospect of establishing a legal parent-child relationship.

**Case Summary: Vagdalt v. Hungary (ECtHR, Application no. 9525/19)**

The applicant, István Vagdalt (born 1961), had an extramarital relationship with E.R. (married to Cs.H.) from 2000 to 2005. Their daughter C. was born on 27 September 2002 and registered as the child of E.R. and Cs.H. under the old Family Act’s presumption that a child born in wedlock is fathered by the mother’s husband. The applicant maintained regular contact with C. until the relationship ended in 2005.

Unable to initiate proceedings himself, the applicant in May 2006 asked the Guardianship Authority to appoint a guardian ad litem for C. to challenge Cs.H.’s paternity. Initial refusals (on grounds that C.’s status was settled and challenge was not in her best interests) were reversed after Supreme Court remittal. In August 2008, a guardian was appointed based on expert psychological opinions finding C. had an emotional attachment to the applicant, was aware of paternity uncertainties, and that clarification served her healthy development and best interests (per Family Act s. 1(2)). Courts, including the Supreme Court (January 2010), upheld this, noting ongoing conflicts harmed C. despite her stable family environment.

The guardian sued in December 2008. A DNA test confirmed the applicant as biological father. In November 2010 (upheld April 2011), the Sopron District Court annulled Cs.H.’s paternity and ordered deletion from the register.

In May 2011, the applicant declared paternity, but without E.R.’s consent it had no effect. On 3 June 2011, Cs.H. (with E.R.’s consent) made a full-effect paternity declaration; the registrar re-entered him as father on 7 July 2011. The applicant had no avenue to challenge these non-decisional acts. His prosecutor’s request (dismissed 2016) and criminal complaint for document forgery (discontinued 2012, as registrars need not verify biology) failed.

Further requests for proceedings followed. After remittals, a 2012 Guardianship Authority decision (citing C.’s confusion from early belief the applicant was her father and resulting psychological harm) appointed a guardian, who sued to challenge Cs.H. A court later ordered withdrawal; the Kúria (May 2014) reversed, holding clarification in C.’s best interests. A new guardian was appointed in August 2014 to seek annulment of Cs.H.’s paternity and establishment of the applicant’s.

In May 2015, the guardian sued only to establish the applicant’s paternity (omitting challenge to Cs.H., contrary to the mandate). The Sárvár District Court initially granted it (July 2015), but the High Court dismissed (paternity not vacant due to Cs.H.’s 2011 declaration) and the Kúria upheld (January 2017). A Constitutional Court complaint was dismissed (September 2018).

In March 2017, the guardian sued to annul Cs.H.’s paternity. The Veszprém District Court dismissed it as time-barred (February 2018, upheld June 2018): under the new Civil Code (in force March 2014), a minor child’s action must be brought within one year of learning relevant facts (here, from the August 2014 appointment); prior proceedings on a different subject did not interrupt the limit. Transitional rules applied old-law time-limits only until March 2017.

The applicant initiated further civil proceedings in 2018 (still pending as of February 2023). The case concerns his inability, under Article 8, to contest Cs.H.’s declaration and establish his own paternity, due to delays, remittals, guardian failures, and time-barring that extinguished prospects of success despite confirmed biology and findings that proceedings served C.’s best interests. The case of Vlahović v. Montenegro (Application no. 62444/10) concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic court judgment and two administrative decisions issued in 2010 in the applicant’s favour. The applicant, Zoran Vlahović, a Croatian national living in Split, is a co-owner of two plots of land (nos. 1084/4 and 1084/10) in Herceg Novi, Montenegro, registered as an uncategorised road. He holds one-third and one-half shares respectively. Another co-owner, M.D., held smaller shares at the relevant time.

In June 2005, M.D. constructed a sewage collection system on the plots and paved the road with concrete, without the consent of other co-owners or municipal authorisation. The applicant and another co-owner initiated civil proceedings against M.D. An expert witness found that the concrete paving accelerated rainwater flow, that existing drainage was inadequate, and that unregulated runoff risked flooding, soil deposits and erosion damaging adjacent land (including the claimants’). The sewage system also lacked authorisation and might not meet construction standards.

On 26 February 2010 the Herceg Novi Court of First Instance held that M.D. had unlawfully violated the applicant’s property rights and ordered him to remove the constructions within 15 days. On 29 and 30 March 2010 the municipal police issued two decisions requiring removal of the sewage system and concrete paving; these were upheld on 27 April 2010. The civil judgment became final on 8 February 2011 after the High Court upheld the relevant parts.

On 18 May 2010 M.D. transferred his ownership shares to the municipality free of charge. The municipality then sought expropriation of the plots to regularise an access road. From late 2010 onwards the municipal police repeatedly postponed enforcement of their own decisions; all such postponements were quashed by the Chief Administrator. An enforcement order issued on the civil judgment in April 2011 was quashed in October 2011 because M.D. was no longer a co-owner and expropriation proceedings were pending. In 2012 the courts refused to treat the municipality as the successor debtor, advising the applicant to bring fresh civil proceedings against it.

Expropriation requests were rejected or stayed. In April 2015 an interim measure prohibited removal of the constructions pending expropriation, on the ground that enforcement would leave occupants without road access or water/sewage services and cause nearly irreparable harm. The Supreme Court later stated that expropriation proceedings could not obstruct enforcement of the removal orders. In April 2021 the Court of First Instance terminated enforcement of the 2010 judgment, citing the change in ownership; this was upheld on appeal. The applicant repeatedly invoked statutory provisions allowing enforcement against a successor in title, but these arguments were initially rejected.

As of December 2023 the 2010 judgment and the two police decisions remained unenforced, the interim measure was still in force, and expropriation proceedings were pending before the Administrative Court. The applicant’s constitutional appeal against non-enforcement was dismissed in 2022, although a later Constitutional Court decision found that one first-instance ruling had failed to address the successor-liability provision.

These facts form the basis of the complaints under Article 6 § 1 (right of access to court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) concerning the unjustified failure to enforce final and binding decisions in the applicant’s favour. A prior unilateral declaration by the Government (leading to the case being struck out in 2016) had not been honoured, resulting in restoration of the application in 2020.

Montenegro (Application no. 62444/10) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a final 2010 domestic judgment and two contemporaneous administrative decisions in favour of the applicant, Zoran Vlahović. The land was registered as an uncategorised road. An expert found the works accelerated rainwater runoff, risking flooding, soil deposits and erosion of adjacent plots, and lacked proper authorisation or construction standards.

On 18 May 2010 M.D. transferred his remaining shares to the municipality free of charge. The municipality then sought expropriation so an access road could be built. Between late 2010 and 2019 the municipal police issued repeated postponements of its own removal decisions; all were quashed. An April 2011 enforcement order on the court judgment was quashed in October 2011 because M.D. was no longer owner and expropriation was pending. The applicant’s request that the municipality itself enforce the judgment was dismissed in 2012 on the ground that the municipality had not been a party; he was told to sue it separately.

Expropriation was first rejected in 2012, then stayed in 2015. In April 2015 an interim measure (still in force) prohibited removal pending expropriation, citing “nearly irreparable damage” to occupants who had no other access or utility connections. Enforcement of the judgment was formally terminated in April 2021 (upheld September 2021) because the named debtor was no longer owner; the applicant was again directed to new proceedings against the municipality. The Constitutional Court dismissed a 2017 appeal in January 2022 but, in June 2023, quashed a 2019 first-instance decision for failing to examine whether successor liability applied under the Enforcement Act.

A 2021 expropriation decision was quashed in November 2022; fresh proceedings remained pending before the Administrative Court as of December 2023. Throughout, the applicant repeatedly sought enforcement against both M.D. and the municipality, invoking successor provisions of the Enforcement Acts, without success. The 2010 judgment and decisions therefore remained unenforced more than 13 years later. The application, initially struck out in 2016 after a unilateral declaration, was restored in 2020 when the promised enforcement never materialised.

These facts underpin the complaints of unjustified non-enforcement of a final judgment and administrative decisions, violating the right of access to court and the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The case of Kaczmarek v. Poland (Application no. 16974/14) concerns complaints by Honorata Kaczmarek, a Polish national born in 1960 and living in Gdynia, under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding her private life and correspondence. She is the wife of politician J.K., who served as Minister of the Interior during the relevant events.

In 2007, Polish authorities, including the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CAB) and Warsaw Regional Prosecutor, investigated allegations of trading in influence. An entrapment operation planned for 6 July 2007 at the Ministry of Agriculture was leaked, leading to the “land scandal” involving senior politicians. J.K. was accused of warning the Minister of Agriculture, resulting in his dismissal on 8 August 2007.

On 11 July 2007, the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor and Internal Security Agency (ISA) opened a pre-trial investigation (V Ds. 324/07) into hampering the operation, with J.K. as a witness. Materials related to alleged false testimony by J.K. were severed into a separate case (V Ds. 400/07), in which he became a suspect. The ISA conducted covert surveillance of J.K. (operation GAMMA), while the CAB monitored the applicant’s telephone calls. The prosecutor also obtained recordings and transcripts of her calls under operation GWIAZDA 4. Both investigations were discontinued in late 2009, as no criminal offence was established.

On 31 August 2007, Deputy Prosecutors General D.B. and J.E., along with other prosecutors and representatives of the ISA and CAB, held a live-broadcast press conference on public television to discuss the land scandal. J.E. played a recording of a brief telephone conversation between the applicant and K.K., then Chief Police Commandant, in which K.K. asked for her house number (given as “twenty”) and arranged to visit. J.E. identified the applicant as J.K.’s wife, stating no further comments were needed. Permission to disclose the recording had been given orally by the head of the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor’s Office under Article 156 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

In December 2008, Newsweek Polska published an article on the investigation; related proceedings for disseminating investigative material were discontinued in 2010. In spring 2009, Dziennik published articles indicating access to transcripts of the applicant’s intercepted calls, prompting an investigation into disclosure of confidential material that was discontinued in 2010 as no perpetrator could be identified.

The applicant sued J.E. in 2008 for damages and an apology over breach of personal rights. Domestic courts, after remittal by the Supreme Court, ultimately dismissed the claim in 2016, finding the disclosure did not unlawfully infringe her rights, as it did not damage her reputation and occurred in a professional capacity amid public interest.

During the operations, authorities collected transcripts of the applicant’s private conversations with her husband and son. She requested destruction of this material in 2010, but prosecutors refused, citing its status as trial material and inapplicability of destruction provisions. After 2010 amendments to the Code of Criminal Procedure allowing destruction applications, conflicting information was provided. The applicant applied to the Warsaw Mokotów District Court in 2013–2014, which dismissed the request in 2014 (decision classified in part and unappealable). The files remain stored securely as non-archival material subject to a minimum five-year retention.

The Court held that the disclosure of the recording and the storage/retention of data from surveillance (of which the applicant was not a target) constituted interferences with Article 8 rights that were not “in accordance with the law.”

Additionally, in operation GWIAZDA 4, the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor obtained recordings and transcripts of the applicant’s calls. Both investigations were discontinued in late 2009 on the grounds that no criminal offence had been established.

On 31 August 2007, Deputy Prosecutors General (including J.E.), Warsaw Regional Prosecutor’s Office prosecutors, and representatives of the ISA and CAB held a live-broadcast press conference on public television to inform the public about the land scandal. During the conference, J.E. played a recording of a telephone conversation between the applicant and K.K. (then Chief Police Commandant), in which K.K. asked for her house number (“Twenty”) and said he would arrive shortly. The case of Kural v. Türkiye (ECtHR Application no. 84388/17) concerns a deputy chief of police's challenge to an inter-provincial transfer and the authorities' failure to comply with a stay-of-execution order.

At the relevant time the applicant, Suat Kural (born 1965), served as deputy chief of police in Eskişehir with the rank of “chief of police of the second grade.” On 20 January 2014 he was temporarily assigned to the Eskişehir Police Academy. On 3 February 2014 the General Security Directorate of the Ministry of the Interior transferred him to the post of “lecturer chief of police” at the Samsun Police Academy, citing “needs of the service.” His rank, grade and salary remained unchanged.

The applicant brought an action for annulment before the Eskişehir Administrative Court and requested a stay of execution. He contended that the decision was unlawful, taken without regard to the public interest or service needs, and contrary to the Regulation on Appointments and Transfers of Members of the Security Forces. On 10 April 2014 the Administrative Court granted the stay. It held that although the authorities possessed discretion in transfers, they had failed to cite specific circumstances justifying the exercise of that discretion, had made no mention of any negative work-related remarks, and had not shown necessity for an appointment outside the ordinary collective-appointment period. Because the applicant’s family resided in Eskişehir, implementation of the transfer risked damage that would be difficult or impossible to remedy, satisfying the conditions of section 27 of the Administrative Procedure Act (Law no. 2577). An objection by the Directorate was dismissed on 13 May 2014.

Despite the stay, on 23 May 2014 the Directorate re-appointed the applicant to the same Samsun post, invoking section 28 of Law no. 2577 and the absence of a vacant position in Eskişehir. On 1 July 2014 it transferred him to the Erzurum Police Academy on the ground that his turn to serve in the second service region had arrived. On 20 November 2014 the Administrative Court annulled the original February decision, repeating its earlier findings of unlawfulness.

Subsequent Directorate decisions of 7 January and 27 March 2015 purported to reassign the applicant (first temporarily, then permanently) to his former deputy-chief post in Eskişehir. The applicant stated, however, that he never actually resumed duties there and was forced to retire in May 2015 while still in Erzurum.

On appeal the Supreme Administrative Court, on 17 June 2015, quashed the annulment. It held that the authorities could reassign personnel to posts of equal or higher grade without preserving original titles or duties, that both Eskişehir and Samsun lay within the first service region, and that nothing indicated the discretion had been exercised on subjective grounds contrary to the public interest. On 22 December 2015 the Administrative Court, bound by that ruling, dismissed the applicant’s action; the decision became final on 18 February 2016.

Meanwhile, on 12 June 2014 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, alleging a violation of Article 6 of the Convention (and Article 36 of the Constitution) because of non-enforcement of the stay-of-execution order. On 2 June 2017 the Constitutional Court declared the application manifestly ill-founded. Stay-of-execution orders were not final judgments; the right of access to court required only that non-enforcement not render a possible eventual favourable decision impossible or excessively difficult to implement. The applicant had retained his statutory employment rights, had not complained of other rights violations, and the non-compliance had not reached that threshold.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the authorities’ persistent non-compliance with the stay order violated Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention. The Court examined the complaint under the access-to-court limb of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Kural v. Türkiye (Application no. 84388/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right of access to a court) arising from the non-compliance by Turkish authorities with a stay-of-execution order in administrative proceedings over the transfer of a senior police officer.

The applicant, Suat Kural (born 1965), was a deputy chief of police in Eskişehir holding the rank of second-grade chief of police. On 20 January 2014 he was temporarily assigned to the Eskişehir Police Academy. On 3 February 2014 the General Security Directorate of the Ministry of the Interior transferred him to the post of “lecturer chief of police” at the Samsun Police Academy, citing “needs of the service.” His rank, grade and pay remained unchanged.

Kural challenged the decision in the Eskişehir Administrative Court, seeking both annulment and a stay of execution. He argued that the transfer was unlawful, failed to take account of the public interest or service needs, and was not supported by any negative performance remarks.

On 10 April 2014 the Administrative Court granted the stay. It held that while the authorities possessed discretion in transferring security-force personnel, that discretion had to be exercised in accordance with the public interest, service requirements and the Regulation on Appointments and Transfers. The Directorate had cited general provisions of the Regulation and Law no. 657 but had given no specific reasons demonstrating a lawful exercise of discretion. The transfer also fell outside the Regulation’s ordinary period for collective appointments; although exceptions were permitted in cases of necessity, none had been established. Because the applicant’s family lived in Eskişehir, implementation risked damage that would be difficult or impossible to remedy, satisfying the conditions of section 27 of the Administrative Procedure Act (Law no. 2577). An objection by the Directorate was dismissed as final by the Eskişehir Regional Administrative Court on 13 May 2014.

Despite the stay, on 23 May 2014 the Directorate re-appointed Kural to the identical Samsun post, invoking section 28 of Law no. 2577 and the absence of a vacant position. On 1 July 2014 it transferred him instead to the Erzurum Police Academy on the ground that his turn to serve in the second region (as defined by the Regulation) had arrived.

On 20 November 2014 the Administrative Court annulled the original 3 February decision, repeating its earlier findings of unlawfulness. The Directorate then issued decisions on 7 January and 27 March 2015 purporting to return Kural to Eskişehir, first temporarily and then permanently. Kural maintained, however, that he was forced to retire in May 2015 while still in Erzurum and never actually resumed work in Eskişehir.

On 17 June 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the annulment judgment. It ruled that the authorities could reassign personnel to posts of equal or higher grade without preserving original titles or duties, that both Eskişehir and Samsun lay in the first service region, and that there was no indication the discretion had been exercised on subjective grounds contrary to the public interest. Complying with this ruling, the Administrative Court dismissed Kural’s action on 22 December 2015; the decision became final on 18 February 2016.

Kural had already lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court on 12 June 2014 complaining of the non-enforcement of the stay. On 2 June 2017 that court rejected the complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It observed that stay-of-execution orders are not final judgments on the merits and that, in any event, non-compliance had not rendered a potential final decision in Kural’s favour impossible or excessively difficult to implement; he had retained his statutory employment rights and no other fundamental rights were implicated.

Domestic law (Constitution Articles 36, 125 and 138; Law no. 2577, sections 27 and 28) required administrative authorities to implement stay-of-execution decisions without delay and in any event within 30 days. Subsequent legislative amendments that would have conditioned enforcement on the availability of vacant posts were later declared unconstitutional.

These facts form the core of the alleged violation: the authorities’ continued transfers of Kural in the face of a binding stay, thereby undermining the effectiveness of judicial protection of his access to court.

The case of Kural v. Türkiye concerns the non-compliance by Turkish authorities with a stay-of-execution order issued in administrative proceedings over the transfer of a police officer, which the applicant alleged violated his rights under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention (access to court and effective remedy).

The applicant, Suat Kural (born 1965), was a deputy chief of police in Eskişehir holding the rank of second-grade chief of police. On 3 February 2014 the General Security Directorate transferred him to serve as lecturer chief of police at the Samsun Police Academy, citing “needs of the service.” His rank, grade and salary remained unchanged.

He sought annulment of the decision and a stay of execution in the Eskişehir Administrative Court, arguing that the transfer was unlawful and failed to take account of the public interest or service needs. On 10 April 2014 the court granted the stay. It held that while the authorities possessed discretion to transfer security-force members, that discretion had to be exercised in accordance with the public interest, service needs and the applicable Regulation. The authorities had given no concrete reasons, cited no negative performance remarks, and had acted outside the Regulation’s ordinary appointment window without demonstrating necessity. Because the move was inter-provincial and the applicant’s family lived in Eskişehir, implementation risked damage that would be difficult or impossible to remedy, satisfying the statutory conditions for a stay.

The Directorate’s objection was dismissed by the Eskişehir Regional Administrative Court on 13 May 2014. Nevertheless, on 23 May 2014 the Directorate issued a fresh appointment to the same Samsun post, relying on a statutory provision and the claimed absence of a vacant position. On 1 July 2014 it transferred him instead to the Erzurum Police Academy, asserting that his turn had come to serve in the second region of the country.

On 20 November 2014 the Administrative Court annulled the original transfer, repeating its earlier findings of unlawfulness. The Supreme Administrative Court later quashed that judgment (17 June 2015), holding that both Eskişehir and Samsun lay in the first region and that the authorities’ discretion had not been shown to have been exercised on subjective or improper grounds. The Administrative Court accordingly dismissed the action (22 December 2015); the decision became final on 18 February 2016.

Although subsequent Directorate decisions of January and March 2015 purported to return the applicant to Eskişehir, he maintained that he was never able to resume duties there and was forced to retire in May 2015 while still in Erzurum.

On 12 June 2014 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court complaining of the non-enforcement of the stay. That court dismissed the application as manifestly ill-founded (2 June 2017), reasoning that stay-of-execution orders are not final judgments and that non-compliance had not rendered any eventual merits decision impossible or excessively difficult to implement, the applicant having retained his statutory employment rights.

Domestic law (Constitution Arts. 36, 125 and 138; Law no. 2577 ss. 27–28) required authorities to give effect to stay-of-execution decisions without delay, subject only to limited statutory exceptions later declared unconstitutional.

These facts—the grant of a stay, the authorities’ subsequent re-appointments that circumvented it, and the domestic courts’ ultimate dismissal of the underlying action—form the core of the alleged violations of the right of access to court.
001-231550:
The case of Association of People of Silesian Nationality (in liquidation) v. Poland (application no. 26821/17) concerns a complaint under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the dissolution and liquidation of the applicant association. The association, registered in Poland in 2011, aimed to promote Silesian national consciousness, culture, and heritage among those identifying as Silesian. Silesia is a historic region in south-western Poland with a layered past involving Polish, Bohemian, Habsburg, Prussian, German, and post-World War II Polish control. A 2011 national census recorded over 800,000 people declaring Silesian nationality, either solely or alongside Polish identity.

On 21 December 2011, the Opole District Court registered the association. Its memorandum of association referred to “Silesian nationality” (but not a “Silesian nation” or “national minority”) and explicitly stated that it would not register electoral lists. Membership was open to anyone declaring affiliation with Silesian nationality. The association acquired legal personality upon registration in the National Court Register.

The Opole regional prosecutor appealed, arguing that the memorandum violated section 2 of the 2005 Act on National and Ethnic Minorities and Regional Language. That Act lists recognized national and ethnic minorities but does not include Silesians. The prosecutor contended that referencing a non-existent “Silesian nationality” and conditioning membership on it was unlawful.

On 7 September 2012, the Opole Regional Court dismissed the appeal. It held that registration did not create a Silesian nationality or minority, nor confer electoral privileges reserved for registered national-minority organizations under the Electoral Code (such as exemption from the 5% vote threshold for parliamentary seats). The memorandum’s explicit refusal to register electoral committees further supported this view.

The prosecutor appealed to the Supreme Court. On 5 December 2013, the Supreme Court quashed the Regional Court’s decision and remitted the case. It found the association’s name misleading, as media reports suggested judicial confirmation of a “Silesian nation.” This could weaken the Polish State’s unity and integrity. The Court also feared the association might later claim Electoral Code privileges despite its memorandum. Drawing on prior case-law, including Gorzelik and Others v. Poland, the Supreme Court stressed that nationality choice applies only to objectively existing nations formed historically. Neither the 2011 census nor the 2005 Act recognized a Silesian nation or minority.

The case returned to the District Court. After the association refused to amend its name and key memorandum provisions referring to “Silesian nationality” (despite amending other clauses at an extraordinary general meeting), the District Court on 9 January 2015 dissolved the association and ordered its liquidation under the Law on Associations. It cited a flagrant, repeated failure to comply with the law and no prospect of reform. The court again invoked Gorzelik, holding that references to an unrecognized nationality breached the 2005 Act and Electoral Code.

The Regional Court dismissed the association’s appeal on 18 June 2015, noting unchanged circumstances and continued refusal to amend. The Supreme Court refused a cassation appeal on 12 October 2016.

The applicant association alleged that these measures violated its Article 11 right to freedom of association. The European Court of Human Rights later found that the dissolution and liquidation were not based on relevant and sufficient reasons and that the Polish authorities had failed to demonstrate a pressing social need for the interference.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) case Association of People of Silesian Nationality (in liquidation) v. Poland (Application no. 26821/17, judgment of 14 March 2024) concerned the forced dissolution of a Polish association registered in 2011. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 11 (freedom of association) of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from Polish court orders dissolving the group and placing it into liquidation.

Silesia is a historic region now located in south-western Poland. It passed through Polish, Bohemian, Habsburg, Prussian and German control before most of it was incorporated into Poland after the Second World War. A 2011 national census recorded 430,798 people declaring both Polish and Silesian nationality and a further 375,635 declaring exclusively Silesian nationality.

On 21 December 2011 the Opole District Court registered the association under the name “Association of People of Silesian Nationality.” Its memorandum of association (as later amended) stated that it would operate throughout Poland, would not register electoral lists, and pursued cultural and educational aims such as awakening Silesian national consciousness, restoring Silesian culture, promoting knowledge of the region and preserving its heritage. Ordinary membership was open to anyone who declared an affiliation to Silesian nationality. The association described itself as “an organisation of persons declaring their affiliation to Silesian nationality.”

The Opole regional prosecutor appealed the registration, arguing that the memorandum contravened the 2005 Act on National and Ethnic Minorities and Regional Language because it referred to a “Silesian nationality” that does not exist in Polish law and made membership contingent on that nationality. On 7 September 2012 the Opole Regional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that registration neither created a Silesian nation or minority nor entitled the association to electoral privileges reserved for recognised national minorities; the memorandum expressly forbade the registration of electoral committees.

The Supreme Court quashed that decision on 5 December 2013 and remitted the case. It ruled that the association’s name was misleading: press reports had treated registration as judicial confirmation of a Silesian nation, which risked undermining the unity of the Polish State and might allow the group to claim an exemption from the 5 % electoral threshold granted to recognised national-minority organisations. Relying on the ECHR’s earlier judgment in Gorzelik and Others v. Poland, the Supreme Court held that freedom to choose a nationality applies only to nations that exist objectively as the product of historical processes. Neither the 2011 census results nor the 2005 Act (which does not list Silesians) established the existence of a Silesian nation.

Following remittal, the Opole District Court on 9 January 2015 dissolved the association and ordered its liquidation under section 29 of the Law on Associations. The association had been invited to amend its name and all references to “Silesian nationality” but had refused to do so at an extraordinary general meeting in October 2014. The court considered that the group’s continued use of those terms constituted a flagrant and repeated breach of the 2005 Act and the Electoral Code, and that there was no prospect of reform. The Opole Regional Court upheld the dissolution on 18 June 2015; the Supreme Court refused a cassation appeal on 12 October 2016.

The ECHR later held that the dissolution was not based on relevant and sufficient reasons and that the Polish authorities had failed to demonstrate a pressing social need for the measure.

The ECtHR case Association of People of Silesian Nationality (in liquidation) v. Poland (no. 26821/17) concerned the 2015–16 dissolution and liquidation of a Polish association registered in 2011. The applicant alleged that this interfered with its Article 11 right to freedom of association.

Silesia is a historic region in south-western Poland. A 2011 census recorded 430,798 people declaring dual Polish-Silesian nationality and 375,635 declaring Silesian nationality alone. On 21 December 2011 the Opole District Court registered the Association of People of Silesian Nationality. Its memorandum avoided the phrases “Silesian nation” or “Silesian national minority,” referred only to “Silesian nationality,” and expressly stated that the association would not register electoral lists. Membership was open to anyone declaring affiliation to Silesian nationality. Statutory aims included awakening Silesian national consciousness, restoring Silesian culture, promoting knowledge of the region, and fostering contacts among Silesians. The association acquired legal personality upon registration.

It found the association’s name misleading: media reports had treated registration as judicial confirmation of a Silesian nation, which risked weakening the Polish State’s unity and integrity and might enable the association to invoke minority electoral privileges. The Court relied on its earlier case-law and the ECtHR’s Grand Chamber judgment in Gorzelik and Others v. Poland, stressing that freedom to choose nationality exists only in respect of nations that have arisen through an objective historical process; the 2011 census and the 2005 Act supplied no such recognition.

The association had been invited to amend its name and the clauses referring to “Silesian nationality” but had refused (an October 2014 general meeting altered only minor aims). The court characterised this as a flagrant, repeated breach of the law and of the memorandum, with no prospect of reform. It again invoked Gorzelik and held that continued use of “Silesian nationality” violated both the 2005 Act and the Electoral Code. The Regional Court upheld the dissolution on 18 June 2015; the Supreme Court refused cassation on 12 October 2016.

These facts—registration of an association whose identity and membership criteria were premised on a nationality unrecognised by Polish law, subsequent judicial findings that the name was misleading and potentially destabilising, the association’s refusal to amend, and the resulting dissolution—constituted the interference complained of under Article 11. The ECtHR later held that the interference was not shown to pursue a pressing social need and was therefore not based on relevant and sufficient reasons.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered its judgment in B.T. v. Russia (Application no. 15284/19) on 19 March 2024 (final 19 June 2024). The case concerns sex-based discrimination in parental-leave entitlements for male versus female police personnel under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) taken with Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the Convention.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1982 and residing in Vladikavkaz, served in the internal-affairs agencies from August 2008 until July 2017. From December 2013 he was head of the road police for the Digorskiy District, supervising traffic-safety, public-order and road-crime functions. He married T.S. on 14 April 2017; their daughter was born on 26 May 2017. The next day T.S. formally refused to care for the infant. She received gynaecological treatment from 2 to 15 June 2017. The applicant collected the child from the maternity hospital on 9 June and obtained a notarised certificate of the mother’s refusal on 10 June.

On 14 June 2017 he applied to his superior for parental leave until the child reached three years of age, citing the mother’s refusal and hospitalisation and enclosing the marriage and birth certificates plus the notarised refusal. The request was rejected the following day under section 56(8) of Federal Law No. 342-FZ on Service in Internal Affairs Agencies, on the ground that there was no evidence the child lacked maternal care for “objective reasons.” The applicant then stopped attending work. T.S. commenced divorce proceedings the same day, asking that the child’s residence be fixed with the applicant and that she be granted limited contact. The applicant was disciplined and dismissed on 7 and 11 July 2017 for unauthorised absence.

He challenged both the leave refusal and the dismissal in the Digorskiy District Court. Meanwhile the marriage was dissolved on 2 October 2017; residence was awarded to the applicant and T.S. received visiting rights on Sundays. On 9 November 2017 the District Court dismissed the claims. It relied on Constitutional Court rulings stressing the special public-service character of police work and the need to exclude any interruption that might harm public safety. Section 56(8) entitles a female officer who is a mother to parental leave in accordance with ordinary labour legislation, but a male officer who is a father may obtain it only if he is actually raising the child and the child lacks maternal care for objective reasons (the mother’s death, deprivation of parental authority, or prolonged hospitalisation, among others). The court examined the living-conditions report, paediatric records showing the applicant’s exclusive care, and T.S.’s testimony that she had not wanted the pregnancy for health reasons and had formally refused the child. It found, however, that her hospitalisation had ended on 15 June, later hospital records were unreliable, she had not been deprived of parental rights, and the visiting-rights order demonstrated her continued involvement. Consequently there was no objective absence of maternal care after 15 June, and the dismissal was lawful. Appeals to the republican Supreme Court and the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation were rejected in 2018.

The European Court applied its earlier findings in Gruba and Others v. Russia. It held that the sex-based difference in treatment pursued the legitimate aim of preserving police operational effectiveness but lacked a reasonable relationship of proportionality and therefore lacked a reasonable and objective justification. A violation of Article 14 taken with Article 8 was accordingly found.

The case of B.T. v. Russia concerns alleged sex discrimination under Article 14 taken with Article 8 of the Convention, arising from unequal parental-leave entitlements for male versus female police personnel.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1982, served in the internal-affairs agencies from August 2008 until July 2017. From December 2013 he headed the road-police unit in Digorskiy District, North Ossetia-Alania, supervising traffic safety, public order and related offences.

He married T.S. on 14 April 2017. Their daughter was born on 26 May 2017. The next day T.S. formally refused to care for the child. She was hospitalised in the gynaecology department from 2 to 15 June 2017. On 9 June the applicant collected the infant from the maternity hospital; a notarised certificate of T.S.’s refusal was issued the following day.

On 14 June the applicant applied for parental leave until the child turned three, stating that his wife refused to raise the child, was receiving medical treatment, and that he alone was providing care. He enclosed the marriage and birth certificates and the notarised refusal. The request was refused the next day under section 56(8) of Federal Law No. 342-FZ on Service in Internal Affairs Agencies, on the ground that there was no proof the child lacked maternal care for objective reasons. The applicant then stopped attending work.

On the same day T.S. petitioned for divorce, asking that the child’s residence be fixed with the applicant because of her poor health and lack of income, while seeking limited Sunday contact. The applicant was disciplined and dismissed on 7 and 11 July 2017 for unauthorised absence.

He challenged the leave refusal and dismissal in the Digorskiy District Court. Meanwhile, on 2 October 2017 the marriage was dissolved, the child’s residence was assigned to the applicant and T.S. was granted visiting rights.

On 9 November 2017 the District Court dismissed the claims. Citing Constitutional Court decisions, it stressed that police service is a special public-interest function whose operational effectiveness requires that personnel remain available; limitations on rights are therefore constitutionally permissible. Section 56(8) entitles female officers to parental leave automatically, but male officers only if they are actually raising a child who has no maternal care for objective reasons (mother’s death, deprivation of parental rights, prolonged hospitalisation, etc.). After examining the living-conditions report, medical records, paediatric visits and T.S.’s testimony, the court found that T.S. had not been deprived of parental authority, that later hospital-stay entries were unreliable, and that the divorce judgment showed she continued to participate in the child’s upbringing. Consequently there was no objective lack of maternal care after 15 June 2017 and the dismissal was lawful.

The republican Supreme Court and the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation rejected subsequent appeals in 2018.

The statutory distinction—automatic leave for policewomen versus conditional leave for policemen—underpins the discrimination complaint. The Court later applied its reasoning in Gruba and Others v. Russia, holding that the difference lacked a reasonable relationship of proportionality to the aim of maintaining police operational effectiveness.

The case of B.T. v. Russia (Application no. 15284/19) concerns alleged sex discrimination under Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 8, arising from differing parental leave entitlements for male and female police personnel.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1982, served in the internal affairs agencies from 2008 to 2017. From December 2013 he headed the road police in Digorskiy District, North Ossetia-Alania, supervising traffic policing for road safety, public order and related crimes.

He married T.S. on 14 April 2017. Their daughter A.T. was born on 26 May 2017. The next day T.S. refused to care for the child. She received gynaecological treatment from 2–15 June 2017. The applicant collected the child from hospital on 9 June; a notarised document of 10 June recorded T.S.’s refusal.

On 14 June 2017 the applicant requested parental leave until the child turned three, citing his wife’s refusal, her hospitalisation and his sole care of the infant. He enclosed marriage and birth certificates plus the notarised refusal and sought urgent action.

The request was refused on 15 June under section 56(8) of Federal Law no. 342-FZ on Service in Internal Affairs Agencies, for lack of proof that the child was without maternal care for objective reasons. The applicant then ceased attending work. That same day T.S. petitioned for divorce, citing poor health and no income, and asked that the child reside with the applicant (with Sunday contact for her).

The applicant was disciplined and dismissed on 7 and 11 July 2017 for unauthorised absence. He challenged the refusal of leave and his dismissal in the Digorskiy District Court.

On 2 October 2017 the marriage was dissolved; the child’s residence was fixed with the applicant and T.S. given Sunday visiting rights.

On 9 November 2017 the District Court dismissed the claims. It invoked Constitutional Court rulings that police service is a special public function justifying restrictions on rights, and that denying parental leave to fathers who raise children jointly with the mother balances public and private interests. Section 56(8) grants leave to male personnel only if they raise a child without maternal care for objective reasons (mother’s death, loss of parental authority or prolonged hospitalisation). Evidence of the applicant’s care (hospital collection, paediatric visits) was noted, but T.S. had not been deprived of parental rights, some hospital records were unreliable, she was not hospitalised when he stopped work, and the divorce order showed her continued involvement via contact rights. Thus no objective absence of maternal care existed and the dismissal was lawful.

Appeals to the republican Supreme Court and the Russian Supreme Court failed.

Under the relevant law, female police employees who are mothers receive parental leave until the child is three in accordance with labour legislation. Male employees who are fathers receive it only if the child lacks maternal care for objective reasons, together with associated benefits provided they do not conflict with the service law.

The European Court applied its earlier findings in Gruba and Others v. Russia. It held there was no reasonable relationship of proportionality between the legitimate aim of preserving police operational effectiveness and the difference in treatment between male and female personnel. The difference therefore lacked reasonable and objective justification, amounting to a violation of Article 14 taken with Article 8.

The applicant, born in 2006, was placed in the Šaltinėlis foster home (run by nuns) from 2008 to 2013 after his parents’ rights were restricted. In late 2018 his subsequent guardian reported that the applicant had disclosed being sexually abused there by three older boys (A.K., K.S. and A.D.). Police opened a pre-trial investigation for sexual assault of a young child.

Investigators tapped the phones of the former director (E.) and the three boys, who were questioned as special witnesses and denied any abuse. E. recalled only a single vague complaint about A.K. that she had discussed with him. The 12-year-old applicant, interviewed by a judge with a psychologist present, stated that K.S. had anally raped him once while the others watched and laughed; he had told E., who replied “that is enough” and later gave him a toy car. A psychologist at a specialist children’s centre concluded that the applicant’s reactions were consistent with intimate trauma and raised a reasonable supposition of sexual violence. A forensic medical examination found no physical traces of anal penetration; any constipation was attributed to functional or psychosocial causes.

In April 2019 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, holding that no crime had been established. Numerous witnesses from the home had given no corroboration; the four persons implicated had denied everything; the medical report was negative; and the psychologist’s findings were merely probabilistic. No negligence by E. could be shown.

The applicant appealed, stressing Lithuanian Supreme Court case-law that, in child-sexual-abuse cases typically lacking eyewitnesses, a comprehensive court-ordered forensic psychiatric-psychological examination of the victim is essential to assess credibility, trauma and the capacity to testify. He argued that the existing psychological evaluation was insufficient and that the suspects had obvious motives to lie. The chief prosecutor rejected the appeal, stating that all feasible steps had been taken and that remaining doubts had to be resolved in the suspects’ favour.

The Kaunas District Court likewise dismissed the complaint without addressing the request for a forensic examination. It found the applicant’s account insufficiently detailed, noted the lapse of time, and accepted that no “objective” evidence existed beyond the child’s statements. The Kaunas Regional Court, in a final ruling, similarly held that further measures would serve no purpose, again without examining the necessity of the specialised forensic assessment the applicant had repeatedly invoked.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the authorities’ refusal to order the forensic examination, and the higher prosecutor’s and courts’ failure even to discuss that request, rendered the investigation into his arguable claim of sexual ill-treatment ineffective, in breach of the procedural limb of Article 3.

The case of E.L. v. Lithuania (Application no. 12471/20) concerns a complaint under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the Lithuanian authorities’ alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation into claims of sexual ill-treatment of a minor at a foster home.

The applicant, born in 2006, had his biological parents’ rights limited indefinitely in 2012. He resided at the Šaltinėlis foster home (run by the Sisters of the Immaculate Conception) from 2008 to 2013, after which Ms V.T. was appointed his guardian. In November 2018, following statements by the then-12-year-old applicant to V.T., the Kaunas childcare authority complained to police. This prompted a pre-trial investigation into sexual assault of a young child under Article 150 § 4 of the Criminal Code. The applicant alleged that, between 2008 and 2013, three older boys at the home—A.K. (born 1996), K.S. (born 1998) and A.D. (born 1992)—had sexually abused him, including one instance of anal rape by K.S. while the others watched. He claimed to have reported this to the home’s director, E., who punished the boys by restricting computer access and bought him a toy.

Investigative measures included court-authorised telephone tapping of E., A.K., K.S. and A.D. (who were questioned as “special witnesses” and denied any abuse); interviews with numerous former residents and staff, none of whom corroborated the claims; a psychological evaluation at the Užuovėja Children’s Assistance Centre, which found reactions consistent with possible intimate trauma sufficient to raise a reasonable suspicion of sexual violence; and a forensic medical examination, which found no physical evidence of anal intercourse (attributing constipation issues to functional/psychological factors, possibly linked to family trauma). The applicant was interviewed by a pre-trial judge in the presence of a psychologist and others, repeating his account.

In April 2019, a Kaunas regional prosecutor discontinued the investigation, concluding no crime had been established. The decision emphasised the lack of corroboration from witnesses (including E., who denied being informed of abuse and provided photos claiming the toy was a christening gift), the medical findings, and the psychologist’s conclusions being merely probabilistic. It invoked in dubio pro reo and the presumption of innocence.

The applicant, via V.T., appealed, arguing the investigation was incomplete. Citing Lithuanian Supreme Court case-law on child sexual abuse cases (typically lacking witnesses), he stressed that key evidence comprises the child’s testimony, statements from confidants, and—crucially—a comprehensive court-ordered forensic psychiatric and psychological examination to assess credibility, mental state and ability to testify. He noted the prosecutors’ reliance on potentially biased denials from possible suspects and those responsible for his safety, and their failure even to discuss such an examination.

The chief prosecutor, Kaunas District Court and Kaunas Regional Court successively upheld the discontinuation. They found all necessary steps taken, no “objective evidence” beyond the applicant’s “insufficiently detailed” statements, and gathering proof hindered by the time elapsed. None explicitly addressed the repeated requests for a forensic psychiatric-psychological examination or the Supreme Court precedents, stating that prosecutors independently decide on investigative actions and further steps would serve no purpose.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 procedural violation: an arguable claim of sexual ill-treatment of a vulnerable child in state care was met with an investigation that omitted a key forensic tool repeatedly sought, with higher authorities failing to engage with this omission.

**E.L. v. Lithuania (ECHR, Application no. 12471/20, Judgment of 9 April 2024)**

The applicant, a Lithuanian national born in 2006, complained under Article 3 of the Convention that Lithuanian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into his claims of sexual abuse while living at the Šaltinėlis foster home (run by the Sisters of the Immaculate Conception) from 2008 to 2013. His biological parents’ rights were limited in 2012, and the foster home served as his guardian. In December 2013, the Marijampolė Region District Court appointed Ms V.T. as his guardian after he developed a positive relationship with her and her partner; the foster home supported the transfer. He left the home in May 2013.

In November 2018, Kaunas police opened a pre-trial investigation into sexual assault of a young child (Article 150 § 4 of the Criminal Code) following a complaint by the Kaunas childcare authority. This was based on the applicant’s statements to V.T. that three older boys at the home—A.K. (b. 1996), K.S. (b. 1998), and A.D. (b. 1992)—had sexually abused him. He claimed he informed the then-director, E., who punished the boys by restricting computer access and bought him a toy.

Investigators tapped the phones of E., A.K., K.S., and A.D. (who were questioned as special witnesses and denied any involvement). E. stated she became director in July 2010; the applicant once reported an inappropriate request by A.K., after which she spoke to A.K. but received neither confirmation nor denial. In January 2019, the applicant (then 12) spent several days at the Užuovėja Children’s Assistance Centre. A psychologist concluded that his reactions suggested possible intimate trauma and that there was a reasonable supposition of sexual violence. A medical examination by the State Forensic Medicine Service found no physical evidence of forced anal intercourse; any constipation issues were deemed functional (physiological, psychological, or stress-related). The applicant, interviewed by a pre-trial judge in the presence of a psychologist and others, stated he had been anally raped once by K.S. while the others watched (one laughing), after which E. said “that is enough” and gave him a red toy car.

On 26 April 2019, a Kaunas regional prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding no crime. Witnesses from the foster home provided no corroboration. The three boys and E. denied the events. The psychologist’s report was treated as probabilistic and insufficient, and the medical findings offered no objective support. V.T.’s account derived solely from the applicant. No negligence by E. was established.

The applicant (via V.T.) appealed, arguing the investigation was incomplete. He cited Lithuanian Supreme Court case-law emphasizing that child sexual-abuse cases often lack witnesses and rely on the child’s testimony, statements of confidants, and especially court-ordered forensic psychiatric and psychological examinations. He stressed that no such comprehensive examination had been ordered, contrary to established practice, and that the statements of potential perpetrators or those responsible for his safety (who had motives to conceal events) could not justify discontinuation.

The chief prosecutor rejected the appeal on 28 May 2019, holding that all necessary steps had been taken, no corroborating evidence emerged (including from phone taps), and the *in dubio pro reo* principle applied. On 3 July 2019, the Kaunas District Court dismissed a further appeal, agreeing there was no objective evidence beyond the applicant’s “not sufficiently detailed and concrete” statements and noting the passage of time. It did not address the requested forensic examination, stating prosecutors decide on investigative steps. On 27 August 2019, the Kaunas Regional Court upheld this, finding no purpose in further actions and again omitting explicit discussion of the forensic examination despite the applicant’s reiterated arguments.

The case thus centered on the authorities’ reluctance to order a forensic psychiatric-psychological examination and the higher prosecutor’s and two levels of courts’ failure to engage with the applicant’s specific arguments on its necessity, despite arguable claims of sexual ill-treatment and relevant domestic case-law.
