001-231606:
The case of Almeida Arroja v. Portugal (Application no. 47238/19) concerned the applicant’s criminal conviction for comments broadcast on television, which he alleged violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

The applicant, an economist and university professor, regularly provided political commentary on a daily news programme on the private channel Porto Canal. He also chaired the J. association, which sought to fund and construct a paediatric wing at São João Hospital in Porto as a donation from the Portuguese community. In 2014–2015, the hospital obtained legal advice from law firm C., whose director was P.R., a well-known lawyer, university professor, politician and Member of the European Parliament. A lawyer at the firm drafted a tripartite Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) setting out the rights and duties of the association, the construction companies and the hospital. After the association rejected a first draft, a second draft was sent in April 2015. Disagreement over its terms, which protected the hospital’s interests, led to the project being halted.

On 25 May 2015, during the news programme, the applicant stated that “politics got in the way” of the works via law firm C. and P.R. He described the MoU as a “legal joke” that caused internal division at the hospital and halted construction for four weeks, leaving children in inadequate facilities. He accused P.R. of mixing politics and legal practice by soliciting State-sector clients (including the hospital) and producing a politically motivated document “to reward the hand that feeds them,” rather than a professional one. He claimed politicians, including P.R. (from the governing party), opposed the project because it made them look bad by highlighting State inaction. He linked P.R. (and another lawyer from the firm) to the Porto Commercial Association’s absence from a charity gala and used terms such as “second-class politicians” and “grubby lawyers.” He invited P.R. to debate the issue on air, declared the project a personal mission, and urged viewers not to vote for P.R. or his party if they accepted children remaining in “shacks.”

P.R. and the law firm filed a criminal complaint for aggravated defamation (Articles 180, 183 and 184 of the Criminal Code) and causing offence to a legal person (Article 187). They also sought civil damages. The Matosinhos public prosecutor charged the applicant. On 12 June 2018 the Matosinhos Criminal Court convicted him of offending the law firm, finding that he had knowingly made untrue factual allegations about the MoU’s political nature and the reasons for the halt (which he knew stemmed from disagreement over terms protecting the hospital, not from P.R.’s influence; P.R. had not even drafted the document). The court imposed a €4,000 fine and €5,000 in non-pecuniary damages. It acquitted him of defaming P.R., treating the remarks as a mix of facts and value judgments (mostly opinions) on a matter of public interest, for which politicians enjoyed a reduced right to reputation.

Both sides appealed. On 27 March 2019 the Porto Court of Appeal upheld the conviction regarding the firm and additionally convicted the applicant of aggravated defamation of P.R. It held that certain assertions were untrue statements of fact (that the firm’s document, driven by P.R.’s political motives rather than the hospital’s interests, had halted the works) for which there were no serious grounds; the same facts could not be treated as mere opinions vis-à-vis P.R. An aggregate fine of €7,000 was imposed, plus €5,000 damages to the firm and €10,000 to P.R. A dissenting judge considered that public-interest debate, even if factually distorted, should have prevailed and that the applicant may have believed his remarks lawful. Further appeals were rejected.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the convictions and sanctions unjustifiably restricted his freedom of expression.

The case of Almeida Arroja v. Portugal (App. no. 47238/19) concerns the applicant’s 2018–2019 criminal conviction in Portugal for comments made on a private television news programme, which he alleged violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

The applicant, an economist, university professor and chair of the J. association (formed to fund a paediatric wing at Porto’s São João public hospital), regularly provided political commentary on Porto Canal. In 2014–2015 the hospital obtained legal advice from the well-known law firm C., whose director P.R. was a prominent lawyer, politician and sitting Member of the European Parliament. A draft tripartite memorandum of understanding (MoU) prepared by a lawyer at C. protected the hospital’s interests so thoroughly that the association and construction companies refused to sign; the project stalled.

On 25 May 2015 the applicant discussed the impasse live on air. He asserted that “politics got in the way” through C. and P.R., that the MoU was a “legal joke” produced to serve political rather than professional ends, that P.R. used his political office to solicit State clients, and that the stalling of a €20 million gift for sick children (then housed in “shacks”) was intended to prevent politicians from looking bad. He invited P.R. to debate the following week, used terms such as “second-class politicians” and “grubby lawyers,” and urged viewers not to vote for P.R.’s party if they wanted children treated in proper facilities. The broadcast reached more than 9,500 viewers and remained online.

P.R. and C. lodged a private criminal complaint for aggravated defamation (Articles 180, 183 and 184 of the Criminal Code) and causing offence to a legal person (Article 187). They also claimed civil damages. The Matosinhos Criminal Court found the applicant had knowingly made untrue factual assertions that the MoU itself (rather than the parties’ disagreement) had halted the works and that political motives had driven the drafting. It convicted him of offending the legal person, imposing a €4,000 fine and €5,000 damages, but acquitted him of defaming P.R., classifying most remarks as value judgments on a matter of public interest against a politician whose reputation enjoyed reduced protection.

On appeal the Porto Court of Appeal reversed the acquittal. It held that the same remarks constituted false statements of both external fact (the MoU caused the halt) and internal fact (P.R. acted from political self-interest rather than professional duty). It found no “serious grounds” for the imputations, noted that the applicant knew they were untrue, and rejected any distinction between the firm and its politically active director. The applicant was convicted of both offences, sentenced to an aggregate €7,000 fine and ordered to pay a further €10,000 to P.R. Further appeals were refused. A dissenting judge considered the remarks, however unfair, part of a legitimate public debate that P.R. had declined to join.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the convictions and damages awards disproportionately restricted political speech on a matter of public concern. The Court later held that the domestic courts had failed to apply the criteria required by its case-law, had not given relevant and sufficient reasons, and had imposed sanctions capable of producing a chilling effect, thereby exceeding the narrow margin of appreciation and violating Article 10.

**CASE OF ALMEIDA ARROJA v. PORTUGAL (Application no. 47238/19, ECtHR Fourth Section, Judgment of 19 March 2024)**

The applicant, José Pedro Almeida Arroja (born 1954), is a Portuguese economist, university professor, and political commentator who appeared regularly on the Monday edition of a daily news programme on the private television channel Porto Canal. He also chaired the J. association, established to raise funds for constructing a paediatric wing at São João Hospital in Porto as a gift from the Portuguese community (estimated cost €20 million). In 2014–2015 the hospital obtained legal advice from law firm C., directed by P.R., a well-known lawyer, politician, and Member of the European Parliament. Lawyer F.M. at the firm drafted a tripartite Memorandum of Understanding setting out rights and duties of the association, construction companies, and hospital. The association rejected the first draft; a second was sent on 16 April 2015. Construction then halted.

On 25 May 2015 the applicant discussed the project on air (audience over 9,500 viewers; later viewed online more than 2,000 times and reproduced on blogs). He stated that “politics got in the way” via law firm C. and P.R.; that the firm’s document caused the hospital (particularly one worried administrator) to halt work and created division within its administration; that the document was a “legal joke” produced for political reasons because politicians (including P.R., belonging to the party in government) felt the civil-society gift made them “look bad”; that P.R. solicited State-sector clients (hospitals, city halls, ministries) for his firm; that the document was a “political document to reward the hand that feeds them”; that the firm and P.R. had invented “jokes (palhaçadas)” claiming the association could not gift the work and reserving the hospital’s right to sue; that this served “political goals” so citizens would not see politicians as inactive; and that “no second-rate politician or grubby lawyers” would stop him. He invited P.R. to debate the “legal joke” the following Monday and urged voters against P.R.’s party if they wanted children hospitalised “in a shack.” He also noted P.R. and another firm lawyer sat on the board of the Porto Commercial Association, which had declined to attend a charity dinner.

P.R. and law firm C. filed a criminal complaint. The Matosinhos public prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated defamation (Criminal Code Arts. 180, 183, 184) and causing offence to a legal person (Art. 187). The plaintiffs also claimed civil damages (€50,000 each) for non-pecuniary harm. On 12 June 2018 the Matosinhos Criminal Court convicted the applicant of the offence against the law firm (fine of €4,000 plus €5,000 damages). It found he knew the hospital administration (not the firm, whose role was to protect its client) had halted the project, that he had lied about political influence (the MoU was drafted by F.M., not P.R.), and that the untrue statements damaged the firm’s prestige, credibility, and trust. It acquitted him of defamation against P.R., treating most remarks as value judgments/opinions on a matter of public interest, with politicians enjoying reduced protection of honour.

The Porto Court of Appeal (27 March 2019) upheld the conviction regarding the firm and additionally convicted the applicant of aggravated defamation of P.R. (aggregate fine €7,000 plus €5,000 to the firm and €10,000 to P.R.). It held that certain assertions were untrue statements of fact (external: the document halted construction for political rather than legal-protection reasons; internal: P.R. prioritised politics over professional ethics or children’s welfare) made without serious grounds, even if some remarks were value judgments. One judge dissented, finding no defamation given the public-interest context and invitation to debate. Further appeals were rejected.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR under Article 10 of a disproportionate interference with freedom of expression. The Court held that the domestic courts’ balancing exercise failed to conform to Convention criteria, lacked relevant and sufficient reasons, and that the conviction plus damages were manifestly disproportionate, capable of a chilling effect, and exceeded the narrow margin of appreciation, violating Article 10.
001-231609:
The case of K.J. and Others v. Russia concerns three North Korean nationals (K.J., C.C., and S.K.) and alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention arising from their actual or threatened removal to North Korea and related detention in Russia.

K.J. and C.C. were arrested in Russian waters in 2018, convicted of illegal fishing and imprisoned. Upon K.J.’s release on 24 January 2020, a district court immediately ordered his detention pending expulsion for breach of migration rules, without specifying any term. He did not appeal in time; a later request to restore the time-limit was refused. In 2021 a cassation court upheld the expulsion order, finding no sufficient evidence of persecution risk and not addressing the detention complaint. K.J. remained in immigration detention until February 2022, when he was released after the statutory two-year maximum. C.C. was similarly detained from February 2020 until February 2022.

S.K. arrived in 2019 as a student at a Vladivostok university. North Korean consular officials routinely collected students’ documents and supervised them. After his first year S.K. decided not to return, contacted UNHCR and a lawyer, and moved to a pastor’s home. On 10 September 2020, after he received a certificate of registration for identification, police officers detained him at the pastor’s residence. He was taken to an undisclosed location and, according to police statements, handed over the same day to North Korean consular officials with FSB assistance. No arrest records, fingerprints or photographs were made, and police stations denied holding him. An interim measure under Rule 39 was indicated the same day, prohibiting his removal. Subsequent criminal complaints alleging abduction produced three successive refusals to open a case (later set aside in part), with authorities maintaining that S.K. had simply been “located and handed over” because of his nationality. No investigation established a legal basis for the transfer, located S.K., or verified compliance with the interim measure. The Government initially denied any handover or departure from Russia.

Human-rights reports (UN, Human Rights Watch, US State Department, Amnesty International and others) document that North Korean returnees—especially those who overstay studies, contact foreign organisations or convert to Christianity—are treated as traitors. They face incommunicado detention in political prison camps, systematic torture (stress positions, beatings, starvation), forced labour, possible execution and “guilt-by-association” punishment of families. No effective domestic procedure examined these risks before the transfers or detentions.

These facts underpin the claims that S.K.’s unacknowledged, legally baseless transfer by Russian agents exposed him to a real risk of death or ill-treatment without any prior assessment or investigation, and that K.J.’s (and C.C.’s) multi-year detention pending expulsion lacked periodic review of whether removal remained realistic and exceeded what was reasonably required.

The case of K.J. and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 27584/20 and 39768/20) involved two North Korean nationals, K.J. and C.C., plus the Institute for Human Rights acting on behalf of a third, S.K. They alleged that Russia violated Articles 2, 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention through unlawful detention, an unacknowledged handover, failure to examine risks of expulsion to North Korea, and lack of effective investigation or remedies.

K.J. and C.C. were captured in Russian waters in July 2018, convicted of illegal fishing and imprisoned. Upon K.J.’s release in January 2020 the Shkotovskiy District Court immediately ordered his detention pending expulsion, without specifying any term. He remained in a foreigners’ detention centre until February 2022, when the same court released him after the two-year statutory maximum. C.C. was detained on similar grounds from February 2020 until February 2022. K.J.’s late appeal against the expulsion order was rejected by the regional court and later confirmed by the cassation court, which found no sufficient evidence of persecution risk and held that expulsion was justified to prevent further offences. The cassation court did not address his detention complaint. No other court ever reviewed the continuing necessity of his detention.

S.K. arrived in Vladivostok in September 2019 as a student. After completing his first year he decided to seek asylum rather than return home. In late August 2020 he left the university campus, contacted UNHCR and a lawyer, and moved in with a local pastor. North Korean consular officials normally collected students’ documents and supervised their movements; a missing-person report was filed with the police the day he left campus. On 8 September 2020, while registering for an identification procedure, S.K. was confronted by five North Korean officials demanding his handover; he escaped. On 10 September, after receiving a certificate confirming his registration, he was taken by police from the pastor’s home. His lawyer was first told he would be at a Vladivostok station, then that he had been handed to North Korean consular officials with FSB assistance. S.K. himself telephoned from Artyom police station. The same day the European Court indicated an interim measure forbidding his removal. Subsequent police statements confirmed the handover but recorded no arrest, fingerprints or photographs. Repeated criminal complaints about his disappearance produced three refusals to open an investigation (one later quashed as unlawful). Courts repeatedly declined to examine the refusals on standing grounds. The Government first denied any handover and claimed S.K. remained in Russia; later they stated his location was unknown. No effective investigation was ever conducted.

Independent reports document systematic torture, starvation, forced labour and political imprisonment in North Korea, especially for those who contact foreigners, seek asylum or practise Christianity—acts treated as treason. These facts formed the basis of the claims that S.K. had been subjected to unacknowledged, legally baseless detention and illegal transfer; that all three applicants faced a real risk of death or ill-treatment if returned; that no competent authority examined those risks; and that K.J.’s two-year detention pending expulsion lacked periodic review and exceeded what was reasonably required.

The ECHR case K.J. and Others v. Russia (applications 27584/20 and 39768/20) involves North Korean nationals K.J., C.C., and S.K. (the latter represented by the Institute for Human Rights). It concerns risks of expulsion to North Korea under Articles 2 and 3 ECHR, lack of effective remedies (Article 13), and detention issues under Article 5.

K.J. and C.C. were arrested in Russian waters in July 2018 for illegal fishing, convicted, and imprisoned (K.J. for two years; C.C. for two years and one month). Upon K.J.’s release on 24 January 2020, the Shkotovskiy District Court ordered his detention pending expulsion without specifying a term. He did not initially appeal. In July 2020 he sought to appeal out of time (citing language barriers and COVID restrictions on lawyer access), but this was refused. The 9th Cassation Court in February 2021 upheld the expulsion, finding insufficient evidence of persecution risk compared to other North Koreans and ignoring detention complaints. K.J. was released on 4 February 2022 after the two-year maximum. C.C. was detained pending deportation from 27 February 2020 until 14 February 2022. Neither received periodic reviews of whether removal remained realistic.

S.K. arrived in Vladivostok in September 2019 to study. North Korean consular officials supervised students and held their documents. After his first year he decided to seek asylum, moved in with a pastor, and contacted UNHCR and lawyer Ms T. in late August 2020. He expressed determination not to return, noting possible surveillance due to church attendance. A missing-person report (presumed from North Korean officials) followed.

On 8 September 2020, at a migration office to register for identification, North Korean officials demanded S.K.’s handover; he escaped. On 10 September, police detained him at the pastor’s home without explanation and claimed he would go to Vladivostok police station no. 4 (he was not there). He briefly called from Artyom police station. Police later confirmed handover to North Korean consular officials with FSB assistance. No arrest, fingerprint, or presence records existed at any station.

The ECHR immediately indicated an interim measure against removal. Ms T. filed a criminal complaint for abduction. Authorities issued repeated refusals to open a case, stating S.K. was located on 27 August and handed over as a North Korean national with no arrest records. Prosecutors later set some refusals aside as unlawful, ordering inquiries (including locating S.K. and contacting the DPRK consul), but new identical refusals followed. Courts initially dismissed lawyer complaints on representation grounds (later corrected). No effective investigation occurred. Russia initially denied any handover and claimed S.K. remained in the country; later his whereabouts were unknown.

A 2016 Russia–North Korea readmission agreement provides for rapid transfer of illegal residents without notice or appeal rights. Extensive reports (HRW, UN OHCHR, US State Department, Amnesty, UN Special Rapporteur) document that North Korean returnees—especially those who left without permission, sought asylum, or engaged in religious activity—face treatment as traitors: incommunicado detention in political camps, systematic torture (beatings, stress positions, starvation), forced labour, possible execution, and no fair process. These facts form the basis of the alleged violations of unlawful unacknowledged transfer without risk assessment or investigation (S.K.) and excessive unreviewed detention (K.J.).

The case of Tzioumaka v. Greece (Application no. 31022/20) concerns the alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to the Greek authorities’ failure to enforce domestic court decisions granting the applicant, Chrysovalanto Tzioumaka, custody of her two minor daughters and ordering their father, K.K., to return them to her.

The applicant married K.K. in 2011. Their daughters were born in 2012 and 2015. In April 2016, while visiting the applicant’s family, K.K. took the children to his parents’ home in Kolokythas (Amaliada region) and thereafter blocked all contact. He and his family displayed aggression toward the applicant, who was unable to see or speak to the children.

In July 2016 an interim decision awarded K.K. temporary custody and sole parental responsibility, citing parental conflict. Contact arrangements were later set, but the applicant’s attempts to see the children were obstructed (including an alleged assault). In September 2018 the Amaliada court dissolved the marriage, awarded the applicant custody (with shared parental responsibility), and ordered K.K. to hand over the children or face a €1,000 fine and one month’s detention. The court found that the children’s reluctance stemmed from K.K.’s passivity and his parents’ hostility, while praising the applicant’s efforts to maintain ties despite the distance. K.K.’s appeal was dismissed in May 2020; the appellate court held him unfit, noting that the children were effectively raised by his parents.

The appellate decision was served on 9 June 2020 with an order to deliver the children at the Amaliada police station on 11 June 2020. K.K. failed to appear. Executory titles were issued, but further civil attempts (including a September 2020 provisional contact order requiring three weekly visits) collapsed: the children cried and refused, K.K. claimed the applicant was absent, and she later returned to her distant home. Subsequent civil applications were repeatedly adjourned or withdrawn.

The applicant immediately filed criminal complaints against K.K. and relatives for kidnapping a minor (by omission, given the legal duty to deliver the children after 11 June 2020) and related offences. Police searches of residences and businesses (June and October 2020), some with judicial presence, failed to locate the children. Arrests occurred under expedited procedures, but the children remained hidden. Files were merged; K.K. was referred for felony trial (kidnapping of children under 14 by omission) and relatives for abetting. Hearings were adjourned repeatedly (last known dates in late 2023/early 2024). Separate perjury proceedings against a witness instigated by K.K. resulted in convictions. The applicant also petitioned prosecutors, complaining of inadequate police help in a small village where the children had been seen, and of K.K.’s tactic of filing then withdrawing interim-measure requests to undermine the custody rulings.

Despite the applicant’s persistent requests and the existence of enforceable titles, the authorities conducted only unsuccessful searches, allowed prolonged delays in both civil enforcement and criminal trials, and failed to take effective, timely measures to secure the children’s return. This inaction permitted the children to become further integrated into their paternal grandparents’ household, consolidating a de facto situation that permanently frustrated the applicant’s custody rights. The Court held that the authorities thereby breached their positive obligation under Article 8 to act with the requisite diligence to restore family life.

001-233410:
The case of A.K. v. Russia (Application no. 49014/16) concerns the 2014 dismissal of a music teacher from a St Petersburg state school for students with special needs, which she alleged violated her rights to private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights and amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation under Article 14 taken with Article 8.

A.K., born in 1987, began working as a music director in October 2011. On 25 November 2014 she was summoned to a meeting with the school principal and a district official. They presented a “dossier” compiled by a representative of the NGO “Parents of Russia.” The file consisted of roughly ten pages reviewing her social-media profile, group subscriptions and friends list, together with screenshots of photographs. The images—posted in a restricted-access album visible only to her friends—showed her embracing and kissing female partners (without nudity) and one photograph in which she made a middle-finger gesture. Accompanying commentary highlighted her same-sex relationships, criticised the photographs as incompatible with “a teacher’s good name” and asserted that they could harm children and the school’s reputation. Officials told her she had engaged in “propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation” and must resign. She refused.

On 8 December 2014 she submitted written comments stating that no complaints had ever been received from pupils or parents, that she had never promoted any sexual orientation at school, and that the action against her was motivated solely by her sexual orientation. The same day the principal dismissed her under Article 81(8) of the Labour Code for having committed “immoral acts incompatible with the continued performance of educational child-rearing functions.” A subsequent letter from twelve parents supported the dismissal, citing “indecent photos” and possible access by children to “harmful information promoting non-traditional sexual relations.”

A.K. challenged the dismissal in the domestic courts, arguing that no immoral act had been proved and that the sole ground was her sexual orientation—an unlawful distinction under the Constitution and the Labour Code. She emphasised that the photographs had never been publicly accessible and that she had never discussed her private life at work. The school countered that she had publicly displayed “lesbian scenes and indecent gestures,” that she performed in a “lesbian club,” and that her conduct was incompatible with her role.

On 21 April 2015 the Kirovskiy District Court upheld the dismissal. It characterised the photographs as a “public display of immoral, unethical and unacceptable private conduct,” including “unethically close same-sex relations.” While stating that sexual orientation itself was irrelevant, the court held that even private conduct could be immoral if it involved posting such images. Professional competence and awards were deemed legally irrelevant. The St Petersburg City Court dismissed her appeal on 3 September 2015, affirming that the employer enjoyed a wide discretion to classify conduct as immoral and that her actions diminished educators’ authority and promoted “non-traditional sexual views.” Discrimination claims were rejected as unproven. Cassation appeals to the City Court and the Supreme Court were refused in March and April 2016.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centre on the use of private, restricted-access photographs of same-sex affection (and one vulgar gesture) as the exclusive basis for the most severe disciplinary sanction, without any evidence of classroom impact, prior complaints or consideration of less drastic measures, and against a background of explicit official and parental references to her sexual orientation.

The case of A.K. v. Russia (Application no. 49014/16) involves the dismissal of a music teacher from a state school for students with special needs in St. Petersburg, alleged to violate Articles 8 and 14 of the ECHR due to interference with private life and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

The applicant, a Russian national born in 1987, began work as a musical director on 7 October 2011. On 25 November 2014, she met the school principal and a municipal official. They presented a “dossier” from a representative of the NGO “Parents of Russia” reviewing her social-media profile: subscriptions, friends lists, and screenshots of photos from a restricted-access album inaccessible to the public. The photos showed travel, partying, embracing and intimately kissing other women (without nudity), plus one image of her making a middle-finger gesture. Accompanying comments highlighted her sexual orientation, criticised the images as incompatible with a teacher’s reputation, and claimed they could harm children and the school.

She was told to resign for alleged “propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation” and damaging the teaching profession. She refused and later submitted comments stating there had been no prior complaints from students or parents, she had never promoted any sexual orientation, and the action was discriminatory, based solely on her orientation.

On 8 December 2014 the principal terminated her contract under Article 81(8) of the Labour Code for an “immoral act incompatible with continued performance of teaching activities.” Twelve parents subsequently sent a letter supporting the dismissal and voicing concern that children might access “harmful information promoting non-traditional sexual relations.”

The applicant sued, arguing there was no evidence of any immoral act, the photos came from a private restricted album, she had never mentioned her orientation at school, and the dismissal was discriminatory. The school replied that she had publicly displayed “lesbian scenes and indecent gestures” and noted her membership in a music band that performed in a “lesbian club” with songs of “lesbian content.”

On 21 April 2015 the Kirovskiy District Court dismissed her claim. It held that the photos constituted a public display of immoral, unethical conduct—indecent gestures, poses and “unethically close same-sex relations”—even though posted only to a restricted group. The court stated that her sexual orientation itself was irrelevant; the legal issue was the conduct of a person performing educational functions. Her professional competence, awards and the absence of complaints were of “no legal consequence.”

The St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment on 3 September 2015. It observed that the Labour Code contains no definition of an “immoral act,” so the employer may decide according to the circumstances. Expert reports were cited as concluding that the photos diminished educators’ authority, promoted indecent conduct and formed “non-traditional sexual views,” incompatible with the applicant’s duty to develop students’ aesthetic taste and emotional sphere. Students model themselves on teachers, the court noted. Discrimination arguments were rejected; the ground for dismissal was the unethical conduct, not orientation.

Cassation appeals to the City Court and the Supreme Court of Russia were dismissed in March and April 2016. These facts underpin the complaints that the dismissal constituted a disproportionate interference with private life (the photos being neither obscene nor publicly accessible) and amounted to discrimination based solely on sexual orientation.

The case of A.K. v. Russia (Application no. 49014/16) before the European Court of Human Rights involves a music teacher’s 2014 dismissal from a St. Petersburg special-needs school, alleged to violate Article 8 (private life) and Article 14 (discrimination) of the Convention due to her sexual orientation.

A.K., born in 1987, had worked at the school since October 2011 with no prior complaints. On 25 November 2014 the principal and a municipal official presented a dossier compiled by an activist from the NGO “Parents of Russia.” It contained screenshots from her restricted-access social-media album showing her embracing and kissing female partners (no nudity) plus one image of her making a middle-finger gesture. Officials accused her of promoting “non-traditional sexual orientation” and bringing the teaching profession into disrepute, demanding her resignation. She refused.

On 8 December 2014 she submitted a written statement denying any promotion of sexual orientation or workplace misconduct and alleging discrimination. That same day she was dismissed under Article 81(8) of the Labour Code for “immoral acts incompatible with continued performance of teaching activities.” Twelve parents later wrote in support, fearing children might access “harmful information.”

A.K. sued, arguing the photos were private, she had never discussed her orientation at school, and the sole motive was her sexuality. The school replied that the images constituted public “lesbian scenes and indecent gestures” and noted her performances in a “lesbian club.”

On 21 April 2015 the Kirovskiy District Court upheld the dismissal. It held that even restricted online posting of “indecent gestures, poses and unethically close same-sex relations” amounted to immoral conduct for an educator; her orientation itself was legally irrelevant and her professional awards carried no weight. The St. Petersburg City Court affirmed on 3 September 2015, stating that the employer alone decides what is “immoral,” that her actions undermined educators’ authority and modelled “non-traditional” views for pupils, and that discrimination had not been proved. Cassation appeals were rejected in 2016.

These facts underpin the claims that the most severe sanction was applied immediately to private, non-obscene expressions of affection and a single gesture, without considering lesser disciplinary measures, and that the treatment was based solely on sexual orientation without convincing justification.
001-233985:
The case of *Pisanski v. Croatia* (Application no. 28794/18) concerns a fine imposed on a lawyer for contempt of court based on remarks in an appeal, alleged to violate Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression).

The applicant, Viktor Pisanski, represented creditor J.C. in Zagreb Municipal Civil Court enforcement proceedings seeking to recover a debt of HRK 2,457,005.19 (EUR 326,100.63) plus interest via bank account seizure. The claim derived from a 2009 notary enforcement order assigned to J.C. via a notarized contract. On 11 May 2016, the Municipal Court (decision prepared by clerk V.P.V. and approved by Judge E.M.S.) dismissed the application, holding that the assignment contract was not a “public or publicly certified document” as required by the Enforcement Act for transferring an enforceable debt.

On 31 May 2016, the applicant lodged an appeal with the Municipal Court (as required before second-instance review). He argued that a notarized assignment contract was plainly a publicly certified document under sections 2 and 32(1) of the Enforcement Act. Criticizing the Municipal Court’s contrary view (which followed Zagreb County Court precedent in another case), he wrote that this “peculiar” approach would “justifiably provoke both outrage and ridicule” absent higher-court endorsement, which had made the matter “dramatically serious.” He analogized the court’s persistence to a “superior” insisting “the sea is red, the sky is yellow, and the sun is green” despite contrary evidence from a “subordinate.” He decried “conformism” and “uncritical acceptance” of “manifestly incorrect” case-law in a non-precedent system, calling it “a most severe form of arbitrary adjudication” that caused “immense damage,” especially given the large claim. He added that while one party “will have nothing to live on tomorrow,” the courts would “safely sheltered” maintain “the sun is green. Because they can.”

The Osijek County Court (Judge J.T.B.) allowed the appeal on 18 August 2016, quashing the decision and remitting the case, but instructed the Municipal Court to examine the remarks for contempt. After the applicant’s 4 October 2016 apology (noting harsh words were not directed at that court), the Municipal Court issued a writ of execution on 7 November 2016; the claim was later fully satisfied and proceedings discontinued.

On 9 November 2016, the Municipal Court (again involving clerk V.P.V., now approved by Judge M.A.D.) fined the applicant HRK 2,000 (EUR 265) under the Civil Procedure Act (applied via the Enforcement Act) for insulting the court. It held that parties, especially lawyers bound by Bar ethics, must address courts politely; the remarks expressed dissatisfaction impermissibly by insulting the court, describing it as a “centre of power,” and failing to use available remedies.

The applicant appealed, invoking Article 10 and ECHR contempt case-law. He argued the remarks mainly targeted Zagreb County Court precedent, were not offensive (the “outrage and ridicule” comment was hypothetical), were justified (as the appeal succeeded), and that courts as a branch of power could be portrayed as such. He noted the Municipal Court had not initially found the remarks offensive and raised impartiality concerns regarding both county courts, seeking a transfer. The Supreme Court refused the transfer. On 12 September 2017, the Osijek County Court (again Judge J.T.B.) dismissed the appeal, agreeing the remarks were offensive. The Constitutional Court declared a subsequent complaint inadmissible on 5 December 2017. The fine was collected from the applicant’s account on 31 January 2018 (disputed by him).

Parallel Bar Association disciplinary proceedings (for alleged ethics breaches) resulted in acquittal: the Disciplinary Court (27 November 2018) and High Disciplinary Court (8 July 2020) found no intent to insult or undermine authority. The remarks were unusual legal argument criticizing case-law (not a specific judge) in a private appeal of high-stakes importance, falling within lawyers’ duty to challenge potentially incorrect law and courts’ wider tolerance for criticism.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 10: the remarks did not exceed acceptable criticism; domestic courts failed to contextualize them within appellate proceedings; reasons were insufficient and not aligned with ECHR criteria; no fair balance was struck, rendering the interference unnecessary in a democratic society.

The case of Pisanski v. Croatia (Application no. 28794/18) concerns a Croatian lawyer, Viktor Pisanski, who was fined for contempt of court over remarks in an appeal. He alleged a violation of his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

In 2016, Pisanski represented a creditor seeking enforcement of a substantial debt (approximately €326,000 plus interest) in the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court. The claim derived from an assigned enforcement order, supported by a notary-certified assignment contract. The court dismissed the application, holding that the contract was not a “publicly certified document” under the Enforcement Act, as required to transfer the debt.

Pisanski appealed to the Osijek County Court (via the first-instance court, as required). His appeal strongly criticised the legal approach as “peculiar” and potentially provocative of “outrage and ridicule” (had a higher court not previously adopted it). He accused the courts of “conformism” in uncritically accepting manifestly incorrect case-law, analogised the situation to a superior insisting “the sun is green” despite evidence to the contrary, and described it as “arbitrary adjudication” causing “immense damage,” particularly given the large sum at stake.

The Osijek County Court upheld the appeal on the merits, quashed the dismissal, and remitted the case (which later succeeded, with the debt fully recovered). However, it instructed the Municipal Court to consider whether the remarks constituted contempt.

The Municipal Court fined Pisanski HRK 2,000 (about €265) under the Civil Procedure Act (applied mutatis mutandis in enforcement proceedings). It found the remarks insulting, as they portrayed the court as a “centre of power,” showed disrespect, and failed to address the court politely, contrary to lawyers’ professional duties. Pisanski apologised in subsequent submissions, noting the remarks targeted the higher court’s approach more than the first-instance court.

He appealed the fine, arguing the comments were not offensive, were justified (as confirmed by the successful merits appeal), and were made in an emotionally charged context involving a large client claim. He also raised impartiality concerns, as the same Osijek judge who flagged the contempt issue later dismissed his appeal against the fine (after the Supreme Court refused a transfer). The Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible, as the decision was not subject to review. The fine was collected from his bank account.

Separately, the Croatian Bar Association instituted disciplinary proceedings but acquitted Pisanski. It held that, viewed in context, the unusual wording criticised (possibly incorrect) case-law rather than insulting courts or judges, with no intent to undermine authority. As a lawyer performing his duty, he was entitled to robust advocacy, especially in a high-stakes, non-public appeal that succeeded. Courts must tolerate wider criticism than individuals.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 10. Pisanski’s remarks, though strongly worded, did not exceed acceptable criticism of judicial approaches in an internal, non-public appellate document. Domestic courts failed to place them in context (lawyer’s role, large claim, successful outcome, no personal attacks) or provide relevant and sufficient reasons, thus not striking a fair balance. The interference was not “necessary in a democratic society.”

The case of Pisanski v. Croatia (Application no. 28794/18) concerns a Croatian lawyer, Viktor Pisanski, who was fined for contempt of court over remarks in an appeal, raising an Article 10 complaint of unjustified interference with his freedom of expression.

The Osijek County Court (Judge J.T.B.) allowed the appeal on 18 August 2016, quashing the dismissal and remitting the case, but directed the Municipal Court to consider whether the remarks constituted contempt. Enforcement was eventually granted and the debt collected in full.

It held that lawyers must address courts politely and that his remarks insulted the court by portraying it as an unaccountable “centre of power,” expressing dissatisfaction in an “impermissible and inappropriate way.” Non-payment would trigger collection by the payments agency FINA.

Pisanski appealed, invoking Article 10 and ECHR case-law. He argued the remarks were not insulting, targeted mainly the higher court’s legal approach (only secondarily the Municipal Court’s “conformism”), were justified (as later confirmed on the merits), and had been submitted internally rather than publicly. He also questioned the impartiality of both county courts and sought a transfer. The Supreme Court refused the transfer. On 12 September 2017 Judge J.T.B. (who had earlier instructed the contempt examination) upheld the fine. The Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible in December 2017.

Parallel disciplinary proceedings before the Croatian Bar Association ended in Pisanski’s acquittal (first instance 2018, upheld 2020). The disciplinary courts found no intent to insult or undermine judicial authority; the language, though unusual, constituted legitimate (if vigorous) criticism of case-law in a private appellate submission of high-stakes importance to his client, and the appeal had succeeded. Courts, they noted, must tolerate wider criticism than ordinary citizens.

The European Court later held that the fine constituted an interference with Article 10 that was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The remarks, made in a non-public appellate context by a lawyer discharging his duty to represent a client vigorously, did not exceed acceptable criticism of judicial reasoning; the domestic courts had failed to place them in proper context or to give relevant and sufficient reasons meeting Convention criteria, thus failing to strike a fair balance.
001-233833:
The case of Zarema Musayeva and Others v. Russia concerns three Russian nationals: Zarema Musayeva (first applicant, born 1969, diabetic requiring daily insulin), her husband Sayda Yangulbayev (second applicant, born 1958, former Chechen Supreme Court judge), and their daughter Aliya Yangulbayeva (third applicant, born 2000). The family fled Chechnya in 2017 after alleged torture of the second applicant and sons Abubakar and Ibrahim by State agents due to opposition activities. Ibrahim sought asylum in Norway. In December 2021, Abubakar (a human rights defender with the Committee Against Torture) was questioned by Chechen police in another region as a terrorism witness, prompting his flight from Russia. The remaining applicants, living in Nizhniy Novgorod (official address Zavolzhye), planned to leave Russia on 21 January 2022, fearing abduction.

On 20 January 2022, five or six Chechen police officers arrived at their home, demanding the first and second applicants for questioning in a fraud case based on a summons sent to a non-existent address. Local police offered no help. Officers later broke in, shoving the third applicant to the floor and the second aside, dragging the first applicant out without medication, clothes, shoes or passport. She lost consciousness on the stairs and was forced barefoot through snow into a car. She was driven non-stop ~2,000 km to Grozny over 24 hours, deprived of insulin and food, forced to relieve herself barefoot in snow, verbally abused and punched in the face. The second and third applicants suffered facial and head injuries (medically confirmed) and fled Russia on 22 January. The second applicant later lost judicial status and immunity.

Upon arrival on 21 January, the first applicant was questioned briefly at a Grozny police station (filmed barely conscious by the Chechen Ombudsman). She was then accused of disorderly conduct (“petty hooliganism”) for alleged insults and scratching an officer, and of violence against an official. That evening, the Leninskiy District Court convicted her in absentia of prosecutor and lawyer, imposing the maximum 15-day administrative detention; she lost consciousness mid-hearing. No proper medical exam occurred despite diabetes. She received food only on 22 January, was denied visitors until 4 February, and later denied making a statement refusing counsel. Pre-trial detention followed (extended repeatedly), with her confined in a metal cage during hearings. She was convicted in 2023 of violence and fraud, receiving a five-year sentence (upheld on appeal). Lawyers’ appeals faced delays and erroneous rejections.

From 21 January 2022, Chechen President Ramzan Kadyrov and officials (including parliamentary speaker Daudov, deputy PM Vismuradov, Duma member Delimkhanov and police heads) issued repeated public death threats via Telegram, Instagram and VKontakte, promising imprisonment or death, a “blood feud,” hunting the family (including abroad), beheading and elimination. A Grozny demonstration featured thousands stomping and burning family photos amid threats. Russian authorities took no preventive action or investigation despite complaints, amid a documented climate of impunity and human rights abuses in Chechnya.

The Court indicated interim measures (Rule 39) requiring medical treatment for the first applicant, fortnightly updates and rights safeguards, but the Government ceased providing information after early March 2022. Complaints of ill-treatment and home violation were dismissed without opening a criminal case.

These facts underpin alleged violations of Articles 2 (unaddressed life threats), 3 (ill-treatment and no investigation), 5 (arbitrary detention), 18 (ulterior retaliatory purpose against activist relatives), 6 (unfair administrative proceedings lacking participation and impartiality) and 34 (hindering application via non-compliance with measures). International bodies, including the EU, PACE, UN rapporteurs and European Parliament, condemned the events as politically motivated retaliation.

The case of *Zarema Musayeva and Others v. Russia* (Application no. 4573/22) concerns events in January 2022 involving the first applicant (Zarema Musayeva, a diabetic requiring daily insulin), her husband (the second applicant, a former Chechen Supreme Court judge), and their daughter (the third applicant). The family had fled Chechnya in 2017 after alleged torture of the second applicant and their sons by State agents due to opposition activities. Their sons included human-rights activist Abubakar Yangulbayev (who fled Russia after Chechen police questioning in December 2021) and opposition blogger Ibrahim Yangulbayev (who had sought asylum in Norway). In January 2022 the applicants, then in Nizhniy Novgorod, planned to leave Russia.

On 20 January 2022 Chechen police officers arrived at the applicants’ home, claiming the first and second applicants were required for questioning in Grozny on a fraud matter. After producing a defective summons to a non-existent address, officers broke into the flat, used force (shoving the third applicant to the floor and the second applicant aside), and dragged the first applicant out without her insulin, clothing, shoes or passport. She lost consciousness on the stairs and was forced barefoot through snow into a car. She was then driven non-stop for approximately 24 hours (2,000 km) to Grozny, deprived of medication and food, forced to relieve herself by the roadside in snow, verbally abused and punched in the face. Medical examinations the next day confirmed facial and head injuries to the second and third applicants, who fled Russia on 22 January 2022. Domestic complaints about the raid and ill-treatment led to refusals to open a criminal investigation.

Upon arrival in Grozny on 21 January the first applicant was briefly questioned, after which police alleged she had committed disorderly conduct and scratched an officer. That evening the Leninskiy District Court convicted her of petty hooliganism in a hearing held without a prosecutor or her lawyer; she lost consciousness during the hearing and was sentenced to the maximum 15 days’ administrative detention. She received no visitors for two weeks and was later charged criminally with violence against an officer and fraud, convicted in 2023 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. Pre-trial detention hearings saw her confined in a metal cage. Appeals against the administrative conviction remained pending or were initially dismissed on technical grounds.

From 21 January 2022 onwards President Ramzan Kadyrov and other senior Chechen officials (including a State Duma member, the parliamentary speaker and police chiefs) issued repeated public death threats via social media and videos, declaring the family would face “imprisonment or death,” a “blood feud,” beheading or hunting, and urging their expulsion from abroad. A mass demonstration in Grozny featured similar threats. Russian authorities took no investigative or protective steps despite complaints. The Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39 requiring medical care, regular updates and safeguards for the first applicant; the Government initially responded but then ceased providing the requested information.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: a real and immediate risk to life from unpunished official death threats in a climate of impunity (Art. 2); police ill-treatment during the raid, transfer and detention without effective investigation (Art. 3); arbitrary administrative detention (Art. 5 § 1) pursued for the ulterior purpose of retaliating against the family’s human-rights and opposition activities (Art. 18 + Art. 5); an unfair administrative hearing in which the first applicant could not participate and the court lacked impartiality through the prosecutor’s absence (Art. 6 § 1); and hindrance of the right of individual petition through non-compliance with interim measures (Art. 34).

The case of Zarema Musayeva and Others v. Russia (Application no. 4573/22) arose from the January 2022 forcible transfer of the first applicant from Nizhniy Novgorod to Grozny and related events targeting her family. The first applicant (Zarema Musayeva, born 1969, diabetic and requiring daily insulin) is married to the second applicant (Sayda Yangulbayev, born 1958, a former Chechen Supreme Court judge). The third applicant is their daughter Aliya (born 2000). The family had three sons, including human-rights lawyer Abubakar Yangulbayev (who worked with the Committee Against Torture) and opposition blogger Ibrahim Yangulbayev. After alleged torture of the second applicant and sons by Chechen agents in 2015–2017 due to their opposition to local leadership, the family fled Chechnya for Nizhniy Novgorod (some 2,000 km away). Ibrahim later sought asylum in Norway. In December 2021 Chechen police questioned Abubakar in another region about alleged terrorism links tied to an opposition Telegram channel; he then fled Russia.

On 20 January 2022, as the remaining applicants packed to leave Russia, five or six Chechen police officers arrived at their Nizhniy Novgorod apartment. They produced a summons (sent to a non-existent address) for a 14 February witness interview in a fraud case and demanded to take the first and second applicants to Grozny. After the second applicant identified himself as a retired federal judge, the officers said only the first applicant would be taken. Local police and NGO representatives proved unable to intervene. Officers then forced entry, shoved the second and third applicants (who later received medical confirmation of facial and head injuries), dragged the first applicant out without medication, warm clothes, shoes or passport, and forced her barefoot through snow into a car. She was driven non-stop for approximately 24 hours to Grozny, denied insulin and food, verbally abused, punched in the face, and made to relieve herself by the roadside in freezing conditions.

Upon arrival on 21 January she was briefly questioned, then immediately accused of public-order offences and of scratching an officer’s cheek. That evening the Leninskiy District Court (sitting without a prosecutor or her lawyer) convicted her of petty hooliganism and imposed the maximum 15-day administrative detention; she fainted during the hearing. She received no insulin until hours later and no food until the next day. Criminal charges followed for violence against an official and later for fraud. She was remanded in custody (repeatedly extended) and, in 2023, convicted and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment (reduced on appeal). She was held in a metal cage during several detention hearings, initially denied visitors, and given only limited medical attention despite her diabetes.

From 21 January onward, Chechen President Ramzan Kadyrov and other senior officials (including a State Duma member, deputy prime minister and police chiefs) issued repeated public death threats against the entire family via Telegram, Instagram and videos. They described a “blood feud,” promised to “hunt” and behead them, called for their killing if they resisted, and urged Chechens in Europe to locate them. A large Grozny demonstration featured similar threats and the burning of family photographs. No investigation was opened despite complaints. The second and third applicants fled Russia on 22 January; the second applicant was later stripped of judicial status.

The applicants alleged these events violated Articles 2 (life), 3 (ill-treatment), 5 (liberty), 6 (fair trial), 18 (ulterior purpose) and 34 (hindrance of the individual application). The Court later found violations on all those grounds, noting a climate of impunity, the absence of any protective measures or effective investigation, and the authorities’ failure to comply with interim measures requiring medical updates.

The case of Oleg Balan v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 25259/20) arose from a defamation claim brought by the applicant, Moldova’s Minister of the Interior from February 2015 to January 2016, after opposition politician Renato Usatîi published a purported official document on Facebook. On 10 November 2015 Usatîi posted that he had received “an interesting document” and attached a three-page “information note” dated 22 May 2015, bearing SIS letterhead, “Secret” stamps and an addressee of the then-President. The note accused Balan of placing personal image above institutional reform, dismissing named officials and replacing them with loyalists, selling posts, protecting smuggling, demoralising staff and causing Sweden to withdraw €2 million in aid.

SIS immediately denied authorship or transmission of any such document; the President’s office likewise denied receipt. Several media outlets republished the note or its contents. Balan demanded a public retraction and apology; receiving none, he sued Usatîi, Usatîi’s party and various media for defamation.

The Chișinău District Court twice found for Balan (2017 and 2018), holding that the note contained specific accusations of criminal conduct, that Usatîi had produced no evidence of their truth, and that he had made no genuine attempt to verify authenticity before publication. The Court of Appeal upheld these findings. The Supreme Court of Justice, however, remitted the case on procedural grounds relating to mail logs. After the President’s incoming-mail register (produced years later) showed no receipt and SIS stated it could not identify any originating unit, the Court of Appeal again ruled for Balan.

In a final judgment of 4 December 2019 the Supreme Court quashed the lower decisions and dismissed the claim entirely. It classified Usatîi’s Facebook post as “journalistic activity,” treated him as both an investigative journalist and a “public person,” and applied the statutory presumption of good faith that domestic law accords to investigative journalists. The court emphasised the public-interest character of alleged corruption, Balan’s status as a minister obliged to tolerate heightened criticism, the practical impossibility of verifying a classified SIS document, the “time-sensitive” nature of news, and the chilling effect that liability would produce. It concluded that any residual doubt about authenticity had to be resolved in Usatîi’s favour and that he had merely disseminated third-party information.

The European Court of Human Rights held that these reasons failed to strike a fair balance between Balan’s Article 8 right to reputation and Usatîi’s Article 10 freedom of expression. The domestic courts had, without explanation, assimilated a political actor to an investigative journalist and thereby imported a presumption of good faith that the Convention does not automatically extend to politicians. They had not examined with the required care the concrete elements of the case—Usatîi’s lack of verification, the gravity and specificity of the criminal allegations, and the official denials—thereby offering insufficient protection to the applicant’s reputation. A violation of Article 8 was therefore found.

The case of Oleg Balan v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 25259/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that Moldovan courts failed to protect his reputation after dismissing his defamation claim. Balan, born in 1969 and resident in Chișinău, served as Minister of the Interior from 18 February 2015 to 20 January 2016.

On 10 November 2015, Renato Usatîi, leader of an opposition party and mayor of Bălți, posted on his personal Facebook page that he had received “an interesting document” by post, attaching a three-page “information note” dated 22 May 2015. The Note, bearing the letterhead of the Security and Information Service (SIS), stamps reading “Secret” and a control date of 29 May 2015, was addressed to then-President Nicolae Timofti. It accused Balan of prioritising his personal image over the Ministry’s reputation, dismissing or inducing officials and police officers to leave (listing names) and replacing them with loyalists (again listing names), selling positions, protecting unlawful smuggling, demoralising staff, and causing Swedish partners to withdraw €2 million in aid due to inept leadership.

The post and Note (or summaries thereof) were widely republished by Moldovan news outlets. One portal, deschide.md, disclosed that it had received an identical envelope months earlier but declined to publish after unsuccessful attempts to authenticate the document. The same day, the SIS issued a press release stating it had neither prepared any such “operative study” nor sent any such letter to the President. The following day the President’s office denied receiving the Note or any similar information.

Balan wrote to Usatîi and his party on 31 December 2015, citing the official denials, demanding a public declaration that the Note’s contents were false, an apology and MDL 500 000 (approximately €23 280) in non-pecuniary damages. Receiving no reply, he sued Usatîi, the party and several media outlets on 15 January 2016.

The Chișinău District Court (Buiucani) initially found for Balan on 10 February 2017 and again on 10 January 2018 after a remittal, holding that the Note contained specific allegations of criminal conduct that Usatîi had failed to prove true and that official denials established falsity. Usatîi was ordered to apologise and pay MDL 50 000; media defendants were ordered to retract. The Court of Appeal upheld this in June 2018, emphasising Usatîi’s failure to attempt pre-publication verification. The Supreme Court of Justice quashed the judgment in January 2019 for non-production of SIS and presidential mail logs (which could be examined under secrecy safeguards) and remitted the case.

After further examination, the Court of Appeal again found for Balan in April 2019, noting that SIS logs could not be identified from the Note’s details and that presidential incoming-mail logs contained no record of the document. On 4 December 2019 the Supreme Court of Justice reversed and dismissed the action. It classified Usatîi’s Facebook post as journalistic activity entitled to the “public-watchdog” protection of investigative journalism, especially on alleged corruption. Domestic law required any doubt as to a journalist’s good faith to be resolved in the journalist’s favour. As a public official Balan had to tolerate heightened criticism concerning his official duties. Verification of a secret SIS document was deemed impractical and time-sensitive news made prior contact with the authorities unrealistic. Delayed production of logs created sufficient doubt, triggering a presumption that Usatîi had published truthful information in good faith. Restricting the republication of third-party material would gravely impair journalistic freedom. Usatîi was therefore treated simultaneously as a journalist (via social media) and a “public person.”

Balan complained that the courts had failed to strike a fair balance between his Article 8 right to reputation and Usatîi’s Article 10 rights, in particular by treating a political actor as an investigative journalist without justification and by applying an unwarranted presumption of good faith. The Court later found a violation of Article 8 on precisely those grounds.

The case of Oleg Balan v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 25259/20) involves a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Oleg Balan, alleged that Moldovan courts failed in their positive obligation to protect his right to reputation by dismissing his defamation action against statements published by an opposition politician.

Balan served as Minister of the Interior from 18 February 2015 to 20 January 2016. On 10 November 2015, Renato Usatîi, leader of an opposition party and then mayor of Bălți, posted on his personal Facebook page: “Received an interesting document in the post. Again our Timofte knew everything and kept silent about it.” He attached a three-page “information note” dated 22 May 2015, purporting to be a secret “operative study” prepared by the Security and Information Service (SIS) and addressed to the President. The Note accused Balan of prioritizing his personal image over the Ministry’s, dismissing or forcing out named officials at various levels and replacing them with loyalists (also named), selling positions, protecting unlawful smuggling schemes, demoralizing Ministry and police staff, and causing Swedish partners to withdraw €2 million in aid due to inept leadership. The document bore official letterhead, “Secret” stamps, and a control marking.

Several news outlets republished or summarised the Note. One portal disclosed that it had received a similar envelope months earlier but declined to publish after failing to authenticate it. The same day, the SIS issued a press release denying it had prepared or sent any such document. The next day the President’s office similarly denied receipt of the Note or comparable information.

Balan wrote to Usatîi and his party on 31 December 2015, citing the official denials, demanding a public retraction, apology and MDL 500,000 (approximately €23,280) in non-pecuniary damages. Receiving no reply, he sued Usatîi, the party and several media outlets on 15 January 2016 for defamation.

The first-instance court initially found for Balan in February 2017, holding that the Note alleged specific criminal acts, that Usatîi had produced no evidence of their truth (including any conviction), and that the SIS and Presidency had disavowed the document. It ordered an apology and MDL 50,000 damages. After a procedural remittal, the district court and Court of Appeal again found against Usatîi, stressing his failure to attempt verification before publication.

The Supreme Court of Justice ultimately dismissed the claim on 4 December 2019. It treated internet publication as journalistic activity and classified Usatîi as both an investigative journalist and a “public person.” Domestic law required any doubt about a journalist’s good faith to be resolved in the journalist’s favour, creating a rebuttable presumption. The court emphasised the public-interest nature of allegations of corruption, the applicant’s status as a serving minister who must tolerate heightened criticism, the purported secrecy of the document (making verification “impossible”), and the value of reporting third-party information. It concluded that Usatîi had acted in good faith and that the information was therefore to be treated as truthful until proven otherwise.

The European Court held that the Supreme Court had failed to strike a fair balance between the applicant’s Article 8 right to reputation and Usatîi’s Article 10 rights. It had applied the journalist’s good-faith presumption without adequate explanation of why Usatîi qualified as an investigative journalist, and it had not conducted a careful analysis of the concrete elements of the case relevant to protecting Balan’s reputation.

001-233990:
The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) impaired his right of access to a court by declaring inadmissible his action for State compensation arising from a Court of Cassation judgment previously found by the ECHR to have violated that same provision.

In 1992 the applicant concluded a private-law contract of indefinite duration as an auxiliary official at the Greek embassy in Germany. He later sued the State in the civil courts for an increase in his expatriation allowance in respect of two dependent children for the period 1 January 1993–31 May 1998. The first-instance court dismissed the claim, holding that the relevant legislation and ministerial decisions applied only to permanent public-law employees and that the distinction did not breach equality principles. The Court of Appeal partially allowed the claim for the period after a 1998 legislative change that equalised the status of the two categories of staff, but upheld the dismissal for the earlier period. In 2001 the Court of Cassation rejected as “vague” the applicant’s grounds of appeal on points of law concerning that earlier period, on the basis that he had not set out the terms of his contract or the number and ages of his children, even though those facts appeared in the case file.

In Zouboulidis v. Greece (no. 77574/01, 14 March 2007) the ECHR held that this constituted excessive formalism and a disproportionate restriction on access to a court, in violation of Article 6 § 1. It awarded non-pecuniary damages but declined to speculate on the outcome had the Cassation examined the merits.

On 13 December 2007 the applicant brought an action in the administrative courts under Article 105 of the Introductory Law to the Civil Code, seeking compensation for the pecuniary loss he alleged would not have occurred had the Cassation not unlawfully dismissed his grounds of appeal. In 2014 the SAC plenary (judgment 1501/2014) held that, although Article 105 did not apply directly to judicial acts, the Constitution required that damage caused by any State organ be capable of compensation; pending specific legislation, Article 105 should therefore be applied by analogy to “manifest errors” of the judiciary. The first-instance and appellate administrative courts applied that case-law, examined the action on the merits and dismissed it, finding no manifest error.

The applicant’s further appeal reached the SAC plenary. In judgment 800/2021 of 4 June 2021 the SAC reversed its earlier approach. It held that Article 105 could not be applied analogously (or at all) to judicial bodies; the Constitution merely obliged the legislature to enact specific rules on the conditions, extent and competent courts for such liability. Until that occurred, claims were not justiciable. Distinguishing EU-law cases (in which analogical application was required for uniformity), the SAC declared the action inadmissible of its own motion for lack of jurisdiction. It characterised the change as an ordinary development of case-law that did not undermine legal certainty, noting that the 2014 judgment had not been well-established when the applicant lodged or pursued his claim.

The new interpretation, applied for the first time in the applicant’s case and without a perceptible line of departing case-law, rendered his (and all similar) claims ineligible for judicial review for an indeterminate period pending hypothetical legislation. The ECHR found that this created legal uncertainty, imposed a disproportionate burden and impaired the very essence of the right of access to a court.

The applicant, a Greek national employed under a private-law contract as auxiliary staff at Greece’s embassy in Germany, sought an increased expatriation allowance for two dependent children covering 1993–1998. The first-instance civil court dismissed the claim, holding that the relevant legislation and ministerial decisions applied only to permanent public-law employees and that the distinction did not violate equality principles. The Court of Appeal partially granted the claim for the brief period after a 1998 law equated the two categories of staff, but upheld the dismissal for the earlier period. The applicant’s appeal on points of law to the Court of Cassation was rejected in 2001 as “vague” because it allegedly failed to set out the employment-contract terms and the children’s details, even though those facts were in the case file.

In Zouboulidis v. Greece (no. 77574/01, 2007) the European Court found that this rejection constituted excessive formalism violating Article 6 § 1 and awarded non-pecuniary damages (but not pecuniary damages, as it could not speculate on the outcome had the merits been examined). The Committee of Ministers later closed supervision after Greece paid just satisfaction and publicised the judgment.

In December 2007 the applicant sued the State in the administrative courts under Article 105 of the Introductory Law to the Civil Code, claiming compensation for the pecuniary loss he said flowed from the Cassation judgment’s unlawfulness (as established by the Strasbourg Court). He argued that a merits examination would have led to payment of the full allowance.

In 2014 the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) plenary held (judgment 1501/2014) that, pending specific legislation, Article 105 should apply by analogy to judicial acts that constituted a “manifest error,” because the Constitution forbids leaving damage caused by any State organ uncompensated. The first-instance and appeal administrative courts applied this ruling but found the Cassation error not “manifest” and dismissed the action.

On the applicant’s further appeal, the SAC plenary reversed course in 2021 (judgment 800/2021). It now held that Article 105 cannot apply—even analogically—to judicial bodies; the Constitution requires the legislature to enact a dedicated regime specifying conditions, scope and competent courts. Until that occurs, no compensation claim for judicial error is justiciable and the administrative courts lack jurisdiction. Distinguishing a same-day ruling that allowed analogical application for breaches of EU law, the SAC declared the action inadmissible of its own motion. It also ruled that the sudden change of case-law did not violate legal certainty or legitimate expectations, because the 2014 analogical approach had been recent, sparsely followed and post-dated the applicant’s original filing.

The applicant complained that this interpretation closed the courts to his claim indefinitely, impairing the very essence of his right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1. The Strasbourg Court agreed, finding the restriction disproportionate and productive of legal uncertainty.

**The applicant, a Greek national employed under a private-law contract at the Greek embassy in Germany, sought an increased expatriation allowance for his dependent children (1993–1998). Greek civil courts dismissed most of his claim, citing different legal statuses of permanent versus contract staff. His 2001 appeal on points of law to the Court of Cassation was rejected in part as “vague” for insufficiently detailing his contract and family circumstances (despite those facts being in the file).**

In *Zouboulidis v. Greece* (no. 77574/01, 2007), the European Court of Human Rights found this constituted excessive formalism violating Article 6 § 1 (access to court). It awarded non-pecuniary damages but declined pecuniary compensation, as it could not speculate on the outcome had the appeal been examined on the merits. The Committee of Ministers closed supervision after Greece paid just satisfaction and disseminated the judgment.

In December 2007 the applicant sued the State in the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance under Article 105 of the Introductory Law to the Civil Code (ILCC) (State liability for unlawful acts of its organs). He claimed the Cassation judgment’s formalism caused him pecuniary loss (unpaid allowance plus interest), arguing that a merits examination would have succeeded in light of later case-law. He relied on the 2007 Strasbourg finding.

In 2014 the Supreme Administrative Court (SAC) plenary, in an unrelated case (no. 1501/2014), held that Article 4 § 5 of the Constitution required compensation for damage caused by any State organ, including the judiciary. Pending specific legislation, Article 105 ILCC should apply by analogy to “manifest errors” by judicial bodies (an error’s manifest character depending on the case’s specifics). Subsequent SAC and lower-court decisions applied this approach.

The first-instance administrative court (2015) and Court of Appeal (2017) applied Article 105 by analogy but dismissed the claim on the merits, finding the Cassation Court’s approach—even if formalistic—was not a “manifest error” given civil-procedure requirements for precision in cassation appeals and the need for legal certainty.

The applicant appealed to the SAC. In plenary judgment no. 800/2021 (4 June 2021) the SAC reversed course. It held that Article 105 could not apply (directly or by analogy) to judicial acts, because the Constitution required the legislature first to enact specific rules on conditions, extent of liability, procedure and competent courts. Until then, such claims were not justiciable. The administrative courts therefore lacked jurisdiction; the action was declared inadmissible *ex officio*. (The same day, in no. 799/2021, the SAC applied Article 105 by analogy to last-instance judicial breaches of EU law, to ensure uniform application of EU rules.)

The SAC acknowledged its departure from the 2014 plenary ruling but said a change of interpretation is inherent in the judicial function, does not violate legal certainty or legitimate expectations unless arbitrary, and need not be postponed except in limited cases (none of which applied). It noted the 2014 line had been followed only sporadically and that the applicant’s action predated it.

The applicant complained to the Court that the 2021 ruling, by creating an absolute and indefinite bar to judicial review of his State-liability claim pending unspecified future legislation, violated his right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1. The Court agreed, holding that the novel, unforeseeable interpretation imposed a disproportionate and permanent obstacle, generated legal uncertainty, and impaired the very essence of the right.
