The case of M.C. v. Türkiye concerns a Georgian national (born 1978) wanted in Russia for voluntary homicide allegedly committed in October 2000. He was arrested at Istanbul Atatürk Airport on 23 May 2017 while attempting to leave Türkiye. The following day, a magistrates’ court ordered his provisional detention under Law no. 6706 and the European Convention on Extradition, based on a Russian Interpol Red Notice and an in-absentia arrest warrant from 2000.

He was released on 2 July 2017 after Russia failed to submit required extradition documents and the 40-day maximum for provisional detention expired. Two days later, however, the same court ordered his re-detention under Article 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing the gravity of the offence, strong suspicion, evidence, and flight or evidence-tampering risks. The applicant had argued that Russia had not pursued the case for over 17 years, that he faced ill-treatment upon extradition, and that less restrictive measures should be used.

On 16 August 2017 the Bakırköy Tenth Assize Court declared the extradition request admissible. The applicant repeated his fears of persecution, claimed the request lacked documents required by the Extradition Convention, and asserted that the offence was time-barred under Turkish law (a point on which the Ministry of Justice had earlier opined that an assessment was required). The court held that evidence on limitation was insufficient and that the issue belonged to the Russian courts; it continued detention and transferred him to prison.

An appeal to the Court of Cassation reiterating these points, including the Ministry’s view on limitation, was dismissed on 18 December 2017 with a brief statement that the Assize Court’s judgment was lawful. On 5 January 2018 the applicant applied to the Constitutional Court, adding that he had served in the Georgian army and fought in Abkhazia (1992–93) against Russian-backed forces; combined with the charge of killing a Russian national this created a real risk of ill-treatment. He also cited his hepatitis C and claimed that poor Russian prison conditions would deny him treatment, amounting to ill-treatment. He further argued that detention had exceeded lawful maxima, that extradition proceedings violated domestic and international law, and that detention was arbitrary and excessively long. The Constitutional Court refused an interim measure on 11 January 2018, finding the risks unsubstantiated and noting Russian diplomatic assurances of a fair trial limited to the charged offence, no torture, and permission to leave after any sentence. Subsequent similar requests were likewise rejected.

In June 2018 the applicant developed serious cardiac and respiratory problems (infectious endocarditis, pneumonia, acute respiratory failure). Hospital reports stated that his condition precluded extradition. He applied to the European Court on 4 July 2018 seeking an interim measure against extradition (granted on 7 August) and release on health grounds. Further medical reports confirmed the need for hospital care and postponement of any sentence.

On 18 December 2018 the applicant sought release under Article 16 of Law no. 6706 because extradition had not been effected within one year of the final admissibility decision. He was released the next day and left for Georgia on 22 December 2018. The Constitutional Court later struck out his application for failure to supply requested information.

The alleged violations centred on Articles 2 and 3 (risk of death or ill-treatment from health, possible political persecution, and Russian prison conditions) and Article 5 § 1 (unlawful and arbitrary detention pending extradition lasting some 17 months). The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 5 § 1(f) because the detention failed the requirements of non-arbitrariness and due diligence: domestic courts did not adequately address serious arguments concerning lawfulness (including limitation under Turkish law, given Türkiye’s reservation to the Extradition Convention), did not demonstrate that removal remained a realistic prospect, and did not show that proceedings were conducted with the requisite speed and without serious delay.

He applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 4 July 2018, alleging that extradition would violate Articles 2 and 3 (risk of death or ill-treatment due to health and Russian conditions) and that his detention pending extradition was unlawful and arbitrary under Article 5 § 1. The Court indicated an interim measure on 7 August 2018 prohibiting extradition.

On 19 December 2018 he was released because extradition had not occurred within one year of the admissibility ruling becoming final. He left Turkey for Georgia on 22 December 2018. The Constitutional Court later struck out his application for failure to provide requested information.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: a realistic risk of extradition despite health deterioration, persecution claims linked to the Abkhazia conflict, and lengthy detention (May 2017–December 2018) during which domestic courts did not adequately examine arguments on time-bar, missing documents, delay, or the continuing realistic prospect of removal.

The case of M.C. v. Türkiye concerns a Georgian national detained in Türkiye from 2017 pending possible extradition to Russia on charges of voluntary homicide allegedly committed on 19 October 2000. The applicant, born in 1978, was arrested on 23 May 2017 at Istanbul Atatürk Airport. The next day, a magistrates’ court ordered his provisional detention under Article 14 of Law no. 6706 and Article 16 of the European Convention on Extradition, relying on an Interpol Red Notice and a 2000 Russian in absentia arrest warrant. Provisional detention is limited to 40 days.

On 2 July 2017 he was released because Russia had not submitted the required extradition documents and the 40-day limit had expired. Two days later, however, he was re-detained under Article 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court cited the gravity of the offence, strong suspicion, the evidence and a risk of absconding or tampering with evidence, rejecting the applicant’s arguments about the 17-year prosecutorial delay, a real risk of ill-treatment in Russia and the availability of less restrictive measures.

On 16 August 2017 an assize court declared the extradition request admissible. The applicant had argued that the request lacked documents required by the Extradition Convention, that the offence was time-barred under Turkish law (a point the Ministry of Justice had itself flagged), and that he faced persecution because of his combat service in Abkhazia and the fact that the alleged victim was Russian. The court held that the limitation question was for the Russian courts and continued the detention. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision on 18 December 2017 with a one-sentence statement that it was lawful.

The applicant then applied to the Constitutional Court, adding that his hepatitis C and the conditions in Russian prisons would amount to ill-treatment or even death, contrary to Articles 2 and 3. Interim-measure requests were refused on the basis of diplomatic assurances given by Russia. In June–July 2018 his health deteriorated sharply; he was hospitalised with hepatitis C, pneumonia, infectious endocarditis and acute respiratory failure. Medical reports stated that his condition precluded travel.

He lodged an application with the European Court on 4 July 2018; an interim measure prohibiting extradition was indicated on 7 August 2018. On 19 December 2018 he was released because no extradition decision had been taken within one year of the admissibility ruling becoming final (Article 16(3) of Law no. 6706). He left Türkiye for Georgia three days later.

The applicant alleged that extradition would violate Articles 2 and 3 because of his health and a real risk of ill-treatment, and that his detention pending extradition was unlawful and arbitrary under Article 5 § 1. Domestic courts had failed to examine his serious arguments on the time-bar (Türkiye’s reservation to the Extradition Convention), missing documents and the 17-year delay, and the authorities had not shown that removal remained a realistic prospect or that the proceedings had been conducted with the requisite due diligence.

The case of T.V. v. Croatia (Application no. 47909/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the death of the applicant’s partner, V.D., a Slovenian national with schizophrenia, during a Croatian police intervention on 16 November 2017, as well as the alleged ineffectiveness of the subsequent criminal investigation. The applicant invoked Articles 2, 3 and 13 of the Convention.

V.D. had absconded from a Slovenian psychiatric institution on 11 November 2017. Croatian border police were promptly informed by their Slovenian counterparts, based on information from V.D.’s father, that he posed a danger to himself and others and might be heading to Opuzen. On 16 November, after V.D. fought with a hotel guest, staff summoned the Metković police, describing a mentally distressed man attacking others. Responding officers already knew of the earlier alert.

Around 2.20 p.m. four officers found V.D. sitting on his car in the hotel car park, mumbling incoherently. He emptied his pockets when ordered but refused to turn and spread his legs. He produced a telephone, shouted that he would “blow up” the officers if they approached, then sat on the ground still holding the device. An officer twice ordered him to drop the phone and warned of force. When V.D. remained seated, pepper spray was used—an action excluded under Croatian law for passive resistance. V.D. collapsed onto his side, biting his lips and tongue and spitting blood. Three officers then forced him face-down, pinned him and handcuffed his hands behind his back while he struggled, struck his head on the pavement and bit off part of a finger. A fifth officer joined them. They held him in that position for approximately twelve minutes until an ambulance arrived at 2.47 p.m. (called at 2.35 p.m.).

The doctor administered a sedative, noting facial cyanosis, bleeding and the self-amputated fingertip. V.D. was placed face-down on the stretcher and strapped. During the 90-minute journey to the nearest suitable hospital the doctor and nurse sat in front; three officers sat in the back. A second sedative was given after the ambulance stopped because V.D. remained restless. Shortly thereafter he was found dead. The coroner recorded natural death by cardiac arrest.

An official autopsy found no evidence of violent death, five broken ribs attributed to a fall, and no causal link between the injuries and death. A police internal report deemed the force lawful and proportionate. The applicant commissioned a second autopsy in Slovenia that recorded additional findings (knocked-out teeth, lung and brain swelling, myocardial fibrosis). Her criminal complaint against the officers (serious bodily injury resulting in death) and ambulance staff (medical negligence) was rejected in February 2019 on the basis of the official autopsy.

After hierarchical review, further interviews occurred in 2020 and a forensic report was obtained in 2021. That report concluded V.D. had died a violent death from mental trauma: self-harm, prone restraint and pressure on his back had produced grave injury, shock and cardiac arrest. It found no medical negligence but criticised the absence of continuous bedside monitoring. Prosecutors again rejected the complaint, holding the force proportionate. The Croatian Constitutional Court later dismissed the applicant’s challenge, describing the investigation as independent and thorough despite its length.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: police awareness of V.D.’s psychiatric history yet failure to summon medical assistance first (contrary to domestic guidelines); use of pepper spray against passive resistance; prolonged prone restraint (a recognised asphyxia risk) both at the scene and in the ambulance; inadequate monitoring; and an investigation that was delayed, dismissed contrary medical evidence and ultimately classified the death as non-violent.

The Constitutional Court dismissed a complaint in 2023, finding the (delayed) investigation independent and thorough. Civil damages proceedings remain pending.

These facts underpin alleged violations of Article 2 (substantive failure to protect life through unnecessary force, including pepper spray contrary to domestic rules on passive resistance, prolonged prone restraint, and inadequate medical coordination/training; and procedural ineffectiveness of the investigation) as well as Articles 3 and 13. The Court later found Article 2 violations on both limbs.

The investigation was delayed, initially dismissed official findings without the later forensic view, and deemed ineffective. Civil damages proceedings remain pending.

001-234138:
The case of RFE/RL Inc. and Others v. Azerbaijan (applications nos. 56138/18, 48735/19, 51207/19 and 58694/19) concerns the wholesale blocking of four Azerbaijani online news outlets—azadliq.org (operated by RFE/RL Inc.), anaxeber.az (founded and edited by journalist Talibov), az24saat.org (operated by 24Saat.org Ltd, founded and edited by journalist Alakbarov), and xural.com (operated by newspaper Khural, founded and edited by Zeynalov)—following 2017 amendments to the Law on Information, Informatisation and Protection of Information (IIPI Law) and the Code of Civil Procedure. These amendments empowered the Ministry of Transport, Communication and High Technology (MTCHT) to identify “prohibited” content on internet resources (such as information promoting violence, extremism, incitement to hostility or riots, forcible constitutional change, libel, false or misleading material, or other unlawful acts under the Law on Mass Media) and to seek court orders restricting access, with urgent temporary blocks possible.

For azadliq.org, a 27 March 2017 Prosecutor General’s letter alleged (without examples) that the site and others regularly breached the IIPI Law through “destructive actions” aimed at changing the constitutional order, violating stability, calling for riots, or promoting radical groups. That same day, the MTCHT imposed an immediate temporary block under the new urgent-threat provisions, citing unspecified “prohibited information” threatening state and public interests, then applied to court. The Sabail District Court (12 May 2017) ordered a permanent block, relying on four articles (from February–March 2017, some predating the amendments) containing critical remarks on a 2016 constitutional referendum, economic/social crises and protests, a “caviar diplomacy” corruption scandal, and a “false state/democracy.” Higher courts (Baku Court of Appeal, 19 December 2017; Supreme Court, 4 June 2018) upheld this, interpreting prohibited “open calls” to include indirect “between the lines” statements perceivable as such by individuals, treating continued online availability as a continuing violation (no retroactivity bar), deeming a delayed hearing (beyond the five-day rule) reasonable, and finding an advance warning futile given the outlet’s denials.

For anaxeber.az, the MTCHT emailed a warning on 5 August 2018 (unseen by the applicant, then abroad) about libellous/false/misleading articles, applying to court (apparently the same day). The Sabail District Court (7 August 2018, in the applicant’s absence) blocked the entire site based on three June–July 2018 articles criticising healthcare officials as “butchers,” alleging clan clashes over vice-presidential posts, and attributing Ganja riots to official tyranny rather than radicals. Appeals (Baku Court of Appeal, 21 September 2018; Supreme Court, 20 December 2018) were dismissed; the MTCHT could act on its own initiative without prior defamation claims or judgments, and the Ganja article risked inciting hatred/panic.

Similar processes applied to az24saat.org and xural.com. Warnings (6 and 7 August 2018) alleged libellous/false content in articles on a presidential assistant’s dismissal/clan struggles, a Nakhchivan official’s affairs, hospital mistreatment, a Ganja official’s conduct, and political prisoners. The MTCHT applied immediately (sometimes before the eight-hour removal deadline), with hearings offering little notice or adjournment. Courts (7–8 August 2018) blocked the full sites, finding breaches of IIPI Law Article 13-2.3.11 and Mass Media Law Article 10; higher courts (September 2018–February 2019) upheld this, confirming the MTCHT’s independent identification power. Applicants argued the articles were protected political speech/criticism, not unlawful, with no affected-person complaints.

In all cases, entire domains were blocked (not just specific content or pages), orders were immediately enforceable without suspensive appeals, and domestic remedies failed. Applicants alleged these measures arbitrarily restricted freedom of expression.

The case of RFE/RL Inc. and Others v. Azerbaijan (nos. 56138/18, 48735/19, 51207/19 and 58694/19) concerns the wholesale blocking of four online media outlets—azadliq.org (operated by RFE/RL Inc.), anaxeber.az (founded and edited by journalist Talibov), az24saat.org (operated by 24Saat.org Ltd, founded and edited by journalist Alakbarov), and xural.com (operated by newspaper Khural, founded and edited by journalist Zeynalov)—on the grounds that certain articles they published contained allegedly unlawful content. The applicants complained under Article 10 of the Convention (freedom to receive and impart information), as well as Articles 6, 13 and 18 in some instances.

In March–April 2017, Azerbaijan amended the Law on Information, Informatisation and Protection of Information (IIPI Law) to regulate “internet information resources.” Article 13-2.3 prohibited owners from placing specified content, including information promoting violence or religious extremism, openly calling for ethnic/racial/religious hostility, a forcible change in the constitutional order, violation of territorial integrity, forcible seizure/retention of power, or mass riots (13-2.3.2); insulting or libellous information or that breaching private life (13-2.3.9); and “other information prohibited by the laws” (13-2.3.11). Owners were required to remove prohibited information upon discovery or notification (13-2.4). Article 13-3 empowered the relevant executive authority (the Ministry of Transport, Communication and High Technology, or MTCHT) to issue a written warning upon identifying prohibited content and, if not removed within eight hours, to apply to a district court for a blocking order. In urgent cases threatening State or public interests, the MTCHT could impose a temporary block pending court review. Concurrent amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure (Chapter 40-6) required courts to examine such applications within five days, with judgments immediately enforceable (appeals did not suspend execution). The Law on Mass Media (Art. 10) similarly prohibited using mass media for false, misleading or libellous publications or other illegal acts.

For azadliq.org, the Prosecutor General’s Office wrote to the MTCHT on 27 March 2017 stating that the site (among others) had “regularly breached” the IIPI Law through “destructive actions” aimed at forcibly changing the constitutional order, violating social stability, calling for mass riots, and promoting radical religious groups—without citing specific examples. The MTCHT immediately imposed a temporary block under Arts. 13-2.3 and 13-3.3, then applied to the Sabail District Court. The court, on 12 May 2017, ordered a full block after quoting short extracts from four articles (published February–March 2017, some predating the amendments) containing: a journalist’s criticism of 2016 constitutional changes granting the President exclusive appointment powers; an opposition figure’s remarks on economic crisis, political prisoners, corruption and the need for protests; references to a “caviar diplomacy” corruption scandal; and an emigrant’s comments on Azerbaijan as a “false State” with a “false democracy.” The court found a breach of Art. 13-2.3.2. Appeals to the Baku Court of Appeal (19 December 2017) and Supreme Court (4 June 2018) failed. Higher courts held that prohibited content need not be “in open text” but could include indirect “in between the lines” expressions perceivable as such by individuals; they dismissed arguments on retroactivity (ongoing public accessibility created a continuing situation), lack of prior warning (futile given the applicant’s denial of unlawfulness), and the court’s delay beyond five days.

In August 2018, the MTCHT sent warning emails to the remaining applicants (one unused for years) alleging libellous, false and misleading articles, then applied to the same court (in one instance the same day, before the eight-hour period expired). Blocking orders followed on 7–8 August 2018 for entire sites, based on 3–4 articles each: criticism of healthcare officials as “butchers”; alleged clan struggles for vice-presidential posts; Ganja riots attributed to official “tyranny,” unemployment and land seizures rather than religious radicals (with appellate remarks that this could incite hatred, panic or repeat events amid ongoing investigations); rumours about an Assistant to the President (dismissal, clan conflicts, false information to the President); a Nakhchivan official’s alleged extramarital affairs and gifts; a hospital described as a “morgue”; insults and persecution by a Ganja official; and claims of over 160 political prisoners with implications of wrongful convictions or poor treatment. Courts invoked Arts. 13-2.3.9/13-2.3.11 of the IIPI Law read with Art. 10 of the Mass Media Law. They rejected arguments that no defamation claims or prior court findings existed (MTCHT could act on its own initiative under Art. 13-3.1) and that the content was protected political speech/criticism. Procedural complaints included hearings in absence (one applicant abroad), extremely short notice (hours), refusal of adjournments, and failure to consider post-warning article removals. Appeals to the Baku Court of Appeal and Supreme Court (final decisions December 2018–February 2019) were dismissed, upholding the first-instance reasoning.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 10 violations: entire sites were blocked indefinitely based on a handful of critical/political articles, with domestic law applied in an unforeseeable, overly broad manner lacking safeguards against arbitrariness (no requirement to target specific content, immediate unappealable effect, MTCHT’s unilateral initiative). Additional complaints addressed fair-trial delays/absences, lack of effective remedies, and possible ulterior political motives (especially for RFE/RL, given prior raids, tax probes and journalist prosecutions).

The case of RFE/RL Inc. and Others v. Azerbaijan (applications nos. 56138/18, 48735/19, 51207/19 and 58694/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the wholesale blocking of four independent Azerbaijani online news outlets (azadliq.org, anaxeber.az, az24saat.org and xural.com) in 2017–2018. The blocks were imposed because certain articles allegedly contained unlawful content, raising complaints under Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression, including to receive and impart information) as well as Articles 6, 13 and 18.

RFE/RL Inc., a US-funded non-profit operating azadliq.org since 2004, had already faced prior pressure (FM broadcasting ban, office raid, tax probe). In March 2017, shortly after legislative amendments introducing a new Chapter III-I of the Law on Information, Informatisation and Protection of Information (IIPI Law) and corresponding Civil Procedure Code provisions on restricting internet resources, the Prosecutor General’s Office wrote to the Ministry of Transport, Communication and High Technology (MTCHT). It alleged that azadliq.org and other sites “regularly” published material aimed at forcibly changing the constitutional order, inciting riots or promoting extremism, without citing specific examples. The same day the MTCHT imposed an immediate temporary block under the “urgent cases” clause of Article 13-3.3 IIPI Law, again without identifying any particular content, then applied to the Sabail District Court. On 12 May 2017 the court granted a permanent blocking order, quoting four short extracts from articles (criticism of 2016 constitutional changes expanding presidential powers, an opposition figure’s remarks on crisis and the need for protest, reporting on a “caviar diplomacy” corruption scandal, and comments describing Azerbaijan as a “false State”). Appeals were dismissed. The appellate court held that even “between-the-lines” statements that individual readers might perceive as indirect calls for unrest fell within the prohibition of Article 13-2.3.2 IIPI Law; it also rejected arguments that the block was retroactive, that no prior warning had been given, and that the statutory five-day hearing deadline had been missed.

The three later cases followed a similar pattern in August 2018. Journalist Mehman Talibov (anaxeber.az) received an eight-hour warning e-mail (which he did not see because he was abroad) alleging libellous, false and misleading material. The MTCHT then obtained a block based on three articles criticising the health minister, speculating about clan rivalries over vice-presidential posts, and attributing Ganja riots to official tyranny rather than religious radicalism. The courts treated the content as prohibited under Article 13-2.3.11 IIPI Law read with Article 10 of the Mass Media Law, even though no defamation claims had been brought by any named individual.

24Saat.org Ltd and its editor Vugar Alakbarov faced a warning and same-day court application over four articles discussing rumours about the President’s assistant (possible dismissal, internal “clan” struggles, alleged misinformation of the President). The hearing notice arrived only hours in advance; an adjournment request was refused. Khural newspaper and its editor Avaz Zeynalov received a warning at an unused e-mail address. After learning of four articles (alleged extramarital gifts by a Nakhchivan deputy prime minister, criticism of a Baku hospital, comments on a Ganja official, and a list of “political prisoners”), the editor immediately removed them, yet the court still ordered a wholesale block the next day.

In all four sets of proceedings the domestic courts upheld the complete blocking of entire websites rather than the removal of specific items, relying on the MTCHT’s own initiative to identify “prohibited information.” The applicants argued that the measures lacked a sufficiently precise legal basis, were unforeseeable, afforded no effective safeguards against arbitrariness, and were disproportionate. The Strasbourg Court ultimately found a violation of Article 10 on the ground that the blocking was not “prescribed by law.”
001-233992:
The 16 Azerbaijani applicants deposited funds (in AZN, USD or EUR) into savings accounts at the Baku branch of private bank T. between various dates, receiving official savings books and receipts signed by branch head Z.Y., the accountant and treasurer, and sealed with the branch stamp. These confirmed 1% monthly interest under written deposit contracts.

On 30 September 2008, criminal proceedings began against Z.Y. and staff for fraud, embezzlement, abuse of office, forgery and related offences (Criminal Code Arts. 178, 179, 308, 313, 320). Z.Y. allegedly formed a group that accepted deposits from 2005–2008 without transferring all funds to the bank treasury, using them for personal businesses while issuing false documents to create an appearance of valid contracts. Extra interest (3–6%) was sometimes paid. An expert report found large sums missing or undisclosed.

Applicants in two cases (nos. 46579/14 and 46596/14) sued the bank in civil proceedings in 2008–2009. First-instance courts (2008–2009) partly granted claims, ordering return of principal (and limited interest in one case) under Civil Code Arts. 944.1, 946.1, 947.2 and 1099.1. They held that official documents created valid contracts; employee misconduct did not relieve the bank of liability. Proceedings were later stayed pending the criminal case.

In the criminal trial, Z.Y. admitted taking funds for personal use but denied an organised group. Some applicants knew him personally or received extra-interest promises; most denied receiving extra sums and sought repayment from the bank (one from both). The Court of Serious Crimes convicted Z.Y. et al. on 27 April 2010, sentencing them to imprisonment. It held the accused (not the bank) liable for all depositors’ losses, allocating Z.Y.’s attached properties (wedding hall, house, non-residential building) toward compensation. It dismissed bank-liability arguments without detailed reasoning, citing CCrP Art. 183.2.

Applicants appealed, arguing the offences targeted the bank (using official documents while on duty), so the bank was vicariously liable under Civil Code Art. 1099. They cited CCrP Arts. 180.2 and 188 and CCP provisions on civil claims. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed appeals on 30 March 2011. The Supreme Court quashed and remitted (2011–2012), holding that employees acted in official roles using bank documents, triggering bank liability under Art. 1099; lower courts failed to examine whether the correct respondent was identified and ignored some civil claims against the bank.

On remittal, the Court of Appeal (22 May 2013) upheld the trial judgment, ruling the acts were criminal fraud against depositors (who dealt with Z.Y. as a businessman and received extra interest), not a civil delict by employees; the bank itself was an injured party. The Supreme Court dismissed further cassation appeals on 22 November 2013.

Civil proceedings resumed for some applicants; appellate and Supreme Court decisions (2011–2012) overturned first-instance awards, relying on the criminal judgment (CCP Art. 82.4). The remaining applicant (no. 58873/14) obtained a first-instance order against the bank (2013) that was overturned on similar grounds; the Supreme Court upheld this in 2014.

The bank’s licence was revoked in 2016. Limited recovery occurred: one non-residential property (valued at AZN 230,000) was transferred in 2017 to four applicants, covering some deposits fully or partially. Z.Y.’s father later recovered the other properties. Most applicants recovered nothing or only part of the sums awarded against the convicts.

These facts underpin the alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (inadequate reasoning, failure to address bank-liability arguments or follow Supreme Court instructions, inconsistent application of civil vs. criminal liability) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (inability to recover deposits despite official bank documentation).

The case of Abbasali Ahmadov and Others v. Azerbaijan (applications nos. 46579/14, 46596/14 and 58873/14) concerns 16 Azerbaijani nationals who, on various dates, opened savings accounts at the Baku branch of private bank T. They deposited sums in Azerbaijani manats, US dollars and/or euros at a 1% monthly interest rate. Official savings books and receipts, signed by branch head Z.Y., the accountant and treasurer and sealed with the branch stamp, confirmed the deposits.

On 30 September 2008 criminal proceedings were opened against Z.Y. and several staff members for fraud, embezzlement, official forgery and related offences. The indictment alleged that, between 2005 and 2008, they formed an organised group that accepted deposits without transferring them to the bank’s treasury, used the funds for Z.Y.’s personal business, paid some depositors extra interest above the contractual rate, and issued forged official documents to create the appearance of valid contracts.

Most applicants brought civil actions against the bank in 2008–2009 seeking return of the principal and interest. First-instance courts, relying on Civil Code Articles 944.1, 946.1, 947.2 and 1099.1, largely granted the claims. They held that written deposit contracts had been formed through the official documents, that the bank remained liable even if an employee had diverted the funds, and that internal irregularities did not relieve the bank of its contractual obligations. Interest was generally refused because the contracts had not yet expired. The civil proceedings were then stayed pending the criminal trial.

In the criminal case the applicants were recognised as injured parties; some lodged civil claims naming the bank (or, in one instance, Z.Y.) as respondent. At trial several applicants stated they knew Z.Y. personally or had been recommended to the branch; a few mentioned promises of extra interest, though most denied receiving any. All requested repayment from the bank. An expert report established large shortfalls in the branch treasury and undisclosed deposits. On 27 April 2010 the Court of Serious Crimes convicted Z.Y. and co-accused, sentenced them to imprisonment, and ordered them (not the bank) to compensate the depositors, allocating Z.Y.’s attached properties for that purpose. The court dismissed requests directed at the bank without detailed reasoning.

Applicants appealed, arguing that the convicted employees had appropriated the bank’s money while acting in an official capacity, so the bank was vicariously liable under Civil Code Article 1099 and remained contractually bound. They invoked the Law on Banks and Convention rights. The Supreme Court initially quashed the appellate judgment, holding that the employees had acted within their posts using official documents, that the bank was therefore liable, and that the lower courts had failed to examine the civil claims or consider substituting the proper respondent.

On remittal the Baku Court of Appeal nevertheless upheld the trial judgment. It characterised the acts as criminal fraud against the depositors rather than a civil delict, noted that the bank itself was an injured party, and found that the applicants had given money to Z.Y. as a businessman in return for extra interest. The Supreme Court later dismissed cassation appeals as unsubstantiated.

Some stayed civil proceedings were resumed and dismissed by reference to the now-final criminal judgment (Civil Procedure Code Article 82.4). A separate civil action by one applicant was likewise rejected. The bank’s licence was later revoked. Enforcement against the convicts’ assets recovered only a fraction of the sums (one property was transferred to four applicants; other properties were restored to Z.Y.’s father). By 2022 most applicants had recovered nothing, or only part of their deposits.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints that the domestic courts failed to address their arguments on contractual and vicarious liability, provided inadequate reasoning, and thereby rendered the proceedings unfair, leaving them unable to recover their savings.

The case of Abbasali Ahmadov and Others v. Azerbaijan concerns 16 Azerbaijani applicants who, on various dates, opened savings accounts at the Baku branch of private bank T., depositing sums in AZN, USD and/or EUR at a 1% monthly interest rate. They received official savings books and receipts confirming the deposits, signed by branch head Z.Y., the accountant and treasurer, and sealed with the branch’s official stamp.

On 30 September 2008, criminal proceedings were initiated against Z.Y. and several staff members for offences including fraud, embezzlement, abuse of office, forgery and falsification of documents. They were accused of forming an organised group that accepted deposits between 2005 and 2008 without transferring the funds to the bank’s treasury, instead using the money for personal business activities while paying some depositors extra interest (3–6%) above the contractual rate, and of forging documents to allocate unauthorised loans.

The applicants (or most of them) brought civil proceedings against the bank in 2008–2009 seeking return of their deposits plus interest. First-instance courts largely granted the claims, citing Civil Code provisions on bank deposit contracts (Arts. 944.1, 946.1, 947.2) and employer liability for employees’ acts (Art. 1099.1). They held that valid contracts existed, the bank remained responsible even if staff had misappropriated funds, and interest was generally not due because deposits were withdrawn early. These civil cases were later suspended pending the criminal outcome.

In the criminal proceedings, the applicants were recognised as injured parties; some lodged civil claims against the bank (or, in one case, Z.Y.). At trial, Z.Y. admitted taking deposits for his own use and paying extra interest to certain depositors (including some applicants). Some applicants stated they knew Z.Y. personally or had been promised additional benefits, though most denied receiving extra interest. An expert report identified millions of AZN missing from the branch.

On 27 April 2010 the Court of Serious Crimes convicted Z.Y. and others and, applying Art. 183.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, ordered the convicted persons (not the bank) to repay all deposited amounts. Z.Y.’s attached properties were allocated for compensation. The applicants appealed, arguing that the offences had been committed against the bank in the course of official duties, so the bank was liable under Civil Code Art. 1099 and should repay them (then recoup from the employees). They also relied on their right to pursue separate civil claims.

The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals. The Supreme Court quashed those decisions (2011–2012), holding that the employees had acted in their official capacity using bank documents, that the bank was therefore liable under Art. 1099, and that the lower courts had failed to examine properly who the correct civil respondent was or whether claims needed to be redirected. The case was remitted.

On 22 May 2013 the Court of Appeal nevertheless upheld the original conviction and compensation order. It characterised the acts as fraud against the depositors personally (not a civil delict by the bank), noted that some applicants had known Z.Y. as a businessman and received extra interest, and found the bank itself an injured party. It did not address the Supreme Court’s instructions. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicants’ further cassation appeals on 22 November 2013, describing their bank-liability argument as unsubstantiated.

Resumed civil proceedings of some applicants were then dismissed by reference to the criminal judgment’s findings (under Code of Civil Procedure Art. 82.4). A separate civil claim by one applicant met the same fate. The bank’s licence was later revoked. Only limited recovery occurred from one confiscated property; other properties were restored to Z.Y.’s father. Most applicants recovered nothing.

The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to give adequate reasons, ignore their arguments and the Supreme Court’s binding instructions, and thereby denied them a fair hearing, as well as under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning their inability to recover the deposited funds.

The case of Bluks Savickis v. Latvia (no. 44570/19) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that Latvian courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for his prolonged pre-trial detention.

The applicant, born in 1962, was convicted in January 2013 of procuring and storing large quantities of narcotics for distribution and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. While still serving that sentence he allegedly continued to organise narcotics distribution through intermediaries V.R. and M.L. After his release on 10 November 2017 he was arrested five days later on suspicion of the same offence committed as part of an organised group; he was under the influence of drugs at the time of arrest.

On 17 November 2017 the Riga City Ziemeļu District Court ordered detention, citing a reasonable suspicion of a particularly serious offence punishable by imprisonment, a risk of further offending stemming from the applicant’s character, and the public interest. The Riga Regional Court upheld the order on 4 December 2017, stressing that the public interest in a grave offence outweighed personal liberty and that the applicant’s still-unexpunged prior conviction created a re-offending risk.

Detention was successively extended on 10 January, 6 March, 2 May and 27 June 2018. Each decision repeated the same factors: the nature and gravity of the offence, participation in an organised group, the applicant’s character and criminal record, and the consequent risk of re-offending. Non-custodial alternatives were considered but rejected as insufficient to guarantee fair and speedy proceedings or to protect the public. On 27 June the court offered release on bail of EUR 25 000 (the applicant having proposed EUR 12 000), reasoning that only that sum would neutralise the high re-offending risk and safeguard society from narcotics; the applicant did not pay and remained in custody.

After indictment on 20 April 2018 the trial opened on 15 August 2018. Defence applications to replace detention with a non-custodial measure were refused on 15 August, 8 October and 19 December 2018 and again on 25 April and 28 June 2019. The courts held that the original grounds had neither disappeared nor changed, that detention remained necessary to prevent absconding or obstruction, and that less restrictive measures would not ensure a fair and speedy trial. Public-interest considerations—preventing drug distribution and protecting society, especially the young—were repeatedly invoked. The applicant’s family, employment and residence circumstances, and his limited means (he could raise only EUR 5 000–6 000), were dismissed as insufficient to alter the measure. The earlier bail offer, which had been declined, was also cited against him.

On 12 September 2019, with the statutory maximum approaching, the Riga District Court found that the grounds for detention no longer obtained and released the applicant subject to residence-notification and travel-ban conditions. On 15 January 2020 he entered a plea bargain, admitted the organised-group narcotics offence and received a six-year sentence that became final on 11 February 2020.

The relevant provisions of the Latvian Criminal Procedure Law (ss. 244, 249, 272, 274–275, 277, 281) require courts to base detention on specific facts, to consider alternatives, to review necessity periodically and to observe strict time-limits (normally 24 months, extendable by three-month increments). The domestic decisions, however, largely recycled the same general justifications throughout the almost two-year period of detention.

The case of Bluks Savickis v. Latvia (Application no. 44570/19) concerned the applicant’s pre-trial detention from November 2017 until September 2019 and the alleged failure of Latvian courts to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for its repeated extensions, in violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1962, had been convicted in January 2013 of unauthorised procurement and storage of large quantities of narcotics for distribution and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. While serving that sentence he continued to organise narcotics trafficking through intermediaries V.R. and M.L. After his release on 10 November 2017 he was arrested on 15 November 2017, while under the influence of drugs, on suspicion of the same type of offence committed as part of an organised group. On 17 November 2017 the Riga City Ziemeļu District Court ordered his pre-trial detention, citing a reasonable suspicion of a particularly serious offence punishable by imprisonment and a risk, based on his character, that he would continue criminal activity. The measure was held to be proportionate and in the public interest.

An appeal was dismissed on 4 December 2017 by the Riga Regional Court, which emphasised the public interest in light of the gravity of the offence and the fact that the applicant’s earlier conviction remained on his record, creating a risk of re-offending. Detention was extended on 10 January 2018 and again on 6 March 2018 by first-instance courts that repeated the same grounds: the nature and seriousness of the offence, participation in an organised group, the applicant’s character and criminal history, and the public interest. Non-custodial alternatives were considered but rejected as insufficient to ensure the proper conduct of proceedings.

After indictment on 20 April 2018 the necessity of detention was reviewed on 2 May and 27 June 2018. The courts again relied on the risk of re-offending, noting that the applicant’s drug use on the day of arrest showed he had not changed his lifestyle. On 27 June the court offered release on bail of EUR 25,000 (higher than the EUR 12,000 suggested by the applicant) because of the seriousness of the offence and the high risk of re-offending; the applicant did not pay and remained in custody.

The trial opened on 15 August 2018. Defence requests to replace detention with a non-custodial measure were refused on 15 August, 8 October and 19 December 2018 and on 25 April and 28 June 2019. The courts consistently held that the original grounds had not disappeared or changed, that detention was necessary to prevent absconding or further offences, and that less restrictive measures would not guarantee a fair and speedy trial. They repeatedly invoked the public interest in combating drug trafficking, the applicant’s prior conviction and the organised nature of the alleged crime, while stating that his family, employment or residential situation did not justify a change. In June 2019 the court also noted that an earlier bail offer had been declined and that the applicant lacked the means to pay a sufficient sum.

On 12 September 2019, shortly before the statutory maximum period expired, the court found that the grounds for detention no longer obtained and released the applicant subject to residence-notification and travel-restriction conditions. He later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment.

Throughout the period of detention the domestic courts relied on largely formulaic references to the seriousness of the offence, the applicant’s criminal record and a generalised risk of re-offending, without demonstrating a continuing, individualised necessity for deprivation of liberty or adequately explaining why alternatives had become or remained inadequate.

The case of Namazli v. Azerbaijan (no. 8826/20) concerns a lawyer’s complaint that prison staff inspected his documents and seized a client’s written statement, interfering with lawyer-client confidentiality under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicant, Fariz Namazli, a member of the Azerbaijani Bar Association, represented prisoner A.H. in domestic criminal proceedings and before the European Court of Human Rights. On 10 August 2018 he visited Gobustan Prison to discuss A.H.’s pending Court cases. Staff inspected his documents at the entrance despite his protests that the action was unlawful. During the meeting (12:35–17:20) A.H. handed him a five-page written statement intended for the Court.

On leaving, the applicant was personally searched and his documents re-inspected. Staff removed the statement to show the prison governor and later refused to return it on the governor’s instructions. No record of the seizure was drawn up.

The applicant immediately complained to the prison service of the Ministry of Justice, alleging unlawful inspection and seizure that breached professional privilege. The service replied on 11 September 2018 that no document belonging to A.H. had been taken and that no interference with confidential communications had occurred.

He also lodged an administrative complaint. The prison governor wrote to the court stating that the applicant’s briefcase had undergone only a general inspection, not censorship, and that no statement had been seized. The applicant contested this, asserting he had carried the documents in his hands and that they had been read. He requested the checkpoint video recordings and that A.H. be heard as a witness. On 5 March 2019 the first-instance court refused to examine the claim for lack of evidence. Appeals were dismissed: the videos had been automatically deleted after one month, and A.H. could not testify because the events had not occurred in his presence. The Supreme Court’s final decision was served on 30 July 2019.

Azerbaijani law on advocates protects lawyer confidentiality, prohibits questioning lawyers about professional matters and bars seizure of their files by investigative or judicial bodies; it also requires confidential meetings with detained clients. Nevertheless, the Code on Execution of Punishments and the Internal Prison Disciplinary Rules authorise the administration to inspect all persons entering or leaving a prison and their belongings. Lawyers must present identity and professional documents but, unlike judges or certain international officials, they are not exempt from inspection. No detailed rules distinguish lawyers from other visitors, require reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing, or provide procedural safeguards against abuse.

The European Prison Rules require that consultations and correspondence between prisoners and their legal advisers remain confidential, with restrictions permitted only in exceptional, judicially authorised circumstances to prevent serious crime or major security breaches.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation: an inspection and seizure of privileged material carried out without any suspicion of misconduct, under general provisions that disregarded lawyers’ special status in the administration of justice and lacked a clear framework or safeguards against arbitrariness. Complaints under Articles 6 and 13 were also notified to the Government. The Court later held that the interference was not “in accordance with the law.”

**CASE OF NAMAZLI v. AZERBAIJAN (Application no. 8826/20)**

The applicant, Fariz Namazli, an Azerbaijani lawyer and Bar Association member, represented client A.H. in domestic criminal proceedings and before the European Court of Human Rights. On 10 August 2018, he visited Gobustan Prison to discuss A.H.’s pending cases before the Court.

According to the applicant, prison staff inspected his documents at the entrance before allowing the meeting, despite his objections that this was unlawful. During the meeting, A.H. provided a five-page written statement intended for submission to the Court. After the meeting, staff conducted a personal search of the applicant and inspected his documents again as he exited. They removed the written statement to show the prison governor. Approximately 30 minutes later, staff informed the applicant they could not return it on the governor’s instructions. No record of the seizure was made.

The applicant lodged complaints the next day (11 August 2018) with the Ministry of Justice prison service and the Baku Administrative-Economic Court No. 1. He argued the inspections and seizure unlawfully breached lawyer-client confidentiality and his professional rights.

The prison service replied on 11 September 2018 that no document belonging to A.H. had been taken and there had been no interference with confidential communications. In a 20 September 2018 letter to the court, the prison governor stated the applicant had met A.H. from 12:35 p.m. to 5:20 p.m., that his briefcase had undergone only a general inspection (not censorship), and that no written statement or complaint by A.H. had been seized.

The applicant requested the first-instance court obtain security-camera footage from the checkpoint and hear A.H. as a witness. He contested the governor’s account, stating he had carried documents in his hands (not a briefcase) and that staff had read the papers and seized the statement.

On 5 March 2019, the Baku Administrative-Economic Court No. 1 declined to examine the claim, holding that the applicant had provided no supporting evidence of censorship or seizure. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 25 April 2019. The Supreme Court rejected his cassation appeal on 16 July 2019 (served 30 July 2019), confirming that the applicant had submitted no evidence. It noted that requested video recordings had been automatically deleted after one month (as stated by the prison representative) and that A.H. could not give admissible evidence because the alleged inspection and seizure occurred at the checkpoint outside his presence.

The case concerns alleged interference with the applicant’s private life and correspondence under Article 8 of the Convention, arising from the inspection of a lawyer’s documents (before and after a privileged prison meeting) and the claimed seizure of a client statement, in the absence of any suspicion of wrongdoing. Domestic law (including the Law on Advocates, the Code on Execution of Punishments, and Internal Prison Disciplinary Rules) permitted general inspections of persons and belongings entering or leaving prisons, with limited exceptions (e.g., for judges or certain international representatives) but no specific distinction or safeguards for lawyers.

The case of Spišák v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 13968/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged discrimination under Article 14 of the Convention (taken together with Article 5) arising from the frequency of automatic judicial review of the applicant’s pre-trial detention. The applicant, Pavel Spišák (born 2003), was 17 years old when arrested on 20 November 2020 on suspicion of robbery, grievous bodily harm and, later, attempted murder. He was already serving a suspended sentence and was on probation. Prosecution proceeded against him as a juvenile.

On 23 November 2020 the Prague 4 District Court remanded him in detention from the date of arrest, citing risks of interference with justice and re-offending (Article 67(b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”) and section 46(1) of the Juvenile Justice Act (“JJA”)). He was informed of his right to apply for release at any time. A complaint against the remand order was dismissed.

By mid-February 2021 the detention ground of interference with justice had expired, leaving only the risk of re-offending. On 24 March 2021 the applicant applied for release, arguing that the three-month automatic-review period in Article 72 § 1 CCP had elapsed on 23 March without a judicial decision, requiring his immediate release. The prosecutor refused and referred the matter to court. On 15 April 2021 the Prague-East District Court dismissed the application after a hearing. It held that the JJA, as lex specialis, displaced the CCP: section 47(1) JJA set a six-month maximum for juveniles prosecuted for particularly serious offences (with possible one-time extension), a limit that had not yet expired. The court found the re-offending risk still present and declined to impose any alternative measure.

A complaint against this ruling was dismissed by the Prague Regional Court on 11 May 2021. Meanwhile the applicant was indicted. On 28 April 2021 the Prague High Court, on the Regional Court’s application, extended detention to 20 November 2021 under section 47(1) JJA, citing the violent nature of the charges, the complexity of the investigation and the continuing risk of re-offending. The applicant challenged the extension, arguing that treating the JJA as overriding the three-month CCP review deprived juveniles of the more frequent protection afforded to adults charged with the same category of offences and contradicted the JJA’s purpose of more favourable treatment. The Supreme Court dismissed the complaint on 2 June 2021, finding the extension conditions met and declining to examine the interplay between the two statutes.

A plea bargain was approved on 19 May 2021; the applicant began serving an 18-month sentence on 21 May 2021, with the entire period of pre-trial detention (20 November 2020–20 May 2021) set off against it. Subsequent constitutional complaints yielded mixed results: the initial remand order was quashed for lack of territorial jurisdiction, but later decisions on release and extension were left intact.

The core of the alleged violation is the age-based difference in automatic judicial control of detention. Adults prosecuted for particularly serious offences receive a mandatory review every three months under Article 72 § 1 CCP; failure to review requires immediate release. Juveniles in the same situation are governed by the JJA’s six-month ceiling (extendable once by a further six months). Domestic courts consistently treated the JJA as a special law that excluded the CCP’s more frequent review. The applicant contended that this produced less favourable treatment contrary to the JJA’s stated aims of individualisation, social reintegration and the shortest possible deprivation of liberty for juveniles. The Court later found no objective and reasonable justification for the disparity, holding it incompatible with the protective purpose of the juvenile-justice regime.

The case of Spišák v. the Czech Republic (application no. 13968/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned alleged discrimination in the automatic judicial review of pre-trial detention for a juvenile compared to adults, in violation of Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 5.

The applicant, Pavel Spišák, a Czech national born in 2003, was arrested on 20 November 2020 at age 17 on suspicion of robbery and grievous bodily harm. Prosecution as a juvenile followed the next day, later extended to include attempted murder. He had a prior suspended sentence and was on probation. On 23 November 2020, after a hearing, the Prague 4 District Court remanded him in detention from 20 November 2020 under Article 67(b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) and section 46(1) of the Juvenile Justice Act (JJA), citing risks of interfering with justice and reoffending. He was informed of his right to apply for release at any time under CCP Article 71a. A complaint against the remand was rejected on 23 December 2020.

From 20 February 2021, detention continued solely on the reoffending ground. On 24 March 2021, the applicant applied for release, arguing that the three-month automatic review deadline under CCP Article 72 § 1 had expired on 23 March without a decision, requiring immediate release. The prosecutor refused, and the Prague-East District Court dismissed the application on 15 April 2021 after a hearing. It held that the JJA, as lex specialis, governed via section 47(1), which set a six-month maximum for detention in particularly serious offences (not yet expired), rendering the CCP three-month rule inapplicable. Grounds for detention under CCP Article 67(c) persisted due to reoffending risk, with no alternative measures specified. A complaint was dismissed by the Prague Regional Court on 11 May 2021.

On 22 April 2021 the applicant was indicted. The Regional Court sought a six-month extension under JJA section 47(1), granted by the Prague High Court on 28 April 2021 until 20 November 2021, citing the violent “particularly serious” offences, reoffending risk, and investigation complexity without delays. The applicant’s complaint argued that applying JJA section 47(1) over CCP Article 72 § 1 disadvantaged juveniles contrary to the Constitution and the protective purpose of juvenile legislation. The Supreme Court dismissed this on 2 June 2021, finding extension conditions met and declining to address the review-period arguments.

A plea bargain was approved on 19 May 2021, after which the applicant began an 18-month prison sentence on 21 May 2021; the pre-trial period (20 November 2020 to 20 May 2021) was credited against it. The Constitutional Court quashed the initial remand on 20 July 2021 for lack of territorial jurisdiction (by which time detention had ended) but dismissed a later appeal on 2 November 2021 concerning the April/May 2021 decisions, citing an incomplete complaint, the subsequent court’s proper jurisdiction, and the detention’s expiry.

The applicant claimed State-liability compensation in January 2022. Pecuniary damages were granted on 26 September 2023, but non-pecuniary damages were refused as the detention had been set off against the sentence (appeal pending).

Relevant CCP provisions require authorities to review detention grounds continuously (Article 71) and mandate automatic judicial review every three months in pre-trial proceedings for remaining in detention or release (Article 72 § 1), failing which immediate release follows. JJA section 47(1) instead caps juvenile detention at two months generally or six months for particularly serious offences, extendable once before and during trial by up to the same periods in exceptional cases. JJA section 48 requires ongoing review of grounds and consideration of alternatives. Domestic case-law treated JJA as lex specialis, excluding the CCP’s three-month rule. A 2006 Constitutional Court judgment viewed the formally longer JJA interval as not necessarily harsher, given continuous-review duties, release applications, and overall proportionality.

The applicant alleged that subjecting juveniles prosecuted for serious offences to six-month rather than three-month automatic reviews constituted unjustified age-based discrimination, undermining the JJA’s aim of more favourable, individualised treatment focused on rehabilitation and shortest possible deprivation of liberty. The Court found the difference contrary to that aim, lacking objective and reasonable justification.

The Supreme Court dismissed the complaint on 2 June 2021 without examining the interaction of the two provisions.

Subsequent constitutional complaints were unsuccessful or became academic once detention had ended. Domestic case-law (Supreme Court decisions of 2004–2019) consistently treated sections 47 and 48 JJA as the exclusive regime for juvenile detention reviews, so that the three-month automatic review applicable to adults under the CCP did not apply. The Constitutional Court had earlier held that the six-month interval was not necessarily more severe because of other safeguards (ongoing duty to re-examine grounds, right to apply for release at any time, and the overall maximum duration).

The applicant’s compensation claim for the period of detention (later found unlawful on jurisdictional grounds by the Constitutional Court) remained pending at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

The ECHR case of Suprun and Others v. Russia (2024) concerns five applications by historians, researchers, a Wallenberg relative, and NGO International Memorial alleging Article 10 violations from Russian restrictions on accessing, copying, or photographing Soviet-era archival records of political repression.

Historian Mikhail Suprun, head of a university history department, signed a 2007 contract with police archives, the German Red Cross, and a research society to process up to 40,000 records of interned, repressed, or deported ethnic Germans and related groups. Data (names, birth details, addresses, professions, family composition, deportation dates, charges, etc.) was to be scanned into a database for a bilingual memorial book, limited to humanitarian/academic use with no internet publication or commercial transfer without consent. Suprun processed over 8,000 records in 2007–2008. In 2009, FSB-linked investigators charged him with unlawfully acquiring and transferring personal data of 20 special settlers without consent (heirs named as injured parties). Some heirs called the information a “shameful secret”; others did not. In 2011, a district court convicted him under Criminal Code Article 137 of collecting personal/family secrets that could harm reputations, but exempted him due to expired limitation. Appeals failed, with courts holding the data constituted private secrets despite no legal definition of “private life” and arguments that it concerned public-authority interactions (arrests, imprisonment, sanctions).

In 2017, she requested unredacted copies of 1945–1947 Lubyanka/Lefortovo prison registers (interrogations, transfers, belongings, alphabetical lists). FSB refused, citing third-party private data unrelated to Wallenberg and prior partial access. Courts dismissed her 2017 claim, finding no rights infringement.

These denials of access/copies/photography, plus Suprun’s conviction, formed the alleged Article 10 interferences with gathering historical data for public debate.

The case of *Suprun and Others v. Russia* (applications nos. 58029/12 and 4 others) concerns restrictions imposed by Russian authorities on access to State archives documenting Soviet political repression, including the Great Terror, Gulag, deportations, NKVD operations, and the fate of Raoul Wallenberg. The applicants—historians, researchers affiliated with the Iofe Foundation, Wallenberg’s great-niece, and the NGO International Memorial—alleged violations of Article 10 of the Convention (freedom to receive information) due to refusals of access, copying, or photography of documents, as well as one criminal conviction for collecting data.

In 2009, FSB-initiated criminal proceedings accused him of unlawfully collecting and transferring personal data of 20 individuals without consent. The 2011 district court convicted him under Article 137 of the Criminal Code for gathering “personal and family secrets” that could harm reputations, though he was exempted due to the expired statute of limitations. Appeals failed, with courts holding the information related to identifiable private lives despite arguments that it concerned public interactions with authorities (arrests, deportations, convictions).

The FSB refused, citing private data of unrelated third parties. Moscow courts dismissed her 2017 administrative claim, ruling that prior partial disclosures to researchers sufficed and that documents contained non-public personal information, without assessing public interest in Wallenberg’s historical fate.

Researchers Ms. Yevgeniya Kulakova, Ms. Olga Startseva, and Ms. Yelena Kondrakhina reviewed FSB investigative files in St. Petersburg in 2019 but were denied copies or photography, limited by the Rehabilitation Act to rehabilitated victims and heirs. St. Petersburg courts upheld this as lawful, rejecting claims of disproportionate restrictions on historical research.

Historian Mr. Sergey Prudovskiy, studying NKVD “ethnic operations” (e.g., the 1937 Harbin campaign), received redacted 1930s files hiding officers’ identities (classified as state secrets until 2044 per a 2014 commission). He was denied copies of execution reports for publication and access to a non-rehabilitated officer’s file. Moscow courts confirmed the refusals, citing state secrets laws, the 2006 access regulations (excluding non-relatives), and lack of consent.

The FSB and Prosecutor’s Office refused, limiting copies to rehabilitated persons and invoking the Personal Data Act (private-life details). Karelian and Moscow courts dismissed challenges, finding no overriding public interest and that official roles did not justify disclosure of identifying information.

These measures, grounded in the Rehabilitation Act (1991), Archives Act (2004), Personal Data Act (2006), and State Secrets Act (1993), blocked researchers’ preparatory work for publications and public debate on Soviet-era crimes, despite documents relating primarily to official acts rather than personal lives.

The case of *Suprun and Others v. Russia* comprises five applications by historians, researchers, a relative of Raoul Wallenberg, and the NGO International Memorial. The case of Vlaisavljevikj v. North Macedonia (ECHR Application no. 23215/21) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life). The applicant, Velimir Vlaisavljevikj (born 1953, resident in Skopje), claimed that domestic authorities failed in their positive obligation to protect him from a private heat supplier’s unlawful collection and use of his personal data.

From January 2013 onward, heat supply company B. repeatedly issued invoices and payment-order requests to the applicant for a “standing heating charge.” This charge applied under 2012 Heat Energy Supply Regulations to users disconnected from a heating network. The applicant insisted he had never been connected: no heating pipes existed in his apartment, and he had never contracted with any heat supplier. He refused payment and successfully challenged multiple payment orders in civil courts. Between 2014 and 2022, first- and second-instance civil courts issued numerous judgments (the latest covering January–July 2021) confirming that the applicant was not a user, had never been disconnected, and owed nothing because no contract existed.

On 15 February 2016 the applicant complained to the Personal Data Protection Directorate. He argued that company B. possessed and processed his personal data (name, address, apartment size, and heating-related details) without his provision or consent, solely to generate invoices and pursue collection. Company B. explained that it had obtained the data via a 2013 contract from the previous supplier C., pursuant to its public-interest licence and section 154-a of the Energy Act, which authorised processing for invoicing, payment collection, and judicial proceedings. The applicant was classified as a “disconnected user.”

An inspector first stayed the proceedings, treating the applicant’s user status as a preliminary proprietary question. After the Administrative Court quashed that stay, the inspector dismissed the complaint on 16 October 2017. She found the data had been collected and processed lawfully under sections 5 and 6 of the Personal Data Protection Act (fair processing for specified legal purposes, fulfilment of a legal obligation, public-interest activities, or legitimate interest). The supplier’s duty to invoice under energy rules and the Energy Act supplied a legitimate basis; whether the applicant actually owed money was a civil-court matter and irrelevant to data-protection law.

The Administrative Court quashed this decision in January 2019, noting that the previous supplier C. itself could not have lawfully obtained the data if the applicant had never been connected. The Higher Administrative Court, however, overturned that judgment on 2 October 2020 and reinstated the inspector’s ruling. It held that processing was authorised by the supplier’s licence, the data-transfer contract, and the Energy Act; the creditor–debtor relationship was irrelevant.

The applicant maintained that the authorities never examined the core issue: how his data had been collected at all given that he had never been a user, and how continued processing remained lawful after repeated civil-court findings that he was not a consumer. He therefore alleged that the State had failed to protect his personal data against unlawful private-sector processing, in breach of Article 8.

The case of Vlaisavljevikj v. North Macedonia (no. 23215/21) concerns the alleged failure of domestic authorities to protect the applicant from a private heat supplier’s collection and use of his personal data, in breach of Article 8 ECHR (private life, positive obligations).

The applicant, Velimir Vlaisavljevikj (born 1953, living in Skopje), received repeated invoices and payment-order requests from heat supplier B. from January 2013 onward for a standing heating charge under the 2012 Heat Energy Supply Regulations. He had never contracted with B. or any predecessor, his apartment had no heating pipes or connection to the network, and he was not a (disconnected) user. Civil courts repeatedly accepted his objections (judgments of 1 December 2014, 17 September 2015 and others through 2022), holding he owed nothing.

On 15 February 2016 he complained to the Personal Data Protection Directorate that B. had unlawfully obtained and processed his data (name, address, apartment size, heating-related figures) without consent or legal basis. B. replied that it had received the data from previous supplier C. under a 2013 transfer contract, pursuant to its licence, public-interest duties and Energy Act s. 154-a (permitting processing for invoicing, collection and litigation).

An inspector first stayed the case (1 April 2016) pending resolution of the applicant’s user status; the Administrative Court quashed this (29 June 2017), directing a decision on data-protection, not proprietary, issues. On 16 October 2017 the inspector dismissed the complaint: data collection and processing were lawful and fair under Personal Data Protection Act ss. 5 and 6(1)(3),(5),(6) because they served B.’s legal obligation and legitimate interest in invoicing and litigating under the Energy Act and 2012 Regulations; the applicant’s non-user status was irrelevant.

The Administrative Court quashed that decision (11 January 2019). It accepted that B. had received the data from C., but questioned how C. had originally obtained them given that the applicant had never been connected; C. therefore had no right to collect, retain or transfer them. The court cited the 2015 civil judgment and a February 2018 Supreme Court opinion that never-connected persons are not “disconnected users”.

The Higher Administrative Court reversed (2 October 2020) and restored the inspector’s decision. Processing was lawful under the energy licence, street-based user allocation, the transfer contract and the cited statutory provisions; the creditor–debtor relationship was irrelevant to data-protection proceedings.

The applicant argued before the Strasbourg Court that the authorities had thereby failed to examine the core of his complaint—that his data had never been lawfully collected in the first place—and thus failed to protect him against continued unlawful use.

The case of Vlaisavljevikj v. North Macedonia (Application no. 23215/21) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the North Macedonian authorities failed to protect him from a private heat supplier’s allegedly unlawful collection and use of his personal data. The applicant, born in 1953 and residing in Skopje, received repeated invoices and payment-order requests from heat supplier B. beginning in January 2013 (continuing until at least 2023) for a standing heating charge. This charge applied, under 2012 Heat Energy Supply Regulations, to users disconnected from a private heating system. The applicant objected throughout that he had never been a user of the supplier’s services: no heating pipes were installed in his apartment, and he had never contracted with the company or any predecessor.

On 15 February 2016 the applicant complained to the Personal Data Protection Directorate that supplier B. had obtained and processed his personal data (name, address, apartment size and related heating details) without his provision or consent. He attached first-instance civil judgments of 2014 and 2015 in which courts had accepted his objections to payment orders. Supplier B. explained that it had received the data from previous supplier C. under a 2013 contract, pursuant to a public-interest licence issued by the Energy Regulatory Commission and section 154-a of the Energy Act (authorising processing for invoicing, collection and judicial proceedings). It treated the applicant as a disconnected user.

An inspector first stayed the complaint pending determination of the applicant’s user status, but the Administrative Court quashed that stay, directing a decision on the data-protection claim itself. On 16 October 2017 the inspector dismissed the complaint, holding that the data had been lawfully transferred and processed under the Personal Data Protection Act (fair collection for specified lawful purposes, fulfilment of a legal obligation or legitimate interest) and energy legislation. The inspector regarded the applicant’s never having contracted or been connected as irrelevant to data-processing lawfulness; any dispute over the underlying debt belonged in the civil courts.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the data had been obtained unlawfully (“stolen”) because he had never been connected and therefore could not be a disconnected user, and that a private company lacked a legitimate interest. The Administrative Court quashed the inspector’s decision on 11 January 2019. It accepted that supplier B. had received the data via the 2013 contract but found it unresolved how predecessor C. had originally obtained them, given the applicant’s lack of connection. The court cited a 2015 civil judgment and a 2018 Supreme Court legal opinion confirming that persons never contracted with a supplier and lacking installed heating do not qualify as disconnected users.

The Directorate appealed. On 2 October 2020 the Higher Administrative Court overturned the Administrative Court’s judgment and reinstated the inspector’s dismissal. It held that the data had been processed in accordance with the energy-supply licence, the contract transferring them, and the relevant statutory provisions; the creditor-debtor relationship was irrelevant.

Meanwhile, in nine separate sets of civil proceedings between 2014 and 2022, first- and second-instance courts repeatedly upheld the applicant’s objections to payment orders covering periods up to July 2021. They found he had never been a user of the heating network, had never been disconnected from it, and had never contracted with any supplier, so he owed no standing charge.

The European Court of Human Rights subsequently found a violation of Article 8 because the domestic authorities, particularly the Higher Administrative Court, failed to examine the core of the applicant’s complaint: whether the initial collection and continued use of his personal data were lawful given that he had never been a heating-system user.
