The case of Oghlishvili v. Georgia (no. 7621/19) concerns Georgia’s alleged failure to protect the applicant’s daughter E.N. from domestic violence and to investigate her death effectively. Complaints were lodged under Articles 2, 3 and 13 of the Convention.

E.N. married R.G. around 2013 and lived with him, their child and mother-in-law T.G. Relations deteriorated after two years because E.N. worked late; T.G. accused her of infidelity. On 12 October 2017 E.N. telephoned police reporting physical assault by T.G. and her husband. Officers interviewed the family. E.N. described a verbal and physical row with T.G., who punched her face after E.N. spent a night at a friend’s house; she sought restraining measures against T.G. but said her husband had never abused her and she had named him only in distress. T.G. and R.G. claimed E.N. had attacked T.G. and that R.G. had intervened. A same-day medical examination found a minor bruise on E.N.’s left shoulder and no injuries on T.G. No further protective action followed.

On 18 October 2017 E.N. was found hanged, naked from the waist down, in the family wine cellar around 08:00 by her brother-in-law G.G., who reported the matter only at 08:40. An investigation into incitement to suicide (Criminal Code Art. 115) was opened immediately. External examination recorded bruises and lesions on the knees, face and throat. A later comprehensive forensic report (8 November 2017) identified numerous additional injuries (jaw, arms, abdomen, hips, thighs, buttocks, vulva, legs and foot), some 6–7 days old and others inflicted immediately before death by hitting, grabbing or similar violence. Death resulted from asphyxia by strangulation, occurring at least 17 hours before the examination.

Family, friends, neighbours and others (over 25 witnesses) were questioned. They confirmed frequent arguments, E.N.’s emotional instability, a prior hanging attempt in the same cellar in August 2017, and G.G.’s late-night visits even when R.G. was absent. One neighbour saw G.G. near the house at 06:30 on the morning of the death. At the funeral G.G. himself attempted suicide. R.G. thereafter accused G.G. of rape and murder, citing a possible revenge motive arising from R.G.’s affair with G.G.’s former fiancée. Forensic tests found no semen on or in the body, unidentified male DNA on cellar trousers, a bra cut by a sharp object, and blue fibres matching G.G.’s denim trousers under E.N.’s nails and on her clothing (though not vice versa). Telephone records identified a male acquaintance with whom E.N. had spoken at length, including the day before her death; another number could not be traced.

The applicant was granted victim status in December 2017. After February 2019 the investigation, still open as of April 2022, produced no significant steps beyond granting her file access in 2022. The offence was classified as a less-serious “domestic crime” subject to a six-year limitation period. That period expired because of prolonged inactivity attributable to the authorities.

The Court held that the investigation violated Article 2 (procedural limb): it failed to pursue all credible lines of inquiry, displayed lengthy unjustified inactivity, allowed the limitation period to lapse (rendering further inquiry futile), and lacked the particular diligence required in cases of violence against women, amounting to unwillingness to establish the truth.

The case of Oghlishvili v. Georgia concerns the alleged suicide of the applicant’s daughter, E.N., amid domestic tensions, and the Georgian authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation. E.N. had lived since 2013 with her husband R.G., their child and mother-in-law T.G. in Shilda. After two years, relations deteriorated because E.N. kept late hours; T.G. accused her of infidelity.

She denied that R.G. had ever abused her and requested a restraining order against T.G. T.G. and R.G. countered that E.N. had struck T.G. and that R.G. had intervened. The body showed bruises and lesions on the knees, face, throat and elsewhere. External examination occurred between 11 a.m. and 12.10 p.m.; a full forensic autopsy began at 3 p.m., more than 17 hours after death. The cause was asphyxia by strangulation. Numerous injuries (face, jaw, abdomen, thighs, vulva, legs, etc.) had been inflicted while E.N. was still alive, most immediately before death and some six or seven days earlier; they were consistent with hitting, pushing or grabbing. The case of B.A. v. Cyprus concerns a Syrian national who entered Cyprus irregularly in early 2019 and sought international protection. On 8 February 2019 he and two relatives presented themselves at a crossing point and were processed by immigration authorities. A background check yielded no adverse information, but completed forms raised suspicions of involvement in irregular immigration. The applicant formally lodged his asylum claim on 11 February 2019 and received written confirmation of his right to remain in government-controlled areas pending a final decision.

That same day he was interviewed. Authorities noted old wounds he attributed to Syrian army fire, his age, origin in a conflict zone, and prior residence in an ISIS-controlled area. Inspection of his phone (to which he eventually consented) revealed an encrypted application containing photographs of him and his relatives holding Kalashnikov rifles and wearing military uniforms. A search warrant was obtained. Further inquiries showed one relative’s father held a Cypriot identity document and had previously been linked to hosting Muslim preachers. On these grounds the Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department issued a detention order under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law, citing the need to protect national security. The applicant was arrested on 12 February 2019 and held, first at a police station and then at Menoyia Detention Centre, until his release on 30 November 2021—a period of two years and nine months.

He immediately challenged the detention. A recourse to the Administrative Court was dismissed on 25 April 2019; the court held the order lawful, based on a specific investigation, and found no effective alternatives. An appeal to the Supreme Court, lodged on 7 May 2019, was not decided until 20 July 2021. The Supreme Court declined to second-guess the executive’s national-security assessment and considered detention compatible with both EU law and Article 5 of the Convention.

Parallel habeas-corpus petitions attacking the length of detention were also unsuccessful. The first (July 2019) was dismissed after the court found the authorities had acted with reasonable diligence. A second petition (January 2020) and its appeal (decided June 2021) likewise failed; the courts treated the still-pending asylum proceedings as sufficient justification and regarded twelve months as not excessive. Internal reviews conducted in late 2019, early 2020, February 2021 and May 2021 simply restated the original national-security grounds.

Meanwhile the Asylum Service rejected the protection claim on 28 May 2019, finding the applicant individually responsible for war crimes. His subsequent recourse to the Administrative Court of International Protection remained pending (with suspensive effect) throughout the detention period.

The European Court of Human Rights later found the detention arbitrary under Article 5 § 1 (f). The national-security rationale lacked a sufficiently close connection to the prevention of unauthorised entry, was not tied to the outcome of the asylum application, and operated as a general preventive measure. The duration was also unjustified. Under Article 5 § 4 the Court held that the more-than-two-year appeal proceedings reviewing the detention’s lawfulness failed the “speediness” requirement, noting unjustified delays, including a ten-month period of inaction before the Covid-19 pandemic.

The case of B.A. v. Cyprus (Application no. 24607/20) concerns a Syrian national born in 1996 who entered the government-controlled areas of Cyprus irregularly on 8 February 2019 after arriving from Türkiye via the occupied north. He and two relatives presented themselves at the Ledras Palace crossing, expressed intent to seek international protection, and were processed by the Aliens and Immigration Service. They were transferred to the Pournara reception centre. On 11 February 2019 the applicant formally lodged an asylum application and received confirmation of his right to remain pending a final decision.

That same day he was interviewed by immigration officers, criminal investigators, intelligence services and counter-terrorism personnel. The authorities noted old shrapnel and bullet wounds, his age, departure from a war zone, and prior residence in an ISIS-controlled area of Daraa province. Inspection of his phone (to which he eventually consented) revealed password-protected images of the applicant and his relatives holding Kalashnikov rifles while wearing military uniforms. Additional intelligence indicated that a relative’s father, who held a Cypriot identity card, had previously hosted Muslim preachers. On these grounds the Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department issued a detention order under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law, citing national-security requirements. The applicant was arrested in the early hours of 12 February 2019, held first at Lakatamia police station and then transferred on 22 February 2019 to Menoyia Detention Centre for Prohibited Immigrants.

He remained in administrative detention for two years and nine months. Internal reviews conducted in late 2019, January 2020, February 2021 and May 2021 repeatedly confirmed that the original national-security grounds persisted; no less-restrictive alternatives were considered viable. The detention order was finally revoked on 30 November 2021, after which the applicant was released subject to thrice-weekly police reporting and an address-notification obligation.

Parallel asylum proceedings unfolded. After an interview on 22 April 2019 the Asylum Service rejected the claim on 28 May 2019 (notified 3 July 2019) on the basis that the applicant had incurred individual responsibility for war crimes. He lodged a recourse before the Administrative Court of International Protection on 31 July 2019; that challenge remained pending with suspensive effect throughout the detention period.

The applicant challenged the lawfulness of his detention through successive judicial avenues. A first-instance recourse to the Administrative Court (filed 27 March 2019) was dismissed on 25 April 2019 after the court inspected classified security-service material that was withheld from the applicant. An appeal to the Supreme Court (filed 7 May 2019) was not decided until 20 July 2021. Two habeas-corpus petitions followed: the first (18 July 2019) was rejected on 8 August 2019; the second (17 January 2020), which also sought disclosure of classified documents, was rejected on 11 March 2020. The appeal against the second habeas refusal (filed 24 April 2020) was dismissed by the Supreme Court sitting in plenary on 8 June 2021. These review proceedings themselves lasted more than two years and were marked by periods of administrative inactivity, including approximately ten months of delay before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations under Article 5 §§ 1(f) and 4 of the Convention are therefore the issuance and prolongation of detention solely on national-security grounds that were never linked to the pending asylum claim or to any concrete risk of unauthorised entry, the absence of any periodic individualised re-assessment that could have led to release or alternatives, the extraordinary overall duration of more than 33 months, and the protracted, delayed character of the domestic judicial reviews that failed to produce a speedy determination of lawfulness.

The applicant, a Syrian national born in 1996, entered Cyprus irregularly on 8 February 2019 via occupied areas after travelling from Türkiye with two relatives. At the Ledras Palace crossing they sought international protection and were processed by the Aliens and Immigration Service (AIS), with notification to the Counter Terrorism Office and Cyprus Intelligence Service. Initial checks found nothing of note, though irregular-immigration suspicions arose; they were sent to the Pournara reception centre.

On 11 February 2019 the applicant formally lodged an asylum claim and received a confirmation document entitling him to remain in government-controlled areas pending a final decision. The same day, interviews (with AIS, criminal investigators and intelligence services) revealed old injuries he attributed to Syrian army fire. Authorities considered he fitted a foreign-fighter profile: he was 23, had left Damascus for ISIS-controlled Al-Harra, and (after initial resistance) permitted inspection of his phone, which contained an encrypted application showing him and relatives posing with Kalashnikovs in military uniform. Further enquiries linked a relative’s father (holder of a Cypriot identity card) to earlier suspicions of hosting Muslim preachers. On these grounds the Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department issued a detention order under s. 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law for national-security reasons. The applicant was arrested on 12 February 2019, held first at Lakatamia police station and then (from 22 February) at Menoyia Detention Centre until his release on 30 November 2021—more than two years and nine months.

He immediately challenged the order. A recourse (no. 442/19) filed on 27 March 2019 was dismissed by the Administrative Court on 25 April 2019 after the court inspected classified security material (not disclosed to the applicant) and a FRONTEX handbook; the court held the order lawful, specific and necessary, with no viable alternatives. An appeal lodged on 7 May 2019 was dismissed by the Supreme Court only on 20 July 2021; the court declined to second-guess the executive’s security assessment and cited CJEU case-law confirming compatibility with the Reception Directive.

In parallel asylum proceedings the applicant was interviewed on 22 April 2019; his claim was rejected on 28 May 2019 for alleged war-crimes involvement. He filed a recourse (no. 74/2019) on 31 July 2019; that challenge remained pending (with suspensive effect) throughout his detention.

The applicant also sought habeas corpus on grounds of excessive length. The first petition (18 July 2019) was dismissed on 8 August 2019. Internal reviews in November 2019–January 2020 confirmed the original risk assessment. A second petition (17 January 2020), including a request for disclosure of the classified material, was refused on 11 March 2020; the court considered twelve months not excessive while asylum proceedings were pending. The ensuing appeal (24 April 2020) was dismissed by the Supreme Court (plenary) on 8 June 2021. Further administrative reviews in February and May 2021 reiterated the same national-security grounds. Upon release the applicant was subjected only to thrice-weekly reporting and an address-notification obligation.

These facts form the basis of the complaints that detention was arbitrary (lacking a sufficiently close link to preventing unauthorised entry or to the asylum process itself) and that the review of its lawfulness was not speedy.

The case of Savinovskikh and Others v. Russia (Application no. 16206/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the termination of a transgender applicant’s custody and foster care of two minors solely on the basis of his “transsexualism” diagnosis and gender transition, raising issues under Article 8 (family life) of the Convention.

The applicant, Yulia Savinovskikh (born 1977), is a transgender man assigned female at birth who identifies as male. He has three biological children and, at the relevant time, was married to a man (E.S.). In 2014 and 2016, municipal social services in Yekaterinburg placed two unrelated minors—D.D. and K.K., both born in 2012—into his guardianship under a foster-care agreement. The children’s biological parents had been deprived of parental rights; both children had serious health issues (HIV, developmental delays, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability) and had lived in public care from birth. At placement, the applicant’s legal gender remained female and the household was presented as a traditional family.

On 3 July 2017 a medical commission diagnosed the applicant with “transsexualism” and found no psychiatric contraindications to gender-affirming treatment. He underwent a double mastectomy on 21 July 2017 and began presenting as male on social media. Social services learned of these facts on 24 August 2017. An official visit on 27 August recorded unsatisfactory sanitary conditions; the applicant disclosed his diagnosis, transition plans and an asylum application abroad. On 28 August 2017 social services issued orders terminating custody, citing a conflict of interests. The children were removed on 30 August and have had no contact with the applicant since.

Social services then sued to dissolve the foster-care agreement, stating that “the main reason” was the applicant’s transsexualism because “the children were initially placed in a traditional family.” The applicant counter-claimed, denying any intention to complete transition, describing his social-media activity as artistic and asserting that he continued to fulfil a maternal role. On 5 February 2018 the District Court terminated the agreement. It accepted that transsexualism was not an automatic bar to fostering, yet held that the applicant’s male identification, while married to a man, violated Russian family-law principles (marriage only between man and woman), societal traditions and mentality. The court also relied on the applicant’s failure to notify social services of “significant circumstances” (diagnosis, surgery, male presentation) that allegedly affected the children’s physical, spiritual and moral development, plus the recorded sanitary deficiencies and claimed educational neglect of K.K.

On appeal the Regional Court (15 May 2018) upheld the termination, reiterating poor hygiene, insufficient attention to K.K.’s development and the “legal impossibility of same-sex couples being foster parents.” An expert report submitted by the applicant diagnosed only “gender identity disorder, unspecified,” noted his social adaptability, heterosexual marriage and child-rearing, and found no danger to the children; the courts disregarded it. Cassation appeals were dismissed. Meanwhile an investigating authority, after inspecting the home, concluded living conditions were satisfactory and parental duties had been properly performed, refusing to open a criminal case.

The applicant later fled Russia with his husband and biological children and obtained asylum. D.D. and K.K. were subsequently placed with another foster family. The applicant lodged the Strasbourg application on his own and the children’s behalf, arguing that the authorities had failed to conduct an in-depth, individualised assessment of the family situation or the actual impact of his gender identity on the children’s welfare, relying instead on abstract legal and cultural considerations.
001-235016:
The case of Hanovs v. Latvia (no. 40861/22) involves an alleged homophobic attack on Deniss Hanovs, a Latvian national born in 1977, and the subsequent investigation, raising issues of ineffective prosecution and discrimination under Articles 3, 8 and 14 of the Convention.

On 8 November 2020, Hanovs and his male partner were walking their dog in Riga when they encountered two intoxicated men. One, later identified as JP, shouted a vulgar homophobic slur (“долбаная задница,” roughly “an ass that has been pounded”). The second man kicked Hanovs in the buttocks (perceptible but not forceful). After Hanovs threatened to call police, JP mockingly stated “I want to have sex with you.” JP then tried to punch Hanovs, who fled into a flower shop and locked the door. JP pursued him with sexually explicit language, demanding he come out. Hanovs’s partner called police. When Hanovs later exited, JP rushed at him again, forcing him back inside. The second man tried to force the door, verbally abused Hanovs, and exposed himself while shouting. Both men left. A florist salesperson confirmed Hanovs hid while holding the door shut and that one attacker exposed himself.

Police arrived, obtained descriptions, located the men, but did not detain them or properly identify the second (whose given name matched no records). Criminal proceedings began for hooliganism under Criminal Law s. 231(1). Hanovs and his partner identified JP from photos.

JP, interviewed as a suspect, admitted seeing the pair walking closely and holding each other, assuming they were gay and feeling offended by the “overt display.” He used slurs (“faggots, have you lost your f...ing minds?!”), chased Hanovs after alleged provocation, tried (unsuccessfully) to kick him, and threatened punishment. He denied witnessing exposure or hating homosexuals, claiming only anger at public affection.

On 18 May 2021 police terminated the criminal case, finding no disturbance of public peace or business, and referred it to administrative proceedings. On 19 June 2021 JP was convicted of petty hooliganism (Administrative Penalties Law s. 11(1)) and fined EUR 70, without addressing bias motives. He did not appeal.

Hanovs appealed the termination, arguing the acts constituted a hate crime under Criminal Law s. 150 given JP’s admitted motivation. Supervising and higher prosecutors upheld termination: s. 150 requires verbal/written calls to incite hatred against a group with direct intent, not an individual-directed act lacking publicity. After one higher prosecutor briefly remitted the case for s. 150(3) investigation, police re-interviewed JP (who repeated his account and claimed “neutral” views on homosexuals) and terminated again in January 2022, finding no intent to incite enmity or sufficient publicity. Further prosecutorial appeals failed. Prosecutors acknowledged prejudice but held there was no incitement: the encounter was fortuitous, JP targeted only Hanovs (not his partner) without urging others to hate, and the salesperson perceived no orientation-based attack or incitement.

The facts thus centre on a homophobic physical and verbal assault (slurs, kick, attempted punch, exposure, threats) whose bias motivation was admitted yet never prosecuted as a hate offence; instead, a minor administrative fine was imposed that ignored the prejudice.

The case of Hanovs v. Latvia (Application no. 40861/22) concerns an allegedly ineffective investigation into a homophobic attack on the applicant, a gay man, raising issues under Articles 3, 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding positive obligations, effective investigation and discrimination based on sexual orientation.

On 8 November 2020 in Riga, the applicant and his male partner were walking their dog when they encountered two intoxicated men, one later identified as JP. JP shouted a highly vulgar homophobic slur at them (“an ass that has been pounded”). The second man kicked the applicant in the buttocks (a perceptible but not forceful blow). After the applicant threatened to call police, JP stated “I want to have sex with you” and attempted to punch him. The applicant fled into a nearby flower shop and held the door shut. JP pursued, demanding he come out while using sexually explicit language. The applicant’s partner called the police. When the applicant later emerged, JP rushed at him again, forcing him to hide once more. The second man tried to open the door, verbally abused the applicant and exposed himself. A florist’s salesperson witnessed the events, confirming that the applicant had to barricade himself inside and that one man exposed himself. Police arrived, obtained descriptions and located the men but failed to detain or properly identify them; the second man remained unidentified as the name given did not match records.

Criminal proceedings were opened for “hooliganism” under Section 231(1) of the Criminal Law. The applicant and his partner identified JP from photographs. In interview, JP admitted seeing the couple walking closely and holding each other, assuming they were gay and being offended by the public display of affection. He used slurs, chased the applicant and attempted to kick him, employing language that could denote either physical assault or sexual intercourse (which he claimed meant the former). He denied seeing the exposure.

On 18 May 2021 police terminated the criminal case, finding no criminal offence as the actions had not disturbed public peace or business operations, and referred it to administrative proceedings. On 19 June 2021 JP was convicted of “petty hooliganism” under administrative law and fined EUR 70; he did not appeal.

The applicant appealed the termination, arguing the acts constituted a hate crime under Section 150 of the Criminal Law (incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation, including aggravated forms involving violence). Prosecutors initially upheld termination, holding that Section 150 required intent to incite hatred against a group generally, not a personal attack. A higher prosecutor later remitted the case for investigation under Section 150(3). After a further interview in which JP claimed a “neutral” attitude toward homosexuals but anger at public displays, police again terminated proceedings on 26 January 2022, finding no direct intent to incite hatred or sufficient publicity. Subsequent appeals failed. A prosecutor acknowledged prejudice-based motivation but concluded there was no intent to incite hatred, citing the random encounter, targeting of only the applicant (not his partner), and the witness’s failure to perceive it as group-based incitement. The decision became final.

Domestic law at the time defined petty hooliganism as public-order disturbance punishable by a fine of EUR 70–500. Section 150 of the Criminal Law penalised incitement to hatred on grounds including sexual orientation, with aggravated penalties for violence. Relevant domestic case-law included convictions for racially motivated assault and homophobic online incitement.

The applicant alleged that the authorities failed to investigate the homophobic motive, prosecute the attack as a hate-motivated offence, or impose a sanction commensurate with its severity, thereby trivialising the incident and fostering impunity in violation of the State’s positive obligations.

**Hanovs v. Latvia (ECtHR, Application no. 40861/22, 18 July 2024) involved a homophobic street attack on applicant Deniss Hanovs (a gay Latvian man) and his male partner, followed by an investigation that the Court found inadequate under Articles 3, 8 and 14.**

On 8 November 2020 in Riga, Hanovs and his partner were walking their dog when they encountered two visibly intoxicated men (one later identified as JP; the other never identified). JP shouted an extremely vulgar homophobic slur in Russian. The second man kicked Hanovs in the buttocks (perceptible but not strong). After Hanovs warned he would call police, JP made a sexually explicit remark and tried to punch him. Hanovs fled into a nearby flower shop and held the door shut. JP tried to follow, using more explicit language and demanding he come out. The second man approached, attempted to open the door, verbally abused Hanovs, and exposed himself. A florist witnessed Hanovs hiding inside and holding the door, plus the exposure. Police were called by the partner, obtained descriptions, located the men, but recorded names without proper identification or detention; the second man could not be traced.

Criminal proceedings began for hooliganism (Criminal Law s.231(1)). Both victims identified JP from photos. JP, interviewed as a suspect, admitted seeing the pair walking closely and holding waists, assuming they were gay, feeling offended by the “overt display,” and using slurs such as “faggots, have you lost your f...ing minds?” He said Hanovs retorted with a derogatory term, after which JP chased him, tried (unsuccessfully) to kick him, used further slurs, and threatened punishment. He denied seeing exposure or acting with the second man. Police terminated the criminal case on 18 May 2021, finding no disturbance of public peace or business operations sufficient for a crime, and referred it as an administrative offence.

On 19 June 2021 JP was fined EUR 70 for petty hooliganism (Law on Administrative Penalties s.11(1)). Hanovs appealed, arguing the acts constituted a hate crime under Criminal Law s.150 (incitement to hatred/enmity based on gender or other characteristics, including violence-aggravated forms) given JP’s admitted motivation by dislike of homosexuals. Supervising and higher prosecutors upheld termination, stating s.150 required verbal/written calls for hatred with direct intent to incite against a group generally, not a personal confrontation lacking publicity or incitement of others.

A higher prosecutor later quashed the decision and ordered investigation under s.150(3). After a further interview (in which JP claimed a “neutral” attitude to gay men but anger at public affection), police terminated proceedings again on 26 January 2022, finding no direct intent to incite hatred or enmity and insufficient publicity to affect public attitudes. Appeals (citing ECtHR cases Beizaras and Levickas v. Lithuania and Sabalić v. Croatia) failed. Prosecutors acknowledged prejudice against homosexuals but held the encounter fortuitous, targeted only Hanovs (not his partner), involved no urging of others to hate, and was not viewed by the florist as orientation-based incitement. The Prosecutor General’s Office confirmed the termination as final.

Relevant law included Constitution Art. 95 (protection of honour/dignity, prohibition of inhuman/degrading treatment); petty hooliganism as mere public-order disturbance; and Criminal Law provisions on hooliganism versus incitement to hatred (ss.78/150), with domestic examples of racially or homophobically motivated convictions. The applicant alleged these facts showed failure to investigate or prosecute the homophobic motive effectively, treating a violent, slurs-laden attack as a trivial administrative matter.

(The Court later held this breached positive obligations: no effective prosecution of the hate-motivated offence, a manifestly disproportionate EUR 70 fine, and trivialization fostering impunity.)
001-235473:
The case of Tsulukidze and Rusulashvili v. Georgia concerns two Georgian applicants who alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention due to the lack of impartiality of Supreme Court Judge L.M. Both held managerial roles at JSC Telasi, Tbilisi’s primary electricity distributor. In 2016, a company reorganization liquidated their departments. The first applicant, Zurab Tsulukidze (born 1959), was dismissed on 30 August 2016 after declining an alternative post. The second, Levan Rusulashvili (born 1973), was dismissed on 4 March 2016 with compensation of two months’ salary.

The first applicant sued Telasi for reinstatement and salary arrears. The Tbilisi City Court dismissed the claim on 1 November 2018, holding the dismissal lawful given the reorganization. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal upheld this on 23 December 2019. He then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, assigned to a three-judge panel with Judge L.M. as president and rapporteur. On 23 April 2020 he sought L.M.’s recusal under Article 31 § 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure (CCP), noting that L.M.’s judicial assistant G.D. was the daughter of Telasi’s lawyer (also the company’s in-house counsel who had prepared the dismissal). On 4 June 2020 a two-judge panel (excluding L.M.) rejected the request, finding the familial link insufficient to prove influence or bias. On 3 March 2021 the applicant sought recusal of the entire panel, adding that the other judges were acquaintances of the lawyer and citing a prior Supreme Court ruling that had treated an assistant’s marriage to a party’s representative as problematic. On 5 March 2021 the full panel (including L.M.) dismissed the application, reiterating that mere acquaintance or family ties did not automatically imply interest in the outcome, that influence by the assistant had not been shown, and that Article 28 CCP secrecy of deliberations barred assistants from learning judges’ views. The same day the panel, with L.M. participating, declared the appeal inadmissible.

The second applicant similarly sued for reinstatement and arrears. The City Court awarded him partial compensation of 27 360 GEL (approximately €9 500) but refused reinstatement on 26 October 2018; the Court of Appeal confirmed this on 16 July 2020. His cassation appeal was assigned to a three-judge panel that included Judge L.M. (with another judge as rapporteur). On 4 March 2021 he requested recusal of all three judges, stressing the same family link (the lawyer also headed Telasi’s legal department) and alleged close acquaintance of the remaining judges, and referring to Supreme Court practice that judicial assistants of rapporteurs may prepare cases (Article 200 CCP and decision of 30 July 2018). On 5 March 2021 the same panel rejected the request on identical grounds: no proven bias, acquaintanceship insufficient, no evidence of influence, and secrecy of deliberations. On 24 November 2021 the panel, again including L.M., declared the appeal inadmissible.

National law relevant to the impartiality complaint includes Article 63 of the Constitution (judicial independence) and CCP Articles 29–35 (recusal grounds and procedure). Article 31 § 1(d) permits recusal if a judge is personally interested or if any circumstance casts doubt on impartiality. Recusal of a single judge is decided by the remaining members; recusal of a majority is decided by the panel itself. Section 58 of the 1997 Law on Courts of Ordinary Jurisdiction and Articles 200 and 396–408 CCP confer on judicial assistants substantial functions: receiving applications, preparing cases, researching law and practice, drafting documents and performing other case-related duties at the judge’s request. International material cited includes CCJE Opinion No. 22 (2019), which requires judicial assistants to disclose conflicts and contemplates recusal rules analogous to those for judges, and the Bangalore Principles, which extend impartiality to the entire decision-making process.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ claim that Judge L.M.’s continued participation, given his assistant’s close family relationship to opposing counsel and the assistants’ non-administrative role in Georgian procedure, created an objectively justified fear of bias that the Supreme Court had failed to dispel.

The case of Yaylalı v. Serbia (no. 15887/15) concerns the confiscation of jewellery belonging to the applicant’s wife and a fine imposed after he failed to declare it while transiting Serbia, alleged to breach Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). Victim status under Article 34 was also at issue given the circumstances.

On 19 June 2013 the applicant, a Turkish national living in the Netherlands, entered Serbia at the Batrovci crossing from Croatia en route to Turkey. After declaring €1,500 and personal belongings, a personal search uncovered eight second-hand gold bracelets (254 grams) in a belt-bag pouch. The case of Toth and Crișan v. Romania (Application no. 45430/19) concerns two Romanian police officers, Zoltán-Ovidiu Toth and Alin Crișan, who alleged a violation of their Article 8 rights to respect for private life and reputation. They claimed that domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance after dismissing their defamation action against a private individual, C.T., over a Facebook post.

On 8 April 2016, the applicants, officers of the Oradea local police, fined C.T. and her mother for improperly disposing of household waste and related conduct. C.T. later successfully challenged aspects of the fine: courts confirmed she had dumped waste in an unauthorized location but found she had not insulted the officers, while the applicants had behaved inappropriately. A forensic report indicated C.T. sustained minor bodily injuries not requiring treatment, and the fine was reduced.

That same day, C.T. posted on the public Facebook group “Oradea is us” (with over 24,000 members) a narrative of the incident accompanied by a photograph of the applicants in uniform. The post described the officers as aggressively confronting her (while she held a child) and her mother, failing to identify themselves until she threatened to call emergency services, verbally assaulting and pushing them, and preventing her mother from driving away. It questioned their dignity and respect toward women and a child. The photograph showed the officers standing together, one holding a notebook, pen, and phone, with cars and buildings in the background.

The post received around 160 likes, 92 comments, and 73 shares. Applicants estimated it reached over 100,000 views. Comments included insults such as “scumbags,” “idiots,” “uneducated,” and “worthless simpletons,” along with claims of prior abuses by the officers (including videos of the second applicant) and expressions of hostility. In replies, C.T. disclosed the second applicant’s full name and stated she intended only to report the event, not to defame.

Disciplinary and criminal complaints by C.T. or her mother against the applicants were discontinued for insufficient or contradictory evidence.

On 14 February 2017, the applicants sued C.T. in tort, seeking 50,000 RON (about €11,111) in non-pecuniary damages and an apology in newspapers and on the Facebook group. They argued the post distorted facts (claiming they, not C.T., were the aggressors), disseminated their photograph and the second applicant’s name without consent to a wide audience, and provoked offensive comments and threats that harmed their professional and personal reputation. Family, friends, strangers, and their employer questioned their conduct; disciplinary proceedings were opened against them.

The Oradea District Court dismissed the claim on 26 June 2017. It recognized standing due to the photo and name but applied res judicata from the fine-challenge proceedings. The post, it found, generated only trivial comments and caused no harm to their image; C.T. had clarified she did not intend offense.

The Bihor County Court upheld this on 12 January 2018, noting the applicants should have considered the public context of their duties. The post merely conveyed C.T.’s perception of an event in which she was involved and did not launch a defamatory campaign.

The Oradea Court of Appeal dismissed the final appeal on 28 February 2019. Applying ECHR principles on freedom of expression (including to private individuals using social media), it held the post expressed C.T.’s dissatisfaction with the officers’ professional conduct, rested on a sufficient factual basis (confirmed by prior judgments), and did not exceed acceptable limits. C.T. was not liable for third-party comments, as liability is personal. As public servants, the applicants faced wider limits of criticism. Dissemination of the photograph (not undignified) and name caused no additional harm.

The European Court of Human Rights found Article 8 applicable, as the requisite seriousness threshold was met, but concluded that the domestic courts’ balancing of the applicants’ reputation against C.T.’s freedom of expression conformed to its case-law criteria. No violation was found.

The case of Çağıl v. Türkiye (Application no. 19085/18) concerns a complaint by Turkish national Ferat Çağıl under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He alleged unfairness in criminal proceedings because he could not appeal his conviction by the Third Division of the Edremit Criminal Court of First Instance to the Court of Cassation. The fines imposed fell below the statutory appeal threshold, which he claimed impaired the essence of his right of access to a court.

On 5 September 2015, the applicant and his girlfriend G.R.F. quarrelled with T.A. and V.E. at a café in Altınoluk, Balıkesir. The dispute escalated into a fight. On 16 December 2015, the Edremit public prosecutor indicted all four for making threats, public insults, and inflicting actual bodily harm.

On 26 May 2016 the trial court convicted the applicant (together with the others) of public insults, threats, and actual bodily harm. It imposed 87 day-fines totalling TRY 1,740 (approximately EUR 594) for insults, 25 day-fines totalling TRY 500 (approximately EUR 170) for threats, and 120 day-fines totalling TRY 2,000 (approximately EUR 683) for bodily harm. Because each fine was below the TRY 3,000 threshold in provisional section 2 of Law no. 5320 (then in force), the judgment was final and could not be appealed.

On 21 July 2016 the applicant applied to the Constitutional Court, arguing that the lack of an appeal violated his right of access to a court. He paid the threat fine on 31 August 2016 and the remaining fines on 15 December 2016. On 28 December 2017 the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It recalled that the right of access to a court is not absolute and may be limited provided the limitation does not impair the right’s essence, pursues a legitimate aim, is precise and proportionate, and does not impose an excessive burden. The Constitution leaves procedural regulation (including appeal rights) to the legislature and does not guarantee an appeal against every decision. The European Convention itself permits exceptions for minor offences. In view of the nature and modest quantum of the dispute, the statutory limit did not offend the sense of justice; consequently there was no violation of the right of access to a court.

The offences were governed by Articles 86, 106 and 125 of the Criminal Code, which allow either imprisonment or a judicial fine. Judicial fines are entered in the criminal register, archived after execution and erased five years later. The appeal threshold itself originated in former Article 305 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (struck down in part in 2009 because it also covered fines converted from imprisonment) and was restated in Article 272 of the current Code. Its purpose is to relieve the Court of Cassation of minor cases so that more serious disputes can be resolved within a reasonable time. Even below-threshold convictions may exceptionally be reviewed solely on the legal characterisation of the offence, and an extraordinary “appeal in the interests of justice” remains theoretically available, though limited to cases brought to the detriment of the accused and involving offences whose statutory maximum exceeds the threshold.

These facts—the modest financial penalties for relatively minor public-order offences, the automatic finality of the first-instance judgment, the unsuccessful constitutional challenge, and the existence of the statutory filter—constitute the core of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation.

Since their parents’ death the applicant had provided daily practical and psychological support. Both were placed together in a family home with an experienced psychiatric assistant nurse and assigned a special representative and public counsel.

When A.H. turned 18 in January 2017 the municipality ended the family-home placement, finding no sufficiently extensive care needs. A.H. appealed, submitting medical certificates and statements describing anxiety, depression, sleep and concentration problems, anger-management difficulties and repeated self-harm (cigarette burns, wrist-cutting). A.H. was then accommodated at a Migration Agency reception unit with home-care visits five times daily, later moving in March 2017 to institutional accommodation in Vimmerby (270 km from the applicant). Staff reports recorded frustration, aggression, suicidal thoughts, a request for a psychologist (after which he reported feeling better) and a July 2017 incident in which he attempted to throw himself from a balcony. Staff assessed him as not immediately suicidal but requiring increased supervision; they noted trauma, powerlessness and a wish to be closer to his brother. In August 2017 he was transferred to protected housing in Mölndal (near Gothenburg) offering 24-hour non-psychiatric care.

During asylum interviews in April and June 2017 A.H. repeatedly stated that he would commit suicide if refused asylum or expelled, that life had no meaning given his deteriorating vision, and that he had already chosen death. On 23 August 2017 both asylum claims were refused. The applicant was notified on 7 September; A.H. was notified personally on 18 September with an interpreter and information on appeal rights. He confirmed understanding and stated an intention to appeal. No signs of acute distress were recorded at that meeting, and neither brother subsequently contacted the authorities. A.H. died by suicide on 20 September 2017. The Migration Agency’s internal review identified shortcomings in the asylum examination (insufficient investigation of disability and mental health) but did not address the suicide. A subsequent compensation claim before the Chancellor of Justice was refused: although the authorities knew of a general risk linked to a negative decision, there was no indication of a real and immediate risk at the time of notification or in the days immediately preceding the suicide, and the Mölndal placement had been accepted by A.H. as a temporary measure to be near his brother.

One absent civil party (B.N.V.) was examined in Moldova and answered the parties’ written questions, confirming that her passport had been taken, her movements monitored and she had been forced into sexual acts under threat of family exposure. The case of T.A. v. Switzerland (ECHR Application no. 13437/22, Fifth Section judgment of 6 March 2025) concerns the Swiss authorities’ refusal to authorise the applicant’s adoption of a child she found as a newborn in Ethiopia in 2016 and later brought to Switzerland. The applicant, a Swiss national born in Ethiopia in 1967, alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life).

The applicant moved to Switzerland in 1995, adopted an Ethiopian-born son (R.) that year, and later divorced. She regularly visited Ethiopia. On 23 January 2016 she claimed to have found the newborn (later named E.) in Addis Ababa; police declined to take him to an orphanage, so she cared for him. Ethiopian documents indicated locals found the child and police placed him with her via court order on 11 February 2016. In February 2017 an Ethiopian court approved her adoption based on an October 2016 agreement with local women’s/children’s authorities, and a birth certificate named her as mother.

Swiss authorities were alerted in April 2016. The Geneva adoption service (SASLP) investigated after the applicant sought authorisation to foster with a view to adoption. Ethiopian procedures required a two-month search for biological family, police investigation of abandonment, and court scrutiny; these were not followed. Discrepancies included delayed police reporting, an unauthorised local office signing the agreement, same-day court approval without inquiry, and the applicant presenting as Ethiopian (she had lost that nationality). A 2016 Swiss federal directive halted new suitability certificates for Ethiopian adoptions amid fraud concerns.

On 4 October 2016 SASLP refused authorisation, citing the applicant’s inability to work due to frail health, reliance on social benefits, a 49-year age gap (exceeding the 45-year legal maximum, waivable only in the child’s best interests), absence of the required one-year fostering period, and Ethiopian procedural flaws. The decision became final.

Despite this, the applicant brought E. to Switzerland via France in March 2017 and presented the fait accompli to SASLP. Guardianship was granted to SASLP staff (later the applicant and R.), and E. remained with her as being in his best interests given their bond. A 2019 SASLP psycho-social report found adoption suitable and recommended it; TPAE approved, waiving the age gap. However, the Geneva Court of Justice rejected the application in 2020 (upheld 2021), emphasising the applicant’s finances, health, initial refusal, and non-compliance. The Federal Supreme Court confirmed in August 2021: Swiss law applied (Ethiopia not a Hague Convention party), the Ethiopian order was non-compliant, and Article 8 was not absolute. Family life existed but was not severed (no forced separation; they could live in Ethiopia or continue in Switzerland under guardianship). The public interest in enforcing adoption rules—to protect children and prevent illegal faits accomplis disguised as serving best interests—outweighed the applicant’s claim. She had deliberately circumvented procedures.

E. later received a permanent residence permit (eligible for nationality at age 12). The ECHR found no Article 8 violation: the refusal was based on relevant, sufficient reasons; a fair balance was struck; unlawful removal could not be justified by the child’s interests; and family life faced no particular obstacles.

The case of T.A. v. Switzerland (ECtHR, Application no. 13437/22) concerns the Swiss authorities’ refusal to authorize the applicant’s adoption of a child she had found in Ethiopia, alleged to violate Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life).

The applicant, T.A., was born in Ethiopia in 1967 and acquired Swiss nationality after moving to Switzerland in 1995 with her then-husband. They had previously adopted a son, R., from Ethiopia. After divorcing in 2003, she lived in Geneva with R. and regularly visited Ethiopia.

In January 2016, T.A. claimed to have found a newborn boy (E.) in Addis Ababa. Ethiopian police records indicated locals had found the infant and handed him to authorities, who placed him in her care via the Legetafo Court. In February 2017, an Ethiopian court approved her adoption based on an agreement with local authorities, and a birth certificate listed her as the mother.

Swiss authorities learned of the situation in April 2016 when R. contacted Geneva’s adoption authority (SASLP). T.A. applied for authorization to foster E. with a view to adoption. An investigation by Swiss diplomats revealed major irregularities: T.A. had given inconsistent accounts; she delayed reporting the child to police; the local office signing the adoption agreement lacked authority and admitted errors; Ethiopian procedures (including a mandatory two-month search for biological family and proper investigation) were ignored; the court approved the adoption the same day without inquiry; and T.A. presented herself as Ethiopian (having lost that nationality upon becoming Swiss), leading authorities to treat it as a domestic rather than intercountry adoption.

On 4 October 2016, SASLP refused authorization, citing T.A.’s frail health, reliance on social benefits, a 49-year age gap exceeding the legal maximum of 45 years, the absence of a required probationary fostering period, and Ethiopia’s non-compliance with proper procedures. A Swiss federal directive had also halted new Ethiopian adoptions amid reports of fraud. T.A. did not appeal.

In March 2017 she brought E. to Switzerland via France, admitting she had violated the refusal and Swiss law. SASLP then sought guardianship measures. The Geneva Adult and Child Protection Court appointed SASLP officials as guardians but left E. with T.A. due to their established bond. In May 2019, after a positive psychosocial assessment, SASLP granted fostering authorization and recommended adoption; the protection court approved, waiving the age limit.

However, the Geneva Court of Justice rejected the adoption in June 2020, citing T.A.’s finances, health, the initial unauthorized entry, and the age difference. Appeals were dismissed. In August 2021 the Federal Supreme Court upheld the refusal. It confirmed Swiss law applied (Ethiopia not being party to the Hague Adoption Convention). While family life existed, the refusal did not force separation; T.A. and E. could live together in Ethiopia, where she had family ties and spent months each year. Even assuming interference, the public interest in enforcing adoption procedures—to protect children and prevent unlawful faits accomplis—outweighed T.A.’s interest. Her illegal circumvention of the 2016 refusal could not be justified by claims of the child’s best interests.

E. later received a permanent Swiss residence permit (eligible for nationality at age 12). T.A. and R. remain his legal guardians; their relationship was not severed, and no practical obstacles to family life were found. The ECtHR held that a fair balance had been struck, with relevant and sufficient reasons given, finding no violation of Article 8.

Family life under Article 8 existed, but the refusal did not sever the relationship: the applicant and her adult son remained legal guardians, E. later received a permanent residence permit, and the pair could continue living together either in Switzerland or in Ethiopia. The court balanced the applicant’s interest in regularizing a situation she had created by illegally bringing the child into the country against the public interest in enforcing adoption procedures designed to protect children and to prevent faits accomplis. It concluded that the latter interest prevailed.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 8. The refusal was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aims of protecting children and maintaining the integrity of inter-country adoption rules, and was supported by relevant and sufficient reasons. Because guardianship preserved the de-facto family unit and no practical obstacles to their continued cohabitation were shown, a fair balance had been struck between the competing interests.

**F.S.M. v. Spain (ECtHR, Application no. 56712/21, judgment of 13 March 2025) concerns the applicant’s conviction for tax offences amid claims that his age and cognitive impairment rendered the criminal proceedings unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention (fair trial, including adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence).**

The applicant, a Spanish national born in 1948, faced criminal proceedings initiated in December 2013 for alleged tax fraud as sole administrator of two companies in 2007–2008. He was accused of concealing economic activity in VAT declarations (evading over €3.8 million) and failing to file a corporate tax return (evading a further €877,000). Charges were confirmed in 2016, with the case referred for trial.

A 2016 forensic report found these conditions impaired understanding and action, particularly in administrative/economic matters, though not totally; partial guardianship (*curatela*) was recommended for such decisions. In October 2016, a court declared partial incapacitation, requiring guardian consent for contracts or administrative acts creating obligations. The decision noted pending criminal cases, stating any impact on criminal liability would be assessed case-by-case (not automatically exonerating). A guardian was later replaced in 2018 by a foundation with the same limited scope.

In the criminal case, fitness issues arose. At a 2017 preliminary hearing, a forensic expert reported the applicant’s condition was not severe enough to prevent understanding the trial’s purpose. In January 2018, his lawyer sought adjournment or discontinuation, citing inability to grasp administrative concepts, limited defence cooperation from prior counsel, the incapacitation judgment, and reports (including a private one) of restricted capacity. Alternatives included expert assessment, videolink participation, and guardian assistance. The hearing was adjourned; a new forensic exam was ordered.

A May 2018 forensic report confirmed ADHD, personality disorder, and cognitive impairment history but found no current cognitive/volitional disorders or acute psychiatric issues. The applicant could distinguish right from wrong. He was fit to stand trial if adjustments were made (e.g., support person or videolink). After non-appearance, pre-trial detention was ordered (later lifted on conditions); the court deemed him fit based on reports, noted the incapacitation timing relative to charges, and found guardian presence unnecessary.

Requests to discontinue (under Criminal Procedure Act Articles 381/383, for post-offence mental disturbance) or admit further experts were rejected in July 2018 as the reports (including two court-ordered ones) showed sufficient capacity, consistent with the incapacitation judgment. Late evidence was inadmissible, though proposable at hearing. The applicant appointed new lawyers.

A January 2019 request to admit a further forensic report (noting possible impact on answering questions/defence due to memory/orientation issues, though capacity to understand consequences existed) and discontinue was refused at the 16–17 January 2019 hearing. The case of Demirer v. Türkiye (Application no. 45779/18) concerned the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 that her conviction for membership of an armed terrorist organisation lacked a sufficiently reasoned judgment, as the courts allegedly failed to set out grounds or assess her defence on the merits.

Both initially claimed to be Syrian nationals without identification, giving false names and stating they had come for a relative’s wedding, but could provide no supporting details. Fingerprints later revealed their true identities.

Ş.A. confessed to gendarmerie officers (in the presence of a lawyer) that she had attended PYD-YPG training camps in Syria (regarded by Turkey as a terrorist organisation and Syrian branch of the PKK), receiving ideological and weapons training, a Kalashnikov, and a code name. She had then been assigned kitchen duties before being sent back to Turkey with assistance from organisation members. She claimed the group of women, including the applicant, had been told to claim Syrian identity if caught. The applicant denied any terrorist membership. She stated she was from Hakkari, had relatives in Syria, and had crossed illegally (due to family finances, despite holding a passport) to attend her father’s cousin’s wedding in Amude, staying about ten days before attempting to return for an examination. She too claimed a smuggler advised claiming Syrian identity. Both later repeated their accounts to a prosecutor and investigating judge (again with lawyers present). The judge ordered pre-trial detention, forming the view that they had committed the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

An indictment of 31 January 2016 charged both with that offence and with making a false declaration. At trial, the interpreter confirmed that the applicant had called him a “traitor” for “betraying his nation.” The applicant maintained her wedding account and denied knowing Ş.A. beforehand. Ş.A. recanted her confession, alleging threats of violence, rape, and transfer to an ISIS camp, claiming she had gone to Syria for adventure.

On 24 May 2016 the Mardin Assize Court convicted both, sentencing each to nine years’ imprisonment for organisational membership and one year for forgery. It relied on Ş.A.’s initial lawyer-present confession (preferring it over her recantation, which it found unconvincing), incident/arrest reports, the false identities, the applicant’s “traitor” remark, and their joint illegal crossing. It held Ş.A. was clearly a hierarchical member (code name, training, orders followed). The applicant’s wedding explanation was unconvincing; she had acted together with a proven member, and no evidence favoured her. A dissenting judge would have acquitted the applicant for lack of evidence of any prior connection or hierarchical link, noting Ş.A. had said she first met the applicant at the border.

After the verdict the applicant chanted PKK slogans. Her appeal argued Ş.A. had never claimed to know her and that the interpreter’s evidence should not be treated as conclusive. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction on 1 February 2017, finding the evidence properly assessed, facts established, and defences dismissed on credible grounds (without relying on the slogans). The Constitutional Court declared her individual application inadmissible on 7 May 2018, holding there was no arbitrariness in the evidence assessment and that the trial court had sufficiently discussed all relevant accusations and defences (its reasons having been upheld on appeal).

The European Court of Human Rights found the domestic judgments sufficiently reasoned, disclosing no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Backović v. Serbia (No. 2) (Application no. 47600/17) concerns a lawyer’s complaint under Article 10 of the Convention that a fine imposed for contempt of court violated his freedom of expression.

The applicant, Čedomir Backović (born 1956), is a practising lawyer. The relevant events arose from earlier litigation over his status as a Sombor city councillor. In 2008 the Sombor District Court held that his (and fifteen others’) terms of office had ended. In 2011 the Constitutional Court found this violated their electoral rights and directed the Administrative Court to amend the judgment, which it did by dismissing the original action.

On 27 January 2012 the applicant (acting for himself and six others) applied to the Sombor Court of First Instance for enforcement of the Administrative Court judgment, seeking municipal acknowledgement that they remained councillors. On 21 February 2012 a single judge dismissed the request, ruling that the judgment was not an “enforceable document” under the Enforcement Procedure Act.

On 2 March 2012 the applicant lodged a written objection. In addition to arguing misapplication of the Act, he used highly critical language: he described the court’s approach as a “pen-pushing” restrictive interpretation lacking constitutional or legal basis and rooted in outdated, “pre-war” practices that had been universally condemned and should have been abandoned both legislatively and in personnel terms. He asserted that such “pen-pushing actions” of enforcement courts produced “catastrophic consequences” for claimants’ rights, the length of proceedings and legal certainty. He accused enforcement judges of failing to make reasonable efforts to enforce judgments in which other courts and parties had invested years of work, of regarding themselves as “legal geniuses and legal giants” capable of drafting better judgments, of “looking for a needle in a haystack” from the “pedestal of an absolute arbiter” and thereby abusing their function. He labelled the first-instance finding “supreme nonsense” possibly written out of malice or ignorance and incompatible with a professional judiciary in a rule-of-law state, and remarked that challenging the Administrative Court’s status and expertise would be “funny if it were not sad.”

On 7 March 2012 the same judge fined the applicant 100 000 RSD (approximately EUR 910) for contempt, holding that the language insulted the court, enforcement judges and the sitting judge. The court took into account the harshness of the remarks and the fact that they were made by a practising lawyer.

The applicant objected, invoking Article 10 and ECHR case-law (De Haes and Gijsels, Dalban, Krasulya, Lepojić, Filipović). He maintained that he had intended only a sharp critique of the quality of the judicial function and the (un)lawfulness of the decision, not personal insult, and that the statements were value judgments rather than false assertions of fact.

On 4 September 2012 another formation of the first-instance court reduced the fine to 50 000 RSD (approximately EUR 425) but otherwise upheld the finding of insult, concluding that the applicant had not merely challenged the decision but had denied the court’s and judge’s expertise, humiliated them and intended to belittle them, thereby damaging judicial reputation. Freedom of expression, it held, did not cover an intention to insult the court.

The applicant paid the fine in May 2014. His December 2012 constitutional appeal, which repeated the Article 10 arguments and added an Article 6 impartiality complaint (same judge both “insulted” and fining), was rejected by the Constitutional Court on 29 December 2016. The court noted that freedom of expression may be restricted to protect the rights and reputation of others and found the lower courts’ reasoning clear, sufficient and constitutionally acceptable.

(The remainder of the original application was declared inadmissible; only the Article 10 complaint was communicated.)

He distinguished value judgments from factual insults.

The language showed an intent to belittle rather than challenge the decision on legal grounds, and freedom of expression did not extend to insults of courts or judges.

On 2 March 2012 the applicant filed an objection. Besides arguing that the court had misapplied or failed to apply the relevant statutory provisions, he used strongly critical language. He described the decision as a “pen-pushing” restrictive interpretation lacking any constitutional or legal basis, rooted in outdated “pre-war” practices that had produced “catastrophic consequences” for claimants’ rights, the length of proceedings and legal certainty. He asserted that enforcement courts should strive to give effect to judgments even if their “legal geniuses and legal giants” believed they could have drafted a better one, and that the first-instance court’s stance reached the level of “abuse of an entrusted function.” He called the court’s finding “supreme nonsense,” suggested it might have been written “out of malice \ldots or owing to a lack of knowledge,” and said it was incompatible with a professional judiciary in a State governed by the rule of law. He added that questioning the Administrative Court’s status and expertise would be “funny if it were not sad.”

The court found that the objection insulted the court, enforcement judges and the individual judge by denying their expertise and humiliating them. The applicant objected, invoking Article 10, several Strasbourg judgments, and the distinction between value judgments and factual assertions. He maintained that his remarks concerned only the quality of the judicial decision and the application of the law, not any personal characteristic of the judge.

Freedom of expression, it held, did not encompass an intention to insult judges. The applicant paid the fine in May 2014. His subsequent constitutional appeal, which also alleged a lack of impartiality because the same judge had both felt insulted and imposed the sanction, was rejected by the Constitutional Court in December 2016. That court accepted that the lower courts had given clear, sufficient and constitutionally acceptable reasons and that freedom of expression could be restricted to protect the reputation of others, including the judiciary.

The European Court ultimately found no violation of Article 10, holding that the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of maintaining the authority of the judiciary, and was necessary in a democratic society. The domestic courts had subjected the fine to effective review; the language used went beyond acceptable criticism of a judicial decision by accusing judges of abuse of office and belittling their professional capacities; and the modest, reduced fine had no impact on the applicant’s right to practise law. The reasons given by the national courts were relevant and sufficient.

**Case summary: Federici v. France (ECHR Application no. 52302/19)**

Jean-François Federici, a French national born in 1957 and detained at the time of the application, was charged with murder committed as a member of an organised group and conspiracy to commit a crime. In 2011 he absconded after failing to comply with a court supervision order. The Bouches-du-Rhône Assize Court (Aix-en-Provence) convicted him in absentia in December 2014 and imposed a 30-year prison sentence. He was arrested in 2016, placed in pre-trial detention, and retried. In January 2017 the Assize Court again sentenced him to 30 years’ imprisonment plus confiscation. He appealed.

Appeal hearings took place from 3–6 and 9–13 April 2018 in the standard courtroom of the Aix-en-Provence Law Courts. The applicant, assisted by two lawyers, appeared in a glass dock pursuant to Article 318 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, “free and only accompanied by guards to prevent him from escaping.” The dock was a permanent, open-roofed glass enclosure measuring 3.68 m by 2.47 m. It featured two 20 cm-diameter hygiaphones (perforations) at human height for communication with lawyers (whose bench sat directly adjacent and below the openings), two 8 cm × 30 cm slots for passing documents, two fixed microphones on swivel legs, a loudspeaker transmitting courtroom sound at pre-set volume, a glass door to the courtroom, and a solid security door to a secure waiting area.

On 6 April 2018 the applicant was questioned about his personality. He made no complaint of hearing difficulties and did not request to leave the dock. On 10 April, with questioning on the merits scheduled for the next day, his lawyer filed supplementary submissions invoking Article 6 of the Convention, the preliminary Article of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and recital 20 of Directive (EU) 2016/343. The lawyer asked that the applicant appear in the courtroom itself rather than the dock, citing security checks already performed on members of the public and a hearing impairment that “sometimes made it more difficult to hear the questions put to him.”

On 11 April the President of the Assize Court questioned the applicant, who remained inside the dock. In an interlocutory judgment of 13 April 2018 the court dismissed the request. It relied on Articles 318 and D. 294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which require security measures commensurate with the danger posed by the accused and the need to prevent escape. The court noted the gravity of the charges (murder as part of an organised group, carrying a possible life sentence), the applicant’s pre-trial detention after more than four years on the run, and its own observation that, despite alleged hearing problems, he had been able to answer questions and communicate confidentially with counsel while moving freely inside the dock. The placement was therefore lawful, proportionate and necessary; it neither infringed the presumption of innocence, individual dignity, nor the rights of the defence. The same day the court convicted the applicant of a double murder committed as a member of an organised group and imposed a 30-year sentence.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, arguing that the Assize Court had given insufficient reasons and had failed to consider whether available staff and security measures would have permitted him to appear freely at the witness stand. He relied on an April 2018 opinion of the Public Defender’s Office criticising systematic use of glass docks and on the ECHR judgment in Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on 10 April 2019, holding that the Assize Court’s reasoning (based on its unfettered assessment) did not show that the applicant had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers.

These facts—late request, unsubstantiated hearing complaint, detailed dock design permitting movement, confidential lawyer communication and participation, serious violent organised-crime charges, and lengthy absconding—formed the basis of the alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) (fair trial, presumption of innocence, and adequate time and facilities for the defence).

The case of Green v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 22077/19) concerns alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the use of parliamentary privilege to identify the applicant in breach of a court-ordered interim privacy injunction.

The applicant, Philip Nigel Ross Green (born 1952), is a British businessman and former chairman of the Arcadia Group, which included high-street brands such as Topshop. On 16 July 2018, a journalist from the Telegraph Media Group contacted Arcadia, stating an intention to publish serious allegations of sexual harassment, racist abuse and bullying made against Green by former employees of Arcadia and Topshop. Parliamentary privilege (rooted in Article 9 of the Bill of Rights) confers absolute immunity on statements made in proceedings in Parliament. The House of Lords is self-regulating; its Code of Conduct contains no provisions on privilege or the sub judice rule (which, subject to the Lord Speaker’s discretion, generally prohibits reference to active court proceedings). Successive parliamentary committees had noted rare instances of injunctions being breached in Parliament but concluded that the threshold for restricting members’ speech had not been crossed. Comparative material showed that the large majority of Council of Europe states likewise afford absolute protection to parliamentary statements from external legal action.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 6 § 1, 8 and 13, arguing that the disclosure of his identity, made possible by an effectively uncontrolled parliamentary privilege, violated his right to respect for private life, denied him access to court, and left him without an effective remedy.

The case of Green v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 22077/19) concerns a complaint by businessman Philip Green that the United Kingdom failed to protect his Article 8 rights to private life when a Member of the House of Lords used parliamentary privilege to name him as the subject of an interim privacy injunction. Green, chairman of the Arcadia Group (which included brands such as Topshop), had settled employment claims with former employees alleging sexual harassment, racist abuse and bullying. The settlements included non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) under which both sides agreed to keep the complaints and terms confidential, while still permitting legitimate disclosures such as reports of crime. The employees had received independent legal advice.

In July 2018 the Telegraph Media Group indicated it intended to publish details of the allegations. Green, Arcadia and Topshop obtained an interim injunction from the Court of Appeal on 23 October 2018 preventing publication of the material and granting anonymity pending an expedited trial. The Court of Appeal held that substantial parts of the information had likely been obtained in breach of confidence, that NDAs served a legitimate purpose in consensual dispute resolution, and that there was no evidence the agreements had been procured by undue pressure. It also found a real risk of immediate and irreversible commercial harm. The Telegraph published a story the following day that respected the order.

On 25 October 2018, after an unrelated debate, Lord Hain made a short personal statement in the House of Lords. Invoking parliamentary privilege, he named Green as the “powerful businessman” using NDAs and payments to conceal “serious and repeated sexual harassment, racist abuse and bullying.” The statement was widely reported, rendering the anonymity orders pointless; they were later discharged by consent. The underlying details of the allegations remained protected by the injunction. The Lord Speaker subsequently reminded the House of the need for mutual respect between Parliament and the courts.

Green lodged a formal complaint with the House of Lords Commissioner for Standards, alleging breach of the sub judice rule, abuse of privilege and failure to declare an interest. The Commissioner declined to investigate the privilege and sub judice issues because they fell outside the Code of Conduct and therefore outside her remit; she accepted Lord Hain’s explanation of the interest point. Green and Arcadia then sought to pursue the Telegraph for the consequences of the disclosure, but the newspaper invoked Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689, which renders proceedings in Parliament immune from question in any court. The claimants ultimately discontinued the action in January 2019, stating that insufficient confidentiality remained to justify continuing.

Parliamentary privilege in the United Kingdom is absolute in respect of statements made in the course of proceedings. It is protected by Article 9 of the Bill of Rights and is regarded as a constitutional principle of the highest importance, reflecting the separation of powers. The House of Lords is self-regulating; neither the Lord Speaker nor the Commissioner for Standards has power to sanction a Member for a statement made on the floor of the House. A sub judice resolution exists but is likewise internally enforced and subject to the Speaker’s unchallengeable discretion. Breach of an injunction by anyone other than a parliamentarian would constitute contempt of court punishable by imprisonment or a fine; no such sanction is available against a Member acting under privilege.

These facts form the basis of Green’s complaints under Articles 6 § 1, 8 and 13. He argued that the absence of effective ex ante or ex post controls allowed an unaccountable interference with his private life and left him without any judicial or other remedy. The Court examined whether the United Kingdom’s positive obligation under Article 8 required it to introduce additional restrictions on parliamentary speech in order to prevent the disclosure of information protected by privacy injunctions.
