**Case of Tergek v. Türkiye (App. No. 39631/20, ECtHR Second Section, 29 April 2025)**

The applicant, Abdül Samed Tergek (born 1989), a Turkish national serving a sentence in Kocaeli T-Type Prison for membership of the FETÖ/PDY (an armed terrorist organisation), complained that prison authorities’ refusal to deliver internet printouts posted to him by relatives violated Article 10 (freedom to receive information and ideas). Notice was given of the Article 10 complaint; other complaints were declared inadmissible.

On 22 October 2018, the prison letter-reading committee flagged a 31-page letter from the applicant’s sister (containing internet printouts) as objectionable and referred it to the Disciplinary Board. Citing section 68(3) of Law no. 5275, the Board withheld it on grounds of potential threat to prison security, unknown publisher/purpose, and phrases that could facilitate FETÖ/PDY communication. The applicant objected to the Kocaeli enforcement judge, explaining that some documents (sent by his physiotherapist sister) covered exercises for his ankle injury (requiring a cast after 1 October 2018) and others related to his distance-learning real-estate management course/exams. On 19 August 2019 the judge upheld the objection, finding that withholding without specific content assessment was unlawful in light of freedom of communication and expression (citing ECtHR and Constitutional Court case-law). The applicant was notified on 1 October 2019 and received the materials on 25 October 2019 (delayed delivery).

On 18 December 2018, a letter from the applicant’s wife (61 pages of internet printouts, a handwritten note and four pictures) was similarly flagged. The Disciplinary Board withheld the printouts under section 68(3) and a 4 November 2016 Administration and Monitoring Board decision on risks of internet printouts, without addressing their content; the note and pictures were delivered. The applicant objected on 24 December 2018, repeating that the documents concerned physiotherapy and his real-estate studies, essential for rehabilitation and education. The enforcement judge dismissed the objection (citing section 62 of Law no. 5275), holding that printouts of unknown origin, susceptible to interference, were neither “books” nor “correspondence”; prisoners could access publications via the prison library. The Kocaeli Assize Court endorsed this on 17 September 2019.

On 30 October 2019 the applicant applied to the Constitutional Court, alleging breach of respect for correspondence due to delayed delivery of the first letter and seizure of the second. On 16 June 2020 a two-judge panel dismissed the application as manifestly ill-founded, referring to its leading *Diyadin Akdemir* judgment (2015/9562, 4 April 2018). There, photocopied documents fell outside section 62 (“periodicals and non-periodicals”); applying the same inspection criteria would impose an unreasonable burden on prison administrations and courts, and such documents could raise copyright issues.

Relevant domestic law included section 62 of Law no. 5275 (right to receive periodical/non-periodical publications, except those endangering institutional security or containing obscenity; textbooks for studies exempt from inspection) and section 68 (letters monitored; not forwarded if they threaten prison order/security, target officials, permit organisational communication among terrorist/criminal groups, contain panic-inducing falsehoods, or threats/insults). Similar provisions applied via Regulation 91 and to remand prisoners under section 116. An April 2020 amendment to section 62(3) expanded grounds to include disturbance of discipline/order or hindering rehabilitation.

The Court held the refusal proportionate under Article 10. Reviewing large volumes of unscrutinised printouts/photocopies (beyond regular publications) risked overwhelming staff, impeding duties and burdening the judiciary. Official books/periodicals undergo pre-publication scrutiny, unlike printouts, which pose specific security/order risks. Prisoners had other lawful means to obtain publications. National authorities reasonably regulated photocopied/printed documents for efficient prison functioning. The Constitutional Court’s assessment was detailed and balanced; the margin of appreciation was not exceeded. No violation. (The judgment may be referred to the Grand Chamber.)

The case of Iordan v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 10870/15) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Iurie Iordan, a judge at the Chișinău Court of Appeal, claimed that Moldovan courts failed to protect his reputation by refusing to punish journalist B. under administrative offence proceedings for disseminating statements implying the applicant had accepted a bribe.

On 27 March 2013, during a lunch break, B. filmed the applicant leaving the court building. The footage showed the applicant meeting a man and a woman near a car registered in Căușeni. The woman handed him an envelope; he removed its contents, placed them in his pocket, and returned what appeared to be a banknote. While filming, B. provided live commentary questioning whether this was a bribe from litigants, describing the scene as “horrible” and “revolting,” suggesting it warranted investigation by anti-corruption authorities rather than the High Council of the Judiciary (whom he called accomplices), and implying the applicant was funding a car, villa and other luxuries beyond his salary. B. then confronted the applicant on camera as he re-entered the building, asking whether the individuals were litigants or parties in his cases and what they had discussed; the applicant did not reply.

Approximately three hours later, B. posted the video on YouTube under the title “A judge caught while receiving an envelope,” with a description reiterating the events and implying bribery. Comments treated the bribe-taking as fact, calling for the applicant’s resignation and imprisonment while criticising Moldova’s justice system.

Later that day, the woman in the video telephoned B., identifying herself as the applicant’s sister-in-law (her husband also present). She explained that she had handed over a receipt for a land tax bill she had paid on the applicant’s behalf, and that he had reimbursed her. The Chișinău Court of Appeal issued a press release confirming this account and noting that the applicant had not answered B. because B. had been an injured party in a prior case in which the applicant, as rapporteur, had seen the accused acquitted. The release also stated (without citing a legal basis) that judges could not speak to parties outside court sessions.

B. then updated his YouTube post with an “Update” summarising the telephone call and changed the title to “A judge caught while receiving an envelope (they say that there was a receipt inside).” That evening, hosting a live television programme, B. recounted the call, referred to the press release, and replayed an edited version of the video (omitting some of the more accusatory commentary) with a caption stating “They brought him a receipt in an envelope.” He invited viewers to comment; responses largely expressed disgust at the justice system or joked that bribes were now paid with receipts.

On 4 April 2013 the applicant filed a complaint with the Prosecutor General’s Office and police, seeking to hold B. liable under Article 70 of the Code of Administrative Offences (slander: deliberately disseminating false information that defames another person and produces serious consequences). An officer subsequently drew up a report finding B. guilty and imposing a fine of 1,600 Moldovan lei (approximately €85).

B. appealed, arguing that he had not knowingly made untruthful statements but had merely posed questions and voiced assumptions based on what he had observed; the applicant’s refusal to answer had prevented him from obtaining information. After remittal, the Botanica District Court on 22 May 2014 set aside the fine. It held that Article 70 required proof of deliberate dissemination of known falsehoods, which had not been established: B. could not have known the true facts at the time of posting because the applicant had remained silent; B. had asked questions rather than made firm assertions; and the filming had occurred in a public place. The Bălți Court of Appeal upheld this decision on 17 September 2014, adding that B. had lacked the requisite intent and invoking Article 10 of the Convention.

The applicant maintained that the courts’ refusal to sanction B. breached Moldova’s positive obligation under Article 8 to protect his private life and reputation against untrue statements of corruption. (The European Court ultimately found no violation, noting the limited balancing exercise that resulted from the applicant’s choice of an administrative rather than civil remedy, the domestic courts’ application of several Convention criteria, and the absence of a showing that the State had failed to provide effective protection of reputation.)

The case of Sahiner v. Austria (Application no. 21669/21) involves an Austrian national, Ms Özlem Sahiner (born 1996), who alleged that the authorities’ refusal to change her registered forename from “Özlem” to “Lemilia” violated Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

At birth in Austria the applicant received the Turkish forename “Özlem” at her father’s insistence; her mother preferred “Lemilia.” After the parents’ divorce the applicant was raised by her mother, had virtually no contact with her father (apart from one difficult childhood incident) and wished to sever all association with him. She later changed her surname to her mother’s. From birth her mother, friends and colleagues have always called her “Lemilia,” the name with which she identifies and which she had long believed to be her official name. Having to explain that her legal name is “Özlem” caused her significant inconvenience.

On 5 February 2019 she applied to the Innsbruck District Administrative Authority to change her forename under the Name Change Act. After a preliminary check the authority informed her that “Lemilia” did not appear in Austrian registrars’ databases (containing tens of thousands of names registered since 1984) and that a University of Innsbruck linguistics institute had confirmed it existed in neither Italian nor Spanish, appearing instead to be a combination of “Emilia” and a definite article. Because the name was therefore not “common” (gebräuchlich) as required by section 3(1)(7) of the Act, the authority intended to refuse the request.

The applicant submitted that “common” was undefined and that the Act’s purpose (according to the explanatory notes) was merely to ensure gender recognisability. “Lemilia” was clearly female and could be found on social-media platforms and in a Brazilian driving licence she produced. She emphasised her lifelong identification with the name and the interference with her private life that a refusal would cause.

On 27 May 2019 the authority rejected the application. It accepted that a foreign or rarely used name could qualify if it possessed a certain frequency, prominence or commonness, but held that the applicant’s evidence (social-media profiles and one Brazilian licence) was insufficient. Naming practices in Latin America were far less restrictive than in Europe.

The applicant appealed to the Tyrol Regional Administrative Court, arguing that the authority had wrongly treated statistical frequency in Austria as decisive, that her evidence proved the name’s use, and that a single extra letter added to the common name “Emilia” could not render it uncommon. She reiterated her personal history and the daily inconvenience of having two names. After an oral hearing the court dismissed the appeal on 4 December 2019. It interpreted “common” as “customary,” found social-media evidence unreliable (fake names being possible) and a single licence inadequate against the linguistic opinion, and held that the applicant’s identification with “Lemilia,” while understandable, did not make the name customary.

A constitutional complaint alleged that both the decision and the underlying provision were unconstitutional: the interpretation of “common” as “customary” was excessive, no fair balance had been struck under Article 8, and persons born abroad named “Lemilia” would be allowed to keep or register the name, violating Article 14. The Constitutional Court declined to examine the complaint (8 June 2020), referring to its case-law that the legislature may legitimately require names to have a real societal reference point and not be freely invented. It transferred the case to the Supreme Administrative Court, which on 30 September 2020 confirmed that “common” means customary or widespread in Austria or abroad and possesses a genuine link to the social development of names. The lower court’s findings were upheld.

The Name Change Act permits a change “for other reasons” unless a refusal ground applies, including that the requested forename is not common or does not correspond to the applicant’s gender. Explanatory notes indicate that the commonness requirement aims to prevent names that create doubt about gender or that are invented combinations. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claims that the refusal interfered with her identity and private life and treated her less favourably than persons whose names originated abroad.

The case of Sahiner v. Austria (Application no. 21669/21) concerns an Austrian national, Ms Özlem Sahiner (born 1996), who alleged that the authorities’ refusal to change her registered forename from “Özlem” to “Lemilia” violated Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant was registered at birth in Austria with the Turkish forename “Özlem” at her father’s insistence; her mother had preferred “Lemilia.” Following her parents’ divorce, she was raised solely by her mother and has had virtually no contact with her father apart from one difficult childhood encounter. From birth her mother called her Lemilia, and she has been known by that name to family, friends and colleagues. She later changed her surname (originally her father’s) to her mother’s surname, Sahiner, because she wished to have no association with him.

On 5 February 2019 she applied to the Innsbruck District Administrative Authority to change her forename to Lemilia. After checking Austrian registrars’ databases (including an encyclopaedia of forenames and all names registered since 1984) and consulting the University of Innsbruck Institute of Linguistics, the authority informed her that Lemilia did not appear as a recognised forename in Italian or Spanish and was probably a combination of “Emilia” and a definite article. It therefore intended to refuse the request because the name was not “common” (gebräuchlich) as required by section 3(1)(7) of the Name Change Act.

The applicant submitted social-media profiles of persons named Lemilia and a copy of a Brazilian driving licence bearing that forename. She argued that “common” was undefined in the statute and, according to the legislative explanatory notes, served only to ensure gender identifiability; Lemilia was clearly feminine. She further maintained that she had always identified with the name, that her official name caused repeated inconvenience, and that refusal would breach her right to private life.

On 27 May 2019 the District Administrative Authority rejected the application, holding that Lemilia lacked the required degree of frequency, prominence or commonness either in Austria or abroad. Latin-American naming practices were far less restrictive, so isolated examples from that region were irrelevant.

The applicant appealed to the Tyrol Regional Administrative Court, repeating that the commonness requirement existed only to exclude ridiculous, offensive or gender-ambiguous names and that adding a single letter to the common name Emilia should not render it uncommon. After an oral hearing the court dismissed the appeal on 4 December 2019, interpreting “common” as “customary.” Social-media evidence was unreliable (fake names being possible) and a single foreign licence insufficient. While the court accepted the applicant’s personal reasons—non-identification with Özlem, lifelong use of Lemilia, and desire to distance herself from her father—these did not make the requested name customary.

She then lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging that the provision was unconstitutionally vague and that the courts had failed to strike a fair balance under Article 8. She also claimed discrimination under Article 14 because persons born abroad named Lemilia could retain or register that name upon naturalisation. On 8 June 2020 the Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaint, referring to its own case-law that the legislature may require a name to have a genuine societal reference point and not be freely invented; it transferred the case to the Supreme Administrative Court. On 30 September 2020 that court dismissed the appeal on points of law, confirming that a forename must be customary or widespread in Austria or abroad and possess a real reference in the social development of names.

The applicant’s complaints therefore centred on the interference with her private-life identity (Article 8) caused by the refusal to register the name she had always used and with which she identified, and on alleged unequal treatment compared with foreign-born individuals (Article 14).

The case of Sahiner v. Austria (Application no. 21669/21) concerns an Austrian national, Ms Özlem Sahiner (born 1996), who sought to change her registered forename from “Özlem” to “Lemilia.” The applicant was given the Turkish name “Özlem” at birth in Austria at her father’s insistence, against her mother’s preference for “Lemilia.” Following her parents’ divorce, she was raised by her mother, with whom she had almost no contact with her father apart from one difficult childhood incident. Her mother had always called her “Lemilia,” a name by which she was known to family, friends and colleagues. She identified strongly with “Lemilia,” viewed “Özlem” as an unwanted association with her father, and had already successfully changed her surname from her father’s to her mother’s (“Sahiner”).

On 5 February 2019 she applied to the Innsbruck District Administrative Authority to change her forename. The authority conducted a preliminary check and found “Lemilia” absent from Austrian registrars’ databases (covering some 36,000 female forenames registered since 1984) and from linguistic resources. An enquiry to the University of Innsbruck’s Institute of Linguistics confirmed the name existed neither in Italian nor Spanish and appeared to be a hybrid of “Emilia” plus a definite article. The authority therefore indicated that the name failed the “common” (gebräuchlich) requirement of section 3(1)(7) of the Name Change Act and invited submissions.

The applicant argued that “common” was undefined, that the legislative purpose was merely to ensure gender recognisability, and that “Lemilia” was clearly female. She produced social-media profiles of persons named Lemilia and a Brazilian driving licence bearing the name, asserting that the name was sufficiently used abroad and that she had always identified with it. Refusal, she claimed, would violate her right to private and family life.

On 27 May 2019 the authority rejected the request, holding that “Lemilia” lacked the required frequency, prominence or commonness even as a foreign name. Latin-American naming practices were far more permissive and therefore irrelevant. The applicant appealed to the Tyrol Regional Administrative Court, reiterating that the name was a minor variant of the common name Emilia, that social-media evidence demonstrated use, and that the authorities’ insistence on statistical frequency in Austria contradicted their own statements. She emphasised the practical inconvenience of constantly correcting friends and her lack of identification with “Özlem.”

After an oral hearing the Regional Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 4 December 2019. It accepted the applicant’s personal history and identification with “Lemilia” but held that “common” meant “customary” (allgemein üblich). The submitted evidence was insufficient: social-media accounts could be fictitious and a single foreign licence could not rebut the linguistic finding that the name did not exist. A one-letter difference from Emilia did not render it customary.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that both the decision and the Name Change Act itself were unconstitutional. She argued that her father’s patriarchal imposition of “Özlem,” her lifelong use of “Lemilia,” and the serious reasons for the change outweighed any public interest. She also claimed discrimination under Article 14 compared with persons born abroad who could retain or register “Lemilia.” The Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaint (8 June 2020), citing its case-law that the legislature may require names to have a genuine societal reference point rather than being freely invented, and that this was compatible with Article 8. The Supreme Administrative Court likewise dismissed the appeal on points of law (30 September 2020), confirming that “common” required a name to be customary or widespread in Austria or abroad and to possess a real historical or social basis.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that the refusal interfered with her private life and identity without a sufficient legal basis or fair balance of interests.

The case of Kári Orrason and Others v. Iceland (applications nos. 29791/21, 40600/21 and 2281/22) concerned complaints under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention following the applicants’ convictions for disobeying a police order to leave the Ministry of Justice lobby after its closing time during a demonstration.

Peaceful protests over asylum seekers and refugees occurred in Reykjavik in March 2019, including outside the Ministry of Justice from 2 to 5 April 2019, with small groups occasionally entering the lobby. On 5 April 2019, shortly before 4 p.m. (the Ministry’s closing time of 8.30 a.m. to 4 p.m.), nine people including the three applicants entered the first-floor lobby (which also housed a reception and meeting rooms). Staff called police at 3.51 p.m. Surveillance footage showed the group sitting on the floor from 3.38 p.m. Police arrived at 4.02 p.m. and repeatedly ordered them to leave. Four departed at 4.03 p.m., but the remaining five (including the applicants) stayed, lying on the floor; officers attempted to remove them forcibly between 4.06 and 4.09 p.m. They were arrested, held for some hours and released.

The applicants were prosecuted under section 19 of the Police Act (obligation to obey police orders to maintain public order), read with sections 15(2) and 44 (fines for breaches). They refused administrative fines and were tried separately in the Reykjavik District Court, pleading not guilty and invoking their rights to expression and peaceful assembly (seeking a meeting with the Minister of Justice, sitting in protest, chanting and making noise, with some using drumsticks). Police witnesses described four consecutive days of similar sit-ins (removed without further action on prior days); on 5 April the group was noisy. Officers said ample time was given after repeated orders.

The first applicant (Icelandic) said he heard orders more than once but had little time to leave voluntarily. He was convicted on 13 October 2020, fined 10,000 ISK (approx. EUR 74) plus costs of approx. EUR 4,250. Leave to appeal was refused on 30 November 2020 as the outcome lacked general importance or important personal interests and was unlikely to change significantly. The second applicant (Polish) claimed he did not understand Icelandic orders (police did not speak English) despite participating in an earlier similar protest. He was convicted on 18 November 2020, receiving the same fine plus costs of approx. EUR 2,650; leave to appeal was refused on 2 February 2021 on similar grounds. The third applicant (Icelandic) described the orders as irrational and arbitrary. She was convicted on 12 May 2021 (sentence suspended for one year, taking account of delay) plus costs of approx. EUR 315; the District Court held that evidence (including video of repeated orders after closing) showed disobedience of lawful instructions and that Convention/Constitution provisions did not alter this. Leave to appeal was refused on 24 June 2021.

A later Court of Appeal judgment (11 November 2022) in a related case involving another protester from the same incident upheld a similar conviction as compliant with Articles 10 and 11 (and equivalent constitutional provisions), noting the sit-in continued after hours, time was given to leave, other protest avenues existed, and the penalty was a modest fine.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the convictions as an interference with freedom of peaceful assembly (read in the light of freedom of expression). It found the domestic authorities’ view that the applicants had no right to remain inside the building after closing hours was not unreasonable, the police action was moderate, and the lenient fines rendered the interference proportionate.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined applications by three protesters—Kári Orrason (Icelandic), Borys Andrzej Ejryszew (Polish) and Hildur Harðardóttir (Icelandic)—against Iceland. The applicants alleged that their criminal convictions for remaining in the Ministry of Justice lobby after closing time violated Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention (freedom of expression and peaceful assembly).

Peaceful demonstrations concerning asylum seekers and refugees occurred in Reykjavik in March 2019 outside Parliament and, from 2–5 April 2019, outside the Ministry of Justice, with small groups periodically entering its lobby. On 5 April 2019, shortly before 4 p.m. (the Ministry’s closing time), nine people including the applicants entered the first-floor lobby, sat on the floor, chanted, used drumsticks and sought a meeting with the Minister of Justice. Staff called police at 3:51 p.m. Officers arrived at 4:02 p.m. and repeatedly ordered the group to leave. Four persons complied immediately; the remaining five, including the applicants, refused. Video footage showed the group already inside at 3:38 p.m. Police attempted forcible removal between 4:06 and 4:09 p.m. after giving additional time to leave voluntarily. The applicants were arrested, held for some hours and released.

They were charged with breaching section 19 (read with sections 15(2) and 44) of the Police Act for failing to obey orders issued to maintain public order. Because they refused administrative fines they were prosecuted separately in the Reykjavik District Court.

Orrason testified that the group sat protesting and that he heard the leave order more than once but was given little time to comply. Police witnesses described four consecutive days of similar lobby occupations; on 5 April they found nine noisy persons sitting on the floor. After four left, the remainder were removed. On 13 October 2020 Orrason was convicted and fined 10,000 ISK (approximately €74) plus substantial costs. Leave to appeal was refused on 30 November 2020 because the case lacked general importance, did not affect important interests and was unlikely to be altered significantly.

Ejryszew, who had joined an earlier sit-in, claimed the officers shouted only in Icelandic, which he did not understand. The same evidence was presented. On 18 November 2020 he received an identical fine plus costs. Leave to appeal was refused on 2 February 2021 on similar grounds.

Harðardóttir stated she regarded the orders as irrational and arbitrary. On 12 May 2021 she was convicted; the sentence was suspended for one year (taking account of delay) and she was ordered to pay costs. The District Court expressly held that the Convention and the Icelandic Constitution did not alter the finding of disobedience after closing hours. Leave to appeal was refused on 24 June 2021.

A later Court of Appeal judgment concerning another participant in the same incident (who had been granted leave) confirmed that the protesters had no right to remain after 4 p.m., that the police had acted moderately to allow the building to close, that alternative lawful protest venues existed, and that the modest fines were compatible with Articles 10 and 11.

The Strasbourg Court, examining the complaints under Article 11 read in the light of Article 10, accepted that the domestic authorities’ conclusion that the applicants were not entitled to occupy the Ministry after public hours was not unreasonable. The fines were lenient and the interference was therefore proportionate. No violation was found.

The case of Kári Orrason and Others v. Iceland (applications nos. 29791/21, 40600/21 and 2281/22) concerns three applicants convicted of disobeying a police order to leave the lobby of Iceland’s Ministry of Justice after closing time during a demonstration. The applicants alleged that this interfered with their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly under Articles 10 and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Peaceful protests over Iceland’s treatment of asylum seekers and refugees took place in Reykjavik in March 2019, initially outside Parliament. From 2 to 5 April 2019 similar demonstrations occurred outside the Ministry of Justice, with small groups occasionally entering its lobby. On Friday 5 April 2019, shortly before 4 p.m., nine people including the three applicants entered the lobby on the building’s first floor (which also housed a reception area and two meeting rooms). The Ministry’s opening hours were 8.30 a.m. to 4 p.m. The group sat on the floor, chanted, made noise (some using drumsticks) and sought a meeting with the Minister of Justice.

Police were summoned by Ministry staff at 3.51 p.m. and arrived at 4.02 p.m. Officers repeatedly ordered the group to leave. Four people complied at 4.03 p.m.; the remaining five, including the applicants, refused and lay on the floor. Between 4.06 and 4.09 p.m. police removed them by force. The applicants were arrested, held for several hours and then released. They were charged with breaching section 19 of the Police Act (obligation to obey police orders to maintain public order) read with sections 15(2) and 44.

Each was tried separately before the Reykjavik District Court. The first applicant (an Icelandic national) stated that the group had sat in the lobby to protest and obtain a meeting; he heard the order to leave more than once but was given little time to comply. The second applicant (a Polish national) said he had joined a similar sit-in days earlier; the police spoke only Icelandic, which he did not understand. The third applicant (an Icelandic national) described the police instructions as irrational and arbitrary. Police evidence and CCTV footage showed the group already in the lobby at 3.38 p.m., the arrival of officers after closing time, repeated orders, partial compliance, and forcible removal of those who remained. The District Court convicted all three: the first and second applicants were each fined 10,000 Icelandic krónur (approximately €74) plus substantial legal costs; the third applicant received a suspended sentence (taking account of delay) plus costs. The court held that the Ministry was closed, the applicants had disobeyed lawful orders, and the Convention and Icelandic Constitution did not alter that finding.

Applications for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal were refused in each case. The court considered it unlikely that the convictions would be significantly altered, that the outcome did not affect important personal interests, and that the cases lacked substantial general importance. A later Court of Appeal judgment concerning another participant in the same incident reached the same conclusion on the merits, holding that the protesters had no right to remain inside after closing hours, that the police had acted moderately to restore public order, that alternative means of protest existed outside the building, and that the modest fines were proportionate.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that their convictions violated Articles 10 and 11. The Court examined the complaints under Article 11 read in the light of Article 10. It found that the domestic authorities’ assessment—that the applicants were not entitled to continue their protest inside a government building after public closing hours—was not unreasonable, that the police had given the group time to leave, and that the very lenient penalties were proportionate to the legitimate aim of maintaining public order. No violation was found.

**CASE OF SILES CABRERA v. SPAIN (ECtHR, App. no. 5212/23, 17 July 2025)**

The applicant, a Bolivian national born in 1968, has resided in Spain with his wife since 2005. Their son, born in 2012 and also of Bolivian nationality, was diagnosed at age two and a half with autism spectrum disorder and a pervasive developmental disorder. He later developed agranulocytosis/neutropenia requiring hospitalisations. Medical evidence from 2017 confirmed he is non-verbal, requires constant specialised care and monitoring unavailable in Bolivia, and was slowly progressing with local support programmes, schooling, and family input. The family has long depended on social services due to irregular status, limited employment (primarily domestic work), and the son’s needs.

In March 2018 the applicant applied for an initial temporary residence permit on “social roots” (arraigo social/social integration) grounds under Institutional Law 4/2000 and Royal Decree 557/2011. A February 2018 social integration report from Basque authorities was favourable: it noted his housing, family ties, language courses, and the son’s condition, recommending exemption from the usual one-year employment contract requirement. It recorded that he received basic guaranteed income (RGI) plus housing benefit, amounts sufficient for subsistence. The Government Sub-Delegation refused the permit in July 2018, finding he lacked “own means of subsistence” independent of welfare (which did not qualify). He was required to leave Spain within 15 days (extendable to 90 in exceptional cases with proof of means); failure would trigger irregular-stay sanctions.

The applicant appealed, arguing the authorities ignored the non-binding but relevant social report, his son’s constant-care needs (preventing work), family vulnerability, and the risk of helplessness if he (the child’s legal representative) were removed. A 2019 social-services report corroborated long-term dependence on benefits, irregular work/permits, and the son’s additional rare hereditary disease. First-instance and appellate courts (Bilbao Administrative Court 2019; Basque High Court of Justice 2020) dismissed the claims. They held that welfare benefits do not constitute the required “sufficient means of subsistence” without burdening public finances (per established Basque case-law distinguishing genuine/temporary integration from habitual reliance). Exemption from a contract still required proof of own resources. The inability-to-work claim was rejected: the unemployed mother also resided in Spain, and the applicant had no employment record since registering as a job-seeker in 2015 (despite the son’s 2012 birth). Cassation and amparo appeals failed (Supreme Court 2021; Constitutional Court 2022).

Separately, in 2019 (and renewed) the son received a humanitarian/health-grounds residence permit (serious illness; care unavailable in Bolivia). The wife later obtained a 2023 training-purposes permit (no work right). A 2023 social report confirmed the now-11-year-old son’s high dependency/disability (83%/89%), ongoing specialised schooling and treatment, family vulnerability due to the father’s irregular status (blocking some benefits/housing), continued RGI and local aid, and the family’s presence in Erandio. The son had a pending citizenship-by-residence application.

The applicant complained under Article 8 of interference with family life via the refusal, alleging failure to consider the disabled child’s best interests, his care role, and integration. The Court found the decisions had a clear legal basis (foreseeable application of the “own means” criterion, excluding habitual welfare); domestic courts had examined the personal/family/son’s situation; other regularisation routes existed (e.g., humanitarian grounds used by the son); and a fair balance was struck within Spain’s wide margin of appreciation on immigration/resources. No violation.

The case of Siles Cabrera v. Spain (Application no. 5212/23) concerns a Bolivian national, Julio Cesar Siles Cabrera (born 1968), who has lived in Spain since 2005 with his wife. Their son, born in 2012 and also a Bolivian national, was diagnosed at age two-and-a-half with autism spectrum disorder involving a pervasive developmental disorder. In 2017 he was further diagnosed with agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia), requiring repeated hospitalisations. A 2017 medical report stated that the child was non-verbal, intolerant of frustration and separation from his parents, and needed uninterrupted specialised care unavailable in Bolivia. He participated in early-intervention programmes, attended school with support from an autism association, and later (by 2023) had an 83% dependency rating and 89% disability, requiring constant parental supervision that was difficult to combine with flexible employment.

The applicant first registered as a job-seeker in 2015. In March 2018 he applied for an initial temporary residence permit on grounds of “social roots” (arraigo social) under Spain’s Institutional Law 4/2000 and Royal Decree 557/2011. He submitted a favourable social-integration report from Basque authorities, which noted his housing, family ties, Basque-language courses, the son’s medical needs, and receipt of the regional guaranteed minimum income (RGI) plus a housing supplement. The report recommended waiving the usual one-year employment-contract requirement because of the child’s disability.

In July 2018 the Government Sub-Delegation in Biscay refused the permit. It held that the applicant had not proved “own means of subsistence” independent of welfare benefits, which could not be counted. He was ordered to leave Spain within 15 days (extendable to 90 days in exceptional circumstances). The applicant appealed, arguing that the authorities had ignored the social-integration report, his inability to work while providing constant care, and the family’s vulnerability (documented in a 2019 Erandio social-services report). The first-instance administrative court dismissed the appeal in March 2019, finding that welfare payments did not constitute “own resources” under established Basque case-law and that the child’s mother (also unemployed) was present; the applicant had shown no employment activity since 2015.

The Basque High Court of Justice upheld the refusal in May 2020. It emphasised that even when an employment contract is waived, an applicant must still demonstrate personal financial means that do not burden the public treasury. Welfare benefits satisfy the requirement only if they are temporary and follow genuine prior social integration through work. The applicant’s reliance on benefits since 2014 was habitual, not circumstantial. Subsequent cassation and amparo appeals were rejected by the Supreme Court (2021) and Constitutional Court (2022) for lack of objective interest and constitutional relevance.

Meanwhile the son received a humanitarian residence permit on health grounds (first granted 2019, renewed), and the wife obtained a training-purpose permit in 2023. A December 2023 social report confirmed the family remained in Erandio in a vulnerable situation, still receiving RGI and local assistance, with the applicant still irregular. The applicant alleged that the refusal of his permit, given his disabled son’s dependency and the lack of alternative regularisation routes, violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for family life) by failing to take his personal circumstances adequately into account.

The ECHR case Siles Cabrera v. Spain (no. 5212/23) concerns a Bolivian national’s unsuccessful 2018 application for a Spanish temporary residence permit on exceptional “social roots” (arraigo social) grounds. The applicant, Julio Cesar Siles Cabrera (born 1968), has lived in Spain since 2005 with his wife. Their son, born in 2012, was diagnosed at age 2.5 with autism spectrum disorder (pervasive developmental disorder) and later agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia requiring hospitalisations). A 2017 medical report confirmed the child needed uninterrupted specialised care unavailable in Bolivia; he was non-verbal, had limited social tolerance, and participated in early intervention, schooling, and autism-family support. By 2023 he had 83% dependency/89% disability, requiring constant supervision, therapy, medication, and specialised inclusive schooling.

The applicant registered as a job-seeker in 2015. On 27 March 2018 he applied for an initial residence permit under Institutional Law 4/2000 (LOEX) s. 31(3) and Royal Decree 557/2011 Art. 124(2). He submitted a favourable Basque social-integration report (Feb. 2018) documenting three years’ continuous residence, family ties, Basque-language courses, housing, and his son’s needs. The report recommended waiving the one-year employment-contract requirement because of the child’s disability and noted receipt since 2014 of basic guaranteed income (RGI) plus housing benefit, deemed sufficient for subsistence.

On 17 July 2018 the Biscay Government Sub-Delegation refused the permit. It held that welfare benefits did not constitute “own means of subsistence” (medios de vida propios) under LOEX s. 31 and Decree Arts. 47 and 124; the applicant therefore failed the financial-self-sufficiency test required even when a contract waiver was recommended. He was ordered to leave within 15 days (extendable to 90 days if exceptional circumstances and means were shown). Irregular stay thereafter would constitute a serious offence potentially leading to expulsion.

The applicant appealed, arguing that his son’s condition demanded his constant care, rendering employment impossible, and that expulsion of a parent would leave the child helpless. A March 2019 municipal social-services report described long-term family vulnerability, irregular-status barriers to care programmes, and the child’s additional cyclic neutropenia. The first-instance court (March 2019) dismissed the claim: welfare did not prove personal resources (consistent with Basque High Court case-law treating habitual benefits as falling outside the “sufficient-means” concept); the mother also resided in Spain and was unemployed; and the applicant had shown no work activity since 2015. The Basque High Court of Justice (May 2020) upheld the ruling, stressing that social-roots permits still require proof of independent means so as not to burden public finances; benefits satisfy the test only if truly circumstantial after genuine labour-market integration. Cassation and amparo appeals were rejected for lack of interest/relevance.

Meanwhile the son obtained (and renewed) a humanitarian residence permit on health grounds (Art. 126); a nationality application by residence remained pending. The wife received a 2023 training permit (Art. 124(4)). A December 2023 social report confirmed the family still lived in Erandio, receiving RGI and local aid, but the applicant’s lack of status continued to restrict housing, benefits and support, compounding their vulnerability.

The alleged Article 8 violation (positive obligations concerning family life) thus turns on whether the authorities, by rigidly applying the “own-means” criterion without sufficient regard to the child’s exceptional medical needs and the family’s de-facto integration, failed to strike a fair balance between immigration control and the unity/care of a disabled child.

The case of Á.F.L. v. Iceland (no. 35789/22) involved an Icelandic applicant (born 1990) diagnosed in childhood with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and cognitive difficulties (though not testing at intellectual disability level). He alleged that the 2021–2022 decisions depriving him of custody of his daughter V.F. (born February 2019) violated Articles 8 and 14 ECHR, as they were discriminatory on disability grounds and stemmed from a failure to provide reasonable accommodation via necessary child-rearing support.

After V.F.’s birth the family home was unstable, with parental conflict, the applicant’s self-reported violence and the mother’s mental-health issues prompting CPS involvement and police intervention. The parents separated; the mother initially provided most care with YLFA support, but after further incidents the applicant assumed primary care in September 2019 with his mother’s assistance. Both parents consented to V.F.’s placement at Mánaberg, a comprehensive CPS residential diagnosis-and-guidance facility (typically lasting under two months). The applicant joined her there in October 2019 after the mother left. Staff, aware of his impairments from the outset, provided continuous, tailored guidance on all aspects of parenting and independent living, set goals, monitored progress weekly and gradually reduced supervision. Psychological and staff assessments (December 2019–January 2020) noted his affection, insight into his own needs, cooperation and some progress (hygiene, routines, initiative), but found persistent difficulties recognising the child’s needs, transferring skills and coping with change. He required extensive ongoing assistance and was not ready for independent care. The stay was exceptionally prolonged.

In late January 2020 they moved to the paternal grandmother’s home under a support plan (to April 2020, later extended): frequent Mánaberg follow-up visits, twice-weekly (later increased) visits from a specialised YLFA counsellor (a psychologist/developmental therapist experienced with autism), a support family (initially 4, then 7 days/month), counselling and municipal-service applications. YLFA reports (March–June 2020) confirmed attachment to V.F. and basic-care competence but highlighted lack of insight into physical, social and emotional needs, insufficient stimulation, household-task difficulties and emerging child symptoms (poor emotional control, self-stimulation, disinhibited attachment, motor-skill delays) suggestive of neglect or attachment disorder linked to the applicant’s autism. Increased support was provided despite COVID disruptions and the grandmother’s brief absence.

In July 2020 the CPC ordered two-month temporary foster placement, finding tailored supports exhausted without adequate results and the child’s best interests requiring removal pending reassessment. Further expert reports (August 2020 and court-appointed April 2021, the latter considering CRPD rights and Act no. 38/2018 disability services) confirmed limited parenting capacity: slow skill acquisition, inability to meet basic needs or form secure attachment despite goodwill and 24-hour-then-targeted support. V.F. thrived and progressed markedly in foster care (contrasting her agitation with the applicant). Additional measures were deemed insufficient to enable independent care without unjustifiably risking her development; she needed prompt stability.

The District Court (with psychologist lay judge) deprived the applicant of custody in September 2021 (upheld by the Court of Appeal in February 2022; Supreme Court leave refused March 2022), applying child-protection legislation (best interests paramount, least-restrictive measures first) and CRPD principles that disability alone cannot justify deprivation. Extensive individualised supports had been implemented and exhausted; the decision rested on demonstrated unfitness despite them, not disability per se. Contact rights were preserved (later adjusted but maintained). The ECHR found no violation: supports were multiple, flexible and tailored to correct disability-related inequality; parental capacity was assessed with reference to them; domestic analysis was comprehensive and conclusions reasonable.

**CASE OF Á.F.L. v. ICELAND (Application no. 35789/22)**

The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1990 and diagnosed in childhood with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and mild intellectual disability (though later cognitive tests did not place him at intellectual-disability level), had a history of substance abuse but had been sober since 2012. In February 2019 he and his then-girlfriend had a daughter, V.F. The family situation was unstable, involving parental conflict, the mother’s mental-health issues and a police intervention. After the parents separated, the child lived with her maternal grandmother with CPS-arranged support. In September 2019 the CPS placed V.F. at Mánaberg, a residential diagnostic and guidance facility (the most intensive child-protection measure available), with both parents’ consent. The mother left after a short time; the applicant then assumed primary care of the infant at the facility under continuous staff supervision, daily guidance, skill-building and weekly reviews. Staff were aware of his impairments from the outset.

A December 2019 psychologist’s assessment found that, despite goodwill, insight into his own needs and some progress, the applicant required extensive ongoing assistance and could not care independently. Mánaberg reports confirmed difficulties recognising the child’s needs, transferring skills across situations, and performing household tasks, though affection and basic routines improved. The stay was extended well beyond the usual duration. After discharge in late January 2020 the applicant and child moved to his mother’s home. Support included frequent Mánaberg follow-up visits, a specialised YLFA counsellor (a psychologist and developmental therapist experienced with autism) visiting several times weekly, a support family (later increased to seven days per month), continued counselling and cooperation with daycare. YLFA reports from March–June 2020 documented persistent lack of insight into the child’s physical, social and emotional needs, insufficient stimulation, delayed responses, and emerging signs of attachment difficulties or possible autism/ADHD in V.F. (later unconfirmed). The grandmother’s temporary absence and COVID-19 disruptions were noted, after which support intensity was increased.

In July 2020 the Child Protection Committee ordered two-month temporary foster care pending reassessment, citing exhausted tailored measures and the child’s best interests. A further psychologist’s report (August 2020) observed that V.F. appeared a “different child”—agitated with the applicant but calm and communicative in foster care—and concluded that the applicant’s impairments limited insight, skill acquisition and ability to meet basic needs despite extensive help. The child progressed markedly in foster care. The Committee then initiated custody-deprivation proceedings.

A court-appointed expert (2021), consulting a disability-studies specialist and considering the CRPD and Act no. 38/2018 on long-term disability services, confirmed earlier findings: the applicant lacked basic parenting skills, progressed slowly even with 24-hour support, and further daily-guidance measures would not justify returning the child given signs of prior neglect and her subsequent thriving. The District Court (September 2021, with a psychologist lay judge) and Court of Appeal (February 2022) deprived the applicant of custody under the Child Protection Act, holding that the child’s paramount interests required it after exhaustive, individualised supports (including an unusually long Mánaberg placement) had failed to enable adequate care or bonding. Disability was not treated as an automatic bar; additional measures were deemed indefensible. Contact continued, later reduced. Leave to the Supreme Court was refused.

The applicant alleged that the authorities’ failure to provide sufficient reasonable accommodation for his disability (support under the disability-services Act) rendered the custody deprivation discriminatory, violating Articles 8 and 14. The Court examined whether the measures addressed factual inequality created by disability and whether decisions were based solely on disability or on the child’s best interests after supports were exhausted. The case of Á.F.L. v. Iceland (Application no. 35789/22) concerns an Icelandic national born in 1990 who was diagnosed in childhood with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and a mild intellectual disability. Cognitive testing in later parenting assessments did not place him at the level of intellectual disability, though he exhibited related challenges. He had a history of substance abuse but had been sober since 2012. In February 2019 he and his then-girlfriend had a daughter, V.F. Their relationship soon deteriorated amid reports of conflict, the mother’s mental-health difficulties and the applicant’s self-reported violence. Child Protection Services (CPS) became involved.

After the mother assumed primary care and later moved with the child to her own mother’s home, an incident in September 2019 led CPS to place V.F. in the applicant’s care with support from his mother. Both parents consented to a comprehensive plan that included placing the child at Mánaberg, a CPS residential facility offering intensive diagnosis and guidance (normally lasting under two months). The applicant and V.F. resided there from October 2019 until late January 2020—an unusually prolonged stay. Staff, aware of his impairments from the outset, provided continuous, tailored instruction on all aspects of childcare, gradually reducing supervision. Weekly reviews tracked progress. Psychologist reports and staff assessments acknowledged the applicant’s affection, insight into his limitations and some skill acquisition, but concluded he required extensive ongoing assistance, struggled to recognise the child’s needs, generalise skills or manage household tasks, and was not ready for independent care.

Upon discharge the family moved to the paternal grandmother’s home. CPS arranged follow-up visits (initially four times weekly), twice-weekly (later increased) counselling from a YLFA specialist experienced with autism, a support family (rising to seven days per month), continued Centre for Parents and Children sessions, and psychological support. A case-management plan ran until mid-2020, with extensions after COVID-19 disruptions. YLFA reports consistently found that, despite attachment and basic-care competence, the applicant lacked insight into V.F.’s physical, emotional and developmental needs, offered insufficient stimulation, and that the child displayed motor delays and possible attachment-disorder signs that worsened over time. The grandmother’s temporary absence exacerbated concerns. CPS increased intensity of support but, after further meetings, recommended temporary foster care pending reassessment.

In July 2020 the Child Protection Committee (CPC) ordered V.F.’s two-month removal, citing exhausted tailored measures and the child’s best interests. She was placed with a foster family; contact was set at three hours every two weeks. A new psychologist assessment and YLFA report confirmed the applicant’s goodwill and cooperation but reiterated that his impairments prevented him from meeting even basic needs or forming a secure attachment; the child thrived in foster care. The CPC then initiated custody-deprivation proceedings, concluding that available measures had been exhausted and that the child required prompt stability.

A court-appointed expert, after reviewing the file, testing, interviews and CRPD-related advice, validated prior findings. He noted slow skill acquisition even under 24-hour support and that returning the child to try further measures would be contrary to her interests given observed neglect signs. The District Court (including a psychologist lay judge), after hearing nearly 20 witnesses, deprived the applicant of custody in September 2021 under the Child Protection Act, emphasising the child’s paramount interests, the extensive disability-tailored supports already provided, and the absence of realistic additional measures that would not delay stability. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in February 2022, stressing that disability alone was not the basis and that statutory conditions had been met after considering limitations and practical experience of supports. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

Contact continued (later reduced and supervised). The applicant alleged before the European Court that the authorities had failed to provide reasonable accommodation in the form of necessary child-rearing support required by his disability, resulting in a discriminatory deprivation of custody contrary to Articles 8 and 14.
001-243657:
The case of Radobuljac v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 38785/18) involves Croatian lawyer Silvano Radobuljac, who alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. He claimed that domestic authorities unlawfully refused to offset his tax debt against his enforceable claims against the State (unrelated to taxation) and that enforcing tax collection—while the State delayed paying its own debts to him—imposed an excessive individual burden.

In February 2014, the Tax Administration audited the applicant and found he owed HRK 24,260.17 (EUR 3,235) in unpaid VAT, advance income tax and social insurance contributions due to late payments (e.g., contributions for December 2013 due by 15 January 2014). The 3 March 2014 audit report noted these as minor offences and warned of possible professional suspension if unpaid within 10 days.

During the audit and in his objection, the applicant requested a set-off against his claims against the State, established by court decisions from September–November 2013 for fees as officially appointed counsel in criminal proceedings (initially HRK 13,715.25 or EUR 1,828). The Tax Administration did not address this. He later added further claims of HRK 4,625 (EUR 616).

On 10 November 2014, he was fined HRK 6,900 (EUR 920) for the delays. On 1 April 2014, an enforcement order seized funds from his bank accounts. His 15 April 2014 appeal (pending over two years, versus a 60-day statutory limit) repeated the set-off request and argued the debt was extinguished. Meanwhile, the full debt plus interest was collected via seizures between July 2014 and January 2015. The State paid some of its debts to him only later (December 2014–December 2015).

The Ministry of Finance dismissed the appeal on 13 July 2016, stating the first-instance tax authority had jurisdiction over set-off. The Rijeka Administrative Court (21 February 2017) held that section 115(2) of the General Tax Act limited set-off to claims arising in a tax relationship, which these did not. The High Administrative Court (14 June 2017) agreed, reading section 115(3) similarly. The Constitutional Court declared his complaint (invoking Article 1 Protocol 1, alleged unlawfulness given implementing rules, and unfairness, plus ECtHR cases such as Čikanović v. Croatia) inadmissible as unfounded on 17 January 2018.

The General Tax Act defines tax relationships and allows set-off of mutual tax debts (sections 12, 18–19, 24, 115(1)–(2)). Section 115(3) (added 2012) provides for suspending due claims against the State budget to offset recorded tax debts. A 2013 Ordinance implementing it lists eligible claims (including those from enforceable court decisions payable from the State budget) and sets a procedure: State budget beneficiaries notify the Financial Agency of due claims; the Agency checks tax debts with the Tax Administration and withholds the necessary amount for offset, notifying the debtor. Similar rules persist. High Administrative Court rulings (e.g., 2017–2018) consistently interpret set-off as limited to tax-relationship claims, excluding other State debts such as the applicant’s counsel fees.

The applicant argued this interpretation ignored the Ordinance and that the State, as simultaneous debtor, should have allowed set-off rather than force enforcement while delaying its payments.

The case of Radobuljac v. Croatia (No. 2) (application no. 38785/18) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applicant, a practising Croatian lawyer, complained that the authorities' refusal to offset his tax debt against his enforceable claims against the State was unlawful and that enforcement of the tax debt (while the State delayed paying its own debts to him) imposed an excessive individual burden.

In February 2014 a tax audit established that the applicant had failed to pay value-added tax, advance income tax and compulsory social-insurance contributions on time, leaving a total debt of HRK 24,260.17 (approximately EUR 3,235). The audit report warned that non-payment within statutory deadlines constituted a minor offence and that continued non-payment could lead to suspension from professional practice.

During the audit the applicant requested that the debt be extinguished by set-off against his enforceable claims against the State. Those claims, arising from court decisions of September–November 2013 awarding him fees for services as officially appointed defence counsel in criminal proceedings, totalled HRK 13,715.25 (EUR 1,828). He reiterated the request in an objection to the audit report, but the Tax Administration did not address it. He later obtained further enforceable awards amounting to HRK 4,625 (EUR 616).

On 10 November 2014 the Tax Administration fined him HRK 6,900 (EUR 920) for the late payments. Meanwhile, on 1 April 2014 it issued an enforcement order authorising seizure of funds from his bank accounts. The applicant appealed, repeating the set-off request and arguing that, together with certain payments he had already made, the claims extinguished the entire tax debt. Although domestic law required a decision within 60 days, the appeal remained pending for more than two years. During that period (July 2014–January 2015) the authorities collected the full tax debt plus statutory default interest by seizing the applicant’s funds.

The State subsequently settled some of the applicant’s claims: payments were made in December 2014 (on the basis of 2013 and 2014 decisions), November 2015 and December 2015.

In July 2016 the Ministry of Finance dismissed the appeal on the ground that only the first-instance tax authority had competence to decide a set-off request. The Rijeka Administrative Court (February 2017) and the High Administrative Court (June 2017) upheld the refusal, holding that section 115 of the General Tax Act permitted set-off solely of claims arising within a “tax relationship” and that the applicant’s fee awards did not qualify. The Constitutional Court declared the subsequent constitutional complaint inadmissible as unfounded (January 2018).

Relevant domestic law included section 115 of the 2008 General Tax Act (as amended in 2012), which provided for set-off of a tax debtor’s due claims against the State budget. Implementing ordinances of 2013 expressly listed enforceable court decisions among the claims that could be offset and established a procedure involving the Financial Agency and the Tax Administration. Nevertheless, the administrative courts consistently interpreted the provision as limited to purely tax-related claims.

The applicant argued that the refusal was contrary to the statutory scheme and to the Court’s case-law on the State’s duty to honour its obligations, and that the combination of coercive tax collection, a fine and the threat of professional suspension, while the State delayed payment of its own debts, placed a disproportionate burden on him as a lawyer.

The case of Radobuljac v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 38785/18) involves a Croatian lawyer’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that domestic authorities unlawfully refused to offset his tax debt against his enforceable (non-tax) claims against the State, and that enforcing the tax debt (plus instituting minor-offence proceedings) while the State delayed paying its own debts imposed an excessive individual burden.

In February 2014 a tax audit established that the applicant had failed to pay VAT, advance income tax and social-insurance contributions on time, leaving a debt of HRK 24,260.17 (EUR 3,235). The audit report of 3 March 2014 recorded that the late payments constituted minor offences and warned that non-payment within ten days could lead to suspension from practice. During the audit and in his objection to the report the applicant asked the Tax Administration to set the debt off against court decisions of September–November 2013 awarding him HRK 13,715.25 (EUR 1,828) for work as officially appointed counsel in criminal proceedings. The request was ignored.

On 10 November 2014 the Tax Administration fined him HRK 6,900 (EUR 920) for the late payments. Meanwhile, on 1 April 2014 it issued an enforcement order authorising seizure of funds from his bank accounts. In his appeal of 15 April 2014 he repeated the set-off request, added further awards totalling HRK 4,625 (EUR 616) and asserted that, together with payments he had already made, the tax debt had been extinguished. Although domestic law required a decision within sixty days, the appeal remained pending for two years and three months. During that period (July 2014–January 2015) the entire tax debt plus statutory default interest was collected by bank-account seizures.

Between December 2014 and December 2015 the State eventually paid some of the sums it owed the applicant under the 2013 and 2014 court decisions.

On 13 July 2016 the Ministry of Finance dismissed the appeal, holding that only the first-instance tax authority had jurisdiction over set-off. The applicant brought an administrative action arguing that section 115 of the General Tax Act entitled a taxpayer to set off any due claim against the State budget and citing Strasbourg case-law that the State must meet its obligations without forcing claimants to pursue enforcement. The Rijeka Administrative Court (21 February 2017) and the High Administrative Court (14 June 2017) rejected the claim, ruling that set-off under section 115 was confined to mutual obligations arising inside a tax relationship; the applicant’s legal-fee awards did not qualify. The Constitutional Court declared his subsequent complaint inadmissible as unfounded (17 January 2018).

The relevant statutory framework comprised sections 12, 18, 19, 24 and 115 of the 2008 General Tax Act (as amended in 2012). Section 115(3) provided that a tax debtor’s due claim against the State budget would be suspended up to the amount of the recorded tax debt for the purpose of set-off. Implementing Ordinance of February 2013 expressly listed, among eligible claims, those established by enforceable court decisions payable from the State budget. Subsequent High Administrative Court judgments nevertheless consistently interpreted the provision as limited to tax-related claims.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violation: the authorities’ refusal to apply the set-off mechanism to the applicant’s court-awarded fees, the forced collection of the tax debt (and imposition of a fine) while the State remained in arrears, and the resulting burden on a practising lawyer.

The case of Miari v. Denmark (Application no. 2852/24) concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding an expulsion order imposed on a long-term settled migrant. The applicant, Khaled Miari, a stateless Palestinian born in Lebanon in 1972, entered Denmark in 1986 at nearly 13 years of age and obtained permanent residence in 1991. He has resided lawfully in Denmark for over 34 years, completing elementary education through the 10th grade, obtaining a professional bachelor’s degree in special education, and undertaking courses in management and addiction therapy. He previously operated a kiosk, worked at a municipal addiction centre, and managed a socio-educational residential home for vulnerable children. He is divorced with no children; his parents, siblings and approximately 77 other family members live in Denmark. He has no family in Lebanon, speaks only broken Arabic, and maintains virtually no ties there. After financial difficulties, bankruptcy, divorce and depression, he developed a drug addiction and received social welfare. He and his former wife later reconciled, though she would not accompany him if deported.

The applicant has a prior conviction from 1997 for robbery, resulting in a sentence of two years and six months’ imprisonment. In November 2022 the District Court convicted him under Article 191 of the Penal Code of serious drug offences involving 351.88 grams of cocaine, 102.99 grams of heroin and 146 grams of cannabis intended for resale (or sold) between November 2021 and April 2022. He received a three-year prison sentence and an expulsion order accompanied by a six-year re-entry ban. Before the District Court he described his history of running a children’s residential home, subsequent personal decline into addiction, and strong social and family connections in Denmark. The District Court found the statutory conditions for expulsion met under the Aliens Act but concluded that a six-year ban would not “for certain” violate Denmark’s international obligations, given the seriousness of the drug-trafficking offences.

On appeal the High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the conviction and expulsion in May 2023. It accepted that the applicant’s personal and cultural ties to Denmark far exceeded those to Lebanon and that he would not be entirely unequipped to live there. Balancing these factors against the gravity of the latest offences (committed in particularly aggravating circumstances) and the earlier robbery conviction, and noting the absence of family life within the meaning of Article 8, the High Court held that the public interest in expulsion outweighed the applicant’s private-life interests. It expressly reduced the otherwise mandatory permanent re-entry ban to six years because a lifetime ban would breach Article 8. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in September 2023. The applicant was released in April 2024, placed in a deportation centre and later admitted to a psychiatric hospital; the expulsion had not been enforced by the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.

The relevant Danish Aliens Act provisions (as amended) required expulsion and a permanent re-entry ban for sentences exceeding 18 months unless such a measure would “for certain” contravene international obligations, in which case the courts could impose a shorter ban. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found no violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons, properly assessed proportionality in light of Strasbourg case-law, and that the time-limited nature of the ban rendered the interference compatible with the Convention.

The case of Miari v. Denmark (Application no. 2852/24) concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding an expulsion order imposed on a long-term resident following a criminal conviction. The applicant, Khaled Miari, a stateless Palestinian born in Lebanon in 1972, entered Denmark in 1986 at nearly 13 years of age and obtained permanent residence in 1991. By the time of the relevant proceedings, he had resided lawfully in Denmark for over 34 years. He is divorced with no children. His parents, siblings and an extended family of 77 members live in Denmark. He attended school there through the 10th grade, obtained a professional bachelor’s degree in special education, completed courses in management and addiction therapy, operated a kiosk, worked in an addiction centre and managed a socio-educational residential home for children. He speaks Danish fluently but only broken Arabic and has no family or meaningful social ties in Lebanon, having fled that country as a child.

The applicant has a prior conviction from 1997 for robbery, for which he received a sentence of two years and six months’ imprisonment. In November 2022 the District Court convicted him under Article 191 of the Penal Code of serious drug offences involving 351.88 grams of cocaine, 102.99 grams of heroin and 146 grams of cannabis intended for resale (or sold) between November 2021 and April 2022. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. The court also ordered his expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban, finding that the statutory conditions under the Aliens Act were met and that a six-year ban would not “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8.

On appeal the High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the conviction and sentence in May 2023. It accepted that the applicant’s personal and cultural ties to Denmark were far stronger than any remaining links to Lebanon, yet found he would not be wholly unequipped to live there. The High Court emphasised the seriousness of the drug-trafficking offences (aggravated by the earlier robbery conviction), the absence of family life within the meaning of the Convention, and the fact that Danish law prescribed a permanent re-entry ban for sentences exceeding one year and six months. Invoking section 32(5)(i) of the Aliens Act, the court reduced the ban to six years because a permanent ban would have been contrary to Article 8. It concluded that the public-interest considerations in favour of expulsion outweighed the applicant’s strong private-life ties to Denmark once the ban was time-limited.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in September 2023. The applicant was released from prison in April 2024 and placed in a deportation centre; the expulsion order has not yet been enforced. Under the Aliens Act an unenforced expulsion may later be reviewed if material circumstances change, and courts may further shorten a re-entry ban if necessary to comply with international obligations.

The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the interference with the applicant’s private life was proportionate. It noted that the domestic courts had carefully applied the Court’s case-law, identified the length of the re-entry ban as the decisive factor, and reduced it from the statutory permanent duration precisely to avoid a violation. The prospect of lawful re-entry after six years was not theoretical. The Court therefore found that the national authorities had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had duly assessed proportionality, rendering the expulsion compatible with Article 8.
