The case of Miari v. Denmark (Application no. 2852/24) concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Khaled Miari, a stateless Palestinian born in Lebanon in 1972. He alleged that a Danish expulsion order, issued alongside a criminal conviction, unlawfully interfered with his right to respect for private life as a long-term settled migrant.

Miari entered Denmark in 1986 at nearly age 13 and received permanent residence in 1991. He has lived there for over 34 years, completing elementary school (grades 9 and 10), obtaining a professional bachelor’s degree in special education, and completing courses in management and addiction therapy. He previously ran a kiosk, worked at an addiction centre, and managed a socio-educational residential home for children, earning praise from local authorities. He is divorced with no children, though he and his ex-wife (who remains in Denmark and would not accompany him if deported) had run a children’s home together and later reconciled. He has extensive family in Denmark (77 members, including parents and siblings) but virtually none in Lebanon, speaks only broken Arabic, and has no significant social or cultural ties there. He became a drug user after bankruptcy, divorce, and depression.

In 1997 he was convicted of robbery and sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment. On 25 November 2022 the District Court convicted him under Article 191 of the Penal Code of serious drug offences involving 351.88 g of cocaine, 102.99 g of heroin and 146 g of cannabis intended for resale between November 2021 and April 2022. He received a three-year prison sentence plus expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The court found the statutory conditions for expulsion met and held that, despite his long residence, language skills, prior employment and lack of ties to Lebanon, the gravity of the hard-drug offences meant a six-year ban would not “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations (including Article 8).

On appeal the High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 24 May 2023. It noted that expulsion was mandatory unless it would “for certain” violate international obligations. The court accepted that Miari’s personal and cultural ties to Denmark far outweighed those to Lebanon (though he was not entirely unequipped to live there). He had no family life within the meaning of Article 8. Weighing his strong Danish ties against the seriousness of the latest offence (committed while a drug addict receiving social welfare) and his prior robbery conviction, the court found the public-interest reasons for expulsion compelling. It emphasised that the duration of a re-entry ban is decisive under the Court’s case-law. Domestic law prescribed a permanent ban for a sentence exceeding 18 months, but the High Court reduced it to six years because a lifetime ban would breach Article 8. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 29 September 2023.

Miari was released on 16 April 2024 and placed in a deportation centre; he spent July–September 2024 in a psychiatric hospital. The expulsion has not yet been enforced. The European Court later held that the time-limited ban, together with the domestic courts’ detailed proportionality assessment drawing on Strasbourg case-law, rendered the measure compatible with Article 8.
001-244017:
**CASE OF SAKKOU v. CYPRUS (Application no. 4429/23)**

This ECHR Fifth Section judgment of 10 July 2025 (final 10 October 2025) concerned whether the applicant’s drug-offence conviction, based to a decisive extent on accomplice R.’s testimony, violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing). The Court found no unfairness.

The applicant (born 1979, imprisoned in Nicosia) and R. were prosecuted for drug offences. In February 2018 R. bought 2 kg of cannabis (worth €12,500) from the applicant on credit, later paying €6,000. R. left Cyprus owing debts (including the remaining €6,500) and returned in September 2018, isolating himself. In February 2019, T. (the applicant’s acquaintance) proposed a drug-trafficking partnership with R. Upon learning of it, the applicant demanded repayment. T. suggested payment in kind: R. would supply 0.5 kg of MDMA (reducing the debt to €2,000), with T. brokering the deal. On 11 April 2019 (while the applicant was in the Netherlands) T. gave R. the MDMA, which R. hid pending delivery instructions. On 12 April 2019 R. was arrested for an unrelated offence (importing ~1 kg of cocaine from Belgium).

In detention R. was threatened by a person posing as T.’s friend not to speak. He informed YKAN investigators G.M. and O.O. On 15 April he was transferred and informally indicated he might confess if given witness protection and safe detention. On 17 April an informal meeting occurred with the YKAN Commander; an information note recorded R.’s confession, willingness to testify against accomplices, and request for protection plus financial support to leave Cyprus post-trial. On 23 April the Attorney General admitted R. to the witness-protection programme under section 16(2) of the Witness Protection Law 2001. R. then gave a voluntary written statement confessing and detailing other exchanges involving the applicant and T., and showed police where the MDMA was hidden. Two cases were opened, one against the applicant.

R. pleaded guilty to the cocaine import and, on 5 December 2019, received five years’ imprisonment (from 13 April 2019). The court considered his cooperation (providing previously unknown information), confession, rehabilitation and remorse.

The applicant was charged inter alia with selling cannabis on credit and agreeing to receive MDMA for the debt. Trial occurred on 10 June 2020. Prosecution witnesses included R., G.M. and O.O.; the applicant testified in his defence. Unchallenged telecommunications data (numbers linked to R., T. and the applicant) were admitted. G.M. and O.O. described events from R.’s arrest to his statement and denied directing him to incriminate the applicant. R. described the applicant as a major trafficker using multiple SIMs, frequent calls, and a meeting in a side-room at the applicant’s house (which R. described in detail after challenge). He explained confessing from fear after the threat and a desire to leave trafficking, emphasising the importance of protection. In cross-examination he denied fabricating testimony for favourable treatment, noting he disclosed unknown offences (risking a worse position), did not implicate the applicant in everything, and was serving five years.

The applicant denied knowing R. (though T. had mentioned him) but admitted the side-room connected internally (contradicting his counsel’s earlier suggestion). On 29 October 2020 the Limassol Assize Court convicted him on eight charges, sentencing him on 9 November 2020 to six years. It treated R. as an accomplice, examining his testimony with great care, caution and scepticism. It found the testimony consistent, detailed, first-hand, logical and persuasive, with no improper inducement beyond lawful protection (R. received no immunity and served five years). R.’s knowledge of the house layout, multiple phone numbers (admitted by the applicant) and the MDMA hiding place, plus matching telecom data (locations, contacts and a call the day before arrest, contradicting the applicant), reinforced credibility. The court accepted G.M. and O.O. and found the applicant’s evidence inconsistent and showing unexplained drug-trade knowledge.

On 17 December 2020 the President (on the Attorney General’s recommendation) suspended the remainder of R.’s sentence from 21 December, with transfer abroad (return only to testify, under protection). R. later breached terms by not appearing against T.

On appeal the applicant argued unfair reliance on uncorroborated accomplice evidence and that the later suspension indicated a deal. On 20 September 2022 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, citing domestic case-law allowing uncorroborated accomplice evidence if approached with caution (which the Assize Court had done rigorously). Protection did not undermine credibility; the post-conviction suspension did not prove a prior reward or false testimony (distinguishing *Adamčo v. Slovakia*) and the President’s constitutional power was unreviewable. Independent evidence further supported R.

The ECHR held the trial fair: no promise or undue reward beyond the protection programme, courts displayed caution, and independent evidence reinforced the testimony.

The ECHR case Sakkou v. Cyprus examined whether the applicant’s conviction for drug offences violated Article 6 § 1 (fair trial) because it rested decisively on testimony from accomplice R.

In February 2018 R bought 2 kg of cannabis from the applicant on credit for €12,500 and later repaid €6,000. R then left Cyprus owing money, returned in September 2018 and remained isolated. In February 2019 T (a close associate of the applicant) proposed a trafficking partnership; R accepted. When the applicant learned of this he demanded the outstanding €6,500. T suggested R settle the debt in kind. The parties agreed that R would supply 500 g of MDMA (reducing the debt to €2,000), with T brokering the deal. On 11 April 2019 T delivered the MDMA to R, who hid it. The next day R was arrested for an unrelated cocaine importation.

While in detention R was threatened by a man posing as T’s friend. He reported the threat to YKAN investigators and, after being moved, indicated he would confess and testify against others if placed in witness protection. An informal meeting with the YKAN commander followed. On 23 April 2019 the Attorney General admitted R to the statutory witness-protection programme. R then made a voluntary statement confessing his own offences, implicating the applicant and T in multiple transactions, and directing police to the hidden MDMA.

R pleaded guilty to the cocaine charge and, taking account of his cooperation, was sentenced to five years (running from arrest). No immunity was granted.

The applicant was charged with selling cannabis on credit and agreeing to receive MDMA in lieu of debt. At the June 2020 trial the prosecution called R, two investigators and telecom-company employees. Unchallenged call-location data linked the relevant numbers. R portrayed the applicant as a major trafficker who used multiple SIMs, described a meeting in a side-room of the applicant’s house, and explained that fear and the protection programme enabled him to speak. Cross-examination alleged fabrication for leniency; R replied that he had revealed previously unknown offences (risking a heavier sentence) and was himself serving five years. The applicant denied knowing R, yet conceded that the side-room had an internal door and that he used multiple numbers.

On 29 October 2020 the Assize Court convicted the applicant on eight counts and imposed six years. It treated R as an accomplice, applied “great care, deliberation, caution and scepticism,” and found his account consistent, detailed and credible. No improper inducement had been offered beyond the protection programme itself; R received no substantive immunity. Independent evidence (telecom data matching R’s chronology, the discovered MDMA, and the applicant’s own admissions about the house and phones) corroborated the testimony. The court therefore considered corroboration unnecessary.

In December 2020 the President, on the Attorney General’s recommendation, suspended the remainder of R’s sentence and authorised his relocation abroad, subject to return for further testimony. R later breached those terms.

The applicant appealed, arguing that reliance on uncorroborated accomplice evidence and the subsequent suspension proved a secret deal. In September 2022 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It confirmed that Cypriot law permits conviction on an accomplice’s word provided the trial court approaches it with caution; the Assize Court had done so rigorously. A later presidential pardon, exercised under Article 53 of the Constitution, did not demonstrate that the testimony had been false.

The ECHR held that the proceedings remained fair: the domestic courts had displayed the required caution, no undue reward had been promised, and independent evidence reinforced R’s account.

The case of Sakkou v. Cyprus (Application no. 4429/23) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned whether the applicant’s conviction for drug offences violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing) because it relied decisively on testimony from an accomplice, R.

In February 2018, R. purchased 2 kg of cannabis worth €12,500 on credit from the applicant, later repaying €6,000. R. left Cyprus owing money but returned in September 2018. In February 2019, T. (an acquaintance of the applicant) proposed a drug-trafficking partnership with R., who resumed selling. The applicant inquired about R.’s remaining €6,500 debt. T. suggested R. settle it with drugs. They agreed R. would provide 0.5 kg of MDMA (reducing the debt to €2,000), with T. supplying the MDMA. On 11 April 2019 (while the applicant was in the Netherlands), T. delivered the MDMA to R., who hid it pending delivery instructions. The next day, R. was arrested for an unrelated offence: importing ~1 kg of cocaine from Belgium.

In detention, a person posing as T.’s friend threatened R. not to speak. R. reported this to YKAN investigators G.M. and O.O. After transfer to another facility, R. indicated he might confess to other offences if given witness protection and a safe facility. On 17 April 2019, an informal meeting occurred with the YKAN Commander; an information note recorded R.’s confession and willingness to testify, plus his request for protection and eventual financial support to leave Cyprus. On 23 April 2019, the Attorney General admitted R. to the witness protection programme under the 2001 Witness Protection Law. R. then gave a voluntary statement confessing to his arrest offences and detailing other drug dealings involving the applicant and T. He also showed police the hidden MDMA. This led to a case against the applicant (no. 20763/19).

R. pleaded guilty to the cocaine import and, on 5 December 2019, received a 5-year sentence (from arrest), with the court considering his cooperation (disclosing unknown offences and naming individuals), confession, rehabilitation, and remorse.

The applicant’s trial occurred on 10 June 2020. He was charged, inter alia, with selling cannabis on credit and agreeing to receive MDMA in lieu of debt. Prosecution witnesses included R., G.M., and O.O.; the applicant testified in his defence. Unchallenged telecommunications data linked phones of R., T., and the applicant. G.M. and O.O. described events from R.’s arrest to his statement, denying they directed him to incriminate the applicant (as they could not have known the details). R. described the applicant as a major trafficker using multiple SIMs, frequent calls, and a meeting in a side-room at the applicant’s house (which R. described in detail). R. said he testified due to fear (especially after the threat), a desire to escape drug rings, and the security of protection. In cross-examination, he denied fabricating testimony for leniency, noting he received a 5-year sentence, provided previously unknown information at personal risk, and had not implicated the applicant in everything. The applicant denied knowing or speaking to R. (though T. had mentioned him) but admitted the side-room connected internally to his house.

On 29 October 2020, the Limassol Assize Court convicted the applicant on eight charges. It treated R. as an accomplice, approaching his testimony with “great care, deliberation, caution, scepticism and critical assessment.” It found the testimony consistent, detailed, logically coherent, and persuasive (details only a participant could know). No improper inducement existed beyond programme admission; R. received no immunity and served his sentence. The court relied on it even without corroboration, though telecom data matched R.’s account (including calls the day before arrest), the applicant confirmed multiple phones and the internal house connection (contradicting his counsel), and R. had shown the hidden MDMA. Police failure to minute the Commander meeting did not prove encouragement of false testimony. The applicant lacked credibility due to contradictions and unexplained knowledge of drug pricing/import details. He was sentenced to six years on 9 November 2020.

On 17 December 2020, the President (on the Attorney General’s recommendation) suspended the remainder of R.’s sentence from 21 December, requiring relocation abroad (return only to testify in pending cases, with protection). R. later breached this by failing to testify against T.

The applicant appealed, arguing the trial was unfair as the Assize Court relied on R.’s uncorroborated accomplice testimony, and the later suspension evidenced a deal. On 20 September 2022, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. Domestic law permitted reliance on accomplice evidence without corroboration if approached cautiously (as done here, with thorough credibility assessment). Protection did not undermine credibility. The a posteriori suspension did not prove immunity, reward, or false testimony (distinguishing Adamčo v. Slovakia); presidential powers under Article 53 § 4 of the Constitution were not judicially reviewable. Other evidence discredited the applicant and reinforced R.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 6 § 1. No promise or undue reward was offered beyond programme placement. Domestic courts displayed caution in relying on the accomplice and cited independent reinforcing evidence (telecom data, hidden MDMA, house details). There was no unfairness.

The case of Seppern v. Estonia (Application no. 31722/22) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention (fair trial in criminal proceedings). The applicant, Estonian national Alar Seppern, was convicted of tax evasion, document counterfeiting (and related use), fraudulent use of identity documents, fraud, and (on appeal) two counts of incitement to counterfeit documents.

During the investigation, the applicant’s telephone was wiretapped and conversations recorded. At a 21 September 2020 hearing, the Viru County Court declared this material inadmissible. It found that the authorizations by the preliminary investigation judge lacked sufficient reasoning on the ultima ratio requirement (that evidence could not be obtained by other, less intrusive means), violating Article 1261 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court undertook to give fuller reasons in its later judgment.

On 19 October 2020, during the applicant’s cross-examination, the same court (at the prosecutor’s request) disclosed several excerpts from the transcripts of the intercepted calls. This was done solely to test the credibility of the applicant’s trial statements against the recordings. The applicant was given, and accepted, the opportunity to explain the discrepancies.

In its 19 April 2021 judgment the County Court convicted the applicant of some charges and acquitted him of others. It confirmed that the surveillance had been unlawful and the resulting material inadmissible as evidence. However, it held that Article 289 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure nevertheless permitted the use of any document or data recording (including the transcripts) to assess a witness’s credibility, irrespective of the material’s admissibility as evidence. The court stressed that only consistency and coherence of the statements were examined, not the content of the calls themselves. Finding the applicant’s explanations unconvincing, it excluded his trial statements as unreliable.

Both parties appealed. On 12 January 2022 the Tartu Court of Appeal partly quashed and partly upheld the first-instance judgment, adding convictions on the two incitement counts. It rejected the applicant’s complaint about the transcripts, holding that their use complied with Article 289 § 3 even though they were inadmissible as evidence. The court acknowledged the psychological risk of subconscious influence on judges but observed that the same risk exists whenever any prior statement is disclosed; the provision would otherwise be unusable. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 18 April 2022.

The transcripts were used to test credibility only in respect of three charges. For those convictions the courts relied on independent evidence: bank records, witness testimony, handwriting expertise, commercial-register extracts, evidence-inspection reports, employment-registry data, search reports, information obtained through international legal assistance, and contextual analysis of company structures and the roles of the applicant and others (including the fact that a deceased person’s identity documents had been used after his death). The appellate court also noted that the overall picture, including real-life plausibility, supported the findings.

The European Court of Human Rights subsequently found no violation of Article 6. The domestic courts had given thorough, non-arbitrary reasons for the limited use of the excerpts in accordance with national law. Access to the full transcripts had been restricted, constituting a procedural safeguard. The applicant had been able to challenge both the use and the content of the material, and his arguments had been addressed. The surveillance reports were not decisive for the outcome. The applicant had therefore not been deprived of a fair trial.

**Case Summary: Seppern v. Estonia (Application no. 31722/22)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 16 September 2025 (final 9 February 2026) in this case concerning an alleged violation of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing in criminal proceedings). The applicant, Estonian national Alar Seppern (born 1986), complained that evidence obtained through unlawful secret surveillance was used during his trial to test and ultimately exclude as unreliable his own statements, thereby undermining the fairness of the proceedings.

The applicant faced charges including tax evasion, counterfeiting of documents and their use, fraudulent use of identity documents, fraud, and incitement to counterfeit documents. During the pre-trial investigation, authorities wiretapped his telephone and recorded conversations under secret surveillance measures authorized by a preliminary investigation judge.

At a hearing on 21 September 2020 before the Viru County Court, the surveillance material was declared inadmissible. The court found that the authorizations lacked sufficient reasoning as to why the measure was necessary as an ultima ratio (last resort), contrary to Article 1261 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which requires that surveillance be used only when other evidence-gathering methods are impossible, untimely, overly complicated, or prejudicial to the proceedings. Further reasons were reserved for the final judgment.

Nevertheless, during the applicant’s cross-examination on 19 October 2020, the prosecutor requested—and the court granted—disclosure of excerpts from the intercepted-call transcripts solely to assess the credibility of the applicant’s trial testimony under Article 289 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. This provision permits the court, at a party’s request during adversarial examination, to disclose any document or information recording containing a prior statement by the witness that contradicts testimony given in court. The applicant was invited to, and did, explain apparent inconsistencies between his trial statements and the recordings.

In its judgment of 19 April 2021, the Viru County Court convicted the applicant of tax evasion, counterfeiting documents and related offences, while acquitting him of others. Confirming the surveillance’s unlawfulness, the court held the recordings inadmissible as evidence of guilt. It nevertheless ruled that Article 289 § 3 allowed their limited use to test credibility regardless of admissibility as evidence, citing the provision’s explanatory memorandum and legislative intent not to restrict such materials to admissible items. The court emphasized that it examined only consistency of the applicant’s accounts, not the recordings’ substantive content. Finding the applicant’s explanations of discrepancies unconvincing, it excluded his trial statements as unreliable.

Both parties appealed. On 12 January 2022 the Tartu Court of Appeal partially quashed the first-instance judgment, convicting the applicant of two additional counts of incitement to counterfeit documents while otherwise upholding the convictions. It confirmed that use of the transcripts accorded with domestic law. Although acknowledging possible subconscious influence on judges, the court reasoned that this did not invalidate the procedure, as analogous disclosure of pre-trial statements under Article 289 § 1 would otherwise be equally precluded. The Supreme Court refused to examine the applicant’s subsequent appeal on points of law on 18 April 2022.

The recordings were used to assess credibility (and exclude testimony) only in respect of three charges. Convictions on those counts rested on independent evidence, including bank information, witness statements, commercial-register extracts, handwriting expert reports, evidence-inspection protocols, employment-registry data, search reports, telecommunications data, cross-border legal-assistance materials, and contextual analysis of company structures, real-life plausibility, and the applicant’s role (including use of a deceased person’s identity after death). Other charges were supported by similar non-surveillance evidence.

Domestic law (Articles 1261, 289 and 293 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) thus permitted limited disclosure of otherwise inadmissible recordings solely for credibility testing. The applicant argued this use of unlawfully obtained material rendered the trial unfair. The Court later held that the domestic courts had given thorough, non-arbitrary reasons; the applicant had been able to challenge the material; courts had only limited access to full transcripts; and the recordings were not decisive to the outcome. No violation of Article 6 was found.

The case of B.A. v. Iceland (ECtHR Application no. 17006/20) arises from the applicant’s complaints that Icelandic authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention by inadequately investigating her reports of domestic violence and sexual assault, and that this reflected gender-based discrimination contrary to Article 14.

The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1975 and resident in Reykjavík, lodged a police complaint in December 2017 against her former cohabitant, F.Þ. She alleged a pattern of physical, psychological and sexual violence during their cohabitation from 2011 to 2014. According to her account, the relationship began with humiliation, criticism, isolation from family and controlling behaviour, which intensified after she became pregnant and escalated into physical and sexual violence. She described four specific incidents of sexual violence: coercion into sexual stimulation while she was hospitalised during pregnancy; rape during a visit to a rehabilitation clinic; rape in the hallway of their home; and rape while she was asleep, resulting in bruising. She also alleged two physical incidents—a brief chokehold and a headbutt. She had not sought immediate medical attention after any incident.

The police investigation included the applicant’s interview (with an officially appointed legal representative) and F.Þ.’s first questioning on 19 September 2018. He denied all allegations of violence or mistreatment, attributing relationship difficulties to the applicant’s alcohol consumption. He admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied it constituted rape, and acknowledged controlling behaviour only in urging her to stop drinking or working while intoxicated. Eleven witnesses were questioned. Several described changes in the applicant after cohabitation began, including reduced social contact and instances of humiliation or anger by F.Þ. One witness reported hearing the applicant scream and finding her trembling after the alleged chokehold. There were no direct witnesses to the physical or sexual acts; most testimony consisted of the applicant’s later disclosures. Supporting material included a December 2017 certificate from Stígamót (a sexual-abuse support centre) confirming the applicant’s attendance since April 2015 and her reports of severe mental, physical and sexual violence; psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017 noting depression and anxiety; and a February 2019 psychologist’s statement diagnosing post-traumatic stress disorder linked to an alleged sexual offence.

On 11 June 2019 the police discontinued the investigation. For the sexual-violence allegations they found insufficient support in light of F.Þ.’s denial and the available evidence, concluding that further inquiries were unlikely to strengthen the case. For the physical-violence allegations they held that Article 218b of the General Penal Code (introduced in 2016 to address domestic violence as a continuous pattern) could not apply retroactively; the conduct therefore fell only under the older Article 217, whose two-year limitation period had expired. On 25 September 2019 the State Prosecutor upheld the decision, reiterating that Article 218b was not retroactive, that the physical allegations were time-barred, and that the evidence (including witness statements and documentation of the applicant’s distress) was not “sufficient or likely” to secure a conviction on the sexual allegations. Subsequent correspondence confirmed that the Prosecutor’s review had not been limited to the police’s legal classification and that no other offence (such as gross defamation under Article 233b) warranted continuation.

These facts form the core of the alleged violations: a delayed complaint about events occurring years earlier, the absence of contemporaneous medical evidence or eyewitnesses, the resulting insufficiency finding, the statutory time-bar on physical violence, and the authorities’ conclusion that additional investigative steps would not alter the evidentiary position. The applicant further relied on these outcomes, together with broader statistics on high discontinuance rates in Icelandic sexual- and domestic-violence cases, to allege systemic gender bias.

The case of Levon v. Lithuania concerns the applicant's complaint under Article 2 of the ECHR (procedural limb) that Lithuanian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into his father's death in hospital, allegedly caused by medical negligence.

On the morning of 25 December 2020, the applicant's 78-year-old father A. suddenly felt unwell, with difficulty sitting, breathing problems and pallor. The applicant called an ambulance around 8.50 p.m.; it arrived within 25 minutes and transported A. to Šalčininkai municipal hospital (the nearest facility with emergency and intensive-care services). A. died the next evening around 9.30 p.m. The death certificate listed pulmonary oedema as the direct cause, resulting from unspecified chronic cardiovascular disease. No autopsy occurred: the hospital saw no need and the family (including the applicant) objected in writing.

The applicant alleged that the ambulance failed to give adequate urgent care, chose an unsuitable hospital lacking a cardiologist or intensive-care specialist, and provided inaccurate information to hospital staff. At the hospital, he claimed, A. was not properly examined by a doctor, received no measures to ease breathing or identify the cause of his condition, and was left inadequately monitored until it was too late for effective resuscitation.

Internal inquiries by the ambulance service (Šalčininkai PHC) and the hospital found care adequate. Records showed A. had a history of heart-rhythm disorders (including paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed in 2020). The ambulance technician had measured vital signs, given painkillers and oxygen, and taken A. promptly to hospital after he lost consciousness. Hospital records indicated examination on arrival (diagnosed with acute pulmonary heart disease and anaemia), regular monitoring, tests (ECG, blood/urine, COVID-19), medication and oxygen. His condition remained stable until sudden deterioration on the evening of 26 December; resuscitation failed.

In June 2021 the applicant sought compensation from the Commission for the Determination of Damage Caused to Patients’ Health. The Commission (doctors, a nurse, a health-sciences professional and a lawyer) reviewed records and obtained an independent analysis from another hospital’s internal-medicine doctor. That analysis (noting poor-quality copies) found the ambulance assessment accurate, but suggested an intensive-care consultation would have been appropriate (it never occurred because the specialist was busy). It attributed death to worsening chronic conditions (heart failure, atrial fibrillation, infection, kidney disease, anaemia) and a possible delay by the family in seeking help; no professional errors were identified. The Commission unanimously found no causal link and denied compensation.

The applicant then brought civil proceedings in the Vilnius Regional Court seeking EUR 15,000 for non-pecuniary damage, repeating his allegations and criticising the Commission as biased. The court dismissed the claim. Applying the Patients’ Act and Supreme Court case-law, it held that doctors owe an obligation of means (greatest possible care and professionalism), not of result; liability requires unlawfulness, damage, causation and (rebuttable) fault. It found the ambulance acted professionally. Hospital records and the earlier analysis showed examinations, monitoring and treatment; A. had pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Death resulted from those diseases plus delayed help-seeking, not from any unlawful act or omission. The applicant bore the burden of proof and had not discharged it.

On appeal the Court of Appeal upheld the decision. It refused a new expert assessment (requested only on appeal) as untimely and unnecessary; the existing written evidence (records, statements and prior analysis) sufficed. The hospital was the nearest appropriate facility. Allegations of inadequate monitoring or forged records were unsupported. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on points of law.

In parallel, the applicant requested a criminal investigation in August 2022, alleging negligent homicide (Criminal Code Art. 132) and document falsification (Art. 300) because some records appeared dated after A.’s death and the death certificate seemed contradictory. Police opened a pre-trial investigation. The State Accreditation Service found several hospital breaches of regulations (incomplete history, failure to call an intensive-care specialist or arrange certain tests, no resuscitation protocol, limited radiologist availability) and issued a warning. The State Forensic Medicine Service, however, concluded after document review that assistance had been adequate, the likely cause was sudden heart failure from chronic disease, there was no causal link to medical actions, and death was unavoidable. Exhumation would serve no purpose given the elapsed time. A nurse explained that records were sometimes pre-filled due to staff shortages and later corrected; this practice, though inappropriate, lacked criminal intent or dangerousness.

The prosecutor discontinued the investigation in April 2024: regulatory breaches did not establish the required causal link for criminal liability, and the document issues did not meet the threshold of a criminal offence. Appeals to a senior prosecutor, a pre-trial judge and the Vilnius Regional Court were all dismissed; the investigation was found thorough and no objective evidence of crime existed.

These were the facts on which the applicant based his claim that the civil and criminal proceedings had been neither thorough nor impartial.

The case of Levon v. Lithuania concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 2 of the Convention (procedural limb) that domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into his father’s death, which he attributed to medical negligence by ambulance and hospital staff.

On 25 December 2020 the applicant’s 78-year-old father, A., suddenly felt unwell with breathing difficulties. An ambulance was summoned at 8.50 p.m. and took him to the nearest hospital offering emergency and intensive-care services. A. died the next evening. The death certificate listed pulmonary oedema as the direct cause and unspecified chronic cardiovascular disease as the underlying cause. No autopsy was performed because the hospital saw no indication for one and the applicant objected in writing.

The applicant complained that the ambulance had given inadequate care, chosen the wrong hospital and supplied inaccurate information, and that hospital staff had failed to examine A., treat his breathing problems or determine the cause of his condition. Internal inquiries by both institutions concluded that care had been adequate. They noted A.’s pre-existing diagnoses of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and other cardiac problems, the measurements and oxygen given in the ambulance, regular monitoring, tests and medication at the hospital, and a sudden deterioration.

In June 2021 the applicant claimed €5 000 non-pecuniary damage from the Commission for the Determination of Damage Caused to Patients’ Health. After reviewing records and obtaining an independent analysis by an internal-medicine doctor from another hospital, the Commission found no professional errors or causal link. The analysis (based on poor-quality copies) stated that an intensive-care consultation would have been appropriate but the specialist was busy, that the family had delayed seeking help, and that death resulted from worsening chronic diseases.

The applicant then sued the State and municipality in the Vilnius Regional Court for €15 000, repeating his allegations and arguing that the Commission had been biased. He was not legally represented at first instance. The court dismissed the claim. It held that ambulance staff had acted professionally, that hospital care met the “obligation of means” standard given A.’s pre-existing conditions and the delay in seeking help, and that the applicant had failed to prove unlawfulness or causation. Existing records and the Commission’s analysis were sufficient; specialist knowledge was not required for the court to decide.

On appeal the applicant, now represented, criticised the analysis as superficial and contradictory, complained that the first-instance court had not ordered an expert report or advised him to obtain counsel, pointed to possible forgeries in the records, and requested an expert assessment. He also informed the court of a parallel criminal investigation. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, finding the expert request late and unnecessary, the evidence sufficient, the hospital choice lawful, and no duty on the court to suggest representation. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on points of law.

Separately, a criminal investigation was opened into alleged negligent homicide and document falsification. An Accreditation Service report identified several hospital breaches (incomplete records, no intensive-care consultation, missing tests, no resuscitation protocol or 24-hour radiology). A forensic assessment concluded that death was caused by unavoidable sudden heart failure due to chronic disease, that care had been adequate and that there was no causal link. A nurse explained that records were sometimes pre-filled because of staff shortages. The prosecutor discontinued the case for lack of causation and of the required criminal intent. Subsequent appeals were rejected.

The Court found that the civil proceedings had been accessible and adversarial, giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity to present his case, and that the parallel criminal investigation and expert assessments had complemented them and sufficiently clarified the facts. The case of Levon v. Lithuania (Application no. 27121/23) concerns the procedural obligation under Article 2 of the ECHR to conduct an effective investigation into the death of the applicant’s 78-year-old father, A., in hospital on 26 December 2020, allegedly due to medical negligence.

On the morning of 25 December 2020, A. experienced breathing difficulties and weakness. The applicant called an ambulance at 8.50 p.m.; it arrived within 25 minutes and transported A. to Šalčininkai municipal hospital, the nearest facility with emergency and intensive-care services. A. died the following evening at 9.30 p.m. The death certificate listed pulmonary oedema as the direct cause, resulting from unspecified chronic cardiovascular disease. No post-mortem examination occurred, as the hospital saw no need and the family objected.

The applicant complained to the ambulance provider (Šalčininkai Primary Healthcare Centre) and the hospital, alleging failure to provide urgent care, incorrect hospital selection (lacking a cardiologist or intensive-care specialist), inaccurate information transfer, lack of doctor examination, and no measures to aid breathing or diagnose the condition. He noted A. had undergone a health check in January 2020 with no major issues identified and had led a healthy lifestyle.

Internal inquiries established that A. had prior diagnoses of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and other heart-rhythm disorders. The ambulance inquiry, based on the technician’s statement, found that vital signs were measured, painkillers and oxygen administered, and A. taken promptly to the nearest suitable hospital; care complied with regulations. The hospital inquiry recorded examination by the on-duty doctor, hospitalisation in the internal-diseases unit (pending a COVID-19 test), regular monitoring (five file entries), tests (ECG, blood, urine, COVID-19), and medication. Condition remained stable until sudden deterioration around 9 p.m., when unsuccessful resuscitation occurred. Both inquiries deemed care adequate; a precise cause of death could not be determined without autopsy.

In June 2021 the applicant sought €5,000 non-pecuniary compensation from the Commission for the Determination of Damage Caused to Patients’ Health. The six-member Commission reviewed complaints, records, and statements from two attending doctors detailing symptoms (shortness of breath, vertigo, loss of consciousness), diagnoses (acute pulmonary heart disease, anaemia), tests, and monitoring. An independent analysis by an internal-medicine doctor from another hospital (November 2021) noted poor-quality records but concluded that history-taking, tests, diagnosis, treatment (infusion, diuretics, anticoagulants, oxygen), and supervision occurred. An intensive-care consultation would have been appropriate but the specialist was busy. Ambulance care was accurate; family delay in seeking help may have contributed. Death resulted from advanced heart failure, atrial fibrillation, infection, kidney disease and anaemia. No professional errors were found. The applicant contested the analysis (arguing ICU placement was required, ambulance should have chosen a better-equipped hospital, and the on-duty doctor failed to attend when A. lost consciousness). The Commission unanimously found no legal breach or causal link and denied compensation (December 2021).

The applicant then sued the State and municipality in the Vilnius Regional Court for €15,000, repeating allegations of inadequate ambulance choice, lack of urgent hospital measures, delayed resuscitation, ineffective treatment plan, and Commission bias. He signed the claim himself (though a lawyer had assisted preparation) and did not request an expert assessment at first instance. After hearings at which he could make requests (some telephone-data requests were refused), the court dismissed the claim (June 2022). It applied Patients’ Act standards requiring proof of unlawful action, damage, causation and (presumed) fault, assessed against a professional “obligation of means.” Relying on records and the independent analysis, it found ambulance care professional; hospital treatment appropriate given pre-existing hypertensive heart disease and atrial fibrillation; and death caused by those diseases plus delayed help-seeking. No causation was shown.

On appeal the applicant (now represented) criticised the analysis as superficial, based on illegible records, prepared by an unqualified specialist, and contradictory; alleged record forgeries (entries dated after death); argued the first-instance court should have ordered an expert or advised him of his rights given the unrepresented status and public-interest issues; and requested an expert assessment plus stay pending a newly opened criminal investigation. The Court of Appeal refused the expert request as untimely (not made at first instance) and unnecessary, given sufficient written evidence; it found no court duty to prompt the request or appoint counsel (the applicant had indicated awareness of the right). It endorsed the lower court’s findings: ambulance destination complied with “nearest suitable facility” rules; records disproved lack of monitoring or treatment; death stemmed from pre-existing conditions and delay. The Supreme Court declined leave to appeal (March 2023), finding no important legal issues.

In parallel, the applicant prompted a criminal investigation (August 2022) into negligent homicide and document falsification (records dated 27 December and alleged contradictions in the death certificate and file). Police obtained an Accreditation Service report (March 2023) confirming ambulance compliance but identifying hospital breaches: incomplete records and history, failure to summon an intensive-care specialist or order chest X-ray/biochemical tests, inadequate test assessment, self-resuscitation without protocol, and lack of 24-hour radiologist cover. A warning and rectification order followed. A State Forensic Medicine Service expert (March 2024), reviewing history (pulmonary hypertension since 2011 plus later heart disorders) and all materials, concluded the likely cause was sudden heart failure amid chronic cardiovascular disease; precise determination required (unavailable) autopsy; care was adequate with proper diagnosis and tests; no causal link existed; and death was unavoidable. A nurse explained pre-filling of records as a staffing-shortage practice later corrected. The prosecutor discontinued proceedings (April 2024): regulatory breaches lacked the required causal link for homicide liability; pre-filling, though improper, lacked criminal intent or dangerousness; and the death certificate could not be proven false without autopsy. Hierarchical and judicial appeals were rejected as the investigation was thorough and disclosed no offences.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the authorities failed to conduct a sufficiently thorough and impartial inquiry into the death.

The case of Šabanović and Others v. Serbia (ECHR, Third Section, Applications nos. 39819/16 and four others) concerns five Serbian police officers employed by the Ministry of the Interior (MoI) as authorised officers. Between June 2010 and September 2011 they brought civil claims against Serbia seeking unpaid salary supplements for overtime, night work and public-holiday work performed between April 2007 and September 2011. They argued that the MoI had failed to increase their salary coefficients by the 30–50 % required under Article 147 § 1 of the 2005 Police Act and that they were therefore entitled to the supplements under the general Labour Act and the Salaries of Civil Servants Act.

Domestic courts at first instance and on appeal uniformly dismissed the claims. They found that the applicants’ additional coefficients (fixed by the unpublished 2006 Salaries Regulation) already exceeded those of civilian MoI employees of comparable education who did not work unsociable hours by more than 30 %. Article 147 § 3 of the Police Act therefore excluded the general labour rules. Constitutional appeals lodged between 2013 and 2015 were likewise rejected as unfounded, the Constitutional Court relying on its earlier decisions (especially Už-3827/12) that the coefficient comparison was legally correct and that isolated contrary judgments did not demonstrate “profound and long-standing” inconsistency.

The same period saw marked divergence among appellate courts. Some (Kragujevac, Niš, Novi Sad, later Belgrade) allowed identical claims after comparing coefficients with other authorised officers who performed little or no unsociable work; others (including the courts that decided the applicants’ cases) used civilian employees as the comparator and dismissed the claims. A third line of cases succeeded simply because the MoI had never issued individual decisions increasing coefficients.

The Supreme Court first addressed the conflict in a Civil Division opinion of 23 September 2014: the proper comparator was a non-authorised police officer or, failing that, another civil servant of the same education. It declared special appeals on points of law automatically admissible in contrary cases. On 10 November 2015 it amended the opinion, holding that the comparator must be an authorised officer of identical education who did not work unsociable hours. Subsequent Supreme Court rulings consistently applied the new test, quashing dismissals or upholding awards and thereby unifying the case-law within roughly a year.

The applicants’ own requests to reopen their proceedings after the 2015 change were rejected; the Civil Procedure Act contained no ground for reopening based on a later shift in Supreme Court interpretation. Two applicants also invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, claiming that the dismissals amounted to a deprivation of property.

The ECHR examined the complaints under Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing). It held that the domestic system had successfully resolved the inconsistencies through the Supreme Court’s reasonably prompt and binding opinions, that the applicants had enjoyed fully adversarial proceedings in which their arguments were thoroughly examined, and that the courts’ interpretation of Article 147 could not be regarded as arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. No violation was found.

Serbia involves five Serbian police officers (authorised officers of the Ministry of the Interior) who alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention (fair hearing) due to inconsistent domestic case-law on their claims for unpaid salary supplements, as well as (for two applicants) deprivation of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The comparator used was a civilian Ministry employee of equivalent education who performed no unsociable hours. This approach was supported by Constitutional Court decisions such as Už-3827/12 (2012) and Už-4045/12 (2013). Constitutional appeals lodged between 2013 and 2015 were rejected (2014–2016) on the same grounds; one court noted that a single contrary judgment did not prove “profound and long-standing” inconsistency.

Other courts, including those deciding the applicants’ cases, used the civilian comparator and dismissed the claims. A 2014 Supreme Court legal opinion initially endorsed comparison with non-authorised or civilian staff; an amended 2015 opinion required comparison with authorised officers of the same education who performed no unsociable hours. Subsequent Supreme Court rulings quashed dismissals that had used the civilian comparator and ordered retrials or allowed claims.

The case of Helme v. Estonia (Application no. 3023/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing in criminal proceedings). The applicant, Peeter Helme, an Estonian national, complained that his conviction for attempted sexual enticement of a minor relied on evidence obtained through entrapment by an undercover police officer posing as a 12-year-old girl in an online chatroom.

In September 2019, Estonian authorities initiated criminal proceedings based on information indicating that individuals were using websites including www.armastusesaal.org (“hall of love”) to conduct sexual chats with minors under 14 and send them sexual content. On 27 September 2019, a prosecutor authorised the use of an undercover officer on that site pursuant to the Code of Criminal Procedure. From 8 October to 8 December 2019, an officer used the username “Marleen12” and the identity of a 12-year-old girl named Marleen Ilus to participate in chatrooms.

The applicant, using the username “m41tln,” initiated multiple private conversations with “Marleen12,” beginning on 8 October 2019. Early in the first chat, the officer stated she was 12 years old. The applicant repeatedly raised sexual topics, asking about the officer’s physical development, prior sexual experiences, pornography, masturbation, and interest in sex; he also described having had sex with a girl younger than 12. When the officer did not respond immediately, the applicant persisted with greetings. The officer generally gave short, passive replies. Transcripts of these chats were included in a surveillance report later used as evidence.

Separate proceedings were opened against the applicant on 17 November 2019 after he was identified as the user. On 30 November 2020, Harju County Court convicted him. The court reviewed the secret file, confirmed proper authorisation based on reasonable suspicion of offences against minors (which are often hidden), and found the operation justified and proportionate. It held that the officer had not incited the applicant; he had initiated and driven the conversations. The court rejected the applicant’s claim that he believed it was adult role-play, noting the site’s lack of age verification, his frequent use of it, and the content of the chats.

The applicant appealed, arguing there had been no prior suspicion specifically against him; the operation targeted potential offenders generally by using a child’s identity and username “Marleen12,” thereby inciting the offence. On 10 June 2021, Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding the officer remained passive, the applicant always initiated sexual topics, and the operation served to verify existing information about offences on the site rather than to entrap him. The Supreme Court declined to examine a further appeal on 17 August 2021, rendering the conviction final.

The applicant maintained before the ECtHR that the evidence resulted from unlawful incitement, as the police created the opportunity without individualised suspicion and by assuming a child’s role. The Court examined whether the undercover operation amounted to entrapment that rendered the trial unfair.

The case of Helme v. Estonia (Application no. 3023/22) concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial). The applicant, Peeter Helme (born 1978), complained that he was convicted of attempted sexual enticement of a minor based on evidence obtained through online entrapment by an undercover police officer posing as a 12-year-old girl.

In September 2019, Estonian authorities initiated criminal proceedings based on information that individuals were using websites, including www.armastusesaal.org (“hall of love”), for sexual chats with minors under 14 and to send them sexual content. On 27 September 2019, a prosecutor authorised an undercover officer under the Code of Criminal Procedure to gather information on that site. From 8 October to 8 December 2019, an officer used the identity of a 12-year-old girl named Marleen Ilus (username “Marleen12”) in the site’s chatrooms.

A user named “m41tln” (later identified as the applicant) initiated multiple private chats with “Marleen12,” starting on 8 October 2019. Early in the first conversation, the officer stated she was 12. The applicant repeatedly initiated and steered discussions toward sexual topics, asking about the girl’s body, whether she had seen sexual discussions, if she had “boobs,” her knowledge of sex with young children, her sexual experience, pornography, masturbation, orgasms, and sexual interests. He also claimed to have had sex with a girl younger than her. The officer gave mostly short, passive replies and did not initiate sexual topics. On 17 November 2019, separate proceedings were opened against the applicant based on these chats; transcripts were included in a surveillance report later used as evidence.

On 30 November 2020, Harju County Court convicted the applicant of attempted sexual enticement of a minor (Criminal Code Article 179 § 1). The court reviewed the secret surveillance file, confirming proper prosecutorial authorisation based on reasonable suspicion of an offence for which surveillance was permitted. It found the operation justified and proportionate given the hidden nature of crimes targeting minors, where offenders often destroy evidence, and that the ultima ratio principle was respected. Examining the chats, the court held that the officer had not incited the applicant; he had initiated contact, maintained conversations, and introduced all sexual topics. It rejected his claim that he believed he was engaging in adult role-play, noting the site did not require age verification, he used his own age in his username (implying others did likewise), and the content showed he believed he was speaking to a 12-year-old and sought to arouse her sexual interest.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 10 June 2021, agreeing that extracts showed he always initiated sexual discussions while the officer remained passive, giving short answers even when urged. It found the operation aimed at verifying information about the websites’ use for sexual chats with minors, not at inciting the applicant specifically. The Supreme Court declined to examine his further appeal on 17 August 2021, rendering the conviction final.

The applicant argued there was no prior suspicion against him personally; proceedings against him began only after the chats. He claimed the operation targeted “sexual enticers” generally, with the username “Marleen12” chosen to provoke conversations, and that assuming a minor’s identity constituted incitement regardless of who initiated sexual topics. Domestic courts rejected these claims, finding the operation lawful, the evidence admissible, and no incitement.

The ECtHR later examined whether the undercover operation amounted to entrapment affecting the fairness of the trial.

**Helme v. Estonia (App. no. 3023/22), ECtHR (Third Section), 7 October 2025 (final 9 February 2026)**

The applicant, Peeter Helme (born 1978), an Estonian national, alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial in criminal proceedings) due to online entrapment. He was convicted of attempted sexual enticement of a minor after engaging in explicitly sexual conversations with an undercover police officer posing as a 12-year-old girl in an online chatroom; the resulting evidence was used against him.

In 2019, criminal proceedings were opened based on information that persons had used websites including www.armastusesaal.org (“hall of love”) for sexual chats with minors under 14 and to send sexual content. On 27 September 2019 the prosecutor authorised an undercover officer under the Code of Criminal Procedure. From 8 October to 8 December 2019, an officer using the identity of 12-year-old “Marleen Ilus” (username “Marleen12”) operated in the site’s chatrooms.

The applicant, using username “m41tln”, initiated multiple private-message chats with “Marleen12” (starting 8 October 2019). Early in the first chat she stated she was 12. He repeatedly initiated and steered conversations toward sexual topics, inquiring about her body, sexual experience, pornography, masturbation, and related matters, and described his own alleged sexual acts with a younger child. He persisted even when responses were delayed or brief. Transcripts formed part of a surveillance report used as evidence. Separate proceedings identified him as the user.

On 30 November 2020 Harju County Court convicted him of attempted sexual enticement of a minor (Criminal Code Art. 179 § 1). It reviewed the surveillance file, confirmed lawful authorisation based on reasonable suspicion of relevant offences (hidden crimes targeting minors justifying ultima ratio use of an undercover officer), and found the evidence admissible. The officer had not incited the applicant: he initiated chats and all sexual topics; the officer remained largely passive with short replies. The court rejected his claim of adult role-play, finding that as a frequent user he knew the site lacked age verification, his username incorporated his age, and the content showed he believed he was addressing a 12-year-old and sought to arouse her sexual interest.

The Tallinn Court of Appeal (10 June 2021) dismissed his appeal, agreeing there was no provocation: he always initiated sexual talk and urged the passive officer. The operation verified general information about offences on the site rather than targeting or inciting him specifically. The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal (17 August 2021), making the conviction final.

The applicant argued there was no prior suspicion against him personally; proceedings began only after alleged incitement via the undercover role and username chosen to lure those interested in children under 14. Domestic courts and the ECtHR rejected this. The Court found good reasons to initiate the operation based on information about potential sexual enticement of minors on the specific site. In an online context, prior identification of individual suspects was not always feasible. Lack of objective suspicion specific to the applicant was not decisive; there existed an objective suspicion tied to a defined, limited virtual space. Given the context of crimes against minors, the operation did not imply an intent to entrap him. Police actions were not unlawful and did not presume illegal conduct by interlocutors. The officer maintained a passive attitude; the applicant faced no pressure. Use of the undercover officer did not amount to incitement. Thus there was no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case of Fajstavr v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 48303/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing in criminal proceedings). The applicant, Czech national Aleš Fajstavr (born 1957), challenged his 2019 conviction for particularly serious drug manufacturing and trafficking as part of an organised group between January and June 2015. The conviction rested to a decisive extent on testimony from co-accused N.M., who had been granted “cooperating accused” status under Article 178a of the Czech Code of Criminal Procedure and received a markedly more lenient sentence.

Pre-trial proceedings began on 13 July 2016 when police charged N.M. with drug trafficking; she largely confessed. Her ex-partner J.J. stated that the applicant had once been present when co-accused O.K. gave N.M. drugs to transport to Switzerland. On 20 July 2016 N.M. added that her April 2015 trip had been organised by both O.K. and the applicant, who came to her flat, packaged the drugs, drove her to the Prague bus station and later collected the proceeds; they also accompanied her for a June 2015 trip. She later reiterated their joint involvement but could not specify roles. N.M. then requested cooperating-accused status.

On 20 November 2016 charges were brought against N.M., O.K. and the applicant. The applicant, represented by counsel, stated he knew N.M., had accompanied her and O.K. to the bus station once and had visited her flat, but remembered nothing further. N.M. was questioned as a cooperating accused on 16 December 2016 in the presence of all defence lawyers; the applicant’s counsel put detailed questions about her addiction history and the applicant’s alleged role. A psychiatric expert later found N.M. mentally competent (despite long-term drug use since age 14) and able to participate fully in proceedings, recommending only outpatient treatment. Formal indictment followed on 6 October 2017, designating N.M. as cooperating accused.

At the Ústí nad Labem Regional Court trial (hearings April 2018–August 2019), the applicant denied involvement and offered alibis: hospitalisation 15–18 April 2015 (covering the first trip) and a documented car-transport trip to Belgium around 11–15 June 2015 (covering the second). He argued N.M. had motive to lie (a past insult plus hope of sentence reduction) and that her addiction rendered her unreliable. N.M. confirmed her earlier statements, answered questions from the court, prosecutor and defence, and conceded she could not recall whether the applicant had accompanied her once or twice. Defence witness J.V. confirmed loading a car on 11 June and delivering it in Belgium on 13 June but could not pinpoint departure; a request to hear a further witness (H.K.) was refused. The prosecutor acknowledged N.M.’s lack of integrity but noted she had incriminated herself in a more serious offence, described the whole group’s activities and was corroborated by six other witnesses plus objective evidence; he recommended a sentence below the statutory minimum.

On 26 September 2019 the Regional Court convicted the applicant, O.K. and N.M. The applicant received ten years’ imprisonment; N.M. received three years. The court treated N.M.’s consistent pre-trial and trial statements as reliable because they logically described the group’s actions and were corroborated by J.J.’s initial statement, telephone recordings, a search of O.K.’s home, bus-company records and Swiss authorities’ information. It found no history of serious conflict that would motivate false accusation and rejected the alibis (hospitalisation did not preclude presence on 14 April; J.V.’s evidence contradicted the claimed 10 June departure). Appeals to the Prague High Court (dismissed 13 March 2020), Supreme Court (25 November 2020) and Constitutional Court (24 March 2021, as manifestly ill-founded) all failed. The higher courts held that the evidence had been comprehensively examined, the unused witness was redundant even if accepted, and all defence arguments had been addressed.

The cooperating-accused mechanism (introduced 2010) permits a prosecutor to designate an accused who reports facts likely to clarify organised-group offences, freely confesses, and agrees to testify comprehensively. The court then independently assesses whether a reduced or waived sentence is justified, treating such testimony with particular caution regarding motive and requiring corroboration. The applicant was later arrested in Germany on a European arrest warrant and transferred to serve his sentence. The ECtHR ultimately held that reliance on the cooperating witness, after thorough scrutiny and in the presence of corroboration and full opportunity to challenge her, did not render the trial unfair.

These facts centre on the decisive weight given to a cooperating accused’s testimony, the procedural opportunities afforded the defence to test it, the corroborative material relied upon, the applicant’s alibi evidence and the domestic courts’ credibility assessments.

In closing, the prosecutor accepted that N.M. was not a person of integrity but stressed that she had incriminated herself on a more serious charge, described the entire group’s activities, and been corroborated by other evidence (telephone recordings, a house search, bus-company records and Swiss authorities’ information). The prosecutor recommended a sentence below the statutory minimum for her.

On 26 September 2019 the Regional Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment; N.M. received three years. The court found N.M.’s accounts logical, consistent and independently corroborated, saw no mental-health impairment from the psychiatric report, and rejected any motive of personal animosity. It dismissed the alibis as implausible or incomplete. The Prague High Court (March 2020), the Supreme Court (November 2020) and the Constitutional Court (March 2021) all upheld the conviction, holding that the evidence had been comprehensively assessed, that the unheard witness would not have been decisive, and that the cooperating-accused testimony had been subjected to the required critical scrutiny.

The applicant was arrested in Germany on a European arrest warrant and began serving his sentence in November 2021. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately held that the trial had not been rendered unfair.
