The case of Ayala Flores v. Italy (Application no. 16803/21) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for one’s home). The applicant, a Peruvian national born in 1957 and resident in Procida, Italy, challenged the enforcement of a demolition order against a small unauthorized dwelling she had occupied as her home for decades.

In the early 1990s the applicant and her husband constructed a 30-square-metre building on land he owned on the island of Procida, in a highly seismic zone subject to landscape constraints and an absolute building ban by reason of its designation as an area of “specific environmental interest.” They established their home there without the required permit. In 1996 the municipality ordered restoration of the site; a demolition order followed in 1998. Criminal proceedings ensued. In 2002 the couple were convicted of unauthorized construction and of breaking official seals placed on the site; a demolition order formed part of the sentence (five months’ imprisonment, suspended, plus a fine). The conviction became final in 2003. An application for a building amnesty in 2004 was unsuccessful because the site was subject to landscape and environmental restrictions. The applicant’s husband died in 2009; she continued to occupy the structure.

Enforcement of the demolition order began in 2016. The public prosecutor and municipality served notices requiring demolition within 90 days, failing which the work would be carried out at the applicant’s expense. She immediately sought a review of the enforcement order (incidente di esecuzione), initially without relying on Article 8. She later claimed to have filed additional written submissions asserting that the building was her only home, that she had lived there for more than 15 years after conviction, that she faced financial hardship, and that demolition would be disproportionate (citing Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria). The Government disputed that those submissions had been properly filed.

The Naples Court of Appeal, sitting as enforcement court, dismissed the review application in 2018, characterizing the demolition order as a mandatory restorative measure required to restore lawful land use. The Court of Cassation in 2020 declared the subsequent appeal inadmissible for failure to satisfy formal requirements (the additional submissions had not been attached and their filing had not been proved). It nevertheless observed that any Article 8 complaint had been presented only generically, without identification of concrete individual circumstances capable of outweighing the public interest in enforcement. It added that the applicant could have formed no legitimate expectation of remaining in a structure she had always known to be unauthorized, that she had not shown the construction had been erected out of necessity, and that the passage of time did not alter the restorative purpose of the order.

Subsequent municipal inspections (2020, 2022 and 2024) recorded that the building appeared uninhabited, overgrown and in a state more consistent with storage than residential use; unauthorized additions (a fence, shutters and an external storage area) had been made. The applicant produced a residence certificate dating from 2001, evidence of a modest social pension (approximately €552 net per month) and an ISEE household income of €4,943, statements from two local residents that she still lived there and had no alternative accommodation, and a surveyor’s report attributing the lack of maintenance to her age and poverty. She applied for public housing in 2021. As of April 2025 the structure had not been demolished.

The core of the alleged Article 8 violation is therefore the claimed failure of the domestic courts to conduct a sufficiently individualized proportionality review of the demolition’s impact on the applicant’s home, taking account of her long-term occupation, financial circumstances and lack of alternative housing, against the competing public interest in environmental protection and enforcement of building restrictions in a high-risk seismic and landscape-protected zone.

**CASE OF AYALA FLORES v. ITALY (Application no. 16803/21)**

In the early 1990s, Peruvian national Elisabeth Ayala Flores (born 1957) and her husband erected a 30 m² unauthorized dwelling on his land on the island of Procida, Italy, establishing it as their home. The site lay in a highly seismic zone subject to landscape constraints (*vincoli paesaggistici*) under laws protecting areas of outstanding natural beauty, and an absolute construction ban as an area of “specific environmental interest.” In 1996 the municipality of Procida confirmed the lack of required permits and ordered restoration of the site. A demolition order followed in 1998.

The couple were prosecuted for unauthorized construction under section 20(c) of Law no. 47/1985 and for breaking police seals placed on the site (Article 349 of the Criminal Code). In 2002 the Pozzuoli District Court convicted them, imposing a suspended five-month prison sentence plus a €300 fine and ordering demolition. On appeal in 2003 the Naples Court of Appeal upheld the core convictions (some charges being time-barred), reduced the sentence, and lifted a seizure to permit demolition. The judgment became final in October 2003. A 2004 application for a building amnesty was unanswered and, in any event, inapplicable to constrained areas. The husband died in 2009; the applicant continued occupying the structure.

Enforcement resumed in 2016 when the public prosecutor (responsible for executing the criminal demolition order) inquired of the municipality. Eviction and demolition notices followed, requiring the applicant to demolish within 90 days or face demolition at her expense. She asked the municipality to recognize a public interest in retaining the building and, on 2 March 2016, sought review of the enforcement order (*incidente di esecuzione*) before the Naples Court of Appeal, requesting annulment, revocation or a stay. Her initial filings did not invoke Article 8 of the Convention. She later claimed to have submitted additional arguments that the dwelling was her sole home of more than 15 years, that she faced financial hardship, and that demolition would be disproportionate under Article 8 (citing *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*). The Government contested that these submissions were properly filed.

In November 2018 (deposited 2019) the Court of Appeal, sitting as enforcement judge, dismissed the application. It characterized the demolition order as a mandatory restorative measure required to restore lawful land use and compliance with building rules; it did not address the alleged Article 8 arguments. On further appeal the Court of Cassation, in September 2020, declared the appeal inadmissible for failure to attach or prove the additional submissions. It nevertheless recalled that Article 8 requires a proportionality assessment of interference with the home, citing both Strasbourg case-law and its own precedents. It found the applicant’s Article 8 claim generic, lacking concrete individual circumstances capable of outweighing the public interest in environmental protection and restoration of the site. The applicant, it held, had never had a legitimate expectation of remaining in a knowingly unauthorized building, had not shown construction out of necessity, and could not rely on the 15-year delay. Remaining grounds were rejected.

Subsequent municipal inspections (2020, 2022, 2024) recorded the structure as uninhabited, overgrown and later fitted with an unauthorized fence, shutters and an external storage area; interior photographs suggested it was unfit for habitation and more akin to storage. The applicant produced residence certificates dating from 2001, evidence of a modest social pension (€551 net monthly) and low household income (€4,943 annually), witness statements asserting continued occupancy and lack of alternatives, a surveyor’s opinion on her limited means and inability to maintain the property, and photographs of water damage. She applied for public housing in 2021. As of April 2025 the building remained standing.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint solely under Article 8 (right to respect for home). It found that the domestic courts had carried out a proportionality assessment balancing environmental protection against the applicant’s conscious defiance of building restrictions. Any lack of deeper examination of personal circumstances was attributable to the applicant’s vague and unsubstantiated submissions. Italy had not overstepped its margin of appreciation. No violation was found. The judgment became final on 23 January 2026.

The case of Ayala Flores v. Italy (Application no. 16803/21) concerns a Peruvian national, Elisabeth Ayala Flores (born 1957), who alleged that Italy violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by enforcing a demolition order against her home without a sufficient proportionality assessment of its impact on her right to respect for her home.

In the early 1990s, the applicant and her husband erected a 30 m² unauthorized dwelling on the husband’s land on the island of Procida, in a highly seismic zone subject to landscape constraints and an absolute construction ban due to “specific environmental interest.” The municipality of Procida ascertained the violation in 1996 and issued restoration and demolition orders in 1996 and 1998. In 2002, the Pozzuoli District Court convicted the couple of unauthorized construction and of breaking police seals (after they further modified the sealed site). They received a suspended five-month prison sentence, a fine, and a demolition order. The Naples Court of Appeal upheld the core convictions in 2003 (some charges having become time-barred) and lifted a seizure solely to permit demolition; the judgment became final that October.

A 2004 application for a building amnesty went unanswered (such regularizations being unavailable in constrained areas). After her husband’s death in 2009 the applicant continued occupying the structure. In 2016 the public prosecutor initiated enforcement: the municipality served an eviction notice and the prosecutor ordered demolition within 90 days at the applicant’s expense if she failed to comply. She requested the municipality to recognize a public interest in retaining the building and lodged an “incidente di esecuzione” seeking annulment, revocation or stay of the demolition order.

Her initial submissions did not invoke Article 8. She later claimed to have filed additional pleadings asserting that the dwelling was her sole home of more than 15 years, that she faced financial hardship, and that demolition would be disproportionate (citing Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria). The Government disputed that these pleadings were ever filed. In November 2018 the Court of Appeal, sitting as enforcement court, dismissed the application, characterizing the demolition order as a mandatory restorative measure required to restore lawful land use. On appeal, the Court of Cassation (2020) declared the cassation application inadmissible for lack of self-sufficiency (the alleged Article 8 pleadings had not been attached). It nevertheless examined the substance, recalling ECHR case-law that an independent tribunal must assess proportionality in light of personal circumstances. It found the applicant’s Article 8 complaint generic: she had not identified specific circumstances outweighing the public interest in environmental protection and seismic safety, had no legitimate expectation of remaining in a building she knew to be illegal, and had not proved construction out of necessity.

Subsequent municipal inspections (2020–2024) recorded the site as uninhabited, overgrown, and used essentially for storage, with further unauthorized additions (fence, shutters). The applicant produced statements from two acquaintances, a surveyor’s report citing her age and limited means (monthly pension of €551, annual household income of €4,943), a 2001 residence certificate, and photographs of water damage. She also applied for public housing in 2021. As of April 2025 the structure remained standing.

The European Court held that the domestic courts had carried out the required proportionality assessment, balancing the applicant’s asserted home interest against her conscious, repeated defiance of building restrictions in a protected seismic and landscape area. Any lack of more detailed scrutiny was attributable to the vagueness of her submissions. Italy had not overstepped its margin of appreciation.
001-245683:
The case of Vasile Rusu v. Romania (Application no. 53021/20) concerns the applicant’s claim that appeal proceedings examining his conviction for economic and corruption offences were unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention. He alleged that the Timișoara Court of Appeal examined his appeal in absentia after failing to summon him lawfully and then refusing to stay or adjourn the hearing (or later to annul the judgment) despite COVID-19 travel restrictions that prevented him from attending in person from the United Kingdom.

The applicant, a company director born in 1963, was indicted on 25 July 2017 by the Timișoara anti-corruption prosecutor’s office, together with ten co-defendants, on charges of complicity in tax evasion, participation lato sensu in money laundering and membership of an organised criminal group. The charges arose from complex 2009 financial transactions involving petroleum products, fictitious contracts and alleged concealment of tax liabilities. The indictment relied on accounting documents, an expert report, wiretap transcripts and witness statements. The applicant had already been interviewed by prosecutors in March, April and July 2017.

On 2 April 2019 the Arad District Court convicted him of the first two offences (acquitting him of forming an organised criminal group), imposed a six-year sentence that, when combined with activation of a prior suspended sentence, totalled nine years’ imprisonment, and ordered him jointly liable for civil damages of approximately €3 million plus confiscation of a further modest sum. The applicant did not appear at first instance; summonses sent to his last known Romanian addresses went unanswered and he was represented solely by a court-appointed lawyer.

He lodged an appeal by fax on 4 April 2019 and immediately requested that all documents be served at a United Kingdom address evidenced by a December 2018 tenancy agreement he shared with his partner (a former witness in the case). The Court of Appeal complied, sending registered summonses to that address and assigning successive court-appointed counsel after the applicant complained of a conflict of interest. Hearings scheduled for June, September, October and November 2019 were adjourned, in part to allow him to instruct a lawyer of his choice. Registered letters were later reported lost by the British postal service. Letters rogatory were issued; UK police visited the address on three occasions in early 2020, confirmed through neighbours that the applicant resided there, but never obtained a signed receipt or personal service. Emails likewise went unanswered.

On 21 February 2020 the court severed the applicant’s appeal to avoid delaying the remaining appellants and fixed a hearing for 29 April 2020. Further service attempts, including a March 2020 letter rogatory, failed because of emerging pandemic restrictions. On 14–15 April and again on 27 April 2020 the applicant (via his partner’s email and fax) invoked the Romanian state-of-emergency decree of 16 March 2020 and requested either a stay of proceedings or an adjournment, citing cancelled flights, closed UK borders, mandatory quarantine and his wish to appear in person to “clarify the facts and demonstrate [his] innocence.” He indicated he intended to engage private counsel.

At the 29 April hearing the court-appointed lawyer supported the request but reported she had been unable to contact her client. The Court of Appeal refused both a stay (holding that the emergency decree expressly excluded money-laundering cases) and an adjournment (noting multiple prior postponements and viewing the request as dilatory). On 13 May 2020 it upheld the conviction and sentence, confirmed the civil award and cancelled the small confiscation order. The applicant’s subsequent extraordinary appeal for annulment under Article 426 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was dismissed on 8 September 2020: the court found he had been lawfully summoned (he knew the hearing date because he had asked for it to be adjourned) and had been able to inform the court of his absence, so neither statutory ground for annulment was met.

The applicant began serving his sentence in May 2023. These facts formed the basis of his complaint that he had been deprived of an effective opportunity to participate in person in the appeal that determined his conviction.

The case of Vasile Rusu v. Romania concerns alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention, specifically the right to a fair hearing and to defend oneself in person. The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1963, complained that his criminal appeal was examined in absentia due to alleged failures in summoning him properly and subsequent refusals to stay or adjourn proceedings amid COVID-19 travel restrictions, without granting a retrial.

In July 2017, the Timișoara anti-corruption prosecutor indicted the applicant (a company director) and ten others on charges of complicity in tax evasion, improper participation in money laundering, and forming an organised criminal group, arising from complex 2009 financial transactions involving petroleum products. Evidence included documents, an expert report, wiretaps, and statements. The applicant had been interviewed by prosecutors in March, April, and July 2017 after formal notification of charges.

On 2 April 2019, the Arad District Court convicted him of the first two offences (acquitting him of organised crime), imposing six years' imprisonment, plus activation of a prior suspended sentence for a total of nine years. Civilly, he and co-defendants were ordered to pay the State RON 14,195,391 (about EUR 3 million) in damages, with confiscation of excess proceeds (RON 53,067). The applicant was absent throughout first-instance proceedings despite summonses to his known Romanian addresses; he filed no documents or evidence requests and was represented only by a court-appointed lawyer.

The applicant appealed by fax on 4 and 12 April 2019, requesting that the judgment and documents be served at a UK address (supported by a December 2018 tenancy agreement with his partner, a former witness). He stated he no longer lived in Romania and had no contact with occupants of his former address. The Ministry of Finance and prosecutor also appealed, seeking increased damages/sentence and conviction on the organised-crime charge.

The Timișoara Court of Appeal summoned him to the UK address. A 26 June 2019 hearing was adjourned (at his faxed request referencing the date) to allow engagement of counsel, with a warning that this would be the sole such adjournment. On 24 September 2019, he emailed (from a company address, again referencing the next day's hearing) to replace his court-appointed lawyer due to a conflict of interest with a co-appellant; this was granted, and a new lawyer represented him thereafter. Hearings followed in October-November 2019 with registered-mail summonses to the UK (later declared lost by UK postal services). In December 2019, the court ordered letter-rogatory service and emails to addresses he had used. UK police visited the address three times without finding him (neighbours confirmed residency) and received no response to emails; no signed receipt was obtained.

On 21 February 2020, the court severed the applicant's appeal (new file number) to avoid delaying co-appellants, scheduling a hearing for 29 April 2020. Further summonses, including another letter rogatory amid emerging COVID-19, failed (UK authorities later refused due to constraints).

Via emails and faxes from his partner (14-15 and 27 April 2020), the applicant requested a stay under Romania's 16 March 2020 state-of-emergency decree (or adjournment of the 29 April hearing). He cited cancelled flights, closed UK borders (since 20 March), mandatory quarantine, inability to travel without approval pending a 4 June COVID test, and his wish to appear personally, clarify facts, prove innocence, and engage a lawyer. He referenced the new file number.

At the 29 April hearing, his court-appointed lawyer (who reported no communication with him) supported adjournment. The court rejected a stay, as the decree exempted money-laundering cases, and denied adjournment, citing multiple prior postponements and viewing the request as a delay tactic. The lawyer orally sought acquittal (or sentence reduction); no written submissions appear to have been filed. On 13 May 2020, the court upheld the conviction, sentence, and damages (annulling only the small confiscation).

On 5 September 2020, the applicant sought extraordinary annulment, arguing he had not been lawfully summoned (unserved at the UK address, unaware of the new file, no lawyer contact, notice-board display insufficient) and that rejecting his COVID-related requests violated his defence rights.

On 8 September 2020, the Court of Appeal dismissed this. He had been lawfully summoned via Romanian addresses, notice board, and letter rogatory (though not found at the UK address); he knew the 29 April date, as he requested its adjournment. Even if COVID prevented attendance, he had informed the court, failing the second statutory ground for annulment. Any error in rejecting adjournment was at most a judgment error, not a procedural flaw. The applicant began serving his sentence in May 2023.

The case of Vasile Rusu v. Romania (Application no. 53021/20) concerned a complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention that criminal appeal proceedings against the applicant were unfair because they were conducted in his absence. The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1963, was indicted in July 2017 by the Timișoara anti-corruption prosecutor’s office, along with ten others, on charges of complicity in tax evasion, improper participation in money laundering and membership of an organised criminal group. The charges related to complex 2009 financial transactions involving petroleum products and fictitious contracts, evidenced by documents, an expert accountancy report, wiretap transcripts and witness statements. The applicant had been interviewed three times during the investigation.

On 2 April 2019 the Arad District Court convicted him of the first two offences, sentencing him to six years’ imprisonment as a repeat offender and activating a prior suspended sentence for a total of nine years. He was acquitted of forming an organised criminal group. The court also ordered him (jointly with others) to pay approximately €3 million in damages to the State and confiscated a further modest sum. The applicant had been absent throughout the first-instance trial despite summonses to his known Romanian addresses and was represented by a court-appointed lawyer.

The applicant lodged an appeal by fax on 4 April 2019 and requested that documents be served at a United Kingdom address evidenced by a December 2018 tenancy agreement with his partner. The Ministry of Finance and the prosecutor also appealed. The Timișoara Court of Appeal summoned him at the UK address and appointed counsel. Hearings were adjourned in June 2019 to allow the appellants to instruct lawyers and again after the applicant successfully requested a change of counsel owing to a conflict of interest. Subsequent registered-letter summonses were lost in the UK postal system. The court therefore resorted to letters rogatory, emails and, after further unsuccessful attempts by British police, displayed summonses and used known electronic addresses. To avoid delaying the other appellants, the court severed the applicant’s case in February 2020 and fixed a hearing for 29 April 2020.

In April 2020, after COVID-19 travel restrictions were imposed, the applicant (via fax and his partner’s email) requested a stay of proceedings under Romania’s state-of-emergency decree or an adjournment, stating he wished to attend in person, engage a lawyer and give evidence. The court-appointed lawyer supported the request. The Court of Appeal refused both applications on 29 April 2020, holding that the decree excluded money-laundering cases and that further delay was unjustified given prior adjournments. The lawyer then argued for acquittal or a reduced sentence. On 13 May 2020 the court upheld the conviction and sentence, confirmed the damages award and cancelled the small confiscation order.

The applicant’s subsequent extraordinary appeal for annulment, claiming unlawful summons and inability to appear because of the pandemic, was dismissed on 8 September 2020. The Court of Appeal found he had been lawfully summoned (or at least knew the hearing date, having requested its adjournment) and had informed the court of his absence, so the statutory grounds for annulment were not met. He began serving his sentence in May 2023.

The European Court held that the in-absentia examination and refusal of a retrial were not disproportionate. The applicant had been lawfully summoned, possessed concrete knowledge of the proceedings through his own communications, and was represented throughout. Rejection of the COVID-related adjournment request was reasonable in light of earlier delays and the overall fairness of the proceedings.

**Case Summary: Zakaidze v. Georgia (ECtHR, App. no. 42199/22)**

The case concerns the alleged ineffectiveness of Georgian criminal proceedings following a physical assault on the applicant, Mr Besik Zakaidze (born 1973), by three neighbours on 9 February 2021. The altercation began when the applicant demanded repayment of a loan; it ended with all three neighbours beating him. Emergency services recorded speech and swallowing difficulties due to lower-jaw pain and deformation, plus nausea. Hospital diagnosis included bilateral mandibular fractures, nasal excoriations, intracranial trauma and concussion. After two jaw surgeries he was discharged on 16 February 2021. A psychiatrist later recommended psychotherapy.

A criminal investigation opened the same day under Article 126 § 11(b) of the Criminal Code (group violence). The applicant was interviewed in hospital; the three suspects (two of whom were 19 and 20) promptly confessed to verbal and physical assault and were not detained. On-site inspection, photography and witness interviews (including the emergency doctor) followed. On 9 March 2021 the applicant complained of delay and sought details of charges and the supervising prosecutor. Forensic examination of his medical file was ordered on 10 March.

On 19 April the applicant petitioned the Chief Prosecutor and Interior Ministry Inspectorate, arguing that the legal classification was unduly lenient given the group nature of the attack, the need for third-party intervention to stop it, his diminished working capacity, medical costs and psychological harm. He requested reclassification, victim status and information on investigative steps. Victim status was granted on 21 April 2021. He signed a standard form listing his rights under Articles 57–58 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that contained a pre-typed waiver of his right to review the case file or receive progress updates. On 24 May he alleged that the investigator had misled him into signing the waiver, pressured him to minimise the violence in his statement and ignored his complaints; he again sought file access. The complaint went unanswered. The prosecutor declined diversion for the younger suspects because of the seriousness of the acts.

A 1 July 2021 forensic report classified the jaw fractures and concussion as less-severe injuries causing long-term health harm, consistent with the date of the assault; isolated abrasions were deemed minor. On 8 July charges were reclassified to Article 118 § 3 (intentionally causing less-serious harm to health under aggravating circumstances). Fresh victim status was granted.

On 22 July 2021 the Mtskheta District Court held a remote hearing at which the defendants again pleaded guilty. The applicant was not notified and did not attend. Invoking the parties’ agreement not to contest the evidence, the court applied simplified procedure, convicted all three and imposed three-year suspended prison sentences plus a non-contact order. On 2 August the applicant complained to the prosecutor that he had not been heard, that the sentences were disproportionate to his injuries and damage, and that he had been denied file access; he requested an appeal. The first-instance court later refused him a copy of the judgment, stating he should have sought access earlier.

The prosecution appealed for a harsher penalty. The applicant independently asked the Tbilisi Court of Appeal for an oral hearing so that he could give evidence. On 3 November 2021 that court, sitting with the applicant present, increased the sentences to four years’ imprisonment (still suspended) plus 200 hours’ community service. It cited the defendants’ guilty pleas, lack of prior convictions, cooperation and non-reoffending, and held that a victim’s desire for severity could not dictate the penalty. No evidence was examined because the appeal was limited to sentence. The Supreme Court on 30 May 2022 rejected the prosecution’s further appeal, noting that any compensation claim could be pursued separately in civil proceedings and that non-payment of damages was irrelevant to sentencing.

In February 2023 the applicant’s subsequent civil claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage was dismissed for non-payment of court fees; the courts held that the statutory exemption for crime-related compensation did not cover non-pecuniary loss. The decision was upheld on appeal.

The applicant complained to the European Court under Articles 2, 6 and 8, alleging an ineffective investigation and trial that failed to secure an adequate response to a serious assault causing lasting physical and psychological harm, while systematically excluding him from the proceedings. The Court examined the matter principally under the procedural limb of Article 3.

The case concerns an allegedly ineffective investigation and prosecution of a violent assault on the applicant, Besik Zakaidze, by three neighbours. On 9 February 2021, a dispute over unpaid debt escalated into a group beating. An ambulance recorded the applicant’s difficulty speaking and swallowing, jaw deformation and nausea. Hospital diagnosis confirmed bilateral mandibular fractures (fragmentary on the right, linear on the left), nasal abrasions, intracranial trauma and concussion. Two jaw surgeries followed; he was discharged in stable condition on 16 February. A psychiatrist later recommended psychotherapy.

A criminal investigation opened the same day under Article 126 § 11(b) of the Criminal Code (group violence). The applicant was interviewed in hospital; the three suspects (two of whom were 19 and 20) immediately confessed and were not remanded. Scene photographs, an on-site inspection and witness statements (including the emergency doctor) were obtained. On 10 March a forensic examination of the medical file was ordered. The expert report of 1 July classified the jaw fractures and concussion as “less serious bodily harm” causing long-term health damage, caused by a blunt object and consistent with the date of the incident; the abrasions were “minor.”

The applicant repeatedly complained of investigative shortcomings. On 9 March he sought the prosecutor’s identity and details of the charges. On 19 April he asked the Chief Prosecutor and the Interior Ministry Inspectorate to reclassify the offence as more serious, grant him victim status and disclose investigative steps; no reply was received. Victim status was conferred on 21 April, but the applicant later alleged that the investigator had tricked him into signing a waiver of his rights to inspect the file and receive progress updates. A 24 May complaint about this alleged deception, investigator pressure to minimise the violence, and lack of information went unanswered. On 8 July the charges were reclassified to Article 118 § 3 (intentional less-serious harm to health with aggravating circumstances). Fresh victim-status papers again listed his rights.

The Mtskheta District Court held a hearing on 22 July 2021 with the prosecutor and the three defendants appearing online; the applicant was never notified and did not attend. Because the parties accepted the evidence, the court applied simplified procedure, convicted the defendants as charged and imposed three-year suspended prison terms plus a non-contact order. The applicant immediately protested that he had been excluded, that the sentences were disproportionate to the bilateral jaw fractures, concussion and psychological harm, and that he had been denied access to the file. The first-instance court refused access, stating it should have been requested at the pre-trial stage.

The prosecution appealed for a heavier penalty. The applicant wrote directly to the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, repeating his exclusion complaint and requesting an oral hearing at which he could testify. On 3 November 2021 the appeal court, sitting with the applicant present, increased the sentences to four years’ imprisonment (still suspended) plus 200 hours’ community service. No evidence was re-examined; the court merely read the applicant’s written submissions. It reasoned that the offence was “less serious,” that the defendants had confessed, had no prior convictions and had not reoffended, and that a victim’s call for a custodial sentence was not decisive. The Supreme Court on 30 May 2022 declared the prosecution’s further appeal inadmissible, adding that the applicant could pursue separate civil compensation (a later civil claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage was dismissed for non-payment of court fees).

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation and prosecution of the assault, in particular by inadequate legal classification, exclusion of the victim from key stages, and imposition of unduly lenient sanctions.

The court cited the defendants’ guilty pleas, lack of prior convictions, cooperation and family circumstances, observing that a victim’s desire for severity could not dictate the sentence. The Supreme Court on 30 May 2022 declared the prosecution’s points-of-law appeal inadmissible, noting that any compensation claim could be pursued separately in civil proceedings.

A subsequent civil action for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages was dismissed in 2023 for non-payment of court fees; the courts held that the statutory exemption for crime-related claims did not cover non-pecuniary loss.

These facts underpin the applicant’s allegations of a procedurally deficient investigation and prosecution under Article 3 of the Convention: incomplete information and participation rights, delayed and arguably under-classified charges, exclusion from the first-instance hearing, and ultimately suspended sentences that he regarded as inadequate to the gravity of the group assault and its lasting physical and psychological consequences.
001-245701:
The case of Kyrian v. the Czech Republic (App. no. 15956/23) involves a complaint under Article 8 ECHR (private life) by David Kyrian, the biological father of a boy born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship. The mother's husband was presumed the legal father, and the child lived with the legal parents. Kyrian confirmed paternity via DNA in 2015.

Until early 2016, Kyrian had informal contact (2–4 visits monthly). In April 2016 he sought formal contact rights under Civil Code Art. 927 (for persons with a close relationship if the child has a non-temporary emotional bond and lack of contact would harm the child). The Příbram District Court granted Wednesday afternoon visits plus every second Sunday in summer, noting a positive relationship interrupted by the mother. The Prague Regional Court upheld this, acknowledging the child's right to know his biological father.

Conflicts soon arose. Visits became supervised; the child's psychological state worsened. In 2017 Kyrian sought expanded contact; the mother sought a ban, citing verbal abuse, the child's refusals, anxiety and psychologist visits. After a quashed first-instance decision, mediation produced an approved 2018 agreement replicating the earlier schedule. Further refusals, an incident requiring police, and two unsuccessful supervised visits followed. A psychologist reported the child's strong attachment to his legal parents, stress with unfamiliar persons, and advised against forced contact.

In late 2018 the legal parents sought a prohibition. In 2020 the Český Krumlov District Court and České Budějovice Regional Court refused any contact regime: no positive emotional bond existed, and lack of contact was not shown to be harmful. An expert psychologist found the child (who had developmental delay) caught in a parental triangle, mirroring the legal parents' hostility, strongly attached to his legal father, and burdened by Kyrian's persistent pressure. The courts held it in the child's best interests to de-escalate via professional help; contact could be reconsidered later. The Constitutional Court dismissed Kyrian's 2022 appeal as manifestly ill-founded.

In April 2021 Kyrian renewed his request for Wednesday visits. Expert reports of March 2022 described prior visits as traumatic, producing a negative attitude; given the child's delays and family complexity, contact was not recommended (though possible later if Kyrian respected the child's needs). The child's psychologist confirmed anxiety in new settings. At the hearing Kyrian alternatively sought written contact via the guardian ad litem and regular information on the child's development. The legal parents refused, citing ongoing distress and Kyrian's lingering near the kindergarten/home (bordering on stalking). The guardian opposed all requests.

On 24 March 2022 the District Court dismissed the claim, warning the legal parents to respect biological parenthood. Contact failed Art. 927 conditions and was contrary to the child's best interests: no positive bond, coercive tactics by Kyrian, and the child's strong attachment to the legal parents. Information rights belonged to holders of parental responsibility; given the child's attitude, providing data was not in his interests. The Regional Court upheld this (12 September 2022), treating information as incidental to contact under Art. 927 and finding no other justification. The Constitutional Court dismissed a further appeal (24 January 2023).

Subsequent events: the legal parents divorced (April 2022) and shared custody until the mother moved out and resumed her relationship with Kyrian, giving him occasional contact through her. In 2024 custody proceedings the child expressed fear of Kyrian and unwillingness to see his mother because of him. The child was placed with the legal father; the mother's later contact application was refused because she would not meet the child without Kyrian.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 8 interference by denying both personal contact and information about the child.

The case of Kyrian v. the Czech Republic (ECHR Application no. 15956/23) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life). The applicant, a Czech national born in 1982, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the mother. Under legal presumption of paternity, the mother’s then-husband became the child’s legal father; the child lived with the legal parents. The applicant confirmed biological paternity via DNA testing in 2015.

Until February 2016, the applicant had contact with the child two to four times monthly during the mother’s visits. In April 2016, he applied to the Příbram District Court for contact rights under Article 927 of the Civil Code (for persons socially close to the child, requiring a non-temporary emotional bond and harm from lack of contact). A May 2016 judgment (upheld on appeal) granted him Wednesday-afternoon visits plus every second Sunday in summer holidays, noting a positive relationship interrupted by the mother and the child’s right to know his biological father.

Conflicts soon arose between the applicant and the mother (and later the legal father), prompting supervised visits. Visits continued into 2017 but the child’s psychological condition deteriorated. In September 2017, the applicant sought expanded rights; the mother sought prohibition, citing verbal abuse, the child’s refusals, anxiety, and psychologist visits (with allegations of physical assault on the legal father). After further proceedings and mediation, a 2018 agreement restored similar contact, but visits failed due to the child’s refusals, a police-involved incident, and conflicts in supervised settings. An October 2018 psychologist report found the child strongly attached to his legal parents, stressed by unfamiliar people, and potentially harmed by imposed contact.

In 2020 proceedings, courts refused any contact regime. They cited no positive emotional bond and no harm from lack of contact, relying on an expert report: the child (with developmental delay) was caught in a conflictual “relationship triangle,” mirrored the legal parents’ hostility, and was securely attached to the legal father. The applicant’s persistent pressure had burdened the child, fostering a negative attitude. Courts prioritized calming the situation via professional help, leaving future contact possible.

A 2021 application for Wednesday visits was dismissed in March 2022 (upheld on appeal). Expert reports described past visits as traumatic, reinforcing the child’s negative attitude; given developmental delays and family complexity, forced contact was inappropriate. The applicant’s additional request for written contact via the guardian ad litem and regular information on the child’s development/education/health was also refused. Courts held that information rights form part of parental responsibility (which the applicant lacked) and that, absent any positive bond and given the child’s rejection, providing information was not in the child’s best interests. Legal parents opposed it, citing ongoing distress and the applicant’s lingering near the child’s kindergarten/home (bordering on stalking). The child’s guardian ad litem supported dismissal.

The applicant’s constitutional appeals were dismissed as manifestly ill-founded. Subsequent events included the legal parents’ 2022 divorce (with joint custody initially, then exclusive custody to the legal father). The mother resumed a relationship with the applicant (enabling some contact via her), but the child later expressed fear of the applicant and refused contact with the mother unless the applicant was absent.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 8 interference: the courts’ refusals of contact and information, despite the applicant’s biological paternity and initial bond, based on the child’s negative reaction, conflicts, expert assessments of trauma/developmental issues, and prioritization of the child’s best interests and family stability.

The case of Kyrian v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 15956/23) concerns the applicant’s unsuccessful attempts to obtain court-ordered contact with, and information about, his biological son, born in December 2013. The child was conceived during an extramarital relationship; by operation of the legal presumption of paternity the mother’s husband became the legal father and the boy lived with the married couple. A privately obtained DNA test in 2015 confirmed the applicant’s biological paternity.

Until February 2016 the applicant saw the child two to four times a month. In April 2016 he applied under Article 927 of the Civil Code for formal contact rights. The District Court granted limited contact (Wednesday afternoons and alternate Sundays in summer) in a provisionally enforceable judgment of 18 May 2016, later upheld by the Regional Court. The courts noted an emotional bond but also a conflictual relationship between the applicant and the legal parents.

Thereafter relations deteriorated. Visits became sources of conflict; the child displayed anxiety and began seeing a psychologist. The applicant sought more extensive contact while the mother sought its prohibition. After mediation an agreement replicating the earlier schedule was approved in July 2018, yet visits soon failed because of the child’s refusal. Supervised meetings in October 2018 also collapsed amid conflict. A psychologist reported that the child was strongly attached to his legal parents, that imposed contact was stressful, and that he should not be forced to see the applicant.

In December 2018 the legal parents applied to terminate contact. Relying on an expert psychological assessment that described the child (who had developmental delay) as caught in a relational triangle, very attached to his legal father, and mirroring the parents’ hostility, the courts in 2020 declined to set any contact regime. They found no lasting positive emotional bond and concluded that further pressure from the applicant would harm the child. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in October 2022, observing that the situation could be reassessed if relations improved.

In April 2021 the applicant filed a fresh application seeking Wednesday contact, later adding a request for written communication and regular information about the child’s health and education. A 2022 expert report attributed the child’s negative attitude to traumatic earlier visits and developmental difficulties; it advised against any contact at that time. The child’s psychologist confirmed anxiety attacks. The legal parents opposed all contact, citing the child’s distress and the applicant’s lingering near the kindergarten and home. The District Court dismissed the claims in March 2022, holding that Article 927’s conditions were not met, that the applicant’s coercive conduct had prevented de-escalation, and that the child had a strong bond with his legal parents. Information rights, being an aspect of parental responsibility, were also refused as contrary to the child’s interests. The Regional Court and Constitutional Court upheld these conclusions.

Subsequent events confirmed the child’s continuing rejection of the applicant: after the legal parents’ divorce the mother resumed her relationship with him, but the child expressed fear of the applicant and was ultimately placed in the legal father’s sole custody.

The applicant alleged that the persistent refusal of contact and information violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention.
001-246128:
The case of Rasmussen and Others v. Denmark (ECtHR, Application no. 2390/24, judgment of 25 November 2025) arose from the accidental death by drug overdose of prisoner J.F. on 17 November 2017 at Kragskovhede Prison. His mother, wife and child alleged that Denmark had failed to fulfil its positive obligations under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention to protect his life and provide adequate medical care and supervision.

J.F., a known addict to benzodiazepines and other substances serving a sentence, was transferred to the prison on 22 September 2017. On the morning of 16 November he saw the prison nurse and began antibiotics for a dental abscess. That evening, around 7.40 p.m., officer L.R. noted that J.F. appeared intoxicated. Fellow inmate M.V.T. claimed J.F. had stolen a bottle of 100 methadone tablets from the dispensary that morning (when a nurse’s colleague briefly left the room) and had taken too many. L.R. contacted the nurse, who confirmed that methadone bottles were kept but later could not confirm or disprove a missing bottle. J.F. was moved to the medical unit for observation; officers were instructed to call a doctor or emergency services if his condition worsened. Officers M.B. and J.P. spoke with him; he denied taking anything except antibiotics. M.B. took him outside to smoke and to the library for books, assessing that he could walk, light a cigarette and find books without staggering and that his intoxication level was no worse than usual (he often appeared intoxicated). He was placed in a disciplinary cell near the staff office (used provisionally, as the prison lacked approved observation cells). His own cell was searched around 8.45 p.m., revealing cardboard with two lines of powder (later destroyed without analysis). Night-shift officer P.M. observed him hourly from outside the cell (at least at 11 p.m. and 11.55 p.m.); he was snoring or moving. At 12.15 a.m. on 17 November he was unresponsive. Staff administered first aid and called an ambulance; he was pronounced dead at 1.10 a.m.

An autopsy established death from poisoning by methadone, oxycodone, fentanyl and benzodiazepines (J.F. was not on regular opioid treatment). Police discontinued a criminal investigation, finding no offence. The Patient Safety Authority later classified the prison as having major patient-safety problems and issued an enforcement notice on medicine storage and administration. The Prison and Probation Service and Parliamentary Ombudsman criticised failures to follow internal instructions (no doctor called, no set observation times, no stock management, no formal search or urine sample). The prison subsequently tightened dispensary access and stock procedures.

In civil proceedings the District Court found the prison liable: staff should have recognised a significant overdose risk and called a doctor, violating the duty to protect life; it awarded each applicant DKK 150,000 (reduced for J.F.’s contributory negligence in taking the tablets). The High Court reversed. It accepted that J.F. frequently appeared intoxicated, that staff reasonably assessed his condition as not unusually severe after conversations and observation of his abilities, that he repeatedly denied extra drugs, that hourly checks showed no deterioration, and that they followed the nurse’s advice. The actions did not breach Articles 2 or 3 (citing Marro v. Italy and Patsaki v. Greece). Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

The ECtHR held that the domestic courts had thoroughly examined the facts in light of its case-law. It was not established that the authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to J.F.’s life; they had taken basic precautions to protect his health.

The case of Rasmussen and Others v. Denmark arose from the accidental death by drug overdose of prisoner J.F. on 17 November 2017. His mother, wife and child alleged that Denmark had failed in its positive obligations under Articles 2 and 3 ECHR to protect his life and prevent inhuman or degrading treatment.

J.F., a known addict to benzodiazepines and other substances, was transferred to Kragskovhede Prison on 22 September 2017. On the morning of 16 November he saw the prison nurse for a dental abscess and started antibiotics. Around 7.40 p.m. officer L.R. observed him appearing intoxicated. Fellow inmate M.V.T. reported that J.F. had stolen a bottle of 100 methadone tablets from the dispensary that morning (when a colleague left him unattended briefly) and had taken too many. L.R. contacted the nurse; they agreed to transfer J.F. to the medical unit for observation and to call a doctor or emergency services only if his condition deteriorated.

Officers M.B. and J.P. spoke with J.F. in the medical unit. He denied taking anything other than antibiotics. M.B. assessed him as not severely intoxicated (able to walk without staggering, light a cigarette and select books in the library) and similar to his usual medicated appearance. J.F. was placed in a provisional observation cell (a disciplinary cell near the staff office) rather than an approved observation cell. No formal body search or urine test occurred. His own cell was later searched, revealing cardboard with two lines of unidentified powder (destroyed without analysis). Night-shift officer P.M. observed J.F. hourly from outside the cell (at least at 11 p.m. and 11.55 p.m.), noting him snoring or moving. At 12.15 a.m. on 17 November he was unresponsive. Staff administered first aid and called an ambulance; J.F. was declared dead at 1.10 a.m.

Autopsy and toxicology established death from combined poisoning by methadone, oxycodone, fentanyl and benzodiazepines. The dispensary had locked cabinets, but lacked stock monitoring; it could not be confirmed whether a methadone bottle had gone missing.

Police investigated the officers but discontinued proceedings, finding no criminal offence. The Danish Patient Safety Authority inspected the prison, classified it as having major patient-safety problems and issued an enforcement notice on medicine storage and administration. The Prison and Probation Service itself criticised failures to follow internal instructions (no doctor contacted, incomplete observation plan, no search or urine sample, powder destroyed). The Parliamentary Ombudsman noted the criticisms but took no further action. The prison later tightened dispensary access, refurbished facilities and introduced stock-management procedures.

In subsequent civil proceedings the District Court found the authorities liable. It held that staff ought to have recognised a significant overdose risk, that a doctor should have been called, and that the duty to protect J.F.’s life had been breached; it awarded non-pecuniary damages (reduced for J.F.’s contributory negligence). The High Court reversed. It accepted that J.F. frequently appeared intoxicated, that staff had reasonably assessed his condition as no worse than usual on the basis of conversations, behaviour and hourly checks showing no deterioration, that he had repeatedly denied taking drugs, and that a doctor had not been required. It found no breach of Article 2 or 3. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

The European Court of Human Rights, examining the facts in light of its case-law, concluded that the domestic courts had thoroughly reviewed the matter. It had not been established that the prison authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to J.F.’s life, and they had taken basic precautions to protect his health. No violation of Article 2 (substantive) was found.

The case of Rasmussen and Others v. Denmark (ECHR, Application no. 2390/24) arose from the death of prisoner J.F. on 17 November 2017 from an accidental drug overdose at Kragskovhede Prison. His mother, wife and child alleged that Danish authorities failed in their positive obligations under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention to protect his life and prevent ill-treatment through adequate supervision and medical care.

J.F., serving a sentence and known as a long-term abuser of benzodiazepines and other substances, had been transferred to the prison on 22 September 2017. On the morning of 16 November he saw the prison nurse and began antibiotics for a dental abscess. That evening around 7.40 p.m. officer L.R. observed him appearing intoxicated. Fellow inmate M.V.T. reported that J.F. had stolen a bottle of 100 methadone tablets from the unlocked dispensary earlier that day (when a nurse briefly left) and had taken too many.

Staff moved J.F. to the medical unit. Officers M.B. and J.P. spoke with him; he denied taking anything except the antibiotics and attributed his condition to them. They noted he could walk without staggering, light a cigarette and select books from a low shelf, concluding his intoxication matched his usual appearance (he was frequently intoxicated). The nurse confirmed the antibiotics, advised observation and instructed staff to call a doctor or emergency services if he deteriorated. J.F. was placed in a nearby disciplinary cell used provisionally for observation (the prison lacked approved observation cells). His own cell was searched around 8.45 p.m., revealing cardboard with two lines of unidentified powder (later destroyed without analysis). No formal body search or urine test occurred.

Night officer P.M. conducted hourly visual checks from outside the cell (at least at 11 p.m. and 11.55 p.m.); J.F. was seen snoring or moving. At 12.15 a.m. on 17 November he was found unresponsive. First aid was given and an ambulance called, but he was declared dead at 1.10 a.m.

Autopsy and toxicology established death by combined poisoning from methadone, oxycodone, fentanyl and benzodiazepines, at levels consistent with severe or lethal overdose (especially given J.F. was not regularly prescribed opioids). Police investigation found no criminal offence by staff. The Prison and Probation Service criticised its own handling: no medicine stock control (a methadone bottle may have gone missing), no doctor called, observations not strictly timed, no search or urine sample, and the powder destroyed. The Parliamentary Ombudsman endorsed these findings. The Patient Safety Authority later identified major medicine-storage problems and issued an enforcement notice; the prison subsequently improved procedures.

In civil compensation proceedings the District Court found staff should have recognised a significant overdose risk from the inmate’s report and J.F.’s condition, that failure to call a doctor breached the duty to protect life, and awarded each applicant DKK 150 000 (reduced for J.F.’s contributory negligence in taking the tablets). The High Court reversed, holding that staff reasonably assessed J.F.’s intoxication as typical based on his behaviour, repeated denials and the nurse’s confirmation of antibiotics. Hourly observations revealed no deterioration. The authorities’ actions therefore complied with Articles 2 and 3 (citing ECHR case-law such as Marro v. Italy). Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused.

These facts formed the core of the alleged failures to take reasonable steps once a risk of overdose became known.
001-247555:
The case of Vekua v. Georgia (Application no. 43537/22) concerns complaints by Nana Vekua under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention (fair trial and presumption of innocence) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). It arose from administrative proceedings that followed the discontinuation of criminal proceedings against her as time-barred.

In December 1991 the Poti municipality issued a decision transferring two buildings to Interterminali-Poti Ltd, a company founded by the applicant (then head of the municipality’s Economic Affairs Department). The underlying land (3,516 sq. m) was transferred in 1993 and title was registered in the company’s name in 1998. In 2009 the applicant purchased half the plot (1,750 sq. m) from the company.

A criminal investigation opened in 2012 into allegations that the applicant had fraudulently obtained registration of title to State property (then assigned to the Ministry of Defence) by using a forged 1991 municipal decision. The National Agency of State Property was granted victim status. In May 2017 the investigation was discontinued because the limitation period had expired. The prosecutor’s decision nevertheless stated that the applicant had committed aggravated fraud by using the forged document to register title in her company’s name and later acquire half the plot, though she was exempted from liability. Her appeal, in which she maintained her innocence and claimed damage to her reputation, was rejected.

One month later the Property Agency brought proceedings seeking annulment of the 1998 registration and the 2009 purchase agreement, plus damages. The case was split: administrative courts were to examine annulment of the registration (with the applicant joined as a third party), while civil claims against her were suspended. In January 2020 the Poti City Court annulled the registration. It relied extensively on the 2017 prosecutor’s decision, reproducing its evidence and findings that the 1991 decision was forged, that the applicant knew this because it benefited her company, and that she had used it to obtain State property. The court fully agreed with the prosecutor’s factual and legal assessment, treating the unappealable prosecutorial decision as confirmatory evidence of forgery, and considered other material.

The applicant appealed, arguing that there was no independent forensic examination, that the court had treated the prosecutor’s findings as res judicata without its own assessment, and that this breached the presumption of innocence and her property rights. In July 2021 the Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision, recapping the investigation evidence and additional material from the parties and concluding that the 1991 decision was falsified and the 1998 registration therefore unlawful. It did not address the presumption-of-innocence complaint. In March 2022 the Supreme Court rejected her cassation appeal, endorsing that the registration had not complied with the applicable legislation because the company lacked a valid document of title.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations: the administrative courts’ language and heavy reliance on discontinued criminal findings were claimed to impute criminal guilt, undermine overall fairness, and unlawfully interfere with property rights.

The case of Vekua v. Georgia (Application no. 43537/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns complaints by Nana Vekua under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention (fair trial and presumption of innocence) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). These arose from administrative proceedings that followed the discontinuation of criminal proceedings against her as time-barred.

In December 1991, while the applicant served as head of the Economic Affairs Department of Poti municipality, a municipal decision transferred two buildings to Interterminali-Poti Ltd, a company she had founded. The underlying 3,516 sq. m plot of land was transferred to the company in 1993. In December 1998, at her request and based on those documents, the Public Registry registered title in the company’s name. In August 2009 she purchased half the plot (1,750 sq. m) from the company; she later sold her shares.

A criminal investigation opened in June 2012 into allegations that the applicant had fraudulently registered title using a falsified 1991 municipal decision. The buildings were in fact State property assigned to the Ministry of Defence. The National Agency of State Property was granted victim status. In May 2017 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation because the limitation period had expired, but the decision stated that the applicant had committed aggravated fraud under Article 180 § 3(b) of the Criminal Code by using a forged document to register title and obtain pecuniary benefit. She was exempted from liability solely on limitation grounds. The applicant appealed, disputing the findings, maintaining her innocence and arguing that the decision harmed her reputation; the appeal was rejected in June 2017.

One month later the Property Agency brought proceedings seeking annulment of the 1998 registration, the 2009 purchase agreement and damages. The case was split: administrative proceedings (in which the applicant was joined as a third party) concerned annulment of the registration, while civil proceedings concerning the remaining claims were stayed.

In January 2020 the Poti City Court annulled the 1998 registration. It relied heavily on the 2017 prosecutorial decision, quoting that the 1991 document was forged, that the applicant knew this because it conferred a proprietary interest on her company, and that she had prepared and used the forged document to acquire State property. The court stated that it “fully agrees with the factual circumstances, legal assessment and conclusion” of the prosecutor, treating the unappealable prosecutorial decision as conclusive evidence of forgery.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the 1991 decision was not forged (no forensic examination had been conducted), that the court had adopted the prosecutor’s findings as res judicata without independent assessment, and that this violated her presumption of innocence and property rights. In July 2021 the Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision, again reciting the prosecutor’s findings that the document was forged and that the applicant knew this, and concluding that the materials “unequivocally prove” falsification and the unlawfulness of the registration. It did not address the presumption-of-innocence argument. In March 2022 the Supreme Court rejected her cassation appeal as inadmissible, endorsing the conclusion that registration had been unlawful because the company lacked a valid document conferring possession.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s claims that the administrative courts’ extensive reproduction of, and agreement with, the prosecutor’s statements of criminal guilt after discontinuation of the criminal case violated her presumption of innocence, rendered the proceedings unfair, and unlawfully interfered with her property. The European Court later found no violation of Article 6 § 2, holding that the wording, viewed in the context of administrative proceedings, could not reasonably be read as an affirmation of criminal liability.
