The case of Cavca v. the Republic of Moldova concerns disciplinary proceedings that led to the dismissal of Ivan Cavca, head of a territorial subdivision of the Environmental Protection Inspectorate (EPI). Cavca, who had no prior disciplinary record, alleged that he was incited by an undercover state agent to accept a bribe during a professional integrity test, in violation of his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (civil limb).

On 29 February 2019, the National Anti-Corruption Centre (NAC) launched integrity testing of EPI staff under Law no. 325, citing corruption risks identified from prior reports, a Court of Auditors decision, NGO findings, statistics and confirmed cases. A Chișinău Court judge authorised the testing (including its planned random application and subsequent evaluation) on 5 March 2019.

On 22 May 2019 an undercover agent, S., telephoned Cavca’s office to report illegal tree-felling. At the indicated site Cavca found S. with a chainsaw and a felled tree. S. proposed an unofficial resolution and offered various items as a bribe; Cavca refused, recorded an administrative offence and imposed a fine. S. later returned to prove payment. Cavca insisted on confiscating the chainsaw. After a conversation they stepped outside, where (according to the authorities) Cavca indicated he needed the tool and directed S. to leave it in a car. S. secretly recorded the entire sequence.

On 28 January 2020 the same judge reviewed the recordings and other materials from multiple tests and confirmed that Cavca (and others) had failed. The judge stated that the NAC had shown the officials would have acted identically without state involvement, but gave no particulars. Cavca was neither summoned nor heard; only the EPI could appeal the confirmation.

The EPI disciplinary commission, after hearing Cavca, recommended dismissal for breaches of internal rules and the Law on public functions. He was dismissed on 19 May 2020.

Cavca challenged the decision in court, arguing incitement and disproportionality. On 3 November 2020 the Chișinău Court rejected the claim, relying on the videos (said to demonstrate propensity), Cavca’s subsequent reimbursement of the chainsaw’s value, and the 28 January confirmation. It recorded NAC comments on the dialogue but ignored the entrapment plea. The Court of Appeal (12 May 2021) and Supreme Court (27 October 2021, appeal declared inadmissible) upheld the outcome without addressing entrapment or the statutory requirement (section 28 of Law no. 325) that officials be notified in writing, and countersign, that they might be tested. Cavca invoked an earlier Supreme Court ruling (F., 2016) in which lack of notification had rendered a similar dismissal unlawful.

A later application to reopen proceedings, based on a 7 December 2021 Constitutional Court judgment striking down parts of section 17 of Law no. 325 (because officials could not participate in or appeal the confirmation hearing, whose findings bound later courts and thereby impaired the right to a fair trial), was refused.

The Strasbourg Court held that integrity testing is not inherently incompatible with Article 6 § 1, but requires robust procedural safeguards in planning, execution and review. The domestic courts had failed to examine Cavca’s arguable entrapment claim effectively or to respect equality of arms and adversarial process, producing flagrant deficiencies.

The case of Cavca v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 21766/22) concerns alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights in disciplinary proceedings that led to the dismissal of a public official following a professional integrity test. The applicant, Ivan Cavca, born in 1988, served as head of a territorial subdivision of the Environmental Protection Inspectorate (EPI) and had no prior disciplinary sanctions.

On 29 February 2019, the National Anti-Corruption Centre (NAC) initiated integrity testing of EPI employees under Law no. 325 on the assessment of institutional integrity. This followed identification of corruption risks from reports, audits, NGO data, statistics, and prior cases. A Chișinău Court judge authorised the testing on 5 March 2019 after reviewing its necessity and planned random application to EPI officials.

On 22 May 2019, an undercover agent, S., telephoned the applicant’s office to report illegal tree felling. At the site, the applicant found S. using a chainsaw to fell a tree. S. proposed resolving the matter unofficially and offered various items as a bribe. The applicant refused, recorded the administrative offence, and imposed a fine. S. later returned to the applicant’s office with proof of payment. The applicant stated he must confiscate the chainsaw. S. indicated this was not an issue as he possessed another. According to the Government, the applicant gestured for silence to avoid being overheard; they then stepped outside, where the applicant explained he had recorded the offence due to a prior complaint and a local forester’s presence, and promised future assistance if warned in advance. When S. asked if the applicant needed the chainsaw (implicitly offering it as a bribe), the applicant accepted and indicated a vehicle in which to leave it. S. secretly recorded the encounters.

On 28 January 2020, the same judge who had authorised the testing reviewed materials, including audiovisual recordings, for multiple officials. He confirmed that the applicant (and others) had failed the test and stated that the NAC had shown the misconduct would have occurred even without State involvement, without providing details. The applicant was neither summoned nor permitted to make submissions. Only the EPI could appeal this decision.

The NAC then requested that the EPI examine the materials. After hearing the applicant, the EPI disciplinary commission on 8 May 2020 proposed dismissal for failing the integrity test and breaching internal rules, including the Law on public functions. The EPI dismissed the applicant on 19 May 2020, citing actions that damaged the authority’s prestige, breaches of conduct rules, and violations of legal duties.

The applicant challenged the dismissal in court on 18 June 2020, arguing incitement to the disciplinary offence and a disproportionate sanction. On 3 November 2020, the Chișinău Court (Râșcani Office) dismissed the action. It relied on video recordings showing the applicant’s propensity to offend, his subsequent reimbursement of the chainsaw’s cost, and the 28 January 2020 confirmation. It noted a NAC representative’s account of the exchanges but did not address the entrapment claim.

The applicant appealed, emphasising that the recording showed S. actively offering brandy, fish, money, and the chainsaw rather than passively observing an offence. He also argued that the EPI had failed to notify him, as required by section 28 of Law no. 325, that his integrity might be tested and obtain his countersignature. On 12 May 2021, the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance decision for the same reasons, without commenting on entrapment or the notification failure. The Supreme Court of Justice declared a further appeal inadmissible on 27 October 2021, again without addressing these arguments.

A later request to reopen proceedings, based on a 7 December 2021 Constitutional Court decision invalidating parts of section 17 of Law no. 325 (which had excluded officials from the confirmation hearing and bound later courts by its res judicata effect), was rejected. Under the law, integrity-test evidence could not be used in criminal proceedings but was admissible in disciplinary ones if relevant, admissible, and truthful.

These facts underpin the applicant’s claims of incitement by a State agent and flagrant procedural deficiencies, including the inability to contest the test results in an adversarial setting with equality of arms.
001-241571:
The case of Bazhenov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 8825/22 and 19130/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns three gay Russian men who alleged that the authorities failed to protect their private lives and to prevent discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The applicants claimed that private individuals had non-consensually published their personal data, including their sexual orientation, on the social network VKontakte (VK) in explicitly homophobic contexts, and that the ensuing official investigations were ineffective.

Yevgeniy Bazhenov and Aleksandr Semkin, a same-sex couple who ran a chain of board-game shops, posted a statement of non-discrimination on their business VK page on 17 May 2020 (International Day Against Homophobia). Nine days later a homophobic public group styled “OTDG” republished the post under the headline “Board-games shops owned by two openly gay men in a same-sex marriage,” adding the applicants’ names, Bazhenov’s photograph and the shops’ addresses. A well-known “gay-basher” activist, Timur Bulatov, immediately reposted the material and urged followers to leave hostile comments under “two sexual perverts” who dared to equate “faggots and healthy people.”

On 27 May 2020 Bazhenov lodged a criminal complaint with the Moscow Investigative Committee alleging unlawful dissemination of private data (Article 137 of the Criminal Code) and incitement to hatred. He expressed fear of violence against himself or his family. Parallel complaints were sent to the prosecutor about the insults. For months the Committee refused even to confirm receipt. Court challenges to this inaction were dismissed on the basis of purported letters that the applicants denied receiving. After a prosecutor’s intervention the investigator interviewed the couple, requested psychiatric records, and twice asked VK for the poster’s identity, yet repeatedly refused to open a case, citing lack of corpus delicti. Each refusal was quashed as premature or unlawful, but the statute of limitations expired in May 2022 without any identifications or charges.

The third applicant, lawyer Artem Lapov, who regularly represented LGBTI victims of hate crime, discovered on 24 May 2020 that his full name and former registered address (still occupied by his parents) had been posted in anti-LGBT VK groups under the heading “Address list of LGBT activists, paedophiles and other LGBT perverts.” He filed an analogous Article 137 complaint, stressing that the publication also constituted pressure to abandon his professional work. After similar delays and unsuccessful court applications, an investigator interviewed him and requested VK data but refused to open proceedings before receiving any reply. Subsequent refusals were likewise quashed, yet the limitation period again expired in May 2022. Lapov and his husband subsequently fled Russia and obtained refugee status in Europe.

In both instances the authorities never examined whether the disclosures were motivated by homophobia, despite the openly hostile language, the targeting of known LGBTI persons and the existence of an aggravating circumstance for hate-based crime. The applicants therefore argued that Russia had failed in its positive obligation under Article 8 (private life) read with Article 14 (non-discrimination) to investigate effectively and to afford special protection to a vulnerable community.

**The case of Bazhenov and Others v. Russia (applications nos. 8825/22 and 19130/22) concerns three Russian nationals who alleged that domestic authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligation under Article 8 (private life) read with Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the Convention. This arose from inadequate responses to the non-consensual online dissemination of their personal data, including sexual orientation, by private individuals on social media in a homophobic context. The applicants highlighted the vulnerability of LGBTI persons in Russia and the need for effective investigation of possible bias motives.**

Yevgeniy Bazhenov and Aleksandr Semkin, a same-sex couple married abroad who owned a chain of board-game shops, posted a message on 17 May 2020 (International Day Against Homophobia) on their business VKontakte (VK) account affirming dedication to customers irrespective of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation. On 26 May 2020 a homophobic VK group styled as militating “for discrimination” published a post headed “Board-games shops owned by two openly gay men in a same-sex marriage.” It named the applicants, included Bazhenov’s photograph and listed their shop addresses. The same day, activist Timur Bulatov, who presented himself as a “gay basher” and defender of traditional values, reposted the material and urged supporters to leave “correct comments” under the “publication of two sexual perverts.”

On 27 May 2020 Bazhenov lodged a criminal complaint with the Moscow Investigative Committee alleging unlawful dissemination of personal data without consent (Article 137 of the Criminal Code) and possible incitement of hatred. He expressed fear of hate-motivated crime. A parallel complaint about insults was sent to a prosecutor. For months the authorities provided no information. A court challenge to inaction was rejected in October 2020 on the basis of letters the applicant denied receiving. Subsequent refusals to open an investigation (March, June and August 2021, October 2021) cited absence of corpus delicti, even after interviews with the applicants and a belated request to VK for user data. The investigator also sought information on whether the applicants were under psychiatric or narcological supervision. Prosecutors repeatedly quashed the refusals as premature or unlawful, but no effective identification of the posters occurred. The two-year limitation period under Article 137 expired in May 2022. In 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated an “LGBT international public movement” extremist.

Artem Lapov, a homosexual lawyer in a same-sex marriage registered in the United States who had provided legal assistance in high-profile hate-crime cases involving LGBTI persons, discovered on 24 May 2020 that comments on anti-LGBT VK groups listed his full name and registered address (his parents’ home) under the heading “Address list of LGBT activists, paedophiles and other LGBT perverts.” He filed a similar Article 137 complaint on 26 May 2020, adding that the publication constituted pressure to abandon his professional work protecting LGBTI rights (invoking the Federal Law on Advocacy). After delays and a late-received notification, courts initially rejected challenges to inaction. A 2021 court order required an inquiry. The investigator interviewed Lapov and requested VK data but issued refusals in October 2021 and February 2022 claiming no privacy violation, before any reply from VK. Prosecutors quashed these decisions; the limitation period likewise expired in May 2022. Lapov and his husband subsequently left Russia as refugees.

In both instances the authorities conducted no meaningful investigation into whether the postings were motivated by homophobia, despite the explicit context, inflammatory language and known hostility toward LGBTI persons. The applicants submitted that this disregarded the community’s vulnerability and the State’s duty to provide special protection against such interferences with private life.

The ECtHR case Bazhenov and Others v. Russia (apps. 8825/22 and 19130/22, judgment 4 February 2025) concerns three Russian homosexual applicants (Bazhenov and Semkin, a same-sex married couple owning board-game shops; Lapov, a lawyer aiding LGBTI hate-crime victims, also in a same-sex marriage) alleging violations of Article 14 (non-discrimination) taken with Article 8 (private life). They claimed Russian authorities failed their positive obligation to respond adequately to non-consensual online dissemination of their private data (including sexual orientation) by private parties on VKontakte (VK), and failed to investigate possible homophobic motives, ignoring LGBTI vulnerability.

On 17 May 2020 (International Day Against Homophobia), Bazhenov and Semkin posted on their VK business account expressing support for customers regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation. On 26 May, the homophobic VK group “OTDG” (self-described as militating for discrimination) posted their names, Bazhenov’s photograph and shop addresses under the headline “Board-games shops owned by two openly gay men in a same-sex marriage.” Activist Timur Bulatov (self-styled “gay basher” defending “traditional values”) reposted it, urging supporters to leave hostile comments against “two sexual perverts” promoting equality between “faggots and healthy people.”

On 27 May 2020 Bazhenov filed a criminal complaint with the Moscow Investigative Committee under Criminal Code Article 137 (unlawful dissemination of private-life information without consent), attaching screenshots and expressing fear of hate-motivated crime against him or his family; he also complained of insults. Authorities delayed, issued unreceived or inadequate letters, and repeatedly refused to open an investigation (20 March, 25 June, 6 August and 12 October 2021), citing lack of evidence of a crime despite prosecutors repeatedly quashing the refusals as premature, unlawful or unfounded. Investigators interviewed the applicants only after months, requested VK user data but proceeded without replies, and even sought information on whether the applicants were under psychiatric or narcological supervision. No perpetrators were identified and the two-year limitation period under Article 137 expired in May 2022. Courts dismissed challenges to the inaction.

On 24 May 2020 comments appeared on two VK groups (“Against LGBT Propaganda” and another) listing “LGBT activists, paedophiles and other LGBT perverts,” including Lapov’s full name and registered address (his parents’ home). On 26 May he complained under Article 137, noting the posts pressured him (as an advocate under Federal Law on Advocacy s. 18(4)) to abandon LGBTI rights work. After similar delays and unreceived correspondence, courts eventually ordered an inquiry. Investigators interviewed him, requested VK data for account “Maksim Ivanen” but issued refusals to investigate (5 October 2021 and 11 February 2022) before receiving replies, citing no privacy violation. Prosecutors quashed these as unlawful, directing identification and interview of the poster, but Lapov received no further notifications. The limitation period expired in May 2022. He and his husband later fled Russia as refugees.

Relevant domestic law (Constitution Arts. 23–24; Criminal Code Arts. 137–138 and 63(1)(e) on hate-motive aggravation; CCP Arts. 144–145 requiring prompt three-to-thirty-day verification of complaints and a reasoned decision) was not applied effectively. These facts underpin the alleged failures to protect private life or investigate discriminatory motives.
001-241578:
The case of M.B. v. Spain (ECtHR, App. no. 38239/22) concerns the detention of a Moroccan woman born in 1978 who has longstanding mental health issues (including psychotic/schizophrenic disorder, personality disorder, PTSD, anxiety, substance use and auditory hallucinations urging self-harm or arson). On 12 March 2018 she set fire to her rented flat while intoxicated and acting on voices; she was hospitalised then placed in pre-trial detention by the Salamanca investigating judge for aggravated arson (Criminal Code Art. 351). The judge cited her confession, a same-day forensic report of mental disorder posing a risk of harm to self or others, and ordered hospital assessment followed by prison placement. Appeals arguing prison unsuitability and seeking psychiatric hospitalisation were dismissed.

Detention was extended in February 2019. A February 2020 prison report (plus 2018–2019 hospital notes) showed ongoing medication, monitoring and that hallucinations were “almost controlled,” with the applicant living in a respect module. Expert evidence at trial (apparently based mainly on the 2018 report) indicated a need for about three years of monitored inpatient treatment before possible supervised outpatient care.

On 24 February 2020 the Audiencia Provincial found the facts proved but acquitted M.B. as criminally irresponsible (Art. 20) because her disorder plus alcohol fully destroyed her capacity to understand or control her actions. It nevertheless imposed a security measure of detention in a closed psychiatric unit for a minimum of five and maximum of 15 years (replaceable by open-regime care depending on progress), citing the 2018 mental state, danger to society and therapeutic need. Pre-trial detention was extended in May 2020 pending appeal.

The High Court dismissed her appeal in October 2020, holding the measure served both public protection against reoffending and the applicant’s own treatment, with duration linked to the abstract 10–20-year penalty for the offence. The Supreme Court declared her cassation appeal (which also challenged the post-acquittal extension of pre-trial detention as lacking legal basis) inadmissible in May 2021, finding the measure justified by the verified 2018 disturbance and its duration dependent on treatment results. An amparo application was rejected by the Constitutional Court in May 2022 for non-exhaustion and lack of special relevance.

The judgment became final in June 2021; M.B. was transferred to Alicante prison psychiatric hospital in July 2021 (remaining term calculated to 2033). In June 2022, on the basis of later reports showing reduced danger and good treatment response, the measure was converted to placement in an open mental-health centre, though transfer did not occur until November 2023. She was recognised as 65 % disabled in April 2022.

The complaints under Articles 5 and 7 focused on the lawfulness and duration of both the pre-trial detention (especially after acquittal) and the subsequent security measure. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 5 § 1 (e) because the measure was imposed almost two years after the offence solely on the basis of the 2018 assessment, without any contemporary evaluation of whether the applicant’s condition had improved, whether she still posed a danger, what her therapeutic needs were, or any prediction of future behaviour.

The case of M.B. v. Spain (ECHR Application no. 38239/22) concerns a Moroccan national with documented mental health issues (psychotic disorder, likely schizophrenia, personality disorder, PTSD, anxiety, substance use, and auditory hallucinations) who was detained after setting fire to her rented flat on 11-12 March 2018. Influenced by voices commanding her to burn her belongings and after consuming significant alcohol, she started a fire that endangered neighbours. Police took her immediately to hospital; reports noted prior admissions for psychotic symptoms and ongoing treatment, plus alcohol intoxication and claimed voices.

The Salamanca investigating judge ordered pre-trial detention the same day for aggravated arson (Criminal Code Art. 351), citing her confession, a forensic report of mental disorder creating risk of harm to self or others, and need for assessment/treatment. She remained in ordinary prison (later transferred) despite appeals arguing unsuitability for her condition; higher courts upheld detention, stating her mental health had been considered. Detention was extended in 2019 without additional reasoning and again in May 2020 (during appeals, post-acquittal) under Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 504, to a two-year maximum.

In February 2020, after prison medical reports (ongoing monitoring, medication, hallucinations largely controlled, participation in activities) and expert testimony (need for ~3 years monitored treatment to stabilize), the Audiencia Provincial acquitted M.B. She had committed the offence as perpetrator but was fully inimputable (Criminal Code Art. 20) due to a mental disorder that, combined with alcohol, completely diminished her intellectual/volitional capacities at the time of the act (sudden impulse from voices, no planning). Nonetheless, it imposed a security measure of internment in a secure unit for 5–15 years (replaceable by open mental-health treatment based on progress), plus compensation to neighbours. This rested solely on the offence-day disorder.

M.B. appealed the duration (not evidence-based; potential ordinary sentence shorter, max 10–20 years abstractly) and lack of current dangerousness assessment (Criminal Code Arts. 6, 95, 101). The High Court dismissed, holding the measure served dual purposes of societal protection (reoffending risk) and therapy, justified by the proven derangement. The Supreme Court declared cassation inadmissible (May 2021), finding the measure justified by the verified disorder causing acquittal, duration within abstract penalty limits, and actual length dependent on treatment progress; it ignored the post-acquittal detention-extension complaint. The Constitutional Court rejected amparo (May 2022) for non-exhaustion (detention issue) and lack of special relevance.

The judgment became final in June 2021. M.B. was transferred to Alicante prison psychiatric hospital (July 2021); remaining measure time was set to expire March 2033. In 2022, medical reports showing reduced danger, insight, and treatment response led to an order replacing internment with a specialised mental-health centre, but transfer occurred only in November 2023. Disability (65%, paranoid schizophrenia) and a pension were granted in 2022.

These facts underpin alleged violations of Article 5 (unlawful/arbitrary deprivation of liberty, including of a person of unsound mind under §1(e), and post-acquittal pre-trial detention without basis) and Article 7 (security measure as de facto punishment post-acquittal, lacking proper current assessment of dangerousness, improvement, therapeutic needs, monitoring, or future risk, contrary to legality). Domestic courts evaluated her condition only as of the offence (nearly two years earlier) without contemporaneous findings of ongoing unsound mind or necessity.

The case of M.B. v. Spain (ECtHR, 6 February 2025) concerns a Moroccan national born in 1978 who alleged violations of Articles 5 and 7 ECHR arising from her pre-trial detention and a post-acquittal security measure of continued detention on mental-health grounds.

On 12 March 2018 the applicant was arrested after setting fire to her rented flat while intoxicated and acting on auditory hallucinations. She was taken to hospital, where reports noted prior psychotic admissions, ongoing treatment, alcohol intoxication and claims of hearing voices. The Salamanca investigating judge immediately ordered pre-trial detention for aggravated arson (Criminal Code Art. 351), citing her confession and a forensic report indicating a mental disorder posing a risk of harm to herself or others. She was to be assessed in hospital then transferred to prison (ordinary or psychiatric wing). Appeals against detention were dismissed. On 19 February 2019 she was formally accused and detention was extended without additional reasoning.

In January 2020 the Audiencia Provincial obtained a prison medical report listing psychotic and borderline-personality disorders, substance use, current medication and largely controlled hallucinations under external psychiatric monitoring. Two experts (who appear not to have examined her personally) testified that three years of monitored treatment would be needed for stabilisation. On 24 February 2020 the Audiencia Provincial found the facts constituted aggravated arson but acquitted the applicant as inimputable under Art. 20(1) Criminal Code: her capacities had been fully diminished by schizophrenia, voices and alcohol. It nevertheless imposed a security measure of treatment in a closed unit for a minimum of five and a maximum of fifteen years, replaceable by open treatment according to later reports. The court relied exclusively on the 2018 forensic evidence concerning her state on the day of the offence.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the duration lacked evidential basis and exceeded the ten-year maximum sentence that would have applied had she been responsible. On 21 May 2020, while the appeal was pending, detention was extended for a further two years. The Castile and León High Court dismissed the appeal on 15 October 2020, holding that the measure served both public protection and the applicant’s own treatment and that its length was consistent with the abstract penalty (10–20 years). It treated the measure as justified by the verified 2018 disorder and as adjustable according to later progress. An amparo application was declared inadmissible by the Constitutional Court on 24 May 2022.

The 2020 judgment became final on 28 June 2021. The applicant was transferred to Alicante prison psychiatric hospital on 16 July 2021; remaining detention was calculated to expire in March 2033. Internal prison reports (not systematically placed before the courts) documented ongoing hallucinations, frequent medication adjustments, schizophrenia, PTSD and anxiety. In March 2022 the hospital proposed replacement by an open mental-health centre; the Audiencia Provincial so ordered on 14 June 2022 after finding reduced dangerousness and good treatment response. Transfer did not occur until November 2023. She was later recognised as 65 % disabled and granted a pension.

The applicant maintained that both the prolonged pre-trial detention after acquittal and the imposition of the closed-unit measure (based solely on her 2018 condition, without contemporaneous assessment of current mental state, dangerousness, therapeutic needs or future risk) were arbitrary and lacked the safeguards required by Article 5 § 1 (e).

The case of P. v. Poland concerns the 2013 dismissal of a secondary-school teacher (applicant K.P., born 1980) after disciplinary proceedings. He taught Polish and English from 2007–2013, receiving annual prizes as best teacher (2008–2012) and national awards as best form tutor (2010, 2013), with no prior reprimands or complaints. The school principal had suspected his homosexuality since 2010 but viewed him as an excellent teacher.

Two issues triggered proceedings under the 1982 Teacher’s Charter Act (sections 6 and 75–76), which require teachers to perform duties reliably (including student safety), shape moral/civic attitudes, and uphold professional dignity, with penalties ranging from reprimand to dismissal.

First, on two June 2013 school trips (students aged 15–18), the applicant’s same-sex partner accompanied him without prior registration or authorization, contrary to school rules and a 2001 ministerial ordinance. The partner was introduced as a “cousin” and left one event promptly; the applicant claimed he provided full supervision (including night shifts) and sought companionship due to sunburn. The partner was unlisted in trip records.

Second, from April/May 2012 to 1 July 2013, the applicant posted ~100 public entries (often daily) on an adults-only website for homosexual men, using a pseudonym but occasionally his real first name. Content mixed diary-style text (daily life, loneliness, love for his partner, job frustrations, general student comments, and swear words about superiors) with photos of men (alone or interacting: hugging, kissing, nude or semi-nude in non-explicit contexts such as beaches or beds; none showed genitals or intercourse). Several dozen passages had explicit erotic/sexual descriptions. The blog had 39,000 visitors; some staff read it, and at least one student commented publicly identifying him as their teacher. No student/parent complaints arose. On 1 July 2013, after the principal learned of it, she reprimanded him; he deleted the blog the same day, later calling it a “foolish” therapeutic outlet for childhood trauma.

The principal referred the matter, citing unauthorized trip companions (compromising supervision) and a blog “full of eroticism and profanities” rendering him unfit to shape students’ morals. The Disciplinary Commission (16 December 2013) found breaches of professional dignity and section 6 duties, ordering dismissal. Reasoning stressed that teachers must show restraint in public internet activity (no privacy right), that profane/obscene content (photos, erotic texts) undermined dignity regardless of orientation, and that the blog’s public nature exposed the profession.

The applicant appealed, admitting the facts but calling dismissal disproportionate (excellent record, remorse, no student harm) and possibly driven by homophobic stereotypes about his “disturbed” orientation. His lawyer alleged discrimination. The Appellate Commission (24 September 2014) discontinued proceedings, citing admissions, deletion, therapeutic purpose, no proven duty neglect or student impact.

The Ministry disciplinary officer appealed, insisting the issue was indecent public content (erotic texts, obscene photos of the applicant/partner, profanities about staff/school), not orientation, and that the applicant failed basic moral principles. The Szczecin Court of Appeal (7 May 2015) reversed, upholding dismissal. It found trip violations compromised safety (section 6(1)) and the blog’s “profane, obscene and sexual” content (citing 30+ dated entries: work complaints like “school’s prostitute,” student sarcasm, sexual imagery/descriptions, “blow you”) unworthy of the profession and contrary to shaping morals (section 6(5)). Orientation was “irrelevant”; public exposure of profession, colleagues, and students mattered more than lack of proven harm. The sanction was deemed proportionate (career intact elsewhere). No further appeal existed.

The applicant alleged the dismissal violated Articles 8 (private life), 10 (expression), and 14 (discrimination) of the Convention. (Word count: 512)

The case of P. v. Poland (Application no. 56310/15) involved a Polish secondary school teacher (born 1980) dismissed in 2013 for writing an adult-oriented internet blog with sexually explicit content and for allowing an unauthorised companion on school trips. The applicant introduced his partner as a cousin; the partner left one event (a Warsaw ceremony) immediately and joined a camping trip for companionship after the applicant suffered sunburn. The applicant maintained he completed night shifts and supervised students diligently.

Writing under a pseudonym (occasionally using his real first name in the first person), posts resembled a diary with photographs of men (alone or interacting: holding hands, hugging, kissing, posing, some half-dressed or nude but without displayed genitals or intercourse) and texts describing daily life, dreams, love, loneliness, and intimate/erotic thoughts or acts with his partner. It dismissed him, citing the blog’s “erotic character and obscene photos,” profane social media comments undermining dignity (teachers must act with restraint privately, especially online without privacy), and “obscene photographs.” No specific posts were assessed; sexual orientation was explicitly distinguished from the issues.

The blog—profane, obscene, sexual (listing >30 dated entries with excerpts on work (“school’s prostitute”), students (“little psychopaths”), youth rebellion, and explicit sexual imagery/descriptions)—was “unworthy of the teaching profession,” breaching the duty to shape moral attitudes (section 6(5)). Teachers influence conduct/perceptions beyond knowledge transmission; public blogging exposed/discredited the profession, colleagues, and students. Orientation was irrelevant to public obscenities; lack of student harm was immaterial. The sanction was proportionate (harmful yet preserving other career options), considering remorse and record. No further appeal existed.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8, 10, and 14 of the Convention arising from the disciplinary dismissal.

The case of *P. v. Poland* (Application no. 56310/15) involves a secondary school teacher's dismissal, primarily over an adult-oriented internet blog with sexually explicit content (plus unauthorized accompaniment on school trips). It centers on an alleged violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression).

The applicant, a Polish national born in 1980 and qualified in Polish and English, taught at a Koszalin secondary school (students aged 15–18) from September 2007 to December 2013. He received annual “best teacher” prizes (2008–2012) and national awards as best form tutor (2010, 2013), with no prior reprimands or complaints. The principal later noted suspecting his homosexuality since 2010 but viewed him as an excellent teacher.

The partner was introduced as a cousin, unregistered in official records, and the trips treated partly as private—violating known school rules against unlisted third parties. The applicant performed night shifts and student supervision.

From April/May 2012 to 1 July 2013, the applicant posted ~100 entries (often daily) on a public blog hosted on a site for homosexual men, accessible only after users declared adulthood. Writing under a pseudonym (occasionally using his real first name) in diary style, posts included photos of men (alone or interacting; dressed, semi-nude, or nude) in everyday, affectionate, or erotic contexts (e.g., hugging, kissing, holding phallic objects, removing underwear) but without depicting genitals or actual intercourse. Texts covered daily life, emotions, love, loneliness, and intimate desires, with several dozen passages explicitly erotic or describing male sexual acts. Some expressed job frustration, used profanities toward superiors, or referred generally to students. The blog attracted 39,000 visitors. The applicant claimed secrecy from colleagues and students, but staff read it and at least one student commented publicly identifying him as their teacher. No student or parent complaints about the blog were received.

On 1 July 2013, the principal reprimanded the applicant and demanded deletion; he complied immediately. Disciplinary proceedings ensued under the 1982 Teacher’s Charter Act for (1) allowing an unauthorized person on trips (compromising student care/safety) and (2) running a blog with “eroticism and profanities” “unworthy of the teaching profession,” rendering him unfit to shape students’ moral attitudes.

At a 16 December 2013 hearing, the applicant admitted the acts, describing the blog as therapeutic (per psychiatric advice for childhood trauma) and a “foolish mistake.” The Disciplinary Commission found breaches of professional dignity and duties (section 6), dismissing him. It cited erotic texts, “obscene” photos, and profane comments (including Facebook posts about colleagues as “slackers”), stressing teachers must act with dignity even privately, especially online, as they educate a new generation.

The applicant appealed, calling the sanction disproportionate and possibly rooted in homophobic bias. The Appellate Disciplinary Commission quashed the dismissal (24 September 2014), citing his remorse, immediate deletion, lack of proven duty neglect on trips, therapeutic intent, and no evidenced negative impact on students.

The Ministry’s disciplinary officer appealed. On 7 May 2015, the Szczecin Court of Appeal reinstated dismissal. It held the trips neglected duties and compromised safety. The blog’s “profane, obscene and sexual” content (listing 30+ dated entries with excerpts on sexual life, work frustration like calling himself the “school’s prostitute,” sarcastic student comments, and profane terms) was unworthy and breached moral/civic education duties. Sexual orientation was irrelevant; public posting discredited the profession, colleagues, and students. The sanction was deemed proportionate given his record and remaining career options.

No further appeal existed. Statistics showed 109 similar internet-related teacher disciplinary cases (2013–2021), 96 resulting in sanctions.

The ECtHR found an Article 10 violation: authorities lacked relevant/sufficient reasons; private adult blogging did not threaten minors’ morals sufficiently to justify dismissal, nor was it a pressing social need or proportionate.

The case of Romanchenko and Kharazishvili v. Georgia (ECtHR, 18 February 2025) concerned the covert interception of the applicants’ telephone communications during a Georgian criminal investigation. Ana Romanchenko (first applicant), a practising lawyer and Georgian Bar Association member, served as legal representative of the founder and director of Naderi Ltd. Her husband, Nika Kharazishvili (second applicant), had no independent link to the company. On 3 November 2020 the Investigative Service of the Ministry of Finance opened an inquiry into the planned unlawful sale of 400,000 packs of unstamped cigarettes (value approximately €270,000) imported by an Iranian national who had registered Naderi Ltd. The investigation rested initially on “operational information.”

On 7 November 2020 the Prosecutor General’s Office applied to the Tbilisi City Court for a 30-day warrant to intercept eight telephone lines, including two used by the first applicant and one used by the second. The application asserted a reasonable suspicion that both applicants had “criminal links” with others involved in the offence and that they would discuss the sale by telephone. It claimed the measure was necessary in a democratic society, proportionate, and the only practicable means of obtaining essential evidence. The prosecutor stated that neither applicant enjoyed professional immunity. The court granted the warrant the same day, reciting the statutory criteria of Article 1433 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) in generic terms: the offence was of a type permitting covert measures; a reasonable suspicion existed that the applicants were “persons directly connected to an offence” or possessed relevant information; and the measure was a last-resort, proportionate response. The order contained no case-specific reasoning and did not address the first applicant’s status as a lawyer.

Interception by the Operational-Technical Agency lasted from 10 November to 9 December 2020. None of the first applicant’s conversations were deemed relevant and they were not retained; one conversation of the second applicant was recorded and placed on the case file. The applicants were notified more than a year later (10 November 2021 and 24 December 2021 respectively) and given copies of the court order.

The first applicant challenged the warrant, arguing that blanket surveillance of a practising lawyer for a month inevitably captured privileged communications, that “operational information” alone did not meet the reasonable-suspicion threshold, and that the order was wholly unreasoned. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal dismissed the complaint on 29 December 2021, holding that her role in registering Naderi Ltd created a sufficient link and that lawyers enjoy no immunity provided the statutory conditions are met. The second applicant’s appeal, which stressed the absence of any evidence connecting him to the other suspects except his marriage, was likewise dismissed on 27 January 2022; the appeal court treated the group nature of the offence and the “logical link” of operational information as adequate justification and the measure as the only available means. No further appeal lay. Neither applicant was charged and the investigation remained open as of May 2023.

Georgian law (CCP Articles 1431–1437) required prior judicial authorisation, reasonable suspicion, necessity, last-resort character and proportionality, and contained special rules protecting lawyer–client communications. The applicants complained that these safeguards had not been applied in a manner that genuinely assessed necessity and proportionality vis-à-vis each of them, particularly given the first applicant’s professional status. The Court later found a violation of Article 8 on precisely those grounds.

The case concerns complaints by Georgian lawyer Ana Romanchenko (first applicant) and her husband Nika Kharazishvili (second applicant) under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention regarding the interception and recording of their telephone communications during a criminal investigation.

On 3 November 2020 the Investigative Service of the Ministry of Finance opened an investigation into the alleged unlawful sale of 400,000 packs of unstamped cigarettes (valued at approximately €270,000) by Naderi Ltd, a Georgian company registered by Iranian citizen D.N. Operational information indicated the goods had been transferred under the company’s name on 4 November 2020. The first applicant was the legal representative of the company’s founder and director; the second applicant was her husband.

On 7 November 2020 the Prosecutor General’s Office applied to the Tbilisi City Court for a 30-day authorisation (9 November–9 December 2020) to intercept eight persons’ telephone communications, including two lines used by the first applicant and one used by the second. The application asserted a reasonable suspicion that the applicants had criminal links with others planning the offence and that they would discuss implementation by telephone. It claimed the measure was necessary for a comprehensive investigation, would yield essential evidence unobtainable by other means, served a pressing social need (crime prevention and protection of economic interests), and was adequate and proportionate. It stated that neither applicant enjoyed immunity or belonged to a restricted profession. Supporting materials from the investigation file were attached.

The same day the court granted the order. It found the offence eligible for covert measures, a reasonable suspicion that the applicants were persons “directly connected to an offence” or possessing important information, and that they enjoyed no immunity. It accepted that the prosecutor had substantiated necessity by reference to investigating a serious offence, preventing its commission, protecting others’ rights, and the impossibility or excessive difficulty of obtaining essential information otherwise. The order was not appealable except in limited circumstances and required material to be sent to the Investigative Service and the State Inspectorate.

Interceptions were carried out by the Operational-Technical Agency from 10 November to 9 December 2020. None of the first applicant’s conversations were deemed of investigative interest and, after initial retention, they were not recorded. One conversation of the second applicant was recorded and added to the case file.

The applicants were notified of the measures only in November and December 2021 (more than a year later). They received copies of the court order and related material and were informed of their right to challenge lawfulness.

The first applicant appealed on 9 December 2021, arguing the measure was unlawful because she was a practising lawyer and member of the Georgian Bar Association acting as the company’s legal representative; surveillance appeared directed at her professional activities and captured communications covered by legal professional privilege. She also contended that “operational information” alone failed the reasonable-suspicion standard and that both the application and order were unsubstantiated. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 29 December 2021, holding that company-registration documents and the timing of registration created a minimum reasonable suspicion of connection to the offence and that lawyers are not immune provided the statutory conditions are met.

The second applicant appealed on 21 January 2022, arguing that suspicion rested solely on his marital relationship, that no evidence linked him to the other suspects, and that neither the application nor the order explained why less intrusive means were impossible. The appeal was dismissed on 27 January 2022. The court found the group nature of the alleged offence, the first applicant’s representative role, and operational information of a suspicious connection sufficient to establish necessity; the operational information appeared reliable and the measure was the only means of achieving the legitimate aim.

As of May 2023 neither applicant had been charged and the investigation remained open.

These facts underlie the alleged violations: the authorisation procedure failed to guarantee that surveillance was genuinely necessary and proportionate vis-à-vis each applicant; the court order lacked relevant and sufficient reasons and did not consider the first applicant’s status as a practising lawyer; and domestic law, as interpreted and applied, failed to provide reasonable clarity on the scope and manner of the authorities’ discretion.

The case concerns two Georgian nationals, Ana Romanchenko (a practising lawyer and member of the Georgian Bar Association) and her husband Nika Kharazishvili. On 3 November 2020 the Investigative Service of the Ministry of Finance opened a criminal investigation into the planned unlawful sale of 400,000 packs of cigarettes without excise stamps (valued at approximately EUR 270,000). The goods had been imported by an Iranian national, D.N., through his Georgian-registered company Naderi Ltd. Romanchenko acted as the authorised legal representative of Naderi Ltd’s founder and director.

On 7 November 2020 the Prosecutor General’s Office applied to the Tbilisi City Court for a 30-day authorisation (9 November–9 December 2020) to intercept and record the telephone communications of eight persons, including both applicants (two numbers used by Romanchenko and one used by Kharazishvili). The application asserted a reasonable suspicion that the applicants had “criminal links” with others involved in the planned offence and that they would discuss implementation of the plan by telephone. It claimed the measure was required by a pressing social need, was the only means of obtaining essential evidence, and that neither applicant enjoyed professional immunity.

The same day the Tbilisi City Court granted the request. It found that the offence fell within the statutory list permitting covert measures, that a reasonable suspicion existed that the applicants were either directly connected to the offence or possessed relevant information, and that the measure was necessary and proportionate because other investigative methods would be impossible or unreasonably burdensome. The order noted that the applicants did not enjoy immunity and that the resulting material should be sent to the Investigative Service (with a copy of the operative part to the State Inspectorate). The order was not amenable to ordinary appeal.

Interception by the Operational-Technical Agency of the State Security Service took place between 10 November and 9 December 2020. None of Romanchenko’s intercepted conversations were judged of investigative interest and they were not retained. One conversation of Kharazishvili was recorded and placed on the case file.

The applicants were notified of the surveillance in November and December 2021 and given copies of the court order together with the right to challenge its lawfulness. Romanchenko appealed, arguing that the measure had been directed at her professional activities as a lawyer, thereby violating legal professional privilege, that it rested solely on unsubstantiated “operational information,” and that it failed the statutory reasonable-suspicion standard. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 29 December 2021, holding that her role in registering Naderi Ltd created a minimum reasonable suspicion and that practising lawyers are not immune from covert measures if the statutory conditions are met.

Kharazishvili appealed separately, contending that the only basis for targeting him was his marital relationship, that no evidence of any criminal links existed, and that the necessity of intercepting rather than using less intrusive methods had not been demonstrated. His appeal was dismissed on 27 January 2022; the Court of Appeal relied on the group nature of the offence, his wife’s professional role, and the apparent reliability of the operational information.

As of May 2023 neither applicant had been charged and the investigation remained open. These facts form the basis of the complaints that the interception constituted an unjustified interference with private life and correspondence (Article 8) and, in Romanchenko’s case, also raised fair-trial concerns (Article 6) arising from the targeting of legally privileged communications.

The case concerns Azerbaijan’s National Television and Radio Council (NTRC) refusal to award a radio broadcasting licence for the 103.3 FM frequency (covering Baku and the Absheron peninsula) after a November 2010 call for tenders. The applicants—Objective Television and Radio Broadcasting Company (founded 2010 by journalists Mehman Aliyev and Emin Huseynov) plus activist Rasul Jafarov—sought to operate stations (Objective Radio and Alternative Radio) offering mixed programming (news, analysis, culture, education, music and sports) to address perceived lack of pluralism and one-sided political coverage in existing media. A third bidder, Golden Prince LLC, proposed an almost exclusively news-based station (90% news, later rebranded Araz FM).

Three bids were submitted with details of programming, staff and equipment. At an 18 January 2011 NTRC meeting (seven members present), bidders made brief public presentations and answered questions on start dates and staffing. In a subsequent closed session, members discussed bids collectively and unanimously selected Golden Prince, citing its superior equipment, technical/creative capacity, staffing potential and ability to start sooner, plus the “novelty” of a purely news station. Applicants were informed orally but received only a 31 January 2011 letter quoting the Broadcasting Law and noting the novelty factor, plus an extract of the minutes containing solely the operative decision. Requests for full minutes, Golden Prince’s bid documents and representative authorisations were refused as “not expedient” and contrary to other parties’ interests.

Applicants appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal (March 2011), arguing the decision ignored statutory criteria (Broadcasting Law Art. 32.0.1 and Licensing Rules Art. 4.7) requiring priority for educational/cultural programmes, avoidance of overloading airtime with similar content, and evaluation of originality, staff experience and technical/financial resources. They also complained that no properly reasoned written refusal (required by Art. 18.5) had been issued. The court dismissed the claims, holding that non-selection of a bidder was a lawful ground for refusal, that 32% of Golden Prince’s proposed output (cultural/educational news) satisfied the criteria, and that minutes showed relevant factors had been considered. The Supreme Court upheld this in May 2011.

Subsequent information (obtained during litigation and via a 2014 OCCRP investigation) revealed Golden Prince’s formal owner was linked to businesses associated with A.H., long-time head of the Presidential Administration’s Public Policy Department. A.H.’s wife S.V. (an NTRC member since 2007 and later deputy chair) participated in the closed deliberations and vote; their son later appeared as director of Araz FM. A.H. publicly confirmed family ownership of Golden Prince and related entities. The NTRC chairman had previously worked in A.H.’s department. These ties were never disclosed.

The applicants alleged the refusal violated Article 10 (freedom to impart information and ideas). The Court later held the interference was not “prescribed by law”: although the relevant legislation was accessible and sufficiently precise, the NTRC failed to give a duly reasoned decision or conduct a comprehensive, objective evaluation; it exercised virtually unlimited discretion without adequate safeguards against arbitrariness; and the undisclosed conflict of interest of one member fatally undermined the body’s impartiality, rendering the entire procedure arbitrary.

**CASE OF OBJECTIVE TELEVISION AND RADIO BROADCASTING COMPANY AND OTHERS v. AZERBAIJAN (Application no. 257/12)**

The applicants—Objective Television and Radio Broadcasting Company (registered 2010), its journalist founders Mehman Aliyev (also owner/director of Turan Information Agency and editor of contact.az/top.az) and Emin Huseynov (IRFS NGO chairman), plus civil society activist Rasul Jafarov—complained under Article 10 of the Convention about the National Television and Radio Council’s (NTRC) refusal to grant them a radio broadcasting licence.

On 23 November 2010 the NTRC announced a tender for the 103.3 FM frequency covering Baku and the Absheron peninsula. The notice listed required documents but stated no programme-type preferences. Three bids were received. The applicant company proposed “Objective Radio” (20% daily news, 10% analytical, 10% culture news, 15% concerts/arts, 20% educational, 15% music/talk shows, 5% sports; five staff, including Aliyev as chief editor and Huseynov as producer). Jafarov proposed “Alternative Radio” (25% news, 15% talk shows, etc.; eight staff). Golden Prince LLC proposed a station (later Araz FM) consisting of 90% news (50% political, 20% cultural, 12% educational, 5% scientific, 3% sports) plus 10% other content, with twelve staff and “very high-quality” equipment. All bidders supplied equipment details.

On 18 January 2011 the NTRC held an open session (seven members present) in which bidders made brief presentations and answered questions about start dates and staffing. The applicants emphasised the need for greater objectivity and pluralism; they would begin within six months and hire more staff (including from Turan). Jafarov said he would start sooner and add staff. Golden Prince representatives stressed superior equipment and a three-month start. In a subsequent closed session, members (including S.V.) praised Golden Prince’s preparedness, modern equipment, staffing potential and “novelty” of a purely news format, then selected it unanimously.

Applicants received only an oral announcement and, later, an extract from the minutes stating the result (no reasons). The NTRC’s 31 January 2011 letter cited Article 15.5 of the 2002 Broadcasting Law and the novelty of a news station. Requests for the full minutes, Golden Prince’s bid/charter and representatives’ authorisations were refused as “not expedient” and contrary to other parties’ interests. Full minutes and some documents were supplied only during later court proceedings.

Applicants appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal, arguing the decision ignored statutory criteria (Broadcasting Law Article 32.0.1 requiring priority for educational/cultural programmes and prevention of programme-type overload; Licensing Rules Article 4.7 listing originality, cultural/educational volume, staffing/experience, technical/financial resources, etc.). They noted the unannounced preference for news, lack of a reasoned written refusal within 15 days (Article 18.5), and a pattern of favouring state-linked entities. The court dismissed the appeals on 28 March 2011, finding the decision lawful: non-selection was a statutory ground for refusal, the letter supplied reasons, 32% educational/cultural news complied with Article 32.0.1, and minutes showed discussion of originality, staff and technical criteria. The Supreme Court upheld this on 25 May 2011.

Subsequent facts relevant to the complaint included revelations that Golden Prince’s formal owner A.V. was linked to businesses associated with A.H. (long-time head of the Presidential Administration’s Public Policy Department). A.H.’s wife S.V. sat on the NTRC (later deputy chair) and participated in the vote/deliberations; their son was later identified as Araz FM’s general director. An OCCRP investigation and A.H.’s 2014 confirmation established family ownership of Golden Prince and related companies. The NTRC chairman had previously worked in A.H.’s department. Applicants argued these links, never disclosed during the procedure, created an undisclosed conflict of interest.

Domestic law (Broadcasting Law Articles 14–18 and 32; NTRC Licensing Rules; 2002 NTRC Regulations) required competitions taking account of viewers’/state interests, creative/technical capacity, and listed evaluation criteria, while requiring reasoned written refusals. NTRC members were required to be independent and impartial, with incompatibilities for certain office-holders or those engaged in paid activities. Applicants contended the NTRC’s virtually unlimited discretion, absence of a duly reasoned/comprehensive evaluation, and the undisclosed conflict rendered the interference with their freedom to impart information and ideas not “prescribed by law.”

A.H. later publicly confirmed that the companies, including the successful bidder, belonged to his family; their son became general director of Araz FM. These links were never disclosed during the tender.

The domestic legal framework (Broadcasting Law Arts. 15, 18 and 32 and the Licensing Rules) listed numerous evaluation criteria but conferred virtually unlimited discretion on the NTRC, whose members were appointed by the President and whose decisions were not required to be fully reasoned or published. Combined with the undisclosed family ties of a voting member, this rendered the entire procedure arbitrary and the interference with the applicants’ freedom to impart information not “prescribed by law.”

The case of K.M. v. North Macedonia concerns the State's alleged failure under Article 8 of the Convention to protect a 14-year-old girl from sexual abuse through an effective legal framework. The applicant, born on 19 August 1999, was 14 at the time of the events.

On 31 August 2013, Gj.K., a 39-year-old telecommunications employee, visited the family's home to restore internet service. Left alone with the applicant, he complimented her tanned legs and caressed one of them. When she moved away, he followed, remarked that men sent her messages because they loved her and because she had large breasts, massaged her shoulders, and touched one of her breasts. The applicant fled the room. The same day, Gj.K. allegedly also touched the applicant's sister inappropriately.

On 2 September 2013 the applicant's sister filed a complaint with the Ministry of the Interior alleging sexual assault of a minor. A police officer took a statement from Gj.K., who denied any touching. On 28 October 2013 a public prosecutor interviewed the applicant, who confirmed the contact with her shoulders, one breast and leg, as well as the comments, but stated that no force or threats had been used. The prosecutor also interviewed the sister and mother; the latter reported that both girls were frightened and distressed and had been taken to a psychiatrist who prescribed medication. Gj.K. was re-interviewed on 31 October 2013 and again denied the allegations.

On 6 November 2013 the prosecutor rejected the complaint as regards the offence of rape under Article 186 §§ 1 and 4 of the Criminal Code (which covered “other sexual acts” only when committed by force or threat). The prosecutor accepted that the touching and caressing had occurred but held that, absent force or threats, the conduct amounted only to the privately prosecutable offence of insult (Article 173). The applicant and her sister were informed they could take over the prosecution within eight days; they did not do so.

The applicant then brought a civil claim against Gj.K. on 30 November 2013, seeking non-pecuniary damages for insult and harm to honour and reputation. She relied on an expert report of 20 November 2013 finding that she had suffered fear and psychological distress. After remittal, the Tetovo Court of First Instance dismissed the claim on 10 March 2015. It held that the Insults and Defamation Act applied only to expressed opinions, not physical acts, and that after the prosecutor's decision the applicant could have pursued a private prosecution and then sought compensation. The Gostivar Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal on 22 March 2016, finding that the constituent elements of insult had not been established, that no causal link to damage had been shown, and that no statutory provision on civil liability covered the claim. The judgment was served on 8 April 2016.

At the material time Article 188 of the Criminal Code criminalised sexual intercourse or “other sexual acts” with a child under 14, but the applicant had already turned 14. Insults had been decriminalised in 2012 and could be pursued only as a civil claim under legislation that required an intention to demean through an expressed opinion. Section 191 of the Obligations Act provided compensation for victims of certain sexual offences committed by fraud, duress or abuse of dependence, but the courts did not apply it. The Lanzarote Convention, in force for North Macedonia since October 2012, required criminalisation of sexual activities with children below the age of consent or involving coercion or abuse of trust or vulnerability.

The domestic authorities therefore classified the admitted non-consensual sexual touching of a 14-year-old as neither a publicly prosecutable sexual offence nor a compensable civil wrong, leaving the applicant without effective legal protection.

**Case summary: K.M. v. North Macedonia (Application no. 59144/16, ECtHR judgment of 4 March 2025)**

The case concerns North Macedonia’s alleged failure under Article 8 of the Convention to fulfil its positive obligation to protect a 14-year-old girl from sexual abuse. The applicant, born on 19 August 1999, was 14 at the time of the events.

On 31 August 2013, Gj.K., a 39-year-old telecommunications employee, visited the family’s home to restore internet service. Left alone with the applicant, he remarked that her legs were nicely tanned and touched her leg. When she moved away he followed her, commented that men loved her because she had large breasts, massaged her shoulders and touched her breasts. She fled the room. The same day he allegedly also touched her sister inappropriately. The applicant and her sister later saw a psychiatrist and were prescribed medication; they were described as scared and upset.

On 2 September 2013 the sister filed a criminal complaint with the Ministry of the Interior alleging sexual assault of a minor. Police interviewed Gj.K., who denied any touching. On 28 October 2013 a public prosecutor interviewed the applicant (who confirmed the touching of her shoulders, one breast and her leg, together with the comments, and stated that no force or threats were used), her sister and their mother. On 31 October 2013 another prosecutor interviewed Gj.K., who again denied the allegations.

On 6 November 2013 the prosecutor rejected the complaint for the offence of rape under Article 186 §§ 1 and 4 of the Criminal Code (which covered “other sexual acts” only when committed with force or threats). The prosecutor accepted that Gj.K. had touched one of the applicant’s breasts and caressed her leg without force or threats, but held that these acts therefore did not constitute a publicly prosecutable offence. They amounted only to the privately prosecutable offence of insult under Article 173. The applicant and her sister were informed they could take over the prosecution within eight days; they did not do so.

Instead, on 30 November 2013 the applicant (through a lawyer) brought a civil claim against Gj.K. for non-pecuniary damage, alleging that the same acts insulted her and harmed her honour and reputation. She relied on an expert report documenting fear and psychological distress. After remittal, the Tetovo Court of First Instance dismissed the claim on 10 March 2015. It held that the Insults and Defamation Act applied only to expressed opinions, not physical actions, that the applicant could have taken over the criminal prosecution and then sought compensation, and that section 191 of the Obligations Act provided no basis for an award. The Gostivar Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 22 March 2016, finding that she had failed to establish the elements of insult or a causal link to damage and that no statutory provision on civil liability covered the claim. The judgment was served on 8 April 2016.

At the material time the Criminal Code required force or threats for “other sexual acts” (Article 186) and criminalised sexual acts with children under 14 (Article 188); the applicant had just turned 14. Insults had been decriminalised in 2012 and were now civil matters. Civil courts treated the physical acts as falling outside the Insults and Defamation Act (which concerned opinions) and found no other applicable provision. Later 2023 amendments criminalised non-consensual sexual acts and introduced a sexual-harassment offence, but these were not in force at the time.

The applicant complained that the domestic legal framework, as applied, failed to afford her effective protection of her physical and psychological integrity against the sexual abuse. The Court examined the complaint solely under Article 8.

The case of K.M. v. North Macedonia (App. no. 59144/16) concerns North Macedonia’s alleged failure under Article 8 ECHR to protect a 14-year-old girl’s physical and psychological integrity from sexual abuse. The ECtHR held that the domestic legal framework, as applied, did not afford effective protection.

On 31 August 2013 the applicant (born 19 August 1999) was at home when 39-year-old telecom employee Gj.K. arrived to restore internet service. Left alone with her, he remarked that her legs were nicely tanned and caressed her leg. When she moved away he followed, stated that men loved her because she had big breasts, massaged her shoulders and touched her breast. She fled the room. He allegedly also touched her sister inappropriately the same day.

The sister lodged a criminal complaint on 2 September 2013. Gj.K. denied the allegations. The applicant, her sister and their mother were interviewed; the mother described both girls as frightened and upset and said a psychiatrist had prescribed medication. On 6 November 2013 the prosecutor rejected the complaint. Although Gj.K. had touched the applicant’s breast and caressed her leg, the acts were committed without force or threats and therefore did not constitute “rape” (Article 186 §§ 1 and 4 Criminal Code, which required force or threats for “other sexual acts”). They amounted only to the (recently decriminalised) offence of insult, prosecutable solely by private complaint. The applicant was told she could take over the prosecution but did not do so.

On 30 November 2013 she brought a civil claim against Gj.K. for non-pecuniary damage, alleging insult and injury to honour and reputation, supported by a psychological report confirming fear and distress. The first-instance court dismissed the claim (March 2015, after remittal), holding that the Insults and Defamation Act covered only expressed opinions, not physical acts, and that she could have pursued private prosecution; no liability arose under the Obligations Act either. The appellate court upheld the dismissal (March 2016), finding the elements of insult unproven, no causal link established, and no statutory civil-liability provision applicable.

Domestic law protected physical and psychological integrity (Constitution Art. 11) and personal dignity (Art. 25). Criminal liability for non-penetrative sexual acts required force or threats (Art. 186); a separate offence existed only for children under 14 (Art. 188). Insults had been decriminalised in 2012; the Insults and Defamation Act required an intended degrading opinion. The Obligations Act permitted compensation for violations of personal rights and for certain sexual offences involving fraud, duress or abuse of dependence, but the courts did not apply these provisions (or the Convention directly, despite an express statutory mandate).

International standards (UNCRC Art. 19, Lanzarote Convention Art. 18, Istanbul Convention Art. 36) require criminalisation of non-consensual sexual acts with children, including those without physical force or involving abuse of position, and effective civil remedies. The facts demonstrate that, despite the applicant’s age, the isolated setting, the sexual comments and touching, and documented psychological harm, neither the criminal nor the civil system provided redress.
001-242199:
The case of Aytaj Ahmadova v. Azerbaijan (ECHR Application no. 30551/18) concerns alleged failures by Azerbaijani authorities to investigate a journalist’s complaints about the unauthorized online publication of her private photographs and videos, accompanied by insults and threats. These events followed the 2015 seizure of her computer by state officials, raising issues under Article 8 of the Convention regarding positive obligations to protect private life.

The applicant, born in 1993 and living in Baku, worked as a journalist for Meydan TV, an online news portal, from 2015. On 16 September 2015, she was forcibly detained by unidentified persons in civilian clothes and taken to the Organised Crime Department (OCD) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, where she was questioned about Meydan TV. That same day, OCD employees searched her flat without a warrant and seized her computer. The computer was added to the investigation file in criminal proceedings against Meydan TV by the Serious Crimes Investigation Department (SCID) of the Prosecutor General’s Office and remained in state possession despite the applicant’s repeated requests for its return. (Related domestic proceedings concerning the detention, search, and seizure form a separate pending application.)

From 14 September 2016, personal photographs and video-recordings of the applicant—taken at home with her family or at the beach, never previously shared, and stored only on the seized computer—were published on various Facebook accounts appearing to belong to fake individuals. The posts included captions suggesting she should be “hanged by her tongue,” “hanged naked in front of everyone,” and similar threats. When the applicant contacted one poster (E.K.) via Facebook to request deletion of beach photos of her and her mother, E.K. threatened further publication, accused her of betraying her country, and insulted her. The applicant continued to face insults on various Facebook pages.

On 14 October 2016, she complained to the Prosecutor General’s Office, Ministry of Internal Affairs, and State Security Service, asserting that the materials originated from her seized computer (retained for over a year) and that the publications, insults, and threats were linked to her journalistic work. She requested identification of those responsible and commencement of criminal proceedings. Receiving no reply, she repeated the complaint on 14 February 2017 (with a copy of the original) and again on 29 September 2017 (to the Prosecutor General’s Office only), still without response.

On 17 October 2017, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Sabail District Court under the judicial supervision procedure. She reiterated her allegations, treating the prosecuting authority’s silence as a de facto refusal to commence proceedings, and requested: production of the computer for court examination; an expert analysis to determine if it had been accessed, if files had been opened or transferred, or if data had been altered or deleted while in SCID custody; identification of IP addresses of those who posted the materials or threats; and summons of relevant OCD and SCID officials as witnesses. She sought a declaration that the Prosecutor General’s inaction was unlawful, an order to commence proceedings, identification and accountability of perpetrators, and recognition of violations of her Convention rights (including Articles 3, 8, 10, 13, 14, and 18).

The Sabail District Court rejected the complaint on 10 and 28 November 2017, citing Article 449.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It held that examination was impossible because the decision she sought to annul was “uncertain” with no information about its existence, and it did not address her requests or arguments.

The applicant appealed on 29 November 2017, repeating her arguments and complaining that the first-instance court had dismissed the matter without examination, failed to obtain materials from the prosecuting authority, and ignored her inability to produce a non-existent written refusal. On 11 December 2017, the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the decision on the same grounds, adding that the applicant had not proven her complaints were sent and delivered (despite providing copies). It dismissed her requests as irrelevant to the appeal.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: the prosecuting authorities neither commenced nor formally refused criminal proceedings despite repeated, detailed complaints about serious interferences with private life (publication of intimate materials stored solely on a state-retained computer, plus threats and insults potentially linked to journalistic activity). Domestic courts rejected the subsequent complaint in a formalistic manner without examining the substance, requests for evidence, or the authorities’ inaction. The applicant argued this breached positive obligations to investigate and protect her rights.
