001-242052:
**Case summary: Milashina and Others v. Russia (ECHR, Application no. 75000/17, judgment 4 March 2025)**

The applicants were Novaya Gazeta journalists Yelena Milashina (staff journalist and special projects editor), Dmitriy Muratov (editorial council chair and former editor-in-chief), Sergey Kozheurov (editor-in-chief and long-time company director), and the newspaper’s publishing house. On 1 April 2017, Milashina published “Honour Killing,” reporting mass abductions, arbitrary detentions, torture, and killings of men perceived as homosexual by Chechen authorities. Sources included Interior Ministry, FSB, prosecutor’s office, and local activists; a crisis line for victims was mentioned. A 4 April follow-up, “Massacre of Chechen Gays,” detailed survivor accounts of persecution. These reports were later corroborated by UN, OSCE, PACE, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and major media; over 114 people fled Chechnya. Related ECHR cases (N.A. and Others v. Russia; Lapunov v. Russia) confirmed State-agent abductions and disappearances.

Chechen officials and religious leaders responded with public statements broadcast and published widely. On 2 April, Minister Dzhambulat Umarov called the report a “heinous hoax” and warned that any “filth” (LGBTI people) would be “harshly persecuted” by locals, possibly via “more radical measures” by relatives. On 3 April, a 15,000-person meeting at Grozny’s central mosque (attended by 24 community representatives and Islamic leaders) featured advisor Adam Shakhidov branding staff “enemies of our faith and our homeland.” A resolution denounced the article as slander insulting Chechen honour, dignity, traditions, and faith, promising “retribution to the instigators, whoever and wherever they are,” and urging a fight against such “infamy.” It was published on the state-run Grozny-Inform site.

On 14–15 April, Mufti Mezhiyev (Chechen Muslim Spiritual Authority chair) called journalists “creatures” (not people) who insulted the Chechen people and faith, stating they would face legal responsibility plus “retribution of the almighty Allah.” Umarov replied to Muratov’s public appeal (which recalled past Novaya Gazeta killings and sought dialogue) by demanding apologies, accusing ignorance of Chechen traditions (where even mentioning “the sin of Sodom” offends), and warning of others who might act against the paper. On 22 April, Head of the Chechen Republic Ramzan Kadyrov said such journalists “want war in Russia” and should be “chased... far away.”

These statements, viewed as incitement, triggered further anonymous death threats to Milashina via Facebook (usernames suggesting Caucasian/Chechen origin). She received a signal jammer, relocated from home, limited public transport, used a driver, and fled Russia from late April 2017 until year-end due to safety fears and inaction. An envelope with unknown white powder addressed to Kozheurov (marked “Grozny”) arrived at the office on 19 April; police were notified but took no action.

On 18 April, the editorial board and Milashina complained to Russia’s Investigative Committee about murder threats and incitement by Chechen leaders. An initial 17 May refusal to open a case (finding no crime in the resolution and noting the mosque video had been deleted) was quashed. Mufti Mezhiyev was questioned on 6 June; he confirmed the meeting/resolution, explained Islamic/Chechen views on “non-traditional relations” (execution or clan annihilation, though legally banned, with “retribution” meaning Allah’s punishment), and denied threats. Further refusals (12 nearly identical ones through February 2018) cited missing video and Mezhiyev’s explanation. A 2018 court challenge to the last refusal (arguing incomplete inquiry, late video request, no identification of resolution authors, no linguistic analysis, and Article 10 breach) was dismissed by Yessentuki Town Court and Stavropol Regional Court without addressing key points. No criminal case was opened, no charges brought, and no full file disclosed.

Later incidents (not the core 2017 events but cited) included chemical spraying at the Novaya Gazeta office (2021), verbal attacks on Milashina/Novaya Gazeta by Kadyrov (2017–2022), physical assaults on her in Chechnya (2020, 2023), an attack on Muratov (2022, chemical burns; no case opened despite identification), and the paper’s history of five murdered journalists. The applicants alleged these facts showed a concerted intimidation campaign interfering with journalistic work (Article 10), exposing them to violence without protection or investigation (Articles 2/8), and discrimination (Article 14). The Government made no submissions. The Court examined victim status, threats’ chilling effect, and investigative failures.

The case of Milashina and Others v. Russia (Application no. 75000/17) concerns complaints by Novaya Gazeta journalists Yelena Milashina, Dmitriy Muratov and Sergey Kozheurov, together with the newspaper’s publishing house, arising from their 2017 reporting on the persecution of LGBTI people in Chechnya.

On 1 April 2017 Novaya Gazeta published Milashina’s article “Honour Killing”, which detailed mass abductions, arbitrary detention, torture and killings of men perceived as homosexual by Chechen authorities. The piece cited sources inside the Chechen Interior Ministry, FSB, prosecutor’s office and local activists, and noted the creation of a crisis line. A follow-up article on 4 April reproduced survivor testimonies. The allegations were later corroborated by UN, OSCE, PACE, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and other bodies; the Court itself subsequently found in related cases that abducted victims were presumed dead.

Chechen officials reacted immediately. On 2 April the republic’s Minister for National Politics, Dzhambulat Umarov, declared that any “filth” (LGBTI people) appearing in Chechnya would be “harshly persecuted” and that relatives might take “more radical measures”. On 3 April a meeting of 15 000 people in Grozny’s central mosque, addressed by Ramzan Kadyrov’s adviser Adam Shakhidov, branded the journalists “enemies of our faith and our homeland”. The assembly adopted a resolution declaring the articles “absolutely a lie and slander” that insulted Chechen honour and Islam, and promising “retribution to the instigators, whoever and wherever they are”. The resolution was published on the official Grozny-Inform portal.

Further statements followed. Chechen Mufti Salah Mezhiyev, on radio and in print, described the journalists as “creatures” who would face “the reprisal of the almighty Allah” and “retribution \ldots through whom He will do it”. Umarov demanded public apologies and accused the newspaper of ignorance of Chechen traditions. Kadyrov himself, on 22 April, said the journalists “want war in Russia” and should be “chased \ldots far away”. These remarks were broadcast on state television and widely recirculated.

The applicants received immediate threats. Milashina was inundated with anonymous death threats on social media from accounts suggesting Chechen origin. She left her home, restricted her movements and, by late April 2017, fled Russia for the remainder of the year. An envelope containing unidentified white powder, postmarked “Grozny”, arrived at the newspaper addressed to Kozheurov. Subsequent years saw further public verbal attacks by Kadyrov, a toxic-chemical incident at Novaya Gazeta’s Moscow offices, physical assaults on Milashina during reporting trips to Chechnya, and an attack on Muratov in 2022 in which he was doused with a paint-and-acetone mixture. Five Novaya Gazeta journalists had previously been murdered in connection with their work.

Complaints lodged with the Investigative Committee in April 2017 alleging death threats and incitement to hatred produced a succession of refusals to open a criminal case (the last in February 2018). Investigators failed to obtain timely video of the mosque meeting, conducted no forensic linguistic analysis of the resolution, and accepted the Mufti’s explanation that “retribution” referred only to divine punishment. Domestic courts dismissed challenges to these decisions without addressing the applicants’ arguments. No investigation was opened into any of the later incidents.

The Court found that the officials’ statements constituted a concerted campaign of intimidation capable of inciting violence, placing the applicants in fear for their lives and safety and producing a chilling effect on journalistic activity. The authorities’ failure to investigate the threats or to take preventive measures amounted to an unlawful and disproportionate interference with freedom of expression (Article 10) and a failure to protect private life (Article 8). The publishing house itself was recognised as a victim.

The case of Mustafa Aydın v. Türkiye (Application no. 6696/20) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that his conviction for membership of an armed terrorist organisation (YDGH, the youth wing of the PKK) was unfair because the trial court failed to deliver an individualised, reasoned judgment, a defect unremedied by higher courts.

In February 2008, a judge authorised interception of the applicant’s telecommunications and surveillance as part of a wider YDGH investigation. Informant R.S. later provided extensive statements (in exchange for sentence reduction) detailing the organisation’s structure and naming several members of its Aegean branch, but not the applicant. A police report recorded that the applicant, a Dicle News Agency correspondent and journalism student, had connected by telephone to a Roj TV programme to discuss a planned protest march. During a house search of co-suspect M.B., police seized a two-page “Progress Report” listing “Mustafa A.” (alongside two others) as responsible for press affairs.

The applicant was arrested on 20 March 2008 while video-recording a Nowruz gathering. In statements to police, the prosecutor and a judge (always with counsel present), he consistently denied any organisational membership. He explained that he worked under contract for Dicle News Agency, that telephone references to “afiş” with acquaintance E.Y. concerned a café of that name rather than illegal banner-hanging, that he did not know the other named individuals, and that a single Roj TV connection contained no criminal content. He produced his employment contract and a photograph of Afiş Café.

The May 2008 indictment charged him solely with membership under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code. It relied on the seized document (the prosecutor substituting “Mustafa Aydın” for “Mustafa A.” without explanation), intercepted calls, and R.S.’s statements (which did not identify the applicant). Seventeen arson incidents were mentioned, yet the applicant was not charged with them.

At trial the applicant repeated his denials. His lawyer submitted that the prosecution had produced no evidence of any organisational link and had failed even to investigate the alleged banner-hanging.

On 24 January 2014 the İzmir Tenth Specially Authorised Assize Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. Its 82-page judgment reproduced the indictment, all statements and a general list of evidence, then grouped the applicant with six other defendants. For that group the court stated, in a single undifferentiated passage, that intercepted conversations showed they had been in contact with YDGH leaders, that those contacts had produced demonstrations and arsons, and that conviction was therefore justified by the “accusations, defence submissions, transcripts, R.S.’s statements and seized documents.” No specific call involving the applicant was quoted or analysed, his explanations of the “afiş” conversations and the document were not addressed, and R.S. had never mentioned him.

The applicant’s appeal emphasised the absence of any personal link, the lack of identification by R.S., and the unexplained identification of “Mustafa A.” The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction in a brief formula stating that the offence had been correctly characterised and the defence dismissed on credible grounds. The Constitutional Court, in a two-page decision, declared the individual application inadmissible, holding that the proceedings as a whole disclosed no violation of the right to a reasoned judgment and no manifest arbitrariness.

Turkish law (Constitution Art. 141 § 3; CCP Arts. 34, 230 and 232) requires every judicial decision to contain reasons that discuss the evidence relied upon and rejected and that specify the acts found to constitute the offence. The trial court’s generic grouping and the higher courts’ failure to supply the missing individualised reasoning constitute the core of the alleged Article 6 violation.

The case of Mustafa Aydın v. Türkiye (Application no. 6696/20) concerns the alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to the unfairness of criminal proceedings against the applicant. Specifically, the domestic courts failed to conduct an individualised assessment of the evidence against him and to provide sufficient reasons for convicting him of membership in an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code.

In February 2008, a judge authorised the interception of the applicant’s telecommunications and covert surveillance as part of an investigation into the Patriotic Democratic Youth Movement (YDGH), regarded as the youth wing of the PKK. A key witness, R.S., provided detailed statements (in exchange for sentence reduction under active repentance provisions) describing the YDGH’s structure, including its Aegean branch, though he did not specifically implicate the applicant. A March 2008 police report noted that the applicant, a correspondent for the Dicle News Agency, had connected to a Roj TV programme (viewed as PKK-aligned) and discussed a protest march. A search of another suspect’s house yielded a document listing “Mustafa A.” as responsible for the organisation’s press affairs in the Aegean region.

The applicant was arrested on 20 March 2008 while filming a Nowruz gathering where slogans were chanted. In statements to police, the prosecutor, and a judge, he denied any organisational membership. He explained that he was a journalism student and Dicle correspondent (submitting his contract as proof), that intercepted calls with E.Y. referring to “afiş” concerned a café of that name rather than illegal banner-hanging, and that he had no knowledge of the seized document or the named individuals. He was released pending trial.

The May 2008 indictment charged the applicant (among 20 others) with organisational membership, citing R.S.’s statements, the seized document (now identifying him as “Mustafa Aydın”), and phone records, while alleging group involvement in unauthorised demonstrations, arson, and related acts. The applicant’s house yielded no incriminating material, and he was not charged with specific damage offences.

At trial, the applicant reiterated his denials, emphasising his professional and academic status and limited acquaintance with only one co-defendant (E.Y., for translation work). His lawyer argued that the evidence showed only everyday conversations, that police had misinterpreted “afiş” without verifying any illegal activity, and that no link existed between the applicant and the organisation or the seized document.

In its 24 January 2014 judgment (82 pages), the İzmir Assize Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. After reproducing the indictment, statements, and a generic evidence list, the court grouped the applicant with several co-defendants. It referred generally to intercepted conversations showing contact with YDGH leaders, organisational decisions to intensify activities (including vehicle arson), and R.S.’s statements as harmonious with events, concluding that the grouped defendants were members. No specific telephone transcripts involving the applicant were analysed, nor was the identification of “Mustafa A.” explained or his individual defences (such as the café explanation or lack of contact with key figures) addressed.

The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction in 2016, stating only that the offence characterisation was correct and the defence dismissed on credible grounds. The Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s individual application inadmissible in 2019, finding no violation of the right to a reasoned judgment when viewing the proceedings as a whole and no manifest arbitrariness in fact-finding or legal application.

Turkish law (Constitution Article 141 § 3 and Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 34, 230, and 232) requires all judicial decisions to contain reasons, including discussion and assessment of evidence, indication of evidence relied upon or rejected, and individualised conclusions on the defendant’s acts. The trial court’s generic grouping and failure to engage with the applicant’s specific submissions, unremedied by higher courts, formed the core of the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation.

The case of Mustafa Aydın v. Türkiye concerns the applicant’s conviction for membership of an armed terrorist organisation (YDGH, the youth wing of the PKK) under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code. He alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention due to the domestic courts’ failure to provide an individualised assessment or sufficient reasons for his conviction.

In February 2008, a judge authorised interception of the applicant’s telecommunications and covert surveillance as part of a broader investigation. R.S., a former YDGH figure who later received impunity under “active repentance” provisions, provided lengthy statements detailing the organisation’s structure but did not name the applicant. A police report recorded the applicant (a Dicle News Agency correspondent and journalism student) briefly connecting to a Roj TV programme to discuss a protest march. A search of co-suspect M.B.’s house yielded a two-page “Progress Report” listing “Mustafa A.” (later treated by prosecutors as the applicant) as responsible for press affairs in İzmir’s Aegean branch.

The applicant was arrested on 20 March 2008 while filming a Nowruz gathering involving slogans. In statements to police, prosecutors and a judge (all with legal representation), he denied organisational membership. He explained intercepted calls with E.Y. (a university acquaintance) as referring to “Afiş Café,” not illegal banner-hanging, and submitted supporting photographs and his employment contract. He was released pending trial while most co-suspects were detained.

The May 2008 indictment charged 20 people, including the applicant, with organisational membership. It referenced R.S.’s statements, general phone records, the seized report (substituting the applicant’s full name without justification), and various arson incidents, though the applicant faced only the membership charge. At trial, he reiterated his denials and journalist role. His lawyer’s submissions (2010 and 2013) stressed the absence of evidence linking him to any illegal acts, the untested “afiş” interpretation, and lack of verification that he had hung banners or known other suspects beyond E.Y.

The “assessment of evidence” section contained only generalised assertions: that phone transcripts showed contact with YDGH leaders, that meetings occurred, and that this led to unauthorised demonstrations and vehicle-burnings. No specific calls involving the applicant were quoted or analysed, R.S.’s statements (which omitted him) were invoked collectively, and the seized document was not individually attributed. The court listed categories of evidence but offered no discussion of what was accepted or rejected in the applicant’s case, nor any response to his concrete defences.

The applicant’s 2015 cassation appeal highlighted these gaps: no organisational link, no identification by R.S., no meetings or relevant calls, and an unexplained identification from the document. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction in 2016 with boilerplate language that the offence was correctly characterised and proven, without addressing the specific arguments. The Constitutional Court declared his 2017 individual application inadmissible in a two-page 2019 decision, finding no violation of the right to a reasoned judgment when viewing the proceedings as a whole and no manifest arbitrariness.

Turkish law (Constitution Article 141 and Criminal Procedure Code Articles 34, 230 and 232) requires all judicial decisions to contain reasons, including discussion of the evidence relied upon and rejected. The European Court held that the trial court’s failure to deliver an individualised, reasoned judgment was not remedied on appeal, violating Article 6 § 1.
001-242368:
The case of Farhad Mehdiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 36057/18) concerns the rapid revocation of the applicant’s readmission to the Azerbaijani Bar Association (ABA) days after he took the lawyer’s oath. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention, finding a violation of Article 8 because the interference with the applicant’s private life (his professional activity) was not “in accordance with the law.”

The applicant, born in 1974 and resident in Baku, was first admitted to the ABA on 5 August 2009 and affiliated with the Absheron District Law Office. On 23 February 2012 he requested termination of his lawyer status because he was exclusively engaged in academic work; the ABA granted the request on 27 February 2012. In August 2016 he applied for readmission. On 7 September 2016 the ABA Presidium admitted him with immediate effect, assigned him to Baku Law Office no. 11, and administered the lawyer’s oath. Under Article 14 of the Law on Advocates and Advocacy Activity, the oath marked the commencement of his term of office and inclusion in the register of lawyers.

Two days later the head of the Absheron District Law Office wrote to the ABA stating that the applicant had concluded only one contract between 2009 and 2012, had never appeared as a State-appointed lawyer, and owed AZN 1,800 (approximately EUR 1,000) in unpaid membership fees from that earlier period. On 15 September 2016 the Presidium, relying on the letter, revoked its 7 September decision and refused readmission, citing both the alleged lack of practice and the outstanding debt.

The applicant challenged the revocation before the domestic courts. He argued that, having taken the oath, he was a practising lawyer who could be removed only after disciplinary proceedings under Articles 21–22 of the Law. He further contended that any disciplinary action was time-barred (six months from discovery or one year from commission) and that, in any event, Article 23(II) required a court decision before activity could be terminated for non-payment of fees. The first-instance court (10 May 2017), the Baku Court of Appeal (24 August 2017) and the Supreme Court (27 December 2017) all dismissed the claim. They held that Article 23(I) expressly permitted termination for failure to pay membership fees for more than six months without good reason and that the documented debt justified the Presidium’s action. The applicant received the Supreme Court’s decision on 23 January 2018 and lodged his application with the Strasbourg Court on 21 July 2018.

The facts therefore centre on a sequence in which the applicant was formally readmitted and sworn in, only to have that status cancelled eight days later on the basis of a historical debt incurred during a previous, already-terminated membership. The domestic authorities treated the non-payment as an automatic ground for termination under Article 23(I) without instituting disciplinary proceedings or obtaining a court order as contemplated by Article 23(II). These circumstances formed the core of the alleged unlawfulness of the interference with the applicant’s professional life.

**Case of Farhad Mehdiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 36057/18)**

The applicant, Farhad Mehdiyev (born 1974), an Azerbaijani national and law professor living in Baku, was admitted to the Azerbaijani Bar Association (ABA) on 5 August 2009 and affiliated with the Absheron District Law Office. On 23 February 2012 he requested termination of his lawyer status to focus exclusively on scientific and pedagogical work; the ABA granted this on 27 February 2012.

In August 2016 he applied for readmission. On 7 September 2016 the ABA Presidium admitted him with effect from that date, assigned him to Baku Law Office no. 11, and he immediately took the lawyer’s oath. Two days later the head of the Absheron District Law Office wrote to the ABA stating that the applicant had had only one contract between 2009 and 2012, had not appeared as a State-appointed lawyer, and owed AZN 1,800 (approximately EUR 1,000) in unpaid membership fees.

At a Presidium meeting on 15 September 2016 three members relied on this letter to argue that the applicant had not genuinely practised and had outstanding debt. The applicant, present at the meeting, contested the letter and asserted that he had practised. The Presidium revoked its 7 September decision and refused admission.

The applicant challenged the revocation in court on 8 November 2016. He argued it was unlawful because he had been practising since 7 September 2016 after taking the oath; disbarment required disciplinary proceedings under the Law on Advocates and Advocacy Activity; any sanction was time-barred (six months from discovery or one year from commission of the alleged breach); and the decision restricted his professional activity.

On 10 May 2017 Baku Administrative-Economic Court no. 1 dismissed the claim. It cited Article 23 of the Law, which lists grounds for terminating a lawyer’s activity, including failure to pay membership fees for more than six months without good reason, and noted the AZN 1,800 debt. The applicant appealed, repeating that he had been a practising member since 7 September, that disciplinary procedure was required, and that Article 23(II) mandated a court decision (not a mere Presidium act) for termination on unpaid-fees grounds.

The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 24 August 2017, essentially repeating the first-instance reasoning. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal invoking Articles 6, 8, 14 and 18 of the Convention. The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts on 27 December 2017; the decision was served on 23 January 2018. The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2018, complaining under Articles 6 and 8.

The core facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the extremely rapid revocation of a freshly granted admission (eight days later) on the basis of unpaid fees from a prior, voluntarily terminated membership period four years earlier, without initiating disciplinary proceedings or obtaining a court order as the applicant contended the Law required. The domestic courts treated the matter as a straightforward application of Article 23(I) despite the applicant’s intervening readmission, oath-taking and commencement of practice. The European Court later found the interference with the applicant’s private life (professional activity as a lawyer) was not “in accordance with the law.”

The case of Farhad Mehdiyev v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 36057/18) concerns the abrupt termination of the applicant’s right to practise law just days after his readmission to the Azerbaijani Bar Association (ABA). The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1974, had first been admitted to the ABA on 5 August 2009 and affiliated with the Absheron District Law Office. On 23 February 2012 he requested termination of his status as a lawyer in order to devote himself exclusively to academic and teaching work; the ABA granted that request on 27 February 2012.

In August 2016 the applicant applied for readmission. On 7 September 2016 the ABA Presidium admitted him with immediate effect, assigned him to Baku Law Office no. 11, and he took the statutory lawyer’s oath the same day. Under the Law on Advocates and Advocacy Activity, a lawyer’s term of office begins upon taking the oath and the person is entered in the register of lawyers.

Two days later the head of the Absheron District Law Office wrote to the ABA stating that the applicant had concluded only one contract between 2009 and 2012, had never acted as a State-appointed lawyer, and owed AZN 1 800 (approximately EUR 1 000) in unpaid membership fees. At a meeting on 15 September 2016 three Presidium members relied on that letter to argue that the applicant had not genuinely practised and that the debt remained outstanding. The applicant, who was present, disputed both assertions. The Presidium nevertheless revoked its decision of 7 September and refused his application for admission.

The applicant brought administrative proceedings on 8 November 2016. He contended that he had validly become a practising lawyer on 7 September and could be removed only through disciplinary proceedings under Articles 21–22 of the Law. Those provisions impose a six-month time-limit from disclosure of any breach (or one year from its commission) and require an opinion of the disciplinary commission. He further argued that even if non-payment of fees were relied upon, Article 23(II) expressly required a final court judgment excluding him from the ABA; the Presidium had no power to act unilaterally. He claimed the decision unlawfully restricted his professional activity.

Baku Administrative-Economic Court no. 1 dismissed the claim on 10 May 2017, holding that Article 23(I) authorised termination for non-payment of fees for more than six months without good reason and that the debt of AZN 1 800 justified the Presidium’s decision. The Baku Court of Appeal (24 August 2017) and the Supreme Court (27 December 2017) upheld that reasoning. The applicant relied, inter alia, on Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the extremely short interval between formal readmission (including the oath) and revocation, the reliance on a debt incurred years earlier during a previous membership, the absence of any disciplinary procedure or court order as required by the domestic statute, and the domestic courts’ endorsement of the Presidium’s unilateral action. These circumstances form the basis of the complaint that the interference with the applicant’s professional life was not “in accordance with the law”.
001-242532:
The case of *Kulák v. Slovakia* (Application no. 57748/21) concerns the search of a lawyer’s office and prolonged seizure of his work computer, alleged to violate Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life and home).

The applicant, Tomáš Kulák, a practising lawyer, became involved in a wide-ranging NAKA investigation into judicial corruption, including the “Vodári case.” On 21 October 2020 a prosecutor issued a warrant under Article 90 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requiring the applicant to surrender computer data containing specified keywords linked to that case. The warrant’s stated purpose was to obtain evidence that the applicant had drafted a first-instance judgment; it contemplated on-site extraction of only relevant files so as not to disrupt his practice or breach legal professional privilege.

On 27 October 2020 the applicant was charged with interfering with judicial independence. The next morning officers searched his law firm at a secondary address. The Government maintained that they first attended his registered home address, arrested him, and only then learned the true office location, making an immediate search without a written warrant necessary under Article 101 § 3 CCP to prevent destruction of evidence. The applicant asserted that officers arrived directly at the office. The search report invoked urgency but gave no particulars. A prosecutor later recorded that she had given oral consent by telephone.

The search, conducted in the presence of the applicant, his counsel, a Bar Association representative and an independent observer, lasted approximately one hour. Officers seized the entire work computer, which contained data of numerous unrelated clients. The applicant’s representatives objected to the absence of a written search warrant and to the lack of precision concerning the device. They asked that the computer be secured intact. It was retained for almost fifteen months and returned only on 21 January 2022.

An expert subsequently examined the computer and exceeded the original keywords (one of which was the applicant’s own surname), thereby accessing privileged material unrelated to the investigation. Domestic law provided no mechanism for the applicant, his lawyer or the Bar Association to supervise the keyword search or to protect privileged files.

The applicant challenged the operation through prosecutorial complaints and two constitutional complaints. Prosecutors defended the urgency (the office address having been unknown until arrest) and the full seizure (hard-drive size and the applicant’s own request). The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaints, holding that criminal proceedings themselves afforded adequate remedies, that urgency had been established, that keywords sufficiently protected third-party rights, and that the applicant had caused the computer’s wholesale removal.

The European Court held that, although a general legal basis existed, the interference was not “in accordance with the law.” At the material time there was no immediate *ex post facto* judicial review of searches of non-residential premises; the entire computer was seized despite the warrant’s limited purpose; and no procedure existed to isolate or preserve material covered by legal professional privilege. These deficiencies meant that the applicant’s Article 8 rights lacked sufficient safeguards both before and after the search-and-seizure operation.

The case of Kulák v. Slovakia (Application no. 57748/21) concerns a search of the applicant’s law firm and seizure of his work computer, alleged to violate Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life and home). The applicant, Tomáš Kulák, a Slovak lawyer, was implicated in a 2019 National Crime Agency (NAKA) inquiry into judicial corruption, including the “Vodári case.” In March 2020, charges were brought against multiple judges and others. A cooperating witness later alleged that the applicant, as defence counsel, had drafted a first-instance judgment in that case.

On 21 October 2020 a prosecutor issued a warrant under Article 90 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) for the securing and surrender of computer data from the applicant’s devices. The warrant targeted data containing specified keywords linked to the Vodári case and was justified as a targeted measure that would avoid removing devices (thereby minimising interference with the applicant’s practice) and would be executed by an expert. Legal professional privilege was said to be protected by secrecy obligations. The following day the applicant himself was charged with interfering with judicial independence.

On 28 October 2020 officers searched the applicant’s law firm at a secondary address. Accounts diverge: the Government maintain that officers first went to the applicant’s registered home address, arrested him and only then learned of the actual office location, necessitating an immediate move to prevent evidence destruction; the applicant states that officers arrived directly at the office. The search was conducted without a written warrant, under the urgency exception in Article 101 § 3 CCP. The search report contained no particulars of urgency. A Bar Association representative and the applicant’s lawyer were present and both objected to the absence of a warrant and to the imprecise identification of the computer. The entire work computer—containing data of numerous unrelated clients—was seized because on-site extraction was deemed impractical. The prosecutor later recorded that telephone consent had been given that morning.

The applicant challenged the search and seizure through prosecutorial review (Article 210 CCP) and two constitutional complaints. Prosecutors and the Constitutional Court upheld the measures, citing the unforeseen discovery of the office location, the need to prevent remote deletion, the applicant’s own request that the whole computer be taken, and the use of keywords to filter data. The Constitutional Court added that criminal proceedings themselves constituted an adequate remedy and that no warrant could be served because none existed.

An expert report of August 2021 revealed that the examination had exceeded the authorised keywords (including the applicant’s own surname) and had therefore accessed privileged and irrelevant material. Domestic law provided no mechanism for the applicant, his lawyer or the Bar Association to participate in or supervise the keyword search or to isolate privileged files. The computer was returned only on 21 January 2022, almost fifteen months later. The applicant was formally indicted in March 2023; the criminal proceedings remain pending.

At the relevant time Article 101 CCP required a written, reasoned warrant for searches of non-residential premises, to be served at the time of the search (or within 24 hours). The urgency exception applied only when a warrant could not be obtained in advance and delay was impossible; the authority competent to issue the warrant had to be informed immediately. No provision existed for immediate judicial review of such searches, nor for the segregation and prompt return of material unrelated to the investigation or subject to legal professional privilege.

**CASE OF KULÁK v. SLOVAKIA (Application no. 57748/21, ECtHR, 3 April 2025)**

The case concerns alleged violations of Article 8 ECHR (private life and home) arising from a 28 October 2020 search of Slovak lawyer Tomáš Kulák’s law firm and the seizure of his work computer, which was retained for nearly 15 months. The computer likely contained legally privileged client data unrelated to the investigation.

The background was a National Crime Agency (NAKA) inquiry, begun in August 2019, into alleged judicial corruption, bribery, abuse of authority and interference with judicial independence. This included the “Vodári” case. On 9 March 2020, 18 people (including 13 judges) were charged. A cooperating former judge later testified that Kulák, as defence counsel, had drafted a first-instance judgment favouring his client with support from an accused judge.

On 21 October 2020 a Special Prosecutions prosecutor issued a written warrant under Article 90 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the securing and surrender of specified computer data (documents, applications, recordings) from Kulák’s devices matching Vodári-related keywords. The stated purpose was to obtain evidence of the drafted judgment. The warrant emphasised that devices in active use should not be seized so as not to disrupt legal practice, that only keyword-specified data would be taken, and that professional secrecy would be protected by officers’ and experts’ duties of confidentiality. On 27 October Kulák himself was charged with interference with judicial independence.

On the morning of 28 October, officers searched the law firm at Kulák’s secondary address (Družstevná Street). Accounts differed: the Government said officers first went to his registered home/office address, arrested him, then learned of the actual premises and hurried there to prevent evidence destruction or remote deletion; Kulák said they arrived directly at the firm while he was meeting a client. The search report recorded that it was conducted without a written search warrant under the urgency provision of Article 101 § 3 CCP. The prosecutor later noted she had given telephone consent that morning. Five officers (including a forensic technician), an electronics expert and an independent observer participated. A Bar Association representative was notified at 9.25 a.m. and arrived later; Kulák’s lawyer arrived at 10.10 a.m. Both objected to the absence of a written warrant and to insufficient specification of the target computer. The Bar representative stated the urgency conditions were not met and stressed confidentiality. At the request of Kulák and his lawyer the entire work computer was seized “without interference.” The search ended at 11.10 a.m. The computer contained data of multiple unrelated clients.

Prosecutors later justified the lack of prior warrant by the last-minute discovery of the true address and the need to act immediately. They said the hard-drive size prevented on-site extraction, so the whole computer had to be taken; keywords would limit the data retained and unrelated material would be destroyed or returned. An expert appointed in August 2019 was later instructed to examine the seized computer using the keywords. His August 2021 report showed he had gone beyond those keywords (including searching Kulák’s surname), thereby accessing unrelated data. Domestic law provided no mechanism for the lawyer, his counsel or the Bar to participate in or supervise the keyword search or to isolate privileged material.

Kulák lodged complaints with supervising prosecutors (dismissed) and two constitutional complaints (rejected in May and November 2021). The Constitutional Court held that the search was justified by newly discovered facts creating urgency, that any prolonged retention was caused by Kulák’s own request for full seizure, that keywords adequately protected third-party privacy, and that any remaining issues could be addressed in the ongoing criminal proceedings (in which he was formally indicted in 2023). The computer was returned on 21 January 2022.

The ECtHR later found the interference not “in accordance with the law,” citing the absence of a written warrant, lack of immediate ex post judicial review of non-residential searches, seizure of the entire computer despite the warrant’s limited purpose, and the absence of any procedure to safeguard unrelated or privileged material.
001-242862:
The case of Kavečanský v. Slovakia (no. 49617/22) concerns searches of a notary’s office and unoccupied non-residential premises, plus seizure of electronic devices, under Articles 8 and 13 ECHR.

The applicant, a notary since 2009, alleged he was kidnapped from 30 April to 2 May 2021, forced to withdraw and surrender €4 million. He reported this on 2 May and took sick leave from 3 May. Police opened a kidnapping investigation on 10 May. Unannounced Chamber of Notaries inspections in May revealed irregularities; a replacement notary was appointed on 14 June and the applicant suspended. Police searched his unoccupied future office premises on 15 June as part of the kidnapping inquiry.

On 21 and 25 June, an investigator opened embezzlement proceedings after the notary’s office failed to release hundreds of thousands of euros from deposit accounts. These were extended in July. On 16 July the Justice Minister released the applicant from confidentiality regarding the relevant deposits.

On 2 August the investigator issued search warrants (approved by the prosecutor) under Article 101 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the notary’s office and non-residential premises. The warrants cited a reasonable suspicion that evidence of embezzlement (documents on fund transfers July 2020–August 2021, cash proceeds, and computer equipment used for transfers) would be found. They did not address how unrelated or privileged notary-client material would be handled. A judge issued a similar home-search warrant the next day.

On 4 August the applicant was charged with aggravated embezzlement causing €1,084,549.94 damage. Searches occurred that day: the home (9:20 a.m.–12:05 p.m., wife present; seven USB keys, two tablets, one phone and four laptops seized); the notary’s office (1:00–2:23 p.m., caretaker present after the warrant was served on him; five phones, two laptops, two computers and a network storage device seized); and the non-residential premises (6:00–6:30 p.m., mother present after the applicant’s 3:30 p.m. arrest; nothing found). An independent municipal police observer and forensic experts attended. Data copies were later made; devices were returned in September–October 2021. A November 2021 expert report analysing the copied data for betting records and deposit lists (2018–August 2021) was placed on the file. The applicant was indicted on 28 January 2022 for embezzlement of €1,796,975.83; proceedings remain pending.

The applicant’s October 2021 constitutional complaint (Articles 6 and 8) was rejected in June 2022 for non-exhaustion: he could challenge the searches’ legality in the criminal trial.

The Court held that the office and premises searches and seizures interfered with Article 8 rights to private life and home. Although based on domestic law, they lacked prior judicial authorisation and any effective a-posteriori judicial review of the warrants or their execution. Insufficient safeguards therefore rendered the interference not “in accordance with the law.”

The case of Kavečanský v. Slovakia (Application no. 49617/22) concerns complaints under Articles 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from searches of the applicant’s notary office and unoccupied non-residential premises, together with the seizure of his electronic devices. These measures were authorised by search warrants issued by a police investigator and approved by a prosecutor in the course of embezzlement proceedings, without prior judicial authorisation or an effective possibility of subsequent judicial review of either the warrants or the manner of their execution.

The applicant, a practising notary since 2009, reported to police on 2 May 2021 that he had been abducted and extorted of €4 million between 30 April and 2 May 2021. A kidnapping investigation was opened on 10 May 2021. Subsequent unannounced inspections by the Chamber of Notaries revealed serious irregularities in the management of his office and the administration of notarial deposits. On 21 and 25 June 2021 an investigator opened criminal proceedings against the applicant for a particularly serious form of embezzlement after his office failed to release several hundred thousand euros from client deposit accounts. The proceedings were later extended.

On 2 August 2021 the investigator issued written search warrants under Article 101 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the applicant’s notary office on Kmeťová Street and his unoccupied non-residential premises on Rumanová Street (intended as a future office). Both warrants were approved the same day by the prosecutor. They asserted a reasonable suspicion that evidence of embezzlement would be found, specifically documents recording fund transfers (1 July 2020–2 August 2021), cash proceeds of crime, and computer equipment used for transfers. The warrants referred to the existing investigation file but contained no provisions for the identification, isolation or protection of material unrelated to the charges or covered by notary-client privilege. A judicial warrant was obtained only for the applicant’s home.

On 4 August 2021 the applicant was charged with aggravated embezzlement causing damage of approximately €1.08 million. That day police searched his home (judicial warrant), his notary office and the Rumanová Street premises. Multiple electronic devices (laptops, computers, mobile phones, USB keys, tablets and a network storage device) were seized from the home and office; nothing was found at the unoccupied premises. An independent observer and forensic experts were present. The applicant himself was arrested later that afternoon and served with the Rumanová warrant after the office search had already begun. Data copies were subsequently made of the seized devices, after which the physical items were returned to the applicant’s wife in September and October 2021. A forensic expert report based on the imaged data was later added to the investigation file.

The applicant’s complaint against the charging decision was dismissed by the supervising prosecutor. His constitutional complaint alleging violations of Articles 6 and 8 (among others) was rejected on 1 June 2022 for non-exhaustion of ordinary remedies; the Constitutional Court held that challenges to the legality of the searches and seizures could be raised during the still-pending criminal trial. The applicant was subsequently indicted on an increased sum of embezzlement and the criminal proceedings remain ongoing.

Domestic law (Articles 99 and 101 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) permitted an investigator, with prosecutorial consent, to order searches of non-residential premises without prior judicial authorisation. The warrants and the subsequent searches therefore rested solely on prosecutorial approval, with no contemporaneous or prompt judicial scrutiny of necessity, proportionality or the handling of privileged material. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the interference with his private life and home was not “in accordance with the law” and that he lacked an effective remedy.

**The applicant, a notary since 2009, reported a kidnapping and extortion in early May 2021.** An investigation into the abduction opened, but inspections by the Chamber of Notaries soon revealed serious irregularities in his office’s management of client deposits. He was placed on sick leave, suspended from practice, and a replacement notary was appointed. In June 2021, criminal proceedings for aggravated embezzlement were initiated against him over unreleased funds totaling hundreds of thousands of euros from notarial deposit accounts. The proceedings were later expanded.

**On 2 August 2021, a police investigator issued written search warrants** (approved the same day by a prosecutor) under Article 101 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the applicant’s notary office on Kmeťová Street and unoccupied non-residential premises on Rumanová Street (intended as a future office). The warrants cited a reasonable suspicion that evidence of embezzlement would be found, including transfer documents from July 2020 onward, cash proceeds, and computer equipment used for transfers. They asserted that requesting the items without a search risked their loss or devaluation. The warrants did not address how any unrelated or notary-client privileged material would be handled. A judge separately issued a similarly worded warrant for the applicant’s home.

**Searches occurred on 4 August 2021.** The home search (in the wife’s presence, with a municipal police observer and forensic expert) ran from about 9:20 a.m. to 12:05 p.m.; seven USB keys, two tablets, one phone, and four laptops were seized. The applicant was not present (he was undergoing a medical examination). The notary-office search began around 1 p.m. (warrant served on the building caretaker) and ended at 2:23 p.m., with a forensic technician, computer expert, observer, and caretaker present; five phones, two laptops, two computers, and a network device were seized. After the applicant’s arrest that afternoon, the non-residential premises were searched from 6–6:30 p.m. (keys provided via his mother); nothing was found. The applicant disputed details of notice, his whereabouts, requests for a lawyer, and participation.

**Forensic copies of the seized devices were made.** Items were returned to the applicant’s wife in September and October 2021 after imaging. An expert report (using the copies) examined data for betting records, unpaid deposits, and related lists from 2018–2021; it was added to the file. The applicant was charged on 4 August 2021 and later indicted (January 2022) for embezzlement exceeding €1.7 million. Criminal proceedings remain pending.

**The applicant challenged the office and premises searches** (not the home search) via a constitutional complaint alleging violations of private life/home rights. The Constitutional Court rejected it in June 2022 for non-exhaustion, holding that legality (including any constitutional dimension) could be raised during the ongoing criminal process, particularly regarding evidence admissibility at trial. No prior judicial warrant existed for the office/premises searches, nor an effective a-posteriori judicial review of the warrants themselves or their execution (including privileged material). Domestic law provided a general basis for such searches by investigator/prosecutor, but the applicant argued this lacked adequate safeguards.

These facts underpin the Article 8 (private life/home) and Article 13 complaints concerning the searches and seizures. The Court found the interference lacked sufficient judicial safeguards and was therefore not “in accordance with the law.”
001-242861:
The ECHR case Derrek and Others v. Russia (no. 31712/21) arose from a 5 December 2020 police raid on a peaceful LGBT human-rights workshop in Yaroslavl attended by 11 people (including the six applicants). The event began at 1:30 p.m. At 2:40 p.m. police, special forces and the local police chief (K.) entered, filming the operation. Participants were forced to stand facing the wall, arms raised and legs spread, for more than 30 minutes. They were searched (including intimate touching of both men and women by a plain-clothes officer), questioned and had their identity documents checked and filmed. K. used homophobic slurs (“faggots”), slapped the second applicant’s legs, seized the third applicant by the chin, and struck the fifth applicant on the soles of his shoes after the latter telephoned a lawyer. No drugs were found; books belonging to the third applicant were seized. Videos of the raid later appeared on social media.

At 3:20 p.m. all participants were transported to a hospital for compulsory drug testing, although the administrative file contained no written authorisation. Every test was negative. The first, fifth and sixth applicants were released around 6 p.m.; the remaining three were taken to a police station and released around 9 p.m. The third applicant was required to provide a urine sample without being allowed to close the toilet door, in view of a female medical practitioner. The officers were armed and masked, creating an atmosphere of intimidation.

The applicants immediately alleged that the searches, slurs, physical handling and forced testing constituted wilful humiliation motivated by homophobic hatred and therefore degrading treatment and discrimination. They further claimed that their confinement at the venue, the unrecorded transfer to hospital and the subsequent detention at the police station amounted to an unlawful deprivation of liberty lacking any procedural safeguards. Finally, they contended that the raid itself constituted a disproportionate interference with freedom of peaceful assembly, that purported COVID-19 or drug-related justifications were pretextual (no administrative prosecutions followed), and that the episode produced a chilling effect.

On 25 December 2020 the fifth applicant lodged a detailed criminal complaint with the Investigative Committee citing abuse of power, excessive force and discriminatory motive; the other applicants filed analogous complaints. An internal inquiry concluded there had been no misconduct, but the results were never disclosed. Domestic courts dismissed all challenges without examining the merits, holding that they lacked competence in the absence of a criminal investigation. The administrative file recorded an anonymous (and later denied) tip-off about drugs and a report of mask-and-distancing breaches, yet no charges were pursued and no documents authorised the drug tests.

These facts form the factual core of the Court’s subsequent findings of violations of Articles 3 (substantive and procedural) taken with 14, 5 § 1 and 11 of the Convention.

The case of Derrek and Others v. Russia (Application no. 31712/21) before the European Court of Human Rights arose from a police raid on an LGBT workshop held in Yaroslavl on 5 December 2020. The six applicants were among 11 participants (including three invited speakers from the ABC of Activism Project) at the event, which began at 1:30 p.m. At 2:40 p.m., police and special forces, including local police chief K., raided the venue and filmed the operation. Participants were ordered to stand facing the wall for over 30 minutes, during which they were searched, questioned, and had their identity documents checked and filmed. K. refused to explain the raid and called the participants “faggots.” No drugs were found, but books brought by the third applicant were seized. Videos of the raid were later posted on social media.

The applicants described an intimidating atmosphere created by armed, masked officers. At 3:20 p.m., all participants were taken to a local hospital for obligatory drug testing; all tested negative. The first, fifth and sixth applicants were released around 6 p.m. The second, third and fourth applicants were then transferred to a police station for further questioning and released around 9 p.m.

On 25 December 2020 the fifth applicant complained to the Investigative Committee, alleging excessive force, unlawful personal searches and drug testing, and discriminatory, hate-motivated conduct amounting to abuse of power. He described over 30 people (police, special forces, a regulatory official and cameramen) entering the premises without explanation. K. ordered him to the police station, slapped the second applicant’s legs while telling him to spread his feet, grabbed the third applicant’s chin after being asked about the raid’s purpose, and hit the fifth applicant on the soles of his shoes after the latter called a lawyer. A plain-clothes man searched participants, including women, by touching their bodies. Participants stood against the wall with arms raised and legs spread for 30 minutes. They were taken one by one to the lab for testing. The third applicant later added that he was not allowed to close the toilet door during urination and was observed by a female medical practitioner. The other applicants lodged similar complaints.

On 25 January 2021 the regional Ministry of Interior informed the fifth applicant that an inquiry had found no professional misconduct or unlawfulness, without disclosing the results, and advised him of his right to appeal. The Kirovskiy District Court dismissed his challenge on 10 March 2021 without examining the merits, holding that it lacked authority to assess the raid’s lawfulness in the absence of a criminal investigation. The Yaroslavl Regional Court upheld this decision on 4 May 2021. Parallel complaints by the remaining applicants were likewise dismissed without merits review.

The administrative case file recorded a call from M. reporting drug distribution and use at the workshop (M. later denied making the call). A police report cited COVID-19 violations (some participants not wearing masks or maintaining distance). An inspection report noted the seizure of the third applicant’s books. Decisions were issued not to institute administrative proceedings for drug use (owing to negative tests) and to discontinue proceedings against the fourth applicant for COVID-19 non-compliance. None of the applicants were prosecuted. The file contained no decisions authorising the mandatory drug testing.

These events formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints of wilful humiliation and debasement motivated by homophobic hatred (together with an ineffective investigation), unrecorded deprivation of liberty without procedural guarantees, and a disproportionate disruption of a peaceful assembly that produced a chilling effect and lacked justification or redress.

The case concerns a police raid on an LGBT workshop held on 5 December 2020 in Yaroslavl. The event, organized by the local LGBT community for human rights and LGBT activists, involved 11 participants (including three invited speakers) and began at 1:30 p.m. At 2:40 p.m., police and special forces, led by local police chief K. and accompanied by cameramen and others, entered the venue. Participants were forced to stand facing a wall for over 30 minutes with arms raised and legs spread. They underwent personal searches (including by a plainclothes officer who touched their bodies, including those of women), questioning, and identity checks that were filmed. K. used homophobic slurs such as “faggots,” grabbed the third applicant by the chin, slapped the second applicant’s legs while ordering him to spread his feet, and struck the fifth applicant on the soles of his shoes after he contacted a lawyer. No drugs were found, though books belonging to the third applicant were seized. The raid was filmed and videos later appeared on social media.

At 3:20 p.m. the participants were taken to a hospital for obligatory drug and alcohol testing (all results negative). The third applicant was denied privacy during urinalysis, as a female practitioner could observe him. The first, fifth and sixth applicants were released around 6 p.m.; the remaining three were taken to a police station and released around 9 p.m. The process lasted several hours without records of arrest, detention or any documents authorizing the testing. Officers were armed and masked, creating an intimidating atmosphere.

The applicants complained to the Investigative Committee of excessive force, unlawful searches and testing, and homophobic discrimination amounting to abuse of power. An inquiry found no misconduct (without disclosing details). Court challenges were dismissed without merits review on the ground that no criminal investigation existed; appeals failed. Similar complaints by the other applicants were likewise rejected.

The administrative file cited an (unconfirmed and later denied) tip-off from M. about drug distribution at the workshop, plus a police report alleging COVID-19 breaches (failure to wear masks or maintain distance). No administrative charges were pursued against any applicant (one COVID-related case was discontinued). The file contained no authorization for the drug tests.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: degrading treatment and discrimination (Art. 3 + Art. 14) through humiliating searches, testing and slurs motivated by homophobia, plus an ineffective investigation; unlawful deprivation of liberty (Art. 5 § 1) via unrecorded confinement and transfers lacking safeguards; and a disproportionate interference with peaceful assembly (Art. 11) that was not shown to rest on COVID measures or any other pressing need, producing a chilling effect without redress.

001-242957:
The ECHR case Van Slooten v. the Netherlands (no. 45644/18) concerns the 2017 termination of the applicant’s parental authority over her daughter (born 4 August 2014), then aged 2 years and 10 months. The applicant (born 1990) had sole parental authority. Reports of domestic violence between her and the child’s father existed before and after the birth; their relationship ended in February 2015, but unsupervised contact continued, producing further police-reported incidents.

The pair lived in supported housing with multiple care services. Instability, frequent moves, the child’s exposure to violence and the applicant’s mood swings prompted a Child Care and Protection Board investigation in August 2015. A one-year supervision order was issued on 22 October 2015, citing serious developmental risks, the applicant’s mental-health history and her refusal of help. Assessment in a mother-and-child facility was recommended.

After the applicant left a crisis shelter, an emergency care order of 29 October 2015 placed the child with a foster family; it was later extended. The youth-protection institution repeatedly proposed assessment at De Stee Clinic; the applicant refused, citing an alienating atmosphere. In February 2016 a “perspective decision” declared that the child’s future lay with foster carers and reduced contact. The applicant’s alternative assessment plan was rejected by courts in April and June 2016 as insufficiently child-focused and unconvincing. Appeals against the care order failed.

In October 2016 the Regional Court refused return of the child, holding that the applicant had not shown she could resume care. The Court of Appeal confirmed in March 2017 that the “acceptable time” had expired given the child’s age and 17 months in the same foster placement.

On 20 September 2016 the institution asked the Board to seek termination of parental authority. The Board’s March 2017 report found the child thriving in a structured foster environment, contact visits unpredictable, and the applicant uncooperative; it concluded the developmental threat was so serious that authority should end. On 6 June 2017 the Regional Court terminated authority, stressing the child’s vulnerability (witnessed violence in her first year), successful bonding with foster parents, the applicant’s diagnoses (depression, PTSD, panic disorder) and her refusal of assessment. It held that the “acceptable time” had already expired and that independent expert investigation would not serve the child’s interests. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 27 March 2018, adopting the same reasoning and noting that home placement had become “a dead end.”

The applicant did not pursue cassation. She later successfully raised a second child without intervention.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 8 (and Article 6) violations: termination occurred less than 18 months after the emergency placement, family reunification was abandoned at an early stage without an in-depth evaluation of the child’s actual vulnerability or a proper assessment of the applicant’s parenting capacity, and insufficient weight was given to the Convention rights of both mother and child.

The case concerns the 2017 termination of the applicant’s parental authority over her daughter (born 4 August 2014), then aged two years and ten months, alleged to violate Article 8 ECHR (family life) by failing to pursue reunification or adequately assess the mother’s parenting capacity. The father had recognised the child, but the parents’ relationship involved repeated domestic violence reports to Veilig Thuis. It ended in February 2015, though unsupervised contacts continued, producing further incidents.

The applicant held sole parental authority and lived with the child in supported housing with multiple care services. In August 2015 the Child Care and Protection Board investigated after neighbourhood reports. A certified youth-protection institution (GI) became involved by agreement. In September the pair were asked to leave sheltered housing for alleged non-cooperation and entered a six-week crisis shelter.

On 16 October 2015 the Board reported that the child had endured chronic instability, the mother’s mental-health problems (later identified as persistent depressive disorder, panic disorder and PTSD), mood swings and witnessed violence; physical care was adequate but the mother refused to cooperate. A one-year supervision order was made on 22 October. After the applicant left the shelter, an emergency care order on 29 October placed the 15-month-old child with a foster family; weekly supervised contact was allowed.

The GI repeatedly proposed assessment in a 24-hour mother-and-child facility (De Stee Clinic). The applicant refused, citing an alienating atmosphere and fear of unfair evaluation, and offered an alternative plan. Courts in April and June 2016 found the plan inadequate, unfocused on the child’s needs and lacking methodological clarity. In February 2016 the GI issued a “perspective decision” that the child’s future lay with the foster family and halved contact. Subsequent applications to return the child or transfer supervision were dismissed; by March 2017 the Court of Appeal held that the “acceptable time” (six months for a child under five under then-applicable guidelines) had expired because the child had bonded with the foster parents.

On 20 September 2016 the GI asked the Board to seek termination of parental authority. The Board’s March 2017 report noted the child’s positive development in a structured foster placement, unpredictable contact visits (later reduced to monthly), the mother’s non-cooperation and the expiry of acceptable time. The Regional Court (6 June 2017) terminated authority, stressing the child’s vulnerability from early trauma, the need to protect her attachment to the foster parents and the paramountcy of her best interests under the UNCRC. It dismissed a request for an independent expert under Article 810a of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court of Appeal (27 March 2018) adopted that reasoning, observing that cooperation had been “difficult” (a 2015 GI email had itself damaged trust) yet the mother had failed to use the opportunities offered. Cassation advice indicated no realistic prospect of success.

The applicant later had a second child whom she raised without intervention. The facts relevant to the Article 8 complaint are therefore the early abandonment of reunification (less than 18 months after removal), the absence of any in-depth assessment of the mother’s actual parenting capacity once she declined the clinic, the heavy yet unanalysed weight placed on the child’s “vulnerability”, and the courts’ reliance on the mere passage of “acceptable time” rather than a concrete demonstration that continued family ties were incompatible with the child’s best interests.

The case of Van Slooten v. the Netherlands (ECtHR, 15 April 2025) concerns the termination of the applicant’s parental authority over her daughter (born 4 August 2014), then aged two years and ten months. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention, focusing on the authorities’ handling of family reunification.

The child’s parents had a history of verbal and physical domestic violence reported to Veilig Thuis. After their relationship ended in February 2015, they continued unsupervised contact, resulting in further incidents. The applicant held sole parental authority and lived with the child in supported housing with additional services. In August 2015, the Child Care and Protection Board began investigating the unstable home environment after reports of stress, mood swings, and developmental risks to the child, despite her good physical condition and the applicant’s affection. The applicant was seen as uncooperative.

On 22 October 2015, a children’s judge issued a one-year supervision order, recommending assessment in a mother-and-child facility. Days later, after the applicant left a crisis shelter (citing safety concerns), the GI obtained an emergency care order on 29 October 2015. Police removed the 15-month-old child, placing her with a foster family; contact was limited to weekly supervised visits. The order was later extended.

The GI proposed assessment at the De Stee Clinic, which the applicant refused, citing an alienating atmosphere and fears of a biased evaluation. She submitted an alternative plan, deemed inadequate by the Regional Court (28 April 2016) and Court of Appeal (28 June 2016) for lacking focus on the child’s needs. A February 2016 “perspective decision” concluded the child’s future lay with the foster family, reducing contact. Courts later held that the “acceptable time” for reunification had expired, given the child’s age, time in care (from October 2015), and developing attachment to foster parents; further assessment would disrupt this.

In March 2017, the Board recommended terminating parental authority, citing the child’s vulnerability from early exposure to violence, unpredictable contact with the applicant, her non-cooperation, and the expired “acceptable time.” On 6 June 2017, the Regional Court terminated authority and appointed the GI as guardian, prioritising the child’s stability and attachment under Articles 3 and 20 of the UNCRC. It dismissed a request for an independent expert under Article 810a of the Code of Civil Procedure as contrary to the child’s interests. The Court of Appeal upheld this on 27 March 2018, finding cooperation had been difficult (despite some GI failings) and reunification a “dead end.” No cassation appeal followed.

The ECtHR found an Article 8 violation: authorities failed to analyse the child’s vulnerability in depth despite relying on it, sought termination less than 1.5 years after placement, abandoned reunification too early without adequately assessing the applicant’s parenting capacity, and gave insufficient weight to the family’s Article 8 rights. The applicant later successfully raised a second child independently.
001-242864:
The case of Ţîbîrnă and Others v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 67593/14), decided by the ECtHR on 30 April 2025, concerns the State's alleged responsibility for non-enforcement of a final judgment in the applicants' favour. The applicants, investors in a pyramid scheme operated by company I., invoked Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair trial, encompassing effective enforcement of judgments) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). They claimed that a State agent's failure to implement a seizing order enabled alienation of the debtors' assets, rendering the judgment largely unenforceable.

The applicants were civil parties in criminal proceedings against C.V., director of company I. On 22 November 2002 the Chișinău District Court convicted C.V. and awarded the applicants' claims in full against C.V. and the company as joint debtors. The judgment became final on 7 June 2006 after the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed C.V.'s appeal.

Although the company's assets had been ordered seized during the trial, investigating officer A.C. failed to comply and permitted their dissipation. A.C. was convicted of abuse of power on 2 July 2010 (final on 9 April 2013). The conviction established that A.C. acted outside his competence, discrediting the authorities and making it impossible to repair the damage caused by C.V. In September 1999 A.C. arranged for C.V. to be escorted from prison to company premises, allowing unrestricted disposal of assets. Between October and December 1999 C.V., with A.C.'s illegal permission, systematically alienated the assets to unidentified persons, thereby causing material loss to the civil parties.

Enforcement of the 2002 judgment began in 2005. After sale of remaining company assets and a State-allocated building, the applicants recovered only about 20 per cent of the awards. In 2013 the bailiff returned the partially executed titles because no further assets could be located. A 2016 resubmission by 124 creditors, including some applicants, yielded only negligible additional sums; the titles were again returned for lack of attachable property.

In 2012 the applicants sued the State under Law no. 87, arguing that A.C.'s failure to execute the seizure had caused irrecoverable damage and made enforcement impossible. The Chișinău District Court partially upheld the claims on 5 June 2013, but the Chișinău Court of Appeal dismissed them on 27 November 2013, holding that the debtor was a private person for whom the State bore no responsibility and that the bailiff had taken all necessary steps. The Supreme Court of Justice confirmed this ruling on 2 April 2014.

These facts underpin the applicants' contention that the investigator's misconduct, for which the State is accountable, frustrated the practical realisation of a final judicial award, thereby violating their Convention rights to effective judicial protection and peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The case of Ţîbîrnă and Others v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 67593/14) originated in an application lodged on 26 September 2014. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the State was responsible for the non-enforcement of a final judgment in their favour against private debtors. This stemmed from a State agent's failure to comply with a seizing order, which allowed the alienation of the debtors' assets.

The applicants had invested in company I., later identified as a pyramid-type financial scheme. In criminal proceedings against its director, C.V., they were admitted as civil parties seeking recovery of sums equivalent to their investments. On 22 November 2002 the Chișinău District Court convicted C.V. and granted the civil claims in full against him and company I. as joint debtors. The judgment became final on 7 June 2006 after the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed C.V.'s appeal on points of law.

During the trial the company's assets were ordered seized. It subsequently emerged that the investigating officer, A.C., had not complied with the order and had permitted their alienation. On 2 July 2010 the Chișinău District Court convicted A.C. of abuse of power; the conviction became final on 9 April 2013. The court found that A.C. had acted outside his competence, discredited the public authority he represented and placed the authorities in a position of impossibility to repair the material damage caused by C.V.'s actions. In September 1999 A.C. had instructed police officers to escort C.V. from prison to the company's headquarters, thereby granting C.V. unrestricted opportunity to dispose of the assets. Between October and December 1999 C.V., systematically escorted there, alienated the assets to unidentified persons. A.C. thereby caused material damage to the injured parties, including the applicants.

Enforcement proceedings in respect of the 2002 judgment were opened by a bailiff in 2005. After the sale of company I.'s remaining assets and of a building allocated by the State, the applicants received approximately 20 per cent of the sums awarded. In 2013, following distribution of the collected funds, the bailiff returned the partially executed enforcement titles because no further assets of company I. could be traced. In 2016 one hundred and twenty-four creditors, including some of the applicants, resubmitted the titles. Relatively insignificant additional sums were recovered and distributed before the titles were again returned for lack of traceable assets.

In 2012 the applicants sued the State under Law no. 87, seeking compensation for the non-enforcement. They argued that the State was liable for the investigator's failure to comply with the seizing order, which had caused them material damage and rendered enforcement of the judgment impossible. On 5 June 2013 the Chișinău District Court partially allowed the claims. On 27 November 2013 the Chișinău Court of Appeal rejected the arguments and dismissed the action, holding that the debtor was a private person for whom the State was not responsible and that the bailiff had taken all adequate and necessary enforcement measures. The Supreme Court of Justice upheld that decision on 2 April 2014.

These circumstances formed the basis of the applicants' allegation that the State's failure, through its agent's misconduct, to preserve the seized assets had prevented full enforcement of a final judgment, thereby engaging the State's responsibility under the Convention.

On 5 June 2013 the Chișinău District Court partially allowed the claims.
