001-243081:
The case of Radelić v. Croatia (Application no. 12432/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the confiscation of alleged proceeds of crime from the applicant personally, even though those proceeds had been obtained for the benefit of a limited liability company of which he was the sole shareholder and director, after that company had gone bankrupt and ceased to exist.

The applicant, Dražen Radelić, controlled Radelić d.o.o. Bankruptcy proceedings against the company opened in November 2010 and concluded the following month; it was struck off the commercial register in March 2011 and thereby ceased to exist. On the same day, the Split Municipal State Attorney’s Office indicted him for business fraud and forgery of documents. The charges alleged that, between August 2003 and February 2004, he had presented 36 cheques drawn on foreign banks, falsely representing them as payment for services rendered by the company, with the intent of obtaining significant pecuniary gain for the company.

In April 2014 the Split Municipal Court convicted him of forgery (suspended prison sentence of 18 months) but acquitted him of fraud. After an appeal by the prosecution, the fraud count was remitted. In April 2017 the Municipal Court convicted him of business fraud (suspended one-year sentence) and, pursuant to Article 77 of the 2011 Penal Code, ordered confiscation from him personally of HRK 854,743.39 (approximately EUR 113,440). Payment into the State budget was imposed as a condition of the suspension; failure would convert it into immediate imprisonment. The court reasoned that, because the company had been dissolved without a legal successor, the proceeds had to be taken from the applicant as sole founder, shareholder and authorised representative who had controlled the company’s accounts.

The applicant appealed, stressing that the sums had been credited to the company’s account, that the company had paid tax on them and used them for ordinary operations, and that he had received no personal benefit. The Split County Court dismissed the appeal in September 2017. It held that the applicant, through his criminal acts, had enabled the company to retain the money and that confiscation from him personally was justified by analogy with section 252(5) of the Commercial Companies Act (liability of directors to creditors when a company cannot meet its debts). A representative of the County State Attorney’s Office had itself argued at the hearing that the confiscation was unlawful; later the same office proposed (unsuccessfully) that the Principal State Attorney seek protection of legality before the Supreme Court, on the ground that the applicant had never been charged with, or shown to have received, a personal gain.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint, invoking the right of ownership, was dismissed by the Constitutional Court in October 2021. Enforcement of the confiscation order later failed because of insufficient funds in his accounts.

The Strasbourg Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Penal Code did not authorise confiscation from the perpetrator when the proceeds had been acquired for another person (natural or legal). Domestic Supreme Court case-law consistently refused such confiscation in analogous business-fraud cases. The measure was therefore neither foreseeable nor consistent with the nature of the offence of which the applicant had been convicted, and the interference with his possessions was not “provided for by law”.

The case of Radelić v. Croatia (Application no. 12432/22) before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerns an alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The applicant, Dražen Radelić, was the sole shareholder and director of the limited liability company Radelić d.o.o. Bankruptcy proceedings against the company opened on 12 November 2010 and concluded on 12 December 2010; it was struck off the commercial register on 4 March 2011 and ceased to exist.

On the same date, the applicant was indicted for business fraud and forgery of documents. The charges alleged that, between August 2003 and February 2004, intending to obtain significant pecuniary gain for the company, he presented 36 forged foreign-bank cheques to a Croatian bank as payment for services rendered abroad. In April 2014 he was convicted of forgery (one-and-a-half years’ imprisonment, suspended) and acquitted of fraud. On appeal the acquittal was quashed and the fraud charge remitted. In April 2017 the Municipal Court convicted him of business fraud (one year’s imprisonment, suspended for four years) and ordered confiscation from him personally of HRK 854,743.39 (approximately EUR 113,440) as proceeds of crime, to be paid into the State budget within six months, failing which the suspended sentence would be revoked. The court reasoned that, because the company no longer existed and had no legal successor, the proceeds had to be taken from the applicant as its sole founder, shareholder and authorised representative.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the funds had been paid into the company’s account, not his personal account; the company had paid all taxes and used the money for ordinary operations; and he himself had derived no benefit. The County Court dismissed the appeal in September 2017, analogising the applicant’s position to the statutory liability of management-board members under the Commercial Companies Act. A proposal by the County State Attorney’s Office that the Principal State Attorney seek protection of legality (on the ground that confiscation from the natural person was unlawful when the gain had been acquired for the company) was never lodged. The applicant’s constitutional complaint, relying inter alia on the constitutional right of ownership, was dismissed in October 2021. Enforcement proceedings were later initiated but remained unexecuted for lack of funds.

Domestic law (Article 77 of the 2011 Penal Code) provided that no one may retain proceeds of crime and that they must be confiscated from the person who acquired them or to whom they were transferred (except in good faith). Supreme Court case-law consistently held that proceeds could not be confiscated from the perpetrator when they had been acquired for the benefit of another (including a legal person). The offence of which the applicant was convicted (business fraud) required intent to obtain unlawful gain for a legal entity he represented. The confiscation measure was therefore neither foreseeable nor consistent with the nature of the offence, rendering the interference with the applicant’s possessions not “provided for by law.”

**CASE OF RADELIĆ v. CROATIA (Application no. 12432/22, ECtHR, 13 May 2025)**

The applicant, Dražen Radelić (born 1973), was the sole shareholder and director of the limited liability company Radelić d.o.o. In November 2010, the Split Commercial Court opened bankruptcy proceedings against the company; these concluded in December 2010. The company was struck off the commercial register on 4 March 2011 and thereby ceased to exist, with no legal successor.

On the same date, the Split Municipal State Attorney’s Office indicted the applicant for business fraud and forgery of documents. The indictment alleged that, between August 2003 and February 2004, he had presented 36 cheques drawn on foreign banks to a Croatian bank for cashing, falsely representing them as payment for services rendered by the company abroad, with the intent of obtaining significant pecuniary gain for the company.

In April 2014, the Split Municipal Court convicted him of forgery of documents, imposing a suspended sentence of 18 months’ imprisonment. It acquitted him of business fraud. On appeal, the Split County Court in October 2014 upheld the forgery conviction but quashed the acquittal and remitted the fraud charge for retrial.

In April 2017, following retrial, the Municipal Court convicted the applicant of business fraud and imposed a suspended sentence of one year’s imprisonment. It additionally ordered confiscation of HRK 854,743.39 (approximately EUR 113,440) from him personally as proceeds of crime, to be paid into the State budget within six months of the judgment becoming final, failing which the suspended sentence would be revoked. The court relied on Article 77 of the 2011 Penal Code (providing that no one may retain proceeds of crime) and reasoned that, because the company had been struck off with no successor, the proceeds had to be confiscated from the applicant as its sole founder, shareholder and representative authorised to dispose of its funds.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the sums had been paid into the company’s account (not his personal account), that the company had paid all applicable taxes and used the funds for its operations, and that he had obtained no personal benefit. The County Court dismissed the appeal in September 2017. It held that the company no longer existed, so the illegally obtained gain should be confiscated from the applicant. It analogised to section 252(5) of the Commercial Companies Act, under which a management-board member who grossly violates the duty of care can be liable to the company’s creditors if they cannot recover from the company.

The County State Attorney’s Office later proposed (but the Principal State Attorney did not lodge) a request for the protection of legality, arguing that confiscation from the applicant personally was unlawful: the indictment charged him with obtaining gain for the company, not himself; no evidence showed transfer of the proceeds to him; and there was no identified injured party for a damages order.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint invoking, inter alia, the constitutional right of ownership. The Constitutional Court dismissed it in October 2021, finding no breach. Enforcement of the confiscation order was later sought but remained unenforced owing to insufficient funds in the applicant’s accounts.

The Penal Code’s confiscation provisions (Articles 5 and 77) and the offence of business fraud (Article 247, which requires intent to obtain unlawful gain for a legal entity) did not provide for confiscation from the perpetrator when the proceeds had been acquired for another person or entity. Supreme Court case-law consistently held that proceeds could not be confiscated from the perpetrator in such circumstances. The applicant complained that the confiscation therefore interfered with his peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case of Russ v. Germany (ECHR, Application no. 44241/20, judgment 20 May 2025)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined the criminal conviction of German national Benjamin Russ for wearing a homemade plastic visor at a 2015 demonstration. The Court found a violation of Article 11 of the Convention (freedom of peaceful assembly), read in light of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The applicant had also invoked Article 7, but the Court focused on the assembly and expression complaints.

On 18 March 2015, during the opening of the European Central Bank headquarters in Frankfurt am Main, the Blockupy alliance organised protests, including a demonstration under the slogan “colourful, loud – but peaceful.” The applicant joined this event for several hours and wore a relatively hard but flexible transparent plastic sheet (thinner than Plexiglas), fastened with a rubber band over his forehead and eyes. He had written “smash capitalism” on it. Other participants wore similar visors. Police present at the demonstration neither warned him, asked him to remove it, nor fined him on the spot.

Separately, from early morning, violent groups in the Ostend district (near the ECB site) blocked streets, erected and burned barricades, damaged and burned cars and police vehicles, threw stones and bottles, and attacked police, bystanders, firefighters and medical personnel. The applicant’s demonstration itself remained peaceful.

German authorities later issued a penalty order against the applicant for violating sections 17a(1) and 27 of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions. These provisions ban carrying “protective weapons” (or objects suitable and intended as such to ward off law-enforcement measures) at public outdoor assemblies, with limited exemptions (e.g., religious events, traditional festivals) and possible further exemptions if no threat to public safety exists. Legislative history defined protective weapons as objects typically manufactured for defence against attacks, such as shields, armour, police/military equipment (steel helmets, gas masks) or martial-arts items, because of their aggression-stimulating appearance. The ban was not meant to cover mere symbolic use for expressing opinion.

The Frankfurt District Court convicted the applicant, finding the visor a protective weapon designed to shield eyes from pepper spray or similar police measures and thus prolong the wearer’s ability to resist. It saw no other “civil” purpose and held that the slogan did not change its character; the applicant could have worn it on the back of his head to display the message without violating the ban. After a hearing, the court imposed a fine (adjusted for a prior conviction). The Regional Court upheld the conviction (reducing the penalty because the prior sentence had already been served), reiterating that the visor was manufactured and used to defend against pepper spray, not solely for expression. It rejected any unavoidable mistake of law, citing the applicant’s experience as a demonstration spokesperson. Higher courts (Court of Appeal and Federal Constitutional Court) refused further review.

The ECHR held that the conviction interfered with the applicant’s right to peaceful assembly. Domestic courts failed to provide sufficient reasons: they did not adequately balance the applicant’s rights against the ban’s aims (preventing violence and maintaining order), consider possible exemptions, or assess the overall circumstances—including the demonstration’s explicitly peaceful nature, the visor’s simple construction and political inscription, the lack of on-site police action, and the absence of any violence by the applicant or his group. The interference was therefore not “necessary in a democratic society.”

The judgment became final on 20 August 2025.

The case of Russ v. Germany (Application no. 44241/20) before the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) concerned the applicant’s criminal conviction and fine for wearing a plastic visor at a demonstration, which German courts held breached a statutory ban on “protective weapons” at public outdoor assemblies. The Court examined the matter under Article 11 of the Convention (freedom of peaceful assembly), read in the light of Article 10 (freedom of expression), and found a violation.

On 18 March 2015 the European Central Bank opened its new headquarters in Frankfurt am Main. The Blockupy alliance organised protests that day, including a demonstration held under the slogan “colourful, loud – but peaceful.” The applicant, a German national born in 1985, took part for several hours. He fastened a sheet of relatively hard but flexible transparent plastic (thinner than Plexiglas) over his forehead and eyes with a rubber band and wrote “smash capitalism” on it. Several other participants wore similar visors. Police officers present neither warned him, requested removal of the visor, nor issued an on-the-spot fine.

Separately, from the early morning, groups prepared to use violence gathered in the Ostend district. They blocked streets, erected and set fire to barricades, damaged and burned vehicles, threw stones and bottles at police, and attacked bystanders, firefighters and medical personnel. The applicant’s own demonstration remained peaceful.

In June 2016 the Frankfurt am Main District Court issued a penalty order imposing a fine of 40 daily rates of €10. After the applicant objected, a hearing took place. The court convicted him and imposed a cumulative sentence of 60 daily rates of €30 (taking account of a prior conviction). It held that the visor violated sections 17a(1) and 27 of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions, which prohibit carrying protective weapons or objects suitable for and, in the circumstances, intended to ward off law-enforcement measures at outdoor public events. Drawing on legislative materials, the court defined protective weapons as objects used for defence against attacks and ordinarily given that purpose at manufacture (examples: shields, homemade armour, steel helmets, NBC gas masks, martial-arts equipment). The visor, though simple, was capable of shielding the eyes from liquids or gases such as pepper spray and thereby of prolonging the wearer’s ability to resist police coercive measures; no other “civil” use was imaginable. The inscription did not alter its character as a protective weapon; the applicant could have worn it on the back of his head merely to display the slogan.

The Frankfurt am Main Regional Court reduced the penalty to 10 daily rates (the prior conviction having already been served) but otherwise upheld the conviction. It confirmed that the visor had been manufactured and used to defend against pepper-spray attacks, not solely for expression. The applicant, an experienced demonstration spokesperson, could not claim an unavoidable mistake of law; he could have sought clarification from police beforehand. Further appeals on points of law and a constitutional complaint were unsuccessful.

The statutory ban (section 17a(1)) applies while present at or travelling to outdoor assemblies and carries a penalty of up to one year’s imprisonment or a fine (section 27). Limited exemptions exist for religious processions, funerals and traditional festivals; the competent authority may grant further exemptions if no threat to public safety or order is feared and may issue exclusion orders. Parliamentary materials from 1985 emphasised that such items create an appearance of martial readiness, stimulate aggression in crowds and therefore threaten public order irrespective of individual intent; mere symbolic use for expression of opinion was said not to be covered.

The Court held that the domestic courts had not supplied sufficient reasons, had failed to balance the applicant’s rights against the legitimate aims of the ban or to consider the available exemptions, and had not adequately assessed the overall (peaceful) circumstances of the demonstration. The interference was therefore not “necessary in a democratic society.”

The case of Russ v. Germany (Application no. 44241/20) before the European Court of Human Rights arose from the applicant’s criminal conviction for wearing a plastic visor at a public demonstration, which German courts treated as a breach of a statutory ban on “protective weapons” at outdoor assemblies. The applicant invoked Articles 7, 10 and 11 of the Convention.

On 18 March 2015, coinciding with the opening of the European Central Bank’s new headquarters in Frankfurt am Main, the Blockupy alliance organised protests under the slogan “colourful, loud – but peaceful.” These included a demonstration featuring peaceful blockades. The applicant joined the morning demonstration and, for approximately three hours, wore a relatively hard but flexible sheet of transparent plastic (thinner than Plexiglas) fastened with a rubber band so that it covered his forehead and eyes. Several other participants wore similar visors. He had written the words “smash capitalism” on his visor. Police officers present neither warned him, fined him, nor required him to remove it.

Separately, from around 5 a.m. until midday, groups intent on violence assembled in the Ostend district (where the demonstration occurred). They blocked streets, erected and set fire to barricades, damaged and burned cars, threw stones and bottles at police, attacked bystanders, firefighters and emergency services, damaged property, set fire to police vehicles and inflicted bodily harm on officers.

On 28 June 2016 the Frankfurt am Main District Court issued a penalty order imposing a fine of 40 daily rates of €10 each. It found that the applicant had worn the visor at the demonstration to protect himself against police measures such as pepper spray. After he objected and a hearing was held, the District Court convicted him and imposed a cumulative sentence of 60 daily rates of €30 each (taking into account a prior conviction). It held that the visor violated sections 17a(1) and 27(2) of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions, which prohibit carrying protective weapons or objects suitable for use as such (and intended in the circumstances to ward off law-enforcement measures) at outdoor public assemblies. Drawing on legislative materials, the court defined protective weapons as objects used for defence against attacks and usually given that purpose at manufacture (examples: protective shields, self-made armour, police/military equipment such as steel helmets or NBC gas masks, or martial-arts items). It concluded that the visor, despite its simple construction, was such a weapon because it could prevent eyes from being exposed to liquids or gases (especially pepper spray) and thereby preserve or prolong the wearer’s ability to resist police coercive measures. No other “civil” use was imaginable; the inscription did not alter its character, as the visor could have been worn on the back of the head to display the slogan without constituting a protective weapon.

The Frankfurt am Main Regional Court, on appeal, reduced the penalty to 10 daily rates (the prior conviction having already been served) but otherwise upheld the conviction. It likewise classified the visor as a protective weapon whose purpose (defence against pepper spray) had been assigned at manufacture, as evidenced by the inscription. It rejected any claim of unavoidable mistake of law, citing the applicant’s experience as a spokesperson in the protest scene and the fact that he could have sought clarification from police beforehand. The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal on points of law. On 18 March 2020 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit a constitutional complaint, without reasons.

Section 17a(1) of the Assemblies Act generally prohibits carrying such items at outdoor assemblies, with exemptions for religious services, funerals, weddings and traditional festivals, and a possibility of further exemptions if no threat to public safety or order exists. Violation is punishable by up to one year’s imprisonment or a fine. Legislative history from 1985 indicated that such items pose a threat by their martial appearance and aggression-stimulating effect, irrespective of individual intent to use them against police, while purely symbolic use for expression of opinion was not intended to be covered.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the conviction interfered with his rights to freedom of assembly and expression without sufficient justification.

The ECHR case of Vachik Karapetyan and Others v. Armenia (applications nos. 15736/16, 24649/16 and 25718/16) concerns three Armenian nationals who alleged that domestic courts denied them access to higher courts by applying appeal time-limits in an unforeseeable and formalistic manner, in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right of access to a court). Time-limits under the relevant codes of civil, administrative and criminal procedure ran from the date of pronouncement of the impugned decision rather than from actual service, even though service often occurred after the statutory period (immediately or the next day for first-instance and appeal decisions). Constitutional Court rulings of 16 October 2012 and later (including 2016–2017 decisions applying the same logic across procedure codes) required that delayed service trigger de jure restoration of the full time-limit, without judicial discretion, so that appellants had a genuine opportunity to become acquainted with the decision.

Mr Karapetyan (first applicant) faced a civil eviction claim. The Lori Regional Court granted the claim on 12 March 2015. The Civil Court of Appeal partly allowed his appeal on 30 June 2015 (dismissing eviction but otherwise upholding the judgment). The decision was dispatched on 2 July and received on 3 July 2015. On 3 August he lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation, expressly requesting restoration of the one-month limit by reference to the 2012 Constitutional Court decision, stating the receipt date and enclosing the service envelope. On 26 August 2015 the Cassation Court declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time, asserting that no restoration request had been made.

Mr Shakaryan (second applicant) was fined for an administrative offence arising from a 2013 protest. The Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 26 June 2015. The decision was sent on 29 June and received on 30 June. He appealed to the Cassation Court on 30 July, requesting restoration, but the appeal contained formal defects (unsigned, missing documents). After the court returned it on 26 August and granted three days to correct, he resubmitted a compliant version on 9 September (within the working-day limit), again requesting restoration of the original one-month period on the basis of the Constitutional Court ruling and enclosing proof of receipt. On 14 October 2015 the Cassation Court rejected the appeal as out of time, treating the restoration request as relating only to the three-day correction period.

Ms Davtyan (third applicant) sued for defamation. The Ararat Regional Court dismissed her claim on 24 June 2015. The judgment was sent on 2 July and received on 6 July. She appealed on 6 August, noting the receipt date, citing the Constitutional Court decision and providing evidence of service. On 27 August the Civil Court of Appeal refused restoration and declared the appeal out of time, wrongly recording service as 1 July and lodging as 7 August. She challenged that ruling; the Cassation Court later found no merit. After she resubmitted the appeal, the Court of Appeal admitted it on 15 September but, on 11 December 2015, dismissed it without examining the merits, acknowledging the true dates yet holding itself bound by its earlier (erroneous) inadmissibility decision. A further cassation appeal was rejected for lack of merit.

In each instance the contested decisions had not been served within the period prescribed by domestic law, the calculation method generated uncertainty, and the higher courts either ignored or mischaracterised explicit restoration requests. These facts formed the core of the applicants’ complaints that the very essence of their right of access to a court had been impaired by excessive formalism and the imposition of an undue burden arising from the courts’ own procedural errors.

The case of Vachik Karapetyan and Others v. Armenia (applications nos. 15736/16, 24649/16 and 25718/16) concerns three Armenian nationals who alleged that they were denied access to higher courts in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention due to the unforeseeable and formalistic application of procedural time-limits. Time-limits under domestic law (the former Code of Civil Procedure, Code of Administrative Procedure and related rules) generally ran from the date of pronouncement of a judgment or decision, which entered into force after one month. However, copies had to be served immediately or the next day (or within three days in some criminal/administrative contexts). The applicants relied on Constitutional Court decisions (notably of 16 October 2012 and subsequent rulings) holding that time-limits must start from actual service if delayed beyond the statutory period, with missed deadlines restored de jure (automatically) rather than at judicial discretion when the delay was beyond the party's control.

The first applicant, Vachik Karapetyan, faced a civil eviction claim. On 12 March 2015 the Lori Regional Court granted the claim and dismissed his counterclaim. The Civil Court of Appeal partially allowed his appeal on 30 June 2015 (dismissing eviction but otherwise upholding the judgment). The decision was sent on 2 July 2015 and received on 3 July 2015. On 3 August 2015 he lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation, noting the receipt date, attaching proof of service, citing the Constitutional Court decision, and expressly requesting restoration of the one-month time-limit so that 3 August would be treated as the last day. On 26 August 2015 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time, stating that no restoration request had been made.

The second applicant, Mr Shakaryan, was fined 50,000 AMD (approx. EUR 90) by the Administrative Court on 4 July 2014 for disobeying a police order during a protest. The Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 26 June 2015; the decision was sent on 29 June and received on 30 June 2015. He lodged an appeal on points of law on 30 July 2015 (with formal defects). The Court of Cassation returned it on 26 August 2015, allowing three days from service to correct it; he received this on 4 September 2015 and resubmitted a complete appeal on 9 September 2015 (excluding the weekend), again requesting restoration of the original time-limit on Constitutional Court grounds and attaching proof of service. On 14 October 2015 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time, interpreting the restoration request as relating only to the three-day correction period.

The third applicant, Ms Davtyan, brought a civil defamation claim that was dismissed by the Ararat and Vayots Dzor Regional Court on 24 June 2015. The judgment was sent on 2 July and received on 6 July 2015. She appealed on 6 August 2015, noting the receipt date, citing the Constitutional Court and providing proof. On 27 August 2015 the Civil Court of Appeal refused restoration and declared the appeal out of time, wrongly stating that the judgment had been served on 1 July 2015 (requiring an appeal by 1 August) and that it had been lodged on 7 August. After her further appeal was dismissed by the Court of Cassation, she resubmitted the appeal. The Civil Court of Appeal admitted it on 15 September 2015 but, on 11 December 2015, dismissed it without examining the merits, holding that its earlier inadmissibility decision precluded review even though it now accepted the correct dates (service 6 July, appeal 6 August). The Court of Cassation later declared her appeal on this point inadmissible for lack of merit.

These facts illustrate delays in service beyond prescribed periods, calculation of time-limits from pronouncement rather than service, failure to address restoration requests in substance, factual errors by the courts, and the imposition of an excessive burden on the applicants arising from those errors.

The case of Vachik Karapetyan and Others v. Armenia concerns three applications by Armenian nationals alleging violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right of access to a court) due to domestic courts' application of procedural time-limits for appeals. The first and second applicants complained of the Court of Cassation rejecting their appeals on points of law as out of time; the third complained of the Civil Court of Appeal dismissing her appeal without examining its merits.

The first applicant, Mr Karapetyan, faced a private civil claim for eviction from a house, against which he lodged a counterclaim. On 12 March 2015, the Lori Regional Court granted the eviction and dismissed the counterclaim. The Civil Court of Appeal, on 30 June 2015, partially allowed his appeal by dismissing the eviction claim but otherwise upholding the first-instance judgment. That decision was sent on 2 July 2015 and received by him on 3 July 2015. He lodged an appeal on points of law on 3 August 2015, explicitly noting the service date, requesting restoration of the one-month time-limit by reference to a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling, and enclosing proof of service. On 26 August 2015 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time, stating that no restoration request had been made (despite the applicant's explicit request).

The second applicant, Mr Shakaryan, was detained for over three hours after a public protest on 2 December 2013 for allegedly disobeying a police order. The police sought an administrative penalty. On 4 July 2014 the Administrative Court imposed a fine of AMD 50,000. The Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 26 June 2015; the decision was sent on 29 June and received on 30 June 2015. He lodged an appeal on points of law on 30 July 2015, requesting restoration of the time-limit, but it lacked a signature and certain documents. The Court of Cassation returned it on 26 August 2015, allowing three days from service to correct the defects (he received the return decision on 4 September). He resubmitted a corrected appeal on 9 September 2015 (within three working days), again requesting restoration by reference to the 2012 Constitutional Court decision and providing proof of service of the appealed decision. On 14 October 2015 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible as out of time, treating the restoration request as relating only to the three-day correction period rather than the original one-month limit.

The third applicant, Ms Davtyan, brought a civil defamation claim. On 24 June 2015 the Ararat and Vayots Dzor Regional Court dismissed it. The judgment was sent on 2 July and received on 6 July 2015. She lodged an appeal on 6 August 2015, asserting it was timely by reference to the 2012 Constitutional Court ruling and providing proof of service. On 27 August 2015 the Civil Court of Appeal refused restoration and declared the appeal out of time, erroneously recording service as having occurred on 1 July (making the deadline 1 August) and the appeal as lodged on 7 August. She challenged that decision unsuccessfully before the Court of Cassation. She then resubmitted the appeal on 11 September 2015. The Civil Court of Appeal initially admitted it on 15 September but, on 11 December 2015, dismissed it without examining the merits. Although it now accepted the correct dates (service on 6 July, appeal on 6 August), it held that its earlier inadmissibility ruling deprived it of authority to review the first-instance judgment. A further appeal on points of law was declared inadmissible by the Court of Cassation on 6 April 2016.

In all three cases the applicants relied on Constitutional Court case-law holding that appeal time-limits must run from actual service (or be restored de jure) when service occurs after the statutory period following pronouncement, to avoid depriving parties of a genuine opportunity to appeal. The domestic courts instead calculated time-limits from the date of pronouncement and applied a formalistic approach that disregarded or mischaracterised the applicants' restoration requests and, in the third case, relied on factually incorrect dates.

The case of Bayramov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 45735/21) concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life) arising from the filming of the applicant, a practising lawyer, during a traffic-related incident and the subsequent publication of that footage, as well as the domestic courts’ handling of his related civil claim.

On 20 October 2018, according to the applicant, he had consumed a small amount of alcohol at a family gathering and used a professional “sober driver” service to return home. After the driver parked the car approximately 70 metres from his house, the applicant later approached the vehicle. State Traffic Police officers suddenly stopped him, demanded documents without identifying themselves, ignored his explanation that he had not driven, and took him to the Narcology Centre of the Ministry of Health. Officers filmed the medical examination that concluded he was intoxicated, while stating their intention to release the footage to the media to embarrass him. He was released around 1 a.m.

The Government maintained that the applicant had been stopped for driving without a seatbelt while under the influence of alcohol.

On 22 October 2018 the footage, showing the applicant arriving at the centre in a police car and undergoing examination, was broadcast on television channels and uploaded to YouTube. Multiple websites published articles citing the Press Service of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, under headlines such as “Well-known advocate arrested drunk” and “Well-known advocate stopped while drink-driving.”

Administrative-offence proceedings were opened against the applicant for driving without a seatbelt and drink-driving. He denied having driven after drinking and complained that he had not received a copy of the report. District courts repeatedly returned the case file to the police because of procedural defects (unsigned medical report, absence of named signatory, lack of attesting witnesses, and failure to serve documents). The proceedings were eventually terminated for lack of evidence and later discontinued as time-barred.

In August 2019 the applicant brought a civil action against the State Traffic Police. He alleged unlawful filming and distribution of the footage in breach of domestic procedural rules and Article 8, claiming damage to his professional reputation, loss of legal-service contracts, ongoing harm from the footage remaining online, and emotional distress. He sought a public retraction and compensation of AZN 300,000.

The first-instance court dismissed the claim, holding that the applicant had admitted being drunk and had failed to prove either defamation or that the police had supplied the material to the media. The Court of Appeal initially awarded modest non-pecuniary damages on the ground that the offence had not been proved, but the Supreme Court quashed that decision. On remittal the Court of Appeal again dismissed the claim, finding insufficient proof that the police had distributed the footage (despite a website attribution to the Ministry’s Press Service), referring to a police denial letter and a television channel’s statement that it had later removed the video. It also held that the police were the wrong defendant and that the termination of the administrative proceedings was irrelevant. The Supreme Court upheld this reasoning.

The European Court found a violation of Article 8 on account of the domestic courts’ failure to provide adequate reasoning when dismissing the lawyer’s complaint concerning the allegedly unlawful filming and subsequent publication of the footage.

The case of Bayramov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 45735/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life) arising from the filming of the applicant, a lawyer, by State Traffic Police (STP) during a 20 October 2018 traffic stop for suspected drink-driving and the subsequent publication of the footage. The applicant, Bahruz Front oglu Bayramov, practised as an advocate in Azerbaijan since 2007.

According to the applicant, after consuming a small amount of alcohol at a family event, he used a “sober driver” service to return home. The driver parked the car approximately 70 metres from his house. After visiting a nearby shop, the applicant returned to move the vehicle into his yard when STP officers stopped him without identifying themselves. Despite his explanation that he had not been driving, he was forced into their vehicle, taken to the Narcology Centre for an intoxication examination (which found him drunk), filmed throughout, and told the footage would be used to embarrass him in the media. He was released by taxi at 1 a.m. The Government’s account was that he was stopped for driving without a seatbelt and found to be drink-driving.

On 22 October 2018, video footage of the applicant arriving at the Narcology Centre in a police car, entering the building and undergoing examination was broadcast on television channels and uploaded to YouTube. Several websites, citing the Press Service of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, published articles with stills and headlines such as “Well-known advocate arrested drunk” and “Well-known advocate stopped while drink-driving.”

Administrative-offence proceedings were opened under Articles 329.1 and 333.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for driving without a seatbelt and drink-driving. The applicant refused to sign the report. Courts repeatedly returned the file to the STP because of procedural defects (unsigned medical report lacking the examiner’s name, no proof of service on the applicant, and absence of required attesting witnesses under CAO Articles 69.2–69.4 and 96). The proceedings were eventually terminated for lack of evidence and later discontinued as time-barred.

In August 2019 the applicant brought a civil action against the STP, alleging breaches of CAO procedural rules (no disqualification or examination report, no witnesses, no copy of the offence report) and unlawful filming and distribution of footage without his consent, contrary to CAO Article 51.2, Article 32 of the Constitution and Article 8 of the Convention. He claimed reputational harm, loss of legal work for a month and continuing professional damage from the online footage, seeking a public retraction and 300,000 AZN in damages.

The Yasamal District Court dismissed the claim on 15 October 2019, holding that the applicant had admitted being drunk and had failed to prove either defamation or that the STP had supplied the material to the media. The Baku Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal on 12 February 2020, awarding 1,000 AZN for non-pecuniary damage on the basis that the offence had not been proved, but finding no evidence that the STP had distributed the footage. The Supreme Court quashed that judgment on 21 July 2020 and remitted the case, citing among other things the identity of the proper defendant (Ministry of Finance) and the later termination decision. On remittal the Court of Appeal on 6 October 2020 upheld the first-instance dismissal, repeating that distribution by the police had not been proved (despite one website citing the Press Service), referring to an STP denial letter and a television channel’s independent upload, noting the wrong defendant, and stating that the grounds for terminating the administrative proceedings were irrelevant. The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal on 1 April 2021.

The European Court found a violation of Article 8 on account of the domestic courts’ failure to give adequate reasoning when dismissing the applicant’s complaints about the filming and publication.

The case of Bayramov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 45735/21) concerns an Azerbaijani lawyer’s complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention arising from police filming during a traffic stop for alleged drink-driving, the subsequent media publication of that footage, and the domestic courts’ dismissal of his related civil claim without adequate reasoning.

On 20 October 2018 the applicant attended a family gathering and consumed a small amount of alcohol. He used a “sober driver” service to return home. After the driver left the vehicle parked near his house, police officers of the State Traffic Police (STP) approached him as he prepared to move the car a short distance. They demanded documents without identifying themselves, ignored his explanation that he had not driven while intoxicated, and took him to the Narcology Centre. Officers filmed the medical examination that concluded he was drunk and told him they intended to release the footage to embarrass him publicly. He was released around 1 a.m.

The Government maintained that the applicant had been stopped for driving without a seatbelt while under the influence of alcohol.

On 22 October 2018 video footage showing the applicant arriving at the Centre in a police vehicle and undergoing examination appeared on television channels and YouTube. Websites, citing the Ministry of Internal Affairs Press Service, published accompanying articles with headlines such as “Well-known advocate arrested drunk” and “Well-known advocate stopped while drink-driving.”

Administrative-offence proceedings were opened under the Code of Administrative Offences for driving without a seatbelt and drink-driving. The applicant denied having driven after drinking. The first-instance court twice returned the file because the medical report lacked the examiner’s name, no copy had been served on the applicant, and no attesting witnesses had been recorded. The STP later terminated the proceedings for lack of evidence (no video, audio or witnesses) and subsequently discontinued them as time-barred.

In August 2019 the applicant brought a civil action against the STP. He alleged that officers had filmed him and distributed the footage without consent, in breach of domestic procedural rules, Article 32 of the Constitution and Article 8 of the Convention. He claimed the publication had damaged his professional reputation, preventing him from concluding legal-services contracts, and sought a public retraction plus AZN 300 000 in damages.

The Yasamal District Court dismissed the claim, holding that the applicant had admitted being drunk and had failed to prove that the STP itself supplied the material to the media. The Baku Court of Appeal initially awarded AZN 1 000 for non-pecuniary damage, finding the STP responsible for its officers’ unlawful conduct because the offence had not been established, but not for the publication. The Supreme Court quashed that judgment, noting that the Ministry of Finance rather than the STP should be the proper defendant for State damages and that the later time-barred discontinuation of the administrative case had to be taken into account. On remittal the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance dismissal, again finding no proof that the police had distributed the footage and that the claim had been brought against the wrong defendant. The Supreme Court confirmed that decision on 1 April 2021.

The European Court held that the domestic courts had failed to give adequate reasons for rejecting the applicant’s complaint about the filming and publication, thereby violating the State’s positive obligations under Article 8 to protect private life.

**The case of Martinez Fernandez v. Hungary (ECtHR, Application no. 30814/22) concerns the six-day involuntary psychiatric detention and treatment of an 83-year-old woman with dementia, raising issues under Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to liberty, specifically detention of persons of unsound mind).**

The applicant, a Hungarian national born in 1937, had lived with dementia for years and received 24-hour home care from a paid caregiver and family. On 1 September 2020, after feeling unwell, emergency services took her to a general hospital on suspicion of accidental medication overdose. Tests confirmed no overdose, but she was transferred to a psychiatric hospital due to restlessness and disorientation. At the psychiatric emergency department she was uncooperative (singing, shouting, demanding release), allegedly punched a paramedic, and spoke overly familiarly to staff. She received antipsychotic and sedative injections and was admitted involuntarily. The admission report noted no suicidal thoughts or intentions; she was diagnosed with dementia and organic mood disorder.

Her son was not promptly informed of the transfer, and her phone was confiscated, preventing contact. When he located her, he explained that her agitation and uncooperativeness toward strangers were typical of her dementia, but staff refused release and sought judicial approval of hospitalization. The applicant had given her son power of attorney to represent her. A hospital representative telephoned him at 10 a.m. the next day, informing him that a court hearing would occur in one hour at the hospital.

The 17-minute hearing took place on 3 September 2020. The judge, already having appointed a guardian ad litem, maintained that appointment despite being informed of the power of attorney, citing the son’s lack of legal qualifications. The guardian was ordered to inform the applicant and her son of the proceedings and rights; the applicant had no comments. The hospital representative described the admission and treatment. The applicant gave brief, confused answers about her identity and situation. Her son noted that she appeared worse than the previous day. A psychiatric expert, relying on observation and records, diagnosed “confusion connected to mental deterioration” and deemed admission justified due to imminent danger from symptoms (confusion, disorientation, impaired impulse control, restlessness, incoherence). The expert also supported continued detention as symptoms were unchanged. The guardian ad litem stated that the procedure complied with law and agreed to involuntary treatment. The court approved emergency hospitalization and compulsory treatment on the basis of the expert’s report of imminently dangerous behavior.

The applicant was released on 7 September 2020 after her condition stabilized. She appealed, arguing that her chronic dementia did not constitute an emergency requiring hospital rather than home care; that she had been heavily sedated at the hearing in breach of Healthcare Act section 199(4), impairing assessment of her condition; and that representation was inadequate (late notice to her son and a passive guardian). The Budapest High Court dismissed the appeal, finding the first-instance court not responsible for late notification, the guardian’s appointment proper, the son’s presence sufficient, and the expert-supported finding of imminent danger well-founded.

The Kúria (supreme court) upheld this, noting limits on its review (no specific complaint under evidence-assessment rules) and holding that the applicant had not disproved imminent danger (citing suspected overdose, aggression, and confusion). It found no proof of sedation preventing examination and noted that the guardian had informed the parties, with no request for postponement. A constitutional complaint was dismissed as unfounded. The Constitutional Court accepted the expert’s view of impulse-control issues meeting the statutory “imminently dangerous conduct” threshold, observed that the expert knew of the medication, and held that representation deficiencies (despite the guardian’s formal rather than substantive role) did not violate the Fundamental Law, as the son was present and informed.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 5 § 1 violation: the detention’s lawfulness and lack of arbitrariness, particularly the guardian ad litem’s failure to visit the applicant beforehand or substantively represent her interests (a systemic issue of overly formalistic guardianship), lack of consideration of medication’s effect on her hearing participation, short notice, and whether her chronic condition truly met the imminent-danger criterion for emergency involuntary measures rather than less restrictive home care. Domestic proceedings were found not to have ensured the required procedural safeguards. (Word count: 512)

001-243188:
**Summary of Gevorgyan v. Armenia (ECtHR, Application no. 231/16)**

Journalist Ani Gevorgyan (born 1988) alleged violations of Articles 3 and 10 of the ECHR arising from police actions on 12 February 2014 while she covered an event on Mashtots Avenue in Yerevan. Supporters of the opposition Armenian National Congress (ANC) were distributing leaflets about an upcoming demonstration. Rival supporters of the ruling Republican Party approached and disrupted the event through aggressive behaviour, including pushing and grabbing leaflets. Police arrived and began arresting individuals from both groups.

Video footage showed police officers (identified as V.G., later A.A. and G.M.) attempting to pull an object from Gevorgyan’s hand as she resisted and shouted that she was a journalist and to let go of her camera. Officer V.G. was heard saying “Let go of it.” The incident occurred on a road lane near the pavement, where police cars were parked and a crowd had gathered, blocking traffic. Gevorgyan, who had a press card attached to her bag, was arrested on suspicion of hooliganism, placed in a police car with her journalist brother S.G., and taken to Kentron police station. There she was searched; her camera and memory cards were seized for inspection. She was released after about three hours and signed a receipt for the return of her belongings.

On 13 February 2014, criminal proceedings for hooliganism were opened against a group including Gevorgyan for allegedly disrupting public order. These were later discontinued for lack of intent. On 15 February 2014, Gevorgyan filed a complaint with the Special Investigative Service alleging that officer V.G. had obstructed her journalistic work by pulling and hitting her hand to seize her camera, causing injury, and that officer S.M. had seized a memory card from her camera that was never returned; three other memory cards containing footage were returned damaged. A forensic examination recorded a small haematoma (0.6 x 0.5 cm) on her right wrist, described as not meeting the criteria for light damage to health; the expert did not rule out it resulting from officers grabbing and pulling her hand.

Criminal proceedings were opened against the officers for obstruction of a journalist’s lawful activities (committed by a public official) and exceeding official authority with violence. Police officers denied attempting to seize the camera, stating they had intervened in an altercation, that Gevorgyan had obstructed traffic, yelled, interfered with arrests, and failed to obey orders, prompting them to grab her hands to move her off the road for public order and her safety. They claimed not to have known she was a journalist and that no press card was visible. Bystander witnesses described seeing a woman resisting on the road but not officers grabbing a camera or using violence. Other journalists present stated officers had tried to grab Gevorgyan’s camera (and one journalist’s phone) and continued attempts in the police car. Confrontations and further interviews produced conflicting accounts. A technical examination of the memory cards confirmed they no longer worked but could not determine the cause.

On 24 June 2014 the investigator discontinued the case for lack of corpus delicti, finding the officers had acted lawfully under the Police Act to restore order, that force was limited to grabbing and pulling her hands (causing only a minor injury), that there was no obstruction of journalism (she was arrested for public-order violations, not her profession), and that allegations of seized or damaged memory cards were unproven. Prosecutors and domestic courts (District Court, Court of Appeal, and Court of Cassation) upheld the decision. Courts noted other journalists had worked unobstructed, video evidence showed officers moving her off the road rather than seizing equipment, and she had signed a receipt listing her belongings without noting damage at the time. They acknowledged procedural shortcomings (failure to grant her victim status) but found she had been able to participate and challenge the outcome.

The ECtHR examined the complaints of physical force under Article 3 (finding the force used to seize the camera did not reach the threshold of degrading treatment and was manifestly ill-founded) and the related obstruction of journalistic work, arrest, and seizure/inspection of equipment under Article 10 (finding an unjustified interference with her professional duties).

She stated she had displayed a press card and that further attempts to seize cameras occurred in the car and station.

Proceedings were opened against officers under Criminal Code provisions on obstructing a journalist’s lawful activities (abuse of position) and exceeding official authority with violence. Officers and attesting witnesses stated that the camera was examined in her presence with no card found in it, that five cards from her pockets/bag were neither copied nor inserted into devices, and that belongings were sealed and sent onward. Confrontations produced no change in accounts. Officer V.G. said he and colleagues intervened in a brawl, arrested her for obstructing traffic, yelling and interfering with arrests (not because she was a journalist), and pulled her hands only to move her off the road; he denied seeing a press card or trying to seize the camera. Bystanders described seeing a woman resist being pulled from the road but did not see camera-grabbing or blows. Other journalists, including S.G., corroborated attempts to seize her camera (and one colleague’s phone) while she filmed arrests, continuing in the car; S.G. heard her demand return of a card at the station.

A technical examination found the cards no longer functioned but could not determine the cause. On 24 June 2014 the investigator discontinued the case for lack of corpus delicti, holding that officers lawfully restored order under the Police Act, used limited force (grabbing/pulling hands) justified by her resistance and traffic obstruction, caused only a minor injury, did not target her as a journalist, and that card allegations were unproven. A prosecutor upheld this.

The applicant appealed, arguing the investigator ignored video evidence of force and obstruction, failed to grant her victim status (shifting the burden of proof), and that police actions exceeded authority and hindered her professional duties, resulting in lost footage. The District Court rejected the appeal, finding the video and “neutral” witnesses confirmed officers merely moved her from the road without grabbing the camera or obstructing journalism (other journalists worked unhindered); card claims were contradicted by officers, attesting witnesses and her signed receipt (which listed items without noting damage). It noted she should have been treated as a victim and officers as suspects but held she had participated equally and could challenge the decision. Higher courts, including the Court of Cassation (decision notified 3 June 2015), endorsed this. The applicant lodged her ECHR application on 3 December 2015, alleging interferences with her journalistic work (Article 10), use of force and an ineffective investigation (Article 3), and related issues under Article 8.

The case of Zuvić v. Serbia (application no. 3592/17) concerns a Serbian national’s inability to obtain a judicial ruling on disciplinary proceedings that led to his discharge from professional military service. In 2002 the applicant, then a lieutenant in the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia stationed in Podgorica (Montenegro), faced both criminal charges for abuse of office and parallel disciplinary proceedings for the same conduct. On 26 December 2002 a Military Disciplinary Court imposed the penalty of “loss of rank,” which automatically entailed dismissal from service. After the Federal Republic was reconstituted as the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, the High Military Disciplinary Court twice confirmed the penalty (June and November 2003). Enforcement followed on 20 April 2004, when the applicant was formally discharged.

On 29 June 2004 the Supreme Military Court annulled the High Court’s judgment, quashed the first-instance decision and ordered a complete retrial. By then organisational changes had abolished the original disciplinary court; the case was therefore transferred to the Military Disciplinary Court in Podgorica on the basis of the unit’s location. That court recused itself because its judges had already sat in the related criminal case, prompting a further transfer to the Military Disciplinary Court in Belgrade. The Belgrade court declined to proceed, stating that the applicant was no longer a serving soldier and that the discharge order first had to be revoked by the Chairperson of the Supreme Defence Council—the only authority competent to do so.

Montenegro’s declaration of independence on 3 June 2006 dissolved the State Union and extinguished the Supreme Defence Council. Although Serbia declared itself the sole successor State, the President of Serbia’s office forwarded the entire case file to the President of Montenegro on 17 July 2006. Thereafter Serbian military courts repeatedly disclaimed jurisdiction, citing both the applicant’s discharge and the existence of parallel criminal proceedings still pending in Montenegro. The High Court in Podgorica acquitted the applicant of the criminal charges on 24 September 2010. Montenegro’s Ministry of Defence returned the file in April 2014, observing that the applicant had never been a member of the Montenegrin armed forces.

The applicant made successive requests (2009, 2012) that the Serbian disciplinary courts either resume the proceedings or discontinue them on limitation grounds. Those courts, confirmed by the High Military Disciplinary Court and later by the Administrative Court (1 October 2015), maintained that they lacked both subject-matter and territorial competence. Two constitutional complaints were lodged. On 21 April 2016 the Constitutional Court awarded the applicant EUR 900 for the excessive length of the proceedings but rejected his complaint that he had been denied access to a court.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the obstacles that prevented any determination of the disciplinary dispute originated inside the judicial system itself and were beyond the applicant’s control. After the dissolution of the State Union, Serbia retained jurisdiction; the transfer of the file to Montenegro and the courts’ overly rigid insistence that the discharge order first be revoked therefore impaired the very essence of the right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1.

001-243249:
The ECtHR case ARB SHPK and Others v. Albania (applications 39860/19, 38996/20, 6142/22 and 27370/22) concerns complaints under Article 6 § 1 (reasonable time) and Article 13 of excessive delays in Albanian civil and administrative proceedings, plus the practical ineffectiveness of the 2017 acceleratory/compensatory remedy (CCP Arts 399/1 et seq.).

ARB SHPK (a private enforcement company) filed two similar damages claims against banks for allegedly obstructing enforcement. The first (May 2014) was dismissed by the Tirana District Court (April 2015) and Court of Appeal (April 2016). A cassation appeal reached the Supreme Court in May 2016 and was declared inadmissible only in November 2024. While it was pending, the company applied under Art 399/1 in December 2020. After no timely ruling, it appealed to the Constitutional Court (April 2021). In Decision 34/2021 (November 2021) that court treated the Supreme Court delay as rendering the remedy ineffective for exhaustion purposes, found the length prima facie excessive and attributable to the authorities (not the applicant or case complexity), but held there was no violation: the commercial claim carried no high personal risk and the 2016 judicial-vetting reform had created an unavoidable backlog. Later Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rulings (including a 2024 tied vote) reached the same result. The second claim followed an identical path (started May 2014, appeal dismissal March 2017, cassation September 2017, inadmissible September 2024) and produced an identical Constitutional Court outcome (Decision 33/2021).

Llagami sued in March 2014 for compensation after alleged unlawful dismissal. The first-instance court awarded damages (May 2014); the Administrative Court of Appeal reduced them (April 2016). Cassation succeeded in May 2023. In June 2021, while the case was still at the Supreme Court, he lodged an Art 399/1 complaint; that court rejected it in September 2021, attributing the delay to the reform and calling it “objectively impossible” to avoid. He did not appeal to the Constitutional Court.

Gazidedja challenged a 2016 Social Insurance decision that cancelled his mineworker’s pension (received since 2001) and refused an old-age pension. First-instance judgment (October 2016) favoured him; the Administrative Court of Appeal (November 2017) remitted a factual issue to the civil courts and limited repayment. Cassation was filed in December 2017. After an Art 399/1 application (September 2020) went unanswered, the Constitutional Court (Decision 35/2021, November 2021) found a violation, ordered the Supreme Court to decide within six months (it remitted the case in January 2022) and declined jurisdiction over damages. Gazidedja then sued the ministries for compensation (April 2022). The District Court awarded roughly EUR 3 600 plus costs (April 2024, written October 2024) and ordered provisional enforcement, but the authorities appealed; by February 2025 the decision remained unenforced and the appeal was pending.

The 2017 remedy requires a superior court to decide length complaints within 45 days (or three months) and, if a violation is found, to accelerate the underlying case; a subsequent first-instance action then determines compensation. Transitional extensions applied to pending cases. In practice the Supreme Court and appeal courts faced massive backlogs (Supreme Court still had 18 665 cases at end-2024; the Administrative Court of Appeal exceeded 23 000), largely caused by vetting vacancies. The High Judicial Council adopted a 2024 backlog-reduction strategy, but clearance rates and staffing remain inadequate. The Constitutional Court itself later recognised that delays in the compensation stage can render the whole remedy ineffective.

These timelines and unsuccessful or delayed uses of the 2017 mechanism form the factual core of the alleged Convention breaches.

Albania (applications 39860/19, 38996/20, 6142/22 and 27370/22) concerns four complaints of excessive delays in Albanian civil and administrative proceedings, plus questions over the effectiveness of a 2017 statutory remedy (Articles 399/1 et seq. of the Code of Civil Procedure). That remedy first allows a request to a higher court to declare a “reasonable-time” breach and order acceleration; a subsequent first-instance action can then seek compensation.

In the first two applications the same private-enforcement company sued two banks in May 2014 for damages after the banks allegedly obstructed enforcement of judgments. First-instance and appeal courts dismissed both claims as unfounded (2015–2017). Cassation appeals reached the Supreme Court in 2016 and 2017 and remained pending until de-plano inadmissibility rulings in November 2024 and September 2024 respectively. While those appeals were still pending, the company lodged Article 399/1 complaints in December 2020. The Supreme Court issued no timely decision. The Constitutional Court, seised in April 2021, held in November 2021 that the length appeared excessive on its face, that the applicant had not contributed to delay and that the authorities bore responsibility for planning the 2016 judicial reform that had produced a large Supreme Court backlog. It nevertheless found no violation, emphasising the commercial (non-personal) nature of the claims, their complexity and the incomplete composition of the Supreme Court. Later Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rulings reached the same conclusion; one 2024 Constitutional challenge ended in a 4–4 split and therefore failed.

The third applicant, Llagami, sued a state body in March 2014 over his dismissal. After a first-instance award of damages was reduced on appeal, the Supreme Court in May 2023 restored the original award. In June 2021, while the cassation appeal was pending, Llagami filed an Article 399/1 request. The Supreme Court rejected it in September 2021, attributing delay to the same judicial reform and describing the delay as “objectively unavoidable.” He did not take the matter to the Constitutional Court.

The fourth applicant, Gazidedja, a former miner, applied in 2015 for an additional old-age pension. The Social Insurance Directorate rejected the request, cancelled his existing miner’s pension and demanded repayment of sums paid since 2001. Judicial proceedings began in May 2016. After mixed rulings the Supreme Court, acting on a December 2017 cassation appeal, remitted the case in January 2022; it remains pending before the Administrative Court of Appeal. In September 2020 Gazidedja lodged an Article 399/1 complaint. The Constitutional Court in November 2021 found a violation, noted that the issues were not complex and that the applicant had not caused delay, and ordered the Supreme Court to decide within six months (which it did). Gazidedja then brought a compensatory action in April 2022. In April 2024 a district court awarded him approximately €4 000 plus costs and ordered provisional enforcement. The written judgment appeared only in October 2024; the authorities appealed both the merits and the enforcement clause. As of February 2025 the award remains unpaid and the appeal is still pending.

Across the cases the principal delays occurred at the Supreme Court (seven to ten years) against a background of a 2016 vetting process that removed many judges, created vacancies and produced a national backlog of tens of thousands of cases. The 2017 remedy itself generated further delay in the fourth application, where even the compensation stage lasted nearly three years and remains unresolved.

The case of ARB SHPK and Others v. Albania concerns four applications alleging violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a hearing within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention, arising from lengthy civil and administrative proceedings in Albania and shortcomings in a 2017 domestic remedy designed to address such delays.

The first two applications were lodged by ARB SHPK, a company providing private enforcement services. In May 2014 it brought two similar damages claims against banks that had allegedly hindered enforcement procedures. First-instance and appellate courts dismissed both claims as unfounded in 2015–2017, finding no unlawful conduct or damage. Cassation appeals reached the Supreme Court in 2016 and 2017. Those appeals remained pending for years and were ultimately declared inadmissible in late 2024. While they were pending, the company applied to the Supreme Court in December 2020 under the 2017 remedy (Articles 399/1 et seq. of the Code of Civil Procedure) seeking a finding of unreasonable delay and expedition. When the Supreme Court failed to decide within the statutory 45-day period, the company appealed to the Constitutional Court. In November 2021 the Constitutional Court held the appeals admissible because the Supreme Court’s inaction had rendered the statutory remedy ineffective, but it found no violation of the reasonable-time requirement. It acknowledged delays not attributable to the applicant, yet emphasised the commercial nature of the claims (no personal rights at stake), the complexity of the cases, and a large backlog caused by the 2016 judicial-vetting reform that had removed many judges. Subsequent Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rulings (including a 4–4 split in 2024) reached the same conclusion.

The third application was brought by Llagami, who in March 2014 sued a state authority for compensation after his alleged unlawful dismissal. He succeeded at first instance in May 2014; the appellate court reduced the award in 2016. His cassation appeal was decided by the Supreme Court only in May 2023. In June 2021, while the case was still pending, he invoked the 2017 remedy. The Supreme Court rejected the length complaint in September 2021, attributing the delay to the same judicial reform and describing it as objectively unavoidable. Llagami did not appeal that ruling to the Constitutional Court.

The fourth application concerned Gazidedja’s pension entitlements. After receiving a mineworker’s pension from 2001, he applied in 2015 for an additional old-age pension. The Social Insurance Directorate rejected the request in 2016, revoked the original pension and demanded repayment of sums received since 2001. Judicial proceedings began in May 2016. The first-instance court ruled in his favour; the appellate court in 2017 remitted factual issues and limited repayment to three years. A cassation appeal filed in December 2017 led the Supreme Court, in January 2022 (after a Constitutional Court order), to quash and remit the case, which remained pending before the appellate court as of February 2025. Gazidedja had invoked the 2017 remedy in September 2020. The Constitutional Court, in November 2021, found a violation of the reasonable-time requirement (the case was not complex and the delay was not the applicant’s fault) and ordered the Supreme Court to decide within six months, but held it lacked jurisdiction to award damages. Gazidedja then sued the State for compensation. In April 2024 a first-instance court awarded approximately €3,600 plus costs and ordered provisional enforcement. The written judgment appeared only in October 2024; the authorities appealed both the merits and the enforcement clause. As of February 2025 the compensation proceedings were still pending on appeal and the award had not been paid.

The 2017 legislation created a two-stage remedy: an application to the competent higher court (or a different Supreme Court formation) for a finding of delay and an acceleration order, followed by a separate damages claim before a first-instance court. Statutory time-limits were 45 days for the first stage and three months for the second. Transitional provisions extended those periods for already-pending cases. In practice the Supreme Court frequently missed the 45-day deadline, prompting Constitutional Court intervention. Broader systemic data showed persistent backlogs (over 18,000 cases at the Supreme Court at the end of 2024 and more than 23,000 at the Administrative Court of Appeal in 2023), low grant rates for length complaints, and delays even in the compensation stage of the remedy itself.

001-243551:
The applicants are B.T., a woman of Roma origin born in 1976, and her son B.K.Cs., born 3 May 2014 (considered Roma by his parents). B.T. had five older children (born 1997–2010) placed under child protection in September 2010 for non-attendance at school and inadequate medical care. They entered temporary institutional/foster placements in June 2011 and temporary foster care in December 2011.

In December 2013, when B.T. was four months pregnant, the local health visitor reported to the Child Welfare Service and Guardianship Authority that the pregnancy was unplanned. B.T. lived alone on social benefits (participating in obligatory public work), smoked, missed check-ups, and had not altered her attitude or conditions since her older children entered care. The report recommended against releasing the newborn with her. Neither B.T. nor the father M.Cs. were informed. Days later, the Authority noted improvements (decent housing, father’s employment, municipal support) and returned one daughter from care but retained the sons, citing the new pregnancy. B.T.’s request to end the sons’ care was refused in March 2014 for the same reason.

In February 2014 the health visitor again (unbeknownst to the parents) advised the hospital not to release the baby, citing the other children’s placements and B.T.’s smoking. After the birth, B.T. was discharged on 6 or 7 May 2014 without the infant. On 6 May the Child Welfare Service and a hospital nurse asked the Guardianship Authority to prevent the baby going home, describing the mother as in “crisis” owing to irresponsibility, non-cooperation and the older children’s placements. On 7 May the Authority immediately suspended both parents’ rights and placed B.K.Cs. with a foster mother. It cited B.T.’s “irresponsible lifestyle,” the earlier placements caused by living conditions, and serious endangerment of the newborn’s development. No prior hearing of the parents occurred.

B.T. appealed, arguing that the assessment rested on outdated 2011 facts, ignored the December 2013 findings of improvement, and that Roma children were disproportionately removed in the locality. The County Authority upheld the order, listing continued smoking, missed antenatal care, past school/medical neglect, dirty clothing, smoking-related illness in siblings and unsuccessful counselling. The father’s income was discounted because he did not share the household; public work was viewed merely as a benefit condition. Judicial review by the Administrative Court, the Kúria (May 2015) and the Constitutional Court (January 2016) likewise dismissed her claims. The Kúria held that later improvements could not be considered and, even if considered, were insufficient; the Constitutional Court found the restriction necessary and proportionate to the child’s protection.

Subsequent reviews converted the placement to long-term foster care (2015), limited contact to one hour monthly, and required proof of changed parental attitudes, particularly toward schooling. After a court remittal for incomplete fact-finding, B.K.Cs. was returned to his parents on 1 April 2016 once adequate housing, income, cooperation and contact were established.

The applicants also brought unsuccessful or only partially successful civil damages claims alleging failure of supportive services, delayed reviews, hospital separation without a decision, and ethnic bias. They complained under Articles 3, 8, 13 and 14 that the immediate removal (without genuine balancing of the child’s and parents’ interests, without current in-depth assessment, and relying solely on past conduct) constituted a disproportionate interference with family life, degrading treatment, lack of effective remedy and discrimination against Roma families.
