**Case Summary: B.T. and B.K.Cs. v. Hungary (ECHR, Application no. 4581/16)**

The applicants are B.T. (born 1976, of Roma origin) and her son B.K.Cs. (born 3 May 2014, considered Roma by his parents). They alleged violations of Articles 3, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention arising from the second applicant’s placement in temporary State care immediately after birth.

B.T. had five older children (born 1997–2010). In September 2010 they were placed under child protection because the older children missed school and the younger ones lacked medical care. They entered temporary institutional or foster care in June 2011 and temporary foster care in December 2011.

During B.T.’s pregnancy with B.K.Cs., a local health visitor reported in December 2013 (when B.T. was four months pregnant) that the pregnancy was unplanned, B.T. lived alone on benefits, smoked, missed check-ups, and had not improved her situation since her other children entered care. The visitor recommended against releasing the baby to the mother after birth. Neither parent was informed. A similar uncommunicated recommendation was sent to the hospital in February 2014. In December 2013 the guardianship authority noted some improvements in housing and support and returned one daughter, but maintained the sons’ placement partly because of the new pregnancy.

B.K.Cs. was born on 3 May 2014. B.T. was discharged around 6–7 May without her son. On 6 May the child-welfare service and hospital reiterated that the baby should not go home, citing the mother’s “crisis,” prior placements, and lack of cooperation. On 7 May the Tiszaújváros District Guardianship Authority suspended both parents’ rights and placed the newborn in temporary care with a foster mother. It cited B.T.’s “irresponsible lifestyle,” prior placements of three children, and serious endangerment of the baby’s development.

B.T. appealed, arguing the findings reflected only the 2011 situation, that later official decisions had noted positive changes (decent housing, the father’s work, municipal support), and that Roma children were disproportionately removed in the locality. The county authority upheld the decision on 24 June 2014, emphasising smoking, missed check-ups, earlier educational and medical neglect of the other children, and the father’s absence from the household. Judicial review by the Miskolc Administrative and Labour Court (October 2014) and the Kúria (May 2015) confirmed the placement, relying on past conduct and the father’s distant workplace. The Constitutional Court dismissed a complaint in January 2016, finding the measure necessary and proportionate to protect the child.

In January 2015 the child was transferred to long-term foster care; after remittal and further review, he was returned to his parents on 1 April 2016 once living conditions, cooperation and contact were deemed adequate. Separate civil damages claims produced mixed results: some awards for procedural delays and inadequate support services, but no finding of discrimination.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations centre on the immediate post-birth removal without contemporaneous evidence of danger to the newborn, reliance on historical shortcomings rather than a fresh, balanced assessment of current circumstances or the child’s short- and long-term interests, lack of parental involvement or notification of the pre-birth reports, and the applicants’ claim that Roma origin played a role. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 8 on the grounds that the authorities failed to conduct a genuine balancing exercise or an in-depth assessment, based decisions primarily on the mother’s prior conduct, and thereby disproportionately interfered with family life.

The case of B.T. and B.K.Cs. v. Hungary concerns the placement of the second applicant (B.K.Cs., born 3 May 2014 and of Roma origin) into temporary State care immediately after birth, alleged to violate Articles 3, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention (primarily family life and non-discrimination).

The first applicant (B.T., Roma, born 1976) had five older children (born 1997–2010) placed under child protection in September 2010 for non-attendance at school and lack of medical care. They entered temporary foster care in 2011. During B.T.’s unplanned sixth pregnancy, the local health visitor wrote to child welfare and guardianship authorities in December 2013 (at four months) and February 2014 (at six months), citing her smoking, missed check-ups, prior children in care, lack of attitude change, solitary living on benefits, and “crisis” status. The visitor recommended against releasing the newborn with the mother. Neither B.T. nor the father (M.Cs.) was informed of these reports.

A December 2013 review noted positive changes (decent housing, father’s employment, municipal support) and returned one daughter, but retained the sons in care due to the pregnancy. B.T.’s request to terminate the sons’ care was refused in March 2014 for the same reason.

B.K.Cs. was born on 3 May 2014. B.T. was discharged on 6 or 7 May without the baby and without being shown a decision or given reasons. On 6 May, child welfare and hospital staff reiterated that the child should not go home, citing the health visitor’s assessment, prior placements, and non-cooperation. On 7 May the Tiszaújváros District Guardianship Authority issued an immediately enforceable order suspending both parents’ rights and placing the newborn with a foster mother. It relied on B.T.’s “irresponsible lifestyle,” the 2011 placements of three children, and asserted serious endangerment of the infant’s development.

B.T. appealed, arguing the decision rested on outdated 2011 facts, ignored documented improvements, and reflected disproportionate removal of Roma children. The county authority upheld the order on 24 June 2014, emphasising continued smoking, missed prenatal care, and historical neglect of the older children (school absence, hygiene, unattended wandering). Judicial review by the Miskolc Administrative and Labour Court (October 2014) and the Kúria (May 2015) dismissed her claims, treating later positive developments as irrelevant to the original decision’s lawfulness and insufficient in any event. A constitutional complaint was rejected in January 2016 as a necessary and proportionate protection of the child’s interests.

Subsequent long-term foster-care proceedings (2015) likewise cited insufficient change in parental attitude; a court later remitted the case for incomplete fact-finding. After further review, B.K.Cs. was returned to his parents on 1 April 2016 once living conditions, cooperation and income were deemed adequate. Parallel civil damages actions produced mixed results: some awards for delays and inadequate support services, but no finding of ethnic discrimination.

The applicants contended that the authorities failed to balance the child’s interests against those of the biological family, conducted no contemporaneous in-depth assessment of current risks (relying instead on past conduct and pregnancy-related reports of which the parents were unaware), and afforded the mother no meaningful participation before the immediate post-birth removal. They further alleged that the measure was motivated by anti-Roma bias, given statistical over-representation of Roma children in Hungarian care. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 8 on the basis of these procedural and proportionality shortcomings.
001-243566:
The case of Krpelík v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 23963/21) concerns the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings against the applicant, an intellectually disabled man, under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention. The applicant complained that he lacked legal assistance during initial police interviews and a site visit, despite his vulnerability due to intellectual disability.

The applicant, born in 1984, had a history of similar burglaries. On 2 April 2016, he received a summons to explain one such incident, noting his right to a lawyer under the Code of Criminal Procedure. He failed to appear and was arrested on 19 May 2016 without prior prosecutorial approval due to urgency. The arrest report, signed by him, informed him of his right to choose a lawyer.

That day, he was questioned as a suspect from 2:57 p.m. to 3:05 p.m. The report noted his elementary education and prior questioning. He signed a page detailing rights, including legal assistance, and a pre-printed form confirming understanding without needing clarification. He then gave a further explanation from 3:18 p.m. to 4:39 p.m., again informed of rights including a lawyer and remaining silent, confirming via form he would speak. He admitted multiple burglaries, stating he forgot details. On 20 May 2016, during a site visit with an independent observer, he directed police and explained entries and stolen items.

The same day, prosecution commenced for theft and trespass. Questioned as a charged person, he received two pages of rights information, including choosing a lawyer. He signed confirming understanding, waived complaint against prosecution, declined a lawyer, and admitted charges, stating good health and no psychiatric treatment since age 13.

On 22 May 2016, at a detention hearing, he confirmed his confession. After a detention order, he requested an appointed lawyer, who was provided that day. The lawyer later complained of psychological pressure and unlawful arrest, rejected by the prosecutor citing the waiver.

On 4 July 2016, with his lawyer present, the applicant remained silent. At an 11 August 2016 detention hearing, he declined to change his prior statements. His lawyer requested a psychological report on his capacity, rejected as no doubts existed.

Indicted on 13 September 2016, the applicant at trial on 11 October 2016 recanted, claiming confusion, fear, and signing without understanding due to police coercion. Police officers denied coercion, with some noting he appeared "mentally weaker" or communication awkward.

A January 2017 psychiatric expert found slight mental disability (IQ 60-70), inability to grasp complex texts, easy influence, and statements not matching his capacity. The District Court acquitted him in February 2017, deeming pre-trial evidence inadmissible without required legal assistance under Article 36 § 2 CCP.

The Regional Court quashed this, requiring further evidence. Additional experts confirmed IQ around 67, diminished capacities, manipulability, but some found him able to represent himself. In July 2018, the District Court convicted him, finding no assistance required, statements admissible (even if police-formulated), and later court repetitions with lawyer sufficient.

Appeals followed: Regional Court dismissed; Supreme Court quashed partly for insufficient corroboration on unconfessed offences but endorsed no required assistance. Reconvicted in November 2019 except three offences, to two years' imprisonment. Further appeals failed. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in November 2020 as manifestly ill-founded, noting courts assessed his capacity via experts, considering simple offences and prior experience.

These facts highlight the alleged violations: questioning and site visit without counsel, reliance on complex forms for a vulnerable person with IQ 60-70 who could not understand rights or appreciate waiver consequences, no additional assistance despite police observations of mental weakness, and courts' later findings of capacity despite contradictory experts, using unremedied pre-trial detriment for conviction.

The case of Krpelík v. the Czech Republic (no. 23963/21) concerned the fairness of criminal proceedings against Oldřich Krpelík, a man with slight intellectual disability (IQ 60–70), who was convicted of burglaries and related offences. He alleged a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) ECHR because he lacked legal assistance during key pre-trial stages despite his vulnerability.

In April 2016, police summoned Krpelík (born 1984, elementary education only, prior criminal experience) over similar burglaries. After he failed to appear, they arrested him on 19 May 2016 without prior prosecutor approval (deemed urgent). The arrest report and subsequent documents informed him of his right to a lawyer via pre-printed forms, which he signed confirming understanding and that no further explanation was needed. He was first questioned briefly as a suspect without counsel, then gave a longer explanation confessing to multiple burglaries (claiming he forgot most details). He signed the record after it was read to him.

On 20 May, police conducted a site visit (with a local observer) where Krpelík directed them to locations, explained entries, and identified stolen items—again without a lawyer. Later that day, he was formally charged, informed of rights (including remaining silent and choosing counsel) via two pages of pre-printed text, waived any complaint against prosecution, declined a lawyer, and admitted the charges. He confirmed he felt physically and mentally well, with no psychiatric treatment since age 13.

A lawyer was appointed only on 22 May after a detention hearing, where Krpelík confirmed his confession was voluntary and waived appeal. The lawyer later complained of psychological pressure and sought a psychological expert report on Krpelík’s capacity to self-represent (under CCP Article 36 § 2, requiring counsel if doubts exist about defence due to disabilities). Police rejected this, citing no such doubts. Krpelík then remained silent in later questioning with counsel present.

At trial, Krpelík recanted, claiming confusion, fear, and signing without understanding half the text due to police coercion and conviction of his guilt. Police officers denied pressure; some noted he seemed “mentally weaker” or communication awkward, but not “retarded.” A court-commissioned psychiatrist (M.P.) found him slightly disabled, unable to grasp complex texts or self-represent effectively, easily manipulable, and that recorded statements exceeded his capacities. A psychologist (P.V.) similarly noted high manipulability and inability to understand rights information without simplification. Later review experts (R.G. and G.Z.) concluded he could represent himself, understand proceedings, and that reports were not verbatim.

The District Court initially acquitted, excluding uncounselled statements and the site visit as inadmissible (police should have sought appointed counsel). After prosecutor appeal and further experts, it convicted him (31 July 2018, later adjusted to two years’ imprisonment after Supreme Court intervention on some counts), finding no mandatory counsel requirement given simple offences, prior experience, and no health complaints. Appeals courts and the Constitutional Court upheld this, treating capacity as a factual issue resolved by experts and noting the confession was corroborated and not retracted with counsel present (at one detention hearing).

The ECtHR held the trial unfair overall: authorities had to treat Krpelík as vulnerable due to disability; complex forms left him unaware of representation rights and consequences of uncounselled questioning; additional assistance was needed; the waiver lacked commensurate safeguards; restriction of assistance lacked compelling reasons; courts failed to assess waiver capacity; and pre-trial detriment was unremedied.

The case of *Krpelík v. the Czech Republic* (App. No. 23963/21) involved a Czech national with a slight intellectual disability (IQ 60–70, elementary education only, prior psychiatric treatment as a child) who alleged that his criminal conviction for burglaries violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) ECHR. The core complaint was that he lacked legal assistance during initial police questioning and a site visit, despite his vulnerability, and that his purported waivers of counsel were invalid.

On 19 May 2016, police arrested the applicant (without prior prosecutor approval, citing urgency) after he failed to appear on a summons for similar past burglaries. The arrest report and subsequent interrogation records contained pre-printed information on rights, including the right to a lawyer under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant signed forms confirming he understood these rights, did not wish to remain silent or consult counsel, and felt well. In a brief initial questioning, he acknowledged suspicion of burglaries. A longer session followed in which he confessed to multiple break-ins, though he could not recall details. The statements were read to him; he signed them (with a misspelling). Police noted his limited schooling and prior questioning experience.

The next day, without counsel, police conducted a site visit (with a local observer) during which the applicant directed officers, demonstrated entry methods, and identified stolen items. He was then charged with theft and trespass. Similar pre-printed forms were used; he again waived counsel and a complaint against prosecution, confirmed good health (denying recent treatment), and admitted the charges. Only after a 22 May detention hearing—where he confirmed his confession and requested appointed counsel—was a lawyer provided.

The lawyer later challenged the proceedings, alleging psychological pressure (exacerbated by an allegedly unlawful arrest) and requesting a psychological expert to assess the applicant’s capacity to self-represent under CCP Article 36 § 2. Police rejected this, citing no doubts about his mental state. At trial, the applicant recanted, claiming confusion, fear, coercion, and inability to understand half the documents. Police witnesses denied coercion but noted he appeared “a bit weaker mentally” or awkward, though not “retarded,” with some outlandish comments. An observer described normal behavior.

Multiple expert reports followed. One psychiatrist found the applicant slightly disabled, easily influenced, unable to grasp complex texts or represent himself effectively, and capable of irrational confessions under stress; the recorded statements’ syntax did not match his abilities. A psychologist noted high manipulability, cognitive issues, and inability to understand unsimplified rights information without help. A later review (psychiatrist and psychologist) concluded he could stand trial, understand proceedings, represent himself, and even distort facts, though statements were likely police-formulated. The District Court initially acquitted, deeming uncounseled statements and the site visit inadmissible due to disability and failure to appoint counsel. After remittal and further experts, it convicted him (later reduced after Supreme Court intervention on some counts), finding no mandatory counsel requirement, sufficient capacity (supported by prior criminal experience and offense simplicity), and corroboration from the site visit. Appeals, including to the Supreme and Constitutional Courts, were dismissed; the latter held the assessment non-arbitrary.

The ECtHR held that authorities were required to treat the applicant as vulnerable. Complex pre-printed forms did not ensure he understood his rights or the consequences of uncounseled questioning. The waiver lacked minimum safeguards; no compelling reasons justified restricting assistance; domestic courts failed to properly assess waiver capacity; and pre-trial detriment was not remedied, rendering the trial as a whole unfair.
001-243553:
The case K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited v. Türkiye (Application no. 41120/17) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by a Cypriot company established in 1967, whose shareholders and directors are of Greek Cypriot origin. The company owned a building complex in the fenced-off area of Famagusta in northern Cyprus. It abandoned this property after the 1974 Turkish military intervention.

On 23 July 2010 the company applied to the Immovable Property Commission (IPC), the mechanism established in the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (TRNC) to deal with such claims. It sought restitution of the immovable property, compensation for loss of use together with statutory interest, compensation for non-pecuniary damage, and legal costs. When the TRNC authorities failed to respond, the company applied on 1 November 2010 for a default judgment.

Hearings on the default application took place between December 2010 and June 2012. At each hearing the TRNC Attorney General obtained adjournments on the ground that the Land Registry had not yet produced a report on the property. In October 2012 the applicant complained of these delays. The Attorney General then disclosed that a preliminary assessment indicated the property was registered in the name of the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, an Islamic vakıf managed by the Evkaf Administration and originally endowed in the eighteenth century. On 23 November 2012 the IPC admitted the Evkaf Administration as a third party.

The applicant challenged both the delays and the third-party joinder before the TRNC Administrative Court. On 6 November 2015 that court held that Evkaf could not be joined because its participation would render restitution impossible, but declined jurisdiction over the delay complaint. Both sides appealed. On 29 November 2016 the High Administrative Court ruled that it possessed exclusive jurisdiction over all IPC-related matters, that delays were not subject to judicial review, and that Evkaf must be admitted, relying on a 27 December 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment that had declared the foundation the owner of a list of properties in the Varosha-Famagusta area.

TRNC authorities finally filed their defence submissions on 11 December 2019. From January 2020 the applicant and its representative refused to attend further IPC hearings. Although a representative appeared once in February 2024 and indicated willingness to consider any compensation proposal, the company later stated that any settlement would have to occur before the Strasbourg Court. The IPC proceedings remain pending.

These facts form the basis of the alleged violations. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the joinder of a religious foundation whose claim derived from an eighteenth-century title, rather than 1974 land-registry records, rendered the proceedings unfair and unbalanced, and that the High Administrative Court lacked impartiality. It further alleged that the IPC’s handling of the claim—marked by repeated adjournments, delayed joinder of a third party, and an overall duration exceeding fourteen years—constituted a failure to act with the coherence, diligence and expedition required by Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, thereby interfering with the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. Additional complaints under Articles 13 and 14 concerned the absence of an effective remedy for the delays and alleged discrimination. The Court ultimately examined the fairness of the third-party participation, the overall fairness of the proceedings, and the IPC’s delay in examining the property claim.

The applicant, K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited (a Cypriot company established in 1967 with Greek Cypriot shareholders and directors), owned a building complex in the fenced-off Varosha area of Famagusta in northern Cyprus. It abandoned the property following the 1974 Turkish military operation.

On 23 July 2010, the company applied to the Immovable Property Commission (IPC) under Law 67/2005, seeking restitution of the property, compensation for loss of use (with statutory interest), non-pecuniary damages, and costs. When the “TRNC” authorities did not respond, it applied for a default judgment on 1 November 2010. Between December 2010 and June 2012, the IPC granted multiple adjournments at the request of the Attorney General’s office, which cited the absence of a required land registry report.

On 23 October 2012, the company complained of delays. The Attorney General then indicated that a preliminary assessment showed the property was registered in the name of the Abdullah Paşa Foundation (a religious vakıf managed by the Evkaf Administration). The IPC admitted Evkaf as a third party on 23 November 2012. The company challenged both the delays and the third-party admission before the “TRNC” Administrative Court.

On 6 November 2015, that court ruled that Evkaf could not be admitted as a party because doing so would render restitution impossible, but it declined jurisdiction over the delay complaint. Both sides appealed. On 29 November 2016, the High Administrative Court held that it had exclusive jurisdiction over IPC matters, that delays were not subject to judicial review, and that Evkaf must be admitted as a party. It relied on a 27 December 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment that had declared the foundation the current registered owner of various properties in the area (based on 18th-century endowment documents). A later High Administrative Court decision in another case confirmed that the IPC could consider only 1974 title deeds and that Evkaf’s participation did not alter claimants’ rights if those deeds were proven.

The “TRNC” authorities filed their defence submissions only on 11 December 2019. From January 2020 the company largely refused to attend IPC hearings (though it briefly appeared in February 2024). The IPC proceedings remain pending more than 14 years after they began.

The complaints centre on the excessive length of the IPC proceedings, the admission of the religious foundation as a third party (which the company argued made restitution impossible and rendered the remedy ineffective), and the alleged lack of impartiality of the High Administrative Court. These issues arise in the specific context of properties in the fenced Famagusta area and engage Articles 6 § 1, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court later found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 on account of the IPC’s lack of coherence, diligence and expedition, while rejecting the Article 6 complaint concerning third-party participation.

**Case Summary: K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited v. Türkiye (Application no. 41120/17)**

The applicant, K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited, is a Cypriot company established in 1967 that conducted business in Nicosia. Its shareholders and directors are of Greek Cypriot origin. It owned a building complex in the fenced-up Varosha area of Famagusta in northern Cyprus. Following the 1974 Turkish military intervention, the company abandoned the property.

On 23 July 2010, the company applied to the Immovable Property Commission (IPC) of the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”) seeking restitution of the property, compensation for loss of use (plus statutory interest), non-pecuniary damages, further interest, and legal costs. When the “TRNC” authorities failed to respond, the company applied on 1 November 2010 for a default judgment.

Between December 2010 and June 2012, multiple hearings on the default application were adjourned at the request of the “TRNC” Attorney General because a required Land Registry report had not been prepared. In October 2012 the company complained of delays. The Attorney General then indicated that preliminary assessment suggested the property was registered in the name of the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, a religious endowment managed by the Evkaf Administration. On 23 November 2012 the IPC admitted the Evkaf Administration as a third party on the ground that it was possibly affected by the claim.

The company challenged both the adjournments and the third-party admission before the “TRNC” Administrative Court on 6 December 2012. On 6 November 2015 that court held that admitting Evkaf would render restitution impossible and therefore refused joinder, while declining jurisdiction over the delay complaint. Both sides appealed to the High Administrative Court.

On 29 November 2016 the High Administrative Court asserted exclusive jurisdiction over IPC matters. It ruled that delays and adjournments were not subject to judicial review. Relying on a 27 December 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment that had declared the Evkaf Administration the owner of various Varosha properties (including on the basis of 18th-century vakıf documents), it ordered that Evkaf be joined as a party.

The “TRNC” authorities filed their defence submissions only on 11 December 2019. From January 2020 the company and its lawyer declined to attend scheduled IPC hearings. Limited contact resumed in February 2024, but the company indicated that any settlement should occur before the European Court. The IPC proceedings remain pending more than 14 years after the original application.

These facts underpin the complaints of excessive length and lack of effectiveness of the IPC remedy (Articles 6, 13 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1), unfairness arising from the forced joinder of the religious foundation (which the company argued made restitution in the fenced-off area impossible), lack of impartiality of the High Administrative Court as appellate body, and discrimination (Article 14). The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 6 § 1 in the third-party participation (holding it necessary for a fair trial and not arbitrary) but a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the IPC had failed to act with coherence, diligence and appropriate expedition. It also indicated under Article 46 the need for general measures to accelerate IPC proceedings and provide an effective remedy for delays.

The case of Cioffi v. Italy (Application no. 17710/15) concerns the alleged inhuman and degrading treatment of Italian national Andrea Cioffi by police at the Virgilio Raniero station in Naples on 17 March 2001, after an anti-globalisation demonstration, plus the ensuing ineffective investigation, under Article 3 ECHR.

Following clashes at a protest against the Third Global Forum, police transferred 85 people—including the applicant, retrieved from hospital—to the station around 12:30–13:00. He was released after 5:30 p.m. A deputy chief coordinated, deploying officers and assigning seniors C.S. and F.C. to oversee detainees in the break room.

The Naples District Court (2010) found proven “egregious conduct”: detainees walked a gauntlet of slaps, kicks, trips, spitting and verbal abuse; knelt hands-behind-head (even if injured); underwent prolonged naked searches on blood- and urine-soaked floors amid further abuse; were beaten, threatened (including sexually, religiously and politically), denied lawyer/family contact, phone use (mobiles seized/damaged), food, water or toilets. This amounted to a “suspension of constitutional guarantees” via an unjustified “sweep” of hospital attendees, including non-demonstrators.

The applicant specifically suffered repeated beatings, was shoved/kicked/punched into a kneeling position facing the wall, and endured “very violent” further assault plus “particularly odious” insults/threats after identifying as a trainee lawyer (“the little lawyer”) and questioning his detention. Officers threatened they knew his address. He underwent two toilet searches (one by officers who fetched him), was forced to sign a false record of a “dangerous” keychain, then given a contradictory record. His phone was damaged.

Thirty-one officers of various ranks were charged with aggravated kidnapping (by officials abusing authority), unlawful searches, property damage, abuse of office, forgery, criminal coercion and bodily harm (including applicant’s head/back contusions, aggravated by official status, numbers, vulnerability and baton use).

The District Court discontinued time-barred charges (bodily harm, coercion, searches, damage). It convicted ten officers of kidnapping (2–2 years 8 months). R.M. and D.T. were also convicted of coercion for using violence/threats to enforce unlawful orders, creating inferiority and “inhuman and degrading” treatment; they knew of (or permitted) abuse but failed to intervene or alert superiors. Some sentences were fully remitted by 2006 pardon; others (and ancillary public-office suspensions) were suspended, with convictions not recorded. Civil parties (applicant plus 19 others) were entitled to damages (to be quantified separately) plus costs. The court noted victims’ delayed complaints stemmed from intimidation.

The Naples Court of Appeal (2013) discontinued remaining kidnapping charges as time-barred and quashed office suspensions. It upheld R.M. and D.T.’s coercion convictions but imposed shorter suspended terms (10 and 6 months) with unrecorded convictions. Civil compensation rights were confirmed without quantification.

The Court of Cassation dismissed officers’ 2015 appeals.

C.S. and F.C. were briefly house-arrested then returned to duty. A 2014 disciplinary probe led to F.C. receiving only a written warning for negligence (failure to detect/investigate blood traces or prevent abuse despite hours on site); C.S. was cleared. F.C.’s appeal was pending in 2016.

Domestic law then lacked a specific torture offence (added 2017). Short limitation periods, pardons, suspended/light penalties and failure to hold all responsible for widespread, documented abuse rendered proceedings ineffective.

The case of Cioffi v. Italy (ECtHR, Application no. 17710/15) concerns alleged police ill-treatment of the applicant, Andrea Cioffi, and an inadequate investigation, raising issues under Article 3 ECHR (substantive and procedural limbs).

On 17 March 2001, following an anti-globalisation demonstration in Naples against a government summit, clashes occurred between protesters and police. Injured persons (and companions) were taken to city hospitals. From around 12:30 p.m., police identified those present in emergency departments and transferred 85 individuals, including the applicant (retrieved between 12:30 and 13:00), to the Virgilio Raniero police station. He was released after 5:30 p.m. A deputy police chief coordinated operations; officers C.S. and F.C. oversaw detainees held in a break room.

Domestic courts later established that arrivals were forced through a gauntlet of officers who slapped, kicked, tripped, spat on and verbally abused them. Detainees, including the injured, were made to kneel with hands behind heads; subjected to prolonged naked, barefoot searches on a floor soiled with blood and urine amid further abuse; denied communication with lawyers or family (phones seized or damaged); beaten; threatened (including over sexual, religious or political affiliations); and refused food, water or toilet access. The applicant specifically endured multiple beatings, was forced to kneel facing a wall, and was shoved, kicked and punched from behind despite requests for an explanation. Identifying himself as a trainee lawyer led to “very violent” further physical and verbal abuse (he was called “the little lawyer” and became a “designated target”), plus threats that officers knew his address and could reach him. He underwent two toilet searches with inconsistent official records (one falsely noting a “keychain” as a dangerous item) and his phone was damaged.

Thirty-one officers of various ranks were charged with offences including aggravated kidnapping, unlawful searches, property damage, abuse of office, forgery, criminal coercion and bodily harm (the latter including contusions to the applicant’s head and back, with aggravating factors such as use of batons and exploiting vulnerability). The applicant joined as a civil party.

In its 23 January 2010 judgment, the Naples District Court found the facts proven as described by victims, amounting to a “suspension of constitutional guarantees” via an unjustified “sweep” of hospital attendees (many unrelated to the demonstration or already identified). It described the overall conduct as “inhuman and degrading.” Proceedings for bodily harm, coercion, unlawful searches and damage were discontinued as time-barred. Ten officers were convicted of kidnapping (sentences of 2–2 years 8 months); two (R.M. and D.T.) were also convicted of coercion for failing to prevent or reporting the abuse they witnessed (R.M. additionally of bodily harm to another victim). Sentences for four officers (including C.S., F.C., R.M. and D.T.) were remitted by a 2006 pardon; remaining penalties were suspended and convictions ordered not to appear on criminal records. Civil parties were granted a right to damages (to be quantified separately).

On 9 January 2013 the Naples Court of Appeal discontinued the kidnapping convictions as time-barred (overturning related ancillary penalties) but upheld the two coercion convictions (sentences reduced to 10 and 6 months, then suspended, with non-recording of convictions). Civil rights were confirmed. Appeals to the Court of Cassation were dismissed on 9 October 2015.

C.S. and F.C. were briefly suspended from duty in 2002. A 2014–2015 disciplinary process found F.C. negligent (written warning issued; he had been inside the station for hours and failed to investigate blood traces) but cleared C.S. F.C.’s administrative appeal against the sanction remained pending.

These facts underpin the alleged Article 3 violations: the established treatment at the station and the investigation’s outcome (prescription of core offences, remitted/suspended sentences and minimal disciplinary consequences).

001-243567:
The case of T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22) concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private life). The applicant, a Czech national born in 1977 and registered as male at birth with a corresponding male personal numerical code (birth number), identifies as non-binary or “intergender.” From an early age, the assigned male identity conflicted with his psychological and social identity. Due to fears of medical complications, he declined irreversible male-to-female gender reassignment surgery (which would have included sterilisation and genital reconstruction). He did undergo hormone therapy to reduce testosterone and certain aesthetic procedures. In 2012 he legally changed his first name and received a new identity card still recording male sex and a male-form birth number.

From 2012 onward the applicant repeatedly asked the Ministry of the Interior to alter the sex/gender marker and birth number on his identity documents to a neutral form or, failing that, a female form. All requests were refused because he had not undergone the surgery required by Article 29 § 1 of the Civil Code and section 21(1) of the Specific Health Services Act. Those provisions defined legal gender reassignment as surgery that disables reproductive function and reconstructs the genitals; only then could the birth number (which encodes sex by adding 50 to the month of birth for women) be changed under the Population Register Act. A 2013 Swiss medical report confirmed that the applicant was receiving clinical treatment for transition toward a female gender, but this was deemed insufficient.

In 2017 the applicant again sought a change of birth number. After administrative dismissal he brought an action for unlawful interference, alleging breaches of Articles 3, 8 and 14. The Prague Municipal Court rejected the claim in 2018, holding that the statutory surgery requirement served the public interests of reliable civil-status records and legal certainty and that those interests outweighed the applicant’s right to gender self-determination. It distinguished the European Court’s judgment in A.P., Garçon and Nicot v. France. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the cassation appeal in 2019, emphasising Czech society’s binary, biologically grounded understanding of gender and stating that any shift away from that understanding was a matter for the legislature, not the courts.

The applicant’s subsequent constitutional complaint sought both individual relief and the annulment of the relevant statutory provisions. In a 2021 plenary judgment (Pl. ÚS 2/20) the Constitutional Court, by one vote short of the required majority, refused to annul the provisions. It observed that the applicant identified as neither male nor female and had requested only a change of numerical code; consequently the surgery requirement was not an obstacle to his self-expression. The Court stressed the State’s need for objective, binary gender data to perform its functions and held that Article 8 did not entitle an individual to have inaccurate information recorded. A later chamber decision in 2022 likewise found no violation, citing a wide margin of appreciation on morally sensitive questions lacking European consensus and warning that judicially imposed change could generate social tension.

(The Constitutional Court later, in 2024, annulled the surgery-and-sterilisation requirement itself, with effect from 30 June 2025, but that ruling post-dated the facts of the present application.)

The European Court found that the authorities’ persistent refusal amounted to a refusal to recognise the applicant’s gender identity. Conditioning legal recognition on surgery that entailed or risked sterilisation against the person’s wishes forced the applicant to choose between the full exercise of the right to private life and the right to physical integrity, thereby upsetting the fair balance required by Article 8.

The case of T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22) concerns the authorities’ refusal to change the applicant’s personal numerical code (birth number) on his national identity card to reflect a non-male gender, on the ground that he had not undergone gender-reassignment surgery required by domestic law. The applicant, a Czech national born in 1977 and living in Prague, was registered as male at birth and given a male name. He identifies as non-binary (“intergender”). From an early age he experienced a mismatch between his assigned male identity and his psychological and social identity. Owing to fears of medical complications he declined irreversible male-to-female surgery (which would have entailed sterilisation). He nevertheless underwent hormone treatment to reduce testosterone and certain aesthetic procedures. In autumn 2012 he changed his first name and received a new identity card that still recorded male sex and a male-form birth number.

From May 2012 the applicant repeatedly asked the Ministry of the Interior to alter the sex/gender marker and birth number to a neutral or at least female form. The Ministry rejected the requests because he had not fulfilled the statutory conditions in Article 29 § 1 of the Civil Code and section 21(1) of the Specific Health Services Act: gender reassignment required surgery that disabled reproductive function and reconstructed the genitals. A July 2013 Swiss medical report confirmed that he was receiving appropriate clinical treatment for transition to female. In 2015 the Public Defender of Rights found no discrimination, holding that the legislation itself required surgery and that any compatibility assessment belonged to the Constitutional Court.

On 11 August 2017 a further request was refused. The applicant brought an administrative action alleging violations of the prohibition of ill-treatment, of the prohibition of discrimination and of the right to respect for private life. The Prague Municipal Court dismissed the action on 14 May 2018, noting that the applicant had not undergone the required surgery. It distinguished A.P., Garçon and Nicot v. France, emphasising the lack of consensus among Council of Europe States and the overriding public interest in the reliability of civil-status records and legal certainty. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment on 30 May 2019, stressing that Czech law and society rest on a strictly binary, medically objective conception of gender; any departure was viewed as disruptive of social order. It was not for the courts to alter that societal consensus.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint seeking annulment of the relevant provisions and alleging breaches of Articles 3, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court’s plenary rejected the annulment request (by one vote) on 9 November 2021. It observed that the applicant sought only a change of birth-number format and identified as neither male nor female, so the surgery requirement was not directly in issue. Birth numbers served to record objective biological sex for the State’s administrative functions; they did not purport to reflect internal identity. The Court expressed doubts about the applicability of the European Court’s gender-recognition case-law, given the absence of a settled European consensus. Seven judges dissented.

On 7 June 2022 the Constitutional Court dismissed the individual appeal, holding that A.P. was distinguishable because the applicant identified as gender-neutral and sought only a format change, not recognition of a genuinely perceived binary identity. The State enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation on morally sensitive questions lacking consensus. The refusal did not upset the fair balance required by Article 8; the entire legal order was premised on a binary approach that reflected the attitude of Czech society.

The European Court later held that the refusal constituted a failure to recognise the applicant’s gender identity. Conditioning legal recognition on surgery that entailed or could entail sterilisation against the person’s wishes made the full exercise of the right to respect for private life contingent on relinquishing the right to physical integrity, thereby disregarding the fair balance that must be struck between the general interest and the interests of the individual.

The case of T.H. v. the Czech Republic (application no. 33037/22) concerns a transgender applicant’s unsuccessful attempts to obtain legal recognition of a change of gender. The applicant, a Czech national born in 1977 and living in Prague, identifies as having a non-binary (“intergender”) identity. Assigned male at birth and given a male name, he experienced a mismatch between his assigned sex and his psychological and social identity from an early age. He underwent hormone treatment to reduce testosterone and certain aesthetic procedures but declined irreversible male-to-female gender-reassignment surgery (which would have included sterilisation) because of concerns about medical complications.

In autumn 2012 he obtained a name change and a new identity card that continued to record male sex and a male-form personal numerical code (birth number). From May 2012 onwards he repeatedly asked the Ministry of the Interior to alter the sex/gender marker and birth number on his identity documents to a neutral form or, failing that, a female form. All requests were refused on the ground that he had not undergone the surgery required by Article 29 § 1 of the Civil Code and section 21(1) of the Specific Health Services Act. A 2013 Swiss medical report confirmed that he was receiving appropriate clinical treatment for transition toward a female gender, but this was not accepted as sufficient.

In August 2017 the applicant again sought a change of birth number. After administrative dismissal he brought an action alleging violations of the prohibition of ill-treatment, the prohibition of discrimination and the right to respect for private life. The Prague Municipal Court dismissed the claim in May 2018, holding that the statutory surgery requirement served the public interest in reliable civil-status records and legal certainty. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that decision in May 2019, emphasising Czech society’s binary, medically objective conception of legal gender and stating that any change should come from the legislature. The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint seeking both individual relief and the annulment of the relevant statutory provisions. The Constitutional Court’s plenary rejected the annulment request in November 2021 (by one vote short of the required majority) and, in June 2022, dismissed the individual complaint. It characterised the State’s interest in a binary legal order as overriding and distinguished the Court’s earlier case-law.

The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that making legal recognition of gender identity conditional on sterilising surgery forced him to choose between his right to physical integrity and his right to private life. He also invoked Articles 3 and 14. The Court later examined the case solely under Article 8, finding that the authorities’ refusal amounted to a denial of recognition of the applicant’s gender identity and that the sterilisation requirement placed him in an impossible dilemma, thereby failing to strike a fair balance between competing interests.

001-243877:
The case of Mustafa and Mustafova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 7428/17) concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention by two Bulgarian siblings, Metin Mustafa Mustafa and Esengyul Mustafova Mustafova. They alleged that domestic courts wrongly declared inadmissible a tort claim they brought on behalf of their late father, thereby denying them access to a court.

The applicants’ brother suffered serious injuries in a road accident on 22 October 2010 and died days later. The driver at fault was convicted in September 2011. Their father sought compensation for non-pecuniary damage arising from his son’s death. After the Guarantee Fund (a body funded by insurers to cover uninsured or unidentified drivers) informed him that the driver was uninsured, the father submitted a written request to the Fund on 25 October 2011 for BGN 100,000 (EUR 51,150). Under Article 288 § 9 of the 2005 Insurance Code, this out-of-court step was obligatory before any court action against the Fund (Article 288 § 11). No equivalent preliminary procedure applied to claims against insurers.

The father died on 10 November 2011. On 28 November 2011 the Fund refused the request, asserting that the driver had in fact been insured with company V., which was therefore liable.

On 3 May 2012 the applicants lodged a court claim against V. (or, alternatively, the Fund) seeking the same sum on their father’s behalf. The Sofia City Court dismissed the claim as inadmissible on 26 February 2013, holding that the right to non-pecuniary compensation was strictly personal and that the father had never himself brought court proceedings. The Sofia Court of Appeal reversed this on 10 April 2013, finding that the father’s Fund application constituted the mandatory first stage of the compensation procedure, so the applicants could continue it.

On 16 June 2014 the Sofia City Court partially allowed the claim against V. The Sofia Court of Appeal, however, quashed that judgment on 2 February 2015 and again declared the claim inadmissible. It held that the father’s personal entitlement had died with him; heirs could pursue only proceedings already pending in court. The Fund request was “insignificant” and not equivalent to a court action. The court relied on a 2009 Supreme Court of Cassation (SCC) decision in a similar case. (Obiter, it noted that the insurance was invalid, so the Fund would have been liable.) The SCC refused leave to appeal on 18 July 2016 because the applicants had not challenged the standing ruling.

Bulgarian case-law had long treated non-pecuniary claims as non-inheritable unless the deceased had already filed a court action. Later SCC rulings (2021–2022) recognised that an out-of-court claim against an insurer or the Fund equally manifested the injured person’s will, rendering the right inheritable. The 2005 Code’s obligatory Fund procedure and the 2016 Code’s analogous insurer procedure formed the relevant statutory background. The applicants consistently argued that their father’s Fund request had already asserted the claim, which therefore formed part of his estate and could be inherited.

The alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 thus centred on whether the domestic courts’ classification of the claim as a new, inadmissible action (rather than a continuation of the father’s already-initiated procedure) unjustifiably restricted the applicants’ access to court.

The case of Mustafa and Mustafova v. Bulgaria (no. 7428/17) concerned access to court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicants, Bulgarian siblings, complained that domestic courts had declared inadmissible a tort claim they brought on behalf of their late father for non-pecuniary damages arising from their brother’s death.

Their brother was seriously injured in a car accident on 22 October 2010 and died days later. The at-fault driver was convicted in September 2011. The applicants’ father sought compensation. After the Guarantee Fund (an institution funded by insurers to cover uninsured or unidentified drivers) informed him in February 2011 that the driver was uninsured, he submitted a written request to the Fund on 25 October 2011 for BGN 100,000 (EUR 51,150). This followed the obligatory out-of-court procedure under Article 288 § 9 of the 2005 Insurance Code; a court action against the Fund was permitted only after refusal, delay, or unsatisfactory payment (Article 288 § 11). No such preliminary step applied to claims against insurers.

The father died on 10 November 2011. On 28 November 2011 the Fund refused, stating the driver had been insured with company V., which was therefore liable.

On 3 May 2012 the applicants sued V. (alternatively the Fund) for the same amount on their father’s behalf. The Sofia City Court dismissed the claim as inadmissible on 26 February 2013, holding that the right to non-pecuniary compensation was strictly personal and the father had never initiated court proceedings.

The Sofia Court of Appeal quashed this on 10 April 2013, finding that the father’s Fund application was the obligatory first stage and that the applicants could continue it without substituting his personal choice. The City Court then partially allowed the claim on 16 June 2014, holding V. liable because the insurance was valid, and ordered the applicants to pay part of the defendants’ costs.

On 2 February 2015 the Sofia Court of Appeal reversed, declaring the claim inadmissible. It ruled that the father’s strictly personal entitlement had extinguished on his death; heirs could only continue an already-filed court action, not start one. The Fund request was not equivalent to a court action. The court relied inter alia on a 2009 Supreme Court of Cassation (SCC) decision in a similar case. In an obiter it noted that the insurance had in fact been invalid, so the Fund would have been liable.

The SCC refused cassation review on 18 July 2016 because the applicants had raised only insurance-validity questions, not standing.

Throughout, the applicants argued that their father had already manifested his will by the obligatory Fund request, that he had been barred from suing until the Fund decided, that he died before notification of the refusal, and that the claim had therefore entered his estate and was inheritable.

Bulgarian practice (consistent SCC and former Supreme Court case-law) treated non-pecuniary claims as non-transferable unless the injured person had already lodged a court action. A 2009 SCC decision had expressly dismissed the relevance of a prior out-of-court request. Subsequent 2022 SCC judgments, however, recognised that an out-of-court assertion of the claim also rendered it inheritable.

The European Court held Article 6 § 1 applicable. The father’s obligatory out-of-court claim was equivalent to initiating court proceedings. The applicants’ action was therefore a continuation of the compensation procedure he had already set in motion. The domestic courts’ restriction of access to court was disproportionate to any legitimate aim and violated Article 6 § 1.

The claim sought compensation for non-pecuniary damage arising from the death of their brother.

After inquiring, he was told in February 2011 by the Guarantee Fund (a body funded by insurers to pay compensation in cases of uninsured or unidentified drivers) that the driver was uninsured. On 25 October 2011, pursuant to Article 288 § 9 of the 2005 Insurance Code, he submitted a written request to the Fund for BGN 100,000 (EUR 51,150) in non-pecuniary damages. This out-of-court step was obligatory; under Article 288 § 11 a court action against the Fund was possible only after three months without a decision, a refusal, or dissatisfaction with any award. (No such prerequisite applied to claims against insurers themselves.)

The father died on 10 November 2011, before any Fund decision. On 28 November 2011 the Fund refused payment, stating the driver had in fact been insured with company V.

On 3 May 2012 the applicants sued V (or, alternatively, the Fund) for the same BGN 100,000 on their father's behalf. The Sofia City Court dismissed the claim as inadmissible (26 February 2013), holding that the right to non-pecuniary damages was strictly personal and the father had never himself brought a court action. The Sofia Court of Appeal quashed this (10 April 2013), ruling that the father's obligatory Fund request constituted the start of the compensation process; the applicants could continue it without substituting their own decision for his.

On remittal the Sofia City Court partially allowed the claim (16 June 2014), finding V liable because the insurance was valid, and ordered payment (while also making the applicants pay some costs). The Sofia Court of Appeal again quashed and dismissed the claim as inadmissible (2 February 2015). It held that the personal right had extinguished on the father's death; heirs could pursue only proceedings already pending in court. The Fund request was “insignificant” and not equivalent to a court action. The court relied on, among other authorities, a 31 March 2009 Supreme Court of Cassation (SCC) decision in a similar case. It added obiter that the insurance had actually been invalid, so the Fund would have been liable.

The SCC refused to hear a further appeal on points of law (18 July 2016). The applicants had raised only issues of insurance validity, not standing.

Throughout, the applicants argued that their father had manifested his will to claim compensation by the obligatory Fund request; he had been legally barred from suing immediately and had died before the refusal. The claim had therefore become part of his estate and inheritable.

(The 2016 Insurance Code later introduced a similar obligatory out-of-court stage for claims against insurers. Subsequent SCC case-law from 2021–2022, not applicable to the present events, treated an out-of-court claim as sufficient to make the right inheritable.)

The applicants' Article 6 § 1 complaint concerned this denial of access to court.
001-248194:
The case of Tatlı v. Türkiye (Application no. 35383/19) concerns the applicant’s inability to obtain judicial review of an administrative decision waiving the environmental impact assessment (EIA) requirement for a dam and hydroelectric power plant on the Solaklı River near Köknar village in Trabzon’s Çaykara district.

On 2 March 2015 the applicant, a Turkish national living in Istanbul with seasonal ties to the village, sought information under the Freedom of Information Act about the project’s EIA status. The Trabzon governor’s office replied on 13 November 2015 that a waiver decision had been issued. On 28 April 2016 the applicant brought annulment proceedings in the Trabzon Administrative Court. He alleged irreparable harm to the local population, biodiversity and ecosystem, and claimed a direct personal interest arising from months spent annually in the village and strong land and community ties (despite not being a permanent resident). He noted he had been a party to two earlier related actions and that subsequent project revisions had not been notified to him.

The court requested details of his residence and any immovable property in Çaykara as of the date the action was filed and, taking account of the prior litigation, commissioned an expert panel (forestry, environmental, construction, mining and geological engineers). The experts concluded that post-revision works would cause no permanent ecological damage, that tree-felling and waste impacts had been reduced, and that the legal and scientific conditions for an EIA waiver were satisfied.

On 10 May 2017 the Administrative Court dismissed the action, holding that the revisions had sufficiently minimised adverse effects and that the waiver was lawful. The applicant appealed, arguing inadequate merits examination and a failure to assess cumulative impacts holistically. On 2 November 2017 the Supreme Administrative Court set aside the first-instance judgment and dismissed the case with final effect for lack of standing. It reasoned that recognising standing for persons who neither resided nor owned property in the vicinity would expose administrative decisions and investors to perpetual litigation, contrary to administrative stability. After an ex-officio search of the National Judiciary Informatics System (UYAP), the court found the applicant had neither resided nor owned immovable property in the area on the date the action was introduced. No further appeal lay.

On 24 January 2018 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, asserting a breach of access to a court. He reiterated his seasonal residence and social-economic ties and submitted jointly inherited title deeds. On 12 November 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded by summary decision.

Domestic law (Administrative Procedure Act, s. 2) grants standing to anyone whose interests are violated by an allegedly unlawful administrative act. Section 20 empowers courts to raise issues of their own motion and to require parties to supply information. EIA Regulation provisions then in force allowed waiver for Annex-II projects after screening if impacts were deemed insignificant or manageable by technical measures.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the standing ruling had denied him access to a court to challenge the EIA waiver. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the limitation pursued a legitimate aim, was foreseeable, and remained proportionate, having particular regard to the applicant’s own omissions and the courts’ consistent application of established case-law.

Disturbed, M.G. and M.C. stood to leave and exchanged heated words with J.C., criticising his humour as unfunny and xenophobic, while he mocked their age, possible retirement status, and understanding of freedom of expression. The incident lasted several minutes.

The applicant company, owner of the channel SIC Radical (known for irreverent youth-oriented programming), later licensed the show from producer C.F. under an agreement in which C.F. assumed responsibility for third-party image rights and warranted that all necessary authorisations had been obtained. The recording formed part of a six-episode documentary series, "The Humourist," about J.C.'s career.

From 29 January 2013, a promotional video aired repeatedly on SIC Radical for at least 45 days, featuring a brief extract of M.G. in close-up complaining that the audience was not laughing. Episode 1 (broadcast 12 times from 4 February 2013) included a short clip showing M.C.'s image and M.G.'s image and voice. Episode 4 (broadcast 13 times from 26 February 2013) featured a nearly three-minute extract reproducing both individuals' images and voices during the altercation. The material was also published on the channel's website and J.C.'s YouTube channel.

In June 2013 M.G. and M.C. requested removal of their images, citing humiliation after family, friends and clients viewed the footage; the company refused. They sued in 2014 for unauthorised use causing distress.

The Cascais Civil Court dismissed the claim in 2018, holding that the licensing assurances sufficed and no further steps were required of the applicant. The Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld this in 2019, finding tacit consent under data-protection law could be presumed from the recording notices, visible cameras and the claimants' attendance and conduct.

On 16 June 2020 the Supreme Court reversed, awarding €40,000 in damages (€15,000 moral, €25,000 punitive to deter) jointly and severally with C.F. (with indemnity reserved) and ordering deletion of all recordings containing the individuals' images or voices, including from the website and via third-party action on YouTube. It held that any tacit consent covered only the ordinary course of the live show, not subsequent editing, out-of-context use or promotional montage that highlighted a negative heated exchange, applied graphic/musical effects and portrayed the claimants in an embarrassing light capable of harming their honour, reputation and dignity. Express, unequivocal consent was required under Civil Code Article 79 (interpreted with Personal Data Protection Law Article 3(h)). The close-up reproduction of their words and voices, without public-interest justification, risked professional and personal prejudice; the company took no steps to mitigate.

The applicant's request for Constitutional Court review, arguing the interpretation of consent unconstitutionally impaired balancing with freedom of expression, was refused.

There was no public-interest element in depicting the private individuals; tacit consent was doubtful; the use was embarrassing and potentially prejudicial; the company failed to minimise effects; the quantum of damages was not excessive; and the injunction appropriately prevented further dissemination. The Saarivuoma Sami Village, a Swedish legal entity representing a traditional reindeer-herding community, alleged that Norwegian authorities violated its rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core complaint concerned the community’s inability to exercise established reindeer-grazing rights in two “contested areas” of Troms County, Norway, for roughly fifty years because of the application of Norwegian legislation that excluded those areas.

Cross-border Sami herding dates to the 1751 Lapp Codicil appended to the Sweden–Norway border treaty. Subsequent bilateral conventions (1883, 1919, 1949) regulated grazing periods and districts. The 1972 convention, implemented in Norway by the 1972 Reindeer Grazing Act, reduced Swedish Sami access in Troms County by approximately 70 percent. The applicant community received a designated (later slightly enlarged) summer-grazing zone. The convention expired in 2002; after a short extension it lapsed in 2005. Norway then enacted the Cross-Border Reindeer Husbandry Act, which unilaterally continued the 1972 spatial and temporal limits pending a new treaty that never materialised. Administrative regulations issued under the 2005 Act therefore still omitted the two contested areas.

The community maintained that it had acquired exclusive private-law grazing rights in those areas through immemorial use (consuetude). In 2018 it sued the Norwegian State and the State-owned landowner Statskog SF, seeking a declaration of those rights and compensation for lost grazing. Lower courts held that the 1972/2005 legislation exhaustively governed Swedish herding irrespective of any private-law title. The Supreme Court, in a 30 June 2021 judgment, declared the action against Statskog inadmissible. As against the State it found, by a 4–1 majority, that the community had in fact established historical-use rights. A further majority of three judges nevertheless refused compensation. They characterised the legislation as a public-law regulation of use rather than an expropriation, aimed at sustainable allocation of scarce summer pasture in the light of Swedish winter-pasture constraints. Pre-2005 restrictions flowed from an international convention; post-2005 restrictions merely prolonged that regime. Two dissenting judges considered the fifty-year exclusion expropriatory in effect and would have awarded damages.

Following the Supreme Court ruling the community was no longer barred from the contested areas. Before the European Court it argued that the decades-long legislative exclusion itself constituted an unlawful, disproportionate interference with its possessions and that the denial of compensation rendered the interference still more severe. The Court ultimately held that the interference had been “in accordance with the law,” pursued a legitimate public-interest aim (balanced, sustainable herding), and remained proportionate; the Supreme Court’s refusal of compensation did not alter that conclusion.

**Case of Saarivuoma Sami Village v. Norway (Application no. 2381/22, ECtHR, 3 March 2026)**

The Swedish Sami village Saarivuoma (the applicant community) alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 14 ECHR arising from Norwegian legislation that prevented it from exercising claimed reindeer grazing rights in two additional “contested areas” of Troms County, Norway, for about 50 years.

Cross-border Sami reindeer herding has long been regulated by the 1751 Lapp Codicil (addendum to the Sweden-Norway border treaty) and later bilateral conventions (1883, 1919, 1949). The 1972 convention, implemented in Norwegian law, reduced Swedish Sami grazing areas in Troms by some 70% (while Swedish authorities viewed remaining areas as sufficient). The applicant community received a designated area, later expanded in 1985. After the 1972 convention expired without replacement (post-2005, following failed negotiations), Norway unilaterally continued the prior rules via the revised Cross-Border Reindeer Husbandry Act and accompanying regulations. These defined the applicant’s permitted grazing areas/periods but excluded the contested areas.

The applicant maintained exclusive private-law rights (based on consuetude/immemorial use) in the contested areas, independent of the public-law legislation. In 2018 it sued the Norwegian Government and Statskog SF (state-owned owner of the land) in Senja District Court for a declaration of those rights plus compensation for members’ losses from denied access. Lower courts (District Court 2018; Hålogaland High Court 2020) held that the Act exhaustively regulated Swedish grazing in Norway irrespective of any private-law rights.

The Supreme Court (30 June 2021) declared the claim against Statskog inadmissible (as the dispute was public-law in nature). Against the Government, a majority preliminarily found that the applicant had established private-law herding rights (including summer grazing) in the contested areas via historical use. It held that the Act did not preclude their exercise, though judges split on the legal basis: two inferred a narrow exception in the preparatory works for court-established private rights; two others held the legislation was never intended to override unacknowledged rights. A 3-2 majority refused compensation. The reporting judge distinguished the 1972–2005 period (based on a bilateral convention, so any shortfall was primarily a Swedish matter) from the post-2005 continuation of the same limits (aimed at sustainable use of scarce resources, matching summer access in Norway to winter pasture available in Sweden). The restriction was not an expropriation but a regulation of use; under Norwegian law, compensation for such interference arises only if it is significant and, overall, unreasonable to accept. Two judges dissenting on compensation analogised the 50-year exclusion (with risks of fees, fines or forced removal if rights were exercised) to expropriation, finding it unreasonable to bear without compensation.

Following the judgment, the applicant community was no longer barred from the contested areas. The ECtHR later held the interference lawful, in the public interest and proportionate, with the refusal of compensation not rendering it disproportionate.

The case of Saarivuoma Sami Village v. Norway (no. 2381/22) concerns a Swedish Sami community's inability to exercise claimed reindeer grazing rights in additional “contested areas” of Norway for about 50 years. This resulted from Norwegian authorities applying the 1972 Act (later the 2005 Cross-Border Reindeer Husbandry Act), which designated only limited grazing zones based on bilateral conventions rather than the applicant’s asserted private-law rights from historical/immemorial use. The community alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property) and Article 14 (discrimination).

Cross-border Sami herding dates to the 1751 Lapp Codicil. Later conventions (1883, 1919, 1949, 1972) regulated times and areas; the 1972 convention cut Swedish Sami access in Troms County by ~70% to balance scarce pastures. Norway implemented this via the 1972 Act (expanded 1985). After the convention lapsed in 2005 without a successor, the 2005 Act unilaterally continued the prior rules, defining zones by regulation. The applicant received one designated area but claimed extra private-law rights in the contested lands owned by state enterprise Statskog SF.

In 2018 the community sued the Government and Statskog for a declaration of exclusive rights and compensation for exclusion losses. Lower courts rejected the claims, holding the public-law Act exhaustively governed locations regardless of private rights.

The Supreme Court (30 June 2021) dismissed the case against Statskog (no public authority; rights uncontested). Against the Government it held the Act did not preclude exercise of any established private-law rights. A 4-judge majority preliminarily found the community had acquired herding rights (including summer grazing) via consuetude. Two judges inferred a special preparatory-work exception allowing court-established private rights to override the Act; two others held the legislation never intended to suspend rights pending judicial confirmation. Compensation was refused by majority: the reporting judge treated the measures as a non-expropriatory restriction (not “significant” or unreasonable overall). The 1972–2005 period rested on a bilateral convention (responsibility lying more with Sweden); post-2005 merely continued sustainability-oriented limits matching Swedish winter pasture capacity. Regulation of rights remained possible on other legal bases. Two judges would have awarded compensation, viewing the 50-year exclusion (with penalty risks) as expropriation-like and unreasonable.

Thereafter the community could access the contested areas. The ECtHR characterised the long exclusion as control of the use of property. It held the interference lawful (pursuant to the Act), in the public interest (sustainable herding and intra-industry balance), and proportionate. The Supreme Court’s denial of compensation, given the conventions’ history, regulatory aims and eventual recognition of the rights, did not render it disproportionate. No violation was found.

The first applicant was refused a permit and a five-year re-entry ban was imposed. The case of V.N. and Others v. Sweden concerns four Azerbaijani nationals who arrived in Sweden on 21 May 2013 and sought asylum. The third applicant (then aged 7) required a pacemaker replacement for a heart condition, which was performed in Sweden in October 2013. Their claims were rejected in June 2014 (upheld on appeal), with deportation ordered to Azerbaijan on the basis that equivalent medical care was available there and family ties were stronger in their country of origin. The family absconded. The first applicant (the husband) returned to Azerbaijan around 2016 before later re-entering Sweden.

The original deportation orders became statute-barred on 1 April 2019. The family reapplied for asylum. In early 2020 the second applicant (the wife) was diagnosed with cervical cancer. On 17 December 2021 the Migration Agency granted the wife, daughter and son temporary residence permits (later extended to January 2025). A MedCOI report confirmed that the wife’s required treatment (Bevacizumab/Avastin) was unavailable in Azerbaijan. The Agency also found that removing the daughter or son would disproportionately interfere with their Article 8 family-life rights given the daughter’s medical needs, the son’s formative years spent in Sweden, and mutual family dependence.

During four interviews he had given a coherent, detailed account (including personal thoughts and emotions) of participating in serious non-political crimes—torture, kidnapping, extortion, bodily harm and threats—while employed by a security company in Azerbaijan (2010–2013). Deportation, accompanied by a five-year re-entry ban, was not considered a disproportionate interference with Article 8. Appeals failed.
