**Case summary (approx. 500 words):** Nederlandse Omroep Stichting and Others v. the Netherlands (ECHR, 21 April 2026) concerns a complaint under Article 10 ECHR by two Dutch broadcasting organisations and a national newspaper (the applicants, acting as journalists) over the partial refusal to disclose State-held documents on the Dutch government’s political and administrative handling of the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 on 17 July 2014. The crash killed all 298 aboard, including 196 Dutch nationals. The Netherlands coordinated recovery/repatriation and co-established a Joint Investigation Team. The national crisis structure activated the Ministerial Crisis Management Committee (MCCb, a Cabinet sub-committee of relevant ministers, chaired by the Prime Minister) and the Interministerial Crisis Management Committee (ICCb, senior officials), which formed the core of the response. Cabinet rules imposed confidentiality on their deliberations to protect policy coherence and free discussion.

In October–November 2014 the applicants requested, under the Transparency of Public Administration Act (Wob) and Article 10, all MCCb/ICCb documents (including minutes) on the handling of MH17. The Minister of Security and Justice identified 255 documents. Initial February 2015 decisions refused 79 entirely and disclosed the rest fully or with redactions, citing Wob grounds: “disproportionate disadvantage” (s. 10(2)(g)) to protect uninhibited MCCb/ICCb deliberations and future decision-making (especially for minutes); “personal opinions on policy” in internal-consultation documents (s. 11(1)), to allow candid advice without fear of publicity (factual data being inseparable); “relations with other States or international organisations” (s. 10(2)(a)), given ongoing joint investigations requiring confidential information-sharing; “respect for personal privacy” (s. 10(2)(e)), redacting names/contact details of non-public-facing officials and private individuals (public-position names left unredacted); and security of personnel in the disaster zone (again s. 10(2)(g)). A list of titles, dates and grounds was provided. The Minister later emphasised that the Wob treats the public-interest-in-disclosure as a self-standing interest, independent of the applicants’ journalist status or the disaster’s societal impact.

Objections were rejected (August 2015) with expanded reasoning. Appeals followed. The Regional Court inspected unredacted documents (with applicants’ consent). Interlocutory judgments (June 2016) found some refusals inadequately reasoned (no section-by-section analysis) and ordered a new decision; they held Wob restrictions compatible with Article 10 § 2 but that journalist “watchdog” status and MH17’s impact could not alter the Wob balancing. The Minister’s August 2016 additional decisions disclosed more (70 documents fully, 147 partially; 38, including all 33 MCCb minutes, withheld). Remaining ICCb redactions invoked the same grounds plus limited “State security” (s. 10(1)(b)) concerning security-service methods. Regional Court judgments (February 2017) still found defects regarding MCCb minutes and certain ICCb passages and ordered their disclosure, upholding the rest.

On further appeal the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State (October 2017), also inspecting unredacted material, reversed the order to disclose MCCb minutes. It held disclosure would jeopardise the MCCb’s (and Cabinet’s) effective functioning, free ministerial discussion, constitutional policy-coherence duty and confidentiality rules; ministers would become more reserved. Personal data could not be replaced by job titles without risking identifiability. On Article 10 it held that Wob grounds generally satisfy Article 10 § 2; applicants must show “very special circumstances” of unjustified interference, which they had not (mere journalist status and high public interest being already weighed in the Wob; substantial information already released via disclosed documents, parliamentary briefings, press conferences and a University of Twente evaluation that had confidential researcher access). The applicants’ appeal failed; the Minister’s succeeded on the MCCb minutes. No further appeal lay. Later, more ICCb passages were released, parliamentary updates continued, and MH17 documents were archived for future accountability.

The applicants alleged an unjustified interference with their Article 10 right to receive/impart information of public interest that was ready and available, for journalistic purposes. A considerable portion of the requested material was ultimately disclosed during domestic proceedings.

**Case Summary: Nederlandse Omroep Stichting and Others v. the Netherlands (App. no. 20066/18, ECtHR Fourth Section, 21 April 2026)**

This case concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 ECHR (freedom of expression, including the right to receive and impart information) arising from the Dutch authorities’ partial refusal to disclose government documents on the political and administrative handling of the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17.

On 17 July 2014, MH17 was shot down over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 people aboard, including 196 Dutch nationals. The Netherlands coordinated recovery efforts and formed a joint investigation team with other states. It activated its national crisis structure, including the Ministerial Crisis Management Committee (MCCb, a Cabinet subcommittee of relevant ministers chaired by the Prime Minister) and the Interministerial Crisis Management Committee (ICCb, of senior officials). These bodies coordinated the response; MCCb decisions required Cabinet approval except in urgency, and a duty of confidentiality applied to Cabinet and committee discussions.

In October–November 2014, the applicants (two Dutch broadcasting organisations and a national newspaper), acting as journalists, requested under the Transparency of Public Administration Act (Wob) and Article 10 all MCCb and ICCb documents relating to the handling of the disaster, including meeting minutes. The Wob established a presumption of disclosure in the public interest unless specific grounds applied, without requiring the requester to show a personal interest and treating all requesters equally (no special regime for journalists).

In February 2015 the Minister of Security and Justice identified 255 documents. He refused 79 entirely and disclosed the rest fully or with redactions, providing a list of titles, dates and grounds. Refusals of MCCb/ICCb minutes (74 documents) and other passages relied on: (i) “disproportionate disadvantage” (Wob s. 10(2)(g)), as disclosure would inhibit free deliberation essential to the committees’ functioning; (ii) “personal opinions on policy in documents for internal consultation” (s. 11(1)), to protect candid exchanges among officials and ministers (factual content was deemed inseparable); (iii) harm to relations with other states/international organisations (s. 10(2)(a)), given the need for confidential cooperation in the ongoing investigation; (iv) respect for personal privacy (s. 10(2)(e)), redacting names/contact details of non-public officials (public-position names were unredacted); and (v) security of Dutch personnel (again s. 10(2)(g)).

The Minister maintained the decisions on objection (August 2015), emphasising that the Wob treated the public-interest disclosure interest as independent of subject-matter (even given MH17’s societal impact) and that redaction of names in minutes (small committees) would still allow identification.

The applicants appealed. The Regional Court, after reviewing unredacted documents with consent, held in interlocutory judgments (June 2016) that Wob restrictions complied with Article 10 § 2 but that journalist status and MH17’s impact were irrelevant under the Wob. It found the blanket refusals of minutes and certain documents inadequately reasoned (no section-by-section assessment) and ordered a new decision.

**Case of Nederlandse Omroep Stichting and Others v. the Netherlands (App. no. 20066/18), ECtHR Fourth Section, 21 April 2026**

Two Dutch broadcasting organisations and a national newspaper (“the applicants”) alleged that the partial refusal of their 2014 request for State-held documents on the political and administrative handling of the MH17 disaster violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom to receive and impart information). They acted as journalists seeking information of public interest that was ready and available.

On 17 July 2014, Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 was downed over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 aboard (196 Dutch nationals). The Netherlands coordinated recovery and repatriation and, with other States, formed a Joint Investigation Team. It activated its national crisis structure, centred on the Ministerial Crisis Management Committee (MCCb, comprising relevant ministers, chaired by the Prime Minister) and the Interministerial Crisis Management Committee (ICCb, comprising senior officials). These bodies coordinated the response; MCCb minutes formed part of Cabinet decision-making, subject to confidentiality rules and the constitutional duty to promote policy coherence.

In October–November 2014 the applicants requested, under the Transparency of Public Administration Act (Wob) and Article 10, all MCCb and ICCb documents (including minutes) on the handling of the disaster. Of 255 identified documents, the Minister of Security and Justice initially refused 79 outright (or disclosed them only with redactions). Grounds included: “disproportionate disadvantage” (uninhibited deliberation and decision-making in the committees would be hindered, especially given ongoing aftermath and investigations); “personal opinions on policy” in internal-consultation documents (to protect candour); harm to relations with other States/international organisations (confidential exchanges needed for the joint investigation); respect for personal privacy (names/contact details of non-public-facing officials); and (later) State security (methods/knowledge of security services and personnel protection in the disaster zone). A list of titles, dates and grounds was provided. The Minister maintained that the protected interests outweighed the public interest in disclosure; the Wob treated that public interest as self-standing and independent of the subject-matter or the applicants’ journalistic status.

After objections (March 2015) the Minister upheld the refusals with fuller reasoning. Appeals followed. The Regional Court (interlocutory judgments, June 2016; final judgments, February 2017), after inspecting unredacted documents, found some refusals inadequately reasoned (especially full non-disclosure of MCCb minutes and certain ICCb passages) and ordered a section-by-section reassessment. An additional Ministerial decision (August 2016) disclosed far more material (70 documents in full, 147 with redactions); 38 documents (including all 33 MCCb minute-sets) remained undisclosed. The Regional Court still found remaining defects and ordered disclosure of the MCCb minutes and certain ICCb passages.

On further appeal the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State (October 2017), also inspecting the unredacted files, allowed the Minister’s appeal on the MCCb minutes. It held that mandatory disclosure would jeopardise the MCCb’s effective functioning and Cabinet confidentiality, causing ministers to become more reserved; the Minister had been entitled to give priority to preventing disproportionate disadvantage. Names could not be replaced by job titles without risk of identification. On Article 10, Wob grounds generally constituted necessary restrictions under Article 10 § 2 unless “very special circumstances” were shown; the applicants had not demonstrated such circumstances. Substantial information had already been disclosed (including via parliamentary briefings, press conferences and a 2015 University of Twente evaluation report prepared with confidential researcher access). The applicants’ status as journalists and the public importance of MH17 did not alter the balance already struck under the Wob. Remaining aspects of the Regional Court’s judgments were upheld. No further appeal lay.

Subsequent public and parliamentary disclosures continued, and MH17-related documents were retained for eventual National Archives transfer. The ECtHR later found the interference “necessary in a democratic society” in pursuit of several legitimate aims, after effective domestic review in adversarial proceedings that yielded considerable additional disclosure; the authorities had remained within their margin of appreciation.

001-249694:
The case of E.H. v. Germany (Application no. 25914/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the fairness of criminal proceedings against a 15-year-old under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant was convicted of aggravated murder of a 14-year-old schoolmate on 7 March 2018. Four days later, police arrived at his home (where his mother held sole custody). Officers separately informed the applicant of his rights to remain silent, consult defence counsel and have his mother present during questioning; he signed a written form. His mother was informed of the suspicion, a search warrant and her right to refuse testimony.

While this occurred, officers asked the applicant about the murder weapon. His mother then confronted him in an officer’s presence; he did not reply. After she left, he disclosed the locations of incriminating items (including the weapon), indicated willingness to make a statement but not in her presence, and began crying. Officers told his mother of his wishes and that she could still attend; she respected them. As he was removed, she shouted that if he had done it he should say so. They travelled separately to the station, where the applicant was observed shaking. His mother entered the interrogation room and confirmed he wished to be questioned alone (citing embarrassment); she then waited outside.

Before a three-hour interview, the applicant (then using an adult-form notice) was again informed of his rights, including that he could request his mother or a lawyer at any time. He confirmed understanding and confessed. A brief post-interview conversation with his mother occurred in an officer’s presence before he was detained.

At trial before the Berlin Regional Court’s Juvenile Division, defence counsel moved to exclude the confession. They argued that German law (Juvenile Courts Act s. 67, police regulations and some lower-court practice) implied a right to prior confidential parental consultation equivalent to the right to counsel. Without private discussion, the 15-year-old could not validly waive rights or decide to confess given his vulnerability. The court rejected the motion, finding comprehensive, age-appropriate information had been given, the mother’s rights had been respected, and any consultation right was not statutory or equivalent to core defence rights. The mother had had (non-private) opportunities to speak. The applicant’s own decision governed. He later made a second, differing confession at trial (especially on premeditation and motive).

On 22 November 2018 the court convicted him, imposing a nine-year youth sentence. It relied in part on the first confession as more credible, treating the second as tactically evasive, particularly regarding aggravating intent and motive.

The Federal Court of Justice dismissed an appeal on points of law (13 August 2019), leaving open whether a private-consultation right existed but holding that any violation would not automatically exclude evidence. Balancing interests (including charge severity) showed no basis for exclusion: the mother had spoken to him, could have attended, and would likely not have advised differently. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit a constitutional complaint (18 November 2020).

The ECHR application alleged that the lack of confidential parental consultation before the first confession (and of information about it) rendered the trial unfair, as the conviction partially rested on that statement. The Court limited its examination to this complaint and found all reasonable steps had been taken to ensure the applicant understood his rights and the consequences of his choices.

**Case of E.H. v. Germany (App. no. 25914/21, ECtHR, 21 April 2026) concerns the fair-trial implications of using a 15-year-old’s police confession in his conviction for aggravated murder.**

The applicant, born in 2002, was suspected of knifing a 14-year-old schoolmate to death on 7 March 2018. On 11 March, six officers arrived at the Berlin home of his mother (who had sole custody). Officers went to his room while another took his mother to the kitchen. He was told of his rights to silence, to consult a lawyer and to have his mother present, and signed a written form. His mother was separately informed of the murder suspicion, a search warrant and her right to refuse testimony.

While she was still being informed, officers asked him about the weapon. Shocked, she entered his room, confronted him in an officer’s presence and received no reply. After she left, he indicated the location of a backpack, clothes and the weapon, said he would speak but not with her present, and began crying. She was told of his wish and that she could still attend; she chose to respect it. As he was led away she shouted that if he had done it he should say so, as the victim’s mother deserved to know. They travelled separately; he shook throughout.

At the station she entered the interrogation room and asked whether he really wanted to be alone; he said yes because it was “too embarrassing.” She left. He was again informed of his rights (using an adult-standard form plus verbal explanation that he could change his mind about her presence at any time). He confirmed understanding and, over about three hours, confessed. Afterwards they had only a brief, officer-supervised conversation before he was detained.

Trial began in the Juvenile Division of the Berlin Regional Court on 25 September 2018. On day three counsel moved to exclude the confession, arguing that German law (Juvenile Courts Act s. 67, police regulation 382) and the minor’s vulnerability required a private parental consultation (analogous to the right to counsel) before any waiver or statement, and that neither he nor his mother had been informed of or given such an opportunity. On day six, after hearing officers, the court refused exclusion: he had been informed of silence, counsel and parental presence in an age-appropriate way; his mother had been informed of her rights; any “right to parental consultation” was not statutory and, even if it existed, she had spoken to him at the flat and station; the decision to speak was his own. He later made a second, partly inconsistent confession in court.

On 22 November 2018 the court convicted him of aggravated murder and imposed nine years’ youth imprisonment, relying especially on the first confession for premeditation and motive (treating the second as tactical). The Federal Court of Justice (13 August 2019) rejected his appeal on points of law, leaving open whether a consultation right existed but holding that any breach would not automatically exclude evidence; his mother had been able to speak to him, could have attended, and would not have advised differently. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to hear his complaint (18 November 2020).

Before the ECtHR the applicant complained solely under Article 6 § 1 that the use of the confession, obtained without prior confidential parental consultation or information about that possibility, violated his right to a fair hearing. The Court recorded that all reasonable steps had been taken to ensure he was fully aware of his defence rights and could appreciate the consequences of his conduct.

The case of Lárus Welding v. Iceland (Application no. 24999/21) before the ECHR concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to an independent tribunal) arising from the appointment and participation of an expert lay judge in the applicant’s criminal trial for fraud by abuse of position.

The applicant, born in 1976 and resident in Reykjavík, was committed for trial on 10 February 2014 before the Reykjavík District Court together with two co-defendants. The three-judge panel comprised professional judges S.S. (presiding) and S.H., plus expert lay judge H.S.B. (chair of undergraduate business studies at Reykjavík University), whom S.S. summoned. The District Court convicted the defendants on 21 December 2015. The Supreme Court quashed the conviction on 1 June 2017 owing to circumstances capable of casting doubt on S.H.’s impartiality and remitted the case.

For the retrial, S.S. again summoned H.S.B. The applicant sought recusal, arguing that the statutory framework and practical implementation of expert lay judges’ selection, appointment and status created legitimate doubts as to the bench’s independence. He later added that ad hoc appointments were professionally and financially appealing, generating incentives to please the presiding judge (who also set remuneration), and that H.S.B. had previously sat with S.S. in the original trial and another trial resulting in the applicant’s conviction, suggesting she had been chosen because of those earlier outcomes.

The District Court rejected recusal on 20 October 2017, finding sufficient safeguards: expert lay judges participated fully in hearings and judgment drafting, enjoyed identical rights and obligations to professional judges, and were bound by the constitutional duty to adjudicate solely according to law. The Supreme Court upheld this on 2 November 2017, reiterating that expert lay judges possessed the same adjudicative authority and that impartiality challenges remained available. The District Court reconvicted the applicant on 21 December 2017. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 26 June 2020; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 26 November 2020.

At the material time the Criminal Procedure Act permitted summoning of one or two expert lay judges (eligible by age, citizenship, health, financial competence and absence of disqualifying convictions) when specialist knowledge was required. They took a sworn declaration of conscientious and impartial performance, sat from the start of the main hearing (parties being notified in advance), and enjoyed equal rights and obligations except that the presiding judge directed proceedings and ruled on most procedural matters. Fees were fixed by the presiding judge. Recusal rules applied equally to professional and expert lay judges and were appealable.

Subsequent 2016–2018 reforms (not applicable to the trial) transferred rostering and designation of expert lay judges to an independent Court Administration following GRECO recommendations that the earlier system afforded insufficient guarantees of independence because of the appointing judge’s wide discretion.

The ECHR held that the appointment and participation of the expert lay judge disclosed no deficiencies of such nature or degree as to undermine the tribunal’s independence or its appearance of independence.

**CASE OF LÁRUS WELDING v. ICELAND (Application no. 24999/21)**

The European Court of Human Rights examined an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to an independent tribunal in criminal proceedings) arising from the appointment and participation of an expert lay judge in the applicant’s fraud trial. The applicant, Lárus Welding (born 1976, resident in Reykjavík), was committed for trial on 10 February 2014 at the Reykjavík District Court together with two co-defendants on charges of fraud by abuse of position.

The original panel comprised two professional judges (S.S. as presiding judge and S.H.) and one expert lay judge, H.S.B. (chair of the undergraduate business studies department at Reykjavík University), whom S.S. summoned. The District Court convicted the defendants on 21 December 2015. On 1 June 2017 the Supreme Court quashed the conviction and remitted the case because of circumstances capable of casting doubt on Judge S.H.’s impartiality.

For the retrial, S.S. again summoned H.S.B. The applicant requested recusal, arguing that the statutory framework and its practical implementation for selecting, appointing and regulating expert lay judges created legitimate doubts as to the bench’s independence. He later added that ad hoc appointments were professionally and financially appealing, generating incentives to please the summoning presiding judge; that expert lay judges depended on that judge for remuneration; and that H.S.B. had previously sat with S.S. in the first trial and in another set of proceedings that had also resulted in the applicant’s conviction, giving the appearance of selection based on prior outcomes favourable to conviction.

On 20 October 2017 the District Court rejected the recusal request, holding that the system contained sufficient safeguards. Expert lay judges participated in the hearing and judgment drafting, enjoyed the same rights and bore the same obligations as professional judges, and were bound by the constitutional duty to adjudicate solely according to law. The Supreme Court upheld this ruling on 2 November 2017, adding that expert lay judges possessed the same adjudicatory authority and that their impartiality could be challenged on appeal.

The District Court convicted the defendants again on 21 December 2017. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 26 June 2020; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 26 November 2020.

At the material time the Criminal Procedure Act allowed an expert lay judge (or two) to sit with professional judges where specialist knowledge was needed. Eligibility required Icelandic citizenship, age 25 or over, financial competence and legal capacity, together with absence of convictions or conduct undermining public trust. Parties were to be informed in advance so they could object. On first service the expert signed a sworn declaration of conscientious, impartial performance according to law. They enjoyed the same rights and obligations as professional judges in the hearing and judgment, although the presiding judge directed proceedings and ruled alone on most procedural matters. Fees were set by the presiding judge. Recusal rules (including circumstances capable of raising justifiable doubts as to impartiality) applied equally; the presiding judge assessed an expert’s competence, and recusal rulings were appealable.

GRECO had earlier criticised the arrangement for conferring wide discretion on the appointing judge and for lacking administrative scrutiny, recommending reforms to guarantee independence, impartiality and transparency. Subsequent legislation (Act on the Judiciary 2016 and related amendments, in force from 1 January 2018) introduced a Court Administration roster, public advertisement or judicial recommendation, fixed terms, and rules on competence and remuneration; those changes did not apply to the applicant’s trial.

The Court concluded that the appointment and participation of the expert lay judge did not disclose deficiencies of such a nature or degree as to be capable of undermining the tribunal’s independence or its appearance of independence.

On 2 November 2017, the Supreme Court upheld the District Court’s decision, emphasizing that expert lay judges have the same authority as professional judges and that their impartiality could be challenged on appeal.

The District Court again convicted the defendants on 21 December 2017. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 26 June 2020, and the applicant’s request for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was rejected on 26 November 2020. The application to the European Court of Human Rights was lodged on 10 May 2021.

At the material time, the Criminal Procedure Act no. 88/2008 allowed expert lay judges to be summoned where specialist knowledge was needed. Eligibility required sufficient maturity, health, Icelandic citizenship, age of at least 25, financial competence, and legal capacity, with exclusions for certain convictions. They took their seats by the start of the main hearing after parties were informed, signed a sworn declaration of conscientious and impartial performance, enjoyed the same rights and obligations as professional judges (except that the presiding judge directed proceedings and ruled alone on most procedural matters), and had their fees determined by the presiding judge. Recusal rules applied equally to professional and expert lay judges, with decisions appealable to the Supreme Court.

Subsequent legislative amendments (Act on the Judiciary no. 50/2016, entering into force on 1 January 2018) transferred designation of expert lay judges for five-year terms to the Court Administration from a roster, following public advertisement or judges’ recommendations, with verification of competence. These changes, which did not apply to the applicant’s trial, responded to GRECO’s 2013 recommendation that the prior wide discretion of the appointing judge and lack of administrative scrutiny failed to provide sufficient guarantees of independence, impartiality, and transparency.

The European Court of Human Rights ultimately held that the appointment and participation of the expert lay judge did not disclose deficiencies of such a nature or degree as to undermine the tribunal’s independence or its appearance of independence.

The case of Y v. Serbia (ECtHR, Application no. 28322/20) concerns the complete severance of contact between the applicant (born 2007) and her younger half-brother X (born February 2014) following X’s intercountry adoption. In 2015 the children’s biological parents, unable to provide adequate care, requested that the Social Care Centre place the four siblings in foster care; staff found serious neglect. The applicant and X were placed together with foster carer Ms L. (who was later appointed their legal guardian), while the other two siblings went to another local family. Weekly sibling contact was maintained. In May 2016 the parents were stripped of parental rights after making no effort to stay in touch, rendering all four children adoptable.

The Centre concluded that long-term adoption was in the children’s best interests and first sought a single family for all four siblings or, failing that, for the applicant and X together. When no suitable domestic adopters were found, an international search began in 2017. A foreign couple expressed interest in both children. Upon turning ten the applicant acquired the statutory right to consent to her own adoption and twice (November–December 2017) refused, stating she wished to remain with Ms L. even if her siblings were adopted. Ms L. then withdrew her earlier consent to X’s adoption. The Centre immediately removed Ms L. as X’s guardian, appointed one of its own lawyers, and proceeded. Expert reports (paediatric, psychological, social-work and ministerial) assessed X as suitable for adoption and the foreign couple as capable of meeting his needs. A short period of introductory contact and adjustment in February 2018 was described as successful. On 14 February 2018 the Ministry authorised the adoption; the Centre confirmed it a week later. Neither decision mentioned any future contact between X and the applicant. Contact ceased immediately and has never resumed.

The applicant was taken to a psychologist shortly afterwards; after an initial period of distress her condition improved. Ms L. subsequently initiated multiple domestic proceedings—seeking reopening of the adoption, its annulment on the ground that it had permanently severed sibling ties, and restoration of contact—none of which succeeded. She was temporarily stripped of guardianship over the applicant (later reinstated by the Constitutional Court) and ultimately lost her status as foster carer. The applicant, upon reaching majority in 2025, confirmed she wished to pursue the application.

These facts form the basis of the alleged Article 8 violation: the authorities’ failure to discharge their positive obligation to respect the applicant’s family life with her half-brother by permitting (and later refusing to restore) any post-adoption contact, despite the siblings’ prior close relationship and the applicant’s repeated opposition to a placement that would end it. The domestic decisions treated the applicant’s refusal as incapable of outweighing X’s long-term interest in a stable adoptive family abroad and gave decisive weight to the adoptive family’s interest in building an undisturbed family life.

Serbia (Application no. 28322/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns alleged violations of the applicant’s right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention (as well as related complaints under Articles 6 and 13). No suitable Serbian adopters were found. In September 2017 (the month the applicant turned ten and acquired the statutory right to consent or refuse adoption) a foreign couple expressed interest in adopting both children. The applicant repeatedly and expressly refused adoption, stating she wished to remain with Ms L even if her siblings were adopted. Ms L, who had initially consented to X’s adoption, then withdrew that consent.

The Centre immediately relieved Ms L of guardianship over X (while she remained his foster carer) and appointed one of its own lawyers as X’s guardian, reasoning that Ms L’s opposition failed to recognise that a permanent adoptive family was in X’s best interests. Subsequent expert reports (January–February 2018) from the Centre, a multidisciplinary team and the Ministry of Labour confirmed that the foreign couple had been properly assessed as suitable, that contact and an adjustment period had gone well, and that international adoption was in X’s best interests given the absence of domestic options. The Ministry and Centre issued the adoption decisions in mid-February 2018. Neither decision mentioned or provided for any post-adoption contact between X and the applicant (or any other biological relatives). Contact between the siblings ceased immediately and has never resumed.

Ms L, acting first as guardian and later in her personal capacity, launched a series of domestic challenges: a request to re-open the adoption procedure (dismissed), an action to annul the adoption on the ground that it had not been in X’s best interests because it severed sibling ties (dismissed for lack of standing after Ms L was temporarily stripped of guardianship over the applicant), and multiple appeals and constitutional complaints. Those proceedings produced mixed procedural outcomes (including later restoration of Ms L’s guardianship by the Constitutional Court) but never resulted in restoration of contact or annulment of the adoption. After X’s adoption the receiving-State authorities informed Ms L that the adoptive parents spoke regularly with X about his origins but that he was not yet ready for contact; they left open the possibility of future contact if he wished it.

The applicant, who turned 18 in 2025, confirmed she wished to pursue the Strasbourg application and approved all steps taken by Ms L. These facts form the basis of the complaint that the Serbian authorities failed in their positive obligation to protect the applicant’s family life by allowing the total rupture of sibling ties without adequate consideration of her interests or any mechanism for future contact.

The case of Y v. Serbia (Application no. 28322/20) concerns the applicant (born 2007), a Serbian national, and her complaint under Article 8 of the Convention regarding the complete severance of contact with her maternal half-brother X (born February 2014) following his intercountry adoption. Complaints under Articles 6 and 13 were also communicated, relating to the fairness of domestic proceedings and the availability of effective remedies.

In 2015 the applicant’s parents requested that their four children be placed in foster care owing to their inability to provide adequate care; the children were found to have been seriously neglected. The applicant and X were placed with foster carer Ms L (who lived with her parents and brother), while the two other siblings were placed with another local family. The children maintained weekly contact. Ms L was appointed legal guardian of the applicant and X in May 2015. The biological parents, having made no effort to maintain contact, were deprived of parental rights in respect of all four children on 16 May 2016, rendering the children eligible for adoption.

The Social Care Centre assessed that long-term adoption was in the children’s best interests and sought a family willing to adopt all four siblings or, failing that, both the applicant and X. After unsuccessful domestic searches, an international search began in September 2017. A foreign couple expressed interest in adopting both children. Upon turning ten, the applicant acquired the right to consent to her own adoption; she refused (orally and in writing in November–December 2017), stating she wished to remain with Ms L even if her siblings were adopted. Ms L, who had initially consented to X’s adoption, then withdrew that consent. On 14 December 2017 the Centre relieved Ms L of guardianship over X, finding that her opposition failed to recognise that a permanent family solution served X’s best interests, and appointed a Centre lawyer as his guardian (Ms L remaining his foster carer).

Positive assessments of the prospective adopters followed, as did a period of contact and adjustment in February 2018 that was reported as successful. On 13 February 2018 a Ministry expert team opined that adoption by the foreign couple was in X’s best interests (no Serbian adopters having been found) and noted that the couple would ensure sibling contact “in accordance with their means, needs and interests.” The Ministry authorised the adoption on 14 February 2018 and the Centre approved it on 21 February 2018; neither decision referred to post-adoption contact. Contact between the applicant and X ceased immediately. In March 2020 the Centre relieved Ms L of guardianship over the applicant, citing her attempts to obstruct the adoption, her involvement of the applicant in litigation, the fostering of false hope that X would be “returned,” and her obstruction of unsupervised interviews with the applicant. The applicant remained in Ms L’s foster care under the Centre’s direct guardianship. Subsequent appeals, stay applications and constitutional complaints followed. A guardian ad litem later declined to support the annulment claim, which was declared inadmissible for lack of standing. In September 2023 the Constitutional Court quashed the decisions removing Ms L’s guardianship over the applicant, holding that her litigation and contact efforts did not constitute abuse. Further applications to reopen the annulment proceedings were dismissed. In 2024 Ms L’s foster-carer status was terminated after an expert assessment found her controlling, uncooperative and lacking necessary skills; that decision was upheld. The applicant attained majority in September 2025, confirmed her wish to pursue the application, and Ms L’s remaining guardianship ended.

After the adoption, Ms L contacted Serbian and foreign authorities and the adoptive parents seeking sibling contact. In December 2021 the receiving-state authorities reported that the adoptive parents regularly discussed X’s origins with him but that he was not yet ready for contact, though this might change as he matured.

The case of Stanković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 11103/23) concerns allegations of discrimination in access to salary compensation during temporary incapacity to work. The applicant, Dragana Stanković (born 1986), is a self-employed lawyer living in Banja Luka. She was affiliated to the compulsory health insurance scheme of the Republika Srpska Health Insurance Fund, governed by the Health Insurance Act 1999 and the Contributions Act 2017.

On 16 August 2019, while on pregnancy-related sick leave, she requested BAM 1,401.18 (approximately EUR 717) in salary compensation for the period from 1 May to 4 July 2019. The Fund rejected the request on 18 September 2019, holding that only “insured employees” (those working under an employment contract) were entitled to such compensation under section 31 of the Health Insurance Act. A second-instance administrative body upheld this decision on 2 December 2019. In judicial review proceedings, the Banja Luka District Court confirmed the refusal on 10 November 2020.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional appeal on 8 January 2021, claiming violations of Articles 13 and 14 of the Convention, Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, and provisions of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (particularly Article 10 on family protection). On 18 October 2022 (served 31 October 2022), the Constitutional Court rejected the discrimination claim. It found that self-employed insured persons were not in a relatively similar situation to employees because the two groups had different rights and obligations. Although the health-insurance contribution rate was uniformly 10.2 percent, the contribution base differed: employees paid on their total taxable income, while self-employed persons paid on a minimum amount equal to the average gross salary in Republika Srpska for the preceding year (BAM 1,358 or approximately EUR 700 in 2018). Given this distinction and the wide margin of appreciation in social-security matters, the Constitutional Court held there had been no discrimination and dismissed the remaining complaints as manifestly ill-founded.

Under the 1999 Health Insurance Act both employees and persons independently performing an economic or professional activity (including liberal professions) were compulsory insured persons entitled to healthcare. Section 4 listed compensation for salary during temporary incapacity as a statutory right, yet section 31 expressly reserved that benefit to insured employees. The first 30 days of compensation were paid by the employer; thereafter the Fund paid up to 12 months. Sections 32–35 set the calculation basis (net salary that would have been earned, capped at the contribution base), the replacement rate (70–90 percent), and the qualifying circumstances (illness, injury, medical examinations, isolation, family care, or organ donation). Self-employed persons were defined separately (sections 11–12) and received no equivalent cash benefit.

A new Health Insurance Act entered into force on 29 September 2022 and extended salary (or equivalent) compensation to both groups without distinction, treating all insured persons equally. The Contributions Act confirmed the differing contribution bases, while the Labour Act 2016 guaranteed employees a right to salary and compensation during absence.

The applicant alleged that the exclusion of self-employed persons from cash benefits available to employees during pregnancy-related incapacity constituted discrimination contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 and Article 14 taken together with Article 8. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately held that the applicant was not in a relatively similar situation to insured employees under the legal framework then in force and therefore found no violation.

Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 11103/23) concerns alleged discrimination against a self-employed lawyer in access to salary compensation during temporary incapacity to work. Both employees under contract and self-employed persons (including those in liberal professions) were covered as insured persons.

The Fund refused on 18 September 2019, citing section 31 of the 1999 Act, which granted the benefit solely to insured employees (in state or private enterprises and institutions). The first 30 days of compensation were payable by the employer, with the Fund covering thereafter (up to 12 months). The second-instance body upheld the refusal on 2 December 2019. The Banja Luka District Court confirmed it on 10 November 2020 in judicial review.

The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal on 8 January 2021, alleging violations of Articles 13 and 14 of the Convention, Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, and ICESCR provisions (notably Article 10 on family protection). On 18 October 2022 the Constitutional Court found no discrimination. It held that the applicant’s situation was not analogous to that of insured employees, given differing rights, obligations and contribution bases. The uniform 10.2% contribution rate applied to all, but employees’ contributions were calculated on total taxable income (paid by the employer), while self-employed persons paid their own contributions on a basis of at least the previous year’s average gross salary (BAM 1,358 or approximately EUR 700 for 2018). The Court invoked the wide margin of appreciation in social-security matters and rejected remaining complaints as manifestly ill-founded. The decision was served on 31 October 2022; the applicant applied to the Court on 28 February 2023.

Under the 1999 Act, compulsory insurance covered all citizens and conferred rights to healthcare, salary compensation during temporary incapacity (illness, injury, medical examinations, family care, isolation or organ donation) and other benefits. Section 31 nevertheless limited salary compensation to employees; calculation was based on the net salary the employee would have earned (capped at the contribution base), at 70–90% thereof. Self-employed persons were defined separately (craft workers, hospitality providers, etc.). The Labour Act 2016 separately entitled employees to salary and related compensation.

A replacement Health Insurance Act entered into force on 29 September 2022 and equalised treatment: both groups now receive compensation (from the 31st day of uninterrupted incapacity, up to 11 months). Calculation uses average gross salary over the preceding six months, at 70–100% according to the ground (100% for pregnancy complications or malignancy). For self-employed persons the payment is drawn from the contribution base, with 30% budget co-financing in pregnancy cases, provided contributions continue to be paid.

The alleged violations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 and Article 14 taken with Article 8 therefore turned on whether the 1999 framework discriminated against self-employed insured persons who, despite participating in the same compulsory scheme, were denied a cash benefit available to employees. The Court ultimately held that the two groups were not in a relevantly similar situation.

**CASE OF MILADZE v. GEORGIA (Application no. 41585/23)**

Irakli Miladze, a Tbilisi-based food courier and self-described civil activist, posted a public-mode TikTok video on 5 December 2022 criticising Tbilisi’s urban transport reforms. The reforms, announced in 2018 and accelerated in 2022, sought to reduce car dependency through bus lanes, pedestrian/cyclist infrastructure and new buses amid public debate over ineffective implementation, overcrowding and alleged misuse of bus lanes by government vehicles (informally called “Škoda-lanes”). Public surveys reflected dissatisfaction.

The short video, which quickly exceeded 100,000 views and 600 shares, featured extremely crude, sexually explicit and repetitive insults directed at the identifiable Tbilisi mayor, City Hall staff, Ministry of Interior officials, State Security Service personnel and patrol police. After a warning about obscene language, the applicant ranted about traffic chaos on Tchavtchavadze Avenue (reduced from three lanes), exemptions for officials in tinted-window vehicles, fines imposed on delivery riders like himself, and officials’ failure to use public transport. Translations capture the vulgar, aggressive tone, including repeated “go fuck your mothers,” “motherfuckers,” and references to the mayor and his “gang.” He framed the remarks as general criticism of policy and impunity, some in conditional/colloquial form.

On 10 December 2022, Tbilisi Police initiated administrative-offence proceedings under Article 166 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disorderly conduct: swearing/insulting in public places disturbing order/peace) and Article 173 § 1 (insulting a law-enforcement officer). TikTok was treated as a “public place.” A separate summons-service incident on 12 December (verbal insults and flight attempt during service of a summons, leading to arrest, detention until 14 December, and a later 2,000 GEL fine conviction under Article 173 § 1, upheld on appeal) was distinct.

In the TikTok video case, Tbilisi City Court (27 January–10 March 2023 hearings) convicted the applicant of both offences, imposing a 2,000 GEL fine (~EUR 720). It classified TikTok as a public forum (citing Supreme Court and appellate precedents), noting social media’s rapid reach (including to minors) and potential harm to dignity/reputation. Balancing Article 10 of the Convention and the Georgian Constitution, the court found the obscene language exceeded protected speech: it constituted wanton verbal aggression and denigration rather than political criticism, satire or contribution to debate, disturbing public order/peace. Article 173 § 1 applied as insults targeted identifiable officers due to their status.

On appeal (11 May 2023), Tbilisi Court of Appeal upheld the Article 166 § 1 conviction but dismissed Article 173 § 1 (insults were general, not directed at officers in the line of duty at the time). The fine was reduced to the minimum 500 GEL (~EUR 180). It confirmed TikTok as a public gathering place affecting order/peace, referenced the Freedom of Expression Act (obscene content lacking value may be regulated), distinguished ECHR cases (e.g., Peradze, Uj) where vulgarity served stylistic purposes, and emphasised viral impact, lack of contribution to debate, and prevention of normalising insults on youth-popular platforms. The sanction was proportionate; no video removal or account restrictions were sought. The applicant continued activism and criticism on social media.

The applicant alleged the conviction violated Article 10 (freedom of expression). Domestic courts conducted a structured balancing exercise finding the interference necessary in a democratic society. The ECHR (Fourth Section, 19 May 2026) later held the conviction and minimum fine proportionate given the crude, non-satirical denigration, medium’s amplification, and thorough domestic reasoning.

**Case of Miladze v. Georgia (ECtHR, App. no. 41585/23, 19 May 2026)** concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) arising from the applicant’s administrative conviction and fine for a public TikTok video containing crude, sexually explicit insults aimed at identifiable public officials.

Irakli Miladze (born 1993), a Tbilisi food courier and self-described civil activist active on social media, posted a short video on 5 December 2022 in unrestricted public mode. It rapidly went viral (over 100,000 views and 600 shares). The video, which opened with a warning about obscene language, criticised Tbilisi’s urban transport reform (initiated in 2018 and accelerated in 2022 to reduce car dependency via public transport, bus lanes and related measures). Public debate had highlighted perceived ineffectiveness, overcrowding and “Škoda-lanes” (alleged use of bus lanes by government/law-enforcement vehicles in white Škodas, contrary to traffic rules). In the video the applicant, speaking after a long snowy workday on his scooter, directed repeated vulgar insults (“go fuck your mothers,” “motherfuckers,” etc.) at the Tbilisi mayor, City Hall staff, Ministry of Interior/State Security Service personnel and patrol police. He accused them of creating chaotic streets (e.g., reducing Tchavtchavadze Avenue to one lane), hypocrisy (officials using bus lanes with tinted windows while fining delivery workers), and superiority, while urging they use crowded public transport themselves. The language was presented as an outburst rather than structured argument or satire.

On 10 December 2022 police opened administrative-offence proceedings under Article 166 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disorderly conduct: swearing/cursing in public places disturbing public order and peace) and Article 173 § 1 (insulting a law-enforcement officer in the line of duty), treating TikTok as a public place. A separate summons-service incident on 12 December led to additional Article 173 proceedings, arrest, brief detention, conviction and a GEL 2,000 fine (upheld on appeal); that conviction was not the focus of the Article 10 complaint.

In the TikTok video case, Tbilisi City Court convicted the applicant of both offences on 10 March 2023 and imposed a GEL 2,000 fine. It held social media (including TikTok) to be a public forum capable of affecting public order, citing Supreme Court and appellate precedents; the obscene language exceeded protected speech, constituting verbal aggression aimed at denigrating officials rather than contributing to debate, and risked normalising such insults (especially among minors). The court balanced this against Article 10 and the Georgian Constitution, noting public officials must tolerate criticism but not gratuitous insults. On 11 May 2023 the Tbilisi Court of Appeal (final) upheld the Article 166 conviction but dismissed Article 173 (insults were general, not directed at specific officers then on duty), reducing the fine to the statutory minimum of GEL 500. It confirmed the video addressed a matter of public interest but found the language served no stylistic/rhetorical/literary purpose and was intended to insult; it distinguished ECtHR cases such as *Peradze and Others v. Georgia* and *Uj v. Hungary*, applied *Delfi AS* and *Skałka*, and emphasised TikTok’s rapid amplification and youth reach. No broader measures (video removal or account restrictions) were taken; the applicant continued his activism.

The ECtHR found the interference prescribed by law and pursuing legitimate aims (protection of public order/peace, rights/reputation of others, and morals). Domestic courts conducted a structured, thorough balancing exercise. The expressions constituted violent verbal aggression for wanton denigration, lacking political/social satire or other justifying purpose. The medium’s algorithmic virality and high youth engagement were significant. The sanction was limited (minimum fine) with relevant and sufficient reasons. The interference was therefore necessary in a democratic society. No violation of Article 10.

001-250279:
The case of Fal v. Spain (Application no. 25828/23) concerns a Moroccan national’s administrative expulsion from Spain with a ten-year re-entry ban, alleged to violate Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private and family life). The applicant, Najib Fal (born 1975), had lawfully resided in Spain since 2006. In 2010 he married a Moroccan national who joined him there; they had two daughters born in Spain in 2013 and 2017.

On 28 March 2019 the National Police arrested him and initiated priority expulsion proceedings under Article 54(1)(a) of the Foreigners Act for a very serious offence of participating in activities contrary to national security. The basis was a report from the General Information Commissioner’s Office, which had been monitoring suspected promoters of Islamist terrorism. The report linked the applicant to two sets of criminal preliminary proceedings before the Audiencia Nacional. In the first (no. 24/2013) police dismantled a Madrid-based cell known as “Brigada Al Andalús” that recruited, radicalised and dispatched mujahideen to Syria and Iraq to join DAESH. The applicant was identified as part of the active nucleus that sent several young people from Madrid. After arrests in June 2015, investigations continued (no. 103/2014) into an alleged organised network of imams using Muslim centres in Madrid for recruitment and indoctrination. The applicant was said to have headed this group, exercising leadership under the legal cover of the centres, sometimes against directors’ opposition, and to have acted as the person responsible for DAESH recruitment.

The initiation decision set out these facts, identified the offence, warned of possible expulsion with a ban of up to ten years, and gave 48 hours to submit observations. The applicant was notified in person with a duty lawyer present but refused to sign. His counsel filed observations on 29 March 2019 denying any evidence or conviction of terrorism-related activity, arguing the decision lacked reasoning, and stressing the disproportionality of separating him from his family, long-term residence and source of income. Supporting documents (marriage and birth certificates, family book, residence permits, municipal registration) were attached.

An investigating officer’s report of 2 April 2019 applied Article 8 criteria from the Court’s case-law, weighing the gravity of the alleged conduct, duration of stay and family circumstances. It noted that expulsion would not alter the status of the wife and daughters; if they accompanied him the children could adapt easily and the wife would return to her country of origin. The applicant had lived his first 31 years in Morocco and could readapt. Lawful residence did not equate to integration when fundamental values (life, health, security) were not respected. The officer concluded that the investigated acts showed a real, current and sufficiently serious threat to society’s fundamental interests, justifying expulsion on imperative public-security grounds, and that the interference with family life was proportionate to preventing terrorist attacks.

On 3 May 2019 the Secretary of State for Security issued a reasoned expulsion order with a ten-year ban, referring to national law, EU law and Article 8 and finding the measure proportionate to protecting national security. The applicant was informed of remedies. The order was enforced on 18 June 2019 and he was removed to Morocco, where he now lives in Casablanca.

He challenged the decision before the Administrative Division of the Audiencia Nacional, alleging breaches of effective judicial protection, the presumption of innocence and Article 8. He submitted further documents including school certificates, his wife’s language-course enrolment and an employment history showing only about seven years of work in 14 years. On 13 January 2021 the court dismissed the appeal. It held that administrative sanctioning law (protecting national security) is distinct from criminal law; the conduct could be established for administrative purposes even without a criminal investigation or charge. Concrete references to recruitment and indoctrination for DAESH sufficed; detailed investigative steps need not be recited. Applying the Court’s settled-immigrant criteria, the court found that family ties had been adequately considered, an acceptable balance struck, and the measure proportionate, as integration is incompatible with conduct that fails to respect the host society’s values. Terrorism was described as one of the gravest attacks on EU foundational values.

An appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court was declared inadmissible on 9 September 2021 (mere disagreement with the factual assessment, excluded from cassation). A subsequent amparo application to the Constitutional Court was rejected on 22 February 2023 for lack of constitutional significance.

(The Court’s judgment of 12 May 2026 found the expulsion justified, with adequate procedural safeguards and adversarial review, and no reason to depart from the domestic proportionality assessment.)

The case of Fal v. Spain (ECtHR, Application no. 25828/23, judgment of 12 May 2026) concerned the administrative expulsion from Spain of a lawfully resident Moroccan national, Najib Fal (born 1975), together with a ten-year re-entry ban, on national-security grounds linked to alleged jihadist activities. The applicant, who had resided in Spain since 2006, married a Moroccan national in 2010; the couple had two daughters born in Spain in 2013 and 2017. He complained principally under Article 8 of the Convention that the measure disproportionately interfered with his private and family life.

On 28 March 2019 the National Police initiated priority expulsion proceedings under Article 54(1)(a) of the Foreigners Act for participation in activities contrary to national security. The decision relied on a classified-style report from the General Information Commissioner’s Office. That report stated that the applicant had been under investigation in two sets of criminal preliminary proceedings before Central Investigating Court no. 5 of the Audiencia Nacional (nos. 24/2013 and 103/2014). In the first, a police operation had dismantled the Madrid-based “Brigada Al Andalús” cell, which recruited, radicalised and dispatched fighters to Syria and Iraq for DAESH; the applicant was identified as belonging to its active nucleus. After arrests in June 2015, investigations continued under the second file, focusing on an organised network of imams operating from Muslim centres in Madrid. The applicant was alleged to have headed recruitment and indoctrination efforts for DAESH, exercising leadership functions even against the opposition of some centre directors.

The initiation decision set out the statutory offence, the possible sanction of expulsion plus a ban of up to ten years, and the 48-hour period for observations. The applicant was notified in person in the presence of a duty lawyer (he refused to sign). Counsel immediately submitted written observations denying any evidence or criminal conviction, arguing that expulsion would irreparably separate him from his family and livelihood, and criticising the decision’s reasoning. Supporting documents (marriage and birth certificates, residence permits, municipal registration) were attached.

An investigating officer’s report of 2 April 2019 applied the Court’s Article 8 criteria (nature and gravity of the conduct, length of stay, family circumstances). It concluded that the alleged acts demonstrated a real, current and sufficiently serious threat to fundamental societal interests, that the family could adapt in Morocco, and that the applicant—who had spent his first 31 years there—could reintegrate. Lawful residence did not equate to integration where fundamental values such as respect for life and security were rejected. On 3 May 2019 the Secretary of State for Security issued a reasoned expulsion order with a ten-year ban, expressly invoking national law, EU law and Article 8. The applicant was expelled to Morocco on 18 June 2019.

He challenged the order before the Administrative Division of the Audiencia Nacional, alleging violations of effective judicial protection, the presumption of innocence and Article 8, and stressing the absence of any criminal charge. Additional evidence included school records, his wife’s Spanish-language enrolment and an employment-history report showing only seven years of work in fourteen. On 13 January 2021 the Audiencia Nacional dismissed the appeal. It held that administrative sanctioning and criminal proceedings pursue distinct aims; the protected interest (national security) did not require a criminal conviction or detailed disclosure of investigative steps, provided the impugned conduct—recruitment and indoctrination for DAESH—was clearly identified. Applying the Court’s settled-immigrant criteria, the court found that the authorities had adequately balanced the competing interests and that the measure was proportionate, given that integration is incompatible with rejection of core societal values and that terrorism gravely undermines the EU’s foundational principles.

A subsequent appeal on points of law was declared inadmissible by the Supreme Court (9 September 2021) as merely contesting factual assessments, and a recurso de amparo was rejected by the Constitutional Court (22 February 2023) for lack of constitutional significance. The ECtHR ultimately found the interference justified, the procedural safeguards adequate and the domestic proportionality assessment unimpeachable.

The case of Fal v. Spain (ECtHR, Application no. 25828/23) concerns the 2019 administrative expulsion from Spain of Moroccan national Najib Fal (born 1975), together with a ten-year re-entry ban, on national-security grounds. Fal alleged that the measure violated Article 8 of the Convention by interfering with his private and family life. He had resided lawfully in Spain since 2006. In 2010 he married a Moroccan woman who joined him there; they had two daughters born in Spain (2013 and 2017).

On 28 March 2019 police arrested Fal and opened priority expulsion proceedings under Article 54(1)(a) of the Foreigners Act for participation in activities contrary to national security. The decision rested on a classified report of the General Information Commissioner’s Office, which had monitored Islamist-terrorism suspects. The report placed Fal in two sets of preliminary criminal investigations before the Audiencia Nacional. In case 24/2013 a police operation dismantled the Madrid-based “Brigada Al Andalús,” which recruited, radicalised and dispatched young men to Syria and Iraq to join DAESH. Fal was identified as a member of the group’s active nucleus and as having maintained contact with its principal figures. After the 2015 arrests, investigation 103/2014 continued against remaining members; it alleged that Fal headed an organised recruitment network operating through imams at several Madrid Muslim centres, using sermons to propagate extremist ideology and to prepare candidates for travel to join DAESH. He was said to have exercised leadership functions under the legal cover of those centres, sometimes over the opposition of their directors.

Fal was notified in person in the presence of a duty lawyer (he refused to sign). He was given 48 hours to comment. Counsel argued that there was no conviction or even a formal criminal charge, that the decision merely recited statutory provisions, and that expulsion would disproportionately sever him from his family and livelihood. Family documents were attached. An investigating officer’s report of 2 April 2019 applied the Court’s Article 8 criteria, concluding that the gravity of the alleged conduct, Fal’s 31 years spent in Morocco before arriving in Spain, and the fact that his wife and children could either remain in Spain or accompany him to Morocco rendered the interference proportionate to the aim of preventing terrorist attacks. The Secretary of State for Security confirmed the expulsion and ten-year ban on 3 May 2019; the order was executed on 18 June 2019.

Fal challenged the decision before the Audiencia Nacional, repeating the lack of a criminal charge and the impact on family life and adding evidence of the children’s schooling, his wife’s Spanish-language course and an employment history showing only about seven years of work in fourteen. On 13 January 2021 the court dismissed the appeal. It held that administrative expulsion for national-security reasons does not require a prior criminal conviction, that the decision sufficiently identified Fal’s alleged leadership role in recruitment and indoctrination, and that the authorities had carried out an acceptable balancing exercise under Article 8. Subsequent cassation and amparo appeals were rejected as inadmissible.

The ECtHR later found the expulsion justified, the procedural safeguards adequate and no reason to substitute its own view for the domestic proportionality assessment.

The case of Ferrieri and Bonassisa v. Italy (Applications nos. 40607/19 and 34583/20) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned two Italian nationals, Matteo Ferrieri (born 1965) and Ornella Bonassisa (born 1977). They alleged that the Italian Tax Authority’s access to and examination of their banking data violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life). The data included bank account details, transaction histories, and other financial operations related to or traceable to them, obtained for tax audit purposes.

On 15 July 2019, Ferrieri’s bank notified him that the Tax Authority had requested such information covering 1 January to 31 December 2017. Bonassisa received a similar notification on 16 July 2020 for the period 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2017. Both banks stated they would comply with their legal duty to disclose the data. Authorizations for the requests had been issued internally by Tax Authority directors under Article 51 § 2 (7) of Presidential Decree no. 633/1972 (VAT) and Article 32 § 1 (7) of Presidential Decree no. 600/1973 (income taxes). These provisions allow tax offices, after prior authorization from a central or regional director (or equivalent for the Revenue Police), to obtain from banks any data, information, or documents on financial relationships, transactions, services, guarantees, or related persons. Requests and replies must be transmitted electronically.

The applicants argued that the legislation granted domestic authorities excessively broad, unfettered discretion over the scope and conditions of such measures, without adequate procedural safeguards against abuse or arbitrariness. In particular, there was no effective ex ante or ex post judicial or independent review.

Under Italian law and Court of Cassation case-law, the authorizations are purely internal, preparatory, or organizational acts. They require no reasoning, need not be notified to the taxpayer, and cannot be challenged independently before the tax courts (whose jurisdiction is limited to an exhaustive list of acts, such as tax assessment notices). A subsequent tax assessment based on the data can be challenged, but only on limited grounds: typically, only a complete absence of authorization that caused specific prejudice to a constitutionally protected right. Recent judgments have further restricted this, holding that even unauthorized acquisition does not automatically invalidate an assessment. The Taxpayer’s Guarantor (established by Law no. 212/2000) may receive complaints of malfunctions or irregularities and recommend self-correction (autotutela), but its decisions are non-binding; it has no power to annul acts or compel the Tax Authority.

Administrative circulars (e.g., nos. 131/1994, 32/E/2006, 25/E/2014, 16/2016) offer non-binding guidance, recommending targeting of high-risk taxpayers (such as evaders or those with unreliable records), requiring substantiation of requests, cost-benefit analysis, and use only after assessing significant discrepancies and initiating an inquiry. These do not create enforceable statutory limits.

The Court held that the interferences were not “in accordance with the law.” The legal framework failed the “quality of law” test by conferring unfettered discretion, lacking sufficient safeguards, and providing no effective independent or judicial review. Under Article 46, it identified a systemic problem requiring Italy to amend its legislation and practice. Specific statutory rules must define the circumstances and conditions for accessing banking data, ensure effective review, and account for international tax cooperation (including EU Directive 2011/16/EU and the OECD/Council of Europe Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters).

Italy (applications nos. 40607/19 and 34583/20) concerns two Italian nationals who alleged a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for private life). Mr Matteo Ferrieri (born 1965) and Mrs Ornella Bonassisa (born 1977, an accountant) complained about the Italian Tax Authority (Agenzia delle Entrate) accessing and examining their banking data—including account information, transaction histories, and other financial operations related to or traceable to them—for tax audit purposes.

On 15 July 2019, Ferrieri’s bank notified him that the Tax Authority had requested such data covering 1 January to 31 December 2017. Bonassisa received a similar notification on 16 July 2020 covering 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2017. Both banks stated they would comply with their legal duty to provide the information. The requests were authorised by Tax Authority directors under Article 51 § 2 (7) of Presidential Decree no. 633/1972 (VAT assessment) and the identical Article 32 § 1 (7) of Presidential Decree no. 600/1973 (income tax assessment). These provisions permit tax offices, after prior authorisation from a central or regional director (or equivalent for the Revenue Police), to demand from banks data, information and documents on any financial relationships or transactions involving clients, plus related guarantees and particulars of persons involved. Requests and responses must be electronic.

The applicants argued that the legislation granted the authorities excessively broad, unfettered discretion over the scope and conditions of such measures, without adequate procedural safeguards against abuse or arbitrariness. In particular, there was no effective ex ante or ex post judicial or independent review.

Domestic practice included administrative circulars (e.g., nos. 131/1994, 32/E/2006, 25/E/2014 and 16/2016) setting selection criteria (such as suspected evasion or unreliable records) and requiring substantiated authorisation requests with a cost-benefit analysis. However, Court of Cassation case-law treated authorisations as purely internal, preparatory or organisational acts that need not be reasoned, need not be notified to the taxpayer, and cannot be challenged independently. They can be contested only indirectly via a later tax assessment notice (under Legislative Decree no. 546/1992, which lists challengeable acts exhaustively), and even then only if the complete absence of authorisation caused specific prejudice to a constitutionally protected interest. The Taxpayer’s Guarantor (under Law no. 212/2000) may request documents or recommend self-correction (autotutela) but cannot issue binding decisions.

The Court found that banking data falls within the scope of “private life” under Article 8, so the access constituted an interference. For the interference to be “in accordance with the law,” the domestic framework must be accessible, foreseeable and afford adequate protection against arbitrary interference (the “quality of law” requirement). The Court held that the framework failed this test: it conferred unfettered discretion as to when, how far and under what conditions data could be obtained; it lacked sufficient procedural safeguards; and there was no effective independent or judicial review of the measures themselves. Consequently the interferences were not in accordance with the law, violating Article 8.

The Court further identified a systemic problem under Article 46, requiring Italy to amend its legislation and practice. Specific rules must indicate the circumstances and conditions for accessing taxpayers’ banking data, provide for effective judicial or independent review, and take account of international tax-cooperation obligations (e.g., under EU Directive 2011/16/EU and the OECD/Council of Europe Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters).

The ECtHR case of Ferrieri and Bonassisa v. Italy (apps. 40607/19 and 34583/20) involved two Italian nationals, Matteo Ferrieri (born 1965) and Ornella Bonassisa (born 1977). They alleged that the Italian Tax Authority’s access to and examination of their banking data violated Article 8 of the ECHR (right to respect for private life).

In July 2019, Ferrieri’s bank notified him that the Tax Authority had requested information on his accounts, transaction histories, and related financial operations for the whole of 2017. In July 2020, Bonassisa received a similar notification covering 2016–2017. The banks stated they would comply. Authorizations for these requests had been issued by Tax Authority directors under Article 51(2)(7) of Presidential Decree 633/1972 (VAT) and the equivalent provision of Presidential Decree 600/1973 (income tax). These provisions allowed tax offices, after high-level authorization, to obtain from banks any data on clients’ relationships, transactions, guarantees, and related persons. Requests and replies were to be electronic; the taxpayer was to be notified by the bank.

Domestic practice and case-law treated such authorizations as purely internal, preparatory, and organizational acts. They required no reasons, need not be notified to the taxpayer, and could not be challenged independently before tax courts (Court of Cassation judgments 14026/2012, 8849/2015, 19564/2018). Challenge was possible only later, against a subsequent tax assessment notice, and then only for total absence of authorization plus proof of specific prejudice to a constitutional right. Administrative circulars (1994–2016) suggested criteria such as suspected evasion, unreliable records, or cost-benefit analysis, and required some substantiation of requests, but these were non-binding. The Taxpayer’s Guarantor could receive complaints and request documents or self-correction but had no binding powers (Cassation 25212/2022). Tax-assessment time limits ran to five or seven years.

The applicants argued that the legal framework conferred excessively broad, unfettered discretion on the authorities regarding the scope and conditions of access, and that it lacked sufficient procedural safeguards against abuse, in particular any effective ex-ante or ex-post judicial or independent review.

The Court held that the interferences with private life (access to and examination of banking data) were not “in accordance with the law.” The domestic provisions failed the “quality of law” test: they afforded the authorities unfettered discretion as to when and how banking data could be obtained, contained no sufficiently precise rules on the circumstances and conditions of access, and provided no adequate procedural safeguards. Contested measures were not subject to effective judicial or independent review either before or after implementation. The Court also identified a systemic problem and indicated, under Article 46, that Italy must amend its legislation and practice to introduce specific rules on access to taxpayers’ banking data, coupled with effective review, taking account of international tax-cooperation contexts.
