The case of Yokuşlu v. Türkiye (Application no. 489/24) involved a Turkish professional footballer, Kutay Yokuşlu (born 1999), who complained under Articles 6 and 8 ECHR about proceedings before the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) Arbitration Committee. The alleged violations focused on the Committee’s lack of independence and impartiality in compulsory arbitration, inadequate access to court and reasoned judgment, and interference with private life.

In May 2023, while playing for Altay Sports Club in the Turkish First League, Yokuşlu’s lawyer notified the club of intended contract termination within 30 days unless outstanding salary was paid. The club paid on 12 June 2023. Unaware of this, the lawyer filed a termination notice with the TFF on 3 July 2023. The TFF registered it on 14 July 2023 and cancelled Yokuşlu’s club registration, giving it legal effect.

On 24 July 2023, Yokuşlu and the club jointly requested retraction of the notice, explaining it resulted from a communication error. On 9 August 2023, the TFF Board of Directors refused, holding that the registered termination created an irreversible “new legal situation” under domestic law. Yokuşlu appealed to the TFF Arbitration Committee on 17 August 2023 seeking to set aside that decision.

The Committee dismissed the appeal on 25 August 2023 via a summary decision stating the Board’s ruling complied with procedures and regulations. Its reasoned decision, served on 4 June 2024, emphasised that professional football contracts and their terminations, once registered with the TFF, produce effects beyond the parties’ control and cannot be revoked. A FIFA ban preventing the club from signing players during the relevant seasons further blocked any recontracting.

Independence concerns were acute because the dispute directly challenged a Board of Directors decision. After the TFF Congress elected a new president and Board in June 2022, the president publicly called for all committees (including the existing Arbitration Committee) to resign for a “clean slate.” Members resigned and the Board appointed a new chair, six regular members and six substitutes on 8 July 2022. A similar episode occurred after 2024 elections: the new president invoked a proverb implying loyalty to the new leadership and requested resignations; new Committee members were promptly announced.

These events occurred despite 2022 legislative reforms (Law no. 7405 amending the TFF Law) that followed the Court’s earlier finding of structural deficiencies in Ali Rıza and Others v. Turkey. The reforms provided a four-year term of office for Arbitration Committee members independent of the Board’s term, appointment of jurists with at least ten years’ experience, written independence declarations, oaths, prohibitions on instructions or concurrent TFF roles, recusal duties in cases of legitimate doubt, and limited personal liability except for serious fault. In practice, however, members still resigned en masse after Board elections, rendering the detached four-year term ineffective.

The Court later held Article 6 applicable to the compulsory arbitration. It found that the remaining safeguards (liability rules and recusal procedure) still fell short of Convention standards identified in Ali Rıza, and that the independence/impartiality deficit was especially pronounced given the direct challenge to the Board itself. Article 8 was inapplicable under the Denisov consequence-based test, as the decision lacked sufficiently serious effects on the applicant’s private life. The Court also indicated under Article 46 that general measures were required to remedy the structural nature of the deficiencies.

The case of Yokuşlu v. Türkiye (no. 489/24) concerns complaints by professional footballer Kutay Yokuşlu under Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention regarding proceedings before the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) Arbitration Committee.

The applicant, born in 1999, played for Altay Sports Club in Türkiye’s First League. On 24 May 2023 his lawyer notified the Club that the applicant would terminate his contract after 30 days if unpaid salary remained outstanding. The Club paid the salary on 12 June 2023. Unaware of this, the lawyer filed a termination notice with the TFF on 3 July 2023. The TFF registered the notice on 14 July 2023 and cancelled the applicant’s registration with the Club, giving it legal effect.

On 24 July 2023 the applicant’s lawyer and the Club jointly requested retraction of the notice, explaining it resulted from a communication failure. On 9 August 2023 the TFF Board of Directors rejected the request, holding that the registered termination had created an irreversible new legal situation under domestic law.

The applicant then applied to the TFF Arbitration Committee on 17 August 2023 seeking to set aside the Board’s decision. On 25 August 2023 the Committee dismissed the application in a summary ruling, stating the Board’s decision accorded with applicable procedures and regulations. Its reasoned decision, served on 4 June 2024, emphasised that professional football contracts and their terminations, once registered by the TFF, produce effects beyond the parties’ private will and cannot be revoked.

A FIFA ban on the Club signing new players (stemming from unpaid debts to former players) remained in force and further prevented the applicant from concluding a new contract with the Club.

The applicant complained that the Arbitration Committee lacked independence and impartiality (particularly as the dispute directly challenged a Board of Directors decision), that he was denied access to a court and a reasoned judgment, and that the outcome interfered with his private and family life.

Relevant contextual facts include statements by successive TFF presidents. After the June 2022 extraordinary Congress elected a new Board, the incoming president publicly called for all TFF committees (including the existing Arbitration Committee) to resign so as to start with a “clean slate”; new members were then appointed. After the July 2024 ordinary Congress, the newly elected president similarly asked all committee members to resign, invoking the proverb “a horse neighs according to its rider”; a new Committee composition was promptly announced.

Although legislative amendments adopted after the Court’s 2020 judgment in Ali Rıza and Others v. Turkey introduced a four-year term of office for Arbitration Committee members formally detached from that of the Board, oaths of impartiality, limited personal liability (except for serious fault), and recusal rules, these safeguards proved ineffective in practice. Mass resignations followed each Board election, allowing the new Board to appoint replacements. The Court found that the regulation of members’ legal liability and the recusal procedure still fell short of the Convention standards identified in Ali Rıza. The structural deficiencies therefore persisted, and the applicant’s fear of a lack of independence and impartiality was especially pronounced given that the impugned dispute attacked a decision of the Board itself.

Article 6 § 1 was applicable to the compulsory arbitration proceedings. Article 8 was not applicable under the consequence-based approach of Denisov v. Ukraine, as the decision did not have sufficiently serious repercussions for the applicant’s private life. Under Article 46 the Court indicated the need for general measures to address the structural nature of the independence and impartiality problems affecting the TFF Arbitration Committee.

The case of Yokuşlu v. Türkiye (App. no. 489/24) arose from a professional footballer's challenge to the TFF Arbitration Committee's independence and impartiality under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (and related complaints under Articles 6 and 8). The applicant, Kutay Yokuşlu (born 1999), played for Altay Sports Club in Türkiye's First League.

On 24 May 2023, his lawyer notified the Club that the contract would terminate in 30 days unless outstanding salary was paid. The Club paid on 12 June 2023. Unaware of this due to a communication lapse, the lawyer filed a termination notice with the TFF on 3 July 2023. The TFF registered it on 14 July 2023, cancelling the applicant's Club registration and giving it legal effect.

On 24 July 2023, the applicant (via counsel) and Club jointly requested retraction of the notice as a mistake. On 9 August 2023, the TFF Board of Directors refused, holding that registration created an irreversible new legal situation under domestic law.

The applicant appealed to the TFF Arbitration Committee on 17 August 2023 seeking to set aside the Board's decision. The Committee dismissed the appeal on 25 August 2023 (summary decision). Its reasoned decision, served 4 June 2024, confirmed that once a termination was filed and registered with the TFF, it could not be revoked, as such contracts (and terminations) had effects beyond the parties' will and were governed by TFF rules.

The Government noted a contemporaneous FIFA ban preventing the Club from signing players (due to unpaid debts), which also blocked any new contract with the applicant.

These events formed the core of the applicant's complaints that the Committee was neither independent nor impartial (especially as it reviewed a Board of Directors decision), that he lacked effective access to a court, that the decision was inadequately reasoned, and that it interfered with his private/family life (Article 8).

The Committee's structure derived from post-Ali Rıza reforms (TFF Law as amended 2022, TFF Statutes, and Arbitration Committee Directive). Members (a chair plus six regular and six substitute jurists with ≥10 years' experience) were appointed by the Board of Directors for a four-year term independent of the Board's term. They swore oaths of independence/impartiality, had to disclose conflicts, recuse themselves if doubt arose, could not hold other TFF or affiliated posts, and faced liability only for serious fault. Decisions on management/discipline of football were final (other decisions challengeable under the Code of Civil Procedure).

In practice, however, after the June 2022 TFF Congress election of a new president and Board, the president publicly called for all committees (including the sitting Arbitration Committee) to resign "to start with a clean slate." Members resigned; the Board appointed replacements on 8 July 2022. After the July 2024 election, the new president similarly asked all committee members to resign (citing a proverb about loyalty to the "rider"); new members, including a new chair, were announced on 22 July 2024.

The Court held Article 6 applicable to the compulsory arbitration. Despite the legislative changes, the combination of Board-appointed members, their practical replacement with each new Board (undermining the four-year term), limited liability/recusal safeguards, and especially the Committee's review of a direct challenge to a Board decision, meant the Committee still lacked sufficient independence and impartiality. Article 8 was inapplicable (no sufficiently serious private-life consequences under the Denisov test). Structural deficiencies required general measures under Article 46.

The case of Biliński v. Poland concerns district court judge Łukasz Biliński’s non-consensual transfer between court divisions and the lack of subsequent judicial review. Appointed in 2016 to the Warsaw-Śródmieście District Court, Biliński was assigned to Criminal Division XI, which handled administrative offences. From 2018 to mid-2019 he decided hundreds of cases involving freedom of assembly and expression, including counter-demonstrations to monthly Smolensk crash commemorations and protests against government judicial reforms. His rulings, which invoked constitutional and Convention standards, attracted media attention and public criticism from ruling-party politicians as unfavourable to the Government.

The District Court president at the time was Judge M. Mitera, appointed in 2018 by Justice Minister Z. Ziobro after secondment to the Ministry; Mitera also sat on the recomposed National Council of the Judiciary (NCJ) and served as its spokesperson. Biliński’s requests in December 2018 and January 2019 for transfer to another criminal division (to broaden his experience) were refused. On 29 March 2019 the Minister of Justice abolished Division XI (among others) with effect from 1 July 2019.

On 17 June 2019 the District Court vice-president sought the obligatory opinion of the Warsaw Regional Court Board on transferring Biliński, against his will, to Family and Juvenile Division III. Biliński asked for an adjournment so he could be heard. The Board postponed its opinion pending a CJEU preliminary ruling on NCJ independence. Nevertheless, on 3 July 2019 the District Court president transferred Biliński to the Family Division without stating legal grounds and without the required Board opinion. A provisional assignment to another criminal-offences unit had been notified days earlier.

Biliński appealed to the NCJ on 10 July 2019, alleging manifest breaches of the 2001 Act on the Organisation of Ordinary Courts (no Board opinion; disregard of statutory criteria of seniority and specialisation) and infringement of judicial independence under the Constitution, the EU Charter and Article 6 of the Convention. He requested postponement of the NCJ session and recusal of Mitera. His lawyers’ requests to attend the session and to inspect the file were refused. The Polish Commissioner for Human Rights asked the District Court president for an explanation, noting that Biliński was the only judge from the abolished division sent to the Family Division (the others remaining in criminal work) and that an experienced family-division judge was simultaneously being moved against her will.

On 22 July 2019 the Warsaw Regional Court president annulled both the provisional and the definitive transfer decisions as unlawful for want of the mandatory Board opinion. Biliński immediately informed the NCJ that the appeal was therefore moot. The NCJ nevertheless dismissed the appeal by unexplained resolution of 25 July 2019 (section 22a(5)–(6) of the 2001 Act as amended in 2018). The three-member panel later disclosed included two judges whose public comments on the very issue of transfers Biliński had sought to exclude. The Regional Court president’s annulment was ignored. Despite the annulment, Biliński remained de facto assigned to the Family Division; his salary was unaffected.

Under the 2018 amendments, appeals against changes in a judge’s duties now lay exclusively with the NCJ; the NCJ was not required to give reasons, hear the judge or disclose its composition, and no further appeal to a court was possible. The Supreme Court’s Chamber of Extraordinary Review and Public Affairs consistently treated such NCJ resolutions as unappealable. These facts underpin the complaint that Biliński was denied access to a court for review of an allegedly arbitrary transfer between divisions dealing with entirely different areas of law.

Nevertheless, on 3 July 2019 the District Court President (himself a recent ministerial appointee and NCJ member) ordered the transfer with immediate effect, citing no legal basis.

Biliński appealed to the NCJ, arguing that the decision violated statutory requirements (absence of the Board’s opinion, disregard of seniority and specialisation), his judicial independence and the prohibition on arbitrary transfers. He sought an adjournment, recusal of conflicted NCJ members and the right to be heard. The NCJ denied those requests, examined the appeal in camera and, on 25 July 2019, dismissed it by an unreasoned resolution. The panel included two judges who had already commented publicly on the case. Meanwhile, on 22 July the Regional Court President had annulled the transfer as unlawful; the NCJ ignored that annulment. Biliński was nevertheless assigned de facto to the Family Division, where he remained. No further domestic appeal lay against the NCJ resolution; the Supreme Court’s Extraordinary Review Chamber consistently treated such challenges as inadmissible.

The 2018 amendments to the 2001 Act on Ordinary Courts had shifted competence for appeals against changes in judicial duties from court boards to the NCJ, eliminated the requirement to hear the judge or give reasons, and excluded any subsequent court review (except in same-area transfers). The applicant therefore had no access to an independent tribunal capable of examining the lawfulness of a transfer between distinct branches of law. These facts form the core of the alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 (access to court).

The case of Biliński v. Poland (ECtHR, Application no. 13278/20, judgment of 15 January 2026) concerns a Polish district court judge's non-consensual transfer between court divisions and his inability to obtain judicial review of that decision, raising issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (access to court).

The applicant, Łukasz Biliński, was appointed a judge at the Warsaw-Śródmieście District Court in 2016 and assigned to Criminal Division XI, which handled administrative offences. Between 2018 and mid-2019 he decided hundreds of cases involving freedom of assembly and expression, including counter-demonstrations against monthly Smolensk commemoration events and protests against judicial reforms. His rulings, which invoked constitutional and Convention standards, drew media attention and were publicly criticised by ruling-party politicians as unfavourable to the Government.

The court's president at the time, Judge M. Mitera, had been appointed by Justice Minister Z. Ziobro and previously seconded to the Ministry; he also served on the recomposed National Council of the Judiciary (NCJ). In late 2018 and early 2019 the applicant unsuccessfully requested a transfer to another criminal division to broaden his experience. On 29 March 2019 the Minister of Justice abolished Criminal Division XI (effective 1 July 2019). On 17 June 2019 the vice-president sought the obligatory opinion of the Warsaw Regional Court's Board on transferring the applicant (who withheld consent) to the Family and Juvenile Division. The Board postponed its opinion pending a CJEU preliminary ruling on NCJ independence. Nevertheless, on 3 July 2019 the president transferred the applicant to the Family Division without the Board's opinion and without stating legal grounds.

The applicant immediately appealed to the NCJ, arguing breaches of the 2001 Act on the Organisation of Ordinary Courts (transfer without the required opinion, disregard of seniority and specialisation criteria), infringement of judicial independence, and violation of Article 6 § 1. He requested a stay pending the CJEU ruling and recusal of certain NCJ members. The NCJ refused to hear him or his lawyers and, on 25 July 2019, dismissed the appeal by an unreasoned resolution (later revealed to have been adopted by a panel including two judges who had publicly commented on the case). Meanwhile, on 22 July 2019 the Regional Court president had annulled the transfer as unlawful for want of the Board's opinion; the NCJ ignored this. Although the applicant remained de facto assigned to the Family Division, no further domestic appeal was available.

The Court held that Article 6 applied under its civil limb because a genuine dispute existed over the applicant's "right" as a judge to protection against arbitrary transfer between divisions adjudicating different areas of law. The Eskelinen test's first condition (access to court not expressly excluded by domestic law for the category of staff in question) was met; the second (the exclusion being justified on objective grounds in the State's interest) was not. Exclusion of judicial review was not justified, given the lack of independence of the reformed NCJ, the absence of any hearing or reasons, and the overall insufficiency of procedural safeguards. Consequently the very essence of the applicant's right of access to a court was impaired.

**Summary of Pešić v. Serbia (Application no. 4545/21, ECtHR, 13 January 2026)**

Vesna Pešić, a Serbian national born in 1940 and a former politician and long-time political activist living in Belgrade, brought complaints under Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 6 § 1 (fair trial and access to court) of the European Convention on Human Rights. She alleged that damages awarded against her in civil defamation proceedings initiated by a public official unjustifiably interfered with her expression rights. She further claimed the civil proceedings were unfair because she could not put certain questions to the plaintiff, the Constitutional Court’s judgment was inadequately reasoned, and the Supreme Court of Cassation’s refusal to consider her appeal on points of law violated her right of access to a court.

The relevant events began in the early hours of 25 April 2016, when unidentified perpetrators used heavy machinery to demolish numerous structures in Belgrade’s Savamala neighbourhood as part of a construction project. They unlawfully detained several people present and released them only after the demolition. Those affected contacted police, who failed to respond. An investigation into the events remained ongoing.

On 12 May 2016, Interior Minister N.S. publicly addressed the incident, stating that police would not intervene or enter an area until any threat to officers’ safety (such as cut electrical cables) had been neutralised.

The next day, 13 May 2016, Pešić published an article titled “Adding Salt (Dosoljavanje)” on the website of the citizens’ association Peščanik, to which she regularly contributed. The piece strongly criticised N.S., describing his “stupidity” as unsurpassed and unpredictable, questioning why he was given the role of “playing the fool,” calling his remarks “quite a stupid statement” and “the most stupid,” and accusing him of suggesting that police exist to protect themselves rather than citizens. She argued that the minister had downplayed the demolition of illegal buildings, ignored criminal acts by masked men, and implied citizens (described as those acquiring wealth through political-tycoon collusion) deserved any harm, including electrocution. She also dismissed his promise of an investigation.

On 27 July 2016, N.S. sued Pešić, Peščanik, and its editors-in-chief before the Belgrade High Court, seeking 200,000 Serbian dinars (RSD) in non-pecuniary damages for mental distress caused by an alleged attack on his honour and reputation.

At a 27 April 2018 hearing, both N.S. and Pešić testified. The judge twice directed Pešić to confine her remarks to relevant matters and avoid political speeches. The court disallowed certain questions to N.S. as irrelevant.

On 10 July 2018, the High Court found for N.S. It held that Pešić’s remarks about the minister’s “stupidity” exceeded acceptable criticism of a public official’s statements and actions, constituting a personal insult. The court concluded she had maliciously and inaccurately represented his words, that the article neither contributed to public debate on the Savamala events nor addressed a genuine issue, and that it was instead aimed at denigrating N.S., subjectively attacking his dignity, reputation and honour, thereby causing mental distress. It rejected her argument that the expressions were value judgments based on the factual context of the demolitions. Relying on Article 200 of the Obligations Act, the court ordered the defendants jointly to pay RSD 200,000 (approximately EUR 1,710) plus costs.

Pešić appealed, invoking Article 10 and relevant case-law. On 17 October 2018, the Belgrade Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals but reduced damages to RSD 150,000 (approximately EUR 1,280) plus reduced costs. It stated that not all manners of conveying ideas fall within freedom of expression, as that freedom cannot contradict its own purpose. The article had not contributed to public debate but appeared intended solely to offend N.S. While value judgments are generally permitted, defamatory ones not in the public interest are impermissible.

Pešić lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court of Cassation on 5 December 2018 and a constitutional appeal on 20 December 2018. On 21 March 2019, the Supreme Court dismissed the points-of-law appeal, holding that Pešić and co-defendants lacked standing because the Court of Appeal had reduced the award; only N.S. could have appealed.

Pešić filed a further constitutional appeal on 8 August 2019 concerning access to court. On 4 June 2020, the Constitutional Court rejected her appeals, finding they presented no valid constitutional arguments but merely sought a legality review beyond its jurisdiction, and agreeing that she lacked standing for the points-of-law appeal.

After the application was communicated to the Government, the Constitutional Court on 11 March 2024 (in proceedings brought by Peščanik and the editors) found that the Supreme Court’s dismissal of the points-of-law appeal had violated the right to a fair trial, quashed the decision, and directed re-examination. It stated the ruling applied equally to Pešić as she was in the same legal situation. The outcome of the resumed Supreme Court proceedings remained unknown as of November 2025.

The ECtHR later held that the interference with Pešić’s Article 10 rights was not necessary in a democratic society, as the national courts failed to strike a fair balance, provide relevant and sufficient reasons, apply Convention standards, or base their decisions on an acceptable assessment of the facts. The applicant, Vesna Pešić (born 1940), a Serbian national, former politician and long-time political activist living in Belgrade, alleged violations of Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial, including access to a court) of the Convention. He declared that the fact that the main news item in Serbia is the demolition of three illegal buildings in Savamala is just ‘spin’... That was quite a stupid statement, but what followed was the most stupid... he said that the police couldn’t act because it wasn’t permitted to endanger the lives of officers! ... we’ve ended up with a situation where the police exist to protect themselves! It agreed the applicant lacked standing for the cassation appeal. The decision was served on 16 June 2020.

After the application was communicated to the Government, on 11 March 2024 the Constitutional Court (in a decision on Peščanik et al.’s related appeal) found that the Supreme Court of Cassation had infringed the right to a fair trial by dismissing their cassation appeal. The case of Ramishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 4100/24) concerns the European Court of Human Rights’ finding of a violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life) arising from Georgian courts’ dismissal of a civil defamation claim. The applicant, Mikheil Ramishvili, a well-known defence lawyer, had represented the family of Sandro Girgvliani in a notorious 2006 murder case that implicated high-ranking officials. At the relevant time he was also defending Archil Mamaladze in another high-profile prosecution (the “Cyanide case”) involving the attempted murder of the Georgian Patriarch’s secretary. Father I., a prominent Orthodox clergyman and prosecution witness in the Mamaladze trial, intervened by telephone during a live evening broadcast on the private channel Iberia on 21 September 2017. He described the applicant as Father Petre’s “snitch,” claimed he had been “planted” in the Girgvliani case as a “provocateur,” and alleged that he had supplied information to the former head of the Constitutional Security Department.

Ramishvili sued for defamation, seeking a retraction and modest non-pecuniary damages. He argued that the remarks conveyed concrete, verifiable accusations of professional betrayal and collaboration with state security services, thereby damaging his honour and standing as counsel. The Tbilisi City Court upheld the claim in December 2018, characterising the statements as assertions of fact that Father I. had made no attempt to substantiate. The Court of Appeal reversed that judgment in November 2022, re-classifying the remarks as value judgments uttered in a matter of intense public interest. It emphasised that both men were public figures and that Georgian law therefore required the plaintiff to prove not only falsity and harm but also actual knowledge of falsity or gross negligence. The Supreme Court confirmed this reasoning in June 2023. It treated the word “snitch” as purely evaluative, regarded the “planted provocateur” comments as contextual opinion rather than factual allegation, and held that testimony from the Girgvliani family and a co-counsel attesting to the applicant’s professional conduct could not disprove the accusations. The court also accepted Father I.’s claim that he had believed the conversation to be private.

The Strasbourg Court held that Article 8 was engaged because the statements were capable of undermining the applicant’s professional reputation and of generating lasting prejudice in both legal and social circles. It found that the domestic courts had failed to require any factual foundation for the gravest accusations, had placed an unattainable burden of proof on the applicant to disprove allegations of covert collaboration, and had thereby neglected to strike a fair balance between the applicant’s right to reputation and Father I.’s freedom of expression. The judgment became final on 3 May 2026.

The case involves Georgian lawyer Mikheil Ramishvili, a publicly known defence counsel who represented the victim’s family in the high-profile Girgvliani murder case and the defendant in the Mamaladze attempted-murder case (the “Cyanide case”). On 21 September 2017 Father I., a prominent Georgian Orthodox clergyman and prosecution witness in the Mamaladze case, intervened live by telephone on the television programme “Axali Ambebi.” He described the applicant as an “informer,” “provocateur” and “Father Petre’s snitch,” asserting that the applicant had been “planted” in the Girgvliani case and had fed information to the former head of the Constitutional Security Department.

The applicant brought a civil defamation action on 20 October 2017, claiming the remarks contained substantially false information that damaged his honour and professional reputation. He sought a retraction and 2 000 GEL in non-pecuniary damages. Father I. counter-claimed that the statements were protected value judgments under the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act.

The Tbilisi City Court (11 December 2018) found for the applicant. It held that the remarks conveyed specific, verifiable facts presented as confirmed realities (that the applicant had been planted by the security services and had acted as an informer). Father I. offered no source or basis for the assertions. The court ordered a public retraction and symbolic damages of 1 GEL.

The Tbilisi Court of Appeal (16 November 2022) reversed. It classified the statements as value judgments made about a public figure on a matter of public interest. Under the Act the plaintiff (a public figure) bore the burden of proving falsity, damage and malice or gross negligence. Any residual doubt was to be resolved in favour of treating the remarks as opinion. The court also accepted that Father I. may not have realised the conversation was being broadcast live.

The Supreme Court (23 June 2023) upheld the appellate decision. It characterised “snitch” as purely evaluative and the remaining accusations as subjective assessments inseparable from Father I.’s criticism of the applicant’s defence of “murderers.” Even the more factual-sounding references to being “planted” and feeding information did not allege criminal conduct. Testimony from the Girgvliani victim’s family and co-counsel attesting to the applicant’s professionalism was dismissed as merely subjective and insufficient to disprove the allegations. The applicant had therefore failed to establish the required fault. The court further accepted that Father I. had believed the exchange was private.

The Freedom of Speech Act defines “thought” as a value judgment containing no confirmable fact and grants such statements absolute privilege. Defamation requires a substantially false fact that harms reputation. Doubts are resolved in favour of opinion status and against restriction of speech. For public figures the plaintiff must additionally prove the speaker knew the statement was false or acted with gross negligence.

These facts—particularly the courts’ classification of concrete accusations as unassailable opinions, the reversal of the burden of proof onto the applicant, and the absence of any requirement that the speaker demonstrate a factual basis—form the core of the alleged Article 8 violation concerning protection of reputation.

The case of Cuculovic v. Switzerland (Application no. 28865/17) concerns an alleged violation of Article 5 § 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Swiss national Nebojsa Cuculovic (born 1995), claimed that his pre-trial detention was improperly extended on new, unrelated factual and legal grounds after the original charges were dropped, without a personal hearing.

On 15 October 2016, Cuculovic was arrested on suspicion of common assault and making threats against B., as well as violating the Narcotics Act. The public prosecutor applied for pre-trial detention. On 18 October 2016, the Compulsory Measures Court of the Canton of Aargau heard the applicant in person and rejected the application for lack of a specific ground for detention, ordering his immediate release. The prosecutor appealed. On 20 October 2016, the Court of Appeal granted the appeal suspensive effect and ordered continued detention pending its decision.

On 27 October 2016, B. withdrew all criminal complaints in writing. The prosecutor notified the Court of Appeal the next day. On 7 November 2016, the prosecutor submitted new facts and grounds relating to the applicant driving without a licence and committing serious traffic violations. The applicant received a copy of this letter.

On 18 November 2016, B. confirmed the withdrawal during an interview. That same day, the applicant requested immediate release, arguing that the offences of common assault and making threats required a formal complaint to proceed and that the necessary prerequisites had therefore ceased. He did not comment on the new facts.

On 21 November 2016, the Court of Appeal upheld the prosecutor’s appeal on the basis of the new facts and grounds. It overturned the Compulsory Measures Court’s order and imposed three months’ provisional pre-trial detention. It found no remaining urgent suspicion regarding the original charges due to the final withdrawal of complaints. However, because there was no prohibition on new arguments or evidence, the newly ascertained facts could be considered. These established both a strong suspicion of guilt and a risk of recidivism.

The applicant appealed to the Federal Supreme Court. On 19 December 2016, that court upheld the appeal in part. It held that the applicant’s detention from 28 October to 21 November 2016 had not been based on a judicial decision meeting Article 5 § 1 requirements. The Court of Appeal should have lifted the detention upon learning of the complaint withdrawals. New facts should have prompted a fresh application to the Compulsory Measures Court, which would have had to respect the applicant’s Article 5 § 3 rights. Nonetheless, the Court of Appeal (having full jurisdiction) could review detention in light of the facts known at the time of its assessment. Because the 7 November 2016 submissions had been served on the applicant, there was no violation of the right to be heard. The new grounds were correctly approved.

On 5 January 2017, the Federal Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s request for revision. He had argued that he had not been personally heard by the Court of Appeal and that the proceedings had amounted to a (re)ordering of detention rather than a review of an existing deprivation of liberty.

The relevant Swiss Code of Criminal Procedure provisions at the time (Articles 220, 222, 228, 390 and 397) governed the definition of pre-trial detention, appellate remedies, applications for release, and the predominantly written nature of appeal proceedings, with hearings possible but not mandatory. The law has since been amended, notably to restrict who may contest detention orders.

These facts form the core of the alleged Article 5 § 3 violation: the extension of detention on entirely new, unrelated charges after the original ones lapsed, without the applicant being heard in person by the court that ordered the continued deprivation of liberty.

The core of the complaint before the Strasbourg Court was therefore that the extension of detention on wholly new, unrelated grounds, after the original charges had been dropped, had taken place without an in-person hearing of the applicant, contrary to Article 5 § 3.

The case of Cuculovic v. Switzerland (Application no. 28865/17) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1995, claimed that his pre-trial detention was unlawfully extended on entirely new and unrelated factual and legal grounds after the original charges were dropped, without him being heard in person by the relevant court.

On 15 October 2016, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of common assault and making threats against B., as well as violations of the Narcotics Act. The public prosecutor applied for pre-trial detention. On 18 October 2016, the Compulsory Measures Court of the Canton of Aargau heard the applicant in person and rejected the application, finding no specific ground for detention and ordering his immediate release.

The public prosecutor appealed. On 20 October 2016, the Court of Appeal granted the appeal suspensive effect and ordered the applicant’s continued detention pending a decision. On 27 October 2016, B. withdrew all criminal complaints against the applicant. The prosecutor informed the Court of Appeal of this on 28 October 2016.

On 7 November 2016, the prosecutor submitted entirely new facts and grounds for detention to the Court of Appeal, relating to the applicant driving without a licence and committing serious traffic offences. A copy of this letter was provided to the applicant. On 18 November 2016, B. confirmed the withdrawal of the complaints in an interview. The same day, the applicant applied for immediate release, arguing that the offences of common assault and making threats required a formal complaint, which had now been withdrawn, so the procedural prerequisites for prosecution no longer existed. He did not address the new allegations.

On 21 November 2016, the Court of Appeal upheld the prosecutor’s appeal on the basis of the new facts. It overturned the Compulsory Measures Court’s decision and ordered three months’ pre-trial detention. The court accepted that there was no longer an urgent suspicion regarding the original charges because of the withdrawal of complaints. However, it held that new arguments and evidence could be introduced on appeal. It found a strong suspicion of guilt and a risk of recidivism in respect of the traffic offences.

The applicant appealed to the Federal Supreme Court. On 19 December 2016, that court partially upheld the appeal. It found that the applicant’s detention from 28 October to 21 November 2016 had not been based on a judicial decision satisfying Article 5 § 1, as the Court of Appeal should have ordered his release upon learning of the withdrawal of complaints. The prosecutor ought to have made a fresh application to the Compulsory Measures Court, which would have been required to respect the applicant’s rights under Article 5 § 3. Nevertheless, the Federal Supreme Court held that the Court of Appeal, having full jurisdiction, could assess the detention in the light of the facts known at the time of its decision. Because the new submissions had been served on the applicant, there was no violation of the right to be heard. The new grounds for detention were upheld.

On 5 January 2017, the Federal Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s request for revision, in which he argued that he had not been personally heard by the Court of Appeal and that the proceedings amounted to a re-ordering of detention rather than a mere review.

The core issue is that, after the original charges collapsed, detention was continued and then formally ordered on wholly unrelated new grounds at the appeal stage, without a personal hearing of the applicant by the court taking that decision. Under the applicable Swiss procedural rules, appeal proceedings were conducted in writing, with an oral hearing being optional rather than mandatory.

The case of Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (No. 2) (Application no. 16613/23) arose from the applicant’s ineligibility to stand for election as President or Vice-President of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr Zlatan Begić, born in 1975 and living in Tuzla, is a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front and a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He does not declare affiliation with any of the constitutionally defined “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats or Serbs) and therefore falls into the residual category of “Others.”

In early 2023 three delegates belonging to the “Others” caucus of the Federation House of Peoples nominated him for the Presidency or Vice-Presidency. On 2 February 2023 the Central Election Commission rejected the nomination because it failed to satisfy the statutory conditions set out in Article IV.B.2 of the Federation Constitution and sections 9.13–9.15 of the Election Act: a candidate must be nominated by eleven delegates from one of the three constituent-people caucuses and must himself declare affiliation with that people. The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina upheld the rejection on 8 February 2023.

The applicant and his nominators lodged constitutional appeals. On 23 January 2025 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina joined the cases. It first held that the President and Vice-Presidents of the Federation do not constitute a “legislature” within the meaning of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Those offices lack the power to initiate or adopt legislation, to control the legislative process, or to censure the Parliament; their functions are essentially executive (representation of the Entity, proposal of laws that only Parliament can enact, signature of treaties subject to parliamentary ratification, limited power of dissolution, and the grant of certain amnesties). Consequently the complaints under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, taken alone or together with Article 14 of the Convention, were declared inadmissible.

The Constitutional Court nevertheless found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. The relevant provisions of the Federation Constitution and Election Act treat persons in otherwise identical situations differently solely on the ground of ethnic origin: members of the three constituent peoples may stand for the Presidency or Vice-Presidency, while “Others” may not. Relying on the Court’s earlier Grand Chamber judgment in Sejdić and Finci and on its own 2015 decision U-14/12, the Constitutional Court concluded that this difference in treatment no longer pursues a legitimate aim by proportionate means. The original post-Dayton justification of preserving peace by exclusive ethnic power-sharing had been overtaken by Bosnia and Herzegovina’s subsequent democratic development, its international human-rights obligations, and the explicit constitutional commitment to equality and pluralism. Exclusion of “Others” could therefore no longer be regarded as the only, or even a necessary, method of maintaining stability. The Constitutional Court accordingly held that the discrimination lacked an objective and reasonable justification and directed the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federation Parliament to adopt the necessary constitutional and legislative amendments.

The European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Chamber of the Fourth Section, examined the same facts and the same legal framework. It confirmed that the applicant’s ineligibility stemmed exclusively from his refusal to declare affiliation with a constituent people and that the resulting difference in treatment, being based on ethnic origin, required particularly weighty justification. No such justification had been shown to exist more than thirty years after the Dayton Agreement. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The case of Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (No. 2) (Application no. 16613/23) concerns complaints by Zlatan Begić, a Bosnian citizen born in 1975 and living in Tuzla, of discrimination in his ineligibility to stand for election as President or Vice-President of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Begić, a high-ranking Democratic Front official and member of the Parliamentary Assembly’s House of Representatives, does not declare affiliation with any of the three “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats or Serbs) and thus falls into the residual constitutional category of “Others.”

In February 2023 three “Others” delegates in the Federation’s House of Peoples nominated him for the posts. On 2 February 2023 the Central Election Commission rejected the nomination because it failed to satisfy the statutory rules: a candidate must be put forward by 11 delegates from one of the constituent-peoples’ caucuses and must himself declare affiliation with that people. The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina upheld the rejection on 8 February 2023.

Begić and his nominators lodged constitutional appeals. On 23 January 2025 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina joined the cases. It held that the President and Vice-Presidents do not constitute a “legislature” within the meaning of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, so that provision (taken alone or with Article 14 of the Convention) was inapplicable. Relying on Sejdić and Finci and its own earlier case-law, however, it found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. The difference in treatment between “Others” and members of the constituent peoples was based solely on ethnicity and lacked an objective and reasonable justification. Peace-preservation could no longer be regarded as requiring the total exclusion of “Others.” The court therefore ordered the Parliamentary Assembly and the Federation Parliament to amend the relevant constitutional and electoral provisions.

Under Article IV.B.2 of the Federation Constitution any group of 11 delegates from a constituent-people caucus in the House of Peoples may nominate a candidate of that people; the House of Representatives and then the House of Peoples must approve a three-person list comprising one candidate from each constituent people. The three elected persons then decide among themselves who will be President. The House of Peoples itself consists of 23 members for each constituent people and 11 for “Others.”

The President is head of the Federation’s executive, represents the Entity, proposes draft laws (though only Parliament may adopt them), signs enacted laws (and may refuse only if the required majorities have not been obtained), may dissolve Parliament in limited circumstances, grants certain amnesties, and signs international treaties (subject to parliamentary ratification). These powers, while significant, do not confer legislative authority.

The applicant’s complaints before the European Court therefore centred on the ethnically based barrier to candidacy for an important executive office, a barrier that the domestic Constitutional Court had already characterised as unjustified discrimination contrary to Protocol No. 12.

**Case summary (approx. 500 words):** The case concerns Zlatan Begić (born 1975, resident in Tuzla), a high-ranking Democratic Front official and member of the House of Representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Parliamentary Assembly. He belongs to the constitutional category of “Others,” as he does not declare affiliation with any of the three “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats or Serbs).

Three “Others” delegates in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s House of Peoples nominated him for President or Vice-President of the Federation. On 2 February 2023 the Central Election Commission rejected the nomination for failure to meet statutory requirements under Article IV.B.2 of the Federation Constitution and sections 9.13–9.15 of the Election Act: he had not been nominated by 11 delegates from constituent-people caucuses and he himself declared no such affiliation. The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina upheld the rejection on 8 February 2023.

The applicant and nominators lodged constitutional appeals on 20 February 2023. On 23 January 2025 the Constitutional Court joined the cases. It held that the President and Vice-Presidents are not a “legislature” within Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (they cannot initiate or adopt legislation, nor exercise wide control over the legislative process or censure the legislature), rendering that provision (alone and with Article 14) inapplicable. It found, however, a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. Differential treatment excluding “Others” from candidacy for these posts, solely on ethnic grounds, lacked objective and reasonable justification. The Court relied on its earlier ruling in U-14/12 (2015) and ECHR case-law (notably Sejdić and Finci). Given Bosnia and Herzegovina’s post-Dayton democratic progress, international human-rights obligations, and the constitutional commitment to pluralism, equality and peaceful relations in a multi-ethnic society, ethnic exclusion could no longer be regarded as the only means of preserving peace. More than nine years after U-14/12, neither the State nor Federation Constitutions had been amended. The Court therefore directed the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federation Parliament to take all necessary measures to eliminate the incompatibility with the Convention.

The relevant constitutional scheme requires that any group of 11 delegates from each constituent-people caucus of the House of Peoples (23 members per constituent people plus 11 “Others”) may nominate a candidate from that people. A list of three candidates—one from each constituent people—must then be approved by both Houses of the Federation Parliament. The three elected persons decide among themselves who becomes President (or the House of Representatives decides if they cannot agree). The President is head of the executive and represents the Federation; the two Vice-Presidents must come from the other two constituent peoples. Powers include proposing (but not adopting) draft laws, signing laws only if approved by the requisite majorities, dissolving Parliament in limited circumstances, granting certain amnesties, and signing treaties (subject to parliamentary ratification). Legislative power remains with Parliament.

These facts demonstrate that eligibility for a senior executive office is reserved to persons who declare affiliation with a constituent people, producing a difference in treatment of persons in analogous situations based solely on ethnicity. The European Court of Human Rights, in its 3 February 2026 judgment, likewise found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, confirming the absence of objective and reasonable justification.

The case of Erol Aksoy v. Türkiye (no. 58919/18) concerns the non-enforcement of Supreme Administrative Court judgments annulling the Fund’s valuation, tender and sale of Viva TV-Radio Viva, media assets of companies in the Erol Aksoy Group.

In 2001, during an economic crisis, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Board transferred İktisat Bank to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund. The applicant held 61.8% of Avrupa ve Amerika Holding A.Ş. (which owned 95.19% of the Bank) plus 1.01% personally; his family controlled 99.6% of the holding. Auditors later found former shareholders, including the applicant and family members, had misappropriated Bank resources. The Fund sought recovery of TRY 726 million. In May 2006 the applicant (personally) and the Erol Aksoy Group (including various media companies) signed a Liquidation Protocol accepting joint and several liability for all debts. In 2008 the Fund declared default, took over management of the group companies and proceeded to realise assets.

Several group companies owned Viva TV and Radio Viva. The applicant’s disclosed direct shareholding was minimal (e.g., 0.62% in one company); remaining interests were indirect via holdings. In 2007–2009 the Fund consolidated the assets into economic units, obtained valuations (2007: Radio Viva USD 4.26 m, Viva TV USD 0.37 m; 2009: Radio Viva USD 5.78 m, Viva TV USD 0.13 m) and ultimately offered the combined unit at a USD 6 m reserve. After an unsuccessful first tender, a 2011 auction attracted only one bidder. Following negotiation the unit was awarded and transferred in May 2012 for USD 5 m.

On 7 February 2011 the applicant challenged the 13 January 2011 valuation/tender decision before the administrative courts, asserting standing as Protocol signatory, personal guarantor and because the Fund controlled his companies. After a first-instance dismissal, the Supreme Administrative Court’s General Assembly (7 July 2015) annulled the decision: the USD 6 m figure rested on the outdated 2009 report without a fresh market assessment. The Fund refused enforcement (April 2016), citing the completed transfer to a bona-fide purchaser, use of the proceeds, loss of control over the assets and impossibility of restoring the status quo.

Separately, the applicant sought annulment of the sale itself. After initial dismissal, the Supreme Administrative Court (30 June 2017), relying on the 2015 judgment, held that all subsequent acts were invalid and annulled the sale. The Fund again refused enforcement on identical grounds.

The applicant applied to the Constitutional Court (September 2017) complaining of non-enforcement; the application was declared inadmissible as out of time.

He then lodged the present application under Article 6 (civil limb) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging that the Fund’s persistent refusal to implement the final annulment judgments deprived him of effective judicial protection and interfered with his property rights as shareholder and Protocol debtor.

The case of Erol Aksoy v. Türkiye concerns the non-enforcement of two final Supreme Administrative Court judgments that annulled the valuation, tender and sale of Viva TV and Radio Viva. These media assets belonged to companies within the Erol Aksoy Group, in which the applicant held (mostly indirect) shares.

In March 2001, amid Turkey’s economic crisis, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Board transferred İktisat Bank to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund after finding the bank insolvent and its assets diverted. In May 2006 the Fund and the Erol Aksoy Group (the applicant personally, family members and numerous group companies) signed a Liquidation Protocol under which all debtors assumed joint and several liability. In 2008 the Fund declared default, assumed management of the group companies and resolved to sell their assets.

Several of those companies owned Viva TV and Radio Viva. The Fund consolidated the relevant assets into two economic units, later merged into a single unit. Valuations by the Industrial Development Bank of Türkiye produced figures of USD 4.258 million (Radio Viva) and USD 373 400 (Viva TV) in 2007, and USD 5.782 million and USD 132 000 respectively in 2009. After unsuccessful tenders the Fund set a reserve of USD 6 million based on the 2009 report and, following negotiations with a single bidder, sold the unit in May 2012 for USD 5 million. The purchaser paid the price and received title the same day.

The applicant, asserting standing as protocol signatory, personal guarantor and shareholder, brought two sets of administrative proceedings. In the first he challenged the 13 January 2011 decision that had authorised the tender and fixed the USD 6 million reserve. The 13th Chamber dismissed the claim in 2014, but the General Assembly of the Supreme Administrative Court annulled the decision on 7 July 2015 because the Fund had relied on an outdated valuation without a fresh market assessment. The judgment became final in January 2016. In the second set of proceedings he attacked the sale itself. After initial dismissals, the 13th Chamber, citing the General Assembly’s ruling, annulled the sale on 30 June 2017 as legally dependent on the now-void valuation decision.

The applicant promptly requested enforcement of both judgments. The Fund refused, stating that the sale had been completed, the purchase price used to pay creditors, control of the assets transferred to a bona-fide third party, and restoration of the status quo both legally and practically impossible. An individual application to the Constitutional Court alleging breaches of the rights to property and a fair trial was declared inadmissible as out of time.

These facts form the basis of the complaints under Article 6 (non-enforcement of final judgments affecting civil rights) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (interference with possessions).

The case of Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (no. 5067/23) concerns Mr Zlatan Begić, a 1975-born BiH citizen living in Tuzla and a high-ranking Democratic Front official serving as a member of the House of Representatives (the State Parliament’s first chamber). He does not declare affiliation with any of the Constitution’s “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats or Serbs) and thus falls into the residual category of “Others.” On 1 December 2022 two fellow members nominated him for Chair or Deputy Chair of the House. The nomination was never put to a vote because it conflicted with the House’s Rules of Procedure, which implement Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution: each chamber must elect one Serb, one Bosniac and one Croat to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs on a rotating basis. No comparable ethnic restriction applies to ordinary membership of the House.

The Constitution, an annex to the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, divides BiH into two Entities plus the Brčko District and embeds extensive ethnic power-sharing: a vital-interest veto, an Entity veto, a second chamber (House of Peoples) composed solely of five delegates from each constituent people, and a three-member Presidency likewise reserved for one member of each group. These devices were inserted late in the Dayton negotiations at the insistence of the warring parties, even though the mediators recognised their likely incompatibility with human-rights norms. Article II § 2 was therefore inserted to give the Convention and its Protocols “priority over all other law,” with the expectation that the ethnic arrangements would be phased out. They have never been amended.

The applicant’s complaint—brought under Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention, Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12—centres on this blanket exclusion of “Others” from the House’s presiding offices. The Constitutional Court has repeatedly declined to review the Constitution itself against the Convention, holding that the latter does not prevail over the former and that the Court lacks jurisdiction to strike down constitutional text. After the Court’s judgments in Sejdić and Finci, Zornić and Pilav, it has simply declared similar applications inadmissible on the ground that only a constitutional amendment (which the political institutions have failed to adopt) can remove the incompatibility.

The Venice Commission and other international bodies have long criticised the resulting system as both inefficient and discriminatory: it privileges ethnic identity over citizenship, excludes persons of mixed or non-constituent origin from key offices, and makes effective government dependent on perpetual ethnic consensus. The Government has not shown any objective and reasonable justification for continuing to bar “Others” from the Chair/Deputy Chair posts once they have already been elected to the House itself. The Fourth Section therefore found a violation of the general prohibition of discrimination in Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The case of Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 5067/23) concerns a complaint by Zlatan Begić, a Bosnian citizen born in 1975 and resident in Tuzla, regarding his exclusion from standing for the positions of Chair or Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives (the lower chamber of the State Parliamentary Assembly). Begić, a senior official of the Democratic Front party and an elected member of the House, does not declare affiliation with any of the three constitutionally designated “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats or Serbs). He therefore falls into the residual category of “Others.”

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 1995 Constitution, annexed to the Dayton Peace Agreement, structures the State around ethnic power-sharing. The country comprises two Entities (the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska) plus the Brčko District. Key institutions—including the tripartite Presidency and the House of Peoples—are reserved exclusively for members of the constituent peoples. Although election to the House of Representatives itself carries no ethnic qualification, Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution requires that each chamber select “one Serb, one Bosniac, and one Croat” from among its members to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the chairmanship rotating among them. The House’s Rules of Procedure (Article 4) implement this rule by mandating the election of “a representative from each constituent people.”

On 1 December 2022 two fellow Representatives nominated Begić for Chair/Deputy Chair. The nomination was not put to a vote because it failed to satisfy the ethnic requirement in the Rules of Procedure. Begić alleged that this exclusion constituted discrimination contrary to Article 14 of the Convention, Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination), as well as an abuse of rights under Article 17.

The Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina has repeatedly declined jurisdiction to examine whether these constitutional provisions themselves violate the Convention, holding that the Convention does not prevail over the Constitution. Earlier Strasbourg judgments (Sejdić and Finci, Zornić, Pilav) had already found analogous ethnic restrictions on the Presidency and House of Peoples to be discriminatory; the domestic court thereafter treated such complaints as already decided and therefore inadmissible.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined the case solely under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. It recalled that the Dayton arrangements, while originally intended as a temporary post-conflict mechanism, had never been amended despite the Court’s prior rulings and the Constitution’s own provision (Article II § 2) giving the Convention priority over “all other law.” The Court found no objective and reasonable justification for continuing to bar “Others” from the House’s presiding offices more than three decades after Dayton. The restriction therefore violated the general prohibition of discrimination. The judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention.

The case of Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina concerns the applicant Zlatan Begić, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1975 and resident in Tuzla. A high-ranking official of the Democratic Front party and an elected member of the House of Representatives (the first chamber of the State Parliamentary Assembly), Begić does not declare affiliation with any of the three constitutionally defined “constituent peoples” (Bosniacs, Croats and Serbs). He therefore falls into the residual constitutional category of “Others.”

The nomination was not put to a vote because it failed to satisfy Article 4 of the House’s Rules of Procedure, which implement Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution. That provision requires each chamber to select from its members “one Serb, one Bosniac, and one Croat” to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs, the chairmanship rotating among them. Consequently, persons who decline to identify with a constituent people are automatically ineligible for these leadership posts, even though no ethnic criterion applies to membership of the House itself.

The Constitution, annexed to the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, established an elaborate consociational architecture intended to protect the three constituent peoples after the 1992–95 war. In addition to the ethnic composition of the House of Peoples and the tripartite Presidency, it introduced vital-interest and Entity vetoes that make it impossible to adopt decisions against the will of any constituent people. Although the international mediators recognised that these arrangements were likely to conflict with human-rights norms, they inserted Article II § 2, which gives the European Convention and its Protocols “priority over all other law,” in the expectation that the ethnic privileges would be phased out. They have never been amended.

After the Strasbourg Court’s judgments in Sejdić and Finci, Zornić and Pilav—which found analogous ethnic restrictions on access to the Presidency and the House of Peoples to be discriminatory—the Constitutional Court began dismissing similar complaints as already decided, while emphasising that only a constitutional amendment by the Parliamentary Assembly can remove the incompatibility.

The Venice Commission has repeatedly criticised the same power-sharing mechanisms as making effective government extremely difficult and as forcing citizens of mixed or other origin either to identify artificially with one of the three peoples or to remain excluded from key offices. It has recommended progressive replacement of ethnic representation by civic representation, while acknowledging that the vital-interest veto cannot be abolished overnight.

Begić’s complaint, brought under Article 14 of the Convention, Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, therefore centres on the absence of any objective and reasonable justification for denying an elected member of the House of Representatives eligibility for its chairmanship solely because he refuses to declare affiliation with a constituent people. The case thus continues the line of Strasbourg jurisprudence examining whether the Dayton arrangements, originally designed as a transitional peace settlement, remain compatible with the Convention’s prohibition of discrimination more than three decades later.
001-248591:
The case of Đaković v. Serbia concerns an application by Croatian national Vilko Đaković alleging that Serbian authorities violated Article 2 of the Convention by failing to conduct an effective investigation into the 1991 killing of his father, P.Đ., during the armed conflict in Croatia.

On 10 October 1991, the Yugoslav People’s Army, together with locally recruited territorial defence forces, police and volunteers, shelled and captured the village of Lovas. P.Đ. was shot and killed in the assault.

In November 2007 the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor indicted 14 persons for war crimes against civilians committed in Lovas in October 1991. Four were initially charged with P.Đ.’s killing; an amended indictment in 2011 left only Ž.K. (then local police commander) charged with that offence. He was alleged to have organised and participated in the 10 October attack on D.L.’s orders. The group used indiscriminate fire and grenades, killing seven civilians including P.Đ. The remaining accused faced charges relating to later events. During the proceedings a prosecutor recorded serious concerns about D.L.’s liability but decided the issue should be examined only after the case against the direct perpetrators.

In June 2019 the Belgrade High Court convicted eight defendants, including Ž.K. for the 10 October events, finding he had acted on D.L.’s orders. In November 2020 the Court of Appeal acquitted Ž.K. and another defendant and reduced other sentences.

On 2 November 2016 the Humanitarian Law Centre filed a criminal complaint on the applicant’s behalf against D.L. for war crimes, alleging he had ordered the 9–10 October attacks that killed 21 civilians, including P.Đ. The complaint relied on evidence already gathered in the first set of proceedings. The prosecutor confirmed that a preliminary investigation was under way. Between February 2017 and October 2018 five written prompts were sent seeking progress; an October 2018 objection alleging inactivity was dismissed, as was a further objection to the Public Prosecutor.

The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal in December 2018 complaining that two years after the complaint no witnesses or suspects had been questioned, no evidence collected and no formal investigation opened, despite the availability of existing case files. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal in March 2022, noting that statements had been taken from D.L. and retired officers, relevant files reviewed, and a formal investigation opened against D.L. on 5 February 2021.

D.L. was indicted in September 2022 for war crimes including the killing of 21 civilians. The trial opened in December 2022 and remains pending at first instance, with 19 hearings scheduled (14 held, five postponed) as of January 2026. The applicant was summoned twice in 2024 but was unable to testify.

These facts demonstrate prolonged inactivity from the 1991 killing, delayed first proceedings (indictment 2007, final decision 2020), a 2016 complaint that produced a formal investigation only in 2021, and still-unconcluded proceedings in 2026, all relevant to the alleged lack of promptness and reasonable expedition.

The village was captured that day by the Yugoslav People’s Army, together with locally recruited territorial defence forces, police and volunteers, following an assault involving indiscriminate gunfire, grenades and executions of civilians. Seven civilians, including P.Đ., died.

He was alleged to have directed the assault on orders from Yugoslav People’s Army commander D.L. During the trial an official note recorded serious concerns about D.L.’s own liability, but prosecutors decided to address it only after proceedings against the direct perpetrators concluded. In June 2019 the Belgrade High Court convicted Ž.K. (and others). In November 2020 the Court of Appeal acquitted him.

On 2 November 2016 the Humanitarian Law Centre lodged a criminal complaint on the applicant’s behalf against D.L. for war crimes, relying on evidence already contained in the earlier case file. The Prosecutor’s Office confirmed a preliminary investigation was under way. Between February 2017 and October 2018 the Centre sent five written reminders and then a formal objection alleging inactivity; both the War Crimes Prosecutor and the Public Prosecutor dismissed the objection.

The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal in December 2018, complaining that two years after the complaint no witnesses or suspects had been questioned, no evidence collected and no formal investigation opened, despite the case’s limited complexity and the existence of a complete prior file. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal in March 2022. It accepted the Prosecutor’s account that statements had been taken from D.L. and retired officers, that the earlier case files had been examined, and that a formal investigation had been opened against D.L. on 5 February 2021.

D.L. was indicted on 12 September 2022 for war crimes that included the killing of 21 civilians, among them P.Đ. Trial began in December 2022 and remains pending at first instance. The applicant was summoned as a witness in 2024 but was unable to give evidence.

The core facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the long interval between the 2016 complaint (supported by an existing investigative file) and the opening of a formal investigation in 2021, the even later indictment, and the still-unfinished trial more than nine years after the complaint and 34 years after the killing.

The case of Đaković v. Serbia (application no. 30749/22) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by Croatian national Vilko Đaković. He alleged a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention, claiming that Serbian authorities failed to conduct an effective official investigation into the 1991 killing of his father, P.Đ., during the armed conflict in Croatia.

P.Đ. was shot and killed in the assault. In November 2007 the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor indicted 14 individuals for war crimes against civilians committed in Lovas that October. Four of the accused were initially charged, inter alia, with P.Đ.’s killing. An amended indictment in December 2011 dropped those charges against three of them; only Ž.K., then commander of the local police station, remained charged with the killing. He was accused of organising and participating in the 10 October attack on the orders of Yugoslav Army commander D.L. The attack, carried out without military necessity by an armed group using indiscriminate gunfire and grenades, killed seven civilians including P.Đ.

In June 2019 the Belgrade High Court convicted eight defendants of war crimes; Ž.K. was found guilty of directing the 10 October assault on D.L.’s orders. In November 2020 the Belgrade Court of Appeal acquitted Ž.K.

On 2 November 2016 the Humanitarian Law Centre lodged a criminal complaint on the applicant’s behalf against D.L. for war crimes against the civilian population, alleging that he had ordered the 9–10 October attacks that killed 21 civilians including P.Đ. The complaint relied on evidence already contained in the first set of proceedings. The War Crimes Prosecutor’s Office stated that a preliminary investigation was under way. Between February 2017 and October 2018 the Centre submitted five written prompts seeking information and progress, followed by formal objections alleging inactivity; all were dismissed.

The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal in December 2018, complaining that two years after the complaint no injured parties or suspects had been questioned, no evidence collected and no investigation opened, despite the case’s simplicity and the existence of relevant evidence in the earlier file. He argued that the prolonged inactivity breached the requirement of an effective investigation. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal in March 2022. It noted that after receipt of the complaint the prosecutor had taken statements from D.L. and retired officers, reviewed the earlier case file (which itself contained an official note recording serious concerns about D.L.’s liability that were to be addressed only after the first trial concluded), and formally opened an investigation against D.L. on 5 February 2021.

D.L. was indicted on 12 September 2022 for war crimes including the killing of 21 civilians. The trial began in December 2022 and remains pending at first instance, with 19 hearings scheduled of which 14 have been held. The applicant was summoned twice as a witness in 2024 but did not testify, once because a video link could not be organised and once because of illness.

The applicant maintained that the investigation into his father’s death lacked the promptness and reasonable expedition required by Article 2. The Court examined these delays against the background of the earlier, protracted proceedings concerning the same events.
