The case of Tishkina v. Bulgaria (Application no. 4711/20) concerns a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that the Bulgarian authorities failed to take reasonable measures to protect the applicant’s house from irreparable structural damage caused by illegal coal mining by private individuals. The applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1957, inherited a 52-square-metre house in Pernik’s Rudnichar district (purchased by her mother in 1995). Pernik has a long mining history; an underground mine operated from 1906 until its closure in 1962 due to depletion. In 2003 a concession covering the entire city (approximately 14,000 hectares) was granted to Mini Otkrit Vagledobiv EAD, which was obliged to operate safely, prevent landslides and compensate for damage from poor practices.

Illegal small-scale underground mining by groups of (often former) miners using basic tools began around 1996–1998 in areas not being exploited by the concessionaire. It persisted despite police filling of pits/tunnels, awareness campaigns and some fatalities from collapses or gas. Activity declined around 2008–2010 but resurged after a May 2012 earthquake exposed shallow deposits; estimates indicated 150–400 people extracting 60–70 tonnes of coal daily for the black market, endangering houses and infrastructure. Police checks numbered 52 in 2013 and 83 in 2014, typically resulting only in short-term custody. Pre-2017 theft prosecutions (illegal mining was not then a specific offence) were discontinued due to the low value of seized coal.

From 2010 the applicant and her mother observed tunnels (entrances on adjacent mining-company land) running directly beneath their hillside house, with nocturnal voices, pickaxe sounds and vibrations. Cracks appeared in walls (later widening to 5–12 cm), tiles, window frames (causing leaks) and outdoor ground; part of the floor sank and the street subsided. The mother lodged repeated complaints from late 2011 onward with the municipality, mining company, police, Ombudsman and Parliament, reporting distress, threats, reopened tunnels and further damage. Limited earthquake-repair aid was received in 2012. After her mother’s death in August 2013 the applicant inherited the property, vacated it as unsafe (despite her prior repairs) and moved elsewhere. A July 2015 landslide (followed by smaller ones) caused additional damage; by a 2018 expert inspection the house was tilted, irreparable and uninhabitable. Illegal mining continued in the area in 2017–2018.

Municipal authorities had discussed the problem since 2009 and appointed a commission in 2012. They exchanged letters with the Ministry of Economy (which confirmed damage but assigned primary control of unlicensed extraction to the mayor under section 90(5) of the Underground Resources Act), police and the mining company, urging action. The company filled tunnel entrances several times (2012, 2014, 2015) but they were reopened; it cited proximity of houses and utilities as limiting more comprehensive work and requested state help. The mayor imposed modest fines (BGN 50–70) on some miners from 2015–2017 under a municipal ordinance. After the 2015 landslide an emergency was declared, houses evacuated and a 24-hour police post established. A December 2015 geological report confirmed two long parallel galleries (5–15 m deep) caused by illegal mining had destabilised the terrain; it recommended filling and sealing tunnels. Works occurred only after later government funding, with the emergency lifted in December 2017. An expert later found no technical barrier to earlier intervention.

In 2017 the applicant brought unsuccessful tort proceedings against the municipality, claiming it had failed to act under section 90(5) despite knowledge of the risks (2011–2015). Domestic courts held the concessionaire primarily responsible, viewed the mayor’s letters and fines as adequate (an obligation of means, not result) and dismissed the claims (house value plus other losses). The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this in July 2019. The applicant argued these measures were too late, fragmented and ineffective, reflecting unclear responsibilities, inadequate legal tools and failure to prevent foreseeable, serious property damage.

Progressive damage included widening cracks (5–12 cm), deformed windows, sinking floors and land holes. By 2018 an expert found the house irreparably tilted and uninhabitable. A major landslide on 1 July 2015 (plus smaller ones later) caused further damage; the house was among those declared uninhabitable.

The municipality sent multiple letters (2012–2015) urging the Ministry of Economy, prosecutors, police and the mining company to act. The Ministry confirmed damage, cited the Underground Resources Act (s. 90(5)) assigning the mayor control over unlicensed extraction, and pressed the company. Police confirmed ongoing mining and urged municipal action. The company filled tunnel entrances repeatedly (2012, 2014, 2015) but they were reopened; it cited nearby buildings/infrastructure as limiting factors and requested state help. The mayor imposed small fines (BGN 50–70) on some miners in 2015–2017 under a local ordinance.

After the 2015 landslide an emergency was declared, houses evacuated and a 24-hour police post established (until December 2017). A December 2015 geological report confirmed illegal tunnels (5–15 m deep) had destabilised the terrain, causing the surface damage, and recommended filling/sealing. She claimed the house’s value plus other losses. 001-248884:
The case of Sungur v. Türkiye concerns events during the Gezi Park protests in Istanbul on 28 May 2013. Applicant Ceyda Sungur, then a university research assistant, joined a sit-in opposing plans to redevelop the park into a shopping centre. During a police intervention, officer F.Z. of the Rapid Response Force sprayed tear gas directly at her head from less than one metre away. He continued spraying as she turned her back to protect herself. Photographs of the incident, in which she wore a red dress, circulated widely, earning her the nickname “the woman in red.” She experienced burning on her face and breathing difficulties but, in shock, did not seek immediate medical attention. She later reported pain lasting about an hour with no lasting physical effects; the injury was treatable by simple medical care and left no marks.

Administrative inquiries began promptly. Inspectors identified F.Z. and concluded he had used tear gas unnecessarily and unlawfully against the applicant (who offered no resistance) and others, in breach of the Directive on tear-gas weapons (which prohibits spraying from under one metre or against non-resisting persons). A disciplinary investigation reached the same findings. The Istanbul Police Disciplinary Committee imposed only a warning (a lighter sanction than the indicated reprimand) citing F.Z.’s clean record. The governorship authorised a criminal investigation.

The public prosecutor indicted F.Z. for abuse of duty. In her statement the applicant described unprovoked spraying without warning after she had fallen. At trial F.Z. claimed he acted on a superior’s order, that his launcher had malfunctioned, and that some protesters had been violent; he attributed inconsistencies in his accounts to initial failure to recognise himself in footage. Commanding officers gave conflicting evidence: one denied issuing any order, another said a superior had instructed use of gas against protesters attempting to breach a barricade. Video evidence confirmed F.Z. had targeted the applicant’s face at close range and continued after she turned away.

On 10 June 2015 the Istanbul Criminal Court of First Instance convicted F.Z. of intentionally causing bodily harm by exceeding his authority (Article 86 § 2 of the Criminal Code) and of abuse of duty toward other protesters, imposing two ten-month prison terms. It noted that tear gas is classified as a weapon and that F.Z. had abused his position. However, citing his good trial behaviour and lack of prior convictions, the court suspended pronouncement of the judgment for five years under Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on condition he committed no further intentional offence. It also required him to plant and tend 300 trees as a rehabilitative measure. The applicant’s objection, arguing that the suspension created impunity, was rejected. F.Z. completed the tree-planting obligation. In 2023 the court cancelled the judgment entirely after he remained offence-free.

Parallel proceedings against F.Z.’s superiors for issuing unlawful orders resulted in one acquittal and discontinuation of another case on limitation grounds. The applicant also complained to the Constitutional Court of a violation of the prohibition of inhuman treatment. In 2019 that court found the use of force unnecessary but held it could not assess proportionality because the applicant had not obtained a medical report and had shown limited diligence. It further held that the criminal process had been prompt and thorough, the sentence (though suspended) harsher than the statutory minimum, and the additional measures (trees plus disciplinary warning) sufficiently deterrent and proportionate. It therefore found no violation of Article 17 of the Constitution.

The European Court of Human Rights later examined the same facts under Article 3 of the Convention, focusing on whether the close-range spraying constituted degrading treatment and whether the domestic response provided adequate redress and deterrence.

Türkiye (no. 56462/19) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns an alleged violation of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) arising from a police officer's use of tear gas against the applicant during the 2013 Gezi Park protests.

On 28 May 2013, applicant Ceyda Sungur, then a 27-year-old urban planning research assistant, joined a peaceful sit-in in Istanbul's Gezi Park protesting government plans to replace the park with a shopping centre. During the police intervention, officer F.Z. sprayed tear gas directly at her head from under one metre, continuing as she turned away. She had shown no resistance or aggression. She suffered breathing difficulties and facial burning but, in shock, sought no immediate medical care. Widely circulated photos of her in a red dress made her a protest symbol ("the woman in red"). The injury was later classified as non-serious, treatable by simple medical care, with no lasting marks.

Inspectors promptly identified F.Z. as having used tear gas unnecessarily and unlawfully, breaching directives that prohibit spraying from under one metre, without warning, or against non-resistant persons. A disciplinary committee imposed only a warning (lighter than the indicated reprimand, citing his clean record).

Criminal proceedings followed. F.Z. was indicted for abuse of duty. He claimed superior orders, a launcher malfunction, protestor violence, and shoulder pain, but video evidence contradicted this. In 2015 the Istanbul Criminal Court convicted him of intentionally causing the applicant bodily harm by exceeding authorised force (and of abuse of duty toward others). It imposed 10-month prison terms (above the minimum, due to weapon use and abuse of office) but suspended pronouncement of the judgment for five years, requiring him to plant and tend 300 trees. The applicant objected that this produced impunity and lacked deterrence, but the Assize Court upheld the decision. After five offence-free years, the judgment was cancelled in 2023. Related proceedings against superiors ended in acquittal or were time-barred.

The applicant's 2015 Constitutional Court application alleged a violation of the prohibition of ill-treatment. In 2019 that court found the force unnecessary given her non-violent conduct but declined to assess proportionality, citing her failure to obtain a medical report or pursue her complaint diligently. Procedurally, it held that the prompt investigation, above-minimum (though suspended) sentence, disciplinary warning and tree-planting provided sufficient redress and deterrence.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the close-range spraying constituted degrading treatment, as the force was not rendered strictly necessary by the applicant's conduct. Domestically there was a failure to afford sufficient redress; application of the criminal-law system produced the perpetrator's impunity without the requisite deterrent effect. Thus both the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3 were violated.

The case of Sungur v. Türkiye (no. 56462/19) concerns alleged violations of Article 3 of the Convention (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) in both its substantive and procedural limbs. The applicant, Ceyda Sungur (born 1986), a research assistant, attended a peaceful sit-in protest on 28 May 2013 in Istanbul’s Gezi Park against plans to replace it with a shopping centre. This event initiated the wider Gezi Park protests. During the police intervention, Rapid Response Force officer F.Z. sprayed tear gas directly at her head from under one metre, continuing even after she turned away. Widely circulated photographs of her in a red dress made her a symbol of the protests. She experienced breathing difficulties and facial burning but, in shock, sought no immediate medical care. She later described only brief pain with no lasting effects or marks, consistent with injury treatable by simple medical intervention.

Administrative inspectors quickly identified F.Z. and found his actions unnecessary and unlawful: Sungur had shown no resistance, and he had violated the Directive on tear-gas weapons (prohibiting use from under one metre or against non-aggressive persons). A disciplinary committee imposed only a warning (reduced from a reprimand owing to his clean record). The Istanbul Public Prosecutor charged F.Z. with abuse of duty. In his statements he initially denied involvement, later claiming a superior’s order, launcher malfunction, shoulder pain and protester violence. Commanding officers gave conflicting accounts of any order. Video evidence confirmed the close-range, unprovoked spraying without warning.

The Istanbul Criminal Court convicted F.Z. of intentionally causing minor bodily harm by exceeding his authority to use force (and of abuse of duty regarding other protesters), imposing two ten-month prison terms. It noted that force was permissible only when strictly necessary and that an unlawful demonstration did not justify it absent violence. Nevertheless, citing F.Z.’s good trial behaviour and lack of prior convictions, the court suspended pronouncement of the judgment for five years under the Code of Criminal Procedure, on condition he commit no further intentional offence, and ordered him to plant and tend 300 trees. Sungur’s objection that this produced impunity was rejected. After five years the conviction was cancelled entirely. Parallel complaints against superiors and senior officials resulted in non-prosecution, acquittals or discontinuation on limitation grounds.

Although the force was unnecessary, the applicant’s failure to obtain a medical report or pursue her complaint diligently prevented a proportionality assessment. Procedurally, the prompt ex officio investigation, collection of evidence, above-minimum sentence (even if suspended), disciplinary warning and tree-planting measure were deemed proportionate and deterrent.

The European Court found both a substantive and a procedural violation of Article 3. The spraying was not rendered strictly necessary by the applicant’s conduct and amounted to degrading treatment. Domestic authorities failed to afford sufficient redress: the criminal-law response produced the perpetrator’s impunity and lacked the required deterrent effect.

The case of *Manjani v. Albania* (ECtHR, Third Section, Application no. 32283/23, judgment of 10 March 2026) concerns a violation of Article 8 of the Convention arising from the refusal to admit the applicant to magistrate training on the basis of a spent juvenile conviction.

Shiqiri Manjani, an Albanian national born in 1991, applied in February 2020 to the School of Magistrates for the three-year prosecutor-profile initial training programme. He disclosed that in 2006, at age 15, he had been convicted of theft and legally rehabilitated as of 1 December 2014. After a preliminary assessment confirming he met the admission criteria, he passed the entrance examination. Background and asset verification followed.

The underlying 2006 offence occurred in September of that year. During a meeting between Manjani’s father and a potential land buyer (D.), the 15-year-old applicant was left alone in D.’s car. He opened the glove compartment, took 1,000,400 Albanian leks, and hid the money nearby among rubbish. Upon D.’s return the money was missing; the applicant initially denied taking it but later admitted the act at the police station, explaining he had felt awkward confessing in front of others. The money was immediately recovered and returned. The Bulqizë District Court convicted him of theft (Criminal Code Article 134) and imposed an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for three years. The court emphasised the applicant’s admission of guilt, low social danger, minimal consequences, minor age, educational needs, and the prompt restitution. The judgment became final on 1 December 2006. Under Article 69 of the Criminal Code he was thereafter treated as never having been convicted.

On 17 December 2020 the High Prosecutorial Council (HPC) nevertheless refused admission by a 7–2 majority. It interpreted section 28(d) of the Status of Judges and Prosecutors Act (then requiring that a candidate “has not been convicted by a final criminal judgment”) as an absolute bar covering an individual’s entire criminal history, irrespective of rehabilitation, in order to protect the integrity of the judiciary. Dissenting members noted that the legislature had omitted any explicit exclusion of rehabilitation.

Manjani’s appeals failed. The Administrative Court of Appeal (18 March 2021) held that section 28(d), as a special law, referred to the fact of conviction regardless of the Criminal Code’s rehabilitation provisions. The Supreme Court (17 March 2022) acknowledged the provision’s original lack of clarity but concluded that even before its 2021 amendment (which expressly disregarded rehabilitation for offences discrediting a magistrate’s image) it had always intended a lifetime ban. Theft, being intentional, permanently undermined public trust; the applicant’s age at the time of the offence was irrelevant. The Constitutional Court (23 March 2023) found no arbitrary interpretation, a legitimate aim of protecting judicial integrity, and no significant interference with private life, since other professions remained open. A dissenting judge criticised the absence of any individualised balancing that took account of the applicant’s juvenile status and subsequent 2017 juvenile-justice reforms.

At the time of the refusal Manjani was working as a judicial police officer. The Court held that Article 8 applied because the absolute, permanent exclusion had a serious impact on his choice of professional and private life, social identity and relationships with others. Domestic authorities failed to give sufficient weight to his age at the time of the offence or to conduct a thorough, individualised assessment of his personal circumstances. The measure, imposed at an early stage of his career and lasting indefinitely, was therefore disproportionate.

The case of *Manjani v. Albania* (Application no. 32283/23) before the ECHR Third Section concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life). The money was immediately recovered. On 21 November 2006 the Bulqizë District Court convicted him of theft under Article 134 of the Criminal Code and imposed an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for three years under Article 59. The court cited his minor age, low social danger, admission of guilt, minimal consequences, and need to continue education. The judgment became final on 1 December 2006. Under Article 69 of the Criminal Code he was rehabilitated as of 1 December 2014 and thereafter treated as having no conviction.

He disclosed the 2006 conviction and rehabilitation, submitted supporting certificates, passed the admission examination and was initially listed as meeting the criteria. Background verification followed. The HPC construed the provision as covering an individual’s entire criminal history, irrespective of rehabilitation, in order to protect judicial integrity. Dissenters noted that rehabilitation under Article 69 meant the applicant was legally regarded as unconvicted.

Manjani appealed. The Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed the claim on 18 March 2021 (2–1), holding that the special statutory criterion prevailed over general rehabilitation rules and referred to the fact of conviction itself. Dissenting judges criticised the domestic reasoning for effectively applying later or draft amendments retroactively, failing to conduct an individualised proportionality assessment, ignoring the applicant’s age and limited culpability, and disregarding Albania’s 2017 Juvenile Justice Code (which prioritises reintegration, privacy, diversion and the best interests of the child) as well as international standards (UN CRC Articles 3 and 40, CoE recommendations on juvenile records and rehabilitation). At the time of the proceedings the applicant worked as a judicial police officer (since 2019) after earlier private-sector legal practice.

The refusal therefore constituted an absolute, permanent barrier at an early stage of the applicant’s professional life, affecting his choice of career, social identity and relationships, without adequate consideration of rehabilitation, the trivial nature and circumstances of the offence, or subsequent conduct.

The applicant’s age at the time of the offence was treated as irrelevant. Dissenting judges at every level criticised the failure to take account of the applicant’s age, the rehabilitative purpose of juvenile justice, the limited gravity of the offence and the absence of any individualised assessment of current risk or integrity. At the time of the proceedings Manjani was working as a judicial police officer after earlier private legal practice.

These facts form the core of the complaint: an absolute, lifelong exclusion from a chosen profession imposed at an early stage of adult life, without regard to rehabilitation or the applicant’s juvenile status, thereby affecting his professional identity, social relations and private life.
001-249529:
The case of H.D. v. Italy concerns a Burkinabe national born on 1 January 2006 who arrived in Italy as an unaccompanied minor migrant on 24 June 2023. He was immediately placed in the Sant’Anna C.A.R.A. Regional Hub, an adult reception and asylum-seeker centre in Isola di Capo Rizzuto. A residence permit confirming his minority and an internal centre card stating his age were issued on 31 July 2023. He remained there for over five months until 6 December 2023, during which time he claimed he could not leave the facility.

On 19 October 2023 his representatives filed an urgent application under Article 700 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Catanzaro District Court. They alleged de facto detention in an adult-only centre marked by overcrowding and inadequate conditions, seeking recognition of the unlawfulness of his stay and an order for transfer to a suitable facility for unaccompanied minors. No hearing had been scheduled by the time they applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 1 December 2023 under Rule 39. The Court indicated an interim measure on 5 December 2023 requiring transfer to a centre providing the assistance required for an unaccompanied minor. The applicant was moved the following day to a minors’ facility in Lamezia Terme.

Notice of a hearing fixed for 19 December 2023 reached the representatives on the day of transfer. The hearing was later postponed to 9 January 2024. On 20 December 2023 the representatives informed the domestic court of the transfer and of their consequent loss of interest, requesting that the case be struck out. The Catanzaro District Court did so on 14 February 2024.

The applicant described the Sant’Anna centre as intended solely for adults, yet chronically housing unaccompanied minors in a situation of severe overcrowding (approximately 830 residents, including 200 minors, against a capacity of 641). He alleged poor material and hygienic conditions, absence of dedicated services, unrestricted contact with adults, and inability to leave or to meet his lawyers. Supporting material included replies from the Prefecture of Crotone and the Questura confirming that the centre was not designed for unaccompanied minors but hosted them temporarily in a separate area during emergency arrivals. A February 2023 report of the National Guarantor documented extremely poor conditions, the chronic rather than exceptional presence of minors, lack of specific services, free movement between adult and minor areas, and incidents of harassment; on the day of inspection the minors’ area was being used as a mixed module. A January 2023 Save the Children report described the former military site (barbed wire, barred windows) as severely overcrowded, while an ASGI on-site check in June 2023 recorded 238 unaccompanied minors.

The Government maintained that overall conditions were adequate and that an addendum to the management contract of 20 September 2023 provided for increased staff and services for minors.

Domestic law prohibited the refusal of entry or expulsion of unaccompanied minors except in limited circumstances. Following significant arrivals, Decree-Law no. 133 of 5 October 2023 (the Cutro Decree) authorised, from that date, the provisional placement of minors aged 16 or over in a dedicated area of adult centres for up to 90 days (extendable by 60 days) when dedicated facilities were unavailable. Article 13 of the Constitution requires a reasoned judicial order for any restriction of personal liberty. Article 700 of the Code of Civil Procedure offers a residual urgent measure, while Article 2043 of the Civil Code permits claims for damages arising from unlawful acts. Constitutional Court and Court of Cassation case-law treats Article 700 as an autonomous, albeit atypical, remedy capable of protecting fundamental rights, and recognises the availability of compensation under Article 2043 for unlawful detention.

These facts underpin the complaints of unlawful and unjustified detention lacking a clear legal basis and information as to its reasons, of insufficiently expeditious domestic proceedings, of inhuman and degrading treatment arising from the placement of a vulnerable minor in inadequate adult-centre conditions without age-appropriate services, and of the absence of an effective remedy.

**Case Summary: H.D. v. Italy (Application no. 41645/23)**

H.D., a Burkinabe national born on 1 January 2006, arrived in Italy on 24 June 2023 as an unaccompanied minor. He was immediately placed in the Sant’Anna C.A.R.A. Regional Hub, an adult reception centre and asylum-seeker facility in Isola di Capo Rizzuto, Crotone, with a stated capacity of 641. He remained there for over five months until 6 December 2023. A residence permit identifying him as a minor and an internal centre card confirming his age were issued on 31 July 2023. The applicant stated he could not leave the centre during this period.

The applicant’s representatives lodged an urgent application on 19 October 2023 under Article 700 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure before the Catanzaro District Court. They alleged de facto detention in a facility intended solely for adults, citing overcrowding (around 830 occupants, including approximately 200 minors), poor material and hygienic conditions, lack of separation from adults, absence of dedicated services for minors, and inability to meet lawyers. The application sought recognition of the unlawful detention and transfer to an appropriate unaccompanied-minors facility. On 1 December 2023, with domestic proceedings still pending and no hearing scheduled, the applicant requested an interim measure from the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. On 5 December 2023 the Court indicated that he should be transferred to a suitable unaccompanied-minors centre offering necessary assistance. He was transferred on 6 December 2023. The domestic hearing was later scheduled for 19 December 2023 (postponed to 9 January 2024); after notification of the transfer and withdrawal of interest, the District Court struck the case from the list on 14 February 2024.

The applicant described the Sant’Anna centre as a former military facility retaining barbed-wire fencing and barred windows, characterised by severe overcrowding, inadequate hygiene, unrestricted contact between minors and adults (despite a designated minors’ area), and no specialised services or freedom of movement for unaccompanied minors. Supporting evidence included replies from the Prefecture of Crotone and local police confirming the centre was not intended for unaccompanied minors except in emergencies (when they were housed separately); a February 2023 National Guarantor report documenting chronically poor conditions, routine (not exceptional) presence of unaccompanied minors, lack of specific services, unrestricted adult-minor contact, and reported harassment of minor females; a January 2023 Save the Children report on structural features and overcrowding; and a June 2023 ASGI report noting 238 unaccompanied minors. The Government maintained that overall conditions were adequate and submitted a September 2023 contractual addendum authorising increased staff and services for minors.

Relevant domestic law included Article 13 of the Italian Constitution (inviolability of personal liberty, requiring judicial authorisation and legal basis for restrictions); Article 700 of the Code of Civil Procedure (urgent interim measures to prevent irreparable harm); Article 2043 of the Civil Code (liability for unlawful damage); and Legislative Decree no. 286/1998 (prohibiting refusal of entry or expulsion of unaccompanied minors except in limited cases). Provisions on reception of unaccompanied minors (summarised in prior case-law) were later amended by Decree-Law no. 133/2023 (the “Cutro Decree,” converted into Law no. 176/2023), which from 6 October 2023 permitted, in cases of significant arrivals and unavailability of dedicated facilities, provisional placement of minors aged 16 or older in designated areas of adult centres for up to 90 days (extendable by 60 days).

These facts underpin the alleged violations: placement amounting to unlawful detention lacking a clear, accessible legal basis and not justified under Article 5 § 1 (f); failure to inform the applicant of the legal reasons for detention; insufficiently expeditious domestic proceedings (Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4); inhuman and degrading treatment arising from confinement of a vulnerable unaccompanied minor in inadequate adult-centre conditions without age-appropriate services (Article 3); and the absence of effective remedies (Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3). The Court indicated an interim measure that was complied with, after which the domestic application was discontinued.

**Summary of H.D. v. Italy (ECHR, Application no. 41645/23)**

The applicant, a Burkinabe national born on 1 January 2006, arrived in Italy as an unaccompanied minor on 24 June 2023 and was immediately placed in the Sant’Anna C.A.R.A. Regional Hub, an adult reception centre and asylum-seekers’ facility in Isola di Capo Rizzuto, Crotone. A residence permit noting his minority was issued on 31 July 2023. He remained there for over five months, until 6 December 2023, during which he alleged he was unable to leave.

On 19 October 2023 his representatives filed an urgent application under Article 700 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Catanzaro District Court, seeking recognition of his de facto detention and transfer to a suitable facility for unaccompanied minors. They cited the centre’s exclusive designation for adults, overcrowding, and inadequate conditions, while limiting the claim to the detention issue. No hearing was scheduled promptly. On 1 December 2023 the applicant requested an interim measure from the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. On 5 December the Court indicated that he should be transferred to an appropriate centre for unaccompanied minors. Transfer occurred the next day. The domestic hearing, scheduled for 19 December 2023 and later postponed to 9 January 2024, became moot; the court struck the case out on 14 February 2024 after being informed of the transfer and the applicant’s consequent lack of interest.

The applicant described the Sant’Anna centre as intended solely for adults yet chronically housing unaccompanied minors (around 200 at the relevant time, against a capacity of 641 and an occupancy of some 830). He reported severe overcrowding, poor material and hygienic conditions, unrestricted contact with adults, absence of age-appropriate services, inability to leave, and difficulties meeting lawyers. Supporting material included official replies confirming that the centre was not designed for unaccompanied minors (though they were housed in a “separate area” during emergencies), a February 2023 report by the National Guarantor for the rights of detained persons documenting chronic (not exceptional) presence of minors, lack of dedicated services, free movement between adult and minor areas, mixed modules, and reported harassment, plus NGO reports (Save the Children, January 2023; ASGI, June 2023) describing military-style features, barbed wire, barred windows, and 238 unaccompanied minors present. The Government maintained that conditions were adequate overall and pointed to a September 2023 contractual addendum providing for increased staff and services.

These facts underpinned the complaints of unlawful detention (Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4) arising from the absence of a clear, accessible legal basis for holding an unaccompanied minor in an adult facility for more than five months, the lack of justification under Article 5 § 1(f), failure to inform him of the legal reasons for detention, and the lack of sufficiently expeditious domestic review. They also founded the Article 3 claim of inhuman and degrading treatment stemming from placement in inadequate conditions without services commensurate with his age and vulnerability, together with the Article 13 complaint of no effective remedy. Relevant domestic law included Article 13 of the Constitution (inviolability of personal liberty), Article 700 of the Code of Civil Procedure (urgent protective measures), general civil-liability rules, and provisions on unaccompanied minors (including the October 2023 “Cutro Decree” permitting limited temporary placement of 16-year-olds in adult facilities). The Court later found violations of all invoked provisions.
001-249531:
**Summary of Novák v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 6656/24)**

The applicant, a Czech national and father of two daughters (born 2014 and 2018), lived with their mother in Brno until April 2021. Upon separation they agreed to share custody. In September 2021 the mother petitioned for divorce and sole custody; the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022 the mother refused shared arrangements, though the applicant maintained regular weekly and weekend contact. The family attended counselling without reaching agreement.

While proceedings on the merits were pending, the applicant obtained an interim shared-custody order from the Brno Municipal Court on 18 May 2022. The Brno Regional Court overturned it on 14 June 2022, finding no necessity because the children were properly cared for and the applicant had regular contact.

On 14 July 2022 the Municipal Court awarded weekly shared custody, relying on counselling reports and the guardian ad litem’s view that both parents had positive relationships with the children and were capable of raising them. The mother’s appeal had suspensive effect.

On 28 August 2022 the mother unilaterally relocated the children to Prague (more than 200 km away), enrolled them in a new school, and proposed reduced contact (every other weekend plus holidays). She later sought court authorisation for the move. The applicant immediately informed the social-welfare authority, which classified the children as “endangered.” On 7 September 2022 he applied for interim measures granting him custody (with the mother having fortnightly contact) and ordering the children’s return to Brno and their original schools, arguing the move breached Article 877 of the Civil Code.

On 12 September 2022 the Municipal Court dismissed both applications. It referred to the June 2022 Regional Court ruling, noted the applicant still had access and the mother provided good care, and found no urgent need to alter the status quo. A deposit technicality (later cured) was also cited. A renewed return application was dismissed on 21 September 2022; the court saw no endangerment requiring an immediate order and deferred the residence/schooling issue to the merits.

The Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeals on 2 December 2022. Although acknowledging the mother’s unauthorised relocation, it held that the applicant had not shown serious impairment of the children’s care, that further upheaval was not in their best interests, and that no urgent interim adjustment was required. The Constitutional Court rejected a challenge as manifestly ill-founded on 5 April 2023.

On 20 April 2023 the Regional Court quashed the July 2022 shared-custody judgment and awarded the mother sole custody, granting the applicant contact every second weekend and during holidays. It cited the children’s eight-month adaptation to Prague, proximity to other family, the impracticality of weekly travel and dual schooling given the distance, and the children’s expressed preference to remain with their mother. The applicant’s subsequent constitutional complaint was dismissed in October 2023.

The applicant later faced repeated refusals of contact (prompted in part by an unsubstantiated criminal complaint by the mother), leading to enforcement proceedings, fines against the mother, and her 2025 conviction for obstructing contact. The core complaint under Article 8, however, concerns the courts’ handling of the interim applications and the April 2023 custody decision: they failed to restore the status quo or prevent consolidation of the mother’s unlawful unilateral relocation, rendering any realistic prospect of shared or sole custody for the applicant merely theoretical. The domestic courts thereby failed to strike a fair balance between the parties’ interests and did not give sufficient reasons for dismissing the urgent interim measures.

**Case Summary: Novák v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 6656/24)**

The applicant, Stanislav Novák, is the father of two daughters (born 2014 and 2018). After separating from the children’s mother in April 2021 in Brno, the parents initially agreed to shared custody. In September 2021 the mother petitioned for divorce and sole custody; the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022 the mother refused to implement shared custody. The applicant had regular contact (weekly overnight visits plus alternate weekends) and both parents attended counselling, but no agreement was reached.

While awaiting a decision on the merits, the applicant applied for an interim shared-custody order. The Brno Municipal Court granted it in May 2022, but the Regional Court overturned it in June 2022, holding that no interim measure was needed because the children were well cared for by the mother and the applicant had regular contact. In July 2022 the Municipal Court awarded weekly shared custody, citing a counselling report and the guardian ad litem’s view that both parents were capable and the children had positive relationships with them. The mother appealed (with suspensive effect).

On 28 August 2022 the mother unilaterally relocated the children to Prague (more than 200 km away), enrolled them in a new school, and offered the applicant only alternate-weekend and holiday contact. She then applied for court authorisation of the relocation. The applicant notified the social-welfare authority (guardian ad litem), which declared the children “endangered.” On 7 September 2022 he applied for two interim measures: one granting him custody (with the mother having fortnightly contact) and another ordering the children’s return to Brno and their original schools, arguing the mother had breached Civil Code Article 877 § 1 by deciding an important matter (residence and education) without his consent or a court ruling.

The Municipal Court dismissed both applications on 12 September 2022. It relied on the June 2022 Regional Court decision, noted the applicant still had access and the mother provided good care, and found no urgent need for an interim adjustment. The return application was also dismissed because a required deposit had not been paid on the day of filing (it arrived the next day). A fresh return application on 20 September was dismissed the following day: the court saw no endangerment sufficient to justify even a temporary order determining residence and schooling, stating the issue would be resolved on the merits. Appeals were dismissed on 2 December 2022. The Regional Court acknowledged the mother’s unauthorised relocation but held that the applicant had not shown serious impairment of the children’s care, that they had settled, and that further change was not in their best interests. The Constitutional Court later dismissed a challenge as manifestly ill-founded.

The Regional Court delayed the merits hearing. In April 2023 it overturned the July 2022 shared-custody judgment and awarded the mother sole custody, granting the applicant contact every second weekend and during holidays. It reasoned that the children had adapted well after eight months in Prague (near other family), that the distance made weekly shared custody impractical and burdensome, and that the children’s expressed wishes favoured remaining with the mother. Although the mother had relocated without consent, the court treated the new status quo as decisive.

Subsequent enforcement proceedings revealed ongoing difficulties: the mother withheld the children after lodging an unsubstantiated criminal complaint against the applicant, prompting fines, a later order for enforcement, supervised visits, and her eventual conviction for obstructing contact. Later expert evidence found no risk from the applicant.

The alleged Article 8 violation centres on the courts’ handling of the unilateral, unlawful relocation. Interim-measure refusals repeatedly invoked the pre-relocation situation and the absence of “urgent” endangerment, providing limited reasoning why the mother’s breach of joint parental responsibility (Civil Code Articles 858, 865, 876–877) did not require prompt restoration of the status quo or an interim adjustment. By the time of the April 2023 merits decision the eight-month delay had allowed the children to settle, which the courts then treated as a decisive change of circumstances precluding shared (or sole) custody for the applicant. The decisions thus consolidated and legitimised the situation created by the mother’s unlawful act, rendering the applicant’s prospects of meaningful custody merely theoretical and failing to strike a fair balance between the parties’ interests and the children’s best interests. **CASE OF NOVÁK v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC (Application no. 6656/24)**

The applicant, a Czech father of two daughters (born 2014 and 2018), alleged a violation of Article 8 (right to family life) arising from domestic courts’ handling of custody after the mother unilaterally relocated the children. In April 2021 the parents, who had lived together in Brno, separated and initially agreed to shared custody. In September 2021 the mother petitioned for divorce and sole custody; the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022 she refused shared arrangements, though the applicant maintained regular weekly overnight and weekend contact. A counselling centre and the children’s guardian ad litem reported that both parents were capable and the children had positive relationships with each.

In May 2022 the Brno Municipal Court granted the applicant an interim shared-custody order; the Regional Court overturned it in June, finding no urgency because the children were well cared for and contact occurred. On 14 July 2022 the Municipal Court awarded weekly shared custody on the merits, citing the counselling report. The mother’s appeal had suspensive effect.

On 28 August 2022 the mother informed the applicant by email that she had moved the children to Prague (over 200 km away), enrolled them in new schools, and proposed only fortnightly weekend contact plus holidays. She applied for court authorisation of the relocation. The social-welfare authority (guardian ad litem) declared the children “endangered.” On 7 September the applicant applied for interim measures: (i) granting him custody with the mother having fortnightly contact, and (ii) ordering the children’s immediate return and re-enrolment in their original schools, arguing the move breached Civil Code Article 877 § 1 (joint decision on important matters such as residence and education).

The Municipal Court dismissed both applications on 12 and 21 September 2022. It relied on the June Regional Court ruling, noted that the mother provided good care and the applicant still had access, and found no urgent need or sufficient endangerment to justify interim intervention; the return application was also rejected for a technical deposit delay (later re-filed and again dismissed). The Regional Court upheld the dismissals on 2 December 2022, observing that although the relocation lacked agreement or court approval, the applicant had not shown serious impairment of care, contact continued, and further disruption was not in the children’s interests. The issue of residence could be decided on the merits. The Constitutional Court later dismissed a related appeal as manifestly ill-founded.

Despite the applicant’s requests to expedite the merits (hearings delayed until March 2023), the Regional Court on 20 April 2023 reversed the shared-custody judgment. It awarded the mother sole custody and the applicant contact every second weekend plus holidays. After eight months the children had adapted well to Prague, were near other family, and (per a social-welfare report) preferred remaining there; the distance made weekly shared custody impractical (travel burden and two schools). The court assigned the mother responsibility for some collection and travel costs, noting her unlawful move. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, finding the reasoning convincing.

Subsequent enforcement proceedings revealed the mother repeatedly withheld the children (prompting fines and her later criminal conviction for obstruction). Courts confirmed no substantiated risk from the applicant and eventually enforced contact, but they refused to alter the custody status quo or return the children, treating the new Prague arrangement as established. The applicant’s efforts to obtain sole or shared custody thus became theoretical. The ECtHR later held that the courts had failed to strike a fair balance, that the interim dismissals lacked sufficient reasons, and that the decisions had consolidated and legitimised the mother’s unlawful relocation.

The case of Mlinarević v. Croatia concerns an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial by an impartial tribunal) arising from the composition of the Croatian Constitutional Court panel that dismissed the applicant’s constitutional complaint in high-profile criminal proceedings known as the “Planinska” case.

On 31 August 2012 the Office for the Suppression of Corruption and Organised Crime indicted the applicant, former Prime Minister I. Sanader, S.F., P.Č. and two companies (M. and C.) before the Zagreb County Court. The charges related to abuse of power and authority (or instigating/aiding it) in connection with the sale to the government of a property co-owned by the companies on Planinska Street in Zagreb. The indictment was confirmed on 13 December 2012 and the case sent to trial; proceedings against P.Č. were later separated. S.F. and the companies pleaded guilty, while the applicant and Sanader denied the charges.

By a final judgment of 4 April 2019 the Supreme Court found all remaining accused guilty, partly upholding and partly reversing the Zagreb County Court’s 7 April 2017 judgment. The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting abuse of power, sentenced to one year’s imprisonment (replaced by community service) and ordered, jointly and severally with co-accused, to pay compensation of approximately 1.98 million euros.

On 27 June 2019 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging unfairness in the criminal proceedings. The Constitutional Court examined it jointly with Sanader’s complaint and dismissed both by decision of 26 November 2020 (served on 7 December 2020). The Court sat as a six-judge panel presided over by Judge R.M., who also acted as rapporteur. Two other judges (including the usual panel president) recused themselves.

The impartiality complaint centres on Judge R.M.’s connections to counsel for co-defendants. Prior to his appointment to the Constitutional Court on 7 June 2016, R.M. had practised as a lawyer with his own office. Upon appointment, that office (i.e., ongoing representation in unrelated cases in which he had been lead counsel) was “taken over” by lawyers from the law firm representing the M. company (one of the applicant’s co-defendants; the applicant also asserted the firm represented S.F.). During a period overlapping with the proceedings, R.M.’s son was employed at that same firm as a trainee lawyer and thus stood in a position of dependence and subordination to the lawyer representing a co-defendant.

Judge R.M. did not inform the President of the Constitutional Court of these circumstances and made no attempt to recuse himself. Under the applicable domestic rules (Constitutional Court Act and Rules of Procedure, applied mutatis mutandis with the Code of Criminal Procedure), a judge who becomes aware of circumstances calling impartiality into question must notify the court president so that a substitute can be designated; recusal is mandatory in certain family or prior-representation situations and discretionary where other doubts arise.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s claim that the Constitutional Court lacked objective impartiality. The Court later held that the applicant’s doubts were objectively justified.

001-249807:
The case of Antonov v. Estonia concerns Andrei Antonov (born 1972), detained continuously since 18 October 1994. He received 15-year sentences in May 1995 and May 1996, then life imprisonment in August 1996. While serving this, he was convicted on 30 January 2004 of attempted murder (sentence start dated to that day) and on 14 March 2013 of causing damage to another prisoner’s health plus physical abuse (sentence start remaining 30 January 2004).

On 9 July 2021 the Viru County Court convicted him of causing damage to another prisoner’s health in 2019 and imposed 1 year 3 months’ imprisonment. Applying Criminal Code Articles 64 § 4 and 65 § 2, it added the “unserved part” of the prior life sentence, producing an aggregate life sentence. It treated the entire period from 18 October 1994 to 8 July 2021 as already served, so the aggregate sentence began on 9 July 2021. This reset the 25-year minimum term (Article 77, reduced from 30 years in 2019) that must elapse before parole eligibility can be considered.

The applicant appealed, arguing the start date should remain 30 January 2004 and citing other life prisoners whose subsequent convictions had not reset their start dates (including his own 2013 conviction). The Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 10 November 2021, holding that Article 65 § 2 required the start date of any aggregate sentence to be the date of the latest judgment, relying on Supreme Court case 3-1-1-104-15.

The Supreme Court rejected his further appeal on 10 June 2022. It reasoned that a life sentence has no diminishing “unserved portion”; any new offence therefore produces a fresh aggregate life sentence whose start date is necessarily the date of the newest judgment. Two justices dissented, contending that life sentences lack a measurable unserved portion, so the original start date should persist unless a new life sentence is imposed. They highlighted statutory ambiguity, inconsistent earlier case-law, the automatic reset’s failure to distinguish offence gravity or time already served, and the resulting dependence of parole eligibility on the length of new proceedings.

Article 76 lists the individualised factors courts must weigh when deciding parole (offence circumstances, personality, conduct, living conditions, etc.). Presidential clemency (Constitution Article 78 and the 2007 Decree) exists but is discretionary, non-public and lacks the procedural guarantees associated with a genuine “prospect of release.”

The applicant’s complaint under Article 3 is that the rigid, automatic reset rendered his life sentence de facto irreducible: review would occur only 50 years after the original imposition. Domestic courts had applied the aggregation rules inconsistently over time, making the mechanism unforeseeable. The reset ignored the modest severity of the 2019 offence, the modest new term imposed, and the decades already served, thereby unduly postponing any review of continued detention. (The Court later held this violated Article 3 but stressed the finding does not entitle the applicant to imminent release.)

Andrei Antonov (born 1972) has been detained since 18 October 1994. He received two 15-year sentences (May 1995 and May 1996) before being sentenced to life imprisonment in August 1996. While serving that sentence he was convicted of attempted murder on 30 January 2004 (the court then set the sentence start date as 30 January 2004) and, on 14 March 2013, of assaulting another prisoner (the 2004 start date was left unchanged). On 9 July 2021 the Viru County Court convicted him of causing damage to another prisoner’s health in 2019 and imposed one year and three months’ imprisonment. Applying Articles 64 § 4 and 65 § 2 of the Criminal Code, it added the “unserved part” of the existing life sentence, imposed an aggregate life sentence, treated the period from 18 October 1994 to 8 July 2021 as already served, and therefore fixed 9 July 2021 as the new starting date.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the start date should remain 30 January 2004 and pointing to other life prisoners whose start dates had not been reset after later convictions. The Tartu Court of Appeal (10 November 2021) and the Supreme Court (10 June 2022) upheld the reset, holding that a life sentence has no diminishing “unserved portion,” so any aggregate life sentence must start on the date of the latest judgment. Two dissenting justices contended that this reading was not required by the statutory text, ignored earlier inconsistent case-law, treated every new offence identically regardless of gravity, and made parole eligibility depend on the length of subsequent proceedings.

Estonian law (Article 77 § 1 of the Criminal Code, as amended in 2019) allows a court to consider a life prisoner for parole only after 25 years have actually been served. The 2021 reset therefore postponed eligibility until 2046—more than 50 years after the original sentence began. The presidential clemency procedure (Constitution Art. 78 § 19 and the 2007 Presidential Decree) was available but lacked binding criteria, publicity or judicial review.

The European Court held that the automatic, non-individualised reset of the 25-year minimum term—applied irrespective of the new offence’s seriousness, the additional sentence imposed or time already served—unduly delayed any prospect of review and rendered the life sentence de facto irreducible. Combined with the unforeseeable and inconsistent domestic practice and the inadequacy of clemency as a substitute review mechanism, this constituted a violation of Article 3. The finding does not entitle the applicant to imminent release.

The case of Antonov v. Estonia (Application no. 48721/22) concerns an Estonian national born in 1972 who has been continuously detained since 18 October 1994. He received consecutive 15-year sentences in May 1995 and May 1996, followed by a life sentence in August 1996. While imprisoned he incurred further convictions: attempted murder on 30 January 2004 (the operative part of that judgment fixed the starting date of his sentence as 30 January 2004) and offences of causing bodily harm and physical abuse on 14 March 2013 (the 2004 starting date was left unchanged).

On 9 July 2021 the Viru County Court convicted him of a 2019 prison assault and imposed a sentence of one year and three months. Applying Articles 64 § 4 and 65 § 2 of the Criminal Code, the court aggregated that term with the “unserved part” of the existing life sentence, producing a new aggregate life sentence. It treated the entire period from 18 October 1994 to 8 July 2021 as already served and therefore declared that the applicant had begun serving the aggregate life sentence only on 9 July 2021. The practical effect was to restart the 25-year minimum term that, under Article 77 § 1 of the Criminal Code (in force since 1 July 2019), must elapse before a life prisoner may apply for parole.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the starting date should remain 30 January 2004 and that time served between 1994 and 2004 should count. He pointed to earlier domestic judgments in which other life prisoners convicted of new offences had not had their starting dates reset. The Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 10 November 2021, holding that Article 65 § 2 and Supreme Court precedent (case 3-1-1-104-15) required the starting date of any aggregate sentence to be the date of the latest conviction. The Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on points of law on 10 June 2022. It reasoned that a life sentence has no diminishing “unserved portion”; consequently every new offence committed during its currency produces a fresh aggregate life sentence whose starting date can only be the date of the newest judgment. Two dissenting justices contended that this interpretation was not compelled by the statutory text, contradicted prior practice in many cases, automatically reset the 25-year clock regardless of the gravity of the new offence or time already served, and made eligibility dependent on the unpredictable length of subsequent criminal proceedings.

Under Estonian law a life prisoner becomes eligible for parole only after 25 years have been “actually served” from the starting date fixed by the last judgment. Presidential clemency (Constitution, Art. 78(19)) exists as a residual possibility, but the procedure (Decree No. 13 of 2007) lacks binding criteria, publicity or an enforceable right to reasoned consideration and is therefore regarded as insufficient to supply a realistic “prospect of release.” The combination of an automatic, non-individualised reset of the 25-year term and the absence of any other reliable review mechanism meant that, as a result of the 2021 judgment, the applicant’s life sentence would not become reviewable until 50 years after its original imposition. This calculation, applied inconsistently across time and cases, formed the factual core of the alleged violation of Article 3.
001-249966:
The case of Gerovska-Popchevska v. North Macedonia (No. 2) concerns professional misconduct proceedings before the State Judicial Council (SJC) against the applicant, a retired judge. Snezhana Gerovska-Popchevska served as a judge at Skopje Court of First Instance No. 1 until her dismissal in May 2007. In its 2016 judgment in Gerovska Popčevska, the ECHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1 owing to the SJC’s lack of impartiality and independence, as the President of the Supreme Court and Minister of Justice had participated in the dismissal decision. The applicant retired in February 2016 and, in May 2016, sought reopening of the proceedings in light of that judgment.

The SJC granted reopening in February 2018, appointed its then-President as complainant, and in April 2018 formed a five-member Commission (including member V.B.) to gather evidence. On 22 May 2019 the SJC established that the applicant had acted unconscientiously and unprofessionally in a civil case, amounting to professional misconduct under the 2006 Courts Act, but did not dismiss her as she was no longer a sitting judge. She appealed, arguing the SJC lacked jurisdiction over a retired judge. On 8 October 2019 an Appeal Panel of the Supreme Court quashed the decision and remitted the case. It held that the relevant provisions permitted only dismissal of sitting judges, not a purely declaratory finding of misconduct, and that the SJC had failed to identify the applicable versions of the Courts Act and SJC Act.

Following remittal the SJC replaced all Commission members except V.B. The Commission heard the applicant and complainant in December 2019 and proposed dismissal. V.B.’s term expired that month. At a February 2020 session attended by 12 of 14 members (the Minister of Justice and Supreme Court President being absent, two members recused, and the complainant abstaining from the vote), the SJC amended the proposal. It established professional misconduct rather than dismissal, applying the 2018 amendments to the SJC Act (which it considered applicable) and relying on provisions allowing it to establish unprofessional performance of judicial functions. The decision was adopted by nine votes.

The applicant appealed again in March 2020, contending that the SJC had ignored the Appeal Panel’s instructions, applied inconsistent versions of the legislation, lacked jurisdiction over a former judge, and that certain members had been improperly recused or replaced. The SJC rejected the appeal as inadmissible under section 96(4) of the 2018 SJC Act, which made its post-remittal decision final after “assessing” the Appeal Panel’s instructions. A subsequent constitutional challenge to that provision was also rejected.

These facts underpin the applicant’s Article 6 § 1 complaints: that Commission members who had prepared the report voted on the final decision in breach of rules requiring their exclusion; that a replacement of a Commission member after remittal was irregular; that the SJC lacked jurisdiction to issue a declaratory ruling against a retired judge; and that domestic law barred any appeal against the post-remittal decision, leaving the Appeal Panel unable to verify compliance with its earlier instructions.

The applicant, a former first-instance judge dismissed from office in 2007, obtained an ECtHR judgment in 2016 finding a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the State Judicial Council (SJC) that dismissed her lacked impartiality (the Supreme Court President and Minister of Justice having participated). She retired in February 2016 and then sought reopening of the SJC proceedings in light of that judgment.

The SJC granted reopening in 2018, designated its President as complainant, and formed a five-member Commission (including member V.B.) to gather evidence. After recusing one SJC member, the SJC in May 2019 found that the applicant had committed professional misconduct through unconscientious and unprofessional performance of judicial functions in a civil case, but imposed no dismissal because she had already retired. She appealed, arguing that the SJC lacked jurisdiction over a non-sitting judge.

An Appeal Panel of the Supreme Court quashed the decision and remitted the case. It held that the relevant provisions of the Courts Act permitted only dismissal of a sitting judge for professional misconduct, not a purely declaratory finding against a retired judge, and that the SJC had failed to identify which versions of the applicable statutes it had applied.

The SJC then replaced four of the five Commission members (retaining only V.B.). The Commission heard the parties and proposed dismissal as the sole available outcome. V.B.’s term expired in December 2019; the applicant unsuccessfully requested a new Commission hearing. In February 2020 the SJC, sitting with 12 of its 14 members (excluding the Minister of Justice and Supreme Court President, plus two recused members and the non-voting complainant), received the Commission’s report. After deliberations it instructed the Commission President to amend the proposal orally so as to record a finding of unprofessional and unconscientious performance rather than dismissal. Nine members then voted to adopt that finding, relying on a 2018 amendment that expressly empowered the SJC to “establish unprofessional or unconscientious performance of judicial functions.”

The applicant again appealed, repeating her jurisdictional objection, complaining that the SJC had ignored the Appeal Panel’s instructions and had applied the wrong version of the SJC Act, and questioning the voting majority and participation of recused or ineligible members. The SJC rejected the appeal as inadmissible under a 2018 provision that rendered its post-remittal decision final once it had “assessed” the Appeal Panel’s instructions.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that (i) Commission members who had prepared the report later voted on the final decision in breach of procedural rules requiring their exclusion from the vote; (ii) an SJC member who had sat in the earlier phase was replaced after remittal by a member who had not previously participated; (iii) the SJC lacked competence to make a declaratory finding against a retired judge; and (iv) domestic law barred any appeal against the post-remittal decision, thereby rendering even the first-instance appeal ineffective.

The Court held that Article 6 applied because the proceedings directly affected the applicant’s civil right to reputation. Although the SJC constituted a “tribunal,” it was not “established by law”: members of the Commission that had reported on the case voted on the final decision in contravention of the SJC Act. In addition, the inability of the Appeal Panel to verify compliance with its own earlier instructions after remittal deprived the applicant’s right of access to that Panel of any practical substance, impairing the very essence of the right of access to a court.

**Case summary: Gerovska-Popchevska v. North Macedonia (No. 2) (App. no. 30989/20)**

The applicant, a former judge of Skopje Court of First Instance No. 1, was dismissed in 2007. In 2016 the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1 in those dismissal proceedings because of the participation of the then President of the Supreme Court and the Minister of Justice in the State Judicial Council (SJC). She retired in February 2016 and thereafter practised as a lawyer. In May 2016 she requested reopening of the SJC proceedings in light of the Court’s judgment.

The SJC reopened the case in 2018, appointed its then President as complainant, and established a five-member Commission (including member V.B.) to gather evidence. In May 2019 the SJC found that the applicant had committed professional misconduct (unconscientious and unprofessional performance in a civil case) under the Courts Act but did not dismiss her, as she was no longer a sitting judge. One SJC member had been recused.

The applicant appealed, arguing among other things that the SJC lacked jurisdiction to issue a declaratory finding of misconduct against a person who was no longer a judge. In October 2019 an Appeal Panel of the Supreme Court quashed the decision and remitted the case. It held that the relevant provisions of the Courts Act and SJC Act permitted only dismissal of a sitting judge for professional misconduct, not a purely declaratory ruling, and noted that the SJC had not specified which versions of the repeatedly amended legislation it had applied.

After remittal the SJC replaced four of the five Commission members (retaining V.B.). The Commission heard the applicant and the complainant and, in December 2019, proposed dismissal as the only available outcome. V.B.’s term of office then expired. The applicant requested a new Commission hearing and proposal; the Government later stated that V.B. was never replaced.

In February 2020 the SJC (14 members at the time) sat with 12 members present. The Minister of Justice and President of the Supreme Court (ex officio members) were absent; two members (including one previously recused) were recused and the complainant did not vote. The Commission president presented the report proposing dismissal. After deliberations the SJC amended the proposal because the applicant had already retired, and by nine votes it found that she had committed professional misconduct while performing judicial functions, relying on the 2018 amendments to the SJC Act (which it held applicable). Section 60(3) of that Act required Commission members to participate in deliberations but to be exempted from voting on the final decision.

The applicant appealed again, repeating that the SJC could not issue a declaratory ruling, that it had not followed the Appeal Panel’s instructions, that the 2018 Act was inapplicable, and that voting irregularities (recusals and ineligibility) required verification of the majority. The SJC rejected the appeal as inadmissible, citing section 96(4) of the 2018 SJC Act, under which a decision after remittal is final once the SJC has “assessed” the Appeal Panel’s instructions. No further judicial review of compliance with those instructions was possible.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that: (i) Commission members who had prepared the report later voted on the final decision, contrary to procedural rules, so the SJC was not a tribunal established by law; (ii) an SJC member who had sat before remittal was later replaced by a member who had not; (iii) the SJC lacked jurisdiction over a retired judge; and (iv) domestic law barred any appeal against the post-remittal decision, rendering the earlier appeal to the Appeal Panel meaningless because that body could not verify compliance with its own instructions.
