The applicants are the Word of Life Church (registered in Armenia since 1993) and its senior pastor Artur Simonyan. In 2011 a scandal involving actress A.S. and leaked intimate photographs led to media speculation that she belonged to the applicants’ church. On 19 October 2011 the newspaper Iravunk Hetaqnnutyun published an article headed “The Story of the Sect Involving Pornographic Photographs Has ‘Blossomed’ into Charges of Paedophilia.” It described Word of Life as Armenia’s largest “sect,” labelled A.S. a “sectarian,” linked the church to allegations of incest and paedophilia, and claimed the organisation exerted influence over television and officials. Two digitally altered images depicted Simonyan as a priest leaning toward a scantily clad A.S. in a nun’s headdress and A.S. posing for a “Word of Life” mug-shot. A Russian-language weekly reprinted the material under the title “A Story of Sectarianism and Pornography.” Later issues of Iravunk called for a public “war” against the “ringleader of the secretive Word of Life Sect.” A.S. subsequently appeared on television and denied any affiliation with the church.

The applicants sued the publisher in the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court for defamation and insult, seeking retraction and an apology. They contended that the articles deliberately associated them with criminality without verification, tarnished Simonyan’s honour and the church’s reputation, and that the term “sect” (and its derivatives) carried pejorative connotations of heresy, clandestine activity and social danger capable of inciting ridicule, hostility and religious hatred. They submitted linguistic, legal and sociological material showing that Armenian society understood the word as an insult.

The defendant obtained a letter from the Catholicos of the Armenian Apostolic Church stating that Word of Life had no connection with the national church and was a “sect” because its doctrines had “deviated from the true faith, canons and traditional principles.” A protest featuring anti-sect banners and an Apostolic priest took place outside the first hearing. An independent expert report concluded that the publications were intended to portray the applicants as clandestine and anti-social and that the use of “sect” was humiliating.

On 31 July 2012 the District Court dismissed the action. It held that the articles constituted protected journalistic comment employing exaggerated language, that the applicants (as public actors) were required to tolerate criticism, and that “sect” was a value judgment rather than a statement of fact. The court relied on a dictionary definition of “sect” as deviation from the dominant church, on Article 8.1 of the Constitution recognising the Apostolic Church’s exclusive national mission, on internet videos and on the Catholicos’s letter to find that the applicants’ rituals indeed departed from Apostolic canons. Consequently the term had been used without intent to insult.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the first-instance court had itself labelled them “sectarians,” thereby violating Article 9 of the Convention, and had given preference to the Apostolic Church by treating the Catholicos’s legally irrelevant opinion as decisive. On 8 November 2012 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, noting that the applicants had not denied doctrinal deviation and therefore bore the burden of proving falsity.

On 3 December 2012 the applicants lodged an appeal on points of law. The cover page correctly identified the Court of Appeal decision of 8 November 2012 and enclosed that decision together with proof of service. The final paragraph, however, asked the Court of Cassation to quash the District Court’s judgment of 31 July 2012—a typographical error. On 16 January 2013 the Cassation Court declared the appeal inadmissible under Article 222 § 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure because a first-instance judgment is not amenable to cassation. The applicants promptly re-filed a corrected version, explained the obvious clerical mistake and requested restoration of the time-limit. On 6 March 2013 the Cassation Court rejected the request as unfounded and declared the appeal out of time.

These facts underpin the two alleged Convention violations: (i) that the domestic courts, by endorsing the Apostolic Church’s characterisation of Word of Life as a “sect,” breached the State’s duty of neutrality and impartiality in religious matters (Article 9); and (ii) that the Cassation Court’s rigid application of formal requirements to a patent typographical error, without affording an opportunity to correct it, constituted excessive formalism that denied the applicants access to court (Article 6 § 1).

The applicants are the Word of Life Church of Christians of Evangelical Faith in Armenia, a registered religious organisation since 1993, and its senior pastor Artur Simonyan. In 2011 an investigation into dissemination of private pornographic photographs of actress A.S. generated public speculation that she belonged to the applicants’ church. On 19 October 2011 the weekly Iravunk Hetaqnnutyun published an article headlined “The Story of the Sect Involving Pornographic Photographs Has ‘Blossomed’ into Charges of Paedophilia.” It identified Word of Life as Armenia’s largest “sect,” labelled A.S. a “sectarian,” described the church as a “sectarian union” exerting influence over media and officials, and accompanied the text with digitally altered images of Simonyan as a priest leaning toward a scantily clad A.S. in a nun’s headdress and of A.S. posing in a nun’s habit holding a “Word of Life” sign. A similar article and images appeared in a Russian-language weekly. A.S. later stated on television that she had never been a member of any religious organisation. Subsequent publications by the same newspaper called for a public campaign against the applicants under headlines such as “Join the War” and “The Ringleader of the Secretive Word of Life Sect.”

On 18 November 2011 the applicants sued the publisher in the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court for defamation and insult. They sought an apology and retraction of statements linking them to A.S., arguing that the articles, published without verification, created a false and damaging association, insulted Simonyan’s honour and the church’s reputation, and used the terms “sect” and “sectarian” which, they submitted with supporting research, carried strongly negative connotations capable of inciting ridicule, harassment and religious hostility. They later supplemented their claim to emphasise that calling a legally registered religious organisation a “sect” was both defamatory and insulting.

The defendant wrote to the head of the Armenian Apostolic Church asking whether the applicants’ organisation was a sect; the Catholicos replied that it was, because its beliefs had “deviated from the true faith.” A protest organised outside the first hearing featured banners reading “Say no to sects” and “Word of Life is a sect,” with an Apostolic priest present. An independent expert report commissioned by the applicants concluded that the contested language was debasing and aimed to portray the church as clandestine and antisocial.

On 31 July 2012 the District Court dismissed the action. It held that the publications constituted protected, if exaggerated, journalistic comment on a matter of public debate; that the applicants, having entered public controversy, were required to tolerate criticism aimed at defending the beliefs of the Armenian Apostolic Church; and that “sect” was a value judgment. The court cited a dictionary definition, Article 8.1 of the Constitution recognising the Apostolic Church’s exclusive national mission, internet material and videos submitted by the defendant, and the Catholicos’s letter as evidence that the applicants’ rituals “deviated” from Apostolic doctrine. Consequently the use of “sect” was neither insulting nor defamatory.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the District Court had itself labelled them a sect, thereby violating their freedom of religion, and had improperly privileged the Apostolic Church by relying on the Catholicos’s legally irrelevant opinion. On 8 November 2012 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, noting that the applicants had not denied their deviation from Apostolic beliefs and therefore bore the burden of proving the publications untrue.

On 3 December 2012 the applicants lodged an appeal on points of law. The first page correctly identified the Court of Appeal decision of 8 November 2012 as the contested ruling and enclosed a copy of that decision; the body of the appeal attacked its reasoning. The final paragraph, however, requested cassation of the District Court’s 31 July 2012 judgment. On 16 January 2013 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible because it had been directed against a first-instance judgment not amenable to cassation. The applicants promptly resubmitted a corrected version, explaining the discrepancy as a typographical error and seeking restoration of the time-limit. On 6 March 2013 the Court of Cassation rejected the request as unfounded and declared the amended appeal out of time.

These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints that the domestic courts failed to remain neutral and impartial in religious matters (Article 9) and that the Court of Cassation’s refusal to examine their cassation appeal, caused by an obvious clerical error they were given no chance to correct, denied them access to court (Article 6 § 1).

The applicants are the Word of Life Church of Christians of Evangelical Faith in Armenia (a religious organisation registered since 1993) and its senior pastor, Artur Simonyan. The article and images were reprinted (with minor changes) in a Russian-language weekly under the title “A Story of Sectarianism and Pornography.” Further publications followed, including calls to join a campaign against the applicants with headlines such as “The Ringleader of the Secretive Word of Life Sect.”

On 18 November 2011 the applicants sued the publisher (Iravunk Media Ltd) in the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan for defamation and insult, seeking an apology and retraction. They argued that the articles created an unfounded association with the scandal, disseminated insulting disinformation that tarnished Simonyan’s honour and the organisation’s reputation, and aimed to depict them as dangerous. They later supplemented the claim, asserting that the terms “sect” and “sectarian” were defamatory and insulting: legally the organisation was a “religious organisation,” the words carried negative societal connotations capable of inciting ridicule, harassment, religious hatred and hostility, discouraged potential followers, and damaged their standing. They submitted research on the terms’ meanings.

An independent expert opinion (requested by the applicants) concluded that the terms were debasing, insulting and humiliating and that the publications sought to portray the organisation as clandestine and antisocial.

On 31 July 2012 the District Court dismissed the claims. It held that the publications contained no defamatory or insulting statements, were protected by journalistic freedom of expression (which permits exaggerated and provocative language), and showed no defamatory intent. The applicants, having entered public debate, were required to tolerate criticism aimed at an open discussion of religious ideas and at preventing deviation from Apostolic Church beliefs. “Sect” was a value judgment; dictionary definitions confirmed it meant a belief deviating from a given church or the main religion of a country. The Constitution recognised the Apostolic Church’s exclusive national mission. Evidence (including internet materials, videos and the Catholicos’s letter) showed the applicants’ activities and rituals deviated from Apostolic principles; thus the term expressed an opinion, not an insult.

On 8 November 2012 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. It noted that the applicants had not denied deviation from Apostolic beliefs (which did not restrict religious freedom or constitute discrimination) and that they bore the burden of proving the disseminated information was untrue.

The front page correctly identified the Civil Court of Appeal decision of 8 November 2012 as the impugned ruling; copies were sent to that court and the respondent; extensive arguments attacked that decision; and supporting documents (the decision itself and postal receipts) were enclosed. However, the final paragraph erroneously requested reversal of the District Court’s 31 July 2012 judgment. On 16 January 2013 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible under Article 222 § 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure because it was directed against a first-instance judgment not amenable to cassation. The applicants promptly resubmitted an amended version correcting the last paragraph, explained the error as typographical (supported by the appeal’s first page and substance), and requested restoration of the time-limit. On 6 March 2013 the Court of Cassation rejected the amended appeal as out of time and dismissed the restoration request as unfounded. The Code required an appeal on points of law to identify the Court of Appeal decision by name and date, provided for possible correction of errors within a set time-limit, and rendered appeals against non-amenable decisions inadmissible.
001-249971:
The case of Jurić v. Croatia (Application no. 51771/21) concerns the alleged violation of the applicant’s right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (and her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1) after domestic courts dismissed as time-barred her claim for compensation for land taken for an unclassified road.

The applicant inherited several plots in Rijeka in 2013 from her aunt B.J. and registered her title. An access road (a cul-de-sac serving several houses and used by third parties) had been built on one plot in the 1970s and asphalted in 2000. The 2011 Roads Act, which entered into force on 28 July 2011, provided that unclassified roads (surfaces used for vehicular traffic, accessible to many users and not classified as public roads) became public property owned by the relevant local authority and were to be recorded as such in the land register regardless of existing entries.

In 2014 the cadastral authority applied to the Rijeka Municipal Court. On 4 July 2014 a land-registry clerk divided the applicant’s plot, merged part of it with other land and recorded the resulting plot as an unclassified road owned by the Town of Rijeka. On 1 October 2015 the applicant sued the Town for compensation for unjust enrichment, arguing that part of her land had been appropriated without an expropriation decision or payment.

On 24 May 2019 the Municipal Court dismissed the claim as time-barred. It accepted that the land had been taken, that an asphalt road existed and that neither the applicant nor B.J. had ever been compensated. Under section 33 of the Property Act she was entitled to compensation as if the land had been expropriated. However, because the road had been built in 1978, equipped with drainage, sewerage and lighting, and last asphalted in 2000, the land could no longer be restored; ownership had therefore passed and the five-year limitation period under section 225 of the Obligations Act had begun to run, expiring at the latest on 1 January 2006. The court relied inter alia on a 2017 Constitutional Court decision. The applicant was ordered to pay the Town’s costs of approximately EUR 3,584.

The Šibenik County Court dismissed her appeal on 15 September 2020, holding that ownership had already been lost by her predecessor and that the limitation period ran from the moment of appropriation, irrespective of later land-register entries. The Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible on 10 March 2021, finding no constitutional issue and considering the outcome foreseeable.

A parallel request for compensation lodged with the county property office in 2016 was rejected because no formal expropriation order existed; the applicant was directed to civil proceedings. That decision became final in 2021.

The applicant contended that nothing had indicated a transfer of title or given her (or her predecessor) reason to know of the deprivation before the 2014 land-register decision. Pre-2011 legislation on unclassified roads was unclear and incomplete; such roads had not automatically been State-owned. The manner in which the courts calculated the limitation period was therefore unforeseeable, denied her any possibility of obtaining compensation and impaired the very essence of her right of access to a court.

**The case of Jurić v. Croatia (Application no. 51771/21, ECtHR, 7 May 2026) concerns the taking of the applicant’s inherited land for an unclassified access road and the subsequent dismissal of her compensation claim as time-barred.**

Vanessa Jurić, a Croatian national born in 1982, inherited several plots in Rijeka from her aunt B.J. in 2013 and recorded her ownership in the land register. One plot contained a house; another had an access road (a cul-de-sac serving several houses and third parties) built in the 1970s and asphalted in 2000. On 28 July 2011 the Roads Act entered into force. It provided that unclassified roads—those used for vehicular traffic, accessible to many users and not classified as public roads—became public property in general use, owned by the relevant local authority and to be recorded as such in the land register regardless of existing entries.

In 2014 the cadastral authority initiated land-registry proceedings. On 4 July 2014 a clerk of the Rijeka Municipal Court divided the relevant plot, merged part of it into a new cadastral plot and recorded that plot as an unclassified road owned by the Town of Rijeka. On 1 October 2015 the applicant brought a civil action against the Town for unjust enrichment, arguing that part of her land had been taken without an expropriation decision or compensation.

The Rijeka Municipal Court dismissed the claim as time-barred on 24 May 2019. It accepted that the land had been appropriated, that an asphalt road existed and that neither the applicant nor her predecessor had received compensation. Applying section 33 of the Property Act, it held she was entitled to compensation as if the land had been expropriated. However, it found that once the road had been asphalted (last in 2000) and equipped with drainage, sewerage and lighting, it could no longer be returned; ownership had therefore been lost then. The five-year limitation period under section 225 of the Obligations Act had thus expired by 1 January 2006 at the latest. The court relied on a 2017 Constitutional Court decision. The applicant was also ordered to pay the Town’s costs of approximately €3,584.

The Šibenik County Court dismissed her appeal on 15 September 2020, endorsing the view that ownership had already been taken from her predecessor when the road was asphalted and that the limitation period ran from the moment of appropriation, irrespective of later land-register entries. On 10 March 2021 the Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible, finding no constitutional issue, that the lower courts’ reasoning was sufficient and non-arbitrary, and that the time-bar had been foreseeable.

Separately, in October 2016 the applicant sought compensation from the county property office. The request was declared inadmissible in January 2017 because no formal expropriation order existed; she was directed to civil proceedings. Her administrative appeal was dismissed in January 2021 and she did not seek judicial review.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (access to court) that the time-barred dismissal disproportionately restricted her right, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) concerning the taking of her land without compensation. Relevant domestic law showed that the legal status of unclassified roads had been unclear before 2011; earlier Roads Acts treated public roads as unownable or State-owned, while the 2011 Act transferred unclassified roads to local authorities by operation of law. Supreme Court practice generally started the limitation period when a road was completed and could no longer be returned, though a 2024 practice direction allowed an exception where an owner learned of the change only later for justified reasons. A 2017 Constitutional Court decision treated the 2011 Act as a mere reclassification of already State-owned roads and indicated that former owners could still claim compensation under the Property Act.

The Court later found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the domestic courts’ calculation of the limitation period was unforeseeable, that no circumstances indicated the land had been transferred to the State before the 2014 registration decision, and that the applicant had thereby been denied any possibility of compensation, impairing the very essence of her right of access to court.

The case of Jurić v. Croatia (Application no. 51771/21) concerns the applicant’s unsuccessful attempt to obtain compensation after part of her inherited land was recorded as an unclassified public road owned by the Town of Rijeka. Vanessa Jurić, a Croatian national born in 1982, inherited several plots in Rijeka from her aunt in 2013 and registered her ownership. One plot contained a house; another had hosted an access road (a cul-de-sac serving neighbouring houses and third parties) since the 1970s, last asphalted in 2000.

The 2011 Roads Act, which entered into force on 28 July 2011, reclassified all unclassified roads—surfaces used for vehicular traffic and accessible to many users but not designated public roads—as public property owned by the relevant local authority. Such roads were to be entered in the land register as such, irrespective of prior ownership entries. In 2014 the cadastral authority initiated land-registry proceedings. On 4 July 2014 a clerk of the Rijeka Municipal Court subdivided the applicant’s plot, merged part of it with other land, and recorded the new plot as an unclassified road belonging to the Town of Rijeka.

On 1 October 2015 the applicant sued the Town for unjust enrichment, claiming de-facto expropriation without any formal decision or payment. The Rijeka Municipal Court dismissed the action as time-barred on 24 May 2019. It accepted that the land had been appropriated and that neither the applicant nor her predecessor had received compensation; under section 33 of the Property Act she was therefore entitled to compensation equivalent to that payable on expropriation. However, the court held that once the road was asphalted and put into public use in 2000 the land could no longer be restored, so the five-year limitation period under section 225 of the Obligations Act began then and expired by 1 January 2006. The court relied inter alia on a 2017 Constitutional Court decision. The applicant was also ordered to pay the Town’s legal costs of HRK 27 000 (approximately EUR 3 584).

The Šibenik County Court upheld the dismissal on 15 September 2020, confirming that appropriation had occurred years earlier and that the limitation period ran from the moment the land became an unclassified road, irrespective of the date of land-register entry. The Constitutional Court declared the subsequent constitutional complaint inadmissible on 10 March 2021, finding no constitutional issue and observing that the claim had been foreseeably doomed.

Separately, in October 2016 the applicant applied to the county property office for expropriation compensation. The request was rejected in January 2017 because no expropriation order existed; she was told to pursue a civil claim. Her administrative appeal was dismissed in January 2021 and she did not seek judicial review.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the manner in which the domestic courts calculated the limitation period was unforeseeable. Nothing indicated that title had passed to the State before the 2014 land-register decision, nor any circumstance from which the applicant could reasonably have learned of the deprivation earlier. By treating the claim as time-barred from 2000 the courts denied her any realistic opportunity to obtain compensation, thereby impairing the very essence of her right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. (The Court also noted the related complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 but concentrated its reasoning on the access-to-court issue.)

The judgment became final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention.
001-249973:
The case of Konstantinou v. Cyprus (Application no. 36862/23) concerns the applicant’s inability to obtain judicial review of a decision by Cyprus’s transitional Supreme Council of Judicature (SCJ) refusing to promote him to district court president.

In 2022 Cyprus enacted judicial reforms creating a new Supreme Constitutional Court (SCC) and Court of Appeal, while restructuring the SCJ to include non-voting legal professionals and giving it authority over judicial appointments and promotions. The reforms, originally due to take effect in January 2023, were postponed until 1 July 2023. During the intervening period a transitional SCJ, composed of the then-Supreme Court judges plus non-voting participants, operated from August 2022 to June 2023.

The applicant, a Cypriot national born in 1968, had served as a temporary district court judge since 2004 and as a senior district court judge since January 2019. On 3 February 2023 the transitional SCJ advertised 17 vacancies for district court president. The applicant applied on 8 February among 23 candidates (almost all senior district court judges). After a preliminary assessment he was interviewed on 2 March 2023. Although he ranked first in seniority among serving senior district court judges, the transitional SCJ on 3 March appointed 17 other candidates. No member voted for or even commented on the applicant’s qualifications.

The applicant requested the procedural records; the request was refused. The transitional SCJ later explained that it had relied on the administrative presidents’ opinions, the candidates’ CVs and interview performances, and had found no significant difference in seniority. It regarded the other candidates as stronger in personality, judicial conduct and professional contribution.

On 12 May 2023 the applicant lodged a recourse in the Administrative Court, complaining that the transitional SCJ had disregarded prescribed procedure, acted opaquely and arbitrarily, failed to give due weight to seniority, denied him access to the records, and thereby breached domestic law and Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention.

On 27 June 2023 the Administrative Court dismissed the recourse as premature. It treated the transitional SCJ and the new SCJ as the same body and held that review would become available once the SCC began operating on 1 July 2023. Neither party appealed, so the decision became final.

On 3 July 2023 the applicant filed a complaint with the SCC sitting as second-tier judicial council, repeating his earlier arguments and additionally alleging that the SCC was not impartial because its members had sat on the transitional SCJ. On 11 July 2023 the SCC unanimously dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction. It ruled that the transitional SCJ was a distinct temporary body that had ceased to exist on 30 June 2023 and that the legislature had deliberately omitted any right of review of its decisions, unlike the new SCJ whose decisions were reviewable by the SCC. The distinction was said to reflect the mutual control between the two supreme judicial bodies that was intended to operate only after 1 July 2023.

The applicant was nevertheless promoted to district court president on 1 November 2024.

The alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 is the complete absence of any effective judicial review of the transitional SCJ’s refusal to promote him.

The case of Konstantinou v. Cyprus (Application no. 36862/23) concerns a Cypriot senior district court judge’s unsuccessful challenge to a 2023 decision of a transitional judicial council refusing his promotion. The applicant, Kostas Konstantinou (born 1968), had served as a temporary district judge since 2004 and as a senior district judge since 2019. Implementation was postponed from January to July 2023; a transitional SCJ, composed of the then-Supreme Court judges plus non-voting participants, therefore operated from August 2022 to 30 June 2023.

He passed the preliminary screening, ranked first in seniority among senior district judges, and was interviewed on 2 March. In a 22 March letter the council stated that it had relied on administrative presidents’ opinions, curricula vitae, interview performance, personality, judicial conduct and professional contribution, and that the other candidates were stronger; seniority differences were regarded as insignificant.

On 12 May 2023 the applicant lodged a recourse (judicial-review application) in the Administrative Court, alleging that the council had disregarded the published seven-stage promotion procedure, acted arbitrarily and without transparency, failed to give reasons or to weigh seniority, and denied access to records in breach of domestic rules and of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. On 27 June the court dismissed the application as premature, holding that the transitional and new SCJs were in substance the same body and that review would become available before the SCC once it began operating on 1 July. No party appealed, so the ruling became final.

On 3 July the applicant therefore complained to the SCC sitting as second-tier judicial council, repeating his earlier arguments and adding that the SCC was not impartial because its members had sat on the transitional council. On 11 July the SCC unanimously rejected the complaint for lack of jurisdiction. It held that the transitional body had ceased to exist on 30 June, that the legislature had deliberately omitted any right of objection against its decisions (in contrast to the express provision for review of the new SCJ’s decisions), and that the two councils were distinct. The applicant was later promoted to district-court president in November 2024.

The facts thus centre on the complete absence of any judicial forum competent to examine the transitional council’s promotion decision, despite the applicant’s seniority ranking, the existence of published procedural rules, and the Administrative Court’s earlier suggestion that review would be available.

The case of Konstantinou v. Cyprus (Application no. 36862/23) concerns a Cypriot senior district court judge who alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights due to the lack of any judicial review of a decision refusing his promotion.

In 2022 Cyprus enacted major judicial reforms creating a new Supreme Constitutional Court (SCC) and Court of Appeal, distinct from the existing Supreme Court, and restructuring the Supreme Council of Judicature (SCJ) with expanded membership including non-voting legal professionals. The reforms, originally due in January 2023, were postponed until July 2023. During the interim, a transitional SCJ composed of sitting Supreme Court judges plus non-voting participants operated from August 2022 to June 2023.

The applicant, a judge since 2004 and senior district court judge since 2019, applied in February 2023 for one of 17 vacancies as district court president announced by the transitional SCJ. He ranked first in seniority among 23 candidates (almost all senior judges), passed the preliminary assessment, and was interviewed. On 3 March 2023 the transitional SCJ appointed 17 other judges; none of its members voted for or even commented on the applicant. His request for access to the procedure records was refused. The transitional SCJ later explained that it had relied on administrative presidents’ opinions, CVs, interview performance, personality, judicial conduct and professional contribution, finding other candidates stronger and noting no significant seniority differences.

On 12 May 2023 the applicant brought a recourse before the Administrative Court, arguing that the transitional SCJ had failed to follow the prescribed seven-stage promotion procedure, acted without transparency, produced an arbitrary and unreasoned decision, ignored his seniority, and denied him access to records, in breach of equality and Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. On 27 June 2023 the Administrative Court dismissed the application as premature. It treated the transitional SCJ and the forthcoming enlarged SCJ as the same body whose decisions would become reviewable by the SCC once that court began operating on 1 July 2023. No party appealed, so the decision became final.

On 3 July 2023 the applicant lodged a complaint with the SCC sitting as second-tier judicial council, repeating his earlier arguments and adding that the SCC lacked impartiality because its members had sat on the transitional SCJ. In a unanimous judgment of 11 July 2023 the SCC declined jurisdiction. It held that the transitional SCJ (which ceased to exist on 30 June 2023) was a distinct body from the new SCJ; the legislature had deliberately omitted any right of objection against transitional decisions, unlike the explicit review mechanism created for post-1 July 2023 SCJ decisions. The applicant was later promoted to district court president in November 2024.

The Court held that Article 6 § 1 applied because the applicant had a genuine and serious dispute over a right under domestic law to a fair promotion procedure. The second limb of the Eskelinen test was not met: the exclusion of judicial review was not in the interest of a State governed by the rule of law. Given the link between the integrity of judicial appointments and judicial independence, and the importance of procedural safeguards plus an appeal possibility for decisions affecting a judge’s career, there were no exceptional and compelling reasons justifying the total absence of review. The very essence of the right of access to a court was therefore impaired.
001-250024:
The applicants—the Trade Union of Social Sector Workers (representing essential social-sector employees) and three of its members—complained under Articles 11 and 13 of the Convention that protracted court proceedings to determine the minimum services required during planned strikes rendered those strikes ineffective, thereby violating their freedom of association.

On 17 December 2019 the applicant union, together with another public-sector union, announced a series of one-day strikes on 11 specified dates throughout 2020. The purpose was to press for improved pay, working conditions, pension rights and a national labour round-table. Under section 4(3) of the 1989 Strike Act, a strike in an essential service may proceed only after the parties agree on, or a court finally determines, the “sufficient” level of services that must be maintained. The unions submitted their proposed minimum-service schedule to the Ministry of Human Resources the same day. On 15 January 2020 the Ministry rejected the proposal and demanded a new one.

On 6 February 2020 the unions applied to the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court for a judicial determination. The court first rejected the application as incomplete, then, on 19 February, discontinued the proceedings on the ground that negotiations had not been shown to have failed. The Budapest High Court quashed that ruling on 6 March and remitted the case, holding that negotiations had indeed ended without agreement.

A COVID-19 emergency court recess was declared, but the first-instance court quickly lifted its own suspension, finding the recess inapplicable to non-contentious strike proceedings. On 18 March it set a minimum-service level by amending the unions’ proposal in light of pandemic-related submissions from the Government. The Government appealed. The case file then travelled back and forth between the two courts three times (14 April, 20 April and 7 May) solely for the correction of formal errors in the notice of appeal. Only on 25 May 2020 did the High Court rule: it quashed the first-instance decision and dismissed the application, reasoning that the unpredictable duration of the pandemic made it impossible to decide when a strike could lawfully be held or what services would then be required.

The unions petitioned the Kúria for review on 9 July. After a further delay caused by an extension granted to the Government for its observations, the Kúria, on 25 November 2020, restored the first-instance ruling. It held that the High Court had erred in treating the pandemic as rendering the planned strikes unlawful, that the statutory five-working-day time-limits had been grossly exceeded, and that the Government had failed to submit a meaningful counter-proposal. The Kúria’s decision was not notified to the unions until 31 January 2021.

By that date every announced strike day had long passed. The applicants therefore argued that the cumulative delays—far beyond the five-day statutory deadlines at each instance—had stripped the proposed industrial action of any practical relevance, constituting a disproportionate interference with their Article 11 rights that could not be regarded as necessary in a democratic society.

The applicants—the Trade Union of Social Sector Workers (representing essential-service providers) and three members—complained under Articles 11 and 13 ECHR of protracted court proceedings to fix the minimum services that had to be maintained during planned strikes. Those delays, they argued, rendered the industrial action meaningless.

On 17 December 2019 the union (joined by another organisation) announced a series of one-day strikes throughout 2020 (12 February, 13 March, 1 April, 13 May, 10 June, 15 July, 19 August, 16 September, 21 October, 18 November and 9 December) in support of better pay, pensions, working conditions and a national labour round-table. Hungarian strike law required the parties first to agree, or a court to determine, the “sufficient service” that must continue during any stoppage of essential activities. The unions therefore submitted their proposed minimum-service package to the Ministry of Human Resources the same day. The Ministry rejected it on 15 January 2020 and demanded a fresh offer.

On 6 February the unions applied to the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court to set the minimum services. After an initial rejection for incompleteness, a corrected application was lodged on 12 February. On 19 February the court discontinued the case, holding that negotiations had not yet failed—a statutory precondition for judicial intervention. The unions appealed; on 6 March the Budapest High Court quashed that ruling and remitted the matter, finding that talks had in fact ended without agreement.

COVID-19 then intervened. An extraordinary court recess was declared, but the first-instance court ultimately treated the non-contentious strike procedure as unaffected. It held that the unions had fulfilled their statutory duty to propose minimum services while the Ministry had not, and it therefore adopted an amended version of the unions’ proposal (taking pandemic needs into account). The Government appealed on 25 March. Procedural defects in the appeal notice caused the file to shuttle back and forth for corrections until 14 May.

On 25 May the High Court reversed, dismissing the application altogether: because the pandemic’s duration could not be predicted, it was impossible to know when any of the listed strike days would be lawful and therefore impossible to fix the corresponding minimum services. The unions sought review by the Kúria on 9 July (and also filed a constitutional complaint, which was rejected). After further delay caused by the Government’s late observations, the Kúria on 25 November 2020 quashed the High Court’s judgment and reinstated the first-instance decision. It criticised both the lower court’s failure to decide the case on the law as it stood when the application was filed and the Government’s failure to make a meaningful proposal. The Kúria ruling reached the unions only on 31 January 2021—well after every announced strike date had passed.

The sequence of incomplete filings, remittals, COVID-related interruptions, appeal-notice defects and late governmental submissions stretched a procedure that statute required to be completed in a matter of days into more than a year. By the time a final, enforceable determination of minimum services existed, the industrial-action timetable had elapsed, stripping the planned strikes of any practical effect.

The case of Trade Union of Social Sector Workers and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 33144/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerned complaints under Articles 11 and 13 of the Convention. The applicants—the Trade Union of Social Sector Workers (representing essential-service social workers) and three of its members—alleged that protracted compulsory arbitration proceedings to determine the minimum services required during strikes violated their rights to freedom of association and to an effective remedy.

The action sought better working conditions, pay and pension rights for social-sector employees together with the establishment of a national labour roundtable. Pursuant to section 4(3) of the Strike Act, the unions submitted a proposal for the minimum services that would be maintained during the strikes. The Ministry of Human Resources rejected the proposal on 15 January 2020 and required a fresh offer.

The unions therefore applied to the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court on 6 February 2020, asking it to fix the minimum-service level. The court first rejected the application as incomplete, then discontinued the proceedings on 19 February on the ground that negotiations had not yet failed. That ruling was quashed by the Budapest High Court on 6 March 2020 and the case remitted. Despite a COVID-19-related court recess, the first-instance court continued the non-contentious procedure, held that the unions had fulfilled their statutory duty to propose minimum services, noted that the Ministry had failed to submit its own proposal, and on or about 19 March 2020 set a minimum-service level by amending the unions’ offer while taking pandemic exigencies into account.

The Government appealed on 25 March 2020. The case file was thereafter shuttled repeatedly between the first-instance and appellate courts for the correction of formal errors in the notice of appeal (14 April, 20 April, 7 May and 14 May 2020). On 25 May 2020 the High Court overturned the first-instance decision, holding that it was impossible to predict when the pandemic would end and therefore impossible to determine when a strike could lawfully take place or what minimum services would then be required.

After further delay occasioned by an extension of time granted to the Government, the Kúria on 25 November 2020 quashed the High Court’s judgment and reinstated the first-instance ruling. It emphasised that the exceptionally short statutory time-limits applicable to strike-related proceedings had been exceeded, that the second-instance court should have decided the case on the law as it stood when the application was lodged, and that the Government had never submitted a meaningful counter-proposal. The Kúria’s decision was transmitted to the first-instance court only on 23 December 2020 and notified to the unions on 31 January 2021.

By that date every one of the originally announced 2020 strike days had already passed. The Court later found that these successive delays had rendered the proposed industrial action meaningless, thereby imposing a disproportionate restriction on the applicants’ Article 11 rights that was not necessary in a democratic society.
001-250201:
The case of Idris Akhundov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 22824/21) concerns the discontinuance of the applicant’s lifetime old-age pension as a former police officer. Born in 1967, Akhundov served in various roles at the Khachmaz District Police Office under Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) from June 1993 until May 2016. Upon reaching retirement age, he was relieved of duties and granted an old-age pension for life effective 8 May 2016, pursuant to the Law on Work Pensions.

Following retirement, Akhundov alleged persecution by MIA employees due to his participation in opposition party events criticizing the political regime and law-enforcement agencies. He left Azerbaijan for Germany in 2017 and resides in Mainz. On an unspecified date, the MIA requested that the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) under the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection discontinue his pension payments, citing his alleged grant of political asylum in Germany. Payments ceased as of 1 November 2017.

On 21 October 2018, Akhundov initiated proceedings in Baku Administrative-Economic Court no. 1 against the MIA (later designating the SSPF as defendant and MIA as third party). He sought an order for the SSPF to resume payments from 31 October 2017, arguing the discontinuance was unlawful. The SSPF objected, noting payments had continued until 31 October 2017 but stopped thereafter based on the MIA request. Relying on the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees (defining a refugee as someone outside their country owing to well-founded fear of persecution, unwilling to avail themselves of its protection), the SSPF claimed Akhundov had voluntarily refused Azerbaijan’s protection and obtained asylum due to persecution; thus, the stoppage was lawful and justified, as he could not benefit from two States’ social protection systems.

The first-instance court dismissed the claim on 17 July 2019, endorsing the SSPF’s reasoning. Akhundov appealed, denying refugee status and arguing that even if granted, it could not revoke acquired social rights; he cited misinterpretation of the 1951 Convention and failure to apply Article 38 of the Constitution (right to social security). The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3 October 2019.

Akhundov’s cassation appeal to the Supreme Court reiterated these points and noted the absence of evidence of asylum. On 18 December 2019, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal in part and remitted the case, finding the lower courts had failed to examine all factual circumstances (per Articles 12.1 and 58.7 of the Code of Administrative Procedure) and based decisions on assumptions. There was no evidence of asylum, and neither the MIA nor the courts cited any legal provision authorizing discontinuance.

On remittal, the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal on 21 July 2020. It noted Akhundov’s departure on 18 November 2016, a Prosecutor General’s Office letter indicating criminal proceedings against him for organizing illegal migration and document forgery/unlawful production/sale/use, his failure to explain four years’ residence in Germany despite denying asylum, and his voluntary renunciation of Azerbaijan’s protection. The Supreme Court dismissed his further cassation appeal on 27 October 2020.

Relevant domestic law includes Article 38 of the 1995 Constitution (right to social security upon reaching age or in specified cases). The 2006 Law on Work Pensions provides for lifetime old-age pensions (Article 32.1) and annual indexation (Article 29). Article 37.8 permits discontinuance only upon death, a widow’s remarriage, or circumstances failing to meet grant conditions. Article 43.1 allows Azerbaijani citizens abroad to receive pensions via transfer to a domestic bank account or (at their expense) in their state of residence. The Code of Administrative Procedure requires courts to independently examine all relevant facts and evidence comprehensively.

These facts underpin the alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The pension constituted a possession; its discontinuance interfered with that right. Domestic courts failed to identify any provision of domestic law permitting stoppage on grounds of alleged asylum, rendering the interference non-compliant with “conditions provided for by law.” No evidence of asylum was adduced, and foreign residence or refugee status is not among the statutory grounds for discontinuance; indeed, the law expressly contemplates payments to those living abroad.

The case of Idris Akhundov v. Azerbaijan (no. 22824/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the discontinuance of the applicant’s lifetime old-age pension as a former police officer. The alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions) arose because domestic courts identified no provision of Azerbaijani law permitting termination on the ground that he had supposedly obtained political asylum in Germany, rendering the interference not “in accordance with the law.”

The applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1967 and residing in Mainz, Germany, served in the Khachmaz District Police Office of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) from June 1993 until May 2016. Upon reaching retirement age he was granted an old-age pension for life with effect from 8 May 2016. He maintains that after retirement he was persecuted by MIA personnel because he had taken part in opposition-party events criticising the regime and the law-enforcement agencies; he therefore left Azerbaijan for Germany in 2017 (the appellate court later recorded the departure date as 18 November 2016).

On an unspecified date the MIA asked the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) to stop the pension on the asserted basis that the applicant had been granted political asylum in Germany. Payments ceased from 1 November 2017. On 21 October 2018 the applicant sued in Baku Administrative-Economic Court no. 1, later substituting the SSPF as defendant, seeking a declaration that the discontinuance was unlawful and an order to resume payments from 31 October 2017.

The SSPF replied that the applicant had been paid until 31 October 2017 and that termination followed the MIA request. Invoking the 1951 Refugee Convention, it argued that he had voluntarily rejected Azerbaijan’s protection by obtaining asylum on persecution grounds and therefore could not continue to receive Azerbaijani social benefits.

The first-instance court dismissed the claim on 17 July 2019, endorsing the SSPF’s reasoning. The applicant appealed, denying that he was a refugee, asserting that even refugee status could not extinguish social rights already acquired in the country of origin, and complaining that Article 38 of the Constitution (right to social security) had been ignored. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3 October 2019.

In cassation the Supreme Court, on 18 December 2019, remitted the case. It held that the lower courts had failed to examine the facts of their own motion (Articles 12.1 and 58.7 of the Code of Administrative Procedure), had relied on unproven assumptions, had produced no evidence that asylum had actually been granted, and—crucially—had cited no legal provision authorising discontinuance of a lifetime pension on that ground.

On re-examination the Court of Appeal, on 21 July 2020, again dismissed the claim. It noted the applicant’s unexplained four-year residence in Germany, referred to a Prosecutor General’s letter indicating criminal proceedings against him for illegal migration and document offences, and repeated that he had voluntarily renounced Azerbaijan’s protection and could not enjoy the social-security systems of two States Parties to the 1951 Convention simultaneously. The Supreme Court rejected a further cassation appeal on 27 October 2020.

Azerbaijani law (Law on Work Pensions, Articles 32.1, 37.8 and 43) provides that an old-age pension is granted for life, may be discontinued only on death, remarriage or failure to meet statutory conditions, and may be paid to citizens living abroad. Neither the Constitution nor the pension statute contains any ground corresponding to the grant of political asylum. The administrative courts nevertheless terminated the pension without identifying any such legal basis, which is the core factual predicate of the alleged Convention violation.

The case of Idris Akhundov v. Azerbaijan (no. 22824/21) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the discontinuance of the applicant’s lifetime old-age pension. Akhundov, born in 1967 and living in Mainz, Germany, served as an officer of Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) from June 1993 to May 2016 in the Khachmaz District Police Office. Upon reaching retirement age, he was granted an old-age pension for life effective 8 May 2016 under the Law on Work Pensions.

Akhundov claimed that after retirement he faced persecution by MIA employees due to his participation in opposition-party events criticising the political regime and law-enforcement agencies. He left Azerbaijan for Germany in 2017. On an unspecified date the MIA requested the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) to discontinue his pension on the ground that he had been granted political asylum in Germany. Payments stopped from 1 November 2017.

On 21 October 2018 Akhundov brought administrative proceedings against the MIA (later designating the SSPF as defendant), arguing the discontinuance was unlawful and seeking resumption of payments from 31 October 2017. The SSPF objected, relying on the 1951 Refugee Convention’s definition of a refugee. It asserted that Akhundov had voluntarily refused Azerbaijan’s protection and obtained asylum on the basis of persecution; otherwise asylum would not have been granted. The first-instance court dismissed the claim on 17 July 2019, finding the decision lawful. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 3 October 2019, repeating the same reasoning.

Akhundov’s cassation appeal succeeded in part. On 18 December 2019 the Supreme Court remitted the case, holding that the lower courts had failed to comply with Articles 12.1 and 58.7 of the Code of Administrative Procedure. There was no evidence that asylum had actually been granted, the courts had proceeded on assumptions, and neither the MIA nor the appellate court had cited any domestic legal provision authorising discontinuance on that ground.

On remittal the Court of Appeal again dismissed the claim on 21 July 2020. It found that Akhundov had left Azerbaijan on 18 November 2016, referred to a Prosecutor General’s letter indicating criminal proceedings against him for illegal migration and document forgery, and noted that he had offered no alternative explanation for his four-year residence in Germany. The court concluded he had voluntarily renounced Azerbaijan’s protection, could not simultaneously benefit from the social-protection systems of two States parties to the 1951 Convention, and therefore the pension stoppage was justified. The Supreme Court rejected a further cassation appeal on 27 October 2020.

Domestic law (Constitution Article 38; Law on Work Pensions Articles 32.1, 37.8 and 43) guarantees the right to social security, provides that an old-age pension is granted for life, lists exhaustive grounds for discontinuance (death, remarriage of a widow/widower, or failure to meet statutory conditions), and expressly permits transfer of pensions to citizens living abroad. No provision authorises cessation because of alleged refugee status or asylum abroad.

The Court held that the pension constituted a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The interference was not “in accordance with the law” because the domestic courts never identified any statutory basis permitting discontinuance on the ground of alleged political asylum. The application therefore succeeded on that complaint.
001-250110:
The case of Lena Hakobyan and Others v. Armenia (applications nos. 13721/23 and 34245/23) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns complaints by several Armenian nationals about the excessive duration of civil and administrative court proceedings in which they were parties, lasting between seven and thirteen years, in alleged breach of the reasonable-time requirement in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicants in one of the applications also complained under Article 13 of the lack of an effective domestic remedy for such delays.

The relevant facts centre on the applicants’ involvement in various civil and administrative disputes whose length they considered unreasonable. In 2014 and 2015 Armenia amended its Civil Code (Articles 162.1 and 1087.2) to create a right to claim compensation from the State budget for non-pecuniary damage arising from violations of fundamental rights, including the right to a fair trial. The amendments, which entered into force in 2016, allow claims either together with a request to establish the violation or after a judicial finding of violation, subject to a one-year time-limit. Compensation is independent of fault, must be reasonable, equitable and proportionate, and is subject to a statutory cap (normally 2 000 times the minimum wage, approximately AMD 2 million) that may be exceeded only in “exceptional cases” involving serious consequences. Court fees are payable separately for the non-pecuniary claim establishing the violation and the pecuniary compensation claim; fee relief is possible but discretionary.

Domestic practice, as illustrated by the Government’s examples, shows that first-instance courts (principally the Yerevan Court of General Jurisdiction) have frequently dismissed compensation claims. Courts have required claimants to produce extensive evidence—such as audio recordings of virtually every hearing—to prove that adjournments were unjustified, that delays were attributable solely to the court rather than external factors or the claimant’s own conduct, that the case was not complex, and that the delay caused concrete harm. Incomplete evidence has routinely led to findings that the length was not shown to be unreasonable. The ECtHR case of Lena Hakobyan and Others v. Armenia (applications 13721/23 and 34245/23) arose from complaints by several Armenian nationals that civil and administrative court proceedings in which they were parties had lasted an unreasonably long time, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Some applicants also alleged a violation of Article 13 on account of the absence of an effective domestic remedy for such delays. The proceedings in question, whose precise dates appear in an unpublished appendix, ranged from seven to thirteen years.

Armenian law had been amended in 2014–2015 (effective 2016) to create a statutory right to non-pecuniary damages for violations of Convention rights, including the right to a fair trial. Under Civil Code Articles 162.1 and 1087.2, a claimant must first obtain a judicial finding that a State body or official has breached the right; compensation is then payable from the State budget irrespective of fault. Awards are limited to 2 000 times the minimum wage (approximately AMD 2 million) unless “exceptional circumstances” producing “severe consequences” are proved. Claims must be brought within one year of knowledge of the violation or of a final judicial confirmation of it. Court fees are levied separately on the declaration-of-violation claim (fixed fee) and the pecuniary compensation claim (3–5 % of the sum sought); relief from fees is discretionary and rarely granted automatically.

Domestic case-law submitted by the Government revealed that compensation actions for delay are routinely dismissed. First-instance courts have insisted that claimants produce complete audio recordings of every hearing, proof that every adjournment was attributable solely to the court, evidence of the case’s lack of complexity, and demonstration of concrete prejudice suffered. In one typical decision a claim concerning 4½-year administrative proceedings plus a two-year delay in serving judgment was rejected for incomplete recordings. In another, a six-year property-partition case stalled by an expert report was dismissed because the claimant had not shown that similar cases were resolved faster. Successful claims have been rare and modest: AMD 300 000 was awarded after five-year pension proceedings, and AMD 800 000 after four-year criminal proceedings ending in acquittal. Even these “successful” compensation actions themselves lasted between 1½ and more than four years across three instances; several remained pending after five years.

The Constitutional Court (2020–2021) acknowledged systemic delays, the need for both preventive and compensatory mechanisms, and the vagueness of the “exceptional circumstances” proviso, but left the design of remedies to the legislature and did not strike down the existing scheme.

The Court found that the applicants’ own proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time. It further held that the Civil Code remedy was ineffective: the high evidential burden, the risk of substantial irrecoverable fees, the modest statutory ceiling, and the protracted character of the compensation proceedings themselves rendered it incapable of providing adequate and prompt redress. Consequently Article 13, taken together with Article 6 § 1, had also been violated.

Under Article 46 the Court indicated that Armenia must, as a matter of priority, introduce a dedicated compensatory (and possibly acceleratory) remedy meeting the Court’s established criteria for length-of-proceedings complaints.

The case of Lena Hakobyan and Others v. Armenia (applications nos. 13721/23 and 34245/23) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns complaints by multiple Armenian nationals about the excessive duration of civil and administrative proceedings to which they were parties. These proceedings lasted between seven and thirteen years, which the applicants argued breached the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicants in one of the applications additionally invoked Article 13, complaining of the absence of an effective domestic remedy through which they could obtain redress for the delays.

In 2014 the Armenian Civil Code was amended (Articles 162.1 and 1087.2) to permit claims for non-pecuniary damage arising from violations of certain Convention rights by State or municipal bodies or officials. A further amendment effective 1 January 2016 extended this possibility to breaches of the right to a fair trial. Compensation is payable from the State budget irrespective of fault and independently of any pecuniary loss. The amount is fixed by the court according to principles of reasonableness, equity and proportionality, taking into account the nature, degree and duration of suffering, consequences, personal circumstances and other factors. A statutory ceiling of 2 000 times the minimum wage (AMD 1 000) applies, although this may be exceeded in “exceptional cases” involving “severe consequences.” A claim may be lodged either together with an action seeking a finding of a rights violation or within one year of a final judicial confirmation of such a violation. Court fees are levied separately on the non-pecuniary claim (fixed multiples of the base fee) and on any ancillary pecuniary claim (a percentage of the amount sought). Limited fee relief is available on grounds of financial hardship.

The Armenian Constitutional Court has examined related provisions. In 2020 it held that every violation of fundamental rights is inherently exceptional and that courts enjoy discretion to decide whether consequences are “severe,” without imposing a disproportionate burden of proof on claimants. In 2021 it acknowledged a systemic problem of lengthy proceedings, noted the existence of the compensatory mechanism under Article 162.1, and observed that the State must also put in place preventive frameworks; the precise choice of measures was left to the legislature.

The Government submitted examples of domestic compensation claims brought under the 2016 amendments. The large majority were dismissed. Typical reasons included the claimant’s failure to produce audio recordings of every hearing, insufficient evidence of the parties’ conduct or of the case’s complexity, inability to prove that adjournments or long intervals between hearings were attributable solely to the court rather than external factors, and lack of proof of personal harm or of what was at stake. Compensation proceedings themselves frequently lasted two to four years across three instances, and several were still pending after comparable periods. In the few successful cases awards were modest (AMD 300 000 for five-year pension proceedings; AMD 800 000 for four-year criminal proceedings that ended in acquittal). Claimants were required to pay fees on both the recognition and the compensation elements of their claims.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ allegations that their original proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time and that the available compensatory remedy was ineffective.

The case of Skrcheski v. North Macedonia (no. 37954/21) concerns proceedings in which the State Judicial Council (SJC) established professional misconduct by the applicant, a retired judge, and the fairness of those proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The Court held Article 6 applicable because the proceedings directly affected the applicant’s civil right to a good reputation. Given the SJC’s central role in safeguarding judicial independence and public confidence, the proceedings as a whole failed to meet the requirements of a fair trial. A violation of Article 6 § 1 was therefore found.

**Case Summary: Skrcheski v. North Macedonia (Application no. 37954/21)**

The case concerns Mr Trajche Skrcheski, a retired judge born in 1956 and residing in Ohrid, North Macedonia. He alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the fairness of disciplinary proceedings before the State Judicial Council (SJC). These proceedings established professional misconduct in his judicial functions and directly implicated his civil right to a good reputation. The European Court of Human Rights found Article 6 applicable and held that the proceedings as a whole failed to meet fair trial standards due to the SJC’s non-compliance with a binding higher decision on applicable law, undermining the rule of law, judicial independence, and public trust in the SJC.

Proceedings began on 14 July 2017 when the Council for Establishing Facts initiated a professional misconduct case against the applicant before the SJC. On 18 June 2019, the SJC dismissed him from judicial office. It determined that in 2015 and 2016 he had failed to draft or deliver judgments within statutory deadlines in more than 240 assigned cases. This constituted professional misconduct under sections 75(1)(2) and (10) of the 2010 Courts Act: unconscientious, slow or negligent performance of judicial functions in specific cases, and a severe breach of the Judicial Code of Conduct damaging the reputation of the judicial function.

The applicant appealed to an Appeal Panel of the Supreme Court on 17 July 2019. He argued that the SJC should have applied the 2019 Courts Act (in force from 25 May 2019), which was more lenient. Under the 2019 Act, section 74 permitted disciplinary measures short of dismissal and restricted dismissal to cases of intentional or obviously negligent misconduct causing serious consequences. Section 76 also redefined unprofessional and unconscientious performance, excluding mere failure to draft or timely deliver judgments from that category. He maintained that no such aggravating circumstances existed in his case.

On 11 November 2019 the Appeal Panel quashed the SJC decision. It held that sections 75(1)(2) and (10) of the 2010 Act were no longer in force after 25 May 2019 and directed the SJC to apply the more lenient 2019 law in accordance with the principle of lex mitior. The applicant retired on 29 April 2020 and his mandate was formally terminated on 7 May 2020.

In the remitted proceedings the applicant and his lawyer repeated the arguments concerning the 2019 Act, including the requirement of intent or obvious negligence. Nevertheless, on 24 December 2020 the SJC again found professional misconduct under the 2010 Act (sections 75(1)(2) and (10) in conjunction with section 74(1)(2)). It acknowledged the Appeal Panel’s indication that the 2019 Act was more lenient and referred to section 76(1) of that Act (unsatisfactory professional competence or lack of conscientiousness affecting quality and promptness), but concluded that the 2010 Act remained applicable. It noted that the applicant had not denied the underlying facts and applied the 2006 State Judicial Council Act (as amended) for procedural purposes. The decision was served on 4 February 2021.

The applicant’s complaint centred on the SJC’s refusal to follow the Appeal Panel’s explicit ruling on the applicable substantive law, despite the 2018 amendments to the SJC Act requiring the SJC, on remittal, to take the Appeal Panel’s instructions into account. This created an inconsistency incompatible with the proper administration of justice. The Court emphasised the constitutional prohibition on retroactive legislation except where more favourable to the individual (Article 50 § 4 of the Constitution) and the SJC’s institutional role in safeguarding judicial independence. The proceedings therefore violated Article 6 § 1. The judgment, adopted on 31 March 2026 and delivered on 12 May 2026, may become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention.

The SJC’s central role in safeguarding judicial independence and public confidence made the overall proceedings incompatible with fair-trial requirements.

On 18 June 2019 the SJC dismissed him from office, finding that in 2015–2016 he had failed to draft or deliver judgments within statutory time-limits in more than 240 cases. The SJC’s second decision disregarded those instructions, thereby creating an inconsistent application of the law in a matter that went to the heart of judicial accountability. The Court concluded that this failure rendered the proceedings as a whole unfair.

The case of Samet Kaya v. Türkiye (Application no. 42109/22), decided by the ECtHR Second Section on 26 May 2026, concerns the applicant’s dismissal from prosecutorial office by the Council of Judges and Prosecutors (HSK) on health grounds. A Turkish law graduate born in 1993, the applicant passed the judicial candidate exam in June 2017 and was appointed prosecutor in Karabük on 5 November 2018. After a divorce, he experienced personal difficulties and was diagnosed with depression on 25 April 2019 at Ankara Kahramankazan State Hospital.

On 29 April 2019 he suffered a nervous breakdown at the courthouse, exhibiting insomnia, restlessness, disorganised behaviour, paranoid delusions and suicidal thoughts. He was diagnosed with “schizophrenia-like acute psychotic disorder” at Karabük University Hospital and admitted, but discharged against medical advice on 8 May 2019. Further inpatient treatment at Ankara University Gülhane Hospital followed a “psychosis” diagnosis; he was discharged on 27 May 2019 in the absence of active psychopathology, with a doctor’s note referring to “anxiety disorder” and one month’s leave. The HSK then appointed him judge rapporteur at the Court of Cassation in June 2019 to facilitate treatment in Ankara. He remarried in December 2019 and was transferred, at his request, as prosecutor in Hatay in June 2020.

On 25 June 2019 the HSK Professional Admission Office opened an inquiry into whether his health precluded judicial service. The HSK Second Chamber referred him to the Forensic Medicine Institute (FMI) on 3 October 2019 for an expert opinion on his ability to perform duties continuously nationwide. After six examinations between November 2019 and May 2021, the FMI Fourth Specialised Board reported on 11 August 2021 that, although no significant psychopathology was present and the applicant remained in remission, the severity of the initial diagnoses and risk of stress-induced recurrence rendered him unfit. On 7 September 2021 the Second Chamber terminated his tenure under section 8(g) of Law no. 2802 (requiring absence of any illness hindering continuous nationwide service).

The applicant obtained a 10 September 2021 report from Hatay University Hospital concluding full recovery and no impairment. He sought review, prompting referral to the FMI High Board, which on 14 December 2021 reaffirmed the earlier conclusion after reviewing the file. The Second Chamber rejected the review request on 28 December 2021. The applicant objected to the HSK Plenary, submitting a further hospital report of 9 March 2022 and arguing that a preliminary investigation of actual professional performance was a mandatory prerequisite to FMI referral. The Plenary dismissed the objection on 6 April 2022 (notified 9 May 2022).

Article 159 of the Constitution and section 33(5) of Law no. 6087 exclude judicial review of HSK decisions other than dismissals for misconduct. The applicant therefore had no access to a court to challenge the factual or legal basis of his termination. These facts underpin the complaints under Article 6 § 1 (lack of access to court) and Article 8 (private-life implications of the health-based dismissal). The Court held that Article 6 applied, that a genuine dispute existed over an arguable right against arbitrary dismissal, and that HSK internal procedures lacked sufficient guarantees, thereby impairing the very essence of the right of access to a court.

The case of Samet Kaya v. Türkiye (Application no. 42109/22) concerns the premature termination of a young prosecutor’s tenure by Türkiye’s Council of Judges and Prosecutors (HSK) on health grounds, without any possibility of external judicial review. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, holding that the complete exclusion of judicial oversight impaired the very essence of the right of access to a court.

The applicant, born in 1993, graduated from law school, passed the 2017 judicial candidate examination and oral interview, and was appointed a prosecutor in Karabük on 5 November 2018. Shortly after taking office his marriage ended in divorce. He experienced personal difficulties, took sick leave and was diagnosed with depression on 25 April 2019. On 29 April 2019, while at the courthouse, he suffered an acute nervous breakdown, exhibiting insomnia, restlessness, disorganised behaviour, paranoid delusions and suicidal ideation. He was diagnosed with a “schizophrenia-like acute psychotic disorder” and hospitalised. After discharge against medical advice he was re-admitted elsewhere with a diagnosis of psychosis; by late May 2019 active psychopathology had resolved and he was released on outpatient treatment for an anxiety disorder.

At his request the HSK transferred him to Ankara as a judge rapporteur to facilitate treatment. He remarried in December 2019 and was later posted to Hatay. Meanwhile, on 25 June 2019 his medical records were referred to the HSK. The Second Chamber sought an expert opinion from the Forensic Medicine Institute (FMI) on whether he could continuously perform judicial duties nationwide. After six examinations the FMI reported in August 2021 that the applicant showed no significant current psychopathology and remained in remission, yet, attaching decisive weight to the original diagnoses and the theoretical risk of stress-induced recurrence, concluded he was unfit. On 7 September 2021 the HSK terminated his tenure under section 8(g) of Law no. 2802 (physical or mental illness preventing continuous service).

The applicant obtained a contrary report from Hatay University Hospital stating he had fully recovered. The HSK referred him to the FMI High Board, which reached the same unfavourable conclusion. His request for review was rejected on 28 December 2021. An objection to the HSK Plenary, supported by a further hospital report and an argument that a preliminary investigation of actual professional performance was a legal prerequisite, was dismissed on 6 April 2022.

Under Article 159 of the Constitution and section 33 of the HSK Law, HSK decisions—other than dismissals for misconduct—are immune from judicial review; only internal re-examination and Plenary objection are available. The Court held that Article 6 § 1 applied because there was a genuine, serious dispute over an arguable civil right to protection against arbitrary dismissal. The first limb of the Eskelinen test was satisfied, but the second was not: the State had not shown that excluding judicial review served a legitimate interest, the HSK’s internal procedures lacked sufficient procedural guarantees, and no exceptional circumstance justified the exclusion. The absence of any independent determination of the factual and legal basis for the termination therefore violated Article 6 § 1. (The Court also received an Article 8 complaint but the provided materials focus on the access-to-court issue.)

The judgment underscores that even health-based removals of judges and prosecutors must remain subject to effective judicial scrutiny in order to safeguard both individual rights and the independence of the judiciary.

Türkiye (Application no. 42109/22) before the European Court of Human Rights concerns the premature termination of the applicant’s tenure as a prosecutor by Türkiye’s Council of Judges and Prosecutors (HSK) on health grounds, without subsequent judicial review. The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1993, alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right of access to a court) and Article 8 of the Convention.

Subsequent treatment at another hospital produced a diagnosis of “psychosis”; by 27 May 2019 no active psychopathology remained, and he was discharged with a one-month medical leave note referring to an “anxiety disorder.”

At the applicant’s request the HSK then appointed him as a judge rapporteur at the Court of Cassation in Ankara to facilitate continued treatment. He later remarried and, again at his request, was transferred as a prosecutor to Hatay in June 2020. On 7 September 2021 the HSK terminated his tenure, citing loss of the health-related qualifications required by section 8(g) of Law no. 2802.
